This section asks what the brain does with it next, and why seeing, as its illusions show, is far less direct than it feels. Inference or direct pickup: the theories Perception is the selection, organisation and interpretation of sensory signals into meaningful objects and events: sensation gives you a pattern of light, perception your mother's face. Bottom-up processing (data-driven) builds the percept from features of the stimulus; top-down processing (conceptually driven) lets knowledge, expectation and context shape how those features are read. The theories differ in the weight they give each. For Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894), perception was unconscious inference : rapid, automatic conclusions from sensory evidence plus past experience. Richard Langton Gregory (1923 to 2010) built this into the constructivist approach , the indirect or top-down theory ( Eye and Brain , 1966), in which a percept is a best-guess hypothesis; that is why a hollow mask looks like a normal, convex face. The Bayesian approach puts the idea in probabilities: the percept combines prior beliefs with sensory evidence, and the weaker the evidence, the more the priors decide. The classic bottom-up theory is the direct perception (ecological) approach of James Jerome Gibson (1904 to 1979). The light reaching a moving observer, he argued, specifies the world without inference: optic flow streams outwards from the point you are heading for, and objects offer affordances , possibilities for action perceived directly (a chair affords sitting). Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012) joined the two directions in his perceptual cycle (1976): a schema directs exploration, and the information sampled modifies the schema. Exam trap Unconscious inference and probabilistic reasoning define the constructivist approach. The computational approach (Marr, below ) asks what each stage of vision computes, and the information-processing approach describes a chain of stages; neither centres on inference. Bayesian perception rests on prior beliefs and sensory evidence , not genes, culture or emotion. The bottom-up theorist, and the coiner of affordances, is James J. Gibson : Helmholtz and Gregory are top-down, Wertheimer is a Gestalt psychologist, and Gibson's wife Eleanor built the visual cliff. The apperceptive mass (Herbart's term, often credited to Wundt; Section 1.1) is not unconscious inference. Gestalt organisation: figure, ground and grouping No school has contributed more to perception than Gestalt psychology (Section 1.2), launched in 1912 by Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) with Kurt Koffka (1886 to 1941) and Wolfgang Köhler (1887 to 1967). Its claim is that the whole is different from the sum of its parts. First the field splits into a figure , which stands out, and a ground behind it. As Edgar Rubin (1886 to 1951) described in 1915, the figure is thing-like (high in object character), clearly outlined, usually smaller and in front; the ground is shapeless, diffuse and seems farther away. Rubin's vase is a reversible figure: it flips into two faces although the stimulus never changes, so the perceiver does the organising. Elements are then grouped (Figure 1.4). By the law of proximity , elements close together in space or time belong together. By similarity , alike elements group; by the law of closure , gaps are filled, so a broken outline is seen as a circle; by good continuation (continuity), elements on a smooth path group; by common fate , elements moving together group, like a flock of birds. Symmetry, common region (a shared enclosure) and connectedness (joining lines) group elements too. The master law is Prägnanz (good figure, simplicity): every pattern is seen in the simplest, most complete organisation the conditions allow, so two overlapping rings look like two circles. Proximity three pairs of columns Similarity seen as rows, not columns Closure gaps filled: one circle Good continuation one line and one curve Common region (top) and connectedness (bottom) Common fate dots moving together group Figure 1.4 Six grouping laws you can watch in your own perception. In each panel the elements are physically identical or evenly spaced in some respect, yet you see definite groups; the grouping is supplied by your visual system. Exam trap Close in space and time is proximity . The tendency to complete a figure is closure ; continuation and continuity both name the smooth-path law. Organised "in the best possible whole form" is Prägnanz . The school that contributed most to perception is Gestalt , not structuralism, behaviourism or psychoanalysis. Interposition is a depth cue, interpolation fills in between known points, extrapolation extends beyond them; one paper keyed structuring for working out a rule from incomplete evidence and picking the items that fit it. Depth cues and the visual cliff How does a flat retinal image give you three dimensions? The brain combines depth cues, and only two are binocular cues , needing both eyes. In retinal disparity , the eyes, about 6 centimetres apart, receive slightly different views, and the nearer the object, the greater the difference; fusing the two gives the solid depth of stereopsis. In convergence , the eyes turn inwards to fixate a near object, and the brain registers how far they have turned. All other cues are monocular cues , available to one eye (Table 1.5). Most are static pictorial cues, the ones a painter uses to put depth on a flat canvas. In the texture gradient , pebbles look smaller and more densely packed with distance; engineers exaggerate it by painting stripes ever closer together before a toll plaza or on an exit ramp, so that drivers feel their speed and slow down. Motion parallax needs movement: from a train, nearby poles flash past while distant hills crawl. Table 1.5 Depth cues classified. Cue Type Depth signal Retinal disparity Binocular Images differ more when near Convergence Binocular, oculomotor Eyes turn in more when near Accommodation Monocular, oculomotor Lens thickens for near objects Motion parallax Monocular, movement Near objects sweep past faster Interposition (overlap) Monocular, pictorial A partly hidden object is farther Relative and familiar size Monocular, pictorial Smaller image, farther object Linear perspective Monocular, pictorial Parallel lines converge Texture gradient Monocular, pictorial Texture finer and denser Aerial perspective Monocular, pictorial Distant objects hazy, bluish Height in the field Monocular, pictorial Nearer the horizon, farther Shading Monocular, pictorial Shadows reveal shape Key study: The visual cliff (Gibson and Walk, 1960) Question. Can infants perceive depth before learning it from falls? Method. Eleanor Jack Gibson (1910 to 2002) and Richard Walk (1920 to 1999) built a visual cliff : glass over a checkerboard lying just beneath one half (the shallow side) and far below the other (the deep side). Mothers called 36 infants aged 6 to 14 months across it. Results. Of the 27 who left the centre board, only three crept onto the deep side; newborn animals avoided it too. Conclusion. Depth perception is present by crawling age. Criticism. Crawlers have already had months of visual experience, so innateness is not proved. Exam trap The binocular cues are only retinal disparity and convergence . Interposition, accommodation, motion parallax and aerial perspective are all monocular. Assimilation (Piaget's term) is no depth cue. The cliff tested depth perception , not object permanence, colour or imprinting, and showed it present by crawling age , not fully formed at birth or only after age two. One paper keyed 180 degrees for each eye's visual field; the better figure is about 160 degrees, with about 200 for both eyes together. Perceptual constancy Perceptual constancy is the perception of objects as stable despite changing sensory input. Hold one hand at arm's length and the other halfway to your face: the far hand's retinal image is half the size, yet both look alike. This size constancy follows size-distance invariance : perceived size is retinal size scaled by perceived distance, a rule that Emmert's law (1881) shows with afterimages, which look larger on a farther wall. Shape constancy keeps an opening door rectangular; brightness constancy keeps coal black in sunlight, because lightness depends on the ratio of an object's light to its surroundings'; colour constancy keeps a banana yellow under any lamp; location constancy keeps the world still as the eyes jump in saccades. Tiny saccades also refresh the retinal image, which would otherwise fade, and so ensure constant perception. Exam trap The outstretched hand is size constancy , not shape constancy, motion parallax or depth perception. Lateral inhibition (Section 1.3) enhances edges; it does not dull them. A fixation is the pause between saccades, and sensory adaptation the fading they prevent. Illusions and what they reveal An illusion is a misinterpretation of a stimulus that really exists. The error lies in perception, not sensation: the retinal image is accurate. Indian textbooks contrast personal illusions , which vary with observer and occasion (a rope seen as a snake at dusk), with permanent or universal illusions, which everyone sees every time (railway tracks converging). In the Müller-Lyer illusion , published in 1889 by Franz Carl Müller-Lyer (1857 to 1916), a shaft ending in outward fins looks longer than an equal shaft ending in arrowheads (Figure 1.5). Gregory (1963) blamed inappropriate constancy scaling : arrowheads suggest the near outside corner of a building, fins the far inside corner of a room, and size constancy enlarges the "farther" shaft on a flat page. Marshall Segall , Donald Thomas Campbell (1916 to 1996) and Melville Jean Herskovits (1895 to 1963) showed that experience matters (1963, 1966): by their carpentered-world hypothesis , people raised among rectangular buildings are more susceptible than people raised among round huts. The Ponzo illusion, the Ames room (a distorted room that looks rectangular through a peephole, shrinking a person in its far corner) and the moon illusion (terrain makes the horizon moon seem farther) are misapplied size scaling too: whatever is registered as farther is seen as bigger. The Ebbinghaus illusion (Titchener circles) is size contrast, and the Zöllner, Poggendorff and Hering figures distort lines. The Necker cube is an ambiguous figure that flips in depth; the Penrose triangle is an impossible figure. Müller-Lyer the shafts are equal Ponzo the two bars are equal Ebbinghaus centre circles are equal Zöllner the long lines are parallel Poggendorff the diagonals are one line Hering both lines are straight Figure 1.5 Six classic geometric illusions. In every panel the caption underneath is physically true, yet you see something else: the finned shaft looks longer, the upper bar looks longer, the circle among small circles looks larger, the long lines look tilted, the diagonal looks broken and the straight lines look bowed. Check them with a ruler. Exam trap Rails converging for everyone is a permanent illusion (visual too, but the item tests the classification), not a personal one or the Müller-Lyer. Illusions distort perception , not sensation, adaptation or "translation" (transduction). The Müller-Lyer is strongest with buildings with corners and best explained by misapplied size constancy , not disparity (it works with one eye), lateral inhibition or figure-ground reversal. Illusion, hallucination and delusion An illusion misinterprets a real external stimulus. A hallucination is a perception without an adequate external stimulus, such as a voice in an empty room. A delusion is not a perception at all but a false belief held with unshakeable conviction. Psychopathology adds the sensory distortion, a real object perceived but altered in size, intensity or quality (micropsia), and imagery, a picture in the mind's eye under voluntary control. Déjà vu is the illusion of having seen something before; déjà entendu, of having heard it before. Exam trap Illusions are a misinterpretation of stimuli arising from an external object , or distortions of existing stimuli . "Without an adequate external stimulus" and "not based on external reality" are hallucinations ; "a real object perceived in a distorted way" is a sensory distortion; "vivid mental images" is imagery; "innate mechanisms" fails because learning shapes illusions. Clear memory of the past is hypermnesia; involuntary repeated speech is palilalia (Psychiatric Disorders chapter). Motion perception Real motion is signalled by direction-selective neurons, concentrated in area MT (V5). Apparent motion is seen where nothing moves: in Wertheimer's phi phenomenon (1912) two lines flashed in quick succession look like one line moving (strictly, smooth object motion is beta movement), and films give stroboscopic motion. In induced motion a still object seems to move because its frame moves, like the moon behind racing clouds. In the autokinetic effect a still light in darkness seems to wander for lack of a frame of reference; Muzafer Sherif (1906 to 1988) used it in 1935 to study how group norms form. The motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) is a still scene drifting opposite to a motion just watched. Pattern and object recognition Recognising an A in any handwriting defeats template matching , comparison with exact stored copies, so feature analysis uses parts instead. In the Pandemonium model of Oliver Selfridge (1959), image demons record the pattern, feature demons shout when they find their line or curve, cognitive demons (one per letter) shout in proportion to their matching features, and a decision demon picks the loudest. David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel found such feature detectors, cells tuned to lines of one orientation, in cat visual cortex from 1959. A prototype , in the work of Eleanor Rosch (born 1938), is an idealised average member of a category. The recognition-by-components theory of Irving Biederman (1987) builds objects from about 36 three-dimensional geons, and David Marr (1945 to 1980) traced vision from a primal sketch through a viewer-centred 2.5-D sketch to an object-centred 3-D model. Prosopagnosia (face blindness) is a selective loss of face recognition. In the word superiority effect ( Gerald Reicher , 1969), a letter is identified better in a word than alone: knowledge helps from the top. Set, culture, subliminal perception and ESP A perceptual set is a readiness to perceive in a particular way. Jerome Seymour Bruner (1915 to 2016) and Leigh Minturn (1955) found one shape read as B among letters and as 13 among numbers, a context effect. Bruner's New Look stressed needs: with Cecile Goodman in 1947 he found that poor ten-year-olds overestimated coin sizes more than rich ones, and Elliott McGinnies (1949) found that taboo words needed longer exposures (perceptual defence). Experience reshapes perception. Perceptual learning sharpens discrimination; George Malcolm Stratton (1865 to 1957) showed perceptual adaptation by adjusting to lenses that turned his world upside down (1896, 1897); and S.B., given sight at 52 and studied by Gregory and Jean Wallace (1963), could not at first judge distance. Culture matters too, as the carpentered world showed. Herman Witkin (1916 to 1979) found a perceptual style, field dependence-independence (rod-and-frame and embedded figures tests): field-dependent people are swayed by the surrounding field, field-independent people separate items from it. Subliminal perception is the processing of stimuli too faint or brief to be noticed. James Vicary 's 1957 "Eat Popcorn" cinema study was a hoax, admitted in 1962, but in masked semantic priming ( Anthony Marcel , 1983) an unseen word speeds responses to a related one, and in blindsight ( Lawrence Weiskrantz , 1974) patients with damaged primary visual cortex deny seeing yet locate targets above chance. Extrasensory perception claims perception with no sensory input: telepathy (mind to mind), clairvoyance (hidden objects) and precognition (the future), studied with psychokinesis (mind over matter) by parapsychology. Joseph Banks Rhine (1895 to 1980) used Zener cards at Duke (chance is 5 hits in 25), and later researchers the Ganzfeld procedure, guessing a target picture in a uniform sensory field. The results do not replicate, so most scientists remain sceptical. Exam trap Semantic priming studies subliminal perception , not field dependence-independence (Witkin), locus of control (a personality variable) or signal detection (Section 1.3). Failing to notice obvious changes is change blindness, an attention topic (Section 1.5), not a failure of constancy. Deprivation and coin size is Bruner and Goodman , not Segall, Herskovits, or K. D. Answers: (1) top-down, (2) affordances, (3) closure, (4) convergence, (5) scaling, (6) hallucination, (7) geons, (8) coins. 1.5 Attention and Consciousness High yield · 61 Qs Attention selects the small part of the world that reaches awareness, and consciousness, the awareness itself, changes state many times a day and night: in sleep and dreams, under hypnosis, in meditation and on drugs. What attention is: span and determinants William James (1842 to 1910) defined attention in 1890 as the mind "taking possession ... in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought": selection plus concentration, needed because the brain's capacity is limited. Classical texts give it five characteristics: selectivity , shifting to a new object, a limited span , fluctuation (attention to an unchanging object waxes and wanes, as a faint ticking watch seems to fade and return) and division between tasks. The span of attention is the number of objects apprehended in one brief glance. William Stanley Jevons (1871), glancing at handfuls of beans, was never wrong with three or four; tachistoscope studies, using displays flashed for a fraction of a second, put the span at about six to eight unrelated items. External determinants of attention are properties of the stimulus (intensity, size, contrast, change, movement, novelty, repetition); internal determinants are properties of the person (motives, interests, attitudes and mental set , a temporary readiness to perceive something). Exam trap Number plates carry about four digits plus a few letters because of the span of attention , not selective, divided or sustained attention. Miller's memory span of seven (Section 1.7) is a different process. Selective attention: filters, attenuators and spotlights The British engineer Colin Cherry (1953) named the cocktail party problem: how do we follow one conversation among many? Hearing your own name from a conversation you were ignoring is the cocktail party phenomenon . Key study: Cherry's shadowing experiments (1953) In dichotic listening a different message goes to each ear, and the listener repeats one aloud as it arrives ( shadowing ). People recalled almost nothing of the unattended message's meaning, missing even a switch from English to German, yet noticed physical changes such as a male voice turning female. Neville Moray (1959) then found that a word list repeated 35 times in that ear left no memory, yet a third of listeners noticed their own name there. Donald Broadbent 's filter model (1958), the first major information-processing theory, passes one message on a physical feature (ear, pitch) and blocks the rest before meaning is analysed: early selection , with the filter as a bottleneck . Anne Treisman 's attenuation model (1964) turns unattended messages down, not off. Each word in a mental dictionary has a threshold, and important words such as your name have permanently low thresholds, so they fire even from the weakened channel. J. Anthony Deutsch and Diana Deutsch (1963) instead proposed late selection , at the response, after every message is analysed for meaning (Table 1.6). Table 1.6 Theories of selective auditory attention. Theory Theorist and year Where selection happens Filter (switch) Broadbent, 1958 Early; the rest is blocked Attenuation Treisman, 1964 Early but leaky Late selection Deutsch and Deutsch, 1963 At the response, after meaning Pertinence Donald Norman , 1968 Late; signal strength plus relevance Multimode William Johnston and Steven Heinz , 1978 Flexible; later costs more effort Perceptual load Nilli Lavie , 1994 to 1995 Early if the task is demanding, late if easy Vision has the same limits. Michael Posner likened covert attention, moved without moving the eyes, to a spotlight (others prefer a zoom lens , wider but less detailed). In his cueing task (1980) a central arrow directs voluntary endogenous attention, a peripheral flash captures reflexive exogenous attention, and after about 300 milliseconds the flashed spot is answered more slowly ( inhibition of return ). In Treisman and Garry Gelade 's feature integration theory (1980), features register in parallel at a preattentive stage, so a red letter pops out among green ones, but binding them into objects needs serial focused attention, so conjunction search slows with every added item; unattended features can combine wrongly (illusory conjunctions). Missing a person in a gorilla suit while counting basketball passes ( Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris , 1999) is inattentional blindness , missing an unexpected object in plain view; missing a large change made across a blink or flicker is change blindness ; missing a second target 200 to 500 milliseconds after a first is the attentional blink . Exam trap "Filter-attenuation theory" is Treisman (1964), not Broadbent, Johnston or Heinz, and her attenuator model, not Broadbent's switch model, best explains the cocktail party effect. A bottleneck is a narrow processing stage, not the cocktail party phenomenon. Failing to notice obvious changes is change blindness , not inattentional blindness or perceptual constancy (Section 1.4). Divided attention, automaticity, Stroop and vigilance Divided attention asks how far we can do two things at once. Daniel Kahneman 's capacity model ( Attention and Effort , 1973) treats attention as one limited pool of mental effort; Christopher Wickens 's multiple resource theory (1984) adds separate pools by modality, code and stage, so dissimilar tasks interfere less: driving combines better with the radio than with texting, though even a hands-free phone conversation impairs it. Practice helps because some processes stop needing capacity. An automatic process runs without intention, awareness or interference with other activity (Posner and Charles Snyder, 1975). Richard Shiffrin and Walter Schneider (1977) contrasted fast, parallel, effortless and inflexible automatic processing, learned through consistent practice, with slow, serial, effortful and flexible controlled processing . In Patricia Devine 's model (1989), stereotypes are activated automatically in everyone, but low-prejudiced people use controlled processing to refute them (Chapter 3). Key study: Stroop's colour-word experiments (1935) John Ridley Stroop (1897 to 1973) asked people to read colour words printed in a conflicting ink (RED printed in green) or to name the ink colour of such words. Reading was barely slowed, but naming the inks took about 74 per cent longer than naming plain colour patches, and errors rose. The Stroop effect is this slowing of colour naming when word and ink conflict. Reading is automatic, so the word cannot be shut out, and its name competes with the controlled naming of the ink at the response stage. The effect thus shows a limit of selective attention : interference in reaction time from conflicting information, one attribute of the stimulus (the word) dominating the other (the ink). Watching radar for hours for a rare blip demands sustained attention , or vigilance . Norman Mackworth (1948) had observers watch a clock pointer for occasional double jumps; detection fell across the two-hour watch, the vigilance decrement . In an oddball task, where a rare target appears among frequent non-targets, the brain produces a positive event-related potential about 300 milliseconds later, the P300 , which indexes the allocation of attention to the target and is reduced in schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Attention fails in ADHD, in hemispatial neglect (ignoring the left side of space after right parietal damage) and in delirium (Chapter 8). Exam trap The Stroop effect is an attention phenomenon (selective attention; interference in reaction time from conflicting information), not long-term memory retrieval, working memory, procedural memory, perception or language development. RML 2024 asks what it is "an account of" and keys stimulus dominance : the printed word dominates its ink colour. "Semantic dominance" tempts because the word is meaningful; "instructional" and "conceptual" dominance are not terms used for it. Air traffic controllers and radar readers exemplify sustained attention , not selective, divided or "perceptual" attention. Consciousness: James's stream and Freud's levels Consciousness is our awareness of ourselves and our environment at a given moment. Its level, from coma to alert waking, depends on the brainstem reticular activating system and is scored on the Glasgow Coma Scale (eye, verbal and motor responses; 3 to 15). The structuralists analysed its contents into elements by introspection (Section 1.1); James objected that consciousness "does not appear to itself chopped up in bits ... it flows": it is a stream of consciousness (1890), personal, ever changing, continuous and selective. Its most researched feature is daydreaming , which Jerome L. Singer showed to be normal and nearly universal. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) held that most mental life never enters the stream. His topographic model (1900) has three levels: the conscious, the small tip of present awareness; the preconscious , accessible memories recallable at will (your mobile number); and the much larger unconscious , repressed wishes known only indirectly, through dreams, symptoms and Freudian slips , errors of speech that betray unconscious impulses. By psychic determinism , no mental event is accidental. In his structural model (1923) the id works on the pleasure principle and the ego on the reality principle (Chapter 4). The psychodynamic perspective holds that behaviour is driven by unconscious inner forces largely beyond our control and shaped in early childhood. Research has not supported the Oedipus complex, but it does support the concept of an unconscious mind. Modern psychology adds the cognitive unconscious , processing outside awareness that is automatic, not repressed, such as the unconscious stereotyping measured by the Implicit Association Test (Anthony Greenwald and colleagues, 1998). Processes never open to awareness, such as blood-pressure control, are nonconscious . David Chalmers (1995) called the question of why brain processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all the hard problem of consciousness . An altered state of consciousness , a term made standard by Charles Tart (1969), is a temporary, qualitative change in the overall pattern of mental functioning, arising naturally (sleep), psychologically (hypnosis, meditation) or chemically (drugs). Exam trap "Stream of consciousness" is William James (1890), not Carl Jung, Wilhelm Wundt or B. F. Skinner; its most researched feature is daydreaming , not gender differences, brain-wave patterns or eye movements. Memories recallable at will are preconscious , not unconscious. The three levels form the topographic model (1900); id, ego and superego the structural model (1923). Indian context The Mandukya Upanishad names four states: jagrat (waking), svapna (dreaming), sushupti (dreamless sleep) and turiya , "the fourth", pure consciousness witnessing all three, identified with the Atman , the true self or soul, eternal consciousness (Section 1.2). Biological rhythms and the suprachiasmatic nucleus A circadian rhythm is a biological cycle of about 24 hours, such as sleep and waking or body temperature. Without time cues, in caves, human rhythms persist but drift slightly beyond 24 hours, so they come from an internal clock, reset daily by zeitgebers ("time givers"), above all light. The clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, just above the optic chiasm: animals without it sleep the usual total amount but at random times. Light reaches it directly along the retinohypothalamic tract , and it drives the pineal gland to secrete melatonin in darkness. Jet lag and shift work put the clock out of step with the day. Ultradian rhythms are shorter than a day (the 90-minute sleep cycle), infradian rhythms longer (the menstrual cycle). Exam trap The SCN is the master circadian pacemaker ; its lesions disrupt circadian rhythms, not total sleep. It is not the hunger and satiety centre (lateral and ventromedial hypothalamus), the thermoregulation centre (preoptic area), the paraventricular stress nucleus, the controller of anterior pituitary hormones, or a seat of memory (hippocampus, mammillary bodies), language or pain perception. The stages and cycles of sleep Sleep opened to study after Hans Berger published the first recordings of the human electroencephalogram (EEG) in 1929: neurons firing independently give small, fast, desynchronised waves, neurons firing together large, slow, synchronised ones. In 1953 Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman found recurring bursts of rapid eye movement with a waking-like EEG, from which woken sleepers usually reported vivid dreams; William Charles Dement and Kleitman (1957) then described the cycle of stages. Sleep thus divides into REM sleep and NREM sleep, whose old stages 1 to 4 became N1, N2 and N3 in 2007 (Table 1.7). Table 1.7 EEG waves and the stages of sleep. Why we sleep, and sleep disorders Recuperation theories say sleep restores what waking runs down; adaptation theories say evolution timed sleep to keep animals safe and save energy; memory consolidation theories note that sleep after learning reduces forgetting (Section 1.7). Sleep loss brings sleepiness, low mood and lapses of sustained attention, including microsleeps of a few seconds. Volunteers woken at every REM onset tried to enter REM ever more often, then showed REM rebound , extra REM (Dement, 1960). In cataplexy , part of narcolepsy, strong emotion triggers a sudden loss of muscle tone in full wakefulness: REM atonia while awake. Treatments for insomnia, such as stimulus control and Viktor Frankl's paradoxical intention (trying to stay awake), are in Chapter 7. Dreams: Freud, Jung and the brain Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) called dreams "the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious". Each dream is a wish fulfilment , the disguised fulfilment of a repressed wish. The manifest content is the dream as remembered, the latent content its hidden meaning, and the dream work disguises one as the other by condensation (several ideas in one image), displacement (feeling shifted to a trivial object), symbolisation (thoughts made into images) and secondary revision (tidying it into a story). Carl Gustav Jung (1875 to 1961) saw dreams as undisguised symbolic messages that compensate for a one-sided conscious attitude. He held that the unconscious has two levels: a personal (individual) unconscious of forgotten and repressed experience and, beneath it, the collective unconscious , an inherited layer shared by all humanity, which he explained by evolution, through the similar brain structure of all human races. It holds archetypes , universal images recurring in myths: the persona (social mask), the shadow (disowned dark side), the anima (the feminine side of a man) and the animus (the masculine side of a woman). Jung also devised the word association test, in which hesitations reveal unconscious complexes (Chapter 4). In the activation-synthesis hypothesis of J. Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley (1977), the pons fires randomly during REM and the cortex synthesises a story from the activation, which is why dreams are visual, bizarre and soon forgotten. Information-processing views link dreams to the overnight consolidation of recent experience, and Antti Revonsuo 's threat-simulation theory (2000) says dreams evolved to rehearse responses to danger. In a lucid dream the dreamer knows he is dreaming, confirmed by pre-arranged eye-movement signals from REM sleep ( Stephen LaBerge ). Hypnagogic imagery comes while falling asleep, hypnopompic imagery while waking. Exam trap The Interpretation of Dreams : 1900 (printed November 1899). The collective unconscious is from Carl Jung , not Sigmund Freud, Alfred Adler or Karen Horney; his two levels are collective and individual , not anima and animus or extraversion and introversion. Hypnosis, meditation and psychoactive drugs Hypnosis is a social interaction in which one person's suggestions of changes in perception, memory or behaviour are experienced by the other as real and involuntary. Its crux is suggestibility , and it is not sleep. Franz Anton Mesmer 's animal magnetism (1770s) was put down to imagination by a royal commission in 1784. The Scottish surgeon James Braid coined "hypnotism" ( Neurypnology , 1843). Jean-Martin Charcot took hypnotisability for a sign of hysteria; the Nancy school of Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault and Hippolyte Bernheim showed it was normal suggestion. Freud learned from both, published the mechanism of hysteria with Josef Breuer (1893; Studies on Hysteria , 1895), then replaced hypnosis with free association , the patient on the couch reporting whatever comes to mind. Susceptibility is measured by the Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scales ( André Weitzenhoffer and Ernest Ropiequet Hilgard , 1959). Hypnosis can relieve pain and produce posthypnotic suggestions (acted on at a cue after hypnosis ends) and posthypnotic amnesia, but it cannot give superhuman strength or recover memories reliably, since it raises false recall and confidence together. Hilgard's neodissociation theory holds that hypnosis splits consciousness, a hidden observer registering pain that the hypnotised person denies; the social-cognitive theory of Theodore Xenophon Barber and Nicholas Spanos says hypnotised people enact an expected role. Meditation trains attention. Concentrative meditation holds it on one object, such as the repeated mantra of transcendental meditation , introduced by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi in the 1950s; mindfulness meditation (opening-up) observes whatever arises without judging it, from Buddhist vipassana. Herbert Benson showed that meditation's slowed heart rate and breathing, the relaxation response (1975), follow from any similar technique. Surveys showing that regular meditators are less stressed are correlational, however: without random assignment, calmer people may simply meditate more, and only an experiment can show cause (Chapter 9). In McGill University's sensory deprivation studies (1954), students lying in a cubicle with goggles and gloves mostly quit within two or three days, and many hallucinated. A psychoactive drug alters perception, mood or consciousness by acting on the nervous system (Table 1.9). With repeated use, tolerance means a larger dose is needed for the same effect, dependence means the drug is needed to function, and withdrawal is the unpleasant reaction, usually opposite to the drug's effects, on stopping (Chapter 8). This section runs from the simplest learning, through conditioning, to the maps, insights and imitation that conditioning alone could not explain. What learning is The standard definition descends from Gregory Kimble (1961): learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour, or in the potential for behaviour, that results from experience. "Potential" matters because learning is inferred from performance , what an organism actually does, and the two can come apart. "Experience" rules out maturation , change on a biological timetable (a baby walks when her body is ready), as well as fatigue, drugs, motivation and instinct. Nikolaas Tinbergen (1907 to 1988) showed that a male stickleback attacks any crude model with a red belly: a fixed action pattern , an unlearned, stereotyped sequence triggered by a sign stimulus and run to completion. The simplest learning involves one stimulus and is called non-associative. In habituation the response to a repeated, harmless stimulus decreases: trains outside a new hostel room wake you the first night but not by the end of the week. It is stimulus-specific and shows dishabituation (a novel strong stimulus restores the response), proof that it is learning, not fatigue. Its near opposite, sensitisation , is an increased response to many stimuli after a strong or noxious one. Eric Kandel (born 1929) traced both to synapses of the sea slug Aplysia (Physiological Psychology chapter). In infants, habituation reveals discrimination before speech ( Robert Fantz , 1964): a baby bored with one picture who looks longer at a new one can tell them apart. Between instinct and ordinary learning lies imprinting , the rapid, unrewarded and largely irreversible attachment to the first suitable moving object, possible only within a critical period : in 1935 Konrad Lorenz (1903 to 1989) reported incubator-hatched greylag goslings following him as their mother. Everything else here is associative learning: learning that two events go together. Exam trap Fixed action patterns are innate , not products of classical or operant conditioning. The near opposite of habituation is sensitisation ; "habitation" and "inhabitation" are sound-alikes. Pavlov and classical conditioning Ivan Petrovich Pavlov (1849 to 1936), a physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for work on digestion, collected his dogs' saliva through a tube in the cheek. In the late 1890s he noticed that they salivated before food arrived, at the sight of the dish or the attendant's footsteps. From about 1897 he studied these "psychic secretions": a metronome was sounded, meat powder followed, and after several pairings the metronome alone produced salivation. This is classical conditioning (Pavlovian or respondent conditioning): learning in which a neutral stimulus, repeatedly paired with a stimulus that already produces a response, comes to produce a similar response itself. Five terms describe it. The unconditioned stimulus (UCS) produces a response without learning (food in the mouth), and that unlearned response is the unconditioned response (UCR: salivation to food). A neutral stimulus (NS), the metronome on day one, does not produce it. After pairing, the metronome is a conditioned stimulus (CS), and its learned response is the conditioned response (CR: salivation to the metronome). So the metronome is an NS before conditioning and a CS after it, and salivation is a UCR to food but a CR to the metronome. The fundamental element is association, the pairing of two stimuli close in time. Table 1.10 adds three cases; each response is involuntary. Table 1.10 Three classical conditioning situations broken into their parts. Situation UCS UCR CS CR Little Albert Loud clang Startle and fear White rat Fear of the rat Student who lost a match Defeat and humiliation Distress The sports ground Anxiety at the ground Cancer patient Chemotherapy drug Nausea Hospital smell Nausea on arrival Timing matters. In delay conditioning the CS begins first and is still on when the UCS arrives; this is the most effective arrangement, because the CS works as a warning. Trace conditioning, the other forward arrangement, leaves a gap between CS and UCS and is weaker; simultaneous conditioning gives no warning and is weak; backward conditioning (UCS first) is the weakest of all. Exam trap The bell is a neutral stimulus before pairing and a conditioned stimulus after ; never a UCS, never an "operant stimulus". It becomes a CS by repeated pairing with a UCS , not by reward, punishment or random occurrence. "Delay" does not mean slow: delay conditioning is the most effective; trace has the gap. The CR grows during acquisition, quickly at first and then more slowly. If the CS is then presented repeatedly without the UCS, the CR fades: extinction . (Pavlov called the UCS the "reinforcement", so withdrawing reinforcement means omitting the UCS.) Extinction suppresses rather than erases learning (Pavlov saw it as active inhibition): after a rest the CR returns with no new pairings ( spontaneous recovery ); a novel distracting stimulus restores it briefly (disinhibition); so does the UCS alone (reinstatement) or a return to the original context (renewal). Hence fears can relapse after therapy. Responding to stimuli similar to the CS, the more so the more similar they are (a generalisation gradient), is stimulus generalisation ; responding only to the CS, learned when a similar stimulus is never followed by the UCS, is stimulus discrimination . A dog whose circle-versus-ellipse discrimination Shenger-Krestovnikova (1921) made impossible became agitated and lost even easy discriminations: experimental neurosis , the first laboratory model of anxiety. In higher-order conditioning an established CS acts as the UCS for a new stimulus (a black square paired only with the metronome comes to produce salivation), which is how the word "exam" alone can make a heart race. In sensory preconditioning ( W. J. Brogden , 1939) two neutral stimuli are paired first; when one is later conditioned, the other also produces the CR. Exam trap Omitting the UCS produces extinction . Spontaneous recovery needs only time, disinhibition a novel stimulus, reinstatement the UCS alone and reconditioning new pairings; sensitisation is no comeback. Avoiding a black cat but playing with a tabby is discrimination , not extinction, successive approximation (shaping) or negative transfer. Conditioned fear and its therapies John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958), the founder of behaviourism, set out with Rosalie Rayner to show that emotions are conditioned. In 1920 they paired a white rat seven times with the clang of a steel bar behind the head of an eleven-month-old infant, "Albert B.". Afterwards the rat alone made him cry and crawl away, and the fear generalised to a rabbit, a dog and a fur coat but not to his wooden blocks: a conditioned emotional response. With one infant and no control, the study would be unethical today. Can fear be unconditioned? In 1924 Mary Cover Jones (1897 to 1987) treated Peter, a boy who feared rabbits: while he ate a favourite food, a caged rabbit was brought a little closer each day until he let it nibble his fingers. This is counterconditioning : replacing a conditioned response with an incompatible one, so that the client learns the stimulus is no longer threatening. Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997) borrowed a physiologist's term for the principle, reciprocal inhibition : a response incompatible with anxiety, made to occur in the presence of the feared stimulus, weakens the bond between them. His systematic desensitisation ( Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition , 1958) has three steps: relaxation training, usually the progressive muscle relaxation of Edmund Jacobson (1888 to 1983); an anxiety hierarchy, its items rated on Wolpe's 0 to 100 Subjective Units of Disturbance Scale (SUDS); and desensitisation proper, in which the relaxed client imagines each item in turn, moving up only when it no longer arouses anxiety. A relaxed student who pictures himself on the stage, then introducing himself, then giving his feared talk, is being desensitised. In flooding , another conditioning therapy, the client stays in the most feared situation at full intensity, with no steps or relaxation, until anxiety subsides: extinction with escape blocked. Implosive therapy ( Thomas Stampfl ) is flooding in imagination. Aversion therapy pairs a cue such as the taste of alcohol with a nausea-producing drug, and in covert sensitisation ( Joseph Cautela , 1967) the behaviour and an unpleasant outcome are both imagined. Exposure and response prevention ( Victor Meyer , 1966) exposes a person with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) to the feared cue and blocks the compulsion, so that anxiety falls by habituation and extinction (Clinical Psychology chapter). Exam trap Systematic desensitisation is Wolpe's and rests on reciprocal inhibition , not operant extinction, shaping, habituation, the law of effect, catharsis or vicarious reinforcement. Relaxation is Jacobson's ; hierarchy ratings use SUDS , not the Fear Survey Schedule, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory or Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. Graded steps with relaxation is desensitisation, full intensity is flooding, and imagined behaviour plus imagined unpleasantness is covert sensitisation. Exposure and response prevention rests on habituation and extinction ; "graded exposure" is a procedure, not a principle. Symptom substitution is not a technique but the psychoanalytic prediction that a removed symptom will be replaced. Prediction and preparedness Conditioning was long thought to need only contiguity, the CS and UCS close together in time. In 1968 Robert Rescorla (1940 to 2020) showed that rats did not fear a tone if shocks were as likely without it as with it: conditioning depends on contingency, how well the CS predicts the UCS. In blocking ( Leon Kamin , 1969), rats already afraid of a noise learned almost nothing about a redundant light added to it. In overshadowing the most salient part of a compound CS takes most of the learning; in latent inhibition ( Robert Lubow and A. U. Moore , 1959) a stimulus often met alone beforehand conditions slowly. The Rescorla-Wagner model (Rescorla and Allan Wagner , 1972), ΔV = αβ(λ − ΣV), says that an animal learns only when surprised. A CS gains associative strength (ΔV) in proportion to the prediction error, the gap between the most the UCS can support (λ) and what all stimuli present already predict (ΣV), scaled by salience and learning rate (αβ). The error shrinks as the UCS becomes expected, so each trial adds less; in blocking it is zero from the start. In the 1990s Wolfram Schultz found dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area signalling exactly this error. The CS is thus a signal that predicts the UCS, not, as Pavlov's stimulus substitution theory held, a substitute for it. Key study: Garcia and Koelling's "bright, noisy, tasty water" (1966) Question. Are all stimuli equally easy to associate with all consequences? Method. John Garcia (1917 to 2012) and Robert Koelling let rats drink saccharin-flavoured water whose every lick also produced a flash and a click; then some were made ill, others shocked. Result. Ill rats avoided the taste but not the light and click; shocked rats avoided the light and click but not the taste. Conclusion. Taste "belongs" with illness, and sights and sounds with pain; the finding so contradicted theory that Garcia struggled to publish it. Such conditioned taste aversion forms in a single trial, even when illness follows the taste by hours, and refutes equipotentiality, the assumption that any stimulus can be associated with any consequence equally easily. Martin Seligman (born 1942) called the principle preparedness (1970): each species is biologically prepared to learn some associations easily, which is why phobias of snakes and heights are common and phobias of electric sockets rare. Chemotherapy patients are given a novel "scapegoat" food to protect their usual diet, and advertisers pair a brand with a beloved film star so that the liking transfers. Exam trap Taste aversion is classical conditioning (taste = CS, illness = UCS), not operant, second-order conditioning or a "spurious association" (a statistical term). It illustrates biological preparedness , defying equipotentiality and contiguity. Prediction error is signalled by dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area , not serotonin, GABA or acetylcholine. Latent inhibition is not Tolman's latent learning . Thorndike, Skinner and consequences Most behaviour, however, is emitted rather than elicited, and its consequences decide whether it recurs. Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949) shut hungry cats in puzzle boxes ( Animal Intelligence , 1898). Each cat scrambled until it hit the release by accident, and over trials its escape time fell gradually, not suddenly: trial-and-error learning. His law of effect (1911) states that responses followed by satisfaction are strengthened and those followed by discomfort weakened. His connectionism, which treats learning as forming stimulus-response bonds, added the law of exercise (use strengthens a bond), later abandoned, and the law of readiness (acting when ready is satisfying). The radical behaviourist Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990), in The Behavior of Organisms (1938), separated respondent behaviour, elicited by a stimulus, from operant behaviour, emitted by the organism and operating on the environment. In operant conditioning the probability of a response is changed by its consequences (Thorndike's trial-by-trial version is often called instrumental conditioning). In the Skinner box a rat pressed a lever freely while a cumulative recorder plotted its rate. A discriminative stimulus, such as a chai stall's "Open" board, signals that a response will be reinforced, bringing it under stimulus control. Applied behaviour analysis and functional analysis, which ask what a problem behaviour gets the person or lets him escape, rest on these principles; merely recording a behaviour often changes it (reactivity). Two questions classify every consequence (Table 1.11): does the behaviour increase (reinforcement) or decrease (punishment), and is a stimulus added (positive) or removed (negative)? Positive and negative mean plus and minus, not good and bad. A friend's warm agreement with an opinion you voice is positive reinforcement, so the attitude strengthens. Pressing a lever to switch off a shock already on is negative reinforcement . A fine for jumping a red light is negative punishment. A parent who buys a sweet to end a tantrum positively reinforces the tantrum and is negatively reinforced for giving in. Table 1.11 The four kinds of operant consequence. Effect on behaviour Stimulus added (positive) Stimulus removed (negative) Increases (reinforcement) Positive reinforcement: something wanted is given (praise) Negative reinforcement: something unpleasant is taken away (a headache ends) Decreases (punishment) Positive punishment: something unpleasant is given (a scolding) Negative punishment: something wanted is taken away (time-out, response cost) Food is a primary reinforcer, effective without learning. Money and praise are secondary reinforcers , neutral stimuli that became reinforcing through association with primary ones; one linked with many primary reinforcers, as money is, is a generalised reinforcer. (Harry Harlow's infant monkeys preferred a cloth mother to a wire one that fed them: attachment rests on contact comfort, not secondary reinforcement.) In the 1960s Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin built the token economy at Anna State Hospital, Illinois: long-stay psychiatric patients earned tokens for self-care and ward work and exchanged them for privileges ( The Token Economy , 1968). Escape learning terminates an aversive stimulus already present; avoidance learning prevents its arrival. Orval Hobart Mowrer (1907 to 1982) explained avoidance with his two-factor theory (1947): a warning signal comes to elicit fear by classical conditioning, and avoiding it is negatively reinforced by fear reduction, an operant process that also keeps the fear from extinguishing. Compulsive washing in OCD is such an escape or safety behaviour. Time-out (brief removal from a setting where reinforcement is available) and response cost (loss of a reinforcer already held) are negative punishment. As William Kaye Estes (1919 to 2011) showed in 1944, punishment suppresses a response without erasing it; it also breeds fear of the punisher and models aggression. New behaviour is built by shaping , reinforcing successive approximations to a target: facing the lever, approaching it, touching it, finally pressing it. Shaping works on a response's speed and force and needs no words. Chaining links responses into a sequence; a prompt adds a cue and fading withdraws it. Operant extinction, the fading of a response no longer reinforced, often begins with an extinction burst of harder, more varied responding (jabbing at a lift button), after which responding falls back to its operant level, the rate before reinforcement. Exam trap The law of effect is Thorndike's (not Skinner's, Pavlov's or Watson's), not modelling, insight or unconscious drive. Operant conditioning works through reinforcement and punishment , not modelling or cognitive dissonance. Negative reinforcement is not punishment , and it too increases behaviour, though one real item keyed only positive reinforcement. Removing a desirable stimulus to reduce behaviour is response cost , not negative reinforcement, positive punishment or extinction; time-out is negative punishment . OCD compulsions are escape (avoidance) behaviours , not conditioned stimuli, unconditioned responses or positively reinforced acts. Exam trap The token economy is operant (secondary reinforcement), the therapy not derived from classical conditioning, and Ayllon and Azrin's (Amity 2023 keyed Skinner, who supplied only the principles). Stickers that buy a homework exemption are tokens , not primary or generalised reinforcers or "prepotent" (dominant) responses. Ignoring tantrums is extinction , not "operant escape" (another wrong Amity 2023 key). Shaping is not chaining, prompting, fading or the law of effect; RML 2024 keyed its principles as speed, power and non-verbal. Schedules and other operant effects A schedule of reinforcement is the rule deciding which responses are reinforced. Continuous reinforcement, after every correct response, teaches fastest but extinguishes fastest; partial reinforcement makes behaviour persist far longer once reward stops (the partial reinforcement extinction effect). Reward may depend on the number of responses (ratio) or on time elapsed (interval), fixed or variable, giving the four schedules that Charles Ferster and Skinner mapped in 1957 (Figure 1.7). Fixed ratio (FR), as in piece-rate pay: high, steady responding with a brief post-reinforcement pause. Variable ratio (VR), as in slot machines: the highest, steadiest rate and the greatest resistance to extinction. Fixed interval (FI), as in checking a dish due out of the oven: a pause, then faster and faster responding, the scallop. Variable interval (VI), as in checking for a reply to a message: moderate, very steady responding. Exam trap "Number" means ratio, "time" interval, "unpredictable" variable. Reinforcement after every response is continuous , the least resistant to extinction. Sheena's chocolate "for every 45 minutes" of study is keyed fixed interval . Differential reinforcement extinguishes a problem behaviour while reinforcing other behaviour, that is, its absence (DRO), an incompatible (DRI) or alternative (DRA) behaviour, or a low rate of it (DRL). The Premack principle of David Premack (1959) holds that a more probable activity can reinforce a less probable one: homework first, then video games. Skinner's pigeons, fed every 15 seconds whatever they did (1948), developed odd rituals: superstitious behaviour, strengthened by accidental reinforcement. Key study: Learned helplessness (Seligman and Maier, 1967) Martin Seligman and Steven Maier gave dogs shocks they could switch off, identical shocks they could not control (the yoked group), or none. Later, in a shuttle box, most yoked dogs passively took shocks they could have escaped by jumping a barrier. Lack of control, not shock, produced learned helplessness : passive acceptance of aversive events, even avoidable ones, after repeated unavoidable ones. It became a model of depression, later recast in attributional terms (Psychiatric Disorders chapter). Biology limits operant learning too: Keller Breland and Marian Breland (1961) found raccoons trained to bank coins rubbing them together as if washing food (instinctive drift). Richard Herrnstein 's matching law (1961) states that responses are divided among options in proportion to the reinforcement each yields. Rats that Leo Crespi (1942) shifted to a medium reward ran slower if shifted down, and faster if shifted up, than rats always given it: contrast effects, too abrupt to be learning, showing that reward size changes motivation. In biofeedback a bodily process is measured and displayed so that changes in the desired direction are reinforced, following Neal Miller 's (1909 to 2002) claim that autonomic responses can be operantly conditioned. Electromyographic (EMG) biofeedback suits tension headache, and Arnold Kegel 's perineometer (1948) was an early form. Exam trap Premack: high-probability behaviour reinforces low-probability behaviour , never the reverse. Learned helplessness is Seligman and Maier's , not Beck's, Sullivan's or Kahneman's. The Crespi effect is a change in motivation when reward size changes , not retroactive inhibition, extinction or insight. Autonomic control by operant conditioning is biofeedback , not hypnosis, sublimation or desensitisation. Table 1.12 compares the two conditionings. They are not "entirely different" but interact constantly: Albert's fear was classical, but had he crawled away and felt relief, his avoidance would have been operant. The hallmark of behaviour therapy is the use of both to eliminate unwanted behaviour, not a search for underlying causes, insight, cognitive restructuring, dream analysis or free association. Latent learning, insight and learning sets Against the view that learning is only stimulus-response connections stamped in by reward, Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959), a purposive behaviourist, argued that animals learn knowledge. Key study: Tolman and Honzik's latent learning experiment (1930) Tolman and Charles Honzik ran three groups of hungry rats through a maze daily for seventeen days: one always found food in the goal box, one never did, and one found food only from day 11. The third group made as many errors as the unrewarded rats for ten days, then at once matched the always-rewarded rats. It had learned the maze all along; reward merely gave it a reason to show it, so learning and performance differ. This is latent learning : learning without obvious reinforcement that stays hidden until there is an incentive to show it. Tolman (1948) said the rats had formed a cognitive map , a mental representation of the layout; rats learn places and expectancies of what leads to what, not only turns. Wolfgang Köhler (1887 to 1967), a founder of Gestalt psychology (Section 1.2), studied chimpanzees on Tenerife (1913 to 1920). Sultan, unable to reach a banana with either of two short sticks, later fitted one into the other and at once raked it in; others stacked boxes. Such insight learning , the sudden grasp of a solution by perceiving the relations among a problem's elements, is abrupt, smooth once found, well retained and readily transferred; its flash of understanding is the aha experience. Harry Harlow (1905 to 1981) found that monkeys given hundreds of discrimination problems came to solve each new one in a single trial: a learning set, or learning to learn (1949), suggesting that apparent insight rests on earlier, gradual learning. Concept formation (Section 1.8) runs from observing instances, through discriminating them from non-instances and generalising to all that share the essential features, to abstracting the defining properties. Exam trap Latent learning and the cognitive map are Tolman's , not Bandura's, Skinner's, Köhler's or Harlow's (Gould studied honeybee navigation). Sultan means insight , and the realisation is the "aha" experience , not the "light bulb"; insight graded in a mental status examination is psychiatric. Concept formation runs observation, discrimination, generalisation, abstraction ; assimilation is Piaget's term. Observational learning Most complex skills, from rolling a chapati to a cover drive, are learned largely by watching. This is observational learning (social learning, modelling): learning by watching others, called models, and the consequences of their behaviour. John Dollard (1900 to 1980) and Neal Miller (1941) held that imitation must itself be reinforced, the early social learning theory; Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) showed that it need not be. Key study: Bandura, Ross and Ross's Bobo doll experiment (1961) Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross let 72 nursery-school children watch an adult punch, kick and hammer an inflatable Bobo doll. Left later with the doll, these children copied the model's specific acts and words far more than children who saw a quiet model or none, with no reinforcement at all. In 1965 children who saw the model punished imitated less, until offered a reward for showing what the model had done, when all groups did equally well. Criticism. Bobo is made to be hit, and only short-term effects were measured. The model's consequences, then, affect performance, not learning: seeing a model rewarded increases imitation (vicarious reinforcement), and seeing one punished reduces it. Bandura's four processes are attention (noticing the model), retention (storing the act in images and words), motor reproduction (turning the memory into action) and motivation (a reason to perform). The first three govern learning and the fourth performance, so reinforcement is not necessary, and the model must actually demonstrate the target behaviour. Modelling is also a therapy (Clinical Psychology chapter). With Richard Walters (1963) Bandura developed later social learning theory, renamed social cognitive theory in 1986. Its reciprocal determinism (1978) holds that the person (beliefs, expectations), behaviour and environment influence one another in both directions, against Skinner's view that environment alone shapes behaviour. Self-regulation means that most behaviour is guided by self-set standards and self-reward rather than external rewards. The theory's central motivational construct is self-efficacy (1977), a person's belief in his capability to carry out the actions a specific task requires. ( Julian Rotter 's separate social learning theory of 1954 belongs to the Personality chapter: behaviour potential, the likelihood of a behaviour in a given situation in relation to a reinforcement, depends on expectancy and reinforcement value. Social learning frameworks in general explain behaviour by expectancies, situational demands and incentives rather than by reinforcement history alone.) Exam trap The four processes are attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation , not sensory-perceptual or memory stages; the one NOT necessary is reinforcement , a view that is Bandura's , not Skinner's, Tolman's or Miller and Dollard's. Reciprocal causation belongs to social cognitive theory , not two-factor, drive-reduction or constructivist theory, and is neither reciprocal inhibition nor reciprocal altruism. Self-efficacy (Bandura, not Beck, Ellis or Skinner) is not self-esteem, external locus of control or Adlerian striving; it, not goal difficulty, rewards or drives, is the motivational core of social cognitive theory. Most behaviour stems from self-regulation , not "reciprocal dualism" or "behavioural determinism". Match: Dollard and Miller, early social learning; Bandura and Walters, later; Skinner, radical behaviourism; Maslow, self-actualisation. Other theorists and learning in practice The grand theories divided on two questions: is what is learned a stimulus-response connection, as the stimulus-response (S-R) behaviouristic approach holds, or knowledge (Tolman, Köhler); and does learning need only contiguity, or reinforcement too? Edwin Ray Guthrie (1886 to 1959) chose contiguity: a stimulus combination that accompanied a movement will tend to be followed by it again, at full strength after one trial. A habit is broken by attaching a new response to its cue: present the cue too weakly to trigger the habit and strengthen it gradually, as with a light blanket before a saddle (threshold method); repeat the response to exhaustion (fatigue method); or present the cue while a competing response occurs (incompatible response method). Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) chose reinforcement, defined as drive reduction: reaction potential equals habit strength multiplied by drive ( S E R = S H R × D). Table 1.13 adds Estes and Robert Mills Gagné (1916 to 2002). Mowrer and his wife devised the bell-and-pad for bed-wetting (1938), and constructivists (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner) hold that learners actively build knowledge. William James (1890) and Thorndike refuted formal discipline, the belief that Latin trains the mind; Thorndike's identical elements theory ties transfer to elements the tasks share. Sidney Leavitt Pressey built the first teaching machine (1920s); Skinner's programmed instruction (1954) used small steps, active responses, immediate feedback and self-pacing. Answers: (1) sensitisation, (2) conditioned, (3) reciprocal inhibition, (4) negative, (5) variable ratio and (6) motor reproduction. 1.7 Memory: Encoding, Storage, Retrieval and Forgetting High yield · 111 Qs Memory, the capacity to retain information and use it later, is not one thing. After encephalitis destroyed both his hippocampi in 1985, the British musician Clive Wearing could follow a conversation only while it lasted and had lost almost every episode of his past, yet he could still sight-read and conduct. To see how, begin with how memory was first measured. Ebbinghaus and the measurement of memory Cognitive psychology treats the mind as an information processor (Section 1.2) and divides remembering into encoding (turning information into a code the system can hold), storage and retrieval . Encoding needs attention: fewer than half of the adults tested by Raymond Nickerson and Marilyn Adams (1979) could pick out the correct drawing of a coin they had handled thousands of times. Details never attended to are never encoded ( encoding failure ) and so cannot be retrieved. The first memory experiments were made by Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909), his own sole participant. To escape the associations of real words he invented the nonsense syllable (DAX, BUP), learned lists to one perfect recitation and relearned them later. Relearning was faster even when nothing could be recalled. The savings method expresses this as original learning time minus relearning time, divided by original learning time, multiplied by 100: a list learned in 20 readings and relearned in 12 shows (20 minus 12) divided by 20, or 40 per cent, savings. His forgetting curve ( Über das Gedächtnis , 1885) falls steeply, losing more than half within an hour and about two thirds within a day, then levels off without reaching zero. He also first noted the spacing effect and the advantage of a list's beginning and end. Retention is measured by recall , which is free (any order), serial (original order) or cued (from a hint); paired-associate learning , introduced by Mary Whiton Calkins in 1894, is cued recall of pairs, such as a Kannada word and its English meaning. Recognition , picking old items from new ones as in a multiple-choice question, is easier than recall. Relearning is the most sensitive measure. The reconstruction method hands back the presented items shuffled for the person to put in order. Exam trap Items presented, scrambled and put back in order (RML 2024) is the reconstruction method, a measuring technique, not Bartlett's reconstructive memory. Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud were independent pioneers, not laboratory founders, and each devised a new method (nonsense syllables; questionnaires and word association; free association). RML 2020 keys "independent pioneers" alone, as Ebbinghaus's method was experimental, not observational; a bank version keys "(a) and (c)", adding "novel observational methods". The multi-store model In 1968 Richard C. Atkinson and Richard M. Shiffrin proposed the multi-store model , also called the modal or stage model: attended information passes from sensory memory to short-term memory, and rehearsed information passes on to long-term memory, from which it is retrieved when needed. Attention and rehearsal are control processes that the person chooses. The first store, sensory memory (the sensory register), briefly holds a large amount of raw, pre-categorical information, one store per sense. Ulric Neisser named the visual store iconic memory and the auditory store echoic memory in 1967; a touch store, haptic memory, is little studied. Key study: Sperling's partial report (1960) Shown twelve letters for 50 milliseconds, people report only four or five but insist they saw more. George Sperling sounded a tone just after the flash to signal which of the three rows to report. People gave about three of the four cued letters, so about nine of the twelve had been briefly available. Delaying the tone by about one second removed the advantage: the icon fades within roughly 250 to 500 milliseconds. Echoic memory lasts two to four seconds, as the "three-eared man" study of Christopher Darwin , Michael Turvey and Robert Crowder (1972) showed. Short-term memory (STM) holds a little information for seconds unless it is rehearsed. George Armitage Miller put its span at "the magical number seven, plus or minus two" (1956) meaningful units, or chunks. Grouping items into larger meaningful units is chunking : I N D I A I I T I S R O is twelve letters but three chunks (INDIA, IIT, ISRO). Without chunking and rehearsal, capacity is nearer four chunks ( Nelson Cowan , 2001). In the Brown-Peterson technique ( John Brown , 1958; Lloyd Peterson and Margaret Peterson , 1959), counting backwards blocked rehearsal, and recall of a consonant trigram fell from about 80 per cent at 3 seconds to about 10 per cent at 18, hence a duration of 18 to 30 seconds; Geoffrey Keppel and Benton Underwood (1962) traced the loss to interference, not decay. STM codes mainly by sound: Reuben Conrad (1964) found people writing V for B, and Alan Baddeley showed in 1966 that sound-alike words confuse immediate recall and meaning-alike words delayed recall. Long-term memory (LTM) codes mainly by meaning (Table 1.14). Table 1.14 The three stores of the multi-store model compared. "Icon and echo" are always sensory memory, and the store that "lasts only a few seconds" is sensory memory, not eidetic imagery. Free recall gives the U-shaped serial position effect , or primacy-recency effect ( Bennet Murdock , 1962; Figure 1.8). The primacy effect reflects extra rehearsal of early items into LTM; the recency effect reflects the last items still sitting in STM.
