Answers: (1) need, drive, (2) lower, (3) belongingness and love, (4) press, (5) relatedness, (6) hygiene. 1.11 Emotion and Stress High yield · 74 Qs Your heart pounds as the question paper is handed out. Is that pounding the fear itself, or something your mind has still to interpret? This section takes emotion apart, then turns to stress and coping. What an emotion is An emotion is a brief, whole-person response to an event that matters to you, with three components: physiological arousal (a pounding heart, sweating palms), expressive behaviour (face, voice, posture, action) and conscious experience ("I am afraid"). The theories that follow quarrel mainly about the order of these three. A feeling is the subjective part of an emotion. An emotion lasts seconds to minutes and has an object (you are angry at someone); a mood lasts hours or days, is weaker and often has no object. Affect is the umbrella term for your present good or bad feeling state and, clinically, its observable expression, rated for quality, range and reactivity; persistence is what defines mood. Temperament is the inborn style of emotional reactivity (Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess's easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up types are in the Developmental chapter). Are there basic emotions, innate and universal, each with its own face? Paul Ekman (born 1934) and Wallace V. Friesen found six with universally recognised expressions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust, with contempt added in 1986. Silvan Tomkins (1962) listed nine innate affects; Carroll Izard 's differential emotions theory (1977) listed ten, including shame and guilt; and Robert Plutchik 's wheel (1980) set eight primaries opposite one another (joy and sadness, trust and disgust, fear and anger, surprise and anticipation), with neighbours blending into dyads such as love (joy plus trust). Dimensional models place emotions in a space instead: Wundt's three-dimensional theory of feeling (Section 1.1) and the circumplex of James Russell (1980), a circle of valence (pleasant to unpleasant) by arousal. Exam trap Jealousy, shame, guilt, pride and love are not among Ekman's six. Shame and guilt are Izard's, trust and anticipation Plutchik's. "Our current mood and feelings" is affect , not mood. Body first or label first Common sense says you see a bear, feel afraid, and therefore tremble. William James (1842 to 1910) in 1884 and the Danish physician Carl Georg Lange (1834 to 1900) in 1885 reversed the order. The James-Lange theory holds that the stimulus first triggers bodily changes and that the emotion is our perception of them: "we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble." The textbook sequence is stimulus, arousal, awareness ("interpretation") of the arousal, then emotion (Figure 1.14, top row), where the "interpretation" is just the brain noticing what the body is doing. Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945) objected in 1927 that emotion survives when the viscera are cut off from the brain; that the same visceral changes accompany fear, anger, fever and exercise; that the viscera are too insensitive and slow for quick, fine distinctions; and that injected adrenaline produces symptoms without real emotion. In the Cannon-Bard theory , developed with Philip Bard (1898 to 1977), the thalamus signals the cortex and the body at once, so feeling and arousal occur simultaneously and independently (second row). If arousal is so similar across emotions, what tells fear from joy? In 1962 Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer answered with the two-factor theory : emotion is physiological arousal, which sets its intensity, plus a cognitive label drawn from the situation, which names it. Key study: Schachter and Singer's adrenaline experiment (1962) Students given adrenaline (epinephrine), described as a vitamin, were told its true effects, told nothing or misinformed; a placebo group got saline. Each then waited with a stooge acting euphoric or angry. The aroused but uninformed caught the stooge's mood most; the informed, who could blame the injection, least. Criticism. The effects were small, and in replications unexplained arousal simply felt anxious. A label can be wrong. In misattribution of arousal people mistake the source of their arousal: in 1974 Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron found that men approached by an attractive woman on the swaying Capilano suspension bridge telephoned her far more often than men on a low, solid bridge. Fear had been read as attraction. Dolf Zillmann 's excitation transfer theory (1970s) adds that leftover arousal from one event intensifies the next emotion. Exam trap Match theory to sequence. Common sense: emotion, then body (the view James rejected). James-Lange: body first, then emotion. Cannon-Bard: emotion and visceral reaction simultaneous , via the thalamus. Schachter-Singer: cognition plus arousal , and the only one that explains misattribution. No classic theory makes the somatic nervous system the seat of emotion, and "emotions are learned through reinforcement" is behaviourism. Appraisal, faces and opposing processes Richard S. Lazarus (1922 to 2002) put thought first. In his cognitive appraisal (cognitive-mediational) theory, primary appraisal asks "Does this matter to me?" (harm-loss, threat or challenge), secondary appraisal asks "What can I do about it?", and reappraisal revises both (Figure 1.14, bottom row). Robert Zajonc (1923 to 2008) argued for affective primacy ("preferences need no inferences", 1980; debated with Lazarus in 1984): by the mere exposure effect, repeated exposure raises liking even for shapes seen too briefly to be recognised, so affect can come first. The facial feedback hypothesis , rooted in Tomkins's work, says that our own expressions modulate our feelings; in the pen study of Fritz Strack , Leonard Martin and Sabine Stepper (1988), holding a pen in the teeth, which forces a smile, made cartoons seem funnier, an effect now judged real but small. Charles Darwin 's The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) founded the evolutionary view of expressions as inherited adaptations. Richard Solomon 's opponent-process theory (1974) holds that every strong emotion triggers a slow, opposite after-reaction that grows with repetition: a drug's high fades while withdrawal deepens. The emotional brain and body The body's side of emotion is run by the autonomic nervous system. Its sympathetic division prepares for fight or flight: it dilates the pupils, speeds the heart and breathing, dries the mouth, halts digestion and releases adrenaline from the adrenal medulla, and its sweating lowers skin resistance (the galvanic skin response). The parasympathetic division ("rest and digest") reverses each effect, constricting the pupils. Heartbeat and breathing themselves are paced by the medulla of the hindbrain; the hypothalamus only orchestrates them. Bard's cats, with the cortex removed, showed sham rage , an undirected hissing fury that vanished only when the hypothalamus was removed too: the hypothalamus organises rage and the cortex restrains it. In 1937 James Papez (1883 to 1958) proposed an emotional loop, the Papez circuit : hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus, entorhinal cortex and back to the hippocampus. Paul MacLean (1913 to 2007) added the amygdala and other structures in 1952 and named the whole the limbic system , the classic "seat of emotion", which regulates emotion, motivation and memory (Table 1.23). Its key member is the amygdala , deep in each temporal lobe. When Heinrich Klüver and Paul Bucy removed both anterior temporal lobes of rhesus monkeys (1937, 1939), wild animals became tame. Klüver-Bucy syndrome is placidity (loss of fear, even of snakes), psychic blindness or visual agnosia, hyperorality, hyperphagia and hypersexuality; human cases often add aphasia and amnesia, because nearby temporal cortex is damaged too. The amygdala detects threat, drives fear conditioning and gives emotional events their extra memorability, an advantage that disappears when noradrenaline is blocked with propranolol (Cahill and McGaugh, 1994). Joseph LeDoux (born 1949) found a fast, crude low road from the thalamus straight to the amygdala and a slower, detailed high road through the cortex. Such subcortical routes probably explain affective blindsight, the recognition of emotional faces shown in a cortically blind field. The prefrontal cortex regulates emotion ( Phineas Gage 's rod injury of 1848; Antonio Damasio 's somatic markers, 1994). Damage to its control of the brainstem, after stroke, multiple sclerosis, ALS or brain injury, can cause pseudobulbar affect : sudden, involuntary laughing or crying out of proportion to the actual mood, which is not depression. The polygraph records arousal, not lies, so frightened innocent suspects can fail it; David T. Expression and four emotions The Fore of Papua New Guinea, who had seen no films or magazines, matched Ekman and Friesen's faces to stories far above chance (1971), confusing only fear with surprise. Cultures differ instead in display rules , learned norms for when an emotion may be shown. The Facial Action Coding System (1978) codes faces as muscle action units, and a genuine Duchenne smile engages the muscles around the eyes. Posture, gesture and voice carry emotion too. Women are, on average, more facially expressive, largely through socialisation. Fear answers a present danger; anxiety is diffuse and future-oriented; a phobia is a persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation. The catharsis hypothesis, that venting anger drains it, fails: hitting a punching bag while thinking of an insulter increased aggression ( Brad Bushman , 2002). Disgust guards against contamination ( Paul Rozin and April Fallon , 1987). Ed Diener (1946 to 2021) defined subjective well-being (1984) by three components: life satisfaction (cognitive), frequent positive affect and infrequent negative affect. Good fortune fades: by Harry Helson 's adaptation-level theory (1964) and the hedonic treadmill of Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell (1971), lottery winners are no happier than others a year or so later, and relative deprivation ( Samuel Stouffer , 1949) makes us judge ourselves against others. Barbara Fredrickson 's broaden-and-build theory (1998) says positive emotions widen thought and build lasting resources. Savoring ( Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff , 2007) is enhancing and prolonging the enjoyment of positive experiences. Exam trap Diener: life satisfaction, not physical, spiritual or social wellness. Fredrickson: broaden-and-build; flow is Csikszentmihalyi, cognitive distortions Beck, psychodynamic theory Freud. Savoring is not avoiding negatives, relaxing or reflecting on trauma. How emotions develop and are regulated Katharine Banham Bridges (1932) saw the newborn's general excitement split first into distress and delight , and only then into anger, fear, elation and the rest. Primary emotions are present by about six months. The self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, shame, guilt) need a sense of self, so they appear after 12 months, from about 18 months. Edward Tronick 's still-face procedure (1978), in which a mother suddenly freezes her face, shows that even young infants expect emotional give-and-take. In the process model of James Gross (1998), emotion regulation has five families of strategies, in the order an emotion unfolds: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment (distraction, rumination), cognitive change, chiefly cognitive reappraisal ("my racing heart is my body getting ready"), and response modulation, which includes expressive suppression. Alexithymia ( Peter Sifneos , 1973) is difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, not anhedonia (loss of pleasure). Daniel Goleman 's emotional intelligence (1995; Section 1.9) has five domains: knowing one's emotions, managing them, motivating oneself, recognising others' emotions and handling relationships (later relabelled self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills); empathy has emotional, cognitive and empathic-concern components. Exam trap Reappraisal is cognitive change ; suppression is response modulation. First infant emotions: distress and delight (Bridges); fear, rage and love are Watson's. Goleman: if the 1995 list (knowing and managing one's emotions, motivating oneself, recognising others' emotions, handling relationships) and the later self-awareness relabelling both appear, choose the 1995 wording. Stress and the body's emergency systems Stress has been defined as a stimulus (the stressor), as a response (Selye's "nonspecific response of the body to any demand") and as a transaction in which demands are appraised as exceeding one's resources. Cannon's fight-or-flight response (1915) is the fast route: within seconds the sympathetic nerves act and the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline. What if the emergency never ends? Hans Selye (1907 to 1982) found that every noxious agent he gave rats, from tissue extracts to cold, produced the same triad: enlarged adrenal glands, shrunken immune tissue and stomach ulcers. In 1936 he proposed the general adaptation syndrome ( The Stress of Life , 1956), with three stages in fixed order. In the alarm reaction the body mobilises, as in fight or flight. In the stage of resistance cortisol stays high and the body adapts, at a cost. In the stage of exhaustion adaptive capacity runs out and diseases of adaptation such as ulcers and hypertension appear. He later (1974) separated eustress , beneficial stress, from distress. Resistance runs on the slower hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA axis): the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), the anterior pituitary adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), and the adrenal cortex cortisol, which feeds back on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary to switch the system off. Shelley E. Taylor (2000) added tend-and-befriend: females especially meet stress by protecting offspring and seeking allies, a pattern linked to oxytocin. Exam trap Alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Illness is not a stage, and the stages are Selye's, not life events theory, the health belief model or protection motivation theory. The adrenal glands are the stress glands; the pituitary only releases ACTH, and the posterior pituitary is not in the HPA axis. Insulin (pancreas), thyroxine (thyroid) and melatonin (pineal) are distractors. Sources of stress and the transactional model Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe 's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (1967) scores 43 life events in life change units, from death of a spouse (100) through marriage (50) to minor violations of the law (11); because change itself is the stressor, even holidays count. Allen Kanner , Lazarus and colleagues (1981) showed that daily hassles , the irritations of everyday life, predict symptoms better than major events, while uplifts, the small pleasures that offset them, matter less. An acute stressor is brief (a pop quiz); a chronic one lasts (HIV disease, cancer, marital discord); a cataclysmic one, such as a flood or war, strikes many people at once. Frustration and conflict are covered under motivation (Section 1.10). At work, organisational stressors are task, role and interpersonal demands, structure and leadership, as distinct from environmental (political uncertainty) and individual (family, money) factors. Role conflict (incompatible expectations) and Robert Karasek 's high-demand, low-control jobs (1979) can end in burnout ( Herbert Freudenberger , 1974), which Christina Maslach 's inventory (1981) measures as exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced accomplishment. In Lazarus and Susan Folkman 's transactional model of stress (1984), stress is a person-environment relationship appraised as taxing or exceeding one's resources: primary appraisal judges harm-loss, threat or challenge, secondary appraisal judges the resources for coping, and coping and reappraisal follow. In one exam hall, Ananya appraises the paper as a threat and her preparation as thin, and shakes; Kiran sees a challenge, trusts his practice, and feels keyed up but focused. The diathesis-stress model ( Paul Meehl , 1962; Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring , 1977) explains why stress makes one person ill and spares another: a disorder appears when a pre-existing vulnerability, often biological, is triggered by stress; usually neither is enough alone. Exam trap The SRRS measures life events , not hassles, physiological reactions or cognitive change. Secondary appraisal is the resources question; "coping resource assessment" is not the model's term. Diathesis-stress is not "genes only", "environment only", "unconscious conflicts only", "learned experiences alone" or supernatural; humanistic, sociocultural and cognitive models blame blocked growth, social forces and faulty thinking. Coping, personality and health Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor (a revision plan); emotion-focused coping acts on the feelings (reappraisal, support, acceptance, but also denial). The best choice fits controllability: plan while the exam can still be prepared for, reappraise once the result is out. Approach coping beats avoidance in the long run. Defence mechanisms (Personality chapter) differ in being unconscious: repression involuntarily blocks painful feelings (suppression is deliberate); displacement redirects anger to a safer target (anger at a husband shouted at a child); sublimation channels it into a valued outlet (kickboxing); projection attributes one's own feelings to others; isolation of affect strips the feeling from an idea (a gruesome fantasy told calmly), whereas denial rejects the reality; rationalisation offers a plausible excuse; and reaction formation turns a feeling into its opposite. Social support protects both directly and as a buffer when stress is high ( Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Wills , 1985). Robert S. Weiss (1973) separated emotional isolation , lacking a deep attachment to one specific person, from social isolation, lacking a circle of friends. Suzanne Kobasa 's hardiness (1979) is commitment, control and challenge; Aaron Antonovsky 's sense of coherence (1979) is comprehensibility, manageability and meaningfulness; resilience is bouncing back from adversity. Dispositional optimism ( Michael Scheier and Charles Carver , 1985), a general expectancy of good outcomes, aids coping and recovery. Martin Seligman and Steven Maier (1967) found that dogs given inescapable shock stopped trying to escape, learned helplessness (Section 1.6), which Seligman later reversed into learned optimism. In 1959 the cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman described the Type A behaviour pattern : competitive striving, time urgency and hostility. In their Western Collaborative Group Study, Type A men developed coronary heart disease about twice as often as relaxed Type B men; later work found hostility to be the toxic component. A cancer-prone Type C, unassertive and suppressing negative emotion, has weak support. Johan Denollet 's Type D personality (mid-1990s) is negative affectivity plus social inhibition, and predicts a poor outlook in heart disease. George Engel 's biopsychosocial model (1977) explains illness through biological, psychological and social factors together. Psychoneuroimmunology began when Robert Ader and Nicholas Cohen (1975) conditioned immune suppression in rats by pairing saccharin with an immunosuppressive drug; chronic stress suppresses immunity and slows healing. Three models predict health behaviour: the health belief model ( Irwin Rosenstock and colleagues, 1950s: perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers and cues to action), Ronald Rogers 's protection motivation theory (1975: threat appraisal and coping appraisal) and Icek Ajzen 's theory of planned behaviour (1985: attitude, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control, close to Albert Bandura's self-efficacy, belief in one's capability to act). Stress management (Clinical chapter) includes Edmund Jacobson 's progressive muscle relaxation (1929), tensing and releasing muscle groups in turn; Herbert Benson 's relaxation response (1975); biofeedback, learning to control a bodily signal displayed on a monitor; meditation, as in Jon Kabat-Zinn 's mindfulness-based stress reduction (1979); regular aerobic exercise; and cognitive restructuring, replacing distorted thoughts with realistic ones, which Donald Meichenbaum combined with coping skills in stress inoculation training (1970s). Exam trap Type A is competitiveness, impatience and hostility; options with "non-competitiveness" are wrong, and introversion or extraversion is no risk factor. Offered both Type A and hostility, RML 2024 keyed Type A; for the toxic component , answer hostility. Type D is not hostility, optimism or perfectionism. Learned helplessness is Seligman and Maier, not Beck, Sullivan or Kahneman. Biopsychosocial means social, not cultural. Emotional isolation is not incompetence or low self-esteem. The Case of Max Friedrich's Key, Revisited Go back to the winter of 1879 and the student pressing his key. You can now take his act apart with the whole chapter. The stimulus had to cross a threshold (Section 1.3) and be organised into an object (Section 1.4); apperception was attention bringing it into focus (Section 1.5); practice shortened the times, which is learning (Section 1.6); the instruction was held in memory (Section 1.7); choosing when to press was a small decision (Section 1.8); observers differed in speed, one root of the study of individual differences and intelligence (Section 1.9); and the readiness and strain of waiting were motivation and emotion (Sections 1.10 and 1.11). Friedrich's numbers are forgotten, but his question, how long a mental act takes and what it is made of, runs through every section of this chapter. Chapter summary 1.1 Psychology as a Science: Roots, Founders and the First Schools. Psychology, once the study of the soul, is now the scientific study of behaviour and covert mental processes. Its long past lies in philosophy (Plato's nativism, Aristotle's laws of association, Descartes' dualism, Locke's tabula rasa , the associationists, Leibniz and Herbart on apperception, Kant) and in physiology (Muller, Helmholtz, localisation), with Darwin and Galton adding function and individual differences. Fechner's psychophysics (1860) and Donders' chronometry measured the mind. Wundt founded the first laboratory at Leipzig in 1879 and taught voluntarism through controlled introspection. Titchener 's structuralism sought the elements of consciousness; James 's functionalism asked what the mind is for, and Witmer opened the first clinic (1896). 1.2 Schools and Systems, the Cognitive Revolution and Indian Psychology. From about 1900 to 1960 psychology was a preparadigmatic field of rival schools. Watson founded behaviourism in 1913; Tolman, Hull, Guthrie and Skinner refined it. Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer's phi phenomenon, 1912; Kohler; Koffka) held that the whole differs from the sum of its parts, and Lewin defined the life space. Psychoanalysis was the first force, humanism (Maslow, Rogers) the third and transpersonal psychology the fourth, beside existential psychology and Seligman's positive psychology. The cognitive revolution (1956 onwards) restored the mind. Sengupta and Bose pioneered modern psychology at Calcutta; Indian psychology rests on Samkhya's purusha, prakriti and three gunas, Patanjali's eight limbs, the four states and the five koshas. 1.3 Sensation and Psychophysics. Sensation is the detection and transduction of physical energy; perception is its interpretation, so illusions distort perception. Muller's specific nerve energies and the all-or-none law explain how quality and intensity are coded, and every sense but smell relays through the thalamus. Fechner's psychophysics (1860) defines the absolute threshold as 50 percent detection and the JND as the smallest detectable change; Weber's law, Fechner's logarithmic law and Stevens' power law link stimulus to sensation, and signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d′) from response bias. Rods serve scotopic vision and foveal cones colour and acuity; colour is trichromatic then opponent; pitch is coded by place and timing; gate control explains pain. 1.4 Perception: Organising and Interpreting the World. Perception is the selection, organisation and interpretation of sensory signals. Constructivist theories (Helmholtz's unconscious inference, Gregory's hypotheses, the Bayesian union of priors and evidence) treat it as top-down inference; Gibson's direct, ecological theory, with its affordances, is the classic bottom-up account, and Neisser's perceptual cycle joins the two. The Gestalt laws, crowned by Prägnanz, organise the field into figure, ground and groups. Depth comes from two binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence) and many monocular ones; the visual cliff (Gibson and Walk, 1960) showed depth perception by crawling age. Constancies keep objects stable, while illusions such as the Müller-Lyer reveal misapplied size scaling and differ from hallucinations and delusions. 1.5 Attention and Consciousness. Attention selects the little that reaches awareness; its span, studied by Jevons (1871) and with the tachistoscope, is about six to eight items. Cherry's dichotic listening (1953) led to Broadbent's early filter (1958), Treisman's attenuation model (1964) and late selection (Deutsch and Deutsch, 1963). In the Stroop effect (1935) automatic reading defeats selective attention, and vigilance declines over a watch (Mackworth). James described a stream of consciousness, Freud conscious, preconscious and unconscious levels. The suprachiasmatic nucleus times sleep, whose NREM and REM stages cycle every 90 minutes, four to six times a night. Dreams are explained by Freud, Jung and activation-synthesis; hypnosis rests on suggestibility. 1.6 Learning: Conditioning, Cognition and Observation. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour, or its potential, resulting from experience (Kimble). In classical conditioning (Pavlov) a neutral stimulus paired with a UCS becomes a CS; extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination follow. Watson's Little Albert showed conditioned fear, and Jones and Wolpe reversed it through counterconditioning and systematic desensitisation (reciprocal inhibition). Rescorla, Kamin and Garcia showed that conditioning depends on prediction and preparedness. In operant conditioning (Thorndike's law of effect, Skinner) consequences change behaviour: reinforcement increases it, punishment decreases it, and schedules shape its pattern, variable ratio most strongly. Tolman's latent learning, Köhler's insight and Bandura's observational learning showed much learning without direct reinforcement. 1.7 Memory: Encoding, Storage, Retrieval and Forgetting. Memory is studied as encoding , storage and retrieval ; Ebbinghaus (1885) measured forgetting with nonsense syllables and savings. Atkinson and Shiffrin's multi-store model (1968) separates sensory, short-term (seven plus or minus two chunks, mainly acoustic) and long-term memory, and Baddeley and Hitch (1974) recast short-term memory as working memory : central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and, from 2000, the episodic buffer. Depth of processing, Tulving's episodic and semantic memory, implicit memory, schemas and Bartlett's reconstruction, encoding specificity, decay, interference and repression explain remembering and forgetting, while H.M., Korsakoff's syndrome and Lashley's search for the engram reveal its biology. 1.8 Thinking, Problem Solving, Reasoning, Decision Making and Language. Thinking manipulates internal representations: images (Shepard and Metzler's mental rotation; Paivio's dual coding), concepts (Bruner's hypothesis testing for artificial concepts, Rosch's prototypes for natural ones) and propositions. Problems yield to algorithms, heuristics or Gestalt insight, and are blocked by functional fixedness (Duncker, 1945) and mental set (Luchins, 1942). Deduction runs from theory to data, induction from data to theory. Simon's bounded rationality and satisficing, and Tversky and Kahneman's heuristics and prospect theory, describe real decisions. Creativity is divergent production passing through Wallas's four stages. Language is built from phonemes and morphemes; Chomsky's LAD, the critical period, Whorf's linguistic relativity and Vygotsky's inner speech complete the picture. 1.9 Intelligence: Theories, Measurement, Heredity and Environment. Intelligence has been defined as judgement (Binet), what the tests test (Boring) and Wechsler's aggregate or global capacity (1944). Binet and Simon's 1905 scale introduced mental age; Stern coined the IQ (1912), Terman's Stanford-Binet (1916) made the ratio IQ famous, and Wechsler's deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15) replaced it. The WAIS-IV has four indices; Raven's matrices test fluid intelligence, and Bhatia's Battery suits illiterate Indian children. Spearman's g, Thurstone's primary abilities, Guilford's cube, Cattell's fluid and crystallised intelligence, Gardner's multiple intelligences and Sternberg's triarchic theory offer rival structures. Heritability is a population statistic, and intellectual disability requires adaptive deficits as well as low IQ. 1.10 Motivation. Motivation energises and directs behaviour: a need produces a drive that pushes, while incentives pull. McDougall's instincts gave way to Hull's drive reduction (1943), which could not explain curiosity; Hebb proposed optimal arousal, and the Yerkes-Dodson law (1908) makes performance an inverted U of arousal with a lower optimum for complex tasks. Maslow's hierarchy of needs runs physiological, safety, belongingness, esteem, self-actualisation; Alderfer reduced it to ERG. Murray's needs and press underlie the TAT; McClelland studied achievement, power and affiliation. Self-efficacy, self-determination theory and flow explain intrinsic motivation. Lewin classified conflicts; the VMH is the satiety centre, the LH the feeding centre; Herzberg, Vroom and Locke explain work. 1.11 Emotion and Stress. An emotion joins arousal, expression and conscious experience; a mood is longer and diffuse, and affect is the current feeling state. Ekman named six universal basic emotions. James-Lange puts bodily change before feeling, Cannon-Bard makes them simultaneous via the thalamus, Schachter and Singer add a cognitive label (explaining misattribution), and Lazarus puts appraisal first. The limbic system , above all the amygdala , organises fear. Stress runs through Selye's alarm, resistance and exhaustion and the HPA axis; life events, hassles and appraisal shape it, and coping, support, hardiness and Type A or D personality link it to illness. Stanley Hall ✓ Answer: (c) William James William James, Principles of Psychology (1890) The concept The school Functionalism asked what the mind is for : how mental processes help us adapt, not what they are made of. Which is the correct order of the last four of Patanjali's eight limbs? (NIMHANS 2026 recall) a Dharana, pratyahara, dhyana, samadhi b Pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi c Pratyahara, dhyana, dharana, samadhi d Dhyana, dharana, pratyahara, samadhi ✓ Answer: (b) Pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi Patanjali's eight limbs of yoga The concept Turning inward The senses are first withdrawn inward ( pratyahara ), then the mind is fixed on one point ( dharana ). Going deeper The fixing becomes an unbroken flow ( dhyana ) and finally absorption ( samadhi ). Exam tip Each wrong option swaps two of these steps; remember the order withdraw, fix, flow, absorb . Why the other options are wrong (a) Dharana, pratyahara, dhyana, samadhi Swaps the first two: pratyahara (withdrawing the senses) must come before dharana (fixing the mind). (c) Pratyahara, dhyana, dharana, samadhi Swaps the middle two: dharana (fixing on one point) must come before dhyana , its unbroken flow. (d) Dhyana, dharana, pratyahara, samadhi Swaps the first and third: it starts with dhyana , but sense withdrawal ( pratyahara ) comes first. Which statement is INCORRECT? (Amity 2023) a Cones are most prevalent in the central retina b Cones are sensitive to moderate to high levels of light c Cones provide only monochromatic information d Cones provide excellent acuity ✓ Answer: (c) Cones provide only monochromatic information Rods versus cones in the retina The concept Why it is false Cones , with three pigments, give colour vision , so they are not monochromatic. Who is monochromatic It is the rods , with one pigment ( rhodopsin ), that give colourless scotopic vision. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Cones are most prevalent in the central retina True: cones are packed in the fovea , at the centre of the retina. (b) Cones are sensitive to moderate to high levels of light True: cones work in moderate to bright light, while the rods handle dim light. (d) Cones provide excellent acuity True: cones give excellent acuity , sharpest in the fovea where they are packed. In signal detection theory, the ability to distinguish a stimulus from background noise is: (IHBAS 2025) a Sensitivity (d′) b Criterion (β) c ROC curve d JND ✓ Answer: (a) Sensitivity (d′) Signal detection theory: sensitivity, d′ The concept What it is d′ is the separation between the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions. Why this one It does not depend on the observer's willingness to say "yes", so it measures the ability to detect alone. Why the other options are wrong (b) Criterion (β) The observer's willingness to say "yes" ( response bias ), not the ability to detect. (c) ROC curve A graph that plots hit rate against false alarm rate , not the ability itself. (d) JND The just noticeable difference belongs to classical psychophysics, not signal detection theory. Among monocular cues for depth perception is (JEMAS 2025) a Convergence b Retinal disparity c Assimilation d Interposition ✓ Answer: (d) Interposition Monocular depth cue: interposition (overlap) The concept What it is In interposition , an object that partly hides another is seen as nearer. Why monocular One eye is enough to see the overlap, so it is a monocular cue . Why the other options are wrong (a) Convergence A binocular cue (the eyes turn inward for near objects); convergence and retinal disparity are the only two binocular cues. (b) Retinal disparity The other binocular cue: each eye gets a slightly different image, so it needs both eyes. (c) Assimilation Not a depth cue at all; it is Piaget 's term for fitting new experience into existing schemas. Illusions are (JEMAS 2025) a misinterpretation of stimuli arising from an external object b real perceptual object perceived in a distorted way c vivid mental images d perception without an adequate external stimulus ✓ Answer: (a) Misinterpretation of stimuli arising from an external object Definition of an illusion The concept What it is In an illusion a real external stimulus is present but is misread. Exam tip Contrast a hallucination , which is perception without an adequate external stimulus. Why the other options are wrong (b) real perceptual object perceived in a distorted way A sensory distortion such as micropsia , where a real object looks changed (smaller). (c) vivid mental images Imagery , produced by the mind with no stimulus being misread. (d) perception without an adequate external stimulus The definition of a hallucination , not an illusion. The Stroop effect demonstrates interference in (JEMAS 2025) a Long-term memory retrieval b Working memory c Selective attention d Procedural memory ✓ Answer: (c) Selective attention Stroop effect: selective attention The concept How it works Word reading is automatic , so it cannot be filtered out while naming the ink colour . Why this one The task therefore shows a failure of selective attention . Why the other options are wrong (a) Long-term memory retrieval A memory distractor: no stored memory is being retrieved from long-term memory . (b) Working memory A memory distractor: nothing is being rehearsed in working memory ; the clash is in attention. (d) Procedural memory A memory distractor: procedural memory is skill memory, and no stored skill is being retrieved here. According to Freud, the ___ mind includes accessible memories, which can be recalled at will (RML 2020) a Conscious b Preconscious c Unconscious d Psychic determinism ✓ Answer: (b) Preconscious Freud's topographical model of the mind The concept What it is Freud's preconscious holds memories outside current awareness that can be recalled at will. The other levels The conscious holds only what is in awareness now; the unconscious cannot be recalled at will. Why the other options are wrong (a) Conscious Holds only what is in awareness now, not stored memories waiting to be recalled. (c) Unconscious Its contents cannot be recalled at will, so it does not fit "accessible memories". (d) Psychic determinism A principle (no mental event is accidental), not a level of mind. Systematic desensitization technique is based upon the idea of: (IHBAS 2025) a Reciprocal inhibition b Law of effect c Habituation d Adaptation to stress ✓ Answer: (a) Reciprocal inhibition Wolpe, reciprocal inhibition The concept How it works Wolpe paired each step of an anxiety hierarchy with relaxation . Why it works Relaxation is a response incompatible with anxiety, so the anxiety bond weakens: reciprocal inhibition . Why the other options are wrong (b) Law of effect Thorndike 's operant principle: behaviour followed by satisfaction is strengthened. (c) Habituation Underlies exposure and response prevention , which uses no competing response such as relaxation. (d) Adaptation to stress Belongs to stress theory , not to the learning principle behind desensitization. Among the following schedules of reinforcement, which typically produces the highest rate of response and is most resistant to extinction? (Real PYQ 2024) a Fixed Ratio b Variable Ratio c Fixed Interval d Variable Interval ✓ Answer: (b) Variable Ratio Skinner, schedules of reinforcement The concept Why ratio Ratio schedules reward fast responding: the more responses, the more reinforcers. Why variable Unpredictability removes any reason to pause and makes it hard to tell that reinforcement has stopped, as with slot machines . Why the other options are wrong (a) Fixed Ratio Fast too, but shows a pause after each reinforcer and gives up sooner in extinction, since the end of reward is easier to spot. (c) Fixed Interval Produces a scallop : little responding just after a reinforcer, speeding up as the next one nears. (d) Variable Interval Gives only a moderate, steady rate, because responding faster does not earn reinforcement sooner. The famous patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) underwent surgical removal of the medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus, to treat severe epilepsy. While he retained most of his intellectual abilities and working memory, his primary and most profound deficit was in: (Real PYQ 2024) a Procedural memory b Semantic memory c Anterograde amnesia d Retrograde amnesia ✓ Answer: (c) Anterograde amnesia Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), 1953 operation The concept What was lost After the 1953 operation H.M. could not form new declarative memories : a profound anterograde amnesia . What survived His intelligence, digit span and childhood memories survived. Why the other options are wrong (a) Procedural memory Spared: he learned mirror tracing , improving with practice though he did not remember the sessions. (b) Semantic memory Old semantic knowledge was intact; his loss was in forming new memories. (d) Retrograde amnesia Present but limited: his retrograde amnesia covered only the years before surgery. Which of the following terms refers to difficulty recalling information due to interference from new information? (IHBAS 2024) a Retroactive interference b Proactive interference c Decay theory d Retrieval failure ✓ Answer: (a) Retroactive interference Interference theory of forgetting The concept What it is In retroactive interference , new learning reaches back to disrupt older memories. Memory trick RETRO : new disrupts old, acting backwards in time. Why the other options are wrong (b) Proactive interference The reverse: old learning disrupts new learning. (c) Decay theory Decay blames the passage of time, not competition from new learning. (d) Retrieval failure Retrieval failure blames a mismatch of cues, not competition from new learning. In which method does the researcher gather data, look for patterns, and then generate a theory or hypothesis? (RML 2023) a Deductive reasoning b Hypothetico-deductive method c Inductive reasoning d Abductive reasoning ✓ Answer: (c) Inductive reasoning Inductive reasoning: data first, theory last The concept What it is Induction runs from specific observations to a probable generalisation. Why this one Data come first and theory last, as in most qualitative research . Why the other options are wrong (a) Deductive reasoning Deduction runs the other way, from a theory to a tested prediction. (b) Hypothetico-deductive method Also runs from a theory to a tested prediction: form a hypothesis , deduce a result, then test it. (d) Abductive reasoning Abduction infers the best explanation of a surprising fact, rather than generalising from patterns. What is the primary difference between Piaget and Vygotsky's theories of language development? (RML 2021) a Piaget argued thought depends on language while Vygotsky argued language depends on thought b Vygotsky argued thought depends on language while Piaget argued language depends on thought c Vygotsky was concerned with early language development while Piaget was concerned with later language development. d None of the above ✓ Answer: (b) Vygotsky argued thought depends on language while Piaget argued language depends on thought Piaget versus Vygotsky on thought and language The concept Piaget For Piaget , language expresses concepts already built through action, so language depends on thought. Vygotsky For Vygotsky , thought and speech merge at about two, after which thought becomes verbal and depends on language. Why the other options are wrong (a) Piaget argued thought depends on language while Vygotsky argued language depends on thought Swaps the names: it is Vygotsky, not Piaget, who made thought depend on language. (c) Vygotsky was concerned with early language development while Piaget was concerned with later language development. False: both studied the same preschool years. (d) None of the above Fails because (b) states the difference correctly. The term IQ was invented by (JEMAS 2025) a Lewis Termon (sic) b Gordon Allport c William Stern d John Watson ✓ Answer: (c) William Stern William Stern, 1912 The concept What he proposed Stern proposed the intelligence quotient in 1912: mental age divided by chronological age. Who spread it Terman multiplied the quotient by 100 and popularised it in the 1916 Stanford-Binet , but did not coin it. Why the other options are wrong (a) Lewis Termon (sic) Terman is the tempting wrong answer: he popularised the IQ but did not coin it. (b) Gordon Allport Allport is known for traits ; he never worked on the IQ. (d) John Watson Watson is known for behaviourism ; he never worked on the IQ. A 10-year-old child from a rural area, with no formal schooling, is brought for an intellectual assessment due to academic struggles. The child is illiterate and has had minimal exposure to formal testing materials. Which of the following tests would be the MOST appropriate to use to minimize cultural and educational bias? (Real PYQ 2024) a Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence b Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV) c Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale (5th ed.) d Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) ✓ Answer: (a) Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests The concept Why this one Its five performance subtests need no reading, so an illiterate child is not penalised. Norms It has Indian rural norms , which fit a rural child with no formal schooling. Why the other options are wrong (b) Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV) Rests on school-built verbal knowledge and foreign norms, so it is biased against this child. (c) Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale (5th ed.) The SB5 also rests on school-built verbal knowledge and foreign norms. (d) Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) The tempting Indian option, but half of it is verbal , adapted from the WISC. The ‘satiety centre’ of the brain is located in the: (RML 2024) a Lateral hypothalamus b Ventromedial hippocampus c Lateral thalamus d Ventromedial hypothalamus ✓ Answer: (d) Ventromedial hypothalamus Stellar's dual-centre theory (1954) The concept The evidence Bilateral VMH lesions make rats overeat and grow obese ( Hetherington and Ranson , 1940). The theory So Stellar 's dual-centre theory (1954) called the ventromedial hypothalamus the satiety centre. Why the other options are wrong (a) Lateral hypothalamus The opposite, the feeding centre : its destruction causes aphagia ( Anand and Brobeck , 1951). (b) Ventromedial hippocampus Invented by changing one word; the hippocampus serves memory, not satiety. (c) Lateral thalamus Invented by changing one word; the thalamus is a sensory relay, not a hunger centre. According to Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which of the following factors are considered motivators that lead to job satisfaction? (RML 2023) a Salary and benefits b Job security and work conditions c Recognition and opportunities for advancement d Company policies and interpersonal relationships ✓ Answer: (c) Recognition and opportunities for advancement Herzberg's two-factor theory The concept Motivators Herzberg 's motivators lie in the content of the work: achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement and growth. Hygiene factors Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction when good but do not by themselves motivate. Why the other options are wrong (a) Salary and benefits Salary and benefits are hygiene factors : good pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not by itself motivate. (b) Job security and work conditions Job security and working conditions are hygiene factors , part of the setting rather than the content of the work. (d) Company policies and interpersonal relationships Company policies and relationships are hygiene factors ; good ones prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate. The seat of emotion is to be found in _________________. (RML 2024) a Reticular formation b Hind brain c Limbic system d Forebrain ✓ Answer: (c) Limbic system MacLean's limbic system (1952), after Papez The concept What it is MacLean 's limbic system (1952), built on Papez 's circuit, is the classic seat of emotion. Key part It includes the amygdala , central to fear and emotional learning. Why the other options are wrong (a) Reticular formation Governs arousal and wakefulness, not emotion. (b) Hind brain Paces heartbeat and breathing, basic life functions rather than emotion. (d) Forebrain Too broad: the limbic system lies within the forebrain , but so does much else. 'Psychological disorders develop when a biological predisposition is set off by a stressful situation', is proposed by (JEMAS 2025) a Humanistics existential models. b Socio-cultural model. c Diathesis-stress model. d Cognitive model. ✓ Answer: (c) Diathesis-stress model Diathesis-stress model (Meehl, 1962; Zubin and Spring, 1977) The concept What it is A pre-existing vulnerability ( diathesis ) set off by a stressful trigger ( stress ) is the model's definition. Who proposed it Meehl (1962) and Zubin and Spring (1977) set out the model. Why the other options are wrong (a) Humanistics existential models. Humanistic-existential models blame blocked growth, not predisposition plus stress. (b) Socio-cultural model. Sociocultural models blame social forces, not a biological predisposition. (d) Cognitive model. Cognitive models blame faulty thinking; none is defined by predisposition plus stress. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Systematic desensitisation (Joseph Wolpe, Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition , 1958) rests on reciprocal inhibition : relaxation, a response incompatible with anxiety, is paired step by step with a graded anxiety hierarchy. asked 17 times Working memory (Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch, 1974) has four components: the central executive (an attentional controller that stores nothing, loaded by random number generation), the phonological loop (auditory-verbal information), the visuospatial sketchpad (visual and spatial information, including mental rotation) and the episodic buffer, added in 2000, which binds information into coherent episodes. asked 11 times The token economy is operant conditioning with tokens as secondary reinforcers, developed by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin ( The Token Economy , 1968); it is the listed therapy not derived from classical conditioning. asked 10 times Abraham Maslow 's hierarchy of needs (1943, 1954), bottom to top: physiological, safety, belongingness and love (social), esteem, self-actualisation. Physiological and safety needs are the lower needs; ego is not a level. asked 10 times Korsakoff's syndrome follows thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency in chronic alcoholism, often after Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus); it damages the mammillary bodies and mediodorsal thalamus and causes dense anterograde amnesia, extensive retrograde amnesia and confabulation, sincere false stories that fill memory gaps. asked 8 times The empty chair technique belongs to Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls, with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman), an experiential here-and-now therapy that is not the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Kohler and Koffka. asked 7 times Variable ratio reinforcement gives the highest, steadiest rate and the greatest resistance to extinction; fixed ratio gives high rates with a post-reinforcement pause, fixed interval the scallop, variable interval moderate steady rates, and continuous reinforcement the fastest learning and fastest extinction. asked 7 times Extinction is the fading of a conditioned response when the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS, or of an operant response that is no longer reinforced; a parent who ignores tantrums is using extinction, not operant escape. asked 7 times Reinforcement always increases behaviour and punishment decreases it; positive adds and negative removes a stimulus, so switching off a shock is negative reinforcement , while time-out and response cost are negative punishment . asked 7 times H.M. (Henry Molaison) had both medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus and amygdala, removed by William Beecher Scoville in 1953; Scoville and Brenda Milner (1957) reported a profound anterograde amnesia for declarative memory, with normal short-term memory, limited retrograde amnesia and spared procedural learning (mirror tracing). asked 7 times Raymond Cattell (with John Horn) split g into fluid intelligence (Gf), reasoning with novel problems independently of acquired knowledge and measured best by Raven's Progressive Matrices, and crystallised intelligence (Gc), the repertoire of information, cognitive skills and strategies, measured by vocabulary and information. asked 7 times The limbic system is the classic "seat of emotion": Paul MacLean named it in 1952, enlarging James Papez's 1937 circuit, and it regulates emotion, motivation and memory; hunger and thirst belong to the hypothalamus. asked 7 times The amygdala is the structure for fear and aggression: it detects threat, drives fear conditioning and gives emotional events their extra memorability, while the hippocampus stores the facts. asked 7 times The hippocampus is the structure damaged in anterograde amnesia and is critical for consolidating new declarative memories; it is not the store of remote memories. asked 6 times Narendra Nath Sengupta set up India's first psychology laboratory (1915) and first Department of Psychology (1916) at the University of Calcutta and is the father of modern psychology in India; keys naming Bose or Uma Chaudhuri for the first laboratory are wrong. asked 5 times Humanistic psychology (Maslow, Rogers) is the third force , after psychoanalysis (first) and behaviourism (second); transpersonal psychology is the fourth force. asked 5 times The Stroop effect (John Ridley Stroop, 1935): naming the ink colour of a conflicting colour word (RED printed in green) is slowed because automatic word reading interferes; it shows a limit of selective attention (interference in reaction time), not a memory effect. asked 5 times Proactive interference : earlier learning disrupts newer learning (dialling your old phone number); retroactive interference : newer learning disrupts older memories. RML 2024 keys English grammar intruding on newly learned Spanish as retroactive, but it is proactive. asked 5 times Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to probable generalisations (gather data, find patterns, build theory: the logic of theory development and qualitative research); deductive reasoning starts from a theory and tests its predictions against observations. asked 5 times Graham Wallas ( The Art of Thought , 1926): preparation, incubation, illumination, verification; incubation (setting the problem aside) is second and illumination (the insight) third. asked 5 times Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker's candle problem, 1945) is seeing an object only in its usual use; mental set (Abraham Luchins's water jars, 1942) is reusing a strategy that worked before, and was keyed as the most basic and common obstacle to problem solving. asked 5 times Henry Murray 's need-press theory (1938) underlies the Thematic Apperception Test (Morgan and Murray, 1935), a projective test whose stories reveal the teller's needs, conflicts and motives. asked 5 times Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879 (not Vienna, Paris or Cambridge); Galton's London laboratory (1884) was anthropometric. asked 4 times Patanjali's eight limbs , in order: yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana (concentration on one point), dhyana (unbroken meditation), samadhi (absorption); karma and jnana are not limbs. asked 4 times Tamas is the guna of inertia, lethargy, darkness, dullness and ignorance; a person who has stopped eating and cannot get herself to act shows tamas alone. asked 4 times Every sense except smell relays through the thalamus on its way to the cortex (vision via the lateral geniculate nucleus, hearing via the medial geniculate nucleus); the olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) bypasses it. asked 4 times The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the master circadian pacemaker, entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract; SCN lesions abolish circadian rhythms, not total sleep. asked 4 times REM (paradoxical) sleep : a desynchronised, fast, low-voltage EEG like waking, rapid eye movements, atonia of the core muscles, genital arousal and vivid dreams; EEG synchrony and delta waves belong to N3, spindles and K-complexes to N2. asked 4 times Carl Jung split the unconscious into a personal (individual) unconscious and the collective unconscious , an inherited layer of archetypes shared by all humanity, which he explained by the similar brain structure of all human races. asked 4 times William Stern coined the intelligence quotient in 1912; Lewis Terman 's Stanford-Binet (1916) multiplied it by 100, giving the ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, so a mental age of 8 at age 10 gives an IQ of 80. asked 4 times

title: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 2: Psychological Assessment
text: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 2: Psychological Assessment Chapter 2 of the one-volume Final Exam Textbook, all nine JSS subjects in one book. Both A4 PDFs hold the whole book with the same page numbers. A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (975 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (975 pages) Chapter 2 Psychological Assessment In this chapter 2.1 Psychological Testing: Nature, History, Types and Ethics : Define a psychological test and assessment, trace testing from Chinese civil-service examinations to the MMPI, classify tests (objective versus subjective, speed versus power, maximum versus typical performance), list the characteristics of a good test, recognise the errors of clinical judgement and apply the ethics of test use. 2.2 Building a Test: Items, Item Analysis, IRT and Response Bias : Write and format test items, run a classical item analysis (difficulty, discrimination, item-total correlations, distractors, ceiling and floor effects), explain item response theory and the item characteristic curve, and recognise response sets and rater errors such as acquiescence and halo. 2.3 Reliability: Consistency and the Standard Error of Measurement : Explain how classical test theory defines reliability, choose and compute the right estimate (test-retest, parallel forms, split-half with Spearman-Brown, Rulon, Flanagan, KR-20, KR-21, alpha, kappa) and put a standard-error band around one person's score. 2.4 Validity and the Accuracy of Test Decisions : Define validity in its classical and unified senses, tell face, content, criterion-related (concurrent and predictive) and construct validity apart by their evidence, link validity to reliability through the validity ceiling, and judge test decisions with sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, base rates and ROC curves. 2.5 Norms, Standard Scores and Interpreting a Score : Interpret any test score by placing it against norms: tell norm- from criterion-referenced scores, judge a norm sample, and convert between percentiles, z, T, stanine, sten, scaled scores and deviation IQs on the normal curve. 2.6 Intelligence Tests: Binet, Wechsler, Non-verbal and Indian Scales : Identify and compare the major intelligence tests (the Binet scales, the Wechsler family, the Kaufman and Das-Naglieri batteries, non-verbal and culture-fair tests and the Indian scales), say what an IQ test can and cannot tell you, and choose the right test for a given person. 2.7 Assessing Development, Adaptive Behaviour and Disability : Explain how development, social maturity and adaptive behaviour are measured (DQ, SQ, Gesell, Bayley, Denver, VSMS, Vineland and the Indian scales), how intellectual disability and global developmental delay are assessed, and how intellectual disability, specific learning disability and autism are certified in India. 2.8 Aptitude, Achievement, Creativity, Interest and Attitude Measures : Tell achievement, aptitude and intelligence tests apart, name the main aptitude batteries, creativity tests and interest and value inventories, and explain how Thurstone, Likert, Guttman, Bogardus, semantic differential and implicit attitude measures are built and scored. 2.9 Objective Personality Inventories : Distinguish objective inventories from projective tests, name Cattell's L-, Q- and T-data, match inventories to their construction strategy, interpret the MMPI's validity and clinical scales and its revisions, and identify the authors, items, scales and scores of the 16PF, EPQ, NEO-PI-R, MBTI, EPPS, CPI, MCMI, STAI, Rep test and Q-sort. 2.10 Projective Techniques : Explain the projective hypothesis, sort projective techniques by Lindzey's five categories, describe how the Rorschach and TAT are given, scored and interpreted, recognise the completion, expressive and choice techniques with their authors, and weigh the evidence on their reliability and validity. 2.11 Neuropsychological Assessment and Clinical Rating Scales : Explain what neuropsychological assessment measures and how, recognise the main batteries and the memory, visual-motor, executive, attention and language tests and bedside screens, and match each clinical rating scale to its author, format, rater and purpose. Weightage. 336 of the 3180 questions mapped in this book (10.6%) test this chapter, 136 of them from real past papers. 2 of its 11 sections are High yield. London, 1884. Among the displays on diet, dress and sanitation at the International Health Exhibition in South Kensington stood a long, narrow room unlike anything else in the show. For threepence a visitor could walk along a counter of instruments while attendants measured height, arm span, weight, breathing power, strength of squeeze, keenness of sight and hearing, colour sense and speed of reaction. The figures went onto a card: the visitor kept one copy and the laboratory kept the other. By the time the exhibition closed, 9,337 people had passed through Francis Galton 's Anthropometric Laboratory. Galton was not running a sideshow. He had argued in Hereditary Genius (1869) that ability is inherited, and he believed that an able mind showed itself in keen senses and quick reactions. Measure the senses accurately enough, in enough people, and you would be measuring intelligence. His data were superb: taken the same way for every visitor and from thousands of people, they showed how human traits spread around an average, and to analyse them Galton worked out the idea of correlation. At the University of Pennsylvania, James McKeen Cattell built the same kinds of measure into a battery and in 1890 gave it a name: the mental test. Then, in 1901, Cattell's student Clark Wissler asked the obvious question. Did the tests predict anything that mattered? At Columbia University they barely related to students' grades. Careful, precise measurement had captured the wrong thing. That gap, between measuring something consistently and measuring what matters, runs through this whole chapter, and at its end we return to Galton's counter of instruments. 2.1 Psychological Testing: Nature, History, Types and Ethics Lower yield · 11 Qs Later sections each study one kind of test or one property of tests. This one builds their frame: what a test is, where testing came from, how tests are sorted and judged, how clinicians reason from scores, and testing ethics. What a test is Anne Anastasi (1908 to 2001), author of the standard text Psychological Testing (1954), defined a psychological test as "essentially an objective and standardized measure of a sample of behavior". Objective : the score does not depend on who gives or scores it. Standardised : everyone meets the same items, instructions, time and scoring. Sample : the test observes a small, chosen part of behaviour and infers the rest, as a doctor judges your blood from one drop. Lee J. Cronbach (1916 to 2001) stressed comparison: a test is "a systematic procedure for comparing the behavior of two or more persons". Measurement assigns numbers to attributes by rules (Ravi scored 42); evaluation judges the number against a standard (42 is a pass); testing obtains a behaviour sample with a standardised instrument; and assessment , the widest, answers a referral question by integrating tests with interview, observation, history and records. A test yields a score; an assessment yields a reasoned conclusion about a person. The psychometric approach measures individual differences with standardised tests, and its logic of fixed items, norms, reliability and validity serves intelligence, symptoms of psychopathology and neurological or cognitive deficits alike. Levels of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) are taught in Chapter 9. From Chinese examinations to the MMPI Testing is older than psychology: China examined candidates for public office under the Han dynasty (206 BC to AD 220), and under the T'ang dynasty written civil-service examinations became the rule. Modern testing has two nineteenth-century roots, one clinical: the French psychiatrist Jean-Étienne Esquirol (1772 to 1840) separated mental retardation from mental illness, grading retardation by the person's use of language, and Édouard Séguin (1812 to 1880), who trained retarded children through sensory and motor exercises, left us the form board , a performance task of fitting shapes into matching holes. The other root is individual differences. Francis Galton (1822 to 1911) argued in Hereditary Genius (1869) that ability is inherited and, believing that all knowledge enters through the senses, measured sensory discrimination and reaction time in his London Anthropometric Laboratory of 1884 (the scene that opened this chapter). His idea of correlation became, in the hands of Karl Pearson (1857 to 1936), the product-moment correlation coefficient. Galton is called the father of mental testing and of psychometrics. James McKeen Cattell (1860 to 1944), who had worked with Wundt and Galton, coined the term mental test in his 1890 paper "Mental Tests and Measurements"; his tests, too, were sensory and motor. In 1901 Clark Wissler (1870 to 1947) found that they barely correlated with Columbia students' grades. Measuring the senses precisely was not measuring intelligence. The breakthrough came in Paris, where Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911) and Théodore Simon tested judgement, comprehension and reasoning instead (Table 2.1). From the 1960s, the period of accountability, American courts heard challenges to tests as biased against minorities and women. Indian tests (Kamat 1934, Bhatia 1955, Malin 1969, the NIMHANS and PGIMER batteries) appear in Sections 2.6, 2.7 and 2.11. Table 2.1 Milestones of the testing century. Year Who Milestone 1905 Binet and Simon Binet-Simon scale, the first practical intelligence test 1912 William Stern Intelligence quotient: mental age divided by chronological age 1916 Lewis Terman Stanford-Binet; IQ = MA/CA × 100 1917 Robert Yerkes , using Arthur Otis 's group items Army Alpha (literate recruits) and Army Beta (non-verbal) group tests 1917 Robert S. Woodworth Personal Data Sheet, the first personality inventory 1921 Hermann Rorschach Inkblot test 1927 Edward K. Strong Strong Vocational Interest Blank 1928 to 1929 L. L. Thurstone Attitude scaling; later multiple factor analysis 1935 Christiana Morgan and Henry Murray Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) 1938 Oscar Buros First Mental Measurements Yearbook of test reviews 1939 David Wechsler Wechsler-Bellevue scale for adults 1943 Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) Exam trap "Mental tests" was coined by Cattell (1890), not Binet (first practical intelligence test, 1905), Terman (Stanford-Binet, 1916) or Wechsler (1939). Galton is the father of mental testing; Stern proposed the intelligence quotient and Terman multiplied it by 100. Woodworth's data sheet, built in 1917 to 1918, is dated 1919 or 1920 in some books. Kinds of tests Four ways of sorting tests matter most; Table 2.2 gives the rest. Scoring. On an objective test a fixed key leaves no room for the scorer's judgement, so any two scorers agree: multiple-choice items, rating scales and self-report inventories such as the MMPI are objective. On a subjective test (an essay, an interview rating, a projective test such as the Rorschach) the scorer judges each free response. "Projective" names a technique of ambiguous stimuli (Section 2.10); "introjective" is no kind of test (introjection is a defence mechanism, Chapter 4). Time. A speed test has easy items of similar difficulty under a time limit so strict that few finish; the score is how many are done, as in a clerical checking test. A power test gives generous time, or none, but its items climb in difficulty until some are too hard for anyone; the score reflects the hardest level mastered (Figure 2.1). Most real tests are speeded tests , a blend of both. Speed test Power test Difficulty Time up answered not reached Items, in order Easy items, strict time limit Difficulty Limit of the ablest examinee failed by all Items, easy to hard Generous time, rising difficulty Figure 2.1 Speed versus power. Left: easy items, and time runs out first (white items are never reached). Right: time for everything, but difficulty rises until the white items defeat everyone. What is asked. Cronbach, in Essentials of Psychological Testing (1949), separated tests of maximum performance , which ask you to do your best under standard conditions (intelligence, aptitude and achievement tests: the ability tests ), from tests of typical performance , which ask how you usually feel or act (personality, interest and attitude measures). An IQ test is an ability test. Purpose. An intelligence test measures general mental ability; an aptitude test , the potential to learn a specific skill; an achievement test , what has already been learned; a personality test , traits, emotions, attitudes and motives; an interest inventory, liking for activities and occupations; a neuropsychological test , brain-behaviour functions in suspected brain damage; and a diagnostic test, specific weaknesses such as reading errors. Table 2.2 Ways of classifying tests. Basis Types The difference Administration Individual; group One person, trained examiner (WAIS); many at once (Army Alpha) Item content Verbal; non-verbal; non-language Words in items; pictures, words only in instructions (Raven's); gesture only (Army Beta) Medium Paper-and-pencil; performance Written answers; handling blocks or form boards Construction Standardised; teacher-made Fixed procedures and norms; classroom use, no norms Reference Norm-referenced; criterion-referenced Against other people; against a mastery standard (Section 2.5) Culture Culture-fair Minimal language and schooling (Section 2.6) Delivery Computerised; computer-adaptive On screen; items chosen by earlier answers (Section 2.2) Exam trap Speed versus power concerns time limit and item difficulty only, not reaction time and not individual versus group administration; and it is power items that rise in difficulty. "Maximum performance" means an ability test : speed and power tests are ability tests differing in timing, and a personality inventory measures typical performance. Characteristics of a good test A good test has five characteristics: Objectivity : freedom from the examiner's judgement in administration, scoring and interpretation, so that different examiners agree. Reliability : consistency of scores over occasions, forms and scorers (Section 2.3). Consistency is a criterion of good measurement; high cost, low reliability and subjectivity mark poor measurement. Validity : measuring what the test claims to measure (Section 2.4). Reliability is necessary but not sufficient: head size can be measured consistently, yet it is a worthless intelligence test. Norms : a representative sample's performance, against which a raw score is read (Section 2.5). Practicability (usability): reasonable time, length, cost and ease of scoring. Standardisation means fixing uniform procedures for administration and scoring (the same instructions, materials, time limits and key for everyone) and establishing norms, so that scores are comparable across people and occasions. It is a precondition of validity, not a guarantee of it; it does not remove cultural bias; and it has nothing to do with computer administration. Exam trap RML 2024 keyed objectivity as the most important characteristic of a psychological test, following Indian texts such as A. K. Singh's that list it first: without it the score reflects the examiner. Most textbooks, and the 2014 Standards ("the most fundamental consideration"), name validity , since an objective test of the wrong thing is useless. On RML papers expect objectivity; elsewhere choose validity. Subjectivity and rationality are not test characteristics. The top row builds and selects the items; the bottom row checks the scores, and the manual reports it all. Tests serve selection (choosing applicants), classification and placement (assigning people to categories or programmes), diagnosis and treatment planning, self-knowledge and guidance, programme evaluation and research. Their limitations: they can invade privacy; a label such as "retarded" or "gifted" may stick after the person has changed; they sample only limited aspects of behaviour; test anxiety depresses some scores; and fixed keys penalise creative examinees whose unusual answers earn no credit. Clinical judgement and its errors Clinicians treat assessment information as samples, correlates or signs. A sample directly resembles the behaviour of interest: how a client tackles a frustrating puzzle samples how she meets frustration. A correlate has a statistically demonstrated link with something outside the test, as a high depression-scale score goes with clinicians' ratings of depression. A sign is read as an indicator of a hidden state, as when a Rorschach response is taken to signal disordered thinking. Interpretation can be nomothetic , placing the person against norms for everyone (her anxiety is at the 95th percentile), or idiographic , tracing what is unique to her (what this worry means in her life); good assessment uses both. In Clinical versus Statistical Prediction (1954) Paul E. Meehl (1920 to 2003) compared clinical prediction , combining the data in the clinician's head, with actuarial prediction , combining them by a formula derived from past cases. The formula usually equalled or beat the clinician, and later reviews agree. Judgement also errs systematically. Confirmatory bias covers ignoring information that does not support one's hypothesis, ignoring information that does not fit one's stereotypes, and reading ambiguous information as support (confirmation bias in general: Chapter 1). Illusory correlation is perceiving a relation that is not there (Key study). Overconfidence grows with more data even when accuracy does not, and neglect of base rates over-diagnoses rare conditions (Section 2.4). The Barnum effect is accepting vague, universally true descriptions as uniquely accurate: in 1949 Bertram Forer (1914 to 2000) tested his students, then gave each the same "personal" sketch, largely from an astrology book ("You have a great need for other people to like and admire you"); they rated it 4.26 out of 5 for accuracy. Meehl named the effect in 1956 after the showman P. T. Barnum. Key study: Illusory correlation (Chapman and Chapman, 1967 and 1969) Clinicians believed Draw-a-Person signs, such as large eyes meaning suspiciousness, that research did not support. Loren Chapman and Jean Chapman showed naive students drawings, each paired at random with a symptom statement. The students "found" the very relations clinicians reported, though none existed, because the pairs were already linked in their minds (eyes go with suspicion). In 1969 they found the same for Rorschach signs: popular invalid signs were seen and valid ones missed. The safeguards are multimethod assessment (tests, interview, observation, records), multiple informants (client, family, teachers), actuarial aids and a deliberate search for disconfirming evidence. Assessment ends in a written report (referral question, background, tests, behaviour, results, interpretation, recommendations) and feedback the client can understand. Interviewing, the mental status examination and behavioural assessment are in Chapter 7. Exam trap All three statements describe confirmatory bias: answer "All of the above". Assessment information is conceived as samples, correlates or signs ; the other triads offered (factual, hypothetical or imaginary; predictions, estimates or suggestions; examples, prototypes or categories) are invented. Ethics and responsible test use Tests can harm as well as help. The rules are the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing of the American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association and National Council on Measurement in Education (AERA, APA and NCME; 2014 edition), Section 9 (Assessment) of the APA Ethics Code and, in India, the code of the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI), where clinical psychologists register (ethics and law in full: Chapter 7). The main duties: Competence. Use only tests you are trained for. Publishers sell by test-user qualification levels : Level A (achievement and proficiency tests) needs only the manual; Level B (group intelligence, aptitude and interest tests) needs training in test construction and statistics; Level C (individual intelligence tests, clinical personality inventories, projective techniques) needs an advanced degree and supervised experience. Informed consent. Explain purpose, nature, fees, who sees results and the limits of confidentiality, unless law or a court orders the testing. Confidentiality and release of test data. Results go only to the client, those the client authorises, or as law requires; raw data may be withheld to prevent harm or misuse. Test security. Items, manuals and protocols are kept from the public; a leaked test measures nothing. Current editions and relevant norms. Obsolete tests and outdated or foreign norms mislead. Fairness. A test is biased when its scores mean different things for different groups (Section 2.4). Disability. Accommodations (Braille or large print, a sign-language interpreter, extra time, a scribe) remove barriers unrelated to what is measured; the report records them. Translation. A translated test is back-translated into the original language by an independent translator and the versions compared; reliability, validity and norms must then be re-established. Explaining results and labelling. Clients are owed an understandable explanation; labels are used sparingly, because they stigmatise and can fulfil themselves. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks.
