Accepting a vague, universal description as uniquely one's own is the effect. Answers: (1) sample, (2) James McKeen Cattell, (3) speed, (4) maximum, (5) standardisation, (6) signs, (7) Barnum. 2.2 Building a Test: Items, Item Analysis, IRT and Response Bias Lower yield · 11 Qs A test begins as a pile of draft items, and most will not survive. The constructor writes far more than needed, tries them out and keeps those of the right difficulty that separate people high and low on the trait. Then come the biases that test-takers and raters add. Writing items An item is the smallest scorable unit of a test, a question or task with a scoring rule. A good item measures only its trait, is unambiguous, gives no clues, is of suitable difficulty and discriminates. Essay items (free-response items) tap organisation and evaluation but are scored slowly and subjectively. Objective items , once called new-type items, are scored alike by anyone. In supply type items the examinee produces the answer (short answer, completion); in selection type items he chooses it: true-false or alternative response (a 50 percent guessing chance), matching (more responses than stems, to block elimination), rearrangement (put steps in order) and the multiple-choice item , with a stem (the question), a key (the correct option) and distractors , wrong options that attract those who do not know. The writing rules make the trait alone decide the answer: one idea per item ("I enjoy parties and sports" defeats someone who likes only one), clear wording, no double negatives, no clues such as a longer key or specific determiners ( always and never suggest false), plausible distractors and, on personality scales, balanced keying (half the items keyed "agree", half "disagree"). Item formats, scoring and guessing Psychological tests use the wider formats of Table 2.3. Table 2.3 Item formats in psychological tests. Format The respondent Dichotomous Chooses between two answers (true or false) Polytomous Chooses among three or more Likert format Rates agreement, usually on five points (Section 2.8) Category format Rates on numbered categories, often 1 to 10 Visual analogue scale Marks a point on an unbroken line Adjective checklist Ticks the adjectives that apply Forced choice Picks between options matched for desirability Q-sort Sorts statements from most to least like me (Section 2.9) Answers are scored with a stencil key (overlay key: a card with holes at the correct answers, laid over the sheet) or a strip key (the answers in a column laid beside the test's). A correction for guessing removes lucky hits: S = R - W / (n - 1), with R right, W wrong (omissions excluded) and n options. A blind guesser on four options gets one right per three wrong, so 60 right and 30 wrong give S = 60 - 10 = 50. The formula assumes, wrongly, that every error is a blind guess. Item difficulty, ceiling and floor Item analysis uses tryout data to decide which items to keep, revise or discard, judging each by its difficulty, its discrimination and its distractors. The item difficulty index (p) is the proportion passing the item (120 of 200 gives 0.60), so a high p means an easy item. An item everyone passes or everyone fails tells no one apart. The variance of a pass-fail item, p × q, peaks at p = 0.50, which gives maximum variance and discrimination. Guessing raises the target: for multiple choice the optimum lies midway between chance and 1.00, about 0.62 for four options, 0.75 for true-false (texts aiming at maximum reliability give 0.74 and 0.85). Most tests keep p between 0.30 and 0.70. A ceiling effect occurs when a test is too easy: most respondents score near the maximum, so it cannot discriminate among high performers or register further gains; scores are negatively skewed (Figure 2.3). A floor effect is the reverse: the test is too difficult, scores pile up near the minimum (positively skewed) and low performers cannot be told apart. Both shrink the spread of scores, lowering reliability and validity. Floor effect: test too hard Positively skewed Ceiling effect: test too easy Negatively skewed 0 Max 0 Max Score Score Figure 2.3 Floor and ceiling effects: scores pile up at the minimum (test too hard) or the maximum (too easy), and the piled-up people cannot be told apart. Exam trap "The test is too difficult for everyone" is a floor effect. A ceiling effect does not mean "scores are normally distributed" (they are negatively skewed) or "perfect reliability": no reliability coefficient exceeds 1, and bunched scores lower it. Item discrimination and distractors The item discrimination index (D) asks whether high scorers on the whole test did better on this item. Take the top and bottom 27 percent by total score, the split that Truman Lee Kelley (1884 to 1961) showed in 1939 best balances extremeness against group size; then D = p upper - p lower , ranging from -1 to +1. If 40 of 50 upper and 15 of 50 lower examinees pass, D = 0.80 - 0.30 = 0.50 (and p = 0.55). Robert L. Ebel 's guide: 0.40 and above, very good; 0.30 to 0.39, reasonably good; 0.20 to 0.29, marginal; below 0.20, poor. A negative D means the lower group did better: the item is miskeyed, ambiguous (able examinees see a second defensible answer) or otherwise faulty, and must be revised or discarded. Exam trap D = -0.20 does not mean "well-functioning", "too easy" or "at ideal difficulty": difficulty is p, not D. A negative D says the item works backwards; check the key first. Discrimination can also be an item-total correlation : point-biserial r (pass-fail item against a continuous total), biserial r (the pass-fail split assumed to cut a normal ability), phi (two true dichotomies) or tetrachoric r (two artificial dichotomies). Since the item is part of the total, the correlation is inflated, most in short tests; the corrected form uses the other items. The item's correlation with an outside criterion, times its standard deviation, is the item validity index . Distractor analysis checks each option: a working distractor draws more of the lower group; a non-functioning one draws almost nobody; one drawing the upper group signals ambiguity or miskeying. Plausible distractors make an item harder and usually more discriminating. Difficulty caps discrimination: at p = 1.00 or 0, D must be 0, and D can approach 1 only near p = 0.50, though an ambiguous item can sit at p = 0.50 with D near zero. These indices assume a power test ; in a speed test the last items are reached only by fast workers, so their p and D reflect speed, not content. Item response theory All this is classical test theory (CTT; X = T + E, Section 2.3), whose p and D depend on the sample: an item with p = 0.90 among postgraduates may have p = 0.30 in Class 8. Item response theory (IRT), or latent trait theory, models each item instead. It assumes an unobservable latent trait , θ (theta), and expresses the probability of a correct (or keyed) response as a function of the person's θ and the item's parameters. Graphed, this is the item characteristic curve (ICC): the probability of a correct response plotted against the examinee's level on the latent trait, not against time taken, number of examinees or reliability. It is an S-shaped ogive (Figure 2.4). Its location on θ is the difficulty, b (where the probability reaches 0.50, or halfway between c and 1); its slope there is the discrimination, a ; its lower asymptote is the pseudo-guessing parameter, c , the chance that a very low-θ examinee still succeeds. 0 0.5 1.0 -3 -1 0 +1 +3 Latent trait level, θ Probability of correct response b = -1 b = +1 c = 0.20 Item B is steeper: higher a Item A (easy) Item B (hard) Figure 2.4 Item A (solid) lies left, so it is easy (b = -1). Item B (dashed) lies right (b = +1), rises more steeply (higher a) and never drops below its guessing floor, c = 0.20. The Rasch model , or one-parameter logistic model (1PL), published in 1960 by the Danish mathematician Georg Rasch (1901 to 1980), estimates difficulty only. The two-parameter model adds discrimination and the three-parameter model adds guessing; Allan Birnbaum set out these logistic models in 1968, building on the work of Frederic M. Lord (1912 to 2000) from 1952. IRT assumes unidimensionality (one trait) and local independence (at a fixed θ, responses to different items are unrelated). An item information function shows how precisely an item measures at each θ, peaking near b; summed, they give the test information function. When the model fits, item parameters are sample-invariant and θ does not depend on which items were given, since persons and items share one scale. This allows computerised adaptive testing (CAT), which picks each next item to suit the current estimate of θ and so needs far fewer items; item banking; test equating across forms; and detection of differential item functioning (DIF), or item bias, when equally able people from two groups have different ICCs for an item (Table 2.4). Rating scales and rater errors When another person judges the trait, bias moves to the rater. Rating scales may be numerical (numbered points), graphic (a line to mark), descriptive (a phrase per level), percentage (a percentile band), standard or man-to-man (known people as anchors), cumulated points or checklist (ticked statements summed) or forced-choice (equally favourable statements, curbing leniency). The behaviourally anchored rating scale (BARS) of Patricia Cain Smith and Lorne M. Kendall (1963) anchors each point with a concrete behaviour. Ranking orders people; paired comparison compares every pair. The halo effect (halo error), named by Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949) in 1920 from officers' ratings of soldiers, is judging a person on the basis of one attribute or a general impression that colours every other rating: a clinician who sees anxiety improve rates depression improved too. A psychological test is a scale for something invisible, so the first question about any score is the same: measured again, would it come out the same? What follows separates score from error, estimates the error four ways, and puts an honest band around one person's score. True scores, error and the meaning of reliability In 1904 Charles Spearman proposed the model on which classical test theory rests: every observed score is a true score plus error, X = T + E . The true score is the average a person would earn over endless independent testings. The model assumes that errors are random, averaging zero; that they are uncorrelated with true scores; and that errors on one test are uncorrelated with errors on another. The variances therefore add: observed variance = true variance + error variance. The reliability coefficient (r xx ) is the share of observed-score variance that is true-score variance: r xx = σ 2 T / σ 2 X = 1 - σ 2 E / σ 2 X . If scores vary with variance 100, of which 80 is true and 20 error, reliability is .80. It runs from 0 (all error) to 1 (no error). The domain-sampling model sees a test's items as a sample from a large domain, such as all the words a spelling test could use; the score on the whole domain is the universe score. The more items sampled, the closer the test score comes to it, so longer tests are more reliable. Only random error (a lapse of attention, a lucky guess, a noisy hall), which moves scores unpredictably, lowers reliability. A systematic error moves every score the same way, like a scale that always reads two kilograms heavy; being consistent, it leaves reliability intact but biases the scores and so threatens validity. Reliability therefore means consistency , dependability and freedom from measurement error . It is distinct from validity (measuring what the test claims) and sensitivity (detecting a condition or a change), both in Section 2.4, from generalizability (findings extending to other people and settings), and from fairness to groups (Section 2.1). A standardised test has uniform administration and scoring (Section 2.1); a normed test is read against a reference group (Section 2.5). Exam trap Reliability is "freedom from measurement error, consistency and dependability": all of the above . A study is reliable when its measures are stable on different occasions . "Conducted by a reputable researcher" is trust in a person, "findings can be generalised to other settings" is external validity, and "methods stated clearly enough to be repeated" is replicability (Chapter 9). Stability and equivalence: test-retest and parallel forms In test-retest reliability the same test is given to the same people on two occasions and the scores are correlated, giving the coefficient of stability . Giving a new anxiety scale to students twice, two weeks apart, and correlating the scores is the classic case. It detects time-sampling error: changes in health, mood and conditions between sittings. Too short an interval lets memory and practice inflate the coefficient; too long lets real change lower it, so a fortnight to a few weeks is usual. The method suits traits expected to stay stable over the interval, such as intelligence and personality, not rapidly changing states such as current mood, where a low coefficient reflects true change. Exam trap Test-retest reliability means the test gives consistent results over time . Correlating two halves is split-half reliability; two raters scoring one protocol is inter-rater reliability; correlating with a future criterion, or "measuring what it claims", is validity (Section 2.4); the client doing better the second time is a practice effect . It fits stable traits, not mood states, single-item measures or open-ended interviews. A second method, alternate-forms reliability ( parallel-forms reliability ), uses two versions built to one blueprint: the same number, kind, content and format of items, equal difficulty, and equal means and variances. Given in one session, their correlation is a coefficient of equivalence , which detects content-sampling error; given weeks apart, it is a coefficient of stability and equivalence , the most demanding estimate. Parallel forms avoid remembered answers and suit retesting and speed tests, but they are costly to write, rarely truly equivalent, and practice on the type of task still carries over. Split-half reliability and the Spearman-Brown formula Can reliability come from one sitting? Methods that do so estimate internal consistency reliability : how well the parts of a test agree with each other within one administration. In split-half reliability one test is scored as two halves, which are then correlated. First half against second half is a poor split, since warming up, fatigue and rising difficulty make the halves unequal; an odd-even split, or random halves matched for content and difficulty, is better. The major challenge is dividing the test into two nearly equivalent halves, and different splits give different answers. The half correlation describes a test half as long, so it underestimates the whole. Spearman and William Brown published the correction independently in 1910. The Spearman-Brown prophecy formula steps the half correlation up: r full = 2r half / (1 + r half ), so halves correlating .60 give 1.20 / 1.60 = .75 . Its general form predicts reliability when length changes by a factor k (new length over old): r new = kr / [1 + (k - 1)r] . Adding parallel items (k above 1) raises reliability, because true-score parts add up while random errors partly cancel; shortening (k below 1) lowers it. Rearranged, the length needed for a target is k = r target (1 - r) / [r(1 - r target )]. Table 2.7 works four cases, and Figure 2.5 shows the diminishing returns. Doubling gains .15, tripling only .07 more, and .90 needs six times the items. Spearman-Brown assumes parallel halves, with equal means and variances; when the half variances differ it overestimates. Two formulas need no step-up. Phillip Rulon (1939) treated the difference between a person's two half-scores as error: Rulon's formula is r = 1 - σ 2 d / σ 2 X , the variance of the differences over the variance of totals. John Flanagan (1937) used the half variances: r = 2[1 - (σ 2 a + σ 2 b ) / σ 2 X ] ( Louis Guttman gave the same formula in 1945). If each half has variance 6, totals 20 and differences 4, Rulon gives 1 - 4 / 20 = .80 and Flanagan 2(1 - 12 / 20) = .80; the halves correlate .67, which Spearman-Brown also steps up to .80. Exam trap Spearman-Brown estimates full-test reliability from a split-half correlation, or predicts reliability when length changes ; it raises reliability by adding parallel items, not by removing items, making them ambiguous or shrinking the sample. It does not estimate rater agreement, correct validity for unreliability, estimate a speed test's reliability from one sitting, or predict validity, effect sizes or factor structure. Rulon needs variances : SDs of 3 (differences) and 6 (totals) give 1 - 9 / 36 = .75. Odd-even splitting suits a power test : graded items, generous time. On a pure speed test of easy items the score is how far a person gets, so whoever reaches item 60 has about 30 odd and 30 even right. The halves match by construction and the correlation nears 1.00 spuriously, as do KR-20 and alpha from one timed sitting. Speed tests need test-retest, parallel forms or separately timed halves , each given with half the time and stepped up with Spearman-Brown. Projective and many neuropsychological tests lack comparable, objectively scored items to split. Every internal consistency method shares one limitation: a single administration says nothing about stability over time. Exam trap The limitation of internal consistency methods: they measure consistency within a single administration only . Needing several items and falling with mixed content are conditions of use, so a mock offering "all of the above" still keys the single administration. Kuder-Richardson formulas and coefficient alpha Why trust one arbitrary split? In 1937 G. Frederic Kuder and Marion Richardson derived an internal consistency coefficient from item statistics. KR-20 suits items scored dichotomously (right or wrong, yes or no) that may vary in difficulty: KR-20 = [k / (k - 1)] × [1 - Σpq / σ 2 X ] , where k is the number of items, p the proportion passing an item, q = 1 - p, and σ 2 X the variance of total scores. The product pq is the item's variance: an item passed by 30 percent has pq = .30 × .70 = .21, and the maximum is .25 at p = .50. Items measuring one thing covary, so total variance far exceeds the summed item variances. For 20 items with Σpq = 3.2, mean 12 and variance 16: 3.2 / 16 = .20, 1 - .20 = .80, and × 20 / 19 gives .84 . KR-21 assumes equal item difficulty, replacing Σpq with M(k - M) / k, so it needs only k, mean and variance: KR-21 = [k / (k - 1)] × [1 - M(k - M) / (kσ 2 )]. For the same test, 12 × 8 = 96, 96 / (20 × 16) = .30, 1 - .30 = .70, and × 20 / 19 gives .74 . When item difficulties differ, KR-21 is lower than KR-20: a quick, conservative estimate. Lee Cronbach (1951) generalised KR-20 to items with several score points, such as Likert ratings. The resulting coefficient alpha is α = [k / (k - 1)] × [1 - Σσ 2 i / σ 2 X ]: five Likert items with variances summing to 6 and total variance 20 give 1.25 × .70 = .875 . For 0 or 1 items σ 2 i = pq, so alpha equals KR-20. Cronbach showed that alpha is the mean of all possible split-half coefficients (each by Rulon's or Flanagan's formula); averaging over every split increases the accuracy of the estimate. Cyril Hoyt (1941) reached the same value by analysis of variance of persons by items: r = (MS persons - MS residual ) / MS persons . For alpha, as for any reliability coefficient, about .70 is acceptable for research and group comparisons, decisions about an individual patient need .80 to .90 or more, and .40 is poor: the items do not hang together. Alpha rises with test length, very high values can mean redundant items, and a high alpha does not prove that a test measures a single trait. Exam trap Cronbach's alpha measures internal consistency reliability : how well a scale's items hang together. It is not validity of any kind (content, construct, concurrent, predictive or criterion), not test-retest, parallel-forms or inter-rater reliability, and not a variance or regression statistic. KR-20 differs from alpha only in being limited to dichotomous items, whatever their content. Agreement between scorers Scorer or inter-rater reliability is the degree to which two or more clinicians agree when independently scoring or interpreting the same test responses. It matters wherever judgement enters, since scorer disagreement becomes error in the score: projective protocols, essays, behaviour observation and psychiatric diagnosis. Agreement of two tests on one construct is convergent validity, predicting future behaviour is predictive validity, and items relating to each other is internal consistency. Simple percentage agreement flatters raters, since some agreement is chance. Jacob Cohen (1960) corrected for it with Cohen's kappa for categorical judgements: κ = (P o - P e ) / (1 - P e ). Two clinicians classify 100 patients: both say depressed for 40 and not depressed for 30, so observed agreement P o = .70. Clinician A calls 50 depressed and B calls 60, so chance agreement P e = (.50 × .60) + (.50 × .40) = .50, and κ = .20 / .50 = .40 . Seventy percent raw agreement is only fair beyond chance. J. Richard Landis and Gary Koch (1977) labelled kappa below 0 poor, .00 to .20 slight, .21 to .40 fair, .41 to .60 moderate, .61 to .80 substantial and .81 to 1.00 almost perfect, so .85 is almost perfect. The standard error of measurement A reliability coefficient describes a group. A psychologist facing Ravi, whose IQ came out at 110, needs to know how far his true score might lie from 110. The standard error of measurement (SEM), the standard deviation of the errors one person's scores would show over many retestings, answers that: SEM = SD × √(1 - r xx ) . With SD 15 and reliability .91, SEM = 15 × √.09 = 15 × .30 = 4.5 ; with reliability .80, SEM = 15 × √.20 = about 6.7 . At r = 1 the SEM is 0; at r = 0 it equals the SD. The true score lies within ±1 SEM of the observed score about 68 percent of the time and within ±1.96 SEM 95 percent of the time, so Ravi's true IQ is probably 105.5 to 114.5 (68 percent) or 101.2 to 118.8 (95 percent), as Figure 2.6 shows. 95 100 105 110 115 120 125 Observed IQ 110 68% SEM = 15 × √(1 - .91) = 4.5 ±1 SEM, 68%: 105.5 to 114.5 ±1.96 SEM, 95%: 101.2 to 118.8 Figure 2.6 Confidence bands around an observed IQ of 110 (SD 15, reliability .91). The narrow band holds the true score about two times in three; the wide band, 19 times in 20. Exam trap SEM = SD × √(1 - r) , used to estimate the range within which a person's true score falls . Wrong options: SD × √r, SD × r (15 × .91 = 13.65), SD × (1 - r) without the root (1.35), √(1 - r) alone (.30), SD / r, SD × (1 + r), reliability × validity, mean minus SD. It does not correlate two tests, index item difficulty (Section 2.2) or predict performance. Clinical link DSM-5 places the IQ criterion for intellectual disability at about 70 ± 5 (65 to 75), a margin for measurement error. Report bands, never a single number treated as exact. Comparing two scores needs the standard error of the difference , √(SEM 1 2 + SEM 2 2 ). For two index scores (SD 15) with reliabilities .91 and .84, the SEMs are 4.5 and 6.0 and the standard error of the difference is √56.25 = 7.5, so the scores must differ by about 1.96 × 7.5 ≈ 15 points to be trusted at 95 percent. A difference score is unreliable when its two tests correlate highly: r dd = [(r xx + r yy ) / 2 - r xy ] / (1 - r xy ), so reliabilities .90 and .80 with a correlation of .70 give .15 / .30 = .50, because the shared true score cancels and the errors remain. A composite score from several positively correlated tests is usually more reliable than its parts. The index of reliability , √r xx , is the correlation between observed and true scores (√.81 = .90) and caps validity (Section 2.4). The estimated true score , M + r xx (X - M), regresses towards the mean: an IQ of 130 with reliability .90 gives 100 + .90 × 30 = 127, because extreme scores contain some luck. Spearman's (1904) correction for attenuation , r xy / √(r xx r yy ), estimates the correlation between perfectly reliable measures: a predictor and criterion correlating .36, with reliabilities .81 and .64, give .36 / (.90 × .80) = .36 / .72 = .50 (Section 2.4). Divide by the root; multiplying (.26) or dropping the root (.69) are the usual slips. What raises or lowers reliability Reliability belongs to scores from a particular group under particular conditions, not to a test for all time. Length. More parallel items raise it, as Spearman-Brown predicts. Group heterogeneity. A wide range of ability raises r; restriction of range (testing only admitted students) lowers it. Item difficulty and discrimination. Items near p = .50 with high item-total correlations add most; items everyone passes or fails add nothing (Section 2.2). Guessing. It adds random error, most on true-false items. Speededness and interval. Speed inflates single-session estimates; a longer retest interval lowers test-retest coefficients. Scoring and conditions. Objective keys raise reliability; subjective scoring, ambiguous items, noise, fatigue and low motivation lower it. Cronbach and Goldine Gleser (1965) applied the bandwidth-fidelity dilemma from information theory to testing: a test covering many traits briefly (wide bandwidth) measures each with low precision (fidelity), while a narrow test measures one trait precisely but says little else. Beyond classical theory Classical theory lumps all error into one E; generalizability theory , from Cronbach, Gleser, Harinder Nanda and Nageswari Rajaratnam (1972), uses analysis of variance to split observed-score variance into persons and facets such as raters, items and occasions. A G study estimates these variance components; a D study (decision study) forecasts dependability under other designs, such as two raters instead of one. The result is a generalizability coefficient , of which classical reliability is a special case. Item response theory, which models each item's response curve, replaces one reliability for everyone with test information , which varies along the trait (Section 2.2). Table 2.9 gathers the methods. Section 2.3 asked whether a test measures consistently; this section asks whether it measures the right thing, and then follows its scores into the decisions they drive. What validity means The classic definition, associated with Henry Edward Garrett (1894 to 1973), is that validity is the extent to which a test measures what it claims (purports) to measure. Validity is specific to a purpose and a population (a test valid in one culture need not be valid in another), it is a matter of degree, and every new use needs new evidence. The American Psychological Association's Technical Recommendations of 1954 named content, predictive, concurrent and construct validity, and the 1966 Standards merged predictive and concurrent into criterion-related validity, giving the classical trinity of content, criterion-related and construct validity. In 1989 Samuel Messick replaced the trinity with a unified view of validity : one integrated judgement of how well evidence and theory support the interpretations and uses of scores, so validity belongs to an inference drawn from scores, not to the test itself. The 2014 Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing list five sources of evidence: test content, response processes, internal structure, relations with other variables, and the consequences of testing. Face validity and content validity Face validity is the appearance of validity: on superficial inspection a test seems to measure what it claims, because its questions intuitively seem relevant, as when a depression questionnaire asks "I feel sad most of the day". It is judged by test takers and lay people, not by experts or by any statistic, so it is not validity in the technical sense. It still earns rapport and acceptance, but an obvious purpose makes faking good or faking bad easy, which is why some inventories use subtle items (Section 2.9). Content validity is how adequately the items sample the whole domain: a depression scale should cover mood, interest, sleep, appetite, energy, guilt, concentration and suicidal thinking, not sadness alone. The developer drafts a table of specifications (test blueprint), a grid of content areas against objectives that fixes the number of items in each cell, and experts then judge every item. C. H. Lawshe quantified their judgement in 1975 with the content validity ratio , CVR = (n e − N/2) / (N/2), where n e of N experts rate an item essential; it runs from −1 to +1. Item validity means each item belongs to the domain; sampling validity means the items together cover all of it. The two threats are construct under-representation (part of the domain left out) and construct-irrelevant variance (scores also reflecting something else, as when a mathematics test set in English partly measures reading). Content validity is the main evidence for achievement tests. Exam trap Face validity has nothing to do with faces: "facial expressions used for diagnosis" and "a scale of emotional responding" are invented distractors, and "a hypothetical attribute that may not be directly observable" defines a construct ( 2.4.5 ). Face validity is judged by lay people; content validity by experts against a blueprint. Criterion-related validity: concurrent and predictive A criterion is an independent, external measure of the attribute, such as a psychiatrist's diagnosis, a gold-standard scale, grades or job ratings, and criterion-related validity is the correlation between test and criterion. Its two types differ only in timing. In concurrent validity test and criterion are measured at about the same time. The classic design gives a new intelligence test together with an established one; likewise, a new 20-item depression questionnaire that correlates r = 0.85 with a gold-standard scale completed the same day shows concurrent validity. A high correlation with an established measure of the same attribute shows that the test reflects present status. In predictive validity the criterion is measured later, as when entrance scores are correlated with first-year marks. Selection tests need it, and it usually runs lower than concurrent validity because people change in the interval. A criterion recorded before the test gives postdictive validity. The correlation is the validity coefficient; its square, the coefficient of determination, is the share of criterion variance the test explains (r = 0.60 explains 36 percent). The standard error of estimate, SE est = SD y √(1 − r 2 ), is the error of an individual prediction: with r = 0.60 and a criterion SD of 10 marks it is 8 marks. It is not the standard error of measurement (Section 2.3). Exam trap Concurrent and predictive are the two criterion-related types; face, content, factorial and construct validity are not criterion based. RML 2024 keyed "predictive validity" as the one NOT criterion based: that key is wrong. Of its options, face validity (appearance only) and factorial validity (construct evidence) are not criterion based; face validity is the safer mark. RML 2021 defined concurrent validity as "scores correlate highly with scores from tests that measure the same attribute"; "two tests done at the same time" is only the timing, "two clinicians agree" is inter-rater reliability, and split-half or retest correlations are reliability (Section 2.3). Criteria, cut-offs and cross-validation A coefficient is no better than its criterion, and finding a good one is the criterion problem. A good criterion is relevant, reliable (an unreliable one caps the coefficient, 2.4.6 ), free from bias and available at reasonable cost. In criterion contamination the criterion is influenced by knowledge of the predictor scores, or includes predictor-related content, so the correlation is inflated artificially: supervisors who know employees' selection-test scores tend to rate high scorers highly. The cure is blind ratings. Criterion deficiency is the opposite flaw, a criterion that omits important parts of performance, and plain random error in the criterion lowers rather than inflates the coefficient. Restriction of range also lowers validity: grades exist only for students the entrance test admitted, and their narrow band of scores underestimates the test. Items chosen because they correlated with the criterion in one sample capitalise on chance, so the coefficient falls in a fresh sample. Re-checking it there is cross-validation , and the fall is shrinkage, largest with small samples and many items tried for few kept. An expectancy table shows the chance of criterion success at each band of test scores. A cut-off score divides those selected or diagnosed from the rest, and since no test is perfectly valid every cut-off makes some errors ( 2.4.8 ). Incremental validity ( Lee Sechrest , 1963) is the prediction a test adds beyond measures already available, such as school marks. Synthetic validity, a term of Lawshe's, infers validity for a job too small to study directly from known validities for its components. Construct validity What is the criterion for anxiety? Many attributes have none. A construct is a hypothetical or inferred attribute, such as intelligence, anxiety or extraversion, that cannot be directly observed but is used to explain behaviour. Construct validity , introduced in the 1954 recommendations and set out by Lee Joseph Cronbach (1916 to 2001) and Paul Everett Meehl (1920 to 2003) in 1955, is the degree to which a test measures the theoretical construct it claims to measure. They placed each construct in a nomological network , the web of lawful relations the theory predicts with other constructs and with behaviour. Validation then tests whether scores behave as the network predicts. Convergent validity is a high correlation with other measures of the same construct; discriminant validity (divergent validity) is a low correlation with measures of theoretically unrelated constructs. A new resilience scale should correlate highly with an established resilience measure and weakly with an unrelated trait. Donald Thomas Campbell (1916 to 1996) and Donald W. Fiske showed in 1959 how to test both at once. Key study: Campbell and Fiske's multitrait-multimethod matrix (1959) Does a score reflect the trait, or only the way it was measured? Campbell and Fiske measured two or more traits, each by two or more methods (self-report, peer rating, observation), and intercorrelated everything in a multitrait-multimethod matrix . The monotrait-heteromethod values (same trait, different methods) should be high, showing convergence, and higher than the heterotrait-monomethod values (different traits, same method). When different traits correlate highly merely because both were self-reported, the matrix has exposed method variance, which proved common in the published matrices they examined. Criticism: the criteria are judged by eye, without a single statistical test, so confirmatory factor analysis is now used to model the matrix. Factorial validity is shown when items load on the expected factor in exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis, evidence of internal structure (the technique is in Chapter 9). In the known-groups method (contrasted groups) the test separates groups known to differ, such as depressed inpatients and community volunteers. Scores should also change with development as the theory expects and move with experimental interventions (anxiety scores falling after therapy). Internal consistency (Section 2.3) supports a construct claim but cannot establish it alone. Consequential validity , Messick's addition, weighs the social consequences of using the scores; ecological validity is how well test performance represents everyday functioning, a key question in neuropsychology. The validity of research designs (internal, external, statistical conclusion and the construct validity of a manipulation) belongs to Chapter 9. Exam trap Construct validity was keyed as "the degree to which a test measures what it claims to measure" (RML 2025) and as "the level to which the theoretical construct is related to other similar measures" (RML 2021); in the 2021 paper "scores correlate highly with tests of the same attribute" defined concurrent validity. The 2025 wording is Garrett's general definition, which fits because the unified view treats all validity as construct validity. The distractors are reliability (consistency across administrations or among items), content validity (the whole domain) and inter-rater reliability (rater agreement). For discriminant validity choose the weak correlation with an unrelated construct; a high correlation with an established measure of the same construct is convergent, "covers all facets" is content and "predicts future coping" is predictive. Reliability and validity together A test can be reliable without being valid: a scale with high internal consistency but low criterion validity consistently measures something, but not the intended construct. It cannot be valid without being reliable, because scores that are mostly random error correlate with nothing. Reliability is therefore necessary but not sufficient for validity; consistency does not make a test valid, and validity is more than consistency. A validity coefficient cannot exceed √(r xx × r yy ), the square root of the product of the test and criterion reliabilities. With a perfectly reliable criterion this validity ceiling is √r xx , the index of reliability: r xx = 0.81 allows at most 0.90. Run in reverse, the logic gives the correction for attenuation of Charles Edward Spearman (1863 to 1945), published in 1904, which estimates the correlation if both measures were perfectly reliable: r c = r xy / √(r xx × r yy ). An observed 0.36 with reliabilities of 0.81 and 0.64 becomes 0.36 / 0.72 = 0.50. One apparent conflict remains. Very high homogeneity maximises internal consistency but narrows coverage, so a broad criterion is often predicted better by a heterogeneous test with moderate inter-item correlations: the bandwidth-fidelity trade-off of Section 2.3 seen from the validity side. Exam trap The TRUE statement (RML 2024) is "a test can be reliable without being valid". "If a test measures what it is intended to measure, then by definition it is reliable" is the near-miss: a valid test must be reliable, but not by definition. Validity need not come "first chronologically". The ceiling is the square root of reliability, not reliability itself, its square or reliability minus the SEM. Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values Once a test is used to decide (depressed or not, select or reject), validity shows up as right and wrong calls. Crossing the test result with the true state, set by a gold-standard diagnosis, puts every person in one of four cells (Figure 2.7): a true positive, a false positive (positive without the condition), a false negative (the condition missed) or a true negative. True state (gold-standard diagnosis) Has the condition Does not have it Test positive Test negative True positive (TP) False positive (FP) False negative (FN) True negative (TN) Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) true positive rate Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) true negative rate PPV = TP / (TP + FP) NPV = TN / (TN + FN) Figure 2.7 The four outcomes of a diagnostic decision. Sensitivity and specificity read down the columns; the predictive values read across the rows. Only the diagonal cells are correct decisions. Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) is the true positive rate: the proportion of people who have the condition whom the test correctly identifies. Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) is the proportion of people without the condition whom the test correctly clears. Both describe the test itself at a given cut-off. A screen with sensitivity 90 percent and specificity 70 percent calls 90 percent of depressed people depressed and 70 percent of healthy people healthy. A high false positive rate means normal people are diagnosed as disordered; false negatives leave disordered people undetected. The proportion of all decisions that are correct is the hit rate. The clinician, though, holds a result, not a diagnosis, and needs the rows. The positive predictive value , PPV = TP / (TP + FP), is the probability that a positive result is correct, and the negative predictive value, NPV = TN / (TN + FN), the probability that a negative one is. Both depend heavily on the base rate (prevalence) of the condition in the people tested, as Meehl and Albert Rosen showed in 1955 (Table 2.10). A sign is worth using only if it improves on the base rate. Exam trap TP / (TP + FP) is the PPV, not sensitivity. "Probability that a positive test reflects true disease" is the PPV; "probability of disease prior to testing" is the base rate. Sensitivity of 90 percent does not mean 90 percent of positive results are correct. The PPV is most affected by the base rate, not by sensitivity alone, specificity alone or the number of items. An over-strict diagnosis produces false negatives, not false positives. Cut-offs, ROC curves and selection Sensitivity and specificity hold only for one cutting score. Lower the cut-off and sensitivity rises while specificity falls; raise it and the reverse happens. The choice weighs the costs of the two errors: missing a suicidal patient is worse than a false alarm, so screens use lenient cut-offs. The receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC curve), borrowed from signal detection theory, plots sensitivity (true positive rate) against 1 − specificity (false positive rate), one point for each possible cut-off (Figure 2.8). A useless test follows the diagonal; a better one bows toward the top-left corner. Is that good? Until you know how hard the items were and how other ten-year-olds do, the raw score (items passed or points earned) means nothing; it needs a frame of reference. There are two such frames, and the commoner one, comparison with other people, rests on norms, on derived scores and on the normal curve that ties them together. Norm-referenced and criterion-referenced scores In norm-referenced interpretation a score is compared with those of a norm group or standardisation sample , a representative sample of the people the test is meant for. "Higher than 90 per cent of her peers", "5th in his class" and "1 standard deviation (SD) above the mean" are norm-referenced: they rank a person among others, as selection requires. In criterion-referenced interpretation the score is compared with a fixed standard, whatever others do: "85 per cent of the addition problems correct, meeting the mastery cut-off". Robert Glaser drew the distinction in 1963. A criterion-referenced test asks what a person can do, so a whole class can pass it, or no one. A domain-referenced test samples items from a defined domain (all two-digit additions, say), so the percentage correct estimates how much of the domain the person commands; a mastery test adds a cut-off and reports pass or fail, like a driving test. Norms are not standards : they describe how people do perform, not how they should, so matching the norm of a poorly taught school is not being good enough. An ipsative score compares a person with no one else: it expresses one trait relative to the same person's other traits, as in forced-choice inventories (Section 2.9), and cannot be compared across people. Exam trap Of the usual options, only "85 per cent correct, meeting the mastery cut-off" is criterion-referenced; percentile standing, class rank and "1 SD above the mean" are norm-referenced. Norm-referencing compares with a representative standardisation sample, not with a cut-off, an absolute criterion or the person's own earlier scores. Standardisation and the norm sample The process of standardisation means giving and scoring a test identically for everyone (same instructions, materials, time limits and scoring rules) and giving it so to a large sample whose scores become the norms . The test maker defines the target population , the people the test is meant for, and samples it: simple random sampling is ideal but rarely practical, so stratified sampling (quotas matching the census on age, sex, region, residence and socio-economic status) or cluster sampling (whole schools chosen at random) is used (Section 9.3). Good norms are large, representative , recent (the Flynn effect, a rise of about 3 intelligence quotient (IQ) points a decade, makes old norms too easy; Section 1.9), relevant to the person tested and fully described in the manual. Hence national norms , local norms (one region or school) and subgroup norms (by age, sex, grade, language or occupation). American norms compare an Indian child with American children, so Indian versions of Western tests were renormed (Section 2.6). Standardisation lets the clinician do all three of the following: see where a client's score falls on the test's distribution of scores; estimate from it whether the client might meet the diagnostic criteria for a disorder (an IQ about 2 SD below the mean is one criterion for intellectual disability, Section 2.7); and estimate how probable that diagnosis is. Computers now score tests against the norm tables and write narrative reports (as for the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory-2, MMPI-2), saving time and errors, though not replacing clinical judgement. Age and grade norms; ratio and deviation IQ The oldest derived scores express performance as the age or school grade at which it is typical. An age-equivalent norm is the average performance at each age; Alfred Binet 's 1908 scale grouped items by age, and the age level a child reached was the mental age (MA). A grade-equivalent norm does the same for school grades, interpolating in-between values. Both mislead. Growth is uneven (faster at 2 than at 14), so a year is not a fixed unit; traits such as personality do not grow with age; grade equivalents in different subjects are not comparable; and a Class 4 child with an arithmetic grade equivalent of 7.2 has not mastered Class 7 work, only scored on a Class 4 test as an average Class 7 pupil is estimated to. William Stern divided MA by chronological age (CA) in 1912, and Lewis Madison Terman multiplied by 100 in the 1916 Stanford-Binet: the ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, so MA 8 and CA 10 give 80. It fails for adults, because mental age stops rising in the late teens (a 40-year-old with an MA of 16 would score 40). David Wechsler 's Wechsler-Bellevue scale (1939) introduced the deviation IQ , a standard score comparing a person with same-age peers, with a mean of 100 and an SD of 15 at every age (Sections 1.9 and 2.6). Exam trap MA 8 and CA 10 give 80; 125 inverts the ratio (CA ÷ MA). The deviation IQ is not "only for adults", is not less reliable and is not built from unstandardised raw scores: it is a standard score against age peers. Percentile ranks The percentile rank (PR) is the percentage of the norm group scoring below a given raw score (some books say "at or below"). If 70 per cent of the sample scored below Meera's 65, her PR is 70 and her score is the 70th percentile (P 70 ). It is not the percentage correct , a raw score: 70 per cent correct could be the 30th percentile on an easy test and the 99th on a hard one. The quartiles cut the distribution into four (Q 1 = P 25 ; Q 2 = P 50 , the median; Q 3 = P 75 ) and deciles into ten (D 5 = P 50 ). Percentiles are ordinal , with unequal units. Scores crowd around the middle of a normal distribution, so a small raw difference there jumps many percentile points while a large one in the tails moves few: the 50th to the 60th percentile is a quarter of an SD (IQ 100 to 104), the 90th to the 99th more than a whole SD (IQ 119 to 135). So percentiles exaggerate differences near the middle, hide them in the tails and should not be averaged; equal-unit standard scores solve this. The z score A standard score states how far a score lies from the mean in SD units. The basic one is the z score : z = (X − M) ÷ SD, with X the raw score and M and SD those of the norm group. z scores have a mean of 0 and an SD of 1; z = +1.0 is exactly one SD above the mean, and negative values lie below it. Their great use is comparing results from different distributions. Arjun scores 60 in psychology (mean 50, SD 5) and 70 in statistics (mean 60, SD 10). The raw scores favour statistics, but psychology is z = +2.0 and statistics z = +1.0, so psychology was his better paper. Look-alikes answer other questions (Sections 9.8 and 9.9). The variance (SD squared) and the semi-interquartile range , (Q 3 − Q 1 ) ÷ 2, measure the spread of a whole distribution; the coefficient of variation , (SD ÷ M) × 100, compares spread across distributions in different units; the standard error is the SD of a sampling distribution, such as that of sample means (the standard error of measurement is in Section 2.3); the median, not z, describes the centre of a skewed distribution. Only z places one person within a distribution. Exam trap The measure of how far a data point lies from the mean in SD units, which lets scores from different distributions be compared, is the z score. It is not a measure of variability or of the central tendency of a skewed distribution. The normal curve: from z to percentile Why does z = +1 always mean the 84th percentile? Because test scales are built on the normal curve , the symmetrical bell in which mean, median and mode coincide, and its areas are fixed: about 34.1 per cent of cases lie between the mean and 1 SD on each side, 13.6 per cent between 1 and 2 SD and 2.1 per cent between 2 and 3 SD. So about 68 per cent fall within ±1 SD, 95 per cent within ±2 SD and 99.7 per cent within ±3 SD (Figure 2.9). On a Binet-type scale with an SD of 16, an IQ of 136 is z = 36 ÷ 16 = 2.25; the z table gives .9878 below it, so about 98.8 per cent score lower (98.7 if the entry is truncated). Exam trap ±2 SD holds about 95 per cent (exactly 95 within ±1.96, so 97.5 per cent lies below +1.96); ±1 SD holds 68 and ±3 SD 99.7. The z table comes from the normal distribution, not from the SD, t scores or random sampling. The 84th percentile is z = +1, not +1.5 (93rd) or +2 (98th). Linear and normalised scores; the T score z scores carry signs and decimals, so other standard scores rescale them: new score = new mean + (new SD × z). This is a linear transformation (new = a + b × old), as are z itself and the deviation score X − M; it keeps the raw distribution's shape, so skewed raw scores stay skewed. A normalised standard score (an area, or non-linear, transformation) instead turns each raw score into its percentile rank, looks up the z that cuts off that percentage of the normal curve and rescales it, forcing a normal shape. Stanines, stens, the C scale, normalised T scores and most modern intelligence-test scales are normalised, which is justified only with large samples and when the skew lies in the test, not the trait. The T score of William A. McCall (1922) has a mean of 50 and an SD of 10: T = 50 + 10z, usually 20 to 80 (±3 SD). Computed from z it is linear; McCall's own scale was normalised. T scores are the metric of the MMPI and most personality inventories, including the Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEO-PI-R; Section 2.9). T 70, 2 SD above the mean (about the 98th percentile), was the original MMPI's clinical cut-off; the MMPI-2 uses T 65, 1.5 SD above (about the 93rd). Exam trap T scores have a mean of 50 and an SD of 10, not 100 and 15 (IQ), 0 and 1 (z) or 500 and 100 (CEEB). T 70 = +2 SD, T 65 = +1.5 SD, T 60 = +1 SD. Stanines, stens and the C scale The stanine ("standard nine"), developed by the United States Army Air Forces in World War II, runs from 1 to 9 with a mean of 5 and an SD of about 2. Stanines are assigned by rank: the lowest 4 per cent of the norm group get 1, the next 7 per cent 2, and so on in the proportions 4, 7, 12, 17, 20, 17, 12, 7 and 4 per cent. Each band but the open-ended 1 and 9 is half an SD wide. Stanine 5 spans z = −0.25 to +0.25, the 40th to 60th percentile, and holds 20 per cent of cases; stanine 4 covers about the 23rd to 40th percentile, and 9 begins at the 96th (Figure 2.9). Built from percentile ranks, stanines are a normalised, non-linear transformation. Stanines 1 to 3 are below average, 4 to 6 average and 7 to 9 above average; single digits are easy to record but coarse. The sten ("standard ten") runs from 1 to 10 with a mean of 5.5 and an SD of 2. It has no middle band: stens 5 and 6 lie just below and above the mean, and 4 to 7 cover the middle 68 per cent. Stens are the scale of Raymond Bernard Cattell 's Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF, 1949), not of the Wechsler scales, the Stanford-Binet or the Rorschach. J. P. Guilford 's C scale (1954) extends the stanine to 11 units (0 to 10; mean 5, SD 2) by splitting off about the extreme 1 per cent at each end. Exam trap Stanine 5 holds 20 per cent, not 17 (stanines 4 and 6). Of z, 50 + 10z, X − M and the stanine, only the stanine is a non-linear transformation. Scaled scores, deviation IQs and CEEB scores Each Wechsler subtest is reported as a scaled score (mean 10, SD 3, range 1 to 19), and the index scores and Full Scale IQ as deviation IQs (mean 100, SD 15). A scaled score of 10 is exactly average, the 50th percentile; 7 is 1 SD below (about the 16th percentile, like an IQ of 85), which the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, fourth edition (WAIS-IV), calls low average; 13 is 1 SD above (84th); 4 is 2 SD below (2nd), the borderline region. The Stanford-Binet used an SD of 16 from Form L-M (1960) through the fourth edition (1986), returning to 15 in the fifth (2003), and Cattell's Culture Fair Intelligence Test also uses 16. So IQ 130 is z = +2.0 (97.7th percentile) on a Wechsler scale but +1.875 (97th) on an SD-16 scale: compare tests through z. A CEEB score (College Entrance Examination Board) has a mean of 500 and an SD of 100, as on the older SAT and Graduate Record Examinations (GRE). Tables 2.11 and 2.12 summarise them all. Answers: (1) criterion, (2) 80, (3) 95, (4) +1, (5) 1.5, (6) 20, (7) 16PF. 2.6 Intelligence Tests: Binet, Wechsler, Non-verbal and Indian Scales Medium yield · 35 Qs In 1904 the French education ministry asked which Paris schoolchildren could not keep up without special help. The answer, a list of graded tasks, founded psychology's most used family of tests. This section follows it through the Binet, Wechsler and Kaufman scales, the non-verbal tests and the Indian adaptations; theories of intelligence and the IQ itself were introduced in Section 1.9. What an intelligence test can and cannot do An individual test is given by one examiner to one person, who can be watched and questioned (the Stanford-Binet, the Wechsler scales); a group test is given to many people at once. A verbal test uses language in its items; a non-verbal test keeps language out of the items; a performance test asks the person to handle materials, such as blocks or a form board, usually against the clock. What does a good IQ test offer? High test-retest reliability, high internal consistency (both above .90 for the major full-scale IQs) and good validity for predicting school achievement (it correlates about .5 with grades). It does not offer a good prediction of behaviour in general: honesty, persistence and social skill depend on personality, motivation and circumstance. Intelligence tests diagnose intellectual disability and giftedness, guide educational placement, set a neuropsychological baseline and document eligibility for a disability allowance, but not for housing benefit (an income question), suicide risk (a clinical risk assessment, Chapter 7) or, with an adult scale, a child's special educational needs. The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) is an intelligence test, not a personality, aptitude (predicting future success), attitude or achievement (measuring past learning) test (Sections 2.8 and 2.9), and it does not look for neurological soft signs, subtle non-localising signs such as clumsiness. Exam trap "An IQ test does NOT provide ..." is answered by "a good predictor of behaviour". High test-retest reliability, high internal consistency and good validity (for school achievement) are exactly what it does provide. The Binet scales Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911) and the physician Theodore Simon (1872 to 1961) published the first practical intelligence test in 1905: 30 items in order of difficulty. In 1908 they grouped the items by the age at which most children pass them, creating the first age scale ; the highest level a child reaches is the mental age . The 1911 revision, the year Binet died, extended it to adults. Lewis Madison Terman (1877 to 1956) standardised it at Stanford University as the Stanford-Binet (1916), using William Stern's ratio IQ (mental age ÷ chronological age × 100): the original Stanford-Binet used the ratio IQ, not a deviation IQ, percentile rank or T-score (Section 2.5). Later editions (Table 2.13) moved away from mental age: parallel Forms L and M with Maud Merrill (1937); Form L-M (1960), with a deviation IQ of SD 16; and the SB4 (1986) of Robert L. Thorndike , Elizabeth Hagen and Jerome M. Sattler , a point scale (each subtest scored by items passed, whatever their age level) reporting Standard Age Scores, SD 16. The Stanford-Binet Fifth Edition (SB5, 2003) of Gale H. Roid covers ages 2 to 85 and over, with mean 100 and SD 15. Its five factors, Fluid Reasoning, Knowledge, Quantitative Reasoning, Visual-Spatial Processing and Working Memory, are each tested in a verbal and a non-verbal domain: 10 subtests yielding Full Scale, Verbal and Nonverbal IQs. Two routing subtests (Object Series/Matrices and Vocabulary) set the starting level for the rest. Within a subtest the examiner finds a basal level , below which all items are assumed passed, and a ceiling level , where failures stop testing. The SB5's factors are not "sensory, motor, memory, attention, language" (a neuropsychological checklist) or "Verbal and Performance IQ only" (old Wechsler). Wechsler, the deviation IQ and the WAIS-IV David Wechsler (1896 to 1981), chief psychologist at Bellevue Hospital in New York, found the Stanford-Binet unsuited to the adults he tested. It had little appeal for adults; it put too much emphasis on word manipulation; it stressed speed over accuracy; and it relied on mental age, which stops growing in the late teens, so an adult's ratio IQ falls with every birthday. His Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale (1939) answered each flaw: a point scale with a Performance scale of non-verbal tasks beside the Verbal scale, scored by a new deviation IQ , also called the standard IQ because it is a standard score. The deviation IQ compares the actual score with the expected mean score for the person's age group: IQ = 100 + 15 × (score minus age-group mean) ÷ age-group SD. Scoring at your age group's mean gives 100 at any age; one SD above gives 115. Wechsler defined intelligence (1944) as "the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally, and to deal effectively with his environment". Exam trap Wechsler's new method was the deviation ("standard") IQ, not a mental-age, physical-age or age-relative formula IQ; mocks write it as actual score ÷ expected mean score for age. His target flaws were no appeal for adults, word manipulation, speed over accuracy and mental age, never "children", "physical age" or "accuracy over speed". The adult line runs from the WAIS (1955; 6 verbal and 5 performance subtests) through the WAIS-R (1981) and WAIS-III (1997), which still gave Verbal, Performance and Full Scale IQs, to the WAIS-IV (2008; ages 16:0 to 90:11), which dropped the first two. It yields a Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) from 10 core subtests and four index scores , composites for narrower abilities: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Perceptual Reasoning (PRI), Working Memory (WMI) and Processing Speed (PSI) (Figure 2.10). Five supplemental subtests can replace a spoiled core subtest. The VCI reflects verbal reasoning and acquired knowledge; the PRI, reasoning with visual, non-verbal material. The Working Memory Index , built on holding and manipulating digits and mental sums, reflects attention, concentration and mental control; the Processing Speed Index , how quickly simple visual material is scanned and acted on. The optional General Ability Index (GAI, VCI plus PRI) estimates reasoning with less weight on memory and speed; the Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI) pairs WMI and PSI. The WAIS-5 (2024) splits perceptual reasoning into Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning: five primary indices. "VIQ, PIQ, FSIQ and Memory Quotient" mixes the WAIS-III with the Wechsler Memory Scale (Section 2.11); "crystallised, fluid, visual, auditory (or quantitative)", "VIQ, PIQ, memory, attention" and "cognitive, behavioural, emotional, adaptive" are not WAIS-IV indices. The WISC-V (2014; ages 6:0 to 16:11) has five primary indices, Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory and Processing Speed, from 10 primary subtests, and takes the FSIQ from seven; Information, Arithmetic and Letter-Number Sequencing are among its secondary subtests. Digit Span, Symbol Search and Matrix Reasoning are core or primary in both, so mark Letter-Number Sequencing, but Information and Arithmetic truly fit the stem. Which ability does each subtest tap? Vocabulary and Information measure crystallised intelligence, knowledge acquired through schooling and culture. Matrix Reasoning (completing a visual pattern) measures fluid reasoning, solving novel problems without learned knowledge; Block Design (copying a design with coloured cubes) measures visuospatial analysis and construction; Coding (formerly Digit Symbol: copying number-paired symbols at speed) measures processing speed. The FSIQ is placed in a descriptive band (Table 2.15). Below 70 is extremely low, but intellectual disability also requires deficits in adaptive behaviour (Section 2.7). Scores of 70 to 84 straddle borderline (70 to 79) and low average (80 to 89); older systems called 71 to 84 borderline intellectual functioning. The examiner then studies index discrepancies , differences between index scores, and scatter , unevenness among subtest scores. A VCI of 115 beside a PSI of 82 is interpreted only if the gap is statistically significant and rare in the norm sample; the FSIQ then averages over a real split, and the separate indices or the GAI tell more. Kaufman and Nadeen L. Kaufman built their tests on theory. The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (K-ABC, 1983) used Alexander Luria's sequential processing (handling items in serial order) and simultaneous processing (integrating many at once), and scored achievement apart from ability. The KABC-II (2004, ages 3 to 18) lets the examiner choose a Luria model or a Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) model. The Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test (K-BIT, 1990; KBIT-2, 2004, ages 4 to 90) is a quick screen with a Verbal or Crystallised scale and a Nonverbal or Fluid scale (matrices). Reading, mathematics, quantitative and analytical scales belong to achievement and scholastic aptitude tests, such as the ACT, SAT and GRE admission tests (Section 2.8); an "EQ scale" belongs to emotional intelligence (Section 1.9). The Indian-born J. P. Das and Jack A. Naglieri turned Luria's three functional units of the brain into the PASS theory (Planning, Attention, Simultaneous and Successive processing), measured by their Cognitive Assessment System (1997). The Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Cognitive Abilities ( Richard W. Woodcock and Mary Bonner Johnson , 1977) are, in current editions, built on CHC theory. Non-verbal and culture-fair tests Vocabulary items reward schooling and language as much as intelligence. A culture-free test would leave culture out entirely; none exists, since even a pattern on paper assumes familiarity with pictures and timing. A culture-fair test merely minimises language, reading and specific knowledge, so that people from different backgrounds start more nearly level. The classic is Raven's Progressive Matrices by John Carlyle Raven (1902 to 1970). Each item is a pattern with a piece missing. The Standard Progressive Matrices (1938) has 60 items in five sets, A to E, growing progressively harder; the Coloured version (1947) serves children of 5 to 11, elderly people and disabled people; the Advanced version serves able adults. Raven aimed at Spearman's g through eductive ability , seeing relations in confusion, as against recalling learned information. The test measures fluid, non-verbal reasoning by abstract pattern completion with minimal language, and is one of the strongest single markers of g. Exam trap Raven's measures fluid intelligence; it is culture-fair, not culture-free, and does not measure crystallised, verbal or social intelligence, reading comprehension or memory alone. Offered "general intelligence" beside "fluid", choose fluid: Raven's marks g, but its content is fluid and non-verbal. "Both" is wrong. Raymond Bernard Cattell (1905 to 1998) named his test the Culture Free Intelligence Test (1940), then renamed it Culture Fair. Its three Scales are graded by age and ability; Scales 2 and 3 use four figural subtests: series, classification, matrices and conditions. Other tests remove speech from the task: the Leiter International Performance Scale of Russell Graydon Leiter (1929; Leiter-3, 2013) gives its instructions by pantomime, for deaf or autistic children; the Columbia Mental Maturity Scale needs only pointing to the drawing that does not belong, suiting children with cerebral palsy; and the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test of Lloyd M. Dunn (1959) measures receptive vocabulary as the person points to the picture the examiner names. The simplest non-verbal test is a pencil and the request "draw a man". Florence Laura Goodenough (1886 to 1959) noticed that children add details to drawings in a regular developmental order. Her Draw-a-Man test (1926) credits up to 51 details as a non-verbal estimate of intellectual maturity and visual-motor ability; Dale B. Harris revised it in 1963. Because it asks so little, it works with a client too disorganised for verbal or performance subtests. Karen Machover 's Draw-a-Person uses the same request projectively, to read personality (Section 2.10). Exam trap A disorganised client who cannot manage verbal or performance tasks is asked to draw a person: the domain targeted is visual-motor integration and cognitive estimation (Goodenough), not projective personality assessment (Machover), verbal comprehension or processing speed. Group testing arrived with the First World War. In 1917 a committee led by Robert Mearns Yerkes (1876 to 1956) built the Army Alpha, a verbal test for literate recruits, and the Army Beta, a non-verbal one for illiterate and non-English-speaking recruits. Arthur Otis , Terman's student, devised the multiple-choice group format the Alpha borrowed (today's Otis-Lennon School Ability Test). The Primary Mental Abilities tests of Louis Leon Thurstone (1887 to 1955) score seven primary abilities separately instead of giving one IQ. Performance tests and Indian scales India needed tests that did not lean on literacy or on one language, so its psychologists normed performance tests and adapted Western scales (Table 2.16). In the Kohs Block Design test ( Samuel C. Kohs , 1920; book 1923) the person arranges coloured cubes to copy a printed design; Wechsler borrowed it as Block Design. In the Alexander Pass-Along test ( W. P. Alexander , 1932) blocks are slid along a tray, never lifted, to reach a target pattern. The Seguin Form Board, a teaching device of Edouard Seguin (1812 to 1880) for children with intellectual disability, became a test in Henry Herbert Goddard 's version: a child replaces 10 shapes over three trials, and the shortest time converts to a mental age. In the Gesell Drawing Test of Arnold Gesell (1880 to 1961) a child copies geometric figures mastered at typical ages. C. M. Bhatia assembled Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (1955), standardised on Indian children. Its five subtests are Kohs Block Design, Alexander Pass-Along, Pattern Drawing, Immediate Memory (digits, the one non-performance task) and Picture Construction; the Seguin Form Board is not among them. Needing no reading or writing, it is the test of choice for an illiterate child or adult from a rural area, because it minimises cultural and educational bias; the WISC-IV and SB5 carry Western verbal content, and MISIC is half verbal and assumes schooling. Being visual, it cannot serve a patient with cortical blindness. Exam trap For an illiterate rural 10-year-old, choose Bhatia's Battery over the WISC-IV, SB5 or MISIC. Its population is illiterate or rural Indians, adolescents and adults included, not urban English speakers or preschoolers only. The adaptations follow their parents. The Binet-Kamat Test ( V. V. Kamat , 1934; revised 1967) adapted the 1916 Stanford-Binet; it is a heavily verbal age scale giving a mental age and ratio IQ. Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC; Arthur J. Malin , Nagpur, 1969) adapted the WISC for ages 6 to 15, so it can be given from 6 years, and yields Verbal and Performance Quotients and a Full Scale IQ. The Wechsler Adult Performance Intelligence Scale (WAPIS; P. Ramalingaswamy , 1974) adapted the WAIS performance subtests for Indian adults. Pramila Phatak of Baroda produced Indian norms for the Draw-a-Man test, and Raven's matrices also have Indian norms. Pearson's Indian editions of the WISC-IV and WAIS-IV are newer and poorly documented. Exam trap A mock keys "WAIS-IV India edition" as the Indian WAIS common in clinics. Answers: (1) behaviour, (2) ratio, (3) Arithmetic, (4) 16:11, (5) routing, (6) free, (7) WISC. 2.7 Assessing Development, Adaptive Behaviour and Disability Lower yield · 21 Qs An intelligence test asks how well a person reasons when tested. Two other questions matter as much. Has this infant reached the milestones expected for her age? And how well does a child or adult actually manage everyday life? Their answers decide who is diagnosed with intellectual disability and who in India is certified as disabled. Beyond IQ: quotients, adaptive behaviour and informants An infant cannot follow test instructions, so you measure how far she has come along the expected path. A developmental scale lists milestones at the ages most children reach them. The level reached is the developmental age (DA), and the developmental quotient is DQ = DA / CA × 100, CA being chronological age. A social maturity scale gives a social age (SA) and a social quotient , SQ = SA / CA × 100: if 6-year-old Ravi (72 months) manages daily life like a typical child of 54 months, his SQ is 75. Modern scales replace these crude ratios with deviation scores, mean 100 and SD 15 (Section 2.5). Why measure everyday competence apart from IQ? Because one child scoring 65 dresses, shops and takes the bus alone, while another scoring 75 cannot look after herself. The American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD, formerly the AAMD) defines adaptive behaviour as the conceptual (language, money, number), social (relationships, rules, avoiding victimisation) and practical (self-care, safety, travel, work) skills that people learn and perform in everyday life. Since it is what a person habitually does, not what he can do at his best, it is usually rated by an informant , a parent, caregiver or teacher, which also suits infants and the severely disabled. A screening test is short, is given to many children and only flags those needing a closer look; a diagnostic test is longer and individual, and yields a level on which a diagnosis can rest. And because symptoms vary across contexts (the boy restless in a noisy classroom may be calm at home), clinicians use multi-informant assessment , combining parents, teachers, the child and clinic observation. Key study: Achenbach's cross-informant correlations (1987) Thomas M. Achenbach and colleagues pooled studies in which several people rated the same children. Similar informants, such as two parents, agreed moderately (mean correlation about 0.60); different kinds, such as parent and teacher, only weakly (about 0.28). Disagreement, they argued, reflects real differences between settings, so each informant adds valid information: the logic of Achenbach's parallel parent Child Behavior Checklist, Teacher's Report Form and Youth Self-Report. Criticism: it does not say whose report should decide. Exam trap Multi-informant assessment is recommended because symptoms may vary across contexts , not because parents over-report, teachers add nothing or clinic observation alone is insufficient. Infant and preschool developmental scales Arnold Gesell (1880 to 1961) of the Yale Clinic of Child Development filmed thousands of infants and turned the timing of their behaviour into norms (1925, 1940). His Gesell Developmental Schedules place observed behaviour at an age level in four fields: motor, adaptive (solving problems with objects, not adaptive behaviour in the Vineland sense), language and personal-social, each giving a DQ. Nancy Bayley (1899 to 1994) built the leading diagnostic infant test, the Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID, 1969). The BSID-II (1993) gave a Mental Development Index (MDI) and a Psychomotor Development Index (PDI). The Bayley-III (2006), renamed Infant and Toddler Development, and the Bayley-4 (2019) have five scales: cognitive, language and motor, tested with the child, and social-emotional and adaptive behaviour, reported by the caregiver. Its range since 1993, the first month to 42 months, is its signature. For screening, the Denver Developmental Screening Test of William K. Frankenburg and Josiah B. Dodds (1967; Denver II, 1990) covers birth to 6 years in four sectors: personal-social, fine motor-adaptive, language and gross motor. The result is normal, suspect or untestable, never a quotient. The McCarthy Scales of Children's Abilities ( Dorothea McCarthy , 1972; 2½ to 8½ years) yield a General Cognitive Index. Virginia Apgar 's newborn score (1953) and T. Berry Brazelton 's Neonatal Behavioral Assessment Scale (1973) are taught in Chapter 6. The Indian Developmental Screening Test (DST) of J. Bharath Raj (Mysore, 1977, 1983) places 88 milestones on Indian norms from birth to 15 years and gives a DQ. The Developmental Assessment Scales for Indian Infants (DASII) of Pramila Phatak and colleagues (Baroda) restandardised the Bayley on Indian infants from birth to 30 months, giving motor and mental DQs. The Trivandrum Developmental Screening Chart of M. K. C. Nair and colleagues (1991), built from the Baroda norms, screens children under 2 in minutes. Exam trap The scale for birth to 42 months across cognitive, language and motor domains is the Bayley , not the WPPSI (from 2½ years), the Stanford-Binet (from 2; both Section 2.6) or the McCarthy (from 2½). Do not confuse Bharath Raj's Indian DST with the American Denver, or the DASII (the Indian Bayley) with the TDSC (a Kerala screening chart). Social maturity: the Vineland Social Maturity Scale Intelligence tests missed something institution staff saw daily: residents of the same mental age differed hugely in self-care. Edgar Arnold Doll (1889 to 1968), director of research at the Vineland Training School in New Jersey, measured that difference with the Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS, 1935), the first standardised measure of social competence, or adaptive behaviour. Its 117 items run in the order in which they are usually achieved, grouped year by year through childhood and in wider bands up to "25 and above", so the scale spans birth to adulthood. They fall into eight categories: self-help general, self-help eating, self-help dressing, self-direction, occupation, communication, locomotion and socialisation. The scale is not given to the person: an informant who knows him well is interviewed, habitually performed items are credited under standardised scoring rules, and the total converts to a social age and an SQ. The Indian version, Malin's VSMS , is by Arthur J. Malin of Nagpur, who also adapted the WISC as MISIC (Section 2.6). It keeps the eight categories but has 89 items for birth to 15 years on Indian norms, and its SQ is used with IQ in Indian disability certification. Exam trap The VSMS was devised by Doll , not Malin (the Indian adaptation), Bharath Raj (the DST), C. M. Bhatia (a performance battery), Terman, Wechsler or Binet. It yields social age and social quotient , not mental age and IQ, developmental age and DQ, or emotional age and EQ. Its items run past 25 years, so "applicable from 0 to 25 years only" is false; age-graded items set out in age-level groups (the "separate forms for different age groups" of the options) and standardised scoring are genuine features. Malin VSMS: 89 items, SQ; Bharath Raj DST: 88 items, DQ; both 0 to 15 years. Adaptive behaviour scales and structured interviews Sara S. Sparrow , David A. Balla and Domenic V. Cicchetti rebuilt Doll's scale as the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (1984; Vineland-II, 2005; Vineland-3, 2016); the current edition covers birth to 90 years. They measure adaptive functioning in daily life in four domains, communication, daily living skills, socialisation and motor skills (for young children), plus an optional maladaptive behaviour domain; the first three form the Adaptive Behavior Composite (mean 100, SD 15). Given as a caregiver interview or parent and teacher forms, the Vineland supplies the adaptive half of an intellectual disability diagnosis. The older AAMD Adaptive Behavior Scale ( Kazuo Nihira and colleagues, 1969) rates adaptive skills in Part One and maladaptive behaviour in Part Two. The Vineland belongs to a family of clinician-administered instruments with the K-SADS (Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia; Joaquim Puig-Antich , 1978), a semi-structured psychiatric interview of parent and child, and the ADI-R and ADOS-2 for autism ( below ). Table 2.17 compares this section's scales. Exam trap The Vineland measures adaptive behaviour , not IQ or verbal IQ, personality, psychopathology, psychotic symptoms, neurological soft signs, memory deficits or suicidal ideation. The Vineland-3, K-SADS, ADI-R and ADOS-2 are interviews and observation schedules , not EEG paradigms, projective techniques or self-report cognitive tests. (A) Deficits in intellectual functions such as reasoning and learning, confirmed by clinical assessment and individual standardised testing: about 2 SD below the mean, an IQ of about 65 to 75 allowing for measurement error (Section 2.3).
