Severity (mild, moderate, severe, profound) is graded by adaptive functioning , not IQ, since that decides the support needed. Older systems used IQ bands (Table 2.18): ICD-10's mild 50 to 69, moderate 35 to 49, severe 20 to 34, profound below 20, and DSM-IV-TR's overlapping bands. ICD-11 (in force 2022) renamed the condition disorders of intellectual development , adding a provisional level. Old educational labels set expectations: mild was educable (academics to about sixth grade by the late teens), moderate trainable (about second grade), severe and profound custodial. So an IQ of about 50, at the mild-moderate border, legitimately predicts learning to about fifth grade, not lifelong institutional care, constant supervision or high-school graduation. And borderline intellectual functioning (IQ about 71 to 84) is not intellectual disability, and an FSIQ of 70 without adaptive deficits is no diagnosis. Disability certification in India The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (RPWD Act) recognises 21 disabilities, up from 7 under the 1995 Act, among them intellectual disability, specific learning disabilities, autism spectrum disorder and mental illness. Forty percent or more of a specified disability is a benchmark disability , which opens reservations and other benefits. Guidelines notified under the Act in 2018 set out how each disability is assessed. For intellectual disability, IQ comes from Indian or Indian-normed tests (Binet-Kamat, MISIC, WAPIS, Bhatia's battery, the Seguin Form Board, Raven's matrices: Section 2.6), the social quotient from the VSMS, and a DQ for children under 5, who are certified with global developmental delay. A medical board that includes a clinical psychologist certifies. The percentages widely quoted for each IQ band (Table 2.18) come from earlier guidelines; check them against the current notification. A specific learning disability (dyslexia, dysgraphia, dyscalculia; Chapter 8) is assessed and certified only from 8 years of age, since before then ordinary variation in learning to read, write and calculate cannot be told apart from a disorder. An intelligence test shows that general ability is not the problem, and the NIMHANS Index for Specific Learning Disabilities , with curriculum-based tests, measures the deficits. Disability from mental illness is rated with IDEAS, the Indian Disability Evaluation and Assessment Scale (Section 2.11). Exam trap The minimum age for assessing specific learning disability under the RPWD guidelines is 8 years , not 7, 10 or 14. Assessing autism: ISAA, CARS and the diagnostic pair Two rating scales dominate Indian autism assessment (the disorder is in Chapter 8). In the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) of Eric Schopler , Robert J. Reichler and Barbara Rochen Renner (North Carolina; 1980, manual 1988; CARS-2, 2010), the clinician observes the child, hears the parents and rates 15 areas, such as relating to people and imitation, from 1 (normal for age) to 4 (severely abnormal). Totals run from 15 to 60; 30 and above indicates autism. The Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (ISAA) was developed in 2009 by the National Institute for the Mentally Handicapped, Secunderabad, partly from CARS items. Its 40 items cover six domains (social relationship and reciprocity, emotional responsiveness, speech-language and communication, behaviour patterns, sensory aspects, cognitive component), each rated 1 (rarely) to 5 (always) from observation and parent interview. Totals run from 40 to 200: below 70 is not autism, and higher scores grade mild, moderate or severe autism with a disability percentage. ISAA is the instrument prescribed for certifying autism in India. Diagnosis pairs the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R; Michael Rutter , Ann Le Couteur and Catherine Lord , 2003), a 93-item parent interview, with the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2; Lord and colleagues, 2012), structured play and conversation in one of five modules. The M-CHAT-R/F ( Diana Robins and colleagues, 2009) screens toddlers of 16 to 30 months with 20 parent questions. Not autism tools: the Children's Global Assessment Scale (CGAS; David Shaffer , 1983), a single 1 to 100 rating of overall functioning, and the Child Behavior Checklist (Section 2.11). Exam trap IHBAS papers of 2020 and 2024 key CARS for severity and disability in autism, even for "the Indian tool" with ISAA offered. CARS is American; the Indian instrument prescribed for certifying autism disability is ISAA , which drew on CARS. Choose ISAA when offered. DAAS, PAAS, CGAS and the CBCL are distractors. The marks show what each has learnt, but not what each could still learn, how original each is, what each enjoys or how each feels about a career in engineering. Each of those questions has its own family of tests. Aptitude, achievement and intelligence An achievement test measures what a person has already learnt: the knowledge and understanding gained in a specific academic area, usually through instruction. An aptitude test looks forward, estimating how well a person will learn or succeed in a specific area in future, such as mechanical, musical or clerical work. An intelligence test samples general ability and gives one broad score (Section 2.6). Achievement looks back and aptitude looks ahead, so achievement tests rest mainly on content validity and aptitude tests on predictive validity (Section 2.4). Anne Anastasi (1908 to 2001) stressed that the difference is one of degree: all ability tests measure developed ability, and they lie on a continuum by how specific and how controlled the underlying learning is. Course-based achievement tests (a term of algebra) sit at one end; broad achievement tests, verbal aptitude and intelligence tests, and non-verbal tests follow; culture-fair tests, drawing on the least controlled everyday experience, sit at the other. A teacher-made test serves one class and has no norms; a standardised achievement test has tried-out items, fixed administration and norms. By purpose, a survey test gives an overall level of attainment, a diagnostic test pinpoints specific weaknesses (exactly which kinds of subtraction a child gets wrong), and a prognostic test forecasts success in a later course. Clinicians use individual batteries: the Wide Range Achievement Test ( Joseph Jastak , 1946; reading, spelling and arithmetic), the Peabody Individual Achievement Test ( Lloyd Dunn and Frederick Markwardt , 1970; many items answered by pointing), the Wechsler Individual Achievement Test (1992) and the Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Achievement ( Richard Woodcock and Mary Bonner Johnson , 1977). The last two are co-normed with ability tests to assess the ability-achievement discrepancy : achievement well below what measured intelligence predicts has traditionally signalled a specific learning disability (Section 2.7). Exam trap The primary purpose of an achievement test is to measure understanding and knowledge in specific academic areas. "Future success potential" is aptitude, "cognitive abilities related to brain function" is neuropsychological testing (Section 2.11), and "unconscious conflicts" belong to projective techniques (Section 2.10). Aptitude batteries and special aptitude tests One intelligence score told a careers counsellor little. After Louis Leon Thurstone (1887 to 1955) split intelligence into primary mental abilities (Section 1.9), the 1940s produced the multiple aptitude battery : separately normed subtests that give a profile instead of one number. The Differential Aptitude Tests (DAT) of George K. Bennett , Harold G. Seashore and Alexander G. Wesman (1947), built to guide secondary school students, has eight subtests: verbal reasoning, numerical ability, abstract reasoning, clerical speed and accuracy, mechanical reasoning, space relations, spelling and language usage. Verbal reasoning plus numerical ability indexes scholastic aptitude, and J. M. Ojha adapted the DAT for India. The General Aptitude Test Battery (GATB) of the United States Employment Service (1947) measures nine aptitudes, from general learning ability to finger and manual dexterity, to match people to occupations, and the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (1968) serves US military recruitment. A special aptitude test measures one narrow talent; an early classic is the Measures of Musical Talents of Carl Seashore (1866 to 1949), published in 1919 (Table 2.19). Tests in the guidance programme These batteries serve guidance, the organised help a school gives students in educational and vocational choices. A guidance programme's tools are the case study (an in-depth picture of one pupil from all sources), the interview (a face-to-face conversation to gather information and advise), the cumulative record (a running file of marks, test scores, health and activities kept over the years), observation, and tests of intelligence, aptitude, achievement and interest. Counselling then draws on them all. Exam trap Guidance textbooks call counselling "the heart of the guidance programme", so choose counselling whenever it is offered. RML 2022 offered only case study, interview, cumulative record and aptitude test, and keyed the aptitude test, which no standard text supports: an aptitude test only predicts trainability. With exactly those four options, choose the interview, counselling's chief instrument and itself called the heart of the counselling process (Section 7.10), and expect some keys to differ. Creativity and divergent thinking Intelligence tests reward convergent thinking , narrowing information down to one correct answer. In his presidential address to the American Psychological Association in 1950, Joy Paul Guilford (1897 to 1987) tied creativity to divergent thinking , producing many varied answers to an open problem, the operation he called divergent production in his Structure of Intellect model (Section 1.9). His Alternate Uses task asks for uses of an object such as a brick. If Kavya writes wall, house, doorstop, paperweight and red powder for rangoli, her fluency (number of ideas) is five; her flexibility (number of categories: building, weighting, pigment) is three; her originality is the statistical rarity of each idea (rangoli powder scores, a wall does not); and elaboration is the detail she adds. Ellis Paul Torrance (1915 to 2003) standardised such tasks in the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (1966), with verbal and figural (picture-completing) forms. Sarnoff Mednick (1962), in his associative theory, held that creative people reach remote associations easily. His Remote Associates Test (RAT) is a timed paper-and-pencil test of about 40 minutes in which the examinee finds one word linking three cue words: cottage, Swiss, cake gives "cheese". Michael Wallach and Nathan Kogan (1965), testing children in relaxed, game-like conditions, found creativity largely independent of intelligence. The Indian tests are the verbal and non-verbal Tests of Creative Thinking of Baqer Mehdi (1973) and the six Passi Tests of Creativity ( B. K. Passi , 1979). Exam trap "A timed, 40-minute paper-and-pencil test" is the RAT. Each item has one right answer, so its format is convergent, unlike the TTCT. The Alternate Uses task is Guilford's, not Torrance's. Interest inventories and value scales An interest inventory asks which activities, subjects and occupations a person likes. On the empirical route an item joins an occupational scale if people in that occupation answer it differently from people in general, whatever its content; on the homogeneous route items are grouped by content into interest areas. Edward Kellogg Strong Jr. (1884 to 1963) took the empirical route in the Strong Vocational Interest Blank (1927), revised by David Campbell as the Strong-Campbell Interest Inventory (1974) and now the Strong Interest Inventory. G. Frederic Kuder (1903 to 2000) took the homogeneous route in the Kuder Preference Record (1939): the person marks the most and least liked activity in each forced-choice triad, and the answers score ten areas (outdoor, mechanical, computational, scientific, persuasive, artistic, literary, musical, social service, clerical). As each choice raises one area by lowering another, the scores are ipsative : they show relative strengths within the person, not standing against others (Section 2.5). The later Kuder Occupational Interest Survey compares people with occupational groups. John L. Holland (1919 to 2008), in a theory first published in 1959 and set out fully in 1973, sorted people and work environments into six RIASEC types (Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional) arranged on a hexagon: adjacent types are alike, opposite ones (Realistic and Social) least alike. His self-scored Self-Directed Search (1971) gives a three-letter code matched to occupations. For values, the Study of Values of Gordon Allport (1897 to 1967) and Philip Vernon (1931; with Gardner Lindzey from 1951; revised 1960) measures six values from the types of Eduard Spranger (1882 to 1963): theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political and religious. Milton Rokeach (1973) had people rank 18 terminal values (end states such as freedom) and 18 instrumental values (conduct such as honesty). Thurstone and Likert scales An attitude is an evaluative disposition towards an object such as a group or an idea (its components and theories are in Chapter 3). An attitude scale infers it from responses to statements, combined into one score from unfavourable to favourable. The classic scales differ in how the statements are chosen and how the score is formed. Thurstone and Ernest J. Chave (1929), measuring attitude towards the church, devised the method of equal-appearing intervals . Judges sorted over a hundred statements into 11 piles from most unfavourable to most favourable, without giving their own opinion. A statement's scale value is the median pile; its ambiguity is Q, the interquartile range of the placements, and high-Q statements are dropped. About 20 statements with evenly spread values form the scale. The respondent ticks those they agree with and scores the median (or mean) of their values: agreeing with statements valued 7.2, 8.1 and 8.4 gives 8.1, a favourable attitude. This is laborious. Rensis Likert (1903 to 1981) offered a short cut in 1932, the method of summated ratings . A Likert scale is a set of closed-ended statements, each with a fixed number of ordered alternatives, classically five from strongly agree to strongly disagree, scored 5 to 1 (reversed for unfavourable statements). Respondents rate their own agreement on this symmetric continuum, and item scores are summed with equal weights. No judges are used: items are kept by item analysis if high and low total scorers answer them differently (Section 2.2). Easier to build and usually as reliable, Likert scales dominate questionnaires; strictly ordinal, their scores are usually treated as interval. Figure 2.12 contrasts the two methods. Thurstone: equal-appearing intervals Likert: summated ratings 1. Write 100+ opinion statements 2. Judges sort each into 11 piles 3. Scale value = median; high Q dropped 4. Keep about 20 evenly spaced items 5. Score = median value of items agreed 1. Write many opinion statements 2. Respondents rate each item 1 to 5 3. Item analysis keeps good items 4. Score = sum of ratings, equal weights Figure 2.12 The step shaded alike is the key difference: Thurstone's judges pre-scale the statements, whereas Likert's respondents rate their own agreement and the ratings are summed. Exam trap A summated rating scale is a Likert scale, never a Thurstone, Guttman or equal-appearing interval scale. Likert items are closed-ended with a fixed number of ordered alternatives, neither open-ended nor dichotomous. Judges pre-scaling statements is Thurstone; respondents rating their agreement, summed with equal weights, is Likert; a sentence-completion stimulus belongs to projective techniques (Section 2.10). Likert is a type of attitude scale, whereas nominal, ordinal and interval are levels of measurement (Chapter 9). Guttman, Bogardus and the semantic differential Louis Guttman (1916 to 1987) built a one-dimensional cumulative scale by scalogram analysis (1944). Statements are ordered so that endorsing a stronger one implies endorsing every weaker one ("I would accept a de-addiction centre in my city", "in my locality", "on my street"), so the total score reveals the exact pattern of answers. Fit is judged by the coefficient of reproducibility , which should be 0.90 or more. The social distance scale of Emory Bogardus (1882 to 1973), published in 1925, is generally regarded as the oldest attitude scale. For each group the respondent marks the closest relation they would accept, on seven steps: close kinship by marriage, club chums, neighbours, co-workers, fellow citizens, visitors only, and exclusion from the country. In the semantic differential of Charles Osgood , George Suci and Percy Tannenbaum (1957), a concept such as "the police" is rated on seven-point bipolar adjective pairs (good to bad, strong to weak, fast to slow), which factor into evaluation, potency and activity; evaluation is the attitude proper. In paired comparisons each object is paired with every other and one of each pair is chosen; Thurstone's law of comparative judgement (1927) converts the choices into scale values, and rank ordering is a quicker variant. Allen Edwards and Franklin Kilpatrick (1948) combined Thurstone judging, Likert item analysis and Guttman scaling in the scale-discrimination technique . Table 2.20 compares the main scales. Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962) put the psychiatrist's screening questions on paper, and the personality inventory was born. Ever since, psychologists have argued over how to choose the questions and how far to trust the answers. Objective tests and Cattell's three kinds of data An objective personality test fixes the items, the answer format (true or false, yes or no, a rating) and the scoring key, so any two scorers get the same result. Rating scales and personality inventories (long self-report questionnaires scored on several scales) are objective; projective tests (Section 2.10) use ambiguous stimuli, free responses and interpretive scoring. Raymond Bernard Cattell (1905 to 1998), whose trait theory is taught in Chapter 4, accepted a trait only if it appeared in three kinds of data: L-data (life record data): actual behaviour in everyday life, from school performance, work and criminal records, and ratings by observers who know the person. Q-data (questionnaire data): self-report ratings of one's own characteristics, attributes and interests. T-data (objective test data): behaviour in a controlled test situation whose purpose the person cannot see, and so cannot easily fake, such as a laboratory task scored for a trait he does not know is being measured. Exam trap Cattell's scheme has exactly three letters, L, Q and T : there is no P-data (projective) or Z-data. School and criminal records are L-data; self-report questionnaires are Q-data; projective-test performance and Q-sort responses are not L-data. Q-data is not the Q-sort ( 2.9.7 ). Four ways to build an inventory The logical-content or rational strategy reasons out how people with a trait (anxiety, say) describe themselves and writes items whose content plainly reflects it, trusting face validity. Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet (built in 1917, published in 1919 and often dated 1920), the first personality inventory, asked 116 yes-no questions about symptoms and gave one score of emotional instability; Hugh M. Bell 's Adjustment Inventory (1934) scored home, health, social and emotional adjustment. Its weakness: respondents see what each item is after, and the method assumes insight and honesty. The theoretical strategy writes items for the constructs of a personality theory: the Edwards Personal Preference Schedule (Henry Murray's needs), the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (Carl Jung's types) and the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory (Theodore Millon's theory). Empirical criterion-group keying ignores content. A large item pool goes to a criterion group (say, patients diagnosed with depression) and a normal control group; only the items the two groups answer differently survive, whatever they say, and the scale is cross-validated on fresh groups. If depressed patients happened to answer "true" to "I like mechanics magazines" more often than controls, that item would join the depression scale. The MMPI, the California Psychological Inventory and the Strong Vocational Interest Blank (Section 2.8) were built this way. The factor-analytic strategy factor-analyses the correlations among many items, keeps the items that load on each factor and names the factor afterwards: the 16PF, the Eysenck inventories, the NEO-PI-R, the Guilford-Zimmerman Temperament Survey ( J. P. Guilford and Wayne Zimmerman, 1949; 300 items, ten traits such as sociability and restraint) and the Comrey Personality Scales ( Andrew L. Comrey , 1970; 180 items, eight factors such as trust and orderliness). Modern inventories, such as the NEO-PI-R and the MCMI, use combined strategies . Against response sets (Section 2.2) and deliberate faking, test makers use rapport and confidentiality, forced-choice items pairing statements of equal social desirability, disguised items, and validity scales and correction keys. Exam trap The MMPI was derived by finding items that discriminate between criterion and control groups, not by the rational method or by assuming traits and writing questions for them. Comrey's 180-item test is factor-analytic . "Correlational" and "experimental" are research designs (Chapter 9), and criterion-referencing is a way of interpreting scores (Section 2.5), not of choosing items. The MMPI and its validity scales Around 1940, at the University of Minnesota Hospitals, the psychologist Starke R. Hathaway (1903 to 1984) and the neuropsychiatrist J. Charnley McKinley (1891 to 1950) set out to aid psychiatric diagnosis. They gave over a thousand statements to patient groups with known diagnoses and to about 700 "Minnesota normals", mostly hospital visitors, and kept for each scale only the items that separated that patient group from the normals. The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI, 1943) had 550 different statements (566 printed, 16 repeated), answered true, false or cannot say. It is "multiphasic" because its items cover physical health, mood, family, sexual, religious and social attitudes, fears and unusual experiences. The MMPI is therefore an objective personality inventory of personality and psychopathology , used mainly for psychiatric diagnosis. It is not a projective test, intelligence test, aptitude battery, interest inventory or neuropsychological screening battery, nor a tool for educational, career or physical-health assessment, and it does not measure unconscious drives (projective tests), the Big Five (the NEO) or leadership potential (the CPI). Because self-reports can mislead, it carries validity scales: Cannot Say (?) : items left blank or marked both ways; 30 or more make the record doubtful. L (Lie) scale : small faults nearly everyone admits, of the kind "I get angry sometimes". Answering "false" to them asserts a degree of personal virtue rarely seen in our culture, so a high L marks a naive attempt to look good by denying common minor faults. F (Infrequency) scale : items fewer than one normal person in ten endorses. A high F flags random or careless responding, over-reporting of symptoms (faking bad) or severe psychopathology; on the MMPI-2 an F above T 100 suggests random responding or gross exaggeration. K (Correction) scale : added by Paul E. Meehl (1920 to 2003) and Hathaway in 1946 to catch subtle defensiveness. A fraction of K is added to clinical scales 1, 4, 7, 8 and 9 (the K-correction ) to compensate for defensive responding. The MMPI-2 added VRIN (Variable Response Inconsistency: contradictory answers to similar item pairs, a sign of random responding), TRIN (True Response Inconsistency: answering "true", or "false", regardless of content), F(B) (Back F, for later items), F(p) (Infrequency-Psychopathology, items rare even among psychiatric inpatients, which separates faking bad from real disorder) and S (Superlative Self-Presentation). Exam trap The three classic validity scales are L, F and K (four if Cannot Say is counted, as some texts do); VRIN, TRIN and S came later. L is naive faking good, K is subtle defensiveness plus a correction, and F is rare responding (random answers, faking bad or severe pathology). A very high F never means faking good, defensiveness or an excellent profile. Clinical scales, profiles and the MMPI family The MMPI has ten clinical scales (Table 2.21): not 4, 13 or 16 (the 13 "basic scales" are the ten plus L, F and K). Eight were keyed against psychiatric diagnostic groups; scales 5 and 0 were not. Scales 1, 2 and 3 form the neurotic triad ; 6, 7, 8 and 9 the psychotic tetrad . The MMPI-2 ( James N. Butcher and colleagues, 1989) has 567 items, rewrote outdated ones, was normed on 2,600 US adults and added content and supplementary scales (such as health concerns and the MacAndrew alcoholism scale). The old clinical scales intercorrelate because all share a general distress factor, demoralisation . Auke Tellegen and colleagues (2003) extracted it first as RCd and rebuilt the Restructured Clinical (RC) scales (such as RC2 low positive emotions and RC4 antisocial behaviour) so that each measures a distinctive dimension. RC scales are the core of the MMPI-2-RF ( Yossef S. Ben-Porath and Tellegen, 2008; 338 items) and the MMPI-3 (2020; 335 items). The MMPI-A (1992; 478 items) serves adolescents aged 14 to 18. Indian context H. N. Murthy 's Multiphasic Questionnaire (MPQ; 1964) is a short (100-item) Indian adult inventory built from MMPI-type items, with a Lie scale and seven clinical scales such as hysteria, depression, anxiety, paranoia and schizophrenia. An elevated MPQ Lie scale indicates all of these: a tendency to fake and manipulate, social desirability, and mistrust (a guarded person who admits no flaw to the examiner). Factor-analytic inventories: 16PF, Eysenck and NEO Cattell turned his source traits into the Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF), first published in 1949; the fifth edition (1993) has 185 three-choice items for ages 16 and over. It scores 16 primary factors found by factor analysis and labelled by letter (A warmth, B reasoning, C emotional stability, E dominance, and so on to Q4 tension), plus five global, second-order factors (extraversion, anxiety, tough-mindedness, independence, self-control) that approximate the Big Five. Scores are stens (standard tens: 1 to 10, mean 5.5, SD 2). Factor B is a brief reasoning scale, but the 16PF measures personality traits, not fluid, crystallised or general intelligence (Section 2.6). Exam trap The 16PF is Raymond B. Cattell's : Kelly is to the Rep test as Cattell is to the 16PF. Hans Eysenck built the EPQ, Costa and McCrae the NEO-PI-R, Henry Murray the TAT, Gordon Allport the Study of Values, William Sheldon a body-type scheme, and Freud no inventory. Hans Jurgen Eysenck (1916 to 1997), at the Maudsley Hospital, London, built three inventories. The Maudsley Personality Inventory (1959; 48 items) scored extraversion (E) and neuroticism (N); the Eysenck Personality Inventory (1964, with Sybil B. G. Eysenck ; 57 items) added a Lie scale; and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ, 1975; 90 items) added psychoticism (P), giving PEN plus L. The EPQ-R followed in 1985. Paul T. Costa Jr. and Robert R. McCrae built the NEO Personality Inventory on the Five-Factor Model (Chapter 4). The NEO-PI-R (1992) has 240 items on a five-point agree-disagree scale and scores five domains, Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism (OCEAN), each with six facets (30 in all), as T scores. The 60-item NEO-FFI scores domains only; the NEO-PI-3 (2005) simplified the wording. The NEO is not based on Cattell's 16 factors, Eysenck's PEN, Murray's needs or MBTI types (personality-disorder scales belong to the MCMI), and OCEAN is neither the four humours (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic; Chapter 4) nor achievement, affiliation and power motives (Chapter 1). Shorter Big Five measures include the 44-item Big Five Inventory (Oliver John and colleagues, 1991); the HEXACO inventory of Kibeom Lee and Michael Ashton adds a sixth factor, Honesty-Humility. Theory-based, clinical and Indian inventories The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) of Katharine Cook Briggs (1875 to 1968) and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers (1897 to 1980), first issued in 1943, is directly based on Carl Gustav Jung 's theory of psychological types. Forced-choice items place people on four dichotomies, extraversion-introversion, sensing-intuition, thinking-feeling and judging-perceiving, giving 16 types such as INTP. It is popular in counselling and team building but psychometrically weak: continuous scores that bunch near the middle are forced into types, and many people get a different type on retest weeks later. The Edwards Personal Preference Schedule (EPPS) of Allen L. Edwards (1953, manual 1954; revised 1959) measures 15 needs from Henry A. Murray 's list, such as achievement, order, affiliation, dominance and aggression. To control social desirability, every item is a forced choice between two statements matched for desirability (225 pairs: 210 different and 15 repeated for a consistency score). The scores are therefore ipsative : each need is strong only relative to the person's other needs, so people cannot be compared directly. The California Psychological Inventory (CPI) of Harrison G. Gough (1921 to 2010), published in 1956 (manual 1957), is the normal person's MMPI: largely criterion-keyed, with many MMPI items, but scoring folk concepts , everyday trait ideas found in all cultures, such as dominance, sociability, responsibility and self-control. It began with 480 items (now 434) and predicts achievement, leadership and delinquency. The Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory (MCMI) of Theodore Millon (1928 to 2014), first published in 1977, follows Millon's theory and the DSM, measuring personality disorders and clinical syndromes in patients (175 items; 195 in the MCMI-IV of 2015). It reports base rate scores , anchored to how common each disorder is in clinical samples rather than to normal T scores. The State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) of Charles D. Spielberger (1927 to 2013) and colleagues (1970; Form Y 1983) has 40 items: 20 ask how you feel right now (state anxiety, passing) and 20 how you generally feel (trait anxiety, a stable proneness). Its purpose is to differentiate state from trait anxiety. Measuring psychoticism, extraversion and neuroticism is the EPQ's job; "normal and abnormal personality" fits broad inventories such as the MMPI and CPI; checking response validity is the job of validity scales. The older Taylor Manifest Anxiety Scale of Janet A. Taylor (1953) used 50 MMPI items judged to express overt anxiety. Indian context Common Indian tools include Sinha's Comprehensive Anxiety Test (A. K. P. Sinha and L. N. K. Sinha), Hindi adaptations of Bell's Adjustment Inventory (Saxena, 1959; Mohsin and Hussain, 1981), the PGI Health Questionnaire N-1 (N. N. Wig and S. K. Verma, PGIMER Chandigarh), a neuroticism screen derived from the Cornell Medical Index, and Hindi versions of the MPI and EPQ. Idiographic and situational methods Some methods study how one person construes the world. In the Role Construct Repertory Test (Rep test, 1955) of George A. Kelly (1905 to 1967), the person names people who fill roles in his life (mother, a liked teacher, someone disliked). Shown three at a time, he says how two are alike and differ from the third; each answer ("generous versus selfish") is a bipolar personal construct , and a repertory grid of figures by constructs maps his construct system (theory in Chapter 4). In the Q-sort , set out by William Stephenson (1902 to 1989) in 1953, a person sorts statements, such as self-descriptions, into piles from least to most characteristic, with a fixed number per pile forming a forced, quasi-normal distribution (Figure 2.14). Since every sort has the same mean and spread, it shows which statements are more characteristic of this person : within-person, not between-person, variation. Carl Rogers (1902 to 1987) had clients sort for the real self and the ideal self; Butler and Haigh (1954) found the mean real-ideal correlation rose from about zero before client-centred therapy to about .3 after it (.34 at the end, .31 at follow-up). Jack Block (1924 to 2010) built the 100-item California Q-set for observers. The Q-sort complements inventories; it never replaced the MMPI. On an adjective checklist , such as Gough's Adjective Check List of 300 adjectives, the person ticks every word that applies. Situational tests watch behaviour in staged real-life tasks. In the Character Education Inquiry, Hugh Hartshorne and Mark A. May (1928) gave schoolchildren natural-seeming chances to cheat, lie and steal; honesty in one situation predicted honesty in another only weakly. The US Office of Strategic Services (OSS) selected World War II agents through stressful staged tasks; in the leaderless group discussion candidates tackle a problem with no appointed leader while assessors rate who leads, as India's Services Selection Board still does. Judging inventories Inventories offer objective scoring, large norms, good reliability and economy (one psychologist can test a hundred people at once). Their weaknesses are those of self-report: response sets and faking, limited self-insight, the reading level they demand, and cultural bias when items and norms from one country (rural Minnesota in 1940) travel to another. Walter Mischel (1968) added that trait scores predict behaviour in any one situation only weakly, a debate for Chapter 4. Table 2.22 compares the main inventories. One person sees two dancers, another a crushed bat, a third "blood, because it is red". The blot is the same, so the differences must come from the viewers. That idea produced clinical psychology's most famous and most disputed tests. This section explains it, sorts the tests into five families, works through the Rorschach and the Thematic Apperception Test, then the smaller techniques and the evidence on their worth. The projective hypothesis The objective inventories of Section 2.9 ask clear questions and score fixed answers. A projective technique reverses that logic. It presents an ambiguous, unstructured stimulus (an inkblot, a vague picture, half a sentence, a blank page), gives minimal instructions and accepts any answer. Because the stimulus supplies so little structure, whatever structure appears in the response is assumed to come from the person. This is the projective hypothesis : faced with an ambiguous stimulus, a person projects needs, conflicts, unconscious processes and a characteristic perceptual style into the response, usually without knowing it. The word comes from Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939), for whom projection was a defence that attributes one's own unacceptable impulse to someone else (Section 4.3). Testing borrowed a broader sense: everyone reads their inner world into an unclear outer one. Lawrence K. Frank coined the term projective methods in 1939, likening them to an X-ray that shows inner structure without opening the body. Projective tests share four features: an ambiguous stimulus ; an open response , with almost unlimited possible answers; a disguised purpose , so the person cannot tell how answers will be read; and global interpretation of the whole personality rather than one trait. They therefore claim to reveal unconscious processes , not intellectual attainment, parenting style or career aptitude. Their main advantage follows from the disguise: a person who cannot tell what a "good" answer is cannot easily fake one, so the tests avoid the self-report biases of inventories (social desirability, faking, defensiveness). Exam trap The advantage is avoiding self-report bias . "They let people use the defence of projection" twists the theory; superior retest reliability and numerical data are strengths of objective inventories. Beside the EPQ, 16PF, MMPI-2, NEO-PI-R, MBTI or MCMI-III, only the Rorschach and TAT are projective: the rest are objective self-report inventories (Section 2.9). Intelligence tests and direct observation are not projective either. Lindzey's five families Gardner Lindzey (1959) sorted the many techniques by the kind of response they demand (Figure 2.15). In association techniques the person reports the first word, image or percept the stimulus calls up. In construction techniques the person builds a product, usually a story with a past, present and future. In completion techniques the person finishes an incomplete stimulus. In choice or ordering techniques the person picks or ranks items by preference, a step towards objective testing. In expression techniques the person produces something freely (a drawing, a painting, play), and the manner of production counts as much as the product. Anchor one test per family: Rorschach, TAT, sentence completion, Szondi, Draw-A-Person. Frank (1939) had grouped methods by what the person does with the material: constitutive (structuring formless material, as in finger painting), constructive (building a directed product), interpretive (giving material personal meaning, as in the TAT), cathartic (releasing emotion, as in play) and refractive (personality refracted through a conventional medium, as in handwriting). The categories overlapped, and Lindzey's replaced them. Exam trap The TAT is construction , the Rorschach association , sentence completion completion and Draw-A-Person expression. RML 2021 keyed the word association test as "not a projective test". That key is wrong: Lindzey lists word association as an association technique, and Galton's word association (1879) is usually called the first projective technique. By the standard classification all four options (word association, Rorschach, TAT, sentence completion) are projective, so no option is correct. Learn word association as projective; if the identical item returns, the paper's key was word association. The Rorschach: ten cards and how they are given Hermann Rorschach (1884 to 1922), a Swiss psychiatrist, published the test in Psychodiagnostik (1921). From many blots he kept the ten that best separated psychiatric groups, then died the next year, aged 37. The Rorschach Inkblot Test has ten bilaterally symmetrical cards (not 12, 15 or 20), always shown in the same order. Five are achromatic, black and grey (I, IV, V, VI, VII); two are black and red (II, III); three are multicoloured (VIII, IX, X), as Figure 2.16 shows. Hence the textbook phrase "five black-and-white and five coloured". Fixed order of presentation, Card I to Card X I II III IV V VI VII VIII IX X Achromatic: I, IV, V, VI, VII (5) Black and red: II, III (2) Multicoloured: VIII, IX, X (3) Chromatic in all: 2 + 3 = 5 Figure 2.16 The ten Rorschach cards. Five are achromatic; the other five carry colour, two only as red patches on black and three as full pastel colour. Administration has three phases. In the response phase (free association, or performance proper) the examiner asks "What might this be?", records every response verbatim with its reaction time, and does not prompt. In the inquiry phase , after all ten cards, the examiner goes back through each response to clarify where on the blot it was seen (location) and what made it look that way (determinants), using non-leading questions ("What made it look like that?"). Optional testing the limits follows: the examiner asks directly, for example, whether the person can see a common percept they missed. A longer reaction time, rejection or confusion on the coloured cards than on the achromatic ones is colour shock , read as a sign of emotional disturbance. The Rorschach assesses personality, cognition and perception: how a person organises an ambiguous field, how they think, and whether thinking is disordered. Rorschach built it as a diagnostic aid, so it is used to detect thought disorder, help identify mental illness and infer unconscious intentions. It does not interpret dreams, record conscious desires, measure IQ, memory or brain size, or diagnose physical illness. Exam trap The inquiry clarifies each response without leading questions ; cards are never shuffled, responses are recorded from the first card, and inquiry is not "scoring only". Ten cards, Hermann Rorschach, 1921: not 20 by Henry Murray, 15 by John Exner or 5 by Carl Jung, and no blank card (that is TAT card 16). Five chromatic and five achromatic, not three and seven. RML 2025 keyed "five black and white and five multi-colored cards": the five-five split is right but the wording is loose, since the achromatic cards are black and grey and only VIII, IX and X are fully multicoloured (II and III are black and red). It is still the only correct option; "only black and white", "only coloured" and "ten multicoloured" are wrong. Scoring and reading a Rorschach record Each response is coded first for its location , the part of the blot used: W the whole blot, D a common detail, Dd an unusual detail, and S white space (always coded with another location, as WS or DS). In Exner's system many W responses, especially well-organised ones, reflect organisational and integrative effort , the drive to pull a complex field into one meaningful whole. Developmental quality grades that integration: synthesised (+), ordinary (o) or vague (v). The determinants record what feature of the blot shaped the percept (Table 2.23); the colour determinants index emotional reactivity and impulse control. It is the main index of reality testing : many minus responses mean perception driven by inner preoccupation rather than by the stimulus, as in psychosis. Content codes what was seen: H (whole human), Hd (human detail), A (animal), An (anatomy), Bl (blood) and others. A popular response (P) is one given very often, such as a bat or butterfly on Card V, and shows conventional perception; an original response is rare, a sign of creativity when well formed and of bizarre thinking when not. Two further signs matter. An absence of human responses suggests poor interpersonal orientation , little interest in or understanding of people (not apathy or lack of empathy as such). A confabulatory response (DW) generalises from one detail to the whole blot ("a crab, because of these claws, so the whole thing is a crab"), and indicates impaired reality testing , not a regressed ego, cognitive immaturity or lack of empathy. Exam trap Shape alone is F ; "blood because it is red", with no form, is pure C . FC and CF mix form and colour; Cn only names the colour. M is human movement only (FM animal, m inanimate); C' is achromatic. Scoring systems: Exner, R-PAS and Holtzman Rorschach left no full scoring system, and five American ones grew up in parallel: those of Samuel Beck , Bruno Klopfer , Marguerite Hertz , Zygmunt Piotrowski , and David Rapaport with Roy Schafer . Their codes differed, so research could not be compared. John E. Exner (1928 to 2006) combined their best-supported elements in his Comprehensive System (1974). It standardised administration, required at least 14 responses for a valid record, and tallied the codes into a Structural Summary of ratios and indices compared with norms. Lambda compares pure F responses with all others; a high Lambda suggests a simplifying, avoidant style. Experience Balance (EB) weighs human movement against colour: an introversive person (more M) works things out internally, an extratensive person (more colour) through feeling and action. Constellations flag specific risks: PTI (Perceptual-Thinking Index, formerly the Schizophrenia Index, SCZI), DEPI (depression), S-CON (suicide), CDI (coping deficit) and HVI (hypervigilance). The system gives no IQ score . After Exner's death, Gregory Meyer and colleagues published the Rorschach Performance Assessment System (R-PAS, 2011). It keeps only research-supported variables, asks for two or three responses per card ("prompt and pull") so records are comparable in length, and reports standard scores against international norms. Wayne Holtzman had earlier solved the length problem differently: the Holtzman Inkblot Technique (1961) has two parallel forms of 45 cards each and allows one response per card, so every record is the same length and alternate-form reliability can be computed. Exam trap There is no "Murray system" of Rorschach scoring: Henry Murray gave us the TAT. The Comprehensive System is Exner's (not Beck's, Klopfer's or Piotrowski's) and scores the Rorschach, not the MMPI, TAT or Wechsler scales. The Thematic Apperception Test The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) was introduced in 1935 by Christiana Morgan (1897 to 1967) and Henry Alexander Murray (1893 to 1988) at the Harvard Psychological Clinic; Murray's manual followed in 1943. To apperceive is to perceive in the light of past experience. The theory is Murray's need-press theory of psychogenic needs ( Explorations in Personality , 1938; Section 4.6), not personal constructs (George Kelly), operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner) or cognitive distortions (Aaron Beck). For each picture of people in an ambiguous social scene, the person tells a dramatic story: what led up to it, what is happening, what the characters think and feel, and how it ends. The full set has 31 cards : 30 pictures plus blank card 16 , on which the person imagines a scene. Classically 20 cards were given over two sessions; in practice a clinician selects about 5 to 12 per session. The interpreter assumes the storyteller identifies with the hero and lends the hero their own needs , such as need for achievement (n Ach), affiliation (n Aff) and aggression (n Agg). The press is the force of the environment on the hero: alpha press as it really is, beta press as the person perceives it. A recurring need-press combination is a thema , and the outcome (success, failure, rescue) shows the person's expectations. Leopold Bellak later systematised this scoring, and David McClelland scored stories for the achievement motive (1953). The TAT therefore reveals unconscious thoughts, conflicts and motives, and a client's characteristic ways of thinking, feeling and behaving in close relationships; when stories about ambiguous pictures are wanted, it is the test of choice. It is a projective personality test, not an intelligence, achievement or neuropsychological test, and it does not measure vocabulary or memory. Unlike the Rorschach, the TAT uses ambiguous social scenes with characters, not symmetrical inkblots, and asks for stories, not percepts; it shows the content of motives and relationships more than the structure of thought. Its descendants adapt the pictures to the teller. The Children's Apperception Test (CAT; Leopold and Sonya Sorel Bellak , 1949) has 10 cards of animals in human situations for children of 3 to 10, who identify readily with animals; the CAT-H (1965) uses human figures and the CAT-S is a supplement. The Bellaks' Senior Apperception Technique (1973) serves older adults, and the Roberts Apperception Test for Children (1982) adds normed scoring. Gerald Blum 's Blacky Pictures (1950) show a dog family in scenes built around Freud's psychosexual stages, and Edwin Shneidman 's Make-A-Picture-Story test (MAPS, 1947) lets the person place cut-out figures on backgrounds before telling the story. Exam trap TAT: Murray and Morgan, 1930s , a construction technique. Not Freud, Jung, Skinner, Rorschach, Exner or Bellak (Bellak made the CAT). The CAT differs mainly in its animal figures designed for children ; it is not objective, not an intelligence test and uses no inkblots. Indian context Uma Chowdhury adapted the TAT (1960) and the CAT for India, with Indian figures, dress and settings. Udai Pareek adapted the Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study (below); do not swap them. Completion and verbal techniques The oldest projective method is the word association test . Francis Galton tried it on himself in 1879. Carl Gustav Jung made it clinical (1910) with 100 stimulus words, timing each reply and watching for complex indicators (a delayed reaction, no reply, repeating the stimulus word, an odd answer) that betray an emotionally charged complex (Section 4.4). Grace Kent and Aaron Rosanoff published a 100-word list in 1910 with frequency norms from 1,000 normal adults, so a reply could be scored as common or idiosyncratic. The sentence completion method grew from Hermann Ebbinghaus 's completion method: the person finishes stems such as "My father..." or "I regret...". The Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank ( Julian Rotter and Janet Rafferty , 1950) has 40 stems, each rated for conflict or positive adjustment and summed into one adjustment score. The Sacks Sentence Completion Test ( Joseph Sacks and Sidney Levy , 1950) has 60 items covering 15 attitude areas in four groups: family, sex, interpersonal relationships and self-concept. The Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study ( Saul Rosenzweig , 1945; some Indian texts give later dates) shows 24 cartoon-style frames of everyday frustrations; the respondent writes what the frustrated character says in an empty speech balloon. Replies are scored for direction of aggression : extrapunitive (blame turned outward), intropunitive (blame turned on oneself) or impunitive (blame avoided, the frustration glossed over); and for type of reaction : obstacle-dominance (the obstacle stands out), ego-defence (protecting the self) or need-persistence (seeking a solution). The Group Conformity Rating shows how often the person gives the commonest reply. Expressive and choice techniques In Karen Machover 's Draw-A-Person test (1949) the person draws a person, then one of the other sex. Her body-image hypothesis holds that the drawing reflects the drawer's self-concept and unconscious attitudes, so size, placement, erasures and omitted parts are read as signs; it is not a test of fine motor skill alone, academic achievement or brain lesions. Contrast Florence Goodenough 's Draw-a-Man, which counts details as an index of intellectual maturity (Section 2.6). John Buck 's House-Tree-Person test (1948) asks for a house (home and family), a tree (deeper feelings about the self) and a person (self-concept and relationships), first in pencil (achromatic phase), then in crayon (chromatic phase), each followed by questioning. In the Kinetic Family Drawing ( Robert Burns and S. Harvard Kaufman , 1970) the child draws everyone in the family doing something, revealing perceived closeness and conflict. Elizabeth Koppitz listed emotional indicators in children's figure drawings, such as a tiny figure or gross asymmetry. Max Hutt read the copying of the Bender designs projectively (Section 2.11). The Szondi Test ( Leopold Szondi , 1947) is the classic choice technique: from 48 photographs of psychiatric patients, in six sets of eight, the person picks the faces they like and dislike most; its genetic theory is unsupported. Margaret Lowenfeld 's World Technique (a world built in a sand tray) and Mosaic Test (patterns from coloured pieces), the Hand Test ( Edward Wagner , 1962: "What might this hand be doing?", read for acting-out tendencies), play, finger painting and graphology (handwriting analysis, with little validity) complete the expressive family. Exam trap House-Tree-Person is John Buck 's, not Aaron T. Beck's (cognitive therapy), David D. Burns's (author of Feeling Good ) or Karen Machover's (Draw-A-Person). Kinetic Family Drawing is Robert Burns's, a different Burns. How good are projective tests? The case against them is psychometric. Many techniques have competing scoring systems, so two clinicians may not be giving the same test. Inter-scorer reliability is acceptable only with structured systems such as Exner's or Rotter's; retest reliability is weak, because stories and percepts change between occasions. Global, intuitive interpretation has poor validity, and even scored variables show doubtful incremental validity : they add little to an interview and an inventory. Defenders reply that some Rorschach indices, notably of thought disorder and perceptual accuracy, hold up, and that the tests generate rich clinical hypotheses; they remain in clinical training and practice in India. They paired figure drawings with symptom statements at random and showed them to students, who "discovered" the links clinicians reported, such as odd eyes with suspiciousness, though the real correlation was zero. In 1969 the same happened with invalid Rorschach signs, while valid signs went unnoticed. This illusory correlation comes from expectation, not data. Is it depression, early dementia or a small stroke, and which abilities are gone? Neuropsychological tests profile what the brain can still do; clinical rating scales measure how severe symptoms are and whether treatment helps. What neuropsychological assessment measures Neuropsychological assessment infers how the brain is working from behaviour: each standardised task samples one function, and a characteristic pattern of failures points to the damaged system. Its domains are orientation and consciousness, attention and concentration, processing speed, memory, language, visuospatial and constructional skill, executive functions (planning, shifting, inhibiting and monitoring goal-directed behaviour) and motor and sensory function; mood is checked too, because it colours every score. Opinions, attitudes and reactions are not neuropsychological domains. The purposes are diagnosis, localisation, a baseline for measuring change, rehabilitation planning and judgments of capacity. Localisation itself is in Section 5.11. A fixed battery gives every patient the same tests scored against norms (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska); a flexible battery adds tests to a core to fit the referral question. The process approach of Edith Kaplan (1924 to 2009) in Boston holds that how a patient fails matters as much as the score (a piecemeal copy and an incomplete one may score alike). Its roots lie in the qualitative method of Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977), who used no norms but watched exactly where a function broke down. A score needs a standard. The normative comparison (nomothetic) standard compares the patient with healthy people of the same age and education. The individual comparison standard compares present performance with the person's own estimated premorbid level , which one Indian paper calls the 'ideometric' approach: an engineer who now scores average has declined. David Wechsler (1896 to 1981) noticed that some subtests 'hold' with age and illness (Vocabulary, Information, Picture Completion, Object Assembly) while others 'don't hold' (Digit Span, Similarities, Digit Symbol, Block Design). His deterioration index or quotient, (hold minus don't hold) divided by hold, estimates how far brain or psychiatric illness has eroded cognitive and intellectual ability. The National Adult Reading Test ( Hazel Nelson , 1982) predicts premorbid IQ from reading aloud 50 irregular words such as 'debt', a skill that survives early dementia. Such profiles replaced the old screening question 'organic or functional?', once answered with a single test such as the Bender-Gestalt. Exam trap Estimating the impact of brain or psychiatric illness on intellectual ability means the deterioration quotient . Distractors: a mediation index belongs to statistics (Chapter 9), sense of coherence to Aaron Antonovsky 's salutogenesis (Section 7.9), theory of mind to social cognition (Chapter 6). The 'ideometric' approach weighs premorbid functioning against current status; comparison with population norms is the normative approach, and neither quantitative scoring nor emotional well-being is meant. Neuropsychological batteries The classic fixed battery began with Ward Halstead 's studies of frontal-lobe patients (1947) and was validated by his student Ralph Reitan (1922 to 2014). The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery is used for comprehensive neuropsychological assessment: to detect and localise brain dysfunction and gauge its severity. Its tests are the Category Test (abstract reasoning and concept formation); the Tactual Performance Test (the blindfolded patient fits blocks into a form board, then draws it from memory, giving time, memory and localisation scores); the Seashore Rhythm Test ; the Speech-Sounds Perception Test ; the Finger Tapping (Finger Oscillation) Test of motor speed; and the Trail Making Test , Parts A and B. Reitan added the Reitan-Indiana Aphasia Screening Test, a sensory-perceptual examination, grip strength and lateral dominance. A Halstead Impairment Index (the proportion of key scores in the impaired range) of 0.5 or more suggests brain damage. The Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery gave Luria's methods American norms: Anne-Lise Christensen compiled them (1975), and Charles Golden , Thomas Hammeke and Arnold Purisch standardised them (1978; manual 1980). Form I has 269 items scored 0 to 2 in 11 clinical scales, from motor and rhythm to memory and intellectual processes; high T scores mean impairment. The Indian NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery (Bangalore; adult manual by Shobini Rao , D. K. Subbakrishna and K. Gopukumar, 2004, plus a children's battery) is a set of individually normed tests with Indian norms by age, sex and education: colour trails, digit vigilance, N-back, WCST, Tower of London, Stroop, verbal fluency, auditory verbal learning and a complex figure. The PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction (PGIMER, Chandigarh; Dwarka Pershad and colleagues) combines the PGI Memory Scale, verbal and performance intelligence tests (the latter built on C. M. Bhatia 's, Section 2.6), the Nahor-Benson perceptual test and the Bender-Gestalt. The PGI Memory Scale (Pershad and N. N. Wig , 1977) has 10 subtests: remote and recent memory, mental balance, attention and concentration, delayed and immediate recall, retention for similar and for dissimilar pairs, visual retention and recognition. Exam trap The Halstead-Reitan assesses brain function, not personality, vocational interest, attachment, self-reported depression or unconscious conflict, and it is not a projective test. The Rorschach is never part of it (the WAIS and MMPI are often given alongside). Luria did not write the Luria-Nebraska. PGI means Chandigarh; NIMHANS means Bangalore. Memory and visual-motor tests The Wechsler Memory Scale (Wechsler, 1945) began as seven brief subtests summed into a memory quotient . The WMS-IV (2009) gives five indices: Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory, Immediate Memory and Delayed Memory . Verbal and Performance IQ, like crystallised and fluid scores, belong to intelligence tests (Section 2.6); Mechanical Reasoning is a Differential Aptitude Tests subtest (Section 2.8). In the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test ( André Rey , Geneva) the examiner reads 15 words over five trials, then an interference list, then asks for the first list again immediately and after a delay; a flat learning curve or heavy delayed loss signals a memory disorder. The California Verbal Learning Test (1987) uses a 16-word 'shopping list' of four categories, showing whether the person groups words by meaning. Visual memory is tested by the Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure , a detailed drawing first copied (planning and construction) and later drawn from memory, and by the Benton Visual Retention Test ( Arthur Benton , 1946), in which 10 designs are each shown briefly and drawn from memory. The classic visual-motor test is the Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test (1938) of Lauretta Bender (1897 to 1987). She adapted nine figures (A and 1 to 8) from designs the Gestalt psychologist Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) had used to study perceptual organisation. Copying them requires perceiving each design as a whole and reproducing it by hand, so the test assesses visual-motor integration . Its errors screen for organic brain damage and neurological dysfunction in adults and for developmental immaturity in children, scored by Elizabeth Koppitz 's developmental system (1963). The Bender-Gestalt II (2003) has 16 designs and a recall phase. Max Hutt also read the drawings projectively, a secondary use. Simplest of all is digit span . Repeating digits in the order heard (forward span, about seven in adults) measures attention span. Repeating them in reverse (backward span) forces the person to hold and rearrange the digits at once, so it measures working memory (Section 1.7), not long-term, sensory or procedural memory. Exam trap The Bender does not test verbal intelligence, vocational interest, personality, unconscious conflict, depression, schizophrenia, ADHD, reading, auditory or working memory, verbal abstraction or premorbid intelligence (that is the NART). Bender (1938) means copying nine figures; Benton (1946) means drawing ten designs from memory. Executive function, attention, thinking and language The most widely used test of executive function is the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) of David Grant and Esta Berg (1948), with a clinical manual by Robert Heaton (1981). The patient sorts 128 response cards under four stimulus cards by colour, form or number, told only 'right' or 'wrong', and after ten correct sorts the rule changes without warning (Figure 2.17). A healthy person notices the run of 'wrong' and shifts; a frontal patient keeps sorting by the old rule. The scores are perseverative errors , categories achieved and failure to maintain set. The WCST measures set-shifting and cognitive flexibility and is most sensitive to dysfunction of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex . 1 red triangle 2 green stars 3 yellow crosses 4 blue circles 2 red circles By colour (red): under card 1 By number (two): under card 2 By form (circles): under card 4 Figure 2.17 The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test. Each response card fits more than one rule; clinging to a rule after it has changed is perseveration. Key study: Milner and the frontal lobes (1963) In Montreal Brenda Milner gave the WCST to patients having brain surgery for epilepsy. Those with dorsolateral frontal excisions achieved few categories and made many perseverative errors, some while saying the rule had changed; temporal and posterior cases did not. Criticism: perseveration also follows damage elsewhere and occurs in schizophrenia, so the test is sensitive to frontal damage but not specific to it. Exam trap The 'Minnesota Number Ordering Test' and 'Manhattan Card Sorting Test' do not exist. The WCST does not measure memory, language, reading, visual acuity, mood or manual dexterity, and its region is the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, not the hippocampus, primary motor cortex or cerebellum. The Trail Making Test , from the Army Individual Test Battery (1944), has two parts: Part A joins 25 numbered circles in order (attention and speed), and Part B alternates numbers and letters (1, A, 2, B and so on), adding set-shifting. In children with ADHD it assesses inattention; impulsivity, over-activity and social skills are better judged from continuous performance errors and rating scales. The Stroop Colour-Word Test ( John Ridley Stroop , 1935) asks for the ink colour of conflicting colour words ('RED' printed in green), measuring response inhibition . The Tower of London ( Tim Shallice , 1982), moving beads on three pegs to a goal in the fewest moves, measures planning, as does the Tower of Hanoi. Verbal fluency asks for words beginning with a letter in a minute (the Controlled Oral Word Association or FAS test) or from a category such as animals. Sustained attention is tested by the Continuous Performance Test ( H. Enger Rosvold and colleagues, 1956): in a long stream of letters the person responds only to a target, so omissions reflect inattention and commissions impulsivity. The Test of Everyday Attention measures sustained, selective and divided attention through everyday tasks such as map searching. Neither shows which side of the body is affected; Benton's Finger Localization Test does. The patient, without looking, identifies fingers the examiner touches, and consistently more errors on one hand point to the opposite hemisphere. Concept formation, and with it thought disorder , is assessed by sorting. In the Object Sorting Test of Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965) and Martin Scheerer (1941) the patient groups everyday objects and explains why they belong together; concrete, bizarre or loose groupings expose disordered thinking directly. The Rorschach reveals it only indirectly (Section 2.10), the TAT taps needs and conflicts, and the Bender visual-motor skill. Proverbs and similarities test abstract against concrete thinking in the same way. Language tests include the Boston Naming Test (60 line drawings), the Token Test of Ennio De Renzi and Luigi Vignolo (1962), which checks comprehension with commands such as 'touch the small red circle', and the Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination and Western Aphasia Battery. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) of Marshal Folstein , Susan Folstein and Paul McHugh (1975) takes about ten minutes and is scored out of 30: orientation (10), registration (3), attention by serial sevens (5), recall (3), and language and copying (9). A score of 23 or below (cut-off 23/24) suggests impairment. It screens for and tracks global cognitive impairment and dementia, not personality, depression or IQ. Because it is verbal and education-bound, Mary Ganguli built the Hindi Mental State Examination (1995) for rural, largely illiterate older Indians. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) of Ziad Nasreddine (2005) is also out of 30 and takes about ten minutes, but adds executive tasks (a short trail, fluency, abstraction), cube copying and clock drawing ; 26 and above is normal. It is therefore more sensitive than the MMSE to mild cognitive impairment. Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination III extends the idea to 100 points. Staging scales grade severity. The Glasgow Coma Scale of Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett (1974) rates level of consciousness from the best eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6), totalling 3 to 15; 8 or below means severe injury or coma. In dementia the Clinical Dementia Rating grades six domains of cognition and daily function from 0 to 3, the Global Deterioration Scale ( Barry Reisberg , 1982) describes seven stages, and the Hachinski Ischemic Score separates vascular from Alzheimer-type dementia (Section 8.10). Exam trap The Glasgow Coma Scale measures consciousness, not attention, memory or intelligence, and its minimum is 3, not 0. The MoCA's advantage over the MMSE is sensitivity to mild impairment, not brevity, and neither is reserved for neurologists. Rating scales for depression and anxiety Rating scales grade symptom severity and track change. What matters first is who completes them. In a self-report inventory the patient rates himself; in a clinician-rated scale a trained interviewer rates the patient from interview and observation. Structured diagnostic interviews (SCID, PSE) are in Section 7.2, and life-event scales such as Holmes and Rahe's in Section 1.11. The Beck Depression Inventory of Aaron Temkin Beck (1921 to 2021), first published in 1961, is the most used self-report depression measure. The BDI-II (1996) has 21 items, each rated 0 to 3 for the past two weeks, so totals run from 0 to 63: 0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate, 29 to 63 severe . For a patient with two months of sadness, anhedonia and worthlessness, the BDI is the instrument for further evaluation, not the Rorschach (projective), the MMPI (broad personality, Section 2.9) or the WAIS (IQ). Clinician-rated alternatives are the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression ( Max Hamilton , 1960) and the Montgomery-Asberg scale, which is sensitive to treatment change; the Zung scale (1965) and PHQ-9 are brief self-report screens, and Beck's Hopelessness Scale and Scale for Suicide Ideation assess suicide risk. For anxiety, the clinician-rated Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale pairs with the self-report Beck Anxiety Inventory and GAD-7. The Fear Survey Schedule of Joseph Wolpe and Peter Lang (1964) lists feared situations; the SUDS rating used in exposure is in Section 7.4. Exam trap RML 2025 keyed the BDI as 'typically used for neuropsychological assessment' against a Likert scale (an attitude-scaling format, Section 2.8), the 16PF (a personality inventory, Section 2.9) and the Peabody Individual Achievement Test (an achievement test, Section 2.8). The BDI is a self-report depression inventory, not a neuropsychological test; neuropsychologists add it to see whether low mood is depressing test scores. Choose it only because the others are further off. Scales for OCD, psychosis, substances, children and forensic work The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) of Wayne Goodman and colleagues (1989) is the standard clinician-rated measure of OCD severity. After a symptom checklist, ten core items rate obsessions (five) and compulsions (five) on the same five dimensions, time, interference, distress, resistance and control, each 0 to 4, for a total of 0 to 40. It does not rate depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, PTSD or suicidal ideation. For psychosis the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale ( John Overall and Donald Gorham , 1962) covers general psychopathology, and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) of Stanley Kay , Abraham Fiszbein and Lewis Opler (1987) measures symptom severity in schizophrenia with 30 items: 7 positive, 7 negative and 16 general psychopathology. Nancy Andreasen 's SANS and SAPS rate negative and positive symptoms separately; the Young Mania Rating Scale rates mania. General screens such as the General Health Questionnaire ( David Goldberg , 1972) and Leonard Derogatis 's SCL-90-R detect distress without making a diagnosis. For substance use there are the WHO's Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT), CAGE (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener), the Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test (MAST), the CIWA-Ar for alcohol withdrawal, the SADQ for dependence severity and the Fagerstrom Test for nicotine dependence. The Clinical Global Impression rates severity and improvement from 1 to 7; the Global Assessment of Functioning, dropped in DSM-5, gave way to the WHO's WHODAS 2.0. In India, disability from mental illness is certified with IDEAS , the Indian Disability Evaluation and Assessment Scale (Indian Psychiatric Society, 2002). Children are rated with the Conners Rating Scales (ADHD), Thomas Achenbach 's Child Behavior Checklist and its Indian adaptation, Savita Malhotra 's Childhood Psychopathology Measurement Schedule (PGIMER); the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (1987) screens new mothers. In forensic work the Psychopathy Checklist-Revised of Robert Hare (1980, revised 1991) rates 20 items 0 to 2 from interview and case records.
