Galton's Anthropometric Laboratory, Revisited Look again at Galton's counter with this chapter behind you. Every visitor met the same instruments, instructions and recording, so his procedures were standardised and objective (Section 2.1). Measures such as height and grip strength are highly reliable (Section 2.3), yet Wissler showed that sensory and motor tests of this kind had almost no criterion validity for academic success (Section 2.4): consistency is necessary, not sufficient. Galton's thousands of cards were among the first large norms, and his spread of scores around an average foreshadowed standard scores (Section 2.5). Binet's turn to judgement and reasoning founded the intelligence tests of Section 2.6, and every later test has had to prove what Galton assumed. His belief in inherited ability, which fed eugenics, is one reason testing now carries rules of fairness. Chapter summary 2.1 Psychological Testing: Nature, History, Types and Ethics. A psychological test is an objective, standardised measure of a sample of behaviour (Anastasi); assessment integrates tests with interview, observation and records. Testing runs from Chinese examinations through Galton's laboratory (1884), Cattell's 'mental tests' (1890) and Wissler's disproof (1901) to Binet and Simon (1905), the Army Alpha and Beta, Woodworth's inventory and the MMPI (1943). Tests are objective or subjective, speed or power, of maximum or typical performance. A good test is objective, reliable, valid, normed and practicable; standardisation fixes procedures and norms. Clinicians read data as samples, correlates or signs; actuarial prediction usually beats clinical judgement, which suffers confirmatory bias, illusory correlation and the Barnum effect. 2.2 Building a Test: Items, Item Analysis, IRT and Response Bias. Items are essay or objective (supply or selection type), and guessing is corrected by S = R - W/(n - 1). Item analysis gives difficulty p (proportion passing; ideal 0.50, about 0.62 for four options) and discrimination D = p upper - p lower on Kelley's 27 percent groups; a negative D flags a miskeyed item. Ceiling and floor effects stop a test discriminating at the top or bottom. In IRT the item characteristic curve plots success against the latent trait θ (b, a, c; Rasch 1PL to 3PL), and sample-invariant parameters allow adaptive testing. Acquiescence , social desirability and halo (Thorndike, 1920) bias scores. 2.3 Reliability: Consistency and the Standard Error of Measurement. Reliability is the consistency of a measure: dependability and freedom from measurement error. In Spearman's classical test theory (1904) every observed score is a true score plus random error, and reliability is the ratio of true-score to observed-score variance. Test-retest correlation gives the coefficient of stability, for stable traits; parallel forms give the coefficient of equivalence. Single-sitting internal consistency methods are split-half (stepped up by the Spearman-Brown formula, so .60 becomes .75), Rulon and Flanagan, KR-20 and KR-21 for right-wrong items, and Cronbach's alpha (1951). Cohen's kappa measures rater agreement beyond chance. The standard error of measurement , SD × √(1 - r), bands one person's score. 2.4 Validity and the Accuracy of Test Decisions. Validity is the extent to which a test measures what it claims to measure; since Messick (1989) it is a unified judgement about the interpretations and uses of scores. Face validity is mere appearance; content validity is adequate sampling of the domain (blueprint, Lawshe's CVR). Criterion-related validity is concurrent (criterion measured now) or predictive (criterion measured later). Construct validity (Cronbach and Meehl, 1955) rests on convergent and discriminant evidence and the multitrait-multimethod matrix (Campbell and Fiske, 1959). A test can be reliable without being valid, and validity cannot exceed the square root of reliability. Sensitivity and specificity describe the test; predictive values depend on the base rate. 2.5 Norms, Standard Scores and Interpreting a Score. A raw score means nothing without a frame of reference. Norm-referenced interpretation compares a person with a representative standardisation sample; criterion-referenced interpretation (Glaser, 1963) compares with a fixed mastery standard. Good norms are large, representative, recent and relevant. The ratio IQ (MA ÷ CA × 100) gave way to Wechsler's deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15). Percentile ranks are ordinal. The z score (mean 0, SD 1) and the normal curve (68, 95, 99.7 per cent within 1, 2, 3 SD) link T scores (50, 10), stanines (5, 2), stens (5.5, 2), scaled scores (10, 3) and CEEB scores (500, 100). 2.6 Intelligence Tests: Binet, Wechsler, Non-verbal and Indian Scales. Intelligence tests are reliable and predict school achievement but not behaviour in general. Binet and Simon (1905) built the first test; Terman's Stanford-Binet (1916) used the ratio IQ, and the SB5 (Roid, 2003) measures five factors in verbal and non-verbal domains. Wechsler's Bellevue scale (1939) introduced the deviation IQ; the WAIS-IV (2008; 16:0 to 90:11) gives an FSIQ and four indices (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI) from 10 core subtests, and the WISC-V covers 6:0 to 16:11. Raven's Progressive Matrices measures fluid reasoning and is culture-fair. In India, Bhatia's performance battery suits illiterate people, while the Binet-Kamat, MISIC and WAPIS adapt the Stanford-Binet, WISC and WAIS. 2.7 Assessing Development, Adaptive Behaviour and Disability. Development and everyday competence are scored apart from IQ as DQ (developmental age / CA × 100) and SQ (social age / CA × 100), from several informants because symptoms vary across contexts. Infant scales include the Bayley (1 to 42 months), Gesell's schedules, Denver II and the Indian DST, DASII and TDSC. Doll's VSMS (1935; 117 items; SQ) and Malin's Indian version (89 items) measure social maturity; the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales , adaptive functioning. DSM-5 intellectual disability needs IQ and adaptive deficits, with severity graded adaptively; global developmental delay is for under-5s. Under the RPWD Act 2016, learning disability is certified from 8 years, autism with ISAA . 2.8 Aptitude, Achievement, Creativity, Interest and Attitude Measures. An achievement test measures what has been learnt in a specific academic area; an aptitude test predicts future learning in a specific area, and Anne Anastasi placed both on one continuum. Multiple aptitude batteries (the DAT with eight subtests, 1947; the GATB with nine aptitudes) serve guidance. Guilford's divergent thinking is scored for fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration (TTCT; Mednick's RAT). Strong keyed interests empirically, Kuder used ipsative forced-choice triads and Holland proposed RIASEC. Thurstone's equal-appearing intervals use judges and median scale values; Likert's summated ratings sum respondents' agreement ratings; Guttman's cumulative scale needs reproducibility of 0.90; Bogardus measured social distance; the IAT measures implicit attitudes by reaction time. 2.9 Objective Personality Inventories. An objective personality test fixes items, answer format and scoring. Cattell accepted three data sources: L-data (life records), Q-data (questionnaires) and T-data (objective tests). Inventories are built rationally (Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet, 1917), theoretically (EPPS, MBTI, MCMI), by empirical criterion keying (MMPI, CPI) or by factor analysis (16PF, EPQ, NEO-PI-R, GZTS, Comrey). The MMPI (Hathaway and McKinley, 1943) assesses personality and psychopathology with validity scales L, F and K and ten clinical scales; the MMPI-2, MMPI-2-RF (RC scales) and MMPI-3 followed. The Rep test and Q-sort study one person at a time. 2.10 Projective Techniques. Projective techniques rest on the projective hypothesis (term coined by Frank, 1939): faced with an ambiguous stimulus, people project needs, conflicts and unconscious processes into their answers, which resists self-report bias. Lindzey (1959) grouped them as association, construction, completion, choice or ordering and expression. The Rorschach (1921) has 10 cards (5 achromatic, 2 black-red, 3 multicoloured), a response and inquiry phase, and codes for location, determinants and form quality; Exner's Comprehensive System (1974) and R-PAS (2011) standardised it. The TAT (Morgan and Murray, 1935; 31 cards) is read for needs and press. Sentence completion, the Rosenzweig P-F, figure drawings and the Szondi complete the family, all psychometrically weak. 2.11 Neuropsychological Assessment and Clinical Rating Scales. Neuropsychological assessment infers brain function from behaviour across attention, memory, language, visuospatial, executive, motor and sensory domains, using fixed batteries ( Halstead-Reitan , Luria-Nebraska), flexible batteries or Kaplan's process approach, and comparing scores with norms or with the person's own premorbid level (Wechsler's deterioration quotient , the NART). India has the NIMHANS and PGI batteries. Key tests are the WMS-IV, Rey AVLT, the Bender-Gestalt (visual-motor integration), backward digit span (working memory) and the WCST (set-shifting, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex). The MMSE, MoCA and Glasgow Coma Scale screen and stage. Rating scales are self-report (BDI) or clinician-rated (Hamilton scales, Y-BOCS, PANSS, PCL-R). Negative Syndrome Scale, Psychopathy Checklist-Revised From the past papers The primary difference between a "speed test" and a "power test" in psychological assessment is that a speed test: (Real PYQ 2024) a Has items of increasing difficulty, while a power test has items of uniform difficulty. b Has a strict time limit that prevents most test-takers from completing all items, while a power test has items so difficult that no one can answer them all correctly. c Measures reaction time, while a power measures cognitive ability. d Is administered individually, while a power test can be administered in groups. ✓ Answer: (b) Has a strict time limit that prevents most test-takers from completing all items, while a power test has items so difficult that no one can answer them all correctly. Speed test versus power test distinction The concept Speed test A speed test uses easy items under a time limit so strict that few finish. Power test A power test allows generous time, but its items grow so hard that no one passes them all. Exam tip Speed: easy items, tight time limit . Power: hard items, ample time. Why the other options are wrong (a) Has items of increasing difficulty, while a power test has items of uniform difficulty. Reverses the two: items growing harder is the mark of a power test , while a speed test uses easy items. (c) Measures reaction time, while a power measures cognitive ability. Confuses a timed test with reaction time ; a speed test counts items finished under a time limit. (d) Is administered individually, while a power test can be administered in groups. Confuses timing with individual versus group administration , which is a separate way of classifying tests. Which of the following is the most important characteristic of a psychological test? (RML 2024) a Objectivity b Subjectivity c Validity d Rationality ✓ Answer (as keyed): (a) Objectivity A. K. Singh and other Indian texts (RML key) The concept Why this one RML follows Indian texts such as A. K. Singh , which list objectivity first. What it means Objectivity means a score must not depend on who gives or scores the test. Other papers Most textbooks and the 2014 Standards call validity the most fundamental property, so on other papers choose (c). Why the other options are wrong (b) Subjectivity A defect, not a virtue: subjectivity lets the scorer's judgement change the score, the opposite of objectivity. (c) Validity The answer most textbooks and the 2014 Standards give; choose it on other papers, but RML keys objectivity. (d) Rationality Not a test characteristic at all; rationality does not appear in lists of test properties. Which of the following refers to the notion of the confirmatory bias? (RML 2021) a Clinicians ignore information that does not support their hypothesis b Clinicians ignore information that does not support their stereotypes. c Clinicians interpret ambiguous information as supporting their hypothesis. d All of the above ✓ Answer: (d) All of the above Confirmatory bias in clinical judgement The concept What it is Confirmatory bias is the tendency to notice, weigh and interpret information so that it confirms what one already believes. Why all three Ignoring contrary evidence, ignoring evidence against one's stereotypes and reading ambiguity as support are all forms of it. Why the other options are wrong (a) Clinicians ignore information that does not support their hypothesis True: ignoring contrary evidence is one form of the bias, but only one of three. (b) Clinicians ignore information that does not support their stereotypes. True: ignoring evidence against one's stereotypes is the same bias applied to beliefs about groups; only part of the answer. (c) Clinicians interpret ambiguous information as supporting their hypothesis. True: reading ambiguity as support is the interpretive side of the bias; only part of the answer. The improvement in anxiety may sometimes spuriously improve depression. This is called: (RML 2024) a Halo effect b Ceiling effect c Hawthorne effect d Therapeutic effect ✓ Answer: (a) Halo effect Halo effect in rating The concept What it is In the halo effect , one attribute colours the rating of another. Here The improved anxiety colours the depression rating, so the depression rating improves although the depression has not. Why the other options are wrong (b) Ceiling effect A ceiling effect is a test too easy to register further gains, not one rating colouring another. (c) Hawthorne effect The Hawthorne effect is change because people know they are being studied. (d) Therapeutic effect A therapeutic effect is real improvement from treatment; here the depression has not actually improved. A response style or bias, in which there is tendency to agree with test items regardless of their contents is called: (RML 2024) a Halo effect b Central tendency effect c Social desirability effect d Acquiescence effect ✓ Answer: (d) Acquiescence effect Acquiescence response style (yea-saying) The concept What it is Acquiescence ( yea-saying ) is agreeing with items regardless of their content. How it is controlled It is controlled by balanced keying : some items are worded so that agreeing scores in the opposite direction. Why the other options are wrong (a) Halo effect Halo is a rater's error, not a test-taker's response style. (b) Central tendency effect Central tendency is choosing the middle of the scale, not agreeing with everything. (c) Social desirability effect Social desirability depends on content: choosing the answer that looks good. The tendency of the rater/interviewer to judge an individual on the basis of one single attribute is referred to as : (IHBAS 2024) a Similarity error b Central tendency error c Contrast error d Halo error ✓ Answer: (d) Halo error Thorndike, halo error (1920) The concept What it is In halo error , one attribute or a general impression colours every other rating of the person. Who named it Thorndike named it in 1920. Why the other options are wrong (a) Similarity error Similarity error favours people who are like the rater. (b) Central tendency error Central tendency error rates everyone as average. (c) Contrast error Contrast error rates others as opposite to the rater. Which of the following is assessed by Cronbach's alpha? (RML 2021) a Concurrent validity b Inter-rater reliability c Test retest reliability d Internal consistency ✓ Answer: (d) Internal consistency Lee Cronbach, coefficient alpha (1951) The concept What it is Alpha ( Lee Cronbach , 1951) estimates how well a scale's items hang together. Key point It needs only one administration , which is what makes it a measure of internal consistency . Why the other options are wrong (a) Concurrent validity Concurrent validity needs an outside criterion, not agreement among a scale's own items. (b) Inter-rater reliability Inter-rater reliability needs two scorers and is indexed by kappa or the intraclass correlation. (c) Test retest reliability Test-retest reliability needs two occasions, whereas alpha uses one administration. A test developer administers a new anxiety scale to a group of college students and, two weeks later, administers the same scale again to the same group. She then correlates the two sets of scores. This process is used to establish: (Real PYQ 2024) a Split-half reliability b Inter-rater reliability c Test-retest reliability d Parallel forms reliability ✓ Answer: (c) Test-retest reliability Test-retest reliability, coefficient of stability The concept The design Same scale, same people, two occasions, scores correlated. What it gives That correlation is the coefficient of stability , the index of test-retest reliability . Why the other options are wrong (a) Split-half reliability Split-half correlates two halves of one sitting, not two occasions. (b) Inter-rater reliability Inter-rater reliability compares scorers, not occasions. (d) Parallel forms reliability Parallel forms would need a second, equivalent version of the scale; here the same scale was repeated. Odd-even method of splitting the test to estimate split-half reliability is MOST appropriate for : (RML 2022) a Projective tests b Neuropsychological tests c Power tests d Speed tests ✓ Answer: (c) Power tests Odd-even split-half method The concept Why power tests In a power test items are graded and time is generous, so odd and even halves are fair parallel samples. Why not speed tests On a speed test the halves match by construction and the coefficient is spuriously high. Why the other options are wrong (a) Projective tests Projective tests lack comparable, objectively scored items to split into halves. (b) Neuropsychological tests Many neuropsychological tests lack comparable, objectively scored items to split. (d) Speed tests The trap: on a speed test odd and even halves match by construction, so the coefficient is spuriously high. To determine whether a newly developed intelligence test truly accurately measures intelligence or not, it is necessary to administer the test with one that has been in the field for some time. Which of the following needs to be looked for? (JEMAS 2025) a Construct validity b Concurrent validity c Content validity d Predictive validity ✓ Answer: (b) Concurrent validity Criterion-related validity, concurrent type The concept What it is Correlating a new test with an established test given at about the same time is concurrent validity . Where it fits It is one type of criterion-related validity ; the established test serves as the criterion. Why the other options are wrong (a) Construct validity Construct validity rests on a network of evidence rather than one established test. (c) Content validity Content validity concerns sampling of the domain, not agreement with another test. (d) Predictive validity Predictive validity needs a criterion measured later, not a test given at the same time. Which of the following statements is TRUE? (RML 2024) a A test can be valid without being reliable b A test can be reliable without being valid c If a test measures what it is intended to measure, then by definition it is reliable d If a test gives consistent scores when administered repeatedly then it is valid ✓ Answer: (b) A test can be reliable without being valid Reliability versus validity The concept Why this one A test can be reliable without being valid : it can consistently measure the wrong thing. The rule A test cannot be valid without being reliable, so reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Why the other options are wrong (a) A test can be valid without being reliable The reverse of the rule: a test cannot be valid without being reliable. (c) If a test measures what it is intended to measure, then by definition it is reliable Overstates the link: a valid test must be reliable, but this is not true by definition . (d) If a test gives consistent scores when administered repeatedly then it is valid Consistency alone never proves validity ; a test can consistently measure the wrong thing. A high false positive rate in diagnosis means : (IHBAS 2025) a Diagnosis is too strict b Normal people are diagnosed as disordered c Diagnosis has low reliability d Disordered people go undetected ✓ Answer: (b) Normal people are diagnosed as disordered False positives and specificity The concept What it is A false positive is a positive call on someone without the condition: a normal person diagnosed as disordered. Key link A high false positive rate is the mark of low specificity . Why the other options are wrong (a) Diagnosis is too strict An over-strict diagnosis produces false negatives , the opposite problem. (c) Diagnosis has low reliability Reliability is a different property: the consistency of a diagnosis, not its error type. (d) Disordered people go undetected Undetected disordered people are false negatives , not false positives. Which statistical measure tells us how far individual data points are dispersed from the mean expressed in standard deviation units? (Real PYQ 2025) a Variance b Z-score (Standard score) c Coefficient of variation d Standard error ✓ Answer: (b) Z-score (Standard score) Standard score, z = (X − M) ÷ SD The concept The formula z = (X − M) ÷ SD states how many SDs one score lies from the mean. Why it is useful With every score in standard deviation units , scores from different distributions can be compared. Why the other options are wrong (a) Variance Variance (SD squared) describes the spread of a whole distribution, not where one score lies. (c) Coefficient of variation The coefficient of variation compares spread across distributions, not one score's distance from the mean. (d) Standard error The standard error is the SD of a sampling distribution, not of individual scores. IQ if any body has a mental age of 8 and a chronological age of 10 is: (RML 2020) a 108 b 125 c 80 d 92 ✓ Answer: (c) 80 Ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100 The concept The formula Ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100 = (8 ÷ 10) × 100 = 80. Sense check A mental age below the chronological age must give an IQ below 100. Why the other options are wrong (a) 108 Above 100, which is impossible when mental age (8) is below chronological age (10). (b) 125 The tempting trap: it inverts the ratio, (CA ÷ MA) × 100 = (10 ÷ 8) × 100. (d) 92 Below 100, but not what the formula gives: (8 ÷ 10) × 100 is exactly 80. Which of the following is a non-linear transformation of raw scores? (Recall set) a z-score b 50 + 10z c Stanine d Deviation score (X − M) ✓ Answer: (c) Stanine Stanines, a normalising area transformation The concept What a stanine is Stanines are assigned from percentile ranks in fixed proportions: 4, 7, 12, 17, 20, 17, 12, 7, 4 per cent. Why non-linear This is a normalising, area transformation that forces a normal shape on the scores. The contrast z, the T score 50 + 10z and the deviation score X − M all apply one multiply-and-add rule to every score, so they are linear and keep the raw distribution's shape. Why the other options are wrong (a) z-score Linear: the z-score applies one multiply-and-add rule to every score, so it keeps the raw distribution's shape. (b) 50 + 10z The T score , a linear rescaling of z, so it keeps the raw distribution's shape. (d) Deviation score (X − M) Linear: subtracting the mean shifts every score by the same amount and keeps the shape. In the WAIS-IV (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale - Fourth Edition), how many core subtests are there in the Verbal Comprehension Index and the Perceptual Reasoning Index respectively? (Real PYQ 2025) a 3 verbal, 4 performance b 3 verbal, 3 performance c 4 verbal, 3 performance d 2 verbal, 4 performance ✓ Answer: (b) 3 verbal, 3 performance Wechsler, WAIS-IV core subtests The concept VCI core The Verbal Comprehension Index core is Similarities, Vocabulary and Information; Comprehension is supplemental. PRI core The Perceptual Reasoning Index core is Block Design, Matrix Reasoning and Visual Puzzles; Figure Weights and Picture Completion are supplemental. Exam tip Counting a supplemental subtest as core produces the tempting 4. Why the other options are wrong (a) 3 verbal, 4 performance Counts a supplemental PRI subtest ( Figure Weights or Picture Completion ) as core; the PRI core is three. (c) 4 verbal, 3 performance Counts Comprehension , a supplemental VCI subtest, as core; the VCI core is three. (d) 2 verbal, 4 performance Undercounts the VCI and overcounts the PRI; each index has three core subtests. A 10-year-old child from a rural area, with no formal schooling, is brought for an intellectual assessment due to academic struggles. The child is illiterate and has had minimal exposure to formal testing materials. Which of the following tests would be the MOST appropriate to use to minimize cultural and educational bias? (Real PYQ 2024) a Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence b Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV) c Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale (5th ed.) d Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) ✓ Answer: (a) Bhatia's Battery Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests (Indian norms) The concept Why this one Bhatia's Battery has five performance subtests that need no reading, so an illiterate, unschooled child is not penalised. Norms It carries Indian norms , so the child is compared with the right group. Why the other options are wrong (b) Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV) The WISC-IV rests on Western verbal content and norms, which penalise an unschooled Indian child. (c) Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale (5th ed.) The SB5 also rests on Western verbal content and norms. (d) Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) MISIC is Indian, but it is half verbal and assumes schooling. An IQ test does NOT provide which of the following? (RML 2021) a High test retest reliability b Good predictor of behaviour c High internal consistency d Good validity ✓ Answer: (b) Good predictor of behaviour Psychometric strengths and limits of IQ tests The concept Why this one IQ tests predict school achievement well, but how a person behaves in general depends on personality , motivation and circumstance. Their strengths IQ tests do have high test-retest reliability , high internal consistency and good validity. Why the other options are not the answer (a) High test retest reliability True: IQ scores are stable on retesting, so IQ tests have high test-retest reliability . (c) High internal consistency True: IQ test items hang together well, giving high internal consistency . (d) Good validity True: IQ tests have good validity for predicting school achievement. Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) is a measure of : (RML 2022) a Mental age and Intelligence quotient b Social age and social quotient c Developmental age and developmental quotient d Emotional age and emotional quotient ✓ Answer: (b) Social age and social quotient Doll, Vineland Social Maturity Scale The concept How it works Doll's VSMS converts the items an informant credits into a social age . The quotient The social quotient is SQ = SA / CA × 100. Why the other options are wrong (a) Mental age and Intelligence quotient Mental age and IQ come from intelligence tests , not a social maturity scale. (c) Developmental age and developmental quotient Developmental age and DQ come from developmental scales such as Gesell's or the DST. (d) Emotional age and emotional quotient Not a VSMS score; an emotional quotient belongs to emotional intelligence measures, while the VSMS yields social age and SQ. A key differentiation between global developmental delay and intellectual disability is (JEMAS 2025) a Age of assessment (under 5 years for GDD, 5 years and above for ID) b Presence of social deficits c Language delay alone d Motor impairment ✓ Answer: (a) Age of assessment DSM-5, global developmental delay versus intellectual disability The concept The rule DSM-5 reserves global developmental delay for children under 5 who are too young for reliable standardised testing. What happens next These children must be reassessed; from 5 years the diagnosis is intellectual disability . Why age is the key The deficits are of the same kind , so only age separates the two. Why the other options are wrong (b) Presence of social deficits Social deficits are of the same kind in both, so they do not separate them. (c) Language delay alone Language delay is of the same kind in both, so it does not separate them. (d) Motor impairment Motor impairment is of the same kind in both, so it does not separate them. Name of the Indian tool to assess the severity and disability of children with autism : (IHBAS 2024) a CGAS b Childhood Autism Rating Scale c CBCL d ISAA ✓ Answer: (d) ISAA NIMH Secunderabad, ISAA (2009) The concept What it is The Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (NIMH Secunderabad, 2009; 40 items) is the Indian instrument prescribed for certifying autism. What it gives Besides severity, it gives the disability percentage used for certification. Key note The paper keys (b) CARS , the American scale of Schopler and colleagues on which ISAA partly drew; ISAA is the Indian tool asked for. Why the other options are wrong (a) CGAS The CGAS rates global functioning, not autism severity. (b) Childhood Autism Rating Scale CARS is the American scale of Schopler and colleagues, not Indian; the paper keys it, but ISAA only partly drew on it. (c) CBCL The CBCL rates general behaviour problems, not autism severity. Summated rating scale is also known as : (RML 2022) a Likert scale b Thurstone scale c Guttmann scale d Equal appearing interval scale ✓ Answer: (a) Likert scale Likert, summated ratings (1932) The concept How it works Likert (1932) had respondents rate their agreement with each statement and summed the ratings. The name Summing the ratings gives summated ratings , hence the name. Why the other options are wrong (b) Thurstone scale The Thurstone scale is a judge-scaled method, one and the same as the equal-appearing interval scale. (c) Guttmann scale The Guttman scale is cumulative, not summated. (d) Equal appearing interval scale Another name for the Thurstone scale , a judge-scaled method, not summated ratings. The Implicit Association Test is designed to measure: (RML 2022) a Verbal ability b Unconscious stereotyping c Hidden mathematical ability d Dream content ✓ Answer: (b) Unconscious stereotyping Greenwald, McGhee and Schwartz, IAT (1998) The concept What it is Greenwald, McGhee and Schwartz (1998) built the IAT to reveal implicit attitudes and stereotypes. How it works It reads these from reaction times in a sorting task. Why the other options are wrong (a) Verbal ability The IAT is not an ability test of any kind. (c) Hidden mathematical ability Again an ability, and the IAT is not an ability test of any kind; 'hidden' is not the same as implicit. (d) Dream content Dream content is not its target; the IAT works from reaction times in a sorting task. What is the primary purpose of achievement tests in psychological assessment? (RML 2025) a To measure future success potential b To assess cognitive abilities related to brain function c To measure understanding and knowledge in specific academic areas d To evaluate unconscious conflicts and emotions ✓ Answer: (c) To measure understanding and knowledge in specific academic areas Achievement versus aptitude tests The concept What it is Achievement tests look back at what has been learnt in specific academic areas. The contrast Aptitude tests look forward to future potential. Why the other options are wrong (a) To measure future success potential Future potential is the aim of aptitude tests , which look forward, not back. (b) To assess cognitive abilities related to brain function Brain-related abilities are the aim of neuropsychological tests . (d) To evaluate unconscious conflicts and emotions Unconscious conflicts are the target of projective techniques . Which of the following statements is TRUE with respect to Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI)? (RML 2022) a It utilizes rational method of test construction b It is constructed by assuming specific personality traits and formulating questions to answer them c It is derived by finding items that discriminate between criterion and control groups d It is true with respect to both a and b ✓ Answer: (c) It is derived by finding items that discriminate between criterion and control groups Hathaway and McKinley, MMPI empirical criterion keying The concept How it was built Hathaway and McKinley kept only items that separated patient groups from normal controls, whatever their content. The name This is empirical criterion keying . Why the other options are wrong (a) It utilizes rational method of test construction The rational , logical-content strategy of Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet , not the MMPI. (b) It is constructed by assuming specific personality traits and formulating questions to answer them Also the rational, logical-content strategy of Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet: items written to fit assumed traits. (d) It is true with respect to both a and b Both (a) and (b) describe the rational strategy, which is not how the MMPI was built. According to Raymond Cattell's classification of personality data sources, which of the following is NOT recognized as a legitimate data type? (Real PYQ 2025) a Q-data (Questionnaire data) b L-data (Life record data) c T-data (Objective test data) d P-data (Projective data) ✓ Answer: (d) P-data Raymond Cattell, L-, Q- and T-data The concept The three sources Cattell recognised only three sources of personality data: L-data , Q-data and T-data . Why this one There is no P-data in his scheme, so it is the one not recognised. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Q-data (Questionnaire data) Recognised: Q-data are self-report questionnaires. (b) L-data (Life record data) Recognised: L-data are life records such as school and criminal records, and observer ratings. (c) T-data (Objective test data) Recognised: T-data come from objective tests in controlled situations whose purpose is hidden. Elevated Lie scale on Multiphasic Questionnaire (MPQ) is indicative of: (IHBAS 2020) a Tendency to fake and manipulate b Social desirability c Mistrust d All the above ✓ Answer: (d) All the above Lie scale, denial of common faults The concept What it means A high Lie score means the person denies common minor faults. Why all three That denial is an attempt to fake a good impression , a pull towards social desirability , and a guarded mistrust that admits no flaw to the examiner. Why the other options are wrong (a) Tendency to fake and manipulate True: denying common faults is an attempt to fake a good impression, but only one of three. (b) Social desirability True: the denial reflects a pull towards social desirability ; only part of the answer. (c) Mistrust True: guarded mistrust admits no flaw to the examiner; only part of the answer. How many Rorschach cards are coloured? (RML 2022) a 10 b 5 c 3 d 4 ✓ Answer: (b) 5 Rorschach inkblot cards and colour The concept The colour cards Two cards ( II, III ) are black with red and three ( VIII, IX, X ) are multicoloured, so five carry colour. The rest The other five (I, IV, V, VI, VII) are achromatic . Why the other options are wrong (a) 10 Ten is the whole set, not just the coloured cards. (c) 3 Counts only the fully coloured cards (VIII, IX, X) and misses the two black-and-red ones. (d) 4 Matches no grouping of the cards: two black-and-red plus three multicoloured make five. Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) is based on which technique of psychological testing? (RML 2022) a Expressive technique b Construction technique c Association technique d Completion technique ✓ Answer: (b) Construction technique Lindzey's classification of projective techniques The concept Lindzey's scheme Lindzey grouped projective techniques by what the person must do with the material. Why construction In the TAT the person constructs a story about each picture. Why the other options are wrong (a) Expressive technique Expression is drawing and play, not storytelling. (c) Association technique Association is the Rorschach and word association. (d) Completion technique Completion is sentence completion and the Rosenzweig P-F. Absence of 'Human' Response on Rorschach Psychodiagnostics Test indicates: (IHBAS 2020) a Apathy b Poor interpersonal orientation c Lack of empathy d All the above ✓ Answer: (b) Poor interpersonal orientation Rorschach human content The concept What it means Human content reflects interest in and understanding of people. So its absence Its absence points to poor interpersonal orientation . Why the other options are wrong (a) Apathy Apathy is not the standard reading of absent human content. (c) Lack of empathy Lack of empathy is not the standard reading either. (d) All the above Fails because apathy and lack of empathy are not standard readings, so 'All the above' is wrong as well. One of the most widely used tests to assess executive functioning: (Amity 2023) a Wisconsin Card Sorting Test b Minnesota Number Ordering Test c Manhattan Card Sorting Test d None of the above ✓ Answer: (a) Wisconsin Card Sorting Test Grant and Berg, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (1948) The concept What it measures Grant and Berg's WCST (1948) measures set-shifting and cognitive flexibility. How it works The sorting rule changes unannounced, and perseverative errors show a failure to shift. Brain link It is most sensitive to dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction. Why the other options are wrong (b) Minnesota Number Ordering Test An invented distractor; no standard executive test goes by this name. (c) Manhattan Card Sorting Test An invented distractor that borrows the 'card sorting' wording of the real WCST. (d) None of the above Wrong too, because the WCST is a real and widely used test of executive functioning. Which of the following is a clinician-rated questionnaire? (RML 2022) a Beck Depression Inventory b Beck Anxiety Inventory c Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale d Both b and c ✓ Answer: (c) Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale Max Hamilton, Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (1959) The concept What it is Max Hamilton's 14-item anxiety scale (1959) is completed by a trained clinician . How it is rated The clinician rates from interview and observation , not from the patient's own answers. Why the other options are wrong (a) Beck Depression Inventory Self-report: on the Beck Depression Inventory the patient rates his own symptoms. (b) Beck Anxiety Inventory Self-report: on the Beck Anxiety Inventory the patient rates his own symptoms. (d) Both b and c Fails because (b) is a self-report Beck inventory, not clinician-rated. Impact of psychiatric illness on one's cognitive and intellectual abilities can be estimated on the basis of: (IHBAS 2020) a Deterioration quotient b Mediation index c Sense of coherence index d Theory of Mind index ✓ Answer: (a) Deterioration quotient Wechsler, deterioration quotient (hold versus don't hold) The concept How it works Wechsler compared 'hold' subtests (Vocabulary, Information, Picture Completion, Object Assembly) with 'don't hold' subtests (Digit Span, Similarities, Digit Symbol, Block Design). What it shows The gap between the two sets estimates loss from illness: the deterioration quotient . Why the other options are wrong (b) Mediation index Mediation is a statistical concept , not an estimate of cognitive loss. (c) Sense of coherence index Sense of coherence is Antonovsky's health concept, not a measure of cognitive loss. (d) Theory of Mind index Theory of mind concerns understanding others' minds, not intellectual deterioration. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Cattell's (1949; fifth edition 1993, 185 items): 16 primary source traits found by factor analysis and five global factors, scored in stens; it measures personality traits, not intelligence. asked 7 times Reliability means consistency, dependability and freedom from measurement error (all of these): a reliable measure gives stable results on different occasions. asked 6 times SEM = SD × √(1 - r) , which estimates the range within which a person's true score probably falls: with SD 15 and r = .91 the SEM is 4.5 (±1 SEM 68 percent, ±1.96 SEM 95 percent). asked 6 times The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (Sparrow, Balla and Cicchetti, 1984; Vineland-3, 2016) measure adaptive functioning in daily life (communication, daily living skills, socialisation, motor skills), not IQ, personality or psychopathology. asked 6 times The MMPI (Hathaway and McKinley, 1943; 550 items) is an objective personality inventory that assesses personality and psychopathology for psychiatric diagnosis, covering mood, physical concerns and social attitudes; it is not projective, an intelligence test or an aptitude battery. asked 6 times Projective tests present ambiguous stimuli to reveal unconscious processes ; their main advantage is that they avoid self-report biases and are hard to fake. asked 6 times John Exner's Comprehensive System (1974) is the standard Rorschach scoring system: it codes location, determinants, form quality and content, gives no IQ, and there is no 'Murray system' of Rorschach scoring. asked 6 times The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (David Grant and Esta Berg, 1948) is the most widely used test of executive function: it measures set-shifting and cognitive flexibility through perseverative errors and is most sensitive to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex dysfunction. asked 6 times A test can be reliable without being valid but cannot be valid without being reliable: reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. asked 5 times Wechsler scaled scores have a mean of 10 and an SD of 3 (range 1 to 19): 10 is the 50th percentile, 7 is 1 SD below (about the 16th, low average), 13 is 1 SD above and 4 is 2 SD below. asked 5 times The Rorschach (Hermann Rorschach, Psychodiagnostik , 1921) has 10 symmetrical inkblot cards: 5 achromatic (I, IV, V, VI, VII), 2 black and red (II, III) and 3 multicoloured (VIII, IX, X), so five achromatic and five chromatic. asked 5 times The Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test (Lauretta Bender, 1938; nine figures adapted from Wertheimer, 16 in Bender-Gestalt II, 2003) assesses visual-motor integration and screens for organic brain damage and developmental immaturity; it is not a personality test. asked 5 times The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery (Halstead 1947; Reitan) is a fixed battery for comprehensive neuropsychological assessment (Category Test, Tactual Performance, Seashore Rhythm, Speech-Sounds Perception, Finger Tapping, Trail Making); an Impairment Index of 0.5 or more suggests brain damage, and the Rorschach is not part of it. asked 5 times The BDI-II (Aaron Beck, 1996) is a self-report inventory of 21 items rated 0 to 3 for the past two weeks: 0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate, 29 to 63 severe. asked 5 times Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN), the proportion of people with the condition whom the test correctly identifies; specificity = TN / (TN + FP), the proportion without it whom the test correctly clears. asked 4 times Construct validity (Cronbach and Meehl, 1955) is the degree to which a test measures the theoretical construct it claims to measure; convergent validity is a high correlation with measures of the same construct and discriminant validity a low correlation with measures of unrelated constructs. asked 4 times T scores (McCall, 1922) have a mean of 50 and an SD of 10 (T = 50 + 10z) and are used on the MMPI and NEO-PI-R; T 70 is 2 SD above the mean (original MMPI cut-off) and T 65 is 1.5 SD above (MMPI-2 cut-off). asked 4 times The z score , z = (X − M) ÷ SD, has a mean of 0 and an SD of 1, expresses a score's distance from the mean in SD units and lets results from different distributions be compared. asked 4 times Stanines run from 1 to 9 (mean 5, SD about 2) in the proportions 4, 7, 12, 17, 20, 17, 12, 7, 4 per cent; stanine 5 holds 20 per cent, the 40th to 60th percentile (mean ± 0.25 SD), and is a normalised, non-linear transformation. asked 4 times The Vineland Social Maturity Scale was devised by Edgar A. Doll (1935, Vineland Training School): 117 items from birth to adulthood (25 and above), given by informant interview, yielding social age and social quotient (SQ = SA / CA × 100). asked 4 times A Likert scale is a summated rating scale (Rensis Likert, 1932): closed-ended statements with a fixed number of ordered alternatives, usually five from strongly agree to strongly disagree, rated by respondents and summed with equal weights. It is a type of attitude scale, not a level of measurement. asked 4 times

title: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 3: Social Psychology
text: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 3: Social Psychology Chapter 3 of the one-volume Final Exam Textbook, all nine JSS subjects in one book. Both A4 PDFs hold the whole book with the same page numbers. A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (975 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (975 pages) Chapter 3 Social Psychology In this chapter 3.1 Social Psychology: History, Theories, Concepts and Methods : Define social psychology and set it apart from its neighbours, trace its history from Le Bon, Triplett and Lewin to the replication crisis, use the sociological ideas of anomie, socialisation, status and role, match the main theories to their founders, and outline the field's methods and research ethics. 3.2 Social Cognition and First Impressions : Explain how people think about the social world (cognitive misers, dual processes, schemas, priming, heuristics and the errors of social thought), recognise the self-fulfilling prophecy and the halo effect, and describe how first impressions form, how accurate thin slices are and how people manage the impressions they make. 3.3 Communication, Nonverbal Cues and Attribution : Trace a message through the communication process and its classic models, read nonverbal cues and personal space, explain behaviour with the attribution theories of Heider, Jones and Davis, Kelley and Weiner, and recognise each attributional bias from its description. 3.4 Attitudes, Persuasion and Cognitive Dissonance : Define attitudes, their components, strength and functions, explain how they form and when they predict behaviour (reasoned action, planned behaviour, MODE), analyse persuasion through the Yale factors and the elaboration likelihood model, explain resistance (reactance, forewarning, inoculation), and apply balance and cognitive dissonance theory with its classic paradigms and rivals. 3.5 Stereotypes, Prejudice and Intergroup Relations : Distinguish stereotype, prejudice and discrimination, explain where prejudice comes from (personality, frustration, learning, realistic conflict and social identity), describe the processes that sustain stereotypes and the barriers they create at work, and state when contact reduces prejudice. 3.6 Affiliation, Attraction and Close Relationships : Explain why people affiliate and compare themselves with others, what draws them together, how exchange, equity and investment theories account for staying or leaving, and how self-disclosure, love, break-up and loneliness are described and measured. 3.7 Social Influence: Conformity, Compliance, Obedience and Power : Tell apart conformity, compliance and obedience, explain why people conform or resist, and recall the classic studies of Sherif, Asch, Milgram and Zimbardo, Cialdini's compliance principles and tactics, and French and Raven's bases of power. 3.8 Prosocial Behaviour: Why and When People Help : Explain why and when people help: the empathy-altruism, egoistic, evolutionary and normative accounts, the bystander effect with its five-step model and its two classic explanations, and the situations, personalities and recipient reactions that raise or lower helping. 3.9 Aggression: Its Roots, Causes and Control : Define aggression and its forms, compare the instinct, biological, frustration-aggression, learning and General Aggression Model explanations, link each major cause of aggression to its researchers, and judge which methods of control work and why catharsis fails. 3.10 Groups: Structure, Performance, Decisions and Leadership : Define a group and its structure, map a group with sociometry, order Tuckman's stages, predict when the presence of others raises or lowers effort and performance, diagnose and prevent group polarisation and groupthink, and compare the main theories of leadership. 3.11 Applied Social Psychology: Law, Culture and Social Work : Apply social psychology to health, environment, eyewitnesses, juries and offenders, and name the roots, methods, models, principles and pioneers of social work, from case work and group work to culturally sensitive practice, child welfare and the first Indian school. Weightage. 136 of the 3180 questions mapped in this book (4.3%) test this chapter, 93 of them from real past papers. 0 of its 11 sections are High yield. In the early hours of 13 March 1964, Catherine "Kitty" Genovese, a 28-year-old bar manager, parked her car near her flat in Kew Gardens, a quiet neighbourhood of Queens, New York, and started the short walk home. A stranger, Winston Moseley, chased her and stabbed her. A neighbour shouted from a window and Moseley fled, but about ten minutes later he came back, found her lying wounded in a hallway at the back of her building, and attacked her again. She died on the way to hospital. Two weeks later The New York Times put the killing on its front page. For more than half an hour, it reported, 38 respectable, law-abiding citizens had watched a killer stalk and stab a woman, and not one had telephoned the police during the attack. The story went round the world as proof of big-city apathy. Two young psychologists in New York, John Darley and Bibb Latane, suspected another explanation: perhaps each witness, knowing that others could also hear, assumed that someone else would act. They staged an emergency in the laboratory, reported in 1968, in which students talking over an intercom heard another student apparently have a seizure. The more listeners a student believed were present, the less likely that student was to go for help. The finding became one of the most famous in psychology, yet the newspaper story behind it was badly wrong. Later investigations, among them a 2007 review by the psychologists Rachel Manning, Mark Levine and Alan Collins, found no 38 watching witnesses: few neighbours saw any part of the attacks, most heard only a cry in the night, and one, Sophia Farrar, went down and held Kitty in her arms as she lay dying. In 2016 the Times itself conceded that its report had exaggerated the number of witnesses and what they saw. One night in Queens thus holds social psychology in small: how the presence of others changes what each of us does, and how a whole society can come to share a story that is not quite true. 3.1 Social Psychology: History, Theories, Concepts and Methods Lower yield · 6 Qs Why do you drive more carefully with your father beside you? Social psychology asks how other people, present or imagined, shape what we think, feel and do. This section defines the field, traces its history, and covers its sociological roots, theories and methods. What social psychology studies The classic definition is that of Gordon Willard Allport (1897 to 1967), from 1954: social psychology studies how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others: an audience in the hall, a mother whose frown you picture, a "No smoking" sign left by strangers. Robert A. Baron and Nyla R. Branscombe call it the scientific study of the nature and causes of individual behaviour, feeling and thought in social situations: scientific because evidence settles questions, individual because the unit is the person, even in a crowd. Behaviour reflects the person-situation interaction : a student silent in class talks freely among friends. Psychological social psychology studies the individual's mental processes, mostly by experiment; sociological social psychology studies how groups, roles and social structure shape people, mostly by surveys and observation, drawing on symbolic interactionism ( below ). Sociology proper studies groups and societies, and personality psychology stable differences between people (Chapter 4); social psychology asks how situations make different people act alike. Common sense has a proverb for every outcome ("birds of a feather flock together", yet "opposites attract"), and hindsight bias (Section 1.8) makes findings look obvious afterwards; only testing shows which holds when. Exam trap "Actual, imagined or implied presence of others" is Gordon Allport (1954), though Baron and Branscombe credit it to his brother Floyd (1924). "Nature and causes of individual behaviour ... in social situations" is Baron and Branscombe . Founders and landmarks Two roots, crowds and experiments, fed the field (Table 3.1). Le Bon's crowd mind, Ringelmann's rope pullers (each pulled less hard as the team grew) and Triplett's children, who wound fishing reels faster in pairs than alone in what is usually called the first social psychology experiment, are taught in Section 3.10. The first two textbooks (1908) pulled opposite ways: the British psychologist William McDougall traced social behaviour to inborn instincts, the American sociologist Edward Alsworth Ross to imitation and suggestion in crowds. Floyd Henry Allport (1924) made the field experimental and individual-centred, and Muzafer Sherif (1935, 1936) watched group norms form as people judged the apparent movement of a light in the dark (Section 3.7). Table 3.1 Landmarks in the history of social psychology. Year Who Landmark 1895 Gustave Le Bon The Crowd : contagion, the crowd mind 1898 Norman Triplett First experiment: others speed us up 1908 McDougall; Ross First textbooks: instinct; imitation 1913 Max Ringelmann Rope pulling: effort falls in groups 1924 Floyd Allport Experimental, individual-centred text 1935, 1936 Muzafer Sherif Norm formation (autokinetic effect) 1939 Lewin, Ronald Lippitt , Ralph K. White Leadership climates 1945 to 1947 Kurt Lewin Group dynamics, action research, T-groups 1950 Theodor W. Adorno and colleagues The Authoritarian Personality 1951 Solomon Asch Conformity to a wrong majority 1953 Carl Hovland and colleagues Yale persuasion research 1954, 1957 Leon Festinger Social comparison; cognitive dissonance 1958 Fritz Heider The Psychology of Interpersonal Relations 1961 Serge Moscovici Social representations 1963 Stanley Milgram Obedience 1971 Philip Zimbardo Stanford prison study 1973 Kenneth Gergen "Social psychology as history" 2010s Many teams Replication crisis Kurt Lewin Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947), a Gestalt-trained refugee from Nazi Germany, is called the father of modern experimental social psychology. His field theory (Section 1.2) states B = f(P, E): behaviour is a function of the person and the environment, together the life space , the person plus the psychological environment as it exists for that person at that moment, not society, the group or the physical setting. Lewin wanted research to change real life. In 1945 he founded the Research Center for Group Dynamics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT); group dynamics is the study of forces within groups. In 1946 he described action research , done with the people affected, as a spiral of steps, each a circle of planning, action and fact-finding about the results (Figure 3.1). A 1946 workshop produced the T-group (training group), whose members learn from frank feedback on their behaviour in the group, spread by the National Training Laboratories (1947) as sensitivity training. His motto: "There is nothing so practical as a good theory." Cycle 1 Cycle 2 Plan Act Fact-find results shape the next plan Revised plan Act Fact-find next cycle Done with the people affected, not on them Figure 3.1 Lewin's action research (1946): fact-finding about each action feeds a revised plan. Exam trap Life space = person + psychological environment, not society, group or physical environment. Lewin founded action research , not psychoanalysis (Freud), psychophysics (Fechner) or functionalism (James). Crisis and new directions After 1945 the field grew around the war's questions: persuasion, prejudice, conformity and obedience (Table 3.1). By the late 1960s a crisis had set in: laboratory experiments on students looked artificial, ethically doubtful and culture-bound, and Kenneth J. Gergen argued in "Social psychology as history" (1973) that its findings describe one society at one moment, not timeless laws. Europeans made the field more social: Henri Tajfel (1919 to 1982) studied group identity (Section 3.5), and Serge Moscovici minorities and shared knowledge. Then came the social cognition era of the 1970s and 1980s (Section 3.2), social neuroscience (the brain activity behind social thought), implicit processes (automatic attitudes outside awareness, measured by the Implicit Association Test, 1998) and cultural psychology (how culture shapes social thought and behaviour). In the 2010s the replication crisis broke: when 100 published psychology studies were repeated in 2015, only about a third gave the original result. Sociological roots: Durkheim to Mead Emile Durkheim (1858 to 1917), founder of French sociology, treated society as a reality in its own right. Social facts are ways of acting, thinking and feeling that exist outside individuals and constrain them, such as laws and customs; collective representations are the ideas and symbols a society shares. His most examined idea is anomie : normlessness, a state in which social norms are unclear, weak or no longer apply, so people no longer know what is expected of them. He introduced it in The Division of Labour in Society (1893); in Suicide (1897), anomic suicide rises when sudden change, a crash or a windfall, unsettles the norms. Robert King Merton (1910 to 2003) recast anomie as strain (1938), a gap between cultural goals such as wealth and the legitimate means to them, met by conformity, innovation (illegitimate means such as fraud), ritualism (rules kept, goal dropped), retreatism (both rejected) or rebellion (both replaced). Exam trap Anomie = normlessness. The progression from traditional to modern society is modernisation : Durkheim's mechanical solidarity (bonds of sameness) giving way to organic solidarity (interdependent specialists), or Ferdinand Tonnies 's (1887) Gemeinschaft (community) giving way to Gesellschaft (society). Adapting to a dominant culture's values is assimilation or acculturation ; internalising society's norms is socialisation . A second root is symbolic interactionism : people act towards things according to the meanings those things have for them, and meanings, and the self, are built in interaction through symbols, above all language. George Herbert Mead (1863 to 1931) founded it; students published his lectures as Mind, Self and Society (1934), and Herbert Blumer named it in 1937. Charles Horton Cooley (1864 to 1929) added the looking-glass self (1902: we imagine how we appear to others, imagine their judgement and feel pride or shame; Chapter 4) and the primary group (1909), such as the family. Socialisation and resocialisation Socialisation is the lifelong learning of a society's norms, values and roles until they become one's own: primary in childhood within the family, secondary through school, peers, work and the media, the other agents of socialisation (gender socialisation is in Chapter 6). Merton's anticipatory socialisation is adopting a group's norms before joining it, as a medical aspirant already talks like a doctor. Resocialisation is unlearning old norms, values and roles and learning new ones after a major transition: college, migration, marriage, the army or prison. A student's first weeks at college, before she finds friends and fits in, are a mild case. It is most intense in the total institutions described by Erving Goffman (1922 to 1982) in Asylums (1961), such as prisons, mental hospitals and barracks, which cut people off from society, manage all of daily life and strip away the old identity. Clinical link Long-stay inmates may develop institutionalisation : apathy, lost initiative, submissiveness and dependence on routine. Russell Barton called it institutional neurosis (1959), a product of the institution rather than the illness (Chapter 7). Exam trap A newcomer adapting to college, a new country or the army shows resocialisation , not the looking-glass self (a self-image built from imagined judgements), self-awareness (attention turned on oneself) or institutionalisation (the dependent apathy of long-stay inmates). Status and roles A status is a position in a group: ascribed if given at birth (sex, caste), achieved if earned (doctor), in Ralph Linton 's distinction (1936). A role is the behaviour expected of whoever holds a status. Table 3.2 separates the easily confused terms; Zimbardo's prison study shows the power of roles (Section 3.7). Table 3.2 The vocabulary of roles. Term Meaning Example Role expectation What others expect of the person in a position Patients expect a doctor to listen Role taking (Mead) Seeing a situation from another's viewpoint: one person at a time (play stage), all the players at once (game stage), then the community, the generalised other A fielder reading the bowler and wicketkeeper Playing at a role A young child's imitative make-believe Playing "teacher" to dolls Role playing (role enactment) The behaviour a person actually engages in while enacting a role A new teacher taking her first class Role conflict Clashing demands: inter-role (between roles) or intra-role (within one) Mother and employee on a sick child's day Role strain ( William J. Goode , 1960) Felt difficulty in meeting one role's obligations A student with too many deadlines Role set (Merton, 1957) All the role partners of one status A student's teachers, classmates, parents Role ambiguity Unclear expectations A job with no job description Exam trap "The behaviour an individual engages in while enacting a role" is role playing . Role taking is mental (seeing through another's eyes), playing at a role is a child's make-believe, and role expectation lies in other people, not in the performer. Theoretical perspectives The field works with several theories (Table 3.3), most taught where they are used. Table 3.3 Theoretical perspectives in social psychology. Theory Theorist, year Core idea Field theory Kurt Lewin B = f(P, E) Cognitive consistency Heider (1958); Festinger (1957) We strive for consistent beliefs Social exchange George C. Homans (1961); John Thibaut and Harold Kelley (1959); Peter Blau (1964) Relationships weighed by rewards and costs Social learning, social cognitive Albert Bandura Learning by observing models Psychoanalytic group psychology Sigmund Freud (1921) Members idealise the leader and identify with one another Sociobiology, evolutionary Edward O. Wilson (1975) Natural selection shapes social behaviour; kin selection Social representations Serge Moscovici (1961) Shared common-sense theories Social identity Tajfel and John Turner (1979) Self-esteem from group membership Uncertainty-identity Michael A. Hogg Group identity reduces self-uncertainty Need to belong Roy F. Baumeister and Mark R. Leary (1995) A basic drive for lasting bonds Sociometer Mark R. Leary Self-esteem gauges acceptance Role theory Mead; Ralph Linton (1936) Behaviour follows the roles people occupy Social constructionism Kenneth Gergen (1985) Knowledge is built socially, not discovered Dual-process models Petty and Cacioppo, others Fast automatic versus slow deliberate thinking Liberation psychology Ignacio Martin-Baro Psychology from the viewpoint of the oppressed A social representation is a shared, changing system of values, ideas and practices, a common-sense theory through which a group makes the unfamiliar familiar: a collective successor to Durkheim's collective representations. Key study: Moscovici and psychoanalysis in France (1961) Serge Moscovici (1925 to 2014), a Romanian-born French psychologist, asked in La Psychanalyse, son image et son public (1961) how a scientific theory becomes common sense. Surveying Parisians and analysing the Catholic, Communist and popular press, he found each group remaking psychoanalysis by anchoring , fitting the unfamiliar into a familiar category (analysis seen as a kind of confession), and objectification , turning an abstract idea into a concrete thing (a "complex" became something a person has , like a cold). Critics find the concept too broad to test precisely. Exam trap Social representations = Serge Moscovici . Michael A. Hogg is social identity and uncertainty-identity theory; Baumeister and Leary proposed the need to belong, and Leary the sociometer. Methods and ethics Social psychology uses the methods of Chapter 9 (Table 3.4). A theory predicts; results support or revise it, never prove it. Table 3.4 Research methods in social psychology. Method What it does, and its catch Systematic observation Records behaviour, often in natural settings (naturalistic); participant observers join the group, and may alter it Survey Questions large samples; self-report bias Correlational Measures how two variables co-vary; correlation is not causation Laboratory experiment Manipulates an independent variable, measures a dependent variable; shows cause, can be artificial Field experiment Experiment in a natural setting; realistic, less control Quasi-experiment Compares existing groups without random assignment; cause uncertain Archival Analyses existing records; no reactivity Cross-cultural Compares cultures; tests generality Meta-analysis Statistically combines many studies into one overall effect size Random assignment, giving every participant an equal chance of any condition, lets an experiment show cause. Elliot Aronson and J. Merrill Carlsmith (1968) separated experimental realism , how far a study absorbs participants, from mundane realism , how far it resembles everyday life; Milgram's study had much of the first, little of the second. External validity is how far results generalise. A mediating variable explains how or why one variable affects another (a violent film raises aggressive thoughts, which raise aggression); a moderating variable changes when or for whom it does (more in people already angry). Deception, misleading participants about a study's purpose so they behave naturally, needs two safeguards: informed consent beforehand (what they will do, and that they may leave at any time) and debriefing afterwards, by dehoaxing (revealing the deception) and desensitising (removing distress, such as the belief that one is cruel). The Milgram and Zimbardo controversies made both standard (Section 3.7). Participants also respond to demand characteristics , cues revealing what the experimenter hopes to find ( Martin Orne , 1962), and experimenters bias results through expectancy effects ( Robert Rosenthal , 1966); double-blind procedures guard against both. Indian context Gardner Murphy led a UNESCO study of social tensions in India, In the Minds of Men (1953). Durganand Sinha (1922 to 1998) urged indigenising psychology (Section 1.2), Jai B. P. Sinha proposed the nurturant-task leader (Section 3.10) and Udai Pareek (1925 to 2010) studied role stress. Research centres on caste, communal relations and poverty. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Allport: the actual, imagined or presence of others. Lewin's life space is the person plus the environment. Lewin founded research: planning, action and fact-finding. Durkheim's term for normlessness is . Unlearning old norms and learning new ones at college is . Behaviour performed while enacting a role is role . Social representations theory (1961) is 's. Cues revealing the experimenter's hypothesis are characteristics. Answers: (1) implied, (2) psychological, (3) action, (4) anomie, (5) resocialisation, (6) playing, (7) Serge Moscovici, (8) demand 3.2 Social Cognition and First Impressions Lower yield · 7 Qs A stranger sits down at your hostel mess table, and within seconds you have judged him friendly, clever or arrogant; from then on you notice what fits. This section follows social thought from the frameworks that store it, through the shortcuts and tilts that bend it, to the impressions we form of others and manage in ourselves. The social thinker Social cognition is how we interpret, analyse, remember and use information about the social world. Susan Fiske and Shelley Taylor (1984) called people cognitive misers : with limited capacity and a flood of social information, we save effort with shortcuts and settle for good-enough answers. In their 1991 revision the thinker became a motivated tactician , choosing shortcuts or careful thought according to goals and stakes: you skim a passing stranger but study an interviewer's face. That choice is dual-process thinking. Automatic processing is fast, effortless, unintended and often unconscious; controlled processing is slow, effortful, deliberate and conscious (System 1 and System 2, Section 1.8). Fatigue and time pressure push us onto the automatic track. The dominant account of how people organise social information in memory and use it to understand behaviour is the schema approach . Exam trap "How people organise information in memory and use it to understand behaviour" = the schema approach . A motivational approach explains social thought by needs and goals; a perceptual approach treats knowing people like perceiving objects (Asch's Gestalt view, below); "organisational approach" merely echoes the stem's verb. Schemas, priming and perseverance A schema is an organised mental framework, built from experience, that holds our knowledge about a person, group, role or event and guides how we take in new information (Bartlett's idea, Section 1.7). Table 3.5 lists the kinds. Table 3.5 Kinds of social schema. Schema What it holds Example Person schema Traits and goals of a person or type Your cautious uncle Self-schema Beliefs about oneself ( Hazel Markus , 1977; Chapter 4) "I am a good debater" Role schema Expected behaviour in a role What a professor does Event schema or script The usual sequence of an event ( Roger Schank and Robert Abelson , 1977) Eating at a restaurant Group schema or stereotype Traits assumed of a group (Section 3.5) "Engineers are logical" Schemas steer attention towards what fits, shape encoding (consistent information is stored readily, though a sharply inconsistent event stands out) and bias retrieval towards schema-consistent details. Recently activated schemas dominate. Priming is a temporary rise in a schema's availability: after a violent film, a driver who takes your parking spot looks aggressive. Automatic priming works below awareness: John Bargh , Mark Chen and Lara Burrows (1996) had students unscramble sentences containing words linked to old age (bingo, Florida), and they then walked down the corridor more slowly. It failed to replicate: Stéphane Doyen and colleagues (2012), timing walkers with infrared sensors, found slowing only when experimenters expected it. A primed schema fades by unpriming once it is expressed in thought or action (Betsy Sparrow and Daniel Wegner, 2006). Schemas also resist disconfirmation, the perseverance effect . In the classic study of belief perseverance , Lee Ross , Mark Lepper and Michael Hubbard (1975) gave students false feedback that they were good or poor at telling real suicide notes from fakes; told later that the feedback was invented, they still rated their ability in line with it. Confirmation bias (Section 1.8) keeps schemas alive. Even figures of speech prime schemas: in reasoning by metaphor we grasp an abstract idea through a concrete one ("our relationship is on the right track"), and the metaphor shapes the judgement. Worst of all, a schema can make itself come true. The self-fulfilling prophecy The sociologist Robert King Merton (1910 to 2003) named and formalised the self-fulfilling prophecy in 1948: "a false definition of the situation evoking a new behaviour which makes the originally false conception come true." A rumour that a sound bank is failing starts a run on it, and it fails. In social psychology the term covers any expectation, about oneself or another, that leads us to act in ways that make the expected event or behaviour more likely (Figure 3.2). 1. Perceiver's belief "This child will bloom" 2. Perceiver's behaviour More warmth, praise and challenge 3. Target's response Child engages and improves 4. Belief confirmed "I knew she was bright" the cycle repeats Figure 3.2 The self-fulfilling prophecy: the perceiver's expectation draws matching behaviour from the target, which seems to prove it. Key study: Pygmalion in the Classroom (1968) Robert Rosenthal (born 1933) and Lenore Jacobson tested every child in a Californian elementary school and told teachers that about 20 percent, in fact chosen at random, would soon "bloom" academically. Eight months later these children had gained more IQ points than their classmates, most clearly in the first two grades; teachers had given them more warmth and challenge. Critics questioned the IQ measures; later reviews find expectancy effects real but usually small. A high expectation that raises performance is the Pygmalion effect (Rosenthal effect), after the sculptor whose statue came to life; a low one that depresses it is the Golem effect (Elisha Babad, Jacinto Inbar and Rosenthal, 1982). A perceiver's expectation drawing matching behaviour from the target is behavioural confirmation . Mark Snyder , Elizabeth Tanke and Ellen Berscheid (1977) gave men a photograph, attractive or not, of the woman they would telephone (it was not her); judges hearing only the women's side rated the "attractive" women warmer and more sociable. Carl Word, Mark Zanna and Joel Cooper (1974) found that white interviewers sat farther away and ended interviews sooner with Black applicants; white applicants treated this coolly then performed worse. Exam trap Acting on an expectation until it comes true = self-fulfilling prophecy . Confirmation bias only seeks confirming evidence and changes nothing in the world; the base-rate fallacy ignores how common something is (Section 1.8); "motivational reaction" is not a term. Merton formalised it, not Erving Goffman (dramaturgy, below; stigma, 1963; total institutions), Charles Horton Cooley (1864 to 1929; looking-glass self, 1902; primary group) or Émile Durkheim (1858 to 1917; anomie, a state of normlessness). Heuristics in social judgement Why shortcuts? Because of information overload : demands exceed our capacity, so we use heuristics , simple rules giving quick, usually adequate judgements ( Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman , 1974; Section 1.8). Representativeness judges a quiet, bookish neighbour a librarian, ignoring that managers far outnumber librarians (base-rate neglect). Availability judges by ease of recall: people who recalled six of their own assertive acts rated themselves more assertive than those asked for a harder twelve ( Norbert Schwarz and colleagues, 1991). Anchoring and adjustment starts from a value, such as an asking price, and adjusts too little. The status quo heuristic ("what is, is good") favours the established: the same chocolate tasted better when said to be on sale since 1937 rather than 2003. The affect heuristic (Paul Slovic) lets a feeling of liking or dread stand in for judging risk and benefit.
