Ironic rebound arises because an automatic monitoring process keeps checking for the forbidden thought, and so keeps it primed. Terror management theory (Jeff Greenberg, Sheldon Solomon and Tom Pyszczynski, 1986) holds that awareness of certain death creates anxiety we buffer with cultural world-views, self-esteem and supernatural beliefs. Feeling also steers thought. In mood-congruent judgement we notice, recall and judge in line with our mood (Section 1.7). Using affect as information we ask "how do I feel about it?": people telephoned on sunny days reported more life satisfaction than on rainy days, unless first asked about the weather, which let them discount their mood (Schwarz and Gerald Clore, 1983). Joseph Forgas 's affect infusion model (1995) adds that mood seeps into judgements we must construct, but hardly into ready-made or goal-driven ones. Forming impressions Impression formation is the combining of information about a person into an overall judgement. Its founding experiment used only adjectives. Key study: Asch's warm and cold stranger (1946) Solomon Asch (1907 to 1996), a Gestalt thinker, read participants a stranger's traits: intelligent, skilful, industrious, warm , determined, practical, cautious. Others heard cold instead. The warm stranger was judged far more generous, happy and sociable; swapping polite for blunt changed little. Warm-cold were central traits , which reorganise the whole impression; polite-blunt were peripheral traits . Traits, Asch concluded, form an integrated whole rather than a sum. Critics later showed that centrality depends on context. Asch also showed a primacy effect : a person described as "intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious" was liked more than one given the same words in reverse, because early traits set the meaning of later ones. Harold Kelley (1950) told students a guest lecturer was "rather cold" or "very warm"; after the same class, the warm group rated him more considerate and sociable, and more of them joined the discussion. Such leaps rest on implicit personality theories , unspoken beliefs about which traits go together ("warm people are generous"), a term of Jerome Bruner and Renato Tagiuri (1954). Their best-known product is the halo effect : an overall impression, or one salient positive trait, colours ratings of other, unrelated traits. Edward Lee Thorndike named it in 1920: army officers who rated a soldier high on physique also rated him high on intelligence, loyalty and leadership. The negative version is the horns effect . "What is beautiful is good" is a halo from attractiveness (Section 3.6); in rating scales the halo is a rater error (Chapter 2). Exam trap Halo effect = an overall impression or one positive trait influencing ratings of other, specific traits. Not judging by group membership (stereotyping, Section 3.5); not initial impressions shaping later judgements (primacy, or anchoring); not overlooking a liked person's faults (a consequence of a halo, not its definition); not crediting oneself for success and circumstances for failure (self-serving bias, Section 3.3); not overestimating how far others share our opinions (false consensus, Table 3.6). In Norman Anderson 's information integration theory (1965) each trait has a value and a weight. An additive model sums them, so adding "punctual" to "brilliant, generous" should help; a weighted averaging model , which the evidence mostly favours, averages them, so the impression dips. By the negativity effect , negative traits weigh more because bad behaviour seems more revealing. Thin slices and first impressions How fast and how good is a first impression? Nalini Ambady and Rosenthal (1992) named thin slicing : accurate inferences about people from very brief samples of behaviour. In 1993 they showed students silent clips of college teachers lasting 30 seconds or less (later as little as six); ratings of the clips predicted the teachers' end-of-semester student evaluations. Malcolm Gladwell popularised the idea in Blink (2005). Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov (2006) found that a 100-millisecond look at a face yields trait judgements, trustworthiness above all, that correlate highly with unhurried ones; longer looks mainly raise confidence. Thin slices beat chance but are not infallible. Exam trap A teacher who watches two students for under a minute and correctly picks the class leader shows thin slicing . Not social facilitation (better performance of well-learned tasks before others, Section 3.10), not a self-fulfilling prophecy (her expectation did not create the leadership), not the fundamental attribution error (over-explaining others' behaviour by disposition, Section 3.3). Managing the impressions we make We also try to control the impressions others form of us: impression management , or self-presentation . Erving Goffman (1922 to 1982) framed it as theatre in The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959). In his dramaturgy , on the front stage we play a role before an audience (the doctor's calm on the ward); back stage we drop it (doctors joking in the staff room). Face-work maintains one's own and others' face, the positive social value claimed in an encounter. Tactics are self-enhancement , raising one's own appeal (grooming, recounting achievements), or other-enhancement , making the target feel good, chiefly ingratiation , winning liking through flattery and agreement, analysed by Edward E. In self-handicapping people create an obstacle in advance to excuse possible failure: Steven Berglas and Jones's (1978) students, given unearned success on unsolvable problems, chose a drug said to impair performance before a retest. By the spotlight effect we overestimate how much others notice us: students in an embarrassing T-shirt guessed half the room noticed, when about a quarter did (Gilovich, Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky, 2000). The illusion of transparency overestimates how well others read our inner states, such as nervousness. Does it work? Usually: applicants who use it get higher interview ratings. Merton, (4) downward, (5) central, (6) halo; Edward Thorndike, (7) thin slicing. 3.3 Communication, Nonverbal Cues and Attribution Lower yield · 12 Qs A friend answers your long message with one word: "ok." Is she busy, annoyed, or simply brief? Two processes are at work: communication, which carries meaning from one head to another through words, faces, gestures and distances, and attribution, by which you decide why someone acted as they did. This section follows the message first, then turns to the rules, and the biases, by which we explain behaviour. The communication process and its models Communication is the process by which a person or group transmits information, ideas and feelings to another through shared symbols. Every exchange has the same parts (Figure 3.3). The sender, or source, first performs encoding , turning an idea into symbols such as words or a gesture. The message travels through a channel , the medium that carries it (speech, print, a phone screen, the face). The receiver, or recipient, performs decoding , turning the symbols back into meaning, and replies with feedback . Anything that distorts the message on the way is noise . Noise (distortion) Sender (source) Encoding idea to code Channel the medium Recipient (receiver) Decoding code to idea Feedback: the recipient responds Figure 3.3 The communication process: encoding, channel, recipient, decoding. Noise (dashed arrow) distorts the message in the channel; feedback (dotted line) makes the exchange two-way. Exam trap The sequence is encoding, channel, recipient, decoding : a message must be encoded before it can enter a channel, and received before it can be decoded. Table 3.8 compares four classic models: those of Harold Lasswell (1902 to 1978); Claude Shannon (1916 to 2001) and Warren Weaver (1894 to 1978); Wilbur Schramm (1907 to 1987), for whom a message is understood only where the parties' fields of experience (language, culture, knowledge) overlap; and David Berlo (1929 to 1996), whose SMCR model adds the source's and receiver's skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture. Table 3.8 Four classic models of communication. Model Year Elements Remembered for Lasswell 1948 Who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect Verbal, linear; no feedback Shannon and Weaver 1949 Source, transmitter, channel, noise, receiver, destination Linear; introduced noise Schramm 1954 Each party encodes, interprets and decodes Circular; field of experience Berlo (SMCR) 1960 Source, message, channel, receiver Skills, attitudes, knowledge, culture Verbal communication uses words; nonverbal communication uses everything else. In one-way communication (a lecture, a notice) the receiver cannot reply; in two-way communication feedback flows back, which is slower but more accurate. Barriers are semantic (words or jargon understood differently), physical (noise, distance, a poor network), psychological (anxiety, anger, prejudice, inattention) and cultural (different norms for gestures, eye contact and directness). In the communication networks studied by Alex Bavelas (1913 to 1993) in 1950 and Harold Leavitt (1922 to 2007) in 1951, small groups solved problems by passing notes along fixed links. The centralised wheel , everyone linked only to a hub, was fastest and most accurate on simple tasks, and the hub became leader, but the others were least satisfied. The chain was intermediate. The decentralised circle was slower, with no clear leader but the highest morale, and in the later all-channel network everyone talks to everyone, which suits complex problems (Section 3.10). Nonverbal channels and personal space Nonverbal communication is the exchange of information through facial expression, gaze, body movement, posture, touch, voice and even scent, apart from the meaning of words. Such cues are hard to suppress, so hidden feelings leak through them. As Section 1.11 showed, Paul Ekman (born 1934) and Wallace Friesen found six universally recognised expressions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust), with contempt added in 1986, while cultures differ in display rules about when and how strongly an emotion may be shown. The facial feedback hypothesis is also in Section 1.11. Eye contact usually signals liking, and avoided eyes suggest dislike or shyness, but staring , gaze held regardless of what the other person does, signals hostility and makes people leave. Body language includes posture (an open posture signals ease, frequent self-touching nervousness) and gestures, the most specific being emblems with a fixed meaning in one culture, such as the namaste or the Indian head wobble meaning "all right". Ray Birdwhistell (1918 to 1994) founded kinesics , the study of body movement as communication ( Introduction to Kinesics , 1952). Touch conveys affection, care or dominance depending on who touches whom and where. Paralanguage is the voice apart from the words (pitch, tone, loudness, rate, pauses), which is why "fine" can mean its opposite. Even scent is a channel: subtle changes in body odour, such as those across the menstrual cycle, can affect others who do not consciously notice them. Edward T. Hall (1914 to 2009) coined proxemics (1963), the study of how people use interpersonal distance, and in The Hidden Dimension (1966) described four zones (Figure 3.4). He measured them among Americans; contact cultures (Arab, Latin American) stand closer. In Beyond Culture (1976) he contrasted high-context cultures , where meaning lies largely in the setting, the relationship and nonverbal cues, so speech is indirect (India, Japan, China), with low-context cultures, where explicit words carry it (the United States, Germany). An Indian "I will try to come" may be a polite no. Learn the boundaries: 18 inches, 4 feet, 12 feet and 25 feet. Detecting deception Can nonverbal cues expose a lie? Four help. Microexpressions are fleeting facial expressions, lasting a fraction of a second, that leak a concealed emotion before it is masked. Interchannel discrepancies are mismatches between channels: a liar may control the face but not the voice or hands. Eye contact changes: liars blink more, have more dilated pupils, and show too little or unusually much eye contact. Exaggerated expressions, an overdone smile or excessive regret, are the fourth sign, and vocal pitch tends to rise. Yet a meta-analysis of more than 200 studies by Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo (2006) found accuracy of only about 54 percent, barely above chance, and truths were spotted more often than lies because people assume honesty. Exam trap Averted eyes do not reliably mark a lie: liars may stare to look honest. No single cue betrays a lie, and most judges stay near chance. Heider, Jones and Davis: from acts to causes Attribution is the process by which people infer the causes of their own and others' behaviour. Fritz Heider (1896 to 1988), in The Psychology of Interpersonal Relations (1958), described people as amateur scientists; his naive psychology (common-sense psychology) concerns the implicit rules they use to infer causes. His key distinction: a dispositional attribution (internal) locates the cause in the person (traits, abilities, attitudes, effort), while a situational attribution (external) locates it outside (the situation, other people, the environment, luck, roles, culture). "He failed because he is lazy" is dispositional; "the paper was unusually hard" is situational. Exam trap Causes resting on the actor's personality traits are dispositional ; situational, environmental and cultural causes are all external. Matching: Heider = implicit rules of attribution; Fred Fiedler (1922 to 2017) = contingency theory of leadership (Section 3.10); Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) = unconscious conflict; Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) = social learning theory. Edward E. Jones and Keith Davis asked when an act reveals a trait. By their correspondent inference theory (1965), we infer that behaviour corresponds to a stable disposition when it is (1) freely chosen; (2) produces non-common effects , outcomes that only the chosen option yields, which pinpoint the motive; and (3) low in social desirability, since out-of-role behaviour is more revealing: a guest who calls your mother's biryani too salty reveals more than one who praises it. Hedonic relevance (the act affects us) and personalism (it seems aimed at us) strengthen the inference. Kelley's covariation model and causal schemas Harold Kelley (1921 to 2003) asked whether a cause lies in the person, the stimulus or the circumstances. His covariation model (1967) says that, observing behaviour over several occasions, we attribute it to the cause it covaries with, using three kinds of information: Consensus : do other people react to this stimulus in the same way? Consistency : does this person react this way to the stimulus on other occasions? Distinctiveness : does this person react differently to other stimuli? Ananya laughs at a comedian. If few others laugh, she laughs at him every time and she laughs at every comedian (low, high, low), the cause is Ananya. If everyone laughs, she always does and she laughs at no other comedian (all high), the comedian is funny. If she has never laughed at him before (low consistency), a passing circumstance is responsible. Consistency is high in both main patterns, so only consensus and distinctiveness separate internal from external (Table 3.9). Table 3.9 Kelley's covariation model. Consensus Consistency Distinctiveness Attribution Low High Low Internal: the person High High High External: the stimulus Low High High Person and stimulus together Any Low Any A temporary circumstance For a single observation, Kelley (1972) proposed causal schemas. By the discounting principle , a cause gets less weight when other plausible causes exist (a film star is paid to praise a brand); by the augmenting principle , it gets more weight when the effect occurs despite an obstacle (a student tops the class while working nights). Weiner's three dimensions Bernard Weiner (born 1935), studying achievement from the 1970s, classified causes by locus (internal or external), stability and controllability . Ability is internal, stable and uncontrollable; effort is internal, unstable and controllable; task difficulty is external and stable; luck is external and unstable. Stability shapes expectations, and the dimensions shape emotion: success put down to internal causes brings pride; failure from low ability brings shame, from low effort guilt. Another person's misfortune seen as controllable ("he drank") provokes anger, and an uncontrollable one ("a lay-off") pity and helping (Section 3.8). Clinical link In the attributional reformulation of learned helplessness, Lyn Abramson , Martin Seligman (born 1942) and John Teasdale (1978) proposed that people who explain bad events by internal ("it is me"), stable ("it will last") and global ("it spoils everything") causes are most vulnerable to depression (Section 1.6; Chapter 8). Attributional biases Our attributions tilt in predictable directions (Table 3.10). The strongest tilt is the fundamental attribution error (FAE), named by Lee Ross (1942 to 2021) in 1977: overestimating dispositional and underestimating situational causes of other people's behaviour. A man arrives late and spills his coffee; we call him clumsy, not delayed and hurried. The correspondence bias , inferring dispositions that correspond to behaviour even when situational causes are present, is usually treated as a synonym (reviewed in 1995 by Daniel Gilbert , born 1957, and Patrick Malone ). Key study: Jones and Harris, the Castro essays (1967) Method. Jones and Victor Harris had participants read essays for or against Fidel Castro, telling some that the writer chose the side and others that it was assigned. Result. Even with assigned sides, pro-Castro writers were judged fairly pro-Castro. Conclusion. People underweight a situational constraint they know about. Criticism. Readers may assume nobody argues well for a view he rejects, but the bias replicates across many tasks. Why does it happen? The actor is perceptually salient while the situation fades into the background. In Gilbert's two-step model we first make an automatic dispositional inference, then effortfully correct it for the situation; under cognitive load the correction fails. For our own behaviour the tilt reverses. The actor-observer effect (Jones and Richard Nisbett , 1971) is attributing our own behaviour to situations and others' to dispositions: he trips because he is clumsy, I trip because the floor was wet. The actor sees the situation; the observer sees the actor. Michael Storms (1973) reversed the effect by showing actors and observers videotapes shot from the opposite viewpoint. The self-serving bias concerns our own outcomes: successes go to internal causes, failures to external ones (an unfair paper, bad luck); it protects self-esteem and is weaker in collectivist cultures. The just-world hypothesis of Melvin Lerner (1965, 1980) holds that people need to believe the world is orderly, predictable and fair, a place where people get what they deserve. An innocent person's suffering threatens the belief, which is restored by deciding the victim deserved it: victim blaming. In Lerner and Carolyn Simmons 's experiment (1966), women who watched a fellow student receive apparent electric shocks, and could not end or compensate her suffering, derogated her. Zick Rubin and Letitia Anne Peplau measured the belief with their Just World Scale (1975). Exam trap Just-world victim blaming comes from the need to believe that the world is orderly, predictable and fair , not from sadism, not from the FAE itself (it looks dispositional, but the motive is protecting the belief), and not from downward social comparison with someone worse off (Section 3.6). The optimism bias is in Section 3.2. Culture and applications Is the FAE truly fundamental? It is strongest in individualist cultures, which see the person as an independent agent, and weaker in collectivist ones, which see behaviour as embedded in roles and relationships. Indian context Joan Miller (1984) compared Hindu Indians in Mysore with Americans, aged 8, 11, 15 and adult, asking them to explain good and bad acts of people they knew. American adults gave far more dispositional explanations; Hindu adults gave more situational ones (roles, relationships, circumstances). At age 8 the groups barely differed and the gap grew with age: attributional style is learned from culture. Similarly, Michael Morris and Kaiping Peng (1994) found that The New York Times explained two 1991 American mass murders by the killers' personalities, while a Chinese-language newspaper stressed their situations (isolation, conflicts at work, easy access to guns). Because attributions shape feelings and effort, changing them helps. In attribution retraining , Timothy Wilson and Patricia Linville (1982) showed worried first-year students evidence that grades usually improve after the first year, inviting an unstable explanation for poor grades; they later earned better grades and dropped out less than controls. Attributional therapy for depression teaches people to credit themselves for success and to stop blaming lasting flaws for failure. Happy couples credit a partner's kindness to disposition and excuse lapses as situational; distressed couples do the reverse (Section 3.6). And computer-mediated communication, stripped of faces and tone, gives the correspondence bias free rein: a terse "ok." reads as rudeness, not haste. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. This section follows attitudes from their origins to behaviour, persuasion, resistance and dissonance. What an attitude is In 1935 Gordon Willard Allport (1897 to 1967) called the attitude "the most distinctive and indispensable concept in contemporary American social psychology". An attitude is a learned, fairly lasting evaluation of an attitude object (a person, group, thing or idea) along a like-dislike dimension. The tricomponent model (ABC model) of Milton J. Rosenberg and Carl Hovland (1960) gives it three parts: affect (feelings: "chai cheers me up"), behaviour or conation (action tendencies: "I stop at the stall daily") and cognition (beliefs: "tea is good for me"). Attitude strength combines extremity, certainty, accessibility (how fast the attitude comes to mind) and importance. Ambivalence, holding positive and negative evaluations of one object at once, weakens an attitude's hold on behaviour. Explicit attitudes are conscious and self-reported; implicit attitudes are automatic evaluations measured from reaction times, as in the Implicit Association Test (Section 3.5), and the two can disagree. Daniel Katz (1903 to 1998) named four functions of attitudes in 1960: utilitarian or adjustive (gaining rewards, avoiding punishments), knowledge (organising a confusing world), ego-defensive (protecting self-esteem from threatening truths, as when scorn for an outgroup props up a shaky self) and value-expressive (displaying central values). In 1956 M. Brewster Smith , Jerome Seymour Bruner and Robert W. White had named object appraisal (sizing up objects for one's interests), social adjustment (easing relations with valued people) and externalisation (projecting inner conflicts onto outside objects). Measurement belongs to Section 2.8: Bogardus's social distance scale (1925), Thurstone's equal-appearing intervals (1928), Likert's summated ratings (1932), Guttman's cumulative scale and Osgood's semantic differential (1957). How attitudes form Most attitudes are learned (Section 1.6). In classical conditioning a neutral object takes on the feeling of what accompanies it: Arthur W. Staats and Carolyn K. Staats (1958) paired nationality names such as "Dutch" and "Swedish" with pleasant or unpleasant words, and the pleasantly paired names were later rated more favourably. In subliminal conditioning the pairing works without awareness: Jon A. Krosnick and colleagues (1992) flashed pleasant or unpleasant pictures too briefly to be noticed before photographs of a stranger, who was then liked more after the pleasant ones. In instrumental conditioning, views that are praised or agreed with are strengthened, which is why children echo their parents' opinions until adolescence. We also copy the attitudes of models (observational learning) and adopt those of reference groups, the groups whose standards we judge ourselves by, through social comparison, which Leon Festinger (1954) described as evaluating our own opinions and abilities against other people's. Mere exposure is taught in Section 3.6. Identical twins share more attitudes than fraternal twins, and Abraham Tesser (1993) found highly heritable attitudes more accessible and harder to change. Online word of mouth (reviews, ratings, posts) now carries the weight of peers. Exam trap Praise or agreement from a friend strengthens an expressed attitude, never weakens it: positive reinforcement raises the likelihood of whatever it follows. When attitudes predict behaviour Key study: LaPiere's travels (1934) In the early 1930s, a time of open anti-Asian prejudice, Richard Tracy LaPiere (1899 to 1986) toured the United States with a young Chinese couple. Of about 250 hotels and restaurants, one refused them. Afterwards he wrote to the same places asking whether they would serve Chinese guests, and over 90 percent of those replying said no. Critics note that different staff may have answered the letters. In 1969 Allan W. Wicker 's review found attitude-behaviour correlations rarely above .30. Research then asked when attitudes do predict behaviour. Strong attitudes predict best. Extremity often reflects vested interest : John Sivacek and William D. Crano (1982) found that 47 percent of students who would be barred by a higher drinking age agreed to campaign against it, against 12 percent of unaffected students. Certainty (clarity plus a sense of correctness), personal relevance and knowledge about the object also help. So does direct experience. During a Cornell University housing shortage, Dennis T. Regan and Russell H. Fazio (1977) found that students forced to sleep on lounge cots acted on their attitudes (petitions, committees) far more consistently than students who had only heard about it, and Fazio and Mark P. Zanna (1981) showed that direct experience makes attitudes clearer and more accessible. Attitudes formed by indirect experience predict worst. Specificity must also match. The principle of compatibility of Icek Ajzen and Martin Fishbein (1977) requires attitude and behaviour to correspond in action, target, context and time. In Andrew Davidson and James Jaccard's (1979) study, general attitude towards birth control correlated .08 with women's pill use over the next two years, but attitude towards using the pill in that period correlated .57. Finally, situational constraints and perceived norms intervene: Deborah A. Prentice and Dale T. Miller (1993) found Princeton students privately less comfortable with heavy drinking than they believed their peers were, and the men's attitudes drifted towards that imagined norm. Exam trap Behaviour is hardest to predict from attitudes formed by indirect experience (hearsay, media). Direct experience, personal relevance, knowledge of the object, certainty and matching specificity all strengthen the link. Reasoned action, planned behaviour and MODE For deliberate behaviour, the theory of reasoned action (Fishbein and Ajzen, 1975) makes behavioural intention the immediate predictor of behaviour. Intention rests on the attitude towards the behaviour (beliefs about its outcomes, weighted by their value) and the subjective norm (what important others want, weighted by the motivation to comply). Ajzen (1985, 1991) added perceived behavioural control , the belief that one can perform the act, close to Albert Bandura's self-efficacy, making the theory of planned behaviour ; control affects intention and also behaviour directly. It is the standard model of health behaviours such as condom use and quitting smoking; the health belief model and protection motivation theory are in Section 7.9. Spontaneous behaviour works differently. In Fazio's attitude-to-behaviour process model (1986), an event automatically activates an accessible attitude, which together with knowledge of norms shapes how the situation is defined, and that definition drives behaviour. His MODE model (1990: Motivation and Opportunity as DEterminants) unites the accounts: people deliberate only when motivated and given the opportunity (time, capacity); otherwise accessible attitudes act automatically. Exam trap Planned behaviour's predictors of intention are attitude, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control, often worded as self-efficacy (RML 2023). Genetics, personality, socio-economic status, cultural beliefs, social support, health literacy, physical environment, emotional intelligence and coping are not in the model. Persuasion: who says what to whom Persuasion is attitude change produced by messages. At Yale University Carl Iver Hovland (1912 to 1961), Irving Lester Janis (1918 to 1990) and Harold H. Kelley (1921 to 2003) summarised their programme in Communication and Persuasion (1953). The Yale communication approach asks who says what to whom (Section 3.3) and varies source, message, audience and channel (Table 3.11). Credibility means expertise plus trustworthiness. Need for cognition , the enjoyment of effortful thinking ( John T. Cacioppo and Richard E. Petty , 1982), makes people weigh arguments rather than cues. William J. McGuire (1925 to 2007) explained why moderate self-esteem and intelligence persuade best with his information-processing chain of attention, comprehension, yielding, retention and behaviour: able, confident people comprehend more but yield less. In the sleeper effect , a low-credibility message gains impact over time because the discounting cue (its source) is forgotten while the content is remembered. Hovland and Walter Weiss (1951) found that a message credited to the physicist Robert Oppenheimer persuaded more than the same message credited to the Soviet paper Pravda , but four weeks later the difference had almost vanished. Exam trap "Receiver characteristics" (printed "receiver-operant characteristics" in IHBAS 2025) are audience factors influencing persuasion, not sensory thresholds or the receiver operating characteristic, the signal-detection curve of hits against false alarms (Section 1.3), not reinforcement controlling recall, and not biases in interpreting messages (biased assimilation, 3.4.7 ). Two routes to persuasion Why do these factors work? In the elaboration likelihood model (ELM) of Petty and Cacioppo (1981, 1986), elaboration is thinking about a message's arguments, and it depends on motivation (personal relevance, need for cognition) and ability (time, knowledge, no distraction). With both, people take the central route : systematic processing with careful attention to argument quality, giving durable change that resists attack and predicts behaviour. Without them they take the peripheral route , using mental shortcuts triggered by cues such as an attractive source, the number of arguments or a good mood, and the change is temporary (Figure 3.5). In a 1981 study by Petty, Cacioppo and Goldman, argument quality decided students' views on a comprehensive-examination proposal due next year, but source expertise decided them when it was a decade away. Persuasive message Motivated and able to think about it? Yes No Central route careful scrutiny of arguments Lasting change, resists attack, predicts behaviour Peripheral route cues: source, mood, number of arguments Temporary change, easily reversed Figure 3.5 The elaboration likelihood model (Petty and Cacioppo, 1986). Motivation and ability decide the route; only central-route change lasts. Shelly Chaiken 's heuristic-systematic model (1980) contrasts systematic processing with heuristic processing by rules of thumb ("experts are right"), and lets both run at once. Exam trap Systematic processing is the central route and involves careful attention; heuristic processing is the peripheral route and uses mental shortcuts. The ELM has exactly two routes: there is no "emotional" or "situational" route (IHBAS 2020). Resisting persuasion Audiences also push back. Jack Williams Brehm (1928 to 2009) defined reactance in 1966 as the unpleasant state, and motivation, to restore a freedom that is threatened, often by wanting or doing the forbidden thing more; hard selling may even produce a boomerang effect , change opposite to the one advocated. Reactance is not compliance (changing behaviour at a direct request), conformity (following group norms) or obedience (following authority), all in Section 3.7, nor social comparison ( 3.4.2 ). Forewarning of persuasive intent aids resistance: Jonathan L. Freedman and David O. Sears (1965) found teenagers warned ten minutes ahead of a talk against teenage driving were persuaded less than those warned two minutes ahead or not at all, because they had time for counterarguing, generating thoughts that refute the message. People also practise selective avoidance of challenging information and selective exposure to agreeable information. In inoculation (McGuire, 1961), a weak attack plus its refutation (refutational defence) protects a belief better than supportive arguments alone, as a vaccine does. Charles G. Lord , Lee Ross and Mark R. Lepper (1979) showed biased assimilation: supporters and opponents of capital punishment read the same mixed evidence, each rated the agreeing study as stronger, and both became more extreme ( attitude polarisation ). Ego depletion, tiredness after a demanding task, weakens resistance. Exam trap Reactance (Brehm, 1966) is the motivation to restore a threatened freedom, so the restricted option grows more attractive. It is not complying with requests or authority, following norms or the majority, the effect of persuasive messages, or comparing one's abilities with others. Clinical link Lecturing a client to stop drinking can provoke reactance; motivational interviewing (Section 7.6) avoids it by letting the client voice the reasons for change. Consistency theories and cognitive dissonance Much resistance reflects a drive for consistency. In the balance theory of Fritz Heider (1896 to 1988; 1946, 1958), a person (P), another person (O) and an object (X) form a triad of positive or negative relations. It is balanced when the product of the three signs is positive, and imbalanced, motivating change, when it is negative (Figure 3.6). In the congruity theory of Charles E. Osgood and Percy H. Tannenbaum (1955), when a source endorses an object we rate differently, as when an admired cricketer promotes a disliked brand, both evaluations move towards each other. If your friend hates the cricket you love (dashed line), you may like cricket less, like the friend less, or win the friend over. Leon Festinger (1919 to 1989) proposed cognitive dissonance theory in 1957. Dissonance is the aversive tension of holding inconsistent cognitions, especially of acting against one's own attitude; it grows with the importance of the cognitions and with the ratio of dissonant to consonant ones. People reduce it by: changing the attitude, the usual outcome when the behaviour cannot be undone; changing the behaviour; adding consonant cognitions and seeking supportive, not conflicting, information; trivialisation , deciding the inconsistency does not matter ( Linda Simon , Jeff Greenberg and Brehm, 1995); self-affirmation , bolstering self-worth through other values while the inconsistency stays ( Claude Mason Steele , 1988); denying responsibility. Take a case. Arvind detests smoking; his grandfather died of lung cancer. At a party his friends smoke, and so does he. "Smoking is deadly" and "I smoked" clash, both matter to him, and he feels dissonance. He cannot unsmoke the cigarette, so he may soften his attitude ("one is harmless"), add a cognition ("I did it for my friends"), blame the pressure, or vow never again. This is not effort justification (valuing what cost effort), an increased drive to smoke, or drive reduction (Hull's need-reduction principle, Section 1.10). Exam trap Cognitive dissonance is Festinger's theory, not Milgram's (obedience), Asch's (conformity) or Zimbardo's (prison simulation), and not operant conditioning, classical conditioning or social learning theory (Section 1.6). Trivialisation and self-affirmation reduce dissonance, not compliance, reactance or self-regulation (control of one's own behaviour towards goals). Dissonance is likeliest when one must decide or act against one's beliefs, not when thoughts and behaviour agree, after praise or during happy memories. Dissonance paradigms and rival explanations Key study: Festinger and Carlsmith (1959) Festinger and James Merrill Carlsmith had students do an hour of dull tasks (turning pegs, loading spools), then paid them $1 or $20 to tell the next participant the tasks were interesting. The $20 group, like controls who told no lie, later rated the tasks dull; the $1 group rated them more enjoyable. Lacking adequate external justification, they reduced dissonance by changing their attitude. This is induced compliance (forced compliance) with insufficient justification, and its result is the less-leads-to-more effect . Table 3.12 sets out the other classic paradigms. Elliot Aronson (born 1932) proposed self-consistency: behaviour that threatens a decent, competent self-concept. The new look of Joel Cooper and Fazio (1984) required personal responsibility for foreseeable aversive consequences. Daryl J. Bem 's self-perception theory (1967, 1972) denied any tension: when attitudes are vague we infer them from our own behaviour, as an observer would ("I praised it for a dollar, so I must like it"). How do ordinary people come to think less of whole groups, and what undoes it? Stereotype, prejudice and discrimination Bias has three components, matching the ABC of attitudes (Section 3.4). A stereotype is cognitive: a belief about the traits typical of a group's members, what the journalist Walter Lippmann called "pictures in our heads" ( Public Opinion , 1922). Daniel Katz and Kenneth Braly (1933) measured them with an adjective checklist: Princeton students agreed strongly on the traits of ten ethnic groups, including groups they had seldom or never met. Prejudice is affective: a negative attitude toward people because they belong to a group, in Gordon Willard Allport 's words ( The Nature of Prejudice , 1954) "an antipathy based upon a faulty and inflexible generalization". Discrimination is behavioural: unfair negative action toward a group's members. William Graham Sumner ( Folkways , 1906) named the in-group ("we") and the out-group ("they") and defined ethnocentrism , judging other groups by the standards of one's own, placed at the centre and above the rest. Allport ranked prejudice in action in five steps of rising harm ( Allport's scale ): antilocution (hostile talk), avoidance , discrimination , physical attack and extermination . Prejudice is named by its target: racism , sexism and ageism (against the old; coined by Robert Neil Butler in 1969). In India, casteism is prejudice and discrimination based on caste, a hereditary, endogamous ranking (untouchability is abolished by Article 17 of the Constitution), and communalism joins loyalty to one's own religious community with hostility toward others. Exam trap Stereotype = belief, prejudice = feeling, discrimination = action. "Pictures in our heads" is Lippmann, not Allport. Allport's scale starts with antilocution, not avoidance. Ethnocentrism is Sumner (1906). Where prejudice comes from Early explanations looked inside the prejudiced person. Theodor Adorno , Else Frenkel-Brunswik , Daniel Levinson and Nevitt Sanford ( The Authoritarian Personality , 1950) described an authoritarian personality : rigid, conventional, submissive to authority and hostile to minorities, shaped by harsh, punitive parenting, and measured by the F-scale (F for fascism). Its modern heirs are Bob Altemeyer 's right-wing authoritarianism (1981: authoritarian submission, authoritarian aggression, conventionalism) and Jim Sidanius and Felicia Pratto 's social dominance orientation , a preference for a hierarchy in which some groups rank above others. Scapegoat theory holds that frustration is displaced onto a weak, visible minority (Section 3.9): Carl Hovland and Robert Sears (1940) found that lynchings in the American South rose as cotton prices fell. In the social learning view , children absorb prejudice from parents, peers and media and are rewarded with approval for voicing it. At the group level, realistic conflict theory (named by Donald Thomas Campbell in 1965, argued by Muzafer Sherif in 1966) holds that competition for scarce resources breeds hostility. Often what hurts is relative deprivation , having less than one feels entitled to compared with others: in The American Soldier (1949), Samuel Stouffer and colleagues found fast-promoted Air Corps men less satisfied with promotion than slow-promoted military police. Walter Garrison Runciman (1966) separated egoistic (personal) from fraternal (group) deprivation; the fraternal kind fuels prejudice and collective action such as protest. Ted Robert Gurr ( Why Men Rebel , 1970) traced rebellion to the gap between what people expect and what they get. Key study: The Robbers Cave experiment (1954) Question. Does competition create intergroup hostility, and what removes it? Method. Sherif and colleagues took 22 unacquainted boys aged about 11 to 12, in two matched groups, to a summer camp at Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma. Phase 1, in-group formation : each group lived apart and named itself (the Eagles, the Rattlers). Phase 2, competition and friction : a tournament with prizes for the winners. Phase 3, reduction of conflict . Result. Competition brought name-calling, a burned flag and cabin raids. Mere contact (shared meals, films) failed and even made things worse: meals became food fights. Hostility fell only with superordinate goals , which both groups wanted but neither could reach alone: restoring the water supply, pooling money to rent a film, pulling a stalled truck. Criticism. The boys were all white, Protestant and middle class, and staff stage-managed events. The report appeared in 1961. Exam trap Superordinate goals requiring cooperation reduced the hostility. Mere contact failed, more competition is what created the hostility, and no dominant leader was assigned. Robbers Cave is not Sherif's autokinetic study of norms (Section 3.7). Social identity theory Sherif's boys traded insults as soon as they learned of each other, before any contest. Is competition even needed? Henri Tajfel (1919 to 1982), a Polish Jew who lost most of his family in the Holocaust, looked for the minimal conditions for discrimination. In the minimal group paradigm (Tajfel, Billig, Bundy and Flament, 1971), Bristol schoolboys were told they had been grouped by a preference for Paul Klee or Wassily Kandinsky (in truth, at random), then divided points worth money between two anonymous others. Groups with no history, contact or competition still produced in-group favouritism, and many boys chose to maximise the difference between groups even at a cost to their own group's absolute gain. Tajfel and John Turner (1947 to 2011) explained this with social identity theory (1979, 1986): a large part of our self-concept and self-esteem comes from the groups we belong to. Besides a personal identity (one's own traits, achievements and preferences) we have a social identity derived from group memberships (Indian, Kannadiga, psychology student). Three processes link membership to bias (Figure 3.7): social categorisation into in-groups and out-groups, social identification with the in-group, and social comparison with out-groups. Since self-esteem rides on the comparison, we seek positive distinctiveness : our group must come out ahead. Prejudice thus arises from categorisation itself, with no clash of interests required. 1 Social categorisation us and them 2 Social identification adopt its identity 3 Social comparison us versus them Positive distinctiveness in-group favoured Unfavourable comparison? Three responses Social mobility leave the group Social creativity change the comparison Social competition challenge the out-group Figure 3.7 Social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner 1979): three processes, and three responses when the in-group compares badly. When the comparison is unflattering, members may leave for a higher group ( social mobility , if boundaries are permeable), change the comparison by picking a new dimension or a lower group ( social creativity : "poorer but kinder"), or challenge the higher group directly ( social competition ). The self-categorisation theory of Turner and colleagues (1987) explains when we see ourselves as individuals and when as interchangeable group members: the category that best fits the situation becomes salient. Marilynn Brewer 's optimal distinctiveness theory (1991) holds that we balance a need to belong against a need to be different, so we identify most with groups that are inclusive yet distinctive. Exam trap In social identity theory, identity and prejudice come from group membership and categorisation into in-groups and out-groups , driven by the need for a positive social identity. Wrong options: competition for scarce resources (realistic conflict); birthplace, prejudice experienced, economic status, personal achievements, preferences or attributes (personal identity); internal or external attributions (Section 3.3); cognitive dissonance (Section 3.4); social facilitation (Section 3.10); genetic kin selection (Section 3.8); operant reinforcement (Chapter 1). How stereotypes work in the mind Categorisation also distorts perception. In the out-group homogeneity effect "they are all alike": George Quattrone and Edward Ellsworth Jones (1980) found Princeton and Rutgers students generalised more from one rival student's choice to his whole university than from an in-group member's; the reverse is in-group differentiation . An illusory correlation is a perceived group-trait link the data do not support: David Hamilton and Robert Gifford (1976) gave a large and a small group the same proportion of undesirable acts, yet people paired the two distinctive things, minority and rare bad acts, and judged the small group worse. Thomas Pettigrew 's ultimate attribution error (1979) extends the fundamental attribution error (Section 3.3) to groups: an out-group's failings are put down to its nature, its successes to luck. Stereotypes persist because they save effort: C. Neil Macrae , Alan Milne and Galen Bodenhausen (1994) found that people given stereotype labels recalled more traits and did better on a simultaneous second task, so stereotypes are energy-saving devices . They also resist disconfirmation. Renee Weber and Jennifer Crocker (1983) compared bookkeeping (each exception nudges the stereotype), conversion (one dramatic case overturns it) and subtyping (exceptions are fenced off as atypical, leaving it intact); disconfirmations spread over many typical members changed it most. The stereotype content model of Susan Fiske , Amy Cuddy , Peter Glick and Jun Xu (2002) places groups on warmth and competence , each combination evoking its own emotion (Figure 3.8). Stereotypes can also impair performance through stereotype threat , the fear of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group. Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson (1995) found that Black Stanford students scored below equally able White students on hard verbal items only when these were presented as a test of ability; Steven Spencer , Steele and Diane Quinn (1999) found the same for women on a hard mathematics test. Pity the elderly, the disabled paternalistic prejudice Admiration the in-group, close allies little prejudice Contempt the poor, the homeless contemptuous prejudice Envy the rich, businesswomen envious prejudice High warmth Low warmth Low competence High competence Figure 3.8 The stereotype content model (Fiske and colleagues 2002): warmth and competence decide the emotion a group evokes, so much prejudice is mixed. Automatic and controlled processes Nearly everyone knows the cultural stereotypes; is everyone then prejudiced? Patricia Devine 's (1989) dissociation model says no. High- and low-prejudiced White Americans knew the stereotype of Black Americans equally well, and after stereotype-related words were flashed too fast to see, both judged an ambiguous man as more hostile: activation by automatic processing (fast, unintended, outside awareness) happens in everyone. Given time to list their thoughts, however, low-prejudiced people wrote more egalitarian ones. Devine concluded that low-prejudiced people use controlled processing (slow, deliberate, effortful) to inhibit the activated stereotype and replace it with egalitarian beliefs, much like breaking a bad habit. Automatic associations can be measured without asking. The Implicit Association Test (IAT) of Anthony Greenwald , Debbie McGhee and Jordan Schwartz (1998) times how fast people sort faces and words with two response keys. Being faster when one group shares a key with "good" words than with "bad" words reveals an implicit, unconscious association ( implicit prejudice or stereotyping) that people may be unwilling or unable to report. In the bona fide pipeline of Russell Fazio and colleagues (1995), a briefly shown Black or White face primes a good-or-bad judgement of adjectives; faster responses to negative words after Black faces reveal an automatic negative attitude. Exam trap Low-prejudiced people show controlled processing that refutes the stereotype . Automatic processing with involuntary stereotyping is the first stage, shared by all and left unchecked by high-prejudiced people; "automatic, voluntary" is self-contradictory; controlled processing prevents involuntary stereotyping rather than causing it. The IAT measures implicit associations by reaction time: not verbal or hidden mathematical ability, and not dream content (psychoanalysis). Why do we seek company at all, why these people rather than others, and what keeps a relationship alive or ends it? This section moves from the need to affiliate, through attraction and the theories of close relationships, to love, break-up and loneliness. The need to affiliate Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary argued in 1995 that the need to belong , a drive to form and keep a few lasting, positive relationships, is a fundamental human motive. People differ in its strength; the stable trait is the need for affiliation (nAff), listed by Henry Murray and measured by David McClelland (Section 1.10). The older word is gregariousness , the urge to be with others and live in groups. William McDougall listed a gregarious instinct in 1908, but gregariousness is now classed as a social motive : a secondary, learned or psychosocial motive, like affiliation, achievement and power, that arises and is satisfied in interaction with others. Biological (primary) motives such as hunger and thirst serve bodily survival instead. Exam trap Gregariousness has a social motive. "Biological" tempts because McDougall called it an instinct, but instinct theory collapsed (Section 1.10). "Psychological" is not a standard separate class, and personal motives are an individual's own habits, interests and aspirations. Key study: Schachter's anxiety and affiliation experiment (1959) Stanley Schachter (1922 to 1997) had women students met by a fictitious "Dr Gregor Zilstein", who warned of electric shocks that would be painful (high anxiety) or feel like a tickle (low anxiety). Offered a wait alone or with others, about two-thirds of the high-anxiety women chose company, against about one-third of the low-anxiety women, and they wanted only others facing the same shocks: "misery doesn't just love any kind of company, it loves only miserable company". No shocks were given. Why do frightened people want each other? All three usual answers hold: we affiliate to obtain information about what is happening, to reduce anxiety , and to compare ourselves with similar others . Craig Hill (1987) found four affiliation motives: positive stimulation , emotional support , attention and social comparison . The need shows most sharply when thwarted. Ostracism , being ignored and excluded, was studied by Kipling Williams with Cyberball (2000), an online ball-tossing game in which the other "players" soon stop throwing to the participant; minutes of exclusion by strangers lower mood and threaten belonging, self-esteem, control and meaningful existence. Feelings shape liking too: in the reinforcement-affect model of Donn Byrne and Gerald Clore (1970) we like people who make us feel good and, by classical conditioning, even strangers merely present when something pleasant happens. Social comparison Leon Festinger (1919 to 1989) proposed social comparison theory in 1954: people are driven to evaluate their opinions and abilities, and when no objective standard exists they compare themselves with others, preferably similar others. A mark of 85 percent means little until you know how your classmates scored. Upward social comparison , with someone better off, can inspire but often brings envy; downward social comparison , with someone worse off, was described by Thomas Wills (1981) as a route to self-enhancement when self-esteem is threatened. Abraham Tesser 's self-evaluation maintenance model (1988) adds closeness and relevance: if your cousin tops the medical entrance and medicine matters to you, the comparison process stings and you may distance yourself; if she wins a dance contest you do not care about, the reflection process lets you bask in her glory. Social media supply an endless upward stream of other people's best moments. Andrew Przybylski and colleagues (2013) defined the fear of missing out (FOMO) as a pervasive apprehension that others might be having rewarding experiences from which one is absent; it goes with heavier social media use and lower mood. FOMO is a social comparison phenomenon. Exam trap FOMO is linked to social comparison , not classical conditioning (learning by pairing stimuli), operant extinction (a response fading when reinforcement stops) or "cognitive dissonance only" (discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, Section 3.4). Nearness and familiarity The plainest force of attraction is nearness. In 1950 Festinger, Schachter and Kurt Back studied Westgate West, married-student housing at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology where flats were assigned at random. Of next-door neighbours, 41 percent were named as close friends, against 22 percent of those two doors away and 10 percent of those at the far end of the corridor. Functional distance , how often architecture brings paths together, mattered too: residents beside the stairs and mailboxes made more friends upstairs. Mady Segal (1974) found that police trainees seated alphabetically befriended those with neighbouring surnames. This is the propinquity effect : the more we see and interact with a person, the more likely he or she is to become our friend or partner. The mechanism is largely the mere exposure effect of Robert Zajonc (1968): repeated exposure to a stimulus, without interaction or reward, increases liking for it, whether nonsense words, Chinese-like characters or faces. Richard Moreland and Scott Beach (1992) had four women attend a class 0, 5, 10 or 15 times without speaking; students liked them more the more often they came. Theodore Mita and colleagues (1977) found that women preferred mirror images of their own faces, the version they see daily, while friends preferred the true image. A stimulus disliked at first, however, can become more disliked. Exam trap "The more we see and interact with someone, the more likely they become our friend or partner" is the propinquity effect . The exposure effect is narrower (mere exposure to any stimulus raises liking) and is its mechanism; matching and reciprocity are taught below. For mere exposure, "performing better when observed" is social facilitation, "attitude change after inconsistent behaviour" is cognitive dissonance and "riskier group decisions" is the risky shift (Sections 3.4 and 3.10). Looks, similarity and reciprocity Appearance acts first. Karen Dion , Ellen Berscheid and Elaine Hatfield (then Walster) showed in 1972 that attractive people are judged kinder, more sociable and more successful: the what is beautiful is good stereotype. At a 1966 computer dance at the University of Minnesota, Walster and colleagues paired students at random; the only predictor of wanting another date was the partner's attractiveness. Judith Langlois and Lori Roggman (1990) found computer-averaged faces more attractive than most faces composing them (averageness); symmetry also attracts. Yet most people must settle: the matching hypothesis (Walster and colleagues 1966; tested by Berscheid and colleagues 1971) holds that we pair with partners of roughly our own attractiveness to avoid rejection, and Bernard Murstein (1972) found real couples closer in attractiveness than chance. Similarity matters more over time. Theodore Newcomb measured transfer students' attitudes by post, housed them together, and found that those initially similar became friends ( The Acquaintance Process , 1961). Byrne's "bogus stranger" experiments gave his law of attraction (1971): attraction rises with the proportion of similar attitudes. Milton Rosenbaum 's repulsion hypothesis (1986), that dissimilarity repels while similarity adds nothing, overstates the case, though dissimilarity does weigh slightly more. Robert Winch 's (1958) complementarity of needs , opposites attracting (dominant with submissive), has found little support. We also like those who like us ( reciprocity of liking ). In the gain-loss effect of Elliot Aronson and Darwyn Linder (1965), participants who overheard a confederate's evaluations liked her most when they turned from negative to positive, more than when consistently positive, and least when they turned from positive to negative. Exchange, equity and investment Why do people stay in some relationships and leave others? Social exchange theory , from John Thibaut and Harold Kelley (1959) and George Homans (1961), treats a relationship as a trade: rewards minus costs. The outcome is judged against the comparison level (CL), what one feels one deserves from past relationships, which sets satisfaction, and the comparison level for alternatives (CLalt), the best outcome available elsewhere, which decides staying. Meera may be dissatisfied with Arjun (below her CL) yet stay because every alternative looks worse (above her CLalt). Table 3.16 sets this beside three relatives. Caryl Rusbult 's investment model explains staying when unhappy: years together, children or a shared home cannot be recovered, so commitment stays high, as in women who return to abusive partners. Margaret Clark and Judson Mills showed that tit for tat suits exchange relationships with strangers; in communal relationships with family and close friends, prompt repayment can even reduce liking. Self-disclosure Relationships deepen through self-disclosure , revealing personal information about oneself to another. Sidney Jourard (1926 to 1974), in The Transparent Self (1964), saw being fully known by someone as a mark of healthy personality; his Jourard Self-Disclosure Questionnaire asked how much people had told mother, father, friends and spouse about areas such as tastes, work, money and body. Irwin Altman and Dalmas Taylor 's social penetration theory (1973) pictures the self as an onion: relationships grow in breadth (range of topics) and depth (intimacy), moving from outer layers to the core. Disclosure invites matching disclosure ( disclosure reciprocity ), and we like those who confide in us. T. L. Morton (1978), followed by the textbook of Shelley Taylor , Letitia Anne Peplau and David Sears , separated descriptive self-disclosure , revealing facts and information about oneself (where you grew up), from evaluative self-disclosure , revealing one's personal feelings, opinions and judgements (that you feel lonely). Evaluative disclosure is more intimate and comes later. Exam trap IHBAS 2020 keyed "descriptive self-disclosure" for communicating one's feelings. By the standard definitions that is evaluative ; descriptive disclosure is about facts. Learn the standard pair, and know that this paper's key reversed it. "Prescriptive" and "non-evaluative" self-disclosure are not standard types. Love Zick Rubin (1970) built separate Liking (respect, affection) and Loving Scales (attachment, caring, intimacy); high scorers on loving gazed at each other longer. Berscheid and Hatfield separated passionate love , an intense, aroused longing for union with the other (measured by Hatfield and Susan Sprecher 's Passionate Love Scale, 1986), from companionate love , the calmer affection we feel for those with whom our lives are deeply entwined. Robert Sternberg 's triangular theory of love (1986) builds love from intimacy (closeness), passion (physical attraction and arousal) and commitment (the decision to maintain the love); their combinations give eight kinds (Table 3.17). Love also carries the stamp of early attachment (infants in Chapter 6). Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver (1987) classified adults as secure , avoidant (uneasy with closeness) or anxious-ambivalent (craving closeness, fearing abandonment), just over half secure, much as in infants. David Buss and colleagues (1992) reported men more upset by sexual and women by emotional infidelity, an evolutionary reading that critics say depends on question wording. Indian context In Jaipur, Usha Gupta and Pushpa Singh (1982) found that couples who married for love reported less love after about five years, while those in arranged marriages reported more love once past the newlywed years. When relationships fail Rusbult classified responses to dissatisfaction as active or passive and constructive or destructive: exit (active, destructive: leaving), voice (active, constructive: discussing problems), loyalty (passive, constructive: waiting faithfully) and neglect (passive, destructive: letting things decay). Steve Duck (1982) traced dissolution through four phases: intrapsychic (brooding privately on the partner's faults), dyadic (confronting the partner), social (telling friends and family) and grave-dressing (building an acceptable story of the break-up). John Gottman 's "four horsemen" are taught with couple therapy in Chapter 7. Loneliness Peplau and Daniel Perlman (1982) defined loneliness as the unpleasant experience that occurs when a person's network of social relationships is deficient in quantity or quality. It is subjective: one can be lonely in a crowd. Robert Weiss (1973) separated two kinds. Emotional isolation (emotional loneliness) is the lack of a close, intimate attachment to one specific person, felt by a widow though friends surround her. Social isolation (social loneliness) is the lack of a wider network of friends and associates, felt by a newcomer to a city even in a happy marriage. Exam trap Emotional isolation means no deep attachment to one specific person ; social isolation means too few friends or associates . Incompetence, inadequacy and low self-esteem are correlates of loneliness, not Weiss's types. The UCLA Loneliness Scale of Daniel Russell , Peplau and colleagues (1978, revised 1980) has 20 statements such as "I lack companionship". Loneliness goes with depression, poorer health and shorter life ( John Cacioppo and colleagues), and lonely people often benefit from social skills training (starting conversations, disclosing appropriately) and from challenging the negative expectations that keep them withdrawn. You join the queue at a chai stall, lend a friend your notes, fall silent when the invigilator orders it. This section follows influence from the unspoken norm through direct requests to outright commands, then turns to the roles and the bases of power behind them. Kinds of social influence Social influence is any effort by one or more people to change the behaviour, attitudes or feelings of others (persuasion, changing attitudes by messages, is in Section 3.4). Three forms differ in how directly pressure is applied (Table 3.18). Conformity is changing your behaviour or beliefs to match a group or its norms, although nobody has asked you to. Compliance is changing in response to a direct request, which you may accept or refuse. Obedience is changing in response to a command from an authority. Textbooks add symbolic social influence : absent people still steer us through our mental image of them. Table 3.18 The forms of social influence. Form Source of pressure Example Conformity Group norms; no request Standing for the national anthem Compliance A direct request A friend asks to borrow your notes Obedience A command from an authority A doctor orders a nurse to give a drug Symbolic influence Mental image of absent others Studying because you picture a parent's disappointment Herbert Kelman (1958) graded how deep the change goes. In compliance (his sense) a person goes along outwardly to gain reward or avoid punishment, and only while watched. In identification he adopts the behaviour to be like an admired person or group. In internalisation he adopts it because it fits his own values, and it lasts. The same contrast appears as public compliance (going along outwardly while privately disagreeing) versus private acceptance (truly coming to believe what the group believes). Exam trap "Changing your behaviour to match others in a group" is conformity . Norming is a stage of Bruce Tuckman 's group development (forming, storming, norming, performing; Section 3.10); standardisation means uniform test procedures (Chapter 2). Conformity is change under group pressure with nobody asking; compliance answers a direct request. Conformity is not "always involuntary", and neither term means obedience. Social norms Social norms are rules indicating how people are expected to behave in a situation. Explicit norms are written or stated ("No Parking"); implicit norms are unstated yet known to all (do not talk during a concert). Robert Cialdini , Raymond Reno and Carl Kallgren (1990) distinguished descriptive norms , what most people actually do, from injunctive norms , what is approved or disapproved, what ought to be done. In their littering study, people found a handbill on their car windscreen. More dropped it where the ground was already littered; fewest did where the ground was clean and a confederate conspicuously dropped one, because the lone litterbug highlighted the descriptive norm that nobody litters here. Making the injunctive norm salient (a passer-by picking up litter, in a follow-up) cut littering even in a littered setting. Their focus theory of normative conduct holds that a norm guides behaviour only when it is focal, salient at the moment of acting. Prescriptive norms tell people what they ought to do (greet elders); proscriptive norms tell them what not to do (do not cheat). A perceived norm is a person's belief about what others do or approve, which may be wrong: students who overestimate their classmates' drinking drink more. Societies whose norms break down suffer anomie (Section 3.1). Exam trap Norms telling people how they ought to behave are prescriptive (injunctive) norms. "Idealistic norms" is not a standard type; descriptive norms describe what is done; perceived norms are beliefs about norms. Sherif and Asch: the classic studies How does a norm form? Muzafer Sherif (1935, 1936) used the autokinetic effect : in a dark room a stationary point of light seems to move, because there is no frame of reference. Alone, people gave widely different estimates of the movement. In small groups over several sessions their estimates converged on a shared group norm, which each person kept when later tested alone. In an ambiguous situation people used one another as information and privately accepted the answer. Robert Jacobs and Donald Campbell (1961) had confederates set an exaggerated norm, then replaced members one at a time; the arbitrary norm was handed down for several "generations" after the confederates had gone. Solomon Asch (1951, 1956) asked the harder question: will people conform when the answer is obvious? Key study: Asch's line judgements (1951, 1956) Method: one real participant sat among about seven confederates and said aloud, near the end of the row, which of three comparison lines matched a standard line (Figure 3.10). On 12 of 18 trials, the critical trials , every confederate gave the same wrong answer. Result: alone, people almost never erred (under 1 percent of judgements); in the group, conformity occurred on about 37 percent of critical trials. About three quarters (76 percent in Baron's account) conformed at least once; about a quarter never did. Conclusion: the answer was obvious, so people yielded to avoid standing out: normative influence towards an incorrect majority, mostly public compliance. Criticism: only male American students were tested, and such conformity has since declined. A. The task 1 2 3 Standard Comparison lines Correct: 2. Confederates all say 1 B. Size of the majority Conformity Levels off after 3 or 4 1 2 3 4 8 Number of unanimous confederates Figure 3.10 Asch's conformity task. (A) The match is obvious, yet on critical trials every confederate named a wrong line. (B) Conformity rose steeply as the unanimous majority grew to three, then levelled off (schematic, after Asch's group-size variation). Asch's variations show what drives the effect. Conformity rose with the size of the majority up to three or four, then levelled off. A single dissenting partner cut it sharply, even one giving a different wrong answer: unanimity is what matters. Written, private answers cut it steeply too. Richard Crutchfield (1955) mechanised the method: people in separate booths saw others' supposed answers as lights on a panel, so no confederates were needed. Rod Bond and Peter Smith 's (1996) meta-analysis of 133 Asch-type studies in 17 countries found more conformity in collectivist cultures and a decline in the United States since the 1950s. Exam trap Asch tested the limits of conformity (not social perception, leadership or coercive power) and showed normative influence towards an incorrect majority : not obedience (nobody gave orders), the bystander effect or diffusion of responsibility (Section 3.8), or cognitive dissonance (Section 3.4). Private answers lowered conformity. Sherif's dot of light: ambiguity, informational influence, norm formation (not obedience or implicit bias, Section 3.5). Why people conform Morton Deutsch and Harold Gerard (1955) named two motives. Normative social influence rests on the desire to be liked and accepted; it produces public compliance and is strongest when a valued group is watching, as in Asch's study. Informational social influence rests on the desire to be correct; it produces private acceptance and is strongest when the situation is ambiguous or we lack expertise, as in Sherif's study. Conformity rises with the group's cohesiveness (how much we are attracted to it and want to belong), its size up to a point, its unanimity, its members' status or expertise, public responding, a difficult or ambiguous task, and a collectivist culture. Gender differences are small: Alice Eagly and Linda Carli 's (1981) review found women slightly more influenceable, mainly under face-to-face group pressure. Conformity keeps traffic and queues orderly, but its downside is that it can lead ordinary people into cruelty (see the power of roles ). Exam trap Normative influence is the desire to be accepted and liked ; informational influence, the desire to be correct . "Personal beliefs and values" describe internalisation; "power and authority" describe obedience and the bases of power. Resisting the majority; minority influence Conformity pressure can be resisted. C. R. Snyder and Howard Fromkin (1980) proposed a need for uniqueness ; later studies found that people told they are "exactly average" resist the majority more. The related desire for individuation , to stand out as a distinct person, works the same way. People reminded of a time they held power over others conform less, and pressure that threatens freedom can provoke reactance (Section 3.4). Can a minority sway a majority? Serge Moscovici , Elisabeth Lage and Martine Naffrechoux (1969) showed groups of four participants and two confederates blue slides. When the confederates consistently called every slide "green", about 8 percent of the majority's judgements became "green", and in a later private test participants labelled more blue-green discs green; an inconsistent minority had almost no effect. In his conversion theory (1980) Moscovici argued that majorities win quick public compliance, whereas a consistent minority makes people think and produces slower, genuine private conversion. Edwin Hollander (1958) explained safe dissent: by conforming early a member earns idiosyncrasy credits , goodwill he can later spend on deviation. The most basic influence may be emotional contagion , the automatic catching of another's mood, which Elaine Hatfield , John Cacioppo and Richard Rapson (1994) traced to our mimicry of others' faces and postures. Compliance tactics and cults Cialdini worked undercover among "compliance professionals" (salespeople, fund-raisers, advertisers) and in Influence (1984) traced their tactics to six principles: reciprocity (we repay favours and concessions), commitment and consistency (we act in line with what we have agreed to), social proof or social validation (we copy similar others), liking or friendship, authority (we defer to real or apparent experts) and scarcity (we want what is rare or running out).
