Commitment to a friendly exchange Key study: The foot-in-the-door (1966) Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser demonstrated the foot-in-the-door technique by asking Californian homeowners to put a large, ugly "Drive Carefully" sign on their lawns. About 17 percent of those approached cold agreed, but about 76 percent of those who, two weeks earlier, had agreed to show a small "Be a safe driver" sign. Two explanations: consistency (refusing now feels inconsistent) and self-perception (watching yourself agree, you infer "I support good causes"; Section 3.4). The door-in-the-face technique reverses the order. Cialdini and his colleagues (1975) asked students to counsel juvenile delinquents two hours a week for two years; all refused. Asked next to take delinquents on a two-hour zoo trip, about 50 percent agreed, against under 17 percent asked only the small favour. The retreat looks like a concession, and reciprocity demands one back (reciprocal concessions). In the low-ball technique the initial commitment does the work: a car buyer who agreed to a bargain still buys when the "manager" cancels the discount. Exam trap Foot-in-the-door: small, then large . Door-in-the-face: large, refused, then small . Low-ball: yes first, then the deal worsens. That's-not-all: the deal improves before any yes. "Reward" is not one of Cialdini's six principles, and "conformity technique" is not a compliance tactic: conformity involves no request. Cults use these principles at full strength. Recruiters begin with love-bombing , flooding a newcomer with affection and attention; they escalate commitment step by step (a free dinner, a retreat, a donation, then residence); they isolate recruits from family and former friends, control their information and build an us-versus-them identity. Robert Jay Lifton (1961), studying Chinese Communist "thought reform", described such total environments, including milieu control (control of all communication). At Jonestown, Guyana (1978), more than 900 followers of Jim Jones died in a mass murder and suicide he ordered. Talking with recruits' families is exactly what cults avoid. Obedience: Milgram's experiments Would you shock an innocent stranger because a man in a laboratory coat told you to? Stanley Milgram (1933 to 1984) asked this partly to understand how ordinary people carried out the Holocaust. Key study: Milgram's obedience study (1963) Method: at Yale, 40 men aged 20 to 50 joined a supposed study of punishment and memory. A rigged draw made each the teacher ; the learner , a likeable confederate, sat strapped in next door. For each error the teacher moved one switch up a generator from 15 to 450 volts in 15-volt steps, labelled up to "Danger: severe shock" and "XXX". No real shocks were given. At 300 volts the learner pounded on the wall, then fell silent. When teachers hesitated, the experimenter used four standard prods, from "Please continue" to "You have no other choice, you must go on." Result: psychiatrists had predicted that about one in a thousand would go to the end. All 40 reached 300 volts and 26 (65 percent) went to 450 volts, many sweating, trembling and protesting. Conclusion: most ordinary people obey a legitimate authority even to the point of apparently harming another person. His variations ( Obedience to Authority , 1974) show what raises and lowers obedience (Table 3.20). Table 3.20 Milgram's variations: percentage who went to 450 volts. Condition Full obedience Remote: learner unseen, pounds on wall (baseline) 65% Voice feedback: protests heard 62.5% Proximity: learner in the same room 40% Touch-proximity: teacher presses learner's hand onto plate 30% Orders given by telephone About 20% Run-down Bridgeport office, no link to Yale About 48% An ordinary man gives the orders 20% Two peer teachers rebel 10% Women as teachers 65% Milgram's explanation was the agentic state : within a hierarchy a person stops acting autonomously and becomes the agent of another's wishes, transferring responsibility to the authority. The authority seemed legitimate (Yale, the coat, science); demands escalated gradually, each step barely worse than the last; and events moved too fast for reflection. Obedience falls when people are reminded that they are responsible, see disobedient models, question the authority's expertise and motives, and know about this research. Diana Baumrind (1964) attacked the study's ethics: participants were deceived and severely stressed. Milgram replied that all were debriefed and 84 percent were glad to have taken part. Burger (2009) ran a safer partial replication, stopping at 150 volts (beyond which nearly all of Milgram's obedient men went to the end): about 70 percent were willing to continue past it. Hannah Arendt (1963), reporting the trial of the Nazi official Adolf Eichmann , described the banality of evil : monstrous crimes done by ordinary people doing their jobs. Clinical link Charles Hofling and colleagues (1966) had an unknown "doctor" telephone hospital nurses and order 20 milligrams of an unfamiliar drug, "Astroten", twice the maximum dose on its label. Of 22 nurses, 21 began to give it before being stopped. Exam trap Milgram's baseline: 65 percent (26 of 40) to 450 volts, all 40 to 300 volts; not 10, 35 or 100 percent. The lesson is the power of the situation, not personality, and it concerns obedience to authority, not conformity when an answer is ambiguous. The power of roles Key study: The Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) Method: Philip Zimbardo , with Craig Haney and Curtis Banks , randomly made 24 psychologically healthy male students guards or prisoners in a mock prison in Stanford's psychology basement. Prisoners were "arrested" at home and known only by numbers; guards wore uniforms and mirrored sunglasses. Result: the guards became abusive, and the prisoners, after a brief rebellion, passive and distressed. Planned for two weeks, the study was stopped after six days. Conclusion: social roles and situational forces can turn ordinary people cruel. Criticism: demand characteristics (guards may have acted as they thought was wanted), Zimbardo's double role as researcher and prison superintendent, and ethical harm. In the BBC Prison Study (2006), Stephen Reicher and Alexander Haslam found that guards who did not identify with their role did not turn tyrannical, and prisoners who shared a group identity challenged them: roles shape behaviour when people identify with them. In The Lucifer Effect (2007) Zimbardo applied his analysis to American soldiers' abuse of Iraqi prisoners at Abu Ghraib. Exam trap "The power of roles" is Zimbardo's prison experiment , showing situational forces, not genetics, conditioning or reinforcement schedules (Chapter 1). Not the Robbers Cave experiment (Sherif's intergroup conflict study, Section 3.5); not Milgram's message experiment , the small-world study (1967), whose letters reached a stranger through about six acquaintances ("six degrees of separation"), nor his lost-letter technique; not "Zilstein's shock research", the fictitious Dr Gregor Zilstein of Stanley Schachter 's (1959) affiliation study (Section 3.6). Was this proof that city people no longer cared? Two young psychologists suspected that the number of witnesses was itself the problem. Their answer, the bystander effect, is the heart of this section. First, though: why does anyone help at all? Prosocial behaviour, helping and altruism Any action that benefits others, such as sharing, comforting, donating or rescuing, is prosocial behaviour . Prosocial behaviour that intentionally benefits a particular person is helping . Defined by motive rather than act, altruism is helping with no expected reward, often at a cost to oneself, purely for the other's welfare. In cooperation , people work together towards a goal that benefits all of them, so nobody need be the giver. A student who lends her notes is helping; if she expects nothing back and loses revision time, she may be acting altruistically; if two friends split the syllabus and swap notes, they are cooperating. Does true altruism exist? The doctrine of psychological egoism says no: every helpful act ultimately serves the helper, by winning praise, avoiding guilt or feeling good. This egoism versus altruism debate was fought hardest over empathy. Empathy and the egoism versus altruism debate The act of perceiving, understanding and responding to another person's emotional state and ideas is empathy . Its emotional side, affective empathy , is feeling with the person; cognitive empathy , or perspective taking, is accurately understanding what they think and feel; empathic concern is the warm, other-oriented compassion that follows. Mark H. Davis measured these with his Interpersonal Reactivity Index (1980), whose four scales are perspective taking, fantasy, empathic concern and personal distress (one's own anxiety at another's suffering). Feeling concern or pity for someone, rather than feeling with them, is sympathy . Empathy is a foundation of helping, and a core condition a counsellor offers a client (Chapter 7). Exam trap "Perceiving, understanding and responding to the emotional state and ideas of another person" is empathy , not sympathy. Transference (a client redirecting feelings about past figures onto the therapist) is a therapy term (Chapter 7); displacement (shifting an impulse onto a safer target) is a defence mechanism (Chapter 4). C. Daniel Batson 's empathy-altruism hypothesis (1981; The Altruism Question , 1991) holds that empathic concern produces truly altruistic motivation, a wish to relieve the other's suffering for their sake, whereas personal distress produces only an egoistic wish to escape. To tell the two apart, Batson made escape easy. Key study: Elaine and the shocks (Batson and colleagues 1981) Women students watched "Elaine" react badly to electric shocks and were asked whether they would take her remaining shocks. Some were led to feel high empathy (Elaine shared their values). With easy escape they could leave after watching two of ten trials; with difficult escape they had to watch all ten. Low-empathy participants helped when escape was hard but mostly left when it was easy, as egoists would. High-empathy participants helped at high rates even when they could walk away. Criticism: they might still be avoiding guilt. Robert Cialdini and colleagues replied with the egoistic negative-state relief model (1981, 1987): seeing suffering, or being sad for any reason, makes us feel bad, and we help to lift our own mood. Empathic people helped less when told that a drug had "fixed" their mood, so helping could not make them feel better. The empathic joy hypothesis ( K. D. Smith , J. P. Keating and Ezra Stotland 1989) says we help for the pleasure of seeing the person relieved: empathic participants helped only if they expected to learn how their help had worked. Batson kept finding helping that these motives cannot explain, and most psychologists now accept that both altruistic and egoistic motives exist. Genes, status and norms How could a costly urge to help survive natural selection? William D. Hamilton 's kin selection theory (1964) answers that helping a relative helps copies of your own genes, so helping is favoured when relatedness multiplied by the benefit exceeds the cost. Eugene Burnstein , Christian Crandall and Shinobu Kitayama (1994) found that people would help close kin more than distant kin or strangers, and young relatives more than old ones, most clearly when life was at stake. For non-relatives, Robert Trivers proposed reciprocal altruism (1971): helping pays when the favour is likely to be returned. Two accounts are frankly strategic. According to competitive altruism ( Charlie Hardy and Mark Van Vugt 2006), people help to gain status: players gave more when giving was public, and the most generous were preferred as partners. Helping an out-group to reduce its threat to one's in-group is defensive helping ( Arie Nadler and colleagues 2009): students offered more help to a rival school said to outscore them, as if to keep it dependent. Finally, norms. The norm of reciprocity ( Alvin Gouldner 1960) says we should help those who helped us; the social responsibility norm ( Leonard Berkowitz and L. R. Daniels 1963) says we should help those who depend on us, whether or not they can repay. A personal norm , one's own felt moral obligation to act, predicts helping better than vague social norms. The bystander effect In the early hours of 13 March 1964, Kitty Genovese (1935 to 1964), aged 28, was stabbed near her apartment building in Kew Gardens, Queens, New York. The New York Times reported that 38 neighbours had seen or heard the attack without calling the police. The figure was later shown to be exaggerated (few saw the attack clearly, and some did call or go to her), but the story shocked the country, and commentators blamed big-city apathy. Bibb Latané (born 1937) and John Darley (1938 to 2018) suspected that the witnesses failed to act because there were so many of them. Their experiments (1968) and book The Unresponsive Bystander (1970) established the bystander effect : the more bystanders present at an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help, and the slower the help that comes. People are more likely to help when alone. Key study: a seizure over the intercom (Darley and Latané 1968) New York University students talked over an intercom from separate booths. One voice, a tape, began choking and begging for help as if having a seizure. Participants believed that only they, or they and one other, or they and four others could hear. Before the fit ended, 85 percent of those who thought they were alone left the booth to help, 62 percent with one other listener, and 31 percent with four others (Figure 3.11). Non-helpers were not apathetic; many were trembling. Criticism: a distressing deception. In the smoke-filled room (Latané and Darley 1968), students filling in questionnaires saw smoke pour through a vent. Alone, 75 percent reported it; beside two passive confederates who kept writing, 10 percent did; in groups of three naive students, someone reported it in 38 percent of groups. In the lady in distress study (Latané and Judith Rodin 1969), a woman was heard falling next door: 70 percent of people alone went to help, but only 7 percent of those sitting with an unresponsive confederate. Seizure over the intercom % helping before the fit ended Smoke-filled room % reporting the smoke 100 50 0 85 62 31 75 38 10 Alone 1 other 4 others Alone 3 naive students 2 passive confederates Figure 3.11 The bystander effect in two classic 1968 studies by Darley and Latané. The more people present, the less likely any one person is to act. Exam trap The research followed the murder of Kitty Genovese , not Martin Luther King Jr. (assassinated 1968), Emmett Till (a Black teenager lynched in 1955) or Malala Yousafzai (shot by the Taliban in 2012). People help more when alone ; seeing others not help makes intervention less likely. Groups did notice the smoke a little later, but the effect is about helping, not noticing. Five decisions, and why bystanders fail Latané and Darley (1970) traced the failure to five decisions, each of which must be answered yes before help is given (Table 3.22). Table 3.22 Latané and Darley's decision model of helping. Step The bystander must Obstacle at this step 1 Notice the event Distraction, hurry, overload 2 Interpret it as an emergency Ambiguity; pluralistic ignorance 3 Assume responsibility Diffusion of responsibility 4 Know how to help Lack of competence 5 Decide to help Audience inhibition; costs Two obstacles carry the bystander effect. The first, diffusion of responsibility (step 3), is the spreading of responsibility across all the bystanders, so that each feels less personally obliged and assumes someone else will act. In the intercom study nobody could see anyone else, so diffusion alone explains the result. The second, pluralistic ignorance (step 2), occurs when bystanders use the behaviour of others to decide whether help is needed and mistakenly conclude that it is not. Among strangers, nobody knows for sure what is happening; each stays calm to avoid looking foolish, reads the others' calm as evidence that all is well, and the whole group hesitates and does nothing, as in the smoke-filled room. A third obstacle, audience inhibition (evaluation apprehension), is the fear of being judged for overreacting or helping clumsily. Push a familiar scene through the model. A woman is beaten in a busy street while a crowd films it on phones and nobody calls for help. Each sees many others who could act (diffusion), sees nobody stepping in and half concludes it is a private quarrel (pluralistic ignorance), and fears looking foolish (audience inhibition). That is the bystander effect, not social loafing or group polarisation. Exam trap The two classic explanations are diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance; asked for one, the key is diffusion of responsibility. Pluralistic ignorance is not ignoring others or eyewitnesses, nor being suggestible about the cause: it is relying on others and wrongly deciding, from their calm, that help is unnecessary. "Someone else will do it" is diffusion; "nobody looks worried, so it must be nothing" is pluralistic ignorance. Table 3.23 defines the terms most often offered in their place. A meta-analysis by Peter Fischer and colleagues (2011) found it much weaker in dangerous emergencies, which are quickly recognised as real and in which other bystanders become physical support. Weighing costs: the arousal: cost-reward model Why do bystanders sometimes help at once? In 1969 Irving Piliavin , Judith Rodin and Jane Allyn Piliavin staged collapses on New York subway trains. A man with a cane who seemed ill was helped in 95 percent of trials, usually within seconds, and larger groups did not help less; a man who smelled of alcohol and carried a bottle was helped in only about half. Their arousal: cost-reward model (developed fully in 1981) says that seeing someone in distress causes unpleasant arousal, which bystanders reduce by whichever response costs least. The costs of helping (effort, danger, embarrassment) are weighed against the costs of not helping (guilt, blame, the victim's suffering). The drunk man raised the costs of helping and, seeming responsible for his plight, lowered the guilt of walking away (Figure 3.12). Cost of helping Low High Cost of not helping: high Cost of not helping: low Direct help quick and likely Indirect help (call police), or reinterpret the event Varies with norms and person No help leave, deny or ignore Figure 3.12 Predictions of the arousal: cost-reward model. Help is most likely when helping is cheap and not helping is costly. Situations that raise or lower helping We help people who are similar to us, partly because similarity raises empathic concern. We help less when victims seem responsible for their plight : in Bernard Weiner 's attribution analysis (Section 3.3), a controllable cause such as drinking invites anger, an uncontrollable one such as illness invites sympathy and help. Key study: the Good Samaritan (Darley and Batson 1973) Princeton Theological Seminary students, some preparing a talk on the parable of the Good Samaritan, were told they had time to spare, were on time, or were already late. On the way they passed a man slumped and groaning in a doorway. Of those in no hurry, 63 percent helped; moderate hurry, 45 percent; great hurry, 10 percent. The topic of the talk made no reliable difference. Being in a hurry , not character, decided who stopped. Stanley Milgram (1970) proposed urban overload : city dwellers face so much stimulation that they screen much of it out, people in need included, and helping is lower in big cities than in small towns. Mood matters. Alice Isen and Paula Levin (1972) found that students given a cookie were more willing to help, and that people who had just found a dime in a public telephone were far more likely to help a stranger pick up dropped papers (about 88 against 4 percent). This feel good, do good effect fades if helping would spoil the mood. Guilt also raises helping, as people repair their self-image. Goodness is contagious. Motorists stopped more often for a woman with a flat tyre if they had just passed another woman being helped ( James Bryan and Mary Ann Test 1967): a prosocial model shows what to do and that helping is the norm. After playing a prosocial video game such as Lemmings, 57 percent helped pick up spilt pencils, against 33 percent after a neutral game ( Tobias Greitemeyer and Silvia Osswald 2010). Watching an act of kindness produces elevation , an uplifted feeling described by Jonathan Haidt (2000) that makes the watcher want to help. Gratitude raises future helping. Adam Grant and Francesca Gino (2010) had students comment on a stranger's job application letter; when he thanked them, about twice as many helped again. Being thanked raised the helpers' self-worth (feeling valued by others) and self-efficacy (feeling competent), but only self-worth carried the rise in helping. Exam trap Gratitude raises helping by enhancing helpers' self-worth and self-efficacy ; pairs built on self-esteem or self-confidence are wrong. If asked which one did the work, it is self-worth. Helping falls after social exclusion , which drains empathy (people told they would end up alone gave less to a student fund; Jean Twenge and colleagues 2007); in darkness and other conditions of anonymity , which remove the approval helping earns ( Chen-Bo Zhong and colleagues 2010); and when people think of their time in money terms ( Sanford DeVoe and Jeffrey Pfeffer 2010). Who helps, and how help is received The altruistic personality is a consistent tendency to help others across situations, rather than helping only when one feels like it, calculating costs and benefits, or being ready only in emergencies. Hans Werner Bierhoff , Renate Klein and Peter Kramp (1991) compared people who had given first aid at road accidents with people who had not, and found five components in the helpers: empathy, belief in a just world, social responsibility, internal locus of control and low egocentrism. Samuel Oliner and Pearl Oliner (1988) interviewed more than 400 rescuers of Jews in Nazi Europe: compared with non-rescuers, their parents had modelled caring and disciplined by reasoning, and they felt responsible for people beyond their own group. In volunteering, Allen Omoto and Mark Snyder (1995) found five motives among AIDS volunteers (values, understanding, personal development, community concern, esteem enhancement); the self-oriented ones best predicted who kept serving. Help is not always welcome. The threat-to-self-esteem model (Nadler and Jeffrey Fisher 1986) holds that aid carries both support (someone cares) and threat (you are inferior and dependent). It threatens most when the helper is a similar peer, the task is central to one's self-image and the help cannot be repaid; then people resent help or avoid seeking it. Nadler also contrasted dependency-oriented help , which hands over the full solution, with autonomy-oriented help , which gives the tools to solve the problem oneself. The helper's perceived motive matters too: help that seems freely chosen and caring is welcomed; help that seems forced by a role or given for show is resented. Are helping and aggression, then, opposites? Not quite. Their motives overlap (people help to gain status or keep rivals dependent), their acts can look alike (a surgeon's knife), and unwanted help can harm. Section 3.9 takes up aggression. All three are aggression, yet their roots differ. This section traces those roots, the triggers, and the methods that actually reduce aggression. What counts as aggression Robert A. Baron and Deborah R. Richardson (1994) define aggression as behaviour directed toward the goal of harming another living being who is motivated to avoid such treatment. So hateful thoughts alone are not aggression (it is behaviour); accidental harm is not, though a punch that misses is (it is intended); and kicking a door or a wanted surgical cut is not (the target must be living and unwilling). Anger is an emotion, aggression a behaviour: you can be furious and do nothing, and the hired killer aggresses without anger. The main distinction is by goal. In hostile aggression (reactive or affective aggression) harm is the end in itself: hot, impulsive, a reply to provocation. In instrumental aggression (proactive aggression) harm is a means to another end, such as money or status: cold and planned. Table 3.24 adds the other cuts. The term relational aggression comes from Nicki R. Crick and Jennifer K. Grotpeter (1995), who found that girls used it more than boys; studies that counted only hitting had made girls look unaggressive. Table 3.24 Further forms of aggression. Form What it is Example Physical Harm by bodily force or weapons A slap Verbal Harm by words Insults, threats Direct Face to face; the aggressor is known A shove Indirect Through others or in secret An anonymous complaint Relational Damages the victim's friendships and status Exclusion, gossip Instinct, evolution and biology The oldest answer is that aggression is built in. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) proposed in 1920 a death instinct , thanatos , opposing the life instinct (eros): a drive toward self-destruction that is turned outward as aggression (Chapter 4). The ethologist Konrad Lorenz (1903 to 1989), in On Aggression (1966), saw an inherited fighting instinct that spaced animals out and let the strongest males breed. His hydraulic model pictured aggressive energy building like water in a tank until a releasing stimulus, or eventually none at all, lets it out. Well-armed animals evolved ritualised fighting (stags shove with locked antlers rather than gore) and appeasement gestures (a beaten wolf bares its throat) that stop the winner's attack; weakly armed humans evolved weak inhibitions, and our weapons now kill beyond the reach of appeasement. Critics note that aggression varies too much across cultures to be one pressure-cooker drive. Both views fed the catharsis idea ( 3.9.8 ). Evolutionary psychology recasts instinct as inherited potential: aggression that won mates and resources was passed on. It predicts that young men commit most violence, mostly against rival men ( male competition ), and that sexual jealousy is a leading cause of violence between partners. The clearest chemical finding is that low serotonin activity, shown by low levels of its breakdown product 5-HIAA in cerebrospinal fluid, is linked to impulsive aggression; serotonin helps restrain impulses. Testosterone correlates modestly with dominance and aggression. Table 3.25 sets out the usual distractors. The amygdala fuels anger, the hypothalamus organises attack and the prefrontal cortex applies the brakes (Chapter 5). Genes act through environments: in the New Zealand cohort of Avshalom Caspi and colleagues (2002), maltreated boys became antisocial adults far more often if they carried the low-activity form of the MAOA gene, which codes the enzyme that breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine; without maltreatment the variant carried little risk. Testosterone is a hormone, not a neurotransmitter. Frustration-aggression and its reformulation Social psychologists moved the drive's source outside the person. The frustration-aggression hypothesis , put forward at Yale in 1939 by John Dollard , Leonard W. Doob , Neal E. Miller , O. H. Mowrer and Robert R. Sears , claimed that frustration, the blocking of a goal (Section 1.10), always leads to aggression, and that aggression always comes from frustration. Neither holds: frustration often brings sadness or problem solving, and the hired killer is not frustrated. Miller (1941) soon withdrew the first claim: aggression is only one of several responses to frustration. The group also explained the target. When the frustrator is powerful or absent, aggression shifts to a safer target ( displacement : scolded by his boss, a clerk shouts at his children); when that target is a weak minority blamed for the trouble, displacement becomes scapegoating (Section 3.5). Leonard Berkowitz (1926 to 2016) reformulated the hypothesis in 1989, in what became his cognitive neoassociationist model . Frustration causes aggression only to the extent that it produces negative affect , so unexpected or unfair frustrations provoke most. And any aversive event (pain, heat, foul smells, noise) does the same. Negative affect automatically primes both fight (rudimentary anger) and flight (rudimentary fear); the situation, past learning and later appraisal decide which wins (Figure 3.13). Stimuli associated with violence act as aggressive cues , tipping an angry person toward fight. Key study: The weapons effect (Berkowitz and LePage, 1967) In the study by Berkowitz and Anthony LePage , male students, angered or not by a partner's electric shocks, could shock him back while a shotgun and a revolver, or badminton racquets, or nothing lay nearby. Angered men beside the guns gave the most shocks. "The finger pulls the trigger, but the trigger may also be pulling the finger." Some replications failed, but meta-analyses support a modest weapons effect . Arousal from elsewhere also feeds aggression. In Dolf Zillmann 's excitation transfer theory (1971), arousal fades slowly, so arousal left over from one event (a near miss on the Mysuru ring road, a gym session) is misattributed to the next, and a minor annoyance produces rage, especially when the leftover arousal goes unnoticed. Exam trap The reformulation is Berkowitz's (1989), not Dollard's (the 1939 original), Miller's (the 1941 softening) or Lazarus's (Richard Lazarus: appraisal and stress, Section 1.11). Weapons effect: Berkowitz and LePage; leftover arousal: Zillmann. Learning, scripts and the General Aggression Model Learning theories ask where the particular ways of aggressing come from. Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) answered: largely from watching others. Key study: The Bobo doll experiments (1961 to 1965) Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila A. Ross (1961) let 72 nursery-school children watch an adult punch, kick and shout at an inflatable Bobo doll, or play quietly. Left with the doll, those who had seen aggression copied the model's specific acts and words, unrewarded. Filmed and cartoon models worked almost as well (1963). In 1965, children who saw the model punished (vicarious punishment) imitated less than those who saw it rewarded (vicarious reinforcement), yet a reward for reproducing the acts made all groups equal: consequences to the model affect performance, not learning. Criticism. Bobo is built to be hit. This is observational learning through modelling , with no direct reinforcement of the learner (Bandura's four processes are in Section 1.6). Exam trap Bobo doll = observational learning of aggression through modelling . Not operant conditioning (no child was reinforced for hitting), not classical conditioning of fear (Little Albert, Section 1.6), not sensory deprivation (the McGill isolation studies, Section 1.5). Repeated observation builds aggressive scripts ( L. Rowell Huesmann ): stored programmes for how a conflict unfolds and how to respond ("if disrespected, hit back"), retrieved fast when provoked. The General Aggression Model of Craig A. Anderson and Brad J. Bushman (2002) integrates these theories (Figure 3.14): person and situation inputs shape the present internal state (affect, cognition, arousal); a quick appraisal yields impulsive action, a considered one thoughtful action; and each outcome feeds back, making the next aggressive episode easier. Heat, alcohol and other aversive conditions Aversive conditions act as Berkowitz predicted. The hot temperature effect is real: across 50 US cities from 1950 to 1995, hotter years brought more murders and assaults but not more property crime (Anderson and colleagues). Yet in Baron's laboratory, very hot, angry participants became less aggressive. The negative affect escape model of Baron and Paul A. Bell explains this: discomfort raises aggression up to a moderate level, beyond which escape takes priority, an inverted U. Alcohol raises aggression in both sexes. In the alcohol myopia account of Claude M. Steele and Robert A. Josephs (1990), alcohol narrows attention to the salient cue (the insult) and pushes out distant ones (consequences, norms). Crowding, uncontrollable noise and pain act likewise, through negative affect. Bullying, cyberbullying and workplace aggression Dan Olweus , pioneer of school research in Norway ( Bullying at School , 1993), defined bullying as intentional, repeated aggression against a victim with less power. He distinguished bullies, victims (often anxious and friendless) and bully-victims (provocative victims who also bully, and fare worst); his whole-school programme of supervision, clear rules and consistent action roughly halved bullying. Online, cyberbullying follows victims home and reaches vast audiences; anonymity and the unseen victim produce online disinhibition , a cousin of deindividuation (Section 3.10). Workplace aggression is mostly verbal, indirect and covert, and perceived injustice often triggers it. Preventing and controlling aggression Punishment deters only when it is prompt, certain, strong and seen as justified, conditions courts rarely meet; unfair punishment acts as fresh provocation, and physical punishment models aggression. The catharsis hypothesis , rooted in Freud, adopted by Dollard's group (1939) and revived by Lorenz, holds that venting anger safely (punching a pillow, shouting) drains the drive and reduces later aggression. It fails. Key study: Venting feeds the flame (Bushman, 2002) Bushman angered about 600 students with harsh feedback on their essays. One group then hit a punching bag while thinking about the critic, a second while thinking about fitness, and a third sat quietly. When all could blast the critic with noise, the rumination group was angriest and most aggressive; doing nothing produced the least aggression. What works? Cognitive interventions : a sincere apology ; pre-attribution , a warning that someone is ill or stressed, so later rudeness is blamed on circumstances; and a delay that lets arousal fade. Exposure to non-aggressive models who stay calm under provocation. Social skills training in negotiating and complaining without attack. Baron's incompatible response technique , which induces empathy or humour, feelings that cannot coexist with anger. Strengthened self-regulation , which fatigue, stress and alcohol deplete (Baumeister). And forgiveness , which ends the cycle of revenge. Exam trap Which method is not supported? What turns people into a group, how do groups grow, how do others change our effort, why do groups decide badly, and what makes a leader effective? What makes a group A group is two or more people who interact, depend on one another for their goals, see themselves as belonging together and share a structure of roles and norms. People at a bus stop share a place, not a group. Entitativity , Donald T. Campbell 's (1958) term, is how far a collection of people is seen as one coherent unit; frequent interaction, shared goals and similarity raise it, and highly entitative groups such as families matter most to their members. Table 3.27 sorts the kinds of groups. Table 3.27 Kinds of groups. Distinction Who Meaning Primary versus secondary Charles Horton Cooley (1909) Primary: small, intimate, face-to-face (family). Secondary, the later contrast: large, impersonal, goal-based (a company) Formal versus informal Set up with assigned roles (a ward team) versus arising on its own (lunch friends) Membership versus reference Herbert Hyman (1942) Groups you belong to versus groups whose standards you judge yourself by In-group versus out-group William Graham Sumner (1906) "Us" versus "them"; root of ethnocentrism (Section 3.5) Intimacy groups, task groups, social categories, loose associations Brian Lickel and colleagues (2000) Most to least entitative: a family; a work team; "women"; a bus queue A reference group can remake attitudes. In Theodore Newcomb 's Bennington College study (late 1930s, published 1943), women from conservative homes who adopted the liberal college as their reference group became more liberal, and most stayed so 25 years later. Formed versus natural groups and social group work are in Section 3.11. Group structure and membership Every lasting group develops a structure with four parts. Roles are behaviours expected of a position. Kenneth Benne and Paul Sheats (1948) distinguished task roles that move the work on (initiator, information seeker, coordinator, evaluator-critic), maintenance roles or socio-emotional roles that hold members together (encourager, harmoniser, compromiser, gatekeeper) and self-oriented roles that serve the individual at the group's cost (aggressor, blocker, recognition seeker, dominator). Role differentiation follows as members specialise, often one leading the task while another keeps the peace. Status is rank within the group; high-status members talk more and may deviate more. Norms are the group's rules, often unspoken. Cohesiveness is the sum of forces holding members in: liking, commitment to the task and pride. Cohesive groups demand more conformity (Section 3.7) and satisfy members more, but perform better only when their norms favour effort, and very high cohesion feeds groupthink . People join for belonging, goals, self-knowledge, status and identity (Section 3.5), and pay in freedom, time and effort. A high price even raises a group's value: women who passed an embarrassing initiation liked a dull group more ( Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills , 1959), a dissonance effect (Section 3.4). Richard Moreland and John Levine (1982) described group socialisation as five phases in which group and person evaluate each other: investigation (prospective member), socialisation (new member), maintenance (full member), resocialisation (marginal member, as commitment falls) and remembrance (ex-member). Entry, acceptance, divergence and exit mark the transitions. Sometimes the whole group breaks. A schism is the splintering of a group into distinct factions. Fabio Sani (2005) found that clergy who left the Church of England after it first ordained women in 1994 felt the change had subverted its identity, and that their protests would go unheard. Exam trap Splintering into factions is a schism . A chapter is a local branch, division an everyday word and deviation one member breaking a norm. Sociometry: mapping who chooses whom A hostel's room list shows its official structure; how would you find the real one? Jacob Levy Moreno (1889 to 1974) answered with sociometry , a method of measuring an individual's social behaviour and relations in a group from the attractions and rejections among its members. He set it out in Who Shall Survive? (1934), with Helen Hall Jennings , after regrouping a girls' training school by the residents' own choices. In the sociometric test each member privately names whom he or she would choose, and sometimes reject, for working, living or playing together. Answers fill a sociometric matrix , choosers down the side and the chosen across the top; a column total divided by the number of other members (N minus 1) is a sociometric index of choice status. Drawn out, the matrix becomes a sociogram , a diagram of choices and rejections that shows attraction, social distance and patterns of choice within a group (Figure 3.15). A star receives many choices, an isolate none; a neglectee receives few but is not rejected; a rejectee draws rejections. A mutual pair choose each other, a chain runs A to B to C, and a clique chooses within itself. The sociogram thus captures implicit and explicit communication and interaction patterns; teachers use it to find isolated children. Moreno also founded psychodrama (Chapter 7). A B C D E R I K L M Star Mutual pair Rejectee Isolate Clique chooses rejects Figure 3.15 A sociogram. A is the star, A and C a mutual pair, K, L and M a clique; R is rejected and nobody chooses I. Exam trap Sociometry, not the sample method (Chapter 9), the interview method or the Verstehen method (interpretive understanding of social action, Wilhelm Dilthey , Max Weber ), measures social behaviour in a group. A sociogram does not measure IQ, a leader's personality or economic status. A genogram is a three-generation family tree (Chapter 7), an ecomap a family's links with its environment (Section 3.11), a cognitive map Tolman's mental map (Section 1.6). How groups develop In 1965 Bruce Tuckman reviewed studies of therapy, training and laboratory groups and proposed four stages; with Mary Ann Jensen in 1977 he added a fifth (Figure 3.16). In forming , members orient themselves, are polite and unsure, and depend on the leader. In storming , conflict and resistance surface as members struggle over leadership, roles and the group's definition. In norming , cohesion grows, norms and roles are agreed, and the group clarifies its purpose and strategy for reaching its goals. In performing , the work gets done. In adjourning , the group disbands, often with a sense of loss. Forming orientation; polite, unsure; lean on leader Storming conflict over leadership and group's aims Norming cohesion; norms, roles, purpose agreed Performing energy goes into the task; work gets done Adjourning task ends; group disbands (added 1977) Figure 3.16 Tuckman's stages of group development, in their fixed order. Real groups do not always march in step. Connie Gersick (1988) found that project teams with deadlines show punctuated equilibrium : inertia, a burst of change near the midpoint of their time, then focused work. The Boston model used in social group work is in Section 3.11. Exam trap Proximity is not a stage of group formation; it is a cause of attraction (Section 3.6). "Clarified its purpose and strategy" is norming ; "struggle over leadership and group definition" is storming . The order is forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning. Performing in front of others Does an audience help you or hurt you? The question is as old as experimental social psychology. Key study: Triplett's fishing reels (1898) Norman Triplett noticed in cycling records that riders were faster when paced or racing a rival than when riding alone against the clock. He then had children wind a fishing reel as fast as possible, alone or beside another child doing the same; many wound faster in company, though some did worse. Published in 1898, it is often called the first social psychology experiment. Criticism: the gains were small and uneven. Floyd Henry Allport named the effect social facilitation (1920, 1924), better performance when others are present, and called working side by side on the same task coaction. Yet others sometimes made people worse, called social inhibition or impairment. Robert Zajonc resolved the puzzle in 1965 with drive theory : the mere presence of others raises arousal, and arousal strengthens the dominant response , the one most likely in that situation. On a simple or well-learned task the dominant response is correct, so performance improves; on a complex or new task it is likely wrong, so performance worsens (Figure 3.17). Push a case through it. Tim has trained his voice for years but has hardly danced, and his school musical needs both. The audience raises his arousal: his singing improves and his dancing deteriorates. An audience helps most on easy, well-learned tasks, not novel, difficult, creative or first-time ones. Zajonc, Alexander Heingartner and Edward Herman (1969) found it even in cockroaches: watched by other roaches, they ran a straight runway faster but a maze more slowly. Presence of others Arousal (drive) rises Dominant response strengthened Easy, practised task dominant response is correct Performance improves (Tim's singing) Hard or new task dominant response is often wrong Performance worsens (Tim's dancing) Figure 3.17 Zajonc's drive theory (1965): one rise in arousal, two opposite outcomes. Two rivals refine the account. In evaluation apprehension ( Nickolas Cottrell and colleagues, 1968), concern about being judged does the arousing: a blindfolded audience produced no facilitation. In distraction-conflict theory ( Robert S. Baron , 1986), attending to both task and onlookers creates conflict that arouses and narrows attention. The arousal-performance curve is the Yerkes-Dodson law (Section 1.10). Exam trap Triplett used fishing reels . Rope pulling is Ringelmann, the shock generator Milgram (Section 3.7), a maze with food reward animal learning (Section 1.6). Diffusion of responsibility explains bystanders not helping (Section 3.8). Social loafing and deindividuation Now pull a rope with seven others: nobody can tell how hard you pull. The French engineer Max Ringelmann found that the bigger the team, the less each member pulled (published 1913). Part of this Ringelmann effect is coordination loss, but Alan Ingham and colleagues (1974) showed that blindfolded people who merely believed others were pulling also pulled less: motivation falls too. That loss is social loafing : less effort when individual efforts are pooled than when working alone. Bibb Latané , Kipling Williams and Stephen Harkins (1979) had blindfolded students in headphones clap and shout alone or in supposed groups of two, four or six: each person's output fell as the group grew. Steven Karau and Williams's collective effort model (1993) explains why: people work hard only when they expect their effort to matter for an outcome they value. Loafing therefore falls when each contribution is identifiable and evaluated, the task is challenging, appealing or involving, members are friends or committed, effort is believed to bring valued rewards, and the group is small. A teacher such as Miss Pooja should grade both the group and each member; group grades alone, random assignment or optional presentations leave individual effort hidden. Exam trap "Groups loaf less when evaluation apprehension is absent" is false : removing the fear of judgement lets people loaf. Social loafing's other name is the Ringelmann effect ; the free-rider effect is a related but separate term (Table 3.28). The Triplett effect is social facilitation, the McGurk effect is lips changing the speech sound heard (Section 1.3), and the sleeper effect is delayed persuasion (Section 3.4). Loafing is not universal. P. Christopher Earley (1989, 1993) found that Chinese management trainees worked harder in a group than alone, where Americans loafed: social striving , typical of collectivist cultures. Philip Zimbardo (1969) found that hooded women gave longer shocks than name-tagged women, and Edward Diener and colleagues (1976) saw anonymous Halloween trick-or-treaters in groups take extra sweets far more often than named children alone. Cyberbullying and online disinhibition, cruelty behind a screen name, are deindividuation, not social facilitation, polarisation or the bystander effect (bullying is in Section 3.9). Group decision making Do several heads beat one? James H. Davis (1973) showed that group decisions follow social decision schemes : majority wins on opinions, truth wins when one member can demonstrate a correct answer, and first shift , where the group follows the first member to change position, as in deadlocked juries. Groups are often more extreme, not more moderate. In 1961 James Stoner found that groups recommended riskier courses than their members had alone, the risky shift , but later studies found that groups that began cautious became more cautious. Serge Moscovici and Marisa Zavalloni (1969) showed the general rule: French students' liking for de Gaulle and dislike of Americans both grew after discussion. This is group polarisation : discussion pushes members towards a more extreme version of their initial leaning, through persuasive arguments (more arguments heard for the favoured side), social comparison (wanting to look better than average on the valued side) and social identity (converging on the group's prototype). Exam trap More extreme group decisions are group polarisation . "Extremity" is not a technical term, groupthink is cohesive suppression of dissent, and conformity is yielding to a norm (Section 3.7). Irving Janis , in Victims of Groupthink (1972; revised 1982), analysed fiascoes such as Kennedy's Bay of Pigs invasion (1961) and the ignored warnings before Pearl Harbor (1941); later analysts added the 1986 Challenger launch. Groupthink is a mode of thinking in highly cohesive groups in which the drive for unanimity overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives: collective decision making that discourages dissent and leads to poor decisions. Antecedents are high cohesion, insulation, a directive leader, high stress and no methodical procedures. The eight symptoms are an illusion of invulnerability (excess optimism and risk), collective rationalisation (warnings explained away), belief in the group's morality, stereotyped views of out-groups, direct pressure on dissenters, self-censorship of doubts, an illusion of unanimity (silence read as agreement) and self-appointed mindguards who screen out contrary information. Remedies: the leader stays impartial and withholds his or her view early, appoints a devil's advocate or a subgroup to critique the plan, invites outside experts, uses subgroups and holds a second-chance meeting. Exam trap To curb groupthink, the leader should ask a subset of the group to critique the plan. Team-building raises cohesion, stating his view first steers the group, and forbidding argument silences dissent: all make it worse. Groupthink is not individual thinking, brainstorming or mere peer pressure, and it yields poor decisions. Groups also waste what members know. Garold Stasser and William Titus (1985) spread facts so that the best student-body candidate stood out only if members pooled unshared facts, a hidden profile ; groups discussed mainly shared facts (biased information sampling) and chose worse. In brainstorming , popularised by Alex Osborn , members produce many ideas with criticism postponed, yet as many people working alone produce more, because of production blocking : one person speaks at a time and ideas fade while waiting. The nominal group technique has members write ideas silently, share them in turn and vote privately; the Delphi technique , from the RAND Corporation, polls experts anonymously over rounds with feedback until opinion converges. Escalation of commitment is continuing to invest in a failing course to justify past costs. Cooperation, conflict and fairness In a social dilemma , each person gains by acting selfishly but all lose if everyone does. In the prisoner's dilemma , two suspects questioned apart each do best by betraying the other, yet both do worse if both betray than if both stay silent. Garrett Hardin 's tragedy of the commons (1968) is the many-person version: each herder adds cows to the shared pasture until it is ruined, as with groundwater or fish stocks today. Communication, trust, small groups and sanctions raise cooperation. Conflict yields to bargaining , best ending in an integrative agreement that gives both sides more than a split by trading on issues each values differently; to superordinate goals that neither side can reach alone (Sherif's Robbers Cave, Section 3.5); and to Charles Osgood 's GRIT (graduated and reciprocated initiatives in tension reduction, 1962), small announced concessions that invite reciprocation. Conflict is often about fairness: distributive justice is fair outcomes, judged in J. Stacy Adams 's equity theory (1965) by comparing our outcome-to-input ratio with others'; procedural justice is fair procedures; transactional or interactional justice is courteous treatment and honest explanation. Leadership Leadership is influencing group members towards shared goals. The great-person theory held that leaders are born with special traits, but Ralph Stogdill 's 1948 review found traits only weakly linked to leadership: a leader in one situation may not lead in another. Attention turned to what leaders do. Key study: Lewin, Lippitt and White (1939) Kurt Lewin , Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White had adults lead clubs of ten-year-old boys in three styles. Under autocratic leaders, who made every decision, boys worked while watched but stopped when the leader left, and grew hostile or apathetic. Under democratic leaders, who guided group decisions, work was more original, continued without the leader, and the boys liked this style best. Under laissez-faire leaders, who left the boys alone, little was done. Criticism: small American samples. The Ohio State studies, using the Leader Behaviour Description Questionnaire (LBDQ), found two independent dimensions: initiating structure (organising work and roles) and consideration (warmth and concern for subordinates); one leader can be high on both. The Michigan studies contrasted job-centred with employee-centred supervisors. Robert Blake and Jane Mouton 's managerial grid (1964) crosses concern for production with concern for people, from impoverished (1,1), country club (1,9), authority-compliance (9,1) and middle of the road (5,5) to the ideal, team management (9,9). Contingency theories match leader to situation. In Fred Fiedler 's contingency model (1967), leaders rate their least preferred co-worker (LPC): rating even that person kindly (high LPC) marks a relationship-oriented leader, rating harshly (low LPC) a task-oriented one. Situational favourableness comes from three dimensions: leader-member relations , task structure and position power (the leader's formal power and authority to reward and punish); good relations count most. Task-oriented leaders do best in very favourable or very unfavourable situations, relationship-oriented leaders in between; since style is fixed, Fiedler advised changing the situation. This closing section follows that wish into hospitals and crowded cities, police stations and courtrooms, and then into social work, the profession that helps individuals, groups and communities. Health, environment, work and happiness Why does the same stress make one person ill and leave another well? Partly because of other people. Social support is the perception or experience of being loved, cared for and part of a network of mutual help. Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Ashby Wills (1985) contrasted two models. In the main-effect model, social integration benefits health at any level of stress. In the stress-buffering hypothesis , support protects chiefly under high stress, by making the stressor seem less threatening and by softening the reaction to it. Loneliness is in Section 3.6, and health behaviour models in Chapter 7. Places matter too (personal space is in Section 3.3). Daniel Stokols (1972) separated density, a physical count of people per unit of space, from crowding , the unpleasant feeling that there are too many people, with lost control and privacy: a festival is dense yet enjoyable, while a lift with three strangers feels crowded. In 1962 John B. Calhoun let rats breed with ample food but limited space. Their society collapsed into a behavioural sink of neglected young, soaring infant mortality, aggression and withdrawal. In people, density harms mainly when it removes control. Irwin Altman (1975) described territoriality , the marking and defending of places: primary territories are owned and central to life (a home), secondary territories are used regularly but shared (a canteen table) and public territories are open to anyone for a while (a park bench). Noise, likewise, harms most when it is unpredictable and uncontrollable. At work, social psychology informs motivation (Herzberg, Section 1.10), the Hawthorne effect, in which people change their behaviour because they know they are being studied (Chapter 9), and leadership (Section 3.10). Ed Diener (1946 to 2021) defined subjective well-being as a person's own evaluation of life: high life satisfaction, frequent positive feelings and infrequent negative ones. Eyewitness testimony Why do defence lawyers so often protest the use of eyewitness testimony? Witnesses are not especially forgetful, and poor eyesight is rarely the issue; the trouble is that a memory can be vivid, confident and false. Source monitoring is the process of judging where a memory came from: seen, heard about or imagined ( Marcia Johnson and colleagues, 1993). A source monitoring error attaches a genuine memory to the wrong origin, so a face seen in a mugshot album, on the news or as an innocent bystander is taken for the culprit's. In one celebrated case a rape victim identified the psychologist Donald Thomson , who had been on the live television programme she was watching when she was attacked: his alibi was the source of her memory. Misleading questions act the same way. In the 'smashed' versus 'hit' study of Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer (1974; Section 1.7), the wording of a question changed what witnesses remembered, down to broken glass that was never there. A confident witness is not usually right: across studies, confidence predicts accuracy only weakly, and it grows after the event. In the post-identification feedback effect ( Gary Wells and colleagues, 1998), witnesses told 'Good, you identified the suspect' later claimed a better view and more certainty, even when they had picked an innocent person. Some sources of error the legal system cannot control. In weapon focus a visible weapon draws attention away from the face; in own-race bias people recognise faces of their own race more accurately than faces of other races; and high stress during the crime usually impairs identification. Other sources it can control, chiefly the lineup (Table 3.30). Table 3.30 Lineup reforms that reduce false identifications. Reform What is done Why it helps Double-blind The officer running it does not know the suspect No unintended hints or feedback Sequential lineup Faces shown one at a time, each judged yes or no Stops choosing the closest match Unbiased instructions Witness told the culprit may not be present Removes pressure to choose someone Fair fillers Others match the witness's description The suspect does not stand out Confidence recorded at once Certainty noted in the witness's words Before feedback inflates it The cognitive interview of Ronald Fisher and Edward Geiselman (first tested in 1984) gives four instructions: reinstate the context (mentally return to the scene and your feelings), report everything , however trivial, change the order (recall backwards as well as forwards) and change the perspective (describe what another person present would have seen). Because a memory has several retrieval routes, it draws out much more correct detail than a standard police interview, with few added errors. Exam trap Defence lawyers protest eyewitness testimony because source errors can cause a false identification , not because witnesses forget more, see poorly or are usually right when confident. The Ronald Fisher of the cognitive interview is not Ronald Aylmer Fisher, the statistician. Juries, profiling and rehabilitation In the story model of Nancy Pennington and Reid Hastie (1986), jurors faced with conflicting evidence build a narrative of what happened from the evidence and their own knowledge of how such events go, then choose the verdict that fits the most coherent story; evidence presented in story order persuades best. Pretrial publicity against the accused raises guilty verdicts, and instructions to ignore it help little. Attractive defendants are more often acquitted and given lighter sentences, unless their looks aided the crime, as in a swindle. Stereotypes about race, sex and class bias verdicts (Section 3.5), though careful deliberation weakens them. Offender profiling infers the characteristics of an unknown offender from the crime. FBI agents such as Robert Ressler and John Douglas interviewed convicted murderers and built a top-down typology. Organised offenders plan, control the scene, bring and remove a weapon and are socially competent; disorganised offenders act on impulse, leave a chaotic scene and a weapon of opportunity, and are socially inadequate. David Canter 's investigative psychology works bottom-up, from statistical patterns across many solved cases; his 1986 profile helped catch England's 'railway rapist'. Support for the organised-disorganised split is weak. Profiling and the cognitive interview help to catch offenders; rehabilitation tries to change them. After Robert Martinson 's 'nothing works' (Key study), meta-analyses from the late 1980s built the 'what works' evidence. Successful programmes are community-based rather than institutional, keeping offenders tied to work, family and prosocial peers; they are cognitive-behavioural , structured and multimodal. They follow the risk-need-responsivity (RNR) principles of Don Andrews and James Bonta (1990): match treatment intensity to the risk of reoffending ( risk ); target criminogenic needs, the changeable causes of crime such as antisocial attitudes, antisocial peers and substance misuse ( need ); and teach in the way the offender learns best ( responsivity ). Punishment alone does not reduce reoffending. Key study: Martinson and 'nothing works' (1974) Question: does rehabilitation reduce reoffending? Method: Martinson and colleagues reviewed 231 controlled evaluations of correctional programmes. Result: 'with few and isolated exceptions', rehabilitation had had no appreciable effect on recidivism; the press shortened this to 'nothing works', and policy turned to punishment. Criticism: many programmes were weak or badly run, and Martinson himself withdrew the strong claim in 1979. Exam trap A quality of successful offender rehabilitation is being community-based . Cognitive interviews and offender profiling are investigative tools, not treatment, and a focus on the relationship with parents is not a defining quality. Social work: definition, roots and methods The 2014 global definition of the International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) and the International Association of Schools of Social Work (IASSW) calls social work a practice-based profession and academic discipline that promotes social change and development, social cohesion, and the empowerment and liberation of people. Its lens is the person-in-environment : problems arise between people and their families, neighbourhoods and institutions, so help may target either side. It has two roots. The Charity Organisation Society (London, 1869) sent 'friendly visitors' to investigate applicants and coordinate relief, the seed of case work. The settlement houses placed educated volunteers among the poor to press for reform: Toynbee Hall (London, 1884, under Samuel Barnett ) and Hull House (Chicago, 1889, founded by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr ), the seed of group work and community organisation. The primary methods , or direct methods, are social case work, social group work and community organisation; the secondary or auxiliary methods are social welfare administration, social action and social work research. Direct practice , face-to-face work with clients, has historically been conceptualised as case work and case management, as individual psychotherapy (clinical social work) and as generalist practice. Policy practice, shaping laws and agency rules, is indirect or macro practice. India's first school of social work, and Asia's, was the Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work , opened in Bombay in 1936 under the American missionary Clifford Manshardt ; in 1944 it was renamed the Tata Institute of Social Sciences . The Delhi School of Social Work followed in 1946, and psychiatric social work training grew up at Ranchi and at NIMHANS, Bengaluru. Exam trap 'Tata Institute of Social Profession' and 'Tata Institute of Social Service' are invented, and the Tata Institute of Social Sciences is the 1944 name; the first school was the Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work . Policy practice is not a form of direct practice. Social case work Social case work , the oldest method, helps one person or family at a time with problems of social functioning, through a professional relationship and community resources. Its founder, Mary Ellen Richmond (1861 to 1928), gave it a method in Social Diagnosis (1917), which taught workers to gather evidence systematically before judging, and defined it in What Is Social Case Work? (1922) as the processes that develop personality through adjustments consciously effected, individual by individual, between people and their social environment. The process runs in phases (Figure 3.18): intake (can this agency help?), study (gathering the facts), assessment or social diagnosis (defining the problem and its causes), intervention or treatment, evaluation , and termination with follow-up . Content analysis, the coding of themes in texts, is a research technique, not a phase. The worker's techniques are interviewing (the central one), observation , counselling , supportive techniques (reassurance, encouragement), home visits , collateral contacts (speaking, with consent, to relatives, teachers or employers), environmental modification (changing the client's surroundings, such as arranging a pension) and referral . Lobbying legislators belongs to social action, not case work. 1 Intake and study Facts gathered 2 Assessment Social diagnosis 3 Intervention Plan carried out 4 Evaluation Were goals met? 5 Termination Planned ending 6 Follow-up Do the gains last? Goals unmet: reassess Figure 3.18 The social case work process. When evaluation finds goals unmet, the worker returns to assessment (dashed arrow). By the 1930s case work had split into the diagnostic school , built on Freud, and the functional school , built on Otto Rank's will therapy (Table 3.31). Florence Hollis developed the diagnostic school into the psychosocial approach, and Charlotte Towle 's Common Human Needs (1945) taught that every welfare applicant has the same basic needs as anyone else. Approach Key names Central idea Diagnostic (psychosocial) Gordon Hamilton (1940); Hollis (1964) Understand the personality, diagnose, then treat; the client as person-in-situation Functional Jessie Taft , Virginia Robinson (Pennsylvania) The client's will drives change, within the agency's function and time limits Problem-solving Helen Harris Perlman (1957) Four Ps: a person with a problem comes to a place for a process of help Task-centred William Reid and Laura Epstein (1972) Brief, time-limited work on agreed problems through concrete tasks Whatever the school, the relationship carries the help. Felix Biestek (1957) set out seven principles of the casework relationship: individualisation (each client is unique), purposeful expression of feelings , controlled emotional involvement (responding with feeling without being swept away), acceptance , a non-judgemental attitude , client self-determination (the right to make one's own choices) and confidentiality . Key study: Fischer, 'Is casework effective?' (1973) Question: does professional case work help clients? Method: Joel Fischer reviewed the controlled studies comparing clients who received professional case work with control groups who did not. Result: there was no good evidence that case work worked, and in some studies treated clients did worse. Impact: the review shook the profession and pushed it toward empirical, evidence-based practice. Criticism: the studies often had vague goals and crude outcome measures. Exam trap Richmond founded case work; Joel Fischer studied its effectiveness. Irwin Epstein wrote on social work research, John Goyder on survey nonresponse, and Jacob Cohen was the statistician of kappa, effect size and power (Chapter 9). Not part of the case work process: content analysis . Not a case work technique: lobbying . Social group work Social group work uses the group itself as a helper: members gain from one another as well as from the worker. Grace Longwell Coyle (1892 to 1962), whose Social Process in Organized Groups appeared in 1930, established group work as a method within social work. Gisela Konopka (1910 to 2003) later carried it into treatment settings such as institutions and child guidance clinics. Harleigh B. Trecker listed ten principles: planned group formation, specific objectives, a purposeful worker-group relationship, continuous individualisation, guided group interaction, democratic group self-determination, flexible functional organisation, progressive programme experiences, resource utilisation and evaluation. Three models dominate. The social goals model, from the settlements, builds social consciousness and responsible citizenship. The remedial model of Robert Vinter uses the group to treat individual members, with the worker as change agent. The reciprocal, or mediating, model of William Schwartz makes the group a mutual-aid system, with the worker mediating between members and between the group and society. Ronald Toseland and Robert Rivas distinguish formed groups , deliberately convened by a worker or agency for an identified purpose, usually with a professionally trained leader and an agency auspice (a support group for caregivers), from natural groups , which come together spontaneously out of friendship, shared interest or circumstance (a circle of friends, a street gang). All groups share certain properties: a purpose, stages of development and criteria for their composition, along with structure, norms, roles and cohesion (Section 3.10). No group needs an 'analytic base'. Some members serve the group in hidden ways. Lawrence Shulman described the scapegoat, blamed for what the group dislikes in itself; the deviant member, whose odd behaviour often voices what others feel; the gatekeeper , who blocks or diverts the group, by joking or changing the subject, whenever talk nears a painful topic; the internal leader, who takes initiative from within; the defensive member, who denies having a problem; the quiet member; and the monopoliser, who dominates the talk. Groups also change over time. The Boston model of James Garland , Hubert Jones and Ralph Kolodny (1965) has five stages: pre-affiliation (approach and avoidance), power and control, intimacy, differentiation and separation. Tuckman's forming to adjourning sequence is in Section 3.10. Exam trap Group work as a method: Grace Coyle , not Mary Richmond (case work), Charlotte Towle ( Common Human Needs ) or Gisela Konopka (group work in treatment settings).
