Chapter summary 3.1 Social Psychology: History, Theories, Concepts and Methods. Social psychology studies how individuals' thoughts, feelings and behaviour are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others ( Gordon Allport , 1954). It grew from Le Bon's crowd (1895), Triplett's first experiment (1898) and the 1908 texts of McDougall and Ross; Kurt Lewin , its modern father, added the life space (person plus psychological environment), group dynamics and action research . A crisis around 1970, European work and the social cognition era followed. From sociology came Durkheim's anomie (normlessness), symbolic interactionism, socialisation and resocialisation , status and role. Its theories include Moscovici's social representations (1961); its methods run from observation to experiment, with debriefing after deception. 3.2 Social Cognition and First Impressions. Social cognition is how we interpret, remember and use social information. As cognitive misers (Fiske and Taylor, 1984) we lean on automatic processing, schemas (scripts, self-schemas, stereotypes), priming and heuristics. Schemas persist (belief perseverance) and can fulfil themselves: Merton's self-fulfilling prophecy (1948), the Pygmalion effect (Rosenthal and Jacobson, 1968) and the Golem effect. Social thought tilts towards negativity, optimism, the planning fallacy, counterfactuals, magical thinking, false consensus and the illusion of control. Asch's central traits (warm-cold) and the halo effect (Thorndike, 1920) shape impressions; thin slices (Ambady and Rosenthal) are surprisingly accurate; impression management follows Goffman's dramaturgy and Jones and Pittman's strategies. 3.3 Communication, Nonverbal Cues and Attribution. Communication runs encoding, channel, recipient, decoding , with feedback and noise; the classic models are Lasswell (1948), Shannon and Weaver (1949), Schramm (1954) and Berlo's SMCR (1960). Nonverbal channels include face, gaze, body language, touch and paralanguage; Hall's proxemics sets intimate, personal, social and public zones, and lies are detected with only about 54 percent accuracy. Attribution theory began with Heider (1958): dispositional versus situational causes. Jones and Davis explained correspondent inferences, Kelley used consensus, consistency and distinctiveness, and Weiner added stability and controllability. The fundamental attribution error (Ross 1977), actor-observer effect, self-serving bias and just-world hypothesis tilt our explanations, more so in individualist cultures. 3.4 Attitudes, Persuasion and Cognitive Dissonance. An attitude is a learned evaluation of an object with affective, behavioural and cognitive parts (Rosenberg and Hovland, 1960), serving Katz's utilitarian, knowledge, ego-defensive and value-expressive functions. LaPiere (1934) exposed the attitude-behaviour gap; strong, specific attitudes formed by direct experience predict best, and the theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen) adds perceived control to attitude and subjective norm. Persuasion depends on source, message and audience (the Yale approach) and runs by the central or peripheral route (Petty and Cacioppo). Reactance (Brehm, 1966), forewarning and inoculation aid resistance. Festinger's cognitive dissonance (1957) explains why $1 beat $20; Bem's self-perception theory is its main rival. 3.5 Stereotypes, Prejudice and Intergroup Relations. A stereotype is a belief about a group, prejudice a negative attitude (Allport, 1954) and discrimination unfair action. Prejudice has been traced to the authoritarian personality, displaced frustration, social learning, realistic conflict (at Robbers Cave only superordinate goals ended hostility) and relative deprivation. Tajfel's minimal groups showed that categorisation alone breeds in-group favouritism; social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner, 1979) says much of our self-esteem comes from our groups. Low-prejudiced people inhibit automatically activated stereotypes by controlled processing (Devine, 1989); the IAT measures implicit bias. Social roles (Eagly) shape gender stereotypes, which build glass ceilings and sticky floors. Contact reduces prejudice under Allport's conditions. 3.6 Affiliation, Attraction and Close Relationships. The need to belong (Baumeister and Leary 1995) is fundamental; gregariousness is a social motive. Schachter (1959) showed that anxiety raises affiliation with others in the same plight, and we affiliate for information, anxiety reduction and social comparison (Festinger 1954), which also explains FOMO. Attraction grows from propinquity and mere exposure (Zajonc 1968), looks, matching, similarity and reciprocity. Exchange, equity and investment theories explain staying or leaving. Self-disclosure deepens relationships (descriptive facts, evaluative feelings). Love is passionate or companionate, triangular (Sternberg 1986) and shaped by attachment style. Weiss separated emotional from social loneliness. 3.7 Social Influence: Conformity, Compliance, Obedience and Power. Social influence takes three forms: conformity (matching a group with no request), compliance (yielding to a direct request) and obedience (following an authority's command). Norms may be descriptive or injunctive, prescriptive or proscriptive. Sherif's autokinetic study showed norms forming through informational influence; Asch's line studies showed normative conformity to an obviously wrong majority (about 37 percent of critical trials). Consistent minorities can convert majorities (Moscovici). Cialdini traced compliance tactics such as the foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face to six principles. In Milgram's study 65 percent obeyed to 450 volts; Zimbardo's prison study showed the power of roles. French and Raven named six bases of power. 3.8 Prosocial Behaviour: Why and When People Help. Altruism is helping with no expected reward, at a cost to oneself. Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis (the Elaine study) claims true altruism; Cialdini's negative-state relief model and the empathic joy hypothesis are egoistic, while kin selection (Hamilton), reciprocal altruism (Trivers), competitive altruism, defensive helping and norms add other motives. After the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese , Latané and Darley showed the bystander effect : people help more when alone (seizure study, 85 versus 31 percent). Their five-step model locates its two classic causes, diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance . Costs (Piliavin), hurry, mood, models, gratitude, the altruistic personality and the threat-to-self-esteem model complete the picture. 3.9 Aggression: Its Roots, Causes and Control. Aggression is behaviour aimed at harming a living being who wants to avoid it (Baron and Richardson, 1994): hostile or instrumental , physical or verbal, direct, indirect or relational . Freud's thanatos and Lorenz's hydraulic instinct gave way to biology (low serotonin , MAOA with maltreatment) and to the frustration-aggression hypothesis (Dollard and colleagues, 1939), softened by Miller (1941) and reformulated by Berkowitz (1989) as negative affect plus aggressive cues (the weapons effect). Bandura's Bobo doll studies showed observational learning; the General Aggression Model integrates these. Provocation, exclusion, media violence, honour cultures, heat and alcohol raise aggression; catharsis fails, while apology, incompatible responses and self-regulation help. 3.10 Groups: Structure, Performance, Decisions and Leadership. A group is two or more interacting, interdependent people with a shared identity and a structure of roles, status, norms and cohesiveness. Moreno's sociometry (1934) maps choices in a sociogram of stars, isolates and cliques. Groups pass through Tuckman's forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Others' presence brings social facilitation on easy tasks and impairment on hard ones (Triplett 1898; Zajonc 1965); pooled effort brings social loafing (Ringelmann), reversed as social striving in collectivist cultures; anonymity brings deindividuation . Discussion causes group polarisation , and cohesion with insulation causes Janis's groupthink . Leadership theory runs from traits and styles to Fiedler's contingency model and transformational leadership. 3.11 Applied Social Psychology: Law, Culture and Social Work. Social support protects health, chiefly as a stress buffer (Cohen and Wills, 1985); crowding is felt, density is counted (Stokols). Defence lawyers challenge eyewitnesses because source monitoring errors cause false identifications and confidence predicts accuracy weakly; double-blind sequential lineups and the cognitive interview help. Jurors build stories; effective rehabilitation is community-based, cognitive-behavioural and follows risk-need-responsivity . Social work grew from the Charity Organisation Society and settlements. Mary Richmond founded case work (intake to follow-up); Fischer (1973) doubted its effectiveness. Grace Coyle established group work ; Trecker gave its principles and Shulman its member roles. (RML 2022) a Serge Moscovici b Michael A. Hogg c Roy F. Baumeister d Mark E. Leary ✓ Answer: (a) Serge Moscovici Serge Moscovici, social representations theory (1961) The concept The founding study Moscovici launched social representations theory in 1961 by studying how psychoanalysis became French common sense. How it works A new idea becomes common sense through anchoring (tying it to familiar categories) and objectification (turning it into a concrete image). Why the other options are wrong (b) Michael A. Hogg Known for work on social identity and his uncertainty-identity theory , not social representations. (c) Roy F. Baumeister With Mark R. Leary, proposed the need to belong (1995), a theory of motivation, not of shared common sense. (d) Mark E. Leary Proposed the sociometer theory of self-esteem and, with Baumeister, the need to belong (1995); the theorist is Mark R. Leary. Which one refers to the behaviour that an individual engages in while enacting a role? (RML 2020) a Role taking b Role playing c Playing at a role d Role expectation ✓ Answer: (b) Role playing Role theory: role enactment The concept What it is Role playing (also called role enactment ) is the actual behaviour of the person performing a role. Why this one The stem asks for the behaviour shown while enacting a role: the doing, not the thinking or the expecting. Why the other options are wrong (a) Role taking Mead 's mental act of seeing a situation from another person's viewpoint; it is thinking, not behaving. (c) Playing at a role A young child's make-believe , pretending at a role rather than actually performing one. (d) Role expectation What other people expect of the role occupant, not what the occupant actually does. Some students experience an intense period of adaptation when they leave their old school environment and start college, especially during those initial days before they find companions, start to fit in and feel comfortable. This process is best described as: (RML 2021) a Looking-glass self b Self-awareness c Institutionalisation d Re-socialisation ✓ Answer: (d) Re-socialisation Resocialisation after a major transition The concept What it is Resocialisation is unlearning old norms and roles and learning new ones. Why this one It follows a major transition such as starting college: the student drops old-school ways and learns the new setting's. Why the other options are wrong (a) Looking-glass self Cooley 's self-image built from others' imagined judgements of us, not adapting to a new setting. (b) Self-awareness Just attention turned on oneself ; it says nothing about learning new norms. (c) Institutionalisation The apathetic dependence of long-stay inmates on an institution, not fitting into a new life. A tendency to act in a way that is consistent with one's own belief, expectation, or cognition about an event or behavior, thereby increasing the likelihood that the event or behavior will occur, is termed as: (IHBAS 2020) a Self-fulfilling prophecy b Confirmation bias c Motivational reaction d Base-rate fallacy ✓ Answer: (a) Self-fulfilling prophecy Merton, self-fulfilling prophecy (1948) The concept What it is A self-fulfilling prophecy is acting on an expectation in ways that make it come true. Who named it Merton coined the term in 1948. The belief changes behaviour, and the behaviour changes the outcome . Why the other options are wrong (b) Confirmation bias Only seeks evidence that fits a belief; it changes nothing in the world, so the event is not made more likely. (c) Motivational reaction Not a recognised term in psychology; a made-up distractor. (d) Base-rate fallacy Ignoring how common something is (its base rate) when judging likelihood. What is the halo effect? (IHBAS 2024) a The tendency to judge others based on their group membership b The influence of a positive trait on the perception of other traits c The tendency to overlook negative behaviors in individuals d The effect of initial impressions on subsequent judgments ✓ Answer: (b) The influence of a positive trait on the perception of other traits Thorndike, halo effect (1920) The concept What it is In the halo effect , one salient positive trait or an overall impression colours ratings of unrelated traits . Who named it Thorndike named it in 1920. Why the other options are wrong (a) The tendency to judge others based on their group membership Stereotyping : judging a person by the group they belong to. (c) The tendency to overlook negative behaviors in individuals A consequence of a halo, not its definition; the halo is one trait spreading to others. (d) The effect of initial impressions on subsequent judgments The primacy effect (or anchoring), where early information weighs most. A teacher watches two students interact for less than a minute and correctly infers who is the class leader. This example best illustrates: (IHBAS 2025) a Social facilitation b Self-fulfilling prophecy c Thin slicing d Fundamental attribution error ✓ Answer: (c) Thin slicing Ambady and Rosenthal, thin slices of behaviour The concept What it is Thin slicing is making accurate judgements from very brief samples of behaviour. The evidence Ambady and Rosenthal showed that silent clips of 30 seconds or less yield accurate judgements. Why the other options are wrong (a) Social facilitation Better performance of well-learned tasks in front of others; it is about performing, not judging. (b) Self-fulfilling prophecy The teacher's expectation did not create the leadership; the teacher only perceived it. (d) Fundamental attribution error Over-explaining behaviour by disposition ; here the brief judgement was accurate, not an error. Arrange the process of communication in sequence (RML 2020) a coding, decoding, recipient, channel b channel, encoding, recipient, decoding c channel, decoding, recipient, encoding d encoding, channel, recipient, decoding ✓ Answer: (d) encoding, channel, recipient, decoding Sender-receiver model of communication The concept Sending The sender first encodes the idea into symbols, and the message travels through a channel . Receiving It reaches the recipient , who then decodes it. So: encoding, channel, recipient, decoding. Why the other options are wrong (a) coding, decoding, recipient, channel Puts decoding before the message is sent through the channel or received. (b) channel, encoding, recipient, decoding Sends the message through the channel before it is encoded. (c) channel, decoding, recipient, encoding Starts with the channel and decodes before the recipient gets it, leaving encoding last. The tendency of people to attribute their own behavior to external causes and other’s behavior to internal causes is referred to as : (IHBAS 2024) a Self-serving bias b Fundamental attribution error c Actor-Observer effect d Stereotyping ✓ Answer: (c) Actor-Observer effect Jones and Nisbett, actor-observer effect (1971) The concept What it is As actors we explain our own behaviour by the situation; as observers we explain others' by their dispositions. Who found it Jones and Nisbett described it in 1971. Exam tip The stem contrasts self and others ; only this effect covers both sides. Why the other options are wrong (a) Self-serving bias Concerns our own successes and failures , not the self-versus-other split in explaining behaviour. (b) Fundamental attribution error Concerns only other people's behaviour; it has no self-versus-other contrast. (d) Stereotyping A generalised belief about a group, not an attribution pattern. The "just-world hypothesis" explains victim-blaming as a result of: (Real PYQ 2024) a People's inherent sadism and desire to see others suffer. b The need to believe that the world is orderly, predictable, and fair. c A fundamental error in attributing behavior to dispositional factors. d The process of social comparison with a less fortunate other. ✓ Answer: (b) The need to believe that the world is orderly, predictable, and fair Melvin Lerner, just-world hypothesis The concept The belief Melvin Lerner held that people need to believe the world is orderly, predictable and fair . Why victims get blamed An innocent person's suffering threatens this belief, so observers restore it by deciding the victim deserved it . Why the other options are wrong (a) People's inherent sadism and desire to see others suffer. Observers are distressed by the suffering, not sadistic; blaming defends their belief. (c) A fundamental error in attributing behavior to dispositional factors. The dispositional blame is the result of the belief, not its cause. (d) The process of social comparison with a less fortunate other. Downward social comparison is a different process, not a defence of a belief in fairness. Arvind is a college student who has strong negative feelings about smoking cigarettes. His grandfather died of lung cancer and he believes smoking is disgusting. One night at a party, Arvind's friends all go outside for a cigarette and he decides to smoke as well. What will he most likely experience as a result? (RML 2021) a Justification of efforts b Increased drive to smoke c Cognitive Dissonance d Drive Reduction ✓ Answer: (c) Cognitive dissonance Festinger, cognitive dissonance theory The concept What it is Cognitive dissonance is Festinger 's aversive tension felt when actions clash with beliefs. Why here Arvind acts against a strong, important attitude (smoking is disgusting), so he will feel this tension. Why the other options are wrong (a) Justification of efforts A different paradigm, effort justification : valuing what cost us effort; nothing here involved effort. (b) Increased drive to smoke Nothing in the story suggests a stronger urge to smoke; he dislikes smoking. (d) Drive Reduction Hull 's motivation theory, not a reaction to acting against an attitude. In which of the following scenarios would it be most difficult to predict behaviour from attitudes? (RML 2021) a When the attitude has a great deal of personal relevance for the individual b When the attitude is formed by indirect experience c When the individual has a lot of knowledge about the attitude object d When the attitude is formed by the individual's direct experience ✓ Answer: (b) When the attitude is formed by indirect experience Regan and Fazio (1977), attitude-behaviour link The concept Why this one Hearsay-based attitudes, formed by indirect experience , are weak and less accessible , so they predict behaviour poorly. The evidence Regan and Fazio (1977) showed that direct experience strengthens the attitude-behaviour link. Why the other options are wrong (a) When the attitude has a great deal of personal relevance for the individual High personal relevance strengthens the attitude-behaviour link, so prediction is easier. (c) When the individual has a lot of knowledge about the attitude object More knowledge of the object strengthens the link, so prediction is easier. (d) When the attitude is formed by the individual's direct experience Direct experience makes the attitude strong (Regan and Fazio, 1977), so prediction is easiest. In Social Psychology, reactance is : (IHBAS 2024) a The tendency to comply with direct requests b The motivation to restore freedom when it is threatened c The effect of persuasive messages on attitude change d The tendency to follow social norms without question ✓ Answer: (b) The motivation to restore freedom when it is threatened Brehm, psychological reactance (1966) The concept What it is Reactance is the motivation to restore a freedom when it is threatened. Key note Brehm (1966) defined it; it often makes the forbidden option more attractive. Why the other options are wrong (a) The tendency to comply with direct requests That is compliance (complying with requests), the opposite of pushing back against a threat to freedom. (c) The effect of persuasive messages on attitude change Persuasion : attitude change driven by a message. (d) The tendency to follow social norms without question Conformity , going along with group norms. According to social identity theory, prejudice arises primarily due to : (IHBAS 2025) a Competition for scarce resources b Cognitive dissonance c Categorization into in-groups and out-groups d Social facilitation ✓ Answer: (c) Categorization into in-groups and out-groups Tajfel, social identity theory (minimal groups) The concept The evidence Tajfel 's minimal groups showed in-group favouritism with no resources at stake. The conclusion So categorisation plus the need for positive distinctiveness is enough to produce prejudice. Why the other options are wrong (a) Competition for scarce resources Sherif 's realistic conflict theory , not social identity theory. (b) Cognitive dissonance Festinger 's theory of inconsistent cognitions; unrelated to this account of prejudice. (d) Social facilitation Performance in the presence of others ; unrelated to prejudice. Low-prejudiced people engage in: (IHBAS 2020) a Automatic information processing resulting in involuntary stereotyping b Controlled information processing resulting in refuting stereotype c Controlled information processing resulting in involuntary stereotyping d Automatic information processing resulting in voluntary stereotyping ✓ Answer: (b) Controlled information processing resulting in refuting stereotype Devine (1989), automatic and controlled stereotyping The concept Stage 1: automatic Devine (1989) found stereotypes are activated automatically in high- and low-prejudiced people alike. Stage 2: controlled Low-prejudiced people then use controlled processing to inhibit the stereotype. Why the other options are wrong (a) Automatic information processing resulting in involuntary stereotyping The first stage , common to all; low-prejudiced people go on to override it. (c) Controlled information processing resulting in involuntary stereotyping Pairs the processes wrongly: controlled processing is what inhibits stereotyping, not what produces it. (d) Automatic information processing resulting in voluntary stereotyping Pairs the processes wrongly: automatic processing gives involuntary, not voluntary, stereotyping. The phenomenon where a qualified individual is prevented from advancing to higher positions in their career due to an invisible barrier based on gender or minority status is called: (Real PYQ 2024) a The Matthew Effect b The Glass Ceiling Effect c The Halo Effect d The Pygmalion Effect ✓ Answer: (b) The Glass Ceiling Effect Wall Street Journal article (1986), glass ceiling The concept What it is The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier of attitudes and organisational bias near the top. Origin The term was popularised by a 1986 Wall Street Journal article. Why the other options are wrong (a) The Matthew Effect Accumulated advantage (Merton, 1968), not a barrier to advancement. (c) The Halo Effect Concerns impressions , not career barriers. (d) The Pygmalion Effect Concerns expectations , not career barriers. 'The more we see and interact with a person, the more likely he or she is to become our friend or sexual partner.' This denotes: (IHBAS 2020) a Propinquity effect b Exposure effect c Matching hypothesis d Reciprocity ✓ Answer: (a) Propinquity effect Festinger, Schachter and Back (1950) The concept What it is The propinquity effect : nearness and frequent interaction breed friendship. The study Festinger , Schachter and Back (1950) showed this. Why the other options are wrong (b) Exposure effect Narrower: mere repeated exposure to any stimulus raises liking; it is the mechanism behind propinquity. (c) Matching hypothesis Choosing partners of similar attractiveness . (d) Reciprocity Liking those who like us . Emotional isolation means: (IHBAS 2020) a Feeling a lack of deep emotional attachment to one specific person b Suffering from a lack of friends/associates c Suffering from feelings of incompetence d Feeling a sense of inadequacy and low self-esteem ✓ Answer: (a) Lack of deep attachment to one specific person Robert Weiss (1973), emotional versus social isolation The concept Two kinds Robert Weiss (1973) separated emotional isolation from social isolation . The difference Emotional isolation is lacking a deep attachment to one specific person; social isolation is lacking a wider network of friends and associates. Why the other options are wrong (b) Suffering from a lack of friends/associates This is social isolation , Weiss's other type. (c) Suffering from feelings of incompetence Incompetence is a correlate of loneliness, not one of its types. (d) Feeling a sense of inadequacy and low self-esteem Low self-esteem is a correlate of loneliness, not one of its types. Which concept is closely related to FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) in social media research? (JEMAS 2025) a Social comparison b Classical conditioning c Operant extinction d Cognitive dissonance only ✓ Answer: (a) Social comparison Przybylski and colleagues (2013); Festinger (1954) The concept What FOMO is FOMO (Przybylski and colleagues 2013) arises from constant upward comparison with others' curated experiences. The root theory It sits in the tradition of Festinger 's social comparison theory (1954). Why the other options are wrong (b) Classical conditioning A learning process , not comparison with others. (c) Operant extinction A learning process , not comparison with others. (d) Cognitive dissonance only A consistency process , not comparison with others. Which of the following is an example of the power of roles? (IHBAS 2024) a Robber's Cave Experiment b Milgram's message experiment c Zilstein's shock research d Zimbardo's prison experiment ✓ Answer: (d) Zimbardo's prison experiment Zimbardo, prison experiment The concept What happened Students randomly made guards or prisoners took on their roles so fully that the study was stopped after six days. Why this one Ordinary people changed because of the role they were given: the power of roles. Why the other options are wrong (a) Robber's Cave Experiment Studied intergroup conflict (Robbers Cave), not the power of roles. (b) Milgram's message experiment Was the small-world study, not a study of roles. (c) Zilstein's shock research Dr Zilstein was the fictitious experimenter of Schachter 's affiliation study, not research on roles. What is normative social influence? (IHBAS 2024) a Influence based on the desire to be correct and accurate b Influence based on the desire to be accepted and liked by others c Influence based on personal beliefs and values d Influence based on perceived power and authority ✓ Answer: (b) The desire to be accepted and liked Deutsch and Gerard (1955) The concept What it is Normative social influence is going along with others out of the desire to be accepted and liked . Its contrast Deutsch and Gerard (1955) contrasted it with informational influence , the desire to be correct. Why the other options are wrong (a) Influence based on the desire to be correct and accurate Informational influence , the other half of Deutsch and Gerard's pair. (c) Influence based on personal beliefs and values Describes internalisation (personal values), not influence from others' approval. (d) Influence based on perceived power and authority Describes obedience . According to Cialdini, techniques for gaining compliance rest to a large extent on six basic principles. These do NOT include: (RML 2022) a Scarcity b Social validation c Friendship/liking d Reward ✓ Answer: (d) Reward Cialdini, six principles of influence The concept The six Cialdini 's six are reciprocity , commitment and consistency, social validation (social proof), friendship or liking, authority and scarcity. Why reward Reward is not on the list. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Scarcity One of the six: things seem more valuable when they are rare or running out. (b) Social validation One of the six, also called social proof : we follow what others are doing. (c) Friendship/liking One of the six: we say yes more readily to people we know and like . The bystander effect, where the presence of others inhibits helping, is primarily explained by two factors: (Real PYQ 2024) a Social loafing and deindividuation b Diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance c Social comparison and normative influence d Group polarization and groupthink ✓ Answer: (b) Diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance Latané and Darley, bystander effect The concept Diffusion of responsibility Latané and Darley 's first mechanism: each bystander assumes someone else will act . Pluralistic ignorance Their second: each bystander reads the others' calm as a sign that nothing is wrong. Key note The other pairs are group phenomena of other kinds (Sections 3.6, 3.7 and 3.10). Why the other options are wrong (a) Social loafing and deindividuation Social loafing (slacking in a group effort) and deindividuation (losing self-awareness in a crowd) do not explain failing to help. (c) Social comparison and normative influence Social comparison (judging ourselves against others) and normative influence (conforming to be liked) are broader processes, not the two named mechanisms. (d) Group polarization and groupthink Group polarisation (discussion pushing views to extremes) and groupthink (cohesive groups suppressing dissent) concern group decisions, not helping. A state that occurs when bystanders in an emergency situation use the behaviour of others to determine whether help is actually required is called: (IHBAS 2020) a Pluralistic ignorance b Group conformity c Group compliance d Crowd behavior ✓ Answer: (a) Pluralistic ignorance Pluralistic ignorance in emergencies The concept What happens In an emergency, bystanders look to one another to decide whether help is needed. Why no one helps Seeing calm faces , each wrongly concludes help is not needed: pluralistic ignorance . Why the other options are wrong (b) Group conformity Conformity : yielding to group pressure, not misreading others' calm in an emergency. (c) Group compliance Compliance : yielding to a direct request. (d) Crowd behavior The collective action of a large gathering, not bystanders reading one another. Altruistic Personality is characterized by: (IHBAS 2020) a Offering help only when one feels like b Consistently helping others c Calculating the cost and benefits of helping d Readiness to help in an emergency ✓ Answer: (b) Consistently helping others Bierhoff, Klein and Kramp (1991) The concept What it is The altruistic personality is a stable tendency to help across situations . Its components Bierhoff , Klein and Kramp (1991) found them to be empathy, belief in a just world, social responsibility, internal locus of control and low egocentrism. Why the other options are wrong (a) Offering help only when one feels like Helping only when in the mood is situational helping , not a stable trait. (c) Calculating the cost and benefits of helping Cost-benefit calculation describes situational helping , not a stable trait. (d) Readiness to help in an emergency Readiness only in emergencies describes situational helping ; the trait shows across situations. Who reformulated the "frustration-aggression hypothesis"? (RML 2022) a Dollard b Miller c Berkowitz d Lazarus ✓ Answer: (c) Berkowitz Leonard Berkowitz, reformulated frustration-aggression hypothesis (1989) The concept The reformulation Leonard Berkowitz (1989) said frustration leads to aggression only to the extent that it produces negative affect . Role of cues Aggressive cues in the setting then tip the balance. Why the other options are wrong (a) Dollard Dollard and colleagues proposed the original hypothesis (1939), not the reformulation. (b) Miller Only softened the original (1941); the full recasting came later from Berkowitz. (d) Lazarus Richard Lazarus is known for appraisal and stress, not aggression. Albert Bandura's Bobo doll experiment is a classic demonstration of: (RML Practice 1) a Operant conditioning through direct reinforcement b Observational learning of aggression through modeling c Classical conditioning of fear d The effects of sensory deprivation ✓ Answer: (b) Observational learning of aggression through modelling Bandura, Bobo doll study The concept What happened Children copied an aggressive adult's specific acts toward the doll. Why observational They were never reinforced , so the learning came from watching a model . Why the other options are wrong (a) Operant conditioning through direct reinforcement No reinforcement was given, so it is not operant conditioning . (c) Classical conditioning of fear Conditioned fear is the Little Albert study, not Bobo doll. (d) The effects of sensory deprivation Studied in the McGill isolation research, not Bobo doll. Low levels of which neurotransmitter leads to aggression (Entrance Mock 1) a Serotonin b Dopamine c Epinephrine d Norepinephrine ✓ Answer: (a) Serotonin Low serotonin (5-HIAA) and impulsive aggression The concept The link Low serotonin activity is linked to impulsive aggression . How it shows It appears as low 5-HIAA , a serotonin breakdown product, in cerebrospinal fluid. Why the other options are wrong (b) Dopamine Concerns reward and movement , not this aggression link. (c) Epinephrine Marks arousal in any strong emotion, not aggression in particular. (d) Norepinephrine Like epinephrine, marks arousal in any strong emotion, not aggression in particular. Which of the following is not a stage of group formation? (JEMAS 2025) a Storming b Proximity c Norming d Performing ✓ Answer: (b) Proximity Tuckman, stages of group development The concept The stages Tuckman 's stages are forming , storming, norming, performing and adjourning . Why proximity Proximity is a cause of interpersonal attraction, not a stage of group development. Why the other options are wrong (a) Storming A real stage, the second: conflict over roles and leadership. (c) Norming A real stage, the third: the group settles its norms and cohesion. (d) Performing A real stage, the fourth: the group gets on with its task . Tim would like to participate in his high school's musical. He has been taking vocal lessons for years and is an excellent singer, but does not have much experience as a dancer. The director gives him a part where he has to sing and dance. Based on the theory of social facilitation, how will the presence of an audience affect Tim's performance? (RML 2021) a His dancing will improve, but his singing will be impaired b Both his singing and dancing will improve c His singing will improve, but his dancing will be impaired d Both his singing and dancing will be impaired ✓ Answer: (c) His singing will improve, but his dancing will be impaired Zajonc, drive theory of social facilitation The concept How it works By Zajonc 's drive theory, an audience raises arousal , which strengthens the dominant response . Applied to Tim The dominant response is correct on a well-learned task (singing) and often wrong on an unpractised one (dancing). Why the other options are wrong (a) His dancing will improve, but his singing will be impaired Reverses the prediction: arousal helps the well-learned task (singing) and hurts the unpractised one (dancing). (b) Both his singing and dancing will improve Ignores that the effect depends on how well learned the task is; his dancing is unpractised. (d) Both his singing and dancing will be impaired Ignores that the effect depends on how well learned the task is; his singing is well practised. A group of scientists is deciding on the use of live animals in research; most of the group has used live animals. How might the leader reduce groupthink? (RML 2021) a Make a cohesive team-building exercise a mandatory part of the meeting b Relate his opinion at the beginning of the discussion c Ask a subset of individuals in the group to critique animal research d Ask the group members not to argue with one another's opinions ✓ Answer: (c) Ask a subset to critique animal research Janis, remedies for groupthink The concept The remedy Janis 's remedies include a devil's advocate or critical subgroup . Why this one Asking a subset to critique animal research builds in the dissent that groupthink suppresses. Why the other options are wrong (a) Make a cohesive team-building exercise a mandatory part of the meeting Team-building raises cohesion , which worsens groupthink. (b) Relate his opinion at the beginning of the discussion A leader stating views first steers the group , which worsens groupthink. (d) Ask the group members not to argue with one another's opinions Forbidding argument suppresses dissent , which worsens groupthink. Defense attorneys often protest the prosecutor's use of eyewitness testimony because: (Amity 2023) a Eyewitnesses are more prone to forgetting b A confident witness is usually right c Source errors may cause an eyewitness to make a false identification d Poor eyesight of eyewitnesses tends to invalidate their testimony ✓ Answer: (c) Source errors may cause an eyewitness to make a false identification Source misattribution in eyewitness memory The concept What it is A source error is remembering a face but placing it in the wrong context. How it misleads A face met elsewhere (a mugshot , the news, a bystander) is misattributed to the crime. Why the other options are wrong (a) Eyewitnesses are more prone to forgetting Witnesses are not unusually forgetful . (b) A confident witness is usually right False: confidence predicts accuracy only weakly and grows after feedback. (d) Poor eyesight of eyewitnesses tends to invalidate their testimony Eyesight is rarely the issue. Which of the following is not a part of the social case work process? (RML 2020) a Content analysis b Treatment c Assessment d Evaluation ✓ Answer: (a) Content analysis Stages of the social case work process The concept The process Case work runs intake and study , assessment (social diagnosis), treatment or intervention, evaluation, termination and follow-up. Why content analysis Content analysis , coding themes in texts, is a research technique , not a case work step. Why the other options are wrong (b) Treatment A real stage: treatment or intervention , which follows assessment. (c) Assessment A real stage, also called social diagnosis . (d) Evaluation A real stage, coming before termination and follow-up. Who among the following established group work as a method within the profession of social work? (RML 2020) a Mary Richmond b Charlotte Towle c Grace Coyle d Geisla Konopka ✓ Answer: (c) Grace Coyle Grace Coyle, Social Process in Organized Groups (1930) The concept Her contribution Grace Coyle 's Social Process in Organized Groups (1930) founded group work as a method. Exam tip Link each name to one method: Richmond with case work, Coyle with group work. Why the other options are wrong (a) Mary Richmond Founded case work , not group work. (b) Charlotte Towle Wrote Common Human Needs ; she did not establish group work . (d) Geisla Konopka Konopka carried group work into treatment settings later, building on it rather than establishing it. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The fundamental attribution error (named by Lee Ross, 1977), also called the correspondence bias , is the tendency to overestimate dispositional and underestimate situational causes of other people's behaviour. asked 6 times Leon Festinger proposed cognitive dissonance theory (1957): holding inconsistent cognitions, or acting against one's attitude, produces aversive tension that people reduce, usually by changing the attitude when the behaviour cannot be undone. asked 6 times Diffusion of responsibility is the main explanation of the bystander effect: responsibility spreads across all the bystanders, so each feels less personally obliged and assumes someone else will act (Latané and Darley). asked 6 times Social loafing , also called the Ringelmann effect, is reduced effort when individual efforts are pooled (Latané, Williams and Harkins 1979); it falls when each contribution is identifiable and evaluated, so a teacher should grade both the group and each member. Its collectivist reversal is social striving (Earley). asked 6 times Social identity theory (Henri Tajfel and John Turner, 1979): a large part of our self-concept and self-esteem comes from the groups we belong to, and prejudice arises from categorisation into in-groups and out-groups and the need for positive distinctiveness, not from competition for resources. asked 5 times Solomon Asch (1951, 1956): among about seven confederates unanimously giving an obviously wrong line judgement, participants conformed on about 37 percent of critical trials and about three quarters conformed at least once; this is normative influence towards an incorrect majority, not obedience. asked 5 times Pluralistic ignorance : in an ambiguous emergency each bystander uses the calm behaviour of the others to decide whether help is needed, and mistakenly concludes that it is not (the smoke-filled room). asked 5 times Bruce Tuckman (1965) ordered group development as forming, storming (conflict over leadership and the group's definition), norming (cohesion; purpose and strategy clarified) and performing; adjourning was added with Mary Ann Jensen in 1977. Proximity is not a stage. asked 5 times Social facilitation began with Norman Triplett's 1898 fishing-reel study; Zajonc's drive theory (1965) says the presence of others raises arousal and strengthens the dominant response, improving easy, well-learned tasks and impairing new or difficult ones. asked 4 times The halo effect (Edward Thorndike, 1920): an overall impression or one positive trait influences ratings of a person's other, unrelated traits; the negative version is the horns effect. It is not primacy, stereotyping, self-serving bias or false consensus. asked 3 times Normative social influence rests on the desire to be liked and accepted; informational social influence on the desire to be correct (Deutsch and Gerard, 1955). Sherif's autokinetic study shows informational influence and the formation of group norms. asked 3 times The bystander effect : the more bystanders present, the less likely any one is to help and the slower the help; people help more when alone (seizure study: 85 percent alone versus 31 percent with four others). asked 3 times A sociogram , the tool of Jacob Moreno's sociometry (1934), maps choices and rejections to show social distance and patterns of choice in a group (stars, isolates, cliques); it captures implicit and explicit interaction patterns and does not measure IQ, personality or economic status. asked 3 times Groupthink (Irving Janis 1972) is a mode of thinking in highly cohesive groups where the drive for unanimity overrides realistic appraisal, discouraging dissent and producing poor decisions; a devil's advocate or critical subgroup and an impartial leader reduce it. asked 3 times Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947), father of modern social psychology: in B = f(P, E) the life space is the person plus the psychological environment, and he founded action research (1946) and group dynamics. asked 2 times The self-fulfilling prophecy was named and formalised by the sociologist Robert K. Merton (1948): a false definition of a situation evokes behaviour that makes it come true. It is not confirmation bias or the base-rate fallacy. asked 2 times Melvin Lerner's just-world hypothesis explains victim blaming by the need to believe that the world is orderly, predictable and fair. asked 2 times In the elaboration likelihood model (Petty and Cacioppo), systematic processing with careful attention to argument quality is the central route ; reliance on mental shortcuts and cues is the peripheral route . There is no emotional or situational route. asked 2 times Reactance (Jack Brehm, 1966) is the motivation to restore a threatened freedom, often by wanting the forbidden behaviour more. asked 2 times The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier that stops qualified women and minorities from rising to top positions; the term was popularised by a 1986 Wall Street Journal article. asked 2 times Intergroup hostility falls with cooperation: at Robbers Cave (Sherif, 1954) only superordinate goals ended it, and Allport's contact hypothesis (1954) requires equal status, common goals, cooperation and support of authorities, law or custom. asked 2 times The propinquity effect : the more we see and interact with a person, the more likely he or she becomes our friend or partner (Festinger, Schachter and Back 1950); its mechanism is Robert Zajonc's mere exposure effect (1968), in which repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking for it. asked 2 times Conformity is changing to match a group with no direct request; compliance is changing in response to a direct request; obedience is following a command from an authority. asked 2 times In Milgram 's 1963 baseline study, 26 of 40 men (65 percent) obeyed to the maximum 450 volts, and all went to 300 volts. asked 2 times Zimbardo 's Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) demonstrates the power of social roles and situational forces; planned for two weeks, it was stopped after six days. asked 2 times Cialdini 's six compliance principles are reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity (not reward); the foot-in-the-door (Freedman and Fraser, 1966) starts with a small request, then a larger one. asked 2 times The two classic explanations of the bystander effect are diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance, not social loafing, deindividuation, group polarisation or groupthink. asked 2 times Social case work was founded by Mary Ellen Richmond ( Social Diagnosis , 1917); its process is intake and study, assessment (social diagnosis), intervention, evaluation, termination and follow-up, and its techniques include interviewing, observation, counselling, home visits, collateral contacts and referral, but not content analysis or lobbying. asked 2 times Grace Coyle established group work as a method within social work; formed groups are convened for an identified purpose with a trained leader and an agency auspice, whereas natural groups come together spontaneously. asked 2 times In Lawrence Shulman's terms the gatekeeper blocks or diverts the group from painful topics; Trecker's principles include democratic group self-determination, flexible functional organisation and progressive programme experiences. asked 2 times

title: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 4: Personality
text: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 4: Personality Chapter 4 of the one-volume Final Exam Textbook, all nine JSS subjects in one book. Both A4 PDFs hold the whole book with the same page numbers. A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (975 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (975 pages) Chapter 4 Personality In this chapter 4.1 What Personality Is: Definitions, Approaches and Early Type Theories : Define personality and its neighbouring terms, map the approaches and the six questions on which they differ, name the determinants and research methods, and describe the early type theories from the four humours to Sheldon's somatotypes. 4.2 Freud's Psychoanalysis: Instincts, Structure and Psychosexual Stages : Trace how Freud built psychoanalysis from the study of hysteria, and use his methods, instincts, topographic and structural models, types of anxiety and psychosexual stages to explain personality, judging which of his ideas research supports. 4.3 Defence Mechanisms: How the Ego Protects Itself : Define defence mechanisms and their shared features, tell repression from its look-alikes, name the classic mechanisms from everyday vignettes, place them in Vaillant's four-level hierarchy, and match characteristic defences to particular disorders. 4.4 Jung's Analytical Psychology and Adler's Individual Psychology : Explain how Jung's analytical psychology and Adler's individual psychology broke with Freud, and attribute each of their concepts (collective unconscious, archetypes, attitudes and functions, inferiority complex, fictional finalism, style of life, birth order) correctly. 4.5 Horney, Fromm, Sullivan and the Object-Relations Theorists : Explain how Horney, Fromm and Sullivan rooted personality in culture and relationships, and how ego psychology, object relations (Klein, Winnicott, Fairbairn, Mahler, Kernberg), Kohut's self psychology and Lacan revised Freud. 4.6 Traits I: Allport, Cattell and the Lexical Search : Explain the trait approach and the lexical hypothesis, Allport's personal dispositions, idiographic method, functional autonomy and proprium, and Cattell's surface and source traits, ergs and sentiments, L-, Q- and T-data and the 16PF. 4.7 Traits II: Eysenck, the Big Five and the Biology of Personality : Explain Eysenck's PEN model and its biology, the other biological temperament models, the Big Five with its facets and In 1920 a 22-year-old American named Gordon Allport was travelling home after a year teaching at Robert College in Istanbul. He stopped in Vienna to see one of his brothers and, on an impulse, sent a note to Sigmund Freud asking whether he might call. Freud, then in his sixties and already world famous, invited him over. When Allport entered the study, Freud said nothing at all. He simply sat and waited for the young visitor to explain why he had come. The silence stretched until Allport, desperate for something to say, described an incident he had just seen on the tram. A small boy had seemed terrified of dirt: everything looked dirty to him, he changed his seat, and he told his mother not to let a dirty man sit beside him. Freud studied the neat, carefully groomed young man in front of him and asked, "Was that little boy you?" Allport was shaken. He had told the story only to fill a silence; Freud had heard it as a disguised confession of his visitor's own unconscious fears. Allport denied for the rest of his life that he was the little boy, yet 47 years later he still wrote that his "single encounter with Freud was traumatic". The meeting convinced him that psychoanalysis dug too deep, and that psychology should first take people's conscious motives at face value. In 1922 he finished a Harvard dissertation on personality traits, the first research on traits in the United States, and went on to found the trait approach. Two great personality theorists had heard the same small story and seen entirely different things in it. Which of them was right is a question this whole chapter keeps asking. 4.1 What Personality Is: Definitions, Approaches and Early Type Theories Lower yield · 4 Qs You call a cousin moody and a friend a born leader, and you use those labels to predict what each will do next. Personality psychology does the same job with evidence. This section defines personality and its neighbouring terms, maps the approaches that fill this chapter, and ends with the oldest answers, which sorted people into types by body fluids, faces and physiques. Persona and Allport's definition The word personality comes from the Latin persona , the mask a Roman actor wore to show which character he was playing. The origin points to the public face we show others, and it raises the question every theory in this chapter must answer: is personality the mask, or what lies behind it? The most quoted definition is that of Gordon Willard Allport (1897 to 1967), who weighed some 50 earlier definitions and offered his own in 1937: personality is "the dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his unique adjustments to his environment". In 1961 he replaced the last phrase with "characteristic behavior and thought". Dynamic organisation means personality grows, but in an organised way; psychophysical means mind and body work together; determine means it actively directs behaviour. A working definition: personality is the relatively enduring, distinctive pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviour that characterises a person, with internal aspects (motives, emotions) and external aspects (what others see), consistent across situations and over time. "Relatively" matters: a calm friend may still panic in an exam hall. Temperament, character, trait and type Temperament is the biologically based, early-appearing and relatively stable style of emotional reacting: how easily a person is aroused, how strongly they respond and what their usual mood is. Allport counted it, with physique and intelligence, as the inherited raw material of personality; infant temperament (Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess's easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up babies) is in Chapter 6. Character is personality judged against moral standards; in Allport's phrase, "character is personality evaluated, and personality is character devaluated". A trait is a stable dimension along which people differ consistently, such as sociability; a type is a discrete category into which a person is placed, such as "melancholic". Duane Schultz and Sydney Ellen Schultz compare theorists on six questions: free will versus determinism (do we direct our lives?), nature versus nurture (inheritance or upbringing?), past versus present (is the adult fixed by childhood, the view called historical determinism ?), uniqueness versus universality , equilibrium versus growth (do we only reduce tension, or strive to grow?) and optimism versus pessimism (are people basically good?). Freud gave the darkest answers (Figure 4.1): behaviour determined by instincts and the first five years, life a struggle to reduce tension, people seen pessimistically; on nature-nurture and uniqueness he took a middle position. The humanists stand near the opposite pole: Carl Rogers saw people as free, shaped more by the present than by childhood, growing and basically good. Determinants of personality Heredity supplies temperament and more: twin studies (identical versus fraternal twins) and adoption studies (children compared with biological and adoptive parents) suggest genes account for up to about half the variation in traits (Section 4.7). Environment shapes the rest: the family (parenting style, parental models, and birth order, which Alfred Adler stressed; Section 4.4), culture (individualist and collectivist societies reward different traits) and social class (opportunities, stresses and values). Surprisingly, the environment siblings share matters less than each child's own experiences. The situation matters too: the student talkative in the canteen is silent in the viva. Walter Mischel's 1968 critique began a twenty-year person-situation debate (Section 4.9) that ended in interactionism : behaviour depends on the person, the situation and their interaction. How personality is studied and assessed The clinical method builds theory from the case study , a detailed history of one person from many sources; Freud, Jung and Adler built their theories from patients this way. It gives depth, but its data are subjective and open to the therapist's bias. The experimental method manipulates an independent variable and measures its effect on a dependent variable with all else held constant, so it alone shows cause; Skinner and Bandura worked this way, at the price of studying narrow slices of behaviour. The correlational method measures how strongly two variables go together, such as anxiety and exam marks, so it cannot prove cause. Its extension, factor analysis , finds the few factors underlying many intercorrelated measures; Raymond Cattell and Hans Eysenck built their trait theories with it. The German philosopher Wilhelm Windelband (1848 to 1915) named a second divide in 1894. Nomothetic research (Greek nomos , law) seeks general laws from groups; idiographic research (Greek idios , one's own) studies the single individual in depth, the approach Allport championed (Section 4.6). Assessment uses self-report inventories (MMPI-2, 16PF, NEO-PI-R, EPQ), projective techniques that ask for interpretations of ambiguous material (Rorschach inkblots, the Thematic Apperception Test or TAT), interviews, behavioural observation and life records such as diaries and letters. Each is useful only if reliable (consistent) and valid (measures what it claims); the tests are in Chapter 2. Humours and the four temperaments The Greek physician Hippocrates (about 460 to 377 BC) taught that health depends on the balance of four bodily fluids, or humours : blood, yellow bile, black bile and phlegm. Galen (AD 129 to about 216), a Greek physician in Rome, is credited with turning this into a theory of temperament: the dominant humour sets a person's emotional style (Table 4.3). The chemistry is wrong, but the idea of a biological temperament was ahead of its time, and Hans Eysenck later fitted the four temperaments into the quadrants of his extraversion and neuroticism dimensions (Section 4.7). Body types: Kretschmer, Sheldon and later typologies The German psychiatrist Ernst Kretschmer (1888 to 1964) thought his patients' illnesses went with their build. In Physique and Character (1921) he described the pyknic type, short and round, with a cyclothymic temperament swinging between cheer and gloom and a liability to manic-depressive illness; the asthenic or leptosomic type, tall and thin, with a reserved, withdrawn schizothymic temperament and a liability to schizophrenia; the athletic type, muscular; and the dysplastic type, a disproportioned mix. One flaw: his manic-depressive patients were older, and people grow rounder with age. The American physician William Herbert Sheldon (1898 to 1977) replaced boxes with dimensions. In The Varieties of Human Physique (1940) he rated thousands of standardised photographs of male college students on three components, named after the embryonic layers that form the dominant tissues: endomorphy (soft and round, digestive organs prominent), mesomorphy (muscle and bone) and ectomorphy (thin and fragile, a large skin surface for the body's mass). Each is rated from 1 to 7, so a somatotype is three numbers: 4-4-4 is the average build, 7-1-1 the extreme endomorph, 1-7-1 the extreme mesomorph and 1-1-7 the extreme ectomorph. In The Varieties of Temperament (1942) he matched each component to a temperament (Table 4.4). Table 4.4 Sheldon's somatotypes and temperaments. Most of us call these accidents. Sigmund Freud did not. To him every slip, dream and symptom had a hidden cause, and personality was an uneasy truce between inborn urges, the outside world and the morality we absorb as children. His system, psychoanalysis , was the first formal theory of personality and is still the best known: at once a theory of personality and a method of treating mental disorder. We follow it from hysteria to the verdict of research. Freud's life and the birth of psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) was born in Freiberg, Moravia (now Příbor in the Czech Republic), and from the age of four lived in Vienna for almost 80 years. He qualified in medicine at Vienna in 1881 and began his career as a neurologist , not a psychiatrist or philosopher; "psychoanalyst" was a profession he had yet to invent. Neurologists were sent the patients nobody could explain, those with hysteria : genuine physical symptoms such as paralysis, blindness or loss of feeling (anaesthesia) in a limb, with no damage to the nerves. Freud came to see these as bodily reactions to emotional trauma, produced by painful memories kept out of awareness. Three teachers pointed the way. In Paris (1885 to 1886) the neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot (1825 to 1893) showed him hysterical symptoms produced and removed by hypnosis, and hinted that their roots were sexual. At Nancy, which Freud visited in 1889, Hippolyte Bernheim (1840 to 1919) showed that hypnosis worked through suggestion. In Vienna the physician Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925) had found that a patient lost her symptoms when she talked through their origins under hypnosis. Breuer and Freud reported this in "On the Psychical Mechanism of Hysterical Phenomena: Preliminary Communication" (1893), expanded into Studies on Hysteria (1895): hysterics, they wrote, suffer mainly from reminiscences. Key study: Anna O. and the talking cure (Breuer and Freud, 1895) Anna O., really Bertha Pappenheim (1859 to 1936), was a bright young Viennese woman who fell ill while nursing her sick father: blurred vision, weakness of her right arm and both legs, and trouble speaking. Breuer took one symptom at a time; under hypnosis she traced it back to the moment it began, relived the feeling, and the symptom faded. She called this the "talking cure". Breuer and Freud named the release of pent-up emotion catharsis (Greek for purification) and concluded that symptoms carry hidden meaning. Criticism: she was Breuer's patient, not Freud's, and she was not cured when treatment ended in 1882; she spent months in a Swiss sanatorium and took years to recover before becoming a pioneering social worker. Freud went further than Breuer. By the mid-1890s he held that the buried trauma was always sexual: his seduction theory traced neurosis to sexual abuse in childhood, usually by an older male relative. In 1897 he abandoned it, deciding that many such memories were fantasies and that the wishes behind them mattered more than events. The same year he began a lifelong self-analysis through his own dreams, recovering childhood hostility to his father and attachment to his mother, the seed of the Oedipus complex. The major works followed (Table 4.5). He fled the Nazis to London in 1938 and died there in September 1939, after sixteen years of cancer of the mouth. Exam trap The 1893 paper and Studies on Hysteria are Freud and Breuer , never Freud with Charcot, Adler or Jung (Adler and Jung were later followers who broke away; Section 4.4). Freud began as a neurologist . To Freud, hysteria meant physical symptoms produced by emotional trauma ; a phobia of horses is the case of Little Hans, and an unresolved Oedipus complex or oral behaviour are unrelated ideas. The father of psychoanalysis is Freud, not Bernheim, Adler or Jung. Freud's methods: free association, dreams and slips Many patients could not be hypnotised, so Freud had them lie on a couch, with himself out of sight, and gave them one fundamental rule : say whatever comes to mind, however trivial, embarrassing or painful, without censoring or rearranging it. This is free association , a kind of daydreaming aloud, and it became the central technique of psychoanalysis. Because of psychic determinism ( below ), nothing in the chain was random; each idea led closer to the buried conflict. The chain often stalls: the patient falls silent or changes the subject. This is resistance , the unconscious refusal to let painful material surface, which Freud took as a sign that the analysis was near the source. Patients also come to feel toward the analyst as they once felt toward their parents: transference . Both are worked through in therapy (Chapter 7). Dream analysis was the second road in; Freud called the interpretation of dreams "the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious". What you remember is the manifest content ; its hidden meaning, a disguised wish, is the latent content . The dream-work that turns one into the other is taught in Section 1.5. The third window was everyday mistakes. A parapraxis (plural parapraxes), popularly a Freudian slip , is a slip of the tongue or pen, a forgotten name or appointment, or a misplaced object that betrays an unconscious thought or wish. A student who writes to his professor "I look forward to missing your lecture" has, in Freud's eyes, said what he meant. Parapraxes are mistakes that reveal the unconscious; they need not be sexual. Their meaning is found as a symptom's is, through free association. Freud reported his work as case studies , detailed histories of single patients: Anna O. (hysteria, Breuer's patient), Dora (hysteria, 1905), Little Hans (1909, a small boy's phobia of horses, read as Oedipal fear of his father), the Rat Man (obsessional neurosis, 1909), Schreber (paranoia, 1911, analysed only from his published memoir) and the Wolf Man (1918, a childhood dream of wolves). The method is rich but weak as evidence, as the evaluation shows. Exam trap Lying on the couch saying whatever comes to mind is free association , not dreaming, narration or storytelling, and it is the central technique of psychoanalysis , not of behaviour, person-centred or cognitive therapy (Chapter 7). Freudian slips are analysed through free association : case studies are how Freud reported patients, behaviour analysis records observable acts and their consequences, and a sleep study records sleep stages, not meanings. A slip is not a defence mechanism (an unconscious strategy against anxiety; Section 4.3), a cognitive distortion (Aaron Beck's errors of thinking, such as overgeneralisation) or a speech disorder (such as stuttering). Instincts and psychic energy What powers the mind? Freud's answer was the instincts (German Triebe , sometimes translated "drives"): the powerful innate forces that motivate all behaviour and set its direction. An instinct is the mental representation of a bodily need, the wish that hunger becomes in the mind. In "Instincts and Their Vicissitudes" (1915) Freud gave every instinct a source (the bodily need), an aim (to remove the excitation, that is, satisfaction), an object (whatever achieves the aim, the most changeable part) and an impetus or pressure (its strength). The aim is always tension reduction, so the model is homeostatic. Freud grouped the instincts into two classes. The life instincts , or Eros , serve survival of the individual and the species: hunger, thirst and above all sex, which Freud defined broadly to include almost any bodily pleasure and affection. Their energy is the libido . In Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), shaken by the slaughter of the First World War, he added the death instinct , an unconscious drive toward decay and a return to the inanimate state, which his followers named Thanatos , a word Freud himself did not use in his writings. Turned inward it is self-destruction; turned outward it becomes the aggressive drive to destroy, conquer and kill, so wars and violence are, for Freud, evidence of the death instinct. Sex and aggression are what the id wants; the pleasure and reality principles ( below ) are the rules by which the id and the ego pursue them. Libido can be attached to anything. Cathexis is the investment of psychic energy in the mental representation of an object, person or idea: if you adore a cricketer, your libido is cathected to him. An anticathexis is the opposing investment by which the ego or superego blocks an id cathexis; keeping a wish repressed costs energy. The cost matters because Freud saw the mind as a closed energy system , a fixed quantity of psychic energy that can be shifted but never added to, so whatever the ego spends holding back the id is lost to work and love. Beside it stands psychic determinism , the principle that every mental event has a cause, so no slip, dream or symptom is an accident. Exam trap Freud's innate motivating forces are instincts ; needs are Maslow's and Henry Murray's term, drives Clark Hull's, and the id is the reservoir that holds the instincts. Investing energy in an object is cathexis . Its neighbours: libido is the energy itself, fixation is libido left stuck at a childhood stage, sublimation channels it into socially valued work, displacement shifts an impulse to a safer target and repression keeps threatening material out of awareness (the last three are defences; Section 4.3). The levels of the mind: the topographic model Freud's first map, the topographic model (1900), sorts mental contents by how accessible they are. The conscious holds whatever you are aware of at this moment. The preconscious holds accessible memories, thoughts and perceptions that are not in awareness now but can be recalled at will: your mobile number, what you ate last night. The unconscious , by far the largest, holds instincts, repressed wishes and painful memories that cannot be recalled at will and show themselves only indirectly, in dreams, slips and symptoms. Freud likened the mind to an iceberg: the conscious is the small tip above the water, the preconscious lies just below the waterline, and the unconscious is the vast hidden mass, the real driving power of behaviour (Figure 4.2). Exam trap Accessible memories recalled at will are preconscious , not conscious (in awareness now) or unconscious (not recallable at will). Psychic determinism is a principle, not a level of the mind. Id, ego and superego: the structural model In The Ego and the Id (1923) Freud replaced the three levels with three interacting structures, the structural model . The levels became properties of the structures (Figure 4.2). The id is the reservoir of unorganised instinctual drives, present at birth, wholly unconscious and the source of all psychic energy. It operates on the pleasure principle : seek pleasure and avoid pain, now. Impulsive, irrational, selfish and amoral, it demands the immediate gratification of primitive needs and tolerates no delay ("Just do it"). Having no contact with reality, it can satisfy a need only by reflex or by primary process thought , forming a wish-fulfilling image of the object it lacks, as a hungry infant pictures the breast. This wish fulfilment also drives dreams. Images feed no one, so from the id grows the ego , the rational part of personality, which works on the reality principle . Using secondary process thought (perception, memory, judgement and planning) and reality testing , it decides when, where and how the id's wishes can safely be met. It does not block the id; it postpones and redirects ("Wait till later"). Freud compared it to a rider guiding a stronger horse. It is called the executive of personality because it directs the energies supplied by the id and mediates between the id's desires, the superego and reality or social rules. The ego is partly conscious, partly preconscious and partly unconscious. The superego is the moral arm, working on the moral principle. It forms at about five or six, when the Oedipus complex is resolved and the child internalises parental and social standards, so that parental control becomes self-control. It has two parts. The conscience is built from behaviours for which the child was punished and enforces them with guilt; the ego-ideal is built from good, correct behaviours for which the child was praised and rewards with pride. Like the id it admits no compromise: it seeks not to delay forbidden impulses but to stop them ("Don't do it"), and it strives for perfection. The ego is the executive ; "superordinate" and "subordinate" are not Freud's labels, and congruence is Carl Rogers's term for a match between self and experience (Section 4.8). The conscious and unconscious mind are levels, not principles. The self and the libido are not Freudian structures, and the superego's two parts are the conscience and the ego-ideal , not the id and the ego. "Do your own thing" and "Oh, sit on it" are not Freudian mottoes. Anxiety: the ego's danger signal Squeezed by three masters, the ego feels anxiety , fear without a clear object. In Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety (1926) Freud made anxiety a signal that warns the ego of danger, with the overwhelming stimulation of birth as its prototype. He named three kinds by their source. Reality anxiety (objective anxiety) is fear of a real danger in the outside world, such as a speeding lorry; it is useful and fades when the danger passes. Neurotic anxiety , a conflict between id and ego, is the unconscious fear that id impulses will break through and bring punishment. Moral anxiety , a conflict between id and superego, is fear of one's own conscience, felt as guilt or shame. When realistic action cannot remove the threat, the ego turns to unconscious defence mechanisms, the subject of Section 4.3. The psychosexual stages Freud believed adult personality was largely set by about the age of five, and his psychosexual stages ( Three Essays , 1905) explain how. At each stage the libido centres on a different erogenous zone , a part of the body that gives pleasure, and each stage brings a conflict between the child's pleasure and the parents' demands. If a stage goes badly, part of the libido stays invested there: fixation . It results from frustration (needs unmet) or overindulgence (needs so richly met that the child will not move on), and it stamps a recognisable adult character. Under stress a person may show regression , a return to the behaviour of an earlier stage, usually the one where libido is fixated. Table 4.7 gives the sequence; the ages are approximate and differ between textbooks (some give oral birth to 1 year, anal 1 to 3, phallic 4 to 5 and latency 5 to puberty). In the oral stage (birth to about 18 months) pleasure comes from the mouth, through sucking, biting and swallowing, and the central conflict is feeding and weaning . Its first mode, oral-incorporative (taking in), produces adults preoccupied with eating, drinking, smoking, kissing and nail-biting, who are dependent and gullible ("swallowing" whatever they are told). The later oral-aggressive or oral-sadistic mode, which comes with painful teething, leaves adults who are sarcastic ("biting" remarks), critical, hostile and argumentative. Freud linked alcohol dependence to oral fixation. In the anal stage (about 18 months to 3 years) pleasure comes from holding back and expelling faeces, and toilet training is the first time society regulates an instinct. A child who defies it by soiling may become an anal-expulsive (anal-aggressive) adult: messy, wasteful, disorganised, even cruel. A child who resists by holding back may become anal-retentive : orderly, stingy, obstinate and compulsively neat. The phallic stage (about 3 to 5 or 6 years) centres on the genitals and on incestuous fantasies. The boy faces the Oedipus complex , named after the king in Sophocles' play who unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother: he desires his mother and sees his father as a rival. Fearing that the father will cut off his penis ( castration anxiety ), he represses the desire and achieves identification with the same-sex parent, adopting his father's manner and standards; this gives him his sex role and creates the superego. The girl's first love is also her mother, but on finding she lacks a penis she feels penis envy , blames her mother and turns to her father; she resolves the conflict, less completely in Freud's view, by identifying with her mother. Freud called this the female Oedipus complex. Carl Gustav Jung (1875 to 1961) named it the Electra complex in 1913, after the Greek heroine who persuades her brother to kill their mother. Freud rejected the term, yet exams pair Electra with girls and Oedipus with boys. In the latency period (about 6 to puberty) the sexual instinct is dormant, sublimated into school, sport, hobbies and friendships with children of the same sex; Freud did not count it as a true psychosexual stage, since no new zone appears. The genital stage (puberty onwards) reawakens sexuality, now directed to mature love. Its achievements are sex-role identity, adult social relationships and the capacity for love and work. Oral aggression is oral, not anal, and "genital identity confusion" is not a Freudian concept. Incestuous fantasies, the Oedipus complex and the emergence of the superego belong to the phallic stage; sublimation of the sex instinct is latency ; sex-role identity and adult relationships are genital . Evaluating Freud Which parts of the theory survive testing? The strongest support is for an unconscious mind. In subliminal perception studies, stimuli flashed too briefly to be seen still shape thought: Howard Shevrin (1977) showed people a picture of a bee they could not report, and their free associations then included "sting" and "honey". Implicit memory (experience shaping performance without recollection) and priming point the same way. Some defences, such as repression, projection and displacement, have experimental support (Section 4.3), and Michael Motley (1987) found that men made anxious about an electric shock said "damn shock" for "sham dock", a laboratory Freudian slip. Reviewing some 2,500 studies, Seymour Fisher and Roger Greenberg (1977, 1996) judged the id, ego, superego, libido and death instinct untestable, found weak support for oral and anal character types and some Oedipal ideas, and found no support for the psychosexual stages or for dreams as disguised wishes. The criticisms are heavy. Many concepts are unfalsifiable : if a man loves his mother it is Oedipal, and if he hates her he is defending against Oedipal love, so no result can count against the theory. The data came from Freud himself and a small, biased sample, a dozen or so published cases, mostly young, educated, well-off Viennese women. His notes were written from memory hours later, and patients' recollections were not corroborated. His account of women (penis envy, a weaker superego) is sexist, a charge led by Karen Horney (Section 4.5). His view of human nature is pessimistic and over-sexualised, and personality plainly goes on developing after five. Still, Freud gave psychology its first comprehensive theory of personality, the ideas of unconscious motivation, defence and the weight of childhood, and the talking cure from which every psychotherapy descends. On the six questions about human nature (Section 4.1) Freud is a determinist (though analysis widens choice), takes a middle ground on nature and nurture (inborn id and stages, learned ego and superego), stresses the past (the first five years), sees both universality (shared instincts and stages) and uniqueness (the content of ego and superego), makes equilibrium (tension reduction) life's goal, and is a pessimist. In India, Girindrasekhar Bose, founder of the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922), corresponded with Freud and proposed his own theory of opposite wishes (Section 1.2). Exam trap Research has begun to support the unconscious mind , not the existence of an id, ego and superego (untestable), the order of the psychosexual stages or a universal Oedipus complex.
