Within an hour he has told his friends that statistics is useless for a clinician anyway, and he has snapped at his younger brother over nothing. He is not lying, at least not knowingly. In the terms of Section 4.2, his ego is under threat: anxiety is signalling danger, and when the ego cannot remove a danger by realistic means it falls back on unconscious tricks that disguise it. This section defines those tricks, studies the most basic of them, repression, walks through the full catalogue, ranks them from psychotic to mature, and shows which ones mark particular disorders. What defences are and what they share Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) wrote of defence from his first papers on hysteria in the 1890s, although for years he spoke almost only of repression. In Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety (1926) he returned to the wider term: anxiety is a signal of danger to the ego, and defence is the name for every technique the ego uses to keep that danger out of awareness. Formally, defence mechanisms are unconscious strategies the ego uses to protect itself against anxiety by denying or distorting reality. It was his daughter Anna Freud (1895 to 1982) who turned the idea into a catalogue. In The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936) she listed ten mechanisms (regression, repression, reaction formation, isolation, undoing, projection, introjection, turning against the self, reversal and sublimation), described others such as identification with the aggressor, and moved the ego to the centre of psychoanalysis. The standard list you learn today owes its full articulation to her. The mechanisms differ in detail, but they share six features: They operate unconsciously. The person neither chooses a defence nor knows that one is working; if we knew we were lying to ourselves, the lie would no longer protect us. They deny or distort reality, either outer reality (a diagnosis, a loss) or inner reality (a wish, a feeling). They protect the ego and reduce anxiety. That is their whole function, and we usually use several at once. They have adaptive value in moderation. Freud held that everyone defends all the time and that we could not survive long without defences. They become pathological when they are rigid, overused or used where realistic action is needed; then they produce neurotic or even psychotic symptoms. They are not rational. A defence does not solve the problem; it changes how the problem is seen. Exam trap Asked which statement does NOT describe defence mechanisms, the answer is "rational unconscious protective measures". "Having adaptive value", "pushing painful experiences out of consciousness" and "resulting in a distorted view of reality" are all true. The single word rational makes the option false. Defence should not be confused with coping , the conscious, deliberate, flexible and reality-oriented effort to manage stress (problem-focused and emotion-focused coping are taught in Section 1.11). If Arjun draws up a revision timetable he is coping; if he decides the subject is useless he is defending. The line blurs only at the top of the maturity ladder ( see below ), where suppression and anticipation look much like good coping. Repression, the primary defence Freud called the theory of repression "the corner-stone on which the whole structure of psycho-analysis rests" (1914). In full, repression is the involuntary, unconscious blocking of threatening or anxiety-provoking memories, wishes and feelings from awareness, or the barring of them from ever reaching it. Freud separated two forms: primal repression , which keeps instinctual ideas from ever becoming conscious, and repression proper (after-pressure), which pushes out material that was once conscious and is now linked with the forbidden. Repression is the primary defence against anxiety: it is the most basic and most frequently used, the other mechanisms are often described as back-ups when it fails, and Freud saw it in all neurotic behaviour. It can act on memories, on perception (we may fail to see a disturbing event in front of us) and even on bodily function, as when a man represses his sexual drive so strongly that he becomes impotent. What is repressed is not destroyed; it stays active in the unconscious and returns in disguise as dreams, slips and symptoms. In memory terms, then, repression is an unconscious process that removes unpleasant memories from awareness. It is not a conscious effort to forget, not a strengthening of memory traces and not the deliberate recall of traumatic events. Several neighbouring terms are easily confused with it, and Table 4.8 sets them side by side. Table 4.8 Repression and its look-alikes. Term Conscious? What it is Example Repression No, involuntary Blocks threatening material from awareness No memory of a childhood humiliation Suppression Yes, deliberate Puts a worry aside to face later; mature in Vaillant's scheme "I will think about the result after the exam" Inhibition No Gives up an ego function (work, eating, sex) to avoid anxiety (Freud, 1926) Cannot bring himself to start any work Denial No Refuses to accept an outer reality that is perceived "The biopsy report must be wrong" Motivated forgetting Can be either The broad memory term: any forgetting driven by a motive (Chapter 1) Includes both repression and suppression Depression Not a defence A mood state and disorder (Chapter 8) Persistent sadness, loss of interest Exam trap Stems that say "involuntary", "unconscious" or "unable to gain access to conscious awareness" (Deepika cannot bring the threatening material into awareness) want repression . "Decides to put it out of mind" is suppression . Depression sounds similar but is a mood, not a mechanism, and "motivated forgetting" is the wider memory label, not the psychoanalytic defence. The recovered memory controversy. From the late 1980s, adults in therapy began to "recover" memories of childhood sexual abuse, and some accused relatives were tried and imprisoned on that evidence. Elizabeth Loftus (born 1944) and others showed how easily suggestion, hypnosis and dream interpretation can implant vivid memories of events that never happened. Abuse is real and can go unrecalled for years, but Loftus, reviewing the evidence in 2006, concluded that there is little support for the idea that trauma is commonly banished from awareness and later reliably recovered. Repression remains a clinical concept rather than a proven memory mechanism (misinformation and false memory are taught in Chapter 1). Repression, hysteria and dissociation. The concept was born in Studies on Hysteria (1895), written by Freud with Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925). Hysterical symptoms, they argued, came from painful memories pushed out of awareness that found expression through the body. For the same reason most psychodynamic theorists hold that dissociative symptoms (amnesia, fugue, multiple identities) are produced by repression: a whole segment of experience is walled off from consciousness. Conflict is what sets defence going, not the mechanism itself; "ego states" describe the split-off parts rather than the process that splits them; and gender identity has no bearing on dissociation. Five defences that redirect or disguise Most questions on defences give a short story and ask you to name the mechanism. Five defences carry most of these stories. Three of them move an impulse somewhere, so the key question is where it goes; Figure 4.3 follows one impulse through all five. Forbidden impulse Anger at a harassing boss she cannot attack Five routes the ego can take Displacement: new target Picks a fight with her husband instead Sublimation: valued activity Pours the anger into kickboxing Projection: another person "My boss is the angry one, not me" Reaction formation: opposite Is excessively sweet to the boss Rationalisation: good reason Rude later: "I was only being frank" Figure 4.3 One impulse, five disguises. Notice what changes in each: the target (displacement), the activity (sublimation), the owner (projection), the direction (reaction formation) or the stated reason (rationalisation). In displacement a feeling, usually anger, is redirected from a threatening target to a safer one that cannot hit back. The impulse stays the same; only its object changes. The woman angry with her husband shouts at her child; the teenager furious with a teacher goes home and shouts at his younger sibling; the man upset with his girlfriend yells at his dog; the woman harassed by her boss picks a fight with her husband. Because the substitute never discharges the tension as fully as the real target would, undischarged tension builds up. Displacement of fear, rather than anger, is the classic mechanism of phobias ( see below ). In projection a person attributes his or her own unacceptable thoughts and impulses to someone else. The person says, in effect, "I don't hate him; he hates me." A husband who struggles with his own wish to stray accuses his faithful wife of flirting. The impulse is still expressed, but as somebody else's, which feels far less threatening. In sublimation , sexual or aggressive energy is rechannelled into a socially valued activity. Roshan, who is full of anger and frustration, enrols in a kickboxing class; aggressive drives go into competitive sport, and frustrated sexual energy goes into painting or poetry. Displacement changes only the target, whereas sublimation transforms the impulse's aim into something society admires. Freud saw art, science and civilisation itself as built on sublimation and treated it as the healthiest defence; Vaillant later placed it among the mature ones. The term rationalisation , introduced by Freud's follower Ernest Jones (1879 to 1958) in 1908, means a logical, socially acceptable reason invented after the act for behaviour that was really driven by unconscious or unacceptable motives. Clare complains about her duties, rarely finishes her tasks and is regularly late; when she is fired she says a co-worker badmouthed her. Arjun's "statistics is useless anyway" is the "sour grapes" form, after the fox in the fable who decides that the grapes he cannot reach are sour. Unlike a lie, the excuse is believed by the person who gives it. In reaction formation the opposite of a threatening impulse is expressed: someone troubled by sexual longings becomes a crusader against pornography, and a child who resents a new baby smothers it with exaggerated affection. The giveaway is the excessive, rigid quality of the displayed feeling. Exam trap Read the stem for its landing place: a safer target is displacement, a socially valued activity is sublimation, another person's mind is projection. Clare blames a co-worker, which tempts you towards projection or displacement, and she plays down her failings, which tempts you towards denial. But she does not deny the dismissal, and she moves no anger onto a safer target; she supplies an after-the-fact excuse that protects her self-esteem: rationalisation. Do not confuse rationalisation (an excuse) with intellectualisation (abstract thinking that keeps feeling away). The wider catalogue Beyond the big five lies a long list drawn from Freud, Anna Freud, Alfred Adler (1870 to 1937) and the object-relations school. Three belong together because all appear in obsessional neurosis: isolation of affect keeps the idea in awareness but removes its emotion, intellectualisation goes further and buries the emotion under abstract analysis, and undoing adds an act that magically "cancels" the thought. Plain identification copies another's behaviour, and identification with the aggressor , Anna Freud's special case, copies the very person one fears; introjection goes deeper and swallows another's values whole, so that they feel like one's own. Note too that regression , a retreat to the behaviour of an earlier stage, is a general response to stress rather than the mark of any one disorder, and dissociation , though dramatic, is ranked neurotic rather than immature by Vaillant. In the same way, conversion (Freud's term from his work on hysteria) produces a single symbolic symptom such as paralysis or blindness, whereas somatisation is a general tendency to express distress through the body. Finally, splitting , described by Melanie Klein (1882 to 1960) in the infant's paranoid-schizoid position (Section 4.5), keeps good and bad images apart so that the bad cannot spoil the good; projective identification , also Klein's, adds the push that makes the other person actually carry the projected feeling. Adler's compensation is treated fully in Section 4.4. Projection, introjection, empathy and denial apart Projection has a broad sense as well as the narrow defensive one. Freud also used the word for any externalising of inner states, and in this broad sense projection is any distorting or selective effect of a person's inner world on his perception or conception of the outer world. This broad sense underlies the projective hypothesis : given an ambiguous stimulus, people read their own needs and conflicts into it. Lawrence K. Frank named such tests projective methods in 1939 (they are taught in Chapter 2). The neighbouring terms run in other directions. Introjection moves something from outside to inside, the reverse of projection. By contrast, empathy is perceiving and sharing another person's feelings from that person's point of view; it is an accurate act of understanding, not a defence, and it distorts nothing. And denial blocks a particular, unwelcome fact of outer reality ("my son cannot be dead"); it does not colour perception in general. Exam trap RML 2024 asked for "any distorting or selective effect of a person's inner world on his perception or conception of the outer world" and keyed denial . That wording is the broad definition of projection , the basis of the projective hypothesis, so the key is doubtful. Denial refuses a specific reality; introjection takes the world in; empathy reads others accurately. If the same stem appears, projection is the defensible answer. Vaillant's hierarchy of maturity Are some defences healthier than others? George Eman Vaillant (born 1934), an American psychiatrist, answered with decades of life-history data (see the Key study box) and arranged the defences in four levels of maturity (Table 4.10). Table 4.10 Vaillant's four levels of defence (1977). Level Defences Hallmark I Psychotic Delusional projection, psychotic denial, distortion Reality testing lost; normal in dreams and early childhood II Immature Projection, schizoid fantasy, hypochondriasis, passive aggression, acting out Normal in adolescence; in adults, common in personality disorders III Neurotic (intermediate) Intellectualisation, isolation, repression, displacement, reaction formation, dissociation Common in healthy adults under stress; private, inner distortions IV Mature Altruism, anticipation, humour, sublimation, suppression Integrate reality, feelings and relationships; most adaptive Several names appear only in this ladder. At Level I, delusional projection hardens projection into a frank, usually persecutory delusion ("the neighbours are poisoning my water"); psychotic denial denies outer reality itself, as when a widow insists her husband is alive; distortion grossly reshapes reality to fit inner needs, as in a belief in one's own divine powers. At Level II, schizoid fantasy is retreat into private daydreams to avoid conflict and people, and hypochondriasis turns reproach towards others (after bereavement or loneliness) into complaints of illness. At Level IV, altruism gains satisfaction from constructive service to others, humour expresses painful feelings openly without hurting anyone, anticipation is realistic planning for future discomfort, and suppression is the conscious decision to postpone attention to a worry. Key study: Vaillant and the Grant Study men (1977) Question: do the defences a person habitually uses predict how well his life turns out? Method: the Grant Study of Adult Development has followed 268 Harvard men since 1938 through interviews, questionnaires and medical examinations. For Adaptation to Life (1977), judges rated the defences the men showed in crises over more than three decades. Result: the maturity of defences predicted adult adjustment: men who relied on mature defences had better marriages, careers, and physical and mental health, and defences tended to mature with age. Criticism: the sample was all male, mostly white and privileged, and the ratings rest on judges' inferences from life histories. Some psychiatry textbooks extend the lists, calling Level I narcissistic and adding, for example, rationalisation and inhibition to the neurotic group and regression and somatisation to the immature group. The DSM-IV Defensive Functioning Scale (1994) later spread the defences over seven levels, from the high adaptive level down to defensive dysregulation, placing splitting and projective identification at the major image-distorting level. Exam trap Repression, projection and reaction formation are not mature; only altruism, anticipation, humour, sublimation and suppression are. Splitting (primitive), sublimation (mature) and projection (immature) are not neurotic, so intellectualisation is the neurotic choice. Dissociation is neurotic , not immature. Denial, distortion and delusional projection together mark the psychotic level. No defence is "conscious" as a class; suppression is the one deliberate exception, and it sits in the mature group. Freud concluded that Hans's Oedipal fear of his father had been displaced onto horses, whose blinkers and dark muzzles recalled the father's spectacles and moustache; a horse, unlike a father, can simply be avoided. Criticism: the evidence came from a sympathetic father asking leading questions, and Joseph Wolpe and Stanley Rachman (1960) argued that the phobia was conditioned after Hans saw a horse fall in the street. The logic behind the table is worth knowing. In obsessional neurosis the disturbing idea stays fully conscious (that is what an obsession is), but its feeling is isolated, compulsions undo it, and excessive cleanliness or kindness stands in reaction to it; hysteria, by contrast, represses the idea itself. In phobia, a fear is displaced onto an object that can be avoided, as in Little Hans. In paranoia, the forbidden feeling is projected, so that hatred within becomes persecution from without. Otto Kernberg (born 1928) made splitting and projective identification the core of borderline personality organisation, which is why the person with borderline personality disorder swings between idealising and devaluing the same person; regression, undoing and sublimation are not characteristic. In depression, following Freud's Mourning and Melancholia (1917), the lost person is introjected and the anger meant for them is turned against the self. Exam trap "Which defence is used in OCD: isolation, undoing, reaction formation, displacement?" Three options are true. When the key is undoing (RML 2024), take it: undoing is the defence most directly tied to compulsive rituals. When the stem asks which is NOT typical of OCD, the answer is repression . Asked where displacement is typically seen, answer phobias (IHBAS 2020), not hysteria, OCD or depression. Development, research and clinical use Defences have a developmental order. Phebe Cramer , coding children's Thematic Apperception Test stories (1987), found that denial dominates in early childhood, projection rises in later childhood, and identification takes over in adolescence, as Figure 4.4 shows. Each step demands more cognitive skill: denial needs only a refusal, projection needs a sense of other minds, identification needs a stable self that can borrow from others. A later study of pupils from Grade 2 to college found the same pattern: denial and projection fell with age while identification rose. Denial Dominant in early childhood Projection Rises in later childhood Identification Takes over in adolescence Age and cognitive complexity increase from left to right Figure 4.4 Cramer's developmental sequence. Simpler defences come first and give way to ones that need more cognitive skill. Laboratory evidence for repression is debated. Sam Glucksberg and L. J. King (1967) paired some words with electric shock and found that people later forgot those words and related ones, which looks like repression. Others have found that habitual "repressors", people low in reported anxiety but high in defensiveness, recall fewer negative childhood memories. Yet David S. Holmes (1990), reviewing sixty years of studies, found no convincing controlled evidence that repression works as Freud described, and the recovered memory debate has kept the question open. In everyday life defences are neither rare nor shameful: they soften losses, protect self-esteem and buy time. Clinically, they matter in two ways. The defences a person habitually uses help a clinician gauge the level of personality organisation, and in psychodynamic therapy defences show up as resistance, which the therapist gently interprets so that the patient can face what is being avoided and replace rigid, immature defences with mature ones (therapy is taught in Chapter 7). Answers: (1) 1936, (2) repression; suppression, (3) displacement, (4) sublimation, (5) isolation, (6) neurotic; mature, (7) splitting, (8) identification. 4.4 Jung's Analytical Psychology and Adler's Individual Psychology Medium yield · 25 Qs In March 1907 a 31-year-old Swiss psychiatrist, Carl Jung, met Sigmund Freud in Vienna, and the two talked for almost thirteen hours. Six years later they were no longer speaking, and Alfred Adler had already walked out of Freud's circle. Each rebel kept part of Freud's framework but rebuilt the theory of personality at the point where he thought Freud had gone wrong. The neo-Freudians and the break with Freud The neo-Freudians began inside psychoanalysis, kept its belief in unconscious processes and in the weight of childhood, and then rebuilt the theory. The usual list is Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, Karen Horney, Erich Fromm, Harry Stack Sullivan and Erik Erikson (Horney, Fromm and Sullivan are in Section 4.5, Erikson in Chapter 6). Their changes ran one way: less sex and instinct; more social, cultural and conscious forces; and a person pulled toward goals, not only pushed by the past. Adler left first. A member of Freud's circle from 1902 and president of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, he argued that inferiority and social striving, not sexuality, lay behind neurosis. In 1911 he resigned with 9 of the 23 members, and in 1912 he founded the Society for Individual Psychology. Jung was Freud's chosen successor. Freud called him his "crown prince", took him on the 1909 lecture trip to Clark University in Massachusetts, and saw him become first president of the International Psychoanalytic Association in 1910. But Jung would not accept that libido was purely sexual, and they parted in 1913 (Table 4.12). Table 4.12 Freud, Jung and Adler compared. Jung's psyche: energy, ego and complexes Carl Gustav Jung (1875 to 1961), a Swiss pastor's son, worked from 1900 at the Burghölzli hospital in Zurich under Eugen Bleuler. His analytical psychology begins with energy. Jung widened libido from sexual energy to general psychic energy, the energy of all perceiving, thinking, feeling and wishing; sex is only one of its uses. It obeys three principles borrowed from physics. By the principle of opposites , conflict between polarities, such as love and hate, generates energy. By the principle of equivalence , energy withdrawn from one interest reappears in another of equal value, as when a retired cricketer's passion flows into coaching. By the principle of entropy , energy flows from stronger to weaker parts of the personality, tending toward a balance that is never reached. The psyche has three levels (Figure 4.5). The ego is the conscious mind, the centre of awareness. Below it lies the personal unconscious , material once conscious but forgotten or suppressed, much like Freud's preconscious. There related memories and feelings gather into complexes. A complex is an emotionally charged cluster of ideas organised around a theme, such as a mother complex or a power complex; its owner rarely notices it, though others do. To detect complexes Jung developed, from 1904 with Franz Riklin , the word association test . Key study: Jung's word association test (1904 onwards) Question: can a hidden complex be detected objectively? Method: Jung read out 100 stimulus words (head, green, water, death), the patient answered each with the first word that came to mind, and Jung timed every reply and recorded physiological signs such as breathing and skin resistance. Result: certain words produced complex indicators: a long delay, no answer, repeating the stimulus word, the same reply to different words, a slip, or a bodily reaction. These marked the theme of a complex. Legacy and criticism: the test fed projective testing and lie detection, but its interpretation stays subjective. Francis Galton and Wilhelm Wundt had studied word association earlier; as a clinical tool for complexes it is Jung's. Exam trap Word association test: Jung. Not Henry Murray (the Thematic Apperception Test, Chapter 2), not Freud (free association, talking freely with no stimulus words) and not Donald Winnicott (object relations: the transitional object and the good enough mother, Section 4.5). The collective unconscious and the archetypes Freud's unconscious was essentially personal. Jung held that the unconscious exists on two levels, the personal (individual) and the collective. The collective unconscious is the deepest layer of the psyche: inherited, universal, the same in every human being, the deposit of the experience of our human and pre-human ancestors. Jung accounted for it through evolution: the brain has the same structure in all human races, so it carries the same inherited predispositions. His evidence was that the same symbols (the dragon-slaying hero, the great flood, the sacred circle) recur in the myths of cultures that never met and in the dreams of patients who had never read those myths. We inherit readiness, not memories: not a fear of snakes, but the potential to fear them. Person A Person B Person C Ego conscious mind Ego Ego Personal unconscious complexes Personal unconscious Personal unconscious Collective unconscious inherited and universal: the archetypes persona, shadow, anima, animus, self, hero Individual, acquired in one lifetime Shared, inherited by every human Figure 4.5 Jung's model of the psyche. Each person has an ego and a personal unconscious of his or her own, but all rest on the same collective unconscious, the inherited store of archetypes. The contents of the collective unconscious are archetypes , which Jung also called primordial images: universal patterns that shape how we respond to life's recurring experiences, such as mother, birth and death (Table 4.13). The persona is the social mask; trouble starts when the ego mistakes it for the whole person. The shadow , the most powerful archetype, is the disowned animal side, the source of evil but also of vitality and creativity. The anima is the feminine side of a man and the animus the unconscious masculine side of a woman. The self , the archetype of wholeness and unity, is the centre of the whole psyche (the ego is only the centre of consciousness), symbolised by the mandala , a circle usually divided into four. Exam trap The collective unconscious is not repressed personal memories (the personal unconscious), not socially learned attitudes and not ruled by the reality principle (Freud's ego, Section 4.2). It is inherited, universal and archetypal, and it is Jung's, not Freud's, Adler's or Horney's. Asked for the two levels of the unconscious, answer collective and individual: anima and animus are archetypes, extraversion and introversion are attitudes, and intuitive and perceptive are type labels. Attitudes, functions and the eight types In Psychological Types (1921) Jung asked why people meet the same world so differently. His first answer was two attitudes, his own terms for the direction of psychic energy. In extraversion it flows outward, to people and things: the extravert is sociable and assertive. In introversion it flows inward, to one's own thoughts and feelings: the introvert is reserved and reflective. Everyone has both; one dominates consciousness, while the other sinks into the personal unconscious and still leaks out, as when a shy student is drawn to a loud friend. His second answer was four functions in two opposed pairs (Figure 4.6). Thinking judges true or false; feeling judges pleasant or unpleasant. Because both evaluate, they are the rational functions . Sensing registers what is there, like a camera; intuiting grasps possibilities and hunches beyond the evidence. Because both perceive without evaluating, they are the irrational functions (also called nonrational). One function dominates; the other member of its pair, the inferior function , stays undeveloped and largely unconscious, so a strong thinker may be clumsy with feelings. Two attitudes times four functions give Jung's eight psychological types, from the extraverted thinking type (logical, rule-bound) to the introverted intuiting type (the visionary daydreamer). Thinking Feeling Sensing Intuiting Ego Rational pair (judging) Irrational pair (perceiving) Two attitudes extraversion or introversion × 4 functions Eight types extraverted thinking ... One function is dominant; its opposite is inferior Figure 4.6 Jung's four functions form two opposed pairs: thinking and feeling judge (rational, vertical axis); sensing and intuiting perceive without judging (irrational, horizontal axis). Crossed with the two attitudes they give eight types. Katharine Cook Briggs (1875 to 1968), who read Jung's book in 1923, and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers (1897 to 1980), neither trained in psychology, turned the types into the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), whose first form appeared in 1943. It scores four dichotomies, extraversion-introversion (E-I), sensing-intuition (S-N), thinking-feeling (T-F) and judging-perceiving (J-P, their own addition), giving 16 types such as INTP. Hugely popular in workplaces, it is psychometrically weak: it forces continuous traits into either-or boxes, and its test-retest reliability is poor, with many people (in some studies about half) typed differently when retested a few weeks later. Researchers prefer trait inventories (Section 4.7; Chapter 2). Exam trap Jung's two attitudes are extraversion and introversion; thinking, feeling, sensing and intuiting are functions; rational and irrational label the pairs of functions. The inventory based directly on Jung's types is the MBTI, not the MMPI (an empirically keyed clinical inventory), the 16PF (Raymond Cattell's factors, Section 4.6) or the NEO-PI-R (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae's Big Five, Section 4.7). Individuation, method and evaluation of Jung Freud thought personality was largely settled by five; Jung's crucial period was middle age, the time of his own breakdown after 1913. In the first half of life energy goes outward, to education, career and family, under consciousness and extraversion. Between about 35 and 40 many successful people feel empty. Jung saw this midlife crisis as natural, a signal to turn inward, from the material to the spiritual and from extraversion toward introversion. The goal of the second half of life is individuation , becoming a whole, undivided individual by integrating conscious and unconscious: dethrone the persona, accept the shadow, express the anima or animus, and transcend, so that the self, not the ego, becomes the centre. Such self-realisation is rarely complete. Synchronicity , a meaningful coincidence with no causal link, belongs to the same mystical side of Jung. Jung assessed patients by word association, symptom analysis (free associations to the symptoms) and dream analysis. He studied series of dreams, saw them as prospective (preparing for the future) and compensatory (balancing a one-sided conscious attitude), and used amplification : circling back to one dream image and enlarging it with repeated associations and parallels from myth, instead of following free associations away from it. Critics call his evidence (myth, alchemy, the occult, his own visions) mystical, his writing obscure and the collective unconscious unfalsifiable. Yet introversion-extraversion (Section 4.7), complexes, word association, the midlife transition and individuation, a forerunner of Abraham Maslow's self-actualisation, all lasted. Adler: the individual as a goal-seeking whole Alfred Adler (1870 to 1937), born near Vienna, was a sickly second son with rickets who nearly died of pneumonia at four and envied a healthy older brother. A physician, he joined Freud's circle as a colleague, never a pupil, and after the break founded individual psychology ; he died on a lecture tour in Scotland. Individual here means indivisible: each person is a unique, unified whole, not an id, ego and superego at war, and the whole person moves toward a goal. The basic assumption of individual psychology is that human behaviour is purposeful and goal-directed: Freud explained behaviour by past causes, Adler by future goals that pull us forward. The goals are social. In place of Freud's sexual instinct, Adler held that people are motivated primarily by social urges, the need to belong and to count among others. He gave the conscious more weight than the unconscious and saw people hopefully, as free to shape themselves. Exam trap The basic assumption is purposeful, goal-directed behaviour. Optimism is a feature of Adler's view, not its basic assumption; "social beings understood through their relationships" describes his social emphasis but fits Sullivan's interpersonal theory better (Section 4.5); lifelong development with ego identity at the centre is Erik Erikson (Chapter 6). The motive is social urges: not conscious drives (drive is Freud's language), not neurotic needs (Karen Horney, Section 4.5) and not empathic understanding (a therapist condition of Carl Rogers, Section 4.8). Individual psychology is Adler's, not Horney's, Jung's or Erikson's. Inferiority, compensation and striving for superiority Adler's Study of Organ Inferiority and Its Psychical Compensation (1907) argued that a weak organ or body part drives the person to make up for it, sometimes overshooting into strength, as the Greek orator Demosthenes overcame a stutter. This idea of organ inferiority grew into a theory of all motivation. Every child starts small and dependent among powerful adults, so inferiority feelings are universal and normal, and they are the source of all human striving. The effort to overcome them is compensation ; going beyond the deficit, as the frail boy who becomes an athlete does, is overcompensation (Figure 4.7). When compensation fails, the feelings harden into an inferiority complex , Adler's term: a lasting lack of self-worth, with helplessness, hopelessness and avoidance of challenge. It has three childhood sources: organ inferiority, pampering (the spoilt child crumbles when school does not revolve around him) and neglect (the unwanted child learns that others are hostile). Children with organic defects or born into minority groups are therefore at risk. Overcompensation can instead produce a superiority complex , an exaggerated self-importance shown in boasting, vanity and belittling others. Inferiority feelings universal in childhood Intensified by organ inferiority, pampering or neglect compensation succeeds Striving for superiority growth toward perfection compensation fails Inferiority complex helpless, hopeless, avoids overcompensation Superiority complex boastful, vain, belittling Figure 4.7 Adler's account of inferiority. Universal inferiority feelings drive all striving; successful compensation becomes striving for superiority, failure an inferiority complex, and overcompensation a superiority complex. Neither complex is striving for superiority , the healthy, innate drive toward perfection (completion) that Adler called the fundamental fact of life: an effort to perfect oneself and one's community, not to dominate others. Exam trap The inferiority complex and the superiority drive are Adler's, not Jung's, Viktor Frankl's (logotherapy, Chapter 7) or Erikson's. Adler coined the term, not Franz Alexander (psychosomatic medicine), Gordon Allport (traits, Section 4.6) or Jung; obituaries wrongly credited Freud and Jung with it. Organ inferiority is Adler's too, not Sullivan's, Melanie Klein's (both Section 4.5) or Anna Freud's (Section 4.3). Overcompensation, lack of self-worth and hopelessness go with the complex; certainty in decision making is its opposite. Fictional finalism, style of life and social interest What goals pull us? Adler borrowed from the philosopher Hans Vaihinger (1852 to 1933), whose The Philosophy of "As If" (1911) argued that people live by useful fictions, unprovable ideas acted on as if they were true, such as "all people are created equal". Adler's fictional finalism is the idea that each person is guided by an imagined final goal, a subjective ideal of success or completeness; he preferred the terms subjective final goal or guiding self-ideal. Each person pursues the goal through a unique style of life , the characteristic pattern of traits, habits and attitudes by which one strives for superiority. It grows from the child's compensations, birth order and parenting, and is largely fixed by four or five. Yet it is not fate: through the creative power of the self each child interprets heredity and environment and builds its own style. The test of a healthy style is social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefühl , community feeling), an innate potential to cooperate with others for personal and social goals, which the mother must nurture. It is needed for the three life tasks of work, friendship and love, and its absence underlies neurosis and crime. Crossing social interest with degree of activity, Adler described four styles of life (Table 4.14). Table 4.14 Adler's four styles of life. Birth order, early recollections and Adler's legacy For Adler, siblings raised by the same parents do not grow up in the same family, because each birth position is a different situation (Table 4.15). The first-born rules alone until a new baby dethrones it, and so knows power and wants it back; the second has a pacesetter ahead and, Adler said, behaves as if in a race. "Overachieving" is too narrow (the second child may instead give up), "resentful of the older child's freedom" is not his description, and inferiority feelings are universal, not the mark of the middle child. Adler's entrance gates to mental life were birth order, dreams and early recollections , a person's earliest memories which, true or imagined, reveal the style of life, because we remember what fits our present view of ourselves. Dreams, for him, rehearse solutions to present problems. His counselling methods are in Chapter 7. Critics call Adler commonsensical and unsystematic, but Abraham Maslow, Julian Rotter (social learning theory) and Albert Ellis (rational emotive therapy) built on his stress on goals and beliefs, and Karen Horney (Section 4.5) on his social emphasis. Karen Horney, Erich Fromm and Harry Stack Sullivan moved the source of personality from instinct to culture and relationships. Others kept more of Freud and asked how the ego adapts, how loved people become figures inside the mind, how a cohesive self is built and how language shapes the unconscious. Jung and Adler are in Section 4.4. Horney: basic anxiety and the neurotic trends Karen Horney (1885 to 1952), a Berlin-trained analyst who taught in the United States from 1932, argued in The Neurotic Personality of Our Time (1937) that personality is shaped primarily by social and cultural factors, above all the child's relationships with its parents, not by biological instincts, unconscious sexual conflicts or classical conditioning. The helpless infant's overriding need is the childhood need for safety and security : to feel wanted and protected. What damages a child is parental indifference , a lack of genuine warmth shown through favouritism, unfair punishment, broken promises or ridicule. The child feels basic hostility towards such parents but must repress it, out of helplessness, fear, the wish to keep even counterfeit love, or guilt. The buried hostility returns as basic anxiety , in Horney's words an "insidiously increasing, all-pervading feeling of being lonely and helpless in a hostile world". It is the foundation on which every later neurosis is built. Exam trap Pervasive loneliness and helplessness, the foundation of neurosis, is basic anxiety . Neurotic anxiety is Freud's fear that id impulses will break through (Section 4.2); existential anxiety is dread of death, freedom and meaninglessness (Section 4.8); "innate anxiety" is not a technical term. Instincts, sexual conflicts or conditioning are never Horney's answer. To quiet basic anxiety the child seizes a strategy (winning affection, submitting, gaining power or withdrawing), and used rigidly a strategy hardens into a need. Horney listed ten neurotic needs , irrational defences against anxiety that become permanent parts of the personality: affection and approval, a dominant partner, power, exploitation, prestige, admiration, achievement, self-sufficiency and independence, perfection, and narrow limits to life. Everyone feels them at times; they are neurotic when pursued compulsively as the only route to safety. In Our Inner Conflicts (1945) she grouped them into three neurotic trends (Figure 4.8). The compliant person moves toward people, seeking love and leaning on others; the aggressive person moves against people, treating life as a struggle; the detached person moves away from people, keeping an emotional distance. A healthy person uses all three flexibly; the neurotic is locked into one, and the clash among them is the core of neurosis. Parental indifference no warmth or security Basic hostility repressed Basic anxiety lonely and helpless in a hostile world Moving toward people: compliant affection and approval, a dominant partner Moving against people: aggressive power, exploitation, prestige, admiration, achievement Moving away from people: detached self-sufficiency, perfection, narrow limits to life Figure 4.8 Horney's account of neurosis. Repressed hostility becomes basic anxiety, managed by one of three neurotic trends; the small text lists the neurotic needs in each. Indian context For basic anxiety "in the Indian context" the key is Sudhir Kakar (born 1938), the psychoanalyst of Indian childhood and society ( The Inner World , 1978; Section 1.2). He wins as the only psychoanalyst offered: Anand C. Paranjpe co-edited the Handbook of Indian Psychology (2008), Durganand Sinha (1922 to 1998) urged the indigenisation of psychology, and "Kamala Chaudhuri" is a garbled name. Horney on the idealised self, women and "momism" In Neurosis and Human Growth (1950) Horney turned to the self. A healthy self-image rests on a realistic appraisal of strengths and weaknesses. The neurotic, torn between incompatible trends, builds an idealised self-image of flawless virtue and tries to become it. The result is the tyranny of the shoulds ("I should be the perfect student, never tired, never angry"), demands no one can meet, which end in self-hatred. Horney also challenged Freud's view of women. From 1922 she rejected Freud's penis envy as an idea drawn from neurotic women and seen through male eyes. Men, she countered, may feel womb envy , envy of women's power to bear children, which they sublimate into achievement. In her feminine psychology , women's inferiority feelings have cultural causes, such as economic dependence and narrow roles, not anatomical ones. Her Self-Analysis (1942), drawn from her own lifelong practice, argued that people can ease many of their own neurotic conflicts without an analyst. A fashion of the 1940s blamed mothers instead. Momism is the blaming of over-protective, idealised mothers for their sons' weakness. The writer Philip Wylie coined it in Generation of Vipers (1942), and the psychiatrist Edward Strecker took it up in Their Mothers' Sons (1946), blaming "moms" for the young men found unfit for military service in the Second World War. Exam trap "Mom-ism" was coined by Wylie; when Wylie is not an option, the key is Edward Strecker , not Freud, Jung or Horney. Fromm: escape from freedom and the existential needs Erich Fromm (1900 to 1980), a German analyst trained also in sociology, called his approach humanistic psychoanalysis and studied whole societies. In Escape from Freedom (1941), written as fascism spread, he argued that modern people have won freedom from the old ties of church, clan and guild but pay for it with isolation. Many flee it through three mechanisms of escape : authoritarianism (submitting to a leader or dominating others), destructiveness (attacking the threatening world) and automaton conformity (becoming exactly what society expects). The healthy answer is positive freedom through spontaneous love and productive work. In The Sane Society (1955) Fromm named five distinctly human existential needs , arising from our awareness of being separate from nature (Table 4.16). Table 4.16 Fromm's five existential needs. Need What it is Healthy versus unhealthy answer Relatedness Union with others Productive love versus narcissism Transcendence Rising above passive existence Creating versus destroying Rootedness Feeling at home in the world Brotherliness versus clinging to mother and clan Sense of identity Knowing oneself as a separate being Individuality versus herd conformity Frame of orientation (consistent orientation) A stable way of making sense of the world Reason versus irrational belief Exam trap Safety, love and belonging, esteem and self-actualisation are Maslow's (Section 1.10 compares the lists); competence, autonomy and relatedness are Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory; hunger, thirst and shelter are physiological needs. Fromm's character orientations ( Man for Himself , 1947) describe how people relate to the world. Four are nonproductive: the receptive person waits to be given all good things; the exploitative person takes them by force or cunning; the hoarding person holds on to possessions, feelings and thoughts; and the marketing person packages the self as a commodity for sale. The productive orientation is the healthy ideal: using one's own powers in love, reason and work. Sullivan's interpersonal theory The American psychiatrist Harry Stack Sullivan (1892 to 1949) went furthest. His interpersonal theory ( The Interpersonal Theory of Psychiatry , published in 1953, after his death) holds that personality exists only in relations with other people, real or imagined: it is "the relatively enduring pattern of recurrent interpersonal situations which characterize a human life". Anxiety, again, is the engine. It passes by empathy from the "mothering one" to the infant: a tense mother makes a tense baby. To avoid it the child builds a self-system , the organisation of experience that guards security, using security operations such as selective inattention, which ease anxiety but block learning. It forms personifications , images of self and others: the good-me (experiences met with tenderness), the bad-me (experiences met with the mother's anxiety) and the not-me (experiences so dreadful that they are dissociated, surfacing in nightmares and schizophrenia). Experience matures through three modes. The prototaxic mode is the infant's undifferentiated flow of sensations. The parataxic mode links events that occur together as cause and effect, the prelogical thinking behind superstition. The syntaxic mode is logical and consensually validated through shared language. Sullivan's developmental epochs run from infancy and childhood through the juvenile era (the need for peers), preadolescence, and early and late adolescence to adulthood. Preadolescence brings the chum , a same-sex friend whose welfare matters as much as one's own: the first intimacy. Exam trap A practice-mock key for "Sullivan's interpersonal theory" is "personality as an open system interacting with the environment". Accept it by elimination, but "open system" is Allport's phrase ( The Open System in Personality Theory , 1960; Section 4.6). "Unconscious processes" is Freud, "observable behaviour" is behaviourism, and "social structures and institutions" is sociology, nearer Fromm. The eight stages from oral-sensory to maturity are Erikson's (Chapter 6), never Sullivan's. Ego psychology: Anna Freud, Hartmann and Erikson Ego psychology kept Freud's structural model but gave the ego more power. Anna Freud (1895 to 1982), Freud's youngest daughter, catalogued the defences in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936; Section 4.3) and pioneered child analysis. Heinz Hartmann (1894 to 1970), the father of ego psychology, argued in Ego Psychology and the Problem of Adaptation (1939) that perception, memory, motor skill, language and thinking develop in a conflict-free ego sphere , not out of conflict with the id. These functions give the ego autonomy, and its task is adaptation to an "average expectable environment". Erik Erikson (1902 to 1994), analysed by Anna Freud, carried the ego across the life span. His epigenetic principle holds that development unfolds by a ground plan, each part having its own time of special ascendancy, as organs form in an embryo. His stages are psychosocial, not psychosexual: each is a crisis between the growing person and society's demands, not a shift of libido to a new body zone, and they continue into old age. The adolescent identity crisis is his term; the eight stages are in Chapter 6. Object relations and Melanie Klein In psychoanalysis an object is the target of a drive or feeling: almost always a person, or the mental image of one, beginning with the mother. Object relations are the internalised mental representations of self and others (objects) and the relationships between them. A child does not just live with a mother; it carries a mother inside, coloured by love and hate, and later relationships are lived through these inner figures. The term does not mean the relationship among id, ego and superego, the use of defences, or the genital stage (Sections 4.2 and 4.3). The school's founder was Melanie Klein (1882 to 1960), who worked in Berlin and, from 1926, London. Klein analysed very young children through her play technique , treating play with small toys as free association. At first, she concluded, the baby relates to part objects : the gratifying "good breast" and the frustrating "bad breast", felt as two different beings. In the paranoid-schizoid position of the first months, the infant protects the good by splitting it off from the bad, keeping love and hate apart, and projects its rage into the bad object, which then seems to persecute it. From about the middle of the first year, as the infant grasps that the loved and hated mother are one person, it enters the depressive position : it feels guilt over the harm its rage may have done and makes reparation through loving acts. Klein spoke of positions, not stages, because adults move between them all their lives (Table 4.17). In projective identification a person puts unwanted parts of the self into someone else and then treats that person as if they had them. Envy ( Envy and Gratitude , 1957) is the infant's wish to spoil the good breast because it has what the infant lacks. Table 4.17 Klein's two positions. Feature Paranoid-schizoid position Depressive position Begins First months of life About the middle of the first year Object Part objects: good breast, bad breast Whole object: one mother, good and bad Anxiety Persecutory: fear of being attacked Depressive: fear of having harmed the loved one Main processes Splitting, projection, projective identification Guilt, mourning, reparation Exam trap Klein's defence in paranoia is splitting : the paranoid-schizoid position rests on it, and projection works on what splitting has already separated. Projection is Freud's classic mechanism of paranoia (the Schreber case, 1911). Reaction formation (turning a feeling into its opposite) and suppression (conscious putting aside) are in Section 4.3. Winnicott and the later object-relations theorists The English paediatrician Donald Winnicott (1896 to 1971) held that the infant needs not a perfect mother but a good-enough mother , who meets its needs almost completely at first and then fails it in small, bearable ways, so that it learns to tolerate frustration. She provides a holding environment of physical and emotional security. As the infant learns that the mother is separate, it adopts a transitional object , the teddy or blanket that is neither wholly "me" nor "not-me" and comforts it when she is away. Good-enough care lets a spontaneous true self develop; without it the infant builds a false self , a compliant shell that gives others what they expect. Ronald Fairbairn (1889 to 1964) made the cleanest break with Freud: libido is object-seeking, not pleasure-seeking. Margaret Mahler (1897 to 1985) traced the infant's psychological birth through separation-individuation , from fusion with the mother to a separate self (Chapter 6). Otto Kernberg (born 1928) described borderline personality organisation : intense early frustration and aggression leave the person unable to unite good and bad images, so splitting persists into adulthood, identity is diffuse and others are all good or all bad, though reality testing is largely kept. John Bowlby (1907 to 1990), trained in this tradition, turned the infant's tie to its mother into attachment theory, an offshoot taught in Chapter 6. Kohut's self psychology Heinz Kohut (1913 to 1981) founded self psychology , which drew on object relations, in The Analysis of the Self (1971) and The Restoration of the Self (1977). Where Freud saw narcissism as love withdrawn from others, Kohut saw healthy narcissism as a normal line of development. The self grows through selfobjects , people experienced as part of the self because they perform functions the child cannot yet perform alone. Three selfobject needs must be met: mirroring , the gleam in the mother's eye that confirms the child's "Look at me!" and so sustains the grandiose self ; idealising , merging with a calm, strong parent (the idealised parent imago); and twinship (alter ego), added later, feeling essentially alike with others. When parents respond well but imperfectly, each bearable failure leads the child to take over the selfobject's soothing function; this transmuting internalisation builds a cohesive self. When mirroring and idealising fail chronically, the self stays fragmented and enfeebled: empty and dependent on others to hold it together. Failed mirroring above all leaves the archaic grandiose self unintegrated, and it returns in adulthood as narcissistic pathology : grandiosity, a constant hunger for admiration and little empathy, as the person still seeks the mirroring that never came. Exam trap Grandiosity, a need for constant admiration and a lack of empathy trace to failed parental mirroring . Failed idealising leaves a person searching for someone perfect to admire; twinship (alter ego) is the need to feel alike; "confrontation" is a therapist's technique, not a selfobject need. Clinical link A client says she is "no one", feels "empty inside", dreads abandonment and has intense, unstable relationships. Self psychology reads this as a fragmented self from failed parental mirroring and idealising. It is not oral fixation or an unresolved Oedipus complex with castration anxiety (Freud's psychosexual explanations, Section 4.2), nor guilt from a harsh superego, a neurotic conflict rather than a deficit of self. The borderline disorder itself is in Chapter 8. Lacan, the "French Freud" Jacques Lacan (1901 to 1981), the Paris analyst called the "French Freud", led a return to Freud, a close rereading of Freud's own texts against ego psychology's taming of them. In the mirror stage , between about 6 and 18 months, the infant delights in its unified mirror image; the ego is born from this identification with an outside image, and so is partly an illusion. Drawing on structural linguistics, Lacan taught that the unconscious is structured like a language. Experience moves in three registers: the Imaginary (images and identifications), the Symbolic (language, law and social order) and the Real (whatever resists being put into words). Exam trap The other options are earlier French psychiatrists. Jean-Étienne Esquirol gave hallucination its modern meaning and described monomania. Each one claims that you behave in a characteristic way across situations and across years. Trait theorists set out to make a science of this everyday habit. This section follows two of them, who began from the same dictionary and went opposite ways: Gordon Allport, who studied the unique individual, and Raymond Cattell, who used statistics to find the dimensions on which everyone differs. Eysenck and the Big Five follow in Section 4.7. The trait approach and the lexical hypothesis The trait approach describes personality through specific psychological attributes along which individuals differ in consistent and stable ways. A trait is one such attribute: an enduring dimension, such as sociability, on which everyone has a position. The approach assumes stability over time (the talkative child becomes a talkative adult), consistency across situations (sociable at a wedding and in the canteen alike) and individual differences (people sit at different points on the same dimension, so they can be compared and their behaviour predicted). Three neighbouring ideas must be kept apart. A type sorts people into broad, discrete categories, such as Sheldon's body types (Section 4.1), and so describes personality through broad patterns; typing shades into stereotyping, a set of expected behaviours based on similarities among members of a group. Situationism holds that characteristics of the situation, not of the person, largely determine behaviour (Walter Mischel's challenge, Section 4.7). A state is a temporary condition: Charles Spielberger (1927 to 2013) separated state anxiety, a passing tension, from trait anxiety, a stable proneness to anxiety, and measured both with his State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (1970). Where should one look for the traits that matter? The lexical hypothesis answers: in language. Differences between people that matter in daily life get noticed and named, so the important traits are already encoded as words, and the more important a trait, the more words a language has for it. In 1936 Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert searched an unabridged English dictionary and culled 17,953 words that distinguish one person's behaviour from another's. Only about 4,500 named stable traits (honest, sociable); the rest described temporary states (flustered), evaluations (admirable), or physical features and abilities. This list fed the whole factor-analytic tradition (Figure 4.9). Such a list can be used in two ways. The nomothetic approach (Greek nomos , law) studies many people on the same dimensions to find general laws. The idiographic approach ( idios , one's own) studies one person intensively to grasp his or her unique pattern. The terms are Wilhelm Windelband's (Section 4.1). Cattell went nomothetic; Allport preferred the idiographic path. Exam trap The trait approach focuses on specific psychological attributes along which individuals differ in consistent and stable ways . "Broad patterns" describes the type approach; "expected behaviour based on similarities" describes stereotyping; "situational characteristics determine behaviour" is situationism, the critique of trait theory. Allport: traits as real structures Gordon Willard Allport (1897 to 1967) did more than anyone to make personality a recognised field. In 1920 he called on Sigmund Freud in Vienna and, to fill an awkward silence, described a small boy he had just seen on a tram who was terrified of dirt. Freud looked at his neat, meticulous visitor and asked, "Was that little boy you?" Allport decided that psychoanalysis digs too deep and that psychology should take conscious, present motives seriously. Back at Harvard, from 1924, he taught what was probably the first American college course on personality, and his Personality: A Psychological Interpretation (1937) established the field. It defined personality as "the dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his unique adjustments to his environment" (Section 4.1). For Allport a trait was not a convenient label but a real neuropsychic structure . It renders many stimuli functionally equivalent and guides consistent behaviour: a friendly man greets the stranger at the bus stop, the new colleague and the neighbour's guest with the same warmth. Traits therefore cause behaviour rather than merely summarising it. Allport distinguished common traits , shared in varying degrees by the members of a culture so that people can be compared on them, from individual traits, which he later renamed personal dispositions ( Pattern and Growth in Personality , 1961): characteristics peculiar to one person. Personal dispositions differ in how much of a life they govern, and Allport set them on three levels (Table 4.18). A cardinal trait is the most pervasive and powerful kind: a single ruling passion that dominates a whole life. Few people have one, and those who do often lend it a name: Machiavellian, narcissistic, Christlike. Central traits are the handful, five to ten, of outstanding traits that describe a person's behaviour, the words you would put in a reference letter. Secondary traits are the least important, displayed inconspicuously and inconsistently, such as a taste for filter coffee, and noticed only by close friends. Table 4.18 Allport's three levels of personal dispositions. Level What it is Who has it Examples Cardinal The most pervasive and powerful trait; one ruling passion Few people Machiavellian, narcissistic, Christlike Central The handful (5 to 10) of outstanding traits that describe a person Everyone Honest, sociable, cynical: a reference letter Secondary The least important; shown inconspicuously and inconsistently Everyone, many of them Food or music preferences, passing attitudes Exam trap Allport's levels are cardinal, central and secondary . "Primary, secondary, tertiary" is invented; "cognitive, emotional, physiological" are components of emotion; "id, ego, superego" is Freud's structure (Section 4.2). Match the definitions: most pervasive and powerful, cardinal; handful of outstanding traits, central; least important and inconsistent, secondary; shared by members of a culture, common traits. The idiographic approach Because every personality is unique, Allport argued, its science must study the individual case and not only group averages, which describe nobody in particular. He therefore preferred the idiographic approach to the nomothetic search for laws, with its factorial designs (several variables crossed over many subjects) and group statistics such as chi-square (Chapter 9). Later he called his approach morphogenic , the study of how traits are patterned within one person. His main method was the personal-document technique : analysing diaries, letters and autobiographies for the traits they reveal. Key study: Letters from Jenny (1965) Over twelve years a woman Allport called Jenny, the mother of his college roommate, wrote more than 300 letters to Allport and his wife. Thirty-six judges read them and listed nearly 200 trait names, which Allport reduced to eight clusters, among them quarrelsome-suspicious, self-centred and dramatic-intense. A later computer count of her words by one of his students found much the same eight. Criticism: the method rests on judges' interpretations, and one case is hard to generalise. Allport was not purely idiographic. With Philip Vernon (1931), and later with Gardner Lindzey , he built the Study of Values , a nomothetic self-report test of the relative strength of six values taken from Eduard Spranger's types: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political and religious. With Vernon he also showed (1933) that expressive behaviour, such as handwriting, gesture and voice, is consistent across tasks. Exam trap Allport preferred the idiographic approach. The nomothetic approach, factorial designs and chi-square are the group methods he criticised. Nor did he use factor analysis: that is the hallmark of Cattell and Eysenck. Functional autonomy, the proprium and maturity Freud explained adult motives by tracing them to childhood. Allport's reply was functional autonomy : the motives of a mature adult become independent of the experiences in which they began, as a grown tree no longer needs its seed. A girl made to practise the veena to escape scolding may, as a woman, play for hours for its own sake. Perseverative functional autonomy covers low-level routines that persist without reward, such as addictions and daily rituals. Propriate functional autonomy covers motives bound up with one's values, self-image and lifestyle, and is the key to adult motivation. "Propriate" comes from the proprium , Allport's word for the self. It develops through seven aspects: (1) the bodily self, (2) self-identity and (3) self-esteem, in about the first three years; (4) self-extension ("my house, my school") and (5) the self-image, actual and ideal, at about four to six; (6) the self as a rational coper, from six to twelve; and (7) propriate striving, the long-range goals of adolescence. The self returns in Section 4.10. If childhood needs for affection and security are met, the result is the mature adult, marked by six criteria: (1) extension of the sense of self beyond oneself; (2) warm relating to others; (3) emotional security and self-acceptance; (4) realistic perception, skills and commitment to work; (5) self-objectification, meaning insight together with humour; and (6) a unifying philosophy of life. In 1960 Allport described personality as an open system , taking in energy and information and growing, not merely reducing tension. Critics note that functional autonomy says that motives become independent but not how, that the sharp break between child and adult personality is doubtful, and that the theory produced little research. Cattell: surface and source traits Raymond Bernard Cattell (1905 to 1998) studied chemistry in London and then took a PhD in psychology in 1929 under Charles Spearman. Spearman had applied factor analysis to mental abilities; Cattell resolved to apply it to personality. He moved to the United States in 1937 and worked mostly at the University of Illinois. His goal was prediction: "Personality is that which permits a prediction of what a person will do in a given situation" (1950). Factor analysis examines the correlations among many measures and finds the few underlying factors that account for them: if people rated talkative are also rated sociable and cheerful, one factor may lie beneath all three. Cattell took Allport and Odbert's 4,500 stable-trait words, merged synonyms to leave 171, found that ratings on these formed about 35 clusters, and factor-analysed ratings, questionnaires and tests down to the 16 factors of his Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire, the 16PF (Figure 4.9). 17,953 trait words culled from a dictionary (Allport and Odbert, 1936) About 4,500 words for stable traits 171 terms once Cattell merged synonyms About 35 correlated clusters: surface traits 16 source traits: the 16PF (1949) factor analysis 5 global second-order factors factored again Figure 4.9 The lexical search, from dictionary to questionnaire. Each step keeps fewer, deeper units: the correlated surface clusters give way to the source traits beneath them. The clusters and the factors give Cattell's most examined distinction. Surface traits are clusters of behaviours that correlate and appear together; anxiety, indecision and irrational fear, for example, form a surface trait one might call neuroticism. Because they arise from several sources, they are less stable and less important. Source traits are the stable, unitary factors beneath them, revealed by factor analysis: the building blocks of personality, as atoms are of matter. By origin, source traits are either constitutional traits , rooted in biology, or environmental-mold traits , learned from social and physical surroundings. Cattell also separated common traits, which everyone has in some degree, from unique traits belonging to one or a few people (a passion for old coins), and divided traits by function into ability traits (how efficiently we pursue goals), temperament traits (emotional style) and dynamic traits (the motivating forces). Dynamic traits come in two kinds. Ergs are innate drives, such as hunger, sex, fear, curiosity, gregariousness and self-assertion. Sentiments are learned patterns of attitudes centred on an important object, such as career, religion, family or the self; the self-sentiment integrates the rest. A specific attitude ("I want to revise tonight") serves a sentiment, which in turn serves ergs, a chain Cattell called subsidiation . The web of such links is the dynamic lattice (Figure 4.10). Attitudes specific interests Sentiments learned Ergs innate drives Revise for the exam Buy textbooks Visit grandmother Cook for the family Career sentiment Family sentiment Self-assertion Security (fear) Protectiveness Gregariousness Subsidiation: each attitude serves a sentiment, and each sentiment serves ergs Figure 4.10 A simplified dynamic lattice. Read it from left to right: everyday attitudes are subsidiary to learned sentiments, which are subsidiary to innate ergs. Exam trap Cattell's pair is surface and source traits . Cardinal and central traits are Allport's; openness and conscientiousness are Big Five factors (Section 4.7); id and ego are Freud's. An Amity 2023 item says Cattell divided "attitudes" into source and surface: the key is right, but the stem garbles traits as attitudes. Its option "egos and sentiments" garbles Cattell's ergs and sentiments , the two kinds of dynamic trait. "Traits and types" are two approaches; defence and coping mechanisms belong to Sections 4.3 and 1.11. L-data, Q-data and T-data A factor found in only one kind of data might be an artefact of method, so Cattell required source traits to reappear across three kinds (Table 4.19). L-data (life-record data) capture everyday behaviour through records or the ratings of observers who know the person: school performance, absences from work, a criminal record. Q-data (questionnaire data) are self-report ratings of one's own characteristics, attributes and interests, limited by poor self-knowledge and by faking. T-data (objective test data) come from controlled test situations whose purpose is hidden, so responses are hard to fake. The four 16PF factors labelled Q1 to Q4 appeared only in questionnaire data, hence the Q. Table 4.19 Cattell's three sources of personality data. "P-data" (projective data) and "Z-data" do not exist; Cattell classed hard-to-fake tasks such as inkblots as T-data, and projective responses are never L-data. Q-data is not the Q-sort, in which a person sorts self-descriptive cards from "most like me" to "least like me" (Rogers, Section 4.8). Nor is it the P-technique , a research design that factor-analyses one person measured on many occasions (the usual R-technique correlates many people measured once). Self-report is Q-data; school and criminal records are L-data; the 16 source traits are results, not data. The Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire Cattell packaged his source traits in the Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF), first published in 1949; the fifth edition (1993) has 185 items for people aged 16 and over. It measures normal personality on 16 primary factors (Table 4.20), lettered roughly by their size in Cattell's early rating studies; D, J and K are missing because those factors did not reappear reliably in adult questionnaire data. Factor B is a brief reasoning scale, but the instrument measures personality, not intelligence. Factoring the 16 again yields five second-order global factors : extraversion, anxiety, tough-mindedness, independence and self-control. These approximate the Big Five (extraversion, neuroticism, low openness, low agreeableness and conscientiousness; Section 4.7). Sten-score norms, reliability and validity are in Chapter 2. Eysenck also used factor analysis but found three dimensions (the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire, EPQ); Costa and McCrae built the NEO-PI-R for five factors; Allport built the Study of Values; Sheldon rated body types; Murray devised the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT); Freud and Rogers proposed no trait dimensions at all. The 16PF measures normal personality traits, not fluid, crystallised or general intelligence (Cattell's fluid and crystallised intelligence and Spearman's g are in Section 1.9), and it is not a personality-disorder scale, a Q-sort or a projective test. Heredity, development and the wider trait family Comparing twins and ordinary siblings reared together and apart, Cattell concluded that about one third of personality is genetically based and two thirds environmental, though intelligence (factor B) and boldness (factor H) looked about 80 percent hereditary. He proposed six life-span stages: infancy (birth to 6, the major formative period), childhood (6 to 14), adolescence (14 to 23), maturity (23 to 50), late maturity (50 to 65) and old age. His specification equation predicts a response in a given situation as the sum of the person's trait scores, each weighted by its relevance to that situation. The main criticism is that factor analysis is less objective than it looks: the researcher chooses the measures and names the factors, which may be why others could not replicate all 16. Hans Eysenck thought three were enough and looked for them in the brain; Paul Costa and Robert McCrae settled on five, the answer that now dominates. This section follows both, then asks how much of a trait is inherited and whether traits predict what you will actually do tomorrow. Eysenck's three superfactors Hans Jurgen Eysenck (1916 to 1997) left Berlin for London in 1934 and spent his career at the Maudsley Hospital and Institute of Psychiatry. Like Cattell he used factor analysis, but he distrusted purely statistical factors: a real dimension of personality must also show up in laboratory experiments and have a biological cause. Factor analysis joined to experiment and biology is his signature. His hierarchical model has four levels (Figure 4.11). At the bottom are specific responses : today you chat with a stranger at the bus stop. Responses that recur become habitual responses : you chat at every bus stop. Correlated habits form traits (sociability, liveliness, activity), and correlated traits form a type or superfactor, here extraversion. An Eysenck type is a broad continuous dimension, not a box people fall into. Type Traits Habitual responses Specific responses Extraversion (type) Sociability Liveliness Activity HR HR HR HR HR HR Figure 4.11 Eysenck's hierarchical model. Specific responses (dots) recur as habitual responses (HR), correlated habits form traits, and correlated traits form a type such as extraversion. His early analyses ( Dimensions of Personality , 1947) found two superfactors; a third was added in the 1970s, giving the PEN model : E, extraversion versus introversion . Extraverts are sociable, lively, active, talkative, assertive and sensation seeking; they enjoy parties and large gatherings and look for stimulation. Introverts are quiet, reserved and reflective; they prefer a few close friends, plan before acting and, in the popular phrase, gain energy from solitude while crowds drain them. Introversion is not unfriendliness, aggression or even shyness (Eysenck listed shyness under N). N, neuroticism versus emotional stability. High scorers are anxious, moody, tense, guilt-prone and emotionally reactive, with low self-esteem; low scorers are calm and even-tempered. P, psychoticism versus impulse control. High scorers are aggressive, cold, egocentric, impersonal, impulsive, antisocial and tough-minded, though sometimes creative. P is not psychosis; the scale is closer to psychopathy. Exam trap Eysenck's three are E, N and P . "Extraversion, sensing-intuition, thinking-feeling" smuggles in the Myers-Briggs dichotomies from Carl Jung's types (Section 4.4); "psychoticism-conscientiousness" borrows a Big Five factor. His earliest model had only E and N: not openness and conscientiousness (Big Five), not inferiority and superiority striving (Alfred Adler, Section 4.4), not internal and external locus of control (Julian Rotter, Section 4.9). "Aggressive and dominant" never describes the introvert: dominance goes with E, aggression with P. Arousal, the visceral brain and the four temperaments Why should one student crave the roar of a cricket stadium while her roommate hides in the library? Eysenck's answer ( The Biological Basis of Personality , 1967) was arousal. The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) in the brainstem sets the level of cortical arousal . Introverts, he proposed, have a higher baseline arousal, so extra stimulation overloads them and they avoid it; extraverts sit below their comfortable level and seek stimulation to climb up to it. The laboratory bore him out: given a few drops of lemon juice on the tongue, introverts salivate more than extraverts, and they are more sensitive to faint stimuli, tolerate pain less and condition faster. Later work confirmed these differences more firmly than the arousal explanation. Neuroticism rests on the visceral brain , an older name for the limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulum, septum, hypothalamus), which drives the sympathetic nervous system; in high-N people this alarm fires at mild stress and settles slowly. For P he suggested male hormones, since men score higher; this biology is the weakest. Because E and N are independent, crossing them gives four quadrants, and Eysenck pointed out that these reproduce the four temperaments of Galen (Section 4.1): the stable extravert is sanguine , the unstable extravert choleric , the unstable introvert melancholic and the stable introvert phlegmatic (Figure 4.12).
