Each quadrant matches one of Galen's temperaments; the trait words under each name are Eysenck's. Eysenck's questionnaires, many built with his wife Sybil B. G. Eysenck , are the Maudsley Personality Inventory (MPI, 1959; E and N), the Eysenck Personality Inventory (EPI, 1964, or 1963 in some sources; E, N and a Lie scale), the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ, 1975), which added P and kept the Lie scale (L) that catches faking good, and the EPQ-R (1985) with an improved P scale. Twin studies supported his view that the dimensions are largely inherited, E and N more than P, and all three appear in over 35 nations. In Crime and Personality (1964) he argued that offenders score high on E and N, adding P in later editions: extraverts condition poorly, so they are slow to acquire the conditioned anxiety that serves as conscience. The P link is the most consistent; the full theory has only modest support. Other biological models of temperament Eysenck opened the way to a biology of temperament, the inherited, early-appearing emotional style (Section 4.1) now seen as the biological core of personality. Table 4.22 sets out four successors. Jeffrey Alan Gray (1934 to 2004) rotated Eysenck's E and N axes in his reinforcement sensitivity theory : anxiety runs from stable extravert to neurotic introvert, impulsivity from stable introvert to neurotic extravert. C. Robert Cloninger (1987, extended 1993) tied temperaments to neurotransmitters. Jerome Kagan (1929 to 2021) found that about one baby in five reacts to novelty with thrashing and crying, and these high-reactive infants tend to become shy, cautious children, showing behavioural inhibition . Arnold Buss and Robert Plomin (1984) proposed three heritable temperaments. Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess's infant categories are taught in Chapter 6. Researchers who reanalysed trait ratings, following the lexical hypothesis of Section 4.6, kept arriving at five. Donald Fiske (1949) found five factors in ratings on Cattell's variables; Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal (1961) found five recurrent factors in US Air Force ratings; Warren Norman (1963) replicated them; and Lewis Goldberg named them the Big Five (1981), "big" meaning broad, not important. The NEO-PI-R (1992) has 240 items, eight per facet, covering five domains with six facets each, 30 facets in all. The NEO belongs to the trait approach : it measures stable dispositions, not learned responses (behaviourist), thought processes (cognitive) or unconscious conflict (psychodynamic). Its psychometric properties are in Chapter 2. Exam trap The NEO-PI-R rests on the Five-Factor Model : five domains, six facets each. It is not Cattell's 16 source traits (16PF, Section 4.6), Eysenck's three PEN dimensions (the EPQ), the MBTI's 16 types (Section 4.4), Henry Murray's needs and press (Section 4.6) or eleven personality-disorder scales (a clinical inventory, Chapter 2). The Big Five across life and cultures McCrae and Costa built the factors into five-factor theory (1996). The traits are basic tendencies : biologically based capacities that upbringing does not shape. What life shapes are characteristic adaptations : the habits, attitudes, skills, roles, relationships and self-concept through which a tendency is expressed in a particular culture. High E is a basic tendency; joining the college cultural committee in Mysuru is one adaptation of it. The factors replicate in more than 50 nations, India among them, suggesting a common human structure. Critics note that most samples are urban and literate, that a remote Bolivian tribal group did not show the five clearly, and that lexical studies in some languages find six factors. How stable are the factors? People keep their rank order, more so with age, but mean levels shift: from adolescence into middle age, conscientiousness and agreeableness rise while neuroticism falls, the maturity principle . Costa and McCrae borrowed William James 's 1890 phrase that by about 30 character is "set like plaster"; later work shows the plaster can still be chipped. Twin studies put the heritability of each factor at about 40 to 50 percent. The factors also predict outcomes. High conscientiousness and low neuroticism go with better health and longer life. Lewis Terman began following about 1,500 bright Californian children in 1921; when Howard Friedman and colleagues (1993) traced their deaths, those rated conscientious and prudent as children had lived longer. Conscientious people exercise, wear seat belts, avoid smoking and follow medical advice. High N predicts distress and is the broadest personality risk factor for anxiety and depressive disorders (Chapter 8). Conscientiousness also predicted job performance in every occupational group in the meta-analysis of Murray Barrick and Michael Mount (1991). Exam trap The health pair is high C plus low N . "Low agreeableness and low neuroticism" swaps in low A, which as hostility (the toxic core of the Type A pattern; Type A and Type D are in Section 1.11) predicts heart disease, not health. "Neuroticism exclusively" is backwards, since high N harms health, and "introversion exclusively" has no such link. Beyond five: HEXACO and the Dark Triad Not everyone accepts five. Michael Ashton and Kibeom Lee reanalysed trait words across many languages (from 2004) and found six factors, the HEXACO model: H onesty-Humility (sincere, fair, modest versus greedy, boastful, manipulative), E motionality (fearful, anxious, sentimental; close to N), e X traversion, A greeableness, C onscientiousness and O penness to experience. Honesty-Humility, the genuinely new factor, is low in offenders; the 100-item HEXACO-PI-R measures all six. Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams (2002) described the Dark Triad , three overlapping, socially aversive but subclinical traits: narcissism (grandiosity, entitlement, hunger for admiration), Machiavellianism (cold, cynical, strategic manipulation) and psychopathy (callousness, impulsive thrill seeking, lack of remorse). All three share low agreeableness and low honesty-humility. The Dark Tetrad adds everyday sadism , enjoying others' suffering (Paulhus and colleagues, 2013). Genes, environments and evolution How can genes be separated from upbringing? Behaviour genetics uses two natural experiments. Identical (monozygotic) twins share all their genes and fraternal (dizygotic) twins about half, so greater similarity in identical pairs points to genes. In adoption studies, resemblance to the biological parents points to genes, resemblance to the adoptive parents to family environment. The heritability of a trait is the proportion of its variation within a population that is due to genetic differences; it says nothing about how "genetic" one person's trait is. Key study: the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart (from 1979) Question: if identical twins grow up in different homes, how alike are they? Method: Thomas Bouchard and colleagues brought more than 100 sets of twins and triplets reared apart to the University of Minnesota for about a week of tests. Result (reported in 1990): identical twins reared apart were about as similar in personality as those reared together; heritability came to about 0.40 to 0.50 for personality and about 0.70 for IQ. Criticism: some pairs grew up in similar homes or had met before testing, and the sample was small and self-selected. The same studies held a surprise: growing up in the same family adds almost nothing to personality similarity, and adoptive siblings reared together are scarcely more alike than strangers. Plomin and Denise Daniels (1987) asked why children in the same family are so different, and answered that what matters is the non-shared environment : different friends, teachers, illnesses, accidents and differential treatment by parents. The shared environment (the same home, parents, income and religion) has only a weak effect on adult personality. Genes and environments are also entangled. Sandra Scarr and Kathleen McCartney (1983) described three kinds of gene-environment correlation . In the passive kind, parents give a child both genes and a matching home (musical parents, a house full of music); it is strongest in infancy. In the evocative kind, a child's inherited traits draw responses from others (a smiling baby is picked up more). In the active kind, or niche picking, people seek settings that suit them (the extravert joins the drama club); it grows with age. In gene-environment interaction , by contrast, a gene's effect depends on the environment: a vulnerable genotype may raise the risk of depression only after severe stress. Why does variation persist at all? David Buss (born 1953) treats traits as adaptive individual differences : the Big Five summarise what our ancestors most needed to know about one another (who will lead, cooperate, work hard, panic or innovate), and different trait levels pay off in different environments. He is not Arnold Buss of the EAS model. The person-situation debate Traits assume consistency: an honest child should be honest in class, at play and at home. Hugh Hartshorne and Mark May tested this and found it largely missing (Key study below). Forty years later Walter Mischel (1930 to 2018) generalised the point in Personality and Assessment (1968). Trait measures, he found, correlated with behaviour in a given situation, and behaviour in one situation with behaviour in another, rarely above about 0.30, a ceiling he called the personality coefficient ; it explains less than 10 percent of the variation in behaviour. His critique: situational factors often override traits in determining behaviour. So began the person-situation debate . Key study: Hartshorne and May's honesty studies (1928) Question: is honesty a consistent trait? Method: in the Character Education Inquiry, thousands of American schoolchildren were given secret chances to cheat, lie or keep money in classroom, party, athletic and home settings. Result: honesty in one setting predicted honesty in another only weakly; a child who copied answers might still return a coin. Conclusion: honesty looked situation-specific. Criticism: single acts are unreliable samples; summed over many tests, the scores showed much more consistency. Trait theorists replied in three ways. First, aggregation : Seymour Epstein (1979) showed that a single act is as unreliable as a single test item; averaged over many occasions, behaviour becomes far more stable, so traits predict most of the people much of the time. Second, a strong situation (a red traffic light, a funeral, an exam hall) has clear rules that make everyone behave alike, while a weak situation (a party, a free afternoon) lets traits show. Third, interactionism ( Norman Endler and David Magnusson , 1976): behaviour depends on the person, the situation and their interaction. Mischel himself rebuilt consistency as stable if-then patterns in his cognitive-affective personality system (Section 4.9). Traits predict behaviour averaged across time and situations well, single acts poorly. Exam trap Mischel's critique was that situations often override traits . He did not say that personality is entirely biological (closer to Eysenck), that traits outpredict situations (the opposite of his point), or that traits cannot be measured reliably: trait questionnaires were reliable; they simply predicted single behaviours poorly. By the 1950s a group of American psychologists objected that neither left room for what people experience most directly: choosing, hoping and trying to become someone. The humanists, Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow, asked what a person could grow into. The existentialists, from Heidegger to Rollo May and Viktor Frankl, asked how a person faces freedom, anxiety and death. The humanistic image of the person The humanistic approach to personality rests on four assumptions. People have free will and answer for their choices. Every person has an innate tendency to grow and develop, to reach his or her maximum potential . A person must be understood as a whole , not as a bundle of parts. What matters most is conscious, present experience , studied from the inside through the person's phenomenological field : the world as he or she perceives it, which may differ from the world as it is. Table 4.25 sets this image beside its rivals. Humanism does not explain people by unconscious conflict (the psychodynamic view), conditioned responses (behaviourism) or information processing (the cognitive perspective), nor judge them against statistical norms , the "average is normal" yardstick of trait measurement and of one definition of abnormality (Chapter 8). Its founders were Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers, with Charlotte Buhler (1893 to 1974), who studied the goals that organise the whole life course, and Rollo May, who brought in existential ideas. How it became psychology's "third force" is told in Section 1.2. Table 4.25 Five images of the person. Perspective The person is Behaviour explained by Disorder seen as Psychodynamic Driven by hidden forces Unconscious conflict, childhood Repressed conflict Behavioural A product of learning Conditioned responses, reinforcement Faulty learning Cognitive An information processor Thoughts, beliefs, schemas Distorted thinking Humanistic Free, whole, growing Conscious experience, the urge to grow Blocked growth Existential Free, responsible, mortal Choices made facing anxiety and death Inauthentic, meaningless living Disorder, on this view, is blocked growth : conditional love, unmet needs or a false self thwart the push to grow. Cure needs neither a reinforcement schedule nor the interpretation of buried conflict, but a relationship in which the therapist believes in the client's potential, offers positive regard and treats the client with respect (Chapter 7). Critics reply that "actualisation" and "potential" are vague and nearly untestable, and that the focus on the individual's inner world misses the wider social and cultural contexts that shape experience and identity: the autonomous, self-made individual is a Western, individualist ideal. Exam trap Maximum potential, an innate tendency to grow, free will and personal growth all point to humanistic . Maslow and Rogers propose the humanistic approach, not the existential (May, Frankl), cognitive or behavioural one. "Availability of reinforcement" is the behavioural view of disorder. The standard criticism is neglect of social and cultural context: "too much focus on cognition" fits the cognitive approach, "too much focus on past experience" fits psychoanalysis, and "neglecting personal experience" is the opposite of what humanists do. Rogers: the self and its conditions of worth Carl Ransom Rogers (1902 to 1987) built his theory from what clients told him about their own experience. Its single motive is the actualising tendency , the innate drive of every organism to maintain and enhance itself: it keeps the toddler walking despite falls, and later powers psychological growth. Once a self has formed, part of it becomes the self-actualising tendency , the push to actualise the self as perceived. From infancy, experience is judged by the organismic valuing process : what enhances the organism feels good and is sought, what hinders it feels bad and is avoided. Each person lives in a private phenomenal field , also called the experiential world: all experience as the person perceives it, the only reality that counts for behaviour. Part of it is gradually set apart as "I" and "me": the self-concept , the organised picture of who one is. Beside it grows the ideal self , the self one would most like to be. With the self comes a universal need for positive regard (warmth, love and acceptance from important others) and later a need for positive self-regard , approval from within. Unconditional positive regard values the child whatever he or she does: the act may be disapproved of, the child never is. Conditional positive regard is love with strings attached. The child then introjects (takes in as his or her own) the parents' standards as conditions of worth : "I am worthy only when I ...". These work much like Freud's superego, and experience is now valued not by the organismic valuing process but by whether it earns approval. The result is incongruence : a split between what the organism actually experiences and a self-concept burdened by conditions of worth, felt as tension, anxiety and confusion. Its opposite, congruence , is a close match between self-concept and experience. Threatening experience is kept out by distortion (admitting it in a changed form) or denial (keeping it out of awareness). Arjun, praised at home only when he tops the class in science, believes "I am the future doctor". When he finds he loves designing furniture and finds anatomy dull, he distorts it ("I am just tired") or denies it; tension builds and anxiety appears without a nameable cause. Figure 4.13 traces both routes. Actualising tendency + need for positive regard Unconditional positive regard Conditional positive regard No conditions of worth; organismic valuing intact Conditions of worth introjected Congruence toward fully functioning Incongruence: anxiety distortion and denial Figure 4.13 Two routes in Rogers's theory: the same need for positive regard leads to congruence when love is unconditional, and to incongruence and defence when it is conditional. Exam trap "A split between the organismic valuing process and a self-concept burdened by conditions of worth, producing tension and confusion" is incongruence . Introjection is only how conditions of worth get in (and a defence mechanism, Section 4.3); conflict is a general term (id, ego and superego in Section 4.2, approach-avoidance in Section 1.10); the actualising tendency is the growth force that incongruence blocks. The fully functioning person and the Q-sort A child given unconditional positive regard stays congruent and moves toward what Rogers called the fully functioning person , "a direction, not a destination" ( On Becoming a Person , 1961). Five features mark such a person: openness to experience , nothing distorted or denied; existential living , fully in each moment; organismic trusting , relying on one's own reactions; experiential freedom , a felt freedom to choose and responsibility for the choice; and creativity . Rogers stated the theory as 19 propositions in Client-Centered Therapy (1951), beginning with the claim that each person lives at the centre of a continually changing world of experience and reacts to it as perceived. Therapy restores congruence; its core conditions are taught in Chapter 7. Rogers also made the self measurable. The Q-sort , devised by the British psychologist William Stephenson ( The Study of Behavior , 1953) and adopted by Rogers's group at Chicago, has the person sort self-descriptive statements ("I feel helpless", "I am emotionally mature") from "most like me" to "least like me" into a forced, roughly normal distribution: a few cards at each extreme, most in the middle. Because the statements are ranked against one another for the same person, the Q-sort captures within-person rather than between-person variation. Sorting once for the real self and once for the ideal self gives a self-ideal correlation, an index of congruence. Key study: the case of Mrs Oak (Rogers, 1954) Does successful therapy bring the perceived self closer to the ideal? Mrs Oak's self-ideal correlation rose from +.36 before client-centred therapy to +.79 a year after it, and in 25 clients studied by Rogers's associates J. M. Butler and G. V. Haigh (1954) the average rose from .01 before therapy to +.31 after it. Criticism: Q-sorts are self-reports, open to the wish to please the therapist, and a rising correlation can come from a lowered ideal as well as a changed self. Research supports Rogers in part: conditionally loved children show unstable self-esteem, and large self-ideal gaps go with anxiety and depression. Critics note his reliance on conscious self-report and an actualising tendency assumed rather than shown; his lasting gifts were recorded therapy sessions as research data and the self-concept as a variable. Exam trap The Q-sort was devised by Stephenson and used by Rogers to measure the self-concept and self-ideal congruence. It did not replace the MMPI (Chapter 2), and it is neither a test of infant reflexes nor a diagnostic test for schizophrenia. Maslow: deficiency, being and the self-actualiser Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970) asked what the healthiest people are like. His hierarchy of needs (physiological, safety, belongingness and love, esteem, self-actualisation, with lower needs stronger and prepotent) is taught in Section 1.10; here we follow what it implies for personality. The four lower levels are deficiency needs (D-needs): a lack creates tension that drives us to fill it, and once filled they stop motivating. Behaviour driven by them is D-motivation . Once they are met, a person is moved differently. Maslow called this metamotivation (also B-motivation, from Being), the distinct motivation of self-actualisers: not making up a lack but growing and expressing oneself, even seeking tension. Its objects are being needs, the metaneeds or B-values, such as truth, goodness, beauty, justice, wholeness and meaningfulness. Frustrated metaneeds produce metapathology : cynicism, apathy and a sense of meaninglessness that the sufferer cannot trace to any lack (Table 4.26). Table 4.26 Maslow's deficiency and being realms. Feature Deficiency (D) Being (B) Needs Physiological, safety, belonging, esteem Metaneeds (B-values): truth, beauty, justice Motivation D-motivation: fill a lack Metamotivation: grow and express Tension Reduced Sought and enjoyed When thwarted Illness, anxiety Metapathology: cynicism, apathy Typical of Most people Self-actualisers (1 percent or fewer) Self-actualisation is the striving to fulfil one's potential, to become everything one is capable of becoming. The neurologist Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965) coined the term in The Organism (German 1934, English 1939); Maslow made it the summit of his hierarchy. Finding almost none among students, he studied older people and historical figures, among them the later Abraham Lincoln , Thomas Jefferson , Albert Einstein and Eleanor Roosevelt , and estimated that 1 percent of people or fewer self-actualise. They showed efficient perception of reality; acceptance of self, others and nature; spontaneity; problem-centring (a mission outside themselves); a need for privacy; autonomy and resistance to enculturation; freshness of appreciation; peak experiences; social interest (Adler's term, Section 4.4); deep but few relationships; a democratic character; and creativity. A peak experience is a brief, intense moment of ecstasy and awe in which the sense of self is transcended; late in life Maslow added the plateau experience , a calmer, longer-lasting and more voluntary serenity. Why do so few self-actualise? Besides unmet lower needs and poor upbringing, Maslow blamed the Jonah complex , the fear of one's own greatness, named after the prophet who ran from God's call. The Personal Orientation Inventory (POI) of Everett Shostrom (1964) later measured self-actualisation with 150 paired statements. Critics note that the sample was small and hand-picked by Maslow's own values, and that his terms are vague. The transpersonal "fourth force" he foresaw is in Section 1.2. Exam trap The distinct motivation of self-actualisers is metamotivation ; D-motivation drives everyone else, and "E-motivation" and "F-motivation" do not exist. "The striving for fulfilment of one's potential" is self-actualisation , not the self-concept (one's picture of oneself), the ideal self (the self one wishes to be) or self-efficacy (Bandura's belief that one can perform a task, Section 4.9). Existential roots: Dasein and the three worlds Both schools reject determinism, but humanism assumes an inner nature, a seed of potential waiting to unfold, and existentialism denies even that. It grew from the Danish philosopher Soren Kierkegaard (1813 to 1855), who wrote of the anxiety of choosing oneself; the German Martin Heidegger (1889 to 1976), author of Being and Time (1927); and the French Jean-Paul Sartre (1905 to 1980), whose slogan was existence precedes essence : we exist first and then make ourselves by our choices. Nothing fixes the meaning of a life in advance, so each person must continually recreate himself or herself, and the meaning of existence keeps changing. This is existential psychology: not humanistic psychology, which assumes a potential to fulfil, nor experimental psychology, which seeks general laws by controlled experiment, nor philosophy alone, since it carries the philosophers' ideas into the study and treatment of persons. Heidegger's key term was Dasein (German, "being there"): human existence as being-in-the-world . A person is not a mind looking out at a separate world but one unit with it, so Dasein expresses the basic unity of person and environment. Behaviourists, cognitivists and psychoanalysts all split person from world; existentialists refuse the split. The Swiss psychiatrists Ludwig Binswanger (1881 to 1966) and Medard Boss (1903 to 1990) applied Heidegger to patients as Daseinsanalysis , describing each patient's world rather than explaining symptoms. Binswanger, and after him May, described three modes of being-in-the-world, lived at once (Figure 4.14). The Umwelt ("world around") is the biological and physical world: body, drives, sleep and death. The Mitwelt ("with-world") is the world of relationships with others. The Eigenwelt ("own world") is one's relationship with oneself. Modern people, May argued, are alienated in all three. Dasein: being-in-the-world (person and world as one unit) Umwelt world around body, drives, physical nature Mitwelt world with others relationships, community Eigenwelt own world relation to oneself, self-awareness All three modes are lived at once, not in stages Figure 4.14 Dasein is the whole, the unity of person and world; Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt are three sides of it that every person lives simultaneously. Exam trap Dasein and being-in-the-world are existential , not behavioural, cognitive or psychoanalytic. Dasein is the unity of person and environment; Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt are its three modes, so none of them is "the basic unity". The modes are not id, ego and superego, not conscious, preconscious and unconscious (both Section 4.2), and not Piaget's sensorimotor, preoperational and concrete operational stages (Chapter 6). Rollo May: anxiety, the daimonic and love Rollo May (1909 to 1994) brought existential psychology to America. After months in a tuberculosis sanatorium, unsure whether he would live, he wrote The Meaning of Anxiety (1950). For May anxiety is ontological , part of being itself: it arises whenever our existence, or a value we identify with, might be destroyed, and its root is awareness of nonbeing , death but also loss of self in conformity. Normal anxiety is proportionate to the threat, involves no repression and can be faced and used creatively; there is no freedom without it. Neurotic anxiety is disproportionate, involves repression and is handled by blocking off awareness. In Love and Will (1969) May added three ideas. Intentionality is the structure that gives meaning to experience and lets a person decide about the future; it underlies will. The daimonic is any natural function that can take over the whole person, such as sex, anger or the craving for power: directed, it fuels creativity; unintegrated, it destroys. Love takes four forms: sex (biological release), eros (the longing to create and unite), philia (intimate, non-sexual friendship) and agape (selfless concern for another's welfare). In Freedom and Destiny (1981) he argued that freedom has meaning only against destiny , the givens of body, history and death; healthy people accept their destiny and use their freedom within it. Frankl and the existential constructs The Viennese psychiatrist Viktor Emil Frankl (1905 to 1997) survived Auschwitz and observed that prisoners who held on to a reason to live were the likelier to endure. In Man's Search for Meaning (German original 1946) he argued that the primary human motive is neither the will to pleasure (Freud) nor the will to power (Adler) but the will to meaning . Frustrated, it leaves an existential vacuum of emptiness and boredom. If symptoms follow, the result is a noogenic neurosis (Greek noos , mind or spirit), arising from an existential problem such as loss of meaning or a clash of values rather than from conflict between drives; its anxiety is noogenic anxiety. Frankl's therapy, logotherapy, is taught in Chapter 7. Across the existential writers five constructs recur: coming to terms with anxiety; confronting the universal fear of death; accepting freedom and the responsibility it brings; understanding our ultimate isolation, since no one can live or die for us; and facing meaninglessness by creating meaning. Irvin Yalom's four ultimate concerns restate the list for therapy (Chapter 7). Existentialists do not dig for unconscious fears and desires; that is the psychoanalytic aim. Critics find existential writing vague and hard to test. Exam trap Noogenic neurosis and noogenic anxiety are Frankl's and belong to the existential school, not the humanistic, Gestalt (the school of perception in Section 1.2, or Perls's Gestalt therapy in Chapter 7) or psychodynamic school. The theorists of this section ask what he has learned, what he expects and how he reads the situation. The story runs from Skinner, who denied any inner person, through the social learning theorists who put expectation and thought back in, to George Kelly, for whom personality is a way of construing the world. Skinner: personality without a self Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990) gave the most radical answer: personality is only a collection of learned behaviour patterns , each kept alive by its consequences. This is radical behaviourism : thoughts and feelings are behaviour obeying the same laws, and inner causes explain nothing ("he shouts because he is aggressive" is circular, since the only evidence of aggressiveness is the shouting). Skinner distinguished two kinds of behaviour. Respondent behaviour is elicited by a specific stimulus: the knee-jerk to a tap, or salivation to Pavlov's bell after conditioning. Operant behaviour is emitted spontaneously or voluntarily and operates on the environment to change it: the rat presses a lever and food drops, the child cries and a parent comes. Most human behaviour is operant, so a personality is a history of reinforcement. Reinforcement and its schedules are taught in Section 1.6. Shaping (successive approximation) builds a new response by reinforcing closer and closer approximations to it. Superstitious behaviour is behaviour strengthened by accidental reinforcement: pigeons fed every 15 seconds, whatever they did, kept repeating whatever they happened to be doing when food arrived, as a batsman clings to the bat that once scored a century. Self-control , for Skinner, is not willpower but control of the outside variables that control us, by four techniques: stimulus avoidance (studying away from the phone), self-administered satiation (eating sweets until sick of them), aversive stimulation (announcing a diet so that lapses bring ridicule) and self-reinforcement. Walden Two (1948) is his novel of a utopian community run by positive reinforcement; Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971) argued that freedom is an illusion and that cultures should design their contingencies deliberately. The approach is precise, testable and the source of behaviour modification and token economies; critics say it ignores cognition, heredity and inner experience and generalises too freely from rats and pigeons. Exam trap "Behaviour emitted spontaneously or voluntarily that operates on the environment to change it" is operant behaviour (Skinner). The distractors are other theorists' terms: the opposition principle is Jung's (psychic energy arises from conflict between opposites; Section 4.4), behaviour potential is Rotter's (below) and personal dispositions are Allport's individual traits (Section 4.6). Dollard and Miller: Freud in learning terms Earlier, two Yale scholars had married psychoanalysis to learning theory. John Dollard (1900 to 1980) and Neal Elgar Miller (1909 to 2002) restated Freud's clinical insights in the drive-reduction terms of Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952), in Social Learning and Imitation (1941) and Personality and Psychotherapy (1950): the early social learning theory . Learning needs four things ("want something, notice something, do something, get something"): a drive , a strong stimulus that impels action; a cue , which signals when, where and how to respond; a response ; and reinforcement , the drive reduction that strengthens the cue-response link. Their key idea was the learned drive . Fear is learned: Miller's rats, once shocked in a white box, learned to turn a wheel to escape it with no shock present, reinforced by fear reduction alone. Freud then translates easily. Repression is learned not-thinking: a forbidden thought arouses fear, dropping it reduces fear, and the relief reinforces not-thinking. Neurotic conflict is competing approach and avoidance tendencies. Both grow stronger nearer the goal, but the avoidance gradient is steeper, so in an approach-avoidance conflict a person approaches a mixed goal from afar, retreats near it and hovers where the two gradients cross (the other conflict types are in Section 1.10). With Yale colleagues they also proposed the frustration-aggression hypothesis (1939): frustration always leads to some form of aggression, and aggression always presupposes frustration (Chapter 3). Bandura: reciprocal determinism and self-regulation Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) began where Dollard and Miller stopped. With Richard Walters he wrote Social Learning and Personality Development (1963): people learn much of what they do by watching models, without performing the act or being reinforced, which is observational or vicarious learning (its four processes and the Bobo doll studies are in Section 1.6). In Social Foundations of Thought and Action (1986) he renamed the approach social cognitive theory , stressing that thought, not reinforcement alone, guides action. Its organising principle is reciprocal determinism (Figure 4.15): person (cognitive) factors such as beliefs and expectations, behaviour and the environment each influence the other two, in both directions. The master is not the environment (Skinner), the genes (biological theories) or the unconscious (psychodynamic theory). A student who believes she can master statistics (person) joins a study group (behaviour); its praise (environment) lifts her confidence, and she picks harder problems, changing the environment again. Person (P) beliefs, expectations, self-efficacy Behaviour (B) actions, choices Environment (E) models, rewards triadic reciprocal causation (Bandura, 1986) Figure 4.15 Reciprocal determinism. Each pair of factors is joined by arrows running both ways, so no single factor is the master cause. Exam trap Reciprocal determinism is central to social cognitive theory , not psychodynamic, humanistic or biological theory, and it means two-way influence, not control by environment alone or genes alone, nor a denial of social reinforcement. Bandura's constructs are reciprocal determinism and observational (vicarious) learning, not reciprocal inhibition (Joseph Wolpe: a response incompatible with anxiety, such as relaxation, suppresses it; the basis of systematic desensitisation), reciprocal altruism (Robert Trivers: helping those who will help in return) or the invented "reciprocal interpretation" and "reciprocal dualism". Bandura noticed that most behaviour occurs with no external reward or punishment in sight: nobody pays a novelist per page. Most behaviour must therefore stem from self-regulation . People adopt standards, largely from models such as parents and teachers, and run three processes: self-observation (watching their own performance), judgement (comparing it with the standard) and self-response (pride when they meet it, self-criticism when they fall short). Rewarding or punishing oneself this way is self-reinforcement . It is neither negative reinforcement (removal of an unpleasant stimulus, still an external consequence) nor Skinner's behavioural determinism. The machinery can also be switched off: moral disengagement silences self-condemnation during cruelty through moral justification, euphemistic labels, displaced responsibility and dehumanising the victim. Self-efficacy: believing you can At the centre of Bandura's theory sits self-efficacy : a person's belief in his capability to organise and execute the actions needed to achieve a specific goal. Bandura introduced it in 1977 as a unifying theory of behavioural change, a cognitive-behavioural account of how people change in therapy (his concept, not Aaron Beck's, Albert Ellis's or Skinner's). It is the key motivational factor of social cognitive theory, ahead of external rewards, biological drives or goal difficulty (goal-setting theory, Section 1.10): people attempt what they believe they can do, aim higher and persist after failure. Bandura separated two expectations (Figure 4.16). An outcome expectancy is the belief that a behaviour will produce an outcome ("steady revision gets a good rank"); an efficacy expectancy is the belief that one can perform it ("I can revise three hours a day"). Only the second is self-efficacy, and it is task-specific: confident at chess, helpless in a viva. Mastery experience Vicarious experience Verbal persuasion Physiological state Person efficacy beliefs Behaviour Outcome Can I do it? efficacy expectation Will it pay? outcome expectation Figure 4.16 Efficacy versus outcome expectation. The four sources feed only the first, "Can I do it?". Efficacy beliefs come from four sources, the first being the strongest: Performance (enactive) mastery : one's own past successes; early failures weaken efficacy most. Vicarious experience : seeing someone similar succeed ("if she can, so can I"). Verbal persuasion : being told "you can do it", which helps only if realistic. Physiological and emotional states : calm is read as readiness, a pounding heart as inability. Key study: mastering snake phobia (1969) Bandura, Edward Blanchard and B. Ritter treated adults with intense snake phobia by a film of models approaching snakes, by systematic desensitisation, or by participant modelling : watching a live model handle a snake, then being guided, at first in gloves, to touch and hold it. Participant modelling, which gives direct mastery, worked best, removing the phobia in almost everyone. In later studies (1977) clients' efficacy beliefs after treatment predicted how close they would approach a snake, whichever treatment they had received. Critics reply that efficacy ratings may be predictions of behaviour rather than causes. Collective efficacy is a group's shared belief that together it can succeed, as in a cricket team or a village self-help group. Bandura later framed the theory around human agency : people are agents who plan, anticipate, regulate and reflect on themselves, not puppets. Table 4.28 separates self-efficacy from its look-alikes. Four concepts answer: Behaviour potential : "the potentiality of any behaviour occurring in any given situation as calculated in relation to any single reinforcement or set of reinforcements". Expectancy : the subjective probability that the behaviour will bring that reinforcement. Reinforcement value : how much he prefers that reinforcement to others, expectancies being equal. Psychological situation : the situation as the person perceives it, which shapes both expectancy and value. Behaviour potential is a function of expectancy and reinforcement value, BP = f(E & RV), often read as a product: a student who prizes a seat at NIMHANS but believes no study will win it will not study. There is no "punishment value" in the theory. Expectancies carried across many situations are generalised expectancies , which give personality its consistency; the best known are locus of control and interpersonal trust (belief that others' word can be relied on; Interpersonal Trust Scale, 1967). Locus of control is a generalised expectancy about whether one's outcomes are controlled by internal efforts or external forces. A person with an internal locus of control believes outcomes depend on his own effort, ability and preparation, like the student who credits his exam result to his own work. One with an external locus of control credits luck, fate, chance, powerful others or an easy examiner. Rotter's Internal-External (I-E) Scale (1966) has 29 forced-choice pairs, 23 scored and 6 fillers; higher scores mean more externality. Internals, on average, achieve more, seek information, look after their health and cope actively; externals report more anxiety. Warm, consistent parents who praise achievement and encourage independence tend to raise internals. Hanna Levenson (1973) later split it into three separate dimensions: internality , powerful others and chance (her IPC scale). Exam trap Locus of control has two poles, internal and external ; there is no "neutral" or "situational" locus. It concerns external forces versus internal efforts , not cognitive schemas (Beck), genetic predisposition or social status. It is not self-efficacy: locus of control asks "do outcomes depend on what I do?", self-efficacy asks "can I do it?". Attribution theory, with its own locus dimension, is in Section 1.10. Mischel's cognitive-affective personality system Walter Mischel (1930 to 2018) is known for the person-situation critique of trait theory (Section 4.7): people behave less consistently across situations than traits predict. His positive answer, with Yuichi Shoda , was the cognitive-affective personality system (CAPS, 1995), a stable network of five kinds of units: encodings (how one construes self, others and situations), expectancies and beliefs , affects , goals and values , and competencies and self-regulatory plans . Different situations activate different units, so what is stable is not an average level of behaviour but a behavioural signature of if-then relations: Ravi is aggressive if teased by classmates and meek if scolded by a teacher, every time. His delay of gratification research shows self-regulatory competencies at work (the marshmallow test is in Chapter 6). Kelly: the person as scientist George Alexander Kelly (1905 to 1967) set out the most purely cognitive theory in The Psychology of Personal Constructs (1955). Ordinary people, he argued, behave like scientists: they form theories, predict events and revise the theories when predictions fail. The theories are personal constructs , bipolar ways of construing events, such as friendly versus hostile. A construct may be permeable (admitting new events, open to revision) or impermeable (rigid whatever the evidence, as in prejudice). Since no one is trapped in one construal, people can always re-construe their lives: constructive alternativism . The theory has a fundamental postulate , "a person's processes are psychologically channelised by the ways in which he anticipates events", and eleven corollaries (Table 4.29). Since anticipation itself drives behaviour, Kelly needed no separate motivation theory, and he redefined emotions through constructs. Anxiety is recognising that events lie outside the range of one's constructs; threat is awareness of imminent comprehensive change in one's core constructs; fear is the same for an incidental change; guilt is perceiving oneself dislodged from one's core role; hostility is continued effort to extort evidence for a prediction that has already failed. This last section turns from personality seen from outside to the self as people experience it, then to narrow traits and the strengths that positive psychology studies, and ends with India's oldest personality theory, the three gunas, and its bodily cousin, the Ayurvedic doshas. The self: James, Cooley and Mead The modern study of the self begins with William James (1842 to 1910), whose Principles of Psychology (1890) split it in two. The I is the self as knower, the subject doing the thinking; the me is the self as known, everything a person can call his own. James divided the me into three parts. The material self is the body, clothes, family, home and possessions, which is why losing a phone can feel like losing a piece of yourself. The social self is the recognition one gets from others; a person has as many social selves as there are groups whose opinion he cares about. The spiritual self is the inner world of dispositions, conscience and faculties, the most intimate and enduring part. James also gave a formula: self-esteem = success / pretensions . A student who aimed only to pass is content with 55 percent; one who pretended to the first rank is crushed by the second (James's example was a man ashamed to be only the second-best boxer in the world). So self-esteem rises in two ways: succeed more, or lower the pretensions. For Charles Horton Cooley (1864 to 1929), writing in Human Nature and the Social Order (1902), the self is social from the start. His looking-glass self is the self-concept we build by seeing ourselves in other people as in a mirror, in three steps (Figure 4.17): we imagine how we appear to the other person, we imagine that person's judgement of that appearance, and we develop a self-feeling, such as pride or shame, from that imagined judgement. Every step is imagined, so the mirror can distort. 1. I imagine how I appear to you 2. I imagine your judgement of me 3. I feel pride or shame Self-concept: who I am builds next encounter Figure 4.17 Cooley's looking-glass self. Notice that all three steps happen in the imagination: the self is built from what we think others think of us. George Herbert Mead (1863 to 1931), whose lectures appeared after his death as Mind, Self and Society (1934), explained how the mirror gets inside us. With Cooley he founded the tradition later called symbolic interactionism : the self emerges through social interaction and shared symbols, above all language. Mead's "I" is the spontaneous, creative, unpredictable response of the person; his "me" is the organised set of others' attitudes that the person has taken in, the socialised self. The child builds the me by taking roles. In the play stage the child takes the role of one particular other at a time, playing at being mother or policeman. In the game stage , organised games demand holding everyone's role at once: a fielder in cricket must anticipate bowler, batter and captain within shared rules. The organised attitudes of the whole group, and finally of the community, form the generalised other , the standpoint from which the person judges himself. Exam trap Looking-glass self = imagined appearance, imagined judgement, self-feeling. The distractors are other theories: innate, unconscious drives (Freud, Section 4.2); comparing ourselves with similar others (Leon Festinger's social comparison theory, 1954, Chapter 3); resolving psychosocial crises (Erik Erikson, Section 6.10); operant reinforcement of self-statements (Section 4.9); solitary introspection or genetic inheritance (Cooley's self is neither private nor inborn). James's I is the knower, Mead's the spontaneous actor; the generalised other is Mead's. Self-concept, self-esteem and the self-system Two terms that are often blurred need separating. The self-concept is the cognitive description of who one is, the organised set of beliefs about one's own attributes: "I am a Kannadiga, a fast bowler, shy, good at maths." Self-esteem is the evaluative and affective component, how one feels about that self: "and I am worthwhile", or "and I am a failure." Two students may share the self-concept "I am shy", one at peace with it and one ashamed of it. The standard measure of global self-esteem is the ten-item Self-Esteem Scale (1965) of Morris Rosenberg (1922 to 1992), with statements such as "On the whole, I am satisfied with myself" rated from strongly agree to strongly disagree. Nor is self-esteem the same as self-efficacy (Albert Bandura), the belief that one can carry out a specific task such as a statistics problem (Section 4.9), or self-actualisation (Kurt Goldstein's term, made famous by Abraham Maslow), the striving to fulfil one's potential (Section 4.8). The reversed pairing is wrong, the two are not identical, and the individual versus collective self (a self defined by personal traits versus one defined by group memberships) is a different distinction altogether. Limited-domain traits: sensation seeking and explanatory style A limited-domain theory studies one trait in depth rather than the whole person. Marvin Zuckerman (1928 to 2018) defined sensation seeking as the need for varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences, and the willingness to take physical, social, legal and financial risks for them. His Sensation Seeking Scale (SSS; first form 1964, later the 40-item Form V) offers forced choices such as "I would like to try parachute jumping". Factor analysis yielded four components: Thrill and adventure seeking: a desire for speed, danger and defying gravity, as in bungee jumping or scuba diving. Experience seeking: novel experience through travel, music, art or a nonconformist lifestyle. Disinhibition: release through wild parties, drinking and risky sex. Boredom susceptibility: an aversion to routine, repetition and predictable people. Sensation seeking is strongly heritable and belongs within Eysenck's extraversion, with its impulsive form also tied to psychoticism (Section 4.7). It rises in adolescence, falls with age and is higher in men. High sensation seekers have low levels of monoamine oxidase (MAO), the enzyme that breaks down dopamine and the other monoamines, which Zuckerman linked to a strong dopamine-driven approach system. Martin E. P. Seligman (born 1942) reached optimism by way of learned helplessness (Section 1.6), in which dogs given inescapable shock later failed to escape avoidable shock. People, he found, differ in how far helplessness spreads, depending on how they explain bad events to themselves. This habitual way of explaining is the explanatory style , which Learned Optimism (1990) describes by three Ps. Permanence : is the cause lasting ("I will always fail") or temporary ("I was tired that day")? Pervasiveness : does it spoil everything ("I am useless") or one area ("I am weak in statistics")? Personalisation : is it me ("I am stupid") or outside me ("the paper was unusually hard")? The pessimist explains bad events as permanent, pervasive and personal, and good events as temporary, specific and lucky; the optimist does the reverse, and is less prone to depression, illness and giving up. The Attributional Style Questionnaire (ASQ; Christopher Peterson, Seligman and colleagues, 1982) measures it: the respondent names the main cause of imagined good and bad events and rates it as internal, stable and global. Being learned, the style can be retrained. Dispositional optimism and hardiness belong to stress (Section 1.11). Well-being: hedonic and eudaimonic Positive psychology (its founding, flow and PERMA are in Sections 1.2 and 1.10) asks what makes a life go well, and two traditions answer differently. Hedonic well-being equates the good life with pleasure: positive feelings, comfort, enjoyment and satisfaction with life. Ed Diener (1946 to 2021) measured it as subjective well-being (SWB): high life satisfaction, frequent positive affect and infrequent negative affect, with life satisfaction assessed by his Satisfaction With Life Scale (1985). Eudaimonic well-being goes back to Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE), for whom eudaimonia , flourishing, came from living by virtue and realising one's best potential. Here well-being means cultivating personal strengths, meaning and growth and contributing to the greater good, whether or not it feels pleasant at the moment. Carol Ryff (1989) gave it six dimensions of psychological well-being : self-acceptance, personal growth, purpose in life, environmental mastery (managing one's surroundings and demands), autonomy (self-determination and independence from social pressure) and positive relations with others. A holiday of films and good food yields hedonic well-being; one spent teaching village children to read may leave you tired but richer in eudaimonic well-being. The two correlate but are distinct. Exam trap Eudaimonic = cultivating strengths, growth and contribution to the greater good. "Pleasure and relaxation" and "pleasure and happiness" describe hedonic well-being. "Income and material possessions" is a material yardstick that neither tradition accepts as well-being itself. Character strengths, grit and sportsmanship Christopher Peterson (1950 to 2012) and Seligman wrote Character Strengths and Virtues (2004) as a "manual of the sanities", a positive counterpart to the DSM. Surveying moral and religious traditions across the world, they found six virtues valued almost everywhere, each reached through specific character strengths , 24 in all (Table 4.31). These are measured by the VIA Inventory of Strengths (VIA stands for Values in Action); a person's top few are his signature strengths . Key study: Grit (Duckworth and colleagues, 2007) Why do some equally able people achieve more? Duckworth's team gave a Grit Scale to adults, to cadets entering West Point's gruelling first summer and to Scripps National Spelling Bee finalists. Grit predicted educational attainment, which cadets completed the summer and how far spellers advanced, over and above measures of ability. Criticism: a later meta-analysis found grit so close to conscientiousness (Section 4.7) that it may be an old trait under a new name. The same strengths define character in sport. Sportsmanship is playing hard within the rules and with respect for opponents: the true sportsman is persistent (perseverance), keeps self-control under provocation (self-regulation), stays optimistic after a defeat (hope) and plays fair (fairness). Focusing on winning at all costs, by cheating, injuring or gamesmanship, is its opposite: the batter who walks after edging the ball shows character; the bowler who tampers with the ball does not. The triguna theory of personality The triguna theory comes mainly from the Samkhya school, attributed to the sage Kapila , together with the Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14, 17 and 18), with earlier hints in the Upanishads. It does not come from Nyaya (the school of logic), Mimamsa (the school of Vedic ritual) or the materialist Charvaka. Samkhya divides reality into purusha, pure consciousness, the passive witness, and prakriti, primordial nature, from which body and mind evolve (Section 1.2 gives the full scheme, the inner instrument and the koshas). The three gunas (strands or qualities) belong to prakriti, not purusha; the Gita calls them "born of prakriti" (14.5). Because the mind evolves from prakriti, the gunas are the stuff of personality: Sattva is clarity, goodness, light, calm, balance and knowledge; the sattvic person is truthful, self-controlled, content and wise. Rajas is activity, passion, desire and restlessness; the rajasic person is ambitious, driven and attached to results, and tips into over-activity, greed, anger and anxiety. Tamas is inertia, dullness, darkness, lethargy and ignorance; the tamasic person is heavy, careless and confused, sleeps too much and cannot bring himself to act. Every jiva , every embodied individual self, has all three in shifting proportions. None is ever absent; the dominant guna colours the personality (Figure 4.18), and the Gita traces that colouring through daily conduct (Table 4.32). Yama cannot be her problem, alone or with tamas, because it is not a mental state but the first limb of Patanjali's yoga, the ethical restraints; pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses, the fifth limb) and jnana (the path of knowledge) are practices, not afflictions. Exam trap The only gunas are sattva, rajas and tamas. Not gunas: ahimsa (non-violence, the first of the yamas); yama, pratyahara and samadhi (absorption, the eighth limb), all limbs of yoga; jnana (knowledge); samskara (the latent impression a past act leaves on the mind); ahamkara (the I-maker or ego, a product of prakriti); prakriti itself; vata (an Ayurvedic dosha). The gunas belong to prakriti, not to purusha, atman (the true self), Brahman (ultimate reality), ahamkara, samadhi or samskara. Distractor triads: prakriti, purusha and kshetra (the "field", the body that the self knows); atman, Brahman and maya (appearance), the Vedanta triad; karma, dharma and moksha (action, duty and liberation). The gunas have been turned into questionnaires: David Wolf 's Vedic Personality Inventory (VPI, 1998) and Indian instruments such as the Mysore Triguna Scale score sattva, rajas and tamas separately. Such studies tend to link sattva with mental health and life satisfaction, and tamas with depression and poor adjustment. Ayurvedic constitution and Indian typologies Ayurveda, India's classical medicine, adds a bodily typology. One of its foundational texts, the Charaka Samhita of Charaka , describes three doshas (the tridosha ), bodily forces each built from two of the five elements (Table 4.33). Their proportions at conception fix a person's prakriti in the Ayurvedic sense: one's inborn bodily and mental constitution, a second meaning quite different from Samkhya's primordial nature. Ayurveda also describes a mental constitution in terms of the gunas, and calls rajas and tamas the two doshas of the mind. Table 4.33 The three doshas and their Western parallels. Dosha Elements Body Temperament Rough parallel Vata Air and space Thin, light, dry Quick, restless, anxious, creative Ectomorph Pitta Fire and water Medium, muscular, warm Sharp, ambitious, irritable Choleric; mesomorph Kapha Earth and water Heavy, solid Calm, steady, slow Phlegmatic; endomorph The parallels with the four humours of Greek medicine and with William Sheldon's somatotypes (Section 4.1) are real: all three systems tie a bodily fluid or build to a temperament. What are Indian typologies worth as personality science? They are holistic, joining body, diet, routine and mind; the guna model is dimensional, since everyone has all three in varying amounts, which is closer to modern trait thinking than to rigid boxes; and they point to change, since diet, routine, yoga and right action are meant to raise sattva. Their limits are those of all typologies: people get forced into types, the scales rest mostly on self-report with limited validation, what they add to the Big Five is unsettled, and body-temperament links, like Sheldon's, have little experimental support. The Boy on the Vienna Tram, Revisited Return to Allport's tram story with the whole chapter behind you. Freud's question was psychoanalysis in one line: an innocent anecdote read as the surface of hidden conflict (Sections 4.2 and 4.3). Allport's reply became the trait approach: take conscious motives seriously and describe the stable dispositions a person actually shows (Sections 4.6 and 4.7). Adler would have seized on the "generalized inferiority feeling" Allport admitted to (Section 4.4); Rogers would have asked how the young man saw himself (Section 4.8); Bandura and Mischel would have pointed to the situation, an awkward silence in a famous man's study (Section 4.9). The modern answer is interactionism: a neat, orderly young man, in a situation that made him anxious, telling a story that revealed something of both. Chapter summary 4.1 What Personality Is: Definitions, Approaches and Early Type Theories. Personality, from the Latin persona (the actor's mask), is the relatively enduring, distinctive pattern of thought, feeling and behaviour; Allport (1937) called it the dynamic organisation of psychophysical systems. Temperament is its biologically based, early-appearing emotional core; character is personality evaluated; traits are dimensions, types are categories. Theories describe, explain, predict and generate research, and differ on Schultz's six questions about human nature. Personality reflects heredity, environment and the situation in interaction, and is studied by clinical, experimental and correlational methods, nomothetically or idiographically (Windelband). The early type theories, the four humours, physiognomy, Kretschmer's body types and Sheldon's somatotypes , did not survive testing. 4.2 Freud's Psychoanalysis: Instincts, Structure and Psychosexual Stages. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939), a Viennese neurologist, built psychoanalysis from hysteria: Charcot's hypnosis, Bernheim's suggestion and Breuer's Anna O. (catharsis; Studies on Hysteria , 1895). Free association, dream analysis and parapraxes open the unconscious. Instincts (Eros and its libido; the death instinct, 1920) supply energy invested by cathexis. The topographic model divides conscious, preconscious and unconscious; the structural model (1923) sets the id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle, the executive) and superego (conscience and ego-ideal) in conflict, and anxiety (reality, neurotic, moral) signals danger. Fixation at the oral, anal or phallic (Oedipus) stage shapes adult character; latency and the genital stage follow. Research supports unconscious processes, not the stages. 4.3 Defence Mechanisms: How the Ego Protects Itself. Defence mechanisms are the ego's unconscious, reality-distorting strategies against anxiety, described by Sigmund Freud and catalogued by Anna Freud in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936); they are adaptive in moderation, pathological when rigid, and never rational. Repression , the involuntary blocking of threatening material from awareness, is the primary defence; suppression is its conscious, mature counterpart. Displacement changes the target, sublimation the activity, projection the owner, reaction formation the direction and rationalisation the stated reason. George Vaillant (1977) ranked defences as psychotic, immature, neurotic and mature. Obsessive-compulsive disorder favours isolation, undoing and reaction formation; phobias, displacement; hysteria, repression; borderline personality disorder, splitting. 4.4 Jung's Analytical Psychology and Adler's Individual Psychology. Jung and Adler were the first neo-Freudians to break with Freud (Adler in 1911, Jung in 1913). Jung's analytical psychology widened libido into general psychic energy and placed, beneath the personal unconscious and its complexes (detected with the word association test), an inherited collective unconscious of archetypes: persona, shadow, anima, animus and self. His two attitudes and four functions give eight types, the basis of the MBTI, and individuation belongs to midlife. Adler's individual psychology sees behaviour as goal-directed: universal inferiority feelings drive compensation and striving for superiority, shaped by fictional finalism, the style of life, social interest and birth order. 4.5 Horney, Fromm, Sullivan and the Object-Relations Theorists. Karen Horney traced neurosis to basic anxiety , the feeling of being lonely and helpless in a hostile world, managed by ten neurotic needs grouped into moving toward, against and away from people; she added the idealised self, the tyranny of the shoulds and womb envy . Erich Fromm described mechanisms of escape from freedom, five existential needs and character orientations; Harry Stack Sullivan saw personality as recurrent interpersonal situations. Ego psychology (Anna Freud, Hartmann, Erikson) strengthened the ego. Object relations are internalised images of self and others: Klein's splitting and two positions, Winnicott's good-enough mother. Kohut's selfobjects and Lacan's mirror stage complete the section. 4.6 Traits I: Allport, Cattell and the Lexical Search. The trait approach describes personality through stable, consistent dimensions of individual difference, unlike types, states or situationism. The lexical hypothesis led Allport and Odbert (1936) to cull 17,953 trait words from a dictionary. Gordon Allport treated traits as real neuropsychic structures, separated common traits from personal dispositions (cardinal, central, secondary), preferred the idiographic study of single cases ( Letters from Jenny ), and proposed functional autonomy , the proprium and six marks of maturity. Raymond Cattell factor-analysed the lexicon into surface and source traits , described ergs and sentiments, required L-, Q- and T-data, and built the 16PF (1949). 4.7 Traits II: Eysenck, the Big Five and the Biology of Personality. Hans Eysenck joined factor analysis to experiment and biology: a hierarchy from specific responses to types, and three superfactors, extraversion (cortical arousal set by the ARAS), neuroticism (the visceral brain) and psychoticism; crossing E and N gives Galen's four temperaments. Gray, Cloninger, Kagan, and Buss and Plomin extended the biology of temperament. The Big Five (OCEAN) came from lexical and questionnaire research; Costa and McCrae's NEO-PI-R has 240 items and 30 facets. High conscientiousness and low neuroticism predict health. HEXACO adds honesty-humility. Heritability is about 40 to 50 percent, with the non-shared environment mattering most. Mischel (1968) argued that situations often override traits; aggregation and interactionism replied. 4.8 Humanistic and Existential Theories: Rogers, Maslow and May. The humanistic approach stresses free will, an innate tendency to grow toward one's maximum potential, the whole person and conscious experience; disorder is blocked growth, and critics call it vague and blind to culture. Rogers's actualising tendency , organismic valuing process , conditions of worth and incongruence explain how conditional love splits self from experience; the fully functioning person is the ideal, and the Q-sort measures self-ideal congruence. Maslow contrasted D-motivation with metamotivation and described self-actualisers, peak experiences and the Jonah complex . Existentialists (Heidegger, Sartre, Binswanger, May, Frankl) describe Dasein in the Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt, normal and neurotic anxiety, the will to meaning and noogenic neurosis. 4.9 Behavioural, Social-Cognitive and Cognitive Theories. Skinner 's radical behaviourism treats personality as learned operant behaviour (emitted, acting on the environment) with no inner causes. Dollard and Miller (1950) recast Freud in Hull's drive, cue, response and reinforcement: early social learning. Bandura (later social learning, with Walters) proposed reciprocal determinism among person, behaviour and environment, self-regulation and self-efficacy (1977), fed by mastery, vicarious experience, persuasion and arousal. Rotter : behaviour potential = f(expectancy, reinforcement value); internal versus external locus of control (I-E Scale, 1966). Mischel 's CAPS gives if-then signatures. Kelly (1955): the person as scientist, bipolar constructs, the Rep test and fixed-role therapy . Witkin: field dependence; Kagan: reflection-impulsivity. 4.10 The Self, Positive Traits and Indian Approaches to Personality. William James (1890) split the self into the knowing I and the known me (material, social and spiritual selves) and defined self-esteem as success divided by pretensions. Cooley's looking-glass self (1902) builds the self-concept from imagined appearance, imagined judgement and self-feeling; Mead (1934) added the play and game stages and the generalised other. Self-concept is cognitive, self-esteem evaluative (Rosenberg, 1965). Zuckerman's sensation seeking and Seligman's explanatory style are limited-domain traits. Hedonic well-being is pleasure; eudaimonic well-being is strengths, growth and contribution (Ryff's six dimensions).
