Sheldon's theory that people with different body types have different personalities has been: (RML 2020) a supported by research b discredited c shown to be accurate for thin people but not overweight people d shown to be accurate for women but not for men ✓ Answer: (b) discredited Sheldon, body type (somatotype) theory The concept The theory Sheldon claimed that body type predicts temperament. Why it failed He rated physique and temperament himself, so his expectations inflated the correlations. Independent studies found only weak links . Why the other options are wrong (a) supported by research The opposite: independent studies found only weak links once Sheldon's own biased ratings were removed. (c) shown to be accurate for thin people but not overweight people Invented subgroup: the theory holds for no subgroup, thin or overweight. (d) shown to be accurate for women but not for men Cannot be right: his subjects were men, and the theory holds for no subgroup. Physiognomy, an early approach to personality study, was based on : (IHBAS 2025) a Brain localization of functions b Dreams and unconscious motives c Handwriting style analysis d Facial features as indicators of character ✓ Answer: (d) Facial features as indicators of character Physiognomy: reading character from the face The concept What it is Physiognomy treated facial features as outward signs of inner character. Exam tip Match each early method to its clue: face is physiognomy , skull bumps phrenology , handwriting graphology . Why the other options are wrong (a) Brain localization of functions This is phrenology ( Gall ), which read brain localisation from skull bumps, not from the face. (b) Dreams and unconscious motives This belongs to psychoanalysis , which reads dreams as clues to unconscious motives. (c) Handwriting style analysis This is graphology , a separate method. According to Freud, fixation at which stage of development is associated with sarcasm, criticalness, overeating, and nail-biting in adults? (RML 2020) a Oral b Anal c Phallic d Latency ✓ Answer: (a) Oral Freud, psychosexual stages (oral fixation) The concept Two oral types Overeating and nail-biting are oral-incorporative habits. Sarcasm and criticalness are oral-aggressive (biting) traits. Where it comes from Both come from problems of feeding and weaning in the oral stage. Why the other options are wrong (b) Anal Fixation here gives orderliness, stinginess and obstinacy, or messiness and cruelty, not mouth-centred habits. (c) Phallic Fixation here is tied to the Oedipus complex , not to feeding or weaning. (d) Latency Not a fixation point at all, so it cannot explain adult habits. According to Freud, which term refers to the part of the personality that mediates between desires and social rules? (IHBAS 2024) a Id b Superego c Ego d Self ✓ Answer: (c) Ego Freud, structural model (ego) The concept What it is Working on the reality principle , the ego is the executive of the personality. What it balances It mediates between the id 's desires, the superego and reality or social rules. Why the other options are wrong (a) Id Pure desire, run on the pleasure principle ; it wants, it does not mediate. (b) Superego Internalised morality , one of the forces the ego has to balance. (d) Self Not one of Freud's structures (id, ego, superego). In psychoanalytic theory, what term describes the mental representation of psychic energy being invested or attached to a particular object, person, or idea? (Real PYQ 2025) a Libido b Cathexis c Fixation d Sublimation ✓ Answer: (b) Cathexis Freud, psychic energy (cathexis) The concept What it is Cathexis is the investment of psychic energy in an object, person or idea. Key note The energy itself is libido ; cathexis is where that energy gets attached. Why the other options are wrong (a) Libido The energy itself, not its investment in an object. (c) Fixation Libido left stuck at a psychosexual stage . (d) Sublimation Channelling the energy into socially valued activity. A woman harassed by her boss at work, initiates an argument with her husband. She is using which of the following ego's defense mechanisms: (RML 2024) a Projection b Identification c Sublimation d Displacement ✓ Answer: (d) Displacement Freudian defence mechanism: displacement The concept What it is Displacement redirects a feeling from a threatening target onto a safer one. Why this one Her anger at the boss, who could punish her, is redirected onto a safer target, her husband. Why the other options are wrong (a) Projection She would attribute her own anger to someone else, not redirect it. (b) Identification She would take on another's qualities, not redirect anger. (c) Sublimation She would channel the anger into a socially valued activity, not into a fight. Which type of defence mechanism is dissociation? (NIMHANS 2026 recall) a Mature b Immature c Neurotic d Conscious ✓ Answer: (c) Neurotic Vaillant's hierarchy of defences (1977) The concept The hierarchy Vaillant (1977) ranked defences in levels from immature to mature. Level III is the neurotic level. Neurotic defences Level III groups dissociation with intellectualisation, isolation, repression, displacement and reaction formation. Why the other options are wrong (a) Mature The top level (Level IV): sublimation, humour, altruism, suppression; dissociation is not among them. (b) Immature This level holds projection, acting out and the like, not dissociation. (d) Conscious Defences are not conscious as a class; only suppression is deliberate. Which of the following defense mechanisms is not involved in obsessive-compulsive disorder? (IHBAS 2020) a Reaction formation b Repression c Isolation d Undoing ✓ Answer: (b) Repression Freud, defences in obsessional neurosis The concept In OCD In obsessional neurosis the disturbing idea stays conscious ; the defences work on its feeling and meaning instead. Hysteria contrast Repression , which pushes the idea itself out of awareness, is the hallmark of hysteria . Why the other options are wrong (a) Reaction formation Involved: it turns the disturbing idea into its opposite . (c) Isolation Involved: the idea stays conscious but its feeling is isolated from it. (d) Undoing Involved: rituals undo the idea, as if cancelling it. Who believed that the universe of the collective unconscious could be accounted for by evolutionary theory, through the similarity of brain structure evident in all human races? (Amity 2023) a Freud b Jung c Horney d None of these ✓ Answer: (b) Jung Jung, collective unconscious The concept What it is The collective unconscious is Jung 's inherited, universal layer of the psyche. Why evolution He explained it by the same brain structure in all human races. Why the other options are wrong (a) Freud His unconscious was personal , not inherited and universal. (c) Horney She stressed social and cultural forces, not inherited contents. (d) None of these Fails because Jung fits exactly. The basic assumption of Adler's individual psychology is (JEMAS 2025) a human behaviour is purposeful and goal directed. b an optimistic view of human life. c human beings are social beings who could be understood in terms of their relationship with others. d development is a lifelong process and ego identity is granted a central place in the process. ✓ Answer: (a) Human behaviour is purposeful and goal directed Adler, individual psychology (goal-directed behaviour) The concept Basic assumption Adler explained behaviour by future goals that pull us forward, not past causes that push us. Exam tip Optimism and the social emphasis are real features of his view, but the goal-directed assumption is the base. Why the other options are wrong (b) an optimistic view of human life. Optimism is a feature of his view, not its basic assumption. (c) human beings are social beings who could be understood in terms of their relationship with others. The social emphasis is a feature of his view, not its basic assumption. (d) development is a lifelong process and ego identity is granted a central place in the process. This is Erikson 's theory, with ego identity at the centre of lifelong development. According to Adler, middle children tend to be: (RML 2022) a Overachieving b Competitive c Resentful of the freedom of the older child d Filled with feelings of inferiority ✓ Answer: (b) Competitive Adler, birth order The concept The middle child With a pacesetter always ahead, the middle (second) child behaves as if in a race. Result So the typical middle child is ambitious and competitive . Why the other options are wrong (a) Overachieving Not the typical mark: such a child is driven to compete, and may instead give up and underachieve . (c) Resentful of the freedom of the older child Not Adler's picture: the middle child races to catch the older one rather than resenting their freedom. (d) Filled with feelings of inferiority Inferiority feelings are universal in Adler's theory, not the mark of the middle child. Karen Horney emphasized personality development as influenced primarily by (JEMAS 2025) a Social and cultural factors. b Biological instincts exclusively. c Unconscious sexual conflicts exclusively. d Classical conditioning only. ✓ Answer: (a) Social and cultural factors Karen Horney, basic anxiety The concept The break Horney broke with Freud's instinct theory . Basic anxiety Basic anxiety grows from parental indifference and the culture around the child. Why the other options are wrong (b) Biological instincts exclusively. Freud's emphasis, the very instinct theory Horney broke with. (c) Unconscious sexual conflicts exclusively. Also Freud's emphasis, which Horney rejected as the main driver. (d) Classical conditioning only. Conditioning belongs to behaviourism , not psychoanalysis. In paranoia, the ego's defense mechanism as given by Melaine Klein is seen as: (RML 2024) a Reaction formation b Splitting c Suppression d Projection ✓ Answer: (b) Splitting Melanie Klein, paranoid-schizoid position The concept The position Klein 's paranoid-schizoid position rests on splitting good from bad objects. Then projection Projection then puts the bad part outside, but splitting comes first. Why the other options are wrong (a) Reaction formation An unrelated defence that turns an impulse into its opposite. (c) Suppression An unrelated defence: deliberately pushing a thought aside. (d) Projection Freud 's classic mechanism of paranoia; in Klein it follows splitting, which is primary. A client tells you that they are "no one" and feels "empty inside." They report chronic fears of abandonment and have a history of intense, unstable relationships. According to psychoanalytic object relations theory, this pathology of the self is most likely a result of: (Real PYQ 2024) a Fixation at the oral stage of psychosexual development. b A failure in parental mirroring and idealizing, leading to a fragmented self. c Unresolved Oedipal complex and castration anxiety. d Harsh superego demands leading to constant guilt. ✓ Answer: (b) A failure in parental mirroring and idealizing, leading to a fragmented self Kohut, self psychology The concept Whose theory This is Kohut 's self psychology : the child needs parents as selfobjects who mirror and can be idealised. What goes wrong Unmet selfobject needs leave an empty, fragmented self : the client who feels like 'no one'. Why the other options are wrong (a) Fixation at the oral stage of psychosexual development. Oral fixation is a classical Freudian conflict explanation, not a deficit of the self. (c) Unresolved Oedipal complex and castration anxiety. The Oedipus complex is a classical Freudian conflict, not a deficit of the self. (d) Harsh superego demands leading to constant guilt. Superego guilt is a classical Freudian conflict explanation, not a deficit of the self. Cattlell (sic) distinguished between which two types of traits? (JEMAS 2025) a Openness and Conscientiousness b Cardinal and central traits c Surface traits and Source traits d Id and Ego ✓ Answer: (c) Surface traits and source traits Raymond Cattell, factor-analytic trait theory The concept Surface traits Surface traits are clusters of correlated behaviours. Source traits Source traits are the stable underlying factors that factor analysis reveals. Why the other options are wrong (a) Openness and Conscientiousness Two of the Big Five factors, not Cattell's distinction. (b) Cardinal and central traits Allport 's trait levels, not Cattell's. (d) Id and Ego Freud 's personality structures, not traits. Allport believed that traits could be organised into three levels: (RML 2020) a primary, secondary, tertiary b cognitive, emotional, physiological c id, ego, superego d cardinal, central, secondary ✓ Answer: (d) cardinal, central, secondary Allport, trait theory The concept Cardinal A cardinal trait is a ruling passion, found in few people. Central and secondary Central traits are the five to ten that describe a person; secondary traits are minor and inconsistent. Why the other options are wrong (a) primary, secondary, tertiary Invented: there is no primary-secondary-tertiary scheme in Allport. (b) cognitive, emotional, physiological Not a trait scheme at all, and not Allport's levels. (c) id, ego, superego Freud 's structure of the mind (id-ego-superego), not traits. According to Raymond Cattell's classification of personality data sources, which of the following is NOT recognized as a legitimate data type? (Real PYQ 2025) a Q-data (Questionnaire data) b L-data (Life record data) c T-data (Objective test data) d P-data (Projective data) ✓ Answer: (d) P-data Raymond Cattell, L-, Q- and T-data The concept Three sources Cattell used exactly three: L-data (life records), Q-data (questionnaires) and T-data (objective tests). The trap He classed hard-to-fake tasks such as inkblots as T-data, so there is no projective category. His P-technique is a research design, not a data type. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Q-data (Questionnaire data) Legitimate: self-report from questionnaires, one of Cattell's three sources. (b) L-data (Life record data) Legitimate: life records, one of the three sources. (c) T-data (Objective test data) Legitimate: objective, hard-to-fake tests; this is where Cattell put inkblots. Hans Eysenck proposed which three dimension of personality? (JEMAS 2025) a Extraversion-Introversion, Neuroticism-Stability, Psychoticism b Extraversion-Introversion, Sensing-Intuition, Thinking-Feeling c Openness, Extraversion, Judging, Perceiving d Extraversion-Introversion, Neuroticism-Stability, Psychoticism-Conscientiousness ✓ Answer: (a) Extraversion-Introversion, Neuroticism-Stability, Psychoticism Hans Eysenck, PEN model The concept The model These are Eysenck 's PEN superfactors: Psychoticism , Extraversion-Introversion and Neuroticism-Stability. Why the other options are wrong (b) Extraversion-Introversion, Sensing-Intuition, Thinking-Feeling Sensing-intuition and thinking-feeling are Myers-Briggs dichotomies from Jung 's types, not Eysenck's. (c) Openness, Extraversion, Judging, Perceiving Judging and perceiving are Myers-Briggs dichotomies, and openness is a Big Five factor: a mix of other models. (d) Extraversion-Introversion, Neuroticism-Stability, Psychoticism-Conscientiousness Close, but conscientiousness is a Big Five factor, not part of Eysenck's model. Which personality trait is linked to better health outcomes? (JEMAS 2025) a Low Agreeableness and Low Neuroticism b Neuroticism exclusively c Introversion exclusively d High conscientiousness and Low neuroticism ✓ Answer: (d) High conscientiousness and low neuroticism Conscientiousness and health (Terman's sample) The concept Conscientiousness Conscientious people look after their health and lived longer in Terman 's sample. Low neuroticism Low neuroticism means less distress. Why the other options are wrong (a) Low Agreeableness and Low Neuroticism Half wrong: low neuroticism helps, but low agreeableness ( hostility ) predicts heart disease. (b) Neuroticism exclusively The reverse: high neuroticism harms health. (c) Introversion exclusively Introversion alone has no health advantage. Mischel's critique of personality traits mainly emphasized that : (IHBAS 2025) a Situational factors often override traits in determining behavior b Personality is entirely biologically based c Traits are more important than situations in predicting behavior d Traits cannot be measured reliably ✓ Answer: (a) Situational factors often override traits in determining behaviour Mischel, Personality and Assessment (1968) The concept The finding In Personality and Assessment (1968) Mischel found trait-behaviour correlations rarely above about 0.30 . Why this one So situational factors often override traits in determining behaviour. Why the other options are wrong (b) Personality is entirely biologically based He did not claim personality is biological; his point was about situations. (c) Traits are more important than situations in predicting behavior The opposite of his point. (d) Traits cannot be measured reliably Trait questionnaires were reliable ; they simply predicted single acts poorly. In existential psychology, Dasein encompasses three fundamental psychological dimensions of human existence. Which of the following correctly identifies these three modes of being-in-the-world? (Real PYQ 2025) a Id, Ego, and Superego b Umwelt, Mitwelt, and Eigenwelt c Conscious, Preconscious, and Unconscious d Sensorimotor, Preoperational, and Concrete Operational ✓ Answer: (b) Umwelt, Mitwelt, and Eigenwelt Binswanger and May, existential psychology The concept Who Binswanger and May describe three modes of being-in-the-world ( Dasein ). The three worlds Umwelt is the biological and physical world, Mitwelt the world of relationships, Eigenwelt one's relation to oneself. Why the other options are wrong (a) Id, Ego, and Superego Freud 's structural model, not modes of existence. (c) Conscious, Preconscious, and Unconscious Freud's topographic model, running from conscious to unconscious. (d) Sensorimotor, Preoperational, and Concrete Operational Piaget 's stages of cognitive development. Noogenic anxiety is described under: (IHBAS 2020) a Humanistic School b Gestalt school c Existential school d Psychodynamic school ✓ Answer: (c) Existential school Viktor Frankl, noogenic neurosis The concept What it is Viktor Frankl 's noogenic neurosis and anxiety arise from a frustrated will to meaning . Why existential A loss of meaning is an existential problem, not a drive conflict. Why the other options are wrong (a) Humanistic School Humanistic theory explains distress as blocked growth, not frustrated meaning. (b) Gestalt school Gestalt ideas do not explain noogenic anxiety. (d) Psychodynamic school This school traces anxiety to drive conflict , not to a lack of meaning. A split between the organismic valuing process and a self-concept burdened by conditions of worth which results in feelings of tension and confusion: (Amity 2023) a Conflict b Incongruence c Introjection d Actualizing tendency ✓ Answer: (b) Incongruence Carl Rogers, incongruence The concept What it is Incongruence is Rogers 's term for the gap between experience and a self-concept shaped by conditions of worth . How it feels When the organismic valuing process and the self-concept split, the person feels tension and confusion. Why the other options are wrong (a) Conflict A general term, not Rogers's specific concept. (c) Introjection How conditions of worth are taken in, the step before incongruence. (d) Actualizing tendency The growth force that incongruence blocks. Which concept is central to Bandura's Personality Theory? (JEMAS 2025) a Self-efficacy b Inferiority complex c Collective unconscious d Congruence ✓ Answer: (a) Self-efficacy Albert Bandura, social cognitive theory The concept What it is Self-efficacy is the belief that one can organise and execute the actions needed for a specific goal . Why central It is the core of Bandura 's social cognitive theory . Why the other options are wrong (b) Inferiority complex Adler 's concept, not Bandura's. (c) Collective unconscious Jung 's concept, not Bandura's. (d) Congruence Rogers 's concept, not Bandura's. Which of the following best describes the concept of 'reciprocal determinism' as proposed by Albert Bandura? (RML 2025) a Individual behavior is solely controlled by environmental factors. b Cognitive processes influence both behavior and the environment in a bidirectional manner. c Personality develops strictly from genetic inheritance and biological predispositions. d Social reinforcement has no impact on self-concept formation. ✓ Answer: (b) Cognitive processes influence both behavior and the environment in a bidirectional manner. Albert Bandura, reciprocal determinism The concept What it is In reciprocal determinism , person (cognitive) factors, behaviour and environment influence one another in both directions. Why this one Option (b) is the only one that keeps the influence two-way. Why the other options are wrong (a) Individual behavior is solely controlled by environmental factors. Environment alone is Skinner 's position, not Bandura's two-way model. (c) Personality develops strictly from genetic inheritance and biological predispositions. Genes alone is a biological position, not Bandura's. (d) Social reinforcement has no impact on self-concept formation. False: Bandura never denied the role of social reinforcement. Julian Rotter's concept of locus of control describes whether individuals believe that their outcomes are controlled by : (IHBAS 2024) a External forces or internal efforts b Their cognitive schemas c Genetic predisposition d Social status ✓ Answer: (a) External forces or internal efforts Julian Rotter, locus of control The concept What it is Locus of control is a generalised expectancy about what decides one's outcomes. Two ends Internal : outcomes depend on one's own effort. External : they depend on luck, fate, chance and powerful others. Why the other options are wrong (b) Their cognitive schemas These belong to Beck , not to Rotter's construct. (c) Genetic predisposition Genes are not part of the construct. (d) Social status Not part of the construct. The "looking-glass self," a concept introduced by Charles Horton Cooley, posits that our self-concept is primarily formed by: (Real PYQ 2024) a Our innate, unconscious drives. b Comparing ourselves to others who are similar. c Imagining how we appear to others and how they judge us. d Successfully resolving psychosocial crises at each life stage. ✓ Answer: (c) Imagining how we appear to others and how they judge us Charles Horton Cooley, looking-glass self The concept Three steps Cooley 's steps: imagined appearance , imagined judgement , and a self-feeling such as pride or shame. Key idea Others act as a mirror : the self-concept is built from how we imagine they see us. Why the other options are wrong (a) Our innate, unconscious drives. Freud 's idea, not Cooley's. (b) Comparing ourselves to others who are similar. Festinger 's social comparison, not the looking-glass self. (d) Successfully resolving psychosocial crises at each life stage. Erikson 's psychosocial crises, not Cooley's. Which of the following best describes the concept of "self-esteem" in contrast to "self-concept"? (Real PYQ 2024) a Self-esteem is the cognitive appraisal of one's traits, while self-concept is the evaluative and emotional component. b Self-esteem is the evaluative and affective component of the self (how one feels about oneself), while self-concept is the cognitive description of who one is. c Self-esteem and self-concept are identical and can be used interchangeably. d Self-esteem is a collective term for the self in relation to others, while self-concept is the individual self. ✓ Answer: (b) Self-esteem is evaluative and affective; self-concept is the cognitive description of who one is Evaluative versus descriptive self The concept Self-concept Self-concept is the cognitive description of who one is. Self-esteem Self-esteem is the evaluative and affective part: how one feels about oneself. Why the other options are wrong (a) Self-esteem is the cognitive appraisal of one's traits, while self-concept is the evaluative and emotional component. Reverses the two: self-esteem is the evaluative part, self-concept the cognitive part. (c) Self-esteem and self-concept are identical and can be used interchangeably. They are not identical: one describes, the other evaluates. (d) Self-esteem is a collective term for the self in relation to others, while self-concept is the individual self. The individual versus collective self is a different distinction altogether. Bavisha lost her job. Since then she is stressed, has stopped eating properly and cannot get herself to do anything. According to yogic philosophy, the main issue she is dealing with is: (NIMHANS 2026 recall) a Yama alone b Tamas alone c Both yama and tamas d Rajas alone ✓ Answer: (b) Tamas alone Yogic gunas: tamas The concept The gunas Yogic philosophy describes three gunas : sattva, rajas and tamas . Why this one Not eating, withdrawal and the inability to act are the inertia and lethargy of tamas. Why the other options are wrong (a) Yama alone Not a mental state at all but the first limb of Patanjali 's yoga, the ethical restraints. (c) Both yama and tamas Fails because yama is not a mental state, so it cannot be part of her problem. (d) Rajas alone Would show as restless over-activity and agitation, not lethargy. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The id works on the pleasure principle and the ego on the reality principle ; the ego is the executive that mediates between the id's desires, the superego and reality or social rules. asked 7 times The Big Five are Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism (OCEAN); psychoticism, intelligence, intuition, sensing, anxiety (a facet of N) and sense of humour are not Big Five factors. asked 7 times The three gunas are sattva (clarity, calm, balance, knowledge), rajas (activity, passion, desire, restlessness) and tamas (inertia, darkness, lethargy, ignorance); a person sunk in withdrawn inertia who cannot act shows tamas alone. asked 7 times Free association (the fundamental rule: on the couch, say whatever comes to mind) is the central technique of psychoanalysis, and Freudian slips ( parapraxes ), mistakes that reveal the unconscious, are analysed through it. asked 6 times Repression is the primary defence: the involuntary, unconscious blocking of threatening memories, wishes and feelings from awareness. Suppression is its conscious, deliberate counterpart and is mature in Vaillant's scheme. asked 6 times Vaillant (1977) ranked defences in four levels: psychotic (delusional projection, psychotic denial, distortion), immature (projection, schizoid fantasy, hypochondriasis, passive aggression, acting out), neurotic (intellectualisation, isolation, repression, displacement, reaction formation, dissociation) and mature (altruism, anticipation, humour, sublimation, suppression). asked 6 times Displacement redirects feelings from a threatening target to a safer one (the woman harassed by her boss who picks a fight with her husband); it is the classic defence of phobias. asked 6 times Alfred Adler coined the inferiority complex (helplessness, hopelessness, lack of self-worth; from organ inferiority, pampering or neglect) and paired it with the striving for superiority; organ inferiority (1907) is also his. asked 6 times Incestuous fantasies, the Oedipus complex and the emergence of the superego belong to the phallic stage ; the girls' counterpart was named the Electra complex by Jung in 1913. asked 5 times Projection attributes one's own unacceptable thoughts and impulses to others; in its broad sense it is any distorting effect of a person's inner world on his perception of the outer world. asked 5 times Carl Jung 's collective unconscious is the deepest, inherited, universal layer of the psyche, containing the archetypes; with the personal unconscious it forms his two levels of the unconscious. asked 5 times The Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF) was developed by Raymond B. Cattell (1949), who used factor analysis to derive 16 primary source traits; not Eysenck, Allport, Sheldon, Murray or Costa and McCrae. asked 5 times Smoking, drinking (alcohol dependence), overeating, nail-biting, sarcasm and criticalness indicate oral fixation, which arises from problems of feeding and weaning. asked 4 times The id is the wholly unconscious reservoir of unorganised instinctual drives; impulsive and irrational, it alone seeks immediate gratification of primitive needs ("Just do it"), whereas the superego says "Don't do it". asked 4 times Sublimation rechannels sexual or aggressive energy into a socially valued activity such as kickboxing, competitive sport or art; Freud's healthiest defence and mature in Vaillant's scheme. asked 4 times Rationalisation (Ernest Jones, 1908) is a logical, socially acceptable reason invented after the act for behaviour driven by unconscious or unacceptable motives. asked 4 times In Jung's theory the anima is the feminine side of a man and the animus the unconscious masculine side of a woman; the persona is the social mask and the shadow the dark, disowned side. asked 4 times Cattell's three sources of personality data are L-data (life records and observers' ratings, such as school performance and criminal records), Q-data (self-report questionnaires) and T-data (objective tests whose purpose is hidden); P-data and Z-data do not exist. asked 4 times The NEO-PI-R (Costa and McCrae, 1992) is a trait-approach inventory of the Five-Factor Model: 240 items, five domains with six facets each, 30 facets in all. asked 4 times The humanistic perspective (Maslow and Rogers) emphasises free will, personal growth and an innate tendency in everyone to grow toward their maximum potential, not unconscious conflict, conditioned responses or statistical norms. asked 4 times Self-efficacy (Bandura, 1977), a person's belief in his capability to organise and execute the actions needed to achieve a specific goal, is the central concept of Albert Bandura 's social cognitive theory and its key factor in motivation. asked 4 times The basic assumption of Adler's individual psychology is that human behaviour is purposeful and goal-directed; people are motivated primarily by social urges. asked 3 times Jung's two attitudes are extraversion and introversion (thinking, feeling, sensing and intuiting are his functions), and the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator is built directly on his psychological types. asked 3 times Karen Horney held that personality is shaped primarily by social and cultural factors; her basic anxiety is the all-pervading feeling of being lonely and helpless in a hostile world, the foundation of neurosis. asked 3 times Dasein (Heidegger's being-in-the-world, the basic unity of person and environment) is existential; its three modes are the Umwelt (biological and physical world), Mitwelt (relationships with others) and Eigenwelt (relation to oneself). asked 3 times Existential psychology holds that existence precedes essence, so meaning is never fixed; Frankl's noogenic neurosis and anxiety belong to the existential school, and uncovering unconscious fears and desires is psychoanalytic, not existential. asked 3 times Reciprocal determinism (Bandura): person (cognitive) factors, behaviour and environment influence one another in both directions; it is central to social cognitive theory and is not reciprocal inhibition (Wolpe) or reciprocal altruism (Trivers). asked 3 times Julian Rotter 's locus of control (I-E Scale, 1966) is either internal (outcomes depend on one's own effort and preparation) or external (luck, fate, chance, powerful others); there is no neutral or situational locus. asked 3 times Cooley's looking-glass self (1902): we imagine how we appear to others, imagine their judgement, and develop a self-feeling such as pride or shame. asked 3 times The gunas belong to prakriti , not purusha, and come mainly from the Samkhya school (Kapila) with the Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14, 17 and 18). asked 3 times

title: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 5: Physiological Psychology
text: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 5: Physiological Psychology Chapter 5 of the one-volume Final Exam Textbook, all nine JSS subjects in one book. Both A4 PDFs hold the whole book with the same page numbers. A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (975 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (975 pages) Chapter 5 Physiological Psychology In this chapter 5.1 Biopsychology and the Organisation of the Nervous System : Explain behaviour from the biological perspective, name the six divisions of biopsychology, and map the nervous system: central and peripheral, somatic and autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic), the reflex arc, spinal and cranial nerves, and the meninges, cerebrospinal fluid and blood-brain barrier that protect the brain. 5.2 The Brain: Brainstem, Diencephalon and Cerebral Cortex : Name the brain's five developmental divisions and state where the medulla, pons, cerebellum, midbrain, reticular formation, thalamus, hypothalamus, limbic system, basal ganglia, cortical lobes, Brodmann areas and fibre systems lie and what each does. 5.3 Neurons, Neural Conduction, Synapses and Neurotransmitters : Describe the neuron and the glial cells, explain the resting potential, the all-or-none action potential, refractory periods and saltatory conduction, follow synaptic transmission from Ca2+-triggered release to receptor binding and deactivation, and name the main neurotransmitters with their receptors, source nuclei and functions. 5.4 Drugs, Reward and Psychopharmacology : Explain how psychoactive drugs reach and act on the brain, how tolerance, dependence and addiction develop, how the mesolimbic reward pathway and the four dopamine pathways work, and how antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilisers, anxiolytics and drugs for alcohol dependence act and what side effects they cause. 5.5 Research Methods, Behaviour Genetics and the Developing Brain : Choose the right method for studying brain structure, activity or timing, reason through Mendelian and behaviour-genetic designs, identify the main single-gene and chromosomal disorders, and trace how the nervous system develops, prunes itself and stays plastic. 5.6 Sensory Pathways and the Motor System : Trace each sense from receptor to cortex, locate a lesion from the visual field it destroys, and follow a movement down from association cortex through the motor cortex, descending tracts, basal ganglia, In the night before Easter Sunday the pharmacologist Otto Loewi woke with an idea, switched on the light and jotted a few notes on a slip of thin paper. At six in the morning he knew he had written down something important, but he could not read his own scrawl. The question behind it was an old one. Physiologists knew that stimulating the vagus nerve slows the heart, but how does a nerve tell a muscle what to do? Most assumed the message simply crossed as electricity. Loewi had long wondered whether the nerve might instead release a chemical, but he had never found a way to test it. The next night, at three o'clock, the idea came back. This time he got up, went straight to his laboratory and ran the experiment. The design was simple enough to fit on that slip of paper. Loewi kept two frog hearts beating in small chambers of salt solution, the first with its vagus nerve attached. He stimulated the vagus, and the first heart slowed. Then he drew off the fluid that had bathed it and gave it to the second heart, which had been isolated without its nerves. The second heart slowed too. Something had passed from the nerve endings into the fluid, and that something, not an electric current, had carried the message. Loewi called it Vagusstoff , 'vagus substance'. It was later identified as acetylcholine , and in 1936 Loewi shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with the British scientist Henry Dale for discoveries about the chemical transmission of nerve impulses. Loewi's two frog hearts hold this chapter in miniature. A change in what an organ does had a physical cause that could be isolated, carried from one heart to another and named. Physiological psychology studies behaviour in that spirit: through the nerves that carry messages, the cells and chemicals that pass them on, the drugs that interfere with them, and the brain systems behind sensation, movement, emotion, sleep, memory and language. 5.1 Biopsychology and the Organisation of the Nervous System Lower yield · 21 Qs Loewi's second frog heart slowed because a nerve had released a chemical. To see how such simple events add up to fear, memory and speech, you need a point of view that explains behaviour through the body, and a map of the machinery. This section supplies both; the structures inside the brain follow in section 5.2. The biological perspective The biological perspective , also called the neurobiological approach, holds that behaviour and mental processes are produced by the body: the brain and nervous system, hormones and genes. Every psychological event, from a memory to a mood, is assumed to have a physical basis in neural activity, so changing the body with a drug, a lesion or a hormone changes the mind. Three neighbouring approaches (Chapter 1) sharpen the contrast. The psychophysical approach relates the physical intensity of a stimulus to the sensation it produces; the cognitive approach explains behaviour by mental processes such as perceiving, remembering and thinking; the neo-behaviouristic approach explains it by learned stimulus-response connections, with intervening variables such as habit strength inside the organism. The science built on this view, biopsychology, owes its emergence largely to Donald Hebb 's The Organization of Behavior (1949), the first comprehensive theory of how thought and memory could arise from brain activity (section 5.9). Exam trap Asked which system the biological perspective links behaviour to, answer the body : the mind is the cognitive answer, the soul a dualist one and the unconscious the psychodynamic one. Behaviour "governed by the brain and nervous system" names the neurobiological approach. Biopsychology as a neuroscience Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour. For John P. J. Pinel and Steven J. Barnes ( Biopsychology , 11th edition, 2021) it is a neuroscience: biopsychologists bring expertise in behaviour to what neuroanatomy, neurochemistry and neurophysiology discover. Their research falls into six divisions (Table 5.1). Table 5.1 The six divisions of biopsychology (Pinel). In an experiment the researcher assigns subjects to conditions and varies one independent variable, so only an experiment shows cause. A quasi-experimental study compares groups already exposed to a condition in real life, such as heavy drinkers and abstainers, so confounding variables remain. A case study examines one person in depth (Chapter 9). Key study: converging operations and Korsakoff's syndrome Because each method has weaknesses, progress comes from converging operations : aiming several approaches at one problem so that each covers the others' weaknesses. Korsakoff's amnesia (section 5.9) was first blamed on alcohol from quasi-experiments with heavy drinkers; case studies of malnourished people who drank little, and experiments in which thiamine-deficient rats developed similar memory loss, then pointed to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. Behind all this lies the mind-brain problem. René Descartes (1596 to 1650) proposed dualism : the body, brain included, is a machine obeying natural laws, while a nonphysical mind controls it, the two meeting, he suggested, at the pineal gland. Monism holds that only one kind of substance exists; its materialist form, the working view of biopsychology, treats mental events as brain activity. The divisions of the nervous system The nervous system is a system of twos (Figure 5.1). The central nervous system (CNS), the brain and spinal cord, lies inside the skull and spine; the peripheral nervous system (PNS) is all the nerves outside them. The PNS has two divisions. The somatic nervous system deals with the outside world: its afferent nerves carry sensory signals from skin, eyes and ears to the CNS, and its efferent nerves carry commands to the skeletal muscles, which are under voluntary control (afferent arrives, efferent exits). The autonomic nervous system (ANS) regulates the internal environment, controlling smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands largely involuntarily. Exam trap The parts of the ANS are the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. "Central and peripheral" divide the whole nervous system, "voluntary and involuntary" describe somatic versus autonomic, and "cerebrospinal and cortical" is no division at all. The brain and spinal cord form the CNS . The autonomic nervous system Each division of the ANS reaches its targets through two neurons: a preganglionic neuron from the CNS synapses in an autonomic ganglion on a postganglionic neuron that runs to the organ. The sympathetic division mobilises and spends energy. Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945) described its emergency role in 1915 as the fight-or-flight response : the heart races, pupils and airways widen, blood shifts to the muscles and the liver releases glucose. Its preganglionic neurons leave spinal segments T1 to L2, the thoracolumbar outflow ; their short fibres end mostly in the sympathetic chain, a string of ganglia beside the spine, from which long postganglionic fibres run to the organs. Acetylcholine is the transmitter at the ganglia, noradrenaline (norepinephrine) at most targets. Some preganglionic fibres go straight to the adrenal medulla, the core of the adrenal gland, which acts like a sympathetic ganglion and releases adrenaline (epinephrine) and some noradrenaline into the blood. This sympathetic adrenal-medullary system is the fast arm of the stress response. The parasympathetic division serves rest and digest: it slows the heart, narrows the pupils and promotes digestion, conserving and storing energy. Its preganglionic neurons leave the brainstem in cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and the spinal cord at S2 to S4, the craniosacral outflow . Their long fibres end in ganglia near or inside the organ, and both synapses use acetylcholine. The vagus nerve (X) carries most of these fibres, supplying the heart, lungs and most of the gut. Most organs receive both divisions ( dual antagonistic innervation ), so your heart rate reflects the balance of sympathetic acceleration and vagal braking; sweat glands and most blood vessels are sympathetic only, and in sexual response the two cooperate (Table 5.2). The enteric nervous system , a network of neurons in the gut wall, runs local reflexes of gut movement and secretion on its own. Table 5.2 The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions compared. The enteric system cannot slow the heart or narrow the pupils, and the pituitary-thyroid axis is endocrine, setting metabolic rate rather than the emergency response (section 5.7). Grey matter, white matter and the spinal cord Slice fresh brain or spinal cord and you see two tissues. Grey matter is mainly neuron cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons and synapses, where information is processed. White matter is mainly myelinated axons, the wiring between areas; myelin is a fatty insulating sheath (section 5.3), and its fat makes the tissue white. A cluster of cell bodies is a nucleus in the CNS but a ganglion in the PNS; a bundle of axons is a tract in the CNS but a nerve in the PNS. (The basal ganglia, despite the name, are CNS nuclei.) In the spinal cord (Figure 5.2) a butterfly-shaped core of grey matter, with dorsal and ventral horns, is surrounded by white columns of ascending and descending tracts: the reverse of the cerebral cortex, which is grey outside. Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves attach to the cord: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal. Each joins it by two roots. The dorsal root is purely sensory, its cell bodies sitting just outside the cord in the dorsal root ganglion ; the ventral root is purely motor, its cell bodies lying in the ventral horn. This is the Bell-Magendie law , named after Charles Bell (1774 to 1842), who reported the motor role of the ventral roots in 1811, and François Magendie (1783 to 1855), who demonstrated both halves of the law in 1822. Exam trap White matter is myelinated axons ; cell bodies and unmyelinated axons are grey, and dendrites are never myelinated. Cell bodies in the PNS form ganglia (nuclei in the CNS); tracts and nerves are bundles of axons. Neurons by function and the reflex arc Neurons fall into three functional classes. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry signals from receptors to the CNS. A motor neuron (efferent) carries commands from the brain and spinal cord to muscles and glands. An interneuron (connector or association neuron), by far the commonest kind, lies wholly within the CNS and links the two. Muscles and glands are effectors: targets, not neurons. Together they form the reflex arc of an automatic response. Touch a hot pan and the signal runs: receptor in the skin, afferent neuron through the dorsal root, interneuron in the spinal grey matter, efferent neuron through the ventral root, effector muscle that pulls your hand away (Figure 5.2). The arc closes in the spinal cord, so you withdraw before you feel the pain. This withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic . The knee-jerk, a stretch reflex, is monosynaptic : the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron, with no interneuron. A cell carrying information from the brain to muscles and glands is a motor neuron : "effector cell" names the target and "connector neuron" the interneuron. Three are sensory (I, II, VIII), five are motor (III, IV, VI, XI, XII) and four are mixed (V, VII, IX, X). Protecting the CNS The CNS is encased in bone and wrapped in three meninges : from outside in, the tough dura mater, the web-like arachnoid mater and the thin pia mater, which clings to the brain's surface. Between arachnoid and pia lies the subarachnoid space. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), made by the choroid plexus (networks of capillaries in the ventricles), fills the brain's four ventricles, the central canal of the spinal cord and the subarachnoid space. It flows from the two lateral ventricles, the largest, to the third ventricle, through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth, and out into the subarachnoid space, and is absorbed through the arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses of the dura. CSF cushions the brain, which floats in it. If its flow is blocked, for example at the aqueduct, the ventricles swell and compress the brain: hydrocephalus , treated with a draining shunt. The blood-brain barrier exists because the endothelial cells of brain capillaries are sealed together by tight junctions, supported by the end-feet of astrocytes (star-shaped glial cells). Small fat-soluble molecules such as oxygen, alcohol and nicotine pass; glucose is carried across by active transport; large or water-soluble molecules, many toxins and many drugs are kept out (section 5.4). Weak spots include the area postrema in the floor of the fourth ventricle, which detects poisons in the blood and triggers vomiting. Exam trap The barrier is tight junctions plus astrocyte end-feet : not the pia mater (a meninx), microglia (immune scavengers) or oligodendrocyte myelin (around axons). CSF is made by the choroid plexus and absorbed by the arachnoid granulations, and the ventricles hold CSF, not blood, myelin or "synaptic fluid". Directions and planes Anterior (rostral) means toward the nose, posterior (caudal) toward the tail. Dorsal means toward the back or the top of the head, ventral toward the belly or the bottom of the head; because humans stand upright, this axis bends at the brainstem, so dorsal is up in the brain but back in the spinal cord. Medial means toward the midline, lateral away from it. Ipsilateral means on the same side, contralateral on the opposite side: each hemisphere controls the contralateral hand. A horizontal section is parallel to the ground, a frontal (coronal) section parallel to the face and a sagittal section parallel to the midline; the midsagittal section runs exactly between the hemispheres. Location is everything. This section tours the brain from the bottom up: the plan that names its five divisions, the hindbrain and midbrain that keep you alive and awake, the diencephalon that relays and regulates, and the cortex that perceives, plans and thinks. Five divisions from three swellings The brain's tongue-twisting names come from its development. The embryonic nervous system begins as a fluid-filled neural tube, and three swellings appear at its front end: the forebrain (prosencephalon), midbrain (mesencephalon) and hindbrain (rhombencephalon). Before birth the forebrain divides into the telencephalon and diencephalon , and the hindbrain into the metencephalon and myelencephalon , giving the five divisions of Table 5.4. Exam trap The corpus callosum lies just above the thalamus, so it is often filed under the diencephalon. It is the white matter of the cerebral hemispheres, so it belongs to the telencephalon . The diencephalon is the thalamus and hypothalamus, the mesencephalon the midbrain, the metencephalon the pons and cerebellum. The hindbrain: medulla, pons and cerebellum The medulla oblongata is where the spinal cord widens into the brain. Much of it is tracts: on its front surface two ridges, the pyramids , carry the corticospinal motor tract, which crosses sides at the lower medulla (Section 5.6). It also holds the vital centres : the cardiovascular centre for heart rate and blood pressure, the respiratory centre that generates the rhythm of breathing, and reflex centres for swallowing, coughing, sneezing and vomiting. So medullary damage is the brain injury most likely to kill, and an overdose of alcohol or opioids kills by silencing its respiratory centre. Above it, the pons (Latin "bridge") bulges from the front of the brainstem; its nuclei relay signals from the cortex across to the cerebellum. It also helps set the rhythm of breathing, and its reticular nuclei contribute to arousal, sleep and REM sleep (Section 5.8). Behind the pons sits the cerebellum ("little brain"): about 10 percent of the brain's mass but more than half its neurons. It does not start movements; the primary motor cortex does. It makes them accurate, comparing the intended movement with the actual one and correcting the error. So it coordinates and smooths movement, keeps balance and posture, times rapid sequences and supports motor learning, such as the practised timing of a cricket stroke. Damage produces ataxia : clumsy, uncoordinated movement and a wide, staggering gait, like drunkenness. It does not produce language (Broca's area), store declarative memories (hippocampus and cortex) or regulate emotion (amygdala); its circuitry is in Section 5.6. Exam trap Heartbeat and respiration are modulated by the hindbrain (medulla and pons). The hypothalamus adjusts them for homeostasis but does not pace them; the amygdala is for fear; the cerebellum, though in the hindbrain, does not keep you breathing. Damage most likely to cause death : the medulla, not the pons, cerebellum or reticular formation (whose damage causes coma). The midbrain and the reticular activating system Two words organise the midbrain. The tectum ("roof") is its back surface, with two pairs of bumps: the superior colliculi turn your eyes and head towards a sudden flash (visual orienting), and the inferior colliculi relay hearing (superior for sight, inferior for sound). The tegmentum beneath holds the substantia nigra , whose dopamine neurons feed the basal ganglia and die in Parkinson's disease; the red nucleus , a motor nucleus; the periaqueductal grey , which suppresses pain and mediates opioid analgesia; and the ventral tegmental area , source of the dopamine reward pathway (Section 5.4). On the front, the cerebral peduncles are thick stalks of axons descending from the cortex. Through the core of the whole brainstem, from medulla to midbrain, runs the reticular formation , a net-like web of about 100 small nuclei ( reticulum , "little net"). Its ascending part, the reticular activating system (RAS), projects through the thalamus and directly to the cortex. It regulates arousal, wakefulness, attention and consciousness , filtering stimulation so that a parent sleeps through traffic yet wakes at a baby's cry. Destroy it and the result is coma . Its descending parts help control muscle tone and cardiac and respiratory reflexes. Key study: Moruzzi and Magoun (1949) Giuseppe Moruzzi and Horace Magoun stimulated the reticular formation of sleeping cats electrically. The cats woke, and their EEG changed from the slow, synchronised waves of sleep to the fast, desynchronised pattern of alertness. With brainstem transection and lesion findings, this led them to propose that low reticular activity produces sleep and high activity wakefulness. Later work showed that sleep is also actively generated elsewhere (Section 5.8). Exam trap RAS questions offer its neighbours. Fine motor coordination, balance and posture belong to the cerebellum, emotional memory to the amygdala, episodic memory to the hippocampus, motor planning to premotor and prefrontal cortex, reading comprehension to Wernicke's area and the angular gyrus. The RAS means arousal, wakefulness, attention and consciousness. The diencephalon: thalamus and hypothalamus The thalamus is the large two-lobed structure at the top of the brainstem, one lobe on each side of the third ventricle. It is the brain's relay station : every sense except smell synapses in a thalamic nucleus before reaching cortex. The lateral geniculate nucleus relays vision, the medial geniculate nucleus hearing (lateral for light, medial for music), and the ventral posterior nucleus touch, pain, temperature, body position and taste. Smell goes from the olfactory bulb directly to olfactory cortex. Nor is the thalamus a passive switchboard: each relay nucleus receives feedback from its cortex, and other nuclei relay motor loops (basal ganglia and cerebellum to motor cortex) and association loops (to prefrontal cortex). Just below the front of the thalamus ( hypo , "below") lies the almond-sized hypothalamus , master regulator of homeostasis , the maintenance of a stable internal environment. It controls hunger, thirst, body temperature, the sleep-wake cycle, sexual behaviour, and emotion and aggression, acting through the autonomic nervous system, through motivated behaviour and through the endocrine system. The pituitary gland hangs from its underside, and the hypothalamus directs it, with releasing hormones carried in local blood vessels to the anterior pituitary and axons to the posterior pituitary (Section 5.7). The pituitary is the "master gland", but the hypothalamus is its master: the control centre integrating the endocrine, autonomic and visceral systems. Its nuclei are named here and taught later: the suprachiasmatic nucleus , the circadian clock above the optic chiasm; the lateral and ventromedial areas and arcuate nucleus in feeding (both Section 5.8); the preoptic area in temperature and sexual behaviour; and the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, which make oxytocin and vasopressin (Section 5.7). On its underside sit the two mammillary bodies , part of the limbic memory circuit and damaged in Korsakoff's syndrome (Section 5.9). Behind the thalamus, the epithalamus holds the pineal gland , which secretes melatonin at night. Exam trap "Relays every sense except smell" is the thalamus . "Homeostasis", "master regulator", "controls the pituitary" and "integrates the endocrine, autonomic and visceral systems" are the hypothalamus . The brainstem runs autonomic reflexes without integrating them with hormones; the spinal cord carries messages and simple reflexes; the pineal makes melatonin; the corpus callosum, basal ganglia and hippocampus relay no senses. The limbic system and basal ganglia Beneath the cortex lie two loose groupings. The limbic system is a ring of midline structures circling the thalamus ( limbus , "border"): the hippocampus of the medial temporal lobe (forming new declarative memories and spatial maps), the almond-shaped amygdala in front of it (emotion, especially fear, and emotional memory), the cingulate cortex above the corpus callosum, the fornix (the main limbic tract, arching from hippocampus to mammillary bodies and septum), the septum and the mammillary bodies. Together they serve emotion, motivation and memory (Sections 5.7 and 5.9). The basal ganglia are large nuclei deep in each hemisphere. The tail-like caudate nucleus and the putamen receive cortical input; both look striped, so together they are the striatum . Its output goes to the globus pallidus ("pale globe"). The subthalamic nucleus and the substantia nigra, whose dopamine input to the striatum fails in Parkinson's disease, are functional partners; older texts also counted the amygdala. The basal ganglia select and initiate voluntary movements, build habits and support procedural learning (pathways in Section 5.6). Exam trap "Which is NOT a basal ganglia structure?" The red nucleus , a motor nucleus of the midbrain tegmentum (source of the rubrospinal tract). The caudate and globus pallidus are core members; the subthalamic nucleus belongs to the circuit. The cerebral cortex: layers and landmarks The cerebral cortex ("bark") is a sheet of grey matter a few millimetres thick over the hemispheres, with white matter (myelinated axons) beneath. It is crumpled into ridges, gyri , and grooves, sulci ; the deepest grooves are fissures . The longitudinal fissure separates the hemispheres. The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal lobe, with the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) in front and the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) behind. The lateral fissure (Sylvian fissure) separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. The calcarine sulcus , on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, is lined by primary visual cortex (Figure 5.4). About 90 percent of human cortex is neocortex ("new cortex", or isocortex), the most recently evolved part, with six layers numbered I to VI from the surface. Large pyramidal cells send long axons out of the area; small stellate cells are interneurons. Layer IV receives thalamic input, so it is thick in sensory cortex; layer V holds the large pyramidal output cells projecting to brainstem and spinal cord, so it is thick in motor cortex, where it contains the giant Betz cells . The neocortex is the seat of higher cognitive functions: perception, language, reasoning, planning and voluntary movement. The older allocortex has fewer layers: the hippocampus (three) and olfactory cortex. Everything in front is prefrontal cortex : planning, problem solving, reasoning, working memory, intellectual functioning, personality and social behaviour. In the parietal lobe, posterior parietal cortex integrates touch, vision and body position into a sense of where objects and limbs are. Primary visual cortex is called striate cortex for the white stripe in its layer IV. Cortex is also graded by distance from the senses. Primary sensory cortex receives most of its input directly from a thalamic relay nucleus; secondary sensory cortex mostly from primary cortex of the same sense. Association cortex receives input from more than one sensory system and integrates it; it makes up most of human cortex (prefrontal, posterior parietal, temporal). In 1909 the German neuroanatomist Korbinian Brodmann (1868 to 1918) divided the cortex into numbered areas by cytoarchitecture , the size, density and layering of its cells. Vision and V1 are occipital ; auditory processing is temporal ; motor commands and language production are frontal. Fibre systems: wiring the parts together The white matter comes in three kinds. Commissural fibres cross the midline to connect the hemispheres. The largest commissure is the corpus callosum , an estimated 200 million axons linking the left and right hemispheres; the smaller anterior commissure links the temporal lobes and olfactory regions. Association fibres stay within one hemisphere: short U-fibres join neighbouring gyri, and long bundles such as the arcuate fasciculus link the frontal and temporal lobes (Broca's and Wernicke's areas). Projection fibres connect cortex with lower centres in both directions, from thalamus to cortex and from cortex to brainstem and spinal cord. They funnel through the internal capsule between the thalamus and basal ganglia, so a small stroke there can paralyse the opposite side of the body. Three pairs of cerebellar peduncles link the cerebellum to the brainstem. Cutting the corpus callosum produces the split brain (Section 5.10). Exam trap The corpus callosum connects the left and right hemispheres . The wrong options name other fibre systems: brainstem and cerebellum (cerebellar peduncles), frontal and temporal lobes (arcuate fasciculus), thalamus and cortex (projection fibres). This section follows one message from start to finish: how a neuron is built, how it holds a charge at rest, how that charge flips into an action potential that races down the axon, and how chemicals carry the signal across the synapse. The neuron: the basic unit In the early 1870s the Italian physician Camillo Golgi (1843 to 1926) found that silver chromate stains a few neurons in a slice completely black, showing single cells in silhouette for the first time: the Golgi stain . Golgi held that the nervous system is one continuous net of fused fibres, the reticular theory . The Spanish histologist Santiago Ramón y Cajal (1852 to 1934), using Golgi's own stain, showed that it is built of separate cells that touch but do not fuse: the neuron doctrine . The rivals shared the Nobel Prize in 1906, and Cajal was right. The neuron is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system; a dendrite is only part of one, the brain is an organ made of billions of them, and glial cells support neurons rather than carry their messages. Figure 5.5 shows the parts. The cell body (soma) holds the nucleus and keeps the cell alive. Branching dendrites , studded with tiny dendritic spines , receive most incoming synapses. The cone-shaped axon hillock joins the soma to the axon , the long fibre that carries signals away from the soma; action potentials begin here (strictly, Pinel notes, in the axon initial segment just beyond it). A fatty myelin sheath wraps many axons, broken at intervals by bare gaps, the nodes of Ranvier . The axon ends in fine branches, the telodendria , each tipped by an axon terminal (terminal button) whose synaptic vesicles store and release the transmitter. Dendrites Spines Axon hillock Myelin sheath Node of Ranvier Telodendria Cell body (soma) Axon Axon terminals Figure 5.5 A multipolar neuron. Signals flow from the dendrites and soma, through the hillock and down the myelinated axon, to the terminals, whose vesicles (dots) hold the transmitter. A multipolar neuron (one axon, many dendrites) is by far the commonest type and includes motor neurons. A bipolar neuron has two processes, one at each end, as in the retina. A unipolar neuron has a single process that splits in two, as in most somatosensory neurons. Exam trap Transmitter is released from the axon terminals . The telodendria are the branches leading to them, the axon hillock is where the spike starts, and myelin only insulates. The basic unit is the neuron, not the dendrite, the brain or the glial cell. Glial cells Neurons share the nervous system with glial cells (glia, "glue"). They are not ten times as numerous as neurons, as is often claimed: Pinel puts it at about two glia for every three neurons. Glia do not fire action potentials, but they do far more than hold neurons in place (Table 5.7). Table 5.7 The glial cells. Oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS (brain, spinal cord, basal ganglia) and Schwann cells the PNS; options that swap them are wrong. Astrocytes never conduct action potentials. The resting membrane potential Push a fine electrode into a resting neuron and its inside reads about 70 millivolts more negative than the outside: the resting membrane potential , about -70 mV (range about -60 to -80 mV). The neuron is polarised because ions are unevenly spread: sodium (Na + ) and chloride (Cl - ) ions are concentrated outside, potassium (K + ) ions and negatively charged proteins inside. Two forces act on each ion: the concentration gradient , from crowded to scarce, and electrostatic pressure , as like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Both push Na + inwards, yet little enters, because at rest the membrane is far more permeable to K + than to Na + : K + channels are open, Na + channels closed. K + leaks out until the negative charge inside holds the rest back. The sodium-potassium pump , powered by ATP, exchanges three Na + out for every two K + in , preserving the gradients against the leak. The Nernst equation gives one ion's equilibrium potential; the Goldman equation combines several ions. Key study: Hodgkin and Huxley's squid giant axon (1952) Alan Hodgkin (1914 to 1998) and Andrew Huxley (1917 to 2012) recorded inside the giant axon of the squid, up to 1 mm across. In 1952 they described the action potential as a timed rise in Na + and then K + permeability, in equations that won a Nobel Prize in 1963. Criticism: the large, simple squid axon fits many mammalian neurons only roughly. Exam trap The resting potential is about -70 mV, inside negative: not -40 mV and never positive. It rests on high K + permeability (not equal Na + and K + permeability) plus the pump. Open Na + channels, Ca 2+ influx and Cl - channels are distractors. Postsynaptic potentials and the action potential Transmitter binding nudges a neuron's membrane potential. A depolarisation (say from -70 to -67 mV) makes firing more likely and is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP); a hyperpolarisation (to -72 mV) makes it less likely and is an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP). Both are graded potentials , sized in proportion to the input, and they spread fast but decrementally, fading like ripples on a pond. Whether a neuron fires depends on the sum of thousands of PSPs reaching the axon initial segment, a process called integration . In spatial summation , PSPs arriving together from different synapses add up (an EPSP and an IPSP cancel); in temporal summation , PSPs arriving in quick succession at one synapse add up. If the total reaches the threshold of excitation , about -65 mV in Pinel (many texts say -55 mV), an action potential follows. The action potential (AP, spike) is a massive reversal of the membrane potential lasting about 1 millisecond (Figure 5.6). At threshold, voltage-gated Na + channels open and Na + rushes in, driving the membrane from -70 to about +50 mV . The Na + channels then close and inactivate, while voltage-gated K + channels (the delayed rectifiers) let K + out, repolarising the membrane. They close slowly, so the membrane is briefly hyperpolarised before it returns to rest. +50 0 -70 Membrane potential (mV) 0 1 2 3 4 5 Rising phase (Na+ in) Peak, about +50 mV Repolarisation (K+ out) Hyperpolarisation Threshold, about -65 mV Absolute refractory Relative refractory Time (milliseconds) Figure 5.6 An action potential. A depolarisation that reaches the threshold line fires a full spike; the bars show when no stimulus can fire another (absolute) and when only a stronger one can (relative). Unlike PSPs, action potentials obey the all-or-none law : once threshold is reached, the spike fires at full, constant size whatever the stimulus strength; below threshold, nothing fires. Squeeze a gun's trigger hard or gently and the bullet leaves at the same speed. A strong stimulus is signalled instead by firing more often: intensity is coded by frequency, the rate law . Exam trap Only action potentials obey the all-or-none law. EPSPs and IPSPs are graded, and the resting potential is a steady baseline that does not vary with the stimulus. Stronger stimuli give more spikes, not bigger ones; sub-threshold stimuli give no "miniature" spikes; and the law says nothing about neighbouring neurons firing together or one spike per second. Refractory periods and conduction For about 1 to 2 milliseconds after a spike begins, no stimulus, however strong, can fire another: the absolute refractory period , during which the voltage-gated Na + channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises. In the relative refractory period that follows, K + channels are still open and the membrane is hyperpolarised, so only a stronger than normal stimulus works. Two consequences follow. A spike cannot turn back onto the axon it has just left, so it travels one way, soma to terminals: orthodromic conduction (backward, antidromic travel is seen mainly under artificial stimulation). And firing is capped at about 1,000 spikes per second, intense stimulation refiring the cell as soon as the absolute period ends. In an unmyelinated axon the spike is regenerated at each Na + channel in turn: continuous conduction , which never weakens but is slow, about 1 m per second in thin axons. In a myelinated axon ions can cross only at the nodes of Ranvier, where voltage-gated Na + channels are concentrated, so the spike is regenerated node by node and seems to jump: saltatory conduction (Latin saltare , to leap). The function of myelin is thus to increase conduction speed, up to about 100 m per second in the largest axons (Pinel cites up to 60 m per second for human motor neurons); wider axons are faster too. Multiple sclerosis destroys CNS myelin and slows or blocks conduction (Section 5.11). Exam trap The absolute refractory period reflects inactivated Na + channels , not pump failure, inactivated K + channels or Cl - influx. Myelin speeds conduction; it does not support the neuron, store transmitter or generate spikes. Saltatory conduction needs Na + channels clustered at the nodes, not spread evenly along the axon. How a synapse works A synapse is the junction where one neuron passes its message to another across a narrow gap, the synaptic cleft , in four steps. Synthesis and packaging. Small-molecule transmitters are made and packed into vesicles in the terminal; neuropeptides are made in the soma and carried down the axon on microtubules. Release. The arriving action potential opens voltage-gated Ca 2+ channels ; Ca 2+ entry makes vesicles fuse with the membrane and spill their contents into the cleft: exocytosis . Binding. Transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. Deactivation. Reuptake or an enzyme ends the message ( below ). Most synapses are axodendritic (often onto a spine) or axosomatic . Axoaxonic synapses facilitate or inhibit a single terminal button, and dendrodendritic synapses can often transmit both ways. Most are directed synapses , with release site and receptors side by side. At nondirected synapses , Pinel's string-of-beads synapses, transmitter is released from varicosities , swellings along the axon, and spreads to distant targets; most monoamine neurons work this way. Some neurons are linked by gap junctions , protein channels (connexins) joining their cytoplasm to form electrical synapses, faster than chemical ones. And one button often holds a small-molecule transmitter and a neuropeptide together: coexistence . Exam trap Release is triggered by Ca 2+ influx , not by K + efflux (which repolarises), closure of the pump, or Cl - influx (which makes IPSPs). Varicosities are non-directed synapses that release monoamines . Receptors and deactivation A transmitter acts by binding a receptor , a membrane protein shaped for it, and most transmitters have several receptor subtypes , so one chemical can send different messages to different places. An ionotropic receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel that opens at once (Na + in gives an EPSP; Cl - in or K + out an IPSP), so its effect is fast and brief. A metabotropic receptor is coupled to a G protein, which opens a nearby channel or triggers a second messenger such as cyclic AMP that can alter the cell's metabolism and even its genes; these receptors are more common, and their effects slower, longer lasting and more varied. Small-molecule transmitters bind both kinds, but virtually all neuropeptides bind only metabotropic receptors. Metabotropic receptors on the releasing neuron itself, autoreceptors , sense its own transmitter and cut release when levels are high. Transmitter left in the cleft would jam the line. Reuptake by transporters, the commoner route, returns monoamines and amino acids to the button. In enzymatic degradation an enzyme breaks the transmitter apart: acetylcholine is deactivated solely by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft, and its choline is recycled. Monoamines are degraded by monoamine oxidase (MAO-A: serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine; MAO-B: dopamine and phenylethylamine) and by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). Exam trap Ionotropic receptors bind small transmitters only . The transmitter cleared exclusively by an enzyme is acetylcholine ; dopamine, GABA and glutamate are taken back up. MAO never acts on GABA, glutamate, glycine or acetylcholine. GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the main inhibitory transmitter of the brain: an amino acid, not a hormone, neuropeptide or catecholamine. The nucleus basalis of Meynert in the basal forebrain supplies the cortex with ACh and is depleted in Alzheimer's disease, hence treatment with cholinesterase inhibitors. Curare blocks nicotinic receptors and botulinum toxin blocks ACh release, both paralysing; in myasthenia gravis, antibodies attack muscle nicotinic receptors, causing weakness that worsens with use. Exam trap Inhibitory: GABA (brain) and glycine (spinal cord). Excitatory: glutamate . GABA-A is the ionotropic, ligand-gated Cl - channel (fast IPSPs), not a voltage-gated or excitatory channel; GABA-B is metabotropic. NMDA is ionotropic, needs depolarisation and admits Ca 2+ , not Cl - .
