The section runs from the principles of drug action and addiction, through recreational drugs and the reward circuit they hijack, to the drugs prescribed for schizophrenia, depression, mania and anxiety. Psychoactive drugs and their route to the brain A psychoactive drug is a substance that alters mood, cognition, perception or behaviour by acting on the nervous system; the term does not mean a drug-induced hallucination, a particularly active psychopath or the psychology of physical activity. Drugs are taken in four ways. Oral ingestion is easy and safe but unpredictable, because food in the stomach alters absorption. Injection (subcutaneous, intramuscular or intravenous) is fast, strong and predictable, but an intravenous overdose cannot be recalled. Inhalation through the lung capillaries (tobacco, cannabis, anaesthetics) makes the dose hard to regulate. Absorption through mucous membranes of the nose, mouth or rectum is how snorted cocaine enters. From the blood a drug must cross the blood-brain barrier (Section 5.3), which small, fat-soluble molecules pass most easily. Most drugs are then deactivated by liver enzymes, a process called drug metabolism , whose products usually can no longer penetrate the barrier. Agonists, antagonists and synaptic mechanisms Drugs that facilitate the effects of a particular neurotransmitter are its agonists ; drugs that reduce them are its antagonists . A drug can act at any step in a transmitter's life. Agonists may increase synthesis (L-dopa, the precursor of dopamine), increase release (amphetamine), block reuptake (cocaine, SSRIs), block degradation (MAO inhibitors) or activate receptors (nicotine, morphine). Antagonists may block synthesis, empty the vesicles so the transmitter leaks out and is destroyed (reserpine), block release, or occupy receptors without activating them, as receptor blockers do (chlorpromazine, naloxone). Presynaptic autoreceptors normally slow release, so a drug that blocks them increases release and one that activates them reduces it. An allosteric modulator binds a site on the receptor other than the transmitter's own and changes the receptor's response to the transmitter; benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of the GABA-A receptor. A partial agonist activates a receptor only partly, raising activity when the transmitter is scarce but lowering it when the transmitter is plentiful; buspirone at the serotonin 5-HT1A receptor is an example. Tolerance, withdrawal and addiction Drug tolerance is decreased sensitivity to a drug that develops through exposure to it: a given dose has less effect, or more drug is needed for the same effect. The dose-response curve shifts to the right (Figure 5.7). Metabolic tolerance comes from changes that reduce the amount of drug reaching its sites of action (a heavy drinker's liver clears alcohol faster); functional tolerance comes from changes that reduce the reactivity of those sites, such as fewer receptors, and accounts for most tolerance to psychoactive drugs. Exposure to one drug also brings tolerance to others that act by the same mechanism, called cross tolerance : a heavy drinker needs more of a benzodiazepine or barbiturate, because all three enhance the GABA-A receptor. Tolerance may develop to some effects but not others, and some effects may instead grow with repeated use: drug sensitisation (amphetamine's motor effects in rats). Shift right Before repeated use After repeated use Drug dose (log scale) Size of drug effect Figure 5.7 Tolerance as a rightward shift of the dose-response curve. After repeated use the same dose has less effect, and a larger dose is needed for the same effect. When a drug that has been in the body for days is suddenly removed, a withdrawal syndrome follows whose effects are almost always opposite to the drug's: sleeping pills leave insomnia, alcohol leaves tremor, seizures and delirium tremens. The compensatory neural changes that produced tolerance are now unopposed. Suffering withdrawal on stopping defines physical dependence ; psychological dependence is a compulsive craving for the drug's effects without bodily withdrawal. Neither defines drug addiction : habitual use that continues despite harm to health and social life and despite repeated efforts to stop. Key study: Siegel's heroin overdose rats (1982) Shepard Siegel treated each dose as a Pavlovian conditioning trial: the usual room and paraphernalia become conditioned stimuli that elicit compensatory responses opposite to the drug's effect, so tolerance is strongest where the drug is usually taken ( conditioned drug tolerance ). Siegel and colleagues (1982) made rats tolerant to heroin in one environment, then gave a large dose there or in a novel one. Many more died in the novel environment, where no compensatory responses opposed the drug, which may explain human overdoses in unfamiliar places. Criticism: some drug cues elicit drug-like rather than opposite responses. Exam trap Cross tolerance means exposure to one drug reduces the effect of another acting by the same mechanism; it is not "no addiction to any drug". Withdrawal is usually the opposite of the drug's effect, and physical dependence is not addiction: detoxified users still relapse. Sedative-hypnotics: alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates Sedatives calm and hypnotics induce sleep; both are broad classes covering alcohol, barbiturates, benzodiazepines and newer sleeping pills, not one chemical family. These drugs depress the central nervous system mainly by enhancing GABA, the brain's main inhibitory transmitter, at the GABA-A receptor , a chloride (Cl-) channel whose opening hyperpolarises the neuron. Alcohol is a positive modulator, functionally an agonist, at the GABA-A receptor, and also blocks the NMDA glutamate receptor, so it raises inhibition and lowers excitation. Drinking in pregnancy causes fetal alcohol syndrome (Chapter 6), and the thiamine deficiency of chronic drinkers causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (Section 5.9). The benzodiazepines form one chemical class: diazepam (Valium), alprazolam (Xanax), flunitrazepam (Rohypnol), triazolam (Halcion) and chlordiazepoxide. They are used as anxiolytics, hypnotics and anticonvulsants. The older barbiturates (phenobarbital) bind another site on the same receptor. As Figure 5.8 shows, a benzodiazepine increases the frequency of Cl- channel opening and works only when GABA is present, so its effect has a ceiling; a barbiturate increases the duration of each opening and at high doses opens the channel by itself. Hence barbiturates, and benzodiazepines taken with alcohol, are dangerous in overdose, whereas a benzodiazepine overdose alone is rarely fatal and is reversed by the antagonist flumazenil . Withdrawal from any of these drugs is rebound excitation (anxiety, insomnia, tremor, seizures) and can kill. Benzodiazepines make the channel open more often; barbiturates keep each opening longer. Exam trap Frequency goes with benzodiazepines and duration with barbiturates, never the reverse. Both act on GABA-A, not GABA-B or NMDA receptors, and the receptor benzodiazepines modulate binds GABA, not glutamate, acetylcholine or glycine (the spinal cord's inhibitory transmitter). Valium, Xanax, Rohypnol and Halcion are all benzodiazepines; "sedatives" and "hypnotics" are too broad. Opioids, stimulants, cannabis and hallucinogens Opium is the dried sap of the opium poppy's seed pods; its natural alkaloids are morphine, codeine, thebaine and papaverine. Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is not one of them: it is made by adding two acetyl groups to morphine, a semisynthetic opioid that enters the brain faster. Methadone and fentanyl are fully synthetic. Opioids act mainly at mu opioid receptors , the receptors for the body's endorphins (Section 5.3): they relieve pain, cough and diarrhoea, bring euphoria, and in overdose suppress breathing. Naloxone (short acting, the emergency reversal of overdose) and naltrexone (long acting, oral) are opioid antagonists. Opioid withdrawal mirrors the drug: dilated pupils, runny nose, sweating, gooseflesh and diarrhoea; miserable but rarely fatal. Table 5.10 covers the other classes. Reward circuits and theories of addiction Key study: Olds and Milner's 'pleasure centre' (1954) In 1954, at McGill University, James Olds and Peter Milner let rats press a lever that delivered brief electrical stimulation through an electrode in their own brains. With electrodes in the septal area and along the medial forebrain bundle , rats pressed thousands of times an hour, ignoring food, until exhausted. This intracranial self-stimulation seemed to reveal sites that mediate the pleasure of food, water and sex: 'pleasure centres'. Later work found no single centre; self-stimulation depends largely on dopamine axons running in the medial forebrain bundle. Those axons form the mesolimbic pathway , from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) of the midbrain to the nucleus accumbens in the ventral striatum and other limbic sites. It is the core reward pathway of addiction: natural rewards and almost every addictive drug raise dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, directly (cocaine, amphetamine) or indirectly (opioids, alcohol, nicotine), and dopamine antagonists reduce self-stimulation. The reward transmitter is dopamine, not serotonin, noradrenaline or acetylcholine. With chronic use, control of drug taking shifts to the dorsal striatum (habit), and weakened prefrontal control makes stopping harder. Physical-dependence theories said addicts take drugs to escape withdrawal, but detoxified users relapse months later, and cocaine causes little withdrawal distress. Positive-incentive theories replaced them: people take drugs for their anticipated pleasure. Yet addicts often crave a drug they no longer enjoy. The incentive-sensitisation theory of Terry Robinson and Kent Berridge (1993) explains this: in addiction-prone people repeated use sensitises the drug's incentive value ('wanting') while tolerance develops to its pleasure ('liking'). Mesolimbic dopamine signals wanting more than liking. Exam trap The reward pathway is mesolimbic (VTA to nucleus accumbens), not nigrostriatal (movement), tuberoinfundibular (prolactin) or the raphe serotonergic pathway. Olds and Milner's sites were the septal area and medial forebrain bundle , not the cerebellar tonsils, the lateral geniculate nucleus (a visual relay) or the globus pallidus (a motor nucleus). The cerebellar vermis and vestibular nuclei serve balance, not addiction. Antipsychotics (neuroleptics) are the front-line treatment for schizophrenia; CBT, stress management and social skills training are adjuncts (Chapter 7), and neuroleptics are not mainly for depression or anxiety. Akathisia is subjective inner restlessness with an urge to pace; tardive dyskinesia comes last and may be irreversible; neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare emergency. Drug-induced conditions such as akathisia are secondary movement disorders , with an identifiable external cause; Huntington's chorea (inherited) and Parkinson's disease are primary. This section surveys those methods, then asks how genes are inherited and studied, which genetic errors derail development, and how the brain builds and keeps rewiring itself. Imaging the living brain Ordinary X-rays show little of the soft brain, so contrast X-ray techniques inject a substance that absorbs X-rays differently: in cerebral angiography a radio-opaque dye in a cerebral artery outlines the blood vessels, revealing vascular damage and, by displaced vessels, tumours. Computed tomography (CT), introduced in the early 1970s by Godfrey Hounsfield , passes X-rays through the head from many angles and computes horizontal slices. It is fast and shows fresh blood, so it is the first scan after acute head injury. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves: hydrogen atoms then emit signals that differ between structures. With the highest spatial resolution (precision about where), MRI gives the most detailed view of brain structure. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), an MRI method, follows water diffusing along axons to map the white matter tracts. CT and plain MRI are structural; functional imaging shows activity. Positron emission tomography (PET) injects a radioactive tracer such as 2-deoxyglucose (FDG in human PET), which active neurons absorb like glucose but cannot metabolise, so the scan maps metabolic activity. Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) maps blood flow with a gamma-emitting tracer, more cheaply but less sharply. Functional MRI (fMRI) needs no injection: it detects the BOLD signal (blood-oxygen-level-dependent; Seiji Ogawa , 1990), which rises as active regions draw oxygenated blood. Its spatial resolution is good but its temporal resolution (precision about when) only moderate, because blood flow takes seconds to respond. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measures cortical oxygenation with light shone through the scalp; it is portable and suits infants. Table 5.14 compares the methods. Subtraction revealed regions more active in the resting baseline than during tasks: the default mode network (DMN), after the "default mode" of brain function described by Marcus Raichle and colleagues in 2001. Its hubs are the medial prefrontal cortex, the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and the lateral parietal cortex. It is most active at rest, during mind-wandering and self-referential thought, deactivates during externally focused, goal-directed tasks (moving, seeing, calculating), and is altered in depression, Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia. Exam trap The functional techniques are PET and SPECT (and fMRI), not CT or plain MRI, so "all of the above" is wrong. For brain structure after head injury choose MRI ; CT is the quick emergency scan for bleeding. EEG, PET and fMRI record activity, not structure. Recording electrical activity Imaging shows where; electrical recording shows when. The electroencephalogram (EEG), first reported in humans by Hans Berger in 1929, records through scalp electrodes the summed electrical activity of cortical neurons. The brain's counterpart of the electrocardiogram (ECG), it has the highest temporal resolution, in milliseconds, but poor spatial resolution, and it is the standard test for epilepsy and sleep (wave bands in Section 5.8). Magnetoencephalography (MEG) records the magnetic fields of the same currents: as fast, better at localising, far costlier. In animals, a microelectrode records one neuron's action potentials ( single-unit recording ) or a larger electrode the firing of many neighbours ( multiple-unit recording ). The response to a single click is lost in the background EEG, so the EEG after hundreds of clicks is averaged ( signal averaging ): random activity cancels and the time-locked event-related potential (ERP) remains, named by polarity (P or N) and latency in milliseconds. In the oddball paradigm , a rare target among frequent standard stimuli evokes a large positive wave about 300 ms later, the P300 , first described by Samuel Sutton and colleagues in 1965. Skin conductance (electrodermal activity, the galvanic skin response ) rises as sympathetic arousal activates the sweat glands. Heart rate and blood pressure are other autonomic indices; the polygraph records several at once and, as a "lie detector", detects arousal, not lies. Lesions, stimulation and genetic tools Invasive methods, used mostly in animals, begin with stereotaxic surgery : a stereotaxic atlas gives each structure's coordinates, and a stereotaxic instrument holds the head and guides an electrode or cannula to them. A lesion destroys tissue to reveal its function by what is lost: aspiration sucks away cortex, radio-frequency current heats small subcortical areas, knife cuts sever tracts, and cryogenic blockade (cooling) makes a reversible lesion. Neurotoxins are selective: kainic acid kills cell bodies but spares passing axons, and 6-hydroxydopamine destroys dopamine and noradrenaline neurons. Bilateral lesions usually have far larger effects than unilateral ones. Conversely, electrical stimulation or chemical stimulation (a microinjected transmitter or agonist) can evoke behaviour. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) applies continuous current through implanted electrodes, chiefly in Parkinson's disease. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) induces current in the cortex from a coil on the scalp, a non-invasive "virtual lesion"; repeated TMS treats depression. Optogenetics inserts genes for light-sensitive ion channels into one type of neuron, so light switches those neurons on or off. Microdialysis samples extracellular fluid in behaving animals to measure transmitter release. In humans, neuropsychological tests (Chapter 2) also map damage. Genetic methods alter genes. A gene knockout mouse lacks a working gene; a knock-in replaces or adds one; a transgenic animal carries another species' gene, such as a human disease gene. CRISPR-Cas9 , developed by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier in 2012 (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2020), uses a guide RNA to lead the Cas9 protein to a chosen DNA sequence, where it edits the gene or switches it on or off. Other tools do not edit: the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of Kary Mullis copies DNA millions of times, gel electrophoresis separates DNA or proteins by size, and Western blotting detects a particular protein. Mendel, chromosomes and epigenetics Gregor Mendel (1822 to 1884), a monk who crossed pea plants and published in 1866, found that each trait depends on a pair of inherited factors, now called genes , one from each parent. The alternative forms of a gene are alleles : two alike make an organism homozygous (DD or dd), two different heterozygous (Dd). The genotype is the alleles carried, the phenotype the trait shown. A dominant allele is expressed even in a heterozygote; a recessive trait appears only in the homozygote, as the Punnett square in Figure 5.9 shows. Blending occurs only in incomplete dominance (red and white snapdragons give pink) and codominance (blood group AB shows both), so with a stated dominant allele "blue-green" is wrong. Every Dd child has blue eyes. (The alleles are hypothetical.) Genes lie on chromosomes , strands of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) whose base sequence codes for proteins. Human cells have 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and the sex chromosomes , XX in females and XY in males. Meiosis makes eggs and sperm with 23 single chromosomes, and crossing over (paired chromosomes swapping segments) makes each one unique. A mutation is an accidental change in a gene. X-linked recessive sex-linked traits , such as red-green colour blindness, are commoner in males, who have no second X to mask them. Epigenetics studies changes in gene expression without any change in the DNA sequence: DNA methylation usually silences genes, and histone modification loosens or tightens the packaging of DNA, making genes more or less readable. Experience, such as early stress or maternal care, alters these marks. Separating heredity and environment Family studies ask whether risk rises with closeness of kinship, but relatives share homes as well as genes. Twin studies compare monozygotic twins (MZ), from one fertilised egg that splits, who have the same heredity and share virtually all their genes, with dizygotic twins (DZ), who share about 50 percent like other siblings. The concordance rate is the percentage of pairs in which, when one twin has a disorder, the other has it too: for schizophrenia, about 48 percent in MZ and 17 percent in DZ twins in the pooled data of Irving Gottesman (1991). Adoption studies ask whether adoptees resemble their biological parents (genes) or adoptive parents (environment). Key study: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart From 1979, Thomas Bouchard and colleagues (main report in Science , 1990) gave adult MZ and DZ twins separated in infancy about 50 hours of intelligence and personality tests. MZ twins reared apart were about as alike as those reared together, and more alike than DZ twins, on almost every measure. Critics note that adoptive homes vary less than homes in general. Exam trap Twins reared apart combine twin and adoption logic (Pinel even calls the Minnesota study an adoption study), but the keyed answer is twin studies , because comparing MZ with DZ pairs defines the design. Choose adoption studies only if twin studies is not offered. Linkage studies trace a DNA marker inherited along with a disorder through affected families, locating the gene nearby. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) compare hundreds of thousands of variants across the genome in thousands of patients and controls, usually finding many genes of tiny effect. Heritability is the proportion of variation in a trait, in a given population and environment, due to genetic differences; it describes populations, not individuals, and changes when environments change. Diagnoses are too broad to map onto genes, so Gottesman and Todd Gould (2003) popularised the endophenotype : a measurable, heritable intermediate trait between genes and symptoms, through which genetic risk produces a disorder. P50 gating, P300 and smooth-pursuit eye-tracking deficits in schizophrenia are examples, also found in unaffected relatives. By contrast, the phenotype is the observable symptoms, the genotype the genes, and molecular genetics the study of DNA itself. The diathesis-stress model is taught in Chapter 8. Single-gene and chromosomal disorders Phenylketonuria (PKU), discovered in 1934 by the Norwegian Ivar Asbjørn Følling , is an autosomal recessive lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase , the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine . Phenylalanine accumulates and damages the developing brain, but newborn screening and a low-phenylalanine diet prevent the intellectual disability. In a trinucleotide repeat disorder a three-base sequence is repeated too often; in genomic imprinting a gene is expressed only from one parent's copy, so one deletion causes different syndromes depending on its parent of origin (Table 5.16). Building the nervous system After fertilisation the zygote divides into a solid ball (the morula ) and then a hollow ball that implants (the blastocyst ); these stages (Chapter 6) contain no nervous tissue. The nervous system begins at gastrulation , in the third week, when the embryo forms three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Induced by the mesoderm beneath, a patch of ectoderm becomes the neural plate , which folds into the neural groove, whose lips fuse into the neural tube , forerunner of the brain and spinal cord. Failures of this neurulation cause spina bifida (tail end) and anencephaly (head end). Development then proceeds in phases: proliferation in the ventricular zone lining the tube, migration of young neurons along radial glial cells , aggregation into structures, and axon growth led by growth cones . Roger Sperry , who rotated frogs' eyes and found that regenerating optic axons regrew to their original targets, proposed the chemoaffinity hypothesis (1963): each target releases a chemical label that attracts its axon. After synapses form, far more neurons exist than survive; in apoptosis (programmed cell death) those that fail to obtain neurotrophins from their targets die. Rita Levi-Montalcini discovered the first, nerve growth factor (Nobel Prize 1986). In synapse rearrangement , surviving axons take over the vacated sites. Exam trap The nervous system begins forming at the gastrula stage. Zygote, morula and blastocyst come earlier. Pruning, myelination and lifelong plasticity The young brain overproduces synapses; childhood synaptic density far exceeds the adult level. Synaptic pruning (neural pruning) then eliminates unused connections and keeps those in use: "use it or lose it". It is heaviest in childhood and continues in the prefrontal cortex through adolescence, partly carried out by microglia , which engulf unwanted synapses. Myelination also continues into early adulthood, the prefrontal cortex last, one reason judgement and impulse control mature late. Exam trap Pruning is the elimination of unused connections , a process of neuronal development and plasticity. It is not memory consolidation, not long-term potentiation or any strengthening of pathways (both Section 5.9), not neurotransmitter release (Section 5.3), not the growth of new neurons and not an increase in brain size. Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change its structure and function throughout life with experience, learning and injury; it is not a protective coating (skull, meninges or myelin), memory loss or cell death. In the 1960s Mark Rosenzweig and colleagues found that rats reared in enriched environments developed a thicker, heavier cortex than rats in barren cages. Plasticity peaks in critical periods : when David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel sewed one eye of a young kitten shut ( monocular deprivation ), the visual cortex permanently lost its responses to that eye, whereas adult cats were barely affected. Adults still make new neurons ( adult neurogenesis ) in the hippocampal dentate gyrus and, in rodents, the olfactory bulb; Peter Eriksson and colleagues confirmed it in the human hippocampus in 1998. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) supports synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival (it prevents apoptosis) and hippocampal neurogenesis, not action potential firing (Section 5.3) or myelin synthesis. This section follows their signals into the brain, then traces motor commands back out to the muscles. Principles of sensory systems Every sensory system begins with transduction , the conversion of physical energy into neural signals by receptors. A neuron's receptive field is the area of the sensory surface (a patch of retina or skin) in which a stimulus changes its firing. The systems are hierarchical: receptors, thalamic relay nuclei, primary sensory cortex (input mainly from the thalamus), secondary sensory cortex (input mainly from primary cortex of the same sense) and association cortex (input from several senses). Each level contains areas with different jobs ( functional segregation ), and information flows along several routes at once ( parallel processing ). Refractive errors The cornea and lens must focus the image on the retina; their failures are refractive errors , optical rather than neural faults. In myopia (near-sightedness) distant objects blur because the eyeball is too long, so their image focuses in front of the retina; a concave lens corrects it. In hypermetropia (far-sightedness) a short eyeball focuses near objects behind the retina; a convex lens corrects it. Astigmatism is an irregularly curved cornea that blurs some orientations, and presbyopia the stiffening of the ageing lens that brings reading glasses after about 40. Visual field defects, by contrast, are blind areas left by pathway damage ( 5.6.4 ). Retinal circuits and lateral inhibition The retina is built inside out (the inverted retina ): light passes the ganglion, amacrine, bipolar and horizontal cells, in that order, before reaching the rods and cones at the back. Signals return along the through pathway , receptors to bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve, while horizontal and amacrine cells carry signals sideways. Where the axons leave, at the optic disc, there are no receptors: the blind spot, filled in by completion . Stephen Kuffler (1953) found that cat ganglion cells have circular receptive fields with an opposing centre and surround: an on-centre cell fires to light on its centre and is inhibited by light on its surround, and an off-centre cell does the reverse. Such cells signal contrast, not even illumination. The mechanism is lateral inhibition , the suppression of a neuron by its active neighbours, analysed by Haldan Keffer Hartline in the eye of the horseshoe crab Limulus (Nobel Prize 1967). At a light-dark border, a receptor just on the bright side has dark neighbours, receives less inhibition and signals "brighter still"; one just on the dark side receives extra inhibition and signals "darker still". The result is the illusory bright and dark strips called Mach bands ( Ernst Mach , 1865). Exam trap Mach bands come from lateral inhibition, not the rod-cone dichotomy (dim-light versus colour vision), the opponent process (colour afterimages) or temporal summation (adding weak signals over time). From retina to striate cortex At the optic chiasm , fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross; temporal fibres do not. Because nasal hemiretinas see the outer visual fields, the left visual field reaches the right hemisphere . Each optic tract ends in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus, the visual relay (hearing uses the medial geniculate nucleus, touch the ventral posterior nucleus, and smell no thalamic relay). The LGN has six layers. Layers 1 and 2 are magnocellular : large, fast, colour-blind cells with large receptive fields, for motion, contrast and depth. Layers 3 to 6 are parvocellular : small, slower cells for colour and fine detail. Koniocellular cells lie between the layers. Optic radiations carry the output to the primary visual cortex (V1, striate cortex, area 17) around the calcarine fissure. V1 is retinotopic , and the tiny fovea claims about a quarter of it. Field loss therefore locates damage (Figure 5.10). An optic nerve lesion blinds one eye. A pituitary tumour pressing on the chiasm cuts the crossing fibres: bitemporal hemianopia . Damage behind the chiasm (tract, radiations or V1) causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia , the same opposite half-field lost in both eyes. A posterior cerebral artery stroke of V1 often spares central vision ( macular sparing ), because the occipital pole also draws blood from the middle cerebral artery. A small V1 lesion leaves a scotoma , an island of blindness often hidden by completion; in blindsight , studied by Lawrence Weiskrantz in the patient D.B. (1974), people point accurately at stimuli in the scotoma that they deny seeing. Visual cortex and the two streams In V1, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel (Nobel Prize 1981; Section 1.4) found simple cells , responding to a line of one orientation in one exact position, and complex cells , responding to that orientation anywhere in a larger field, often only when it moves. V2 (area 18) elaborates contours and feeds specialised areas: V4 for colour (damage causes cerebral achromatopsia , a grey world) and V5, or MT, for motion (damage causes akinetopsia , movement seen as still frames). Leslie Ungerleider and Mortimer Mishkin (1982) grouped these areas into two streams leaving V1. The dorsal stream runs to the posterior parietal cortex: "where" things are. The ventral stream runs to the inferotemporal cortex: "what" they are, faces included (the fusiform face area, Section 5.11). Melvyn Goodale and David Milner (1992) recast the dorsal stream as "how", vision for guiding action such as grasping, and the ventral stream as vision for conscious perception. Exam trap The streams are not colour against motion (motion is dorsal) or hearing against vision, and they diverge from V1 rather than converging on it. Hearing, touch, pain, smell and taste The hair cells of the organ of Corti transduce mechanically: basilar membrane movement bends their stereocilia, opening cation channels through which potassium from the endolymph flows in and depolarises the cell. Inner hair cells supply almost all auditory nerve signals; outer hair cells amplify the vibration. The pathway runs from the cochlear nuclei to the superior olives on both sides, where the two ears' signals first meet and are compared to locate sounds, then to the inferior colliculi, the medial geniculate nucleus and the primary auditory cortex in Heschl's gyrus (areas 41 and 42), which is tonotopic (each frequency has its own place). Conductive deafness arises in the outer or middle ear, sensorineural deafness in the hair cells or auditory nerve. The anterolateral system (spinothalamic tract and others) carries nociceptive pain and temperature; it crosses in the spinal cord near the level of entry. Both relay in the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus to primary somatosensory cortex (SI; postcentral gyrus, areas 3, 1 and 2). Wilder Penfield and Theodore Rasmussen (1950) mapped its somatosensory homunculus by stimulating patients' cortex during surgery: the hands, lips and tongue, used for fine discrimination, have the largest areas, the trunk, hips and feet small ones. Secondary somatosensory cortex (SII), below SI, receives input from both sides of the body. Pain has no single cortical centre; the anterior cingulate cortex tracks its unpleasantness. It can be blocked from above: David Reynolds (1969) operated on rats with no pain relief but electrical stimulation of the periaqueductal grey (PAG) ( stimulation-produced analgesia ). Opioid receptors were then found in the PAG, endorphins were isolated, and a descending analgesia circuit was traced from the PAG through the serotonergic raphe nuclei to the dorsal horn, where interneurons block incoming pain (compare the gate-control theory of Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall, 1965, Section 1.3). Phantom limbs reflect cortical reorganisation: Vilayanur Ramachandran showed the face area of SI invading the lost hand's territory, and his mirror box eases phantom pain. Smell alone reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay: the olfactory bulb projects to the piriform cortex and amygdala, and on to the orbitofrontal cortex. Taste travels in cranial nerves VII, IX and X to the solitary nucleus of the medulla, the ventral posterior thalamus and the gustatory cortex in the insula. Exam trap Pain uses free nerve endings (Merkel, Meissner and Ruffini receptors serve touch) and the anterolateral system (not the route for proprioception, vibration and touch). Hair cells work by mechanical bending and potassium entry, not sodium-channel closure (the photoreceptor's response to light), GABA or chemical signalling. Phantoms are cortical remapping, not nerve regrowth, denial or cerebellar damage. The sensorimotor hierarchy and mirror neurons The motor system is a hierarchy run in reverse, from goals down to muscles. At the top, posterior parietal cortex integrates where the body and nearby objects are (damage causes apraxia and neglect, Section 5.11), and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex decides to initiate voluntary responses. Secondary motor cortex , the premotor cortex and supplementary motor area (area 6), programmes patterns of movement and fires just before movement starts. Primary motor cortex (area 4, precentral gyrus), the main cortical exit, is laid out as a motor homunculus with outsized hands and mouth. Brainstem nuclei and spinal circuits execute. Primary, secondary and supplementary areas thus all control movement. The levels are functionally segregated and parallel, output is guided by sensory feedback, and practice hands control down to lower levels. Key study: Rizzolatti's mirror neurons (1990s) Giacomo Rizzolatti and colleagues found neurons in area F5 of macaque ventral premotor cortex that fired both when the monkey grasped an object and when it watched an experimenter grasp it: mirror neurons , active for performing and for observing the same action. Humans show a mirror system in premotor cortex, Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) and the inferior parietal lobule, proposed to support imitation, action understanding and empathy. Criticism: human single-cell evidence is scarce, and the "broken mirror" theory of autism is debated. Exam trap Mirror neurons fire for doing and watching, not one alone, and not in REM sleep. The system is not in the hippocampus, amygdala or cerebellum. Descending pathways and spinal circuits Four tracts descend from the motor cortex (Table 5.18). The corticospinal, or pyramidal, tract passes through the pyramids of the medulla, and at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla about 85 to 90 percent of its fibres cross, so each hemisphere moves the opposite side of the body. Basal ganglia and cerebellum Neither the basal ganglia nor the cerebellum sends commands to the muscles; both modulate the cortex through the thalamus. In the basal ganglia, the striatum (caudate and putamen) receives cortical input, and the output nuclei, the internal globus pallidus (GPi) and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), constantly inhibit the thalamus (Figure 5.11). In the direct pathway , cortex excites striatal D1 neurons, which inhibit GPi and SNr; the thalamus, released, excites the cortex and movement is facilitated. In the indirect pathway , striatal D2 neurons inhibit the external globus pallidus (GPe), freeing the subthalamic nucleus (STN) to excite GPi; the thalamus is inhibited and movement suppressed. Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites the direct and inhibits the indirect pathway. Its loss causes the slow, scarce movement of Parkinson's disease, a hypokinetic disorder; loss of indirect-pathway neurons causes the chorea of Huntington's disease, a hyperkinetic one (Section 5.11). The basal ganglia thus perform action selection , initiate and gate voluntary movement, and learn habits, motor sequences and rewarded actions. Depth perception, memory consolidation and cardiorespiratory control belong to the visual cortex, hippocampus and medulla. GPi and SNr brake the thalamus; the direct pathway lifts the brake, and the indirect pathway, through GPe and STN, tightens it. Dopamine favours movement through both. The cerebellum compares intended with actual movement and corrects the error: climbing fibres from the inferior olive carry error signals to its Purkinje cells. It coordinates and times movement, maintains balance, and supports motor adaptation and eyeblink conditioning (Section 5.9). Answers: (1) lateral inhibition, (2) bitemporal, (3) magnocellular, (4) inferotemporal, (5) anterolateral, (6) pyramidal decussation, (7) Purkinje. 5.7 The Endocrine System, Stress and the Emotional Brain High yield · 46 Qs A bus swerves towards you on a Mysuru road. Before you have thought a word, your heart pounds and your palms are wet, and an hour later you are still shaky: nerves reacted in milliseconds, but hormones in your blood kept you on edge for hours. This section follows the hormones from the hypothalamus to the glands and the stress systems they build, then the brain circuits that turn a threat into fear. Glands, ducts and hormones Glands come in two kinds. Exocrine glands are duct glands : they deliver their secretions through ducts onto a surface or into a cavity, and those secretions are not hormones. Sweat, salivary, tear and digestive glands are exocrine. Endocrine glands are ductless : they release hormones , chemical messengers carried by the blood to distant cells that have receptors for them. The pancreas is both: most of it sends digestive enzymes down a duct, while islands of cells within it release insulin into the blood. Hormones belong to three chemical classes. Amino acid derivatives are made in a few steps from one amino acid (adrenaline, thyroxine, melatonin). Peptide and protein hormones are short and long chains of amino acids (insulin, oxytocin, vasopressin, growth hormone, ACTH). Steroid hormones are made from cholesterol: the gonadal hormones (testosterone, oestrogens, progesterone) and the adrenal cortex hormones (cortisol, aldosterone). Most hormones act on receptors in the cell membrane, but steroids, small and fat-soluble, also enter the cell, bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus and change gene expression directly, so their effects are the most diverse and long-lasting. Exam trap Exocrine glands are duct glands ; endocrine glands are ductless . "Primary" is no class of gland, and sweat, saliva and tears are never hormones. The hypothalamus and the pituitary The pituitary gland , a pea-sized gland hanging from the base of the brain, is called the master gland because most of its hormones are tropic hormones , which make other glands release theirs; it also releases growth hormone, which regulates growth. Yet the master gland has a master: the hypothalamus above it (Section 5.2), which integrates the endocrine, autonomic and visceral systems. In an emergency the hypothalamus supervises the fight-or-flight response, driving the sympathetic nervous system and the pituitary at once. The pituitary is really two glands, controlled in two different ways (Table 5.21). The anterior pituitary ( adenohypophysis ) is glandular tissue that releases growth hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), the gonadotropins (follicle-stimulating hormone, FSH, and luteinising hormone, LH) and prolactin, yet no nerve fibres reach it. How, then, does the hypothalamus command it? Geoffrey Harris (1913 to 1971) proposed in 1955 that hypothalamic neurons release releasing and release-inhibiting hormones into a network of blood vessels, the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system , which carries them down the pituitary stalk; cutting the portal veins halted anterior pituitary release until they regrew. In the late 1960s Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally separately isolated one, thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), sharing the 1977 Nobel Prize. The posterior pituitary ( neurohypophysis ) is neural tissue, an outgrowth of the hypothalamus, and makes nothing itself. Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised in neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, carried down their axons and released from the posterior pituitary into the blood. Vasopressin , or antidiuretic hormone (ADH), makes the kidneys reabsorb water; its failure causes diabetes insipidus , with copious dilute urine and constant thirst. Oxytocin contracts the uterus in labour, ejects milk during suckling and promotes bonding. Table 5.21 How the hypothalamus runs the pituitary. Supervisor of fight or flight: the hypothalamus, not the pituitary, the adrenal gland or the parasympathetic system. The anterior pituitary is reached by portal blood , not by axons, cerebrospinal fluid or the vagus nerve. Not anterior pituitary: oxytocin (posterior) and melatonin (pineal). The posterior pituitary only stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin; orexin (a hypothalamic wakefulness peptide, Section 5.8), noradrenaline and "vasodilators" are impostors. Oxytocin and vasopressin are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, not the suprachiasmatic nucleus (body clock), the arcuate nucleus (feeding; the dopamine that inhibits prolactin) or the mammillary bodies. Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin ejects it. The other endocrine glands Three facts about the remaining glands (Table 5.22) recur: the adrenal glands run the stress response, the thyroid sets the metabolic rate and the pancreas controls blood glucose. Each adrenal gland sits on a kidney and is two glands in one. The outer adrenal cortex makes steroids: cortisol , the chief glucocorticoid and the stress hormone; aldosterone, for salt and water balance; and adrenal androgens. The inner adrenal medulla , a modified sympathetic ganglion, releases adrenaline and noradrenaline when sympathetic nerves fire. Adrenaline and epinephrine are two names for one hormone (Latin and Greek for "on the kidney"), as noradrenaline is norepinephrine. The thyroid gland releases thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which set the body's metabolic rate and energy expenditure; the thyroid itself is controlled by TSH. In the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas, beta cells release insulin , which lowers blood glucose by letting cells take it up, and alpha cells release glucagon, which raises it. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of the beta cells, usually in childhood. Type 2 diabetes , far commoner and widespread in India, is a disorder of insulin resistance : it runs in families, but it is most strongly associated with poor diet, obesity and a sedentary lifestyle. In Cushing's syndrome , excess cortisol (from a tumour or steroid medicines) brings a round "moon face" and central obesity and, most commonly, depression, anxiety, irritability and poor memory and concentration; a minority develop mania or psychosis (not catatonia or loss of smell). Amity 2023's "Which controls the thyroid gland? Metabolism" means what the thyroid controls; the thyroid itself obeys TSH, glucose uptake is insulin's job and emotion the limbic system's. The adrenal secretes both cortisol and epinephrine; melatonin, thyroxine and insulin are distractors, and noradrenaline and dopamine are adrenaline's relatives, not its other name. For type 2 diabetes genetics matters, and stress and toxins contribute less, but the keyed answer is poor diet and sedentary lifestyle. Two stress systems, feedback and allostasis The hypothalamus answers a threat through two systems (Figure 5.12). In the fast sympathetic adrenal-medullary system (SAM), sympathetic nerves fire and the adrenal medulla pours adrenaline and noradrenaline into the blood within seconds: the fight-or-flight response named by Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945; the autonomic wiring is in Section 5.1). The slower hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA axis) works by hormones. The paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) into the portal blood, the anterior pituitary answers with ACTH, and ACTH in the general circulation makes the adrenal cortex release cortisol over minutes. Cortisol mobilises glucose and dampens inflammation and immunity. It also switches the axis off by negative feedback on the hypothalamus (less CRH) and the anterior pituitary (less ACTH), helped by the hippocampus, whose dense glucocorticoid receptors let it restrain the axis. The thyroid and gonadal axes work the same way. Hans Selye 's general adaptation syndrome, what follows when the axis stays switched on, is taught in Section 1.11. Stressor Hypothalamus the supervisor Sympathetic nerves Adrenal medulla Adrenaline, noradrenaline fast: seconds CRH, portal blood Anterior pituitary ACTH, blood Adrenal cortex Cortisol slower: minutes Negative feedback SAM system HPA axis Figure 5.12 The two stress systems. Solid arrows drive; the dashed line is cortisol's negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. The posterior pituitary and pineal gland play no part. Brief cortisol surges help; chronic ones harm. Prolonged high cortisol shrinks hippocampal dendrites, and a damaged hippocampus brakes the axis less well, so cortisol climbs further. Chronic stress also suppresses immunity and slows wound healing. The study of such links between mind, nervous system and immune system is psychoneuroimmunology . Cannon also named the goal of these systems: homeostasis (popularised in The Wisdom of the Body , 1932), keeping the internal state stable around fixed set points, as a thermostat holds a room's temperature. Peter Sterling and Joseph Eyer (1988) argued that the brain also predicts demands and shifts the set points in advance, raising blood pressure as you stand and cortisol before an examination. They called this allostasis , "stability through change": the brain regulating its own stress responses by controlling hormone release. Bruce McEwen and Eliot Stellar (1993) added allostatic load , the cumulative wear and tear when these responses are overused or fail to switch off: high blood pressure, abdominal fat, insulin resistance and hippocampal damage. Exam trap The HPA chain is hypothalamus (CRH), anterior pituitary (ACTH), adrenal cortex (cortisol) . ACTH comes from the anterior pituitary, not from the adrenal gland it targets; the posterior pituitary and adrenal medulla are not in the axis, and "pineal, pituitary, thyroid" is no axis; the cerebellum plays no part. Cortisol feeds back on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary , not the pineal, posterior pituitary, adrenal medulla or vagal motor nucleus (parasympathetic output). "The brain regulating its own stress responses by controlling hormone release" is allostasis , not homeostasis (fixed set points), neuroplasticity (rewiring with experience, Section 5.5) or circadian rhythm (Section 5.8). Clinical link In melancholic depression the HPA axis is often overactive: in the dexamethasone suppression test , a night dose of synthetic glucocorticoid fails to suppress next morning's cortisol (Chapter 8). Because endocrine disease mimics depression and anxiety, hormones are checked before a psychiatric diagnosis. Emotion and the autonomic nervous system Fear and anger bring one broad sympathetic pattern: heart rate, blood pressure and breathing rise, the pupils dilate, blood shifts to the muscles, glucose enters the blood and sweating increases. Sweat conducts electricity, so skin conductance rises and skin resistance falls (the galvanic skin response). Pupil constriction is parasympathetic. The polygraph records heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and skin conductance together; it detects arousal, not lies. Whether each emotion has its own autonomic pattern divides the James-Lange, Cannon-Bard and Schachter-Singer theories (Section 1.11). Exam trap Odd one out among signs of sympathetic activation: pupil constriction . "Lowered skin resistance" is sympathetic: it is the same event as raised skin conductance. From sham rage to the limbic system Which part of the brain makes emotion? In 1929 Philip Bard found that decorticate cats, their cortex removed, raged at the lightest touch, arching their backs, hissing and baring their teeth, but excessively and at no target. He called this sham rage . It survived removal of everything down to the hypothalamus but vanished once the hypothalamus went too. The hypothalamus organises rage; the cortex inhibits and directs it. In 1937 James Papez (1883 to 1958) proposed a circuit for emotion (Figure 5.13). The Papez circuit runs from the hippocampus through the fornix to the mammillary bodies, by the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nucleus, on to the cingulate cortex, through the cingulum to the entorhinal (parahippocampal) cortex and back to the hippocampus. Emotion, he argued, is expressed through the hypothalamus and experienced through the cortex. The loop is now thought to serve memory more than emotion (Section 5.9), but it began the search for an emotional brain. Hippocampus Fornix Mammillary bodies Anterior thalamic nucleus Cingulate cortex Entorhinal cortex mammillothalamic tract Papez circuit (1937) cingulum Figure 5.13 The Papez circuit, a closed loop. Loops through the caudate, putamen, globus pallidus or substantia nigra (basal ganglia), from retina to visual cortex, or through the cerebellum are other circuits. Paul MacLean (1913 to 2007) enlarged the circuit in 1952, adding the amygdala, septum and other structures, and named it the limbic system (Latin limbus , border, because it rings the thalamus at the inner edge of the cortex); later it became the middle layer of his triune brain. Its members are the hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, fornix, septum and mammillary bodies, with the hypothalamus and anterior thalamus closely tied in. It is the classic "seat of emotion", regulating emotion, motivation and memory. Exam trap "Seat of emotion", "emotion and motivation", "emotional behaviour": limbic system ; offered single parts (hippocampus, thalamus, hypothalamus) beside it, choose the system. Not the reticular formation (arousal), hindbrain (breathing, heart rate), whole forebrain (too broad), pituitary (hormones), cerebellum (motor coordination), corpus callosum (joins the hemispheres), frontal lobe (voluntary movement, decisions), thalamus and sensory cortex (sensory processing), visual cortex (acuity) or Broca's area (syntax). Hunger, thirst and hormone regulation are hypothalamic, so Amity 2023 keys "regulation of emotions", not "both". The amygdala and fear The amygdala (Greek for almond), a cluster of nuclei in each anterior medial temporal lobe, is the key emotional structure: it detects threat, gives events emotional salience, triggers fear and defensive aggression, and learns what predicts danger. Its role was mapped by fear conditioning: after a tone has preceded mild shocks, the tone alone makes a rat freeze, heart racing. Signals enter through the lateral nucleus , where tone and shock are associated, and leave through the central nucleus for the hypothalamus (autonomic and hormonal responses) and the periaqueductal grey of the midbrain (freezing). Amygdala lesions abolish conditioned fear. Joseph LeDoux (born 1949) traced two routes in (Figure 5.14). The low road , from the sensory thalamus straight to the amygdala, is fast and crude: you jump back from a coiled shape before you know what it is. The high road , from the thalamus through the sensory cortex to the amygdala, is slower but accurate: it tells you the shape is a rope. (Adolphs and colleagues, 1994) Does the human amygdala matter for emotion? Ralph Adolphs and colleagues tested S.M., whose amygdalae had been destroyed on both sides by Urbach-Wiethe disease, a rare genetic disorder that calcifies the amygdala and nearby medial temporal lobe. She recognised faces and most expressions but not fear, and could not produce a fearful expression herself. Later work found she barely feels fear, reaching for snakes in a pet shop (Justin Feinstein and colleagues, 2011). Criticism: one rare patient. In affective blindsight , described by Beatrice de Gelder and colleagues in 1999, patients blinded in part of the visual field by damage to the primary visual cortex guess well above chance which emotion a face shown there expresses, while insisting they see nothing. The signal is thought to travel subcortically, from the superior colliculus through the pulvinar of the thalamus to the amygdala. "Affect neglect", "emotional neglect" and "motivational blindsight" are not established terms. Exam trap Fear and aggression, emotion processing, threat detection, fear conditioning: amygdala . Not the hippocampus (conscious recall, declarative memory, Section 5.9), thalamus (relay), hypothalamus (executes the amygdala's orders), frontal lobe (verbal working memory), brainstem (vital functions), cerebellum and basal ganglia (starting movement, motor sequence learning) or suprachiasmatic nucleus (circadian rhythm). "Slower, more accurate identification" is the high road; conscious vision and voluntary motor output are cortical. Klüver-Bucy syndrome and other influences What happens to an animal without its amygdalae? In 1937 and 1939 Heinrich Klüver and Paul Bucy removed both anterior temporal lobes, amygdalae included, in rhesus monkeys. Unmanageable monkeys became tame and placid, approaching snakes without fear. They showed psychic blindness , a visual agnosia (seeing objects without recognising their meaning); examined everything by mouth ( hyperorality ); ate almost anything, even meat, which rhesus monkeys normally refuse ( hyperphagia and dietary change); directed sexual activity at inappropriate partners and objects ( hypersexuality ); and attended compulsively to every sight ( hypermetamorphosis ). This Klüver-Bucy syndrome follows mainly from loss of the amygdala. Answers: (1) ducts, (2) portal, (3) paraventricular, (4) ACTH, (5) allostasis, (6) sham, (7) low, (8) Klüver-Bucy. 5.8 Sleep, Biological Rhythms, Hunger, Thirst and Sex Medium yield · 31 Qs Why does a student who revised all night still feel alert in the evening, hungry at lunchtime however large breakfast was, and thirsty after salty chaat? The answers lie in small clusters of neurons, mostly in the hypothalamus. Biological rhythms and the master clock A circadian rhythm (Latin circa diem , about a day) repeats about every 24 hours, like the sleep-wake cycle; ultradian rhythms are shorter (the 90-minute sleep cycle) and infradian rhythms longer (the menstrual cycle). Circadian rhythms are entrained, locked to the world, by zeitgebers ("time givers"), above all light. Without cues, in a cave or windowless laboratory, they persist as free-running rhythms slightly longer than 24 hours (about 24.2 in humans). Jet lag and shift work put the clock out of step with the day; eastbound flights, which demand a phase advance, are the harder. Curt Richter found in 1967 that large medial hypothalamic lesions disrupted the daily cycles of eating, drinking and activity in rats; smaller lesions located the clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), just above the optic chiasm. SCN lesions abolish the circadian timing of sleep but not its total amount. Key study: the SCN transplant (Ralph and colleagues, 1990) Martin Ralph and colleagues transplanted SCN tissue from fetal mutant hamsters with a 20-hour free-running cycle into normal adults whose 25-hour rhythms SCN lesions had abolished. Rhythms returned with the donor's 20-hour period (and the reverse transplant gave 25 hours): the SCN sets the period. It is the master clock, though most body cells carry clock machinery that it keeps in step. Light reaches the SCN by the retinohypothalamic tract , from retinal ganglion cells containing the photopigment melanopsin , not from rods or cones. The clock itself is a molecular loop: clock genes such as period , timeless and clock are transcribed, and their proteins build up and switch off their own transcription over about 24 hours, as Jeffrey Hall , Michael Rosbash and Michael Young showed in fruit flies (Nobel Prize, 2017). The SCN drives the pineal gland , a small endocrine gland of the epithalamus, to secrete melatonin at night, the "hormone of darkness"; light suppresses it. Melatonin promotes sleepiness, and taken at bedtime in the new time zone it eases jet lag. Exam trap The master circadian pacemaker is the SCN of the hypothalamus , not the paraventricular or ventromedial nucleus or mammillary bodies, and no centre for hunger, temperature, anterior pituitary release, memory, language or pain (Table 5.25). Yet RML 2022 ("which gland regulates circadian rhythm") and RML 2023 ("which structure regulates the body's internal clock") keyed the pineal gland , which turns the clock's signal into melatonin. Choose the SCN whenever it is offered; for a gland, or "hypothalamus" against "pineal", these keys want the pineal. The pituitary (Section 5.7), cerebellum and thalamus keep no clock. The EEG of sleep and REM sleep When cortical neurons fire independently, the electroencephalogram (EEG) is desynchronised (small, fast waves); when they fire together it is synchronised (large, slow waves). Stages 3 and 4 together form slow-wave sleep , merged as N3 in the 2007 scoring rules of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (Table 5.24). The NREM stages and a REM period make a cycle of about 90 minutes, four to six a night (Section 1.5). Table 5.24 The EEG of waking and sleep. REM is paradoxical sleep : the EEG looks awake while the body is deeply asleep. The switches for sleep, waking and dreams In 1936 Frederic Bremer cut cats' brainstems between the colliculi (the cerveau isolé, "isolated forebrain"), and the cortex showed almost constant slow-wave sleep; a cut at the bottom of the brainstem (the encéphale isolé, 1937) left the sleep-wake cycle intact. Something between the cuts keeps the forebrain awake. Giuseppe Moruzzi and Horace Magoun (1949) found that stimulating the brainstem reticular formation woke sleeping cats: it is the reticular activating system . It is now seen as several ascending arousal systems named by transmitter: noradrenaline (locus coeruleus), serotonin (raphe nuclei), histamine (tuberomammillary nucleus), acetylcholine (basal forebrain and pons) and orexin , or hypocretin (lateral hypothalamus, in its posterior, wake-promoting part). Slow-wave sleep begins when GABA neurons of the ventrolateral preoptic area (VLPO) become active and inhibit these systems. The chemical of drowsiness is adenosine , a by-product of the brain's energy use that builds up during waking and falls during sleep: it is the homeostatic sleep pressure, and caffeine keeps you awake by blocking its receptors. Orexin, acetylcholine and serotonin promote arousal instead. Alexander Borbély 's two-process model (1982) joins this process S, rising with time awake, to the circadian process C from the SCN. REM has its own switch: REM-on neurons of the sublaterodorsal nucleus in the pons and REM-off neurons of the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey inhibit each other. In REM the sublaterodorsal nucleus drives medullary neurons that inhibit motor neurons, producing atonia. In the activation-synthesis hypothesis of J. Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley (1977; Section 1.5), the cortex weaves a dream from random pontine activity. In REM the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is relatively inactive, so dreams lack organisation, planning, logic and a sense of time; the amygdala is active, so they are emotional; and the extrastriate visual association cortex is active while the striate (primary visual) cortex is quiet, so we see vivid images without input from the eyes. The somatosensory cortex plays no special part. Sleep disorders and why we sleep In narcolepsy the orexin neurons of the lateral (posterior) hypothalamus are lost. Its signs are excessive daytime sleepiness with sleep attacks; cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion, in full consciousness; sleep paralysis; hypnagogic hallucinations while falling asleep; and sleep-onset REM. All but the sleepiness are REM breaking into waking. In REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD), REM atonia is lost and patients act out their dreams; it often precedes Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia by years (Section 5.11). Sleepwalking (somnambulism), night terrors and bedwetting are NREM parasomnias, arising from partial arousal out of N3 early in the night; nightmares are frightening REM dreams, mostly late in the night. In sleep apnoea, breathing stops repeatedly during sleep. Insomnia and its treatment are in Chapters 7 and 8. Exam trap Sleepwalking and night terrors: N3 , not REM, N1 or N2 (a body in REM is paralysed). RBD is loss of REM atonia, not an inability to enter REM, not bedwetting in N3 and not daytime sleepiness without night-time symptoms. Why sleep at all? Recuperation theories say sleep restores what waking depletes; adaptation theories say it evolved to keep animals inactive and safe when they need not forage. Sleep also aids memory consolidation (Section 5.9). Hunger: set points and positive incentives Most people assume hunger works like a thermostat. On this set-point assumption , eating starts when energy falls below a set point and stops when it is restored: Jean Mayer 's glucostatic theory (1953) made blood glucose the regulated quantity, and the lipostatic theory made it body fat. John Pinel and colleagues argue instead for positive-incentive theory : we eat mainly for the anticipated pleasure of food, shaped by taste, learning and company, and body weight drifts to a settling point. The circulating hormone that triggers hunger is ghrelin , from the empty stomach. Satiety signals come from the gut and from fat. In 1973 James Gibbs , R. C. Young and Gerard Smith injected cholecystokinin (CCK), released by the duodenum as food arrives, into hungry rats, which then ate smaller meals: the classic satiety peptide. Insulin, released by the pancreas as blood glucose rises, is both a satiety and a body-fat signal. Key study: the ob/ob mouse and leptin (1994) Mice of the ob/ob strain overeat and grow up to three times normal weight. In 1994 Jeffrey Friedman 's group cloned the mutated gene: expressed only in fat cells, it codes a hormone they named leptin , which ob/ob mice lack, and leptin injections cut their eating and fat. Released in proportion to fat stores, leptin is the long-term regulator of body weight and fat. Yet obese humans usually have high leptin and do not respond to injections (leptin resistance). The long-term fat signal is leptin, not the hypothalamus (a brain area, not a hormone), oestrogen or cortisol. The hypothalamus and the arcuate nucleus Section 1.10 told how two lesion studies built the dual-centre hypothesis . In 1940 Albert Hetherington and Stephen Ranson destroyed the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) of rats, which overate (hyperphagia) and grew grossly obese, first in a dynamic phase of rapid gain, then in a static phase holding the new weight. In 1951 the Indian physiologist Bal Krishan Anand and John Brobeck found that lateral hypothalamus (LH) lesions caused aphagia, a fatal refusal to eat; Philip Teitelbaum and Alan Epstein (1962) showed that it comes with adipsia, a refusal to drink, and that tube-fed rats partly recover. Eliot Stellar (1954) made the LH the feeding centre and the VMH the satiety centre. The model has since been revised: VMH lesions raise blood insulin, so food is turned into fat and the rats overeat because they are getting fat, not the reverse; cut fibres from the paraventricular nucleus explain much of the syndrome; and LH lesions cause broad motor and sensory deficits. Feeding centre: LH ; its lesion gives aphagia, adipsia and weight loss (Lateral, Lose). "Ventromedial hippocampus" and "lateral thalamus" are invented; the cerebrum and basal ganglia are not hunger centres. The arcuate nucleus is not for motor coordination, memory or circadian rhythm. NPY triggers eating; leptin, CART and CCK are satiety signals. Learned influences on eating, and thirst What is on the plate, and who is at the table, matter too. In the portion size effect , people eat more when served larger portions: Barbara Rolls and colleagues (2002) served lunches of macaroni and cheese in different sizes, and the bigger the portion, the more people ate, without feeling fuller. In sensory-specific satiety , a food loses its appeal as you eat it while other foods stay attractive, so a new dish restarts eating. A small first course increases hunger (the appetiser effect), and a cafeteria diet of varied, palatable foods made rats eat 84 per cent more calories. Through social facilitation we eat more with others than alone, though we also eat less when companions do. Prader-Willi syndrome is in Section 5.5, eating disorders in Chapter 8. Thirst has two triggers. In osmotic thirst the salt concentration of body fluid rises, as after a salty meal: water leaves the cells, and hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense this cellular dehydration, start thirst and trigger the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) so the kidneys keep water. In hypovolaemic thirst blood volume falls, as after bleeding: the kidneys release renin, which forms angiotensin II, and angiotensin II acts on the subfornical organ to start drinking. When ADH fails, in diabetes insipidus, the kidneys pass large volumes of dilute urine and the person is constantly thirsty. Hormones, sexual development and sexual response The organisational effects of hormones act early in development and permanently shape body and brain; activational effects act in adulthood, only while the hormone is present. Charles Phoenix and colleagues (1959) drew this distinction after female guinea pigs exposed to testosterone before birth mounted like males when given testosterone as adults. The default course of a fetus is female. The SRY gene on the Y chromosome turns the primitive gonads into testes, which secrete testosterone, masculinising the body, and Müllerian-inhibiting substance, which makes the female ducts degenerate; Alfred Jost found that fetuses deprived of their gonads develop female ducts whatever their chromosomes. From puberty the pituitary gonadotropins, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone, make the gonads secrete androgens (chiefly testosterone), oestrogens (oestradiol) and progestins (progesterone). Both sexes make all three, in different amounts; hence Pinel's attack on the mamawawa , the men-are-men-and-women-are-women assumption that the sexes are separate, opposite categories. In congenital adrenal hyperplasia, the adrenal glands of XX fetuses make excess androgens, partly masculinising girls' genitals; in androgen insensitivity syndrome, XY individuals with testes but unresponsive androgen receptors develop a female body without a uterus. The medial preoptic area, whose sexually dimorphic nucleus is several times larger in male rats ( Roger Gorski , 1978), is critical for male sexual behaviour, the VMH for female. In 1991 Simon LeVay reported that INAH3, a nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus, was smaller in gay than in heterosexual men, nearer the size in women; the finding has not been consistently replicated, and reading it as a "female-like" brain is mamawawa thinking. William Masters and Virginia Johnson (1966) observed volunteers in the laboratory and described a four-phase sexual response cycle : excitement, plateau (arousal levels off near its peak), orgasm and resolution, with a male refractory period after orgasm. Helen Singer Kaplan (1979) put desire first, in a three-phase model of desire, excitement and orgasm. Exam trap Masters and Johnson: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution . A sequence that starts with plateau, or inserts desire anywhere, is not theirs: desire first is Kaplan, and the refractory period lies within the male resolution phase rather than being a phase of its own. Where, and how? The answers come from patients whose memory broke in revealing ways, from animal lesion studies, and from the synapse itself. Section 1.7 treated memory as a psychological process; here the subject is its biology. Amnesia: forward and backward in time Clinically, amnesia is a pathological loss of memory, far beyond ordinary forgetting. It usually follows brain damage or disease (head injury, stroke, surgery, encephalitis, thiamine deficiency); more rarely its cause is psychological, as in dissociative amnesia (Chapter 8). It is a disorder of memory, not a behavioural disturbance, a depressed mood or impaired perception. Amnesias come in two directions in time from the onset (Figure 5.17). The first, anterograde amnesia , is the inability to form new long-term memories after the injury or onset: the patient chats normally, yet ten minutes later the conversation is gone. The second, retrograde amnesia , is the loss of memories formed before it. It usually has a temporal gradient : recent memories are lost most completely while remote ones survive, a pattern Théodule Ribot (1839 to 1916) described in Les maladies de la mémoire (1881), hence Ribot's law . The gradient shows that memories grow sturdier with age, through consolidation ( 5.9.4 ). In source amnesia you remember a fact but not where or when you learned it, a lapse common in old age and after frontal lobe damage. Injury or onset Remote memories kept Retrograde loss Anterograde loss time childhood, school years recent past lost most new events not stored (gradient: Ribot's law) Figure 5.17 Amnesia is named by its direction from the onset. Retrograde loss is worst for the most recent past; anterograde loss blocks everything that follows. Exam trap Anterograde means forward from the injury: no new memories . It is not "temporary memory loss" (transient global amnesia, Table 5.27), a visual deficit, or an inability to speak or recognise faces. Losing memories from before a concussion or stroke, or failing to retrieve old memories, is retrograde amnesia; dissociative amnesia is the psychological kind. The search for the engram If learning changes the brain, the change must be somewhere. In 1904 the German zoologist Richard Semon (1859 to 1918) named it the engram : the physical trace an experience leaves in the brain. It is not a process of forgetting, a retrieval failure or a type of explicit memory. Its most determined hunter, Karl Spencer Lashley (1890 to 1958), trained rats on mazes and then removed different parts of their cortex, expecting one lesion to erase the habit. None did. In Brain Mechanisms and Intelligence (1929) he stated two principles: mass action (the deficit depended on how much cortex was removed, not where) and equipotentiality (within a functional area, any part could do the work of any other). His review "In search of the engram" (1950) concluded that memories are not held in one place but distributed throughout the cortex. His former student Donald Olding Hebb (1904 to 1985) explained why in The Organization of Behavior (1949). A memory is held by a cell assembly , a network of neurons linked because they fired together during an experience; spread across the cortex, it survives any single lesion in part. The links form at a Hebbian synapse : when neuron A repeatedly helps to fire neuron B, the connection from A to B strengthens ("cells that fire together wire together", a later summary). Long-term potentiation, found in 1973, bore him out ( 5.9.7 ). The Montreal neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield (1891 to 1976), stimulating the temporal lobes of awake epileptic patients, sometimes evoked vivid recollections, now regarded as reconstructions rather than stored replays. Exam trap Lashley placed memories throughout the cortex : not in specific localised regions, the hippocampus alone or only the frontal and temporal lobes. The engram is the physical trace of a memory; the term is Semon's, the search Lashley's. H.M. and the medial temporal lobes Section 1.7 told H.M.'s story; here is the neural detail. Henry Gustav Molaison (1926 to 2008) had severe epilepsy that drugs could not control, apparently arising in both medial temporal lobes. In 1953, when he was 27, the neurosurgeon William Beecher Scoville (1906 to 1984) performed a bilateral medial temporal lobectomy , removing the inner parts of both temporal lobes: most of the hippocampus, the amygdala and adjacent cortex. The seizures eased. Scoville and the psychologist Brenda Milner (born 1918) reported the cost in 1957. H.M. was left with severe anterograde amnesia for declarative memory (explicit memory: consciously recalled facts and events). He never learned his new address or recognised doctors he met after surgery, and he reread magazines with fresh interest. He had some retrograde amnesia for the few years before surgery. Spared were his intelligence (above average), language, personality, working memory (a normal digit span of about six) and remote memories, such as people and events from his childhood. Most surprising, he could learn skills. Tracing a star while watching his hand only in a mirror, ten times a day on three days, he made fewer errors each day, yet each day denied ever doing the task. He also improved at rotary pursuit (keeping a stylus on a moving target), identified fragmented drawings sooner on the incomplete-pictures test (priming) and acquired a conditioned eyeblink: all implicit (nondeclarative) memory. Three lessons followed. The medial temporal lobes consolidate new declarative memories but do not store remote ones, since his old memories survived. Short-term and long-term memory are separable. Explicit and implicit memory dissociate. Key study: Scoville and Milner (1957) Their report on H.M. and other patients established medial temporal amnesia as a distinct syndrome. Criticism: the lesion also took the amygdala and nearby cortex, so the case alone could not show which structure mattered. Exam trap H.M.'s most profound deficit was anterograde amnesia for declarative memory, not retrograde amnesia or a loss of procedural, semantic or working memory. Improving mirror drawing shows preserved procedural memory, not episodic, declarative or semantic memory. The surgery removed the medial temporal lobes , not prefrontal, parietal (angular gyrus) or occipital (lingual gyrus) cortex. It did not abolish motor coordination, selectively erase semantic memory, or cause "global retrograde amnesia with intact new learning", the reverse of his case. The hippocampus: consolidation and space Which structure mattered? Patient R.B., described by Stuart Zola-Morgan , Larry Squire and David Amaral (1986), suffered ischaemia (interrupted blood supply to the brain) at 52, when a pump failed during heart bypass surgery. His anterograde amnesia was milder than H.M.'s, and after his death the only obvious damage was to pyramidal cells in field CA1 of the hippocampus. Hippocampal damage alone, then, causes anterograde amnesia: a man who since a road accident remembers his past but not what he said ten minutes ago has probably injured his hippocampus. The hippocampus is needed for consolidation , the conversion of fragile new memories into stable long-term ones, especially episodic and spatial declarative memories. In standard consolidation theory , it binds the scattered cortical pieces of an experience and replays them, partly during sleep (5.8), until cortical connections can hold the memory alone; remote memories then no longer need it. This explains both H.M.'s intact childhood and Ribot's gradient. It is also the brain's map. In 1971 John O'Keefe (born 1939) and Jonathan Dostrovsky found place cells in the rat hippocampus, each firing only when the rat is in one particular spot; O'Keefe and Lynn Nadel argued in The Hippocampus as a Cognitive Map (1978) that the hippocampus builds a cognitive map of the environment. May-Britt Moser (born 1963) and Edvard Moser (born 1962) in 2005 found grid cells in the entorhinal cortex, the hippocampus's main input, each firing in a regular triangular grid of locations, a coordinate system for space. The three shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Eleanor Maguire and colleagues (2000) found enlarged posterior hippocampi in London taxi drivers, larger the longer they had driven. K.C., Kent Cochrane (1951 to 2014), studied by Endel Tulving (1927 to 2023), suffered diffuse brain damage including the medial temporal lobes in a motorcycle accident in 1981. He lost episodic, autobiographical memory for his whole life and could not imagine his future, yet his semantic knowledge, skills (chess, card games) and working memory survived: episodic and semantic memory are separable. Clive Wearing (born 1938), a British musician, lost both hippocampi and more to herpes simplex encephalitis in 1985; left with a memory span of seconds, he could still play the piano and conduct. Exam trap The hippocampus forms and consolidates new declarative memories (especially episodic and spatial); remote memories end up in the wider cortex. It does not control temperature (hypothalamus), balance (cerebellum), speech (Broca's area, 5.10), procedural memory (basal ganglia, cerebellum), smell transduction (olfactory receptors, 5.6) or voluntary movement (motor cortex). Failure to form new memories after head injury points to the hippocampus , not the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, cerebellum, thalamus, hypothalamus, pituitary, brainstem, reticular formation (arousal) or spinal cord (reflexes). Memory systems and the amygdala Memory, then, is several systems, each with its own structures (Table 5.26). Skills and habits depend on the cerebellum, basal ganglia and motor cortex, spared in H.M. but damaged in Parkinson's and Huntington's disease, which impair skill learning. Mortimer Mishkin (1926 to 2021) and Jean Delacour (1975) devised the delayed nonmatching-to-sample test : a monkey sees a sample object, then after a delay must choose the new object rather than the sample to find food. Monkeys with medial temporal lesions failed at longer delays, an animal model of H.M.; later lesions traced this object-recognition memory chiefly to the perirhinal cortex.
