Korsakoff's syndrome and its look-alikes The second classic site of amnesia is the medial diencephalon. Korsakoff's syndrome (Korsakoff's psychosis), described in the 1880s by the Russian neuropsychiatrist Sergei Korsakoff (1854 to 1900), is an amnesic disorder caused by deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1) , classically in chronic alcoholism with a poor diet: alcohol supplies calories without vitamins and impairs thiamine absorption. It also occurs in malnourished non-drinkers, so the vitamin, not the alcohol, is the main cause. Thiamine is needed to metabolise glucose, so energy-hungry neurons die first. It usually follows Wernicke's encephalopathy , described by Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) in 1881: an acute emergency with a triad of confusion (disorientation, lapses of attention), ataxia (loss of muscle coordination) and ophthalmoplegia (paralysis of eye movements), often with nystagmus (jerky eye movements). Attention and coordination are both impaired. Untreated survivors settle into Korsakoff's amnesia, and the continuum is called Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome . Damage centres on the mammillary bodies and the mediodorsal (dorsomedial) thalamus, a diencephalic amnesia , though it is diffuse. The result is dense anterograde amnesia, severe retrograde amnesia with a temporal gradient reaching back decades, confusion, apathy, poor insight and confabulation : detailed, plausible but false stories that fill memory gaps, told sincerely without intent to deceive. Malingering, by contrast, is deliberate faking for gain; delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness; confusion is muddled thinking without invented stories. Thiamine supplements for heavy drinkers help prevent it. Treatment is high-dose thiamine given before any glucose (a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy); it halts damage, but established amnesia is largely permanent. Exam trap Korsakoff's: vitamin B1 (thiamine) , not B12, niacin, B6, folate or vitamin D, hypoxia or lead. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome impairs both attention and muscle coordination. Memory loss with confabulation and nystagmus in a heavy drinker is Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, not Alzheimer's, vascular or frontotemporal dementia. Eric Kandel (born 1929) chose Aplysia because its large neurons can be identified one by one. A touch to its siphon makes it withdraw its gill. Repeated harmless touches weaken the reflex ( habituation ) because sensory neurons release less transmitter onto motor neurons; a tail shock strengthens it ( sensitisation ) because interneurons release serotonin onto the sensory terminals, raising cyclic AMP and transmitter release. Long-term forms need the transcription factor CREB, protein synthesis and new synapses. Kandel shared the 2000 Nobel Prize. In mammals the breakthrough came in 1973: Timothy Bliss (born 1940) and Terje Lømo (born 1935) stimulated the perforant path into the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus in anaesthetised rabbits. After a brief burst of high-frequency (tetanic) pulses, single test pulses produced larger responses for hours, and in later work for weeks or months. This long-term potentiation (LTP) is a lasting strengthening of synaptic transmission after high-frequency stimulation. Four properties fit a memory mechanism: longevity (it lasts); input specificity (only the stimulated synapses strengthen); cooperativity (several inputs must be active together); and associativity (a weak input active with a strong one is potentiated too, a cellular version of pairing a conditioned with an unconditioned stimulus). The secret lies in the receptors for glutamate, the brain's main excitatory transmitter (Figure 5.18). AMPA receptors carry ordinary fast excitation. The NMDA receptor is special: at resting potential its channel is plugged by a magnesium ion (Mg 2+ ), so glutamate alone lets almost nothing through. Only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic membrane is already depolarised is the magnesium expelled, letting calcium (Ca 2+ ) flood in. The NMDA receptor is thus a coincidence detector of presynaptic and postsynaptic activity: Hebb's rule in molecular form. (Glycine must also bind as a co-agonist but cannot open it alone; the receptor is excitatory and postsynaptic, so it does not trigger vesicle release.) In the dendritic spine, calcium activates CaMKII (calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II), which strengthens AMPA receptors and inserts extra ones, so the same glutamate release produces a larger response. Late LTP, lasting days or more, needs CREB-driven gene expression, new proteins and growth of more and larger dendritic spines; LTP does not involve fewer spines, glutamate depletion or neuron death (apoptosis). Richard Morris and colleagues (1986) tied it to behaviour: rats given AP5, an NMDA receptor blocker, showed no hippocampal LTP and were badly impaired at learning where a platform lay hidden in the Morris water maze, a pool of opaque water. 1 Glutamate only, at rest Presynaptic terminal AMPA AMPA receptor NMDA receptor pore plugged Little calcium enters No LTP 2 Glutamate plus depolarisation Presynaptic terminal + + AMPA AMPA AMPA receptors NMDA open extra one inserted calcium flows in Calcium activates CaMKII More AMPA receptors: LTP glutamate magnesium ion calcium ion Figure 5.18 The NMDA receptor as a coincidence detector: magnesium plugs it when glutamate arrives alone (left) and leaves when the membrane is also depolarised (+ +), letting calcium in (right). Exam trap LTP is a lasting strengthening after high-frequency stimulation, not a weakening (that is LTD), neuron death or myelination, and it is linked to memory , not thermoregulation, circadian rhythm or sleep. Its induction depends on NMDA receptors , not AMPA receptors alone, muscarinic M1 or GABA-A receptors. Magnesium blocks the NMDA channel, not the AMPA channel. LTD and the dopamine teaching signal Synapses that could only strengthen would saturate. LTP's counterpart, long-term depression (LTD), is a lasting weakening of synaptic transmission. Serena Dudek and Mark Bear (1992) produced it in hippocampal field CA1 with prolonged low-frequency stimulation, about 1 Hz for 15 minutes. LTD there also needs NMDA receptors, but the modest, sustained calcium rise activates phosphatases (enzymes that remove phosphate groups) rather than kinases, and AMPA receptors are pulled out of the membrane. A large, fast calcium surge gives LTP; a small, slow one gives LTD. LTD is not cell death, presynaptic GABA release, magnesium block of AMPA receptors or glutamate release without postsynaptic effect; high-frequency stimulation with NMDA receptors blocked produces neither LTP nor LTD. Learning also needs a signal saying what is worth learning. Wolfram Schultz recorded from dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra in monkeys learning that a light predicted juice. Before learning, the neurons burst when juice arrived unexpectedly. After learning, they burst at the light and ignored the expected juice; if the juice was withheld, firing paused when it should have come. Schultz, Peter Dayan and Read Montague (1997) identified this as a reward prediction error : reward received minus reward expected, positive for a pleasant surprise, zero for a predicted reward, negative for a disappointment. It is the surprise term of the Rescorla-Wagner model (Chapter 1), and the dopamine released strengthens the striatal synapses that were just active. Drug reward is covered in 5.4. Exam trap The prediction-error signal comes from dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area , not serotonin release, GABA inhibition or acetylcholine release. That finding raised the two questions of this section: why do the hemispheres do different jobs, and where is language produced and understood? Discovering the dominant hemisphere Cerebral lateralisation is the tendency of a function to depend more on one cerebral hemisphere than on the other. In 1836 Marc Dax , a French country doctor, reported that none of his 40 or so patients with speech loss had damage confined to the right hemisphere, but nobody took notice. In 1861 Paul Broca (1824 to 1880) described Louis Victor Leborgne, nicknamed 'Tan' because it was almost the only syllable he could utter. Leborgne understood speech; at autopsy his lesion lay in the left inferior frontal cortex, and by 1864 Broca had seen the same in more patients. Because language, and later skilled movement, proved to depend on the left hemisphere, it was called the dominant hemisphere or major hemisphere, and the right the minor hemisphere . The second label is outdated. Two tests reveal the language hemisphere of a living person. In the Wada test (sodium amytal test) of Juhn Atsushi Wada (1949), the barbiturate sodium amytal is injected into one carotid artery, anaesthetising that hemisphere for a few minutes; if it holds language, the patient falls mute. It is used before brain surgery. The harmless dichotic listening test plays different words or digits to the two ears at once. Doreen Kimura (1961) found that most people report more right-ear items, a right-ear advantage for words, because each ear's stronger pathway runs to the opposite hemisphere and the left hemisphere handles language; for melodies the advantage passes to the left ear. About 90 percent of people are right-handed, and handedness is loosely tied to language. Language is in the left hemisphere in about 95 percent of right-handers and in most left-handers (roughly 70 percent); the rest have it on the right or in both hemispheres. Exam trap The left hemisphere is the major (dominant) hemisphere. 'Spatial and pattern sense' and 'centre of musical ability' describe the right hemisphere, and 'minor hemisphere' is the old name for the right. Most left-handers are still left-dominant for language. What each hemisphere does best Table 5.28 summarises the asymmetries. Phonological processing means handling the sound structure of words; right-hemisphere control of spatial attention explains why neglect follows right parietal damage (5.11). Table 5.28 Functional asymmetries in most right-handers. Each is a relative bias, not a monopoly. Left hemisphere Right hemisphere Speech, phonology, grammar and syntax Emotional prosody; understands simple words Reading, writing, arithmetic Visuospatial processing; spatial and pattern sense Analytic, sequential processing Holistic processing of whole patterns Verbal memory Non-verbal (visual, spatial) memory Speech sounds Music, melody, non-speech sounds Skilled, complex movement Faces; emotional expression; spatial attention One right-hemisphere skill lies inside language itself. Prosody is the melody of speech: the intonation and emotional tone that let 'Oh, great' mean delight or sarcasm. Emotional prosody depends on right-hemisphere regions homotopic to the language areas, that is, in their mirror-image positions. Elliott Ross (1981) described the aprosodias : damage opposite Broca's area leaves speech flat and monotonous, and damage opposite Wernicke's area leaves the patient deaf to the emotion in other voices, while words and grammar are spared. The hemispheres differ in structure too. Norman Geschwind (1926 to 1984) and Walter Levitsky (1968) found the planum temporale , auditory cortex behind Heschl's gyrus that includes part of Wernicke's area, larger on the left in about two thirds of 100 brains. Popular talk of logical 'left-brained' and creative 'right-brained' people is a myth. Lateralisation is a matter of degree (the right-ear advantage is slight), every complex skill, creativity included, uses both hemispheres together, and imaging finds no 'left-brained' individuals. Exam trap The function most reliably lateralised to the right is visuospatial processing and prosody ; phonological processing, grammatical syntax and verbal memory are left-hemisphere. Speech intonation depends on right-hemisphere regions homotopic to the language areas , not Broca's area, the primary motor cortex or the occipital lobe. The split brain The most striking evidence came from cutting the corpus callosum, the largest commissure linking the hemispheres (5.2). In 1953 Ronald Myers and Roger Wolcott Sperry (1913 to 1994) cut both the corpus callosum and the optic chiasm of cats, so each eye fed one hemisphere. A cat trained on a visual task with one eye patched had to relearn it from scratch with the other eye, as if it had two brains: the corpus callosum transfers learning between hemispheres. From the 1960s surgeons cut the corpus callosum in people with intractable epilepsy, to stop seizures spreading between hemispheres. This corpus callosotomy (often called commissurotomy) reduced the seizures and left patients almost unchanged in daily life. Sperry and his student Michael Gazzaniga (born 1939) then tested them, work that won Sperry the Nobel Prize in 1981. Key study: Sperry and Gazzaniga's split-brain patients (1960s) Method: the left visual field projects to the right hemisphere and the right field to the left (5.6). In tachistoscopic presentation the patient fixates a central dot while a picture is flashed to one side for about a tenth of a second, too fast for an eye movement. Each hand, hidden from view, reports to and is controlled by the opposite hemisphere. Result: objects flashed to the right visual field were named at once. Objects flashed to the left field reached only the non-speaking right hemisphere: the patient said he saw nothing, yet his left hand picked out the object by touch (Figure 5.19). Neither eye nor field was blind. Criticism: the patients were few, and long-standing epilepsy may have reorganised their brains. + SPOON APPLE Left visual field Right visual field Left hemisphere speech; right hand Right hemisphere no speech; left hand corpus callosum cut Says "apple" Left hand finds the spoon but cannot name it Figure 5.19 The split-brain test. Each visual field reaches only the opposite hemisphere, so the object seen by the right hemisphere can be found by the left hand but not named. Four conclusions followed. Each hemisphere perceives, learns and remembers independently: shown two pictures at once, each hand fetches the object its own hemisphere saw. Language is not bilateral: in right-handers speech comes from the left hemisphere, and the right cannot speak, though it understands simple words. The right hemisphere is better at spatial tasks. And each hemisphere completes what it sees: shown chimeric figures , photographs joining halves of two different faces, patients of Jerre Levy , Colwyn Trevarthen and Sperry (1972) reported one whole face, naming the right-field half but pointing to the left-field half. In Gazzaniga's best-known demonstration, one patient's left hemisphere saw a chicken claw and his right hemisphere a snow scene; his right hand chose a chicken, his left a shovel. Asked why, he said at once that the shovel was for cleaning out the chicken shed. Gazzaniga called this the left-hemisphere interpreter , which invents plausible reasons for behaviour whose real cause it does not know. A few patients show intermanual conflict : one man's left hand would switch off a television programme he was enjoying. Outside the laboratory both hemispheres share the same eyes, ears and body, and some information crosses through the brainstem or by cross-cueing (one hemisphere signalling to the other with a frown). Cutting the corpus callosum therefore does not kill, blind or abolish language; its cost is difficulty coordinating activities that need both hemispheres. Exam trap An object in the left visual field cannot be named but can be selected with the left hand; the patient is not blind in that eye or field and has not forgotten the object. The Nobel Prize went to Roger Sperry, not to Karl Spencer Lashley (1890 to 1958; the engram, 5.9), Wilder Graves Penfield (1891 to 1976; cortical stimulation mapping and the homunculus, 5.6) or Donald Olding Hebb (1904 to 1985; cell assemblies, 1949). Broca's area and Wernicke's area Lateralisation tells you which side; localisation tells you where within it. Broca's area lies in the left inferior frontal gyrus, in the pars opercularis and pars triangularis (areas 44 and 45, 5.2), just in front of the face area of the primary motor cortex. This frontal-lobe area serves speech production: programming articulation and assembling grammatical sentences. It is not the seat of comprehension, memory consolidation (the hippocampus, 5.9) or motor coordination (the cerebellum, 5.6). In 1874 Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) described patients who spoke fluently but understood little, with damage further back. Wernicke's area is the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (area 22), the classic centre for comprehending spoken and written language. In front of it, in Heschl's gyrus, the primary auditory cortex registers sounds without understanding them. The arcuate fasciculus , a bundle of association fibres, joins the two language areas. Behind Wernicke's area, where the temporal, parietal and occipital lobes meet, the angular gyrus (area 39) links a word's seen form to its sound and meaning, so it is vital for reading. The usual decoys have other jobs: the occipital pole holds primary visual cortex, the postcentral gyrus primary somatosensory cortex, the right parietal lobe spatial attention, and the anterior cingulate attention and error monitoring. Exam trap Ria speaks slowly and laboriously in keywords that make sense. 'Frontal lobe' is true but too broad, and a temporal-lobe (Wernicke's area) lesion leaves speech fluent: the answer is Broca's area , also the site after a left frontal stroke with non-fluent speech. For comprehension the answer is Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus), never the inferior frontal gyrus, Heschl's gyrus or the angular gyrus. The Wernicke-Geschwind model and the dual streams In 1965 Geschwind revived the ideas of Broca, Wernicke and Dejerine as the Wernicke-Geschwind model , a left-hemisphere circuit of seven parts (Figure 5.20). To repeat a heard word, the primary auditory cortex passes the sound to Wernicke's area, where it is understood; the arcuate fasciculus carries it to Broca's area, which selects an articulation programme; and the face area of the motor cortex drives the speech muscles. To read aloud, the primary visual cortex sends the written word to the angular gyrus, which converts it into its auditory code for Wernicke's area, and the same output path follows. Damage to each box or link predicts a particular aphasia. Front Back Motor cortex (face area) Speech Broca's area areas 44, 45 Wernicke's area area 22 arcuate fasciculus Angular gyrus area 39 Auditory cortex Heschl's gyrus Visual cortex area 17 Heard word to speech Extra steps for reading Figure 5.20 The Wernicke-Geschwind model, left hemisphere, front at the left. The solid route repeats a heard word; reading aloud enters by the dashed route and then follows the same output path. The model's limits are serious. Removing Broca's area alone often leaves no lasting aphasia, real lesions are large and include white matter, and almost every aphasic patient has both expressive and receptive problems. Modern research favours the dual-stream model of Gregory Hickok and David Poeppel (2007). A ventral stream along the temporal lobe maps speech sounds onto meaning in both hemispheres; a dorsal stream from the temporoparietal junction to the frontal lobe, including the arcuate fasciculus, maps sounds onto articulation and is strongly left-lateralised. That is why damage to the dorsal route can spare understanding but ruin repetition. Aphasia and its syndromes Aphasia is an acquired disturbance of language function due to organic brain disease, most often a left-hemisphere stroke, and is the common term for all types of language loss. Dysphasia is often used for partial loss, dyslexia is a disorder of reading, and 'lexphasia' is not a term. Aphasia is a disorder of language, not of intellect, abstract thinking or memory, which fail in dementia and amnesia (5.9, 5.11). Clinicians classify aphasias by fluency, comprehension, repetition and naming (Table 5.29). Broca's aphasia (expressive or non-fluent aphasia) is primarily a deficit of speech production. Speech is slow, effortful, poorly articulated and telegraphic, made of content words with the small grammatical words missing ( agrammatism ): 'Yes ... Monday ... Dad and Dick ... Wednesday nine o'clock ... doctors ... and ... teeth.' The keywords make sense, comprehension is relatively preserved, repetition is impaired, and the patient knows it and is frustrated. Right hemiparesis is common because the motor cortex lies next door. Wernicke's aphasia (receptive or fluent aphasia) is the mirror image: fluent, grammatical speech that is empty of meaning, full of paraphasias (wrong words or sounds) and neologisms (invented words), sometimes reaching word salad, with severely impaired comprehension, poor repetition and little awareness. Reading, writing and speech beyond aphasia Alexia is an acquired loss of reading and agraphia of writing. Joseph Jules Dejerine (1849 to 1917) linked alexia with agraphia to the left angular gyrus in 1891, and in 1892 described alexia without agraphia (pure alexia) after damage to the left occipital cortex and the splenium, the rear of the corpus callosum. His patient could write but not read what he had written: words seen by the intact right visual cortex could not cross to the left-hemisphere language areas. Such patients often cannot name colours either. Acalculia is an acquired loss of calculation. Gerstmann syndrome ( Josef Gerstmann , 1920s) follows left angular gyrus damage and combines finger agnosia, left-right confusion, agraphia and acalculia. Not every speech problem is aphasia. Dysarthria is faulty articulation from weak or uncoordinated speech muscles, and apraxia of speech is faulty programming of articulatory movements; in both, language itself is intact. Developmental dyslexia and other language-based learning difficulties are present from childhood despite adequate intelligence and teaching. Their core weakness is phonological, linked to the left perisylvian language network including Broca's area rather than to the occipital lobe (vision), cerebellum (coordination) or amygdala (emotion); the disorders are in Chapter 8. Finally, deaf signers with left-hemisphere damage develop sign-language aphasias of the Broca and Wernicke types, while right-hemisphere damage spares signing: the left hemisphere is specialised for language, not for sound. This section covers how brains are damaged, the major neurological diseases and the classic neuropsychological syndromes. Causes of brain damage Brain damage has six main causes. A brain tumour (neoplasm) is a mass of cells growing independently of the rest of the body. About 20 percent are meningiomas , encapsulated in their own membrane between the meninges, harmful only by pressure and almost always benign. Most others are infiltrating , growing diffusely into brain tissue and usually malignant; gliomas , from glial cells, are the commonest. About 10 percent are metastatic , seeded through the blood from cancers elsewhere, often the lungs. A stroke is a sudden-onset cerebrovascular disorder. Around the dead tissue (the infarct) lies the penumbra , tissue that may recover or die over the next few days and that treatment tries to save. Cerebral haemorrhage is bleeding from a ruptured vessel, often an aneurysm. Cerebral ischaemia is a blocked blood supply, from thrombosis (a plug formed on the spot), embolism (a plug carried from elsewhere) or arteriosclerosis (walls narrowed by fat deposits). Starved neurons release excess glutamate, which overactivates NMDA receptors and floods neighbouring neurons with Na + and Ca 2+ , killing them over a day or two: excitotoxicity (Section 5.3). A closed-head traumatic brain injury leaves the skull intact. A contusion (bruised brain) forms where the brain strikes the skull, at the site of the blow (coup) and often on the opposite side ( contrecoup injury ). Concussion , now called mild traumatic brain injury, disturbs consciousness without structural damage, but repeated ones produce chronic traumatic encephalopathy , the dementia of boxers and American football players. The confused period after a head injury in which new memories are not stored is post-traumatic amnesia ; its length is the best single guide to severity. Infection causes encephalitis (brain inflammation): herpes simplex encephalitis attacks the medial temporal lobes (Clive Wearing, Section 5.9), bacteria cause meningitis, neurosyphilis causes general paresis (psychosis and dementia) and HIV can cause dementia. Neurotoxins include lead, mercury, alcohol (Korsakoff's syndrome, Section 5.9) and antipsychotic drugs (tardive dyskinesia, Section 5.4). Genetic causes include recessive genes, the dominant gene of Huntington's disease and the extra chromosome 21 of Down syndrome. Whatever the cause, neurons die by necrosis , passive swelling and bursting within hours that inflames nearby tissue, or by apoptosis , programmed shrinkage over a day or two without inflammation. Epilepsy Epilepsy is a disorder of recurrent, spontaneous seizures arising from chronic brain dysfunction; a single seizure from a high fever does not count. Neurons discharge in synchronous bursts, often because GABA inhibition fails, and the EEG shows high-amplitude spikes. Many patients first sense an aura (a strange smell, déjà vu), which betrays where the seizure starts. Generalised seizures involve the whole brain, focal (partial) seizures only part of it (Table 5.30). Simple focal seizures are sometimes called Jacksonian after John Hughlings Jackson (1835 to 1911), whose Jacksonian march is jerking that spreads from fingers to arm to face as the discharge crosses the motor homunculus. Complex focal seizures usually begin in the temporal lobe ( temporal lobe epilepsy ) and bring automatisms such as fumbling with buttons. The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) classification of 2017 grades focal seizures by awareness instead: focal aware (simple) and focal impaired awareness (complex). Exam trap Epilepsy is a neurological disorder but not a neurodegenerative one . Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and Huntington's diseases are progressive losses of neurons; epilepsy is episodic, often with normal function between seizures. Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases Parkinson's disease , described in 1817 by James Parkinson (1755 to 1824) as the "shaking palsy", affects 1 to 2 percent of people over 65. Its signs are resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia (slowness) or akinesia (difficulty starting movement), postural instability, a masked face and a shuffling gait; loss of smell and depression may come years earlier, and dementia often follows. Dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta die, so the nigrostriatal pathway no longer delivers dopamine to the striatum (Figure 5.21); in 1960 Oleh Hornykiewicz found the patients' striatum almost empty of dopamine. Surviving nigral neurons hold Lewy bodies , clumps of alpha-synuclein. L-dopa , the dopamine precursor, which unlike dopamine crosses the blood-brain barrier, and dopamine agonists relieve symptoms for some years; deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus helps when drugs fail. In 1982 young drug users in California who injected a "synthetic heroin" contaminated with MPTP developed permanent parkinsonism (reported by J. William Langston in 1983); MPTP destroys nigral dopamine neurons in monkeys too, giving the best animal model of the disease. Exam trap Parkinson's disease is dopamine loss from the substantia nigra pars compacta . It is not degeneration of the locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), raphe nuclei (serotonin), spinal motor neurons (motor neuron disease, polio), hippocampal pyramidal cells (memory) or cholinergic basal forebrain (Alzheimer's), nor a serotonin, acetylcholine or GABA deficiency. The subthalamic nucleus is the stimulation target, not the lesion. Huntington's disease , described by George Huntington in 1872, is rarer (about 1 in 7,500): chorea (jerky, dance-like involuntary movements), psychiatric symptoms and cognitive decline ending in dementia, beginning at about 40. An autosomal dominant expanded CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4 (Section 5.5) kills the GABA neurons of the striatum, caudate first. Parkinson's is hypokinetic, Huntington's hyperkinetic. Alzheimer's disease and other dementias Dementia is an acquired, usually progressive decline of global intellect (memory, abstraction, judgement) that disrupts daily life; its criteria belong to Chapter 8, and "senile dementia" and "atrophy" are vague older labels. The commonest cause is Alzheimer's disease , described in 1906 by Alois Alzheimer (1864 to 1915) in his patient Auguste Deter . Onset is insidious and progression gradual: recent episodic memory fails first, then language (anomia), visuospatial and executive functions. The brain shows amyloid plaques (beta-amyloid, outside cells), neurofibrillary tangles (tau, inside cells) and neuron loss that begins in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus. Death of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert leaves the cortex short of acetylcholine, so treatment uses cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) and memantine , an NMDA receptor antagonist. The APOE e4 allele raises risk; rare early-onset families carry APP or presenilin mutations, and because APP lies on chromosome 21, almost everyone with Down syndrome has plaques and tangles by 40. Exam trap Acetylcholine deficiency means Alzheimer's disease , not "senile dementia", "atrophy" or Korsakoff's syndrome (thiamine deficiency, Section 5.9). Hard scars, sclerotic plaques , form in the white matter, disseminated in time and space . It usually starts in early adulthood with a relapsing-remitting course of visual disturbance, weakness, numbness and fatigue, and is commoner in women and far from the equator. In prosopagnosia (face blindness), faces are seen as faces but not recognised, even those of close family, who are known at once by voice. It follows bilateral or right-sided damage to the fusiform gyrus at the occipitotemporal junction, the fusiform face area identified by Nancy Kanwisher and colleagues in 1997. Simultanagnosia , seeing only one object at a time, is part of Bálint's syndrome after bilateral posterior parietal damage. Anosognosia ( Joseph Babinski , 1914) is unawareness of one's own deficit. Astereognosis is failure to recognise objects by touch, and auditory agnosia failure to recognise sounds. Exam trap Prosopagnosia is inability to recognise faces . The IHBAS 2024 key gives "distinguish tastes", which is wrong (loss of taste is ageusia); it is also not loss of facial expression or of object recognition. Face-recognition loss after a stroke is an agnosia , not aphasia, apraxia or ataxia, and prosopagnosia beats the broader "visual agnosia". The lesion is fusiform, not in the primary motor cortex (movement), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (executive function) or cerebellar vermis (balance). Apraxia ( Hugo Liepmann , 1900) is inability to perform learned purposeful movements despite intact strength, sensation, coordination and comprehension. In ideomotor apraxia the patient cannot mime an act on command (show how you use a comb) though he does it naturally; in ideational apraxia he cannot sequence the steps of an act such as brushing his hair. Constructional apraxia spoils copying and block building, dressing apraxia putting on clothes. The lesion is usually left parietal or frontal. Exam trap "Impairment in motor performance and coordination" is dyspraxia (developmental coordination disorder; Amity 2023 key). Apraxia is acquired loss of skilled movement with coordination intact; ataxia is cerebellar incoordination; anomia is failure to name, alexia to read. Hemispatial neglect After right posterior parietal damage, patients with hemispatial neglect ignore the left side of space and of their own body. They eat from the right of the plate, shave only the right side of the face, bisect lines to the right and miss left targets on cancellation tests (Figure 5.22). In extinction , a left stimulus is noticed alone but missed when paired with a right one, and anosognosia is common. Left neglect is far commoner and more severe than right neglect, because the right hemisphere attends to both sides of space. Neglect is inattention, not blindness: in homonymous hemianopia the patient knows half the visual field is lost and compensates. Bilateral damage to primary visual cortex causes cortical blindness (bilateral homonymous hemianopia), sometimes denied in Anton's syndrome ; hemiplegia (one-sided paralysis) follows motor cortex or internal capsule damage. Phineas Gage and the prefrontal syndromes Key study: Phineas Gage (1848) In 1848 an explosion drove a tamping iron through the left cheek and frontal lobe of Phineas Gage (1823 to 1860), a 25-year-old railway construction foreman in Vermont. His speech, memory and intelligence survived, but the reliable foreman became impulsive, profane and poor in judgement, and soon lost his job. His physician John Martyn Harlow reported the case in 1848 and, in 1868, that friends found him "no longer Gage". In 1994 Hanna Damasio and colleagues reconstructed the injury from his skull and placed it in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex . Criticism: the record is thin, and Gage later drove stagecoaches in Chile for several years before dying in San Francisco, so he may have partly recovered. Gage is the classic evidence that the frontal lobes govern personality and social behaviour. Damage to different prefrontal regions produces different frontal lobe syndromes (Table 5.33). Dorsolateral damage causes the dysexecutive syndrome : executive functions (planning, sequencing, set-shifting and inhibition, using working memory) break down, and the patient shows perseveration , repeating a response after it has stopped working. In the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test of David Grant and Esta Berg (1948) cards are sorted by colour, shape or number, the rule being learned only from feedback and changed without warning; in 1963 Brenda Milner showed that frontal patients keep sorting by the old rule. Planning is tested by the Tower of London of Tim Shallice (1982), inhibition by the Stroop test, and verbal fluency by naming words that begin with a given letter. The Wisconsin test detects dorsolateral dysfunction, not hippocampal (long-term declarative memory), motor cortex or cerebellar damage, colour perception (visual cortex) or reflexes (spinal cord). Orbitofrontal damage gives disinhibition, not pure aphasia, cortical blindness or hemiplegia. Impaired executive function is the hallmark of the frontal lobe syndrome, not of obsessive-compulsive disorder, catatonic schizophrenia (Chapter 8) or temporal lobe epilepsy. Recovery and plasticity after damage When an axon is cut, its distal segment breaks up within days ( anterograde degeneration , or Wallerian degeneration, after Augustus Waller , 1850), while retrograde degeneration creeps back to the cell body. Peripheral axons often regenerate , guided by Schwann cells; central axons rarely do, blocked by oligodendrocyte inhibitors and glial scars. Instead, healthy neighbouring axons grow branches into vacated synapses ( collateral sprouting ), and neighbouring cortex takes over lost territory ( cortical reorganisation ). Recovery is best with small lesions and young patients, and people with high cognitive reserve (roughly, education and intelligence) compensate better. In constraint-induced movement therapy ( Edward Taub , 1993) a stroke patient's good arm is restrained while the weak arm is trained intensively, enlarging its cortical representation. Loewi's Two Frog Hearts, Revisited Every section of this chapter has passed through Loewi's laboratory. The nerve he stimulated was the vagus, the main parasympathetic nerve, whose rest-and-digest outflow slows the heart (5.1). The slowing was a chemical message crossing a synapse: acetylcholine binding to receptors and then broken down by acetylcholinesterase (5.3). Drugs act by imitating, boosting or blocking such messages (5.4), and Loewi's logic of changing one thing and measuring another runs through the methods of 5.5. The opposite state, the pounding heart of fear, belongs to the sympathetic division and the adrenal medulla (5.7). His idea surfaced at night, out of sleep (5.8). And when Alzheimer's disease strips the cortex of acetylcholine, the drugs prescribed are cholinesterase inhibitors, which keep Vagusstoff working longer (5.11). Chapter summary 5.1 Biopsychology and the Organisation of the Nervous System. The biological perspective explains behaviour through the body, brain and nervous system. Biopsychology (Pinel) has six divisions and progresses by converging operations ; Descartes's dualism opposes monism. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; the PNS has somatic (voluntary) and autonomic divisions. The sympathetic division (fight or flight, Cannon 1915; T1 to L2; adrenal medulla) spends energy; the parasympathetic (rest and digest; craniosacral; vagus; acetylcholine) conserves it. A reflex arc runs afferent neuron, interneuron, efferent neuron. White matter is myelinated axons; PNS cell-body clusters are ganglia; dorsal roots are sensory, ventral roots motor. Twelve cranial nerves, the meninges, CSF and the blood-brain barrier complete the map. 5.2 The Brain: Brainstem, Diencephalon and Cerebral Cortex. The embryonic forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain become five divisions: telencephalon (cortex, limbic system, basal ganglia, corpus callosum ), diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus), mesencephalon, metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla). The medulla holds the vital centres for breathing and heart rate; the cerebellum coordinates movement and balance; the reticular activating system maintains arousal (Moruzzi and Magoun, 1949). The thalamus relays every sense except smell, and the hypothalamus governs homeostasis through the pituitary. Six-layered neocortex, about 90 percent of cortex, serves higher cognition across frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes, mapped by Brodmann (1909); commissural, association and projection fibres connect it. 5.3 Neurons, Neural Conduction, Synapses and Neurotransmitters. The neuron is the basic unit of the nervous system (Cajal's neuron doctrine; Nobel 1906, shared with Golgi); glia include astrocytes, microglia and the myelin makers, oligodendrocytes (CNS) and Schwann cells (PNS). The resting potential, about -70 mV, rests on K+ permeability and the pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in). Summed EPSPs reaching threshold fire an all-or-none action potential (Na+ in, K+ out, peak about +50 mV), then refractory periods. Myelin gives fast saltatory conduction . Ca2+ influx triggers release; ionotropic and metabotropic receptors respond; reuptake or enzymes clear the transmitter. Glutamate excites, GABA inhibits, acetylcholine drives muscle, monoamines arise in brainstem nuclei, and endorphins control pain. 5.4 Drugs, Reward and Psychopharmacology. Psychoactive drugs act as agonists or antagonists at synapses. Tolerance (metabolic, functional, cross and conditioned, as in Siegel's 1982 heroin study) and withdrawal are distinct from addiction. Benzodiazepines raise the frequency and barbiturates the duration of GABA-A channel opening; heroin is a semisynthetic opioid; THC acts at CB1 receptors. Olds and Milner (1954) found self-stimulation sites in the septal area, and the mesolimbic pathway (VTA to nucleus accumbens) is the core reward circuit. Antipsychotics block D2, and nigrostriatal blockade causes extrapyramidal effects ending in tardive dyskinesia. SSRIs work after 2 to 4 weeks; lithium (Cade 1949) is the gold-standard mood stabiliser; disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase. 5.5 Research Methods, Behaviour Genetics and the Developing Brain. Structural imaging (contrast X-ray, CT , MRI , DTI) shows anatomy; functional imaging ( PET , SPECT , the BOLD signal of fMRI, fNIRS) shows activity, and paired-image subtraction revealed the default mode network , active at rest. EEG has the best temporal resolution, and averaging it yields ERPs such as the P300 to oddball targets. Lesions, stimulation (DBS, TMS, optogenetics), microdialysis, knockouts and CRISPR-Cas9 manipulate the brain. Mendelian inheritance and epigenetics underlie twin, adoption, linkage and GWAS designs, heritability and endophenotypes. PKU, Huntington's, fragile X, Down, Turner, Klinefelter and Prader-Willi syndromes show genetic errors. The neural tube forms at gastrulation; pruning, myelination and neuroplasticity continue for years. 5.6 Sensory Pathways and the Motor System. Sensory systems transduce energy, build receptive fields and climb from receptors through thalamic relays to primary, secondary and association cortex. In the inverted retina, lateral inhibition sharpens edges and creates Mach bands. Nasal fibres cross at the optic chiasm ; the LGN's magnocellular layers carry motion, its parvocellular layers colour and detail, to V1, whose damage gives contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing. Dorsal 'where/how' and ventral 'what' streams leave V1. Hair cells, two somatosensory pathways and PAG analgesia complete the senses. Corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation ; mirror neurons fire for doing and watching; the basal ganglia select actions and the cerebellum corrects errors. 5.7 The Endocrine System, Stress and the Emotional Brain. Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood; exocrine glands use ducts. Hormones are amino acid derivatives, peptides or steroids. The hypothalamus controls the pituitary , the master gland: releasing hormones reach the anterior lobe (GH, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, prolactin) through portal blood, while oxytocin and vasopressin, made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, travel down axons to the posterior lobe. The adrenals run stress: the fast SAM system releases adrenaline, and the slower HPA axis (CRH, ACTH, cortisol) is braked by negative feedback. Allostasis is stability through change. Sham rage, the Papez circuit and the limbic system led to the amygdala , the hub of fear. 5.8 Sleep, Biological Rhythms, Hunger, Thirst and Sex. Circadian rhythms are timed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract, which drives night-time melatonin from the pineal gland. Sleep EEG runs from beta and alpha waking through theta (N1) and spindles (N2) to delta slow-wave sleep (N3); REM is paradoxical, with a waking-like EEG and atonia. Sleep begins when the VLPO inhibits the arousal systems; adenosine builds sleep pressure, and orexin, lost in narcolepsy, holds waking. Ghrelin starts hunger, CCK and leptin bring satiety, VMH lesions cause obesity and LH lesions aphagia, and arcuate NPY neurons trigger eating. Masters and Johnson described excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution. 5.9 The Biology of Learning, Memory and Amnesia. Amnesia is a pathological loss of memory: anterograde (no new memories after the onset) or retrograde (loss of earlier memories, worst for recent ones, Ribot's law). Lashley's search for Semon's engram found memories distributed across the cortex, which Hebb explained with cell assemblies. H.M.'s bilateral medial temporal lobectomy (1953) showed that the hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories but not skills; R.B., place and grid cells, K.C. and Clive Wearing refined the picture, and the amygdala strengthens emotional memories. Korsakoff's syndrome follows thiamine deficiency and damages the mammillary bodies and mediodorsal thalamus. At the synapse, NMDA-dependent LTP strengthens and LTD weakens connections, while dopamine signals reward prediction errors. 5.10 Lateralisation, the Split Brain and Language. Dax (1836) and Broca (1861, patient Leborgne, 'Tan') tied language to the left, dominant hemisphere; the Wada test (1949) and Kimura's dichotic listening right-ear advantage (1961) confirm it in about 95 percent of right-handers and most left-handers. The right hemisphere leads in visuospatial processing, faces, music and emotional prosody . Split-brain studies (Myers and Sperry 1953; Sperry and Gazzaniga, Nobel 1981) showed each hemisphere working independently. Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus, areas 44 and 45) serves speech production; Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus, area 22) comprehension. Aphasia is acquired language loss from organic brain disease: Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction, global, transcortical and anomic types. 5.11 Brain Damage, Neurodegeneration and Neuropsychological Syndromes. Brain damage comes from tumours (encapsulated meningiomas , infiltrating gliomas, metastases), strokes (haemorrhage or ischaemia, with glutamate excitotoxicity in the penumbra ), closed-head injury (contusions, contrecoup, chronic traumatic encephalopathy), infections, neurotoxins and genes; neurons die by necrosis or apoptosis. Epilepsy (tonic-clonic, absence, focal seizures) is neurological but not neurodegenerative. Parkinson's disease is dopamine loss from the substantia nigra pars compacta; Huntington's disease kills striatal GABA neurons; Alzheimer's disease brings plaques, tangles and acetylcholine loss. Multiple sclerosis is autoimmune demyelination. Agnosia (prosopagnosia), apraxia, right parietal left neglect and the prefrontal syndromes (Gage, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test) complete the section. Which of the following is the correct path of a reflex arc? (Amity 2023) a Afferent neuron to interneuron to afferent neuron b Afferent neuron to afferent neuron to interneuron c Afferent neuron to interneuron to efferent neuron d Efferent neuron to interneuron to the brain ✓ Answer: (c) Afferent neuron to interneuron to efferent neuron Spinal reflex arc The concept How it works The signal enters the spinal cord by a sensory ( afferent ) neuron, crosses an interneuron in the grey matter and leaves by a motor ( efferent ) neuron to the effector. Exam tip Afferent arrives, efferent exits. The knee-jerk even skips the interneuron. Why the other options are wrong (a) Afferent neuron to interneuron to afferent neuron Ends in an afferent neuron; an arc must end in an efferent neuron to reach the effector. (b) Afferent neuron to afferent neuron to interneuron Two afferent neurons and no way out; the arc must end in an efferent neuron. (d) Efferent neuron to interneuron to the brain Runs to the brain, but the arc closes in the spinal cord , not the brain. White matter is primarily composed of (JEMAS 2025) a Myelinated axons. b Myelinated dendrites. c Cell bodies. d Unmyelinated axons. ✓ Answer: (a) Myelinated axons Myelin and white matter The concept Why white The fat of the myelin sheath around axons makes the tissue look white. The contrast Grey matter is made of cell bodies and unmyelinated axons. Why the other options are wrong (b) Myelinated dendrites. Dendrites are not myelinated, so they cannot make white matter. (c) Cell bodies. Cell bodies make up grey matter , not white. (d) Unmyelinated axons. Unmyelinated axons belong to grey matter ; without myelin there is no white. What it does It keeps the cortex awake and alert; its destruction causes coma . Why the other options are wrong (a) Fine motor coordination Belongs to the cerebellum , not the RAS. (c) Emotional memory Belongs to the amygdala . (d) Balance and posture Belongs to the cerebellum . Which brain structure would most likely result in death if damaged? (Amity 2023) a Cerebellum b Medulla c Reticular formation d Pons ✓ Answer: (b) Medulla Medulla oblongata, vital centres The concept Why this one The medulla oblongata holds the vital centres for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, so its damage is the most likely to kill. Why the other options are wrong (a) Cerebellum Cerebellar damage causes ataxia , not death. (c) Reticular formation Reticular damage causes coma ; the vital centres sit in the medulla. (d) Pons Helps set the breathing rhythm but is not the main vital centre. (Real PYQ 2025) a Cerebellum b Hypothalamus c Thalamus d Brainstem ✓ Answer: (b) Hypothalamus Hypothalamus, homeostasis The concept What it does The hypothalamus controls the autonomic nervous system and directs the pituitary . Why this one So it integrates neural and hormonal control of the body for homeostasis . Why the other options are wrong (a) Cerebellum Coordinates movement , not endocrine or autonomic control. (c) Thalamus The sensory relay , not an integrator of body systems. (d) Brainstem Carries out autonomic reflexes without integrating them with the endocrine system. (JEMAS 2025) a Norepinephrine b GABA c Dopamine d Epinephrine ✓ Answer: (b) GABA GABA, main inhibitory transmitter The concept What it is GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter of the brain. (d) Epinephrine Adrenaline , a catecholamine; none of these is the standard inhibitory transmitter. Which of the following is NOT a type of glial cell? Key note Strictly it is also a catecholamine neurotransmitter , released by a few adrenergic brainstem neurons, so treat this as an odd-one-out question. Why the other options are wrong (a) Dopamine A classic brain monoamine transmitter. (b) Serotonin A classic brain monoamine transmitter. (c) Nor-epinephrine Noradrenaline , a classic brain monoamine transmitter. (d) Hypnotics A broad functional label that also covers alcohol and barbiturates, not a chemical class. Which of the following substances is NOT a natural alkaloid compound? A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia has been on antipsychotic medication for years. This condition is most likely: (Real PYQ 2024) a Akathisia b Acute Dystonia c Tardive Dyskinesia d Parkinsonism ✓ Answer: (c) Tardive Dyskinesia Tardive dyskinesia, late extrapyramidal effect The concept What it is Involuntary orofacial movements after months or years of neuroleptic treatment are tardive dyskinesia ( tardive means late). (RML 2025) a fMRI b PET scan c EEG d CT scan ✓ Answer: (c) EEG EEG, millisecond temporal resolution The concept Why this one EEG records the brain's electrical activity directly, so it follows changes millisecond by millisecond . Key term Temporal resolution is how precisely a method tracks when activity happens. Why the other options are wrong (a) fMRI Depends on a blood-flow response that takes seconds. (b) PET scan Depends on tracer uptake over a minute or more. (d) CT scan A still structural image with no temporal resolution at all. (Real PYQ 2025) a Urea b Tyrosine c Tryptophan d Histidine ✓ Answer: (b) Tyrosine Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (PKU) The concept How it works Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine into tyrosine . A male child presents with tall stature, small testes, and learning difficulties. Karyotype analysis shows an extra X chromosome. This condition is : (IHBAS 2025) a Klinefelter syndrome b Turner syndrome c Prader-Willi syndrome d Down syndrome ✓ Answer: (a) Klinefelter syndrome Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY The concept What it is Klinefelter syndrome is an extra X in a male ( 47,XXY ). The Mach bands phenomenon is best explained by : (IHBAS 2025) a Rod-cone dichotomy in the fovea b Opponent-process theory of color vision c Lateral inhibition in the retina d Temporal summation in photoreceptors ✓ Answer: (c) Lateral inhibition in the retina Lateral inhibition, Mach bands The concept Key term Lateral inhibition means neighbouring retinal cells suppress each other. How it works At a light-dark border, cells on the bright side receive less inhibition from their dark neighbours and cells on the dark side receive more. The result The edge is exaggerated into a brighter and a darker strip: the Mach bands . Why the other options are wrong (a) Rod-cone dichotomy in the fovea Concerns dim-light versus colour vision , not edges. (b) Opponent-process theory of color vision Explains colour coding and afterimages, not brightness at an edge. (d) Temporal summation in photoreceptors The adding of weak signals over time , not contrast at an edge. (d) Visual Field Defects Blind areas caused by damage to the visual pathway , not focusing errors. Which of the following areas of the brain is involved in controlling movements of the body? (Amity 2023) a Primary b Secondary c Supplementary d All of the above ✓ Answer: (d) All of the above Motor cortex hierarchy The concept The executor Movement is controlled by a hierarchy. Primary motor cortex (area 4, precentral gyrus) is the main cortical output. The planners Secondary motor cortex , the premotor cortex and supplementary motor area , programmes the patterns of movement that primary cortex executes. Why all No single area does the job alone. Why the other options are wrong (a) Primary The main output, but it executes patterns the secondary areas programme. (b) Secondary Programmes movement patterns but needs primary cortex to execute them. (c) Supplementary Part of secondary motor cortex; it programmes movement but does not act alone . (d) Reticular formation Serves arousal ; it does not consolidate memory. According to Karl Lashley's research on memory storage, where did he conclude that memories are primarily stored in the brain? (Real PYQ 2025) a In specific localized brain regions dedicated to particular memories b Distributed throughout the entire brain cortex c Exclusively in the hippocampus d Only in the frontal and temporal lobes ✓ Answer: (b) Distributed throughout the entire brain cortex Karl Lashley, mass action and equipotentiality The concept The finding No cortical lesion erased a maze habit in Lashley 's rats; he found no localised engram . Two principles The deficit depended on how much cortex was removed ( mass action ), not where ( equipotentiality ). Why the other options are wrong (a) In specific localized brain regions dedicated to particular memories The opposite of his result: he found no localised engram . (c) Exclusively in the hippocampus The hippocampus 's role in forming memories emerged only later, with H.M. (d) Only in the frontal and temporal lobes The deficit depended on how much cortex was removed, not which lobes. The cost The hemispheres cannot share information , which shows up in tasks needing both. Why the other options are wrong (a) Die Patients stay alive after the surgery. (b) Become blind Patients stay sighted . (c) Be unable to speak or understand language Patients can still speak, because the left hemisphere still speaks. Ria has difficulty enunciating words correctly and speaks in a slow and laboured way; her speech often makes sense, but it includes only keywords. Which part of her brain is damaged? (RML 2022) a Wernicke's area b Broca's area c Temporal lobe d Frontal lobe ✓ Answer: (b) Broca's area Broca's (non-fluent) aphasia The concept Why this one Slow, effortful, telegraphic speech that still makes sense is Broca's (non-fluent) aphasia . Why the other options are wrong (a) Wernicke's area Damage here gives fluent, empty speech with poor comprehension, the opposite pattern. (c) Temporal lobe Damage here gives fluent, empty speech with poor comprehension. (d) Frontal lobe True but too broad ; Broca's area is the specific answer. Prosopagnosia results in an inability to : (IHBAS 2024) a Recognize faces b Distinguish tastes c Express feelings through facial expressions d Recognize objects ✓ Answer: (a) Recognize faces Prosopagnosia, fusiform gyrus damage The concept What it is Prosopagnosia is a visual agnosia for faces after fusiform gyrus damage. Key note The source key gives (b), which is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (b) Distinguish tastes Loss of taste is ageusia ; the source key's choice here is an error. (c) Express feelings through facial expressions A motor sign, like the masked face of Parkinson's disease. (d) Recognize objects Failure to recognise objects is object agnosia , not the face-specific form. A patient presents with an inability to perform coordinated, purposeful movements, despite having intact motor function, sensation, and comprehension of the task. When asked to brush their hair, they cannot sequence the movements. This deficit is best described as: (Real PYQ 2024) a Agnosia b Ataxia c Apraxia d Alexia ✓ Answer: (c) Apraxia Apraxia (ideational type) The concept What it is Apraxia is loss of learned purposeful movement with strength, sensation, coordination and comprehension intact. This case It is ideational apraxia: the steps cannot be sequenced. Why the other options are wrong (a) Agnosia A failure of recognition , not of movement. (b) Ataxia Cerebellar incoordination, but coordination is intact here. (d) Alexia Loss of reading . Which of the following neurological conditions is NOT classified as a neurodegenerative disorder? (Real PYQ 2025) a Parkinson's disease b Alzheimer's disease c Epilepsy d Huntington's disease ✓ Answer: (c) Epilepsy Epilepsy, an episodic disorder The concept What it is Epilepsy is recurrent seizures from synchronous neural discharge . Why this one It is an episodic disorder with normal function between attacks, not a progressive loss of neurons. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Parkinson's disease Neurodegenerative: progressive loss of substantia nigra dopamine neurons. (b) Alzheimer's disease Neurodegenerative: progressive loss of cortical and hippocampal neurons. (d) Huntington's disease Neurodegenerative: progressive loss of striatal GABA neurons. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Korsakoff's syndrome is caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, classically in chronic alcoholism; it damages the mammillary bodies and mediodorsal thalamus and causes dense anterograde amnesia, severe retrograde amnesia and confabulation. asked 13 times Extrapyramidal side effects come from D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway and appear in order: acute dystonia (hours to days), akathisia (days to weeks, inner restlessness), parkinsonism (weeks) and tardive dyskinesia (months to years, orofacial movements, may be irreversible); akathisia is a secondary movement disorder. asked 10 times Damage to Broca's area (left inferior frontal gyrus, pars opercularis and triangularis, areas 44 and 45) causes Broca's aphasia: non-fluent, effortful, telegraphic speech with relatively preserved comprehension and impaired repetition. asked 9 times The hippocampus consolidates new declarative (especially episodic and spatial) memories; its damage, as after a head injury, causes anterograde amnesia while remote memories survive. asked 8 times The ANS has two divisions: the sympathetic mediates fight or flight (Walter Cannon, 1915) together with the adrenal medulla, which releases adrenaline, and spends energy; the parasympathetic (rest and digest) conserves energy, slowing the heart and constricting the pupils mainly through the vagus nerve and acetylcholine. asked 7 times The limbic system , named by Paul MacLean in 1952, is the classic seat of emotion, regulating emotion, motivation and memory; hunger and thirst belong to the hypothalamus. asked 7 times The adrenal glands run the stress response: the cortex releases cortisol at the end of the HPA axis (hypothalamus CRH, anterior pituitary ACTH, adrenal cortex cortisol, with negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary), and the medulla releases adrenaline, also called epinephrine. asked 7 times The ventromedial hypothalamus was the satiety centre: its lesions cause hyperphagia and obesity (Hetherington and Ranson, 1940), whereas lateral hypothalamus lesions cause aphagia and adipsia (Anand and Brobeck, 1951). asked 7 times H.M. (Henry Molaison) had both medial temporal lobes (hippocampus, amygdala, adjacent cortex) removed by William Scoville in 1953; he was left with severe anterograde amnesia for declarative memory but improved at mirror drawing (preserved procedural memory). asked 7 times The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia: mesolimbic dopamine (D2) hyperactivity produces positive symptoms and mesocortical hypoactivity negative symptoms; its original support was that typical antipsychotics' clinical potency correlates with their D2 affinity. asked 6 times The amygdala is the key structure for fear, aggression, threat detection and fear conditioning; not the locus coeruleus, raphe nuclei or cholinergic basal forebrain. asked 6 times The mesolimbic pathway , from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum), is the core reward pathway of addiction, and dopamine is the reward transmitter. asked 5 times Oxytocin and vasopressin (ADH) are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary; neither oxytocin nor melatonin is an anterior pituitary hormone. asked 5 times Long-term potentiation (Bliss and Lømo, 1973) is a lasting strengthening of synaptic transmission after high-frequency stimulation; its induction needs NMDA receptors, which pass calcium only when glutamate binds and the depolarised membrane expels their magnesium block. asked 5 times Wernicke's area is the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (area 22), the classic region for comprehending spoken and written language; damage gives fluent, empty speech with poor comprehension. asked 5 times The medulla oblongata (hindbrain) holds the vital centres for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure; its damage is the brain injury most likely to cause death. asked 4 times GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter of the brain (glycine in the spinal cord); glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter of the CNS. asked 4 times All-or-none law : once threshold is reached, an action potential fires at full, constant amplitude whatever the stimulus strength, and intensity is coded by firing frequency; EPSPs, IPSPs and the resting potential do not obey it. asked 4 times Saltatory conduction : in myelinated axons the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, where voltage-gated Na+ channels cluster;
