title: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 6: Developmental Psychology
text: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 6: Developmental Psychology Chapter 6 of the one-volume Final Exam Textbook, all nine JSS subjects in one book. Both A4 PDFs hold the whole book with the same page numbers. A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (975 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (975 pages) Chapter 6 Developmental Psychology In this chapter 6.1 Foundations: The Lifespan View, Key Issues and Ecological Contexts : Define development, growth and maturation, explain the lifespan perspective, the principles and enduring issues of development and the difference between critical and sensitive periods, and place a child's settings in Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems. 6.2 Heredity, Prenatal Development, Birth and the Newborn : Explain how genes are inherited and expressed, how heredity and environment are separated and combined, how prenatal development unfolds and what threatens it, and how the newborn is assessed, including the Apgar scale and the newborn reflexes. 6.3 Infancy: Brain, Body, Motor Skills and Perception : Describe growth and brain development in infancy, apply the principles, milestones and theories of motor development, explain how infant perception is studied and what it reveals (senses, visual cliff, affordances), and order the early learning, imitation and milestone sequence. 6.4 Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development : Explain Piaget's constructivist theory, from schemes, assimilation, accommodation and equilibration through the four stages and their landmark tasks (object permanence, conservation, the pendulum), and judge how later research and postformal theorists have revised it. 6.5 Vygotsky, Bruner, Information Processing and Theory of Mind : Explain Vygotsky's sociocultural theory (the zone of proximal development, scaffolding, private speech) and how it differs from Piaget's, Bruner's modes of representation, the information-processing view of development, and how theory of mind and social perspective taking develop. 6.6 Emotional Development, Temperament and Self-Regulation : Trace emotional development from Bridges' first emotions through the self-conscious emotions, stranger and separation anxiety and the still face, and classify temperament (Thomas and Chess, Rothbart and Bates, Kagan) and self-regulation (Kopp, Mischel's marshmallow test). 6.7 Attachment: Imprinting, Bowlby, Ainsworth and Beyond : Explain why infants form attachments, trace the phases of attachment over the first three years, classify Strange Situation patterns by reunion behaviour, and weigh the evidence on deprivation, culture and adult attachment. 6.8 Parenting, Family, Play and Gender in Childhood : Compare Baumrind's parenting styles on demandingness and responsiveness, recognise the forms of maltreatment and neglect, trace how play develops from Piaget to Parten, and explain how children acquire gender through socialisation, Kohlberg's stages and gender schemas. 6.9 Moral Development: Piaget, Kohlberg, Gilligan and Beyond : Trace moral development from Piaget's heteronomous and autonomous morality through Kohlberg's three levels and six stages, place any moral reason at its level, and weigh the critiques from Gilligan, cross-cultural research and later theories. 6.10 Erikson's Psychosocial Stages, Identity and Adolescence : Name all eight of Erikson's psychosocial stages with their ages, crises, virtues and maldevelopments, and explain adolescent identity (Marcia's statuses), Elkind's adolescent egocentrism, puberty and the adolescent brain, and modern views of adolescence. 6.11 Adulthood, Ageing, Death and Dying : Trace adult development from emerging adulthood through midlife and old age to death and grief, naming the theorist behind each stage model, type of marriage and theory of ageing, and telling the climacteric apart from general physical ageing. Weightage. 230 of the 3180 questions mapped in this book (7.2%) test this chapter, 101 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 11 sections is High yield. Southern France, January 1800. On a winter morning a boy walked out of the woods near the village of Saint-Sernin-sur-Rance, in the district of Aveyron, looking for food. He was naked but for the rags of a shirt, scarred, about twelve years old, and he could not speak. Local people had glimpsed a wild child in the forests for years, and more than once he had been caught and had escaped. This time he stayed. Within months he was in Paris, the most talked-about child in France, and learned men came to see what a human being is like when society has had no hand in shaping him. The verdict of the greatest authority was harsh. Philippe Pinel , reformer of the Paris asylums, examined the boy and judged him an incurable idiot, perhaps abandoned because he was defective from birth. A 26-year-old physician at the Paris institution for deaf-mutes, Jean-Marc-Gaspard Itard , disagreed. The boy, he argued, was backward because he had grown up alone; give him the experiences he had missed and he would become fully human. Itard named him Victor and, with his carer Madame Guérin, worked with him daily for about five years, training his senses, his attention and his feelings, and trying above all to teach him language. The results, reported in 1801 and 1806, were mixed. Victor came to recognise written words, follow instructions, show affection for Madame Guérin and protest when he was punished unjustly. But he never learned to speak more than a word or two, and Itard ended the lessons disappointed. Victor lived quietly with Madame Guérin in Paris until his death in 1828, aged about forty. Was his failure born or made, and had the teaching simply come too late? This chapter gives you the tools to answer. 6.1 Foundations: The Lifespan View, Key Issues and Ecological Contexts Lower yield · 13 Qs Before the story of how a fertilised cell becomes an ageing adult, you need its frame: what developmental change means, what drives it, the questions still argued over, and the contexts in which every child grows. The science of change and stability Developmental psychology is the scientific study of change and stability from conception to death. It takes the developmental perspective , the approach concerned with the changes that occur as people mature. The other perspectives of Section 1.2 ask other questions: the psychoanalytic about unconscious conflicts rooted in childhood, the biological about genes, brain and hormones, and the humanistic about free choice and self-actualisation. Keep two kinds of change apart. Growth is quantitative change, an increase in size or amount: height, weight, vocabulary. Development is qualitative change in structure and organisation, an orderly, progressive series of changes towards maturity: the child does not just know more words but starts combining them into sentences. Change runs through three interacting domains: physical (body, brain, motor skills), cognitive (memory, language, thinking) and psychosocial, or socioemotional (emotions, personality, relationships). The lifespan is divided into periods, but the divisions are a social construction, an idea a society shares rather than a fact of nature: adolescence became a recognised stage only with industrialisation. Indian courses follow Elizabeth Hurlock (1898 to 1988), whose Developmental Psychology: A Life-Span Approach marks ten periods (Table 6.1). Table 6.1 Hurlock's ten periods of the lifespan. Period Age span Period Age span 1 Prenatal Conception to birth 6 Puberty 10 or 12 to 13 or 14 2 Infancy Birth to 2 weeks 7 Adolescence 13 or 14 to 18 3 Babyhood 2 weeks to 2 years 8 Early adulthood 18 to 40 4 Early childhood 2 to 6 years 9 Middle age 40 to 60 5 Late childhood 6 to 10 or 12 10 Old age 60 onward Older texts treated development as ending with adolescence. Paul Baltes (1939 to 2006) countered in 1987 with the lifespan perspective : development is lifelong (no age holds supremacy), multidimensional (physical, cognitive and social strands), multidirectional (some abilities rise while others fall), plastic (open to change at every age), contextual (embedded in history and culture) and multidisciplinary , and every age brings both gains and losses (an older adult loses speed but may gain wisdom). Baltes named three kinds of influence. Normative age-graded influences are tied to age and shared by most people (puberty, retirement). Normative history-graded influences are shared by a cohort, a generation, because of when it lived (Partition, the COVID-19 pandemic). Non-normative influences are unusual events in one life (a parent's early death). Longitudinal, cross-sectional and cross-sequential designs, which separate age changes from cohort effects, are in Chapter 9; infant research methods are in Section 6.3. From philosophers to baby biographies Two philosophers framed the debate. John Locke (1632 to 1704) held that the newborn mind is a tabula rasa , a blank slate written on by experience: the root of the nurture view. Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712 to 1778), in Émile (1762), saw the child as a noble savage, born good, whose natural plan of growth unfolds in stages: the root of the nature, maturation and stage views. Scientific observation began with the baby biography , a detailed diary of one child. Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) published one on his first son in 1877, and Wilhelm Preyer (1841 to 1897) followed with The Mind of the Child (1882), often taken as the start of scientific child psychology. G. Stanley Hall (1844 to 1924) led the child study movement with questionnaires given to large numbers of children; his Adolescence (1904) called the teens a time of storm and stress (Section 6.10) and proposed recapitulation , the idea that each child's development replays the evolutionary history of the species. Hall's student Arnold Gesell (1880 to 1961) took the normative approach , observing many children to find the typical age, or norm, of each behaviour. Against him stood the behaviourist John B. Watson (1878 to 1958), who boasted that he could train any healthy infant into any kind of specialist. Maturation and learning Gesell's lasting idea is maturation , the biological unfolding of genetic potential: changes that appear on a genetic timetable with little dependence on practice. Learning is change through experience and practice. Maturation supplies readiness; learning builds on it. Three terms that depend on experience are not maturation: socialisation , acquiring the values, norms and behaviour of one's society; accommodation, Jean Piaget's term for changing a mental scheme to fit new information (Section 6.4); and conditioning, learning by association (Section 1.6). Key study: Gesell and Thompson's co-twin control (1929) Can practice hurry an unready body? Gesell and Helen Thompson studied identical twin girls, T and C, holding heredity constant: the method of co-twin control . Twin T practised stair climbing daily for six weeks from 46 weeks of age. Twin C's training began only at 53 weeks, yet after two weeks she had caught up. Maturation, not early training, set the pace. Criticism: one pair of twins and a narrow set of skills. Myrtle McGraw (1899 to 1988) refined the point in Growth: A Study of Johnny and Jimmy (1935). Intensive training from infancy did not hurry Johnny's phylogenetic skills, those common to the species (crawling, walking), but it advanced ontogenetic skills particular to the individual (swimming, roller skating) once he was ready; his twin Jimmy was left untrained. So a child's increasing skill at using his muscles is due mainly to maturation, not to the opportunity to exercise, pushing by parents or learning. Gesell turned such observations into age norms and developmental schedules for motor, adaptive, language and personal-social behaviour (the scales are in Chapter 2). Exam trap "The biological unfolding of genetic potential" is maturation (Gesell), never socialisation, accommodation or conditioning. A child's growing muscular skill is credited to maturation , not exercise, parental pushing or learning. Growth is quantitative (size, amount); development is qualitative (structure, organisation). Principles of development and developmental tasks Development follows regularities that hold across cultures (Table 6.2). Two give the direction of physical growth: cephalocaudal , from head to tail (head control comes before walking), and proximodistal , from the centre outwards (arms before fingers). Motor milestones are in Section 6.3. Table 6.2 Principles of development (Hurlock and standard texts). Principle Meaning and example Orderly, predictable pattern Same sequence in all children: sit, stand, walk Cephalocaudal Head to foot Proximodistal Centre to extremities General to specific (mass to specific) Whole-body wriggling comes before one hand reaching Continuous but uneven in rate Never stops; spurts in infancy and puberty Individual differences Same sequence, different rates: walking at 10 or at 15 months Maturation and learning interact Reading needs both readiness and practice Early foundations are critical Early patterns tend to persist Each stage has its own pattern Characteristic behaviour, hazards and social expectations Robert J. Havighurst (1900 to 1991), in Developmental Tasks and Education (1948), defined a developmental task as one that arises at about a certain period of life; success brings happiness and success with later tasks, while failure brings unhappiness, social disapproval and later difficulty. Tasks arise from physical maturation (walking), cultural pressure (reading) and personal values (choosing a vocation). Early childhood tasks include walking, talking, taking solid food and controlling elimination; middle childhood brings the skills of ordinary games, getting along with age-mates, and reading, writing and arithmetic. Adolescent and adult tasks are in Sections 6.10 and 6.11. The enduring issues Every theory takes a stand on the issues of Table 6.3. On nature versus nurture (heredity or environment?) today's answer is interaction: a genetic tendency shows itself only in some environments, and inherited traits help select the environments a child meets (Section 6.2). Continuity versus discontinuity asks whether development is gradual, quantitative accumulation, a ramp, or a series of qualitatively different stages, a staircase. Table 6.3 The core issues of developmental psychology. Issue The question Typical answers Nature versus nurture Heredity or environment? Rousseau, Gesell (nature); Locke, Watson (nurture); today, interaction Continuity versus discontinuity Gradual change or stages? Learning theory (continuous); Freud, Piaget, Erikson (stages) Stability versus change Do early traits persist? Freud (personality set by 5 or 6); Baltes (plastic for life) Early versus later experience Do the first years decide? Freud, Bowlby (early); Clarke and Clarke (later can repair) Active versus passive child Does the child shape development? Piaget (active builder); Watson (moulded by environment) Universal versus context-specific One path everywhere? Piaget (universal stages); Vygotsky, Bronfenbrenner (culture) Try a worked example. In one Native American tribe, mothers answer an infant's distress at once and hold the baby almost constantly for three years; for generations the children have grown up quiet, even-tempered, obedient and respectful. Is the calm inborn? No: it follows a child-rearing practice handed down in the culture, so it is learnt behaviour , acquired through experience. Innate behaviour appears without experience, as reflexes do. The calm is also overt behaviour (observable action), not covert behaviour (private thoughts and feelings), and "complex behaviour" describes how many parts an act has, not where it comes from. Exam trap Behaviour that follows a child-rearing practice handed down in a culture is learnt ; stability across generations is not proof of heredity. Stage theorists (Freud, Piaget, Erikson) take the discontinuity side; learning and information-processing theorists take the continuity side. Critical and sensitive periods A critical period is a fixed window in which a particular experience must occur for normal development; if it passes without that experience, the effects are largely irreversible. The model case comes from ethology, the study of behaviour in its evolutionary setting: Konrad Lorenz (1903 to 1989) reported in 1935 that greylag goslings imprint on the first moving object they see after hatching, even Lorenz himself (Section 6.7). In human development the clearest critical periods are in the embryo: each organ forms within a brief window, so a teratogen such as thalidomide or rubella seriously damages an organ only if it strikes while that organ is forming, mostly in weeks 3 to 8 (Section 6.2). A sensitive period is an optimal but more flexible window: the experience matters most then, but some development remains possible later (Figure 6.1). First language is the standard case. Eric Lenneberg (1967) proposed a critical period for language from about age two to puberty (Section 1.8); the evidence now favours a sensitive period. Genie, found in Los Angeles in 1970 at 13 after years of isolation, learned many words but never mastered grammar. Such lasting limits after early language deprivation support sensitive periods. They say nothing about semantics (word meaning) or syntax (rules of word order), which are levels of language, or about nativism, the view of Noam Chomsky (born 1928) that language ability is innate. Critical window Sensitivity to experience Early Later Age window closes Some late recovery possible Critical: fixed, irreversible Sensitive: optimal, flexible Figure 6.1 A critical period (solid line) opens and closes sharply; a sensitive period (dashed line) peaks early but never falls to zero. Can later experience repair a poor start? Ann Clarke and Alan Clarke argued that it often can in Early Experience: Myth and Evidence (1976). The strongest test is the English and Romanian Adoptees study led by Michael Rutter (1933 to 2021): children adopted into British homes from Romanian orphanages after 1989 caught up almost fully if adopted before about six months, and greatly, though some kept lasting difficulties, if adopted later (Section 6.7). Later experience compensating for earlier deficits contradicts the strict critical-period view. Sensitive periods allow late recovery by definition; continuity concerns gradual versus stepwise change, and stability whether traits persist. Exam trap RML 2024 asked for the strongest evidence for critical periods "in the case of human development" and keyed imprinting . Imprinting is the classic critical period, but it is animal evidence. Within human development the clearest critical periods are in embryonic development (teratogen timing); language shows a sensitive period, and vocational interests show none. Expect imprinting as the key; know why embryonic development is the better human answer. The grand theories at a glance Six families of theory answer these issues differently (Table 6.4), each taught in full elsewhere. Psychoanalytic and cognitive theories propose stages; learning theories see continuous, environment-driven change; ethology stresses evolved behaviour and critical periods; ecological and dynamic systems theories stress context and many interacting causes. In the dynamic systems theory of Esther Thelen (1941 to 2004), a new skill self-organises out of body, task and environment. Table 6.4 The grand theories of development. Family Key theorists Where taught Psychoanalytic Sigmund Freud (psychosexual stages); Erik Erikson (psychosocial stages) Chapter 4; Section 6.10 Learning John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner, Albert Bandura Section 1.6 Cognitive Jean Piaget; Lev Vygotsky; information processing Sections 6.4, 6.5 Ethological Konrad Lorenz, Nikolaas Tinbergen, John Bowlby Section 6.7 Ecological Urie Bronfenbrenner Below Dynamic systems Esther Thelen Section 6.3 Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems Most theories put the child under a microscope; Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917 to 2005) widened the lens. His ecological systems theory , set out in The Ecology of Human Development (1979), places the child inside environmental systems nested like Russian dolls (Figure 6.2), each affecting the child and affected in turn. The microsystem is the innermost layer: the settings in which the child takes part directly, face to face, such as family, school, peer group and neighbourhood. Influence is bidirectional: parents shape the child, and the child shapes the parents. The mesosystem is the set of links between microsystems: home and school (a parent-teacher meeting), family and peers. It is a relationship between settings, not a setting. The exosystem holds settings the child is not in that still affect the child: a parent's workplace (a night shift), the school board, the mass media, extended family. The macrosystem is the overarching culture: values, laws, ideology and the economic system. The chronosystem , added later, is time: transitions such as parental divorce and historical events such as a pandemic. Macrosystem Exosystem Family School Peers Neighbourhood Child Macrosystem culture, values, laws Exosystem without the child: parent's workplace Microsystem direct, two-way settings Mesosystem links between settings Chronosystem: time (divorce, a pandemic) Figure 6.2 Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems. The dashed mesosystem lines are links between microsystem settings, not a setting; the exosystem holds settings without the child. Later Bronfenbrenner gave biology more weight. In the bioecological model , developed with Stephen Ceci (1994) and later with Pamela Morris (1998), development is the product of Process-Person-Context-Time (PPCT). Its engine is the proximal process : regular, increasingly complex, two-way interaction between the child and nearby people, objects and symbols, such as a parent reading with a child every night. Person characteristics (temperament, abilities) shape these processes, context is the five systems, and time runs from moments to history. Bronfenbrenner also helped found Head Start (1965), the American preschool programme for poor children. Exam trap Family, school and peer group are all microsystem ; the immediate family is never meso-, exo- or macrosystem. The mesosystem is a link (school-family, parent-teacher), not a setting. The exosystem does not contain the child (the parent's workplace). Culture is macrosystem; divorce is chronosystem. Nested systems are Bronfenbrenner's , not Skinner's (operant learning), Gesell's (maturation) or Hall's (child study). Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Increase in size or amount is growth; qualitative change in structure and organisation is . The biological unfolding of genetic potential is called . Gesell and Thompson held heredity constant with the method of control. Head control before walking illustrates the principle. Events shared by a whole generation, such as a pandemic, are normative -graded influences. A fixed window with irreversible effects is a period. Links between a child's home and school belong to the . A parent's workplace belongs to the . Answers: (1) development, (2) maturation, (3) co-twin, (4) cephalocaudal, (5) history, (6) critical, (7) mesosystem, (8) exosystem. 6.2 Heredity, Prenatal Development, Birth and the Newborn Lower yield · 7 Qs Every life begins as one cell; nine months later a newborn arrives able to suck, startle and grip. This section follows that journey, from genes to the newborn's first reflexes. Genes, chromosomes and conception The nucleus of each body cell holds 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent. A chromosome is a long strand of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid); a gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a protein. Twenty-two pairs are autosomes ; the twenty-third, the sex chromosomes , is XX in females and XY in males. Body cells multiply by mitosis into identical copies; sperm and ova form by meiosis , which halves the number to 23 and reshuffles genes, so siblings differ. At conception, usually in a fallopian tube, sperm and ovum unite into one cell, the zygote ; since every ovum carries an X, the father's X or Y sperm decides the child's sex. A zygote that splits yields monozygotic twins (identical, sharing all their genes); two ova fertilised by two sperm yield dizygotic twins (fraternal, sharing about half, like any siblings). Patterns of inheritance Each gene comes in alternative forms called alleles . The alleles a person carries are the genotype ; the observable traits, shaped also by the environment, are the phenotype . Two identical alleles make a person homozygous for that gene; two different ones, heterozygous . In dominant-recessive inheritance , the pattern Gregor Mendel (1822 to 1884) reported from pea plants in 1866, a heterozygote shows only the dominant allele's trait; the recessive allele is masked but can be passed on, so the person is a carrier . Let blue eyes (D) be dominant and green (d) recessive: DD and Dd children have blue eyes, dd children green. Figure 6.3 shows why two blue-eyed Dd parents can have a green-eyed child. Two carriers thus face a one-in-four risk, in each pregnancy, of a child with a recessive disorder: phenylketonuria (PKU), cystic fibrosis (thick mucus clogs lungs and pancreas), sickle-cell anaemia or Tay-Sachs disease (fatal nervous system degeneration in early childhood). In PKU the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase is missing, so phenylalanine builds up and damages the brain; newborn screening and a low-phenylalanine diet prevent the intellectual disability. A dominant disorder needs one copy: Huntington's disease (chorea and dementia) appears in midlife, often after it has been passed on. Genetic counselling estimates such risks from family history and tests. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is intermediate (sickle-cell carriers sickle mildly when oxygen is low); in codominance both alleles are fully expressed (A and B alleles give blood group AB). In X-linked inheritance a recessive allele on the X is usually masked by a female's second X, but a male has none, so haemophilia, red-green colour blindness and Duchenne muscular dystrophy strike mainly males, through carrier mothers. Polygenic inheritance , many genes of small effect, underlies continuous traits such as height and intelligence. In genomic imprinting one parent's allele is chemically silenced, so the effect depends on which parent it came from. A mutation is a sudden, permanent change in DNA, spontaneous or caused by radiation or chemicals. Chromosomal abnormalities Whole chromosomes can be extra or missing, usually because a pair fails to separate in meiosis (nondisjunction), and parts can be lost (deletion). Down syndrome , described by John Langdon Down (1828 to 1896) in 1866, is usually trisomy 21 , three copies of chromosome 21; its risk rises with maternal age. Heredity and environment How far is a trait inherited? (The nature-nurture debate itself is in Section 6.1.) Family studies are weak evidence, since relatives share homes as well as genes. Adoption studies ask whether adopted children resemble their biological or adoptive parents; twin studies , whether identical (MZ) twins are more alike than fraternal (DZ) twins. Most informative are MZ twins adopted by different parents : identical genes, different homes, so their similarities reflect heredity and their differences environment. MZ twins reared together share genes and home, confounding the two; DZ twins or siblings adopted apart share only about half their genes. Albert Stunkard and colleagues (1990) found identical twins reared apart nearly as alike in body-mass index as those reared together. Heritability , the proportion of variation in a trait within a population due to genetic differences, describes groups, not individuals (IQ figures: Section 1.9; behaviour genetics: Chapter 5). Genes and environment also work together. Sandra Scarr and Kathleen McCartney (1983) described three kinds of gene-environment correlation : passive (parents supply both genes and a matching home: musical parents, a musical house), strongest in infancy; evocative (a child's traits evoke responses: a cheerful baby draws more play); and active , or niche-picking (children seek settings that suit them), which grows with age. In gene-environment interaction one environment affects genotypes differently: an ordinary diet harms only the child with PKU. Irving Gottesman 's (1963) reaction range is the band of outcomes a genotype permits, the environment deciding where in it a person falls. Conrad Hal Waddington 's (1905 to 1975) canalisation is heredity's channelling of some traits, such as early motor milestones, to the same outcome in almost any environment. Epigenetics studies how experience switches genes on or off (for example by DNA methylation) without changing the DNA sequence. The three prenatal periods Prenatal development lasts about 38 weeks from conception, in three periods (Figure 6.4). In the germinal period , about the first two weeks, the zygote divides (cleavage) as it travels down the fallopian tube, becoming a solid ball, the morula (about day 4), then a hollow blastocyst (about day 5), whose inner cell mass becomes the baby and outer layer the placenta. Implantation in the uterine wall ends the period. The embryonic period (weeks 3 to 8) opens with gastrulation , when the inner cell mass forms three germ layers: ectoderm (nervous system, skin), mesoderm (muscle, bone, heart, blood) and endoderm (gut, lungs, glands). The nervous system begins here: the neural plate arises from ectoderm and folds into the neural tube , the future brain and spinal cord, by about week 4. Because every major organ forms now ( organogenesis ), this period is the most vulnerable to teratogens. The embryonic , not the fetal, period is the most vulnerable. Teratogens, maternal factors and prenatal tests A teratogen is any environmental agent that harms the developing child. Its effect depends on timing (each organ has its own critical period, as Figure 6.4 shows), dose , the genetic susceptibility of mother and child, and delayed effects that surface years later. Birth and assessing the newborn Labour has three stages: dilation of the cervix (the longest), delivery of the baby, and delivery of the placenta . Its main danger is anoxia , too little oxygen (as when the cord is squeezed), which can damage the brain and cause cerebral palsy. A preterm baby is born before 37 weeks, perhaps at a weight right for its age; a baby small for gestational age weighs less than expected for its age, even at term, and usually fares worse. Low birth weight means under 2,500 g. Kangaroo care , skin-to-skin holding on a parent's chest, steadies temperature, breathing and heart rate and improves survival. The Apgar scale , devised in 1952 (published 1953) by the anaesthesiologist Virginia Apgar (1909 to 1974), rates five signs 0, 1 or 2 (total 10) at 1 and 5 minutes: a ppearance (colour), p ulse, g rimace (reflex irritability), a ctivity (muscle tone) and r espiration. Peter Wolff (1966) distinguished the newborn's states of arousal : regular (non-REM) sleep, irregular (REM) sleep, drowsiness, quiet alertness, and waking activity and crying. Newborns sleep about 16 to 18 hours a day, half of it REM sleep. Sudden infant death syndrome (unexplained death of a sleeping infant under one year) fell sharply after back-to-sleep campaigns taught parents to lay babies on their backs. A year later she walks across the room and picks a grain of rice off the floor between thumb and finger. This section follows that change through brain, body, movement and the senses, and asks how we can know what a baby who cannot speak perceives and learns. Physical growth in the first two years Birth weight roughly doubles by about 5 months and triples by the first birthday. Growth has two directions. In the cephalocaudal trend (Latin, "head to tail") the head grows first and fastest; it is a quarter of body length at birth but an eighth in adulthood. In the proximodistal trend growth runs from the centre outward, trunk before arms and arms before hands. Breast milk is the ideal food. Severe malnutrition causes marasmus , wasting of the whole body from too little food of any kind, usually in the first year, or kwashiorkor , a protein deficiency after weaning in which belly and limbs swell with fluid. The developing brain Neurogenesis , the birth of new neurons, is largely prenatal. Why, then, does the brain grow so much after birth? Because existing neurons form connections and gain insulation. In synaptogenesis the infant brain forms far more synapses than it will keep, and synaptic pruning then removes the rarely used ones and keeps those used often: "use it or lose it". Pruning is a process of neuronal development and plasticity that fits circuits to the child's own experience, continuing in the prefrontal cortex through adolescence (Section 5.5). Myelination , the wrapping of axons in fatty myelin that speeds conduction, reaches the prefrontal cortex last, continuing into early adulthood. Together these take the brain from about 25 percent of adult weight at birth to about half by 6 months, 75 percent by age 2 and 90 percent by age 5 to 6 (Figure 6.5). adult weight (100%) 0 25 50 75 100 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 Age (years) Percent of adult brain weight birth: about 25% 6 months: about 50% 2 years: about 75% 5 to 6 years: about 90% Figure 6.5 Brain weight as a percentage of adult weight (approximate values joined by a smooth line). The curve climbs most steeply in the first two years. William Greenough and colleagues (1987) distinguished two kinds of plasticity. Experience-expectant plasticity depends on experiences every member of the species can count on, such as patterned light and speech; the brain overproduces synapses in readiness and keeps those the expected input uses. Hence sensitive periods: a cataract left untreated in an infant's eye leaves lasting poor vision. Experience-dependent plasticity builds connections from experiences unique to the individual and continues for life. Exam trap Synaptic pruning belongs to neuronal development and plasticity , not memory consolidation (stabilising a new memory, Section 1.7), neurotransmitter release (the moment-to-moment signal at a synapse) or long-term potentiation (lasting strengthening of a synapse by repeated stimulation, Chapter 5). Half of adult brain size is keyed at about 6 months , not birth, 1 year or 3 years; some texts imply nearer the first year, so treat these percentages as approximate. Principles and milestones of motor development Motor control follows the same two directions as growth (Figure 6.6). By the cephalocaudal principle it spreads from head to foot: the infant holds up her head before she sits, and sits before she stands. By the proximodistal principle it spreads from the centre of the body to the extremities: she swings her whole arm at a toy months before her fingers can pick it up. Development also runs from gross motor skills (large movements of trunk and limbs, such as walking) to fine motor skills (precise movements of hands and fingers), and from mass to specific : shown a toy, a young infant waves, kicks and wriggles all at once, and only later reaches with one hand. Finally, motor development shapes social and behavioural expectations: a child who walks and feeds herself is treated differently and expected to do more. "Distal to proximal" reverses it and is the false option; cephalocaudal, gross to fine, mass to specific, and shaping social and behavioural expectations are all true principles. Fine motor skills: from reflex to pincer grasp The hand tells the proximodistal story in miniature. The newborn's palmar grasp reflex closes her fingers round anything pressed into her palm. Her prereaching is poorly aimed swiping at objects in view, fading after about 2 months. At 3 to 4 months voluntary reaching brings the first voluntary grasp, the ulnar grasp : the fingers close clumsily against the palm, holding the object on the little-finger (ulnar) side. By 4 to 5 months she transfers objects from hand to hand. Control then shifts to the thumb side in radial grasps (the radius is the forearm bone on the thumb side), and by about 9 to 12 months the pincer grasp , thumb against forefinger, lifts that grain of rice. Exam trap The keyed first grasp is the ulnar grasp , the first voluntary one; the palmar grasp at birth is a reflex. Texts order the middle steps differently (one even puts a clumsy palmar grip before the ulnar grasp), but the pincer grasp always comes last. Explaining motor development Why do babies sit, crawl and walk in this order? Arnold Gesell (1880 to 1961) gave the maturational view : motor development unfolds a genetically programmed sequence as nerves and muscles mature, so practice adds little (his co-twin study is in Section 6.1). Experience matters more than he thought. Wayne Dennis and Marsena Dennis (1940) found that Hopi infants bound to cradleboards walked at about the same age as unbound Hopi infants, which seemed to favour maturation; but in Iranian orphanages, where babies lay on their backs with almost no chance to move, Wayne Dennis (1960) found many 3- and 4-year-olds who could not walk alone. Cultures that train sitting and walking, such as the Kipsigis of Kenya, see these skills earlier. Maturation is necessary but not sufficient. The modern account is dynamic systems theory , applied to motor skills by Esther Thelen (1941 to 2004): a skill is assembled from the body's current size and strength, the task and the support the environment offers. Take the newborn stepping reflex, which seems to vanish at about 2 months. It vanishes, Thelen showed, because the legs grow heavier faster than the muscles grow stronger: with her legs held in water, the infant steps again. Methods for studying infant perception How can you know what a baby perceives? Watch where she looks, how hard she sucks and how her brain responds. Robert Fantz (1961) used preferential looking : two stimuli are shown side by side and an observer times the looking at each. Infants from a few days to 6 months old looked longest at a face, then at patterns such as newsprint and a bull's-eye, and least at plain discs: they prefer patterns, and faces most of all. The habituation-dishabituation method needs no favourite. Show a picture again and again and looking falls ( habituation , the simplest form of learning); show a new one, and if looking recovers ( dishabituation ) the infant has noticed the difference. It is the standard test of discrimination and categorisation before language: habituate a baby to many cats, then show a new cat and a dog, and extra looking at the dog shows a category "cat". In high-amplitude sucking , strong sucks on a recording dummy switch on a sound, and sucking revives when a new sound is noticed. In the violation-of-expectation method of Renée Baillargeon (1985), infants look longer at an impossible event than a possible one, revealing what they expect of objects (Section 6.4). Evoked potentials , electrical brain responses recorded from the scalp, show whether the brain registers a difference when behaviour shows nothing. Exam trap Habituation paradigms assess discrimination and categorisation before language , not long-term declarative memory (recognition here lasts minutes within one session), object permanence specifically (tested by violation of expectation) or moral reasoning (Section 6.9). The infant's senses Every sense works at birth, but vision is the least mature. Newborn visual acuity , the sharpness of sight, is poor (about 20/200 to 20/600, against the adult 20/20) but improves rapidly over the first year. Colour vision is present by about 2 to 3 months, and newborns already prefer faces. Hearing works before birth. Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer (1980) found that newborns under 3 days old sucked in whichever pattern played their own mother's voice rather than another woman's. DeCasper and Melanie Spence (1986) had mothers read The Cat in the Hat aloud in late pregnancy; after birth the babies sucked to hear that story rather than a new one. Infants at first hear speech-sound contrasts their own language does not use, then lose them: perceptual narrowing . Janet Werker and Richard Tees (1984) found that most English-learning infants of 6 to 8 months heard the Hindi contrast between a dental and a retroflex "ta", but few did by 10 to 12 months. Taste and smell are keen at birth: newborns relax at sweet tastes and grimace at bitter, and breastfed babies about a week old turn towards a pad their own mother has worn. Touch is well developed, and newborns feel pain. Intermodal perception , combining several senses into one event, appears early: Elizabeth Spelke (1976) showed 4-month-olds two films side by side with one soundtrack, and they looked longer at the film that matched the sound. Depth, locomotion and affordances Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk (1960) built the visual cliff , a glass-topped table with a checkerboard just under the glass on the shallow side and far below it on the deep side (full study in Section 1.4). Infants of crawling age, about 6 months onward, crossed the shallow side to their mothers but refused the deep side. Depth perception is therefore present by the time infants crawl: not fully formed at birth, not delayed until age 2 and not taught in words. Chicks and young goats tested within a day of birth also avoided the drop, which Gibson and Walk read as evidence that depth perception is largely innate. Is the crawler's fear inborn? Joseph Campos and colleagues measured heart rate on the cliff. Two-month-olds on the deep side showed a slowing heart rate, a sign of interest; crawlers showed a quickening one, a sign of fear, and the more weeks an infant had crawled, the warier she was. Locomotor experience brings wariness of heights. The ecological view of James J. Gibson (1904 to 1979) and Eleanor Gibson explains why: we perceive the world in terms of what we can do in it. An affordance is an action possibility the environment offers a particular perceiver: a slope affords crawling down to an experienced crawler but a fall to a novice. Because affordances depend on the perceiver's abilities, the change that most transforms them is independent locomotion : once the infant crawls and walks, distant toys become reachable and drops dangerous. Starting to speak, the attachment relationship and new caretaking reshape her social world, but none changes what her surroundings afford her actions nearly as much. Exam trap The visual cliff tested depth perception , present by crawling age , not colour perception, object permanence (Section 6.4), language comprehension, imprinting (Section 6.7) or audio-visual integration (intermodal perception). Toddlers' affordances change most with independent locomotion . Learning, imitation and the milestone sequence Infants learn from birth. Newborns can be classically conditioned: stroke a newborn's forehead just before giving sweet water and soon the stroke alone sets off sucking. In Carolyn Rovee-Collier 's operant studies a ribbon tied a 2- or 3-month-old's ankle to a mobile, so kicking made it move; days later infants kicked again at the sight of the same mobile, showing memory long before language. Key study: Meltzoff and Moore's imitating newborns (1977) Question. Can newborns imitate gestures they cannot see themselves make? Method. Andrew Meltzoff and M. Keith Moore showed infants 12 to 21 days old an adult protruding the tongue, opening the mouth and protruding the lips; coders blind to the gesture scored videotapes. Result. Infants made more of whichever gesture they had seen; imitation was later reported within hours of birth. Conclusion. Imitation is an important early feature of infant learning, appearing long before 1 year (and before the 8 to 12 months Jean Piaget expected), and not only for tongue protrusion. Criticism. Later studies often found only tongue protrusion matched, so the finding is debated. Deferred imitation is in Section 6.4. Table 6.10 gathers the milestones of the first two years. She is not careless; she is reasoning with the tools she has. A Swiss biologist built the most influential theory of children's thinking on mistakes like hers. This section follows it from method and core concepts through four stages and beyond, then weighs the evidence. Piaget and his method Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980) was a biologist first, with a 1918 doctorate on molluscs. Around 1920, in the Paris laboratory of Théodore Simon , co-author with Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911) of the first intelligence scale (1905; Section 1.9), he scored children's answers to reasoning items. The wrong answers fascinated him: children of the same age made the same kinds of error, so younger children seemed not duller than older ones but to think differently. In Geneva from 1921 he pursued one question for sixty years: how does knowledge grow? He called the field genetic epistemology , the study of the origins (genesis) of knowledge. His tool was the clinical method ( méthode clinique ), a flexible interview that follows each answer with further questions to uncover the reasoning behind it; for infancy he observed his own three children closely. His name-year books are The Language and Thought of the Child (1923), The Moral Judgment of the Child (1932; Section 6.9), The Origins of Intelligence in Children (1936) and The Construction of Reality in the Child (1937); his stages of play are in Section 6.8. Piaget treated intelligence as biological adaptation : as a species adapts through bodily structures, a child adapts through ever better mental structures. In his constructivism the child is an active "little scientist" who builds knowledge by acting on objects, first physically and later mentally. Exam trap Piaget = intelligence as a biological adaptation, and the stages of cognitive development. Free association is Sigmund Freud 's (1856 to 1939), operant conditioning Burrhus Frederic Skinner 's (1904 to 1990) and aggression as learned social behaviour Albert Bandura 's (1925 to 2021). Psychosocial stages belong to Erik Erikson (1902 to 1994) and moral stages to Lawrence Kohlberg (1927 to 1987). Schemes, adaptation and equilibration The unit of knowledge is the scheme (often called a schema), an organised pattern of action or thought for dealing with a class of experiences: a newborn's sucking and grasping, a ten-year-old's adding and classifying. Two functional invariants shape schemes at every age. Organisation combines simple schemes into larger systems, as looking and grasping merge into reaching for what one sees. Adaptation adjusts schemes to the environment through two complementary processes. In assimilation the child fits new experience into an existing scheme: a two-year-old whose "doggie" scheme means "four-legged animal" calls a cow "doggie". In accommodation the child changes the scheme, that is, his way of thinking, to fit experience that will not fit: the cow moos, an adult says "cow", and the scheme splits in two. Assimilation keeps knowledge stable; accommodation makes it grow. When schemes handle events, the child is in equilibrium . A misfit produces disequilibrium , an uncomfortable cognitive conflict, resolved by assimilating and accommodating until a new, more advanced balance is reached. This self-regulating process, equilibration (Figure 6.7), drives the child from stage to stage. Mature schemes become operations : internalised mental actions that are reversible (they can be undone in thought) and organised into logical systems; the stage names describe the child's relation to them. Equilibrium schemes fit experience Disequilibrium a new event does not fit Adaptation assimilate and accommodate New equilibrium at a higher level Equilibration: the cycle repeats, each time at a higher level Figure 6.7 Equilibration. A misfit between schemes and experience creates disequilibrium; assimilation and accommodation restore balance at a more advanced level. Piaget named four factors in development: maturation of the nervous system; experience , both physical (properties of objects, such as weight) and logico-mathematical (relations one's own actions create, such as ten pebbles staying ten in any order of counting); social transmission (being taught); and equilibration, which coordinates the other three. Development thus comes from maturation and learning together, never from either alone, and not from social and cultural practice alone, which is nearer Vygotsky's emphasis (Section 6.5). Exam trap Piaget's two basic processes of learning and adaptation are assimilation and accommodation ; encoding and retrieval are memory processes (Section 1.7), and attention and perception, or sensory input and motor output, are not his pair. Changing one's way of thinking to fit new experience is accommodation , not assimilation, conservation (below) or habituation , the decline in responding to a repeated stimulus (Section 6.3). The four stages at a glance Piaget's stages are qualitatively different ways of thinking, not simply more knowledge. Every child passes through them in the same invariant sequence , none skipped or reversed, each built on the last. The ages are approximate; the order is what the theory fixes. Table 6.11 maps the rest of this section. Table 6.11 Piaget's four stages of cognitive development. Hypothetico-deductive reasoning is not a stage ; it is the hallmark of the formal operational stage. Preoperational = 2 to 7 years; concrete operational begins at about 7. Sensorimotor stage and object permanence For the first two years, Piaget argued, infants think with senses and actions rather than mental symbols: the sensorimotor stage . Its motor is the circular reaction , an action the infant hits on by chance and repeats because the result is interesting; its target moves outward from her own body (primary) to objects (secondary) to deliberate experiment (tertiary), as Table 6.12 shows. By 8 to 12 months acts are intentional, one scheme serving as the means to another (pushing a cushion aside to reach a toy). By 18 to 24 months she represents the world mentally: she solves problems by sudden insight, pretends, and shows deferred imitation , copying an action seen hours or days earlier. Table 6.12 The six sensorimotor substages. Substage Months What the infant does Object permanence 1 Reflexes 0 to 1 Exercises inborn reflexes: sucking, grasping None 2 Primary circular reactions 1 to 4 Repeats chance actions on own body (thumb sucking); coordinates schemes across senses (looks towards a sound) Looks briefly where it vanished 3 Secondary circular reactions 4 to 8 Repeats interesting effects on objects (shakes a rattle) Retrieves a partly hidden object 4 Coordination of secondary schemes 8 to 12 Intentional, goal-directed, means-end acts Searches for a fully hidden object; A-not-B error 5 Tertiary circular reactions 12 to 18 Varies actions to see what happens Follows visible moves; fails invisible ones 6 Mental representation (invention of new means) 18 to 24 Insight, deferred imitation, symbolic thought, pretend play Complete: solves invisible displacements The stage's best-known achievement is object permanence , the understanding that objects go on existing when they can no longer be seen, heard or touched. To a 4-month-old, Piaget claimed, a toy covered by a cloth has ceased to be. Search for a fully hidden object begins in substage 4, about 8 to 12 months, with a revealing mistake. Hide a toy under cloth A several times and let the infant find it; then, as she watches, hide it under cloth B. She searches under A. This A-not-B error shows that object permanence is still incomplete: the object belongs where her action last succeeded. At 12 to 18 months she follows visible moves but not invisible ones (the toy, hidden in a hand, is slipped under a cushion); only at 18 to 24 months does she infer where it must be, and object permanence is complete. Adele Diamond (1985) showed that the A-not-B error grows with the delay between hiding and search, and later tied its disappearance to maturation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports working memory and inhibition of a prepotent (habitual, previously rewarded) reach. Key study: Baillargeon's drawbridge (1985, 1987) Renée Baillargeon used the violation-of-expectation method: infants look longer at events that surprise them. A screen rotated like a drawbridge towards a box placed behind it. In the possible event it stopped at the hidden box; in the impossible event it swung through the box's space. Five-month-olds (1985), and later some infants of 3.5 to 4.5 months (1987), looked longer at the impossible event, as if they knew the hidden box still existed. Criticism: longer looking may reflect novelty or perceptual preference rather than knowledge. Exam trap Object permanence is a sensorimotor achievement, never preoperational, concrete or formal, and not to be confused with conservation. Keyed ages: it begins about 8 to 12 months (substage 4, A-not-B error) and is fully established by 18 to 24 months ; 2 months, 4 to 6 months, 8 to 10 months (onset only) or 3 years are wrong for full mastery. The A-not-B error reflects incomplete object permanence with a prepotent reach, not centration or failed reversibility. Preoperational thought Around the second birthday the symbolic function appears: the ability to make one thing (a word, image or gesture) stand for another, seen in language, pretend play (a banana becomes a telephone) and drawing. The preoperational stage (2 to 7) is named for what the child cannot yet do: perform operations. It has a symbolic function substage (2 to 4) and an intuitive thought substage (4 to 7), when children ask endless "why" questions and judge by intuition rather than logic. Judy DeLoache (1987) found that children under about 3 cannot use a scale model of a room to find a toy hidden in the real room: they lack dual representation , treating an object both as a thing and as a symbol for something else. In the Piagetian view, then, preschoolers are unable to reason properly, and their thought shows a family of related limits: Egocentrism : the inability to distinguish one's own visual or conceptual perspective from another person's; a cognitive limit, not selfishness. Animism : attributing life and feelings to inanimate things ("the sun is following me"). Artificialism : believing natural things were made by people ("someone painted the sky"). Centration : focusing on one salient feature while ignoring the others. A 5-year-old who sorts a deck of cards by colour but cannot then re-sort the same deck by suit is centring on colour. Irreversibility : the inability to run an action backwards in the mind, with a focus on states, not transformations : the child compares before and after and ignores the pouring between. Transductive reasoning : reasoning from particular to particular with no general rule. Piaget's daughter, having missed her nap, announced, "It isn't afternoon." Failure of class inclusion : shown wooden beads, mostly brown, and asked "More brown beads or more wooden beads?", the child says "more brown", comparing subclasses instead of a subclass with the whole. Lack of conservation, the subject of the next subsection. Key study: The three mountains task Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder (1913 to 1997) seated children before a model of three mountains (one snow-capped, one with a house, one with a red cross) and asked them to pick the photograph showing the view of a doll sitting elsewhere. Four-year-olds usually picked their own view; correct choices became common only around 7 to 8. Piaget read this as egocentrism. Criticism: the task is unfamiliar and spatially hard; meaningful versions show perspective taking much earlier ( Evaluating Piaget ). Exam trap Centration = focusing on one salient feature while ignoring others (the card sorter; judging liquid by height), not egocentrism, animism, transductive reasoning, irreversibility or the reversible operation behind conservation. Coordinating schemes across senses is a sensorimotor achievement, not centration. "Preschoolers cannot reason properly" is the Piagetian view, not that of Arthur Robert Jensen (1923 to 2012, Level I and Level II abilities), Joy Paul Guilford (1897 to 1987, structure of intellect) or a "holistic" view (Section 1.9). Conservation Conservation is the understanding that a quantity stays the same despite changes in shape or arrangement, so long as nothing is added or taken away. Every task follows one script (Figure 6.8). The child agrees that two identical short, wide glasses hold equal water. One is then poured, as she watches, into a tall, thin glass, where the water stands higher (it does not stay at the same height; that is the point). The preoperational child now says the tall glass has more: her judgement is swayed by one dimension, height, and she ignores the narrower width. 1. Equal amounts 2. Pour B into C 3. Same amount? A B Child agrees: same A C Water stands higher in C Preoperational (about 5): "C has more water, it is taller." centration on height Concrete operational (7+): "Same water, none added." identity "Taller but thinner." compensation "Pour it back: equal." reversibility Figure 6.8 The liquid conservation task. Beaker C is half as wide as A, so the same water stands twice as high; only the conserving child sees that the amount is unchanged, and justifies it in one of three ways. The conserving child gives one of three justifications, exactly the operations the preoperational child lacks: Identity : "It's the same water; you didn't add any or take any away." The principle of identity is the recognition that certain characteristics of an object remain fixed even when its appearance changes. Compensation : "It's taller, but it's thinner." A change in one dimension is offset by a change in another. Reversibility (negation): "If you pour it back, it will be the same as before." Conservation is several achievements, mastered in a typical order (Table 6.13). A child who conserves substance at 7 or 8 may fail with weight until 9 or 10, though both need the same operation. Piaget called this horizontal décalage (French for "gap"): one operation, applied to different contents, mastered at different ages within a stage. Vertical décalage is the same achievement recurring at a higher level in a later stage: a toddler finds her way round the house by action but maps it only years later. Conservation of liquid, loosely called liquid volume, differs from volume by displacement, which comes last; all count as concrete operational achievements. In the liquid task the liquid does not stay at the same height, and the test is not only for under-5s. Concrete operational stage At about 7 children begin to perform true operations on real objects and events: the concrete operational stage (7 to 11). Shown the clay ball rolled into a sausage, the child now says it is still the same amount, and can say why. The gains behind this are: Decentration : attending to several features at once, such as height and width. Reversibility: mentally undoing an action, which first appears in this stage. Seriation : arranging items along a dimension (sticks from shortest to longest) systematically, not by trial and error. Transitive inference (transitivity): if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C, without comparing A and C directly. Classification by more than one attribute, and success on class inclusion ("more wooden beads"). Reduced egocentrism in perception and conversation. The limit is in the name: the concrete thinker reasons logically about real, picturable things but balks at the purely hypothetical. Told "If all dogs were pink and Bruno is a dog, what colour is Bruno?", she objects that dogs are not pink. Exam trap In the concrete stage reduced egocentrism, transitive inference and conservation of mass are present, object permanence is long established and deferred imitation dates from infancy. What the concrete operational child struggles with, and does not attain, is hypothetico-deductive reasoning . Formal operations and postformal thought From about 11 or 12 the formal operational stage frees thought from the concrete. Adolescents reason about abstractions (justice, infinity), about the possible as well as the real, and about propositions , statements whose conclusions follow from their form ("If A then B; A; therefore B"). The signature is hypothetico-deductive reasoning : deducing hypotheses from a general theory and testing them systematically, one variable at a time. With it come counterfactual reasoning (from premises contrary to fact: "If the moon were made of cheese..."), combinatorial reasoning (generating every possible combination of factors) and metacognitive reflection, thinking about one's own thinking. Inhelder and Piaget's tasks appear in The Growth of Logical Thinking from Childhood to Adolescence (1958). In the pendulum problem the child must find what controls how fast a pendulum swings: string length, weight, height of release or force of push. The concrete thinker changes several things at once; the formal thinker varies one at a time and finds that only length matters. In the chemical combination task the adolescent mixes colourless liquids in every combination to find which turns yellow. The new power brings idealism (measuring the real world against ideal ones) and adolescent egocentrism (Section 6.10). Nor is the stage universal: many adults do not reason formally on unfamiliar content. Is formal logic the end point? Several theorists proposed postformal thought , adult reasoning that accepts contradiction, uncertainty and context (Table 6.14). Its core is dialectical reasoning : seeing that opposing views each hold part of the truth and integrating them in a synthesis. Table 6.14 Postformal thought. Theorist Year Idea Klaus Riegel 1973 Dialectical operations, "the final period of cognitive development": integrating contradiction William Perry 1970 College students move from dualism (right versus wrong) through relativism to commitment Patricia Arlin 1975 Problem finding: a fifth stage beyond formal problem solving Michael Basseches 1984 Dialectical thinking: seeing systems in constant change and interaction Gisela Labouvie-Vief 1980 Pragmatic thought: logic adapted to real-life limits and emotion Jan Sinnott 1998 Relativistic thought: choosing among logics, each valid in its context Exam trap The stage of abstract thought is the formal operational stage. It includes hypothetical, hypothetico-deductive, propositional, counterfactual, combinatorial and metacognitive reasoning. Dialectical reasoning is postformal (Riegel, Basseches), not formal operational. Evaluating Piaget Piaget's broad picture survives: children actively construct knowledge, thinking changes in kind as well as amount, and his sequence recurs across cultures. His timing and stages have fared worse. First, he underestimated infants and preschoolers . Baillargeon credited infants with object knowledge months early, and many preschool failures came from the task rather than the mind. Margaret Donaldson (1926 to 2020) drew the lesson in Children's Minds (1978): children reason well when a task makes "human sense" to them. Key study: Policemen and a naughty teddy Martin Hughes (1975) asked children of 3.5 to 5 to hide a boy doll from two policeman dolls among crossing walls; about 90 percent succeeded, though the task needs two perspectives at once, because hiding makes sense to them. James McGarrigle and Donaldson (1974) let a "naughty teddy" disarrange one row of the number-conservation task as if by accident; far more 4- to 6-year-olds conserved than when the adult changed the row on purpose. Criticism: some may have ignored the accidental change rather than truly conserved. Second, development is less stage-like than claimed: décalage is the rule, and abilities grow gradually, domain by domain. Third, culture and schooling matter more than he allowed, the core of Lev Vygotsky's critique (Section 6.5). Fourth, he did not separate competence , the understanding a child has, from performance , what she shows on a task with its own language, memory and attention demands. Neo-Piagetian theories keep the stages but explain them by growing processing capacity. Juan Pascual-Leone (1970) proposed M-space , the number of schemes a child can hold in mind at once, which grows with age. Robbie Case (1944 to 2000) traced stage progress to more efficient use of limited working memory as skills become automatic. Kurt Fischer (1943 to 2020) proposed skill theory (1980): skills develop through levels, separately in each domain, and run higher with support than alone. Exam trap Spot the false statement: "Cognitive structures of children under 7 reflect abstract mental operations" is false ; their thought is preoperational. True Piagetian statements: children construct knowledge by acting on objects physically or mentally; infant schemes are organised patterns of action; older children's operations let them see that quantities are conserved despite changes in appearance. Yet a real child learning to tie her shoelaces usually has an older sister kneeling beside her. Vygotsky and Bruner put that helper back into the picture; the information-processing approach treats the mind as a computer that gets faster and smarter; and research on theory of mind asks when children discover that other people have minds of their own. Vygotsky's sociocultural theory Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky (1896 to 1934), a Russian psychologist who died of tuberculosis at 37, saw cognitive growth as a socially mediated activity: children acquire new ways of thinking through cooperative dialogue with more skilled members of their culture. This is his sociocultural theory , set out in Thinking and Speech (1934) and known to English readers mainly through Mind in Society (1978), an edited collection of his essays. Vygotsky separated elementary mental functions, natural capacities we share with animals (simple attention, perception, involuntary memory), from higher mental functions such as voluntary attention, deliberate memory and verbal reasoning, which are human and cultural. What turns the first into the second is mediation : we act on the world, and on our own minds, through tools. Each culture supplies tools of intellectual adaptation , signs such as number systems, writing, maps and memory aids, that let children use their basic functions more adaptively; a knot tied in a handkerchief to remember an errand is a sign steering one's own memory. Language is the master tool. How does a tool that exists between people get inside one head? The general genetic law of cultural development states that every higher function appears twice: first between people (interpsychological), then within the child (intrapsychological). This passage from outer to inner is internalisation . A mother who asks "Where did you last see your bag?" remembers together with her son; years later he asks himself silently. Joint work rests on intersubjectivity , the process by which two people who begin a task with different understandings arrive at a shared one. Inter-subjectivity therefore precedes intra-subjectivity. Development, Vygotsky added, must be studied at four interrelated levels: microgenetic (change over minutes or days), ontogenetic (over a lifetime), phylogenetic (over evolution) and sociohistorical (change in the culture's values and technologies). Exam trap For Vygotsky, inter-subjectivity precedes intra-subjectivity . "Intra precedes inter" reverses the law, and "children do not engage in inter-subjectivity" contradicts it. "The two are related" is true but empty: the law is about their order. The zone of proximal development and scaffolding Vygotsky described two children who, working alone, both solve test problems set for eight-year-olds. Given hints, one solves problems set for twelve-year-olds, the other only those for nine-year-olds. The distance from eight to twelve, or from eight to nine, is what he called the zone of proximal development (ZPD): the gap between the child's actual developmental level, shown by independent problem solving, and her level of potential development, shown by problem solving under adult guidance or with more capable peers. That helper is now called the more knowledgeable other . As a range of tasks, the ZPD holds those too difficult to master alone but achievable with help (Figure 6.9). Teaching should aim inside it, at functions still ripening. Now Can do alone (actual level) Zone of proximal development: with help Out of reach, even with help today's help becomes tomorrow's skill Later Can do alone New zone Out of reach Task difficulty Figure 6.9 The zone of proximal development. As the child internalises what she first did with help, the zone moves towards harder tasks. Teaching within the ZPD is now usually called scaffolding : support fitted to the learner's current level and withdrawn as competence grows. The term is not Vygotsky's: it comes from David Wood , Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross (1976). Key study: Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976) A tutor helped 3- to 5-year-olds build a pyramid of interlocking wooden blocks, a task too hard for them alone. Good tutoring recruited interest, simplified the task, kept the goal in view, marked critical features, controlled frustration and demonstrated, stepping in only as far as the child needed. Criticism: the metaphor implies a fixed structure built by the adult, whereas real tutoring is a two-way exchange. Barbara Rogoff ( Apprenticeship in Thinking , 1990) described development as an apprenticeship built on guided participation : children learn by taking part, beside adults and peers, in their community's valued activities. In reciprocal teaching ( Annemarie Palincsar and Ann Brown , 1984), teacher and pupils take turns leading discussion of a text through questioning, summarising, clarifying and predicting, the teacher fading as pupils take over. Dynamic assessment (test, teach, retest) measures how much a child gains from help, as in Reuven Feuerstein 's Learning Potential Assessment Device (1979). Exam trap The ZPD is the gap between independent and assisted performance , a term coined by Vygotsky (not Piaget, Bruner, Kohlberg, Bronfenbrenner, Erikson, Skinner or Freud). Wrong options name something else: tasks done alone (the actual level), too simple, too hard even with help, or learned without instruction; innate abilities, structures or the language acquisition device (Section 1.8); a critical, optimal or language-learning period (Section 6.1) or the usual age for a milestone; a stage of logical operations or object permanence (Section 6.4); a fixed capacity or genetic ceiling; mental age minus chronological age (Section 1.9); a brain or adolescent growth spurt; a neural region; a peer group. Thought, speech and concepts On language the two theorists disagreed most clearly. For Piaget thought comes first, and language expresses concepts already built through action; the preschooler's talk to no one, his egocentric speech ( The Language and Thought of the Child , 1923), mirrors egocentric thought and simply fades. For Vygotsky thought and language have separate roots: prelinguistic thought (a toddler using a stick to reach a toy) and preintellectual speech (babbling). At about age 2 they merge; thought becomes verbal, and from then on language shapes thought. So thought depends on language for Vygotsky, and language depends on thought for Piaget. Speech then turns inward. Social speech, used to communicate, comes first. From about 3 children talk aloud to themselves as they work ("the red one goes... no, here"). Vygotsky saw this talk, now called private speech , as social speech turned to guiding one's own actions; at school age it goes underground as inner speech , silent verbal thought. Laura E. Berk 's studies in the 1980s and 1990s supported him: children use more private speech on hard tasks and after errors, those who use it more tend to improve, and it fades to whispers before going inward. Exam trap Vygotsky: thought depends on language; Piaget: language depends on thought. The reversed option swaps the names, and "one studied early, the other later language" is false. Private speech guides and regulates behaviour and becomes inner speech. It is not a regression to "autistic" (undirected, wishful) thinking, a word Piaget used, nor mere imitation, a language disorder or egocentrism that fades with schooling. Vygotsky traced concept formation with block-sorting tasks. Young children form heaps (syncretic groupings), objects lumped together by chance impression. Next come complexes, groups built on concrete, shifting links (a red block, then a red triangle, then any triangle). The most advanced complex, the pseudoconcept , looks like a true concept (every triangle gathered) but rests on visible likeness, not an abstract rule. True concepts mature in adolescence. Vygotsky linked them to the distinction between the acting "I" and the reflecting "I" (the self that does and the self that thinks about its doing), to the problems and developmental tasks society sets adolescents, and to participation in its institutions. Gender differences play no part. Piaget and Vygotsky compared Both men were born in 1896, both saw the child as active, and neither held that development is solely environmental or predetermined.
