Jerome Bruner: representation and discovery Jerome Seymour Bruner (1915 to 2016), an American leader of the cognitive revolution, shared Vygotsky's interest in culture and teaching. In 1966 he proposed three modes of representation . The enactive mode represents knowledge through action (a baby knows a rattle as a shaking movement); the iconic mode, through images (picturing the route to school); the symbolic mode, through language, numbers and other arbitrary symbols. They appear roughly in that order from infancy to the school years, but unlike Piaget's stages none is left behind. In The Process of Education (1960) Bruner argued that any subject can be taught in some intellectually honest form to any child at any stage. Hence the spiral curriculum , which returns to the same big ideas at rising levels of complexity, and discovery learning , in which learners find principles for themselves by working on problems. His language acquisition support system (LASS) is covered in Section 1.8. Information processing: the mind as a computer The information-processing approach likens the mind to a computer: information comes in, is held and transformed, and leaves as an answer. Development means better hardware (the brain and nervous system) and better software (attention, memory strategies and problem-solving routines), and it is continuous: many small quantitative gains, not qualitative stages. The hardware speeds up. Robert V. Kail (1991) showed that processing speed rises steeply in childhood and more slowly in adolescence, at a similar rate across very different tasks, which suggests a general biological cause such as myelination. Attention grows more selective, working memory holds more, and the executive functions of the prefrontal cortex mature: inhibitory control (stopping a dominant response), working memory (holding and updating information) and cognitive flexibility (switching rules or viewpoints). The software improves too. Memory strategies appear in order: rehearsal (repeating items) from about 7, organisation (grouping items by meaning) in middle childhood and elaboration (linking items through an image or sentence) mostly in adolescence. A child with a production deficiency , John H. Flavell 's term, can use a strategy when told but does not produce it spontaneously; one with a utilisation deficiency ( Patricia H. Miller ) produces it but at first gains little from it. Flavell (1979) also made metacognition , knowledge and control of one's own thinking, central; its memory part is metamemory , such as knowing that a long list needs more study. Knowledge matters as much as capacity: Michelene Chi (1978) found that child chess experts recalled board positions better than adult novices, who still recalled digit lists better. Robert S. Siegler 's overlapping waves model (1996) holds that children always have several strategies (for 3 + 5: counting on fingers, counting on from the larger number, simply retrieving 8) whose frequencies shift gradually, like overlapping waves, rather than in stages. In fuzzy-trace theory ( Charles Brainerd and Valerie Reyna , 1990) we store separate verbatim and gist traces and rely more on gist with age. Theory of mind A theory of mind is the understanding that people have mental states (beliefs, desires, intentions) that guide their actions and can differ from one's own and from reality. The term comes from David Premack and Guy Woodruff (1978), who asked whether a chimpanzee has one. Its precursors appear late in the first year: joint attention (following another's gaze or point to a shared object), social referencing (Section 6.6) and intention reading (treating a reach as aimed at a goal). Gyorgy Gergely and Gergely Csibra (from 1995) call this early framework the teleological stance : around the end of the first year infants read an action as efficient and goal-directed, expecting an agent to take the most direct route its situation allows. In the philosopher John Searle 's (1983) terms, toddlers understand intentions in action , the goal visible in an ongoing act. They have moved beyond mere contingencies (this event follows that one) but not yet to prior intentions (plans formed before acting) or mental states such as belief and desire. Henry Wellman (1990) traced the next steps: a desire psychology at about 2, explaining actions by wants, then a belief-desire psychology at 3 to 4, in which actions follow from what people want and what they believe, even falsely. The test is the false-belief task : the child must predict the action of someone whose belief the child knows is wrong. In Heinz Wimmer and Josef Perner 's original (1983), Maxi puts his chocolate in one cupboard and goes out; his mother moves it. Where will Maxi look? In the Smarties (unexpected-contents) task of Perner, Susan Leekam and Wimmer (1987), a child who expected sweets in a Smarties tube is shown pencils and asked what a friend will think is inside. Three-year-olds answer from reality; most children pass at about 4, in the preoperational years. Flavell's appearance-reality distinction comes at a similar age: shown a sponge painted like a rock, a 3-year-old says it looks like a sponge, while a 5-year-old says it looks like a rock but is really a sponge. 1 Sally marble in basket basket box 2 Sally leaves basket box 3 Anne moves it to box basket box 4 Sally returns Where will she look? basket box Pass: "the basket" (Sally's false belief) Fail: "the box" (where the marble really is) Figure 6.10 The Sally-Anne task. To pass, the child must answer from Sally's mistaken belief, not from what she herself knows. Key study: Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith (1985) Simon Baron-Cohen , Alan Leslie and Uta Frith acted out the Sally-Anne task with dolls (Figure 6.10). About 85 percent of typically developing preschoolers and 86 percent of children with Down syndrome answered "the basket", but 80 percent of autistic children, though of higher verbal mental age than the Down syndrome group, pointed to the box. The authors proposed a specific theory-of-mind deficit in autism, later called mindblindness (Chapter 8). Criticism: the task also loads on language and memory, and some autistic children pass it. Exam trap False-belief tasks (Maxi, Sally-Anne, Smarties) assess theory of mind and are passed at about age 4 , in the preoperational period: not at 12 months (only the teleological stance), age 8 (concrete operations) or adolescence. They are not the A-not-B task (object permanence), a conservation task (both Section 6.4), the Strange Situation (attachment, Section 6.7) or a working memory test. Recursive thought and social perspective taking Passing a false-belief task is first-order reasoning: "Sally thinks the marble is in the basket." A second-order theory of mind nests one belief inside another ("John thinks that Mary thinks the ice-cream van is in the park"); Perner and Wimmer (1985) found it at about 6 to 7. The ability to nest perspectives is recursive thought , a form of perspective taking that views a situation from at least two perspectives, reasoning simultaneously about what two or more people are thinking ("I think that you think that I think..."). Patricia Miller, Frank Kessel and Flavell (1970) showed it growing through the school years. It is not referential style , Katherine Nelson 's term for toddlers whose first words mostly name objects; not reversibility , Piaget's mental undoing of an operation (Section 6.4); and not reconstruction , the rebuilding of memories (Section 1.7). Robert L. Selman (1976, 1980) studied social perspective taking , understanding another person's thoughts and feelings, through dilemmas. In the best known, Holly has promised her father not to climb trees, then finds a friend's kitten stuck in one. From the answers Selman described five levels (Table 6.16), a progression from egocentric to multiple, mutual perspective taking. Alongside this shared timetable runs an individual style, temperament, and the growing capacity to manage it, self-regulation. The first emotions What can a newborn feel? In the differentiation theory of Katharine Banham Bridges (1932), built from observing infants of different ages, the newborn has only a diffuse general excitement . Within about three months this splits into two poles, distress and delight , which are therefore the first emotions infants express. Each pole then divides again, distress into anger, disgust and fear, delight into elation and affection, until by two years most adult emotions can be seen (Figure 6.11). Two rival views differ. John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958) held that only fear, rage and love are innate and all other emotions are conditioned onto them. Carroll Izard (1923 to 2017), in his differential emotions theory , held that each basic emotion is a separate innate system with its own facial expression, switched on by maturation (Section 1.11). Pairs such as "pain and anger" or "fear and euphoria" belong to no one's scheme. Birth By about 3 months Later in first year General excitement Distress Delight Anger Disgust Fear Elation Affection Figure 6.11 Bridges' differentiation of emotion (1932): general excitement divides first into distress and delight, then into specific emotions. Modern research, much of it by Michael Lewis , places the primary emotions (joy, interest, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger and fear) within the first six months; none needs a sense of self. Is the first smile joy? Not yet. The reflexive smile (endogenous smile) of the first weeks comes from internal states, mostly in sleep. The social smile , a smile in response to a human face or voice, appears at about 6 to 10 weeks, and laughter at about 3 to 4 months (Figure 6.12). Self-awareness and the self-conscious emotions A second family of emotions must wait for a self. Embarrassment, pride, shame, guilt, envy and empathy are self-conscious emotions (secondary or self-evaluative emotions): each involves judging yourself through others' eyes or against a standard, so each needs self-awareness and appears only after 12 months, from the second half of the second year. Lewis places embarrassment, envy and empathy at about 18 to 24 months, once the child recognises himself, and pride, shame and guilt at about two and a half to three years, once he has rules to judge himself by. Joseph Campos (2009) and Jerome Kagan (1929 to 2021; 2010) agree on this timing. Key study: the rouge test (Lewis and Brooks-Gunn, 1979) Michael Lewis and Jeanne Brooks-Gunn secretly dabbed rouge on infants' noses and placed them before a mirror. A baby who touches her own nose, not the reflection's, knows the face is hers. Infants under a year treated the image as another baby; nose-touching was typical by 18 to 24 months. This mirror self-recognition marks the arrival of the self, just as embarrassment appears. Exam trap Self-conscious emotions appear after 12 months (from the second half of the second year), never at 3 months, 6 to 9 months or "before 9 months". Those early ages belong to the primary emotions. Strangers, separations and the still face In the second half of the first year emotion turns sharply social. Stranger anxiety , wariness or crying when an unfamiliar adult approaches, emerges at about 6 to 8 months; René Spitz (1887 to 1974) called it eight-month anxiety (Section 6.7). Separation protest (separation anxiety), crying when the caregiver leaves, follows; Kagan found the same curve in several very different cultures, rising from about 8 months, peaking at about 13 to 15 months and then declining. Both fears therefore peak within roughly 8 to 15 months, because the baby now has a specific attachment figure and enough memory to notice an unfamiliar face or an absent caregiver. Excessive distress far beyond this age is separation anxiety disorder (Chapter 8). Exam trap Stranger anxiety and separation anxiety peak at about 8 to 15 months , not at 1 to 2 months (the age of the social smile), 3 years or 6 years. Infants also learn to use others' emotions as information. In social referencing , from about 8 to 12 months, an infant facing an uncertain situation reads a trusted adult's face and lets it guide her. James Sorce , Campos and colleagues (1985) placed 12-month-olds on a visual cliff (Section 6.3) with a drop just deep enough to make them hesitate: when the mother looked happy, about three in four crossed; when she looked afraid, none did. Key study: the still-face paradigm (Tronick and colleagues, 1978) Are young infants simply soaked in their caregivers' mood, or partners in the exchange? Edward Tronick and colleagues filmed mothers with infants a few months old in three episodes: normal face-to-face play; a still face, in which the mother keeps looking at the baby with a blank, unresponsive face; and reunion. Faced with the still face, babies first tried to restart the exchange with smiles, coos and reaching, then turned their gaze away, slumped and became distressed and disorganised. The still-face paradigm showed that even very young infants actively expect and seek affective reciprocity (emotional give-and-take); it is now used to study the effects of maternal depression. Exam trap The still face shows infants as active partners who expect reciprocity , distressed and disorganised when it stops. They are not passive recipients of caregiver mood and do not habituate at once; the paradigm says nothing about fathers versus mothers, preferring strangers, or face recognition before 12 months. From soothing to self-regulation Caregivers first manage a baby's feelings by rocking and feeding. Emotion regulation , the processes by which we monitor and adjust the intensity and timing of our emotional reactions, develops as a handover to the child: by a few months babies avert their gaze from overstimulation or suck a thumb. Claire Kopp (1982) described three steps: control (about 12 to 18 months: complying with caregivers' demands), self-control (from about 2 years: complying without being watched) and self-regulation (from about 3 years: flexibly guiding one's own behaviour). Children also learn display rules , a culture's norms for when, where and how much emotion may be shown (Section 1.11): in many Indian homes a child learns early to hide anger before elders. What temperament is Some babies take a new face in their stride; others scream. Temperament names these differences. In Mary Rothbart 's definition, it is constitutionally based individual differences in reactivity (how quickly and strongly a child is aroused) and self-regulation (how she modulates that arousal). It appears early, within the first months. It is moderately stable: a fearful infant often becomes a cautious child, but many change. And it is generally considered biologically and genetically based: identical twins are more alike in temperament than fraternal twins. The environment does not create temperament but shapes its expression, the idea of goodness of fit ( below ). Temperament is the raw material of adult personality (Chapter 4). Exam trap Asked what temperament is "generally considered to be", choose genetically (biologically) based . "Learned behaviour", "a result of parenting" and "environmentally influenced" are the distractors: the environment modulates temperament but is not its origin. Thomas and Chess: the New York Longitudinal Study In 1956 the psychiatrists Alexander Thomas (1914 to 2003) and Stella Chess (1914 to 2007), husband and wife, launched the New York Longitudinal Study (NYLS), following children from infancy into adulthood. At a time when psychiatry blamed children's problems on parents, they asked whether babies arrive with behavioural styles of their own. They interviewed parents , asking not for impressions ("a good baby") but for concrete descriptions of feeding, bathing, a new food or a stranger's visit, and they observed the babies to check the reports. The easy child (about 40 percent) is regular in eating and sleeping, cheerful, approaches new things and adapts quickly. The difficult child (about 10 percent) has irregular biological rhythms, a generally negative mood and intense reactions, withdraws from new stimuli and is slow to adapt. The slow-to-warm-up child (about 15 percent) is low in activity, withdraws from new stimuli at first with mild rather than intense negativity, and adapts slowly but gradually with repeated exposure. The remaining 35 percent or so showed mixed patterns: they are unclassified, not a fourth named type. Picture the first week at a Mysuru playschool. Ananya plays at once and naps on schedule: easy. Kabir screams, flings his snack and still protests a fortnight later: difficult. Meera clings quietly to her mother's dupatta, watches from the edge and joins in by the second week: slow-to-warm-up, because her withdrawal is mild and gives way. The difficult child syndrome means that some infants are difficult even in the first few weeks after birth, before parenting could have produced it. It is a temperament, not a later behaviour problem (though such children run a higher risk of one), and has nothing to do with auditory discrimination (turning the head to one sound and not another) or a delay in voluntary control. Why do some difficult children do well? Thomas and Chess's answer was goodness of fit : the match between a child's temperament and the demands and expectations of caregivers and the wider environment. A difficult child whose parents stay patient and consistent often thrives; the same child with impatient, punitive parents tends to develop problems. Exam trap Thomas and Chess are known for temperament , not human sexuality, needs and drives or marital therapy. Their three types are easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up . Distractors: sanguine, choleric, melancholic and phlegmatic (Hippocrates' humours, Galen's temperaments; Chapter 4); Type A, B and C (behaviour patterns linked to heart disease and cancer; Section 1.11); "inconsistent", "sensitive, resilient, withdrawn" and "inhibited only" (inhibition is Kagan's construct, below); and "insecurely attached", an attachment category (Section 6.7). Goodness of fit is never IQ differences between twins, the number of siblings or parent-child genetic concordance. Rothbart and Bates, Kagan, Buss and Plomin Later researchers condensed the overlapping nine dimensions. Mary Rothbart, who built the parent-report Infant Behavior Questionnaire (1981), and John Bates proposed a structural model of temperament (1998) with exactly three broad dimensions. Surgency , or extraversion, covers approach, activity, positive anticipation, smiling and sociability. Negative affectivity covers fear, frustration, sadness, discomfort and difficulty being soothed. Effortful control is the capacity to focus and shift attention voluntarily and to inhibit a dominant response; it is the self-regulatory side of temperament and matures in the preschool years. Kagan studied reaction to the unfamiliar. Shown novel mobiles, voices and smells, about one 4-month-old in five thrashed and cried. These high-reactive infants tended to become inhibited , shy and wary children, while low-reactive infants tended to become uninhibited , bold and sociable. Behavioural inhibition , the tendency to withdraw from and be distressed by the unfamiliar, is Kagan's construct; he traced it to an easily excited amygdala. Its stability is moderate: many inhibited toddlers grow less shy. Arnold Buss and Robert Plomin (1984) proposed the EAS model of three heritable temperaments: emotionality (how easily a child becomes distressed), activity (tempo and vigour) and sociability (preference for company). Effortful control and the marshmallow test Effortful control is the core of self-regulation , the ability to manage attention, emotion and action in pursuit of a goal; its most famous test asks a child to wait. Key study: the marshmallow test (Mischel, from the late 1960s) Walter Mischel (1930 to 2018) tested preschoolers at the Bing Nursery School at Stanford University. A child could eat one treat now or have two if she waited, up to 15 minutes, for the experimenter to return; ringing a bell brought him back at once, but then she got only one. The marshmallow test measures delay of gratification : giving up a smaller immediate reward for a larger later one. Follow-ups found that longer waiters were rated more competent as adolescents and scored higher on the SAT, the American college admission test ( Yuichi Shoda , Mischel and Philip Peake , 1990). A larger, more diverse replication by Tyler Watts , Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan (2018) found the link about half as strong, and weaker still once family background was controlled. Waiting turned out to be a skill of attention. Children waited longer when the treats were covered or when they distracted themselves by singing. Dwelling on the treat's hot features (sweet, chewy) made waiting almost impossible; thinking of its cool , abstract features ("puffy, like a cloud") made it easier. Mischel later described a hot, emotional "go" system and a cool, cognitive "know" system that matures with age. Keep delay of gratification apart from three neighbours. Sustained attention is keeping focus on one task over time. Resistance to temptation is obeying a prohibition when no one is watching, studied with the forbidden-toy paradigm : the child is told not to touch an attractive toy and left alone with it, with no bigger reward for complying. Impulse control in social settings is holding back an unacceptable act such as grabbing or interrupting. The marshmallow task draws on all three, but its defining feature is the choice between a smaller-sooner and a larger-later reward. Mischel's personality theory is in Chapter 4. Exam trap The marshmallow test primarily measures delay of gratification , not sustained attention, resistance to temptation (the forbidden toy) or impulse control in social settings. She cries when her mother walks out, crawls to her the moment she returns and, within a minute, is back among the toys. That small drama is attachment, the first close relationship of life. This section asks why the bond forms, how it unfolds over the first three years, how its quality is measured, what its absence does and how it echoes into adulthood. What attachment is: four theories An attachment is a strong, enduring emotional bond to a specific person who cannot be swapped for anyone else. Four behaviours reveal it: the infant keeps close to the person (proximity seeking), explores from her as a secure base , runs back to her as a safe haven when frightened, and shows separation distress when she leaves. A baby who smiles at everyone is sociable; one who protests when one particular person leaves is attached. Why does the bond form? Four answers compete (Table 6.19). For Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) it was feeding: the mother gratifies oral needs, so the infant loves her; Erik Erikson (1902 to 1994) added that responsive care builds basic trust (Section 6.10). The learning theorists John Dollard and Neal Miller (1950) and Robert Sears said the same in behavioural terms: the mother, paired again and again with hunger reduction, becomes a secondary reinforcer, so attachment is a learned secondary drive , nicknamed 'cupboard love'. The cognitive-developmental view adds a precondition: a baby must tell familiar people from strangers and know that people go on existing when out of sight, an achievement called person permanence (Section 6.4). The ethological theory of John Bowlby holds that attachment is an evolved behavioural system that kept helpless infants near a protector and so alive. Geese and monkeys, as the next two subsections show, undermined the feeding theories, and the ethological theory is the predominantly accepted account today. Theory Key figures Why the infant attaches Status Psychoanalytic Freud; Erikson Feeding gratifies oral needs; care builds trust Feeding overrated Learning (secondary drive) Dollard and Miller; Sears Mother becomes a secondary reinforcer ('cupboard love') Refuted by Harlow Cognitive-developmental Builds on Piaget Needs person permanence Explains timing only Ethological Bowlby, after Lorenz Evolved system for survival Predominantly accepted Exam trap The ethological theory is today's predominantly accepted account, not the psychoanalytic, learning or cognitive-developmental one. 'Cupboard love' is the learning view. Lorenz and imprinting Key study: Lorenz's goslings (1935) Konrad Lorenz (1903 to 1989), an Austrian zoologist, split a clutch of greylag goose eggs. Half hatched under their mother; half hatched in an incubator, where the first moving thing the goslings saw was Lorenz. The incubator goslings followed him everywhere, and when the two broods were mixed and released, each gosling ran to its own 'mother', goose or man. Lorenz called this imprinting : a rapid, largely irreversible following response to the first moving object, formed only within a narrow critical period after hatching (Section 6.1). It needs no practice and no food reward. It also lasts: birds imprinted on humans later courted humans, a long-term effect called sexual imprinting. Eckhard Hess (1916 to 1986) timed the window in mallard ducklings: imprinting peaked at about 13 to 16 hours after hatching and then fell away sharply. Later work found the window more flexible than Lorenz thought, so many now say sensitive period. Lorenz shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Karl von Frisch . Human babies do not imprint, but Lorenz gave Bowlby two ideas: early bonds are biologically prepared, and they have a critical period. Exam trap Imprinting is rapid, largely irreversible and limited to a critical period : not slow, reversible lifelong learning, operant conditioning with food or a purely visual system unrelated to attachment. Nor is it habituation (Section 6.3), newborn reflexive smiling (Section 6.6) or same-sex playmate preference at 5 (Section 6.8). Lorenz , not Ainsworth, Bowlby or Erikson, argued that newborn creatures imprint during a critical period. Harlow's surrogate mothers If feeding builds the bond, an infant should love whoever feeds it. Harry Harlow (1905 to 1981) tested this at the University of Wisconsin with his wife and colleague Margaret Harlow . Key study: 'The Nature of Love' (Harlow, 1958) Infant rhesus monkeys, taken from their mothers at birth, were raised with two surrogate mothers: a bare wire-mesh figure and one covered in terry cloth. For some infants only the wire mother held a feeding bottle. Whichever fed them, they spent most of the day clinging to the cloth mother and visited the wire one only to feed. Frightened by a mechanical toy, they fled to the cloth mother, calmed, then turned to explore; in a strange room they explored only when she was present. Conclusion: contact comfort , not feeding, is the primary basis of attachment, and the cloth mother served as safe haven and secure base. Criticism: the work is ethically troubling, and monkeys are not children. Monkeys reared in total isolation for six months to a year grew up rocking, clasping themselves and unable to play or mate normally; isolate females who later had infants became 'motherless mothers', neglecting or abusing them. Even a cloth mother could not produce normal social development. Yet Stephen Suomi and Harlow (1972) found that housing isolates with younger 'therapist' monkeys, which clung and played without threat, restored much social behaviour. Early deprivation is serious but partly reversible, a theme the human studies below repeat. Exam trap Harlow showed contact comfort, not feeding , as the basis of attachment: not conditioned reinforcement, operant shaping of clinging, classical conditioning of hunger or innate fear of strangers. He did not show imprinting in primates, critical periods for language or genetic determinism, and his isolates show that maternal absence harms even when nutrition is met. Bowlby's attachment theory John Bowlby (1907 to 1990), a British psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, wove these threads into attachment theory. In Forty-Four Juvenile Thieves (1944) he found that 14 of the young thieves at his London clinic showed affectionless psychopathy (no guilt, no affection for others), and 12 of those 14 had suffered prolonged early separation from their mothers. His 1951 World Health Organization report, Maternal Care and Mental Health , set out the maternal deprivation hypothesis : an infant needs a warm, continuous relationship with the mother or a permanent substitute, and its prolonged disruption in the early years does lasting harm. The trilogy Attachment (1969), Separation (1973) and Loss (1980) completed the theory. Its claims are these. Attachment is an evolved behavioural system: crying, smiling, clinging and following bring a caregiver close; the system switches on under threat or separation, and when the infant feels safe it explores from its secure base. Monotropy means that one bond, usually with the mother, is special and qualitatively different from the rest. The bond must form within a critical period, roughly the first two and a half years. And the infant builds an internal working model : a mental representation of the self (am I lovable?), of attachment figures (will they come?) and of relationships, built from early experience, that serves as a prototype, a schema, for later relationships yet can be revised by new experience. What does a broken bond look like? Bowlby's colleague James Robertson filmed A Two-Year-Old Goes to Hospital (1952) and later, with Joyce Robertson , other brief separations. Young children passed through a protest-despair-detachment sequence: protest (crying, searching), despair (listless misery) and detachment (seeming recovery, but coolness to the mother on her return). Bowlby applied a similar sequence to grief (Section 6.11). Exam trap Attachment theory is Bowlby's , not Freud's, Rogers's or Bandura's. The internal working model is a revisable representation of self, others and relationships. It is not the proximity-seeking mechanism or the attachment system itself (which the model guides), a 'bio-social relationship model' (not Bowlby's term), Tolman's cognitive map (Chapter 1), a hippocampus-amygdala circuit, a genetic fear template, a reflex repertoire, a language substrate or object permanence. Phases of attachment: Bowlby, Schaffer and Emerson, Mahler Attachment assembles itself over the first two years. Bowlby described four phases (Figure 6.13): Pre-attachment (birth to 6 weeks): signals bring adults close; the baby knows her mother's smell and voice but does not mind strangers. Attachment-in-the-making (6 weeks to 6 to 8 months): she prefers familiar people but does not yet protest at separation. Clear-cut attachment (6 to 8 months to 18 months to 2 years): clear preference for the primary caregiver, separation protest, stranger anxiety (Section 6.6) and secure-base behaviour. Formation of a reciprocal relationship , the goal-corrected partnership (from 18 months to 2 years onwards): language lets the toddler understand and predict the parent's comings and goings, so protest gives way to negotiation. Rudolph Schaffer and Peggy Emerson (1964) followed 60 Glasgow infants at home, monthly through the first year and again at 18 months, recording protest at everyday separations and fear of strangers. They found four stages: asocial (0 to 6 weeks), indiscriminate (6 weeks to about 7 months, accepting comfort from anyone), specific attachment (from about 7 months, with separation protest and stranger fear) and multiple attachments (soon after; most infants had several by 18 months). Infants attached most strongly to whoever responded most sensitively to them, not necessarily the person who fed them. Margaret Mahler (1897 to 1985), a psychoanalyst, traced how the child separates psychologically within the bond ( The Psychological Birth of the Human Infant , 1975, with Fred Pine and Anni Bergman ). A normal autistic phase (the first weeks) and a symbiotic phase (to about 5 months, mother and infant felt as one) give way to separation-individuation in four subphases: differentiation or hatching (about 5 to 10 months: turning outward, first stranger reactions); practising (about 10 to 16 months: delighted exploration on new legs); rapprochement (about 15 to 24 months: aware now of being separate, the toddler alternates independent exploration with returns to the caregiver for emotional refuelling , and the clash of autonomy and closeness brings the clinging and tantrums of the rapprochement crisis); and consolidation (about 24 to 36 months), when object constancy , a stable inner image of the mother, lets the child bear her absence. Her developmental theory of schizophrenia and childhood psychosis belongs to Chapter 8. Exam trap Clear preference, separation protest and stranger anxiety mark Bowlby's clear-cut phase (6 to 8 months to 2 years; '6 months to 2 years' in keys), not pre-attachment, attachment-in-the-making or the goal-corrected partnership. Schaffer and Emerson's specific attachment starts at about 7 months . Rapprochement (15 to 24 months) is exploration alternating with refuelling: not symbiotic merger, the first stranger reactions (differentiation) or full object constancy. Ainsworth and the Strange Situation Bowlby's theory said every infant attaches; it did not say how well. That measure came from Mary Ainsworth (1913 to 1999), who worked with Bowlby in London and then watched mothers and babies at home in Uganda and Baltimore. To capture differences in security in one short session she devised the Strange Situation (Ainsworth and Barbara Wittig , 1969; reported in full in Patterns of Attachment , 1978, with Mary Blehar , Everett Waters and Sally Wall ). Over eight episodes of about three minutes each, a 12- to 18-month-old explores a playroom with the caregiver, meets a stranger, is left with the stranger, is reunited, is left alone, is joined by the stranger and is reunited again. Observers score exploration, separation distress, reaction to the stranger and, above all, reunion behaviour, which best reveals what the infant expects of the caregiver. Ainsworth's maternal sensitivity hypothesis explains the differences: security grows from noticing the baby's signals, reading them correctly and answering them promptly and appropriately. In Baltimore, mothers who answered crying promptly in the early months had securely attached one-year-olds; later studies confirm a real but more modest link. Exam trap Ainsworth (not Bowlby, Harlow, Lorenz, Piaget or Erikson) devised the Strange Situation, and she is known for attachment, not cognitive, moral or language development. Bowlby is to attachment as Ainsworth is to the Strange Situation; the Bobo doll is Albert Bandura's, Little Albert is John Watson and Rosalie Rayner's, and the visual cliff is Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk's (Section 6.3). Four patterns of attachment, and culture Ainsworth's infants fell into three groups, A, B and C; Mary Main and Judith Solomon (1986, 1990) added a fourth, D (Table 6.20). Secure attachment (B) is the commonest, about 60 to 70 percent of samples. Insecure-avoidant attachment (A, about 20 percent) follows rejecting care: an infant whose bids for comfort are rebuffed learns to suppress them. Insecure-resistant attachment (C), or ambivalent (about 10 to 15 percent), follows inconsistent care: never sure that comfort will come, the infant clings and protests. Disorganised attachment (D), or disoriented, abounds among maltreated infants and those with a frightened or frightening caregiver, who is both the source of fear and its only refuge. Marinus van IJzendoorn and Pieter Kroonenberg (1988) pooled 32 studies from eight countries: secure was the commonest type everywhere, and variation within cultures was about one and a half times that between them. Northern German samples ( Klaus Grossmann and Karin Grossmann , Bielefeld) held many avoidant infants because parents valued early independence, which lowers visible distress and reunion seeking. Japanese infants, rarely apart from their mothers, and Israeli kibbutz infants, who seldom met strangers, showed more resistant attachment. Deprivation and privation René Spitz (1887 to 1974) compared babies in a foundling home, fed and clean but rarely held, with babies cared for by their own mothers in a prison nursery. The foundling babies fell behind, sickened and many died, a syndrome he called hospitalism (1945). He also described anaclitic depression (1946): infants separated from their mothers in the second half of the first year turned weepy, then withdrawn, lost weight and stopped developing, recovering if the mother returned within a few months. Michael Rutter (1933 to 2021), in Maternal Deprivation Reassessed (1972), distinguished deprivation (losing a bond already formed) from privation (never forming one), the more harmful of the two. Barbara Tizard and Jill Hodges followed children raised in London residential nurseries by many changing carers: those later adopted formed close bonds with their new parents, closer than children returned to birth families, yet at 16 still had more difficulty with peers. Rutter's English and Romanian Adoptees study found that Romanian orphans adopted into British homes before about 6 months caught up almost fully, while later adoptees more often kept cognitive deficits and disinhibited attachment. Privation harms, but early rescue repairs much. Donald Winnicott (1896 to 1971) added the good-enough mother , reliably responsive rather than perfect, and the transitional object , a blanket or soft toy that comforts the child on the way to independence. Clinical link Severe early neglect can produce reactive attachment disorder (a withdrawn child who rarely seeks comfort) or disinhibited social engagement disorder (indiscriminate, overfamiliar approach to strangers); both are taught in Chapter 8. Exam trap Hospitalism and anaclitic depression are Spitz's , not Piaget's, Skinner's or Eysenck's. Deprivation is losing a bond; privation is never having one. Attachment beyond infancy Mary Main's Adult Attachment Interview classifies adults by how coherently they discuss their childhood: secure-autonomous (balanced), dismissing (idealises parents, recalls little), preoccupied (still angrily entangled) and unresolved (incoherent about loss or abuse). These parallel infant types B, A, C and D, and a parent's classification predicts her infant's well above chance. Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver (1987) found secure, avoidant and anxious-ambivalent styles in adult romantic love, in proportions resembling the infant ones. Kim Bartholomew and Leonard Horowitz (1991) crossed positive or negative models of self and of others into four adult styles: secure, preoccupied, dismissing and fearful. Monotropy, finally, has softened. Fathers are attachment figures in their own right, and most infants have several attachments by 18 months, as in any Indian joint family; responsiveness, not feeding, decides to whom. On day care, Jay Belsky (1986) warned that over 20 hours a week in the first year raises the risk of insecurity, but the large Study of Early Child Care run by the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) found that day care alone does not; risk rises only when poor or very long care meets insensitive mothering. A parent sets her limits, siblings and grandparents crowd round, she plays beside and then with other children, and in almost everything she is learning what it means to be a girl. This section follows those threads; attachment, which comes first, is Section 6.7. Baumrind's parenting styles Why do some children grow up confident and self-controlled while others become anxious or unruly? In the 1960s Diana Baumrind (1927 to 2018) observed preschoolers at nursery school and at home and interviewed their parents. In papers from 1966 to 1971 she described three patterns of parenting style , the overall emotional climate in which a parent raises a child. Authoritative parenting combines warmth and emotional support with clear boundaries: rules are explained, discipline is reasoned, children are held accountable for their behaviour and their growing autonomy is encouraged. Authoritarian parenting makes high demands with little warmth: strict obedience, rules without reasons ("because I said so") and often harsh punishment. Permissive parenting , also called indulgent, is warm and accepting but makes few demands and sets few rules. In 1983 Eleanor Maccoby (1917 to 2018) and John Martin recast the styles as combinations of two independent dimensions: demandingness (control: expecting mature behaviour, supervising, disciplining) and responsiveness (warmth: acceptance and attention to the child's needs). The cell low on both became a fourth style, neglectful parenting (uninvolved): detached parents who do little beyond meeting basic needs. Figure 6.14 shows the four styles. Children of authoritative parents are the most self-reliant, competent and achievement-oriented; those of authoritarian parents tend to be anxious, withdrawn and unhappy, and those of permissive parents impulsive, with poor self-control; children of neglectful parents fare worst, with low self-esteem, poor schoolwork and later delinquency. Demandingness (control) High Low Authoritarian Strict obedience, little warmth Child: anxious, withdrawn Authoritative Warm, firm, reasons given Child: self-reliant, competent Neglectful (uninvolved) Detached, few demands Child: poorest outcomes Permissive (indulgent) Warm, few rules or demands Child: impulsive, low control Low High Responsiveness (warmth) Figure 6.14 Maccoby and Martin's two dimensions give four parenting styles; only authoritative parenting is high on both. Culture shifts the picture. Ruth Chao (1994) showed that Chinese-American parents score as authoritarian on Western scales, yet their children do well at school: their strictness expresses the Chinese idea of training ( chiao shun ), devoted involvement that children read as care. Many Indian families show a similar warm control , firm expectations of obedience inside close affection. Control harms mainly when it comes without warmth. Exam trap Authoritative is the best style; authoritarian is strict and cold. "Emotional support, clear boundaries and accountability", "high demandingness and high responsiveness" and "reasoned discipline with autonomy support" all mean authoritative. Permissive is low demandingness with high responsiveness; neglectful is low on both and was added by Maccoby and Martin, not Baumrind. New labels, discipline and the family Helicopter parenting is over-involved parenting: parents hover, monitor and step in to solve problems the child could handle alone. The image comes from Haim Ginott (1922 to 1973), whose 1969 book Between Parent and Teenager quotes a teenager whose mother hovers over him like a helicopter. It has several roots at once: parental anxiety, parents' unfulfilled wishes lived out through the child, and parents' own personality traits such as perfectionism. Tiger parenting (after Amy Chua 's 2011 memoir) is strict and achievement-driven; free-range parenting grants age-appropriate independence with little supervision. Martin Hoffman 's (1967) three kinds of discipline, induction (explaining how the behaviour affects others), power assertion (force, threats) and love withdrawal (withholding affection), are compared in Section 6.9. Parents are one part of a family system in which every member affects every other. Siblings are companions, teachers and rivals; the claim that birth order shapes personality belongs to Alfred Adler (Chapter 4). Only children, despite the "spoilt" stereotype, match others in achievement and adjustment. E. Mavis Hetherington , following families for decades (2002), found that most children adjust to divorce within two to three years, though about 25 percent show serious problems against about 10 percent from intact families; remarriage brings a second adjustment. Maternal employment does not in itself harm children, and day care matters through its quality. Indian context In a joint family several generations share a home and its childcare, so the child has many attachment figures, more adults to obey and a strong sense of interdependence. Urbanisation has made the nuclear family (parents and children only) the commonest household, with day care or grandparents filling the gap. Child maltreatment and neglect In 1962 the paediatrician C. Henry Kempe (1922 to 1984) and colleagues described the battered child syndrome : young children with fractures at different stages of healing that their parents' accounts did not explain. Child maltreatment has four types: physical abuse (non-accidental injury), sexual abuse (any sexual activity with a child), emotional abuse (persistent rejecting, belittling or terrorising) and neglect , failure to meet a child's basic needs and the most often reported form. Neglect has five categories: physical (failure to provide proper nutrition, housing and clothing), supervisory (children left unattended), health or medical (failure to immunise, seek proper care or follow medical directions), educational (not enrolling the child, chronic absence) and emotional (withholding affection and attention). Exam trap Using licensed day care is not neglect: it is approved, supervised care, the odd one out beside nutrition, supervision and immunisation. Risk factors include parents who were themselves maltreated (about a third repeat it), young, depressed or misusing substances; premature, disabled or difficult children; and poverty, domestic violence and isolation. Effects include disorganised attachment (Section 6.7), aggression, school failure, depression and post-traumatic stress. Management and India's Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 are in Chapter 7. The development of play Play is activity chosen freely and done for its own sake. Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980) saw it as pure assimilation, the child bending reality to fit existing schemes, so play follows the cognitive stages (Section 6.4). The first form, in infancy during the sensorimotor stage, is functional play (practice or sensorimotor play): simple actions repeated for the pleasure of mastering them. With the preoperational symbolic function comes symbolic play (pretend play), and in the concrete operational stage games with rules . In 1968 the Israeli psychologist Sara Smilansky added constructive play , making or building something. Table 6.21 gives the standard definitions. Table 6.21 Types of play, in the order they appear. "Transforming the physical environment into a symbol" is symbolic play; "combining sensorimotor or practice play with symbolic representation of ideas" is constructive play; "interaction with peers" is social play. Bullying , as defined by the Norwegian psychologist Dan Olweus (1931 to 2020), is repeated, intentional aggression against someone less powerful; his whole-school programme roughly halved it in Norway. Gender concepts and gender socialisation Gender research needs exact terms. Sex is biological: chromosomes, hormones and anatomy. Gender is the psychological and social meaning a culture attaches to being male or female. Gender identity is one's own sense of being male, female or another gender; a gender role is the behaviour a culture expects of each sex. A gender stereotype is a rigid, oversimplified belief about what males and females are like ("boys don't cry"); gender stereotyping applies it to individuals. Gender typing is the process by which children adopt the preferences and behaviours their culture considers right for their sex. Gender socialisation is the process by which children learn this "gender map" from the people and institutions around them. Parents come first: pink or blue, dolls or trucks, indoor or outdoor chores, much of it taught unconsciously because their own gender orientations are so deeply embedded. Peers, school and media reinforce the map. Gender construction , by contrast, is the sociological view that a society creates gender categories and their meanings, and gender structuralisation is not a standard developmental term. From about three, children prefer same-sex playmates; this gender segregation peaks in middle childhood, so that, as Maccoby put it, boys (large groups, rough play) and girls (small groups, talk) grow up in two cultures. Exam trap Parents passing on the "gender map" (pink and blue, toys, chores), consciously or unconsciously, is gender socialisation . Gender stereotyping is a belief applied to people, not a learning process; gender construction and gender structuralisation are distractors. Theories of gender development The biological view points to prenatal hormones: girls with congenital adrenal hyperplasia , exposed to high androgen levels before birth, prefer boys' toys and rough play more than other girls, although raised as girls. In the psychoanalytic view the child of three to six identifies with the same-sex parent (Chapter 4). Social learning theory , applied to gender by Walter Mischel (1930 to 2018) in 1966, holds that children are reinforced for gender-appropriate behaviour and imitate same-sex models. Kay Bussey and Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) extended this in 1999 into a social cognitive theory: reinforcement and modelling build internal gender standards by which children regulate themselves. Either way, shaping from outside comes first. Lawrence Kohlberg (1927 to 1987) reversed the order in his cognitive-developmental theory of 1966: "I am a boy, therefore I want to do boy things." Understanding comes first, and children then socialise themselves. It grows in three steps (Figure 6.15): basic gender identity (about two to three: labelling oneself and others), gender stability (about three to five: a boy will become a man) and gender constancy or consistency (about five to seven: a boy in a frock is still a boy). These are his only stages; "gender-role achievement" is not one. Ronald Slaby and Karin Frey (1975) supported him: watching a split-screen film of a man and a woman doing the same things, children high in constancy looked longer at the same-sex adult. Yet children prefer gender-typed toys by about two, long before constancy. Basic gender identity About 2 to 3 years "I am a girl" Gender stability About 3 to 5 years "I will be a woman" Gender consistency About 5 to 7 years "Still a boy in a frock" Gender schema theory: self-socialising starts Kohlberg: fully committed self-socialiser Figure 6.15 Kohlberg's three steps in understanding gender. Gender schema theory starts self-socialisation at the first step; on the stricter reading of Kohlberg, it is complete only at the third. Gender schema theory , proposed in 1981 by Sandra Bem (1944 to 2014) and independently by Carol Martin and Charles Halverson , explains this. A gender schema is an organised set of beliefs about what goes with each sex. As soon as children have basic gender identity, they sort toys, activities and people into "for boys" and "for girls" and attend to and remember what fits their own group: shown a girl sawing wood, many later recall a boy doing it (Martin and Halverson, 1983). Earlier, Bem (1974) had treated masculinity and femininity as separate dimensions, so a person can be high on both: androgyny , measured by the Bem Sex Role Inventory (Chapter 2). Many textbooks are stricter: for Kohlberg, children become fully committed self-socialisers only at gender consistency (constancy), and it is gender schema theory that starts self-socialisation at basic gender identity. John, called to dinner, opens a door and accidentally smashes fifteen cups standing on a tray behind it. Henry, reaching for jam while his mother is out, breaks one cup. Who is naughtier? The six-year-old usually says John, since fifteen cups are worse than one; a ten-year-old says Henry, who was doing wrong. What has changed is not knowledge about cups but reasoning about right and wrong. This section follows that change through Piaget, Kohlberg and Gilligan, then meets the researchers who widened the picture. Three sides of morality Moral development is the growth of the standards by which a person judges right and wrong, and of the feelings and actions that go with them. Morality has three sides, and each tradition studied one. The emotional side is guilt, shame and empathy (their emergence in toddlers is traced in Section 6.6). Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) placed it in the superego , the conscience formed at about five or six when the child resolves the Oedipus complex by identifying with the same-sex parent; it punishes misdeeds with guilt (Chapter 4). The behavioural side is what people do when tempted. Social learning theorists led by Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) held that moral conduct is learned through reinforcement, punishment and above all modelling ; in 1963 Bandura and Frederick McDonald even shifted children's judgments between consequences and intentions simply by letting them hear adults judge the other way. The cognitive side, moral reasoning , is how a person thinks a moral problem through; it belongs to Piaget and Kohlberg. The study below shows why reasoning and conduct need separate study. Key study: the Character Education Inquiry (1928 to 1930) Hugh Hartshorne and Mark May asked whether children have a general trait of honesty. They gave more than 10,000 schoolchildren rigged chances to lie, cheat and steal at school, at home, at parties and in games. Most children cheated in some situations and not in others, and cheating in one setting only weakly predicted cheating in another. Honesty, they concluded, is largely situation-specific , not a fixed trait, and moral knowledge barely predicted honest conduct. Piaget: from moral realism to autonomy Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980) turned from logic (Section 6.4) to morality in The Moral Judgment of the Child (1932). He asked Swiss boys playing marbles where the rules came from and whether they could be changed, and he read children paired stories like John and Henry's, in which one child does more damage by accident and another less damage while misbehaving. He described a premoral period , before about age 5, when children pay little attention to rules, followed by two stages (Table 6.24). In heteronomous morality (Greek for "ruled by another"), also called moral realism , from about 5 to 10 (some books say 9), rules come from adults and are sacred and unchangeable: a new marble rule is cheating even if every player agrees. Acts are judged by their consequences, not intentions, which Piaget called objective responsibility , so John is naughtier. The child believes in immanent justice , that the world itself punishes wrongdoing (a boy who stole apples falls through a rotten bridge "because he stole"), and favours expiatory punishment , severe and unrelated to the offence. From about 10, cooperation among equal peers brings autonomous morality , or moral relativism . Rules become agreements that players may change by consent; intentions outweigh consequences, so Henry is naughtier; fairness means equality; and reciprocal punishment should fit the misdeed and repair it (the child who broke a window pays for it). Piaget underestimated preschoolers, who do use intentions when a story makes them clear, but his idea that moral reasoning grows with cognition and peer experience became Kohlberg's starting point. Piaget did not use the Heinz dilemma. Kohlberg's method: the Heinz dilemma Lawrence Kohlberg (1927 to 1987) carried Piaget's approach into adolescence. For his 1958 doctoral study he interviewed 72 Chicago boys aged 10, 13 and 16, and re-interviewed many of them every three or four years for about 20 years. His method was to pose hypothetical moral dilemmas, stories in which two moral values collide, to children and adolescents of different ages. The most famous is the Heinz dilemma : A woman is dying of cancer. A druggist has a drug that might save her, but he charges $2,000 for a dose that cost him $200 to make. Her husband, Heinz, can raise only about $1,000, and the druggist will not sell it cheaper or let him pay later. Heinz breaks in and steals the drug. Should he have done that? Why? The decisive word is "why". Kohlberg scored the reasoning , not the choice: "steal" and "don't steal" can come from the same stage, and the same answer from different stages. His interview and scoring system became the Moral Judgment Interview . The theory describes moral reasoning, not moral behaviour. Exam trap Kohlberg studied morality by posing moral dilemmas to children of different ages , not through daily journals, court records of delinquents, or making people perform legal and illegal acts (watching real cheating was Hartshorne and May's method). His stages concern moral reasoning ; language acquisition (Chapter 1), motor skills (Section 6.3) and psychosexual conflict (Freud, Chapter 4) belong to other theories. Three levels, six stages Kohlberg grouped the reasons into three levels of two stages each (Table 6.25, Figure 6.16), named by the person's relation to conventions , society's rules and expectations. At the preconventional level (Level I), typical of children under about 9, morality is under external control: the child obeys rules to avoid punishment or gain rewards, so rewarded acts are right and punished acts wrong. Stage 1 , the punishment-and-obedience orientation , judges an act by the punishment it brings. Stage 2 , instrumental purpose and exchange (naive hedonism), counts as right whatever serves one's own interest: what is in it for me? At the conventional level (Level II), reached by most adolescents and where most adults stay, the person conforms to social rules to be a good group member and maintain the social order. Stage 3 , the good boy-nice girl orientation , counts as right whatever wins the approval of close others; intentions matter, and the golden rule guides relationships. Stage 4 , the law-and-order orientation , takes the whole society's view: do your duty, respect authority and obey laws, because society would collapse if everyone broke them. At the postconventional level (Level III), reached by a minority of adults and rarely before 20, principles can stand above a particular law. Stage 5 , the social-contract orientation , sees laws as instruments that express the will of the majority and further human welfare, to be changed by democratic agreement when they fail. Stage 6 , universal ethical principles , follows self-chosen principles of justice and human dignity, even against an unjust law. Keeping a promise because society depends on it , or obeying a law because laws keep society functioning , is stage 4: conventional . It becomes stage 5 only when the speaker asks whether the agreement serves people's rights and welfare, and would change it if not. How sound is Kohlberg's theory? Kohlberg held that the stages form an invariant sequence : everyone climbs them in the same order, without skipping, and regression is rare; the 20-year Chicago data largely agreed. Each stage needs a cognitive base that is necessary but not sufficient: postconventional reasoning needs formal operations (Section 6.4), yet many formal-operational adults never reach it. It also needs role-taking , seeing a problem from other people's viewpoints (Robert Selman's levels of social perspective taking, Section 6.5), which grows through discussion and education. Stage 6 proved so rare that Kohlberg later dropped it from his scoring manual. Because his interview needs trained scorers, James Rest built the Defining Issues Test in the 1970s, a questionnaire in which people rate and rank prepared statements about each dilemma. Three criticisms dominate. The first is cultural bias . John Snarey (1985) reviewed 45 studies from 27 cultural areas: stages 1 to 4 appeared in order almost everywhere, but stage 5 mainly in urban, educated groups and hardly ever in village societies, whose communal reasoning the scoring missed. Richard Shweder , studying Hindu families in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, argued that the scale measures only an ethic of autonomy (harm, rights, justice) and misses an ethic of community (duty, hierarchy) and an ethic of divinity (purity, sanctity). The second is the gap between reasoning and behaviour : higher-stage reasoners act morally only somewhat more often. The third is gender bias : the founding sample was all male. Indian context Shweder's Oriya Brahmin informants judged it a serious moral wrong for an eldest son to get a haircut and eat chicken the day after his father's death; Chicago informants saw a personal choice. Joan Miller , comparing Hindu Indians in Mysore with Americans, found that Indians treated helping family, friends and even strangers as moral obligations , where Americans saw many of the same acts as personal decisions. A scale built around individual rights scores such duty-based reasoning as merely conventional. Gilligan: the ethic of care Carol Gilligan (born 1936), who had worked with Kohlberg at Harvard, noticed that women often scored at stage 3, apparently below men. In In a Different Voice (1982) she argued that his scale rests on a male ethic of justice , reasoning from rights, rules and fairness, and misses the ethic of care more often heard in women, reasoning from relationships and responsibility, wanting no one hurt. Her 11-year-old Jake solved Heinz like "a math problem with humans": life outweighs property. Amy worried that if Heinz went to jail his wife would have no one, and wanted them to talk it out. From interviews with 29 women deciding about abortion, Gilligan described three levels of care: an orientation to individual survival (caring only for oneself), goodness as self-sacrifice (caring for others at one's own expense) and the morality of nonviolence (caring for self and others, hurting no one). Is there a sex difference? Lawrence Walker 's 1984 review found little difference in Kohlberg scores once education and occupation were allowed for, and later meta-analyses found only small differences in care and justice orientation: both sexes use both voices. Exam trap The pairing is fixed: females, ethic of care; males, ethic of justice . Options that reverse it are wrong, and "males have an ethic of justice", though part of her argument, is what Kohlberg already measured; her departure is the female ethic of care. Gilligan added a voice; she did not replace Kohlberg. Beyond the stage theories Elliot Turiel 's social domain theory (1983) holds that children build separate kinds of social knowledge from early on: the moral domain (harm, fairness, rights), the social-conventional domain (agreed customs such as dress codes or forms of address) and the personal domain (choices such as friends or hairstyle). Even preschoolers say hitting would be wrong in a school with no rule against it, but calling the teacher by her first name would then be fine: they already separate moral from conventional rules. Nancy Eisenberg studied prosocial moral reasoning , about helping at a cost to oneself (should Mary, on her way to a party, stop to help a girl who has fallen?). Children move through five levels: hedonistic, needs-oriented, approval-oriented, empathic and finally internalised reasons. Martin Hoffman saw empathy as the main motive of moral action and traced four stages: global empathy in the first year (an infant cries when another cries), egocentric empathy in the second (a toddler fetches his own mother to comfort a crying friend), empathy for another's feelings from about 2 or 3, and in late childhood empathy for another's life condition (for the poor as a group). He also compared three kinds of discipline. Power assertion (force, threats, removing privileges) and love withdrawal (coldness, ignoring the child) produce compliance out of fear or anxiety. Induction , explaining how the child's act affects others ("Riya is crying because you snatched her book"), recruits empathy and guilt and so best fosters internalisation , behaving well when no one is watching (parenting styles are in Section 6.8). Finally, Jonathan Haidt 's social intuitionist model (2001) reverses the cognitive tradition: moral judgments are fast gut intuitions, and reasoning mostly follows to justify them. Erik Erikson put that question at the centre of a theory that runs from the first feed to the last years, and he gave it a name now used everywhere: the identity crisis. His eight stages come first; then identity is followed into adolescence itself, with its identity statuses, its egocentrism, its changing body and brain, and the old argument over storm and stress. Erikson and the psychosocial approach Erik Homburger Erikson (1902 to 1994) lived his own theory. Born in Frankfurt to a Danish mother who never told him who his father was, he carried his stepfather's surname, Homburger, and wandered Europe as an artist in his late teens. At 25 he began teaching at a small school in Vienna, was analysed by Anna Freud (1895 to 1982), and became a psychoanalyst without any university degree. He moved to the United States in 1933 and later treated Second World War veterans whose trouble seemed to be a confused sense of who they were rather than repressed conflict. His key books are Childhood and Society (1950), which set out the eight stages, Young Man Luther (1958), Identity: Youth and Crisis (1968) and Gandhi's Truth (1969). Erikson belonged to ego psychology , which treats the ego as a partly independent, adaptive part of the personality rather than a servant of the id. Development follows the epigenetic principle : like an embryo whose organs appear on a fixed timetable ( epi means "upon"), the personality unfolds through a built-in sequence of stages, while society decides how each turns out. Each stage poses a psychosocial crisis , a turning point between two opposed tendencies set off by new social demands; it is a choice of direction, not a catastrophe. A favourable resolution leaves the ego with a basic strength, or virtue . Favourable means a balance tilted towards the positive pole, not the absence of the negative: a child who trusts everyone is gullible. An unresolved crisis makes later ones harder but not hopeless, because development continues across the whole lifespan. Erikson coined the term identity crisis for the adolescent struggle to know who one is. His own labels for the eight stages of the life cycle run from the oral-sensory stage through the muscular-anal, locomotor-genital, latency, puberty and adolescence, young adulthood and adulthood stages to the stage of maturity. The first four echo Freud's oral, anal, phallic and latency stages; the adult stages are Erikson's own. Exam trap The identity crisis, and the eight stages from the "oral-sensory stage" to the "stage of maturity", are Erikson's. Freud described five psychosexual stages, Harry Stack Sullivan developmental epochs from infancy to adulthood, and Melanie Klein the paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions of infancy (all Chapter 4). John Bowlby is attachment (Section 6.7); Eric Berne is transactional analysis (Chapter 7). Indian context Gandhi's Truth (1969) is a psychohistory, a great life read through Erikson's stages and psychoanalytic ideas. Centred on the 1918 Ahmedabad textile mill strike, it asks how one man's identity struggle became a nation's method of nonviolent protest, as Young Man Luther had asked of Martin Luther. It won the Pulitzer Prize. The eight stages Table 6.27 is the map to memorise: for each stage an age, a crisis named by its two poles, the virtue a good resolution leaves, and the people who matter most, a "radius of significant relations" that widens from one mother to all of humankind. Trust versus mistrust. The helpless infant learns whether the world is dependable. Reliable feeding, comfort and contact build basic trust, an expectation of "consistency, continuity and sameness"; neglect or inconsistency breeds suspicion. The virtue is hope, a lasting confidence that wishes can be met. 2. Autonomy versus shame and doubt. The walking, talking toddler wants to do things alone. Erikson's key acts are holding on and letting go, and the classic battleground is toilet training. Patient parents leave the child with will, the determination to choose and to restrain oneself; harsh or overprotective ones leave shame and self-doubt. 3. Initiative versus guilt. The preschooler plans, explores, asks endless questions and acts out adult roles in play. Encouraged, the child gains purpose, the courage to pursue goals; punished or mocked for each venture, the child learns guilt. 4. Industry versus inferiority. School brings tools, tasks and classmates to compare oneself with. Finishing tasks and earning recognition build industry and competence; repeated failure, or being made to feel behind one's peers, brings inferiority. 5. Identity versus role confusion. With puberty and new choices, the young person must fuse childhood identifications, skills, values and future roles into one answer to "Who am I?" Success brings fidelity, loyalty to freely chosen values and people; failure brings role confusion (see Identity, moratorium and Marcia's statuses ). 6. Intimacy versus isolation. With an identity in hand, the young adult can risk merging it with another's, in friendship and love, without losing it. The virtue is love, mutual devotion; failure brings isolation and self-absorption. 7. Generativity versus stagnation. Erikson's generativity is concern for establishing and guiding the next generation: raising children, mentoring juniors, teaching, building work that lasts (parenthood is neither necessary nor sufficient). Its failure is stagnation , a sense of having achieved little and having little to offer the next generation, with boredom and self-indulgence. The virtue is care. 8. Ego integrity versus despair. Looking back, the older person either accepts the one life lived, failures included, as meaningful ( ego integrity ), or feels regret, bitterness and fear of death because there is no time to start again (despair). The virtue is wisdom, a detached concern with life itself in the face of death. Some personality texts put the adult boundaries at 35 and 55. The first four outcomes depend mainly on what others do to the child; in the last four the person increasingly chooses. Exam trap An 18-month-old has been keyed to autonomy versus shame and doubt, yet another key gives trust versus mistrust as 0 to 18 months. Eighteen months is the boundary, so read the options; when both stages are offered for a child of exactly 18 months, the keyed answer has been autonomy. For sequence items, write the stage number under each option. In one mock item they run (a) 1, 2, 5, 7; (b) 2, 4, 5, 7; (c) 3, 4, 5, 8; (d) 1, 3, 6, 8. All rise, so the item is flawed; the key is (a), trust, autonomy, identity, generativity: of the two series that start at stage 1, it skips fewer stages. Virtues in order: hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care, wisdom. Applying the stages, and how they go wrong The stages are easiest to see in people. Mrs Rao, 52, finds her deepest satisfaction in training young engineers: generativity. Her colleague of the same age, who feels he has achieved little and has nothing to pass on, is stagnating. Her father, 78, would live his life the same way again, mistakes and all: integrity. His neighbour broods over wasted chances and dreads death: despair. Her niece in Class 4, measuring herself against classmates while mastering long division, is in industry versus inferiority. Exam trap Erikson's term for the mid-life feeling of having achieved little and having little to offer the next generation is stagnation ; generativity is the healthy pole. "Mid-life crisis" is a popular term, not Erikson's (Section 6.11), and presbyopia is the age-related loss of near focusing in the eye's lens. A crisis can also be resolved too one-sidedly. In The Life Cycle Completed (1982) Erikson split this maldevelopment two ways. Too much of the positive pole, with none of the negative, gives a maladaptive tendency ; too much of the negative pole gives a malignant tendency , the more serious (Table 6.28). He thought maladaptations could lead towards neurosis and malignancies towards psychosis, and that therapy could correct both, later experience the milder maladaptations.
