Childhood identifications (my father's son, a good student, a cricketer) must be sorted, kept or dropped, and fused with new abilities, sexual maturity and choices of work, beliefs and love into an ego identity : a sense of being the same person across time and situations, recognised by the people who count. Society helps by granting a psychosocial moratorium , a socially sanctioned delay of adult commitments in which the young can try out courses, friendships and causes before choosing; college years and Erikson's own wandering years are examples. When the work fails the result is identity confusion (role confusion in Erikson's earlier wording; also identity diffusion): inner fragmentation, little or no sense of where one's life is headed, and an inability to gain the support of a social role or vocation. Some young people instead seize a negative identity , built from the roles their family or community holds up as most undesirable, such as the delinquent, on the logic that it is better to be somebody bad than nobody. Adolescence, then, is a true developmental stage and a moratorium, the fifth of eight and not the last. Exam trap "Inner fragmentation, no sense of direction, no support from a social role or vocation" is identity confusion . Incongruence is Carl Rogers's gap between self-concept and experience (Chapter 4); dissociation is a break in the integration of memory, identity and consciousness (Chapter 8); "conflict" is too general. Key study: Marcia's identity status interview (1966) James E. Marcia asked whether Erikson's identity could be measured. He interviewed male college students about occupation, religion and politics and scored two dimensions: crisis or exploration , a period of actively weighing alternatives, and commitment , a firm investment in a choice. Crossing them gave four identity statuses (Figure 6.17) that predicted behaviour: achieved students coped best with a stressful task, foreclosed students endorsed authoritarian values most. Criticism: an all-male first sample, and a person can hold different statuses in different areas of life. Commitment absent Commitment present Exploration (crisis) present Exploration (crisis) absent Moratorium exploring now, not yet committed Achievement explored, then committed Diffusion neither exploring nor committed Foreclosure committed without exploring Arrows: a common route to achievement Figure 6.17 Marcia's identity statuses cross exploration (crisis) with commitment. Foreclosure and moratorium are mirror images: commitment without exploration, and exploration without commitment. Neither exploration nor commitment is identity diffusion . The young person drifts; adjustment is poorest. Commitment without exploration is foreclosure . Choices are taken over ready-made, often from parents, like the son who becomes a doctor because the family always assumed he would; such youth tend to be rigid and conforming. Exploration without commitment is moratorium . The person is in the middle of the crisis, anxious and actively trying options. Exploration followed by commitment is identity achievement , the most mature status, with the highest self-esteem. Statuses are not fixed stages. Achievement grows through late adolescence and young adulthood, and adults reopen settled questions after a divorce, a job loss or migration and then close them again: the MAMA cycles (moratorium, achievement, moratorium, achievement) described by Marcia and colleagues in 1992. Jean Phinney applied the same logic to ethnic identity , from unexamined through exploration to achieved; a secure ethnic identity goes with higher self-esteem in minority youth. Exam trap Foreclosure is commitment WITHOUT exploration; moratorium is exploration WITHOUT commitment; achievement has both; diffusion neither. Marcia's dimensions are crisis (exploration) and commitment, not IQ and emotional intelligence, locus of control (Chapter 4) or approach and avoidance motivation (Chapter 1). Adolescent egocentrism Formal operational thought (Section 6.4) lets adolescents think about thinking, including other people's. David Elkind argued in 1967 that this power brings a new adolescent egocentrism : the teenager fails to separate what others are thinking about from his or her own preoccupations. It shows in two mental constructions. The imaginary audience is the belief that everyone is watching and judging: the boy who will not enter class with a pimple on his chin, sure that all forty classmates will notice. The personal fable is the belief that one's experiences and feelings are unique, that no one, least of all a parent, could understand them ("You don't know what it's like to be me"), and with it a sense of invulnerability ("It won't happen to me") that feeds reckless riding. Some notes list the invulnerability strand separately as the "mythological fable". Both are strongest in early adolescence and fade by the late teens. Exam trap Adolescent egocentrism = imaginary audience ("everyone is looking at me") plus personal fable ("my experiences are unique"). Conservation and reversibility are concrete operational (Section 6.4), inner speech and scaffolding are Vygotsky's (Section 6.5), and object permanence and stranger anxiety belong to infancy (Sections 6.4 and 6.6). Puberty and the adolescent brain Adolescence begins with puberty , the biological changes that bring sexual maturity; adolescence itself is the wider psychological and social transition. The hormones come in two waves. In adrenarche , from about 6 to 8, the adrenal glands raise their output of weak androgens. In gonadarche , from about 9 or 10, the hypothalamus and pituitary switch on the ovaries and testes, which pour out oestrogens and testosterone (Chapter 5). The visible result is the growth spurt, a rapid gain in height and weight that starts about two years earlier in girls (around 10) than in boys (around 12), so that for a while many girls are taller than boys of their age. The primary sex characteristics are the reproductive organs themselves (ovaries, uterus and vagina; testes, penis and scrotum); secondary sex characteristics are the other visible signs (breasts, body and facial hair, a deeper voice, wider hips or shoulders). In girls, menarche , the first menstrual period, comes late in the sequence, at about 12 or 13; spermarche , the first ejaculation, at about 13 or 14. Better nutrition and health have pulled menarche earlier, from about 16 or 17 in mid-nineteenth-century Europe to about 12 or 13 today, and made adults taller: the secular trend . Timing matters too. Early-maturing boys tend to be confident and popular, though they try alcohol and delinquency earlier; late-maturing boys are often more anxious. Early-maturing girls carry the greatest risk: looking older than they feel, they attract older friends and show more depression, poor body image, eating problems and substance use. Inside the skull, regions mature at different speeds. Laurence Steinberg 's dual systems model (2008) pairs a reward system in the limbic system and ventral striatum, which becomes sharply more responsive around puberty, with a cognitive control system centred on the prefrontal cortex, which matures slowly into the mid-twenties (Figure 6.18). In mid-adolescence the accelerator is pressed while the brakes are still being fitted, so risk-taking peaks, above all among peers. 10 15 20 25 Age (years) Relative strength gap: peak risk-taking Reward system Cognitive control Figure 6.18 Steinberg's dual systems model (schematic). Key study: risk with friends watching (Gardner and Steinberg, 2005) Margo Gardner and Steinberg had adolescents (13 to 16), college-age youths and adults play a video driving game in which they could brake at an amber light or gamble on getting through, alone or with two friends watching. Friends' presence roughly doubled the adolescents' risk-taking, raised the youths' by about half and left the adults' unchanged. Criticism: a laboratory game, though it matches teen drivers' higher crash rates with teen passengers. Storm and stress, tasks, parents and peers Must adolescence be turbulent? G. Stanley Hall (1844 to 1924), in Adolescence (1904), said yes: the teens were a biologically driven period of storm and stress , of mood swings, conflict with parents and risk-taking. Margaret Mead (1901 to 1978) answered from the field. In Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) she described Samoan girls passing smoothly into adulthood in a relaxed culture with many caring adults, and concluded that turmoil is made by culture, not biology. Derek Freeman (1983) later attacked her fieldwork, but modern surveys support a middle view: most adolescents cope well and share their parents' basic values, while a minority run into serious trouble. Conflict and moodiness do rise in early adolescence; storm and stress is real but not universal. Robert J. Havighurst (1900 to 1991) listed the developmental tasks of adolescence (the idea itself is in Section 6.1): new and more mature relations with age-mates of both sexes; a masculine or feminine social role; accepting one's body; emotional independence from parents and other adults; preparing for marriage and family life; preparing for a career; a set of values and an ethical system to guide behaviour; and socially responsible behaviour. Emotional separation from parents, strong peer identification and heterosexual peer interest are therefore all tasks of adolescence. Relations with parents are renegotiated, not cut. The older psychoanalytic view of Anna Freud and Peter Blos held that healthy adolescents must detach from their parents. Research now shows that autonomy grows best inside continued connection: teenagers who stay securely attached explore more confidently and adjust better, so it can be healthy for interdependence to continue. Detachment does not typically happen earlier, in middle childhood; peers do not simply replace parents, who keep their influence on values, education and career while peers sway dress, music and leisure; and parents' goals differ across families and cultures, many Indian families valuing lasting interdependence. Dexter Dunphy (1963), observing teenagers in Sydney, distinguished cliques , small groups of close friends, from crowds, larger groups formed when several cliques join for parties and outings. He traced five stages: isolated same-sex cliques; same-sex cliques beginning to interact; their leaders forming the first mixed-sex clique; a full crowd of mixed-sex cliques; and the crowd loosening into groups of couples. Conformity to peers rises in early adolescence, peaks at about 14 and then declines as autonomy matures. Exam trap Today's view of adolescents and parents: continued interdependence can be healthy. A Mysuru engineer of 24 unsure of his career, his mother of 50 nursing an ailing father, and his grandfather of 80 trimming his circle of friends are all still developing. Emerging adulthood and adult development In 2000 Jeffrey Jensen Arnett named the years from about 18 to 25 emerging adulthood , a period created in industrialised societies by later marriage, parenthood and settled work. Its five features are identity exploration (in love and work), instability, self-focus, feeling in-between (neither adolescent nor adult) and possibilities (life can still go many ways). Its Eriksonian task, intimacy versus isolation, is in Section 6.10. Daniel Levinson (1920 to 1994) drew the best-known map of what follows. In The Seasons of a Man's Life (1978), built on interviews with 40 men aged 35 to 45, each man has a life structure , the underlying pattern of his life at a given time, built mainly around work and family. Overlapping eras alternate stable periods, when a structure is built, with transitions of about five years, when it is questioned and remade (Figure 6.19): the early adult transition (17 to 22) leaves adolescence behind, and the age-30 transition (28 to 33) revises the first adult structure. The young man pursues the Dream , a vision of the adult he hopes to become, helped by a mentor, an older guide at work. In the midlife transition (about 40 to 45) he reappraises the Dream against what he has achieved. Table 6.30 adds four other theorists. Indian context Most Indian marriages are still arranged by families, now usually with the couple's consent; love is expected to grow after the wedding, and the marriage joins two families. Elsewhere more adults cohabit, divorce is commoner, and a first child usually lowers marital satisfaction for a while. Work is the other pillar. Eli Ginzberg (1911 to 2002; Occupational Choice , 1951) described three periods of career choice: fantasy (to about 11), wishing without regard to ability; tentative (about 11 to 17), weighing interests, capacities and values; and realistic (17 to the early twenties), exploring, crystallising and specifying one choice. Donald Super 's career stages are in Chapter 7. Middle adulthood: the climacteric and midlife From about 40 the body changes slowly. Near vision blurs as the lens stiffens ( presbyopia ), hearing for high pitches fades (presbycusis), bone mass falls (especially in women after menopause), hair recedes and greys, muscle strength and agility decline, and reaction time and manual dexterity slow. All of this is general physical ageing. The climacteric is narrower: the end of ovulation and termination of reproductive capacity. In women it culminates in menopause , the last menstrual period (confirmed after 12 months without one), as ovarian oestrogen falls. The average age is about 51 in Western samples and about 46 to 47 in Indian surveys. The male climacteric, or andropause , is a slow decline in testosterone; most men stay fertile into old age. Exam trap Climacteric means the end of ovulation and termination of reproductive capacity (JEMAS 2025). Lost strength, receding or greying hair, and slower reactions and dexterity are general ageing. Menopause is the event within the climacteric, not a synonym. Elliott Jaques (1917 to 2003) coined midlife crisis in 1965, from creative artists confronting mortality in their mid-thirties. Large surveys find that only a minority report one, usually after illness or job loss. Midlife is more often a peak of competence and generativity (Section 6.10). The empty nest , when the last child leaves, more often brings relief than depression. The sandwich generation are middle-aged adults, usually women, caring for children and ageing parents at once. K. Warner Schaie 's Seattle Longitudinal Study (begun 1956) found that most mental abilities peak in middle adulthood, while perceptual speed declines from early adulthood. Late adulthood and the biology of ageing Gerontology studies the biological, psychological and social sides of ageing; geriatrics is the medicine of old age. Robert Butler (1927 to 2010) coined ageism , prejudice against people because they are old, in 1969. Older adults are divided into the young-old (65 to 74), old-old (75 to 84) and oldest-old (85 and over). Life span is the maximum possible length of life, about 120 years ( Jeanne Calment lived 122); life expectancy is the average number of years a person born in a given year can expect to live, about 70 in India. Primary ageing is gradual, inevitable and universal bodily decline. Secondary ageing comes from disease, disuse and lifestyle, so it is partly preventable. Tertiary ageing is the rapid loss shortly before death; its cognitive form, a sharp fall in test scores, is the terminal drop ( Robert Kleemeier , 1962). Programmed theories say the genes set ageing's timetable. Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead (1961) found that human cells in culture divide only about 40 to 60 times (some textbooks say 75 to 80), the Hayflick limit , apparently because telomeres, the caps on chromosome ends, shorten with each division. Elaine Cumming and William Henry 's disengagement theory ( Growing Old , 1961) said old people and society withdraw from each other by natural, mutual consent. Research disagreed: withdrawal is usually forced by illness or loss, and it lowers well-being. Cognition, retirement and elder care Fluid intelligence declines from early adulthood while crystallised intelligence holds or rises into old age (Section 1.9). Timothy Salthouse 's processing-speed theory (1996) traces much of the loss to a general slowing of processing. Episodic and working memory decline; semantic and procedural memory hold. Paul Baltes's Berlin wisdom paradigm defines wisdom as expert knowledge about the fundamental pragmatics of life, judged by factual and procedural knowledge, lifespan contextualism, value relativism and managing uncertainty; it reflects experience more than age. Dementia is disease, not normal ageing (Chapters 5 and 8). Retirement is a process: Atchley described a honeymoon, then possible disenchantment, reorientation and stability; it goes best when chosen, healthy and funded. Widowhood falls mostly on women, who live longer and usually marry older men. Indian context As joint families shrink, the law has stepped in. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 obliges children (or, for the childless, heirs) to maintain parents and senior citizens (60 and over). Tribunals can order up to Rs 10,000 a month, and abandoning a senior citizen is punishable by up to three months in prison, a Rs 5,000 fine, or both. Death, dying and grief Death was once the stopping of heart and breathing. Life support broke that link, so India (Transplantation of Human Organs Act 1994) and most countries also recognise brain death : irreversible loss of all brain function or, in Indian law, of all brainstem function. In a persistent vegetative state the brainstem still works. Maria Nagy (1948) questioned 378 Budapest children aged 3 to 10. Under about 5, death was a departure or sleep, and reversible; from 5 to 9 it was final but personified, a "death-man" who could be escaped; after 9 it was universal and inevitable. Mark Speece and Sandor Brent (1984) named three parts of a mature concept, irreversibility, universality and nonfunctionality (all functions stop), grasped by most children at about 5 to 7. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross 's five stages of dying ( On Death and Dying , 1969) are denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance (Section 7.9). John Bowlby (1907 to 1990) saw mourning as a broken attachment (Section 6.7) with four phases: numbness, yearning and searching, disorganisation and despair, and reorganisation. Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut 's dual process model (1999) replaces fixed stages with oscillation between loss-oriented coping (grief work, yearning) and restoration-oriented coping (new tasks and roles, time off from grief). Cicely Saunders (1918 to 2005) opened St Christopher's Hospice, London, in 1967; hospices give palliative care , aiming at comfort and dignity rather than cure (Section 7.9). Euthanasia is active when a lethal act ends life and passive euthanasia when life support is withheld or withdrawn; India permits only the passive kind. In Aruna Shanbaug v Union of India (2011), about a Mumbai nurse left vegetative by a 1973 assault, the Supreme Court refused the plea but allowed passive euthanasia with High Court approval. Common Cause v Union of India (2018) held that dying with dignity is part of the right to life (Article 21) and upheld the living will , an advance directive refusing life support. Pinel and Itard were arguing nature versus nurture (Section 6.1), and the modern answer is that each may have been partly right: Victor may have had a developmental disability, perhaps autism, before he was abandoned (Sections 6.2 and 6.3). His failure to speak after years of teaching fits a sensitive period for language that had largely closed (Section 6.1), while his growing problem solving and his bond with Madame Guérin show cognition and attachment still developing (Sections 6.4 to 6.7). His protest at unjust punishment touches moral development (Section 6.9), the turmoil puberty brought him touches adolescence (Section 6.10), and his quiet life to about forty is a reminder that development runs across the whole lifespan (Section 6.11). Chapter summary 6.1 Foundations: The Lifespan View, Key Issues and Ecological Contexts. Developmental psychology studies change and stability from conception to death. Growth is quantitative, development qualitative, and maturation is the biological unfolding of genetic potential (Gesell; co-twin control, 1929). Hurlock divides life into ten periods; Baltes's lifespan perspective (1987) sees development as lifelong, multidirectional and plastic, shaped by age-graded, history-graded and non-normative influences. Development runs cephalocaudally and proximodistally, with Havighurst's developmental tasks at each period. Core issues include nature versus nurture and continuity versus discontinuity. A critical period is fixed and irreversible (imprinting, embryonic organ formation); a sensitive period is flexible (language). Bronfenbrenner (1979) nests the child in micro-, meso-, exo- and macrosystems, with the chronosystem added later. 6.2 Heredity, Prenatal Development, Birth and the Newborn. Each body cell carries 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; meiosis halves them in sperm and ovum, which unite as a zygote . In dominant-recessive inheritance a heterozygote shows the dominant trait, while incomplete dominance, codominance, X-linked, polygenic inheritance and genomic imprinting vary the pattern. Chromosomal errors include Down (trisomy 21), Klinefelter (47,XXY), Turner (45,X) and Prader-Willi (paternal 15q11-q13 deletion). MZ twins reared apart best separate heredity from environment, which also correlate and interact. Prenatal life runs through germinal, embryonic (gastrulation, neural tube, greatest vulnerability to teratogens ) and fetal periods. Newborns are scored on the Apgar scale and show primitive reflexes such as the Moro and Babinski. 6.3 Infancy: Brain, Body, Motor Skills and Perception. Birth weight doubles by about 5 months and triples by 1 year, and growth and motor control run cephalocaudal and proximodistal (never distal to proximal). Neurons are mostly made before birth; synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning and myelination take the brain from about 25 percent of adult weight to half by about 6 months. The first voluntary grasp is ulnar; the pincer grasp follows by 9 to 12 months. Gesell stressed maturation, Dennis experience and Thelen dynamic systems. Looking methods reveal face preference and perceptual narrowing; the visual cliff shows depth perception by crawling age, when independent locomotion transforms affordances. Newborns imitate (Meltzoff and Moore, 1977), and comprehension leads production. 6.4 Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development. Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980) saw intelligence as biological adaptation: the child, an active little scientist, builds schemes and adapts them by assimilation (fitting experience into existing schemes) and accommodation (changing schemes), driven by equilibration . Four stages follow in invariant order: sensorimotor (birth to 2; object permanence begins at 8 to 12 months with the A-not-B error and is complete by 18 to 24), preoperational (2 to 7; egocentrism, centration, no conservation), concrete operational (7 to 11; conservation, reversibility, transitivity) and formal operational (11 or 12 onward; hypothetico-deductive reasoning). Dialectical reasoning is postformal. Baillargeon, Donaldson and the neo-Piagetians showed he underestimated young children. 6.5 Vygotsky, Bruner, Information Processing and Theory of Mind. Lev Vygotsky 's sociocultural theory holds that higher mental functions arise in social interaction, mediated by cultural tools (language the master tool): every function appears first between people, then within the child. The zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do alone and with a more knowledgeable other; support there is scaffolding (Wood, Bruner and Ross, 1976). For Vygotsky language shapes thought and private speech becomes inner speech. Bruner described enactive, iconic and symbolic representation. Information-processing research tracks speed, strategies and metacognition. False-belief tasks are passed at about 4, and Selman traced perspective taking from egocentric to societal. 6.6 Emotional Development, Temperament and Self-Regulation. Bridges (1932) held that the newborn's general excitement differentiates first into distress and delight ; primary emotions are present within six months, the social smile at 6 to 10 weeks, and the self-conscious emotions only after 12 months. Stranger and separation anxiety peak at about 8 to 15 months, and Tronick's still face shows that infants expect affective reciprocity. Temperament is early, moderately stable and biologically based: Thomas and Chess gave nine dimensions, the easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up types and goodness of fit; Rothbart and Bates reduced it to surgency, negative affectivity and effortful control; Kagan studied behavioural inhibition. Mischel's marshmallow test measures delay of gratification . 6.7 Attachment: Imprinting, Bowlby, Ainsworth and Beyond. Attachment is an enduring bond shown by proximity seeking, secure-base and safe-haven behaviour and separation distress. Lorenz's imprinting and Harlow's contact comfort undermined the feeding-based psychoanalytic and secondary-drive theories, leaving Bowlby's ethological theory (an evolved system, monotropy, a critical period, the internal working model ) predominant. Bowlby's four phases, Schaffer and Emerson's stages and Mahler's separation-individuation chart the first three years. Ainsworth's Strange Situation sorts infants by reunion behaviour into secure (B), avoidant (A) and resistant (C), plus Main and Solomon's disorganised (D). Spitz, Rutter and the adoption studies show privation harms but is partly reversible. 6.8 Parenting, Family, Play and Gender in Childhood. Diana Baumrind described authoritative, authoritarian and permissive parenting; Maccoby and Martin (1983) crossed demandingness with responsiveness and added the neglectful style. Authoritative parenting, high on both, gives the best outcomes, though warm control also works in Chinese and Indian families. Helicopter parenting has several roots, and the family acts as a system. Neglect is physical, supervisory, medical, educational or emotional; licensed day care is not neglect. Piaget's play runs from functional to symbolic play to games with rules, Smilansky added constructive play, and Parten traced solitary to cooperative play. Children learn the gender map through socialisation; Kohlberg and gender schema theory explain how they then socialise themselves. 6.9 Moral Development: Piaget, Kohlberg, Gilligan and Beyond. Morality has emotional (guilt, empathy, the superego), behavioural (social learning; Hartshorne and May found honesty situation-specific) and cognitive sides. Piaget (1932) traced a shift from heteronomous morality (fixed rules, judging by consequences, immanent justice, expiatory punishment) to autonomous morality (rules as agreements, intentions, reciprocal punishment). Kohlberg posed dilemmas such as Heinz's and scored the reasoning: preconventional (punishment, exchange), conventional (approval, law and order) and postconventional (social contract, universal principles). Critics cite cultural bias (Snarey, Shweder, Miller), the reasoning and behaviour gap and gender bias; Gilligan added the female ethic of care . Turiel, Eisenberg, Hoffman and Haidt widened the field. 6.10 Erikson's Psychosocial Stages, Identity and Adolescence. Erik Erikson (1902 to 1994), an ego psychologist, proposed eight psychosocial stages governed by the epigenetic principle, each a crisis whose favourable resolution yields a virtue: trust (hope), autonomy (will), initiative (purpose), industry (competence), identity (fidelity), intimacy (love), generativity (care) and integrity (wisdom). One-sided resolution gives maladaptive or malignant tendencies. Adolescence is a psychosocial moratorium whose failure is identity confusion. James Marcia (1966) crossed exploration with commitment to give diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium and achievement. David Elkind described the imaginary audience and personal fable. Puberty, Steinberg's dual systems model and modern research temper Hall's storm and stress: connection with parents stays healthy. 6.11 Adulthood, Ageing, Death and Dying. Arnett's emerging adulthood (about 18 to 25) leads into Levinson's life structures, eras, transitions and Dream, joined by Havighurst's developmental tasks, Vaillant, Gould, Neugarten's social clock and Peck. Hurlock's marriages are traditional, companionship or collegial (comradeship with different roles). The climacteric is the end of ovulation and reproductive capacity, culminating in menopause; the midlife crisis (Jaques, 1965) is not universal. Ageing is explained by programmed theories (Hayflick limit, telomeres) and damage theories (free radicals), and adapted to through disengagement, activity, continuity, socioemotional selectivity or SOC. Speed and fluid abilities fall; crystallised knowledge holds. Grief follows Bowlby's phases or Stroebe and Schut's dual process; India allows passive euthanasia and living wills.
