genetic potential? (IHBAS 2025) a Maturation b Socialization c Accommodation d Conditioning ✓ Answer: (a) Maturation Arnold Gesell, maturation The concept What it is Maturation is change that unfolds on a genetic timetable , largely independent of practice. Who to name Arnold Gesell is the theorist linked with maturation: the biological side of development, as opposed to change that depends on experience. Why the other options are wrong (b) Socialization Socialisation is learning the norms and roles of one's society, so it depends on experience, not a genetic timetable. (c) Accommodation Accommodation is Piaget's adjustment of a scheme to fit new experience, so it depends on experience. (d) Conditioning Conditioning is learning by association, so it depends on experience, not genetic unfolding. The fact that people can use later experiences to compensate for earlier deficits is a contradiction of which element of earlier developmental psychology? (IHBAS 2020) a Critical periods b Continuity c Sensitive periods d Stability ✓ Answer: (a) Critical periods Clarke and Clarke (1976); English and Romanian Adoptees study The concept What it is A strict critical period is a window in which an experience must happen; if it is missed, the loss is irreversible . The evidence Recovery through later experience ( Clarke and Clarke , 1976; the English and Romanian Adoptees study) shows early deficits can be made up, which contradicts a strict critical period. Why the other options are wrong (b) Continuity Continuity asks whether development is gradual or stage-like, a different question from whether early deficits can be reversed. (c) Sensitive periods Sensitive periods allow late recovery by definition, so compensation fits them rather than contradicting them. (d) Stability Stability asks whether individual differences persist over time, a different question from reversibility. In the case of human development, the strongest evidence for the critical period hypothesis is found in: (RML 2024) a Imprinting b Language acquisition c Embryonic development d Development of vocational interests ✓ Answer (as keyed): (a) Imprinting Lorenz, imprinting The concept Why this one Imprinting ( Lorenz ) is the textbook critical period : a young bird follows the first moving object it sees in a short window after hatching. Key note Imprinting is animal evidence . Within human development the clearest critical periods are in embryonic development , where teratogen timing decides which organ is damaged, so (c) is the stronger human answer; the paper keys (a). Why the other options are wrong (b) Language acquisition Language shows a sensitive period , not a strict critical period, so it is weaker evidence. (c) Embryonic development The clearest human critical periods: teratogen timing decides which organ is damaged; arguably the better answer for human development, but not the key. (d) Development of vocational interests Vocational interests show no critical period at all. If a blue eye allele (D) is dominant and a green eye allele (d) is recessive, what is the phenotype of a heterozygous (Dd) child? (Real PYQ 2025) a Green eyes b Blue eyes c Blue-green eyes d Cannot be determined ✓ Answer: (b) Blue eyes Mendelian dominant-recessive inheritance The concept How it works In dominant-recessive inheritance a heterozygote (Dd) carries one dominant and one recessive allele and shows the dominant allele's trait. Apply it D (blue) is dominant, so a Dd child has blue eyes . Why the other options are wrong (a) Green eyes Green is recessive, so it needs the dd genotype; a Dd child does not show it. (c) Blue-green eyes A blend would need incomplete dominance , but here dominance is complete. (d) Cannot be determined The phenotype can be determined because dominance is stated in the question. During embryonic development, the nervous system begins forming at the : (IHBAS 2025) a Zygote stage b Morula stage c Gastrula stage d Blastocyst stage ✓ Answer: (c) Gastrula stage Gastrulation, week 3 of embryonic development The concept What happens At gastrulation , in week 3, the three germ layers form: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Nervous system The neural plate arises from ectoderm and folds into the neural tube by about week 4. Why the other options are wrong (a) Zygote stage The single fertilised cell, the earliest stage, with no germ layers yet. (b) Morula stage A solid ball of cells formed by early cell division; an earlier stage with no germ layers yet. (d) Blastocyst stage A hollow ball of cells that implants in the uterus; still earlier than gastrulation, with no germ layers yet. A child with hyperphagia, obesity, short stature, and hypotonia is found to have a deletion on chromosome 15 (15q11-q13). This syndrome is : (IHBAS 2025) a Fragile X syndrome b Turner syndrome c Prader-Willi syndrome d Klinefelter syndrome ✓ Answer: (c) Prader-Willi syndrome Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion (genomic imprinting) The concept What causes it Loss of the paternal 15q11-q13 region gives Prader-Willi syndrome : hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity and short stature. Key note Loss of the maternal copy of the same region gives Angelman syndrome , so which parent's copy is missing decides the syndrome. Why the other options are wrong (a) Fragile X syndrome An FMR1 disorder on the X chromosome, not a chromosome 15 deletion. (b) Turner syndrome 45,X , one X chromosome missing in a girl; short stature overlaps, but there is no 15q deletion or hyperphagia. (d) Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY , an extra X chromosome in a male, who is usually tall; not a 15q deletion. Human motor development is governed by certain basic principles. Which of the following is Not a basic principle of motor development? (RML 2021) a Maturation of the motor system proceeds from gross motor to fine motor behaviours. b Motor development is from cephalo-to-caudal or from head to feet. c Motor development proceeds from the distal to the proximal or from the extremities to the central part of the body. d Motor development plays a major role in social and behavioural expectations. ✓ Answer: (c) Distal to proximal Proximodistal principle of motor development The concept The principle The proximodistal principle says motor control runs from the centre of the body to the extremities: trunk and shoulders before fingers. Why this one Option (c) says distal to proximal, which reverses the real direction, so it is not a principle. Why the other options are wrong (a) Maturation of the motor system proceeds from gross motor to fine motor behaviours. True: the genuine gross to fine principle; large-muscle control such as sitting comes before fine finger skills. (b) Motor development is from cephalo-to-caudal or from head to feet. True: the genuine cephalocaudal principle; head control comes before control of the legs and feet. (d) Motor development plays a major role in social and behavioural expectations. True: a genuine principle; motor development shapes the social role of the child and what others expect of them. What is the principal factor that changes the affordances available to the toddler, compared with the infant? (RML 2022) a Independent locomotion b Starting to speak c The attachment relationship d New kinds of caretaking ✓ Answer: (a) Independent locomotion Gibson, affordances (ecological approach to perception) The concept What it is Affordances are the action possibilities the environment offers a perceiver, so they depend on what that perceiver can do. Why locomotion They change most when the child's own action abilities change: crawling and walking make toys reachable and drops dangerous. Why the other options are wrong (b) Starting to speak Speech changes the child's social world , not what the surroundings afford action. (c) The attachment relationship Attachment changes the child's social world , not the action possibilities in the surroundings. (d) New kinds of caretaking Caretaking changes the social world around the child, not what the environment affords the child's own actions. The process of synaptic pruning is most closely associated with : (RML 2023) a Memory consolidation b Neuronal development and plasticity c Neurotransmitter release d Long-term potentiation ✓ Answer: (b) Neuronal development and plasticity Synaptic overproduction and pruning in brain development The concept What happens The young brain overproduces synapses , then prunes the little-used ones. Why this one Pruning fits circuits to experience, which is the developmental sculpting of circuits: neuronal development and plasticity . Why the other options are wrong (a) Memory consolidation Memory consolidation is how new memories become stable, working at existing synapses, not the developmental sculpting of circuits. (c) Neurotransmitter release Neurotransmitter release is how signals cross existing synapses, not the removal of unused ones. (d) Long-term potentiation Long-term potentiation strengthens existing synapses with repeated use; a memory mechanism, not developmental pruning. Which is not attained in Piaget's concrete operational stage of cognitive development? (JEMAS 2025) a Reduced egocentrism b Deferred imitation c Hypothetico deductive reasoning d Transitive inference ✓ Answer: (c) Hypothetico deductive reasoning Piaget, formal operational stage (11 or 12 onward) The concept Why this one Hypothetico-deductive reasoning , forming hypotheses and testing them systematically, is the hallmark of Piaget's formal operational stage, from 11 or 12 onward. So It is not yet attained in the concrete operational stage, which comes before it. Why the other options are wrong (a) Reduced egocentrism True gain: reduced egocentrism is a concrete operational achievement. (b) Deferred imitation Attained earlier, at 18 to 24 months in the sensorimotor stage, so it is present rather than missing in concrete operations. (d) Transitive inference True gain: transitive inference (if A is taller than B and B taller than C, A is taller than C) is a concrete operational achievement. A 5-year-old child is asked to sort a deck of cards. The cards can be sorted by color (red/black) or by suit (hearts, spades, etc.). The child successfully sorts by color but cannot then re-sort the same deck by suit. This inflexibility is an example of: (Real PYQ 2024) a Egocentrism b Animism c Centration d Transductive reasoning ✓ Answer: (c) Centration Piaget, preoperational stage The concept What it is Centration is focusing on one salient feature and ignoring the others, typical of the preoperational child. In this case The child centres on colour and ignores suit , so the same deck cannot be re-sorted. Why the other options are wrong (a) Egocentrism Egocentrism is failure to take another's perspective; no other person's view is involved here. (b) Animism Animism is giving life to objects, which has nothing to do with sorting. (d) Transductive reasoning Transductive reasoning runs from particular to particular, an error in reasoning, not inflexibility in sorting. Formal operational reasoning involves all the following EXCEPT: (RML 2022) a hypothetical reasoning b counterfactual reasoning c dialectical reasoning d metacognitive reasoning ✓ Answer: (c) Dialectical reasoning Postformal thought: Riegel (1973), Basseches (1984) The concept What it is Dialectical reasoning , integrating opposing views, is postformal thought , a level beyond Piaget's final stage. Who said so Riegel (1973) and Basseches (1984) described it, so it is not part of formal operations. Why the other options are not the answer (a) hypothetical reasoning True: hypothetical reasoning , thinking about possibilities, belongs to Piaget's formal operational stage. (b) counterfactual reasoning True: counterfactual reasoning , reasoning about what is contrary to fact, belongs to Piaget's formal operational stage. (d) metacognitive reasoning True: metacognitive reasoning , thinking about one's own thinking, belongs to Piaget's formal operational stage. Vygotsky's concept of the 'zone of proximal development' (ZPD) refers to: (RML 2025) a The difference between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with guidance. b A measure of a person's fixed learning capacity across cognitive domains. c A developmental stage characterised by logical reasoning capability. d The optimal period during which specific cognitive skills must develop. ✓ Answer: (a) The difference between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with guidance Vygotsky, zone of proximal development The concept What it is The ZPD runs from the actual developmental level (independent problem solving) to the level reached with a more knowledgeable other . Key note It is not fixed: it moves as skills are internalised. Why the other options are wrong (b) A measure of a person's fixed learning capacity across cognitive domains. A fixed capacity is the opposite of the ZPD, which moves as skills are internalised. (c) A developmental stage characterised by logical reasoning capability. Sounds like Piaget's stages of logical operations ; the ZPD is a gap between two levels of performance, not a stage. (d) The optimal period during which specific cognitive skills must develop. Describes a critical or optimal period , a time window; the ZPD is a gap between two levels, not a period. What is the primary difference between Piaget and Vygotsky's theories of language development? (RML 2021) a Piaget argued thought depends on language while Vygotsky argued language depends on thought b Vygotsky argued thought depends on language while Piaget argued language depends on thought c Vygotsky was concerned with early language development while Piaget was concerned with later language development. d None of the above ✓ Answer: (b) Vygotsky argued thought depends on language while Piaget argued language depends on thought Vygotsky versus Piaget on thought and language The concept Piaget's view For Piaget language expresses concepts already built through action, so language depends on thought . Vygotsky's view For Vygotsky thought and speech have separate roots that merge at about 2, after which language shapes thought. Why the other options are wrong (a) Piaget argued thought depends on language while Vygotsky argued language depends on thought Swaps the names : Piaget made language depend on thought, and Vygotsky had language shape thought. (c) Vygotsky was concerned with early language development while Piaget was concerned with later language development. False: both studied the speech of young children, egocentric speech for Piaget and private speech for Vygotsky. (d) None of the above Fails because option (b) states the difference correctly. In the 'teleological stance', toddlers can understand: (RML 2022) a Contingencies b Intentions in action c Prior Intentions d Mental states such as belief and desire ✓ Answer: (b) Intentions in action Gergely and Csibra, teleological stance The concept What it is In Gergely and Csibra 's teleological stance , infants near the end of the first year read an action as efficient and goal-directed. Why this one So they grasp the goal visible in an ongoing act, the intention in action , without yet representing mental states. Why the other options are wrong (a) Contingencies Mere contingencies are what these infants have already moved beyond; the teleological stance reads goals. (c) Prior Intentions Prior intentions are plans formed before acting, which infants do not yet represent. (d) Mental states such as belief and desire These come later: desire psychology at about 2 and belief-desire psychology at 3 to 4. Which of the following is a key characteristic of the "slow-to-warm-up" temperament category in the Thomas and Chess model? (Real PYQ 2024) a Positive approach to new stimuli and high regularity of biological functions. b Negative withdrawal from new stimuli, slow adaptability, and mild intensity of reactions. c Intense and frequent negative emotional reactions with irregular routines. d A mix of easy and difficult characteristics with no clear pattern. ✓ Answer: (b) Negative withdrawal from new stimuli, slow adaptability, and mild intensity of reactions Thomas and Chess, temperament types The concept What it is The slow-to-warm-up child withdraws from new things at first, but mildly , and adapts gradually. The model Thomas and Chess described easy , difficult and slow-to-warm-up children; roughly 35 percent fitted no single type. Why the other options are wrong (a) Positive approach to new stimuli and high regularity of biological functions. Describes the easy child , not the slow-to-warm-up one. (c) Intense and frequent negative emotional reactions with irregular routines. Describes the difficult child , whose reactions are intense, unlike the mild slow-to-warm-up child. (d) A mix of easy and difficult characteristics with no clear pattern. Describes the roughly 35 percent who fitted no single type, not a category of its own. Which among the following is not included within the classification of structure of temperament given by Rothbart and Bates (RML 2022) a Extraversion b Inhibition to the unfamiliar c Negative affectivity d Effortful control ✓ Answer: (b) Inhibition to the unfamiliar Rothbart and Bates, three dimensions of temperament The concept The model Rothbart and Bates have exactly three dimensions: surgency (extraversion), negative affectivity and effortful control . Why this one Inhibition to the unfamiliar is not one of them; it is Jerome Kagan 's behavioural inhibition. Why the other options are wrong (a) Extraversion Included: this is surgency , one of the three Rothbart and Bates dimensions. (c) Negative affectivity Included: one of the three Rothbart and Bates dimensions. (d) Effortful control Included: one of the three Rothbart and Bates dimensions. According to experts on socioemotional development like Campos (2009) and Kagan (2010), self-conscious emotions appear at which age? (RML 2022) a 6-9 months b Before 9 months c After 12 months d 3 months ✓ Answer: (c) After 12 months Campos (2009) and Kagan (2010), self-conscious emotions The concept What they are Self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, shame, guilt, envy and empathy) need self-awareness . When Self-awareness arrives in the second half of the second year, shown by mirror self-recognition at 18 to 24 months, so these emotions come after 12 months. Why the other options are wrong (a) 6-9 months An age for the primary emotions , which come before self-awareness. (b) Before 9 months Too early: this period belongs to the primary emotions , not self-conscious ones. (d) 3 months Far too early: an age for the primary emotions , long before self-awareness. Children, who are distressed by their parent's absence, seek interaction but also reject it when offered. How can the reaction be categorised? (RML 2021) a Insecure-avoidant b Insecure-resistant c Insecure-disorganized d Secure-resistant ✓ Answer: (b) Insecure-resistant Ainsworth, Strange Situation, type C The concept What it is Ainsworth 's type C (ambivalent or resistant) infants are very distressed at separation. On reunion They seek contact yet resist it , which is exactly the pattern in the question. Why the other options are wrong (a) Insecure-avoidant Avoidant (A) infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver. (c) Insecure-disorganized Disorganised (D) infants show contradictory or freezing behaviour, not a consistent seek-then-resist pattern. (d) Secure-resistant Not a type: secure and resistant are separate categories. According to the schema theory, which hypothetical construct provides a prototype for subsequent attachments and can be adapted through more experience? (RML 2021) a Proximity-seeking mechanism b Attachment system c Bio-social relationship model d Internal working model ✓ Answer: (d) Internal working model Bowlby, internal working model The concept What it is Bowlby 's internal working model is a schema of self, attachment figures and relationships, built from early experience. How it works It acts as a prototype for later relationships and can be revised by new experience. Why the other options are wrong (a) Proximity-seeking mechanism Proximity seeking is a behaviour the attachment system produces, not a mental model. (b) Attachment system The evolved control system itself, not the schema built from experience. (c) Bio-social relationship model Not Bowlby 's term; a made-up distractor. Which theory of attachment is currently considered the predominantly accepted theory by developmental psychologists? (IHBAS 2020) a Psychoanalytic b Learning c Cognitive-developmental d Ethological ✓ Answer: (d) Ethological Bowlby, ethological theory of attachment The concept What it says Bowlby 's ethological theory treats attachment as an evolved behavioural system that keeps the infant near a protector. Why it won Feeding-based theories were undermined by Harlow 's contact comfort findings: infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother rather than a wire one that fed them. Why the other options are wrong (a) Psychoanalytic Freud's view rests on feeding , which Harlow's contact comfort findings undermined. (b) Learning Secondary drive ('cupboard love') theory: the mother is loved because she feeds; Harlow's findings undermined it. (c) Cognitive-developmental Explains only the timing of attachment, not attachment itself. Which parenting style is characterized by the combination of giving emotional support, setting clear boundaries, and maintaining accountability for children's behavior? (Real PYQ 2025) a Authoritarian parenting b Authoritative parenting c Permissive parenting d Neglectful parenting ✓ Answer: (b) Authoritative parenting Baumrind, parenting styles The concept What it is Baumrind 's authoritative style combines warmth (emotional support) with firm, reasoned control (boundaries, accountability). Two dimensions It is high on both demandingness and responsiveness . Why the other options are wrong (a) Authoritarian parenting High control without warmth : demanding but not responsive. (c) Permissive parenting Warmth without control : responsive but not demanding. (d) Neglectful parenting Lacks both warmth and control: low on demandingness and responsiveness . According to Jean Piaget's theory of play development, what is the first stage of child play that emerges during infancy? (Real PYQ 2025) a Symbolic play b Functional play c Games with rules d Constructive play ✓ Answer: (b) Functional play Piaget, stages of play The concept What it is Functional play (practice or sensorimotor play) is repeating actions for the pleasure of exercising sensorimotor schemes , like shaking a rattle again and again. Why first It comes first, in infancy , because it needs only action, not symbols. Why the other options are wrong (a) Symbolic play Needs the preoperational symbolic function , so it comes after infancy. (c) Games with rules Belongs to the concrete operational years. (d) Constructive play Added later by Smilansky , not part of Piaget's own sequence. The starting point for self-socialization, according to Kohlberg's cognitive-developmental theory of gender-role development, is: (IHBAS 2020) a Gender consistency b Basic gender identity c Gender stability d Gender-role achievement ✓ Answer: (b) Basic gender identity Kohlberg, cognitive-developmental theory of gender The concept Kohlberg's chain Kohlberg 's chain runs basic gender identity, gender stability, gender consistency; labelling oneself a boy or girl is the first link. Key note Answered as keyed. Many textbooks say Kohlberg's children become full self-socialisers only at gender consistency , and that it is gender schema theory that starts self-socialisation at basic gender identity. Why the other options are wrong (a) Gender consistency The third link; many textbooks name it as Kohlberg's real start of self-socialisation , but it is not the keyed answer. (c) Gender stability The second link (gender stays the same over time), after basic gender identity, so not the starting point. (d) Gender-role achievement Not one of Kohlberg's stages. What is the focus of Kohlberg's preconventional level of moral development? (IHBAS 2025) a Social contract b Avoiding punishment and gaining rewards c Obeying laws d Ethical principles ✓ Answer: (b) Avoiding punishment and gaining rewards Kohlberg, Level I (preconventional morality) The concept What it is At Level I (preconventional) morality is under external control . The two stages Stage 1 obeys to avoid punishment; stage 2 seeks rewards and fair deals. Why the other options are wrong (a) Social contract Stage 5, at the postconventional level. (c) Obeying laws Stage 4, at the conventional level. (d) Ethical principles Stage 6, at the postconventional level. Jean Piaget's theory of moral development suggests that children in the stage of 'heteronomous morality' (typically ages 5-10) base their moral judgments on: (Real PYQ 2024) a Intentions and equality b Rules as being unchangeable and the consequences of actions c Social contracts and individual rights d Abstract principles of justice ✓ Answer: (b) Rules as being unchangeable and the consequences of actions Piaget, heteronomous morality (moral realism) The concept What it is Heteronomous children ( moral realism ) treat adult rules as sacred and unchangeable. How they judge They judge acts by the damage done ( objective responsibility ), so breaking many cups by accident seems worse than breaking one while misbehaving. Why the other options are wrong (a) Intentions and equality Belongs to Piaget's autonomous stage, when rules become flexible and intentions count. (c) Social contracts and individual rights Kohlberg's stage 5 , not Piaget's heteronomous stage. (d) Abstract principles of justice Kohlberg's stage 6 , not Piaget's heteronomous stage. Carol Gilligan departs from Kohlberg's theory on moral development by highlighting which of these differences? (RML 2022) a Males have ethics of care b Males have ethics of justice c Females have ethics care d Females have ethics of justice ✓ Answer: (c) Females have an ethic of care Carol Gilligan, In a Different Voice (1982) The concept Her argument In In a Different Voice (1982) Gilligan argued that Kohlberg 's scale captures a male ethic of justice . What it misses It misses the ethic of care , reasoning from relationships and responsibility, more often heard in women. Why the other options are wrong (a) Males have ethics of care Reverses the pairing : Gilligan linked care with women, not men. (b) Males have ethics of justice This is what Kohlberg already measured, so it is not Gilligan's departure. (d) Females have ethics of justice Reverses the pairing : Gilligan linked justice with the male voice, not women. According to Erik Erikson's psychosocial development theory, a child who is 1.5 years old (18 months) would be in which developmental stage? (Real PYQ 2025) a Trust vs. Mistrust b Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt c Initiative vs. Guilt d Industry vs. Inferiority ✓ Answer: (b) Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt Erikson, psychosocial stage 2 The concept Why this one Eighteen months is the boundary between Erikson's first two stages, and the keyed answer places the toddler in autonomy versus shame and doubt . The reason The toddler is now walking and facing toilet training . Why the other options are wrong (a) Trust vs. Mistrust The first stage, infancy; 18 months is only its outer boundary, the trap. (c) Initiative vs. Guilt Begins at about 3, so too late. (d) Industry vs. Inferiority Begins at school age , far too late. According to Erikson, the state of ______ involves feelings of inner fragmentation, little or no sense of where one's life is headed, and an inability to gain the support of a social role or vocation. (Amity 2023) a Conflict b Identity confusion c Incongruence d Dissociation ✓ Answer: (b) Identity confusion Erikson, identity versus role confusion (stage 5) The concept What it is Identity confusion is the negative pole of Erikson's fifth stage, identity versus role confusion . What it feels like The person feels fragmented, with no sense of direction and no social role or vocation to lean on, the state described in the stem. Why the other options are wrong (a) Conflict Too general a term; not Erikson's name for this state. (c) Incongruence Carl Rogers 's gap between self-concept and experience, not an Erikson term. (d) Dissociation A break in the integration of memory and identity, not Erikson's crisis. Which term was used by Erikson to refer to the feeling experienced by some individuals in mid-life that they have achieved very little or nothing and have little to offer to the next generation? (RML 2020) a Stagnation b Generativity c Presbyopia d Mid-life crisis ✓ Answer: (a) Stagnation Erikson, generativity versus stagnation (middle adulthood) The concept What it is Stagnation is the negative pole of generativity versus stagnation , Erikson's stage of middle adulthood . In plain terms The stagnant adult feels they have achieved little and have little to offer the next generation. Why the other options are wrong (b) Generativity The healthy pole of the same stage (guiding the next generation), the opposite of the feeling described. (c) Presbyopia Age-related loss of near focusing in the lens , a physical change, not Erikson's term. (d) Mid-life crisis A popular term, not Erikson 's. In adulthood climacteric refers to (JEMAS 2025) a loss of muscular strength and agility. b receding hairlines and greying of hair in adults. c the end of ovulation and termination of reproductive capacity. d gradual decline in reaction time and manual dexterity. ✓ Answer: (c) the end of ovulation and termination of reproductive capacity Definition of the climacteric The concept What it is The climacteric is the midlife winding down of reproductive capacity . In women It culminates in menopause , when ovulation ends. Why the other options are wrong (a) loss of muscular strength and agility. Lost strength and agility is a real midlife change, but general physical ageing , not the climacteric. (b) receding hairlines and greying of hair in adults. Real midlife changes, but general physical ageing , not the climacteric. (d) gradual decline in reaction time and manual dexterity. Slower reaction time and dexterity are real midlife changes, but general physical ageing , not the climacteric. The type of marriage in which comradeship and sharing are emphasized, but husband and wife assume responsibility for different roles is known as (JEMAS 2025) a Traditional marriage. b Collegial marriage. c Companionship marriage. d Satisfactory marriage. ✓ Answer: (b) Collegial marriage Hurlock, types of marriage The concept What it is In Hurlock 's typology the collegial marriage stresses comradeship and sharing. The twist Each spouse still takes responsibility for different, complementary roles . Why the other options are wrong (a) Traditional marriage. Separates roles without stressing comradeship . (c) Companionship marriage. Shares the same roles , not different ones. (d) Satisfactory marriage. Not a type in Hurlock's typology. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Object permanence is a sensorimotor achievement: search for a fully hidden object begins at about 8 to 12 months (substage 4, with the A-not-B error) and object permanence is complete by 18 to 24 months. asked 10 times Erikson's crisis of adolescence (about 12 to 18) is identity versus role confusion , and its virtue is fidelity. asked 10 times The zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do independently (the actual developmental level) and what the learner can achieve with guidance from a more knowledgeable other: tasks too hard to master alone but achievable with help. asked 8 times Conservation (quantity stays the same despite changes in shape or arrangement, as with the clay sausage or the tall glass) is mastered in the concrete operational stage (7 to 11), number first and volume last. asked 7 times Hypothetico-deductive reasoning and abstract thought define the formal operational stage (11 or 12 onward); it is not a stage itself, and the concrete operational child does not attain it. asked 7 times Thomas and Chess (New York Longitudinal Study, 1956) found three types: easy (about 40 percent: regular, positive, adaptable, approaches), difficult (about 10 percent: irregular rhythms, negative mood, intense reactions, withdrawal, slow adaptation) and slow-to-warm-up (about 15 percent: low activity, mild intensity, initial withdrawal, slow gradual adaptation); about 35 percent fitted no single type. asked 6 times Harry Harlow ('The Nature of Love', 1958): infant rhesus monkeys clung to a terry-cloth mother that gave no milk rather than a wire mother that fed them, so contact comfort, not feeding , is the primary basis of attachment. asked 6 times In the Strange Situation, reunion behaviour decides the type: secure (B) infants seek contact, are readily comforted and return to play; insecure-avoidant (A) infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver; insecure-resistant or ambivalent (C) infants are very distressed, seek contact yet resist it and cannot be soothed. asked 6 times Authoritative parenting (Baumrind) is high in demandingness and high in responsiveness: emotional support, clear boundaries, reasoned discipline and accountability, with the best child outcomes; authoritarian is high demand and low warmth, permissive low demand and high warmth, and neglectful (added by Maccoby and Martin, 1983) low on both. asked 6 times Kohlberg's preconventional level (stage 1 punishment-and-obedience, stage 2 instrumental purpose and exchange, or self-interest) is morality under external control: rules are obeyed to avoid punishment or gain rewards, so rewarded acts are right and punished acts wrong. asked 6 times Kohlberg's conventional level is conformity to social rules and maintenance of the social order: stage 3 good boy-nice girl (approval, interpersonal expectations, the golden rule) and stage 4 law and order (duty, respect for authority; Papalia's social concern and conscience). Obeying a law or keeping a promise because society depends on it is conventional. asked 6 times In Bronfenbrenner 's ecological systems theory (1979), the microsystem holds the child's direct settings (family, school, peers), the mesosystem is the links between them (home-school), the exosystem holds settings without the child (parent's workplace), the macrosystem is culture and the chronosystem (added later) is time. asked 5 times Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation (with Barbara Wittig, 1969; Patterns of Attachment, 1978): Bowlby is to attachment theory as Ainsworth is to the Strange Situation. asked 5 times Centration is the preoperational focus on one salient feature while ignoring others, as in the 5-year-old who sorts cards by colour but cannot re-sort them by suit. asked 4 times The term zone of proximal development was coined by Lev Vygotsky (not Piaget, Bruner, Kohlberg, Bronfenbrenner, Erikson, Skinner or Freud); scaffolding , the support given within it, is a term from Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976). asked 4 times The fourth pattern, disorganised or disoriented (D) , was added by Mary Main and Judith Solomon (1986, 1990): no one clear pattern, with contradictory, freezing, dazed or apprehensive behaviour on reunion, often after maltreatment. asked 4 times Kohlberg's three levels are preconventional, conventional and postconventional ; Level III (Papalia: morality of autonomous moral principles) holds stage 5, the social-contract orientation (laws as instruments expressing the majority's will and furthering welfare), and stage 6, universal ethical principles. Unconventional, formal conventional and amoral are not Kohlberg levels, and premoral is Piaget's period before rules matter. asked 4 times Erikson's virtues in order: trust gives hope , autonomy will , initiative purpose , industry competence , identity fidelity , intimacy love , generativity care , integrity wisdom . asked 4 times Marcia's identity statuses cross crisis (exploration) with commitment : diffusion (neither), foreclosure (commitment without exploration), moratorium (exploration without commitment), achievement (both). asked 4 times Middle adulthood is generativity versus stagnation : mentoring and guiding the next generation is generativity; feeling one has achieved little and has little to offer is stagnation. asked 4 times Erikson's first stage is trust versus mistrust in infancy (birth to about 1, some texts 18 months); a child of 18 months is keyed to autonomy versus shame and doubt. asked 4 times A critical period is a fixed window in which an experience must occur for normal development, with largely irreversible effects (Lorenz's imprinting; embryonic organ formation); later experience compensating for early deficits contradicts it. asked 3 times Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk (1960) used the visual cliff to test depth perception: infants of crawling age (about 6 months onward) refused the deep side, so depth perception is present by the time infants crawl. asked 3 times Piaget's stage ages: sensorimotor birth to 2, preoperational 2 to 7, concrete operational 7 to 11, formal operational 11 or 12 onward. asked 3 times False-belief tasks (Wimmer and Perner's Maxi task, 1983; Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith's Sally-Anne task, 1985) assess theory of mind and are typically passed at about age 4 , in the preoperational years. asked 3 times Bowlby's internal working model is a mental representation of self, attachment figures and relationships, built from early experience, that serves as a prototype for later relationships and can be revised by new experience. asked 3 times Konrad Lorenz (1935): greylag goslings imprint on the first moving object after hatching, a rapid, largely irreversible following response formed within a narrow critical period. asked 3 times Late adulthood (65 onward) is ego integrity versus despair : accepting the life one has lived versus regret and fear of death; the virtue is wisdom. asked 3 times Maturation (Arnold Gesell) is the biological unfolding of genetic potential; a child's increasing skill at using his muscles is due mainly to maturation, not exercise, parental pushing or learning. asked 2 times Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is a tall male with small testes, infertility and learning difficulties; Turner syndrome (45,X) is a short female with a webbed neck and ovarian failure. asked 2 times

title: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 7: Clinical Psychology
text: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 7: Clinical Psychology Chapter 7 of the one-volume Final Exam Textbook, all nine JSS subjects in one book. Both A4 PDFs hold the whole book with the same page numbers. A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (975 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (975 pages) Chapter 7 Clinical Psychology In this chapter 7.1 The Profession: History, Models, Ethics and Indian Law : Define clinical psychology and tell it apart from neighbouring professions, trace its history in the West and in India, compare the models of abnormality, apply the APA ethical principles and the Tarasoff duty, and state the main provisions of India's mental health and disability laws. 7.2 The Clinical Interview, Mental Status Examination and Formulation : Conduct and record a clinical assessment: choose an interview format, use the core interviewing microskills, take a case history, carry out and write a mental status examination, assess suicide and violence risk, run a functional analysis, build a 5 Ps formulation, and use DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 with an eye on reliability and labelling. 7.3 Psychodynamic Therapies and Their Descendants : Explain how Freud's psychoanalysis works as a treatment and how its descendants (ego, object relations and self psychology, brief dynamic therapy, interpersonal psychotherapy, Jungian and Adlerian therapy, transactional analysis and supportive therapy) differ in theory, technique and evidence. 7.4 Behaviour Therapy : Trace the origins and assumptions of behaviour therapy and describe, attribute and choose among its classical, operant, modelling, relaxation and self-management techniques, from systematic desensitisation, flooding and ERP to token economies, habit reversal and parent training. 7.5 Cognitive and Cognitive-Behavioural Therapies, and the Third Wave : Explain and compare Ellis's REBT and Beck's cognitive therapy, describe the other cognitive-behavioural and third-wave therapies (DBT, ACT, MBCT and others) with their founders and techniques, and weigh the evidence for CBT. 7.6 Humanistic, Existential, Experiential and Brief Therapies : Explain person-centred, Gestalt, existential, reality, experiential and brief therapies, motivational interviewing with the stages of change, and the helping-skills models, naming each founder and signature technique. 7.7 Family, Couples and Group Therapies : Explain why families are treated as systems, what the double bind and expressed emotion research found, how the Bowen, structural, strategic, Milan, experiential and later family, couples and sex therapies work, and how group therapy, psychodrama, self-help groups and therapeutic communities help, naming who devised each. 7.8 Does Psychotherapy Work? Evidence, Common Factors and the Alliance : Explain how psychotherapy outcome is evaluated, from Eysenck's challenge and meta-analysis to RCTs, empirically supported treatments and clinical significance, and weigh the evidence for common factors, the alliance and therapist and client variables. 7.9 Health, Community, Crisis and Rehabilitation Psychology : Explain health psychology and the models of health behaviour, the psychology of physical and chronic illness, community mental health and prevention, crisis intervention and suicide prevention, and psychosocial, neuropsychological and addiction rehabilitation. 7.10 Working with Children, Older Adults and Special Settings : Adapt assessment and therapy to children, adolescents, older adults and counselling, forensic, creative and digital settings, naming each method's originator and the Indian laws that apply. Weightage. 366 of the 3180 questions mapped in this book (11.5%) test this chapter, 191 of them from real past papers. 4 of its 10 sections are High yield. Paris in the 1790s. On the southern edge of the city stood La Bicêtre, a huge hospice for poor, old, sick and criminal men. In its wards for the insane, men were kept in chains, some of them for years, and treated more like dangerous animals than patients. The story most books tell is that in 1793, at the height of the French Revolution, the hospital's physician, Philippe Pinel , ordered the irons struck off, and that men who had not seen the sky for years walked calmly into the courtyard. Nineteenth-century painters made the scene famous. The real story, pieced together by historians, is less heroic and more useful. The chains at Bicêtre were first removed not by the doctor but by Jean-Baptiste Pussin , the lay superintendent of the ward, who had seen what irons did to the men in his care and had begun to treat them as people: he spoke with them, kept them occupied and replaced irons with gentler restraint. Pinel's contribution was to recognise that Pussin's methods worked, to record his patients' histories carefully and count who recovered, and to take the approach, with Pussin himself, to the women's hospital, the Salpêtrière. Their moral treatment rested on three things: a relationship, a daily routine and careful observation of results. Keep both men in mind: the attendant who knew how to be with a frightened, disturbed person, and the physician who wrote down what happened and checked whether it helped. Between them they hold the whole of clinical psychology: understanding and assessing a person, building a relationship that heals, choosing treatments by their evidence, caring for people in their communities and protecting their dignity in law. This chapter follows each of these threads, and at its end we return to Bicêtre. 7.1 The Profession: History, Models, Ethics and Indian Law Medium yield · 39 Qs Before learning how a clinical psychologist interviews, tests or treats, you need to know who this professional is, where the profession came from, which theories of abnormality it uses, and which ethical rules and Indian laws bind it. What clinical psychology is The American Psychological Association's Division 12, the Society of Clinical Psychology, describes a field that "integrates science, theory, and practice to understand, predict, and alleviate maladjustment, disability, and discomfort as well as to promote human adaptation, adjustment, and personal development". A clinical psychologist therefore researches, assesses, treats and promotes well-being. In India the profession is defined by qualification and registration: under the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) Act, a clinical psychologist holds an RCI-recognised qualification and is on the RCI's register, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 likewise defines one by an RCI-recognised qualification. The work spans psychological assessment, diagnosis, psychotherapy, research, teaching and supervision, consultation and administration, in hospitals, rehabilitation centres, schools, universities, courts, prisons, the armed forces, private practice and online. Table 7.1 separates the clinical psychologist from four neighbours. Table 7.1 The clinical psychologist and neighbouring professions in India. Profession Training Main work Prescribes? Clinical psychologist Psychology degree, then two-year M.Phil (now the RCI MA); RCI registration Assessment, psychodiagnosis, psychotherapy, research No Psychiatrist MBBS, then MD, DNB or DPM in psychiatry Medical diagnosis, medication, ECT Yes Counselling psychologist Master's in psychology or counselling Adjustment, career and relationship problems of relatively healthy people No Psychiatric social worker MSW, then M.Phil in psychiatric social work Family and social assessment, casework, rehabilitation No Psychiatric nurse Nursing degree, psychiatric specialisation Ward care, medicines, monitoring, psychoeducation No From demons to moral treatment How people explained strange behaviour decided how they treated it. The oldest explanation, the supernatural model , blamed possession, sin or sorcery. Some Stone Age skulls show trephining , a hole chipped through the skull, perhaps to let an evil spirit out. The Greek physician Hippocrates (460 to 377 BC) made the first break, finding natural causes in the brain and body. His humoral theory , developed by the Roman physician Galen (about AD 129 to 198), held that health is a balance of blood, yellow bile, black bile and phlegm, and that excess black bile causes melancholia. Medieval Europe swung back to demonology, and outbreaks of mass madness such as St Vitus's dance and tarantism were taken as signs of possession. From the sixteenth century the mentally ill were confined in asylums that were more prisons than hospitals; London's Bethlehem Hospital, shortened to Bedlam , was so notorious that its name now means uproar. Reform came at the end of the eighteenth century. In Paris the physician Philippe Pinel (1745 to 1826) and the superintendent Jean-Baptiste Pussin (1746 to 1811) removed the chains from patients at La Bicêtre (in 1793, by the usual account) and then at the Salpêtrière. In England the Quaker William Tuke (1732 to 1822) opened the York Retreat in 1796, where patients lived and worked in a calm, family-like house. Both reforms practised moral treatment ("moral" meaning psychological): kindness, routine, work and social contact. From the 1840s the American schoolteacher Dorothea Dix (1802 to 1887) persuaded legislatures to build state hospitals, but they filled faster than they could be staffed and moral treatment decayed into custodial care. Then a former patient, Clifford Beers (1876 to 1943), described his abuse in hospital in A Mind That Found Itself (1908) and, through the mental hygiene societies he founded in 1908 and 1909, launched the mental hygiene movement for prevention, early treatment and child guidance. Medicine meanwhile built the biological (medical) model . Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926), in a textbook first published in 1883, treated mental disorders as distinct syndromes with their own symptoms, course and outcome, separating dementia praecox (renamed schizophrenia by Eugen Bleuler in 1908) from manic-depressive insanity; modern classification descends from him. Exam trap Pinel gets the credit, but Pussin had begun the humane regime before Pinel arrived at Bicêtre (1793; some textbooks print 1791), persuaded him to follow, and himself banned the chains there, a step historians date to 1797. "Mental hygiene movement" usually means Beers (1908 to 1909), though some textbooks also give the name to Dix's crusade; check the date. Witmer to Vail: a profession is born The profession began in 1896, when Lightner Witmer (1867 to 1956), a former student of Wundt, opened the first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania for children with learning problems. In 1907 he founded the journal The Psychological Clinic and in it first used the term clinical psychology in print. For decades the work was mainly testing: Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon published the first practical intelligence scale in 1905, and in 1917 Robert Yerkes (1876 to 1956) led the testing of about 1.75 million American recruits with the Army Alpha , a written test for literate men, and the non-verbal Army Beta for those who could not read English. After the Second World War, psychological casualties far outnumbered psychiatrists, and from 1946 the Veterans Administration (VA) paid to train clinical psychologists as therapists. How should they be trained? The Boulder conference (Colorado, 1949) chose the scientist-practitioner model : a PhD training clinicians equally in research and practice, so that they consume research, evaluate their own work and create new knowledge. The Vail conference (Colorado, 1973) endorsed the practitioner-scholar model and the PsyD (Doctor of Psychology), a professional degree centred on practice. Richard McFall 's 1991 "Manifesto for a Science of Clinical Psychology" set out the stricter clinical science model : training grounded in research, and only scientifically supported methods in practice. The APA formed a clinical section in 1919, which became Division 12 when the APA reorganised into divisions in 1945. The newest debate is over prescription privileges for psychologists trained in psychopharmacology: supporters cite shortages of psychiatrists, opponents doubt the training and fear a loss of psychological identity. New Mexico (2002) and Louisiana (2004) were the first American states to grant them; in India clinical psychologists do not prescribe. Exam trap The first clinic and the first printed "clinical psychology" are Witmer's, not Wundt's (first laboratory, 1879), G. Stanley Hall's (first APA president, 1892), James McKeen Cattell's (coined "mental test", 1890), Freud's, Erikson's, Rogers's or Skinner's. Boulder 1949 = scientist-practitioner, PhD; Vail 1973 = practitioner-scholar, PsyD. Salt Lake City hosted a later conference on graduate education (1987), and Adelphi is a university; neither names a training model. Clinical psychology in India Girindrasekhar Bose (1887 to 1953) founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society at Calcutta in 1922 (Chapter 1). Formal training began at the All India Institute of Mental Health, Bangalore (founded 1954), which began training clinical psychologists in 1955 and became NIMHANS (National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences) in 1974; the Hospital for Mental Diseases, Ranchi, now the Central Institute of Psychiatry (CIP), had a clinical psychology department from the late 1940s and started its diploma course in 1962. Their post-MA training in medical and social psychology became the two-year M.Phil in Clinical Psychology , for decades the only qualifying degree. The Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP) was founded in 1968. The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) began in 1986 as a registered society; the RCI Act 1992 made it a statutory body (from 22 June 1993), and the Act was amended in 2000. The RCI regulates rehabilitation and disability professionals, clinical psychologists among them, so it sits under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment rather than the Health Ministry. It recognises courses, sets syllabi and keeps the Central Rehabilitation Register (CRR); practising without registration is an offence under the Act. After the National Education Policy 2020 ended the M.Phil, the RCI replaced it with a two-year professional MA in Clinical Psychology from 2025-26. Exam trap 1968 is the IACP. NIMHANS dates from 1974 and its community psychiatry unit from 1975; it was made an Institute of National Importance by an Act of Parliament in 2012; the PsyD is the American degree from Vail. RCI: society 1986, statutory body under the 1992 Act; Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, not Health. Registration is mandated by the RCI Act, not the Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 or the mental health Acts. What is abnormal, and why? The models No single criterion marks behaviour as abnormal. The statistical criterion calls rare behaviour abnormal, but genius is rare too. The social norm criterion flags rule-breaking, but norms vary: a devotee in trance at a temple festival is following custom. The maladaptiveness criterion asks whether behaviour stops a person meeting daily demands, the personal distress criterion whether the person suffers (a manic person may feel wonderful). Marie Jahoda (1907 to 2001) in 1958 defined ideal mental health instead: positive self-attitude, growth and self-actualisation, integration, autonomy, accurate perception of reality and environmental mastery. Textbooks now condense the criteria into the four Ds : deviance , distress , dysfunction and danger to self or others. A model then says why a disorder arose and so what will help. Beyond the supernatural and biological models, the psychodynamic model of Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) blames unconscious childhood conflict; the behavioural model maladaptive learning; the cognitive model faulty beliefs; the humanistic-existential model blocked growth and lost meaning, answered with respect, empathy, unconditional positive regard and faith in human potential; the sociocultural model poverty, culture and social labels; and the family systems model disturbed family interaction, with the patient as symptom bearer. Table 7.2 lines them up. Table 7.2 Models of psychopathology. Model Key names Cause of disorder Treatment Supernatural Ancient belief Spirits, sin, sorcery Exorcism Biological Hippocrates, Kraepelin Brain, genes, neurotransmitters Drugs, ECT Psychodynamic Freud Unconscious conflict Insight (7.3) Behavioural Pavlov, Skinner Faulty learning, reinforcement Relearning (7.4) Cognitive Ellis, Beck Irrational, distorted thinking Change thinking (7.5) Humanistic-existential Rogers, Maslow, Frankl Blocked growth, lost meaning Growth, choice (7.6) Sociocultural Szasz Poverty, culture, labels Social change (7.9) Family systems Bateson, Minuchin Family interaction Family therapy (7.7) Since each model explains only some cases, two integrative models dominate. In a 1977 paper in Science , the psychiatrist George L. Engel (1913 to 1999) argued that the biomedical model cannot explain why two people with the same lesion fare so differently, and proposed the biopsychosocial model : every illness arises from interacting biological, psychological and social factors, and treatment must address all three. The diathesis-stress model explains who falls ill and when. A diathesis is a predisposition, usually genetic but sometimes psychological (a pessimistic style, an early loss); stress is the triggering event. Neither alone suffices. Paul Meehl (1920 to 2003) applied the idea to schizophrenia in 1962, and Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring formalised it in 1977 as the vulnerability-stress model : everyone has a threshold, and the more vulnerable you are, the less stress it takes to cross it (Figure 7.1). Adding protective factors (social support, coping skills, continued medication), which raise the threshold, gives the vulnerability-stress-protective factor model used in relapse prevention. Stress Vulnerability (diathesis): low to high Disorder: stress exceeds the person's threshold No disorder Person A falls ill Person B stays well Threshold With protective factors Same stressor Figure 7.1 The diathesis-stress (vulnerability-stress) model. The same life event pushes highly vulnerable Person A over the threshold but not Person B; protective factors raise the threshold. Exam trap "Predisposition plus trigger" is diathesis-stress, not the neurodevelopmental model (faulty early brain development in schizophrenia; Chapter 8); "clinical-reductionist" and "syndrome-sign" are not models. Single-cause options (genes, stress, learning, unconscious conflict or spirits alone) are wrong. The biopsychosocial model is Engel's, not Kraepelin's, Bleuler's, Beck's, Freud's, Walter Cannon's (fight or flight) or Richard Lazarus's (stress appraisal). Reinforcement is behavioural, never humanistic. Ethical principles and practice The APA's Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct (2002, amended 2010 and 2016) has two layers: five aspirational General Principles (A to E) that guide judgement but cannot be enforced, and ten sections of enforceable Ethical Standards (on competence, confidentiality, research, assessment, therapy and more). Respect for People's Rights and Dignity Privacy, confidentiality, self-determination Respect for autonomy Behind any code lie two ways of reasoning. A deontological ethic ( Immanuel Kant ) judges an act by its intrinsic rightness: a duty such as keeping a confidence binds whatever the consequences. A utilitarian ethic ( Jeremy Bentham , John Stuart Mill ) weighs costs against benefits and chooses the greatest good for the greatest number. Competence means working only within one's training and supervised experience and referring beyond it; ethical competence means knowing the codes, recognising, analysing and resolving dilemmas, and taking responsibility for one's actions. Informed consent is free agreement by a capable person who has been told, understandably, the nature and course of treatment, fees, the limits of confidentiality and the right to withdraw. A child cannot consent legally, so a guardian gives permission and the clinician seeks the child's assent . Research participants must be told the purpose, procedures, risks and benefits and their right to decline or withdraw (the consent form merely records this). Deception is allowed only when justified and must end in debriefing , a full explanation of the study's true purpose after participation. Research ethics go beyond legal compliance: protection from harm, confidential data, ethics committee approval and honest reporting; fabricating or manipulating data is misconduct. Confidentiality is the clinician's ethical duty not to reveal a client's disclosures; privileged communication is the client's legal right to bar the clinician's testimony in court, which the client may waive. Neither is absolute. Disclosure is allowed or required with the client's consent; when there is serious risk of suicide or of harm to an identifiable person; when child abuse is suspected (India's POCSO Act 2012 makes reporting sexual offences against children mandatory); under a court order, including evidence of guilt or innocence in a criminal case; when clients sue the clinician or put their mental state at issue; and in emergencies. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 grants patients confidentiality with similar exceptions. Key study: Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (1974, 1976) In 1969 Prosenjit Poddar , a graduate student from India at Berkeley, told his university therapist he intended to kill a young woman who had rejected him, readily identifiable as Tatiana Tarasoff . Campus police questioned and released him; no one warned her, and two months later he killed her. The California Supreme Court ruled in 1974 that therapists have a duty to warn an identifiable victim, and in 1976 widened it to a duty to protect (warning, informing police, hospitalisation): "The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins." Critics fear it deters dangerous clients from speaking openly. Exam trap Duty to warn comes from Tarasoff. The M'Naghten (1843) and Durham (1954) rules are insanity tests, and the Daubert standard (1993) governs expert testimony (7.10). "There are never exceptions to confidentiality" is always false. A multiple (dual) relationship exists when a psychologist in a professional role with someone also holds another role with that person or someone close to them, or promises one: treating a friend, employee or relative, or doing business with a client. Under APA Standard 3.05 it is unethical when it risks impaired objectivity, exploitation or harm. Co-therapy by two psychologists, a client seeing two therapists or a psychologist working in two clinics is not a dual relationship. Sexual intimacy with a current client is forbidden, and with a former client for at least two years after therapy and even then only in the most unusual circumstances. Thomas Gutheil and Glen Gabbard (1993) distinguished a boundary crossing , a harmless departure from the usual frame (a brief self-disclosure, seeing a client at the workplace for exposure work), from a boundary violation , which exploits or harms the client to serve the therapist, such as a romantic relationship or business deal. Finally, records must be accurate, secure and open to clients. In assessment , psychologists use valid tests, explain results, release test data (raw scores and responses) to the client or whoever the client names, and guard test security by never releasing manuals or items to untrained people. Teletherapy requires technical competence, secure platforms, consent covering privacy risks, confirming the client's location and an emergency plan. Trainees work under supervision , clients are told so, and the supervisor carries responsibility. The RCI Act lets the Council prescribe a code of ethics, and misconduct can remove a professional from its register. Exam trap A romance with a current client is a boundary violation; rapport and convenient appointments are just good practice. The APA has five General Principles; "equity" is not one. Integrity is APA's, not one of Beauchamp and Childress's four (autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice). Non-maleficence is refraining from harm; doing good is beneficence. Consent comes before a study, debriefing after. Indian mental health law and policy The Indian Lunacy Act 1912 was custodial, built around detaining "lunatics" in asylums. The Mental Health Act 1987 (in force 1993) modernised terms and licensing but gave few rights, exempted government hospitals from licensing and left attempted suicide a crime under section 309 of the Indian Penal Code. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (MHCA, in force 2018) replaced it with a rights-based law aligned with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Rights. A right to access mental healthcare (section 18) from government services, free below the poverty line, with rights to community living, dignity, equality (including insurance parity with physical illness, section 21(4)), confidentiality, information, legal aid and medical records. Choices. Every person, including one with mental illness, is presumed capable (section 4), and treatment needs informed consent. An adult may write an advance directive (section 5) on how to be treated, or not treated, in a future illness and appoint a nominated representative (NR, section 14). A minor can do neither; a minor's NR is the legal guardian unless the Board orders otherwise (section 15). Under section 87 a minor is admitted only on the NR's application after two independent examinations, with the minor's wishes taken into account, is kept apart from adults with the NR or an attendant always present, and is treated with the NR's consent; the Board is informed within 72 hours and must review any stay beyond 30 days. Prohibitions (section 95). No ECT without anaesthesia and muscle relaxant (unmodified ECT is never lawful, and section 94 bars any ECT as emergency treatment); no ECT for minors unless a psychiatrist judges it necessary, the guardian consents and the Board gives prior permission; no sterilisation as treatment; no chaining. Section 97 also bans seclusion and solitary confinement and allows physical restraint only as a last resort authorised by the psychiatrist. Bodies. The Central Mental Health Authority and State Mental Health Authorities register all mental health establishments, government or private, and professionals; Mental Health Review Boards , each for a district or group of districts, chaired by a serving or retired District Judge and including a psychiatrist, a medical practitioner and two service-user or carer members (section 74), register advance directives, appoint NRs, review admissions and hear complaints. Section 115. Anyone who attempts suicide is presumed, unless proved otherwise, to have severe stress and is not punished; in effect, decriminalisation, with a government duty to provide care. Professionals. Section 2 defines a clinical psychologist by an RCI-recognised qualification in clinical psychology, or a postgraduate degree plus a two-year M.Phil in Clinical or Medical and Social Psychology with supervised clinical training; registered with the State Authority, the clinical psychologist is a mental health professional under the Act. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (RPwD, in force 2017) replaced the Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 (7 disabilities) with 21 specified disabilities, including mental illness, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder and specific learning disabilities. At least 40 percent of a specified disability is a benchmark disability , qualifying for reservation (4 percent of government posts, 5 percent of higher education seats). The clinician will interview him, take his history, examine his mental state, judge his safety and build a formulation: the steps this section follows. Purposes and types of clinical interview The clinical interview is a conversation with a professional purpose: it gathers information, tests hypotheses and begins a working relationship at once. Interviews are named by purpose: the intake interview (first contact: why now, how urgent?), the case-history interview, the diagnostic interview (symptoms checked against criteria), the mental status examination, the crisis interview (brief, active, focused on safety; Section 7.9) and the termination interview (reviewing progress and planning relapse prevention). They also differ in structure. In an unstructured interview the clinician chooses the questions: flexible and good for rapport, but two clinicians may reach different diagnoses. A semi-structured interview fixes topics and core questions but lets a trained clinician rephrase, probe and judge. A fully structured interview fixes every word and scoring rule, so a lay interviewer or computer can give it. Structure buys reliability (interviewers agree) at the cost of flexibility and rapport, but not validity : interviewers can agree and still be wrong, and a schedule misses what it does not ask. Rapport , the trust that makes disclosure possible, grows from explaining the purpose and the limits of confidentiality and starting with neutral topics. Attending behaviour shows that you are listening; Gerard Egan ( The Skilled Helper , 1975) summed it up as SOLER : face the client S quarely, O pen posture, L ean forward, E ye contact, R elaxed, though steady eye contact feels intrusive to many Indian clients. Restating in different words is paraphrasing , not questioning, empathy (the broader capacity) or nonverbal communication. "Tell me about" is an open-ended question , even inside an ethnographic interview (learning a culture in the insider's terms) or theory-guided inquiry (questions chosen from a theory). Common errors are leading questions ("You've been depressed, haven't you?"), double-barrelled questions (two in one), accusing "why" questions, premature reassurance and premature closure on an early hypothesis. With children, use play, drawing and concrete words and add parents' and teachers' reports; with older adults, check hearing and vision before inferring confusion (Section 7.10); with resistant clients, acknowledge that coming was not their idea; with suicidal clients, ask directly, since asking does not plant the idea. Across cultures, elicit the client's explanatory model (his name for the problem, its cause, the cure he expects), as Arthur Kleinman (1980) urged, and respect idioms of distress such as "tension". Use a trained interpreter, never a relative or child. The case history The case history, the story of person and illness, follows a fixed order: Identifying data (age, education, occupation, marital status, religion, socioeconomic status), then the informant and the account's reliability (relationship, closeness of contact, consistency). Chief complaints , in the patient's own words, each with its duration ("Low mood, 3 months"). History of present illness : onset (abrupt, acute or insidious), course, precipitating factors and treatment so far. Past psychiatric and medical history , and family history drawn as a genogram (three generations; squares for males, circles for females). Personal history : birth and development, education, occupation, marital and sexual life, substance use and forensic record. Premorbid personality : the person before the illness, the baseline for judging change. The MSE: behaviour, mood, thought and perception The mental status examination (MSE) is a snapshot of mental functioning during the interview. It records appearance and behaviour , attitude towards the examiner (cooperative, guarded, hostile), psychomotor activity (retardation, agitation) and speech (rate, volume, tone, reaction time, relevance, coherence). Mood is the sustained emotion the patient reports: subjective, the climate. Affect is the emotion the examiner observes: objective, the weather. Affect is rated for range, reactivity, appropriateness and stability: it may be blunted (markedly reduced), flat (virtually absent), labile (shifting rapidly) or inappropriate (laughing about a death). Thought has four headings: stream (speed and flow), form of thought (thought process: how ideas connect; Table 7.7), content of thought (what is thought: delusions, obsessions, overvalued ideas, phobias, suicidal or homicidal ideas) and possession (whose thoughts they feel to be). A delusion is a false, unshakeable belief out of keeping with the person's culture: persecutory, of reference (chance events carry a personal message), grandiose, nihilistic (the self, body or world does not exist), of jealousy, erotomanic (a person of higher status is secretly in love with one), of guilt or somatic (the body is diseased or changed). An overvalued idea is an understandable belief held with excessive emotion but without delusional fixity. An obsession is an intrusive thought recognised as one's own and resisted (Indian case formats file obsessions under possession, as lost control of thinking); a phobia is an excessive fear of a specific object, situation or idea. In thought alienation thoughts feel inserted, withdrawn or broadcast; these are among the first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia listed by Kurt Schneider (1887 to 1967; Chapter 8). The MSE: cognition, insight and judgement Cognitive functions are tested in order: consciousness (alert to coma); orientation to time, place and person (time is lost first); attention and concentration (digit span, serial sevens from 100, months backwards); memory , immediate (repeat three words), recent (recall them after five minutes) and remote (childhood events); intelligence and general information ; abstract thinking (proverbs, similarities: literal answers are concrete); and judgement , personal (plans), social (conduct) and test ("What would you do if you saw smoke in a cinema?"). Insight is the patient's awareness and understanding of his own illness, graded on six levels: (1) complete denial; (2) slight awareness of illness while still denying it; (3) awareness, but blamed on others or physical causes; (4) awareness of something unknown within oneself; (5) intellectual insight , accepting the illness without changing behaviour; (6) true emotional insight , awareness that leads to change. Risk assessment: suicide and violence Suicide risk factors include a previous attempt (the strongest predictor), depression, substance use, schizophrenia, hopelessness, male sex (women attempt more often), living alone, chronic illness, recent loss and access to means such as pesticides. Protective factors include family support, responsibility for children, religious objections and reasons for living. The SAD PERSONS mnemonic (Patterson and colleagues, 1983) scores one point each for Sex (male), Age (under 19 or over 45), Depression, Previous attempt, Ethanol abuse, Rational thinking loss, Social support lacking, Organised plan, No spouse and Sickness. It aids memory but predicts poorly: suicide is rare, so scales raise many false alarms yet miss many who act. Ask instead about ideation, intent, plan and means, and build a safety plan. For violence, past violence is the best predictor, with youth, male sex, substance misuse and threats. Structured professional judgement such as the HCR-20 (Historical, Clinical and Risk management items) beats unaided judgement; dynamic factors, unlike static history, can be treated. Behavioural assessment Behavioural assessment asks what a behaviour does for the person here and now. Its core, functional analysis , rests on the operant conditioning of Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990): consequences maintain behaviour. The target behaviour is defined operationally and its ABC recorded: A ntecedent, B ehaviour, C onsequence. A boy who throws his glass when told to clear it, and so escapes the chore, is being reinforced. The SORC model adds O rganism variables (biology, thoughts, learning history) between S timulus and R esponse. Data come from behavioural interviews (what, when, how often), self-monitoring (the client's own diary, essential for private acts such as purging), role play (the client enacts a problem situation, such as refusing a request, while the clinician watches), and observation that is naturalistic (home, school), analogue (a simulated clinic situation) or participant (by a parent, teacher or nurse already present). Event recording counts occurrences; interval recording notes whether the behaviour occurred in each short interval; time sampling observes at chosen moments. Reactivity is behaviour changing because it is observed; observer drift is observers' gradual shift in applying definitions, corrected by retraining. Exam trap Functional analysis is based on operant conditioning , not classical conditioning (Section 7.4), humanistic or psychodynamic principles. Its ABC is Antecedent, Behaviour, Consequence ; Albert Ellis's ABC is Activating event, Belief, Consequence (Section 7.5). A case formulation is an individualised, testable hypothesis about why this person has these problems now (causes, triggers, maintaining factors), revised as therapy proceeds.
