Answers: (1) furthering, (2) semi-structured, (3) circumstantiality; form, (4) subjective; objective, (5) true emotional, (6) Consequence; operant, (7) perpetuating. 7.3 Psychodynamic Therapies and Their Descendants High yield · 39 Qs Every therapy in this section assumes that hidden forces pushing against one another (hence dynamic ) shape what we feel and do, and that bringing them into awareness relieves suffering. The idea began with one patient in Vienna, became Freud's psychoanalysis, and then branched into a large family. Freud's psychoanalysis as a treatment Key study: Breuer's Anna O. (1880 to 1882) The physician Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925) treated Bertha Pappenheim, a young woman with hysterical paralyses and weeks in which she could not drink water. When, in a self-induced trance, she talked through the moment a symptom began and released the feeling she had swallowed then, the symptom eased: her "talking cure". Breuer and Freud published her as "Anna O." in Studies on Hysteria (1895). Criticism: she was not in fact cured, and spent months in sanatoria afterwards. Breuer's procedure was the cathartic method : hypnotise the patient, take her back to the moment a symptom began and let her relive it. Abreaction is the discharge of the emotion attached to a particular repressed memory by reliving it; catharsis (Greek, "purging") is the release and relief that follow. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939), the father of psychoanalysis, then dropped hypnosis: many patients could not be hypnotised, its cures faded, and it went round resistance instead of exposing it. At Nancy in 1889 he had watched Hippolyte Bernheim (1840 to 1919) recover "forgotten" memories from waking patients. The aim of analysis is to make the unconscious conscious, or, in Freud's formula of 1933, "Where id was, there ego shall be". Change comes through insight , an emotionally felt understanding of how present feelings repeat past conflicts, and the target is character, not just the symptom. The patient lies on a couch with the analyst out of sight behind, four or five times a week for years; once- or twice-weekly, face-to-face work on the same principles is psychodynamic psychotherapy. Every analyst first undergoes a training analysis. The patient's one duty is the fundamental rule : say whatever comes to mind, however trivial or embarrassing, without censoring it. Following the rule is free association , the defining technique of psychoanalysis. When conscious steering relaxes, Freud argued, thoughts follow paths laid down by unconscious wishes, and the places where association stalls point to what is repressed. The analyst brings evenly suspended attention; neutrality , taking no side in the patient's conflicts and giving no advice (the "blank screen"); and abstinence , declining to gratify the patient's wishes for love, praise or comfort so that they stay alive to be understood. Abstinence here has nothing to do with alcohol. Dreams, Freud wrote in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900), are "the royal road" to the unconscious. The manifest content , the dream as remembered, disguises the latent content , the hidden wish, through the dream-work: condensation, displacement, symbolisation and secondary revision. The patient free-associates to each element to recover it. Sooner or later the patient arrives late, forgets a session or changes the subject just as something painful approaches. This is resistance : everything in the patient that opposes the treatment and access to unconscious material. It is repression showing itself in the room, so in analysis of resistance the analyst points out the obstruction and explores with the patient what it protects against. Interpretation links what the patient says or does to its unconscious meaning; it is prepared by confrontation and clarification and aimed at the defence before the content it hides. Because one insight rarely changes a lifelong pattern, working through (Freud, 1914) re-examines the same conflicts and interpretations in context after context until lasting change in behaviour and character follows. Remember Origin of disorder by school: psychodynamic, unconscious conflict from childhood emotional experience; behavioural, faulty learning (Section 7.4); cognitive, disturbed thought patterns (Section 7.5); humanistic, failure to fulfil one's potential (Section 7.6). Exam trap Saying whatever comes to mind, uncensored, is free association; systematic desensitisation, flooding and modelling are behaviour therapy (Section 7.4), and paradoxical intention is Frankl's and Adler's. Obstructing the analysis while the therapist explores why is analysis of resistance. Working through is never "giving the interpretation once", advice or ending after one insight. Transference and countertransference In the Dora case (1905) Freud saw that patients come to feel about the analyst as they once felt about their parents. Transference is the patient's unconscious redirection onto the therapist of feelings and expectations that belong to significant figures from the past. It may be positive (affection, idealisation, erotic love) or negative (hostility, suspicion). When the patient's neurosis is re-created around the analyst, it becomes a transference neurosis , whose resolution is, in classical theory, the cure. Countertransference , named by Freud in 1910, is the therapist's emotional reaction to the patient arising from the therapist's own unresolved conflicts, a blind spot to be recognised (hence the training analysis). Since Paula Heimann 's paper of 1950 the term also covers all the therapist's feelings towards the patient, used as information about the patient. Negative countertransference is the therapist's hostility, irritation or boredom towards a patient; positive countertransference is over-involvement or a wish to rescue. Both differ from the working alliance ( Ralph Greenson , 1965), the patient's rational collaboration with the therapist (Section 7.8). Exam trap Direction decides the term: patient to therapist is transference; therapist to patient is countertransference. "The therapist's emotional reaction to the client" is never transference, "the client's projection onto the therapist" is never countertransference, and a therapist's negative feelings are negative countertransference, not negative transference. Fear of the unknown or low motivation are sources of resistance, not countertransference. Managing both is the hallmark of psychodynamic models, not of behaviour modification, CBT or solution-focused therapy. Defences and psychic energy In Freud's language of psychic energy, libido is the energy of the sexual (later, life) drive; cathexis is its investment in the mental representation of a particular object, person or idea; fixation is libido left attached to an earlier psychosexual stage; and sublimation redirects a drive into a socially valued aim. Defence mechanisms are the ego's unconscious strategies against anxiety. Their theory is in Chapter 4; Table 7.9 shows how a clinician meets them. Table 7.9 Defences as the clinician meets them. Exam trap Energy invested in a particular object, person or idea is cathexis, not libido, fixation or sublimation. Projection gives your feeling to someone else; displacement keeps it yours but moves its target. The primary defence, and the psychodynamic source of dissociation, is repression, not conversion, isolation or "ego state" (Paul Federn's term, later Berne's). Ego psychology, object relations and self psychology Freud's successors kept the unconscious but changed what they listened for. Ego psychology turned from the id to the ego. Anna Freud (1895 to 1982), in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), made the analysis of defences central and pioneered child analysis; Heinz Hartmann (1894 to 1970) described a conflict-free ego sphere that develops for adaptation (1939); and Erik Erikson (1902 to 1994) added psychosocial stages and the adolescent identity crisis (Chapters 4 and 6). Object relations theory holds that the mind is built from internalised representations of self and others ("objects") and of the relationships between them. Melanie Klein (1882 to 1960) analysed children through play. In her paranoid-schizoid position the infant manages terror by splitting the world into wholly good and wholly bad objects and by projective identification (placing unwanted parts of the self in another and then controlling that person); in the later depressive position good and bad are seen as one person, bringing guilt and reparation. Paranoia revives the first position, so its defence is splitting. Donald Winnicott (1896 to 1971) described the good-enough mother , closely attuned at first and then failing tolerably, who lets a true self grow; the transitional object , a blanket or soft toy that bridges inner and outer reality; and therapy as a holding environment , as reliable as a mother's arms. Ronald Fairbairn (1889 to 1964) held that libido is object-seeking, not pleasure-seeking. Margaret Mahler (1897 to 1985) traced separation-individuation : a normal autistic phase, a symbiotic phase of fusion with the mother, then differentiation, practising, rapprochement and object constancy by about three years. Her theory of psychosis (1952) traces schizophrenia to these first phases: the person remains in the autistic phase and fails to develop an adequate, stable symbiosis (Silvano Arieti, Ping-Nie Pao and Edith Jacobson wrote other analytic accounts of psychosis). Otto Kernberg (born 1928) described borderline personality organisation (identity diffusion, splitting, intact reality testing) and developed transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP), which interprets the split images of self and others as they appear in the transference. Heinz Kohut (1913 to 1981) founded self psychology with The Analysis of the Self (1971). The child needs selfobjects who provide mirroring (confirming the child's worth), an idealised figure to look up to and merge with and, in his later work, twinship (feeling like others). Chronic failure of mirroring and idealising leaves a fragile self that fragments into emptiness and rage. In therapy these needs return as mirror, idealising and twinship transferences, met by the analyst's empathic attunement . Relational psychoanalysis ( Stephen Mitchell , 1946 to 2000, with Jay Greenberg, 1983) treats therapy as a two-person process in which the analyst cannot be neutral. John Bowlby 's (1907 to 1990) attachment theory inspired attachment-based therapies in which the therapist is a secure base for revising internal working models. Mentalisation-based treatment (MBT), by Anthony Bateman and Peter Fonagy for borderline personality disorder (first trial 1999), strengthens mentalisation, understanding one's own and others' behaviour in terms of feelings, wishes and intentions, a capacity that collapses under attachment stress. Exam trap "Object relations" means internalised representations of self and others and their relationships, not the id-ego-superego relation, defences or the genital stage. A client who feels empty, "no one", afraid of abandonment and hungry for admiration is explained by failed parental mirroring and idealising leading to a fragmented self: that is Kohut's self psychology even when the stem says "object relations". Oral fixation, an unresolved Oedipus complex and a harsh superego are classical Freudian explanations of neurotic conflict and guilt (Chapter 4). For paranoia "as given by Klein", answer splitting; projection is Freud's classical explanation of paranoia. Brief psychodynamic psychotherapies Brief dynamic therapies keep the psychodynamic ideas but use one agreed focus, a limited number of sessions (usually 12 to 40), an active therapist who questions and confronts instead of waiting for free association, and early work on the transference. David Malan of the Tavistock Clinic ( The Frontier of Brief Psychotherapy , 1976) supplied their map (Figure 7.3): the triangle of conflict (hidden feeling, anxiety, defence) and the triangle of person (others now, the therapist, parents then). Table 7.10 lists the models of Malan, Peter Sifneos (1920 to 2008), Habib Davanloo (born 1927), James Mann (1973), Lester Luborsky (1984), and Hans Strupp and Jeffrey Binder (1984). Rooted in the ideas of Adolf Meyer, Sullivan and Bowlby, it works on current relationships rather than childhood conflict, does not interpret the transference, and treats depression as a medical illness, giving the patient the sick role. IPT runs 12 to 16 weekly sessions in three phases. The initial phase diagnoses and explains depression, reviews key relationships (the interpersonal inventory) and picks one or two of four problem areas: grief (complicated bereavement), interpersonal role disputes (with a spouse, parent or employer), role transitions (marriage, a new job, retirement, illness) and interpersonal deficits (social isolation). The middle phase works on that area through encouragement of affect, clarification, communication analysis (who said what, exactly), role play and decision analysis. Termination treats ending as a small grief and credits the patient's own competence. IPT matched cognitive therapy in the NIMH depression trial (Section 7.8), meta-analyses rate it about equal to CBT, and adaptations treat depressed adolescents (IPT-A), perinatal depression and bulimia. Exam trap Asked what IPT does NOT include beside grief, role conflict and role transition, choose "role playing and role reversal": the other three are its problem areas. The fine print: IPT therapists do use role play after communication analysis; role reversal is psychodrama's (Jacob Moreno, Section 7.7). IPT is Klerman and Weissman's; MBT, Bateman and Fonagy's; TFP, Kernberg's; Lorna Smith Benjamin developed interpersonal reconstructive therapy. Jung, Adler, Horney and Sullivan as therapists Freud's early dissenters built their own therapies (their personality theories are in Chapter 4). Carl Gustav Jung (1875 to 1961) founded analytical psychology. Beneath the personal unconscious he placed a collective unconscious of inherited archetypes: the persona (the social mask), the shadow, the anima (the unconscious feminine side of a man), the animus (the unconscious masculine side of a woman) and the self. Jung read dreams as direct, creative messages, not disguises. In amplification the analyst enlarges a dream image with parallels from myth and religion; in active imagination the patient, awake, holds a dialogue with a dream or fantasy figure. The goal is individuation , becoming a whole, integrated self. Alfred Adler (1870 to 1937) left Freud in 1911 and called his school individual psychology . From organ inferiority (1907: compensation for a weak organ) he moved to universal feelings of inferiority that drive a striving for superiority; when they become overwhelming they form an inferiority complex . Therapy is an equal, educational partnership. Lifestyle assessment explores the family constellation, birth order (the dethroned first-born, the competitive second, the pampered youngest) and early recollections, which reveal the present style of life. Its techniques are encouragement , the core one; acting as if (behaving as though one already had the feared ability); spitting in the client's soup (exposing a behaviour's hidden payoff so that it loses its appeal); the push-button technique (Harold Mosak: picturing a pleasant and then an unpleasant memory to show that we create our own feelings); and paradoxical intention. Adlerians do not analyse transference. Karen Horney (1885 to 1952) traced neurosis to basic anxiety, met by moving towards, against or away from people; her therapy dismantled the idealised self-image and its "tyranny of the shoulds". Harry Stack Sullivan (1892 to 1949) made the therapist a participant observer of interpersonal patterns, including parataxic distortion (seeing others through the template of earlier relationships), and so influenced IPT. Exam trap Analysis of transference is the technique an Adlerian counsellor would not use; acting as if, the push button and encouragement are all Adlerian. Collective unconscious, anima and animus: Jung. Individual psychology, inferiority complex, organ inferiority: Adler, not Jung, Horney, Frankl (logotherapy, Section 7.6) or Erikson. Transactional analysis Transactional analysis (TA) was founded by Eric Berne (1910 to 1970), who took the term ego state from his analyst Paul Federn, in Transactional Analysis in Psychotherapy (1961) and Games People Play (1964). It proceeds through structural, transactional, game and script analysis. Personality has three ego states . The Parent holds attitudes and behaviour copied from parents and parental figures, critical or nurturing; the Adult processes present reality objectively; the Child holds feelings and responses from childhood, free or adapted. A transaction is a stimulus from one ego state and a response from another (Figure 7.4). Complementary transactions run parallel and talk continues. Crossed ones stop it: "Where are my keys?" (Adult to Adult) answered by "Why do you always blame me?" (Child to Parent). Ulterior transactions carry a hidden message beneath the social one. Complementary: lines parallel Crossed: lines cross P A C P A C P A C P A C Person 1 Person 2 Person 1 Person 2 stimulus response Figure 7.4 Ego states (P, Parent; A, Adult; C, Child). Left: Adult to Adult and back, so talk goes on. Right: the reply comes from Child to Parent, the lines cross and communication stops. People need strokes , units of recognition, and prefer negative strokes to none. A game is a series of ulterior transactions with a predictable payoff of bad feelings, such as "Why Don't You, Yes But", in which every suggestion is rejected. A life script is an unconscious life plan decided in childhood under parental injunctions ("Don't be close", "Don't grow up", sent nonverbally from the parent's Child) and counterinjunctions ("Be perfect", "Work hard", spoken from the parent's Parent); Bob and Mary Goulding's redecision therapy helps clients revise them. Scripts rest on one of four life positions : I'm OK, you're OK (the healthy one); I'm OK, you're not OK; I'm not OK, you're OK; and I'm not OK, you're not OK, the first made famous by Thomas Harris 's best-seller I'm OK, You're OK (1969). Exam trap Injunctions, counterinjunctions, games, scripts and strokes all mean transactional analysis, not Gestalt, REBT or person-centred therapy (Sections 7.5 and 7.6). The ego state copied from parents is the Parent; "persona" is Jung's archetype, not an ego state. Supportive therapy, hypnosis, narcoanalysis and the evidence Psychodynamic work runs along a continuum from expressive (uncovering conflict by interpretation, for patients with ego strength) to supportive. Supportive psychotherapy strengthens defences instead of dismantling them, through a warm relationship, reassurance, advice, encouragement, ventilation of feelings, education and practical changes in the environment. It is the mainstay when the ego is overwhelmed: in crisis management, bereavement, acute psychosis and severe physical illness. Hypnotherapy uses hypnosis, focused attention with heightened suggestibility. It descends from Franz Anton Mesmer 's (1734 to 1815) "animal magnetism" and was named by James Braid in 1843. Today it assists the treatment of pain, habits and anxiety, but memories "recovered" under it are unreliable. Narcoanalysis gives a slow intravenous barbiturate (sodium amobarbital or thiopentone) so that a mute, stuporous or amnesic patient talks and abreacts, as in Second World War battle neuroses. It is no "truth serum": drugged people can still lie and fantasise. Indian context In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) the Supreme Court held compulsory narcoanalysis, polygraph and brain-mapping unconstitutional (Articles 20(3) and 21); they need consent, and the statements made are not admissible as evidence. Critics from Hans Eysenck (1952; Section 7.8) to the philosopher Karl Popper , who called its theory unfalsifiable, attacked psychoanalysis as unproven, long and costly. Yet meta-analyses reviewed by Jonathan Shedler (2010) show psychodynamic therapy matching other evidence-based therapies, with gains that grow after treatment ends; short-term dynamic therapy and IPT work for depression, and MBT and TFP for borderline personality disorder. Answers: (1) fundamental, (2) cathexis, (3) countertransference, (4) 12, (5) deficits, (6) crossed. 7.4 Behaviour Therapy High yield · 88 Qs A child terrified of rabbits, a woman who washes until her hands bleed, a boy with autism who cannot ask for water: behaviour therapy sees in each of them learned behaviour that can be unlearned or replaced. Building on the learning principles of Section 1.6, we trace where the approach came from, then take its techniques family by family. Origins, assumptions and functional analysis Behaviour therapy is the application of experimentally established principles of learning to the assessment and treatment of psychological problems. Its spur was a 1952 paper by Hans Jürgen Eysenck (1916 to 1997) of the Maudsley Hospital, London, which claimed that about two-thirds of neurotic patients improved within two years whether or not they had psychotherapy (the debate belongs to Section 7.8). If talking did no better than time, Eysenck argued, the clinic needed a treatment derived from learning theory, aimed at the symptom and testable. His creed was blunt: get rid of the symptom and you have eliminated the neurosis. The new therapy grew from three roots in the 1950s. In Johannesburg, Joseph Wolpe, Arnold Allan Lazarus (1932 to 2013) and Stanley Rachman worked from classical conditioning. At the Maudsley, Eysenck supplied the theory and Monte Bernard Shapiro the method of treating each patient as a single-case experiment. In the United States, Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990) and his students carried operant methods onto hospital wards and into schools, a strand later called applied behaviour analysis (ABA): operant principles, carefully measured, used to change socially important behaviour. The name behaviour therapy first appeared in a 1953 hospital report by Ogden Lindsley, Skinner and Harry Solomon, reached a journal in Lazarus's 1958 paper and was popularised by Eysenck's 1959 paper. The shared assumptions all contradicted psychoanalysis. Problem behaviour is learned by the same principles as normal behaviour and can be unlearned. The behaviour is the problem, not the symptom of a hidden conflict, so therapy aims to eliminate it and build adaptive behaviour in its place. What maintains a problem now matters more than how it began, and everything is defined and measured. Applied to anxiety, this gives the learning model of disorder , best known as the two-factor theory of O. Hobart Mowrer (1947): a fear is acquired by classical conditioning and maintained because avoiding the feared object reduces fear and is therefore negatively reinforced. Avoidance stops the person ever learning that the object is harmless, which is why exposure works. Every case starts with a functional analysis : identifying the observable events that trigger and maintain a specific problem behaviour. Its simplest form is the ABC model of Antecedents, Behaviour (defined so that two observers would agree) and Consequences; Frederick Kanfer and George Saslow (1965) expanded it into SORKC (stimulus, organism, response, contingency, consequence). After recording a baseline , the frequency, duration or intensity of the behaviour before treatment, the therapist asks what the behaviour achieves. If Arjun's tantrums at homework time get him sent to his room, they are rewarded by escape, and the "punishment" feeds them. Treatment follows the function, not the form. Exam trap Behaviour therapies apply learning principles to eliminate the unwanted behaviour ; "treat the underlying causes" is the psychodynamic aim, "improve learning and insight" that of insight therapies and "communication and social sensitivity" that of encounter groups (Section 7.7). Behaviour analysis rests on operant conditioning , not classical conditioning, modelling, cognitive learning or dream analysis. Systematic desensitisation Can a learned fear be unlearned? In 1924 Mary Cover Jones (1897 to 1987), a student of John Watson, treated Peter, a boy of almost three who was terrified of rabbits. He watched other children play happily with a rabbit (modelling), and while he ate a favourite food a caged rabbit was brought a little closer each day, never so close that he stopped eating, until he let it nibble his fingers. This is counterconditioning : attaching to a stimulus a new response that is incompatible with the old one, so that the person learns the stimulus is no longer threatening. Key study: Wolpe's cats (late 1940s) Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997), a South African psychiatrist, shocked cats in a small cage until they were too anxious to eat there even when hungry. He then fed them in a room very unlike the laboratory, then in rooms progressively more like it, and finally in the cage, until the anxiety vanished. A response incompatible with anxiety, evoked while the anxiety was weak, had eliminated it. Cats are not neurotic patients, which is why later trials with people mattered. Wolpe borrowed a term from the physiologist Charles Sherrington. Reciprocal inhibition is the principle that two incompatible responses cannot occur together, so a response antagonistic to anxiety, evoked in the presence of anxiety-provoking stimuli, suppresses the anxiety and weakens its bond to them. His main inhibitor was deep relaxation; others were assertion, sexual arousal and, in children, eating. On it he built systematic desensitisation ( Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition , 1958), which has three steps. Relaxation training. The client learns Edmund Jacobson's progressive muscle relaxation over about six sessions, practising 10 to 15 minutes twice a day. Hierarchy construction. An anxiety hierarchy ranks 10 to 20 feared situations from least to most frightening, each rated on the subjective units of distress scale (SUDS), Wolpe's self-rating from 0 (calm) to 100 (the worst imaginable), also called units of disturbance or discomfort. Desensitisation proper , the step of gradual exposure. With the client relaxed (SUDS below about 25) the therapist describes the lowest item; at any anxiety the client raises a finger and relaxation is restored. Only when an item evokes no anxiety does the client move up (Figure 7.5). Hierarchy item SUDS goal start A stray dog runs at him in a lane 100 Patting a calm dog on a lead 85 Three metres from a leashed dog 70 A leashed dog across the road 55 A dog barking nearby 40 A video of dogs playing 25 A photograph of a puppy 10 0 50 100 SUDS rating Figure 7.5 An anxiety hierarchy for Ravi, a Mysuru student bitten by a stray dog as a child. Treatment starts at the bottom and climbs only when the current item evokes no anxiety. Wolpe worked in imagination, called in vitro desensitisation (Latin, "in glass", that is, in the consulting room); in vivo desensitisation ("in life") climbs the hierarchy in real situations, which generalises better, while imagination suits fears that cannot be staged, such as flying. Gordon Paul (1966) found desensitisation better than insight therapy for fear of public speaking, but dismantling studies showed that it worked without relaxation or a strict hierarchy, never without exposure. Reciprocal inhibition is Wolpe's theory of why it works, not a proven mechanism. Exam trap Systematic desensitisation is Wolpe's (not Skinner's, Pavlov's, Watson's, Rogers's, Perls's, Beck's, Freud's or Bandura's) and rests on reciprocal inhibition , not operant extinction, shaping, the law of effect, habituation alone, generalisation, vicarious reinforcement, punishment, adaptation to stress or catharsis. Its relaxation is Jacobson's ; cognitive restructuring is not one of its steps; it treats phobia , not hallucination, delusion or depression. SUDS is keyed to desensitisation (IHBAS 2020), though all exposure therapies now use it; multimodal therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy and mindfulness-based stress reduction belong to Section 7.5. The Fear Survey Schedule (Wolpe and Peter Lang, 1964), State-Trait Anxiety Inventory and Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale are questionnaires (Chapter 2), not the hierarchy scale. Exposure, flooding and response prevention If exposure is the active ingredient, why not go straight to it? Exposure therapy is repeated or prolonged confrontation with a feared stimulus, without escape, until the fear subsides. It works through habituation , the reduction in anxiety through repeated or prolonged encounter with a stimulus, and through extinction, as the stimulus keeps appearing without the feared outcome. Exposure may be graded or intense, in vivo or imaginal. Interoceptive exposure deliberately provokes feared bodily sensations (spinning in a chair, overbreathing) in panic disorder, and virtual reality exposure uses computer-generated scenes for fears of flying, heights or combat. Flooding exposes the client at once, in real life or in imagination, to the most feared stimulus at full intensity, with no hierarchy and no relaxation, preventing escape until the anxiety peaks and subsides: the person afraid of heights stands on the balcony for as long as it takes. Implosive therapy ( Thomas Stampfl , 1966; set out with Donald Levis in 1967) is imaginal flooding with exaggerated, horrific scenes enriched with presumed psychodynamic themes; it is now rare. Both work by extinction, and both are so unpleasant that clients must choose them knowingly. Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the first-line behavioural treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Victor Meyer described it in London in 1966, and Edna Foa and colleagues refined and tested it. The client touches the "contaminated" object and is prevented from washing. The ritual brings quick relief, so it is negatively reinforced, and it stops the person learning that the anxiety would pass anyway (Figure 7.6). Blocking it allows habituation and extinction, and ERP helps more than 70 percent of patients. Foa also built prolonged exposure for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): imaginal reliving of the trauma memory plus in vivo exposure to safe but avoided reminders. Anxiety (SUDS) 100 50 0 0 30 60 90 Minutes after touching the trigger Washing: quick relief No washing: habituation Next session: lower peak Figure 7.6 Why response prevention works. Washing ends anxiety within minutes and so negatively reinforces the ritual; without it, anxiety peaks and falls by itself, and the next session peaks lower (habituation within and between sessions). A debated relative of exposure is eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR), which Francine Shapiro (1948 to 2019) developed from a 1987 observation and published in 1989, initially for PTSD. The client holds a traumatic image, its negative belief and its body sensation in mind while following the therapist's fingers back and forth; this bilateral stimulation (eye movements, taps or tones) comes in sets of about 15 to 30. Shapiro's standard protocol has eight phases , always in this order: (1) history taking, (2) preparation, (3) assessment of the target image, negative belief and distress rating, (4) desensitisation with the eye movements, (5) installation of a positive belief, (6) body scan for leftover tension, (7) closure and (8) re-evaluation at the next session. EMDR works about as well as trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy, but the eye movements seem to add little, since holding the memory in mind is itself imaginal exposure. As critics put it, what is effective in EMDR is not new, and what is new is not effective. Exam trap Flooding means full intensity with no hierarchy and no relaxation , in vivo or imaginal; pairing the feared stimulus with relaxation step by step is desensitisation, pairing it with shock is aversion therapy, and replacing irrational beliefs (Ellis) or cognitive restructuring is cognitive therapy (Section 7.5). ERP rests on habituation and extinction , not counterconditioning or reciprocal inhibition, and is first-line for OCD , not phobia, panic, depression, schizophrenia or personality disorder. EMDR is Shapiro's , for PTSD ; prolonged exposure is Foa's, cognitive processing therapy Patricia Resick's and dialectical behaviour therapy Marsha Linehan's (Section 7.5). Bessel van der Kolk researches trauma, Pat Ogden founded sensorimotor psychotherapy and Joseph LeDoux maps the brain's fear circuits. Aversion therapy, covert sensitisation and the bell and pad Counterconditioning can also run in reverse. Aversion therapy pairs an unwanted behaviour, or the stimulus that tempts it, with an unpleasant stimulus, so that by classical conditioning it loses its appeal: a nausea-inducing drug is given just before the patient tastes alcohol (chemical aversion), or a brief shock accompanies a cigarette or a deviant sexual image (electrical aversion). It has been used for alcohol use, smoking and paraphilias. It inflicts pain, loses many clients, often fades outside the clinic and was misused against homosexuality, so today it needs informed consent and is tried only after milder methods fail. Joseph Cautela (1967) moved the procedure into the imagination. In covert sensitisation the client imagines lifting a glass of whisky, then vividly imagines vomiting over himself in front of his family, then the relief of turning away; no real aversive stimulus is used. Exam trap An undesirable behaviour imagined together with an imagined unpleasant consequence is covert sensitisation (Cautela), not flooding, implosion or desensitisation. Aversion therapy works by pairing ( classical conditioning ), not by intermittent reward, ignoring the behaviour (extinction) or restructuring beliefs. The oldest classical technique is the bell-and-pad method for bed-wetting (nocturnal enuresis), built in 1938 by Orval Hobart Mowrer and Willie Mae Mowrer . Urine reaching a pad under the sheet completes a circuit and rings a bell; after repeated pairings, bladder tension alone wakes the child. Treatment takes 6 to 12 weeks, and the alarm remains first-line. Operant techniques that build behaviour Operant techniques work on consequences (the grid of reinforcement and punishment, and the schedules, are in Section 1.6). In therapy, positive reinforcement means giving something the person values immediately after a target behaviour, every time while the behaviour is new and then intermittently so that it lasts. A behaviour that never occurs must be built. Shaping is reinforcing successive approximations to a target behaviour: for a silent child with autism, first eye contact, then any sound, then "wa", then "water". Chaining links the steps of a task, such as dressing, into a sequence; in backward chaining the last step is taught first, so every practice ends in success. A prompt is an extra cue (a hint, a gesture, a guiding hand) that makes the right response likely, and fading withdraws it gradually until the natural cue alone controls the behaviour. The Premack principle of David Premack (1959) states that a more probable activity can reinforce a less probable one: video games after homework, or grandma's rule, vegetables before dessert. A token economy rewards target behaviours with tokens (points, stars, chips) that are later exchanged for backup reinforcers such as snacks or privileges. Tokens are secondary reinforcers , valued only for what they buy, and they bridge the delay between behaviour and reward. Key study: Ayllon and Azrin's token economy (1968) Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin ran a ward of chronic psychotic women at Anna State Hospital, Illinois. Tokens earned for self-care and ward jobs bought privileges such as privacy or a walk in the grounds. When tokens were handed out regardless of work, the work almost stopped; when the contingency returned, so did the work. Their book The Token Economy (1968) launched the method, though gains often fade outside the ward, and basic needs must never become backup reinforcers. Contingency management systematically arranges reinforcing consequences for target behaviours, as when clients with substance use disorders earn vouchers for drug-free urine samples. A contingency contract puts the arrangement in a signed agreement: "Ravi studies two hours each weekday; his parents allow cricket on Sunday." Exam trap The token economy is operant (secondary reinforcers), so it is the treatment NOT derived from classical conditioning; flooding, desensitisation and aversion therapy are classical. Its developers were Ayllon and Azrin ; Amity 2023 keyed Skinner, who supplied only the principles. Premack runs one way: the high -probability behaviour reinforces the low -probability one, never the reverse; it is a behaviour modification technique for children, not a theory of relationships, language or parenting. "Pleasant consequences make a behaviour likely to recur" is Thorndike's law of effect, and continuous reinforcement is the least resistant to extinction (Section 1.6). Operant techniques that reduce behaviour, and ABA To reduce a behaviour, therapists start with the least restrictive method. Extinction withholds the reinforcer that maintains a behaviour: parents who rewarded tantrums with attention now ignore them. Expect an extinction burst , a temporary rise when reinforcement stops; giving in at its peak teaches that louder tantrums pay. Both are negative punishment . Overcorrection , from Richard Foxx and Azrin (1972), requires restitution (restoring the disturbed scene to better than before) or positive practice (repeating the correct behaviour many times); it is used for aggressive, disruptive and self-stimulatory behaviour in autism and intellectual disability. In satiation a reinforcer is given so freely that it loses its value: Ayllon (1963) gave a towel-hoarding patient towels until she threw them out. Positive punishment suppresses quickly but breeds fear, aggression and avoidance and teaches nothing new, so it is a last resort, used with consent and monitoring. Combined into an intensive, data-driven programme, these methods are ABA, best known in autism. Its core is discrete trial training : a skill is broken into small units, each trial being an instruction, a prompt if needed, the child's response and an immediate consequence. In functional communication training a child whose tantrums win breaks from work learns to ask for a break with a word or a picture card instead. Key study: Lovaas's early intervention for autism (1987) Ole Ivar Lovaas (1927 to 2010) at the University of California, Los Angeles, gave 19 young children with autism 40 or more hours a week of one-to-one treatment for at least two years. Nine (47 percent) reached normal intellectual and educational functioning, against 2 percent of controls. Groups were not randomly assigned and aversives such as slaps were used, but the "Lovaas programme" became the best-known behavioural treatment for autism. Exam trap Deliberately ignoring tantrums is extinction (not generalisation or discrimination, Section 1.6). Amity 2023 keyed "operant escape", which is wrong: escape ends an unpleasant stimulus already present and avoidance prevents one (Section 1.6). Time-out and response cost are negative punishment ; negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant and increases behaviour. Overcorrection targets repetitive aggressive behaviour in autism; bed-wetting needs the bell and pad. Lovaas treated autism , not aphasia, depression or alcoholism, and a picture card to request a break is ABA , not CBT, play therapy or psychoanalysis. Modelling, assertiveness and social skills Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) turned observational learning into therapy. In live modelling the client watches a real person perform the feared or missing behaviour; in symbolic modelling the model appears on film or in a story; in participant modelling the therapist models the behaviour and then physically guides the client through it. For snake phobia (Bandura, Edward Blanchard and Brunhilde Ritter, 1969), participant modelling beat both symbolic modelling and systematic desensitisation. In behavioural rehearsal the client practises the new behaviour in role-play, with feedback, before trying it in life. Assertiveness training , pioneered by Andrew Salter ( Conditioned Reflex Therapy , 1949) and developed by Wolpe and Lazarus, teaches people to express wishes and feelings directly while respecting others. Passive behaviour surrenders one's rights (silence when someone jumps the bus queue), aggressive behaviour violates other people's (shouting abuse), and assertive behaviour defends one's own without attack ("Please join the queue; we were here first"). Social skills training teaches eye contact, conversation and refusal through instruction, modelling, rehearsal, feedback and homework, in autism, social anxiety and schizophrenia, where antipsychotic medication remains front-line. Relaxation, biofeedback and self-management Several methods teach control of one's own body. Edmund Jacobson 's progressive muscle relaxation (1929, enlarged in 1938) tenses and releases muscle groups in turn; Johannes Heinrich Schultz 's autogenic training (1932) uses self-suggestions of heaviness and warmth; breathing retraining slows the overbreathing of panic; and the applied relaxation of Lars-Göran Öst (1987) trains rapid relaxation on cue, used at the first sign of anxiety in panic, generalised anxiety and phobias. Biofeedback makes a bodily process the person cannot normally sense visible or audible, so that he can learn to control it. Its basis was Neal Miller 's 1960s report that rats could change heart rate and other autonomic responses through operant conditioning: the autonomic nervous system could come under voluntary control. Electromyographic (EMG) feedback of muscle tension treats tension-type headache and back pain, thermal feedback of hand temperature treats migraine and Raynaud's disease, and EEG neurofeedback of brain waves is used for ADHD and epilepsy. An early device was the perineometer of Arnold Kegel (1948), a pressure gauge that let a patient watch her pelvic floor squeeze. Habit reversal training (HRT), from Azrin and Gregory Nunn (1973), is the treatment of choice for tics and habits such as hair pulling and nail biting. Awareness training teaches the client to detect each occurrence and the urge before it; competing response training teaches a response physically incompatible with the habit, inconspicuous and held for about a minute or until the urge passes (clenching the fists against hair pulling); motivation comes from reviewing the habit's costs and from family praise. A variant, regulated breathing, was applied to stuttering. In negative practice (massed practice), proposed by Knight Dunlap (1932), the habit is performed deliberately and repeatedly until fatigue makes it aversive. Thought stopping , popularised by Wolpe, interrupts an unwanted thought with "Stop!", first shouted, later silent; it has faded because suppressed thoughts rebound. Self-monitoring , the systematic recording of one's own target behaviour, often changes that behaviour before treatment begins; this reactivity spoils the baseline but helps therapy. In self-reinforcement the client rewards himself on meeting his own goal, completing Kanfer's sequence of self-monitoring, self-evaluation and self-reinforcement. Behavioural activation (BA) treats depression by re-engaging clients in meaningful, rewarding activities. Peter Lewinsohn proposed in the 1970s that depression follows a loss of response-contingent positive reinforcement. Neil Jacobson and colleagues (1996) found the activation component of cognitive therapy as effective as the whole package, and Jacobson and Christopher Martell developed BA in its own right: activity monitoring, scheduling and graded tasks that replace avoidance. For insomnia, stimulus control ( Richard Bootzin , 1972) re-links the bed with sleep: bed only when sleepy and only for sleep and sex, leave it if not asleep within about 10 to 20 minutes, a fixed rising time and no naps. Sleep restriction ( Arthur Spielman , 1987) limits time in bed to the time actually slept, extending it as sleep consolidates. Paradoxical intention , from the logotherapist Viktor Frankl (Section 7.6), asks the person to do or wish for the very thing he fears: the insomniac tries hard to stay awake, which removes the performance anxiety that kept him awake. Frankl's dereflection instead turns attention away from the symptom. Exam trap Operant control of autonomic functions is biofeedback , not hypnosis (Section 1.5), sublimation (a defence mechanism) or desensitisation; EMG feedback suits tension-type headache , and Kegel's perineometer was early biofeedback. Repeating a habit to fatigue is negative practice , not the competing response of habit reversal. HRT is for tics ; OCD needs ERP. Doing or wishing the opposite of the goal is paradoxical intention , not stimulus control, sleep restriction, dereflection, negative practice or reciprocal inhibition. Behavioural activation means engaging in meaningful activity , not analysing childhood, relaxation or hypnosis. Parents, classrooms and an evaluation Gerald Patterson of the Oregon Social Learning Center described a coercive cycle at home: a parent makes a demand, the child whines or hits, the parent gives in (negatively reinforcing the aggression) and the child stops (negatively reinforcing the surrender). Parent management training (PMT) teaches parents to give clear commands, attend to and praise good behaviour, reward it with points or stickers, ignore minor misbehaviour, and use brief time-out or loss of privileges for serious misbehaviour; negative reinforcement is what it removes, not what it teaches. Classroom management applies the same principles at school: clear rules, praise, planned ignoring, token systems, daily report cards and group contingencies such as the Good Behaviour Game. Behaviour therapy is a first choice for specific phobias, OCD, panic, enuresis, tics and habits, insomnia, conduct problems and skills in autism, and behavioural activation rivals cognitive therapy for depression; in psychosis and personality disorder it is an adjunct. Psychoanalysts predicted symptom substitution : remove a symptom without resolving its underlying conflict and another will take its place. Follow-ups from Paul's 1966 trial onwards found little sign of it. Aversive methods raise the sharpest ethical questions: they demand informed consent, the least restrictive alternative first, supervision and special protection for children and institutionalised patients. One is disappointed and studies her mistakes; the other decides he was never good enough and stops opening his books. Same event, opposite reactions: what differed was what each made of the score. That observation underlies every therapy in this section, from the founders, Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck, to the "third wave", which asks clients not to argue with their thoughts but to change their relationship with them. The cognitive turn and the three waves The term cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) covers a family of treatments that share three propositions: thinking affects emotion and behaviour; thinking can be monitored and changed; and changing maladaptive thought patterns relieves distress, even when the events that triggered it cannot be changed. The idea is old. The Stoic philosopher Epictetus (about 50 to 135 CE) wrote that people are disturbed not by things but by the views they take of them. In the 1950s and 1960s two therapists, Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck, independently concluded that faulty thinking drives emotional disturbance, and both are counted as founders of the cognitive tradition. Behaviour therapists (Section 7.4) joined them in the 1970s; Donald Meichenbaum's Cognitive-Behavior Modification (1977) gave the hybrid its name. Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021) supplied a bridge in 1977 with self-efficacy , a person's belief that he or she can carry out the actions a situation demands. He argued that all effective treatments work largely by raising it, which made self-efficacy the classic cognitive-behavioural explanation of how people change. In 2004 Steven C. Hayes (born 1948) described three waves. The first, behaviour therapy (1950s onwards), applied learning principles to behaviour. The second, the cognitive therapies of Ellis and Beck, changed the content of thoughts from irrational or distorted to realistic. The third wave (from the 1990s: dialectical behaviour therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, and compassion-focused, metacognitive and functional analytic therapies) changes a person's relationship to thoughts and feelings: noticing and accepting them while acting on one's values. All CBTs are time-limited, focused on present problems, structured, collaborative and educational; they rely on homework and measure symptoms throughout. Exam trap "Third-wave CBT includes all EXCEPT": psychoanalysis (Section 7.3), which belongs to no wave. REBT and Beck's therapy are second wave; token economies are first wave. Self-efficacy is Bandura 's concept, not Beck's, Ellis's or Skinner's (Skinner rejected cognitive explanations). Ellis's rational emotive behaviour therapy Albert Ellis (1913 to 2007) treated his own shyness first: as a young man he made himself talk to a hundred women in New York's Bronx Botanical Garden in one month, and learned that rejection was unpleasant, not terrible. After a PhD at Columbia University (1947) he practised psychoanalysis until about 1953, frustrated that insight rarely made patients better. Drawing on Stoic philosophy, he began rational therapy in 1955; it became rational-emotive therapy (RET) and, in 1993, rational emotive behaviour therapy (REBT), a name that acknowledged its behavioural homework. His Reason and Emotion in Psychotherapy (1962) is the classic text, and REBT is usually called the first cognitive-behavioural therapy. Its core is the ABC model : A , the activating event; B , the person's beliefs about A; C , the emotional and behavioural consequences. Common sense says A causes C; Ellis says A contributes, but B is the main cause. The two students shared an A, but "one mock does not decide my future" produced disappointment and study, while "I must score well, or I'm a failure" produced depression and avoidance (Figure 7.7). A rational belief is a flexible preference that fits reality, follows logically and serves the person's goals; an irrational belief is a rigid, absolute demand. A rational belief about a real loss still produces a healthy negative emotion (sadness, concern), whereas an irrational one produces an unhealthy emotion (depression, anxiety). Common-sense view: A causes C A: Activating event Scored 48 of 90 on a mock test B: Belief "I must do well; I am a total failure" C: Consequence Depression; stops studying D: Disputing the belief Logical: does it follow? Empirical: where is the proof? Pragmatic: does it help me? E: Effective belief "I'd prefer to pass; I can stand failing" F: sadness, not despair Ellis's chain Common sense Figure 7.7 Ellis's ABC model extended to D (disputing), E (an effective new philosophy) and F (new feelings and behaviour). The dashed arrow is the common-sense view that events cause feelings directly; Ellis's chain runs through the belief. Irrational thinking takes four forms. The root is demandingness, turning preferences into musts, shoulds and oughts, which Ellis called musturbation (also spelt musterbation). From it follow awfulising (rating a setback as more than 100 percent bad, close to Beck's catastrophising), low frustration tolerance ("I can't stand it") and global rating of self or others ("I failed, so I am a failure"). Ellis's three major musts concern the self ("I must do well and win approval, or I am no good"), others ("Others must treat me fairly, or they are rotten") and the world ("Life must give me what I want, quickly and easily"). They breed, respectively, anxiety and depression, anger and rage, and self-pity and procrastination. The active ingredient is D, disputing the irrational belief. A logical dispute asks whether it follows ("You want to pass; why must you?"), an empirical dispute asks for evidence ("Where is the proof that you are a total failure?") and a pragmatic dispute asks whether it helps ("Where does this belief get you?"). Success yields E, an effective new philosophy, and F, new feelings and behaviour. The antidote to global rating is unconditional self-acceptance : one's acts can be rated, one's whole self cannot. Ellis extended it to others and to life; unlike Carl Rogers (Section 7.6), he thought therapist warmth unnecessary, and his style was famously blunt. REBT mixes cognitive techniques (disputing, self-help forms, reading), emotive techniques and behavioural homework set at almost every session (in vivo exposure, rewards and penalties). In rational emotive imagery , adopted from the psychiatrist Maxie C. Maultsby Jr. , the client imagines the activating event, feels the unhealthy emotion, changes it to its healthy counterpart and notes the self-statement that did it. In a shame-attacking exercise the client does something harmless but embarrassing in public (Ellis's example was calling out station names in a subway train) to learn that disapproval is bearable. REBT is clear, brief and teachable, but its evidence is thinner than Beck's: a 1991 meta-analysis of 70 studies found it better than control groups and baseline, and a 2008 trial found it comparable with cognitive therapy and medication for depression. Its chief criticism is that it can be direct and confrontational, so clients may find it intimidating; the therapist's idea of "rational" may also impose his own values, and its philosophical claims are hard to test. A focus on sexuality is a criticism of Freud, not of Ellis. Exam trap ABC stands for activating event, beliefs, consequences: B is the belief about the activating event , not behaviour, baseline, bias or "beliefs about oneself", and C is the consequence of that belief, not "critical analysis". D = disputing , not desensitisation, drama or "discuss"; E = effective new philosophy. The behavioural ABC of antecedent, behaviour, consequence is functional analysis (Section 7.4), and affect, behaviour, cognition is the ABC of attitudes (Chapter 3). Musts, musturbation and shame attacking signal Ellis, not Freud, William James, Rogers, Adler, Beck, DBT or Glasser's reality therapy (Section 7.6). Beck's cognitive model and the distortions Aaron Temkin Beck (1921 to 2021), a psychoanalytically trained psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania, noticed in the late 1950s that his patients had a second, barely noticed stream of quick, believable, self-critical thoughts ("He won't like me") that came before their feelings. He called them automatic thoughts . Depressed patients' dreams, expected to show anger turned inward, showed loss and defeat instead. Beck set out the model in Depression (1967) and the treatment in Cognitive Therapy of Depression (1979, with colleagues). He built cognitive therapy for depression and later extended it to anxiety, personality disorders, substance use and psychosis. At its centre is the cognitive triad : negative views of the self ("I am worthless"), the world or current experience ("everything is against me") and the future ("it will never get better"). Remember it as self, world, future: not past, present, future; not self, others, environment; not the thoughts, feelings and behaviours that CBT links in its cognitive model; and not id, ego and superego. Cognition runs on three levels. The deepest are core beliefs , or schemas: rigid, global beliefs formed in childhood ("I am unlovable"). From them grow intermediate beliefs , also called dysfunctional assumptions: the rules, attitudes and assumptions that follow ("If I am not perfect, I will be rejected"). When a situation activates these, automatic thoughts appear and drive emotion and behaviour. A dormant schema can be woken by a critical incident such as a loss, so the model is a diathesis-stress one. Beck's daughter Judith S. Beck laid out these levels in Cognitive Therapy: Basics and Beyond (1995). Negative thinking is kept going by cognitive distortions , systematic errors in processing information. Beck named arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralisation, magnification and minimisation, personalisation and dichotomous thinking; the psychiatrist David D. Burns popularised the rest of Table 7.12 in Feeling Good (1980). Table 7.12 The cognitive distortions, with an example of each. Distortion What happens Example Arbitrary inference A conclusion without evidence A friend does not greet you: "He dislikes me now" Selective abstraction (mental filter) One detail taken out of context, the rest ignored A teacher sees two bored students: "My class dislikes me" Overgeneralisation A broad rule from one or a few events "I failed statistics, so I fail at everything" Magnification and minimisation Faults enlarged, strengths shrunk One slip "ruins" the talk; praise "means nothing" Personalisation Blaming oneself for events one did not cause "The guests left early because of me" Dichotomous (all-or-nothing) thinking Only two extremes "If I don't top the exam, I have failed" Labelling A global label for one act "I'm a loser", not "I made a mistake" Mind reading Assuming one knows what others think "She thinks I'm stupid" Fortune telling Predicting a bad outcome "I'll freeze in the interview" Emotional reasoning A feeling taken as proof "I feel useless, so I am useless" Should statements Rigid rules for self and others "I should never make mistakes" Catastrophising Expecting the worst to happen "If I fail this exam, my life is over" Disqualifying the positive Good events "don't count" "They praised me only to be polite" Exam trap A man whose friend fails to acknowledge him and who concludes "he doesn't like me any more" shows arbitrary inference ; mind reading and fortune telling are later, narrower names for such jumps, so choose arbitrary inference when they are not offered. Selective abstraction , also called selective attention or the mental filter, is fixing on one detail and ignoring the whole, like the teacher with two bored students; overgeneralisation is a broad rule from a few events. Catastrophising is worrying that the worst will always happen; all-or-nothing thinking is extreme categories; personalisation is taking things personally. Cognitive therapy in practice Cognitive therapy treats thoughts as hypotheses to be tested, not facts to be argued away. In collaborative empiricism therapist and client investigate together, making objective assessments of beliefs against evidence. The main method is Socratic questioning , or guided discovery: open questions that help the client discover and attend to previously overlooked information, so that the discovery is the client's own rather than an interpretation from the therapist ("What is the evidence? How else could you see it? If it were true, what would it mean?"). The therapist neither interprets nor tells the client what to think. Collaborative empiricism, Socratic dialogue and guided discovery are the approach's fundamental concepts; free association and dream analysis belong to psychoanalysis (Section 7.3). The dysfunctional thought record (1979) has columns for the situation, the emotion (rated 0 to 100), the automatic thought, a balanced response and the outcome; with it clients learn to identify, examine and restructure their own automatic thoughts. Behavioural experiments test predictions in real life ("If I speak in class, everyone will laugh"). Activity scheduling plans the week and rates each activity for mastery and pleasure; graded task assignment breaks a daunting task into small steps so that success comes early. The downward arrow technique asks repeatedly "If that were true, what would it mean to you?" to descend from an automatic thought to the core belief. Decatastrophising (the "what if" technique) weighs how likely and how bad the feared outcome is and how the client would cope; reattribution spreads responsibility fairly when the client blames himself for everything. A session runs in a set order: mood check, bridge from the last session, agenda, homework review, work on the agenda, new homework, then summary and feedback. Progress is measured with Beck's scales: the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI, 1961; BDI-II, 1996), the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI, 1988) and the Beck Hopelessness Scale (BHS, 1974), described in Chapter 2. Exam trap The BDI and BAI are self-report ; the Hamilton depression and anxiety scales of Max Hamilton are clinician-rated . So "Which is clinician-rated?" is the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, not "both". The downward arrow is not a 0 to 10 distress rating or an exposure hierarchy (Section 7.4). Ellis and Beck share the central assumption that emotional disturbance arises mainly from how people think about events, not from the events themselves, and both therapies are active, brief and built on homework. His self-instructional training , first used with impulsive children in 1971, moves guidance inward in five steps: the therapist performs the task while talking aloud; the child performs it while the therapist instructs aloud; then the child instructs himself aloud, then in a whisper, then silently. His stress inoculation training , named after vaccination, builds resistance by coping with manageable doses of stress, in three phases: conceptualisation (how appraisals and self-talk create stress), skills acquisition and rehearsal (relaxation, cognitive restructuring, problem solving, coping self-statements) and application and follow-through (practice in imagery, role-play and real life, with relapse prevention). Problem-solving therapy , introduced by Thomas J. D'Zurilla and Marvin R. Goldfried (1971) and extended to depression by Arthur M. Nezu , teaches a positive problem orientation and a sequence: define the problem, brainstorm alternatives, choose one, act and check the result. Arnold A. Lazarus (1932 to 2013) built multimodal therapy , which assesses the BASIC I.D. (Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal relationships, Drugs and biology) and borrows techniques from any school (technical eclecticism, Section 7.8). In fixed-role therapy , from the personal construct theory (1955) of George Alexander Kelly (1905 to 1967), the client lives for about two weeks as a new character sketched by the therapist, to try out new constructs and new relationships. For clients who failed standard CBT, especially those with personality disorders, Jeffrey E. Young developed schema therapy (1990). It targets 18 early maladaptive schemas, enduring themes such as abandonment, mistrust, defectiveness and unrelenting standards, formed when childhood needs went unmet, and schema modes, the states a person switches between (vulnerable child, angry child, punitive parent, detached protector, healthy adult). Its signature is limited reparenting , meeting some unmet childhood needs within professional limits, with imagery rescripting and chair work. Anthony Ryle 's cognitive analytic therapy (CAT, Britain, 1980s) is a brief therapy, often 16 sessions, joining cognitive therapy to psychoanalytic object relations through a reformulation letter and a diagram of the client's reciprocal roles. Exam trap Fixed-role therapy is George Kelly 's, not Beck's, Ellis's or Fritz Perls's; BASIC I.D. is Lazarus 's; schema therapy, with its schema modes and limited reparenting, is Jeffrey Young 's, not DBT's. Disorder-specific CBT: panic, social anxiety, trauma, psychosis Beck's cognitive specificity hypothesis (each disorder has its own theme: loss in depression, danger in anxiety) led to disorder-specific models. Panic. David M. Clark (1986) traced panic attacks to the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations: a racing heart read as a heart attack raises anxiety, which intensifies the sensations, in a vicious circle. Paul M. Salkovskis (1991) added safety behaviours , such as gripping a shopping trolley or sitting down, which seem to avert disaster but stop the client learning that it would not have happened. Treatment provokes the feared sensations and gradually drops safety behaviours, as experiments that test the catastrophic beliefs. In the model of social anxiety by Clark and Adrian Wells (1995), self-focused attention and safety behaviours maintain the fear; effective CBT for social phobia combines exposure, cognitive restructuring and social skills training. Trauma. Prolonged exposure (PE), developed by Edna B. Foa , combines imaginal exposure (repeatedly retelling the trauma) with in vivo exposure to avoided but safe reminders. Cognitive processing therapy (CPT), developed by Patricia A. Resick for rape survivors, challenges "stuck points" about blame, safety, trust, power, esteem and intimacy. Trauma-focused CBT (TF-CBT) for children, by Judith A. Cohen , Anthony P. Mannarino and Esther Deblinger , teaches coping skills first; its central aim is to build and process the trauma narrative and so desensitise the traumatic memories. With eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) of Francine Shapiro (Section 7.4), these are the first-line trauma treatments. Exam trap PE comes from Edna Foa and colleagues , CPT from Resick , EMDR from Shapiro , DBT from Linehan. For survivors of sexual assault, pick the option naming trauma-focused CBT and EMDR (psychodynamic therapy is also commonly used, with less evidence); DBT, ACT, mindfulness-based therapy and interpersonal psychotherapy (Section 7.3) are not trauma-focused treatments. In panic, safety behaviours are dropped, never prescribed. Psychosis. CBT for psychosis (CBTp), developed in Britain in the 1990s by David Kingdon , Douglas Turkington and others, normalises unusual experiences, tests delusional beliefs collaboratively and teaches ways of coping with voices. It is an adjunct, not an alternative: antipsychotic medication remains the front-line treatment for schizophrenia (Chapter 8), with CBTp, social skills training and stress management as psychosocial add-ons. Dialectical behaviour therapy Marsha M. Linehan (born 1943) developed dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT; manuals 1993) for chronically suicidal women, most with borderline personality disorder (BPD; Chapter 8). Standard CBT's constant push for change felt invalidating to them and they dropped out, yet acceptance alone left the self-harm untouched. DBT's dialectic synthesises the two: full acceptance of the client together with a firm push for change. The acceptance side, including core mindfulness, came from Zen Buddhism, which Linehan practised; the change side came from behaviour therapy. Her biosocial theory sees BPD as pervasive emotion dysregulation arising when a biological emotional vulnerability (high sensitivity and reactivity, slow return to baseline) meets an invalidating environment that dismisses or punishes the child's emotions. Standard DBT has four modes: individual therapy, a weekly skills group (usually for a year), telephone coaching in crises and a therapist consultation team. Individual work targets life-threatening behaviour first, then therapy-interfering and then quality-of-life-interfering behaviour. The four skills modules are core mindfulness (observing without judgement and finding "wise mind" between reasonable mind and emotion mind), distress tolerance (surviving crises through distraction, self-soothing and radical acceptance), emotion regulation (naming emotions, acting opposite to unhelpful urges) and interpersonal effectiveness (asking and refusing while keeping relationships and self-respect). Key study: Linehan's DBT trials (1991 and 2006) Linehan and colleagues randomly assigned chronically parasuicidal women with BPD to a year of DBT or treatment as usual; the DBT group made fewer and less medically serious parasuicidal acts, spent fewer days in hospital and dropped out less (1991). Critics cited the small sample and weak control, so in 2006 Linehan compared DBT with treatment by community experts in psychotherapy, and DBT still halved suicide attempts. Exam trap DBT is Marsha Linehan's. Its four skills modules are mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness; cognitive restructuring and relaxation are not among them. Family genogram construction is a Bowen technique (Section 7.7), not a DBT mode. DBT's mindfulness is Zen, not Stoic. DBT was built for borderline personality disorder with chronic suicidality, not for schizophrenia, phobias or OCD. ACT, mindfulness and the rest of the third wave Hayes, with Kirk D. Strosahl and Kelly G. Wilson , developed acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT, said as the word "act"; their book appeared in 1999). It rests on relational frame theory , Hayes's account of language: because humans relate events to one another through words, a thought carries the sting of what it stands for, so remembering a failure hurts like failing. The usual response, experiential avoidance (trying to escape unwanted thoughts and feelings), backfires and narrows life. ACT therefore aims not at symptom elimination but at psychological flexibility , acting on one's values with whatever thoughts and feelings are present. It builds flexibility through the six processes of the hexaflex (Figure 7.8): acceptance, cognitive defusion (seeing thoughts as words, as in "I'm having the thought that I'm a failure"), contact with the present moment, self-as-context (the observing self), values and committed action. Psychological flexibility Acceptance open up to feelings Present moment be here now Values know what matters Committed action do what it takes Self-as-context the observing self Cognitive defusion thoughts are words Figure 7.8 The hexaflex of acceptance and commitment therapy. Each process has an opposite that produces inflexibility: experiential avoidance, cognitive fusion, living in the past or future, attachment to a conceptualised self, unclear values, and inaction or impulsivity. Jon Kabat-Zinn (born 1944) brought mindfulness (attention paid on purpose, in the present moment and non-judgementally) into medicine with mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR), founded in 1979 at the University of Massachusetts Medical School: an eight-week group course of body scan, meditation and gentle yoga for chronic pain and stress. Zindel V. Segal , J. Mark G. Williams and John D. Teasdale merged it with cognitive therapy as mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT; 2002), an eight-week group for recovered patients designed to prevent relapse in recurrent major depression by teaching decentering: seeing thoughts as passing mental events, not facts. Key study: MBCT and depressive relapse (Teasdale and colleagues, 2000) Recovered patients with recurrent depression were randomly assigned to usual treatment or usual treatment plus MBCT and followed for 60 weeks. For those with three or more past episodes, relapse fell from 66 to 37 percent; for those with two, MBCT made no difference. MBCT is a relapse-prevention treatment, not a treatment for acute illness. Compassion-focused therapy (CFT) of Paul Gilbert , built for shame and self-criticism, describes three emotion-regulation systems: threat (protection, anxiety, anger), drive (seeking resources and achievement) and soothing (contentment, safeness, affiliation); compassionate mind training strengthens the soothing system, which self-critical people lack. Metacognitive therapy (MCT) of Adrian Wells targets not what people think but how they respond to thinking. Its central concept, the cognitive attentional syndrome , is persistent worry and rumination, threat monitoring and unhelpful coping (thought suppression, avoidance), driven by metacognitive beliefs such as "Worrying helps me cope" and "My worry is uncontrollable"; attention training and detached mindfulness loosen it. Functional analytic psychotherapy (FAP) of Robert J. Kohlenberg and Mavis Tsai (1991) uses the therapy relationship itself: the client's problem behaviours and improvements appear in session, and the therapist naturally reinforces the improvements. Behavioural activation grew from Peter M. Lewinsohn 's view that depression follows a loss of response-contingent positive reinforcement; when Neil S. Jacobson and colleagues (1996) found that the activation component of Beck's therapy worked as well as the whole package, scheduling valued activity and tackling avoidance became a treatment in its own right (Section 7.4). Exam trap ACT comes from Steven Hayes and colleagues, not Linehan, Beck or Ellis. Its hexaflex (acceptance, defusion, present moment, self-as-context, values, committed action) is not DBT's list of skills, and ACT aims at psychological flexibility through six core processes, not symptom elimination, insight into childhood conflicts or disputing beliefs. MBSR is Kabat-Zinn's; MBCT prevents depressive relapse and is not a treatment for acute psychosis or phobias. How well does CBT work? CBT is the most researched psychotherapy. A 2006 review of 16 meta-analyses, co-authored by Beck, found large effects for depression, generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social phobia, post-traumatic stress disorder and childhood depression and anxiety. CBT is first-line for most anxiety disorders and for depression, where it matches antidepressants and better protects against relapse after treatment ends; it is also first-line for bulimia nervosa and insomnia, and an adjunct to medication in bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. Its methods travel: in Goa, lay counsellors delivering behavioural activation helped depressed primary-care patients in a 2017 trial led by Vikram Patel . It has limits. Many clients do not fully recover or later relapse; trial samples are more selected than clinic patients; it needs literacy and homework; critics say it neglects social causes such as poverty and assumes a Western, individualist outlook; and against other well-conducted therapies the differences are often small (Section 7.8). Computerised and internet-delivered CBT (iCBT), such as Beating the Blues in Britain and MoodGYM in Australia, delivers modules, thought records and homework on screen. Guided versions approach the results of face-to-face therapy, whereas unguided ones lose many users. It suits stepped care, in which low-intensity help comes first (telepsychology in India, Section 7.10). Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Asking "If that were true, what would it mean to you?" to reach a core belief is the technique.
