Answers: (1) 1993, (2) disputing, (3) triad, (4) arbitrary inference, (5) downward arrow, (6) application and follow-through, (7) biosocial, (8) flexibility. 7.6 Humanistic, Existential, Experiential and Brief Therapies High yield · 49 Qs By the 1950s psychotherapy had two systems: psychoanalysis (Section 7.3) and behaviourism (Section 7.4). Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970) called the movement against both the third force . Its core, humanistic psychology, studies the whole person from his or her own viewpoint and assumes an inborn drive toward growth; Maslow (Chapter 4) and Carl Rogers, who built the therapy, were its leading proponents. Existential therapists share its respect for freedom but make the person face death, isolation and meaninglessness; experiential therapists work with feeling as it happens in the session. Together these humanistic-experiential psychotherapies aim to promote a more fluid and integrated organisation of the self, not to resolve deep-seated conflicts (the psychodynamic aim), change maladaptive behaviours (the behavioural aim) or train interpersonal skills. Rogers: the self, conditions of worth and incongruence Carl Ransom Rogers (1902 to 1987) gave his therapy three names: non-directive therapy in Counseling and Psychotherapy (1942), because the counsellor does not advise, interpret or steer; client-centred therapy in Client-Centered Therapy (1951), which added a theory of personality; and the person-centred approach from the 1970s. A "client", unlike a patient, keeps responsibility for his or her own life. The theory starts from the actualising tendency , the inborn tendency of every organism to develop its capacities in ways that maintain and enhance it (not Maslow's self-actualisation). Infants judge experience by an organismic valuing process : food is good when hungry, pain is bad. Part of experience becomes the self-concept, the organised picture of "I" and "me", beside an ideal self, the self one would like to be. With the self comes a need for positive regard, and parents rarely give it without strings ("we love you when you top the class"). The child introjects these rules as conditions of worth and starts valuing experience by whether it earns approval. The result is incongruence , a mismatch between self-concept and experience: a split between the organismic valuing process and a self burdened by conditions of worth, felt as tension, anxiety and confusion. Ananya, raised as "the doctor of the family", comes alive only when she draws, so she distorts the experience ("I am just tired") or denies it awareness (Figure 7.9). Rogers's 19 propositions (1951) state the theory: behaviour follows the world as perceived (the phenomenal field), and experience inconsistent with the self is denied or distorted until, in complete safety, it can be admitted. Growth heads toward the fully functioning person , a direction rather than a state: open to experience, living fully in each moment, trusting his or her own organism, free and creative. Incongruence (before therapy) Greater congruence (after therapy) Self- concept Experience overlap = congruence (small) much experience denied or distorted congruence Self- concept Experience experience admitted to awareness and the self-concept enlarged to fit it Figure 7.9 Rogers's model of incongruence. The overlap of self-concept and actual experience is the area of congruence; therapy enlarges it by letting denied and distorted experience into awareness. Exam trap "A split between the organismic valuing process and a self-concept burdened by conditions of worth" is incongruence . Introjection is how conditions of worth get in, conflict has no special place in the theory, and the actualising tendency is the growth force that incongruence blocks. The core conditions and person-centred practice The cure, then, is a relationship without conditions of worth. In a 1957 paper Rogers listed six necessary and sufficient conditions of personality change: (1) two persons are in psychological contact; (2) the client is incongruent, vulnerable or anxious; (3) the therapist is congruent; (4) the therapist feels unconditional positive regard; (5) the therapist empathically understands the client's internal frame of reference and communicates this; (6) the client perceives this empathy and regard, at least minimally. "Necessary and sufficient" means no change without them and nothing more needed. Conditions 3 to 5 are the three core conditions (Table 7.14): unconditional positive regard , a term coined in 1954 by Rogers's student Stanley Standal ; congruence , which Rogers later called the most basic; and empathy. Table 7.14 Rogers's three core conditions. Core condition Also called What it means What it is not Congruence Genuineness, realness Feelings, awareness and words match; no façade Disclosing every feeling; playing the expert Unconditional positive regard Acceptance, prizing, warmth Valuing the person without conditions of worth Approving every act; praise; reassurance Accurate empathic understanding Empathy Sensing the client's world "as if" one's own, never losing the "as if", and saying so Sympathy; identification; interpretation The therapist responds from inside the client's frame of reference, above all by reflection of feeling : putting into words the feeling the client is expressing and offering it back to be checked. To "I am not sure this course is mine", advice ("Talk to your parents") directs and analysis ("Perhaps you resent your father") imposes theory; a reflection ("You doubt whether this course is really yours") stays with the client's meaning. Interpretation, advice, diagnosis, testing and aversive conditioning (Section 7.4) have no place. Exam trap The core conditions are empathy, unconditional positive regard and congruence ("all of the above" when all three are listed). Interpretation, transference and free association are psychoanalytic; reinforcement and shaping are behavioural; disputation and homework belong to Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck (Section 7.5); confrontation and paradoxical intention belong to Gestalt therapy and logotherapy. Edward Bordin's working alliance (1979: goals, tasks and bond; Section 7.8) is not Rogerian; person-centred therapy is the approach least likely to use the term, preferring the "real relationship" and the core conditions. Key study: the Q-sort and the self-ideal gap (Chicago, 1954) Question. Does therapy bring the perceived self closer to the ideal self? Method. The Q-sort was devised by the British psychologist William Stephenson ( The Study of Behavior , 1953) and adapted by Rogers's group. A person sorts about 100 self-statements ("I am a submissive person") from "most like me" to "least like me" into a forced, roughly normal distribution, once for the real and once for the ideal self; correlating the sorts captures within-person variation. Results. For John Butler and Gerard Haigh's clients (1954) the mean self-ideal correlation rose from about zero (minus .01) before therapy to .34 after it, and stood at .31 at follow-up. Criticism. Falling ideals or learning the "healthy" answer could shrink the gap; samples were small. Using rating scales of empathy, warmth and genuineness, Charles Truax and Robert Carkhuff (1967) found that clients of high-scoring therapists improved more. The conditions help in every therapy (Section 7.8) but are rarely sufficient: a severe phobia still needs exposure. Rogers also championed the encounter group ( Carl Rogers on Encounter Groups , 1970): a small, loosely structured group whose principal role is personal growth and self-change through self-disclosure and honest feedback, not socialising, team building or diagnosis. Kurt Lewin's T-groups and other group formats are in Section 7.7. Gestalt therapy Fritz Perls (1893 to 1970), a German-born psychoanalyst, founded Gestalt therapy with his wife Laura Perls and the writer Paul Goodman ; the founding book, Gestalt Therapy (1951), was by Perls, Ralph Hefferline and Goodman, and Perls's workshops at the Esalen Institute (1964 to 1969) made it famous. Therapy stays in the here and now. Its goal is awareness of what one is doing and feeling, and how, not why; with awareness comes responsibility, so clients say "I won't" rather than "I can't". Needs organise experience as figure and ground : the most pressing need stands out, is met and recedes. A feeling never expressed and completed (an unsaid goodbye to a dead parent) remains as unfinished business , an incomplete gestalt that intrudes on the present. Health needs good contact at the boundary between self and environment. Perls, Hefferline and Goodman's five disturbances of contact ended with egotism; the five of Erving and Miriam Polster (1973), the list most textbooks use, drop egotism and add deflection (Table 7.15). Table 7.15 The contact boundary disturbances of Gestalt therapy. Disturbance What happens Example Introjection Swallowing others' views whole, undigested "Good girls never get angry", held as one's own rule Projection Disowning a part of oneself by placing it in others Blaming the professor for an exam one did not study for Retroflection Doing to oneself what one wants to do to others Biting one's nails instead of expressing anger Deflection Turning aside from direct contact Joking, vagueness, talking about someone instead of to them Confluence Self-other boundary blurred; a high need for acceptance and liking leads to enmeshment "We feel exactly the same about everything" Egotism Excessive self-monitoring; watching oneself instead of engaging Judging every sentence while talking The techniques are experiments in awareness. In the empty chair technique the client speaks to an absent person, or a part of the self, imagined in an empty chair, often switching seats to reply: the classic way to finish unfinished business. In the two-chair technique each side of an inner split gets a chair, typically the top dog (the righteous "you should" voice) and the underdog (the apologetic voice that wins by stalling). On the hot seat one workshop member worked with Perls while the group watched. In dream work every person and object in a dream is a projection of a disowned part of the dreamer, so the client speaks as each part, in the present tense, instead of having the dream interpreted. The Gestalt prayer (1969) begins: "I do my thing and you do your thing. I am not in this world to live up to your expectations." Exam trap Gestalt therapy is not Gestalt psychology, the perception school of Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka (Chapter 1), which rejected Perls's borrowing of its terms. The empty chair always means Gestalt therapy, never person-centred therapy, CBT, REBT, dialectical behaviour therapy, psychoanalysis or Bowen's family systems therapy, though emotion-focused therapy later borrowed it. Existential therapy and logotherapy Existential therapy is more a view of life than a set of techniques. Its chief philosophical source is Martin Heidegger , whose Being and Time (1927) described human existence as Dasein ("being there"), a being-in-the-world: a person is never a thing apart from a world. It begins from the existential givens, which Irvin Yalom (born 1931) named in Existential Psychotherapy (1980) as four ultimate concerns : death, freedom (with its responsibility), isolation and meaninglessness. Anxiety about them is normal; trouble starts when people flee it into inauthentic living, and the therapist helps the client face the givens and choose. The Swiss psychiatrists Ludwig Binswanger (1881 to 1966) and Medard Boss (1903 to 1990; Psychoanalysis and Daseinsanalysis , 1963) applied Heidegger to psychiatry as Daseinsanalysis. Binswanger described three simultaneous modes of being-in-the-world: the Umwelt (world around: body, drives and physical environment), the Mitwelt (with-world: relationships with others) and the Eigenwelt (own-world: one's relation to oneself); Emmy van Deurzen later added the Überwelt of spiritual values. Rollo May (1909 to 1994; The Meaning of Anxiety , 1950; Existence , co-edited 1958) brought these ideas to America. For May, existential anxiety is the anxiety of a being who knows it is free and will die: normal anxiety is proportionate, not repressed and usable; neurotic anxiety is disproportionate, repressed and paralysing. Existential-humanistic therapy (May, James Bugental) is the American blend. Viktor Emil Frankl (1905 to 1997), a Viennese psychiatrist who survived Auschwitz and other Nazi camps, wrote Man's Search for Meaning (German original, 1946). His logotherapy (Greek logos , meaning), the "third Viennese school", holds that the primary human motive is not Freud's will to pleasure or Adler's will to power but the will to meaning . Its frustration brings an existential vacuum of emptiness and boredom and sometimes a noogenic neurosis (Greek noos , mind or spirit): one rooted in an existential problem rather than in conflict between drives. Meaning comes from creating or doing (creative values), from experiencing or loving (experiential values), and from the stand one takes toward unavoidable suffering (attitudinal values). In paradoxical intention , used for anticipatory anxiety in phobias, obsessions and insomnia, the client deliberately wishes for the feared symptom: a doctor afraid of sweating is told to show people how much he can really sweat, and the fear collapses. In dereflection , which counters hyper-reflection (excessive watching of oneself), attention is turned outward, as when a man anxious about his sexual performance attends to his partner instead. Socratic dialogue, the main technique, uses questions to help clients discover their own meanings. Exam trap The will to meaning, noogenic neurosis or anxiety, paradoxical intention and dereflection all belong to Frankl's logotherapy, an existential therapy: not REBT, acceptance and commitment therapy (Section 7.5) or the broader existential-humanistic therapy. Dereflection is not sensate focus, the graded touching exercise of Masters and Johnson (Section 7.7). Yalom's four ultimate concerns are not his group therapeutic factors (Section 7.7). Reality therapy, focusing, emotion-focused and positive therapies William Glasser (1925 to 2013), an American psychiatrist, refined reality therapy with delinquent girls at the Ventura School and published Reality Therapy in 1965. Its base, control theory, later renamed choice theory ( Choice Theory , 1998), holds that we choose nearly all behaviour to meet five basic, genetically built-in needs: survival, love and belonging, power (achievement), freedom and fun. Behaviour is chosen "total behaviour" (acting, thinking, feeling, physiology), so Glasser spoke of "depressing" rather than being depressed; acting is the easiest part to change. The therapist is warm but firm: present behaviour, responsibility, no excuses, no punishment. Robert Wubbolding summed up the method as WDEP : Wants, Doing (and direction), Evaluation (is it working?) and Planning. Eugene Gendlin (1926 to 2017), working with Rogers, found that improving clients attended to their inner bodily experiencing, and taught this skill as focusing (1978): attending to the vague bodily felt sense of a problem until a fitting word or image brings a "felt shift". Leslie Greenberg joined person-centred empathy to Gestalt tasks in process-experiential therapy, now emotion-focused therapy . Adaptive emotions are used, maladaptive ones changed by evoking a healthier emotion, and secondary ones (anger covering hurt) explored; two-chair work treats self-critical splits, the empty chair unfinished business. Greenberg and Susan Johnson also built emotionally focused couples therapy (Section 7.7). "Positive psychotherapy" has two meanings. Martin Seligman (born 1942) launched positive psychology as president of the American Psychological Association in 1998; his positive psychotherapy builds strengths and well-being (PERMA: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment) through exercises such as listing three good things daily. The idea of flow , total absorption when challenge matches skill, comes from Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021), not from Rogers, Maslow or Frankl. The Iranian-born German psychiatrist Nossrat Peseschkian (1933 to 2010) founded a separate, transcultural Positive Psychotherapy in the 1970s (Latin positum , the given): it starts from capacities, uses stories from many cultures, balances four areas of life (body, achievement, contact, future) and runs in five stages (observation, inventory, situational encouragement, verbalisation, broadening of goals). Narrative and solution-focused brief therapy These brief therapies grew from family therapy and social constructionism: no account of a life is the single true one, and the client is the expert. Narrative therapy was created by Michael White (1948 to 2008) in Adelaide, Australia, and David Epston in New Zealand ( Narrative Means to Therapeutic Ends , 1990). Clients arrive with a thin, problem-saturated story; the therapist practises externalising the problem ("the person is not the problem; the problem is the problem"), searches for unique outcomes when the problem did not win, and helps the client re-author the self story around them. The solution-focused brief therapy (SFBT) of Steve de Shazer (1940 to 2005) and Insoo Kim Berg (died 2007) was developed at the Brief Family Therapy Center in Milwaukee (founded 1978). It ignores causes and builds, through questions (Table 7.16), on what the client wants and what already works; the miracle question (de Shazer, 1988) is its signature. Brief strategic therapy (the Mental Research Institute in Palo Alto; Jay Haley), with reframing and paradoxical directives such as prescribing the symptom, is in Section 7.7. Miller in 1983 for problem drinkers and developed with Stephen Rollnick in Motivational Interviewing (1991; later editions 2002, 2013 and 2023). It is a collaborative, person-centred but goal-directed way of strengthening a person's own motivation by resolving ambivalence, wanting and not wanting change at once; arguing for change only makes the client defend the status quo. The spirit (2013 edition) is PACE: Partnership, Acceptance, Compassion and Evocation (drawing out the client's own reasons). The four processes are engaging, focusing, evoking and planning, and the core skills are OARS: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections and Summaries. The 2002 edition gave four principles: express empathy, develop discrepancy between behaviour and the client's own goals, roll with resistance (now split into sustain talk for the status quo and discord in the relationship) and support self-efficacy. The counsellor strengthens change talk : DARN (Desire, Ability, Reasons, Need), then CAT (Commitment, Activation, Taking steps). MI's home ground is substance use; it is also used for smoking, treatment adherence and other health behaviours. The meta-analysis of Burke, Arkowitz and Menchola (2003) found adapted MI effective for alcohol, drug, and diet and exercise problems (central in diabetes care), but not for smoking or HIV-risk behaviour; obsessive-compulsive disorder was not reviewed. Exam trap MI was developed by Miller and Rollnick, not by Prochaska and DiClemente (stages of change), Albert Bandura (self-efficacy) or Alan Marlatt (relapse prevention, Section 7.9). Asked what MI is used to manage, choose substance abuse, its original field, over treatment adherence. Asked which problem Burke and colleagues (2003) did not list, choose obsessive-compulsive disorder: smoking was reviewed (with weak results), OCD not at all. MI is often paired with the transtheoretical model of James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente , built from studies of how smokers quit on their own (1983). People pass through stages of change (Figure 7.10): precontemplation (no intention to change within six months), contemplation (intending to, but ambivalent), preparation (acting within a month; small steps taken), action (changed under six months ago), maintenance (change kept over six months) and termination (no temptation, full confidence). Relapse is recycling to an earlier stage, not failure, so progress is a spiral. Ten processes of change drive movement: experiential ones (consciousness raising, dramatic relief, environmental and self-re-evaluation, social liberation) help most early, behavioural ones (self-liberation or commitment, counterconditioning, stimulus control, contingency management, helping relationships) in action and maintenance. Decisional balance (pros and cons) and self-efficacy track progress; the health belief model is in Section 7.9. Counselling and the helping skills Counselling and psychotherapy overlap so much that Rogers used the words interchangeably. Counselling usually helps fairly well-functioning people with developmental, educational, vocational or situational problems, briefly and in the present; psychotherapy treats more severe or long-standing disorders, seeking deeper, slower personality change. Allen Ivey 's microcounselling (late 1960s) teaches interviewing one skill at a time. His microskills hierarchy rises from ethics and multicultural competence, through attending behaviour (culturally appropriate eye contact, vocal quality, verbal tracking, body language) and the basic listening sequence (questions, encouraging, paraphrasing, reflecting feeling, summarising), to focusing, empathic confrontation, reflection of meaning and influencing skills, and finally integration into a personal style. Carkhuff's model ( Helping and Human Relations , 1969) has the helper attend, respond, personalise and initiate, moving the client through exploration, understanding and action; on his five-level empathy scale, level 3 is interchangeable with what the client said. Gerard Egan 's The Skilled Helper (1975) has three stages. Stage I asks "What is going on?" (the current picture: telling the story, seeing blind spots, choosing the key issue); Stage II asks "What do I want instead?" (the preferred picture: possibilities, goals, commitment); Stage III asks "How do I get there?" (strategies, a plan and action). The helper attends with SOLER: face the client Squarely, Open posture, Lean forward, Eye contact, Relaxed. Egan separates primary empathy, understanding what the client has said and felt, from advanced empathy , voicing what the client only hints at or half sees, which is a form of challenge. Exam trap Advanced empathy is inappropriate in an initial session: without trust and enough information it feels like an intrusive interpretation. Primary empathy is right from the first minute, and culturally sensitive empathy is always appropriate. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Answers: (1) incongruence, (2) unconditional positive regard, (3) confluence, (4) meaninglessness, (5) dereflection, (6) fun, (7) solution-focused brief. 7.7 Family, Couples and Group Therapies Medium yield · 28 Qs For most of its history psychotherapy meant one patient and one therapist. In the 1950s clinicians noticed that patients who recovered in hospital often relapsed soon after going home, and that when one family member improved another sometimes fell ill. Perhaps the problem lay partly in the relationships. This section follows that idea from the family to the couple and the group. The family as a system The idea came from biology. Ludwig von Bertalanffy (1901 to 1972) proposed a general systems theory : a system is a set of interacting parts whose whole is more than their sum, so a change in one part changes the whole. Norbert Wiener 's cybernetics (1948) added self-regulation by feedback. A family tends toward homeostasis , a balance it defends as a thermostat defends a room temperature. Negative feedback restores the old balance and positive feedback amplifies change; neither word means good or bad. Systems thinking replaces linear causality (A causes B, so someone is to blame) with circular causality , in which each person's behaviour is both cause and effect of the others' (Figure 7.11). The member brought for treatment is the identified patient , the visible sign of a troubled system rather than its cause; the symptom may even serve the system, as when a son's misbehaviour unites quarrelling parents, and a child made to carry the family's problems is its scapegoat. Families also pass through a family life cycle : Betty Carter and Monica McGoldrick described six stages (leaving home, the new couple, families with young children, with adolescents, launching children, and later life), and symptoms cluster at the transitions. Linear view: each blames the other Her account He withdraws I nag His account She nags I withdraw Circular view: one loop, no culprit She nags He withdraws each act is both cause and effect Figure 7.11 Linear and circular causality. Each partner says the other started it; the systems therapist treats the loop and blames no one. Families and schizophrenia: from blame to expressed emotion The first family research asked whether families cause schizophrenia. In 1948 Frieda Fromm-Reichmann (1889 to 1957) blamed a dominating, rejecting schizophrenogenic mother . In 1956 the anthropologist Gregory Bateson (1904 to 1980), with Don Jackson (1920 to 1968), Jay Haley and John Weakland at Palo Alto, proposed the double bind : a person in a vital relationship repeatedly receives two contradictory messages at different levels (typically words contradicted by manner) and can neither comment on the contradiction nor leave, so every response is wrong. Key study: Bateson's double bind (1956) A young man recovering from an acute schizophrenic episode put his arm round his visiting mother, and she stiffened. He withdrew it; she asked, "Don't you love me any more?" When he blushed she said, "Dear, you must not be so easily embarrassed and afraid of your feelings." After she left he assaulted an aide. Whatever he did was wrong, and he could not say so. Criticism: anecdotal and never predictive, it is not accepted as a cause. Theodore Lidz (1910 to 2001) at Yale described marital schism , open conflict in which each parent undermines the other and courts the child, and marital skew , in which one disturbed parent dominates while the other pretends all is normal. Lyman Wynne (1923 to 2007) described pseudomutuality (1958), a facade of harmony that hides distance and leaves no room for a separate identity. None of these survived as a cause of schizophrenia (Chapter 8), and the schizophrenogenic mother is discredited. What survived concerned relapse . In London George Brown found that discharged patients who spent long hours with their relatives relapsed more often. The emotional climate of the home, the attitudes relatives express about the patient, is called expressed emotion (EE) and is rated from the Camberwell Family Interview. High EE has three components: critical comments , hostility and emotional over-involvement (intrusive, self-sacrificing concern). Brown, James Birley and John Wing (1972) showed that high EE predicts relapse. Key study: Vaughn and Leff (1976) Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff followed patients with schizophrenia for nine months after discharge. About half of those returning to high-EE homes relapsed, against about one in eight in low-EE homes. In high-EE homes, regular medication and less than 35 hours a week of face-to-face contact each lowered the risk. Hence family psychoeducation : teaching relatives about the illness, medication and warning signs, training calm communication and problem solving, and cutting contact hours where the climate will not change (Leff's programmes; Ian Falloon 's behavioural family management). It lowers relapse (Section 7.9). Exam trap High EE predicts relapse , not onset, negative symptoms or violence. Warmth is rated in the interview but is not a high-EE dimension. Reducing contact hours manages high EE. One parent sending two conflicting messages is double bind communication; first-rank symptoms are Kurt Schneider's (Chapter 8). Indian context In the 1950s Vidya Sagar at Amritsar Mental Hospital had families camp on the grounds and share in care. Indian families show the lowest rates of high EE in cross-cultural comparisons (Jenkins and Karno, 1992), and closeness that looks like over-involvement by Western norms may be ordinary support. A therapist unaware of a family's culture and customs will misread it and make wrong assessments. Bowen's family systems therapy Murray Bowen (1913 to 1990), who admitted whole families to hospital wards in the 1950s, founded the transgenerational school. Its master concept is differentiation of self : separating thinking from feeling, and staying oneself while emotionally connected; the poorly differentiated are fused and reactive. Under stress a two-person relationship draws in a third person, usually a child: triangulation . Table 7.17 lists all eight concepts. Bowen worked as a calm coach who stayed out of the family's triangles, and mapped three or more generations in a genogram (squares for males, circles for females, lines for marriages, conflicts and cutoffs). Minuchin's structural family therapy Salvador Minuchin (1921 to 2017) worked with poor families of delinquent boys ( Families of the Slums , 1967) and then at the Philadelphia Child Guidance Clinic ( Families and Family Therapy , 1974). He studied the family's present structure : its subsystems (spousal, parental, sibling), a hierarchy with parents in charge, and boundaries that should be clear, firm yet permeable. Diffuse boundaries produce enmeshment (over-involvement, intrusion, little autonomy); rigid boundaries produce disengagement (isolation, little support), as Figure 7.12 shows. Psychosomatic Families (1978) described families of children with anorexia, diabetes and asthma as enmeshed, overprotective, rigid and unable to resolve conflict. The therapist begins by joining , accommodating to the family's style, then maps its structure and asks for an enactment : the conflict acted out in the room rather than described. Unbalancing (siding with one member, often an overruled parent, to shift power), boundary making and reframing then restructure the family. Exam trap Enmeshment means diffuse boundaries; rigid boundaries mean disengagement. Enmeshment is not a complete lack of communication, nor scapegoating. Structural is Minuchin, strategic is Haley, multigenerational is Bowen, experiential is Satir. A therapist's boundary violation with a client is professional ethics (Section 7.1). Strategic, systemic and other family therapies Jay Haley (1923 to 2007), influenced by the hypnotherapist Milton Erickson , made therapy strategic: the therapist plans how to remove the presenting problem through directives (tasks) and does not seek insight. With resistant families he used paradoxical intervention , such as prescribing the symptom (a quarrelling couple told to quarrel at a set hour); in ordeal therapy (1984) the client performs a harmless but tiresome ordeal every time the symptom occurs. Cloe Madanes (1981) added pretend techniques: the child pretends to have the symptom and the parent pretends to help. At the Mental Research Institute in Palo Alto (founded by Jackson, 1959), Paul Watzlawick , Weakland and Richard Fisch offered brief therapy of about ten sessions. In Change (1974) they argued that attempted solutions keep problems going: a wife nags her husband to exercise, he resists, she nags more. Trying harder is first-order change , within unchanged rules; the goal is second-order change , a change in the rules themselves. The Milan group ( Mara Selvini Palazzoli , Luigi Boscolo , Gianfranco Cecchin and Giuliana Prata ; Paradox and Counterparadox , 1978) worked as a team behind a one-way mirror. Their positive connotation recasts everyone's behaviour, symptom included, as serving the family's unity, and prescribed rituals interrupt the family's game. Their three guidelines were hypothesising (a provisional systemic explanation, revised each session), circularity (exploring relationships and differences) and neutrality (siding with no one), and circular questioning asks one member about the relationship between others: "Who is most upset when Anu won't eat?" Among the experiential therapists, Virginia Satir (1916 to 1988; Peoplemaking , 1972) named four stances that protect low self-esteem under stress: placating (always agreeing), blaming, computing or super-reasonable (cold logic) and distracting or irrelevant, against congruent, levelling communication in which words, feelings and body match. In family sculpting she posed members physically to show their relationships. Carl Whitaker (1912 to 1995) practised spontaneous, often absurd symbolic-experiential therapy with a co-therapist. Couples and sex therapy When a couple's distress keeps an individual problem going, the pair is treated together. For depression bound up with marital discord, marital and couple therapy is the better choice: behavioural marital therapy relieves the depression about as well as individual cognitive therapy and also mends the marriage. Behavioural couples therapy ( Neil Jacobson and Gayla Margolin , 1979) increases positive behaviour exchange and teaches communication and problem solving. Jacobson and Andrew Christensen 's integrative behavioural couple therapy adds acceptance of differences that will not change. John Gottman , filming couples in conflict, found that his four horsemen predict divorce: criticism (attacking character), contempt (mockery; the strongest predictor), defensiveness and stonewalling (withdrawal). Stable couples keep at least five positive interactions for every negative one, the 5:1 ratio, and his Sound Relationship House builds from love maps and fondness up to shared meaning, on walls of trust and commitment. Emotionally focused couple therapy ( Sue Johnson , 1980s) uses attachment theory: fights are protests at a threatened bond, locked in cycles such as pursue and withdraw. William Masters and Virginia Johnson ( Human Sexual Inadequacy , 1970) treated the couple as the patient, with a male and female co-therapist team. Their sensate focus is graded, non-demand touching with intercourse at first banned, removing performance anxiety; for premature ejaculation they taught the squeeze technique (firm pressure where the head of the penis joins the shaft, just before ejaculation). The stop-start technique, pausing stimulation before the point of no return, is James Semans 's (1956). Helen Singer Kaplan ( The New Sex Therapy , 1974) blended these tasks with psychodynamic work in brief sex therapy. Jack Annon 's PLISSIT model (1976) grades help: Permission, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions, Intensive Therapy. Exam trap Contempt, not criticism, is Gottman's best predictor of divorce. Squeeze is Masters and Johnson's; stop-start is Semans's (Masters and Johnson adapted Semans's method, so some textbooks credit Semans with both). Emotionally focused couple therapy (Johnson) is not Greenberg's individual emotion-focused therapy (Section 7.6). Group therapy: Yalom's factors and group stages Why do groups help? Irvin Yalom 's The Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy (first edition 1970) sets out eleven therapeutic factors (Table 7.19). Of these, universality , discovering that one is not alone in one's suffering, is often a newcomer's first relief. Table 7.19 Yalom's eleven therapeutic factors. The group is a social microcosm, where members soon behave as they do in life, so the leader works with interactions in the session: first experiencing them, then illuminating the process by reflecting on what just happened. The leader creates and maintains the group, builds its norms, and activates and illuminates the here-and-now. Bruce Tuckman (1965) traced group development through forming (polite testing), storming (conflict), norming (cohesion) and performing, adding adjourning with Mary Ann Jensen in 1977. A closed group keeps the same members for a fixed term and bonds quickly; an open group admits new members as others leave. Exam trap "Not alone" is universality ; seeing others recover is hope; helping is altruism; venting is catharsis. The here-and-now does not ban talk of outside life; it makes the group's own interactions, experienced and then reflected upon, the engine of change, and it is not didactic teaching or disputing irrational beliefs (Section 7.5). Free association, token reinforcement and schema work are not Yalom factors. Yalom's four ultimate concerns belong to existential therapy (Section 7.6). Psychodrama, encounter and self-help groups, therapeutic communities Jacob Levy Moreno (1889 to 1974), who coined the term group psychotherapy, opened a Theatre of Spontaneity in Vienna in 1921. In psychodrama the protagonist acts out scenes on a stage , guided by the therapist as director , with members as auxiliary egos playing significant others and an audience that shares afterwards. In role reversal the protagonist plays the other person; in doubling an auxiliary voices the protagonist's unspoken feelings; in mirroring someone replays the protagonist's behaviour for them to watch. Moreno's sociometry measures attraction and rejection in groups, and its sociogram draws members as points and choices as arrows, revealing the group's explicit and implicit communication patterns. Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947) inspired the T-group (training or sensitivity group, National Training Laboratories, 1947), in which members learn group dynamics and their effect on others. The encounter group , championed by Carl Rogers , encourages therapy and self-growth through open disclosure and interaction. Self-help groups are run by members, not professionals: Alcoholics Anonymous, founded in 1935 by Bill Wilson and Bob Smith , works through twelve steps, sponsors and anonymity, and Narcotics Anonymous adapted the steps to drugs. In milieu therapy the whole ward environment, staff, routine and fellow patients, is the treatment. Its democratic form, the therapeutic community , was pioneered by Maxwell Jones (1907 to 1990) at Belmont Hospital in Surrey, whose unit later became the Henderson Hospital: staff and patients share decisions in daily community meetings, hierarchy is flattened, and every interaction becomes feedback. Addiction communities are in Section 7.9. Exam trap Maxwell Jones means the therapeutic community . Milieu therapy is the broader idea; group analysis is S. H. Foulkes 's psychoanalytic group therapy; encounter groups are Rogers's and psychodrama Moreno's; the token economy, aversion therapy and EMDR belong to behaviour therapy (Section 7.4), and logotherapy is Frankl's (Section 7.6). Evidence, Common Factors and the Alliance Lower yield · 12 Qs Sections 7.3 to 7.7 described a crowded marketplace of therapies. Does any of it help, and if so, why? The story runs from Eysenck's attack, through the statistics that answered him, to a debate that continues: does the technique heal, or the relationship, the client and the therapist? Eysenck's challenge and the meta-analytic answer In 1952 Hans Jürgen Eysenck (1916 to 1997) reviewed the published outcome reports. Neurotic patients given psychoanalysis improved at about 44 percent and those given eclectic therapy at about 64 percent, but comparable patients without psychotherapy (insurance-disability claimants seen by general practitioners, and state-hospital discharges) improved at about 72 percent. Roughly two-thirds of neurotic patients, he concluded, improve within two years with or without therapy, through spontaneous remission : recovery driven by time, life events and ordinary support. Critics attacked his method: the groups differed in severity, "improved" meant different things in different studies, and the "untreated" patients had received reassurance and sedatives. Allen E. Bergin (1971) showed that counting dropouts differently lifted psychoanalysis to about 85 percent improvement among those who completed it; Michael J. Lambert (1976) showed that Eysenck had inflated untreated improvement, putting spontaneous remission nearer 40 percent. The decisive answer came from a new statistic. Gene V. Glass coined the term meta-analysis in 1976 for pooling many studies statistically instead of counting how many "worked". Each comparison of a treated with a control group yields an effect size ( d ): the difference between the group means divided by a standard deviation. Effect sizes, all in the same unit, can then be averaged across studies and compared across therapies. A d of 0.85 places the average treated client above about 80 percent of untreated people (Figure 7.13). d = 0.85 80% Untreated group Treated group -3 -2 -1 0 +1 +2 +3 +4 Outcome, in standard deviations (higher is better) Figure 7.13 What an effect size of 0.85 means. The average treated client (solid curve) scores better than the shaded 80 percent of the untreated group (dashed curve). Key study: Smith and Glass (1977) Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass pooled 375 controlled studies. The average effect size was 0.68: the typical client was better off than 75 percent of untreated people, and types of therapy differed little. With Thomas Miller ( The Benefits of Psychotherapy , 1980) they reached 475 studies and 0.85 (80 percent). Eysenck called it "mega-silliness": good and bad studies pooled ("garbage in, garbage out"), unlike outcomes averaged ("apples and oranges"). Exam trap Eysenck said therapy adds nothing to spontaneous remission, not that it harms. 0.68 and 75 percent is Smith and Glass (1977); 0.85 and 80 percent is Smith, Glass and Miller (1980). The dodo bird verdict and common factors Smith and Glass also found the rival schools roughly equal. Saul Rosenzweig (1907 to 2004) had predicted this in 1936: diverse therapies succeed through implicit common factors, he argued, quoting the Dodo in Alice in Wonderland : "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes." In 1975 Lester Luborsky , Barton Singer and Lise Luborsky reviewed the comparative trials and named the dodo bird verdict : bona fide therapies, competently delivered, produce roughly equivalent outcomes, because change comes mainly from the common factors they share (the alliance, empathy, hope) rather than from specific techniques. Specific-effects researchers, holding a medical model in which each therapy has active ingredients like a drug, point to exceptions: exposure beats non-exposure therapies for obsessive-compulsive disorder, phobias and panic. Common-factors researchers reply that most comparisons of bona fide therapies show differences near zero (at most about 0.2 in a 1997 meta-analysis) and that apparent winners often reflect allegiance ( 7.8.4 ). Bruce E. Wampold formalised this view as the contextual model ( The Great Psychotherapy Debate , 2001; in its fullest form in the 2015 edition with Zac Imel): therapy works through a real relationship; through expectations created by a convincing explanation and treatment plan; and through specific ingredients that help because they get the client doing healthy things, not because they correct a specific deficit. Its root is Jerome David Frank (1909 to 2005), whose Persuasion and Healing (1961) compared psychotherapy with religious healing and placebo. Clients arrive demoralised , and every healing method restores morale through four shared features: The client has an emotionally charged, confiding relationship with a helper. Help takes place in a healing setting (a clinic, a temple, a consulting room). A rationale or "myth" plausibly explains the symptoms and how to overcome them. A ritual or procedure, believed in by both, requires the client's active participation. Exam trap "Healing and Persuasion" is Frank's Persuasion and Healing with the title reversed. Distractors: Gerald Klerman co-developed interpersonal psychotherapy and Donald Winnicott was an object-relations analyst (both 7.3); Alfred Pritz is the Austrian psychotherapist who was founding president of the World Council for Psychotherapy (1995). The dodo verdict never says therapy is ineffective, that only psychoanalysis lasts or that medication always wins: bona fide therapies tie. Lambert (1992) estimated, in his famous pie (Figure 7.14), that about 40 percent of improvement comes from client and extratherapeutic factors, 30 percent from relationship factors, 15 percent from expectancy (placebo and hope) and only 15 percent from model-specific techniques: rough judgements from the literature, not statistical results. 40% 30% 15% 15% Client and extratherapeutic: 40% strengths, support, life events Relationship: 30% empathy, warmth, alliance Expectancy (placebo): 15% hope that therapy will help Model-specific techniques: 15% the school's own methods Figure 7.14 Lambert's (1992) rough estimates of what produces improvement. Technique, the slice the schools argue about, is the smallest. The therapeutic alliance and the core conditions The alliance idea began in psychoanalysis. Elizabeth Zetzel (1956) spoke of the therapeutic alliance and Ralph Greenson (1965) of the working alliance, the patient's rational, cooperative tie to the analyst as distinct from transference; Greenson also described the real relationship , the genuine person-to-person bond. Edward S. Bordin (1979) made the therapeutic alliance pantheoretical: a collaborative relationship with three parts, agreement on goals , agreement on the tasks that reach them, and a bond of trust and respect. A working relationship is thus a contract to work together realistically and collaboratively, visible in how well the two actually work together and resting on a committed belief in the helping relationship; it needs no particular theory. Adam Horvath and Leslie Greenberg's (1989) Working Alliance Inventory (36 items, with a 12-item short form) measures goals, tasks and bond. Across meta-analyses the alliance correlates about 0.28 with outcome: modest but robust. Jeremy D. Safran and J. Christopher Muran described alliance ruptures : withdrawal (the client falls silent, goes vague, over-agrees) and confrontation (the client complains or attacks). Repair means noticing the strain, talking openly about what is happening between the two and owning one's part; repaired ruptures predict good outcomes. Carl Ransom Rogers (1957) held that his core conditions (empathy, unconditional positive regard, congruence; 7.6) were necessary and sufficient. Research supports a weaker claim: empathy correlates about 0.3 with outcome, positive regard and congruence a little less (roughly 0.2 to 0.3): facilitative in every therapy, but not sufficient. Exam trap Bordin's alliance is not a Rogerian concept; Rogers' terms are the actualising tendency, conditions of worth and unconditional positive regard (7.6). Person-centred therapy is the school least likely to say "therapeutic alliance": it treats the relationship and unconditional positive regard as the therapy itself, whereas psychoanalysis coined the term and cognitive-behavioural and interpersonal therapists use Bordin's version. The alliance is not an outcome score, not two clinicians agreeing on a diagnosis (inter-rater reliability, Chapter 2) and not the client's ability to do homework alone. What a working relationship does NOT need: "a psychodynamic theory base". Therapist, client and allegiance effects Consistent differences between individual therapists' outcomes, whatever their approach, are called therapist effects ; they account for about 5 percent of outcome variance (roughly 3 in controlled trials, 7 in routine practice), far more than the differences between treatments. An allegiance effect appears when researchers find their own favoured therapy superior; Luborsky and colleagues (1999) showed that researcher allegiance predicted most of the outcome differences in comparative trials. Client factors carry the biggest slice of the pie. William Schofield ( Psychotherapy: The Purchase of Friendship , 1964) noted that therapists prefer, and do best with, the YAVIS client: young, attractive, verbal, intelligent and successful. YAVIS describes patient characteristics, not a technique, an illness or a therapist quality; its opposite, HOUND (homely, old, unattractive, nonverbal, dumb), names neglected clients. Readiness to change (stages of change, 7.6) and realistic expectations of outcome (hope) and of role (what a client does) also predict benefit. In the hello-goodbye effect , described by Starke R. Hathaway , clients exaggerate distress at intake (to justify seeking help) and well-being at the end (to thank the therapist), so before-and-after self-reports overstate improvement. Testing outcome: efficacy, effectiveness and ESTs Research on efficacy asks whether a treatment can work under ideal, controlled conditions (internal validity); research on effectiveness asks whether it does work in routine practice (external validity), as in Martin E. P. Seligman 's (1995) Consumer Reports survey, in which most readers reported benefit (Table 7.20). Table 7.20 Efficacy and effectiveness studies. Feature Efficacy study Effectiveness study Clients Homogeneous, one disorder Mixed, often comorbid Assignment Random assignment to treatment or control Often not random Therapist Controlled by a manual Flexible Sessions Fixed number Set by need In analogue research , clinical questions are studied under conditions that only resemble therapy, usually with healthy, non-clinical participants (students with a mild fear of snakes standing in for phobic patients): control is high, generalisation uncertain. It is neither outcome research on a clinical population nor comparative research pitting two treatments against each other. In the randomised controlled trial (RCT), chance decides who receives which condition, so the groups differ only in treatment. Its safeguard, allocation concealment , hides the upcoming allocation sequence from the recruiter until each participant is enrolled, preventing selection bias. Blinding hides the assigned condition after allocation; in psychotherapy only outcome assessors can be blind. The comparison group decides what a trial can show (Table 7.21). Control Group receives Controls for Waiting list Treatment after a delay Time, spontaneous remission Placebo-attention Credible contact, no active ingredient Attention and expectancy Treatment as usual Routine care Usual care; shows added benefit Trials follow treatment manuals (Aaron Beck's 1979 manual for cognitive therapy of depression was an early model) and check treatment fidelity : adherence to the manual and competence in delivering it. In 1995 an APA Division 12 (Clinical Psychology) task force chaired by Dianne L. Chambless began listing empirically supported treatments (ESTs). A well-established treatment needed at least two good between-group experiments, by independent teams, showing it superior to a pill or psychological placebo or another treatment, or equal to an established one (or a large single-case series), with a manual and clearly described clients. A probably efficacious treatment needed only two experiments beating a waiting list, or strong trials from one team. Chambless and Steven Hollon (1998) refined the criteria; most listed treatments were cognitive-behavioural. The APA's 2006 task force defined evidence-based practice in psychology more broadly: "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences." Exam trap Efficacy studies use manuals, homogeneous samples and random assignment; "therapist flexibility is encouraged" marks effectiveness research. Allocation concealment (before enrolment) is not blinding (after allocation). Landmark trials, dose and clinical significance Key study: NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program (1989) Irene Elkin 's trial randomly assigned about 250 depressed outpatients at three sites to 16 weeks of cognitive-behavioural therapy, interpersonal psychotherapy, imipramine or a pill placebo (the last two with clinical management). All groups improved and the two psychotherapies did not differ; only in severe depression did imipramine clearly beat placebo, with interpersonal therapy showing some advantage. Re-analyses found that the alliance predicted outcome in every arm, and that therapists differed more than treatments. Project MATCH (1997) assigned about 1,700 people with alcohol problems to twelve-step facilitation, cognitive-behavioural coping-skills therapy or four-session motivational enhancement therapy, to test whether matching clients to treatments helps. All three worked about equally; matching effects were scarcely found. Kenneth I. Howard and colleagues (1986), pooling about 2,400 outpatients from 15 studies, described the dose-effect relationship (Figure 7.15): about 50 percent had improved by 8 sessions, 75 percent by 26 and 85 percent by 52. The curve is negatively accelerated; Howard's later phase model reads it as quick remoralisation, then remediation of symptoms, then slow rehabilitation. 8 sessions: 50% 26 sessions: 75% 52 sessions: 85% 0% 25% 50% 75% 100% 0 8 26 52 78 104 Number of sessions Clients improved Figure 7.15 The dose-effect relationship (Howard and colleagues, 1986), a smooth curve through the published milestones: most of the benefit comes early. A large sample can make a small average gain statistically significant while many clients stay unwell. Neil S. Jacobson and Paula Truax (1991) therefore judged clinical significance client by client, with two tests. The reliable change index (RCI), the change divided by the standard error of the difference (derived from the test's reliability), must exceed 1.96, so the change is unlikely to be measurement error; and the client must cross a cut-off from the dysfunctional into the functional range. Both tests passed means recovered; reliable change alone, improved; reliable worsening, deteriorated. Take Meena, who falls from 32 to 12 on a depression scale with a standard deviation of 8 and reliability of 0.84. The standard error of measurement is 8 × √0.16 = 3.2, the standard error of the difference √2 × 3.2 ≈ 4.5, so her RCI is 20 ÷ 4.5 ≈ 4.4: reliable. With a functional cut-off of 14, she has recovered. A fall from 32 to 27 (RCI about 1.1) is not reliable change. Therapy can also harm. Bergin (1966) named the deterioration effect : roughly 5 to 10 percent of adult clients get worse, which is why Lambert's Outcome Questionnaire-45 feeds each client's progress back to the therapist. Process research and psychotherapy integration Where outcome research asks whether therapy works, process research studies what happens within sessions and how it produces change. Therapy has a beginning (assessment, alliance, goals, contract, teaching the client's role), a middle or working phase (the main interventions and working through) and a planned termination (consolidating gains, preparing for setbacks, handling the ending). Many clients end in premature termination , leaving before goals are met and against the therapist's advice: near half of outpatients in a 1993 meta-analysis, about one in five in a 2012 one, more often with young and poor clients, weak alliances and mismatched expectations. Classical analysts shunned therapist self-disclosure and humanistic therapists value it; it helps when brief, rare, client-focused and about resolved issues. Homework, central to cognitive and behavioural therapy, carries therapy into the client's week; completing it predicts better outcome. Psychotherapy integration takes four routes (Table 7.22). In technical eclecticism techniques are borrowed without their theories; theoretical integration fuses theories into a new framework; assimilative integration keeps one home theory and absorbs techniques into it. Culture-sensitive therapy and therapy in India Western therapy prizes autonomy, insight and an equal, non-directive relationship. A therapist unaware of a family's culture and customs risks wrong assessments and misinterpretations, such as calling a joint family's shared decisions enmeshment. A culturally adapted therapy modifies an evidence-based treatment's language, metaphors, content, goals and methods to fit the client's culture ( Guillermo Bernal 's ecological validity framework), and meta-analyses find adapted versions modestly more effective. N. C. Surya , writing with S. S. Jayaram (1964), argued that Indian patients are more dependent than Western ones and less inclined to integrate inner processes, so the therapist should use the patient's own language and give direct, situational support rather than intrapsychic interpretation. Jaswant Singh Neki (1973) proposed the guru-chela relationship as an Indian therapeutic paradigm: a wise, warm, guiding therapist and a client who accepts a phase of dependence, normal in Indian relationships, which the guru gradually turns into self-reliance. Families usually accompany patients and join sessions, so therapists work with them as allies (7.1). Yoga-based programmes have been tested at NIMHANS as add-on treatment for depression and schizophrenia, and mindfulness is taught in familiar forms alongside pranayama and meditation. Training, supervision and the therapist's self-care Clinical supervision builds a trainee's skill and protects clients. Developmental models (Cal Stoltenberg's) trace trainees from anxious dependence to autonomy; psychotherapy-based models supervise in the language of the therapy taught; Janine M. Bernard 's (1979) discrimination model has the supervisor switch between teacher, counsellor and consultant roles across intervention, conceptualisation and personalisation. In parallel process the trainee re-enacts with the supervisor what is happening with the client. Carl Gustav Jung 's image of the wounded healer , after the wounded centaur Chiron, holds that a therapist's understood wounds deepen empathy while unexamined ones become countertransference. The risk of burnout , which Christina Maslach described as emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced personal accomplishment, makes self-care (supervision, personal therapy, boundaries, manageable caseloads, rest) an ethical duty. Most deaths in India now come from illnesses driven partly by behaviour, and most people with a mental illness never see a specialist. This section follows the psychologist onto the ward, into the community, into crises and into rehabilitation. Health psychology and the sick role In 1980 Joseph D. Matarazzo , first president of the American Psychological Association's Division of Health Psychology (Division 38, founded 1978), defined health psychology as the aggregate of psychology's educational, scientific and professional contributions to promoting and maintaining health, preventing and treating illness, and identifying the causes and correlates of health and illness. It is one discipline's field, leaning towards promotion and prevention. Behavioural medicine ( Gary Schwartz and Stephen Weiss , 1978) is an interdisciplinary field that integrates behavioural and biomedical knowledge and techniques for prevention, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation. Both apply George Engel 's biopsychosocial model (1977; Section 7.1). What a person does with a symptom, ignoring chest pain for a week or rushing to casualty, is illness behaviour ( David Mechanic , 1962). Once accepted as ill, a person enters the sick role of Talcott Parsons ( The Social System , 1951), with two rights (exemption from normal duties; no blame for the illness) and two obligations (to want to get well; to seek competent help and cooperate with it). It fits acute illness better than chronic or stigmatised illness. Seeking the sick role itself is the motive in factitious disorder; malingering seeks external gain (Chapter 8). Exam trap Behavioural medicine, not health psychology, is the interdisciplinary field integrating behavioural and biomedical interventions (JEMAS 2025). Options such as "only uses medication" are nonsense. Health psychology is Division 38; clinical psychology, Division 12. Models of health behaviour and adherence Models of health behaviour explain why knowing the risks is not enough (Table 7.23). The health belief model grew from a 1950s puzzle, the poor uptake of free tuberculosis X-rays, studied by Godfrey Hochbaum , Irwin Rosenstock and Stephen Kegeles in the United States: people acted when they felt susceptible, judged the disease severe, saw benefits outweighing barriers and met a cue to action. Rosenstock gave it its classic statement (1966), and Marshall Becker (1974) extended it to sick-role behaviour and adherence. Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen 's theory of reasoned action (1975) made intention the immediate cause of behaviour; Ajzen's theory of planned behaviour added perceived behavioural control (Figure 7.16). Ronald Rogers 's protection motivation theory (1975) shows that fear appeals work only when coping appraisal is also high, and Ralf Schwarzer 's health action process approach (1992) adds planning to turn intention into action. Exam trap "Susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers" is always the health belief model (JEMAS 2025). RML 2023 keyed the theory of planned behaviour as "attitude, subjective norms and self-efficacy": pick it, though strictly the third factor is perceived behavioural control, which Ajzen (1991) likened to Bandura's self-efficacy; the other options are not its constructs. Medicine most needs adherence , following an agreed treatment; the older word compliance implied obedience (in social psychology it means yielding to a direct request, Chapter 3). Only about half of chronically ill patients in developed countries take treatment as prescribed (World Health Organization, 2003). Clear written instructions, simple regimens, reminders, family involvement and a good relationship all help. Thomas Szasz and Marc Hollender (1956) ranged patient-practitioner relationships from activity-passivity (the unconscious patient) through guidance-cooperation to mutual participation, best for chronic illness. Stress and physical illness Stress itself is taught in Section 1.11: Hans Selye 's general adaptation syndrome (alarm, resistance, exhaustion), the life-events scale of Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe , and psychoneuroimmunology, begun when Robert Ader and Nicholas Cohen (1975) conditioned immune suppression in rats. Health psychology adds that an acute stressor is brief with a clear end (a pop quiz), a chronic stressor persists (marital discord, HIV disease, colon cancer), and chronic stress is what suppresses immunity. Franz Alexander ( Psychosomatic Medicine , 1950) proposed that a specific unconscious conflict acting on a vulnerable organ caused each of seven psychosomatic disorders , the "holy seven": peptic ulcer, essential hypertension, bronchial asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, neurodermatitis and thyrotoxicosis. The specificity idea failed (most ulcers proved bacterial, from Helicobacter pylori ), but psychological factors are now known to shape the course of every illness (Table 7.24). Wilbert Fordyce (1976) treated pain behaviours (grimacing, resting, asking for pills) as operants: his operant approach rewards well behaviour, raises activity by quotas and gives analgesics on a fixed schedule, not on complaint. Cognitive-behavioural therapy adds coping skills, pacing and challenges to catastrophising, usually in multidisciplinary pain clinics. Exam trap Offered both, RML 2024 keyed Type A (the whole pattern) for coronary risk; later research found hostility its toxic component, so answer hostility only when the stem asks for the component. For Type 2 diabetes the key is diet and inactivity, the strongest modifiable cause, not genes, stress or toxins. Behavioural medicine and lifestyle change Biofeedback displays a bodily signal (muscle tension, finger temperature, skin conductance, brain waves) so that a person can learn to control it, as in tension headache or migraine, though it often does no better than relaxation: Edmund Jacobson 's progressive muscle relaxation, Johannes Schultz 's autogenic training or Herbert Benson 's relaxation response (1975). Stress management adds cognitive restructuring and problem solving (Section 7.5). Chronic insomnia is treated first with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia : stimulus control ( Richard Bootzin , 1972: the bed only for sleep and sex; leave it if awake for about 20 minutes), sleep restriction ( Arthur Spielman , 1987: time in bed cut to time asleep) and cognitive work on sleep worries. Sleep hygiene (no evening caffeine, a dark quiet room, regular hours) is not enough alone. Smokers are helped by the five As (ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange follow-up) and nicotine replacement. Drinkers are screened with the World Health Organization's Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT, 1989): 10 items scored 0 to 40, with 8 or more suggesting hazardous or harmful use and 20 or more possible dependence. A positive screen earns a brief intervention, a few short sessions in the style of motivational interviewing (Section 7.6). Weight management relies on self-monitoring, stimulus control and a modest 5 to 10 percent loss; exercise lasts when it is enjoyable, shared and planned. Chronic illness, dying and grief Chronic illness is self-managed for life; depression is common and worsens self-care, so psychologists teach self-management and involve the family. When cure is impossible, palliative care seeks comfort and quality of life for patient and family. It began with Cicely Saunders 's St Christopher's Hospice, London (1967), which treated "total pain": physical, emotional, social and spiritual. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross ( On Death and Dying , 1969) described five stages in dying patients: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. They are neither fixed nor universal, came from the dying rather than the bereaved, and have weak research support. J. William Worden (1982) proposed four tasks of mourning , in their current wording: accept the reality of the loss, process the pain of grief, adjust to a world without the deceased, and find an enduring connection with the deceased while embarking on a new life. Most grief is normal and runs its course with ordinary support; counselling adds little. Complicated grief , intense yearning that persists and disables (prolonged grief disorder, Chapter 8), needs intervention, usually one to one. Exam trap "Crisis-related bereavement should always be considered traumatic grief" is the false statement (RML 2020): grief is usually normal, and "always" gives it away. Worden's are tasks, not stages. Community mental health and prevention President John F. Kennedy 's Community Mental Health Centers Act (1963) funded local centres to replace state hospitals. With antipsychotic drugs it sped deinstitutionalisation , but too few centres were built, and many discharged patients became homeless, imprisoned or caught in a "revolving door" of readmissions. Community psychology (Swampscott conference, 1965) turned to prevention and social change. Gerald Caplan ( Principles of Preventive Psychiatry , 1964) brought public health's three levels to mental health. Primary prevention lowers new cases (incidence) among the healthy: vaccination, health education. Secondary prevention lowers prevalence by early detection and prompt treatment. Tertiary prevention limits the disability of an established disorder: rehabilitation. Robert Gordon (1983) classified prevention by its target instead: universal (everyone), selective (high-risk groups, such as children of depressed parents) and indicated (individuals with early signs). Caplan (1970) also named four types of mental health consultation , helping another professional rather than the client: client-centred case, consultee-centred case, programme-centred administrative and consultee-centred administrative. Julian Rappaport (1981) preferred empowerment , people gaining control over their own lives. Where specialists are scarce, task-shifting trains lay counsellors to deliver structured care under supervision. In Zimbabwe, Dixon Chibanda 's Friendship Bench has lay health workers, many of them grandmothers, offer problem-solving therapy on clinic benches. In Goa, Vikram Patel 's MANAS trial (2010) showed that lay counsellors in public primary-care clinics improved recovery from common mental disorders, and his group's PRIDE programme took lay-counsellor problem solving to adolescents in Indian schools. Stigma ( Erving Goffman , 1963) deters help-seeking; contact with people who have recovered reduces it best. These attack the treatment gap, as do India's National Mental Health Programme (1982) and District Mental Health Programme (1996), modelled on a NIMHANS pilot in Bellary, Karnataka (Section 7.1). Exam trap Promoting vaccination is primary prevention (JEMAS 2025). Treating a diagnosed illness, surgery for chronic disease and rehabilitation after injury come later (secondary or tertiary). Caplan's levels say when you intervene; Gordon's types say whom you target. Crisis intervention and suicide prevention Key study: Lindemann and the Cocoanut Grove fire (1944) On 28 November 1942 a fire at Boston's Cocoanut Grove nightclub killed 492 people. Erich Lindemann interviewed 101 bereaved people and in 1944 described acute grief as a syndrome (bodily distress, preoccupation with the dead, guilt, hostility) that most work through within weeks by "grief work", while some develop delayed or distorted grief. Timely brief help, he concluded, could prevent lasting disorder: the seed of crisis intervention. Criticism: impressionistic data and too short a time course for grief. Caplan defined a crisis as an obstacle to important life goals that is, for a time, insurmountable by customary problem solving, followed by disorganisation; it usually resolves, for better or worse, within four to six weeks. Crises are developmental (retirement) or situational. Situational events are large-scale (floods, earthquakes, tornadoes) or small-scale, striking one person or family: violence (child abuse, domestic abuse, crime), psychopathology that triggers a crisis (a suicide attempt, an overdose) and personal catastrophe (a car accident, a life-threatening illness). Crisis intervention is brief, active, directive and focused on the here and now, aiming to restore previous functioning. Its stance is supportive therapy (listening, reassurance, problem solving, mobilising support), not exploratory work, and it is often named the treatment of choice for adjustment disorder (Chapter 8), a short reaction to an identifiable stressor. Albert Roberts 's seven stages are: assess lethality, establish rapport, identify the major problems, deal with feelings, explore alternatives, make an action plan, and follow up. Suicide risk is assessed by asking directly about thoughts, plans and means (Chapter 2). The safety plan of Barbara Stanley and Gregory Brown (2012) is a written list of warning signs, coping strategies, distracting people and places, people to ask for help, professionals and crisis lines, and ways to make the environment safe. Means restriction (pesticide bans cut suicides sharply in Sri Lanka), gatekeeper training for teachers and police, and helplines such as Tele-MANAS (14416) work at population level. After disasters, psychological first aid (World Health Organization, 2011) offers practical support: look (for safety and needs), listen (without forcing talk), link (to services and loved ones). It replaced critical incident stress debriefing ( Jeffrey Mitchell , 1983), a single group session retelling the event, which does not prevent post-traumatic stress disorder and may harm (Cochrane review), so it is not recommended. Trauma-informed care (US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2014) asks services to realise, recognise and respond to trauma and to resist re-traumatising people. Exam trap Crisis management needs supportive therapy (IHBAS 2020), not acceptance and commitment, expressive or cognitive behaviour therapy. A tornado or flood is a large-scale event; personal events are small-scale. Rehabilitation Rehabilitation aims at function and a valued life, not cure. Psychosocial rehabilitation of severe mental illness offers a ladder of services (Table 7.25); its vocational rehabilitation rungs, sheltered workshops and supported employment, aim at paid work. Service What it offers Day care Daytime treatment and activity; the person sleeps at home Halfway house Supervised transitional home between hospital and independent living Sheltered workshop Paid work in a protected setting Supported employment A real job first, then support on the job (place, then train) Assertive community treatment Mobile team, about 10 clients per worker, round the clock Social skills training Modelling, role play, feedback and homework Family psychoeducation Teaches families about the illness, lowers expressed emotion and relapse Clubhouse model Member-run community with a work-ordered day (Fountain House, New York, 1948) Leonard Stein and Mary Ann Test (1980, Madison, Wisconsin) randomly assigned patients to community treatment instead of hospital; they spent less time in hospital and worked more. This became assertive community treatment . Case management links a person with long-term, complex needs to services and coordinates them; it seeks skill training, environmental accommodations and empowerment, never cure. Its models are often contrasted as provider-driven, in which the agency sets the client's tasks and the worker controls access to services, and client-driven, in which the worker allies with the client in advocacy and empowerment. After brain injury, neuropsychological rehabilitation takes two routes. The restorative approach retrains the damaged function by graded practice (cognitive retraining), as in the attention process training of McKay Moore Sohlberg and Catherine Mateer (1987), which drills sustained, selective, alternating and divided attention. The compensatory approach works around the deficit with memory aids (diaries, alarms, phone reminders). Errorless learning ( Alan Baddeley and Barbara Wilson , 1994) prevents mistakes during learning, because amnesic patients cannot remember, and so cannot correct, their errors. For substance users, detoxification (medically managed withdrawal) is only the start. G. Alan Marlatt and Judith Gordon 's relapse prevention (1985) sees relapse as failed coping in a high-risk situation (negative emotions, interpersonal conflict, social pressure). Coping raises self-efficacy; without it, self-efficacy falls, a lapse (first use) follows, and the abstinence violation effect , the guilt and "I have blown it" thinking after one slip, turns the lapse into relapse. Clients rehearse coping and treat lapses as lessons. Therapeutic communities , from Synanon (California, 1958), use the community itself (peer confrontation, graded responsibility, mutual help) as the method of change. The Rehabilitation Council of India, a statutory body under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, regulates the training and registration of rehabilitation professionals, including clinical psychologists; disability certification under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 is covered in Section 7.1. Exam trap Case management aims at function, skills, environmental accommodation and empowerment, not cure (RML 2020). The same paper's "task or role performance" model (structure-function theory at the organisational level; fiduciary and humanitarian obligations; authority to provide, deny or withdraw services as the client complies with tasks) is, whatever its label, provider-driven, so the exception is the power alliance with the client, a client-driven idea. The Rehabilitation Council of India is under Social Justice and Empowerment, not Health, Education or Labour. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Alexander's holy seven include peptic ulcer, essential hypertension and bronchial . Caplan's prevention lowers the number of new cases. Psychological first aid rests on look, listen and .
