Answers: (1) medicine, (2) control, (3) asthma, (4) primary, (5) link, (6) violation. 7.10 Working with Children, Older Adults and Special Settings Lower yield · 16 Qs Most therapies in this chapter assume an adult who talks and who chose to come. Many clients do not fit: a six-year-old who will not discuss his bed-wetting but will bury a toy tiger in a sand tray; a grandmother who asks each evening when her dead husband is coming home; a youth whose lawyer asks whether he was "of unsound mind". This section adapts therapy to them. Children as clients, and play therapy Children differ from adult clients. Their developmental level limits what therapy can ask, so clinicians work through play and parents; adults make the referral; and school is a second home. Assessment is therefore multi-informant assessment (parents, teachers, the child, observation in clinic, home and class), not because parents over-report or teachers lack information but because symptoms vary across contexts : a child with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may be calm in a quiet clinic and unmanageable in a class of fifty. Clinic observation alone falls short for the same reason. Play therapy uses the child's natural language. Melanie Klein (1882 to 1960) treated play as the equivalent of free association and interpreted it early and deeply; Anna Freud (1895 to 1982) began with a preparatory phase to win trust, involved parents and gave the analyst an educative role. Virginia Axline (1911 to 1988) carried Carl Rogers' ideas into the playroom ( Play Therapy , 1947; Dibs: In Search of Self , 1964). Her non-directive play therapy rests on eight principles: build warm rapport; accept the child exactly as he is; create permissiveness so that feelings flow freely; recognise feelings and reflect them back; respect the child's ability to solve his own problems; let the child lead; do not hurry; and set only the limits that anchor therapy to reality. Table 7.26 lists later forms, including filial therapy and sandplay . Table 7.26 Later forms of play therapy. Approach Founder Core idea Relationship play therapy Clark Moustakas (1950s) The living relationship itself heals Child-centred play therapy Garry Landreth The modern form of Axline's model Filial therapy Bernard Guerney and Louise Guerney (1964) Parents are trained to hold the play sessions at home Sandplay Dora Kalff (1950s), from Margaret Lowenfeld 's World Technique (late 1920s) The child builds a scene in a sand tray with miniatures; Jungian Exam trap Axline is Rogerian, not Freudian. Klein, not Anna Freud, equated play with free association. Sandplay is Kalff's; the World Technique is Lowenfeld's. In filial therapy parents run the sessions. Parent training and behaviour change at home and school Why does defiance worsen in loving homes? Gerald Patterson (1926 to 2016) answered with coercion theory ( Coercive Family Process , 1982). A mother orders the television off, her son screams, and she gives in. His screaming is negatively reinforced (the demand goes away), and so is her giving in (the screaming stops; Figure 7.17). Each trains the other, and the exchanges escalate. 1. Parent gives a command 2. Child screams 3. Parent gives in 4. Screaming stops Child reinforced: demand removed Parent reinforced: screaming ends Figure 7.17 Patterson's coercion cycle. Both sides are negatively reinforced, so each round makes the next tantrum likelier. The treatment, parent management training (PMT), reverses the trap. Parents give clear commands, attend to and praise good behaviour and reward it on a token chart, ignore minor misbehaviour ( extinction ; expect a brief extinction burst), and use time-out and response cost (Section 7.4). Named programmes include Russell Barkley 's Defiant Children (1987); Carolyn Webster-Stratton 's Incredible Years, which teaches parent groups with videotaped scenes; and Sheila Eyberg 's parent-child interaction therapy (PCIT, ages two to seven), which coaches the parent live through an earpiece, first in child-directed play, then in discipline. At school, teachers add token economies (Section 7.4) and the daily report card: the teacher rates a few target behaviours daily and the child earns rewards at home. For repetitive aggression, often in autism or intellectual disability, Richard Foxx and Nathan Azrin devised overcorrection : restoring the damaged scene to better than before (restitution) and rehearsing the correct act (positive practice). For anxious children of 7 to 13, Philip Kendall 's 16-session Coping Cat (1990) teaches the FEAR plan (Feeling frightened? Expecting bad things? Attitudes and actions that help; Results and rewards), then graded exposure. Family work (Section 7.7) runs through all of these. Exam trap Deliberately ignoring tantrums is extinction ; some keys wrongly mark "operant escape". Escape (ending an aversive stimulus already present) and avoidance (preventing it) are negative reinforcement, which strengthens behaviour. Nor is negative reinforcement a PMT technique; PMT breaks that trap. Elimination problems, school refusal and ADHD Enuresis (wetting from age five) is treated best with the bell-and-pad of O. Hobart Mowrer and Willie Mae Mowrer (1938): urine completes a circuit and rings a bell until bladder tension alone wakes the child, and overlearning cuts relapse. Encopresis (soiling from age four) is usually retentive, with constipation and overflow; laxatives are combined with scheduled toilet sitting and rewards. In school refusal the child refuses out of anxiety, with the parents' knowledge; in truancy the child hides the absence, shows no anxiety and often has conduct problems. Christopher Kearney and Wendy Silverman classified refusal by its function: avoiding distress caused by school, escaping social or evaluative situations, seeking the parents' attention, or gaining tangible rewards outside school. Treatment centres on an early, graded return to school. Key study: the MTA study (1999) The US National Institute of Mental Health randomly assigned 579 children with ADHD, aged 7 to 9, to 14 months of managed medication, intensive behavioural treatment, both, or community care. Medication and the combination beat the others on core symptoms; the combination added small social and family gains at lower doses. Criticism: the advantage faded after the trial. Hence the rule: behavioural treatment plus medication. Autism, intellectual disability and learning disability Autism was first described in 1943 by Leo Kanner (1894 to 1981) of Johns Hopkins, in eleven children with extreme aloneness and an anxious insistence on sameness (the disorder is in Chapter 8). Treatment is early and behavioural, based on applied behaviour analysis (ABA), which applies operant principles to socially important behaviour. Ole Ivar Lovaas (1927 to 2010), at the University of California, Los Angeles, pioneered early intensive behavioural intervention using discrete trial training : a skill is broken into small steps, each taught in repeated trials (instruction, response, prompt, reinforcement), with prompts faded. In functional communication training, a child whose tantrums serve to escape demands learns an acceptable substitute, such as handing over a picture card that says "break". Table 7.27 lists other programmes. Key study: Lovaas (1987) Nineteen autistic children under four received about 40 hours a week of one-to-one behavioural treatment for two years or more. Nine (47 percent) reached normal intellectual and educational functioning, against 2 percent of controls; a 1993 follow-up found the gains kept. Criticism: no random assignment, a narrow outcome measure, and early use of aversives. Table 7.27 Other named programmes for autism. India's National Trust Act 1999 covers exactly four conditions (autism, cerebral palsy, mental retardation, multiple disabilities) and provides legal guardians. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (Section 7.1) lists 21 disabilities, including intellectual disability, specific learning disabilities and autism, but not ADHD. Autism is certified with the 40-item Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (ISAA), developed in 2009 by the National Institute for the Mentally Handicapped (now NIEPID): each item is rated 1 to 5 across six domains, a total of 70 or more indicates autism, and the total grades severity (above 153 is severe) and the disability percentage. Specific learning disability is treated by remedial teaching with multisensory methods, such as Orton-Gillingham phonics and Grace Fernald 's tracing method (see, say, hear and trace each word), plus accommodations: extra time, a scribe, exemption from a third language. Exam trap Kanner (1943) first described infantile autism; Hans Asperger (1944) described more able children, and Eugen Bleuler coined "autism" in 1911 for withdrawal in schizophrenia. The Indian autism tool is the ISAA ; some keys mark the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), which is American (Schopler). The CBCL is Thomas Achenbach 's Child Behavior Checklist; the CGAS rates global functioning. Child abuse, POCSO and the adolescent client Child abuse (physical, sexual, emotional, neglect) entered medicine with C. Henry Kempe 's "battered child syndrome" (1962). Safety and reporting come first. The best-supported therapy is trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (TF-CBT) of Judith Cohen , Anthony Mannarino and Esther Deblinger , for ages 3 to 18, with a non-offending parent. Its PRACTICE components (psychoeducation, relaxation, affect modulation, cognitive coping, trauma narrative, in vivo mastery, conjoint sessions, safety) build coping skills first, but the central goal is the trauma narrative: retelling the trauma desensitises the memories and corrects beliefs such as "it was my fault". (Emotion regulation and mindfulness skills define dialectical behaviour therapy, Section 7.5.) Indian context The POCSO Act 2012 (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) covers everyone under 18 and is gender-neutral. Reporting is mandatory (section 19): anyone, psychologists included, who knows of an offence or fears one is likely must inform the Special Juvenile Police Unit or the local police, and failing to do so is punishable under section 21 (up to six months' imprisonment, a fine or both). It also sets up Special Courts and child-friendly procedures. Adolescence, Erik Erikson's stage of identity versus role confusion (Chapter 6), is the peak age for risk behaviour such as substance use, unsafe sex and self-harm. Anna Freud and Peter Blos held that healthy teenagers must detach from parents; research now shows that continuing interdependence is healthy, so parents remain allies. Engagement comes first: be collaborative and see the teenager alone for part of each session. The limits of confidentiality with minors are explained at the start: privacy holds except for risk to life, abuse or legal duties such as POCSO, and the teenager is told before anything is shared; guardians give consent. Schools offer counsellors and WHO life skills education. Adolescent depression is treated with CBT or interpersonal psychotherapy, adding fluoxetine with monitoring for suicidal thinking; self-harm calls for a safety plan, restricted means, family involvement and adolescent dialectical behaviour therapy. Older adults: dementia care, depression and capacity The field of geropsychology applies clinical psychology to older adults. Robert Butler (1927 to 2010) coined "ageism" (1969) and described reminiscence as a healthy life review (1963). In India families, mostly women, give most dementia care; their caregiver burden , objective (time, money) and subjective (distress, guilt), is measured with the Zarit Burden Interview and eased by psychoeducation, behaviour-management training, support groups and respite. Life review, unlike plain reminiscence, is evaluative and covers the whole life. Late-life depression often shows as bodily, sleep and memory complaints rather than sadness. Depressive pseudodementia mimics dementia, but it begins abruptly, the person complains of poor memory and answers "I don't know", and it lifts with treatment. The 30-item Geriatric Depression Scale ( Jerome Yesavage ) omits bodily symptoms. CBT, problem-solving therapy, antidepressants and electroconvulsive therapy all help. A person's decision-making capacity is presumed, and judged for one decision at one time. Paul Appelbaum and Thomas Grisso (1988) named four abilities: to understand the information, appreciate how it applies to oneself, reason about the options and communicate a choice. India's Mental Healthcare Act 2017 uses a similar test. Counselling and career guidance Guidance helps people make educational and vocational choices through information, tests and advice. Counselling is a face-to-face relationship that helps a basically healthy person resolve a problem of living and reach his own decision. Psychotherapy treats more disturbed clients, longer and deeper (Section 7.6). Counselling is called the heart of the guidance programme, and its instrument, the interview, was called the heart of the counselling process by Ruth Strang . Other tools are the cumulative record (a school-long file of each pupil's background, health, tests and achievement), the case study (an in-depth picture of one pupil drawn from all sources) and tests. Exam trap One key names the aptitude test "the heart of the guidance programme". The sources are not uniform: Indian guidance texts give that title to counselling, Strang gave "heart of the counselling process" to the interview, and a few lesser sources use similar words for the cumulative record, but no standard text found gives it to the aptitude test, which only predicts trainability. If counselling is not offered, choose the interview, and expect some keys to differ. Frank Parsons (1854 to 1908), father of vocational guidance, set out the trait-factor approach in Choosing a Vocation (1909): know yourself, know the world of work, and match them by "true reasoning". The counselling process runs from relationship building through assessment, goals and intervention to termination (microskills are in Section 7.2). Areas include school, career, marital, rehabilitation, de-addiction, grief and HIV counselling (before and after testing, under the five Cs: consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct results, connection to care). Affirmative therapy for LGBTQ+ clients affirms their identities, addresses minority stress and rejects conversion therapy, which India's National Medical Commission called professional misconduct in 2022. John Holland (1919 to 2008) sorted people and work environments into six RIASEC types (Figure 7.18); satisfaction follows from congruence between person and environment. Donald Super (1910 to 1994), in his life-span, life-space theory , saw a career as lifelong self-concept implementation through five stages (growth to 14, exploration to 24, establishment to 44, maintenance to 64, then decline) and many life roles, drawn as the Life-Career Rainbow; readiness for choice is career maturity. Neighbouring types are most alike; opposite types (Realistic and Social) are least alike. Forensic clinical psychology Forensic psychology answers legal questions for a client that is often the court, so confidentiality is limited. An accused must have competence to stand trial : the present ability to understand the proceedings and help his lawyer ( Dusky v. United States , 1960). Criminal responsibility concerns his mind at the offence: the insanity defence (Table 7.29). It began in 1843, when Daniel M'Naghten , deluded that he was persecuted, shot Prime Minister Robert Peel's secretary; his acquittal produced the M'Naghten rules , which section 84 of the Indian Penal Code (now section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023) follows. Irresistible impulse: could he control ? ALI: both, softened to "substantial capacity". Durham: was the act a product of illness? India's section 84 is M'Naghten-based. Competence concerns the mind at trial; insanity, the mind at the offence. Risk assessment predicts violence or reoffending; unaided clinical prediction was right in at most one case in three ( John Monahan , 1981), so structured tools such as the HCR-20 and Robert Hare 's Psychopathy Checklist-Revised are used. Custody evaluation follows the best interests of the child (in India, the child's welfare, under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890). An expert witness, unlike others, may give opinions (Section 45, Indian Evidence Act 1872; now Section 39, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023). The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015 sends a child in conflict with law to a Juvenile Justice Board and a child in need of care and protection to a Child Welfare Committee. A 16- to 18-year-old accused of a heinous offence (minimum seven years' imprisonment) may, after the Board's preliminary assessment of his mental and physical capacity to commit the offence and his grasp of its consequences, with psychologists' help, be tried as an adult. In correctional psychology, effective offender programmes follow the risk-need-responsivity model of Donald Andrews and James Bonta (intensity matched to risk, criminogenic needs targeted, cognitive-behavioural methods) and are community-based. The cognitive interview of Ronald Fisher and Edward Geiselman , which aids eyewitness recall, and offender profiling, which infers an unknown offender's traits from the crime, are investigative tools, not treatments. Neuropsychology, creative therapies and telepsychology Clinical neuropsychology, which assesses the effects of brain damage on behaviour, is covered in Chapters 2 and 5; rehabilitation psychology is in Section 7.9. Art therapy has two founders: Margaret Naumburg (1890 to 1983) treated art as symbolic speech from the unconscious (art psychotherapy), and Edith Kramer (1916 to 2014) held that the creative process heals through sublimation (art as therapy). Music therapy uses listening and making music; dance and movement therapy (founded by Marian Chace , 1896 to 1970) uses movement and mirroring; drama therapy uses role play (psychodrama is in Section 7.7); bibliotherapy is guided reading. Modern animal-assisted therapy began in the 1960s with Boris Levinson (1907 to 1984), whose dog Jingles drew a withdrawn child into talk. In India yoga and meditation are common adjuncts, and NIMHANS trials support yoga in schizophrenia and depression. Telepsychology delivers care by phone, video, messaging or apps. Guided internet CBT rivals face-to-face CBT for depression and anxiety, while apps vary widely in quality. The Unchaining at Bicêtre, Revisited Look back at Bicêtre with what this chapter has taught. Pinel, recording his cases and counting recoveries, was a scientist-practitioner a century and a half before Boulder, and his case notes were ancestors of the interview, mental status examination and formulation of section 7.2. Pussin's conversations and routines anticipated what outcome research found in section 7.8: much of what heals in psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive and humanistic therapy alike is the relationship and the other common factors. Chapter summary 7.1 The Profession: History, Models, Ethics and Indian Law. Clinical psychology joins science and practice to understand, predict and relieve distress; in India it rests on an RCI-recognised qualification and RCI registration. Care moved from supernatural ideas and the humours through the asylums to Pinel and Pussin's moral treatment , Dix and Beers. Witmer opened the first clinic (1896); Boulder (1949) set the scientist-practitioner model and Vail (1973) the PsyD. In India the IACP dates from 1968 and the RCI Act from 1992. Engel's biopsychosocial and the diathesis-stress models integrate the older models. Ethics rests on five APA principles, consent, confidentiality and its limits (Tarasoff) and boundaries; the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 adds rights, advance directives and section 115. 7.2 The Clinical Interview, Mental Status Examination and Formulation. The clinical interview may be intake, diagnostic, crisis or termination, and unstructured, semi-structured (SCID, PSE and SCAN, K-SADS, ADIS) or fully structured (DIS): structure buys reliability, not validity. Microskills include SOLER attending, open questions, furthering, paraphrasing and reflection of feeling. The case history runs from identifying data to premorbid personality. The MSE records appearance, speech, mood (subjective) and affect (objective), the stream, form, content and possession of thought, perception, cognition and insight (six grades). SAD PERSONS aids memory but cannot predict suicide. Functional analysis (ABC, SORC) is operant. A formulation (5 Ps, biopsychosocial) explains, a diagnosis classifies; kappa measures diagnostic reliability, and Rosenhan (1973) exposed labelling. 7.3 Psychodynamic Therapies and Their Descendants. Psychodynamic therapies hold that unconscious conflict drives symptoms. Freud's psychoanalysis grew from Breuer's cathartic method with Anna O.; it relies on the fundamental rule and free association , dream analysis, interpretation, analysis of resistance and of transference and countertransference , and working through , under neutrality and abstinence. Ego psychology, object relations (Klein, Winnicott, Mahler, Kernberg), Kohut's self psychology and mentalisation-based treatment changed what analysts listen for. Brief dynamic therapies (Malan, Sifneos, Davanloo, Mann, Luborsky, Strupp and Binder) and Klerman and Weissman's interpersonal psychotherapy shortened treatment. Jung, Adler, Horney, Sullivan and Berne's transactional analysis offered rival techniques, alongside supportive therapy, hypnosis and narcoanalysis. 7.4 Behaviour Therapy. Behaviour therapy applies learning principles to problem behaviour. Spurred by Eysenck's 1952 critique, it grew from Wolpe's Johannesburg, the Maudsley and Skinner's operant work, and every case starts with a functional analysis. Classical techniques include Jones's counterconditioning, Wolpe's systematic desensitisation (reciprocal inhibition, a SUDS-rated hierarchy), flooding, implosion, exposure and response prevention for OCD, aversion therapy, covert sensitisation, the bell and pad and the debated EMDR. Operant techniques build behaviour (shaping, chaining, the Premack principle, Ayllon and Azrin's token economy) or reduce it (extinction, time-out, response cost, overcorrection), as in ABA for autism. Modelling, assertiveness, relaxation, biofeedback, habit reversal, behavioural activation, insomnia methods and parent training complete the toolkit. 7.5 Cognitive and Cognitive-Behavioural Therapies, and the Third Wave. Cognitive-behavioural therapies hold that emotional disturbance follows mainly from how people interpret events. Albert Ellis's REBT (1955; renamed 1993) uses the ABC model, disputes irrational musts and aims at unconditional self-acceptance. Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy targets the cognitive triad, core and intermediate beliefs, automatic thoughts and distortions through collaborative empiricism, Socratic questioning and the thought record. Meichenbaum's stress inoculation, problem-solving and multimodal therapy, Kelly's fixed-role therapy, Young's schema therapy and disorder-specific models for panic, trauma and psychosis followed. The third wave (DBT, ACT, MBSR, MBCT, CFT, MCT, FAP, behavioural activation) changes the relationship to thoughts. CBT is the most researched psychotherapy, now also delivered online. 7.6 Humanistic, Existential, Experiential and Brief Therapies. Carl Rogers 's person-centred therapy holds that conditions of worth create incongruence between self-concept and experience, and that six necessary and sufficient conditions, above all empathy, unconditional positive regard and congruence , are enough for change. Fritz Perls 's Gestalt therapy works on here-and-now awareness, unfinished business and the empty chair . Existential therapists (Binswanger, Boss, May, Yalom) confront death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness, and Frankl 's logotherapy rests on the will to meaning. Reality, focusing, emotion-focused, positive, narrative and solution-focused therapies follow. Motivational interviewing (Miller and Rollnick) resolves ambivalence alongside Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change, and Ivey, Carkhuff and Egan model the helping skills. 7.7 Family, Couples and Group Therapies. Family therapy grew from general systems theory : families keep homeostasis through feedback, causality is circular, and the identified patient signals a troubled system. Theories that families cause schizophrenia (the schizophrenogenic mother, Bateson's double bind , Lidz's schism and skew, Wynne's pseudomutuality) failed, but high expressed emotion predicts relapse, which psychoeducation reduces. Bowen stressed differentiation and triangles, Minuchin boundaries, Haley directives and paradox, the MRI second-order change, the Milan team circular questioning. Couples work runs from behavioural therapy to Gottman's four horsemen; Masters and Johnson founded sex therapy. Groups heal through Yalom's eleven factors; Moreno created psychodrama and Maxwell Jones the therapeutic community. 7.8 Does Psychotherapy Work? Evidence, Common Factors and the Alliance. Eysenck (1952) claimed that about two-thirds of neurotic patients improve without therapy ( spontaneous remission ); Smith and Glass's meta-analysis (1977, effect size 0.68; 0.85 in 1980) answered him. Rival therapies tie (the dodo bird verdict : Rosenzweig 1936; Luborsky and colleagues 1975), which points to common factors: Frank's Persuasion and Healing (1961), Wampold's contextual model, Lambert's pie and Bordin's alliance of goals, tasks and bond. Outcome is tested in efficacy and effectiveness studies, RCTs with waiting-list, placebo-attention and usual-care controls, EST criteria and evidence-based practice (APA 2006), and judged by the dose-effect curve and the reliable change index. Integration, culturally adapted therapy (Neki's guru-chela relationship), supervision and self-care complete the picture. 7.9 Health, Community, Crisis and Rehabilitation Psychology. Health psychology (Matarazzo, 1980) is psychology's contribution to health; behavioural medicine (Schwartz and Weiss, 1978) is interdisciplinary. Parsons's sick role carries two rights and two duties. The health belief model, the theory of planned behaviour and protection motivation theory explain health behaviour and adherence. Alexander's holy seven, Type A hostility, Fordyce's operant pain treatment, CBT for insomnia and the AUDIT link mind and body; Kübler-Ross and Worden describe dying and grief. Caplan supplied prevention levels, consultation and crisis theory: crisis work is brief and supportive, and debriefing is not recommended. Rehabilitation uses assertive community treatment, case management, errorless learning and relapse prevention. 7.10 Working with Children, Older Adults and Special Settings. Children are assessed through several informants because symptoms vary across contexts , and treated with play therapy (Klein, Anna Freud, Axline's non-directive principles, filial therapy, sandplay), parent management training built on Patterson's coercion theory , the bell-and-pad for enuresis, behavioural treatment plus medication for ADHD (the MTA study) and applied behaviour analysis for autism (Lovaas 1987). TF-CBT treats abuse, and the POCSO Act 2012 makes reporting mandatory. Dementia care uses reality orientation, reminiscence, life review, validation and cognitive stimulation therapy. Holland's RIASEC and Super's life-span, life-space theory guide careers.
