Perinatal causes include asphyxia and extreme prematurity; postnatal ones, meningitis, encephalitis, lead, head injury and severe deprivation. Communication disorders Language disorder is persistent difficulty acquiring and using language: small vocabulary, simple sentences, poor discourse. Speech sound disorder is difficulty producing speech sounds, making speech hard to understand, without a physical cause such as cleft palate or deafness. Childhood-onset fluency disorder (stuttering) breaks the flow of speech with repetitions, prolongations, broken words and blocks; 80 to 90 percent of cases begin by age 6. Social (pragmatic) communication disorder is difficulty using language socially (adjusting to the listener, taking turns, grasping hints and idioms) without the repetitive behaviour of autism. Ask why a child does not communicate. In mutism , as in an inherently mute person, there is no capacity for speech: language itself is the barrier. In selective mutism , an anxiety disorder (Section 8.6), the child speaks at home but not in feared settings, so anxiety is the barrier. In autism the barrier is the social use of language; in specific learning disorder, reading and writing. Autism spectrum disorder Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) coined autism (Greek autos , self) in 1911 for the withdrawal seen in schizophrenia. In 1943 Leo Kanner (1894 to 1981) published "Autistic disturbances of affective contact", on eleven children with extreme aloneness and insistence on sameness, and soon called the condition early infantile autism . In 1944 Hans Asperger (1906 to 1980) described boys with fluent speech but odd social behaviour and narrow interests. Bruno Bettelheim 's (1903 to 1990) "refrigerator mother" theory (1967) blamed cold parenting; it was discredited when autism proved largely genetic. Lorna Wing (1928 to 2014) and Judith Gould (1979) described a triad of impairments : social interaction, communication and imagination. DSM-5 (2013) merged autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, PDD-NOS and childhood disintegrative disorder (two or more years of normal development, then loss of skills; Theodor Heller , 1908) into autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Rett syndrome ( Andreas Rett , 1966) was left out as a genetic condition (MECP2): girls regress after early normal development, losing speech and hand use, with hand-wringing. Criterion A : persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, in all three of social-emotional reciprocity, nonverbal communication (eye contact, gesture) and relationships. Criterion B : restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour , interests or activities, at least two of stereotyped movements or speech (hand-flapping, lining up toys, echolalia or echoing others' words), insistence on sameness, intense restricted interests, and sensory hyper- or hyporeactivity. Symptoms start early (though they may show only as social demands rise) and impair functioning. Severity is rated per domain: level 1 "requiring support", level 2 "requiring substantial support", level 3 "requiring very substantial support". Specifiers note accompanying intellectual impairment or language impairment, a known genetic or medical condition, and catatonia; many former Asperger's cases are now ASD without either impairment. Exam trap ASD needs social-communication deficits plus repetitive behaviour; delayed speech alone, IQ below 70 and hyperactivity are not required. No eye contact, delayed language and repetitive movements spell ASD, not ADHD, conduct disorder or SLD. Kanner first described infantile autism; Bleuler only coined the word, and Kurt Schneider (Section 8.4) and Cameron, Goldstein and Jaspers (Section 8.2) are distractors. The research deficit is in encoding social cues ; trouble deceiving follows from mindblindness, and anger control and memory retrieval are not core deficits. ASD affects about 1 to 2 percent of people, three to four males per female (DSM-5-TR says 3:1; girls are under-recognised). Outside the communication disorders themselves, language development is compromised more often in ASD than in any other neurodevelopmental disorder. The commonest co-occurring conditions are intellectual disability and ADHD (diagnosable alongside ASD only since DSM-5), then anxiety, depression and epilepsy. Heritability is about 80 percent (estimates 37 to over 90); some cases carry de novo (new, uninherited) mutations, and older parents, extreme prematurity and prenatal valproate add risk. Autistic people show deficits in encoding social cues such as faces, gaze and tone of voice, and find deliberate deception hard, while rote memory is often a strength. Simon Baron-Cohen (born 1958), Alan Leslie and Uta Frith (born 1941) proposed a deficit in theory of mind (Chapter 6), or "mindblindness". Frith's weak central coherence (1989) is a bias to detail over the whole; executive dysfunction explains rigidity; Baron-Cohen's extreme male brain theory casts autism as strong systemising with weak empathising. Key study: the Sally-Anne test (1985) Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith tested 20 autistic, 14 Down syndrome and 27 typical children. Sally puts a marble in her basket and leaves; Anne moves it to her box. Where will Sally look? About 85 percent of typical and Down syndrome children said the basket; 80 percent of autistic children, despite higher verbal mental age than the Down group, said the box, failing to represent Sally's false belief. Criticism: a fifth passed, the deficit is not unique to autism, and it cannot explain repetitive behaviour. In 1998 Andrew Wakefield linked the MMR vaccine to autism in a 12-child Lancet paper; it was retracted in 2010, he was struck off the medical register, and large studies find no link. Treatment is behavioural and educational: Ivar Lovaas 's applied behaviour analysis (1987), TEACCH and PECS (Sections 7.4 and 7.10). Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder In 1902 George Frederic Still (1868 to 1941) described restless, inattentive children with a "defect of moral control". Later labels were minimal brain dysfunction, hyperkinetic reaction of childhood (DSM-II, 1968), attention deficit disorder (DSM-III, 1980) and ADHD (DSM-III-R, 1987). ICD-10's hyperkinetic disorder (F90) is overactivity, distractibility, short attention span and impulsivity; social withdrawal is not a feature. DSM-5-TR attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) needs six of nine inattention and/or six of nine hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (Table 8.11; five from age 17) for at least 6 months; several present before age 12 (DSM-IV: 7) and in two or more settings; and impairment. The presentation is combined, predominantly inattentive or predominantly hyperactive-impulsive. Table 8.11 The 18 DSM-5-TR symptoms of ADHD (each "often"). Inattention (A1) Hyperactivity-impulsivity (A2) Careless mistakes Fidgets or squirms Cannot sustain attention Leaves seat Does not seem to listen when spoken to directly Runs about or climbs Does not follow through Cannot play quietly Disorganised "On the go", "driven by a motor" Avoids sustained mental effort Talks excessively Loses things Blurts out answers Easily distracted Cannot wait turn Forgetful Interrupts or intrudes Exam trap "Does not seem to listen when spoken to" is an inattention item; squirming, not playing quietly and talking excessively are hyperactivity items. The onset age is now 12, not 7. ADHD is not a learning disability (dyslexia, dysgraphia and auditory processing disorder are), though the two often co-occur. About 7 percent of children and 2.5 percent of adults have ADHD, boys about twice as often as girls; hyperactivity fades, but inattention and impulsivity often persist into adulthood. Heritability is about 74 percent. Dopamine and noradrenaline in frontostriatal circuits are implicated; risks include prenatal smoking and alcohol and low birth weight. Russell Barkley 's (born 1949) behavioural inhibition model (1997) makes poor response inhibition the core deficit. Stimulants such as methylphenidate are first-line drugs, with the non-stimulant atomoxetine as the main alternative (Section 7.10). Specific learning disorder DSM-5 merged reading, mathematics and written expression disorders into one specific learning disorder (SLD): difficulty in reading, spelling, writing or mathematics persisting at least 6 months despite targeted intervention , achievement well below age expectation on standardised tests, onset in the school years, and no better explanation in intellectual disability, sensory loss or poor teaching. Intelligence is usually average (IQ above about 70 plus or minus 5), hence "unexpected underachievement". It affects 5 to 15 percent of schoolchildren. The specifiers are impairment in reading (word-reading accuracy, fluency and comprehension), whose core pattern of poor word recognition, decoding and spelling is called dyslexia ; in written expression, often called dysgraphia ; and in mathematics, dyscalculia . The Glasgow eye surgeon James Hinshelwood (1859 to 1919) described "congenital word-blindness" (a book of that title in 1917), and Samuel Torrey Orton (1879 to 1948) in the 1920s blamed incomplete cerebral dominance. The modern phonological deficit theory locates dyslexia in linking speech sounds (phonemes) to letters. The old IQ-achievement discrepancy model waited for a child to fail; response to intervention (RTI) identifies children who do not respond to good teaching. Auditory processing disorder , difficulty interpreting heard sounds despite normal hearing, is grouped with the learning difficulties though DSM-5-TR omits it. India's RPwD Act 2016 covers specific learning disabilities (Section 7.1). Exam trap SLD means roughly average intelligence with persistent academic difficulty; IQ below 50 points to intellectual disability, "only attention deficit" to ADHD and "motor coordination deficit only" to dyspraxia. Dyslexia is difficulty reading and decoding words, not understanding speech (language disorder) or concentrating in lectures (ADHD). Motor disorders and tics Developmental coordination disorder ( dyspraxia ) is impaired acquisition and execution of coordinated motor skills: clumsiness and slowness in catching, using scissors, handwriting or cycling, without a neurological cause. It differs from syndromes acquired through brain damage (Chapter 5): apraxia , loss of learned purposeful movement despite intact strength; agnosia , failure to recognise despite intact sensation; anomia , inability to name. Stereotypic movement disorder is repetitive, driven, purposeless movement (rocking, head-banging, self-biting), with or without self-injury. A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic motor movement or vocalisation (blinking, shrugging, sniffing, throat-clearing). Seizures are abnormal electrical discharges that cannot be held back, dissociation disrupts consciousness or identity (Section 8.7), and Parkinson's tremor is rhythmic. Tics are often preceded by a premonitory urge and can be briefly suppressed; they begin at 4 to 6 years and peak at 10 to 12. All tic disorders need onset before 18 (Table 8.12). Tourette's disorder was described in 1885 by Georges Gilles de la Tourette (1857 to 1904); coprolalia (involuntary obscenities) occurs in a minority and is not required. Tics often accompany OCD and ADHD; habit reversal training treats them (Section 7.4). Table 8.12 The DSM-5-TR tic disorders. Schizophrenia is the central psychotic disorder; its neighbours differ from it mainly in duration. We follow the concept's history, symptoms, criteria, causes and drug treatment. From dementia praecox to schizophrenia In the 1850s the French physician Benedict Morel (1809 to 1873) used démence précoce , early loss of mind, for young patients who deteriorated. Ewald Hecker described hebephrenia (silly, disorganised behaviour beginning in youth) in 1871, and Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum described catatonia (stupor, posturing and excitement) in 1874. Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926) united these pictures, with paranoid forms, under the Latin dementia praecox , 'premature dementia', in 1893. In the sixth edition of his textbook (1899) he separated it from manic-depressive insanity by course: dementia praecox began early and deteriorated, while manic-depressive insanity came in episodes with recovery between them. These two clinical types still divide Sections 8.4 and 8.5. Despite the name, dementia praecox is the ancestor of schizophrenia, not of Alzheimer's disease or frontotemporal dementia (Section 8.10). The Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) saw that not every patient deteriorated or fell ill young. In a 1908 lecture and his 1911 monograph, Dementia Praecox or the Group of Schizophrenias , he coined schizophrenia (Greek schizein , to split, and phren , mind) for a splitting between thought, emotion and behaviour, not a split personality. His fundamental symptoms, the four As , were present in every case: Loosening of Associations : thoughts lose their logical links. Blunted or incongruous Affect , such as smiling at sad news. Ambivalence : opposite feelings or wishes held at once towards the same object, a term Bleuler coined. Autism : withdrawal into an inner world (not the developmental disorder of Section 8.3). Hallucinations and delusions were only accessory symptoms , because they occur in other illnesses too. Exam trap Auditory hallucinations are not one of the four As. Ambivalence was coined by Bleuler, not Kraepelin, Freud or Fromm-Reichmann. Alogia, avolition and anhedonia are later negative-symptom As (8.4.2); apathy, anxiety, aphasia, amnesia, attention and anosognosia are not Bleuler's. Bleuler's symptoms were hard to rate reliably. The German psychiatrist Kurt Schneider (1887 to 1967) listed instead, in Clinical Psychopathology (English edition 1959), first-rank symptoms (FRS) that, in the absence of brain disease, strongly suggest schizophrenia. Their common theme is a failure of the boundary between self and world: Three kinds of voices : audible thoughts ( Gedankenlautwerden , thought echo), voices arguing or discussing the patient in the third person, and voices giving a running commentary on the patient's actions. Thought alienation : thought insertion, thought withdrawal and thought broadcasting. Passivity phenomena (delusions of control): made feelings, made impulses, made volitional acts, and somatic passivity (bodily sensations imposed from outside). Delusional perception : a normal perception suddenly given a private delusional meaning (a traffic light turns red, and he 'knows' he has been chosen). His second-rank symptoms were other hallucinations, perplexity, sudden delusional ideas, mood changes and emotional blunting. FRS are typical of schizophrenia but not specific: they also occur in mania, so DSM-5 gives them no special weight. Exam trap Not first-rank: depersonalisation , loose associations (Bleulerian), delusions of self-reference , catatonic signs such as echolalia, negative symptoms, olfactory hallucinations and memory loss. Delusions of control are first-rank. FRS are Schneider's: Karl Jaspers ( General Psychopathology , 1913) described primary delusions (Section 8.2), and Bateson and Wynne are family theorists (8.4.7). Positive, negative and cognitive symptoms Positive symptoms are the presence of something abnormal, an excess or distortion of normal function: delusions, hallucinations (commonest in schizophrenia, mostly voices, though mania and psychotic depression can bring them too), disorganised speech and grossly disorganised behaviour. Negative symptoms are the absence or reduction of something normal: affective flattening (less emotional expression in face, voice and gesture), alogia (poverty of speech), avolition (little self-started purposeful activity), anhedonia (reduced pleasure) and asociality . ICD-10 lists its negative symptoms as marked apathy, paucity of speech, and blunting or incongruity of emotional responses. A third, cognitive dimension (poor attention, working memory and executive function) best predicts work and social functioning. Timothy Crow (1980) proposed Type I schizophrenia (positive symptoms, acute onset, good response to neuroleptics, normal brain structure, dopamine D2 overactivity) and Type II (negative symptoms, chronic course, poor drug response, enlarged ventricles, intellectual decline). Peter Liddle (1987) found three syndromes: reality distortion (delusions, hallucinations), disorganisation (thought disorder, inappropriate affect) and psychomotor poverty (poverty of speech, flat affect, slowed movement). Symptoms are rated with Nancy Andreasen 's SANS and SAPS (Scales for the Assessment of Negative and of Positive Symptoms) and the 30-item PANSS (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale, 1987); see Chapter 2. Exam trap Delusions, hallucinations and disorganised speech or behaviour are positive ; flat affect is negative , never positive. Ambivalence is Bleulerian, not a negative symptom. Positive means the presence of something unusual, negative the absence of something normal, never the reverse. Diagnostic criteria: DSM-5-TR, ICD-10 and ICD-11 DSM-5-TR (2022) diagnoses schizophrenia when these are all met: A. Two or more of five symptoms, each present for a significant part of a 1-month period (less if successfully treated): delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, and negative symptoms. At least one must be one of the first three. B. Functioning in work, relationships or self-care falls markedly below the earlier level. C. Continuous signs last at least 6 months, including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms; the rest may be prodromal or residual phases, showing only negative or attenuated symptoms (odd beliefs, unusual perceptions). D to F. Schizoaffective and mood disorders, substances and medical conditions are excluded; after childhood autism, prominent delusions or hallucinations must last 1 month. DSM-5 (2013) dropped the DSM-IV subtypes (paranoid, disorganised, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual) and the rule that one bizarre delusion or one Schneiderian voice was enough. ICD-10 (F20) needs one very clear symptom from groups (a) to (d), or symptoms from two of groups (e) to (h), present most of the time for 1 month or more: (a) thought echo, insertion, withdrawal or broadcasting; (b) delusions of control or passivity, and delusional perception; (c) voices commenting on or discussing the patient; (d) persistent, culturally impossible delusions; (e) persistent hallucinations with delusions; (f) breaks in the train of thought, incoherence or neologisms; (g) catatonic behaviour; (h) negative symptoms. Its subtypes were paranoid (the commonest), hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, post-schizophrenic depression, residual and simple schizophrenia (insidious negative symptoms without overt psychosis). The spectrum: duration, delusions, mood and catatonia Symptoms identical to those of schizophrenia can be short-lived, so DSM-5-TR separates the disorders largely by duration (Figure 8.5). Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning; one symptom suffices if it is delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech. Specifiers: with marked stressors (brief reactive psychosis), without marked stressors, or with peripartum onset (in pregnancy or within 4 weeks after delivery). Schizophreniform disorder has the full Criterion A picture for at least 1 month but less than 6 months and needs no decline in functioning. Six months or more is schizophrenia. The same psychotic symptoms are named by how long they last; delusional disorder also starts at 1 month. Exam trap One keyed answer (IHBAS 2025) calls psychosis lasting 1 to 6 months 'brief psychotic disorder'. It is schizophreniform disorder : brief psychotic disorder ends within a month. Delusional disorder , Kraepelin's paranoia , is one or more delusions lasting 1 month or more (ICD-10 and ICD-11: about 3 months) in someone who has never met Criterion A for schizophrenia; hallucinations are not prominent, and apart from the delusion functioning is not markedly impaired. Types follow the theme: erotomanic (another person, usually of higher status such as a film star, is secretly in love with the patient), grandiose (an unrecognised great talent or discovery), jealous (the partner is unfaithful), persecutory (being plotted against, spied on or poisoned; the commonest), somatic (bodily functions, such as emitting a foul odour), mixed and unspecified. Schizoaffective disorder needs an uninterrupted period in which a major mood episode coincides with Criterion A of schizophrenia, plus delusions or hallucinations for 2 weeks or more without a major mood episode, with mood episodes present for most of the illness; it has bipolar and depressive types. Psychotic depression and mania belong to Section 8.5. Schizotypal disorder , eccentricity below the psychotic threshold, is listed in this DSM-5-TR chapter but described in Section 8.11; ICD-10 placed it beside schizophrenia as F21, and ICD-11 keeps it there as 6A22. Psychosis caused directly by a drug, medication or toxin is substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder ; psychosis caused by a medical illness is psychotic disorder due to another medical condition . Catatonia requires three or more of twelve signs: stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia and echopraxia. DSM-5 makes it not an independent disorder but a specifier across several disorders (catatonia associated with schizophrenia, depression and others), plus catatonic disorder due to another medical condition and unspecified catatonia. Attenuated psychosis syndrome (Section III, for further study) means weaker psychotic symptoms with insight retained, at least weekly for a month. ICD-10 acute and transient psychotic disorders (F23) begin within 2 weeks and usually resolve within 2 to 3 months; ICD-11 6A23 keeps the 2-week onset, with rapidly changing symptoms lasting at most 3 months. They are common in India and recover well. Folie à deux ( Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret , 1877) is a delusion transmitted from a dominant primary case with an established psychotic disorder to a more passive, often socially isolated secondary partner in a close relationship, usually a relative. Separation often lets the secondary partner's belief fade. In folie imposée the delusion is imposed on a healthy partner; in folie simultanée two predisposed people fall ill together; folie à trois involves three. ICD-10 coded it F24 induced delusional disorder , DSM-IV shared psychotic disorder . DSM-5 dropped the category: the partner receives delusional disorder if its criteria are met, otherwise other specified schizophrenia spectrum disorder ('delusional symptoms in the context of relationship with an individual with prominent delusions'). ICD-11 has no separate code either: it describes 'shared or induced delusional disorder' (folie à deux) as a rare form of 6A24 delusional disorder , in its block 'schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders'. Exam trap A belief shared by a whole cultural or religious group is not folie à deux; nor are two independent psychotic episodes, or a stress psychosis in two relatives. ICD-10 F24 is induced delusional disorder; F21 is schizotypal disorder. ICD-11 puts it under neither schizoaffective nor schizotypal disorder: it is a form of delusional disorder among the other primary psychotic disorders. Epidemiology, course and prognosis The lifetime risk is usually quoted as about 1 percent ; DSM-5-TR gives 0.3 to 0.7 percent. Schizophrenia is above all a disorder of young adults : psychosis emerges between the late teens and the mid-30s, peaking in the early to mid-20s in men and the late 20s in women, with a second peak in women in midlife, around the menopause. Prevalence is about equal in the two sexes, but men have more negative symptoms and worse outcomes. A prodrome of withdrawal and odd ideas precedes the active phase. In the WHO International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (1973, nine countries including India) and the later Determinants of Outcome study, patients in developing countries had a better course, often linked to family support. Schizophrenia is commoner in the lowest social classes: social causation says poverty and stress produce it; social drift says the illness pushes people down the social ladder. Risk rises with the genes shared with an affected relative, but even an identical co-twin falls ill only about half the time. The dopamine hypothesis holds that positive symptoms reflect excess dopamine activity at D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway. Arvid Carlsson showed that dopamine is a neurotransmitter and that antipsychotics act on its system (Nobel Prize, 2000); amphetamine, which releases dopamine, can cause a paranoid psychosis, and L-dopa for Parkinson's disease can cause hallucinations (it does not relieve negative symptoms). The original support came in 1976, when Philip Seeman and colleagues, and Ian Creese, David Burt and Solomon Snyder , showed that the clinical potency of typical antipsychotics correlates with their affinity for D2 receptors. Dopamine runs in four pathways, so a drug that blocks D2 everywhere both helps and harms (Table 8.15). Table 8.15 The four dopamine pathways. Pathway Route Role in schizophrenia and treatment Mesolimbic Ventral tegmental area (VTA) to nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum) and limbic areas; reward Overactive: positive symptoms; D2 blockade treats them Mesocortical VTA to prefrontal cortex Underactive: negative and cognitive symptoms Nigrostriatal Substantia nigra to caudate and putamen; voluntary movement D2 blockade: extrapyramidal symptoms, parkinsonian rigidity Tuberoinfundibular Hypothalamus to median eminence and pituitary D2 blockade: raised prolactin Kenneth Davis and colleagues (1991) revised the hypothesis: too much subcortical dopamine for positive symptoms, too little prefrontal dopamine for negative ones. Oliver Howes and Shitij Kapur (2009) located the core fault in increased presynaptic dopamine synthesis in the striatum, a final common pathway to psychosis. Phencyclidine and ketamine block NMDA glutamate receptors and produce positive and negative symptoms, suggesting NMDA receptor hypofunction; atypical antipsychotics add blockade of 5-HT2A serotonin receptors. The neurodevelopmental hypothesis ( Daniel Weinberger , 1987; Robin Murray and Shon Lewis, 1987) proposes that an early brain lesion stays silent until adolescent maturation unmasks it. The evidence: enlarged lateral ventricles , first shown on CT by Eve Johnstone and colleagues (1976); reduced grey matter; hypofrontality , low prefrontal activity during tasks; obstetric complications, prenatal influenza and winter-spring birth; and, later, adolescent cannabis use. Family and psychological theories Early family theories blamed parents. Frieda Fromm-Reichmann (1948) described the cold, dominating schizophrenogenic mother ; the idea is discredited and caused families needless guilt. Gregory Bateson , with Don Jackson, Jay Haley and John Weakland (1956), proposed the double bind : a person repeatedly receives contradictory messages at two levels from a significant other, and can neither comment on the contradiction nor escape. Key study: Bateson's double bind (1956) A young man, fairly well recovered from an acute schizophrenic episode, put his arm round his visiting mother; she stiffened. He withdrew, and she asked, 'Don't you love me any more?' He blushed, and she said, 'Dear, you must not be so easily embarrassed and afraid of your feelings.' After she left he assaulted an aide. Bateson called this the symptomatic double bind : every response was wrong. No controlled study has shown that double binds cause schizophrenia. The group's cybernetic and homeostatic views of the family belong to family therapy (Section 7.7). Theodore Lidz (1957) described marital schism (parents in open conflict, undermining each other) and marital skew (one dominant, disturbed parent whose distortions the other accepts). Lyman Wynne (1958) described pseudomutuality , a façade of harmony that forbids individuality, and later communication deviance , vague and fragmented parental speech. Ronald David Laing led anti-psychiatry , which saw schizophrenia as an understandable response to an unliveable family situation. Where these theories sought causes and failed, expressed emotion (EE) predicts relapse. EE is the emotional climate of a key relative towards the patient, rated from the Camberwell Family Interview on three dimensions: critical comments , hostility and emotional over-involvement . Warmth and positive remarks are also rated, but they are not high-EE dimensions. Key study: Expressed emotion and relapse (1972, 1976) George Brown , James Birley and John Wing (1972) followed patients discharged to their families: relapse was about four times commoner in high-EE homes. Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff (1976) replicated this and found relapse highest when a patient spent more than about 35 hours a week face to face with a high-EE relative and took no medication. Criticism: the data are correlational; a more disturbed patient may provoke more criticism. In WHO studies in Chandigarh, Indian relatives were far less often high in EE than London relatives, one suggested reason for better outcome in India. High EE is managed by family psychoeducation and by reducing face-to-face contact hours. Table 8.16 summarises the psychodynamic theories; the vulnerability-stress model that integrates these causes is in Section 8.1. Exam trap High EE predicts relapse of psychotic illness, not its onset, negative symptoms or violence; relapse is more precise than a vague 'poor treatment outcome'. It means critical, hostile or over-involved relatives, not overwhelmingly positive comments, a family without emotion, or a patient who cannot talk about feelings. Neuroleptics are used chiefly for schizophrenia (and in mania), not for depression or anxiety. The era began in 1952, when Jean Delay and Pierre Deniker in Paris gave chlorpromazine to psychotic patients. Typical antipsychotics (first-generation), such as chlorpromazine and haloperidol, act mainly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors (not D1); chlorpromazine also blocks muscarinic (M1) receptors, causing dry mouth and constipation. Atypical antipsychotics (second-generation), such as risperidone, olanzapine and clozapine , block 5-HT2A as well as D2 and cause fewer movement effects; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Because a typical drug blocks D2 in the nigrostriatal pathway too, it produces extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), in a fixed order: Acute dystonia , within hours to days: sustained muscle spasms, a twisted neck, eyes forced upwards. Akathisia , within days to weeks: a subjective inner restlessness with a compelling need to pace or move. Drug-induced parkinsonism , within weeks: tremor, rigidity and slowed movement. Tardive dyskinesia , after months to years: involuntary orofacial movements such as lip-smacking, tongue movements and grimacing; the last to appear and the most likely to be irreversible. Other dangers are neuroleptic malignant syndrome , a rare emergency of high fever, 'lead-pipe' rigidity, unstable pulse and blood pressure and clouded consciousness; hyperprolactinaemia from tuberoinfundibular blockade (breast enlargement, milk secretion, missed periods); metabolic syndrome (weight gain, diabetes, raised lipids) with atypicals, especially clozapine and olanzapine; and agranulocytosis with clozapine, which demands regular blood counts. DSM-5-TR lists these reactions as medication-induced movement disorders and other adverse effects of medication. Exam trap Akathisia and tardive dyskinesia are secondary (drug-induced) movement disorders; Huntington's chorea (inherited) and Parkinson's disease (nigral degeneration) are primary . Tardive dyskinesia follows neuroleptics, not antidepressants, anxiolytics or barbiturates. Typicals cause EPS by blocking nigrostriatal D2 receptors, not by blocking serotonin reuptake (SSRIs), stimulating GABA-A receptors (benzodiazepines) or blocking mesolimbic receptors selectively. A mood disorder (affective disorder) is a low or high mood, with changed sleep, energy, thinking and behaviour, that takes over a life for weeks or years. Such disorders are built from three kinds of episode, so the episodes come first. Mood episodes: the building blocks A disorder with depressive episodes only is unipolar ; one in which mood swings between the extremes, mania or hypomania as well as depression, is bipolar . DSM-5 (2013) split DSM-IV's "mood disorders" into two chapters, bipolar and related disorders and depressive disorders , placing bipolar disorders between the psychotic and depressive chapters as a bridge. Mania and hypomania differ in degree, not kind: hypomania is shorter, and though others notice it, it never causes marked impairment or hospitalisation; psychotic features make an episode manic by definition. DSM-5 also dropped the bereavement exclusion , which had barred a diagnosis of depression in the 2 months after a death, because grief-triggered depression proved to be like any other. Exam trap Specific phobias and euphoric mood are not symptoms of a major depressive episode; anhedonia and appetite change are. Social phobia and fear of weight gain (anorexia, Section 8.8) are not manic symptoms, and hallucinations, though possible in severe mania, are not among its seven. Mania lasts longer than hypomania and need not follow depression; hypomania must be observable by others. Depressive disorders Major depressive disorder (MDD), one or more major depressive episodes with no mania or hypomania, is marked by persistent sadness and loss of interest; it may be a single episode or recurrent. Called the common cold of psychiatry , it affects about 16 percent of people in a lifetime (estimates run 15 to 20 percent), and rates are rising, fastest among the young. Onset grows likelier at puberty, after which women are affected about twice as often as men (in children the ratio is about equal). Episodes are often triggered by a stressful event, and the more severe the depression, the higher the suicide risk. Exam trap Asked which statement least accurately describes depression, pick "men are more vulnerable than women": the reverse is true. Widespread and rising incidence, stress triggers and the severity-suicide link are all accurate. Persistent depressive disorder (PDD), formerly dysthymia, merges dysthymic disorder and chronic major depression. Mood is depressed most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years in adults or 1 year in children and adolescents , with two or more of six symptoms: appetite change, sleep change, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration and hopelessness. The person is never symptom-free for more than 2 months and has never had mania or hypomania. Dysthymia is persistent mild depression, less severe than MDD but longer . A major depressive episode on top of it is double depression . Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD), new in DSM-5, means severe temper outbursts grossly out of proportion to the provocation, three or more times a week, with persistently irritable mood between them, for 12 months, in two of three settings (home, school, peers). Onset is before age 10 and diagnosis between 6 and 18. It was added to curb the over-diagnosis of bipolar disorder in children, who in fact grow up to have depression and anxiety. Exam trap A 12-year-old whose temper outbursts have just begun cannot have DMDD, because onset must come before age 10. Bipolar disorder, conduct disorder and ADHD (Sections 8.3 and 8.11) all remain possible. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) needs five or more symptoms, at least one of them mood swings, irritability, depressed mood or anxiety, in the week before menses in most cycles, easing within a few days after menses begin. Depression caused by a drug, or by an illness such as hypothyroidism, is substance-induced or due to another medical condition (Section 8.10). The "hybrid" disorder is ICD-10's mixed anxiety and depressive disorder (F41.2): anxiety and depression both present, neither enough for its own diagnosis. ICD-11 keeps it among the depressive disorders; DSM-5 does not. (Multiple personality, borderline and schizoid disorders belong to Sections 8.7 and 8.11.) René Spitz (1887 to 1974) described anaclitic depression in 1946: infants separated from their mothers in the second half of the first year grew weepy, then withdrawn, lost weight and stopped developing, recovering if the mother soon returned. His term hospitalism named the graver, sometimes fatal, decline of infants reared in impersonal institutions. (Piaget, Skinner and Eysenck are known for cognitive stages, operant conditioning and personality dimensions.) Masked depression presents as bodily complaints while sadness is denied, common in Indian primary care; depressive pseudodementia is covered in Section 8.10. Norman Rosenthal and colleagues described seasonal affective disorder in 1984: depression each autumn or winter, lifting in spring, with oversleeping and carbohydrate craving, commoner at high latitudes. It responds to bright light therapy. Exam trap Seasonal affective disorder is the "with seasonal pattern" specifier of recurrent major depressive or bipolar disorder: not a separate, anxiety or personality disorder, and not confined to women. "With limited prosocial emotions" belongs to conduct disorder (Section 8.11), not mania. Bipolar and related disorders The two-pole idea came from 1850s France: Jean-Pierre Falret (1794 to 1870) described folie circulaire and Jules Baillarger (1809 to 1890) folie à double forme , mania and melancholia alternating in one patient (Falret's son Jules gave us folie à deux). Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926) united recurrent mood illness as manic-depressive insanity in 1899, apart from dementia praecox, and Karl Leonhard split unipolar from bipolar forms in 1957. Bipolar I disorder needs at least one manic episode; major depressive and hypomanic episodes are common but not required, and subthreshold depressive periods are allowed. Bipolar II disorder needs at least one hypomanic and one major depressive episode and never a full mania, which would make it bipolar I. Bipolar II is not milder, since its depressions are frequent and disabling, and it needs no psychotic features. Cyclothymic disorder is the chronic low-grade form: for at least 2 years (1 in the young), numerous hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet episode criteria, never absent for more than 2 months. Swinging between the poles is what makes a disorder bipolar (Figure 8.7). Bipolar disorder affects about 1 percent of people, men and women equally, usually beginning around age 20. Exam trap Bipolar I is defined by mania, so "bipolar I includes hypomania" is the incorrect statement: hypomania defines bipolar II and is optional in bipolar I, which may also include depressive periods, even subthreshold ones. Rapid cycling and psychotic depressions occur in both, and bipolar II has no manic episodes at all, only shorter hypomanias; a full manic episode is what separates I from II. Its depressive episode lasts 2 weeks and is graded mild, moderate or severe by how many symptoms are present, three of them typical (depressed mood, loss of interest, reduced energy). Mild and moderate episodes are coded with or without the somatic syndrome , ICD-10's counterpart of melancholic features. Criticism: one city, women only, and life events recalled after the fact. First-line drug treatment For depression, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as fluoxetine are first line, safer in overdose than tricyclics (imipramine) and monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs, which need a low-tyramine diet). For bipolar disorder the gold standard is lithium ( John Cade , 1949), used for acute mania and for prophylaxis (preventing further episodes), and it lowers suicide risk. Its therapeutic range is narrow, so blood levels are monitored; toxicity brings coarse tremor, vomiting, unsteadiness and confusion. Valproate, carbamazepine and lamotrigine are alternatives, and atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone) are first line for acute mania; haloperidol and lorazepam are adjuncts for agitation only. Electroconvulsive therapy and the psychotherapies are in Chapter 7. Exam trap Fluoxetine is not a first-line treatment for acute mania: an antidepressant given alone in bipolar disorder can trigger a switch into mania or rapid cycling. Lithium, valproate and atypical antipsychotics are first line. Suicide Suicidal ideation is thinking of killing oneself; a plan fixes method, place and time; intent is how much the person wants to die; an attempt is a self-injurious act with some intent to die that is survived; completed suicide ends in death. Lethality is the medical danger of the method, so the mode of an attempt (hanging or pesticide against a few tablets) shows its lethality, while intent is inferred from planning and precautions against rescue. Norman Kreitman coined parasuicide (1969) for non-fatal deliberate self-injury or overdose whatever its intent, later called deliberate self-harm. Non-suicidal self-injury (cutting or burning without intent to die) is a DSM-5 condition for further study. The World Health Organization counts over 700,000 suicides a year. India's National Crime Records Bureau recorded about 1.71 lakh in 2022, about seven in ten of them men and most aged 18 to 45, with family problems (about a third) and illness the leading recorded causes. Women attempt suicide more often, but men die by it more often, using more lethal methods: the gender paradox. Émile Durkheim (1858 to 1917), in Suicide (1897), traced suicide to social ties: egoistic (too little integration, the isolated person), altruistic (too much, dying for the group as in hara-kiri), anomic (too little regulation, sudden upheaval such as losing a fortune) and fatalistic (too much regulation, as for slaves or prisoners). Edwin Shneidman (1918 to 2009), founder of suicidology, saw suicide as escape from psychache , unbearable psychological pain. In Thomas Joiner 's interpersonal theory (2005) the wish to die comes from perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belongingness , but lethal attempts also need an acquired capability , fearlessness of pain and death built by exposure such as self-harm. Marie Åsberg (1976) found that depressed patients with low cerebrospinal fluid 5-HIAA , the serotonin metabolite, made more frequent and more violent suicide attempts. The strongest single predictor of suicide is a previous attempt . Other risk factors are depression and other mental disorders, alcohol, hopelessness (Beck's Hopelessness Scale predicts better than depression severity), male sex, older age, living alone, chronic illness, a family history of suicide and access to means such as pesticides. Social support, children at home, religious objection and restricted means protect. Risk is highest when high lethality, a specific plan, frequent ideation and family history converge. SAD PERSONS (Patterson and colleagues, 1983) is in Section 7.2, and the decriminalisation of attempted suicide by the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 in Section 7.1. Exam trap The mode or method of an attempt indicates lethality ; intentionality is the wish to die, and conviction and survival are not standard dimensions. A man who has avoided buses for three years since he panicked on one, or a woman who washes for three hours a day to cancel a thought of germs, has crossed into disorder. This section sets out the anxiety disorders and why they develop, then obsessive-compulsive disorder and its relatives. Fear, anxiety and the old neuroses Fear is the alarm response to danger that is present now: a surge of autonomic arousal and the urge to escape. Anxiety is apprehension about a future threat, felt as muscle tension, vigilance and cautious avoidance. Both are normal, and moderate anxiety even helps performance (the Yerkes-Dodson law, Section 1.10). Anxiety becomes pathological when it is out of proportion to the danger, developmentally inappropriate, persistent (typically six months or more) and impairing. The Scottish physician William Cullen coined the word neurosis in 1769 for disorders of sense and motion arising from the nervous system without fever or local disease. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) narrowed neurosis to a non-psychotic disorder of unconscious conflict, with insight preserved, and in 1895 described an "anxiety neurosis". DSM-III (1980) dropped the term because it implied Freud's theory. DSM-5 (2013) split the old anxiety group into three chapters: anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, and trauma- and stressor-related disorders (Section 8.7). ICD-10 kept the umbrella block F40 to F48, "neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders", running from phobic anxiety (F40), other anxiety (F41) and OCD (F42) to somatoform (F45) and other neurotic disorders (F48). ICD-11 follows DSM-5, with separate "anxiety or fear-related" and "obsessive-compulsive or related" groupings. The anxiety disorders and their time rules DSM-5-TR orders the anxiety disorders by typical age of onset and separates them by what is feared (Table 8.21); six months is the usual duration. Anxiety caused by a drug or its withdrawal, or by an illness such as hyperthyroidism, is diagnosed instead as substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder or anxiety disorder due to another medical condition. A specific phobia is a persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation, out of proportion to the danger, provoked almost every time and avoided or endured with dread: an anxiety disorder, not a mild stress reaction, a personality disorder or a passing hallucination. Its five types are animal, natural environment (heights, storms, water), blood-injection-injury, situational (aeroplanes, lifts, enclosed places) and other (choking, vomiting). Most phobics show sympathetic arousal, but the blood-injection-injury type shows a diphasic vasovagal response : heart rate and blood pressure rise briefly, then drop, and the person may faint. Social anxiety disorder is fear of situations of possible scrutiny (conversation, eating in public, a speech) because one may act in a way that is negatively evaluated or embarrassing; in children it must occur with peers. The performance only specifier covers fear confined to speaking or performing in public. Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is excessive anxiety and worry about a number of events or activities, more days than not for at least six months, that the person finds hard to control, with three or more of six symptoms (only one in children): restlessness, easy fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension and sleep disturbance. Hopping from health to money to a child's journey home, it is continued, free-floating apprehension about unspecified things. ICD-10 asks for anxiety on most days for several weeks at a time, usually several months; its research criteria fix six months. ICD-11 asks for at least several months, more days than not, with no fixed number. Exam trap GAD is continued apprehension about unspecified things , defined by persistent, excessive worry. "Fear of fear" is panic disorder, flashbacks PTSD and safety checking OCD; mania and mood swings are mood symptoms (Section 8.5), hallucinations psychotic (Section 8.4). GAD needs at least 6 months in adults and specific phobia typically 6 months, not 1 week or 1, 3 or 12 months. Panic attacks, panic disorder and agoraphobia A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes (literally a few minutes; not seconds, half an hour or hours), with four or more of thirteen symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills or heat sensations, paraesthesias (numbness or tingling), derealisation or depersonalisation, fear of losing control or "going crazy", and fear of dying. Expected attacks have an obvious cue (a spider); unexpected ones come out of the blue. A panic attack is not itself a disorder; in other disorders it is a specifier ("PTSD with panic attacks"). Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks, at least one followed by a month or more of persistent worry about further attacks or their consequences (a heart attack, going mad), a maladaptive change in behaviour (avoiding exercise), or both. One attack is not panic disorder. Agoraphobia , literally "fear of the marketplace", is marked fear of two or more of five situations: public transport, open spaces, enclosed places (shops, cinemas), queues or crowds, and being outside the home alone, because escape might be difficult or help unavailable if panic-like symptoms strike. The situations are avoided, endured with dread or faced only with a companion, typically for six months. Since DSM-5, agoraphobia is diagnosed independently of panic disorder; a person meeting both receives both. In 1978 Alan Goldstein and Dianne Chambless argued that after a few attacks people come to fear the bodily sensations of anxiety themselves. This fear of fear marks panic disorder and agoraphobia. Exam trap Agoraphobia is the irrational fear of public places . Hearing voices is psychotic, nervousness in a lift is claustrophobia, fear of tall trees or buildings a fear of heights, and re-experiencing trauma PTSD. Panic disorder is recurrent unexpected attacks, not one attack, worry about many things (GAD) or fear of panicking in enclosed spaces. Anxiety is moderately heritable, though what is inherited is a general anxious tendency. Benzodiazepines calm anxiety by boosting GABA, the main inhibitory transmitter, so the GABA-benzodiazepine system is the classic anxiety system; noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus drives the alarm, serotonin modulates it, and the amygdala is the hub of the fear circuit. Jerome Kagan (1929 to 2021) found that behavioural inhibition , shyness and withdrawal from novelty visible by four months of age, predicts later anxiety. Learning. The two-factor theory of O. Hobart Mowrer (1907 to 1982), set out in 1947, explains why fears last. A neutral stimulus paired with a frightening one becomes a conditioned stimulus for fear (classical conditioning, as with Little Albert, Section 1.6); avoiding it then reduces fear, so avoidance is negatively reinforced and the fear is never unlearned. Martin Seligman (born 1942) explained why snakes and heights are feared more than electric sockets with preparedness (1971): evolution has prepared us to learn ancestral fears quickly and keep them. Stanley Rachman (1977) explained phobias with no frightening memory through three pathways: direct conditioning, vicarious learning and information. Cognition. David M. Clark (1986) traced panic to the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations: a skipped heartbeat is read as a heart attack, and fear and sensations feed each other (Figure 8.8). Catastrophic thinking in general means worrying that the worst will always happen. It differs from other distortions (Section 7.5): dichotomous thinking (everything extremely good or extremely bad), selective abstraction (seeing only the negative) and personalisation (taking things personally). Steven Reiss 's anxiety sensitivity , the belief that anxiety symptoms are harmful, predicts panic. For GAD, Thomas Borkovec held that verbal worry avoids the vivid imagery and arousal of fear and is reinforced by that avoidance; Adrian Wells ' metacognitive model adds positive and negative beliefs about worry itself; and Michel Dugas stressed intolerance of uncertainty . The suffocation alarm. Donald F. Klein 's suffocation false alarm theory (1993) proposes an evolved suffocation monitor that in panic disorder is oversensitive, firing at harmless rises in carbon dioxide; carbon dioxide inhalation and lactate infusion do trigger attacks far more readily in panic patients. It explains panic disorder, not Down syndrome, autism (Section 8.3) or delirium (Section 8.10). David H. Barlow 's triple vulnerability theory then combines a generalised biological vulnerability (an anxious temperament), a generalised psychological vulnerability (a sense that events are uncontrollable) and a specific psychological vulnerability (learning that certain things are dangerous). Psychodynamic view. Freud later treated anxiety as signal anxiety (1926), a warning to the ego that a forbidden impulse is near, which sets defences going. The defence of phobia is displacement , shifting feeling from a threatening object to a safer one. Each classic neurosis had a signature defence: repression in hysteria, displacement in phobia, isolation, undoing and reaction formation in OCD, introjection in depression. Key study: Little Hans (Freud, 1909) Hans, aged five, would not go out for fear that a horse would bite him. Freud, working mainly through the boy's father, read the fear as an Oedipal fear of the father displaced onto horses, which, unlike a father, could be avoided. Critics noted that the evidence came from a father devoted to Freud, and that Hans had seen a horse fall in the street, which suggests simple conditioning. Exam trap Displacement is the defence of phobias , not of hysteria, OCD or depression. Catastrophic thinking is expecting the worst , not dichotomous thinking, selective abstraction or personalisation. Obsessive-compulsive disorder Obsessions are recurrent, persistent, intrusive and unwanted thoughts, urges or images that cause anxiety and that the person tries to ignore, suppress or neutralise. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours (washing, checking, ordering, tapping) or mental acts (praying, counting) performed in response to an obsession or by rigid rules, to reduce anxiety or prevent a dreaded event, though not realistically connected to it. The cardinal DSM-5 feature is obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming (more than 1 hour a day) or cause significant distress or impairment . Merely having obsessions is not enough, and there is no six-hour or two-week rule. Priya, 22, after touching a door handle, fears she will carry germs that kill her mother and washes three hours a day: this is OCD. GAD worry concerns realistic matters without rituals, illness anxiety disorder is fear of having a disease (Section 8.7), and a specific phobia simply avoids an external object. Obsessions are ego-dystonic : intrusive, unwanted and inconsistent with the self-concept, neither part of one's identity nor pleasurable. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (Section 8.11), a separate disorder, is ego-syntonic : perfectionism and control felt as right, without true obsessions or compulsions. The insight specifier runs from good or fair through poor to absent insight/delusional beliefs (certain the house will burn unless the stove is checked 30 times; 4 percent or fewer). A tic-related specifier marks a current or past tic disorder. Symptoms cluster in four dimensions: contamination and washing, doubt or harm and checking, symmetry with ordering and counting, and taboo (aggressive, sexual, religious) thoughts. Hoarding is no longer an OCD compulsion, since DSM-5 made hoarding disorder separate. Twelve-month prevalence is about 1.2 percent, and onset is in childhood or early adulthood (mean 19.5 years; boys earlier). Exam trap Tapping, washing and checking are compulsions; hoarding is not . OCD is ego-dystonic , OCPD ego-syntonic; obsessions are not always reality-grounded, OCD is not confined to childhood, and total unawareness that obsessions are unreasonable is absent insight. Grandiosity and need for admiration mark narcissistic personality disorder (Section 8.11). Biology. OCD responds to clomipramine and the SSRIs, which block serotonin reuptake, implicating the central serotonin (5-HT) system ; GABA is the anxiety system, and glutamate and dopamine play lesser parts. Imaging implicates the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit : the orbitofrontal cortex and anterior cingulate signal "something is wrong", the caudate nucleus fails to filter the signal, and the thalamus loops it back. Susan Swedo (1998) described PANDAS , sudden childhood OCD or tics after streptococcal infection, thought to be an autoimmune attack on the basal ganglia. First-degree relatives have about twice the rate, ten times after childhood onset. Learning. Mowrer's two-factor theory applies directly (Figure 8.9): the obsession acquires anxiety by classical conditioning, the compulsion relieves it, and the relief negatively reinforces the compulsion. Compulsive acts are thus escape or avoidance responses (safety behaviours): not conditioned stimuli (the contaminating thought is the stimulus), not unconditioned responses (unlearned reflexes), not positively reinforced (distress is removed, nothing pleasant added) and not involuntary. Conditioning is the general mechanism; escape is the pattern. Exposure and response prevention blocks the ritual (Section 7.4). Cognition and psychodynamics. Nearly everyone has odd intrusive thoughts; Paul Salkovskis (1985) argued that OCD begins when they are appraised as signs of inflated responsibility for harm, which must be neutralised. Rachman added thought-action fusion , the belief that thinking of an act is as bad as doing it or makes it likelier. Freud's Rat Man (1909), tormented by the thought of rats gnawing into his father, is the classic case of "obsessional neurosis", which Freud traced to regression to anal-stage conflicts over control, dirt and aggression. Its defences are isolation of affect (the thought stays, its feeling goes), undoing (an act that symbolically cancels a forbidden thought, the most characteristic), reaction formation (scrupulous cleanliness against a wish to soil) and intellectualisation. Repression is the defence of hysteria. Exam trap Isolation, undoing and reaction formation are all OCD defences. For a single answer choose undoing , the defence of obsessive-compulsive neurosis (not depression, mania or schizophrenia). The defence NOT used in OCD is repression . The related disorders Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others, with repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (comparing). Specifiers record insight and muscle dysmorphia , the belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular. Enrico Morselli called it dysmorphophobia in 1891. DSM-IV listed BDD among the somatoform disorders; DSM-5 placed it in obsessive-compulsive and related disorders , not with somatic symptom, anxiety or personality disorders. It concerns appearance, unlike somatic symptom disorder (distressing bodily symptoms), illness anxiety disorder (fear of serious illness) and conversion disorder (neurological symptoms without matching disease), all in Section 8.7. Hoarding disorder is persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, from a perceived need to save them, so that clutter blocks the use of living spaces. Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder), named by François Hallopeau in 1889, is recurrent hair pulling causing hair loss, with repeated attempts to stop; excoriation disorder is the same with skin picking and lesions. These body-focused repetitive behaviours are not driven by obsessions. Substance/medication-induced OCRD and OCRD due to another medical condition complete the chapter. ICD-11's obsessive-compulsive or related group also includes olfactory reference disorder (a conviction of emitting a foul body odour) and hypochondriasis (health anxiety), and calls trichotillomania and excoriation body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders. Finally, an obsession is resisted as intrusive and usually recognised as excessive; a GAD worry concerns real-life matters and brings no ritual; a delusion is a false belief held as simply true. This section follows hysteria as it split into the trauma-related, dissociative and somatic symptom disorders, and ends with illness that is feigned. Hysteria, from Hippocrates to DSM-III The word hysteria comes from the Greek hystera , womb: Hippocrates (about 460 to 370 BCE) and his followers blamed its fits and paralyses on a "wandering womb". At the Salpêtrière in Paris, Jean-Martin Charcot (1825 to 1893) showed that hysterical phenomena such as loss of feeling in a limb or fainting could be produced and removed by hypnosis and suggestion, so their cause was psychological, not a lesion. His pupil Pierre Janet (1859 to 1947) named the mechanism désagrégation (1889), now called dissociation : under strain, a cluster of memories and functions splits off from consciousness and runs on its own. The phrase la belle indifférence , the calm unconcern some patients show about a dramatic symptom, is usually credited to Janet. In Vienna Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925) relieved "Anna O." of her paralyses by letting her talk through their origins under hypnosis, her "talking cure", and with Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) published Studies on Hysteria (1895). For Freud, hysteria was physical reactions to emotional trauma: a painful memory is pushed out of awareness by repression and its energy converted into a bodily symptom, hence conversion . Most psychodynamic theorists still see repression behind both conversion and dissociative symptoms. The symptom gives primary gain , relief from the anxiety of the conflict, and often secondary gain , attention or escape from a duty. Key study: Hilgard's hidden observer Ernest Ropiequet Hilgard (1904 to 2001) gave hypnotised volunteers a suggestion that they would feel no pain and put their hands in iced water. They reported little pain, yet a hidden observer , addressed by a prearranged cue, reported nearly normal pain. His neodissociation theory ( Divided Consciousness , 1977) holds that awareness can split into parallel streams. Critics such as Nicholas Spanos argued that the instructions create the observer. In 1980 DSM-III divided hysteria into somatoform and dissociative disorders (Figure 8.10); ICD-10 kept them together as dissociative (conversion) disorders, F44. Exam trap Freud's hysteria is physical reactions to emotional trauma ; a phobia of horses is Little Hans, and the Oedipus complex and oral traits belong to Chapter 4. The psychodynamic mechanism of dissociative symptoms is repression : conflict is what gets repressed. Charcot used both hypnosis and suggestion. La belle indifférence is credited to Janet , not Freud, Anna Freud (who catalogued the defence mechanisms, Chapter 4) or Hippocrates. Posttraumatic and acute stress disorders First World War soldiers who shook, froze or went mute were said to have shell shock; Abram Kardiner (1891 to 1981) described The Traumatic Neuroses of War (1941), and DSM-III named posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in 1980. DSM-5 moved it from the anxiety disorders into a new trauma- and stressor-related chapter. The event must involve actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, experienced directly, witnessed in person, learned of as happening to a close family member or friend, or met through repeated exposure to aversive details, as by police officers hearing about child abuse. Symptoms fall into four clusters: Intrusion (1 of 5): distressing memories, nightmares, flashbacks (acting or feeling as if the event were recurring), distress at reminders. Avoidance (1 of 2) of trauma-related thoughts and feelings or of outside reminders. Negative alterations in cognitions and mood (2 of 7): amnesia for part of the event, self-blame, "no one can be trusted", guilt, detachment, no positive emotions. Alterations in arousal and reactivity (2 of 6): irritability, recklessness, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, poor concentration, poor sleep. Symptoms must last more than 1 month . Specifiers are the dissociative subtype (persistent depersonalisation or derealisation) and delayed expression (full criteria met only 6 months or more after the event); children 6 and younger have separate criteria. Acute stress disorder covers 3 days to 1 month after the trauma and needs nine of fourteen symptoms from five categories. DSM-IV required dissociative symptoms for it; DSM-5 dropped that rule, so timing now separates it from PTSD, and both sit in the trauma chapter. ICD-11 places PTSD among disorders specifically associated with stress, which require an extremely threatening or horrific event, and keeps three core elements: re-experiencing in the here and now, avoidance, and a persistent sense of current threat. Complex PTSD adds disturbances in self-organisation (affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship difficulties), usually after prolonged, inescapable trauma such as torture or childhood abuse. An acute stress reaction is a normal response, not a disorder. Who develops PTSD depends first on the dose and type of trauma (most prisoners of war do; interpersonal violence is worse than accidents), then on vulnerability: earlier anxiety, family instability and peritraumatic dissociation (feeling dazed or unreal during the event) raise risk, while social support protects. Conditioning attaches fear to reminders and avoidance blocks extinction. The amygdala is overactive, the hippocampus smaller and the HPA (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal) stress axis dysregulated. Prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy and EMDR are covered in Sections 7.4 and 7.5. Trauma can also bring post-traumatic growth , which Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun (1996) measured in five domains: appreciation of life, relating to others, personal strength, new possibilities and spiritual change. Exam trap PTSD has four clusters (DSM-IV had three). Magical thinking and ideas of reference belong to schizotypal personality and psychosis (Sections 8.4 and 8.11), and "denial, anger, bargaining" are Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's stages of dying (Chapter 6). PTSD lasts more than 1 month; acute stress disorder 3 days to 1 month; delayed expression begins at 6 months. Adjustment, grief and attachment disorders An adjustment disorder is an emotional or behavioural reaction to an identifiable stressor, such as divorce or job loss, with disproportionate distress or impaired functioning; it begins within 3 months of the stressor and ends within 6 months after the stressor or its consequences end. Its subtypes are with depressed mood, with anxiety, with mixed anxiety and depressed mood, with disturbance of conduct, with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct, and unspecified. Being brief and tied to a present stressor, it is best treated by brief psychotherapy and crisis intervention (Section 7.9). Prolonged grief disorder , added in DSM-5-TR (2022), is intense yearning for or preoccupation with the deceased, with symptoms such as identity disruption, disbelief and meaninglessness, at least 12 months after the death (6 months in children and adolescents; ICD-11 needs 6), beyond cultural norms. Ordinary bereavement is not a disorder. After severe neglect or institutional rearing, a child with reactive attachment disorder is inhibited and emotionally withdrawn, rarely seeking comfort, while one with disinhibited social engagement disorder shows indiscriminate sociability, readily going off with strangers. Dissociative identity disorder (DID), called multiple personality disorder until DSM-IV (1994), requires two or more distinct personality states, or an experience of possession, and recurrent gaps in the recall of everyday events, personal information or trauma beyond ordinary forgetting, not explained by accepted religious practice. The identity most often encountered, carrying the person's real name, is the host ; the others are alters , which may differ in age, gender and voice, and changing between them is a switch . The amnesia shows in daily life: a woman finds clothes she does not remember buying. About 90 percent of patients report childhood abuse or neglect. Corbett Thigpen and Hervey Cleckley 's The Three Faces of Eve (1957) and Sybil (1973), a case later criticised as shaped by the therapist, frame the debate on causes. The trauma model sees identities as states split off to escape unbearable abuse. The sociocognitive model of Nicholas Spanos (1942 to 1994) sees them as roles shaped in suggestible people by therapists' questions, hypnosis and media; in a 1985 experiment, over 80 percent of students playing an accused murderer produced an "alter" when interviewed. Exam trap "Multiple personalities in one body" is DID, not schizophrenia , whose "split" is between thought and emotion (Section 8.4). Bipolar disorder alternates moods, and borderline personality disorder an unstable self-image, not separate identities with amnesia. The identity with the real name is the host ; "ghost" and "mixed" identities do not exist. Dissociative amnesia, fugue and depersonalisation Dissociative amnesia is an inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually traumatic or stressful, too extensive to be ordinary forgetting and not due to a substance or a neurological or medical condition. It is a potentially reversible, mainly retrograde failure of retrieval, in five forms: Localised : a circumscribed period, such as the hours of an assault (the commonest form). Selective : some, but not all, events of that period. Generalised amnesia : one's entire life history, often with identity. Systematised : one category, such as everything about a violent sibling. Continuous : each new event, as it occurs. Fugue, a separate diagnosis in DSM-IV, is now the specifier with dissociative fugue : apparently purposeful travel or bewildered wandering with amnesia for identity, as in the man found working in another city with no memory of who he is. Organic amnesias differ. Transient global amnesia is a sudden, hours-long loss of new learning in an older adult who keeps their identity but repeats the same questions; Korsakoff syndrome is thiamine-deficiency amnesia with confabulation in chronic alcohol use; Alzheimer's disease begins with gradually failing new learning (Section 8.10); amnesia from head injury or another medical condition is mainly anterograde. In all of these, personal identity is lost last; in dissociative amnesia it can go first. Depersonalisation/derealisation disorder means persistent or recurrent experiences of either kind, or both. Depersonalisation is detachment from oneself: being an outside observer of one's own thoughts, feelings, body or actions, or feeling no longer one's normal self. Derealisation is unreality of the surroundings, which seem dreamlike, foggy or distorted. Reality testing stays intact ("it is as if I were dreaming"), which separates it from psychosis. Exam trap Self unreal is depersonalisation ; world unreal is derealisation . Multiple personality, fugue and amnesia are hysterical dissociative states, but déjà vu (a new situation feels already lived) is not: it is a disorder of recognition memory, seen in healthy people and temporal lobe epilepsy. A hallucination is perception without a stimulus (Section 8.2). Other specified dissociative disorder covers possession without amnesia, identity change after brainwashing, acute reactions lasting under a month, and dissociative trance , an acute narrowing or loss of awareness of the surroundings with profound unresponsiveness, outside accepted cultural practice. ICD-10 adds dissociative stupor and trance and possession disorders , in which a spirit or deity seems to take over; possession states are among the commonest dissociative presentations in India, though within an accepted ritual they are not disorders. Ganser syndrome , described by Sigbert Ganser (1853 to 1931) in 1898 in prisoners awaiting trial, combines approximate answers (a cow has "five" legs), clouding of consciousness, pseudohallucinations and conversion symptoms. Somatic symptom and illness anxiety disorders Somatoform disorders (DSM-III and DSM-IV) were conditions with symptoms suggesting a medical condition without evidence of physical pathology. They included somatisation disorder , earlier Briquet's syndrome after Paul Briquet (1796 to 1881), who in 1859 described patients returning with endless lists of complaints; hypochondriasis ; pain disorder ; and conversion. Neurasthenia ("lack of nerve strength"), named by George Miller Beard (1839 to 1883) in 1869 for unexplained exhaustion, survives in ICD-10. DSM-5 renamed the class somatic symptom and related disorders and defined it by positive features. Somatic symptom disorder needs one or more distressing somatic symptoms with excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours: disproportionate thoughts about their seriousness, high health anxiety, or excessive time and energy spent on them, typically for more than 6 months. The symptoms may have a medical cause: a woman with real arthritis who spends hours a day researching it qualifies. Exam trap "Physical symptoms without a medical cause" is the old somatoform idea, which DSM-5-TR calls "problematic". Against hallucinations, delusions and obsessions it is still the keyed answer for somatic symptom disorder, but the DSM-5-TR feature is excessive response to distressing symptoms. Illness anxiety disorder (formerly hypochondriasis) is preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness when somatic symptoms are absent or mild, with high health anxiety and excessive checking or avoidance, for at least 6 months. It has care-seeking and care-avoidant types. ICD-11 keeps the name hypochondriasis but places it among obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, and replaces somatoform disorders with bodily distress disorder , distressing bodily symptoms with excessive attention to them. Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions covers stress or behaviour that worsens a real disease (Section 7.9). Exam trap Chronic fatigue syndrome, or systemic exertion intolerance disease , has no DSM-5-TR criteria . The US Institute of Medicine (2015) requires fatigue for 6 months or more, not relieved by rest; post-exertional malaise; unrefreshing sleep; and cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance. Weight change is not a criterion. Conversion: functional neurological symptom disorder Hysteria's direct heir is functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder): one or more symptoms of altered voluntary motor or sensory function, with clinical findings incompatible with recognised neurological or medical conditions. The symptoms are not intentionally produced. They include paralysis; abnormal movements such as astasia-abasia (cannot stand or walk, yet moves the legs normally in bed); globus , a lump in the throat; aphonia ; psychogenic non-epileptic seizures ; glove anaesthesia , ending sharply at the wrist where no nerve territory ends; and tunnel vision or functional blindness , explained by psychological factors with no damage to eye, optic nerve or cortex. Diagnosis rests on positive signs. In Hoover's sign a "paralysed" leg cannot press down on request, yet presses down when the patient lifts the healthy leg against resistance. A woman whose arm becomes paralysed after an argument, with a normal examination and the remark "it's not really bothering me", is the classic picture: sudden onset after a stressor, motor or sensory loss, and la belle indifférence. DSM-5-TR no longer requires a stressor and calls la belle indifférence non-specific: in one review 21 percent of conversion patients showed it, against 29 percent with organic disease. ICD-11 calls the condition dissociative neurological symptom disorder . Conversion differs from hypochondriasis: neurological-like symptoms without organic basis, versus fear of having a serious illness. Exam trap La belle indifférence points to conversion disorder , not malingering, factitious disorder, somatic symptom disorder or illness anxiety. Conversion symptoms "affect motor or sensory function, begin suddenly and follow a stressor" (the classic picture, though DSM-5-TR no longer requires the stressor); "suggest a medical disorder" fits any somatic disorder, and normal investigations alone never make the diagnosis. Factitious disorder and malingering In factitious disorder the person falsifies signs or symptoms, or induces injury or disease, with deception and presents as ill even without obvious external rewards; the motive is to assume the sick role. The severe form imposed on self , with dramatic stories and many admissions, was named Munchausen syndrome by Richard Asher (1912 to 1969) in 1951, after the tall tales of Baron Munchausen . In factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen by proxy, Roy Meadow , 1977) a carer induces illness in a dependent person, like the nursing assistant who secretly injects insulin into elderly patients; the perpetrator receives the diagnosis. DSM-5 lists it in the somatic symptom chapter, but it was never a somatoform disorder: DSM-IV gave it a chapter of its own. Malingering is intentionally producing false or grossly exaggerated symptoms for external incentives such as compensation, drugs, or escape from work, military duty or prosecution.
