The eating disorders, above all anorexia nervosa, threaten life most and come first; the elimination and sleep-wake disorders follow. Pica, rumination and ARFID DSM-5-TR's feeding and eating disorders are persistent disturbances of eating that impair health or psychosocial functioning. Three of the six begin mostly in childhood and involve no body-image concern. Pica is the persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances (chalk, soil, paper, hair, paint) for at least 1 month , inappropriate to the developmental level and not culturally sanctioned, and is diagnosed from about age 2. It is linked with iron or zinc deficiency, pregnancy, intellectual disability and autism. In rumination disorder food is repeatedly regurgitated for at least 1 month, then re-chewed, re-swallowed or spat out, without a medical cause such as reflux; it occurs in infants and in intellectual disability. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) is food avoidance (for texture or smell, lack of interest, or fear of choking) causing weight loss, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or tube feeding, or psychosocial interference; mere picky eating does not qualify. ARFID has no disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced , which separates it from anorexia. Anorexia nervosa: history and criteria In 1873 two physicians described young women who starved themselves while insisting they were well. In London Sir William Withey Gull (1816 to 1890) named the illness anorexia nervosa (in a paper read in 1873 and printed in 1874); in Paris Ernest-Charles Lasègue (1816 to 1883) called it anorexie hystérique . The name misleads: anorexia means loss of appetite, yet most patients are hungry and driven by fear of fatness. Hilde Bruch (1904 to 1984), in The Golden Cage (1978), described a compliant, high-achieving girl who feels ineffective and finds in control of her body the one thing truly hers. Anorexia nervosa (AN) has three DSM-5-TR criteria: Restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight for age, sex, development and physical health. Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behaviour that interferes with weight gain, even at a low weight. Disturbance in how weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of weight or shape on self-evaluation, or persistent failure to recognise the seriousness of the low weight. Subtypes describe the last 3 months. The restricting type has had no recurrent binge eating or purging; weight is lost by dieting, fasting or excessive exercise. The binge-eating/purging type has had recurrent binges or purging (vomiting, or misuse of laxatives, diuretics or enemas). Adult severity uses body mass index (BMI, weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared): mild 17 or more, moderate 16 to 16.99, severe 15 to 15.99, extreme below 15. Exam trap DSM-5 dropped amenorrhoea as a criterion and sets no BMI cut-off : a BMI of 17 marks mild severity, not eligibility. ICD-10 used BMI 17.5 or less; ICD-11 uses below 18.5. Purging does not exclude anorexia; it defines a subtype. The core is fear of weight gain with restriction, not obsession with cleanliness (obsessive-compulsive disorder, Section 8.6). The starving body and the anorexic personality Most physical signs are the body's defences against starvation, so think "slow and low". Metabolism slows, giving bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypotension and hypothermia . Fine downy hair called lanugo grows on the body. Falling hormones produce amenorrhoea , the absence of menstrual periods, and in time osteoporosis . Vomiting adds hypokalaemia (low potassium), which can trigger fatal arrhythmias. Hyperthyroidism, tachycardia, hyperkalaemia and polyphagia (overeating) all point the wrong way. Anorexia nervosa is the most lethal eating disorder and has one of the highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder. DSM-5-TR puts its crude mortality at about 5 per cent per decade, from medical complications (cardiac arrhythmia among them) and from suicide. It usually begins in adolescence, far more often in women. The personality behind it is strikingly consistent: perfectionism , obsessionality, rigidity and anxiety; the patient is over-controlled. Impulsivity belongs to bulimia, while avoidance and dependence define the avoidant and dependent personality disorders (Section 8.11). Exam trap Amenorrhoea is no longer required but is still common , so it remains a correct "finding in anorexia". It means absence of menstrual periods, not fear of weight gain or excessive exercise. Bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder The London psychiatrist Gerald Russell named bulimia nervosa (BN) in 1979, calling it "an ominous variant of anorexia nervosa". DSM-5-TR requires: Recurrent binge eating : eating, in a discrete period (about 2 hours), an amount definitely larger than most people would, with a sense of loss of control . Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviour against weight gain: self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics or other medicines, fasting or excessive exercise. Both on average at least once a week for 3 months (DSM-IV asked for twice a week). Self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape and weight. Not occurring only during episodes of anorexia nervosa. Secret binges, often set off by low mood, are followed by shame and purging, in repeating cycles. Because purging undoes only part of a binge, people with bulimia are usually of normal weight or overweight . Vomiting leaves marks: eroded dental enamel, swollen parotid glands, hypokalaemia and Russell's sign , calluses on the back of the hand from the teeth. The typical trait is impulsivity . Binge-eating disorder (BED), a full diagnosis only since DSM-5, is binge eating at least once a week for 3 months, with marked distress and three of five features: eating very rapidly, until uncomfortably full, when not hungry, alone from embarrassment, and with disgust or guilt afterwards. There is no regular compensatory behaviour . Figure 8.11 shows how the three disorders are told apart. Anorexia and bulimia share a psychology: a distorted body image , an intense fear of being fat , and eating regulated by psychological rather than physiological processes (rules, fear and mood instead of hunger and fullness). Exam trap Significantly low body weight separates anorexia from bulimia. Purging, fear of fatness and damage to health occur in both. Weight is asked first, so a low-weight person who binges and purges has anorexia (binge-eating/purging type), not bulimia. Causes and other specified eating disorders Risks pile up. Sociocultural : they cluster where a thin ideal is prized, as in modelling and ballet. Dieting starts most histories, and restraint provokes bingeing as the body defends its weight (set-point theory, Section 1.10). Family : Salvador Minuchin's enmeshed, overprotective, rigid, conflict-avoiding psychosomatic family (Section 7.7) features in anorexia. Personality : perfectionism in anorexia, impulsivity in bulimia. Biology : twin studies put heritability near one half, and low serotonin activity is linked with impulsivity and binge eating. Presentations fitting no full pattern are other specified feeding or eating disorder (OSFED), for example atypical anorexia nervosa (every criterion met except low weight: despite significant weight loss, weight is within or above the normal range), bulimia or binge-eating disorder of low frequency or short duration, purging disorder (purging without binge eating) and night eating syndrome (eating after waking at night, or excessively after the evening meal, with recall). Enuresis and encopresis The elimination disorders are the repeated passage of urine or faeces into inappropriate places by a child developmentally old enough to control them, voluntary or not. Enuresis is repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes, at least twice a week for 3 consecutive months or with significant distress or impairment, at an age of at least 5 years , and not caused by a substance (a diuretic) or a medical condition (diabetes, epilepsy). It is nocturnal only (the commonest), diurnal only, or both. In primary enuresis the child has never been dry; secondary enuresis returns after a dry period, usually between 5 and 8 years, often after stress. About 5 to 10 per cent of 5-year-olds wet the bed; most outgrow it. The bell-and-pad alarm is described in Section 7.4. Encopresis is repeated passage of faeces into inappropriate places (clothing, the floor) at least once a month for 3 months , at age 4 or older . It is specified with constipation and overflow incontinence , the commoner form, in which painful defecation leads to withholding and leakage around impacted stool, or without constipation , often with oppositional or conduct problems. It too may be primary or secondary. Exam trap Lack of bowel control is encopresis ; lack of bladder control is enuresis . Anorexia is an eating disorder, and "analism" is not a recognised elimination disorder. Ages: urine 5, faeces 4. The sleep-wake disorders and insomnia The sleep stages, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stages N1 to N3 and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, are taught in Section 1.5. DSM-5-TR's sleep-wake disorders , ten disorders or groups (Table 8.25), share a complaint about the quality, timing or amount of sleep with daytime distress. ICD-11 moved them out of the mental disorders into their own chapter, Chapter 7. Four follow a rule of threes, at least three times a week for 3 months: insomnia, hypersomnolence, narcolepsy and restless legs syndrome. Insomnia disorder is difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early waking, on at least 3 nights a week for 3 months despite adequate opportunity for sleep . Its treatment, cognitive behaviour therapy with stimulus control, sleep restriction and paradoxical intention, is in Section 7.4. In hypersomnolence disorder the person is excessively sleepy despite a main sleep of at least 7 hours, with daytime lapses into sleep, unrefreshing sleep of over 9 hours, or difficulty waking fully. In the breathing-related sleep disorders breathing falters in sleep: the upper airway collapses (obstructive sleep apnoea hypopnoea), the brain stops driving breathing (central sleep apnoea), or shallow breathing lets carbon dioxide rise (sleep-related hypoventilation). In the circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders the body clock is out of step with the required schedule: sleep comes too late or too early (delayed or advanced phase), is scattered across the 24 hours (irregular type), drifts later each day (non-24-hour type, common in blind people) or clashes with working hours (shift work type). Exam trap Cataplexy is a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion, in full consciousness, and it marks narcolepsy. Catalepsy is the reverse, a posture held for long periods with the waxy flexibility of catatonia (Section 8.4). Parasomnias and restless legs Parasomnias are abnormal behaviours or experiences arising from sleep, and timing identifies them: deep N3 sleep fills the first third of the night, while REM periods lengthen towards morning. The NREM sleep arousal disorders are incomplete awakenings, usually from N3, in the first third of the night , with little dream recall and amnesia ; they are commonest in children. In sleepwalking ( somnambulism ) the person sits up, walks about or performs complex acts while asleep, blank-faced and hard to wake. In sleep terrors ( pavor nocturnus ) the sleeper wakes abruptly with a panicky scream, intense fear and autonomic arousal (racing heart, rapid breathing, sweating, dilated pupils), and cannot be comforted. REM parasomnias come later. Nightmare disorder is repeated, extended, extremely dysphoric dreams, usually in the second half of the night; the dreamer wakes alert and remembers vividly . In REM sleep behaviour disorder the normal muscle atonia of REM fails, so the person acts out dream content , shouting, punching or kicking. Commonest in men over 50, it often precedes Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or multiple system atrophy, often by more than a decade (about 75 per cent of idiopathic cases within 10 to 15 years). Restless legs syndrome (Willis-Ekbom disease) is an urge to move the legs, with creeping sensations, that starts at rest, is relieved by movement and worsens in the evening. A substance/medication-induced sleep disorder follows intoxication or withdrawal. Kleine-Levin syndrome , recurrent hypersomnia with hyperphagia and hypersexuality, mostly in adolescent boys, is a separate diagnosis in the International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD-3); DSM-5-TR names it only as an example of other specified hypersomnolence disorder. Exam trap Sitting, walking or complex behaviour while asleep is somnambulism ; screaming terror is sleep terrors; acting out dreams is REM sleep behaviour disorder , from loss of REM atonia, not absence of REM; uncomfortable leg sensations are restless legs. A man who ejaculates too soon, a person aroused by shoes, a child who insists she is a boy and a contented gay man in 1970 have all been diagnosed; only some would be today. We start with normal sexual response, take the three DSM-5-TR groups in turn, and end with homosexuality's exit from the manuals. The sexual response cycle and the language of gender Disorder is judged against the normal picture drawn by the gynaecologist William Howell Masters (1915 to 2001) and his research partner Virginia Eshelman Johnson (1925 to 2013). In Human Sexual Response (1966), from laboratory recordings of nearly 700 volunteers, they described a four-phase sexual response cycle . In excitement , blood engorges the genitals, producing erection or vaginal lubrication. In plateau , arousal levels off just before climax. Orgasm is a peak of rhythmic muscular contractions, with ejaculation in men. In resolution the body returns to rest, and men pass through a refractory period in which another orgasm is impossible; many women have none and can have multiple orgasms. Helen Singer Kaplan (1929 to 1995) saw patients whose bodies worked but who did not want sex, and in Disorders of Sexual Desire (1979) put a desire phase first (desire, excitement, orgasm), giving the linear sequence of Figure 8.12; dysfunctions are still sorted by the phase they disturb. Rosemary Basson argued in 2000 that this fits many women in long relationships poorly. In her circular model a woman often starts from sexual neutrality, is receptive for the sake of intimacy, is aroused by sexual stimuli and only then feels responsive desire ; satisfaction feeds back into intimacy. DSM-5 merged women's desire and arousal disorders partly for this reason. Right: Basson's circle, in which desire can follow arousal. Four terms must be kept apart. Sex is biological (chromosomes, gonads, hormones, genitals); gender identity is the inner sense of being a man, a woman or another gender; gender role is the behaviour a culture expects of each gender; sexual orientation is the gender of those one is attracted to. Androgyny , in the 1974 work of Sandra Lipsitz Bem (1944 to 2014) with her Bem Sex Role Inventory, means scoring high on both masculine and feminine traits; it describes a flexible personality, not a disorder. Sexual dysfunctions A sexual dysfunction is a clinically significant disturbance in the ability to respond sexually or to experience sexual pleasure. Most of DSM-5-TR's eight share one template: the problem occurs on almost all occasions (about 75 to 100 percent), has lasted at least about 6 months, causes clinically significant distress, and is not better explained by another mental disorder, severe relationship distress, a substance or a medical condition. Specifiers give the course: lifelong (present since sexual activity began) or acquired (after a period of normal function), and generalised or situational (only with certain partners, stimulation or situations). Erectile disorder has the strongest medical ties: diabetes, vascular disease, smoking and age. The substance/medication-induced form follows drugs: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) most often delay orgasm or ejaculation, and antipsychotics, antihypertensives and chronic alcohol use are frequent culprits. Masters and Johnson ( Human Sexual Inadequacy , 1970) described performance anxiety , fear of failing, and spectatoring , mentally watching and judging one's own performance, so that attention leaves erotic sensation and one failure breeds the next. Relationship conflict, past abuse, depression and religious prohibitions add to the picture. Premature ejaculation is the dysfunction most tied to anxiety, and is commoner in men with anxiety disorders, especially social anxiety disorder. Treatment is in Section 7.7; here, match tool to problem. The stop-start technique of James Semans (1956), halting stimulation just before the point of no return, and Masters and Johnson's squeeze technique , firm pressure where the head of the penis meets the shaft, teach ejaculatory control. Sensate focus , graded non-demanding touch with intercourse at first forbidden, removes performance anxiety in many dysfunctions. Vaginismus is treated with relaxation and graded dilators, erectile disorder often with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil. Exam trap Stop-start and squeeze treat premature ejaculation , not erectile disorder, inhibited male orgasm (delayed ejaculation, the opposite problem) or vaginismus. Premature ejaculation is most commonly associated with an anxiety state : masturbation does not cause it (a myth that also fuels dhat syndrome, Section 8.1), diabetes is the classic link of erectile disorder, and personality disorder has no special tie. Paraphilias and paraphilic disorders DSM-5-TR calls any intense and persistent sexual interest other than in genital stimulation or fondling with physically mature, consenting human partners a paraphilia . The key DSM-5 move was to separate interest from disorder. A paraphilic disorder is a paraphilia that currently causes distress or impairment, or whose satisfaction has involved harm, or risk of harm, to others. Criterion A gives the interest, recurrent and intense for at least 6 months in fantasies, urges or behaviours; Criterion B the consequences. A shoe fetish that troubles no one is a paraphilia but not a disorder; exposing oneself to strangers meets Criterion B even without distress. The eight named disorders (Table 8.27) fall into two groups. Anomalous activity preferences are the courtship disorders , distorted pieces of courtship (looking, showing, touching), and the algolagnic disorders , which involve pain. Anomalous target preferences are pedophilic, fetishistic and transvestic disorder. Most sets allow the specifiers in a controlled environment (such as prison) and in full remission (no acting on urges and no distress for 5 years outside such settings). Ray Blanchard coined autogynephilia in 1989: a male's recurrent, intense sexual arousal by the thought or image of himself as a woman. It anchors his controversial typology of male-to-female gender dysphoria, and in men with transvestic disorder it raises the likelihood of gender dysphoria. Exam trap Autogynephilia is arousal by the image of oneself as a woman ; arousal by prepubescent children is pedophilia, by being humiliated is masochism, and mere arousal by oneself is not autogynephilia. An inanimate object means fetishism: necrophilia needs a corpse, frotteurism a non-consenting person, voyeurism an unsuspecting one. Why do paraphilias form? Learning theorists cite classical conditioning : Stanley Rachman (1966) conditioned mild arousal to a picture of women's boots in the laboratory. John Money (1921 to 2006) proposed the lovemap , a childhood template of the ideal lover and erotic scene that early experience can distort. Kurt Freund (1914 to 1996), in his courtship disorder hypothesis , saw voyeurism, exhibitionism, frotteurism and preferential rape as disturbances of successive courtship phases (searching, pre-touch interaction, touching, intercourse), which is why they cluster. Gender dysphoria and gender incongruence Gender dysphoria in DSM-5-TR is a marked incongruence between one's experienced or expressed gender and one's assigned gender, lasting at least 6 months and causing clinically significant distress or impairment. A child needs six of eight indicators, one of which must be a strong desire to be, or insistence that one is, the other gender; others include cross-gender clothing, play and playmates and dislike of one's anatomy. An adolescent or adult needs two of six, such as a strong desire to be rid of one's sex characteristics or to be treated as the other gender. Specifiers: 'with a disorder/difference of sex development' and, for adults, 'posttransition'. DSM-III (1980) introduced transsexualism for adults (a historic term for a person seeking social and often bodily transition to the other sex) and gender identity disorder of childhood. DSM-IV (1994) merged them into gender identity disorder , a condition in which one's experienced gender identity does not match one's assigned sex. That made the identity itself the disorder, so DSM-5 (2013) renamed it gender dysphoria, moving the focus from identity to distress. ICD-10 listed transsexualism (F64.0), dual-role transvestism (F64.1) and gender identity disorder of childhood (F64.2) under F64. ICD-11, in force from 1 January 2022, renamed the condition gender incongruence , of adolescence or adulthood and of childhood (about 2 years' persistence in children), and moved it out of the mental disorders chapter into a new Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health : being transgender is not a mental illness, but a code lets people obtain gender-affirming care. The sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders moved there too. The paraphilic disorders stayed in Chapter 6, now built around non-consent: exhibitionistic, voyeuristic, pedophilic, coercive sexual sadism disorder and frotteuristic, plus other paraphilic disorder involving non-consenting individuals and paraphilic disorder involving solitary or consenting individuals with marked distress or risk. Consensual fetishism, fetishistic transvestism and sadomasochism were removed (Table 8.28). DSM-5's gender dysphoria corresponds to ICD-11's gender incongruence. Homosexuality: pathologised, then depathologised Pathologisation is classifying a behaviour or identity as a mental disorder; depathologisation is removing that classification (not changing orientation, the aim of discredited conversion therapies, nor coming out). Homosexuality is the clearest case. DSM-I (1952) placed it under sociopathic personality disturbance as a sexual deviation; DSM-II (1968) kept it among the sexual deviations. Alfred Charles Kinsey (1894 to 1956), in Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948), rated behaviour on the Kinsey scale from 0 (exclusively heterosexual) to 6 (exclusively homosexual), showing same-sex experience to be common and graded. Key study: Hooker's blind judges (1957) Evelyn Hooker (1907 to 1996) asked whether homosexual men are more maladjusted. She matched 30 homosexual and 30 heterosexual men, none in therapy, for age, IQ and education and gave them projective tests, including the Rorschach. Expert judges blind to group could not tell them apart beyond chance, and rated their adjustment alike. Criticism: a small, non-random sample; but earlier claims had rested on patients in treatment. With this evidence and activist pressure, the board of the American Psychiatric Association voted in December 1973 to remove homosexuality. The seventh printing of DSM-II (1974) substituted sexual orientation disturbance for people distressed by their orientation; DSM-III (1980) renamed it ego-dystonic homosexuality , and DSM-III-R (1987) dropped it. ICD-10 (endorsed in 1990) no longer listed homosexuality, stating that orientation by itself is not a disorder, but kept F66, including egodystonic sexual orientation; ICD-11 deleted F66. On his third dry day he is trembling, picking at the sheets and swatting at insects only he can see. Months later, sober, he forgets a nurse within minutes and fills the gap with invented stories. He spans both halves of this section: the disorders drugs produce, and the failures of cognition that drugs, disease and age produce. The language of substance use A psychoactive substance is a drug that alters mood, cognition, perception or behaviour by acting on the brain; the word has nothing to do with a drug-induced hallucination or an "active psychopath". Intoxication is the reversible syndrome of recent use. Withdrawal is the syndrome that follows stopping or cutting down after heavy, prolonged use, and it usually mirrors intoxication: a sedative leaves an agitated brain behind, a stimulant a slowed one. Tolerance is needing markedly more of a drug for the same effect: metabolic tolerance when the liver breaks the drug down faster, pharmacodynamic tolerance when receptors and neurons adapt. Cross-tolerance is tolerance that extends to other drugs, especially of the same class, so a heavy drinker needs large doses of benzodiazepines or barbiturates. In cross-dependence one drug suppresses another's withdrawal. Together these are why alcohol-dependent patients are detoxified with a long-acting benzodiazepine such as chlordiazepoxide, and why methadone can replace heroin. Sensitisation (reverse tolerance) is the opposite: repeated cocaine or amphetamine use brings paranoia or seizures at ever lower doses. Physical dependence shows itself in a withdrawal syndrome; psychological dependence is a compelling need to use for pleasure or relief. Addiction, compulsive drug seeking despite harm, is different again: a cancer patient on morphine is physically dependent but not addicted. Craving is an intense urge to use, often cued by places and objects linked to the drug, and relapse is a return to use after abstinence (Chapter 7). ICD-10 codes these disorders F10 (alcohol) to F19 (multiple drugs), and the digit after the point gives the clinical pattern: .0 acute intoxication, .1 harmful use (use that is actually damaging health), .2 dependence syndrome, .3 withdrawal state, .4 withdrawal with delirium, .5 psychotic disorder, .6 amnesic syndrome and .7 residual and late-onset psychotic disorder. The dependence syndrome was described for alcohol in 1976 by Griffith Edwards and Milton Gross : a narrowed drinking repertoire, drink given priority over everything else, tolerance, repeated withdrawal, drinking to relieve it, a felt compulsion, and rapid reinstatement after abstinence. DSM-IV split this ground into substance abuse and substance dependence. DSM-5 (2013) and DSM-5-TR (2022) merge them into one substance use disorder : at least 2 of 11 criteria within 12 months, in four groups. Impaired control covers using more or longer than intended, failed efforts to cut down, much time spent, and craving; social impairment covers failed roles, interpersonal problems and activities given up; risky use covers hazardous situations and use despite known harm; the pharmacological criteria are tolerance and withdrawal. Severity is mild with 2 or 3, moderate with 4 or 5, and severe with 6 or more. Craving was added and legal problems dropped. "Addiction" is not a DSM-5-TR diagnosis. DSM-5-TR also includes gambling disorder (four or more of nine criteria in 12 months, such as chasing losses) as its only behavioural addiction; internet gaming disorder is a condition for further study. ICD-11's block "disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours" codes each drug as an episode of harmful use, a harmful pattern of use, or dependence, and adds gambling disorder and gaming disorder : gaming with impaired control, given priority over other interests despite harm. Exam trap "Drug abuse" is not an ICD-10 pattern: abuse was a DSM-IV category, and ICD-10's nearest term is harmful use. Gaming disorder sits in ICD-11's substance use and addictive behaviours block, not under stress-associated, mood or impulse control disorders. Cross-tolerance is tolerance carried over to a related drug, not freedom from addiction. Why drugs capture the brain Every drug of abuse, by its own route, ends up raising dopamine in the mesolimbic dopamine system , from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens in the ventral striatum (Chapter 5). It is the circuit most consistently altered in substance use disorders; the cerebellar vermis (gait), lateral geniculate nucleus (vision) and vestibular nuclei (balance) are not reward structures. Drugs are positive reinforcers because they give pleasure and negative reinforcers because they remove withdrawal, anxiety or pain (Chapter 1). In the opponent-process theory of Richard Solomon and John Corbit (1974), every drug high (the a-process) triggers an opposing low (the b-process). With repetition the b-process strengthens: the high shrinks (tolerance), the crash deepens (withdrawal), and the user takes the drug to escape misery rather than to feel good. Using Swedish adoption records in 1981, C. Robert Cloninger and colleagues separated type I alcoholism (onset after about 25, guilt, binges with loss of control, both sexes, shaped by environment) from type II (early onset, novelty seeking, antisocial behaviour, inability to abstain, mainly men, highly heritable). Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) saw alcohol-dependent people as fixated at the oral stage (Chapter 4). Elvin Morton Jellinek (1890 to 1963) argued in The Disease Concept of Alcoholism (1960) that alcoholism is a disease with five "species": alpha (psychological reliance, no loss of control), beta (physical damage without dependence), gamma (tolerance, withdrawal and loss of control: once started, the drinker cannot stop), delta (inability to abstain) and epsilon (periodic binges). Key study: Kandel's stages of drug use (1975) Denise Kandel surveyed New York State high-school students twice and found a regular order: beer or wine, then cigarettes or spirits, then marijuana, then other illicit drugs. Few reached heroin or cocaine without marijuana, so in this gateway hypothesis marijuana is the drug most often cited as the gateway, although alcohol and tobacco come first. Criticism: a sequence is not a cause, and shared risk factors could explain it. Drugs differ in addictive liability, the chance that a user becomes dependent. Nicotine (tobacco) ranks highest: a larger share of people who try it become dependent than of those who try heroin, cocaine, alcohol or marijuana. DSM-5-TR notes that withdrawal begins within about 4 to 12 hours of the last drink, peaks on the second day and eases markedly by the fourth or fifth. Its complications keep only a rough clock (Figure 8.13): tremor, sweating and insomnia within the first day (roughly 6 to 24 hours); seizures at about 12 to 48 hours; alcoholic hallucinosis , hallucinations (usually voices) in clear consciousness, at about 12 to 48 hours; and delirium tremens at about 48 to 72 hours, with clouded consciousness, fever, racing pulse, coarse tremor and vivid visual and tactile hallucinations of insects, small animals or tiny (Lilliputian) people. Fewer than 1 in 10 people in withdrawal reach this stage, but it can kill, so benzodiazepines are given to prevent it, with thiamine against Wernicke's encephalopathy. day 2: withdrawal peaks Tremor, sweating 6 to 24 h Hallucinosis 12 to 48 h Seizures 12 to 48 h Delirium tremens 48 to 72 h 0 24 48 72 96 120 Hours after the last drink Figure 8.13 Approximate onset windows of alcohol withdrawal features. Tremor comes first and delirium tremens, the most dangerous, last; timing varies between people. Chronic drinkers may develop alcoholic jealousy, a delusion that the partner is unfaithful; fetal alcohol syndrome is in Section 8.3, and the CAGE and AUDIT questionnaires in Chapter 2. Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde accumulates after a drink and causes flushing, nausea and palpitations. Naltrexone, an opioid antagonist, blunts alcohol's reward and craving, and acamprosate, acting on glutamate, eases protracted withdrawal. Opium's natural alkaloids are morphine, codeine, thebaine, papaverine and noscapine. Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is made from morphine, so it is semi-synthetic; methadone, pethidine, fentanyl and tramadol are synthetic. Intoxication brings pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression, reversed by naloxone. Withdrawal is miserable but rarely dangerous: yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, dilated pupils, piloerection ("cold turkey"), diarrhoea and aches. Methadone or buprenorphine substitution stabilises dependent users. Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake and amphetamines release dopamine, giving euphoria, energy and, at high doses, paranoia; amphetamine psychosis can resemble paranoid schizophrenia, and a dysphoric crash follows a binge. MDMA (ecstasy) is an amphetamine derivative that releases serotonin. Formication , tactile hallucinations of insects crawling on or under the skin ("cocaine bugs"), is most characteristic of stimulant intoxication and of alcohol or sedative withdrawal, not of depression, phobia or generalised anxiety. Cannabis acts through delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC); in India it is used as bhang (leaves), ganja (flowering tops) and charas (resin). Heavy use is linked to an amotivational syndrome of apathy and to a raised risk of psychosis. LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide), whose effects Albert Hofmann (1906 to 2008) discovered in 1943, psilocybin and mescaline alter perception in clear consciousness; some users later re-experience trails and halos (hallucinogen persisting perception disorder, or flashbacks). Inhalants intoxicate like alcohol and damage organs. Nicotine acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors; caffeine use disorder is only a condition for further study. Benzodiazepines and barbiturates are cross-tolerant with alcohol, and their withdrawal can also bring seizures and delirium. Exam trap Alcohol is a GABA agonist. Heroin is the odd one out among opium alkaloids because it is semi-synthetic. Opioid intoxication gives pinpoint pupils, withdrawal dilated ones. Disulfiram works by aversion through aldehyde dehydrogenase; reducing reward is naltrexone's action and glutamate modulation acamprosate's. Neurocognitive disorders: terms and domains ICD-10 groups disorders of failing cognition as organic mental disorders (F00 to F09). DSM-5 renamed them neurocognitive disorders (NCDs), acquired declines from a previous level. It kept delirium and replaced dementia and amnestic disorder with major neurocognitive disorder , a significant decline in one or more of six domains (complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor function, social cognition) that costs independence in daily life, and mild NCD, a modest decline with independence kept. One impaired domain is enough, so pure amnesia now counts as major NCD. Older terms name the function each disorder chiefly affects: dementia, a global decline that includes abstraction and judgement; amnesia, memory; aphasia, alexia and acalculia, language and symbolic function; apraxia, skilled purposeful movement (motor skills); and agnosia, recognition despite intact senses (Chapter 5). Delirium Delirium is a disturbance of attention and awareness (clouded consciousness) that develops over hours to days, fluctuates through the day, and brings disorientation, memory loss or perceptual disturbance, often visual hallucinations. The sleep-wake cycle may reverse, and confusion worsens in the evening ( sundowning ). DSM-5-TR specifies acute or persistent delirium and hyperactive, hypoactive (quiet and easily missed) or mixed types. Motor signs include asterixis (a flapping tremor of outstretched hands), multifocal myoclonus, tremor, abnormal tone and reflexes, and carphologia or floccillation, picking at the bedclothes: all can occur. The electroencephalogram (EEG) shows diffuse slowing. Delirium always has a physical cause: infection, metabolic or electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, drugs, intoxication or withdrawal, or surgery. It affects 11 to 51 percent of older people after operations, and it is the commonest psychiatric syndrome after cardiac surgery, ahead of depression, anxiety and schizophrenia. Heavy drinkers eat poorly and absorb thiamine (vitamin B1) badly, and neurons need thiamine to use glucose. Acute deficiency causes Wernicke's encephalopathy , described by Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) in 1881: confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia with nystagmus, an emergency treated with thiamine before glucose. Untreated, it leaves Korsakoff's syndrome (Korsakoff's psychosis), described by Sergei Korsakoff (1854 to 1900) in 1887: severe anterograde and retrograde amnesia, apathy, and confabulation , fluent false accounts filling memory gaps without intent to deceive. Immediate memory and intelligence are relatively spared. Together these form Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, with lesions in the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus. Exam trap Memory loss, confabulation and nystagmus in a heavy drinker is Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. The cause is thiamine deficiency, not vitamin B12, vitamin D, folate, hypoxia or lead. Alzheimer's, Pick's, Parkinson's, Huntington's and Creutzfeldt-Jakob diseases are not caused by drinking. Disorders due to another medical condition Physical disease can present psychiatrically, so DSM-5-TR has diagnoses such as depressive disorder due to another medical condition (ICD-10 F06 and F07, the "organic" syndromes). Cushing's syndrome (excess cortisol) mainly causes depression, anxiety and cognitive impairment, occasionally mania or psychosis; Addison's disease (cortisol deficiency) causes apathy and depression. Hypothyroidism causes depression and, when severe, a psychosis called "myxoedema madness"; hyperthyroidism causes anxiety. Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, neurosyphilis (general paresis, with grandiose delusions), HIV and systemic lupus erythematosus can all cause mood change, psychosis or dementia. Epilepsy can bring an interictal psychosis, and head injury lasting personality change. The conditions here describe how a person habitually thinks, feels and relates, year after year. We define personality disorder, sort the ten types into clusters, study borderline and antisocial personality closely, meet the dimensional models, and end with the disorders of conduct and impulse control. When personality becomes a disorder Everyone has personality traits, enduring ways of perceiving, relating to and thinking about the world and oneself; they become a personality disorder (PD) only when inflexible and maladaptive. DSM-5-TR defines a PD as an enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from the expectations of the person's culture and shows in two or more of four areas: cognition (how self, others and events are perceived), affectivity (the range, intensity, lability and appropriateness of emotion), interpersonal functioning and impulse control . The pattern is pervasive and inflexible, stable, traceable to adolescence or early adulthood, causes distress or impairment, and is not better explained by another disorder, a substance or a medical condition. A PD can therefore disturb thinking, mood and relationships alike. The traits are usually ego-syntonic : they feel like "just me", so informants become essential. The median prevalence of any PD is about 10 percent (10.5 percent in DSM-5-TR's review). Diagnosis before 18 needs features present for at least a year, because childhood traits often fade; antisocial PD is never diagnosed before 18. DSM-IV recorded PDs on Axis II (Section 8.1). DSM-5-TR keeps the categorical model , PDs as distinct syndromes, while noting the dimensional model , PDs as extreme variants of normal traits that shade into normality ( see the newer models ). The ten disorders in three clusters DSM-5-TR groups its ten specific PDs into three clusters by descriptive similarity (Table 8.32): Cluster A , odd or eccentric; Cluster B , dramatic, emotional or erratic; Cluster C , anxious or fearful (weird, wild, worried). Among paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal and borderline, the odd one out is borderline (Cluster B). Borderline personality disorder Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, with marked impulsivity, beginning by early adulthood. Its signature is emotional instability and impulsivity, not detachment, perfectionism or paranoid ideation. Five or more of nine criteria are needed: Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment. Unstable, intense relationships alternating between idealisation and devaluation. Identity disturbance: a markedly and persistently unstable self-image. Impulsivity in at least two self-damaging areas (spending, sex, substances, reckless driving, binge eating). Recurrent suicidal behaviour, gestures or threats, or self-mutilation. Affective instability from marked reactivity of mood, episodes lasting hours, rarely days. Chronic feelings of emptiness. Inappropriate, intense anger or difficulty controlling anger. Transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociation. Adolph Stern coined "borderline" in 1938 for patients between neurosis and psychosis. Otto F. Kernberg (born 1928) recast it as borderline personality organisation : identity diffusion, primitive defences and generally intact reality testing. The primary defence is splitting : self and others are seen as all good or all bad, so today's idealised rescuer becomes tomorrow's betrayer. With it come projective identification (disowned feelings are placed in another person, who is pressed into feeling them), primitive idealisation and devaluation. Repression (pushing wishes out of awareness), sublimation (channelling them into valued activity), rationalisation (plausible excuses), regression (retreat to earlier behaviour) and undoing (an act that symbolically cancels another) are not the BPD defence (Chapter 4). Heinz Kohut (1913 to 1981), founder of self psychology , held that a child needs mirroring (a parent's delighted reflection of its worth) and a calm figure to idealise ; when both fail, the self stays fragmented, felt as emptiness and being "no one". He built the theory mainly to explain narcissism. Marsha M. Linehan (born 1943) proposed the biosocial theory : biological emotional vulnerability meets an invalidating environment that dismisses the child's feelings, so regulation is never learned. Treatments (Chapter 7): her dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based treatment, Kernberg's transference-focused psychotherapy and schema therapy. ICD-10 calls BPD emotionally unstable personality disorder , impulsive or borderline type. Two differentials. BPD mood shifts last hours and follow interpersonal triggers; bipolar episodes last days to weeks, and both may coexist. Conduct disorder is diagnosed under 18 and centres on rule violation and aggression; BPD is an adult pattern of identity and affective instability and fear of abandonment, and childhood conduct disorder leads to ASPD, not BPD. Clinical link BPD is diagnosed more often in women in clinical samples, though not in community samples. Self-harm is common; about 6 percent of hospitalised patients died by suicide over 24 years. Exam trap BPD mood is reactive and unpredictable, never "regular and predictable"; eccentric, odd thinking is schizotypal; cruelty to animals and rule-breaking before 15 are conduct disorder. A 2023 paper asking which is NOT a BPD feature offered both "regular and predictable changes in mood" and "eccentric behaviour with odd thinking"; both are strictly correct, but the key is the mood option, the direct inversion of BPD's affective instability. A 2024 paper keys "failure of parental mirroring and idealising, leading to a fragmented self" under object relations theory : strictly it is Kohut's self psychology , a cousin of the object relations school of Melanie Klein (1882 to 1960) and Kernberg. Choose it; oral fixation, Oedipal conflict and a harsh superego are classical Freudian answers. Antisocial personality disorder and psychopathy Antisocial personality disorder (ASPD) is a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, occurring since age 15, shown by three or more of seven criteria: failure to conform to laws; deceitfulness and conning; impulsivity; irritability and aggressiveness; reckless disregard for safety; consistent irresponsibility; and lack of remorse. The person must be at least 18, with evidence of conduct disorder beginning before 15 (Figure 8.14). ICD-10 calls it dissocial personality disorder . Antisocial behaviour often remits by about age 40. Philippe Pinel (1745 to 1826) described manie sans délire (mania without delirium) in 1801: impulsive rages with intact reasoning. James Cowles Prichard (1786 to 1848) named moral insanity in 1835. Hervey Cleckley (1903 to 1984), in The Mask of Sanity (1941), listed 16 characteristics of the psychopath, among them superficial charm, absence of nervousness, untruthfulness and lack of remorse: a normal mask over an emotional void. Robert D. Hare (born 1934) developed the Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R, 1991), built on Cleckley: 20 items scored 0 to 2 from interview and records (total 40; 30 or more is the usual cut-off for psychopathy), with an interpersonal-affective factor (glibness, grandiosity, callousness) and an antisocial-lifestyle factor (impulsivity, irresponsibility, early behaviour problems). Psychopathy is defined by traits, ASPD mostly by behaviour: most men in prison meet ASPD criteria, but only a minority are psychopaths. Causes combine genes with adverse rearing (abuse, neglect, erratic discipline). In Deviant Children Grown Up (1966), Lee Nelken Robins (1922 to 2009) found that adult sociopathy almost never arose without childhood antisocial behaviour: the root of the conduct-disorder rule. The underarousal hypothesis adds that psychopaths have low autonomic arousal (low resting heart rate and skin conductance) and seek stimulation. Key study: Lykken's fearless psychopaths (1957) David Thoreson Lykken (1928 to 2006) had primary psychopaths, other prisoners and controls learn a "mental maze" in which some wrong choices brought a shock. Psychopaths learned the maze as well but avoided the shocked errors less, reported less anxiety and showed smaller skin conductance responses to a signal paired with shock. Conclusion, the fearlessness hypothesis : punishment teaches psychopaths little. Criticism: small samples, one laboratory task. Exam trap The PCL-R is Hare's , built on Cleckley's description; not Cleckley alone, Aaron Temkin Beck (1921 to 2021; cognitive therapy) or Hans Jürgen Eysenck (1916 to 1997; the PEN model). In ASPD the pattern dates from 15, the diagnosis waits until 18, and conduct disorder must begin before 15, not 18. An option reading "conduct disorder before 15 and disregard for others' rights from 18" is loosely worded but still the answer: 18 is the minimum age for the diagnosis. Histrionic, narcissistic and the rest of Cluster B Histrionic personality disorder is excessive emotionality and attention seeking: discomfort when not the centre of attention, seductive or provocative behaviour, shallow and rapidly shifting emotion, impressionistic speech lacking detail, theatricality, suggestibility, and seeing relationships as more intimate than they are. Narcissistic personality disorder rests on a core triad of grandiosity , need for admiration and lack of empathy , with fantasies of unlimited success, the belief that one is special and understood only by high-status people, entitlement, exploitation, envy and arrogance. Kohut saw narcissism as arrested development after parents failed to mirror, to be met with empathy; Kernberg saw a pathological grandiose self defending against rage and envy toward cold parents, to be confronted. Dependent personality disorder is an excessive need to be taken care of: needing reassurance for everyday decisions, never disagreeing for fear of losing support, urgently seeking a new relationship when one ends. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is a preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and mental and interpersonal control at the expense of flexibility, openness and efficiency: lists swallow the task, perfectionism stops it being finished, work crowds out friends, morals are rigid, worthless objects are kept and money is hoarded. The motive is control , not achievement or autonomy; efficiency is what it sacrifices. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) described the same trio in the anal character (1908): orderly, parsimonious and obstinate. OCPD is ego-syntonic, with limited insight and no true obsessions or compulsions; OCD is ego-dystonic, its intrusive obsessions and compulsions felt as alien and resisted (Section 8.6). Newer models: ICD-11 and the AMPD ICD-11 abolished the ten types: one diagnosis of personality disorder is graded mild, moderate or severe , with personality difficulty below that threshold. Five trait domain qualifiers describe its style: negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition and anankastia (rigid perfectionism and control), plus a borderline pattern specifier . DSM-5's Section III offers the Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD). Criterion A rates the level of personality functioning from 0 to 4 on identity and self-direction (self) and empathy and intimacy (interpersonal); at least moderate impairment is needed. Criterion B requires one or more pathological traits, organised in five domains: negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition and psychoticism. Six types survive: antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive and schizotypal, plus personality disorder-trait specified. Oppositional defiant and conduct disorder The disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders, failures of emotional and behavioural self-control, mostly begin in childhood and are commoner in boys. Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) is angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behaviour, or vindictiveness for at least 6 months, with four or more of eight symptoms shown with someone other than a sibling. Most children with ODD never develop conduct disorder. Conduct disorder (CD) is a repetitive, persistent pattern violating the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate norms: three or more of 15 criteria in the past 12 months, one in the past 6 months, from four groups: aggression to people and animals , destruction of property , deceitfulness or theft and serious violations of rules (staying out at night or truancy before 13, running away). The childhood-onset type shows a symptom before age 10, the adolescent-onset type none. The specifier with limited prosocial emotions , applied to CD alone, needs two or more of four traits for 12 months: lack of remorse or guilt, callous lack of empathy, unconcern about performance, and shallow or deficient affect. These callous-unemotional traits mark more severe, planned aggression. Terrie E. Moffitt (1993) explained the two onsets. Life-course-persistent antisocial behaviour is rare, starts in early childhood from neuropsychological deficits meeting adverse homes, and continues into adult crime. Adolescence-limited antisocial behaviour is common, begins at puberty as teenagers copy older peers, and fades in early adulthood. Pyromania is planned fire setting for gratification; IED is impulsive aggression beyond the trigger. Each began with signs and symptoms, the vocabulary of Section 8.2, and ended with onset, course and prognosis, the terms of Section 8.1. The line the cards drew still divides schizophrenia (8.4) from the bipolar and depressive disorders (8.5), and DSM-III turned his method into explicit criteria, which is why every disorder from 8.3 to 8.11 arrives as a criterion set, often with a minimum duration. Yet his deeper hope, that each pile would prove to be a separate brain disease, has not come true. Risk genes for schizophrenia are shared with bipolar disorder and depression, comorbidity is the rule, and the diathesis-stress model explains more than any single cause. So DSM-5 added severity ratings and spectra to his categories, and ICD-11 grades personality disorder by severity. Chapter summary 8.1 Abnormality, Causes and the Classification of Mental Disorders. No single criterion defines abnormality: clinicians weigh the four Ds , Wakefield's harmful dysfunction and the DSM-5-TR definition, which excludes expectable grief and mere social deviance. Psychopathology has its own vocabulary of aetiology, onset, course, prognosis, prevalence, incidence and comorbidity . Genes, endophenotypes and stress meet in the diathesis-stress model and Engel's biopsychosocial model . Classification is syndromal and prototypical, judged by reliability and validity. The DSM (APA; DSM-5 dropped the axes; DSM-5-TR, 2022, is current) and the ICD (WHO; ICD-10 F codes; ICD-11 Chapter 6) are the two systems, and cultural concepts of distress such as dhat and latah show culture shaping distress. 8.2 Descriptive Psychopathology: Signs and Symptoms. Descriptive psychopathology , founded by Karl Jaspers ( General Psychopathology , 1913), describes experiences phenomenologically, separating form from content, primary from secondary symptoms and signs from symptoms. An illusion misreads a real stimulus; a hallucination , a disorder of perception, has no stimulus; hypnagogic hallucinations are normal. Flight of ideas, loosening, tangentiality and circumstantiality are disorders of the form of thought. Persecution is the commonest delusion ; Capgras, Fregoli, Cotard, Othello and de Clérambault name delusional themes. Confabulation fills memory gaps without intent to deceive. Affect is observed and momentary, mood sustained; elevated mood runs euphoria, elation, exaltation, ecstasy. Insight has six grades. 8.3 Neurodevelopmental Disorders. Neurodevelopmental disorders begin in the developmental period and often co-occur, so assessment uses several informants. Intellectual disability needs intellectual deficits (IQ about two SD below the mean, 65 to 75), adaptive deficits and early onset; DSM-5 grades severity by adaptive functioning, and global developmental delay is used under age 5. Causes include trisomy 21, fragile X, PKU and fetal alcohol syndrome. Autism spectrum disorder (Kanner, 1943) needs social-communication deficits plus restricted, repetitive behaviour, not low IQ. ADHD needs six of nine symptoms in a domain, several before 12, in two settings. Specific learning disorder occurs with average intelligence; Tourette's needs motor and vocal tics for over a year. 8.4 Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders. Kraepelin's dementia praecox (1893), separated from manic-depressive insanity by its deteriorating course, became Bleuler's schizophrenia (1908, 1911), defined by four As; Schneider's first-rank symptoms stress voices, thought alienation, passivity and delusional perception. Symptoms are positive, negative or cognitive. DSM-5-TR needs 6 months including 1 month of active symptoms; ICD-10 and ICD-11 need 1 month. Brief psychotic disorder lasts 1 day to under 1 month, schizophreniform disorder 1 to under 6 months. Risk is about 48 percent for an identical twin. Positive symptoms reflect mesolimbic dopamine excess; high expressed emotion predicts relapse. Antipsychotics are first-line; nigrostriatal D2 blockade causes dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism and, last, tardive dyskinesia. 8.5 Depressive and Bipolar Disorders, and Suicide. Mood disorders are built from three episodes: a major depressive episode (5 of 9 symptoms for 2 weeks), a manic episode (1 week; marked impairment or psychosis) and a hypomanic episode (4 days, no marked impairment or psychosis). MDD affects women twice as often as men; dysthymia is milder but lasts 2 years; DMDD begins before age 10. Specifiers include mixed features, rapid cycling, melancholic, atypical, peripartum and seasonal. Bipolar I needs mania; bipolar II needs hypomania plus major depression; cyclothymia is subthreshold. Causes range from monoamines and kindling to Beck's cognitive triad . Lithium is the gold-standard mood stabiliser. A previous attempt is the strongest predictor of suicide. 8.6 Anxiety and Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders. Fear answers present danger, anxiety a future threat. DSM-5 split the old neuroses into anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and trauma chapters. Most anxiety disorders need about 6 months ; panic disorder and selective mutism need 1 month. A panic attack peaks within minutes with 4 of 13 symptoms; agoraphobia needs 2 of 5 situations and GAD 3 of 6 symptoms. Causes include the GABA system, Mowrer's two-factor theory, Clark's catastrophic misinterpretation, Klein's suffocation alarm and displacement (Little Hans). OCD needs ego-dystonic obsessions or compulsions taking over an hour a day or causing distress; compulsions are negatively reinforced escape responses and undoing its typical defence. BDD, hoarding, trichotillomania and excoriation are its relatives. 8.7 Trauma, Dissociative and Somatic Symptom Disorders. Charcot, Janet, Breuer and Freud explained hysteria by hypnosis, dissociation and repression , and DSM-III (1980) split it into somatoform and dissociative disorders. PTSD needs a qualifying trauma and symptoms in four clusters for more than 1 month; acute stress disorder lasts 3 days to 1 month, and ICD-11 adds complex PTSD . DID combines two or more personality states with amnesic gaps; dissociative amnesia, fugue and depersonalisation/derealisation complete the class. Somatic symptom disorder is an excessive response to symptoms, conversion a neurological-like loss incompatible with disease, and factitious disorder and malingering are deliberate, differing in external reward. 8.8 Feeding, Eating, Elimination and Sleep-Wake Disorders. DSM-5-TR's feeding and eating disorders include pica (non-food eating for at least 1 month), rumination disorder and ARFID, which restricts food with no body-image concern. Anorexia nervosa (Gull and Lasègue, 1873) needs restriction to a significantly low weight, fear of weight gain and disturbed body experience; amenorrhoea was dropped, severity is graded by BMI, and it is the most lethal eating disorder. Bulimia nervosa (Russell, 1979) pairs binges with compensation weekly for 3 months at normal weight; binge-eating disorder lacks compensation. Enuresis starts at age 5, encopresis at 4. Among sleep-wake disorders, narcolepsy brings cataplexy, N3 brings sleepwalking and sleep terrors, and REM brings nightmares and REM sleep behaviour disorder. 8.9 Sexual Dysfunctions, Paraphilic Disorders and Gender Dysphoria. Masters and Johnson's sexual response cycle (1966: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution, with a male refractory period) gained Kaplan's desire phase (1979) and Basson's circular model (2000). Most DSM-5-TR sexual dysfunctions need symptoms on 75 to 100 percent of occasions for about 6 months with distress; premature ejaculation is tied to anxiety and treated with stop-start and squeeze. A paraphilic disorder is a paraphilia plus distress, impairment or harm to others; DSM-5-TR names eight. Gender dysphoria replaced gender identity disorder, and ICD-11 moved gender incongruence to Chapter 17 while paraphilic disorders stayed in Chapter 6. The APA removed homosexuality in 1973. 8.10 Substance-Related, Addictive and Neurocognitive Disorders. A psychoactive substance alters mood, cognition or behaviour; tolerance, cross-tolerance , withdrawal and dependence describe how use becomes disorder. ICD-10 codes F10 to F19 patterns (harmful use, Edwards and Gross's dependence syndrome ; 'drug abuse' is not one), DSM-5-TR merges abuse and dependence into substance use disorder (2 of 11 criteria), and ICD-11 adds gambling and gaming disorder. Drugs converge on the mesolimbic dopamine system. Alcohol is a GABA-A agonist; heroin is semi-synthetic. Delirium is acute, fluctuating and clouded, unlike dementia; NCD subtypes differ in course and pathology; depression causes pseudodementia; thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome . 8.11 Personality Disorders, Conduct and Impulse-Control Disorders. A personality disorder is an enduring, pervasive, inflexible pattern deviating from cultural expectations in two or more of cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning and impulse control, beginning by adolescence or early adulthood; usually ego-syntonic, it affects about 10 percent. DSM-5-TR's ten types form Clusters A (odd), B (dramatic) and C (anxious). Borderline PD (5 of 9 criteria) is instability of relationships, self-image and affect with impulsivity, its defence splitting. Antisocial PD needs age 18 and conduct disorder before 15; Hare's PCL-R measures psychopathy. ICD-11 and the AMPD grade severity and traits.
