(Amity 2023) a Dhat Syndrome b Koro c Suchi-bai d Latah ✓ Answer: (d) Latah Latah, a Malaysian and Indonesian culture-bound syndrome The concept What Latah is Latah is an exaggerated startle with echolalia , echopraxia , automatic obedience and blurted obscenities. Why this one It belongs to Malaysia and Indonesia , not India, so it is the syndrome not reported here. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Dhat Syndrome Reported in India: anxiety over semen loss . (b) Koro Reported in India: fear that the genitals are retracting, with epidemics in north-east India . (c) Suchi-bai Reported in India: obsessional cleanliness in Bengal. The diathesis-stress model of psychopathology suggests that mental disorders result from: (RML 2023) a Genetic factors only b Environmental factors only c A combination of genetic predisposition and environmental stressors d Neurobiological abnormalities only ✓ Answer: (c) A combination of genetic predisposition and environmental stressors Zubin and Spring, vulnerability-stress model (1977) The concept What it is The diathesis is a genetic, biological or psychological vulnerability. It produces disorder only when a stressor sets it off. Who named it Zubin and Spring (1977) called this the vulnerability-stress model . Exam tip Every option ending in 'only' names a single cause , the one-dimensional thinking the model replaced. Why the other options are wrong (a) Genetic factors only Names a single cause ; genes can be the diathesis, but without a stressor the model predicts no disorder. (b) Environmental factors only Names a single cause ; a stressor needs an existing vulnerability to set off. (d) Neurobiological abnormalities only Names a single cause ; a biological abnormality is one kind of diathesis, which still needs a stressor. A high false positive rate in diagnosis means: (IHBAS 2025) a Diagnosis is too strict b Normal people are diagnosed as disordered c Diagnosis has low reliability d Disordered people go undetected ✓ Answer: (b) Normal people are diagnosed as disordered Definition of a false positive The concept What it is A false positive wrongly labels a healthy person as ill. Why it happens It happens when diagnostic criteria are too loose , so normal people get swept in. Why the other options are wrong (a) Diagnosis is too strict Over-strict criteria cause the opposite error, false negatives , where real cases are missed. (c) Diagnosis has low reliability Low reliability means clinicians disagree with each other, a separate problem. (d) Disordered people go undetected These are false negatives , the result of over-strict criteria. Hypnagogic hallucinations most commonly occur in: (RML 2024) a Schizophrenia b Delirium c Drug dependence d Normal ✓ Answer: (d) Normal Hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations as normal experience The concept What they are Hypnagogic hallucinations occur while falling asleep; hypnopompic ones occur on waking. Who gets them They lie within normal experience and are commonest in healthy people. Narcolepsy also features them. Why the other options are wrong (a) Schizophrenia The hallucinations of schizophrenia are mainly auditory and occur in clear consciousness. (b) Delirium Delirium brings visual and tactile hallucinations; hypnagogic ones are still commonest in healthy people. (c) Drug dependence Drugs bring visual and tactile hallucinations; hypnagogic ones are still commonest in healthy people. Our current mood and feelings are best described by the term: (RML 2024) a Emotion b Mood c Affect d Feeling ✓ Answer: (c) Affect Definition of affect versus mood The concept What affect is Affect is the immediate, observed, moment-to-moment expression of emotion: the weather . Versus mood Mood is the sustained state the person reports: the climate . Why the other options are wrong (a) Emotion The broader term for a brief reaction , not the observed moment-to-moment expression. (b) Mood The sustained state the person reports (the climate), not the current moment. (d) Feeling The experienced side of an emotion, not its observed expression. Choose the correct arrangement of these stages of elevated mood based upon severity: i) Elation, ii) Exaltation, iii) Euphoria, iv) Ecstasy. (Amity 2023) a i, ii, iii & iv b iii, i, ii & iv c iv, iii, ii & i d None of the above ✓ Answer: (b) iii, i, ii & iv Grades of elevated mood, euphoria to ecstasy The concept Lower grades Elevated mood rises from euphoria (mild; hypomania) through elation (moderate; mania). Upper grades Next comes exaltation (intense, with grandiosity; severe mania), then ecstasy (rapture; stuporous or delirious mania). Why this one So the order is iii (euphoria), i (elation), ii (exaltation), iv (ecstasy). Why the other options are wrong (a) i, ii, iii & iv Puts elation first, but euphoria is the mildest grade. (c) iv, iii, ii & i Reverses the scale, putting ecstasy , the most severe grade, first. (d) None of the above Fails because option (b) gives the correct order. Which is NOT a core symptom to diagnose as autism in children as per DSM- 5? (IHBAS 2024) a Communication skills b Unusual repetitive behavior c Social reciprocity d I.Q. is below 70 ✓ Answer: (d) I.Q. is below 70 DSM-5 autism, two core domains The concept Two core domains DSM-5 autism rests on two core domains: social communication and reciprocity , and restricted, repetitive behaviour . Where IQ fits Intellectual impairment is only a specifier (with or without), not a core symptom. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Communication skills Core: part of the social communication domain. (b) Unusual repetitive behavior Core: the restricted, repetitive behaviour domain. (c) Social reciprocity Core: part of the social communication and reciprocity domain. In which of the following situations would a diagnosis of "global developmental delay" be inappropriate? (RML 2022) a The patient is a child who is too young to fully manifest specific symptoms or to complete requisite assessments. b The patient, a 7-year-old boy, has a full-scale IQ of 65 and severe impairment in adaptive functioning. c The patient's scores on psychometric tests suggest intellectual disability, but there is insufficient information about the patient's adaptive functional skills. d The patient's impaired adaptive functioning suggests intellectual developmental disorder, but there is insufficient information about the level of cognitive impairment measured by standardized instruments. ✓ Answer: (b) The 7-year-old with full-scale IQ 65 and severe adaptive impairment Global developmental delay, provisional label under age 5 The concept What it is Global developmental delay is a provisional label for children under 5 whose severity cannot yet be reliably assessed. Why this one A testable 7-year-old who meets both criteria (IQ 65, severe adaptive impairment) has intellectual disability , so the provisional label does not fit. Why the other options are wrong (a) The patient is a child who is too young to fully manifest specific symptoms or to complete requisite assessments. Appropriate: a child too young to be assessed is exactly the provisional case the label exists for. (c) The patient's scores on psychometric tests suggest intellectual disability, but there is insufficient information about the patient's adaptive functional skills. Appropriate: without adaptive data, severity cannot yet be reliably assessed . (d) The patient's impaired adaptive functioning suggests intellectual developmental disorder, but there is insufficient information about the level of cognitive impairment measured by standardized instruments. Appropriate: without standardised cognitive testing, severity cannot yet be reliably assessed . Within attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, which of the following is NOT classified as a problem relating to hyperactivity/impulsivity? (RML 2021) a Experiences difficulties in playing quietly. b Rather than sitting still, squirms in seat and fidgets. c Talks excessively. d Doesn't appear to listen when being told something or spoken to ✓ Answer: (d) Doesn't appear to listen when spoken to ADHD criteria, nine inattention items The concept Two symptom lists ADHD symptoms fall into two lists: inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity . Why this one Not seeming to listen when spoken to directly is one of the nine inattention items , so it is not a hyperactivity-impulsivity problem. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Experiences difficulties in playing quietly. A hyperactivity-impulsivity item, so it does belong on that list. (b) Rather than sitting still, squirms in seat and fidgets. A hyperactivity-impulsivity item (squirming and fidgeting), so it belongs on that list. (c) Talks excessively. A hyperactivity-impulsivity item, so it belongs on that list. "First rank symptoms" of schizophrenia given by Schneider include all except (JEMAS 2025) a Depersonalization b Hallucinatory voice in the form of running commentary c Delusional perception d Thought broadcasting ✓ Answer: (a) Depersonalization Kurt Schneider, first-rank symptoms The concept What they are Kurt Schneider listed first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia, including running-commentary voices, delusional perception and thought broadcasting. Why this one Depersonalisation , like loose associations and delusions of self-reference, is not a first-rank symptom. Why the other options are wrong (b) Hallucinatory voice in the form of running commentary On Schneider 's list: one of his first-rank auditory hallucinations. (c) Delusional perception On Schneider 's list: a normal perception suddenly given a delusional meaning. (d) Thought broadcasting On Schneider 's list: the belief that one's thoughts are being made known to others. The ICD-10 duration criterion for schizophrenia requires symptoms to persist for at least: (IHBAS 2025) a 6 months b 2 weeks c 3 months d 1 month ✓ Answer: (d) 1 month ICD-10 and ICD-11 schizophrenia duration criterion The concept The rule ICD-10 and ICD-11 require schizophrenia symptoms to last at least 1 month . Do not mix up DSM-5-TR uses a longer total of six months instead, so the two systems differ. Why the other options are wrong (a) 6 months The DSM-5-TR total, including 1 month of active-phase symptoms, not the ICD figure. (b) 2 weeks The 2-week onset window of acute and transient psychotic disorders , not schizophrenia. (c) 3 months Matches neither system: ICD needs 1 month, DSM-5-TR 6 months in total. High EE (Expressed Emotion) is known to cause: (IHBAS 2020) a Poor treatment outcome b Relapse of psychotic illness c Negative symptoms of schizophrenia d Violent behavior in schizophrenic patients ✓ Answer: (b) Relapse of psychotic illness Brown, Birley and Wing (1972); Vaughn and Leff (1976) The concept What EE is Expressed emotion (EE) means critical, hostile or over-involved attitudes in a patient's relatives. The evidence Brown, Birley and Wing (1972) and Vaughn and Leff (1976) showed that such relatives predict relapse after discharge. Why the other options are wrong (a) Poor treatment outcome Too vague: the research finding is specifically relapse after discharge, the better answer. (c) Negative symptoms of schizophrenia EE does not cause the illness or its negative symptoms ; it predicts relapse. (d) Violent behavior in schizophrenic patients EE does not cause violence ; its established link is with relapse. Which of the following statements concerning Bipolar disorder is INCORRECT? (RML 2022) a Bipolar-I Disorder includes mania b Bipolar-II Disorder includes hypomania c Bipolar-I Disorder includes hypomania d Bipolar-I Disorder includes periods of depression even if these do not reach the threshold for major depressive disorder ✓ Answer: (c) Bipolar-I Disorder includes hypomania Bipolar I versus bipolar II definitions The concept Bipolar I Bipolar I is defined by at least one manic episode ; hypomania is optional in it. Bipolar II Hypomania is the defining high of bipolar II , so claiming it as a bipolar I feature is the incorrect statement. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Bipolar-I Disorder includes mania True: at least one manic episode defines bipolar I. (b) Bipolar-II Disorder includes hypomania True: hypomania is the defining high of bipolar II. (d) Bipolar-I Disorder includes periods of depression even if these do not reach the threshold for major depressive disorder True: bipolar I may include depressive periods , even below the major depressive threshold. A 12-year-old boy begins to have new episodes of temper outbursts that are out of proportion to the situation. Which of the following is NOT a diagnostic possibility in this patient? (RML 2022) a Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder b Bipolar Disorder c Conduct Disorder d Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder ✓ Answer: (a) Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder DMDD onset criterion: before age 10 The concept The rule DMDD requires onset before age 10 , with diagnosis made between 6 and 18. Why this one Outbursts that begin at 12 rule it out, so DMDD is not a possibility here. Why the other options are not the answer (b) Bipolar Disorder Possible: bipolar disorder can begin or present at this age. (c) Conduct Disorder Possible: conduct disorder can begin or present at this age. (d) Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder Possible: ADHD can present at this age. Suicidal risk is assessed to be highest when the following criteria are met in comparison to others, the 'time' factor being the same for all (JEMAS 2025) a High lethality, specific plan, frequent suicidal ideas, family history b Disrupted biological functioning, no recent attempt, no suicidal ideation c Adequate biological functioning, no previous attempt, moderate intent d Frequent suicidal ideation, recent suicide attempt, low lethality, absence of family history ✓ Answer: (a) High lethality, specific plan, frequent suicidal ideas, family history Convergence of suicide risk markers The concept Key idea Risk is highest when several markers converge . The markers A highly lethal method , a specific plan , frequent ideation and a family history of suicide. Why the other options are wrong (b) Disrupted biological functioning, no recent attempt, no suicidal ideation Lacks ideation and a recent attempt, so the key markers are missing. (c) Adequate biological functioning, no previous attempt, moderate intent Lacks a previous attempt , and intent is only moderate. (d) Frequent suicidal ideation, recent suicide attempt, low lethality, absence of family history Has low lethality and no family history, so fewer markers converge despite the recent attempt. The following defense mechanisms are used in obsessive-compulsive disorder: (RML 2024) a Isolation b Undoing c Reaction formation d Displacement ✓ Answer: (b) Undoing Classic OCD defences, undoing as the key The concept OCD defences Isolation , undoing and reaction formation are all classic OCD defences. Why undoing Undoing , an act that symbolically cancels a forbidden thought, is the most characteristic, so it is the key. Why the other options are wrong (a) Isolation A classic OCD defence too (cutting a thought off from its feeling), but less characteristic than undoing . (c) Reaction formation Also a classic OCD defence (acting opposite to an unacceptable impulse), but undoing is the most characteristic. (d) Displacement The defence of phobias , as in Freud's Little Hans case. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a pervasive condition in which the sufferer experiences: (IHBAS 2024) a Continued apprehension about unspecified things b Fear of fear c Continual flashbacks to past events d A desire to check that the environment is safe ✓ Answer: (a) Continued apprehension about unspecified things GAD: free-floating worry for 6 months The concept What GAD is GAD is excessive, hard-to-control, free-floating worry about many matters. Duration The worry must last at least 6 months . Why the other options are wrong (b) Fear of fear Fear of fear marks panic disorder and agoraphobia , not GAD. (c) Continual flashbacks to past events Flashbacks mark PTSD , not GAD. (d) A desire to check that the environment is safe Checking marks OCD , not GAD. A client with OCD washes their hands excessively to neutralize the anxiety caused by intrusive thoughts of contamination. This hand-washing behavior is BEST conceptualized as a(n): (Real PYQ 2024) a Conditioned stimulus b Unconditioned response c Avoidance response / Safety behavior d Operant behavior maintained by positive reinforcement ✓ Answer: (c) Avoidance response / Safety behavior Mowrer, two-factor theory The concept Two-factor theory In Mowrer 's two-factor account, fear is learned by classical conditioning and kept going by avoidance . Why washing persists The washing removes anxiety, so it is negatively reinforced : an avoidance response or safety behaviour. Why the other options are wrong (a) Conditioned stimulus The contamination thought is the conditioned stimulus; the washing is the response to it. (b) Unconditioned response An unconditioned response is an unlearned reflex ; hand-washing is learned. (d) Operant behavior maintained by positive reinforcement Nothing pleasant is added; anxiety is removed, so it is negative , not positive, reinforcement. The term 'la Bella indifference' seen in hysteria was first used by: (RML 2024) a Sigmund Freud b Anna Freud c Pierre Janet d Hippocrates ✓ Answer: (c) Pierre Janet Pierre Janet, hysteria as dissociation The concept The term La belle indifférence is the calm unconcern some conversion patients show about their symptoms. Who used it The phrase is usually credited to Pierre Janet , who explained hysteria as dissociation . Why the other options are wrong (a) Sigmund Freud Freud explained hysteria by repression and conversion; the phrase is usually credited to Janet. (b) Anna Freud Anna Freud catalogued the defences, not hysterical unconcern. (d) Hippocrates Hippocrates blamed hysteria on a wandering womb. When an individual has dissociative amnesia it is usually associated with several types of memory disturbances. In contrast, in generalized amnesia: (RML 2022) a There is a failure of recall of the entire past week b There is a failure of recall that encompasses the person's entire life c There is a failure of recall that encompasses the person's childhood d There is a failure of recall for traumatic events ✓ Answer: (b) Failure of recall that encompasses the person's entire life Dissociative amnesia, generalised type The concept Generalised amnesia Generalised amnesia covers the whole life history, often with identity . Other types Loss of a set period is localised amnesia; loss of one category of information is systematised . Why the other options are wrong (a) There is a failure of recall of the entire past week Loss of a set period such as a week is localised amnesia. (c) There is a failure of recall that encompasses the person's childhood Covers only one period, not the whole life history, so it is not generalised . (d) There is a failure of recall for traumatic events Describes dissociative amnesia in general, not the generalised type. The difference between malingering and factitious disorder lies in: (IHBAS 2025) a The presence or absence of external rewards b Whether the individual believes the symptoms are real c The severity of symptoms d Age of onset ✓ Answer: (a) The presence or absence of external rewards Malingering versus factitious disorder: external incentive The concept What they share In both malingering and factitious disorder people deliberately falsify symptoms and know they are false. The difference The malingerer seeks an external incentive such as money or escape from duty. Factitious disorder persists without obvious external reward, to occupy the sick role . Why the other options are wrong (b) Whether the individual believes the symptoms are real Both know their symptoms are false , so belief does not separate them. (c) The severity of symptoms Not the distinguishing feature; the difference is whether an external reward is sought. (d) Age of onset Not the distinguishing feature; what separates them is motive , external reward or the sick role. Unlike people with anorexia, individuals with bulimia (RML 2022) a Often purge themselves to stay thin b Are obsessed with being too fat c Can do damage to their health d May appear normal in weight ✓ Answer: (d) May appear normal in weight Anorexia nervosa criterion: significantly low body weight The concept Key difference Significantly low body weight is a criterion of anorexia nervosa . Bulimia People with bulimia are usually of normal weight or overweight. Why the other options are wrong (a) Often purge themselves to stay thin Purging occurs in both: the binge-eating/purging type of anorexia purges too. (b) Are obsessed with being too fat Fear of fatness occurs in both disorders, so it does not distinguish them. (c) Can do damage to their health Damage to health occurs in both disorders, so it does not distinguish them. In narcolepsy, which of the following is most characteristically present? (IHBAS 2025) a Both cataplexy and catalepsy equally b Cataplexy, sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions c Neither cataplexy nor catalepsy d Catalepsy, maintenance of imposed posture with waxy flexibility ✓ Answer: (b) Cataplexy Narcolepsy type 1, loss of hypocretin (orexin) The concept What cataplexy is Cataplexy is brief, sudden, bilateral loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness, triggered by laughter or joking. Why narcolepsy It marks narcolepsy type 1 , caused by loss of hypocretin (orexin) neurons. Why the other options are wrong (a) Both cataplexy and catalepsy equally Fails: catalepsy belongs to catatonia, not narcolepsy. (c) Neither cataplexy nor catalepsy Fails: cataplexy is the characteristic feature of narcolepsy type 1. (d) Catalepsy, maintenance of imposed posture with waxy flexibility Catalepsy , a held posture with waxy flexibility, belongs to catatonia . Lack of bowel control in children is known as: (RML 2024) a Encopresis b Analism c Enuresis d Anorexia ✓ Answer: (a) Encopresis Encopresis criteria (from age 4) The concept What it is Encopresis is repeated passage of faeces into inappropriate places. Criteria It must happen at least once a month for 3 months , from age 4 . Why the other options are wrong (b) Analism Not a recognised elimination disorder . (c) Enuresis The urinary counterpart of encopresis, diagnosed from age 5. (d) Anorexia An eating disorder , not an elimination disorder. Premature ejaculation is most commonly associated with: (RML 2024) a Diabetes mellitus b Masturbation c Personality disorder d Anxiety state ✓ Answer: (d) Anxiety state Premature ejaculation and performance anxiety The concept Cause Premature ejaculation is mostly psychogenic and most tied to performance anxiety . The link It is commoner in men with anxiety disorders . Why the other options are wrong (a) Diabetes mellitus Diabetes is the classic link of erectile disorder , not premature ejaculation. (b) Masturbation A myth: masturbation does not cause it. (c) Personality disorder Personality disorder has no special association with it. Autogynephilia is defined by: (RML 2022) a Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to prepubescent children b Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to thoughts, images, or thoughts about oneself as a woman c Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to oneself d Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to being humiliated ✓ Answer: (b) Attraction to thoughts or images of oneself as a woman Ray Blanchard, 1989 The concept What it is Autogynephilia is sexual attraction to thoughts or images of oneself as a woman. Origin Ray Blanchard coined the term in 1989, and DSM-5-TR uses it as a specifier of transvestic disorder. Why the other options are wrong (a) Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to prepubescent children Defines pedophilia , not autogynephilia. (c) Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to oneself Mere attraction to oneself is not autogynephilia; the term needs the image of oneself as a woman . (d) Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to being humiliated Defines masochism , not autogynephilia. When gender incongruence moved out of the mental disorders chapter in ICD-11, which of these stayed in Chapter 6 (Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders)? (NIMHANS 2026 recall) a Sexual dysfunctions b Paraphilic disorders c Sexual pain disorders d Gender incongruence of childhood ✓ Answer: (b) Paraphilic disorders ICD-11, Chapter 6 versus Chapter 17 The concept What moved ICD-11 moved gender incongruence (of childhood as well as of adolescence or adulthood), the sexual dysfunctions and the sexual pain disorders into Chapter 17 , Conditions related to sexual health. What stayed Only the paraphilic disorders , now centred on non-consent , stayed in Chapter 6. Why the other options are wrong (a) Sexual dysfunctions Moved to Chapter 17 , Conditions related to sexual health. (c) Sexual pain disorders Moved to Chapter 17 along with the sexual dysfunctions. (d) Gender incongruence of childhood Moved to Chapter 17 , along with gender incongruence of adolescence or adulthood. A patient presents with severe memory deficits, confabulation, and nystagmus, with a history of chronic alcohol use. This clinical picture is classic for: (Real PYQ 2024) a Alzheimer's Disease b Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome c Vascular Dementia d Frontotemporal Dementia ✓ Answer: (b) Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, thiamine deficiency The concept Cause Thiamine deficiency in chronic drinkers damages the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus. The two parts Nystagmus belongs to Wernicke's encephalopathy ; amnesia with confabulation to Korsakoff's syndrome . Why the other options are wrong (a) Alzheimer's Disease Gradual memory decline from plaques and tangles ; not caused by alcohol and does not produce this triad. (c) Vascular Dementia Decline after strokes or small-vessel disease; not caused by alcohol and does not produce this triad. (d) Frontotemporal Dementia Early change in personality and behaviour ; not caused by alcohol and does not produce this triad. Which of the following substances is NOT a natural alkaloid compound? (Amity 2023) a Morphine b Heroin c Codeine d Papaverine ✓ Answer: (b) Heroin Opium alkaloids versus semi-synthetic opioids The concept Why heroin Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is made by chemically modifying morphine, so it is semi-synthetic . Natural alkaloids Morphine, codeine and papaverine all occur naturally in opium . Why the other options are not the answer (a) Morphine A natural opium alkaloid, and the starting material for heroin. (c) Codeine A natural opium alkaloid. (d) Papaverine A natural opium alkaloid, though a smooth-muscle relaxant rather than a narcotic. A key of distinguishing feature of dementia vs. delirium is : (IHBAS 2025) a Delusions in dementia but not delirium b Onset gradual in delirium vs. acute in dementia c Hallucinations in dementia but not delirium d Impaired memory in dementia vs. fluctuating consciousness in delirium ✓ Answer: (d) Impaired memory in dementia, fluctuating consciousness in delirium Delirium versus dementia: consciousness The concept Delirium Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness. Dementia Dementia is an insidious decline in memory and cognition in clear consciousness . Why the other options are wrong (a) Delusions in dementia but not delirium Delusions occur in both, so they do not distinguish them. (b) Onset gradual in delirium vs. acute in dementia Reverses the two onsets : delirium is acute, dementia insidious. (c) Hallucinations in dementia but not delirium Hallucinations occur in both, so they do not distinguish them. Borderline Personality Disorder is most characteristically associated with which primary defense mechanism? (Real PYQ 2025) a Repression b Splitting c Sublimation d Rationalization ✓ Answer: (b) Splitting Kernberg, borderline personality organisation The concept What splitting is Splitting means seeing self and others as all good or all bad. Why BPD Kernberg placed this primitive defence at the centre of borderline personality organisation . Why the other options are wrong (a) Repression The classic neurotic defence; it does not define BPD. (c) Sublimation A mature defence; it does not define BPD. (d) Rationalization Means giving a plausible excuse ; it does not define BPD. Identify the 'odd one out' from the groups: (Amity 2023) a Paranoid personality disorder b Schizoid personality disorder c Schizotypal personality disorder d Borderline personality disorder ✓ Answer: (d) Borderline personality disorder Personality disorder clusters A and B The concept Cluster A Paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal form Cluster A (odd or eccentric). The odd one Borderline belongs to Cluster B (dramatic, emotional or erratic). Why the other options are wrong (a) Paranoid personality disorder Cluster A (odd or eccentric), with schizoid and schizotypal. (b) Schizoid personality disorder Cluster A , with paranoid and schizotypal. (c) Schizotypal personality disorder Cluster A , with paranoid and schizoid. A client reports a persistent pattern of seeking admiration, but their behavior is characterized by excessive emotionality, attention-seeking, and seductive behavior, rather than grandiosity. This presentation is more characteristic of: (Real PYQ 2024) a Narcissistic Personality Disorder b Histrionic Personality Disorder c Borderline Personality Disorder d Dependent Personality Disorder ✓ Answer: (b) Histrionic Personality Disorder Histrionic personality disorder criteria The concept What defines it Excessive emotionality , attention seeking and seductive behaviour define histrionic PD. Why not narcissistic Narcissistic PD also seeks admiration, but rests on grandiosity, which this client lacks. Why the other options are wrong (a) Narcissistic Personality Disorder Also seeks admiration, but rests on grandiosity and lack of empathy, absent here. (c) Borderline Personality Disorder Centres on instability and fear of abandonment. (d) Dependent Personality Disorder Centres on a need to be taken care of . orofacial, often irreversible); akathisia and tardive dyskinesia are secondary, drug-induced movement disorders. asked 6 times Folie à deux (Lasègue and Falret, 1877) is a delusion transmitted from a dominant psychotic primary case to a passive partner in a close relationship; ICD-10 F24 induced delusional disorder, DSM-IV shared psychotic disorder; ICD-11 describes it under 6A24 delusional disorder. asked 6 times A major depressive episode needs 5 or more of 9 symptoms in the same 2-week period, at least one being depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure; phobias and euphoric mood are not among them. asked 6 times La belle indifférence , calm unconcern about a dramatic symptom, is the classic but non-diagnostic sign of conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder); the term is usually credited to Pierre Janet . asked 6 times Factitious disorder (Munchausen syndrome, Asher 1951; imposed on another, Meadow 1977) and malingering both feign illness on purpose; they differ in the absence or presence of external rewards , and malingering is not a mental disorder. asked 6 times The diathesis-stress model explains disorder as a predisposition (a genetic, biological or psychological diathesis) set off by stress; Meehl applied it to schizophrenia in 1962, and Zubin and Spring named it the vulnerability-stress model in 1977. asked 5 times Dissociative amnesia is inability to recall important, usually traumatic autobiographical information beyond ordinary forgetting; generalised amnesia covers the whole life history, and fugue (purposeful travel with loss of identity) is now a specifier. asked 5 times Bulimia nervosa needs recurrent binges with loss of control plus compensatory behaviour (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, exercise), both at least once a week for 3 months ; binge-eating disorder needs binges once a week for 3 months with marked distress, three of five features and no regular compensation. asked 5 times Cotard syndrome (Jules Cotard, 1880) is a nihilistic delusion that one is dead, does not exist, or has lost organs or blood; nihilistic delusions are characteristic of severe psychotic depression. asked 4 times Depression, the common cold of psychiatry , is characterised by persistent sadness and loss of interest; it is widespread and increasing, often triggered by stress, linked to suicide risk by severity, and about twice as common in women as in men. asked 4 times OCD obsessions are ego-dystonic (intrusive, unwanted, inconsistent with the self-concept); obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is ego-syntonic perfectionism without true obsessions or compulsions. asked 4 times Generalised anxiety disorder is excessive, hard-to-control worry about many events, more days than not for at least 6 months , with 3 of 6 symptoms (restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance; 1 in children): continued apprehension about unspecified things. asked 4 times Undoing is the most characteristic OCD defence, alongside isolation of affect and reaction formation; repression is the defence of hysteria and displacement that of phobias. asked 4 times Depersonalisation is feeling detached from or unreal in oneself ('not my normal self'); derealisation is the surroundings feeling unreal or dreamlike; reality testing stays intact. asked 4 times DSM-5-TR anorexia nervosa : restriction leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain (or behaviour blocking gain) and disturbed experience of weight or shape; amenorrhoea was dropped and no BMI cut-off is required; the restricting type has no recurrent bingeing or purging in the last 3 months. asked 4 times Anorexia nervosa is the most lethal eating disorder (crude mortality about 5 per cent per decade in DSM-5-TR), with lanugo, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, amenorrhoea and hypokalaemia, and the trait of perfectionism . asked 4 times

title: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 9: Research Methodology
text: The Final Exam Textbook, Chapter 9: Research Methodology Chapter 9 of the one-volume Final Exam Textbook, all nine JSS subjects in one book. Both A4 PDFs hold the whole book with the same page numbers. A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (975 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (975 pages) Chapter 9 Research Methodology In this chapter 9.1 Science and the Research Process: Problems and Hypotheses : Distinguish science from other ways of knowing, inductive from deductive reasoning and the main types of research, and turn a research problem and literature review into a well-formed hypothesis of the right type. 9.2 Variables, Experimental Control and the Validity of Research : Identify and classify the variables in a study, define them operationally, choose the right technique of control, recognise participant and experimenter artefacts and what blinding controls, and judge a study's statistical conclusion, internal, construct and external validity and the threats to each. 9.3 Sampling: Populations, Probability and Non-Probability Methods : Define population, sample, parameter and statistic, tell probability from non-probability sampling, recognise every major sampling method from a description (simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster and multistage, quota, purposive, convenience, snowball), and distinguish sampling error from bias. 9.4 Research Designs: Experimental, Single-Case and Non-Experimental : Distinguish experimental, quasi-experimental, single-case, non-experimental and developmental designs, and judge which conclusions each one licenses. 9.5 Clinical Epidemiology, Randomised Trials and Evidence Synthesis : Calculate and interpret prevalence, incidence, relative risk, odds ratio, NNT, sensitivity, specificity and predictive values, tell the epidemiological designs and trial analyses apart, and explain meta-analysis and the reporting guidelines. 9.6 Methods of Data Collection and Qualitative Research : Choose and critique the main tools of data collection (observation, interview, questionnaire and schedule, content analysis, sociometry), place a study in its research paradigm, and tell the qualitative traditions, their analysis and their quality criteria apart. 9.7 Research Ethics and Writing the Research Report : Trace research ethics from the abuses that produced it to its codes and core principles (informed consent, protection from harm, confidentiality, deception and debriefing, the 3Rs, honest publication), and describe the structure and style of an APA research report and of a research proposal. 9.8 Measurement Scales, Organising Data and Descriptive Statistics : Classify any variable by Stevens's four levels of measurement, process, tabulate and graph raw data, choose and compute averages and measures of variability, read skewness and kurtosis, and use the normal curve to convert scores through z into percentiles and standard scores. 9.9 Sampling Distributions and the Logic of Hypothesis Testing : Explain how psychologists reason from samples to populations: the sampling distribution and standard error, the central limit theorem, confidence intervals, the steps of a significance test, the p-value, Type I and Type II errors, power and effect size. 9.10 Comparing Groups: t-Tests, ANOVA and Non-Parametric Tests : Choose the right test for comparing groups from the design and the level of measurement (t-tests, one-way and factorial ANOVA with post hoc tests, ANCOVA and MANOVA, chi-square and the rank tests) and work out its degrees of freedom. 9.11 Correlation, Regression and Factor Analysis : Choose and interpret the right correlation coefficient, read and use a regression equation, and decide how many factors to retain and how to rotate them in a factor analysis. Weightage. 320 of the 3180 questions mapped in this book (10.1%) test this chapter, 175 of them from real past papers. 2 of its 11 sections are High yield. Berlin, 1904. A retired schoolteacher named Wilhelm von Osten puts a question to his horse: what is three plus five? Hans taps his hoof eight times and stops. Von Osten had spent years teaching him, and Hans now seemed able to add, subtract, multiply and divide, to work with fractions, tell the time and answer questions about German words, all by tapping. He answered strangers as well as his owner, so deliberate fraud seemed unlikely. In September 1904 a commission that included the psychologist Carl Stumpf watched him perform and found no trick. The newspapers called him Clever Hans. Stumpf passed the puzzle to his student Oskar Pfungst, who treated it as a research problem rather than a marvel. Pfungst set out rival explanations (trickery, genuine reasoning, cues from the people present) and tested them by changing one condition at a time. When the questioner knew the answer, Hans was nearly always right; when the questioner did not, Hans was nearly always wrong. With blinkers that hid the questioner, or with the questioner standing far off, Hans failed again. The horse was not counting; he was watching. Pfungst found the signal: once the question was put, the questioner bent forward slightly to watch the hoof, and Hans began to tap; when the right count was reached, the questioner's head lifted a fraction and the tension left his body. Hans stopped at that release. None of the questioners, von Osten included, knew they were doing it. Pfungst published his study in 1907. He even took the horse's part himself in the laboratory, tapping out answers for human questioners, and found that they gave him the same small, unwitting signals. The lesson has outlived the horse: what an observer expects can leak into the very data meant to test it. This chapter is about the methods science has built to stop that from happening. 9.1 Science and the Research Process: Problems and Hypotheses Medium yield · 21 Qs Why should you believe a psychologist's claim? Not because the psychologist is famous or certain, but to the degree that the claim was reached by a method that could have shown it to be wrong. This section describes that method, the reasoning it uses, the kinds of research it produces, and the first two steps of every study: finding a problem and stating a hypothesis. Ways of knowing In "The Fixation of Belief" (1877) the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce (1839 to 1914) described four ways in which people settle what they believe, and Fred N. Kerlinger (1910 to 1991) made them standard in Foundations of Behavioral Research (1964). By the method of tenacity you hold a belief because you always have; by the method of authority , because a respected source says so; by the a priori method , because it seems self-evidently reasonable (intuition). Only the method of science settles belief by public observation that anyone can repeat, so only science corrects its own mistakes. Older traditions stand behind the list (Table 9.1). Socrates (about 470 to 399 BCE) used the elenchus , a question-and-answer cross-examination that draws out a person's beliefs until they contradict one another (the Socratic method). Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) observed and classified nature; René Descartes (1596 to 1650) trusted reason and intuition (rationalism); Galileo Galilei (1564 to 1642) experimented; and Francis Bacon (1561 to 1626) argued in Novum Organum (1620) for building knowledge inductively from observations. Table 9.1 Ways of knowing. Only the last corrects itself. Way of knowing Linked with Belief is settled by Elenchus Socrates Questioning that exposes contradictions Observation, classification Aristotle Watching and sorting nature Intuition, reason Descartes Thinking alone Experiment, induction Galileo; Bacon Varying conditions; generalising Tenacity Peirce Habit and repetition Authority Peirce An expert or text A priori Peirce What "stands to reason" Science Peirce Public, repeatable observation What makes research scientific Kerlinger defined scientific research as "systematic, controlled, empirical and critical investigation of hypothetical propositions about the presumed relations among natural phenomena". Unpacked, that gives its characteristics. Empiricism : claims are settled by observation, not by argument or rank. Objectivity through systematic, controlled observation: the result should not depend on who observes it. Replicability and reproducibility: the study can be repeated, and gives the same results when it is. When the Open Science Collaboration (2015) repeated 100 published psychology studies, about 97 percent of the originals but only about 36 percent of the repetitions were significant. Parsimony : prefer the simpler of two explanations that fit equally well. This is Occam's razor, after William of Ockham (about 1287 to 1347); in animal psychology it is Lloyd Morgan's canon (1894), after Conwy Lloyd Morgan (1852 to 1936): never explain an action by a higher mental faculty if a lower one will do. Falsifiability : Karl Popper (1902 to 1994), in Logik der Forschung (1934), noted that a thousand white swans cannot prove "all swans are white" but one black swan disproves it. A statement is scientific only if some possible observation could show it false; psychoanalysis, which explains any behaviour after the event, was his example of a theory that risks nothing. Determinism and tentativeness: behaviour has natural causes and so is lawful, yet every conclusion is provisional. A. K. Singh adds three assumptions of science (nature is lawful, behaviour is determined, nature is understandable) and six attitudes of the scientist: open-minded, tolerant of uncertainty, aware of being fallible, cautious (a finding is evidence, never "proof"), sceptical and ethical. The goals of science are to describe, explain, predict and control behaviour. Exam trap "A characteristic of good research" is reproducibility of results . The distractors are the opposites of the real criteria: good research has clear objectives, unbiased findings, adequate scope and ethical conduct. Science builds with the terms in Table 9.2. A hypothesis is a guess about one relation, a law a confirmed regularity, a theory an explanatory system; "just a theory" misuses the word. Table 9.2 The building blocks of scientific knowledge. Term Meaning Example Fact An observation others can verify Pavlov's dogs salivated before feeding Concept An abstraction naming a class of observations Reward, aggression Construct A concept invented for science, inferred and not directly observed Anxiety, intelligence Theory Interrelated constructs and propositions that explain and predict (Kerlinger) Beck's cognitive theory of depression Law A highly confirmed, usually narrow regularity Weber's law Model A simplified representation or analogy Atkinson and Shiffrin's memory model Popper said how science ought to work; Thomas S. Kuhn (1922 to 1996) described how it does, in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962). Scientists usually do normal science inside a paradigm , a shared package of theory, methods and assumptions. Anomalies pile up, crisis follows, and a scientific revolution installs a new paradigm (a paradigm shift), as when the cognitive revolution displaced behaviourism. Induction, deduction and abduction Induction runs from specific observations to broad generalisations, bottom-up. You interview twenty hostel students in exam week, notice that the poorest sleepers worry most, and generalise. Induction builds theory, so it belongs to the theory-development stage and is typical of exploratory and qualitative research. Its weakness, noted by David Hume (1711 to 1776), is that no number of cases guarantees the rule. Deduction runs top-down, from theory to hypothesis to the observation that tests it: if the cognitive theory of depression is right, depressed patients should recall more negative words, so you test them. It is typical of quantitative, experimental research. Abduction , Peirce's term, is inference to the best explanation: from a surprising fact to the hypothesis that would best account for it, as when Oskar Pfungst guessed that Clever Hans was reading his questioners (see the chapter opening). The hypothetico-deductive method joins them: propose a hypothesis, deduce a prediction, test it, then keep, revise or drop the hypothesis. Clark L. Hull (1884 to 1952) built Principles of Behavior (1943) this way. Figure 9.1 shows the cycle. Theory Hypotheses Observations Empirical generalisations deduce predictions test against data summarise patterns build theory INDUCTION data up to theory DEDUCTION theory down to data Figure 9.1 The research cycle, after Walter Wallace's "wheel of science" (1971). Deduction carries theory down to data (right); induction carries data back up to theory (left), at the theory-development stage. Exam trap "Starts with a theory and tests it with observations" is deductive reasoning ; the hypothetico-deductive method (the whole conjecture-and-test cycle) is the distractor. "Gathers data, finds patterns, then generates a theory", "specific observations to broader generalisations" and "associated with qualitative research" are all inductive reasoning , used at the theory-development stage, not in formulating hypotheses, collecting data or reviewing literature. Experimental design and quantitative analysis go with deduction; qualitative analysis is a way of handling data, not a direction of reasoning. Methodology, methods and the steps of research Research methods are the techniques for collecting and analysing data: an interview, an experiment, a t-test. Research methodology is the wider study of the logic behind choosing them: why this method suits this problem, and what its results can show. As C. R. Kothari puts it in Research Methodology: Methods and Techniques , methods are part of methodology, so methodology has the wider scope. Research advances theory, informs government policy, guides practice (which therapy works) and, in business, provides insights for decision-making, a role broader than profit and far from merely academic. Kothari's criteria of good research are a clearly defined purpose, a procedure described well enough to be repeated, a design planned for objective results, frankly reported flaws, adequate analysis, and conclusions confined to what the data justify. Singh's eight steps are: (1) identifying the problem, with the literature review; (2) formulating hypotheses; (3) identifying, manipulating and controlling variables (9.2); (4) the research design (9.4); (5) devices for observation and measurement (9.6); (6) summarising results (9.8); (7) statistical analysis (9.9 to 9.11); and (8) drawing conclusions. Kothari's flow runs: problem, literature survey, hypotheses, research design, sample design (9.3), data collection, execution, analysis, hypothesis testing, generalisation and interpretation, and the report (9.7), which raises the next problem. Types of research One study has a place on each axis of Table 9.3: a randomised trial of yoga for anxiety in a Bengaluru hospital is applied, explanatory, quantitative, experimental, field-based and longitudinal. Table 9.3 Ways of classifying research. Basis Types What separates them Purpose (also Kothari) Basic (pure, fundamental) versus applied Knowledge for its own sake versus a practical problem Depth Exploratory, descriptive, explanatory Generates hypotheses; describes; tests causes Kothari Descriptive versus analytical Describes things as they are versus critically evaluates available facts Kothari Quantitative versus qualitative Amounts versus qualities and meanings (9.6) Kothari Conceptual versus empirical Abstract ideas versus observation or experiment Kerlinger Experimental versus non-experimental Independent variable manipulated versus measured Setting Laboratory versus field Control versus realism Time Cross-sectional versus longitudinal One occasion versus followed over time (9.4) Focus Nomothetic versus idiographic General laws versus the unique individual Basic research seeks knowledge for its own sake; applied research solves a practical problem. Action research , an applied form, was introduced by Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947), often called the father of modern social psychology, in 1946. It is research done by or with the people in a setting to solve a specific local problem there, in cycles now drawn as plan, act, observe and reflect: a ward team studies why patients miss follow-up visits, changes the reminders and measures again (participatory action research is in 9.6). Evaluation research judges whether a programme works; Michael Scriven (1967) separated formative evaluation, which improves a running programme, from summative evaluation, which judges it at the end. Exploratory research probes a poorly understood area without firm hypotheses, so it is hypothesis-generating. Descriptive research observes and describes what exists without manipulating variables. Explanatory research (causal research) tests hypotheses about why, most strongly by experiment, a variable-manipulating study. A case study is a design for one case (9.4). Wilhelm Windelband (1848 to 1915) in 1894 separated sciences seeking general laws from those seeking to understand the unique case. The nomothetic approach (Greek nomos , law) finds laws across many people through experimental and quasi-experimental methods; the idiographic approach ( idios , one's own) studies one person in depth through case studies, ethnography and other qualitative methods. Gordon W. Allport (1897 to 1967) brought the pair into personality psychology in 1937 and preferred the idiographic approach (Chapter 4). Exam trap Both experimental and quasi-experimental methods are nomothetic; when both are offered, the expected answer is the experimental method . Qualitative methods and ethnography are idiographic. Allport preferred the idiographic approach; factorial design (9.4) and chi-square (9.10) are a design and a test, not approaches. Action research is " research carried out to solve a specific problem ": it is applied but need not be longitudinal, so "all of the above" fails. Lewin founded action research, not psychoanalysis, psychophysics or functionalism (Chapter 1). The research problem A research problem is a felt difficulty sharpened until data can answer it: "students seem stressed" becomes "Is sleep duration related to test anxiety in first-year students?" Kerlinger's criteria are that it relates two or more variables, is stated clearly as a question, and implies empirical testing. A good research question is clear, answerable, connected to earlier work and worth answering. Problems come from experience, theory and earlier findings, which reveal a gap, contradictory results, or an isolated unexplained fact, such as the apparent movement that Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) studied as the phi phenomenon, which led to Gestalt psychology. Pauline V. Young (1956) named documentary sources, key informants and library sources; Baker and Keller add programmed activities, research proposals, government policies and social values. A problem should be novel, significant, feasible (time, money, participants), within the researcher's interest and competence, supported by available data and instruments, and ethical. It must also be solvable by empirical observation. An unsolvable problem ("Is there a divinity that shapes our ends?") is metaphysical: unstructured, with terms that cannot be operationally defined and data that cannot be collected. Singh's steps in formulating a problem are: choose a broad area, divide it, select a subarea, raise questions, turn them into objectives, assess their feasibility, and double-check. Reviewing the literature The literature is the body of prior work related to a research problem; it is not an archive (a store of historical records) or a repository (a storage place for documents and data). The review of literature evaluates it. Its primary purpose is to provide a theoretical framework, from which hypotheses are deduced; it also avoids duplication, locates gaps, refines the problem and suggests variables, designs and tools. Singh's five types are primary (traces a topic's development), content (links a study to related work), methodological (compares methods), integrative or systematic (combines empirical results; see 9.5) and theoretical (compares theories). Sources include peer-reviewed journals, books, review articles, abstracts ( Psychological Abstracts , begun in 1927, now PsycINFO), indexes, PubMed, dissertations (Shodhganga in India), the internet and grey literature , material without an ISBN or ISSN such as theses and government reports. A review is written as critical synthesis organised by theme, with each source annotated, not as a string of summaries. Exam trap The primary objective of a literature review is to provide a theoretical framework . Establishing the researcher's credibility is a secondary purpose Singh mentions; summarising your own findings belongs in the results, and ignoring earlier research is the opposite of a review. The hypothesis: meaning, criteria and functions The problem asks; the hypothesis answers. Kerlinger (1973) called it "a conjectural statement of the relation between two or more variables", always declarative: a tentative, testable statement. "Is sleep related to test anxiety?" is a problem, interrogative and not directly testable; "Students who sleep under six hours will report higher test anxiety" is a hypothesis, declarative and testable. Hypotheses can be recast as "if (antecedent), then (consequent)". A good hypothesis is testable and falsifiable, conceptually clear, specific, consistent with known facts, parsimonious, and related to theory and to available techniques. William J. Goode and Paul K. Hatt ( Methods in Social Research , 1952) named three difficulties in formulating one: no clear theoretical framework (or ignorance of it), inability to use that framework logically (Singh renders this as not knowing what theoretical evidence is available), and unfamiliarity with research techniques. Hypotheses come from theory, observation, earlier research, analogy (learned helplessness in dogs suggested a model of human depression), intuition and culture. A hypothesis guides data collection and analysis (what to collect, what to ignore), delimits the study, suggests the design and links theory to observation. It is never meant to prove the researcher's view or steer the results, and it does not replace the literature review it grows from. A supported hypothesis is retained, never proved. Types of hypotheses Table 9.4 lists the types. The null hypothesis (H 0 ) states no difference or relationship in the population; the alternative hypothesis (H 1 ) states that one exists, and is accepted when the null is rejected. An alternative is a directional hypothesis if it names the direction (one-tailed test) and a non-directional hypothesis if it predicts only a difference (two-tailed); statistical hypotheses and their testing are in 9.9. A universal hypothesis holds for all values of the variables at all times and places; an existential hypothesis holds for at least one case. Universal hypotheses are preferred because they predict more. Table 9.4 Types of hypotheses. Type States Example Universal All values, all times and places Adequate light increases reading efficiency Existential At least one case At least one patient improves untreated Causal One variable causes another Boring content causes channel changing Descriptive A feature of behaviour, no cause Viewers alone change channels more Simple One independent, one dependent variable Reward improves learning Complex More than two variables Class and gender jointly affect adjustment Research Prediction derived from the theory CBT beats usual care for depression Working Provisional guess, revised as data arrive Dropout may depend on distance Null (H 0 ) No difference or relationship No difference between male and female incomes in the population Alternative (H 1 ) A difference or relationship Male and female incomes differ Directional Names the direction Reinforcement will have a positive effect on performance Non-directional A difference only Boys and girls differ in aggression Exam trap "Reinforcement will have a positive effect on performance" predicts an effect ( alternative , not null) and its direction ( directional ). The statement that "sounds like a null" is the one of no difference : "there is a correlation", "the coin is not fair" and "the defendant is guilty" all claim an effect (the courtroom null is "innocent"). For universal hypotheses, options about "two" or "some" values are invented: universal means all values everywhere. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Peirce's four methods of fixing belief are tenacity, authority, a priori and . Socrates' cross-examination that exposes contradictions is the . For Popper, a scientific statement must be . Specific observations to general theory is reasoning. Allport preferred the approach. Action research was founded by . A literature review chiefly provides a . "Reinforcement will improve performance" is an alternative, hypothesis. Answers: (1) science, (2) elenchus, (3) falsifiable, (4) inductive, (5) idiographic, (6) Kurt Lewin, (7) theoretical framework, (8) directional 9.2 Variables, Experimental Control and the Validity of Research Medium yield · 22 Qs Suppose a counsellor at a Mysuru college runs a six-week yoga course for forty anxious students, and their anxiety falls. Did the yoga do it, or did the examinations end, or did the students relax because someone was watching? Deciding needs the language of variables, measurement, control, guards against bias and the idea of validity. (Hypotheses are Section 9.1; designs, Section 9.4.) Variables and their kinds A variable is any characteristic that can take two or more values; one with a single value in a study is a constant . A concept is an abstraction from observed events (honesty, courage), and a construct is a concept deliberately invented for scientific use, such as intelligence ( Fred N. Kerlinger , 1910 to 1991, Foundations of Behavioral Research , 1964). Measurability is what separates a variable from a concept. The independent variable (IV) is the presumed cause, manipulated by the experimenter or, where that is impossible, selected. The dependent variable (DV) is the measured outcome, expected to change with the IV. Find the IV by asking what is presumed to cause what, not by word order: in "old age home residents who have heart disease die earlier than those who do not", the IV is having heart disease, the DV is age at death, and the old age home is a constant. Heart disease cannot be handed out, which illustrates Kerlinger's split between active variables , which the researcher manipulates (dose, instructions), and attribute variables , which participants bring and which can only be measured or selected (age, sex, diagnosis). With an attribute IV random assignment is impossible, so causal claims are weaker. Attribute variables are also called organismic, the O in Robert S. Woodworth 's (1869 to 1962) stimulus-organism-response scheme. Table 9.5 lists the other contrasts. Table 9.5 Ways of classifying variables. Distinction Meaning Example Stimulus, organismic, response Feature of the task or setting; of the person; the behaviour measured Noise; age; reaction time Explanatory and response IV and DV in observational studies Smoking; lung disease Predictor and criterion IV and DV in correlation and regression Entrance score; MA marks Continuous and discrete Any value in a range; separate, countable values Reaction time; siblings Quantitative and qualitative Differ in amount; differ in kind (categorical) Anxiety score; diagnosis True and artificial dichotomy Two natural categories; a continuum cut in two (biserial correlation, Section 9.11) Alive or dead; pass or fail Exam trap The IV is the presumed cause (having heart disease), not the first-mentioned variable (dying early) or the setting (the old age home, a constant). "Manipulated by the experimenter" defines the IV; "measured as the outcome" defines the DV; "randomly assigned" describes participants, not a variable. Extraneous, confounding, moderator and mediator variables An extraneous variable is any variable other than the IV that may affect the DV: subject or organismic variables (age, intelligence, motivation), task variables (difficulty, instructions), environmental variables (noise, light) and situational variables (time of day, the experimenter's manner). One that varies randomly only adds noise. One that varies systematically with the IV and also affects the DV is a confounding variable : it influences both, and its effect cannot be separated from the IV's. If the yoga volunteers were also more motivated, and motivation lowers anxiety, motivation is confounded with treatment. Reuben M. Baron and David A. Kenny (1986) separated two other third variables (Figure 9.2). A moderator changes the direction or strength of the IV-DV relationship, saying when or for whom: if yoga helps mild but not severe anxiety, severity moderates the effect (statistically an interaction, Section 9.10). A mediator is the mechanism through which the IV acts: yoga slows breathing, which lowers anxiety. An intervening variable is such a link that can only be inferred, never observed, such as learning or fatigue. Confound Mediator Moderator C X (IV) Y (DV) no causal link X (IV) M Y (DV) direct path (no M) X (IV) Y (DV) Z Z acts on the arrow itself Figure 9.2 A confound (C) drives both X and Y; a mediator (M) carries the effect from X to Y; a moderator (Z) changes how strongly X affects Y. Exam trap A variable that "only affects the DV" is merely extraneous; a confound must also vary with the IV, which is why it "influences both". Hook: mediator = mechanism (how); moderator = more for some (when, for whom). Operational definitions and measuring the DV An operational definition defines a variable by the operations used to manipulate or measure it: anxiety is the score on a named inventory; hunger is hours without food. This operationism comes from the physicist Percy Williams Bridgman (1882 to 1961) in The Logic of Modern Physics (1927); Stanley Smith Stevens (1906 to 1973) brought it into psychology in 1935. It makes research objective and replicable, though no single operation captures a whole construct. The DV can be measured by direct observation of behaviour, by indirect physiological measures or reaction time, by judgements about a stimulus, or by self-report. A good DV is reliable, valid and sensitive. Scores bunched at the bottom of a scale because the task is too hard show a floor effect ; scores bunched at the top because it is too easy show a ceiling effect . Both hide real differences. Control and the MAXMINCON principle Control means holding constant, or otherwise neutralising, the influence of extraneous variables on the DV, so that conditions differ only in the IV. Kerlinger summed up the aim of design in the MAXMINCON principle : maximise systematic (experimental or primary ) variance, the variance due to the IV, by making its levels as different as possible; minimise error variance , the random variance from individual differences and measurement error, by reliable measures and steady conditions; and control extraneous ( secondary ) variance, the systematic variance from other variables, by the techniques that follow. Exam trap MAXMINCON reads primary, error, secondary; "true variance" belongs to test theory (Chapter 2). One real paper defines control as holding constant "the possible influence of the dependent variable". The stem is careless (extraneous variables are what is held constant), but control is still the answer. Standard deviation is a statistic (Section 9.8); an experiment is the whole procedure (Section 9.4). Techniques of control Elimination removes an extraneous variable (a sound-proof room removes noise). Constancy of conditions holds it at one value for all (same room, time and instructions), at some cost to generality. Matching pairs participants on a relevant variable and splits each pair between groups. Balancing spreads a known variable equally across groups, as with equal numbers of men and women in each. When the same people serve in every condition, order effects arise: practice, fatigue and carry-over. Counterbalancing varies the order so that each condition appears equally often in each position: complete (every order: 2 for two conditions, 6 for three, 24 for four), partial (a subset, such as a Latin square, Section 9.4) or ABBA (one order, then its reverse). Psychophysics controls primacy and recency effects the same way, by counterbalancing the order of presentation. The most powerful technique is randomisation , or random assignment: every participant has an equal chance of being placed in any group. It makes the groups alike at the start on known and unknown variables, so that the main difference between them is the treatment, and is the chief guard against selection bias and confounding. That is why an HIV vaccine trial randomly assigned over 16,000 volunteers to vaccine or placebo: not to reduce non-response or sampling variability (Section 9.3), and not to blind anyone. It does nothing about measurement error (reliable measures reduce that), recall bias (faulty memory of past exposures) or publication bias (selective publishing of positive results; both Section 9.5). Figure 9.3 separates it from random sampling. Population Random selection Sample Random assignment Treatment group Control group compare Selection buys external validity; assignment buys internal validity. Figure 9.3 Random selection decides who enters the study; random assignment decides who gets which condition. Finally, a within-subjects design uses participants as their own control : stable individual differences drop out, but order effects enter. Statistical control removes a measured extraneous variable in the analysis (ANCOVA, Section 9.10; partial correlation, Section 9.11). A control group , untreated or given a placebo, shows what would have happened anyway. Exam trap Equal probability of being assigned to a treatment group is randomisation. Random sampling decides who enters the study, stratification splits a population into subgroups before sampling, and randomness is mere unpredictability. In the psychophysics item, "pairing" is matching, and randomisation only scatters order effects by chance. "Double-bind technique" is most likely a misprint for double-blind; the double bind proper is a theory of contradictory family messages in schizophrenia (Chapter 8). None of these balances order, so counterbalancing is the answer. Bias and artefacts Bias is any influence that distorts a study's results away from the truth. (Control is its remedy; sample and population are the people studied, Section 9.3.) Distortions created by the research situation itself are called artefacts; the lesser ones are in Table 9.6. The best known is the Hawthorne effect : people change their behaviour because they know they are being observed, whatever the intervention. Key study: The Hawthorne studies (1924 to 1932) The Western Electric Hawthorne Works near Chicago studied workers' output. In the illumination experiments output rose when lighting was increased, but also in the control group, and sometimes when the light was dimmed. The studies, associated with Elton Mayo (1880 to 1949), were reported by Fritz J. Roethlisberger (1898 to 1974) and William J. Dickson in Management and the Worker (1939); Henry A. Landsberger coined the term in 1958. Reanalyses find the data weaker than the legend. Martin T. Orne (1927 to 2000) argued in 1962 that participants are active problem-solvers. Demand characteristics are the cues in a setting (rumours, instructions, procedure, the experimenter's manner) that tell participants what is expected and so shape their behaviour. Stephen J. Weber and Thomas D. Cook (1972) described good (confirming), faithful (literal), negativistic (opposing) and apprehensive subjects, the last showing evaluation apprehension , anxiety to be judged favourably ( Milton J. Rosenberg , 1965). From the other side, Robert Rosenthal (born 1933), in Experimenter Effects in Behavioral Research (1966), showed that researchers' expectations change how participants are treated and responses scored: the experimenter expectancy effect , or experimenter bias. Key study: Pygmalion in the classroom (1968) Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson gave the pupils of Oak School (a pseudonym), a Californian elementary school, an IQ test and told teachers that it had picked out certain pupils, in fact chosen at random (about 20 percent), as about to bloom intellectually. Retested on the same IQ test at the end of the year, these children, especially in grades one and two, had gained more IQ points than their classmates: the Pygmalion effect , a self-fulfilling prophecy. Replications find it real but smaller. The halo effect , described by Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949) in 1920, is one salient attribute colouring ratings of others. When a patient's anxiety improves and the rater therefore scores depression as improved too, that is halo: not a ceiling effect (a scale limit), not Hawthorne (a change in the participant) and not a therapeutic effect (a genuine benefit of treatment). Blinding In a single-blind study participants do not know their condition, which controls their expectancy and demand, but the experimenter can still bias the results. In a double-blind study neither the participants nor the experimenters who treat and assess them know who is in which group, so it minimises both experimenter bias and expectancy effects. Random assignment equalises groups, but the experimenter still knows who got what; a control group hides nothing; demand characteristics are a bias, not a control; single-blinding leaves the experimenter free; pretest instructions hide nothing. Double-blind does not mean two control groups or running the study twice. The four kinds of validity of a study Here validity belongs to a study, not a test (Chapter 2). Donald T. Campbell (1916 to 1996) first set internal against external validity in 1957 and, with Julian C. Stanley (1918 to 2005), listed the threats to each in 1963; Cook and Campbell (1979) and William R. Shadish , Cook and Campbell (2002) gave four types: Statistical conclusion validity : is the IV-DV relationship real, or did low power, violated assumptions or many tests mislead? Internal validity : did the IV cause the change in the DV? Campbell and Stanley called it the basic minimum for interpreting an experiment. Construct validity : do the manipulation and measures represent the intended constructs? Giving plain versus barbecue-flavoured chips does not manipulate anxiety. External validity : the extent to which findings generalise to other people (population validity), settings ( ecological validity ) and times (temporal validity). Glenn H. Bracht and Gene V Glass (1968) split it into population and ecological validity. The two main kinds trade off: tight laboratory control raises internal validity but makes the setting unlike life, while a busy clinic is realistic but loosely controlled. Researchers establish an effect under control, then replicate it in the field. Alan Bryman , in Social Research Methods (2001), judges studies by reliability (measures of concepts stable on different occasions), replicability (methods stated clearly enough to repeat) and validity (generalising to other social settings is external validity). The researcher's reputation is no criterion. Exam trap In the chips item, internal validity tempts, but no rival variable explains the result; the manipulation simply is not anxiety, so construct validity fails. "Statistical validity" loosely means statistical conclusion validity; "empirical validity" is an old name for a test's criterion-related validity (Chapter 2). Causation is internal validity; internal consistency and reliability belong to measures. Threats to internal and external validity A threat to internal validity is any rival explanation for a change in the DV.
