You will test a few hundred of the crores who exist, then speak about all of them. Whether that leap is justified depends almost entirely on how the few hundred were chosen. Populations, samples and parameters A population (or universe) is the whole, well-defined group about which you want to draw conclusions. The target population is the group you would like to generalise to (all school students in India); the accessible population is the part you can actually reach (students in the Mysuru schools that admit you). Each member about whom data are collected is an element ; a sampling unit is whatever is selected at a step of sampling, either an element or a whole group such as a school. The sampling frame is the actual list used for selection (a school register, a voters' list), and the sample is the smaller set chosen from it by some rule or plan. Studying every element is a census ; studying a part in order to describe the whole is a sample survey. A number describing a population is a parameter , written with Greek letters (mean μ, standard deviation σ); the same number computed from a sample is a statistic , written with Roman letters (M or X̄, s). A parameter is fixed but usually unknown; a statistic is known but varies from sample to sample. Sampling exists to estimate the first from the second. Exam trap "A statistical measure based upon a population" is a parameter ; one based upon a sample is a statistic . Pair the initials: Population with Parameter, Sample with Statistic. Sampling is needed because it saves time and money, often measures more accurately (a few trained investigators beat an army of hasty ones), is the only option for huge or infinite populations, and is unavoidable when testing destroys what is tested. Its principles: a statistic usually differs somewhat from its parameter; parameters are estimated through sampling distributions; and a random sample mirrors its population more closely as it grows. Its aims: a representative sample, unbiased estimates and a known margin of error. A good sample therefore shows representativeness (population characteristics in the same proportions), adequacy (enough cases), independence (choosing one element does not affect choosing another) and homogeneity (its units are of the same kind as the population's). Probability versus non-probability sampling Following the sociologist Hubert M. Blalock (1926 to 1991), whose Social Statistics appeared in 1960, sampling methods fall into three families (Figure 9.4). Probability sampling methods clearly specify the likelihood of inclusion of each element: every element has a known, non-zero chance of selection, and a random mechanism does the choosing. In non-probability sampling that chance cannot be known, because a person (researcher, interviewer, volunteer or friend) does the choosing. Mixed sampling combines features of both: Indian texts following Blalock place systematic sampling here, since only its start is random, and the term also covers designs that join a purposive stage to a random one. Why does the random mechanism matter? It removes the researcher's personal bias from selection, and because selection follows the laws of chance, the size of the chance error can be calculated (Section 9.9), which is what licenses inferential statistics. Probability sampling is therefore the method most likely to yield a representative sample: likely, not certain, since a random draw can still come out lopsided. Non-probability samples allow neither randomisation nor a calculated sampling error. Sampling methods (Blalock, 1960) Probability known, non-zero chance Mixed features of both Non-probability chance unknown Simple random Systematic (most texts) Stratified random Cluster (area) Multistage cluster Multiphase (double) Systematic random start, then a fixed rule Convenience (accidental) Volunteer (self-selected) Purposive (judgemental) Quota Snowball (chain referral) Saturation, dense Figure 9.4 The three families of sampling methods. Systematic sampling appears twice: most texts call it probability sampling, Indian texts following Blalock call it mixed. Exam trap A past paper keys "random sampling guarantees a representative sample". Choose it, since the other options (it ensures personal bias, reduces the sample needed, makes data collection harder) are plainly wrong, but know the exact fact: it makes representativeness likely and error calculable , never guaranteed. "Statistical" and "empirical" sampling are not Blalock's families; methods that specify each element's chance of inclusion are probability methods. Simple random and systematic sampling Simple random sampling (unrestricted random sampling) is the foundation of the others: every element has an equal and independent chance of selection. Equal means none is favoured; independent means one draw does not alter another's chance. Randomness comes from the lottery or fishbowl method (names on identical slips, drawn blind), a table of random numbers (the most popular: elements are numbered 1 to N, and numbers above N and repeats are skipped) or computer generation for large populations. Returning each drawn element before the next draw is sampling with replacement ; psychologists usually sample without replacement . The method needs no knowledge of the population's make-up and its error is easy to compute, but it requires a complete frame and may, by bad luck, miss small subgroups. Systematic sampling takes every kth (or nth) element after a random start, with the interval k = N/n. For 100 students from a register of 2,000, k = 20, so a random start of 7 gives the 7th, 27th, 47th student and so on. It is quick and spreads the sample evenly, but beware periodicity : if a hostel list runs room by room, four to a room with the prefect always first, k = 4 yields every prefect or none. Chance decides only the start, hence the label mixed in Indian texts following Blalock; it is never a non-probability method. Stratified random sampling Suppose a university has 1,000 PhD, 2,000 MA and 7,000 BA students, and research anxiety may differ by level. Stratified random sampling first divides the population into strata , mutually exclusive and exhaustive subgroups formed on a variable related to the study, then draws a random sample from every stratum. In proportionate stratified sampling each stratum gets the same sampling fraction, so a sample of 100 holds 10 PhD, 20 MA and 70 BA students and mirrors the population. In disproportionate stratified sampling small strata are deliberately over-sampled (say 40, 30 and 30) so that each can be analysed on its own, and results are weighted back for the whole. Optimum allocation takes more cases from strata that are larger, more variable and cheaper to sample, giving the most precise estimate for a fixed cost; Jerzy Neyman (1894 to 1981) gave its classic form, weighing stratum size and variability, in 1934. Stratification guarantees that every important subgroup appears. When strata are internally homogeneous and differ from one another, it is also more precise than a simple random sample of the same size, because chance can no longer hand you too many BA students. Its costs: every element's stratum must be known in advance, and in a homogeneous population it gains nothing. Exam trap Stratified sampling is preferred over simple random sampling when important subgroups must be represented . It does not help a homogeneous population, is not chosen to minimise sample size, and needs more knowledge of the frame, not less (with no list of individuals, use cluster sampling). Every nth case is systematic; intact schools are cluster; volunteers are non-probability. Cluster, multistage and multiphase sampling No list of every school student in India exists, and a simple random sample would scatter interviewers across thousands of villages. Cluster sampling (area sampling) solves both problems: the population is divided into naturally occurring groups (districts, villages, schools, wards), a random sample of these clusters is drawn, and units inside the chosen clusters are studied. Only a list of clusters is needed. It began in agricultural research and now drives large surveys. In one-stage cluster sampling everyone in each chosen cluster is studied; in two-stage cluster sampling a random sample is taken within each chosen cluster; in multistage sampling , associated with the British statistician Claus Moser (1922 to 2015), selection descends through more levels. Randomly select 5 districts from each state, then 10 schools per district, then 30 students per school: districts and schools are intact groups picked at random, so this is multistage cluster sampling, the logic of India's National Family Health Surveys. The price is precision. Students in one school are alike, so each extra student from a chosen school adds less new information than one drawn from the whole country. For the same n, a cluster sample usually has a larger sampling error than a simple random sample, and a stratified sample a smaller one; cluster sampling buys cheapness, not a larger sample. Ideal clusters are miniatures of the population, the reverse of ideal strata (Table 9.9, Figure 9.5). Table 9.9 Stratified versus cluster sampling. Two relatives remain. In multiphase sampling (with two phases, double sampling ) the same kind of unit is sampled repeatedly: a large first-phase sample answers a cheap screening question, and a smaller subsample drawn from it gets the detailed study (screen 2,000 students with a brief anxiety scale, then interview 200). Units change across the stages of a multistage design but stay the same across phases. In panel sampling one sample is studied repeatedly over time (longitudinal designs are in Section 9.4). Exam trap A stem saying researchers "divide a population into smaller groups, and then randomly select from these groups" is a stock definition of cluster sampling and is keyed so: the groups themselves are picked at random. Some groups taken and the rest skipped means cluster; every group contributing a random sample means stratified. In the districts, schools, students stem every state contributes, so states act as strata (strictly, stratified multistage cluster sampling), but the keyed answer is cluster . "Two-stage" points to cluster sampling, not to proportionate or disproportionate stratified sampling, and two-stage is not two-phase (double) sampling. Non-probability methods Non-probability methods give up the random mechanism for speed, low cost or access. In all of them the chance of selection is unknown, randomisation is impossible, sampling error cannot be calculated, and generalisation rests on judgement (Table 9.10). Convenience sampling (accidental or incidental sampling) takes people who are available, volunteer or can easily be recruited: your own classmates, shoppers passing a mall. It is the quickest, cheapest and least controlled method. In a volunteer or self-selected sample people answer an advertisement or online poll; volunteers are usually more interested and motivated than others. In purposive sampling (judgemental sampling) the researcher's knowledge and judgement hand-pick cases thought typical, expert or information-rich, such as senior nurses she considers typical of their wards. Quota sampling , "a common and poor version of stratified sampling", fixes how many people of each kind are needed to mirror population proportions (60 men and 40 women, say), then lets interviewers fill each quota with whoever they find. The interviewer, not chance, picks people within quotas, so bias enters there. Cheap and needing no frame, it is widely used in market research and opinion polls. In snowball sampling (chain-referral sampling) a few people with the characteristic of interest recruit others like them, so existing participants recruit future participants. It is the route into hidden populations that have no list, such as drug users or sex workers. In saturation sampling the researcher includes as many available members of a limited group as possible (900 of a school's 1,000 students); in dense sampling all or nearly all of the accessible population is taken. Both are rare. Qualitative purposive strategies (theoretical sampling, maximum variation, typical and extreme case, criterion sampling, sampling to saturation) belong to Section 9.6. That description is purposive sampling; quota wins only as the one non-probability option beside simple random, stratified and cluster. Rule: judgement of typical cases, purposive; fixed numbers per category, quota; whoever is available, convenience; participants recruit participants, snowball. Offered both purposive and quota for a judgement stem, choose purposive. Sampling error, bias and the Literary Digest Sampling error is the chance difference between a statistic and its parameter; Everet Franklin Lindquist (1901 to 1978) defined it in 1940 as "the difference between a parameter and an estimate of that parameter which is derived from a sample". It implies no mistake. It falls as n rises (the standard error of the mean is σ divided by the square root of n, so quadrupling n halves it) and as population variability falls, is zero in a census, and can be calculated only for probability samples. Non-sampling error afflicts a census too: coverage error (the frame misses part of the population), non-response error (non-repliers differ from repliers), measurement error (poor questions, interviewer effects) and processing error (coding and entry mistakes). Error that pushes results consistently one way is sampling bias . Random error shrinks as n grows; bias does not, and a bigger biased sample is only a more confident wrong answer. Key study: The Literary Digest poll (1936) Question. Who would win the 1936 United States presidential election? Method. The magazine Literary Digest mailed about 10 million ballots to names from its subscriber lists, telephone directories and car registrations; over 2 million came back. Result. It predicted a comfortable win for the Republican challenger; the sitting president won by a landslide, carrying all but two states. A young pollster, George Horace Gallup (1901 to 1984), with a far smaller sample, called it correctly. Why. In the Depression, telephone and car owners were richer than average (coverage bias), and those who returned ballots differed from those who did not (non-response bias). Lesson. Size cannot cure bias. Exam trap Random sampling decides who enters the study and supports generalisation (external validity). Random assignment decides who gets which condition and supports causal conclusions (internal validity; Section 9.2). A true experiment needs random assignment and can survive a convenience sample. How large should a sample be? The size needed rises with population variability, with the precision and confidence level wanted, with smaller effects to detect, with higher power (conventionally .80), with the number of subgroups to analyse separately and with expected non-response; cost, time and the planned analysis set the ceiling. Rules of thumb call 30 or more a large sample and about 100 adequate for most educational research, but the modern answer is a power analysis before data collection (Section 9.9). A parameter can be estimated as a single value ( point estimation ) or as a range likely to contain it ( interval estimation , the confidence interval); both rest on the sampling distribution, taught in Section 9.9. Answers: (1) parameter, (2) non-zero, (3) systematic; periodicity, (4) stratified random, (5) multistage cluster, (6) quota, (7) snowball, (8) bias. 9.4 Research Designs: Experimental, Single-Case and Non-Experimental Medium yield · 21 Qs A counsellor in Mysuru believes that slow breathing before class lowers exam anxiety. She could ask 500 students whether they practise it, follow one anxious student as the practice starts and stops, or let chance decide which half of a class practises. Each is a research design , a plan fixing who is studied, what is done to them and when they are measured, and each licenses different conclusions. We begin with the only design that can establish cause. What makes an experiment An experiment has three features: manipulation of the independent variable (IV) by the researcher (variables are defined in Section 9.2), control of everything else, and random assignment , in which chance (a lottery, random numbers), not the researcher or the participant, decides who enters which condition. The experimental group receives the treatment; the control group is treated identically but receives no treatment, and shows what would have happened anyway. Random assignment makes the groups equivalent at the start, spreading every characteristic, even unmeasured ones, evenly by chance. If equivalent groups end unequal on the dependent variable (DV), only the IV can explain it. Creating equivalence among participants is therefore vital for experimental research; the issue does not arise in correlational or descriptive research, where nobody is assigned. John Stuart Mill (1806 to 1873) gave the logic in A System of Logic (1843). By his method of agreement , a circumstance shared by every case of an effect is probably its cause; by his method of difference , if cases with and without the effect differ in only one circumstance, that circumstance is the cause, which is exactly what an experiment arranges. Causal inference needs covariation , temporal precedence (cause before effect) and elimination of alternative explanations . Only the experiment secures all three, so only it licenses cause-and-effect conclusions. Ronald Aylmer Fisher (1890 to 1962), in The Design of Experiments (1935), gave three principles of experimental design: replication (several units per treatment, so that chance variation can be estimated), randomisation (every participant has an equal chance of assignment to any group) and local control (blocking: grouping similar units so that their differences leave the error term). Homogeneity is not one of the three. Exam trap Random selection (sampling, Section 9.3) decides who enters a study; random assignment decides who gets which condition. A survey of 10,000 randomly selected adults finding regular meditators less stressed has no assignment: people chose to meditate, and calmer people may be the ones who do. Large or random samples never turn an observational study into an experiment, so neither this study nor one linking exercise and depression in 30,000 adults supports a causal conclusion. Campbell and Stanley's designs Donald Thomas Campbell (1916 to 1996) and Julian C. Stanley (1918 to 2005) catalogued designs in 1963 in a notation still used: R is random assignment, X the treatment and O an observation; each row is a group and time runs left to right. They grouped designs by how well they rule out threats to internal validity such as history and maturation (Section 9.2), as Table 9.11 shows. Pre-experimental designs have no random assignment and little or no comparison; true experimental designs have R and a control group. A pretest has a hidden cost, pretest sensitisation : a questionnaire on mental illness may make students more responsive to an anti-stigma film that follows. Richard L. Solomon (1949) answered with the Solomon four-group design , which runs the pretest-posttest and posttest-only designs together with four random groups, so the effect of pretesting and its interaction with treatment are measured and controlled. Maturation and selection are already handled by any randomised control group, and researcher bias by blinding (Section 9.2). A quasi-experiment manipulates the IV but uses intact groups (classes, wards) without random assignment. Its main forms are the nonequivalent control group design , the interrupted time-series design (one group measured many times before and after the intervention) and the regression discontinuity design (Donald Thistlethwaite and Campbell, 1960), which assigns treatment by a cut-off score and looks for a jump in the regression line at the cut-off. Noise was manipulated, so it is not a correlational study or naturalistic observation; no child was randomly assigned, so it is not a true experiment. It is a quasi-experiment . Between, within and mixed designs In a between-subjects design each participant receives one condition: two randomised groups; a multigroup design (one IV at three or more levels, which shows the shape of its effect); or the matched-groups or randomised block design , in which participants are matched on a variable correlated with the DV and the members of each block are randomly assigned to conditions, Fisher's local control in practice. In a within-subjects or repeated-measures design everyone receives every condition and serves as his or her own control, so fewer participants are needed and individual differences leave the error term. The cost is order effects (practice, fatigue) and carry-over effects (a drug still acting in the next condition), handled by counterbalancing the order (Section 9.2). A Latin square arranges orders so that each condition appears once in every position: four conditions need four orders instead of 24. Latin squares thus control order effects in repeated-measures designs; they are not correlational, and "equal group sizes" or "one IV with several levels" describe balanced and multigroup designs. A mixed design has a between factor and a within factor (group × time). In a crossover design each participant receives both treatments in sequence, half in each order. Exam trap Patients take a placebo for four weeks and a viral medication for four more, or the reverse. The researchers assigned the treatments, so this crossover study is an experiment , and the explanatory variable (the one that explains changes in the response) is the type of treatment; symptom improvement is the response. Factorial designs A factorial design studies two or more IVs at once, every level of each combined systematically with every level of the others. Each IV is a factor , each of its values a level , and each combination a treatment combination or cell . Count the numerals for factors and multiply them for cells: 2 × 3 is two factors and six cells; 2 × 2 × 2 is three factors and eight cells. A main effect is one factor's effect averaged over the levels of the others; a simple effect is its effect at one level of another; an interaction effect exists when one factor's effect depends on the level of another, shown by non-parallel lines (Figure 9.6). There noise adds 2 errors on an easy task and 8 on a hard one: a main effect of 5 errors that hides an interaction only a factorial design can reveal. Two factors give two main effects and one interaction; three give three main effects, three two-way and one three-way interaction (factorial ANOVA, Section 9.10). Laboratory, field and natural experiments A laboratory experiment , as defined by Leon Festinger and Daniel Katz (1953), is one in which the investigator creates exactly the conditions he wants, controlling some variables and manipulating others: high internal validity, but limited external validity, that is, generalisation to real life (Section 9.2). A field experiment manipulates an IV in a natural setting, as when Irving Piliavin and colleagues (1969) staged a collapse on New York subway trains to see who helped. Its advantage is higher external validity; the laboratory keeps higher internal validity and easier control, and both can use between-participants designs. A field study manipulates nothing but studies relations as they exist in a factory or school; Katz (1953) divided field studies into exploratory (finding the variables) and hypothesis-testing types. In a natural experiment nature or policy does the manipulating: people conceived at the height of the Dutch famine of 1944 to 1945 later showed about twice the usual risk of schizophrenia. With no random assignment, it remains quasi-experimental. Analogue studies are covered in Section 9.5. Single-case and small-N designs The single-subject design (single-case or N = 1 design) asks whether a treatment changes one person's behaviour, by measuring it repeatedly while treatment is switched in planned phases; with a few participants it becomes a small-N design . Such designs grew from the intensive study of a few animals by Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990). Murray Sidman 's Tactics of Scientific Research (1960) argued that a group average may fit no individual and that generality comes from replication, and Alan E. Kazdin (1982) systematised the designs for clinical work. Behaviour is recorded (by frequency, duration or time intervals) through a baseline , phase A, until stable, which predicts what would happen untreated; B is the treatment and C a second treatment. An A-B design shows one change and cannot rule out coincidence. The withdrawal design (A-B-A) removes the treatment to see behaviour return; the reversal design (A-B-A-B) reinstates it, the clearest demonstration (Figure 9.7). Withdrawal is unethical for self-injury and useless for skills, such as reading, that do not reverse; the multiple-baseline design avoids it by starting treatment at staggered times across behaviours, participants or settings (Table 9.12). Non-experimental designs In non-experimental or observational research variables are measured as they exist and nothing is assigned. The commonest form, correlational research , measures two or more variables in the same people (Section 9.11) and allows prediction but not causation. The directionality problem (does poor sleep cause depression, or the reverse?) means it cannot determine the direction of influence; the third-variable problem means an unmeasured factor such as loneliness may cause both. It needs no random assignment and is among psychology's most used designs. No sample, however large or random, cures these two problems. Fred N. Kerlinger (1910 to 1991) defined survey research as studying populations by selecting samples, to discover the relative incidence, distribution and interrelations of sociological and psychological variables, but not the causal factors of an event. A survey of an entire population is a census (the Census of India is the classic survey); of a part, a sample survey . Modes are interview, mail, telephone, online and the panel technique (the same respondents surveyed repeatedly). In Kerlinger's ex post facto research ("after the fact"), also called causal-comparative research , the IV has already occurred or cannot be manipulated, so pre-existing groups such as smokers and non-smokers are compared; self-selection and the post hoc fallacy are its risks. Historical research uses primary sources (eyewitness records) and secondary sources (accounts by people not present). Its evidence faces external criticism , which tests authenticity (is the document genuine?), and internal criticism , which tests credibility (is it accurate, its author honest and informed?). The designs and numbers come from epidemiology , the study of how disorders are distributed in populations and what determines them; evidence synthesis pools the answers. In epidemiology the independent variable is called the exposure and the dependent variable the outcome . Counting cases: prevalence and incidence A disorder's prevalence counts existing cases, old and new together, as a proportion of a population. Its narrowest form, point prevalence , is the number of existing cases on a specific date divided by the total population on that date (40 cases among 2,000 Mysuru adults on 1 March: 2 percent). Period prevalence counts everyone who was a case at any time during a stated period, such as the past 12 months, and lifetime prevalence everyone who has ever met the criteria. By contrast, incidence counts only new cases arising during a period among people free of the disorder at its start, either as cumulative incidence (new cases divided by the population at risk) or as an incidence rate (new cases per person-time at risk, such as per 1,000 person-years). For a stable condition, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration . Schizophrenia has a low incidence but lasts for years, so its prevalence is relatively high; a brief adjustment disorder can have many new cases yet a low point prevalence. Incidence is used to find causes, prevalence to plan services. A morbidity rate expresses illness (its incidence or prevalence) per unit of population over a stated time, and a mortality rate gives deaths per unit of population, usually per 1,000 or 100,000 a year. Exam trap "Existing cases on a specific date out of the total population" is point prevalence . Plain "prevalence" is less specific, "periodic prevalence" covers a stretch of time, and "incidence" counts new cases only. Epidemiological designs The designs differ in where the researcher starts and which way the inquiry runs in time (Table 9.14). An ecological study correlates group-level data, such as suicide and unemployment rates across Indian states; inferring individual behaviour from such correlations is the ecological fallacy , demonstrated by William S. Robinson in 1950. A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one moment, as prevalence surveys do, so it cannot show which came first. A case-control study starts from the outcome: cases who have the disorder and matched controls who do not are compared on past exposure. For a rare dissociative disorder and childhood trauma, a cohort would need thousands of children followed for decades, whereas a case-control study starts from the cases a hospital already has: for rare outcomes it is the most feasible design. It cannot measure incidence, so it yields the odds ratio, and it is prone to recall bias , because ill people search their memories harder than healthy controls. A cohort study classifies people who are free of the outcome as exposed or unexposed and follows them to see who develops it, which gives incidence and the relative risk. A prospective cohort runs forward from now. In the British Doctors Study, begun by Richard Doll (1912 to 2005) and Austin Bradford Hill (1897 to 1991), British doctors were questioned about smoking in 1951, again in 1957, 1966 and repeatedly up to 2001, and their deaths were traced: lung cancer mortality rose with the number of cigarettes smoked. Nobody was assigned to smoke, so the study is observational; it ran forward, so it is prospective. The Framingham Heart Study of a Massachusetts town (from 1948) is another. A retrospective cohort (historical cohort) uses existing records but still reasons from exposure to outcome. Cohorts are slow and costly, and they lose people to attrition. The British Doctors Study is a prospective observational study, not retrospective, not a sample survey (9.3) and not an experiment. "Rare outcome plus past exposure" means case-control : trauma cannot be randomised, and a cross-sectional study cannot show which came first. Measures of association and effect Any exposure and yes-or-no outcome fit a 2 × 2 table. In a trial, 200 people recovering from depression receive maintenance cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) and 200 receive treatment as usual (TAU); 50 and 80 of them relapse. Risk is the proportion who develop the outcome: 0.25 with CBT, 0.40 with TAU (the control event rate). The relative risk or risk ratio (RR) divides the risks: 0.25/0.40 = 0.625. The odds ratio (OR) divides the odds, odds being those with the outcome over those without: (50/150)/(80/120) = 0.50. A ratio of 1.0 means no association . Above 1 the exposure increases risk (an RR of 2.0 means double the incidence); below 1 it is protective, as CBT is here. A case-control study gives only the OR, there phrased as the odds of exposure among cases over that among controls; it approximates the RR when the outcome is rare. Absolute measures show size. The attributable risk (risk difference) is the risk in the exposed minus the risk in the unexposed; in a trial it becomes the absolute risk reduction (ARR): 0.40 − 0.25 = 0.15. The relative risk reduction (RRR = ARR/control risk = 1 − RR) is 37.5 percent, a grander-sounding figure. The number needed to treat ( NNT = 1/ARR ) is how many patients must receive the treatment instead of the control for one additional patient to benefit: 1/0.15 = 6.7, rounded up to 7. An NNT of 8 for an antidepressant means treating 8 patients for one extra to benefit; the ideal is 1. The number needed to harm (NNH) is 1 divided by the absolute risk increase of an adverse effect: a side effect in 30 percent on the drug and 10 percent on placebo gives NNH = 5. Exam trap NNT = 1/ARR. The distractors 1/RRR, 1/RR, RR × control event rate (that gives the treated group's event rate), OR − 1, OR × 100, RRR × 100 and "enrolled ÷ events" are all wrong. An NNT of 8 does not mean the drug works in 8 percent of patients or that 8 must drop out, and there is no NNT threshold for drug approval. RR or OR = 1.0 means no association : not protective (below 1), not "doubles the risk" (2.0), not "causes the outcome" and not "perfect correlation" (r = 1, 9.11). Screening and diagnostic accuracy Against a gold standard such as a clinical interview, a screening test sorts people into four cells (Table 9.15): true positives, false positives (healthy people flagged), false negatives (cases missed) and true negatives. A test's sensitivity , TP/(TP + FN), is the true positive rate : the proportion of real cases it catches. Its specificity , TN/(TN + FP), is the proportion of non-cases it correctly clears. A depression test with sensitivity 90 percent and specificity 70 percent therefore identifies 90 percent of depressed people as depressed and 70 percent of healthy people as healthy. Both are computed among people whose true status is known, so they do not change with prevalence. Table 9.15 A screening test against the true diagnosis. The positive predictive value (PPV), the proportion of positive scorers who truly have the disorder, and the negative predictive value (NPV), the proportion of negative scorers who truly lack it, answer it, and they depend on the prevalence or base rate , the pre-test probability. Apply the 90/70 test to 1,000 clinic patients, 20 percent depressed: 180 true and 240 false positives give PPV = 180/420 = 43 percent. Where only 5 percent are depressed, 45 true and 285 false positives give PPV = 14 percent. The test is unchanged; the base rate fell. Paul Everett Meehl (1920 to 2003) and Albert Rosen warned in 1955 that with rare conditions a test's cutting score can make more errors than predicting from the base rate alone. Lowering a cut-off score raises sensitivity and lowers specificity. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve , from signal detection theory, plots sensitivity (y-axis) against 1 − specificity (x-axis) across all possible cut-offs (Figure 9.9). The area under the curve (AUC) runs from 0.5 (chance) to 1.0 (perfect discrimination). "A positive test reflects true disease" is PPV, "probability of disease before testing" is prevalence, "true negatives correctly identified" is specificity, and TN/(TN + FN) is NPV. PPV is most affected by prevalence , not by sensitivity or specificity alone or by the number of items (Chapter 2). ROC curves do not plot Type I against Type II error (9.9), predictor against outcome (9.11), item difficulty against discrimination, validity against reliability, score against age, or means against standard deviations. The randomised controlled trial A randomised controlled trial (RCT) is a true experiment on patients: participants are randomly allocated to a treatment or a comparison condition and compared on an outcome named in advance. Randomisation gives everyone the same chance of each arm, balancing measured and unmeasured characteristics. Next, allocation concealment hides the upcoming allocation sequence from those enrolling participants until each is irreversibly enrolled, using central randomisation or sealed opaque envelopes, so that a clinician cannot steer a promising patient into the treatment arm; it prevents selection bias. Blinding works after allocation, hiding the arm from the participant (single-blind), also from those treating and assessing (double-blind), and also from the analysts (triple-blind); see 9.2. Psychotherapy trials cannot blind patients or therapists, only assessors and analysts. Controls may receive a placebo (an inert, identical pill) or an active established treatment; psychotherapy trials also use waiting-list, attention-placebo and treatment-as-usual controls (Chapter 7). Exam trap Allocation concealment is not blinding. Concealment hides the upcoming allocation from recruiters before enrolment; blinding hides the actual arm after it. "Blinding the patient to the assigned arm", "hiding outcome assessors' identity", "sealing the analysis dataset", "concealing the primary outcome from the statistician" and "keeping investigators unaware of the hypothesis" are all wrong. Analysing, designing and registering trials In intention-to-treat analysis (ITT) every participant is analysed in the group to which they were randomised, regardless of adherence, drop-out or crossover. A per-protocol analysis keeps only those who completed the treatment as planned (completers), and as-treated analysis groups people by the treatment they actually received. Drop-outs differ between arms, so discarding them reintroduces selection bias and usually flatters the treatment; ITT preserves randomisation and gives a conservative, real-world estimate. Attrition , the loss of participants, reduces power, and when it differs between arms it destroys the balance that randomisation created. Exam trap ITT analyses everyone in their randomised group . "Only completers" and "excluding protocol deviators" are per-protocol; "by actual treatment received" is as-treated; "only responders" or "only the control group" is no analysis at all. Most trials are parallel-group : each person receives one condition. In a crossover trial each person receives both conditions in random order, with a washout between, which fails when effects carry over (9.4). A cluster randomised trial randomises whole groups such as schools or villages. A superiority trial asks whether the new treatment is better; a non-inferiority trial whether it is no worse than the standard by more than a preset margin; an equivalence trial whether the difference lies within that margin in both directions. Drug trials run in phases: phase I tests safety and dose in about 20 to 100 mostly healthy volunteers; phase II seeks first evidence of efficacy in up to several hundred patients; phase III runs confirmatory RCTs in roughly 300 to 3,000 patients, the basis for approval; phase IV is post-marketing surveillance for rare and long-term harms. Trial registration records planned outcomes publicly before enrolment; the Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI), run by the Indian Council of Medical Research since 2007, has been mandatory since 2009. Finally, efficacy is whether a treatment works under ideal conditions (an explanatory trial) and effectiveness whether it works in routine care (a pragmatic trial; Chapter 7). Analogue research In analogue research , a clinical phenomenon is modelled under conditions that only resemble the clinical situation, usually with healthy, non-clinical participants (often students) or simulated conditions: snake-fearful undergraduates standing in for phobic patients, or sadness induced in the laboratory. It offers control, easy recruitment and fewer ethical obstacles, but its findings may not generalise to patients (external validity, 9.2). It is not research on clinical populations, nor an efficacy or comparative effectiveness trial. Systematic reviews, meta-analysis and the evidence hierarchy A systematic review uses explicit, pre-specified, reproducible methods to find, appraise and synthesise all the studies on one question, unlike a narrative review whose author picks the studies. A meta-analysis is its statistical step: it summarises the results of many studies by pooling their effect sizes (9.9) into one weighted average. Gene V. Glass (born 1940) coined the term in 1976. Key study: Smith and Glass (1977) Hans Eysenck (1916 to 1997) had claimed in 1952 that neurotic patients improve about as often without psychotherapy as with it. Mary Lee Smith and Glass pooled 375 controlled studies of psychotherapy: the average effect size of 0.68 meant that the average treated client was better off than about 75 percent of untreated controls. Critics, Eysenck foremost, replied that pooling poor studies gives a precise but wrong answer ("garbage in, garbage out"). Exam trap One real paper (IHBAS 2024) keys "to conduct a single large experiment" as the purpose of meta-analysis. That is wrong: a single experiment, however large, is primary research. Meta-analysis exists to summarise findings from multiple studies ; it collects no primary data and does not analyse individual case studies. A forest plot shows each study as a square (its effect, sized by its weight) on a line (its 95 percent confidence interval), with a vertical line of no effect and a diamond for the pooled estimate. Heterogeneity , variation between studies beyond chance, is tested with Cochran's Q and expressed as I 2 . Pooled effects are inflated by publication bias , the preferential publication of significant results; Robert Rosenthal (born 1933) named its extreme form the file-drawer problem in 1979: null results stay in researchers' drawers. A funnel plot of effect size against precision is symmetrical without bias and lopsided when small null studies are missing. The hierarchy of evidence for treatment questions runs from systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs at the top, through single RCTs, cohort studies, case-control studies and case series or reports, down to expert opinion. Reporting guidelines Reporting guidelines are design-specific checklists telling authors how to write a study up so that readers can judge it (Table 9.16). CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) adds a flow diagram accounting for every randomised participant; PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) governs a systematic review, such as one on CBT for insomnia. This section takes those tools and their errors, then the paradigms beneath them, and ends with qualitative research. Data sources and observation Primary data are collected first-hand for the present study, by observation, interview, questionnaire or test. Secondary data were collected by others for another purpose and are re-used: census records, hospital files, archives, published surveys. They are cheap, large and non-reactive, but the researcher controls neither what was recorded nor how accurately. Observation is the systematic watching and recording of behaviour without manipulating it; it alone does not depend on what people say they do. In participant observation the observer joins the group's life; in non-participant observation the observer stays outside. Structured observation codes predefined categories; unstructured observation keeps open field notes. Naturalistic observation records behaviour in its usual setting (play in a school yard); controlled observation arranges standard conditions (mother and child behind a one-way mirror). Overt observers are known to the group; covert observers are not, which raises consent problems (Section 9.7). James P. Spradley (1933 to 1982), in Participant Observation (1980), described three narrowing phases: descriptive observation, broad, to grasp the field; focused observation, on the processes found relevant; and selective observation, near the end, seeking further evidence for specific practices. Its two errors are reactivity , behaviour changing because people know they are watched (reduced by habituation and one-way mirrors), and observer bias , seeing what one expects (reduced by blind observers and inter-observer agreement). The participant observer may also "go native", losing critical distance. Time and event sampling of behaviour are covered in Section 9.4. Interviews and ethnographic inquiry An interview is a purposeful conversation in which the interviewer asks questions and records the answers. A structured interview fixes the wording and order of every question: reliable and comparable, but rigid. A semi-structured interview follows a topic guide but lets the interviewer rephrase and probe; an unstructured interview fixes only the aim, trading reliability for depth. An in-depth interview is a long one-to-one exploration of experience; a focus group is a moderated discussion among about 6 to 10 similar people whose interaction is itself the data, though dominant members can sway it. An open-ended question lets respondents answer in their own words ("Tell me about..."); a closed-ended question restricts the answer to yes or no or a fixed choice ("Did you sleep well?"). Probes are neutral follow-ups ("Could you say more?", an expectant pause) that draw out a fuller answer without suggesting one. Spradley's The Ethnographic Interview (1979) treats the respondent as an informant, an expert on their own cultural world, asked to explain its meanings to an outsider through descriptive, structural and contrast questions. "Can you tell me why this band is so popular among your age group?" is an ethnographic interview question: the teenager explains the culture of the peer group. Other styles of inquiry differ: psychodynamic inquiry (feelings, early relationships, hidden motives: "What does this remind you of?"), task-focused inquiry (completing a defined task), strength-based inquiry (resources and past successes: "What has helped you cope?") and theory-guided inquiry (questions set by one theory, such as cognitive therapy). The interviewer is part of the instrument, so errors arise from the interviewer's attitudes and expectations, from their sex, age, caste or status, from confusing or overlong questions, coldness and unmotivated respondents, and from interviewers recording similar answers differently. Training and standard wording reduce them. Exam trap "Tell me about..." is an open-ended question , not an ethnographic technique. The band question is ethnographic inquiry because it asks an insider to explain a culture. Questionnaires and schedules A questionnaire is answered by respondents themselves; a schedule is asked and filled in by the investigator or enumerator face to face, as in the census, so it suits respondents who cannot read. Items are open (own words; rich but slow to code) or closed: dichotomous (yes or no), multiple choice, ranking, rating, and the contingency question that routes respondents ("If no, go to question 12"). Attitude scales (Likert, Thurstone, Guttman) are taught in Chapter 2. Table 9.17 lists the wording faults; presuming and hypothetical questions are avoided too. Table 9.17 Faults in question wording. Fault Example Double-barrelled question : two questions, one answer "How often and how much time do you exercise?" Leading: suggests the answer "Don't you agree therapy should be free?" Loaded: emotive words "Should lunatics roam the streets?" Ambiguous or vague "Do you drink regularly?" Double negative "Do you not agree patients should not be told?" The funnel sequence moves from broad, easy questions to narrow ones, with sensitive items last. A good questionnaire is short and relevant, states its purpose, asks one idea per item in simple, neutral words, follows a logical order, looks neat and has been pilot-tested. Mailed questionnaires are cheap and anonymous but cannot clarify questions, and by one survey estimate about 70 percent are never returned; because non-responders differ from responders, a low response rate biases the sample. Every tool thus has its own error: reactivity and observer bias, interviewer bias, response sets and non-response, records of unknown accuracy. Careful studies combine tools ( triangulation ). Content analysis, sociometry and Verstehen Content analysis studies communications (letters, diaries, case notes, films) rather than people. Bernard Berelson (1912 to 1979) defined it in 1952 as "the objective, systematic and quantitative description of the manifest content of communication". Manifest content is what is plainly there; latent content, the underlying meaning, is left to qualitative versions. His method, as set out in his 1954 handbook chapter (the date A.K. Singh gives): specify the universe (the content and its categories), choose the unit of analysis (word, theme, item, character, or space and time) and quantify by counting, ranking or rating. Sociometry measures an individual's social behaviour and relations within a group. Jacob Levy Moreno (1889 to 1974), founder of psychodrama, introduced it in Who Shall Survive? (1934). Members name whom they would choose for an activity, and the sociogram draws the choices as arrows, showing stars (chosen by many), isolates (chosen by none) and mutual choices. Verstehen ("understanding") is the interpretive grasp of the meaning an action has for the actor. Wilhelm Dilthey (1833 to 1911) argued in 1883 that the natural sciences explain from outside while the human sciences must understand from inside; Max Weber (1864 to 1920) made Verstehen the method of interpretive sociology. It is an interpretive stance, not a measure of social behaviour; nor is the "sample method", which is simply sampling (Section 9.3). Q-methodology ( William Stephenson , 1935), which factor-analyses persons through Q-sorts and bridges the two traditions, is covered in Chapter 2. Research paradigms Every method rests on a paradigm, a set of basic beliefs. Egon Guba (1924 to 2008) and Yvonna Lincoln (1994) defined paradigms by three questions: ontology (what is the nature of reality?), epistemology (what is the relation between the knower and the known?) and methodology (how should the inquirer find out?). Table 9.18 gives their four paradigms. Table 9.18 Guba and Lincoln's (1994) paradigms. Qualitative versus quantitative research Qualitative research studies meaning, experience, process and context through words, images and observed action, analysed by interpretation; quantitative research measures variables and tests hypotheses statistically. Qualitative work seeks the insider's view and treats the researcher as the instrument, which calls for reflexivity, an open account of the researcher's influence. It values language and discourse, process and human individuality, and claims neither objective truth nor the researcher's authority over participants' meanings (Table 9.19). The qualitative traditions Ethnography ("writing about a people") describes a culture or group from the inside through long immersion in its setting, mainly by participant observation and key informants; the researcher's role is to understand from the insider's perspective, not to manipulate variables, test large samples or reanalyse official statistics. The linguist Kenneth Pike (1912 to 2000) coined emic (insiders' own categories) and etic (outsiders' comparative categories) in 1954: "tension" as an idiom of distress is emic, "generalised anxiety disorder" etic. Clifford Geertz (1926 to 2006) made thick description the aim (1973): behaviour recorded with the context that gives it meaning, which alone tells a wink from a twitch of the eyelid. Key study: Malinowski in the Trobriand Islands (1915 to 1918) Stranded in Australian territory by the First World War, Bronislaw Malinowski (1884 to 1942) pitched his tent in a Trobriand village off New Guinea, learned the language and joined daily life for about two years. Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922) set ethnography's goal: "the native's point of view". Criticism: his diary, published in 1967, revealed contempt for the people he studied. Grounded theory generates theory from data. Barney Glaser (1930 to 2022) and Anselm Strauss (1916 to 1996) launched it in The Discovery of Grounded Theory (1967). Constant comparison of each new incident with earlier ones drives it; theoretical sampling picks whom to study next from the emerging categories; collection stops at theoretical saturation, when new data add nothing new; and memos record the analyst's developing ideas. The coding stages are those of Strauss and Juliet Corbin (1990), shown in Figure 9.10: open coding breaks the data apart and labels concepts; axial coding weaves the data back together around categories; selective coding integrates everything around one core category. Phenomenology studies lived experience as it appears to the person. Edmund Husserl (1859 to 1938) asked researchers to describe it after bracketing (epoché), suspending their own assumptions; his former assistant Martin Heidegger (1889 to 1976) replied (1927) that we are always immersed in the world, so all understanding is interpretation (hermeneutic phenomenology). Jonathan Smith 's interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA, 1996) follows the hermeneutic line: the researcher makes sense of participants making sense of their experience. Most methods texts call the two lines descriptive (Husserl) and interpretive or hermeneutic (Heidegger) phenomenology. One source used for this book renames them, contrasting a direct approach (Husserlian: a detached researcher lights up the foreground, participants' mental representations) with an indirect approach (Heideggerian: an involved observer, immersed in the everyday world, lights up its background). Exam trap "Direct" and "indirect" are not standard labels, and sources disagree on them. The safe fact is that the detached, bracketing approach is Husserl's (descriptive) and the involved one Heidegger's (interpretive). This book's source calls detached direct and involved indirect ("direct; indirect"); one practice key reverses them ("indirect; direct"). "Semi-direct" is not an approach. This section follows the scandals that produced ethical rules, the rules themselves, and honest reporting. Why research needs ethics Modern research ethics was written in response to abuse. After Nazi physicians' lethal experiments on concentration camp prisoners, the verdict of the Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg (1947) set out ten principles, the Nuremberg Code . Its first point reads: "The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential"; another lets the subject stop at any time. In 1964 the World Medical Association adopted the profession's own code, the Declaration of Helsinki , which puts the participant's welfare above the interests of science and later required independent committee review. From 1932 to 1972 the United States Public Health Service ran the Tuskegee syphilis study: about 600 poor Black men, 399 with syphilis, were told they had "bad blood", and penicillin was withheld even after it became the standard cure. Its exposure in 1972 led to the Belmont Report (1979) and its three principles, each with one application. Respect for persons (treat people as autonomous and protect those with reduced autonomy) is applied through informed consent; beneficence (do no harm, maximise benefits and minimise harms) through risk-benefit assessment; and justice (share research's burdens and benefits fairly) through fair selection of participants, the principle Tuskegee violated most plainly. Psychology's own debated cases matter here for their ethics only (Section 1.6, Chapter 3). John B. Watson (1878 to 1958) and Rosalie Rayner (1898 to 1935) conditioned fear in an infant, Little Albert (1920), and never removed it. Philip Zimbardo (1933 to 2024) cast 24 male students as guards or prisoners in his Stanford prison study (1971); planned for two weeks, it was stopped after six days as guards turned abusive, with Zimbardo himself acting as superintendent. Key study: Milgram's obedience study (1963) and Baumrind's critique Stanley Milgram (1933 to 1984) ordered 40 men, told the study concerned punishment and learning, to give rising "shocks" up to 450 volts to a learner who was really an unharmed confederate; 26 (65 per cent) went to the maximum. Diana Baumrind (1927 to 2018) argued in 1964 that the deception and stress were unjustified, and critics add that prods such as "you have no other choice, you must go on" undercut the right to withdraw. Milgram replied that all were debriefed and 84 per cent were glad to have taken part. Codes and ethics committees Psychologists follow the APA Ethics Code , the American Psychological Association's Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct (2002, amended 2010 and 2016). Its five aspirational general principles are (A) beneficence and nonmaleficence, (B) fidelity and responsibility, (C) integrity, (D) justice, and (E) respect for people's rights and dignity; beneath them, enforceable standards set specific rules, Standard 8 covering research and publication. In India, the Indian Council of Medical Research issued the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants (2017), which cover behavioural research in health. Under either system no study may begin until an independent institutional ethics committee (in the United States, an institutional review board or IRB) has approved its protocol. The Rehabilitation Council of India's code for clinical psychologists is in Section 7.1. Exam trap The APA has five general principles. Competence and confidentiality are enforceable standards, the usual intruders in "which is NOT a general principle". Informed consent and voluntary participation Informed consent is the principle that participants are told enough about a study (its purpose, procedures, duration, risks, benefits, the protection of their data, and their rights) to decide voluntarily whether to take part, and agree before it begins. It needs understandable information , voluntariness and capacity , the ability to understand, weigh and communicate a choice. The consent form is only the signed record of that agreement; a signature extracted with jargon or pressure is not informed consent. Suppose a Mysuru student reads that your exam-anxiety study takes 20 minutes, may stir up worry (a counsellor's number is given), codes answers by number and can be left at any point without effect on marks. If she then agrees, she has given informed consent; her signed form merely documents it. Children cannot give legal consent, so a parent or guardian consents and the child gives assent , an age-appropriate agreement of his or her own; a child's refusal is normally respected. An adult lacking capacity needs a legally authorised representative's consent, though a diagnosis alone does not remove capacity. Voluntary participation rules out coercion (a threat to grades, treatment or parole) and undue inducement (a payment large enough to distort judgement about risk). It continues as the right to withdraw at any time, without a reason or penalty, including withdrawal of one's data. Exam trap "Told enough about the research to decide whether to take part" and "permission obtained after informing them of the purpose and procedures" both define informed consent , given before participation. The consent form is the record, not the principle. Expectation management (a business phrase) and de-concealment are not research-ethics terms; revealing a deception is dehoaxing, part of debriefing. Random assignment is a design procedure (Section 9.2), not an ethical principle. Harm, risk and confidentiality Participants should leave no worse off than they came. Protection from harm covers physical harm but in psychology chiefly psychological harm (anxiety, guilt, lowered self-esteem) and social harm such as stigma. Above minimal risk (no more than in daily life), the committee makes a risk-benefit analysis : are risks as low as possible, outweighed by benefits to participants or society, and covered by safeguards? The duty most often used to sum up research ethics is ensuring the confidentiality of data: the researcher knows who gave the data but does not disclose it, coding names, storing data securely and reporting only group results. Anonymity is stricter: no one, not even the researcher, can link data to a person, because no identity is recorded. Confidentiality has limits, stated at consent, such as a serious risk of harm to self or others. Ethics asks more than following the law, and manipulating data to fit a hypothesis (falsification) or ignoring consent is its opposite. Vulnerable populations , people less able to protect their own interests, need extra safeguards: children, prisoners, people with severe mental illness or intellectual disability, pregnant women, the very poor, and anyone dependent on the researcher, such as students or patients. Justice forbids loading risky research onto them, but also excluding them from research that could benefit them. Exam trap Confidential means the researcher could identify you but will not; anonymous means nobody can. A face-to-face interview or a longitudinal study can be confidential but never anonymous. Deception and debriefing Obedience or conformity cannot be studied if participants know the hypothesis. Deception is misleading participants about a study's purpose or procedures, actively (a cover story, a confederate, false feedback) or passively (withholding the hypothesis). APA Standard 8.07 permits it only when the study has significant scientific, educational or applied value; no effective non-deceptive method is feasible; nobody is deceived about anything expected to cause physical pain or severe emotional distress; and the deception is explained as early as feasible, no later than the end of data collection, with the option to withdraw one's data. That explanation is debriefing : after participation, participants receive full information about all aspects of the study, including its true purpose and any deception, and are checked for distress. David S. Holmes (1976) named its two parts. Dehoaxing convinces participants that the false information was false (the learner received no shocks); desensitising helps them deal with distress or unwelcome self-knowledge (that they obeyed). Debriefing is good practice even without deception, but cannot excuse an unjustified deception. It is not description or explanation (goals of science, Section 9.1), nor interpretation, which belongs to a report's Discussion. Figure 9.11 places each safeguard on the participant's path. Before Informed consent: purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, rights free agreement Child: assent plus parent's consent During Voluntary throughout: free to withdraw without penalty Protection from harm Data kept confidential After Debriefing: full information on all aspects of study Dehoaxing: reveal any deception Desensitising: ease any distress Figure 9.11 The participant's path. Informed consent comes before participation, the right to withdraw and protection last throughout, and debriefing comes after. Animal research and the 3Rs Animals cannot consent, so animal research ethics rests on justification and welfare. William Russell and Rex Burch , in The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique (1959), proposed the 3Rs : replacement (non-animal methods, such as cell cultures or computer models, wherever possible), reduction (the fewest animals that give a valid answer) and refinement (less pain and distress, through anaesthesia and better housing). Misconduct, plagiarism and giving credit Research misconduct means fabrication (inventing data or results), falsification (manipulating materials, procedures or data, or omitting results, so that the record misrepresents the research) and plagiarism (presenting another person's ideas, words or results as one's own). Honest error is not misconduct. Table 9.21 gives the forms of plagiarism. Table 9.21 Forms of plagiarism, and the one practice that is not plagiarism. Form What it is Copying Using someone's words verbatim without quotation marks or citation Patchwriting Reworking a source's sentences by swapping synonyms and word order Mosaic plagiarism Stitching phrases from several sources together without credit Collusion Submitting unauthorised joint work as individual work Ghost-writing Submitting work someone else wrote Self-plagiarism Reusing one's own published text or data as if new Citation (not plagiarism) Openly acknowledging the source: the cure for plagiarism A citation is the brief acknowledgement in the text where an idea is used, such as (Milgram, 1963). Its primary purpose is to give credit to the original authors, and it also lets readers trace the idea; avoiding legal trouble is a side effect. Referencing is listing the full details of every source used at the end of the report, so that readers can find each one; it is not adding footnotes, presenting raw data or sorting data into categories (Section 9.8). Under data sharing (Standard 8.14), published data must not be withheld from competent professionals who wish to verify the findings by reanalysis. Exam trap "Which is NOT a form of plagiarism?" Citation. Collusion, patchwriting and ghost-writing are all plagiarism. Citing gives credit to the original authors; referencing lists the sources used. Writing the research report The purpose of a research report is to communicate the findings: what was done, why, what was found and what it means, so that others can evaluate and replicate the work. Collecting and analysing data come before it, and it summarises raw data rather than presenting them. In psychology the format is set by the APA Publication Manual, now in its 7th edition (released in 2019, dated 2020). Its sections form an hourglass (Figure 9.12); Table 9.22 lists their contents. The research proposal A research proposal is the detailed plan of a study, an architect's blueprint, written to win approval and often funding. A. K. Singh gives nine steps: (1) the problem, in testable terms; (2) definitions (operational definitions, Section 9.2), assumptions, limitations and delimitations; (3) a selective review of related literature; (4) hypotheses; (5) methods: participants, procedure and data analysis; (6) a time schedule; (7) expected results, with alternative outcomes; (8) references; (9) an appendix of instruments and instructions. Assumptions are statements the researcher believes but cannot prove. Limitations are conditions beyond the researcher's control that may weaken the conclusions, such as a low response rate. Delimitations are boundaries the researcher deliberately sets, such as studying only first-year students in Mysuru colleges, and they decide to whom the findings apply. Before any hypothesis can be tested (Sections 9.9 to 9.11), you must decide what kind of numbers you have, put them in order and describe them. This section does those jobs, ending with the normal curve and the z-score. Levels of measurement Measurement is the assignment of numbers to objects or events according to rules. But numbers mean different things: the 2 on a cricketer's shirt, 2nd rank in class, 2°C and 2 kg are all "2", yet only the last can be doubled meaningfully. In 1946 the Harvard psychophysicist Stanley Smith Stevens (1906 to 1973) sorted these meanings into four levels of measurement ("On the theory of scales of measurement", Science ). Each level adds one property: identity (a number names a category), magnitude (order), equal intervals (a unit means the same amount anywhere on the scale) and an absolute zero (zero means none of the attribute). A nominal scale has identity only: labels name unordered categories such as marital status, eye or car colour and gender, and coding "married" as 2 does not make it more than "single" at 1. An ordinal scale adds magnitude: cases are ranked, but the distances between ranks are unknown. Class ranks, socioeconomic status categories and any task in which respondents place items along a continuum by preference or degree of agreement give ordinal data. A single Likert item (strongly disagree 1 to strongly agree 5) is strictly ordinal, though a total over many items is conventionally treated as interval. An interval scale adds equal intervals (20°C to 30°C is the same rise as 30°C to 40°C), but its zero is arbitrary , a reference point rather than the absence of the quantity: 0°C is just the freezing point of water. Differences are meaningful, ratios are not; 40°C is not twice as hot as 20°C. Celsius temperature, calendar years and most test scores, IQ included, are treated as interval. A ratio scale adds a true zero: height, weight, reaction time and the number of books a person owns (zero books is no books, and 6 is twice 3). The level decides which statistics are permissible (Table 9.23), and each level keeps every statistic of the levels below it (memory hook: NOIR). The key is wrong: an arbitrary zero defines the interval scale, and the ratio scale has a true zero. Some Indian texts cite "Stevens (1951)", his handbook chapter; the scales date from 1946. Key study: Stevens and the scales of measurement (1946) Can sensations be measured at all? A committee of the British Association for the Advancement of Science had debated it for years without agreeing, its physicists doubting it (final report, 1940). Stevens replied by defining measurement broadly, as assigning numbers by rule, and by classing scales according to the transformations that leave their information intact: any one-to-one relabelling (nominal), any order-preserving change (ordinal), a linear change, aX + b (interval), and multiplication by a constant (ratio). The result was the four levels and their permissible statistics. Critics such as Frederic Lord (1953, "On the statistical treatment of football numbers") replied that the numbers do not remember where they came from, so scale type should not ban a statistic outright; the debate continues. Two further classifications cut across the levels. A categorical variable (qualitative) sorts cases into classes; a quantitative one records an amount. A discrete variable takes separate values, usually counts (books owned, so a count can be discrete yet ratio); a continuous variable can take any value in a range (height, reaction time). Nominal variables are always categorical. Ordinal variables are strictly ordered categories, but because ranks are taken to lie on an underlying continuum (anxiety, agreement) they are usually analysed as continuous. Exam trap "Ordered variables are considered ____, nominal variables ____" is keyed continuous, categorical . Take the key, knowing that some books call nominal and ordinal variables alike qualitative. "Discontinuous" simply means discrete. A good measure is reliable , that is, consistent (it gives the same result when the same thing is measured again), valid (it measures what it claims to), practical (cheap, quick, easy to interpret) and sensitive to small differences. Objectivity belongs here too; high cost, low reliability and subjectivity mark a poor measure. Test reliability and validity are treated in Chapter 2. Processing data and statistical software Filled-in questionnaires become analysable data through four processing operations, in this order, as set out in C. R. Kothari 's Research Methodology . Editing examines raw data to detect and correct errors, omissions and inconsistencies (an age of 210, a blank item). Field editing is done by the investigator soon after the interview; central editing is done at the office, by one editor or team, once all forms are in. Coding assigns numerals or other symbols to answers so that responses fall into a limited number of exhaustive, mutually exclusive categories (male 1, female 2); the key to the codes is the codebook. Classification arranges the data into groups or classes sharing a characteristic, by attribute (urban or rural) or by class interval (ages 20 to 29). Tabulation arranges the classified data in rows and columns: a simple (one-way) table shows one characteristic, a complex table two or more. Graphs, charts and diagrams present the same data visually instead. On computer, data entry is followed by data cleaning: hunting for out-of-range values (7 on a 1-to-5 scale), duplicates and missing-value codes. Exam trap Coding assigns symbols (the "assigning numerical values" option); classification groups data into classes. One real paper keys "organising data into categories or groups" for both: it is exact for classification and the nearest option for coding. Editing corrects errors; tabulation uses rows and columns. IBM SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences), first released in 1968 and owned by IBM since 2009, is psychology's standard package; its primary purpose is data analysis, from descriptive statistics to factor analysis. R, SAS, Stata and the free JASP are alternatives. Microsoft Excel is a spreadsheet for data entry, tabulation, charts and calculation: =AVERAGE(A1:A10) gives the mean; SUM, MAX, MIN, MEDIAN and MODE do what they say; STDEV gives the sample SD, CORREL Pearson's r and COUNT the number of numeric cells. Word (report writing), Photoshop (photo editing), Illustrator (drawing) and InDesign (page layout) are not analysis tools. Frequency distributions and graphs A list of raw scores, the scores as first recorded, says little. A frequency distribution shows how many cases (f) obtained each score (ungrouped) or fell in each class interval (grouped), the intervals being of equal width, usually 10 to 20 of them. An interval's apparent limits (25 to 29) are those written down; its exact limits (24.5 to 29.5) extend half a unit beyond, because a score of 29.4 is recorded as 29. The midpoint (27) stands for every score in it. Cumulative frequency (cf) is the running total up to an interval's top, and percentages restate f and cf out of 100 (Table 9.24). A line graph shows change over time; a scatter plot shows the relationship and spread of two continuous variables (Section 9.11). Measures of central tendency A measure of central tendency is one score that represents the whole distribution. The arithmetic mean (M = ΣX / N) is the balance point: deviations from it sum to zero, the sum of squared deviations about it is a minimum (least squares), and adding a constant to every score adds it to the mean, while multiplying every score by a constant multiplies the mean by it. Using every score makes it the most stable average across samples, but also lets one extreme score pull it: 4, 7, 7, 9 and 13 have a mean of 8, and adding a 40 lifts it to 13.3. It cannot be computed for an open-ended top class. A combined mean weights each group by its size: 30 boys averaging 60 and 20 girls averaging 70 give (1800 + 1400) / 50 = 64. The median is the middle score of the ordered set, the 50th percentile (for 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, 40 it is 8). Depending only on position, it resists extreme scores, so it is the average for skewed data: community income, where a few rich households inflate the mean, and anxiety or symptom scores, where most people score low and a few very high. It also suits ordinal data. The mode is the most frequent score and the only average for nominal data. One peak makes a distribution unimodal and two bimodal; when two or more scores share the highest frequency it is multimodal. The geometric mean (the Nth root of the product of N scores) suits growth rates; the harmonic mean (N divided by the sum of the reciprocals) suits rates such as speeds. Remember Symmetrical interval or ratio data: mean . Skewed data, outliers or ordinal data: median . Nominal data: mode . Exam trap Range, standard deviation, variance and mean deviation measure variability, not central tendency. Mean deviation is the favourite decoy because it contains the word "mean". Measures of variability Two classes may share a mean of 50 while one spans 45 to 55 and the other 10 to 90; variability (dispersion) describes this spread. The range (highest minus lowest score) rests on the two most extreme scores. The interquartile range (IQR = Q 3 − Q 1 ) covers the middle 50 per cent; half of it is the quartile deviation or semi-interquartile range, Q = (Q 3 − Q 1 ) / 2, the partner of the median. The mean deviation is the average absolute deviation from the mean, Σ|X − M| / N. The variance squares the deviations instead: for a population σ² = Σ(X − μ)² / N, and the standard deviation (SD, σ) is its square root, back in the original units: the typical distance of a score from the mean. For 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5; the deviations −3, −1, −1, −1, 0, 0, 2, 4 square to 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, a sum of squares (SS) of 32. So σ² = 32 / 8 = 4 and σ = 2 (32 is the SS, 2 the SD, 5 the mean). To estimate a population's variance from a sample, divide SS by N − 1: s² = Σ(X − M)² / (N − 1). Deviations from a sample's own mean run slightly small, so dividing by N underestimates. The fix is Bessel's correction, after the astronomer Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel (1784 to 1846), and N − 1 is the degrees of freedom : once the mean is fixed, only N − 1 deviations can vary freely. For the sample 3, 5, 7: SS = 8 and s² = 8 / 2 = 4 , so s = 2 (dividing by N gives 2.67). The coefficient of variation , CV = (SD / M) × 100, compares spread across different units but needs a ratio scale. Adding a constant to every score shifts the mean but leaves the SD and variance unchanged; multiplying by c multiplies the SD by c and the variance by c². With variance 4 and scores multiplied by 3 and then increased by 10, the new SD is 6 and the new variance 4 × 9 = 36 (not 12, which multiplies the variance by 3 only, nor 46, which also adds the 10). Remember Affected by extreme scores: range, mean deviation, variance, SD and the mean. Resistant: IQR, quartile deviation and the median. Skewness and kurtosis Skewness is asymmetry, and it is named after the long tail. In positive (right) skew most scores are low and a few high ones trail right (income, a very hard test); in negative (left) skew most are high and a few low ones trail left (a very easy test). The mean, which uses every score's value, is dragged furthest into the tail, the mode stays at the hump and the median lies between. So positive skew gives mode < median < mean and negative skew mean < median < mode , the mean lying left of the median (Figure 9.14). Karl Pearson (1857 to 1936) measured it as Sk = 3(Mean − Median) / SD, zero for a symmetrical curve.
