The mean is pulled furthest into the tail, the mode stays at the peak and the median lies between them. Kurtosis is peakedness relative to the normal curve: leptokurtic (more peaked), mesokurtic (normal) or platykurtic (flatter). The percentile coefficient Ku = Q / (P 90 − P 10 ) is 0.263 for the normal curve; above it is platykurtic, below it leptokurtic. On the moment measure the normal curve scores 3, and SPSS prints excess kurtosis (minus 3), so 0 means mesokurtic. The normal probability curve The normal probability curve was derived by Abraham de Moivre (1667 to 1754) in 1733 as the limit of the binomial distribution. Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749 to 1827) developed it, and Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777 to 1855) used it in 1809 for errors in astronomical measurement, hence the Gaussian curve. Adolphe Quetelet (1796 to 1874) applied it to human characteristics, and Francis Galton (1822 to 1911) to human ability. Exam trap "Who propounded the normal curve?" is keyed Carl Gauss , after whom it is named; mark Gauss, but know that de Moivre came first (1733). Siméon Denis Poisson (1781 to 1840) gave the distribution of rare events, Jacob (James) Bernoulli the law of large numbers (1713), and Wilhelm Reich (1897 to 1957) was a psychoanalyst. The curve is bell-shaped, symmetrical and unimodal, with mean, median and mode coinciding at the centre; a two-peaked curve cannot be normal. Its tails are asymptotic, nearing the baseline without touching it. The total area under it is 1 (100 per cent), so areas read as probabilities. Its points of inflection lie at ±1 SD, and it is defined by its mean and SD alone. The areas are therefore fixed (Figure 9.15). On each side, 34.13 per cent of cases lie between the mean and 1 SD, 13.59 per cent between 1 and 2 SD and 2.14 per cent between 2 and 3 SD. About 68 per cent fall within ±1 SD, 95 per cent within ±2 SD (exactly 95 within ±1.96) and 99.7 per cent within ±3 SD. Which is better? A z-score states how many SDs a score lies from its mean: z = (X − M) / SD. Statistics gives z = +1.5 and English z = +0.5, so the lower raw score is the better performance. That is the purpose of z-scores: they let you compare results from different distributions. A z of +1 lies one SD above the mean, −1 one SD below, and 0 at the mean itself. A set of z-scores has mean 0 and SD 1, and because the conversion is linear, a skewed set stays skewed. A z-score shows relative position. It is not a measure of variability (the SD, variance or quartile deviation) or of central tendency, nor the coefficient of variation, nor the standard error (the SD of a sampling distribution, Section 9.9). The z table, derived from the normal distribution, converts z into percentiles. A percentile rank is the percentage of cases below a score. Quartiles split the distribution into four (Q 1 = P 25 , Q 2 = the median, Q 3 = P 75 ), deciles into ten. On the normal curve z = 0 is the 50th percentile, +0.5 about the 69th, +1 the 84th, +1.28 the 90th, +1.5 the 93rd, +1.96 the 97.5th, +2 about the 98th and +3 the 99.9th; z = −1 is the 16th and −2 the 2nd. Percentile units are unequal (crowded in the middle), so they are never averaged. Clinical link An IQ of 70 lies two SD below the mean, near the 2nd percentile. DSM-5 places the intellectual deficits of intellectual disability at about this point, roughly 65 to 75 once measurement error is allowed for (Chapter 8). Ronald Aylmer Fisher (1890 to 1962) turned the claim into the opening example of The Design of Experiments (1935): eight cups, four made each way, in random order. A pure guesser would sort all eight correctly only 1 time in 70 (p = .014). That is the whole logic of this section: assume nothing is going on, work out how probable the result would be by chance, and reject chance when the result would be rare. From describing to inferring Descriptive statistics summarise the scores you have (section 9.8). Inferential statistics reason from a sample to the population it came from, drawing on two things: the sample data, and knowledge of how random processes behave. Their question is how plausible it is that a random process alone, drawing samples from a population in which nothing is going on, could produce results as extreme as those obtained. Inference always runs from the observed sample to the unobserved population, never the reverse. If a therapy group improves by 6 points and a control group by 4, part of the gap is chance, because two random samples almost never have identical means. What statistics (applied to health data, biostatistics ) tells the psychologist is whether an observed difference is larger than chance would usually produce. Only a statistical test can show a reliable difference between groups; norms (a reference group's typical scores), reliability (consistency) and validity (measuring what is claimed) are properties of tests (Chapter 2). Exam trap "Inferential statistics make statements about samples based on observing populations" is the FALSE option: it reverses the logic. Statistics does not choose patients for therapy, design interviews or plan therapeutic exercises; it judges whether differences are due to chance. Probability: the language of chance A probability runs from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Classical probability is worked out in advance from equally likely outcomes, favourable outcomes divided by all outcomes: a die shows a six with probability 1/6. Empirical probability is the observed relative frequency over many trials: if 30 of 200 discharged patients relapse, p(relapse) is about .15. The addition rule handles "or": for mutually exclusive events p(A or B) = p(A) + p(B), so a one or a two on a die is 2/6. The multiplication rule handles "and": for independent events p(A and B) = p(A) × p(B), so ten heads in a row has probability 1/1024. For dependent events you multiply by a conditional probability , p(B given A); remember it when you meet the p-value. The binomial distribution gives the probability of each number of successes in N independent two-outcome trials with fixed probability p (mean Np, SD √Npq): ten coin tosses average 5 heads, yet exactly 5 occurs only about one time in four. As N grows the binomial becomes bell-shaped, as Abraham de Moivre (1667 to 1754) showed in 1733. The normal distribution is therefore the probability model of inference: area under it is probability, and since 95 percent lies within ±1.96 SD (section 9.8), a chance value beyond those points has probability .05. The sampling distribution and the standard error Draw a random sample of 36 students, compute their mean, replace them, and repeat thousands of times. The means vary, and the theoretical distribution they form is the sampling distribution of the mean . You never build it, but three facts about it let you judge your one real sample. Its mean equals the population mean, μ. Its standard deviation is the standard error of the mean , SE = σ/√N (estimated as s/√N): for IQ (σ = 15), samples of 25 give SE = 3 and samples of 100 give 1.5, so halving the SE takes four times the sample. And its shape is normal once N is large. That last fact is the central limit theorem : with a sufficiently large sample, conventionally 30 or more (A.K. Singh says above 50), the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal whatever the shape of the population, centred on μ, with a spread that shrinks as N grows (Figure 9.16). De Moivre's coin result was its first case and Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749 to 1827) generalised it. It is why tests on means can use the normal curve even though psychological scores are often skewed. Population: skewed Sampling distributions of the mean mean 10 0 10 20 30 40 0 5 10 15 20 25 mean 10 N = 30 SE = 1.8 N = 4 SE = 5 Individual scores (SD = 10) Sample means Figure 9.16 The central limit theorem. Means of samples from a skewed population cluster around its mean; with N = 30 they are nearly normal and far narrower (SE about 1.8) than with N = 4. Sampling error is the gap between one sample's statistic and the parameter (M − μ); it is a random error, unsystematic and averaging to zero. The standard error is the typical size of that gap across all samples. The law of large numbers ( Jacob Bernoulli , 1655 to 1705, published 1713) says only that a sample mean gets closer to the population mean as N grows; it says nothing about the shape of the sampling distribution. Exam trap The standard error is the SD of the sampling distribution of the mean : not the SD of the sample (which does not shrink with N) and not M − μ (sampling error). As N rises the sampling distribution approaches normal; it does not grow skewed, does not become identical to the population distribution, and its SE gets smaller. "Normal distribution theorem" and "sampling distribution theorem" are invented names. Estimation and confidence intervals A point estimate is a single value, such as a sample mean of 52 for μ. An interval estimate, the confidence interval (CI), adds a margin: M ± 1.96 SE for 95 percent and M ± 2.58 SE for 99 percent. With M = 52, SD = 12 and N = 36, SE = 2, so the 95 percent CI runs from 48.08 to 55.92 and the 99 percent CI, wider, from 46.84 to 57.16. Higher confidence, a larger SD and a smaller N all widen the interval. The population mean is fixed, so the confidence belongs to the procedure: if the sampling were repeated many times, 95 percent of the intervals so built would contain the true mean. If a 95 percent CI for a difference includes zero, the difference is not significant at α = .05 (two-sided): a mean difference of 0.4 with a CI of −0.1 to 0.9 is non-significant. That is not proof of no effect, since the interval also allows 0.9; a wide CI signals an imprecise estimate. For ratios the null value is 1 (section 9.5). Exam trap A 95 percent CI is NOT "a 95 percent probability that μ lies in this interval", NOT "95 percent of individual scores fall in it" and NOT "a 95 percent chance of significance". A CI crossing zero means non-significant, not a difference of exactly zero. The logic and steps of a significance test A significance test assumes the null hypothesis (H 0 : no difference or effect), asks how probable the data would be if H 0 were true, and rejects H 0 in favour of the alternative hypothesis (H 1 ) if they would be rare (wording hypotheses: section 9.1). The steps: State H 0 and H 1 ; choose a one-tailed or two-tailed test. Set the significance level (α), usually .05 or .01, before seeing data. Compute the test statistic (z, t, F, chi-square): the observed effect over its standard error. Compare it with the critical value bounding the critical region, or compare p with α. Reject H 0 or fail to reject (retain) it; report the effect size and CI. A stress scale has a population mean of 50 and SD of 12; after a mindfulness course 36 students average 55. Then z = (55 − 50)/(12/√36) = 2.5: beyond 1.96, so significant at .05 two-tailed (p about .012), but short of 2.58, so not at .01. Table 9.26 gives the cut-offs. They explain the rough rule that a score is significant when it lies more than two standard deviations from the mean : about 95 percent of a normal distribution lies within two SDs, so a value beyond is in the outer 5 percent, while values within one SD, or between one and two, are ordinary chance results. Table 9.26 Critical values of z. α Two-tailed One-tailed Matching CI .05 ±1.96 1.645 95 percent .01 ±2.58 2.33 99 percent A two-tailed test (non-directional H 1 ) splits α between the tails, .025 each. A one-tailed test (directional H 1 ) puts all of α in one tail, so z = 1.80 is significant one-tailed but not two-tailed. It is more powerful in the predicted direction, blind in the other, and legitimate only if the direction was fixed in advance. Tests other than z also need degrees of freedom (df), the number of values free to vary once a constraint is fixed: five scores with a set mean of 10 leave four free, df = N − 1 = 4. Critical values of t, F and chi-square depend on df (section 9.10). The p-value and what it is not The p-value is the probability of obtaining the observed result, or one more extreme, if H 0 is true: the probability, revealed by a statistical test, that a random process (random samples of a given size from a given population) could produce that outcome. If p ≤ α, reject H 0 : with α = .05, p = .03 is statistically significant and H 0 is rejected. Because p assumes H 0 and asks about the data, it is not the probability that H 0 (or H 1 ) is true, which would need Bayes' theorem. Nor is it the effect size (a huge sample makes a trivial effect give tiny p), the probability of replication, or power. It is continuous: p = .049 and p = .051 are essentially the same evidence, because .05 is a convention, not a natural boundary. Two distractors share a letter: the q-value , the false-discovery-rate analogue of p used when thousands of tests are run (brain imaging, genetics), and Tukey's studentised range q (section 9.10). Exam trap The key is always "the probability of the data (or more extreme) if H 0 is true "; the favourite wrong option reverses it, "the probability that H 0 is true". Nor is p the magnitude of a correlation or the sample size, and p = .001 does not mean a large, clinically important or certain-to-replicate effect. Type I and Type II errors A decision from a sample can go wrong in two ways (Table 9.27). A Type I error (alpha error) is rejecting a true null hypothesis: a false positive. Its probability is α, so the significance level is the probability of a Type I error, in analysis of variance as in every test; it does not certify that F is correct, and the Type II risk is β, not α. A Type II error (beta error) is retaining, or loosely "accepting", a false null hypothesis: a false negative, a real effect missed. Its probability, β, is not chosen; it follows from N, the true effect, α and variability. Table 9.27 The four outcomes of a significance test. The procedure fuses two rival traditions. Fisher ( Statistical Methods for Research Workers , 1925) treated p as graded evidence against a single null hypothesis and offered .05 as a convenient cut-off. Jerzy Neyman (1894 to 1981) and Egon Pearson (1895 to 1980), in papers of 1928 and 1933, recast testing as a decision between H 0 and H 1 with fixed error rates, giving us Type I and II errors and power. Exam trap Swapped wordings ("accepting a false null" offered as Type I) are the commonest wrong options. Type III error is informal: the right answer to the wrong question, or rejecting H 0 but in the wrong direction; "Type IV" is rarer still. Low power, sample size (too small, too large or "large sample bias"), a wide CI, a misused one-tailed test, sampling error, standard error and confounding (section 9.2) are not definitions of these errors, though several change their risk. Statistical power Power (1 − β) is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis, of finding an effect that is really there; the convention is at least 0.80. Power rises with a larger true effect, a larger N (it shrinks the SE, pulling the curves of Figure 9.17 apart), a larger, less strict α (at the price of more Type I errors), lower variability (homogeneous samples, standard procedures, repeated measures, reliable measures) and a correctly predicted one-tailed test. It falls when N shrinks, α becomes stricter or variability grows. Power analysis , done before a study, fixes α, the desired power and the smallest effect worth detecting, and solves for N. Jacob Cohen (1923 to 1998) made it routine in Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd edition, 1988): detecting a medium effect (d = 0.5) with an independent-samples t-test at α = .05, two-tailed, and power .80 needs about 64 people per group. Effect size and practical significance Significance says an effect is probably not zero; effect size says how big it is, independent of N. Cohen's d is the standardised difference between two means, (M 1 − M 2 )/pooled SD, with benchmarks 0.2 small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. The mindfulness example gives d = 5/12 = 0.42, between small and medium, despite p = .012. The correlation r is also an effect size (.10, .30, .50); its sign gives only direction, so r = −.30 is a medium negative relationship, not "none", not perfect (−1.00) and not causal (section 9.11). A month later the groups' recall scores differ a little. Is the difference real, or the wobble any three groups would show by chance? Section 9.9 gave the logic of significance testing; here are the tools. Choosing one always comes down to three questions: what kind of data, how many groups, and are the groups independent or made of the same (or matched) people? Parametric or non-parametric? A parametric test estimates population parameters (means and variances) and rests on four assumptions: the scores come from a normally distributed population; the groups have roughly equal variances ( homogeneity of variance ); observations are independent of one another; and the dependent variable (DV) is measured on an interval or ratio scale, so that means make sense. The z-test, t-tests, ANOVA's F-test and Pearson's r are parametric. When data are normal with equal variances, a parametric test is the right choice, because it uses the actual distances between scores and so has the most power. A non-parametric test , also called a distribution-free test , makes few assumptions about the population's shape and works on ranks, signs or frequency counts. Sidney Siegel (1916 to 1961) brought these tests into psychology with Nonparametric Statistics for the Behavioral Sciences (1956). They suit ordinal data (ranks), nominal data (counted categories), very small samples and clearly violated assumptions (heavy skew, outliers, very unequal variances). Rank order is thus the classic non-parametric data, whereas height, weight and Celsius temperature are interval or ratio measures (9.8). Chi-square is not a third family: it is the non-parametric test for nominal frequencies. The price is power, because ranking discards the distances between scores. Siegel measured the cost as power-efficiency : the sample a parametric test needs, as a percentage of the sample a non-parametric test needs for equal power. If a t-test needs 95 cases to match what the Mann-Whitney test does with 100, Mann-Whitney is 95 percent power-efficient. Under normality the Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests reach about 95 percent; the sign test only about 63 percent in large samples. Exam trap "Which is non-parametric data?" Rank order, not height, weight or Celsius temperature (Celsius has an arbitrary zero but equal intervals: interval data). "Distribution-free" is just another name for non-parametric. For normal data with equal variances the answer is parametric tests, never "chi-square tests" or "distribution-free tests". Checking the assumptions Normality is tested with the Shapiro-Wilk test (the usual choice) or the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test , which compares the sample's cumulative distribution with a normal one; it is inspected with a Q-Q plot (quantile-quantile plot), where normal data hug a straight diagonal, and with skew and kurtosis values near zero (9.8). Homogeneity of variance , or homoscedasticity , is tested with Levene's test ( Howard Levene , 1960), which stays accurate when data are not normal; Bartlett's test , more powerful but upset by non-normality; or Hartley's F-max , the largest group variance divided by the smallest (near 1 is fine). These checks precede a t-test, an ANOVA or a regression. Independence has no test: it is secured by random sampling and assignment, and its violation is the most damaging. Repeated-measures ANOVA adds sphericity : equal variances of the difference scores between every pair of conditions. It matters only with three or more conditions, is tested by Mauchly's test , and when violated the df are reduced by the Greenhouse-Geisser correction (more conservative) or the Huynh-Feldt correction (less so). ANCOVA adds homogeneity of regression slopes ( 9.10.6 ). Read these tests backwards: their null hypothesis is that the assumption holds, so a non-significant result (p > .05) is good news. Exam trap Shapiro-Wilk tests normality, NOT homogeneity of variance, so it is the odd one out beside Levene's and Bartlett's tests. Levene's test checks equal variances, not normality, independence or equal group sizes. Equal group sizes are not an assumption, though they make ANOVA more forgiving of unequal variances. The t-tests A z-test compares means using the population standard deviation, which you almost never know (older texts allow it above about 30 cases). Estimating the standard deviation from the sample adds a second source of error, and the statistic then follows the t distribution. Key study: "Student" at the Guinness brewery (1908) William Sealy Gosset (1876 to 1937), a chemist at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, had to judge barley and stout from tiny samples. He worked out the exact distribution of a mean divided by its estimated standard error. Guinness barred staff from publishing under their own names, so his 1908 Biometrika paper appeared as "Student", hence Student's t. (Some Indian texts print 1915; the paper is from 1908.) The t distribution is a family of curves, one for each number of degrees of freedom (df). Like the normal curve it is symmetrical and bell-shaped around zero; unlike it, it has heavier tails and a lower peak, so its variability and kurtosis are greater. As df rise it closes in on the normal curve (Figure 9.18), which is why critical t values shrink towards 1.96 in large samples. -3 -2 -1 0 1 2 3 distance from the mean in standard units normal curve (z) t with df = 10 t with df = 2 heavier tails in t Figure 9.18 The t distribution against the normal curve. All are symmetrical, but with few df t has a lower peak and heavier tails, so a larger t is needed for significance; by df = 10 it is already close to normal. There are three t-tests, each with its own df. The one-sample t-test compares one sample mean with a known population value; df = N - 1, since once the mean is fixed the last score cannot vary. N = 20 gives 19; N = 30 gives 29. The independent-samples t-test (unpaired t) compares the means of two separate groups, using their pooled variance. Its df = N1 + N2 - 2: 25 per group gives 48. If Levene's test shows unequal variances, Welch's t-test is used; it does not pool the variances and lowers the df. The paired-samples t-test (dependent or matched-pairs t) is for the same people measured twice, pre and post, or for matched pairs. It tests whether the mean difference score is zero; df = pairs - 1. Each person acts as their own control, so individual differences leave the error term and power rises. Why not run three t-tests on three groups? Each carries a 5 percent Type I risk (9.9), and the risks accumulate. With c tests the chance of at least one false positive, the family-wise error rate , is 1 - (1 - .05) c : about .14 for three tests and .26 for the six that four groups need. ANOVA tests all the means at once at one alpha. Exam trap One-sample df: N - 1. Independent: N1 + N2 - 2 (25 per group gives 48, not 24, 49 or 50). Paired: pairs - 1. The t curve shares only its symmetry with the normal curve; its kurtosis and variability are larger. One-way ANOVA: partitioning variance Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was developed by Ronald Aylmer Fisher (1890 to 1962) for agricultural trials at Rothamsted Experimental Station and published in Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925); George Waddel Snedecor (1881 to 1974) named its statistic F in Fisher's honour. A one-way ANOVA compares the means of independent groups formed by one independent variable (IV, or factor) on one continuous DV. It is used when more than two means are compared, though it works for two as well, where F = t 2 . ANOVA compares means by analysing variances. The deviations of all scores from the grand mean sum to zero, so they are squared and added to give the total sum of squares . Fisher split it into exactly two parts. The between-groups sum of squares reflects how far each group mean lies from the grand mean: treatment effect plus chance. The within-groups sum of squares reflects how far each person lies from their own group mean: since a group was treated alike, this is pure chance or error. SS total = SS between + SS within, and each part has its own df: between = k - 1 (k groups), within = N - k, total = N - 1. Three groups of 10 give 2, 27 and 29. Each SS divided by its df is a mean square (MS), a variance. MS within is the pooled error variance , and it is the denominator of the F ratio : F = MS between / MS within. If the null hypothesis is true, both estimate the same chance variance and F is about 1; a real effect swells only the numerator. So an F below 1, such as 0.99, can never be significant whatever the df, and as variability due to chance falls, F rises. Figure 9.19 and Table 9.29 work through the revision study. But F is an omnibus test : it says at least one mean differs, not which. Being a ratio of two variances, the F distribution is never negative and is positively skewed, its shape set by two df (numerator and denominator); the test is one-tailed, because only a large F counts against the null. Exam trap F's denominator is MS within (the pooled error variance), not MS between. One-way ANOVA has two sources of variance, each with its own df; "error variance" is the within-groups part, not a third source, and "information variance" does not exist. F = 0.99 is never significant; F is never negative. ANOVA tests means, not "variance only", and unequal variances violate its assumption. After a significant F: post hoc tests Post hoc tests (a posteriori or multiple comparison tests) compare groups pair by pair while holding the family-wise error rate down. They are used only after a significant F; after a non-significant F you stop. With k groups there are k(k - 1)/2 pairs: 3 for three groups, 6 for four, 10 for five. The tests differ in how conservative they are, that is, how hard they make it to call a difference significant (Table 9.30). Table 9.30 Common post hoc tests. The simplest guard for any set of comparisons is the Bonferroni correction , after Carlo Emilio Bonferroni (1892 to 1960): divide alpha by the number of comparisons. Six comparisons are each tested at .05/6 = .0083, keeping the family-wise Type I error rate at .05 or below. The cost is power: Bonferroni is conservative, raising Type II risk as comparisons multiply. A single planned comparison needs no correction. Exam trap Duncan, Newman-Keuls, Tukey and Scheffé are used only when F is significant. Bonferroni divides alpha, never multiplies it (software may multiply each p-value by the number of tests, the same rule). It controls family-wise Type I error; it does not raise power, fix unequal sample sizes or transform skewed data (skew calls for a log or square-root transformation, or a rank test). Factorial, repeated-measures and covariance designs A factorial ANOVA (two-way or higher) crosses two or more IVs so that every level of one meets every level of the other; a 2 × 3 design has two factors and six cells. It tests a main effect of each IV (averaged over the other) and an interaction effect , present when the effect of one IV depends on the level of another: plotted, the lines are not parallel. Of the familiar techniques only factorial ANOVA detects interactions; a t-test has one two-level IV, chi-square tests association between two categorical variables, and correlation measures how two variables move together. A significant interaction is interpreted before the main effects. Repeated-measures ANOVA tests the same people under three or more conditions, extending the paired t-test. It accounts for the correlation among each person's scores by removing individual differences from the error term, so it needs fewer people; but it is still parametric, assuming normality, plus sphericity. A randomised block design uses different people grouped into homogeneous blocks (by pre-test, age or IQ) and randomly assigned to treatments within each block, so block differences leave the error term. With one person per treatment per block, error df = (treatments - 1)(blocks - 1): 4 treatments and 5 blocks give 3 × 4 = 12. A mixed (split-plot) ANOVA combines a between-subjects and a within-subjects factor. Clinical link Most therapy trials are mixed designs: group (therapy or waitlist) by time (pre, post, follow-up). Evidence that therapy worked is the group × time interaction, not either main effect. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), also Fisher's, builds a regression into ANOVA. A covariate (a continuous variable such as pre-test score or IQ) predicts the DV, its effect is removed, and groups are compared on adjusted means. This raises power and statistically equates groups that started unequal, though it cannot replace random assignment. ANCOVA keeps ANOVA's assumptions and adds a linear covariate-DV relation, a covariate measured reliably before treatment, and above all homogeneity of regression slopes : the covariate must predict the DV equally in every group, so the regression lines are parallel. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) tests groups on two or more DVs at once, avoiding the Type I error of many separate ANOVAs; its statistics are Wilks' lambda (most reported; smaller means a bigger effect), Pillai's trace (most robust), Hotelling's trace and Roy's largest root. MANCOVA adds covariates. In all these names, M means more than one DV and C means a covariate. Exam trap The assumption ANCOVA adds to ANOVA is homogeneity of regression slopes. Homogeneity of variance and homoscedasticity (one idea, two names) belong to both; equal sample sizes to neither. Repeated-measures ANOVA is not non-parametric, still assumes normality and is not limited to two conditions. Chi-square: comparing frequencies Nominal data offer no means, only counts of people in categories. For these, Karl Pearson (1857 to 1936) introduced the chi-square test (χ²) in 1900. It compares the observed frequency (O) in each category with the frequency expected (E) under the null hypothesis: χ² = Σ (O - E)²/E. Being squared, it is never negative and its distribution is positively skewed. It is a non-parametric test for categorical frequencies, not for interval, ratio or parametric data. The goodness-of-fit test asks whether one variable's frequencies match a hypothesised pattern (do students prefer four brands of chai equally?); df = k - 1 for k categories. The test of independence asks whether two categorical variables in a contingency table are associated (is gender related to treatment preference?). Each expected frequency is row total × column total / N, and df = (rows - 1)(columns - 1), because once the margins are fixed only that many cells can vary: 2 × 2 gives 1, 3 × 4 gives 6, 4 × 5 gives 12. Chi-square needs raw counts (not percentages), each person in one cell only, and an expected frequency of at least 5 per cell. For 2 × 2 tables with small expected values, Frank Yates (1902 to 1994) proposed the Yates' correction for continuity in 1934, subtracting 0.5 from each |O - E| before squaring, while Fisher's exact test computes the exact probability of a small table. Paired yes-or-no data (the same people before and after) need the McNemar test ( Quinn McNemar , 1947), which counts only those who changed. Chi-square shows whether an association exists, not its strength; for that report phi (2 × 2), the contingency coefficient or Cramér's V (9.11). Exam trap Contingency df is a product, (rows - 1)(columns - 1): 3 × 4 gives 6, not 12, 7 or 11; 4 × 5 gives 12, not 20 or 9. It is not N - 1 (one-sample t) or N - 2 (independent t), and it subtracts 1, not 2. Rank tests and choosing the right test Each parametric test has a rank-based partner. The Mann-Whitney U test ( Henry Berthold Mann and Donald Ransom Whitney , 1947) pools and ranks the scores of two independent samples and asks whether one group's ranks run higher. It is the non-parametric equivalent of the independent-samples t-test, and identical to the Wilcoxon rank-sum test . For two related samples, the Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test ( Frank Wilcoxon , 1945) ranks the size of each pair's difference and reattaches the signs, using both direction and magnitude; the sign test counts only pluses and minuses (direction) and is weaker. For three or more independent groups, the Kruskal-Wallis H test ( William Kruskal and W. Allen Wallis , 1952) is the one-way ANOVA by ranks, H being read against chi-square with k - 1 df. For three or more related samples or repeated measures, the Friedman test of the economist Milton Friedman (1912 to 2006), devised in 1937, ranks conditions within each person: the two-way ANOVA by ranks. The median test splits independent groups at the combined median and applies chi-square. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sample test compares two samples' whole cumulative distributions, so it also catches differences in shape and spread. The Wald-Wolfowitz runs test counts runs of the same group in the pooled, ordered scores; few runs mean the groups differ. Cochran's Q extends McNemar to three or more related yes-or-no samples. Is a satisfied worker a productive one? Such questions concern quantities that rise and fall together, not the group means of Section 9.10. Correlation measures how strongly two variables go together, regression turns that association into a prediction, and factor analysis asks how many underlying dimensions produced a whole table of correlations. Correlation: direction, strength and form A correlation is an association between two variables measured on the same people. It has a direction , positive when both rise together (study hours and marks) and negative when one rises as the other falls (stress and sleep quality); a strength , how closely the scores keep to the pattern; and a form , straight or curved. Sir Francis Galton (1822 to 1911), studying heredity, described such "co-relations" in 1888, and his protégé Karl Pearson (1857 to 1936) gave them an exact formula in 1896: the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient , r . So r measures association; it is not a mean, a variance or a ratio. Correlational data are graphed as a scatterplot (scatter diagram), with one variable on each axis and each person a single dot (Figure 9.20). A rising cloud is a positive correlation, a falling cloud a negative one, and a shapeless cloud no relationship. The last panel is a warning: a clear inverted U gives r = 0, because r detects only straight-line relations. Do not confuse the scatterplot with the bell curve or a skewed distribution, which describe a single variable (Section 9.8), or with chi-square, which is a test, not a graph (Section 9.10). r = +.90 Strong positive (linear) r = -.85 Strong negative (linear) r = .00 No relationship r = .00 Curvilinear: r misses it Figure 9.20 Four scatterplots; each dot is one person. The curved relation in the last panel is strong, yet r is zero. Reading Pearson's r Pearson's r runs from -1.00 through 0 to +1.00. Its sign gives the direction; its size , ignoring the sign, gives the strength. So r = -0.85 between stress and sleep quality is a strong negative (inverse) relationship, exactly as strong as +0.85: the more stress, the worse the sleep, and the scores keep closely to that pattern. The range of r is never 0 to 1 (that is the range of r 2 and of multiple R ), never -0.04 to +0.04, and never 0 to 100 or -100 to +100. Table 9.32 gives the usual verbal labels; effect-size conventions are in Section 9.9. Table 9.32 Interpreting the size of r (the sign gives only direction). If study hours and marks correlate +0.90, r 2 = 0.81: 81 per cent shared variance, not 90. This is why correlation is related to prediction: the nearer r is to plus or minus 1, the better one variable predicts the other, and at 0 it predicts nothing. Correlation does not, however, imply causation. Y may cause X, or a third variable may drive both (ice-cream sales and drownings both follow summer heat). Only a randomised experiment (Section 9.4) licenses a causal claim, so r = +0.90 shows a strong positive linear association: it neither proves that X causes Y nor shows that they are causally unrelated. Key study: the happy, productive worker (1985, 2001) Managers long assumed that satisfied workers perform better. In 1985 Michelle Iaffaldano and Paul Muchinsky pooled the studies in a meta-analysis (Section 9.5) and found a mean correlation of only about .17. In 2001 Timothy Judge and colleagues, pooling more than 300 samples and correcting for measurement error, put it at about .30. Job satisfaction and performance thus show a weak (modest) positive correlation: not zero, not negative, not strong, and silent on which causes which. Exam trap A minus sign never means weak: -0.85 is strong. And r = +0.90 is neither "90 per cent of the variance" (it is 81 per cent) nor proof that X causes Y. Assumptions, limits and testing r Pearson's r is the technique for two continuous (interval or ratio) variables, such as stress level and sleep duration. Chi-square (association between categories), the t-test, analysis of variance (ANOVA) and the Mann-Whitney U test (differences between groups) answer other questions (Section 9.10). Pearson's r assumes linearity ; homoscedasticity , an equal scatter of Y at every value of X, whose violation, heteroscedasticity , shows as a fan-shaped cloud; bivariate normality , for significance tests; and independence of cases. Observations that depend on earlier ones, such as daily mood ratings, show autocorrelation : a variable correlated with itself over time. Homogeneity of variance is the group version of homoscedasticity, equal variances across groups. r is also distorted by restriction of range (entrance scores predict grades poorly among admitted students alone, whose scores span a narrow band), by outliers, by curvilinear relations and by pooling unlike groups. A sample r is tested with t = r √(N - 2) / √(1 - r 2 ) on N - 2 degrees of freedom: r = .30 fails with 20 people but passes with 100. To compare two correlations, Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher (1890 to 1962) devised Fisher's r-to-z transformation , z' = 0.5 ln[(1 + r )/(1 - r )], which removes the skew in the sampling distribution of r . Fisher's z-test then divides the difference between the two z' values by its standard error, √[1/(N 1 - 3) + 1/(N 2 - 3)]. A t-test compares two means, ANOVA several, and Pearson's r measures a single association; none compares two correlations. Matching the coefficient to the data When the data are ranks or categories, another coefficient is used. The key distinction is between a true dichotomy , two natural categories (alive or dead), and an artificial dichotomy , a continuous variable cut in two (pass or fail from marks). Charles Spearman (1863 to 1945) introduced the rank-difference method in 1904. Spearman's rho , ρ = 1 - 6ΣD 2 / N(N 2 - 1), where D is each person's difference in ranks, correlates ranks; it therefore suits ordinal data and monotonic (steadily rising or falling) but non-linear relations, and it resists outliers. Kendall's tau , from Maurice Kendall (1938), counts agreeing and disagreeing pairs of ranks and suits small samples with many ties. Partial, semi-partial and multiple correlation Ordinary r is a zero-order correlation: nothing is held constant. Marital stress may rise with length of marriage partly because long marriages have more children. The partial correlation , r 12.3 , is the correlation between two variables after a third variable's influence has been removed statistically from both ; partialling out the number of children gives the stress and length relation among couples with equally many children. Holding one variable constant gives a first-order partial, two a second-order partial. A semi-partial correlation (part correlation) removes the third variable from only one of the two, usually the predictor; its square is a predictor's unique contribution in multiple regression, and it is never larger than the partial. The multiple correlation ( R , from 0 to 1) links one variable with the best weighted combination of several others. Linear (ordinary) correlation, biserial correlation and multiple correlation remove nothing. Exam trap "Controlling for", "holding constant" or "subtracting out the influence of" a third variable always means partial correlation. Simple linear regression Regression also began with Galton. In 1886 he found that children of very tall parents were tall, but less extremely so, and called it "regression towards mediocrity". This regression to the mean follows whenever two measures correlate imperfectly: extreme scores on one pair with less extreme scores on the other (a threat to validity, Section 9.2). Simple linear regression predicts a criterion Y from a predictor X with the line Y = a + bX (Figure 9.21). The intercept a is the predicted Y when X is zero; the regression coefficient b is the slope, the change in Y for each one-unit rise in X. b = r (SD Y /SD X ) and a = M Y - bM X , where SD is the standard deviation and M the mean. If hours and marks correlate .60, the SD of marks is 10 and the SD of hours 2, then b = 3 marks per hour; with means of 5 hours and 50 marks, a = 35, so 8 hours predicts 35 + 24 = 59 marks. X (predictor) Y (criterion) 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 a (intercept) 1 b (slope) Y = a + bX residual Figure 9.21 A least-squares regression line. The dashed verticals are the residuals whose squared sum the line minimises. The method of least squares , published by Adrien-Marie Legendre (1752 to 1833) in 1805 and developed by Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777 to 1855), chooses the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals (actual minus predicted Y). Their typical size is the standard error of estimate , SD Y √(1 - r 2 ). Regression assumes linearity, independence of residuals, normality of residuals and equal residual variance (LINE). Correlation is symmetrical and unit-free; regression is directional and gives an equation in real units. A researcher therefore uses regression to predict the value of one variable from another, not to find a mean, count frequencies or estimate sampling error. Exam trap In Y = a + bX the slope is b ; a is the intercept, X the predictor and Y the predicted score. Multiple regression and multicollinearity Multiple regression uses several predictors, Y = a + b 1 X 1 + b 2 X 2 + ..., each b holding the others constant. Standardised beta weights (β) let predictors be compared. R 2 is the variance all predictors explain together, and adjusted R 2 corrects its rise with every added predictor. Entry may be simultaneous (all at once), hierarchical (theory-ordered blocks, testing the change in R 2 ) or stepwise (chosen by the computer, which capitalises on chance). When predictors correlate highly with each other, the result is multicollinearity . Anxiety and neuroticism scores correlating .90 carry the same information, so R 2 stays high but the weights become unstable, their standard errors inflate and signs may flip. A variance inflation factor (VIF) above 10 (above 5 on a stricter rule) or a tolerance (1/VIF) below .10 flags it; the cure is to drop or combine predictors. Exam trap Multicollinearity is correlation among predictors, not between a predictor and the outcome. Heteroscedasticity is unequal residual spread, autocorrelation is residuals correlated over time, homogeneity of variance is equal group variances, a categorical outcome calls for logistic regression, and "assumptions are violated" defines nothing. A dichotomous outcome (relapsed or not) calls for logistic regression , which models the log of the odds, estimates weights by maximum likelihood, expresses each as an odds ratio (above 1 raises the odds, below 1 lowers them) and tests it with the Wald test. Regression, the t-test, ANOVA and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) are all cases of the general linear model: factorial designs are analysed by ANOVA, and ANCOVA blends ANOVA with regression, using the covariate's correlation with the outcome (Section 9.10). Mediation and moderation are tested by regression, following Reuben Baron and David Kenny (1986), with the Sobel test of Michael Sobel (1982) for indirect effects (Section 9.2). Discriminant analysis predicts membership of known groups from continuous variables. Path analysis , devised by Sewall Wright (1889 to 1988) in 1921, chains regressions to test a diagram of directional paths, and structural equation modelling (SEM) adds latent variables, joining a confirmatory factor analysis to a path model. Factor analysis: the dimensions behind correlations Twenty tests yield 190 correlations, and factor analysis asks how few underlying factors could produce them: if verbal tests correlate among themselves and numerical tests among themselves, two factors may explain the whole table. It serves data reduction and construct validation (Chapter 2). Spearman invented it in 1904 to argue for a general factor, g (Chapter 1). Louis Leon Thurstone (1887 to 1955) extended it in the 1930s into multiple factor analysis, with the goal of simple structure : each variable loading highly on one factor and near zero on the others. A factor loading is a variable's correlation with a factor; about .30 to .40 or more counts. A variable's squared loadings summed across factors give its communality (h 2 ), and 1 - h 2 is its uniqueness. A factor's squared loadings summed down the column give its eigenvalue , the variance it explains in units of one variable. Before factoring, the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy should be at least .60 and Bartlett's test of sphericity significant (the correlation matrix is not an identity matrix), with at least 10 cases per variable and ideally 300 or more. Of the extraction methods, principal components analysis ( Harold Hotelling , 1933) analyses total variance for data reduction, whereas principal axis factoring and maximum likelihood analyse only common variance, to model latent factors. Retaining, rotating and confirming factors How many factors? The Kaiser-Guttman rule ( Louis Guttman , 1916 to 1987, and Henry Kaiser ) keeps eigenvalues above 1.0, since a factor below 1 explains less than one variable; it tends to keep too many. The scree test of Raymond Cattell (1905 to 1998), published in 1966, keeps the factors above the elbow of the eigenvalue plot, where the slope flattens into "scree", the rubble below a cliff. John Horn 's parallel analysis (1965), the most accurate, keeps factors whose eigenvalues beat those of random data. Factor rotation turns the factor axes towards simple structure without changing the variance explained. An orthogonal rotation keeps factors uncorrelated: varimax (Kaiser, 1958) simplifies each factor, quartimax each variable, and equimax compromises. An oblique rotation (promax, direct oblimin) lets factors correlate, as psychological constructs usually do. A second-order factor is extracted from the correlations among first-order factors (general ability above verbal, numerical and spatial factors, a hierarchical model), so it needs an oblique rotation such as promax; orthogonal factors leave no correlations to factor. Exam trap Second-order factor analysis needs promax (oblique). Varimax, quartimax and equimax are all orthogonal. All of this is exploratory factor analysis (EFA): data-driven, with no prior model. By contrast, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), developed by Karl Jöreskog in 1969, tests a pre-specified structure, fixing which items load on which factor, and judges fit by the comparative fit index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), about .95 or above, the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), about .06 or below, and the standardised root mean square residual (SRMR), .08 or below, with modification indices suggesting changes. It needs no rotation, takes continuous or categorical items, and is the measurement model of SEM. The Case of Clever Hans, Revisited Pfungst's investigation is a compact course in this chapter. He turned a marvel into a research problem with rival, falsifiable hypotheses and preferred the simplest explanation that fitted, as Lloyd Morgan's canon advises (9.1). He varied one condition at a time while holding the others constant, and exposed the questioner's expectation as a hidden variable that undermined every earlier demonstration (9.2). His study of one horse was a single-case experiment (9.4); he observed systematically (9.6) and honestly reported a result that deflated a celebrity (9.7). His verdict rested on counts of right and wrong answers compared across conditions (9.8 to 9.10). And the blinding of modern clinical trials (9.5), in which those who assess outcomes do not know who was treated, exists so that no one plays von Osten again. Chapter summary 9.1 Science and the Research Process: Problems and Hypotheses. Science differs from tenacity, authority and the a priori method (Peirce, 1877) because it fixes belief by public, repeatable observation. Scientific research is empirical, objective, replicable, parsimonious (Occam's razor, Lloyd Morgan's canon), falsifiable (Popper, 1934) and tentative; Kuhn (1962) described paradigm shifts. Induction builds theory from observations (theory development, qualitative research); deduction tests theory against data; abduction infers the best explanation. Methodology is wider than methods. Research is basic or applied (including Lewin's action research), exploratory, descriptive or explanatory, nomothetic or idiographic (Allport). A clear problem and a literature review (which provides a theoretical framework) yield hypotheses: null or alternative, directional or non-directional, universal or existential. 9.2 Variables, Experimental Control and the Validity of Research. A variable takes two or more values; the independent variable is the presumed cause (manipulated or selected) and the dependent variable the measured outcome. A confound varies with the IV and affects the DV; a moderator changes the strength of an effect and a mediator carries it (Baron and Kenny, 1986). Control follows Kerlinger's MAXMINCON principle (maximise primary, minimise error, control secondary variance), above all through random assignment . Hawthorne, demand (Orne), expectancy and Pygmalion (Rosenthal) and halo (Thorndike) effects distort results; double-blinding controls expectancy on both sides. Studies are judged by statistical conclusion, internal, construct and external validity (Campbell and Stanley, 1963; Cook and Campbell, 1979). 9.3 Sampling: Populations, Probability and Non-Probability Methods. A parameter describes a population and a statistic a sample. Following Blalock (1960), sampling methods are probability, non-probability or mixed. In probability sampling every element has a known, non-zero chance of selection, so sampling error can be calculated and the sample is likely, though not guaranteed, to be representative: simple random, systematic (every kth after a random start), stratified (random sampling within every stratum) and cluster sampling (random choice of whole natural groups, multistage when repeated down levels). In non-probability sampling (convenience, purposive, quota, snowball, saturation, dense) the chance is unknown. Sampling error shrinks as n rises; bias, as in the 1936 Literary Digest poll, does not. 9.4 Research Designs: Experimental, Single-Case and Non-Experimental. Only an experiment , with manipulation, control and random assignment that makes the groups equivalent, licenses cause-and-effect conclusions; Fisher's (1935) principles are replication, randomisation and local control. Campbell and Stanley (1963) classed designs as pre-experimental, true experimental (including Solomon's four-group design, which controls pretest sensitisation) and quasi-experimental (intact groups, no random assignment). Experiments may be between-subjects, within-subjects (order effects controlled by counterbalancing and Latin squares), mixed or crossover; factorial designs reveal interactions. Single-case designs (A-B-A-B, multiple baseline) test a treatment in one person. Correlational, survey (a census is a survey) and ex post facto designs cannot establish cause; longitudinal designs suffer attrition, cross-sectional designs cohort effects. 9.5 Clinical Epidemiology, Randomised Trials and Evidence Synthesis. Epidemiology counts disorder as prevalence (existing cases: point, period, lifetime) or incidence (new cases); prevalence is roughly incidence times duration. Cross-sectional studies give prevalence, case-control studies (best for rare outcomes) give odds ratios, and cohort studies, such as Doll and Hill's prospective British Doctors Study, give relative risk; a ratio of 1 means no association, and NNT = 1/ARR. Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test, but predictive values depend on the base rate (Meehl and Rosen, 1955). Trials rely on randomisation, allocation concealment, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis. Meta-analysis (Glass, 1976) pools many studies; CONSORT reports trials and PRISMA systematic reviews. 9.6 Methods of Data Collection and Qualitative Research. Data are primary or secondary . Observation is participant or non-participant, structured or unstructured, naturalistic or controlled, overt or covert. Interviews run from structured to unstructured, with open-ended questions, probes and Spradley's ethnographic inquiry . A questionnaire is self-answered, a schedule filled in by the enumerator; items must not be double-barrelled , leading or loaded. Berelson's content analysis, Moreno's sociometry and Dilthey's Verstehen follow. Guba and Lincoln's paradigms run from positivism (naive realism) to constructivism (relativism). Qualitative research is naturalistic, inductive and emic; ethnography, grounded theory (open, axial , selective coding) and phenomenology lead its traditions, judged by trustworthiness and strengthened by triangulation . 9.7 Research Ethics and Writing the Research Report. Research ethics grew out of abuse: the Nazi experiments produced the Nuremberg Code (1947), and the Tuskegee study (1932 to 1972) led to the Belmont Report (1979: respect for persons, beneficence, justice). The APA Ethics Code (2002) has five general principles, and in India the ICMR guidelines (2017) require ethics committee approval. Informed consent tells participants enough to decide voluntarily before taking part; debriefing gives full information afterwards (dehoaxing and desensitising). Confidentiality differs from anonymity, deception needs strict justification, and animal research follows the 3Rs . Misconduct means fabrication, falsification and plagiarism; citation is not plagiarism. A research report communicates findings, and its Discussion, not its Results, interprets them. 9.8 Measurement Scales, Organising Data and Descriptive Statistics. S. S. Stevens (1946) gave four levels of measurement: nominal (unordered categories), ordinal (ranks), interval (equal intervals, arbitrary zero, as in Celsius) and ratio (true zero, as in height). Raw data are edited, coded, classified and tabulated, analysed in SPSS or Excel, and shown as frequency distributions and graphs. The mean suits symmetrical data, the median skewed data and the mode nominal data; the SD, the square root of the variance, measures spread. The normal curve holds about 68, 95 and 99.7 per cent of cases within 1, 2 and 3 SD, and z = (X − M)/SD converts any score into a percentile or another standard score. 9.9 Sampling Distributions and the Logic of Hypothesis Testing. Inferential statistics use sample data and the laws of chance to judge whether a result could be due to chance. The sampling distribution of the mean centres on the population mean, its SD is the standard error (σ/√N), and by the central limit theorem it is near normal once N is about 30. A 95 percent CI is M ± 1.96 SE. A test assumes H0 and rejects it when p ≤ α. A Type I error rejects a true H0 (α); a Type II error retains a false one (β). Power is 1 − β; Cohen's d of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 is small, medium and large. 9.10 Comparing Groups: t-Tests, ANOVA and Non-Parametric Tests. Parametric tests (z, t, F) assume normality, equal variances, independence and interval or ratio data; non-parametric or distribution-free tests (Siegel, 1956) handle ranks, categories and small or skewed samples. Gosset's t tests one or two means (df N - 1, N1 + N2 - 2 or pairs - 1). Fisher's ANOVA splits variance into between and within parts, F = MS between / MS within , about 1 under H0; a significant F is followed by post hoc tests or a Bonferroni correction. Factorial ANOVA detects interactions; ANCOVA adds homogeneity of regression slopes. Chi-square handles frequencies, with df (r - 1)(c - 1), and rank tests partner each parametric test. 9.11 Correlation, Regression and Factor Analysis. Correlation (Pearson's r , 1896) measures the direction (sign) and strength (size) of a linear association from -1 to +1. It is graphed as a scatterplot; r squared is shared variance (+0.90 means 81 per cent), and correlation aids prediction but never proves causation. Spearman's rho, point-biserial, biserial, phi and tetrachoric suit other data; partial correlation removes a third variable from both. Regression (Y = a + bX) predicts one variable from another; multiple regression is undermined by multicollinearity among predictors. Factor analysis (Spearman, 1904) reduces correlated variables to a few factors, retained by eigenvalues above 1 or the scree elbow and rotated orthogonally (varimax) or obliquely (promax).
