second-order factor, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis From the past papers 'Reinforcement will have positive effect on performance,' which type of hypothesis is this? (RML 2024) a Null and directional b Alternate and directional c Null and non-directional d Alternate and non-directional ✓ Answer: (b) Alternate and directional Definition of an alternative, directional hypothesis The concept Which hypothesis The statement predicts an effect, so it is the alternative hypothesis . The null hypothesis would predict no effect. Why directional It also says which way the effect goes ( positive ), so it is directional and would be tested one-tailed . Why the other options are wrong (a) Null and directional Right on direction, but a null predicts no effect, and this statement predicts one. (c) Null and non-directional Wrong twice: the statement predicts an effect (so not null) and names its direction (so not non-directional). (d) Alternate and non-directional Right that it is the alternative hypothesis, but it names a direction (positive), so it is directional, not non-directional. Nomothetic approach of study is involved in (JEMAS 2025) a Qualitative method b Experimental method c Quasi-experimental method d Ethnography ✓ Answer: (b) Experimental method Nomothetic versus idiographic approach The concept What it is The nomothetic approach seeks general laws that hold across many people. Why this one The experiment is its purest method, testing cause and effect across groups of people. The opposite Idiographic work studies particular cases in depth, as qualitative methods and ethnography do. Why the other options are wrong (a) Qualitative method Studies particular cases in depth, so it is idiographic , the opposite of nomothetic. (c) Quasi-experimental method Quasi-experiments are nomothetic too, but the weaker choice; the true experiment is the purest nomothetic method. (d) Ethnography Like other qualitative methods, ethnography studies particular cases in depth, so it is idiographic . In which method does the researcher start with a theory and then test it with observations? (RML 2023) a Inductive reasoning b Deductive reasoning c Abductive reasoning d Hypothetico-deductive method ✓ Answer: (b) Deductive reasoning Deductive reasoning: theory to observation The concept How it works Deduction runs top-down : from theory, to hypothesis, to observation. Why this one The stem starts with a theory and then tests it with observations, which is exactly that direction. Why the other options are wrong (a) Inductive reasoning Induction runs the other way, from observations up to theory. (c) Abductive reasoning Abduction infers the best explanation for a surprising fact; it does not start from a theory and test it. (d) Hypothetico-deductive method The whole cycle of conjecture and test, not the direction of reasoning asked for; the trap is the word deductive in its name. Maximization of ____ variance, minimization of ____ variance, control of ____ variance. Select the appropriate option. (JEMAS 2025) a secondary, true, error b true, primary, secondary c primary, error, secondary d primary, true, error ✓ Answer: (c) primary, error, secondary Kerlinger's MAXMINCON principle The concept The principle Kerlinger 's MAXMINCON principle: MAXimise one kind of variance, MINimise another, CONtrol a third. Each part Maximise primary (experimental) variance due to the IV, minimise error variance, and control secondary (extraneous) variance. Why the other options are wrong (a) secondary, true, error Scrambles the order and brings in true variance , which belongs to test theory, not to this principle. (b) true, primary, secondary Uses true variance (a test-theory term) and would minimise primary variance, the very variance the experimenter wants to maximise. (d) primary, true, error Starts right, but true variance belongs to test theory, error variance is minimised rather than controlled, and secondary variance is left out. Which of the following can help control experimenter's bias? (RML 2022) a Double-blinding b Randomly assigning subjects to groups c Using control groups d Demand characteristics ✓ Answer: (a) Double-blinding Double-blind procedure against experimenter expectancy The concept How it works In a double-blind design, the experimenters who treat and assess participants do not know who is in which condition. Why it works Because they do not know, their expectations cannot shape the results, which removes experimenter bias . Why the other options are wrong (b) Randomly assigning subjects to groups Random assignment equalises the groups, but the experimenter still knows who got what, so expectations can still shape results. (c) Using control groups A control group gives a comparison, but the experimenter still knows who got what. (d) Demand characteristics A source of bias (cues telling participants what the study expects of them), not a control for it. A researcher is interested in the impact of anxiety on performance. To manipulate anxiety, some subjects were given plain chips to eat while others were given barbecue flavoured chips to eat. The most obvious problem with this experiment is a lack of: (RML 2022) a Statistical Validity b Empirical Validity c Internal Validity d Construct Validity ✓ Answer: (d) Construct Validity Construct validity of the manipulation The concept What it is Construct validity asks whether an operation really represents the construct it is named for. Why this one Chip flavour does not manipulate anxiety , so the operation does not represent the construct named. Why the other options are wrong (a) Statistical Validity Concerns whether the statistical conclusions drawn from the data are sound; it does not name this flaw. (b) Empirical Validity An old name for a test's criterion-related validity , so it does not name this flaw. (c) Internal Validity Internal validity fails when a rival variable explains the result, and no rival variable does here; the flaw is the manipulation itself. A researcher wants to study the prevalence of test anxiety among all school students in India. Due to feasibility, they first randomly select 5 districts from each state, then randomly select 10 schools from each district, and finally randomly select 30 students from each school. This sampling technique is known as: (Real PYQ 2024) a Stratified Random Sampling b Quota Sampling c Cluster Sampling d Purposive Sampling ✓ Answer: (c) Cluster Sampling Multistage cluster sampling The concept What it is Cluster sampling picks intact groups at random rather than individual people. Why this one Intact groups (districts, then schools) are chosen at random at successive levels, which is multistage cluster sampling. Why the other options are wrong (a) Stratified Random Sampling Stratified sampling would draw individuals from every stratum, not intact groups chosen at random level by level. (b) Quota Sampling Involves no random selection at all; the researcher simply fills set quotas of each kind of person. (d) Purposive Sampling Involves no random selection at all; the researcher hand-picks cases by judgement . Which of the following sampling methods relies on the researcher's judgment to select participants who are "typical" or "representative" of the population, and does NOT allow for the calculation of sampling error? (Real PYQ 2024) a Simple Random Sampling b Stratified Random Sampling c Quota Sampling d Cluster Sampling ✓ Answer: (c) Quota Sampling Non-probability sampling: quota sampling The concept Why this one It is the only non-probability method offered, so its sampling error cannot be calculated; the other three are probability methods. Key note Strictly, a judgement-based choice of typical cases describes purposive sampling , which would be the better answer if it were offered. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Simple Random Sampling A probability method in which every member has an equal chance of selection, so sampling error can be calculated. (b) Stratified Random Sampling A probability method (random draws within each stratum), so sampling error can be calculated. (d) Cluster Sampling A probability method (random choice of whole groups), so sampling error can be calculated. A statistical measure based upon a population is known as: (IHBAS 2020) a Statistic b Parameter c Sample d None of the above ✓ Answer: (b) Parameter Definition of parameter versus statistic The concept What it is A parameter describes a population , and is written with Greek letters such as mu (μ) and sigma (σ). The contrast A statistic is computed from a sample and is written with Roman letters. Why the other options are wrong (a) Statistic Computed from a sample , not a population, and written with Roman letters. (c) Sample A group of people, not a measure at all. (d) None of the above Fails because parameter is exactly the right term. In experimental design, the principle that ensures every participant has an equal chance of being assigned to any group is: (Real PYQ 2025) a Replication b Local control c Randomization d Homogeneity ✓ Answer: (c) Randomization Ronald Fisher, The Design of Experiments (1935) The concept What it is Randomisation gives every participant an equal chance of assignment to any group. Who said so It is one of Ronald Fisher 's three principles ( The Design of Experiments , 1935), alongside replication and local control . Why the other options are wrong (a) Replication One of Fisher's other two principles: repeating the treatment across several units, not equal-chance assignment. (b) Local control Fisher's third principle, also called blocking : grouping similar units together, not equal-chance assignment. (d) Homogeneity Not one of Fisher's three principles at all. Researchers studying meditation contacted over 10000 randomly selected adults in 10 nations. The results showed that those who meditated on a regular basis were less likely to suffer from stress than adults who meditate less regularly or not at all. Can we conclude that meditation lowers stress? Why? (RML 2021) a Yes, because the sample size was large b Yes, because the adults were randomly selected c Yes, because the adults were randomly assigned d Not necessarily, because this wasn't an experiment ✓ Answer: (d) Not necessarily, because this wasn't an experiment Correlation is not causation: no random assignment The concept What they did The researchers only measured who already meditated; nobody was randomly assigned to meditate. Why it matters So meditators may differ in other ways that lower stress, and the study cannot show that meditation is the cause . Why the other options are wrong (a) Yes, because the sample size was large A large sample helps generalisation , not causal inference. (b) Yes, because the adults were randomly selected Random selection helps generalisation, not causal inference; the trap is confusing it with random assignment. (c) Yes, because the adults were randomly assigned Describes something the study did not do: nobody was randomly assigned to meditate or not. Longitudinal and cross-sectional designs can be used to study how behaviour changes as a function of age. A disadvantage of cross-sectional studies is that the result can be influenced by : (IHBAS 2024) a Random assignment b Socio-economic factors c Cohort difference d Participant attrition ✓ Answer: (c) Cohort difference Cohort effect in cross-sectional designs The concept How it works A cross-sectional study compares different age groups at one time. The flaw So generational ( cohort ) differences can masquerade as age changes . Why the other options are wrong (a) Random assignment Plays no part in age comparisons, since people cannot be assigned to an age. (b) Socio-economic factors A general confound in many studies, not the characteristic flaw of the cross-sectional design. (d) Participant attrition Attrition (drop-out over time) is the problem of longitudinal studies, which follow the same people; a cross-sectional study tests each person once. A famous study examined the smoking habits of British doctors and whether or not the doctors development various types of cancers. Participants responded to questionnaires about their smoking habits and health in 1951, 1957, 1966 and many more times all the way up to 2001. What type of observation study is this? (RML 2021) a A retrospective observational study b A prospective observational study c A sample survey d None of these. It's an experimental study. ✓ Answer: (b) A prospective observational study Doll and Hill, British Doctors Study (from 1951) The concept The study This is Doll and Hill 's British Doctors Study . Why observational Nobody was assigned to smoke, so it is observational rather than experimental. Why prospective The doctors were followed forward from exposure (smoking in 1951) to outcome, so it is a prospective cohort . Why the other options are wrong (a) A retrospective observational study A retrospective study looks back from outcome to past exposure; these doctors were followed forward from 1951. (c) A sample survey A sample survey describes a population at one point in time, but these doctors were followed for decades. (d) None of these. It's an experimental study. Nobody was assigned to smoke, so it is observational, not experimental. What is the main purpose of using meta-analysis in clinical psychology? (IHBAS 2024) a To summarize findings from multiple studies b To conduct a single large experiment c To analyze individual case studies d To collect primary data ✓ Answer: (a) To summarize findings from multiple studies Meta-analysis: pooling effect sizes across studies The concept What it is Meta-analysis statistically pools the effect sizes of many existing studies. Key note The paper's key gives (b), which is wrong: a single experiment, however large, is primary research . Why the other options are wrong (b) To conduct a single large experiment The paper's keyed answer, but wrong: a single experiment, however large, is primary research, not a pooling of studies. (c) To analyze individual case studies Meta-analysis pools many studies; it does not analyse individual case studies. (d) To collect primary data Meta-analysis works on existing studies; it does not collect primary data . In a cohort study investigating the association between a new psychological intervention and relapse rates in schizophrenia, the risk ratio is calculated as 1.0. This finding indicates that: (Real PYQ 2024) a The incidence of relapse in the exposed group is double that of the unexposed group. b The intervention has a significant protective effect against relapse. c There is no difference in the risk of relapse between the intervention and control groups. d The odds of exposure are equal in both the relapse and non-relapse groups. ✓ Answer: (c) There is no difference in the risk of relapse between the groups Risk ratio in a cohort study The concept What it is A risk ratio divides the risk in one group by the risk in the other. Reading it So 1.0 means equal risks: no difference between the groups. Why the other options are wrong (a) The incidence of relapse in the exposed group is double that of the unexposed group. Double the incidence would give a risk ratio of 2.0, not 1.0. (b) The intervention has a significant protective effect against relapse. A protective effect would show as a risk ratio below 1.0; 1.0 means no effect. (d) The odds of exposure are equal in both the relapse and non-relapse groups. How a case-control study's odds ratio is phrased, not what a cohort's risk ratio measures. 'Can you tell me why this band is so popular among your age group?' is an example of: (RML 2020) a psychodynamic inquiry b a task-focused inquiry c an ethnographic inquiry d a strength-based inquiry ✓ Answer: (c) An ethnographic inquiry Spradley's ethnographic interview The concept What it is An ethnographic inquiry treats the person as an informant on the culture of their own group. Why this one The question asks the teenager to explain the culture of their own peer group, as in Spradley 's ethnographic interview. Why the other options are wrong (a) psychodynamic inquiry Psychodynamic inquiry probes feelings and hidden motives, not the culture of a peer group. (b) a task-focused inquiry Task-focused inquiry explores a defined task, not what a peer group values. (d) a strength-based inquiry Strength-based inquiry explores the person's resources , not their group's culture. Uniting various qualitative methods with quantitative methods can be called as: (IHBAS 2020) a Coalition b Triangulation c Multidimensional approach d Co-operative inquiry ✓ Answer: (b) Triangulation Denzin (1970), methodological triangulation The concept What it is Triangulation means combining methods so that each one's errors are offset by the others. Who named it Denzin (1970) called this methodological triangulation . Why the other options are wrong (a) Coalition Coalition is not a research term at all; the trap is that it sounds like joining things together. (c) Multidimensional approach Merely studies several aspects of a problem; it says nothing about combining methods. (d) Co-operative inquiry Heron 's participatory method, not a way of combining qualitative and quantitative methods. Which one of the following does not apply to qualitative research? (IHBAS 2020) a Recognition of the role of language and discourse b Emphasis on objective truth c Understanding of processes d Concern for human individuality ✓ Answer: (b) Emphasis on objective truth Constructivism versus positivism The concept The idea Qualitative research rests on constructivism , which sees realities as constructed and multiple. Why this one Objective truth belongs to positivist , quantitative work, so it does not apply to qualitative research. Why the other options are wrong (a) Recognition of the role of language and discourse True of qualitative research: language and discourse are among its hallmarks . (c) Understanding of processes True: understanding processes is a hallmark of qualitative research. (d) Concern for human individuality True: concern for individuality is a hallmark of qualitative research. 'The ethical principle that research participants should be told enough about a piece of research to be able to make a decision about whether to participate in it.' Which research principle is this a glossary definition of? (RML 2021) a Informed consent b Debriefing c Expectation management d De-concealment ✓ Answer: (a) Informed consent Informed consent (research ethics) The concept What it is Informed consent means being told enough to decide, before taking part, whether to participate. Why the other options are wrong (b) Debriefing Debriefing comes after participation, not before the decision to take part. (c) Expectation management Not a research-ethics principle. (d) De-concealment Not a research-ethics principle; revealing a deception is called dehoaxing . The principle of ethical research under which the subjects should be given full information about all aspects of the research study after it is done is known as: (IHBAS 2020) a Debriefing b Description c Explanation d Interpretation ✓ Answer: (a) Debriefing Debriefing (research ethics) The concept What it is Debriefing gives participants full information about the study after participation. Its parts It reveals any deception ( dehoaxing ) and helps with any distress ( desensitising ). Why the other options are wrong (b) Description A goal of science , like explanation, not an ethical principle. (c) Explanation A goal of science , like description, not an ethical principle. (d) Interpretation Belongs to a report's Discussion section, not to research ethics. Which of the following is NOT a form of plagiarism? (RML 2023) a Collusion b Citation c Patchwriting d Ghost-writing ✓ Answer: (b) Citation Citation versus plagiarism The concept Why this one Citing openly acknowledges a source and gives credit to its authors, so it is the cure for plagiarism . Why the other options are not the answer (a) Collusion A form of plagiarism: unauthorised joint work presented as one's own. (c) Patchwriting A form of plagiarism: source text only lightly reworded . (d) Ghost-writing A form of plagiarism: work written by someone else . Arbitrary zero is the characteristic of which scale? (RML 2024) a Ratio scale b Ordinal scale c Interval scale d Nominal scale ✓ Answer: (c) Interval scale Stevens' levels of measurement: interval scale The concept What it is An interval scale such as Celsius has equal intervals but an arbitrary zero , so ratios are meaningless. The contrast A ratio scale is defined by a true zero . Key note The source keys (a), which is wrong. Why the other options are wrong (a) Ratio scale The source's keyed answer, but wrong: a ratio scale is defined by a true zero, not an arbitrary one. (b) Ordinal scale Ranks only, with no meaningful zero or equal intervals at all. (d) Nominal scale Names categories only, with no meaningful zero or equal intervals at all. A person wants to determine the representative income of the people living in a community. He would be best advised to use the (JEMAS 2025) a Mean b Median c Mode d Standard deviation ✓ Answer: (b) Median Median for skewed data The concept The problem Income is positively skewed : a few very rich households pull the mean upward. Why the median The median depends only on position, so it stays with the typical family. Why the other options are wrong (a) Mean Pulled upward by a few very rich households, because income is positively skewed. (c) Mode Unstable, so a poor guide to the typical income. (d) Standard deviation Measures spread , not central tendency. In a negatively skewed distribution, the position of the mean with reference to the median is: (RML 2022) a Left of the median b Right of the median c Same as median d Same as a mode ✓ Answer: (a) Left of the median Skewness and the order of mean, median, mode The concept How it works In negative skew the long tail points to low scores and drags the mean furthest into it. The order From low to high the order is mean, median, mode , so the mean lies left of the median. Why the other options are wrong (b) Right of the median True of positive skew , where the tail points to high scores. (c) Same as median Mean and median coincide only in a symmetrical distribution. (d) Same as a mode The mean, median and mode coincide only in a symmetrical distribution. Type II error occurs : (RML 2022) a whenever a true null hypothesis is accepted b whenever a false null hypothesis is rejected c whenever a false null hypothesis is accepted d whenever a true null hypothesis is rejected ✓ Answer: (c) whenever a false null hypothesis is accepted Type II error (β): a false negative The concept What it is A Type II error (β) misses a real effect: a false negative . In decision terms The null hypothesis is false, but the test accepts it. Why the other options are wrong (a) whenever a true null hypothesis is accepted A correct decision : the null really is true, so accepting it is right. (b) whenever a false null hypothesis is rejected A correct decision : the null is false, so rejecting it finds a real effect. (d) whenever a true null hypothesis is rejected Rejecting a true null is a Type I error (α), a false positive. The statistical theorem states that given a sufficiently large sample size, the sampling distribution of the mean for a variable will be approximately normally distributed, regardless of that variable's distribution in the Population. What is this definition of? (RML 2021) a The normal distribution theorem b The central limit theorem c The sampling distribution theorem d The law of large numbers ✓ Answer: (b) The central limit theorem Central limit theorem The concept What it says With N of about 30 or more, the distribution of sample means is near normal whatever the population's shape. Why the other options are wrong (a) The normal distribution theorem Not a standard theorem; the trap is that the central limit theorem is about a normal shape. (c) The sampling distribution theorem Not a standard theorem; the sampling distribution of the mean is what the central limit theorem describes. (d) The law of large numbers Says only that a sample mean approaches the population mean as N grows, nothing about the shape of the distribution. What is the p-value in statistical testing? (IHBAS 2024) a The probability of the null hypothesis being true b The probability of obtaining the observed data if the null hypothesis is true c The effect size of the experiment d The power of the study ✓ Answer: (b) The probability of obtaining the observed data if the null hypothesis is true Definition of the p-value The concept What it is p is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming H 0 is true. The trap It is not the probability that H 0 is true; that reverses the conditional . Why the other options are wrong (a) The probability of the null hypothesis being true Reverses the conditional: p assumes H 0 is true, so it cannot give the probability that H 0 is true. (c) The effect size of the experiment Effect size is a separate quantity: how big an effect is, which p does not tell you. (d) The power of the study Power (1 − β) is a separate quantity: the probability of detecting a real effect. Which non-parametric test is equivalent to the independent samples t-test? (RML 2023) a Mann-Whitney U test b Kruskal-Wallis test c Wilcoxon signed-rank test d Friedman test ✓ Answer: (a) Mann-Whitney U test Mann-Whitney U test The concept How it works The Mann-Whitney U test ranks the pooled scores of two independent groups . Why this one It is the rank partner of the independent t-test . Why the other options are wrong (b) Kruskal-Wallis test For three or more independent groups , the rank partner of one-way ANOVA. (c) Wilcoxon signed-rank test For two related samples , the rank partner of the paired t-test. (d) Friedman test For three or more related samples , the rank partner of repeated-measures ANOVA. Which of the following is a pooled variance estimate that constitutes the denominator of an F-ratio? (RML 2021) a The between-cells mean square (MSB). b The mean of the sampling distribution. c The sum of the deviations from the grand mean. d The within-cells mean square (MSw). ✓ Answer: (d) The within-cells mean square (MSw) F-ratio: MS between over MS within The concept The formula F = MS between / MS within . Why within MS within pools the error variance inside the groups, so it is the denominator. Why the other options are wrong (a) The between-cells mean square (MSB). MS between is the numerator of F, not the denominator. (b) The mean of the sampling distribution. Plays no part in F. (c) The sum of the deviations from the grand mean. Deviations from the grand mean always sum to zero , which is why they are squared. A researcher wants to calculate the degrees of freedom (df) for a 3 x 4 contingency table in a Chi-square test. The df is: (Real PYQ 2025) a 12 b 7 c 6 d 11 ✓ Answer: (c) 6 Chi-square df for a contingency table The concept The formula For a test of independence , df = (rows - 1)(columns - 1) . Worked here A 3 x 4 table gives 2 x 3 = 6 . Why the other options are wrong (a) 12 Multiplies the raw dimensions (3 x 4); twelve is the number of cells, not the df. (b) 7 Adds the raw dimensions (3 + 4) instead of using (rows - 1)(columns - 1). (d) 11 The number of cells minus 1, not the df for a test of independence. A researcher uses a Scree plot to determine the number of factors to retain in an EFA. The plot shows a sharp drop from eigenvalue 3.5 to 1.8, followed by a gradual plateau where eigenvalues are 0.9, 0.7, and 0.5. According to the Kaiser-Guttman rule and the Scree plot, how many factors should ideally be retained? (Real PYQ 2024) a 5 b 3 c 2 d 1 ✓ Answer: (c) 2 Kaiser-Guttman rule plus Cattell's scree test The concept Kaiser rule The Kaiser-Guttman rule keeps factors with eigenvalues above 1.0 : only 3.5 and 1.8 qualify. Scree plot Both lie above the elbow at the third factor, so the two rules agree on two factors. Why the other options are wrong (a) 5 Counts every eigenvalue, though 0.9, 0.7 and 0.5 fall below 1.0. (b) 3 Wrongly keeps the elbow factor (0.9), which falls below 1.0. (d) 1 Keeps only the largest (3.5), though 1.8 also exceeds 1.0. When two variables that are being used as predictors in a statistical analysis have a high correlation with each other, this statistical problem is known as: (Real PYQ 2025) a Heteroscedasticity b Multicollinearity c Autocorrelation d Homogeneity of variance ✓ Answer: (b) Multicollinearity Multicollinearity in regression The concept What it is Multicollinearity means the predictors are highly intercorrelated. Why it matters It makes regression weights unstable and inflates their standard errors ; it is flagged by a VIF above 10. Why the other options are wrong (a) Heteroscedasticity Unequal spread of the residuals , not correlated predictors. (c) Autocorrelation Residuals correlated over time, not predictors correlated with each other. (d) Homogeneity of variance Equal variance across groups , an ANOVA assumption, not a problem between predictors. Which of the following correlation methods is used when one variable is continuous and the other is dichotomous? (RML 2023) a Pearson correlation coefficient b Spearman's rank correlation coefficient c Point-biserial correlation coefficient d Biserial correlation coefficient ✓ Answer: (c) Point-biserial correlation coefficient Point-biserial correlation for a true dichotomy The concept When to use A continuous variable paired with a true (natural) dichotomy calls for point-biserial correlation. Exam tip Ask whether the dichotomy is natural or cut from a continuous variable: natural means point-biserial, cut means biserial . Why the other options are wrong (a) Pearson correlation coefficient For two continuous variables. (b) Spearman's rank correlation coefficient For ranks , not a continuous variable paired with a dichotomy. (d) Biserial correlation coefficient For an artificial dichotomy cut from a continuous variable, not a true one. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. A z-score , (X − M)/SD, states a score's distance from the mean in SD units (mean 0, SD 1) so scores from different distributions can be compared; on the normal curve z = 0, +1, +1.5 and +2 lie at about the 50th, 84th, 93rd and 98th percentiles, so deviation IQs of 85, 100 and 130 sit at the 16th, 50th and 98th. asked 12 times A Type I error (α) is rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive); a Type II error (β) is retaining, or accepting, a false null hypothesis (false negative). The significance level α is the probability of a Type I error, in ANOVA as in every test. asked 11 times Stevens (1946) : nominal = unordered categories (marital status, car colour); ordinal = rank order (preference or agreement); interval = equal intervals with an arbitrary zero (Celsius); ratio = equal intervals with a true zero (height, number of books). asked 9 times One-way ANOVA compares the means of three or more independent groups on one IV with a continuous DV (it also works for two, where F = t squared); repeated t-tests would inflate the family-wise Type I error. asked 9 times The Mann-Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney, 1947; the same as the Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is the non-parametric equivalent of the independent-samples t-test; Wilcoxon signed-rank partners the paired t, Kruskal-Wallis the one-way ANOVA and Friedman the repeated-measures ANOVA. asked 9 times The p-value is the probability of obtaining the observed result, or one more extreme, if H0 is true; it is not the probability that H0 is true. If p ≤ α (p = .03 with α = .05), reject H0. asked 8 times Chi-square (Karl Pearson, 1900) is a non-parametric test for nominal frequency data; the test of independence asks whether two categorical variables are associated, with df = (rows - 1)(columns - 1): 3 x 4 gives 6, 4 x 5 gives 12. asked 8 times The standard deviation is the square root of the variance and measures variability; it is affected by extreme scores (the IQR and quartile deviation are not), and multiplying every score by c multiplies the variance by c² while adding a constant changes nothing (variance 4, scores × 3 + 10: variance 36). asked 7 times Cluster sampling randomly selects whole natural groups (districts, schools) and studies all or some units inside them; districts, then schools, then students is multistage cluster sampling, whereas stratified random sampling samples randomly within every stratum. asked 6 times In non-probability sampling (convenience, purposive, quota, snowball) the chance of selection is unknown, randomisation is impossible and sampling error cannot be calculated; quota sampling, the commonest option-list answer, fills proportional quotas non-randomly. asked 6 times The normal curve is symmetrical and unimodal with mean = median = mode, and about 68, 95 and 99.7 per cent of cases lie within ±1, ±2 and ±3 SD of the mean; a bimodal curve is not normal. asked 6 times The median is the average for skewed data (community income, anxiety scores), the mode the only one for nominal data; range, SD and mean deviation are measures of variability, not central tendency. asked 6 times Cohen's d , the standardised difference between two means, is small at 0.2, medium at 0.5 and large at 0.8; for r the benchmarks are .10, .30 and .50, so r = −.30 is a medium negative relationship. asked 6 times F = MS between / MS within ; MS within, the pooled error variance, is the denominator. F is about 1 when H0 is true, so an F below 1 (0.99) is never significant; F rises as chance variability falls, can never be negative, and the test is one-tailed. asked 6 times Post hoc tests (Tukey's HSD, Scheffé the most conservative, Newman-Keuls, Duncan, Fisher's LSD the least conservative) are used only after a significant F; k levels give k(k - 1)/2 pairs (4 levels give 6); the Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the number of comparisons to control family-wise Type I error. asked 6 times Induction moves from specific observations to broad generalisations and builds theory (the theory-development stage; typical of qualitative research); deduction starts with a theory and tests it against observations (typical of quantitative, experimental research). asked 5 times Degrees of freedom : one-sample t = N - 1 (N 20 gives 19); independent t = N1 + N2 - 2 (25 per group gives 48); one-way ANOVA within = N - k (3 groups of 10 give 27); randomised block error = (treatments - 1)(blocks - 1) (4 and 5 give 12). asked 5 times r = -0.85 is a strong negative relationship: the sign of r gives the direction and its size gives the strength. asked 5 times A double-blind study keeps both the participants and the experimenters who treat and assess them unaware of the conditions, so it controls both experimenter bias and participant expectancy effects. asked 4 times In probability sampling every element has a known, non-zero chance of selection, so sampling error can be calculated and the sample is likely, not guaranteed, to be representative. asked 4 times Only a true experiment (manipulation, control, random assignment) licenses cause-and-effect conclusions; correlational and observational studies cannot, however large or randomly selected the sample, because of the directionality and third-variable problems. asked 4 times NNT = 1/ARR , where the absolute risk reduction is the control event rate minus the treated event rate; an NNT of 8 means treating 8 patients for one additional patient to benefit. asked 4 times Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN), the true positive rate; specificity = TN/(TN + FP). Sensitivity 90 percent and specificity 70 percent means the test correctly identifies 90 percent of ill and 70 percent of healthy people. asked 4 times Qualitative research is naturalistic, context-specific and inductive (bottom-up evidence), seeks meaning, process and the insider's view, and claims neither objective truth nor the researcher's authority; the survey is quantitative, whereas case study, ethnography and grounded theory are qualitative. asked 4 times Random assignment (randomisation) gives every participant an equal chance of being placed in any group, making groups equivalent on known and unknown variables so the main difference is the treatment; it controls selection bias and confounding and is not random sampling. asked 3 times The independent variable is the presumed cause, manipulated or selected (having heart disease in 'residents with heart disease die earlier'); the dependent variable is the measured outcome expected to change. asked 3 times Stratified random sampling divides the population into mutually exclusive strata and samples randomly within each; it is preferred when important subgroups must be represented and is more precise than simple random sampling when strata are internally homogeneous. asked 3 times A longitudinal design studies the same people repeatedly over time and is the best design for examining change over time; its problems are attrition, practice effects, cost and time. asked 3 times A relative risk or odds ratio of 1.0 means no association between exposure and outcome; above 1 marks a risk factor, below 1 a protective one. asked 3 times Intention-to-treat analysis analyses every participant in the group to which they were randomised, regardless of adherence, drop-out or crossover, and so preserves randomisation. asked 3 times

A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (821 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (821 pages) Chapter 1 Psychology as a Science: Roots, Founders and the First Schools In this chapter 1.1 What Is Psychology? : define psychology as it has been defined across history, state its four goals, separate basic from applied work and name the main fields, including the one that studies animals. 1.2 Philosophical Roots: A Long Past : trace nativism, rationalism, empiricism and associationism from Plato to Kant, and lay out the classic positions on the mind-body problem. 1.3 Physiological and Biological Roots : explain how nerve physiology, brain localisation, Darwin's evolution and Galton's study of individual differences prepared the ground for a laboratory science. 1.4 Measuring the Mind: Psychophysics and Mental Chronometry : show how Weber, Fechner, Donders and Ebbinghaus proved that mental events could be measured. 1.5 Wilhelm Wundt and the Founding of Experimental Psychology : describe Wundt's laboratory, his voluntarism, his theory of feeling, his method and his folk psychology, and name his famous students. 1.6 Structuralism and Its European Rivals : explain Titchener's structuralism, its method and its errors, and the challenges from Wurzburg, Brentano, Stumpf and G. E. Muller. 1.7 Functionalism and the American Pioneers : explain why functionalism arose, what James, Dewey, Angell, Carr and Woodworth contributed, and who built American psychology's institutions. 1.8 Reading the History: Zeitgeist, Great Persons and "Fathers" : compare the two ways of explaining history, master the "father of" and "first" questions, and trace the arrival of psychology in India. Weightage. 46 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (5.6%) test this chapter, 12 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 8 sections is High yield. Leipzig, in the winter of 1879. In a small room of an old university building known as the Konvikt, a doctoral student named Max Friedrich sits in front of a clockwork timer called a Hipp chronoscope, a machine built to measure intervals in thousandths of a second. A stimulus is presented; Friedrich presses a telegraph key. Then the procedure is changed: now he must press the key not the instant he senses the stimulus, but only once he has clearly grasped what it is. The second kind of reaction takes longer, and the extra time, Friedrich and his supervisor reasoned, is the time the mind needs to apperceive , to bring an impression into the clear focus of attention. Trial after trial, the numbers go into a notebook. His supervisor was a 47-year-old professor of philosophy, Wilhelm Wundt. When Wundt had arrived in Leipzig four years earlier, the university had given him this room to store the apparatus he used in lecture demonstrations. By the winter of 1879 it had become something new: a place where students carried out original experiments on the mind and published them as research. Friedrich's study of the duration of apperception became the first dissertation to come out of that room, and historians who later combed the Leipzig archives dated the start of the work to the last weeks of 1879. Here is the puzzle that should bother you. Almost nothing in that room was new. The chronoscope had been built for physicists and astronomers. The idea of measuring the time taken by mental acts came from a Dutch physiologist. The word apperception came from a German philosopher who had died in 1716. And at Harvard, in 1875, the same year Wundt got his room, an American named William James had also been given space for psychological apparatus. So why does every textbook in the world, and nearly every entrance paper in India, treat Leipzig in 1879 as the moment psychology was born? The answer to that question is the subject of this chapter. To find it you need to know where the parts in that room came from: the philosophers who argued for two thousand years about where knowledge comes from, the physiologists who timed nerves and mapped brains, the naturalists who put human beings back among the animals, and the physicists who dared to measure sensation. Then you need to see what Wundt and his students built from those parts, and what the next generation, in Germany and in America, did with it. Remember Max Friedrich pressing his key; we will come back to him at the end of the chapter. 1.1 What Is Psychology? Medium yield · 5 Qs Ask ten people at a chai stall what psychology is and you will hear ten answers: reading minds, treating madness, understanding why people do what they do. Ask ten textbooks and you will get fewer answers, but you will notice something odd: the textbooks of 1890, 1920 and today do not agree with one another either. The definition of psychology has changed several times, and each change tells you which school was in charge. Entrance papers love these definitions, so we start with them. From soul to behaviour: a definition that kept changing The word itself is Greek: psyche (breath, soul) and logos (study or reasoned account). Literally, then, psychology began as "the study of the soul". The Greek philosophers did not use the word as the name of a subject; it first appears in Latin book titles of the sixteenth century (the German scholar Rudolf Goclenius used it in 1590), and the philosopher Christian Wolff (1679 to 1754) made it standard with two books, Psychologia empirica (1732) and Psychologia rationalis (1734). For the Greeks and the medieval scholars, the soul was the principle of life and reason; Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) wrote the first systematic treatise on it, De Anima ( On the Soul ), which is why some older Indian textbooks call him the "father of psychology". From the seventeenth century, philosophers spoke less of the soul and more of the mind : its ideas, its reasoning, its sensations. When psychology became a laboratory science in the nineteenth century, the definition narrowed again. For Wundt and his student Titchener, psychology was the science of conscious experience , studied by trained observers looking inward. William James, in 1890, opened his great textbook with the sentence "Psychology is the Science of Mental Life, both of its phenomena and of their conditions." Then came the revolt. In 1905 and again in 1908 the British psychologist William McDougall (1871 to 1938) defined psychology as the positive science of the conduct or behaviour of living creatures, and in 1913 John B. Watson declared that psychology should drop consciousness altogether and study only behaviour , by which he meant anything an organism does that can be observed and measured from outside. (Watson and behaviourism are the subject of Chapter 2.) The new definition spread through the textbooks. Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962), whom you will meet again in Section 1.7, defined psychology as the scientific study of the activities of the individual in relation to the environment. The definition you will most often find credited in Indian textbooks, "psychology is the scientific study of behaviour", is attributed to the American textbook writer Norman L. Munn . Watson's definition won battles but lost the war. By the 1960s psychologists were again studying memory, imagery and thinking, and today's standard definition reunites the two halves: psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes . Each phrase in that definition is doing work. Behaviour is overt: speaking, walking, blushing, pressing a key. By contrast, mental processes are internal and covert: perceiving, remembering, thinking, dreaming, feeling. You cannot see a student remembering the year of Wundt's laboratory, but you can infer it from what he writes. And scientific means that claims are tested against systematic, public observation that someone else could repeat, not against authority or intuition. An old classroom quip sums up the whole story: first psychology lost its soul, then it lost its mind, then it lost consciousness, and now it has behaviour, of a sort. Table 1.1 puts the sequence in order. Table 1.1 How psychology has been defined. Period Psychology is the study of Associated with Ancient Greece the soul (psyche) Plato, Aristotle ( De Anima ) 17th to 19th century the mind Descartes, Locke, the associationists 1879 to about 1910 conscious experience; "mental life" Wundt, Titchener; James (1890) 1905 to 1913 onward conduct, behaviour McDougall (1905, 1908); Watson (1913) Textbook definitions activities of the individual in relation to the environment; the scientific study of behaviour Woodworth; N. L. Munn Today behaviour and mental processes most modern textbooks Exam trap "In the definition of psychology, mental processes mean ..." The answer is internal, covert processes . "Outward behaviour" and "overt actions and reactions" describe the other half of the definition, and "only animal behaviour" describes neither. A related bank question asks who "first proposed and established psychology as the scientific study of behaviour" and keys N. L. Munn , because Indian textbooks quote that definition from Munn. Historically McDougall (1905, 1908) and Watson (1913) came first; if Watson appears as an option alongside Munn, read the stem closely: "established" behaviourism points to Watson, "the definition" points to Munn. Do not confuse William James (science of mental life) with any behaviour definition. The four goals: describe, explain, predict, control Every science tries to do four things with the events it studies, and psychology is no exception. Take one example and push it through all four: a student who "blanks out" in the examination hall at Mysuru even though he knew the material the night before. Describe. First we must say exactly what happens, and to whom: racing heart, sweaty palms, a mind that will not retrieve answers, perhaps in the first ten minutes only. Careful description separates this from simple lack of preparation. Explain. Next we ask why. Perhaps very high arousal and catastrophic thoughts ("If I fail, everything is over") compete with retrieval for limited attention. An explanation is a cause that can be tested. Predict. A good explanation lets us forecast who will blank out and when: students with high scores on a test-anxiety scale, under time pressure, on high-stakes papers. Control (many textbooks now say influence or change ). Finally we use the knowledge to change the outcome: practice under timed conditions, relaxation training, rehearsing realistic self-statements. This goal is where clinical psychology lives. Some textbooks add a fifth goal, improving the quality of life, but the four above are the classic list. Watson put prediction and control at the very centre of his definition, a point we will return to in Chapter 2. Basic and applied research Psychologists who study a problem only to understand it are doing basic research ; those who study it to solve a practical problem are doing applied research . When Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of meaningless syllables in the 1880s to discover how quickly memories fade, he was doing basic research; when Lightner Witmer opened a clinic in 1896 to help a boy who could not learn to spell, he was doing applied work. The line is not a wall: Witmer's clinic drew on the basic science of the laboratory, and applied problems constantly raise new basic questions. You will see in Section 1.7 that the split between "pure" and "applied" psychology was one of the main arguments between the first two schools. The fields of psychology Modern psychology is a family of specialities. You will study several of them in other books of this series, so here we need only a map (Table 1.2). Two of them deserve a sentence more, because entrance papers test the boundary between them. Put simply, clinical psychology is the assessment, diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders and distress; its practitioners work with conditions ranging from anxiety to schizophrenia, in hospitals, clinics and private practice. counselling psychology overlaps heavily but has traditionally focused on people in the normal range who face adjustment problems: career choice, relationships, study difficulties, life transitions. In India, the Rehabilitation Council of India licenses clinical psychologists, not counsellors, to work with psychiatric disorders, which is one reason your interviewers will care whether you understand the difference. The branch that studies the behaviour of animals is comparative psychology : it compares species, often in the laboratory, to understand how behaviour and learning evolved and what is common to humans and other animals. Its biological cousin, ethology , studies animal behaviour in natural settings and is associated with the zoologists Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. You will see in Section 1.3 that comparative psychology grew directly out of Darwin's work. Three more names in Table 1.2 are easily confused. The first, evolutionary psychology , explains present-day behaviour and mental mechanisms as adaptations shaped by natural selection, that is, as part of our genetic inheritance from ancestors who faced recurring problems of survival and reproduction. The second, behaviour genetics , asks a narrower question: how much of the variation among people in a trait is due to differences in their genes, studied mainly through twins, families and adoption. The third, differential psychology , is the study of individual differences in abilities and personality; the German psychologist William Stern (1871 to 1938) named it in 1900, but its founder in practice was Francis Galton (Section 1.3). Table 1.2 The main fields of psychology. Field What it studies Clinical Assessment, diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders Counselling Adjustment problems of people in the normal range: career, relationships, transitions Health How behaviour, stress and beliefs affect physical illness and recovery Developmental Change across the lifespan, from conception to old age Social How people think about, influence and relate to one another Industrial-organisational Behaviour at work: selection, training, motivation, leadership, organisations Educational and school Learning and teaching; children's learning problems in schools Forensic Psychology applied to law: testimony, criminal behaviour, competence Comparative Animal behaviour, compared across species Neuropsychology Brain-behaviour relations, often through people with brain damage Abnormal The nature and causes of psychological disorders (psychopathology) Experimental Basic processes (sensation, learning, memory) studied by experiment Differential Individual differences in ability and personality Evolutionary Behaviour and mind as products of natural selection Exam trap "Which branch focuses on the study of animal behaviour?" is comparative psychology . Abnormal psychology studies disorders; differential psychology studies individual differences among people; social psychology studies people in relation to others. "What does clinical psychology primarily focus on?" is the assessment and treatment of mental illness ; industrial applications and organisational management belong to industrial-organisational psychology, and behavioural changes in animals to comparative psychology. The bank question asking which branch studies "behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance" keys evolutionary psychology ; if behaviour genetics is ever offered as an option, prefer it for questions about heritability. With a definition and a map in hand, we can ask how this discipline came to exist at all. The German memory researcher Hermann Ebbinghaus put the answer in one famous sentence in 1908: "Psychology has a long past, but only a short history." The long past is two thousand years of philosophy and a century of physiology; the short history begins in rooms like Wundt's. Figure 1.1 lays out the short history; the next three sections trace the long past that made it possible. Roots: 1850 to 1890 Schools and institutions: 1892 to 1925 1850 Helmholtz times the nerve impulse; Fechner's insight (22 October) 1859 Darwin, On the Origin of Species 1860 Fechner, Elements of Psychophysics 1861 Broca: speech area (patient Tan) 1869 Galton, Hereditary Genius 1873/74 Wundt, Principles of Physiological Psychology 1879 Wundt's Leipzig laboratory: research begins 1883 Hall: first US research laboratory (Johns Hopkins) 1885 Ebbinghaus, On Memory 1890 James, Principles of Psychology; Cattell coins "mental test" 1892 APA founded at Clark; Hall first president 1894 Washburn: first woman PhD in psychology 1896 Witmer's clinic (Pennsylvania); Dewey's reflex arc paper 1898 Titchener names structuralism 1905 Calkins: first woman APA president 1906 Angell, The Province of Functional Psychology 1913 Watson's behaviourist manifesto 1915/16 Calcutta: first Indian laboratory and department 1922 Bose founds the Indian Psychoanalytic Society 1925 Indian Psychological Association founded Figure 1.1 The short history of psychology at a glance. Notice how the roots (left) cluster in German physiology and British biology, and how quickly the institutions (right) followed once Wundt's laboratory opened in 1879. 1.2 Philosophical Roots: A Long Past Medium yield · 5 Qs Long before anyone measured a reaction time, philosophers had asked the three questions that still organise much of psychology. Where does knowledge come from? How are ideas connected to one another? And how is the mind related to the body? Psychology inherited all three, and the answers given between ancient Athens and eighteenth-century Germany are examined every year in Indian entrance papers. Let us define the main positions first, then meet the people who held them. On the first question, there are two classic answers. The first, nativism , holds that some knowledge, ideas or abilities are inborn, present before any experience. The second, empiricism , holds that all knowledge comes from experience, delivered through the senses. A third term, rationalism , is often paired with nativism: it holds that reason, not the senses, is the chief source of knowledge, and that the senses can deceive. Keep the two contrasts apart. Nativism versus empiricism is a question about origins (inborn or learned?). Rationalism versus empiricism is a question about the route to knowledge (reasoning or sensing?). In practice the rationalists were usually nativists, and the empiricists were nearly always anti-nativists, which is why exam setters sometimes treat the pairs as one. Plato and Aristotle Plato (about 427 to 347 BCE) was a nativist and a rationalist. In his dialogue Meno , Socrates draws a theorem of geometry out of an uneducated slave boy simply by asking him questions, and concludes that the boy was not learning but recollecting knowledge his soul already possessed. For Plato, the senses show us only shifting copies of the true, unchanging Forms; real knowledge comes from reason turning inward. He also divided the soul into three parts (reason, spirit and appetite), an early model of conflict within the mind that you may hear echoed when you study Freud. Plato's student Aristotle disagreed. In De Anima he treated the soul not as a separate thing trapped in the body but as the form or function of a living body, the way seeing is the function of an eye. And he was an empiricist: the mind at birth, he wrote, is like a writing tablet on which nothing has yet been written, and knowledge begins with the senses. (Hold on to that tablet; John Locke will pick it up two thousand years later.) Aristotle also gave psychology its first theory of how one idea leads to another. In his short work On Memory and Recollection he observed that when we try to recall something we start from a thing that is similar to it, contrary to it, or was contiguous with it (close to it in time or place). These are the laws of association : similarity , contrast and contiguity , to which later writers added frequency (ideas experienced together often are linked more strongly). Try it on yourself. Hear the name "Sachin" and "Tendulkar" follows by contiguity, because you have always met the two words together; "Virat Kohli" may follow by similarity (another great Indian batsman); and the thought of the slowest batsman you ever watched may follow by contrast. Exam trap Aristotle is the empiricist of the pair and Plato the nativist ; students often reverse them because Aristotle is called the "father of psychology" (for De Anima ) and they assume he must have founded everything. Aristotle's three laws are similarity, contrast, contiguity . David Hume's three laws (below) are resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect . If a question lists "contrast", it is Aristotle; if it lists "cause and effect", it is Hume. Rene Descartes: the body as a machine As a young man early in the seventeenth century, Rene Descartes (1596 to 1650) walked in the royal gardens at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris, where hydraulic statues moved, played music and even sprayed water at visitors who stepped on hidden plates in the path. The statues seemed alive, yet they were only pipes, water and valves. Descartes drew a bold conclusion: perhaps the living body is the same kind of machine. Nerves could be tubes, and "animal spirits", a fine fluid stored in the brain's cavities, could flow through them to inflate the muscles. Using this model, Descartes gave the first clear description of the reflex : an automatic, unlearned response to a stimulus that needs no mind at all. Put your hand near a fire, he said, and the heat moves particles in the skin, which tug on a thread inside the nerve, which opens a tiny valve in the brain, which releases animal spirits that flow back down to the arm muscles and pull the hand away. The details were wrong, but the idea that much behaviour is mechanical stimulus and response would run, through the Russian physiologists, all the way to behaviourism. The body, then, is a machine, and animals, which Descartes believed had no souls, are nothing but machines (automata). But the human being has something more: a mind, a thinking thing that has no size or location and cannot be doubted. "I think, therefore I am" (in French, je pense, donc je suis ), he wrote in his Discourse on Method (1637). This is dualism : mind and body are two different kinds of substance, the thinking substance and the extended (physical) substance. And because the two plainly affect each other (a pinprick causes pain; a decision moves an arm), Descartes was an interactionist. He placed the meeting point in the pineal gland , a small structure deep in the brain, chosen because, unlike most brain structures, it is single rather than paired and sits near the centre of the brain. His last book, The Passions of the Soul (1649), described how bodily events stir the emotions through this gland. Descartes was also a rationalist and a nativist. He held that certain innate ideas are not learned from experience but are built into the mind: the ideas of God, of the self, of infinity, and the axioms of geometry. You will see why this matters when we reach Kant and, in Chapter 2, the Gestalt psychologists. Remember Descartes left psychology four legacies: (1) mechanism and the reflex, which led through reflex physiology to Pavlov and behaviourism; (2) innate ideas , which led through Kant to the nativism of the Gestalt school; (3) dualism , which created the modern mind-body problem; and (4) rationalism , against which the British empiricists reacted. A practice question asks what Descartes' dualism "influenced" and keys behaviourism and Gestalt psychology on exactly this reasoning. "Empiricism and rationalism" is the wrong pairing because Descartes was himself a founder of modern rationalism, and empiricism was the reaction against him. The British empiricists: Hobbes, Locke, Berkeley and Hume Across the English Channel a very different tradition grew up, one that insisted the mind contains nothing that did not come in through the senses. Thomas Hobbes (1588 to 1679), best known for his political book Leviathan (1651), was its blunt forerunner. Hobbes was committed to materialism , the view that only matter exists; he held that sensations are motions in the body caused by motions outside it, and that thinking is a "train of thoughts" in which one motion follows another in the order in which they were first experienced. He also argued that human action is driven by the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain. Many historians call him the founder of British empiricism. The philosopher who made empiricism a full theory of mind was John Locke (1632 to 1704). Locke tells us that his great book began when a group of five or six friends met in his rooms to discuss a philosophical problem and got nowhere; it struck him that before arguing about what we know, they ought to examine what the human understanding is capable of knowing. Nearly twenty years later he published An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690). Its central claim is that the mind at birth is "white paper, void of all characters", the idea usually summed up by the Latin tabula rasa (blank or scraped tablet). There are no innate ideas. Every idea comes from one of two sources: sensation (experience of the outside world) or reflection (the mind's experience of its own operations, such as thinking and doubting). Locke divided ideas into simple ideas , which cannot be broken down further (the redness, sweetness and roundness of an apple), and complex ideas , which the mind builds by combining simple ones (the idea "apple" itself). This is the beginning of the "mental chemistry" that runs through the rest of this chapter: complex mental life built from simple elements. He also distinguished two kinds of qualities in objects. The primary qualities (solidity, extension or size, shape, motion and number) exist in the object itself, and our ideas of them resemble the object. The secondary qualities (colour, sound, taste, smell and warmth) exist only as powers to produce sensations in a perceiver. Locke's own demonstration is worth doing. Put one hand in hot water and the other in cold water for a minute; then plunge both into a bowl of lukewarm water. The same water feels cold to the first hand and warm to the second. Since the water cannot be both hot and cold, warmth must be in the perceiver, not in the water. Its size and shape, by contrast, feel the same to both hands. Finally, in the fourth edition of the Essay (1700) Locke added a chapter titled "Of the Association of Ideas", giving psychology the phrase. Interestingly, he used association mainly to explain irrational connections: ideas joined by chance or custom (a room where something terrible happened becomes unbearable) that produce prejudice and what he did not hesitate to call a kind of madness. Indian context In 1688 the Irish scientist William Molyneux wrote to Locke with a puzzle: if a man born blind, who had learned to tell a cube from a sphere by touch, were suddenly given sight, could he tell which was which by looking alone? Locke, a good empiricist, said no: the link between seen and felt shape must be learned. For three centuries "Molyneux's problem" could not be tested. Then, in a study published in 2011, Richard Held, Pawan Sinha and colleagues working with Project Prakash in India tested children who had been blind from birth with treatable cataracts. Immediately after surgery the children could see the shapes clearly but could not pick out by sight the shape they had just felt; within days, the link appeared. Locke's answer was largely right, and the learning was fast. George Berkeley (1685 to 1753), an Irish bishop, pushed Locke's argument to a startling end. If colour and warmth exist only in the perceiver, why not size and shape too? All we ever know are our own perceptions. To exist, for any object, is to be perceived: in Latin, esse est percipi . This position is called subjective idealism or mentalism. Berkeley also made a lasting contribution to the psychology of perception. In An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision (1709) he argued that we are not born able to see distance; we learn it, by associating visual cues (such as the feeling of the eyes converging on a near object, or blur) with the experience of reaching and walking. This is the first empiricist theory of depth perception, and the nativist reply to it is one of the threads of Chapter 4. David Hume (1711 to 1776), a Scot, published A Treatise of Human Nature in 1739 and 1740. He divided the contents of the mind into impressions (vivid, immediate experiences) and ideas (faint copies of impressions, as when you remember a taste). Ideas are joined, he said, by three laws of association: resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect. He thought of association as a kind of gentle mental force, the mind's equivalent of Newton's gravity. Then he turned the analysis on causation itself and found that we never see one event make another happen; we see only that the two have always been joined (constant conjunction), and the mind forms the habit of expecting one after the other. Even the self, Hume said, is nothing but "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". Hume's scepticism woke the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, as we shall see. Associationism: Hartley, the two Mills and Bain Out of British empiricism grew a doctrine with a name of its own. Its name, associationism , refers to the view that complex mental life, including memory, thought and emotion, is built up by linking simple elements (sensations and ideas) according to a few laws, above all contiguity and frequency. Four writers turned it into a system. David Hartley (1705 to 1757), a physician, published Observations on Man in 1749. He was the first to give association a physiological basis: sensations are vibrations in the nerves and brain, and they leave behind miniature vibrations, which he called vibratiuncles , that are ideas. When two vibrations occur together often, they become linked, so that one later sets off the other. Contiguity, strengthened by repetition, was for Hartley the master law, and he distinguished simultaneous from successive associations. Historians usually credit him with founding associationism as a formal doctrine. James Mill (1773 to 1836) took the doctrine to its most mechanical extreme in Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind (1829). For him a complex idea is nothing more than the sum of the simple ideas that compose it: the idea of a house is the ideas of bricks, mortar, windows and so on, added together, and the idea of "everything" is all the other ideas at once. This view is called mental mechanics . His son, John Stuart Mill (1806 to 1873), saw the flaw. In A System of Logic (1843) he argued that ideas can fuse into a whole with properties that none of the parts possessed, just as hydrogen and oxygen combine into water, which is like neither gas. His favourite example was Newton's colour disc: paint the colours of the spectrum on a wheel and spin it, and you see white, which is not experienced as "seven colours added". This is mental chemistry . Think of masala chai. James Mill would say your idea of its taste is tea plus milk plus ginger plus cardamom plus sugar; John Stuart Mill would say the taste of good chai is a new whole that is in none of the ingredients. The younger Mill's idea anticipates both Wundt's creative synthesis (Section 1.5) and the Gestalt slogan that the whole is different from the sum of its parts (Chapter 2). The last of the associationists, the Scot Alexander Bain (1818 to 1903), brought the tradition to the edge of modern psychology. His The Senses and the Intellect (1855) and The Emotions and the Will (1859) were the standard British textbooks of psychology for half a century, and they tied every mental process to what was then known of the nervous system. Bain described how a random ("spontaneous") movement that happens to bring pleasure is retained and repeated, a trial-and-error account of learning that anticipates Thorndike. In 1876 he founded Mind , the first journal devoted to psychology and philosophy. Exam trap Mental mechanics belongs to the father, James Mill; mental chemistry to the son, John Stuart Mill. Do not mix up James Mill with William James, or John Stuart Mill with John Locke. "Tabula rasa" is Locke , not Plato (nativist), Descartes (innate ideas) or Kant (innate categories). If asked the source of knowledge "as per empiricists", the answer is sensory experience ; "logical reasoning" and "contemplation" are the rationalists' routes. The continental rationalists: Leibniz, Herbart and Kant While the British were building the mind out of sensations, philosophers in Germany insisted that the mind is active, organised and partly unconscious. Their ideas reached Wundt directly, so we need them in some detail. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646 to 1716), co-inventor of the calculus, pictured reality as made of countless monads : simple, indivisible, active units of force, each of which mirrors the whole universe from its own point of view. Monads do not act on one another (they are "windowless"); they are kept in step by a harmony that God arranged in advance. Applied to mind and body, this "pre-established harmony" is a form of parallelism, which we will meet below. More important for psychology was Leibniz's theory of consciousness. He argued that we receive many perceptions too weak to notice individually, which he called petites perceptions (small perceptions). Standing on a beach, you hear the roar of the sea, yet that roar is made of the sounds of thousands of single waves, none of which you could hear on its own. When enough small perceptions add up, they cross into clear awareness, a step Leibniz called apperception . Consciousness is therefore a matter of degree, not all or none, and much mental activity goes on below awareness. Against Locke he wrote, in his New Essays on Human Understanding , that there is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses, "except the intellect itself". Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776 to 1841), who succeeded to Kant's chair at Konigsberg, turned Leibniz's ideas into a kind of mental mechanics with mathematics. Ideas, he said, have strength, and they compete: incompatible ideas push each other down. An idea that is pushed down does not vanish; it sinks below a boundary he called the threshold of consciousness (a limen), where it remains active and strives to return. Fechner would borrow the idea of a threshold for psychophysics, and Freud's repressed ideas that push to return to awareness have a family resemblance to it. The ideas currently in consciousness form an organised body that Herbart called the apperceptive mass . A new idea is understood, or apperceived, only by being taken up into this mass of existing ideas; an idea that finds nothing related to attach to is not grasped at all. Herbart was also a great educational theorist, and the classroom lesson follows directly: teach new material by linking it to what the child already knows. (His followers later turned this into the "formal steps" of lesson planning, which teacher-training colleges in India still teach.) You have experienced this yourself: the term "apperception" is far easier to learn now, attached to Leibniz's sea and Herbart's competing ideas, than it would be as an isolated word in a list. Herbart said psychology could be empirical and mathematical, but he did not believe it could be experimental, and he kept it separate from physiology. Within forty years both claims would be overturned in Leipzig. Exam trap An IHBAS 2025 question asks what the "apperceptive mass" constitutes and keys pure perception and pre-existing ideas , meaning a new perception taken up into the store of ideas already in the mind. The term is Herbart's ; Wundt took over and reworked the idea of apperception, which is why the question names him. The distractors each belong to someone else: "a compound of elemental processes bound by association" is the associationist (and structuralist) picture of the mind; "sensation and pure perception" leaves out the existing ideas that are the whole point; "sensation plus unconscious inference" is Helmholtz's theory of perception (Section 1.3). Apperception as a word was coined by Leibniz. The most influential German philosopher of all, Immanuel Kant (1724 to 1804), answered Hume in his Critique of Pure Reason (1781). Hume had shown that experience alone can never give us necessary connections such as causality. Kant replied that the mind does not wait passively for experience to write on it; it imposes its own built-in forms on whatever the senses deliver. Space and time are the forms through which we must perceive anything, and categories such as causality, unity and substance are the frames through which we must think about it. We never know things as they are in themselves, only as our minds organise them. This is nativism of a sophisticated kind, and it passed through the perceptual nativists of the nineteenth century into Gestalt psychology. Kant also issued a challenge. Psychology, he argued, could never be a true natural science, because mental events cannot be measured, cannot be put to experiment, and are distorted by the very act of observing them. The history in the rest of this chapter can be read as a series of replies to Kant: Herbart made psychology mathematical, Fechner made it measurable, and Wundt made it experimental. The answers given over the next three centuries form a small set of positions that every psychology student must be able to name (Figure 1.2). The first, interactionism , is Descartes' own answer: mind and body are different substances that causally affect each other. Its weakness is the one Descartes never solved, namely how something with no physical properties can push on something physical. Some of his followers, notably Nicolas Malebranche, proposed occasionalism : mind and body never act on each other, and God produces the bodily event on each occasion of the mental one, and the reverse. The second, psychophysical parallelism , holds that mental events and bodily events run side by side, perfectly correlated, but neither causes the other. Leibniz's picture was two clocks that keep identical time because they were set together at the start, not because one drives the other. Parallelism was attractive to the first experimental psychologists because it let them correlate mental events with physiological ones without worrying about causation; Wundt and Titchener both held versions of it. The third, epiphenomenalism , holds that bodily (brain) events cause mental events, but mental events cause nothing; consciousness is a by-product. Its best-known advocate, the English biologist Thomas Henry Huxley (1825 to 1895), compared consciousness to the whistle of a steam engine: it accompanies the work of the engine but does nothing to drive it. Finally, monism denies that there are two substances at all. Materialist monism (Hobbes) says only matter exists and mind is a process of the body. Idealist monism (Berkeley) says only minds and their perceptions exist. And double-aspect theory , associated with the Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza (1632 to 1677), says there is one underlying reality that shows itself in two ways: seen from the inside it is mind, seen from the outside it is body, as the same curved line is concave from one side and convex from the other. Fechner, the founder of psychophysics, held a view close to this one.
