A word on the philosophy of science Questions about the mind sit inside larger philosophical questions about what exists and how we can know it, and a few terms from the philosophy of science turn up in psychology papers. The term ontology (from the Greek for "being") names the branch of philosophy that deals with existence: what kinds of things are real? Is the mind a thing, a process, or an illusion? By contrast, epistemology deals with knowledge: how do we know what we know, and what counts as good evidence? The nativist-empiricist debate above is an epistemological debate. In the nineteenth century the French philosopher Auguste Comte (1798 to 1857) founded positivism , the view that genuine knowledge comes only from observable, verifiable facts, and that speculation about unobservable causes should be abandoned. Comte rejected introspection on the ground that the mind cannot observe itself, any more than the eye can see itself, an objection you will meet again when Wundt's method comes under fire. Post-positivism , associated with the twentieth-century philosopher Karl Popper, accepts that all scientific knowledge is fallible and provisional, so that theories are tested by trying to refute them rather than by piling up confirmations. Scientific realism holds that the unobservable entities described by our best theories (electrons, genes, perhaps memory traces) really exist. Of these terms, only ontology is defined by the question of existence. Philosophy, then, handed psychology its questions and some brilliant guesses. What it could not supply was a way to settle the arguments. For that, psychology had to borrow the methods of a different parent: experimental physiology. 1.3 Physiological and Biological Roots Lower yield · 1 Q By the middle of the nineteenth century, physiologists in Germany, France and Britain were doing something philosophers never had: cutting, stimulating, timing and measuring living nervous systems. Their findings did two things for the future psychology. They showed that the machinery of mind could be studied by experiment, and they gave Wundt, who trained as a physiologist, his methods and his confidence. Nerves carry the message The first great discovery was about the wiring. In 1811 the Scottish anatomist Charles Bell (1774 to 1842) described, in a privately printed pamphlet, evidence that the nerve roots entering the spinal cord at the front and at the back have different functions. In 1822 the French physiologist Francois Magendie (1783 to 1855) showed it decisively in experiments on young animals. The result is the Bell-Magendie law : the dorsal (back) roots of the spinal nerves carry sensory information in, and the ventral (front) roots carry motor commands out. The nervous system, in other words, has separate input and output channels, an anatomical basis for the distinction between sensation and movement, and ultimately for the stimulus-response unit. (The two men's quarrel over who deserved credit is a classic example of simultaneous discovery, which we discuss in Section 1.8.) The most influential physiologist of the age was Johannes Muller (1801 to 1858) of Berlin, whose Handbook of Human Physiology (published in parts from 1833 to 1840) summarised the field for a generation. Muller's best-known idea is the doctrine of specific nerve energies : the quality of a sensation depends not on the stimulus but on which nerve is stimulated. The optic nerve, however it is excited, produces only sensations of light; the auditory nerve only sound. You can test this now: close your eyes and press gently on the outer corner of one eyelid. You will see a patch of light, though no light has entered your eye; pressure on the optic pathway is "read" as light. A blow to the head makes a boxer "see stars" for the same reason. Muller's idea meant that we never perceive the world directly, only the state of our own nerves, a physiological version of the philosophers' point that experience is not the same as the object (the modern form of the idea, "labelled lines", is covered in Chapter 3). Muller's students included Hermann von Helmholtz and Emil du Bois-Reymond, and Wundt himself spent a semester in his Berlin laboratory. Muller believed that the speed of the nerve impulse was so great that it might never be measured. His student proved him wrong within a decade. Key study: Helmholtz times the nerve impulse (1850) Question. Is the nerve impulse effectively instantaneous, like light, or does it take measurable time? Method. Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) used a frog's nerve with the muscle still attached. He stimulated the nerve first at a point far from the muscle and then at a point near it, and timed the delay before the muscle twitched. Result. Stimulation farther from the muscle produced a later twitch, and dividing the difference in distance by the difference in time gave a speed of only about 27 metres per second, roughly the speed of a car on a highway. Conclusion. Nervous activity is a physical process that takes time. If nerve conduction takes time, so may perceiving and deciding, and those times can be measured. Caveat. When Helmholtz tried to measure reaction times in human beings, the results varied so much from trial to trial and person to person that he gave up, an early hint of the individual differences that Galton and Cattell would later study. Helmholtz was perhaps the greatest scientist of the century, and three more of his ideas reach psychology. First, his theory of unconscious inference : perception is not a simple copy of sensation but a conclusion the mind draws, quickly and without awareness, from sensory data and past experience. When you see a distant elephant as huge though its image on your retina is tiny, you are "inferring" its size from its distance. This made Helmholtz an empiricist about perception, and it is the ancestor of modern ideas of perception as hypothesis-testing (Chapter 4). Second, building on a suggestion made by the English physician Thomas Young (1773 to 1829) in 1802, Helmholtz developed the trichromatic theory of colour vision, the Young-Helmholtz theory, which holds that colour vision depends on three types of receptor, most sensitive to different parts of the spectrum. Third, he proposed a resonance (place) theory of hearing. All three are developed in Chapters 3 and 4. For this chapter, remember that Wundt worked as Helmholtz's assistant at Heidelberg for several years. Exam trap "Helmholtz gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision" is the keyed answer to the bank question about him. The distractors are carefully chosen. The just noticeable difference belongs to Weber and Fechner (Section 1.4); the law of effect to Thorndike (Chapter 6). "Proposed the concept of the unconscious" is a trap because Helmholtz did propose unconscious inference , but the concept of the unconscious mind in the psychodynamic sense belongs to Freud (and its philosophical roots to Leibniz and Herbart). Mapping functions onto the brain If the nerves are wires, is the brain a single organ that does everything everywhere, or a collection of specialised parts? The modern answer, localisation of function , emerged through a strange mixture of quackery and careful science. The quackery came first. The Viennese physician Franz Joseph Gall (1758 to 1828) was a skilled brain anatomist, but he is remembered for a bolder claim: that the brain is made up of separate organs for separate mental faculties (such as acquisitiveness, combativeness or love of offspring), that a well-developed faculty means a larger organ, and that a larger organ pushes out the skull above it. By feeling the bumps on a person's head, therefore, one could read his character. Gall's collaborator Johann Gaspar Spurzheim (1776 to 1832) popularised the system under the name phrenology and carried it across Europe and America, where "phrenological parlours" read heads for a fee. Phrenology was wrong in its method (skull shape does not reflect the brain beneath, and Gall chose his evidence selectively), but it was right in its central assumption that different parts of the brain do different things. Phrenology's first scientific critic was the French physiologist Pierre Flourens (1794 to 1867). In the 1820s he used the method of ablation (also called extirpation): surgically removing a part of the brain of an animal, usually a pigeon or rabbit, and observing what behaviour was lost. He found real localisation at the level of large structures: damage to the cerebellum disrupted the coordination of movement, damage to the medulla stopped breathing and heartbeat, and removal of the cerebral hemispheres abolished perception and voluntary action. But within the cerebral hemispheres he found no faculties in particular places: the effects of damage seemed to depend on how much tissue was removed, and the cortex seemed to act as a whole. Flourens' ablation method became standard in physiological psychology, and his view of the cortex as acting as a whole was revived a century later by Karl Lashley (covered in the Physiological Psychology book). Localisation within the cortex was finally demonstrated through language. In 1861 the French surgeon Paul Broca (1824 to 1880) examined a patient named Leborgne, known in the hospital as "Tan" because that was nearly the only syllable he could say. Tan understood much of what was said to him but could not produce speech. When he died, Broca's autopsy found damage in the left frontal lobe, in a region now called Broca's area, and by 1865 Broca had concluded that "we speak with the left hemisphere". In 1874 the 26-year-old German neurologist Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) described the opposite pattern: patients with damage to the left temporal lobe who spoke fluently but meaninglessly and could not understand speech. Broca's aphasia is effortful, non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension; Wernicke's aphasia is fluent speech with poor comprehension. (The aphasias, including the transcortical and conduction forms, are covered in the Physiological Psychology book.) Meanwhile, in 1870, the German physicians Gustav Fritsch (1838 to 1927) and Eduard Hitzig (1838 to 1907) applied weak electric currents to the exposed cortex of dogs and found a strip of the frontal lobe where stimulation produced movements of specific body parts on the opposite side of the body: the motor cortex. Electrical stimulation now joined ablation and clinical autopsy as a method of mapping the brain. Table 1.4 brings the localisation story together. Table 1.4 The localisation pioneers. It had a plausible theory, confident practitioners, satisfied customers and an apparently huge body of supporting cases, yet it was false, because its evidence was gathered selectively and never put to a fair test. Every assessment tool you will learn to use, from an intelligence test to a projective test, must earn its place by evidence of reliability and validity (the Assessment book), not by the confidence of the person using it. Charles Darwin: the human animal Physiology showed that the mind had machinery. Biology showed where the machinery came from. When Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) published On the Origin of Species in 1859, he proposed that species change over generations through natural selection : individuals vary, some variations help their owners survive and reproduce, and those variations become more common in later generations. In The Descent of Man (1871) he applied the theory to human beings, and in The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) he argued that facial expressions of emotion are inherited and universal, shared with other animals because they once served adaptive purposes (baring the teeth in anger is a remnant of preparing to bite). He even published a diary of his infant son's development (1877), one of the first "baby biographies". Darwin gave psychology three gifts, and each grew into a branch of the discipline. Continuity between species. If humans evolved from other animals, then animal minds differ from ours in degree, not kind, and studying animals can tell us about ourselves. This is the foundation of comparative psychology and of all later animal research on learning. Function. If a trait exists because it helped survival, then the right question to ask about any mental process is what it is for . This question is the heart of functionalism (Section 1.7), and through functionalism, of today's evolutionary psychology. Variation. Natural selection works on differences between individuals, so those differences are worth measuring. This idea was taken up by Darwin's own half-cousin. Francis Galton and the measurement of individual differences Francis Galton (1822 to 1911) shared a grandfather, the physician-poet Erasmus Darwin, with Charles Darwin. Independently wealthy, he never held a university post, and he could not see anything without wanting to count it: he once tried to make a "beauty map" of Britain by secretly tallying attractive and unattractive women he passed in different towns. After reading the Origin , he devoted himself to human variation, and in doing so he founded the study of individual differences . His first major book, Hereditary Genius (1869), traced the families of eminent judges, statesmen, scientists and others, and found that eminence ran in families far more than chance would predict. Galton concluded that ability is inherited. The flaw is obvious to you now: eminent families also pass on wealth, education and connections, so his data could not separate heredity from environment. Galton saw the problem himself and, in 1875, proposed studying twins to separate the effects of "nature and nurture" (a phrase he popularised). He was the first to use twin studies for this purpose. Key study: Galton's anthropometric laboratory (1884) Question. How much do people differ in basic physical and mental capacities? Method. At the International Health Exhibition in London in 1884, Galton set up an anthropometric laboratory where, for threepence, visitors were measured on height, weight, arm span, breathing capacity, strength of grip, swiftness of a blow, keenness of sight and hearing, colour discrimination, reaction time and the highest pitch they could hear (tested with a whistle he designed). More than 9,000 people passed through. Reasoning. Following the empiricist logic that all knowledge enters through the senses, Galton assumed that people with sharper senses and quicker reactions would be more intelligent. Result. He obtained the first large body of data on human individual differences, and to analyse it he had to invent new statistics. Criticism. The assumption linking sensory keenness to intelligence turned out to be wrong, as Cattell's followers discovered (Section 1.7); intelligence testing had to wait for Binet's very different approach (Chapter 9). The statistics may be Galton's greatest legacy. Studying the heights of parents and children (and, earlier, the sizes of sweet-pea seeds), he noticed that very tall parents tend to have children who are tall but less extreme than themselves, a phenomenon now called regression to the mean (1886). From this he developed the idea of correlation , a measure of how closely two variables vary together (1888); his younger colleague Karl Pearson (1857 to 1936) later produced the formula for the correlation coefficient that you will use in the Research Methodology book. Galton also pioneered the questionnaire (asking people to describe the vividness of their mental image of that morning's breakfast table), and in 1879 he devised the word association test: he read a word and noted the first association it called up, and was startled to find how many of his own associations reached back to childhood and revealed thoughts he would rather not publish. Carl Jung later developed word association into a clinical technique (the Personality book). There is a darker side. In 1883 Galton coined the word eugenics for the programme of improving the human stock by encouraging the "fit" to have more children and discouraging the "unfit". Eugenics was later used to justify forced sterilisation and, in Nazi Germany, mass murder. Galton's statistics are permanent tools of psychology; his eugenics is a permanent warning. Animal minds: from anecdote to Morgan's canon Darwin's idea of continuity invited a new question: how intelligent are animals? Darwin's young friend George John Romanes (1848 to 1894) set out to answer it, and his Animal Intelligence (1882) is usually treated as the first book of comparative psychology. Romanes gathered stories, from naturalists, pet owners and newspaper readers, of animals doing clever things: a cat that opened a door latch, a dog that seemed to plan. This anecdotal method had two weaknesses. Anecdotes are selected (no one writes in to report a dog doing something stupid), and they invite anthropomorphism , reading human thoughts and feelings into animal behaviour. The correction came from the British psychologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan (1852 to 1936). Morgan's own fox terrier, Tony, learned to open the garden gate by lifting the latch with his head. A visitor who saw only the finished act would have credited Tony with understanding how latches work, but Morgan had watched the learning: it came slowly, through many chance successes while Tony poked his head through the railings. In An Introduction to Comparative Psychology (1894) Morgan stated the rule now called Morgan's canon : "In no case may we interpret an action as the outcome of the exercise of a higher psychical faculty, if it can be interpreted as the outcome of the exercise of one which stands lower in the psychological scale." It is a principle of parsimony : prefer the simplest explanation that fits the facts. Key study: Clever Hans (1904 to 1907) The claim. In Berlin, a retired schoolteacher, Wilhelm von Osten, exhibited a horse called Hans that seemed to add, subtract and answer questions by tapping its hoof. A commission that included the psychologist Carl Stumpf found no trickery in 1904. Method. Stumpf's student Oskar Pfungst then tested Hans systematically, varying whether the questioner knew the answer and whether Hans could see the questioner. Result. Hans answered correctly only when the questioner knew the answer and was visible. Without meaning to, questioners tensed as the taps began and relaxed slightly, or raised their heads, when the right number was reached, and Hans had learned to stop at that cue. Conclusion (published 1907). The horse was clever, but at reading people, not at arithmetic: a perfect illustration of Morgan's canon. The "Clever Hans effect" is why modern experiments use observers who do not know which condition a participant is in. Comparative psychology soon moved from anecdote into the laboratory. Edward Thorndike's puzzle-box studies of cats (1898, Chapter 6) and Margaret Floy Washburn's textbook The Animal Mind (1908, Section 1.7) carried it into the twentieth century, and Watson would build behaviourism on it. Clinical link Morgan's canon is good clinical sense. A child who will not read aloud in class may have a reading disability, poor eyesight, anxiety or a hearing problem before we conclude that he is "defiant" or "lazy". Test the simpler, lower-level explanations first. You will see in Section 1.7 that the first patient at the world's first psychological clinic turned out to have exactly such a simple problem. The proof, when it came, came from two professors at the University of Leipzig, and it took the form of a simple idea: you cannot put a ruler against a sensation, but you can measure the stimuli that produce it and find the rule that links the two. This section covers that idea and the parallel discovery that mental acts take measurable time. The full treatment of thresholds and psychophysical laws is in Chapter 3; here we need only enough to see why they made a science of mind possible. Ernst Weber and the just noticeable difference Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795 to 1878) was a Leipzig physiologist who studied the sense of touch. Touch two points of a pair of compasses to your fingertip and you will feel two points even when they are only a few millimetres apart; touch them to the middle of your back and they must be several centimetres apart before you feel two rather than one. This "two-point threshold" was one of Weber's discoveries. The more important one came from lifting weights. Weber asked people to compare a standard weight with slightly heavier ones and found the smallest difference they could detect, the just noticeable difference (JND). The JND was not a fixed amount but a fixed proportion of the standard weight. A worked example makes the point. Suppose that for lifted weights the proportion is one-fortieth. If you are holding 40 grams, you will just notice the change when one gram is added. If you are holding 400 grams, adding one gram is now undetectable; you need ten. In symbols, the JND (written delta I) divided by the original intensity (I) is a constant, k. Fechner later named this relation Weber's law . You know it from daily life: a single candle lights up a dark room, but carried into a brightly lit wedding hall it makes no visible difference. Gustav Fechner and the founding of psychophysics Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801 to 1887) was a professor of physics at Leipzig who suffered a long and severe breakdown in the late 1830s and early 1840s, made worse by damage to his eyes from gazing at the sun through coloured glass while studying afterimages. When he recovered he turned to philosophy, and in particular to the relation between mind and matter, which he believed to be two sides of one reality. On the morning of 22 October 1850, lying in bed, he had the insight that would make his name: the relation between the bodily and the mental could be expressed as a mathematical law. If equal ratios of stimulus intensity produce equal steps in sensation (as Weber's data implied), then sensation must grow with the logarithm of the stimulus. This is Fechner's law , usually written S = k log I, where S is the strength of the sensation and I the intensity of the stimulus. Push a case through it. Switch on one bulb in a dark room, then a second: the room gets noticeably brighter. To get the same apparent increase again you need not three bulbs but four, and then eight, then sixteen. Sensation climbs in equal steps while the stimulus doubles at each step. That is what a logarithmic relation means. Fechner spent ten years testing his insight and published the results as Elements of Psychophysics in 1860. He defined psychophysics as the exact science of the functional relations between body and mind, and he gave it three methods that are still taught today: the method of limits, the method of constant stimuli and the method of adjustment (average error), together with the concepts of the absolute threshold and the difference threshold (all in Chapter 3). Researchers in psychophysics still celebrate 22 October as "Fechner Day". One point about thresholds is worth fixing now, because it matters for perception as much as for psychophysics. Whether a stimulus is perceived depends not only on how strong it is but on how long it lasts. A faint flash of light, or the contour (edge) of a briefly shown shape, is seen only if the stimulation reaches a minimum intensity and is present for a minimum exposure time; for very brief exposures the two trade off, so that a weaker flash must last longer to be seen (Bloch's law, 1885). This is why the early laboratories controlled exposure time so carefully with the tachistoscope. Reaction time, by contrast, measures how quickly a person responds once a stimulus has been perceived (as you will see below); it is not a condition for perceiving anything. Why does Fechner matter so much to the history? Because he answered Kant. He showed that mental events could be measured, indirectly but precisely, and that measurement could be repeated by anyone. Wundt, Ebbinghaus and G. E. Muller all built on his book. The historian Edwin Garrigues Boring (1886 to 1968) even argued that 1860, not 1879, could be taken as the founding date of experimental psychology. The convention, however, is clear: Fechner founded psychophysics; Wundt founded psychology as an independent experimental discipline. Exam trap The "founder of psychophysics" is Fechner , not Weber (whose work Fechner built on and named), not Wundt (who founded the laboratory) and not Ebbinghaus (who applied Fechner's spirit to memory). The JND is Weber's concept; S = k log I is Fechner's law. Keep 1850 (the insight, 22 October) separate from 1860 (the book). The personal equation and mental chronometry The second line of measurement began in an observatory. In 1796 the Astronomer Royal at Greenwich, Nevil Maskelyne, dismissed his assistant David Kinnebrook because Kinnebrook's timings of the moment a star crossed a hair line in the telescope were consistently later than his own, by most of a second. Some twenty-five years later the German astronomer Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel compared the timings of several experienced astronomers and found that each had his own systematic error. No one was simply right; every observer took a characteristic amount of time to see and respond. Astronomers called the correction for each observer his personal equation . Here, in effect, was the first measurement of individual differences in reaction time, and the first hint that perceiving takes time. Helmholtz had shown that nerves take time. The Dutch physiologist Franciscus Cornelis Donders (1818 to 1889) asked whether the time taken by a mental process itself could be measured, and in 1868 he devised a way. His subtraction method compares reaction times in tasks that differ by exactly one mental stage (Figure 1.3). In the a-reaction (simple reaction time), one light appears and the participant presses a key as fast as possible: the task needs only detection and response. In the c-reaction (go/no-go), one of two lights appears and the participant must respond to one of them only: now the stimulus must also be identified. In the b-reaction (choice reaction time), each light has its own key: the stimulus must be identified and a response must be chosen. Subtract the a-time from the c-time and you have the time needed to identify the stimulus; subtract the c-time from the b-time and you have the time needed to choose the response. a-reaction (simple) one light, one key Detect Respond c-reaction (go/no-go) respond to one light only Detect Identify Respond b-reaction (choice) two lights, two keys Detect Identify Choose Respond c-time minus a-time = time to identify the stimulus b-time minus c-time = time to choose the response The method assumes that adding a stage leaves the other stages unchanged ("pure insertion"). Figure 1.3 Donders' subtraction method (1868). Each task adds one mental stage to the one above it, so subtracting reaction times isolates the duration of the added stage. Donders had founded mental chronometry , the measurement of the time course of mental processes through reaction time (the interval between the onset of a stimulus and the beginning of the response). Its weak point is marked at the foot of Figure 1.3: the method assumes that inserting a stage leaves the other stages exactly as they were, which is often untrue. A century later the cognitive psychologist Saul Sternberg replaced it with a subtler method that does not need this assumption (Chapter 8). But the idea that the mind can be studied by timing it was immediately taken up in Leipzig. When Max Friedrich pressed his key in the winter of 1879, he was running a version of Donders' experiment, trying to measure the time taken by apperception. Hermann Ebbinghaus: the higher processes measured Wundt, as you will see, believed that the higher mental processes such as memory and thought could not be studied by experiment. A young German scholar proved him wrong without ever working in his laboratory. Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909) came across a second-hand copy of Fechner's Elements of Psychophysics while travelling in France and England in the late 1870s (accounts differ on whether the bookshop was in Paris or London), and resolved to do for memory what Fechner had done for sensation. To remove the effect of meaning and prior knowledge, he invented nonsense syllables , consonant-vowel-consonant combinations such as DAX or BOK, and memorised lists of them himself, under strictly controlled conditions, for several years. He measured memory by the savings method : how much less time it took to relearn a list than it had taken to learn it the first time. The result, published in On Memory (1885), included the first forgetting curve , showing rapid loss in the first hour and slower loss thereafter. Ebbinghaus worked alone, at Berlin and later at Breslau, outside any school, and he is the author of the sentence quoted at the end of Section 1.1 ("Psychology has a long past, but only a short history", 1908). You will meet his curve and his methods properly in Chapter 7. Exam trap "What do Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common?" The options are (a) each worked independently and was a pioneer, (b) each founded a formal psychology laboratory, (c) each developed novel methods to study how the mind works, and (d) (a) and (c). Option (b) is false: Freud never founded a laboratory. Both (a) and (c) are true: Ebbinghaus invented nonsense syllables and the savings method, Galton invented the questionnaire, word association and correlation, and Freud invented free association. So the best answer is (d) , which is how the Panwar bank keys it. The RML 2020 paper printed the same question and keyed (a) . Since (a) alone leaves out a true statement, (d) is the more defensible answer; if you meet this question again, choose (d), and do not be shaken if a key prefers (a). By 1870, then, all the parts were on the bench. Philosophy had supplied the questions and the idea of mental elements and their association; physiology had supplied the experimental method and the reaction-time technique; biology had supplied the idea of function and the interest in individual differences; and psychophysics had shown that the mind could be measured. What was missing was someone to declare that these belonged together as a new, independent science, and to build an institution for it. 1.5 Wilhelm Wundt and the Founding of Experimental Psychology Medium yield · 6 Qs Psychology does have a founder in the way that few sciences do, a single person who set out deliberately to create it. Wundt is remembered as the father of experimental psychology, and also, without qualification, as the father of psychology as a science. To understand why, you need to know what he did and what he believed. From physiologist to psychologist Wilhelm Maximilian Wundt (1832 to 1920) was born on 16 August 1832 at Neckarau, near Mannheim in south-western Germany, the son of a Lutheran pastor. He was a lonely, daydreaming schoolboy who did poorly at first, but he became an intensely hard-working student of medicine at Heidelberg, with a semester in Berlin in Johannes Muller's laboratory. After qualifying in medicine he chose research over practice and spent several years at Heidelberg as an assistant to Helmholtz. During those Heidelberg years his plan took shape. In Contributions to the Theory of Sensory Perception (published in parts from 1858 to 1862) he called for an experimental psychology; in 1862 he began teaching a course on psychology as a natural science; and in 1863 he published Lectures on the Human and Animal Mind . His decisive book was Principles of Physiological Psychology ( Grundzuge der physiologischen Psychologie ), published in two parts in 1873 and 1874. Its preface announced that the work was "an attempt to mark out a new domain of science". Historians rank it among the most important books in the history of modern psychology, and Wundt revised it through six editions. After a year at Zurich, Wundt moved in 1875 to Leipzig as professor of philosophy, the post he held for the rest of his career. The room for apparatus followed, then in 1879 the research of students like Max Friedrich, then a journal, Philosophische Studien ( Philosophical Studies ), founded in 1881 to publish the laboratory's work and usually counted as the first journal of experimental psychology. Wundt also wrote a shorter textbook, Outlines of Psychology (1896), and, in his last twenty years, the ten volumes of his Volkerpsychologie (1900 to 1920). Boring later calculated that Wundt published more than 50,000 printed pages in his lifetime. He died on 31 August 1920, shortly after finishing his memoirs. Exam trap Wundt's 1873 to 1874 book is Principles of Physiological Psychology ; William James's 1890 book is The Principles of Psychology . Questions asking who wrote "Principles of Psychology" want James . And "physiological psychology" in Wundt's title did not mean the study of the brain. It meant psychology that borrows the experimental methods of physiology. Do not answer a question about Wundt's lab with "brain research". What Wundt studied: immediate experience and voluntarism Every science, Wundt said, studies experience, but from different standpoints. The physicist studies mediate experience: experience used as a means of learning about something else, filtered through instruments and concepts. Psychology studies immediate experience : experience as it is directly lived, before interpretation. Look at a red hibiscus. A physicist describes the light it reflects as electromagnetic radiation of a certain wavelength; a psychologist in Wundt's sense describes the experience itself, the quality of the redness, its intensity, how long it lasts, whether it is pleasant. Wundt's analysis of immediate experience found two kinds of elements. Sensations are the elementary contents produced when a sense organ is stimulated, varying in quality and intensity. Simple feelings are the subjective accompaniments of sensations, such as the pleasantness of a taste or the strain of waiting. Elements combine into compounds: ideas, emotions, acts of will. Psychology's task was to analyse conscious processes into their elements, to discover how the elements are connected, and to state the laws of those connections. So far this sounds like British associationism in a laboratory coat. But Wundt insisted that the mind is not a passive meeting place where elements stick together by contiguity. It is active, and the activity is that of attention and will. He called his system voluntarism , from the Latin voluntas (will). The central active process is apperception, the term he took from Leibniz and Herbart and made his own. Wundt distinguished the broad field of consciousness from its narrow focus . Contents that merely enter the field are perceived ; contents brought into the focus by attention are apperceived . Sit in an examination hall: the whirr of the ceiling fans, a cough two rows back and the invigilator's footsteps are all perceived, at the edge of consciousness; the question in front of you is apperceived, held in the clear focus where you can work on it. Apperception does more than select; it also combines. Wundt's principle of creative synthesis (also called the law of psychic resultants) states that when elements are combined by apperception, the result has properties that none of the elements possessed. A melody is not just the sum of its notes, since the same notes in a different order make a different tune; the word "SAHIL" is not just five letters. This is John Stuart Mill's mental chemistry placed at the centre of a psychology, and it is why Wundt cannot fairly be called a mere elementist. Remember Wundt's own name for his system was voluntarism . Many Indian textbooks list Wundt as the founder of structuralism , because Titchener carried his work to America and gave it that name; in exam questions that pair "structuralism" with Wundt and Titchener, accept the pairing. But if a question asks for the system that stresses will, attention and apperception, the answer is voluntarism, and the person is Wundt. The tridimensional theory of feeling One of Wundt's best-known ideas came from listening to a metronome. As he attended to its clicks, he noticed that some rhythmic patterns felt more pleasant than others; that while he waited for the next click he felt a slight strain, which was released when the click came; and that a fast tempo felt stirring while a slow one felt calming. From these self-observations he concluded, in 1896, that simple feelings vary along three independent dimensions: pleasure versus displeasure , tension versus relaxation , and excitement versus depression (sometimes translated excitement versus calm). This is the tridimensional theory of feeling (Figure 1.4). Any feeling can be described as a point in this three-dimensional space, and an emotion is a sequence of feelings moving through it over time. Waiting outside the result board after an examination, for example, might be unpleasant, tense and excited all at once; the moment you find your roll number, the feeling swings to pleasure and relaxation. pleasure-displeasure excitement-depression tension-relaxation neutral Pleasure Displeasure Excitement Depression (calm) Tension Relaxation Figure 1.4 Wundt's tridimensional theory of feeling (1896). Every simple feeling is a point on three independent axes; an emotion is a path through this space. Titchener later kept only the pleasure-displeasure axis. The theory was controversial in its day; Titchener's observers at Cornell could find only pleasantness and unpleasantness, and he rejected the other two dimensions. But notice how modern it looks. Twentieth-century research on emotion and on the meanings of words repeatedly found two or three broad dimensions, most often pleasantness (valence) and arousal, very close to Wundt's first and third axes. (Emotion theories are covered in Chapter 11.) The method: experimental introspection How do you study immediate experience? You have to ask the person having it. Wundt's method is called introspection (literally "looking within"), but it was very different from the armchair reflection of the philosophers, which Wundt distrusted as much as Comte had. His word for the armchair kind was Selbstbeobachtung (self-observation); the kind he accepted he called innere Wahrnehmung (internal perception), and it was usable only under strict experimental control. (English textbooks often call Wundt's version "experimental self-observation", which is why the terms confuse students; the point is the contrast between uncontrolled and controlled looking within.) Wundt laid down four rules for it: The observer must be able to tell when the process to be observed begins (the experimenter presents the stimulus at a signalled moment). The observer must be in a state of readiness, with attention fully concentrated. Each observation must be repeatable many times under the same conditions. The conditions must be variable, so that the stimulus can be systematically changed and the effect on experience noted. Observers were trained, and most of their reports were short and quantitative: whether a stimulus was present or absent, louder or softer, longer or shorter, the same or different, together with reaction times measured by the chronoscope. Wundt did not ask his observers for long descriptions of their inner life; that style of introspection belongs to Titchener and, in a different form, to the Wurzburg school, as Section 1.6 will show. Exam trap "Who is most associated with the technique of introspection?" is Wundt . "Which school used introspection as its method of analysis?" is structuralism . In the analogy "Charles Spearman is to factor analysis as Wilhelm Wundt is to ...", the answer is introspection (Spearman, himself a Wundt student, invented factor analysis; psychoanalysis is Freud's, functionalism is James's, humanism is Maslow's and Rogers'). Wertheimer, Watson and James are wrong answers to the first question: Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology, Watson attacked introspection, and James used casual introspection but is not known for a technique of it. Volkerpsychologie: the other half of Wundt Wundt believed that the laboratory could reach only the simpler processes: sensation, feeling, reaction, attention. The higher mental processes, such as thinking, language, morality and religious belief, are shaped by culture and history, and an individual sitting in front of a chronoscope cannot reveal them. They must be studied instead through their collective products: the languages, myths, customs, arts, laws and religions of whole peoples. Wundt devoted the last twenty years of his life to this second psychology, publishing it in ten volumes between 1900 and 1920 as Volkerpsychologie , usually translated as "folk psychology" and better understood today as cultural psychology . A one-volume summary, Elements of Folk Psychology , appeared in 1912. For most of the twentieth century American textbooks ignored this half of Wundt, partly because few of his American students read the later volumes, and the picture of Wundt as a narrow laboratory elementist owes much to that neglect. Today he is often praised as a forerunner of cultural psychology, which matters for a country like India where psychologists have long argued that Western laboratory findings cannot simply be transplanted. Exam trap "Who gave the concept of folk psychology?" (RML 2024) is Wilhelm Maximilian Wundt . The distractors: Freud founded psychoanalysis; Pavlov discovered classical conditioning; Wilhelm Roentgen was a physicist who discovered X-rays in 1895, included only because his first name matches. Be aware that in modern philosophy of mind "folk psychology" means something else (our everyday explanations of behaviour in terms of beliefs and desires); in history questions it is Wundt's Volkerpsychologie . Leipzig as a training ground Wundt's laboratory was above all a school. Students came from across Europe and, in great numbers, from America, took doctorates under him, and went home to found laboratories, journals and departments of their own. Wundt supervised well over a hundred doctoral students in psychology, and the first generation of professional psychologists in several countries learned the trade in his rooms. Two stories show the atmosphere. James McKeen Cattell later recalled walking into Wundt's office and announcing that Wundt needed an assistant and that he would be it; Wundt agreed, though he called Cattell's interest in individual differences in reaction time "ganz Amerikanisch" (typically American). And G. Stanley Hall, who studied at Leipzig in 1879 and 1880, liked to call himself Wundt's first American student. Table 1.5 lists the students who matter most for examinations. The version that reached America first, and that gave the first school its name, was carried by a young Englishman who had spent two years in Leipzig and who spent the rest of his life defending what he believed was Wundt's programme in its pure form. Edward Bradford Titchener at Cornell Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927) was born in Chichester, England, studied at Oxford, and took his doctorate under Wundt in 1892. Finding no opening for an experimental psychologist in England, he accepted a post at Cornell University in New York State that same year and stayed there until his death 35 years later. He was a commanding and formal figure who lectured in his Oxford academic gown, ran his laboratory as an absolute ruler, and translated several of Wundt's books into English. His own books, especially An Outline of Psychology (1896), the laboratory manuals Experimental Psychology (1901 to 1905) and A Text-book of Psychology (1909 to 1910), trained a generation. In 1904 Titchener formed his own small society, "the Experimentalists", for researchers who shared his approach; it barred women from its meetings until after his death. The irony is sharp, because his first doctoral student was a woman, Margaret Floy Washburn, whom you will meet in Section 1.7. Titchener supervised more than fifty doctoral students in all. The structuralist programme Titchener named his approach in an 1898 article, "The Postulates of a Structural Psychology", and the name stuck: structuralism is the school that studies the structure of conscious experience by analysing it into its basic elements. Titchener drew the analogy with chemistry himself. Just as the chemist analyses compounds into elements and arranges them in the periodic table, the psychologist should analyse consciousness into its elements and catalogue them. He defined his subject carefully. Consciousness is the sum of mental processes occurring at any given moment; mind is the sum of mental processes accumulated over a lifetime. And he set psychology three problems: What? Analyse conscious processes into their simplest elements. How? Discover how the elements combine, and the laws of their combination. Why? Connect the elements with the physiological conditions that accompany them. (Titchener was a psychophysical parallelist: nervous processes accompany mental ones but do not cause them, so the "why" was correlation, not causation.) Titchener found three kinds of elements, one more than Wundt. Sensations are the elements of perceptions; images are the elements of ideas (such as the image of your mother's face when she is not present); and affections are the elements of emotions. Each element has attributes, its basic dimensions of variation: quality (what distinguishes red from cold), intensity (how strong), duration (how long), clearness (how vivid in attention) and extensity (how spread out in space, possessed by sight and touch). Affections, he argued, have quality, intensity and duration but lack clearness: when you try to attend closely to a feeling of pleasantness, it fades. And he recognised only one dimension of affection, pleasantness versus unpleasantness, rejecting Wundt's tension and excitement. Working through his manuals, his laboratory catalogued more than 44,000 distinguishable qualities of sensation, the great majority of them visual and auditory. Introspection, the stimulus error and the meaning of meaning Titchener's method was introspection, but in a more demanding form than Wundt's. He defined it as a highly specialised form of self-observation in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. His observers were trained for months to report not short judgements but detailed descriptions of their experience in terms of elements and attributes. The commonest fault of an untrained observer, Titchener said, was the stimulus error : describing the object instead of the experience. Shown an apple, the untrained person says "a red apple". But "apple" is not an experience; it is knowledge about the object. The trained observer reports what is actually in consciousness: a patch of red of a certain brightness and saturation, a bright highlight near the top, a certain extensity, perhaps a faint image of sourness and a mild pleasantness. Try this yourself with any object on your desk, and you will discover how hard it is not to name things. If consciousness is only elements, where does meaning come from? Titchener's answer was the context theory of meaning . A sensation by itself has no meaning; it acquires meaning from the context of other sensations and images that the mind attaches to it. The core (say, the sound of the word "home") means something because it calls up a context of images: a kitchen, a voice, the smell of food. Often, Titchener thought, the context was kinaesthetic, made of faint sensations of movement and posture. On the same reasoning, he defined perception as a complex of sensory and imaginal processes: sensations from the object plus images supplied by past experience. This definition is the answer to an IHBAS question that asks who defined perception in exactly these terms. Exam trap "Introspection is a highly specialised form of ..." is self-observation (Titchener), not self-perception (that is Daryl Bem's later social-psychological theory), not "self-thinking" and not attention. "Perception is a complex of sensory and imaginal processes" is Titchener ; Jerome Bruner and Roy Schafer, two of the other names in that question, belong to the "New Look" research on perception of the 1940s and later (Chapter 4), and Gregory Kimble is known for work on learning. The aim of structuralism was to build a "periodic table" of the elements of experience; "to study behaviour and not mind" is behaviourism, so "all of the above" is wrong. "To understand the nature of consciousness" is too general to be the answer: it fits Wundt, James and the Wurzburg school just as well, whereas the periodic table of elements is structuralism's distinctive aim. The Wurzburg school and imageless thought The first serious challenge to the structuralist picture came not from America but from one of Wundt's own former assistants. Oswald Kulpe (1862 to 1915) served as Wundt's assistant for several years, then moved to the University of Wurzburg in 1894. Unlike Wundt, he believed that thinking itself could be studied by experiment, and he extended introspection to it. His method, often called systematic experimental introspection, gave the observer a task (for example, to judge, to associate, or to answer a question) and then asked for a full, retrospective description of everything that had passed through consciousness while the task was done. The results shocked everyone. In 1901 August Mayer and Johannes Orth reported that their observers, giving associations to words, often experienced vague states of hesitation, doubt or certainty that contained no sensations or images at all; they called these "conscious attitudes". Karl Marbe, in the same year, had observers judge which of two weights was heavier and found that they could describe the sensations of lifting perfectly well but could report nothing about how the judgement itself was made; it simply appeared. Karl Buhler later argued that thoughts themselves are elements of experience. The conclusion was imageless thought : thinking can proceed without any sensory or imaginal content in consciousness, which directly contradicted Titchener's claim that consciousness consists only of sensations, images and affections. The Wurzburgers also discovered how much thinking is directed by the task. Henry J. Watt showed that the instruction or task, which he called the Aufgabe , determines what association a word produces. Narziss Ach (1905) called the unconscious influence that steers thinking toward the goal of the task the determining tendency , and the readiness it creates a set (in German, Einstellung ). An example: hear the word "Mysuru" with the task "name a building" and you will think "palace"; hear the same word with the task "name its state" and you will think "Karnataka". The stimulus is identical; the set prepared before it arrived decides the answer, and you are not aware of the set doing its work. Titchener replied that the Wurzburg observers were poorly trained and had committed the stimulus error; their "imageless" thoughts, he said, were really faint kinaesthetic sensations and images that a trained observer would detect. Wundt, for his part, dismissed the Wurzburg procedures as sham experiments, because the observer, not the experimenter, controlled what was observed. The quarrel, known as the imageless thought controversy, was never resolved, and that was the real damage: two laboratories using the same method reported different contents of consciousness, and introspection had no way to decide between them. Kulpe's influence lived on, however. The concept of set is basic to the study of problem solving, and one of Kulpe's doctoral students at Wurzburg was Max Wertheimer, the founder of Gestalt psychology (Chapter 2). Act psychology: Brentano, Stumpf and G. E. Muller A different German-speaking tradition rejected the idea of conscious contents altogether. In 1874, the same year Wundt completed his Principles , the philosopher Franz Brentano (1838 to 1917) published Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint . Brentano argued that psychology should study mental acts , not mental contents. When you see a red flower, the redness is a physical phenomenon; what is mental is the act of seeing it. This is act psychology . Brentano's key idea was intentionality : every mental act is directed at, or refers to, some object beyond itself. You never just see; you see something. You never just love or fear; you love or fear someone or something. He grouped acts into three classes: ideating (sensing, imagining), judging (accepting or rejecting, perceiving, recalling) and loving-hating (feeling, wishing, resolving). His method was careful empirical observation of experience rather than laboratory experiment. Brentano taught in Vienna for two decades, where his students included Carl Stumpf, the philosopher Edmund Husserl (founder of phenomenology), Christian von Ehrenfels (whose "form qualities" anticipated Gestalt psychology) and, as an auditor of his lectures, the young Sigmund Freud. Carl Stumpf (1848 to 1936), Brentano's student, studied the perception of musical tones in his Psychology of Tone (two volumes, 1883 and 1890) and argued with Wundt over who was the better judge of tones: Stumpf trusted trained musicians, Wundt trusted trained laboratory observers. From 1894 Stumpf directed the psychological institute at the University of Berlin, where he favoured describing experience as it naturally occurs (a phenomenological approach) rather than breaking it into elements. Three of his students, Wolfgang Kohler, Kurt Koffka and Kurt Lewin, became leaders of Gestalt psychology. You have already met Stumpf on the Clever Hans commission. Finally, Georg Elias Muller (1850 to 1934) ran the second great German laboratory, at Gottingen, for forty years. Muller was a rigorous experimentalist rather than a theorist of acts, and he is grouped here because he stood outside Wundt's system. He refined Fechner's psychophysical methods, extended Ebbinghaus's memory research (with his assistant Friedrich Schumann he developed the memory drum for presenting syllables at a fixed rate), and, with Alfons Pilzecker in 1900, described retroactive interference and proposed that memories need time to consolidate (Chapter 7). His students included Edgar Rubin, whose figure-ground drawings you will meet in Chapter 4. The decline of structuralism, and what it left behind Structuralism died with Titchener in 1927; no one carried it on. The reasons for its decline are examined in almost every paper, so it pays to know them as a list. Introspection was unreliable. Trained observers in different laboratories reported different things (the imageless thought controversy), and since each observer's experience is private, there was no way to settle disputes. Observing changes what is observed. As Comte had warned and William James repeated, attending to an experience alters it, and describing it afterwards depends on memory. Elementism missed the whole. The Gestalt psychologists argued that experience comes organised in wholes that analysis destroys. Its subject matter was too narrow. It excluded animals, children, the mentally ill, individual differences and the unconscious, which Freud was making impossible to ignore. It refused to be useful. Titchener regarded applied work as technology, not science, just as American society was demanding a useful psychology. And yet structuralism mattered. It made psychology a laboratory discipline with standards of training and control, and it gave every later school something definite to argue against. Its topics have also come back. The modern approach most closely aligned with the structuralists in its interest in consciousness, mental imagery and thought processes is cognitive psychology , which studies the same subjects with reaction times, error patterns and brain imaging instead of trained introspection. Neuroscience studies the brain rather than the contents of experience; behaviourism banished consciousness; and functionalism, as you will now see, asked a different question altogether. Clinical link Introspection never left the clinic. Every self-report questionnaire, every mental status interview question ("What is going through your mind right now?") and every thought record in cognitive behaviour therapy asks a person to observe and report his own consciousness. Titchener's problems come with it: patients describe interpretations rather than experiences (a cousin of the stimulus error), and their reports are shaped by memory, expectation and the way the question is asked. Good clinicians, like good structuralists, train the observer, which is exactly what learning to separate a situation, a thought and a feeling in therapy does. 1.7 Functionalism and the American Pioneers High yield · 15 Qs Structuralism asked what the mind is made of. The question that dominated American psychology from the 1890s was different: what is the mind for ? functionalism is the school that studies the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. Notice the order of words, which a bank question tests: the mind functions in adapting the organism . Functionalists studied mental processes and behaviour not as collections of elements but as activities that help a living creature survive and solve problems. Why functionalism grew in America Three forces made America receptive. The first was Darwin, whose theory had become enormously popular in the United States, partly through the evolutionary philosophy of the British writer Herbert Spencer: if traits exist because they are useful, the obvious question about consciousness is what use it is. The second was the American philosophy of pragmatism , which judged ideas by their practical consequences. The third was the character of the country itself: a rapidly growing nation with expanding schools, factories and cities, and universities that had to justify their new psychology departments by doing something useful. Functionalism was never a tightly organised school with a single founder and creed. It was an attitude, shared by people at Harvard, Chicago and Columbia, and it was Titchener, in his 1898 article, who gave it its name, as the opposite of his own "structural" psychology. William James William James (1842 to 1910), the elder brother of the novelist Henry James, is the father of American psychology and the inspiration, though not the formal founder, of functionalism. He qualified in medicine at Harvard in 1869 but never practised. Around that time he fell into a deep depression, from which he dragged himself, he said, partly by reading the French philosopher Charles Renouvier on free will and deciding that his first act of free will would be to believe in free will. He began teaching at Harvard, and in 1875 he offered what is usually called the first course in scientific psychology in America and set up a small room of apparatus for classroom demonstrations, the room mentioned at the start of this chapter. James disliked laboratory drudgery and had little patience with Fechner's psychophysics, but his teaching produced the first American doctorate in psychology (G. Stanley Hall, 1878). In 1878 James signed a contract to write a psychology textbook in two years. It took twelve. The Principles of Psychology (1890), in two volumes, is the most widely read book in the history of the discipline, and its ideas are tested constantly. A shorter version followed in 1892, which students nicknamed "Jimmy" to distinguish it from the full "James". Four ideas from it matter most for you. The first is the stream of consciousness . Against the structuralists' picture of consciousness as a mosaic of elements, James wrote: "Consciousness, then, does not appear to itself chopped up in bits. Such words as 'chain' or 'train' do not describe it fitly ... It is nothing jointed; it flows. A 'river' or a 'stream' are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described." He listed its characteristics: thought is personal (always someone's), always changing (no state ever recurs exactly), sensibly continuous (even across gaps such as sleep), concerned with objects outside itself, and selective, choosing among the things it could attend to. The phrase passed into literature, where novelists such as James Joyce and Virginia Woolf adopted a "stream of consciousness" style. Consciousness, for James, was selective precisely because it was useful: it is a fighter for ends, which is a functionalist claim. The second is habit . James argued that the "plasticity" of nervous tissue lets repeated actions wear grooves in the nervous system, so that they become automatic and free attention for other things. "Habit is thus the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent." His practical advice for forming a new habit is still quoted by therapists: launch the new habit with as strong an initiative as possible, never allow an exception until it is firmly rooted, and seize the very first opportunity to act on a resolution. The third is the self . James divided the self into the "Me" (the self as known) and the "I" (the self as knower). The Me has three parts: the material self (one's body, clothes, family, home and possessions), the social self (the recognition one gets from others; a man "has as many social selves as there are individuals who recognize him") and the spiritual self (one's inner dispositions, faculties and conscience). The I is the pure ego , the sense of personal identity that continues through the stream. He even offered a formula: self-esteem equals success divided by pretensions. Raise your aspirations without raising your achievements and your self-esteem falls; give up a pretension and it rises. The fourth is his theory of emotion: in an 1884 article James argued that we do not cry because we are sorry; we are sorry because we cry. The Danish physiologist Carl Lange (1834 to 1900) proposed a similar theory independently in 1885, so it is known as the James-Lange theory (Chapter 11). After the Principles , James turned to philosophy. He developed pragmatism, the doctrine (first stated by his friend Charles Sanders Peirce) that the meaning and truth of an idea lie in its practical consequences, in Pragmatism (1907); he also wrote Talks to Teachers (1899) and The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902). Exam trap "Stream of consciousness" is William James (not Wundt, Jung or Skinner). "Functionalism is how people work, play and adapt to their surroundings; this viewpoint was given by ..." is William James : Wundt (misspelt "William Wundt" in one paper) is the voluntarist, Darwin inspired functionalism but was not a psychologist of any school, and Watson founded behaviourism. When a question asks which psychologist functionalism is "most closely associated with", the expected answer is James, not Titchener (structuralism), Watson (behaviourism) or G. Stanley Hall (who was a functionalist in spirit but is examined for institutions and adolescence). If Dewey or Angell appears as an option in a question about the formal founding of the functionalist school at Chicago, choose them. The Chicago school: Dewey, Angell and Carr Functionalism became a school, with a home and a programme, at the University of Chicago. Its founding document was a paper by the philosopher John Dewey (1859 to 1952), "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology", published in the Psychological Review in 1896. The reflex arc is the physiologists' unit of behaviour: a stimulus excites a sensory (afferent) nerve, a central process connects it to a motor (efferent) nerve, and a response follows. Psychologists had adopted it as the model for all behaviour: sensation, then idea, then action. Dewey argued that this chops a single, continuous act into three disconnected pieces, "a patchwork of disjointed parts". He made the argument with an example from James: a child sees a candle flame, reaches for it, is burnt, and pulls back. On the reflex-arc view, two separate arcs have occurred: light-reach, then burn-withdraw. Dewey pointed out that the seeing was never a bare stimulus. It was already part of a coordinated act of looking-in-order-to-reach, and the burn does not end the story; it changes the meaning of the seeing, so that next time the child sees a flame as "a light that burns" (Figure 1.5). Stimulus and response are not separate events but phases of one continuous coordination, in which each response alters the next stimulus. Behaviour, Dewey concluded, must be studied as a whole adaptive act in its context. The reflex arc Dewey attacked Stimulus: sight of flame Central process: idea Response: reach out separate pieces, patched together Dewey (1896): a coordination Seeing the flame Reaching for it Burn: pain and withdrawal Seeing anew: light that burns each act changes the next stimulus Figure 1.5 Dewey's critique of the reflex arc. On the left, the traditional view treats stimulus, idea and response as separate links in a chain; on the right, Dewey's child-and-candle example shows a continuous circuit in which the burn transforms the meaning of the next sight of a flame. Dewey went on to become the most influential American philosopher of education. At Chicago he founded a Laboratory School where children learned by doing, and he served as president of the American Psychological Association in 1899. He left Chicago for Columbia in 1904. Exam trap "According to John Dewey, ____ is the connection between sensory stimuli and motor responses." The answer is the reflex arc , the concept his 1896 paper examined and criticised. "Efferent" describes only the outgoing, motor half of the arc (afferent nerves carry signals in, efferent nerves carry them out), so an "efferent arc" cannot connect stimulus to response; "association arc" and "dynamic arc" are invented distractors, the second borrowing a word from Woodworth's Dynamic Psychology . Remember that Dewey attacked the reflex arc as the unit of behaviour; he did not invent it. The man who turned Dewey's attitude into a working department was James Rowland Angell (1869 to 1949). In his presidential address to the American Psychological Association in 1906, "The Province of Functional Psychology" (published in 1907), Angell gave the school its clearest statement. Functional psychology, he said, is (1) the psychology of mental operations , as opposed to mental elements; (2) the study of the fundamental utilities of consciousness, the mind being what mediates between the environment and the needs of the organism; and (3) psychophysical psychology, which treats mind and body as a single functioning organism rather than two parallel series. Angell's Chicago department trained many students, among them a young man named John B. Watson, who took his doctorate there in 1903. Angell later became president of Yale University. Under Angell's successor, Harvey A. Carr (1873 to 1954), Chicago functionalism reached its mature form. In Psychology: A Study of Mental Activity (1925), Carr defined the subject as mental activity: the acquisition, fixation, retention, organisation and evaluation of experiences, and their use in guiding conduct. His unit of analysis was the adaptive act , made up of a motive (a stimulus that persists until it is dealt with, such as hunger), a sensory situation, and a response that changes the situation so as to satisfy the motive. By Carr's time functionalism was less a rebel school than the ordinary way American psychologists worked. The Columbia school: Cattell, Woodworth and Thorndike At Columbia University in New York, functionalism took a still looser form, focused on measurement and individual differences. Its senior figure was James McKeen Cattell (1860 to 1944), Wundt's self-appointed assistant. After Leipzig, Cattell worked with Galton in England and absorbed his interest in measuring individual differences. In 1888 he became professor of psychology at the University of Pennsylvania, often described as the first such title anywhere, and in 1891 he moved to Columbia, where he stayed until 1917, when he was dismissed for opposing the conscription of soldiers in the First World War. In an 1890 article in Mind , Cattell coined the term mental test . His tests followed Galton's logic: strength of grip, speed of movement, two-point threshold, sensitivity to pain, discrimination of weights, reaction time to sound, time to name colours, accuracy in bisecting a line, judging a ten-second interval, and the number of letters remembered after one hearing. He hoped such tests would reveal mental ability. In 1901 his student Clark Wissler showed that scores on them bore almost no relation to college grades, and the sensory approach to intelligence collapsed. Cattell's lasting contributions lay elsewhere: in reaction time and reading research (he showed, for example, that a familiar word can be recognised about as quickly as a single letter), in the ranking method of measurement, and above all as an organiser and editor who did more than anyone to make American psychology a profession. Robert Sessions Woodworth, whom you met in Section 1.1, spent his career at Columbia and became the great systematiser of functionalism. In Dynamic Psychology (1918) he insisted that psychology must study not only the mechanisms of behaviour (how it happens) but also its motivation (why), and he introduced the term "drive" to psychology (Chapter 10). He also proposed adding the organism to the stimulus-response formula. The S-O-R formula (stimulus, organism, response) states that the same stimulus produces different responses depending on the state of the organism: a plate of biryani means one thing to a hungry person and another to someone who has just eaten. Woodworth's Experimental Psychology (1938) was so widely used that students called it "the Columbia Bible", and his Contemporary Schools of Psychology (1931) taught a generation how to compare the systems you are studying now. (His Personal Data Sheet, an early personality questionnaire, belongs to the Assessment book.) Columbia's third functionalist was Edward Lee Thorndike, who began studying the learning of chicks in William James's basement at Harvard and completed his doctorate under Cattell at Columbia in 1898 with the famous puzzle-box experiments on cats. His law of effect and his work on educational psychology are taught in Chapter 6; for now, notice that he came out of the functionalist tradition, as Watson did. The builders: Hall, Witmer and Munsterberg Functionalism's practical spirit produced the institutions of American psychology and its first applied fields. Three Wundt-trained men did most of the building. Granville Stanley Hall (1844 to 1924) was a founder of almost everything. He received the first American doctorate in psychology (Harvard, 1878), studied in Leipzig in 1879 and 1880, and in 1883 opened at Johns Hopkins University the first American psychological laboratory devoted to research (James's 1875 room had been for demonstration). In 1887 he founded the American Journal of Psychology , the first American psychology journal, and in 1889 he became the first president of the new Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts. In July 1892 a small group of psychologists meeting at Clark founded the American Psychological Association (APA) , with Hall as its first president; its charter members numbered only a few dozen. Hall was also a pioneer of child and developmental psychology: he launched the child-study movement, using questionnaires to learn what children knew and thought, and in Adolescence (1904) he described the teenage years as a period of "storm and stress" (from the German Sturm und Drang ). He explained development through recapitulation theory , the idea that each child, in growing up, passes through the stages of the evolution of the human race (a theory now abandoned; the Developmental Psychology book covers adolescence). In 1909 he invited Sigmund Freud and Carl Jung to lecture at Clark, Freud's only visit to America, which did much to spread psychoanalysis there. Lightner Witmer (1867 to 1956) studied under Cattell at Pennsylvania, took his doctorate under Wundt in 1892, and returned to succeed Cattell at Pennsylvania. In March 1896 he opened there the world's first psychological clinic . At the APA meeting in December of that year he proposed a new field, which he called clinical psychology; in 1907 he founded the journal The Psychological Clinic and, in an article titled "Clinical Psychology" in its first issue, became the first person to use the term in print. His clinic dealt mainly with children who had learning and behaviour problems, and he insisted that clinical work rest on the methods and findings of experimental psychology. Key study: The first case at the first clinic (1896) The problem. A schoolteacher brought Witmer a fourteen-year-old boy she described as a "chronic bad speller". He was not lazy and not dull, yet he could not learn to spell. Method. Witmer examined the boy as a scientist would: testing his vision, his memory, his reading and his performance under different conditions, instead of simply labelling him. Finding. Part of the problem turned out to be a defect of vision that made printed words hard to see clearly; with corrected vision and patient, individual teaching, the boy made progress. Conclusion. Witmer took two lessons from the case, and they define the profession you are entering: begin with careful assessment before treatment, and look for the simplest, most concrete cause first (Morgan's canon, applied to a child). Hugo Munsterberg (1863 to 1916), another Wundt graduate, was invited by William James in 1892 to run the Harvard laboratory. Munsterberg became the great popular champion of applied psychology. In On the Witness Stand (1908) he argued that eyewitness testimony and memory are unreliable and that psychology could help the courts, making him a founder of forensic psychology. In Psychology and Industrial Efficiency (1913) he applied psychological methods to selecting workers (telephone operators, tram drivers) and to advertising, making him a founder of industrial psychology. He also wrote on psychotherapy and on the psychology of film. He died in 1916 while lecturing at Radcliffe College. Clinical link Witmer is the father of clinical psychology, and the model of the clinical psychologist that Indian training programmes follow, the scientist-practitioner who assesses carefully, treats on the basis of evidence and evaluates the results, is recognisably his. Notice too what Witmer's clinic did not do: it did not begin with psychoanalysis or with psychiatric diagnosis. Clinical psychology was born out of experimental psychology and education, not out of medicine, and that history explains why assessment remains its distinctive skill. Exam trap The first psychological clinic and the term "clinical psychology" are Witmer's (clinic 1896; term proposed 1896, first in print 1907). Freud founded psychoanalysis, Wundt the laboratory, G. Stanley Hall the APA and the first US research laboratory, Cattell the mental test, and Erik Erikson the psychosocial stages. The APA was founded in 1892 ; 1896 is the year of Witmer's clinic and Dewey's paper, so do not let it pull you. Hall was the APA's first president; Calkins its first woman president. The women pioneers Women were excluded from most universities and all of Titchener's meetings, yet several of the founders of American psychology were women, and their stories are examined often. Mary Whiton Calkins (1863 to 1930) studied psychology at Harvard with William James and Hugo Munsterberg in the early 1890s, attending as a guest because Harvard did not admit women. By 1895 she had completed every requirement for the doctorate, and her examiners recommended the degree, but Harvard refused to award a PhD to a woman; she later declined the offer of a degree from Radcliffe, Harvard's college for women. She taught at Wellesley College, where she founded a psychology laboratory in 1891, invented the paired-associate technique for studying memory (learning pairs of items so that one cues the other), and developed a "self psychology" that treated the self as the centre of all psychology. In 1905 she became the first woman president of the American Psychological Association , and later the first woman president of the American Philosophical Association as well. Margaret Floy Washburn (1871 to 1939) was the first woman to be awarded a PhD in psychology, at Cornell in 1894, as Titchener's first doctoral student. She taught for most of her career at Vassar College, and her book The Animal Mind (1908) was the standard text of comparative psychology for a quarter of a century, gathering the experimental evidence on the sensory and mental capacities of animals. She also proposed a motor theory of consciousness, in which thought depends on small, incipient movements. In 1921 she became the second woman president of the APA. Leta Stetter Hollingworth (1886 to 1939), who trained under Thorndike at Columbia, used experiments to demolish two beliefs used to keep women out of education and work. In Functional Periodicity (1914) she tested women on mental and motor tasks across the menstrual cycle and found no impairment at any phase. She also attacked the "variability hypothesis", the claim that men vary more than women and therefore produce more geniuses, showing that the evidence did not support it and that the difference in eminence was explained by social opportunity. She later became a leading authority on gifted children, and worked as one of the early clinical psychologists in New York. Exam trap Calkins was the first woman APA president (1905); Washburn the first woman PhD in psychology (1894) and the second woman APA president (1921). Calkins completed every requirement for a Harvard doctorate in 1895 but was refused the degree; Washburn had received hers from Cornell in 1894, so she holds the "first PhD" title. Hollingworth is examined for the psychology of women and the gifted. Karen Horney, sometimes offered as a distractor, was a psychoanalyst who challenged Freud's view of women (the Personality book) and was never APA president. The legacy of functionalism Functionalism did not fade like structuralism; it dissolved into the mainstream. Its interests (learning, motivation, individual differences, development, abnormal behaviour, animals) became the ordinary subject matter of psychology, and its willingness to be useful created educational, industrial, forensic and clinical psychology. It also produced its own successors. Watson, Angell's student, took the functionalist interest in adaptive behaviour and animals to its logical end by dropping consciousness altogether; the aim of behaviourism, as Watson put it, was that given the stimulus, psychology should be able to predict the response, and given the response, to specify the stimulus that caused it (Chapter 2). And the functionalist question, what is a mental process for, inherited from Darwin, is the founding question of today's evolutionary psychology. Table 1.6 sets the two first schools side by side.
