The historical perspective that "gave rise to the evolutionary perspective" is functionalism . The aim "given the stimulus, to predict the response, and given the response, to predict the antecedent stimulus" is behaviourism , and John B. Watson is the founder of behaviourism (not functionalism, rationalism or structuralism). Rationalism, remember, is the philosophical view of Descartes and Leibniz, not a psychological school. The chronoscope and the habit of timing observers came from physics and astronomy; the idea that a mental act takes measurable time came from Helmholtz and Donders; the word apperception came from Leibniz and Herbart; the conviction that the mind can be measured came from Fechner. So the puzzle from the start of the chapter can now be put sharply. If nearly everything in that room was borrowed, in what sense did Wundt found anything, and why do we give the credit to one man, one city and one year? Historians answer questions of this kind in two broad ways. The answers matter for more than history, because they decide which names end up in textbooks as "fathers", and so which names end up in your question paper. Two ways of explaining history The first way puts individuals at the centre. In a series of lectures given in London in 1840 and published the next year as On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History , the Scottish writer Thomas Carlyle (1795 to 1881) declared that "the history of the world is but the biography of great men". This is the great-person theory of history, still often called by Carlyle's own phrase, the great-man theory: progress happens because exceptional individuals, through genius and force of will, change the course of events, and without them it would not have happened, or would have happened very differently. Applied to our story, psychology began in Leipzig because Wundt was Wundt. It took a man who would publish more than 50,000 printed pages, supervise well over a hundred doctorates and work at his desk for more than sixty years to turn a scattered set of techniques into a discipline. Historians call this the personalistic view of history. The second way puts the times at the centre. Zeitgeist is German for "the spirit of the times" ( Zeit , time; Geist , spirit or mind): the whole climate of ideas, knowledge, techniques, values and social conditions of a period. On the Zeitgeist view, a discovery is made when the time is ripe for it, and if one person had not made it, someone else soon would have. Individuals still matter, but as the agents through whom their age does its work; the times choose the person more than the person chooses the times. Historians call this the naturalistic view. Its great champion in psychology was Edwin G. Boring, whose A History of Experimental Psychology (1929; second edition 1950) shaped how generations of students, and of examiners, learned the story you have just read. For Boring the founding of psychology in the 1870s was no accident. You saw at the end of Section 1.4 that by 1870 all the parts were already on the bench; someone was bound to assemble them. What evidence could decide between the two views? The strongest argument for the Zeitgeist is the frequency of multiple discovery : the same discovery made independently by two or more people at about the same time. You have already met several in this chapter. Charles Bell (1811) and Francois Magendie (1822) both separated the sensory and motor roots of the spinal nerves, and quarrelled for years over the credit. William James (1884) and the Danish physiologist Carl Lange (1885) proposed the same theory of emotion without knowing of each other's work. The most famous case of all is evolution itself. In 1858, while Darwin was still writing his great book, he received from the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace (1823 to 1913), then collecting specimens in the Malay Archipelago, an essay setting out the same theory of natural selection, and papers by both men were read together at a meeting of the Linnean Society in London that July. Outside the life sciences, Newton and Leibniz each invented the calculus. In 1922 two American sociologists, William Ogburn and Dorothy Thomas, listed 148 such cases, and the sociologist of science Robert K. Merton later argued that "multiples" are the normal pattern of science, not the exception. If great discoveries depended entirely on unique geniuses, such coincidences should be rare. That they are common suggests that the state of knowledge makes certain discoveries almost inevitable. The other side of the same coin is the discovery made too early. In 1866 the monk Gregor Mendel published the laws of heredity he had worked out by breeding pea plants in his monastery garden at Brno. Almost nobody noticed. In 1900 three botanists, working separately, arrived at the same laws and only then found Mendel's paper: a multiple discovery that rescued a premature one. The Zeitgeist also works against ideas. When two Cambridge scholars proposed a laboratory for psychophysics in 1877, the university turned them down; one objector is said to have complained that it would "insult religion by putting the human soul in a pair of scales". At that very moment the same science was flourishing in Leipzig. The ideas were identical; the climate was not. The spirit of the times includes forces that have little to do with ideas, which historians call contextual forces , and you have met three of them already. The first is economic opportunity : American universities, schools and factories wanted a useful psychology, and functionalism, mental testing and the first clinic grew to meet the demand (Section 1.7). The second is war : Cattell lost his Columbia chair in 1917 for opposing conscription, while the same war gave American psychologists their first mass testing programme, the Army Alpha and Army Beta tests of 1917 (Chapter 9). The third is prejudice : Mary Whiton Calkins was refused the doctorate she had earned because she was a woman, Titchener's Experimentalists barred women from their meetings, and Leta Hollingworth spent the first part of her career disproving claims that were used to keep women out of education and work. Who becomes a "great person" depends partly on who is allowed into the room. Most historians now conclude that neither view is enough on its own, and the clearest way to see why is to push one event through both. Take Lightner Witmer's clinic of 1896. The great-person version is easy to tell: a schoolteacher brought a boy who could not spell, and Witmer, unlike his colleagues, decided that a psychologist ought to try to help him. Now tell it the Zeitgeist way. American states were making schooling compulsory, so classrooms were filling with children who could not keep up; G. Stanley Hall's child-study movement had made children a respectable subject of research; Cattell had just introduced mental tests; and functionalism had made usefulness a scientific virtue. Someone was likely to open a clinic for schoolchildren around the turn of the century. Both versions are true. The Zeitgeist explains why a clinic appeared in America in the 1890s; the person explains why it appeared in Philadelphia in 1896, and why it took the shape it did, built on careful assessment rather than on medicine or hypnosis. A useful summary: the Zeitgeist decides what can happen; persons decide when, where and how it does. Exam trap Zeitgeist means "spirit of the times". It is not "spirit of the place", not "worldview" (that is Weltanschauung ) and not "form" or "organised whole" (that is Gestalt , Chapter 2). The historian who championed the Zeitgeist view of psychology's history is Boring ; the "great man" view goes back to Carlyle (1841). If a question asks which view best explains simultaneous discoveries, such as Darwin and Wallace (1858), Bell and Magendie, or James and Lange, the answer is the Zeitgeist or naturalistic view. The great-person view is the personalistic one. Why Germany, why Wundt, why 1879? The Zeitgeist explains a good deal about where psychology was born. Why Germany, and not Britain, France or America, all of which had brilliant scientists? Three features of German academic life made the difference. First, the German universities, reformed on the model of the University of Berlin (founded in 1810), were built around research as well as teaching. Professors were expected to discover things and enjoyed Lehrfreiheit , the freedom to teach whatever their research led them to; students enjoyed Lernfreiheit , the freedom to move between universities in search of the best teachers. Because the German states had many universities competing for prestige, a new field could find a chair, a room and a budget somewhere. Second, the German word for science, Wissenschaft , covered every kind of systematic knowledge, history and philology included, so a "science of mind" sounded natural rather than contradictory. Third, as Section 1.3 showed, experimental physiology was stronger in Germany than anywhere else; Muller, Helmholtz, Weber and Fechner were all German, and their methods were exactly the ones psychology needed. Britain, by contrast, had brilliant individuals but no institutional home for them. Darwin and Galton, the two British giants of this chapter, were men of independent means who never held university posts, and the ancient universities, as the Cambridge refusal shows, were slow to accept new sciences. France had a powerful clinical tradition, and French psychology grew up in the hospital and the school rather than the laboratory: first in the study of hysteria and hypnosis, and then in the work of Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911), who with Theodore Simon produced the first practical intelligence test in 1905 (Chapter 9). America had energy and money, but in 1879 it had no research laboratory, and its universities were still learning the German model; G. Stanley Hall, like so many others, crossed the Atlantic to study in Leipzig. The Zeitgeist cannot, however, explain why it was Wundt rather than one of the many Germans who had the same knowledge. Here historians draw a useful distinction between a founder and a precursor (or pioneer). Weber, Fechner, Helmholtz and Donders all did experiments that we now count as psychology, but none of them set out to create a new discipline. Weber was a physiologist of the senses; Helmholtz thought of himself as a physicist and physiologist; Donders was an eye specialist; Fechner was trying to prove a philosophy of mind and matter. Wundt alone did all four of the things that turn a set of methods into a science. He declared it, in print, in the preface to his Principles (1873 to 1874). He gave it a place , the Leipzig laboratory. He gave it a voice , the journal Philosophische Studien (1881). And he gave it people : the stream of students who carried it to Wurzburg, Cornell, Columbia, Philadelphia, Harvard and, as you will see shortly, Calcutta. A founder is not the first person to have an idea. He is the person who turns the idea into an institution that outlives him. That leaves the year. Why 1879, when James had a room of apparatus at Harvard in 1875 and Fechner's book had appeared in 1860? Because 1875 was a room for showing known effects to students, and 1860 was a book. The winter of 1879 is the first time that students did original, publishable research in a room set aside for psychology. The date is a convention, fixed by later historians (the university did not formally recognise the laboratory as one of its institutes until some years afterwards), but it is a sensible convention, and it is the one every question paper expects. Exam trap "Who established the first laboratory for experimental psychology?" is Wundt (Leipzig, 1879). Each distractor is tied to a different "first" or to no laboratory at all. Galton opened the first anthropometric laboratory (London, 1884), a centre for measuring individual differences, not a research school. Weber was a physiologist whose experiments on touch and lifted weights came before any psychology laboratory existed. Jung turned Galton's word association test into a clinical tool in Zurich (the Personality book). James had a demonstration room at Harvard in 1875. If the question asks for the city, it is Leipzig : not Heidelberg (where Wundt assisted Helmholtz), not Zurich (where he spent one year), not Vienna (Brentano and Freud), not Paris (Charcot's clinic and Binet's tests), and not Cambridge, which is both the town in Massachusetts that is home to Harvard and the English university that refused a psychophysics laboratory in 1877. The first American research laboratory is Hall's (Johns Hopkins, 1883). Fathers, founders and firsts Indian entrance papers have a favourite question form: "Who is the father of ...?" The difficulty is that "father" is used loosely, to mean at least four different things. It can mean the founder of an institution : Wundt founded the laboratory, Witmer the clinic. It can mean the person who named a field or school: Titchener named both structuralism and functionalism, though he founded only the first; Witmer named clinical psychology; William Stern named differential psychology. It can mean the most influential early figure , as James is for American psychology. And it can mean the first person to do something in one country , as Sengupta is for India. Two habits will protect you. Read the qualifying word in the stem ("experimental", "American", "modern", "formal", "in India"), because it often decides between two good candidates. And when two candidates are both defensible, choose the one that standard textbooks name, which is the one given in Table 1.7. Names attached to discoveries can mislead in a second way. Hyphenated names are often a fossil record of multiple discovery: the Bell-Magendie law, the James-Lange theory, the Young-Helmholtz theory (Thomas Young's suggestion of 1802, developed by Helmholtz half a century later) and, in Chapter 11, the Cannon-Bard theory. And some names were given by other people: "Weber's law" was named by Fechner, and Morgan's canon restates, for animal psychology, the much older rule of parsimony usually credited to the fourteenth-century philosopher William of Ockham ("Ockham's razor"). If psychology has fathers, it also has a family tree, and seeing the tree whole is the quickest way to remember who trained whom (Figure 1.6). Notice how much of it grows from one root. Wundt's students founded the Wurzburg school, structuralism, the first American research laboratory, the Columbia school, the first psychological clinic and applied psychology at Harvard. Their students, in turn, include the founder of Gestalt psychology, the first woman to earn a doctorate in psychology, the first woman to lead the APA and the founder of modern psychology in India. A Zeitgeist historian would add that a network like this is exactly how the spirit of an age travels: not through the air, but through people who learned in the same rooms. Psychology comes to India Reflection on the mind in India is far older than anything in this chapter. The Upanishads, the Samkhya and Yoga systems, Buddhist analyses of consciousness and the medical tradition of Ayurveda all contain detailed accounts of perception, attention, emotion and the self, and they are the subject of Sections 2.8 and 2.9. What reached India in the early twentieth century was something narrower and newer: the laboratory psychology of Leipzig and its American descendants. It arrived, as so much of modern Indian science did, through the University of Calcutta (now Kolkata). The first step was a syllabus. In 1905, by the usual account, the philosopher Brajendranath Seal (1864 to 1938) drew up a course in experimental psychology for the University of Calcutta, taught within its philosophy curriculum. The person who turned the syllabus into a science was Narendra Nath Sengupta (1889 to 1944; also spelt Sen Gupta). After his studies in Calcutta, Sengupta went to Harvard, where he trained in experimental psychology under Hugo Munsterberg, himself a Leipzig graduate, so that the line in Figure 1.6 runs unbroken from Wundt's room to Bengal. Back in Calcutta, he set up in 1915 the first laboratory of experimental psychology in India, and in 1916 the University of Calcutta opened the first independent department of psychology in the country, with Sengupta as its moving spirit. (Some sources date the laboratory to 1916 as well; the department is 1916, and the place is always Calcutta.) His early research followed the Leipzig agenda of attention and perception, but he also turned to society: with the sociologist Radhakamal Mukerjee he wrote Introduction to Social Psychology: Mind in Society (1928), one of the first Indian books in the field. He took the lead in founding the Indian Psychological Association in 1925, and later moved to Lucknow University, where he built another department. He is the person Indian papers call the founder, or father, of modern psychology in India. The second founder came to psychology from medicine. Girindrasekhar Bose (1887 to 1953; also written Girindra Shekhar Bose) qualified as a doctor, then took a master's degree in the new Calcutta department, and in 1921 earned what is usually counted as the first doctorate in psychology awarded by an Indian university, for a thesis published as The Concept of Repression (sources differ by a year on the date of the degree). He had been treating patients by psychoanalytic methods, and in 1921 he wrote to Freud, beginning a correspondence that lasted many years. In 1922 Bose founded the Indian Psychoanalytic Society in Calcutta, one of the earliest psychoanalytic societies outside Europe and North America, and it was soon affiliated to the International Psychoanalytical Association. Bose did not simply copy Freud. In his theory of opposite wishes he argued that every wish is accompanied by its opposite (the wish to beat by the wish to be beaten, for example), and he drew on Indian philosophy to explain how such conflicts resolve; Freud read his ideas with interest but was not persuaded. Bose later headed the Calcutta department, and in 1947 he founded the journal Samiksa . He is the father of psychoanalysis in India. (His theory is taken further in Section 2.8 and in the Personality book.) Other centres followed. In 1923 psychology was given its own section, together with educational science, at the annual Indian Science Congress. In 1924 M. V. Gopalaswamy , who had trained in London, started the department of psychology at the University of Mysore. In 1925 the Indian Psychological Association was founded, and in 1926 it launched the Indian Journal of Psychology . Over the following decades departments opened at universities across the country. Reading old history with care One last lesson concerns the reader rather than the past. It is tempting to judge old ideas by what we know now: to laugh at phrenology, to dismiss introspection as naive, to treat Wundt as a dull cataloguer of sensations. In 1965 the historian George Stocking made the standard name for this habit familiar to historians of the behavioural sciences: presentism , interpreting and judging the past by the standards and concerns of the present. Its opposite, historicism , tries to understand past thinkers on their own terms: what questions they were asking, what evidence they had, what their contemporaries believed. Presentism is not always wrong (we do want to know which old ideas turned out to be true), but a purely presentist history becomes a story of heroes and fools, and it gets the facts wrong. Phrenology, judged historically, was a serious theory that got localisation right and method wrong; introspection was abandoned because it could not settle disputes, not because its users were foolish. The fate of Wundt's reputation is the classic case. For much of the twentieth century American students met Wundt mainly through Titchener, who translated him, presented his own structuralism as the faithful continuation of Wundt's programme, and was far more of an elementist than Wundt ever was. Few Americans read the ten volumes of the Volkerpsychologie , and the most influential history of the period was written by Boring, who had taken his doctorate under Titchener at Cornell. The result was a Wundt who was narrow, mechanical and introspective in Titchener's style. Only in the 1970s did historians who went back to Wundt's own German texts, among them Arthur Blumenthal in "A Reappraisal of Wilhelm Wundt" (1975), recover the Wundt you met in Section 1.5: a voluntarist who stressed attention, will and creative synthesis, who limited introspection to short, controlled judgements, and who wrote a whole second psychology of culture. Translation was part of the problem, which is why the German terms in Table 1.10 are worth knowing exactly. Examiners like to put them side by side as options. The case of Max Friedrich's key, revisited Go back to the winter of 1879 and look again at the doctoral student pressing his telegraph key. You can now name the ancestry of almost everything in that room. The clockwork chronoscope belonged to the physicists, and the very idea that observers differ in how long they take to respond had been forced on the astronomers by the personal equation. The logic of the experiment, comparing a simple reaction with one that requires an extra mental act and subtracting the times, was Donders' subtraction method of 1868. The mental act being timed, apperception, had been named by Leibniz and given its psychological meaning by Herbart. The belief that a mental process could be measured at all was Fechner's answer to Kant, and the assumption that each mental event has a bodily partner running alongside it was the psychophysical parallelism that Wundt inherited from Leibniz. Even the plan of asking a trained observer to report under controlled, repeatable conditions was laid down in Wundt's four rules of experimental introspection. So what was new? Not the parts but the purpose. For the first time, a student was doing original research on the mind, in a room set aside for it, under a professor who had announced a new science and would soon give it a journal, a textbook tradition and a stream of students. That is the whole answer to the puzzle the chapter began with, and it needs both theories of history from Section 1.8: the Zeitgeist had put every part on the bench, and one determined person assembled them into an institution. Friedrich's own measurements are long forgotten, and the hope of timing apperception by simple subtraction did not survive the problem of pure insertion described in Section 1.4. But the room outlived its first experiment. Within a generation its graduates had carried it to Wurzburg, Cornell, Columbia, Pennsylvania and Harvard. In Philadelphia in 1896 one of them, Lightner Witmer, brought the same patient, measuring attitude to a boy who could not spell, and in 1915 a student of another, Munsterberg, carried the laboratory to Calcutta. The clinical psychology you are preparing to study is a direct descendant of that winter in Leipzig. Chapter summary 1.1 What Is Psychology? The word comes from the Greek psyche (soul) and logos (study); Christian Wolff made it standard in the 1730s, and Aristotle's De Anima was the first treatise on the soul. The definition has changed with each school: the soul, then the mind, then conscious experience (Wundt and Titchener; James's "science of mental life", 1890), then behaviour (McDougall, 1905 and 1908; Watson, 1913; Woodworth; the definition Indian textbooks credit to N. L. Munn). Today psychology is the scientific study of behaviour, which is overt, and mental processes, which are internal and covert. Its four goals are to describe, explain, predict and control (or influence). Basic research seeks understanding for its own sake; applied research solves practical problems. Clinical psychology assesses and treats psychological disorders, while counselling psychology serves people in the normal range with adjustment problems. Comparative psychology studies animal behaviour across species, ethology studies it in natural settings, evolutionary psychology explains behaviour as the product of natural selection, behaviour genetics asks how much variation is due to genes, and differential psychology studies individual differences. 1.2 Philosophical Roots: A Long Past. Nativism holds that some knowledge is inborn and empiricism that all knowledge comes from experience; rationalism makes reason the chief route to knowledge. Plato was a nativist and rationalist who saw learning as recollection; Aristotle was an empiricist who gave the first laws of association (similarity, contrast, contiguity). Descartes treated the body as a machine, described the reflex, held innate ideas and proposed dualism with interaction through the pineal gland. The British empiricists followed: Hobbes the materialist; Locke with the tabula rasa, sensation and reflection, simple and complex ideas, and primary and secondary qualities; Berkeley with esse est percipi and a learned theory of depth; Hume with impressions, ideas and the laws of resemblance, contiguity and cause and effect. The associationists Hartley, James Mill (mental mechanics), John Stuart Mill (mental chemistry) and Bain built the mind out of linked elements. On the continent, Leibniz proposed monads, petites perceptions and apperception, Herbart the threshold of consciousness and the apperceptive mass, and Kant innate categories and the claim that psychology could never be a science. The mind-body positions are interactionism, psychophysical parallelism, epiphenomenalism (Huxley), materialist and idealist monism, and Spinoza's double-aspect theory. Ontology concerns existence and epistemology knowledge; Comte's positivism rejected introspection. 1.3 Physiological and Biological Roots. The Bell-Magendie law (1811, 1822) separated sensory dorsal roots from motor ventral roots. Johannes Muller's doctrine of specific nerve energies held that the quality of a sensation depends on the nerve stimulated. Helmholtz measured the speed of the nerve impulse in 1850 (about 27 metres per second) and proposed unconscious inference and the trichromatic theory. Localisation of function came through Gall and Spurzheim's phrenology (right idea, wrong method), Flourens' ablation studies, Broca's patient Tan (1861), Wernicke's sensory aphasia (1874) and Fritsch and Hitzig's electrical mapping of the motor cortex (1870). Darwin's natural selection (1859) and his book on emotional expression (1872) gave psychology continuity between species, the question of function and an interest in variation. His half-cousin Galton founded the study of individual differences with Hereditary Genius (1869), twin studies, the anthropometric laboratory (1884), regression, correlation, word association and the questionnaire, and coined eugenics (1883). Romanes' anecdotal method invited anthropomorphism, which Lloyd Morgan's canon of parsimony (1894) corrected, as Pfungst's study of Clever Hans (1907) showed. 1.4 Measuring the Mind: Psychophysics and Mental Chronometry. Weber found that the just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the standard stimulus (Weber's law). Fechner, after his insight of 22 October 1850, proposed that sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity (S = k log I), published Elements of Psychophysics in 1860, gave the three classical psychophysical methods and is the founder of psychophysics; Boring argued that 1860 could even be taken as psychology's founding date. The astronomers' personal equation revealed individual differences in reaction time. Donders' subtraction method (1868) compared simple, go/no-go and choice reactions to time the stages of identification and choice, founding mental chronometry, though it assumes "pure insertion" of stages. Ebbinghaus extended measurement to memory with nonsense syllables, the savings method and the forgetting curve ( On Memory , 1885). 1.5 Wilhelm Wundt and the Founding of Experimental Psychology. Wundt (1832 to 1920), trained in medicine and physiology and once Helmholtz's assistant, published Principles of Physiological Psychology (1873 to 1874), moved to Leipzig in 1875, began laboratory research in 1879 and founded Philosophische Studien in 1881. Psychology for Wundt studied immediate experience, analysed into sensations and simple feelings. His system was voluntarism: the mind actively organises experience through attention and will, apperception brings contents into the focus of consciousness, and creative synthesis produces wholes with new properties. His tridimensional theory of feeling (1896) described feelings as pleasure-displeasure, tension-relaxation and excitement-depression. His method was controlled internal perception ( innere Wahrnehmung ), not armchair self-observation ( Selbstbeobachtung ), governed by four rules. Higher mental processes he studied through language, myth and custom in the ten-volume Volkerpsychologie (1900 to 1920). His students included Hall, Cattell, Munsterberg, Kulpe, Titchener, Witmer, Kraepelin, Spearman and, briefly, Bekhterev. 1.6 Structuralism and Its European Rivals. Titchener carried a stricter version of Wundt's programme to Cornell and named it structuralism (1898). He sought the elements of consciousness (sensations, images and affections) and their attributes (quality, intensity, duration, clearness, extensity), kept only the pleasant-unpleasant dimension of feeling, and trained observers to avoid the stimulus error. Meaning came from context, and perception was a complex of sensory and imaginal processes. Kulpe's Wurzburg school found imageless thought and showed how the Aufgabe, the determining tendency and set (Einstellung) direct thinking; the resulting controversy exposed the unreliability of introspection. Brentano's act psychology (1874) studied mental acts and their intentionality, Stumpf studied tone and trained the Gestalt founders, and G. E. Muller extended psychophysics and memory research at Gottingen. Structuralism declined because introspection could not settle disputes, observation altered experience, elementism missed wholes, its subject matter was narrow and it refused application; cognitive psychology later revived its topics. 1.7 Functionalism and the American Pioneers. Functionalism studied the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment, drawing on Darwin, pragmatism and American practicality. James's Principles of Psychology (1890) described the stream of consciousness, habit, the material, social and spiritual selves and the pure ego, and the James-Lange theory of emotion. Dewey's reflex arc paper (1896) founded the Chicago school, Angell's "Province of Functional Psychology" (1906) defined it and Carr's adaptive act matured it. At Columbia, Cattell coined "mental test" (1890), Woodworth gave the S-O-R formula and dynamic psychology, and Thorndike began the study of animal learning. Hall took the first American doctorate (1878), opened the first American research laboratory (1883), founded the American Journal of Psychology (1887) and the APA (1892), and described adolescence as storm and stress. Witmer opened the first psychological clinic (1896) and named clinical psychology; Munsterberg founded forensic and industrial psychology. Calkins became the first woman APA president (1905), Washburn the first woman PhD in psychology (1894), and Hollingworth disproved claims about women's inferiority. Functionalism dissolved into the mainstream and led to behaviourism, applied psychology and evolutionary psychology. 1.8 Reading the History: Zeitgeist, Great Persons and "Fathers". The great-person (personalistic) theory, stated by Carlyle in 1841, explains history through exceptional individuals; the Zeitgeist (naturalistic) theory, championed by Boring, explains it through the spirit of the times, citing multiple discoveries (Bell and Magendie, Darwin and Wallace, James and Lange), premature discoveries such as Mendel's, and contextual forces such as economic opportunity, war and prejudice. Psychology began in Germany because of its research universities, its broad idea of Wissenschaft and its experimental physiology; it began with Wundt because he, unlike the precursors, declared the science, gave it a laboratory, a journal and students; and 1879 marks the start of original student research. "Father" can mean founder, namer, chief influence or first in a country, so the qualifier in the question decides. In India, Seal drew up a syllabus in 1905, Sengupta set up the first laboratory (1915) and the first department (1916) at Calcutta and is the founder of modern psychology in India, Bose earned the first Indian doctorate (1921) and founded the Indian Psychoanalytic Society (1922), Mysore's department began in 1924 under Gopalaswamy, and the Indian Psychological Association followed in 1925. In the nature versus nurture debate, which early philosopher argued that the mind was a "tabula rasa" or blank slate at birth? (IHBAS 2024) a Plato b Rene Descartes c John Locke d Immanuel Kant ✓ Answer: (c) John Locke John Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) The concept The blank slate In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) Locke described the mind at birth as " white paper ", with nothing written on it yet. Where ideas come from Every idea comes from sensation or reflection , so Locke stands on the nurture (empiricist) side of the debate. Why the other options are wrong (a) Plato Nativist: thought learning was recollection of inborn knowledge. (b) Rene Descartes Nativist: believed in innate ideas . (d) Immanuel Kant Nativist: held that the mind imposes innate forms and categories on experience. ____ is a source of knowledge as per Empiricists. (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) a Logical reasoning b Theories c Sensory experiences d Contemplations ✓ Answer: (c) Sensory experiences Empiricism: knowledge comes through the senses The concept What it says Empiricism holds that all knowledge comes from experience delivered through the senses . The rival view The rationalists (Plato, Descartes, Leibniz) put reasoning and contemplation first. Why the other options are wrong (a) Logical reasoning The rationalists' route to knowledge (Plato, Descartes, Leibniz), not the empiricists'. (b) Theories Products of knowledge rather than its source. (d) Contemplations Also a rationalist route: knowledge reached by thinking, not through the senses. According to Wundt 'apperceptive mass' constitutes ___________ . (IHBAS 2025) a Compound of elemental processes bound by association b Sensation and pure perception c Pure perception and preexisting ideas d Sensation plus unconscious inference ✓ Answer: (c) Pure perception and preexisting ideas Herbart's term, reworked by Wundt The concept What it is The apperceptive mass is the organised body of ideas already in the mind, into which a new perception is taken up and understood. Why this one So it joins a fresh pure perception to preexisting ideas ; both halves are needed. Whose term The term is Herbart 's; Wundt reworked the idea of apperception. Why the other options are wrong (a) Compound of elemental processes bound by association The associationist and structuralist picture of the mind, not apperception. (b) Sensation and pure perception Leaves out the existing ideas , which are the whole point of the apperceptive mass. (d) Sensation plus unconscious inference Helmholtz 's theory of perception, not Wundt's apperception. Herman von Helmholtz (1821-94): (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) a He was a proponent of the just noticeable difference b He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision c He proposed the concept of the unconscious d He gave the law of effect ✓ Answer: (b) He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory (Young, 1802) The concept The theory The trichromatic theory explains colour vision by three receptor types . (d) He gave the law of effect Thorndike 's law, not Helmholtz's. What do Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common? (RML 2020) a Each of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology b Each of them founded a formal psychology laboratory c Each of them developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works d (a) and (c) ✓ Answer: (d) (a) and (c) Ebbinghaus, Galton, Freud: lone pioneers who invented methods The concept Why (a) holds All three worked largely alone and were pioneers . Why (c) holds Each invented methods: Ebbinghaus nonsense syllables and the savings method, Galton the questionnaire, word association and correlation, Freud free association. Other papers The RML 2020 key printed (a), but since (c) is also true, (d) is the more defensible answer and is the one the Panwar bank keys. (b) Each of them founded a formal psychology laboratory False: Freud never founded a laboratory. (c) Each of them developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works True, but (a) is also true, so the full answer is (d).
