In 1913 a twenty-six-year-old German psychologist named Wolfgang Kohler sailed to Tenerife, in the Canary Islands, to take charge of a small research station that the Prussian Academy of Sciences kept there for the study of chimpanzees. He expected a short posting. Then the First World War broke out, the sea lanes closed, and he stayed until 1920. For six years he had little to do but watch apes think. His most gifted subject was a chimpanzee called Sultan. One day Kohler placed a banana outside the bars of Sultan's cage, beyond reach. Inside the cage lay two hollow bamboo sticks, one thin enough to slide into the other, but each too short to reach the fruit on its own. Sultan tried one stick, then the other. He pushed one stick out with the second, so that the first touched the banana, but he could not draw it in. After more than an hour Kohler gave up and left a keeper to watch. Sultan sat on a box, idly playing with the two sticks. By chance he found himself holding them in a line, and he pushed the thin one into the end of the thick one. According to Kohler's record, he jumped up at once, ran to the bars and raked in the banana with his new long stick. When the sticks came apart, he joined them again without hesitation. What had happened inside Sultan? Kohler was sure he knew: the ape had suddenly seen the situation in a new way, the two sticks reorganised in his perception into one tool. But in the very year Kohler reached Tenerife, a young American at Johns Hopkins University, John B. Watson, was telling psychologists that "inside" questions of this kind had no place in a science at all; all that could be studied was what the animal did. In Vienna, Sigmund Freud would have asked a different question again: what hidden wish does the behaviour serve? Forty years later, a cognitive psychologist would describe Sultan as an information-processing system searching a "problem space", and today a researcher trained in the Indian tradition might ask about the state of attention in which the solution arrived. Same ape, same sticks, five different stories. That is what this chapter is about. Between about 1900 and 1960 psychology was divided into rival schools , each with its own idea of what psychology should study, how it should study it, and what a human being is. You will meet each school in turn, see why it arose, what it discovered, and why it declined or was absorbed. Remember Sultan; you will meet him again at the end of the chapter. 2.1 Schools, Systems and Paradigms Lower yield · 3 Qs Chapter 1 ended with the first two schools of scientific psychology, structuralism and functionalism. This chapter picks up the story where they left it. Before we meet the newcomers, though, it helps to be clear about what a "school" actually is, because the word is used loosely, and the vocabulary of the field matters as much as its content. What makes a school of thought A school of thought is a group of psychologists who share a common set of assumptions about what psychology should study (its subject matter), how it should study it (its method), and what kind of explanation counts. A school usually has a recognisable founder or leader, a statement of its programme (often called its manifesto), a university or laboratory that serves as its home, a journal in which its members publish, a stream of students who carry its ideas into other institutions, and, just as important, a rival school against which it defines itself. Behaviourism, for example, had Watson as its founder, his 1913 paper as its manifesto, and structuralism's introspection as its enemy. Two classic books gave the age of schools its shape. Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962) of Columbia University surveyed the rivals in Contemporary Schools of Psychology (1931), and Edna Heidbreder (1890 to 1985) described Seven Psychologies (1933). Notice their dates. The schools flourished roughly between the 1890s and the 1950s; after that, as you will see in Section 2.7, psychology gradually traded rival schools for overlapping "perspectives". Two related words are worth separating. A system of psychology is an organised and internally consistent body of assumptions, methods and theory that tries to cover the whole field; a theory is narrower, an explanation of one set of facts (a theory of forgetting, a theory of colour vision). Courses called "Systems and Theories" study both: the great systems, and the theories they produced. Kuhn's paradigms and a preparadigmatic science Why did psychology split into warring schools when physics and chemistry did not? A helpful answer comes from a physicist turned historian, Thomas Samuel Kuhn (1922 to 1996). In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), Kuhn argued that a mature science works within a paradigm : a shared framework of assumptions, problems, methods and model solutions that all workers in the field accept. Under a paradigm, scientists do what Kuhn called normal science : puzzle-solving within the accepted framework. Over time, results accumulate that the paradigm cannot explain (anomalies). When they pile up, the field enters a crisis; a new framework appears; and if it wins, the result is a scientific revolution, or paradigm shift . Newton's physics giving way to Einstein's is Kuhn's model case. A field that has no single accepted paradigm, but several competing schools, each with its own problems and methods, is in Kuhn's term a preparadigmatic science . Kuhn himself noticed this in the social sciences. In the preface to his book he recalled a year spent among social scientists and how struck he was by the number and extent of their open disagreements about what the legitimate problems and methods even were. The age of schools in psychology fits that description well: a structuralist and a behaviourist did not merely disagree about results, they disagreed about what counted as data. Whether psychology has since acquired a paradigm (or whether the cognitive revolution was a true Kuhnian revolution) is still debated, and we return to the question at the end of Section 2.7. The four forces You will often read that psychology has had three or four "forces". The numbering comes from the humanistic psychologists of the 1960s, above all Abraham Maslow, who called their own movement the third force to set it against the two forces that, in their view, dominated mid-century psychology. Table 2.1 sets out the sequence. Notice that the numbers describe a sequence of influence in the eyes of the humanists, not strict dates of birth: psychoanalysis (from the 1890s) is the first force and behaviourism (1913) the second. Table 2.1 The forces in psychology. Force School Key figures Picture of the person First Psychoanalysis Freud and his successors Driven by unconscious conflict and early childhood Second Behaviourism Watson, Skinner Shaped by the environment through conditioning Third Humanistic psychology Maslow, Rogers Free, growth-seeking, capable of self-actualisation Fourth Transpersonal psychology Maslow, Sutich, Grof Capable of experiences that go beyond the individual self Figure 2.1 lays the schools out in time, so that you can see which ones overlapped and which ones replaced each other. Keep it in mind as you read; each bar is the subject of one part of this chapter. Structuralism (1879) Functionalism (1890s) Psychoanalysis, the first force (1890s) Gestalt (1912) Behaviourism (1913) Neobehaviourism Humanistic (third force) Cognitive (1956) Transpersonal (1969) Positive psychology (1998) Indian Psychology movement (2002) 1880 1900 1920 1940 1960 1980 2000 Figure 2.1 The schools of psychology in time. Each bar runs from a school's founding event to the point where it stopped being a dominant, separate school (bars reaching the right edge are still active traditions). Notice how Gestalt and behaviourism were born a year apart, and how the cognitive and humanistic movements grew up side by side in the 1950s. Exam trap "Which is the fourth force?" The answer is transpersonal psychology . In counselling textbooks, however, Paul Pedersen (1991) called multiculturalism the "fourth force" in counselling. If both appear in the options, read the stem: "in psychology" points to transpersonal; "in counselling" may point to multiculturalism. "Experiential" psychology is not one of the numbered forces. 2.2 Behaviourism: From Watson's Manifesto to Skinner Medium yield · 9 Qs In 1913, structuralism (Wundt and Titchener) and functionalism (James, Dewey and Angell) were still arguing about consciousness: what its elements were, or what it was for. Both relied on introspection, the trained observation of one's own experience. A young professor at Johns Hopkins decided that the whole argument was a mistake. Psychology, he said, should stop studying consciousness altogether. To understand how anyone could say such a thing in 1913, and be applauded for it, you need to see the ground that had been prepared. The ground prepared: animal psychology and Russian objective psychology The first preparation came from the study of animals. After Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) argued for continuity between humans and other species, animal minds became a serious topic. George John Romanes (1848 to 1894) collected stories of clever animals (his anecdotal method), and Conwy Lloyd Morgan (1852 to 1936) answered with his canon of 1894: never interpret an action as the result of a higher mental faculty if it can be explained by a lower one (both are covered in Chapter 1). Jacques Loeb (1859 to 1924), a physiologist who taught Watson at Chicago, went further and explained animal movement as tropisms , forced, mechanical orientations toward or away from light, gravity and chemicals, with no mind required. And Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949), in his 1898 dissertation Animal Intelligence , put hungry cats in puzzle boxes and showed that they escaped not by reasoning but by gradual trial and error, stamped in by satisfying consequences: his law of effect (Chapter 6). If animal behaviour could be studied so precisely without asking what the animal was conscious of, why not human behaviour too? The second preparation came from Russia, where a tradition of objective psychology had grown out of physiology. Ivan Mikhailovich Sechenov (1829 to 1905), in Reflexes of the Brain (1863), argued that all acts of conscious and unconscious life are reflexes in their origin. Ivan Petrovich Pavlov (1849 to 1936), who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on digestion, discovered around the turn of the century that his dogs began to salivate to signals that preceded food; he called these conditioned reflexes and spent the rest of his life studying them (Chapter 6). Vladimir Mikhailovich Bekhterev (1857 to 1927) studied what he called association reflexes, conditioning motor responses such as withdrawing a limb from an electric shock, and named his whole approach reflexology ; his Objective Psychology appeared between 1907 and 1912. Bekhterev's motor conditioning, more than Pavlov's salivation, gave Watson a method he could use on people. The third preparation was home-grown. American functionalism had already pulled psychology toward practical questions (education, testing, industry) and toward the study of what organisms do to adapt. Behaviourism, in a sense, was functionalism with the mind removed. Watson's manifesto (1913) John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958) grew up poor in South Carolina, earned his doctorate at the University of Chicago in 1903 with a study of learning in rats, and moved to Johns Hopkins in 1908. He had never been comfortable with introspection; he later admitted that he hated serving as a subject in introspective experiments and preferred animals, which could not be asked what they were experiencing. Early in 1913 he gave a lecture at Columbia University, published that March in Psychological Review as "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It". It is the founding document of behaviourism , the school that defines psychology as the science of observable behaviour. Key study: "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" (1913) Watson's paper opens with a sentence every student of the history of psychology should know almost by heart: psychology as the behaviourist views it "is a purely objective experimental branch of natural science. Its theoretical goal is the prediction and control of behavior. Introspection forms no essential part of its methods." He added that the behaviourist "recognizes no dividing line between man and brute". The paper made four claims. (1) Subject matter : behaviour, not consciousness. (2) Method : objective observation, never introspection. (3) Goal : prediction and control, which made psychology useful to education, business and medicine. (4) Continuity : the same principles apply to humans and animals. In later books Watson phrased the goal precisely: given the stimulus, to predict the response, and given the response, to identify the stimulus that produced it. Watson was elected President of the American Psychological Association in 1915, only two years later; the manifesto had found an audience ready for it. What methods did Watson allow? Four: observation, with or without instruments; testing (he liked tests as samples of behaviour, not as measures of mental capacities); the verbal report method, in which speech is treated as behaviour, so that what a person says counts as data but is not taken as a window on consciousness; and, from 1915, the conditioned reflex method borrowed from Pavlov and Bekhterev. Watson's programme: thinking, emotion and the "twelve infants" A science of behaviour has to say something about the things introspectionists cared about, such as thought and feeling. Watson had an answer for each, and his answers show you the spirit of the school. Thinking as subvocal speech. Watson argued that thinking is nothing but talking to oneself so quietly that the movements cannot be seen: thought is subvocal speech , small movements of the tongue and larynx (he called them laryngeal habits). This view is called peripheralism , because it locates mental life in the peripheral muscles rather than in central brain processes. It led Watson to divide behaviour into explicit (overt) responses that anyone can see, and implicit (covert) responses such as subvocal speech, which cannot be seen by an observer but can, in principle, be measured with instruments. This is exactly the sense in which modern textbooks say covert behaviour is measurable but not directly observable, and why the "mental processes" in today's definition of psychology (the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes) are internal, covert processes. Was Watson right about thought? A dramatic test came in 1947, when Scott Smith and his colleagues at the University of Utah gave Smith himself a dose of curare large enough to paralyse every skeletal muscle, keeping him alive on a respirator. If thinking were movement of the speech muscles, Smith should have been unable to think. He reported afterwards that he had remained fully aware, had understood what was said to him and could remember it. Peripheralism did not survive. Emotion. Watson held that infants show just three unlearned emotional reactions: fear (to loud noises and sudden loss of support), rage (to hampering of movement) and love (to stroking and gentle handling). Every other emotion, he argued, is built from these three by conditioning. Environmentalism. Watson's most quoted words appeared in his popular book Behaviorism (1925). "Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed, and my own specified world to bring them up in and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select: doctor, lawyer, artist, merchant-chief and, yes, even beggar-man and thief, regardless of his talents, penchants, tendencies, abilities, vocations, and race of his ancestors." This is environmentalism in its purest form: the belief that behaviour is shaped almost entirely by experience rather than heredity. What is usually left out is the next sentence, in which Watson conceded that he was "going beyond my facts", adding that so had the advocates of the contrary view, and they had been doing it for thousands of years. Consistent with this, Watson first accepted, and then by the mid-1920s rejected, the idea of human instincts. Little Albert. To show that emotions are conditioned, Watson and his graduate student Rosalie Rayner (1898 to 1935) conditioned fear in an eleven-month-old infant, "Albert B.", in 1920, pairing a white rat with a loud noise made by striking a steel bar behind his head. Albert came to fear the rat, and the fear generalised to a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat and a Santa Claus mask. The study, its method and its ethical problems are told in full in Chapter 6. The same year, Watson's affair with Rayner became public; he was forced to resign from Johns Hopkins, married Rayner, and spent the rest of his working life in advertising at the J. Walter Thompson agency. His academic career had lasted barely twenty years, but the school he named outlived him by decades. Exam trap Who defined psychology as the science of behaviour? Watson (1913) made behaviour the subject matter of psychology, so for "founder of behaviourism" and "Watson defined psychology as the science of ..." the answers are behaviourism and behaviour (not soul, mind or consciousness: the soul was the subject matter of the ancient philosophers, the mind that of later philosophers, and consciousness that of Wundt and Titchener). One Panwar item, however, keys N. L. Munn as the first to establish psychology as "the scientific study of behaviour": Norman Leslie Munn's widely used textbooks popularised that wording. If Watson is an option, prefer Watson; if the options are Munn, Woodworth and Wundt, the key is Munn. Woodworth is remembered for the S-O-R formula and a quip often credited to him: psychology first lost its soul, then its mind, then consciousness. Rationalism is a philosophical position (Descartes), not a school Watson founded. Functionalism belongs to James, Dewey and Angell; structuralism to Titchener. Three meanings of "behaviourism" As the school matured, it became clear that "behaviourism" could mean three different things, and the three are easily confused. The difference lies in what each says about the mind. Table 2.2 Three kinds of behaviourism. Kind What it says about mental events Typical figures Metaphysical (eliminative) Minds and conscious states do not exist as anything other than behaviour Watson in his most extreme statements Methodological Mental events may exist, but they are private and cannot be studied scientifically; only public behaviour counts as data Watson in practice; most neobehaviourists Radical Private events (thoughts, feelings) are real and are themselves behaviour, obeying the same laws; but they are not the causes of overt behaviour Skinner, who adopted the term in 1945 (Mary Whiton Calkins had first used it, for Watson's view, in 1921) The word "radical" in radical behaviourism does not mean "extreme". Skinner meant it in its root sense: thoroughgoing, going to the roots. Ironically, radical behaviourism is the only one of the three that lets thoughts and feelings into the science; methodological behaviourism simply sets them aside. Neobehaviourism: logical positivism and operationism Watson's crusading behaviourism dominated American psychology from about 1913 to 1930. Historians of psychology usually describe what followed as a second stage, neobehaviourism (about 1930 to 1960), and a third, sociobehaviourism or social learning theory (about 1960 onward). The neobehaviourists, Tolman, Hull, Guthrie and Skinner, kept Watson's demand for objectivity but wanted to make behaviourism more rigorous and more theoretical. They drew on two ideas from the philosophy of science. The first was logical positivism , the philosophy of the Vienna Circle of the 1920s, which held that a statement is meaningful only if it can be verified by observation (or is true by definition). Talk of unobservable "minds" was therefore not false but meaningless unless it could be tied to observables. The second was operationism , proposed by the American physicist Percy Williams Bridgman (1882 to 1961) in The Logic of Modern Physics (1927): a scientific concept means nothing more than the set of operations used to measure it. The psychologist S. S. Stevens brought the idea into psychology in 1935. The legacy is the operational definition that every research methods course still teaches: "hunger" in a rat experiment is defined as "twenty-three hours without food", and "intelligence" as "the score on this test". Edward Chace Tolman's purposive behaviourism. Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959) of the University of California at Berkeley was the behaviourist who let cognition in by the back door. He called his system purposive behaviourism and set it out in Purposive Behavior in Animals and Men (1932), a book he dedicated, with typical humour, to the white rat. Tolman insisted on studying molar behaviour , whole goal-directed acts such as a rat running a maze or a person going home, rather than Watson's molecular behaviour , the individual muscle twitches and glandular secretions that make up an act. Molar behaviour, Tolman observed, "reeks of purpose": a rat that finds its usual route blocked takes another, so what it has learned is not a chain of movements but where the food is. To explain this without returning to introspection, Tolman introduced the intervening variable in the mid-1930s: an unobserved process inferred between the observable stimulus and the observable response and defined operationally by the conditions that produce it. Hunger, expectancy and demand are intervening variables. On one side sit the independent variables (environmental stimuli, hours of deprivation, heredity, previous training, age); on the other, behaviour; in between, the processes that link them. In effect, Watson's S-R formula became S-O-R, the formula Woodworth had used to insert the organism between stimulus and response. Tolman's most famous intervening variable was the cognitive map , a mental representation of the layout of the environment, which he described in "Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men" (1948). The best evidence for it was latent learning , learning that occurs without reinforcement and stays hidden until there is a reason to show it. In the classic experiment of Tolman and Charles Honzik (1930), rats that explored a maze for ten days without food made many errors; once food appeared in the goal box on day 11, their errors fell by the very next day to the level of rats rewarded from the beginning. They had been learning the maze all along (the full study is in Chapter 6). For Tolman, rats learn what leads to what (expectancies), not stimulus-response habits. Clark Leonard Hull's hypothetico-deductive system. If Tolman was the playful neobehaviourist, Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) of Yale University was the system-builder. Hull admired Newton's Principia and wanted a psychology built the same way, by the hypothetico-deductive method : state a small set of postulates, deduce precise testable predictions (theorems) from them, test the predictions experimentally, and revise the postulates when they fail. His Principles of Behavior (1943) made him for two decades the most cited psychologist in the world. At the centre of Hull's theory is drive reduction . A biological need (for food, water, relief from pain) produces a drive (D), an aroused state that energises behaviour; any response that reduces the drive is reinforced. Reinforced repetitions build habit strength , written S H R , the strength of the learned bond between a stimulus and a response, which grows with the number of reinforced trials. Habit alone does not produce behaviour; it must be energised by drive. Hull's 1943 formula for reaction potential , the tendency to make the response, was therefore multiplicative: S E R = S H R × D The multiplication matters: if either habit or drive is zero, there is no behaviour, however strong the other. A well-trained but completely satiated rat does not run the maze. Later versions added incentive motivation (K, the size of the reward) and stimulus intensity (V), and subtracted inhibition (fatigue-like reactive inhibition and conditioned inhibition). Hull's students, especially Kenneth Spence, Neal Elgar Miller and O. Hobart Mowrer, carried his ideas into many fields. One famous offshoot was John Dollard and Neal Miller's Personality and Psychotherapy (1950), which translated Freud's ideas into Hull's vocabulary of drive, cue, response and reinforcement; it is usually called the early social learning theory, as distinct from the later social learning theory of Albert Bandura and Richard Walters (1963). Edwin Ray Guthrie's contiguity theory. Edwin Ray Guthrie (1886 to 1959) of the University of Washington offered the simplest theory of all, in The Psychology of Learning (1935). His one law was contiguity : a combination of stimuli that has accompanied a movement will, on its recurrence, tend to be followed by that movement. Reinforcement is not needed; what matters is only that stimulus and movement occur together. Learning is one-trial learning : a stimulus-movement association reaches full strength on its first pairing. Why, then, does practice help? Because a skill is made of many movements, each attached to many stimuli, and practice attaches the act to more and more of the situations in which it must occur. Guthrie also gave practical advice on breaking habits (the threshold, fatigue and incompatible-response methods, Chapter 6). Burrhus Frederic Skinner's radical behaviourism. Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990) of Harvard became the most famous psychologist of the twentieth century; a 2002 survey ranking the most eminent psychologists placed him first, ahead of Piaget and Freud. Skinner distinguished respondent behaviour, elicited by a preceding stimulus as in Pavlov's experiments, from operant behaviour, emitted by the organism and controlled by its consequences. His tools (the operant chamber or "Skinner box", the cumulative recorder) and findings (reinforcement schedules, shaping) are covered in Chapter 6. Here what matters is his system. Skinner was a radical behaviourist (Table 2.2) and also an anti-theorist. In a 1950 paper he asked whether theories of learning were necessary at all and answered no: psychology should describe functional relations between environmental events and behaviour, without inventing intervening variables, drives or cognitive maps. This is why Skinner's approach is sometimes called descriptive behaviourism, or the "empty organism" approach (a description Skinner disliked, since he never denied that the organism has insides; he denied that inner events explain anything). His major books are worth knowing by title and year: The Behavior of Organisms (1938); Walden Two (1948), a novel about a utopian community run on reinforcement principles; Science and Human Behavior (1953); Verbal Behavior (1957), which treated language as operant behaviour shaped by a verbal community; and Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971), which argued that the idea of an autonomous, free person is a pre-scientific fiction we can no longer afford. Zing-Yang Kuo, the behaviourist who abolished instinct. The most extreme environmentalist of all was a Chinese psychologist trained at Berkeley, Zing-Yang Kuo (1898 to 1970). In "Giving Up Instincts in Psychology" (1921) he argued that the concept of instinct explains nothing. He backed the claim with an elegant experiment (1930): kittens reared alone, kittens reared watching their mothers kill rats, and kittens reared together with rats. Most of the kittens that watched their mothers became rat-killers, while only a small minority of those raised alongside rats ever killed one, and some seemed to treat rats as companions. "Rat-killing instinct," Kuo concluded, depends on rearing. Table 2.3 sets the main behaviourists side by side. Table 2.3 The behaviourists compared. Theorist Label Signature ideas Key work Watson Classical (methodological) behaviourism Prediction and control; peripheralism; fear, rage, love; environmentalism "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" (1913); Behaviorism (1925) Tolman Purposive behaviourism Molar behaviour; intervening variables; cognitive maps; latent learning; expectancy Purposive Behavior in Animals and Men (1932) Hull Hypothetico-deductive neobehaviourism Drive reduction; habit strength; S E R = S H R × D Principles of Behavior (1943) Guthrie Contiguity theory Contiguity without reinforcement; one-trial learning The Psychology of Learning (1935) Skinner Radical (descriptive) behaviourism Operant conditioning; no inner causes; anti-theory The Behavior of Organisms (1938); Verbal Behavior (1957) Exam trap Cognitive map and latent learning are Tolman's, not Kohler's (insight), not Harlow's (learning sets), not Skinner's and not Bandura's (observational learning). Gould , the fourth option in one Panwar item, did not propose the concept either: the ethologist James L. Gould tested Tolman's idea in insects, asking in 1986 whether honeybees have cognitive maps, and the evolutionary biologist Stephen Jay Gould is known for The Mismeasure of Man (1981), a critique of intelligence testing. Guthrie's one-trial learning (any stimulus-movement pairing) is not the same thing as the one-trial learning in Garcia's taste-aversion studies (Chapter 6). Dollard and Miller = early social learning theory (Hull plus Freud, 1950); Bandura and Walters = later social learning theory (1963). Walden Two is a novel, not a research report. Thorndike's "connectionism" (stimulus-response bonds) is not the connectionism of modern neural-network models (Section 2.6). Criticism, decline and legacy By the 1950s behaviourism had won American psychology, and it was beginning to lose. The criticisms came from several directions at once. It could not explain language: Noam Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior , discussed in Section 2.6, argued that children produce sentences they have never heard and never been reinforced for. It ignored biology: two of Skinner's own former students, Keller and Marian Breland, reported in 1961 that the animals they trained for commercial shows kept "misbehaving", drifting back toward instinctive food-getting actions (instinctive drift), and John Garcia showed that rats learn some associations far more easily than others (Chapter 6). Its central concepts strained against its own evidence: Tolman's rats seemed to carry maps in their heads, and Kohler's apes seemed to reason. And it seemed to many to leave out exactly what makes us human: purpose, meaning and freedom. The humanists (Section 2.5) attacked from that side, the cognitive psychologists (Section 2.6) from the other. Yet behaviourism did not so much die as dissolve into the rest of psychology. Its demand for objective, operationally defined, replicable measurement became simply the way psychology is done. Its laws of learning remain the core of Chapter 6. And it gave clinical psychology one of its most effective toolkits. Clinical link Behaviour therapy applies learning principles to psychological problems. Mary Cover Jones (1896 to 1987) removed a small boy's fear of rabbits in 1924 by gradually bringing a rabbit closer while he ate. Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997), in Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958), developed systematic desensitisation : relaxation, which is incompatible with anxiety, is paired with an imagined hierarchy of feared situations. (The method is Wolpe's, not Skinner's, Watson's or Pavlov's.) Skinner's operant principles produced token economies and applied behaviour analysis, now widely used with children with autism. The therapies themselves are taught in the Clinical book. 2.3 Gestalt Psychology and Kurt Lewin High yield · 16 Qs Behaviourism rebelled against structuralism by throwing out consciousness. A second rebellion, in Germany, began a year earlier and took the opposite route: it kept consciousness but threw out the idea that consciousness is built from elements. Where Titchener had analysed experience into sensations, images and feelings, and Watson analysed behaviour into reflexes, the Gestalt psychologists argued that both had made the same mistake. They had taken the whole apart and assumed that the parts were more real than the whole. Wertheimer and the phi phenomenon (1912) Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) was born in Prague and trained under Oswald Kulpe at Wurzburg. As the story is usually told, in the summer of 1910 he was travelling by train to a holiday in the Rhineland when an idea about seen motion struck him so forcefully that he got off at Frankfurt, bought a toy stroboscope (a device that creates the impression of movement from a series of still pictures), and began experimenting in his hotel room. Historians suspect the story has been polished over the years, but what followed is well documented. At the Psychological Institute in Frankfurt, Wertheimer used a tachistoscope (an instrument that flashes visual displays for precisely controlled intervals) to study apparent motion. His two main observers were younger psychologists, Wolfgang Kohler and Kurt Koffka. The three of them became the founders of Gestalt psychology, and Wertheimer's 1912 paper on the experimental study of seen motion is the school's founding document. The experiment was simple. Two lines were flashed one after the other in slightly different positions. When the interval between them was very short (around 30 milliseconds), observers saw two lines at once; when it was long (around 200 milliseconds), they saw one line and then the other. But at intervals in between (around 60 milliseconds), they saw a single line move from one position to the other. Wertheimer called this apparent movement the phi phenomenon . (He distinguished "pure phi", a sense of motion without any moving object, from the smooth movement of the object itself, later called beta movement; the details belong to Chapter 4.) Why did such a small effect launch a school? Because the motion was not in either stimulus. Each line, analysed on its own, was stationary. An elementist, adding up two static sensations, could never arrive at movement. The perceived motion was a property of the whole pattern of stimulation in time, and it was as real in experience as anything else. If something as basic as seen motion could not be built from elements, perhaps nothing in perception could. The idea was not entirely new. In 1890 the Austrian philosopher Christian von Ehrenfels (1859 to 1932), whose lectures Wertheimer had attended in Prague, had described form qualities (Gestaltqualitaten): a melody played in a different key consists of entirely different notes, yet we hear the same melody. The melody, then, is something more than its notes. Ehrenfels, however, treated the form quality as an extra element added to the sensations. Wertheimer's radical step was to reverse the order: the whole comes first, and the parts get their character from their place in it. The German word Gestalt means form, shape or configuration, an organised whole. Kohler: insight, transposition and isomorphism Wolfgang Kohler (1887 to 1967), born in Reval (now Tallinn in Estonia), took his doctorate in Berlin under Carl Stumpf and was the school's scientist and chief spokesman. You have already met him on Tenerife (1913 to 1920). His observations there, published in German in 1917 and in English as The Mentality of Apes (1925), challenged Thorndike's trial-and-error account of animal problem-solving. Thorndike's cats, Kohler argued, had been put in puzzle boxes whose mechanisms they could not see; of course they fumbled. Give an animal a problem whose elements are all in view, and it may solve it by insight : a sudden reorganisation of the perceptual field so that the relations needed for a solution are seen. Sultan's two sticks, and the boxes his companions stacked to reach fruit hung from the roof, were Kohler's showpieces. Insightful solutions, he noted, appear suddenly, are carried out smoothly once found, are retained, and transfer readily to similar problems. Insight learning as a type of learning is treated in Chapter 6. Key study: Kohler's chickens and transposition (1918) The question. When an animal learns to choose one of two stimuli, does it learn the absolute properties of the stimulus (this particular shade of grey) or a relation between stimuli (the darker of the two)? The method. Kohler trained hens to peck grain from the darker of two grey papers; grain on the lighter one was out of bounds. Then he gave them a test pair: the old "correct" darker grey, now beside an even darker new grey. The result. Most of the time the hens pecked at the new, darker grey, the one they had never been rewarded on, and ignored the shade that had been reinforced. Kohler found the same with chimpanzees. The conclusion. The animals had learned a relation ("the darker one"), not an absolute stimulus. Kohler called this transposition , by analogy with a melody transposed to a new key. It was a direct challenge to the stimulus-response view that a specific stimulus becomes bonded to a response. The criticism: Kenneth Spence (1937) later showed that a stimulus-response account combining generalisation gradients of excitation and inhibition could predict transposition too, and that transposition breaks down when the test pair is far from the training pair. Kohler's most ambitious idea was physiological. In Die physischen Gestalten ("Physical Gestalten", 1920) he proposed isomorphism : the organisation of experience corresponds in structure (not in literal copy) to the organisation of electrical field processes in the brain. A perceived circle does not mean a circle drawn on the cortex, but a pattern of brain activity with the same relational order. The theory was tested in the 1950s. Karl Lashley and his colleagues laid strips of gold foil across the visual cortex of monkeys (1951), and Roger Sperry inserted mica plates and tantalum wires into the cortex of cats (1955), to short-circuit or block any such electrical fields. Perception was essentially unaffected. The field version of isomorphism did not survive, although the broader idea that experience and brain activity share a structure lives on in cognitive neuroscience. Kohler became director of the Psychological Institute at the University of Berlin in 1922, the most prestigious post in German psychology. When the Nazis began dismissing Jewish professors in 1933, he published a newspaper article in their defence, one of the last openly critical pieces to appear in Germany, and resisted the regime's interference with his institute until he resigned and emigrated in 1935. He spent the rest of his career at Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania and was President of the American Psychological Association in 1959. Koffka: development and the behavioural environment Kurt Koffka (1886 to 1941) was the school's great communicator. His Growth of the Mind (German 1921, English 1924) applied Gestalt ideas to child development, arguing that infants perceive organised wholes from the beginning rather than assembling them from sensations. In 1922 he introduced Gestalt psychology to American readers in an article in the Psychological Bulletin titled "Perception: An introduction to the Gestalt-theorie". The article was so influential that for years Americans assumed Gestalt psychology was only about perception, which the founders found frustrating. Koffka moved to Smith College in Massachusetts in 1927, and his Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935) is the school's most systematic textbook. Koffka's most memorable lesson is a German legend he retold in the Principles . On a winter evening, in a driving snowstorm, a man on horseback rode across a wide, wind-swept plain and arrived at last at an inn. The innkeeper, astonished, asked where he had come from. The rider pointed back across the plain. "Do you know," said the innkeeper, "that you have ridden across Lake Constance?" The rider dropped dead at his feet. In what environment, Koffka asks, did the rider's behaviour take place? In the geographical environment , the physical world, he crossed thin ice over deep water. But he behaved as if he were crossing solid ground, because his behavioural environment , the world as perceived, was a frozen plain. Behaviour, Koffka argued, is governed by the behavioural environment. It is one of the cleanest arguments in psychology for studying the world as the person experiences it. The three founders, together with the neurologist Kurt Goldstein and the psychiatrist Hans Gruhle, launched the school's journal, Psychologische Forschung ("Psychological Research"), in 1921. The central ideas of Gestalt psychology The whole is different from the sum of its parts. This is the school's slogan, and it is usually quoted as "the whole is greater than the sum of its parts". Koffka himself thought "greater" was the wrong word: in the Principles he wrote that it is more correct to say the whole is something else than the sum of its parts, because summing is a meaningless procedure, whereas the whole-part relationship is meaningful. A square drawn with four lines is not "more" than four lines; it is a different kind of thing, with properties (squareness, closedness, an inside) that none of the lines possesses. Textbooks use both versions for the Gestalt principle. Field theory. The Gestalt psychologists borrowed the concept of a field from nineteenth-century physics, where Faraday and Maxwell had shown that electrical and magnetic events are properties of a whole field of forces rather than of isolated particles. Field theory in psychology holds that perception, thought and behaviour are determined by the whole field of interacting forces present at the moment, not by isolated stimuli. Iron filings around a magnet do not each "decide" where to go; the field organises them. Organisation and Pragnanz. Because experience is organised into wholes, the Gestalt psychologists set out the laws by which the organisation happens. Wertheimer's 1923 paper on the laws of perceptual organisation described proximity, similarity, closure, good continuation and common fate, all governed by an overarching law of Pragnanz : perceptual organisation will always be as "good" (simple, regular, symmetrical, stable) as the conditions allow. Figure-ground organisation, first analysed by the Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin (1886 to 1951) in 1915, was adopted as a cornerstone: the figure is seen as a thing, nearer, with a clear contour and shape, usually smaller and more memorable, whereas the ground seems shapeless, diffuse, farther away and to continue behind the figure. The laws themselves, with demonstrations, are taught in Chapter 4. Productive thinking. Wertheimer's last book, Productive Thinking (published in 1945, two years after his death), brought Gestalt ideas to problem-solving and education. He distinguished reproductive thinking , the blind application of a memorised method, from productive thinking , in which the thinker grasps the structure of the problem and sees why a solution works. His favourite example came from a school classroom. Children taught the formula for the area of a parallelogram (base times height) by rote could apply it to the textbook figure but were helpless when the figure was turned on its side. A child who saw that the triangle "sticking out" at one end could be moved to fill the gap at the other, turning the parallelogram into a rectangle, understood the formula and could never be fooled by a rotation. Wertheimer also interviewed Albert Einstein at length about how the theory of relativity had been discovered. Karl Duncker's work on functional fixedness (1945) continued this line (Chapter 8). Notice the method row. The Gestalt psychologists did not use Titchener's trained introspection, which taught observers to report sensations and to avoid the "stimulus error" of naming the object. They wanted exactly what Titchener forbade: a description of experience as it naturally presents itself to an untrained observer, a book as a book and not as patches of colour. This descriptive approach is called phenomenological, and it links Gestalt psychology to the phenomenology of Husserl (Section 2.5). Exam trap Founders. The Gestalt trio is Wertheimer (founder), Kohler and Koffka. Watson, William James and Pavlov are favourite distractors. Lewin is Gestalt-influenced but is not one of the founders. Most important school for perception? Gestalt psychology. "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts and the parts are related to each other and to the whole" in a management or organisational stem refers to systems theory , associated with Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory, not to Gestalt psychology, motivation theory, contingency theory or Fayol's administrative theory. Read the options. The Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (Lauretta Bender, 1938) borrowed its designs from Wertheimer's 1923 figures, but it is a test of visual-motor integration (Assessment book), not a Gestalt theory. Kurt Lewin: field theory applied to the person The Gestalt founders worked mainly on perception and thinking. It was a younger colleague at the Berlin Institute, Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947), who carried field theory into motivation, personality and, finally, social life. Lewin's starting point was that behaviour at any moment is a function of the whole psychological situation. He expressed it in a formula that appears in his Principles of Topological Psychology (1936): B = f(P, E) Behaviour (B) is a function (f) of the person (P) and the environment (E). The person and the environment are not independent: they form one interdependent field, which Lewin called the life space (LSp), the totality of facts that determine a person's behaviour at a given moment. So the formula is often written B = f(LSp). The life space contains the person and the psychological environment, the environment as it exists for that person (Koffka's behavioural environment again), not the physical world as a geographer would map it. A rule a student has never heard of is not in her life space; an exam she fears is, even though it is a week away. To describe the life space, Lewin borrowed from a branch of mathematics called topology, which deals with regions, boundaries and connections rather than distances and sizes; hence topological psychology . The life space is divided into regions (activities, goals, groups) separated by boundaries, some of which act as barriers. Movement from one region to another, in thought or action, is called locomotion. Because topology alone cannot express direction and strength, Lewin added two dynamic concepts. A valence is the attracting (positive) or repelling (negative) quality a region has for the person; a vector is a force acting on the person, with a direction and a strength, toward or away from a region. Lewin later added hodological space (from the Greek hodos , path), a geometry of paths that represents the routes, including detours, by which a person can reach a goal. Figure 2.2 puts these terms together. The person and the psychological environment together make up the life space. The goal has positive valence and exerts a force (vector) on the person; a barrier blocks the direct route, so the person must find a detour path; a region of negative valence pushes the person away. Notice that everything in the diagram is the situation as the person sees it. Tension systems and the Zeigarnik effect. Lewin proposed that an intention to reach a goal sets up a tension system within the person, which is discharged only when the goal is reached. One prediction follows directly: unfinished tasks should leave tension behind them and so stay active in the mind. According to a story told by his students, Lewin noticed this one evening at a Berlin restaurant, where a waiter remembered every detail of the unpaid orders but could not recall what had been ordered at a table that had already settled its bill. His student Bluma Zeigarnik (1900 to 1988) tested the idea in 1927. Participants were given a series of simple tasks, half of which were interrupted before completion. Afterwards they recalled the interrupted tasks nearly twice as often as the completed ones. Better memory for interrupted than for completed tasks is the Zeigarnik effect . A second student, Maria Ovsiankina (1898 to 1993), showed in 1928 that people given the chance spontaneously go back to interrupted tasks and finish them, the Ovsiankina effect . Remember the pair this way: Zeigarnik, people remember unfinished tasks; Ovsiankina, people resume them. Contemporaneity. A further principle of Lewin's field theory is that only the present field can influence present behaviour. The past matters only to the extent that it has left traces in the life space now; the future, only as present expectations. This principle of contemporaneity is the most direct "here-and-now" idea in Gestalt-derived psychology. Lewin also analysed conflict as a balance of valences (approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance, Chapter 10). Group dynamics and action research. Lewin, who was Jewish, left Germany in 1933, worked briefly at Cornell University and then at the Iowa Child Welfare Research Station, and in 1945 founded the Research Center for Group Dynamics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. There he turned field theory to groups, which he saw as dynamic wholes whose properties are not the sum of their members'. He coined the term group dynamics . With Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White (1939) he compared boys' clubs run under autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire leadership (Social book). He also founded action research , research carried out in partnership with the people affected by a social problem, in a repeating cycle of planning, acting, observing the results and reflecting, then planning again. A summer workshop he led in 1946 gave rise to the T-group (training group) and the National Training Laboratories. His three-stage model of change (unfreezing, moving, refreezing) is still taught in management courses. Lewin is widely called the father of modern social psychology, and his motto summarises his career: "There is nothing so practical as a good theory." Exam trap Life space = the person plus the psychological environment (not society and group, not person and group, not environment and group). Lewin founded action research, group dynamics and modern experimental social psychology; he did not found psychoanalysis (Freud), psychophysics (Fechner) or functionalism (James, Dewey, Angell). Zeigarnik = recall of interrupted tasks; Ovsiankina = resumption of interrupted tasks. Topological = regions and boundaries; hodological = paths. Emigration, legacy, and a different "Gestalt" With the rise of the Nazis, all four leading figures, Wertheimer (1933, to the New School for Social Research in New York), Koffka (already at Smith from 1927), Kohler (1935) and Lewin (1933), ended up in the United States. There they met a psychology dominated by behaviourism, taught at small colleges rather than major research universities, and wrote in a second language. Gestalt psychology never became a dominant American school. Its influence, however, was enormous and lasting. Its account of perceptual organisation is still taught almost unchanged. Its insistence on insight and understanding prepared the ground for cognitive psychology (Section 2.6). And through Lewin, his students (Leon Festinger among them) and Gestalt-minded social psychologists such as Fritz Heider and Solomon Asch, it shaped modern social psychology. One thing Gestalt psychology did not produce is Gestalt therapy. Gestalt therapy was developed in the 1940s and 1950s by Frederick Salomon Perls (Fritz Perls, 1893 to 1970), a German-born psychoanalyst, with his wife Laura Perls and the writer Paul Goodman; the book Gestalt Therapy (1951) was written by Perls, Ralph Hefferline and Goodman. It is an experiential, humanistic therapy that emphasises awareness in the here and now, personal responsibility, and the completion of "unfinished business" (a phrase that echoes Zeigarnik's interrupted tasks). Its best-known technique is the empty chair , in which the client speaks to an imagined person, or a disowned part of the self, placed in an empty chair, and then changes seats to answer. Perls had worked with the holistic neurologist Kurt Goldstein, and he borrowed the word Gestalt and a general holism, but little else. The Gestalt-trained psychologist Mary Henle published a careful comparison in 1978 and concluded that the connection between the two is largely one of name. The therapy itself is taught in the Clinical book. Exam trap Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Kohler, Koffka) is not Gestalt therapy (Perls). The empty chair technique belongs to Gestalt therapy, not to psychoanalysis, CBT or person-centred therapy. Questions sometimes blur the two. An assertion-reason item states "Fritz Perls was a proponent of the Gestalt perspective" with the reason "Gestalt focuses on the wholeness of individuals' experiences in the present moment"; the key treats both as true and the reason as the correct explanation, because "Gestalt perspective" is used loosely there to include the therapy. Similarly, one Panwar item keys "here-and-now" to Gestalt psychology : the idea is most at home in Gestalt therapy (and in existential-humanistic therapy), and within Gestalt psychology proper it corresponds to Lewin's principle of contemporaneity. Psychoanalysis came from somewhere else entirely: the consulting room of a Viennese doctor treating patients whose symptoms made no medical sense. It never really belonged to academic psychology, yet it changed the way the whole twentieth century thought about the mind. This section tells its history as a school; Freud's theory of personality (the stages, defences and dynamics) is taught in full in the Personality book. From neurology to hysteria: Charcot, Bernheim and Breuer Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) did not set out to be a psychologist. He qualified in medicine at the University of Vienna in 1881 after years of research in the physiological laboratory of Ernst Brucke, a leader of the mechanistic school of German physiology, where he studied the nerve cells of fish and other animals under the microscope. Unable to support a family on a researcher's pay, he went into private practice in 1886 as a neurologist , a specialist in diseases of the nerves. Many of the patients who came to him suffered from hysteria , a condition (today classed among the conversion and dissociative disorders) in which people developed paralyses, blindness, loss of feeling or fits with no detectable damage to the nervous system. Three encounters shaped what Freud did with these patients. From October 1885 to February 1886 he studied in Paris with Jean-Martin Charcot (1825 to 1893), the most famous neurologist in Europe, who showed at the Salpetriere hospital that hysterical symptoms could be produced and removed under hypnosis. That meant the symptoms had a psychological, not an anatomical, cause. Charcot's pupil Pierre Janet (1859 to 1947) went on to explain hysteria as dissociation , a splitting off of some mental functions from the rest of consciousness into what he called the subconscious; his ideas ran parallel to Freud's, and the two later disputed priority. In 1889 Freud visited Hippolyte Bernheim (1840 to 1919) at Nancy, the rival French school, which taught that hypnosis was simply heightened suggestibility; Freud was struck by evidence that patients could later recall what had happened under hypnosis when pressed, which suggested that forgotten memories were not lost but kept out of awareness. The third and decisive influence was a senior Viennese physician and friend, Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925). Between 1880 and 1882 Breuer had treated a gifted young woman, known in the literature as Anna O. (her real name was Bertha Pappenheim), who suffered paralysis, disturbances of vision and speech, and periods of altered consciousness. Breuer found that when, under light hypnosis, she talked about the circumstances in which a symptom had first appeared, and expressed the feelings she had held back at the time, the symptom eased. Anna O. called the treatment "the talking cure" and "chimney sweeping". Breuer called it the cathartic method , from the Greek catharsis , purging: emotion that had been "strangulated" was released. Breuer and Freud published Studies on Hysteria in 1895, and that book is usually taken as the beginning of psychoanalysis. (Anna O. was Breuer's patient, not Freud's; she later became a pioneering social worker and campaigner for women's rights.) Freud soon gave up hypnosis, partly because not all patients could be hypnotised. He replaced it first with a "pressure technique" (pressing on the patient's forehead and insisting that a memory would come) and then with free association , in which the patient lies on a couch and reports everything that comes to mind, however trivial, embarrassing or illogical. The places where associations stall, he argued, mark resistance, the mind's defence against painful material. By 1896 he was calling his method psychoanalysis. The Interpretation of Dreams and the growth of a movement In the late 1890s, after the death of his father, Freud undertook a systematic self-analysis, much of it through his own dreams. The result was The Interpretation of Dreams , which appeared in November 1899 but was dated 1900 by its publisher, a fitting debut for the new century. In it Freud argued that every dream is the disguised fulfilment of a wish, and he called the interpretation of dreams "the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious" (dream theory is in Chapter 5). It sold only a few hundred copies in its first years. Yet a circle gathered. From 1902 a small group met at Freud's apartment on Wednesday evenings; in 1908 it became the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, and in 1910 the International Psychoanalytical Association was founded, with Carl Jung as its first president. International recognition came in 1909, when G. Stanley Hall invited Freud to lecture at Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts, as part of the university's twentieth-anniversary celebrations. Freud travelled with Jung and Sandor Ferenczi, gave five lectures in German, and received an honorary doctorate, his first academic honour. William James, by then old and ill, came to hear him. The Clark lectures are the usual marker for the arrival of psychoanalysis in America. Two models of the mind The topographic model. In The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) Freud described the mind as having three regions, a topographic model (topography means the mapping of places). The conscious contains what we are aware of at this moment. The preconscious contains material that is not in awareness now but can easily be recalled, such as your phone number or what you ate this morning. The unconscious contains wishes, memories and impulses that are actively kept out of awareness because they are unacceptable, and that can reach consciousness only in disguised form, in dreams, slips of the tongue and symptoms. The popular image of the mind as an iceberg, mostly below the waterline, illustrates this model, though the image is not Freud's own. The structural model. In The Ego and the Id (1923) Freud added a second map, the structural model , which describes three agencies rather than three regions. The id is the oldest and most primitive part of the personality, present at birth and entirely unconscious; it is the source of instinctual energy and operates on the pleasure principle, demanding immediate gratification and caring nothing for logic, time or morality (impulsive, irrational, pleasure-seeking: these words always point to the id). The ego develops to deal with reality; it operates on the reality principle, delays gratification, and uses realistic thought (secondary process) to find safe ways of meeting the id's demands. The superego is the internalised voice of parents and society, made up of the conscience and the ego-ideal. The ego, caught between the id, the superego and the outside world, protects itself against the anxiety these conflicts produce by means of defence mechanisms such as repression. The two models are not rivals: the ego and superego are partly conscious and partly unconscious, while the id is wholly unconscious. Exam trap Freud began his career as a neurologist , not as a psychiatrist, philosopher or (obviously) a psychoanalyst. Father of psychoanalysis : Freud, not Bernheim (Nancy school of hypnosis), not Adler (individual psychology), not Jung (analytical psychology). Psychosocial theory is Erikson's; psychoanalytic theory is Freud's. Gratification, irrational, impulsive = id. Freud's three anxieties are realistic, neurotic (fear that id impulses will break through and be punished) and moral; "innate anxiety" is not a technical term in any of these theories; Horney's basic anxiety and the existentialists' existential anxiety are different concepts (see Table 2.5 and Section 2.5). Dissenters and neo-Freudians Freud demanded loyalty to the core of his theory, above all to the sexual basis of neurosis, and some of his ablest followers broke away. Alfred Adler left in 1911 and Carl Jung in 1913 to 1914; each founded his own school. A later generation, often called the neo-Freudians , kept the idea of unconscious dynamics but shifted the emphasis from biological instincts to social relationships, culture and the ego. Strictly, Adler and Jung are "dissenters" and Horney, Fromm and Sullivan the neo-Freudians proper, while Anna Freud and Erikson are ego psychologists and Klein the founder of the object relations school; introductory textbooks usually group them all together. Its home was the clinic, not the university; its data were case histories, dreams and free associations, not experiments; and its aim was to relieve suffering as well as to understand it. Its central claims, that much of mental life is unconscious, that childhood experience shapes the adult, and that symptoms have meaning, entered everyday thought so completely that we hardly notice them. It is the first force in psychology (Table 2.1), and the broader psychodynamic perspective descended from it still explains behaviour, and many mental disorders, in terms of unconscious urges and the hidden struggle over their expression. Its critics were just as important to the history of the field. The philosopher Karl Popper (1902 to 1994) argued that psychoanalysis was unscientific because it was unfalsifiable: any behaviour at all could be explained after the event, so no observation could ever count against it. Behaviourists dismissed its concepts as untestable, and later the humanists complained that it built a whole picture of human nature from the study of sick people. Modern psychodynamic research has answered some of these charges with controlled studies, but the debate shaped how all the later schools defined themselves. Clinical link Short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, which focuses on recurring relationship patterns, the transference and avoided feelings, has a growing body of controlled evidence for depression and some anxiety and personality problems. When an interviewer asks you which psychotherapy "school" you find most convincing, remember that modern practice borrows across schools; see eclecticism in Section 2.7. 2.5 The Third Force and Beyond: Humanistic, Existential, Transpersonal and Positive Psychology High yield · 16 Qs By the 1950s, a student of psychology in America could choose between two great pictures of human nature. Psychoanalysis showed a creature driven by blind instincts and scarred by childhood. Behaviourism showed a creature shaped, like a laboratory rat, by its schedule of rewards. Both pictures were deterministic, and to a growing number of psychologists both seemed to leave out what mattered most: the capacity to choose, to grow, to create, to love, to look for meaning. The movement that grew out of this dissatisfaction called itself the third force. The birth of humanistic psychology Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970) began his career as an enthusiastic behaviourist. He took his doctorate at the University of Wisconsin in 1934, studying dominance and sexual behaviour in monkeys, and as a young man he believed Watson's behaviourism could solve the world's problems. Two experiences changed his mind: the Second World War, and the birth of his first child. He later said that holding his baby made him feel small and not really in control, and that anyone who had a baby could not be a behaviourist. Maslow decided to study not sick people, as Freud had done, nor rats, but the healthiest, most fulfilled people he could find. His hierarchy of needs (1943) and his concept of self-actualisation , the fulfilment of one's unique potential, are taught in Chapter 10. His books Motivation and Personality (1954) and Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) became the movement's texts, and it was Maslow who named it the third force. Carl Ransom Rogers (1902 to 1987) came to the same place by a different road, through counselling. In Counseling and Psychotherapy (1942) and Client-Centered Therapy (1951) he argued that every person has an actualising tendency , an innate drive to grow and develop, which flourishes when others offer unconditional positive regard, empathy and genuineness, and is blocked when love is given only on "conditions of worth". His theory is phenomenological: what matters is the person's own perceived world, the phenomenal field. (Rogers's theory belongs to the Personality book and his therapy to the Clinical book.) Two other founders deserve a place. Charlotte Buhler (1893 to 1974), a Viennese developmental psychologist who studied the course of whole human lives through biographies, brought a European lifespan perspective and was an early president of the movement's association. Rollo May (1909 to 1994) brought existential philosophy into American psychology, as you will see below. The movement acquired the trappings of a school quickly. In 1961 Maslow and Anthony Sutich (1907 to 1976) launched the Journal of Humanistic Psychology , and the Association for Humanistic Psychology was formed in the early 1960s (sources differ on the exact year, usually giving 1961 or 1962). In November 1964 a small invitational conference at Old Saybrook, Connecticut, brought together Maslow, Rogers, May, Buhler, Gordon Allport, Henry Murray, George Kelly and others; the Old Saybrook conference is usually treated as the formal birth of humanistic psychology as a movement. In 1971 the American Psychological Association created a Division of Humanistic Psychology. What did the humanists believe? James Bugental (1915 to 2008), the Association's first president, summarised it in five postulates in 1964: Human beings, as human, supersede the sum of their parts; they cannot be reduced to components. Human beings have their existence in a uniquely human context, which is relational: we live among other people. Human beings are aware, and are aware of being aware; awareness is part of what it is to be human. Human beings have choice, and with choice comes responsibility. Human beings are intentional: they seek meaning, value and creativity, and aim at goals. Put simply, humanistic psychology emphasises free will, conscious experience, the whole person, the innate tendency to grow, and the reaching of maximum potential. Its method is phenomenological: understand people from inside their own experience. Its view of psychological disorder follows. Disturbance arises when growth is blocked, when people deny their real feelings to win approval and their self-concept becomes incongruent with their experience. Healing comes from relationships that offer acceptance, respect for the client and belief in the person's potential, not from reinforcement contingencies (a behavioural idea) or the uncovering of unconscious conflict (a psychoanalytic one). Phenomenology Several schools in this chapter call their method "phenomenological", so the word needs a clear definition. Phenomenology is the philosophical method founded by Edmund Husserl (1859 to 1938) for describing experience exactly as it presents itself, before any theory about its causes is applied. Husserl's call was "back to the things themselves". His central technique was bracketing (Greek epoche ): deliberately suspending one's assumptions about the external reality and causes of an experience, in order to describe the experience itself. He took from his teacher Franz Brentano the idea of intentionality , that consciousness is always consciousness of something. Phenomenology fed three streams in psychology: the Gestalt psychologists' description of naive experience (through Carl Stumpf, who also taught Husserl), the existential psychologists, and the humanists' focus on the subjective world of the client. Today interpretative phenomenological analysis is a respected qualitative research method (Research Methodology book). Existential psychology Humanistic psychology was optimistic: people naturally grow toward fulfilment. Existential psychology , its close relative, is more sober. It begins from the "givens" of human existence that no one escapes, death, freedom, isolation and the absence of any ready-made meaning, and asks how people live authentically in the face of them. Its roots are in European philosophy. Soren Kierkegaard (1813 to 1855), the Danish thinker usually called the father of existentialism, analysed anxiety in The Concept of Anxiety (1844) as the "dizziness of freedom" that comes with having to choose. Martin Heidegger (1889 to 1976), in Being and Time (1927), described human existence as Dasein , literally "being there": the human being is not a mind looking at a separate world but is always already being-in-the-world , thrown into a situation not of its choosing and living toward its own death. Jean-Paul Sartre (1905 to 1980) declared that for human beings "existence precedes essence": we are not born with a fixed nature but must continually create ourselves through our choices, so that we are "condemned to be free", and to deny that freedom is bad faith. The statement that "each person must continually recreate himself; the meaning of life is never fixed but constantly changes" is pure existentialism. Two Swiss psychiatrists turned Heidegger's philosophy into a clinical method. Ludwig Binswanger (1881 to 1966) founded Daseinsanalysis (existential analysis), which tries to understand a patient's "world-design". He described three simultaneous modes of being-in-the-world: the Umwelt (the biological and physical world around us), the Mitwelt (the world with others) and the Eigenwelt (one's own world, the relationship with oneself). The existential therapist Emmy van Deurzen later added a fourth, the Uberwelt , the spiritual world of values and beliefs. Medard Boss (1903 to 1990), who worked closely with Heidegger himself, developed Daseinsanalysis further. The most widely read existential psychiatrist is Viktor Emil Frankl (1905 to 1997) of Vienna. Frankl survived Theresienstadt, Auschwitz and Dachau's subcamps; his wife, parents and brother died in the camps. In Man's Search for Meaning (German 1946, English 1959) he described how prisoners who held on to a reason to live, a task to finish or a person to return to, were better able to endure. He founded logotherapy (from the Greek logos , meaning), often called the "third Viennese school of psychotherapy" after Freud's psychoanalysis and Adler's individual psychology. Where Freud saw a will to pleasure and Adler a will to power, Frankl saw the will to meaning as the primary human motive. When it is frustrated, people fall into an existential vacuum , a sense of emptiness and boredom; when the frustration produces symptoms, Frankl called the result noogenic neurosis (from the Greek noos , mind or spirit), a neurosis arising not from psychological conflict or biology but from the spiritual dimension, from problems of meaning. Meaning, Frankl taught, can be found in three ways: by creating a work or doing a deed (creative values), by experiencing something or loving someone (experiential values), and by the attitude we take toward unavoidable suffering (attitudinal values). His techniques include paradoxical intention and dereflection (Clinical book). Rollo May brought European existentialism to American readers in Existence (1958), edited with Ernest Angel and Henri Ellenberger. In The Meaning of Anxiety (1950) he distinguished normal anxiety , which is proportionate to the threat, does not require repression and can be used constructively, from neurotic anxiety , which is disproportionate and involves repression. Existential anxiety, the anxiety of facing death, freedom and meaninglessness, is normal in this sense. Finally, the American psychiatrist Irvin David Yalom (born 1931), in Existential Psychotherapy (1980), organised the field around four "ultimate concerns": death, freedom (with its responsibility), existential isolation, and meaninglessness.
