The fourth world, Uberwelt , is van Deurzen's addition, not Heidegger's. Transpersonal psychology: the fourth force Toward the end of his life Maslow came to believe that humanistic psychology itself was a transitional stage. In the preface to the second edition of Toward a Psychology of Being (1968) he wrote of a still "higher" fourth psychology, transpersonal, centred in the cosmos rather than in human needs and interests. His studies of self-actualising people had shown him that many reported peak experiences , moments of awe, unity and self-transcendence. In 1969 Maslow and Sutich founded the Journal of Transpersonal Psychology . Transpersonal psychology , the fourth force , studies experiences in which the sense of identity extends beyond (trans) the individual person: mystical and peak experiences, meditation and altered states of consciousness, spiritual development and self-transcendence. Its leading figures include the psychiatrist Stanislav Grof (born 1931), who studied non-ordinary states of consciousness, Charles Tart (born 1937), who wrote on states of consciousness, Ken Wilber (born 1949), whose spectrum of consciousness and integral theory tried to unite Western psychology with Eastern traditions, and, earlier, the Italian psychiatrist Roberto Assagioli (1888 to 1974), founder of psychosynthesis. Frankl, with his stress on self-transcendence, is often claimed as a forerunner. Because so much transpersonal psychology draws on yoga, Vedanta and Buddhism, it forms a natural bridge to Indian psychology in Sections 2.8 and 2.9. Positive psychology The last movement in this family is the youngest. The phrase "positive psychology" first appeared as the title of the final chapter of Maslow's Motivation and Personality (1954), but it remained a passing label. The field as it exists today was launched by Martin Elias Peter Seligman (born 1942), the psychologist who had made his name with research on learned helplessness and depression (Chapter 6). Elected President of the American Psychological Association for 1998, he used his presidency to argue that psychology had become a science of repairing damage and had forgotten its other two missions: making the lives of ordinary people more fulfilling, and nurturing talent. Seligman later told how the idea crystallised. He was weeding his garden with his five-year-old daughter Nikki, who was throwing weeds into the air and dancing. He shouted at her. She walked away, came back, and told him that from her third birthday to her fifth she had been a whiner, that on turning five she had decided to stop, that it was the hardest thing she had ever done, and that if she could stop whining, he could stop being such a grouch. Raising Nikki, Seligman realised, was not about correcting her whining but about recognising and nurturing the strength she had just shown. Psychology, he concluded, should do the same. In January 2000 Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021) edited a special issue of the American Psychologist that announced positive psychology : the scientific study of positive experiences, positive individual traits and the institutions that enable them (its "three pillars"). Csikszentmihalyi was already known for his research on flow , the absorbing state of complete engagement in an activity whose challenge matches one's skill. Other landmarks followed. Character Strengths and Virtues (2004), by Christopher Peterson and Seligman, classified 24 character strengths under six virtues as a kind of "manual of the sanities" to set beside the diagnostic manuals. In Flourish (2011) Seligman proposed the PERMA model of well-being: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning and Accomplishment (detail in the Motivation and Emotion chapters). Several research programmes are now considered part of positive psychology. C. R. Snyder's hope theory describes hope as the combination of agency (the will to reach a goal) and pathways (the ways to reach it); promoting hope is a typical positive psychology intervention. Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff (2007) studied savouring , the capacity to attend to, appreciate and deliberately enhance the enjoyment of positive experiences, past, present or anticipated; savouring is to good events what coping is to bad ones. Barbara Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory holds that positive emotions broaden attention and thinking and build lasting personal resources, and Ed Diener's research on subjective well-being measures happiness as high life satisfaction, frequent positive feeling and infrequent negative feeling. Positive psychology interventions, such as writing down three good things each day, using one's signature strengths in a new way, or delivering a gratitude letter, have been tested in randomised trials. How does positive psychology relate to humanism? Seligman was at pains to distance his field from what he saw as the unscientific, self-help side of humanistic psychology; positive psychology is meant to be empirical. Humanistic psychologists replied, with some justice, that positive psychology had rediscovered their themes and given them new names. Most textbooks now treat humanistic psychology as its forerunner. Exam trap Founder of positive psychology : Seligman (with Csikszentmihalyi). Maslow coined the phrase in 1954 but did not found the field. Howard Gardner is multiple intelligences; Steven Pinker is language and evolutionary psychology; Bandura is self-efficacy and social cognitive theory. Savouring = enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences (not avoiding negative ones, not relaxation, not reflecting on trauma). The primary focus of positive psychology interventions is building strengths such as hope, not behaviour therapy, psychoanalysis or DBT. Criticisms of the third force Humanistic psychology has been criticised on four main grounds. First, its concepts (self-actualisation, growth, authenticity) are vague and hard to test; Maslow's description of self-actualisers rested on a small, hand-picked sample of people he admired. Second, its optimism can seem naive in the face of real human destructiveness, a criticism made from inside the movement by Rollo May. Third, it is individualistic: by concentrating so heavily on the individual's inner world, the humanistic and phenomenological approaches miss the wider social, cultural and economic contexts that shape experience and identity, and they reflect a Western, individualist ideal of the self. Fourth, some critics argued that its celebration of self-fulfilment encouraged self-absorption. Positive psychology tried to answer the first criticism with data; cross-cultural and Indian psychologists, as you will see, have pressed the third. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. A second group of critics attacked it for leaving out the mind, and this second attack proved decisive in the laboratories. Between the late 1940s and the late 1960s, the study of memory, attention, language, thinking and perception, all of which behaviourism had pushed to the edges, returned to the centre of experimental psychology. The change was so rapid and so complete that it is usually called the cognitive revolution . Why did it happen when it did? Why behaviourism waned Several pressures converged, and it helps to keep them separate. Anomalies inside behaviourism. You have already met two: Tolman's rats that learned maps without reward, and Kohler's apes that solved problems by insight. A third came from Karl Spencer Lashley (1890 to 1958), once Watson's own student. At the Hixon Symposium on "Cerebral Mechanisms in Behavior" in 1948 (published in 1951), Lashley gave a paper on "The Problem of Serial Order in Behavior". A pianist playing a fast passage, or a person speaking a sentence, produces movements far too quickly for each one to be triggered by sensory feedback from the one before, as a chain of stimulus-response links would require. The sequence must be planned in advance, centrally, and organised hierarchically. In other words, behaviour requires internal plans. The war and its machines. The Second World War posed problems that behaviourism could not answer: how radar operators could stay alert through long watches, how pilots could cope with too many dials and messages at once, how to design controls that people would not misread. Psychologists working on these problems, such as Donald Broadbent in Britain, found themselves talking about attention, capacity and the flow of information through a person. Information, feedback and computers. In 1948 the engineer Claude Elwood Shannon (1916 to 2001) published a mathematical theory of communication that measured information in units called bits, and the mathematician Norbert Wiener (1894 to 1964) published Cybernetics , the science of control and feedback in animals and machines. A machine with a goal and a feedback loop (a thermostat, a guided missile) behaves purposefully, and nobody thinks it is mystical to say so. Then came the stored-program digital computer, and in 1950 Alan Mathison Turing (1912 to 1954) asked whether machines could think. Computers made internal states respectable. A computer's behaviour cannot be understood without reference to its program and its memory, which nobody can see. If a machine could be described in terms of stored symbols and rules for manipulating them, why not a person? Language. The final blow came from linguistics, as you will see shortly. Seen through Kuhn's eyes (Section 2.1), these were anomalies piling up until the old framework entered a crisis. 1956 and after If the revolution has a birthday, it is in 1956. From 10 to 12 September of that year, a Symposium on Information Theory was held at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. George Armitage Miller (1920 to 2012), one of the participants, later dated the birth of cognitive science to its second day, 11 September 1956. On that day Allen Newell (1927 to 1992) and Herbert Alexander Simon (1916 to 2001) described the Logic Theorist , a computer program (written with Cliff Shaw) that proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica , the first program to model human problem-solving. Noam Chomsky (born 1928), a young linguist, presented a paper on formal models of language. And Miller himself spoke about the limits of short-term memory, the subject of his famous 1956 paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two", which showed that people can hold about seven items (between five and nine) in immediate memory, and that the limit can be stretched by grouping items into larger meaningful units, or chunks (Chapter 7). The same year saw the Dartmouth summer research project at which John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and others launched the field of artificial intelligence (McCarthy had coined the term in the 1955 proposal for the meeting), and the publication of A Study of Thinking by Jerome Seymour Bruner (1915 to 2016), Jacqueline Goodnow and George Austin, which analysed the strategies people use to discover concepts (Chapter 8). In 1957 Chomsky published Syntactic Structures , and in 1958 Donald Eric Broadbent (1926 to 1993) published Perception and Communication , which presented the filter model of attention (Chapter 5). Broadbent's book is regarded as the first major theory cast explicitly in information-processing terms: information flows through a series of stages of limited capacity, drawn as a box-and-arrow flow chart. Key study: Chomsky's review of Verbal Behavior (1959) The background. In Verbal Behavior (1957), Skinner had argued that language is operant behaviour like any other: children learn to speak because the verbal community reinforces some sounds and not others, and adult speech is controlled by stimuli and reinforcement histories. The argument. In a long review in the journal Language (1959), Chomsky argued that this could not work. Children acquire the grammar of their language rapidly, at about the same age everywhere, from speech that is fragmentary and full of errors (later called the poverty of the stimulus). They constantly produce and understand sentences they have never heard, so these sentences cannot have been reinforced. Their errors, such as "I goed" or "two mouses", are not imitations of anything adults say; they are over-applications of rules. And when Skinner's terms (stimulus, response, reinforcement) are stretched to cover language, Chomsky argued, they lose their precise laboratory meaning and become a vague paraphrase of ordinary talk. The conclusion. Language is rule-governed, creative and generative, and human beings must come equipped with an innate capacity for acquiring it (Chapter 8). The criticism. Behaviour analysts, notably Kenneth MacCorquodale (1970), replied that Chomsky had misunderstood Skinner's position. Skinner never answered publicly. Whatever its fairness, the review was read as a manifesto for the new cognitive psychology, and it made Chomsky, a linguist rather than a psychologist, one of the movement's heroes. The pieces came together quickly. In 1960 Miller, Eugene Galanter and Karl Pribram published Plans and the Structure of Behavior , which replaced the reflex arc with the TOTE unit (Test, Operate, Test, Exit), a feedback loop in which an organism compares its current state with a goal, acts, and tests again. The same year, Bruner and Miller founded the Center for Cognitive Studies at Harvard. Then, in 1967, Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012) published Cognitive Psychology , the first textbook of the new field, which gave it its name. Neisser defined cognition as "all the processes by which the sensory input is transformed, reduced, elaborated, stored, recovered, and used". He is called the father of cognitive psychology , the study of internal mental processes such as perception, attention, memory, language, problem-solving and reasoning. (Characteristically, Neisser later criticised his own field: in Cognition and Reality , 1976, he argued that laboratory cognitive psychology had lost touch with how people use their minds in real life, its ecological validity.) The approach rests on four assumptions. Mental processes can be broken into a sequence of stages. Each stage has a limited capacity. Processing takes time, so the time a task takes (the reaction time) reveals what stages it involves, an idea that revived Donders's mental chronometry from the nineteenth century (Chapter 1). And mental processes can be described as operations on internal representations (symbols and rules), at the level of the "software", without first knowing the "hardware" of the brain. A worked example shows how the approach thinks. A fast bowler releases a cricket ball at 140 kilometres an hour, and the batsman has about half a second before it reaches him. In information-processing terms: light from the ball is registered by the eyes (sensory input); attention selects the ball from the crowd, the bowler's arm and the sightscreen (selection); the line and length of the delivery are recognised by matching them against patterns stored from thousands of earlier deliveries (pattern recognition, drawing on long-term memory); a shot is selected and its motor program retrieved (decision and response selection); and the bat moves (output). Each stage takes time, and an expert's advantage lies partly in doing some stages faster and partly in anticipating the ball before it is bowled, from cues in the bowler's run-up, which is top-down processing (Chapter 4). Forerunners: Bartlett and Piaget The cognitive revolution was a revolution mainly in America. In Europe, the study of the mind had never stopped, and two European psychologists in particular are treated as forerunners. Frederic Charles Bartlett (1886 to 1969) of Cambridge, in Remembering (1932), asked English students to read and later recall a Native American folk tale, "The War of the Ghosts". Their recall grew shorter, lost its unfamiliar supernatural details and was rationalised into the shape of an English story. Bartlett concluded that remembering is reconstruction guided by a schema , an organised mental structure of knowledge built from past experience (Chapter 7). Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980) of Geneva spent half a century, from the 1920s on, studying how children's thinking develops. He called his field genetic epistemology, the study of the origins and growth of knowledge, and described how children build schemas and adapt them through assimilation (fitting new experience into existing schemas) and accommodation (changing schemas to fit new experience). Piaget studied thinking directly at a time when American psychology refused to, which is why he is often named a pioneer of cognitive psychology; in the 2002 survey of eminent psychologists he ranked second only to Skinner. His stage theory is taught in the Developmental book. Other forerunners include the Gestalt psychologists (insight and productive thinking), Tolman (cognitive maps), the Wurzburg school (thought without images, Chapter 1) and the Russian psychologist Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky (1896 to 1934), who studied the relation between thought and language. Exam trap The first major information-processing theory was Broadbent's (1958), not Treisman's (her attenuation work began around 1960), not Chomsky's (1957 was Syntactic Structures , a work of linguistics), and certainly not Watson's (1920 was Little Albert). Father of cognitive psychology : Neisser (1967), though Miller and Bruner were central figures. Pioneer contributor to cognitive psychology in an Amity item with options Piaget, Kohler, Chomsky and Kohlberg: the key is Piaget , who studied thinking from the 1920s; Chomsky was a linguist whose 1959 review fuelled the revolution; Kohler belongs to Gestalt; Kohlberg studied moral development. Chomsky's review was of Verbal Behavior (1957) and appeared in 1959. Cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience Cognitive psychology soon joined a larger enterprise. Cognitive science is the interdisciplinary study of mind and intelligence, bringing together psychology, artificial intelligence and computer science, linguistics, philosophy, neuroscience and anthropology; it acquired its own journal and, in 1979, a Cognitive Science Society. For its first twenty years cognitive psychology mostly ignored the brain, in keeping with the "software" assumption. That changed in the late 1970s, when, as Michael Gazzaniga (born 1939) tells it, he and George Miller coined the term cognitive neuroscience in the back of a New York taxi. Cognitive neuroscience studies how mental processes are carried out by the brain, combining the experimental tasks of cognitive psychology with methods for measuring brain activity: the study of patients with brain damage, electrical recording (EEG and event-related potentials), positron emission tomography (PET) from the 1980s, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from the 1990s, and transcranial magnetic stimulation. Its methods are taught in the Physiological book. Connectionism and parallel distributed processing The serial, box-and-arrow model had a problem. Brains are made of billions of slow neurons, each firing at most a few hundred times a second, yet people recognise a face in a fraction of a second. A strictly serial process with such slow parts could not be that fast. The answer, many researchers argued, was that the brain does many things at once. Connectionism models the mind as a network of many simple, neuron-like processing units joined by connections of varying strength (weights). Each unit adds up the activation it receives and passes activation on; many units are active at the same time (parallel processing); and a piece of knowledge is stored not in one place but as a pattern of weights spread across the whole network (distributed representation). The landmark was the two-volume Parallel Distributed Processing (1986) by David Everett Rumelhart (1942 to 2011), James Lloyd McClelland (born 1948) and the PDP Research Group, which gave the approach its other name, parallel distributed processing (PDP). Figure 2.3(b) shows a simple network. Networks learn by adjusting their weights. One idea goes back to Donald Hebb (1949), who proposed that a connection between two neurons strengthens when they are active together; another, the back-propagation rule popularised in 1986 by Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, adjusts weights in proportion to the network's errors. Connectionist models have several brain-like properties. They degrade gracefully: damage a few units and performance worsens a little rather than failing completely. They are content-addressable: a partial cue can retrieve a whole memory. And they generalise: Rumelhart and McClelland's 1986 model of the English past tense learned regular and irregular verbs from examples, with no rules written in, and even went through a stage of over-regularising ("goed") as children do. Connectionism has deep roots, in Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts's model neurons (1943) and Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958), and today's deep-learning systems are its descendants. Cognition enters behaviour therapy The cognitive revolution did not stop at the laboratory door. Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021), whose Bobo doll studies you will meet in Chapter 6, moved social learning theory steadily toward cognition. In 1977 he introduced the concept of self-efficacy , a person's belief in his or her capacity to carry out the actions needed to deal with a particular situation, as a unifying explanation of how people change. Expectations, not reinforcements alone, drive behaviour. His mature system is social cognitive theory (1986). At the same time, Albert Ellis (1913 to 2007) developed rational therapy, later renamed rational emotive behaviour therapy, from 1955, and Aaron Temkin Beck (1921 to 2021) developed cognitive therapy for depression in the 1960s, both based on the idea that maladaptive thoughts produce distress. The merger of these ideas with behaviour therapy produced cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), the therapy that focuses on changing maladaptive thought patterns. Clinical link Psychotherapy has gone through three "waves" that mirror this chapter's history: behaviour therapy (the legacy of behaviourism), cognitive therapy and CBT (the legacy of the cognitive revolution), and a third wave of acceptance and mindfulness-based therapies, including acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT), which draw explicitly on Buddhist ideas (Section 2.9). Psychoanalysis is not one of the waves of CBT. Each therapy is taught in the Clinical book. 2.7 Psychology Today: Perspectives, Eclecticism and the Enduring Issues Medium yield · 6 Qs By the 1970s the age of schools was over. Few psychologists now call themselves behaviourists or Gestaltists; instead they speak of perspectives , ways of approaching a question that coexist and complement one another. The difference is real. A school claimed to be the right way to do psychology; a perspective claims only to be a useful angle on a problem that other perspectives also illuminate. The biological perspective , also called the neurobiological perspective, holds that behaviour is ultimately governed by the brain and nervous system. The evolutionary perspective asks what adaptive problem a behaviour helped our ancestors solve; it was developed into evolutionary psychology by researchers such as David Buss, Leda Cosmides and John Tooby. The sociocultural perspective , inspired in part by Vygotsky, studies how culture and social context shape thought and behaviour. The biopsychosocial model was proposed by the American psychiatrist George Libman Engel (1913 to 1999) in a 1977 paper in Science , as an alternative to the purely biomedical model of illness: any illness, physical or mental, must be understood as the product of biological, psychological and social factors acting together. It is now the standard framework of clinical psychology and psychiatry. You will also see "developmental" listed as a perspective in some textbooks, meaning the study of how people change as they mature across the lifespan; strictly, developmental psychology is a field of study that uses all the other perspectives. Within the sociocultural approach, three terms are easily confused. Cross-cultural psychology compares psychological processes across different cultures, usually with the same measures, to find out which are universal and which vary (the work of Harry Triandis, John Berry and Geert Hofstede is typical). Cultural psychology studies, often from within a single culture, how culture and mind "make each other up", treating culture as part of the mind rather than as a variable acting on it. Indigenous psychology builds psychological concepts and theories from within a culture's own traditions instead of importing them; Durganand Sinha's call to indigenise psychology in India, which you will meet in Section 2.8, is an example. Exam trap "Who studies how psychological processes may differ among people of different cultures?" The textbook answer is cross-cultural psychologists . One Panwar item keys social psychologists , presumably because culture is part of the social context; if both appear, cross-cultural psychology is the more precise answer. "Behaviour is governed by the brain and nervous system" = neurobiological (not psychophysical, which is Fechner's study of stimulus-sensation relations, and not neo-behaviouristic). "Unconscious processes and early childhood" = psychodynamic . "Stimulus-response associations through conditioning" = behavioural . "Internal mental processes" = cognitive . "Free will and personal growth" = humanistic . Eclecticism If every perspective captures part of the truth, why choose one? Eclecticism is the practice of selecting concepts, methods or techniques from different schools according to what best fits the problem in hand. Frederick Thorne argued for an eclectic approach to counselling around 1950, and Arnold Lazarus later distinguished technical eclecticism , using techniques from any school without necessarily accepting its theory (his multimodal therapy is the best-known example), from theoretical integration , which tries to combine the theories themselves. A third route looks for the common factors , such as the therapeutic relationship and the instillation of hope, that make different therapies work. Surveys repeatedly find that eclectic or integrative is the most common orientation among practising clinicians. The danger, critics point out, is a shapeless mixture with no principle for choosing. The enduring issues Schools come and go, but the questions that divided them do not. The historian of psychology Robert Irving Watson (1909 to 1980) argued in a 1967 paper, "Psychology: A Prescriptive Science", that since psychology lacks a single paradigm, its history is better organised by prescriptions : contrasting attitudes, held more or less strongly by different psychologists at different times, about what psychology should be and do. He listed eighteen pairs, among them conscious versus unconscious mentalism, determinism versus indeterminism, empiricism versus rationalism, mechanism versus vitalism, molecularism versus molarism, monism versus dualism, nomotheticism versus idiographicism, and peripheralism versus centralism. At the end of Section 2.5 you saw one consequence. Critics charged that even humanistic psychology, for all its talk of the whole person, reflected a Western, individualist ideal of the self. Yet the questions psychology asks (what the mind is, why we suffer, how attention can be trained, what the self really is) were being asked in India more than two thousand years before Wundt opened his laboratory in Leipzig. The Bhagavad Gita is the most famous example. It opens with a warrior, Arjuna, standing in his chariot between two armies. Facing his own teachers and cousins across the field, he tells his charioteer Krishna that his limbs are failing, his mouth is dry, his body trembles and his hair stands on end, that his bow is slipping from his hand and his mind is reeling. He sits down and refuses to fight, because every course open to him seems wrong. The rest of the poem is a dialogue in which Krishna helps him understand his own mind and find his way back to action. A modern reader can hardly miss that it has the shape of a counselling session with a man paralysed by anxiety and moral conflict. This section and the next tell two connected stories. The first is how modern, Western-style psychology came to India in the early twentieth century, and how Indian psychologists gradually moved from copying it to questioning it. The second is what the classical Indian systems actually say about the mind. We begin by separating two phrases that sound almost the same. Psychology in India and Indian psychology Psychology in India means the discipline as it is taught and practised in Indian universities, hospitals and clinics. For most of its first century it was Western psychology carried on in India: laboratories on the Leipzig model, theories from Europe and America, and tests translated or adapted for Indian use. Most of this book is psychology in that sense. Indian psychology , in the sense used by the movement that took shape around the year 2000, is something else: an approach to psychology rooted in the ideas and practices of the classical Indian traditions (the Upanishads, Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, Buddhism and Jainism, the Bhagavad Gita and Ayurveda), joined in later centuries by Indian Sufism and, in the twentieth century, by Sri Aurobindo. It is not the psychology of Indians either; a study of how Indian students cope with examination stress belongs to cross-cultural or cultural psychology (Section 2.7). Its advocates stress that, like the psychology that came out of Germany, it is meant to be universal. Its claims about attention, the self and suffering are claims about human beings anywhere, which happen to have been worked out in India. What makes the approach distinctive? Its leading scholars usually point to five features. It is consciousness-centred. Consciousness is treated as fundamental rather than as a by-product of the brain, and a sharp line is drawn between consciousness itself, the silent witness, and the mind's changing contents and instruments (thoughts, feelings, memories), which are treated as part of nature. It is holistic. Body, mind and spirit are treated as one system, and so are the person, the family and the community; health is a state of balance among them. It is transformative. The aim is not only to describe the mind but to change it, toward freedom from suffering and the realisation of one's true nature (called moksha , kaivalya or nirvana in different systems). Disciplines such as yoga and meditation are its laboratory techniques. It values disciplined first-person methods. Where Western psychology after Watson distrusted introspection, the Indian traditions developed elaborate methods for training and refining it, and they treat the reports of a trained observer as evidence. It is relational and value-laden. The self is understood in relation to others and to dharma , the order of duties that sustains social and moral life, so ethics is part of psychology rather than outside it. Table 2.10 sets these features against mainstream Western psychology. Remember that the contrast is one of emphasis, not a wall. Behaviourists also wanted to change behaviour, humanists also cared about values, and over the last forty years Western psychology has borrowed meditation and mindfulness from India on a large scale (Section 2.9). Not by rejecting modern treatment. Its practitioners combine traditional practices (yoga postures and breathing, meditation, a regulated daily routine and diet, reflection on the values of texts such as the Gita ) with modern psychotherapy and, where needed, medication, and they aim at the well-being of the whole person rather than the removal of a symptom alone. The Ayurvedic and yogic ideas behind this approach are taught in Section 2.9. Exam trap The primary focus of Indian psychology is the integration of Indian philosophical and contemplative traditions with psychological concepts and methods. It is not the exclusive application of Western theories (that is psychology in India at its most imitative), not the study of folklore and mythology, and not meditation without a psychological context. How it differs from Western psychology : it emphasises holistic and spiritual approaches, including family and community, rather than the isolated individual; it does not rely only on ancient texts without modern relevance, and it is Indian (not Western) psychology that stresses spirituality. Atman is the true self, eternal consciousness; not the physical body, not Jung's collective unconscious and not a passing state of mind. The pioneers: how modern psychology came to India The story of psychology in India begins in Calcutta, then the capital of British India and home of its leading university. In 1905, on the initiative of the philosopher Brajendranath Seal (1864 to 1938), the University of Calcutta introduced experimental psychology as a subject within its philosophy curriculum. Seal, a scholar of both Western science and Indian philosophy, wanted Indian students to learn the new laboratory psychology. The university's vice-chancellor, the mathematician and lawyer Asutosh Mookerjee (1864 to 1924), backed him. What was missing was someone trained to run a laboratory. That person was Narendra Nath Sengupta (1889 to 1944; the name is also written Sen Gupta). Sengupta had studied at Harvard under Hugo Munsterberg, who had himself taken his doctorate with Wundt at Leipzig, so there is a direct line of teachers running from Wundt's laboratory to Calcutta. In 1915 Sengupta set up the first psychology laboratory in India at the University of Calcutta, modelled on the German laboratories, and in 1916 the university created a separate Department of Psychology (often called the Department of Experimental Psychology), the first in the country, with Sengupta in charge. With the sociologist Radhakamal Mukerjee he wrote Introduction to Social Psychology: Mind in Society (1928), one of the first social psychology textbooks written by Indian authors, and he later moved to Lucknow University. For his laboratory, his department and the students he trained, Sengupta is called the father, or founder, of modern psychology in India. Among the first generation of Calcutta psychologists was a physician who would take the subject in a completely different direction. Girindrasekhar Bose (1887 to 1953; also written Girindra Shekhar Bose) had qualified in medicine and become fascinated by the mind through his own medical practice. His thesis on the concept of repression, published in 1921 as Concept of Repression , earned him what is usually described as the first doctorate in psychology awarded by an Indian university (some Indian study notes give 1916 or 1922 for this degree; 1921, the year of the thesis, is the date most histories give). He sent a copy to Freud, and the two corresponded for the next sixteen years or so. In 1922 Bose founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society in Calcutta, one of the earliest psychoanalytic societies outside Europe and North America, and in 1947 he launched its journal, Samiksha . When Sengupta left Calcutta, Bose succeeded him as head of the psychology department. He is the father of psychoanalysis in India. Bose did not simply import Freud. His best-known idea, the theory of opposite wishes , holds that every wish comes paired with its opposite: the wish to beat goes with the wish to be beaten, the wish to be male with the wish to be female, the wish to see with the wish to be seen. One member of each pair is expressed in consciousness and behaviour while the other is repressed, and the two can change places. For Bose it was this play of opposites, rather than a fixed Oedipus complex, that lay at the centre of mental life, and he reported that the Oedipal conflict did not hold the same central place in his Indian patients as in Freud's Viennese ones. Freud read his work with interest but was not persuaded. Bose's ideas show an Indian thinker reworking psychoanalysis through his own culture's preoccupation with the reconciliation of opposites, an early example of what would later be called indigenisation. Institutions followed the pioneers. In 1923 the Indian Science Congress opened a section for psychology and educational science. In 1925 Sengupta founded the Indian Psychological Association , and in 1926 the association's Indian Journal of Psychology , the first Indian psychology journal, began publication. From imitation to indigenisation For its first fifty years, psychology in India was largely imitative. Indian psychologists, many trained in Britain or America, repeated Western experiments on Indian participants and used Western tests in translation. Did the results mean what they meant in London or Chicago? Increasingly, the answer seemed to be no. The psychologist who did most to name the problem and chart a way out was Durganand Sinha (1922 to 1998) of the University of Allahabad. In Psychology in a Third World Country: The Indian Experience (1986) he described psychology in India as passing through four broad phases: a period before independence in which the Western academic and experimental tradition was transplanted largely unchanged; a period of rapid expansion after independence, still mostly imitative; a problem-oriented phase from about the 1970s, in which psychologists turned to India's own pressing problems (poverty, deprivation, rural development, social change); and finally a phase of indigenisation , the effort to make psychology's concepts, theories and methods fit the culture in which they are used. Indigenous psychologists distinguish two routes, a pair of terms usually credited to the Filipino psychologist Virgilio Enriquez and used by Sinha in his later writing. Indigenisation from without takes a Western concept or tool and modifies it to suit local conditions. Indigenisation from within builds concepts, theories and methods from the culture itself, from its traditions, texts, languages and everyday life. Test adaptation is the clearest example of indigenisation from without. The pictures of the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), drawn in the United States, showed American faces, clothes and settings, and Indian respondents told thin, guarded stories about them. Uma Chowdhury (the name is also spelled Chaudhuri) of Calcutta redrew the cards with Indian figures and scenes, producing an Indian modification of the TAT around 1960 (the tests themselves are covered in the Assessment book). Two contributions from organisational psychology show indigenisation moving further, toward concepts grown from Indian conditions. Jai B. P. Sinha , studying Indian organisations in the 1970s, found that neither the authoritarian leadership common in Indian offices nor the participative style recommended by American research worked best. In The Nurturant Task Leader (1980) he proposed the nurturant-task leader : a leader who combines a strong task orientation (clear goals, discipline, insistence on hard work) with nurturance (warmth, personal care and guidance, interest in the subordinate's growth), and who makes that nurturance depend on the subordinate's work. The style fits a culture that values hierarchy and personal relationships, and Sinha saw it as a stage through which a work group could move toward fuller participation as subordinates matured (leadership styles in general are covered in the Social book). Udai Pareek (1925 to 2010) of the Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad, was a founder of human resource development in Indian organisations; he developed the concepts and scales of role stress (he identified ten organisational role stressors, among them role overload, role ambiguity and role stagnation) and role efficacy , and, with G. Trivedi, a widely used socio-economic status scale for rural India (1964). Psychoanalysis, too, was reworked from within. Sudhir Kakar (born 1938), a psychoanalyst influenced by Erik Erikson, wrote The Inner World: A Psycho-analytic Study of Childhood and Society in India (1978), which traced how the Indian family, with its long and intense early bond between mother and son and its many caretakers in the joint family, shapes an identity more relational than the Western ideal of the autonomous individual. In Shamans, Mystics and Doctors (1982) he studied India's traditional healers as psychotherapists in their own right. Kakar is the leading figure of a cultural psychoanalysis of India, the field Bose began. Exam trap Two Sinhas. The Indian Psychology movement Indigenisation asked psychology to fit Indian conditions. By the 1990s a growing number of psychologists wanted something bolder: to take the Indian traditions themselves seriously as sources of psychological theory and method, on an equal footing with the Western schools. The turning point came in 2002, when a national conference on yoga and Indian approaches to psychology, held in Pondicherry (now Puducherry), closed with a statement signed by the psychologists present, the Pondicherry Manifesto of Indian Psychology . The manifesto argued that Indian psychologists had too long confined themselves to replicating Western research, that the Indian traditions contain a rich and systematic understanding of consciousness and the self, together with methods for exploring and transforming them, and that this knowledge should be developed into a modern psychology useful anywhere in the world. Notice that Figure 2.1 marks 2002 as the start of the Indian Psychology movement. Several people carried the movement forward. Matthijs Cornelissen , a Dutch-born physician and psychologist long resident at the Sri Aurobindo Ashram, was one of its prime movers and founded the Indian Psychology Institute in Pondicherry, which runs courses and workshops grounded largely in Sri Aurobindo's integral psychology. Koneru Ramakrishna Rao (born 1932), a philosopher and parapsychologist and a former vice-chancellor of Andhra University, became its most prolific theorist; with Anand C. Paranjpe of Simon Fraser University in Canada, author of Self and Identity in Modern Psychology and Indian Thought (1998), and Ajit K. Dalal of the University of Allahabad, he edited the Handbook of Indian Psychology (2008), the movement's first comprehensive reference work, and with Paranjpe he later wrote Psychology in the Indian Tradition (2016). Cornelissen, Girishwar Misra and Suneet Varma , both of the University of Delhi, edited the two-volume Foundations of Indian Psychology (2011), one volume on theories and concepts and one on practical applications. Misra is also one of the most influential scholars of cultural and indigenous psychology in India. The movement has its critics. Some worry that it romanticises the past, that it blurs the line between religion and science, or that claims about pure consciousness cannot be tested. Its defenders answer that the first-person methods of yoga and Buddhism can be made as disciplined as any laboratory technique, that many traditional claims (about meditation, breathing and attention, for example) are now being tested experimentally, and that Western psychology's own assumptions are no less culture-bound for being familiar. The debate is a live one, and you will find both sides in Indian journals today. Exam trap Who led the early-2000s Indian Psychology movement and founded the Indian Psychology Institute? The darshanas: a map of Indian thought Before we open the first of the classical systems, you need a map. Indian philosophy is traditionally divided into schools called darshanas , from a root meaning "to see": each is a way of seeing reality. The schools are sorted into two groups by one criterion, their attitude to the authority of the Vedas, the oldest Indian scriptures. The astika (orthodox) schools accept that authority; the nastika (heterodox) schools reject it. Notice what the criterion is not: it is not belief in God. Classical Samkhya has no creator god, yet it is astika, while Buddhism and Jainism are nastika because they reject the Vedas. Table 2.12 lists the schools; the six astika darshanas are traditionally grouped into three pairs. Table 2.12 The schools of classical Indian philosophy. Group School Traditional founder or text Central concern Astika Nyaya Gautama (Akshapada) Logic and the means of valid knowledge Astika Vaisheshika Kanada Atoms and the categories of reality Astika Samkhya Kapila Dualism of consciousness (purusha) and matter (prakriti) Astika Yoga Patanjali Discipline of the mind, leading to liberation Astika Mimamsa (Purva Mimamsa) Jaimini Vedic ritual and duty (dharma) Astika Vedanta (Uttara Mimamsa) Badarayana's Brahma Sutras ; the Upanishads Brahman, the atman and liberation Nastika Buddhism Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha Suffering, its cause and its end; no permanent self Nastika Jainism Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara Non-violence, karma and the liberation of the soul Nastika Charvaka (Lokayata) Brihaspati (traditional) Materialism: only perception is valid; no soul beyond the body Most of these schools also argued carefully about how we know anything at all. The valid means of knowledge are called pramanas . Samkhya and Yoga accept three: pratyaksha (perception), anumana (inference) and shabda or agama (reliable testimony). Nyaya adds upamana (comparison), and the Charvakas, the materialists of ancient India, accepted perception alone. Indian psychology thus has its own epistemology, its own theory of how knowledge is acquired, built into its foundations. Of all these schools, the one that matters most for psychology is the one whose map of the mind most of the others borrowed: Samkhya. Exam trap Which is an astika system? Advaita Vedanta (and Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa). Buddhism, Jainism and Charvaka are nastika. Sufism is the mystical tradition of Islam and lies outside this classification altogether. Where do the three gunas come from? Mainly Samkhya (with the Bhagavad Gita ), not Nyaya (logic), Mimamsa (ritual) or Charvaka (materialism). Samkhya: purusha and prakriti Samkhya is the oldest of the systematic Indian philosophies of mind. Its name means "enumeration", because it explains the world by counting out its basic principles, twenty-five of them. Tradition names its founder as the sage Kapila , of whom nothing certain is known. Its oldest surviving text is the Samkhya Karika of Ishvarakrishna , a short work of about seventy verses usually dated to around the fourth or fifth century CE. Its ideas, however, are much older; they run through the Upanishads, the Mahabharata and the Gita , and the Yoga of Patanjali takes them over almost entire. The Samkhya Karika begins, as any clinician might, with suffering. Human beings, it says, are tormented by three kinds of suffering: suffering from within ourselves, in body and mind ( adhyatmika ); suffering caused by other beings, people and animals ( adhibhautika ); and suffering from natural and supernatural forces such as floods and storms ( adhidaivika ). Ordinary remedies, medicine or ritual, relieve suffering only for a while. The aim of Samkhya is a lasting cure, and the cure is knowledge of what we really are. What are we? Samkhya's answer is a strict dualism of two ultimate, eternal and independent realities. The first, purusha , is pure consciousness: the seer, the witness ( sakshi ). It does not act, change, think, feel or choose; it simply is aware. It has no qualities, it is neither produced nor productive, and it is untouched by anything that happens. Samkhya holds that there are many purushas, one for each living being, because beings are born, suffer and die at different times. The second, prakriti , is primordial matter or nature: unconscious, active, ever-changing and one. It is the uncaused cause from which everything that is not consciousness evolves, and it is made of three strands or qualities, the gunas, which in its unmanifest state are held in perfect balance. Samkhya explains how the world arises from prakriti by its doctrine that an effect already exists, unmanifest, in its cause ( satkaryavada ), as curd exists potentially in milk or oil in sesame seeds. Evolution is the manifestation of what was latent. When prakriti comes into the presence of purusha, its balance is disturbed and it begins to evolve, unfolding in a fixed order into twenty-three products, or evolutes. The first is mahat , "the great one", which in the individual is buddhi , the intellect. From buddhi comes ahamkara , the "I-maker", the sense of being a separate self. Ahamkara then evolves in two directions. On its sattvic (luminous) side it produces manas , the sensory mind, together with the five organs of perception ( jnanendriyas : hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell) and the five organs of action ( karmendriyas : speech, grasping, movement, excretion and reproduction). On its tamasic (inert) side it produces the five subtle elements ( tanmatras : sound, touch, form, taste and smell as pure potentials), and from them the five gross elements ( mahabhutas : space, air, fire, water and earth), of which the physical world, including the body, is made. Rajas, the active strand, supplies the energy for both lines of evolution. Purusha, prakriti and the twenty-three evolutes together make the twenty-five principles ( tattvas ) of Samkhya. Figure 2.4 lays out the whole scheme. Purusha pure consciousness, witness Prakriti matter: sattva, rajas, tamas presence upsets balance Mahat or buddhi (intellect) Ahamkara (the I-maker) Inner instrument (antahkarana): buddhi + ahamkara + manas sattvic side Manas (sensory mind) 5 jnanendriyas (senses) 5 karmendriyas (organs of action) tamasic side 5 tanmatras (subtle elements) sound, touch, form, taste, smell 5 mahabhutas (gross elements) space, air, fire, water, earth Rajas supplies the energy for both lines of evolution Purusha + prakriti + 23 evolutes = the 25 tattvas Figure 2.4 Samkhya's map of mind and matter. In the presence of purusha, prakriti evolves into intellect, the I-maker, the sensory mind, the ten organs and the elements. Notice that everything below the top row, including thinking, feeling and the sense of "I", is a product of prakriti; only purusha is conscious. Look at Figure 2.4 again and notice something that surprises most Western readers. Intellect, ego and mind, everything a Western psychologist would call mental, are all products of prakriti. They are part of nature, as material as the body, only subtler. Descartes drew the great dividing line between mind and body; Samkhya draws it between consciousness and everything else, with the mind on the side of matter. Why, then, does the mind seem conscious? Because, Samkhya and Yoga answer, it reflects the light of purusha, as a clear crystal placed beside a red flower appears red. Thinking, deciding and feeling are processes in prakriti; the awareness of them belongs to purusha alone. In modern terms, Samkhya separates the contents and operations of the mind, which cognitive psychology studies, from awareness itself, the question at the heart of what philosophers now call the hard problem of consciousness (Chapter 5). Two images from the Samkhya Karika show how the system pictures their relation. Purusha and prakriti are like a lame man who can see and a blind man who can walk: the lame man rides on the blind man's shoulders, and together they find their way. And prakriti is like a dancer who performs for an audience and stops once she has been fully seen. Why do we suffer? Because of aviveka , non-discrimination: consciousness mistakes the activities of prakriti for itself, so that the witness says "I am angry", "I am tired", "I am a failure", when anger, tiredness and failure belong to the body and mind. The cure is viveka , discriminative knowledge, the direct realisation that the seer is not the seen. The result is kaivalya , "aloneness" or isolation: purusha rests in its own nature, free, and prakriti ceases to act for it. The same word names the goal of Patanjali's yoga (Section 2.9). Exam trap Purusha is passive, unchanging and conscious; prakriti is active, ever-changing and unconscious. So "Purusha is described as dynamic and ever-changing" is the false statement in a list about Samkhya; "prakriti is the cosmic material from which all beings emerge", "purusha is the essence of pure consciousness" and "prakriti evolves into the five great elements (pancha mahabhutas)" are all true. Prakriti is the primordial matter from which all forms of life emerge; it is not pure consciousness, not unaffected by change and not the intelligent self. The gunas belong to prakriti , not to purusha, atman or Brahman, and not to samadhi or samskara. Ahamkara is an evolute of prakriti, not a second principle beside it. Samkhya is dualist (many purushas and one prakriti); Advaita Vedanta is monist (Section 2.9). The three gunas If everything in nature, including the mind, is made of prakriti, and prakriti is made of three strands, then every thought, feeling and act is some mixture of the three. This is the doctrine of the three gunas , the best-known idea in Indian psychology. The word guna means a strand, as in the strands twisted together to make a rope, and also a quality. The three strands are always present together and never found alone, in different proportions in different things and at different times. Like the oil, the wick and the flame of a lamp, the Samkhya Karika says, they are opposed in nature yet work together to produce one light. The first, sattva , is the strand of lightness, clarity and illumination. In the mind it shows itself as calm, balance, harmony, knowledge, contentment and goodness. The second, rajas , is the strand of energy, motion and stimulation. In the mind it shows itself as activity, passion, desire, ambition and restlessness, and, when it runs to excess, as anger, greed, anxiety and attachment. The third, tamas , is the strand of heaviness, inertia and obstruction, which covers and darkens. In the mind it shows itself as dullness, lethargy, sleepiness, confusion, ignorance and delusion. The Samkhya Karika links the three to pleasure, pain and dejection respectively, and to three functions, illumination, activity and restraint. A traditional colour code, found as early as the Shvetashvatara Upanishad , makes sattva white, rajas red and tamas black. It is the Bhagavad Gita that turned the gunas into a full psychology of personality. The Gita is a poem of seven hundred verses in eighteen chapters, set within the epic Mahabharata ; its fourteenth chapter is devoted to the gunas, and chapters 17 and 18 classify faith, food, worship, charity, knowledge, action, the doer, the intellect, resolve and happiness into sattvic, rajasic and tamasic kinds. The gunas, Krishna tells Arjuna, are born of prakriti and bind the embodied self: sattva binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by attachment to action, born of craving, and tamas by heedlessness, laziness and sleep. From sattva comes knowledge, from rajas greed, and from tamas negligence, delusion and ignorance. Table 2.13 gathers their signatures. Table 2.13 The three gunas and their behavioural signatures. Three friends in Mysuru face the same entrance examination next week. Ananya has a revision plan, keeps to it, eats simply, sleeps on time and feels a quiet confidence: sattva predominates. Rohan has bought six guidebooks, switches between them every hour, drinks tea after tea, argues with his roommate and lies awake with his heart racing: rajas predominates. Karthik keeps meaning to start, sleeps until noon, scrolls his phone in bed and tells himself there is no point: tamas predominates. Now apply the Gita 's three kinds of happiness. Ananya's hours of revision are hard at first and sweet at the end, when the material falls into place; Rohan's late-night binge of videos is sweet at first and bitter the next morning; Karthik's oversleeping is dull and self-deceiving from start to finish. Notice two further points. First, nobody is purely one guna; the gunas describe proportions, and the same person can be sattvic in the morning, rajasic at noon and tamasic after a heavy lunch. Second, the scheme is not only descriptive but practical, since diet, routine, company and practice can shift the balance toward sattva. The Gita 's ideal is the person who has gone beyond all three, the gunatita , who stays even-minded in pleasure and pain, praise and blame, honour and dishonour. Clinical link The gunas map surprisingly well onto clinical pictures. The person who has stopped eating properly, withdrawn from others and cannot get herself to do anything is in a predominantly tamasic state, which resembles the psychomotor slowing and anergia of severe depression; restless agitation, racing thoughts, irritability and craving are rajasic, as in anxiety and mania. Researchers have built questionnaires to measure the three gunas (David Wolf's Vedic Personality Inventory, from the late 1990s, is one), and in such studies higher sattva scores tend to go with better well-being, and higher rajas and tamas scores with more distress. The disorders themselves are taught in the Disorders book. Exam trap Sattva = harmony, balance, clarity, purity (not passion and desire, which is rajas; not inertia, ignorance, darkness or confusion, which are tamas). Rajas = restlessness, passion, desire, over-activity. Tamas = lethargy, inertia, darkness, dullness, ignorance. The stem "Bavisha lost her job, stopped eating properly and cannot get herself to do anything" points to tamas alone ; yama is the first limb of yoga (an ethical discipline, not a mental state), pratyahara is sense withdrawal and jnana is knowledge (Section 2.9). The three gunas are sattva, rajas and tamas . Distractors that are not gunas: vata (an Ayurvedic dosha), ahimsa (non-violence, a yama), prakriti (the matter the gunas compose), ahamkara (an evolute, the I-maker), and the triads "atman, Brahman, maya", "karma, dharma, moksha" and "prakriti, purusha, kshetra". The antahkarana: the inner instrument Samkhya gives a name to the part of prakriti that does the work of the mind. The antahkarana , literally the "inner instrument", is contrasted with the ten "outer instruments", the five senses and the five organs of action. The Samkhya Karika says the inner instrument is threefold (intellect, I-maker and mind) and the outer tenfold. The Bhagavad Gita uses the same three: Krishna lists earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego as the eightfold division of his lower nature, prakriti. Later Vedanta added a fourth function, chitta , giving the four-part antahkarana of most modern accounts. Each function deserves a careful definition, because the four are easily confused. The first function, manas , is the sensory mind. It receives and coordinates the impressions brought by the senses, directs attention to them, and controls the organs of action. It is also the seat of desire and of doubt: manas weighs alternatives ("is it this or that?") without being able to settle them. The second, ahamkara , is the I-maker. It appropriates experience as "mine": " I see", " I want", "this is my pen". It is the source of individuality, and in excess of egoism and pride. The third, buddhi , is the intellect. It ascertains, judges, decides and discriminates; it is the highest and most sattvic of the evolutes, the one closest to purusha and the one whose clarity makes liberation possible. The fourth, chitta , in the fourfold scheme, is the storehouse of memory, holding the latent impressions ( samskaras ) left by every experience. (In Patanjali's Yoga, as you will see, chitta has a wider sense: the whole mind-stuff, all three inner instruments together.) Table 2.14 summarises the four. Table 2.14 The four functions of the antahkarana. Function Usual translation What it does Manas Sensory mind Receives and coordinates sense impressions, attends, desires, doubts and deliberates Ahamkara Ego, the I-maker Refers experience to a separate self: "I", "me", "mine" Buddhi Intellect Decides, judges, discriminates, knows with certainty Chitta Memory store Holds the impressions (samskaras) of past experience Push one moment through the scheme. You are writing an examination in a silent hall when a phone rings somewhere behind you. Your ears register the sound and manas takes it up: a sound, a ring, a phone, should I attend or ignore it? Chitta supplies the memory: that tune is familiar. Ahamkara claims it: "that is my ringtone!" Buddhi settles the matter: "my phone is switched off in my bag outside the hall, so it cannot be mine; keep writing". And manas sends your hand back to the answer sheet. If you compare this with the information-processing account of the batsman in Section 2.6 (sensory input, recognition from long-term memory, decision, response), the parallel is striking. The difference lies at the very end. For the Indian systems, none of these four functions is the knower. The awareness that witnessed the whole episode belongs to none of them; it belongs to purusha, or, in Vedanta, to the atman. Exam trap Which function is the ego, the I-maker? Ahamkara (not manas, the sensory mind; not buddhi, the intellect; not chitta, memory). The Gita's three elements of mind are manas, buddhi and ahamkara, not "prakriti, purusha, kshetra" ( kshetra , the "field", is the Gita 's word for the body and nature that the self knows), not the purusharthas "dharma, artha, kama", and not the gunas "sattva, rajas, tamas". Do not equate ahamkara with Freud's ego: the Freudian ego is an executive that tests reality, a job closer to buddhi; ahamkara is simply the sense of "I". Some popular study notes, following modern teachers, describe manas as memory and chitta as consciousness; the classical Vedanta assignment is the one in Table 2.14, and ahamkara is the ego in every version.
