The question a clinician asks next is practical: can the mind be changed, and if so, how? The Indian traditions answered with methods, and the most systematic of them is yoga. In September 1893 a young monk from Calcutta, Swami Vivekananda, addressed the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago and became famous overnight; three years later he published Raja Yoga (1896), which presented Patanjali's yoga to Western readers not as a religion or a set of exercises but as a science of the mind. This section follows his lead. It begins with yoga, moves to the Indian theories of the self and its states and sheaths, and then surveys the other great paths of transformation: Buddhist, Sufi and integral psychology, Ayurveda, and the ideas of karma and dharma. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras: stilling the mind The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali are a collection of 195 or 196 aphorisms (the count varies slightly between editions), arranged in four chapters: on absorption ( samadhi ), on practice ( sadhana ), on the extraordinary powers that practice brings ( vibhuti ), and on liberation ( kaivalya ). A sutra is literally a thread, a compressed statement meant to be memorised and unpacked by a teacher, and the oldest surviving commentary, the Yoga Bhashya attributed to Vyasa, has guided readers ever since. Nothing reliable is known about Patanjali the man, and scholars date the compilation anywhere between about the second century BCE and the fourth century CE. Yoga adopts Samkhya's map of purusha and prakriti almost unchanged, adding one thing: Ishvara , a special purusha forever untouched by affliction and karma, who can serve as an object of devotion. For this reason Yoga is sometimes called "Samkhya with God". The second sutra defines the whole discipline in four words: yogas chitta vritti nirodhah . Take them one at a time. Yoga is the subject. Chitta is the mind-stuff, the whole inner instrument of Section 2.8. Vritti means a whirl or fluctuation, any modification of the mind: a perception, a thought, a memory, a mood. Nirodha means restraint, stilling or cessation. So chitta-vritti-nirodha , yoga itself, is the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind. The next two sutras give the reason. When the fluctuations are stilled, "the seer abides in its own nature"; at other times the seer identifies with the fluctuations. The classic image is a lake. When wind ripples its surface, you cannot see the bottom, and the reflection of the moon breaks into a thousand pieces; when the water is still, the bottom is visible and the reflection whole. The goal of the stilling is not a blank mind for its own sake but liberation, kaivalya : consciousness resting in itself, no longer confused with the mind's activity. Notice how far this is from the modern image of yoga as physical fitness. Of the 195 sutras, only three deal with posture. What are the fluctuations? Patanjali lists five kinds of vritti , each of which can be klishta (afflicted, leading to suffering) or aklishta (unafflicted). Pramana , valid cognition, which comes from perception, inference and reliable testimony (the three pramanas of Section 2.8). Viparyaya , error: false knowledge that does not correspond to the real form of its object, like taking a coiled rope in the dusk for a snake. Vikalpa , verbal conceptualisation: an idea that follows words but has no real object, such as "the horn of a hare" or the abstractions we think with but never meet. Nidra , sleep: a fluctuation whose content is the absence of other contents. Smriti , memory: the retention of an object once experienced. Read the list again with a modern eye: perception and reasoning, illusion, imagination and abstraction, sleep, memory. It is very nearly the table of contents of a general psychology textbook, drawn up some two thousand years ago. Patanjali's commentator Vyasa added a description of five levels ( bhumis ) of the mind, which reads like a scale of attentional control. The kshipta mind is restless and scattered, driven by rajas; the mudha mind is dull and stupefied, sunk in tamas; the vikshipta mind is distracted but occasionally steady, the state of most of us most of the time; the ekagra mind is one-pointed, held on a single object; and the niruddha mind is fully restrained and still. Yoga proper begins at the one-pointed level and culminates in the restrained one. How is the stilling achieved? Through two means that work together (sutra 1.12). The first, abhyasa , is practice: repeated effort to rest in stillness, which becomes firmly grounded only when it is kept up for a long time, without interruption and with devotion. The second, vairagya , is non-attachment or dispassion: freedom from craving for objects, whether seen or merely heard of. Practice supplies direction; non-attachment removes the pull of distraction. A modern psychologist would call the first sustained training of attention and the second a kind of acceptance, the willingness to let urges arise and pass without acting on them. Why does the mind keep fluctuating? Because of five afflictions, the kleshas , which Patanjali lists in the second chapter. Avidya , ignorance: taking the impermanent for permanent, the impure for pure, the painful for pleasant and the not-self for the self. It is the field in which all the others grow. Asmita , "I-am-ness" or egoism: identifying the seer with the instruments of seeing, so that one says "I am this body, these thoughts". Raga , attachment: the craving that follows pleasure. Dvesha , aversion: the repulsion that follows pain. Abhinivesha , clinging to life: the fear of death, which, Patanjali notes, is present even in the wise. The afflictions may be dormant, weakened, interrupted or fully active. They generate actions, actions leave latent impressions ( samskaras ) in the chitta, and the impressions give rise to new fluctuations, a self-perpetuating cycle. The cycle can be weakened by kriya yoga , the "yoga of action", which consists of discipline ( tapas ), self-study ( svadhyaya ) and surrender to Ishvara ( ishvara pranidhana ), and the subtler impressions can be dissolved by meditation. Clinical link Two sutras anticipate modern therapy. Sutra 2.33 advises that when the mind is disturbed by harmful thoughts, one should cultivate their opposites ( pratipaksha bhavana ), which is close in spirit to the cognitive therapist's practice of identifying an unhelpful thought and building a balanced alternative (Section 2.6). Sutra 1.33 recommends friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous and equanimity toward the wrongdoer as ways to make the mind clear, attitudes that compassion-focused therapies now teach deliberately. The therapies are taught in the Clinical book. Exam trap The primary goal of yoga according to Patanjali is control of the mind (chitta-vritti-nirodha) leading to liberation (kaivalya): not physical fitness, not cognitive enhancement and not "emotional regulation only", although yoga may bring all three. Do not mix the two lists of five. The five vrittis (pramana, viparyaya, vikalpa, nidra, smriti) are kinds of mental activity; the five kleshas (avidya, asmita, raga, dvesha, abhinivesha) are afflictions that drive them. Abhyasa = practice; vairagya = non-attachment. The eight limbs of yoga The method itself is set out in sutra 2.29 as ashtanga yoga , the yoga of eight limbs ( ashta , eight; anga , limb). The order matters, because each limb prepares for the next, moving from conduct toward others, through the body and breath, to the innermost work of attention. Table 2.15 gives the eight with Patanjali's own definitions. Table 2.15 The eight limbs of Patanjali's yoga, in order. Limb Translation What Patanjali means 1. Yama Restraints Five ethical restraints toward others: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, sexual restraint, non-possessiveness 2. Niyama Observances Five personal disciplines: purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, surrender to Ishvara 3. Asana Posture A seated posture that is steady and comfortable 4. Pranayama Breath regulation Regulating the flow of inhalation and exhalation 5. Pratyahara Withdrawal of the senses The senses withdraw from their objects and follow the mind inward 6. Dharana Concentration Binding the mind to one place or object 7. Dhyana Meditation An unbroken flow of awareness toward that object 8. Samadhi Absorption The object alone shines forth, the mind as if empty of its own form The first two limbs set the ethical foundation. The yamas are ahimsa (non-violence), satya (truthfulness), asteya (non-stealing), brahmacharya (sexual restraint) and aparigraha (non-possessiveness); when they are kept universally, regardless of time, place and circumstance, Patanjali calls them the "great vow". The niyamas are shaucha (purity), santosha (contentment), tapas (austerity or disciplined effort), svadhyaya (self-study, including study of the scriptures) and ishvara pranidhana (surrender to Ishvara). Why begin with ethics? Because a mind full of conflict with others, guilt and greed cannot be stilled by any technique; the yamas and niyamas remove the largest sources of disturbance first. Asana and pranayama then steady the body and the breath. The fifth limb, pratyahara , is the hinge of the system. The word means drawing back ( prati , against, and ahara , food or what is taken in): the senses stop "feeding" on their objects and are drawn inward. The Gita 's image is a tortoise drawing its limbs into its shell. With pratyahara, attention turns from the outer world to the inner. The last three limbs are the stages of meditation proper. The first, dharana , is concentration: fixing the mind on one point, an object, the breath, a mantra, and bringing it back each time it wanders. The second, dhyana , is meditation: the concentration becomes an unbroken flow, so that it no longer needs to be dragged back. The third, samadhi , is absorption: the sense of a separate meditator falls away and only the object remains in awareness. Patanjali calls the three together, practised on one object, samyama . The distinctions between the last four limbs are easy to blur, so push one practice session through them. A student sits to meditate on a candle flame in a hostel room in Mysuru. She stops her attention being pulled by the traffic outside, the smell of the mess and her phone, and turns her senses inward: that is pratyahara. She fixes her gaze and attention on the flame and, each time her mind drifts to tomorrow's class, gently brings it back: dharana. After some minutes the effort drops away and attention flows steadily to the flame without breaks: dhyana. For a moment even the sense "I am meditating" disappears and there is only the flame: samadhi. Patanjali divides the limbs into two groups. The first five are bahiranga , the outer limbs, and the last three, dharana, dhyana and samadhi, are antaranga , the inner limbs; pratyahara is the bridge between them. Samadhi itself has grades. In samprajnata samadhi the mind is absorbed in an object and still has cognitive content; in asamprajnata samadhi there is no object at all, only the latent impressions remain, and these too are finally dissolved. The end is kaivalya in its yogic sense: the gunas, their purpose fulfilled, return to their source, and purusha is established in its own nature. A simple sentence will help you remember the order of the eight: "You Need A Peaceful Place; Do Daily Sitting" (yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi). Clinical link Yoga has become one of India's most studied contributions to mental health, and since 2015 the International Day of Yoga has been observed every 21 June. At NIMHANS in Bengaluru, controlled trials have tested yoga as an add-on to medication for schizophrenia and depression, with encouraging effects on symptoms and functioning, and breathing practices drawn from pranayama are widely used for anxiety. The research question is always the same as for any treatment: does it work better than a credible control? Yoga is used alongside, not instead of, standard care. Exam trap Order of the last four limbs : pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi (not dharana before pratyahara, and not dhyana before dharana). Concentration on a single point = dharana; unbroken flow of meditation = dhyana; turning the senses inward, away from sounds, smells and sights = pratyahara; breath regulation = pranayama; personal observances = niyama. Karma is not one of the eight limbs (karma yoga is a path in the Gita ), and neither is jnana (knowledge). Bahiranga = the first five limbs; antaranga = the last three. The paths of the Gita: action, knowledge and devotion Patanjali's way is the way of meditation. The Bhagavad Gita recognises that people differ, and offers several paths suited to different temperaments. The first, karma yoga , is the path of action: doing one's work and duty in the right spirit. Jnana yoga is the path of knowledge: discriminating the self from the not-self through study and reflection. Bhakti yoga is the path of devotion: love and surrender to God. The sixth chapter of the Gita also describes dhyana yoga , the path of meditation, close to Patanjali's. Vivekananda later presented these as four yogas, karma, jnana, bhakti and raja (his name for Patanjali's yoga). Hatha yoga , the yoga of postures, breathing and cleansing practices systematised in medieval texts such as the Hatha Yoga Pradipika of Svatmarama (fifteenth century), is the ancestor of most yoga classes today. At the heart of the Gita 's psychology of action is one famous verse (2.47): you have a right to your action alone, never to its fruits; do not let the fruits of action be your motive, and do not be attached to inaction either. This is the principle of nishkama karma , desireless or disinterested action: acting fully and well, as one's duty, without attachment to the outcome. The next verses define yoga as evenness of mind in success and failure and as "skill in action". Psychologically, nishkama karma is a cure for the anxiety that comes from fixing one's mind on results one cannot control. Sport psychologists who tell an athlete to focus on the process rather than the scoreboard, and therapists who help clients act on their values whatever the outcome, are teaching something very similar. The Gita also offers one of the earliest analyses of how a passing thought can grow into self-destruction (2.62 to 2.63). Brooding on objects of the senses produces attachment; from attachment arises desire; from frustrated desire, anger; from anger, delusion; from delusion, the loss of memory (of what one knows to be right); from the loss of memory, the destruction of discrimination (buddhi); and with the destruction of buddhi, a person is lost. Set it beside a cognitive therapist's account of how an angry episode escalates and the resemblance is plain. Its ideal is the sthitaprajna , the person of steady wisdom described at the end of the second chapter, who is unshaken by sorrow, free from craving, fear and anger, and who can withdraw the senses from their objects at will. Elsewhere (12.12) the Gita ranks the stages of the path: knowledge is better than mere practice, meditation better than knowledge, and renunciation of the fruits of action better than meditation, because peace follows immediately on renunciation. Indian textbooks often summarise this as a progression from practice ( abhyasa ) through knowledge ( jnana ), meditation ( dhyana ) and renunciation ( tyaga ) to peace ( shanti ). Exam trap The principle of disinterestedness on which the Gita is based is nishkama karma , action without attachment to its fruits. Karma yoga is the broader path of action that applies the principle; jnana yoga (knowledge) and bhakti yoga (devotion) are different paths. If both "karma yoga" and "nishkama karma" appear, the stem's word "principle" points to nishkama karma. The self in Vedanta and the four states of consciousness Who, or what, is the self that all these practices are meant to free? The Upanishads, the philosophical texts at the end of the Vedas (hence Vedanta , "the end of the Veda"), answer with a story. In the Chandogya Upanishad , the gods and the demons hear that the creator Prajapati has spoken of a self that is free from evil, old age, death, grief, hunger and thirst. Each side sends a pupil: Indra for the gods and Virochana for the demons. After thirty-two years of discipline, Prajapati tells them to look at their reflections in a pan of water, dressed in their finest clothes: that, he says, is the self. Virochana goes home satisfied and teaches the demons that the body is the self. Indra, on the way home, has a doubt. If the self is the body, it is blind when the body is blind and perishes when the body perishes. He returns, studies another thirty-two years, and is told that the self is the one who moves about happily in dreams. Again he doubts: in dreams one is chased, beaten and weeps. After thirty-two more years he is told that the self is the one in deep, dreamless sleep. But in deep sleep, Indra objects, one knows neither oneself nor anything else; it is like being annihilated. After five more years, one hundred and one in all, Prajapati teaches him the self that is beyond body, dream and sleep, which only uses the body as its vehicle. The story is a lesson in method: the self is found by examining, one after another, what it is not . The Upanishads call the true self the atman : pure, eternal, unchanging consciousness, the witness of body and mind, distinct from the physical body and from the fleeting contents of thought and feeling. They call the ultimate reality underlying the whole universe Brahman . And their boldest teaching is that the two are one. In the Chandogya , the sage Uddalaka repeats to his son Shvetaketu, " tat tvam asi ", "that thou art"; in the Brihadaranyaka , the realisation is phrased " aham brahmasmi ", "I am Brahman". When asked to describe the self, the Upanishadic teacher Yajnavalkya can only say " neti, neti ", "not this, not this". The most influential interpretation of these texts is Advaita Vedanta , the non-dualism systematised by Adi Shankaracharya (Shankara), who lived in the eighth century CE. For Advaita, Brahman alone is real; the world of many separate things is maya , appearance, neither simply real nor simply unreal; and the individual self ( jiva ) is in truth none other than atman, which is Brahman. Bondage is caused by ignorance ( avidya ), which superimposes the limited body-mind on the self, just as a coiled rope seen in dim light is mistaken for a snake. Liberation ( moksha ) comes not from action but from knowledge ( jnana ) that removes the error; when the light comes on, the snake is not killed, it is simply seen never to have been there. Later Vedantins disagreed: Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism) held that individual souls and the world are real parts of Brahman, and Madhva's Dvaita (dualism) that God and souls are eternally distinct. Notice the contrast with Samkhya too: Samkhya has many purushas and a real prakriti, a dualism, while Advaita has one consciousness and a world of appearance, a monism. Indra's four stages, waking body, dreamer, deep sleeper and the self beyond, have a systematic counterpart in the Mandukya Upanishad , the shortest of the principal Upanishads (just twelve verses), which analyses the self through the four states of consciousness. In jagrat , the waking state, consciousness is turned outward and experiences gross physical objects; the self in this state is called Vaishvanara. In svapna , the dream state, consciousness is turned inward and experiences subtle objects made by the mind itself; the self here is Taijasa, "the luminous". In sushupti , deep dreamless sleep, there is neither desire nor dream; consciousness is an undivided mass, resting in bliss; the self here is called Prajna. The fourth, turiya (literally "the fourth"), is not a further state alongside the others. It is pure consciousness itself, neither inward- nor outward-turned, peaceful and non-dual, the witness present through all three states, and it is identified with the atman. The Mandukya maps the four onto the sacred syllable Om , pronounced A-U-M: A is waking, U is dreaming, M is deep sleep, and the silence that follows is turiya. Table 2.16 sets out the scheme; the modern science of sleep and dreaming is taught in Chapter 5. Table 2.16 The four states of consciousness in the Mandukya Upanishad . State Meaning Name of the self What is experienced Part of Om Jagrat Waking Vaishvanara Gross outer objects A Svapna Dreaming Taijasa Subtle inner images U Sushupti Deep dreamless sleep Prajna No objects, no desire; undivided bliss M Turiya "The fourth" Atman itself Pure, non-dual consciousness, witness of the other three The silence after Why should a psychologist care? Because the scheme makes a claim that can be argued about. When you wake from deep sleep you say "I slept well; I knew nothing". Who knew that nothing was known? Vedanta argues that some witnessing awareness must have persisted through the gap, and that this continuity across waking, dreaming and dreamless sleep is the best evidence that the self is not identical with any of its states. Western psychology describes the states; Vedanta asks what stays the same across them. Exam trap Turiya = "the fourth", pure consciousness, the witness of all three states, not a deeper stage of sleep. Sushupti = deep dreamless sleep; its self is called Prajna , so lists sometimes give the states as jagrat, svapna, prajna and turiya. Svapna = dream, not deep sleep. Texts that speak of avastha-traya ("the three states") count waking, dream and deep sleep, with turiya as what lies beyond them. Atman versus Brahman : atman is the self, Brahman ultimate reality; Advaita says they are one. Advaita Vedanta (Shankara) = non-dualism; Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja) = qualified non-dualism; Dvaita (Madhva) = dualism. The five sheaths and the three bodies If the self is pure consciousness, why do we experience ourselves as bodies with breath, moods and opinions? The Taittiriya Upanishad answers with a second famous story and a model that is now one of the most widely used frameworks in Indian health psychology. The young Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman, and Varuna tells him only to reflect deeply. Bhrigu concludes first that food is Brahman, since beings are born from food, live on food and return to it; dissatisfied, he reflects again and decides that it is breath, then mind, then understanding, and at last bliss. Each answer goes deeper than the one before. The panchakosha ("five sheaths") model turns Bhrigu's progression into a map of the person as five concentric layers covering the self, from the grossest and outermost to the subtlest and innermost. Annamaya kosha , the food sheath: the physical body, built and sustained by food. Pranamaya kosha , the vital sheath: the life-force ( prana ) that animates the body through breath, circulation and the other vital functions, together with the organs of action. Manomaya kosha , the mental sheath: manas with the five senses, the layer of perception, emotion, desire and doubt, where sense impressions are received and processed. Vijnanamaya kosha , the sheath of understanding: buddhi with the senses, the layer of discrimination, judgement, decision and the sense of being the doer. Anandamaya kosha , the bliss sheath: the subtle joy experienced in deep sleep and deep meditation, the layer closest to the self. The atman itself is not a sheath. It is what the sheaths cover, as a scabbard covers a sword or five lampshades of increasing thickness dim a single lamp. A person who identifies with the outermost sheath says "I am fat" or "I am ill"; with the mental sheath, "I am anxious"; with the intellectual sheath, "I am the one who decides". Vedanta teaches discrimination of the self from each sheath in turn, the method Indra used. Vedanta groups the five sheaths into three bodies ( sharira-traya ), and links the bodies to the states of consciousness you have just met. The sthula sharira , the gross body, is the annamaya kosha, and it is the body we experience in waking. The linga sharira (also called sukshma sharira ), the subtle body, consists of the three middle sheaths, pranamaya, manomaya and vijnanamaya, and it is the body we experience in dreams; tradition holds that it is the subtle body that carries the individual from one life to the next. The karana sharira , the causal body, is the anandamaya kosha, experienced in deep sleep. Turiya is the atman, beyond all three. Figure 2.5 puts the whole scheme in one picture. (Samkhya, which does not use the kosha language, describes the subtle body by its components instead: buddhi, ahamkara, manas, the ten organs and the five subtle elements.) Annamaya (food) Pranamaya (breath) Manomaya (mind) Vijnanamaya Anandamaya Atman Bodies and states Gross body (sthula sharira) = annamaya kosha state: waking (jagrat) Subtle body (linga sharira) = pranamaya, manomaya and vijnanamaya koshas state: dream (svapna) Causal body (karana sharira) = anandamaya kosha state: deep sleep (sushupti) Atman (the self) not a sheath: the witness of all three; turiya Outer and grossest at the edge, inner and subtlest at the centre Figure 2.5 The five sheaths (panchakosha) of the Taittiriya Upanishad , with Vedanta's three bodies and the Mandukya 's states of consciousness. Notice that the subtle body is made of three sheaths, and that the atman at the centre is not itself a sheath but the consciousness all of them cover. The model is not only of historical interest. Yoga therapists in Bengaluru built an "integrated approach of yoga therapy" on it, prescribing practices for each sheath (postures and diet for the food sheath, breathing for the vital sheath, meditation and devotional practice for the mental sheath, study and counselling for the sheath of understanding, and practices aimed at contentment for the bliss sheath), and the panchakosha model is often used in India as a framework for holistic, multi-level assessment of well-being, much as the biopsychosocial model (Section 2.7) is used in the West. Exam trap Outermost sheath : annamaya (the food body); then pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya, and innermost , anandamaya. The sheath involved in perceptual processing is manomaya (manas with the senses), not vijnanamaya (intellect and discrimination), pranamaya (vital energy) or anandamaya (bliss). The subtle body (linga sharira) corresponds to the three middle sheaths, pranamaya, manomaya and vijnanamaya. A practice item keys "pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya and atman": the three sheaths are right, but the atman is the witness, never a component of any body. Ahamkara, manas, buddhi and chitta is the antahkarana, not the subtle body as the kosha scheme defines it. Buddhist psychology Of all the Indian traditions, the one that has entered Western clinical psychology most deeply is Buddhism. Its founder, Siddhartha Gautama , the Buddha ("the awakened one"), was born a prince of the Shakya clan at Lumbini, in what is now Nepal; the traditional dates are 563 to 483 BCE, though many historians now place him somewhat later. According to the traditional story, the sight of an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic led him to leave his palace in search of a way beyond suffering. Six years of extreme self-denial brought him close to death but not to freedom, and he turned instead to a "middle way" between indulgence and asceticism. Meditating under a tree at Bodh Gaya, he attained awakening, and in his first sermon, at the Deer Park in Sarnath near Varanasi, he set out the teaching on which all Buddhist psychology rests. The Four Noble Truths have the structure of a physician's consultation: diagnosis, cause, prognosis and treatment. Dukkha : life as ordinarily lived is marked by suffering or unsatisfactoriness, in birth, ageing, illness and death, in separation from what we love, contact with what we dislike and not getting what we want. Samudaya , the origin of suffering: craving ( tanha , literally "thirst"), whether for sensual pleasure, for existence or for non-existence. Nirodha , the cessation of suffering: when craving ends, suffering ends. This state is nirvana (Pali nibbana ), the "blowing out" of the fires of greed, hatred and delusion. Magga , the path to the cessation of suffering: the Noble Eightfold Path. The Noble Eightfold Path is not a sequence of steps but eight factors cultivated together, traditionally grouped into three trainings, as Table 2.17 shows. Table 2.17 The Noble Eightfold Path and its three trainings. Training Path factors What they cultivate Wisdom ( prajna , Pali panna ) Right view (understanding); right intention (thought) Seeing things as they are; wholesome motives Ethical conduct ( sila ) Right speech; right action; right livelihood Harmless, honest living Mental discipline ( samadhi ) Right effort; right mindfulness; right concentration Training of attention and the mind What, according to the Buddha, is the person who suffers? Here Buddhism parts company with the Upanishads. All conditioned things, he taught, bear three marks: impermanence ( anicca ), unsatisfactoriness ( dukkha ) and non-self ( anatta , Sanskrit anatman ). There is no permanent, unchanging self or soul behind experience. What we call a person is a constantly changing process made of five aggregates, the skandhas (Pali khandhas ): form or the body ( rupa ), feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neutral ( vedana ), perception ( samjna ), mental formations such as volitions and habits ( samskara ), and consciousness ( vijnana ). In a famous dialogue from the Milindapanha , the monk Nagasena asks the Indo-Greek King Milinda what a chariot is. Is it the axle? The wheels? The pole? None of them, the king admits, yet "chariot" is not something apart from them either; it is a convenient name for parts in a certain arrangement. So too, says Nagasena, is "Nagasena". Belief in a fixed self is, for Buddhism, a root of craving and therefore of suffering. Modern cognitive science, which also describes the self as a construction assembled moment by moment by many processes, has found the Buddhist view surprisingly congenial. Buddhism also produced one of the world's first systematic psychologies. The Pali canon is divided into three "baskets" ( Tipitaka ): the Vinaya (rules of monastic discipline), the Sutta (the Buddha's discourses) and the Abhidhamma ("higher teaching"). The Abhidhamma analyses experience into momentary states of consciousness ( cittas ) and the mental factors that accompany them ( cetasikas , fifty-two in the Theravada lists), each classed as wholesome, unwholesome or neutral. The three unwholesome roots of action are greed ( lobha ), hatred ( dosa ) and delusion ( moha ), the "three poisons"; their wholesome opposites are generosity, loving-kindness and wisdom. In its ambition to catalogue the elements of mind it resembles Titchener's structuralism, but its purpose is therapeutic: to know which states to cultivate and which to abandon. A later Mahayana school, the Yogacara ("practice of yoga") school of Asanga and Vasubandhu (around the fourth century CE), described a "storehouse consciousness" ( alaya-vijnana ) holding the seeds of past actions below awareness, an idea often compared with the unconscious. Buddhist practice divides meditation into two kinds. Samatha ("calm abiding") develops concentration on a single object, much like Patanjali's dharana and dhyana. The second, vipassana ("insight", literally "seeing clearly"), uses that stability to observe experience as it arises and passes, until its impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and lack of self are seen directly. Its central skill is sati , mindfulness: the Pali word originally meant remembering or keeping in mind, and came to mean a clear, non-reactive, present-moment awareness of whatever is happening. The Satipatthana Sutta describes four foundations of mindfulness: the body, feelings, the mind and mental objects. Alongside these, Buddhism cultivates four boundless attitudes, the brahmaviharas : loving-kindness ( metta ), compassion ( karuna ), sympathetic joy ( mudita ) and equanimity ( upekkha ), the same four Patanjali recommends in sutra 1.33. In modern India, vipassana was revived on a large scale by S. N. Goenka (1924 to 2013), a Burmese-born teacher of Indian descent who began teaching in India in 1969, founded the centre at Igatpuri near Nashik in 1976, and made the ten-day silent residential course famous, including courses held inside Tihar Jail in Delhi in the 1990s. Clinical link Buddhist mindfulness is the root of the third wave of cognitive-behavioural therapy (Section 2.6). Jon Kabat-Zinn (born 1944) built mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) in 1979 and defined mindfulness as paying attention in a particular way: on purpose, in the present moment and non-judgementally. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT; Segal, Williams and Teasdale, 2002) uses it to prevent relapse in recurrent depression. Marsha Linehan (born 1943) developed dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) for chronically suicidal clients and borderline personality disorder; it blends cognitive-behavioural change strategies with acceptance and mindfulness practices drawn from Zen Buddhism and with dialectical philosophy, and teaches four skills modules: core mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness. Steven Hayes's acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) also builds on acceptance and mindful awareness. The therapies are taught in the Clinical book. A word on Buddhism's sister tradition is useful here, because the two are easily confused. Jainism was shaped by Mahavira , an older contemporary of the Buddha whom Jains honour as the twenty-fourth and last tirthankara ("ford-maker"). Unlike Buddhism, it affirms an eternal, conscious soul ( jiva ), one for each living being, and treats karma as a subtle matter that clings to the soul through passions such as anger, pride, deceit and greed. Liberation, a state of perfect knowledge called kevala jnana , comes through the "three jewels" of right faith, right knowledge and right conduct, with ahimsa (non-violence) at the centre of conduct. The Jain doctrine of anekantavada , "many-sidedness", holds that reality has many aspects and every single viewpoint is partial, an ancient lesson in intellectual humility. Exam trap Anatta (Buddhism) is the opposite of atman (Upanishads) : Buddhism denies a permanent self; Vedanta and Jainism affirm one (and Samkhya affirms many purushas). The Abhidhamma is the third basket of the Pali canon, the systematic psychology of mind-states; the Vinaya is monastic discipline and the Sutta the discourses. Mindfulness comes from Buddhist sati and vipassana; samatha is concentration. DBT's core mindfulness skills come from Zen Buddhism (not Stoicism, which influenced Ellis's REBT; not psychoanalysis or existentialism), and DBT blends CBT with mindfulness and acceptance practices and dialectical philosophy (not with free association, drugs or Bowen family systems theory). Its four modules are mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness; cognitive restructuring and relaxation are not modules. Buddhism and Jainism are nastika. Sufi psychology Sufism ( tasawwuf ) is the mystical, inward dimension of Islam, and from about the eleventh and twelfth centuries Sufi teachers made it one of the great spiritual traditions of India. The Chishti order, brought to India by Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, whose shrine at Ajmer still draws millions, and carried on by Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi, became famous for its tolerance and for its use of music ( sama , the ancestor of qawwali ) as a spiritual practice. Like yoga and Buddhism, Sufism contains a detailed psychology of the self and its transformation. The Persian theologian al-Ghazali (1058 to 1111) analysed the "diseases of the heart" (pride, envy, greed, anger) and their cures in terms any counsellor would recognise. Sufi psychology describes the person in terms of the nafs (the self or ego, especially the lower self of appetites and egoism), the qalb (the heart, the organ of spiritual perception), the ruh (the spirit) and the aql (the intellect). Its central teaching is that the nafs can be refined, and it describes the refinement in seven stages, most of whose names come from the Quran. Nafs al-ammara , the commanding or tyrannical self, which incites to evil and is ruled by appetite and ego. Nafs al-lawwama , the self-reproaching or blaming self, which has begun to feel remorse and to struggle against its impulses. Nafs al-mulhama , the inspired self, which begins to receive inspiration and to act from goodness. Nafs al-mutma'inna , the tranquil or serene self, at peace and secure in faith. Nafs al-radiya , the contented self, pleased with whatever comes. Nafs al-mardiyya , the self that is pleasing to God. Nafs al-kamila (also called safiya ), the complete or pure self. The journey is often described as passing through four levels, from the outer to the inner: shariat (the religious law, the outward practice), tariqat (the path of inner discipline), haqiqat (inner truth) and marifat (direct knowledge of God). Along the way the seeker passes through maqamat , "stations" reached by effort and stable once attained, such as repentance ( tawba ), scrupulousness ( wara ), renunciation ( zuhd ), poverty ( faqr ), patience ( sabr ), trust in God ( tawakkul ) and contentment ( rida ), and experiences ahwal , "states" such as love and longing, which come as gifts and pass. The principal practice is zikr ( dhikr ), remembrance through the rhythmic repetition of divine names, together with contemplation ( muraqaba ), under the guidance of a teacher ( murshid or pir ) to whom the disciple ( murid ) is closely bound, a relationship some writers compare with that of therapist and client. The goal is fana , the "annihilation" or passing away of the ego-self in God, followed by baqa , "subsistence", a return to life in the world with the self transformed. Exam trap Lowest stage of the nafs : ammara , the commanding self; next lawwama , the blaming self; the serene self is mutma'inna . Fana = annihilation of the ego in God; baqa = subsistence after it. Maqamat (stations) are earned and lasting; ahwal (states) are given and passing. Sufism is an Islamic tradition: it is neither astika nor nastika. Sri Aurobindo's integral psychology The last of the great Indian psychologies is modern. Sri Aurobindo (Aurobindo Ghose, 1872 to 1950) was born in Calcutta, educated in England from the age of seven and at Cambridge, and returned to India to become one of the leaders of the movement for independence. Arrested in 1908 in the Alipore bomb case, he spent a year in jail awaiting trial, and there, by his own account, had the spiritual experiences that changed the direction of his life. Acquitted in 1909, he withdrew in 1910 to Pondicherry, then a French territory, where he spent the rest of his life writing and practising yoga. His collaborator Mirra Alfassa (1878 to 1973), known as the Mother, organised the Sri Aurobindo Ashram and later founded the international township of Auroville (1968). His major works include The Life Divine , The Synthesis of Yoga and the epic poem Savitri . Aurobindo's integral yoga differs from the classical yogas in one decisive respect. Their aim was release from the world; his was the transformation of life in the world. "All life is yoga", he wrote. He saw evolution as the progressive emergence of consciousness from matter, to life, to mind, and beyond mind to what he called the supermind, and he aimed to integrate the paths of knowledge, works and devotion into one discipline. The psychology built on his writings, which his disciple, the psychologist Indra Sen , is usually credited with naming integral psychology , describes the person along two dimensions. The first is a concentric system, from the surface inward. On the surface is the outer being , made of three parts: the physical, the vital (Aurobindo's term for the life-energy of desires, emotions, sensations and drives) and the mental. Behind it lies a wider inner or subliminal being, with inner physical, vital and mental parts of far greater range than their surface counterparts. And at the centre is the psychic being , the innermost being: the evolving soul, a "divine spark" that grows from life to life and can, once it comes forward, guide the whole personality. The second is a vertical system. Below the waking mind lie the subconscient and the inconscient; above it rises a series of higher planes of consciousness, the higher mind, the illumined mind, intuition, the overmind and, highest, the supermind. Aurobindo described the work of yoga as a triple transformation: a psychic transformation, in which the psychic being comes to the front; a spiritual transformation, in which higher consciousness descends into the person; and a supramental transformation, the final change of the whole nature. Cornelissen's Indian Psychology Institute (Section 2.8) works largely within this framework, and transpersonal theorists such as Ken Wilber (Section 2.5) drew partly on it for their own use of the word "integral". Exam trap The innermost being in the concentric system of integral yoga is the psychic being , not the mind, the vital or the body, which make up the outer being. "The vital" means life-energy, desire and emotion, not the physical body. The supermind belongs to the vertical system, at its top. Ayurveda: the doshas, the gunas and mental health India's classical medicine, Ayurveda ("the knowledge of life"), is set out above all in two great compendia, the Charaka Samhita , on internal medicine, associated with the physician Charaka , and the Sushruta Samhita , on surgery, associated with Sushruta . Ayurveda's definition of health is strikingly psychological. Sushruta calls a person healthy ( svastha ) whose doshas, digestive fire, tissues and excretions are in balance, and whose self, senses and mind are prasanna , clear and content. Health is not merely the absence of disease but balance and contentment in body and mind together. The body, in Ayurveda, is governed by three doshas , functional principles each built from two of the five elements of Samkhya. Every person is born with a characteristic balance of the three, called his or her prakriti or constitution (note that this is a different use of the word from Samkhya's cosmic prakriti), and illness is a departure from that balance. Each constitution has a recognisable psychological signature, set out in Table 2.18. Table 2.18 The three doshas of Ayurveda. Dosha Elements Bodily function Typical temperament (and when out of balance) Vata Space and air Movement: breath, circulation, nerve impulses, elimination Quick, lively, creative, changeable (worry, fear, insomnia) Pitta Fire and water Transformation: digestion, metabolism, body heat Sharp, focused, ambitious (irritability, anger) Kapha Earth and water Structure and cohesion: stability, lubrication, strength Calm, steady, patient, affectionate (sluggishness, possessiveness) Where do the gunas fit? Ayurveda applies them to the mind. The mind ( manas ) is made of the three gunas; sattva is the guna of mental health and clarity, while rajas and tamas are called the two doshas of the mind ( manasa doshas ), the sources of mental disturbance, just as vata, pitta and kapha are the doshas of the body. Charaka described sixteen kinds of mental constitution, seven sattvic, six rajasic and three tamasic, an early typology of personality. Ayurveda also had a branch for mental illness. Bhuta vidya , one of its eight branches, dealt with disorders attributed to possession and mental causes, and the Charaka Samhita describes unmada (insanity) and apasmara (epilepsy), distinguishing disorders arising from deranged doshas within the body from those with external causes. Most remarkable for a clinical psychologist is Charaka's threefold classification of treatment. Daivavyapashraya chikitsa is spiritual or faith-based therapy: prayer, mantras, rituals and offerings. Yuktivyapashraya chikitsa is rational therapy: diet, medicines and physical procedures, reasoned from the cause of the illness. And sattvavajaya chikitsa , "conquest of the mind", is psychotherapy: restraining the mind from harmful objects and strengthening it through knowledge, understanding, courage, memory and concentration. Long before the word existed, Ayurveda recognised a treatment that works through the mind itself. Exam trap Doshas are not gunas. Vata, pitta and kapha are the three doshas of the body (Ayurveda); sattva, rajas and tamas are the three gunas (Samkhya and the Gita ). So vata is the wrong option in any question about the gunas. In Ayurveda, rajas and tamas are the doshas of the mind . Vata = space and air; pitta = fire and water; kapha = earth and water. Ayurveda's prakriti (a person's constitution) is not Samkhya's prakriti (primordial matter). Sattvavajaya is Charaka's psychotherapy. Karma and dharma as psychological ideas Two words from Indian thought have entered every language in the world, usually in a garbled form. Both are psychological ideas, and both shape how millions of people in India explain their lives. The word karma (from the root kri , to do) means action, and by extension the law that every action has consequences for the one who acts. Each deliberate act leaves a latent impression ( samskara ) in the mind; impressions accumulate into tendencies ( vasanas ) that incline us to act the same way again; and actions bear fruit ( phala ), in this life or, the tradition holds, a later one. Vedanta distinguishes three kinds. Sanchita karma is the accumulated store from the past. Prarabdha karma is the portion of that store which has begun to bear fruit and shapes the circumstances of the present life. Agami (or kriyamana ) karma is the new karma being made now, by present choices. Read psychologically, the doctrine of samskaras is a theory of habit: every act strengthens a disposition to repeat it, much as Hull's habit strength (Section 2.2) grows with each reinforced repetition. It is also a theory of moral responsibility and a way of finding meaning in misfortune. That last use cuts both ways. A fatalistic reading ("it is my karma; nothing can be done") can encourage passivity and the acceptance of injustice. An agentic reading ("my present actions shape my future") encourages responsibility and hope, and the distinction between prarabdha and agami karma leaves plenty of room for choice. Indian psychologists, Ajit Dalal among them, have studied how patients explain their illnesses, and found that beliefs about karma and God often stand beside medical explanations rather than replacing them, sometimes helping people to accept what cannot be changed. The word dharma (from the root dhr , to hold or sustain) means that which upholds: the cosmic and social order, and the duties, ethics and right conduct that sustain it. Dharma is sensitive to context. What is right depends on one's stage of life, role and situation; hence svadharma , one's own duty, of which the Gita says it is better to perform one's own dharma imperfectly than another's well. Dharma is the first of the four aims of life, the purusharthas : dharma (virtue and duty), artha (wealth and security), kama (pleasure and love) and moksha (liberation). Unlike Maslow's hierarchy (Section 2.5), the scheme does not climb from lower to higher needs; it places dharma as the regulator of the pursuit of wealth and pleasure, with liberation as the final aim. The tradition also describes four stages of life, the ashramas : the student ( brahmacharya ), the householder ( grihastha ), the retired forest-dweller ( vanaprastha ) and the renunciant ( sannyasa ), a lifespan model that Sudhir Kakar and others have compared with Erikson's psychosocial stages. When duties collide, the result is a dharma-sankata , a dilemma of dharma: a situation in which every available action violates some obligation. Arjuna on the battlefield, bound by his duty as a warrior to fight and by his duty to his family not to kill his kinsmen, is the classic case, and his despair (the first chapter of the Gita is called "the yoga of Arjuna's despair") is the starting point of the whole poem. Krishna's answer combines several ideas you have met in this section: understand that the self is not the body (Vedanta), act according to your svadharma (dharma), and act without attachment to the fruits (nishkama karma). Indian psychologists use the concept of dharma-sankata in the study of moral reasoning and decision-making in Indian families and organisations. Clinical link For a clinical psychologist in India these ideas are not abstractions. Clients explain their distress in terms of karma, fate, dharma and duty to family, and a formulation that ignores those explanations will often fail. Some Indian counsellors draw explicitly on the Gita , treating the Krishna-Arjuna dialogue as a model of a helping relationship that moves from listening to the client's despair, through a change of perspective, to committed action. Whatever framework you use, the rule of the biopsychosocial model (Section 2.7) applies: understand the client's own cultural meanings first. Step back and notice what these Indian systems share, for all their disagreements about the self. Each begins with suffering; each traces it to a mistake about who we are (avidya, aviveka, craving, the commanding nafs); each prescribes a disciplined training of ethics and attention; and each aims at a freedom that is also a transformation of experience. These are exactly the themes that the transpersonal psychologists of Section 2.5 and the third-wave therapists of Section 2.6 later went looking for in India. Exam trap The four purusharthas are dharma, artha, kama and moksha (not the gunas, not the koshas). The four ashramas are brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha and sannyasa. Prarabdha = karma already bearing fruit in this life; sanchita = the accumulated store; agami = karma being made now. Karma as a word means action; it is not one of Patanjali's eight limbs. The case of Sultan's sticks, revisited Go back to Tenerife, to the chimpanzee sitting on his box and idly playing with two bamboo sticks until, suddenly, he fitted one into the other and raked in the banana. You can now tell all five of the stories the opening promised. A strict behaviourist would refuse to say anything about what went on inside Sultan; she would describe the solution as a response that was emitted and then reinforced, and would want to know his history of reinforcement with sticks. Kohler, the Gestalt psychologist, saw insight: a sudden restructuring of the perceptual field, two separate sticks reorganised into one tool, a solution that appeared all at once, was carried out smoothly and was repeated without hesitation. A psychoanalyst would look past the problem to the motive it served. A cognitive psychologist would model Sultan as an information-processing system searching a problem space, holding the goal in working memory and testing operators against it. And a psychologist trained in the Indian tradition would notice what Kohler himself recorded but did not dwell on: the answer came not while Sultan was straining at the bars but after he had given up and sat quietly, when the restless, rajasic effort had subsided, much as many human solvers report that a solution arrives when they stop forcing it (incubation, Chapter 8). The schools did not merely tell different stories; they tested one another. In 1945 Herbert Birch found that young chimpanzees with no previous experience of playing with sticks rarely solved a similar problem, but that after a few days of free play with sticks they did. Insight, it turned out, draws on a learning history, which is exactly what a behaviourist would have predicted, while the sudden reorganisation of that learning is exactly what a Gestalt psychologist would have predicted. That is the lesson of this chapter. Each school saw something real, overreached, and was corrected by its rivals; and psychology today, with its overlapping perspectives, its information-processing models, its third-wave therapies drawn from Buddhist mindfulness and its renewed interest in India's own traditions, is the sum of those corrections. Sultan's two sticks, joined end to end, are not a bad image of it. Chapter summary 2.1 Schools, Systems and Paradigms. A school of thought is a group sharing assumptions about psychology's subject matter, method and explanation, usually with a founder, a manifesto, a home, a journal, students and a rival; Woodworth's Contemporary Schools of Psychology (1931) and Heidbreder's Seven Psychologies (1933) surveyed them. A system is an organised body of assumptions covering the whole field; a theory explains one set of facts. Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) described paradigms, normal science, anomalies, crises and paradigm shifts; a field with competing schools and no shared paradigm is a preparadigmatic science, which fits psychology's age of schools. The humanists numbered the forces: psychoanalysis first, behaviourism second, humanistic psychology third and transpersonal psychology fourth (multiculturalism is Pedersen's "fourth force" in counselling). 2.2 Behaviourism: From Watson's Manifesto to Skinner. Behaviourism was prepared by animal psychology (Darwin, Romanes, Morgan's canon, Loeb's tropisms, Thorndike's puzzle boxes of 1898), by Russian objective psychology (Sechenov, Pavlov and Bekhterev's reflexology) and by functionalism. Watson's 1913 manifesto made psychology "a purely objective experimental branch of natural science" aiming at prediction and control without introspection. He treated thought as subvocal speech (peripheralism), proposed three innate emotions (fear, rage, love), conditioned Little Albert with Rayner (1920) and made the extreme environmentalist "twelve infants" claim (1925). Behaviourism may be metaphysical, methodological or radical. The neobehaviourists drew on logical positivism and Bridgman's operationism (1927): Tolman's purposive behaviourism (molar behaviour, intervening variables, cognitive maps, latent learning), Hull's hypothetico-deductive system (drive reduction, habit strength, reaction potential = habit strength × drive), Guthrie's contiguity and one-trial learning, and Skinner's radical, anti-theoretical behaviourism ( Walden Two , Verbal Behavior 1957, Beyond Freedom and Dignity 1971). Kuo abolished instinct. Dollard and Miller (1950) gave early social learning theory, Bandura and Walters (1963) the later one. Behaviourism declined under attack from Chomsky, the Brelands and Garcia but left operational definition and behaviour therapy (Jones 1924, Wolpe 1958). 2.3 Gestalt Psychology and Kurt Lewin. Wertheimer's 1912 paper on the phi phenomenon (apparent movement, with Kohler and Koffka as observers) founded Gestalt psychology, building on Ehrenfels's form qualities. Kohler's apes on Tenerife (1913 to 1920; The Mentality of Apes , 1917 and 1925) showed insight; his hens showed transposition; his theory of isomorphism was tested and rejected in its field form. Koffka's Growth of the Mind , his 1922 article and his Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935) spread the school, and his Lake Constance story separated the geographical from the behavioural environment. The whole is different from (popularly, greater than) the sum of its parts; field theory, Pragnanz, figure-ground (Rubin, 1915) and productive thinking (Wertheimer, 1945) followed. Lewin's B = f(P, E) located behaviour in the life space (the person and the psychological environment), described with topological and hodological concepts, valences and vectors; his students found the Zeigarnik (recall) and Ovsiankina (resumption) effects; he founded group dynamics and action research. Gestalt therapy (Perls, empty chair) is not Gestalt psychology. 2.4 Psychoanalysis as a School: The First Force. Freud began as a neurologist. Charcot's demonstrations of hysteria under hypnosis (Paris, 1885 to 1886), Janet's dissociation, Bernheim's suggestion (Nancy, 1889) and above all Breuer's treatment of Anna O. (the "talking cure", the cathartic method; Studies on Hysteria , 1895) led Freud to free association and psychoanalysis. The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) called dreams the royal road to the unconscious, and the Clark University lectures (1909) brought psychoanalysis to America. The topographic model divides the mind into conscious, preconscious and unconscious; the structural model (1923) into id, ego and superego. Adler and Jung dissented; Horney, Fromm and Sullivan (the neo-Freudians), Anna Freud and Erikson (ego psychology) and Klein (object relations) followed. Popper criticised psychoanalysis as unfalsifiable. 2.5 The Third Force and Beyond. Maslow (self-actualisation) and Rogers (the actualising tendency, conditions of worth), with Buhler and May, founded humanistic psychology, the third force, which emphasises free will, growth, the whole person and phenomenological understanding; landmarks were the Journal of Humanistic Psychology (1961), the Association for Humanistic Psychology (1961 or 1962), Bugental's five postulates and the Old Saybrook conference (1964). Phenomenology (Husserl) brackets assumptions to describe experience. Existential psychology (Kierkegaard, Heidegger's Dasein, Sartre, Binswanger's Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt, Boss, Frankl's logotherapy, will to meaning and noogenic neurosis, May, Yalom's four ultimate concerns) confronts death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness. Transpersonal psychology (Maslow and Sutich, 1969; Grof, Tart, Wilber, Assagioli) is the fourth force. Positive psychology was launched by Seligman (APA president for 1998) with Csikszentmihalyi (flow) in 2000, and includes PERMA, character strengths, hope and savouring. Humanistic and phenomenological approaches are criticised as vague and as missing social and cultural context. 2.6 The Cognitive Revolution. Behaviourism waned under anomalies (Tolman, Kohler, Lashley's 1948 paper on serial order), wartime problems of attention, information theory (Shannon), cybernetics (Wiener), the computer (Turing, 1950) and linguistics. In 1956 came the MIT symposium (Newell and Simon's Logic Theorist, Chomsky, Miller's magical number seven plus or minus two), the Dartmouth project on artificial intelligence and Bruner's A Study of Thinking ; Broadbent's Perception and Communication (1958) was the first major information-processing theory; Chomsky's 1959 review of Verbal Behavior became a manifesto; and Neisser's Cognitive Psychology (1967) named the field. The information-processing approach treats the mind as a series of limited-capacity stages operating on representations. Bartlett (schema) and Piaget were forerunners. Cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience followed, and connectionism (Rumelhart and McClelland's Parallel Distributed Processing , 1986) modelled knowledge as weights in parallel networks. Bandura's self-efficacy (1977), Ellis and Beck brought cognition into therapy, producing CBT and later its mindfulness-based third wave. 2.7 Psychology Today: Perspectives, Eclecticism and the Enduring Issues. Schools gave way to overlapping perspectives: biological (neurobiological), evolutionary, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, sociocultural and Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977); developmental psychology is a field that uses them all. Cross-cultural psychology compares cultures, cultural psychology studies how culture and mind make each other up, and indigenous psychology builds theory from within a culture. Eclecticism selects from several schools (Lazarus's technical eclecticism versus theoretical integration, and common factors). The enduring issues, which Robert I. Watson (1967) called prescriptions, include mind-body, nature-nurture, free will-determinism, mechanism-vitalism, molar-molecular, nomothetic-idiographic (Windelband, Allport), objectivism-subjectivism and empiricism-rationalism; whether psychology has a Kuhnian paradigm is still debated. 2.8 Indian Psychology I: The Movement, Its Pioneers and Samkhya's Map of the Mind. Psychology in India is the discipline as practised in India; Indian psychology is an approach rooted in classical Indian thought, consciousness-centred, holistic, transformative, relational and open to disciplined first-person methods. Experimental psychology entered the Calcutta curriculum in 1905 (Seal); Sengupta founded the first laboratory (1915) and department (1916) and the Indian Psychological Association (1925), whose Indian Journal of Psychology began in 1926; Bose, father of Indian psychoanalysis, founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922) and proposed the theory of opposite wishes; Gopalaswamy began psychology at Mysore (1924). Durganand Sinha led indigenisation (from without and from within); Uma Chowdhury adapted the TAT; J. B. P. Sinha proposed the nurturant-task leader (1980); Pareek studied role stress; Kakar applied psychoanalysis to Indian childhood. The Pondicherry Manifesto (2002), Cornelissen's Indian Psychology Institute, the Handbook of Indian Psychology (Rao, Paranjpe and Dalal, 2008) and Foundations of Indian Psychology (Cornelissen, Misra and Varma, 2011) launched the Indian Psychology movement. The darshanas are astika or nastika by their acceptance of the Vedas. Samkhya (Kapila; Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika ) is a dualism of passive, conscious purusha and active, unconscious prakriti, which evolves into buddhi, ahamkara, manas, the ten organs, the subtle and the gross elements (25 tattvas); liberation (kaivalya) comes from discriminating the seer from the seen. Prakriti is made of three gunas: sattva (clarity, harmony), rajas (activity, passion, restlessness) and tamas (inertia, dullness, ignorance), elaborated in the Gita . The antahkarana comprises manas (sensory mind), ahamkara (I-maker), buddhi (intellect) and, in Vedanta, chitta (memory). 2.9 Indian Psychology II: Yoga, the Self and the Paths of Transformation. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras define yoga as chitta-vritti-nirodha, aiming at kaivalya; they list five vrittis (pramana, viparyaya, vikalpa, nidra, smriti), two means (abhyasa and vairagya), five kleshas (avidya, asmita, raga, dvesha, abhinivesha) and the eight limbs: yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana and samadhi, the first five outer and the last three inner. The Gita offers the paths of action, knowledge, devotion and meditation, with nishkama karma, action without attachment to its fruits. The Upanishads identify the atman with Brahman; Shankara's Advaita Vedanta treats the world as maya. The Mandukya Upanishad describes waking (jagrat), dreaming (svapna), deep sleep (sushupti) and turiya, the fourth; the Taittiriya describes five sheaths (annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya, anandamaya), grouped into gross, subtle (linga) and causal bodies. Buddhism teaches the Four Noble Truths, the Noble Eightfold Path, anatta and the five skandhas, systematised in the Abhidhamma, with samatha, vipassana and mindfulness (sati) as practices that now underlie MBSR, MBCT, DBT and ACT. Sufi psychology describes seven stages of the nafs and the goal of fana. Sri Aurobindo's integral psychology places the psychic being at the centre of the person. Ayurveda describes three doshas (vata, pitta, kapha), treats rajas and tamas as doshas of the mind and includes Charaka's sattvavajaya psychotherapy. Karma (with samskaras and three kinds of karma) and dharma (svadharma, the purusharthas, the ashramas and dharma-sankata) shape how Indians explain their lives.
