Latent learning was demonstrated by: (IHBAS 2025) a Tolman b Bandura c Skinner d Kohler ✓ Answer: (a) Tolman Tolman and Honzik (1930) The concept The study Tolman and Honzik (1930) let rats run a maze with no reward; they learned it but did not show it. The reveal When food appeared, the rats revealed the learning at once. Learning had been latent , evidence for a cognitive map . Why the other options are wrong (b) Bandura Bandura is observational learning , learning by watching others, not hidden maze learning. (c) Skinner Skinner is operant conditioning , learning through reward; Tolman's point was that rats learned without any reward. (d) Kohler Kohler is insight learning, the sudden solution of a problem, shown in his work with chimpanzees. Gestalt psychology emphasizes: (IHBAS 2025) a Reinforcement and punishment b Neurotransmitter balance c Cognitive distortions d The whole is greater than the sum of its parts ✓ Answer: (d) The whole is greater than the sum of its parts Gestalt school's slogan (Koffka: 'different from') The concept The slogan "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts" is the Gestalt school's slogan: we perceive organised wholes, not piles of separate sensations. Key note Koffka preferred "different from" the sum of its parts, because the whole is a new thing, not just more. Why the other options are wrong (a) Reinforcement and punishment Behaviourist ideas about how consequences shape behaviour, not Gestalt. (b) Neurotransmitter balance Belong to the biological perspective, not to the Gestalt school. (c) Cognitive distortions Belong to Beck 's cognitive therapy , not to the Gestalt school. In Lewin's topological system, emphasis was placed on the study of 'life space,' which includes: (Amity 2023) a Person and psychological environment b Society and group c Person and group d Environment and group ✓ Answer: (a) Person and psychological environment Kurt Lewin, field theory: B = f(P, E) The concept What it is The life space is the person plus the environment as it exists for that person . The formula Hence B = f(P, E) : behaviour is a function of the person and the psychological environment. Key note Groups were a later application of field theory ( group dynamics ), not part of the definition of the life space. Why the other options are wrong (b) Society and group Leaves out the person entirely; groups were a later application of field theory (group dynamics), not part of the life space. (c) Person and group Keeps the person but swaps the psychological environment for the group, which belongs to the later group dynamics work. (d) Environment and group Drops the person, half of B = f(P, E), and adds the group, a later application of field theory. Kurt Lewin is widely titled the father of modern social psychology. Which OTHER field is he also credited with founding? (Amity recall) a Psychoanalysis b Action research c Psychophysics d Functionalism ✓ Answer: (b) Action research Kurt Lewin, founder of action research The concept What it is Action research is a cycle of planning, acting, observing and reflecting . How it works It is done with the people affected, not on them. Lewin founded it. Why the other options are wrong (a) Psychoanalysis Freud 's creation, not Lewin's. (c) Psychophysics Fechner 's field, not Lewin's. (d) Functionalism Belongs to James , Dewey and Angell , not Lewin. Which therapy focuses on "empty chair technique"? (IHBAS 2025) a CBT b Gestalt therapy c Psychoanalysis d DBT ✓ Answer: (b) Gestalt therapy Fritz Perls, Gestalt therapy The concept The technique In the empty chair , the client holds a dialogue with an absent person or a disowned part of the self. Whose it is It is Fritz Perls 's technique, a signature of Gestalt therapy . Exam trap Gestalt therapy is Perls's; it is not the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Kohler and Koffka. Why the other options are wrong (a) CBT Does not use the empty chair as a signature technique. (c) Psychoanalysis Freud's method, built on free association ; it does not use the empty chair as a signature technique. (d) DBT Linehan 's skills-based therapy, which does not use the empty chair as a signature technique. Which perspective in psychology emphasizes unconscious processes and early childhood experiences? (RML 2025) a Behavioral b Psychodynamic c Humanistic d Cognitive ✓ Answer: (b) Psychodynamic Freud's psychodynamic tradition The concept What it is The psychodynamic perspective, descended from Freud , explains behaviour by unconscious conflict . Why this one It also stresses early experience , the second cue in the stem; no other perspective here (behavioural, humanistic, cognitive) centres on both. Why the other options are wrong (a) Behavioral Stresses conditioning , not unconscious conflict or childhood. (c) Humanistic Stresses free will and growth, not unconscious conflict. (d) Cognitive Stresses internal mental processes , not unconscious conflict or childhood. Noogenic anxiety is described under: (IHBAS 2020) a Humanistic school b Gestalt school c Existential school d Psychodynamic school ✓ Answer: (c) Existential school Viktor Frankl, noogenic neurosis The concept What it is Frankl 's noogenic neurosis (and anxiety) arises from frustrated meaning. Why existential Meaning belongs to the spiritual dimension, which places the concept in existential psychology . Exam trap The humanistic school is a close neighbour, but the concept is Frankl's, not Maslow 's or Rogers 's. Why the other options are wrong (a) Humanistic school A close neighbour, but noogenic anxiety is Frankl's concept, not Maslow's or Rogers's. (b) Gestalt school The Gestalt school studied perception and organised wholes; it has no concept of anxiety from frustrated meaning. (d) Psychodynamic school Freud's school explains anxiety by unconscious conflict, not by frustrated meaning. The concept of "Dasein," which refers to human existence as "being-in-the-world," is primarily associated with which school of psychology? (Real PYQ 2025) a Behavioral psychology b Existential psychology c Cognitive psychology d Psychoanalytic psychology ✓ Answer: (b) Existential psychology Heidegger, Being and Time (1927) The concept The term Dasein is Heidegger 's term for human existence as being-in-the-world ( Being and Time , 1927). Into the clinic Binswanger and Boss made it clinical in Daseinsanalysis , a form of existential psychology. Why the other options are wrong (a) Behavioral psychology Does not use the term Dasein; it studies observable behaviour. (c) Cognitive psychology Does not use the term Dasein; it studies mental processes such as memory and thinking. (d) Psychoanalytic psychology Freud's school of the unconscious; it does not use the term Dasein. Viktor Frankl's concept of the "will to meaning," the fundamental motivational force in humans to find purpose in life, is central to which therapeutic school? (Real PYQ 2024) a Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) b Logotherapy c Existential-Humanistic Therapy d Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) ✓ Answer: (b) Logotherapy Viktor Frankl, logotherapy The concept What it is Logotherapy is Frankl 's own school, the "third Viennese school" (after Freud's and Adler's), and it rests on the will to meaning . Exam tip Existential-humanistic therapy is the broad family logotherapy belongs to; choose the most specific answer. Why the other options are wrong (a) Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) Ellis 's therapy, not Frankl's. (c) Existential-Humanistic Therapy The broad family logotherapy belongs to, so it is the tempting but less specific answer. (d) Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) Hayes 's therapy, not Frankl's. Savoring is a concept in Positive Psychology that involves: (IHBAS 2024) a Avoiding negative experiences b Enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences c Minimizing stress through relaxation d Reflecting on past traumas ✓ Answer: (b) Enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences Bryant and Veroff, savouring The concept What it is Bryant and Veroff defined savouring as attending to, appreciating and intensifying positive experiences. When it works It covers positive experiences past, present or anticipated. Key idea Savouring is to good events what coping is to bad ones. Why the other options are wrong (a) Avoiding negative experiences Describes avoidance; savouring moves towards good experiences rather than away from bad ones. (c) Minimizing stress through relaxation Describes relaxation; savouring is about enjoyment, not stress control. (d) Reflecting on past traumas Describes trauma work; savouring deals with positive, not painful, experiences. Who is a pioneer contributor to Cognitive Psychology? (Amity 2023) a Jean Piaget b Kohler c Chomsky d Kohlberg ✓ Answer: (a) Jean Piaget Jean Piaget, studies of thinking from the 1920s The concept Why Piaget Piaget studied the growth of thinking from the 1920s, long before the cognitive revolution . His status So he is treated as a forerunner of cognitive psychology. Why the other options are wrong (b) Kohler A Gestalt psychologist, not a cognitive pioneer. (c) Chomsky A linguist whose 1959 review fuelled the cognitive revolution; tempting, but that came decades after Piaget began. (d) Kohlberg A theorist of moral development , not a pioneer of cognitive psychology. "Third-wave CBT" includes all EXCEPT: (IHBAS 2025) a Acceptance and Commitment Therapy b Dialectical Behavior Therapy c Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy d Psychoanalysis ✓ Answer: (d) Psychoanalysis Third wave of CBT (acceptance and mindfulness therapies) The concept The third wave The third wave comprises acceptance and mindfulness-based therapies, many drawing on Buddhist practice. The earlier waves The first wave was behaviour therapy and the second was cognitive therapy . Why not this one Psychoanalysis is the first force in psychology and is not a wave of CBT at all. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Acceptance and Commitment Therapy True: ACT is a third-wave therapy ( Hayes ) built on acceptance and mindfulness. (b) Dialectical Behavior Therapy True: DBT is a third-wave therapy ( Linehan ) with core mindfulness skills. (c) Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy True: MBCT is a third-wave therapy that joins mindfulness practice to cognitive therapy. In Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), the "core mindfulness" skills are primarily derived from which tradition? (Real PYQ 2025) a Stoicism b Zen Buddhism c Psychoanalysis d Existentialism ✓ Answer: (b) Zen Buddhism Marsha Linehan, DBT The concept Where it comes from Marsha Linehan drew DBT's core mindfulness skills from Zen practice. The balance She balanced this acceptance against cognitive-behavioural change strategies. Why the other options are wrong (a) Stoicism Influenced Ellis 's REBT , not DBT's mindfulness module. (c) Psychoanalysis Unrelated to DBT's mindfulness module, which comes from Zen, not the analytic tradition. (d) Existentialism Also unrelated to DBT's mindfulness module, which is a Zen practice, not existential philosophy. What is the primary focus of Indian psychology? (RML 2025) a The application of Western psychological theories exclusively b The promotion of meditation without psychological context c The study of Indian folklore and mythology d The integration of Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts ✓ Answer: (d) The integration of Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts Indian psychology: Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta, Buddhism The concept What it is Indian psychology draws its concepts and methods from Samkhya , Yoga , Vedanta, Buddhism and related traditions. Why this one So its focus is integrating these philosophical traditions with psychological concepts. Why the other options are wrong (a) The application of Western psychological theories exclusively Describes imitative psychology in India, the opposite of Indian psychology. (b) The promotion of meditation without psychological context Indian psychology is not meditation stripped of theory; its practices sit inside a philosophical framework. (c) The study of Indian folklore and mythology Indian psychology is not mythology; its sources are philosophical schools. Who is regarded as the pioneer of psychology in India, establishing the first Indian psychological laboratory? (IHBAS 2024) a G. S. Rathi b S. K. Mangal c Girindrashekhar Bose d A. K. Singh ✓ Answer (as keyed): (c) Girindrashekhar Bose Girindrashekhar Bose, father of Indian psychoanalysis The concept Why Bose Bose , father of Indian psychoanalysis and Sengupta's Calcutta colleague, is the only pioneer listed. Key note Strictly, the first laboratory was set up by N. N. Sengupta at Calcutta in 1915, and Sengupta is not among the options. Exam tip If Sengupta does appear in the options, choose him for the first laboratory. Why the other options are wrong (a) G. S. Rathi Not credited with founding psychology in India or its first laboratory. (b) S. K. Mangal Mangal is a textbook author, not a pioneer. (d) A. K. Singh A. K. Singh is a textbook author, not a pioneer. Who is considered the father of Indian psychology? (RML 2025) a Narendra Nath Sen Gupta b Sudhir Kakar c Giriswar Misra d G. R. S. Rao ✓ Answer (as keyed): (d) G. R. S. Rao Indian Psychology movement; likely K. Ramakrishna Rao (2008 Handbook) The concept What the key means The key appears to intend a leader of the Indian Psychology movement , most plausibly K. Ramakrishna Rao . His work He co-edited the Handbook of Indian Psychology (2008). Other papers If the question meant modern scientific psychology in India, the answer would be (a) Sengupta . Why the other options are wrong (a) Narendra Nath Sen Gupta The pioneer of modern scientific psychology in India; right if the question meant that, but not the keyed answer. (b) Sudhir Kakar Kakar is a psychoanalyst, not the father of the field. (c) Giriswar Misra Misra is a contemporary scholar of indigenous psychology , not the father of the field. The concept of the three gunas comes mainly from which school of Indian philosophy, alongside the Bhagavad Gita? (NIMHANS 2026 recall) a Nyaya b Charvaka c Samkhya d Mimamsa ✓ Answer: (c) Samkhya Samkhya school, with the Bhagavad Gita The concept The source In Samkhya , prakriti is composed of three gunas: sattva, rajas and tamas. The Gita The Gita builds its psychology of personality on these three gunas . Why the other options are wrong (a) Nyaya The school of logic , not of the gunas. (b) Charvaka The school of materialism , not of the gunas. (d) Mimamsa The school of Vedic ritual and duty , not of the gunas. In Samkhya dualism, the principle of pure consciousness, the passive witness, is Purusha. The three gunas belong to its counterpart, which is: (Amity recall) a Atman b Prakriti c Brahman d Ahamkara ✓ Answer: (b) Prakriti Samkhya dualism: Purusha and Prakriti The concept What it is Prakriti , primordial matter, is made of the three gunas . The pair It is the counterpart of Purusha , pure consciousness, in Samkhya dualism. Why the other options are wrong (a) Atman A Vedantic term for the self, not Purusha's counterpart. (c) Brahman A Vedantic term for ultimate reality , not Purusha's counterpart. (d) Ahamkara One of prakriti's products , not its counterpart. Bavisha lost her job. Since then she is stressed, has stopped eating properly and cannot get herself to do anything. According to yogic philosophy, the main issue she is dealing with is: (NIMHANS 2026 recall) a Yama alone b Tamas alone c Both yama and tamas d Rajas alone ✓ Answer: (b) Tamas alone Theory of the three gunas: tamas The concept The signs Withdrawal, loss of appetite and inability to act are the signature of tamas . What tamas is Tamas is the guna of inertia and dullness . The contrast Rajas would show as restless over-activity. Why the other options are wrong (a) Yama alone The first limb of yoga (ethical restraints), not a mental state, so it cannot describe her condition. (c) Both yama and tamas Fails because yama is an ethical limb of yoga, not a mental state, so only tamas fits. (d) Rajas alone Would show as restless over-activity, the opposite of her withdrawal and inertia. In Indian psychology, the 'inner instrument' (antahkarana) classically has four functions. Which one is the EGO or 'I-maker'? (Amity recall) a Manas b Buddhi c Ahamkara d Chitta ✓ Answer: (c) Ahamkara Antahkarana model: ahamkara, the I-maker The concept What it is Ahamkara refers experience to a separate "I", which is why it is the ego or I-maker. The four The antahkarana has four functions: manas, buddhi, ahamkara and chitta. Why the other options are wrong (a) Manas The sensory mind that doubts and deliberates, not the ego. (b) Buddhi The intellect that decides, not the ego. (d) Chitta The store of memory impressions , not the ego. According to Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, the primary goal of yoga is: (JEMAS 2025) a Physical fitness b Control of the mind (citta vritti nirodha) and liberation (kaivalya) c Cognitive enhancement d Emotional regulation only ✓ Answer: (b) Control of the mind and liberation Patanjali, Yoga Sutra 1.2 The concept The definition Sutra 1.2 defines yoga as the stilling of the mind's fluctuations ( citta vritti nirodha ). The aim Its goal is kaivalya , consciousness resting in itself. Why the other options are wrong (a) Physical fitness May be a by-product of practice, but it is not the goal. (c) Cognitive enhancement Sharper cognition may be a by-product, but it is not the goal. (d) Emotional regulation only Calmer emotions may be a by-product, but they are not the goal, and "only" makes it narrower still. Which is the correct order of the last four of Patanjali's eight limbs? (NIMHANS 2026 recall) a Dharana, pratyahara, dhyana, samadhi b Pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi c Pratyahara, dhyana, dharana, samadhi d Dhyana, dharana, pratyahara, samadhi ✓ Answer: (b) Pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi Patanjali's eight limbs, last four in order The concept First steps The senses must first be withdrawn ( pratyahara ) before attention can be fixed ( dharana ). Deepening Fixed attention becomes an unbroken flow ( dhyana ), and the flow becomes absorption ( samadhi ). Why the other options are wrong (a) Dharana, pratyahara, dhyana, samadhi Puts withdrawal after concentration; the senses must be withdrawn before attention can be fixed. (c) Pratyahara, dhyana, dharana, samadhi Swaps concentration and meditation: attention must be fixed (dharana) before it can flow (dhyana). (d) Dhyana, dharana, pratyahara, samadhi Swaps concentration and meditation and also puts withdrawal after concentration. In the Pancha Kosha model, the five sheaths of the self run from gross to subtle. The OUTERMOST sheath, the physical body sustained by food, is: (Amity recall) a Annamaya kosha b Pranamaya kosha c Manomaya kosha d Anandamaya kosha ✓ Answer: (a) Annamaya kosha Pancha Kosha model, Taittiriya Upanishad The concept The word Anna means food, so annamaya kosha , the food sheath, is the gross body. The order From outer to inner: annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya , anandamaya. Why the other options are wrong (b) Pranamaya kosha The vital sheath of breath, one layer inside the food sheath. (c) Manomaya kosha The mental sheath of perception and emotion, deeper than the body. (d) Anandamaya kosha The innermost bliss sheath , the opposite end of the series. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The empty chair technique belongs to Gestalt therapy , developed by Fritz Perls with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman ( Gestalt Therapy , 1951), which stresses here-and-now awareness; it is not the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Kohler and Koffka. asked 7 times Patanjali's eight limbs (sutra 2.29), in order: yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana (concentration on one point), dhyana (unbroken flow of meditation), samadhi (absorption). Karma and jnana are not limbs. asked 4 times Tamas is the guna of inertia, lethargy, darkness, dullness and ignorance; a person who has stopped eating properly, withdrawn and cannot get herself to act shows tamas alone. asked 4 times Narendra Nath Sengupta set up India's first psychology laboratory (1915) and first Department of Psychology (1916) at the University of Calcutta, and is the father of modern psychology in India. Keys naming Bose or Uma Chaudhuri for the first laboratory are wrong. asked 5 times Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis, the first force; the psychodynamic perspective explains behaviour, and many disorders, by unconscious urges and conflict and by early childhood experience. asked 4 times Indian psychology integrates Indian philosophical and contemplative traditions with psychological concepts; it is holistic and spiritual, includes family and community, and treats mental health by combining traditional practices with modern therapy. asked 3 times Humanistic psychology (Maslow, Rogers) is the third force , after psychoanalysis (first) and behaviourism (second); transpersonal psychology is the fourth force. asked 5 times Humanistic psychology emphasises free will, personal growth , an innate tendency to grow and reaching one's full potential; disorder comes from blocked growth, not from reinforcement or unconscious conflict. asked 4 times The three gunas are sattva, rajas and tamas, the strands of prakriti (not of purusha); the doctrine comes mainly from Samkhya , with the Bhagavad Gita . Ahimsa, vata and prakriti are not gunas. asked 4 times John B. Watson founded behaviourism with "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" (1913): psychology is the science of observable behaviour, its goal prediction and control (given the stimulus, predict the response), learned through stimulus-response conditioning. asked 4 times Viktor Frankl founded logotherapy on the will to meaning ; frustrated meaning produces an existential vacuum and noogenic neurosis, ideas of the existential school. asked 3 times Positive psychology was founded by Martin Seligman (APA president for 1998; American Psychologist special issue with Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, 2000); its interventions build strengths such as hope, and savouring means enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences. asked 3 times Gestalt psychology : the whole is different from (popularly, greater than) the sum of its parts. asked 3 times In Samkhya (Kapila), purusha is pure, passive, unchanging consciousness, and prakriti is active, ever-changing primordial matter, made of the three gunas and evolving into the five great elements. asked 3 times The five koshas ( Taittiriya Upanishad ), outer to inner: annamaya (food body, outermost), pranamaya (vital), manomaya (mind and senses: perception), vijnanamaya (intellect), anandamaya (bliss). The subtle body (linga sharira) is the three middle sheaths. asked 3 times Existential psychology confronts death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness, holds that meaning is never fixed and must be continually created, and uses Heidegger's Dasein (being-in-the-world, 1927); uncovering unconscious desires is a psychoanalytic aim. asked 3 times Kurt Lewin : B = f(P, E); the life space is the person plus the psychological environment; he founded action research and group dynamics and is the father of modern social psychology. asked 2 times Edward Chace Tolman proposed the cognitive map ("Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men", 1948) and demonstrated latent learning (Tolman and Honzik, 1930). asked 2 times Ahamkara is the I-maker (ego) of the antahkarana; manas is the sensory mind, buddhi the intellect, chitta the memory store. The Gita 's three elements of mind are manas, buddhi and ahamkara. asked 2 times Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology with his 1912 paper on the phi phenomenon, with Kohler and Koffka; Gestalt is the school that contributed most to the study of perception. asked 2 times Cognitive psychology studies internal mental processes (attention, memory, problem solving) with the mind-as-information-processor metaphor; Ulric Neisser's Cognitive Psychology (1967) named it. asked 2 times Covert behaviour (thoughts, subvocal speech) is measurable but not directly observable; the "mental processes" in the definition of psychology are internal, covert processes. asked 2 times Sattva = harmony, balance, clarity; rajas = restlessness, passion, desire and over-activity. asked 2 times Girindrasekhar Bose founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (Calcutta, 1922), is the father of psychoanalysis in India, and proposed the theory of opposite wishes. asked 2 times The Indian Psychology movement : Matthijs Cornelissen led it and founded the Indian Psychology Institute (Pondicherry); the Handbook of Indian Psychology (Rao, Paranjpe and Dalal) appeared in 2008; the Pondicherry Manifesto dates from 2002. asked 2 times Patanjali's goal of yoga is chitta-vritti-nirodha, the stilling of the mind's fluctuations (sutra 1.2), leading to liberation (kaivalya). asked once Atman is the true self, eternal pure consciousness, not the body, a passing state of mind or a collective unconscious. asked once Jean Piaget , who studied the growth of thinking from the 1920s (genetic epistemology), is a pioneer contributor to cognitive psychology. asked once Early social learning theory is Dollard and Miller (1950); later social learning theory is Bandura and Walters (1963); radical behaviourism is Skinner's; self-actualisation is Maslow's. asked once The developmental perspective studies how people change as they mature across the lifespan. asked once

distinguish sensation from perception and explain transduction, sensory coding and sensory adaptation. 3.2 Thresholds: how weak a stimulus, how small a difference : define the absolute threshold and the difference threshold (JND) and explain why both are defined as 50 percent points. 3.3 The psychophysical laws: Weber, Fechner and Stevens : state, apply and criticise Weber's law, Fechner's law and Stevens' power law. 3.4 The classical psychophysical methods : describe the methods of limits, constant stimuli and adjustment, their errors and controls, and modern staircase methods. 3.5 Signal detection theory : separate sensitivity (d′) from the response criterion, read a 2 by 2 outcome table and an ROC curve, and apply the theory to real decisions. 3.6 Vision I: light, the eye and the two receptor systems : trace light through the eye and contrast rods with cones, dark adaptation, the Purkinje shift, acuity and lateral inhibition. 3.7 Vision II: colour : explain colour mixing, the trichromatic and opponent-process theories, their dual-process resolution and the forms of colour blindness. 3.8 Hearing : relate the dimensions of sound to pitch, loudness and timbre, follow sound through the ear, and compare the theories of pitch, sound localisation and the types of hearing loss. 3.9 The chemical senses: taste and smell : describe the five basic tastes, papillae and taste buds, the olfactory system, pheromones and flavour. 3.10 The skin senses and pain : describe touch, pressure and temperature, and explain pain through gate control theory, endorphins and phantom limbs. 3.11 The body senses: kinesthesis and balance : distinguish kinesthesis from the vestibular sense and the roles of the semicircular canals and otolith organs. 3.12 Senses in concert and senses deprived : explain sensory interaction, synaesthesia and the effects of sensory deprivation. Weightage. 44 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (5.4%) test this chapter, 16 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 12 sections is High yield. On the morning of 22 October 1850, a forty-nine-year-old former professor of physics lay in bed in Leipzig and worked out how to measure the mind. His name was Gustav Theodor Fechner, and for most of the previous decade he had been too ill to work at all. In the late 1830s Fechner had been studying afterimages, the ghostly colours that linger in your vision after you stare at a bright light, and he had used his own eyes as the instrument, gazing at the sun through coloured glass. The experiments damaged his eyes. A long breakdown followed: he could not bear light, could hardly eat, and could not read. He gave up his chair of physics and spent about three years withdrawn from the world, much of the time in darkened rooms. When he recovered, Fechner turned to an old philosophical puzzle: how are mind and body related? The great philosopher Immanuel Kant had argued that psychology could never become a true natural science, because mental events cannot be measured, and without measurement there is no mathematics and no science. Fechner's insight that October morning was a way around Kant. You cannot hold a ruler against a sensation. But you can measure the physical stimulus that produces it, and you can find out how much that stimulus must change before a person notices any difference at all. If every just-noticeable step in sensation is treated as one unit, sensation can be counted, and the relation between the physical world and the mental world can be written as an equation. Fechner spent the next decade testing the idea, lifting weights, comparing lights and judging distances, thousands of judgements at a time. He found that his Leipzig colleague Ernst Heinrich Weber had already discovered the key regularity, and he generously named it Weber's law. In 1860 Fechner published Elemente der Psychophysik ( Elements of Psychophysics ), and with it founded a new science. Nineteen years before Wilhelm Wundt opened his laboratory, Fechner had shown that the mind could be measured. Psychophysicists still celebrate 22 October as Fechner Day. This chapter explores the territory Fechner opened. It asks how the sense organs turn energy into experience, how weak a stimulus can be before you miss it, how small a change you can notice, and why a "threshold" turns out to be a decision as much as a sensation. It then walks through each sense in turn: vision, hearing, taste, smell, touch, temperature, pain, body position and balance. Keep Fechner's damaged eyes in mind. At the end of the chapter you will see that the afterimages that injured him are now well understood, and that his famous law has been both honoured and revised. 3.1 Sensation and perception: from energy to experience Medium yield · 10 Qs Look up from this page for a moment. You see a room full of objects, each with a colour, a shape and a place. You probably hear something too: a fan, traffic, a voice in the next room. It all seems effortless and immediate, as if the world simply pours into your head. It does not. What actually reaches you is a shower of physical energy (photons striking the back of your eyes, pressure waves in the air, molecules drifting into your nose), and everything you experience is built by your nervous system out of that raw material. This section introduces the first steps of that construction. Sensation versus perception Psychologists traditionally divide the process into two stages. sensation is the process by which sense organs detect physical energy from the environment and convert it into neural signals. perception is the process by which the brain organises and interprets those signals so that they become meaningful objects and events. Think of a batsman at the crease. Light reflected from the ball forms an image on his retinas, and receptors there fire: that is sensation. Recognising, in a fraction of a second, that the ball is a googly spinning the other way: that is perception. The boundary between the two is not sharp, and many modern researchers treat them as one continuous process. But the distinction is useful, and examiners like it, because it tells you where an error happens. Consider an optical illusion such as the Muller-Lyer figure, in which two lines of identical length look unequal because one carries outward-pointing fins and the other inward-pointing fins. Your receptors register the two lines accurately; the image of each line on your retina really is the same length. The error arises later, when the brain interprets the lines in the light of the fins. Optical illusions are therefore distortions of perception, not of sensation (Chapter 4 explains why the brain makes such errors). The idea that experience can be broken into sensory building blocks has a long history. The structuralists, led in America by Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927), treated sensations as the elements of consciousness and hoped to catalogue them the way chemists catalogue elements, a "periodic table" of the elements of sensation; Titchener counted more than 44,000 distinguishable sensation qualities, most of them visual or auditory. For Titchener, a perception was a complex of sensory and imaginal elements: sensations, plus the images that past experience attaches to them, with meaning supplied by this context (Chapter 1 tells the full story of structuralism). A modern descendant of this idea treats perception as inference. Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894), whose work runs through this chapter, argued in the 1860s that perception involves unconscious inference: the brain draws conclusions about the world from incomplete sensory evidence, using past experience. Today this view is formalised in the Bayesian approach to perception , named after the eighteenth-century mathematician Thomas Bayes. According to it, every perceptual experience combines two ingredients: prior beliefs (what you already expect to be out there, learned from experience) and sensory evidence (what the receptors are reporting now). When the evidence is clear, it dominates; when it is weak or ambiguous, the prior carries more weight. Walking down a dimly lit lane at night, you may "see" a dog lying by a gate when it is really a sack of cement, because dogs by gates are common (a strong prior) and the light is poor (weak evidence). Genes, culture and emotional states can all shape a person's priors, but the Bayesian formula itself has just those two inputs: prior beliefs and sensory evidence. Exam trap "Optical illusions result from distortion in ..." The answer is perception , not sensation: the receptors register the stimulus correctly, and the error is in interpretation. "Translation" and "adaptation" are bait. Likewise, "according to the Bayesian approach, perception is influenced by ..." has the answer prior beliefs and sensory evidence ; options naming only genes, culture or emotions describe things that can shape priors, not the approach itself. Receptors and transduction Every sense begins with a receptor , a specialised cell (or the specialised ending of a neuron) that responds to one particular form of energy. The receptor's job is transduction : the conversion of physical energy into the electrical and chemical language of the nervous system. Light, sound and molecules cannot travel along nerves; only neural signals can. So in the eye, light changes the shape of a pigment molecule, which changes the receptor's electrical state; in the ear, the bending of tiny hairs opens ion channels; in the nose, an odour molecule binds to a receptor protein. Each is a different trick for the same task. Table 3.1 groups the receptors by the energy they transduce. Table 3.1 Receptors classified by the energy they transduce. Receptor class Energy detected Examples Sense Photoreceptors Light (electromagnetic) Rods and cones of the retina Vision Mechanoreceptors Mechanical bending, pressure, stretch Hair cells of the cochlea and vestibular organs; skin corpuscles; muscle spindles Hearing, balance, touch, kinesthesis Chemoreceptors Dissolved or airborne molecules Taste receptor cells; olfactory receptor neurons Taste, smell Thermoreceptors Temperature change Warm and cold free nerve endings Temperature Nociceptors Actual or threatened tissue damage Free nerve endings in skin, muscle and organs Pain Receptors can also be classified by where their information comes from. The British physiologist Charles Scott Sherrington (1857 to 1952), in The Integrative Action of the Nervous System (1906), distinguished exteroceptors , which report on the outside world (eyes, ears, skin), interoceptors , which report on the internal organs (a full bladder, a churning stomach), and proprioceptors , which report on the position and movement of the body itself (Section 3.11). Once a receptor has transduced its stimulus, the signal travels toward the central nervous system along afferent (sensory, incoming) nerve fibres. Commands travel outward to muscles and glands along efferent (motor, outgoing) fibres. The simplest complete loop, from receptor through afferent fibre to the spinal cord and back out along an efferent fibre to a muscle, is the reflex arc: the knee jerk is the textbook example. (The philosopher-psychologist John Dewey famously criticised the reflex arc as a model of behaviour in 1896; Chapter 1 explains why.) Sensory coding: specific nerve energies and labelled lines Here is a puzzle that troubled nineteenth-century physiologists. Every sensory nerve carries the same kind of signal: brief electrical impulses called action potentials. An impulse from the eye looks exactly like an impulse from the ear. So how does the brain know whether a message means "red" or "middle C" or "sour"? The German physiologist Johannes Peter Muller (1801 to 1858) gave the classic answer in his Handbook of Human Physiology (1833 to 1840). His doctrine of specific nerve energies states that the quality of a sensation depends on which nerve is stimulated, not on what stimulates it. Each sensory nerve, however it is excited, produces its own characteristic sensation. You can test this yourself. Close your eyes and press very gently on the outer corner of one eyelid: you will see a spot of light (a phosphene), although no light has entered the eye. The pressure excited the optic nerve's receptors, and the optic nerve can only "speak" light. A hard blow to the back of the head makes people "see stars" for the same reason. Muller drew a startling conclusion: we are never directly aware of objects in the world, only of the activity of our own nerves. Helmholtz, Muller's student, later extended the idea within a single sense, proposing that different fibres in the eye and ear carry different colours and pitches (an idea you will meet again in his theories of colour and hearing). Modern neuroscience keeps the core of Muller's insight under the name labelled-line coding : the quality of a sensation is signalled by which neurons are active, because each pathway is wired to a particular brain region, as if each line carried a label. Activity in the visual pathway to the occipital lobe is experienced as sight; activity in the auditory pathway to the temporal lobe is experienced as sound. Within a sense, however, quality is often coded by the pattern of activity across many receptor types rather than by single labelled lines. This across-fibre pattern coding is especially important in taste and smell, where each receptor type responds to many chemicals and a particular flavour or odour corresponds to a particular profile of activity across the whole population. What about intensity? A dim light and a bright light, a whisper and a shout, must also be told apart. Here a basic fact of neurophysiology matters. An action potential obeys the all-or-none law: once a neuron's threshold is reached, the impulse fires at full, constant size and travels along the axon without shrinking, and a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger impulse. A stimulus too weak to reach threshold produces no action potential at all, not a "miniature" one (only small graded changes in voltage that fade away). Intensity therefore cannot be coded by the size of impulses. It is coded instead by rate coding (stronger stimuli make each neuron fire more often) and by recruitment (stronger stimuli activate more neurons, including less sensitive ones). Note one curiosity: signals can also be carried by a decrease in activity. The rods and cones of your retina are most active in darkness, and light actually reduces their activity (Pinel and Barnes's textbook makes this point with some relish). A final piece of wiring is worth knowing for general psychology. Before reaching the cerebral cortex, almost every sensory pathway relays through the thalamus, the brain's sensory switching station: vision through its lateral geniculate nucleus, hearing through its medial geniculate nucleus, and touch, pain and taste through its ventral posterior nuclei. Smell is the exception: olfactory signals run from the olfactory bulb straight to the olfactory cortex and the amygdala without a thalamic relay on the way (Section 3.9). The details belong to the Physiological Psychology book. Explaining experience and behaviour through the workings of the brain and nervous system in this way is the neurobiological (biological) approach to psychology, whose main premise is that behaviour is governed by the brain and nervous system. It differs from the psychophysical approach that fills most of this chapter, which studies the lawful relation between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce without needing to know what the neurons are doing (Chapter 2 compares the approaches). Exam trap The doctrine of specific nerve energies belongs to Johannes Muller , not Helmholtz (Helmholtz extended it) and not Fechner. "The principal sensory relay to the cortex for every sense except smell" is the thalamus ; the hypothalamus regulates drives such as hunger and temperature, the medulla controls breathing and heart rate, the corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, the basal ganglia help to control movement, and the hippocampus serves memory. The lateral geniculate nucleus is visual; the medial geniculate nucleus is auditory ("M for music"). Sensory adaptation When you put on a wristwatch in the morning you feel it on your skin. Ten minutes later you do not, although it is still pressing on exactly the same spot. When you walk into a home where a garland of Mysuru jasmine hangs by the door, the scent is striking; the family who have been sitting there all evening hardly notice it. This is sensory adaptation : a decline in sensitivity (and in receptor response) to a stimulus that remains constant. Adaptation is built into the receptors and the early stages of each sensory pathway, and it is automatic. The English philosopher John Locke (1632 to 1704) described a neat demonstration in 1690. Put one hand in a bowl of hot water and the other in a bowl of cold water for a minute, then plunge both into a bowl of lukewarm water. The same lukewarm water feels cool to the first hand and warm to the second. Each hand has adapted to its starting temperature, so each judges the new water relative to that adapted level. Why should the senses be designed to fade out unchanging stimulation? Because change is what usually matters. A constant stimulus (the pressure of your clothes, the hum of a refrigerator) rarely carries new information, whereas a change (a touch on the shoulder, a sudden silence) may signal something important. Adaptation frees the senses to respond to change. Vision is the dramatic case: if an image is held perfectly still on the retina, it fades from view within seconds, and your eyes avoid this only by moving constantly (Section 3.6). Exam trap Do not confuse sensory adaptation with habituation . Adaptation is a reduced response of the sensory system itself to a constant stimulus. Habituation is a learned decrease in behavioural response to a stimulus that is repeated and proves unimportant (you stop jumping at the ticking clock), and it can be reversed instantly if the stimulus changes (dishabituation). Habituation is the simplest form of learning and is covered in Chapter 6. Adaptation to light and dark is called visual adaptation , not "visual accommodation" (accommodation is the focusing of the lens, Section 3.6). 3.2 Thresholds: how weak a stimulus, how small a difference Lower yield · 2 Qs Fechner's new science, psychophysics , is the study of the quantitative relationship between the physical properties of stimuli and the sensations they produce. It asks two basic kinds of question. The first is about detection: what is the weakest stimulus a person can detect? The second is about discrimination: what is the smallest change in a stimulus a person can notice? The answers are called thresholds. The absolute threshold The absolute threshold is the minimum intensity of a stimulus that a person can detect. The older term for a threshold is limen (Latin for "threshold"), which survives in two words you should know. A stimulus below the absolute threshold is subliminal (below the limen); one above it is supraliminal . At first sight the absolute threshold sounds like a simple switch: below a certain intensity you detect nothing, above it you always detect the stimulus. Experiments show that no such switch exists. If you present a faint tone many times at each of several intensities, there is no single intensity at which "never heard" suddenly becomes "always heard". Instead, the percentage of "yes, I heard it" responses climbs gradually, tracing an S-shaped curve called the psychometric function (Figure 3.1). Why the gradual climb? Because the nervous system is never silent. Neurons fire spontaneously, attention wanders, receptors vary slightly from moment to moment, and even the stimulus itself fluctuates (a very dim light delivers a variable number of light particles from one flash to the next). So the same faint tone is sometimes detected and sometimes missed. Psychophysicists therefore define the absolute threshold statistically: it is the stimulus intensity that is detected on 50 percent of the trials on which it is presented. Not 100 percent, and not "the first time it is noticed", but half the time. 0 25 50 75 100 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 Stimulus intensity (arbitrary units) Percentage of yes responses 50 percent yes = absolute threshold Real observer (ogive) Fixed threshold (step) Observed data Figure 3.1 The psychometric function for detection. Eugene Galanter (1962) gave a set of everyday approximations that appear in almost every introductory text (Table 3.2). They are rough, but they make the point that our senses, at their best, are astonishingly sensitive. Table 3.2 Approximate absolute thresholds for five senses (after Galanter, 1962). Sense Approximate absolute threshold Vision A candle flame seen from about 48 km (30 miles) on a dark, clear night Hearing The tick of a watch from about 6 metres (20 feet) under very quiet conditions Taste One teaspoon of sugar dissolved in about 7.5 litres (two gallons) of water Smell One drop of perfume diffused through a six-room apartment Touch The wing of a bee falling on your cheek from a height of 1 centimetre Key study: How few particles of light can you see? (Hecht, Shlaer and Pirenne, 1942) Question. Light comes in tiny packets called quanta (photons). What is the smallest number of quanta a fully dark-adapted human can detect? Method. Selig Hecht , Simon Shlaer and Maurice Pirenne, working in New York, flashed a very brief spot of blue-green light (wavelength 510 nanometres, close to the peak sensitivity of the rods) onto a rod-rich region of the retina about 20 degrees from the centre of gaze. Observers, including the authors themselves, sat in darkness and reported whether they had seen each flash. Result. At threshold, the flash delivered only about 54 to 148 quanta to the front of the eye. After allowing for light lost in the eye's media and for light that passed through the retina unabsorbed, they calculated that only about 5 to 14 quanta were actually absorbed by rods. Spread across hundreds of rods, this meant that no single rod could have absorbed more than one quantum. Conclusion. A single rod responds to a single quantum of light, and the coincidence of a handful of such events produces the experience of seeing. The human eye at threshold works close to the limit set by physics. Why it matters here. Because the number of quanta in a dim flash fluctuates randomly from flash to flash, some of the variability in "seeing" a threshold flash lies in the light itself. The threshold is probabilistic by its very nature. The difference threshold and the JND Detection is only half of psychophysics. Much of the time we need to tell whether something has changed: whether the dal needs more salt, whether the music has been turned up, whether one mango is heavier than another. The difference threshold (or difference limen) is the smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can detect 50 percent of the time. The amount of change at that threshold is called the just noticeable difference (JND). The terms are effectively interchangeable in examinations: the difference threshold is the JND. Difference thresholds are measured by comparing a fixed standard stimulus with a variable comparison stimulus . If you hold a 100-gram standard weight in one hand and a series of comparison weights in the other, you might find that you can tell 102 grams from 100 grams half the time; the JND at that standard is then 2 grams. Along the way you will find a comparison value that feels exactly equal to the standard; this is the point of subjective equality (PSE), and it need not coincide with the true physical equality point. (A systematic gap between the PSE and the standard is called a constant error.) Ernst Heinrich Weber measured one especially elegant kind of difference threshold on the skin. Touch the skin with the two points of a pair of compasses. If the points are far apart, you feel two touches; bring them closer and, at some separation, the two touches merge into one. The smallest separation at which two points are felt as two is the two-point threshold . Weber found that it varies enormously across the body, from about 2 millimetres on the fingertips and lips to several centimetres on the back and thigh (Section 3.10 explains why). It was while measuring such thresholds, and the JNDs for lifted weights, that Weber noticed the regularity that bears his name. Exam trap "The minimum level of a stimulus that can be detected" is the absolute threshold ; "the smallest change that can be detected" is the difference threshold (JND). "Sensory adaptation point" and "perceptual boundary" are invented distractors, and so is "signal detection of response". A question defining "the point at which a stimulus is strong enough to trigger a response only 50 percent of the time" wants threshold ; response bias is a signal detection term for a person's readiness to say "yes" (Section 3.5), and the phi phenomenon is the illusion of movement produced by lights flashing in sequence, described by Max Wertheimer in 1912 (Chapter 4). 3.3 The psychophysical laws: Weber, Fechner and Stevens Lower yield · 3 Qs Thresholds tell us where sensation begins and how finely it can be graded. The next question is more ambitious: is there a general law relating the size of a stimulus to the size of the sensation it produces? Three answers have been proposed, by Weber, Fechner and Stevens. Each was a real advance, each captures something true, and each fails somewhere. Learn them as a sequence, because each one grew out of the one before. Weber's law: the JND is a constant fraction Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795 to 1878) was a professor of anatomy and physiology at Leipzig. In studies of touch and the muscle sense published in 1834 ( De Tactu ) and 1846, he asked people to compare lifted weights. He noticed, among other things, that discrimination was finer when people actively lifted the weights than when the weights simply rested on a passive hand. His enduring discovery, however, was this: the JND is not a fixed amount. With a light standard weight, a small extra amount is noticed; with a heavy standard, a much larger amount is needed. What stays constant is the ratio of the JND to the standard. In symbols, Weber's law is ΔI / I = k where I is the intensity of the standard stimulus, ΔI (read "delta I") is the increase needed to produce a just noticeable difference, and k is a constant for that sensory dimension, called the Weber fraction (or Weber's constant). A small Weber fraction means fine discrimination; a large one means coarse discrimination. A worked example shows how the law works. Suppose the Weber fraction for lifted weights is about 0.02 (one-fiftieth). Then with a 500-gram standard, the JND is 0.02 × 500 = 10 grams: you will just notice the difference between 500 and 510 grams. With a 5-kilogram standard, the JND is 0.02 × 5,000 = 100 grams. Ten grams added to the heavier load would go completely unnoticed. Or take your morning chai. If a cup sweetened with two teaspoons of sugar needs roughly an extra half teaspoon before anyone notices it is sweeter, then a cup with four teaspoons needs roughly an extra whole teaspoon. The absolute amount needed doubles; the proportion stays the same. The everyday consequences are everywhere. A single candle transforms a dark room but is invisible in sunlight. A shopkeeper knows that a fifty-rupee discount feels generous on a two-hundred-rupee item and trivial on a fifty-thousand-rupee phone. In each case what we notice is proportional change, not absolute change. Table 3.3 gives approximate Weber fractions for several dimensions. Dimension Approximate Weber fraction Change needed on a standard of 100 units Pitch (frequency of a middle tone) About 0.003 (about 1/333) About 0.3 Electric shock About 0.01 About 1 Heaviness of lifted weights About 0.02 (1/50) About 2 Brightness of light About 0.02 to 0.08 About 2 to 8 Loudness (sound intensity) About 0.05 to 0.1 About 5 to 10 Pressure on the skin About 0.14 (1/7) About 14 Taste (salt) and smell About 0.08 to 0.3 About 8 to 30 Where does Weber's law fail? It holds well across the middle range of intensities for most senses, but it breaks down at the extremes. Near the absolute threshold, the Weber fraction rises sharply: when a stimulus is barely detectable, a proportionally much larger change is needed before any difference is noticed. It can also drift at very high intensities, and for pure tones the fraction for loudness declines slowly as intensity increases, a small but systematic departure known as the "near miss" to Weber's law. Weber's law is best regarded as an excellent approximation over the range in which we usually live. Fechner's law: sensation grows with the logarithm of the stimulus Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801 to 1887) took Weber's finding and built it into a law of sensation itself. Weber's law tells you how big a JND is; it says nothing about how strong a sensation is. Fechner's bridge was a single bold assumption: every JND represents the same increase in sensation, no matter where on the scale it occurs . The step from 100 to 102 grams and the step from 1,000 to 1,020 grams are both one JND, so, Fechner assumed, both add one equal unit to the felt heaviness. With that assumption, the strength of any sensation can be measured simply by counting how many JNDs it lies above the absolute threshold. Now combine this with Weber's law. Start at the threshold and climb one JND at a time. Because each JND is a constant fraction of the current intensity, the physical intensities at successive JNDs form a geometric series (each one multiplied by the same factor), while the sensation steps form an arithmetic series (1, 2, 3, 4 units). A quantity that rises arithmetically while another rises geometrically is a logarithm. The result is Fechner's law : S = k log I where S is the magnitude of the sensation, I is the physical intensity (strictly, measured in multiples of the threshold intensity) and k is a constant that depends on the sense. Because it rests on Weber's law, it is often called the Weber-Fechner law. A worked example makes the logarithm concrete. Picture a dark room on Diwali night. Light one diya and the room is transformed. Light a second and the room gets noticeably brighter. To get the same sized step again, Fechner's law says you will need not three diyas but four; then eight; then sixteen; then thirty-two. Each doubling of the physical light adds roughly one equal step of brightness. By the time sixty-four diyas are burning, adding one more makes no visible difference at all. Scales of this kind are familiar from science and engineering: the astronomers' magnitude scale for the brightness of stars (much older than Fechner) and the decibel scale for sound (introduced by telephone engineers in the 1920s; Section 3.8) are both logarithmic, and both fit how our senses actually grade intensity. Fechner's achievement went beyond the equation. In the Elemente of 1860 he coined the word psychophysics, set out the experimental methods for measuring thresholds (Section 3.4), and distinguished "outer psychophysics" (the relation between the stimulus and sensation, which he could study) from "inner psychophysics" (the relation between brain activity and sensation, which he could not). For founding the field he is called the father of psychophysics, and his work showed the young science of psychology that mental events could be measured. One reader who took that lesson to heart was Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909), who came across a second-hand copy of the Elemente and set out to measure memory with the same rigour (Chapter 7). Fechner's method of scaling sensation is called indirect scaling , because it measures sensation indirectly, through discrimination (counting JNDs), rather than by asking people how strong a sensation feels. Where does Fechner's law fail? Its weak point is its founding assumption. There is no direct evidence that all JNDs are subjectively equal, and when people are asked to judge sensory magnitudes directly, their judgements often do not follow a logarithmic curve. For some dimensions, such as electric shock, sensation grows faster than intensity, which no logarithmic law can describe. That is where Stevens enters the story. Stevens' power law: ask people directly Stanley Smith Stevens (1906 to 1973) of Harvard University argued that there was no need to count JNDs: people can judge the magnitude of their sensations directly, and their judgements are lawful. His main method, magnitude estimation , works like this. The experimenter presents a standard stimulus (called the modulus) and assigns it a number, say 10. The observer is then given other stimuli and asked to assign each a number proportional to how intense it seems: a light that looks twice as bright as the standard gets 20; one that looks half as bright gets 5. Across hundreds of studies, Stevens found that the results for every continuum he tested were described by a power function. In 1957 he set out what is now called Stevens' power law : S = k I n where S is the judged magnitude of the sensation, I is the physical intensity, k is a scaling constant and the exponent n is characteristic of each sensory continuum. Taking logarithms of both sides gives log S = log k + n log I : plotted on log-log axes, every power function becomes a straight line whose slope is the exponent. That is how exponents are measured in practice. The exponent tells you how sensation grows. When n is less than 1, sensation grows more slowly than intensity, a pattern called response compression : brightness has an exponent of about 0.33, so to double the apparent brightness of a light you must increase its physical intensity about eightfold (because 2 raised to the power 1/0.33 is 8). When n equals 1, sensation grows in proportion to intensity, as it does for the apparent length of a line. When n is greater than 1, sensation grows faster than intensity, a pattern called response expansion : electric shock has an exponent of about 3.5, so doubling the current makes the shock feel roughly eleven times as intense (2 raised to the power 3.5 is about 11). Continuum Exponent (n) Type of growth Brightness (large target, dark-adapted eye) 0.33 Compression Smell (coffee odour) 0.55 Compression Loudness (3,000 Hz tone, measured as sound pressure) 0.67 Compression Apparent length of a line 1.0 Proportional Taste (sugar) 1.3 Expansion Heaviness of lifted weights 1.45 Expansion Electric shock (through the fingers) 3.5 Expansion Why should the senses differ like this? A plausible functional answer is that compression lets the eye and ear handle an enormous range of physical intensities (the brightest light we can tolerate is billions of times more intense than the dimmest we can see) within a manageable range of experience, whereas expansion makes potentially harmful stimuli, such as electric current, feel alarming quickly. Stevens strengthened his case with cross-modality matching . Instead of using numbers, observers match the intensity of one sense to another: for example, they squeeze a hand grip until the effort feels as strong as a sound is loud. If both senses follow power laws with known exponents, the power law predicts the exponent of the matching function (it should equal the ratio of the two exponents), and the matches came out close to the predictions. This showed that the power law was not merely an artefact of how people use numbers. Stevens was a productive figure in other ways too: in 1946 he proposed the four scales of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio) taught in the Research Methodology book, and in 1936 he defined the sone, a unit of loudness. Where does Stevens' law fail? Magnitude estimates are affected by the range of stimuli presented, by the choice of modulus, by the order of presentation and by individual habits with numbers, so exponents vary from study to study. Some critics argue that magnitude estimation measures how people map sensations onto numbers rather than sensation itself. Even so, the power law describes direct magnitude judgements far better than Fechner's logarithm, and in 1961 Stevens titled a famous paper "To honor Fechner and repeal his law". The two laws are best seen as answers to different questions: Fechner's law describes discriminability (how many just noticeable steps lie between two stimuli), while Stevens' law describes apparent magnitude (how big a sensation seems). Fechner's Elemente described three procedures, and with small changes they are still in use in every vision clinic, hearing clinic and perception laboratory in the world. Each involves a trade-off between speed and accuracy, and each is vulnerable to particular errors. Understanding those errors, and how they are controlled, is as important for examinations as knowing the procedures. A few terms first. In threshold work the experimenter presents stimuli in a series , which may be ascending (starting well below threshold and increasing step by step) or descending (starting well above threshold and decreasing). The point in a series at which the observer's response changes (from "no" to "yes", or the reverse) is the transition point . When two stimuli are compared, the observer may also show a time-order error : a systematic tendency to judge the second of two equal stimuli as different from the first, simply because it comes second. A similar space error arises when a stimulus is judged differently because it appears on the left rather than the right. Errors of this kind are controlled by counterbalancing : arranging the order (or position) of conditions so that each occurs equally often in each place, so that the errors cancel out. The method of limits In the method of limits (Fechner called it the method of just noticeable differences; it is also called the method of minimal changes), the experimenter changes the stimulus in small steps, in alternating ascending and descending series, and records where the observer's response changes. To find the absolute threshold for a faint tone, for example, a descending series starts with a clearly audible tone and lowers it step by step until the observer first says "no"; an ascending series starts with an inaudible tone and raises it until the observer first says "yes". The threshold for each series is taken as the midpoint between the last two responses, and the overall threshold is the average across all series. Table 3.6 shows a worked example. Table 3.6 A worked example of the method of limits for the absolute threshold of a tone (intensity in arbitrary steps). The overall threshold is the mean transition point, 4.0. Notice that ascending transitions are higher than descending ones, the signature of the error of habituation. Series Direction and start Responses Transition point 1 Descending from 9 "Yes" from 9 down to 4, "no" at 3 3.5 2 Ascending from 1 "No" from 1 up to 4, "yes" at 5 4.5 3 Descending from 8 "Yes" from 8 down to 4, "no" at 3 3.5 4 Ascending from 2 "No" from 2 up to 4, "yes" at 5 4.5 The method of limits is quick and intuitive, but it suffers from two opposite errors, both caused by the predictable order of the stimuli. In the error of habituation (also called the error of perseveration), the observer falls into the habit of giving the same response and keeps giving it after the true threshold has been crossed: continuing to say "no" too long in an ascending series (so the ascending threshold comes out too high) and continuing to say "yes" too long in a descending series (so the descending threshold comes out too low). In the error of anticipation (or expectation), the observer, knowing that a change is coming, switches response too early: saying "yes" prematurely in an ascending series and "no" prematurely in a descending series. The two errors push the transition points in opposite directions. The cure is counterbalancing. Ascending and descending series are alternated in equal numbers, so that whatever error inflates the ascending thresholds is balanced by the corresponding error in the descending ones, and the starting point of each series is varied so that the observer cannot simply count steps to the expected change. The same logic applies to other order effects in psychophysical experiments, such as primacy and recency effects: they are controlled by counterbalancing the order of presentation. The method of limits can also measure difference thresholds. The observer compares each comparison stimulus with the standard and responds "greater", "equal" or "less". The range of comparison values judged "equal" is called the interval of uncertainty; its midpoint gives the point of subjective equality, and half its width gives the difference threshold. The method of constant stimuli The method of constant stimuli (Fechner's method of right and wrong cases, also called the frequency method) removes the predictable order altogether. The experimenter first chooses a small set of fixed ("constant") stimulus values, usually five to nine, spaced so that the weakest is almost never detected and the strongest almost always is. Each value is then presented many times, often fifty or a hundred times, in a random order. The proportion of "yes" responses is calculated for each value and plotted against stimulus intensity to give the psychometric function (Figure 3.1). The absolute threshold is the intensity that corresponds to 50 percent detection, read off (interpolated from) the curve. For difference thresholds, each comparison is paired with the standard and the observer says whether it is "heavier" or "lighter" (or "louder", "brighter" and so on). The comparison value judged "heavier" 50 percent of the time is the point of subjective equality. The difference threshold is conventionally taken as half the distance between the 75 percent and 25 percent points. Because the stimuli arrive in random order, the observer cannot anticipate a change or settle into a habit, so the errors of habituation and anticipation disappear. The method of constant stimuli is therefore regarded as the most accurate and reliable of the classical methods. Its cost is time: many trials are needed, and many are spent on stimuli far from threshold, which tell the experimenter little. It also requires pilot work to choose a sensible set of values. The method of adjustment In the method of adjustment (Fechner's method of average error, also called the method of reproduction), the observer controls the stimulus. To measure an absolute threshold, the observer turns a knob until a tone is just audible; to measure a point of subjective equality, the observer adjusts a comparison line until it looks equal in length to a standard. The procedure is repeated many times. The average setting gives the threshold or the point of subjective equality, and the variability of the settings (their average deviation or standard deviation, the "average error" that gives the method its name) is an index of the difference threshold: the more finely a person can discriminate, the more tightly the settings cluster. The method of adjustment is fast and engaging, and it is the natural way to measure the size of an illusion: observers adjust a plain line until it matches the apparent length of the Muller-Lyer line, and the difference between the setting and the true length (the constant error) measures how strong the illusion is. Its weakness is precision. The stimulus changes continuously under the observer's own control, so motor skill, impatience and the observer's beliefs can all creep into the settings, and the experimenter loses control over exactly which stimuli are presented. In a staircase method , the stimulus is made weaker after every "yes" (or correct) response and stronger after every "no" (or incorrect) response. The intensity therefore climbs and descends around the threshold like a person walking up and down a staircase, and the threshold is estimated as the average of the reversal points, the intensities at which the direction changed. The method was popularised in psychophysics by Tom Cornsweet in 1962. Refinements change the rule to target a particular percentage: in the widely used "two-down, one-up" staircase, the stimulus is made harder only after two correct responses in a row, which makes the staircase settle at about 71 percent correct. To stop observers from guessing the rule, experimenters often interleave two staircases, one starting high and one low, at random. A close cousin is the tracking method that Georg von Bekesy (1899 to 1972) built into an audiometer in 1947. The listener holds down a button whenever the tone is audible; while the button is pressed the intensity falls, and when it is released the intensity rises. The result is a zigzag trace that hugs the listener's threshold as the frequency sweeps from low to high, an audiogram drawn by the listener's own responses. Many modern procedures also replace "yes or no" with a forced-choice procedure . In two-alternative forced choice, the stimulus appears in one of two intervals (or locations) and the observer must say which, even when guessing. Chance performance is 50 percent, so the threshold is usually set at the 75 percent correct point, halfway between chance and perfection. The great advantage of forced choice is that it removes the observer's willingness to say "yes" from the measurement. A cautious person and a bold person can no longer differ simply because one says "yes" more readily. That problem, the contamination of thresholds by the observer's decision style, is exactly what signal detection theory was invented to solve. Clinical link Every routine sensory assessment is a psychophysical experiment. Pure-tone audiometry finds the absolute threshold for tones of different frequencies, usually with an ascending method of limits or a staircase. An eye chart measures a visual threshold for detail. Automated perimetry, used to detect glaucoma, maps detection thresholds across the visual field. When a clinical psychologist tests a patient's two-point threshold or pain threshold as part of a neuropsychological examination, the same principles (50 percent points, counterbalanced series, attention to response bias) decide whether the result can be trusted. Exam trap Match the names: method of limits = method of just noticeable differences = minimal changes; method of constant stimuli = method of right and wrong cases = frequency method; method of adjustment = method of average error = reproduction. In the method of limits, the error of habituation means continuing the previous response too long, and the error of anticipation means changing the response too early. Both, along with primacy, recency and time-order effects, are controlled by counterbalancing (alternating ascending and descending series), not by "randomisation", "pairing" or a "double-blind technique". Randomisation is the cure in a different method: constant stimuli. 3.5 Signal detection theory Medium yield · 4 Qs During the Second World War, radar operators sat for hours in front of screens watching for the faint blip that meant an enemy aircraft. The screen was never clean. It sparkled with "noise": random flecks produced by the equipment and the atmosphere. A real aircraft at long range produced a blip barely stronger than the noise. Every few seconds the operator had to make a decision under uncertainty: is that an aircraft or just noise? Say "aircraft" too readily and fighters are scrambled for nothing; say it too reluctantly and the bombers arrive unannounced. Two operators with equally good eyes could perform very differently because they set different standards for raising the alarm. The classical idea of a threshold had no room for this. It assumed that a stimulus is either above the threshold (and detected) or below it (and missed), with the observer passively reporting the result. Yet experimenters had long noticed awkward facts. If they slipped "catch trials" into a detection experiment (trials on which no stimulus was presented), some observers said "yes" anyway. Observers who were paid for each detection reported more stimuli, and their measured thresholds fell, although their eyes and ears had not changed. A threshold, it seemed, measured not only what an observer could sense but also how willing the observer was to say so. The origins of the theory signal detection theory (SDT) began in engineering. In the early 1950s, W. Wesley Peterson, Theodore G. Birdsall and W. C. Fox at the University of Michigan developed a mathematical "theory of signal detectability" for radar and radio receivers, published in 1954. In the same year Wilson P. Tanner Jr. and John A. Swets applied it to human observers in a paper titled "A decision-making theory of visual detection". The definitive statement for psychology came in the 1966 book Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics by David M. Green and John A. Swets. The central claim is simple and powerful: performance in any detection task depends on two independent things, the observer's sensitivity and the observer's decision criterion , and the two can be measured separately. Noise, signals and the four outcomes SDT starts by admitting that the observer's internal state is never quiet. noise , in SDT, is all the random background activity that is present whether or not a signal occurs: static on a screen, hum in a room, and above all the spontaneous firing of the observer's own neurons. On every trial the observer experiences some amount of internal "evidence" for a signal. On trials with no signal, this evidence comes from noise alone, and it varies from trial to trial, forming the noise distribution . On trials with a signal, the signal adds to the noise, so the evidence tends to be larger, forming the signal-plus-noise distribution . The two distributions overlap (Figure 3.3a). Some noise-alone trials produce more evidence than some signal trials, and the observer, who experiences only the evidence, cannot tell which kind of trial produced it. So the observer must adopt a rule: if the evidence on this trial exceeds a certain level, say "yes, a signal was present"; otherwise say "no". That cut-off level is the criterion . Every trial then ends in one of four outcomes, set out in Table 3.8. A hit is saying "yes" when a signal is present. A miss is saying "no" when a signal is present. A false alarm is saying "yes" when only noise is present. A correct rejection is saying "no" when only noise is present. Table 3.8 The four outcomes of a detection trial. Notice what a hit rate alone cannot tell you. A smoke alarm that rings constantly has a perfect hit rate: it never misses a fire. It is also useless, because its false alarm rate is perfect too.
