From the past papers Optical illusions result from distortion in: (Amity 2023) a Translation b Sensation c Perception d Adaptation ✓ Answer: (c) Perception Sensation vs perception, Muller-Lyer illusion The concept What it is An optical illusion is a gap between what is really there and what we experience. In the Muller-Lyer figure, two equal lines look unequal. Where it goes wrong The receptors register the lines correctly; the error arises when the brain interprets them. Interpreting input is the job of perception . Exam tip Sensation is detection and transduction; perception is organising and interpreting. Illusions are errors of the second step. Why the other options are wrong (a) Translation Not a stage of sensory processing at all; it is a distractor that sounds like transduction . (b) Sensation Sensation (detection and transduction) is accurate in an illusion: the receptors register the lines correctly. (d) Adaptation Adaptation is the fading of response to a constant stimulus, not a misreading of a figure. According to the Bayesian approach to perception, our perceptual experiences are influenced by: (RML 2023) a Genetic predispositions b Cultural background c Prior beliefs and sensory evidence d Emotional states ✓ Answer: (c) Prior beliefs and sensory evidence Bayesian inference: prior combined with likelihood The concept What it is The Bayesian approach treats perception as a best guess. It combines the prior (what we expect) with the likelihood (what the senses report). How it works Each source is weighted by its reliability : clear sensory input counts for more, and when input is noisy the prior counts for more. Why the other options are wrong (a) Genetic predispositions Genes may shape a person's priors, but they alone do not define the approach. (b) Cultural background Culture may shape a person's priors, but it alone does not define the approach, which is prior plus sensory evidence. (d) Emotional states Emotion may shape a person's priors, but it alone does not define the approach. Who among the following has defined perception as a complex of sensory and imaginal events? (IHBAS 2024) a Kimbel b Titchener c Bruner d Schafer ✓ Answer: (b) Titchener Titchener, structuralism The concept The definition For the structuralist Titchener , a perception was sensations plus the images that past experience attaches to them: a complex of sensory and imaginal events. Why it fits Structuralism broke consciousness into elements such as sensations and images, so a perception had to be built out of them. Why the other options are wrong (a) Kimbel A distractor name; not linked to this definition of perception. (c) Bruner Bruner is known for the New Look emphasis on needs and expectations in perception (Chapter 4), not this structuralist definition. (d) Schafer A distractor name; not linked to this definition of perception. The minimum level of a stimulus that can be detected is called the: (RML 2025) a Difference threshold b Absolute threshold c Sensory adaptation point d Perceptual boundary ✓ Answer: (b) Absolute threshold Psychophysics: definition of absolute threshold The concept What it is The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus a person can detect. In practice it is the level detected on 50 percent of trials. Key contrast The absolute threshold asks "is anything there?"; the difference threshold asks "has it changed?". Why the other options are wrong (a) Difference threshold The difference threshold ( JND ) is the smallest detectable change between stimuli, not the weakest detectable stimulus. (c) Sensory adaptation point An invented term; no threshold goes by this name. (d) Perceptual boundary An invented term; it is not used in psychophysics. The point at which a stimulus becomes strong enough to trigger a response only 50% of the time is: (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) a Threshold of response b Response bias c Signal detection of response d Phi phenomenon ✓ Answer: (a) Threshold of response Classical psychophysics, the psychometric function The concept Why 50 percent Detection does not switch on at one exact intensity; it rises gradually along the psychometric function . So thresholds are defined as 50 percent points. The answer The level that triggers a response half the time is the threshold of response . Why the other options are wrong (b) Response bias Response bias is the signal detection term for an observer's readiness to say "yes"; a decision tendency, not a stimulus level. (c) Signal detection of response A garbled mix of terms; signal detection theory replaces the fixed threshold with sensitivity and response bias. (d) Phi phenomenon The phi phenomenon is apparent movement between flashing lights ( Wertheimer , 1912), not a threshold. Every Just Noticeable Difference in stimulation constitutes a constant increment in sensation magnitude. Who among the following had given this assumption? (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) a Ebbinghaus b Weber c Tolman d Fechner ✓ Answer: (d) Fechner Fechner, logarithmic law of sensation The concept Weber's finding Weber discovered that the JND is a constant fraction of the standard stimulus. Fechner's assumption Fechner added the assumption that every JND is an equal step of sensation. Adding up those equal steps, he derived his logarithmic law . Why the other options are wrong (a) Ebbinghaus Ebbinghaus applied Fechner's methods to memory ; he made no claim about JNDs as steps of sensation. (b) Weber Weber found the JND is a constant fraction of the standard; the equal-step assumption was Fechner's addition. Classic trap. (c) Tolman Tolman was a learning theorist (purposive behaviourism, cognitive maps), not a psychophysicist. In signal detection theory, the ability to distinguish a stimulus from background noise is: (IHBAS 2025) a Sensitivity (d′) b Criterion (β) c ROC curve d JND ✓ Answer: (a) Sensitivity (d′) Signal detection theory, sensitivity d′ The concept What d′ measures d′ is the separation between the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions. The further apart they are, the easier the signal is to pick out. Why it is pure d′ does not depend on willingness to say "yes", so it measures ability , not bias. Why the other options are wrong (b) Criterion (β) The criterion (β) is the willingness to say "yes" ( response bias ), not the ability to detect. (c) ROC curve The ROC curve is the plot of hit rate against false alarm rate; a graph, not the ability itself. (d) JND The JND belongs to classical psychophysics, not signal detection theory. "Receiver-operant characteristics" in communication studies refer to: (IHBAS 2025) a Physiological thresholds of auditory perception b Reinforcement controlling message recall c Cognitive biases in message interpretation d Factors in the audience influencing persuasion ✓ Answer: (d) Factors in the audience influencing persuasion Persuasion research: receiver (audience) characteristics The concept The receiver In communication research the receiver is the audience. Receiver characteristics such as self-esteem, involvement and initial attitude moderate persuasion (Social Psychology book). The trap The wording echoes the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of signal detection theory, which is a different idea. Why the other options are wrong (a) Physiological thresholds of auditory perception Bait for confusion with the ROC curve of signal detection theory; auditory thresholds are psychophysics, not communication studies. (b) Reinforcement controlling message recall Plays on the word "operant", but receiver factors are audience traits, not reinforcement of recall. (c) Cognitive biases in message interpretation Too narrow: receiver factors are audience traits (self-esteem, involvement, initial attitude) that moderate persuasion, not biases in decoding a message. The visible spectrum wavelength ranges from: (IHBAS 2020) a 380 to 760 nanometres b 200 to 700 nanometres c 400 to 1000 nanometres d 100 to 1000 nanometres ✓ Answer: (a) 380 to 760 nanometres Visible spectrum of light The concept What it is The visible spectrum is the band of wavelengths the human eye can see, about 380 to 760 nanometres. Either side Shorter wavelengths are ultraviolet and longer ones infrared , both invisible to humans. Key note Some books round the range to 400 to 700 nanometres , but no option offers that. Why the other options are wrong (b) 200 to 700 nanometres Starts at 200 nm, inside the ultraviolet , which humans cannot see. (c) 400 to 1000 nanometres Runs to 1000 nm, into the infrared , which humans cannot see. (d) 100 to 1000 nanometres Includes both ultraviolet and infrared ; far too wide. What is the relationship between frequency and wavelength? (RML 2024) a Direct b Collateral c Bilateral d Inverse ✓ Answer: (d) Inverse Wave equation: speed = frequency × wavelength The concept The formula Speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength . Why inverse For light or sound travelling at a fixed speed, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, so the two are inversely related. Why the other options are wrong (a) Direct Wrong direction: at a fixed speed, a higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength, so they move in opposite directions. (b) Collateral Not a mathematical relationship; a distractor. (c) Bilateral Not a mathematical relationship; a distractor. Which of the following act as receptor(s) for scotopic vision? (RML 2024) a Retina b Cones c Iris d Rods ✓ Answer: (d) Rods Rods and rhodopsin, scotopic vision The concept What it means Scotopic vision is dim-light vision. It depends on the rods and their pigment rhodopsin . The contrast Cones serve photopic (daylight, colour) vision. Why the other options are wrong (a) Retina The retina is the tissue that contains both receptor types; it is not itself the receptor. (b) Cones Cones serve photopic (daylight, colour) vision, not dim-light vision. (c) Iris The iris controls the pupil; it is not a receptor. Which statement is INCORRECT? (Amity 2023) a Cones are most prevalent in the central retina b Cones are sensitive to moderate to high levels of light c Cones provide only monochromatic information d Cones provide excellent acuity ✓ Answer: (c) Cones provide only monochromatic information Rods versus cones, colour vision The concept Why (c) is false Cones provide colour vision through three pigments. It is the rods , with one pigment, that give colourless (monochromatic) vision. Exam tip In an INCORRECT item the other options are true; here the other three statements are true of cones. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Cones are most prevalent in the central retina True: cones are packed most densely in the fovea , at the centre of the retina. (b) Cones are sensitive to moderate to high levels of light True: cones need moderate to bright light, which is why they serve photopic (daylight) vision. (d) Cones provide excellent acuity True: little convergence (few cones feed each ganglion cell) gives cones sharp acuity for fine detail. Dark adaptation is the process in which the eyes get more sensitive to: (RML 2024) a Green light b Coloured lights c Light with bright illumination d Light with low illumination ✓ Answer: (d) Light with low illumination Dark adaptation, rhodopsin regeneration in rods The concept What happens In darkness, regeneration of rhodopsin makes the rods thousands of times more sensitive over about 30 minutes. The result The eye becomes far more sensitive to light with low illumination; that is what dark adaptation means. Why the other options are wrong (a) Green light Although rods are most sensitive to blue-green, "green light" misses the point: dark adaptation raises sensitivity to dim light in general. (b) Coloured lights Dark-adapted rods are colour-blind, so sensitivity to coloured lights is not what improves. (c) Light with bright illumination Becoming adjusted to bright light is light adaptation , the reverse process. The process of getting adjusted to different intensities of light is called: (RML 2024) a Visual adaptation b Visual assimilation c Visual accommodation d Visual sensation ✓ Answer: (a) Visual adaptation Visual adaptation: dark and light adaptation The concept What it is Visual adaptation adjusts the eye's sensitivity to the light level. Two directions It works both ways: dark adaptation in dim light and light adaptation in bright light. Why the other options are wrong (b) Visual assimilation Assimilation belongs to Piaget's theory of cognitive development, not vision. (c) Visual accommodation Accommodation is the lens changing shape to focus, not adjusting to light intensity. (d) Visual sensation Sensation is the general detection of stimuli, not the specific adjustment to light levels. The Mach bands phenomenon is best explained by: (IHBAS 2025) a Rod-cone dichotomy in the fovea b Opponent-process theory of color vision c Lateral inhibition in the retina d Temporal summation in photoreceptors ✓ Answer: (c) Lateral inhibition in the retina Lateral inhibition in the retina, Mach bands The concept What you see Mach bands are illusory light and dark bands seen along the edge between two shades. How it works Neighbouring retinal cells inhibit each other ( lateral inhibition ), exaggerating contrast at edges and producing the bands. Why the other options are wrong (a) Rod-cone dichotomy in the fovea Wrong anatomy: the fovea contains no rods at all, so there is no rod-cone split there. (b) Opponent-process theory of color vision The opponent-process theory explains colour afterimages, not brightness bands at edges. (d) Temporal summation in photoreceptors Temporal summation is the adding together of weak signals over time, not contrast between neighbouring regions. Herman von Helmholtz (1821-94): (Panwar Systems & Theories bank) a He was a proponent of the just noticeable difference b He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision c He proposed the concept of the unconscious d He gave the law of effect ✓ Answer: (b) He gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision Helmholtz, Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory The concept The theory Helmholtz developed Young's three-receptor idea into the Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory of colour vision. His other ideas He also proposed the place theory of hearing and unconscious inference in perception. Why the other options are wrong (a) He was a proponent of the just noticeable difference The JND belongs to Weber and Fechner , not Helmholtz. (c) He proposed the concept of the unconscious The dynamic unconscious is Freud's ; the trap is that Helmholtz spoke of unconscious inference , a different idea. (d) He gave the law of effect The law of effect is Thorndike's , a principle of learning. Papillae is responsible for which sensory function? (RML 2024) a Smell b Touch c Taste d Vision ✓ Answer: (c) Taste Papillae and taste buds of the tongue The concept What they are Papillae are the bumps on the tongue that house the taste buds . The types Fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae carry taste buds; filiform papillae lack taste buds and serve touch. Why the other options are wrong (a) Smell Smell receptors lie in the olfactory epithelium of the nose, not on the tongue. (b) Touch Trap: only the filiform papillae serve touch, and they lack taste buds; papillae as a group are known for taste. (d) Vision Vision uses the rods and cones of the retina, not the tongue. Narendra turns around and around in a circle. When he stops, he feels like his head is spinning. What is responsible for this sensation? (RML 2024) a Semi circular canals b Proprioceptors c Otolith organs d Otolith crystals ✓ Answer: (a) Semicircular canals Vestibular sense: semicircular canals The concept What they do The semicircular canals of the inner ear are fluid-filled and sense rotation of the head. Why the spin When Narendra stops, the fluid in the canals keeps moving and bends the hair cells , signalling rotation in the opposite direction. Why the other options are wrong (b) Proprioceptors Proprioceptors report the position of the limbs, not rotation of the head. (c) Otolith organs The otolith organs detect tilt and linear acceleration, not spinning. (d) Otolith crystals The crystals sit inside the otolith organs , so they too serve tilt and linear acceleration, not rotation. What is a key feature of effective learning strategies for individuals with learning difficulties? (RML 2025) a Relying solely on written instructions b Providing multisensory inputs and regular repetition c Avoiding any accommodations or modifications d Focusing only on rote memorization techniques ✓ Answer: (b) Providing multisensory inputs and regular repetition Multisensory integration plus repetition The concept Why it works Combining sight, sound, movement and touch strengthens learning, as the research on multisensory integration predicts. Role of repetition Regular repetition then consolidates what was learned. Why the other options are wrong (a) Relying solely on written instructions Relies on a single channel, which ignores the learner's difficulty. (c) Avoiding any accommodations or modifications Refusing accommodations ignores the learner's difficulty. (d) Focusing only on rote memorization techniques Rote memorisation alone ignores the learner's difficulty. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The thalamus relays every sense except smell to the cortex: vision through the lateral geniculate nucleus, hearing through the medial geniculate nucleus, touch and taste through the ventral posterior nuclei. Smell (olfactory nerve, cranial nerve I) runs from the olfactory bulb straight to the piriform cortex and amygdala. asked 4 times Rods (about 120 million, one pigment, rhodopsin) give scotopic (dim-light) vision and no colour; cones (about 6 to 7 million, three pigments) give photopic vision, colour and fine acuity. "Cones give only monochromatic information" is false. asked twice Dark adaptation makes the eye more sensitive to light of low illumination over about 30 minutes (cones first, a rod-cone break at 7 to 10 minutes, then rods as rhodopsin regenerates). Adjusting to different light intensities is visual adaptation ; accommodation is the lens focusing. asked twice Cones are most concentrated in the fovea centralis , which has no rods and gives the sharpest colour vision; the optic disc has no receptors at all (the blind spot); the peripheral retina is rod territory. asked 3 times The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected on 50 percent of trials; the difference threshold (just noticeable difference, JND) is the smallest change detected 50 percent of the time. asked twice The three semicircular canals detect rotational (angular) acceleration of the head in three planes, so the head seems to spin after you stop turning; the otolith organs (utricle and saccule) detect head tilt and linear acceleration. asked twice In signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966), sensitivity (d′) is the ability to tell a signal from background noise; it is highest when hits clearly exceed false alarms (d′ = z of the hit rate minus z of the false alarm rate). asked twice Edward Bradford Titchener (structuralism) sought a "periodic table" of the elements of sensation and defined perception as a complex of sensory and imaginal elements. asked twice Gustav Theodor Fechner founded psychophysics with Elements of Psychophysics (1860); he assumed that every JND adds an equal unit of sensation and derived S = k log I. asked twice Place theory (Helmholtz, 1863; Georg von Bekesy's travelling wave, Nobel Prize 1961): each frequency peaks at its own place on the basilar membrane, high at the base and low at the apex, and it best explains high pitches. The frequency theory of low pitches is William (not Ernest) Rutherford's (1886). asked twice Charles Bonnet syndrome is complex visual hallucinations in cognitively intact people with significant visual loss who keep their insight (described by Charles Bonnet in 1760). asked twice The visible spectrum runs from about 380 to 760 nanometres . asked once Frequency and wavelength are inversely related (speed = frequency × wavelength), for light and for sound. asked once Papillae on the tongue serve taste: fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae house the taste buds; filiform papillae have none. asked once Optical illusions are distortions of perception , not of sensation: the receptors register the stimulus correctly. asked once The Bayesian approach to perception: every percept combines prior beliefs with sensory evidence. asked once Mach bands (Ernst Mach, 1865) are explained by lateral inhibition in the retina, which exaggerates contrast at edges. asked once "Receiver characteristics" in communication studies are audience factors that influence persuasion; the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) of signal detection theory plots hit rate against false alarm rate. asked once Effective teaching for learning difficulties uses multisensory input (see, say, hear, trace) with regular repetition. asked once The decision parameter that signal detection theory added to classical threshold theory is the response criterion (β or c): liberal observers say "yes" readily, conservative observers rarely. asked once Weber's law (Ernst Heinrich Weber, 1834): the JND is a constant fraction of the standard stimulus, ΔI/I = k, not a fixed amount. asked once Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) gave the trichromatic theory (with Thomas Young, 1802; Helmholtz 1852), the place theory of hearing and unconscious inference; not the JND, the unconscious or the law of effect. asked once Saccades and microsaccades, tiny rapid eye movements, keep the image shifting on the retina and so ensure constant perception; a stabilised image fades. asked once The route of sound: pinna, auditory canal, tympanic membrane , ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), oval window, cochlea, organ of Corti. asked once Cochlear hair cells transduce by direct mechanical bending of their stereocilia, which opens cation channels; potassium flows in and the cell depolarises and releases glutamate. asked once The anterolateral (spinothalamic) system carries pain (nociceptive) and temperature information; the dorsal column-medial lemniscus system carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception. asked once Phantom limb sensation (term coined by Silas Weir Mitchell, 1871) is best explained by cortical reorganisation in the somatosensory cortex (V. S. Ramachandran). asked once The all-or-none law : once threshold is reached, an action potential fires at full, constant amplitude; stimulus intensity is coded by firing rate. asked once John Dewey criticised the reflex arc, the connection between sensory stimulus and motor response, in 1896. asked once The neurobiological approach holds that behaviour is governed by the brain and nervous system. asked once

In 1958 a fifty-two-year-old Englishman, known in the scientific literature only by his initials, S.B., had an operation that gave him back his sight. He had been effectively blind since he was about ten months old. He had learned to get about with confidence and to use tools, and he lived a full, independent adult life by touch and hearing. Then a surgeon replaced the clouded cornea of one eye with a graft, the bandages came off, and light from the world reached a working retina for the first time in half a century. What did he see? Not, as almost everyone expected, the world suddenly laid out before him. He heard the surgeon's voice in front of him, turned towards it, and saw a blur. Only because the voice came from it did he decide that the blur must be a face. The psychologist Richard Gregory and his colleague Jean Wallace, who studied him over the following months, recorded a string of puzzles. S.B. could read the time from a large clock almost at once, because as a blind man he had told the time by feeling the hands of a watch with no glass. He could read capital letters, which he had learned by touch at school, but not lower-case ones, which he had never felt. Looking down from his hospital window, which was several storeys up, he thought he could touch the ground with his feet if he hung from the sill by his hands. The most famous episode came at the Science Museum in London. Gregory and Wallace showed S.B. a lathe in a glass case, a machine he had always wanted to understand. He could make nothing of it. He was then allowed to run his hands over it with his eyes shut. When he opened them again he said, "Now that I've felt it I can see." Think about what that sentence means. The light reaching S.B.'s eyes did not change when he touched the lathe. What changed was what his brain could do with that light. This chapter is about that difference: the difference between light arriving at the eye and a person seeing a lathe, a face or a cliff edge. Keep S.B. in mind; you will meet him again at the end of the chapter. 4.1 What Perception Is: From Sensation to Interpretation Medium yield · 5 Qs Open your eyes and the world is simply there: a cup on the table, a friend across the room, the far wall at its proper distance. It feels as if nothing could be more direct. This section shows you why that feeling is misleading, and introduces the great debate about how perception actually works. Sensation, perception and the inverse problem Chapter 3 followed physical energy as far as the sense organs: light focused on the retina, sound waves moving the basilar membrane, and receptors turning that energy into neural signals. That is sensation , the detection of physical energy by the sense organs and its conversion (transduction) into neural activity. Perception is what the brain then does with those signals: it selects, organises and interprets them so that they become meaningful objects and events. Sensation gives you a pattern of light; perception gives you your mother's face. Why should perception be hard? Because the information at the eye is poorer than the world that produced it. The retina is a curved, nearly flat sheet, so the image on it has only two dimensions, yet you see a three-dimensional world. A small coin held close and a large plate held far away can throw exactly the same-sized image on the retina. A white page in shadow can send less light to your eye than a black page in sunshine. In each case many different states of the world could have produced the same retinal image. Working backwards from the image to the world that caused it is called the inverse problem , and every theory of perception is, at heart, a proposal about how the brain solves it. Bottom-up and top-down processing Two kinds of processing help. Bottom-up processing (also called data-driven processing) starts with the stimulus: receptors register features such as edges, colours and movements, and these are built up step by step into more complex descriptions. Information flows in one direction, from the senses upwards. Top-down processing (conceptually driven processing) runs the other way: knowledge, expectations and context, stored in the brain, shape how the incoming data are interpreted. You can feel both at work when you read a doctor's handwriting on a prescription. Some letters are clear enough to be read from their shapes alone (bottom-up). Others are scrawls that you can read only because you know what word is likely to come next, for example that "Paracet..." is probably followed by "amol" (top-down). Almost all real perception mixes the two. The theories that follow differ in how much weight they give to each. Perception as inference: Helmholtz, Gregory and the Bayesian brain The oldest answer to the inverse problem came from Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894), the German physicist and physiologist who measured the speed of the nerve impulse and wrote the great Handbook of Physiological Optics (completed in 1867). Helmholtz argued that perception is the end point of unconscious inference : the brain draws rapid, automatic conclusions about the world from the sensory evidence plus past experience, much as a scientist draws conclusions from data, except that we are not aware of doing it. His likelihood principle states that we perceive the object that is most likely to have produced the pattern of stimulation we receive. A small retinal image of a person is perceived as a normal-sized person far away, not as a tiny person nearby, because that is by far the likelier cause. A century later the British psychologist Richard Langton Gregory (1923 to 2010) turned this idea into the modern constructivist approach (also called the indirect or top-down approach) in books such as Eye and Brain (1966) and The Intelligent Eye (1970). For Gregory, a perception is a perceptual hypothesis : a best guess about what is out there, constructed from fragmentary sensory data and stored knowledge, and tested against further input. The senses supply evidence; the brain supplies the theory. What is the evidence for this view? Gregory's favourite was the hollow-face illusion . Look at the inside of a hollow mask from a metre or so away and you see a normal face bulging towards you, not a hollow one. Your knowledge that faces stick out is so strong that it overrides the depth information from your two eyes. Illusions (Section 4.5), ambiguous figures that flip between two interpretations, and the effects of expectation (Section 4.8) all fit the idea that perception is an active construction that can be wrong. Critics raised two problems. First, if perception is guesswork from poor data, why is it usually so accurate? Second, most illusions persist even when you know the truth; if perception were a hypothesis open to correction by knowledge, knowing that the lines of the Müller-Lyer figure are equal ought to make them look equal, and it does not. The modern descendant of Helmholtz's idea is the Bayesian approach to perception, named after the English clergyman and mathematician Thomas Bayes (about 1701 to 1761), whose theorem shows how to update a belief in the light of new evidence. On this view the brain combines two things: prior beliefs (how likely each possible state of the world is, learned from experience or built in by evolution) and the likelihood (how well each possibility fits the current sensory evidence). The result, the posterior, is the percept. When the sensory evidence is clear it dominates; when it is weak or ambiguous the priors take over. The Indian-born neuroscientist Vilayanur S. Ramachandran (born 1951) gave a neat demonstration in 1988. Shaded discs that are lighter at the top look like bumps and discs that are lighter at the bottom look like dents, and turning the page upside down swaps them. The brain is applying a prior that light comes from above, because for the whole of our evolutionary history it has. The hollow face is the same story: the prior that faces are convex outweighs weak evidence that this one is concave. Exam trap The approach that "emphasises unconscious inference and probabilistic reasoning" is the constructivist approach (Helmholtz, Gregory); its Bayesian form adds that the percept combines prior beliefs and sensory evidence . Do not pick "genetic predispositions", "cultural background" or "emotional states" for the Bayesian question: they can shape priors, but the definition is priors plus evidence. And do not confuse Helmholtz's unconscious inference with Wundt's apperception: the "apperceptive mass" (a term from Johann Friedrich Herbart that Wilhelm Wundt took over) is the store of existing ideas into which a new perception is absorbed (Chapter 1). Direct perception: Gibson's ecological approach The fiercest critic of the inference view was the American psychologist James Jerome Gibson (1904 to 1979). During the Second World War Gibson worked on how to select and train pilots, and he noticed that the cues listed in textbooks, cues taken from flat pictures viewed by a motionless observer, were of little use in explaining how a pilot lands an aircraft. A pilot is moving, and movement creates information. Over three books, The Perception of the Visual World (1950), The Senses Considered as Perceptual Systems (1966) and The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), he built the theory of direct perception , also called the ecological approach because it studies perception in the animal's real environment rather than in the laboratory. Gibson's central claim is that the light reaching a moving observer is not poor at all. The optic array , the structured pattern of light arriving at the eye from every direction, is rich in information that specifies the layout of the world without any need for inference. Three of his ideas are examined often. Invariants are properties of the optic array that stay constant as the observer moves and so specify the world directly. The texture gradient (Section 4.3) is one: the elements of a surface get smaller and denser with distance in a lawful way. The horizon ratio is another: for objects standing on the same ground, the horizon cuts them at the same proportion of their height whatever their distance, so objects of equal height are seen as equal. Optic flow is the pattern of movement in the optic array as you move through the world. When you walk or drive forward, the scene streams outwards from a single point, the focus of expansion , which marks exactly where you are heading. A pilot landing an aircraft keeps the focus of expansion on the start of the runway. No inference is needed; the information is in the light. Affordances , a word Gibson coined in the 1960s and developed in his 1979 book, are the possibilities for action that an object or surface offers to a particular animal. A chair affords sitting, a handle affords grasping, a ledge at knee height affords climbing for an adult but not for a toddler. Gibson claimed that we perceive affordances directly, so that meaning is picked up from the environment rather than added by the brain. Gibson described the perceiver as "resonating" to this information, as a radio resonates to a broadcast. Because perception is driven by the information in the stimulus and not by stored knowledge, Gibson's theory is the classic example of a bottom-up theory. His approach was a healthy corrective: it put the moving, acting animal back at the centre of perception and inspired work on how we steer, catch and avoid collisions. But it has weaknesses. It has little to say about illusions, which by definition are cases where the information misleads us. It explains poorly how we recognise objects whose meaning depends on culture and learning (a letter box affords posting a letter only to someone who knows what a letter box is). And "resonance" names the process without explaining it. Indian context Watch a fielder at long-on under a skied hit at a cricket match in Bengaluru. He does not calculate the ball's trajectory. Studies of fielders running to catch high balls suggest that they run so as to keep the image of the ball rising smoothly in their field of view; if it starts to accelerate upwards they move back, if it starts to drop they move in. This is Gibsonian perception at its best: action guided directly by a property of the changing optic array. Bringing the two together: Neisser's perceptual cycle and two visual systems Must we choose between Gregory and Gibson? Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012), whose Cognitive Psychology (1967) gave the new field its name, argued in his later book Cognition and Reality (1976) that we need not. His perceptual cycle joins both directions of processing into a loop (Figure 4.1). A schema , an organised body of knowledge about what to expect, directs exploration: where you look, what you listen for, what you reach out to touch. Exploration samples the information actually available in the object or scene. The information sampled then modifies the schema, which directs the next round of exploration. Perception is not a single event but a continuous cycle in which top-down expectation and bottom-up information keep correcting each other. Schema what you expect Exploration looking, moving, touching Object available information directs (top-down) samples modifies (bottom-up) the cycle never stops Figure 4.1 Neisser's perceptual cycle (1976). Notice that top-down and bottom-up processing are not rivals here: each arrow feeds the next, so expectation and information correct each other continuously. A second reconciliation came from the brain. In 1995 David Milner and Melvyn Goodale proposed that the visual system has two streams with different jobs. A ventral stream, running into the temporal lobe, serves vision-for-perception : recognising what objects are, which needs stored knowledge, just as Gregory said. A dorsal stream, running into the parietal lobe, serves vision-for-action : guiding the hand and body in real time, fast and largely unconscious, very much as Gibson described. Their patient D.F., whose ventral stream had been damaged by carbon monoxide poisoning, could not say whether a slot in a disc was horizontal or vertical, yet could turn her hand correctly and post a card through it. The two classic theories may simply be describing two different visual systems (the anatomy is covered in the Physiological book). Two further labels appear as options in examination questions. The information-processing approach treats perception as a series of stages, each transforming the output of the one before, much as a computer program does. The computational approach , associated above all with David Marr, asks what problem each stage of vision has to solve and what calculations would solve it; you will meet it in Section 4.7. The answer is James J. Gibson ; Gregory and Helmholtz are the top-down (constructivist) theorists, and Wertheimer is a Gestalt psychologist. "Affordances" is always Gibson. Do not confuse James J. Gibson (direct perception, affordances) with his wife Eleanor J. Gibson (visual cliff, perceptual learning): they are two different, equally examinable people. Neisser wrote Cognitive Psychology in 1967 but proposed the perceptual cycle in Cognition and Reality in 1976. Clinical link Several studies have found that people with schizophrenia are much less fooled by the hollow-face illusion than other people: they are more likely to see the mask as hollow, as it really is. One interpretation is that the balance between top-down expectation and bottom-up evidence is altered in the disorder. It is a reminder that "seeing correctly" in a laboratory task is not always a sign of a healthy brain. 4.2 Perceptual Organisation: The Gestalt Laws Medium yield · 8 Qs Before you can recognise an object you must first decide which bits of the visual field belong together and which belong to something else. That sounds trivial until you try to explain how it is done. The school that took this problem most seriously, and that has contributed more to the study of perception than any other, was Gestalt psychology. The Gestalt starting point Gestalt psychology was founded in Germany in 1912, when Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) published his experiments on apparent movement, with Kurt Koffka (1886 to 1941) and Wolfgang Köhler (1887 to 1967) as his first subjects and lifelong collaborators (the history of the school is told in Chapter 2). The German word Gestalt means form, shape or configuration. The school's founding claim, aimed squarely at Wundt's and Titchener's attempt to break experience into elementary sensations, was that the whole is different from the sum of its parts. A melody is still the same melody when every note is changed by transposing it into another key; the "melodiness" lies in the relations between the notes, not in the notes themselves. In perception, said the Gestaltists, the brain spontaneously organises the visual field into wholes according to a small set of innate laws, and in 1923 Wertheimer set these out in a famous paper. Figure and ground The most basic act of organisation is to split the field into a figure , the object that stands out and is attended to, and a ground , the background against which it appears. The Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin (1886 to 1951) studied this figure-ground relationship in his 1915 doctoral work and drew the best-known demonstration of it, Rubin's vase : a white vase on a black background which, as you look, becomes two black faces in profile on a white background. Rubin described how figure and ground differ in experience: The figure has a thing-like quality (it looks like an object) and a definite shape; the ground is shapeless and looks like substance or empty space. The contour between them seems to belong to the figure, not the ground. The figure appears nearer and in front; the ground appears farther away, diffuse, and seems to continue behind the figure. The figure is more vivid, more easily named and better remembered. Certain regions are more likely to become figure: smaller regions, enclosed regions, symmetrical and convex regions, and regions in the lower part of the field. Figure-ground organisation is not only visual. At a noisy wedding reception, the voice of the person talking to you is an auditory figure and the din of the hall is ground. The vase and faces is a reversible figure : either region can be seen as figure, but never both at once, and the percept flips back and forth. Notice what this means. The stimulus never changes, yet the perception does. Organisation is something the perceiver does, not something in the picture. Exam trap "Which is not a characteristic of a figure?" The answer is "appears diffused and spatially distant", because that describes the ground . Smaller size, clear outlines and greater object character (thing-like quality) are all properties of the figure. Camouflage works by breaking figure-ground segregation, so that the animal's contour is lost in the ground. The laws of grouping Once figures are separated from ground, elements must be grouped into larger units. The Gestalt laws of perceptual organisation describe how. Look at Figure 4.2 as you read; each panel lets you watch one law at work in your own perception. By the law of proximity , elements that are close together in space or in time are seen as belonging together. In the first panel the dots are equally spaced vertically but not horizontally, so you see three pairs of columns rather than four rows. Proximity in time works the same way: the taps of a drum heard close together form a rhythm group. By the law of similarity , elements that look alike (in colour, shape, size or orientation) are grouped together; in the second panel equal spacing would favour columns, but similarity makes you see rows of filled and open dots. By the law of closure , we tend to complete figures that have gaps, so that the broken outline in the third panel is seen as a circle, not as four separate arcs. The law of good continuation (also called the law of continuity) holds that elements that follow a smooth line or curve are grouped together, so that the fourth panel shows a straight line crossing a curve rather than two odd angular shapes meeting at a point. By the law of common fate , elements moving together in the same direction are grouped together: a flock of birds or a column of marching soldiers is seen as one unit, and in the sixth panel the arrows split the row into two sets. The Gestaltists also described a law of symmetry (symmetrical regions are grouped together and tend to be seen as figure), and Wertheimer added a law of past experience or familiarity (elements that together form a familiar object tend to be grouped). Modern researchers have added two laws. The law of common region , proposed by Stephen Palmer in 1992, states that elements inside a common enclosed region are grouped together, even when proximity says otherwise (fifth panel, top row). The law of connectedness (element connectedness), described by Palmer and Irvin Rock in 1994, states that elements physically joined by lines are seen as a unit (fifth panel, bottom row). In the same 1994 paper Palmer and Rock proposed uniform connectedness: any connected region of uniform colour, texture or lightness is organised as a single perceptual unit. Both kinds of connectedness, and common region, are powerful enough to override proximity and similarity. Table 4.2 brings all the laws together. Proximity three pairs of columns Similarity seen as rows, not columns Closure gaps filled: one circle Good continuation one line and one curve Common region (top) and connectedness (bottom) Common fate dots moving together group Figure 4.2 Six grouping laws you can watch in your own perception. In each panel the elements are physically identical or evenly spaced in some respect, yet you see definite groups; the grouping is supplied by your visual system. It states that every stimulus pattern is seen in such a way that the resulting structure is as simple, regular, stable and complete as the conditions allow. Two overlapping rings could in principle be seen as three oddly shaped pieces, but you see two circles because that is the simplest description. The other laws can be seen as special cases of this one, which is why Prägnanz is called the master law of Gestalt organisation and why a question about a figure "perceived not in parts but organised in the best possible whole form" is answered by Prägnanz. The power of these laws shows most clearly when they create something that is not there. In 1955 the Italian psychologist Gaetano Kanizsa (1913 to 1993) drew three black discs, each with a wedge cut out, arranged so that the wedges face each other. Observers see a bright white triangle lying on top of the discs, complete with sharp edges across empty paper. These illusory contours (subjective contours) show closure and Prägnanz at work: the simplest interpretation of three cut discs is one triangle covering three whole discs. A related process, amodal completion , makes us perceive an object partly hidden behind another as continuing, complete, behind it. How good are the Gestalt laws? They are excellent descriptions; every textbook of design, typography and advertising still uses them. But they are descriptions, not explanations. They do not say why the brain groups this way, and they are vague about what happens when two laws conflict. The Gestaltists' own physiological explanation, that perceptual organisation reflects electrical fields in the brain with the same shape as the percept (Köhler's isomorphism), was not supported by later experiments in which the cortex of animals was filled with metal strips or wires to disrupt any such fields without destroying perception. And research since then has shown that grouping is partly learned: what counts as "similar" or "familiar" depends on experience, as you will see in Section 4.8. Exam trap The tendency to complete a figure is closure , not continuity or continuation (continuity is about smooth paths, not gaps). Items close together in space and time group by proximity . The figure "organised in the best possible whole form" is Prägnanz . The school that contributed most to perception is Gestalt psychology , not structuralism, behaviourism or psychoanalysis. And Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) has nothing to do with Gestalt psychology except the name. Exam trap Do not confuse interposition (a depth cue: a nearer object blocks a farther one, Section 4.3) with interpolation (filling in between known points, as the visual system does when it completes a contour hidden behind an occluder) or extrapolation (extending a trend beyond the known points). One past paper also used structuring for working out a rule or organising principle from incomplete evidence and then picking out the items that satisfy it; that keyed answer fits the Gestalt idea that perception imposes structure on incomplete input. Clinical link In 1938 the American child psychiatrist Lauretta Bender built a test from nine of Wertheimer's grouping designs. The Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test asks the person to copy the designs; distortions, rotations and failures of integration can point to visuoconstructive or organic difficulties. The test itself is covered in the Psychological Assessment book. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Processing driven by knowledge, expectation and context is called processing. Helmholtz described perception as the product of inference. Gregory called a perception a perceptual . The master law of Gestalt organisation, the tendency to see the simplest possible form, is the law of . Answers: (1) inverse, (2) top-down, (3) unconscious, (4) hypothesis, (5) prior, (6) affordances, (7) expansion, (8) schema, (9) reversible, (10) Prägnanz. 4.3 Depth and Distance Perception High yield · 9 Qs Reach out and pick up the cup in front of you. Your hand opens to the right width and stops at exactly the right distance, without a moment's thought. Yet the image of the cup on each retina has no depth at all. How does a flat image give you a world in three dimensions? The problem of the flat retina The problem was posed clearly in 1709 by the Irish philosopher George Berkeley (1685 to 1753) in An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision . Berkeley pointed out that a point at any distance along a line of sight falls on the same point of the retina, so distance cannot be "seen" directly. He concluded that we learn to judge distance by associating visual sensations, such as the strain of turning the eyes inwards, with the experience of reaching and walking. Modern research has replaced Berkeley's short list with a long list of depth cues , sources of information that correlate with distance and that the brain combines to give depth perception , the ability to see the world in three dimensions and to judge how far away things are. The cues fall into families according to what they need: two eyes, one eye, movement, or feedback from the eye's own muscles. Binocular cues: disparity and convergence Binocular cues are depth cues that require both eyes working together. The most important is retinal disparity (also called binocular disparity). Your eyes are about 6 centimetres apart, so each receives a slightly different view of the world. Hold a finger about 20 centimetres in front of your nose and close each eye in turn: the finger jumps from side to side against the background. The difference between the positions of an object's images on the two retinas is its disparity, and the nearer the object, the larger the disparity. Objects at the fixation distance fall on corresponding points of the two retinas and have zero disparity; the imaginary curved surface through all such points is called the horopter . Objects nearer than the horopter have crossed disparity and objects beyond it have uncrossed disparity, so the sign of the disparity tells the brain whether an object is in front of or behind the point being looked at. The vivid impression of solid depth produced by fusing the two images is called stereopsis . The English physicist Charles Wheatstone (1802 to 1875) proved the point in 1838 with his stereoscope , which presented a slightly different drawing to each eye; viewers saw a single solid object. Every 3-D film works the same way, using special glasses to send a different image to each eye. In 1960 the Hungarian-American engineer Béla Julesz (1928 to 2003) went further with random-dot stereograms: two fields of random dots, identical except that a central square of dots is shifted slightly in one of them. Each image alone looks like television snow. Viewed in a stereoscope, a square floats out in depth. Because there is no square to recognise in either image alone, Julesz showed that stereopsis can work before any object is recognised, a purely bottom-up process. The second binocular cue is convergence (vergence): the inward turning of the two eyes to fixate a near object. Look at your fingertip as you bring it towards your nose and you can feel your eyes cross. The brain registers how much the eyes are turned in, from the commands sent to the eye muscles and feedback from them, and the greater the convergence, the nearer the object. Convergence is a binocular cue, because it needs two eyes, and also an oculomotor cue, because it comes from the eye muscles; it is useful only for objects within a couple of metres. Binocular cues can work only where the fields of the two eyes overlap. Each human eye sees roughly 160 degrees horizontally (about 60 degrees towards the nose and about 100 degrees towards the temple); the two together cover roughly 200 degrees, and the central overlap where both eyes see, the binocular field, is about 120 degrees wide. Predators such as cats and owls, and primates such as ourselves, have forward-facing eyes with a large overlap and good stereopsis; prey animals such as rabbits and deer have eyes on the sides of the head, a nearly all-round view, and little binocular overlap. Exam trap A past paper asked for the "approximate visual field covered by each human eye" and keyed 180 degrees . The better textbook figure for one eye is about 160 degrees horizontally; 180 to 200 degrees is the field of both eyes together, and about 120 degrees is the binocular overlap. If you meet that exact item, be aware that the paper's key was 180; if the question clearly says "both eyes", 180 to 200 is right. Monocular cues: what a painter knows Monocular cues are depth cues available to one eye alone. People who have lost an eye still judge depth well, and a flat painting or photograph can look deep, because of them. Most are pictorial cues , so called because artists since the Renaissance have used them to put depth on a flat canvas. Figure 4.3 shows the main ones in a single scene. Relative size : if two objects are known or assumed to be the same size, the one casting the smaller retinal image is seen as farther away. A row of identical lamp posts seems to shrink into the distance. Familiar size : when we know an object's real size, its retinal size tells us its distance. A tiny-looking autorickshaw is seen as a normal autorickshaw far away. Interposition (also called overlap or occlusion): when one object partly blocks the view of another, the blocked object is seen as farther away. Interposition gives only order (nearer or farther), not distance. Linear perspective : parallel lines, such as railway tracks or the edges of a road, appear to converge as they recede, meeting at a vanishing point on the horizon. Texture gradient : a surface with an even texture (pebbles, grass, the sleepers of a railway track, bricks in a courtyard) shows its elements as larger, coarser and more widely spaced nearby, and smaller, finer and more densely packed farther away. This was Gibson's favourite cue, because it specifies distance and the slant of a surface directly. Aerial perspective (atmospheric perspective): distant objects look hazier, less sharp, lower in contrast and often bluer, because light from them passes through more air, dust and moisture. On a clear day after the monsoon, the Nilgiri hills seem nearer than they do in hazy summer. Height in the visual field (relative height or elevation): for objects on the ground below the horizon, those higher in the visual field, that is, closer to the horizon, are seen as farther away; for objects above the horizon, such as clouds, the reverse holds. Shading (light and shadow): the pattern of light and shadow on an object reveals its three-dimensional shape, and shadows cast on the ground show where an object stands. As Section 4.1 showed, the brain assumes the light comes from above. Relative brightness: of two identical objects, the brighter is usually seen as nearer. Aerial perspective: far hills look hazy Linear perspective: edges converge Texture gradient: stripes crowd together Interposition Relative size and height in the field Figure 4.3 Pictorial depth cues in one scene. The road's edges converge (linear perspective), the cross stripes crowd together with distance (texture gradient), the three identical trees shrink and rise towards the horizon (relative size and height in the field), the near house hides part of the far one (interposition), and the distant hills are pale (aerial perspective). Road engineers use these cues deliberately. Stripes painted across the approach to a toll plaza or an exit ramp, with the gaps between them getting smaller, create an exaggerated texture gradient and a heightened sense of speed, so that drivers slow down without being told. Cues from movement and from the eye's own muscles Gibson's complaint that textbook cues were taken from frozen pictures applies with special force to the cues that need movement. The most powerful is motion parallax : when you move, objects at different distances move across your retina at different speeds. Look out of the side window of a moving train. The electric poles beside the track flash past in the direction opposite to your travel, the trees beyond move more slowly, the distant hills crawl, and the moon seems to travel along with you. The relative speed of the images tells you their relative distance. Motion parallax is a monocular cue (one eye is enough) but not a pictorial one, because a still picture cannot show it. A related cue is deletion and accretion: as you move, a nearer surface progressively covers (deletes) and uncovers (accretes) the texture of a farther one, which is interposition in motion. Accommodation is the change in the shape of the lens, controlled by the ciliary muscles, that focuses the image of near or far objects on the retina (Chapter 3). The brain can use the state of these muscles as a rough distance cue for objects within about two metres. Accommodation, like convergence, is an oculomotor cue , but unlike convergence it works with one eye. Table 4.3 classifies every cue in this section by the number of eyes it needs and the family it belongs to. Table 4.3 Depth cues classified. Cue Eyes needed Family How it signals depth Retinal (binocular) disparity Two Binocular Different images in the two eyes; more disparity = nearer Convergence Two Binocular, oculomotor More inward turning of the eyes = nearer Accommodation One Monocular, oculomotor Lens thickens for near objects Motion parallax One Monocular, motion-based Near objects move faster across the retina Interposition (overlap) One Monocular, pictorial Blocked object is farther Relative size and familiar size One Monocular, pictorial Smaller image = farther Linear perspective One Monocular, pictorial Parallel lines converge with distance Texture gradient One Monocular, pictorial Texture becomes finer and denser with distance Aerial perspective One Monocular, pictorial Distant objects are hazy and bluish Height in the visual field One Monocular, pictorial Closer to the horizon = farther Shading One Monocular, pictorial Light and shadow reveal shape Exam trap The binocular cues are only retinal disparity and convergence . Everything else, including accommodation and motion parallax, is monocular. So "a monocular cue" from convergence, retinal disparity, assimilation and interposition is interposition ; "requires both eyes" from motion parallax, aerial perspective, convergence and accommodation is convergence ; and retinal disparity is a binocular cue, not a pictorial, static monocular or motion parallax cue. Assimilation is not a depth cue at all: in Piaget's theory it means fitting new experience into an existing schema (Developmental book), and in perception it names the opposite of contrast, when a colour or grey looks more like its surroundings. Increasing density of stones, pebbles or painted stripes with distance is texture gradient , not aerial perspective (haze) or interposition (overlap). Is depth perception innate? The visual cliff Berkeley thought depth perception had to be learned. Is he right? In the 1950s Eleanor Jack Gibson (1910 to 2002) and Richard Walk (1920 to 1999), at Cornell University, built an apparatus to find out. Key study: The visual cliff (Gibson and Walk, 1960) Question. Can infants and young animals perceive depth before they have had a chance to learn it through falls and bumps? Method. The visual cliff is a large table topped by a sheet of strong glass. Under one half a checkerboard pattern is fixed directly beneath the glass (the shallow side); under the other half the same pattern lies far below the glass (the deep side), so that the table appears to end in a sheer drop, although the glass makes it perfectly safe. A narrow centre board separates the two sides. Thirty-six infants aged 6 to 14 months were placed on the centre board and their mothers called them from the shallow side and from the deep side in turn. Results. Twenty-seven infants moved off the board. All of them crawled onto the shallow side at least once, but only three crept, hesitantly, onto the deep side. Many crawled away from their mothers when called from the deep side, or cried because they could not reach them, and some patted the glass yet still refused to cross. Newly hatched chicks, young goats and lambs placed on the apparatus within a day of birth also avoided the deep side. Conclusion. By the time human infants can crawl, they can perceive depth, and in species that walk from birth, depth perception is present from birth. Criticism. Human infants cannot be tested until they crawl, at around six months, by which time they have had months of visual experience, so the study cannot show that depth perception in humans is innate. Later work divided the question. When Joseph Campos and his colleagues in 1970 lowered infants of about two to three and a half months directly onto the deep side, their heart rate slowed, the sign of interest and attention, not the speeding up that signals fear. Young infants therefore detect the difference in depth long before they fear it. Fear of the drop appears with experience of moving about on one's own: infants of the same age who have begun crawling, or who have been given experience in baby walkers, show fear on the deep side sooner than those who have not. The most balanced conclusion is that the ability to detect depth appears very early and may well be largely built in, while the meaning of a drop, the knowledge that it is dangerous, is learned through self-produced movement. Exam trap The visual cliff was devised by Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk (1960) to study depth perception and whether it is innate. It did not study object permanence (Piaget), colour perception, imprinting (Lorenz) or language. The infants were 6 to 14 months old (crawling age), not newborns and not "3 to 6 months", as some revision notes say. The best summary of the human results is "depth perception is present by the time infants can crawl", not "fully developed at birth" and not "only after age two". Clinical link Children whose eyes are misaligned (strabismus) or who have a lazy eye (amblyopia) in early childhood often grow up stereoblind, because the brain never learns to combine the two eyes' images. The neurobiologist Susan Barry , cross-eyed from infancy, gained stereoscopic vision in her late forties after intensive vision therapy, a case made famous by the neurologist Oliver Sacks (1933 to 2015). Her experience, of suddenly seeing snowflakes floating in depth, shows both how much the brain depends on early experience and how much plasticity remains in adulthood. 4.4 Perceptual Constancy Lower yield · 3 Qs As a friend walks away from you down a corridor, the image of her on your retina shrinks steadily; at twice the distance it is half the height. Yet she does not seem to shrink. When a door swings open, the image it casts changes from a rectangle to a narrower and narrower trapezoid; yet you see a rectangular door turning. This stability is called perceptual constancy : the tendency to perceive objects as having stable, unchanging properties (size, shape, lightness, colour, position) despite large changes in the sensory input they produce. Without constancy the world would be a chaos of swelling, shrinking, stretching, darkening shapes. Size constancy and size-distance invariance Size constancy is the perception of an object as remaining the same size even though the size of its retinal image changes with distance. Try this. Hold one hand at arm's length and the other halfway to your face. The retinal image of the far hand is only about half the size of the near one, yet both look like normal hands of the same size. How is it done? The brain takes account of distance. The size-distance invariance hypothesis states that perceived size is proportional to retinal image size multiplied by perceived distance. If the retinal image halves while the perceived distance doubles, perceived size stays the same. It follows that size constancy should depend on depth cues, and should break down when they are removed. Key study: Holway and Boring (1941) Question. Does size constancy depend on information about distance? Method. Alfred Holway and Edwin Garrigues Boring (1886 to 1968) seated observers at the junction of two long corridors. Down one corridor, at distances from 10 to 120 feet, they placed test discs whose physical size was increased with distance so that every disc cast exactly the same retinal image (one degree of visual angle). In the other corridor was a comparison disc whose size the observer adjusted until it matched the test disc. Observers did this under four conditions: with both eyes, with one eye, with one eye through a small peephole, and finally through a peephole and a long black tunnel that hid almost every cue to distance. Results. With both eyes and full cues, observers matched the discs' physical sizes almost perfectly: size constancy was excellent. As cues were removed, their settings moved steadily towards the retinal size; with the peephole and tunnel, all the discs looked nearly the same size. Conclusion. Size constancy depends on information about distance, just as the size-distance invariance hypothesis predicts. Emmert's law You can test size-distance invariance on yourself with an afterimage. Stare for about thirty seconds at a bright lamp or a coloured square, then look at a sheet of paper in your hand, and then at a distant wall. The afterimage, which is a fixed patch of fatigued retina and therefore has a fixed retinal size, looks small on the paper and large on the wall. This is Emmert's law , described by the Swiss ophthalmologist Emil Emmert (1844 to 1911) in 1881: the perceived size of an afterimage is proportional to the perceived distance of the surface on which it is projected (Figure 4.4). Emmert's law is the size-distance relationship laid bare, because the retinal size is held perfectly constant and only perceived distance varies. Perceived size = retinal size × perceived distance Eye Near wall afterimage looks small Far wall afterimage looks large same retinal image Figure 4.4 Emmert's law. The dashed lines mark one fixed visual angle, the size of the afterimage on the retina. Projected onto a near wall the afterimage looks small; onto a far wall it looks large, because the brain scales retinal size by perceived distance. Size constancy is not perfect, and it depends on experience of distance. From the top of a tall building, people on the street look like ants, because we have little practice in judging vertical distances. In Section 4.8 you will meet a forest dweller who had never seen across open country and who took distant buffalo for insects. And when distance is misjudged, size is misjudged too; this is the key to several famous illusions (Section 4.5). Shape constancy Shape constancy is the perception of an object as keeping its shape even when its orientation to us changes, so that the retinal image changes shape. A round dinner plate on a table casts an elliptical image unless you look straight down on it, and an opening door casts a trapezoid, yet the plate looks round and the door rectangular. The British psychologist Robert Thouless (1894 to 1984) showed in 1931 that constancy is usually a compromise: when observers drew the shape of a tilted circle as it appeared to them, they drew an ellipse that was rounder than the retinal image but not fully round. He called this tendency for perception to lie between the retinal image and the real object phenomenal regression to the real object . Brightness and colour constancy A lump of coal in bright sunlight sends more light to your eye than a sheet of white paper in the shade, yet the coal still looks black and the paper white. Brightness constancy (more precisely, lightness constancy) is the perception of an object's lightness (its whiteness, greyness or blackness) as constant despite changes in the amount of light falling on it. The key, as Hans Wallach (1904 to 1998) showed in 1948, is the ratio principle : perceived lightness depends on the ratio of light reflected from an object to the light reflected from its surroundings. When the illumination changes, object and surroundings change together and the ratio stays the same. White paper reflects about 80 to 90 percent of the light falling on it and coal only a few percent, whatever the lighting. The ratio principle also explains simultaneous contrast : a grey square on a black background looks lighter than an identical grey square on a white background, because the ratio to the surround differs. Part of the neural basis lies in lateral inhibition , the tendency of active neurons in the retina to suppress the activity of their neighbours. Lateral inhibition exaggerates differences at borders and so enhances edge perception. It explains Mach bands , the illusory light and dark stripes seen at the boundaries of a graded strip, described by the Austrian physicist Ernst Mach (1838 to 1916) in 1865, and the grey smudges seen at the intersections of the white lines of the Hermann grid , described by Ludimar Hermann (1838 to 1914) in 1870 (the retinal circuitry is in Chapter 3 and the Physiological book). Colour constancy is the perception of an object's colour as constant under different coloured lights. A ripe banana looks yellow under the bluish light of a tube light, the orange light of a sodium street lamp and the reddish light of sunset, although the light it reflects changes greatly. The brain compares the light from the banana with the light from the rest of the scene and discounts the colour of the illuminant; adaptation of the cones to the prevailing light also helps. Edwin Land (1909 to 1991), the inventor of the Polaroid instant camera, built his retinex theory on demonstrations of this kind. Colour constancy can fail when the brain cannot tell what the illumination is. In February 2015 a photograph of a striped dress divided the internet: some people saw it as blue and black, others as white and gold. The two groups seemed to differ in whether their brains assumed the dress was lit by bluish daylight or by yellowish artificial light, and so discounted different illuminants. Location constancy Every time you move your eyes, the image of the world sweeps across your retina, yet the world stays still. Location constancy (position constancy) is the perception of stationary objects as remaining in the same place despite movements of the eyes, head and body. You can break it yourself with a demonstration that Helmholtz described. Close one eye and press very gently on the outer corner of the other eyelid with a fingertip: the world jumps. When you move your eyes in the normal way, the brain sends a copy of the motor command to the visual system, called a corollary discharge by Roger Sperry (1913 to 1994) and an efference copy by Erich von Holst , both in 1950, and uses it to cancel the expected movement of the retinal image. When your finger moves the eye, there is no command and nothing to cancel, so the movement of the image is attributed to the world. The same mechanism underlies the perception of real motion (Section 4.6). How often does the brain have to make this correction? Several times every second. When you read or scan a scene your eyes do not glide smoothly; they jump from point to point in rapid movements called saccades, separated by brief pauses called fixations, during which information is taken in. Even during a fixation the eyes are never perfectly still: they make a fine tremor, slow drifts and tiny rapid flicks called microsaccades. These small movements are not a flaw. In the 1950s researchers devised ways of keeping an image fixed on the same receptors however the eye moved (a stabilised retinal image), and the image faded from view within seconds, because receptors stimulated without change adapt (sensory adaptation, Chapter 3). By constantly refreshing the image on the retina, saccades and microsaccades ensure constant perception, while the corollary discharge keeps the world from seeming to jump with every one of them. Emmert's law concerns afterimages and their apparent size. Lateral inhibition enhances edges; it does not dull them, lower overall brightness or improve colour vision. Tiny rapid eye movements that keep the retinal image from fading are saccades (strictly, microsaccades), and they ensure constant perception ; a fixation is the pause between saccades, not a movement, and sensory adaptation is the fading they prevent. Constancy is a property of perception, not of sensation: the sensory input changes; the percept does not. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first.
