But a system that works by inference, as Helmholtz and Gregory argued, must sometimes infer wrongly. Those failures are far more than curiosities for puzzle books. A slip of the tongue tells you something about how speech is planned; in the same way, a visual illusion tells you which rules the visual system is following, because it catches the system applying a sensible rule in a place where the rule does not fit. What an illusion is An illusion is a perception that does not correspond to the physical properties of the stimulus: a misinterpretation of a stimulus that really exists in the outside world. Three features mark an illusion in the psychologist's sense. First, there is a real external stimulus; the lines of the Müller-Lyer figure are really there on the page. Second, the error is systematic. Nearly everyone who looks makes the same mistake, in the same direction and by roughly the same amount, so illusions can be measured with the psychophysical methods of Chapter 3. Third, most illusions are stubborn. You can measure the lines with a ruler, satisfy yourself that they are equal, look again, and still see them as unequal. This was the second objection to Gregory's hypothesis theory that you met in Section 4.1, and it tells you that much of the machinery behind illusions runs automatically, below the level that knowledge can reach. Where exactly does the error happen? Not in the eye. Photograph the Müller-Lyer figure and the two lines in the photograph are equal; the image on your retina is just as faithful. The receptors register the light correctly, so sensation is not distorted. What goes wrong is the interpretation of that light, the organising and inferring that turn a retinal image into a seen world. Optical illusions are therefore distortions of perception , not of sensation, which is why textbooks reach for them whenever they want to make the difference between sensation and perception concrete. Illusions are not only visual. Cross your index and middle fingers, close your eyes and roll a small marble between the two fingertips: you feel two marbles (Aristotle's illusion, described more than two thousand years ago). Lift a small box and a large box of exactly the same weight and the small one feels clearly heavier; this size-weight illusion was measured by the French physician Augustin Charpentier in 1891. Listen to a sequence of Shepard tones and the pitch seems to climb for ever without ever getting higher. In each case a real stimulus is correctly registered by the receptors and then misread. Many Indian textbooks of general psychology sort illusions into two classes, and examiners still use the terms. Personal illusions (individual illusions) are private and variable. They depend on the observer's state, expectations and surroundings, so they differ from person to person and from one occasion to the next. The standard example is the coil of rope seen as a snake at dusk: one person sees a snake, the next sees a rope, and the same person may not be fooled the following evening. Universal illusions , also called permanent or general illusions, are experienced by practically everyone, every time, because they arise from the normal working of the perceptual system: railway tracks that seem to converge in the distance, the moon that looks larger at the horizon, the unequal-looking lines of the Müller-Lyer figure. Most of the illusions studied in perception laboratories are universal illusions, and that is exactly what makes them useful. A universal error must come from a universal rule. Indian context The rope mistaken for a snake ( rajju-sarpa ) is one of the oldest illusions in Indian thought. In the Advaita Vedanta of Adi Shankaracharya (eighth century CE) it illustrates adhyasa , superimposition: the mind projects a snake onto the rope, just as, on that view, ignorance projects the world of appearances onto Brahman. Psychologically it is a model personal illusion. It needs dim light (weak bottom-up evidence), a setting in which snakes are expected, and a little fear (top-down influences, Section 4.8); and it vanishes the moment someone shines a torch on the rope. Exam trap "Rail tracks appearing to converge" was keyed as a permanent illusion , with "personal illusion", "visual illusion" and "Müller-Lyer illusion" as the other options. The item is testing the personal versus permanent classification: everyone sees the rails converge, every time, so the illusion is permanent (universal). It is of course also a visual illusion in the broad sense, but when "permanent" is offered alongside "personal", choose permanent. It is not the Müller-Lyer illusion. Strictly, what you are seeing is the depth cue of linear perspective (Section 4.3): the retinal images of the rails really do converge, and the illusion lies only in the impression that the rails themselves draw together. Finally, illusions result from a distortion in perception , not in sensation, adaptation or "translation" (a loose word for transduction, the receptor's conversion of energy into nerve signals, which works perfectly well when you look at an illusion). The Müller-Lyer illusion and the carpentered world The most studied illusion of all was published in 1889 by the German psychiatrist and sociologist Franz Carl Müller-Lyer (1857 to 1916). In the Müller-Lyer illusion , two lines (the shafts) are of equal length. One ends in arrowheads that point outwards, away from the shaft; the other ends in fins that flare outwards like the tail of an arrow. The shaft with the fins looks clearly longer than the shaft with the arrowheads (Figure 4.5, first panel). Look at the figure, then measure it. Müller-Lyer the shafts are equal Ponzo the two bars are equal Ebbinghaus centre circles are equal Zöllner the long lines are parallel Poggendorff the diagonals are one line Hering both lines are straight Figure 4.5 Six classic geometric illusions. In every panel the caption underneath is physically true, yet you see something else: the finned shaft looks longer, the upper bar looks longer, the circle among small circles looks larger, the long lines look tilted, the diagonal looks broken and the straight lines look bowed. Check them with a ruler. Why should a few short strokes at the ends of a line change its apparent length? The best-known answer came from Richard Gregory in 1963, and he called it inappropriate constancy scaling (it is also called the misapplied size constancy theory). The shafts in Figure 4.5 are drawn vertically; take the arrowhead version first. It resembles the outside corner of a building seen from the street: the vertical edge is nearest to you and the walls slope away on either side. The finned version resembles the inside corner of a room: the vertical edge where two walls meet is the farthest point from you, and the edges of the ceiling and floor come towards you. Gregory argued that the visual system reads these depth cues automatically, even in a flat drawing, and then applies size constancy to them (Section 4.4). The shaft that is coded as farther away (the inside corner) is scaled up and looks longer; the shaft coded as nearer (the outside corner) is scaled down and looks shorter. Two lines that cast the same retinal image, one of which is judged to be farther away, must be of different sizes; that is the size-distance invariance hypothesis doing its normal job in a place where it does not belong, a flat page on which both lines are really at the same distance. Gregory reported a striking piece of support: when Müller-Lyer figures are made luminous and shown in a dark room, where the flat surface of the paper cannot be seen, observers see them as three-dimensional corners, receding or approaching in just the way the theory predicts. But the theory has met real criticism. First, the illusion survives when the arrowheads and fins are replaced by small circles or squares at the ends of the lines, shapes that suggest no corner and no depth at all. Second, the figure does not look deep on paper, yet the theory needs depth to be registered. Third, a rival account, defended by the Australian psychologist Ross Day among others, holds that the visual system cannot completely separate the length of the shaft from the length of the whole figure, fins included, and the finned figure as a whole is longer. A fourth finding links back to Section 4.1: in a meta-analysis of 33 studies, Nicola Bruno and colleagues (2008) found that fast pointing movements to the ends of the shafts are much less affected by the illusion than verbal judgements are, as Milner and Goodale's separation of vision-for-action from vision-for-perception would predict. If Gregory is even partly right, the illusion should depend on experience with corners, and therefore on culture. In the late 1950s and early 1960s the psychologists Marshall Segall and Donald Thomas Campbell (1916 to 1996) and the anthropologist Melville Jean Herskovits (1895 to 1963) tested this idea with nearly two thousand children and adults from more than a dozen societies in Africa and the Philippines, and from the city of Evanston in the United States. Their reports (1963, and the book The Influence of Culture on Visual Perception , 1966) set out the carpentered-world hypothesis : people who grow up in a "carpentered" environment, full of rectangular rooms, buildings, windows and furniture made with saws and set squares, learn to read acute and obtuse angles in a drawing as right angles extending in depth, and so are more susceptible to the Müller-Lyer illusion. People raised in a non-carpentered environment, with round huts and few straight edges, should be less susceptible. That is broadly what they found. The urban American sample was among the most susceptible to the Müller-Lyer illusion, and some African samples, such as the San foragers of the Kalahari, were among the least. The rural Zulu, who traditionally lived in round huts with round doorways, became the textbook example of a non-carpentered culture. The same team also found the reverse pattern for the horizontal-vertical illusion (a vertical line looks longer than an equal horizontal line): it was strongest in people who live on open plains, where long stretches of ground recede horizontally into the distance, and weakest in people who live in dense forest, which is just what an experience-based account predicts. The hypothesis is not settled. A rival explanation proposed that people with more densely pigmented retinas (pigmentation tends to go with darker skin) detect contours slightly less sharply and are therefore less affected by such figures; schooling and experience with pictures differ between groups too; and later studies gave mixed results. But the work established the main point that matters for this chapter: susceptibility to illusions is partly learned, so illusions are not purely the product of innate machinery. Exam trap The Müller-Lyer illusion is strongest in cultures with buildings with corners (carpentered environments), not in cultures with "a lot of trees", not in those with "structures without many corners and angles" (that is the low-susceptibility group), and "more men than women" is pure decoration. The carpentered-world hypothesis is Segall, Campbell and Herskovits (1963, 1966). The illusion is "best explained by" misapplied size constancy (Gregory's inappropriate constancy scaling). Binocular disparity cannot be the cause, because the illusion works with one eye shut and on a flat page; lateral inhibition explains Mach bands and the Hermann grid (Section 4.4), not line length; figure-ground reversal is Rubin's vase (Section 4.2). Ponzo, the Ames room and the moon The same size-distance logic explains the second panel of Figure 4.5. The Italian psychologist Mario Ponzo (1882 to 1960) described it in 1911. In the Ponzo illusion , two identical horizontal bars are drawn between two lines that converge towards the top, like railway tracks receding into the distance, and the upper bar looks longer. Linear perspective (Section 4.3) tells the visual system that the upper bar is farther away; it casts the same retinal image as the lower bar; so, by size-distance invariance, it must be bigger. The illusion is strong in photographs of real roads and railway lines, where the depth cues are richer, which is what a depth-scaling account predicts. The most dramatic size illusion is a whole room. The Ames room was first built in 1946 (the commonly cited date; some textbooks cite Ames's account of 1952) by the American scientist Adelbert Ames Jr. (1880 to 1955), a lawyer turned painter turned researcher in physiological optics, developing an idea that Helmholtz had described. Seen through a peephole with one eye, it looks like an ordinary rectangular room. In fact, as Figure 4.6 shows, its back wall slopes away from the viewer, so that one back corner is about twice as far from the peephole as the other, and the walls, floor, ceiling and windows are distorted in exactly the way needed to make the room cast the same retinal image as a rectangular one. Two people of the same height standing in the two back corners now look absurdly different: the one in the near corner looks like a giant and the one in the far corner like a child. A person walking from one corner to the other seems to grow or shrink as they walk. far corner: person looks tiny near corner: person looks huge eye at the peephole plan view, from above real back wall apparent back wall lines of sight Figure 4.6 The Ames room seen from above. The real back wall (solid) slopes away, so the left corner is twice as far from the eye as the right. Each corner lies on the same line of sight as a corner of an ordinary rectangular room (dashed), so the eye assumes that both people stand at the same distance and judges their sizes from their retinal images alone. Why does the room win? Two assumptions are in conflict: that rooms are rectangular, and that people stay the same size. The brain has met far more rectangular rooms than people who change size, yet it keeps the room and sacrifices the person. Ames, whose view of perception became known as transactionalism, argued that every percept is a kind of bet based on our past dealings with the world, and that in a peephole view the bet on rectangular rooms is the safest one available. Familiarity can shift the bet. In 1952 Warren Wittreich reported the "Honi phenomenon", named after a woman nicknamed Honi who saw strangers change size in the room but saw her own husband almost undistorted; in a story often retold in textbooks, a researcher's wife arrived at the laboratory, saw her husband inside the room and said at once that the room was distorted. Ames also built a trapezoidal window that, when rotated steadily, seems to swing back and forth instead. Gordon Willard Allport (1897 to 1967) and Thomas Pettigrew found in 1957 that rural Zulu children, who had grown up with few rectangular windows, were less likely than urban children to see this illusion when the viewing conditions were poor: another sign that the "bet" is learned. The oldest illusion of all hangs in the sky. A full moon rising over the horizon looks enormous; the same moon high overhead a few hours later looks much smaller. This is the moon illusion , and it is purely perceptual. The moon's retinal image is the same size in both positions (about half a degree of visual angle, roughly the size of a pea held at arm's length); photographs show identical discs; and the horizon moon is in fact very slightly farther from you than the overhead moon, by about the radius of the Earth. Contrary to a popular belief, the atmosphere does not magnify it. The leading explanation, the apparent distance hypothesis , goes back about a thousand years to the Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham (about 965 to about 1040), known in Europe as Alhazen. The sky is not perceived as a hemisphere but as a flattened dome, whose horizon seems much farther away than its zenith, because at the horizon we see the moon across a great stretch of terrain filled with depth cues (fields, trees, buildings) while overhead there is only empty sky. A moon of constant retinal size that is registered as farther away must be larger; size-distance invariance again. Lloyd Kaufman and Irvin Rock supported this in 1962 by showing observers the moon through optical arrangements that removed or added the terrain: the horizon moon lost much of its enlargement when the terrain was hidden, and an elevated moon looked larger when it was seen across terrain. There is a puzzle, though. Asked which moon looks nearer, most people say the horizon moon, the opposite of what the theory seems to need. One resolution is that the registered distance that drives size scaling is unconscious, while the conscious judgement of distance is made afterwards from the size that has been seen ("it looks big, so it must be close"). A second explanation, angular size contrast, adds that the horizon moon is seen next to small-looking objects such as trees and roofs, while the overhead moon is dwarfed by the vast expanse of sky, a contrast effect like the Ebbinghaus illusion that follows. Exam trap The Ponzo, Müller-Lyer, Ames room and moon illusions are all explained by size-distance scaling going wrong : something registered as farther away is seen as bigger. The Ames room depends on the assumption that rooms are rectangular and must be viewed with one eye through a peephole , which removes binocular and motion cues. The moon illusion is not caused by the moon being nearer at the horizon (it is slightly farther), nor by atmospheric magnification or refraction; the retinal image is the same. "Apparent distance hypothesis" is the answer for the moon; Kaufman and Rock (1962) are its classic experimenters. Size contrast and bent lines Not every illusion is about depth. In the Ebbinghaus illusion (third panel of Figure 4.5), a circle surrounded by large circles looks smaller than an identical circle surrounded by small ones. It is named after Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909), the pioneer of memory research (Chapter 7), and was made widely known by Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927) in his laboratory manual of 1901, which is why it is also called the Titchener circles. The usual explanation is size contrast: the visual system judges size relative to the neighbours, just as it judges lightness relative to the surround in simultaneous contrast (Section 4.4). In 1995 Salvatore Aglioti, Joseph DeSouza and Melvyn Goodale used poker-chip versions of the figure and found that when people reached out to pick up the central disc, the opening of their finger and thumb fitted the disc's real size even though they saw it as larger or smaller; they summed this up as illusions that "deceive the eye but not the hand". Later studies have argued over how complete this immunity is, but the finding remains a classic piece of evidence for a separate vision-for-action system. A family of nineteenth-century illusions bends or breaks straight lines. In the Zöllner illusion , described in 1860 by the German astrophysicist Johann Karl Friedrich Zöllner (1834 to 1882), long parallel lines crossed by short oblique strokes, slanting in opposite directions on alternate lines, no longer look parallel; they seem to tilt towards and away from each other. When Zöllner sent his figure to the physicist Johann Christian Poggendorff (1796 to 1877), editor of the journal in which it appeared, Poggendorff noticed another distortion in it. In the Poggendorff illusion (1860), a straight diagonal line that passes behind a vertical strip seems to come out at the wrong place, so the two visible parts look misaligned. In the Hering illusion , described in 1861 by the German physiologist Ewald Hering (1834 to 1918), the same man who proposed the opponent-process theory of colour vision (Chapter 3), two straight parallel lines drawn across a pattern of lines radiating from a central point appear to bow outwards; Wilhelm Wundt drew a variant in which the background lines converge the other way and the parallels bow inwards. No single explanation covers this family. One idea is that the visual system tends to overestimate acute angles, perhaps because neurons tuned to neighbouring orientations inhibit one another (an orientation version of the lateral inhibition you met in Section 4.4), so each crossing line pushes the perceived orientation of the long line slightly away from itself. Another is that the figures are again read as perspective drawings: the radiating background of the Hering figure looks like a tunnel or a road stretching away. What these illusions share is the lesson that the visual system does not measure lines one at a time; it codes every element in relation to its context. Ambiguous and impossible figures A different kind of trick produces not a wrong percept but two percepts that take turns. An ambiguous figure (reversible figure) is a single unchanging stimulus that can be seen in two or more different ways, with the percept flipping from one to the other. You have already met Rubin's vase, in which figure and ground swap (Section 4.2). In 1832 the Swiss crystallographer Louis Albert Necker (1786 to 1861) noticed that his drawings of crystals seemed to jump in depth, and the Necker cube , a line drawing of a transparent wire cube, now carries his name: look at it for a few seconds and the face that was in front suddenly lies behind, then jumps forward again. Other famous examples are the duck-rabbit, used by the American psychologist Joseph Jastrow in 1899, and "My wife and my mother-in-law", a cartoon by W. E. Hill published in 1915 and brought into psychology by Edwin Boring in 1930, in which a young woman looking away and an old woman in profile share the same lines. Ambiguous figures are the strongest single argument for Gregory's view of perception as hypothesis testing. The stimulus does not change, so the flipping must come from the perceiver: the brain entertains one hypothesis, then the other, because the evidence fits both equally well. Why does it not settle on one? A popular explanation is that the neural representation of the current interpretation adapts or tires, letting the rival take over; another is that shifts of attention and fixation tip the balance (fixating a particular corner of the Necker cube tends to bring that corner forward). Knowledge matters too. Irvin Rock and his colleagues found in 1994 that young children rarely reverse ambiguous figures spontaneously unless they have been told that there are two interpretations to look for. An impossible figure is a drawing that the visual system reads as a solid object which could not exist in three dimensions. The best known is the Penrose triangle (tribar), whose three beams each look perfectly sensible but join at right angles to make a closed triangle. It was published, together with the never-ending Penrose staircase, in a short paper of 1958 by the British psychiatrist and geneticist Lionel Penrose (1898 to 1972) and his son, the mathematician Roger Penrose (born 1931), later a Nobel laureate in physics; the Swedish artist Oscar Reutersvärd had drawn a version in 1934, and the Dutch artist M. C. Escher built his lithographs Ascending and Descending (1960) and Waterfall (1961) around the Penroses' figures. Impossible figures work because each part is interpreted locally: every corner, taken by itself, is a legitimate piece of a three-dimensional object, and the visual system does not check that the local interpretations add up to a consistent whole. Notice the contrast with ambiguous figures. An ambiguous figure gives one stimulus two possible objects; an impossible figure gives one stimulus a single object that cannot be. Illusions, hallucinations and delusions For a clinical psychologist the most important thing about illusions is what they are not. Three terms are confused constantly, in examinations and in casual speech, and the distinctions between them are part of every mental status examination. An illusion, as you have seen, is a misinterpretation of a real external stimulus. A hallucination is a perception without an adequate external stimulus: the person hears a voice when no one is speaking or sees a figure in an empty room, and the experience has the full vividness of a real perception, is located in outer space and is not under voluntary control. The French psychiatrist Jean-Étienne Esquirol, in the early nineteenth century, was the first to separate the two clearly: in an illusion something is there and is misperceived; in a hallucination nothing is there at all. A delusion is not a perception at all. It is a false belief, held with unshakeable conviction, not open to correction by argument or evidence and out of keeping with the person's cultural and educational background: for example, the conviction that one's neighbours are broadcasting one's thoughts. Illusions and hallucinations are disorders of perception; delusions are disorders of the content of thought. The British psychiatrist Andrew Sims, in his textbook of descriptive psychopathology Symptoms in the Mind , adds a finer distinction that one past paper used as its options. Sensory distortions are changes in the perception of a real object that is perceived as it is but altered in intensity, quality or size: sounds that seem unbearably loud, colours that seem changed, objects that look too small (micropsia) or too large (macropsia). Sensory deceptions are new perceptions that are false, and they include both illusions and hallucinations. So "a real perceptual object perceived in a distorted way" describes a sensory distortion; "misinterpretation of stimuli arising from an external object" is the standard psychopathology definition of an illusion; "perception without an adequate external stimulus" is a hallucination; and "vivid mental images" describes imagery, which is experienced in the mind's eye rather than in outer space and which a person can usually call up or dismiss at will. Psychopathology recognises three kinds of illusion. A completion illusion depends on inattention: you read a misprinted word as the word you expected, and the error disappears as soon as you pay attention. An affect illusion is driven by emotion: a frightened child alone at night sees the coat hanging on the door as a man, and a grieving widow briefly "sees" her husband in a crowd. Pareidolia is the effortless perception of vivid, meaningful images in vague stimuli, such as faces in clouds, animals in the flames of a fire or a face on the front of a car; unlike the other two, it persists, and even grows richer, when you attend to it, and it coexists with knowing perfectly well what the stimulus really is. A last group of "illusions" belongs to memory rather than perception. In déjà vu ("already seen") a new situation feels as if it has been experienced before; in déjà entendu ("already heard") something heard for the first time feels as if it has been heard before; in déjà vécu ("already lived") a whole experience feels relived; and in jamais vu ("never seen") a familiar situation suddenly feels strange, as if it had never been seen. These are illusions of familiarity, occasional in healthy people and frequent in some forms of temporal lobe epilepsy. Do not confuse them with hypermnesia, an unusually vivid and detailed memory for past events, or with disorders of speech such as palilalia, the involuntary repetition of one's own words (Disorders book). Déjà entendu is the illusion of having heard something before; the illusion of having seen it before is déjà vu . A delusional perception , one of Kurt Schneider's first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia, is a normal perception given a sudden delusional meaning; it is not an illusion (Disorders book). Clinical link Illusions and visual hallucinations are common in delirium, the acute confusional state seen in high fever, alcohol withdrawal and severe medical illness, and they typically get worse in the dim light of evening, when bottom-up information is weakest. Elderly people with failing eyesight may develop vivid, silent visual hallucinations (often of small people or patterns) while knowing perfectly well that they are not real, a condition named after Charles Bonnet, the Swiss naturalist who in 1760 described it in his grandfather. Recognising which phenomenon a patient is describing, and whether insight is preserved, is a basic diagnostic skill (Disorders book). 4.6 Motion Perception Lower yield · not asked yet For most animals, movement matters more than anything else in the visual field: it means food, danger or a mate. A hungry frog will ignore dead, motionless flies yet snap at a moving speck, and a rabbit freezes because a predator's eye is drawn to motion. Human beings are no different. A flicker at the edge of your vision pulls your eyes towards it before you know what it is. Yet the perception of motion turns out to be as constructed as the perception of depth, and the illusions of motion are as revealing as the illusions of size. Real motion: two systems and a motion area Real motion is the perception of an object that is physically moving. You might think that seeing it is simply a matter of an image moving across the retina, and sometimes it is. When you hold your eyes still and a car crosses your field of view, its image sweeps across the retina, stimulating one receptor after another. Richard Gregory called this the image-retina system . But now follow a flying kite with your eyes. Its image stays more or less still on your fovea, while the image of the background streams across your retina in the opposite direction; yet you see the kite moving and the background standing still. Here the information comes from what Gregory called the eye-head system : the brain knows the eyes are turning because it issued the commands to turn them (the corollary discharge of Section 4.4), and it attributes movement to whatever the eyes are tracking. This is why the world stays still when you move your eyes normally, and jumps when you push your eyeball with a finger. The image-retina system relies on neurons that respond to movement in a particular direction and not in the opposite one. Such direction-selective cells were found in the retinas of frogs and rabbits and in the visual cortex of cats and monkeys (Section 4.7 describes the work of Hubel and Wiesel). In primates, an area near the junction of the occipital and temporal lobes, the middle temporal area (MT, also called V5), is specialised for motion: nearly all its neurons are direction-selective, and damaging it in monkeys impairs the perception of motion while leaving other aspects of vision intact. Clinical link In 1983 Josef Zihl and his colleagues in Munich described L.M., a woman who had suffered damage to this region on both sides of the brain. She could see shapes, colours and positions but not movement, a rare condition called akinetopsia (motion blindness). Pouring tea was difficult because the stream of liquid looked frozen, like a glacier, and she could not see the level rising in the cup, so it overflowed. Crossing the road was frightening: a car that seemed far away a moment ago was suddenly close, with no movement in between. Conversation was strange because she could not see the speaker's lips move. Her case shows that motion is not inferred from a series of positions; it is computed by its own neural machinery, which can be lost while position perception survives. Motion is also a powerful source of information about what things are. In 1973 the Swedish psychologist Gunnar Johansson (1911 to 1998) attached small lights to the shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees and ankles of a person dressed in black and filmed them walking in the dark. Any single frame of the film looks like a meaningless scatter of a dozen dots. The moment the film runs, every observer sees a person walking, and later studies showed that people can tell from such point-light displays whether the walker is a man or a woman, happy or sad, and even, sometimes, which of their friends it is. This perception of biological motion is an extreme case of the Gestalt law of common fate (Section 4.2): dots that move together in the pattern of a body are grouped into a body. Movement also tells an animal when something will hit it. As an object approaches at a steady speed its retinal image expands, and the Gibsonian psychologist David Lee showed in 1976 that the ratio of the image's size to its rate of expansion, which he called tau, specifies the time remaining before contact, without any need to know the object's distance or speed. Diving seabirds appear to fold their wings at a constant value of tau, and drivers use the expanding image of the car ahead when they brake. Gibson's idea that the optic array carries information directly (Section 4.1) is at its most persuasive here. Apparent motion: phi, beta and the cinema Can you see movement when nothing moves? You do every time you watch a film. Apparent motion is the perception of movement where there is no physical movement at all, produced by stimuli that appear in different places at different times. Its scientific study founded a school of psychology. In 1912 Max Wertheimer, working in Frankfurt with Koffka and Köhler as his observers, flashed two lines one after the other in slightly different places (the history is told in Chapter 2). When the interval between them was very short, about 30 milliseconds, observers saw two lines at once; when it was long, about 200 milliseconds, they saw one line and then the other; at intervals in between, around 60 milliseconds, they saw a single line moving from the first position to the second. The impression of movement was not in either stimulus; it arose from the relation between them, and Wertheimer took this as proof that a perceptual whole can contain something its parts do not. He called the phenomenon phi phenomenon . A subtlety lies behind the name. Wertheimer distinguished two experiences. At some intervals observers saw a smooth, object-like movement of the line from one place to the other; later writers named this beta movement , or optimal movement. At other intervals they reported a pure sensation of movement in the gap between the lines without seeing any object travel across it, which Wertheimer called pure phi. Most introductory textbooks, and most examination papers, now use "phi phenomenon" loosely for any apparent movement of flashing lights. Strictly, the film-like movement of an object is beta movement, and phi is the objectless motion; in 2000 Robert Steinman and his colleagues wrote a paper whose title says it all, "Phi is not beta". In 1915 Adolf Korte showed that apparent motion is lawful: for example, the farther apart the two lights, the longer the interval needed between them for the best movement (Korte's laws). Apparent motion is everywhere once you look for it. The strings of lights that seem to chase each other round a balcony at Diwali, the arrows that seem to slide along a shop sign and the running headlines of a news ticker are all rows of stationary bulbs switching on and off in sequence. Stroboscopic motion is the apparent motion produced when a series of still pictures, each slightly different from the last, is presented in rapid succession. A cinema film shows 24 still frames each second (the projector flashes each frame two or three times, so that the light flickers faster than the eye can follow, Chapter 3), a flip book does the same in your hands, and an animated cartoon is drawn frame by frame. The visual system's motion detectors respond to such sequences much as they respond to real motion, and brain imaging shows that apparent motion activates area MT just as real motion does. Early researchers gave Greek letters to other varieties of apparent movement as well; the one you are most likely to meet is gamma movement, the apparent expansion of a figure when it is suddenly lit and its contraction when the light goes off. Exam trap The phi phenomenon was described by Max Wertheimer in 1912 , and that paper is usually taken as the founding of Gestalt psychology. In loose usage phi means any apparent movement from lights flashed in sequence; strictly, smooth movement of an object is beta movement and objectless "pure" motion is phi . Motion pictures produce stroboscopic motion . None of these involves anything physically moving, which is what separates apparent motion from real motion . Motion parallax (Section 4.3) is a depth cue produced by real movement of the observer; it is not an illusion of motion. Induced motion and the autokinetic effect On a windy night, look at the moon through scattered clouds. The moon seems to race across the sky while the clouds stand still. In reality the clouds are moving and the moon, for the purposes of your perception, is not. This is induced motion : a stationary object appears to move because the frame that surrounds it moves. The German Gestalt psychologist Karl Duncker (1903 to 1940), whom you will meet again in Chapter 8 for his work on problem solving, studied it in 1929. In a dark room he showed observers a luminous dot inside a luminous rectangle and moved the rectangle slowly to one side. Observers saw the rectangle as still and the dot as moving the opposite way. The visual system treats the larger, surrounding frame as the stable background against which smaller things move, which is usually a safe assumption, since rooms, landscapes and skies rarely move. The same rule applies to your own body. Sit in a stationary train at a busy station such as Mumbai Central, and when the train on the next platform pulls out, you feel your own train begin to move, perhaps even sway, until you glance at the platform. The illusion of self-motion produced by a large moving visual field is called vection . It is induced motion with the observer as the "dot" and the neighbouring train as the "frame", and it is the principle behind flight simulators and some forms of motion sickness. Now remove the frame altogether. Sit in a completely dark room and look steadily at a single small, stationary point of light. Within a few seconds the light begins to drift, wander or swing, sometimes by what seems a large distance, even though it is perfectly still. This is the autokinetic effect (autokinesis), long noticed by astronomers watching single stars and by night pilots who have mistaken a solitary star or distant lamp for another aircraft. Its cause is the absence of any frame of reference. In darkness the eyes drift slightly, and the small commands needed to hold fixation steady are not fully accounted for, so the brain cannot tell whether the image or the eye has moved; with no visible background against which to check, it attributes some of the uncertainty to the light. The amount and direction of movement seen differ from person to person and from moment to moment, which made the effect perfect for one of the most famous experiments in social psychology. Key study: Sherif's autokinetic norms (1935) Question. How do social norms form when a situation is ambiguous and there is no objectively correct answer? Method. The Turkish-American social psychologist Muzafer Sherif (1906 to 1988) seated participants in a completely dark room and showed them a stationary pinpoint of light, asking them on each of many trials to say how far it had moved. Some first made their judgements alone and then in groups of two or three, calling out their estimates aloud; others started in groups and were later tested alone. Results. Alone, each person soon settled on a personal range and a typical estimate, and these differed widely from one person to another. In groups, the estimates converged over trials on a common group norm. When people who had formed a norm in a group were later tested alone, they kept to the group's norm. Conclusion. When reality is ambiguous, people use one another as a frame of reference, and the norms they build together become their own private standards (Sherif reported the work in 1935 and in his book The Psychology of Social Norms , 1936). In 1961 Robert Jacobs and Donald Campbell showed that an arbitrary, exaggerated norm planted by a confederate survived for several "generations" of a laboratory group after the confederate had left and members had been replaced one by one. Criticism. Because the movement is wholly illusory, there is no right answer to resist, so the study shows informational influence (using others as a source of information), not the yielding to group pressure on an obvious question that Solomon Asch tested in 1951 with judgements of line length (Social book). Exam trap Sherif used the autokinetic effect to study norm formation; Asch used line-length judgements to study conformity. The autokinetic effect is a stationary light seen moving in darkness , with no frame of reference; induced motion is a stationary object seen moving because its frame moves (the moon "racing" behind clouds, Duncker 1929); vection is illusory self-motion (the train beside yours pulls out). The motion aftereffect In 1834 a visitor to the Scottish Highlands, Robert Addams, stared for some time at the waterfall at the Falls of Foyers, near Loch Ness, and then turned his eyes to the rocks beside it. The rocks seemed to drift slowly upwards, in the direction opposite to the falling water. This motion aftereffect , often called the waterfall illusion, is the illusory movement of a stationary scene in the direction opposite to a movement that has been watched for some time. You can produce it after staring out of the window of a moving train: when the train stops, the platform seems to creep the other way. The explanation is adaptation in direction-selective neurons, and it parallels the colour afterimages of Chapter 3. A stationary scene normally produces roughly equal, low activity in cells tuned to downward and to upward motion, and the brain reads the balance as "no movement". Prolonged watching of downward motion fatigues the downward-tuned cells. When you then look at the still rocks, the upward-tuned cells fire at their normal resting rate while the tired downward cells fire below theirs, the balance tips towards "up", and you see upward drift. Two further observations make the aftereffect especially informative. First, the rocks seem to move without getting anywhere: they drift upwards yet stay in the same place. That paradox shows that the brain codes motion and position separately, just as L.M.'s akinetopsia suggests. Second, if you adapt one eye and then test with the other, a weaker aftereffect is still seen, so at least part of the adaptation must take place in the visual cortex, where cells first receive input from both eyes. A rotating spiral gives a vivid version: after watching a spiral that seems to expand, a friend's face looks as if it is shrinking. Answers: (1) illusion, (2) permanent, (3) scaling, (4) carpentered, (5) Ames, (6) Titchener, (7) hallucination, (8) entendu, (9) autokinetic, (10) aftereffect. 4.7 Pattern and Object Recognition Lower yield · 2 Qs You recognise your mother's voice on a crackling phone line, a friend's face across a crowded platform at Bengaluru City station, and the letter A whether it is printed in a newspaper, scrawled on a blackboard or carved in stone. You do it in a fraction of a second and you cannot say how. Pattern recognition is the process of identifying a sensory pattern by matching it with a representation stored in long-term memory; when the pattern is a three-dimensional thing in the world, psychologists speak of object recognition. The difficulty is variability. The same letter or object almost never produces the same retinal image twice: it changes with size, distance, angle, lighting, partial hiding and, for letters, the hand or font that made it. Any theory of recognition has to explain how a single stored representation can match all of these. This section follows the main attempts, roughly in the order in which they were proposed. Template matching The simplest idea is that memory holds a template for every known pattern: an exact, miniature copy, like a stencil. In template matching , the incoming pattern is compared with the stored templates point by point, and it is recognised as whichever template it overlaps best. Machines work this way when the input is standardised. The numbers printed along the bottom of an Indian bank cheque are in a special magnetic ink and a fixed typeface so that a reader in the clearing house can match them against templates; barcode scanners work on the same principle. For human recognition the theory fails quickly. A template for A matches only an A of the same size, shape, slant and position. To recognise every A you would need a separate template for every variant, an impossible number, and you would still be stuck the first time you met a new handwriting. One could add a preliminary stage that rotates, shrinks or centres the input before matching (normalisation), but to know how to rotate it the system would already have to know what it was. And templates cannot explain why the same shape is read differently in different contexts, as you will see at the end of this section. Template matching survives as a component of some modern theories, but no one now believes it is the whole story. Feature analysis and the Pandemonium model A more flexible idea is that patterns are recognised from their parts. According to feature analysis (feature theories), every pattern can be described as a set of distinctive features , elementary components such as vertical lines, horizontal lines, oblique lines, curves, angles and intersections. An A is two obliques meeting at the top plus a horizontal bar; an H is two verticals plus a horizontal. The perceiver detects the features present in the input and compares this list with the feature lists stored for each pattern. Because features stay the same when a letter changes size or style, the theory handles variability far better than templates do. Two kinds of evidence supported it. When people are shown letters very briefly and asked to identify them, the letters they confuse are those that share many features: P with R, E with F, C with G, while O and X are almost never confused. Eleanor Gibson and her colleagues used such confusions in the 1960s to work out a set of distinctive features for the letters of the alphabet. Ulric Neisser showed in 1964 that it is much faster to find a Z hidden in a list of rounded letters (O, Q, D, C) than in a list of angular ones (X, V, M, W), because in the first list the Z is the only item with straight-line features, while in the second every item shares them. The best-known feature model was proposed in 1959 by the computer scientist Oliver Selfridge (1926 to 2008), one of the founders of artificial intelligence. He called it Pandemonium , after the capital of hell in John Milton's Paradise Lost , because it imagined recognition as the work of crowds of shrieking "demons", each a simple processing unit (Figure 4.7). Image demons record the incoming pattern. Feature demons , each responsible for one feature, inspect the image and shout when they find their feature. Cognitive demons , one for each letter, listen to the feature demons and shout in proportion to how many of their own features are present. A decision demon listens to the cognitive demons and picks the loudest. Presented with R, the demons for P and B shout fairly loudly, because they share many features with R, but the R demon shouts loudest of all. Two features of the model are important. All the demons at each level work at the same time (parallel processing), and the model could learn by adjusting how much weight each cognitive demon gave to each feature, which made it an ancestor of today's neural network models. Neisser's Cognitive Psychology (1967) made it famous among psychologists. Image demon Feature demons Cognitive demons Decision demon R records the input image vertical line horizontal line oblique line curve A: quiet B: louder P: louder R: loudest picks the loudest: it is R each looks for one feature loudness = number of matching features Figure 4.7 Selfridge's Pandemonium (1959) recognising the letter R. Feature demons report the features present; every cognitive demon shouts in proportion to its matching features, so B and P shout too, but R shouts loudest and the decision demon chooses it. Notice that all the demons at each stage work in parallel. Feature theories received spectacular support from the brain. In the late 1950s, at Johns Hopkins University, the neurophysiologists David Hubel (1926 to 2013) and Torsten Wiesel (born 1924) began recording from single neurons in the visual cortex of cats. Key study: Hubel and Wiesel's feature detectors (1959 onwards) Question. What kinds of stimuli make individual neurons in the primary visual cortex fire? Method. Hubel and Wiesel lowered fine microelectrodes into the striate (primary visual) cortex of anaesthetised cats and recorded the activity of one neuron at a time while projecting simple patterns of light onto a screen in front of the animal. Results. For hours, the spots of light that worked so well for retinal cells produced almost nothing. Then, as they slid a glass slide into the projector, one cell began to fire furiously: the faint shadow of the slide's straight edge, sweeping across the screen at a particular angle, was the stimulus it wanted. Systematic work over the next years distinguished simple cells , which respond best to a line or edge of a particular orientation at a particular place in the visual field; complex cells , which respond to a line of a particular orientation anywhere within a larger field, often only when it moves in a particular direction; and hypercomplex (end-stopped) cells, which respond best to lines of a particular length or to corners. Conclusion. The visual cortex contains feature detectors , neurons that respond selectively to particular features of a stimulus, arranged so that simple features are combined into more complex ones as information moves through the system. Hubel and Wiesel shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Roger Sperry. Criticism. Later work showed that such cells are better described as filters tuned to patterns of light and dark at different scales than as detectors of "lines" in the everyday sense, and that their responses are shaped by context and attention. The anatomy is covered in the Physiological book. In the same year, 1959, Jerome Lettvin and his colleagues published "What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain", describing cells in the frog's visual system that responded best to small dark moving spots, nicknamed bug detectors; this is the reason a frog snaps at a moving speck but ignores a dead fly. Further along the primate visual system, cells in the inferior temporal cortex respond to complex shapes such as hands and faces, and in 2005 Rodrigo Quian Quiroga and his colleagues found single neurons in the human medial temporal lobe that fired to many different photographs of one particular film star and not to other people. The brain seems to build complex detectors out of simple ones, much as Pandemonium proposed. Feature theories nevertheless have serious limits. A list of features says nothing about how the features are arranged, yet T, L and + are all one vertical and one horizontal line: the relations between features matter as much as the features themselves, so the stored description must be a structural description, not a list. Features also struggle with three-dimensional objects seen from different angles, and they cannot explain the effects of context that you will meet below. And there is evidence that the whole is often processed before its parts. In 1977 David Navon showed people large letters made up of small letters (a big H made of small S's): they identified the large letter faster than the small ones, and the large letter interfered with naming the small letters more than the reverse. This global precedence is just what the Gestalt psychologists would have expected. Prototypes A third approach replaces exact copies with averages. According to prototype theory , memory stores for each category a prototype : an idealised, abstract representation of the typical member, the central tendency of all the examples one has met, which need not correspond to any example actually seen. An incoming pattern is recognised as belonging to the category whose prototype it most resembles; it does not need to match exactly, only closely enough. Your prototype of a dog is a sort of average dog, and you recognise a new breed as a dog because it is reasonably similar to it. The idea is most closely associated with Eleanor Rosch (born 1938), whose work in the 1970s on natural categories showed that some members of a category are more typical than others (a robin is a better example of a bird than a penguin) and are recognised faster (concepts and categories are treated fully in Chapter 8). The most elegant evidence came from Michael Posner (born 1936) and Steven Keele in 1968. They created random patterns of dots as prototypes, then made distorted versions of each by moving the dots slightly. Participants learned to sort the distortions into categories but never saw the prototypes themselves. In a later test, the never-seen prototypes were classified as accurately as the distortions that had actually been studied, and more accurately than new distortions, and the advantage held up better over time. People had abstracted the prototype from its variants. Prototype theory thus explains recognition of new examples and of typicality, which templates cannot. Its weakness is that it throws away information that people do seem to keep: we know that dogs vary enormously in size and that some birds cannot fly. A rival, exemplar theory, holds that we store many individual examples and compare new items with all of them. Exam trap "An idealised representative object of a category" is a prototype . A template is an exact stored copy that must match point for point; a feature is an elementary part such as a line or curve; geons are Biederman's three-dimensional building-block shapes. Pandemonium is Selfridge's 1959 feature model with image, feature, cognitive and decision demons. Hubel and Wiesel's feature detectors were found first in the cat ; the frog's "bug detectors" are Lettvin's. Recognition-by-components: Biederman's geons Templates, features and prototypes were mostly developed for flat patterns such as letters. How do we recognise solid objects seen from any angle? The most influential answer is the recognition-by-components theory (RBC) proposed in 1987 by the American psychologist Irving Biederman . Its central claim is that every object can be described as an arrangement of a small number of basic three-dimensional shapes, which Biederman called geons (short for geometric ions): blocks, cylinders, spheres, cones, wedges, arcs and so on. He estimated that about 36 geons are enough. That sounds far too few, until you remember that about 44 phonemes are enough to build every word of spoken English. What matters is the combination and arrangement. A cup is an arc attached to the side of a cylinder; a bucket is the same two geons with the arc attached to the top. How are geons found in the image? Biederman proposed that the visual system first extracts the edges of the object and then divides it into parts at regions of deep concavity, the places where the contour bends sharply inwards, such as where the handle of a cup meets its body. Each part is then identified as a geon from non-accidental properties , properties of edges in the image that are very unlikely to arise by accident from a particular viewpoint and that therefore stay the same from almost any angle. He listed five: curvature, parallel lines, cotermination (edges ending at a common point), symmetry and collinearity (points lying along a straight line). A straight edge in the image almost always means a straight edge in the object; parallel edges almost always mean parallel edges. Because geons can be identified from almost any viewpoint, the theory predicts that recognition should be largely viewpoint-invariant: an object should be recognised equally easily from most angles, unless a key geon is hidden. The theory made a striking prediction about damaged pictures. Biederman deleted the same amount of contour from line drawings of objects in two ways. When the deletions were in the middle of line segments, people still recognised the objects easily, because the concavities and non-accidental properties survived. When the deletions removed the vertices and concavities, the objects became almost impossible to identify. Biederman and Peter Gerhardstein (1993) also found that seeing an object primed later naming of the same object almost as well when it was rotated by 135 degrees as when the view was identical, which fits viewpoint invariance. The evaluation is mixed. RBC explains how we tell a cup from a bucket or a dog from a chair, but not how we tell one breed of dog, or one face, from another, because those discriminations depend on fine differences in shape and surface that geons ignore. Recognition is often viewpoint-dependent after all: Michael Tarr and Heinrich Bülthoff (1995), using novel objects learned from particular views, found that recognition was faster and more accurate from the familiar views. Colour and surface texture help recognition more than a pure edge theory allows. And like Marr's theory, below, RBC is almost entirely bottom-up, with little role for expectation and context. Marr's computational theory Biederman built on the work of the British neuroscientist David Marr (1945 to 1980), who worked at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and died of leukaemia at the age of 35; his book Vision was published after his death, in 1982. Marr made two lasting contributions. The first was a way of thinking. Any information-processing system, he argued, must be understood at three levels: the computational level (what problem is being solved, and why), the algorithmic or representational level (what representations and procedures solve it) and the implementational level (how the procedures are carried out in neurons or silicon). This is the computational approach you met by name in Section 4.1. The second was a theory of how vision proceeds, through a series of increasingly rich representations: The primal sketch is a two-dimensional description of the main changes in light intensity in the image: edges, bars, blobs and line endings. Marr divided it into a raw primal sketch (the intensity changes themselves) and a full primal sketch (in which these are grouped, by Gestalt-like principles, into contours and regions). The 2.5-D sketch (two-and-a-half-dimensional sketch) describes the depth and orientation of every visible surface, worked out from cues such as binocular disparity, motion, shading and texture (Section 4.3). It is viewer-centred : it describes the surfaces as they face this observer from this viewpoint, and it says nothing about the hidden back of the object. The 3-D model representation describes the object's three-dimensional shape and the arrangement of its parts in an object-centred frame, independent of the observer's viewpoint, typically as a hierarchy of cylinder-like components arranged along axes. Only at this stage can the object be matched with stored descriptions and recognised from any angle. Marr's achievement was to show how much computation recognition requires, and to inspire a generation of computational models. His theory, however, is overwhelmingly bottom-up (Marr himself admitted that top-down processing is "sometimes used and necessary" but largely left it out), and no one has yet shown how the fully viewpoint-independent 3-D models he proposed could actually be computed.
