Theory Key name and year What is stored Strength Weakness Template matching (Early machine models) Exact copies Works for standardised input Cannot cope with variation Feature analysis Selfridge, 1959; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959 Lists of distinctive features Handles size and style; neural support Ignores relations between features and context Prototype Posner and Keele, 1968; Rosch, 1970s An idealised average Explains new examples and typicality Loses information about variation Recognition-by-components Biederman, 1987 Arrangements of about 36 geons Viewpoint invariance; damaged drawings Poor at fine discriminations; bottom-up only Computational Marr, 1982 3-D model descriptions Precise stages: primal sketch, 2.5-D sketch, 3-D model Neglects top-down processing Exam trap The theory that objects are recognised from geons is Biederman's recognition-by-components theory (1987), not Pandemonium, not prototype theory and not template matching. Marr's stages come in the order primal sketch, 2.5-D sketch, 3-D model ; the 2.5-D sketch is viewer-centred and the 3-D model is object-centred . Marr's book Vision appeared in 1982 , two years after his death. Faces: a special case Faces pose the hardest recognition problem of all. Every face has the same parts in the same arrangement, two eyes above a nose above a mouth, so faces cannot be told apart by listing their features or geons. What distinguishes one face from another is the fine spacing and shape of the parts, their configuration, and there is good evidence that faces are processed holistically, as wholes, more than other objects are. In 1969 Robert Yin showed that turning photographs upside down impairs the recognition of faces much more than the recognition of houses or aeroplanes, the face inversion effect ; inversion seems to disrupt configural processing. In the Thatcher illusion, described by Peter Thompson in 1980, a photograph of Margaret Thatcher with the eyes and mouth cut out and turned upside down looks grotesque when the face is upright but almost normal when the whole picture is inverted. Brain imaging by Nancy Kanwisher and her colleagues (1997) identified a region in the fusiform gyrus of the temporal lobe, the fusiform face area , that responds much more strongly to faces than to other objects. The clearest evidence that face recognition is special comes from people who have lost it. Prosopagnosia (face blindness), named in 1947 by the German neurologist Joachim Bodamer (1910 to 1985) from the Greek for "face" and "not knowing", is a severe difficulty in recognising familiar faces, including one's own in a mirror, with much less impairment in recognising other objects. Acquired prosopagnosia follows damage to the occipitotemporal region, including the fusiform gyrus. Developmental prosopagnosia occurs without any obvious brain damage and may affect up to about 2 percent of people; Oliver Sacks, whom you met in Section 4.3, had it, and the American writer Heather Sellers did not realise until well into adulthood why she sometimes failed to recognise her own mother and husband. People with prosopagnosia recognise others by their voices, hairstyles, clothes and walk. Some of them show covert recognition: their skin conductance rises when they see a familiar face that they insist they do not know, a dissociation between recognition and awareness that anticipates Section 4.9. Clinical link In Capgras delusion, a patient insists that a spouse or parent has been replaced by an identical impostor. One influential explanation, proposed by Hadyn Ellis and Andrew Young in 1990, is that it is the mirror image of covert recognition in prosopagnosia: conscious recognition of the face is intact, but the emotional response that normally accompanies a familiar face is missing, and the patient explains the strange lack of feeling with a delusion. The disorders of face perception show how recognition, emotional familiarity and belief can come apart (Disorders and Physiological books). Top-down help: the word superiority effect and context Every theory so far has been mainly bottom-up, building recognition from the stimulus. Yet recognition is also driven by what we know. The clearest demonstration is with letters and words. As long ago as 1886, James McKeen Cattell (1860 to 1944) found that in a very brief exposure readers could report more letters when the letters formed a word than when they were a random string. The modern version was devised by Gerald Reicher in 1969 and refined by Daniel Wheeler in 1970. A string of letters, such as WORD, a single letter such as D, or a non-word such as ORWD, is flashed for a fraction of a second and then covered by a pattern mask. The participant must say which of two letters appeared in a given position, for example D or K in the fourth position. Both choices are chosen so that they make a word (WORD or WORK), so guessing from knowledge of words cannot help. Even so, the letter is identified more accurately when it is part of a word than when it is part of a non-word, or even when it is shown alone. This is the word superiority effect : a letter is perceived more accurately in a word than in isolation or in a meaningless string. How can a whole word be easier than one of its letters? In 1981 James McClelland and David Rumelhart explained it with their interactive activation model, in which information flows both ways between levels: features activate letters, letters activate words, and activated words send activation back down to their own letters, strengthening them. The letter D in WORD gets support from above; the D in ORWD gets none. The model is a modern, more precise descendant of Pandemonium, with the crucial addition of top-down connections. Context works the same way beyond the page. Selfridge himself drew attention to the phrase THE CAT written with an identical, ambiguous character in the middle of both words, half H and half A: everyone reads it as THE CAT, without noticing that the same shape has been read as two different letters. Stephen Palmer showed in 1975 that after looking at a kitchen scene, people identified a briefly flashed loaf of bread more accurately than a mailbox or a drum of similar shape. In 1970 Richard Warren played listeners a recorded sentence in which one sound in the word "legislatures" had been replaced by a cough; nearly all of them heard the missing sound clearly and could not say where the cough had occurred (phonemic restoration). In all of these, bottom-up information from the stimulus and top-down information from knowledge and context are combined, just as Neisser's perceptual cycle in Section 4.1 proposed. The next section looks more closely at the top-down side: at how expectations, needs, feelings, experience and culture shape what we see. Exam trap The word superiority effect (Reicher, 1969) is better identification of a letter when it appears in a word than when it appears alone or in a non-word; it is evidence for top-down processing. Prosopagnosia is face blindness, linked to the fusiform region; it is not a loss of all object recognition (that is visual object agnosia) and not a memory disorder. The face inversion effect is Yin (1969); the Thatcher illusion is Thompson (1980). 4.8 Perceptual Set, Learning and Culture Lower yield · 1 Q If perception were simply a matter of recording the stimulus, everyone would see the same thing in the same picture. They do not. A hungry person, a frightened person, a person who has just been looking at pictures of animals and a person who grew up in a forest may all look at the same figure and see different things. This section examines the perceiver's contribution to perception, which Section 4.1 described in general terms as top-down processing. Perceptual set: seeing what we expect A perceptual set is a readiness to perceive a stimulus in a particular way: in the definition given in 1955 by the American psychologist Floyd Henry Allport (1890 to 1979), "a perceptual bias or predisposition or readiness to perceive particular features of a stimulus". A set can be created by expectation, context, instructions, recent experience, needs, emotions, values and culture. It works in two ways: it makes us notice some things rather than others (selection, closely linked to selective attention, Chapter 5), and it makes us interpret ambiguous input one way rather than another (interpretation). Look at Figure 4.8. The shape in the middle is identical whichever way you read it, yet read across it is the letter B and read downwards it is the number 13. Jerome Seymour Bruner (1915 to 2016) and Leigh Minturn used exactly this ambiguous figure in 1955: participants who had just seen a series of letters drew it as a B, and those who had just seen numbers drew it as 13. This is the context effect , the influence of surrounding stimuli and of the situation on the perception of a target. read across: the letter B read down: the number 13 Figure 4.8 The context effect. The central shape is physically identical in both readings: between A and C it is seen as the letter B, between 12 and 14 as the number 13 (after Bruner and Minturn, 1955). The stimulus does not decide; the context does. Recent experience creates sets just as powerfully. In 1961 B. R. Bugelski and Delia Alampay showed participants an ambiguous drawing that can be seen either as a rat or as a bald man wearing glasses. Those who had first seen a series of pictures of animals overwhelmingly saw a rat; those who had seen no such series, or pictures of people, mostly saw a man. As early as 1935 Robert Leeper had shown that a brief look at an unambiguous version of the "wife and mother-in-law" figure (Section 4.5) determined which woman people saw in the ambiguous one. The same set makes proofreading so hard: read "Paris in the the spring" quickly and most people miss the repeated word, because they see what they expect a sentence to say. Sets can cross the senses. In 1976 Harry McGurk and John MacDonald dubbed a recording of a voice saying "ba" onto a film of a face saying "ga". Viewers heard "da", a fusion of the two, and went on hearing it even when they knew the trick; with their eyes shut they heard "ba". The McGurk effect shows that speech perception integrates sight and sound automatically, and that what we see changes what we hear. Clinical link Clinicians have perceptual sets too. In 1973 David Rosenhan reported that eight healthy "pseudopatients", admitted to psychiatric hospitals after claiming to hear voices, behaved normally from then on, yet staff interpreted their ordinary behaviour through the diagnosis: one nurse recorded that a patient "engages in writing behaviour" when he was taking notes. Later investigators have questioned how the study was carried out, but the lesson stands. Once a label is applied, it creates a set that shapes what the clinician notices, which is why structured assessment and deliberately considering alternative explanations matter. The same danger, called diagnostic overshadowing, occurs when a physical illness in a person with a psychiatric diagnosis is wrongly put down to the psychiatric condition. Needs, values and emotions: the New Look In the late 1940s Bruner and his colleagues launched what became known as the New Look in perception, the claim that perception is shaped not only by expectation but by the perceiver's needs, values and emotions. The evidence came from a run of ingenious experiments. In 1948 David McClelland and John Atkinson showed dim or even blank slides to sailors at a naval training base who had gone one, four or sixteen hours without food and asked them what they could see; the longer they had gone hungry, the more often they reported food-related objects. Values had similar effects. In 1948 Leo Postman, Bruner and Elliott McGinnies measured the values of their participants with the Allport-Vernon Study of Values and found that words related to a person's strongest values (for example, religious words for people with strong religious values) were recognised at shorter exposure times than words related to weak values. Key study: Bruner and Goodman's coins (1947) Question. Do needs and values change the perceived size of objects? Method. Bruner and Cecile Goodman tested ten-year-old children in Boston. The experimental group, made up of children from a well-off progressive school and children from a settlement house in a poor district, adjusted the size of a circular patch of light until it matched the size of coins (1, 5, 10, 25 and 50 cent pieces) held in the palm of the hand. A control group made the same judgements for cardboard discs of the same sizes. Results. Coins were judged larger than they really were, and on the whole the more valuable the coin, the greater the overestimation; cardboard discs were judged much more accurately. Poor children overestimated the coins considerably more than rich children did. Conclusion. The value of an object and the perceiver's need for it can influence its perceived size: economic deprivation affects perception. Criticism. The samples were small, and the rich and poor children differed in many ways besides income, including familiarity with handling coins. In 1949 Launor Carter and Kermit Schooler found the rich-poor difference when coins were judged from memory but not when they were present, which suggests that the effect may lie partly in memory and judgement rather than in perception itself. The most controversial New Look claim was perceptual defence , the idea that we resist perceiving stimuli that are threatening or emotionally disturbing. In 1949 Elliott McGinnies flashed words in a tachistoscope (a device for presenting visual stimuli for precisely controlled, very short times) at gradually longer exposures until participants could read them. Emotionally loaded taboo words needed longer exposures to be recognised than neutral words. More intriguingly, the galvanic skin response, a measure of emotional arousal, rose for the taboo words before participants reported seeing them, as if some part of the mind had read the word and decided to keep it out of awareness. Critics were quick to respond. Davis Howes and Richard Solomon (1950) pointed out that taboo words are less frequent in print, and less frequent words need longer exposures anyway; and participants, especially students reporting to a stranger in 1949, may simply have hesitated to say such words aloud until they were certain. The opposite tendency, faster recognition of threatening stimuli, is called perceptual vigilance, and it is now the better supported of the two. In 1951 Richard Lazarus (1922 to 2002) and Robert McCleary paired some nonsense syllables with electric shocks; later, when the syllables were flashed too briefly to be identified correctly, the shock-paired syllables still produced larger skin-conductance responses. They called this discrimination without awareness subception , a bridge to the subliminal perception of Section 4.9. Emotions and bodily states shape perception in more everyday ways too. People who are anxious are more likely to interpret ambiguous stimuli as threatening: asked to write down spoken words that sound the same but have different meanings, such as die and dye, anxious people more often write the threatening spelling. Some studies have reported that hills look steeper to people who are tired or carrying a heavy backpack, although other researchers argue that such effects reflect what participants think the experimenter wants rather than a change in what they see. The safest conclusion is that needs, values and emotions certainly influence attention, interpretation and judgement, and probably influence perception itself, but less dramatically than the New Look first claimed. Exam trap "Who demonstrated that economic deprivation affects perception?" Bruner and Goodman (1947, the coin study). Segall and Herskovits (with Campbell) studied culture and illusions (the carpentered world), not poverty. K. D. Broota and H. C. Ganguli are Indian psychologists who wrote on cultural differences in perceptual selectivity in the 1970s, but the classic study of need and perceived size is not theirs. Perceptual defence is McGinnies (1949); subception is Lazarus and McCleary (1951); the New Look is Bruner's movement. A perceptual set is a readiness to perceive in a particular way (Allport, 1955), and the B or 13 figure is Bruner and Minturn (1955). Perceptual learning Expectation and need change perception from moment to moment. Experience changes it for good. Perceptual learning is a relatively lasting improvement in the ability to perceive, especially to discriminate between stimuli, as a result of experience. A tea taster in an Assam garden distinguishes grades of leaf that taste identical to a visitor; a radiologist sees a small tumour in a chest X-ray that a medical student cannot find even when it is pointed out; a cricket umpire judges in an instant whether the ball pitched in line with the stumps; a student of Hindustani music gradually comes to hear the fine differences of pitch between the same note in two different ragas. What changes? In 1955 James and Eleanor Gibson posed the question in a paper titled "Perceptual learning: differentiation or enrichment?" On the enrichment view, held by most psychologists since Berkeley, learning adds associations and memories to an impoverished sensation, so that we come to see more than is there. The Gibsons argued for differentiation: learning makes perception more specific, so that we come to detect more of what is there, picking up distinctive features and variables of the stimulus that we had not noticed before. In their experiment participants were shown a meaningless "scribble", a curly line, and then a long series of similar scribbles that varied in the number of coils, their compression and their orientation, with copies of the original mixed in; their task was to say which were identical to the first. At first they accepted many of the variants as the same; with repeated runs, and without any feedback about which answers were right, they came to pick out exactly the right items, and adults learned faster than children. Eleanor Gibson developed the idea in her book Principles of Perceptual Learning and Development (1969): perceptual learning is the learning of distinctive features, of invariants and of higher-order structure, and it makes attention more economical, so that the expert looks at less but sees more. It is also why, as Section 4.2 warned, what counts as "similar" or "familiar" for the Gestalt laws depends partly on experience. Perceptual adaptation: Stratton's upside-down world How flexible is the adult visual system? In 1896 the American psychologist George Malcolm Stratton (1865 to 1957), who had trained in Wundt's laboratory, put a lens system over one eye that turned the visual world upside down and reversed left and right, and covered the other eye. In a first experiment he wore it for about three days; in 1897 he wore it for eight days, removing it only in darkness or with his eyes closed. At first everything was chaos. He reached for things in the wrong direction, stumbled, felt nauseated, and found that the world swung wildly whenever he moved his head. Day by day his movements became more accurate and the scene less disturbing, and by the end there were periods when things seemed to be in their proper places and he could move about with some ease. When he finally removed the lenses, the normal world looked strange for a while, and his movements were briefly wrong in the opposite direction. Stratton had demonstrated perceptual adaptation : the ability of the perceptual system to adjust to an artificially displaced, distorted or inverted visual input. Later researchers, notably Ivo Kohler at Innsbruck in the 1950s, had participants wear inverting or distorting goggles for weeks; they came to perform complex skilled activities, and the distortions became less noticeable. With prisms that shift the visual world a few degrees to one side, adaptation is much faster: people's reaching errors shrink within minutes, and when the prisms are removed they show a negative aftereffect, reaching too far the other way, which proves that something in the system really changed. How complete the visual change is remains debated. Much of the adaptation seems to lie in the coordination between vision and movement, the felt position of the body, rather than in the picture itself turning the right way up. Movement, it turns out, is essential to that coordination. Richard Held (1922 to 2016) and Alan Hein demonstrated this in a classic experiment of 1963. Key study: Held and Hein's kitten carousel (1963) Question. Is visual experience enough for normal visually guided behaviour to develop, or must the animal produce its own movement? Method. Kittens were reared in darkness and then spent a few hours a day in pairs in a "kitten carousel": a cylinder with vertical stripes on its walls. One kitten walked around freely and actively, pulling a central arm; the other rode passively in a gondola attached to the other end of the arm, so that it received the same visual stimulation but did not produce its own movement. Results. When tested, the active kittens behaved normally: they put out their paws when carried towards a surface, blinked at approaching objects and avoided the deep side of a visual cliff (Section 4.3). The passive kittens did not, until they were allowed to move about freely for some days. Conclusion. The development of visually guided behaviour requires self-produced movement; visual input that is not linked to one's own actions is not enough. Criticism. The passive kittens' movements were restricted in ways other than self-production, and some later studies found a smaller difference; but the result fits the visual cliff finding that fear of heights appears with self-produced locomotion. Experience matters most early in life. When Austin Riesen reared chimpanzees in darkness in the 1940s, they later had great difficulty learning simple visual discriminations, although part of the problem turned out to be damage to the retina from lack of light. When Colin Blakemore and Grahame Cooper (1970) raised kittens for their first months in a cylinder painted only with vertical stripes, the cats later behaved as if blind to horizontal edges, and neurons in their visual cortex responded almost only to vertical orientations. Hubel and Wiesel showed that closing one eye of a kitten during the first few months of life leaves the cortex almost unresponsive to that eye, while the same closure in an adult cat has little effect. There is a sensitive period early in life when visual experience shapes the developing visual brain (Developmental and Physiological books). Exam trap Stratton (1896, 1897) wore inverting lenses : perceptual adaptation . Held and Hein (1963) used the kitten carousel : active versus passive movement. Blakemore and Cooper (1970) reared kittens with vertical stripes only. Gibson and Gibson (1955) argued that perceptual learning is differentiation , not enrichment. Do not confuse perceptual adaptation (adjusting to distorted input) with sensory adaptation (receptors becoming less responsive to an unchanging stimulus, Chapter 3). Restored sight: S.B. and his successors The most direct test of what experience contributes comes from people who gain sight after a lifetime of blindness. The question was put in 1688 by the Irish scientist William Molyneux (1656 to 1698) in a letter to the philosopher John Locke, who printed it in the second edition of his Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1694). Molyneux's question asks: if a man born blind, who has learned to tell a cube from a sphere by touch, were suddenly made to see, could he tell which was which by sight alone, before touching them? Molyneux and Locke both answered no. In 1932 Marius von Senden collected the published reports of people operated on for congenital cataracts and concluded that most could at first see colours and tell figure from ground, but could not recognise even simple shapes by sight, and learned to do so only slowly and with great effort. The case you met at the start of this chapter was reported in 1963 by Richard Gregory and Jean Wallace in their monograph Recovery from Early Blindness . S.B.'s story fits von Senden's conclusion and adds a twist: whatever he had known by touch transferred to vision quickly. He read the time from a clock because he had felt the hands of his watch; he read capital letters but not lower-case ones because he had learned only capitals by touch; he understood the lathe only when he had felt it. His perception of distance was poor, as his belief that he could touch the ground from his high window showed. And Gregory reported that he was less affected than normally sighted people by some of the classic illusions, and that the Necker cube did not reverse in depth for him, as if he lacked the stored depth interpretations on which those effects depend. Modern cases tell a similar story. Mike May, an American blinded in a chemical accident at the age of three and a half, had his sight restored in one eye at 46. When Ione Fine and her colleagues tested him in 2003, he could see colour and motion well, but even years later he struggled to recognise faces and objects from their shape alone and to see depth in flat drawings. Three-dimensional shape, faces and pictorial depth, the most learned parts of perception, were the parts that did not come back. Indian context India has made Molyneux's question testable on a large scale. Project Prakash ("light" in Sanskrit), founded in the mid-2000s by the Indian-born MIT neuroscientist Pawan Sinha , has provided cataract surgery to many blind children and young people in India, most of them from poor rural families, and studied how their vision develops. In 2011 Richard Held, Sinha and their colleagues reported that newly sighted participants could not at first match a shape they had felt with the same shape seen, the answer "no" that Molyneux and Locke had predicted, but that within a few days they learned to do so. Other Prakash studies found that the newly sighted at first had great difficulty separating overlapping shapes, and that motion helped them most to bind parts into objects: common fate (Section 4.2) seems to be one of the first grouping principles available. Culture and perception If experience shapes perception, people who grow up in different physical and cultural environments should perceive differently. You have already met the carpentered-world evidence for illusions (Section 4.5) and the Zulu children who were less fooled by the Ames window. Several other lines of evidence point the same way. The first concerns distance. The British anthropologist Colin Turnbull (1924 to 1994), in The Forest People (1961), described a journey out of the dense Ituri rainforest of the Congo with Kenge, a young BaMbuti man who had spent his whole life in the forest, where one can rarely see more than a few dozen metres. On the open plains Kenge saw a herd of buffalo several kilometres away and asked what kind of insects they were. As they drove towards the herd, the "insects" grew larger, and Kenge, frightened and convinced that witchcraft was at work, could not understand how. Lacking experience of judging great distances, he had no basis for size constancy at that range (Section 4.4). The second concerns pictures. In 1960 the South African psychologist William Hudson showed people a set of simple line drawings in which a hunter aims his spear, with an antelope in the middle distance and an elephant drawn small on a hill far behind it. Most people who had been to school, and who were used to pictures, saw the hunter aiming at the nearby antelope; many unschooled participants said he was aiming at the elephant, interpreting the drawing as flat, without reading its pictorial depth cues. Later, Jan Deregowski found that some African participants preferred "split" drawings of an elephant showing it as if flattened out from above, with all four legs visible, to the perspective drawings that Western viewers prefer. Reading depth in pictures, it seems, is a skill learned through exposure to a pictorial culture. The third concerns what people attend to. In 2001 Takahiko Masuda and Richard Nisbett showed Japanese and American students short animated underwater scenes. Asked to describe them, the Americans tended to begin with the large, fast-moving focal fish; the Japanese more often began with the background ("it looked like a pond") and mentioned the relations between objects and their surroundings. When the focal fish was later shown against a new background, Japanese participants' recognition suffered more. Nisbett argued that East Asian cultures encourage a more holistic, context-sensitive way of seeing and Western cultures a more analytic, object-focused one. A related individual difference, with cultural roots, is field dependence. In a series of studies beginning in the 1940s, the American psychologist Herman Witkin (1916 to 1979) seated people in a dark room and asked them to set a luminous rod to the true vertical while it was surrounded by a tilted luminous frame (the rod-and-frame test), or to find a simple shape hidden within a complex pattern (the embedded figures test). Some people's judgements were strongly pulled by the surrounding frame or pattern; others ignored it and relied on the gravitational feel of their own bodies or on the parts themselves. Witkin called this cognitive style field dependence-independence : field-dependent people perceive in a more global way, strongly influenced by the surrounding field, while field-independent people perceive analytically, separating items from their context. The Canadian cross-cultural psychologist John Berry (born 1939) found in 1966 that Inuit hunters of Baffin Island, whose survival depended on picking out small details in a featureless snowy landscape, were on average more field-independent than Temne farmers of Sierra Leone, whose society stressed conformity; his ecocultural approach holds that each group's ecology and economy shape the perceptual skills it encourages. Indian context Berry's ecocultural approach has been tested extensively in India. Ramesh C. Mishra, Durganand Sinha and John Berry studied Adivasi communities in Bihar, comparing the Birhor, traditionally nomadic hunters and gatherers, with neighbouring groups who had settled into agriculture, and reported their findings in 1996 in the book Ecology, Acculturation and Psychological Adaptation . Their broad conclusion was that a group's ecology and way of life, its degree of acculturation (contact with town life) and schooling were all related to performance on perceptual and cognitive tasks, as the ecocultural model predicts. Exam trap Field dependence-independence is Witkin 's perceptual or cognitive style (rod-and-frame test, embedded figures test), not a procedure for studying subliminal perception; that is semantic priming (Section 4.9). Locus of control is Julian Rotter's personality variable (Personality book), and signal detection ability is measured with the methods of Chapter 3. Kenge and the buffalo is Turnbull (1961); the hunter, antelope and elephant pictures are Hudson (1960); the underwater scenes are Masuda and Nisbett (2001). 4.9 Perception Without Awareness, and Extrasensory Perception Lower yield · 2 Qs Throughout this chapter perception has meant conscious seeing and hearing: the vase you see, the moon that looks large, the letter you read. This last section takes up two claims that stretch that idea in opposite directions. The first is that a stimulus can be perceived, and can influence what you think and do, without your ever being aware of it. The second is that information can be perceived without reaching any sense organ at all. The first claim, after a shaky start, is now well supported. The second, after nearly a century of research, is not. Subliminal perception and the Vicary hoax Chapter 3 introduced the absolute threshold, or limen, and the word subliminal for a stimulus below it. Subliminal perception is the registration and processing of a stimulus that is presented too briefly or too weakly to be consciously perceived, shown by its effects on later behaviour, judgements or physiological responses. Its opposite, a stimulus strong enough to be consciously seen or heard, is supraliminal. The idea burst into public view in 1957. A market researcher named James Vicary (1915 to 1977) announced that during screenings of the film Picnic at a cinema in Fort Lee, New Jersey, he had flashed the messages "Eat Popcorn" and "Drink Coca-Cola" on the screen every few seconds, each for a tiny fraction of a second, far too briefly to be noticed. He claimed that over six weeks the cinema's sales of Coca-Cola had risen by about 18 percent and of popcorn by nearly 58 percent. The announcement caused a sensation and a moral panic about "hidden persuaders"; broadcasters in several countries banned subliminal advertising. But no one could replicate the result, Vicary never published any details, and in 1962 he admitted in a magazine interview that the study had been a gimmick and that he had collected too little data, if any, to mean anything. The Vicary study is now regarded as a hoax. The hoax did not settle whether subliminal perception exists; it only showed that this particular claim was false. Answering the real question turned out to require care about what "unaware" means. In 1984 Jim Cheesman and Philip Merikle distinguished two thresholds. A stimulus is below the subjective threshold when the person says they saw nothing, and below the objective threshold when they cannot even guess its identity better than chance in a forced-choice test. Many early demonstrations used stimuli that were below the subjective threshold only; participants who said they saw nothing might simply have been cautious about saying so, a matter of response criterion in the sense of signal detection theory (Chapter 3). The most influential evidence used priming , the effect of an earlier stimulus (the prime) on the processing of a later one (the target). In semantic priming , a prime makes it easier to recognise a target that is related to it in meaning: in 1971 David Meyer and Roger Schvaneveldt found that people decide that BUTTER is a word faster if they have just seen BREAD than if they have just seen NURSE. Semantic priming became the standard procedure for studying subliminal perception when the British psychologist Anthony Marcel reported in 1983 that primes flashed so briefly and so heavily masked that participants could not tell whether any word had been presented still speeded responses to related target words. A word that was never consciously seen had been processed for its meaning. Later work with stricter tests of awareness has confirmed that masked primes can affect responses, although the effects are small and short-lived. Other studies showed effects on feelings and choices. In 1980 William Kunst-Wilson and Robert Zajonc flashed irregular octagons for one millisecond each. Later, shown pairs of octagons, participants could not tell which ones they had seen (recognition was at chance), yet they reliably said that they liked the previously shown ones better: the mere exposure effect without awareness. In 2006 Johan Karremans and his colleagues flashed the brand name of a soft drink, Lipton Ice, below awareness; afterwards, participants who were thirsty were more likely to choose that drink, while participants who were not thirsty were unaffected. Subliminal influence, in other words, can nudge a goal the person already has; it cannot create one. And the subliminal self-help tapes sold to improve memory or self-esteem fail completely. In 1991 Anthony Greenwald and his colleagues gave volunteers tapes labelled "memory" or "self-esteem", but secretly swapped the labels on half of them. After a month, people believed they had improved in whatever the label said, but objective tests showed no improvement of either kind: a placebo effect of the label, not of the hidden message. Exam trap The procedure called semantic priming (masked priming) is used to study subliminal perception . It is not a method for studying signal detection ability (Chapter 3), field dependence-independence (Witkin, Section 4.8) or locus of control (Rotter, Personality book). Vicary 's 1957 popcorn and Coca-Cola study was a hoax , admitted in 1962; genuine subliminal effects are real but small, brief and dependent on existing goals . Subliminal means below the threshold of awareness; supraliminal means above it. Blindsight and other dissociations The most dramatic evidence for perception without awareness comes from patients. In the early 1970s the British neuropsychologist Lawrence Weiskrantz (1926 to 2018) and his colleagues at Oxford studied D.B., a man who had had part of the primary visual cortex of his right hemisphere removed in an operation to cure severe migraines caused by an abnormal tangle of blood vessels. As expected, he was blind in much of his left visual field: shown a stimulus there, he said he saw nothing at all. But when the researchers insisted that he guess, pointing to where a light might be, saying whether a line was vertical or horizontal, or whether something was moving, he was correct far more often than chance would allow. When he was shown a film of his own accurate performance, he was openly astonished. Weiskrantz named the condition blindsight in 1974: the ability of people with damage to the primary visual cortex to respond accurately to visual stimuli in the blind part of the field while denying any conscious experience of seeing them. How is it possible? Not all visual information goes through the primary visual cortex. Smaller pathways run from the eye to the superior colliculus in the midbrain and onwards to the cortex, and some fibres from the thalamus reach motion-sensitive areas such as MT directly. These routes can support detection, localisation and the sensing of movement, and they feed the dorsal, vision-for-action stream of Section 4.1, which operates largely outside awareness. Some patients even show "affective blindsight", responding differently to happy and fearful faces they cannot see. Sceptics first suggested that blindsight patients were really responding to stray light scattered onto the intact part of the retina, but D.B. could not detect stimuli presented to his natural blind spot, where stray light would have worked just as well. A more serious doubt is that some patients have faint, degraded visual experiences in the "blind" field and are simply very cautious about reporting them; this is the subjective threshold problem again. Even so, blindsight is accepted as a real dissociation between visual processing and visual awareness. You have now met several such dissociations in this chapter: D.F., who could not see the orientation of a slot but could post a card through it (Section 4.1); the hand that is not fooled by the Ebbinghaus illusion (Section 4.5); prosopagnosic patients whose skin conductance recognises faces they cannot name (Section 4.7). Attention produces dissociations of its own in healthy people. In inattentional blindness, an unexpected object in plain view goes unseen because attention is elsewhere; in change blindness, large changes to a scene go unnoticed when they coincide with a blink, a cut or a flicker. These are covered fully in Chapter 5, together with the wider question of what consciousness is. Exam trap Blindsight (Weiskrantz, patient D.B., 1974) follows damage to the primary visual cortex ; the patient denies seeing yet performs above chance on forced-choice tests. Failing to notice significant changes in a scene, even obvious ones, is change blindness ; failing to see an unexpected object while attending to something else is inattentional blindness ; selective attention is the focusing of processing on some stimuli at the expense of others; perceptual constancy (Section 4.4) is a success of perception, not a failure to notice (Chapter 5). Extrasensory perception Extrasensory perception (ESP) is the claimed perception of information without the use of any known sensory channel. It is quite different from subliminal perception: a subliminal stimulus does reach the senses, only too weakly to be noticed, whereas ESP claims that information arrives with no sensory input at all. Three forms of ESP are traditionally distinguished, and a fourth phenomenon is usually studied alongside them (Table 4.9 collects the vocabulary of the field). Telepathy is the direct transfer of thoughts or feelings from one mind to another, mind reading without speech, gesture or any other sensory signal. Clairvoyance is the perception of objects or events that are hidden from the senses or far away, without any other mind knowing them: naming a card lying face down in a sealed envelope, or "seeing" a fire in a distant city. Precognition is the perception of events before they happen; its rarely mentioned partner, retrocognition, is paranormal knowledge of past events. Psychokinesis (PK) is the claimed ability to influence physical objects or events by mental effort alone, such as influencing the fall of dice. It is a claimed power of action, not of perception, so strictly it is not a form of ESP. ESP and psychokinesis together are called psi phenomena, and parapsychology is the field that studies them. Its scientific history begins with Joseph Banks Rhine (1895 to 1980), a botanist by training who came to Duke University in North Carolina in 1927, with his wife and colleague Louisa Rhine, to work with the psychologist William McDougall. Rhine's book Extra-Sensory Perception (1934) made the term famous, and the Duke Parapsychology Laboratory became the centre of the field. Rhine's chief tool was a pack of Zener cards , designed by his Duke colleague, the perception psychologist Karl Zener (1903 to 1964). A pack has 25 cards, five each of five symbols: a circle, a cross, three wavy lines, a square and a star. In a clairvoyance test the participant guesses the order of a shuffled pack; in a telepathy test a "sender" looks at each card in turn; in a precognition test the guesses are made before the pack is shuffled. Pure chance gives an average of 5 correct guesses in 25 (20 percent), and Rhine reported participants who averaged well above that over thousands of trials. Critics found problems with almost every aspect of the early work. The symbols could sometimes be seen faintly through the backs of cheap cards, or reflected in the sender's glasses or cornea; senders could give unintentional cues by their breathing or timing; shuffling was sometimes inadequate; recording errors tended to favour hits; and successful series were more likely to be reported than unsuccessful ones. Laboratories elsewhere generally failed to replicate Rhine's results. The British researcher S. G. Soal produced some of the strongest card-guessing data of the 1940s, but statistical analysis by Betty Markwick in 1978 showed that his records had been manipulated. Modern parapsychologists turned to the Ganzfeld procedure , developed in the 1970s by Charles Honorton (1946 to 1992) and others. Ganzfeld is German for "whole field". The receiver relaxes in a reclining chair with halved table-tennis balls taped over the eyes, a soft red light shining on them and steady hissing noise in headphones, which produces a uniform, featureless sensory field; the idea is that reducing ordinary sensory input makes any faint psi signal easier to notice. In another room, a sender concentrates on a randomly chosen target picture or video clip. Afterwards the receiver is shown four pictures, the target and three decoys, and picks the one that best matches their impressions; chance success is 25 percent. In 1994 the social psychologist Daryl Bem (born 1938) and Honorton published, in a leading journal, an analysis of computer-controlled Ganzfeld studies reporting a hit rate of about 32 percent. But in 1999 Julie Milton and Richard Wiseman analysed 30 newer Ganzfeld studies from several laboratories and found no significant effect, and the debate has swung back and forth since. In 2011 Bem reported nine experiments that appeared to show precognition, for example that people could guess, better than chance, behind which of two curtains an erotic picture would appear before the computer had chosen its position. Several independent teams repeated his procedures and found nothing, and the episode became one of the triggers of psychology's "replication crisis", the realisation that many published effects in psychology were not reproducible (Research Methods book). Why do most scientists remain sceptical? The effects do not replicate reliably. Positive results in one laboratory are followed by null results in others, and the effects tend to shrink as experimental controls become stricter. There is no plausible mechanism. No known form of energy carries information from mind to mind or from the future to the present, and claimed psi effects do not weaken with distance or with time as physical signals do. The history of the field contains sensory leakage, poor randomisation, selective reporting (the file-drawer problem, in which unsuccessful studies are never published) and outright fraud. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. A claim that would overturn much of established physics needs far stronger and more consistent evidence than a claim about, say, the effect of hunger on perception. A large prize offered for decades by the stage magician and sceptic James Randi for any demonstration of paranormal ability under agreed test conditions was never won. Belief can be explained without psi. People remember the one dream that came true and forget the thousands that did not; they underestimate how often coincidences occur by chance (in a group of just 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is better than even); and they notice evidence that confirms what they already believe. The third chapter of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras , the Vibhuti Pada, describes siddhis , powers said to arise from advanced meditation, including knowledge of other minds and of the past and future. Modern parapsychology also put down roots here: a department of psychology and parapsychology was established at Andhra University in Visakhapatnam, associated with K. Ramakrishna Rao, who had worked with Rhine at Duke and later led the institute Rhine founded. The scientific standard is the same everywhere, however: a claimed ability must be demonstrated under controlled conditions that rule out sensory cues and chance, and replicated by independent investigators. Clinical link Belief in telepathy, clairvoyance or a "sixth sense" is common in the general population and, on its own, says nothing about mental health; cultural context always matters. But odd beliefs and magical thinking that go well beyond the person's culture, such as a conviction that one can read other people's minds or that one's thoughts can cause distant events, are part of the description of schizotypal personality disorder, and magical thinking also appears in obsessive-compulsive disorder. Telling a culturally shared belief from a clinically significant one is a matter of careful assessment (Disorders book). Exam trap Telepathy is mind to mind; clairvoyance is perceiving objects or events directly, with no other mind involved; precognition is perceiving the future; psychokinesis is mind over matter and is not a form of ESP, although it belongs to psi. J. B. Rhine (Duke, Extra-Sensory Perception , 1934) used Zener cards (five symbols; chance is 5 out of 25). The Ganzfeld (Honorton) is a mild sensory-deprivation procedure with a chance rate of 25 percent. ESP is not subliminal perception: subliminal stimuli reach the senses, ESP claims no sensory input at all. Perception, then, extends below awareness in ways that are now well established, but not, on present evidence, beyond the senses. Everything you perceive arrives through the sense organs described in Chapter 3 and is organised and interpreted by the processes described in this chapter; what you then select from it, and how much of it reaches consciousness, is the subject of Chapter 5. The case of S.B., revisited You can now see why S.B.'s first months of sight were so puzzling, and why they mattered so much to Richard Gregory. The bottom-up machinery of vision worked from the start: S.B. saw light, colour and movement, and he could pick out a figure from its ground. What he lacked was everything this chapter has shown to depend on stored knowledge. With no experience of seeing distance, he had no size constancy across the space below his window (Section 4.4); with no visual templates, features or prototypes for most objects, he could not recognise them (Section 4.7); with no stored depth interpretations of flat drawings, some illusions and the reversing Necker cube had little hold on him (Section 4.5). Where knowledge existed, it transferred at once, even from another sense. He read a clock because he had felt a watch, and he saw the lathe once his hands had built the schema that Neisser's perceptual cycle says must direct looking (Section 4.1). "Now that I've felt it I can see" is as clear a statement of top-down processing as the literature contains. The story did not end happily. Gregory and Wallace reported that as the months passed S.B. became increasingly disappointed and depressed. The visual world he had imagined turned out to be drab, the flaking paint and blemishes of things troubled him, and he often preferred to sit in the evenings without turning on the light. He died in 1960, less than two years after the operation. Later cases such as Mike May's and the children of Project Prakash show both sides of the lesson: perception in the adult brain is slow to rebuild after a lifetime without sight, yet young brains given sight can learn to see with remarkable speed. Perception, in short, is not a window on the world but a skill, built from the meeting of what arrives at the senses and what the brain already knows. Chapter summary 4.1 What Perception Is. Sensation is the detection and transduction of physical energy; perception is the selection, organisation and interpretation of the resulting signals. Because many states of the world can produce the same retinal image (the inverse problem), perception must combine bottom-up (data-driven) and top-down (conceptually driven) processing. Constructivist theories (Helmholtz's unconscious inference and likelihood principle, 1867; Gregory's perceptual hypotheses, 1966 and 1970, illustrated by the hollow-face illusion) treat perception as inference, and the Bayesian approach treats it as the combination of prior beliefs with sensory evidence (Ramachandran's light-from-above prior, 1988). J. J. Gibson's direct, ecological theory (1950, 1966, 1979) holds that the optic array, with its invariants, optic flow and affordances, specifies the world without inference; it is the classic bottom-up theory. Neisser's perceptual cycle (1976) links schema, exploration and object in a loop, and Milner and Goodale's two visual streams (1995) suggest that the constructivist and direct theories describe vision-for-perception and vision-for-action respectively. 4.2 Perceptual Organisation: The Gestalt Laws. Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler, from 1912) held that the whole is different from the sum of its parts. The field is first split into figure and ground (Rubin, 1915): the figure is thing-like, bounded and in front; the ground is shapeless and behind, and reversible figures such as Rubin's vase show that organisation is done by the perceiver. Elements are grouped by proximity, similarity, closure, good continuation, common fate and symmetry, and by the modern laws of common region (Palmer, 1992) and connectedness (Palmer and Rock, 1994), all governed by the master law of Prägnanz, the tendency to see the simplest, most stable organisation. Kanizsa's illusory contours (1955) show the laws creating edges that are not there. The laws describe rather than explain, and grouping is partly learned. 4.3 Depth and Distance Perception. Berkeley (1709) posed the problem of how a flat retina yields depth. The binocular cues are retinal disparity, which produces stereopsis (Wheatstone's stereoscope, 1838; Julesz's random-dot stereograms, 1960), and convergence. The monocular pictorial cues are relative and familiar size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, aerial perspective, height in the visual field and shading; motion parallax is a monocular cue that needs movement; accommodation and convergence are oculomotor cues. The visual cliff (Gibson and Walk, 1960) showed that infants of 6 to 14 months avoid an apparent drop and that newborn animals of walking species do too; Campos (1970) found that younger infants detect depth before they fear it, and fear grows with self-produced locomotion. 4.4 Perceptual Constancy. Perceptual constancy is the perception of stable object properties despite changing sensory input. Size constancy depends on taking distance into account (size-distance invariance), as Holway and Boring (1941) showed by removing distance cues, and Emmert's law (1881) shows the same relation for afterimages. Shape constancy is a compromise between retinal and real shape (Thouless's phenomenal regression, 1931); lightness constancy follows Wallach's ratio principle (1948), with lateral inhibition producing simultaneous contrast, Mach bands and the Hermann grid; colour constancy discounts the illuminant (Land's retinex theory); and location constancy uses the corollary discharge (Sperry; von Holst, 1950). 4.5 Illusions. An illusion is a systematic misinterpretation of a real stimulus, a distortion of perception rather than sensation; personal illusions vary between people, while universal (permanent) illusions are shared. The Müller-Lyer illusion (1889) is best explained by Gregory's inappropriate constancy scaling (1963), and the carpentered-world hypothesis (Segall, Campbell and Herskovits, 1963, 1966) links susceptibility to experience with rectangular buildings. The Ponzo illusion (1911), the Ames room (1946) and the moon illusion (apparent distance hypothesis; Kaufman and Rock, 1962) are further cases of misapplied size-distance scaling, while the Ebbinghaus (Titchener) illusion reflects size contrast and the Zöllner, Poggendorff and Hering illusions distort orientation. The Necker cube (1832) and other ambiguous figures alternate between interpretations; the Penrose triangle (1958) is an impossible figure. Illusions must be distinguished from sensory distortions, hallucinations (perceptions without an adequate stimulus), imagery and delusions (false fixed beliefs), and from memory illusions such as déjà vu and déjà entendu. 4.6 Motion Perception. Real motion is detected by the image-retina and eye-head systems, using direction-selective neurons and area MT (V5), whose damage causes akinetopsia (patient L.M., 1983); Johansson's point-light displays (1973) reveal biological motion. Apparent motion includes Wertheimer's phi phenomenon (1912), strictly distinguished from beta movement, and the stroboscopic motion of films. Induced motion (Duncker, 1929) makes a stationary object appear to move within a moving frame, and vection is illusory self-motion. The autokinetic effect, apparent movement of a stationary light in darkness, was used by Sherif (1935) to study norm formation. The motion aftereffect, or waterfall illusion (Addams, 1834), results from adaptation of direction-selective neurons. 4.7 Pattern and Object Recognition. Template matching cannot cope with variability. Feature analysis, supported by letter confusions, visual search and Hubel and Wiesel's simple and complex cells (from 1959), is embodied in Selfridge's Pandemonium (1959). Prototype theory (Posner and Keele, 1968; Rosch) stores idealised averages. Biederman's recognition-by-components theory (1987) describes objects as arrangements of about 36 geons identified from non-accidental properties, and Marr's computational theory (1982) proceeds from the primal sketch through the viewer-centred 2.5-D sketch to the object-centred 3-D model. Faces are processed holistically (face inversion effect, fusiform face area), and their recognition can be lost in prosopagnosia (Bodamer, 1947). The word superiority effect (Reicher, 1969) and other context effects show top-down processing. 4.8 Perceptual Set, Learning and Culture. A perceptual set is a readiness to perceive in a particular way (Allport, 1955), created by context (Bruner and Minturn's B or 13, 1955), recent experience (Bugelski and Alampay, 1961) and other senses (the McGurk effect, 1976). The New Look showed effects of need and value: hungry sailors saw food (McClelland and Atkinson, 1948), and poor children overestimated coin sizes more than rich children (Bruner and Goodman, 1947). Perceptual defence (McGinnies, 1949) was challenged on grounds of word frequency and response suppression; subception (Lazarus and McCleary, 1951) showed discrimination without awareness. Perceptual learning is differentiation of distinctive features (Gibson and Gibson, 1955). Stratton's inverting lenses (1896, 1897) demonstrated perceptual adaptation, Held and Hein (1963) showed the need for self-produced movement, and restored-sight cases (Molyneux's question; S.B.; Project Prakash) show which aspects of perception depend on experience. Culture shapes perception of distance (Turnbull's Kenge), pictorial depth (Hudson, 1960), attention to context (Masuda and Nisbett, 2001) and field dependence-independence (Witkin; Berry, 1966). 4.9 Perception Without Awareness, and Extrasensory Perception. Subliminal perception is the processing of stimuli below the threshold of awareness. Vicary's 1957 popcorn study was a hoax, but masked semantic priming (Marcel, 1983), mere exposure without recognition (Kunst-Wilson and Zajonc, 1980) and goal-dependent brand effects (Karremans and colleagues, 2006) show small, short-lived genuine effects, while subliminal self-help tapes are placebos. Blindsight (Weiskrantz, patient D.B., 1974) shows visual processing without awareness after damage to the primary visual cortex. Extrasensory perception comprises telepathy, clairvoyance and precognition, studied with psychokinesis under the name parapsychology; Rhine's Zener-card studies at Duke and the Ganzfeld procedure (Honorton; Bem and Honorton, 1994) have not produced replicable evidence, and most scientists remain sceptical because of failed replications, the absence of a mechanism and the history of methodological flaws. Ganzfeld procedure From the past papers Which approach to perception emphasises the role of unconscious inference and probabilistic reasoning in interpreting sensory information? (RML 2023) a Computational approach b Constructivist approach c Direct perception approach d Information processing approach ✓ Answer: (b) Constructivist approach Helmholtz's unconscious inference; Gregory's constructivism The concept The idea Unconscious inference is Helmholtz 's idea: the brain silently works out what the sensory input most likely means. The approach It is the core of Gregory 's constructivism , which builds the percept from the input plus what we already know. Probabilistic form Its probabilistic, Bayesian form treats the percept as the most likely interpretation of the evidence. Why the other options are wrong (a) Computational approach Marr 's approach, which asks what each stage of vision computes, not how inference shapes the percept. (c) Direct perception approach Gibson 's view, the direct opposite: it denies that inference is needed at all. (d) Information processing approach Describes perception as a series of stages , without stressing inference. According to the Bayesian approach to perception, our perceptual experiences are influenced by: (RML 2023) a Genetic predispositions b Cultural background c Prior beliefs and sensory evidence d Emotional states ✓ Answer: (c) Prior beliefs and sensory evidence Bayes's theorem applied to perception The concept The formula Bayes's theorem combines two things: the prior and the likelihood . The prior The prior is what is likely in the world, learnt from experience or built in by evolution. The likelihood The likelihood is how well each possibility fits the current sensory evidence ; the percept combines the two. Why the other options are wrong (a) Genetic predispositions Genes can shape the priors, but they are not what the Bayesian definition names. (b) Cultural background Culture can shape the priors, but the definition is prior beliefs plus evidence, not culture. (d) Emotional states Emotion can shape the priors, but none of these is the definition. Which psychologist is associated with the concept of "affordances", which refers to the opportunities for action provided by the environment? (RML 2023) a Hermann von Helmholtz b James J. Gibson c Richard Gregory d Ulric Neisser ✓ Answer: (b) James J. Gibson James J. Gibson, ecological theory (1979) The concept What it is An affordance is what the environment offers for action: a chair affords sitting, a handle affords grasping. Whose theory Affordances are central to Gibson 's ecological theory (1979). Why the other options are wrong (a) Hermann von Helmholtz An inference (top-down) theorist, on the opposite side of the debate from Gibson. (c) Richard Gregory Another inference (top-down) theorist, like Helmholtz; affordances are not his idea. (d) Ulric Neisser Proposed the perceptual cycle , a different model; affordances are Gibson's term. According to Wundt, "apperceptive mass" constitutes ___________. (IHBAS 2025) a Compound of elemental processes bound by association b Sensation and pure perception c Pure perception and preexisting ideas d Sensation plus unconscious inference ✓ Answer: (c) Pure perception and preexisting ideas Herbart's term, taken over by Wundt The concept What it is The apperceptive mass is the body of ideas a person already has. How it works A new perception is absorbed into this mass and so made meaningful: pure perception plus preexisting ideas . Whose term The term is Herbart 's; Wundt took it over. Why the other options are wrong (a) Compound of elemental processes bound by association Describes associationist compounds of elements, not a new perception absorbed into existing ideas. (b) Sensation and pure perception Leaves out the existing ideas , which are the whole point of the mass. (d) Sensation plus unconscious inference Mixes in Helmholtz 's unconscious inference , a different theory. The most important school of psychology which has contributed a lot towards perception is: (Amity 2023) a Psychoanalysis b Behaviour school c Structural school d Gestalt psychology ✓ Answer: (d) Gestalt psychology Wertheimer, Koffka and Köhler, phi phenomenon (1912) The concept Where it began Wertheimer , Koffka and Köhler began Gestalt psychology with the phi phenomenon (1912). What it gave It gave perception figure-ground organisation, the grouping laws and Prägnanz . Why this one That is why Gestalt psychology is the school most linked with perception. Why the other options are wrong (a) Psychoanalysis Dealt with the unconscious , not perception. (b) Behaviour school Behaviourism set perception aside as unobservable. (c) Structural school Structuralism analysed sensations into elements; it did not explain how they are organised. According to the law of ______, items which are close together in space and time tend to be perceived as belonging together or forming an organised group. (IHBAS 2024) a Proximity b Continuity c Similarity d Closure ✓ Answer: (a) Proximity Gestalt law of proximity (Wertheimer's grouping laws) The concept What it is Proximity means nearness: items close together in space or time are grouped together. Exam tip The words close together or near in a stem signal proximity. Why the other options are wrong (b) Continuity Groups elements lying on a smooth path , not nearby ones. (c) Similarity Groups elements that look alike , whatever their distance. (d) Closure The completion of gaps in a figure. The tendency to complete a figure is called: (RML 2024) a Continuation b Continuity c Closure d Similarity ✓ Answer: (c) Closure Gestalt law of closure The concept What it is Closure is the tendency to complete a figure by filling in its gaps. Example A circle drawn with gaps is still seen as a complete circle . Why the other options are wrong (a) Continuation Another name for the law of good continuation , which is about smooth paths, not gaps. (b) Continuity Same law as continuation ( good continuation ): smooth paths, not gaps; two names for one law. (d) Similarity Groups look-alike elements; it does not complete figures. Any figure or form not perceived in parts but organised in perception in the best possible whole form is known as: (RML 2020) a Law of proximity b Law of Prägnanz c Law of figure and background d Law of continuity ✓ Answer: (b) Law of Prägnanz Gestalt law of Prägnanz (good figure) The concept What it is Prägnanz , the law of good figure or simplicity, says we see the simplest, most stable and complete organisation possible. Why it is special It is the master law ; the other laws are special cases of it. Why the other options are wrong (a) Law of proximity One particular kind of organisation (nearby items group together), a special case of Prägnanz. (c) Law of figure and background Figure-ground describes one particular kind of organisation (an object standing out from its background), not the best-whole principle. (d) Law of continuity One particular kind of organisation (elements on a smooth path group together), a special case of Prägnanz. Determining a rule of structure from incomplete evidence and then identifying items that fulfil the rule would be a demonstration of: (Amity 2023) a Interpolation b Extrapolation c Interposition d Structuring ✓ Answer: (d) Structuring Definition of structuring The concept What it is Structuring is imposing an organising rule on incomplete input. Second step You then pick out the items that fit the rule, exactly what the stem describes. Why the other options are wrong (a) Interpolation Interpolation fills in between known points; it does not impose a rule of structure. (b) Extrapolation Extrapolation extends a trend beyond the known points. (c) Interposition A monocular depth cue (overlap); the trap is its similar-sounding name. Among monocular cues for depth perception is: (JEMAS 2025) a Convergence b Retinal disparity c Assimilation d Interposition ✓ Answer: (d) Interposition Monocular depth cue of interposition (overlap) The concept What it is In interposition , an object that partly hides another is seen as nearer. Why monocular One eye is enough to see it, so it is a monocular cue . Why the other options are wrong (a) Convergence One of the two binocular cues, so not monocular. (b) Retinal disparity The other binocular cue, so not monocular. (c) Assimilation Not a depth cue at all: it is Piaget 's term, or the opposite of contrast. Retinal disparity, which enables three-dimensional depth perception, is classified as which type of visual depth cue? (Real PYQ 2025) a Monocular static cue b Binocular cue c Motion parallax cue d Pictorial depth cue ✓ Answer: (b) Binocular cue Binocular cue giving stereopsis The concept What it is Retinal disparity is the difference between the two eyes' images. Why binocular It needs two eyes by definition, and it gives stereopsis , so it is a binocular cue . Why the other options are wrong (a) Monocular static cue Monocular static cues are the pictorial ones; disparity needs two eyes. (c) Motion parallax cue Monocular and needs movement ; disparity needs two eyes, not movement. (d) Pictorial depth cue Pictorial cues are monocular and static; disparity needs two eyes. Highway engineers sometimes paint stripes on freeway off-ramps to enhance the perception of depth. This uses the cue of: (RML 2024) a Aerial perspective b Parallax c Overlap d Texture gradients ✓ Answer: (d) Texture gradients Texture gradient depth cue The concept How it works Texture normally looks more crowded with distance: the texture gradient . Why the stripes Stripes that get closer together exaggerate that crowding and heighten the sense of speed . Why the other options are wrong (a) Aerial perspective Haze on distant objects; painted stripes add no haze. (b) Parallax Needs relative movement of objects at different distances, not a painted pattern. (c) Overlap Overlap is interposition, one object hiding another. The density of stones increases as we look farther away. This phenomenon is due to: (RML 2024) a Convergence b Aerial perspective c Interposition d Texture gradient ✓ Answer: (d) Texture gradient Texture gradient depth cue The concept What it is With distance, texture elements look smaller, finer and more densely packed: the texture gradient . Link to stem Stones packed more densely farther away are exactly this cue. Why the other options are wrong (a) Convergence A binocular eye-muscle cue, not a property of the surface. (b) Aerial perspective Haziness of distant objects, not density. (c) Interposition One object blocking another. What is the approximate visual field covered by each human eye? (RML 2024) a 130 degrees b 160 degrees c 180 degrees d 220 degrees ✓ Answer: (c) 180 degrees, as keyed Visual field of one eye, as keyed The concept Keyed answer Choose 180 degrees for this exact item, as the paper keys it. Key note Be careful: the better textbook figure for one eye is about 160 degrees horizontally, about 60 degrees towards the nose and 100 towards the temple. Other papers 180 to 200 degrees is the field of both eyes together, with about 120 degrees of binocular overlap ; recognise 160 if a question is precise about a single eye. Why the other options are wrong (a) 130 degrees Smaller than the standard figures; one eye covers about 160 degrees. (b) 160 degrees The more accurate textbook figure for one eye, but not the keyed answer; choose it when a question is precise about a single eye. (d) 220 degrees More than even the 180 to 200 degrees covered by both eyes together. When you stretch your right hand farther away from your body, you still perceive it to be of the same size as your left hand. This is due to: (IHBAS 2020) a Size constancy b Shape constancy c Motion parallax d Depth perception ✓ Answer: (a) Size constancy Size constancy (size-distance invariance) The concept What happens The far hand's retinal image is smaller. How it works The brain scales it by distance ( size-distance invariance ), so the hand still looks its true size: size constancy . Why the other options are wrong (b) Shape constancy Concerns changes of orientation , not distance. (c) Motion parallax A depth cue from movement, not a constancy. (d) Depth perception What size constancy uses , not the name of the effect. Illusions are: (JEMAS 2025) a misinterpretation of stimuli arising from an external object b real perceptual object perceived in a distorted way c vivid mental images d perception without an adequate external stimulus ✓ Answer: (a) Misinterpretation of stimuli arising from an external object Standard psychopathology definition of illusion The concept What it is An illusion is a misinterpretation of stimuli arising from a real external object . Exam tip Real object, wrong reading: illusion. No adequate external stimulus: hallucination . Why the other options are wrong (b) real perceptual object perceived in a distorted way What Sims calls a sensory distortion , such as micropsia. (c) vivid mental images Describes imagery , not a misperception. (d) perception without an adequate external stimulus The definition of a hallucination . Illusions are: (Amity 2023) a Distortions of existing stimuli b The same as hallucinations c The result of innate mechanisms d Not based on external reality ✓ Answer: (a) Distortions of existing stimuli Definition of an illusion The concept What it is In an illusion , a real stimulus is misperceived. Contrast A hallucination has no adequate external stimulus. Why the other options are wrong (b) The same as hallucinations A hallucination has no adequate external stimulus, while an illusion starts from a real one. (c) The result of innate mechanisms Culture and learning shape susceptibility, as the carpentered-world studies show, so not purely innate. (d) Not based on external reality Describes a hallucination ; an illusion starts from a real stimulus. Optical illusions result from distortion in: (Amity 2023) a Translation b Sensation c Perception d Adaptation ✓ Answer: (c) Perception Müller-Lyer figure: error of interpretation The concept The evidence In the Müller-Lyer figure the retinal image is accurate and the receptors transduce it correctly. Where the error is The error lies in the interpretation , which is perception . Why the other options are wrong (a) Translation Here means transduction , which works normally. (b) Sensation Sensation works normally; the input is registered correctly. (d) Adaptation Sensory adaptation works normally and is not the source of the error. The rail tracks appearing to converge to all of us is an example of: (RML 2024) a Permanent illusion b Personal illusion c Visual illusion d Müller-Lyer illusion ✓ Answer: (a) Permanent illusion, as keyed Personal versus permanent (universal) illusion classification The concept The classification Illusions are classed as personal or permanent (universal). Why permanent An illusion that everyone experiences every time is permanent, as with converging rail tracks; answer as keyed. Key note The convergence itself is the depth cue of linear perspective . Why the other options are wrong (b) Personal illusion Varies between people and occasions, such as a rope seen as a snake . (c) Visual illusion Broadly true, but the item is testing the personal versus permanent classification. (d) Müller-Lyer illusion A different, specific illusion; converging tracks are not the Müller-Lyer figure. It has been found that the Müller-Lyer illusion exists in certain cultures in which there are: (RML 2022) a Lot of trees b Buildings with corners c Structures without many corners and angles d More men than women ✓ Answer: (b) Buildings with corners Segall, Campbell and Herskovits, carpentered world (1963, 1966) The concept The hypothesis The carpentered-world hypothesis comes from Segall, Campbell and Herskovits (1963, 1966). How it works Experience of rectangular buildings teaches people to read angles as corners in depth, increasing susceptibility. Why the other options are wrong (a) Lot of trees Trees are irrelevant to the hypothesis. (c) Structures without many corners and angles The reverse: people living among round huts and few straight edges were less susceptible. (d) More men than women The sex ratio is irrelevant. The Müller-Lyer illusion is best explained by: (Recall set) a Misapplied size constancy (inappropriate constancy scaling) b Binocular disparity between the two eyes' images c Lateral inhibition between neighbouring retinal cells d Figure-ground reversal ✓ Answer: (a) Misapplied size constancy Gregory (1963), inappropriate constancy scaling The concept The theory Gregory (1963) argued that the fins and arrowheads are read as inside and outside corners . The result So one shaft is coded as farther away and scaled up: misapplied size constancy . Why the other options are wrong (b) Binocular disparity between the two eyes' images The illusion works with one eye and on a flat page, which rules out disparity. (c) Lateral inhibition between neighbouring retinal cells Lateral inhibition explains Mach bands and the Hermann grid . (d) Figure-ground reversal Figure-ground reversal is Rubin's vase , a different phenomenon. Déjà entendu refers to: (IHBAS 2025) a Illusion of having seen something before b Memory of past events with clarity c Illusion of having heard something previously d Repetitive involuntary speech ✓ Answer: (c) Illusion of having heard something previously Déjà entendu: entendu means heard The concept The word Entendu means heard , so déjà entendu is the illusion of having heard something before. Exam tip Déjà vu is the seeing version. Why the other options are wrong (a) Illusion of having seen something before Déjà vu , having seen something before. (b) Memory of past events with clarity Hypermnesia , an unusually clear memory of past events. (d) Repetitive involuntary speech A speech disorder such as palilalia . Who demonstrated that economic deprivation affects perception? (IHBAS 2024) a Broota and Ganguli b Bruner and Goodman c Segall d Herskovits ✓ Answer: (b) Bruner and Goodman Bruner and Goodman, coin study (1947) The concept The study In Bruner and Goodman 's 1947 coin study , ten-year-olds judged the sizes of coins. The finding Poor children overestimated coin sizes more than rich children did, so economic deprivation affects perception. Why the other options are wrong (a) Broota and Ganguli Indian psychologists who are not associated with this classic finding. (c) Segall A carpentered-world researcher, who studied culture and illusions. (d) Herskovits Segall's fellow carpentered-world researcher, who studied culture and illusions, not deprivation. The procedure called "semantic priming" is used to study which of the following phenomena? (RML 2022) a Signal detection ability b Subliminal perception c Field dependence-independence d Locus of control ✓ Answer: (b) Subliminal perception Marcel (1983), masked priming The concept The method In semantic priming , masked primes too brief to be consciously seen come before related words. The finding They still speed responses to related words ( Marcel , 1983), showing processing without awareness: subliminal perception . Why the other options are wrong (a) Signal detection ability Measured by d-prime in yes/no detection tasks. (c) Field dependence-independence Measured by Witkin 's rod-and-frame and embedded figures tests. (d) Locus of control Rotter 's concept, measured by personality questionnaires. What term describes the phenomenon where individuals fail to notice significant changes in their environment, even when those changes are obvious? (RML 2023) a Change blindness b Inattentional blindness c Perceptual constancy d Selective attention ✓ Answer: (a) Change blindness Definition of change blindness The concept What it is Change blindness is failing to notice changes , typically when they coincide with a blink, cut or flicker. Exam tip The stem stresses failing to notice changes ; that is the clue (Chapter 5). Why the other options are wrong (b) Inattentional blindness Failing to see an unexpected object while attending to something else; the close trap. (c) Perceptual constancy The stable perception of objects despite changing input . (d) Selective attention The focusing of processing on some stimuli rather than others.
