Answers: (1) span, (2) beans, (3) external, (4) shadowing, (5) early, (6) attenuator, (7) late (at the response stage), (8) inhibition, (9) pop-out, (10) inattentional. 5.4 Divided attention, automaticity, the Stroop effect and vigilance High yield · 10 Qs Selective attention asks how we keep one thing in and other things out. Divided attention asks the reverse question: how far can we do two things at once? You can walk and talk, and an experienced driver can drive and hold a conversation. But a learner driver cannot, and nobody can hold two conversations at the same time. Why do some pairs of tasks combine easily and others not at all? Three answers have been proposed: that we have one limited pool of capacity, that we have several pools, and that practice makes some processes stop needing capacity at all. Kahneman's capacity model (1973) In his book Attention and Effort (1973), Daniel Kahneman (1934 to 2024), later a Nobel laureate in economics, replaced the bottleneck with a different picture. Attention, he proposed, is a single, limited pool of mental effort, or capacity , that can be shared out among activities. This is the capacity model (also called resource or central capacity theory). Two tasks can be performed together as long as their combined demand does not exceed the capacity available; when it does, performance on one or both suffers. The amount of capacity is not fixed: it rises and falls with arousal, so that a drowsy person has less to share out and a moderately alert one has more. How the capacity is divided depends on an allocation policy , which is shaped by four influences: enduring dispositions (built-in tendencies to attend to novel or moving stimuli, or to one's own name), momentary intentions (what you are trying to do right now), the evaluation of demands (the system's judgement of how much each task needs) and the current level of arousal. Kahneman measured effort through the size of the pupil, which widens as a mental task becomes harder. The capacity model explained why difficult tasks interfere more than easy ones, and why practice, which makes tasks easier, makes them easier to combine. But it had a weakness: it predicts that two equally difficult tasks should interfere equally with a third, and they do not. What matters is how similar they are. Multiple resource theory and dual-task interference The study of what happens when people perform two tasks together is called the dual-task paradigm , and its main finding is that interference depends heavily on similarity. In a striking demonstration, Alan Allport, Barbara Antonis and Patricia Reynolds (1972) found that skilled pianists could sight-read music while shadowing speech with little loss on either task, although shadowing two spoken messages would have been impossible. Christopher Wickens captured this in his multiple resource theory (1984, refined in later work). Instead of a single pool, Wickens proposed several separate pools of resources, defined along a few dimensions: the stage of processing (perceptual and cognitive processing versus responding), the modality of input (visual versus auditory), the code of processing (spatial versus verbal) and, within vision, focal versus peripheral (ambient) vision. Two tasks that draw on different pools can be time-shared well; two tasks that compete for the same pool interfere. Driving (visual, spatial, manual) combines reasonably well with listening to the radio (auditory, verbal), and badly with reading a text message (visual, verbal, manual). Practice also changes what can be combined. In a famous study, Elizabeth Spelke, William Hirst and Ulric Neisser (1976) trained two students for several months to read short stories while writing down words dictated to them. At first their reading speed and comprehension collapsed; after weeks of practice they read as fast and understood as well as when reading alone, while writing to dictation. Practice had apparently turned one of the tasks into something that no longer needed much capacity. Multitasking and the phone in the car What people call multitasking is, for most tasks, rapid switching between them. Every switch has a switch cost : responses are slower and more error-prone just after a switch than when the same task is repeated, as Robert Rogers and Stephen Monsell showed in 1995. The real-world consequences are serious. David Strayer and William Johnston (2001) had people perform a simulated driving task while talking on a mobile phone; they missed nearly twice as many red lights and braked more slowly than when driving alone, and a hands-free phone was no better than a hand-held one. Listening to the radio or a recorded book did not have this effect. The problem is the conversation, not the hands. Later work by Strayer's group found that drivers talking on phones were impaired about as much as drivers at the legal limit for alcohol, and that they looked straight at roadside objects and then failed to remember them: inattentional blindness at the wheel. A two-wheeler rider in Bengaluru with a phone wedged inside his helmet is not doing two things well; he is doing two things badly. Automatic versus controlled processing Spelke's students point to the third answer. Some mental processes demand attention and effort; others run off by themselves. In 1975 Michael Posner and Charles Snyder proposed three criteria for an automatic process : it occurs without intention, it occurs without conscious awareness, and it does not interfere with other ongoing mental activity. Two years later Richard M. Shiffrin and Walter Schneider (1977) made the distinction the basis of a major theory. Controlled processes are slow, serial, effortful, limited by capacity, open to awareness and flexible: you can change them at once when the situation changes. Automatic processes are fast, run in parallel, need little or no capacity, are hard to stop once triggered and are inflexible. Table 5.3 lists the contrasts. Key study: Shiffrin and Schneider's search experiments (1977) Participants memorised a set of up to four characters and then searched rapidly presented displays for any of them. In the consistent mapping condition, targets and distractors never swapped roles (for example, targets were always consonants and distractors always digits). In the varied mapping condition, the same characters served as targets on some trials and distractors on others. With consistent mapping, search speed hardly depended on how many items had to be compared: search had become automatic and parallel. With varied mapping, every extra item added time: search was controlled and serial. When participants were trained for 2,100 trials with one set of letters as targets and another as distractors, search became automatic; when the roles were then reversed, it took nearly 1,000 trials before performance recovered even to its starting level. Automatic processes, once learned, are fast but stubborn. Table 5.3 Automatic versus controlled processing (Posner and Snyder, 1975; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977). Feature Automatic processing Controlled processing Effort and capacity Little or none Effortful; limited by capacity Speed and organisation Fast, parallel Slow, serial Intention Triggered without intention; hard to stop Deliberate; can be started and stopped Awareness Usually outside awareness Conscious Flexibility Rigid; hard to modify once learned Flexible; adapts to new situations How acquired Extensive consistent practice Needed for novel or variable tasks Examples Reading a word, an expert's gear change A learner driver, solving a new problem The distinction reaches well beyond the laboratory. Patricia Devine (1989) applied it to prejudice: because cultural stereotypes are learned by everyone in a society, they are activated automatically in high- and low-prejudiced people alike when a member of the group is encountered; what distinguishes low-prejudiced people is that they use controlled processing to override the activated stereotype and replace it with their own egalitarian beliefs. (The social psychology of prejudice is taught in the Social Psychology book.) And the stubbornness of automatic processes produces the most famous interference effect in psychology. The Stroop effect (1935) Key study: Stroop's colour-word experiments (1935) John Ridley Stroop (1897 to 1973), an American psychologist, published "Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions" in 1935, based on his doctoral research at George Peabody College. In one experiment, people simply read aloud colour words printed in conflicting ink colours (the word RED printed in green ink) and were barely slower than when reading the same words printed in black. In another, they had to name the ink colour of such words, saying "green" to RED printed in green, and here performance collapsed: naming the ink colours of 100 conflicting words took about 74 per cent longer than naming the colours of plain coloured patches, and errors rose. A third experiment showed that days of practice reduced the interference but did not abolish it. Stroop himself soon left experimental work to teach the Bible, never knowing that his dissertation would become one of the most cited studies in psychology. The Stroop effect is the slowing of colour naming (and the rise in errors) when the word and the ink colour conflict. Notice its asymmetry. Words interfere strongly with naming colours, but colours hardly interfere with reading words. Why? The most widely accepted explanation is in terms of automaticity. For a literate adult, reading is so overlearned that it is automatic: you cannot look at a familiar word and not read it. Naming an ink colour, by contrast, is a controlled process that needs attention. When the two conflict, the automatically produced word ("red") competes with the deliberately produced colour name ("green") at the stage of choosing a response, and resolving that conflict takes time. A related account, the relative speed of processing explanation, says that words are simply processed faster than colours, so the word's name arrives at the response stage first and must be suppressed. Later connectionist models (Jonathan Cohen, Kevin Dunbar and James McClelland, 1990) recast both ideas in terms of the strength of the pathways involved: the word-reading pathway, trained by years of practice, is stronger. What, then, does the Stroop effect demonstrate? Above all, a limit on selective attention : we cannot completely filter out a stimulus dimension whose processing is automatic, even when we are told to ignore it and it hurts our performance to attend to it. Within a single stimulus, one attribute (the word) dominates the other (the ink colour) in controlling the response. It is also a measure of interference in reaction time due to conflicting information, and of the ability to inhibit a dominant response, which is why the Stroop task is one of the standard tests of the inhibition component of executive function and why it is used clinically to assess frontal lobe and attention problems. The emotional Stroop task applies the same logic: people name the ink colour of emotional and neutral words, and anxious individuals are slower with words related to their worries (a person with a spider phobia slows down on "web" and "hairy"), revealing an attentional bias toward threat. Exam trap The Stroop effect is an attention phenomenon: specifically, a failure of selective attention caused by interference from automatic word reading. It is not primarily about long-term memory retrieval, working memory, procedural memory, perception or language development, which are the usual distractors, and it does not show improved recall for related items or better accuracy under divided attention. One past paper (RML 2024) asks what the Stroop effect is "an account of" and keys stimulus dominance : one dimension of the stimulus (the printed word) dominates the other (its ink colour). "Semantic dominance" is the tempting wrong option because the intruding word is meaningful, but the keyed term describes one attribute of the stimulus overpowering another; "instructional" and "conceptual" dominance are not terms used for this effect. Vigilance and sustained attention Some jobs require attention not to many things at once but to one thing for a very long time, while waiting for something rare to happen. Air traffic controllers watching radar screens, radar operators, airport baggage screeners, lifeguards and nurses monitoring intensive-care displays all depend on sustained attention , the ability to keep attention on a task over a prolonged period; when the events to be detected are infrequent and unpredictable, it is usually called vigilance . Key study: the Mackworth clock (1948) During the Second World War, the Royal Air Force noticed that radar operators hunting for enemy submarines missed more signals as their watches went on. Norman Mackworth built a laboratory model of the problem. A pointer moved around a blank clock face in small regular jumps; occasionally, and unpredictably, it made a double jump, and the observer had to press a key whenever this happened. Over a two-hour watch, detection fell sharply, with the largest drop within the first half hour; a short break or a telephone message restored it. Mackworth had demonstrated the vigilance decrement : the decline in detection over time on a monotonous monitoring task. Two kinds of explanation have been offered for the decrement. One is that boring, understimulating tasks lower arousal, so the observer becomes less alert. The other, now more favoured, is that vigilance is hard mental work that steadily depletes attentional resources; people rate vigilance tasks as surprisingly effortful and stressful. Signal detection analysis (Chapter 3) adds that part of the decrement is a shift in criterion: tired observers become more cautious about saying "yes, there it is". Clinically, sustained attention is measured with the Continuous Performance Test (respond to a rare target letter in a long stream), and it is one of the first functions to suffer from sleep loss, as you will see in Section 5.8. Brain recordings provide another window: when a rare target appears among frequent non-targets (the oddball task), the brain produces a positive event-related potential about 300 milliseconds later, the P300, which indexes the allocation of attention to the target and is reduced in conditions such as schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Exam trap Air traffic controllers and radar readers are the textbook example of sustained attention (vigilance) , not selective attention (choosing one input among several), divided attention (two tasks at once) or "perceptual attention" (not a standard category). The classic experiment is Mackworth's clock test (1948). Clinical link Disorders of attention are among the commonest problems a clinical psychologist assesses. In attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity begin in childhood (the disorder itself is covered in the Disorders book). In hemispatial neglect , usually after damage to the right parietal lobe, patients ignore the left side of space: they eat from only the right half of the plate, shave half the face and bisect a horizontal line far to the right, although their vision is intact. Delirium is defined by an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, and that attentional disturbance, together with its acute onset, fluctuating course and usually identifiable (often reversible) medical cause, is the most reliable feature separating it from dementia, which begins insidiously and progresses slowly, with attention relatively preserved early. Attention is measured with tests such as the Continuous Performance Test, the Test of Everyday Attention, the Stroop and the Trail Making Test (taught in the Psychological Assessment book). 5.5 Consciousness: definitions, levels and the brain High yield · 18 Qs Everything in the last four sections was about how information gets selected. But selected for what? The usual answer is: for awareness. The gorilla that was not attended to was not experienced; the word that broke through the attenuator was. Attention is, very often, the gateway to consciousness. It is time to ask what lies on the other side of the gate. What consciousness is Consciousness is one of those words that everyone understands until asked to define it. A workable definition, used in most introductory texts, is that consciousness is our awareness of ourselves and of our environment: of our sensations, perceptions, thoughts, feelings and memories at any given moment. It helps to separate two meanings. The first is consciousness as a level or state of wakefulness, running from coma through drowsiness to alert wakefulness; this is what a doctor checks at a road accident. The second is consciousness as content : what, in particular, you are aware of right now. The two can come apart. A patient in a vegetative state opens the eyes and has sleep-wake cycles (wakefulness is present) but shows no sign of awareness, whereas a patient with locked-in syndrome , after damage to the brainstem, is fully aware but almost completely paralysed, able to communicate only with eye movements. The level of consciousness is measured clinically with the Glasgow Coma Scale , published by the neurosurgeons Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett in 1974. It scores three responses: eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6), giving a total from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert). A score of 8 or less is generally taken to mean coma. The scale measures consciousness, not attention, memory or intelligence, and it is used every day in emergency rooms across India. William James and the stream of consciousness The founders of experimental psychology tried to study consciousness by breaking it into elements. Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener trained observers to introspect, to report the sensations, images and feelings that made up an experience, much as a chemist breaks a compound into its elements. Titchener described introspection as a highly specialised form of self-observation, and his structuralism set out to describe the components of consciousness, their combinations and their connections (Chapter 1). William James thought this was a mistake. Consciousness, he wrote in 1890, "does not appear to itself chopped up in bits ... It is nothing jointed; it flows. A 'river' or a 'stream' are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described. In talking of it hereafter, let us call it the stream of thought, of consciousness, or of subjective life." The phrase stream of consciousness has belonged to James ever since, and it later gave its name to a style of novel-writing that imitates the flow of thought. James listed five characteristics of this stream. Every thought is part of a personal consciousness: it belongs to someone. Within each person, consciousness is always changing : no state, once gone, can recur exactly. It is sensibly continuous : even after sleep, you know that your thoughts this morning belong to the same self as last night's. It deals with objects independent of itself : thought is always about something. And it is selective : it is interested in some parts of its objects to the exclusion of others, which is James's link between consciousness and attention. One feature of the stream of consciousness has received particularly intense research attention: daydreaming , the spontaneous drift of thought away from the task and the surroundings toward fantasies, memories and plans. From the 1960s the American psychologist Jerome L. Singer (1924 to 2010) showed that daydreaming is not a sign of laziness or disorder but a normal, almost universal part of mental life, and that it can serve planning, creativity and self-reflection. More recently, Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert (2010) used a smartphone app to interrupt thousands of people at random moments; minds were wandering in nearly half of the samples, and people were less happy when their minds wandered than when they were focused, whatever they were doing. Brain imaging has linked mind wandering to the default mode network , a set of midline brain regions that become more active when we are not engaged in an external task. Exam trap "Stream of consciousness" was coined by William James ( Principles of Psychology , 1890), not by Jung, Wundt or Skinner. Wundt studied the elements of consciousness by introspection; James opposed this with the image of a flowing stream, which is why he is linked with functionalism. The feature of the stream that has received the most research attention is daydreaming , not gender differences, brain-wave patterns or eye movements. Levels of consciousness: Freud's iceberg and the modern unconscious James described the stream as it appears to the person having it. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) insisted that most of mental life never appears in the stream at all. In The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) he set out what is now called his topographic model of the mind, which divides it into three regions, usually drawn as an iceberg (Figure 5.3). The conscious is whatever you are aware of at this moment, a small tip above the water. The preconscious holds material that is not in awareness right now but can be recalled at will without difficulty: your mobile number, what you ate yesterday, the name of your school. The unconscious , by far the largest region, holds wishes, impulses and memories that are actively kept out of awareness by repression because they would cause anxiety; they cannot be recalled at will and are known only indirectly, through dreams, slips of the tongue, symptoms and the free associations of the analytic patient. Freud's principle of psychic determinism held that nothing in mental life is accidental: even a slip of the tongue (a parapraxis , popularly a "Freudian slip") is caused by unconscious motives. In 1923 Freud added a second, structural model of id, ego and superego (the id, wholly unconscious, works on the pleasure principle; the ego works on the reality principle; the superego is the internalised conscience); that model, and psychoanalysis as a theory of personality, belong to the Personality book. The picture of behaviour driven by unconscious inner forces that lie largely beyond the person's control, and shaped by early childhood experience, is the heart of the psychodynamic perspective (Chapter 2). waterline Preconscious Unconscious (the largest part) Conscious what you are aware of right now (the sentence you are reading) Preconscious out of awareness, recallable at will (your mobile number, a friend's name) Unconscious kept out of awareness by repression; known only indirectly, through dreams, slips of the tongue and symptoms Figure 5.3 Freud's topographic model drawn as an iceberg. Only the tip is conscious; the preconscious lies just below the surface and can be brought up at will; the much larger unconscious is held down by repression and shows itself only indirectly. Freud's specific claims about repression and the Oedipus complex have fared poorly in research, but the general idea that much mental activity goes on outside awareness has fared very well; it is the part of his thought that modern research most clearly supports. Modern psychologists, however, usually distinguish the dynamic, motivated unconscious of Freud from two other things. The nonconscious refers to processes that are never accessible to awareness at all, however hard you try: the regulation of blood pressure and body temperature, or the early stages of visual processing that compute depth from the two eyes. The cognitive unconscious , a term popularised by John Kihlstrom in 1987, refers to the mental processes that operate outside awareness but are not repressed, simply automatic. You met examples in Section 5.2 (Corteen and Wood's skin responses to unattended words) and Section 5.4 (automatic reading in the Stroop task). Others include priming and implicit memory (Chapter 7), and three findings deserve special mention: Blindsight. Lawrence Weiskrantz (1926 to 2018) studied patients with damage to the primary visual cortex who insist that they see nothing in part of the visual field, yet, when forced to guess, point to objects there and discriminate their orientation far better than chance. Visual information is processed and used without being consciously seen. The "low road" to fear. Joseph LeDoux showed that a fast pathway from the thalamus to the amygdala, bypassing the cortex, allows rapid, crude detection of threat and the start of a defensive response before the threat is consciously recognised (Chapter 11). Implicit attitudes. The Implicit Association Test (Anthony Greenwald and colleagues, 1998) measures how quickly people pair concepts (for example, social groups with good or bad words) and is used to reveal automatic, often unacknowledged stereotyping (taught in the Social Psychology book). Exam trap Accessible memories that can be recalled at will are preconscious , not unconscious. The unconscious cannot be reached at will; that is its defining feature. Psychic determinism is Freud's principle that all mental events are caused, not a level of consciousness. "Subconscious" is a popular word that Freud did not use as a technical term; in exam options prefer conscious, preconscious and unconscious. The model of three levels is the topographic model (1900); id, ego and superego form the later structural model (1923). Consciousness and the brain, and the hard problem Where does consciousness come from in the brain? The first clue about the level of consciousness came in 1949, when Giuseppe Moruzzi and Horace Magoun found that electrically stimulating the reticular formation in the brainstem of a sleeping or anaesthetised cat immediately changed its EEG to the pattern of alert wakefulness. The reticular activating system , a network running from the brainstem through the thalamus to the cortex, maintains arousal; damage to it produces coma. The contents of consciousness, in contrast, seem to depend on widespread, coordinated activity across the cortex and thalamus. Francis Crick and Christof Koch made the search for the neural correlates of consciousness , the minimal brain activity sufficient for a specific conscious experience, a respectable scientific programme from 1990, and Bernard Baars's global workspace theory (1988) proposed that information becomes conscious when it is "broadcast" widely across the brain, so that many specialised systems can use it at once, rather like an actor stepping into the spotlight on a stage watched by a large audience. (The split-brain studies of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga, which bear on the unity of consciousness, are taught in the Physiological Psychology book.) Even a complete map of these correlates would leave one question open. In 1995 the Australian philosopher David Chalmers (born 1966) distinguished the "easy problems" of consciousness, explaining how the brain discriminates stimuli, integrates information, focuses attention and reports on its states, from the hard problem of consciousness : why any of this processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all. Why does the activity of neurons responding to a certain wavelength feel like the redness of a tomato, instead of going on "in the dark"? The easy problems are hard in practice but are problems of mechanism; the hard problem asks why mechanism should produce experience, and there is no agreed answer. Altered states of consciousness Your ordinary waking consciousness is not the only state your mind can be in. An altered state of consciousness (ASC) is a temporary, qualitative change in the overall pattern of mental functioning, such that the person feels that consciousness is radically different from its ordinary state. The definition is associated with the American psychologist Charles Tart (born 1937), whose edited book Altered States of Consciousness (1969) made the term standard; the psychiatrist Arnold Ludwig (1966) listed the features such states tend to share, including disturbed thinking, a changed sense of time, loss of control, changes in emotional expression and body image, perceptual distortion, a sense that experiences are deeply meaningful or indescribable, and increased suggestibility. Some altered states occur naturally every day (sleep and dreaming); others are induced psychologically (hypnosis, meditation, sensory deprivation, rhythmic drumming or chanting) or physiologically (fever, lack of oxygen, fasting and psychoactive drugs). The rest of this chapter examines the most important of them, beginning with the one you enter every night. But sleep is governed by a clock, so we start with the clock. Indian context Indian philosophy analysed states of consciousness long before Western psychology. The Mandukya Upanishad describes four states. In jagrat (waking) consciousness is directed outward to the physical world; in svapna (dreaming) it is directed inward to subtle images; in sushupti (deep, dreamless sleep) there is neither object nor desire, only an undifferentiated rest (the self in this state is called prajna ). The fourth state, turiya (literally "the fourth"), is not a further condition alongside the others but pure consciousness itself, the silent witness present in all three and identified with the Atman , the true self or soul, understood as eternal, unchanging consciousness (as distinct from the perishable body and the passing states of mind). Vedanta texts often speak of avastha-traya , "the three states", with turiya as what lies beyond them. Indian psychology, whose primary focus is the integration of these Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts, is taught in Chapter 2. 5.6 Biological rhythms: the body's clocks Lower yield · 4 Qs If you have ever travelled overnight by train from Mysuru to Delhi and back, you know that the body has opinions about time. You feel sleepy at certain hours whatever you are doing, and alert at others. These opinions come from biological rhythms, regular cyclical changes in physiology and behaviour, and the most important of them is set by a tiny clock deep in the brain. Circadian rhythms A circadian rhythm is a biological cycle of about 24 hours (from the Latin circa diem , "about a day"; the term was coined by the chronobiologist Franz Halberg in 1959). The sleep-wake cycle is the obvious example, but almost every bodily process has one. Body temperature falls through the night and is lowest in the early morning hours, which is why night-shift workers feel coldest and most error-prone around four or five in the morning; it rises through the day. The stress hormone cortisol peaks shortly after waking. The hormone melatonin rises in the evening and is highest in the middle of the night. Are these rhythms just responses to the day outside, or does the body keep time by itself? The test is to remove every time cue. Volunteers have lived for weeks in caves and underground bunkers with no daylight, no clocks and no news, eating and sleeping whenever they wished. Their rhythms persisted, but drifted: under constant conditions human rhythms run with a period slightly longer than 24 hours (about 24.2 hours in careful modern studies), so that each "day" they went to bed a little later. A rhythm that runs on in the absence of time cues is called free-running , and its persistence proves that there is an internal clock. Under normal conditions the clock is reset every day by environmental cues called zeitgebers (German, "time givers"). Light is by far the most powerful; meals, exercise and social activity are weaker zeitgebers. The process of being kept in step with the 24-hour day is called entrainment . The suprachiasmatic nucleus and melatonin The master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a pair of small clusters of neurons in the hypothalamus, sitting just above the optic chiasm (hence "supra-chiasmatic"). The evidence that it is the clock is unusually complete. When the SCN is destroyed in rats and hamsters, circadian rhythms of sleep, activity, eating and drinking disappear: the animals sleep about the same total amount, but at random times of day and night. SCN neurons removed from the brain and kept alive in a dish continue to fire in a 24-hour rhythm. And when Martin Ralph and colleagues (1990) transplanted the SCN from hamsters with a mutant short-period clock into normal hamsters whose own SCN had been destroyed, the recipients took on the donor's rhythm. The clock itself is molecular: in each SCN cell, "clock genes" switch each other on and off in a feedback loop that takes about a day to complete, a discovery recognised by the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2017. How does light reach the clock? Not through the ordinary visual pathway. A special class of retinal ganglion cells containing the photopigment melanopsin responds to overall brightness and sends signals directly to the SCN along the retinohypothalamic tract . (Some blind people whose rods and cones are destroyed still have entrained rhythms because these cells survive.) The SCN, in turn, controls the pineal gland , which secretes melatonin in darkness; light suppresses it. Melatonin, sometimes called the hormone of darkness, signals "night" to the rest of the body and promotes sleepiness, and melatonin taken at bedtime in the new location can help reset the clock after long flights. Exam trap The SCN is the master circadian pacemaker , entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract; SCN lesions disrupt circadian rhythms , not total sleep amount. Do not confuse it with neighbouring hypothalamic regions that are popular distractors: the lateral and ventromedial hypothalamus (hunger and satiety, Chapter 10), the preoptic area (temperature regulation and, in its ventrolateral part, sleep onset; Section 5.7), the paraventricular nucleus (stress hormones), the hypothalamic control of anterior pituitary hormones, and the mammillary bodies (memory). Memory consolidation belongs to the hippocampus, language to Broca's and Wernicke's areas, and long-term memory is not "stored" in the SCN. Jet lag, shift work, larks and owls The clock works well as long as life keeps to a regular schedule. Problems arise when the zeitgebers change suddenly ( jet lag , after flying across time zones) or when work forces us to be awake at the wrong phase of the clock ( shift work ). Both produce sleep disturbance, fatigue, poor concentration and digestive upset, because the internal clock and the external day are out of step, and because different bodily rhythms re-adjust at different speeds. Flying east is harder than flying west. Flying east from London to Bengaluru shortens your day, so you must fall asleep and wake earlier than your clock wants (a phase advance ); flying west lengthens it (a phase delay ), and since the free-running clock naturally runs a little longer than 24 hours, delaying it is easier. Full adjustment takes roughly a day for each time zone crossed. For the same reason, rotating shifts are easier to tolerate when they move forward, from morning to evening to night, than backward; Charles Czeisler and colleagues showed in 1982 that switching a group of industrial workers to forward rotation improved their health and productivity. People also differ in the phase of their clocks. "Larks" (morning types) wake early and peak early; "owls" (evening types) are sluggish in the morning and alert at night. These differences, called chronotypes, are partly genetic, and they shift with age: adolescents drift strongly toward owl-ness, which is why a 7 a.m. coaching class is a biological ordeal for many sixteen-year-olds, while older adults drift back toward larkishness. Sleepiness, finally, is not set by the clock alone. The Swiss researcher Alexander Borbély proposed in 1982 the influential two-process model of sleep regulation. Process S (sleep pressure) is homeostatic: it builds up the longer you are awake (partly through the accumulation of the chemical adenosine in the brain) and dissipates during sleep. Process C is the circadian rhythm from the SCN, which promotes wakefulness during the biological day. You fall asleep easily when sleep pressure is high and the circadian alerting signal is low. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors, hiding sleep pressure for a few hours without removing it. Ultradian and infradian rhythms Not all rhythms are daily. Ultradian rhythms are cycles shorter than a day, repeating more than once in 24 hours. The best known is the roughly 90-minute cycle of sleep stages that you will meet in the next section; Kleitman suggested that a similar 90-minute basic rest-activity cycle continues through the day as well, as fluctuations in alertness, and pulses of many hormones follow ultradian rhythms. Infradian rhythms are cycles longer than a day: the human menstrual cycle of about 28 days is the classic example. Cycles of about a year, called circannual rhythms, include hibernation, bird migration and, in humans, seasonal affective disorder , a form of depression that recurs in the dark months of winter and can be treated with bright-light therapy. For most of history that third was a blank: you closed your eyes, and some hours later you opened them. Sleep could not be studied because the sleeper could not report on it. What changed this was a machine that could listen to the brain. Listening to the sleeping brain: the EEG In 1929 the German psychiatrist Hans Berger (1873 to 1941) published the first recordings of electrical activity from the human scalp, the electroencephalogram (EEG). The EEG picks up the summed activity of millions of cortical neurons. When those neurons fire in an unsynchronised way, each doing its own work, their activity largely cancels out and the EEG shows small, fast waves; when large numbers fire together in rhythm, the waves become large and slow. Waves are described by their frequency (cycles per second, or hertz, Hz) and their amplitude (height, which reflects voltage). The first rhythm Berger described, a regular wave of about 10 Hz seen when a person rests with eyes closed, is still sometimes called the Berger rhythm; we now call it alpha. A modern sleep laboratory records three measures together, a procedure called polysomnography : the EEG, the electrooculogram (EOG), which records eye movements from electrodes beside the eyes, and the electromyogram (EMG), which records muscle tension, usually from under the chin. As sleep deepens, the waves become slower and larger; in REM sleep the EEG returns to a fast, low-voltage, waking-like pattern. The discovery of REM sleep Now return to Eugene Aserinsky and the jerking pens. What Aserinsky and Kleitman reported in 1953 was that the bursts of rapid eye movement coincided with periods of low-voltage, fast EEG, like that of a waking person, and that people woken from these periods usually reported dreams. Their student William Charles Dement (1928 to 2020), then a medical student and later the founder of the world's first sleep disorders clinic at Stanford, joined the work, and in 1957 Dement and Kleitman described the full pattern: the stages of sleep follow one another in a regular cycle of about 90 minutes, repeated through the night, with a period of rapid-eye-movement sleep at the end of each cycle. In their studies, about 80 per cent of awakenings from REM periods produced vivid, story-like dream reports, compared with only a small fraction of awakenings from other stages. In 1959 the French researcher Michel Jouvet (1925 to 2017) found that in cats this state is accompanied by a complete loss of muscle tone and called it paradoxical sleep , because the brain looks awake while the body is more deeply relaxed than at any other time. Sleep researchers therefore divide sleep into two basic kinds. REM sleep (rapid eye movement sleep) is the paradoxical stage. NREM sleep (non-REM sleep) is everything else, and it is subdivided into stages by its EEG. The standard scoring manual of Allan Rechtschaffen and Anthony Kales (1968) recognised four NREM stages, numbered 1 to 4, with stages 3 and 4 together called slow-wave sleep. In 2007 the American Academy of Sleep Medicine merged stages 3 and 4 into a single stage, so that modern texts (including Pinel) describe three NREM stages, N1 , N2 and N3 , plus REM (sometimes labelled R). Many exam questions still use the older numbering, so you must know both. A night's journey through the stages Picture a student going to bed after a long day of revision. As she lies with her eyes closed and relaxes, her EEG shows regular alpha waves. Then, over a few minutes, she passes through the stages of sleep. Stage N1 is the brief transition from waking to sleep, lasting only a few minutes. Alpha waves give way to slower, irregular theta waves of low amplitude, and the eyes may roll slowly. She is easy to wake, and if woken she may insist she was not asleep. This is the stage of the hypnic jerk , the sudden muscle twitch that sometimes jolts us awake with a feeling of falling, and of dreamlike hypnagogic images (Section 5.9). N1 makes up only about 5 per cent of a night's sleep. Stage N2 is light but definite sleep. The EEG is mostly theta, punctuated by two signature waveforms: sleep spindles , short waxing and waning bursts of 11 to 15 Hz waves, and K-complexes , single large sharp waves, a large negative (upward) deflection followed at once by a large positive (downward) one, which often appear when a sound occurs during sleep. Heart rate and breathing slow, body temperature falls and the eyes are still. N2 is the most common stage, about half of an adult's total sleep. Stage N3 is deep sleep. The EEG is dominated by delta waves, the largest and slowest of all, which is why N3 is called slow-wave sleep (SWS). In the older system, stage 3 had 20 to 50 per cent delta and stage 4 more than 50 per cent; together they formed slow-wave sleep. This is the hardest stage to wake from: a person roused from N3 is groggy and confused for several minutes. Breathing and heart rate are slow and regular, the release of growth hormone is at its daily peak, and the brain uses less energy than at any other time. N3 is also when sleepwalking and sleep terrors occur. After N3 the sleeper climbs back up through N2, and then, about 70 to 90 minutes after falling asleep, something remarkable happens. The EEG becomes fast, low-voltage and desynchronised, much like that of an alert, waking person, with bursts of rapid eye movements under the closed lids. This is REM sleep. Its features are a list of paradoxes (Table 5.6 sets them against those of NREM sleep): The brain is highly active: its oxygen use and blood flow in many regions rise to waking levels, and the EEG shows beta and theta waves with characteristic sawtooth waves. The eyes dart rapidly from side to side in bursts. The large skeletal muscles of the body core are almost completely paralysed, a state called REM atonia , produced by brainstem circuits that actively inhibit motor neurons in the spinal cord, although small muscles of the fingers and face may twitch. Heart rate, blood pressure and breathing become irregular, and there is genital arousal (penile erection or clitoral engorgement) in nearly every REM period, whatever the content of the dream; even infants show it. Most vivid, emotional, story-like dreams occur in REM sleep. Despite the waking-like EEG, a person in REM sleep is hard to wake by meaningless sounds, although meaningful ones (their own name, a baby's cry) can wake them easily. The 90-minute cycle and its changes across the night One sequence of NREM stages followed by a REM period is a sleep cycle . Each cycle lasts about 90 minutes (anywhere from about 70 to 110 minutes), so a typical adult night of seven to eight hours contains four to six cycles . But the cycles are not identical, and the way they change is a favourite exam point (Figure 5.5). Early in the night, cycles contain long periods of N3 and very short REM periods; the first REM period may last only about 10 minutes. As the night goes on, N3 shrinks and often disappears altogether in the last cycles, while REM periods lengthen to half an hour or more. Slow-wave sleep is concentrated in the first third of the night; REM sleep in the last third. This is why you are most likely to be woken from a dream by your morning alarm, and why sleepwalking and sleep terrors (N3 events) happen within a few hours of falling asleep. Brief awakenings, usually forgotten by morning, are normal. The standard answer is four to six (about 90 minutes each over seven to eight hours), and that is the keyed answer when it is offered (RML 2024). Some sources give "four to five" or "about five", and one past paper (RML 2022) keys 4 to 7 because 4 to 6 was not among its options; choose the option that contains four to six and excludes the extremes (2 to 4 is too few, 8 to 12 too many). Also remember the direction of change: N3 decreases and REM increases across the night, not the reverse. Sleep across the lifespan Sleep changes dramatically with age, as Howard Roffwarg and his colleagues Joseph Muzio and William Dement showed in a classic paper in 1966 (Figure 5.6). A newborn baby sleeps about 16 hours a day, and about half of that is REM sleep; newborns also often enter REM directly at sleep onset. Total sleep and the proportion of REM fall steeply through infancy and childhood. By adolescence REM makes up about 20 to 25 per cent of sleep, and it stays near that level through adulthood, declining slightly in old age. Roffwarg proposed that the huge amount of REM sleep in infancy provides internally generated stimulation that helps the developing brain mature, an idea known as the ontogenetic hypothesis. Both total sleep and the share of REM fall steeply in early life; REM is half of a newborn's sleep but about a fifth of an adult's. What switches sleep on and off You read in Section 5.5 that the reticular activating system keeps the cortex awake. Sleep is not simply this system running down. It is actively switched on. A group of inhibitory neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area (VLPO) of the hypothalamus, which use the transmitter GABA, become active at sleep onset and shut down the arousal systems of the brainstem and hypothalamus; the arousal systems, in turn, inhibit the VLPO. Because each side suppresses the other, the brain flips quickly between sleep and wakefulness, like a light switch, instead of drifting between them; Clifford Saper and his colleagues called this the "flip-flop switch". The switch is stabilised by orexin (also called hypocretin), a peptide made by neurons in the lateral hypothalamus that keeps the system firmly in the waking position; its loss causes narcolepsy (Section 5.8). REM sleep is generated in the brainstem, particularly the pons. "REM-on" neurons in a region called the sublaterodorsal nucleus trigger REM sleep and, through circuits in the medulla, the atonia that goes with it; "REM-off" neurons in the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey hold REM in check. During REM, waves of activity called PGO waves (ponto-geniculo-occipital) travel from the pons through the visual thalamus to the occipital cortex, a fact that will matter when we come to theories of dreaming. Exam trap Slow-wave (NREM) sleep begins when neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area become active. The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian clock (it decides when sleep is likely, not how it is switched on). The sublaterodorsal nucleus is a REM-on region, and the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey is a REM-off region; both concern REM, not slow-wave sleep. 5.8 Why we sleep, what deprivation does and when sleep goes wrong Medium yield · 4 Qs Sleep is costly. An animal asleep is not eating, mating or watching for predators. Yet every mammal and bird that has been studied sleeps, and even fruit flies and roundworms have sleep-like states. Something so universal and so risky must do something important. But what? Theories of why we sleep Pinel groups the answers into two kinds. Recuperation theories (also called restorative theories), associated with the British psychiatrist Ian Oswald among others, hold that being awake disrupts the body's internal balance in some way and that sleep is needed to restore it: to replenish energy, repair tissue, clear waste products and restore the brain. There is real evidence for restoration. Growth hormone is released mainly during slow-wave sleep. Slow-wave sleep increases after unusually tiring days and after sleep loss. And in 2013 Lulu Xie, Maiken Nedergaard and colleagues showed in mice that the spaces between brain cells widen during sleep, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to flush out waste products, including the protein beta-amyloid that accumulates in Alzheimer's disease, a cleaning system called the glymphatic system. Adaptation theories (Pinel's term; also called adaptive, evolutionary or circadian theories), associated with Wilse Webb and Ray Meddis in the 1970s, hold that sleep is less a response to the wear of waking than a behaviour that evolution timed to keep animals still and safe during the part of the day when activity would be useless or dangerous, and to conserve energy. They explain well why different species sleep such different amounts. Large grazing animals, which must eat for most of the day and cannot hide from predators, sleep only a few hours; animals that are safe in burrows or at the top of the food chain, and that can meet their needs quickly, sleep much longer. They also explain why sleep is so tightly tied to the circadian clock. A third family of theories stresses memory consolidation . As far back as 1924, John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach found that people forgot less of what they had learned if they slept after learning than if they stayed awake (Chapter 7). Modern research suggests that slow-wave sleep helps to consolidate factual, declarative memories, partly by "replaying" the day's patterns of hippocampal activity, while REM sleep helps to consolidate procedural skills and emotional memories; Avi Karni and colleagues (1994) found that improvement on a visual skill overnight disappeared when participants were deprived of REM sleep. Giulio Tononi and Chiara Cirelli have added that sleep may prune back the synaptic strengthening of the day, keeping the brain efficient. These theories are not rivals so much as parts of one answer: sleep probably does several jobs, and its timing has been fitted to each species' way of life. Sleep deprivation Key study: Randy Gardner's 264 hours (1964) In the winter of 1963 to 1964, Randy Gardner, a 17-year-old high-school student in San Diego, set out to break the world record for staying awake as a school science project, kept awake by two friends. William Dement heard about it and joined them. Gardner stayed awake for 264 hours, eleven days. He grew irritable, his speech became slurred, his memory and concentration lapsed, and he had brief perceptual distortions, but he never became psychotic; near the end he held a press conference and conducted himself well. Afterwards he slept for about 14 hours and then returned to his normal schedule. He did not need to recover all the lost sleep, a typical finding. Laboratory studies give a more systematic picture. Even moderate sleep loss produces three consistent effects: increased sleepiness, more negative mood and, above all, poor performance on tasks of sustained attention , the dull vigilance tasks of Section 5.4. Sleep-deprived people suffer microsleeps , episodes of a few seconds in which the eyelids droop, the EEG shows sleep and the person stops responding, even while sitting or standing; at the wheel of a car on a highway, a microsleep can be fatal. Chronic partial deprivation is also harmful: Hans Van Dongen and colleagues (2003) found that people restricted to six hours a night for two weeks performed as badly on attention tests as people kept awake for one or two whole nights, yet they rated themselves as only slightly sleepy. Total deprivation for weeks is lethal in rats (Allan Rechtschaffen's studies in the 1980s), and a rare inherited human prion disease that destroys the thalamus and abolishes sleep, fatal familial insomnia, is invariably fatal. Interpreting human deprivation studies requires caution, however, because sleep loss is so often confounded with stress. REM deprivation and REM rebound In 1960 Dement woke volunteers every time they entered REM sleep, night after night, and woke a control group equally often during NREM sleep. Two things happened. First, the REM-deprived volunteers tried to enter REM more and more often each night, so that they had to be woken ever more frequently. Second, when they were finally allowed to sleep undisturbed, they spent much more time than usual in REM sleep. This compensatory increase is called REM rebound . Dement at first thought REM deprivation also caused anxiety and irritability, but later studies did not confirm serious psychological harm; people taking antidepressants that suppress REM sleep for months show no obvious ill effects. REM rebound is clinically familiar too: alcohol and many sleeping pills suppress REM, and when they are stopped, REM rebounds with intense, often disturbing dreams, which can tempt the person to go back to the drug. Sleep disorders: an overview Sleep disorders fall into a few broad groups: insomnia (difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, or unrefreshing sleep), hypersomnia (excessive sleepiness), breathing-related disorders and the parasomnias , abnormal behaviours or experiences that occur during sleep or the transitions into and out of it. Table 5.7 gives a brief overview; diagnostic criteria and treatment are taught in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Table 5.7 The main sleep disorders in brief. Narcolepsy , named by the French physician Jean-Baptiste-Édouard Gélineau in 1880, is a disorder of hypersomnia in which elements of REM sleep intrude into waking life. Its sufferers fall asleep at inappropriate moments, in the middle of a conversation or a meal, and when they do they often go straight into REM sleep. The most dramatic symptom is cataplexy , a sudden loss of muscle tone during full wakefulness, usually triggered by strong emotion such as laughter or anger: the knees buckle or the person collapses, fully conscious, for a minute or two. It is, in effect, REM atonia switched on while awake. Sleep paralysis (the inability to move for a few moments just as one falls asleep or wakes up) and hypnagogic hallucinations complete the classic picture, although both also occur occasionally in healthy people. The discovery in 1999 and 2000 that narcoleptic dogs carry a mutation in the orexin receptor gene and that human patients have lost most of their orexin-producing neurons explained the disorder. Sleep apnoea often masquerades as insomnia or as daytime fatigue: the sleeper wakes briefly dozens or hundreds of times a night to restart breathing, usually without remembering it. REM sleep behaviour disorder , first described by Carlos Schenck, Mark Mahowald and colleagues in 1986, is the mirror image of cataplexy: the atonia that should accompany REM sleep fails, so the sleeper acts out the dream, sometimes injuring a bed partner. And the contrast between sleep terrors and nightmares is a classic exam point: the first comes from deep NREM sleep early in the night with little recall, the second from REM sleep late in the night with vivid recall. Exam trap Somnambulism means sitting, walking or performing complex behaviour while asleep. Extreme fear, agitation and screaming while asleep describes sleep terrors ; acting out dreams (including nightmares) describes REM sleep behaviour disorder ; uncomfortable sensations in the legs causing movement and lost sleep describe restless legs syndrome . Sleepwalking and sleep terrors arise from N3 (slow-wave) sleep, not REM: a person in REM sleep is paralysed and cannot walk. Sleep talking (somniloquy) can occur in any stage. Clinical link The first-line treatment for chronic insomnia is not a sleeping pill but cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), which outperforms medication in the long run. Its techniques are examined by name. Stimulus control (Richard Bootzin, 1972) re-associates the bed with sleep: go to bed only when sleepy, use the bed only for sleep, get up if not asleep within about 20 minutes, and rise at the same time every day. Sleep restriction (Arthur Spielman) limits the time in bed to the time actually slept, building sleep pressure, and then extends it gradually. Paradoxical intention , a technique from Viktor Frankl's logotherapy, asks the patient to lie in bed in the dark and try as hard as possible to stay awake ; this removes the performance anxiety of "trying to sleep", which is what keeps many insomniacs awake. Dereflection , Frankl's other technique, is different: it redirects attention away from oneself and the symptom toward other meaningful goals. A man told to try to stay awake is receiving paradoxical intention. 5.9 Dreams Medium yield · 8 Qs Every culture has wondered about dreams. In the ancient world they were messages from gods or ancestors; in the Indian epics they foretell victory and disaster; in twentieth-century Vienna they became the key to the unconscious. Sleep research has answered some old questions and sharpened others. Before we look at the theories, let us be clear about what dreams are actually like. What dreams are like A dream is a sequence of images, feelings and thoughts experienced during sleep, usually as a story in which the dreamer takes part. Vivid, emotional, narrative dreams are most common in REM sleep, but mental activity also occurs in NREM sleep, mostly as shorter, more thought-like fragments; late in the night, NREM dreams can be as story-like as REM dreams. Everyone dreams every night, including people who insist they never do: "non-dreamers" have normal amounts of REM sleep and report dreams when woken from it. Early laboratory work tested common beliefs about dreams. Do dreams flash by in an instant? No: in 1957 Dement and Kleitman woke people either 5 or 15 minutes after a REM period began and asked which it had been, judging only from the length of their dream; they were correct in 92 of 111 cases, so dreams unfold in roughly real time. Can outside stimuli enter dreams? Yes: when Dement and Edward Wolpert (1958) sprayed water on sleepers in REM sleep and woke them a few seconds later, the water had been worked into the dream in 14 of 33 cases (a leaking roof, a sudden downpour on a stage). What do people dream about? Calvin Hall, who collected tens of thousands of dream reports, and Robert Van de Castle (1966), who devised a coding system for them, found that most dreams are surprisingly ordinary: familiar settings and people, everyday activities and the dreamer's current concerns. Negative emotions such as anxiety and fear are more common than positive ones, and being chased, falling and failing an exam are among the commonest themes worldwide. Fragments of the previous day's events, which Freud called the day residue , appear often. Why should a brain produce such experiences at all? The theories fall into a few families. Freud: dreams as disguised wishes Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams appeared in November 1899, but the publisher dated it 1900 to mark the new century, and 1900 is the date to remember. Freud called the interpretation of dreams "the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind". His central claim was that every dream is a wish fulfilment : the disguised fulfilment of a repressed wish, often sexual or aggressive and often dating from childhood. During sleep the ego's guard is lowered, and these wishes press toward expression. If they appeared undisguised, the dreamer would be so disturbed that he would wake, so an internal censor disguises them. In this sense, Freud said, dreams are the guardians of sleep. Freud therefore distinguished two levels of every dream. The manifest content is the dream as the dreamer remembers and reports it: the story, the people, the places. The latent content is its hidden meaning, the unconscious wishes and thoughts that gave rise to it. The mental process that turns latent content into manifest content is the dream work , and it uses four main mechanisms: Condensation : several latent ideas are compressed into a single image. A person in a dream who has your teacher's face, your father's voice and your uncle's walk condenses feelings about all three. Displacement : the emotional significance of an important but threatening object is shifted onto a trivial, harmless one. Anger at a parent may appear as anger at a stray dog. Symbolisation (Freud's "considerations of representability"): abstract thoughts are turned into concrete, mostly visual images and symbols, so that a wish to be free of an obligation might appear as a flight from a locked room. Secondary revision (secondary elaboration): on waking and in recall, the mind tidies the confused material into a more coherent, logical-seeming story, hiding the latent meaning further. To interpret a dream, the analyst asks the patient to free associate to each element of the manifest content, retracing the dream work backwards toward the latent thoughts. The theory has been enormously influential in culture and in psychotherapy, but its scientific standing is weak. There is no convincing evidence that dreams systematically disguise wishes; many dreams (the repeated nightmares of trauma survivors, for example) are hard to see as wishes at all, as Freud himself came to accept in 1920; and the brain science on which he built the theory is now obsolete. What has survived is the broader idea that dreams draw on our emotional concerns. Exam trap The Interpretation of Dreams : 1900 (printed in November 1899 but dated 1900). Manifest content is what is remembered; latent content is the hidden meaning. The four mechanisms of the dream work are condensation, displacement, symbolisation (representation) and secondary revision; "sublimation" and "projection" are defence mechanisms, not dream-work mechanisms, and "day residue" is the raw material, not a mechanism. "Royal road to the unconscious" refers to dreams, not to free association or slips of the tongue. Jung: dreams as messages from the psyche Carl Gustav Jung (1875 to 1961), once Freud's closest colleague, broke with him in 1913 partly over dreams. For Jung a dream is not a disguise but a natural, spontaneous self-portrait of the psyche, speaking in the language of symbols. Its chief function is compensatory : it balances a one-sided conscious attitude, so that a man who is outwardly all confidence may dream of being lost and helpless. Dreams can also be prospective , anticipating future development. Here Jung's disagreement with Freud over the unconscious matters. Jung held that the unconscious exists on two levels: a personal (individual) unconscious of the person's own forgotten and repressed experiences, and beneath it the collective unconscious , the inherited layer of the psyche shared by all humanity, which he accounted for in evolutionary terms, through the similar brain structure inherited by all human races. Some dreams draw on the collective unconscious and present universal images, the archetypes (such as the persona, the social mask; the shadow, the disowned dark side; the anima, the feminine side of a man; the animus, the masculine side of a woman; and the wise old man), which Jung found repeated in myths and religions across cultures. Early in his career, at the Burghölzli clinic in Zurich, Jung had also developed the word association test , in which hesitations and odd replies to stimulus words reveal unconscious emotional complexes. Instead of free association, Jung used amplification , enriching a dream symbol by comparing it with parallel images from myth, folklore and religion. (Jung's theory of personality is taught in the Personality book.) Activation-synthesis: dreams from the brainstem The discovery of REM sleep made a purely physiological theory possible. In 1977 the Harvard psychiatrists J. Allan Hobson (1933 to 2021) and Robert McCarley proposed the activation-synthesis hypothesis . During REM sleep, circuits in the pons fire spontaneously and send waves of activation (the PGO waves of Section 5.7) up to the forebrain, stimulating visual, motor and emotional areas more or less at random. That is the activation . The cortex, which is built to make sense of input, does its best with this chaotic barrage and weaves it into a story, drawing on the dreamer's memories and concerns. That is the synthesis . Think of how you see faces and animals in drifting clouds: the clouds are random, but your brain imposes a meaning on them. The hypothesis explains several features of dreams neatly. Dreams are intensely visual because the visual system is activated. They are bizarre, with sudden scene shifts, because the input is random. We dream of running yet being unable to move because motor areas are activated while the body is paralysed. And dreams are quickly forgotten because the brain chemicals that support memory formation (noradrenaline and serotonin) are almost absent in REM sleep. On this view dreams are not disguised messages; any meaning is added by the synthesising brain, although that meaning can still reflect the dreamer's personality. The hypothesis has been criticised: the neuropsychologist Mark Solms showed that patients with certain forebrain lesions stop dreaming although their REM sleep is intact, so dreaming depends on the forebrain, not just the pons, and dreaming also occurs outside REM. Hobson himself later revised the theory, and in 2009 proposed that dreaming is a kind of "protoconsciousness", a virtual-reality rehearsal that helps develop and maintain waking consciousness. Information-processing, memory and threat-simulation theories Information-processing theories see dreaming as a by-product or part of the brain's overnight handling of the day's experiences. In one early, provocative version, Francis Crick (1916 to 2004) and Graeme Mitchison (1983) proposed "reverse learning": REM sleep weakens unwanted, parasitic connections formed during the day, so that, in their phrase, we dream in order to forget. More influential today are memory-consolidation views, which link dreams to the role of sleep in strengthening and integrating memories (Section 5.8): new learning is replayed and connected with older memories, and dream content reflects fragments of this process. When Robert Stickgold and colleagues (2000) had people play the computer game Tetris for hours, many saw falling blocks as they drifted off to sleep, including amnesic patients who could not remember having played. Rosalind Cartwright, studying people going through divorce, argued that dreams also help regulate mood, working through emotional problems overnight. The neurocognitive or continuity view of William Domhoff holds that dreams express our waking concerns and conceptions, using the same cognitive systems that we use when awake; dreams develop gradually in childhood as these systems mature. The Finnish psychologist Antti Revonsuo took an evolutionary approach in his threat-simulation theory (2000). Dreams, he argued, evolved as a virtual training ground in which our ancestors rehearsed responses to threats (being chased, attacked, injured or rejected) safely during sleep, making them better at handling such threats when awake. In support, threatening events are greatly over-represented in dreams relative to waking life, and children who have lived through real danger dream of threats more often. Critics note that many dreams contain no threat, and that the rehearsal would be useless if it is forgotten by morning. Table 5.8 brings the theories of dreaming together. Theory Proposer and year Central idea Wish fulfilment Freud, 1900 Dreams are disguised fulfilments of repressed wishes; manifest content hides latent content Compensation and archetypes Jung Dreams are undisguised symbolic messages that balance conscious attitudes and may show archetypes Activation-synthesis Hobson and McCarley, 1977 The cortex synthesises a story from random brainstem activation during REM sleep Reverse learning Crick and Mitchison, 1983 REM sleep erases unwanted connections; we dream in order to forget Information processing and memory consolidation Stickgold and others Dreams reflect the overnight processing and consolidation of recent experience Continuity (neurocognitive) Hall; Domhoff Dreams express waking concerns using waking cognitive systems Threat simulation Revonsuo, 2000 Dreams evolved to rehearse responses to threats Lucid dreams Sometimes a dreamer realises, within the dream, that he is dreaming, and may even take control of what happens next, choosing to fly or to turn and face a pursuer. This is a lucid dream , a term coined by the Dutch psychiatrist Frederik van Eeden in 1913. For a long time scientists doubted that such dreams were real rather than reports made up after waking. The doubt was settled by an ingenious method. Keith Hearne in Britain in the 1970s, and Stephen LaBerge at Stanford in the early 1980s, asked lucid dreamers to make a pre-arranged pattern of eye movements (left, right, left, right) as soon as they became lucid. Because the eye muscles are not paralysed in REM sleep, the signals appeared clearly on the EOG, in the middle of unmistakable REM sleep. Many people have at least one lucid dream in their lives, and a few have them regularly; lucid dreaming techniques have been tried as a treatment for recurring nightmares. Hypnagogic and hypnopompic imagery The borders of sleep have experiences of their own. Hypnagogic imagery occurs while falling asleep (in N1): flashes of light, geometric patterns, faces, landscapes, snatches of speech or music, or the sensation of falling that may end in a hypnic jerk. The Tetris images described above are hypnagogic. Hypnopompic imagery is similar imagery experienced while waking up, sometimes so vivid that a person sees a figure standing by the bed for a moment after opening the eyes. (The terms are credited to the French scholar Alfred Maury and the British writer Frederic Myers respectively.) Such images are common and normal, and they are distinguished from the hallucinations of psychosis by occurring only at the edges of sleep. When they combine with sleep paralysis, the experience can be terrifying, typically a sense of an evil presence pressing on the chest; many cultures interpret it as an attack by a spirit or ghost. Frequent, intense episodes, together with daytime sleep attacks, should raise the question of narcolepsy. Exam trap Hypnagogic = falling asleep (think "going" to sleep); hypnopompic = waking up. The activation-synthesis hypothesis is Hobson and McCarley (1977) , not Freud or Crick; threat simulation is Revonsuo (2000) ; "we dream in order to forget" is Crick and Mitchison's reverse learning. Lucid dreaming was verified by pre-arranged eye-movement signals during REM sleep (LaBerge), because the eyes are the one set of muscles free to move. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks.
