On stage, the hypnotist swings a watch, the volunteers' eyes close, and moments later grown adults are clucking like hens. Is this a special state of consciousness, or are the volunteers simply playing along? Psychologists have argued about that question for two centuries, and the argument is a good model of how science sorts real effects from wishful thinking. Hypnosis is best defined as a social interaction in which one person, the hypnotist, offers suggestions for changes in perception, feeling, memory or behaviour, and the other person, the participant, experiences those changes as real and as happening by themselves, without deliberate effort. It usually begins with an induction : the participant is asked to focus attention (on the hypnotist's voice or a point on the wall), to relax and to let go of critical evaluation. The essential ingredient, the crux of the whole phenomenon, is suggestibility : a heightened readiness to accept and respond to suggestions. A suggestion is a communication that invites an automatic, non-volitional response, such as "your arm is becoming lighter and is rising by itself". Notice what is not required: neither sleep nor a special swinging watch, and not even a formal induction, since suggestible people respond to many suggestions without one. Exam trap The main crux of hypnosis is suggestibility . The "analytical mind" and "logical mind" are what hypnosis is said to quieten, not what it rests on. Hypnosis is not sleep: the EEG of a hypnotised person is a waking EEG, and people under hypnosis can hear, respond and, in general, refuse. From animal magnetism to the Nancy school: a short history The story begins with the Viennese physician Franz Anton Mesmer (1734 to 1815). From the mid-1770s, Mesmer claimed that health depended on the free flow of an invisible universal fluid through the body, which he called animal magnetism , and that a physician could redirect it to cure disease. In Paris from 1778 he treated fashionable patients in groups around a tub (the baquet ) filled with "magnetised" water and iron rods; many fell into convulsive "crises" and declared themselves cured. In 1784 King Louis XVI appointed a royal commission, which included the American scientist Benjamin Franklin and the chemist Antoine Lavoisier. In some of the first blind experiments in history, they showed that people reacted dramatically to objects they merely believed had been magnetised, and not at all to objects secretly magnetised. The commission concluded that the effects were real but were caused by imagination, not by any fluid. Mesmer was discredited, but "mesmerism" lived on. In the same year one of his followers, the Marquis de Puységur, found that some patients entered not a convulsive crisis but a calm, sleep-like trance in which they spoke and obeyed instructions and afterwards remembered nothing; he called it artificial somnambulism . The name we use came from the Scottish surgeon James Braid (1795 to 1860), practising in Manchester. After watching a travelling mesmerist's demonstration in 1841, Braid concluded that there was no magnetic fluid; the trance was a physiological and psychological effect of prolonged, fixed attention, which he produced by having patients stare at a bright object held above their eyes. He called the state "neuro-hypnotism" (nervous sleep), from Hypnos, the Greek god of sleep, and the shortened form hypnotism (hypnosis) stuck; his book Neurypnology appeared in 1843. Braid later realised that the state was not sleep at all and tried to rename it "monoideism", concentration on a single idea, but it was too late to change the name. Indian context Some of the most remarkable early uses of mesmerism took place in Bengal. James Esdaile (1808 to 1859), a Scottish surgeon with the East India Company at Hooghly, began in 1845 to operate on patients in a mesmeric trance, before chemical anaesthesia had reached India. Over the next few years he reported hundreds of operations, including amputations and the removal of large tumours, performed with little apparent pain and with a lower death rate than usual; the government gave him a small mesmeric hospital in Calcutta, and he described his work in Mesmerism in India (1846). Once ether and chloroform became available, mesmeric surgery quickly disappeared, but Esdaile's reports remain an early documented case of hypnotic analgesia. In the second half of the nineteenth century, hypnosis became the centre of a famous French controversy. At the Salpêtrière hospital in Paris, the great neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot (1825 to 1893) studied hypnosis in his patients with hysteria and concluded that hypnotisability was itself a sign of a diseased nervous system, a pathological state that passed through fixed stages and was found mainly in hysterics. His prestige made hypnosis respectable for scientific study. Against him stood the Nancy school : the country doctor Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823 to 1904), who had treated poor patients with hypnosis for years, and the professor of medicine Hippolyte Bernheim (1840 to 1919), who joined him. They argued that hypnosis is a normal phenomenon, that most healthy people can be hypnotised, and that it works entirely through suggestion. The Nancy view won the argument, and it is essentially the modern view. The young Sigmund Freud learned from both sides: he studied with Charcot in Paris in 1885 to 1886 and visited Bernheim at Nancy in 1889. With the Viennese physician Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925), he used hypnosis to help patients with hysteria recall and emotionally discharge forgotten traumatic experiences, the "cathartic method" first developed with Breuer's patient Anna O. Breuer and Freud reported their ideas on the psychical mechanism of hysterical phenomena in 1893 and in Studies on Hysteria in 1895. Freud soon abandoned hypnosis, because many patients could not be hypnotised and the improvements often did not last, and replaced it with free association , in which the patient, relaxing on a couch, reports whatever comes to mind without censoring it; this became the technique on which psychoanalysis was built. A generation later, the American learning theorist Clark Hull's Hypnosis and Suggestibility (1933) brought hypnosis into the experimental laboratory. Exam trap Mesmer : animal magnetism (1770s and 1780s), not the word hypnosis. Braid : coined hypnotism (1840s; Neurypnology , 1843). Charcot : hypnosis as pathology linked to hysteria (Salpêtrière, Paris). Liébeault and Bernheim : the Nancy school, hypnosis as normal suggestion. Freud and Breuer : the mechanism of hysteria (1893) and Studies on Hysteria (1895); Freud, not Bernheim, is the father of psychoanalysis, and free association replaced hypnosis. Who can be hypnotised? Hypnotic susceptibility People differ greatly in how readily they respond to hypnotic suggestions, a trait called hypnotic susceptibility (or hypnotisability). It is measured by standardised scales in which a standard induction is followed by a graded series of suggestions, from easy to hard, and the person's score is the number passed. The best known are the Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scales , devised by André Weitzenhoffer and Ernest Ropiequet Hilgard (1904 to 2001) at Stanford University (Forms A and B in 1959, Form C in 1962), each with 12 items. An easy item is that an outstretched arm becomes heavy and drops; harder items include hallucinating a buzzing fly, posthypnotic amnesia and failing to see an object that is in plain view. The Harvard Group Scale (Ronald Shor and Emily Orne, 1962) adapts the test for groups. Scores form a roughly bell-shaped distribution: perhaps 10 to 15 per cent of people are highly hypnotisable, a similar proportion respond to almost nothing, and most fall in between. Susceptibility is remarkably stable; in one study it correlated about 0.7 with the same person's score 25 years later. It is not related to gullibility, weakness of will or most personality traits, but it is related to absorption , the tendency to become deeply immersed in imaginative experiences such as a novel, a film or a daydream (Auke Tellegen and Gilbert Atkinson, 1974). What hypnosis can and cannot do Separating the real effects of hypnosis from the myths is one of the most practically useful things a psychologist can do (Table 5.9). Table 5.9 What hypnosis can and cannot do. Hypnosis can Hypnosis cannot Reduce pain substantially (hypnotic analgesia), used in surgery, dentistry, childbirth and burns care Give superhuman strength or endurance; motivated people who are not hypnotised can match the feats Produce posthypnotic suggestions, which are carried out on a cue after hypnosis has ended Reliably recover accurate memories; it increases false recall and confidence together Produce posthypnotic amnesia, which is reversed by a pre-arranged cue Truly regress adults to childhood ways of thinking, or to "past lives" Alter perception, including positive and negative hallucinations in highly hypnotisable people Reliably force people to act against their deeply held values Help as an addition to therapy for pain, irritable bowel syndrome, habit control and anxiety Work equally on everyone; responsiveness depends on susceptibility Hypnotic analgesia is the most robust effect: in highly hypnotisable people it can rival morphine, and in the 1990s Pierre Rainville and colleagues showed that suggestions changing how unpleasant a painful stimulus felt changed activity in the anterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in the emotional side of pain. A posthypnotic suggestion is an instruction given during hypnosis to be carried out later, after hypnosis has ended, in response to a cue: a participant told that she will open a window when the experimenter touches his tie may do so, and then explain, quite sincerely, that the room felt stuffy. Posthypnotic amnesia , forgetting what happened during hypnosis until a cue is given, is instructive because the memories return intact when the cue is given; they were stored all along, and only retrieval was blocked. The memory myths are the most dangerous. Under hypnosis people do report more "memories", but the extra items are as likely to be false as true, and, crucially, hypnosis makes people more confident in everything they recall, a problem called memory hardening. Jean-Roch Laurence and Campbell Perry (1983) suggested to hypnotised people that they had been woken by loud noises on a particular night the previous week; about half later "remembered" the noises, and some insisted on them even after being told of the suggestion. For this reason, many courts treat hypnotically refreshed testimony with great caution or refuse it altogether, and "recovered memories" of abuse produced under hypnosis cannot be trusted without independent evidence. Hypnotic age regression does not make adults think like children; it makes them act as they believe children act. Theories of hypnosis: a special state or a social role? The theoretical debate is between those who think hypnosis involves a special division of consciousness and those who think it is ordinary social and cognitive behaviour. Ernest Hilgard's neodissociation theory , set out in his book Divided Consciousness (1977), revived an idea of the French psychiatrist Pierre Janet. Hilgard proposed that the mind contains several subsystems of control, normally coordinated by a central executive. Hypnotic suggestion splits consciousness into separate streams: one part of the mind carries out the suggestion and has experiences that are walled off from the other, which remains unaware of them. The evidence that made the theory famous came by accident. During a classroom demonstration of hypnotic deafness, a blind student showed no response to loud sounds. A member of the class asked whether "some part" of him might be hearing, so Hilgard quietly told the student that if some part of him could hear, his index finger should rise. It rose. Hilgard called this concealed, aware part of the mind the hidden observer . In later experiments using the cold pressor test, in which a hand is held in ice water, hypnotised participants given analgesia suggestions reported very little pain aloud, while their hidden observer, reporting through automatic writing or key presses, reported pain almost as high as in the normal waking state. The pain was registered, Hilgard concluded, but kept out of the main stream of awareness by an amnesia-like barrier. The social-cognitive theory of hypnosis (also called sociocognitive or role theory) denies that any special state is needed. Its roots lie in Theodore Sarbin's role theory of the 1950s: hypnotised people are enacting the role of "hypnotised subject" as their culture understands it, not faking but absorbed in the role, as an actor can be absorbed in a part. Theodore Xenophon Barber (1927 to 2005) showed in the 1960s that ordinary participants given "task-motivating" instructions (to try their hardest to imagine and experience what is suggested) responded to suggestions almost as well as hypnotised participants. Nicholas Spanos (1942 to 1994) argued that hypnotic responses are goal-directed actions shaped by expectations and by how the situation is interpreted; in a direct challenge to Hilgard, he showed that the hidden observer reported more pain or less pain depending on what participants had been told the hidden observer would experience, suggesting that the hidden observer was itself a product of suggestion. Irving Kirsch added that the expectation of responding is itself a powerful cause of responding. Martin Orne, for his part, used the "real-simulator" design, comparing hypnotised participants with people instructed to fake hypnosis, and found subtle differences, such as "trance logic", the untroubled acceptance of logical contradictions (seeing a hallucinated person and the real person at the same time). Today the two camps have moved closer. Almost everyone agrees that hypnosis is not sleep, that it is not a magical surrender of will, and that expectation and suggestion drive it. But brain imaging shows that, in highly hypnotisable people, suggestion produces real changes in brain activity: Stephen Kosslyn and colleagues (2000) found that the suggestion to see colour in a grey pattern activated colour-processing regions, and Amir Raz, Michael Posner and colleagues (2002) found that a posthypnotic suggestion that words were meaningless symbols greatly reduced the Stroop effect, an effect that, as you saw in Section 5.4, people cannot normally switch off. Yes: a division of consciousness No: ordinary processes of expectation and role enactment Key evidence The hidden observer; cold pressor analgesia Task-motivated controls perform as well; hidden observer reports follow instructions Why responses feel involuntary The executive is unaware of the split-off control Participants interpret their own goal-directed actions as happening by themselves Clinical link Hypnosis has respectable clinical uses, mostly as an addition to other treatment: for chronic and procedural pain, irritable bowel syndrome, smoking and weight control, and anxiety; adding hypnotic techniques to cognitive behavioural therapy has been found to improve outcomes. The idea of dissociation, central to Hilgard's theory, also links hypnosis to the dissociative disorders, such as dissociative identity disorder, which requires two or more distinct personality states with recurrent gaps in memory (covered in the Disorders book). And the history of hypnosis is a reminder of the difference between symptoms produced unconsciously, as in conversion disorder, and symptoms faked deliberately for gain, as in malingering. 5.11 Meditation, sensory deprivation and psychoactive drugs Lower yield · 3 Qs Hypnosis showed that a few words from another person can change experience. The last altered states in this chapter are produced in other ways: by deliberately training one's own attention, by taking stimulation away, and by putting chemicals into the brain. Meditation Meditation is a family of practices that train attention and awareness, usually with the aim of calming the mind and bringing mental processes under greater voluntary control. The many techniques of the world's traditions fall into two broad kinds, which differ in what they do with attention. In concentrative meditation (now often called focused-attention meditation), attention is fixed on a single object: the breath, a repeated word or sound (a mantra ), a candle flame, an image or a prayer. Whenever the mind wanders, as it constantly will, the meditator notices this and gently brings attention back. The best-known modern form is transcendental meditation (TM), introduced by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (1918 to 2008) in India in the mid-1950s and spread worldwide from 1958, especially after the Beatles stayed at his ashram in Rishikesh in 1968. In TM the meditator sits comfortably and silently repeats a personal mantra for about 20 minutes, twice a day. In mindfulness meditation (also called opening-up or open-monitoring meditation), attention is not narrowed but widened: the meditator observes whatever arises, thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations and sounds, with calm, non-judging awareness, noticing each and letting it pass without holding on to it or pushing it away. Its roots are in Buddhist vipassana ("insight") practice. Concentrative meditation is like narrowing the zoom lens of Section 5.3 to a single point; mindfulness is like opening it wide while keeping it steady. What does meditation do? In 1970 Robert Keith Wallace reported that during TM, oxygen consumption, heart rate and breathing rate fell, skin resistance rose (a sign of relaxation) and alpha waves increased. The Harvard cardiologist Herbert Benson (1935 to 2022) then showed that the same changes, which he called the relaxation response (1975), could be produced by any similar technique (sitting quietly, relaxing the muscles and repeating a neutral word) and were not unique to TM. A sceptical review by David Holmes (1984) went further, concluding that meditation reduced physiological arousal no more than simply resting with the eyes closed. Later and better-controlled work has been kinder. Jon Kabat-Zinn (born 1944) developed mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) in 1979 for patients with chronic pain and stress, and Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale combined mindfulness with cognitive therapy in mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT, 2002), which substantially reduces relapse in people who have had three or more episodes of depression. Imaging studies have reported structural and functional brain changes in long-term meditators, for example greater cortical thickness in attention-related regions (Sara Lazar and colleagues, 2005). Meditation research also teaches an important lesson about evidence. Suppose researchers survey 10,000 randomly selected adults in ten countries and find that people who meditate regularly report less stress than people who rarely or never meditate. Can we conclude that meditation lowers stress? Not necessarily. Random selection makes the sample representative, and a large sample makes the estimate precise, but neither makes the study an experiment. Without random assignment of people to meditate or not, the finding is correlational: perhaps calmer people find it easier to keep up a meditation habit, or perhaps a third factor, such as a healthier lifestyle or more free time, produces both. Only an experiment can show that meditation causes the reduction (the logic is taught in the Research Methodology book). Indian context Meditation is among India's oldest contributions to psychology. In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras , the eight limbs of yoga ( ashtanga ) move from ethical restraints and observances ( yama , niyama ), posture ( asana ) and breath control ( pranayama ) to withdrawal of the senses from their objects ( pratyahara ), concentration ( dharana ), meditation ( dhyana ) and absorption ( samadhi ). Dharana and dhyana are close to what psychologists call concentrative meditation, while Buddhist vipassana is the source of mindfulness practice. Sufism describes its process of psycho-spiritual transformation as a comparable journey, from our mundane surface awareness to the depths and heights of self-consciousness, using practices such as dhikr , the rhythmic repetition of divine names. (Indian psychology is taught in Chapter 2.) Sensory deprivation Meditation reduces the variety of what we attend to. What happens if the world's input is taken away almost entirely? In the early 1950s, in Donald Hebb's laboratory at McGill University in Montreal, William Bexton, Woodburn Heron and Thomas Scott (1954) tried to find out. Key study: the McGill sensory deprivation experiments (1954) Male students were paid 20 dollars a day, generous money at the time, to do nothing at all. Each lay on a comfortable bed in a lit cubicle for as long as he could bear, wearing translucent goggles that let in diffuse light but no patterns, cotton gloves and long cardboard cuffs that limited touch, with his head on a U-shaped foam pillow and the steady hum of an air conditioner masking other sounds. He came out only to eat and use the toilet. Although the money was good, most volunteers quit within two or three days. They found it hard to think clearly or concentrate, did worse on simple cognitive tests, became irritable and restless, and many experienced hallucinations, beginning with dots and geometric patterns and developing into whole scenes; Heron later described one volunteer who saw a procession of squirrels with sacks over their shoulders marching across a snowfield. They also became more easily persuaded by recorded talks about the supernatural. The McGill studies, sometimes described as research into the "pathology of boredom", showed that the waking brain needs a steady flow of varied stimulation to function normally, an idea that fed into arousal theories of motivation (Chapter 10). Later researchers softened the picture. The neuroscientist John Lilly developed the flotation tank, in which a person floats in skin-temperature salt water in darkness and silence, and the psychologist Peter Suedfeld showed that short sessions of sensory deprivation , which he called the restricted environmental stimulation technique (REST), are often experienced as deeply relaxing and can help people stop smoking. The clinical relevance is real: hallucinations are common in people with severe visual loss (the Charles Bonnet syndrome), and the monotony of an intensive care unit contributes to confusion in some patients. Psychoactive drugs The most common way people deliberately alter consciousness is chemical: the morning coffee, the evening drink, the cigarette, the cup of bhang at Holi. A psychoactive drug is a chemical substance that changes perception, mood, thought or consciousness by acting on the nervous system, mostly at synapses: some mimic a neurotransmitter, some block its receptors, and some change how much of it is released or how quickly it is removed. (The synaptic mechanisms are taught in the Physiological Psychology book.) Three terms describe what happens with repeated use. Tolerance is the decreasing effect of the same dose with repeated use, so that larger doses are needed to get the original effect; tolerance to one drug often brings tolerance to similar drugs (cross-tolerance, as between alcohol and benzodiazepines). Dependence is a state in which the person needs the drug to function normally. Physical dependence means that the body has adapted to the drug's presence, so that stopping it produces withdrawal; psychological dependence is a compulsive craving to use the drug for its emotional effects. Withdrawal is the set of unpleasant symptoms that follows stopping a drug on which one is physically dependent, and the symptoms are usually the opposite of the drug's effects: anxiety and tremor after alcohol, fatigue and depression after stimulants, and pain, diarrhoea and gooseflesh after opiates. Alcohol, the most widely used, acts largely by enhancing the inhibitory transmitter GABA; at low doses it disinhibits (which is why it can look like a stimulant), at higher doses it impairs judgement, coordination and memory, and at very high doses it can be fatal. Claude Steele and Robert Josephs (1990) described its effect on thought as alcohol myopia : alcohol narrows attention to the most salient cues of the moment, so that a drunk person responds to immediate provocations and forgets distant consequences. The barbiturates (such as phenobarbital and amobarbital) were once widely prescribed as sedatives and sleeping pills, but the margin between an effective and a fatal dose is narrow, and they have largely been replaced by the benzodiazepines , a class that includes diazepam (sold as Valium), alprazolam (Xanax), flunitrazepam (Rohypnol) and triazolam (Halcion). Benzodiazepines are used to reduce anxiety (as anxiolytics), to sedate and to induce sleep (as hypnotics); they are much safer than barbiturates on their own but still cause tolerance and dependence, and they are dangerous when combined with alcohol. Stimulants increase nervous system activity. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors (Section 5.6); nicotine acts on acetylcholine receptors; amphetamines increase the release of dopamine and noradrenaline; cocaine blocks their reuptake, prolonging their action, and is followed by a "crash" of fatigue and low mood. MDMA (ecstasy) is a stimulant with mild hallucinogenic effects that releases large amounts of serotonin. Opiates , derived from the opium poppy (morphine, codeine and heroin) and their synthetic relatives (opioids such as fentanyl), relieve pain and produce euphoria because they mimic the brain's own opioids, the endorphins and enkephalins, at opiate receptors; they produce strong physical dependence, and overdose kills by stopping breathing. Hallucinogens (psychedelics) distort perception and thought. The best known, LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide), was first synthesised by the Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann (1906 to 2008), who discovered its extraordinary effects by accident in 1943; psilocybin (from certain mushrooms) and mescaline (from the peyote cactus) have similar effects, largely through serotonin receptors. Cannabis (marijuana, and in India ganja, charas and bhang) is usually placed in a class of its own because its effects are mixed: its active ingredient, THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), acts on the brain's cannabinoid receptors to produce relaxation and mild euphoria, heightened sensory experience, a slowed sense of time, increased appetite and impaired short-term memory and coordination; at high doses it can produce hallucinations, and heavy use in adolescence raises the risk of psychosis in vulnerable people. Exam trap Valium, Xanax, Rohypnol and Halcion are all benzodiazepines . They are also sedatives and hypnotics in function, which makes those options tempting, but the question asks for the drug class they share, and "sedative" and "hypnotic" describe uses that barbiturates and other drugs share too. They are not barbiturates ; examples of barbiturates are phenobarbital, amobarbital (sodium amytal) and secobarbital. Alcohol is a depressant, not a stimulant, despite its early disinhibiting effect; MDMA is usually classed as a stimulant with hallucinogenic properties. Clinical link Tolerance, withdrawal and craving are the building blocks of substance use disorders, which are among the commonest problems in Indian psychiatric practice (alcohol above all, then cannabis, opioids and tobacco); the diagnostic criteria and treatments are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Two facts from this chapter recur in the clinic: benzodiazepines and alcohol suppress REM sleep, so stopping them brings vivid dreams and broken sleep that tempt relapse, and long-term sleeping-pill use can itself cause insomnia, a reason that CBT-I is preferred. The case of Armond's dancing eyes, revisited Think back to the night in Chicago when the pens of Eugene Aserinsky's old machine began to jerk while his son slept. You can now say exactly what he was seeing. About 70 to 90 minutes after falling asleep, Armond had passed down through N1, N2 and the delta waves of N3, climbed back up, and entered his first period of REM sleep: a desynchronised, waking-like EEG, bursts of rapid eye movements, the large muscles of his body held in atonia by circuits in his brainstem, and, very probably, a dream. Through the rest of the night the pattern returned every 90 minutes or so, four to six times, the REM periods growing longer toward morning. At his age, about a fifth to a quarter of his sleep was REM; as a newborn it had been half. The discovery that Aserinsky first suspected was a machine fault also changed how psychologists think about consciousness. Sleep is not the absence of mind but a sequence of states, switched on by the brain's own circuits and timed by a clock in the hypothalamus. Waking consciousness, too, turned out to be far smaller and more selective than it feels: a narrow stream chosen by attention from a flood of input, while much of the mind's work goes on unseen. Hypnosis, meditation, sensory deprivation and drugs show how far that stream can be bent. Aserinsky's real contribution, in the end, was to wake people up and ask them what they had been experiencing, which is the question this whole chapter has been asking. Chapter summary 5.1 Attention: what it is, how it behaves and what captures it. William James (1890) defined attention as the mind taking possession of one of several possible objects, with focalisation and concentration as its essence. Attention may be involuntary, voluntary or habitual, and Sohlberg and Mateer's clinical model distinguishes focused, sustained, selective, alternating and divided attention. Its characteristics are selectivity, shifting, a limited span, fluctuation and limited division. The span of attention, studied by Jevons (1871) with beans and later with the tachistoscope, is about six to eight unrelated items (about four for errorless subitising), which is why number plates use short groups. Fluctuation is shown by the Masson disc. Attention is determined by external factors (intensity, size, contrast, change, movement, novelty, repetition) and internal factors (motives, interests, mental set, attitudes). 5.2 Selective listening: filters, attenuators and late selection. Cherry (1953) named the cocktail party problem and used dichotic listening with shadowing; listeners noticed physical but not semantic changes in the unattended ear, although Moray (1959) found that about a third heard their own names. Broadbent's filter model (1958), the first information-processing theory, placed an all-or-none filter early. Treisman's attenuation model (1964) turned unattended messages down rather than off, with dictionary units of varying thresholds, and best explains the cocktail party phenomenon. Deutsch and Deutsch (1963) and Norman (1968) placed selection late. Johnston and Heinz (1978) made selection flexible but costly, and Lavie's perceptual load theory showed that high load produces early selection and low load late selection. 5.3 Visual attention: spotlights, binding and blindness to the obvious. Covert visual attention behaves like a spotlight or a zoom lens (Eriksen and St James, 1986). Posner's cueing task (1980) separated endogenous (voluntary, central cues) from exogenous (automatic, peripheral cues) attention and revealed inhibition of return. Treisman and Gelade's feature integration theory (1980) proposed a parallel preattentive stage for features and a serial focused-attention stage that binds them, explaining pop-out, linear conjunction search slopes and illusory conjunctions. Inattentional blindness (Mack and Rock; Simons and Chabris's gorilla, 1999), change blindness (Rensink and colleagues; Simons and Levin) and the attentional blink (Raymond and colleagues, 1992) show how much goes unseen without attention. 5.4 Divided attention, automaticity, the Stroop effect and vigilance. Kahneman's capacity model (1973) treats attention as a single pool of effort allocated by policy; Wickens's multiple resource theory explains why similar tasks interfere more than different ones. Phone use impairs driving even when hands-free. Posner and Snyder (1975) and Shiffrin and Schneider (1977) distinguished fast, parallel, effortless, inflexible automatic processes from slow, serial, effortful, flexible controlled ones. The Stroop effect (1935) shows that automatic word reading interferes with colour naming, a failure of selective attention and a measure of inhibition. Vigilance, or sustained attention, declines over time (Mackworth's clock, 1948), as in radar and air traffic control work. ADHD, neglect and delirium are clinical disorders of attention. 5.5 Consciousness: definitions, levels and the brain. Consciousness is awareness of ourselves and our environment, with a level (measured by the Glasgow Coma Scale) and a content. James (1890) described a personal, changing, continuous, object-directed and selective stream of consciousness, whose most studied feature is daydreaming. Freud's topographic model divides the mind into conscious, preconscious (recallable at will) and unconscious (repressed) levels; modern psychology adds the nonconscious and the cognitive unconscious, supported by blindsight, fast threat processing and implicit attitudes. The reticular activating system maintains arousal; Chalmers's hard problem asks why processing is experienced at all. Altered states of consciousness (Tart, Ludwig) include sleep, hypnosis, meditation and drug states; the Mandukya Upanishad describes waking, dreaming, deep sleep and turiya. 5.6 Biological rhythms: the body's clocks. Circadian rhythms of about 24 hours free-run at about 24.2 hours without time cues and are entrained by zeitgebers, chiefly light. The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the master clock, receiving light through the retinohypothalamic tract and controlling melatonin release from the pineal gland. Jet lag is worse flying east (phase advance), and shift rotations work better forward. Borbély's two-process model combines homeostatic sleep pressure with the circadian signal. Ultradian rhythms (such as the 90-minute sleep cycle) are shorter than a day; infradian rhythms (such as the menstrual cycle) are longer. 5.7 The stages of sleep. Polysomnography records EEG, EOG and EMG. Beta marks alert waking, alpha relaxed waking with eyes closed, theta N1, spindles and K-complexes N2, and delta N3 (slow-wave sleep; stages 3 and 4 in the older system). REM sleep, discovered by Aserinsky and Kleitman (1953) and called paradoxical by Jouvet, combines a desynchronised EEG, rapid eye movements, atonia, autonomic variability, genital arousal and vivid dreams. Cycles of about 90 minutes repeat four to six times a night, with N3 early and REM late. REM forms half of a newborn's sleep and about a fifth of an adult's (Roffwarg and colleagues, 1966). The VLPO switches sleep on; orexin stabilises waking; the pons generates REM. 5.8 Why we sleep, what deprivation does and when sleep goes wrong. Recuperation theories stress restoration and waste clearance, adaptive theories stress safety and energy conservation, and other theories stress memory consolidation. Sleep deprivation (Randy Gardner's 264 hours) mainly impairs mood and sustained attention and produces microsleeps; REM deprivation produces REM rebound. Sleep disorders include insomnia, narcolepsy with cataplexy, sleep apnoea, NREM parasomnias (sleepwalking and sleep terrors, from N3), REM parasomnias (nightmares and REM sleep behaviour disorder) and restless legs syndrome. CBT-I uses stimulus control, sleep restriction and paradoxical intention. 5.9 Dreams. Dreams are most vivid in REM sleep, unfold in roughly real time, incorporate outside stimuli and usually reflect everyday concerns. Freud (1900) saw dreams as disguised wish fulfilments in which the dream work (condensation, displacement, symbolisation, secondary revision) turns latent into manifest content; Jung saw them as compensatory symbolic messages that can carry archetypes. Hobson and McCarley's activation-synthesis hypothesis (1977) explains dreams as the cortex's synthesis of random brainstem activation; information-processing, memory-consolidation and continuity theories link dreams to the handling of experience; Revonsuo's threat-simulation theory (2000) gives them an evolutionary function. Lucid dreams were verified with eye signals; hypnagogic imagery occurs falling asleep and hypnopompic imagery waking up. 5.10 Hypnosis. Hypnosis is a social interaction based on suggestibility. Its history runs from Mesmer's animal magnetism and the 1784 commission through Braid, who coined hypnotism, Charcot's view of it as pathology, the Nancy school's view of it as normal suggestion, and Freud and Breuer's cathartic method. Susceptibility, measured by the Stanford scales, is stable and linked to absorption. Hypnosis can relieve pain and produce posthypnotic suggestions and reversible amnesia, but it cannot give superhuman strength or reliably recover memories. Hilgard's neodissociation theory and hidden observer contrast with the social-cognitive theories of Sarbin, Barber and Spanos. 5.11 Meditation, sensory deprivation and psychoactive drugs. Concentrative meditation (including TM) focuses attention on one object; mindfulness meditation opens it to whatever arises. Meditation produces Benson's relaxation response, and MBSR and MBCT have clinical value, though correlational surveys cannot prove that meditation causes benefits. The McGill sensory deprivation studies (1954) produced impaired thinking and hallucinations, while brief REST can relax. Psychoactive drugs (depressants including alcohol and benzodiazepines, stimulants, opiates, hallucinogens and cannabis) alter consciousness through synaptic actions and produce tolerance, dependence and withdrawal. Why attention Selecting one input and inhibiting another is the job of attention , so the Stroop effect is an attention effect. (c) The increased accuracy of perception under divided attention tasks False: dividing attention reduces accuracy rather than increasing it. (d) The predictive power of schema theory on episodic memory Belongs to memory research on schemas and episodic recall, not to the Stroop task. "Stroop effect" is an account of: (RML 2024) a Stimulus dominance b Semantic dominance c Instructional dominance d Conceptual dominance ✓ Answer: (a) Stimulus dominance Stroop effect as stimulus dominance The concept Two dimensions Each Stroop stimulus has two dimensions: the printed word and its ink colour . One dimension, the word, dominates the other in controlling the response. Why this one One stimulus attribute overpowering another is what stimulus dominance names, and it is the keyed answer. Why the other options are wrong (b) Semantic dominance Tempts because the word is meaningful, but the keyed answer describes one stimulus attribute overpowering another, not meaning as such. (c) Instructional dominance Not a term used for this effect; the dominance is between two attributes of the stimulus, not the instructions. (d) Conceptual dominance Not a term used for this effect; the competing attributes are a word and a colour, not concepts. Air traffic controllers and radar readers provide us with a good example of which of the following phenomena? (RML 2024) a Selective attention b Sustained attention c Divided attention d Perceptual attention ✓ Answer: (b) Sustained attention Vigilance research, Mackworth clock The concept What it is Sustained attention , or vigilance , is watching for rare, unpredictable signals over long periods. How it is studied The classic lab task is the Mackworth clock , where a pointer occasionally makes a double jump the observer must catch. Radar readers and air traffic controllers face the same demand. Why the other options are wrong (a) Selective attention Picks one input among several; the controller's main problem is staying alert for rare signals, not filtering. (c) Divided attention Handles two tasks at once; the defining demand here is long-duration monitoring. (d) Perceptual attention Not a standard term in attention research; perception is involved, but the named phenomenon is vigilance. Why do the number plates of motorbikes and cars carry only four-digit numbers coupled with some letters? (RML 2024) a Selected attention b Span of attention c Divided attention d Sustained attention ✓ Answer: (b) Span of attention Span of attention (span of apprehension) The concept What it is Span of attention is the number of items that can be apprehended at a glance: about six to eight , fewer for accuracy. Why plates So number plates use short groups (four digits plus some letters) that an observer can take in quickly in one look. Why the other options are wrong (a) Selected attention Choosing one input over others; it explains focusing on a plate, not why the plate's length is limited. (c) Divided attention Doing two things at once; plate design is about how much fits in one glance, not task sharing. (d) Sustained attention Staying vigilant over long periods; a glance at a passing plate is brief, not prolonged. Who developed the filter-attenuation theory? (RML 2024) a Broadbent b Treisman c Johnston d Heinz ✓ Answer: (b) Treisman Anne Treisman, attenuation theory (1964) The concept What she changed Treisman (1964) modified Broadbent's all-or-none filter into an attenuator : unattended messages are turned down, not blocked. Why it matters Weakened messages can still get through if they matter, which is why the theory is called filter-attenuation . Why the other options are wrong (a) Broadbent Proposed the original all-or-none filter (1958); Treisman revised it, so naming him is the trap. (c) Johnston With Heinz, proposed the multimode theory (1978), in which the point of selection is flexible. (d) Heinz Co-author with Johnston of the multimode theory (1978), not the attenuation theory. You are at a party and someone calls out your name. Instantly, in the middle of a crowd, you can hear it. This phenomenon is called: (Amity 2023) a Bottleneck effect b Cocktail phenomenon c Divided attention d Sustained attention ✓ Answer: (b) Cocktail party phenomenon Cherry (1953); Moray (1959) The concept What it is The cocktail party phenomenon is picking out your own name from a conversation you were not attending to. Named after Cherry (1953) and shown in the lab by Moray (1959). Why it happens Treisman's low-threshold dictionary units explain it: personally important words like your name need very little signal to be recognised. Why the other options are wrong (a) Bottleneck effect Refers to the narrow stage in attention models where processing is limited, not to this effect. (c) Divided attention Handling two tasks at once; hearing your name is an unattended message breaking through, not deliberate sharing. (d) Sustained attention Staying vigilant over long periods; the name is noticed instantly, without prolonged watching. What term describes the phenomenon where individuals fail to notice significant changes in their environment, even when those changes are obvious? (RML 2023) a Change blindness b Inattentional blindness c Perceptual constancy d Selective attention ✓ Answer: (a) Change blindness Rensink and colleagues; Simons and Levin The concept Spot the cue The stem stresses changes , which points to change blindness : failing to notice that something in a scene has changed. Key studies Rensink and colleagues showed it with flickering pictures; in Simons and Levin's door study, people missed that the stranger they were talking to had been swapped. Why the other options are wrong (b) Inattentional blindness Missing an unexpected object altogether (as in the gorilla study); the stem is about changes, not a new object. (c) Perceptual constancy The stable perception of objects; a perceptual achievement, not a failure to notice. (d) Selective attention The general process of focusing on some inputs; it underlies change blindness but is not the term for it. Low-prejudiced people engage in: (IHBAS 2020) a Automatic information processing resulting in involuntary stereotyping b Controlled information processing resulting in refuting stereotype c Controlled information processing resulting in involuntary stereotyping d Automatic information processing resulting in voluntary stereotyping ✓ Answer: (b) Controlled information processing resulting in refuting stereotype Devine's model of stereotyping (1989) The concept The model In Devine's (1989) model, stereotypes are activated automatically in everyone, high- or low-prejudiced. What differs Low-prejudiced people use controlled , effortful processing to override the activated stereotype, so they refute it. Why the other options are wrong (a) Automatic information processing resulting in involuntary stereotyping Automatic activation happens in everyone; it does not set low-prejudiced people apart, since they go on to override it. (c) Controlled information processing resulting in involuntary stereotyping Contradictory: controlled processing cannot produce involuntary stereotyping. (d) Automatic information processing resulting in voluntary stereotyping Contradictory: automatic processing is not voluntary. The term "stream of consciousness", referring to the flow of thoughts in the human mind, was coined by which psychologist? (IHBAS 2024) a Carl Jung b Wilhelm Wundt c William James d B.F. Skinner ✓ Answer: (c) William James William James, Principles of Psychology (1890) The concept What it means William James described consciousness as a continuous, ever-changing stream of thought rather than a set of separate elements. Where He coined the term in Principles of Psychology (1890). Why the other options are wrong (a) Carl Jung Described the collective unconscious , not the flow of conscious thought. (b) Wilhelm Wundt Analysed consciousness into elements, the opposite of treating it as a continuous stream. (d) B.F. Skinner Rejected the study of consciousness altogether. According to Freud, the ___ mind includes accessible memories, which can be recalled at will. (RML 2020) a Conscious b Preconscious c Unconscious d Psychic determinism ✓ Answer: (b) Preconscious Freud's topographical model of the mind The concept Three levels Freud's topographical model has three levels: the conscious , the preconscious and the unconscious . Why preconscious The preconscious holds memories not in awareness right now but recallable at will, like your phone number. Why the other options are wrong (a) Conscious Holds only what is in awareness now, not stored memories waiting to be recalled. (c) Unconscious Its contents cannot be recalled at will; they are kept out of awareness by repression . (d) Psychic determinism A principle (every mental event has a cause), not a level of mind. The Mandukya Upanishad describes four states of consciousness (avasthas). The "fourth", pure consciousness beyond waking, dream and deep sleep, is called: (Amity recall) a Jagrat b Swapna c Sushupti d Turiya ✓ Answer: (d) Turiya Mandukya Upanishad, four avasthas The concept Three ordinary states The first three avasthas are jagrat (waking), swapna or svapna (dreaming) and sushupti (dreamless deep sleep). The fourth Turiya , literally "the fourth", is the witnessing consciousness present in all three. Why the other options are wrong (a) Jagrat The waking state, the first of the four, not the one beyond them. (b) Swapna The dreaming state (also spelt svapna), the second of the four. (c) Sushupti Dreamless deep sleep, the third state; turiya is the witness present in it too. The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) is crucial for: (IHBAS 2025) a Memory consolidation b Circadian rhythm regulation c Language processing d Pain perception ✓ Answer: (b) Circadian rhythm regulation SCN, the brain's master clock The concept What it is The suprachiasmatic nucleus sits in the hypothalamus , just above the optic chiasm, and is the body's master clock. How it is set Light entrains it through the retinohypothalamic tract , keeping sleep-wake and other daily rhythms in step with day and night. Why the other options are wrong (a) Memory consolidation Depends on the hippocampus , not the SCN. (c) Language processing Depends on Broca's and Wernicke's areas, not the SCN. (d) Pain perception Handled by pain pathways such as the spinothalamic tract and somatosensory cortex, not the SCN. In a typical major sleep period, how many cycles of NREM-REM are there? (RML 2024) a 2 to 4 b 4 to 6 c 6 to 10 d 10 to 12 ✓ Answer: (b) 4 to 6 About 90-minute NREM-REM cycles The concept The maths Each NREM-REM cycle lasts about 90 minutes , so seven to eight hours of sleep hold four to six cycles. Why the other options are wrong (a) 2 to 4 Too few for a full night; it would need cycles much longer than 90 minutes. (c) 6 to 10 Six or more would need cycles far shorter than 90 minutes. (d) 10 to 12 Even further off; it would need cycles far shorter than 90 minutes. During a normal night's sleep, how many times do we pass through the different stages of sleep? (RML 2022) a 8 to 11 b 5 to 8 c 3 to 5 d 4 to 7 ✓ Answer: (d) 4 to 7 Standard four to six sleep cycles The concept Standard figure The standard figure is four to six sleep cycles in a normal night. Why this option No option says 4 to 6 exactly; of the options given, 4 to 7 is the range that contains it. Why the other options are wrong (a) 8 to 11 Far too many; eight or more cycles would not fit a normal night. (b) 5 to 8 Misses part of the usual range: it leaves out four cycles. (c) 3 to 5 Misses part of the usual range: it stops at five and leaves out six. Which of the following characterises slow-wave sleep? (Amity 2023) a Stage 1 to 4 and REM sleep b Stage 3 and 4 c NREM and REM sleep d Stage 1 to 4 ✓ Answer: (b) Stages 3 and 4 Rechtschaffen and Kales staging; N3 since 2007 The concept Old system In the older Rechtschaffen and Kales system, stages 3 and 4, dominated by delta waves , were together called slow-wave sleep . Current system Since 2007 they are merged into a single stage, N3 . Why the other options are wrong (a) Stage 1 to 4 and REM sleep Adds stages 1 and 2, which are light sleep, and REM, which has a fast, desynchronised EEG. (c) NREM and REM sleep Covers all of sleep; REM has a fast, desynchronised EEG and is not slow-wave. (d) Stage 1 to 4 Includes stages 1 and 2, which are light sleep, not slow-wave. Which one of the following characterises somnambulism? (RML 2022) a Sitting, walking or performing complex behaviour while asleep b Extreme fear, agitation, screaming while asleep c Acting out nightmares d Uncomfortable sensations in the legs causing movement and loss of sleep ✓ Answer: (a) Sitting, walking or performing complex behaviour while asleep NREM parasomnia arising from N3 The concept What it is Somnambulism is sleepwalking: sitting up, walking or doing complex acts while still asleep. When it happens It is an NREM parasomnia arising from N3 , deep slow-wave sleep. Why the other options are wrong (b) Extreme fear, agitation, screaming while asleep Sleep terrors , marked by fear and screaming rather than walking. (c) Acting out nightmares REM sleep behaviour disorder , where the normal muscle paralysis of REM is lost and dreams are acted out. (d) Uncomfortable sensations in the legs causing movement and loss of sleep Restless legs syndrome , a sleep-related movement disorder, not a parasomnia. The main crux of hypnosis is: (RML 2020) a Analytical mind b Logical mind c Suggestibility d None ✓ Answer: (c) Suggestibility Hypnotic suggestibility; Stanford scales The concept What it is Hypnosis works through heightened responsiveness to suggestion . How it is measured Suggestibility is measured by scales such as the Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale. Why the other options are wrong (a) Analytical mind The analytical faculty is what hypnotic induction quietens, not its basis. (b) Logical mind Logical thinking is likewise quietened by induction, not the basis of hypnosis. (d) None Fails because suggestibility is the accepted core of hypnosis. Researchers studying meditation contacted over 10,000 randomly selected adults in 10 nations. Those who meditated regularly were less likely to suffer from stress than adults who meditated less regularly or not at all. Can we conclude that meditation lowers stress? Why? (RML 2021) a Yes, because the sample size was large b Yes, because the adults were randomly selected c Yes, because the adults were randomly assigned d Not necessarily, because this wasn't an experiment ✓ Answer: (d) Not necessarily, because this wasn't an experiment Correlation versus causation The concept Why not The study is correlational : it measured who meditated and who was stressed, but nobody was randomly assigned to meditate. Other explanations Calmer people may meditate more ( reverse causation ), or a third factor may cause both. Exam tip Only an experiment with random assignment can show that meditation causes lower stress. Why the other options are wrong (a) Yes, because the sample size was large A large sample improves generalisability, not causal inference. (b) Yes, because the adults were randomly selected Random selection improves generalisability, not causal inference; it is not random assignment. (c) Yes, because the adults were randomly assigned Simply untrue: nobody was randomly assigned to meditate or not. Valium, Xanax, Rohypnol and Halcion are: (Amity 2023) a Benzodiazepines b Barbiturates c Sedatives d Hypnotics ✓ Answer: (a) Benzodiazepines Benzodiazepines: diazepam, alprazolam, flunitrazepam, triazolam The concept The drugs Valium (diazepam), Xanax (alprazolam), Rohypnol (flunitrazepam) and Halcion (triazolam) all belong to one class: the benzodiazepines . Why this one They do act as sedatives and hypnotics , but the class they share is benzodiazepines. Why the other options are wrong (b) Barbiturates An older, more dangerous class, such as phenobarbital ; these four drugs are not barbiturates. (c) Sedatives Describes what they do (calming), not the drug class they share. (d) Hypnotics Describes another effect (inducing sleep), not their shared class. A man with sleep-onset insomnia is told to lie in bed with the lights off and try as hard as he can to stay awake. This technique is: (NIMHANS 2026 recall) a Paradoxical intention b Stimulus control c Sleep restriction d Dereflection ✓ Answer: (a) Paradoxical intention Viktor Frankl, paradoxical intention The concept What it is Paradoxical intention , from Frankl , tells the person to try to do the very thing they fear: here, to stay awake. Why it works It removes the performance anxiety of trying to sleep, so sleep can come on its own. Why the other options are wrong (b) Stimulus control Re-links the bed with sleep (use the bed only for sleep, get up if awake); a behavioural method from Bootzin . (c) Sleep restriction Limits time in bed to build sleep pressure, then extends it as sleep improves. (d) Dereflection Also Frankl's, but turns attention away from the symptom altogether rather than asking the person to pursue it. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The Stroop effect (John Ridley Stroop, 1935): naming the ink colour of a conflicting colour word (RED printed in green) is slowed because automatic word reading interferes. It is a failure of selective attention (interference in reaction time; keyed once as "stimulus dominance"), not a memory effect. asked 5 times The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the master circadian pacemaker, entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract; SCN lesions abolish circadian rhythms, not total sleep. Hunger is the lateral and ventromedial hypothalamus, stress hormones the paraventricular nucleus, memory the hippocampus and mammillary bodies. asked 4 times Carl Jung split the unconscious into a personal (individual) unconscious and a collective unconscious : an inherited layer shared by all humanity, full of archetypes, which he explained by the similar brain structure of all human races. asked 4 times The psychodynamic perspective (Freud) holds that behaviour is driven by unconscious inner forces largely beyond the person's control and shaped by early childhood experience. asked 3 times REM (paradoxical) sleep : desynchronised, fast, low-voltage EEG like waking, rapid eye movements, atonia of the core muscles, genital arousal and vivid, story-like dreams. EEG synchrony and delta waves belong to N3; spindles and K-complexes to N2. asked 4 times Sigmund Freud , the father of psychoanalysis, published the mechanism of hysteria with Josef Breuer in 1893 ( Studies on Hysteria , 1895), replaced hypnosis with free association, and published The Interpretation of Dreams in 1900 (printed November 1899). asked 4 times Freud's topographic model (1900): the conscious (aware now), the preconscious (not in awareness but recallable at will) and the unconscious (repressed; seen in dreams and Freudian slips). The unconscious mind is the part of Freud's theory that research most supports. asked 3 times Sleepwalking (somnambulism: sitting, walking or complex acts while asleep) and sleep terrors arise from N3 early in the night. Nightmares and REM sleep behaviour disorder (loss of REM atonia, so the sleeper acts out dreams) belong to REM. asked 3 times A night holds four to six NREM-REM cycles of about 90 minutes (one paper keys "4 to 7" because 4 to 6 was not offered). N3 dominates the early cycles; REM periods lengthen toward morning. asked twice The Mandukya Upanishad's four states: jagrat (waking), svapna (dreaming), sushupti (deep sleep) and turiya , "the fourth", pure consciousness identified with the Atman , the true self or eternal consciousness. asked twice Anne Treisman 's attenuation (filter-attenuation) model, 1964: unattended messages are turned down, not blocked, so low-threshold dictionary units such as your own name still fire. It best explains the cocktail party effect. asked twice The cocktail party phenomenon (hearing your name across a noisy room) was named by Colin Cherry (1953) using dichotic listening and shadowing; listeners noticed physical changes (male to female voice) in the unattended ear, not its meaning. Moray (1959) showed the own-name effect. asked twice Slow-wave sleep is stages 3 and 4 of the older Rechtschaffen and Kales system (merged as N3 in 2007), dominated by high-amplitude delta waves (about 0.5 to 4 Hz). asked twice William James coined "stream of consciousness" in Principles of Psychology (1890); the feature of the stream most studied by researchers is daydreaming. asked twice Delirium is separated from dementia by acute onset, a fluctuating course and disturbed attention and awareness; dementia begins insidiously, with attention preserved early. asked twice EEG: beta (13 to 30 Hz) alert waking; alpha (8 to 12 Hz) relaxed waking with eyes closed; theta N1; spindles and K-complexes N2; delta N3. asked twice Freud's structural model (1923): the id works on the pleasure principle, the ego on the reality principle. asked twice Jung's anima is the feminine side of a man; the animus is the masculine side of a woman. asked twice Titchener called introspection a highly specialised form of self-observation; structuralism describes the components, combinations and connections of consciousness. asked twice Air traffic controllers and radar readers are the classic example of sustained attention (vigilance); its decline over a watch is the vigilance decrement (Mackworth clock, 1948). asked once Number plates carry about four digits plus letters because of the span of attention : about six to eight unrelated items in one glance (Jevons's beans, 1871). asked once Change blindness is failing to notice obvious changes in a scene (Rensink, O'Regan and Clark, 1997; Simons and Levin's door study); missing an unexpected object in plain view is inattentional blindness (the gorilla, Simons and Chabris, 1999). asked once The crux of hypnosis is suggestibility; hypnosis is not sleep. asked once Valium (diazepam), Xanax (alprazolam), Rohypnol (flunitrazepam) and Halcion (triazolam) are benzodiazepines , depressants that enhance GABA; they are not barbiturates. asked once A survey linking regular meditation with less stress does not show that meditation lowers stress: a large, randomly selected sample is still not an experiment, because nobody was randomly assigned. asked once The primary focus of Indian psychology is integrating Indian philosophical traditions with psychological concepts. asked once Patricia Devine (1989): stereotypes are activated automatically in everyone; low-prejudiced people use controlled processing to refute them. asked once The Implicit Association Test (Anthony Greenwald and colleagues, 1998) measures unconscious stereotyping. asked once Telling an insomniac to lie in the dark and try hard to stay awake is Viktor Frankl's paradoxical intention ; stimulus control (Bootzin) re-links bed and sleep, sleep restriction limits time in bed. asked once Donald Broadbent 's filter model (1958) was the first major theory of information-processing psychology: early, all-or-none selection on physical features. asked once
