Each person's behaviour reinforces the other's: the child learns that screaming produces sweets, and the parent learns that sweets stop screaming. Both behaviours grow. The scolding example makes a related point: a consequence intended as punishment is actually reinforcement if the behaviour increases, which is what often happens when a child starved of attention finds that misbehaviour reliably earns it. Exam trap Negative reinforcement is not punishment. All reinforcement, positive or negative, increases behaviour; all punishment decreases it. A rat pressing a lever to turn off a shock is negative reinforcement (escape conditioning). Time-out and response cost are negative punishment . One real paper asked "which consequence increases the likelihood of a behaviour being repeated?" and offered both positive reinforcement and negative reinforcement; the keyed answer was positive reinforcement, but negative reinforcement increases behaviour too. If you meet such an item, choose positive reinforcement (the intended "reward" answer) and remember that the item, not the principle, is at fault. Operant conditioning motivates behaviour through reinforcement and punishment, not through modelling (Bandura), classical conditioning or cognitive dissonance (Festinger). Primary, secondary and generalised reinforcers Why does a rat work for food, a pigeon for grain, and you for a pay slip? Food is a primary reinforcer (or unconditioned reinforcer): it is reinforcing without any learning, because it satisfies a biological need. Water, warmth, sexual contact and relief from pain are other examples. Money is different. A five-hundred-rupee note is just printed paper; it is reinforcing only because it has been repeatedly associated with things that are reinforcing in themselves. A stimulus that acquires its reinforcing power through association with a primary reinforcer is a secondary reinforcer (or conditioned reinforcer). Grades, praise, a smile, the "click" a dog trainer sounds just before giving a treat, and the ping of a notification are all secondary reinforcers. Notice that the process by which a neutral stimulus becomes a secondary reinforcer is itself classical conditioning: the click is paired with food until it acquires some of food's value. The power of secondary reinforcers was shown dramatically by John B. Wolfe in 1936. Chimpanzees learned to insert poker chips into a vending machine (nicknamed the "Chimp-O-Mat") that dispensed grapes, and then to work at a heavy lever-pulling task to earn the chips. They would work for chips even when the machine was not immediately available, and some hoarded them. A secondary reinforcer that has been paired with many different primary reinforcers, so that it works whatever the person currently needs, is a generalised reinforcer . Money is the obvious example; Skinner also listed attention, approval and affection. These ideas were turned into a treatment method in the early 1960s by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin at Anna State Hospital in Illinois. On a ward of long-stay psychiatric patients, many of whom had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and had become withdrawn and inactive, patients earned tokens for clearly defined behaviours: self-care, making their beds, working on ward jobs. The tokens could be exchanged for backup reinforcers such as a private room, walks in the grounds, extra time with staff, snacks and cigarettes. Participation in the target behaviours rose sharply; when tokens were given regardless of behaviour, participation fell; when the contingency was restored, it rose again. Their book The Token Economy (1968) gave the method its name. A token economy is a behaviour-modification system in which tokens (secondary reinforcers) are earned for target behaviours and exchanged for backup reinforcers. It is an application of operant conditioning, and it has since been used in classrooms, homes for children, prisons and rehabilitation units. Exam trap Who developed the token economy? The historically correct answer is Ayllon and Azrin (Anna State Hospital; book 1968). One real paper (Amity 2023) keyed Skinner , presumably because the method rests on Skinner's operant principles. If both appear, Ayllon and Azrin is the accurate answer; Skinner supplied the principles, not the ward programme. Token economy is based on operant conditioning (secondary reinforcement), never on classical conditioning, observational learning, insight or free association. A teacher's stickers exchangeable for a homework exemption are best called tokens ; they are secondary, not primary, reinforcers. Tokens can also be generalised reinforcers when they buy many different backups, but "token" is the specific answer. A "prepotent response" is simply a dominant, highly probable response (the word echoes Thorndike's law of prepotency of elements), not a kind of reinforcer. Remember Harry Harlow's famous monkeys (1958) were a test of the secondary-reinforcer idea. Many learning theorists held that infants love their mothers because mothers are paired with feeding, so that the mother is a secondary reinforcer (the "cupboard love" or secondary-drive theory). Harlow's infant rhesus monkeys clung to a soft cloth surrogate that gave no milk in preference to a wire surrogate that fed them, and ran to the cloth mother when frightened. Attachment rests on contact comfort, not on conditioned reinforcement from feeding. (The attachment research belongs to the Developmental Psychology book; Harlow's learning-set research is in Section 6.7.) Escape, avoidance and two-factor theory Negative reinforcement comes in two forms. In escape learning , a response terminates an aversive stimulus that is already present: the rat presses a lever to turn off a shock that is on; you step out of the midday sun into the shade. In avoidance learning , a response prevents an aversive stimulus from occurring at all: you leave home early to avoid the traffic jam; you carry an umbrella in the monsoon. Avoidance is usually studied in a shuttle box, a two-compartment box with a low barrier between the halves. A warning signal, such as a light, comes on, and a few seconds later the floor on that side is electrified. At first the animal jumps the barrier only after the shock begins (escape). Soon it jumps as soon as the light comes on, before any shock (avoidance). Avoidance responses are remarkably durable. In 1953 Richard Solomon and Lyman Wynne found that dogs which had learned to avoid a strong shock went on jumping, quickly and calmly, for hundreds of trials after the shock had been disconnected. Avoidance posed a puzzle. In escape, the reinforcer is obvious: the shock goes off. But in successful avoidance nothing happens; the shock never arrives. How can the absence of an event reinforce anything? Orval Hobart Mowrer (1907 to 1982) answered in 1947 with his two-factor theory (two-process theory) of avoidance. In the first factor, classical conditioning, the warning signal is paired with shock and comes to elicit fear. In the second factor, operant conditioning, jumping the barrier takes the animal away from the warning signal, and the reduction in fear negatively reinforces the jump. The animal is not avoiding the shock; it is escaping the fear. The theory also explains why avoidance resists extinction: because the animal always leaves before the shock would have come, it never discovers that the shock has stopped. Two-factor theory became the standard behavioural account of anxiety disorders. A woman who was once trapped in a lift learns to fear lifts (classical); taking the stairs reduces the fear and is negatively reinforced (operant); and because she never rides a lift again, the fear never extinguishes. Obsessive-compulsive disorder fits the same mould. An intrusive thought of contamination produces anxiety; washing the hands reduces the anxiety; the washing is therefore negatively reinforced, and from the standpoint of learning theory compulsions are escape and avoidance behaviours (often called safety behaviours). This is exactly why exposure and response prevention (Section 6.4) works: by blocking the escape response, it allows the anxiety to extinguish and habituate. Exam trap Escape terminates an aversive stimulus that is already present; avoidance prevents its onset. Both are negative reinforcement, not positive reinforcement. Compulsive acts in OCD are best described as escape (avoidance) behaviours maintained by anxiety reduction; one real paper keyed "escape", and "conditioning" is too general to be the best answer. Hand-washing in OCD is an avoidance response or safety behaviour, not a conditioned stimulus, not an unconditioned response, and not behaviour maintained by positive reinforcement. "Two-factor theory" in a learning question means Mowrer's theory of avoidance (do not confuse it with Schachter's two-factor theory of emotion, Chapter 11). Punishment and its problems Punishment is the most widely used and most poorly understood way of changing behaviour. Two forms are used deliberately in clinics and classrooms. Time-out (short for time-out from positive reinforcement) removes the person for a short period from a setting where reinforcement is available: the child who hits is taken out of the game for a few minutes. Response cost removes a specific amount of a reinforcer the person already has, after each instance of the unwanted behaviour: a fine, the loss of tokens, the loss of an hour of television. Both are negative punishment. A third method, overcorrection, requires the person to restore the environment to a better state than before and to practise the correct behaviour repeatedly. Does punishment work? William Kaye Estes (1919 to 2011) gave an early and influential answer in 1944. Rats that had learned to press a lever for food were put on extinction, and some were also given a brief shock whenever they pressed. The punished rats stopped pressing quickly. But when the punishment ended they started pressing again, and by the end of extinction they had made about as many responses in total as unpunished rats. Punishment had suppressed the response, not erased it. Later work by Azrin and others showed that punishment can produce lasting suppression, but only under demanding conditions: it must be immediate, it must follow every instance of the behaviour, it must be intense enough from the start (animals and children adapt to punishment that is gradually increased), and it works best when an alternative behaviour is available and reinforced. Even when it works, punishment has well-documented side effects. It tells the person what not to do but not what to do. It produces fear, and by classical conditioning the fear spreads to the punisher and the setting, so that the child learns to avoid the parent or the school. It can provoke aggression, and physical punishment models aggression for the child to imitate (Section 6.8). It often suppresses the behaviour only while the punisher is present, so that the punisher becomes a discriminative stimulus for not misbehaving. And it is negatively reinforcing for the punisher, because it stops the annoying behaviour at once, so punishment tends to escalate. Skinner argued throughout his career that society should rely on reinforcement instead. Indian context Section 17 of India's Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment of children in schools. The behavioural evidence summarised above, that punishment suppresses rather than teaches and carries fear, avoidance and aggression with it, is part of the scientific case for such laws. Clinical psychologists working with families routinely teach parents to replace smacking with time-out, response cost and, above all, reinforcement of the behaviour they want. Exam trap Removing a desirable stimulus after an undesirable behaviour to reduce it is response cost (a form of negative punishment). It is not negative reinforcement (removal that increases behaviour), not positive punishment (something unpleasant added ), and not extinction (simply no longer delivering the reinforcer that maintained the behaviour). Time-out is technically negative punishment . Shaping, chaining, prompting and fading Reinforcement can strengthen only a behaviour that occurs. How, then, do you teach a rat to press a lever it has never touched, or a child with autism to say a word he has never said? Skinner's answer was shaping , also called the method of successive approximations: reinforcing behaviours that are closer and closer to the target behaviour. To shape lever pressing, the trainer first reinforces the rat for facing the lever, then only for moving towards it, then only for rearing near it, then only for touching it, and finally only for pressing it. At each stage the previous approximation is no longer reinforced (it is put on extinction) while the closer one is. Skinner could shape a pigeon to turn a full circle in a few minutes this way. Shaping can work on any dimension of a response: its form, its speed or rate, its force or intensity, its duration, or how quickly it begins. And because it relies only on reinforcing what the learner does, it needs no verbal instructions at all, which is why it is used to train animals, infants and people with severe intellectual disability or autism. A speech therapist who first reinforces any sound, then a sound beginning with "b", then "ba", and finally "ball" is shaping. Many skills are sequences rather than single responses. A chaining procedure teaches such a sequence by linking responses so that each one produces the discriminative stimulus for the next, with reinforcement coming at the end. Each link's stimulus is therefore both a conditioned reinforcer for the response before it and a signal for the response after it. Chains are often taught backwards (backward chaining): when teaching a child to put on a shirt, the therapist first teaches the last step (pulling it down) so that the child always ends with success, then the step before, and so on. A rat named Barnabus at Brown University in the early 1960s was trained by backward chaining to climb a spiral staircase, cross a drawbridge, climb a ladder, pull a toy car to him, ride it through a tunnel and finally press a lever for food. Two further techniques help get behaviour started. A prompt is an extra stimulus that makes the correct response more likely: a verbal hint, a gesture, a demonstration or physical guidance of the learner's hand. Fading is the gradual removal of the prompt so that, in the end, the natural discriminative stimulus alone controls the behaviour. Exam trap Reinforcing successive approximations is shaping . Linking a sequence of responses is chaining ; adding an extra cue is prompting ; gradually withdrawing the cue is fading . Shaping is not "removing a reinforcer to weaken behaviour", not "pairing two neutral stimuli", not "punishing every incorrect response", not "pigeons pressing a button for food" (that describes operant conditioning in general) and not "any behaviour with pleasant consequences is repeated" (the law of effect). One unusual real item (RML 2024) asked on which "principles" shaping is based and keyed speed, power and non-verbal , excluding "performance". The logic, as far as it can be reconstructed, is that shaping works on the speed and force of responses and needs no verbal instruction; learn the definition first, and treat this item as a one-off. Operant extinction When a response that has been reinforced stops being reinforced, it declines. This is operant extinction, and it follows a characteristic course. At first, responding often gets worse before it gets better: the rate rises, the responses become more forceful and varied, and emotional behaviour such as aggression may appear. This temporary surge is the extinction burst . You have shown one yourself if you have ever pressed a lift button again and again, harder and harder, when the lift did not come. Then responding declines until it returns to its operant level , the baseline rate at which the response occurred before it was ever reinforced. (Because many responses occur occasionally even without reinforcement, extinction brings the rate back to this earlier level, which is not necessarily zero.) After a rest, the extinguished response shows spontaneous recovery, just as in classical conditioning. Key study: Extinguishing a toddler's bedtime tantrums (Williams, 1959) Problem. A 21-month-old boy, recovering from a long illness during which he had received constant attention, screamed and fussed whenever he was put to bed unless a parent stayed in the room until he fell asleep. Method. Carl Williams reasoned that the tantrums were maintained by parental attention, so he advised the parents to put the boy to bed in a relaxed way, leave the room, and not go back in however much he cried. Result. The first night the boy screamed for 45 minutes; the second night he did not cry at all; within ten occasions he was smiling as his parents left. About a week later, when an aunt put him to bed, he cried and she went back in; the tantrums returned (spontaneous recovery, reinforced), and had to be extinguished a second time, after which none occurred for the following two years. Conclusion. Ignoring an attention-maintained behaviour is extinction, and it works if it is consistent. A single "giving in" during the extinction burst puts the behaviour on intermittent reinforcement, which, as Section 6.6 will show, makes it even harder to extinguish. Exam trap "A parent deliberately ignores a child's temper tantrums to discourage them." The correct answer is extinction . The source key for this real item (Amity 2023, repeated in JSS practice sets) marks "operant escape", which is wrong: escape is a response that terminates an aversive stimulus already present (negative reinforcement), and nothing in the parent's ignoring fits that description. Learn the item as extinction. When reinforcement of a previously reinforced behaviour stops and the behaviour fades, the term is extinction, not generalisation, discrimination or shaping. "Habit weakening through the elimination of any reward" is likewise extinction, not negative reinforcement, reciprocal inhibition or flooding. 6.6 Schedules of Reinforcement and Other Operant Phenomena High yield · 25 Qs In the 1930s, Skinner later recalled, he was running short of food pellets, which he made by hand, and he began reinforcing his rats only once a minute instead of after every press to make his supply last. To his surprise the rats kept pressing, and at steady rates. That economy launched one of the most productive research programmes in psychology. With Charles Ferster he spent years mapping how different rules for delivering reinforcement shape the pattern of responding, and their book Schedules of Reinforcement (1957) contains hundreds of cumulative records. The basic findings are few, highly examined and easy to remember once you see the records. Continuous and partial reinforcement A schedule of reinforcement is the rule that determines which responses are reinforced. Under continuous reinforcement (CRF), every correct response is reinforced. Under partial reinforcement (also called intermittent reinforcement), only some responses are. Continuous reinforcement produces the fastest learning, so it is the best way to establish a new behaviour. But behaviour that has been continuously reinforced also extinguishes fastest. When the vending machine that always works suddenly swallows your coin, you stop putting coins in almost at once; when the slot machine that rarely pays fails again, you keep playing. This greater persistence after partial reinforcement is the partial reinforcement extinction effect . It was demonstrated in humans by Lloyd Humphreys in 1939, using conditioned eyeblinks: people for whom the puff of air had followed the signal on only half the trials kept blinking to the signal far longer in extinction than people for whom it had followed every time. The simplest explanation is that it is harder to tell that reinforcement has stopped when it was intermittent to begin with. The practical rule follows: use continuous reinforcement to teach a behaviour, then shift to partial reinforcement to maintain it. The four basic schedules Partial schedules are built from two choices. Reinforcement can depend on the number of responses (a ratio schedule) or on the time that has passed (an interval schedule, in which the first response after the interval is reinforced). And the requirement can be the same every time (fixed) or can vary unpredictably around an average (variable). Crossing the two choices gives four schedules, and each produces its own signature on the cumulative record (Figure 6.4); Table 6.7 summarises them, with continuous reinforcement for comparison. On a fixed-ratio schedule (FR), reinforcement follows a fixed number of responses: FR-10 means every tenth response. Responding is high and steady, because the faster the animal responds, the sooner it is paid, but each reinforcer is followed by a short break, the post-reinforcement pause . The pause lengthens as the ratio grows, and if the ratio is raised too fast responding can break down (ratio strain). Piece-rate work, such as a tailor paid for every ten blouses stitched, and "buy nine coffees, get the tenth free" cards are fixed-ratio schedules. On a variable-ratio schedule (VR), reinforcement follows an unpredictable number of responses that averages a set value. The very next response might pay off, so there is no reason to pause. VR produces the highest and steadiest rate of responding and the greatest resistance to extinction of all the schedules. Slot machines, lottery tickets and a salesperson's cold calls are the classic examples, and they explain why gambling is so hard to stop. On a fixed-interval schedule (FI), the first response after a fixed period is reinforced: FI-60 seconds. Responses during the interval earn nothing, so animals learn to pause after each reinforcer and then respond faster and faster as the end of the interval approaches. The cumulative record shows a curve called the FI scallop. Overall rates are relatively low. You are on something like an FI schedule when a dish is due out of the oven in thirty minutes: you hardly check at first and check more and more often as the time approaches. Students who study little early in term and frantically before a fixed examination date show the same scallop. On a variable-interval schedule (VI), the first response after an unpredictable period, averaging a set value, is reinforced. Because reinforcement could become available at any moment, responding is moderate but very steady, with no scallop, and it is quite resistant to extinction. Checking your phone for a reply to a message, fishing, and preparing for a teacher who sets surprise quizzes are VI schedules. Ratio schedules produce higher rates than interval schedules, because on ratio schedules responding faster brings reinforcement sooner, whereas on interval schedules it does not. And variable schedules produce steadier responding and greater resistance to extinction than fixed ones, because the learner can never predict when the next reinforcer is due, and therefore cannot easily tell when reinforcement has stopped. Put the two rules together and VR comes out on top for both rate and persistence. Exam trap Cue words decide most schedule questions: "number of responses" means ratio; "time" or "minutes" means interval; "unpredictable" means variable. Highest rate and most resistant to extinction: VR . Scallop: FI . High rate with brief pauses after reinforcement: FR . Reinforcement after an unpredictable amount of time: VI . Reinforcement after every correct response: continuous . Continuous reinforcement is the least resistant to extinction. In one real item, Sheena rewards herself with a chocolate "for every 45 minutes" of study; the keyed answer is fixed interval , because the requirement is a constant amount of time. (Strictly, a reward that arrives after a fixed time regardless of responding is a fixed-time arrangement, and the same is true of a monthly salary, the textbook "FI" example; but among the four options, FI is correct.) Differential reinforcement Clinicians rarely want simply to strengthen a behaviour; more often they want to weaken a problem behaviour without the side effects of punishment. Differential reinforcement does this by reinforcing some responses and not others. The main variants are listed in Table 6.8. In each, the problem behaviour is put on extinction while something else is reinforced. Table 6.8 Forms of differential reinforcement. The traditional answer was a list of stimuli: food, water, praise, money. In 1959 David Premack (1925 to 2015) proposed something more radical. Reinforcers, he argued, are not stimuli but activities, and what makes an activity reinforcing is its probability relative to other activities. The Premack principle states that a more probable (preferred) behaviour can be used to reinforce a less probable (less preferred) behaviour. You find out how probable each behaviour is by watching how much time the person spends on it when free to choose. Premack's experiments showed that reinforcement is relative, not fixed. Some children preferred eating sweets to playing a pinball machine, and for them sweets reinforced pinball playing; for children who preferred pinball, the opportunity to play reinforced eating sweets. In rats, access to water reinforced running in a wheel when the rats were thirsty, but when the rats had free water and had been prevented from running, the opportunity to run reinforced drinking. The everyday version is called grandma's rule: "first eat your vegetables, then you can have dessert"; "first finish your homework, then you can play video games." For a child who rarely does homework, letting him play video games only after he finishes it is more effective than vague praise, and it costs nothing. A later refinement, the response-deprivation hypothesis of William Timberlake and James Allison (1974), showed that even a low-probability activity can serve as a reinforcer if the person has been restricted to less of it than they would normally choose. (Premack is also remembered for a quite different idea: in 1978, with Guy Woodruff , he asked whether a chimpanzee has a "theory of mind", a question covered in the Developmental Psychology book.) Exam trap The Premack principle says high-probability behaviour reinforces low-probability behaviour , never the reverse. It does not say that reinforcement works best when intermittent (that is the partial reinforcement effect), that behaviour followed by satisfaction recurs (the law of effect), that complex behaviour is built from successive approximations (shaping), that punishment beats reinforcement, or that continuous reinforcement is most resistant to extinction (it is the least). Some question banks date the principle 1965, the year of Premack's longer statement of it; his first statement was in 1959. Superstitious behaviour Reinforcement strengthens whatever response happens to precede it, whether or not the response produced it. In a 1948 paper titled "'Superstition' in the pigeon", Skinner gave hungry pigeons food every 15 seconds, whatever they were doing. Six of his eight birds developed odd, repetitive rituals: one turned anticlockwise two or three times between feedings, another kept thrusting its head into an upper corner of the cage, two swung their heads from side to side like a pendulum. Each bird, Skinner argued, had happened to be doing something when food arrived; that act was reinforced, became more likely, was therefore more likely to be under way when the next food came, and so on. Superstitious behaviour is behaviour strengthened by accidental (adventitious) reinforcement, with no real relationship between the act and the reinforcer. A batsman who will not change his "lucky" pads during a run of good scores, or a student who takes the same pen to every exam, is showing it. The interpretation has been challenged. When John Staddon and Virginia Simmelhag repeated the experiment in 1971 and watched more closely, they found that the behaviours just before food were mostly the same species-typical, food-related acts in every bird (pecking near the food hopper), which suggests that much of what Skinner saw reflected Pavlovian anticipation of food rather than accidental operant reinforcement. Exam trap Strictly, Skinner's pigeons were on a fixed- time schedule (food every 15 seconds, regardless of behaviour), but many textbooks describe it as fixed-interval reinforcement. Either way, the answer to "what did the superstition experiment demonstrate?" is accidental (adventitious) reinforcement. Learned helplessness What happens to an animal that learns that nothing it does makes any difference? The answer came from a discovery that its investigators did not expect, and it became one of the most influential models in clinical psychology. Key study: Learned helplessness in dogs (Overmier and Seligman, 1967; Seligman and Maier, 1967) Question. Does experience with uncontrollable aversive events change later learning? Method. In the "triadic" design used by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier , dogs were first placed in harnesses in three groups. Dogs in the escape group received shocks that they could switch off by pressing a panel with their heads. Each dog in the yoked group was wired to an escape dog and received exactly the same shocks, at the same times and of the same duration, but nothing it did affected them. A third group received no shocks. A day later all the dogs were placed in a shuttle box where they could escape or avoid shock simply by jumping a low barrier. Result. The escape dogs and the unshocked dogs quickly learned to jump. Most of the yoked dogs did not: after a brief struggle they lay down and whined, taking shock after shock without trying to escape, and even when one did jump by chance it seldom repeated the response. Conclusion. The yoked dogs had learned that their responses and the shocks were independent. This expectation produced three deficits: motivational (they stopped trying), cognitive (they had difficulty learning that a response now worked) and emotional (they appeared depressed). Seligman called this learned helplessness : passive acceptance of aversive events, even avoidable ones, that follows experience with uncontrollable aversive events. Significance. Because the shocks were identical for escape and yoked dogs, the damage was caused not by the shocks but by the lack of control. The first published report was by J. Bruce Overmier and Seligman in 1967, with Seligman and Maier's follow-up in the same year. Later experiments by Donald Hiroto (1974) produced the same pattern in people: university students exposed to loud noise they could not turn off later failed to learn a simple hand movement that would have turned it off. Seligman proposed learned helplessness as a model of depression, because depressed people, like the yoked dogs, often stop trying, find it hard to see that their actions can work, and feel low. The model had a problem: people do not become depressed after every uncontrollable event. In 1978 Lyn Abramson , Seligman and John Teasdale reformulated it in cognitive terms: what matters is how people explain uncontrollable events to themselves. Depression is most likely in people who attribute bad events to causes that are internal ("it's me"), stable ("it will always be like this") and global ("it affects everything I do"). This attributional reformulation, and the hopelessness theory that followed it, are covered with depression in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Fifty years after the original studies, Maier and Seligman (2016) revised their own account using neuroscience: passivity, they now argue, is the brain's default reaction to prolonged aversive events, and what animals learn in the escape condition is that they have control, a discovery that recruits the prefrontal cortex to damp down the stress response. Exam trap Learned helplessness was offered by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier (with Bruce Overmier), not by Aaron Beck (cognitive triad), Harry Stack Sullivan (interpersonal theory) or Daniel Kahneman (heuristics). It is passive acceptance of later aversive events after repeated unavoidable ones. It is not escaping an aversive stimulus, not watching a model rewarded for aggression, and not extinction from loss of reinforcement. One real stem places it "in social learning theory"; the concept actually comes from animal learning research and was later reformulated cognitively, but the answer is unchanged. Instinctive drift and other limits on operant conditioning Just as Garcia showed that classical conditioning is constrained by biology, two of Skinner's own students showed the same for operant conditioning. Keller Breland and Marian Breland set up a business training animals for zoos, fairs and television advertisements, and by the late 1950s they had trained thousands of animals of dozens of species. In 1961 they published a paper wittily titled "The misbehavior of organisms", a play on the title of Skinner's 1938 book. They had trained a raccoon to pick up a coin and drop it into a metal box for food. With one coin all went well. Given two coins, the raccoon began rubbing them together, dipping them into the box and pulling them out again, for minutes at a time, exactly as raccoons rub and wash food, and it never stopped doing so despite losing reinforcement. Pigs trained to carry large wooden coins to a "piggy bank" began, after some weeks, to drop them, root them along the ground with their snouts and toss them in the air, as pigs root for food. The Brelands called this instinctive drift : the tendency of a learned behaviour to drift towards the instinctive, species-typical behaviour associated with the reinforcer. Their conclusion was blunt: operant conditioning cannot be understood without understanding the animal's instinctive repertoire. A related finding is autoshaping. In 1968 Paul Brown and Herbert Jenkins found that if a pigeon's key is simply lit for a few seconds before food is delivered, the pigeon begins pecking the key even though pecking has no effect on the food. A Pavlovian pairing of light and food produced what looks like an operant response. Classical and operant conditioning are separable in principle, but in living animals they constantly interact. Choice: the matching law In everyday life you are rarely choosing whether to respond; you are choosing which of several reinforced activities to do. Richard Herrnstein (1930 to 1994) studied this in 1961 by giving pigeons two keys, each reinforced on its own variable-interval schedule. He found that the proportion of pecks a pigeon made on each key matched the proportion of reinforcers it obtained from that key. This is the matching law : B 1 /(B 1 + B 2 ) = R 1 /(R 1 + R 2 ), where B is the rate of behaviour on each alternative and R is the rate of reinforcement it produces. If the left key yields 40 reinforcers an hour and the right key 20, the pigeon makes about two-thirds of its pecks on the left. People behave similarly: the time we spend with different friends, or on different activities, tends to be proportional to the rewards each provides. Contrast effects: the Crespi effect Does a bigger reward produce better learning, or just more effort? In 1942 Leo Crespi trained rats to run down a runway for food, some for a large amount and some for a small amount, and then shifted all of them to the same intermediate amount. The rats shifted down from a large reward immediately ran slower than rats that had received the intermediate amount all along. The rats shifted up from a small reward immediately ran faster than those rats. Crespi called these the depression and elation effects; in 1949 David Zeaman renamed them negative contrast and positive contrast, and today they are known together as contrast effects , or the Crespi effect. Two conclusions followed. First, the value of a reinforcer is relative to what the organism is used to: a mark of 85 delights a student who usually gets 70 and dismays one who usually gets 95. Second, the changes in running speed were too abrupt to be changes in learning; they were changes in motivation. Reward size affects performance through incentive, a point that forced Clark Hull to add incentive motivation to his equations (Section 6.9). Exam trap The Crespi effect refers to a change in motivation (performance) when the magnitude of reinforcement changes : an increase in reward produces a disproportionate increase in performance (positive contrast) and a decrease produces a disproportionate decrease (negative contrast). The keyed answer in IHBAS 2025 described the positive half. It is not retroactive inhibition (forgetting caused by later learning, Chapter 7), not extinction and not insight. Biofeedback: operant control of the body For decades it was assumed that only skeletal muscles could be operantly conditioned, while heart rate, blood pressure and other autonomic responses could only be classically conditioned. In the late 1960s Neal Miller (1909 to 2002) and his student Leo DiCara reported that rats paralysed with curare, so that they could not use their muscles to influence their hearts indirectly, could learn to raise or lower their heart rates when rewarded with electrical stimulation of the brain's reward areas. Later attempts, including Miller's own, failed to replicate the strongest results, but the idea that autonomic functions can be brought under voluntary control with feedback had already launched a clinical field. Biofeedback is a technique in which a bodily process that is normally outside awareness is measured by an instrument and displayed back to the person, as a tone, a moving line or a number, so that he or she can learn to control it. Each change in the desired direction is reinforced by the feedback itself, so biofeedback is operant conditioning combined with knowledge of results (Section 6.10). Electromyographic (EMG) biofeedback of muscle tension in the forehead and neck is used for tension-type headache and chronic pain; thermal biofeedback of finger temperature is used for migraine; electroencephalographic biofeedback (neurofeedback) has been used for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and epilepsy; and feedback of skin conductance or heart-rate variability is used in anxiety and stress management. The idea is older than the name. In 1948 the gynaecologist Arnold Kegel taught women pelvic-floor exercises with a perineometer, a pressure gauge that let a patient watch her own muscle squeeze on a dial, an early form of biofeedback. Exam trap "The technique based on the idea that the autonomic nervous system can come under voluntary control through operant conditioning" is biofeedback , not hypnosis, sublimation (a Freudian defence mechanism) or systematic desensitisation (Wolpe's counterconditioning). EMG biofeedback is most useful for tension-type headache. Kegel's perineometer was an early form of biofeedback, not aversion therapy, a token economy or desensitisation. Three lines of research, in rats, apes and monkeys, showed that this view left out something essential: what animals learn is often knowledge, a representation of how the world is arranged, which they use flexibly when the occasion demands. This section describes those three lines of research and ends with a brief account of how concepts are formed. Tolman: latent learning and cognitive maps Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959) was a behaviourist in method: he studied rats in mazes and measured only what they did. But he insisted that behaviour is purposive, directed towards goals, and that it should be described at the level of whole, meaningful acts ("running to the food box") rather than muscle twitches. His approach, set out in Purposive Behavior in Animals and Men (1932), is called purposive behaviourism. Tolman argued that between the stimulus and the response there are intervening variables, such as expectancies and knowledge of the environment, that cannot be seen but can be inferred from behaviour. (A similar point had been made by Robert Sessions Woodworth , who proposed replacing the S-R formula with S-O-R, stimulus-organism-response, to show that what the organism brings to the situation shapes its response.) Key study: Tolman and Honzik's latent learning experiment (1930) Question. Do rats learn a maze only when they are reinforced for running it? Method. Tolman and Charles Honzik ran three groups of hungry rats through a complex maze with fourteen choice points, once a day for seventeen days. One group always found food in the goal box. A second group never found food; they were simply removed from the goal box when they reached it. A third group found no food for the first ten days, but from day 11 onwards found food in the goal box. Result. The always-rewarded rats steadily reduced their errors. The never-rewarded rats improved only slightly. The third group made as many errors as the never-rewarded rats for ten days, but the day after food was introduced their errors dropped dramatically, to the level of the always-rewarded group and even slightly below it (Figure 6.5). Conclusion. The third group must have been learning the layout of the maze all along, during the unrewarded days, without showing it. The reward did not create the learning; it gave the rats a reason to display it. Significance. This is the clearest demonstration of the difference between learning and performance. (Hugh Blodgett had reported a similar result in 1929.) 0 2 4 6 8 10 Average errors per run 1 3 5 7 9 11 13 15 17 Days food introduced (day 11) Always rewarded Never rewarded Rewarded from day 11 Figure 6.5 Latent learning, stylised after Tolman and Honzik (1930). The group rewarded only from day 11 (dotted line) performed like the never-rewarded group until food appeared, then immediately matched the always-rewarded group. The learning had been there, unseen, before the reward. Latent learning is learning that occurs without obvious reinforcement and remains hidden until there is an incentive to demonstrate it. What had the rats learned? Tolman's answer, developed in a famous 1948 paper, "Cognitive maps in rats and men", was that they had formed a cognitive map : a mental representation of the spatial layout of the environment. Evidence came from experiments on place learning . In 1946 Tolman and his colleagues trained one group of rats always to find food in the same place in a cross-shaped maze, whichever arm they started from, so that sometimes they had to turn left and sometimes right; another group always had to make the same turn, so the food's location changed. The rats that had to learn a place learned faster than those that had to learn a response, which a pure S-R theory cannot explain. When rats that had learned a roundabout route to food were later offered many straight paths radiating in different directions, many chose the path that pointed most directly towards where the food had been, as if they knew where it was, not just how to get there. Tolman also argued that animals learn expectancies : that a particular goal will follow a particular action. A vivid demonstration had come from Otto Tinklepaugh in 1928. A monkey watched a banana being hidden under a cup; when it lifted the cup and found that the banana had been secretly replaced by lettuce, a food it normally ate happily, it refused the lettuce, searched around and shrieked at the observers. It had expected a banana. Because what is learned in Tolman's view is knowledge of "what leads to what", his position is variously called sign learning theory, expectancy theory and place learning theory. Exam trap Latent learning and the cognitive map belong to Tolman , not Bandura, Skinner, Köhler or Harlow. "A sudden increase in performance upon reinforcement, despite never being reinforced on previous trials" is latent learning, not observational learning, discrimination learning or vicarious reinforcement. Tolman's rats do not show shaping, pure S-R learning or spontaneous recovery. An option naming "Gould" refers to the biologist James Gould, who studied honeybee navigation and asked whether insects might have map-like knowledge; the concept of the cognitive map is Tolman's (1948). Köhler: insight On the other side of the Atlantic, a different challenge to trial-and-error learning was taking shape. Wolfgang Köhler (1887 to 1967) was, with Max Wertheimer and Kurt Koffka, one of the three founders of Gestalt psychology, which holds that experience is organised into wholes that are more than the sum of their parts (Chapters 2 and 4). From 1913 to 1920 Köhler directed a research station for apes on Tenerife in the Canary Islands, where the First World War kept him far longer than planned. There he set chimpanzees problems that could not be solved by any single learned response. In the simplest problems a banana lay on the ground outside the cage, out of reach, and a stick lay inside; the chimpanzees soon used the stick to rake the banana in. In the famous two-stick problem, the banana was farther away, and neither of two sticks was long enough on its own; one stick was hollow, so the other could be fitted into it. The most gifted chimpanzee, Sultan, tried with one stick and then the other, failed, and gave up. Later, while playing idly with the two sticks, he happened to hold them in a line, pushed the thinner one into the hollow end of the thicker, and at once ran to the bars and raked in the banana. In the box problems a banana was hung from the roof of the enclosure, too high to reach by jumping. The chimpanzees jumped in vain, paced about, and then, often quite suddenly, dragged a box under the banana and climbed on it; some later learned to stack two or three boxes. Köhler described this work in a book published in German in 1917 and in English in 1925 as The Mentality of Apes . Insight learning is the sudden grasp of a problem's solution through perceiving the relationships among its elements, a reorganisation of the perceptual field. Köhler identified its features. The change from no solution to solution is sudden, not gradual like Thorndike's curves. It is often preceded by a period of apparent inactivity in which the animal surveys the situation. Once found, the solution is carried out smoothly and without errors. It is remembered well. And it transfers readily to similar problems. It also depends on all the elements of the problem being in view at once: the chimpanzees rarely used a stick that was behind them. The subjective feeling of sudden understanding that accompanies insight is called the aha experience (the German "Aha-Erlebnis", a term usually credited to the psychologist Karl Bühler ). Insight was a powerful argument against the view that all learning is the gradual strengthening of S-R connections. But it has a qualification. In 1945 Herbert Birch found that young chimpanzees who had never handled sticks did not solve stick problems insightfully; after a few days of playing with sticks, they did. Insight, it seems, recombines things that were learned earlier. Harlow's work, described next, explains how. Exam trap Sultan, sticks and stacked boxes mean insight learning (Köhler), not trial-and-error, classical conditioning or latent learning. The sudden realisation of a solution is the "aha" experience , not the "light bulb", "momentary" or "learning". Do not confuse Köhler's insight with insight in psychiatry, the patient's awareness of his own illness, which is rated in the mental status examination on a six-grade scale (with intellectual insight usually placed at grade 5; Clinical Psychology book), or with insight as a goal of psychoanalysis. Harlow: learning to learn Harry Harlow (1905 to 1981), working with rhesus monkeys at the University of Wisconsin, asked what happens when an animal is given not one problem but hundreds of similar ones. In each discrimination problem a monkey was shown two objects it had never seen before, such as a cup and a wooden block, one of which always covered a raisin or a piece of food. The monkey had a few trials to discover which object paid. Then a new pair of objects was introduced, and so on through several hundred problems. On the first few problems the monkeys learned slowly and gradually, in true trial-and-error fashion, and on the second trial of each new problem they were right only about half the time, no better than chance. But each problem was solved a little faster than the last. By the end, the monkeys were right on the second trial of a new problem more than 95 percent of the time: one trial was enough to tell them which object to choose. They had learned a general strategy, which can be described as "if the object you picked paid, stay with it; if not, switch" (win-stay, lose-shift). Harlow, in a 1949 paper, called this a learning set : an improvement in the ability to learn new problems of a given type that results from experience with many problems of that type, or, more simply, learning to learn. Learning sets reconcile Thorndike and Köhler. A naive animal facing a new kind of problem learns by trial and error; an experienced one, armed with learning sets, appears to solve problems by insight. What looks like sudden understanding in an adult may rest on a long history of earlier, gradual learning. Students do the same: the first algebra problem of a new type takes an hour, the twentieth takes a minute. Concept formation A concept is a mental category that groups objects, events or ideas sharing common properties: "dog", "fruit", "democracy". Concepts let us respond to new instances without learning about each one separately. The full cognitive treatment of concepts, including the strategies that Jerome Bruner, Jacqueline Goodnow and George Austin described in 1956 and the later prototype view, is in Chapter 8. Here we need only the stage account of concept formation that is taught in general and educational psychology, in which a concept is built up in four steps. Observation . The learner encounters many instances. A two-year-old in Mysuru sees the neighbour's Labrador, the street dogs outside the temple, a Pomeranian on television. Discrimination . The learner notices how instances differ from non-instances: cows and cats, though they also have four legs and fur, are not dogs. Generalisation . The learner extends the response (the word "dog") to all the instances that share the essential features, however different their size and colour. Abstraction . The learner extracts the common defining properties from the particular instances, so that the concept exists independently of any one dog and can be applied to breeds never seen before. The concept is then named and can be defined. Notice that the stages parallel the conditioning processes of Section 6.3: generalisation and discrimination, which Pavlov studied in dogs, are the raw materials from which human concepts are built. Exam trap The keyed order (JEMAS 2025, repeated in JSS practice sets) is Observation, Discrimination, Generalisation, Abstraction . Options that start with abstraction, or that put generalisation before discrimination, are wrong; so is any option containing assimilation , which is Piaget's term for fitting new experience into existing schemas (Developmental Psychology book), not a stage of concept formation. Some educational psychology texts list the steps as observation, comparison, abstraction and generalisation, followed by naming; if you see that version, accept it too, because "comparison" is discrimination under another name. 6.8 Observational Learning High yield · 17 Qs Imagine learning to drive purely by operant conditioning: you would press pedals and turn the wheel at random, and be reinforced whenever the car happened to move safely forward. You would not survive the first lesson. Most complex human skills, from tying a turban to rolling a round chapati to performing a cover drive, are learned largely by watching someone else do them first. So are many attitudes, fears, habits of speech and ways of handling anger. Observational learning (also called social learning or modelling) is learning that occurs by watching the behaviour of others, called models, and its consequences. Before Bandura: imitation as learned behaviour The first learning theorists to take imitation seriously were Neal Miller and John Dollard (1900 to 1980) at Yale. In Social Learning and Imitation (1941) they argued that imitation is itself an operant response that is learned because it is reinforced. A younger child who follows an older sibling to where the father hands out sweets is rewarded for copying, so copying becomes a habit; they called this matched-dependent behaviour. In Personality and Psychotherapy (1950) they went further and translated Freud's ideas into the language of Clark Hull's learning theory, describing behaviour in terms of drive, cue, response and reward. This work is usually called early social learning theory. Its limitation was that, on their account, imitation still required reinforcement of the observer. The Bobo doll studies Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021), born in a small town in Alberta, Canada, and for most of his career a professor at Stanford University, showed that observers can learn new behaviour without performing it and without any reinforcement at all. Key study: Bandura, Ross and Ross's Bobo doll experiment (1961) Question. Will children imitate aggression they have merely watched, without being reinforced? Method. Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross studied 72 children, aged about three to six, from the Stanford University nursery school. In one condition each child, busy making pictures with potato prints and stickers in a corner of a room, watched an adult model attack a large inflatable "Bobo" clown doll in unusual ways: sitting on it and punching it on the nose, striking it with a mallet, tossing it in the air, kicking it about the room, while saying things like "Sock him in the nose!" and "Pow!". In a second condition the model played quietly with tinker toys and ignored Bobo; a third group saw no model. Each child was then mildly frustrated (shown some very attractive toys and told they were being kept for other children) and left in a room containing various toys, including Bobo and a mallet. Result. Children who had watched the aggressive model reproduced many of the model's specific, novel acts and phrases, far more than children in the other two groups. Boys showed more physical aggression than girls, and the male model was imitated more for physical aggression. Conclusion. New behaviour can be acquired simply by observation, with no reinforcement to either the model or the child. Criticism. A Bobo doll is designed to be hit, so the study may show play rather than aggression towards people; the children may have sensed what the adults expected; and only short-term effects were measured. Two follow-up studies extended the finding. In 1963 Bandura and the Rosses showed that a filmed model, and even a cartoon-like model dressed as a cat, produced as much imitative aggression as a live model, a result that made Bandura a central figure in the debate about violence on television (Social Psychology book). And in 1965 Bandura showed children a film in which the model's aggression was rewarded, punished, or had no consequences. Children who saw the model punished imitated less aggression than the others. But when the experimenter then offered every child an attractive incentive (stickers and fruit juice) for showing what the model had done, the differences disappeared: children in all three groups could reproduce the aggressive acts equally well. The consequences to the model had affected performance , not learning . This is the same learning-performance distinction that Tolman's rats had shown. The 1965 study also illustrates two key terms. Vicarious reinforcement is an increase in an observer's tendency to perform a behaviour after seeing a model rewarded for it; vicarious punishment is a decrease after seeing a model punished. A younger brother who watches his elder sister get scolded for answering back learns, without being scolded himself, not to answer back, at least when the parents are watching. The four processes of observational learning Bandura analysed observational learning into four component processes, all of which must operate for an observed behaviour to be reproduced (Figure 6.6, left). Attention . The observer must notice the model and the relevant features of what the model does. We attend more to models who are attractive, competent, high in status, similar to ourselves, and whose behaviour is distinctive or rewarded. Retention . The observer must store what was seen, in images and in words ("first fold, then tuck"), and rehearse it, because the behaviour may not be performed until much later. Motor reproduction (or production). The observer must be physically able to turn the memory into action, and usually refines the performance with practice and feedback. You can watch Virat Kohli for years and remember every detail of his cover drive without being able to play it. Motivation . Finally, the observer must have a reason to perform the behaviour: direct reinforcement, vicarious reinforcement, or self-reinforcement (the satisfaction of meeting one's own standards). The first three processes govern learning; the fourth governs performance. That is why direct reinforcement is not a necessary condition of observational learning , although it strongly affects whether the learned behaviour is ever shown. It also explains why observational learning helps someone acquire adaptive behaviour only when the model actually demonstrates the target behaviour: a model who acts angrily, playfully or randomly gives the observer nothing useful to attend to and retain. The first three govern whether a behaviour is learned; the fourth (shaded differently) governs whether it is performed. Right: reciprocal determinism. Personal factors, behaviour and environment each influence, and are influenced by, the other two. Exam trap The four processes are attention, retention, motor reproduction (production) and motivation . They are not "sensory, perceptual, cognitive, affective"; not "encoding, storage, retrieval, evaluation" (the stages of memory, Chapter 7); and not "stimulus, response, reinforcement, extinction" (operant conditioning). "Which is NOT necessary for observational learning?" Reinforcement . The view that reinforcement is not required to learn a behaviour by observation is Bandura's , not Skinner's, Tolman's or Miller and Dollard's (who held that imitation must be reinforced). The Bobo doll studies demonstrate observational learning of aggression through modelling, not operant shaping, classical conditioning of fear, negative reinforcement or the effects of sensory deprivation. From social learning to social cognitive theory Bandura's early theory, set out with his student Richard Walters in Social Learning and Personality Development (1963), is often called later social learning theory, to distinguish it from Dollard and Miller's. Over the following decades Bandura gave cognition an ever larger role, and in Social Foundations of Thought and Action (1986) he renamed his position social cognitive theory. Three ideas from this period are heavily examined. The first is reciprocal determinism (Bandura, 1978), which Bandura later called triadic reciprocal causation. Strict behaviourists such as Skinner held a one-way view: the environment determines behaviour. Bandura argued that three sets of factors, the person (beliefs, expectations, self-efficacy), behaviour and the environment, continuously influence one another in both directions (Figure 6.6, right). A student who believes she can master statistics (person) attends classes and practises (behaviour); her practice earns praise and a seat in the advanced group (environment); the new environment strengthens her belief, and so on round the triangle. The second is self-regulation . Bandura noted that most human behaviour occurs in the absence of any immediate external reward or punishment. People set their own standards, observe their own behaviour (self-observation), compare it with the standards (the judgemental process) and reward or criticise themselves accordingly (self-reaction). Much of what keeps a student at her desk at eleven at night is self-regulation, not anyone else's reinforcement. The third is self-efficacy , introduced in a 1977 paper: a person's belief in his or her capability to organise and carry out the actions needed to achieve a particular goal or deal with a particular situation. Self-efficacy is specific to a task: you may have high self-efficacy for public speaking and low self-efficacy for mathematics. It is also different from an outcome expectation, the belief that a behaviour will lead to a result: you may be sure that regular exercise would make you fitter (outcome expectation) and doubt that you could keep it up (efficacy expectation). Bandura identified four sources of self-efficacy: performance attainments (past successes, the most powerful source), vicarious experiences (seeing similar others succeed), verbal persuasion (being told you can do it) and physiological and emotional states (reading a calm body as a sign of competence). Within social cognitive theory, self-efficacy is the most important motivational construct: people with high self-efficacy choose harder tasks, try harder and persist longer. Clinical link Modelling is a therapy technique in its own right. In 1969 Bandura and his colleagues treated people with snake phobia by participant modelling: the therapist first handled the snake while the client watched, then guided the client through closer and closer contact. It worked better than watching a film of models or than systematic desensitisation, and Bandura argued that every successful treatment works by raising the client's self-efficacy. Social skills training, assertiveness training and much of cognitive behaviour therapy use modelling and rehearsal (Clinical Psychology book). Remember: Rotter's social learning theory Julian Rotter (1916 to 2014) developed a separate social learning theory in Social Learning and Clinical Psychology (1954). For Rotter, the behaviour potential (BP) is the likelihood of a particular behaviour occurring in a given situation, calculated in relation to a particular reinforcement or set of reinforcements. It depends on the expectancy (E), the person's subjective probability that the behaviour will lead to the reinforcement, and on the reinforcement value (RV), how much the person wants that reinforcement: BP = f(E and RV), within a given psychological situation. Generalised expectancies about whether outcomes depend on one's own actions became his concept of locus of control (1966), internal or external. Social learning frameworks in general explain behaviour by cognitive variables such as expectancies, situational demands and incentives, rather than by reinforcement history alone. (Rotter's theory is treated fully in the Personality book.) Exam trap Reciprocal determinism (Bandura): cognition, behaviour and environment influence one another bidirectionally; the "reciprocal causation model" belongs to social cognitive theory , not to two-factor theory (Mowrer), drive-reduction theory (Hull) or constructivist theory (Piaget, Vygotsky). Do not confuse it with reciprocal inhibition (Wolpe) or reciprocal altruism (the evolutionary biologist Robert Trivers). Self-efficacy is belief in one's capability for a specific task; it is not overall self-worth (self-esteem), not attributing outcomes to fate or chance (external locus of control, Rotter) and not the striving to overcome inferiority (Adler). The theorist who developed self-efficacy is Bandura, not Beck, Ellis or Skinner. Bandura's claim that most behaviour comes from self-regulation is the right answer when the alternatives are negative reinforcement, "reciprocal dualism" or "behavioural determinism". In a match-the-list question: Dollard and Miller = early social learning; Bandura and Walters = later social learning; Skinner = radical behaviourism; Maslow = self-actualisation. Behaviour that is emitted and operates on the environment is operant behaviour , not Jung's principle of opposites, Rotter's behaviour potential or Allport's personal dispositions.
