Answers: (1) latent, (2) map, (3) Sultan, (4) set, (5) discrimination, (6) reinforced, (7) retention, (8) vicarious, (9) self-efficacy, (10) determinism. 6.9 Other Learning Theorists Lower yield · 1 Q Between about 1930 and 1960, learning was the battleground on which American psychology fought out its biggest theoretical arguments. Pavlov, Thorndike, Skinner, Tolman and Bandura, whom you have already met, were not alone on that field. A handful of other theorists built complete systems that tried to explain all learning with a few principles. None of these "grand theories" survived intact, but their ideas and their vocabulary run all through later psychology, and their names run all through examination papers. The standard guide to them was Theories of Learning (1948) by Ernest Ropiequet Hilgard (1904 to 2001), a book that went through five editions (the later ones with Gordon Bower) and taught generations of students to compare the theories by putting the same few questions to each. (Hilgard is also remembered for his work on hypnosis, Chapter 5.) This section begins with those questions, then takes the theorists one at a time. Two questions that divided the theorists The first question was what is learned . For the stimulus-response theories (S-R theories), what is learned is a connection between a stimulus and a response. Thorndike's bonds, Watson's conditioned reflexes and the theories of Guthrie and Hull below all belong here. They explain learning without any reference to the mind: the organism does not come to know anything; it comes to respond in a new way. Textbooks often call this the stimulus-response behaviouristic approach, and it is the approach that "emphasises learning through stimulus-response associations, mainly via conditioning". For the cognitive theorists, Tolman and the Gestalt psychologists such as Köhler, what is learned is knowledge: an expectancy that one event leads to another, a map of a maze, an insight into how the parts of a problem fit together. The organism then uses that knowledge flexibly. Tolman's place-learning experiment (Section 6.7) was the classic test case. An S-R theorist says the rat learned a turning response; a cognitive theorist says it learned where the food is. The second question was what makes learning happen . Contiguity theorists answered that a stimulus and a response need only occur together. Pavlov's account of conditioning rested on contiguity, and Watson, who regarded Thorndike's talk of "satisfaction" as unscientific, explained learning by two laws of his own: the law of frequency (the response made most often in a situation is the one learned) and the law of recency (the response made most recently is the one that will occur next time). Reinforcement theorists, from Thorndike through Hull to Skinner, answered that a response must be followed by a consequence. Tolman took a third position: learning happens through exploration, with or without reward (latent learning), but reward decides whether what was learned is performed. Skinner, characteristically, refused to play the game. In a 1950 paper titled "Are theories of learning necessary?" he argued that explanations in terms of unobserved events at some other level, whether neural, mental or mathematical, were unnecessary and distracting; a science of behaviour should simply describe how behaviour changes with its environment. That is why Skinner's system is often called descriptive behaviourism. The theorists in the rest of this section disagreed with him. They believed that good theory, the more precise the better, was exactly what the study of learning needed. Exam trap "Which approach emphasises learning through stimulus-response associations, mainly via conditioning?" The answer is the stimulus-response (S-R) behaviouristic approach . The cognitive approach emphasises knowledge, expectancy and insight; the psychoanalytic approach emphasises unconscious conflict (Freud); the existential approach emphasises freedom, choice and meaning. Within learning theory, keep the two dimensions apart: Guthrie is an S-R contiguity theorist, Hull an S-R reinforcement theorist, and Tolman a cognitive theorist. Guthrie: we learn what we do Edwin Ray Guthrie (1886 to 1959) spent his whole career at the University of Washington in Seattle. Trained first in mathematics and philosophy, he wrote clearly, with homely examples from farms, schools and family life, and did few experiments himself. His book The Psychology of Learning (1935, revised 1952) offered the simplest theory of learning ever proposed. It had one law, the law of contiguity : "A combination of stimuli which has accompanied a movement will on its recurrence tend to be followed by that movement." Nothing about satisfaction, reward or drive. If a stimulus pattern and a movement occur together, they become associated, and that is all learning is. Two corollaries follow. The first is one-trial learning : in Guthrie's words, a stimulus pattern gains its full associative strength on the occasion of its first pairing with a response. Learning does not grow bit by bit; each association is made all at once. The second is the recency principle: whatever an organism did last in a situation is what it will do when the situation recurs, because that was the last movement attached to those stimuli. "We learn only what we do," Guthrie said, and teachers have quoted him ever since. A student who reads a chapter passively learns to read passively; if you want her to be able to explain the ideas, she must practise explaining them. If learning is complete in one trial, why does practice help? Guthrie's answer rested on a distinction between movements and acts. A movement is a specific muscle contraction; an act is a class of movements defined by what it achieves, such as playing a cover drive or parking a scooter. An act is made up of thousands of movements, and each movement must be attached to its own stimuli, including the movement-produced stimuli (the sensations from the muscles and joints) generated by the movement before it, which link the movements into a chain. An act must also be performed in many different situations: against fast bowling and slow, on a green pitch and a dry one. Practice attaches the act to more and more of these stimulus combinations. The learning curve for the act is gradual even though every single association is formed in one trial. What, then, does a reward do? For Guthrie, nothing special. A reward simply changes the stimulus situation. When the cat in the puzzle box operates the latch, the door opens and the cat leaves; the last movement it made in the box is therefore preserved, because the cat has no opportunity to do anything else in the presence of those stimuli. If the cat stayed in the box after escaping, it would go on to make other movements, and those would be the ones attached to the box. Forgetting, likewise, is not the fading of an association with time; it occurs only when a new response becomes attached to the old stimuli. Guthrie was one of the first to argue that forgetting is caused by interference rather than decay (Chapter 7). Key study: Guthrie and Horton's cats in a puzzle box (1946) Question. If the last movement before escape is what is learned, will each cat repeat its own particular movement? Method. Guthrie and George P. Horton built a puzzle box with a glass front and a slender pole standing in the middle of the floor. Tilting the pole in any direction opened the door, and a camera triggered by the pole photographed each cat at the instant it escaped. Result. Each cat settled into its own stereotyped way of moving the pole, backing into it, pushing it with a paw, or rubbing against it with its head or flank, and repeated that movement with remarkable consistency, escape after escape, while different cats used different movements. Conclusion. Guthrie and Horton took the photographs as strong support for contiguity and recency: what each cat learned was simply the movement it had happened to make at the moment of escape. Criticism. In 1979 Bruce Moore and Susan Stuttard showed that cats in such a box rub the pole with their heads and flanks whenever a person is in view, even when rubbing never opens the door. Head-rubbing is a feline greeting. Much of what the photographs showed was species-typical behaviour released by the watching experimenters, the same lesson the Brelands drew from instinctive drift (Section 6.6). Guthrie's view of punishment followed directly from his one law. Punishment works, he said, only if it makes the animal do something incompatible with the punished response in the presence of the stimuli that produced it. Slap a dog on the nose as it runs at a passing car, and it recoils, so recoiling becomes attached to the sight of cars; slap it on the rump, and you may simply drive it forward, strengthening the chase. What matters is not the pain but what the pain makes the animal do. Guthrie's methods of breaking habits Guthrie's most practical contribution, and the one most often examined, was his advice on breaking habits. If a habit is a response attached to cues, it cannot be removed by wishing; the only way to break it is to attach a different response to the same cues. He described three methods (Table 6.11). In the threshold method , the stimulus is introduced at an intensity so weak that it does not produce the unwanted response, and is then strengthened so gradually that it always stays below the threshold for that response. Guthrie's example was breaking a horse to the saddle: first a light blanket is laid on its back, then a slightly heavier one, then a light saddle, and so on, each so mild that the horse never bucks. By the time the full saddle and rider arrive, standing quietly has been attached to the feel of weight on its back. In the fatigue method , the stimulus is presented again and again, and the unwanted response is allowed or even made to occur until the organism is so tired that it stops and does something else in the presence of the stimulus. The "bronco buster" rides a bucking horse until it is too exhausted to buck. A child who keeps playing with matches can be made to strike match after match until he is heartily sick of it. In the incompatible response method , the stimulus for the unwanted response is presented together with other stimuli that produce a response incompatible with it, so that the incompatible response becomes attached to the old cue. A small child frightened of a toy panda is given the panda while she sits relaxed on her mother's lap; the warmth and calm that her mother produces cannot coexist with fear, and calm becomes attached to the panda. Guthrie added a fourth piece of advice that is sometimes called sidetracking. Find the cues that start the unwanted habit and practise a different response in their presence. A man who smokes with his morning tea should not try to resist the cigarette at noon, when the urge is weak; he should change what he does with his tea. Guthrie's best-known anecdote makes the same point. A mother complained that her ten-year-old daughter had for two years thrown her hat and coat on the floor every time she came home, despite constant scolding. On a psychologist's advice, the next time it happened the mother made the girl put the coat and hat back on, go outside, come in again and hang them up. A few repetitions cured the habit. Scolding had attached picking up the coat to the mother's voice; the new routine attached it to the cue that really mattered, walking in through the door. Table 6.11 Guthrie's three methods of breaking habits and their descendants in behaviour therapy. Method What you do Guthrie's example Modern parallel Threshold Present the cue so weakly that the habit is not triggered; increase it very gradually Blanket, then saddle, then rider on a young horse Graded exposure; systematic desensitisation Fatigue Make the unwanted response occur over and over until the learner is exhausted Riding a bucking horse until it stops; striking match after match Negative practice (Dunlap); stimulus satiation (Ayllon) Incompatible response Present the cue while a response incompatible with the habit is occurring The feared panda given to a child on her mother's lap Counterconditioning; reciprocal inhibition (Jones, Wolpe) The parallels in the last column are close. The threshold method is, in essence, the graded hierarchy of systematic desensitisation, and the incompatible response method is Mary Cover Jones's treatment of Peter and Wolpe's reciprocal inhibition (Section 6.4). The fatigue method resembles two later techniques. In negative practice, introduced by Knight Dunlap in Habits: Their Making and Unmaking (1932), the person deliberately and repeatedly performs the unwanted habit, as when a typist who habitually types "hte" for "the" practises typing "hte" on purpose. In stimulus satiation, the reinforcer for a habit is supplied in such excess that it loses its value: in 1963 Teodoro Ayllon treated a long-stay psychiatric patient who hoarded towels by giving her towels freely, until several hundred were piled in her room and she began carrying them out herself, after which the hoarding stopped. Exam trap Guthrie's theory is contiguity (stimulus and movement occurring together), with one-trial learning and the recency principle ; reinforcement is not needed. Do not confuse Guthrie's one-trial learning (true, he said, of every association) with the one-trial learning of Garcia's taste aversion (a special, biologically prepared case, Section 6.4). His three methods of breaking habits are threshold (gradual increase below the threshold), fatigue (repeat the response to exhaustion) and incompatible response (pair the cue with a competing response). A question that describes introducing a saddle a little at a time wants the threshold method, not the fatigue method. Guthrie's book is The Psychology of Learning (1935); his cat study was with Horton (1946). Hull: a mathematical theory of habit If Guthrie built the smallest theory of learning, Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) built the largest. Before turning to learning, Hull had written books on aptitude testing (1928) and on hypnosis and suggestibility (1933). At Yale University's Institute of Human Relations from 1929, he set out to make psychology as rigorous as Newton's physics, using the hypothetico-deductive method described in Chapter 2: state a set of postulates, deduce precise predictions from them, test the predictions in experiments and revise the postulates when they fail. Principles of Behavior (1943) presented sixteen postulates; Essentials of Behavior (1951) and A Behavior System (1952), published in the year of his death, revised them. In the 1940s and 1950s Hull was one of the most cited psychologists in experimental research, and the motivational side of his theory, drive reduction, is described in Chapter 10. Here we need its learning side. Hull began from survival. An organism has biological needs, for food, water, air and the avoidance of injury. A need produces a drive (D), an aroused state that energises behaviour. Whatever response reduces the drive is reinforced. This is drive-reduction theory , and for Hull it was the definition of reinforcement: a reinforcer is anything that reduces a drive (or, in later versions, the stimuli that accompany a drive). Primary reinforcement reduces a biological drive directly; secondary reinforcement comes from stimuli that have been associated with drive reduction, the click before the food or the coin before the meal. Each time a response is followed by reinforcement in the presence of a stimulus, the connection between them is strengthened. Hull called the strength of this learned connection habit strength , written S H R . Habit strength grows with the number of reinforced trials, and it grows in a particular way: each reinforcement adds a fixed fraction of the habit strength still to be gained. The early trials therefore add a great deal and the later ones less and less, which is why Hull's theory predicts the negatively accelerated learning curve you saw in Figure 6.3. Once formed, habit strength is permanent; it can be opposed by inhibition, but never unlearned. Habit alone does not produce behaviour. A rat that knows the maze perfectly but has just eaten sits in the start box. Hull therefore distinguished the learned connection from the tendency to act on it, which he called reaction potential ( S E R ). In 1943 the relation was a simple product: S E R = S H R × D The multiplication sign is the heart of the theory. If habit strength is zero (the rat has never been trained), there is no response however hungry the rat is; if drive is zero (the rat is satiated), there is no response however well it is trained. Push numbers through it. A rat with habit strength 0.8 (on a scale from 0 to 1) and moderate hunger (D = 0.5) has a reaction potential of 0.4; double its hunger to D = 1.0 and the reaction potential doubles to 0.8, though it has learned nothing new; feed it to satiation (D = 0) and the reaction potential falls to zero, though it has forgotten nothing. The experiments of the 1940s forced additions. Crespi's rats (Section 6.6) changed their running speed abruptly when the size of the reward changed, far too quickly for habit strength to have changed, so Hull added incentive motivation (K), the motivating effect of the size and quality of the reward. He added stimulus-intensity dynamism (V), the fact that a stronger stimulus evokes a learned response more readily, and he subtracted two kinds of inhibition. In its final form: Effective reaction potential = ( S H R × D × K × V) − (I R + S I R ) Some versions also include J, a factor for delay of reinforcement (Chapter 10, Table 10.4, lists all the symbols). Two last refinements made the theory probabilistic. The effective reaction potential fluctuates randomly from moment to moment (oscillation, S O R ), which is why a well-trained rat sometimes fails to respond; and it must exceed a reaction threshold ( S L R ) before any response occurs. Hull then measured reaction potential by four observable outcomes: how quickly the response begins (latency), how vigorous it is (amplitude), how likely it is, and how many unreinforced trials it takes to extinguish. The two inhibition terms deserve a closer look, because they explain three phenomena at once. Every response, Hull proposed, produces reactive inhibition (I R ), a fatigue-like negative drive that builds up with repeated responding and dissipates with rest. Resting reduces this fatigue-like drive, and drive reduction is reinforcing, so the response of not responding becomes conditioned to the situation; this learned habit of not responding is conditioned inhibition ( S I R ). During extinction, with no reinforcement to offset them, the two kinds of inhibition accumulate until they cancel the reaction potential and responding stops. After a rest, reactive inhibition dissipates but conditioned inhibition remains, so the response returns, but only partly: spontaneous recovery. And because reactive inhibition piles up when trials are crowded together and dissipates when they are spaced out, Hull's theory predicts that distributed practice should beat massed practice and that performance should improve after a rest, two findings you will meet in Section 6.10. Hull's answers to purpose, and Spence's revisions Tolman's rats seemed to act with purpose, to expect food and to know where it was. Hull set out to explain purpose without leaving S-R theory, and three of his concepts are still examined. The goal gradient hypothesis (1932) states that the strength of a response increases the nearer it is to the goal. Rats run faster as they approach the goal box, and in a complex maze they eliminate the blind alleys nearest the goal first and those nearest the start last. The effect is not confined to rats. In a 2006 study by Ran Kivetz and colleagues, customers given a coffee-shop loyalty card bought coffee more and more often as they approached the free cup, an everyday goal gradient. The fractional anticipatory goal response (r G ) was Hull's mechanical version of an expectation. When a hungry rat eats in the goal box, its eating (licking, chewing, salivating) is the goal response. Small fragments of that response become classically conditioned to the stimuli of the maze leading up to the goal, so that the rat makes tiny anticipatory licking and chewing movements as it runs. These fractional responses produce their own internal stimuli (s G ), which guide the rat towards the goal. What Tolman called an expectancy of food, Hull called an r G -s G mechanism. The habit-family hierarchy explained flexibility. Any goal can usually be reached by several routes, and each route has its own habit strength, so they form a family ranked from strongest to weakest. If the preferred route is blocked, the organism takes the next one in the hierarchy. Where Tolman saw a rat consulting a cognitive map, Hull saw a family of habits of different strengths. Hull's most important student, Kenneth Wartinbee Spence (1907 to 1967) of the University of Iowa, refined the system so thoroughly that it is often called Hull-Spence theory. It was Spence who argued for incentive motivation and explained it through the fractional anticipatory goal response: a bigger reward produces a bigger r G , and so more vigour. In his later work Spence concluded that habit strength grows with the number of trials whether or not they are reinforced, and that reinforcement works through incentive. His version was, in effect, a contiguity theory of learning combined with a reinforcement theory of performance. In 1937 Spence also gave a celebrated S-R explanation of transposition, the Gestalt psychologists' favourite evidence for relational learning (Section 6.10). Clinical link If drive multiplies habit, then anxious people, whose general level of drive is high, should condition faster on simple tasks. To test this, Janet Taylor Spence (1923 to 2015), who trained in Spence's laboratory at Iowa and later married him, selected items from the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory to build the Taylor Manifest Anxiety Scale (1953). High scorers did acquire conditioned eyeblinks faster than low scorers. On complex tasks with many competing responses, however, high drive strengthened the wrong responses too, and anxious participants did worse. The finding helps explain why a moderately anxious student may race through simple revision but freeze on a hard, unfamiliar problem (the Yerkes-Dodson law, Chapter 10, makes a related point). How should Hull be judged? His system collapsed under its own weight. Each new finding required a new constant or a new term, and the predictions became so hedged that they could hardly be tested. Drive reduction itself failed as a universal account of reinforcement: rats learned to run for saccharin, which reduces no need, and monkeys worked for the chance to look out of a window (Chapter 10). Latent learning showed that learning can occur without reinforcement at all. Yet Hull's influence was enormous. He showed what a precise, testable theory of behaviour would look like; his intervening variables (habit, drive, incentive) became the common language of motivation research; and his students and colleagues, among them Spence, Neal Miller, John Dollard, Hobart Mowrer, Carl Hovland and Robert Sears, carried his ideas into personality, social psychology, attitude change and therapy. Wolpe's reciprocal inhibition was framed in Hull's terms, and Dollard and Miller's translation of Freud (Section 6.8) used his vocabulary of drive, cue, response and reward. Exam trap Drive-reduction theory is Hull's ( Principles of Behavior , 1943); the word "drive" was introduced earlier by Woodworth (1918), and homeostasis is Cannon's term. Hull's method was hypothetico-deductive . In S E R = S H R × D, E is reaction potential, H habit strength, D drive; K (incentive motivation) was added after Crespi's contrast effects, and V is stimulus-intensity dynamism. Reactive inhibition is Hull's explanation of why spaced practice beats massed practice. The goal gradient and the fractional anticipatory goal response are Hull's; the cognitive map is Tolman's. And the "reciprocal causation model" belongs to Bandura's social cognitive theory, not to drive-reduction theory. Estes: stimulus sampling theory You have already met William Kaye Estes twice: in 1941, with Skinner, he invented the conditioned-suppression measure of fear (Section 6.4), and in 1944 he showed that punishment suppresses a response without erasing it (Section 6.5). Estes had taken his doctorate under Skinner at the University of Minnesota, but in 1950, in a paper titled "Toward a statistical theory of learning", he did something his teacher would never have done. He built a mathematical model of learning, and he built it on Guthrie's ideas. Estes's stimulus sampling theory starts by treating any stimulus situation, such as a Skinner box or a classroom, as a large population of small stimulus elements: a particular sound, a patch of light, a smell, a sensation from the body. On any trial the learner samples, or notices, only a fraction of these elements, a fraction Estes called θ (theta). Following Guthrie, each sampled element becomes connected, completely and at once, to whatever response occurs on that trial (an all-or-none, one-trial process). The probability that the learner will make the response on the next trial is simply the proportion of all the elements in the situation that are now connected to it. From these assumptions Estes derived a learning curve. If P 1 is the probability of the response on the first trial, then on trial n: P n = 1 − (1 − P 1 )(1 − θ) n − 1 Work through it with θ = 0.2 and a response that never occurs at first (P 1 = 0). On trial 2 the probability is 1 − 0.8 = 0.20; on trial 3, 1 − 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.36; on trial 4, 1 − 0.512 = 0.49; on trial 5, about 0.59. Each trial conditions a fifth of the elements not yet conditioned, so the gains shrink as fewer unconditioned elements remain. The result is the familiar negatively accelerated curve, yet every individual element was conditioned in a single step. Notice the family resemblance: Hull's habit strength, Estes's θ and the αβ of the Rescorla-Wagner model (Section 6.4) all describe learning as the capture of a constant fraction of what is still to be learned. The theory explained other phenomena with the same economy. Generalisation occurs because two similar situations share many elements, so a response conditioned to one is partly conditioned to the other. Spontaneous recovery, Estes argued in 1955, occurs because the elements available to the learner fluctuate from session to session: elements that were conditioned during acquisition but happened not to be sampled during extinction drift back into the available set after a rest, carrying the response with them. And the theory predicted a striking pattern called probability matching . Ask people to guess, trial after trial, whether a light will come on, when in fact it comes on at random on 70 per cent of trials, and most of them end up predicting "on" on about 70 per cent of trials, rather than on every trial, which would maximise their score. The first hints of this pattern had appeared in a 1939 experiment by Lloyd Humphreys, and Estes's model predicted it. Stimulus sampling theory, together with the linear models of Robert R. Bush and Frederick Mosteller , launched mathematical learning theory. Estes himself later moved into cognitive psychology, building models of memory and categorisation, and he is one of the few learning theorists whose work bridges the behaviourist and cognitive eras. He made one further point that every reader of learning curves should remember. In 1956 he showed that a curve averaged over many learners can look smooth and gradual even when each individual learner improves in sudden jumps (Section 6.10). Exam trap Stimulus sampling theory is Estes's (1950), a statistical (mathematical) learning theory that formalised Guthrie's contiguity and one-trial ideas; it is not Skinner's. Its key quantity, θ, is the proportion of stimulus elements sampled on a trial. Estes is also examined for conditioned suppression (with Skinner, 1941) and for showing that punishment suppresses rather than eliminates responding (1944). Mowrer: fear, hope and the neurotic paradox Orval Hobart Mowrer, whose two-factor theory of avoidance you met in Section 6.5, was another product of Hull's Yale institute, and his career moved through almost every question in this chapter. His first lasting contribution was practical. In 1938, with his wife Willie Mae Mowrer , he described the bell-and-pad method for treating nocturnal enuresis (bed-wetting). The child sleeps on a pad that completes an electrical circuit at the first drop of urine and rings a bell. In classical-conditioning terms the bell is a UCS that produces waking and contraction of the bladder sphincter (the UCR); the sensations of a full bladder, which immediately precede the bell, are the CS. After a number of pairings the full bladder alone wakes the child or inhibits urination. (Some writers describe the later stages as avoidance learning, since the child learns to prevent the bell.) The enuresis alarm descended from it is still one of the most effective treatments available. In 1947 Mowrer proposed that there are two fundamentally different kinds of learning. Sign learning is classical conditioning: signs (stimuli) become attached to emotional responses, especially fear, which are involuntary and governed by the autonomic nervous system. Solution learning is instrumental learning: skeletal, voluntary responses that solve problems are strengthened because they reduce a drive. Two-factor theory is the combination of the two, fear learned by sign learning and avoidance learned by solution learning. A year later Mowrer used the theory to attack what he called the neurotic paradox : why do people go on behaving in ways that are obviously self-defeating, avoiding what they fear at the cost of jobs, friendships and happiness? A simple law of effect would predict that behaviour with bad consequences should die out. Mowrer's answer was timing. The avoidance response brings immediate relief from anxiety, while its costs are delayed and diffuse, and immediate consequences control behaviour far more strongly than delayed ones. Avoidance also prevents extinction, because the person never stays in the feared situation long enough to discover that nothing terrible happens. The man who leaves every party after ten minutes feels better each time he leaves, and never learns that he could have survived the evening. Two-factor theory was soon challenged. Solomon's dogs (Section 6.5) went on jumping long after they showed any outward signs of fear, which raised the question of what was being reduced. In 1966 Richard Herrnstein and Philip Hineline showed that rats would learn to press a lever that merely lowered the overall frequency of shocks arriving at unpredictable moments, with no warning signal to be afraid of; the avoidance response seemed to be reinforced directly by the reduction in shock. And in 1970 Robert Bolles pointed out that rats learn some avoidance responses in a trial or two (running away, jumping out of a box) but need hundreds of trials to learn others (pressing a lever). Avoidance is learned quickly, Bolles argued, only when the required response is one of the animal's species-specific defence reactions : fleeing, freezing or fighting. Biology constrains avoidance learning just as it constrains taste aversion and operant training. Mowrer, meanwhile, had changed his mind. In Learning Theory and Behavior (1960) he concluded that all learning is sign learning. What organisms learn, he now argued, is to attach emotions to stimuli, including the stimuli produced by their own movements. Four emotions do all the work, depending on whether a stimulus signals the beginning or the end of something painful or something pleasant (Table 6.12). When the feedback from a response has become attached to hope, the organism continues the response; when it has become attached to fear, the organism stops. Even reward and punishment, on this view, work through classically conditioned emotions. Table 6.12 Mowrer's four emotions (1960): what a stimulus comes to signal decides what it comes to make us feel. The stimulus signals Painful event Pleasant event (reward) Onset (it is coming) Fear Hope Termination (it is ending or withheld) Relief Disappointment Mowrer applied learning theory to language too. He suggested that a talking bird, or a babbling infant, first reproduces the sounds of its caregiver's voice because those sounds have been paired with food and comfort and so have become secondary reinforcers; producing them is then self-rewarding. He called this the "autism theory" of speech, using "autism" in its old sense of self (it has nothing to do with autism spectrum disorder). Later still he broke sharply with Freud, arguing that neurotic suffering comes from real guilt over real wrongdoing rather than from repressed impulses, and he founded the confession-based integrity groups of the 1960s (Clinical Psychology book). Exam trap "Two-factor theory" in a learning question is Mowrer's theory of avoidance (1947): classical conditioning of fear plus operant (negative) reinforcement of the avoidance response by fear reduction. It is not Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory of emotion (Chapter 11) and not Herzberg's two-factor theory of work motivation. Sign learning versus solution learning is Mowrer's distinction; but "sign learning theory" is also a name for Tolman's expectancy theory (Section 6.7), in which "signs" are cues to what leads to what. Read the options. The bell-and-pad for enuresis is Mowrer and Mowrer (1938), a classical-conditioning treatment. The neurotic paradox (1948) is Mowrer's question of why self-defeating avoidance persists. Gagné: the conditions of learning The theorists so far wanted one theory for all learning. Robert Mills Gagné (1916 to 2002), an American educational psychologist who had spent much of the 1940s and 1950s in military research on training pilots and technicians, drew the opposite conclusion. In The Conditions of Learning (1965) he argued that there is not one kind of learning but several, and that each requires its own conditions: internal conditions (what the learner must already know or be able to do) and external conditions (what the teacher or the situation must provide). His central claim was that the kinds of learning form a hierarchy. Each type builds on the ones below it, so that a higher type cannot be learned until its prerequisites have been mastered, a view he called cumulative learning. Table 6.13 shows the eight types in order, from the simplest to the most complex. Table 6.13 Gagné's eight types of learning (1965), from simplest to most complex. Type What is learned Example Echoes 1 Signal learning An involuntary, emotional response to a signal A child flinches at the sight of the syringe Pavlov 2 Stimulus-response learning A precise voluntary response to a stimulus, through reinforcement A puppy learns to sit when told "sit" Thorndike, Skinner 3 Chaining A sequence of motor S-R links Starting a scooter: key, choke, kick Skinner's chaining 4 Verbal association Chains of words Learning that "neeru" means water; reciting tables Verbal learning 5 Multiple discrimination Different responses to many similar stimuli Telling each of thirty pupils apart by name Discrimination 6 Concept learning A common response to a class of objects "Triangle", "mammal" Concept formation (6.7) 7 Principle (rule) learning A chain of two or more concepts "Metals expand when heated" Rules 8 Problem solving Combining principles into a new, higher-order principle Freeing a tight steel lid by running hot water over it Thinking (Chapter 8) The hierarchy has a practical message for teachers. If a pupil cannot solve problems about expanding metals, the fault may lie further down: perhaps he never learned the principle, or never mastered the concepts of "metal" and "expansion" from which it is built. Diagnose the missing prerequisite and teach it first. In later editions of the book Gagné recast his scheme as five varieties of learned capability, or learning outcomes: verbal information (knowing that), intellectual skills (knowing how, which include discriminations, concepts, rules and higher-order rules), cognitive strategies (ways of managing one's own learning and thinking), motor skills and attitudes. He also proposed nine "events of instruction" that a good lesson should contain, in order: gain the learners' attention; tell them the objective; stimulate recall of prerequisite learning; present the material; provide learning guidance; elicit performance; provide feedback; assess performance; and enhance retention and transfer. Several of these, feedback and transfer especially, are the subject of Section 6.10. Gagné also distinguished lateral from vertical transfer, a distinction you will meet there. Exam trap Gagné's eight types run signal learning, stimulus-response learning, chaining, verbal association, multiple discrimination, concept learning, principle (rule) learning, problem solving . Signal learning (the lowest) is classical conditioning; problem solving is the highest. Concept learning comes before principle learning, because principles are chains of concepts. Do not mix the eight types with his five learning outcomes (verbal information, intellectual skills, cognitive strategies, motor skills, attitudes) or his nine events of instruction. The book is The Conditions of Learning (1965). The theories side by side By the 1960s the age of grand theories was over. The questions they had argued about did not go away; they were absorbed into cognitive psychology, which took Tolman's side on what is learned, and into the neuroscience of learning, which found that both S-R habits and cognitive maps exist, in different brain systems (Chapter 7 and the Physiological Psychology book). Constructivism is the view that learners do not passively receive knowledge or have responses stamped in, but actively construct their own understanding by fitting new experience to what they already know and revising what they know when it does not fit. Jean Piaget's theory of cognitive development, Lev Vygotsky's account of learning through social interaction, and Jerome Bruner's discovery learning are its main forms (Developmental Psychology book). Constructivist theories share Tolman's and Köhler's conviction that what is learned is knowledge, and they share Bandura's conviction that the learner is an agent, not a passive recipient. Two-factor theory of avoidance : Mowrer. Eight types of learning : Gagné. Reciprocal causation (reciprocal determinism) : Bandura's social cognitive theory, not two-factor theory, drive-reduction theory or constructivist theory. Constructivism : Piaget, Vygotsky and Bruner. The law of effect is Thorndike's and the matching law Herrnstein's; Watson's own laws of learning were frequency and recency . 6.10 Learning in Practice Lower yield · 3 Qs The theories in this chapter were built in laboratories, with rats, pigeons, dogs and cats. But the people who most need to know about learning are not in laboratories. A student with four weeks left before an entrance examination, a nursing trainee learning to give injections, a child learning to read, a batsman remodelling his technique: all of them face the same practical questions. How quickly will I improve, and why have I stopped improving? How much should I practise, and in one long session or many short ones? Should I learn the whole thing at once or in parts? How much does feedback matter? Will what I learn here help me there? Can a machine teach me? Psychologists have been studying these questions since the 1890s, and the answers are among the most useful in this book. Learning curves A learning curve is a graph of performance plotted against the amount of practice, measured in trials, sessions or time. Ebbinghaus's curves of 1885 (Chapter 7) and Thorndike's escape-time curves for his cats (Section 6.5) were among the first. Performance can be measured in many ways: correct responses, words typed per minute, runs scored, or, the other way up, errors made and seconds taken. When errors or time are plotted, a curve of improvement falls instead of rising, as in Tolman's maze data (Figure 6.5). What matters is the shape of the improvement, not which way the line slopes. Three shapes are distinguished (Figure 6.7, left). A negatively accelerated curve (a decelerating curve) rises steeply at first and then more and more slowly, levelling off as performance approaches its limit. Each unit of practice adds less than the one before, a law of diminishing returns. This is the most common shape, especially for simple tasks and for learners who already have the relevant background. Someone learning to type sees huge gains in the first week and tiny ones in the tenth. You have already met three explanations of the shape: in Hull's theory, Estes's theory and the Rescorla-Wagner model, each trial captures a constant fraction of what remains to be learned, and as less remains, each gain shrinks. There is also a simpler reason: learners tend to master the easy parts of a task first, leaving the hard parts for later. A positively accelerated curve (an accelerating curve) does the opposite: progress is slow at first and then speeds up. It appears when a task is difficult or unfamiliar and the learner must first acquire basic components before the real gains can come. An adult beginning a new language spends weeks on sounds and vocabulary with little to show for it; once enough words and grammar are in place, comprehension suddenly takes off. Positively accelerated curves are common in the early stages of complex learning and in learners with little prior knowledge. An S-shaped curve (a sigmoid curve) combines the two: a slow start while the learner gets oriented, a rapid middle phase, and a slowing as performance nears its limit. It is the typical curve when a complex skill, such as driving a car or playing the tabla, is learned from scratch and followed to mastery. Straight-line (linear) curves, in which every trial adds the same amount, are rare. One caution, which comes from William Estes (Section 6.9). In 1956 he showed that a curve averaged over many learners can look smooth and gradual even when each individual learner improves in sudden jumps. If ten students each have their "aha" at a different session, the average of their scores rises gently, though none of them improved gently. A smooth curve in a textbook is therefore not proof that each learner improved bit by bit; Köhler's chimpanzees, plotted one at a time, would have produced steps. Right: a stylised curve with a plateau, after Bryan and Harter's telegraphers. Improvement stalls while letter-by-letter habits become automatic, then resumes as word habits form; a plateau is a pause in the middle of learning, not the final physiological limit. Plateaus and the limits of improvement In the 1890s, at Indiana University, William Lowe Bryan (1860 to 1955) and Noble Harter studied people learning the telegraphic Morse code, measuring each week how many letters per minute they could send and receive. Their reports (1897 and 1899) contain the most famous learning curves in the history of psychology. Sending improved smoothly. Receiving improved rapidly for some weeks, then stopped improving for a long stretch, sometimes for several weeks, and then began to rise again, eventually to the level of an expert operator (Figure 6.7, right). Such a flat stretch in the middle of a learning curve, preceded and followed by improvement, is called a plateau . Bryan and Harter explained it by a hierarchy of habits . A beginner receives code letter by letter. Only when letter habits have become automatic can the learner's attention move on to grasping whole words as units, and later whole phrases. The plateau is the period during which the lower-order habits are being perfected but are not yet automatic enough to free attention for the higher-order ones. When word habits take over, improvement resumes. Later writers listed several other causes of plateaus, which suggest their remedies: A shift from a lower-order to a higher-order method of working, as in the telegraphers, during which neither method is yet efficient. Loss of motivation, boredom or fatigue after the excitement of early rapid progress has worn off. Faulty methods or bad habits that limit performance until they are corrected, such as typing with two fingers. A particularly difficult stage of the task, or a period in which recently learned material is being consolidated. Plateaus can therefore often be shortened: by rest, by changing the method of practice, by setting new goals, by giving precise feedback, and by encouraging the learner, who may be on the verge of a breakthrough without knowing it. They should not be overstated, though. When later researchers looked again at telegraphy and other skills, many found no plateau at all, and in 1958 Fred Keller titled his review of the evidence "The phantom plateau". A plateau is common but not inevitable. A plateau must also be distinguished from the physiological limit , the final ceiling of performance set by the limits of the body and nervous system, beyond which no amount of practice brings improvement. A plateau is temporary and in the middle of the curve; the physiological limit is permanent and at the end. In practice, most people stop practising long before they reach their physiological limit; what they reach is the level that satisfies them. Exam trap Negatively accelerated means rapid early gains and slowing later (the commonest curve); positively accelerated means slow early gains and faster later; S-shaped combines them. A plateau is a temporary flat period of no apparent progress in the middle of learning (Bryan and Harter, telegraphy, 1897 and 1899), explained by a hierarchy of habits ; it is not the physiological limit (the final ceiling), not extinction (the weakening of a response when reinforcement stops) and not forgetting. Do not confuse a learning plateau with the plateau phase of Masters and Johnson's sexual response cycle (Physiological Psychology book). From clumsy to automatic: the stages of skill learning Bryan and Harter's telegraphers were acquiring a skill, and the course of skill learning in general was described by Paul Fitts (1912 to 1965) and Michael Posner (born 1936) in Human Performance (1967). They proposed three stages. In the cognitive stage the learner works out what to do, often talking himself through it ("clutch in, first gear, release slowly"); performance is slow, effortful, inconsistent and full of errors, and it needs all of his attention. In the associative stage the components are linked into smooth sequences, errors fall, and the learner begins to notice and correct his own mistakes. In the autonomous stage the skill runs almost automatically: it is fast, accurate and consistent, needs little attention, and leaves the mind free for other things, so that an experienced rider can weave a scooter through Mysuru traffic while carrying on a conversation. The cost of automaticity is that the expert often cannot say how she does what she does, and finds bad habits hard to change. The stages map onto brain systems described in the Physiological Psychology book. Early, effortful learning depends heavily on the prefrontal cortex. As a skill becomes automatic, control shifts to systems for procedural learning: the cerebellum, which supports error correction and the fine coordination of movement, and the basal ganglia, which support the selection of actions and the formation of habits (procedural memory is in Chapter 7). Overlearning When have you learned something? A natural answer is: when you can do it once without error. Overlearning is practice that continues beyond that point. The classic study was published in 1929 by William C. F. Krueger . Participants learned lists of single-syllable nouns until they could recite a list once without error. Some stopped there; others continued for half as many trials again as they had needed (50 per cent overlearning), or for as many trials again (100 per cent overlearning). Retention was tested after intervals of up to 28 days. Fifty per cent overlearning produced a clear improvement in retention at every interval. Doubling the extra practice to 100 per cent produced a further, smaller gain, so that the benefit per extra trial fell, another example of diminishing returns. Push a case through it. If you need 12 readings to recite a 20-line poem for the first time, 50 per cent overlearning means 6 more readings, and 100 per cent overlearning means 12 more. The first 6 extra readings are well worth the time; the next 6 are worth less. Overlearned material resists forgetting, resists interference from later learning, and, importantly for anyone who has to perform under pressure, resists disruption by stress and anxiety. This is why airline pilots, surgeons and emergency teams drill procedures they already know, and why a dancer rehearses an item long after she can perform it correctly. (Ebbinghaus's savings method, which first revealed the benefits of extra repetitions, is in Chapter 7.) Massed versus distributed practice Suppose you have twenty hours to give to a subject. You could spend them in one long weekend, or as ten two-hour sessions spread over a fortnight. In massed practice , practice sessions are crowded together with little or no rest between them; in distributed practice (spaced practice), the same amount of practice is spread out over time with rest intervals. For both verbal learning and motor skills, distributed practice usually produces better learning and, above all, better long-term retention. The advantage is called the spacing effect, and it is one of the most reliable findings in all of psychology; a 2006 review by Nicholas J. Cepeda and colleagues analysed several hundred experiments on it. Ebbinghaus was the first to show it, in 1885. Twelve years later Adolf Jost stated what is still called Jost's law (1897): if two associations are equally strong but of different ages, a further repetition strengthens the older one more, and the older one is forgotten more slowly. Spaced repetitions, which give each association time to age between repetitions, therefore gain more from each repetition than massed ones. A striking applied study came from Alan Baddeley and D. J. A. Longman in 1978. British postal workers learning to type postcodes on a new keyboard were trained in one or two daily sessions lasting one or two hours each. Those given a single one-hour session a day learned the keyboard in fewer total hours of practice than those on the more massed schedules, though it took them more days; and, interestingly, the workers preferred the massed schedules, which felt more productive. Why does spacing help? Hull's answer was reactive inhibition (Section 6.9): a fatigue-like inhibition builds up when responses are crowded together and dissipates during rest. Hull's theory also explains reminiscence , the improvement in performance after a rest with no further practice, which Philip Boswood Ballard reported in 1913 when schoolchildren recalled more of a poem two or three days after learning it than immediately afterwards. In motor skills, reminiscence is often seen when a learner returns to massed practice after a break and performs better than before the break. Other explanations stress memory: spaced sessions allow consolidation, they encode the material in more varied contexts, and they force effortful retrieval at each new session, a "desirable difficulty" in Robert A. Bjork 's phrase, which strengthens memory more than easy repetition does. Massed practice is not always worse. It is efficient for short, simple tasks; for tasks that require a long warm-up before useful work can begin; and for problems whose solution depends on keeping the whole problem in mind at once, which a break would interrupt. Cramming the night before can also raise performance the next morning. What massed practice does badly is long-term retention: the crammed material is largely gone a month later. Exam trap Overlearning is practice beyond the first errorless performance (Krueger, 1929: 50 per cent overlearning clearly helps; 100 per cent adds less), not learning so much that performance suffers. Distributed (spaced) practice generally beats massed practice , especially for long-term retention; Hull's explanation is reactive inhibition . Reminiscence (Ballard, 1913) is improvement after rest without practice; it is not spontaneous recovery, which is the return of an extinguished conditioned response. Jost's law (1897) says a repetition benefits an older association more than a newer one of equal strength. Whole versus part learning You have to learn a 40-line poem for a recitation, or a long Carnatic composition, or a new bowling action. Should you work through the whole thing each time, or break it into parts? In the whole method , the material is practised as a single unit from beginning to end on every trial. In the part method , it is divided into sections, each section is learned separately, and the sections are then joined. A compromise, the progressive part method , learns the first part, then the first and second together, then the first three, and so on, so that the joins are practised as the learning proceeds. Studies from the early 1900s onwards found that neither method always wins; the answer depends on the material and the learner. The whole method tends to be better when the material is meaningful, well organised and of moderate length, so that its unity helps (a poem with a clear story); when the learner is older, more able and well motivated; and when practice is distributed. It avoids the main weakness of the part method, which is that the parts must later be linked, and the learner tends to stumble at the junctions. The part method tends to be better when the material is very long, difficult or made of loosely connected units (a list of dates, the bones of the hand); and for younger or less able learners. It also gives an early sense of success, which sustains motivation, whereas with the whole method progress may be invisible for a long time. The same principle applies to motor skills. A highly integrated movement, in which each component depends on the others, such as a bowling action, a golf swing or a swimming stroke, is usually best practised whole, perhaps slowed down, because practising its pieces separately destroys their timing. A skill made of fairly independent components, such as a dance with distinct sections or the separate checks of a pre-flight routine, can be practised in parts. Many teachers use a whole-part-whole sequence: show and attempt the whole, practise the difficult parts, then put the whole together again. Exam trap There is no single "best" method. Whole learning favours short or moderate, meaningful, unified material and mature, able learners; part learning favours long, difficult, unconnected material and younger learners; the progressive part method adds each new part to those already learned. Do not confuse whole and part learning (how material is divided for practice) with the whole-report and partial-report methods of Sperling's sensory-memory experiments (Chapter 7). Feedback and goals You saw in Section 6.5 that Thorndike's blindfolded participants, drawing line after line and trying to make each one three inches long, did not improve at all when they were never told how close they had come. Practice alone, without information about its results, taught them nothing. Knowledge of results (KR) is information given to the learner about the outcome of his or her performance; in everyday language it is feedback. In 1932 Margery Trowbridge and Hulsey Cason repeated the line-drawing task with groups that received different kinds of feedback after each line: none, an irrelevant nonsense syllable, a simple "right" or "wrong", or the exact size and direction of the error. The group given no feedback did not improve; the "right or wrong" group improved; the group told exactly how far off they were improved most. Research since then has added several practical rules. Feedback works best when it is precise rather than vague ("two centimetres too long" beats "wrong"), and when it arrives soon after the performance, while the learner can still relate it to what he did. Feedback after every single trial helps performance during practice, but learners who receive it too often can come to depend on it and perform worse when it is withdrawn, so skilled coaches give frequent feedback early and gradually reduce it. Teachers of motor skills distinguish knowledge of results, which concerns the outcome (the ball went for four), from knowledge of performance, which concerns the movement itself (your front elbow dropped). Feedback can also come from the task itself (intrinsic feedback, the feel of a clean strike) or from an outside source (extrinsic feedback, the coach's comment). Feedback works in two ways at once: it is information, telling the learner what to change, and it is a reinforcer and motivator, telling him that his efforts are paying off. Biofeedback (Section 6.6) and programmed instruction (below) are both built on it. Feedback has a natural partner. In 1968 the American psychologist Edwin Locke (born 1938) proposed, and in later work with Gary Latham demonstrated in hundreds of studies, that people who set specific, difficult but attainable goals perform better than people who are told to "do your best" or who set no goal at all. A specific goal directs attention to what matters, mobilises effort, increases persistence and prompts the learner to search for better strategies. Goals and feedback need each other: a goal without feedback leaves the learner unable to tell whether he is on course, and feedback without a goal gives him nothing to compare it with. So practice is most effective when the learner has a specific goal and receives knowledge of results about progress towards it. (Goal-setting theory as a theory of motivation is in Chapter 10; self-efficacy, which decides whether a person will commit to a hard goal, is in Section 6.8.) Exam trap "Learning always leads to efficacy, provided ..." The keyed answer is that the learner has a specific goal (Locke and Latham's goal setting). Ability, aptitude and knowledge help, but on their own they do not make practice purposeful. Knowledge of results is feedback about the outcome; without it, as in Thorndike's line drawing, practice brings no improvement. In a question about what social cognitive theory stresses in motivation, the answer is self-efficacy ; "goal difficulty" belongs to Locke's goal-setting theory, and "external rewards only" and "biological drives" to behaviourist and drive theories. Clinical link The principles of this section are the backbone of teaching children with learning difficulties. Effective programmes present material through several senses at once, a multisensory approach in which the child sees, hears, says and traces a word, as in the method Grace Fernald described in 1943 (visual, auditory, kinaesthetic and tactile, VAKT) and the Orton-Gillingham method; they break skills into small steps, give immediate feedback and reinforcement, and build in regular, spaced repetition and overlearning. Relying solely on written instructions, refusing accommodations, or drilling rote memorisation alone are the opposite of good practice. (Specific learning disorder itself is covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) Transfer of training Nobody learns anything for use in only one situation. You study psychology at a desk in order to use it in a hospital ward; a pilot trains in a simulator in order to fly an aircraft. Transfer of training is the effect that learning one task has on the learning or performance of another. It can take three forms. In positive transfer , earlier learning makes later learning easier: someone who rides a bicycle learns to ride a motorcycle faster, and a student who reads Hindi in the Devanagari script finds written Marathi easy. In negative transfer , earlier learning makes later learning harder, usually because the same stimuli now require different responses: a driver from India, where traffic keeps left, keeps reaching for the wrong side of the road in a country where traffic keeps right, and a driver who switches from a Japanese car to a European one switches on the wipers every time he means to signal a turn. In zero transfer , the first task has no effect on the second: learning to swim neither helps nor hinders learning Sanskrit grammar. Transfer is measured with a simple design. An experimental group learns Task A and then Task B; a control group learns only Task B (often after resting or doing an unrelated task for the same time). If the experimental group learns Task B faster than the control group, transfer was positive; if slower, negative; if the same, zero. Several special kinds of transfer have names. In bilateral transfer , a skill practised with one side of the body improves on the other: people who practise mirror drawing with the right hand also draw better with the left. Gagné distinguished lateral transfer , the application of learning to a new situation at the same level of complexity (calculating the area of the classroom floor after learning to calculate areas of rectangles in a textbook), from vertical transfer , in which lower-level learning makes higher-level learning possible (concepts making principles possible, as in his hierarchy). And Harlow's learning sets (Section 6.7) show non-specific transfer: learning how to learn a kind of problem carries over even when no specific content is shared. Why does transfer occur, and when? For two thousand years educators had a confident answer. According to the doctrine of formal discipline , based on the old faculty psychology, the mind consists of general faculties, such as memory, reasoning, attention and will, that are strengthened by exercise as muscles are. On this view it hardly matters what pupils study, so long as it is hard: Latin, Greek and geometry were taught not for their content but because they were supposed to train the mind for everything else. Three pieces of evidence demolished the doctrine. William James (1842 to 1910) tested it on himself and reported the result in The Principles of Psychology (1890). He learned 158 lines of Victor Hugo's poem Satyr , which took him 131 and five-sixths minutes. He then spent twenty-odd minutes a day for 38 days learning the first book of Milton's Paradise Lost , to train his "memory faculty". Finally he learned another 158 lines of Satyr . It took him 151 and a half minutes: if anything, he was slower. (James had a few friends repeat the experiment, with mixed results, but the point was made.) In 1901 Thorndike and Robert Sessions Woodworth trained people to estimate the areas of rectangles of certain sizes. Accuracy improved for the trained shapes and sizes, but transferred very little to estimating the areas of other shapes, or to related judgements of length and weight. In 1924 Thorndike compared the gains in reasoning test scores of more than 8,000 American high-school pupils over a school year according to the subjects they had studied. The subjects studied made very little difference: the gains that could be credited to Latin or geometry were tiny, and no larger than those from several "practical" subjects. The pupils who took the classical subjects did score higher, but mainly because they had been abler to begin with. In place of formal discipline, Thorndike proposed his identical elements theory : transfer occurs only to the extent that the two tasks share identical elements, whether facts, procedures, stimulus-response connections, attitudes or methods of work. Learning to drive a car transfers to driving a van because nearly all the elements are the same; studying Latin helps with learning Latin-derived English vocabulary but not with reasoning in general. The theory had a large practical effect: if transfer depends on shared content, schools should teach directly what pupils will need, and American curricula became more practical as a result. A second view emphasised understanding. In 1908 Charles Hubbard Judd (1873 to 1946) had two groups of boys throw darts at a target placed under about 12 inches of water. One group had first been taught the principle of refraction, how water bends light so that an object appears displaced; the other had not. Both groups did equally well at first, since practice was what counted. But when the target was moved to a depth of only 4 inches, the boys who understood refraction adjusted quickly, while the others were confused and made many errors. Judd's generalisation theory of transfer holds that what transfers is a general principle or rule that the learner has understood and can apply to new situations. Good teaching, on this view, emphasises principles rather than isolated facts. The Gestalt psychologists offered a third view through the phenomenon of transposition : the transfer of a learned relationship to new stimuli. In 1918 Köhler trained chickens to peck grain from the darker of two grey papers and not from the lighter. He then tested them with the darker grey and a new, still darker one. Most of the chickens pecked at the new paper, the one they had never been rewarded on, because it was now "the darker one". They had learned a relation, not a response to a particular grey. Spence's 1937 S-R reply showed that overlapping generalisation gradients of excitation and inhibition around the two training stimuli could produce the same choice, and the argument between relational and S-R accounts of transposition ran for decades. Finally, Charles Egerton Osgood (1916 to 1991) drew the findings together in 1949. Whether transfer is positive or negative, he showed, depends on the similarity of both the stimuli and the responses in the two tasks. When the stimuli are similar and the responses are the same, transfer is positive, and the more similar the stimuli the more positive it is. When the stimuli are similar but the responses must be different, especially opposite, transfer is negative, and the more similar the stimuli the worse the interference. The driver crossing from left-hand to right-hand traffic faces nearly identical stimuli (roads, junctions, cars) that demand opposite responses, the worst combination of all. Programmed instruction and teaching machines If learning depends on active responding, immediate feedback and practice at the learner's own pace, then an ordinary classroom, with forty pupils listening to one teacher and homework returned a week later, breaks almost every rule. Two psychologists tried to fix this with machines. The first was Sidney Leavitt Pressey (1888 to 1979) of Ohio State University. In the mid-1920s he built a small device, described in 1926, that presented a multiple-choice question in a window. The student pressed one of four keys. In its teaching mode the machine would not move on to the next question until the right key had been pressed, so that every error was corrected at once, and it kept count of errors; it could even be fitted with an attachment that dropped a sweet when the student reached a set score. Pressey predicted an "industrial revolution" in education. It did not come, and his teaching machine , a device that presents material, requires a response and gives immediate knowledge of results, was largely forgotten. The second was Skinner. On 11 November 1953 he visited his younger daughter's fourth-grade arithmetic class on a parents' day and was appalled: every child was being taught at the same pace, whatever his understanding, and no child learned whether an answer was right until long afterwards. From an operant point of view, the reinforcement was too rare and too delayed to shape anything. Within days he had built a prototype machine, and in "The science of learning and the art of teaching" (1954) and "Teaching machines" (1958) he set out the method that came to be called programmed instruction . Its principles are those of shaping, applied to knowledge. Small steps. The material is broken into a long sequence of small units called frames, each a little harder than the last. Active responding. The learner must respond to every frame, usually by writing a word or completing a sentence. Immediate knowledge of results. The correct answer is revealed at once, so that each right answer is reinforced and each wrong one corrected before it can be practised. Self-pacing. Each learner moves through the programme at his own speed. A low error rate. The steps are made so small, with prompts that are gradually faded, that the learner almost always succeeds; Skinner believed that errors are themselves practised and should be avoided. Skinner's design is the linear programme : every learner works through the same fixed sequence of frames, writing his own (constructed) answers. Around 1960 Norman Crowder developed the alternative branching programme (also called intrinsic programming). Each frame presents a larger amount of material followed by a multiple-choice question, and the answer the learner chooses decides where he goes next: a correct answer leads on to new material, while each wrong answer leads to a remedial frame that explains that particular mistake before returning him to the main line. Crowder treated errors as useful diagnostic information rather than something to be avoided; his programmes were often printed as "scrambled textbooks" in which the learner's answer sent him to a different page. Programmed instruction was a sensation in the early 1960s and then faded, partly because many programmes were poorly written and boring, with steps too small for able learners. But its principles survived and spread. Computer-assisted instruction, beginning with the PLATO system at the University of Illinois in 1960, put programmes on screens. Fred Simmons Keller (1899 to 1996), Skinner's friend since their graduate-student days, developed the Personalized System of Instruction in the 1960s, described in his 1968 paper "Good-bye, teacher...", in which university students work through a course in small written units at their own pace and must pass a test on each unit before moving on. The same logic underlies mastery learning and the adaptive learning applications on today's phones, which give small steps, instant feedback and spaced review. Programmed instruction works best for factual material and well-defined skills; it is less suited to teaching open-ended reasoning, discussion and creativity. Exam trap The first teaching machine was Pressey's (1920s); Skinner popularised teaching machines and programmed instruction (1954, 1958), based on operant conditioning (shaping, active responding and immediate reinforcement), not on classical conditioning, insight or observational learning. Linear programmes (fixed sequence, constructed answers, very few errors) are Skinner's; branching (intrinsic) programmes (multiple choice, remedial frames for wrong answers) are Crowder's .
