The case of Little Albert, revisited The chapter opened with three questions about Albert, and you can now answer all of them. How could a placid baby be taught to fear a white rat in a week? Because seven pairings of a neutral stimulus (the rat) with an intense unconditioned stimulus (the clang of the steel bar) were enough to make the rat a conditioned stimulus for fear, especially since the rat appeared just before the noise and was still in view when it came, the most effective delay arrangement. Seligman's idea of preparedness adds a further reason: a furry, moving animal is just the kind of stimulus human beings are prepared to fear, which may be why Elsie Bregman failed when she tried to condition infants to fear wooden blocks. Why did the fear spread to the rabbit, the dog, the sealskin coat, the cotton wool and the Santa Claus mask, but not to the blocks? Because of stimulus generalisation: the more a stimulus resembled the furry white rat, the more fear it produced, while the blocks shared nothing with it. And could the process be run backwards? Mary Cover Jones showed four years later, with Peter and the rabbit, that it could, by counterconditioning, and Wolpe turned her method into systematic desensitisation. A modern clinician would add two warnings. Had Albert been allowed to crawl away and feel relief, his avoidance would have been negatively reinforced, which, on Mowrer's two-factor theory, would have protected his fear from extinction. And even a fear that has been successfully extinguished can return through spontaneous recovery, reinstatement or renewal. One question Watson and Rayner never answered is who Albert was. In 2009 Hall P. Beck and his colleagues, after years of detective work in birth records and census returns, identified him as Douglas Merritte, the son of a wet nurse at the Harriet Lane Home, who died of hydrocephalus in 1925 at the age of six. In 2012 Alan J. Fridlund and colleagues went further and argued, from the film and from Douglas's medical records, that he had been neurologically impaired from birth, which would mean that Watson's "healthy" and "stolid" baby was nothing of the kind. Then, in 2014, Russell A. Powell , Nancy Digdon and their colleagues pointed to another candidate, William Albert Barger, the son of another wet nurse at the same home, whose age, weight and name fitted Watson's records better. Barger, known in later life as Albert Martin, lived until 2007, apparently without ever knowing that he might have been the most famous baby in psychology; a relative recalled that he had always disliked dogs, though nobody can say whether that had anything to do with a white rat and a steel bar. The debate is not settled. What is settled is the lesson of the experiment itself: fears can be learned, they spread to similar things, and they can be unlearned, which is the foundation on which the behaviour therapies described in this chapter were built. No ethics committee today would allow the experiment, and its story is one of the reasons such committees exist. Chapter summary 6.1 What learning is, and what it is not. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour, or in the potential for behaviour, that results from experience (Kimble). It differs from performance, which is what an organism actually does, and from changes caused by maturation, fatigue, drugs, injury or motivation. Fixed action patterns, triggered by sign stimuli (Tinbergen), are innate. The simplest, non-associative learning involves a single stimulus: habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated harmless stimulus, shown to be learning by its stimulus specificity, spontaneous recovery and dishabituation; sensitisation is an increase in responding after a strong stimulus. Kandel traced both to synaptic changes in Aplysia , and Fantz used habituation to study infant perception. Imprinting (Spalding, Lorenz) is rapid, largely irreversible, unrewarded learning confined to a critical period, peaking at 13 to 16 hours in Hess's ducklings. 6.2 Pavlov and the language of classical conditioning. Pavlov, a Nobel Prize-winning physiologist of digestion, noticed "psychic secretions" and from about 1897 studied them as conditioned reflexes; Twitmyer had seen the same thing in the knee jerk. In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus, paired repeatedly with an unconditioned stimulus (UCS) that produces an unconditioned response (UCR), becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) that produces a conditioned response (CR). The CR resembles the UCR but is not identical. Conditioning is strongest in delay (forward) conditioning, where the CS begins first and overlaps the UCS, weaker in trace conditioning, weak in simultaneous conditioning and weakest, often inhibitory, in backward conditioning. 6.3 The phenomena of classical conditioning. Acquisition produces a negatively accelerated rise in the CR; extinction, the omission of the UCS, weakens it. Spontaneous recovery, disinhibition, rapid reacquisition, reinstatement (Rescorla and Heth) and renewal (Bouton) show that extinction suppresses rather than erases learning, which is why fears relapse. Stimulus generalisation produces a generalisation gradient (Hovland); stimulus discrimination is learned by differential conditioning, and an impossible discrimination produced experimental neurosis in Shenger-Krestovnikova's dog. In higher-order conditioning an established CS acts as the UCS for a new stimulus; in sensory preconditioning (Brogden) two neutral stimuli are paired before one of them is conditioned. A conditioned inhibitor signals that the UCS will not occur. 6.4 Fear, prediction and preparedness. Watson and Rayner's Little Albert (1920) showed that fear can be classically conditioned and generalised; Mary Cover Jones's Peter (1924) showed that it can be removed by counterconditioning, the principle that Wolpe developed into reciprocal inhibition and systematic desensitisation (relaxation from Jacobson, a hierarchy rated in SUDS, then graded exposure). Flooding, implosion (Stampfl), aversion therapy, covert sensitisation (Cautela) and exposure and response prevention (Meyer) also rest on conditioning. Rescorla's contingency, Kamin's blocking, overshadowing and Lubow and Moore's latent inhibition showed that a CS must predict the UCS; the Rescorla-Wagner model (1972) formalised learning as driven by prediction error, which dopamine neurons signal (Schultz). The CS acts as a signal rather than a substitute (Siegel's compensatory responses). Garcia and Koelling's taste aversion (1966), learned in one trial and across long delays, refuted equipotentiality and led to Seligman's preparedness (1970), with applications in chemotherapy, wildlife management and advertising. 6.5 Thorndike, Skinner and the consequences of behaviour. Thorndike's cats in puzzle boxes learned by trial and error, and his law of effect (1911) states that satisfying consequences strengthen responses; his connectionism also included the laws of exercise and readiness, and he later abandoned the law of exercise. Skinner distinguished elicited respondent behaviour from emitted operant behaviour, studied it in the Skinner box with the cumulative recorder, and described the three-term contingency of discriminative stimulus, response and consequence. Reinforcement increases behaviour and punishment decreases it; "positive" adds a stimulus and "negative" removes one, so negative reinforcement is not punishment. Secondary and generalised reinforcers (Wolfe's chimpanzees) underlie the token economy (Ayllon and Azrin). Escape terminates and avoidance prevents an aversive stimulus, and Mowrer's two-factor theory explains avoidance and compulsions. Punishment (including time-out and response cost) suppresses rather than teaches and has side effects (Estes). Shaping reinforces successive approximations; chaining, prompting and fading build complex behaviour; extinction produces an extinction burst and a return to the operant level. 6.6 Schedules of reinforcement and other operant phenomena. Continuous reinforcement teaches fastest and extinguishes fastest; partial reinforcement produces the partial reinforcement extinction effect (Humphreys). Fixed-ratio schedules give high rates with post-reinforcement pauses, variable-ratio schedules the highest, steadiest rates and greatest resistance to extinction, fixed-interval schedules a scallop, and variable-interval schedules moderate, steady rates (Ferster and Skinner). Differential reinforcement (DRO, DRI, DRA, DRL, DRH) weakens problem behaviour without punishment. Premack showed that a more probable behaviour reinforces a less probable one. Accidental reinforcement produces superstitious behaviour (Skinner, 1948). Uncontrollable shock produces learned helplessness (Overmier, Seligman and Maier, 1967), a model of depression later reformulated in attributional terms. The Brelands' instinctive drift and Brown and Jenkins's autoshaping show biological limits on operant learning; Herrnstein's matching law describes choice; Crespi's contrast effects show that reward size affects motivation and performance; and biofeedback (Miller, Kegel) brings bodily processes under operant control. Classical and operant conditioning differ in what is associated and in the kind of behaviour involved, but constantly interact. 6.7 Cognitive learning. Tolman's purposive behaviourism held that animals learn expectancies and cognitive maps; in Tolman and Honzik's latent learning experiment (1930) rats rewarded only from day 11 immediately matched always-rewarded rats, showing that reinforcement affects performance rather than learning, and place learning and Tinklepaugh's monkey supported the idea of expectancy. Köhler's chimpanzees, Sultan above all, solved stick and box problems by insight, a sudden perceptual reorganisation accompanied by the "aha" experience, though Birch showed that insight depends on earlier experience. Harlow's monkeys formed learning sets, learning to learn, which reconcile trial-and-error and insight. Concepts are formed in the stages of observation, discrimination, generalisation and abstraction. 6.8 Observational learning. Miller and Dollard (1941) treated imitation as reinforced behaviour. Bandura's Bobo doll studies (1961, 1963, 1965) showed that children learn new aggressive acts simply by watching a live or filmed model, and that the model's consequences affect performance rather than learning. Observational learning requires attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation; reinforcement, direct or vicarious, governs only the last. Bandura's social cognitive theory added reciprocal determinism (person, behaviour and environment influencing one another), self-regulation and self-efficacy (1977), with four sources led by performance attainments. Rotter's separate social learning theory explains behaviour potential through expectancy and reinforcement value. 6.9 Other learning theorists. The grand theories, surveyed in Hilgard's Theories of Learning (1948), divided over whether learning consists of S-R connections or knowledge and whether it requires contiguity or reinforcement. Guthrie's contiguity theory held that learning is complete in one trial and that practice attaches acts to more stimuli; he proposed the threshold, fatigue and incompatible-response methods of breaking habits, and his cat studies with Horton were later reinterpreted as greeting behaviour. Hull's hypothetico-deductive theory made reinforcement equal to drive reduction and reaction potential equal to habit strength multiplied by drive, later with incentive motivation, stimulus-intensity dynamism and reactive and conditioned inhibition; his goal gradient, fractional anticipatory goal response and habit-family hierarchy were S-R answers to Tolman, and Spence extended the system. Estes's stimulus sampling theory (1950) gave learning a statistical form and predicted probability matching. Mowrer developed the bell-and-pad method, two-factor theory with its sign and solution learning, the neurotic paradox, and later a theory of fear, relief, hope and disappointment; Herrnstein and Hineline and Bolles challenged two-factor theory. Gagné's The Conditions of Learning (1965) arranged eight types of learning in a hierarchy from signal learning to problem solving. Constructivism (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner) sees learners as active builders of knowledge. 6.10 Learning in practice. Learning curves may be negatively accelerated (the commonest), positively accelerated or S-shaped, and group averages can hide sudden individual jumps (Estes). Bryan and Harter's telegraphers showed a plateau, explained by a hierarchy of habits; a plateau is temporary, unlike the physiological limit. Skills pass through cognitive, associative and autonomous stages (Fitts and Posner). Overlearning improves retention (Krueger, 1929). Distributed practice usually beats massed practice (Ebbinghaus, Jost, Baddeley and Longman), which Hull explained by reactive inhibition; reminiscence (Ballard) is improvement after rest. Whole learning suits meaningful, unified material and part learning long, difficult material. Knowledge of results is essential (Trowbridge and Cason), and specific, difficult goals improve performance (Locke and Latham). Transfer of training may be positive, negative or zero; formal discipline was refuted by James and Thorndike, and transfer has been explained by identical elements (Thorndike), generalisation of principles (Judd), transposition (Köhler) and the similarity of stimuli and responses (Osgood). Programmed instruction, from Pressey's teaching machine to Skinner's linear and Crowder's branching programmes and Keller's Personalized System of Instruction, applies shaping and immediate feedback to teaching. habituation is termed: (RML 2024) a Sensitisation b Stabilization c Inhabitation d Habitation ✓ Answer: (a) Sensitisation Habituation vs sensitisation (non-associative learning) The concept Habituation Habituation is a decrease in responding to a repeated, harmless stimulus. The opposite Sensitisation is an increase in responding, usually to many stimuli, after a strong or noxious one (Section 6.1). Exam tip Only sensitisation is a real learning term here; the other three options are not learning terms at all. Why the other options are wrong (b) Stabilization Not a learning term; a filler distractor with no meaning in learning theory. (c) Inhabitation Not a learning term; a sound-alike distractor built to look like habituation. (d) Habitation Not a learning term; a sound-alike distractor one syllable short of habituation. In Pavlov's experiment with dogs, the sound of the bell/metronome was the: (RML 2020) a operant stimulus after food was associated b neutral stimulus before the food was associated and conditioned stimulus after food was associated c unconditioned stimulus before the food was associated d conditioned stimulus before the food was associated and neutral stimulus after food was associated ✓ Answer: (b) neutral stimulus before the food was associated and conditioned stimulus after food was associated Pavlov, classical conditioning of salivation The concept Before pairing The metronome alone does not produce salivation, so it is a neutral stimulus . After pairing Once paired with food, it produces salivation on its own, so it is now a conditioned stimulus . Key note Food , not the bell, is the unconditioned stimulus . Why the other options are wrong (a) operant stimulus after food was associated "Operant stimulus" is not a term of classical conditioning ; the label borrows operant language. (c) unconditioned stimulus before the food was associated Food, not the bell, is the unconditioned stimulus ; before pairing the bell produces no salivation. (d) conditioned stimulus before the food was associated and neutral stimulus after food was associated Reverses the order : the bell is neutral first and becomes conditioned only after pairing. Which of the following is most effective in conditioning? (Amity 2023) a Backward Conditioning b Delayed Conditioning c Simultaneous Conditioning d Trace Conditioning ✓ Answer: (b) Delayed (delay) conditioning CS-UCS timing: delay conditioning The concept How it works In delay conditioning the CS begins first and is still present when the UCS arrives. Why it works best The CS serves as a warning that the UCS is coming, so it predicts it most clearly. Why the other options are wrong (a) Backward Conditioning Backward conditioning presents the UCS before the CS; it is the least effective and often makes the CS a signal of safety. (c) Simultaneous Conditioning Simultaneous conditioning starts CS and UCS together, so the CS gives no advance warning. (d) Trace Conditioning Trace conditioning leaves a gap between the CS and the UCS, so it is weaker. A child has learned to avoid a furry, black cat. However, she still plays with her grandmother's short-haired tabby. Her response demonstrates: (RML 2024) a Discrimination b Extinction c Successive approximation d Negative transfer ✓ Answer: (a) Discrimination Stimulus discrimination The concept What it is Discrimination is responding differently to similar stimuli. Applied here She avoids the furry black cat but still plays with the short-haired tabby, so her fear is limited to one kind of cat. Contrast Generalisation would be fearing every cat that resembles the black one. Why the other options are wrong (b) Extinction Extinction would mean the learned fear has faded, but her fear of the black cat has not gone. (c) Successive approximation Successive approximation is shaping , reinforcing closer and closer steps towards a target behaviour; nothing is being shaped here. (d) Negative transfer Negative transfer is earlier learning hindering new learning (Section 6.10), not a pattern of responding to similar stimuli. In reinforcement learning, the "prediction error" signal in the brain is primarily associated with: (JEMAS 2025) a Serotonin release b Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area c GABA inhibition d Acetylcholine release ✓ Answer: (b) Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area Schultz, dopamine reward prediction error The concept What Schultz found Schultz found that dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra fire to an unexpected reward. How it shifts With learning, the firing shifts to a cue that predicts the reward, and it dips when a predicted reward fails to arrive. The link That pattern is the prediction error of the Rescorla-Wagner model (Section 6.4). Why the other options are wrong (a) Serotonin release Serotonin is linked mainly to mood, sleep and appetite; it does not carry the prediction error signal. (c) GABA inhibition GABA is the brain's main inhibitory transmitter; it does not carry the prediction error signal. (d) Acetylcholine release Acetylcholine works at the neuromuscular junction and in attention and memory; it does not carry the prediction error signal. Taste aversion is an example of: (RML 2022) a Classical Conditioning b Second-order conditioning c Operant conditioning d Spurious association ✓ Answer: (a) Classical conditioning Classical conditioning: taste aversion (Garcia effect) The concept How it works The taste is the CS and the illness the UCS. Why it is special They are paired once , often hours apart, yet the aversion still forms; it is also called the Garcia effect . Why the other options are wrong (b) Second-order conditioning Second-order conditioning uses an established CS to condition a new one; no such CS is used here. (c) Operant conditioning Operant conditioning needs a response that is reinforced; no response is reinforced here. (d) Spurious association Spurious association is a statistical term, not a type of learning. Systematic desensitization technique is based upon the idea of: (IHBAS 2025) a Reciprocal inhibition b Law of effect c Habituation d Adaptation to stress ✓ Answer: (a) Reciprocal inhibition Wolpe, reciprocal inhibition The concept The idea Reciprocal inhibition : two incompatible responses cannot occur together, so a calm response suppresses anxiety. How Wolpe used it Wolpe paired each step of an anxiety hierarchy with relaxation, a response incompatible with anxiety (Section 6.4). Why the other options are wrong (b) Law of effect The law of effect is Thorndike 's operant principle, not the idea behind desensitisation. (c) Habituation Habituation underlies exposure and response prevention, not systematic desensitisation. (d) Adaptation to stress Adaptation to stress belongs to stress theory (Chapter 11), not to this therapy. Exposure and response prevention procedure is based on behaviour therapy principal of: (IHBAS 2024) a Counter conditioning b Habituation and extinction c Reciprocal inhibition d Graded exposure ✓ Answer: (b) Habituation and extinction Exposure and response prevention (ERP) for OCD The concept How ERP works The client meets the obsessional cue and is prevented from performing the compulsion . Why it works The anxiety rises, peaks and falls without the escape response, which is habituation and extinction at work. Why the other options are wrong (a) Counter conditioning Counterconditioning trains an incompatible response, as in systematic desensitisation; no incompatible response is trained in ERP. (c) Reciprocal inhibition Reciprocal inhibition also describes systematic desensitisation, which trains an incompatible response; ERP trains none. (d) Graded exposure Graded exposure is a way of presenting stimuli, not the learning principle behind the change. The "law of effect," formulated by Edward Thorndike, states that: (Real PYQ 2024) a Behaviors followed by pleasurable consequences are more likely to be repeated. b Organisms learn by observing and imitating models. c Insight occurs when the elements of a problem are suddenly restructured. d All behavior is motivated by unconscious drives. ✓ Answer: (a) Behaviors followed by pleasurable consequences are more likely to be repeated. Thorndike, law of effect The concept What it says Responses followed by satisfaction are strengthened; those followed by discomfort are weakened (Section 6.5). Where it came from Thorndike 's cats in puzzle boxes escaped faster over trials as the successful response was stamped in. Why the other options are wrong (b) Organisms learn by observing and imitating models. Bandura 's observational learning , learning by watching models, not from one's own consequences. (c) Insight occurs when the elements of a problem are suddenly restructured. Köhler 's insight , a sudden restructuring of the problem, not learning from consequences. (d) All behavior is motivated by unconscious drives. Freud 's idea of unconscious drives, not a learning principle. The behavioral technique that involves removing a desirable stimulus following an undesirable behavior in order to reduce the frequency of that behavior is called: (Real PYQ 2025) a Negative reinforcement b Response cost c Positive punishment d Extinction ✓ Answer: (b) Response cost, Operant conditioning: negative punishment (response cost) The concept What it is Response cost removes a desirable stimulus after an undesirable behaviour, to reduce that behaviour. Where it fits It is a form of negative punishment : negative means something is taken away, punishment means the behaviour decreases. Example Losing tokens or paying a fine for misbehaving. Why the other options are wrong (a) Negative reinforcement Negative reinforcement removes something to increase behaviour; the trap is reading "negative" as punishment. (c) Positive punishment Positive punishment adds something unpleasant; response cost takes something away. (d) Extinction Extinction simply stops delivering the reinforcer that maintained the behaviour; nothing the person already has is taken. The first-grade teacher gives students stickers when they perform well. If they earn five stickers in one day they are exempt from homework. The stickers in this example could also be called: (RML 2024) a Primary reinforcer b Token c Generalized reinforcer d Prepotent responses ✓ Answer: (b) Token Token economy: secondary reinforcers The concept What a token is A token is exchanged for a backup reinforcer ; here, five stickers buy exemption from homework. Its type Stickers used this way are secondary reinforcers , valued for what they buy, not primary ones. Why the other options are wrong (a) Primary reinforcer A primary reinforcer satisfies a biological need, like food or water; stickers matter only for what they buy. (c) Generalized reinforcer A generalised reinforcer buys many different backups (money), whereas these stickers buy only one. (d) Prepotent responses A prepotent response is a dominant response, not a reinforcer. A parent deliberately ignores a child's temper tantrums in an attempt to discourage them. The parent's strategy is in accordance with: (Amity 2023) a Negative reinforcement b Extinction c Operant escape d Operant avoidance ✓ Answer: (b) Extinction Williams (1959), extinction of tantrums The concept What it is Extinction means withholding the reinforcer that maintained a behaviour, so the behaviour fades. Applied here Ignoring withholds the attention that reinforced the tantrums ( Williams , 1959; Section 6.5). Key note The source key marks (c), but that is wrong; the correct answer is extinction. Why the other options are wrong (a) Negative reinforcement Negative reinforcement would increase behaviour, not discourage it. (c) Operant escape Escape terminates an aversive stimulus; the source key marks this, but ignoring a tantrum is not escape. (d) Operant avoidance Avoidance prevents an aversive stimulus; ignoring a tantrum prevents nothing aversive. A client with OCD washes their hands excessively to neutralize the anxiety caused by intrusive thoughts of contamination. This hand-washing behavior is BEST conceptualized as a(n): (Real PYQ 2024) a Conditioned stimulus b Unconditioned response c Avoidance response / Safety behavior d Operant behavior maintained by positive reinforcement ✓ Answer: (c) Avoidance response / Safety behavior Mowrer, two-factor theory of avoidance The concept Two factors In Mowrer 's two-factor theory, fear is learned by classical conditioning and avoidance is kept going by operant conditioning. Applied here Washing reduces anxiety and is therefore negatively reinforced : the second factor (Section 6.5). Why the other options are wrong (a) Conditioned stimulus Washing is a learned response , not a stimulus. (b) Unconditioned response Washing is learned, so it is not an unconditioned response . (d) Operant behavior maintained by positive reinforcement It is maintained by the removal of anxiety , not by positive reinforcement . Sheena is studying for her final exam in her psychology class. For every 45 minutes that she studies, she gives herself a mini chocolate, then goes back to studying. What Schedule of reinforcement is Sheena using? (RML 2021) a Variable ratio schedule b Variable interval schedule c Fixed interval schedule d Fixed ratio schedule ✓ Answer: (c) Fixed interval Schedules of reinforcement: fixed interval The concept Why this one The requirement is a constant amount of time , not a number of responses ( ratio ) and not an unpredictable period ( variable ). Key note Strictly, reward after a fixed time regardless of responding is a fixed-time arrangement, but among these options fixed interval is correct (Section 6.6). Why the other options are wrong (a) Variable ratio schedule Variable ratio rewards after an unpredictable number of responses; Sheena's reward depends on time. (b) Variable interval schedule Variable interval uses an unpredictable period; Sheena's 45 minutes is constant. (d) Fixed ratio schedule Fixed ratio rewards after a set number of responses, not a set amount of time. Among the following schedules of reinforcement, which typically produces the highest rate of response and is most resistant to extinction? (Real PYQ 2024) a Fixed Ratio b Variable Ratio c Fixed Interval d Variable Interval ✓ Answer: (b) Variable ratio Schedules of reinforcement: variable ratio The concept Why ratio Ratio schedules reward fast responding: more responses bring more rewards. Why variable Unpredictability removes any reason to pause and makes it hard to detect that reinforcement has stopped, so it resists extinction . Example Slot machines work this way. Why the other options are wrong (a) Fixed Ratio Fixed ratio produces pauses after reinforcement, so its rate is not the highest overall. (c) Fixed Interval Fixed interval produces a scallop : little responding just after reward, speeding up as the interval ends. (d) Variable Interval Variable interval produces only a moderate rate. According to the Premack Principle, a high-probability behavior (for example, playing video games) can be used to: (Real PYQ 2024) a Reinforce a low-probability behavior (for example, completing homework). b Punish a low-probability behavior. c Reinforce another high-probability behavior. d Extinguish a maladaptive behavior. ✓ Answer: (a) Reinforce a low-probability behavior (for example, completing homework). Premack principle (grandma's rule) The concept What it says A more preferred activity, made available only after a less preferred one, reinforces the less preferred one. Everyday name It is called grandma's rule : eat your vegetables, then you get dessert (Section 6.6). Why the other options are wrong (b) Punish a low-probability behavior. The principle concerns reinforcement , not punishment. (c) Reinforce another high-probability behavior. It runs from high to low probability, not between two high-probability activities. (d) Extinguish a maladaptive behavior. The principle concerns reinforcement, not extinction . Learned helplessness phenomenon is offered by: (JEMAS 2025) a Aaron T. Beck b Martin Seligman and Steven F. Maier c Harry Stack Sullivan d Daniel Kahneman ✓ Answer: (b) Martin Seligman and Steven F. Maier Seligman and Maier, yoked dogs The concept The study Seligman and Maier 's yoked dogs were given inescapable shock . The result Later they failed to escape avoidable shock: they had learned that nothing they did mattered, which is learned helplessness (Section 6.6). Why the other options are wrong (a) Aaron T. Beck Beck is known for the cognitive triad of depression; the trap is that helplessness is also linked to depression. (c) Harry Stack Sullivan Sullivan is known for interpersonal theory . (d) Daniel Kahneman Kahneman is known for heuristics and biases . The Crespi effect in learning experiments refers to: (IHBAS 2025) a Loss of previously learned behavior due to retroactive inhibition b Increase in motivation when the magnitude of reinforcement increases c Decrease in response strength after extinction training d Sudden improvement in performance due to insight ✓ Answer: (b) Increase in motivation when the magnitude of reinforcement increases Crespi, reward-shift (contrast) effects The concept Positive contrast Crespi 's rats shifted from a small to a larger reward ran faster than rats always given the larger reward: positive contrast . Negative contrast The reverse shift, from large to small, produced negative contrast . Why motivation The changes were too abrupt to be learning, so they reflect motivation (Section 6.6). Why the other options are wrong (a) Loss of previously learned behavior due to retroactive inhibition Describes memory interference , not a reward effect. (c) Decrease in response strength after extinction training Describes extinction , not a change in reward size. (d) Sudden improvement in performance due to insight Describes Köhler 's insight , not a reward effect. The technique that is based on the idea that the autonomic nervous system can come under voluntary control through operant conditioning is known as: (JEMAS 2025) a Biofeedback b Hypnosis c Sublimation d Systematic desensitization ✓ Answer: (a) Biofeedback Miller, biofeedback (operant control of autonomic responses) The concept How it works A bodily process is measured and displayed, so changes in the desired direction are reinforced by the feedback. Who showed it Miller argued that autonomic responses can be operantly conditioned (Section 6.6). Why the other options are wrong (b) Hypnosis Hypnosis is an altered state (Chapter 5), not operant conditioning. (c) Sublimation Sublimation is a Freudian defence mechanism . (d) Systematic desensitization Systematic desensitisation is a classical counterconditioning technique, not operant. What is the main difference between classical and operant conditioning? (IHBAS 2024) a Classical conditioning relies on reinforcement; operant conditioning does not b Classical conditioning pairs two stimuli; operant conditioning relies on reinforcement and punishment c Operant conditioning involves cognitive processes; classical conditioning does not d Both are entirely different learning processes ✓ Answer: (b) Classical conditioning pairs two stimuli; operant conditioning relies on reinforcement and punishment Classical vs operant conditioning (Table 6.9) The concept Classical Classical conditioning associates two stimuli, such as bell and food. Operant Operant conditioning associates a response with its consequences, reinforcement and punishment (Table 6.9). Why the other options are wrong (a) Classical conditioning relies on reinforcement; operant conditioning does not Backwards : reinforcement belongs to operant conditioning. (c) Operant conditioning involves cognitive processes; classical conditioning does not False, because classical conditioning depends on prediction (Rescorla), a cognitive process. (d) Both are entirely different learning processes Ignores how constantly the two interact, as in two-factor theory and autoshaping . Latent learning was demonstrated by: (IHBAS 2025) a Tolman b Bandura c Skinner d Kohler ✓ Answer: (a) Tolman, Tolman and Honzik (1930), latent learning The concept The study Tolman and Honzik 's rats found food in the maze only from day 11, yet immediately performed as well as rats rewarded throughout. What it means They had learned the maze without reward and showed it once a reason appeared: latent learning (Section 6.7). Why the other options are wrong (b) Bandura Bandura is observational learning . (c) Skinner Skinner is operant conditioning . (d) Kohler Köhler is insight . Concept formation stages include the following: (JEMAS 2025) a Observation, Discrimination, Generalization, Abstraction b Abstraction, Generalisation, Discrimination, Assimilation c Observation, Generalisation, Discrimination, Abstraction d Observation, Assimilation, Generalisation, Discrimination ✓ Answer: (a) Observation, Discrimination, Generalization, Abstraction Stages of concept formation The concept Steps 1 and 2 The learner observes instances, then discriminates them from non-instances. Steps 3 and 4 Next the learner generalises to all instances sharing the essential features, and abstracts the defining properties (Section 6.7). Why the other options are wrong (b) Abstraction, Generalisation, Discrimination, Assimilation Includes assimilation , which is Piaget's term, not a stage of concept formation, and starts with abstraction, the last stage. (c) Observation, Generalisation, Discrimination, Abstraction Puts generalisation before discrimination; the order is the trap. (d) Observation, Assimilation, Generalisation, Discrimination Includes assimilation , Piaget's term, not a stage of concept formation. According to Albert Bandura, which of the following is NOT a necessary component process for observational learning to occur? (Real PYQ 2024) a Attention b Motivation c Reinforcement d Reproduction ✓ Answer: (c) Reinforcement Bandura, Bobo doll study (1965) The concept Four processes The four processes are attention , retention , motor reproduction and motivation . Bobo doll The 1965 Bobo doll study showed that children learn a model's behaviour whether or not anyone is reinforced. Why not reinforcement Reinforcement affects only whether the behaviour is performed , not whether it is learned (Section 6.8). Why the other options are not the answer (a) Attention True component: attention to the model comes first; without it nothing is learned. (b) Motivation True component: motivation decides whether the learned behaviour is actually performed. (d) Reproduction True component: motor reproduction turns the remembered behaviour into action. Reciprocal causation model has been described under: (IHBAS 2020) a Social cognitive theory b Two-factor theory c Drive reduction theory d Constructivist theory ✓ Answer: (a) Social cognitive theory Bandura, triadic reciprocal causation (reciprocal determinism) The concept The model Bandura 's triadic reciprocal causation (reciprocal determinism) holds that person, behaviour and environment influence one another (Section 6.8). Where it sits It is the core of his social cognitive theory . Why the other options are wrong (b) Two-factor theory Two-factor theory is Mowrer 's account of avoidance. (c) Drive reduction theory Drive-reduction theory is Hull 's. (d) Constructivist theory Constructivism (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner) concerns how learners build knowledge (Section 6.9). Learning always leads to efficacy, provided presence of a significant factor which is: (JEMAS 2025) a The learner has ability. b The learner has aptitude. c The learner has knowledge. d The learner has a specific goal. ✓ Answer: (d) The learner has a specific goal. Locke and Latham, goal-setting theory The concept Goal setting Locke and Latham showed that specific, difficult goals , together with knowledge of results , direct attention, mobilise effort and increase persistence. Why it matters With a goal, practice becomes purposeful, so learning turns into effective performance (Section 6.10). Why the other options are wrong (a) The learner has ability. Ability helps, but on its own it does not turn learning into effective performance. (b) The learner has aptitude. Aptitude helps, but on its own it does not turn learning into effective performance. (c) The learner has knowledge. Knowledge helps, but on its own it does not turn learning into effective performance. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Systematic desensitisation (Joseph Wolpe, Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition , 1958) rests on reciprocal inhibition : relaxation, a response incompatible with anxiety, is paired step by step with a graded anxiety hierarchy. It is counterconditioning, not operant extinction, habituation or the law of effect. asked 17 times The token economy is operant conditioning: tokens are secondary (conditioned) reinforcers exchanged for backup reinforcers. It was developed on a psychiatric ward by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin ( The Token Economy , 1968), and it is the listed therapy NOT derived from classical conditioning. Stickers that earn a reward are tokens. asked 10 times Schedules (Ferster and Skinner, 1957): variable ratio gives the highest rate and greatest resistance to extinction; fixed ratio, high rates with a post-reinforcement pause; fixed interval, the scallop (a reward every 45 minutes of study is keyed fixed interval); variable interval, moderate steady rates; continuous reinforcement, every response reinforced, learns fastest and extinguishes fastest. asked 7 times Extinction : a conditioned response weakens when the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS (classical), or a response fades when it is no longer reinforced (operant), falling back to its earlier operant level. A parent who ignores tantrums is using extinction; the Amity 2023 key "operant escape" is wrong. asked 7 times In Pavlov's experiment the bell or metronome is a neutral stimulus before pairing with food and a conditioned stimulus after ; a neutral stimulus becomes a CS by repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus, and the fundamental element is association . Fear of the ground where you lost a match is classical conditioning. asked 6 times Operant behaviour is emitted and operates on the environment (Skinner), and a response made more frequent by reinforcement is operant conditioning. Reinforcement always increases behaviour and punishment decreases it; positive adds and negative removes, so switching off an ongoing shock is negative reinforcement (escape), not punishment. asked 6 times Shaping (Skinner) is reinforcing successive approximations to a target behaviour; chaining links a sequence of responses, prompting adds a cue and fading withdraws it. asked 5 times Exposure and response prevention (Victor Meyer, 1966) rests on habituation and extinction ; flooding is prolonged full-intensity exposure without relaxation; covert sensitisation (Joseph Cautela, 1967) pairs an imagined behaviour with an imagined unpleasant consequence; counterconditioning teaches that a feared stimulus is no longer threatening. asked 4 times Latent learning : Edward Tolman and Charles Honzik (1930) found that rats unrewarded for ten days and then fed from day 11 almost at once matched rats rewarded throughout. Tolman called what they had learned a cognitive map (1948). asked 5 times Premack principle (David Premack, 1959): a high-probability (preferred) behaviour reinforces a low-probability one, never the reverse (grandma's rule: homework first, then video games). asked 5 times Learned helplessness : Martin Seligman and Steven Maier (1967; first reported by Overmier and Seligman, 1967) found that dogs given inescapable shock later failed to escape avoidable shock; it became a model of depression. asked 4 times Bandura's four processes of observational learning are attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation . Reinforcement is not necessary for learning by observation (it governs performance), and the model must demonstrate the target behaviour. asked 4 times Escape terminates an aversive stimulus already present; avoidance prevents its onset; both are negative reinforcement. On Mowrer's two-factor theory (1947), OCD compulsions such as hand-washing are escape (avoidance) behaviours, or safety behaviours. asked 3 times Behaviour analysis (applied behaviour analysis) and functional analysis are based on operant conditioning : they examine a behaviour's antecedents and consequences. asked 3 times Classical conditioning pairs two stimuli; operant conditioning relies on consequences (reinforcement and punishment). The hallmark of behaviour therapy is the use of classical and operant conditioning techniques to eliminate unwanted behaviour. asked 3 times Reciprocal determinism (triadic reciprocal causation) belongs to Bandura's social cognitive theory : person, behaviour and environment influence one another in both directions. It is not Wolpe's reciprocal inhibition. asked 3 times Time-out and response cost (removing a desirable stimulus after an unwanted behaviour) are both negative punishment . asked 3 times Biofeedback brings autonomic and other bodily processes under voluntary control through operant conditioning with instrument feedback (Neal Miller); EMG biofeedback suits tension-type headache, and Arnold Kegel's perineometer (1948) was an early form. asked 3 times Insight learning (Wolfgang Köhler, Tenerife, 1913 to 1920): Sultan joined two sticks and the chimpanzees stacked boxes to reach bananas; the sudden solution is the "aha" experience . Gestalt psychology holds that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. asked 3 times Harry Harlow (1958): infant rhesus monkeys clung to a cloth surrogate rather than a wire one that fed them, so attachment rests on contact comfort , not on conditioned reinforcement from feeding. asked 4 times Self-efficacy (Albert Bandura, 1977) is a person's belief in his capability to carry out the actions a specific task requires; it is the central motivational construct of social cognitive theory. asked 3 times Law of effect (Edward Lee Thorndike; puzzle-box cats, 1898; classic statement, 1911): responses followed by satisfying consequences become more likely to recur. asked 3 times Bobo doll (Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross, 1961): children who watched an adult attack the doll imitated its specific aggressive acts with no reinforcement at all, which is observational learning . asked 3 times The relaxation in desensitisation is Edmund Jacobson's progressive muscle relaxation, and the client rates each hierarchy scene on Wolpe's 0 to 100 Subjective Units of Disturbance Scale (SUDS) . asked twice Taste aversion (John Garcia and Robert Koelling, 1966) is classical conditioning learned in one trial across long delays; it shows biological preparedness (constraints on learning) and refutes equipotentiality. asked twice Sensitisation (increased responding after a strong stimulus) is the near opposite of habituation (a decreasing response to a repeated harmless stimulus); habituation and dishabituation reveal what infants can discriminate before they can speak. asked twice Little Albert (John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920): seven pairings of a white rat with a loud noise produced classically conditioned fear that generalised to furry objects. asked twice Imprinting (Konrad Lorenz, 1935, greylag goslings) is rapid, largely irreversible attachment to the first moving object, confined to a critical period. asked twice Delay (forward) conditioning , in which the CS begins first and overlaps the UCS, is the most effective timing arrangement; backward conditioning is the least effective. asked once The keyed stages of concept formation are observation, discrimination, generalisation, abstraction . asked once

Weightage. 111 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (13.6%) test this chapter, 72 of them from real past papers. 5 of its 11 sections are High yield. In March 1985, Clive Wearing was at the top of his profession. He was a British musician and musicologist, a producer of music programmes for BBC radio and an authority on the Renaissance composer Orlande de Lassus. Then he fell ill with what looked like a bad flu and a headache that would not go away. It was herpes simplex encephalitis: the same virus that causes ordinary cold sores had invaded his brain, and within days it had destroyed the hippocampus on both sides and damaged large parts of his temporal and frontal lobes. Clive survived, but the man who woke up was trapped inside a moment that lasted only seconds. He could hold a conversation as long as it kept moving, and he could follow a sentence to its end. But a short while after any experience ended, it was gone, and with it any sense that it had ever happened. He felt, continuously, as if he had just regained consciousness for the first time. His diary filled with page after page of entries, each giving the time and announcing that he was now, at last, truly awake; every earlier entry, which he had no memory of writing, was angrily crossed out. When his wife Deborah stepped out of the room for a few minutes and came back, he greeted her with tears of joy, as if they had been apart for years. The damage reached backwards as well as forwards. Almost every particular episode of his earlier life had become inaccessible to him. He knew certain facts, that he was a musician and that he was married to Deborah, but he could bring back almost no specific event from the decades he had lived. And yet some things survived untouched. Seat Clive at a piano or in front of a choir and he could still sight-read, play and conduct with his old skill; the music carried him from one bar to the next for as long as it lasted. Nor did he ever lose his love for Deborah or his recognition of her, although he could not remember a single conversation with her from one visit to the next. Clive Wearing's case raises nearly every question this chapter tries to answer. How can a person hold a thought for a few seconds but not for a minute? How can someone lose his whole personal past and still remember how to play the piano? Is there one memory or many? Where do memories go when we forget them, and why do some of them come back changed? Keep Clive in mind; you will meet him again at the end of the chapter. 7.1 What Memory Is, and How Ebbinghaus Measured It Medium yield · 5 Qs You use memory in everything you do. Reading this sentence requires you to hold its first words in mind until you reach its last ones; understanding it requires the meanings of words you learned years ago; and if you can answer a question about it next week, it is because something of it was kept. memory is the capacity to retain information over time and to use it later. Notice that this definition says nothing about consciousness: as Clive Wearing's piano playing shows, much of what we retain is expressed in what we can do rather than in what we can report. Three processes: encoding, storage and retrieval Psychologists find it useful to break remembering into three processes, an idea that grew out of the information-processing approach of the 1950s and 1960s, which treated the mind as a system that takes in, transforms, stores and outputs information, much as a computer does. The study of mental processes such as attention, memory and problem solving through this information-processor metaphor is cognitive psychology, whose rise is told in Chapter 2. encoding is the transformation of incoming information into a form, or code, that the memory system can hold. storage is the maintenance of encoded information over time. retrieval is the recovery of stored information when it is needed. A library is a fair analogy: books must be acquired and catalogued (encoding), kept on the shelves (storage), and found again when a reader asks for them (retrieval). A book can be missing because it was never bought, because it was lost from the shelf, or because it was shelved under the wrong number and cannot be found; in the same way, a failure to remember can be a failure at any of the three stages. The first stage depends heavily on attention. What you do not attend to is usually never encoded at all. In 1979 Raymond Nickerson and Marilyn Adams asked American adults to pick out the correct drawing of a one-cent coin from fifteen versions; fewer than half chose correctly, although every one of them had handled thousands of such coins. You can try the same test on yourself with a ten-rupee coin. The failure is not forgetting in the ordinary sense but encoding failure : the details were never encoded, because nothing in daily life requires you to attend to them, and what was never stored cannot later be retrieved. Attention itself is the subject of Chapter 5. Ebbinghaus and the first experiments on memory For most of the nineteenth century, memory was a subject for philosophers. Even Wilhelm Wundt, who founded the first psychology laboratory in 1879, doubted that the higher mental processes could be studied by experiment. The person who proved otherwise was Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909), a young German scholar working alone, without a laboratory, who had been inspired by Gustav Fechner's demonstration that sensations could be measured (Chapter 3). If sensations could be measured, Ebbinghaus reasoned, why not memories? His first problem was material. Real words and poems come loaded with associations: a word you already know is not learned from scratch, and some words are far easier than others. So Ebbinghaus invented the nonsense syllable , a pronounceable but meaningless consonant-vowel-consonant combination such as DAX, BUP or ZOL. He built a pool of about 2,300 of them, drew lists at random, and, acting as his own and only participant, read each list aloud at a steady rate until he could recite it without error. Then, after a delay that ranged from twenty minutes to a month, he learned the same list again to the same standard. His measure of what remained was ingenious. Even when he could not recall a single syllable, relearning a list was faster than learning it had been the first time. The savings method expresses this as a percentage: savings equals the time (or number of trials) for original learning minus the time for relearning, divided by the time for original learning, multiplied by 100. Here is a worked example. Suppose a list took 20 readings to learn on Monday and 12 readings to relearn on Friday. The savings are (20 minus 12) divided by 20, multiplied by 100, which is 40 per cent. Forty per cent of the original work did not have to be repeated, so something of Monday's learning survived, even if Friday's attempt at recall produced nothing at all. Key study: Ebbinghaus, Memory (1885) Ebbinghaus published his results in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (On Memory; translated into English in 1913). His central result was the forgetting curve : savings fell steeply at first and then levelled off. After twenty minutes he had already lost about 42 per cent of the original learning; after an hour, more than half; after a day, about two thirds. But after that the loss slowed dramatically, and a month later about a fifth of the learning still survived (Figure 7.1). He also found that a list of about seven syllables could be repeated after a single reading but that the number of readings needed rose steeply for longer lists; that extra repetitions beyond the point of mastery increased later savings; that repetitions spread over several days were more efficient than the same repetitions crowded into one sitting; that syllables at the beginning and end of a list were learned before those in the middle; and that meaningful material (stanzas of poetry) needed far fewer readings than nonsense syllables. The criticisms are obvious and Ebbinghaus knew most of them: one participant, who was also the experimenter; artificial material stripped of meaning; and syllables that were not, in fact, equally meaningless (later researchers measured the "association value" of each syllable). Frederic Bartlett would later argue that by removing meaning Ebbinghaus had removed the most important thing about human memory (Section 7.9). Even so, his curves have been replicated many times, and his work showed that memory could be studied with the same precision as sensation. 0 25 50 75 100 Savings (%) 0 6 12 18 1 10 20 31 Hours after learning Days after learning 58% at 20 minutes 44% at 1 hour 36% at 9 hours 34% at 1 day 28% at 2 days 25% at 6 days 21% at 31 days Figure 7.1 Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, plotted from his 1885 savings data. The time axis is broken: hours on the left, days on the right. Notice how much is lost in the first hour and how little is lost between the sixth and the thirty-first day. Two features of Figure 7.1 are worth fixing in your mind, because examiners return to them. First, the curve is negatively accelerated: forgetting is fastest immediately after learning and slows as time passes. Second, it never reaches zero; Ebbinghaus's savings method detected traces of learning long after recall had failed. Ebbinghaus also left psychology one of its best-known sentences, from a textbook of 1908: "Psychology has a long past, but only a short history." Exam trap A question asks what Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud have in common. All three worked largely independently and were pioneers, and each devised a new method for studying the mind (Ebbinghaus the nonsense syllable and savings, Galton questionnaires and word association, Freud free association). None of them founded a formal psychology laboratory in the sense that Wundt did (Galton's Anthropometric Laboratory, opened in London in 1884, measured physical and sensory traits of the public rather than running psychological experiments). The RML 2020 key gives "each worked independently and were pioneers" alone, while the Panwar bank keys "(a) and (c)". The difference turns on the word "observational": Ebbinghaus's method was experimental, not observational, which is the likely reason the RML key stops at (a). Read the options carefully and choose the statement that is true of all three without qualification. Measuring retention: recall, recognition, relearning and reconstruction Ebbinghaus measured savings, but memory can be measured in several ways, and the same memory can look strong on one test and absent on another. All of the methods below are explicit tests: the person knows that memory is being tested and tries to remember. (Implicit tests, where memory shows itself without any attempt to remember, are described in Section 7.5.) recall requires the person to reproduce information with few or no hints. It comes in three forms. In free recall the person reports the items in any order, as when you list the films you saw last year. In serial recall the items must be reproduced in the order presented, as when you repeat a phone number. In cued recall a hint is given, such as a category name or the first letter. A special and historically important form of cued recall is paired-associate learning , introduced by Mary Whiton Calkins (1863 to 1930) in 1894: the person learns pairs of items (HOUSE and 47, or a Kannada word and its English meaning) and is later given the first member of each pair as a cue for the second. Learning the vocabulary of a new language is paired-associate learning in everyday life. recognition requires the person only to identify previously encountered items among new ones, called distractors or lures. It may take a yes or no form ("Was this face in the set?") or a forced-choice form, like the multiple-choice questions in your exam. A police line-up is a recognition test. Recognition is usually easier than recall, because the item itself is supplied and the person need only judge its familiarity. relearning is Ebbinghaus's savings method: the person learns the material again, and the reduction in time or trials is the measure of what was retained. It is the most sensitive of the measures, because it detects traces too weak to support either recall or recognition. Finally, the reconstruction method presents items in a particular order, then hands them back shuffled and asks the person to put them back into the original order. The score reflects memory for order rather than for the items themselves, which are all in front of the person. Table 7.1 sets the methods side by side. Table 7.1 Measures of explicit retention, roughly from least to most sensitive: the recall tests are the least sensitive and relearning the most. Method What the person does Everyday example Free recall Produces the items in any order, with no cues Writing an essay answer from memory Serial recall Produces the items in their original order Repeating a mobile number Cued recall (including paired associates) Produces an item when given a hint or partner item Giving the English meaning of a foreign word Reconstruction Restores the original order of items that are supplied Putting the steps of a recipe back in sequence Recognition Picks out old items from among new ones A multiple-choice question; a police line-up Relearning (savings) Learns the material again; time saved is measured Revising a subject studied years ago Exam trap The "reconstruction method" (restoring the original order of supplied items) is a measurement technique. "Reconstructive memory" (Bartlett's idea that remembering rebuilds the past from schemas, Section 7.9) is a theory. A question describing items presented in order, then scrambled, then put back in order by the participant is asking for the reconstruction method, not recall, recognition or relearning. And when asked which measure is most sensitive, the answer is relearning (savings); recall, with no cues to help, is the least sensitive. 7.2 The Multi-Store Model High yield · 17 Qs Ebbinghaus studied memory as a single thing that weakens over time. The idea that memory might be made of several different stores is older than experiments on it. William James (1842 to 1910), in his Principles of Psychology (1890), distinguished primary memory, the small amount of information that is still present in consciousness (the sentence you are reading), from secondary memory, the vast store of knowledge that must be brought back into consciousness. In 1965 Nancy Waugh and Donald Norman revived James's terms in an experimental model. Three years later came the version that every textbook teaches. Atkinson and Shiffrin's modal model (1968) In 1968 Richard C. Atkinson and Richard M. Shiffrin proposed the multi-store model of memory. Because so many theorists of the period proposed something similar, it is also called the modal model (the most typical model). It has two kinds of parts. The structural features are three stores through which information passes: sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory. The control processes are strategies that the person can choose to use, such as attending, rehearsing, coding information in a particular way, and searching memory during retrieval. As Figure 7.2 shows, information from the environment enters the sensory stores; what is attended to passes into short-term memory; what is rehearsed there is transferred to long-term memory; and information can be retrieved from long-term memory back into short-term memory when it is needed. Incoming stimuli Sensory memory Short-term memory Long-term memory attention encoding retrieval rehearsal lost by decay lost by displacement interference Large capacity Icon: under 1 s Echo: 2 to 4 s 7 ± 2 chunks About 18 to 30 s Acoustic code No known limit Up to a lifetime Semantic code Figure 7.2 The multi-store (modal) model of Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968). Solid arrows show the flow of information; dashed arrows show how information is lost from each store. The figures beneath each store are the classic textbook values. Sensory memory Wave a lit sparkler in a circle on Diwali night and you see a circle of light, not a moving dot. The circle exists only in your memory: the image of each position persists for a fraction of a second after the sparkler has moved on. sensory memory (also called the sensory register) is a very brief store that holds a large amount of raw, unprocessed sensory information, one store for each sense, just long enough for attention to select some of it for further processing. Its contents are pre-categorical: they are a record of the stimulus, not yet of its meaning. The visual sensory store is iconic memory and the auditory store is echoic memory ; both terms were coined by Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012) in his book Cognitive Psychology (1967), which gave the new field its name. A tactile store, sometimes called haptic memory, has been studied far less. Key study: Sperling's partial-report experiments (1960) When people see an array of twelve letters (three rows of four) flashed for 50 milliseconds, they can report only about four or five of them. Yet they insist that they saw more, and that the rest faded while they were reporting. George Sperling (born 1934) tested this claim with the partial-report procedure . Immediately after the flash, a tone told the participant which row to report: a high tone for the top row, a medium tone for the middle row, a low tone for the bottom row. Because the participant could not know in advance which row would be cued, the proportion of the cued row reported must be true of the whole array. Participants reported about three of the four letters in whichever row was cued, which means that about nine of the twelve letters, roughly 75 per cent, were available at the moment of the tone, about twice as many as the whole-report method suggested. Then Sperling delayed the tone. With every fraction of a second of delay the partial-report advantage shrank, and by about one second it had vanished: performance fell to the level of whole report. Sperling concluded that a rich visual image persists for a few hundred milliseconds after the stimulus ends and fades rapidly, so that whole report underestimates what was seen simply because the image decays while the first letters are being named. A bright visual stimulus that follows the array (a mask) wipes the icon out even faster. Iconic memory therefore lasts roughly 250 to 500 milliseconds (a quarter to half a second, a little longer in some conditions). Echoic memory lasts longer. In 1972 Christopher Darwin, Michael Turvey and Robert Crowder ran an auditory version of Sperling's experiment, the "three-eared man" study: participants heard three different lists of letters and digits at once over headphones, one in the left ear, one in the right ear and one in both ears (which is heard as coming from the middle of the head). A visual cue then indicated which "ear" to report. A partial-report advantage appeared again, and it lasted for up to about four seconds. Echoic memory is generally put at about two to four seconds. You use it every time someone speaks to you while your attention is elsewhere: you say "What did you say?" and then realise you can replay the last few words yourself before they repeat them. The longer life of the echo makes sense, because speech unfolds over time and the end of a word can only be understood together with its beginning. Exam trap Two past papers ask about "the largest capacity" and get different answers. If a question says "largest capacity but shortest duration" (JEMAS 2025), the answer is sensory memory: it registers almost everything that reaches the senses, far more than short-term memory can hold, but for under a second (icon) or a few seconds (echo). If a question asks only which store has "the largest capacity" in the Atkinson and Shiffrin model, the answer is long-term memory, whose capacity has no known limit. Read the second half of the stem. Also note that "icon and echo" belong to sensory memory, never to short-term or working memory; that iconic memory is shorter than echoic memory; and that when a question says "lasts only a few seconds" and offers sensory memory, sensory memory is the intended answer, not eidetic imagery (Section 7.5), which is a rare, long-lasting visual image. Short-term memory: capacity and chunking Information that is attended to passes into short-term memory (STM), a store of very limited capacity that holds information for a matter of seconds unless it is rehearsed. Its capacity is measured by the memory span : the longest sequence of items that a person can repeat back in the correct order immediately after hearing it. Joseph Jacobs measured digit span systematically as early as 1887, and digit span remains part of every major intelligence and memory scale (Psychological Assessment book). In 1956 George Armitage Miller (1920 to 2012) published a paper with one of the most famous titles in psychology, "The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information." Across many tasks, he noted, people could hold about seven items (between five and nine) in immediate memory. But Miller's deeper point was that the limit applies to meaningful units, not to raw items. He called these units chunks, and the process of grouping items into larger meaningful units chunking . Try to hold this string: I N D I A I I T I S R O. Twelve letters is beyond most people's span. Read it as INDIA, IIT, ISRO and it becomes three chunks, well within span. You chunk your mobile number into groups (98450 12345), and your twelve-digit Aadhaar number into three groups of four, for the same reason. Chunking depends on knowledge already stored in long-term memory: IIT is a chunk only for someone who knows what it is. The most dramatic demonstration came from a student known as S.F., studied by Anders Ericsson, William Chase and Steve Faloon (1980). S.F. began with an ordinary digit span of about seven. Over more than 200 hours of practice spread across about twenty months he raised it to around 80 digits, by recoding groups of digits as running times (he was a keen club runner, so 3492 became "3 minutes 49.2 seconds, a near world-record mile"). His span for letters, which he did not practise, stayed at about six. His short-term store had not grown; he had learned to chunk. In the same way, chess masters glancing at a board from a real game for five seconds can reconstruct it almost perfectly, but are no better than novices when the pieces are placed at random (Chase and Simon, 1973). When rehearsal and chunking are prevented, the true capacity of short-term memory appears to be smaller than seven. In 2001 Nelson Cowan reviewed this evidence and argued for "the magical number 4": about four chunks, plus or minus one. Modern textbooks therefore give both figures: Miller's seven plus or minus two for memory span, and Cowan's four for the pure capacity of the store. Short-term memory: duration, forgetting and coding How long does information last in short-term memory if you are prevented from rehearsing it? Two studies answered almost simultaneously: John Brown in Britain in 1958 and, in a paper that every student learns, Lloyd and Margaret Peterson in the United States in 1959. Key study: The Brown-Peterson technique (1958, 1959) Lloyd Peterson and Margaret Peterson read a consonant trigram (such as CHJ) to each participant, followed at once by a three-digit number. The participant had to count backwards by threes from that number (506, 503, 500 ...) until a signal, then recall the trigram. Counting backwards prevented rehearsal. The retention interval varied from 3 to 18 seconds. Recall fell rapidly: from about 80 per cent after 3 seconds to about 10 per cent after 18 seconds. This method of filling the retention interval with a distracting task became known as the Brown-Peterson technique . The Petersons interpreted the result as decay: an unrehearsed trace simply fades in under half a minute, which is the origin of the textbook figure of "about 18 to 30 seconds" for the duration of short-term memory. But the decay interpretation did not survive. In 1962 Geoffrey Keppel and Benton Underwood looked at the very first trial each participant received and found almost no forgetting at all, even after 18 seconds. Forgetting grew only over successive trials, as trigrams from earlier trials piled up and competed with the current one. That is proactive interference (Section 7.8), not decay. Further evidence pointed the same way. Delos Wickens and his colleagues showed in the 1960s and early 1970s that if several Brown-Peterson trials use items from one category (say, fruits), recall declines from trial to trial; but if the category is then switched (to professions), recall jumps back up. This release from proactive interference shows that the earlier items were interfering with the new ones, and, incidentally, that items in short-term memory carry some meaning. Waugh and Norman (1965) presented digits at fast or slow rates and found that forgetting depended on how many items came after the target, not on how much time had passed: new items displace old ones from a store with few slots. The modern view is that short-term forgetting is mostly due to interference and displacement, with decay playing a role, if at all, only over the first few seconds. What form does information take in short-term memory? In 1964 Reuben Conrad showed people strings of letters visually and recorded their recall errors. The errors were acoustic: people wrote V when the letter had been B, or S when it had been X, letters that sound alike but look different. Even visual material, it seemed, was held as sound. Two years later Alan Baddeley (born 1934) gave people short lists of words to recall immediately. Lists of words that sounded alike (man, mad, cap, can, map) were recalled very poorly; lists of words with similar meanings (big, huge, large, broad, great) caused little difficulty. When recall was delayed by twenty minutes, so that it depended on long-term memory, the pattern reversed: similarity of meaning now caused confusion, and similarity of sound did not. The classic conclusion is that acoustic coding dominates in short-term memory and semantic coding in long-term memory. "Dominates" is the right word: short-term memory can also hold visual codes for a second or two, and Wickens's release effect shows that meaning is present too. Long-term memory long-term memory (LTM) is the relatively permanent store of information. Its capacity has no known limit: nobody has ever been turned away from learning a new face because the store was full. Its duration ranges from minutes to a lifetime. Harry Bahrick and his colleagues (1975) tested nearly four hundred American adults on the names and faces of their high-school classmates; even 34 years after graduation, people recognised about 90 per cent of their classmates' faces, although their ability to recall names freely was far poorer and declined steadily. In a later study, Bahrick (1984) found that much of the Spanish people had learned at school was still there fifty years later; he called this stable residue permastore. Information in long-term memory is coded mainly by meaning. Jacqueline Sachs (1967) found that people who had heard a passage could not tell, after a short delay, whether a test sentence matched the exact wording they had heard, but readily detected any change in its meaning: we keep the gist and lose the words. Long-term memory also holds sounds (a song, a voice), images (a face) and movements (how to ride a bicycle), so semantic coding is the typical, not the only, code. Plot the probability of recall against each word's position in the list and you get a U-shaped curve, the serial position effect , also called the primacy-recency effect (Figure 7.3). The superior recall of the first few items is the primacy effect ; the superior recall of the last few is the recency effect . Bennet Murdock (1962) showed how reliable this curve is in free recall across lists of different lengths and presentation rates. The multi-store model explains it neatly. The first items receive more rehearsal than later ones, because each of them is rehearsed alone and then together with the next few, so they are more likely to be transferred to long-term memory: primacy is a long-term memory effect. The last items are still sitting in short-term memory at the moment of recall and are simply read out first: recency is a short-term memory effect. Dewey Rundus (1971) confirmed the first claim by asking people to rehearse aloud; the early items were rehearsed far more often than the rest, and the number of rehearsals predicted recall. Murray Glanzer and Anita Cunitz did exactly that. When recall was delayed by 30 seconds filled with counting (which empties short-term memory), the recency effect disappeared, but the primacy effect was unchanged. When words were presented more slowly (allowing more rehearsal), recall of early and middle items improved, but recency was unaffected. (Section 7.10) and Clive Wearing, have normal digit spans and normal recency effects, but cannot transfer new information into long-term memory: short-term memory intact, long-term learning destroyed. If the stores are truly separate, the opposite pattern should also exist. It does. In 1970 Tim Shallice and Elizabeth Warrington described K.F., a man who had injured the left side of his brain in a motorcycle accident. His digit span was only about two items, and his recency effect was almost absent, yet his long-term learning was essentially normal. When one patient shows damage to function A with function B intact, and another shows the reverse, the result is a double dissociation , the strongest kind of neuropsychological evidence that two functions depend on different systems. Exam trap Who first observed the primacy-recency effect? Ebbinghaus noted in 1885 that the beginning and end of a list were learned first, and many textbooks credit him with the first observation of the serial position effect. The RML 2024 key, however, gives "McCray and Hunter", which refers to J. W. McCrary and W. S. Hunter, who published influential serial position curves for serial learning in 1953. If Ebbinghaus and McCrary and Hunter both appear, remember that the official key for that paper chose McCrary and Hunter, and that the historically earlier observation is Ebbinghaus's. Two more confusables: primacy and recency effects in impression formation and persuasion belong to the Social book, and primacy and recency as order effects in a psychophysics experiment are controlled by counterbalancing (Research Methodology book). Criticisms of the multi-store model The modal model gave memory research a common map, and the distinction between a small, fragile short-term store and a vast, durable long-term store has survived. But nearly every detail has been challenged. First, the stores are not unitary. Short-term memory turned out to have separate verbal and visual parts and an attentional controller, which is why it was replaced by the working memory model (Section 7.3); long-term memory turned out to contain several systems (Section 7.5). Second, rehearsal is not the royal road to long-term memory that the model assumed: simply repeating an item can keep it in short-term memory for as long as you like without making it much more memorable later (Section 7.4). Third, K.F. is a problem as well as a support: if information could reach long-term memory only by passing through short-term memory, his damaged short-term store should have crippled his long-term learning, and it did not. Fourth, the order of the stores is wrong in an important way: we can chunk IIT in short-term memory only because long-term memory has already been consulted, so long-term knowledge acts on information before and during its stay in short-term memory, not merely after it. Finally, the model treats short-term memory as a passive waiting room, when in daily life it is where we calculate, reason and understand. Exam trap "Which of the following is NOT a store in the stage model of memory?" The stage (multi-store) model has three stores: sensory, short-term and long-term. Working memory is not one of them; it is the separate model of Baddeley and Hitch (1974). A related question asks which store information must pass through before reaching long-term memory in the Atkinson and Shiffrin model: short-term memory, which some practice papers write as "short-term (working) memory" because Atkinson and Shiffrin themselves described the short-term store as a working memory.
