You must hold the numbers, carry out the steps, store the partial result (140) while you calculate the next one (28), and then combine them. Short-term memory in the Atkinson and Shiffrin sense, a passive box where items wait to be rehearsed or lost, does not capture what your mind just did. In 1974 Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed that short-term memory is better thought of as a working memory : a limited-capacity system for temporarily holding and manipulating information while we carry out complex tasks such as reasoning, comprehension, mental arithmetic and learning. The dual-task method and the case against a single store Baddeley and Hitch's main tool was the dual-task method : give people two tasks at once and see whether they interfere. The logic is simple. If two tasks need the same limited resource, doing them together will impair one or both; if they draw on different resources, they can be combined with little cost. In their key experiments, participants held a list of up to six digits (a full short-term memory load, by the multi-store account) while solving reasoning problems, such as deciding whether "A follows B" correctly describes the pair BA. If short-term memory were a single store, filling it with six digits should have wrecked the reasoning. It did not. Reasoning slowed somewhat, but accuracy held up. Baddeley and Hitch concluded that short-term memory has several components: a store that was occupied by the digits, and something else, which was still available to do the reasoning. The model that resulted originally had three components, a controlling central executive and two "slave" systems, the phonological loop and the visuospatial sketchpad. In 2000 Baddeley added a fourth, the episodic buffer. Figure 7.4 shows the model in its current form. Central executive attentional controller Visuospatial sketchpad visual cache and inner scribe Episodic buffer (added in 2000) binds information into episodes Phonological loop phonological store and articulatory control process Long-term memory visual semantics episodic long-term memory language Figure 7.4 Baddeley's working memory model (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974; episodic buffer added by Baddeley, 2000). The central executive directs attention but stores nothing; the three subsidiary systems hold information and exchange it with long-term memory. The phonological loop The phonological loop holds and rehearses speech-based, auditory-verbal information. It has two parts. The phonological store, sometimes called the inner ear, holds speech sounds for about two seconds before they fade. The articulatory control process, the inner voice, refreshes the contents of the store by silent rehearsal (the way you repeat a phone number under your breath) and converts written material into a speech code so that it can enter the store. Four findings support this account. The phonological similarity effect : lists of similar-sounding items (B, G, V, P, T) are recalled worse than dissimilar ones (F, W, K, R, Y), because similar sounds are confused in the store. This is Conrad's and Baddeley's finding from Section 7.2, now given a home. The word-length effect : memory span is greater for short words than long ones. Baddeley, Neil Thomson and Mary Buchanan (1975) found that people could recall about as many words as they could say in roughly two seconds, so span for words like "wit, sum, harm" is larger than for "university, opportunity, constitutional". Even words with the same number of syllables but longer spoken durations (Friday, harpoon) are recalled worse than quick ones (bishop, wicket). Digit span depends on language for the same reason: Nick Ellis and Richard Hennelly (1980) showed that Welsh-English bilingual children had smaller digit spans in Welsh, whose digit names take longer to say, than in English. articulatory suppression : if people repeat an irrelevant word aloud ("the, the, the") while studying a list, the articulatory process is occupied. Suppression abolishes the word-length effect, and with visually presented items it also abolishes the phonological similarity effect, because written items can no longer be recoded into sound and so never reach the store. With spoken items, the similarity effect survives, because heard speech enters the store directly. The irrelevant speech effect: background speech, even in a language the listener does not know, impairs serial recall of visually presented digits, whereas non-speech noise of the same loudness does not (Pierre Salamé and Baddeley, 1982). Speech gains automatic access to the phonological store. What is the loop for? Not, mainly, for remembering phone numbers. Baddeley and his colleagues argue that it evolved as a language-learning device: to learn a new word, you must hold its unfamiliar sound sequence long enough to build a long-term representation. A patient known as P.V., whose phonological store was damaged, could learn pairs of words in her own language normally but was almost unable to learn words in Russian, which offered nothing familiar to lean on. The visuospatial sketchpad The visuospatial sketchpad holds and manipulates visual and spatial information: the route from your hostel to the exam hall, the layout of your room in the dark, an image you rotate in your mind. Robert Logie (1995) divided it into a visual cache, which stores form and colour, and an inner scribe, which handles spatial and movement information and rehearses the contents of the cache. When Roger Shepard and Jacqueline Metzler (1971) showed that the time needed to decide whether two drawings show the same object increases steadily with the angle through which one must be mentally rotated, they were measuring the sketchpad at work; any question about the component of working memory that "mentally rotates an object" is asking for the visuospatial sketchpad. The dual-task evidence for a separate sketchpad is elegant. Lee Brooks (1968) asked people to imagine a block capital F and to move around its corners in their mind, classifying each corner as "yes" if it was on the extreme top or bottom and "no" otherwise. They could respond either by saying "yes" or "no" or by pointing to Y and N letters scattered over a sheet of paper. Pointing, which needs spatial control, made the imagery task much slower than speaking. With a verbal task (classifying the words of a remembered sentence), the reverse was true: speaking was slower than pointing. Spatial responses interfere with spatial memory and verbal responses with verbal memory, which is what separate visuospatial and phonological systems predict. Clinically, visuospatial span is measured with the Corsi block-tapping test, in which the examiner taps a sequence of blocks and the patient copies it. The central executive The central executive is the most important and least understood component. It is an attentional control system with no storage of its own. Baddeley (1996) listed its functions as focusing attention, dividing attention between tasks, switching attention, and linking working memory with long-term memory. He modelled it on Donald Norman and Tim Shallice's supervisory attentional system, which takes over from habit whenever a situation is new, difficult or dangerous. Later work by Akira Miyake and colleagues (2000) separated three related executive functions: inhibition of unwanted responses, shifting between tasks, and updating the contents of working memory. The best-known measure of inhibition is the Stroop task (John Ridley Stroop, 1935): naming the ink colour of a colour word printed in a conflicting colour (RED in blue ink) is slow because automatic reading competes with the controlled task of colour naming. The Stroop effect is therefore interference in selective attention, not the interference between memories that causes forgetting (Section 7.8); it is taught fully in Chapter 5. The classic way to load the central executive is random generation. Try saying a random sequence of digits for a minute: you must constantly monitor what you have said, suppress the habitual sequences (1, 2, 3 or your phone number) and decide what to say next. Random number or letter generation disrupts reasoning, planning and the selection of chess moves, and the more demanding the main task, the more random generation suffers. Damage to the frontal lobes, especially the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, produces what Baddeley and Barbara Wilson (1988) called the dysexecutive syndrome: poor planning, distractibility and perseveration, with memory stores themselves intact (Physiological book). The other options in that question each load a different component: continually repeating a word is articulatory suppression (phonological loop), remembering a spatial configuration loads the visuospatial sketchpad, and listening to irrelevant speech reaches the phonological store. Note too that the central executive stores nothing; if an option says it "holds verbal information", it is wrong. The episodic buffer By the late 1990s the three-part model had a problem. People can repeat back a meaningful sentence of fifteen or sixteen words, far more than the five or six unrelated words the phonological loop can hold. Some densely amnesic patients can recall a short prose passage immediately, at normal levels, although they will have forgotten it entirely an hour later. Where is all this information held, and where are words, images and meaning combined into a single experience? In 2000 Baddeley proposed the episodic buffer : a limited-capacity store, holding perhaps four chunks, that uses a multidimensional code to bind information from the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes. It is "episodic" because it holds integrated scenes or episodes, and a "buffer" because it serves as an interface between systems that use different codes. It is controlled by the central executive and is thought to be the place where we are consciously aware of the bound result. Exam trap The four components of working memory are the central executive, the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad and the episodic buffer. Distractors invent plausible-sounding parts: "visual executive loop", "verbal sketchpad", "semantic buffer". The phonological loop handles auditory-verbal information; the sketchpad handles visual and spatial information (including mental rotation); the episodic buffer integrates information into coherent episodes and was the one added in 2000. The original 1974 model had three components. Working memory versus short-term memory Are working memory and short-term memory just two names for the same thing? Not quite. Short-term memory refers to the temporary storage of information, measured by simple span tasks: hear a list, repeat it back. Working memory refers to storage combined with processing, measured by complex span tasks. In the reading span task of Meredyth Daneman and Patricia Carpenter (1980), for example, people read a series of sentences aloud and then try to recall the last word of each one; they must store words while processing sentences. Simple digit span repeated forwards is the classic short-term memory test; digit span repeated backwards requires the person to hold the sequence and reverse it, so it is treated as a working memory test. Working memory capacity, measured by complex span, predicts reading comprehension, reasoning and fluid intelligence far better than simple span does (Chapter 9). In short, short-term memory is a component of the larger working memory system; the multi-store model's single box became Baddeley's set of interacting parts. Clinical link Working memory tasks are central to cognitive assessment. The Wechsler intelligence scales combine forward, backward and sequenced digit span into a working memory index, and the Wechsler Memory Scale, Fourth Edition (WMS-IV), reports five index scores: Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory, Immediate Memory and Delayed Memory. Working memory deficits are prominent in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, schizophrenia and frontal lobe injury, and tests of executive function such as the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test tap the central executive. (Test details are in the Psychological Assessment book.) 7.4 Levels of Processing and the Quality of Encoding Medium yield · 4 Qs The multi-store model said that what gets into long-term memory depends on how long an item is rehearsed in short-term memory. Think about your own studying for a moment. Have you ever read a page five times and remembered nothing, and heard a single striking story once and remembered it for years? If so, you already suspect that the amount of rehearsal is not the whole story. In 1972 Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart turned that suspicion into a theory. Craik and Lockhart's framework (1972) Craik and Lockhart argued that memory is not a series of boxes but a by-product of the way information is processed. Incoming information can be analysed at different depths. At the shallowest level, structural (or orthographic) processing, we attend to physical appearance: is the word printed in capital letters? At an intermediate level, phonemic processing, we attend to sound: does the word rhyme with "weight"? At the deepest level, semantic processing, we attend to meaning: is it a kind of fish? Would it fit the sentence "He met a ___ in the street"? According to the levels of processing framework, deeper processing produces more elaborate, longer-lasting and stronger memory traces. Memory is what is left behind by the analyses that perception and comprehension perform, so the crucial question is not "How long did you rehearse it?" but "What did you do with it?" An important consequence is that the intention to learn matters very little. Thomas Hyde and James Jenkins (1973) gave people word lists with different orienting tasks: some rated each word for pleasantness (a semantic task), others checked whether the word contained the letters E or G (a structural task). Some participants in each condition were warned of a later memory test; others were not. Recall depended strongly on the orienting task and hardly at all on the warning: people who rated pleasantness without trying to learn remembered about as well as people who were deliberately trying to learn. What you do with information determines what you remember, whether or not you mean to remember it. Key study: Craik and Tulving (1975) Fergus Craik and Endel Tulving presented words, each preceded by a question that required one of three levels of processing: a structural question ("Is the word in capital letters?"), a phonemic question ("Does the word rhyme with WEIGHT?") or a semantic question ("Would the word fit the sentence 'He met a ___ in the street'?"). Participants did not know that a memory test would follow. On a later surprise recognition test, memory rose steadily from structural to phonemic to semantic questions, with semantic processing producing performance more than three times as good as structural processing. Words that received a "yes" answer were remembered better than "no" words, especially at the semantic level, because a "yes" word fits into a meaningful structure. Was depth just a disguise for time? Semantic questions take a little longer to answer. Craik and Tulving checked by devising a slow but shallow task (judging the pattern of consonants and vowels in a word). It took longer than the semantic task and still produced poorer memory. In a further experiment, words judged against complex sentence frames ("The great bird swooped down and carried off the struggling ___") were recalled about twice as well as words judged against simple frames ("She cooked the ___"): within the same level, more elaborate processing helped too. Maintenance versus elaborative rehearsal Craik and Lockhart drew a distinction that every student should use. maintenance rehearsal (which they called Type I processing) is the simple repetition of information at the same level, like repeating a phone number until you dial it. It keeps information available in short-term memory but adds little to long-term memory. elaborative rehearsal (Type II processing) links the information to other knowledge: thinking about what it means, how it relates to what you already know, what example illustrates it. It is elaborative rehearsal that builds durable memories. Craik and Michael Watkins (1973) demonstrated the difference neatly. Participants heard lists of words and had to keep in mind the most recent word beginning with a target letter, say G, so that some G-words were held in mind for a long time and others only briefly. On a surprise final recall test, the time a word had spent being maintained made almost no difference to whether it was remembered. Repetition kept words in mind; it did not make them memorable. Two further ideas extend the levels framework. Elaboration refers to the richness of processing within a level, as the complex sentences in Craik and Tulving's study showed. Distinctiveness refers to how different a trace is from other traces; a distinctive memory has fewer competitors at retrieval. Michael Eysenck and Christine Eysenck (1980) asked people to pronounce words with silent letters as they are spelled (the "b" in comb). This was shallow, phonemic processing, yet because it was distinctive it produced recognition as good as semantic processing. (The classic demonstration of distinctiveness, the von Restorff effect, is described in Section 7.8.) The self-reference, generation and dual-coding effects If semantic processing beats phonemic processing, is there anything deeper than meaning? In 1977 T. B. Rogers, Nicholas Kuiper and W. S. Kirker added a fourth orienting question to the classic three: "Does this word describe you?" Adjectives judged in relation to the self were recalled about twice as well as adjectives judged for meaning alone. This self-reference effect , the finding that information is remembered better when it is related to oneself, has been confirmed many times. The usual explanation is that the self is the richest, most organised and most often used body of knowledge each of us has, so linking a word to it provides both elaboration and organisation. Interestingly, in some collectivist cultures, relating words to one's mother produces almost as large an advantage as relating them to oneself, which suggests that what matters is an elaborate, well-organised knowledge structure rather than the self as such. The generation effect is the finding that information you produce yourself is remembered better than information you merely read. Norman Slamecka and Peter Graf (1978) had people either read word pairs (HOT and COLD) or generate the second word from a rule and a cue (an opposite of HOT beginning with C). Generated words were remembered better. The lesson for study is direct: an answer you work out for yourself is worth more than an answer you highlight. A third principle concerns images. Allan Paivio (1925 to 2016) proposed his dual coding theory in 1971: information can be represented in a verbal code and in an imagery code (in his later terms, by logogens and imagens). Concrete words such as "elephant" are easily coded both ways, so they have two routes to retrieval; abstract words such as "truth" are coded mainly verbally. Dual coding explains why concrete words are remembered better than abstract ones and why pictures are remembered better than words (the picture superiority effect), and it underlies the imagery mnemonics of Section 7.11. Exam trap The self-reference effect was demonstrated by Rogers, Kuiper and Kirker (1977); exam keys often write "Rogers and Kuiper". It is not Craik and Lockhart's, although it extends their framework. The other names offered in the RML 2024 question have their own claims: Allan Paivio is dual coding theory; Michael Posner is known for attention research and the letter-matching task (Chapter 5). And the "self-reference effect" is a memory phenomenon; the "sum of a person's impressions of himself", "the beliefs we hold about what we are like" and "the knowledge that we exist as separate individuals" describe self-concept, self-schema and self-awareness (Social and Personality books). Criticisms and transfer-appropriate processing The levels framework was enormously productive, but three criticisms stuck. The first is circularity. How do we know that a task involves deep processing? Because it produces good memory. Why does it produce good memory? Because it involves deep processing. Without an independent measure of depth, the theory cannot be tested properly; Alan Baddeley made this point forcefully in a 1978 critique. The second is that depth, elaboration and distinctiveness were never clearly separated or measured. The third, and most important, is that the framework looked only at encoding and ignored the conditions of retrieval. The third criticism came with an experiment by Donald Morris, John Bransford and Jeffery Franks (1977). Participants answered semantic or rhyme questions about words, as in the levels experiments. Then half of them took a standard recognition test, and half took a rhyming recognition test, in which they had to pick out new words that rhymed with words they had studied. On the standard test, semantic processing won, as usual. On the rhyming test, rhyme processing won. Deep processing is not better in any absolute sense; what matters is the match between the processing done at study and the processing demanded by the test. Morris and colleagues called this transfer-appropriate processing . It is a close cousin of Tulving's encoding specificity principle (Section 7.7), and it explains why practising with past papers in exam format is so valuable: the processing you rehearse is the processing the exam will require. Remember Levels of processing: Craik and Lockhart (1972). The three levels from shallow to deep: structural, phonemic, semantic. Best retention: deep, semantic, elaborate processing. Maintenance rehearsal keeps; elaborative rehearsal stores. Main criticism: circularity. Main rival: transfer-appropriate processing (Morris, Bransford and Franks, 1977). If long-term memory were a single store, this pattern would be impossible. The modern view, built from just such cases, is that long-term memory is a family of systems that store different kinds of information, operate by different rules and depend on different parts of the brain. Episodic, semantic and procedural memory In 1972 the Estonian-born Canadian psychologist Endel Tulving (1927 to 2023) proposed a distinction that is now part of everyday psychology. episodic memory is memory for personally experienced events, each located in a particular time and place: what happened, where it happened and when. Remembering your first day of college, or what you ate for dinner last night, is episodic memory. semantic memory is general knowledge about the world: facts, concepts, word meanings and rules, held without any memory of when or where they were learned. Knowing that Mysuru is in Karnataka, that a sparrow is a bird and that "anterograde" means forward-acting is semantic memory. Semantic memory is often described as a vast network of associated facts and concepts that make up our knowledge of the world (Section 7.6). Because its contents are generalised across many experiences rather than tied to one, some textbooks call it generic memory . Tulving later (1985) tied each kind of memory to a kind of consciousness. Episodic remembering involves autonoetic consciousness ("self-knowing"), the feeling of mentally travelling back in time and re-experiencing an event as one's own. Semantic memory involves noetic consciousness ("knowing"), an awareness of facts without reliving anything. Procedural memory involves anoetic ("non-knowing") consciousness, with no awareness of the memory at all. Tulving turned this into a simple test, the remember-know procedure: when you recognise a word from a list, do you "remember" seeing it (you can recall the moment, what you thought) or do you just "know" it was there? Remember responses reflect episodic recollection; know responses reflect familiarity. The third major kind of long-term memory is procedural memory , memory for how to do things: riding a bicycle, tying shoelaces, typing, playing the piano. The philosopher Gilbert Ryle (1949) had already distinguished "knowing that" from "knowing how", and in 1980 Neal Cohen and Larry Squire used the same contrast to separate declarative from procedural memory. Procedural memories are acquired gradually through practice, are expressed in performance rather than words, and are remarkably resistant both to forgetting and to brain damage that devastates episodic memory. The strongest evidence that episodic and semantic memory are separable is again neuropsychological. Tulving's patient K.C. (Kent Cochrane, 1951 to 2014) suffered a motorcycle accident in 1981 that damaged his medial temporal lobes and other regions. Afterwards his general knowledge, language and intelligence were normal; he knew facts about his own life, such as the address of the family's summer cottage. Yet he could not recall a single event that he had personally experienced, at any point in his life. K.C. was the man who could not travel back in time. The opposite pattern appears in semantic dementia, a degenerative disease of the anterior temporal lobes in which patients progressively lose the meanings of words and concepts while their memory for recent personal events is relatively spared. Table 7.4 summarises Tulving's three kinds of long-term memory. Table 7.4 Tulving's three kinds of long-term memory. Kind Content Type of awareness Example Key evidence Episodic Personal events, located in time and place Autonoetic (re-experiencing) Your first day of college K.C. lost it; semantic spared Semantic General facts and concepts Noetic (knowing) Mysuru is in Karnataka Lost in semantic dementia Procedural Skills and habits Anoetic (no awareness) Riding a bicycle Spared in H.M. and Clive Wearing Explicit and implicit memory A second way of dividing long-term memory cuts across Tulving's. explicit memory involves conscious recollection of information or of the situation in which it was learned; it is tested by recall and recognition. implicit memory is an influence of past experience on behaviour, feelings or thoughts without any conscious recollection of that experience. The terms were introduced by Peter Graf and Daniel Schacter in 1985. Larry Squire's preferred terms, declarative and nondeclarative memory, mean almost the same thing: declarative memory can be "declared" (stated in words); nondeclarative memory is expressed through performance. Implicit memory was discovered through amnesia. In 1911 the Swiss psychologist Édouard Claparède hid a pin in his hand and pricked an amnesic patient as they shook hands. Next time, she refused to shake his hand, although she had no memory of the pinprick and could not say why; when pressed, she offered only that "sometimes pins are hidden in people's hands". In the 1960s and 1970s Elizabeth Warrington and Lawrence Weiskrantz found that amnesic patients who could not recall or recognise a list of words nevertheless identified fragmented versions of those words more easily, and completed word stems with them, just as normal people did. Graf, Squire and George Mandler (1984) sharpened the contrast: given the stem MOT___, amnesic patients told to recall a studied word performed poorly, but told simply to write the first word that came to mind, they produced the studied word (MOTEL) as often as healthy participants. The same memory trace, tested two ways, was absent explicitly and intact implicitly. H.M., the most studied amnesic patient (Section 7.10), showed the same dissociation for skills. Asked to trace a star while watching his hand only in a mirror, he improved steadily over three days of practice, just like anyone else, while denying each day that he had ever done the task before. Squire gathered these findings into the taxonomy shown in Figure 7.5. Declarative memory (episodic and semantic) depends on the hippocampus and the surrounding medial temporal lobe. Nondeclarative memory is a collection of quite different abilities: procedural skills and habits (dependent on the striatum, part of the basal ganglia), priming (dependent on the neocortex), simple classical conditioning (the amygdala for emotional responses, the cerebellum for skeletal responses such as the conditioned eyeblink), and non-associative learning such as habituation and sensitisation (dependent on reflex pathways; Chapter 6). Amnesic patients lose the left branch and keep the right. Exam trap Implicit memory does NOT involve conscious recollection; that is the definition of explicit memory. A "which statement does not accurately reflect these terms" question will usually hide this swap ("implicit memory involves a conscious recollection of the original events"). Also note the matched pairs: explicit = declarative = conscious recollection = recall and recognition; implicit = nondeclarative = performance without awareness = priming, skills, conditioning. Procedural memory is one kind of implicit memory, not a synonym for it. Priming priming is a change in the speed, accuracy or likelihood of processing a stimulus as a result of earlier exposure to the same or a related stimulus, without any intention to remember. In repetition priming (also called direct or perceptual priming), the earlier stimulus is the same item: having read "assassin" on a list, you are more likely to complete the fragment _ss_ss_n correctly later, even if you cannot recognise "assassin" as a word from the list (Tulving, Schacter and Stark, 1982). In semantic priming , the earlier stimulus is related in meaning. David Meyer and Roger Schvaneveldt (1971) asked people to decide as quickly as possible whether strings of letters were words (a lexical decision task). People recognised BUTTER as a word faster when it followed BREAD than when it followed NURSE. The prime activated a region of semantic memory, and activation spread to related concepts (Section 7.6). Priming can occur even when the prime is not consciously seen. In masked priming, a word is flashed for a few milliseconds and immediately covered by a pattern mask, so that people cannot report it; yet it still speeds responses to related words. Anthony Marcel (1983) used this method to argue for semantic processing without awareness, and masked semantic priming became one of the main techniques for studying subliminal perception (Chapter 5). Exam trap An RML 2022 question asks what "semantic priming" is used to study and keys "subliminal perception". Semantic priming is, first of all, a tool for studying the organisation of semantic memory and spreading activation. Its masked (subliminal) form is the standard way of showing that meaning can be processed without awareness, which is why the key chose subliminal perception from options that otherwise belong to other subjects (signal detection is psychophysics, field dependence is a cognitive style, locus of control is personality). If "semantic memory organisation" were offered, it would be the better answer. Autobiographical memory and the reminiscence bump autobiographical memory is memory for the events and facts of one's own life. It contains specific episodes (the day you received your Class 12 results) and personal semantic facts (the name of your school, your father's occupation), organised around the self and its goals. It is the memory that makes you a person with a history. Francis Galton (1879) pioneered its study with the cue-word technique, revived by Herbert Crovitz and Harold Schiffman (1974): give a person a word such as "river" or "fire" and ask for the first specific personal memory it brings to mind, then ask how old they were at the time. When adults over about forty are tested this way and their memories are plotted against age at the time of the event, a characteristic curve appears. Hardly any memories come from the first three or four years (infantile amnesia, Section 7.10). Many come from the last few years (ordinary recency). And there is a surprising hump of extra memories from the ages of about 10 to 30: the reminiscence bump , described by David Rubin, Scott Wetzler and Robert Nebes (1986). Explanations include the many "firsts" of adolescence and early adulthood (first love, first job, leaving home), which are novel and distinctive; the formation of a stable identity in those years, so that events become anchors of the self; the peak of cognitive efficiency; and a cultural life script, which tells us that the major events of a life (marriage, career, children) happen in that period, so that we search our memories accordingly. A handful of people have astonishingly complete autobiographical memories. The first described, A.J. (Elizabeth Parker, Larry Cahill and James McGaugh, 2006), could name the day of the week and the events of almost any date from her adolescence onwards. This highly superior autobiographical memory, or hyperthymesia, is not a general super-memory: such people are ordinary at memorising lists. Prospective versus retrospective memory Almost everything so far concerns retrospective memory , remembering information or events from the past. prospective memory is remembering to carry out an intended action in the future: to take a tablet at 8 p.m., to buy milk on the way home, to pass on a message when you see a friend. Gilles Einstein and Mark McDaniel (1990) distinguished event-based prospective memory, triggered by an external cue (seeing your friend reminds you of the message), from time-based prospective memory, which must be self-initiated at the right time (remembering at 8 p.m. that it is time for the tablet). Time-based tasks are generally harder because nothing in the environment prompts them. Prospective memory failures are the commonest memory complaints of everyday life, and in clinical work they matter enormously: a patient who forgets to take medication is a patient whose treatment fails. Flashbulb memories Many people in India can tell you exactly where they were when they heard about the attacks on Mumbai in November 2008, or when they watched the final of the 2011 Cricket World Cup. In 1977 Roger Brown (1925 to 1997) and James Kulik named such memories flashbulb memory : vivid, detailed and long-lasting memories of the circumstances in which a person learned of a surprising, emotionally significant event. Their main example was the assassination of President John F. Kennedy in 1963. People typically recalled where they were, what they were doing, who told them, how they felt, how others felt and what happened next. Brown and Kulik proposed that a special neural mechanism, which they called "Now Print!" (borrowing the phrase from the neuroscientist Robert Livingston), was triggered by events that were surprising and consequential and fixed the whole scene like a photograph. Key study: Neisser and Harsch and the Challenger disaster (1992) On 28 January 1986 the space shuttle Challenger exploded shortly after launch. The next morning, Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch asked students at Emory University to write down how they had heard the news. About two and a half years later they found 44 of these students and asked them the same questions. The memories had changed dramatically. A typical student who had first written that she heard the news in a religion class, when people started talking, later "remembered" that she had been in her dormitory with her roommate when the news came on television. About a quarter of the students were wrong about every major detail, and few were right about all of them. Yet confidence ratings were high. Some students, shown their own handwritten accounts from the morning after, insisted that their current memory must be the correct one. The same pattern appeared after the attacks of 11 September 2001. On 12 September, Jennifer Talarico and David Rubin (2003) asked 54 students at Duke University to record how they had heard the news, and also to record an ordinary memory from the preceding days, such as a party or a study session. They retested each student 1, 6 or 32 weeks later. Both kinds of memory lost consistency at the same rate: details changed, dropped out or were added. What differed was the experience of remembering. Flashbulb memories stayed far more vivid, and students' belief in their accuracy stayed high, while their accuracy fell. Kathy Pezdek (2003) found that 73 per cent of American students said they had seen the television footage of the first plane hitting the World Trade Center on 11 September itself; no such footage was broadcast that day. So flashbulb memories are special in their vividness and in the confidence they inspire, not in their accuracy. No special "Now Print!" mechanism is needed to explain them. Two ordinary processes do the work: emotional arousal at encoding (which, through the amygdala and stress hormones, strengthens the central features of an experience) and repeated rehearsal and retelling afterwards, through conversation and news coverage, which keeps the story alive while slowly reshaping it. Exam trap Flashbulb memories: Brown and Kulik (1977). Vividness and confidence are very high and stay high; accuracy and consistency decline like those of ordinary memories (Neisser and Harsch, 1992; Talarico and Rubin, 2003, whose title was "Confidence, not consistency, characterizes flashbulb memories"). The current explanation is emotional arousal plus rehearsal, not a special Now Print! mechanism, not freedom from interference and not eidetic imagery. Do not confuse "flashbulb memory" (an emotional autobiographical memory) with "eidetic imagery" (a lingering visual image) or with an "engram" (the physical memory trace, Section 7.10). Eidetic imagery and exceptional memory Is there such a thing as photographic memory? The nearest thing that has been reliably demonstrated is eidetic imagery : a visual image that persists for half a minute or more after a picture is removed, vivid enough that the person can scan it with their eyes and describe details they did not notice while the picture was present. Ralph Haber and Ruth Haber (1964) found it in a small minority of primary school children (estimates range from about 2 to 10 per cent); it is very rare in adults. Even eidetic images are not photographs: they fade, they contain errors, and the children who have them do not have better memories in general. The most famous mnemonist in psychology, the Russian journalist Solomon Shereshevsky, studied for thirty years by Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977) and described in The Mind of a Mnemonist (1968), could reproduce long tables of numbers and lists of words, forwards or backwards, even years later. He did it not with an eidetic image but with intense synaesthesia (words evoked colours, tastes and textures) and by placing images along an imagined street, the method of loci (Section 7.11). His problem was the opposite of ours: he found it hard to forget, and hard to grasp the general meaning of a passage through the crowd of images it evoked. Metamemory: feeling of knowing and the tip of the tongue metamemory is knowledge about one's own memory and the ability to monitor and control it: knowing that you remember lists better if you organise them, judging whether you have learned a chapter well enough, sensing that you know an answer you cannot yet retrieve. The term was introduced by John Flavell (1928 to 2025) in 1971, and metamemory is part of his broader concept of metacognition, thinking about one's own thinking. A person who is very good at planning, monitoring and controlling every phase of the memory system, from what to attend to, to how to rehearse, to how to search memory, is showing good metacognition. Metamemory has two sides: monitoring (judging the state of one's memory) and control (acting on that judgement, for example by restudying what feels weak). Monitoring is often surprisingly accurate. J. T. Hart (1965) asked people general-knowledge questions; when they could not recall an answer, he asked them to rate their feeling of knowing , that is, how likely they were to recognise it among alternatives. Their ratings predicted later recognition well above chance. But monitoring can also mislead: rereading a chapter makes it feel familiar and fluent, which students mistake for having learned it, an illusion of competence that explains why rereading is such a poor study method (Section 7.11). Key study: Brown and McNeill, the tip of the tongue (1966) William James described it in 1890: a gap that is "intensely active", in which the sought name beckons and then retreats. Roger Brown and David McNeill set out to catch the tip-of-the-tongue state in the laboratory. They read out dictionary definitions of rare words, such as "a navigational instrument used in measuring angular distances, especially the altitude of the sun, moon and stars at sea" (sextant). Sometimes participants knew the word at once and sometimes they had no idea, but quite often they were in agony: sure they knew it, unable to produce it. In those states they could guess the first letter and the number of syllables well above chance, and they produced words with similar sounds (secant, sextet) and similar meanings (astrolabe, compass). The memory was clearly stored, and partly accessible; the failure was one of retrieval. Tip-of-the-tongue states become more frequent with age, are more common for proper names than for other words, and are more frequent in bilinguals. They are the best everyday evidence that much forgetting is a failure of retrieval rather than of storage, a theme taken up in Sections 7.7 and 7.8. They are not aphasia: in Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension) and Broca's aphasia (laboured, non-fluent speech), language itself is damaged (Physiological book), whereas the tip-of-the-tongue state is a temporary failure to retrieve one well-known word. 7.6 How Knowledge Is Organised: Networks, Schemas and Scripts Medium yield · 4 Qs Semantic memory holds an enormous amount of knowledge, yet you can answer "Is a canary a bird?" in about a second. That speed is only possible if knowledge is organised. How? Psychologists have proposed several kinds of organisation, from tidy hierarchies to sprawling webs to patterns of connection strength spread across a whole network. The hierarchical network model (Collins and Quillian, 1969) Allan Collins and Ross Quillian (1969) proposed that semantic memory is a network of nodes, each representing a concept, linked into a hierarchy (Figure 7.6). Properties are attached to the nodes they belong to. The hierarchical network model adds one more assumption, the principle of cognitive economy : each property is stored only once, at the highest level in the hierarchy to which it applies. "Has skin" is stored with ANIMAL, not separately with every animal; "can fly" is stored with BIRD; "can sing" with CANARY. Exceptions are stored at the lower node ("cannot fly" with OSTRICH). ANIMAL has skin, can move eats, breathes BIRD has wings can fly has feathers FISH has fins can swim has gills CANARY can sing is yellow OSTRICH has thin legs is tall cannot fly SHARK can bite is dangerous SALMON is pink is edible swims upstream canary can sing: 0 links canary can fly: 1 link canary has skin: 2 links Each property is stored once, at the highest level it applies to (cognitive economy) Figure 7.6 Part of the hierarchical network of Collins and Quillian (1969). To verify "A canary has skin", the search must travel up two links to ANIMAL, so it takes longer than verifying "A canary can sing", which is stored at the CANARY node itself. The model makes a precise prediction. To verify a sentence, you must find the relevant property by travelling along the links, and each link takes time. Collins and Quillian measured how long people took to verify sentences in a sentence verification task. "A canary can sing" (property at the same node, zero links) was verified fastest, "A canary can fly" (one link up) more slowly, and "A canary has skin" (two links up) more slowly still. Category sentences behaved the same way: "A canary is a bird" was faster than "A canary is an animal". Each level added a roughly constant increment of time, just as the model predicted. But the model ran into trouble. First, the typicality effect: Lance Rips, Edward Shoben and Edward Smith (1973) found that "A robin is a bird" is verified faster than "A penguin is a bird", although both are one link apart. Some members of a category are better examples than others (the idea of prototypes, developed by Eleanor Rosch, is taught in Chapter 8). Second, the hierarchy is sometimes violated: a sentence such as "A dog is an animal" is often verified faster than "A dog is a mammal", although "mammal" should be one link closer. Third, Carol Conrad (1972) showed that the apparent effect of hierarchical distance was partly an effect of familiarity: properties such as "can sing" are more often thought about in connection with canaries than "has skin" is. These problems led Smith, Shoben and Rips (1974) to propose a feature comparison model, in which concepts are lists of defining and characteristic features and verification compares feature lists, and led Collins to a more flexible network. Spreading activation (Collins and Loftus, 1975) In 1975 Allan Collins and Elizabeth Loftus (born 1944) abandoned the strict hierarchy. In their spreading activation model, semantic memory is a web of concept nodes, and the length of each link represents how closely the two concepts are related: FIRE ENGINE is close to RED and TRUCK, further from CHERRIES. When a concept is processed, activation spreads outwards along its links, weakening with distance and over time, and partially activates related concepts. A concept that is already partly active is easier to retrieve. This explains semantic priming at once: reading BREAD sends activation to BUTTER, which is then recognised faster. It also explains typicality, because typical members (robin) are closely linked to the category node (BIRD) and atypical members (penguin) are distant. The model's flexibility is also its weakness: with link lengths set to fit the data, it is hard to imagine a result it could not explain. Propositions and connectionist networks Knowledge is not only a set of concepts; it is a set of relations among them. A proposition is the smallest unit of knowledge that can be judged true or false, such as "Ravi studies memory" or "the exam is in October". Propositional network models, such as John R. Anderson's adaptive control of thought (ACT) theory and its successors, represent knowledge as networks of interlinked propositions. Propositions are what we keep when we keep the gist of a sentence and lose its words, as in Sachs's study. (In a question about the "meaningful units" that define working memory capacity, however, the answer is chunks, not propositions, features or scripts.) A more radical alternative came in 1986, when David Rumelhart, James McClelland and the PDP Research Group published Parallel Distributed Processing . connectionism , also called parallel distributed processing (PDP), models memory as a network of simple, neuron-like units (nodes) connected by links of varying strength, or weight. Unlike the earlier semantic networks, a concept is not stored in one node. It is a pattern of activation distributed across many units, and the knowledge of the network lies in its connection weights. Processing is parallel: many units activate one another at the same time. Learning consists of adjusting the weights after experience, a modern version of Donald Hebb's (1949) idea that connections between neurons that fire together are strengthened. Connectionist networks have three properties that resemble human memory. They are content-addressable (any part of a memory can retrieve the rest, as a smell can bring back a whole day). They degrade gracefully (damage to some units blurs memories rather than deleting particular ones, rather like the effect of diffuse brain damage, and recalling Karl Lashley's search for the engram, Section 7.10). And they generalise automatically from examples to new cases. Exam trap "Which model proposes that memory is organised in a network of interconnected nodes?" (IHBAS 2024) keys the connectionist model, although "network model" is also offered. Both Collins and Quillian's semantic network and connectionist models use nodes and links. The distinguishing features of connectionism (parallel distributed processing, Rumelhart and McClelland, 1986) are distributed representation, simultaneous (parallel) activation of many interconnected nodes, and knowledge stored in connection weights. When a question stresses "parallel", "distributed", "simultaneous activation" or "neural network", choose connectionist or PDP; when it stresses a hierarchy, cognitive economy or sentence verification time, choose Collins and Quillian's hierarchical network model; when it stresses activation spreading to related concepts, choose Collins and Loftus. Schemas and scripts Read this passage once: "The procedure is actually quite simple. First you arrange things into different groups. Of course, one pile may be sufficient depending on how much there is to do. If you have to go somewhere else due to lack of facilities, that is the next step..." John Bransford and Marcia Johnson (1972) gave passages like this to students. Without a title it is nearly incomprehensible and is poorly recalled. Told beforehand that it is about washing clothes, students found it easy to understand and recalled about twice as much. (A title given after reading did not help.) The title activated a schema. A schema is an organised body of knowledge, built from experience, about a concept, object, person, event or situation, which guides how new information is perceived, interpreted, encoded and remembered. The term entered memory research through Frederic Bartlett (1932; Section 7.9). Schemas are economical: they let us fill gaps, make predictions and understand quickly. The price is distortion: we remember what fits the schema, add what the schema leads us to expect, and drop or alter what does not fit. William Brewer and James Treyens (1981) asked students to wait for about half a minute in a room they were told was a graduate student's office. Later asked to recall the contents of the room, many "remembered" books, which an office ought to contain but this one did not, while missing unusual objects that did not fit the office schema. The "schema approach" to memory and social understanding is simply the study of how such organised knowledge shapes what we notice and recall. A script is a schema for a familiar, routine sequence of events. The concept was introduced by Roger Schank and Robert Abelson in 1977, whose best-known example is the restaurant script: enter, wait to be seated, read the menu, order, eat, pay, leave. An Indian example is the script for a wedding or for taking a train journey: book the ticket, check the platform, find your coach and berth, show the ticket to the conductor. Gordon Bower, John Black and Terrence Turner (1979) found that when people read stories about routine activities, they later "remembered" script actions that had not been mentioned. Scripts belong to generic (semantic) memory: they are abstracted from many similar episodes, which is why the developmental psychologist Katherine Nelson found that young children can tell you what happens at a birthday party in general well before they can recount a particular party. Exam trap "Which type of memory produces scripts of familiar routines?" Generic memory (RML 2025), the same thing as general, semantic knowledge abstracted from many episodes. Episodic and autobiographical memory hold particular episodes; a script is precisely what is left when the particulars are stripped away. And "how people organise information in memory and use it to understand behaviour" describes the schema approach. Schema theory is Bartlett's (1932), not Wundt's, Titchener's or Watson's. The re-experiencing that accompanies episodic recall is called consciousness. Tulving's patient lost all episodic memory for his life but kept his semantic knowledge. Memory without conscious recollection, such as priming, is called memory. Recognising BUTTER faster after BREAD than after NURSE is an example of priming. The excess of memories from ages 10 to 30 in older adults is the . Remembering to take a tablet at 8 p.m. is memory. Flashbulb memories were named by Brown and in 1977; their accuracy declines, but confidence stays high. Brown and McNeill studied the state, which shows that the failure is one of retrieval. In Collins and Quillian's model, storing each property only at the highest applicable node is called . Answers: (1) semantic, (2) autonoetic, (3) K.C., (4) implicit, (5) semantic, (6) reminiscence bump, (7) prospective, (8) Kulik, (9) tip-of-the-tongue, (10) cognitive economy. 7.7 Retrieval: Cues, Context and State Medium yield · 3 Qs You walk into the kitchen and cannot remember what you came for. You go back to your desk, and the moment you sit down, it comes back: the glass of water. The memory was there all along; what changed was the setting in which you searched for it. This section is about the conditions that make stored information accessible. Availability, accessibility and retrieval cues Endel Tulving and Zena Pearlstone (1966) gave people long lists of words drawn from several categories (animals, fruits, professions and so on). At test, one group simply recalled as many words as they could; the other group was given the category names as prompts. The prompted group recalled far more words. The words the first group failed to recall had not been lost: they were available (stored) but not accessible (retrievable without help). A retrieval cue is any stimulus, internal or external, that helps us gain access to a stored memory: a category name, a smell, a place, a question, a mood. The availability-accessibility distinction also explains why recognition is usually easier than recall. According to the generate-recognise (two-stage) account, recall involves two steps: generating possible candidates from memory, then recognising which of them are correct. A recognition test supplies the candidates, so only the second step is needed. A multiple-choice question is easier than the same question with blanks because the options themselves act as powerful retrieval cues. The encoding specificity principle Which cues work best? In 1973 Endel Tulving and Donald Thomson gave the answer that now organises the whole field. The encoding specificity principle states that a retrieval cue is effective to the extent that the information it contains was encoded together with the memory at the time of learning. Memory traces are not stored in isolation; they are stored together with the context, thoughts and associations present at encoding, and retrieval succeeds when the cue reinstates enough of that encoded package. Tulving and Thomson's evidence was striking. Participants studied target words paired with weak associates (glue and CHAIR). At test, the weak associate (glue) was a better cue for CHAIR than a strong associate such as "table", even though "table" is far more closely linked to "chair" in general knowledge, because "table" had not been part of the encoded event. In a further twist, participants sometimes failed to recognise a target word when it was presented on its own, yet recalled it moments later when given its weak study partner. This recognition failure of recallable words embarrasses the generate-recognise account, which predicts that anything recallable must also be recognisable, and it shows how strongly memory depends on the match between encoding and retrieval. Transfer-appropriate processing (Section 7.4) is the same idea applied to types of processing. Context-dependent memory The external environment is part of what gets encoded. context-dependent memory is the finding that recall is better when the physical context at retrieval matches the context at encoding. Key study: Godden and Baddeley's divers (1975) Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley worked with members of a university diving club. The divers listened to lists of unrelated words either on the beach or several metres under the sea (accounts of the exact depth differ), and later recalled them either in the same environment or in the other one. Words learned underwater were best recalled underwater; words learned on land were best recalled on land. Changing the context reduced recall by roughly a third. The study has become the classic demonstration of context-dependent memory. Five years later, however, the same researchers found that changing the environment had no effect on recognition (Godden and Baddeley, 1980). Context helps mainly when we must generate the memory ourselves; when the test provides the item, the item itself is a strong enough cue. Context effects in everyday settings are real but often small, because rich internal cues (the meaning of the question) usually outweigh the room. One study of real university examinations found no difference between students tested in their usual lecture room and those tested elsewhere. A useful finding for exam candidates is that the context does not have to be physically present: Steven Smith (1979) found that simply imagining the room in which material was learned restored much of the benefit. Mentally reinstating the context is also the first technique of the cognitive interview used with eyewitnesses (Section 7.9). State-dependent memory The internal environment matters too. state-dependent memory is the finding that recall is better when a person's physiological or drug-induced state at retrieval matches their state at encoding. Donald Goodwin and his colleagues (1969) had volunteers learn material either sober or after drinking alcohol, and test it either sober or intoxicated. As expected, alcohol at learning impaired memory overall; but material learned while intoxicated was recalled better when the person was intoxicated again than when sober. Clinical reports describe heavy drinkers who hide money or bottles while drunk, cannot find them when sober, and remember the hiding place when they next get drunk. Similar effects have been found with marijuana, nicotine and other drugs. As with context, state-dependent effects are strongest in free recall and weak or absent in cued recall and recognition, where better cues are available (Eric Eich, 1980). A caution about alcohol "blackouts": heavy intoxication can block the formation of new long-term memories altogether (an alcohol-induced anterograde amnesia), and no change of state can bring back what was never stored. Only memories that were encoded but became inaccessible on sobering up show the state-dependent pattern. Mood-dependent and mood-congruent memory Mood is an internal state as well, and it produces two different effects that students often confuse. In mood-dependent memory, recall is better when one's mood at retrieval matches one's mood at encoding, whatever the emotional tone of the material. In mood-congruent memory , people tend to learn and recall material whose emotional tone matches their current mood: when sad, sad memories come to mind more easily; when happy, happy ones. Gordon Bower (1932 to 2020) reported both effects in 1981, using hypnosis to induce happy or sad moods; later studies found mood-congruent memory to be the more robust of the two. Table 7.5 sets all of these matching effects side by side. Clinical link Mood-congruent memory helps explain why depression feeds itself. A depressed person recalls failures, losses and rejections more readily than successes, which deepens the low mood, which makes negative memories still more accessible. Depressed patients also tend to produce overgeneral autobiographical memories ("I always mess things up") instead of specific episodes when given cue words, a pattern linked to poorer recovery. Cognitive therapy's insistence on examining specific situations and evidence is, among other things, a way of breaking this retrieval cycle (Clinical book). Alcohol-induced amnesia that lifts on re-intoxication is the classic example of state-dependent memory. 7.8 Forgetting High yield · 10 Qs Ebbinghaus showed how fast we forget; he did not show why. Psychologists have offered five main explanations: decay, interference, retrieval failure, motivated forgetting and consolidation failure. Before we examine them, one point is worth making. Forgetting is not simply a defect. A memory that kept everything would drown the important in the trivial, as Shereshevsky found (Section 7.5). By letting unused information fade, forgetting clears the way for current information, reduces interference and helps us abstract general knowledge from particular cases. Retention and forgetting are two sides of one coin: the more that is retained, the less that is forgotten, never the reverse. Decay (trace) theory The oldest and most intuitive explanation is decay theory , also called trace decay theory: learning leaves a physical trace (an engram) in the nervous system, and if the trace is not used, it fades with the passage of time, like a footpath that grows over when nobody walks on it. In psychology, the idea is traditionally credited to Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949), whose law of disuse (the companion of his law of use, together forming the law of exercise; Chapter 6) held that connections not exercised grow weaker. Decay fits the shape of Ebbinghaus's curve and the rapid loss from sensory memory. The trouble is that time never passes empty. While time passes, other things are learned. In 1932 John McGeoch made the classic objection: iron rusts over time, but time does not cause rust; oxidation does. In the same way, forgetting happens over time, but what causes it might be the events that fill the time. The decisive test is to let time pass while reducing those events, and the classic attempt is one of the most quoted studies in memory research. Key study: Jenkins and Dallenbach, sleep versus waking (1924) John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach had two students learn lists of ten nonsense syllables, either late at night just before going to sleep or in the morning before their usual activities. Recall was tested after 1, 2, 4 or 8 hours. After a night's sleep, forgetting was modest and levelled off after about two hours; after eight hours, more than half of the syllables were still recalled. After the same time spent awake, forgetting continued steadily, and after eight hours only about one syllable in ten survived. Since the same amount of time had passed in both conditions, decay could not explain the difference. Jenkins and Dallenbach concluded that forgetting depends less on the passage of time than on "the interference, inhibition or obliteration of the old by the new". Later studies pointed the same way. Cockroaches that were immobilised after learning forgot less than those left free to move about (Minami and Dallenbach, 1946). Baddeley and Hitch (1977) asked rugby players to recall the teams they had played that season; how much they forgot depended on how many games they had played since, not on how much time had passed. One qualification is important: we now know that sleep does more than protect memories from interference; it actively helps to consolidate them (Section 7.10). Exam trap "Who developed the decay theory?" The RML 2024 key is Thorndike, through his law of disuse. Ebbinghaus described the time course of forgetting but did not propose decay as its cause; Tulving is cue-dependent forgetting; Melton and Irwin are the two-factor theory of interference. In short-term memory, the Brown-Peterson studies were first read as evidence for decay and then reinterpreted as interference (Section 7.2). Interference theory interference theory holds that forgetting occurs because other memories compete with or disrupt the one we are trying to retrieve. John Bergström reported the first experiments on interference in the early 1890s, using a card-sorting task in which learning new sorting locations disrupted the old ones. In 1900 Georg Elias Müller and Alfons Pilzecker showed that an activity interpolated between learning and recall impaired memory, and named the effect retroactive inhibition. In the 1930s McGeoch made interference the leading theory of forgetting. There are two directions of interference, and they are among the most examined ideas in this chapter. proactive interference (PI) occurs when earlier learning disrupts the learning or recall of newer information: the old interferes forward with the new. retroactive interference (RI) occurs when newer learning disrupts the recall of older information: the new interferes backward with the old. A simple way to keep them straight: PRO means forward, so in proactive interference old memories push forward and disrupt new ones; RETRO means backward, so in retroactive interference new memories reach back and disrupt old ones. In four words: PRO = old disrupts new; RETRO = new disrupts old. Work through these cases. You change your mobile number and keep giving people your old one: the old number is disrupting the new one, so this is proactive interference. Years later, you cannot remember your old number at all, because the new one has replaced it: retroactive interference. A student studies psychology, then sociology, and finds the psychology getting in the way when she is tested on sociology: the earlier learning disrupts the later, so proactive interference. If instead she is tested on psychology and finds sociology concepts intruding, that is retroactive interference. An English speaker learning Spanish who keeps applying English grammar is suffering from the earlier language disrupting the newer one: proactive interference. In the laboratory, interference is studied with paired-associate lists in which the same stimulus terms are paired with different responses: list A-B (for example, DOG-table) followed by list A-C (DOG-river). Table 7.6 shows the two designs. Notice that the difference between them lies only in which list is tested. Table 7.6 Experimental designs for retroactive and proactive interference. First, interference increases with similarity: John McGeoch and William McDonald (1931) found that an interpolated list of synonyms of the original words produced much more retroactive interference than unrelated words or numbers. Second, proactive interference is the larger cause of forgetting in the laboratory. Benton Underwood (1957) noticed that participants in experiments who had already learned many lists forgot a new list far more quickly over 24 hours than naive participants, and that the forgetting rose steeply with the number of earlier lists. Ebbinghaus, who had learned thousands of lists, was the extreme case: his own forgetting curve was probably steeper than that of a naive learner. Third, interference has two components. Arthur Melton and J. M. Irwin (1940) proposed a two-factor theory: response competition (the A-B and A-C responses compete at recall) and unlearning of the first list during learning of the second, which they called "factor X". Jean Barnes and Underwood (1959) showed that the first-list responses are indeed weakened during second-list learning, and later work showed that they partly recover with time, rather like spontaneous recovery after extinction in conditioning (Chapter 6). Exam trap The RML 2024 question about an English speaker applying English grammar while learning Spanish keys "retroactive interference". That key is wrong. English was learned first and is disrupting the newer learning of Spanish: that is proactive interference by definition, and every standard textbook would classify it so. (Strictly, a learning difficulty caused by earlier habits is also called negative transfer, Chapter 6.) Know the correct answer, and know that this key exists. The reliable test: ask which was learned first and which is being disrupted. Old disrupting new is proactive; new disrupting old is retroactive. "Difficulty recalling information due to interference from new information" (IHBAS 2024) is retroactive interference. Retrieval failure and retrieval-induced forgetting The tip-of-the-tongue state, Tulving and Pearlstone's category cues, and the encoding specificity principle all point to a third explanation: much forgetting is a failure to find information that is still stored. Tulving (1974) called this cue-dependent forgetting and contrasted it with trace-dependent forgetting, in which the trace itself has been lost. Cue-dependent forgetting happens when the cues available at retrieval do not match those encoded with the memory. On this view, much of what we call forgetting is temporary, which is why a smell, a song or a return to a childhood home can bring back memories we believed long gone. Retrieval can also cause forgetting. Michael Anderson, Robert Bjork and Elizabeth Bjork (1994) had people study category-word pairs (FRUIT-orange, FRUIT-banana, DRINK-vodka) and then practise retrieving half of the words from half of the categories (FRUIT-or___). On a final test, the practised words were, unsurprisingly, recalled best. The striking result concerned the unpractised words from practised categories (FRUIT-banana): they were recalled worse than words from categories that had not been practised at all. Retrieving some members of a category had suppressed their competitors. This is retrieval-induced forgetting , and it is thought to reflect inhibition of competing memories during retrieval. It has a practical sting: revising only some topics from a chapter may make the unrevised topics from the same chapter harder to recall than if you had revised none of it. Exam trap An RML 2020 question defines retrieval-induced forgetting as "people remembered practised information better than unpractised information". That is the first half of the finding. The defining half is that unpractised items related to the practised ones are remembered worse than baseline items from unpractised categories: retrieving some memories makes related memories harder to retrieve. Choose the keyed option when it is the only one about practice, but be ready for a better-worded version. The options about names and faces are irrelevant distractors. Motivated forgetting and repression Sigmund Freud proposed that some forgetting is motivated: memories that would provoke anxiety, guilt or shame are actively kept out of consciousness. repression is the unconscious process by which threatening or anxiety-provoking memories and impulses are excluded from awareness; according to Freud, the repressed material is not lost but continues to exert effects, for example in symptoms and slips of the tongue. Repression must be distinguished from suppression, the deliberate, conscious decision not to think about something. (Freud's other defence mechanisms and his model of conscious, preconscious and unconscious mind belong to the Personality book.) Laboratory evidence for repression in Freud's sense is weak; after reviewing decades of studies, David Holmes (1990) concluded that there was no convincing controlled evidence for it. Evidence for conscious, motivated forgetting is much better. In directed forgetting experiments, people told to forget some items remember them less well than items they were told to remember. In the think/no-think paradigm of Michael Anderson and Collin Green (2001), people learned word pairs and then, when shown the first word of some pairs, were told to prevent the associated word from coming to mind; the more often they did so, the worse they later recalled those words, even when offered money for correct answers. Brain imaging shows the prefrontal cortex reducing hippocampal activity during such suppression. Motivated forgetting is real; whether the unconscious repression Freud described is real remains disputed, and the dispute became fierce in the recovered memory controversy (Section 7.9). Exam trap Repression is unconscious; suppression is conscious. "Very threatening material is unable to gain access to conscious awareness" describes repression. "Motivated forgetting" is the broader category that includes both. Do not confuse Freudian repression with the cognitive term "inhibition", which refers to the active weakening of competing memories (as in retrieval-induced forgetting). Consolidation failure The final explanation looks at the biology. New memories are fragile; they become stable only gradually through consolidation , the process by which a memory trace is transformed into a durable form. Müller and Pilzecker introduced the term in 1900, noting that their participants' new associations seemed to "perseverate" and set over time. If consolidation is disrupted, the memory is never fully formed. A blow to the head is the everyday case. American football players who had been concussed could often tell a trainer, immediately afterwards, what play they had been running; a few minutes later they could not, because the memory had not consolidated (Lynch and Yarnell, 1973). Electroconvulsive shock given to rats soon after a learning trial disrupts learning, whereas the same shock given hours later does not (Duncan, 1949), and patients receiving electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for depression often lose memories for events shortly before the treatment course. This kind of memory loss shows a temporal gradient: recent memories are more vulnerable than remote ones. The principle was stated by the French psychologist Théodule Ribot in 1881 and is known as Ribot's law : in progressive memory loss, the new perishes before the old. It is why an elderly person with dementia may forget breakfast but vividly recall their wedding. Consolidation and its brain basis are taken up again in Section 7.10. Classic effects on retention Several named effects reveal what makes a memory last, and examiners love them because their names are easy to swap. In the 1920s, the Gestalt psychologist Kurt Lewin noticed that a Berlin waiter remembered every detail of unpaid orders but forgot them as soon as the bill was settled. His student Bluma Zeigarnik (1900 to 1988) tested the observation in 1927: she gave people a series of simple tasks and interrupted half of them before completion. Later, people recalled the interrupted tasks nearly twice as often as the completed ones. This Zeigarnik effect was explained in Lewinian terms: an unfinished task leaves a state of tension that keeps it active in memory. A year later Maria Ovsiankina showed that people also have a strong tendency to resume an interrupted task when given the chance, even without instructions to do so: the Ovsiankina effect. The Zeigarnik effect is about remembering unfinished tasks; the Ovsiankina effect is about returning to them. Sometimes memory improves with time. In 1913 Philip Ballard had schoolchildren learn poetry and found that many recalled more lines two or three days later than they had immediately after learning, without any further study. This rise in recall after a delay is reminiscence . (A related effect, hypermnesia, is a net increase in recall over repeated tests; Matthew Erdelyi and Jeffrey Becker described it in 1974.) Do not confuse reminiscence with the reminiscence bump of autobiographical memory (Section 7.5). In 1933 Hedwig von Restorff showed that an item that stands out from the rest of a list (a number among syllables, a word printed in red among black words) is remembered better than the same item in a homogeneous list. This von Restorff effect , also called the isolation effect, is the classic demonstration of distinctiveness (Section 7.4); highlighters exploit it, which is also why highlighting everything makes nothing stand out. Two final effects matter more than any others for anyone studying for an exam. The spacing effect is the finding that study sessions spread out over time (distributed practice) produce better long-term retention than the same total study time crowded together (massed practice). Ebbinghaus observed it in 1885, and a large review by Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues (2006) confirmed it across hundreds of studies; the optimal gap grows with how long you need to remember. The testing effect (or retrieval practice effect) is the finding that retrieving information from memory strengthens it more than restudying it. Arthur Gates (1917) found that schoolchildren who spent much of their study time reciting from memory learned more than those who only read. In a modern classic, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke (2006) had students study a prose passage either four times, or once followed by three recall tests. Five minutes later, the repeated-study group did slightly better; a week later, the repeated-testing group recalled about 50 per cent more, although the repeated-study group had predicted they would do better. Schacter's seven sins of memory In 2001 Daniel Schacter organised the ways memory fails into seven "sins", a framework that ties this section to the next (Table 7.8). The first three are sins of omission: something we want to remember is not available. The last four are sins of commission: something is remembered, but wrongly, or remembered when we would rather forget it. Schacter's point is that each sin is a by-product of a feature that usually serves us well: a memory system that kept every detail and resisted all suggestion would be slower, less flexible and far less able to generalise.
