Four of Schacter's seven sins say otherwise. This section tells the story of the research that replaced the recording metaphor with a different one: remembering is less like playing a video and more like a palaeontologist rebuilding a dinosaur from a few bones and a great deal of knowledge about what dinosaurs ought to look like. Bartlett and the War of the Ghosts (1932) At Cambridge in the years around the First World War, Frederic Charles Bartlett (1886 to 1969) set out to study memory in a way that was the opposite of Ebbinghaus's. Instead of meaningless syllables he used meaningful material, and instead of counting items correct he looked at what people did to the material when they remembered it. His most famous material was "The War of the Ghosts", a Native American folk tale from the Pacific north-west recorded by the anthropologist Franz Boas. In it, two young men go down to a river to hunt seals; a canoe of warriors appears out of the fog and invites them to a war party; one goes, is wounded but feels nothing, and realises that his companions are ghosts; he returns home, tells his story, and at sunrise "something black came out of his mouth" and he dies. To English students the story was strange: its logic and its supernatural elements did not fit their expectations. Bartlett used two methods. In repeated reproduction, the same person retold the story after intervals of minutes, days, months and even years. In serial reproduction, one person's version was given to the next, like a message passed along a line of people. His results, published in Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1932), showed consistent changes. The stories became shorter, as details were omitted. They became more coherent and conventional: puzzling elements were explained or dropped, a process Bartlett called rationalisation, so that "something black came out of his mouth" became the man foaming at the mouth, or his soul leaving his body. Unfamiliar details were transformed into familiar ones: canoes became boats, and hunting seals became fishing. Some details became more prominent and acquired a central place. And the supernatural theme, so foreign to Edwardian Cambridge, tended to disappear. Bartlett's explanation was that we do not store and replay experiences. We store a general impression together with a few outstanding details, and at retrieval we rebuild the rest using our schema knowledge (Section 7.6) of how such events usually go. Remembering, he wrote, is an "effort after meaning". reconstructive memory , the view that remembering actively rebuilds the past from fragments and schemas rather than reproducing it, is Bartlett's lasting legacy. Textbooks often describe the changes in his stories with three terms made famous by Gordon Allport and Leo Postman's study of rumour (1947): levelling (the story becomes shorter and simpler), sharpening (a few details are emphasised) and assimilation (details are distorted to fit the listener's expectations and culture). Bartlett's methods were informal: he gave no standard instructions, used no statistics and reported selected examples. When Alan Gauld and Geoffrey Stephenson (1967) instructed participants to be as accurate as possible, many of the errors disappeared, suggesting that some of Bartlett's "distortions" were deliberate guesses rather than true memory changes. But Erik Bergman and Henry Roediger (1999) repeated the War of the Ghosts study under careful control and found that the distortions grew over repeated reproductions, much as Bartlett had said. Exam trap "Rationalisation" has two meanings in psychology. In Bartlett's memory research, it is the reshaping of a story to make it sensible to the rememberer. In psychoanalysis, it is a defence mechanism: offering a plausible, acceptable reason for behaviour after the fact, to hide the real motive (Personality book). Questions about schema and reconstruction belong to Bartlett, not to Wundt, Titchener or Watson. Loftus and the misinformation effect If memories are rebuilt at retrieval, information encountered after an event might be built into the memory. In the 1970s Elizabeth Loftus showed that this happens, and her work changed how courts treat eyewitnesses. Key study: Loftus and Palmer, "smashed" versus "hit" (1974) Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed 45 students seven short films of traffic accidents. Afterwards, each student answered questions, one of which was critical: "About how fast were the cars going when they ___ each other?" The verb varied between groups: smashed, collided, bumped, hit or contacted. The average speed estimates followed the verb: about 41 miles per hour for "smashed", 39 for "collided", 38 for "bumped", 34 for "hit" and 32 for "contacted". Was this just a response bias, or had the memory itself changed? In a second experiment, 150 students saw a film of a multiple-car accident and were asked either the "smashed" question, the "hit" question or no question about speed. A week later, without seeing the film again, they were asked: "Did you see any broken glass?" There was no broken glass in the film. Of those asked the "smashed" question, 32 per cent said yes, compared with 14 per cent of the "hit" group and 12 per cent of the controls. A single word in a question, asked after the event, had altered what people later reported seeing. The broader phenomenon is the misinformation effect : the distortion of memory for an event by misleading information received afterwards, through leading questions, other witnesses' accounts or media reports. In a classic follow-up, Loftus, David Miller and Helen Burns (1978) showed people slides of a car at a stop sign; those later asked a question that presupposed a yield sign were much more likely to "recognise" a slide with a yield sign. Whether misinformation overwrites the original trace or merely creates a competing memory whose source is confused is still debated; Michael McCloskey and Maria Zaragoza (1985) showed that with better test procedures the original memory can often still be found, which supports the source-confusion account. Creating false memories Changing a detail is one thing. Could a whole event that never happened be implanted? Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell (1995) sent participants booklets describing four events from their childhood, supposedly supplied by a relative. Three were true. The fourth, being lost in a shopping mall at about the age of five, crying, and being rescued by an elderly person and reunited with the family, was false, although the relative had confirmed that it fitted the family's history. Over two interviews, about a quarter of the participants came to remember the false event, fully or partly, sometimes adding details of their own. Other researchers implanted memories of spilling a bowl of punch on the bride's parents at a wedding (Ira Hyman and colleagues, 1995) and, using a doctored photograph, of a childhood hot-air balloon ride; in that study about half of the participants came to report some memory of the ride (Kimberley Wade and colleagues, 2002). Merely imagining an event repeatedly increases confidence that it happened, an effect called imagination inflation. A false memory is a recollection of an event, or a detail of an event, that did not occur. The simplest way to produce one in the laboratory is the Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM) paradigm, introduced by James Deese in 1959 and revived by Henry Roediger and Kathleen McDermott in 1995. Read this list once, cover it, and then write down as many words as you can: bed, rest, awake, tired, dream, wake, snooze, blanket, doze, slumber, snore, nap, peace, yawn, drowsy. Did you write "sleep"? It was not on the list. In Roediger and McDermott's experiments, the related but unpresented "critical lure" was recalled about as often as words that had actually been studied, and people often claimed to "remember" hearing it, with the full sense of re-experiencing that Tulving called autonoetic. Every word on the list activated "sleep" (spreading activation, Section 7.6), and at test that internally generated activation was mistaken for a memory of hearing the word. Source monitoring, cryptomnesia and other errors of remembering Why do we confuse what we heard with what we imagined, or what we saw with what we were told? Marcia Johnson and her colleagues (Johnson, Hashtroudi and Lindsay, 1993) proposed that memories do not carry labels stating where they came from. Instead, we infer the source of a memory from its characteristics: memories of perceived events tend to be rich in sensory and contextual detail, while memories of imagined events contain more traces of the thinking that produced them. source monitoring is the set of processes by which we attribute a memory to its origin: when, where, how and from whom it was acquired. A deficit in source monitoring means being unable to recall the relevant contextual elements of an experience and so misattributing it. A special case, studied earlier by Johnson and Carol Raye (1981), is reality monitoring: telling memories of external events from memories of internally generated ones (what you did from what you only thought of doing). Source monitoring is the general framework; reality monitoring is one kind of source judgement. Source errors explain a whole family of memory errors. In source amnesia, a person remembers a fact but not how they learned it; it is common in older adults and in patients with frontal lobe damage. In cryptomnesia , or unconscious plagiarism, a person produces an idea or a tune believing it to be new, when in fact it is a memory of someone else's work. In 1976 a court in the United States ruled that George Harrison's song "My Sweet Lord" had unconsciously copied the melody of an earlier song, "He's So Fine". Alan Brown and Dana Murphy (1989) produced the same effect in the laboratory: after a group generated examples of a category in turn, people later "generated" new examples that had in fact been produced by others. In hindsight bias, described by Baruch Fischhoff (1975), people who know how an event turned out remember their earlier predictions as closer to the outcome than they were: the "I knew it all along" effect. Several experiences of false familiarity and false recall have names that appear in examinations. déjà vu (French for "already seen") is the illusion of recognition: the strong but false feeling that a new situation has been experienced before. It is common and usually harmless, though frequent déjà vu can be an aura of temporal lobe epilepsy. Jamais vu ("never seen") is the reverse: a familiar situation suddenly feels strange and new, as when a common word looks foreign after you have stared at it for a while. confabulation is the production of false memories, often detailed and plausible, to fill gaps in memory, without any intention to deceive; it is typical of Korsakoff's syndrome (Section 7.10). Pseudologia fantastica (pathological lying) is different again: elaborate, often grandiose stories told repeatedly, which the teller may half believe (Psychiatric Disorders book). Exam trap "Being unable to recall the relevant elements of an autobiographical experience" is a deficit in source monitoring (RML 2022); reality monitoring is a narrower case (internal versus external origin), and "personal-monitoring" and "social-monitoring" are invented distractors. The "illusion of recognition" is déjà vu; jamais vu is the illusion of unfamiliarity; confabulation fills memory gaps with false but sincere stories; pseudologia fantastica is pathological lying. Hindsight bias is a memory bias, not a memory store or a physical trace. Eyewitness testimony Few things persuade a jury like an eyewitness who points at the defendant and says, "That is the man." Yet research on reconstructive memory implies that eyewitnesses should be treated with caution, and the evidence of DNA exonerations confirms it: in the United States, mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in roughly 70 per cent of the wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA testing. The problem is not usually poor eyesight or a tendency to forget; it is that memory can be confidently wrong. Many factors affect accuracy. At encoding: extreme stress, brief exposure, poor lighting, and weapon focus, the tendency for a visible weapon to capture attention at the expense of the culprit's face (Loftus, Geoffrey Loftus and Jane Messo, 1987). People are also less accurate at identifying faces of another ethnic group than of their own (the cross-race or own-race effect). After the event: leading questions, conversations with other witnesses and media reports introduce misinformation, and source errors can make a familiar face (seen at the scene, or in a photograph shown by police) feel like the culprit's face. At identification: biased line-ups, suggestive instructions and the investigator's own expectations all increase errors. Confirming feedback after an identification ("Good, you identified our suspect") inflates the witness's confidence, so that by the time of the trial a hesitant witness has become certain (Gary Wells and Amy Bradfield, 1998). Confidence expressed at the first, fair identification is reasonably informative; confidence at trial is not. Young children are especially suggestible when questioned repeatedly with leading questions (Stephen Ceci and Maggie Bruck, 1993). Psychology has also offered remedies. The cognitive interview developed by Ronald Fisher and Edward Geiselman applies memory principles directly: mentally reinstate the context of the event (context-dependent memory), report everything however trivial, recall the events in different orders, and recall them from different perspectives (each provides different retrieval cues). It reliably increases correct recall without much increase in errors. Line-ups conducted by an officer who does not know who the suspect is, with fair fillers and a record of the witness's initial confidence, reduce false identifications. Clinical link Clinical and forensic psychologists are often asked about memory in court. The safest summary of the research is that memory is usually accurate in its gist, often inaccurate in its details, readily altered by suggestion, and that confidence and vividness are poor guides to accuracy. A clinician who interviews a child about possible abuse, or an adult about a traumatic event, must therefore use open, non-leading questions, avoid repeated suggestive questioning, and record exactly what was asked and answered. The recovered memory controversy In the late 1980s and 1990s, a growing number of adults in the United States and elsewhere reported recovering, often during therapy, memories of childhood sexual abuse that they had previously had no awareness of. Some therapists believed that such memories had been repressed and that techniques such as hypnosis, guided imagery, dream interpretation and repeated suggestive questioning could bring them back. Some recovered memories led to accusations, family breakdown and criminal trials. Critics, led by Elizabeth Loftus, argued that the very techniques used to "recover" memories were the techniques known to create false ones, and the term "false memory syndrome" was coined by an organisation founded in 1992 by families who said they had been falsely accused. The resulting dispute became known as the memory wars. The evidence supports a middle position. Genuine abuse can be forgotten for long periods and later remembered: Linda Meyer Williams (1994) interviewed women whose abuse in childhood had been documented in hospital records seventeen years earlier and found that 38 per cent did not report it. (Some of these women may simply have chosen not to disclose it, and ordinary forgetting of early childhood events need not involve repression.) But false memories of traumatic events can also be created, especially through suggestion by an authority figure, imagination and repetition, and hypnosis increases confidence far more than it increases accuracy. A recovered memory is therefore neither automatically true nor automatically false; it needs independent corroboration, and therapists should never try to dig up memories that the client does not report. 7.10 Amnesia and the Biology of Memory High yield · 31 Qs Much of what we know about the organisation of memory has come from people like Clive Wearing whose memories were damaged. This section describes the main forms of amnesia and the classic cases briefly, and outlines what they reveal about consolidation and the brain; the neural detail belongs to the Physiological book. Kinds of amnesia amnesia is a pathological loss of memory, disproportionate to any other cognitive impairment. Take the moment of the brain injury, illness or surgery as a fixed point on a time line. anterograde amnesia (forward-acting) is the inability to form new long-term memories for events after that point: the person cannot learn new names, cannot remember what happened an hour ago. retrograde amnesia (backward-acting) is the loss of memories formed before that point: the person cannot remember events that preceded the injury. Most organic amnesias combine the two, with the anterograde component usually the more disabling. Retrograde amnesia typically follows Ribot's law: the years just before the injury are lost, while remote memories from childhood survive. Amnesia should be distinguished from the other classic disorders that neuropsychologists name with the prefix "a-": aphasia (disorder of language, often listed with alexia, an acquired loss of the ability to read, and acalculia, an acquired loss of the ability to calculate), apraxia (inability to carry out skilled, learned movements despite intact strength), agnosia (inability to recognise objects despite intact sensation) and dementia (progressive decline across several cognitive functions, including memory, judgement and abstraction). H.M.: the man who changed the study of memory Henry Gustav Molaison (1926 to 2008), known for over fifty years only by his initials, had suffered from severe epilepsy since childhood. In 1953, when he was 27, the neurosurgeon William Beecher Scoville removed the medial portions of both of his temporal lobes, including most of the hippocampus, the amygdala and the adjacent cortex, in an attempt to stop his seizures. The seizures were greatly reduced. But H.M. was left with a profound anterograde amnesia. Scoville and the psychologist Brenda Milner (born 1918) described the case in 1957, and H.M. was studied for the rest of his life, especially by Milner and later by Suzanne Corkin. H.M.'s case established four principles. First, memory can be separated from other cognitive abilities: his intelligence, language and perception were normal, and his personality largely unchanged. Second, short-term memory is separate from long-term memory: his digit span was normal, and he could hold a conversation, but as soon as his attention moved on, the content was lost. He read the same magazines again and again with fresh interest and could not learn the address of the house his family moved to after his operation. Third, the medial temporal lobes are needed to form new declarative memories but are not where old memories are stored: his memories of childhood were largely intact, and his retrograde amnesia covered only the years before the surgery (originally estimated at about two years; later testing suggested it reached further back). Fourth, implicit memory is separate from explicit memory: as described in Section 7.5, H.M. learned to trace a star in a mirror, improving over three days just like a healthy person, while having no conscious memory of ever having done the task. He also showed normal priming. After his death in 2008, his brain was preserved and sliced into thousands of sections for study. Exam trap H.M.'s most profound deficit was anterograde amnesia for declarative (explicit) memory; his procedural memory (mirror tracing) was spared, his short-term memory was normal, and his retrograde amnesia was limited. Options saying he lost procedural memory, semantic memory "only", working memory span, or all old memories are wrong. The structures removed were the medial temporal lobes on both sides, including the hippocampus and amygdala, not the frontal, parietal or occipital lobes. The hippocampus is the structure most often linked to anterograde amnesia and to the consolidation of new declarative memories, not the hypothalamus (motivation, temperature, hunger), the pituitary (hormones) or the cerebellum (motor coordination and motor learning). Korsakoff's syndrome and confabulation Korsakoff's syndrome (also called Korsakoff's psychosis, or Korsakoff's amnesic syndrome) is a memory disorder most commonly seen in people with a long history of heavy alcohol use. It was described by the Russian psychiatrist Sergei Korsakoff in the late 1880s, and it is caused mainly by deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1), which commonly accompanies chronic alcoholism because of poor diet and poor absorption. It often follows an acute phase called Wernicke's encephalopathy, described by Carl Wernicke in 1881, marked by confusion, unsteady gait (ataxia) and abnormal eye movements such as nystagmus and paralysis of eye muscles; the two together are called the Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. The damage centres on the medial diencephalon, especially the mammillary bodies and the mediodorsal (also called dorsomedial) nuclei of the thalamus, with more diffuse damage elsewhere. The memory disorder has three features. There is a severe anterograde amnesia for explicit memories. There is also an extensive retrograde amnesia, which grows as the disease progresses and can reach back into childhood, with the usual temporal gradient. And there is confabulation: asked what they did yesterday, patients may give a fluent, detailed and entirely false account, often built from fragments of real older memories, with no intent to deceive and no awareness that it is false. Confabulation must be distinguished from malingering (deliberately faking or exaggerating symptoms for gain), from delirium (an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and consciousness) and from simple confusion. The neurologist Oliver Sacks described a Korsakoff patient, Jimmie G., who in 1975 still believed he was a nineteen-year-old sailor at the end of the Second World War, "the lost mariner". Treatment with thiamine in the acute Wernicke stage can prevent much of the damage, which is why it matters clinically to recognise the syndrome early. Other neurological diseases affect memory in contrasting ways. In Alzheimer's disease, episodic memory for recent events is usually the first to fail and semantic memory declines later. In Huntington's and Parkinson's diseases, which damage the basal ganglia, procedural learning is impaired more than declarative memory, the mirror image of H.M. (Physiological and Psychiatric Disorders books). Other amnesias infantile amnesia , also called childhood amnesia, is the near-total absence, in adults, of memories from the first three or four years of life; the average earliest memory dates from about three to three and a half years. Freud, who named it, attributed it to repression. Current explanations are developmental: the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex are immature in infancy; young children lack the language in which later memories are organised and retrieved; a stable sense of self, needed to organise memories as "things that happened to me", emerges only around the second year (Mark Howe and Mary Courage, 1993); and the schemas through which an adult searches memory differ from those of the infant who encoded it. Transient global amnesia is a sudden, temporary anterograde amnesia, usually in middle-aged or older adults, lasting several hours and never more than a day. The person is alert and knows who they are but asks the same questions over and over; the episode resolves completely, leaving only a gap for the hours it lasted. Post-traumatic amnesia is the period of confusion and failed new learning after a head injury; its length is one of the best predictors of the severity of the injury. Dissociative amnesia, by contrast, is an inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, too extensive to be ordinary forgetting and without a medical cause. It may be localised (a specific period), selective (some events of a period), generalised (the person's whole life history), systematised (a category of information) or continuous (everything from a certain point onwards). It may come with dissociative fugue, purposeful travel or wandering with amnesia for identity, and it is distinct from dissociative identity disorder, in which two or more personality states alternate with gaps in memory. These conditions are taught in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Consolidation, the hippocampus and the search for the engram Where is a memory stored? In 1904 the German biologist Richard Semon coined the word engram for the physical trace that learning leaves in the nervous system. The most determined search for it was made by the American neuropsychologist Karl Spencer Lashley (1890 to 1958). For three decades Lashley trained rats to run mazes and then removed different parts of their cerebral cortex, hoping to find the place where the maze memory was kept. He never found it. Memory loss depended on how much cortex was removed, not on which part; he called this the principle of mass action. And different parts of the cortex seemed able to take over for one another, the principle of equipotentiality (both set out in his 1929 book Brain Mechanisms and Intelligence ). In his 1950 paper "In search of the engram" he wrote, only half joking, that reviewing the evidence sometimes made him feel "that the necessary conclusion is that learning just is not possible." His conclusion was that memories are not localised in single spots but are distributed widely across the cortex. Lashley's student Donald Olding Hebb (1904 to 1985) suggested how a distributed memory could form. In The Organization of Behavior (1949) he proposed that when one neuron repeatedly helps to fire another, the connection between them is strengthened, so that groups of neurons that are active together become linked into cell assemblies, often summarised as "cells that fire together wire together". A physical mechanism of exactly this kind was found in 1973, when Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo showed that brief, high-frequency stimulation of a pathway into the rabbit hippocampus produced a lasting increase in the strength of the synapses. This long-term potentiation (LTP), which depends on NMDA glutamate receptors, is the leading candidate for the cellular basis of learning and memory (Physiological book). Modern methods have even allowed researchers to tag and reactivate the specific "engram cells" that are active during learning in mice, vindicating Semon's term a century later. How do these findings fit with H.M.? The standard account, the standard consolidation theory, is that the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe bind together the scattered cortical elements of a new declarative memory and are needed for that memory for some time; through repeated reactivation, much of it during sleep, the memory is gradually reorganised so that it can be retrieved from the neocortex without the hippocampus (systems consolidation). This explains why damage to the hippocampus prevents new learning and erases recent memories while sparing remote ones. Rival accounts hold that vivid episodic memories always depend on the hippocampus (multiple trace theory, Lynn Nadel and Morris Moscovitch, 1997), and research on reconsolidation (Karim Nader, Glenn Schafe and Joseph LeDoux, 2000) has shown that a consolidated memory, when it is reactivated, becomes fragile again for a time and must be restabilised, a biological counterpart of Bartlett's reconstructive memory. Attention determines what is encoded; meaning, elaboration, self-reference and imagery determine how well it is encoded; organisation and distinctiveness make it findable; spacing and retrieval practice make it last; matching study to test conditions makes it accessible when needed; and sleep consolidates it. The techniques below are those principles put to work. Mnemonic devices A mnemonic is any technique that improves memory by imposing organisation, meaning or imagery on material that lacks them. The oldest is the method of loci . The Roman orator Cicero told how the Greek poet Simonides of Ceos, having stepped out of a banquet hall moments before its roof collapsed, was able to identify the crushed guests by remembering where each had been sitting. Order, Simonides realised, can be held by place. To use the method, you choose a familiar route (your house, the walk from your hostel to the library) and place a vivid image of each item to be remembered at successive locations along it; to recall, you walk the route in imagination and "see" each item where you left it. Shereshevsky used this method, and modern memory champions still do. The peg-word system replaces locations with a memorised list of "pegs" that rhyme with the numbers: one is a bun, two is a shoe, three is a tree, four is a door, five is a hive, and so on. Each item to be learned is linked to its peg by an interactive image: to remember that the third item is "milk", picture milk pouring over a tree. The method gives direct access to any item by number. The keyword method , developed for foreign vocabulary by Richard Atkinson (1975; tested with Michael Raugh on Russian vocabulary), links a foreign word to its meaning through an English word that sounds like part of it. The Spanish word "pato" means duck; it sounds like "pot", so you imagine a duck sitting in a pot. Verbal mnemonics use the first letters of the items. An acronym is a word or pronounceable string formed from the first letters of the items, such as VIBGYOR for the colours of the rainbow or OCEAN for the five broad personality traits. An acrostic is a sentence whose words begin with the first letters of the items, such as "Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit" for the notes on the lines of the treble stave (E, G, B, D, F). Other techniques draw on principles we have met. Chunking groups items into fewer, larger units. Categorical clustering organises a list by meaning; W. A. Bousfield (1953) showed that people spontaneously recall randomly ordered lists in category clusters. Interactive imagery links items in a single scene, and it is the interaction, not bizarreness, that matters (Keith Wollen and colleagues, 1972). Narrative chaining weaves items into a story: Gordon Bower and Michael Clark (1969) had people learn twelve lists of ten words each; those who made up a story for each list later recalled about 93 per cent of the words, while those who simply studied recalled about 13 per cent. Indian context The Vedas were transmitted orally for many centuries before they were written down, with extraordinary fidelity. Reciters learned each text in several forms: the continuous text (samhita patha), word by word (pada patha), in overlapping pairs (krama patha: word 1 and 2, then 2 and 3, then 3 and 4), and in elaborate forward-and-backward weavings (jata and ghana patha). Each recitation pattern acts as a check on the others, so that an error in one would be exposed by the rest. It is one of the most sophisticated memory systems ever devised, and UNESCO recognised the tradition of Vedic chanting as part of the world's intangible heritage in 2003. Study systems: SQ3R and PQRST Two study systems for textbooks build elaboration, self-questioning and retrieval practice into reading. SQ3R , devised by the American educational psychologist Francis P. Robinson in 1946, has five steps: Survey (skim headings and summaries to build a framework), Question (turn each heading into a question), Read (read actively to answer the question), Recite (close the book and state the answer from memory) and Review (go over the whole chapter, testing yourself). PQRST, described by Ellen Thomas and H. Alan Robinson (1972) and widely taught in introductory psychology, is a close variant: Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation and Test. In both, the most important steps are the ones students skip: the questions, which give reading a purpose and a structure, and the recitation, which is retrieval practice. Spacing, testing, overlearning and sleep When John Dunlosky and his colleagues (2013) reviewed the evidence on ten popular study techniques, two were rated as having high utility: practice testing and distributed (spaced) practice. Highlighting, rereading and summarising were rated as having low utility. Rereading feels productive because the material becomes fluent and familiar, but fluency is a poor guide to what can be retrieved later (the illusion of competence, Section 7.5). Retrieval practice works because every successful retrieval strengthens the memory and the route to it, and every failed one shows you exactly what to restudy. Spacing works partly because each return to the material after some forgetting requires effortful retrieval, and partly because material studied in different contexts acquires more varied retrieval cues. Robert Bjork has called such techniques "desirable difficulties": they make learning feel harder and slower, and make it last longer. Mixing different kinds of problems in one practice session (interleaving), rather than practising one kind at a time, is another desirable difficulty: it teaches you to recognise which method a problem needs. Here is a worked example. Suppose you have two days to master a chapter. Massed study would mean reading it four times on the first day. A spaced-retrieval plan would mean reading it once on the first morning; that evening, writing down everything you can recall about each section heading before checking; the next morning, answering the chapter's self-test questions without looking; and the next evening, attempting the past-paper questions and restudying only what you got wrong. The total time is similar. The second plan uses testing, spacing, generation and feedback, and on the evidence reviewed in this chapter it will produce far better retention a week later. Two further aids complete the picture. overlearning , continuing to practise after material has been mastered, increases retention: William Krueger (1929) found that 50 per cent overlearning (half as many extra trials as were needed to learn) produced a clear gain, and 100 per cent overlearning a smaller additional gain, a case of diminishing returns. And sleep after learning reduces interference and actively consolidates new memories, as Jenkins and Dallenbach's results first hinted; studying until the small hours at the expense of sleep is a poor bargain. (Massed versus distributed practice and overlearning in skill learning are also discussed in Chapter 6.) Exam trap SQ3R (Robinson, 1946): Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review. PQRST: Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation, Test. In PQRST the "S" stands for self-recitation, not storing, sequencing or semantics. Clinical link Memory rehabilitation for people with brain injury or dementia applies the same principles in modified form. Because amnesic patients cannot tell their own errors from correct responses, errorless learning (Baddeley and Barbara Wilson, 1994), in which the patient is guided to the correct response from the start rather than encouraged to guess, prevents errors from being learned through intact implicit memory. Spaced retrieval, in which a patient recalls a fact at gradually lengthening intervals, and the method of vanishing cues (Elizabeth Glisky, Daniel Schacter and Endel Tulving, 1986), in which letter cues are withdrawn one at a time, exploit spared implicit learning. The case of Clive Wearing, revisited Go back to Clive Wearing, writing in his diary yet again that he is now, at last, truly awake. You can now describe what happened to him in the language of this chapter. Herpes simplex encephalitis destroyed the hippocampus and much of the medial temporal lobe on both sides, the structures that consolidate new declarative memories. His short-term (working) memory still worked, which is why he could follow a sentence or a conversation for as long as it kept moving. But nothing he experienced could be consolidated into durable long-term memory: he had a dense anterograde amnesia like H.M.'s. Alongside it, and probably because the damage spread well beyond the hippocampus, he had a far more extensive retrograde amnesia than H.M. ever had, one that wiped out almost every particular episode of his past. Without episodic memory he had none of the autonoetic consciousness that lets a person travel back in time and feel himself to be the same person who lived through earlier events. Every moment of awareness seemed to him like the first, and so every earlier diary entry looked like a lie. What survived teaches just as much. Clive kept some semantic knowledge (that he was a musician, that he was married to Deborah), much as Tulving's patient K.C. kept facts about his own life while losing every episode. He kept his procedural memory: sight-reading, playing and conducting, skills that depend on circuits outside the hippocampus, exactly as Squire's taxonomy predicts and as H.M.'s mirror tracing had already shown. And his joy at seeing Deborah, and his love for her, survived without a single remembered conversation to anchor them, a reminder that past experience can shape feeling and behaviour without any conscious recollection. In one life, then, you can see three of this chapter's distinctions: short-term versus long-term memory, episodic versus semantic memory, and explicit versus implicit memory. It also shows what the chapter has argued from Ebbinghaus to Bartlett: memory is not one thing but several, and it is less a recording of the past than the means by which each of us builds a continuing self. Chapter summary 7.1 What memory is, and how Ebbinghaus measured it. Memory is the capacity to retain information over time and use it later. It involves three processes: encoding (turning input into a code the system can hold), storage and retrieval. Encoding depends on attention, and details that were never attended to are lost through encoding failure, as Nickerson and Adams's coin study showed. Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) invented the nonsense syllable, acted as his own participant and measured retention by the savings method: original learning minus relearning, divided by original learning, multiplied by 100. His forgetting curve is negatively accelerated: steep loss in the first hour, then a slow decline that never reaches zero. He also first noted the benefits of overlearning and spaced repetitions, the advantage of the beginning and end of a list, and the ease of meaningful material. Retention can be measured by recall (free, serial and cued, including the paired-associate learning introduced by Calkins in 1894), by recognition, by the reconstruction method (restoring the order of supplied items) and by relearning, which is the most sensitive measure. 7.2 The multi-store model. Building on William James's primary and secondary memory (1890), Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) proposed three stores (sensory, short-term and long-term) worked by control processes such as attention and rehearsal. Sensory memory briefly holds a large amount of pre-categorical information. Sperling's partial-report procedure (1960) showed that about nine of twelve letters are available in iconic memory for roughly a quarter to half a second, and Darwin, Turvey and Crowder (1972) put echoic memory at about two to four seconds. Short-term memory holds seven plus or minus two items (Miller, 1956), or about four chunks (Cowan, 2001), and chunking draws on long-term knowledge. Without rehearsal it lasts about 18 to 30 seconds (Brown, 1958; Peterson and Peterson, 1959), but Keppel and Underwood (1962) showed that the loss came from proactive interference rather than decay. Coding is mainly acoustic in short-term memory (Conrad, 1964; Baddeley, 1966) and semantic in long-term memory, which has no known capacity limit and can last a lifetime (Bahrick). The serial position curve (primacy from long-term memory, recency from short-term memory; Glanzer and Cunitz, 1966) and the double dissociation between H.M. and K.F. support separate stores. Critics point out that neither store is a single unit, that rehearsal is not the main route into long-term memory, and that long-term knowledge acts on information while it is still in short-term memory. 7.3 Working memory. Baddeley and Hitch (1974) used the dual-task method to show that short-term memory has several parts. The central executive controls attention but stores nothing: it focuses, divides and switches attention and links working memory with long-term memory. Random number generation loads it, and the Stroop task measures its inhibitory function. The phonological loop (a phonological store and an articulatory control process) holds speech-based information. Four findings support it: the phonological similarity effect, the word-length effect, articulatory suppression and the irrelevant speech effect. It also helps in learning new words. The visuospatial sketchpad (a visual cache and an inner scribe, in Logie's terms) holds visual and spatial information and carries out mental rotation. The episodic buffer, added in 2000, binds information from the other components and from long-term memory into integrated episodes. Short-term memory is simple storage, measured by simple span; working memory is storage plus processing, measured by complex span and backward digit span, and it predicts comprehension and reasoning. 7.4 Levels of processing and the quality of encoding. Craik and Lockhart (1972) argued that memory is a by-product of processing and that deeper processing (structural, then phonemic, then semantic) leaves more durable traces whether or not the person intends to learn (Hyde and Jenkins, 1973). Craik and Tulving (1975) found the best recognition after semantic questions, and more elaborate processing helped even within one level. Maintenance (Type I) rehearsal keeps information available but adds little; elaborative (Type II) rehearsal builds lasting memories. Distinctiveness, the self-reference effect (Rogers, Kuiper and Kirker, 1977), the generation effect (Slamecka and Graf, 1978) and Paivio's dual coding theory (1971) show other ways of strengthening encoding. The framework was criticised as circular. Morris, Bransford and Franks (1977) showed with a rhyming test that what matters is transfer-appropriate processing, the match between processing at study and processing at test. 7.5 The systems of long-term memory. Tulving (1972) distinguished episodic memory (personal events located in time and place, recalled with autonoetic consciousness) from semantic, or generic, memory (general knowledge, held with noetic awareness). Procedural memory holds skills. K.C. lost his episodic memory but kept his semantic knowledge. Explicit (declarative) memory involves conscious recollection, while implicit (nondeclarative) memory shows itself in performance without awareness (Graf and Schacter, 1985), as in Claparède's pinprick, word-stem completion by amnesic patients and H.M.'s mirror tracing. Squire's taxonomy links declarative memory to the medial temporal lobe, and links procedural skills, priming, classical conditioning and non-associative learning to other structures. Priming may be repetition priming or semantic priming (Meyer and Schvaneveldt, 1971); its masked form is used to study subliminal perception. Autobiographical memory shows a reminiscence bump for ages 10 to 30. Prospective memory (remembering to act, cued by an event or by time) contrasts with retrospective memory. Flashbulb memories (Brown and Kulik, 1977) are vivid and confidently held but no more accurate than ordinary memories (Neisser and Harsch, 1992; Talarico and Rubin, 2003); emotional arousal and rehearsal explain them, not a "Now Print!" mechanism. Eidetic imagery is rare and found mainly in children. Metamemory (Flavell, 1971) covers the feeling of knowing (Hart, 1965) and the tip-of-the-tongue state (Brown and McNeill, 1966), which is a failure of retrieval, not of storage. 7.6 How knowledge is organised. Collins and Quillian's hierarchical network model (1969) stores concepts as nodes in a hierarchy, with each property stored only at the highest level it applies to (cognitive economy), and predicts that verification time rises with the number of links travelled. Typicality effects and familiarity confounds undermined it. They led to the feature comparison model and to Collins and Loftus's spreading activation model (1975), in which activation spreads along links of varying length; this explains semantic priming and typicality. A proposition is the smallest unit of knowledge that can be true or false. Connectionist, or parallel distributed processing, models (Rumelhart and McClelland, 1986) represent knowledge as patterns of simultaneous activation across many interconnected units and store it in connection weights; such networks can retrieve a whole memory from any part of it and degrade gradually when damaged. Schemas are organised bodies of knowledge (Bartlett, 1932) that guide understanding and distort recall (Bransford and Johnson, 1972; Brewer and Treyens, 1981). Scripts are schemas for routine events (Schank and Abelson, 1977) and belong to generic memory. 7.7 Retrieval: cues, context and state. Information may be available but not accessible, and retrieval cues such as category names make it accessible (Tulving and Pearlstone, 1966). Recognition is usually easier than recall because the test supplies the item, as the generate-recognise account says, although the recognition failure of recallable words shows that this is not the whole story. Tulving and Thomson's encoding specificity principle (1973) states that a cue works to the extent that it was encoded with the memory. Its special cases include context-dependent memory (Godden and Baddeley's divers, 1975; merely imagining the original room also helps), state-dependent memory (Goodwin and colleagues, 1969, with alcohol) and mood-dependent memory. Mood-congruent memory, the easier recall of material that matches one's current mood (Bower, 1981), helps to keep depression going. Context and state effects are strongest in free recall and weak or absent in recognition. 7.8 Forgetting. Decay theory, traced to Thorndike's law of disuse, holds that unused traces fade. McGeoch (1932) objected that time itself causes nothing, and Jenkins and Dallenbach (1924) found less forgetting after sleep than after the same time awake. Interference theory distinguishes proactive interference (old learning disrupts new) from retroactive interference (new learning disrupts old), and studies both with A-B, A-C designs. Interference grows with similarity, proactive interference is the larger source of laboratory forgetting (Underwood, 1957), and Melton and Irwin (1940) named response competition and unlearning as its two factors. Tulving's cue-dependent forgetting and retrieval-induced forgetting (Anderson, Bjork and Bjork, 1994) show that much forgetting is a failure of access. Freud's repression is unconscious and lacks controlled evidence; suppression, directed forgetting and the think/no-think paradigm show that conscious motivated forgetting is real. Consolidation failure explains the loss of recent memories after concussion or ECT, with the temporal gradient of Ribot's law (1881). The classic named effects are the Zeigarnik effect (1927), the Ovsiankina effect (1928), Ballard's reminiscence (1913), the von Restorff isolation effect (1933), the spacing effect and the testing effect (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006). Schacter's seven sins (2001) sort memory failures into sins of omission and sins of commission. Retention and forgetting are inversely related: the more is retained, the less is forgotten. 7.9 Memory as reconstruction. Bartlett (1932) used "The War of the Ghosts" to show that remembering is an "effort after meaning": retold stories became shorter and more conventional, and were rationalised to fit the rememberer's schemas. The changes are often described as levelling, sharpening and assimilation (Allport and Postman, 1947). Loftus and Palmer (1974) showed that the verb "smashed" raised speed estimates and later false reports of broken glass, which is the misinformation effect. Whole false events can be implanted (lost in the mall; Loftus and Pickrell, 1995), and the Deese-Roediger-McDermott paradigm produces confident recall of an unpresented critical lure. Source monitoring (Johnson, Hashtroudi and Lindsay, 1993) explains source amnesia, cryptomnesia and misattribution. Déjà vu is an illusion of recognition, and confabulation is the sincere filling of memory gaps. Eyewitness testimony is undermined by weapon focus, the cross-race effect, leading questions, source errors and inflated confidence; the cognitive interview and fair line-ups reduce errors. In the recovered memory controversy the evidence supports a middle position: real abuse can be forgotten and later remembered, and false memories can be created by suggestion. 7.10 Amnesia and the biology of memory. Amnesia is a pathological loss of memory. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after a brain injury; retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before it, usually following Ribot's law. After the removal of both medial temporal lobes, H.M. (Scoville and Milner, 1957) had a severe anterograde amnesia for declarative memory. His short-term memory, intelligence, priming and procedural learning (mirror tracing) were normal, and his retrograde amnesia was limited. Korsakoff's syndrome is caused by thiamine deficiency in chronic alcoholism and is often preceded by Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia and nystagmus). It damages the mammillary bodies and the mediodorsal thalamus and produces anterograde amnesia, an extensive retrograde amnesia and confabulation. Infantile amnesia reflects the development of the brain, language and the self rather than repression. Transient global amnesia and dissociative amnesia (Psychiatric Disorders book) are other forms. Lashley's search for the engram (Semon's term) produced the principles of mass action and equipotentiality and the conclusion that memories are distributed across the cortex; Hebb's cell assemblies (1949) and long-term potentiation (Bliss and Lømo, 1973) suggest the mechanism. The hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories, which in time come to depend on the neocortex. 7.11 Improving memory. Mnemonics add organisation, meaning and imagery to material. The main ones are the method of loci (Simonides), the peg-word system, the keyword method (Atkinson, 1975), acronyms (VIBGYOR), acrostics ("Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit"), chunking, categorical clustering, interactive imagery and narrative chaining (Bower and Clark, 1969). Study systems such as SQ3R (Robinson, 1946: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review) and PQRST (Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation, Test) build questioning and retrieval practice into reading. The best-supported techniques are practice testing and distributed practice (Dunlosky and colleagues, 2013). Other aids are desirable difficulties such as interleaving, overlearning (Krueger, 1929), whose returns diminish, and sleep, which consolidates new learning. Rereading and highlighting feel effective but are not. Memory rehabilitation uses errorless learning, spaced retrieval and the method of vanishing cues. (c) Exclusively in the hippocampus Linked to memory later, by the case of H.M. , and even then as the structure for consolidation , not the exclusive store. (d) Only in the frontal and temporal lobes Also localisation , which Lashley rejected. The famous patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) underwent surgical removal of the medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus, to treat severe epilepsy. While he retained most of his intellectual abilities and working memory, his primary and most profound deficit was in: (Real PYQ 2024) a Procedural memory b Semantic memory c Anterograde amnesia d Retrograde amnesia ✓ Answer: (c) Anterograde amnesia Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), 1953 operation The concept The deficit After his 1953 operation, H.M. could not form new declarative memories : profound anterograde amnesia . Key note Intellect and working memory were kept, so the loss was specific to laying down new long-term memories. Why the other options are wrong (a) Procedural memory Spared: he improved at mirror tracing over three days without remembering the task. (b) Semantic memory His old semantic knowledge was intact, so semantic memory was not selectively lost. (d) Retrograde amnesia Covered only the years before the surgery and was far milder than his anterograde loss. A patient presents with severe memory deficits, confabulation, and nystagmus, with a history of chronic alcohol use. This clinical picture is classic for: (Real PYQ 2024) a Alzheimer's Disease b Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome c Vascular Dementia d Frontotemporal Dementia ✓ Answer: (b) Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome Thiamine deficiency in chronic alcoholism The concept First phase Thiamine deficiency in chronic alcoholism produces Wernicke's encephalopathy : confusion, ataxia and eye signs such as nystagmus. Second phase It is followed by Korsakoff's amnesia with confabulation , which matches this patient. Why the other options are wrong (a) Alzheimer's Disease A gradual dementia of older age, beginning with recent episodic memory , without nystagmus or an alcohol link. (c) Vascular Dementia Typically declines step by step after strokes. (d) Frontotemporal Dementia Begins with changes in personality, behaviour or language (Psychiatric Disorders book). In PQRST method, a method of enhancing memory, what does the alphabet 'S' stand for? (RML 2024) a Storing b Self-recitation c Sequencing d Semantics ✓ Answer: (b) Self-recitation PQRST, a variant of Robinson's SQ3R The concept The acronym PQRST stands for Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation and Test. Its origin A close variant of Robinson's SQ3R (Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review). Why S matters Self-recitation is retrieval practice , the step that does most for retention. Why the other options are wrong (a) Storing Sounds like a memory term but is not a step of the method. (c) Sequencing Sounds like a memory term but is not a step of the method. (d) Semantics Sounds like a memory term but is not a step of the method. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Korsakoff's syndrome (Korsakoff's psychosis) follows chronic alcoholism and thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, often after Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus; together the Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome). It damages the mammillary bodies and mediodorsal thalamus and produces dense anterograde amnesia, extensive retrograde amnesia and confabulation: sincere, false stories that fill memory gaps, not malingering. asked 8 times H.M. (Henry Molaison): both medial temporal lobes (hippocampus and amygdala) removed by William Beecher Scoville in 1953; reported by Scoville and Brenda Milner in 1957. Profound anterograde amnesia for declarative memory, with normal short-term memory, limited retrograde amnesia and spared procedural learning (mirror tracing). asked 7 times The hippocampus (medial temporal lobe) is the structure damaged in anterograde amnesia and is critical for consolidating new declarative memories; it is not the store of remote memories. Amnesia questions offering the hypothalamus, pituitary or cerebellum want the hippocampus. asked 6 times Proactive interference : old learning disrupts new (dialling your old phone number; English grammar intruding on Spanish, although RML 2024 keyed "retroactive"). Retroactive interference : new learning disrupts old. PRO = old disrupts new. asked 5 times Sensory memory (icon about 250 to 500 ms, echo about 2 to 4 s) has the largest capacity and the shortest duration, and "icon and echo" always mean sensory memory. Asked only for the largest capacity in the Atkinson and Shiffrin model, answer long-term memory (no known limit). asked 5 times Endel Tulving (1972) separated episodic memory, personal events with their what, where and when (your first day of college), from semantic memory, the network of facts and concepts. Procedural memory holds skills (riding a bicycle); autobiographical memory is memory for specific episodes of one's own life. Patient K.C. lost episodic memory but kept semantic knowledge. asked 5 times Flashbulb memories (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977) are vivid memories of learning of a shocking event. Confidence and vividness stay very high while accuracy and consistency fall (Neisser and Harsch, 1992; Talarico and Rubin, 2003); emotional arousal plus rehearsal explains them, not a "Now Print!" mechanism. asked 4 times Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after the injury; retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories from before it, usually following Ribot's law; amnesia itself is a pathological loss of memory. asked 4 times Karl Lashley concluded that memories are distributed throughout the cortex (mass action, equipotentiality). The engram (Richard Semon's term, 1904) is the physical memory trace. Long-term potentiation (Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo, 1973) is a lasting strengthening of synapses after high-frequency stimulation, linked with memory. asked 4 times Misinformation effect (Elizabeth Loftus; Loftus and Palmer, 1974, "smashed" versus "hit"): memories are distorted by leading questions or later misleading information. Source errors cause false eyewitness identifications, and failing to recall the contextual elements of an experience is a deficit in source monitoring (Marcia Johnson). asked 3 times George A. Miller (1956), "The magical number seven, plus or minus two": short-term memory span is 7 ± 2 meaningful units called chunks (Nelson Cowan, 2001: about 4 chunks). asked 4 times Serial position effect (primacy-recency effect): the first and last items of a list are recalled better than the middle. Primacy reflects rehearsal into long-term memory; recency reflects items still in short-term memory, and a 30-second filled delay removes it (Glanzer and Cunitz, 1966). asked 4 times Encoding specificity principle (Tulving and Thomson, 1973): recall is best when the cues at retrieval match those at encoding. Context-dependent memory is the same external place (Godden and Baddeley's divers, 1975; Rahul's exam in his usual classroom); state-dependent memory is the same internal state (alcohol). asked 3 times Working memory (Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch, 1974) has a central executive, a phonological loop and a visuospatial sketchpad, plus the episodic buffer added in 2000; a "visual executive loop" does not exist. asked 3 times Random number generation loads the central executive ; backward digit span tests working memory; mentally rotating an object is the job of the visuospatial sketchpad . asked 3 times The Stroop effect (John Ridley Stroop, 1935) is interference in selective attention: automatic reading of the word competes with the controlled task of naming the ink colour. asked 3 times A schema (Frederic Bartlett, 1932, "The War of the Ghosts") is organised knowledge that guides and distorts recall; the schema approach studies how organised knowledge is used to understand behaviour; scripts of familiar routines (Schank and Abelson, 1977) belong to generic memory. asked 3 times The episodic buffer , added by Baddeley in 2000, integrates information from the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad and long-term memory into a single coherent episode. asked 3 times The phonological loop (phonological store plus articulatory control process) stores and rehearses auditory-verbal information. asked 3 times The tip-of-the-tongue state (Roger Brown and David McNeill, 1966) is a temporary inability to retrieve a well-known word: a failure of retrieval, not of storage. asked 2 times The self-reference effect , better recall of information related to oneself, was shown by T. B. Rogers, Nicholas Kuiper and W. S. Kirker (1977); keys write "Rogers and Kuiper". asked 2 times Implicit memory affects performance without conscious awareness (priming, skills); explicit memory involves conscious recollection (Graf and Schacter, 1985). asked 2 times The connectionist or parallel distributed processing model (Rumelhart and McClelland, 1986) treats memory as a network of interconnected nodes activated simultaneously, with knowledge held in the connection weights. asked 2 times In the RML 2025 matching: dementia goes with abstraction, amnesia with memory, aphasia (with alexia and acalculia) with language, and apraxia with skilled movement. asked 2 times Levels of processing (Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart, 1972): structural, then phonemic, then semantic; deep, semantic processing gives the best retention. asked 2 times Repression (Freud) is the unconscious exclusion of threatening memories from awareness; suppression is conscious. asked 2 times The stage (multi-store) model of Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin (1968) has three stores, sensory, short-term and long-term; information must pass through short-term memory to reach long-term memory, and working memory is not one of its stores. asked 2 times RML 2024 keys McCrary and Hunter (1953) for first observing the primacy-recency effect; the earlier observation is Ebbinghaus's (1885). asked once Decay theory is traced to Edward Lee Thorndike's law of disuse (RML 2024 key); Melton and Irwin (1940) proposed the two-factor theory of interference. asked once PQRST is Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation, Test; SQ3R (Francis P. Robinson, 1946) is Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review. asked once
