Alpha is for the literate (verbal); Beta is for the illiterate (non-verbal). 9.3 The IQ and the Modern Tests High yield · 32 Qs The ratio IQ had a fatal flaw, and the way it was fixed gave us the IQ we use today. To see the flaw, push an adult through the formula. From Ratio IQ to Deviation IQ Mental age grows quickly in childhood, slows in adolescence and stops growing in the mid to late teens. Chronological age keeps climbing. Take a perfectly ordinary 40-year-old whose mental age, like that of most adults, levelled off at about 16: the ratio formula gives (16 ÷ 40) × 100 = 40, a score that would label an average adult as severely impaired. Terman patched the problem by treating every adult as if he or she were about 16 years old, but the patch hid a second flaw. Even in childhood, the spread of ratio IQs differs from age to age, so an IQ of 115 might put a 6-year-old in a different position relative to his age-mates than a 12-year-old with the same number. A score that means different things at different ages is a poor score. David Wechsler's solution, introduced with the Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale in 1939, was to abandon mental age altogether. A person's raw score is compared with the scores of a large, representative sample of people of the same age (the norms ), and the IQ simply reports how far above or below the average of that age group the person falls. This is the deviation IQ ; because it is a standard score, some books call it the "standard IQ". The mean of every age group is set at 100 and the standard deviation (SD) , the typical distance of scores from the mean, is set at 15. In formula form, if z is the number of standard deviations a person scores above or below the age-group mean (a z score ): deviation IQ = 100 + 15 z A 40-year-old who scores exactly at the mean of 40-year-olds gets 100; one who scores one standard deviation above them gets 115. The meaning of 115 is now the same at every age: better than about 84 per cent of one's age-mates. Study guides sometimes describe Wechsler's method as "the actual score divided by the expected mean score for the person's age"; that is a loose way of saying the same thing, that the person is compared with the expected performance of his or her own age group, and if you meet that wording as an option, it is the one intended. Other standard scores work the same way with different numbers: the T score used by many personality and neuropsychological tests has a mean of 50 and an SD of 10, and the Wechsler subtest scaled scores have a mean of 10 and an SD of 3. A percentile rank is different again; it is not a standard score but simply the percentage of the norm group scoring below a person. Because IQ scores are approximately normally distributed, the familiar properties of the normal curve let you translate any IQ into a percentile, the percentage of people scoring below it. Now an older Stanford-Binet style question: on a test with a mean of 100 and an SD of 16, a person scores 136. Then z = (136 − 100) ÷ 16 = 2.25, and the normal-curve table gives about 0.987 of the area below z = 2.25, so about 98.7 per cent of people score lower. The SD matters. The Stanford-Binet adopted the deviation IQ in its 1960 revision (Form L-M) with an SD of 16, kept 16 in the fourth edition (1986), and moved to 15, in line with the Wechsler scales, only in the fifth edition (2003). Always check which SD a question gives you. Exam trap Ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, from Stern (1912) and Terman (1916); the original Stanford-Binet used it. Deviation IQ is a standard score with mean 100 and SD 15, comparing a person with same-age peers; Wechsler introduced it in 1939, and modern tests (including the SB5) use it. The deviation IQ is not "only for adults", it does not use raw scores without standardisation, and the ratio IQ is not the more reliable of the two (its meaning shifts from age to age, which is why it was abandoned). The old Stanford-Binet SD was 16, not 15. The Wechsler Scales Wechsler, a Romanian-born American who had tested army recruits in 1918, was chief psychologist at Bellevue Psychiatric Hospital in New York when he built his first scale. He set out to correct several faults he saw in the Stanford-Binet: it was designed for children, so its items had little appeal for adults; it leaned heavily on verbal, word-manipulation tasks; it placed too much weight on speed; and it rested on the concept of mental age, which made no sense for adults. His answer had four features that still define the Wechsler tests. They are point scales rather than age scales : items are grouped by type into subtests, and points are earned within each subtest, rather than items being grouped by the age at which they are passed, as in Binet's ladder. They combine verbal subtests with non-verbal performance tests (block designs, picture puzzles) that require little or no language. They yield subtest and part scores as well as a total, so a clinician can see a profile of strengths and weaknesses. And they use the deviation IQ. The family has grown with every generation (Table 9.4). Until the 2000s each test produced a Verbal IQ , a Performance IQ and a Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) . The newer editions replaced the verbal-performance split with index scores built on factor-analytic research (Section 9.4). Table 9.4 The Wechsler family of intelligence scales. The Working Memory Index, built from Digit Span and Arithmetic, is the one that reflects attention, concentration and mental control. One paper asked which subtest is "core in the WAIS-IV but not found in the WISC-V" and keyed Letter-Number Sequencing. Strictly, Letter-Number Sequencing is a supplemental subtest in the WAIS-IV (it was part of the Working Memory Index in the WAIS-III) and a secondary subtest in the WISC-V; but it is still the best of the options offered, because Digit Span, Symbol Search and Matrix Reasoning are core in both tests. The WISC-V covers 6 years to 16 years 11 months. The Stanford-Binet Today, and Other Individual Tests The Stanford-Binet was revised in 1937 (by Terman and Maud Merrill), in 1960, in 1986 and most recently as the Stanford-Binet Fifth Edition (SB5) (in full, the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition), developed by Gale Roid and published in 2003. The SB5 covers ages 2 to 85 and over and is organised around five factors drawn from the hierarchical Cattell-Horn-Carroll model of Section 9.4, with the working-memory factor also drawing on Alan Baddeley's working-memory model (Chapter 7): Fluid Reasoning, Knowledge, Quantitative Reasoning, Visual-Spatial Processing and Working Memory. Each factor is measured once in a verbal and once in a non-verbal form, giving 10 subtests and a Full Scale IQ, a Verbal IQ and a Nonverbal IQ, all with mean 100 and SD 15. Like the earlier Stanford-Binets, it uses a basal level (the level at which the person passes all items, so easier items need not be given) and a ceiling level (the level at which the person fails all or most items, so testing stops). Several other individual tests appear in questions. Alan and Nadeen Kaufman's Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (K-ABC, 1983) was one of the first major tests built on Luria's neuropsychology (Section 9.5); their Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test, second edition (KBIT-2, 2004), is a 20-minute screening test with just two scales, a Verbal or crystallised scale and a Nonverbal or fluid scale. For infants, intelligence in the adult sense cannot yet be measured, so developmental scales are used instead: the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (Nancy Bayley; the current edition covers roughly the first 42 months) assess cognitive, language and motor development, and the McCarthy Scales of Children's Abilities (Dorothea McCarthy, 1972) cover about 2½ to 8½ years. Developmental scales express results as a developmental quotient (DQ) , developmental age divided by chronological age, times 100, a ratio exactly like Stern's. Detailed administration and scoring belong to the Assessment book. Classifying IQ Scores Test publishers attach descriptive labels to ranges of IQ (Table 9.6). The labels have softened over the decades: the WAIS-IV's "borderline" has become "very low" in the WISC-V and WAIS-5, and the old psychiatric category of borderline intellectual functioning , which DSM-IV-TR placed at IQ 71 to 84, overlaps the "low average" and "borderline" bands. Culture-Fair Tests A vocabulary item asks, in effect, "Have you met this word?", and whether you have met it depends on your home, school and language. Psychologists have therefore tried to build tests whose content is equally familiar, or equally unfamiliar, to everyone. The early hope was a culture-free test , one entirely free of cultural influence; that turned out to be impossible, because even the habit of sitting quietly, working against a clock and treating abstract shapes as a meaningful problem is learned. The realistic goal is a culture-fair test (also called culture-reduced), one that minimises language, reading, specific knowledge and speed so that people from different backgrounds are on a more equal footing. The most famous is Raven's Progressive Matrices , devised by the British psychologist John Carlyle Raven (1902 to 1970), a student of Spearman. Each item shows a pattern of figures arranged in a matrix with one piece missing, and the examinee chooses the piece that completes it. Solving an item requires working out the rule that governs the rows and columns, which is what Spearman called the eduction of relations (Section 9.4). The Standard Progressive Matrices (SPM), published in 1938 (Raven had drafted it by 1936, so some books give that year), has 60 items in five sets of 12 that grow progressively harder, hence the name. The Coloured Progressive Matrices (36 items) are for children and older or impaired adults, and the Advanced Progressive Matrices (48 items) for high-ability adults. Raven's matrices are the classic measure of fluid intelligence, the ability to reason with novel material (Section 9.4), and they are also the best single marker of Spearman's general factor. Raymond Bernard Cattell's Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT), first issued around 1940 as a "culture-free" test and soon renamed, is a group test in three scales for different ages and abilities. Its subtests (series completion, classification, matrices and "conditions", a topological task) use only figures. Other non-verbal and performance tests that reduce the role of language include Florence Goodenough's Draw-a-Man test (1926), the Leiter International Performance Scale, the Porteus Maze Test, Kohs block designs and Alexander's Pass-Along test; the Army Beta was an early example of the same idea. Exam trap Raven's Progressive Matrices measure fluid intelligence; choose "fluid" over "crystallised", "verbal" or "social". If "general intelligence (g)" is offered alongside "fluid", the expected answer is still fluid, although Raven's is also the best single measure of g, because Gf and g are very closely related. Raven's is called culture-fair because it is non-verbal, with minimal language demands; it is not culture-free, and schooling still affects scores. Intelligence Tests in India Most Western tests cannot simply be translated for Indian use: the vocabulary, the general-information items ("Who wrote Hamlet ?") and even the pictures assume a particular culture, and many children who need assessment have had little or no schooling. Indian psychologists responded in two ways: by adapting the Binet and Wechsler tests with Indian content and norms, and by building performance batteries that need no reading at all. Are IQ Tests Reliable and Valid, and What Do They Predict? A test is useful only if it is reliable (it gives consistent scores) and valid (it measures what it claims to measure). The major individual IQ tests are among the most reliable instruments in psychology: the internal-consistency reliability of the WAIS-IV Full Scale IQ is about .98, and retesting after a few weeks typically gives correlations around .9. Individual subtests are much less reliable than the total, which is why clinicians interpret composite scores first. Validity comes in several kinds (the Assessment and Research Methodology books treat them fully). Content validity asks whether the items sample the domain adequately. Criterion-related validity asks whether scores relate to an outside criterion; it is called concurrent validity when test and criterion are measured at about the same time, and predictive validity when the criterion comes later. Construct validity asks whether the test behaves as the theory of the construct predicts, for example correlating with other measures of reasoning but not with unrelated traits. So if a new intelligence test is given alongside a well-established one, and the two sets of scores are correlated, the researcher is checking concurrent validity. What does IQ predict? A great deal, though far from everything. IQ correlates about .5 with school grades and about .55 with the number of years of education completed. In a famous 1998 review of 85 years of research, Frank Schmidt and John Hunter found that general mental ability predicts job performance with a validity of about .5, higher for complex jobs than for simple ones, which makes it the single best predictor of job performance across occupations. Childhood IQ even predicts health and lifespan: in Scotland, people who had been tested at age 11 in the Scottish Mental Survey of 1932 were more likely to be alive decades later if they had scored higher. But a correlation of .5 means IQ accounts for only about a quarter of the variation in grades (.5 squared is .25); motivation, conscientiousness, teaching, opportunity and luck account for the rest. Clinical link Clinical psychologists use intelligence tests to diagnose intellectual disability, to identify specific learning disabilities (where achievement falls well below what ability predicts), to document cognitive decline after brain injury or in dementia, to plan rehabilitation and education, and to establish eligibility for benefits such as a disability allowance or disability certificate. For adults the WAIS is used; for children with special educational needs, the WISC or an Indian equivalent. Every such use rests on current, local norms: a test normed decades earlier inflates scores (the Flynn effect, Section 9.7), which can wrongly deny someone a diagnosis or support. If intelligence is one thing, people who do well on one test should do well on all of them. If it is many things, a person could be strong in one and weak in another. The tool for deciding between these possibilities was invented for the purpose, and it shaped the next hundred years of theory. Factor Analysis in Plain Words Suppose 200 Class 9 students take tests in English, Hindi, mathematics, physics and drawing. You correlate every test with every other and lay out the correlations in a table, a correlation matrix. You notice that English and Hindi correlate highly with each other, mathematics and physics correlate highly with each other, and every test correlates at least a little with every other. Factor analysis is a family of statistical methods that asks how few underlying variables, called factors , are needed to explain such a pattern of correlations. Each test's correlation with a factor is its factor loading . Here you might find one factor on which all five tests load (a general ability), plus a "language" factor and a "mathematics-science" factor. The method does not tell you what the factors mean; the researcher names them by looking at which tests load on them, and different methods of extracting and rotating factors can give different-looking answers from the same data. That is why factor analysts have argued for a century. Spearman's Two-Factor Theory The British psychologist Charles Edward Spearman (1863 to 1945) invented the first form of factor analysis. In 1904, in a paper titled "General Intelligence, Objectively Determined and Measured", he analysed the school marks and sensory-discrimination scores of English schoolchildren (in classics, French, English, mathematics, pitch discrimination and music). He found that all the measures correlated positively with one another, a pattern now called the positive manifold . Moreover, the correlations fell into a neat hierarchy, a regularity Spearman later expressed as "tetrad differences" close to zero, which is exactly what you would expect if a single common factor ran through every measure. He called this common factor general intelligence (g) . Every test, he proposed, measures g plus a specific factor (s) peculiar to that test: the ability to do arithmetic depends partly on g and partly on a specific arithmetical skill. Because it has exactly two kinds of factor, general and specific, this is called the two-factor theory (Figure 9.2). Tests differ in how heavily they are "saturated" with g; Spearman found that tasks requiring abstract reasoning were the most saturated, and simple sensory tasks the least. He interpreted g as a kind of general mental energy, and in 1923 he described three "noegenetic" (knowledge-creating) principles that he thought defined it: the apprehension of experience, the eduction of relations (seeing the relationship between two things) and the eduction of correlates (applying a relationship to generate a new item). Raven's matrices, built by his student, are a direct test of eduction. In The Abilities of Man (1927) Spearman admitted that some tests also share narrower group factors, such as verbal or mechanical ability, but g remained the centre of his theory. Spearman (1904): g plus s g Classics s1 French s2 Maths s3 Music s4 each test score = g + its own s Thurstone (1938): 7 primary abilities Verbal comprehension (V) Word fluency (W) Number (N) Space (S) Associative memory (M) Perceptual speed (P) Reasoning or induction (R or I) Later: the seven correlate (a higher g) Figure 9.2 Two early answers to "one or many?". In Spearman's two-factor model every test draws on the same general factor g plus its own specific factor s. In Thurstone's model there are seven separate primary abilities and no g, although Thurstone later found that the seven themselves correlate, which brings a general factor back at a higher level. Exam trap Spearman's g is a general factor underlying performance on all cognitive tasks; s is the specific factor of each task. Neither is "group factors" (that is Thurstone, Burt and Vernon) nor "genetic predisposition". The two-factor theory is not the triarchic model (Sternberg), multiple intelligences (Gardner), seven primary abilities (Thurstone) or fluid and crystallised intelligence (Cattell). The same Spearman gave us the rank-order correlation coefficient (rho) and, with William Brown, the Spearman-Brown formula used in reliability. Thorndike's Multifactor Theory Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949), the learning theorist of Chapter 6, rejected g. For him intelligence was the product of a vast number of separate stimulus-response connections, and a person was more intelligent simply by having more of them. This multifactor theory is sometimes called the "anarchic" theory, because it allows no governing general factor. Thorndike distinguished three broad kinds of intelligence: abstract intelligence (dealing with ideas and symbols), mechanical intelligence (also called concrete intelligence: dealing with things and tools) and social intelligence (dealing with people). In 1920 he defined social intelligence as the ability to understand and manage men and women, boys and girls, and to act wisely in human relations. His later test, the CAVD (1927), combined four kinds of item, sentence Completion, Arithmetic, Vocabulary and following Directions, and he described intelligence along four dimensions: level (the difficulty of tasks one can solve), range (the number of tasks one can solve at a given level), area (the total of the ranges across levels) and speed. A related idea came from the English-born psychologist Godfrey Hilton Thomson (1881 to 1955), who spent most of his career at Newcastle and then Edinburgh. His sampling theory (first proposed in 1916 and developed in The Factorial Analysis of Human Ability , 1939) showed that the positive manifold does not prove that a single g exists. Suppose the mind contains a huge number of small, independent "bonds" or elementary abilities, and every test calls on a random sample of them. Any two tests will then share some bonds by chance, and so will correlate, even though nothing general exists. Correlation among tests, Thomson pointed out, could come from overlapping samples rather than from one common cause. Versions of this argument are still debated today. Thurstone's Primary Mental Abilities Louis Leon Thurstone (1887 to 1955) of the University of Chicago developed a more powerful method, multiple factor analysis, designed to find several factors at once. In Primary Mental Abilities (1938) he gave 56 tests to 240 university students and extracted seven factors that he called the primary mental abilities : verbal comprehension (V), word fluency (W), number (N), space (S), associative memory (M), perceptual speed (P) and reasoning, also called induction (R or I). Thurstone argued that these seven were distinct abilities, not reflections of g, and he built the Primary Mental Abilities tests (1941, with his wife Thelma Gwinn Thurstone) to give each person a profile across them. Because it replaces one ruler with a small number of group factors, his view is called a group-factor theory (sometimes "oligarchic", rule by a few). The story has a twist. When the Thurstones tested schoolchildren, whose abilities are less differentiated than those of university students, the seven factors correlated substantially with one another. And a set of correlated factors can itself be factor-analysed, yielding a "second-order" general factor. Spearman and Thurstone were, in the end, both partly right: there are several distinct broad abilities, and there is something general that they share. The hierarchical models below formalise that compromise. Exam trap Count carefully. Thurstone: seven primary mental abilities (1938). Gardner: seven intelligences in 1983, eight after the naturalist was added in 1999. Do not mix the lists: "spatial" appears in both, but "word fluency", "perceptual speed" and "associative memory" are Thurstone's, while "musical", "bodily-kinaesthetic" and "intrapersonal" are Gardner's. Thurstone is also the Thurstone of attitude scaling (the method of equal-appearing intervals) in the Social book. In the Indian textbook classification, the unifactor or "monarchic" theory is Binet's (one general ability), the "oligarchic" theory is Thurstone's (a few group factors) and the "anarchic" theory is Thorndike's (many independent abilities). Guilford's Structure of Intellect Joy Paul Guilford (1897 to 1987), who had worked on the selection of aircrew during the Second World War, went furthest in the direction of many abilities. His structure of intellect (SOI) model , set out fully in The Nature of Human Intelligence (1967), classifies every intellectual task along three dimensions, pictured as a cube (Figure 9.3): Operations , the kind of mental process involved (five): cognition, memory, divergent production (generating many possible answers to an open problem, the basis of creativity), convergent production (arriving at the one correct answer) and evaluation. Contents , the kind of material the process works on (four): figural, symbolic, semantic and behavioural. Products , the form the information takes (six): units, classes, relations, systems, transformations and implications. Every combination of one operation, one content and one product defines a separate ability, so the model contains 5 × 4 × 6 = 120 abilities. For example, knowing what words mean is the cognition of semantic units; thinking up as many uses as possible for a brick is the divergent production of semantic units. Guilford later split the figural content into visual and auditory, giving 5 × 5 × 6 = 150 abilities (sources date this to 1977 or 1982), and in 1988 he split memory into memory recording and memory retention, giving 6 × 5 × 6 = 180. OPERATIONS (5), front slice to back slice: cognition, memory, divergent production, convergent production, evaluation PRODUCTS (6) Units Classes Relations Systems Transformations Implications Figural Symbolic Semantic Behavioural CONTENTS (4) operations 5 × 4 × 6 = 120 abilities (1967); later 150, then 180 (1988) Figure 9.3 Guilford's structure of intellect. Each small cell is one ability defined by an operation, a content and a product. The front slice shown is cognition; the shaded cell is the cognition of semantic units (CMU), roughly vocabulary knowledge. Guilford's lasting legacy is the distinction between convergent and divergent thinking, which launched the psychometric study of creativity (Chapter 8). The model itself fared less well. Critics showed that his factor-analytic method could produce "evidence" for almost any structure the researcher had in mind, and that many of the supposedly independent abilities in fact correlate positively, as Spearman would have predicted. Exam trap Guilford's model has three dimensions (operations, contents, products) but 120 abilities (1967), later 150 and then 180. Strictly, then, the model has three dimensions and 120 abilities. One paper (RML 2021) asked "how many dimensions of intelligence" with both "three" and "120" among the options and keyed 120, using "dimensions" loosely to mean abilities. If that exact question returns, 120 is the answer its setters expect; but if a question asks you to name the dimensions, faces or parameters of the cube, the answer is three (operations, contents, products), and if it asks for abilities or factors, it is 120 (or 150 or 180 if the question names the later version). The number of products is six, of operations five, of contents four (later five). Hierarchical Models: Burt and Vernon British psychologists reconciled g with group factors by arranging abilities in a hierarchy, like the branches of a tree. Cyril Lodowic Burt (1883 to 1971) proposed one such model in 1949, and Philip Ewart Vernon (1905 to 1987) produced the best-known version in The Structure of Human Abilities (1950). In Vernon's hierarchical model , g sits at the top. Below it are two major group factors : v:ed (verbal-educational ability) and k:m (spatial, mechanical and practical ability). Below these come minor group factors : verbal fluency and numerical ability under v:ed; spatial, mechanical-information and psychomotor abilities under k:m. At the bottom are the specific factors of individual tests. Vernon's model is essentially Spearman's g and s with group factors inserted between them. Fluid and Crystallised Intelligence Raymond Bernard Cattell (1905 to 1998), a British-born student of Spearman who spent his career in the United States, divided g itself into two. He first sketched the idea in the early 1940s and set it out fully in 1963; his student John Leonard Horn (1928 to 2006) developed it with him from 1966. Fluid intelligence (Gf) is the capacity to reason, see relationships and solve novel problems independently of previously acquired knowledge; it is what you use the first time you meet a puzzle. Crystallised intelligence (Gc) is the repertoire of information, cognitive skills and strategies acquired through education and experience: vocabulary, general knowledge, learned methods. Cattell's investment theory (1971) linked the two: Gf is "invested" in learning experiences, and the knowledge that results "crystallises" as Gc, rather as water freezes into ice. The two can be told apart by how they are measured and by how they change across life (Figure 9.4). Gf is measured by Raven's matrices, matrix reasoning, series completion and other novel-problem tests; Gc by vocabulary, information and comprehension subtests. Gf rises through childhood, peaks in the early twenties and then declines gradually. Gc goes on rising, or at least holds steady, well into the sixties, because people continue to learn. (Note that block design and coding, sometimes offered as options, are measures of visual-spatial ability and processing speed, not of Gc.) 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 Age (years) high low Relative level (schematic) Gf Gc Gf peaks in the early twenties Gc holds or rises into the sixties Fluid intelligence (Gf) Crystallised intelligence (Gc) Figure 9.4 A schematic of the typical lifespan pattern for fluid and crystallised intelligence, after Horn and Cattell. Fluid reasoning peaks early and declines; accumulated knowledge holds up or grows into later life. The curves show the general shape only, not actual test scores. Horn extended the model to nine or ten broad abilities, adding to Gf and Gc visual processing (Gv), auditory processing (Ga), short-term memory (Gsm), long-term storage and retrieval (Glr), processing speed (Gs), decision or reaction speed, quantitative knowledge (Gq) and reading-writing (Grw). Unlike Spearman, Horn did not believe in a single g above them. Exam trap Crystallised = a repertoire of information, cognitive skills and strategies; accumulated knowledge and verbal skill; measured best by vocabulary and information. Fluid = the ability to deal with new problems; measured by matrices. "Practical" and "successful" intelligence are Sternberg's terms; "speed of neural processing" and "working memory capacity" are related to, but not the definition of, either. The Gf and Gc theory belongs to Raymond Cattell (with Horn), not James McKeen Cattell. Carroll's Three Strata and the CHC Model The most thorough factor-analytic study ever made was the work of John Bissell Carroll (1916 to 2003). In Human Cognitive Abilities (1993) he re-analysed more than 460 data sets collected over most of the twentieth century. He concluded that abilities form three layers, or strata (Figure 9.5). Stratum III is a single general factor, g. Stratum II contains eight broad abilities: fluid intelligence, crystallised intelligence, general memory and learning, broad visual perception, broad auditory perception, broad retrieval ability, broad cognitive speediness and processing (decision) speed. Stratum I contains about 70 narrow abilities, such as induction, lexical knowledge, memory span and visualisation. This is the three-stratum theory . Stratum III general Stratum II broad (8) Stratum I narrow g (general intelligence) Gf Gc Gy Gv Gu Gr Gs Gt About 70 narrow abilities, for example: induction, lexical knowledge, memory span, visualisation, reaction time Gf fluid · Gc crystallised · Gy general memory and learning · Gv visual perception Gu auditory perception · Gr retrieval ability · Gs cognitive speediness · Gt decision speed Figure 9.5 Carroll's three-stratum theory (1993). A general factor sits above eight broad abilities, which in turn sit above about 70 narrow ones. Vernon's earlier hierarchy has the same shape, with two major group factors (v:ed and k:m) in place of Carroll's eight. Because Carroll's broad abilities matched Cattell and Horn's so closely, the psychologist Kevin McGrew merged the two models in the late 1990s into the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory . CHC keeps Carroll's g at the top (while noting Horn's doubts about it), recognises roughly ten broad abilities in the middle, and many narrow abilities at the bottom. It is now the dominant framework for test construction: the Woodcock-Johnson batteries, the SB5, the Kaufman tests and the newer Wechsler indices are all organised, more or less explicitly, around CHC abilities. Jensen's Level I and Level II Abilities The American Arthur Robert Jensen (1923 to 2012), a champion of g, proposed a simpler two-level scheme. Level I abilities are associative: rote learning, memory span (repeating digits) and simple association, with little transformation of the input. Level II abilities are conceptual: abstract reasoning, problem solving and the manipulation of concepts, essentially g. Jensen reported that Level I abilities were fairly evenly distributed across social classes and ethnic groups, while groups differed more on Level II tasks. The scheme is famous because of where he published it. His 1969 article in the Harvard Educational Review , "How Much Can We Boost IQ and Scholastic Achievement?", opened with the sentence "Compensatory education has been tried and it apparently has failed." He went on to argue that the heritability of IQ was high and that genetic factors might be partly responsible for the average difference in IQ scores between Black and White Americans. The article provoked a storm of protest (the word "Jensenism" was coined for his position) and one of the longest-running debates in psychology. You will see in Section 9.7 why the step from "heritable within a group" to "genetic differences between groups" is a logical error, and why later research on compensatory education is more encouraging than Jensen claimed. That method has a built-in limit. It can only find structure among the abilities that someone thought to test, and almost everyone tested the abilities that school rewards. From the 1980s onwards a group of theorists asked what a theory of intelligence would look like if it started somewhere else: from the brain, from the study of experts and prodigies, from how people cope with real life, or from the emotions. Gardner's Multiple Intelligences Howard Gardner (born 1943), a Harvard developmental psychologist, spent years in two very different settings: studying artistic development in children with Harvard's Project Zero, and working with adults who had suffered strokes at a Boston aphasia research unit. He was struck by how selectively the brain fails. A stroke could destroy a man's language and leave his musical or spatial abilities intact; a child could be a prodigy at music and ordinary at everything else. In Frames of Mind (1983) he proposed that there is no single intelligence but several relatively independent ones. This is the theory of multiple intelligences . Gardner did not use factor analysis. Instead he set eight criteria that a candidate intelligence should meet: it can be isolated by brain damage; it is shown in exceptional form by savants, prodigies or other exceptional individuals; it has an identifiable core operation; it has a distinctive developmental history ending in expert performances; it has a plausible evolutionary history; it is supported by experimental tasks; it is supported by psychometric findings; and it can be encoded in a symbol system (language, number, musical notation). The theory was enormously popular with teachers, because it promised that every child is intelligent in some way, and schools around the world, including many in India, adopted "multiple intelligence" lesson plans. Researchers were cooler. The criticisms are worth knowing. First, Gardner offered little direct empirical test of the theory; the intelligences were argued for, not measured. Second, when researchers did build tests for them (for example Beth Visser, Michael Ashton and Philip A. Vernon in 2006; this is a different Vernon from the hierarchical theorist of Section 9.4), most of the "cognitive" intelligences correlated substantially with one another and with g, which is the opposite of independence; only the bodily-kinaesthetic and, partly, musical abilities stood apart. Third, critics argued that musical and bodily abilities are better called talents; calling them intelligences changes the word, not the facts. Exam trap Gardner's book is Frames of Mind (1983): seven intelligences; naturalist added in 1999 to make eight; existential considered, not fully accepted; spiritual rejected. "Linguistic, logical-mathematical and spatial" is a Gardner list, never a Sternberg or Cattell one. Gardner used no factor analysis, so a statement that he "derived the intelligences by factor analysis" is false. Sternberg's Triarchic Theory and Successful Intelligence Robert Jeffrey Sternberg (born 1949) has a personal reason to distrust IQ tests: as a primary-school pupil he suffered from such severe test anxiety that he scored poorly on group IQ tests, until a teacher who expected more of him changed how he performed. His triarchic theory of intelligence , set out in Beyond IQ (1985), has three parts, or subtheories (Table 9.10). The componential subtheory describes the mental mechanisms of intelligent thought, the components that analytical intelligence uses. There are three kinds. Metacomponents are executive processes that plan what to do, monitor it while it is being done and evaluate it afterwards. Performance components carry out the plan: encoding the problem, inferring relations, applying them. Knowledge-acquisition components learn new information: selective encoding (picking out the relevant facts), selective combination (putting them together) and selective comparison (relating them to what you already know). This is the kind of intelligence school tests measure best, and Sternberg calls the resulting ability analytical . The experiential subtheory concerns how intelligence relates to experience. Intelligence is shown most clearly at two points: when a task is new, where it shows as the ability to cope with novelty and produce insight, and when a task is becoming familiar, where it shows as the ability to automatise performance so that attention is freed for other things. A person strong here has creative intelligence. The contextual subtheory relates intelligence to the external world. Intelligent behaviour is purposive adaptation to one's environment, shaping the environment to suit oneself and, when neither works, selection of a better environment. A clerk who learns the unwritten rules of her office adapts; one who persuades her manager to change a pointless procedure shapes; one who leaves for a better job selects. The resulting ability is practical intelligence, "street smarts". Table 9.10 Sternberg's triarchic theory (1985). Subtheory Ability (later name) What it involves Everyday example Componential Analytical Metacomponents, performance components, knowledge-acquisition components Solving a textbook problem; analysing an argument Experiential Creative Coping with novelty; automatising the familiar Inventing a new solution; insight Contextual Practical Adapting to, shaping and selecting environments Managing a shop, an office or a family budget In the late 1990s Sternberg extended the triarchic theory into the theory of successful intelligence : the ability to achieve success in life, by one's own standards and within one's culture, by capitalising on strengths and correcting or compensating for weaknesses through a balance of analytical, creative and practical abilities. Central to practical intelligence is tacit knowledge , the practical, usually unspoken know-how that is rarely taught directly but is needed to succeed in a particular setting; Richard Wagner and Sternberg (1985) measured it in business managers and found it predicted their success independently of IQ. A striking illustration came from Brazil, where Terezinha Carraher, David Carraher and Analúcia Schliemann (1985) studied children who sold coconuts and snacks in street markets. The children did complex sums in their heads almost flawlessly while selling, but often failed the same sums presented as school arithmetic. A chaiwala's son who never misses a sale can likewise look "weak in maths" on a school test. Critics, notably Linda Gottfredson (2003), argue that tests of practical intelligence correlate with g more than Sternberg admits and that the evidence for a separate practical ability is thin. Exam trap Componential = analytical; experiential (not "experimental") = creative; contextual = practical. The ability to adapt to the present environment, select a better one or modify (shape) it is contextual . Sternberg's three are analytical, creative and practical, never "verbal, performance and full scale" (Wechsler), "fluid, crystallised and general" (Cattell and Spearman) or "linguistic, logical-mathematical and spatial" (Gardner). The PASS Model A third alternative started from neuropsychology. The Soviet neuropsychologist Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977), studying soldiers with brain wounds, described the brain as three "functional units". The first, based in the brainstem and its reticular activating system, regulates arousal and attention. The second, in the occipital, parietal and temporal lobes, receives, processes and stores information. The third, in the frontal lobes, programmes, regulates and verifies behaviour. Building on Luria, Jagannath Prasad Das (born 1931), an Odisha-born psychologist who spent most of his career at the University of Alberta in Canada, together with Jack A. Naglieri and John R. Kirby , proposed the PASS model of intelligence (set out in their 1994 book). PASS stands for four cognitive processes: Planning : deciding on, carrying out and checking strategies for solving problems (Luria's third unit, the frontal lobes). Attention : focused, selective and sustained attention while resisting distraction, with the necessary arousal (Luria's first unit). Simultaneous processing : integrating separate pieces of information into a whole that can be seen at once, as in understanding a map, a matrix or a sentence like "the boy is taller than the girl" (Luria's second unit, chiefly occipital-parietal). Successive processing : dealing with information in a strict serial order, as in repeating a phone number, following a recipe or sounding out a word (also Luria's second unit, chiefly fronto-temporal). Naglieri and Das turned the model into a test, the Cognitive Assessment System (CAS) (1997; second edition 2014), for school-age children. Because it measures processes rather than acquired knowledge, it shows smaller differences between ethnic and social groups than traditional IQ tests and is designed to link assessment to remediation; Das's PASS Reading Enhancement Programme (PREP) trains successive and simultaneous processing in children with reading difficulties. The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (1983) was also built on Luria's distinction between simultaneous and sequential processing. Indian context The PASS model is one of the few internationally influential theories of intelligence with an Indian-born principal author. J. P. Das's work in the 1970s on simultaneous and successive syntheses led directly to the model, and he also wrote on Indian conceptions of intelligence such as buddhi (Section 9.1). Questions sometimes ask you to expand PASS; it is Planning, Attention, Simultaneous, Successive. Ceci's Bioecological View The American developmental psychologist Stephen J. Ceci argued in 1990 that intelligence is not one general ability but a set of multiple cognitive potentials, each of which develops only when the context (the knowledge domain, the setting, the culture) and the person's motivation call it out. His bioecological model takes its name from Urie Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory (the Developmental book). His favourite evidence came from a 1986 study with Jeffrey Liker of expert racetrack handicappers, men who predicted the odds on horse races. The best of them reasoned using a complex model that weighed many interacting variables at once, a feat of cognitive complexity, yet their IQ scores bore no relation to their expertise. Complex thinking, Ceci concluded, depends on knowledge and context, not on IQ alone. Emotional Intelligence Thorndike's social intelligence of 1920 and Gardner's two personal intelligences were the ancestors of one of the most popular ideas in modern psychology. In 1990 Peter Salovey and John D. Mayer introduced the term emotional intelligence (EI) in its modern sense, defining it as the ability to monitor one's own and others' feelings and emotions, to discriminate among them and to use this information to guide one's thinking and actions. In 1997 they refined it into the four-branch model , which treats EI as a genuine ability, like other intelligences: Perceiving emotions accurately in oneself, in others' faces and voices, and in art. Using emotions to facilitate thought , for example harnessing a good mood for creative work. Understanding emotions : how they blend, change and follow from events. Managing emotions in oneself and others. Their test, the Mayer-Salovey-Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test (MSCEIT, 2002), scores answers against expert or consensus judgements, just as an ability test should. The idea reached the public through the science journalist Daniel Goleman (born 1946), whose bestseller Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ (1995) described five domains: knowing one's own emotions, managing one's emotions, motivating oneself, recognising emotions in others, and handling relationships. In Working with Emotional Intelligence (1998) he relabelled them self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. Goleman's version is a mixed model , because it mixes emotional abilities with personality traits and motivation such as optimism and persistence. Another mixed model came from Reuven Bar-On , whose self-report Emotional Quotient Inventory (EQ-i, 1997) measures intrapersonal, interpersonal, adaptability, stress-management and general-mood scales. Finally, Konstantinos Petrides and Adrian Furnham (around 2000) argued that self-report questionnaires cannot measure an ability at all, only how people see their own emotional dispositions; they renamed this trait emotional intelligence , a personality trait measured by questionnaires such as the TEIQue. In India, the Emotional Intelligence Scale of Anukool Hyde, Sanjyot Pethe and Upinder Dhar (2002) is widely used in research. Table 9.11 compares the four approaches. Ability EI, measured by the MSCEIT, is only modestly correlated with IQ and the Big Five, so it adds something new, and it predicts the quality of social relationships and some aspects of work performance, though modestly. Mixed and trait measures overlap heavily with personality (especially neuroticism, reversed, and extraversion), so much of what they predict is personality under a new name. And Goleman's claim that EI "can matter more than IQ" has not been supported: across most outcomes, including job performance, general mental ability remains the stronger predictor. Exam trap Salovey and Mayer coined the modern concept (1990); Goleman popularised it (1995). Goleman's five parts in the 1995 wording are knowing one's emotions, managing emotions, motivating oneself, recognising emotions in others and handling relationships; the 1998 labels (self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills) describe the same five, so if both appear as options, match the wording the question uses. "IQ, EQ, SQ, CQ" is not anyone's model of EI. Social, Practical, Spiritual and Other Intelligences Once intelligence was allowed to be plural, the list grew. Social intelligence, Thorndike's ability to understand and manage people, was measured as early as 1927 by the George Washington Social Intelligence Test, and appears as Guilford's behavioural content and Gardner's interpersonal intelligence. Practical intelligence and tacit knowledge belong to Sternberg. Spiritual intelligence was proposed by the physicist-philosopher Danah Zohar and the psychiatrist Ian Marshall in SQ: Spiritual Intelligence, the Ultimate Intelligence (2000), as the capacity to address problems of meaning and value; the psychologist Robert Emmons made a similar case the same year. Cultural intelligence (CQ), the ability to function effectively across cultures, was proposed by P. Christopher Earley and Soon Ang (2003). These ideas have practical uses, but none has the measurement base of g. Exam trap Beware the "quotients". IQ is the intelligence quotient; DQ the developmental quotient of infant scales; EQ the emotional quotient (Bar-On's term); CQ cultural intelligence. "SQ" is ambiguous: in the Vineland Social Maturity Scale it is the social quotient (Section 9.8), but in Zohar and Marshall it is spiritual intelligence. Read the context. From the 1970s, psychologists began asking a different question: which basic information-processing operations distinguish people who score high on IQ tests from those who score low? Galton, you may recall, had bet on simple speed and lost. A century later his bet was partly vindicated. Speed of Processing: Reaction Time and Inspection Time In the cognitive-correlates approach , researchers measure performance on simple laboratory tasks and correlate it with IQ. Earl Hunt and his colleagues (1975) showed, for example, that high-verbal university students retrieved the names of letters from memory faster than low-verbal students. Arthur Jensen pursued reaction time (RT). Using a panel of lights and buttons, he measured how quickly people lifted a finger from a home button and pressed the button beside whichever light came on, with one to eight possible lights. Choice reaction time rises as the number of alternatives grows (Hick's law), and Jensen found that higher-IQ people were somewhat faster and, even more clearly, less variable from trial to trial. The correlations are modest, typically about −.2 to −.4 (negative because faster times go with higher IQ), but they are remarkable given that the task involves no knowledge at all. An even purer measure is inspection time , introduced by Ted Nettelbeck and M. Lally in 1976. Two vertical lines of clearly different length are flashed for a few hundredths of a second and then covered by a mask; the person simply says which line was longer. Inspection time is the briefest exposure at which the person can still judge accurately. Shorter inspection times go with higher IQ: across many studies the correlation is about −.3 before correction and about −.5 after statistical correction for unreliability and restricted range. Speed of intake of very simple information, in other words, is part of what IQ tests capture. Working Memory The strongest cognitive correlate of intelligence is working memory capacity , the ability to hold information in an active state while processing it (Chapter 7). In an influential 1990 paper, Patrick Kyllonen and Raymond Christal asked whether reasoning ability is "little more than working-memory capacity" after finding very high correlations between the two at the level of latent factors. Later studies put the relationship lower, but working memory remains closely tied to fluid intelligence and much less to crystallised intelligence, which depends on stored knowledge. One reason is that solving a novel problem, such as a Raven's matrix, requires you to hold several partial rules in mind at once while testing them; lose one and the solution collapses. This is why working memory now has its own index on the Wechsler scales and its own factor on the SB5. Brain Size, Neural Efficiency and Genes Are bigger brains smarter? Nineteenth-century craniologists thought so and were famously biased in how they measured skulls. Modern magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies of living people find a real but modest positive correlation between total brain volume and IQ, about .2 to .4 depending on the meta-analysis. Brain size explains only a small part of the variation, and it says nothing about differences between groups, whose average head sizes differ for many reasons including body size and nutrition. How a brain works may matter more than how big it is. In 1988 Richard Haier and his colleagues used positron emission tomography (PET) to measure how much glucose people's brains consumed while they solved Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices. Surprisingly, the people who scored highest used the least glucose: their brains seemed to work less hard to solve the same problems. In a follow-up, people who practised the computer game Tetris for several weeks became better at it while their brains' glucose use fell. This is the neural efficiency hypothesis : more intelligent brains accomplish a task with less neural effort. The picture is not simple (on very difficult tasks, high scorers sometimes show more activation, because they keep working when others give up), and in 2007 Rex Jung and Haier summarised imaging studies in the parieto-frontal integration theory, which locates the networks most consistently linked to intelligence in the frontal and parietal lobes and the white-matter tracts between them. Finally, the genes. Modern genome-wide studies of hundreds of thousands of people show that intelligence is massively polygenic : it is influenced by thousands of genetic variants, each with a tiny effect. There is no "gene for intelligence". Earlier searches used linkage studies , which track whether a trait travels through families together with known stretches of DNA; that method works well for single-gene disorders such as Huntington's disease but found nothing reliable for intelligence, precisely because no single gene has a large effect. How such genes combine with environments is the subject of the next section. Remember Correlates are not causes. Faster reaction time, shorter inspection time, larger working memory, a slightly larger brain and more efficient glucose use all go with higher IQ, but each could be a cause, an effect (years of schooling and reading change the brain) or a shared result of something else, such as better health and nutrition. 9.7 Heredity and Environment Lower yield · 2 Qs No question in psychology has generated more heat than whether differences in intelligence are inherited. The heat comes from politics; the light comes from a small number of research designs that separate the effects of genes from the effects of environment. Learn the designs first, then the one statistic, heritability, that is most often misunderstood. Family and Twin Studies The simplest evidence comes from family studies : the more closely two people are related, the more similar their IQs. But relatives share homes as well as genes, so family resemblance alone cannot separate the two. Twin studies , first suggested by Galton in 1875, do better. Monozygotic (MZ) twins develop from a single fertilised egg and share virtually all their genes; dizygotic (DZ) twins develop from two eggs and share on average half their genes, like ordinary siblings. If both kinds of twins grow up together, their environments are about equally similar, so if MZ twins are more alike than DZ twins, the extra similarity is attributed to their extra genetic similarity. The most powerful version studies twins who were separated early in life and reared apart, because any similarity between them cannot come from a shared home. In 1981 Thomas Bouchard and Matt McGue pooled 111 studies of family resemblance in IQ. Their weighted averages, shown in Figure 9.6, form a clear gradient: the more genes two people share, the more similar their IQs, and for the same degree of relationship, people reared together are more alike than people reared apart. Both genes and shared environment are visible in the same chart. Identical twins reared apart are more alike than fraternal twins reared together, which points to genes; siblings reared together are more alike than siblings reared apart, and adoptive parents and children resemble each other a little, which points to shared environment. Key study: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart (from 1979) Question. Would identical twins raised in different families turn out alike or different? Method. Thomas J. Bouchard Jr. and his colleagues at the University of Minnesota located twins who had been separated in infancy and brought each pair to Minneapolis for about 50 hours of testing on intelligence, personality, interests and health. Pinel and Barnes report 59 pairs of MZ twins and 47 pairs of DZ twins reared apart, aged 19 to 68, plus many twins reared together. Result. The MZ twins reared apart correlated about .70 on IQ, nearly as high as MZ twins reared together, and in their 1990 report the team concluded that about 70 per cent of the variance in IQ in their sample was associated with genetic variation. The project became famous for anecdotes such as the "Jim twins", separated at a few weeks of age and reunited at 39, who had both married women named Linda and then women named Betty and had both named a son James Alan or James Allan. Criticism. Anecdotes are not data; coincidences are guaranteed when you compare two lives in enough detail. More seriously, many "separated" twins were placed with relatives or similar families, some had met before testing, and all were reared in industrialised countries by families screened for adoption, so the range of environments was narrow. As you will see, a narrow range of environments inflates heritability. Twin research also carries a warning from its history. The British psychologist Cyril Burt, whose hierarchical model you met in Section 9.4, reported very high IQ correlations for MZ twins reared apart from the 1940s to the 1960s. After his death in 1971, Leon Kamin (1974) noticed that Burt's correlations stayed identical to three decimal places (.771) as his sample supposedly grew, a statistical near-impossibility, and that his collaborators could not be traced. Most historians concluded that the later data were fraudulent, although a few writers have defended him. Modern estimates do not depend on Burt: the independent studies agree with one another. Adoption Studies Adoption studies compare adopted children with their biological parents, who gave them their genes but not their upbringing, and with their adoptive parents, who gave them their upbringing but not their genes. Large projects such as the Texas Adoption Project and the Colorado Adoption Project (begun in 1975 by Robert Plomin and John DeFries) produced a consistent and at first surprising result. As adopted children grow older, their IQs come to resemble those of their biological parents more and more, while the resemblance to their adoptive parents fades. Sandra Scarr and Richard Weinberg (1978) found that the IQ correlation between unrelated adolescents reared in the same adoptive home was close to zero. But adoption studies also show something just as important: adoption changes the level of IQ. In a French cross-fostering study, Christiane Capron and Michel Duyme (1989) found that both the social class of the biological parents and that of the adoptive parents made a substantial difference to children's IQ. In another French study, Duyme and his colleagues (1999) followed children with low IQs who were adopted between the ages of 4 and 6; by adolescence, those adopted into high-status homes had gained about 20 points and those adopted into low-status homes about 8. The two findings are not in conflict. Correlations describe who ranks above whom; means describe how high everyone is. Genes can strongly influence the rank order of children within a home while the home raises or lowers the level of all of them. Heritability: What It Is and What It Is Not Heritability (written h 2 ) is the proportion of the variation in a trait, within a particular population at a particular time, that is associated with genetic variation among the members of that population. In symbols, h 2 = genetic variance ÷ total phenotypic variance. A heritability of .6 for IQ means that 60 per cent of the differences among people in that population are associated with their genetic differences. It does not mean that 60 per cent of your intelligence comes from your genes and 40 per cent from your upbringing; for an individual that sentence has no meaning, because every bit of your intelligence comes from genes and environment acting together, as the music of a sitar comes from both the instrument and the player. You can estimate heritability from twin correlations with a simple formula proposed by Douglas Falconer: h 2 = 2 × (r MZ − r DZ ). Push Bouchard and McGue's figures through it: 2 × (.86 − .60) = 2 × .26 = .52. Because MZ twins reared together share all their genes and their home, the rest of their resemblance (.86 − .52 = .34) is attributed to the shared environment , the aspects of the home that make siblings alike, and whatever makes even identical twins differ (1 − .86 = .14) to the non-shared environment and measurement error. Three findings about heritability are essential: It changes with age. The heritability of IQ rises from about .2 in infancy to about .4 to .5 in childhood and .6 or more in adulthood, while the effect of the shared family environment shrinks almost to zero by adulthood. Bouchard named this the Wilson effect, after Ronald Wilson's Louisville twin study. One explanation is that, as people grow up, they increasingly choose environments that suit their genetic tendencies. It depends on the environment. In 2003 Eric Turkheimer and his colleagues studied 7-year-old American twins. In middle- and high-income families the heritability of IQ was about .70; in the poorest families it was close to .10, and the shared environment dominated. Where environments are adequate, genetic differences show; where environments are poor, poverty swamps them. Later meta-analyses found this pattern in the United States but weaker or absent in countries with stronger welfare systems, which is itself evidence that environments matter. Within-group heritability says nothing about between-group differences. The geneticist Richard Lewontin (1929 to 2021) made the point in 1970 with seeds. Take a sack of genetically varied seed corn and plant one handful in rich soil and another in poor soil. Within each tray, differences in height are entirely genetic (heritability 100 per cent), because every plant in the tray received the same soil. Yet the difference between the two trays is entirely environmental. High heritability within groups is therefore no evidence at all that a difference between groups is genetic. Finally, heritable does not mean unchangeable. Phenylketonuria (PKU) , an inherited inability to break down the amino acid phenylalanine, has a heritability close to 100 per cent and once caused severe intellectual disability; a low-phenylalanine diet begun in infancy prevents it. Height is highly heritable too, yet average heights have risen by several centimetres in a few generations as nutrition improved. Exam trap Heritability is a population statistic, not an individual one; it describes differences, not amounts; it is specific to a population and its range of environments; it rises with age; it does not explain differences between groups; and a highly heritable trait can still be changed by the environment. "Individual differences in intelligence are due to genes only" and "environment only" are both wrong: the answer is many factors, genetic and environmental, acting together. Reaction Range and the Interplay of Genes and Environment Behaviour geneticists now speak less of genes versus environment and more of how they work together. In 1963 Irving Gottesman (1930 to 2016) proposed the concept of reaction range : a genotype sets upper and lower limits on how a trait can develop, and the environment determines where within that range a person ends up. A child with a favourable genotype in a deprived home may score lower than a child with a less favourable genotype in a stimulating one. (A related idea is canalisation, the tendency of some traits to develop along the same path across almost any environment.) Genes and environments are also correlated. Sandra Scarr and Kathleen McCartney (1983) described three kinds of gene-environment correlation . It is passive when parents provide both genes and a matching environment (bookish parents pass on genes and fill the house with books). It is evocative when a child's genetically influenced traits draw responses from others (a curious child gets more answers). It is active when people seek out environments that suit them, which Scarr called niche-picking (the curious child grows up and joins the library). Active correlation becomes stronger with age, which helps explain why heritability rises. Turkheimer's finding is an example of gene-environment interaction : the effect of genes depends on the environment. How the Environment Matters Which environmental factors make a difference? The list begins before birth: maternal malnutrition, alcohol (the fetal alcohol syndrome of Section 9.8), infections and toxins can all lower IQ. After birth, nutrition matters. Iodine deficiency is the world's most preventable cause of intellectual impairment; a 1994 meta-analysis found that children in iodine-deficient areas scored about 13 points lower on average, which is why India adopted universal salt iodisation. Exposure to lead, from old paints, fuel and some cookware, lowers IQ even at low levels. Schooling raises IQ. Children's scores drop slightly over long summer holidays, children who start school later fall behind age-mates, and a 2018 meta-analysis of natural experiments by Stuart Ritchie and Elliot Tucker-Drob estimated that each additional year of education raises IQ by about 1 to 5 points. Family environment matters too: the responsiveness of parents, the availability of books and play materials and the amount of conversation a child hears all correlate with later IQ. Robert Zajonc and Gregory Markus's confluence model (1975) even tried to explain small birth-order effects by the "intellectual climate" of the family, which is diluted as more young children are added. Teachers' expectations can matter as well (the Pygmalion effect, covered in the Social book). The most dramatic evidence comes from deprivation and its reversal. In the 1930s Harold Skeels moved a group of apparently retarded toddlers from a bleak Iowa orphanage to an institution where women with intellectual disability doted on them. The transferred children gained, on average, close to 30 IQ points; the children left behind lost ground. Skeels followed them up as adults in 1966: the transferred group were self-supporting, while many of the others were still in institutions. More recently, Michael Rutter's study of children adopted into British homes from grossly depriving Romanian orphanages found that those adopted before about 6 months of age largely caught up, while those adopted later often showed lasting cognitive deficits. Early, severe deprivation does lasting harm; early rescue can undo much of it. Can We Raise IQ? The Intervention Programmes If environments matter, can deliberate programmes raise the intelligence of children from poor homes? This was the question Jensen answered so gloomily in 1969. First, the earlier and more intensive the programme, the more durable the gains in IQ itself; the Abecedarian children, who started in infancy, kept a measurable advantage. Second, even when IQ gains fade (the fade-out effect ), good programmes leave lasting benefits in schooling, employment and behaviour. Jensen's "compensatory education has been tried and it apparently has failed" was premature. The Flynn Effect The most startling evidence for environmental influence came from an unexpected source. In 1984 the political philosopher James Robert Flynn (1934 to 2020), working in New Zealand, showed that Americans had been gaining about 3 IQ points per decade throughout the twentieth century; in 1987 he reported massive gains in 14 nations. Every time a test was renormed, the new sample had to do better than the old one to earn the same IQ of 100. The gains were largest on tests of fluid reasoning such as Raven's matrices (Dutch military conscripts gained about 20 points between 1952 and 1982) and smallest on vocabulary and general information. The rise in average scores across generations is called the Flynn effect , a name coined by Herrnstein and Murray in The Bell Curve (1994); Richard Lynn had noticed the same trend in Japan a little earlier. Genes cannot change that fast, so the cause must be environmental. Candidate explanations include better nutrition and health, more and better schooling, smaller families, a more visually and technologically complex environment and greater familiarity with tests. Flynn's own explanation was that modern life has taught people to put on "scientific spectacles": to classify things abstractly and to take hypothetical problems seriously, exactly what fluid-reasoning tests demand. Since the mid-1990s the effect has stalled or reversed in some countries such as Norway and Denmark; because the reversal appears even within families (younger brothers scoring lower than older ones), it too must be environmental. Clinical link The Flynn effect means test norms go stale. A test normed 15 years ago gives scores about 4 or 5 points too high today. An adult who scores 72 on outdated norms might score 67 or 68 on current norms, and that difference can decide whether a person receives a diagnosis of intellectual disability, a disability certificate or special educational support. In the United States, where the Supreme Court barred the execution of people with intellectual disability in 2002, courts have had to rule on such corrections. Always use the most recent norms available, and say which norms you used in your report. Group Differences and Stereotype Threat In The Bell Curve (1994) the psychologist Richard J. Herrnstein (1930 to 1994) and the political scientist Charles Murray (born 1943) argued that IQ strongly shapes social outcomes such as income, poverty and crime, that American society was stratifying into a "cognitive elite" and a struggling underclass, and that the average difference of about 15 points between Black and White Americans on IQ tests was probably partly genetic. The book sold hundreds of thousands of copies and provoked fierce criticism. In response, the American Psychological Association appointed a task force chaired by Ulric Neisser , whose report "Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns" (1996) remains the most balanced summary. Its main conclusions: IQ tests measure something real and predict school and job performance; the tests predict outcomes about equally well for different groups, so they are not "biased" in that narrow statistical sense; the heritability of IQ within groups is substantial; but there was no direct evidence that the average difference between Black and White Americans is genetic, and Lewontin's argument shows that within-group heritability cannot settle the question. Groups differ in history, income, schooling, health and discrimination, and the Flynn effect shows how large purely environmental changes in IQ can be. Since then the gap has narrowed: William Dickens and Flynn (2006) estimated that Black Americans gained 4 to 7 points on White Americans between 1972 and 2002. One environmental mechanism can act during the test itself. Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson (1995) gave Black and White Stanford University students a set of difficult verbal items from the Graduate Record Examination, with differences in their entrance-test (SAT) scores statistically controlled. When the test was described as a diagnostic measure of intellectual ability, Black students did markedly worse than White students; when the same test was described as a laboratory problem-solving task unrelated to ability, the difference disappeared. Steele called this stereotype threat : the fear of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group, which creates anxiety and uses up the working memory needed for the task. Similar effects were reported for women taking difficult mathematics tests. Later, larger studies have found the effects smaller and less consistent than the early experiments suggested, so stereotype threat is best seen as one contributing factor rather than the whole explanation (the Social book covers it further). What about men and women? On overall measures of general intelligence the average difference is negligible; the tests were deliberately balanced to avoid one, and independent measures agree. There are small to moderate differences in specific abilities, most reliably an advantage for males in mental rotation and for females in verbal fluency and processing speed, and male scores tend to be more variable, with more men at both extremes. Exam trap The Flynn effect is a rise in average scores across generations, not a rise within one person's lifetime, and it is largest on fluid (Raven's-type) tests, not vocabulary. Herrnstein and Murray named it; Flynn documented it. Stereotype threat is Steele and Aronson (1995), not Rosenthal (teacher expectations) or Jensen (Level I and II). The two tails of the curve in Figure 9.1, the 2 per cent below 70 and the 2 per cent above 130, remain the places where intelligence testing matters most to individual lives. Defining Intellectual Disability The name has changed repeatedly, each time because the old name had become an insult. "Idiot", "imbecile" and "moron" gave way to "mental deficiency", then to mental retardation , the term of DSM-IV-TR and of India's Persons with Disabilities Act of 1995, and finally to intellectual disability . DSM-5 (2013) uses intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder), DSM-5-TR (2022) puts the second name first, and ICD-11 speaks of disorders of intellectual development. Across all modern systems, the definition has three parts: Deficits in intellectual functions , such as reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgement and learning, confirmed by clinical assessment and individually administered standardised intelligence testing. This means an IQ about two standard deviations or more below the mean, that is, about 70 or below; allowing for measurement error, DSM-5 speaks of scores of about 65 to 75. Deficits in adaptive functioning. Adaptive functioning means the conceptual, social and practical skills that people need to meet the standards of personal independence and social responsibility expected for their age and culture, such as handling money, communicating, keeping safe and looking after oneself. Onset during the developmental period. DSM-IV-TR required onset before 18; the American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD) extended its own definition to before age 22 in 2021. The biggest change in DSM-5 concerns severity. Under DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10, the four levels (mild, moderate, severe and profound) were defined by IQ ranges (Table 9.13). DSM-5 keeps the four levels but defines them by adaptive functioning in the conceptual, social and practical domains, because it is adaptive functioning that determines how much support a person needs, and because IQ scores become unreliable at the very low end. About 1 per cent of the population has intellectual disability, and about 85 per cent of them are in the mild range. Table 9.13 Levels of intellectual disability.
