Global developmental delay is a provisional diagnosis for children under 5 who fail to meet developmental milestones in several areas but are too young for their severity to be assessed reliably; they must be reassessed later. Unspecified intellectual disability is for people over 5 whose level cannot be assessed because of blindness, prelingual deafness, severe motor disability or severe problem behaviour. So a 7-year-old with a full-scale IQ of 65 and severe adaptive impairment does not receive either label: he is old enough and assessable, and he meets the criteria for intellectual disability itself. Exam trap The DSM-IV-TR criterion for mental retardation was an IQ about two standard deviations below the mean (about 70). DSM-5 defines severity by adaptive functioning , not IQ; IQ cut-offs alone are an old-system answer. Borderline intellectual functioning (IQ about 71 to 84 in DSM-IV-TR) is not intellectual disability. Global developmental delay is for children under 5 only. Measuring Adaptive Behaviour Because the diagnosis depends on everyday functioning, clinicians need a way to measure it. The classic tool was built at the same Vineland Training School where Goddard had worked. Edgar Arnold Doll (1889 to 1968) published the Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) in 1935. It is completed by interviewing someone who knows the person well, and it covers self-help (general, eating and dressing), self-direction, occupation, communication, locomotion and socialisation. The scale yields a social age (SA) , the age level of the person's social competence, and a social quotient (SQ) = (SA ÷ CA) × 100, a ratio exactly like Stern's IQ. A. J. Malin's Indian adaptation of the VSMS is the version most used in Indian clinics and disability certification. Its modern American successor, the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (Sara Sparrow, David Balla and Domenic Cicchetti, 1984; third edition 2016), assesses communication, daily living skills, socialisation and motor skills. Keep the quotients apart: intelligence tests give mental age and IQ; the VSMS gives social age and social quotient; infant scales such as Gesell's and Bayley's give developmental age and developmental quotient. Causes, in Brief Causes are identifiable in perhaps half of all cases, more often in severe than in mild disability. The most common chromosomal cause is Down syndrome , described by John Langdon Down in 1866 and shown by Jérôme Lejeune in 1959 to result from an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21). The most common inherited cause is fragile X syndrome , caused by an expanded repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. Metabolic causes include PKU (first described by Asbjørn Følling in 1934, now prevented by newborn screening and diet) and congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism), linked to iodine deficiency. Environmental causes include fetal alcohol syndrome, prenatal infections such as rubella, birth asphyxia, head injury, severe malnutrition and lead poisoning. Edward Zigler (1967) distinguished an "organic" group with an identifiable cause, usually more severe, from a "familial" or "cultural-familial" group, usually mild, representing the lower end of the normal distribution combined with poverty and deprivation. The disorders themselves are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Indian context The National Trust for the Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act, 1999 covers exactly the four groups in its title, so autism and intellectual disability are both included. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 recognises 21 disabilities and lists specific learning disabilities and autism spectrum disorder under its intellectual disability heading. Disability certification for intellectual disability rests on a standardised IQ test together with an adaptive-behaviour measure such as the VSMS. The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI Act, 1992) regulates the training of the professionals, including clinical psychologists, who carry out such assessments, and the National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities in Secunderabad (founded in 1984) leads national work in the field. Giftedness At the other tail, an IQ of 130 or above (the top 2 per cent) is the most common working cut-off for giftedness , but definitions have broadened. An influential 1972 United States government report listed six areas of giftedness: general intellectual ability, specific academic aptitude, creative or productive thinking, leadership, the visual and performing arts, and psychomotor ability. Key study: Terman's Genetic Studies of Genius (from 1921) Question. What becomes of exceptionally bright children? Popular opinion held that gifted children were frail, odd and doomed to "early ripe, early rot". Method. In 1921 Lewis Terman began screening California schoolchildren and selected about 1,500 (1,528) with Stanford-Binet IQs of about 135 or more, most above 140; their average IQ was about 151. The children, nicknamed the "Termites", were then followed for the rest of their lives, the study being carried on after Terman's death by Melita Oden, Robert Sears and others. Result. As a group the gifted children were healthier, taller, better adjusted and far more successful in education and careers than average; the stereotype of the sickly genius was wrong. Within the group, Terman and Oden found that the most successful men differed from the least successful not in IQ but in persistence, self-confidence, goal-directedness and family background. Textbook summaries add that the social and behavioural problems that did occur were concentrated among those with extremely high childhood IQs, of about 180 or more. Criticism. The sample was selected partly through teacher nomination and was disproportionately white, urban and middle class; many of the women, constrained by their era, never had careers to match their ability. And the screening missed two boys, William Shockley and Luis Alvarez, who were tested but not selected and later won Nobel Prizes in physics, a reminder that an IQ cut-off is not a measure of creative achievement. Terman's contemporary Leta Stetter Hollingworth (1886 to 1939) studied the very top of the range. Her book Children Above 180 IQ , published posthumously in 1942, found that such children often struggled socially, because they had few true peers, and she argued that an IQ of about 125 to 155 was "socially optimal". This is consistent with the Terman finding that adjustment problems clustered above 180. Many researchers now reject the idea that giftedness is simply a high IQ. Joseph Renzulli (born 1936) proposed the three-ring conception of giftedness (1978): gifted behaviour arises from the interaction of above-average (not necessarily exceptional) ability, task commitment and creativity. Françoys Gagné later distinguished gifts (natural abilities) from talents (systematically developed skills), with motivation, environment and chance turning one into the other. The relationship between creativity and intelligence, including the threshold hypothesis that IQ matters for creativity only up to about 120, is taken up in Chapter 8. Savant Syndrome and Prodigies Savant syndrome is the coexistence of a serious developmental disability, often autism or intellectual disability, with an "island" of exceptional ability. Langdon Down coined the term "idiot savant" in 1887; the psychiatrist Darold Treffert, who studied savants for decades, distinguished splinter skills, talented savants and the very rare prodigious savants. Roughly half of savants are autistic, and perhaps one autistic person in ten shows some savant skill. Typical domains are calendar calculation (naming the weekday of any date), rapid arithmetic, music, art and memory. Kim Peek (1951 to 2009), the inspiration for the film Rain Man (1988), memorised thousands of books; the British artist Stephen Wiltshire (born 1974), who is autistic, has drawn detailed panoramas of cities from memory after a single helicopter ride. Gardner used savants as evidence that abilities can be isolated, one of his criteria for separate intelligences. A savant must be distinguished from a prodigy , a child of otherwise typical or high ability who performs at an adult expert level in some domain. India's Shakuntala Devi (1929 to 2013), the "human computer" who in 1980 multiplied two 13-digit numbers in her head at Imperial College London, was a calculating prodigy, not a savant; Arthur Jensen tested her in 1988 and found extraordinary speed on numerical tasks. Clinical link For a clinical psychologist, the lesson of both tails is the same: the score starts the assessment, it does not end it. A child at IQ 68 with good adaptive skills may need classroom support rather than a diagnosis; a child at IQ 145 may need help with anxiety or social isolation more than an accelerated syllabus; and an autistic adult with a savant skill may need adaptive-skills training to live independently. The case of Binet's scale, revisited At the start of this chapter Binet made two claims: that intelligence is complex and a test can only sample it, and that it can be raised. A century of research has been kind to both. The factor theories found that intelligence is neither one thing nor a loose bundle of unrelated things, but a hierarchy: a general factor, broad abilities such as fluid and crystallised intelligence, and many narrow skills, with emotional, practical and creative abilities that standard tests barely touch. And the evidence that it can be raised is overwhelming: the Flynn effect, the gains of adopted children, the effects of schooling, iodine and early intervention, and the recovery of Skeels's toddlers. The hereditarians who borrowed Binet's scale were not wholly wrong either; within a given population, a large share of the differences in adult IQ is associated with genes. What they missed is that heritability is not destiny: it describes differences within one set of environments, it says nothing about differences between groups, and it coexists with large environmental effects on everyone's level. Binet's original purpose, to find the children who need help and then help them, survives in the DSM-5's insistence on adaptive functioning and in India's disability laws, which tie an IQ score to a right to support rather than to a label. Chapter summary 9.1 What is intelligence? Definitions range from Binet's judgement and adaptation, through Terman's abstract thinking, Thorndike's good responses and Boring's operational "what the tests test", to Wechsler's aggregate or global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment (1944), Sternberg's adapting, shaping and selecting, and Gottfredson's 1994 consensus. Achievement tests measure past learning, aptitude tests predict specific future learning, and intelligence tests predict learning in general. Implicit theories matter: Dweck's entity versus incremental theories (fixed versus growth mindset) shape persistence. 9.2 From Galton to Binet. Galton ( Hereditary Genius , 1869; anthropometric laboratory, 1884) measured sensory acuity and reaction time; James McKeen Cattell coined "mental test" (1890), but Wissler (1901) showed such tests did not predict grades. Binet and Simon's 1905 scale of 30 items, revised in 1908 (mental age) and 1911, measured judgement directly. Goddard translated it, Stern coined the intelligence quotient (1912), and Terman's Stanford-Binet (1916) made IQ = MA ÷ CA × 100 famous. Yerkes's Army Alpha (verbal) and Beta (non-verbal) of 1917 began group testing, and their misuse is a lasting warning. 9.3 The IQ and the modern tests. The ratio IQ fails for adults, so Wechsler (1939) introduced the deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15; IQ = 100 + 15z), which converts directly to percentiles. The WAIS-IV has four indices (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI) with 10 core subtests; the WISC-V (6 to 16 years 11 months) has five; the SB5 (2003) has five CHC factors. Raven's matrices (1938) and Cattell's Culture Fair test measure fluid reasoning with minimal language; Indian tests include the Binet-Kamat, MISIC and Bhatia's performance battery. IQ tests are highly reliable and predict school and job performance with correlations around .5. 9.4 Factor theories. Spearman (1904) found a positive manifold and proposed g plus specific s. Thorndike's multifactor theory named abstract, mechanical and social intelligence; Thomson explained correlations by overlapping samples of bonds; Thurstone (1938) found seven primary mental abilities; Guilford's cube had 120, then 150 and 180 abilities. Burt and Vernon arranged g, v:ed, k:m and specific factors in a hierarchy. Cattell and Horn split g into fluid and crystallised intelligence; Carroll's three strata (1993) and the CHC model now organise most tests. Jensen distinguished associative Level I from conceptual Level II abilities. 9.5 Broader views. Gardner (1983) proposed seven, later eight, relatively independent intelligences, attractive to teachers but weakly supported by data. Sternberg's triarchic theory (1985) has componential (analytical), experiential (creative) and contextual (practical) parts and grew into successful intelligence and tacit knowledge. The PASS model of Das, Naglieri and Kirby, based on Luria, measures planning, attention, simultaneous and successive processing with the CAS. Ceci stressed context and knowledge. Emotional intelligence comes in ability (Salovey and Mayer), mixed (Goleman, Bar-On) and trait (Petrides) versions; social, practical and spiritual intelligences extend the list. 9.6 Intelligence, speed and the brain. Higher IQ goes with faster and less variable reaction times, shorter inspection times, larger working memory capacity (especially for fluid intelligence), slightly larger brains and, in Haier's studies, more efficient brain metabolism. Intelligence is highly polygenic. These are correlates, not established causes. 9.7 Heredity and environment. Family, twin and adoption studies (Bouchard and McGue's review; the Minnesota study of twins reared apart) show substantial genetic influence. Heritability is a population statistic that rises with age, falls in poverty (Turkheimer) and cannot explain group differences (Lewontin). Gottesman's reaction range and gene-environment correlation and interaction describe how genes and environments combine. Nutrition, schooling, adoption and early intervention (Abecedarian, Perry, Head Start, ICDS) raise IQ or life outcomes, and the Flynn effect shows large environmental gains across generations. The Bell Curve's genetic claims for group differences are not supported; stereotype threat is one environmental factor in test performance. 9.8 The extremes. Intellectual disability requires deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning beginning in the developmental period; DSM-IV-TR graded it by IQ bands, DSM-5 by adaptive functioning. Adaptive behaviour is measured by the VSMS (social age and social quotient) and the Vineland scales; global developmental delay applies under age 5. Causes include Down syndrome, fragile X and PKU. Giftedness is studied through Terman's longitudinal study, Hollingworth's children above 180 and Renzulli's three rings; savant syndrome pairs disability with islands of exceptional skill. (JEMAS 2025) a Construct validity b Concurrent validity c Content validity d Predictive validity ✓ Answer: (b) Concurrent validity Criterion-related validity, concurrent type (Section 9.3) The concept What was done Giving the new test together with an established test and correlating the two sets of scores. (d) Predictive validity Also criterion-related, but needs a criterion gathered later , such as next year's grades. In the WAIS-IV (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition), how many core subtests are there in the Verbal Comprehension Index and the Perceptual Reasoning Index respectively? (Real PYQ 2025) a 3 verbal, 4 performance b 3 verbal, 3 performance c 4 verbal, 3 performance d 2 verbal, 4 performance ✓ Answer: (b) 3 verbal, 3 performance WAIS-IV core subtests (Table 9.5) The concept VCI core The Verbal Comprehension Index core is Similarities, Vocabulary and Information: 3 subtests. PRI core The Perceptual Reasoning Index core is Block Design, Matrix Reasoning and Visual Puzzles: 3 subtests (Table 9.5). Why not 4 The options with a 4 are tempting because each index also has supplemental subtests (Comprehension for VCI; Picture Completion and Figure Weights for PRI), but these only substitute for core ones and do not count towards the core total of 10 . Why the other options are wrong (a) 3 verbal, 4 performance Counts a supplemental PRI subtest (Picture Completion or Figure Weights) as core; the PRI core is only 3. (c) 4 verbal, 3 performance Counts the supplemental Comprehension subtest as core VCI; the VCI core is only 3. (d) 2 verbal, 4 performance Undercounts the VCI, whose core is 3, and adds a supplemental subtest to the PRI's core of 3. Which of the following subtests is part of the core battery for the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS-IV) but NOT typically found in the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-V)? (Real PYQ 2024) a Digit Span b Symbol Search c Matrix Reasoning d Letter-Number Sequencing ✓ Answer: (d) Letter-Number Sequencing (as keyed) WAIS-IV vs WISC-V subtest structure The concept Shared subtests Digit Span , Symbol Search and Matrix Reasoning are primary subtests in both the WAIS-IV and the WISC-V, so none of them can be the answer. Why this one Letter-Number Sequencing is the only option that is not a primary WISC-V subtest; it is a secondary one there. Key note Strictly, it is a supplemental , not core, subtest of the WAIS-IV (it was core in the WAIS-III ), so the stem is loose, but (d) is clearly the best of the four. Why the other options are not the answer (a) Digit Span A primary Working Memory subtest in both the WAIS-IV and the WISC-V, so it does not separate the two. (b) Symbol Search A primary Processing Speed subtest in both the WAIS-IV and the WISC-V, so it does not separate the two. (c) Matrix Reasoning Primary in both: part of Perceptual Reasoning in the WAIS-IV and Fluid Reasoning in the WISC-V. What is the age range valid for Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, 5th edition (WISC-V)? (RML 2022) a 5 years to 12 years b 6 years to 16 years 11 months c 7 years to 16 years 11 months d 6 years to 15 years 11 months ✓ Answer: (b) 6 years to 16 years 11 months Wechsler age bands (Table 9.4) The concept The range The WISC-V covers 6 years to 16 years 11 months. Where it fits It fills the gap between the WPPSI-IV , which ends at 7 years 7 months, and the WAIS-IV , which begins at 16 years (Table 9.4). Why the other options are wrong (a) 5 years to 12 years Matches no Wechsler scale; the WISC-V starts at 6 and runs to 16 years 11 months. (c) 7 years to 16 years 11 months Moves the lower end up by a year; the WISC-V starts at 6 years . (d) 6 years to 15 years 11 months Moves the upper end down by a year; the WISC-V runs to 16 years 11 months . Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM) is primarily designed to measure which type of intelligence? (Real PYQ 2025) a Crystallized intelligence b Fluid intelligence c Verbal intelligence d Social intelligence ✓ Answer: (b) Fluid intelligence Raven's Progressive Matrices, fluid reasoning (Sections 9.3, 9.4) The concept What each item asks Each item requires working out the rule behind a novel pattern of figures, with almost no language or learned knowledge. Why fluid Solving a new problem without leaning on learned knowledge is fluid reasoning (Sections 9.3 and 9.4). Why the other options are wrong (a) Crystallized intelligence Acquired knowledge , measured by vocabulary and information subtests; crystallised intelligence is what the matrices avoid. (c) Verbal intelligence Exactly what a non-verbal test like the RPM avoids. (d) Social intelligence Thorndike 's ability to understand and manage people; the matrices do not sample it at all. Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (SPM) measure which kind of intelligence? (RML 2022) a Crystallised intelligence b Fluid intelligence c Both a and b d General Intelligence ✓ Answer: (b) Fluid intelligence Raven's SPM (1938), classic measure of Gf The concept What it measures The SPM (1938) is the classic measure of Gf , fluid intelligence. Exam tip Raven's is also the best single marker of Spearman's g , and Gf and g are closely related; but when fluid intelligence is offered, it is the more precise and expected answer. Why the other options are wrong (a) Crystallised intelligence Acquired knowledge, which is precisely what the matrices were designed to keep out . (c) Both a and b Fails because crystallised knowledge is precisely what the matrices were designed to keep out, so only half of it is true. (d) General Intelligence The tempting one: Raven's is the best single marker of Spearman's g , but with fluid intelligence offered, Gf is the more precise answer. A 10-year-old child from a rural area, with no formal schooling, is brought for an intellectual assessment due to academic struggles. The child is illiterate and has had minimal exposure to formal testing materials. Which of the following tests would be the MOST appropriate to use to minimize cultural and educational bias? (Real PYQ 2024) a Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence b Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV) c Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale (5th ed.) d Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) ✓ Answer: (a) Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests (Section 9.3) The concept What it contains Its five performance subtests (Kohs blocks, pass-along, pattern drawing, immediate memory, picture construction) need no reading. Why it fits It has Indian rural norms (Section 9.3), so an unschooled rural child is compared with a fair reference group. Why the other options are wrong (b) Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV) Leans heavily on school-built verbal knowledge and was normed on other populations, not Indian rural children. (c) Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale (5th ed.) Like the WISC, the SB5 leans heavily on school-built verbal knowledge and was normed on other populations. (d) Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) The tempting Indian option, but half of MISIC is verbal, adapted from the WISC's information, comprehension, arithmetic and vocabulary items. The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale can be used to assess eligibility for: (Amity 2023) a Housing benefit b Disability allowance c Suicide risk d Special educational needs ✓ Answer: (b) Disability allowance WAIS Full Scale IQ plus adaptive behaviour (Section 9.3) The concept What it documents A WAIS Full Scale IQ , together with a measure of adaptive behaviour , documents intellectual disability or acquired cognitive impairment. Why this one That evidence supports a disability certificate or allowance (Clinical link, Section 9.3). Why the other options are wrong (a) Housing benefit Depends on income and need , not on cognitive ability. (c) Suicide risk Assessed by clinical interview and specific risk scales , not by an intelligence test. (d) Special educational needs The tempting option, but it concerns children, who are assessed with the WISC or an Indian equivalent rather than the adult scale. Cattell considered crystallised intelligence to be a (an) (RML 2021) a Development Process b Ability to deal with new problems c Repertoire of information, cognitive skills and strategies d Function of brain damage ✓ Answer: (c) Repertoire of information, cognitive skills and strategies Cattell, crystallised intelligence (Gc) as invested ability The concept What Gc is Gc is what fluid ability has "invested" in and crystallised through education and experience . What it holds Vocabulary, general knowledge and learned methods: a repertoire of information, skills and strategies (Section 9.4). Why the other options are wrong (a) Development Process Gc does develop, but "a development process" describes how it grows, not what it is. (b) Ability to deal with new problems The classic swap: this is the definition of fluid intelligence , not crystallised. (d) Function of brain damage Far from it: crystallised abilities such as vocabulary are the ones that hold up best with ageing. According to the Guilford model of intelligence, how many dimensions of intelligence are there? (RML 2021) a Three dimensions b 120 dimensions c 10 dimensions d A variable number depending on I.Q. ✓ Answer: (b) 120 dimensions (as keyed) Guilford's Structure of Intellect cube (1967) The concept The cube Guilford 's cube crosses 5 operations × 4 contents × 6 products = 120 separate abilities (1967), later 150 and then 180 (Section 9.4). Key note The key uses "dimensions" loosely to mean the cells. Strictly, the cube itself has three dimensions (operations, contents and products), so on a literal reading (a) is the correct fact. Exam tip The paper's key nevertheless went to 120, so for this exact question mark (b); whenever a question asks how many abilities or factors, choose 120 . Why the other options are wrong (a) Three dimensions Literally true, as the cube's three dimensions are operations, contents and products; but the key counted the 120 cells, so it loses here. (c) 10 dimensions No basis in the model: ten matches none of Guilford's counts (3 dimensions; 120, 150 or 180 abilities). (d) A variable number depending on I.Q. No basis in the model; the number of abilities is fixed by the cube, not by a person's IQ. Which type of intelligence according to Sternberg's Triarchic theory of intelligence includes the ability to easily adapt to the present environment or select a more favourable environment than the existing one or modify the environment to fit one's need? (JEMAS 2025) a Componential b Contextual c Incremental d Experimental ✓ Answer: (b) Contextual Sternberg's triarchic theory, contextual subtheory (Section 9.5) The concept Three functions Adapting to , selecting and shaping (modifying) the environment are the three functions of the contextual subtheory. Later name Sternberg later called this ability practical intelligence (Section 9.5). Why the other options are wrong (a) Componential The analytical machinery of metacomponents , performance and knowledge-acquisition components, not dealing with the environment. (c) Incremental Belongs to Dweck 's incremental (growth) theory of intelligence, not to Sternberg's triarchic theory. (d) Experimental A corruption of experiential , the subtheory of coping with novelty and automatising, that is, creative intelligence. Individual differences in intelligence are due to: (Amity 2023) a Only genetic factors b Only environmental factors c Genetic and economic factors d Many factors including genetics and environment ✓ Answer: (d) Many factors including genetics and environment Twin and adoption studies, gene-environment interaction (Section 9.7) The concept Genes matter Twin and adoption studies show substantial heritability , but it is well below 1 and varies with age and circumstances. Environment matters Nutrition, schooling, adoption, early intervention and the Flynn effect show large environmental effects. They interact Genes and environment interact , so only a many-factor answer fits (Section 9.7). Why the other options are wrong (a) Only genetic factors Ignores half the evidence: the large environmental effects of schooling, nutrition and the Flynn effect. (b) Only environmental factors Ignores half the evidence: the substantial heritability shown by twin and adoption studies. (c) Genetic and economic factors Names only one environmental factor, socio-economic status , leaving out schooling, nutrition, family environment and the rest. The cardinal DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criterion for Mental Retardation is based primarily on an IQ score: (RML 2021) a Seven standard deviations below the mean b One standard deviation below the mean c Two standard deviations below the mean d Four standard deviations below the mean ✓ Answer: (c) Two standard deviations below the mean DSM-IV-TR, IQ cut-off of about 70 (Section 9.8) The concept The arithmetic With a mean of 100 and an SD of 15 , two SDs below the mean is an IQ of about 70. Why it matters About 70 is the DSM-IV-TR cut-off for significantly subaverage intellectual functioning (Section 9.8). Why the other options are wrong (a) Seven standard deviations below the mean Would be an IQ of about −5, which does not exist on the scale. (b) One standard deviation below the mean An IQ of 85, which is merely low average , not disability. (d) Four standard deviations below the mean An IQ of 40, which already lies at the moderate to severe boundary, far below the cut-off. In which of the following situations would a diagnosis of "global developmental delay" be inappropriate? (RML 2022) a The patient is a child who is too young to fully manifest specific symptoms or to complete requisite assessments. b The patient, a 7-year-old boy, has a full-scale IQ of 65 and severe impairment in adaptive functioning. c The patient's scores on psychometric tests suggest intellectual disability, but there is insufficient information about the patient's adaptive functional skills. d The patient's impaired adaptive functioning suggests intellectual developmental disorder, but there is insufficient information about the level of cognitive impairment measured by standardized instruments. ✓ Answer: (b) The patient, a 7-year-old boy, has a full-scale IQ of 65 and severe impairment in adaptive functioning. DSM-5 global developmental delay, under age 5 (Section 9.8) The concept What it is Global developmental delay is a provisional DSM-5 diagnosis for children under 5 whose severity cannot yet be assessed reliably (Section 9.8). Why (b) The 7-year-old is over 5 and has been fully assessed, with both intellectual and adaptive deficits documented, so he receives a diagnosis of intellectual disability itself. Why the other options are wrong (a) The patient is a child who is too young to fully manifest specific symptoms or to complete requisite assessments. Fits the label: an assessment not yet possible at this age is exactly what the provisional label exists for. (c) The patient's scores on psychometric tests suggest intellectual disability, but there is insufficient information about the patient's adaptive functional skills. Fits the label: the assessment is incomplete (adaptive skills unknown), exactly the situation the provisional label exists for. (d) The patient's impaired adaptive functioning suggests intellectual developmental disorder, but there is insufficient information about the level of cognitive impairment measured by standardized instruments. Fits the label: the assessment is incomplete (cognitive level not measured), exactly the situation the provisional label exists for. Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) is a measure of: (RML 2022) a Mental age and Intelligence quotient b Social age and social quotient c Developmental age and developmental quotient d Emotional age and emotional quotient ✓ Answer: (b) Social age and social quotient Doll, Vineland Social Maturity Scale (1935) The concept What it measures Doll 's VSMS (1935) converts social competence into a social age. The quotient SQ = (SA ÷ CA) × 100 (Section 9.8). Why the other options are wrong (a) Mental age and Intelligence quotient These come from intelligence tests (mental age and IQ), not from a social maturity scale. (c) Developmental age and developmental quotient These come from infant scales such as Gesell's and Bayley's, which give the DQ, not from the VSMS. (d) Emotional age and emotional quotient Not a standard pairing: "emotional age" is not a standard measure, and EQ is Bar-On 's emotional quotient, unrelated to the VSMS. In Terman's study of gifted children, social and behavioural problems were found only in those with: (RML 2022) a IQs of 150 or higher b IQs of 180 or higher c IQs of 180 or higher in adulthood d IQs of 180 or higher in childhood ✓ Answer: (d) IQs of 180 or higher in childhood Terman's gifted study; Hollingworth, Children Above 180 IQ The concept Overall finding As a group, Terman's "Termites" were healthier and better adjusted than average. Where problems were The problems that did occur were concentrated among those whose childhood IQs were about 180 or more, in line with Hollingworth 's Children Above 180 IQ (Section 9.8). Why the other options are wrong (a) IQs of 150 or higher Cannot be right, because 150 is about the average of the whole gifted group. (b) IQs of 180 or higher Right threshold, but omits the key point that the IQs were childhood scores. (c) IQs of 180 or higher in adulthood Wrongly places the testing in adulthood ; the scores of 180 or more were childhood scores. Which of the following disabilities is explicitly covered under the scope of The National Trust Act (1999) in India for the welfare of persons with the disability? (Real PYQ 2024) a Autism Spectrum Disorder b Specific Learning Disability c Intellectual Disability (Mental Retardation) d Both (a) and (c) ✓ Answer: (d) Both (a) and (c) National Trust Act, 1999 (India) The concept Four groups The Act's full title names its four groups: autism , cerebral palsy, mental retardation and multiple disabilities (Indian context, Section 9.8). Why both Autism and intellectual disability (mental retardation) are both named, so (d) is the full answer. Why the other options are wrong (a) Autism Spectrum Disorder Named in the Act, but choosing it alone misses the other named group, mental retardation. (b) Specific Learning Disability Not among the four; it is recognised under the broader Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 . (c) Intellectual Disability (Mental Retardation) Named in the Act, but choosing it alone misses the other named group, autism. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. William Stern coined the intelligence quotient in 1912 (mental age ÷ chronological age); Lewis Terman 's Stanford-Binet (1916) multiplied it by 100, giving the ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, so a mental age of 8 at age 10 gives an IQ of 80. asked 4 times Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (C. M. Bhatia, 1955) has five performance subtests (Kohs blocks, pass-along, pattern drawing, immediate memory, picture construction), needs no reading and has rural norms: the best choice for an illiterate rural Indian child, ahead of the half-verbal MISIC. asked 4 times Fluid intelligence (Gf) is reasoning with novel problems independent of acquired knowledge; crystallised intelligence (Gc) is the repertoire of information, cognitive skills and strategies, measured by vocabulary and information subtests (Raymond Cattell, 1963, with John Horn). asked 4 times Robert Sternberg 's triarchic theory ( Beyond IQ , 1985): componential = analytical, experiential = creative, contextual = practical; adapting to, shaping and selecting environments is contextual intelligence. asked 4 times Raven's Progressive Matrices (John C. Raven; Standard form 1938) is a non-verbal, culture-fair (not culture-free) test of fluid intelligence, and also the best single marker of g. asked 3 times The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale is an individually administered intelligence test (not an aptitude, attitude or achievement test) for adults (WAIS-IV: 16 to 90 years), used among other things to document eligibility for a disability allowance. asked 3 times The WAIS-IV (2008) yields four index scores, Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory and Processing Speed, which combine into the Full Scale IQ; the Working Memory Index (Digit Span, Arithmetic) reflects attention, concentration and mental control. asked 4 times Charles Spearman 's two-factor theory (1904): a general factor g that underlies all cognitive tasks plus a specific factor s for each task, found by factor analysis of the positive manifold. asked 4 times Edgar Doll 's Vineland Social Maturity Scale (1935) gives a social age and a social quotient (SQ = SA ÷ CA × 100); the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales measure adaptive functioning (communication, daily living skills, socialisation). asked 3 times WAIS-IV core subtests: 3 verbal comprehension (Similarities, Vocabulary, Information), 3 perceptual reasoning (Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles), 2 working memory and 2 processing speed, 10 in all; Letter-Number Sequencing is supplemental in the WAIS-IV and secondary in the WISC-V (keyed as "WAIS, not WISC"). asked twice David Wechsler replaced mental age with the deviation ("standard") IQ in the Wechsler-Bellevue (1939): the person's score is compared with the expected score of his or her own age group, mean 100, SD 15. asked 3 times On a deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15), 100 is the 50th percentile, 85 the 16th, 115 the 84th, 130 about the 98th and 70 about the 2nd; with an SD of 16, an IQ of 136 (z = 2.25) is about the 98.7th percentile. asked 3 times Alfred Binet and Théodore Simon published the first intelligence test in 1905 (30 items) for the French ministry; Terman revised it at Stanford as the Stanford-Binet (1916). Piaget did not build the first test. asked twice DSM-IV-TR mental retardation required an IQ about two standard deviations below the mean (about 70); DSM-5 also requires deficits in adaptive functioning and sets severity by adaptive functioning, so an FSIQ of 70 alone is not intellectual disability. asked twice Individual differences in intelligence come from many genetic and environmental factors acting together; twin studies (MZ versus DZ twins, especially twins reared apart) estimate heritability, which is a population statistic. asked twice WAIS-IV bands: 90 to 109 average, 80 to 89 low average, 70 to 79 borderline, 69 and below extremely low; an IQ of 70 to 84 is "low average or borderline, depending on the edition". asked twice The SB5 (Gale Roid, 2003) measures five CHC factors (Fluid Reasoning, Knowledge, Quantitative Reasoning, Visual-Spatial Processing, Working Memory), each in verbal and nonverbal form, drawing on Carroll and Baddeley. asked twice J. P. Guilford 's structure of intellect (1967) has three dimensions (5 operations × 4 contents × 6 products) and so 120 abilities, later 150 and 180; one paper keyed "120 dimensions". asked once The WISC-V (2014) covers 6 years to 16 years 11 months; the WPPSI-IV covers 2 years 6 months to 7 years 7 months and the WAIS-IV 16 to 90 years. asked once DSM-5 global developmental delay is a provisional diagnosis only for children under 5 whose severity cannot yet be assessed reliably. asked once In Terman 's gifted study (from 1921; specific learning disability is not among them. asked once Correlating a new intelligence test with an established one given at the same time tests concurrent validity ; a later criterion would be predictive validity. asked once Keyed answer: the aptitude test is "the heart of the guidance programme" (RML 2022); the textbook phrase belongs to counselling, so choose counselling if it is offered. asked once James McKeen Cattell coined the term "mental test" in 1890. asked once Wechsler built the Wechsler-Bellevue to fix the Stanford-Binet's faults: little appeal for adults, too much word manipulation, too much weight on speed and reliance on mental age. asked once The KBIT-2 (Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test) has two scales: Verbal (crystallised) and Nonverbal (fluid). asked once The Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development assess cognitive, language and motor development up to about 42 months. asked once Daniel Goleman 's five domains of emotional intelligence (1995): knowing one's emotions, managing them, motivating oneself, recognising emotions in others and handling relationships. asked once Carol Dweck 's growth mindset is the belief that intelligence is malleable and can be developed through effort; A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (821 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (821 pages) Chapter 10 Motivation: Why We Do What We Do In this chapter 10.1 What Motivation Is : define need, drive, motive, incentive and goal, trace the motivational cycle, and classify motives as primary or secondary and as intrinsic or extrinsic. 10.2 Instinct Theories : explain the instinct theories of James, McDougall and Freud, the ethologists' fixed action patterns, and why instinct theory declined. 10.3 Drives, Homeostasis and Arousal : describe homeostasis, Hull's drive-reduction theory and its limits, optimal arousal, the Yerkes-Dodson law and sensation seeking. 10.4 The Pull of the Goal: Incentives, Expectancies and Opponent Processes : contrast push and pull theories, explain expectancy-value thinking, and describe the opponent-process theory of acquired motivation. 10.5 Hierarchies of Need: Maslow, Alderfer and Other Lists : state Maslow's hierarchy precisely, distinguish deficiency from growth needs, evaluate the theory, and compare it with Alderfer's ERG theory and other lists of needs. 10.6 Psychosocial Motives and Achievement : explain Murray's needs and press, McClelland's three needs, Atkinson's theory of achievement motivation, fear of success and Weiner's attribution theory. 10.7 Intrinsic Motivation, Competence and the Self : explain curiosity, competence, self-efficacy, the overjustification effect, self-determination theory, flow and the consistency motive. 10.8 Conflict and Frustration : classify motivational conflicts, use Miller's gradients to predict behaviour, and describe the sources of frustration and the ways people react to it. 10.9 Biological Motives: Hunger, Thirst, Sex and Others : explain what starts and stops eating and drinking, how the hypothalamic "centre" theory was revised, and the classic findings on sexual and maternal motivation. 10.10 Motivation in Practice: Work, School and Clinic : apply Herzberg, Vroom, Adams and Locke to work, apply motivation research to the classroom, and describe motivational interviewing. Weightage. 76 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (9.3%) test this chapter, 36 of them from real past papers. 3 of its 10 sections are High yield. In a primate laboratory at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, at the end of the 1940s, a young rhesus monkey sat in its home cage fiddling with a small wooden board. Screwed to the board was a puzzle made of three pieces of hardware: a metal pin, a hook and a hasp. To undo the hasp, the monkey had to pull the pin first, then lift the hook, and only then swing the hasp open. There was nothing behind the hasp. No raisin, no peanut, no sip of juice. The monkey had been fed and watered as usual. Yet it worked at the puzzle, again and again, and when the experimenters put the pieces back together it took them apart again. The experimenters were Harry Harlow, Margaret Kuenne Harlow and Donald Meyer, and in 1950 they reported what they had seen. Monkeys left with assembled puzzles for about two weeks became fast, nearly error-free solvers. Monkeys given the same puzzles already taken apart, so that there was nothing to solve, did not. Harlow even reported that bringing food into the test tended to disrupt the monkeys' smooth performance rather than improve it. The monkeys, the authors concluded, were driven by the activity itself. They called it a manipulation drive. Why should this small observation have caused such a stir? Because in 1950 the most powerful theory in American psychology said it should not happen. According to that theory, an animal learns a response only when the response reduces a biological need: hunger, thirst, pain. Harlow's monkeys were not hungry, not thirsty and not in pain. What need was being reduced? If you have ever done the newspaper Sudoku on a bus to Mysuru, or stayed up past midnight to finish a crossword that nobody will ever check, you already know the answer the theory could not give. This chapter is about that puzzle: why animals and people do what they do. You will meet instincts, drives, arousal, incentives, needs, expectancies and the self, roughly in the order psychology met them. Keep Harlow's monkeys in mind as you read; we will come back to them at the end of the chapter. 10.1 What Motivation Is Medium yield · 7 Qs The word motivation comes from the Latin movere , "to move". In psychology it refers to the processes that start behaviour, give it direction, set its intensity and keep it going until it ends. Notice the four parts of that definition, because questions are built on them. Activation is the starting of behaviour (you get up from your desk). Direction is the choice of one goal over others (you walk to the kitchen, not the television). Intensity is how much effort goes in (you stride, you do not stroll). Persistence is how long the behaviour continues in the face of obstacles (you keep searching after finding the biscuit tin empty). No one has ever seen a motive. You see a student studying until 2 a.m., and you infer that something inside is pushing or pulling him. Motivation is therefore a hypothetical construct, an intervening variable placed between what we can observe (hours without food, a promised reward) and what we can measure (speed, effort, persistence). This is why the history of motivation is a history of competing guesses about what that invisible something is. Need, drive, motive, incentive and goal Five words recur in every theory in this chapter, and the exam treats them as distinct. Take one example, thirst, and follow it through. A need is a state of deficiency or lack within the organism. After a long afternoon in a Mysuru summer, your body is short of water. That shortage is a physiological need, and it exists whether or not you feel it. A drive is the aroused, tense psychological state that a need produces and that energises behaviour. You feel thirsty, restless and irritable. Need is the biological condition; drive is its psychological consequence. The two are not perfectly correlated: a person can have a need without a strong drive (old people can become dangerously dehydrated without feeling very thirsty), and a drive can outlast the need. A motive is the broader term for any internal state that arouses and directs behaviour towards a goal. In practice "drive" is reserved for biologically based states and "motive" for learned, psychological and social ones, such as the motive to achieve or to be liked. John Atkinson used "motive" in a narrower sense still: a stable personality disposition that a person carries from situation to situation. An incentive is an external stimulus or object that attracts (positive incentive) or repels (negative incentive) the organism. A cold bottle of water in a shop window is an incentive; so is the thought of the chai stall after the exam. A goal is the end state towards which motivated behaviour is directed, the incentive as it is represented and pursued: reaching the water and drinking it. The commonly taught shorthand is that drives push from inside and incentives pull from outside. The motivational cycle Put the five terms in order and you get the motivational cycle : a need gives rise to a drive; the drive energises instrumental behaviour , that is, goal-directed activity that is a means to an end; the behaviour reaches the goal or incentive; reaching the goal reduces the drive and brings relief; and after a while the need builds up again and the cycle restarts. Figure 10.1 draws the cycle for thirst. The cycle is a useful teaching device, but notice that it is drawn from one theory, drive reduction, which you will meet in Section 10.3. Much of the rest of the chapter is about behaviour that does not fit it. 1 Need body short of water 2 Drive felt thirst, tension 3 Behaviour walk to the water tap 4 Goal (incentive) drinking water 5 Relief drive reduced, rest The motivational cycle (example: thirst; the need returns later) Figure 10.1 The motivational cycle. A need produces a drive, the drive energises instrumental behaviour, the behaviour reaches the goal, and the drive is reduced until the need builds up again. Notice that this picture is drive-reduction theory in miniature. Classifying motives The most common classification divides motives by their origin. The primary motives , also called biological, physiological or unlearned motives, are rooted in the body's survival needs and are present without learning: hunger, thirst, the need for oxygen, sleep, avoidance of pain, temperature regulation, elimination, sex and, in many textbooks, the maternal drive. Most of them are homeostatic (they correct a bodily imbalance); sex and the maternal drive are the usual exceptions, because no tissue is depleted when they are unsatisfied. The secondary motives , also called psychosocial, social, acquired or learned motives, develop through experience and culture: achievement, affiliation, power, approval, aggression, curiosity about a particular subject, the wish for money. They vary enormously between people and between cultures. Between the two sits a group that some textbooks (following Clifford Morgan and Richard King) call general or unlearned non-homeostatic motives: curiosity, activity, manipulation and the need for contact comfort. They seem to be inborn, like primary motives, yet they repair no tissue deficit. Harlow's monkeys belong here. Table 10.1 sets out the three classes side by side. The personality theorist Henry Murray (you will meet him properly in Section 10.6) drew the same line with his own words. His viscerogenic needs are the primary needs tied to bodily events (air, water, food, sex, urination, avoidance of heat, cold and harm). His psychogenic needs are the secondary needs that arise from mental life and are only loosely connected to the body (achievement, affiliation, dominance, autonomy, order). Motives can also be classified by awareness: conscious motives are ones the person can report, and unconscious motives (the core of Freud's theory) drive behaviour without the person knowing why. Finally, the American personality psychologist Gordon Willard Allport (1897 to 1967) pointed out in 1937 that a learned motive can cut loose from its origins. A man who went to sea to earn a living may, when rich, still long for the sea. Allport called this functional autonomy : a means can become an end in itself, so today's motive need not be explained by the need that started it. Table 10.1 A working classification of motives. Class Other names Examples Key feature Primary Biological, physiological, unlearned, viscerogenic Hunger, thirst, sleep, pain avoidance, sex, maternal drive Rooted in body; mostly homeostatic General Unlearned non-homeostatic, stimulus motives Curiosity, exploration, manipulation, activity, contact comfort Inborn but repair no tissue deficit Secondary Psychosocial, social, learned, acquired, psychogenic Achievement, affiliation, power, approval, gregariousness Learned; vary by person and culture Exam trap Gregariousness , the tendency to seek the company of others, is classed as a social motive (RML 2022 keyed "social motive" over biological, psychological and personal). The bait is that William McDougall listed gregariousness as one of his instincts (Section 10.2). In the textbook classification of motives, the answer is still "social". Similarly, "psychological motive" and "personal motive" are not standard class names; do not be drawn to them. Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation A second, cross-cutting distinction concerns where the reward lies. The desire to do something for its own sake, because the activity itself is interesting, enjoyable or satisfying, is called intrinsic motivation . The desire to do something for a separable outcome (money, marks, praise, or the avoidance of punishment) is called extrinsic motivation . A child who reads comics under the blanket is intrinsically motivated; the same child reading the prescribed textbook to escape a scolding is extrinsically motivated. A classic past-paper example: a toddler goes to great lengths to open a box that she knows is empty. Nothing is inside, so there is no external payoff; the opening is the reward. That is intrinsic motivation. It is not homeostasis (no bodily balance is being restored), not extrinsic motivation (there is no separable reward) and not secondary motivation (nothing learned or social is being served). The two kinds of motivation can interact in surprising ways, and Section 10.7 shows how an external reward can sometimes kill an internal interest. Clinical link The intrinsic-extrinsic distinction is used diagnostically. In malingering a person deliberately produces or exaggerates symptoms for an obvious external incentive (money, avoiding duty, obtaining drugs). In factitious disorder the person also deliberately produces symptoms, but in the absence of obvious external rewards; the motive is internal, typically to occupy the sick role. Same behaviour, different motive, different diagnosis. (The disorders themselves are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) Five ways of explaining motivation Before we take the theories one by one, it helps to see the whole map. Each major school of psychology produced its own answer to "why do we do what we do?", and examiners love questions that ask which school said what. The answer is the psychodynamic model (Freud's instincts working through the unconscious). "Which perspective emphasises free will and personal growth" or "an innate tendency to grow and reach one's maximum potential"? The humanistic perspective. The cognitive model emphasises thinking and beliefs; the behavioural model emphasises conditioning and reinforcement; "statistical norms" belong to the statistical definition of abnormality (Psychiatric Disorders book), not to any school of motivation. Do not confuse "humanistic" with "existential": Maslow and Rogers are the humanistic pair; Frankl, May and Yalom are the existential names. 10.2 Instinct Theories Medium yield · 5 Qs The first scientific answer to the motivation question was the oldest folk answer dressed in new clothes: we do things because we are born to do them. A spider spins a perfect web the first time it tries; a newly hatched turtle heads for the sea. Darwin's theory of evolution (1859) made such inborn behaviour respectable, because a behaviour that helped ancestors survive could be inherited just as a beak or a wing could. Around 1900 it seemed natural to explain human motivation the same way. What counts as an instinct An instinct is a complex, unlearned pattern of behaviour that is characteristic of every member of a species and that appears in full form the first time the triggering situation arises. Four criteria follow from the definition: the behaviour is unlearned (it appears in animals reared in isolation), species-specific or universal within the species, stereotyped (performed the same way each time) and complex (more than a simple reflex such as the knee jerk). Keep these criteria in mind; you will see that most of what was called "instinct" in human beings fails them. William James (1842 to 1910), in his Principles of Psychology of 1890, defined instinct as "the faculty of acting in such a way as to produce certain ends, without foresight of the ends, and without previous education in the performance." James then made a claim that surprised his readers: human beings do not have fewer instincts than animals, they have more . His list included sucking, crying, imitation, rivalry, pugnacity, sympathy, fear, acquisitiveness, constructiveness, play, curiosity, sociability, shyness, modesty, jealousy and parental love. Humans look less instinctive, James argued, because our many instincts conflict with one another and because habit quickly modifies them; an instinct, once acted on, gets bound to particular objects and loses its blind quality. McDougall's hormic psychology The theorist most closely tied to the instinct theory of motivation is the British-born psychologist William McDougall (1871 to 1938), who moved to Harvard in 1920 and later to Duke University. In An Introduction to Social Psychology (1908) McDougall argued that instincts are the prime movers of all human activity: without them, he wrote, the organism would be like a clock without a mainspring. For McDougall an instinct was an inherited disposition with three aspects, corresponding to the old three-part division of mind. It has a cognitive aspect (the animal perceives and pays attention to certain objects), an affective aspect (perceiving the object arouses a particular emotion) and a conative aspect (the animal feels an impulse to act). Each major instinct was paired with a primary emotion, and Table 10.3 shows the famous pairs. Over time, emotions organise around particular objects into sentiments (love of one's country, hatred of a rival), and the most important of these, the self-regarding sentiment, gives character its unity. Table 10.3 McDougall's principal instincts and their primary emotions (1908). Instinct Primary emotion Instinct Primary emotion Flight Fear Self-abasement (subjection) Negative self-feeling Repulsion Disgust Self-assertion (self-display) Positive self-feeling (elation) Curiosity Wonder Parental Tender emotion Pugnacity Anger Also listed Gregariousness, acquisition, construction, reproduction McDougall's list grew across the many editions of his book; by the time of The Energies of Men (1932) he preferred the word "propensities" and listed eighteen of them, which is the figure (18 instincts) you will find in most Indian textbooks. His system is called hormic psychology , from the Greek horme , meaning an urge or impulse, because it put purposive striving at the centre of psychology. McDougall insisted that behaviour is purposive : it is directed towards goals, it persists, it varies its means when blocked, and it stops when the goal is reached. This put him in open conflict with John B. Watson's behaviourism, and the two men debated publicly in 1924. Exam trap "The instinct theory of motivation was developed by" has the keyed answer William McDougall , even though William James also wrote about instincts and Freud built his theory on them. James described instincts; McDougall made them the systematic foundation of motivation and social behaviour. Maslow is the bait from the wrong school (humanistic). A second trap: McDougall's purposive (hormic) psychology is not Edward Tolman's purposive behaviourism . Both stress goals; McDougall explained goals by instincts, Tolman by learned expectancies (Section 10.4). Freud's instincts: life and death Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) also put inborn forces at the root of motivation, though his are better described as drives. His German word was Trieb , a driving force or impulse, which his English translators rendered as "instinct". Freud said every instinct has four features: a source (a bodily need or excitation), an aim (to remove the excitation, which is felt as pleasure), an impetus (the amount of force or pressure it exerts) and an object (the thing or person through which the aim is achieved). Of the four, only the object is learned and changeable, which is why the same hunger can be satisfied by idli in Mysuru and bread in Vienna. In his final theory, set out in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), Freud grouped all instincts into two classes. The life instincts (Eros) serve the survival of the individual and the species: hunger, thirst and above all sex. Their energy is the libido . The death instinct , which his followers named Thanatos, is an unconscious wish to return to the inorganic state; turned outwards it appears as aggression and destructiveness. Freud developed the idea after the slaughter of the First World War, and he read war and violence as evidence of it. The investment of psychic energy in an object, person or idea he called cathexis . The reservoir of all these unorganised instinctual drives is the id , which operates on the pleasure principle. (The id, ego and superego, the defence mechanisms and the psychosexual stages are taught in the Personality book; here we need only Freud's view of motivation.) Exam trap "According to Freud, human beings are motivated by powerful innate forces known as" has the answer instincts , not needs (Maslow, Murray), not drives (Hull's term, though it is a fair translation of Trieb ) and not the id (the id is the reservoir of the instincts, not the forces themselves). "Wars and violence are evidence of" the death instinct ; libido is the energy of the life instincts. Freud himself did not use the word Thanatos in his published writing; it was popularised by his followers. Ethology: fixed action patterns and sign stimuli While instinct theory was fading in human psychology, it was reborn in zoology. The new discipline was ethology , the study of animal behaviour in the natural environment, with an emphasis on its evolution and function. Its founders, the Austrian Konrad Lorenz (1903 to 1989), the Dutch-born Nikolaas Tinbergen (1907 to 1988) and the Austrian Karl von Frisch (1886 to 1982), shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973. The ethologists replaced the vague word "instinct" with precise terms. A fixed action pattern is an unlearned, stereotyped sequence of movements that, once started, runs to completion. A sign stimulus (or releaser) is the simple, specific feature of the environment that triggers it, and the hypothesised neural detector that responds to the sign stimulus was called the innate releasing mechanism . Tinbergen found that a male three-spined stickleback in breeding season attacks crude models of fish as long as their underside is red, while ignoring a realistic model without the red belly. Lorenz and Tinbergen showed that a greylag goose that sees an egg outside its nest stretches its neck and rolls the egg back with the underside of its bill; if the egg is removed mid-roll, the goose finishes the rolling movement over empty ground. A herring gull chick pecks at the red spot on its parent's bill, and the pecking brings up food. Lorenz also described imprinting , the rapid attachment of newly hatched geese to the first moving object they see, during a brief sensitive period (taught in the Learning and Developmental chapters). Why instinct theory declined As an explanation of human motivation, instinct theory had collapsed by the late 1920s, for three reasons. First, naming is not explaining . Why do people form groups? Because of a gregarious instinct. How do we know there is a gregarious instinct? Because people form groups. The argument is circular: the "instinct" is simply the behaviour renamed and then offered as its own cause. Second, the lists grew out of control. Every new behaviour seemed to earn its own instinct, and in 1924 the sociologist Luther Lee Bernard surveyed the literature and counted nearly six thousand proposed human instincts, a reduction to absurdity. Third, the evidence pointed to learning. Anthropologists showed that supposedly universal "instincts" such as pugnacity or acquisitiveness varied enormously between cultures, and the Chinese psychologist Zing-Yang Kuo (1898 to 1970) showed in 1930 that even a cat's "instinctive" killing of rats depended on rearing: most kittens that watched their mothers kill rats became rat killers, while few kittens reared together with rats ever killed one. The idea did not die completely. Ethology showed that fixed action patterns are real in many animals, and modern evolutionary psychology asks how natural selection shaped human motives such as mate preferences and fear of snakes. But psychologists stopped treating a list of instincts as an explanation, and looked for a mechanism. The mechanism they found was the drive. Remember Instinct theory explained behaviour by naming it. Its replacement, drive theory, tried to say how a bodily need turns into action. Whenever a question asks why instinct theory fell, the expected answer is circularity (naming is not explaining), followed by cultural variability and the role of learning. 10.3 Drives, Homeostasis and Arousal Medium yield · 7 Qs Drive theory begins not in psychology but in physiology, with a simple observation: the inside of a healthy body stays remarkably constant while the world outside changes. The air around you may be at 45 degrees on a Rajasthan afternoon or at 5 degrees on a Shimla morning, yet your core temperature stays near 37 degrees Celsius. How? Homeostasis The French physiologist Claude Bernard (1813 to 1878) argued in the second half of the nineteenth century that the cells of the body live in an internal sea of fluids, which he called the milieu intérieur (internal environment). The constancy of this internal environment, he wrote, is the condition for a free and independent life. The American physiologist Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945) of Harvard gave the idea its modern name: he coined the term homeostasis in 1926 and popularised it in his book The Wisdom of the Body (1932). (Some books date the term to 1932, the year of the book; the word itself first appeared in print in 1926.) Homeostasis is the tendency of the body to maintain a stable internal state by detecting deviations and correcting them. The usual model is a thermostat. A set point is the value the system tries to maintain (the temperature you dial in). When a sensor detects a deviation from it, a correction is switched on (the heater), and when the set point is restored the correction is switched off. This is negative feedback : the output of the system feeds back to reduce the deviation that produced it. Some corrections are automatic and need no behaviour at all (sweating, shivering). Others require the whole organism to act: you put on a sweater, walk into the shade or drink water. Those behavioural corrections are what a motivation theory must explain, and that is where Clark Hull came in. Hull's drive-reduction theory The word "drive" entered psychology in 1918, when Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962) of Columbia University used it in Dynamic Psychology for the energy that powers behaviour, as distinct from the mechanisms that steer it. The theory built on the word belongs to Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) of Yale, whose Principles of Behavior (1943) was for a decade the most influential book in American psychology. Hull's drive-reduction theory runs as follows. A physiological need (a departure from homeostasis) creates a drive, an aroused state of tension that energises behaviour. The organism becomes active, and any response that happens to reduce the drive is reinforced , that is, strengthened, so that it is more likely to occur the next time the drive appears. Reinforcement, for Hull, simply is drive reduction. The goal of motivated behaviour is a return to a state of low tension. Two features of the theory are often examined. First, drive energises but does not direct . What decides which response the hungry rat makes is habit strength , the learned stimulus-response connection built up by past reinforcement; drive only multiplies it. Second, drive is general: Hull believed that the energy from any drive pooled together and energised whatever habit was strongest at the moment. Hull expressed all this in a formula. In its later form (by 1952) it reads, in simplified notation: Reaction potential S E R = S H R × D × K × V (minus inhibition) Because the terms multiply, if any one of them is zero the response does not occur. A rat that has learned a maze perfectly (high habit strength) but has just eaten (drive near zero) will sit in the start box. Hull added that reaction potential must exceed a minimum value, the reaction threshold ( S L R ), before any response appears at all, and that above the threshold its strength shows in four measurable ways: a shorter response latency, a greater response (reaction) amplitude , meaning the vigour or size of the response, a higher probability of responding and greater resistance to extinction. Table 10.4 lists the symbols. Table 10.4 The terms in Hull's equation. Symbol Name What it stands for S E R Reaction (excitatory) potential The tendency to make the response S H R Habit strength Learned S-R bond; grows with reinforced trials D Drive Energy from need, for example hours without food K Incentive motivation Size and quality of the reward V Stimulus-intensity dynamism Stronger stimuli evoke the response more readily J Delay of reinforcement Longer delays weaken the response I R and S I R Reactive and conditioned inhibition Fatigue from responding, and learned not-responding Exam trap "The greater the intensity of a stimulus, the greater the probability that a learned response will be elicited" is Hull's stimulus-intensity dynamism (V). Incentive motivation (K) is about the size of the reward, not the strength of the stimulus. Some coaching notes wrongly gloss V as "need"; need belongs to D. Response amplitude and reaction threshold are genuine Hullian terms too, but they name a measure of the response and the minimum reaction potential needed to produce it, not the effect of stimulus intensity. Also note that the word "drive" was introduced by Woodworth (1918) , but drive-reduction theory is Hull's (1943) , and homeostasis is Cannon's term (Bernard's concept was the milieu intérieur). Primary and secondary drives Hull distinguished primary drives , which arise from tissue needs (hunger, thirst, pain, temperature, sex), from secondary drives , which are acquired through learning when a neutral stimulus is repeatedly associated with a primary drive. The clearest demonstration came from Neal Elgar Miller (1909 to 2002), Hull's colleague at Yale, in 1948. Rats were shocked in a white compartment and escaped through a door into a black one. Later, with no shock at all, the rats still hurried out of the white compartment, and they learned a completely new response (turning a wheel to open the door) to get out. Fear had become a learned drive, and reducing it was reinforcing enough to teach new behaviour. The same logic underlies Orval Hobart Mowrer 's (1907 to 1982) two-factor theory of avoidance learning (1947). Factor one is classical conditioning: a warning signal paired with shock comes to evoke fear. Factor two is operant conditioning: the avoidance response is reinforced because it reduces that fear. Mowrer's theory explains why phobic avoidance is so persistent: each escape from the feared situation reduces anxiety, and so strengthens the avoidance (the Learning chapter develops this). What drive reduction cannot explain Drive-reduction theory works well for thirst after a cricket match. It works badly for much else, and the failures pushed psychology towards new ideas. Animals and people seek stimulation. Harlow's monkeys took puzzles apart for nothing (the opening story). Robert Butler showed in 1953 that rhesus monkeys in a closed box would learn a discrimination task for the sole reward of opening a small window and looking out at the laboratory, and would keep doing so for hours. Rewards need not reduce any need. Fred Sheffield and Thornton Roby reported in 1950 that rats learned a maze to obtain saccharin, a sweetener with no nutritional value whatever. Reducing stimulation can be unbearable. At McGill University in 1954, in Donald Hebb's laboratory, Woodburn Heron and his colleagues (Bexton, Heron and Scott) paid students a generous daily wage to lie in a quiet cubicle wearing translucent goggles, gloves and cardboard cuffs, with almost nothing to see, hear or touch. By drive-reduction logic this should have been bliss. Most students quit within two or three days, and many reported difficulty thinking and vivid hallucinations. We eat when we are not hungry , as anyone who has accepted a second sweet at a wedding knows. And people deliberately raise their tension : they climb mountains, ride roller coasters and watch horror films. These findings did not abolish the concept of drive; they showed that tension reduction is only half the story. Sometimes organisms want less stimulation, and sometimes more. The next idea took that seriously. Optimal arousal theory Psychologists use arousal to mean the general level of physiological and psychological activation of the organism, running from deep sleep at one end to frantic excitement at the other. It is regulated by the brainstem's reticular activating system (the Attention and Consciousness chapter, Chapter 5, covers its anatomy). The optimal arousal theory holds that each organism tries to maintain a moderate, optimal level of arousal: when arousal is too low (boredom) it seeks stimulation, and when arousal is too high (anxiety, overload) it seeks to reduce it. The theory was set out most influentially by the Canadian psychologist Donald Olding Hebb (1904 to 1985) in a 1955 paper, "Drives and the C.N.S." (the initials punned on "central nervous system" and "conceptual nervous system"). Hebb argued that arousal acts as a general drive and that performance is best at an intermediate level of it. The theory explains sensory-deprivation distress, curiosity and thrill seeking in one stroke, which drive reduction could not. Optimal arousal theory found its classic evidence in a study that was forty years old by the time Hebb wrote. Key study: Yerkes and Dodson's dancing mice (1908) Question. Does stronger motivation always produce faster learning? Method. Robert Mearns Yerkes (1876 to 1956) and John Dillingham Dodson (1879 to 1955) at Harvard trained "dancing mice" to choose the white compartment of a discrimination box and avoid the black one; a wrong choice brought an electric shock of weak, medium or strong intensity. They also varied how hard the brightness discrimination was. Result. Learning was fastest at an intermediate shock, not the strongest one, and the harder the discrimination, the weaker the shock that produced the fastest learning. Conclusion. The relation between motivation and performance is not linear but rises and then falls, and its peak depends on task difficulty. Criticism. The original study was about shock strength in mice, not "arousal" or "anxiety" in people; the name "Yerkes-Dodson law" and the arousal interpretation came decades later, and the human evidence for a neat inverted U is weaker than textbooks suggest. The Yerkes-Dodson law , as it is now taught, has two parts. First, the relation between arousal (or anxiety) and performance is an inverted U : performance improves as arousal rises from low to moderate, peaks, and then declines as arousal rises further. Second, the optimal level depends on the task: for simple or well-learned tasks the optimum is relatively high, while for complex, difficult or new tasks the optimum is lower. Figure 10.2 shows both curves. In everyday terms, a little exam anxiety sharpens you, and a lot wrecks you, and it wrecks you sooner on a hard numerical problem than on writing your roll number. Simple or well-learned task Complex or new task best for simple task best for complex task high low Performance low high Arousal or anxiety too little: drowsy, careless too much: tense, disorganised Figure 10.2 The Yerkes-Dodson law. Performance is an inverted-U function of arousal, and the peak for a complex or new task (dashed) lies at a lower arousal level than the peak for a simple or well-learned task (solid). Why does too much arousal hurt? One answer came from J. A. Easterbrook in 1959: as arousal rises, attention narrows to fewer cues (his cue-utilisation hypothesis ). At moderate arousal, irrelevant cues are dropped and performance improves; at high arousal, relevant cues are dropped as well and performance falls, and complex tasks, which need more cues, suffer first. The same arousal logic explains a social phenomenon. Norman Triplett noticed in 1898 that cyclists rode faster when racing others than when racing the clock. Robert Zajonc (1923 to 2008) explained such social facilitation in 1965 with a drive theory: the mere presence of others raises arousal, and arousal strengthens the dominant response , the response most likely in that situation. On an easy or well-learned task the dominant response is the correct one, so an audience improves performance; on a new or difficult task the dominant response is often an error, so an audience impairs it. (Social facilitation and social loafing are developed in the Social Psychology book.) Exam trap "The Yerkes-Dodson law states that between performance and anxiety there is" an inverted-U shaped relationship . "Curvilinear" is not false (an inverted U is a kind of curve), but it is less specific, and when both appear the precise answer wins. "Linear" and "M-shaped" are simply wrong. The second half of the law is examined too: on a complex task, performance is best at a moderate arousal level, with the optimum lower than on a simple task. Never choose "very high arousal" or "independent of task difficulty". An option such as "punishment severity and learning rate" describes what the 1908 mouse experiment actually varied, but when "arousal and performance as an inverted U" is offered, that is the law as it is taught. Sensation seeking If each of us has an optimal arousal level, it need not be the same level for everyone. Marvin Zuckerman (1928 to 2018) built a research programme on that idea. In his definition, sensation seeking is the tendency to seek varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences, and to take physical, social, legal and financial risks for the sake of them. Zuckerman's Sensation Seeking Scale (first version 1964) measures four components: thrill and adventure seeking (desire for risky physical activities such as skydiving), experience seeking (novel experiences through the mind, travel, music and a non-conforming lifestyle), disinhibition (seeking release through parties, drinking and varied sexual partners) and boredom susceptibility (intolerance of repetition and routine). High sensation seekers are over-represented among extreme-sport enthusiasts, early drug users and people who drive fast; biologically they tend to have low levels of the enzyme monoamine oxidase (MAO).
