Yet a well-fed guest still eats the gulab jamun because it is there. The theories in this section shift the spotlight outwards, to the goal, and then inwards again to what the person expects about the goal. Incentive theory: push versus pull The incentive theory of motivation holds that behaviour is motivated primarily by the pull of external rewards and the push away from external punishments, rather than by internal tension. Drives push; incentives pull. The theory explains why behaviour depends on the quality of what is on offer, and not only on how deprived the organism is. Two classic observations showed incentives at work. In 1928 Otto Tinklepaugh let monkeys watch while he hid a piece of banana under a cup; then, out of sight, he swapped it for lettuce, which monkeys normally eat readily. When a monkey lifted the cup and found lettuce, it searched about, shrieked and refused the lettuce. The monkey had been working for a specific expected incentive, not for "food". In 1942 Leo Crespi trained rats to run for different amounts of food and then switched them. Rats shifted from a large to a small reward ran more slowly than rats that had always received the small reward, and rats shifted upwards ran faster than rats always given the large one. These contrast effects forced Hull to add K, incentive motivation, to his equation. Pinel and Barnes (Biopsychology) apply the same idea to eating with their positive-incentive perspective : we are drawn to eat mainly by the anticipated pleasure of eating, which depends on the food's taste, our past experience with it, the time since we last ate, and the presence of other people, rather than by energy deficits. Section 10.9 returns to it. Modern neuroscience has refined the idea further. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson distinguish the "wanting" of an incentive (its motivational pull, which depends on dopamine) from its "liking" (the pleasure actually felt). Their incentive-sensitisation theory of addiction (1993) proposes that drugs progressively increase wanting without increasing liking, which is why people with addiction can crave a drug they no longer enjoy. Exam trap "In incentive theory, motivation is primarily driven by" external rewards . The baits each belong to another theory: intrinsic satisfaction (self-determination theory), biological drives (Hull), self-efficacy beliefs (Bandura). Likewise "drive theory primarily explains motivation as a process to" reduce physiological needs ; seeking external rewards is incentive theory, setting long-term goals is goal-setting theory, and increasing social connections is affiliation. Expectancy-value theories Incentives do not pull equally hard on everyone. A promotion pulls hard on someone who thinks he can get it and who wants it, and hardly at all on someone who has given up or who does not care. The label expectancy-value theory covers the family of theories holding that the strength of motivation depends on two things multiplied together: the person's expectancy that an action will lead to an outcome, and the value the person places on that outcome. Because the terms multiply, motivation is zero if either is zero: a highly valued goal that seems impossible does not motivate, and neither does a certain outcome that nobody wants. The idea has several authors. Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959) argued against Hull that animals learn expectancies about what leads to what (his "purposive behaviourism"), and that incentives decide whether this knowledge is shown in performance (latent learning is covered in the Learning chapter). Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947) described goals as having positive or negative valence in a person's psychological field. Julian Bernard Rotter (1916 to 2014), in Social Learning and Clinical Psychology (1954), wrote the most quotable version: the potential for a behaviour to occur in a given situation is a function of the person's expectancy that the behaviour will be reinforced and the reinforcement value of the outcome to that person. Rotter's full theory has four variables: behaviour potential , expectancy, reinforcement value and the psychological situation (the situation as the person perceives it). The same multiplicative logic reappears in John Atkinson's theory of achievement (Section 10.6), in Victor Vroom's expectancy theory of work (Section 10.10) and in Jacquelynne Eccles's model of students' choices, in which value is split into interest, importance, usefulness and cost. Exam trap A bank item reads: "The ______ framework is based on the expectancy, demand and incentive concepts", with the options behavioural, cognitive, social learning and supportive. The wording comes from organisational-behaviour textbooks, which describe three frameworks for explaining behaviour at work: the cognitive framework (built on Tolman's expectancies), the behaviouristic framework (built on reinforcement) and the social learning or social cognitive framework (Rotter, Bandura), which combines the two. The bank keys social learning ; because expectancy is also the defining idea of Tolman's cognitive approach, "cognitive" has its defenders, so read the options carefully. "Supportive" is not a framework at all but one of Keith Davis's models of organisational behaviour (autocratic, custodial, supportive, collegial). Whatever the key, expectancy and incentive are the shared ideas of Tolman, Rotter and every expectancy-value theory in this section. The opponent-process theory of acquired motivation Why do people keep doing things that hurt at first, like parachuting or running marathons, and keep taking drugs that have stopped giving them pleasure? In 1974 Richard Lester Solomon (1918 to 1995) and John D. Corbit proposed an answer in their opponent-process theory , which Solomon later (1980) called the opponent-process theory of acquired motivation. The theory assumes that the brain is built to resist strong emotional departures from neutrality. Any stimulus that produces a strong feeling arouses a primary process (the a-process), which produces the initial state, called state A (pleasant or unpleasant). The a-process automatically triggers an opponent process (the b-process), which produces the opposite feeling, state B. The two have different time courses. The a-process is quick, closely tied to the stimulus and does not change with repetition. The b-process is sluggish: it starts late, builds slowly and decays slowly after the stimulus stops. What we feel is the difference between them. So during the stimulus, state A peaks and then settles to a lower level (as the b-process grows), and when the stimulus ends, the a-process stops at once and the lingering b-process is felt on its own as an after-reaction in the opposite direction. The crucial assumption is that the b-process, unlike the a-process, grows stronger with use : with repeated exposure it starts sooner, becomes larger and lasts longer. Figure 10.3 shows the consequence. After many exposures, state A becomes weak (this is tolerance ), and state B becomes strong and long-lasting (this is withdrawal , or in the case of frightening activities, exhilaration). Motivation shifts from seeking A to escaping B. First few exposures After many exposures A state B state A state B state strong A weak A weak, brief B strong, lasting B baseline stimulus on stimulus on Figure 10.3 The opponent-process theory (after Solomon and Corbit, 1974). The line shows the feeling actually experienced (state A above the baseline, state B below it) while the stimulus is on (black bar) and after it ends. With repetition the opponent b-process grows, so A shrinks (tolerance) and the after-reaction B becomes larger and longer (withdrawal). Solomon and Corbit's favourite examples make the theory concrete. A novice parachutist is terrified during the first jump (state A) and dazed and stony-faced on landing; a veteran feels only tense eagerness during the jump and, afterwards, an exhilaration that lasts for hours (a strengthened state B). A first dose of an opiate brings intense euphoria (A) followed by mild craving (B); after hundreds of doses the euphoria is faint and the withdrawal is agonising, so the person takes the drug mainly to escape B. The same pattern, the theory claims, describes the comfort of a loved one's presence and the grief of separation, and the relief after a sauna. Clinical link Opponent-process theory gives the clinician a vocabulary for addiction: tolerance is a growing b-process, withdrawal is the b-process exposed when the drug wears off, and craving is the motive to escape B. It also explains why the risk of relapse peaks during early abstinence, when B is strongest. Siegel's conditioned-tolerance research (in the Learning chapter) adds that the b-process can become conditioned to the cues that usually accompany the drug. Exam trap There are two "opponent-process theories" in psychology. Ewald Hering's opponent-process theory (1878) is a theory of colour vision (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white; see the Sensation chapter). Solomon and Corbit's (1974) is a theory of acquired motivation and emotion . Match the author to the domain. In Solomon's theory it is the b-process , not the a-process, that strengthens with repetition. 10.5 Hierarchies of Need: Maslow, Alderfer and Other Lists High yield · 17 Qs By the 1950s American psychology had two grand theories of human nature. Psychoanalysis, the "first force", saw people as driven by unconscious sexual and aggressive instincts; behaviourism, the "second force", saw them as products of conditioning. Both, critics complained, had built their pictures of humanity from neurotic patients and hungry rats. The self-styled "third force", humanistic psychology , set out to study healthy, growing people, and to put free will, personal growth and the innate tendency to fulfil one's potential at the centre of psychology. Its two founders were Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970) and Carl Rogers (whose self theory is taught in the Personality book). Of the two, Maslow is the motivation theorist. There is a neat link to the opening of this chapter. Maslow did his doctoral research at the University of Wisconsin under Harry Harlow, studying dominance in monkeys. He left convinced that motivation had to be studied in its highest as well as its lowest forms. The hierarchy of needs Maslow first set out his theory in the paper "A Theory of Human Motivation" in Psychological Review (1943) and developed it in the book Motivation and Personality (1954). His hierarchy of needs arranges human needs in five levels, from the most basic to the most distinctively human: Physiological needs : food, water, oxygen, sleep, warmth, sex. These are the most powerful of all when unmet. Safety needs : security, stability, protection, order, freedom from fear and chaos. Maslow pointed to children's preference for routine and adults' preference for a steady job and insurance. Belongingness and love needs : friends, a partner, children, membership in a group, acceptance. (Some exam questions call this level "social needs".) Esteem needs : self-respect (competence, mastery, independence) and respect from others (status, recognition, appreciation). Self-actualisation : the need to become everything one is capable of becoming. "What a man can be, he must be," Maslow wrote. The organising principle is prepotency : lower needs are stronger than higher needs whenever they are unmet, so they must be at least partly satisfied before the higher needs take over the direction of behaviour. A starving man dreams of food, not of fame. Once food is reliable, safety becomes the dominant concern; once safety is secure, loneliness begins to hurt, and so on upwards. The lower a need stands in the hierarchy, the greater its strength and priority, so physiological and safety needs, at the base, are the lower needs (management writers call them the lower-order needs, and belongingness, esteem and self-actualisation the higher-order needs); the four levels below self-actualisation together form the deficiency needs described below. Maslow called all five levels basic needs , and he described them as instinctoid : inborn in a weak, instinct-like way, although the behaviours used to satisfy them are learned. Two points of precision are often lost in retelling. First, the hierarchy is not all-or-none. In the 1943 paper Maslow suggested that an average person might be about 85 per cent satisfied in physiological needs, 70 per cent in safety, 50 per cent in love, 40 per cent in esteem and 10 per cent in self-actualisation. A higher need emerges gradually as lower ones are partly met. Second, Maslow himself acknowledged exceptions, such as the martyr who gives up life for an ideal, or the creative person who pursues work through poverty. The familiar pyramid diagram, incidentally, is not Maslow's own drawing; it was added later by management writers. Figure 10.4 uses it because it is how the theory is examined. Self- actualisation Esteem respect, achievement Belongingness and love friends, family, acceptance Safety security, order, no danger Physiological food, water, sleep, warmth Deficiency (D) needs Growth or being (B) needs Higher needs Lower needs Figure 10.4 Maslow's hierarchy of needs (1943, 1954). The four lower levels are deficiency (D) needs; self-actualisation is a growth or being (B) need. Lower needs are prepotent: when unmet they dominate behaviour, and they must be largely met before higher needs take charge. Exam trap Memorise the order bottom to top: physiological, safety, belongingness and love (social), esteem, self-actualisation . Distractors swap safety and physiological, or put esteem above self-actualisation. "Which is NOT a level of Maslow's hierarchy?" has the answer ego , which belongs to Freud's structural model. "Maslow considers physiological and safety needs as" lower needs . The bait "greatest potency needs" is cleverly half-true: Maslow did call the lower needs prepotent (strongest when unmet), but the category name for physiological and safety needs is lower (lower-order) needs. "Transformational" is a leadership term (Burns, Bass), not Maslow's. Exam trap RML 2025 asked which need "must be mostly fulfilled before an individual seeks esteem needs". The level immediately below esteem is belongingness and love (social belonging) , so that is the correct answer. The key printed for this question gives physiological needs . Physiological needs must indeed be met first, but so must safety and belonging; the question asks which need precedes esteem, and on Maslow's ladder that is belonging. If the same wording appears, choose social belonging; if only physiological appears among lower levels, choose it. Deficiency needs, growth needs and metamotivation In Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) Maslow drew his most important distinction. The deficiency needs (D-needs) are the four lower levels. They arise from a lack, their satisfaction removes tension, and once satisfied they stop motivating; a fed person is not motivated by food. Behaviour driven by them is D-motivation , and it works much like Hull's drive reduction. The growth needs or being needs (B-needs) are different. They arise not from a lack but from the wish to grow; their satisfaction does not reduce tension but often increases it, and the more they are satisfied, the stronger they become. Maslow called the motivation of self-actualising people metamotivation (also B-motivation): they are not striving to fill a gap but are drawn towards states of being he called metaneeds or B-values, such as truth, goodness, beauty, wholeness, aliveness, uniqueness, justice, order, simplicity, playfulness and meaningfulness. When metaneeds are frustrated, the result is not a neurosis in the ordinary sense but a metapathology : cynicism and mistrust when truth is denied, apathy and loss of zest, a feeling of meaninglessness and despair. Maslow also described the Jonah complex , the fear of one's own greatness that keeps people from attempting to reach their potential. Later Maslow added to his list. In Motivation and Personality he discussed cognitive needs (to know and to understand) and aesthetic needs (for order, symmetry and beauty), which some textbooks insert between esteem and self-actualisation to make a seven-level hierarchy. And in his late writing (around 1969, and in the posthumous The Farther Reaches of Human Nature , 1971) he wrote of self-transcendence : a level beyond self-actualisation at which a person seeks to serve something beyond the self, such as others, a cause, nature or the sacred. An eight-level version (adding cognitive, aesthetic and transcendence needs) circulates widely. Self-actualisers and peak experiences The term self-actualisation was coined by the German neurologist Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965) in The Organism (1939), for the single master motive of any organism to realise its capacities. Maslow made it famous. He studied people he judged to be self-actualising, including historical figures such as Abraham Lincoln, Thomas Jefferson, Albert Einstein, Eleanor Roosevelt, William James, Jane Addams and Albert Schweitzer, and concluded that they made up 1 per cent or less of the population. They shared characteristics such as an efficient perception of reality, acceptance of self and others, spontaneity, a focus on problems outside themselves, a need for privacy, autonomy, a continued freshness of appreciation, deep relationships with a few people, a democratic character, a philosophical sense of humour and creativity. They also reported peak experiences : moments of intense ecstasy, wonder and awe, resembling mystical experiences, in which the sense of self is transcended. (A questionnaire measure of self-actualisation, Shostrom's Personal Orientation Inventory, is described in the Assessment book.) Exam trap "The striving for fulfilment of one's potential is called" self-actualisation . Its look-alikes: self-concept (one's organised picture of oneself, Rogers), ideal self (who one thinks one should be, Rogers), self-efficacy (belief in one's ability to perform a task, Bandura). The motivation proposed for self-actualisers is metamotivation , not D-motivation (and "E-motivation" and "F-motivation" are invented options). Goldstein coined "self-actualisation"; Maslow popularised it; Rogers spoke of an "actualising tendency" in all organisms. Evaluating Maslow Maslow's hierarchy is probably the best-known motivation theory in the world, and one of the least well supported. Four criticisms recur. Method : his self-actualisers were chosen by Maslow himself, according to his own values, so the description of self-actualisers partly describes Maslow's heroes. Evidence : in 1976 Mahmoud Wahba and Lawrence Bridwell reviewed the research and found little support for the ranking of the needs or for the idea that satisfying one level activates the next. Counter-examples : starving artists, hunger strikers and soldiers who die for comrades put higher needs before lower ones. Culture : the ladder reflects an individualistic, Western ideal in which personal fulfilment is the summit; in collectivist cultures, belonging and duty to the group may rank higher, and self-actualisation may be understood in relational terms. A survey of 123 countries by Louis Tay and Ed Diener (2011) found that the needs Maslow named are indeed universal and do predict well-being, but that people gain well-being from social and respect needs even when their basic needs are not fully met: the needs operate largely independently rather than as a strict ladder. Indian context Indian psychologists have often compared Maslow's hierarchy with the four purusharthas , the aims of life in Hindu thought: artha (material welfare), kama (pleasure and desire), dharma (duty and right conduct) and moksha (liberation). The tradition of the renunciant who sets aside bodily comfort in pursuit of liberation is a standard counter-example to strict prepotency, and Maslow's late idea of self-transcendence is the part of his theory closest to Indian ideas of self-realisation. (Indian psychology is covered in Chapter 2.) Alderfer's ERG theory The American organisational psychologist Clayton Paul Alderfer (1940 to 2015) tested Maslow's ideas with workers and in 1969 proposed a simpler, more flexible alternative, ERG theory . He collapsed the five levels into three. Existence needs cover Maslow's physiological and material safety needs (pay, food, working conditions). Relatedness needs cover interpersonal safety, belongingness and the external part of esteem (being respected by others). Growth needs cover the internal part of esteem and self-actualisation. Alderfer then changed the rules of movement. Like Maslow, he accepted a satisfaction-progression principle: satisfying a lower need tends to make the next need more important. Unlike Maslow, he allowed more than one need to operate at once , and he did not insist that lower needs be satisfied before higher ones can matter. And he added the frustration-regression principle: when a higher need is persistently frustrated, the person regresses and puts more effort into the lower need that is easier to satisfy. A clerk with no prospect of growth in his job may become intensely concerned with pay and with office friendships. ERG theory has found more empirical support than Maslow's strict hierarchy, particularly in organisations. Other lists of needs Maslow was not the only theorist to propose a list of basic human needs, and exam setters like to mix the lists. Viktor Frankl (1905 to 1997), the Viennese psychiatrist who survived Auschwitz, argued in Man's Search for Meaning (1946) that the primary motive in human beings is the will to meaning , in contrast to Freud's will to pleasure and Adler's will to power. His therapy is logotherapy , the "third Viennese school" of psychotherapy, and the frustration of the will to meaning produces an "existential vacuum". Table 10.5 collects the other lists. It says much less about why some people strive far harder than others. That question, about individual differences in learned social motives, was taken up at Harvard, beginning with one remarkable man. Murray: needs and press Henry Alexander Murray (1893 to 1988), trained in medicine and biochemistry before turning to psychology, directed the Harvard Psychological Clinic and in Explorations in Personality (1938) set out his personology , a theory of personality built around motivation. A need , for Murray, is a force in the brain that organises perception, thinking and action so as to change an unsatisfying situation; it can be aroused from within or by the environment, it is accompanied by a particular feeling, and it gives behaviour a direction. He distinguished the viscerogenic (bodily) needs from the psychogenic (psychological) needs you met in Section 10.1, and manifest needs, expressed openly in behaviour, from latent needs, expressed only in fantasy and dreams. His list of psychogenic needs, about twenty in the version most textbooks reproduce, is the ancestor of every later list. Table 10.6 gives the most examined ones; note Murray's "n" prefix for need. Table 10.6 A selection of Murray's psychogenic needs. Need What the person strives for n Achievement To accomplish something difficult, overcome obstacles, excel n Affiliation Friendly social contact, companionship, belonging n Dominance To control and influence others n Autonomy Independence, freedom from constraint n Aggression To overcome opposition forcefully, to attack n Nurturance To help, feed and protect the helpless n Succorance To be helped, protected and cared for n Abasement To submit, accept blame, surrender n Exhibition To make an impression, be seen and heard n Order To arrange, organise and keep things tidy Murray's second great idea was that needs cannot be understood apart from the environment. A press is an environmental force or situation that helps or hinders the satisfaction of a need: a strict father, a rival, a supportive teacher. He distinguished alpha press , the environment as it objectively is, from beta press , the environment as the person perceives it, and it is beta press that drives behaviour. The combination of a need and a press, a recurring theme in a person's life, he called a thema . To measure needs that people may not be able or willing to report, Christiana Morgan and Murray published the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) in 1935. The person tells stories about ambiguous pictures of people, and the needs and presses of the story's hero are scored as projections of the storyteller's own. The TAT, its logic and its rivals (the Rorschach inkblots, Jung's word association test, sentence completion tests) are taught in the Assessment book. What matters here is that the TAT became the standard measure of achievement motivation, and that Murray's needs were later measured by questionnaires such as Allen Edwards's Personal Preference Schedule. Exam trap Murray's need-press theory is the conceptual basis of the TAT (not the Rorschach, not the word association test, which is Jung's, not sentence completion). In Murray's system the need for affiliation (n Aff) is the need for social interaction and companionship; power appears in Murray's list as n Dominance (the TAT-scored need for power, n Pow, of McClelland's school descends from it); recognition is n Recognition; achievement is n Ach. "Press" is environmental, "need" is personal, "thema" is their combination. McClelland: achievement, power and affiliation David Clarence McClelland (1917 to 1998) took three of Murray's needs and made them the focus of a forty-year research programme. In The Achievement Motive (1953), written with John Atkinson, Russell Clark and Edgar Lowell, he developed a way of scoring TAT stories for achievement imagery: concern with a standard of excellence, unique accomplishment or long-term involvement. The resulting need for achievement (nAch) is a learned, relatively stable desire to accomplish difficult tasks and to meet standards of excellence through one's own effort. People high in nAch show a characteristic profile. They prefer tasks of moderate difficulty and moderate risk, where success is possible but not certain; they like personal responsibility for outcomes; they want concrete, rapid feedback on how well they are doing; and they are innovative and future-oriented. They are not the gamblers who bet everything on long odds, nor the timid who pick sure things. McClelland argued that such people make good entrepreneurs, and that nAch is learned in childhood: in Marian Winterbottom's studies of the 1950s, mothers who expected early independence and mastery from their sons tended to have sons high in nAch. In The Achieving Society (1961) McClelland went further, claiming that the level of achievement imagery in a nation's children's stories predicted its later economic growth. If nAch is learned and drives economic development, then perhaps it can be taught. Indian context: the Kakinada experiment McClelland put this idea to its most famous test in India. In the mid-1960s, working with the Small Industry Extension Training (SIET) Institute in Hyderabad, his team ran achievement motivation training courses for businessmen in Kakinada, a port town in Andhra Pradesh. Participants learned to think, talk and set goals like high achievers. In follow-up comparisons, the trained men started more new businesses, invested more and created more jobs than comparable untrained men. The work was reported in McClelland and David Winter's Motivating Economic Achievement (1969) and remains the best-known Indian study in motivation psychology. McClelland's other two needs complete his theory of needs (also called acquired-needs or learned-needs theory). The need for power (nPow) is the desire to influence, control and have an impact on others; McClelland and David Winter distinguished personalised power (power used for self-aggrandisement) from socialised power (power used for the benefit of the group). The need for affiliation (nAff) is the desire to establish and maintain warm, friendly relationships. McClelland found that the most effective managers in large organisations show a leadership motive pattern : high nPow, low nAff and high self-control. A manager with very high nAff, by contrast, finds it hard to make unpopular decisions. Dan McAdams later added an intimacy motive , the desire for warm, close, communicative relationships, as a fourth social motive often scored from the same stories. Exam trap McClelland's three needs are achievement, affiliation and power , and McClelland insisted they are learned (acquired), not innate. The baits come from neighbouring theories: "safety, esteem and self-actualisation" (Maslow), "existence, relatedness and growth" (Alderfer), "autonomy, competence and relatedness" (Deci and Ryan). The author of the "hierarchical theory of motivation" is A. H. Maslow , not McClelland, Atkinson or O. H. Mowrer (Mowrer is the two-factor avoidance theorist). Atkinson: the motive to succeed and the motive to avoid failure Why should high achievers prefer tasks of moderate difficulty? McClelland's colleague John William Atkinson (1923 to 2003) answered with an expectancy-value theory, published in 1957, that is one of the most elegant in psychology. Atkinson proposed that every achievement situation arouses two opposing tendencies. The tendency to approach success (Ts) is the product of three terms: the motive to succeed (Ms, a stable personality disposition, the capacity to feel pride in accomplishment), the probability of success (Ps, the person's estimate of the chance of succeeding at this task) and the incentive value of success (Is, the pride that success would bring). Atkinson's key insight was that Is is not independent of Ps: success at an easy task brings little pride, and success at a hard one brings a lot. So Is = 1 minus Ps, and Ts = Ms × Ps × (1 − Ps). The tendency to avoid failure (Taf) is built the same way from the motive to avoid failure (Maf, the capacity to feel shame at failure, usually measured by a test-anxiety questionnaire), the probability of failure and the negative incentive of failure (failing an easy task is the most shameful). The resultant tendency is the difference between the two, and it works out to (Ms − Maf) × Ps × (1 − Ps). Now push some numbers through, as in Table 10.7. Table 10.7 Worked example of Atkinson's theory: the term Ps × (1 − Ps) and what it predicts. Chance of success (Ps) Incentive (1 − Ps) Ps × (1 − Ps) Success-oriented (Ms > Maf) Failure-avoidant (Maf > Ms) 0.1 (very hard) 0.9 0.09 Weak approach Mild avoidance (tolerable) 0.3 0.7 0.21 Stronger approach Stronger avoidance 0.5 (moderate) 0.5 0.25 Strongest approach: preferred Strongest avoidance: shunned 0.7 0.3 0.21 Stronger approach Stronger avoidance 0.9 (very easy) 0.1 0.09 Weak approach Mild avoidance (tolerable) The product Ps × (1 − Ps) peaks at 0.5. So a person whose motive to succeed exceeds his motive to avoid failure is most attracted to tasks of intermediate difficulty, exactly McClelland's observation. A person dominated by fear of failure is most repelled by intermediate tasks, and so, when forced to choose, picks either a very easy task (where failure is unlikely) or a very hard one (where failure is no disgrace, because nobody could succeed). In 1960 Atkinson and George Litwin tested this with a ring-toss game in which students could stand as near to or as far from the peg as they liked. Students high in nAch and low in test anxiety chose intermediate distances; those low in nAch and high in anxiety more often stood very close or very far away. The same logic explains Kurt Lewin's earlier work on level of aspiration , the standard a person sets for his own next performance: success-oriented people raise their aspiration modestly after success, while failure-avoidant people set it unrealistically low or unrealistically high. Remember High achievers: intermediate risk, personal responsibility, feedback, attribute success to ability and effort and failure to lack of effort, persist after failure. Low achievers (high fear of failure): avoid evaluation, choose very easy or very hard tasks, attribute failure to lack of ability, give up. The link between the two halves of this box is Weiner's attribution theory, below. Fear of success Atkinson's theory was built almost entirely on men; women's achievement data were messy and were often set aside. In her 1968 doctoral research at the University of Michigan, Matina Souretis Horner (born 1939) asked why. She gave students the opening line of a story to complete. Women were given: "After first-term finals, Anne finds herself at the top of her medical school class." Men were given the same line about John. About two-thirds of the women wrote stories full of conflict and loss: Anne was lonely, unpopular, unfeminine, or deliberately dropped her grades; a few stories even had her physically disfigured. Fewer than one in ten of the men wrote such stories about John. Horner proposed a fear of success (the motive to avoid success): a learned expectation, stronger in women in her culture, that success, especially in competitive, traditionally male fields, would bring social rejection and doubts about one's femininity. Her paper in the Journal of Social Issues (1972) made the idea famous. Later research was less kind. When men wrote about a man succeeding in a field seen as feminine (nursing, for instance), they produced just as much negative imagery, which suggested that the stories reflected cultural stereotypes about who belongs where, not a stable motive peculiar to women. The concept survives as an example of how social norms shape achievement behaviour. Horner herself went on to become, at 32, the president of Radcliffe College. Weiner: attributions and achievement The newest strand of achievement research asks not "how strong is your motive?" but "how do you explain your successes and failures?" Its roots lie in the work of the Austrian-American social psychologist Fritz Heider (1896 to 1988), who argued in The Psychology of Interpersonal Relations (1958) that people act like naive scientists, explaining behaviour by internal (personal) or external (situational) causes. Such explanations are called attributions . A related idea came from Julian Rotter. His locus of control (1966) is a generalised expectancy about what controls the outcomes in one's life. People with an internal locus of control believe that outcomes depend on their own effort and ability; people with an external locus of control believe that outcomes depend on luck, fate or powerful others. Rotter measured it with his Internal-External (I-E) Scale. A student who believes his results depend on his own preparation rather than on luck or an easy examiner has an internal locus of control. (Low self-efficacy is a different idea, a belief that one cannot perform a task, below; the inferiority complex is Alfred Adler's concept, in the Personality book.) Bernard Weiner (born 1935) of the University of California, Los Angeles, built these strands into an attribution theory of achievement motivation , developed through the 1970s and set out in full in 1985. Weiner proposed that the causes people give for success and failure differ along three dimensions. Locus (borrowed from Rotter) asks whether the cause is internal or external to the person. Stability asks whether the cause is stable over time or variable. Controllability , added later, asks whether the person can control the cause. Table 10.8 places the four classic causes. Table 10.8 Weiner's classification of the causes of success and failure. Cause Locus Stability Controllability Ability Internal Stable Uncontrollable Effort Internal Unstable Controllable Task difficulty External Stable Uncontrollable Luck External Unstable Uncontrollable Each dimension has its own consequences. Locus governs self-esteem emotions : success attributed to internal causes produces pride, while success attributed to luck produces only gratitude or surprise. Stability governs expectancy : if you fail because of a stable cause (low ability, a hard examiner), you expect to fail again and lose hope; if you fail because of an unstable cause (insufficient effort, bad luck), you can expect to do better next time. Controllability governs social emotions : we feel guilt about our own failures due to controllable causes (I did not study) and shame about uncontrollable ones (I am not clever enough); and we feel anger towards others whose failure was controllable and pity or sympathy towards those whose failure was not. Work it through with a student who has failed a statistics test. If he says, "I am useless at maths" (internal, stable, uncontrollable), he feels shame, expects to fail again and is likely to give up. If he says, "I did not practise enough problems" (internal, unstable, controllable), he feels guilty but hopeful and is likely to work harder. Same failure, different attribution, opposite motivation. Seligman's learned helplessness research, reformulated in 1978 by Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale, applies the same logic to depression: people who attribute bad events to internal, stable and global causes are at risk (the Learning chapter and the Disorders book develop this). Exam trap Weiner's three dimensions are locus, stability and controllability . Do not add "globality" (that is the third dimension of the learned-helplessness reformulation, not Weiner's). Locus of control is Rotter's generalised expectancy (1966); locus of causality is Weiner's dimension (borrowed from Rotter). Effort is the only one of the four classic causes that is both internal and controllable, which is why attribution retraining teaches students to attribute failure to effort. 10.7 Intrinsic Motivation, Competence and the Self High yield · 9 Qs We now return to the puzzle in Harlow's monkey cages. If no drive was being reduced, what was going on? Over the 1950s a group of psychologists began to argue that organisms have built-in motives to explore, to understand and to master their surroundings, and that these motives are as basic as hunger. From that argument grew the modern study of intrinsic motivation. Curiosity and exploration Harry Frederick Harlow (1905 to 1981) is better known for his studies of infant monkeys and their cloth and wire "mothers" (in the Developmental book), but his puzzle studies came first. He concluded that a manipulation drive and an exploratory drive are primary, unlearned motives, and in a 1953 paper, "Mice, Monkeys, Men, and Motives", he mocked the attempt to derive all human motives from hunger and thirst. Robert Butler's window-opening monkeys (Section 10.3) showed a matching visual exploration drive. The most systematic account of curiosity came from the British-Canadian psychologist Daniel Ellis Berlyne (1924 to 1976), in Conflict, Arousal and Curiosity (1960). For Berlyne, curiosity is a motive aroused by stimuli with certain collative variables , so called because the organism must collate (compare) the stimulus with what it already knows: novelty , complexity , surprisingness , incongruity and uncertainty. Moderately novel and complex stimuli are the most attractive, in line with optimal arousal theory. Berlyne distinguished perceptual curiosity (the urge to look at or touch something new) from epistemic curiosity (the desire for knowledge), and two kinds of exploration: specific exploration , aimed at resolving uncertainty about a particular thing (what is making that noise?), and diversive exploration , aimed simply at relieving boredom (flicking through television channels). Maslow's cognitive needs to know and understand describe the same territory from the humanistic side. Competence or effectance motivation In 1959 Robert White (1904 to 2001) of Harvard published a long review in Psychological Review called "Motivation Reconsidered: The Concept of Competence". White pulled together the evidence on exploration, play, manipulation and mastery and argued that all of it reflected a single motive: the urge to interact effectively with the environment. He called this effectance motivation , and the feeling it produces, the satisfaction of having an effect, the feeling of efficacy. Watch an infant drop a spoon from a high chair again and again, delighted each time it clatters: the infant is not hungry, it is learning that it can make things happen. White's idea of competence motivation is the direct ancestor of two modern theories: Bandura's self-efficacy and Deci and Ryan's need for competence. Self-efficacy Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021), a Canadian-born psychologist at Stanford, introduced self-efficacy in a 1977 Psychological Review paper. Self-efficacy is a person's belief in his or her capability to organise and carry out the actions required to achieve a particular goal. It is specific to a task (you may have high self-efficacy for cooking biryani and low self-efficacy for public speaking), and it affects which tasks people choose, how much effort they put in, how long they persist in the face of difficulty and how anxious they feel. Bandura distinguished it from outcome expectancy , the belief that a given behaviour will produce a given outcome. A student may be sure that solving past papers would raise his marks (high outcome expectancy) and still doubt that he can make himself do it (low self-efficacy). Bandura named four sources of self-efficacy, in order of power. Mastery experiences (performance accomplishments) are the strongest: succeeding at a task builds belief, especially after overcoming difficulty. Vicarious experiences come from watching similar others succeed ("if she can do it, so can I"). Verbal persuasion is encouragement from others, weaker on its own. Physiological and emotional states are interpreted as signs of capability: a pounding heart before a viva may be read as incapacity unless one learns to read it as readiness. Self-efficacy is the motivational heart of Bandura's social cognitive theory (set out in Social Foundations of Thought and Action , 1986), the expansion of his earlier social learning theory. Its organising model is triadic reciprocal causation , also called reciprocal determinism: personal factors (beliefs, expectations, biology), behaviour and the environment all influence one another, so none is simply cause and none simply effect. Bandura's work on observational learning, with its attention, retention, reproduction and motivation processes, belongs to the Learning chapter. Exam trap "The reciprocal causation model has been described under" social cognitive theory (Bandura), not drive-reduction theory, not constructivist theory, and not "two-factor theory". Be ready for the many two-factor theories: Herzberg (work: motivators and hygiene, 1959), Mowrer (avoidance learning: classical plus operant, 1947), Schachter and Singer (emotion: arousal plus cognitive label, 1962) and Spearman (intelligence: g plus s, 1904). "Social cognitive theory highlights which factor in motivation?" Self-efficacy . Self-efficacy is not self-esteem (a global evaluation of one's worth) and not locus of control (a general belief about what controls outcomes). When rewards backfire: the overjustification effect If intrinsic motivation is real, what happens when you pay someone to do what they already enjoy? Common sense says you get more of it. Edward L. Deci (born 1942) tested this in a study published in 1971. College students worked on Soma puzzles, interesting three-dimensional block puzzles, over three sessions. In the second session, half of them were paid a dollar for each puzzle solved; in the third session nobody was paid. The key measure came when the experimenter left the room for a few minutes, leaving the puzzles and some magazines: how long did students spend on the puzzles in this free-choice period? Students who had been paid spent less free time on the puzzles after the payment stopped than students who had never been paid. Key study: Lepper, Greene and Nisbett's magic markers (1973) Question. Can an expected reward undermine a child's interest in an activity the child already enjoys? Method. Mark Lepper , David Greene and Richard Nisbett observed preschool children at a Stanford nursery school and selected those who, during free play, spent time drawing with magic markers. Each child was then invited to draw in one of three conditions: expected award (told in advance that drawing would earn a "Good Player" certificate with a gold seal and ribbon), unexpected award (given the same certificate as a surprise afterwards) or no award . Result. One to two weeks later, the markers were put out again in the classroom. Children in the expected-award group spent about half as much free time drawing as children in the other two groups, and the drawings they had made for the award were judged lower in quality. Unexpected awards did no harm. Conclusion. An expected, tangible reward for an already enjoyable activity can undermine intrinsic interest. Criticism. The effect depends heavily on conditions; rewards that are unexpected, verbal, or informative about competence do not undermine, and some reviewers (Cameron and Pierce, 1994) argued that the effect is narrower than often claimed. The authors called the result the overjustification effect : when a person is given more external justification for an activity than is needed (a reward for something already enjoyed), the person attributes the behaviour to the reward ("I draw for certificates") rather than to interest ("I draw because I like it"), and when the reward stops, so does the behaviour. A meta-analysis of 128 experiments by Deci, Richard Koestner and Richard Ryan (1999) confirmed that expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing a task reliably reduce intrinsic motivation, while positive verbal feedback tends to increase it. For parents and teachers in a culture of rewards for marks, the message is not "never reward", but "reward in a way that informs rather than controls, and do not pay children for what they already love". Self-determination theory and cognitive evaluation theory Deci and his Rochester colleague Richard M. Ryan (born 1953) built these findings into self-determination theory (SDT), presented in Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Determination in Human Behavior (1985) and now one of the most widely researched motivation theories. SDT proposes three innate, universal psychological needs whose satisfaction is essential for growth, intrinsic motivation and well-being. Autonomy is the need to feel that one's behaviour is self-chosen and volitional, that one is its origin rather than a pawn. Competence is the need to feel effective in dealing with the environment (White's idea). Relatedness is the need to feel close to and cared for by others. Social conditions that support these needs foster intrinsic motivation; conditions that thwart them undermine it. The first part of SDT to be developed was cognitive evaluation theory (CET), which explains when external events help or harm intrinsic motivation. Any reward, deadline, praise or surveillance has two aspects. Its controlling aspect pressures the person to behave in a particular way and shifts the perceived locus of causality from internal to external, lowering autonomy and intrinsic motivation. Its informational aspect tells the person about his competence, and if the information is positive it raises intrinsic motivation. Expected tangible rewards are usually experienced as controlling; unexpected praise for good work is usually experienced as informational. That is the theory behind the magic-marker results. SDT does not treat extrinsic motivation as a single thing. Its organismic integration theory arranges motivation along a continuum of increasing self-determination, shown in Table 10.9 for a student preparing for an entrance examination. The more a person internalises the value of an externally prompted activity, the more autonomous, persistent and satisfying the motivation becomes. Table 10.9 The self-determination continuum (Deci and Ryan). Type Regulation Example: why I study for the entrance Amotivation None; no intention to act "I don't see the point; I just sit there." Extrinsic External regulation "My parents will be angry if I don't." Extrinsic Introjected regulation "I would feel guilty and ashamed if I failed." Extrinsic Identified regulation "I value becoming a clinical psychologist." Extrinsic Integrated regulation "Helping people is part of who I am." SDT also describes stable individual differences, called causality orientations : an autonomy orientation (acting from interest and values), a controlled orientation (acting from rewards, deadlines and others' demands) and an impersonal orientation (feeling that outcomes are beyond one's control, associated with amotivation). Exam trap SDT's three needs are autonomy, competence and relatedness . The usual wrong options swap one of them for affiliation (McClelland), achievement (McClelland), independence , superiority (Adler) or excellence . "Which type of motivation in SDT is driven by internal rewards and personal growth?" Intrinsic motivation ; amotivation is the absence of motivation, and external regulation is the least autonomous form of extrinsic motivation. The overjustification study with magic markers is Lepper, Greene and Nisbett (1973) ; the Soma puzzle study is Deci (1971) . Flow Intrinsic motivation at its most intense has a name. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021), a Hungarian-born psychologist at the University of Chicago, began by asking painters why they worked for hours on canvases they then lost interest in once finished. He went on to interview rock climbers, chess players, dancers and surgeons, and in Beyond Boredom and Anxiety (1975) and Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990) he described flow : a state of complete absorption in an activity, in which action and awareness merge, attention is fully focused, self-consciousness disappears, the sense of time is distorted (hours pass like minutes) and the activity becomes autotelic , rewarding in itself. To study flow in everyday life he and Reed Larson developed the experience sampling method , in which people carry a pager (now a phone) and record what they are doing and feeling whenever it signals at random moments. The central condition for flow is a balance between challenge and skill , at a level that stretches the person, together with clear goals and immediate feedback. When the challenge exceeds skill, the person feels anxiety; when skill exceeds the challenge, boredom. Figure 10.5 shows the "flow channel" and how a learner moves through it. Anxiety challenge exceeds skill Boredom skill exceeds challenge A1 A2 A3 A4 Flow channel (shaded band) A1 beginner, easy rally: flow A2 more skill, same task: bored A3 tougher rival: anxious A4 skill meets challenge: flow Back to flow: raise the challenge (from A2) or build skill (A3) Skill (low to high) Challenge (low to high) Figure 10.5 The flow channel (after Csikszentmihalyi, 1990). Flow occurs when challenge and skill are in balance. A beginning tennis player is in flow at an easy level (A1); as skill grows he becomes bored (A2), and against a much stronger rival he becomes anxious (A3). He regains flow at a higher level (A4) by seeking harder challenges or by building skill. Exam trap "Who introduced the concept of flow?" Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi . The baits are near neighbours: Maslow described peak experiences (brief moments of ecstasy in self-actualisers, not the same as flow, which can occur in ordinary work), Rogers described the fully functioning person , and Frankl described the will to meaning . The consistency motive: cognitive dissonance One more cognitive motive deserves a place here, because it appears in motivation questions although its home is social psychology. Leon Festinger (1919 to 1989) proposed in A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance (1957) that people are motivated to keep their thoughts, beliefs and actions consistent. In his account, cognitive dissonance is the unpleasant state of tension that arises when a person holds two inconsistent cognitions, or acts against his own beliefs; like a drive, it motivates the person to reduce it, usually by changing an attitude, changing the behaviour, or adding a justifying thought. Arvind, who believes that smoking is disgusting because it killed his grandfather, smokes at a party with his friends: he will experience dissonance, and may later tell himself that "one cigarette at a party doesn't count". In Festinger and James Carlsmith's 1959 study, students paid only one dollar to tell a waiting student that a boring task was interesting later rated the task as more enjoyable than students paid twenty dollars; with insufficient external justification, they changed their attitude instead. Notice the family resemblance to the overjustification effect: too much external reward weakens internal interest, too little strengthens internal justification. Effort justification , the tendency to value what we have suffered for (Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills, 1959), is a special case. The theory and its research are developed in the Social Psychology book. Exam trap In the Arvind smoking question, the answer is cognitive dissonance . "Justification of effort" is a specific form of dissonance reduction after a costly choice, not the state itself; "drive reduction" is Hull; "increased drive to smoke" is invented. Dissonance motivates the person to reduce the inconsistency by changing an attitude or behaviour, never to increase it. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Real life is not so tidy. You want the job in Bengaluru and you want to stay near your parents in Mysuru; you want to pass the entrance and you dread another night of revision. Motives collide with each other and with the world, and the study of those collisions is the study of conflict and frustration. It also connects motivation to stress (Chapter 11) and to clinical psychology. Frustration and its sources In psychology, frustration is the blocking or thwarting of goal-directed behaviour, and also the unpleasant emotional state that results. Its sources are usually grouped into three classes. Environmental (external) sources include physical obstacles (a traffic jam, a closed office), natural events (floods, illness in the family), and social and cultural barriers (rules, prejudice, family disapproval, poverty). Personal (internal) sources include physical or mental limitations and, very commonly, a gap between aspiration and ability: the student who sets his heart on a rank his preparation cannot reach. The third source is conflict between one's own motives, taken up below. Delays, lack of resources, losses, failure and a sense of meaninglessness are the everyday forms frustration takes. Frustration is one of several sources of stress that are usually listed together, and questions ask you to tell them apart. Conflict is the presence of two or more incompatible motives. Change is the need to adjust to new circumstances (the life-event research of Holmes and Rahe is in Chapter 11). Finally, pressure is the expectation or demand that one behave in a certain way: pressure to perform (work hard, fast and well) and pressure to conform (meet others' expectations). Ramesh, who must handle a large number of calls at high speed in a call centre, is under pressure ; he is not blocked from a goal (frustration), torn between motives (conflict) or facing an unknowable future (unpredictability). Lewin's types of conflict Kurt Lewin, the German-American founder of field theory, described behaviour as a function of the person and the environment, B = f(P, E), played out in the person's life space . Objects in the life space have positive or negative valences that attract or repel the person, like forces in a physical field. When forces pull in incompatible directions, the result is a conflict . In A Dynamic Theory of Personality (1935) Lewin distinguished three basic types; a fourth was added by later writers (it is often credited to Carl Hovland and Robert Sears in 1938). Table 10.10 summarises them. Table 10.10 Types of motivational conflict. Type Structure Example Typical behaviour Approach-approach Two attractive goals, only one possible Admission offers from two good colleges Easiest to resolve; brief hesitation Avoidance-avoidance Two unpleasant options, one must be chosen Revise a hated subject or fail it Vacillation; tries to leave the field Approach-avoidance One goal with both attractive and unattractive features A well-paid job far from family Ambivalence; approach then retreat Double (multiple) approach-avoidance Two or more goals, each with good and bad features Job A pays well but is far; job B is near but pays less Prolonged vacillation; the most common real-life type In an approach-approach conflict the person is attracted to two goals that cannot both be reached. Such conflicts are the easiest to resolve: once you move even slightly towards one goal, its pull grows and the other's shrinks, so the conflict is unstable and resolves itself. (The medieval puzzle of Buridan's ass, which starved between two equally attractive bales of hay, is a philosopher's joke, not a psychological finding.) In an avoidance-avoidance conflict both options are unpleasant. As the person moves towards one, its repulsion grows and pushes him back towards the other, so he vacillates; if he can, he tries to leave the field altogether, by daydreaming, procrastinating or physically escaping. In an approach-avoidance conflict a single goal both attracts and repels: the cricket fan who wants to watch the final but fears what his boss will say about the day off. The person approaches until the negative features loom large, then retreats, then approaches again. In a double approach-avoidance conflict there are two or more such goals, and every option has its own pros and cons. This is the shape of most important real-life decisions: choosing a course, a job, a partner, a city. Miller's gradients of approach and avoidance Why does the approach-avoidance conflict produce such characteristic vacillation? Neal Miller answered with a model that turned Lewin's descriptions into testable predictions. In a 1944 chapter, "Experimental Studies of Conflict", and later in a fuller statement (1959), Miller proposed a set of postulates about approach and avoidance gradients , the way the strength of each tendency changes with distance from the goal. The tendency to approach a goal grows stronger the nearer the organism is to it (the approach gradient). The tendency to avoid a feared stimulus also grows stronger the nearer the organism is to it (the avoidance gradient). The avoidance gradient is steeper than the approach gradient: fear rises faster than desire as the goal comes closer. The strength of each tendency (the height of each gradient) depends on the strength of the drive on which it is based. When two incompatible tendencies conflict, the stronger one wins. The evidence came from rats wearing small harnesses that measured how hard they pulled. In a 1948 study, Judson Brown found that hungry rats trained to run to food pulled only a little less hard when stopped far from the goal than when stopped near it, while rats shocked at the goal pulled away very hard near it and hardly at all far from it. The gradients really do differ in slope. Now look at Figure 10.6. Far from the goal, approach is stronger than avoidance, so the organism moves forward. Close to the goal, avoidance is stronger, so it retreats. At the point where the gradients cross, the two are equal, and the organism hovers, moving forward and back. This is the vacillation of the bride who longs to marry and panics as the wedding day approaches, and of the student who sits down to start a feared assignment and finds himself, ten minutes later, making tea. Approach (shallow gradient) Avoidance (steep gradient) approach wins: moves closer avoidance wins: retreats vacillation point far from goal at the goal Distance to the goal Strength of tendency Figure 10.6 Miller's gradients in an approach-avoidance conflict. Both tendencies grow stronger nearer the goal, but avoidance (dashed) grows faster. Where the lines cross, the two are equal and the person vacillates; lowering the avoidance line moves the crossing point closer to the goal. Clinical link John Dollard and Neal Miller translated these gradients into therapy in Personality and Psychotherapy (1950). Suppose a client wants a relationship but fears intimacy. Increasing the approach tendency (urging him on, raising the rewards) raises the whole approach line, so the crossing point moves nearer the goal, where avoidance is steepest; he gets closer and suffers more fear and conflict. Reducing the avoidance tendency (lowering fear through reassurance, exposure and relaxation) lets him approach with less distress. Their rule: in an approach-avoidance conflict, work first on reducing fear, not on increasing desire. Modern exposure therapy follows the same logic. Reactions to frustration How do people respond when a goal is blocked? Some responses are constructive: trying harder, changing the approach, finding a substitute goal, or lowering the goal to a realistic level. Others are less adaptive, and four of them are classic in textbooks. Aggression is the most studied (see the frustration-aggression hypothesis, below). It may be direct , aimed at the source of frustration, or redirected onto a safer target when the true source is too powerful or too vague. Such displaced aggression is the clerk who, scolded by his boss, goes home and shouts at his children. When a whole group is blamed for a society's frustrations, displacement becomes scapegoating . In 1940 Carl Hovland and Robert Sears reported that lynchings in the American South rose in years when the price of cotton fell; later reanalyses found the relationship weaker than first claimed, but the study remains the textbook example of displaced aggression. Regression is a return to behaviour typical of an earlier stage of development. In a 1941 study at the University of Iowa, Roger Barker, Tamara Dembo and Kurt Lewin let young children play with ordinary toys, then showed them a room of far more attractive toys and, after a short time, put those toys behind a wire screen where the children could see but not reach them. When the children went back to the ordinary toys, their play became markedly less constructive, more like the play of much younger children. Fixation is the rigid, stereotyped repetition of a response that no longer works. Norman Maier (1900 to 1977) gave rats insoluble discrimination problems on a jumping stand, punishing them unpredictably whatever they chose. Many rats developed a fixed habit, such as always jumping to the left, and kept it even after the problem was made soluble and the correct window was left open in front of them. In Frustration: The Study of Behavior Without a Goal (1949) Maier argued that frustration-induced behaviour is qualitatively different from goal-directed behaviour. Withdrawal and apathy are giving up: the person stops trying, loses interest and may become passive and depressed, as in learned helplessness. Finally, people protect themselves from the anxiety of frustration and conflict with the unconscious strategies Freud called defence mechanisms . Table 10.11 lists the ones most often examined as reactions to frustration (they are taught in full in the Personality book). The psychologist Saul Rosenzweig, who coined the term frustration tolerance for the ability to withstand frustration without maladaptive responses, also classified reactions as extrapunitive (blaming others), intropunitive (blaming oneself) or impunitive (blaming no one), and measured them with his Picture-Frustration Study (in the Assessment book). Table 10.11 Defence mechanisms often listed as reactions to frustration. Mechanism What happens Example Rationalisation A socially acceptable reason is constructed, after the act, for behaviour driven by other motives "I didn't want that seat anyway; the college is overrated." Displacement An impulse is redirected from a threatening target to a safer one Shouting at a younger brother after a bad viva Projection One's own unacceptable impulse is attributed to others A jealous student accuses classmates of jealousy Sublimation Sexual or aggressive energy is re-channelled into socially valued activity Aggression channelled into boxing or surgery Reaction formation An impulse is replaced by its exaggerated opposite Excessive sweetness towards a disliked rival Repression A threatening thought is pushed out of awareness No memory of a humiliating failure Denial An unpleasant reality is refused acknowledgement Insisting the result list must be wrong Regression Return to an earlier developmental level An adult sulking and refusing to eat Compensation Weakness in one area is offset by excelling in another; pushed to excess it is Adler's overcompensation A poor athlete becoming the class topper Exam trap Three bank items describe the same mechanism in different words: "an intellectual reason to justify an action, constructed in the mind after the behaviour is completed", "logical and socially acceptable explanations, after the event, for behaviour actually driven by unconscious motives" and "a socially acceptable reason for actions really based on unacceptable motives". All three are rationalisation . The giveaway is the after-the-fact reason . Re-channelling sexual or aggressive energy into a socially valued outlet is sublimation ; shifting it onto a safer target is displacement ; attributing it to others is projection ; turning it into its exaggerated opposite is reaction formation ; refusing to acknowledge reality is denial ; pushing a thought out of awareness is repression . The frustration-aggression hypothesis In 1939 a group of Yale scholars, John Dollard, Leonard Doob, Neal Miller, Orval Hobart Mowrer and Robert Sears, published Frustration and Aggression . Their frustration-aggression hypothesis made two sweeping claims: aggression is always a consequence of frustration, and frustration always leads to some form of aggression. Both claims proved too strong. Frustration can lead to regression, fixation, withdrawal or constructive problem solving, and aggression can occur without frustration (a hired fighter, a soldier obeying orders). In 1941 Miller himself revised the hypothesis: frustration produces instigations to several kinds of response, one of which is aggression. In 1989 Leonard Berkowitz (1926 to 2016) offered the influential reformulation, which he developed into his cognitive neo-associationist model: frustration produces aggression only to the extent that it produces negative affect , and aversive events of any kind (pain, heat, foul smells, insults) can do the same; cues associated with aggression, such as the weapons in Berkowitz and LePage's 1967 study, make an aggressive response more likely. Aggression as a topic belongs to the Social Psychology book. Exam trap The frustration-aggression hypothesis is Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer and Sears (1939) , not Lewin and not Freud; its revisions are Miller (1941) and Berkowitz (1989). The regression study with toys behind a wire screen is Barker, Dembo and Lewin (1941) ; the fixation study with rats on a jumping stand is Maier (1949) . Lewin described the three basic conflict types; Miller supplied the gradients; the avoidance gradient is steeper , not shallower. "Leaving the field" is the hallmark of avoidance-avoidance conflict; "approach then retreat" is the hallmark of approach-avoidance . 10.9 Biological Motives: Hunger, Thirst, Sex and Others Medium yield · 9 Qs We end the survey of theories where drive theory began, in the body. The biological motives are where psychology and physiology meet, and they are where several of the most famous "facts" in introductory psychology turned out to be only half true. The detailed neuroscience of eating and drinking belongs to the Physiological Psychology book; here the aim is to understand what starts and stops these behaviours, and to know the classic findings and the traps around them. Hunger: from the stomach to the brain The most obvious theory of hunger is that we feel hungry because our stomachs are empty. It was tested in one of the most charming experiments in the history of physiology. Key study: Cannon and Washburn's swallowed balloon (1912) Question. Is hunger the feeling of an empty stomach contracting? Method. Walter Cannon had the idea; his student A. L. Washburn had the ability to swallow a balloon. Washburn swallowed an empty balloon tied to the end of a thin tube; Cannon inflated it and connected the tube to a water-filled U-tube, so that each stomach contraction pushed up the water level, which was recorded. Washburn pressed a key whenever he felt a hunger pang. Result. Large stomach contractions coincided with Washburn's reports of hunger pangs. Conclusion. Cannon and Washburn proposed that hunger is the feeling of stomach contractions and that satiety is the feeling of stomach distension. Criticism. Patients whose stomachs had been surgically removed, with the oesophagus joined directly to the small intestine, still reported hunger and satiety and kept a normal body weight by eating smaller, more frequent meals. The stomach contributes to hunger, but it is not its source. If not the stomach, then what? In the 1940s and 1950s researchers looked for signals in the blood, assuming that eating, like temperature, is regulated around a set point. The glucostatic theory (associated with Jean Mayer, 1953) held that we become hungry when blood glucose falls below its set point and stop eating when it is restored; glucose is, after all, the brain's main fuel. The lipostatic theory (associated with Gordon Kennedy, 1953) held that each person has a set point for body fat, and that deviations from it produce compensating changes in eating. The two were seen as complementary: a short-term glucostatic system for starting and stopping meals and a long-term lipostatic system for body weight. Pinel and Barnes, whose Biopsychology textbook is the standard source on this topic, argue that these set-point theories have several serious problems. They cannot explain the worldwide epidemic of overeating and obesity, since a set-point system should resist it. They fit poorly with the evolutionary pressures on eating: our ancestors faced an unpredictable food supply, so they needed a system that made them eat good food whenever it was available and bank the calories as fat, preventing energy deficits rather than merely responding to them. Their key predictions have not been confirmed: reductions in blood glucose or body fat large enough to trigger eating rarely occur in ordinary life. And they ignore the enormous influence of taste, learning and social factors on eating. Their alternative is the positive-incentive perspective introduced in Section 10.4: we are motivated to eat mainly by the anticipated pleasure of eating, and body weight is regulated loosely around a settling point , the weight at which the many factors that influence intake and expenditure come into balance. Their "leaky barrel" analogy makes the point: the water level in a leaky barrel stays fairly constant not because anything defends a set level, but because a fuller barrel leaks faster. Change the inflow (a more tempting food environment) and the level drifts to a new settling point. This is why dieters' weight drifts back up, and why the same person can stabilise at different weights in different environments. The hypothalamus: two centres and their revision Every entrance paper seems to ask about the "satiety centre". Here is the story behind the term. In 1940 Albert Hetherington and Stephen Ranson reported that large bilateral lesions of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) made rats eat enormously ( hyperphagia ) and become extremely obese. The VMH syndrome has two phases: a dynamic phase of several weeks of gross overeating and rapid weight gain, and a static phase in which the rat eats just enough to maintain its new, high weight, and defends it against both starvation and forced feeding. In 1951 Bal Krishan Anand and John Brobeck at Yale reported that bilateral lesions of the lateral hypothalamus (LH) produced aphagia , a complete refusal to eat that led to death unless the animal was tube-fed, and later work showed that LH lesions also cause adipsia , the refusal to drink. Stimulating the LH made sated animals eat. In 1954 Eliot Stellar put the findings together in the dual-centre theory : the LH is a feeding (hunger) centre and the VMH a satiety centre , working like an accelerator and a brake. Indian context Bal Krishan Anand, the "Anand" of Anand and Brobeck, was an Indian physiologist. After his work at Yale he returned to India and built one of the country's leading neurophysiology departments at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi. With G. S. Chhina and Baldev Singh he also published, in 1961, one of the earliest electroencephalographic studies of yogis in meditation. The "feeding centre" in every psychology textbook carries an Indian name. The dual-centre theory is still the answer examiners want, but you should know that it has been substantially revised, as Pinel describes. VMH-lesioned rats turned out to overeat because they gain weight, rather than gaining weight because they overeat: VMH lesions raise blood insulin, which speeds the conversion of nutrients into fat (lipogenesis) and slows its release (lipolysis), so the rats must keep eating to have enough usable energy. Moreover, many effects of large VMH lesions come from damage to fibres from the nearby paraventricular nucleus (PVN), and lesions of the PVN alone produce overeating. LH lesions, for their part, produce a wide range of motor and sensory deficits, not a specific loss of hunger. Modern research focuses on particular cell groups, especially in the arcuate nucleus , which receives the body's chemical signals about energy.
