Weightage. 73 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (8.9%) test this chapter, 48 of them from real past papers. 3 of its 10 sections are High yield. North of Vancouver, in Canada, a footbridge of wooden planks and wire cable hangs across the Capilano Canyon. It is about 140 metres long and barely a metre and a half wide. It tilts and sways under every step, its cable handrails are low, and the rocks and rapids of the Capilano River lie some 70 metres below. Most people who cross it grip the cables and walk faster than they meant to. In 1974 two psychologists, Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, decided that this frightening bridge would make an excellent laboratory. Their procedure was simple. An attractive young woman stood on the bridge and stopped men aged roughly 18 to 35 who were crossing alone. She explained that she was doing a class project on the effects of scenic places on creativity, and asked each man to fill in a short questionnaire, which included writing a brief story about a picture of a woman. When he had finished, she tore a corner off a sheet of paper, wrote down her name and telephone number, and said that he was welcome to call her if he wanted to talk about the study. Exactly the same thing was done a little further up the river, on a second bridge: a solid cedar structure only about 3 metres above a shallow stream, with high handrails, that did not sway at all. The men on the swaying bridge wrote stories with noticeably more sexual imagery than the men on the solid bridge. And more of them picked up the telephone: nine of the men interviewed on the suspension bridge called the woman, against only two from the solid bridge. When the interviewer was a man, almost nobody called from either bridge. Why should a frightening bridge make a stranger more attractive? The men's hearts were pounding because of the bridge, yet at least some of them seem to have read that pounding as attraction to the woman. Think about what this implies. If the same racing heart can be "fear" on one reading and "attraction" on another, where exactly is an emotion? Is it in the body, in the brain, or in the story we tell ourselves about our body? That question has driven more than a century of research, and it leads directly to the second subject of this chapter: stress, which is what happens when the body's emergency system is switched on and then left on. Keep the men on the Capilano bridge in mind; you will meet them again at the end of the chapter. 11.1 What is an emotion? Medium yield · 4 Qs Everyone knows what an emotion is until asked to define one. You know what it is like to be furious when a scooter cuts across you at a Mysuru signal, or to feel your stomach drop when the question paper is handed out. But what, exactly, has happened in each case? Psychologists answer by taking an emotion apart. The three components of an emotion An emotion is a relatively brief, whole-person response to an event that matters to you, made up of three components that normally occur together. The first is physiological arousal : the bodily changes, most of them controlled by the autonomic nervous system, such as a pounding heart, fast breathing, sweating palms and a dry mouth. The second is expressive behaviour : what can be seen and heard from outside, such as the face, the voice, posture and actions like running or striking. The third is conscious experience : the private, subjective awareness of the state ("I am afraid"), together with the thoughts that go with it. Many modern theorists add two further ingredients that are really part of the same package: an appraisal (an evaluation of what the event means for you) and an action tendency (an urge to do something, such as to flee, attack or approach). Notice how well the three components map onto the theories you are about to meet. The great theoretical quarrels about emotion are mostly quarrels about the order and the causal links among these components. Does the body react first and the feeling follow? Do they occur together? Does a thought have to come first? Keep the three components in view and the theories will sort themselves out. Emotion, feeling, mood, affect and temperament Five words are used loosely in everyday speech but carefully in psychology, and examiners like to test the difference. A feeling is the subjective, consciously experienced part of an emotion: the "what it is like" component. An emotion is short (seconds to minutes) and is usually about something: you are angry at a person, afraid of a dog. A mood is longer, lower in intensity and more diffuse; it often has no clear object or cause, and it colours everything else. You can wake up irritable after a bad night and stay that way all day without being angry at anyone in particular. The word affect has two uses. In research psychology it is the umbrella term for all states that feel good or bad, so emotions, moods and feelings are all forms of affect, and "positive affect" and "negative affect" describe your current feeling state as a whole. In clinical psychology and psychiatry, affect has a narrower meaning: the observable, moment-to-moment expression of emotion, as a clinician sees it in the face, voice and gestures during an interview. Finally, temperament is the biologically based, early-appearing and fairly stable individual difference in how easily a person becomes emotionally aroused and how well he or she calms down. A baby who startles at every noise and is hard to soothe differs in temperament from one who takes the world in her stride. (The famous temperament classification of Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess, easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up, is taught in the Developmental book; the older "four temperaments" of Hippocrates and Galen, sanguine, choleric, melancholic and phlegmatic, belong to the history of personality theory.) Table 11.1 sets the five terms side by side. Table 11.1 Five terms that are easy to confuse. Term What it is Typical time span Example Emotion Brief, multi-component response to a specific event Seconds to minutes Anger when someone pushes ahead in the queue Feeling The subjective, conscious component of an emotion As long as the emotion "I feel humiliated" Mood Diffuse, low-intensity state, often without a clear object Hours to days Gloomy all day for no obvious reason Affect Umbrella term for good or bad feeling states; clinically, the observable expression of emotion Current, moment to moment "Affect restricted, mood low" Temperament Inborn style of emotional reactivity and self-regulation Years to a lifetime A child who is slow to warm up to strangers Clinical link In the mental status examination, clinicians record mood and affect separately. Mood is the patient's sustained, pervasive emotional state, usually in the patient's own words ("I've been low for weeks"); its key feature is its persistence. Affect is what the clinician observes now, and it is described by its quality (anxious, sad, cheerful), its range (full, restricted, blunted or flat), its reactivity or mobility (does it change appropriately as the topic changes, or is it fixed or labile?), its intensity, and whether it is congruent with the mood and appropriate to what is being said. A common teaching image: mood is the climate, affect is the weather. Basic emotions: is there a short list? If emotions are products of evolution, there might be a small set of basic emotions (also called primary emotions): emotions that are innate, appear early in life, are found in all cultures, have distinctive facial expressions, and serve a clear survival function. More complex emotions such as jealousy, pride or nostalgia would then be blends of these or would require more sophisticated thought. Several theorists have proposed such lists, and the lists are a favourite source of exam questions. Silvan Solomon Tomkins (1911 to 1991), in his Affect Imagery Consciousness (first two volumes, 1962 and 1963), proposed an affect theory in which nine innate affects, each with its own facial pattern, are the primary motivators of behaviour: interest-excitement, enjoyment-joy, surprise-startle, distress-anguish, fear-terror, shame-humiliation, anger-rage, disgust and "dissmell" (the reaction to a bad smell). Tomkins argued that the face is the main site of emotion, an idea that led directly to the facial feedback hypothesis (Section 11.3). Two younger researchers whom he mentored and inspired, Ekman and Izard, carried the programme forward. Paul Ekman (born 1934) and his colleague Wallace V. Friesen concluded from cross-cultural research in the late 1960s and early 1970s (Section 11.5) that six emotions have universally recognised facial expressions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust . In 1986 they added a seventh, contempt , whose expression is a one-sided tightening and raising of the lip corner. Carroll Ellis Izard (1923 to 2017) developed differential emotions theory (1971, 1977), which names ten fundamental emotions, each with its own feeling, expression and motivational function: interest, joy, surprise, sadness (distress), anger, disgust, contempt, fear, shame (shyness) and guilt. Izard also built coding systems for reading emotion in infants' faces. Table 11.2 The best-known lists of basic emotions. Theorist Year Number The list John B. Watson 1919 3 Fear, rage, love Silvan Tomkins 1962 9 Interest, enjoyment, surprise, distress, fear, shame, anger, disgust, dissmell Carroll Izard 1971 to 1977 10 Interest, joy, surprise, sadness, anger, disgust, contempt, fear, shame, guilt Paul Ekman 1971 to 1972; contempt 1986 6, then 7 Happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust (then contempt) Robert Plutchik 1980 8 Joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger, anticipation Jaak Panksepp 1998 7 brain systems Seeking, rage, fear, lust, care, panic (grief), play Two more names complete the table. John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958), the founder of behaviourism, held that newborns show only three unlearned emotional reactions, fear, rage and love, and that every other emotion is built from them by conditioning (Chapter 6). Jaak Panksepp (1943 to 2017), working from brain stimulation in animals, identified seven subcortical emotional systems, which he wrote in capitals to show they were brain circuits rather than everyday words: SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, LUST, CARE, PANIC (later PANIC/GRIEF) and PLAY. Indian context The idea of a short list of basic emotions is very old in India. The Natyashastra , the Sanskrit treatise on drama attributed to Bharata Muni (usually dated somewhere between about 200 BCE and 200 CE), describes eight sthayibhavas (enduring emotional states), each of which an audience savours as a rasa : rati (love, giving the erotic rasa shringara ), hasa (mirth), shoka (sorrow), krodha (anger), utsaha (energy or heroism), bhaya (fear), jugupsa (disgust) and vismaya (wonder or astonishment). The philosopher Abhinavagupta (about the tenth to eleventh century) argued for a ninth, shanta (peace). Notice how closely the list overlaps with Ekman's: anger, fear, disgust, sorrow, joy and surprise are all there, nearly two thousand years earlier. Plutchik's wheel of emotions Robert Plutchik (1927 to 2006) offered the most elaborate basic-emotion model in his psychoevolutionary theory of emotion (1980). He proposed eight primary emotions, each tied to an adaptive behaviour that helped our ancestors survive, arranged in a circle so that each emotion sits opposite its psychological opposite: joy opposite sadness, trust opposite disgust, fear opposite anger, and surprise opposite anticipation (Figure 11.1, right). Plutchik's famous three-dimensional "cone" adds intensity: each primary emotion has a milder and a stronger form, so that annoyance intensifies into anger and then rage (Table 11.3). Emotions next to each other mix to form primary dyads : joy and trust give love ; trust and fear give submission ; fear and surprise give awe ; surprise and sadness give disapproval ; sadness and disgust give remorse ; disgust and anger give contempt ; anger and anticipation give aggressiveness ; and anticipation and joy give optimism . Plutchik compared emotions to colours: a few primaries, mixed in different proportions and intensities, produce the whole palette. Table 11.3 Plutchik's eight primary emotions, their intensities, opposites and functions. Primary Milder form Stronger form Opposite Adaptive function Joy Serenity Ecstasy Sadness Reproduction Trust Acceptance Admiration Disgust Incorporation Fear Apprehension Terror Anger Protection Surprise Distraction Amazement Anticipation Orientation Sadness Pensiveness Grief Joy Reintegration Disgust Boredom Loathing Trust Rejection Anger Annoyance Rage Fear Destruction Anticipation Interest Vigilance Surprise Exploration Dimensions instead of categories: Russell's circumplex A rival tradition says that emotions are not separate boxes at all but points in a continuous space. The idea goes back to Wilhelm Wundt (1832 to 1920), whose tridimensional theory of feeling described every feeling by its position on three dimensions: pleasure-displeasure, tension-relaxation and excitement-depression (Chapter 1). The modern version is the circumplex model of James A. Russell (1980). Russell asked people to judge how similar emotion words were and found that the words fell in a circle defined by just two dimensions: valence (how pleasant or unpleasant the state is) and arousal (how activated or calm it is). "Excited" is pleasant and high in arousal; "calm" is pleasant and low; "afraid" is unpleasant and high; "bored" and "sad" are unpleasant and low (Figure 11.1, left). Russell later called the blend of valence and arousal you are in at any moment core affect . A closely related scheme, from David Watson and Auke Tellegen (1985), rotates the same circle by 45 degrees and describes it with two independent axes, positive affect and negative affect, the basis of the widely used PANAS scale (Psychological Assessment book). (a) Russell's circumplex High arousal Low arousal Unpleasant Pleasant Happy Excited Afraid Upset Sad Bored Calm Content Valence across, arousal up and down (b) Plutchik's eight primaries Joy Trust Fear Surprise Sadness Disgust Anger Anticipation Lines join the four opposite pairs Figure 11.1 Two ways of mapping emotion. (a) Russell's circumplex (1980) places every emotion on a circle defined by valence and arousal. (b) Plutchik's model (1980) has eight primary emotions; each sits across from its opposite (joy and sadness, trust and disgust, fear and anger, anticipation and surprise), and neighbours blend into dyads such as love and awe. Which view is right, categories or dimensions? Probably both capture something. Basic-emotion theorists point to universal expressions and to brain circuits such as the fear system of the amygdala (Section 11.4). Dimensional theorists point out that in everyday life emotions blend and shade into one another, and that brain imaging has not found one neat "spot" for each emotion word. The most radical dimensional view is the theory of constructed emotion of Lisa Feldman Barrett (set out in her 2017 book How Emotions Are Made ). Barrett argues that the brain continually produces core affect, and that we construct specific emotions such as "anger" by categorising that core affect with concepts learned from our language and culture. On this view "fear" is less like a reflex and more like a word we have learned to apply, which is why the same pounding heart could be called fear on one bridge and attraction on another. Exam trap Jealousy, shame, guilt, pride, love and envy are not on Ekman's list. Ekman's six are happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust; contempt was added as a seventh in 1986. Jealousy is a complex, social emotion (a blend of fear, anger and sadness about losing a relationship to a rival). Shame and guilt are on Izard's list of ten, not Ekman's. Trust and anticipation appear only in Plutchik's eight. "Dissmell" is Tomkins's. Do not mix up the two-dimension schemes. Russell's circumplex uses valence by arousal; Watson and Tellegen use positive affect by negative affect; Wundt's older theory has three dimensions (pleasure-displeasure, tension-relaxation, excitement-depression). 11.2 The classic theories: from the body to the label Medium yield · 6 Qs Now return to the three components: arousal, expression and experience. Common sense has a firm view of how they are related. You see a snake on a village path, you feel afraid, and because you feel afraid your heart races and you jump back. Feeling comes first and the body follows. The first scientific theory of emotion turned this common sense on its head. The James-Lange theory: we feel afraid because we tremble In 1884 the American psychologist and philosopher William James (1842 to 1910) published an article in the journal Mind with the deceptively simple title "What is an emotion?". A year later, in 1885, the Danish physician Carl Georg Lange (1834 to 1900) independently published a very similar account, so the theory carries both names. James put it memorably in his Principles of Psychology (1890): common sense says that we lose our fortune, are sorry and weep; we meet a bear, are frightened and run. James argued that this order is wrong: "the bodily changes follow directly the perception of the exciting fact, and ... our feeling of the same changes as they occur IS the emotion." In his most quoted line, "we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble." The James-Lange theory , then, says that an emotion-provoking stimulus first triggers bodily responses, autonomic changes in the viscera and actions of the skeletal muscles, and that the emotion we feel is simply our perception of those bodily changes. Take away the racing heart, the trembling and the running, James said, and nothing would be left of fear but a "cold and neutral state of intellectual perception." Lange put more weight on changes in the blood vessels; James included all bodily changes. Notice what the theory implies: if each emotion is the feeling of a particular bodily state, then different emotions must have different bodily patterns. Fear must feel like fear because its pattern of arousal differs from that of anger. Textbooks often draw the James-Lange sequence as stimulus, then bodily arousal, then awareness or "interpretation" of the arousal, then emotion (Figure 11.2, top row). The "interpretation" in this diagram is not a reasoned judgement about the situation. It is just the brain noticing what the body is doing: "my heart is pounding and my knees are shaking." The feeling of those changes is the fear. Is there evidence for James? Some. In 1966 the psychologist George W. Hohmann interviewed men with spinal cord injuries and reported that those with higher injuries, who received less feedback from the body, described their anger and fear as less intense than before. Later and better-controlled studies, however, found that people with severe spinal injuries still experience a full range of emotions, with at most some dampening of fear and anger. In 1983 Paul Ekman, Robert W. Levenson and Friesen found modest differences in autonomic patterns between emotions: anger and fear both raised heart rate, but anger raised finger temperature while fear lowered it. The modern verdict is that bodily feedback is not necessary for emotion but can colour and intensify it, a point you will meet again in the facial feedback hypothesis. Cannon's critique and the Cannon-Bard theory The most powerful attack on James came from the Harvard physiologist Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945), the man who gave us the phrase "fight or flight" (Section 11.8). In a famous paper of 1927, Cannon listed five objections to the James-Lange theory: Cutting the body off from the brain does not abolish emotion. Animals whose viscera had been surgically separated from the central nervous system (Cannon's own sympathectomised cats, and dogs studied earlier by the physiologist Charles Sherrington) still showed rage, fear and pleasure in appropriate situations. The same visceral changes occur in very different emotions and in non-emotional states. A racing heart, faster breathing and sweating accompany fear, anger and excitement alike, and also fever, cold and exercise. Such a general pattern cannot tell fear from anger. The viscera are relatively insensitive. The internal organs have few sensory nerve fibres, so the brain receives only vague information about them, too vague to support fine distinctions among emotions. Visceral changes are too slow. Autonomic responses take a second or more to develop, but we often feel an emotion almost instantly. Producing the bodily changes artificially does not produce the emotion. When the Spanish physician Gregorio Marañón injected 210 people with adrenaline in 1924, about 71 percent reported only bodily symptoms and no emotion at all; the rest described a cold, "as if" state ("I feel as if I were afraid"), but not genuine fear. In place of James's theory Cannon proposed that an emotional stimulus is processed in the thalamus, which then sends signals simultaneously in two directions: up to the cerebral cortex, producing the conscious experience of emotion, and down to the body through the hypothalamus and autonomic nervous system, producing the physiological arousal. His student and collaborator Philip Bard (1898 to 1977) extended the theory and showed that the hypothalamus is critical for the bodily expression of rage (Section 11.4). The Cannon-Bard theory (also called the thalamic theory) therefore holds that the feeling of emotion and the bodily reaction occur at the same time and independently; neither causes the other (Figure 11.2, second row). You see the snake, and your fear and your pounding heart arise together. The Cannon-Bard theory, too, turned out to be only partly right. Its anatomy was wrong in detail (the thalamus is a relay, not the seat of emotion), and the facial feedback and misattribution findings you are about to meet show that bodily states do influence feelings, which the theory denies. But Cannon's criticisms were valuable. They forced the next generation to ask how a single, rather general bodily arousal could give rise to many different emotions. The answer that came next was: through thinking. Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory In 1962 Stanley Schachter (1922 to 1997) and Jerome E. Singer (1934 to 2010) proposed a theory that took something from both sides. Like Cannon, they accepted that physiological arousal is much the same from one emotion to another. Like James, they accepted that arousal matters. Their two-factor theory of emotion (also called the cognitive labelling or cognitive arousal theory) says that an emotion requires two ingredients: physiological arousal , which determines how intense the emotion is, and a cognitive label , an explanation of the arousal drawn from the situation, which determines which emotion it is. When you notice that you are aroused, you look around for a reason; if the reason you find is a growling dog, the arousal becomes fear; if it is a person you like, the same arousal becomes attraction. Students sometimes remember it as the "jukebox" theory: arousal is the coin that makes the machine play, and the situation selects the song. Key study: Schachter and Singer's adrenaline experiment (1962) Question. If people are physiologically aroused but have no explanation for it, will they label the arousal according to the emotional cues around them? Method. Male university students were told the study tested the effects of a vitamin compound, "Suproxin", on vision. Most actually received an injection of adrenaline (epinephrine), which produces a racing heart, trembling hands and a flushed face; a placebo group received saline. The adrenaline groups were told different things: the informed group was correctly told what symptoms to expect; the ignorant group was told nothing; the misinformed group was told to expect irrelevant symptoms such as numb feet and itching. Each participant then waited with a stooge who was supposedly another participant. In the euphoria condition the stooge played paper basketball, flew paper aeroplanes and twirled a hula hoop; in the anger condition the stooge complained bitterly about an insulting questionnaire that both had to fill in (one item asked how many men, other than his father, the participant's mother had had extramarital affairs with) and finally tore it up and stormed out. Results. Participants who were aroused but had no correct explanation for their arousal (the ignorant and misinformed groups) caught the stooge's mood more: they behaved more euphorically and reported feeling happier in the euphoria condition, and acted angrier in the anger condition, than the informed participants, who could put their symptoms down to the injection. Conclusion. Unexplained arousal is labelled using situational cues. Criticisms. The effects were small and some were not statistically reliable; the placebo group did not differ as much from the adrenaline groups as the theory predicted; and later attempts to repeat the study, by Gary Marshall and Philip Zimbardo (1979) and by Christina Maslach (1979), found that unexplained arousal tended to be felt as unpleasant and anxious whatever the stooge did. A review by Rainer Reisenzein (1983) concluded that arousal can intensify emotions but that there is little evidence that it is necessary for them. Table 11.4 summarises the logic of the design. Table 11.4 The logic of Schachter and Singer's design. Group Injection Told about symptoms? Predicted to catch the stooge's emotion? Informed Adrenaline Yes, correctly Least: arousal already explained Ignorant Adrenaline No Most: arousal needs a label Misinformed Adrenaline Yes, wrongly Most (euphoria condition only) Placebo Saline No Little: no arousal to label Misattribution of arousal and excitation transfer If arousal is labelled from the situation, it can be labelled wrongly . Misattribution of arousal occurs when people mistake the true source of their physiological arousal and attribute it to something else that happens to be present. The Capilano bridge study of Donald G. Dutton and Arthur P. Aron (1974), described at the start of this chapter, is the classic demonstration: arousal produced by fear of the bridge was misattributed to attraction to the interviewer. A related experiment by Stuart Valins (1966) showed that even the belief that one is aroused can be enough. Men looked at photographs of women while hearing what they were told was their own heartbeat; when the false heartbeat sped up for certain photographs, the men later rated those women as more attractive. Dolf Zillmann , from the early 1970s onward, developed excitation transfer theory , which explains why arousal from one situation can spill over into the next. Physiological arousal dies away slowly, more slowly than our awareness of its cause. So for a while after one arousing event, residual arousal remains, and if a new emotional event occurs in that window, the leftover arousal is added to the new emotion and intensifies it. In Zillmann's experiments, people who had just pedalled hard on an exercise bicycle and were then provoked retaliated more aggressively than rested people, especially once enough time had passed that they no longer connected their arousal with the exercise. Everyday examples are easy to find: the near miss in traffic that makes you snap at the shopkeeper a few minutes later, or the post-match crowd that turns a minor argument into a fight. Excitation transfer is also the bridge between this chapter and the study of aggression in the Social book. Exam trap Match the theory to its sequence. Commonsense: stimulus, emotion, then arousal. James-Lange: stimulus, arousal, then emotion (the emotion is the perceived bodily change). Cannon-Bard: stimulus, then arousal and emotion simultaneously and independently , via the thalamus. Schachter-Singer: arousal plus a cognitive label. Lazarus: appraisal first (Section 11.3). An option such as "emotions and visceral reactions are simultaneous" describes Cannon-Bard, not James-Lange; "you feel the emotion and then the body responds" is the commonsense view that James rejected. Misattribution of arousal is explained by the two-factor theory , not by James-Lange, Cannon-Bard or facial feedback. What makes Schachter and Singer different from both earlier theories is that their theory includes cognition and arousal . "Two-factor theory" is a name with four owners. Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory of emotion (1962); Spearman's two-factor theory of intelligence (g and s, 1904; Chapter 9); Mowrer's two-factor theory of avoidance learning (classical plus operant conditioning; Chapter 6); and Herzberg's two-factor (motivation-hygiene) theory of job satisfaction (Chapter 10). Read the stem for the subject. Cannon-Bard named the thalamus as the relay; the hypothalamus came in through Bard's later work on sham rage. If an option says "the somatic nervous system is the seat of emotion", reject it: no classic theory says so. 11.3 Appraisal, feedback, evolution and opposing processes Lower yield · not asked yet Schachter and Singer brought thinking into the theory of emotion, but in their account thought arrives after arousal, to explain it. The next step was to ask whether thought comes first: whether we become aroused at all only because we have judged that something matters. Cognitive appraisal: Arnold and Lazarus The word appraisal was introduced into emotion theory by Magda B. Arnold (1903 to 2002) in her book Emotion and Personality (1960). Arnold defined appraisal as an immediate, intuitive evaluation of whether something is good or bad for me, and argued that this evaluation is what turns a perception into an emotion: the snake frightens you only once you have appraised it as dangerous. The idea was developed into the most influential cognitive theory of emotion and stress by the American psychologist Richard S. Lazarus (1922 to 2002), first in Psychological Stress and the Coping Process (1966) and later in Emotion and Adaptation (1991). According to Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory , emotions are produced by the way a person evaluates a situation in relation to his or her own goals and well-being. Lazarus distinguished two kinds of appraisal. In primary appraisal you ask, "Does this matter to me, and how?" The answer may be that the event is irrelevant, that it is benign or positive, or that it is stressful; and a stressful event may be appraised as harm or loss (damage already done), threat (harm expected in the future) or challenge (an opportunity to gain or grow). In secondary appraisal you ask, "What can I do about it?": you evaluate your resources and options for coping. Because situations and resources change, appraisal is continually revised; Lazarus called this reappraisal . The specific emotion depends on the pattern of appraisal. Lazarus summed up each emotion as a "core relational theme": anger is the appraisal of a demeaning offence against me and mine; anxiety is facing an uncertain, existential threat; guilt is having broken a moral rule; sadness is having suffered an irrevocable loss. Because the appraisal stands between the stimulus and the response, Lazarus's account is often called the cognitive-mediational theory of emotion: stimulus, then appraisal, then emotion together with its bodily arousal (Figure 11.2, bottom row). The same theory reappears, with only small changes, as Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model of stress in Section 11.9, which is why the terms primary and secondary appraisal are examined under both emotion and stress. Key study: the subincision film (Speisman, Lazarus and colleagues, 1964) Question. Can changing how people appraise an event change their emotional and bodily response to it? Method. Joseph Speisman, Lazarus and their colleagues showed participants a distressing anthropological film of a painful initiation rite (subincision of the penis) performed on adolescent boys in an Aboriginal Australian community, while recording skin conductance and heart rate. The film was shown with one of four soundtracks: a trauma track that emphasised the pain and mutilation; a denial track that described the boys as willing and the occasion as happy; an intellectualisation track that took a detached, anthropological view; or no soundtrack. Results. Physiological arousal was highest with the trauma track and lowest with the denial and intellectualisation tracks. Conclusion. The same images produced different emotional responses depending on how viewers were led to appraise them. This is the experimental heart of appraisal theory, and it is also the ancestor of the "reappraisal" strategy of emotion regulation (Section 11.7). Does feeling need thinking? The Lazarus-Zajonc debate Not everyone accepted that appraisal must come first. In 1980 the social psychologist Robert B. Zajonc (1923 to 2008) published a paper with the provocative title "Feeling and thinking: Preferences need no inferences." Zajonc argued for affective primacy : affective reactions can occur before, and independently of, any cognitive processing, and are sometimes faster than it. His main evidence came from the mere exposure effect , which he had described in 1968: simply being exposed to a stimulus repeatedly makes people like it more, whether it is a nonsense word, a Chinese character or a face. In a striking version, William Kunst-Wilson and Zajonc (1980) flashed irregular octagons so briefly that participants later could not recognise them better than chance; yet when asked which of two shapes they liked , they chose the previously seen one about 60 percent of the time. Liking had formed without recognition. Lazarus replied in 1982 and again in 1984 ("On the primacy of cognition"), and Zajonc answered in the same year ("On the primacy of affect"), both in the journal American Psychologist . Much of the disagreement turned out to be about definitions. Lazarus insisted that appraisal need not be conscious or deliberate; a fast, automatic evaluation counts as cognition. Zajonc meant by cognition something closer to conscious, deliberate processing. Joseph LeDoux's discovery of a fast subcortical route to the amygdala (Section 11.4) later gave both sides something: there is indeed a rapid emotional evaluation that bypasses the cortex, but it is itself a form of information processing. The modern consensus is that some emotional reactions are quick and automatic while others depend on slower, more elaborate thought. The facial feedback hypothesis Is there anything in the old advice to "put on a happy face"? Charles Darwin thought so, writing in 1872 that "the free expression by outward signs of an emotion intensifies it," while suppressing the outward signs softens it. Tomkins later made the face the centre of his theory of affect, and Izard developed the idea further. The facial feedback hypothesis states that feedback from our own facial expressions influences our emotional experience. In its strong form, the face is necessary to produce emotion; in its weak form, which is the version with evidence behind it, facial expression modulates (strengthens or weakens) emotions that are already under way. You can see that this is a modern descendant of the James-Lange theory, with the face taking the place of the viscera. The best-known test came from Fritz Strack , Leonard Martin and Sabine Stepper (1988). To prevent participants from realising that their faces were being manipulated, they were told the study concerned how people with disabilities might write by holding a pen in the mouth. Some held the pen between their teeth, which forces the muscles of a smile; others held it with their lips, which makes smiling impossible and produces something closer to a pout. Those holding the pen in their teeth rated cartoons as funnier. Other studies found similar effects: people who are made to frown while viewing slides report more anger, and people who hold a smile report more happiness. The story has a modern twist that examiners at postgraduate level increasingly expect you to know. In 2016 a large, pre-registered replication of the pen study, run in 17 laboratories, found no effect at all. Later work suggested that the effect may depend on details such as whether participants know they are being video-recorded, and a 2019 meta-analysis of many facial feedback studies concluded that the effect is real but small. The fair summary is that facial feedback can nudge emotions but is not a powerful cause of them. Clinical link If frowning feeds sadness, could stopping people from frowning help depression? Several small randomised trials have injected botulinum toxin into the frown muscles between the eyebrows of patients with depression and found improvements in mood compared with placebo injections. The results are intriguing but preliminary. The same logic underlies simpler techniques: a therapist may coach a socially anxious client to adopt an open posture and a relaxed face, on the reasoning that expression and feeling influence each other in both directions. The evolutionary view: Darwin's legacy The first major work on the science of emotion was not by a psychologist at all. In 1872 Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) published The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals , in which he argued that emotional expressions are products of evolution, shared across human cultures and continuous with those of other animals. A snarling dog and a sneering man both bare the teeth. To explain expressions, Darwin proposed three principles. The principle of serviceable associated habits holds that expressions began as useful actions: the raised upper lip of disgust and the narrowed nostrils once helped reject a bad smell or taste. The principle of antithesis holds that opposite emotional states are signalled by opposite postures: a dog threatening attack stands tall with ears forward, hair and tail raised, whereas a submissive dog crouches with ears back and tail down, so that the signals cannot be confused. The principle of the direct action of the nervous system holds that some expressions, such as trembling with fear, are simply overflows of nervous excitation. The evolutionary view of emotion that grew from Darwin's book treats emotions as adaptations: packages of physiology, expression and action that solved recurring survival problems. Fear prepares escape from predators, disgust protects against contamination and disease, anger mobilises the defence of resources, and expressions communicate our state to others so that they can respond. Plutchik's psychoevolutionary theory (Table 11.3) and Ekman's work on universal expressions (Section 11.5) are both direct descendants of Darwin's approach. Opponent-process theory: why pleasures fade and pains turn sweet Why does a first-time parachutist feel terror before the jump and an elated high afterwards, while a veteran parachutist feels only mild tension before and a long glow of exhilaration after? Richard L. Solomon (1918 to 1995) and John D. Corbit answered with the opponent-process theory of emotion and acquired motivation (1974). They proposed that any strong emotional reaction (the a-process ) automatically triggers an opposing reaction (the b-process ) that restores emotional balance. The a-process is quick and closely tied to the stimulus. The b-process is sluggish: it starts late, builds slowly and outlasts the stimulus, so when the stimulus ends we are left with an after-reaction opposite to the original emotion. Crucially, the b-process grows stronger with repeated exposure, while the a-process stays the same. This simple machinery explains a great deal. With repetition the strengthened b-process cancels more of the a-process, so the initial reaction weakens (the drug user's high fades, a sign of tolerance), while the after-reaction grows (the drug user's craving and misery when the drug wears off, a sign of withdrawal). For painful experiences the pattern is reversed: the fear of the parachute jump weakens with practice, and the pleasant after-reaction, relief and exhilaration, grows until it becomes the reason for jumping. Solomon used the same idea to explain why separation from a loved one becomes more painful as a relationship matures. Note that this is a different theory from Ewald Hering's opponent-process theory of colour vision (Chapter 3); only the name is shared. This section gives you the essentials; the full anatomy is in the Physiological book. The autonomic nervous system The bodily side of emotion is run mainly by the autonomic nervous system (ANS), the part of the peripheral nervous system that controls the heart, blood vessels, glands and internal organs without our deliberate control. It has two divisions that usually work in opposition. The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for action: it is the "fight or flight" division, most active in fear, anger and excitement. The parasympathetic nervous system conserves and restores energy: it is the "rest and digest" division, dominant when you are calm and after a meal. Table 11.5 lists the main effects. When the sympathetic system activates the sweat glands, even slightly, the skin conducts electricity better. This change is called the galvanic skin response (GSR), now usually called electrodermal activity or skin conductance response: skin resistance falls and skin conductance rises. It is one of the most sensitive measures of emotional arousal available. Where are the bodily responses actually controlled? The vital, involuntary functions of heartbeat, blood pressure and breathing are paced by centres in the medulla oblongata , the lowest part of the brainstem, which belongs to the hindbrain together with the pons and cerebellum. The hypothalamus, higher up, acts as the head ganglion of the ANS: during emotion it sends commands down to these brainstem centres and to the spinal cord. So the hindbrain carries out the adjustments and the hypothalamus orchestrates them. The hypothalamus and sham rage In the late 1920s Philip Bard, Cannon's student, removed the cerebral cortex of cats. The decorticate cats reacted to the slightest touch with a full display of rage: arched back, erect hair, hissing, bared teeth, lashing tail and dilated pupils. But the rage was oddly empty. It was out of all proportion to the provocation, it was not directed at the source of the touch, and it stopped the moment the stimulus stopped. Bard called it sham rage . Sham rage could still be produced when the brain was removed down to, but not including, the hypothalamus; once the hypothalamus was also removed, it disappeared. Bard concluded that the hypothalamus organises the expression of rage, and that a normal function of the cortex is to inhibit and direct it. At about the same time, in Zurich, the Swiss physiologist Walter Rudolf Hess (1881 to 1973) implanted electrodes in the hypothalamus of freely moving cats and found that stimulating certain points produced an attack-like defensive reaction, with hissing, raised hair and dilated pupils, while other points produced calm and sleepiness. Hess shared the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this mapping of the brain's control of the internal organs. The Papez circuit and the limbic system Where, then, does the experience of emotion arise? In 1937 the American neuroanatomist James Papez (1883 to 1958; pronounced "payps") proposed that emotion depends on a loop of interconnected structures on the inner surface of the brain. The Papez circuit runs from the hippocampus through the fornix to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus, then by the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior nuclei of the thalamus, then to the cingulate gyrus (cingulate cortex), and back through the parahippocampal region (entorhinal cortex) to the hippocampus. Papez suggested that emotional expression depends on this circuit's action on the hypothalamus, and emotional experience on its action on the cortex. The French surgeon Paul Broca (1824 to 1880) had already, in 1878, named the ring of cortex bordering the brainstem the "great limbic lobe" (from the Latin limbus , border). In 1949 the American physician Paul D. MacLean (1913 to 2007) called these structures the "visceral brain", and in 1952 he renamed them the limbic system , enlarging Papez's circuit by adding the amygdala, septum, hypothalamus and parts of the prefrontal cortex. MacLean's limbic system theory, which made the limbic system "the seat of emotion", became the textbook view for half a century. MacLean later placed it within his triune brain theory, in which the human brain contains three layers laid down in evolution: a reptilian complex (basal ganglia and brainstem) for instinctive routines, a paleomammalian brain (the limbic system) for emotion, and a neomammalian brain (the neocortex) for reason. Two corrections are needed. First, the Papez circuit is now known to matter more for memory than for emotion: damage to the hippocampus, fornix or mammillary bodies (as in Korsakoff's syndrome) produces amnesia rather than emotional change. Second, the triune brain is an outdated evolutionary story; brains did not evolve by adding new layers on top of old ones, and the limbic system is not a sharply bounded unit. But the core point survives: structures such as the amygdala, hypothalamus and cingulate cortex are central to emotion, motivation and emotional memory. The amygdala: Klüver-Bucy syndrome and emotional memory In 1937, and in full in 1939, the psychologist Heinrich Klüver (1897 to 1979) and the neurosurgeon Paul Bucy (1904 to 1992) described a remarkable change in rhesus monkeys after they removed both anterior temporal lobes. (Klüver had been studying the hallucinogen mescaline, and the surgery began as a test of whether the temporal lobes were involved in its effects.) Monkeys that had been wild and aggressive became tame and placid. They showed no fear of humans or of snakes, which normal monkeys find terrifying. They examined every object by putting it in their mouths, ate things they would normally reject, including meat and inedible objects, attended compulsively to every object in view, and directed sexual behaviour at inappropriate partners and objects. Although they could see, they seemed not to recognise what objects were or meant. This pattern is now called Klüver-Bucy syndrome . Its features are best remembered as a list: psychic blindness or visual agnosia (seeing without recognising); hyperorality (examining things by mouth); hypermetamorphosis (a compulsion to attend to and touch every visual stimulus); dietary change and hyperphagia (overeating, eating inedible things); hypersexuality ; and placidity , that is, loss of fear and anger. Later lesion studies traced the emotional part of the syndrome, the taming and loss of fear, to bilateral damage to the amygdala , an almond-shaped cluster of nuclei deep in each temporal lobe. In humans the syndrome is rare; it follows bilateral temporal damage from herpes simplex encephalitis, head injury or some dementias, and because the surrounding temporal cortex is usually damaged too, human patients often also show amnesia and aphasia (difficulty understanding or producing language). Human cases make the amygdala's role in fear vivid. A woman known as S.M., whose amygdalae were destroyed on both sides by a rare genetic disorder (Urbach-Wiethe disease), cannot recognise fear in other people's faces, and when researchers at the University of Iowa took her to an exotic pet shop and a "haunted house" she showed curiosity but no fear at all. The amygdala is also the brain's tool for making emotional events memorable. When something arousing happens, stress hormones (adrenaline and cortisol) and the amygdala's own activity strengthen the consolidation of the memory by the hippocampus. In one well-known experiment by Larry Cahill , James L. McGaugh and colleagues (1994), people heard either an emotional or a neutral version of a story; the emotional version was remembered better, unless participants had taken propranolol, a drug that blocks noradrenaline receptors, in which case the memory advantage disappeared. This emotional modulation of memory explains why you remember the day of a frightening accident in vivid detail (and why "flashbulb memories", Chapter 7, feel so clear). Key study: a double dissociation of emotional and factual memory (Bechara and colleagues, 1995) Antoine Bechara, Antonio Damasio and their colleagues gave a fear-conditioning task to three patients: S.M., with bilateral amygdala damage; a patient with bilateral hippocampal damage; and a patient with damage to both. A coloured slide (the conditioned stimulus) was paired with a loud, startling boat horn, and the skin conductance response was recorded. S.M. never developed a conditioned skin conductance response to the slide, yet she could tell the researchers exactly which colour had been followed by the horn. The hippocampal patient showed the opposite: a normal conditioned skin conductance response, but no conscious memory of which colour went with the horn. The patient with both lesions showed neither. The amygdala is needed for emotional (conditioned) memory, the hippocampus for declarative memory of the facts. LeDoux's two roads to fear How does the amygdala get its information so quickly? Joseph LeDoux (born 1949), working with rats in auditory fear conditioning (a tone paired with a mild shock), traced the pathways in detail and described them for a general audience in The Emotional Brain (1996). Sounds reach the auditory part of the thalamus (the medial geniculate nucleus). LeDoux found that lesions of the auditory thalamus or of the amygdala blocked fear conditioning to a tone, but lesions of the auditory cortex did not. The reason is that information travels from the thalamus to the amygdala by two routes. The low road runs directly from the sensory thalamus to the amygdala. It is fast (in rats, a matter of milliseconds) but crude, "quick and dirty" in LeDoux's phrase: it can tell that something is sudden or snake-like, but not what it is. The high road runs from the thalamus to the sensory cortex and only then to the amygdala. It is slower but detailed, able to identify the object and its context (Figure 11.3). The amygdala then triggers the fear response through its outputs: to the periaqueductal grey of the midbrain for freezing, to the lateral hypothalamus for sympathetic arousal, and to the paraventricular hypothalamus for the stress hormone response. High road: slower, detailed Sensory cortex Stimulus Sensory thalamus Amygdala Fear responses freeze, pulse up Low road: fast, crude The low road can trigger fear before the cortex identifies the object Figure 11.3 LeDoux's two routes to fear. Signals from the sensory thalamus reach the amygdala directly by the fast, crude low road (solid line) and indirectly through the sensory cortex by the slower, detailed high road (broken lines). On a forest path, the low road makes you freeze at a curved shape; a fraction of a second later the high road tells you whether it is a snake or a stick. The two-road model explains a familiar experience. Walking through a forest you freeze at a long, curved shape on the path, and only a moment later realise it is a stick. The freezing came from the low road; the correction came from the high road. It also explains why phobias and traumatic fears can be so resistant to reasoning: the subcortical route can trigger fear without consulting the cortex, which "knows" that the spider is harmless. A striking related phenomenon is affective blindsight . Beatrice de Gelder and colleagues (1999) studied a patient, G.Y., whose primary visual cortex was damaged on one side, leaving him consciously blind in half of his visual field. When happy, sad, angry or fearful faces were presented in the blind half, he could still guess their emotional expression well above chance, presumably through subcortical routes to the amygdala, although he reported seeing nothing. The prefrontal cortex and the two hemispheres The amygdala raises the alarm; the prefrontal cortex helps decide what to do about it. The classic case is that of Phineas Gage (1823 to 1860), a responsible and well-liked railway construction foreman in Vermont who, in 1848, was tamping explosive into a rock with an iron rod about a metre long when the charge exploded and drove the rod up through his left cheek and out of the top of his skull. Gage survived and kept his intelligence, but he became impulsive, profane and unreliable, so much so that his friends said he was "no longer Gage," as his physician John Martyn Harlow reported in 1868. A computer reconstruction of his skull in 1994 by Hanna Damasio and colleagues placed the damage in the medial (ventromedial) prefrontal cortex of both hemispheres. Antonio Damasio (born 1944) studied modern patients with similar damage, such as a man he called Elliot, whose reasoning and IQ were intact but whose personal and financial decisions became disastrous. In Descartes' Error (1994), Damasio proposed the somatic marker hypothesis : through experience, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex attaches bodily feelings ("somatic markers", a gut feeling of unease) to the likely outcomes of choices, and these markers steer decisions quickly, often before we can say why. In the Iowa Gambling Task, normal participants begin to show skin conductance responses before choosing from risky card decks, and soon avoid them; patients with ventromedial damage show no such anticipatory responses and keep choosing the risky decks. Emotion, on this view, is not the enemy of good decisions but a necessary part of them. The two cerebral hemispheres also differ in emotion. The older right-hemisphere hypothesis held that the right hemisphere is specialised for all emotion; the valence hypothesis holds that the right hemisphere is specialised for negative emotions and the left for positive ones. Richard Davidson's EEG studies support a related approach-withdrawal model: greater left frontal activity accompanies approach-related, mostly positive emotion, and greater right frontal activity accompanies withdrawal-related, mostly negative emotion, and people prone to depression tend to show relatively low left frontal activity. Facial expressions are usually stronger on the left side of the face, which is controlled mainly by the right hemisphere. Clinical link Emotional expression and emotional experience can come apart after brain damage. In pseudobulbar affect (pathological laughing and crying), patients with stroke, multiple sclerosis, motor neurone disease (ALS) or traumatic brain injury have sudden, brief, uncontrollable outbursts of crying or laughing that do not match how they actually feel. Damage to the pathways by which the cortex normally controls the brainstem's emotional-motor centres "releases" the expression from the feeling, much as in Bard's decorticate cats. It is not depression, and it should not be mistaken for it. Table 11.6 gathers the brain structures of this section, with the evidence to remember for each.
