Shelley E. Taylor (born 1946) and her colleagues at the University of California, Los Angeles, pointed out in 2000 that until the mid-1990s women had made up only about 17 percent, fewer than one in five, of the participants in laboratory studies of the physiological stress response. Looking at the evidence from animals and humans with both sexes in mind, they proposed that females, in particular, often respond to stress with a pattern they called tend-and-befriend . Tending means protecting and calming offspring; befriending means seeking out and maintaining social networks that offer protection and support. The evolutionary logic is that a pregnant or nursing female who fights or flees puts her young at risk, whereas one who shields them and gathers allies protects both. The proposed biology centres on the hormone oxytocin, whose effects are enhanced by oestrogen, together with the brain's own opioids, which promote affiliation and calm. Taylor did not claim that women never fight or flee, or that men never seek company; tend-and-befriend is a difference of emphasis that sits on top of the shared fight-or-flight machinery. It also explains part of the protective power of social support, discussed in Section 11.10. Exam trap The order of the GAS is alarm, resistance, exhaustion. "Illness" is not a stage (illness is what exhaustion leads to), and resistance never comes first. Alarm, resistance and exhaustion belong to Selye's general adaptation syndrome , not to life events theory, the health belief model or protection motivation theory (Section 11.10). Match the person to the idea. Cannon: fight or flight (1915) and homeostasis (1926). Selye: general adaptation syndrome (1936; The Stress of Life , 1956) and eustress versus distress (1974). Taylor: tend-and-befriend (2000). McEwen: allostatic load. Cortex versus medulla. Cortisol comes from the adrenal cortex (HPA axis); adrenaline and noradrenaline come from the adrenal medulla (SAM axis). Asked which gland is primarily responsible for the stress response, answer the adrenal glands . The pituitary is the "master gland" and releases ACTH, but it is not the stress gland. Distractor hormones: insulin (pancreas, lowers blood sugar), thyroxine (thyroid, sets metabolic rate), melatonin (pineal, signals darkness and sleep). The HPA sequence is hypothalamus (CRH), then anterior pituitary (ACTH), then adrenal cortex (cortisol); cortisol's negative feedback acts mainly on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and vasopressin and is not part of the HPA axis. Eustress is good stress, not zero stress. 11.9 Sources of stress and the transactional model High yield · 8 Qs What kinds of events cause stress? Researchers have tried three ways of answering: counting the big events in a person's life, counting the small ones, and sorting stressors by how long they last and how many people they strike. Each approach found something real, and each ran into the same awkward fact: the same event affects different people very differently. That fact leads to the transactional model at the end of this section. Life events: Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale In the 1950s and 1960s the psychiatrists Thomas H. Holmes and Richard H. Rahe , at the University of Washington School of Medicine in Seattle, noticed in their patients' case histories that illnesses seemed to follow clusters of major changes in their lives. (The idea of charting a patient's life events alongside the course of illness went back to the psychiatrist Adolf Meyer's "life chart".) In 1967 they published a way of measuring such change. They gave 394 people a list of 43 life events and asked them to rate how much readjustment each one required, compared with marriage, which was arbitrarily given a value of 500. The average ratings, divided by 10, became life change units (LCUs), ranging from 100 for the death of a spouse to 11 for minor violations of the law. The resulting instrument is the Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS). A respondent ticks the events experienced in the past year and adds up their life change units (Table 11.8). Table 11.8 Selected items from Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (1967). Rank Life event Life change units 1 Death of a spouse 100 2 Divorce 73 3 Marital separation 65 4 Jail term 63 5 Death of a close family member 63 6 Personal injury or illness 53 7 Marriage (the anchor event) 50 8 Fired at work 47 10 Retirement 45 12 Pregnancy 40 17 Death of a close friend 37 25 Outstanding personal achievement 28 27 Beginning or ending school 26 32 Change in residence 20 41 Vacation 13 42 Christmas 12 43 Minor violations of the law 11 Look down the list and something stands out. Marriage, pregnancy, outstanding personal achievement, a vacation and Christmas are all there, alongside death and divorce. For Holmes and Rahe the stressor was change itself , whether welcome or not, because any change requires readjustment. This is the stimulus definition of stress in its purest form. In their research, people whose scores totalled more than about 300 in a year were classed as facing a major life crisis and were considerably more likely to fall ill in the following year; scores of 150 to 299 carried a moderate risk. In prospective studies, Rahe gave the scale to US Navy sailors before long tours of duty and found that those with higher life-change scores reported somewhat more illness while at sea. The SRRS was a landmark because it made stress countable, and thousands of studies used it. But it has serious weaknesses, and examiners like them: It lumps good and bad events together. Later research found that it is undesirable, uncontrollable change that predicts illness. The Life Experiences Survey of Irwin Sarason, James Johnson and Judith Siegel (1978) let respondents rate each event as positive or negative and how much it affected them; negative change predicted problems, positive change did not. It ignores meaning and appraisal. A divorce is a catastrophe for one person and a release for another, yet both score 73. It ignores resources and coping , such as social support, which change the impact of the same event. It relies on memory. Recall of events over a year is unreliable, and people who are ill may search their memories harder for causes. Some items are confounded with illness. "Personal injury or illness", "change in sleeping habits" and "change in eating habits" may be early signs or results of illness rather than causes of it. It is culture-bound. Christmas and mortgages of over 10,000 dollars reflect American life in the 1960s. The correlations are small. Most people with high scores do not become ill, so the scale is a weak predictor for any individual. Indian context An American list of life events fits Indian lives imperfectly: few Indian respondents would rate Christmas or a large mortgage as typical stressors, while events such as arranging a daughter's marriage, a family dispute over property or a failed examination may weigh more heavily. In 1984 Gurmeet Singh, Dalbir Kaur and Harsharan Kaur published the Presumptive Stressful Life Events Scale (PSLES), a 51-item life-events scale developed with Indian respondents, in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry . It remains one of the most widely used life-events measures in Indian clinical research. Daily hassles and uplifts Richard Lazarus thought that major life events were the wrong unit of stress. On most days nobody dies, marries or is sacked. But the bus is late, the phone battery dies in the middle of a call, the neighbour's dog barks all night and there are three assignments due on Friday. In 1981 Allen D. Kanner , James C. Coyne, Catherine Schaefer and Lazarus defined daily hassles as the irritating, frustrating and distressing demands that to some degree characterise everyday transactions with the environment, and uplifts as the positive experiences that can offset them, such as relating well with friends, completing a task, getting enough sleep or receiving good news. They built a 117-item Hassles Scale and a 135-item Uplifts Scale and had a group of 100 middle-aged adults complete them every month for most of a year. The most frequent hassles were concerns about weight, the health of a family member, rising prices of common goods, home maintenance, having too many things to do, and misplacing or losing things. The key finding was that hassles predicted psychological symptoms, such as anxiety and depression, better than life-event scores did, and they went on predicting symptoms even when life events were statistically controlled. Later work by Anita DeLongis, Coyne, Lazarus and their colleagues (1982) found that hassles also predicted physical health better than major events. Part of the reason is that big events act partly through small ones: a divorce brings a hundred daily hassles about money, housing and children. Uplifts had weaker and less consistent effects than hassles; the bad, it seems, is stronger than the good. Acute, chronic and cataclysmic stressors Stressors can also be sorted by how long they last. An acute stressor is short-lived, with a clear beginning and end: a surprise test (a "pop quiz"), a job interview, a near miss on the highway. A chronic stressor persists for months or years, often with no foreseeable end: living with HIV disease or cancer, a long-running marital conflict, caring for a parent with dementia, poverty, unemployment or discrimination. The body handles acute stressors well; as Section 11.8 showed, it is chronic stress that produces allostatic load and Selye's exhaustion, and Section 11.10 shows that the two kinds even have opposite effects on immunity. Stressors can be sorted, too, by how many people they strike. Lazarus and Cohen (1977) distinguished three categories. Cataclysmic events are sudden, powerful catastrophes that affect many people at once: earthquakes, floods, wars, terrorist attacks and pandemics, such as the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami on the Tamil Nadu coast or the Kedarnath floods of 2013. Because the suffering is shared, survivors can support one another, and for many people the stress subsides over time, although some develop lasting problems. Personal stressors are major life events, such as bereavement, divorce or job loss, that strike one person or family. Background stressors are the daily hassles of the previous subsection. When a stressor is extreme, involving actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, some of those exposed develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). ICD-11 places PTSD in a group of disorders specifically associated with stress , together with complex PTSD, prolonged grief disorder and adjustment disorder, whose diagnosis requires an identifiable stressor; generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder do not. (The disorders themselves are covered in the Disorders book.) Frustration, conflict, pressure and change Many textbooks, following Wayne Weiten, group the psychological sources of stress into four types: frustration, conflict, change and pressure. You studied the first and second in Chapter 10 (Section 10.8), so a short reminder is enough here. Frustration is the blocking of goal-directed behaviour. Conflict is the simultaneous presence of incompatible motives. Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947) described three basic types in 1935: approach-approach (two attractive goals, such as two good colleges; the mildest and quickest to resolve), avoidance-avoidance (two unattractive options, such as a painful dental visit or a worsening toothache; the person vacillates and tries to "leave the field") and approach-avoidance (one goal with both attractive and repellent features, such as a well-paid job far from home). Later writers added the double approach-avoidance conflict, two goals each with good and bad features, which is the shape of most real-life decisions. Neal E. Miller (1909 to 2002) showed that the avoidance gradient is steeper than the approach gradient, which is why people in approach-avoidance conflicts move towards the goal and then retreat as they near it (Figure 10.6). Approach-avoidance and avoidance-avoidance conflicts are the most stressful; approach-approach conflicts the least. Change is the life-event stress measured by Holmes and Rahe. Pressure is the expectation or demand that one behave in a certain way: pressure to perform (a call-centre worker who must handle a quota of calls at high speed) and pressure to conform (a young adult expected to choose the career or marriage the family has in mind). Stress at work and burnout For most adults the workplace is a major source of stress, and organisational psychologists have catalogued its sources. A widely used scheme from Stephen Robbins's textbook of organisational behaviour sorts potential stressors into three groups. Environmental factors lie outside the organisation: economic uncertainty, political uncertainty and technological change. Organisational factors lie within the job and the organisation: task demands (workload, pace, working conditions, the design of the job), role demands , interpersonal demands (poor relationships with colleagues, lack of support), the structure of the organisation and its style of leadership. Individual factors are those the employee brings from personal life: family problems, economic problems such as debt, and personality. Role demands deserve a closer look. In Organizational Stress (1964), Robert Kahn and his colleagues described role conflict , the presence of incompatible expectations (a supervisor told to cut costs and also to improve service, or a working mother pulled between office and home), and role ambiguity , uncertainty about what one is expected to do, how one's work will be judged or where one's authority ends. To these is added role overload , simply having too much to do. In 1979 Robert A. Karasek proposed the job demand-control model : strain is greatest not in jobs with the heaviest demands but in jobs that combine high demands with low control (little decision latitude). The assembly-line worker, the call-centre agent with a scripted screen and the waiter at a busy restaurant are in "high-strain" jobs; the busy senior executive, who can decide how and when to work, often is not. Jeffrey Johnson and Ellen Hall (1988) later added social support as a third dimension: isolated high-strain jobs are the worst of all. When work stress becomes chronic, the result may be burnout . The term was introduced in 1974 by the psychologist Herbert J. Freudenberger (1926 to 1999), who saw it in himself and in fellow volunteers at a free clinic in New York. Christina Maslach (born 1946), whose research on human-service workers made the concept scientific, and Susan Jackson published the Maslach Burnout Inventory in 1981. It measures three dimensions: emotional exhaustion (feeling drained and used up), depersonalisation (a cynical, detached, even callous attitude towards the people one serves) and reduced personal accomplishment (feeling ineffective). Burnout is most common in the helping professions: nursing, medicine, teaching, social work, policing and counselling, where the emotional labour of Section 11.5 is part of the job. In ICD-11 (2019) the World Health Organisation describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon , not a medical condition, resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, and characterised by exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about one's job, and reduced professional efficacy. Clinical link Clinical psychologists are themselves at high risk of burnout. They spend their working days absorbing other people's distress, often with heavy caseloads and little control over the system they work in, which is Karasek's high-strain recipe. The protections are those this chapter describes: regular supervision and peer support (social support), realistic caseloads and some control over one's schedule (control), and deliberate attention to sleep, exercise and life outside work. Training programmes increasingly treat self-care as a professional skill rather than a luxury. Control and predictability Why do some stressors do so much more damage than others of the same physical size? A series of animal experiments gave an answer that has run through stress research ever since. Key study: executive monkeys and helpless rats (Brady, 1958; Weiss, 1971) In 1958 Joseph V. Brady reported a famous experiment on "executive" monkeys. Pairs of monkeys received electric shocks; the "executive" in each pair could prevent shocks for both of them by pressing a lever at regular intervals, while its yoked partner could do nothing. The executives developed stomach ulcers, and some died; the yoked monkeys did not. The study was taken as proof that the burden of responsibility causes ulcers. But the executives had not been chosen at random: they were the monkeys that had learned the avoidance task fastest in a pretest, and these were probably the most emotionally reactive animals. In 1971 Jay M. Weiss repeated the logic with proper controls, using rats in triads. One rat could avoid or turn off a shock by turning a wheel; a yoked rat received exactly the same shocks but had no control; a third rat received no shocks. The results reversed Brady's: the rats with control developed far fewer stomach ulcers than the helpless yoked rats. Weiss also found that rats that heard a warning tone before each shock developed fewer ulcers than rats shocked without warning. Conclusion. The same physical stressor does less damage when it is controllable and predictable . This is the same lesson as Seligman's learned helplessness experiments (Chapter 6). Human research tells the same story. In the experiments David Glass and Jerome Singer (the same Singer as the two-factor theory) reported in Urban Stress (1972), people exposed to loud, unpredictable bursts of noise afterwards gave up sooner on insoluble puzzles and made more proofreading errors than people exposed to the same noise at predictable intervals. When participants were told they could stop the noise by pressing a button, the after-effects shrank, even though hardly anyone pressed it. Simply believing that one has control helped. In a field study, Ellen Langer and Judith Rodin (1976) gave residents on one floor of a nursing home small choices about their daily lives and a plant to look after; compared with residents on another floor whose lives were managed for them, they became more active and happier, and 18 months later fewer of them had died. Perceived control is a thread you will see again in secondary appraisal, hardiness and self-efficacy. Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model Every finding in this section points the same way. Life events matter less than how they are taken; hassles matter because of how they accumulate in a particular life; control and predictability change the impact of identical shocks. Richard Lazarus drew the conclusion in his appraisal theory of emotion (Section 11.3) and, with Susan Folkman , built it into a full theory of stress in Stress, Appraisal, and Coping (1984). Their transactional model of stress defines psychological stress as "a particular relationship between the person and the environment that is appraised by the person as taxing or exceeding his or her resources and endangering his or her well-being." Stress is a transaction : it exists only in the meeting of a particular person with a particular situation. The model runs through a sequence of appraisals (Figure 11.6). In primary appraisal the person asks, "Is this relevant to my well-being, and how?" The event may be judged irrelevant , benign-positive or stressful , and a stressful event may be appraised as harm or loss (damage already done), threat (harm anticipated) or challenge (an opportunity for gain or growth, which brings eagerness rather than dread). In secondary appraisal the person asks, "What can I do about it?", evaluating his or her coping options and resources: physical (health and energy), social (people who can help), psychological (skills, beliefs, self-efficacy) and material (money, time). Stress is greatest when the demands appraised in primary appraisal seem to outweigh the resources appraised in secondary appraisal. The person then copes (Section 11.10), and the results of coping, together with any new information, feed back into reappraisal , so that the whole transaction keeps changing. Stress arises when demands are appraised as exceeding resources Potential stressor an exam, a quarrel Primary appraisal Does it matter? harm, threat, challenge Secondary appraisal Can I cope? my resources Coping problem-focused or emotion-focused Outcome stress eases or persists; health, morale Reappraisal the results of coping and new information change how the situation is appraised Figure 11.6 Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model of stress (1984). A potential stressor becomes stressful only through primary appraisal (is it harm, threat or challenge?) and secondary appraisal (can I cope?). Coping follows, and its outcome feeds back through reappraisal (the line returning along the bottom). "Primary" and "secondary" name the questions asked, not a fixed order in time. Push two people through the model and its power becomes clear. On the morning of the entrance examination, Ananya and Kiran sit in the same Mysuru hall with the same question paper. Ananya's primary appraisal is threat : "If I fail, my parents will be humiliated and my year is wasted." Her secondary appraisal is bleak: "I never finished revising developmental psychology, and nobody can help me now." Demands far exceed resources, and she is shaking before the first question. Kiran's primary appraisal is challenge : "This matters, but it is my chance to show what I know." His secondary appraisal is reassuring: "I have practised twenty past papers, I know my weak areas, and there is another attempt next year if I need it." He feels keyed up but focused, which is Selye's eustress. Then Ananya reads the first five questions and finds she knows every answer. Her reappraisal ("Maybe I am better prepared than I feared") lowers her stress, and she settles. Same stressor, different transactions, different stress. Later research by Jim Blascovich and his colleagues has shown that challenge and threat appraisals even produce different cardiovascular patterns: in challenge the heart pumps more blood and the blood vessels relax, in threat the vessels constrict. Two features of the model are often misunderstood. First, "primary" and "secondary" do not mean first and second in time, or more and less important; the two appraisals interact continuously, and a good secondary appraisal ("I can handle this") can turn a threat into a challenge. Second, appraisals need not be slow or conscious. As Lazarus argued in his debate with Zajonc (Section 11.3), an appraisal can be an instant, automatic evaluation. Stress meets vulnerability: the diathesis-stress model The transactional model explains why the same event is stressful for one person and not another. A related idea explains why the same amount of stress makes one person ill and leaves another well. The diathesis-stress model holds that psychological disorders develop when a diathesis (from the Greek for "disposition"), a pre-existing vulnerability, is triggered by stress . The diathesis may be genetic or biological (a family history of depression, an overreactive HPA axis), psychological (a negative way of thinking about oneself) or the result of early experience (childhood maltreatment). Neither ingredient is usually enough on its own: a person with a strong vulnerability may stay well in a protected life, and a person with little vulnerability may weather severe stress. The two trade off: the larger the diathesis, the less stress is needed to trigger a disorder. The idea was set out for schizophrenia by Paul E. Meehl (1920 to 2003) in 1962 and developed by Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring as the vulnerability-stress model in 1977; it is now applied to depression, anxiety disorders, PTSD and much else. The diathesis-stress model is often set against single-cause models of abnormality, which examiners use as distractors. The biological model locates disorders in genes and brain chemistry alone; the psychodynamic model in unconscious conflicts; the behavioural model in learned experiences; the cognitive model in maladaptive thinking (Aaron Beck, Albert Ellis); the humanistic-existential model in blocked growth, lack of self-acceptance or failure to find meaning (Carl Rogers, Abraham Maslow, Rollo May); and the sociocultural model in social and cultural forces such as poverty, family structure and discrimination. The oldest view of all, the supernatural (demonological) model, blamed possession by spirits or divine punishment, and no modern model accepts it. The diathesis-stress model is the one that explicitly says a biological or psychological predisposition is set off by a stressful situation . Its broader cousin, the biopsychosocial model, appears in Section 11.10. (The models of abnormality are covered fully in the Disorders book.) Exam trap The SRRS measures life events. Holmes and Rahe (1967) counted major life changes in life change units; death of a spouse scores 100 and marriage, the anchor, 50. It does not measure daily hassles (Kanner, Coyne, Schaefer and Lazarus, 1981), physiological reactions (Selye's tradition) or cognitive appraisal (Lazarus). Positive events such as marriage, vacations and Christmas count, because the scale measures change. Some revision notes credit Holmes and Rahe with "catastrophes and daily hassles" as types of stressor; that threefold scheme (cataclysmic, personal, background) is Lazarus and Cohen's (1977). Hassles beat life events as predictors of symptoms and health. Acute or chronic? A pop quiz, an interview or a near miss is acute; HIV disease, cancer, marital discord, caregiving and poverty are chronic. Secondary appraisal is the assessment of whether one has the resources to cope. Primary appraisal judges relevance and whether the event is harm-loss, threat or challenge. Phrases such as "initial threat evaluation", "coping resource assessment" or "situational capacity evaluation" sound plausible but are not Lazarus and Folkman's terms. Organisational stressors are task demands, role demands, interpersonal demands, structure and leadership. Family and economic problems and the number of dependants are individual factors; political and economic uncertainty are environmental factors. Role conflict means incompatible expectations; role ambiguity means unclear ones. Control reduces damage. Brady's "executive monkeys" (1958) seemed to show the opposite, but the executives were not randomly assigned; Weiss's properly controlled rats (1971) with control got fewer ulcers. Karasek: high demands plus low control produce the most strain. Diathesis-stress means vulnerability plus stress. Options saying "genetic factors only", "environmental factors only", "learned experiences alone", "unconscious conflicts only" or "supernatural influences" are the distractors. Part of the difference lies in what they do about it (coping), part in the people around them (social support), part in stable features of their personalities, and part in what stress does to the heart and the immune system. This final section follows that path, from the first attempt to cope to the cells of the immune system, and ends with what can be done to manage stress. What coping is: problem-focused and emotion-focused Lazarus and Folkman (1984) defined coping as "constantly changing cognitive and behavioral efforts to manage specific external and/or internal demands that are appraised as taxing or exceeding the resources of the person." Notice three things about the definition. Coping is a process : it is what a person actually thinks and does in a particular encounter, and it changes as the encounter unfolds, rather than being a fixed trait. Coping is defined by effort , not by success: a strategy that fails is still coping. And coping may be aimed at the outside demand or at the inner turmoil it causes, which gives the most important distinction in the field. Problem-focused coping is directed at the stressor itself: defining the problem, gathering information, generating and weighing solutions, making a plan, managing time, confronting the person responsible, or learning a new skill. Emotion-focused coping is directed at the emotional response to the stressor: reappraising the situation in a more positive light, seeking sympathy and emotional support, accepting what cannot be changed, distancing oneself, humour, prayer, relaxation and distraction, but also venting, wishful thinking, denial and drinking. In a study of 100 middle-aged adults who described more than 1,300 stressful episodes, Folkman and Lazarus (1980) found that people used both kinds of coping in 98 percent of them. Problem-focused coping rose when people saw something that could be done, such as a difficulty at work, and emotion-focused coping rose when they saw the situation as one that had to be accepted, such as a health problem. Which is better? Neither, in general. The best predictor of good outcomes is the goodness of fit between the strategy and the controllability of the stressor: change what can be changed, and manage your feelings about what cannot. A candidate who learns three weeks before the entrance examination that she is weak in statistics should use problem-focused coping (a revision plan, extra practice papers). The same candidate, the evening after the results are declared, can no longer change the outcome; emotion-focused coping (talking it over with a friend, reappraising the result as one attempt among several) is now what helps. Studying caregivers of partners dying of AIDS in the 1990s, Folkman found that even in the midst of chronic grief they reported positive emotions, which they drew from finding meaning in caregiving, revising their goals and noticing small good moments. She later called this meaning-focused coping : drawing on beliefs, values and goals to find benefit and purpose in a stressful situation that cannot be changed. A second distinction cuts across the first. Approach coping turns towards the stressor and one's reactions to it (seeking information, planning, expressing feelings, reappraisal); avoidance coping turns away (denial, distraction, wishful thinking, withdrawal, substance use). Susan Roth and Lawrence Cohen (1986) reviewed the evidence, and a meta-analysis by Jerry Suls and Barbara Fletcher (1985) gave the most useful summary: avoidance can help in the short term, for example in the hours before an operation, when worrying about details only raises anxiety, but approach coping does better in the long run, and chronic avoidance is linked to poorer mental and physical health. Researchers measure these strategies with questionnaires such as Folkman and Lazarus's Ways of Coping Questionnaire and the COPE Inventory of Charles Carver, Michael Scheier and Jagdish Weintraub (1989). Sigmund Freud introduced the idea, and his daughter Anna Freud systematised it in her book The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), describing defence mechanisms as unconscious , automatic strategies that protect the ego from anxiety by distorting or denying reality. Coping, in Lazarus's sense, is conscious , deliberate and flexible. The two overlap at the edges, and George Vaillant, in Adaptation to Life (1977), arranged defences in a hierarchy from immature (such as projection and acting out) to mature (sublimation, humour, altruism, anticipation and suppression), and found that men who relied on mature defences enjoyed better physical and mental health over decades. The defences examined most often are easy to tell apart by their key words: displacement redirects a feeling from its true target to a safer one (a woman angry with her husband shouts at her child); sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued activity (an angry young man takes up kickboxing); repression is the involuntary banishing of a painful memory or feeling from awareness, whereas suppression is deliberate; projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else; isolation of affect keeps the idea but strips away its feeling (a patient calmly describes a gruesome fantasy); rationalisation offers a plausible excuse; denial refuses to acknowledge a painful reality at all (insisting that a frightening diagnosis must be a mistake); and reaction formation turns a feeling into its opposite. Notice the difference between denial and isolation: the patient who calmly describes a gruesome fantasy is not denying the idea, which he reports in full, but has cut it off from its feeling. The full list is in Table 10.11 and the Personality book. Social support Of all the resources that people bring to stress, the most consistently protective is other people. Social support is the perception or experience that one is loved and cared for, valued and esteemed, and part of a network of mutual help. James House (1981) distinguished four kinds: emotional support (empathy, love, trust and caring), instrumental or tangible support (money, a lift to the hospital, help with the cooking), informational support (advice, suggestions and information) and appraisal support (feedback that helps a person evaluate himself or herself and the situation). An important finding is that perceived support, the belief that help would be there if needed, predicts well-being more consistently than received support, the help actually given. Highly visible help can even backfire, by making the receiver feel indebted or incompetent. How does support protect? Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Wills (1985) reviewed the evidence for two answers. The main-effect (or direct-effect) hypothesis says that support is good for people whether or not they are under stress, because belonging, a sense of being valued and encouragement towards healthy habits are beneficial in themselves. The stress-buffering hypothesis says that support protects mainly when stress is high, by improving secondary appraisal ("I am not alone with this") and by supplying coping resources. Both turned out to be true: measures of how integrated a person is in a social network tend to show main effects, and measures of perceived support that matches the person's needs tend to show buffering. The health effects are large. In the Alameda County study in California, Lisa Berkman and Leonard Syme (1979) followed nearly 7,000 adults for nine years. People with the fewest social ties (marriage, friends and relatives, membership of religious and other groups) had roughly two to three times the death rate of those with the most, even after allowance was made for their initial health and health habits. A meta-analysis by Julianne Holt-Lunstad and her colleagues (2010), combining 148 studies of more than 300,000 people, found that people with stronger social relationships had about a 50 percent greater likelihood of survival over the periods studied, an effect comparable in size to that of giving up smoking. In Sheldon Cohen's laboratory, people with more diverse social networks were less likely to develop colds after being deliberately exposed to a cold virus (1997). Support has a darker twin, too: relationships full of conflict are themselves a major source of stress, a point made clear in the Indian joint family, which can provide abundant support and abundant daily hassles at the same time. The absence of support is loneliness, and the sociologist Robert S. Weiss , in Loneliness: The Experience of Emotional and Social Isolation (1973), showed that it comes in two forms. Emotional isolation (emotional loneliness) is the absence of a close, intimate attachment to one specific person, such as a partner or a confidant; it produces a sense of utter aloneness that no number of acquaintances can cure. Social isolation (social loneliness) is the absence of a wider network of friends, colleagues and community, a place to belong; it produces boredom and a feeling of being on the margins, and a loving partner alone does not cure it. A newly married woman who moves to a new city with her husband may have no emotional isolation but severe social isolation; a widower surrounded by kind relatives may have the reverse. Neither is the same as feeling incompetent or having low self-esteem, which are problems of self-evaluation rather than of attachment. Hardiness, optimism, resilience and sense of coherence Some people seem to stay healthy under stress that flattens others. Four related ideas try to say what they have. The first is hardiness , introduced by Suzanne C. Kobasa in 1979. Kobasa studied middle- and upper-level executives at a large public utility in Chicago (Illinois Bell Telephone) and picked out two groups who had all experienced many stressful life events in the previous three years: those who had fallen ill and those who had stayed well. The healthy executives scored higher on three attitudes, often remembered as the three Cs. Commitment is a sense of involvement and purpose in work, family and life, rather than alienation. Control is the belief that one can influence events, rather than being powerless. Challenge is the tendency to see change as a normal part of life and an opportunity for growth, rather than a threat. A later prospective study by Kobasa, Salvatore Maddi and Stephen Kahn (1982) found that hardiness predicted who would stay healthy in the years that followed. In transactional terms, hardy people appraise stressors as challenges (primary appraisal) and believe they can act (secondary appraisal), and so they tend to cope actively. The main criticism is that hardiness scales overlap heavily with low neuroticism, so part of what they measure may simply be a lack of negative emotionality. The second idea is optimism, studied in two traditions. Michael F. Scheier and Charles S. Carver (1985) defined dispositional optimism as a generalised expectancy that good things rather than bad will happen, and measured it with the Life Orientation Test. Optimists use more problem-focused coping and positive reappraisal and less denial, and in one study by Scheier and colleagues (1989), optimistic men recovered faster after coronary bypass surgery and returned sooner to normal life. The second tradition began with helplessness. Martin E. P. Seligman (born 1942) and Steven F. Maier showed in 1967 that dogs exposed to inescapable shock later failed to escape shock they could have avoided, the phenomenon of learned helplessness (Chapter 6). When the theory was reformulated in 1978 in terms of how people explain bad events, it led to the idea of explanatory style , a person's habitual way of explaining the causes of events. A pessimistic explanatory style explains bad events as internal, stable and global ("It's me, it will always be like this, and it ruins everything"); an optimistic style explains them as external, unstable (temporary) and specific ("That paper was unusually hard, it was one bad day, and it is only one subject"). Christopher Peterson, Seligman and George Vaillant (1988) found that the explanatory style of Harvard graduates at about age 25 predicted their physical health between 45 and 60. In Learned Optimism (1990) Seligman argued that pessimism can be unlearned, by catching and disputing pessimistic explanations, a technique he adapted from Albert Ellis; he called the result learned optimism . One caution: unrealistic optimism, the belief that bad things happen to other people, can lead people to ignore genuine health risks. The third idea is resilience : the process of adapting well, or bouncing back, in the face of serious adversity, trauma or risk. Its classic evidence comes from the Kauai Longitudinal Study of Emmy E. Werner (1929 to 2017) and Ruth Smith, who followed all 698 children born in 1955 on the Hawaiian island of Kauai from before birth into middle age. About a third of the children were at high risk, born into poverty, family discord, parental alcoholism or mental illness, or after a difficult birth. Yet about one in three of these high-risk children grew into competent, confident and caring adults. What protected them was ordinary: an easy-going temperament, at least one close bond with a caring adult (often a grandparent, aunt or teacher rather than a parent), competence in some valued activity, faith, and a supportive community. Ann Masten (2001) summed up such findings by calling resilience "ordinary magic": it comes from ordinary human adaptive systems, not from rare gifts. George Bonanno (2004) showed that after bereavement or trauma, a resilient course, with a short period of disturbance and a steady return to normal functioning, is the most common outcome, not the exception. Resilience is not invulnerability, and it can be strengthened. The fourth idea came from an unusual question. In a 1970 study of the menopause among women in Israel, the medical sociologist Aaron Antonovsky (1923 to 1994) noticed that some of the women had survived Nazi concentration camps, and that, astonishingly, a substantial minority of these survivors (about 29 percent, against about 51 percent of a comparison group who had not been in the camps) were in good emotional health. Medicine, he argued, had always asked what makes people ill ( pathogenesis ); he proposed instead to ask what keeps people healthy, which he called salutogenesis (from the Latin salus , health). His answer, in Health, Stress and Coping (1979) and Unraveling the Mystery of Health (1987), was the sense of coherence (SOC): a pervasive, enduring yet dynamic feeling of confidence that life is comprehensible (events are structured, predictable and explicable), manageable (resources are available to meet its demands) and meaningful (its demands are challenges worth investing in). Meaningfulness, Antonovsky thought, is the motivational heart of the three. People draw on generalised resistance resources , such as money, knowledge, social support and a stable culture, and a strong sense of coherence lets them use these resources well. Two further personal resources, self-efficacy (Albert Bandura, 1977) and an internal locus of control (Julian Rotter, 1966), work in much the same way and are covered in Chapter 10. Exam trap Three-part lists that are easy to swap. Hardiness (Kobasa, 1979): commitment, control, challenge. Sense of coherence (Antonovsky, 1979 and 1987): comprehensibility, manageability, meaningfulness. Diener's subjective well-being: life satisfaction, positive affect, negative affect. Do not give "confidence" or "coherence" as one of Kobasa's Cs. Learned helplessness is Seligman and Maier (1967), later reformulated by Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale (1978). It is not Aaron Beck (cognitive therapy and the negative cognitive triad), Harry Stack Sullivan (the interpersonal theory of psychiatry) or Daniel Kahneman (judgement heuristics and, with Amos Tversky, prospect theory). Dispositional optimism and the Life Orientation Test are Scheier and Carver (1985); learned optimism and explanatory style are Seligman. Emotional isolation (Weiss, 1973) is the lack of a deep attachment to one specific person; the lack of a circle of friends is social isolation . Personality and heart disease: Types A, B, C and D In the mid-1950s two San Francisco cardiologists, Meyer Friedman (1910 to 2001) and Ray H. Rosenman (1920 to 2013), had the chairs in their waiting room reupholstered. The upholsterer remarked that only the front edges of the seats were worn out, as if their patients spent their waiting time perched on the edge, ready to spring up. Friedman later said that he did not grasp the significance of the remark until years afterwards, but he and Rosenman did come to notice that many of their coronary patients shared a distinctive style: hurried, impatient, intensely competitive and quick to anger. In 1959, in the Journal of the American Medical Association , they reported that men showing this pattern had higher blood cholesterol, faster blood clotting and more coronary heart disease than men who did not. They called it the Type A behaviour pattern , and they described three core components. The first is competitive achievement striving : a relentless drive to accomplish more and more, and to win. The second is an exaggerated sense of time urgency ("hurry sickness"): doing two things at once, finishing other people's sentences, fuming in queues and traffic. The third is aggressiveness and hostility , easily aroused. The opposite pattern, Type B , is relaxed, patient and easy-going, unhurried and less driven by competition, although not necessarily less ambitious or less successful. Friedman and Rosenman assessed the pattern mainly with the Structured Interview, in which the interviewer deliberately provokes impatience (by speaking slowly, pausing or interrupting) and codes the person's speech and behaviour as much as the content of the answers; a questionnaire, the Jenkins Activity Survey, was developed later. Their popular book was Type A Behavior and Your Heart (1974). Key study: the Western Collaborative Group Study (1960 to 1969) Question. Does Type A behaviour predict heart disease in men who are healthy at the start? Method. In 1960 and 1961 Rosenman, Friedman and their colleagues classified 3,154 healthy employed men, aged 39 to 59 and working in ten Californian companies, as Type A or Type B using the Structured Interview, and followed them for eight and a half years. Results. Type A men developed coronary heart disease about twice as often as Type B men, and the difference remained after allowing for the standard risk factors of cholesterol, blood pressure and smoking. In 1981 a review panel of the US National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute accepted Type A behaviour as an independent risk factor for coronary heart disease. The twist. Later large studies, notably the Multiple Risk Factor Intervention Trial (1985), found no link between global Type A behaviour and heart disease, and meta-analyses showed that the association had weakened or vanished in later research. The question became: is one ingredient of Type A doing the damage? The answer that emerged in the 1980s was hostility , in particular cynical hostility : a mistrustful, cynical view of other people combined with a readiness to become angry. When the Western Collaborative Group interviews were reanalysed component by component, first by Karen Matthews and her colleagues (1977) and later by Michael Hecker and his colleagues (1988), "potential for hostility" stood out as the strongest predictor of heart disease; in the 1988 analysis it still predicted heart disease after the standard risk factors and the other Type A components were taken into account, and it accounted for much of the link between global Type A and heart disease. John Barefoot, Grant Dahlstrom and Redford B. Williams (1983) traced 255 doctors who had taken the MMPI as medical students 25 years earlier; those with high scores on its Cook-Medley Hostility scale had developed coronary heart disease several times more often, and had a higher death rate from all causes. Williams popularised the finding in Anger Kills (1993), and a meta-analysis by Yoichi Chida and Andrew Steptoe (2009) confirmed that anger and hostility predict coronary heart disease in both healthy and already ill people. How might hostility harm the heart? Hostile people show larger and more frequent surges of blood pressure and stress hormones in everyday encounters; they tend to have poorer health habits; and they drive away the social support that would buffer their stress. The good news is that the pattern can change: in Friedman's Recurrent Coronary Prevention Project (1986), heart attack survivors who received counselling to reduce their Type A behaviour had significantly fewer second heart attacks over the next four and a half years than patients who received only standard cardiological advice. Two later "types" extended the idea to other illnesses. A Type C (cancer-prone) pattern was described in the 1980s, most influentially by the psychologist Lydia Temoshok from her work with patients with melanoma: cooperative, appeasing, unassertive and patient, compliant with authority and, above all, inclined to suppress negative emotions, especially anger. (Some revision notes describe Type C people as introverted, detail-minded perfectionists; the research construct is the emotionally suppressed, unassertive style.) The evidence that personality causes cancer is weak: large prospective studies have not found a reliable link, and the most striking supporting data, from Hans Eysenck and Ronald Grossarth-Maticek, were judged unsafe by an enquiry at King's College London in 2019, after which a number of the papers were retracted. Coping style may, however, affect quality of life after a diagnosis. The most important recent addition is the Type D personality ("D" for distressed), introduced in the mid-1990s by the Belgian psychologist Johan Denollet . Type D is the joint presence of two traits. Negative affectivity is the tendency to experience negative emotions, such as worry, gloom, irritability and tension, across time and situations. Social inhibition is the tendency to inhibit the expression of those emotions and behaviours in social interaction, for fear of disapproval. A Type D person, in other words, feels bad a great deal and keeps it to himself or herself. In Denollet's best-known study, published in The Lancet in 1996, 303 patients with coronary heart disease were followed for six to ten years: 27 percent of the Type D patients died, against 7 percent of the others, and Type D predicted death independently of the severity of the heart disease. Type D is measured with the 14-item DS14 scale. Later and larger studies have found weaker effects than the early ones, and the debate about how much Type D adds to depression and anxiety continues, but it remains the personality type most often examined in cardiac psychology today. That is the classic textbook answer and the one to give when the question is about personality types. Psychoneuroimmunology: how stress gets under the skin For most of the twentieth century medicine worked with a biomedical model : disease is a biological malfunction, to be explained by germs, genes and chemistry. In 1977, in the journal Science , the American psychiatrist George L. Engel (1913 to 1999) argued that this model was too narrow and proposed the biopsychosocial model : health and illness arise from the interaction of biological factors (genes, physiology, infection), psychological factors (emotions, beliefs, coping, behaviour) and social factors (family, relationships, social class, culture, access to care). The model is now the framework of health psychology and of clinical psychology alike. Within it, disorders in which psychological factors play a causal role are often called psychosomatic disorders . Pinel and Barnes point out that so many illnesses, from heart disease and asthma to skin disorders, have turned out to be affected by stress that it is more sensible to think of most medical disorders as psychosomatic to some degree. Gastric ulcers, the classic example, show the point: most are associated with infection by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori , but many infected people never develop ulcers, and stress appears to increase the stomach's vulnerability. The most surprising link between mind and body runs through the immune system. Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI) is the study of interactions among psychological factors, the nervous and endocrine systems, and the immune system. A brief reminder of the immune system helps. The innate immune system reacts quickly and in the same way to all invaders, through inflammation and cells such as phagocytes and natural killer cells. The adaptive immune system is slower but specific and has a memory: its lymphocytes, the T cells and B cells, target particular antigens, and B cells produce antibodies. Until the 1970s the immune system was thought to work on its own, untouched by the brain. The experiment that changed this began as a study of taste aversion. Key study: conditioned immunosuppression (Ader and Cohen, 1975) Background. The psychologist Robert Ader (1932 to 2011), at the University of Rochester, was studying conditioned taste aversion (Chapter 6). Rats drank saccharin-flavoured water and were then injected with cyclophosphamide, a drug that causes nausea, so that they learned to avoid the sweet taste. When he went on giving the rats saccharin water without the drug, to see how long the aversion would last, some of them unexpectedly sickened and died, and the more saccharin they had drunk during conditioning, the more likely they were to die. Ader knew that cyclophosphamide also suppresses the immune system. Could the taste alone have become a conditioned stimulus for immune suppression? Method. With the immunologist Nicholas Cohen , he paired saccharin with cyclophosphamide, then injected the rats with an antigen (sheep red blood cells) and gave some of them saccharin alone. Results. Rats re-exposed to the saccharin produced fewer antibodies than control rats. Conclusion. The immune system can be classically conditioned, so the brain must be able to influence it. Ader and Cohen's paper of 1975 is usually taken as the founding study of psychoneuroimmunology, a name Ader helped establish with his edited book Psychoneuroimmunology (1981). Evidence in people soon followed. Janice K. Kiecolt-Glaser and her husband, the immunologist Ronald Glaser, at Ohio State University, found that the activity of medical students' natural killer cells fell during examinations (1984). In a study published in 1995, they made a small, standard wound on the arm of women who were caring for a relative with dementia and of matched women who were not; the caregivers' wounds took about nine days, or 24 percent, longer to heal. Later they found that a hostile discussion between married partners was enough to slow the healing of such wounds. Sheldon Cohen , David Tyrrell and Andrew Smith (1991) measured psychological stress in 394 healthy volunteers, then gave them nasal drops containing one of five common cold viruses (a further 26 volunteers received plain saline drops) and kept them in quarantine. The higher the stress score, the more likely a person was to develop a cold, in a smooth dose-response pattern. Elissa Epel and her colleagues (2004) found that mothers with the highest levels of perceived stress, many of them caring for a chronically ill child, had telomeres (the protective caps on chromosomes that shorten with age) as short as those of women about a decade older. Does stress, then, simply weaken immunity? Not quite. A meta-analysis of about 300 studies by Suzanne Segerstrom and Gregory Miller (2004) found that the answer depends on the kind of stress. Acute stressors lasting minutes, such as public speaking or a mental arithmetic task, actually boosted parts of the innate immune system, as if preparing the body for injury; this is the biological face of Selye's eustress. Chronic stressors, such as caregiving, unemployment, disability or trauma, suppressed immune function, above all the adaptive (cellular and antibody) system, and the longest-lasting stressors suppressed almost every measure of immunity. Stress acts through two kinds of pathway. The direct pathway is physiological: immune cells carry receptors for cortisol, adrenaline and noradrenaline, so the HPA and SAM axes speak to them directly, and chronic stress also promotes a long-lasting, low-grade inflammation, driven by chemical messengers called cytokines, that is now linked to heart disease, diabetes and depression. The indirect pathway is behavioural: stressed people sleep less, smoke and drink more, exercise less, eat worse and delay seeing a doctor. A caution runs through this literature. Most human studies are correlational, and people under stress may simply notice and report more symptoms, which is why experiments such as Cohen's cold-virus study carry so much weight. Health beliefs and health behaviour Because so much of stress's effect on health runs through behaviour, health psychologists have built models to predict whether people will act to protect their health: get screened, take medicine, stop smoking, exercise. Three are examined most often, and they are frequently offered as wrong options in questions about Selye or life events (Table 11.11). The health belief model was developed in the 1950s by social psychologists in the United States Public Health Service, among them Godfrey Hochbaum and Irwin M. Rosenstock , to explain why so few people took up free screening for tuberculosis. It says that people act to protect their health when they believe they are susceptible to a condition ( perceived susceptibility ), that it would be serious ( perceived severity ), that the recommended action would help ( perceived benefits ) and that its costs are acceptable ( perceived barriers ), and when something prompts them ( cues to action , such as a symptom or a reminder); self-efficacy was added in 1988. Protection motivation theory , proposed by Ronald W. Rogers in 1975 to explain how fear appeals work and revised in 1983, says that motivation to protect oneself depends on a threat appraisal (how severe the danger is and how vulnerable one is) and a coping appraisal (whether the recommended action works, which is response efficacy, and whether one can carry it out, which is self-efficacy). The theory of planned behaviour of Icek Ajzen (1985, 1991) says that behaviour follows from intention, and intention from three factors: the person's attitude towards the behaviour, the subjective norm (perceived social pressure from important others) and perceived behavioural control , a concept very close to self-efficacy (the theory is taught with attitudes in the Social book). The stages-of-change, or transtheoretical, model of Prochaska and DiClemente is in Chapter 10. Table 11.11 Models of health behaviour. The techniques below are the ones most often named in examinations; their use in therapy is covered in the Clinical book. Relaxation training. The American physician Edmund Jacobson (1888 to 1983) noticed in the 1920s that anxious patients carried chronic tension in their muscles, and he reasoned that a relaxed body cannot also be an anxious one. His progressive muscle relaxation (PMR), set out in Progressive Relaxation (1929), teaches people to tense and then release one muscle group after another (hands, arms, face, neck, shoulders, chest, stomach, legs) while attending to the contrast between tension and relaxation, until they can relax deeply at will. Joseph Wolpe (1958) used a shortened version as the response incompatible with anxiety in systematic desensitisation, in which clients rate their anxiety on a 0 to 100 Subjective Units of Distress (SUD) scale as they work up a graded fear hierarchy. The cardiologist Herbert Benson (1935 to 2022), after studying practitioners of Transcendental Meditation, described the relaxation response in a 1975 book of that name: an integrated physiological state that is the opposite of fight or flight, with lower heart rate, breathing rate, oxygen consumption and blood pressure. It can be produced, Benson said, by four simple elements: a quiet environment, a mental device (a word or sound repeated silently), a passive attitude and a comfortable position. Biofeedback. In biofeedback a person is given continuous information, as a tone, a light or a moving line on a screen, about a bodily process that is normally outside awareness, such as muscle tension (recorded by electromyography), skin temperature, skin conductance, heart rate, blood pressure or brain waves (neurofeedback), so that he or she can learn to control it. The idea drew on Neal Miller's reports in the 1960s that autonomic responses such as heart rate could be operantly conditioned in rats, results that later proved hard to repeat. Biofeedback helps with tension headache, migraine (by learning to warm the hands) and some other stress-related conditions, although it is often no more effective than relaxation training alone. Meditation and mindfulness. Concentrative meditation focuses attention on a single object, such as a mantra or the breath; Transcendental Meditation, brought to the West by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, is the best-known example. Mindfulness is the practice of paying attention, on purpose and without judgement, to experience in the present moment, an idea drawn from Buddhist vipassana meditation. In 1979 Jon Kabat-Zinn (born 1944) founded an eight-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction programme at the University of Massachusetts Medical School, and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale, 2002) later adapted it to prevent relapse in depression. Meta-analyses find moderate benefits for anxiety, depression and pain. A caution about evidence applies here, too: a survey showing that regular meditators report less stress than non-meditators cannot show that meditation reduces stress, because calmer people may be the ones who choose to meditate; only experiments with random assignment can establish cause (Research Methods book). Indian context Many of the techniques in this subsection have Indian roots. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras describe an eightfold path whose limbs include asana (posture), pranayama (regulation of the breath), dharana (concentration) and dhyana (meditation); slow, controlled breathing is one of the quickest ways to shift the autonomic balance from sympathetic towards parasympathetic activity. Transcendental Meditation came from an Indian teacher, and the vipassana tradition that inspired mindfulness was revived and taught worldwide from India by S. N. Goenka. Indian research centres, including NIMHANS in Bengaluru, have run clinical trials of yoga-based breathing for depression and anxiety, and yoga is now part of many hospital and workplace stress-management programmes. Exercise. Regular aerobic exercise lowers resting heart rate and blood pressure, reduces the physiological reaction to later stressors, improves sleep and mood, and is an effective treatment for mild to moderate depression. It also offers distraction and a sense of mastery. Cognitive restructuring and stress inoculation. Because stress depends on appraisal, changing appraisals is one of the most powerful tools. Cognitive restructuring means identifying distorted, stress-producing thoughts and replacing them with more realistic ones; it is the core of Albert Ellis's rational emotive behaviour therapy (with its ABC model: an activating event leads to emotional consequences only through the beliefs held about it) and of Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy, and it is reappraisal (Section 11.7) made systematic. Donald Meichenbaum (born 1940) combined it with skills training in stress inoculation training , developed in the 1970s and set out in his book Stress Inoculation Training (1985). The name comes from the logic of vaccination: people are exposed to manageable doses of stress while they build their defences. It has three phases. In the conceptualisation (education) phase, the client learns how stress works and how his or her own appraisals and self-statements feed it. In the skill acquisition and rehearsal phase, the client learns and practises coping skills: relaxation, problem solving and coping self-statements such as "One step at a time; I can handle this." In the application and follow-through phase, the client uses the skills in imagined, role-played and then real, gradually harder situations, with planning to prevent relapse. Clinical link A clinical psychologist assessing a stressed client works through the same transactional map. What are the stressors, acute and chronic? How does the client appraise them, and with what explanatory style? What resources are available: support, money, skills, self-efficacy? Which coping strategies are being used, and do they fit the controllability of the problem? Is there a vulnerability, such as a history of depression, that makes this stress more dangerous? Intervention then targets the weakest link: problem-solving training for the controllable stressors, cognitive restructuring for the threatening appraisals, relaxation or mindfulness for the over-aroused body, and help in mobilising social support. Asking "What do you do when you are under stress?" is one of the most informative questions in any intake interview. Exam trap Who gave which technique? Progressive muscle relaxation: Edmund Jacobson (1920s; Progressive Relaxation , 1929). Systematic desensitisation and the SUD scale: Joseph Wolpe, who borrowed Jacobson's relaxation. Relaxation response: Herbert Benson (1975). Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction: Jon Kabat-Zinn (1979). Stress inoculation training: Donald Meichenbaum, with three phases (conceptualisation, skill acquisition and rehearsal, application and follow-through). Biofeedback gives information about one's own body ; it is not a drug or a form of hypnosis. The biopsychosocial model (George Engel, 1977) integrates biological, psychological and social factors. "Biological, psychological and cultural" is the trap; culture is part of the social. Psychoneuroimmunology began with Ader and Cohen's conditioned immunosuppression in rats (1975), using saccharin and cyclophosphamide. Acute stress tends to boost innate immunity; chronic stress suppresses immunity (Segerstrom and Miller, 2004). Health behaviour models. The theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen) has attitude, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control (an option listing "attitude, subjective norms and self-efficacy" is the keyed answer, because perceived control and self-efficacy are close). The health belief model is about perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers; protection motivation theory about threat and coping appraisal. The case of the Capilano bridge, revisited Go back to the men swaying above the Capilano River in 1974, and you can now say a great deal about what was happening to them. As each man stepped onto the bridge, his low road from thalamus to amygdala flagged the drop as dangerous before he had thought about it, and his sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla, Cannon's fight-or-flight machinery, set his heart pounding and his palms sweating. James would have said that his fear simply was the feeling of those changes; Cannon would have said that feeling and arousal rose together. Then a smiling woman appeared with a questionnaire. Here Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory does the work: a man aroused for one reason found a second, attractive explanation standing in front of him, and some of the arousal was labelled as attraction. Dutton and Aron did not rest on one field study, which had an obvious weakness (perhaps the men who choose a frightening bridge are simply bolder). In a laboratory experiment reported in the same paper, men who expected to receive strong electric shocks found a female confederate more attractive than men who expected only mild ones. The misattribution of arousal, and Zillmann's excitation transfer, have been part of emotion theory ever since. The bridge also illustrates the second half of the chapter. The crossing was an acute stressor, a few minutes of alarm reaction followed by recovery, and for many of the men it was probably eustress, the kind of thrill that tourists pay to experience. Whether a man felt threat or challenge depended on his appraisal and on his secondary appraisal of whether he could cope with the sway, exactly as Lazarus and Folkman would predict. Solomon's opponent-process theory would add that the relief on reaching solid ground was the b-process, and that a man who crossed every day would come to feel less fear and more exhilaration. And if the bridge had been a permanent condition of life, with no far side to reach, the HPA axis, allostatic load and the stage of exhaustion would have taken over from the brief, harmless surge that made a stranger's telephone number so appealing. Chapter summary 11.1 What is an emotion? An emotion is a brief, whole-person response to a significant event, with three components: physiological arousal, expressive behaviour and conscious experience (modern theorists add appraisal and action tendency). A feeling is the subjective component; a mood is longer, weaker and often objectless; affect is the umbrella term for good or bad states and, clinically, the observable expression of emotion (rated for quality, range and reactivity in the mental status examination); temperament is the inborn style of emotional reactivity. Basic-emotion lists include Watson's three (fear, rage, love), Tomkins's nine affects (1962), Izard's ten (differential emotions theory), Ekman's six (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust; contempt added in 1986), Plutchik's eight primaries arranged as opposites on a wheel with dyads such as love and awe (1980) and Panksepp's seven brain systems. Dimensional models include Wundt's tridimensional theory, Russell's circumplex of valence by arousal (1980) and Barrett's theory of constructed emotion. 11.2 The classic theories: from the body to the label. The James-Lange theory (1884, 1885) says that bodily changes come first and that the feeling of them is the emotion ("we feel afraid because we tremble"). Cannon (1927) objected that emotion survives separation of viscera from brain, that visceral changes are similar across emotions, insensitive and slow, and that artificial arousal (Marañón's adrenaline injections) produces bodily symptoms and at most an "as if" emotion; the Cannon-Bard theory holds that the thalamus triggers feeling and arousal simultaneously and independently. Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory (1962) says that emotion requires arousal plus a cognitive label; in their adrenaline experiment, aroused participants without an explanation caught the euphoria or anger of a stooge. Misattribution of arousal (Dutton and Aron's bridge, 1974; Valins's false heartbeats) and Zillmann's excitation transfer follow from the theory. 11.3 Appraisal, feedback, evolution and opposing processes. Arnold (1960) introduced appraisal, and Lazarus built the cognitive appraisal (cognitive-mediational) theory: primary appraisal asks whether an event matters and whether it is harm, threat or challenge, secondary appraisal asks what can be done, and reappraisal revises both; the subincision film study showed that changing appraisals changes arousal. Zajonc argued for affective primacy from the mere exposure effect (1980, 1984), and Lazarus replied that appraisal can be automatic. The facial feedback hypothesis (Tomkins, Izard; Strack, Martin and Stepper's pen study, 1988) holds that expressions modulate feelings, although the effect is small. Darwin (1872) explained expressions by serviceable habits, antithesis and direct nervous action and founded the evolutionary view. Solomon and Corbit's opponent-process theory (1974) explains tolerance, withdrawal and acquired pleasures through a slow, strengthening b-process. 11.4 The emotional brain and body. The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system arouses (dilating the pupils, lowering skin resistance) and the parasympathetic division calms; the medulla of the hindbrain paces heartbeat and breathing, and the hypothalamus orchestrates. Bard's decorticate cats showed sham rage, organised by the hypothalamus; Hess elicited attack by hypothalamic stimulation. Papez (1937) proposed a circuit from hippocampus through fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus and cingulate gyrus; MacLean named the limbic system (1952), the classic "seat of emotion", and the triune brain. Bilateral temporal lobe removal produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome (tameness, psychic blindness, hyperorality, hypersexuality); the amygdala detects threat, supports fear conditioning and enhances emotional memory. LeDoux described a fast low road and a slower high road to the amygdala; affective blindsight shows emotional processing without awareness. Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis gives the ventromedial prefrontal cortex a role in decisions. The polygraph detects arousal, not lies; the guilty knowledge test (Lykken, 1959) is more accurate. 11.5 Expressing and reading emotion. Ekman and Friesen's studies of the Fore of New Guinea supported the universality of six facial expressions, with fear and surprise most often confused; blind athletes produce the same expressions as sighted ones. Display rules, cultural norms for showing emotion, explain cultural differences (Friesen's Japanese and American students, 1972), and emotional labour at work contributes to burnout. Recognition shows an in-group advantage. FACS (1978) codes expressions as muscle action units; the Duchenne smile involves the orbicularis oculi around the eyes; microexpressions may betray concealed feelings, but people detect lies at little better than chance. Body posture can be more informative than the face at high intensity. Women are on average more facially expressive and better at decoding nonverbal cues, differences attributed mainly to socialisation. 11.6 Four emotions up close. Fear is a response to present danger; anxiety is diffuse and future-oriented, and Spielberger separated state from trait anxiety. Anger is an emotion, aggression a behaviour and hostility an attitude; the catharsis hypothesis fails, because venting while ruminating increases aggression (Bushman, 2002). Diener's subjective well-being has three components: life satisfaction, positive affect and low negative affect. Helson's adaptation-level theory and Brickman and Campbell's hedonic treadmill explain why good fortune fades (lottery winners), and relative deprivation (Stouffer, 1949) explains why comparisons matter. Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory says positive emotions widen thought and build resources, and savoring (Bryant and Veroff) prolongs positive experience. Disgust, studied by Rozin, protects against contamination and follows the laws of contagion and similarity. 11.7 Emotional development and regulation. Bridges (1932) described differentiation from general excitement into distress and delight and then into specific emotions; primary emotions appear in the first six months, while self-conscious emotions such as embarrassment, pride, shame and guilt appear after 12 months, once self-recognition develops. Infants use social referencing (the visual cliff) and expect emotional reciprocity (Tronick's still face). Gross's process model (1998) lists five families of regulation strategies: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change (including reappraisal) and response modulation (including suppression); reappraisal is generally healthier than suppression. Alexithymia (Sifneos, 1973) is difficulty identifying and describing one's feelings. Goleman's five domains of emotional intelligence are pointed to Chapter 9. 11.8 Stress and the body's emergency systems. Stress has been defined as a stimulus (the stressor), as a response (Selye: the nonspecific response of the body to any demand) and, most usefully, as a transaction in which demands are appraised as exceeding resources. Cannon described the fight-or-flight response (1915), run by the fast sympathetic-adrenal-medullary axis with adrenaline and noradrenaline, and coined homeostasis. Selye's general adaptation syndrome (1936; The Stress of Life , 1956) has three stages: alarm, resistance and exhaustion, the last bringing diseases of adaptation; he also distinguished eustress from distress (1974). The slower HPA axis runs from hypothalamic CRH to anterior pituitary ACTH to cortisol from the adrenal cortex, with negative feedback; chronic activation produces allostatic load (McEwen). Taylor's tend-and-befriend (2000) describes an affiliative stress response, especially in females, involving oxytocin. 11.9 Sources of stress and the transactional model. Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (1967) scores 43 life events in life change units (death of a spouse 100, marriage 50), counting positive as well as negative change, but it ignores appraisal and predicts illness only weakly; India has its own Presumptive Stressful Life Events Scale. Daily hassles (Kanner, Coyne, Schaefer and Lazarus, 1981) predict symptoms better than major events; uplifts matter less. Stressors may be acute or chronic, and cataclysmic, personal or background (Lazarus and Cohen, 1977). Frustration, conflict (Lewin's types and Miller's gradients), pressure and change are further sources. Work stress arises from environmental, organisational (task and role demands) and individual factors; role conflict, role ambiguity and Karasek's high-demand, low-control jobs are especially harmful, and chronic work stress can lead to burnout (Freudenberger, 1974; Maslach's three dimensions). Control and predictability reduce the damage of stressors (Weiss's rats). Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model (1984) explains stress through primary appraisal, secondary appraisal, coping and reappraisal, and the diathesis-stress model explains disorder as vulnerability triggered by stress. 11.10 Coping, personality and health. Coping is the changing effort to manage demands appraised as taxing. Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor and emotion-focused coping on the feelings; people use both, and the best strategy fits the controllability of the situation. Approach coping wins in the long run over avoidance coping; defence mechanisms are unconscious, coping is conscious. Social support (emotional, instrumental, informational and appraisal) protects health directly and by buffering stress; Weiss separated emotional from social isolation. Hardiness (Kobasa, 1979: commitment, control, challenge), dispositional optimism (Scheier and Carver), optimistic explanatory style and learned optimism (Seligman, building on learned helplessness), resilience (Werner's Kauai study) and Antonovsky's sense of coherence (comprehensibility, manageability, meaningfulness) protect against stress. Friedman and Rosenman's Type A pattern (competitiveness, time urgency, hostility) predicted heart disease in the Western Collaborative Group Study, but hostility is the toxic component; Type B is relaxed, Type C (cancer-prone) has weak support, and Denollet's Type D combines negative affectivity with social inhibition. Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) frames health psychology; Ader and Cohen's conditioned immunosuppression (1975) founded psychoneuroimmunology, and chronic stress suppresses immunity and slows healing, while acute stress can boost innate immunity. Health behaviour is predicted by the health belief model, protection motivation theory and the theory of planned behaviour. Stress management uses progressive muscle relaxation (Jacobson), the relaxation response (Benson), biofeedback, meditation and mindfulness (Kabat-Zinn), exercise, cognitive restructuring and stress inoculation training (Meichenbaum).
