A good record protects the client, because the next clinician will not have to start from nothing, and it protects the clinician, because a record written at the time is the best evidence that she acted with reasonable care. Clinicians put the second point bluntly: if it was not documented, as far as anyone else can tell, it was not done. A clinical record typically contains identifying information and the referral; the consent obtained and the limits of confidentiality that were explained; the history, mental status examination and test results (Chapter 2); the diagnosis and formulation (Section 2.9); the treatment plan; dated progress notes for each contact; every risk assessment, the decision taken and the reasoning behind it; consultations with colleagues; contacts with family or other agencies and the consent for each; and a closing summary. Progress notes are often written in a fixed format such as the SOAP note : Subjective (what the client reports), Objective (what the clinician observes and measures), Assessment (the clinician's interpretation) and Plan (what happens next). What should stay out is just as important: gossip, speculation presented as fact, judgemental language ("manipulative", "attention-seeking"), and intimate details that are not needed for care, since Standard 4.04 asks that only information germane to the purpose be recorded and reported. In the United States, a therapist's private process notes, kept separately from the main record (often called psychotherapy notes ), receive extra protection under the privacy rule of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996. A useful discipline in India is to write every note as though the client will read it, because under Section 25 of the Mental Healthcare Act he has a right to access his basic medical records, subject to narrow exceptions (Section 2.9.9). Records must be kept securely and confidentially "in creating, storing, accessing, transferring, and disposing of" them, whether on paper or electronically (6.02a): locked cabinets, password-protected and encrypted computers, no client files on a personal phone, and identifiers removed when information enters databases that others can access (6.02b). Psychologists also plan ahead for what happens to their records if they leave a job, retire or die (6.02c), so that clients are not stranded. How long should records be kept? The APA's Record Keeping Guidelines (2007) suggest that, in the absence of a stricter legal requirement, full records be kept for seven years after the last service for an adult, and for a minor until three years after he reaches the age of majority or seven years after the last service, whichever is later. India has no single rule for psychologists. The Medical Council of India's ethics regulations of 2002 required doctors to keep the records of in-patients for three years, and hospitals usually set their own, often longer, periods; a psychologist should follow her institution's policy and keep records longer when legal proceedings are possible. Digital records also come under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, whose rules (notified in November 2025) bring its main duties into force in phases, most of them from May 2027: personal data must be processed for a lawful purpose, with the person's consent or for certain other legitimate uses, and protected by reasonable security safeguards. Exam trap The APA code lists five purposes of records (6.01): later services, replication of research, institutional requirements, accurate billing, compliance with law. Records cannot be withheld for non-payment when they are needed for emergency treatment (6.03). Write only what is germane (4.04). In India the client has a right of access to his basic medical records under Section 25 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, and the professional may withhold specific information only if disclosure would cause him serious mental harm or is likely to harm others. The ethics of assessment Psychological tests are powerful precisely because their results are trusted. A report that a child's IQ is 68 can change his school, his future and his family's view of him; a personality profile can decide a custody case or a job. Section 9 of the APA code therefore governs assessment closely. (The tests themselves are taught in the Assessment book; this subsection is about the ethics of using them.) The first rule is about the basis of opinions. Psychologists base their opinions on information and techniques sufficient to support them, and give opinions about a person's psychological characteristics only after an examination adequate to support their conclusions (9.01). This forbids the television expert who diagnoses a politician or a film star from news clips. Psychiatry has a named version of the same rule, the "Goldwater rule", adopted by the American Psychiatric Association in 1973 after a magazine had published the opinions of psychiatrists who had never met the presidential candidate Barry Goldwater about his mental fitness. The second rule is about the instruments. Tests must be used in ways and for purposes supported by evidence; their reliability and validity must have been established for the population being tested, or their limitations must be stated; and they must suit the person's language preference and competence (9.02). Using a test standardised on American children to label a child from rural Bihar, without saying how far the norms apply, violates this rule. Psychologists do not base decisions on obsolete tests or outdated results (9.08): certifying a young adult's intellectual disability today on the basis of a test he took at eight, or using an old edition whose norms are out of date, is an ethical failure as well as a technical one. The code then separates two kinds of material, and the difference is tested often. test data are the person's own raw and scaled scores, his responses to test questions or stimuli, and the psychologist's notes and recordings of what he said and did during the examination; a test form on which the client's answers are written counts as test data. test materials are the manuals, instruments, protocols and the test questions or stimuli themselves. Test data belong, in effect, to the client: with the client's release, psychologists provide test data to the client or to whoever he names, though they may refrain in order to protect the client or others from substantial harm or to prevent misuse, and without a release they provide test data only as required by law or court order (9.04). Test materials must be protected: psychologists make reasonable efforts to maintain the integrity and test security of test materials, consistent with law and contracts (9.11), because a test whose items are known is no longer a valid test. Table 1.23 sets the two side by side. Table 1.23 Test data and test materials in the APA code. Feature Test data (Standard 9.04) Test materials (Standard 9.11) What they are Raw and scaled scores; the client's responses; the examiner's notes on what he said and did Manuals, instruments, protocols, test questions and stimuli Main duty Release to the client or named persons on his release; withhold only to prevent substantial harm or misuse Maintain security and integrity, within law and contracts Without the client's release Only as required by law or court order Not applicable; materials are not the client's Why does security matter so much? In 2009 the ten Rorschach inkblots, together with the responses most commonly given to each, were posted on Wikipedia, and many psychologists protested that the test had been compromised for anyone who read the page before being assessed. The same logic applies in India to photocopied test forms and coaching videos that teach applicants how to "pass" personality tests: a copied test violates copyright, and a test whose stimuli circulate freely can no longer measure what it claims to. The remaining standards protect the person tested. Consent for assessment is required, with the exceptions already described in Section 1.8.6 (9.03); when an interpreter is used, the client must agree to it and the limitations it places on the results must be reported. Psychologists do not encourage unqualified people to use psychological tests, except trainees under supervision (9.07); publishers commonly restrict the sale of tests according to the qualifications needed to use them. Psychologists who use computerised scoring and interpretation services remain responsible for how the results are applied (9.09). And they ensure that results are explained to the person or his representative, unless the nature of the relationship precludes it (as in some pre-employment, security or forensic evaluations) and the person was told this in advance (9.10). How to give feedback well is described in Section 2.9.10. Assessment is also where third-party request s are most common: a school, an employer, a court or an insurer asks for an assessment, or for results. Standard 3.07 requires the psychologist to clarify at the outset her role, who the client is, how the information will probably be used, and the limits of confidentiality. A psychologist engaged by a company to screen job applicants has the company as her client and must tell applicants so; a psychologist engaged by parents to assess their daughter must not hand the report to the girl's school without the parents' consent and the girl's agreement. Section 1.9.11 works through exactly that request. Exam trap Test data (scores, responses, notes on behaviour) are released to the client or to persons he names on his release ; test materials (manuals, items, stimuli) are kept secure . A completed answer sheet containing the client's responses is test data , even though it also shows the items. No opinion about a person's psychological characteristics without an adequate examination (9.01). Do not base decisions on obsolete tests or outdated results (9.08). The psychologist stays responsible for automated interpretations (9.09). Research integrity for clinicians Clinical psychologists in India do research as part of their training (most programmes require a dissertation) and throughout their careers, often with their own clients. Section 1.8.7 covered the protection of participants; the other half of research ethics is honesty about the research itself. Three forms of misconduct are treated as the gravest: fabrication , making up data or results; falsification , manipulating materials, procedures or data, or omitting inconvenient data, so that the record misrepresents what was found; and plagiarism , presenting another person's work or data as one's own. The APA code states the first and third bluntly ("Psychologists do not fabricate data", 8.10; and plagiarism is forbidden "even if the other work or data source is cited occasionally", 8.11), and requires psychologists who discover significant errors in their published data to correct them (8.10b). Fabrication is not a theoretical danger. In 2011 the Dutch social psychologist Diederik Stapel was found to have invented the data for dozens of studies over many years, and more than fifty of his papers were eventually retracted. In clinical research the consequences can be measured in lives: the 1998 Lancet paper by Andrew Wakefield that claimed a link between the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine and autism was retracted in 2010 after it was shown to be fraudulent, and Wakefield was struck off the British medical register, but the vaccine fears it started persisted for years. Credit must also be honest. Authorship goes only to those who actually did or substantially contributed to the work, and the order of authors must reflect their relative contributions "regardless of their relative status"; being head of department does not by itself earn a place on a paper, and a student is normally the principal author of an article based substantially on his dissertation (8.12). Psychologists do not publish the same data twice as if they were new (8.13), they share their data with competent colleagues who want to verify their conclusions (8.14), and as reviewers they respect the confidentiality of the work they review (8.15). In India, clinical trials are registered with the Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI), set up under the ICMR in 2007; registration of regulated trials became mandatory in 2009, and ethics committees and journals now expect trials of psychological treatments to be registered too, so that unfavourable results cannot simply disappear. And when a clinician recruits her own clients into her research, she has created a multiple relationship: Standard 8.04 requires her to protect them from any adverse consequence of declining, so that no client ever feels that his treatment depends on his participation. (Research design, including the ethics of placebo and waiting-list controls, is covered in Section 8.7 and in the Research Methodology book.) Exam trap The three forms of research misconduct are fabrication (inventing), falsification (manipulating or selectively omitting) and plagiarism (taking credit for others' work). "Manipulating data to support hypotheses" is falsification and is never part of research ethics. Plagiarism is not excused by occasional citation. Authorship reflects contribution , not seniority. Duplicate publication of the same data as new is also misconduct. Teletherapy and digital practice Before 2020 video therapy was a specialty; within months of the COVID-19 lockdowns it was ordinary practice, and in India it now reaches clients through private platforms and through the national Tele-MANAS service (Section 1.10). The APA code already covered it, since it applies to work done "in person, postal, telephone, Internet, and other electronic transmissions". More specific guidance came in 2013, when a joint task force of the APA, the Association of State and Provincial Psychology Boards (the association of American and Canadian licensing boards) and the APA Insurance Trust published the Guidelines for the Practice of Telepsychology (the APA approved a revised version in 2024). The 2013 guidelines define telepsychology as the provision of psychological services using telecommunication technologies, and they address eight areas: the psychologist's competence with the technology and with remote work; maintaining the same standard of care as in person; informed consent; confidentiality; the security and transmission of data; the disposal of data and devices; testing and assessment at a distance; and interjurisdictional practice , working across state or national borders. In India, the Telemedicine Practice Guidelines issued in March 2020 apply to registered medical practitioners rather than to psychologists, but the principles they set out (identify the patient, obtain consent, keep records, know when remote care is not enough) are the same ones a psychologist follows. Each area turns into a concrete question. Is this client suitable for remote work? A client in acute suicidal crisis, with severe psychosis, or with no private space may need to be seen in person. What does consent cover? Beyond the usual elements, the client must understand the particular risks of electronic communication (Standard 4.02c), what happens if the connection fails, whether sessions are recorded (they should not be, without explicit permission, Standard 4.03), and how emergencies will be handled. Is the platform secure? A service with end-to-end encryption and no unauthorised recording is acceptable; a session on a shared family laptop, with chat logs that anyone can open, is not. Is the client's space private? In many Indian homes it is not: clients take sessions in a parked car, on the terrace, or in a bathroom with the tap running, and it helps to agree in advance on a signal that someone has come into the room. What is the emergency plan? At the start of each session the psychologist should know where the client actually is, have a local emergency contact, and know the nearest hospital, because a video call cannot call an ambulance to an address no one has recorded. Which law applies? RCI registration is national, so moving between Indian states is not the problem it is in the United States; but a client who has moved to Dubai or Toronto may be subject to that country's rules on who may practise there. Can tests be given remotely? Many standardised tests have never been validated for video administration, and sending stimuli by screen-share puts test security at risk (Section 1.9.6). Return to Shalini from Section 1.9.1. A year into therapy her husband is transferred to Bengaluru, and she asks to continue by video from her in-laws' flat. Continuing is reasonable: the alliance is strong, and finding a new therapist would set her back. But the move requires a fresh consent conversation about the platform and its risks, an agreed time when the flat is empty or a room she can lock, her new address and an emergency contact in Bengaluru, a plan for what happens if her mood drops sharply, and clarity about messaging. Clients who can message their therapist on WhatsApp at midnight will, and a clear policy (messages for scheduling only, replies within working hours, emergencies to a helpline or hospital) protects both sides from a boundary that dissolves without anyone deciding it should. Clinical link A first video session checklist: confirm the client's identity and exact location ; record a local emergency contact and the nearest hospital; check that the client is alone and agree a signal for interruptions; use a secure platform and do not record without written permission; explain what happens if the connection drops ; agree the rules for messages between sessions ; and note in the record that all of this was discussed. Repeat the location check at every session. Supervision and the trainee Every clinical psychologist in India trains under supervision, and supervision has its own ethics. (What supervision is, its functions and its models are covered in Section 8.12; this subsection is about the duties it creates.) The first duty is honesty with the client. Under Standard 10.01(c), when the therapist is a trainee and legal responsibility lies with the supervisor, the client must be told that the therapist is in training and is being supervised, and must be given the supervisor's name. Clients must also know that what they say will be discussed in supervision, and recordings of sessions need their permission (4.03). The supervisor's duties follow from the fact that she shares responsibility for the trainee's clients. She delegates only work the trainee can perform competently with the level of supervision provided, and checks that it is performed competently (2.05). She gives timely and specific feedback through a process explained at the start, and evaluates the trainee on actual performance against established requirements (7.06). She does not require trainees to disclose personal information about their sexual history, abuse, psychological treatment or relationships, unless the programme stated this requirement at admission or the information is needed because the trainee's personal problems are preventing competent work or posing a threat (7.04). Faculty who evaluate a student do not also act as his therapist (7.05), which is why a supervisor who notices that a trainee is struggling personally recommends therapy elsewhere instead of providing it. And sexual relationships with students or supervisees under her evaluative authority are forbidden (7.07). Legally, a supervisor and the institution can be held responsible for a trainee's negligent acts committed in the course of supervised work, under the doctrine of vicarious liability (in Latin, respondeat superior , "let the superior answer"). That is the legal reason supervisors read case notes and check risk assessments, not only the clinical one. The trainee has duties too: not to exceed his competence, to bring his difficulties and mistakes to supervision instead of hiding them, and to tell the supervisor at once about any risk to a client or to others. A trainee who conceals a client's suicidal statement because he is embarrassed not to have asked about it puts the client, the supervisor and himself in danger. Exam trap A client seen by a trainee must be told that the therapist is a trainee , that he is supervised , and the supervisor's name (10.01c). Discussing a case in supervision is not a breach of confidentiality, provided the client was told. A supervisor must not become the trainee's therapist (a multiple relationship; 7.05). Supervisors can be vicariously liable for their trainees' negligence. The RCI code and professional accountability in India The APA code is the one textbooks quote, but the code that binds an Indian clinical psychologist is the Rehabilitation Council of India's. Section 21 of the Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 empowers the Council to prescribe standards of professional conduct and etiquette and a code of ethics for rehabilitation professionals, a category that includes clinical psychologists, and allows its regulations to specify which violations amount to professional misconduct. The Council did so in the Rehabilitation Council of India (Standards of Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Code of Ethics for Rehabilitation Professionals) Regulations, 1998 . The Act also supplies the sanction: after giving the professional a reasonable opportunity to be heard, the Council may remove from the Central Rehabilitation Register the name of anyone who has been convicted of an offence, or found guilty of infamous conduct in a professional respect, or who has violated the prescribed standards or code of ethics, if it considers him unfit to remain on the Register; it may also bar him from re-registration permanently or for a period. Since only registered professionals may practise (Section 1.5), removal from the Register ends a clinical psychologist's right to practise. Indian context An Indian clinical psychologist answers to several authorities at once. The RCI sets the code of ethics and controls registration (RCI Act, 1992, Section 21; Regulations of 1998). The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 defines clinical psychologists, counts them among mental health professionals and imposes legal duties on all professionals who treat persons with mental illness, such as confidentiality (Section 23) and the rules on research (Section 99); Section 1.10 describes the Act. POCSO (2012) imposes mandatory reporting. The courts hear negligence claims, and since the Supreme Court's judgement in Indian Medical Association v. V. P. Shantha (1995), paid health services have been treated as "services" under consumer protection law, so a dissatisfied client may also approach a consumer forum. Professional associations such as the Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists bring practitioners together, but they do not license anyone. Reasoning through an ethical dilemma Codes cannot list every situation, so every profession teaches a method for working through the ones they do not settle. Many such step models have been published, among them those of the American psychologists Gerald P. Koocher and Patricia Keith-Spiegel in their textbook Ethics in Psychology and the Mental Health Professions , and the ten-step model in the Canadian Psychological Association's code. They differ in detail but share a core, condensed in Figure 1.14. Kitchener's two levels (Section 1.8.3) explain why a method is needed at all: when intuition gives a clear and comfortable answer, most decisions are made quickly and well, but when intuition is uncertain or conflicted, the professional must slow down and reason explicitly. 1. Recognise the ethical problem 2. Get the facts; list everyone affected 3. Check the code, the law and policy 4. Consult a supervisor or trusted colleague 5. List the options and weigh their effects 6. Decide, act, and document the reasoning 7. Review the outcome and learn from it Sources: APA code, RCI regulations, MHCA 2017, POCSO 2012, institutional policy Weigh: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, fidelity Feedback loop (left line): step 7 returns to step 1; each dilemma sharpens the next Figure 1.14 A seven-step method for ethical decision making, condensed from published step models. Steps 3 and 5 are where the code, the law and the principles enter; step 4, consultation, is the one that busy clinicians skip and the one that most often prevents a mistake. Three quick self-checks are often added at step 5. Would I be comfortable if this decision were reported in the newspaper or described to my colleagues (publicity)? Would I recommend the same action to another psychologist in the same situation (universality)? Would I treat another client in the same circumstances the same way (justice)? Now push three cases through the method. Case 1: the cousin. Your cousin Ramesh, thirty years old, phones. He has been having panic attacks for months, he trusts only you, he cannot afford private fees, and he does not want anyone in the family to know. Recognise : seeing him would create a multiple relationship (Standard 3.05). Facts : you will meet him at every family function, you know his wife and parents, your own mother will ask how he is, and if therapy goes badly or you have to confront him, family relationships will suffer; on the other side, he is suffering and reluctant to seek help. Sources : the code does not forbid the relationship outright but asks whether it could reasonably impair your objectivity or risk harm, and here it plainly could; principles of beneficence (he needs help) and nonmaleficence (the dual role may harm both the therapy and the family) pull against each other. Consult a colleague. Options : treat him yourself; refuse and leave him to find help alone; or decline the therapist role but act as a cousin, by finding him a competent and affordable colleague, a hospital outpatient department or a low-cost service, and keeping his confidence. The third option meets his need without the dual role. Decide and act : refer, warmly, and explain why the refusal protects him. If you lived in a remote district where no other help existed, a brief, clearly bounded intervention with consultation might be defensible (Standard 2.01d); in a city it is not. Case 2: the school. You have assessed Zoya, the fifteen-year-old from Section 1.8.6, at her parents' request, and found a specific learning disorder with anxiety. The principal of her school phones: "We are deciding whether to promote her. Just tell me her IQ and the diagnosis." Recognise : a third-party request for confidential information (Standards 3.07, 4.05). Facts : your clients are Zoya and her parents, not the school; the school's purpose (a promotion decision) is not one Zoya's family agreed to; a bare IQ figure or diagnostic label, without context, could harm her. Sources : disclosure needs consent (4.05a); only germane information may be shared (4.04); test data go only to persons named in a release (9.04); and the Mental Healthcare Act's right to confidentiality applies. Consult if unsure. Options : refuse everything; give the principal what she asks for; or tell the principal politely that you cannot discuss any client without consent, then discuss the request with Zoya and her parents. Decide and act : with the parents' written consent and Zoya's assent, send a short report that explains her difficulties in plain language and recommends specific accommodations (extra time, a reader, remedial teaching), without raw scores or test items; document the request, the consent and what was sent. Notice how the third option serves Zoya's interests better than either extreme. Case 3: the threat. Nikhil, a 32-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru being treated for depression and heavy drinking, says angrily near the end of a session: "If my team lead humiliates me again in Monday's meeting, I'll finish him. I know where he parks." Recognise : a possible duty to protect an identifiable person (Section 1.8.10). Facts : assess before you act, using the methods of Section 2.7. Has he ever been violent? Does he have a plan beyond these words, any weapon, any history of acting on threats? Is he intoxicated or likely to be on Monday? What does he say when asked, calmly, what he meant? Suppose he has a past assault conviction from a bar fight, has been drinking daily, and repeats the threat when asked. Sources : Section 23(2)(c) and (d) of the Mental Healthcare Act permit release of the information necessary to protect another person, and only that; the code permits disclosure to protect others from harm (4.05b); Tarasoff is not Indian law but shows the professional standard. Consult a senior colleague the same day. Options , from least to most intrusive: explore and de-escalate the anger in the session; increase the frequency of sessions; with his consent, involve his wife; arrange an urgent psychiatric review for his drinking and mood; ask him to take leave or avoid Monday's meeting; consider admission if the danger is high (the Act's admission procedures are described in Section 1.10); and, if he leaves still intending violence, warn the team lead or the company's security, or inform the police, telling them only what is needed to protect the team lead. Decide and act : in this version, with a past assault, ongoing drinking and a repeated specific threat, protective action is required; where possible, tell Nikhil what you are going to do and why, unless doing so would increase the danger. Document the threat in his words, your assessment, the consultation, the options considered and the reasons for your choice. Review at the next session, and with your supervisor. Run the three cases side by side and a pattern appears. The worst choices were nearly always the extreme ones (treat your cousin, or abandon him; tell the school everything, or nothing; ignore the threat, or call the police at the first angry word). The good choice was usually a third option that honoured more than one principle at once, found by slowing down, consulting and asking what the person in front of you actually needs. That is what ethical competence looks like in practice. Exam trap In decision-making models the first step is to recognise that an ethical problem exists; consultation comes before the decision (except in a true emergency), and documentation of the reasoning comes with it. The least intrusive effective option is preferred. When a question asks what to do first about a client's threat, the answer is usually to assess the risk , not to call the police or to do nothing. Beauchamp and Childress's four principles are respect for autonomy, beneficence, justice and . The APA's five General Principles are , whereas its ten sections of Ethical Standards are enforceable. APA Principle C, which emphasises accuracy, honesty and truthfulness, is called . A child's own agreement to treatment, which supplements the consent of a parent, is called . Giving research participants full information about the study after it is over is called . The client's legal right to prevent a professional from testifying about his communications in court is called communication. The 1976 Tarasoff ruling broadened the 1974 duty to warn into a duty to . Gutheil and Gabbard distinguished a harmless boundary from a harmful boundary violation. A client's raw scores and responses are test , which are released on his authorisation, while manuals and test items are test materials, which are kept secure. Answers: (1) utilitarian (consequentialist), (2) nonmaleficence, (3) aspirational, (4) Integrity, (5) assent, (6) debriefing, (7) privileged, (8) protect, (9) crossing, (10) data. 1.10 Mental Health Law and Policy in India High yield · 7 Qs Picture a family in a district town in Karnataka. Their son Bharat, aged 28, has hardly slept for a week. He shouts at the neighbours, has stopped eating at home because he is sure his food is being poisoned, and last night he waved a kitchen knife at his father. In the morning the family bring him to the district hospital and ask the doctor to "keep him inside until he is cured". Who has the power to decide that Bharat must stay in hospital when he says he will not? For how long? Who checks that the decision was right, and which treatments may be given to him while he is there? Every society has to answer these questions, and the answers it chooses say a great deal about how it sees people with mental illness. Indian law has answered them three times in a little over a century and a half. The colonial laws of 1858 and 1912 gave the decision to the magistrate: a person of "unsound mind" was a danger to be removed from society, and the law's business was to confine him safely. The Mental Health Act 1987 renamed the "lunatic" a "mentally ill person" and put doctors at the centre, but it kept much of the old machinery of orders and custody. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 starts from the other end. It presumes that Bharat, like anyone else, can make decisions about his own treatment; it gives him rights that the government must honour; and it lets him be admitted against his wishes only under strict conditions that an independent board can review. Beside these mental health laws stand the disability and rehabilitation laws, which turn mental illness, intellectual disability and autism into grounds for rights and entitlements and decide who may practise as a clinical psychologist, and a set of national programmes that try to bring care within reach of the people the laws protect. Figure 1.15 lays the whole story out in order. A clinical psychologist in India works inside this framework every day, and Indian entrance papers ask about it more often than about almost any other part of the profession. The colonial laws: custody, not care The first Indian laws on mental illness were passed in 1858, the year the British Crown took over the government of India from the East India Company. Three Acts appeared that year. Two of them, the Lunacy (Supreme Courts) Act and the Lunacy (District Courts) Act, dealt with how a court could declare a person to be of unsound mind and appoint someone to look after his property. The third, the Indian Lunatic Asylums Act 1858 (Act 36 of 1858), laid down how asylums were to be established and how people were to be admitted to them. The question these laws asked was who might be confined, on whose order, and what should happen to the confined person's estate. Treatment hardly came into it. In 1912 the colonial government consolidated the law into the Indian Lunacy Act 1912 (Act IV of 1912), which governed Indian psychiatry for the next eighty years. Its vocabulary tells you its outlook. A "lunatic" was defined as "an idiot or a person of unsound mind", so intellectual disability and mental illness were lumped together under one word; the place of care was an "asylum"; and the people in it were lunatics of different legal kinds. The central instrument of the Act was the reception order , defined in the Act as an order "for the reception into an asylum of a lunatic". To obtain one on petition, the husband or wife of the alleged lunatic (or, failing them, the nearest relative) applied to a magistrate, and the petition had to be supported by two medical certificates, one of them from a government medical officer. The magistrate considered the petition, usually examined the person himself, and could order the person's detention while he made up his mind. The police had a duty to take charge of anyone found "wandering at large" whom they believed to be a lunatic, or anyone dangerous by reason of lunacy, and to bring him before a magistrate; a lunatic who was cruelly treated or neglected by the relatives responsible for him could be dealt with in the same way. A criminal lunatic , a person ordered by a criminal court to be detained because of his mental state, came in on that court's order. Finally, the High Courts and District Courts could hold a judicial inquisition into whether a person was of unsound mind and incapable of managing himself and his affairs, and then appoint a guardian of his person and a manager of his estate. There was a door for people who wanted treatment, but it was narrow. A person "desirous of submitting himself to treatment" could be received as a voluntary boarder , but only on his written application and with the consent of two of the asylum's visitors (the official inspectors appointed for each asylum), and he was free to leave again on giving notice in writing. Everything else ran through magistrates, the police and the courts. Laws of this kind are described as following a custodial model : their aim is to protect society from the mentally ill person and to keep him safely confined, not to restore him to health or protect his rights. That is the model the next two Acts set out to replace. Exam trap The 1912 Act is the Indian Lunacy Act (Act IV of 1912); the 1858 law is the Indian Lunatic Asylums Act . Its key words are lunatic ("an idiot or a person of unsound mind"), asylum , reception order and magistrate . Do not assume that voluntary admission was invented in 1987: the 1912 Act already allowed voluntary boarders , though only with the consent of two visitors. The 1912 Act was repealed by the Mental Health Act 1987 , not by the 2017 Act. The Mental Health Act 1987: from lunatics to patients Soon after Independence, the Indian Psychiatric Society, formed in 1947, decided that the 1912 Act had to go, and in 1950 it sent the Government of India a draft Mental Health Bill. Nothing happened for a long time. The government began the formal process only in 1978, when a Mental Health Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha, and after years of revision Parliament passed the Mental Health Act 1987 (Act 14 of 1987), which received the President's assent on 22 May 1987. Even then the wheels turned slowly: the Mental Health Rules were framed in 1990, and the Act came into force in all the states and union territories only on 1 April 1993. Its long title called it "An Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to the treatment and care of mentally ill persons", and the word "treatment" in that title marks the change of direction. It repealed the Indian Lunacy Act 1912. What did the 1987 Act change? First, the language. The "lunatic" became a "mentally ill person", defined as a person who needs treatment because of any mental disorder other than mental retardation, and the "asylum" became a psychiatric hospital or psychiatric nursing home. Second, it created regulators: a Central Authority for Mental Health Services and a State Authority for Mental Health Services in each state, with official visitors to inspect hospitals. Third, it required psychiatric hospitals and psychiatric nursing homes, private as well as public, to be licensed, so that standards could in principle be enforced. Fourth, it made admission at the person's own request the first route into hospital. An adult could ask to be admitted as a voluntary patient (a minor through his guardian); a relative or friend could arrange admission "under special circumstances", without going to court, for a person who needed care but could not express a willingness to be admitted; and the magistrate's reception order was kept for the remaining cases. The Act also stated that a mentally ill person under treatment must not be subjected to indignity or cruelty, and it provided legal aid at state expense in some proceedings. Yet the 1987 Act was still, at heart, a law about hospitals and procedures. Commentators at the time described it as concerned mainly with licensing mental hospitals, regulating admissions and settling guardianship of the person and property, with human rights and the delivery of care treated as afterthoughts. Its procedures were complicated, and some of them, such as the requirement that certificates for admission come from a gazetted government medical officer, were hard to meet in private and general hospitals. Because it excluded mental retardation from its definition, people with severe intellectual disability had no clear place in it. It gave nobody a right to receive treatment, said nothing about community care, rehabilitation or the families who did most of the caring, and was written almost entirely around psychiatrists, medical officers and magistrates, so that clinical psychologists and other mental health professionals had no defined role. Most of all, it assumed that a person with mental illness could not decide for himself. The push to replace it came from outside psychiatry. On 13 December 2006 the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), which came into force on 3 May 2008. The Convention treats disability, including the psychosocial disability that can accompany mental illness, as the product of an interaction between a person's impairment and the barriers society puts in his way, and its Article 12 requires states to recognise that persons with disabilities enjoy legal capacity on an equal basis with others in all aspects of life. India ratified the Convention on 1 October 2007, and a state that ratifies it promises to bring its laws into line. A law built on magistrates' orders and on the assumption of incapacity plainly did not fit. Two new laws followed: the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 for disability (taught later in this section) and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 for mental health care. Exam trap Watch the spelling and the dates. The Mental Health Act (two words) was passed in 1987 but came into force only on 1 April 1993 ; the Mental Healthcare Act (one word, "Healthcare") is the 2017 law, in force from 2018. There is no "Mental Healthcare Act 1987". The RCI Act also came into force in 1993, so "1993" cannot by itself tell you which Act is meant. The 1987 Act had no advance directives, no nominated representatives and no Mental Health Review Boards; its regulators were called the Central and State Authority for Mental Health Services . The Mental Healthcare Act 2017: a rights-based law and its key definitions The new law took nearly four years to pass. The Mental Health Care Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 19 August 2013 by the Union Health Minister of the time, Ghulam Nabi Azad . The Lok Sabha passed it on 27 March 2017, it received the President's assent on 7 April 2017 as the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Act 10 of 2017), and it came into force on 29 May 2018. Section 126 repealed the Mental Health Act 1987. The Act's long title states its purpose in a single sentence that is worth knowing by heart: it is "An Act to provide for mental healthcare and services for persons with mental illness and to protect, promote and fulfil the rights of such persons during delivery of mental healthcare and services". Its preamble then recites the UNCRPD and India's ratification of it, and says that "it is necessary to align and harmonise the existing laws with the said Convention". That is why the Act is called a rights-based approach to mental health law. The 1912 and 1987 Acts asked what society may do to a person with mental illness. The 2017 Act asks what that person is entitled to, and treats every restriction on him as an exception that has to be justified, recorded and open to review. The Act runs to 126 sections in sixteen chapters. You do not need all of them, but you do need to know the shape: definitions and capacity (Chapters I and II, sections 1 to 4), advance directives (Chapter III, sections 5 to 13), nominated representatives (Chapter IV, sections 14 to 17), rights (Chapter V, sections 18 to 28), duties of government (Chapter VI, sections 29 to 32), the Central and State Mental Health Authorities (Chapters VII and VIII), the registration of mental health establishments (Chapter X), the Mental Health Review Boards (Chapter XI, sections 73 to 84), admission, treatment and discharge (Chapter XII, sections 85 to 99), the duties of the police, magistrates and prisons (Chapter XIII), offences and penalties (Chapter XV), and a miscellaneous chapter that contains section 115 on attempted suicide. The definitions in section 2. Several definitions are examined directly, and one of them defines your own profession. Mental illness (section 2(s)) is "a substantial disorder of thinking, mood, perception, orientation or memory that grossly impairs judgment, behaviour, capacity to recognise reality or ability to meet the ordinary demands of life, mental conditions associated with the abuse of alcohol and drugs, but does not include mental retardation". Two things follow. Alcohol and drug conditions are inside the Act, so a man with alcohol dependence has all its rights. Intellectual disability is outside it, and is dealt with by the disability laws later in this section. A clinical psychologist (section 2(g)) is a person with a recognised qualification in clinical psychology from an institution approved and recognised by the Rehabilitation Council of India, or a person with a postgraduate degree in psychology, clinical psychology or applied psychology together with a Master of Philosophy in Clinical Psychology or in Medical and Social Psychology, obtained after a full-time course of two years that includes supervised clinical training, from a university recognised by the University Grants Commission and approved and recognised by the RCI. The definition is tied to the RCI from both directions, which is why the new two-year RCI professional master's degrees described in Section 1.5 fit into it. A mental health professional (section 2(r)) is a psychiatrist; or a professional registered with the State Mental Health Authority under section 55, which is how clinical psychologists, mental health nurses and psychiatric social workers enter the definition; or a professional with a postgraduate degree in the mental health branch of Ayurveda, Homoeopathy, Unani or Siddha. The Act also defines the psychiatric social worker (a postgraduate degree in social work plus a two-year M.Phil in Psychiatric Social Work), the mental health nurse and the psychiatrist . Informed consent (section 2(i)) is consent for a specific intervention, given without force, undue influence, fraud, threat, mistake or misrepresentation, after the person has been told the risks, benefits and alternatives "in a language and manner understood by the person". The ethics of consent are taught in Section 1.8; here the point is that the Act turns them into law. The least restrictive alternative (section 2(j)) is the option for treatment, or the setting for it, that meets the person's needs while imposing the least restriction on his rights. Every admission against a person's wishes must be certified as the least restrictive option available. A mental health establishment (section 2(p)) is any health establishment, government or private, including Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy establishments and general hospitals, where persons with mental illness are admitted and reside for care, treatment, convalescence or rehabilitation; a family home where a person lives with relatives or friends is excluded. A minor (section 2(t)) is anyone who has not completed 18 years. Determining mental illness (section 3). Chapter 2 of this book relies on this section, so state it precisely. Mental illness is to be determined in accordance with nationally or internationally accepted medical standards, including the latest edition of the WHO's International Classification of Diseases, as notified by the Central Government. Nobody may classify a person as mentally ill except for purposes directly related to treatment or as allowed by law. Mental illness must not be determined on the basis of political, economic or social status, membership of a cultural, racial or religious group, or non-conformity with the moral, social, cultural, work or political values or religious beliefs of the person's community. Past treatment or hospitalisation, though relevant, does not by itself justify a present or future finding of mental illness. And a finding of mental illness does not mean that the person is "of unsound mind" unless a competent court has declared him so. Notice how directly this section answers the critics of psychiatric labelling whom Section 1.6 introduced. Capacity (section 4). Now comes the idea on which the whole Act stands. Every person, including a person with mental illness, "shall be deemed to have capacity" to make decisions about his mental health care or treatment if he is able to understand the information relevant to the decision, to appreciate any reasonably foreseeable consequence of making the decision or of not making it, or to communicate the decision by speech, expression, gesture or any other means. The information must be given in simple language that the person understands, or in sign language, visual aids or any other means that help him understand. Then comes the sentence that does the most work: a decision "perceived by others as inappropriate or wrong" does not by itself mean that the person lacks capacity. This is the presumption of capacity . It is not a test of whether the person agrees with his doctors. It is a test of whether he can understand, weigh and communicate (the section joins the three abilities with the word "or", though clinicians usually check all three). Section 14(9) puts the same idea in its strongest form: all persons with mental illness "shall have capacity" to make treatment decisions, but may need varying levels of support from their nominated representative to make them. This is the Act's version of supported decision-making : help the person decide, rather than decide for him. Take an example. Kamala, a 41-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, has bipolar disorder and is now well. Her psychiatrist recommends that she continue lithium; she refuses, because the weight she gained on it was humiliating at school, and she prefers another mood stabiliser that her doctor considers a little less effective. Does Kamala have capacity? She can explain what lithium does and what the alternative is, she knows that stopping it raises her risk of relapse and has weighed that risk, and she can state her decision clearly. She has capacity, and her choice stands, even though the treating team would have chosen differently. If, months later, she becomes manic, cannot follow an explanation of her treatment and cannot hold information long enough to weigh it, she may lose capacity for that decision for as long as the episode lasts. Capacity in the Act is specific to a decision and to a time; it is never a permanent label on a person. Clinical link Capacity is assessed by clinicians, and clinical psychologists are often asked to contribute: a structured interview about what the person understands of his illness, the proposed treatment and the alternatives, together with tests of attention, memory and reasoning where cognition is in doubt. Because the Act defines a registered clinical psychologist as a mental health professional , he can be one of the two professionals who examine a person for a supported admission or for the admission of a minor, and the Act even allows the mental health professional in charge of an establishment, not only the medical officer, to decide on independent admissions. Your reports may therefore end up before a Review Board, so write them as legal documents: what you asked, what the person said, and why you concluded what you did. Exam trap Under the MHCA, a clinical psychologist is defined in section 2(g) by an RCI-recognised qualification (or a postgraduate degree in psychology plus a two-year M.Phil in Clinical Psychology or Medical and Social Psychology with supervised clinical training). A clinical psychologist registered with the State Authority is a mental health professional ; so an option saying "only psychiatrists can provide therapy; psychologists are excluded" is false. The Act's "mental illness" includes conditions associated with alcohol and drug abuse but excludes mental retardation. Capacity is presumed , and a decision that others think "wrong" does not prove its absence. Advance directives and nominated representatives If capacity can come and go, a person who knows his illness may want to decide in advance what should happen when he can no longer decide. Chapter III of the Act gives him that power. Under section 5, every person who is not a minor has a right to make an advance directive in writing, specifying any or all of three things: the way he wishes to be cared for and treated for a mental illness, the way he wishes not to be cared for and treated, and the individual or individuals, in order of precedence, whom he wants to appoint as his nominated representative. He may make it irrespective of his past mental illness or treatment. The directive is invoked only when he ceases to have capacity to make mental health care or treatment decisions, and remains effective only until he regains capacity. Any decision he makes while he has capacity overrides anything he wrote earlier, and a directive that is contrary to any law in force is void from the start (so nobody can direct, for example, that he be given a treatment the Act prohibits). The rest of the chapter makes the directive work. The manner of making it is laid down in regulations of the Central Mental Health Authority (section 6). Every Mental Health Review Board keeps an online register of the advance directives registered with it and makes them available to the professionals concerned (section 7). The person may revoke, amend or cancel his directive at any time (section 8). It does not apply to emergency treatment (section 9). The medical officer in charge and the psychiatrist in charge have a duty to treat the person in accordance with his valid directive (section 10). If a mental health professional, a relative or a care-giver does not want to follow it, he cannot simply ignore it: he must apply to the Board, which hears everyone, including the person who made the directive, and then upholds, modifies or cancels it after asking whether it was made freely, whether the person intended it to apply to the present circumstances, whether he was well informed, whether he had capacity when he made it, and whether it is contrary to law (section 11). The same section gives the legal guardian of a minor the right to make an advance directive for the minor. The Central Authority reviews how directives are being used (section 12), and a professional is not liable for unforeseen consequences of following a valid directive, nor for failing to follow one of which he was not given a copy (section 13). Return to Kamala. While she is well she writes a directive: if she becomes manic she wishes to be treated at a named hospital in Mysuru, with the mood stabiliser she prefers; she does not wish to be given a particular antipsychotic that once made her dangerously stiff; and she names her sister as her nominated representative, with her husband second. She registers it with the Board. Two years later she is admitted in a manic episode, and the team find that she cannot follow an explanation of her treatment. The directive is now invoked. Her husband, alarmed, wants her moved to a different hospital and given the drug she refused. He cannot overrule her written wishes by himself; his remedy is an application to the Board under section 11. And the day Kamala recovers capacity, her own current decisions replace the directive again. The second new figure in the Act is the nominated representative . Under section 14, every person who is not a minor has a right to appoint one, in writing on plain paper, signed or thumb-printed. The nominated representative must not be a minor, must be competent to do the job, and must consent in writing. If the person has not appointed anyone, the Act supplies one in a fixed order of precedence: the individual named in his advance directive; otherwise a relative; otherwise a care-giver; otherwise a suitable person appointed by the Board; and if nobody is available, the Director of the Department of Social Welfare (or his representative), appointed by the Board. While the Board is deciding, a representative of a registered organisation working for persons with mental illness may act temporarily. The person can revoke or change the appointment at any time. Two sub-sections guard against the old assumption of incapacity: appointing a nominated representative, or being unable to appoint one, does not mean that the person lacks capacity (section 14(8)); and every person with mental illness has capacity, though he may need support from his representative to use it (section 14(9)). For minors the rule is different. Section 15 makes the legal guardian the nominated representative of a minor, unless the Board, on an application by a mental health professional or anyone acting in the minor's best interests, finds that the guardian is not acting in those interests or is otherwise unfit, and appoints someone else (or, failing anyone, the state's Director of Social Welfare). A minor therefore cannot appoint his own nominated representative, just as he cannot make his own advance directive. What does the nominated representative actually do? Section 17 lists the duties, and they describe a supporter, not a master. He must consider the person's current and past wishes, life history, values, cultural background and best interests; give particular credence to the person's own views to the extent that the person understands the decision; support the person in making treatment decisions during a supported admission; seek information on diagnosis and treatment; have access to family-based or home-based rehabilitation services on the person's behalf; be involved in discharge planning; apply for admission and, to the Board, for discharge; complain to the Board about violations of the person's rights; appoint an attendant for an admitted minor; and give or withhold consent for research in the limited cases the Act allows. Only in one situation does he decide for the person: when a person in supported admission needs "nearly hundred per cent" support to make a treatment decision, the representative may temporarily consent to the treatment plan on his behalf, and the person's capacity must then be reviewed at regular intervals (you will meet this rule again under admissions). Exam trap Advance directive (section 5) and nominated representative (section 14) both come from the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 . They are not in the Mental Health Act 1987, which had neither; not in the RPwD Act 2016, whose decision-making tool is limited guardianship (its section 14); and not in the RCI Act 1992, which is about training and registering professionals. Advance directives are registered with the Mental Health Review Board , are invoked only when capacity is lost , and do not apply to emergency treatment. Section numbers to keep apart: section 5 is the advance directive, section 14 the nominated representative, section 15 the nominated representative of a minor. Exam trap A 2024 paper asked which statement on the treatment of minors under the MHCA is accurate, and keyed: "A minor has the right to appoint a nominated representative, and their opinion on treatment must be considered in an age-appropriate manner." Only the second half is right. Section 14 gives the right to appoint a nominated representative to "every person who is not a minor", and section 15 makes the legal guardian the minor's nominated representative. What the Act does require is that the minor's wishes be taken into account: admission must be in his best interests "taking into account the wishes of the minor if ascertainable" (section 87). Pick the keyed option as the best of those offered, because the others are wrong: admission does not need the Board's prior consent (the Board is told within 72 hours and reviews admissions lasting beyond 30 days); the option giving the nominated representative "all decisions" overstates his power, because although an admitted minor is treated with the representative's informed consent (section 87), the representative must give particular credence to the minor's views (section 17), ECT for a minor also needs the Board's prior permission (section 95), and the Board can replace an unfit guardian (section 15); and a minor certainly can be admitted against his own wishes on the guardian's application if the conditions of section 87 are met. In a written answer or an interview, say the law correctly. The rights of persons with mental illness and the duties of government Chapter V is the heart of the Act: eleven sections, ten of whose headings begin with the word "right" (the eleventh, section 24, restricts the release of information to the media). The first is the most far-reaching. Section 18 gives every person a right to access mental healthcare and treatment from mental health services run or funded by the government, and spells out what "access" means: services of affordable cost and good quality, in sufficient quantity, geographically accessible, provided without discrimination on the basis of gender, sex, sexual orientation, religion, culture, caste, social or political beliefs, class or disability, and acceptable to persons with mental illness and their families. The services must range from outpatient and inpatient care to halfway homes, sheltered and supported accommodation, support for families, home-based and community rehabilitation, and child and old-age mental health services. Government must integrate mental health into general health care at every level; use long-term institutional care only as a last resort; make at least minimum services available in every district (and pay for treatment elsewhere where they are not); provide basic and emergency care at all community health centres and above; treat people below the poverty line, the destitute and the homeless free of charge; and supply the medicines on an Essential Drug List free at government facilities. A right with duties attached is no longer a hope; it is a claim that can be taken to the Board or the courts. The other rights follow quickly. The right to community living (section 19) is the right to live in, be part of and not be segregated from society, and it forbids keeping anyone in a mental health establishment merely because he has no family, is not accepted by his family, is homeless or lacks community facilities; the government must create less restrictive alternatives such as halfway homes and group homes. Chapter 9 shows what this means for rehabilitation services. The right to protection from cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (section 20) begins with a right to live with dignity and lists what dignity means inside an institution: a safe and hygienic environment, privacy, proper clothing and the right to wear one's own clothes rather than a uniform, leisure, education and religious practice, wholesome food and sanitation including items needed during menstruation, freedom from forced work (and pay for work done), freedom from compulsory tonsuring (shaving of the head), and protection from physical, verbal, emotional and sexual abuse. The right to equality and non-discrimination (section 21) requires that persons with mental illness be treated as equal to persons with physical illness in emergency services, ambulances and living conditions; that a child under three be ordinarily kept with a mother receiving inpatient care; and, in a provision that changed the insurance industry, that every insurer provide medical insurance for mental illness "on the same basis" as for physical illness, which is called insurance parity . The remaining rights concern information and contact. A person and his nominated representative have a right to information about the provision under which he is admitted, his right to apply to the Board, and the nature of his illness and its proposed treatment with its known side effects, in a language he understands (section 22). He has a right to confidentiality, subject to listed exceptions such as release to his nominated representative or treating professionals, to protect another person from harm or violence, to prevent a threat to life, or on the order of a Board or court (section 23); no photograph or information about him may be released to the media without his consent (section 24); and he may see his basic medical records, unless disclosure would cause serious mental harm to him or make harm to others likely (section 25). Chapter 2 teaches sections 22, 23 and 25 in the setting of assessment and record keeping, and Section 1.8 sets them beside the ethical rules on confidentiality. The list ends with rights to personal contacts and communication (section 26), to free legal services (section 27), and to complain about deficiencies in care, first to the officer in charge, then to the Board and then to the State Authority (section 28). Rights mean little unless someone must deliver them, so Chapter VI places duties on the "appropriate Government" (the Central Government for its own establishments, the State Government for the rest): to run programmes that promote mental health, prevent mental illness and in particular reduce suicides and attempted suicides (section 29); to publicise the Act and fund anti-stigma programmes (section 30); to train all medical officers in public health facilities and prisons to give basic and emergency mental health care, and to try to meet international norms for the number of mental health professionals within ten years (section 31); and to coordinate the ministries concerned (section 32). Exam trap Match the right to its section: 18 access to mental healthcare (the flagship right), 19 community living, 20 protection from cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment, 21 equality and non-discrimination (including insurance parity in section 21(4)), 22 information, 23 confidentiality, 25 access to medical records, 27 legal aid, 28 complaints. "Right to information" (what my illness is and how it will be treated) is not the same as "right to access medical records" (seeing the file). Free treatment is guaranteed to people below the poverty line "whether or not in possession of a below poverty line card", and to the destitute and homeless. Authorities, Review Boards and the registration of professionals and establishments A rights-based law needs institutions to enforce it, and the Act creates three. The Central Mental Health Authority (Chapter VII) is chaired by the Secretary or Additional Secretary of the Department of Health and Family Welfare. Besides officials of several ministries and the directors of the central mental health institutions, its members include one clinical psychologist, one psychiatric social worker and one mental health nurse, each with at least fifteen years' experience, and representatives of persons who have had mental illness, of care-givers and of non-governmental organisations. Under section 43 it registers mental health establishments under the Central Government and keeps a national register of all establishments, sets quality norms, supervises central establishments and receives complaints about them, keeps a national register of clinical psychologists, mental health nurses and psychiatric social workers based on state registrations, trains officials and professionals in the Act, and advises the Central Government. Each state has a State Mental Health Authority (Chapter VIII), similarly composed (it too has a clinical psychologist with fifteen years' experience among its members), which must meet at least four times a year. Under section 55 it registers all mental health establishments in the state other than central ones, sets norms, supervises them and receives complaints, and, most important for you, registers clinical psychologists, mental health nurses and psychiatric social workers in the state to work as mental health professionals . This is the registration that makes a clinical psychologist a "mental health professional" within the Act. It is separate from registration with the RCI, which the RCI Act requires before anyone may practise as a clinical psychologist at all (taught later in this section). Section 65 then requires that no person or organisation establish or run a mental health establishment unless it is registered with the relevant Authority. The Central Government may exempt notified categories of existing establishments, but there is no blanket exemption for government hospitals. Running an unregistered establishment attracts a penalty that starts at 5,000 to 50,000 rupees and rises to five lakh rupees for repeated contraventions, and a professional who knowingly works in one can be fined up to 25,000 rupees (section 107). The third institution is the one you will meet in practice. The Mental Health Review Board (Chapter XI) is constituted by the State Authority for a district or a group of districts. Under section 74 each Board consists of a District Judge (or an officer qualified to be one, or a retired District Judge) as chairperson; a representative of the District Collector or District Magistrate; a psychiatrist and a medical practitioner; and two members who are persons with mental illness, care-givers, or representatives of their organisations or of non-governmental organisations working in mental health. Applications to it are free and may be made by the person, his nominated representative or a registered non-governmental organisation with his consent, in exceptional cases even orally or by telephone. Its proceedings are judicial proceedings, held in camera at the establishment where the person is admitted. The Act sets deadlines: challenges to a minor's admission or to a supported admission of up to 30 days, and applications to appoint a nominated representative, must be decided within seven days; challenges to supported admission beyond 30 days within twenty-one days; everything else within ninety days (section 80). The Board's powers (section 82) gather together everything you have read so far: to register, review, alter, modify or cancel advance directives; to appoint nominated representatives; to hear challenges against the decisions of establishments under sections 87, 89 and 90 (the admission of minors and supported admissions); to decide on information withheld from medical records under section 25; to adjudicate complaints about deficiencies in care under section 28; and to visit and inspect prisons and question their medical officers. Where an establishment ignores its orders, the Board or Authority may fine it up to five lakh rupees and recommend cancellation of its registration. Appeals against orders of a Board or Authority go to the High Court (section 83). Table 1.24 gathers the three bodies together. Table 1.24 The three bodies that run the Mental Healthcare Act 2017. Its six members are the judge, the Collector's representative, a psychiatrist , a medical practitioner and two members representing service users or care-givers ; a clinical psychologist sits on the Central and State Authorities but is not one of the Board's prescribed members. A question option saying that "mental health establishments are exempt from registration if government-run" is false: section 65 requires every establishment to be registered with the Central or State Authority, and only the Central Government can exempt a notified category of existing establishments. Admission, treatment and discharge Chapter XII answers the questions with which this section began. Its first rule sets the tone: all admissions shall, as far as possible, be independent admissions, except when conditions make a supported admission unavoidable (section 85). The Act knows four routes into hospital and one route to treatment outside it, and Figure 1.16 shows how they fit together. Independent admission (sections 85, 86 and 88). An independent admission is the admission of a person who has the capacity to make mental health care and treatment decisions or who needs only minimal support to make them. An adult who believes he has a mental illness and wants to be admitted asks the medical officer or mental health professional in charge, who admits him if the illness is severe enough to need admission, he is likely to benefit, and he has understood the nature and purpose of admission and asked of his own free will. A person who needs support "approaching hundred per cent" cannot be admitted this way. The independent patient may not be treated without his informed consent, needs nobody else's consent or presence to be admitted, and may discharge himself. There is one brake. If a mental health professional believes that the person cannot understand his decisions and needs very high support, or has recently threatened or attempted self-harm, behaved violently or caused others to fear harm, or shown an inability to care for himself that puts him at risk, he may prevent discharge for up to 24 hours so that the person can be assessed for a supported admission (section 88). Admission of a minor (section 87). A minor can be admitted only by this procedure. His nominated representative (the legal guardian) applies; two psychiatrists, or one psychiatrist and one mental health professional, or one psychiatrist and one medical practitioner, must examine him independently on the day of admission or in the preceding seven days and both conclude that he has a mental illness severe enough to need admission, that admission is in his best interests "taking into account the wishes of the minor if ascertainable", that his needs cannot be met without admission, and that community alternatives have failed or are unsuitable. He must be housed separately from adults, in surroundings suited to his age. The nominated representative, or an attendant he appoints, must stay with him throughout, and a female attendant must stay with a girl whose representative is male. Treatment is given with the representative's informed consent, and the minor must be discharged if the representative withdraws support. The Board must be told of every admission of a minor within 72 hours, may visit and interview him, must be told if the admission reaches 30 days, and must then review it within seven days and every 30 days after that. Supported admission up to 30 days (section 89). A supported admission is the Act's name for admission without the person's own consent, and its conditions are tight. The nominated representative applies. One psychiatrist and one other mental health professional or medical practitioner must independently examine the person on the day of admission or in the preceding seven days, and both must conclude that his mental illness is so severe that he has recently threatened or attempted (or is threatening or attempting) to harm himself, or has recently behaved violently towards another person or caused another person to fear bodily harm from him, or has recently shown an inability to care for himself that places him at risk of harm. They must also certify, after taking account of any advance directive, that admission is the least restrictive option possible, and the person must be unable to make treatment decisions independently, needing very high support from his representative. Treatment then takes account of his advance directive, or of his informed consent given with his representative's support; only when he needs "nearly hundred per cent" support may the representative temporarily consent on his behalf, and his capacity must then be reviewed every seven days. The establishment must report the admission to the Board within three days for a woman or a minor and within seven days for anyone else; the person, his representative or an NGO acting with his consent may ask the Board to review it, and the Board must give a binding decision within seven days. The admission ends after 30 days, or earlier if the criteria cease to apply, when the person may stay on as an independent patient; a person discharged from a supported admission cannot be readmitted under the same section within seven days. Supported admission beyond 30 days (section 90). If longer inpatient care is needed, two psychiatrists must examine the person and find that the danger to self or others, or the inability to care for himself, has been present "consistently over time"; that admission remains the least restrictive option; and that he still needs very high support. The admission must be reported to the Board within seven days, and the Board must permit it or order discharge within twenty-one days, after asking whether institutional care is really needed and whether care in a less restrictive community setting is possible. The Board may demand a plan for community-based treatment, and nobody may be kept in hospital merely because community services do not exist where he lives. Such admissions run for up to 90 days at first, then up to 120 days, and then up to 180 days at a time, each extension requiring the same procedure. Where the representative is consenting on the person's behalf, capacity is reviewed every fortnight. Emergency treatment (section 94). Outside these admissions, any registered medical practitioner may give emergency treatment, at a health establishment or in the community, with the informed consent of the nominated representative where one is available, when it is immediately necessary to prevent death or irreversible harm to the person's health, serious harm by the person to himself or others, or serious damage to property flowing directly from his mental illness. Emergency treatment includes taking the person to the nearest mental health establishment for assessment. It is limited to 72 hours or until the person has been assessed at an establishment, whichever is earlier (up to seven days during a declared disaster), it may not include treatment unrelated to the emergency, and it may never include electroconvulsive therapy.
