Ravi, 24, male, Hindu, Kannada-speaking, unmarried, B.Com, unemployed (preparing for bank examinations), lower-middle socioeconomic status, from a village near Mandya; lives in a shared rented room in Mysuru. Self-referred with his mother. Informants: Ravi; his mother (46), who speaks to him daily and has stayed with him for the past ten days. Information reliable and adequate. Chief complaints (Ravi): "I feel useless", 3 months; "I can't sleep", 3 months; "nothing goes into my head", 3 months. (Mother): stays in his room and eats little, 2 months; said everyone would be better off without him, 1 week. History of present illness. Onset subacute, over two to three weeks after the bank examination result three months ago; course continuous; progress deteriorating. Precipitants: third failure, in the week his cousin was selected; his father's repeated comparisons. Low mood most of the day, worse in the mornings; loss of interest in studies and in cricket; waking at 3 a.m.; appetite reduced, weight loss of about 5 kg; tiredness; guilt that his parents pledged his mother's gold to pay his coaching fees; hopelessness; a passive wish to be dead, with no plan and no attempt. Stopped going home at weekends two months ago. Negative history: no elated periods, no hearing voices, no head injury, seizures or fever, no alcohol or tobacco. Treatment: a general practitioner prescribed vitamins; his mother made a vow at the village temple. Past history. About a month of sadness and withdrawal at 17 after his second PUC results, which passed without treatment. No significant medical illness. Family history (Figure 2.2): parents are first cousins; maternal uncle treated for depression; paternal grandfather drank heavily. Father critical and proud, mother warm; younger sister studying nursing. Personal history: full-term hospital delivery, milestones normal; nail-biting in childhood; Kannada-medium schooling with high marks ("the bright one" of the family); B.Com first class; six months as an accounts assistant in a cooperative society; heterosexual, no relationships; no substance use; no forensic history. Premorbid personality (from Ravi and his mother): conscientious, perfectionistic, self-critical, shy, a few close friends, devout, usually even in mood, a dutiful eldest son who took criticism to heart. Notice what the history has already done. Before a single question about his present mental state, it has set out a likely sequence (a vulnerable, perfectionistic young man, a family history of depression, a humiliating failure inside a family that measures worth by results), suggested a diagnosis to test (a depressive episode, possibly recurrent), raised a risk to assess (the passive wish to be dead) and flagged something to check (thyroid function and haemoglobin, because tiredness and weight loss have medical causes too). What it cannot tell us is how Ravi is now, in this room. For that the clinician turns from the film to the photograph. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Sullivan's four stages of the interview are the formal inception, reconnaissance, the detailed inquiry and the . When two clinicians reach different diagnoses because they asked different questions, the disagreement is called variance. A semi-structured interview developed for DSM diagnoses is the ; a fully structured interview built for lay interviewers in epidemiology is the . Leaning forward, nodding and saying "umm" are examples of . Restating what the client said in different words is . Voicing what the client has only hinted at is empathy, which is inappropriate in a first session. The tendency to let one salient attribute colour judgements of everything else about a person is the effect. A multigenerational family diagram with squares for males and circles for females is a ; a map of who interacts with whom in a group is a . The person's characteristic way of thinking, feeling and relating before the illness began is the personality. An illness that develops gradually over months has an onset. Answers: (1) termination, (2) information, (3) SCID; DIS (or CIDI), (4) furthering (minimal encouragers), (5) paraphrasing, (6) advanced, (7) halo, (8) genogram; sociogram, (9) premorbid, (10) insidious. 2.4 The Mental Status Examination I: Appearance, Behaviour, Speech, Mood and Affect Lower yield · 1 Q When the clinician called Ravi's name in the waiting room, he did not look up at once. He rose slowly, walked in a step behind his mother, sat on the edge of the chair with his shoulders rounded and his hands pressed between his knees, and studied the floor. His shirt was clean but creased, his chin unshaven. Asked how he was, he paused for several seconds and said, very quietly, "Okay." Nobody had asked him a single question about his symptoms, and the clinician had already started writing his mental status examination. Section 2.1 defined the mental status examination (MSE) as the clinician's systematic description of the client's appearance, behaviour, speech, emotion, thinking, perception and cognition at the time of the interview, and Section 2.3 contrasted it, as a photograph, with the film of the case history. This section and the next two take the photograph apart, heading by heading. This section deals with everything the clinician can observe or hear in the first few minutes: how the person looks, moves and talks, and what he feels. Section 2.5 turns to what he thinks and perceives, and Section 2.6 to cognition, judgement and insight, and to writing the whole thing up. Describing, not diagnosing Why does a clinician need a special vocabulary to describe what a patient looks like and says? Because ordinary words blur exactly the distinctions that matter. "He was confused" might mean that he did not know the date, that his sentences did not hang together, that he was puzzled by his own experiences or that he was drowsy, and each points to a different problem. The precise vocabulary used in the MSE comes largely from one book. In 1913 a young psychiatrist at Heidelberg, Karl Jaspers (1883 to 1969), published General Psychopathology . Jaspers argued that before psychiatry could explain mental illness it had to describe it, accurately and without theory, and that the only way to describe experiences the clinician cannot see (a voice, a conviction, a sense that the world has become unreal) is to question the patient carefully and empathically until the clinician can picture what the experience is actually like from the inside. He called this method phenomenology. The discipline it founded, the precise description of abnormal experience and behaviour without commitment to any theory of its cause, is descriptive psychopathology , and it is the language in which every MSE is written. (Jaspers later left psychiatry for philosophy and became one of the leading existentialist philosophers.) Jaspers also drew a distinction that runs through the rest of this chapter: between the form of an experience and its content . The form is its structure: is this a perception, a belief, a memory, an image? The content is what it is about. If Ravi heard a voice saying "you have failed everyone", the form would be an auditory hallucination and the content would be failure. The content tells you about the person and his life (a Mandya farmer's son who has failed his examinations will hear about failure, a devout woman about sin); the form tells you what kind of disturbance you are dealing with. Diagnosis depends mostly on form. Three working rules follow from Jaspers' approach. First, describe; do not label . "Sat with head bowed, answered in a whisper after long pauses, wept twice while speaking of his father" can be checked, compared with next week's examination and understood by any reader; "depressed" is already a conclusion. Second, record the here and now . The MSE is cross-sectional: what the patient shows and reports at this examination (for experiences such as voices or fears, the clinician also asks about the last few days). The history of how the illness developed belongs in the case history. Third, give examples , and wherever possible quote the patient's own words. The MSE records two kinds of information: signs , which the clinician observes (tearfulness, slowed movement, a tremor), and symptoms , which the patient reports (low mood, hearing voices). Many headings need both. The headings themselves follow a fixed order, shown in Table 2.4. It moves from what can be observed without asking (appearance, behaviour, speech) through what must be asked about (mood, thought, perception) to what must be formally tested (cognition), and ends with the patient's understanding of his own condition. British trainees often remember the headings with the mnemonic ASEPTIC: Appearance and behaviour, Speech, Emotion (mood and affect), Perception, Thought, Insight and judgement, Cognition. American texts often compress the MSE further; Barlow and Durand, for example, describe five categories: appearance and behaviour, thought processes, mood and affect, intellectual functioning and sensorium (awareness of the surroundings, which Section 2.6 calls consciousness and orientation). The contents are the same; only the packaging differs. Table 2.4 The headings of the mental status examination, in the order used in most Indian case records. Heading The question it answers Taught in General appearance and behaviour What does the person look like and how does he behave and relate to me? 2.4 Psychomotor activity Is movement increased, decreased or abnormal? 2.4 Speech How does he talk: rate, volume, tone, amount, latency, coherence? 2.4 Mood and affect What does he say he feels, and what emotion do I see? 2.4 Thought Stream, form, content and possession of thought 2.5 Perception Hallucinations, illusions, depersonalisation and derealisation 2.5 Cognitive functions Consciousness, orientation, attention, memory, intelligence, abstraction 2.6 Judgement and insight Can he judge sensibly, and does he know he is ill? 2.6 Exam trap The MSE is cross-sectional (the present state); the case history is longitudinal . A sign is observed by the clinician; a symptom is reported by the patient. Descriptive psychopathology and the phenomenological method go back to Karl Jaspers' General Psychopathology (1913), who also taught that form , not content, is what matters most for diagnosis. In older American usage "sensorium" means awareness of the surroundings (consciousness and orientation), not the sense organs. General appearance and behaviour The examination starts with what a stranger would notice, organised so that nothing is missed. The clinician records: Apparent age compared with the stated age. Looking much older than one's years suggests long-standing alcohol dependence, chronic physical or mental illness, severe depression or a hard life; looking much younger is less common and is worth a note. Build and nourishment. Thin and wasted (anorexia nervosa, severe depression, self-neglect, physical illness), obese (some antipsychotic and other medicines cause marked weight gain), or showing recent weight loss: a belt pulled to a new hole, a collar that has become too loose. Grooming, hygiene and dress. Well kempt or unkempt; clean or dirty; dressed appropriately for age, sex, season, setting and culture. A man in mania may arrive in a bright shirt with a garland and three rings, talking to everyone in the corridor; a woman with chronic schizophrenia may have uncut nails, matted hair and a body odour she does not notice; a person with dementia may have buttoned his shirt wrongly; a girl with anorexia nervosa may be wearing several loose layers that hide her body; long sleeves in the Mysuru summer can hide the scars of self-harm. Facial expression. Sad, anxious, angry, vacant, perplexed (bewildered, as if trying to make sense of something strange, common early in an acute psychosis and in delirium), smiling to himself, or mask-like and unblinking, as in parkinsonism. Posture and gait. Slumped, stooped, rigid, tense on the edge of the chair, or holding an odd posture (see psychomotor activity below). Physical signs : scars, cuts and burns (note where, how old, how many), injection marks, tremor, the smell of alcohol, a goitre or yellowed eyes. The MSE is not a physical examination, but it should not ignore one in front of it. Hallucinatory behaviour : muttering, smiling or laughing to himself, pausing in mid-sentence as if listening, turning towards a corner of the room, answering when no one has spoken, putting cotton in his ears. These are recorded as observations ("appeared to be listening and muttered in reply twice during the interview"); whether he is actually hallucinating is asked about later (Section 2.5). Level of consciousness , noted in passing: alert, drowsy, fluctuating. Its formal assessment belongs to the cognitive examination (Section 2.6). Every one of these observations has to be read against the person's culture and circumstances, and Indian clinics test this constantly. Vibhuti or kumkum on the forehead, a sacred thread, a black thread or a tabeez worn against the evil eye, a burqa, an uncut beard, a saree draped in the village style or old, much-mended clothes are not eccentricities and not signs of neglect. The useful distinction is between poverty and self-neglect: old clothes that are clean and carefully worn tell you about the family's income; unwashed clothes on a person whose family is well off tell you about the person. Exam trap The MSE records what is observed , so "hallucinatory behaviour" (muttering, smiling to self, listening postures) is noted under appearance and behaviour, while the patient's report of hearing voices goes under perception. "Perplexity" is a facial expression of bewilderment, not a disorder of thought. And remember the cultural rule: religious marks, traditional dress and poverty are not evidence of psychopathology. Attitude towards the examiner, eye contact and rapport The next heading records how the person relates to the clinician. The common descriptions are cooperative, uncooperative, guarded (answers cautiously, gives little away), suspicious (watches the clinician, asks why notes are being taken), hostile or irritable, evasive (avoids certain topics), defensive, ingratiating (eager to please), seductive, over-familiar or disinhibited (calls the clinician by his first name, comments on his clothes, as is common in mania), demanding, and indifferent or apathetic (shows little interest in the interview at all). These are not character judgements. A suspicious attitude may be the first clue to a persecutory belief, an over-familiar one to an elevated mood, an indifferent one to the negative symptoms of a psychosis or to severe depression, and a guarded one simply to a teenager brought by his parents. The clinician's own reaction is information too: feeling irritated, bored, protective or oddly uneasy with a client is worth noticing, though not writing into the record as fact. Eye contact is recorded here: maintained, avoided (eyes down, as in depression, shame or social anxiety), fleeting, staring, or wandering around the room (as in a distractible manic patient or a hallucinating one). Section 2.2 warned that SOLER's "good eye contact" is a cultural rule, and the warning applies to the MSE as well: a young village woman who keeps her eyes lowered before a male doctor is following a social convention. Finally the clinician grades rapport , using the scale you met in Section 2.2: established easily, established with difficulty, or not established. With Ravi it came slowly; he answered more freely after the first fifteen minutes, and his eyes rose from the floor when he talked about cricket. Psychomotor activity and abnormal movements Psychomotor activity is the overall amount and speed of a person's bodily movement, which in mental illness rises and falls with the speed of mental activity. When it is increased, the clinician distinguishes two patterns. Psychomotor agitation is excessive, purposeless motor activity driven by inner tension: hand-wringing, pacing, picking at the skin or clothes, being unable to sit still, getting up and sitting down again. It is common in agitated depression, severe anxiety and delirium. The overactivity of mania is different: it is purposeful but excessive and distractible, a person starting ten tasks and finishing none. When activity is decreased, the term is psychomotor retardation : slowed movement and speech, few spontaneous gestures, a long delay before each answer, an effortful, heavy quality to everything. Barlow and Durand note it as a sign of severe depression, and it is also seen in hypothyroidism and parkinsonism. At its extreme lies stupor , an absence of voluntary movement and speech in a person who is not unconscious (the eyes may follow the examiner, and the patient may later recall what was said). Stupor can be depressive, catatonic, dissociative or organic, and it is a medical emergency, because the patient is not eating or drinking. Some abnormal movements form a cluster with a long history. The German psychiatrist Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum (1828 to 1899) described catatonia in 1874 as a syndrome of motor signs: stupor and mutism alternating with excitement, strange postures, rigidity and imitation. The German psychiatrist Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926) later folded catatonia into his concept of dementia praecox, and for most of the twentieth century it was treated as a subtype of schizophrenia. DSM-5 (2013) abandoned that view. Catatonia is now recognised as a syndrome that occurs with depressive and bipolar disorders, with psychotic disorders and with medical conditions, and DSM-5-TR requires three or more of the twelve signs in Table 2.5 to diagnose it. Several are tested at the bedside. To test for waxy flexibility , the examiner gently moves the patient's arm and feels a slight, even resistance, like bending a candle; in catalepsy a posture that the examiner has placed the patient in is then held against gravity, sometimes for minutes. Older Indian and British texts add further signs: automatic obedience (doing whatever one is told, regardless of consequences), mitgehen (moving a limb in whatever direction the examiner's lightest touch suggests, even after being told to resist), and ambitendency (beginning a movement and stopping it, over and over, as if two opposed impulses were at work). Table 2.5 The twelve signs of catatonia in DSM-5-TR (three or more are needed), with what the clinician sees. Sign What the clinician sees Stupor No psychomotor activity; not actively relating to the surroundings Catalepsy A posture placed by the examiner is held against gravity Waxy flexibility Slight, even resistance when the examiner moves a limb Mutism No, or very little, speech (not due to aphasia) Negativism Opposes or does not respond to instructions Posturing Spontaneously holds a posture against gravity Mannerism Odd, caricatured version of a normal, goal-directed action Stereotypy Repetitive, abnormally frequent movement with no goal Agitation Excitement not influenced by external stimuli (catatonic excitement) Grimacing Fixed or repeated distorted facial expressions Echolalia Repeats the examiner's words Echopraxia Imitates the examiner's movements Notice the difference between two signs that students often confuse. A mannerism is a normal, goal-directed action performed in an odd, stilted or exaggerated way: a man who salutes every time he picks up a glass, or who writes his name with an elaborate flourish of the whole arm. A stereotypy is a repetitive movement with no goal at all: rocking, rubbing the same spot on the thigh for an hour, tapping in a fixed rhythm. Mannerisms decorate purposeful acts; stereotypies replace them. Both differ from a tic , a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic movement or vocalisation (a blink, a shoulder shrug, a sniff) that the person feels as an urge and can suppress only briefly, and from a compulsion , a repetitive act (washing, checking, touching) that the person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety or prevent a feared event. Catatonic excitement, too, is a motor sign: purposeless, excessive activity unconnected with anything around the patient. It is not one of the first-rank symptoms of Section 2.5. Finally, the clinician looks for movements that are caused by treatment, because they are easily mistaken for psychopathology. Antipsychotic medicines can cause an acute dystonia (a sudden, painful muscle spasm that twists the neck or rolls the eyes upwards, usually within days of starting); akathisia , a subjective inner restlessness with an inability to keep still, the patient shifting from foot to foot and crossing and uncrossing his legs; drug-induced parkinsonism , with tremor, rigidity, a shuffling gait and a mask-like face; and, after long use, tardive dyskinesia , involuntary movements of the mouth, tongue and face such as lip-smacking, chewing and tongue protrusion. Akathisia is the dangerous one to miss: it looks like agitation, and if the dose of the drug causing it is increased, the restlessness gets worse. The parkinsonian mask is the other trap, because a face that cannot move looks like an emotion that is not there (see affect, below). Exam trap Waxy flexibility is the slight, even resistance felt as the examiner moves the limb; catalepsy is holding a posture the examiner has imposed; posturing is holding a posture the patient chose himself. A mannerism is an odd version of a goal-directed act; a stereotypy is a repetitive act with no goal. Echolalia echoes words, echopraxia echoes movements. Catatonia was described by Kahlbaum (1874), not Kraepelin or Bleuler, and in DSM-5-TR it is not tied to schizophrenia. Akathisia (a drug side effect) can masquerade as psychomotor agitation, and psychomotor agitation is a sign, not a disorder of thought. Speech The clinician listens to how the person speaks before attending to what he says, because the physical characteristics of speech change early in many conditions and are hard to fake. The usual dimensions are set out in Table 2.6. Table 2.6 The dimensions of speech recorded in the MSE. Dimension Normal description Abnormal descriptions Rate (speed) Normal rate Slow; rapid; pressured Volume (intensity) Audible Loud; soft; whispering Tone, pitch, prosody Normally modulated Monotonous; high-pitched; hoarse Quantity (productivity) Adequate Increased; poverty of speech; mutism Spontaneity Spontaneous Speaks only when questioned Reaction time (latency) Normal Increased; decreased Ease, articulation Fluent, clear Hesitant; stammering; slurred (dysarthria) Relevance, coherence, goal Relevant, coherent, goal-directed Irrelevant; incoherent; not goal-directed Take them in turn. Rate may be slow, as in depression, dementia and hypothyroidism, or rapid, as in mania, anxiety and hyperthyroidism. Pressure of speech is speech that is rapid, increased in amount, often loud, and difficult or impossible to interrupt: the patient talks over the clinician's questions and keeps going after the interview has ended. It is the speech of mania. Volume ranges from loud (excitement, mania, some hearing loss) to soft and barely audible (depression, shyness, a suspicious patient who does not want to be overheard). Tone and prosody concern the melody of speech: the rise and fall of pitch, the stress and rhythm that carry emotion and meaning. Normal speech is modulated; speech that stays on one note is monotonous, as in depression, the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and parkinsonism. Quantity is how much the person says. At one extreme is a flood of talk; at the other is poverty of speech (also called alogia or laconic speech), in which replies are brief, often a single word, and nothing is offered spontaneously ("How have you been?" "Fine." "And your sleep?" "Bad."). Complete absence of speech is mutism , seen in stupor, catatonia, severe depression and some dissociative states; in children who speak freely at home but not at school it is selective mutism. Closely related is spontaneity : does the person ever volunteer anything, or speak only when questioned? Reaction time , or latency, is the time between the end of the question and the beginning of the answer. It is increased in depression, in hypothyroidism and in some patients with schizophrenia, who may pause so long that the clinician wonders whether the question was heard. It is decreased in mania, where the patient may start answering before the question is finished. Ravi's latencies were several seconds long, and the clinician noted that they shortened as rapport grew. Next come ease and articulation . Speech may be hesitant, stammered, or slurred. Dysarthria is a difficulty in articulating words (the speech is slurred, thick or poorly formed) because of a problem with the muscles of speech or their nerve supply, as in intoxication, cerebellar disease, stroke or some drug side effects; the language itself is intact. It must be kept separate from dysphasia (or aphasia), a disorder of language in which the person has trouble finding, choosing or understanding words, because of damage to the language areas of the brain (taught in the Physiological Psychology book). A patient with dysarthria says the right words badly; a patient with dysphasia says the wrong words clearly. Last come relevance, coherence and goal-directedness : whether the answers address the questions asked, whether the speech hangs together as connected discourse, and whether it reaches its point. These three are where speech shades into thought. The clinician cannot see thinking; he infers it from speech. When the answers wander, never arrive, or make no sense, the disturbance is recorded under the form of thought (Section 2.5), with a verbatim sample. A few unusual patterns of speech are worth knowing by name. Verbigeration is the meaningless repetition of the same words or phrases, sometimes for hours, seen in chronic schizophrenia and catatonia. Palilalia is the repetition of one's own last words or phrases, often faster and faster, seen in parkinsonism and other brain disease. Echolalia, repeating the examiner's words, is one of the catatonic signs. Rhyming and punning are common in mania. And talking past the point, giving approximate answers that show the right answer is known ("How many legs does a cow have?" "Five." "What colour is snow?" "Black."), was described by Sigbert Ganser in 1898 in prisoners awaiting trial, and is still called the Ganser syndrome. One practical point matters especially in India. Speech should be assessed in the patient's own language. A Kannada-speaking man answering a clinician's English questions will be slow, hesitant and short in his answers, and that tells you about his English, not about his mind. Exam trap Pressure of speech is a property of speech (rapid, copious, hard to interrupt); flight of ideas (Section 2.5) is a property of thought (rapid jumps between connected ideas). They usually occur together in mania, but they are recorded under different headings. Reaction time is increased in depression and decreased in mania. Dysarthria is a problem of articulation; dysphasia is a problem of language. Poverty of speech is a reduced amount of speech; mutism is its absence. Approximate answers belong to Ganser (1898). Mood: what the patient reports With mood and affect the MSE reaches emotion, and here two words that everyday English treats as near-synonyms acquire precise and different meanings. Mood is the pervasive and sustained emotional state that a person experiences over a period of time, days or weeks rather than minutes, and that colours the way he perceives himself and the world. It is subjective: only the patient can tell you what it is, so it is elicited by asking. Affect , the subject of the next subsection, is the observable expression of emotion from moment to moment during the interview: what the clinician sees in the face, hears in the voice and notices in posture and gesture. A useful analogy: mood is the emotional climate; affect is the emotional weather. A climate can be cold while a particular afternoon is warm, and a depressed patient may laugh at a joke for a moment without his mood having changed at all. The clinician asks about mood with open questions first ("How have you been feeling in yourself?", "How are your spirits these days?") and then specific ones ("Have you been feeling low? Most of the day? Every day?"). The answer is recorded in the patient's own words, in quotation marks, which is the single most informative thing a mood record can contain: Ravi said, "I feel useless, like a burden on my family." Many clinicians also ask the patient to rate his mood from 0 (the worst he has ever felt) to 10 (the best), which gives a number to compare at the next visit; Ravi said "two". The clinician then adds the conventional label. The labels most often used are these. Euthymic mood is mood within the normal range, neither depressed nor elevated; it is what you write for a person whose mood is unremarkable. Depressed mood is sadness, lowness or hopelessness. Dysphoria is an unpleasant mood, often a mixture of sadness, irritability, tension and discontent. Anxious mood is apprehension, worry and tension about what may happen. Irritable mood is being easily annoyed and provoked to anger. Elevated mood is more cheerful than usual, and Indian textbooks grade it in order of increasing intensity: euphoria (a mild elevation, an exaggerated feeling of well-being out of keeping with events, as in hypomania), elation (a moderate elevation, with confidence, enjoyment and increased activity, as in mania), exaltation (intense elation with grandiose ideas, as in severe mania) and ecstasy (a feeling of intense rapture, seen in the most severe, delirious forms of mania and also, sometimes with a sense of union with the divine, in religious experience, in epilepsy and with some drugs). Expansive mood is the lack of restraint in expressing one's feelings, often with an inflated sense of one's own importance. Apathy is the absence of feeling, interest and concern. Two further terms describe what the patient cannot feel. Anhedonia , a word introduced by the French psychologist Théodule-Armand Ribot (1839 to 1916) in 1896, is the loss of the capacity to experience pleasure, a markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities the person once enjoyed. Ravi used to play cricket every Sunday and follow every match on his phone; now, he said, "I don't feel like it. Even when India wins, nothing." In DSM-5-TR, anhedonia and depressed mood are the two core symptoms of a major depressive episode, at least one of which must be present (the episode itself is taught in the Psychiatric Disorders book). Alexithymia , a term introduced by the psychiatrist Peter Emanuel Sifneos (1920 to 2008) in 1973 (some sources say 1972), from Greek words meaning "no words for feelings", is a difficulty in recognising and describing one's own emotions; Sifneos first noticed it in patients with psychosomatic illnesses, who could describe their bodily symptoms in great detail but could say little about what they felt. Beyond the label, the clinician records several features of the mood. Its intensity and pervasiveness : is the patient low all day, every day, or only in certain situations? Its reactivity : does it lift, even briefly, when something good happens, such as a visit from a friend? (Mood reactivity is preserved in what DSM calls depression with atypical features, and lost in melancholic depression.) And its diurnal variation , a regular change over the course of the day: in melancholic depression the mood is characteristically worst in the morning and lifts a little towards evening, while the confusion of delirium is often worst in the evening and at night (sundowning). Ravi's mood was worst in the early mornings, after he woke at three and lay awake. Exam trap Anhedonia is markedly diminished interest or pleasure in nearly all activities (Ribot, 1896). It is not excessive guilt, which is a disturbance of thought content (Section 2.5); not psychomotor agitation, which is a motor sign (described above); and not difficulty concentrating, which is a cognitive symptom (Section 2.6), although all four can appear in the same depressive episode. Alexithymia (Sifneos, 1973) is not being able to put feelings into words; it is not anhedonia. Euthymic means normal mood, not "happy". The grades of elevated mood run euphoria, elation, exaltation, ecstasy. Affect: what the clinician observes While the patient describes his mood, the clinician watches the affect. Because affect is observed, it is described along several dimensions at once, and each dimension has its own vocabulary. The first is quality : which emotion is shown? Sad, anxious, angry, cheerful, fearful, perplexed. The second is range : how many different emotions appear over the interview? A person with a broad (or full) range moves naturally between seriousness, worry, amusement and sadness as the conversation moves. In restricted affect (or constricted affect) the range and intensity of expression are mildly reduced: the person shows some emotion, but less, and of fewer kinds, than you would expect. The third is intensity . Blunted affect is a severe reduction in the intensity of emotional expression: the face is largely immobile, the voice flat, the gestures few, even when the patient talks about things that matter to him. Flat affect is the absence or near-absence of any sign of emotional expression. Restricted, blunted and flat therefore form a sequence of increasing severity, as Figure 2.3 shows, and blunted and flat affect are among the negative symptoms of schizophrenia (DSM-5-TR calls them diminished emotional expression). Some texts add shallow affect, emotion that is expressed but seems to lack depth, and at the other end heightened or exaggerated affect, emotion shown more intensely than the situation warrants. Emotional expression across an interview (up: cheerful; down: sad) Broad (full) normal range Restricted less range, intensity Blunted much less intensity Flat almost no expression Labile sudden, rapid shifts time during the interview Figure 2.3 Affect described by range, intensity and stability. Each trace shows the emotion visible in the patient's face and voice as the interview proceeds. From broad to flat, the swings shrink; in labile affect they are large but abrupt, jumping between extremes without a matching change in the conversation. The fourth dimension is reactivity (sometimes called mobility): does the affect respond to the conversation, softening when a painful topic comes up, brightening at a joke or at the mention of something the patient loves? An affect that stays the same whatever is discussed is described as fixed or unreactive. The fifth is appropriateness (or congruence): does the emotion shown fit what the patient is talking about and the situation he is in? Inappropriate affect (also called incongruous affect) is a mismatch between the emotion expressed and the content of speech or thought: a woman who giggles while describing her mother's death, a man who looks angry while saying he is perfectly content. Older European psychiatry called incongruous affect parathymia (Bleuler's word for it); Indian notes reserve the term for its extreme form, expressing an emotion exactly opposite to what the circumstances call for (laughing at news of a death), and use paramimia for a lack of unity between the different channels of expression (smiling face, tearful voice). Neither word is used in DSM-5-TR, so treat them as exam vocabulary rather than as standard clinical terms. Inappropriate affect is one of the features Eugen Bleuler regarded as fundamental to schizophrenia (Section 2.5). The sixth dimension is stability . Normal affect changes, but in step with the conversation. Labile affect shows repeated, rapid and abrupt shifts between emotions, tears one moment and laughter the next, out of proportion to anything that has been said. It is seen in mania, in some personality disorders and in brain disease. Its most extreme form, emotional incontinence (pathological laughing and crying, also called pseudobulbar affect), is sudden, uncontrollable crying or laughing that the patient does not actually feel, and it occurs after strokes and in diseases such as multiple sclerosis and motor neuron disease. Some formats add a seventh dimension, communicability : can the clinician feel with the patient, or does the emotion fail to reach him? An experienced clinician's sense that he cannot make emotional contact with a patient is itself worth recording. Finally, the clinician compares mood with affect. Usually they match: Ravi said he felt useless and he looked sad. When they do not, the mismatch is important. A patient who says "I am fine, doctor, there is nothing wrong" while tears run down his face has a depressed affect that contradicts his reported mood, and you met the skill for handling this, confrontation, in Section 2.2. Two famous mismatches deserve names. One is la belle indifférence , a striking lack of concern about a dramatic disability, such as a paralysed arm, that is sometimes seen in conversion (functional neurological) disorder, though it is no longer considered a reliable sign of it. The other is the "smiling depression" of a patient who shows a social smile throughout and may be at high risk precisely because no one has noticed (Section 2.7). Table 2.7 The vocabulary of affect. Term Dimension What the clinician sees Broad (full) Range Normal variety of emotions, in step with the conversation Restricted (constricted) Range, intensity Mild reduction in range and intensity Blunted Intensity Severe reduction in intensity of expression Flat Intensity Absence or near-absence of expression Unreactive (fixed) Reactivity Does not change with the topic Inappropriate (incongruous) Appropriateness Emotion does not fit the content or situation Labile Stability Rapid, abrupt shifts out of proportion to events Emotional incontinence Stability Uncontrollable laughing or crying not felt inside Clinical link Before writing "blunted affect", ask three questions. Is the patient on an antipsychotic that could be producing a parkinsonian mask? Is he severely depressed, so that the reduced expression is depressive retardation? Is he from a family or culture in which showing emotion to a stranger, or to a doctor, is simply not done? Each of these can mimic the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, and each leads to a different treatment. The same caution applies in reverse: a patient whose affect looks normal can still be in great distress. Exam trap Mood is subjective (what the patient reports, sustained over time); affect is objective (what the clinician observes, moment to moment). Some Indian case formats write the same pair as "subjective affect" and "objective affect", so read the question carefully. The order of severity is restricted, then blunted, then flat . Labile is a problem of stability (rapid shifts); inappropriate is a problem of fit (emotion that does not match the content). A patient can have labile but appropriate affect, or stable but inappropriate affect. Euthymic describes mood, not affect. Putting it together: the first half of Ravi's MSE Here is how the first part of Ravi's MSE was written, a few minutes after the interview. Notice that it contains no diagnosis, that every judgement has an observation behind it, and that his own words appear wherever they could. Ravi's MSE (first half) General appearance and behaviour. A thin young man who looks his stated age; unshaven, hair uncombed, clothes clean but creased; belt fastened at a new hole. Sat hunched forward with hands between his knees. Eye contact poor initially, mostly towards the floor, improving as the interview went on. No scars or marks of self-harm. No hallucinatory behaviour. Alert. Attitude: cooperative but reticent; rapport established with some difficulty. Psychomotor activity: generally decreased; few spontaneous movements; slowed. No abnormal movements. Speech: soft, slow and monotonous; reduced in quantity; spoke mainly in answer to questions; reaction time increased (several seconds), shortening later; relevant and coherent, goal-directed. Mood: subjectively "I feel useless, like a burden on my family"; rates it 2 out of 10; worst in the early morning; loss of pleasure in cricket ("Even when India wins, nothing"). Affect: depressed; restricted in range; reactive (brief smile when speaking about cricket, tearful when speaking of his mother's gold); appropriate to the content of his thought; stable; congruent with mood. Every word of that record can be checked by another clinician next week, and that is the point. But it is still only the outside of Ravi. What is he thinking about as he sits there, and is he perceiving anything that is not there? Those questions take us inside, to the stream, form, content and possession of thought, and to perception. 2.5 The Mental Status Examination II: Thought and Perception Medium yield · 2 Qs A clinician can watch a patient move and hear him speak, but no one has ever observed a thought. Everything the MSE says about thinking is an inference from what the patient says, and from how he says it. The American psychiatrist Nancy Coover Andreasen (born 1938) made this point the foundation of her work on what is usually called thought disorder: since thought is known only through speech, she argued, the honest name for what clinicians record is a disorder of thought, language and communication. Keep that in mind throughout this section. When you write "flight of ideas" or "delusion of persecution", you are describing a sample of speech and drawing a conclusion about the mind behind it, which is why the MSE asks for the sample, in the patient's own words, alongside the conclusion. This section classifies the disturbances of thought and of perception as the clinician meets and records them, each with a short example of what the patient actually says. The examples are composites, written to show the phenomenon clearly. The disorders in which these phenomena occur (schizophrenia, mania, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder and the rest) are described in the Psychiatric Disorders book; here the aim is to recognise the phenomenon and to name it correctly. Four headings for thought The British descriptive tradition that Indian case records follow, set out in texts such as Frank Fish's Clinical Psychopathology and Andrew Sims' Symptoms in the Mind , examines thought under four headings, and the headings are worth learning precisely because examiners ask which heading a phenomenon belongs to. The stream of thought is its flow: how fast thoughts come (the tempo) and whether the flow is continuous or interrupted (the continuity). The form of thought is its organisation: whether ideas are linked to one another in a logical, understandable sequence that reaches a goal. Disturbances of form are called formal thought disorder . The content of thought is what the person thinks about: his preoccupations, worries, fears and beliefs, including delusions. The possession of thought is the normal, taken-for-granted experience that one's thoughts are one's own and under one's own control. It is disturbed when a patient feels that thoughts are being put into his mind, taken out of it or broadcast to others. American textbooks and many examination keys use a simpler division into two: thought process (the stream and form together: how the person thinks) and thought content (what he thinks, with the possession phenomena counted as delusions of control). The two systems describe the same phenomena; they draw the boundaries differently. Table 2.8 lays them side by side, and Figure 2.4, in the subsection on form, shows how the main disorders of stream and form differ in the path they take from a question to its answer. It is never a disorder of content (it says nothing about what the patient believes), of possession (the patient's thoughts feel entirely his own) or of perception. A complication you should know about: British texts in the tradition of Fish's Clinical Psychopathology put circumstantiality under the stream of thought (its tempo, beside flight of ideas and retardation), and many Indian notes follow it, listing circumstantiality and tangentiality under stream because they change the way thinking flows towards its goal. American texts (Kaplan and Sadock's among them) put all of these, flight of ideas included, under form or thought process. The keyed answer follows the American usage, and this chapter's Table 2.8 does too for circumstantiality and tangentiality. So if "form" or "thought process" is offered, choose it; only if a question offers "stream" and not "form" should you choose stream. Disorders of the stream: tempo and continuity Start with speed. The most famous disorder of tempo is flight of ideas : thoughts follow one another very rapidly, there is no general direction to the thinking, and each idea is linked to the next by chance associations, by rhymes and puns, or by something the patient has just noticed in the room. The crucial point is that every individual link can be understood, even though the train as a whole goes nowhere. Asked how he travelled to the clinic, a man in a manic episode says: "By bus, a big red bus, red like the chillies my mother grows, she grows them for the market, market prices are going up, up, up, I will buy the whole market, I am going into business, doctor, business class, I will fly business class to Dubai, do you want to come?" The clinician can trace every step (bus, red, chillies, market, prices, business, flying), but the question has been left far behind. Flight of ideas is characteristic of mania and usually comes with pressure of speech (Section 2.4). A milder form, in which the patient wanders through many irrelevances but does eventually return to the topic, is called prolixity . Alongside the observed flight goes a subjective experience, pressure of thought or racing thoughts: "My thoughts are going too fast, I can't keep up with them, they are crowding my head." At the other end of the scale, retardation of thought (inhibition of thought, sometimes called bradyphrenia) is a slowing of thinking: fewer ideas come, each one arrives slowly, and the patient finds it hard to think at all. "My mind is slow, like it is full of mud. I try to think and nothing comes." It is common in depression and goes with the psychomotor retardation and long reaction times of Section 2.4. Poverty of thought is a reduction in the number of thoughts, so that the patient's mind feels empty; it shows itself as poverty of speech and is one of the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, though it also occurs in severe depression and dementia. Now continuity. In thought block (thought blocking) the train of thought stops suddenly and completely, often in the middle of a sentence, leaving a blank. After a pause, which may last many seconds, the patient may start again on a different subject, and he cannot say what he was going to say: "My brother came to the hostel and he told me that... [silence of about twenty seconds] ... I don't know. It went. What were you asking?" Everyone occasionally loses the thread when tired or anxious, and that is not thought block. True blocking is sudden, complete and unexplained, and it is seen most characteristically in schizophrenia. Keep it separate from a phenomenon it is often confused with. Thought block is what the clinician observes; if the patient explains the blank by saying that someone or something took his thoughts away, he is describing thought withdrawal , a disorder of possession (see the subsection on possession below). The same observed gap can be one or the other, and only questioning can tell. Perseveration is the persistent repetition of the same word, idea or response beyond the point at which it was relevant, so that it keeps returning in answer to new questions: Clinician: "What is your name?" Patient: "Ramesh." Clinician: "Where do you live?" Patient: "Ramesh." Clinician: "What did you eat this morning?" Patient: "Ramesh... Ramesh." Perseveration strongly suggests organic brain disease, especially of the frontal lobes, and is common in dementia; it also occurs in severe psychosis. It is one of three kinds of repetition you must keep apart. Perseveration repeats the patient's own earlier response when a new one is called for; verbigeration (Section 2.4) repeats meaningless words or phrases, as a stereotypy of speech; and echolalia repeats the examiner's words. Exam trap In flight of ideas each link between ideas is understandable (rhymes, puns, distractions) even though the goal is lost; in loosening of associations (next subsection) the links themselves cannot be followed. Thought block is an observed sudden stop; thought withdrawal is the patient's belief that his thoughts have been removed by an outside force. Perseveration (repeating one's own previous response, typical of organic brain disease) is not echolalia (repeating the examiner) and not verbigeration (repeating meaningless phrases). Disorders of form: when the links break Normal thinking is goal-directed : asked a question, a person moves from the question to the answer by a chain of ideas, each linked logically to the next. The disorders of form are the ways in which that chain bends, wanders or breaks. Figure 2.4 draws them as paths. Each line runs from the question (left dot) towards its answer (right dot) Goal-directed normal Circumstantiality detours, but arrives Tangentiality veers off, never arrives Flight of ideas rapid, linked jumps Derailment links missing Thought block stops dead, new topic blank Figure 2.4 The path from a question to its answer in the main disorders of stream and form. Only goal-directed thinking and circumstantiality reach the answer. In flight of ideas each jump is connected to the one before (the small dots); in derailment the segments do not join at all; in thought block the line simply stops. The idea that the links between ideas can loosen comes from Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939), the Swiss psychiatrist who introduced the word schizophrenia in 1908 and set out his view of the illness in his 1911 monograph Dementia Praecox, or the Group of Schizophrenias . For Bleuler the fundamental disturbance was a "breaking of associative threads", and he listed four fundamental symptoms that students remember as the four As: disturbance of associations , disturbance of affect (blunting and incongruity, Section 2.4), ambivalence (holding opposite feelings or wishes towards the same thing at the same time) and autism (withdrawal into an inner world; Bleuler's word, later borrowed for a quite different developmental condition). In loosening of associations the connection between successive ideas is lost or so remote that the listener cannot follow it. The patient moves from one topic to another with no apparent link, and does not seem to notice: "I have been tired lately. The government should build more temples near the lake. My chappals are from the Bata shop, and the cricket team needs a spinner because the moon is closer this month." Andreasen preferred the term derailment , because "loosening" had come to be used loosely: in derailment the patient's ideas slip off one track onto another that is completely unrelated or only obliquely related. British clinicians sometimes call the abrupt, unexpected jumps "knight's move thinking", after the chess piece that moves sideways as well as forwards. Compare the example with the manic patient's flight of ideas above. There you could trace each step; here you cannot. That is the single most useful distinction in the whole subject. Tangentiality is replying to a question in an oblique, tangential or even irrelevant way. The answer starts somewhere near the question, then heads off in another direction and never returns to it: Clinician: "What brought you to the hospital today?" Patient: "Hospitals in Mysuru are very crowded. My uncle worked in the railway hospital. The railways were built by the British, and the British were very clever people with their clocks." Circumstantiality is also indirect, but it arrives. The patient takes a long, roundabout route full of unnecessary and trivial detail and side-tracks, and the listener grows impatient, but he does eventually reach the point and answer the question: Clinician: "When did your sleep problem start?" Patient: "It was the Dasara holidays, my sister had come home from her engineering college in Hassan, the Hassan bus is always late, it came at nine that night, and my mother had made obbattu, which she makes only for festivals, and I ate three, and that was the week, doctor, about four months ago, that I stopped sleeping." Circumstantiality is seen classically in epilepsy (especially of the temporal lobe), in people with obsessional personalities, in intellectual disability and early dementia, and in anxious or pedantic people; a mild degree is normal in many talkers. The difference from tangentiality is simply whether the goal is reached, as Figure 2.4 shows. At the extreme of disorganisation, speech loses its structure even within sentences. Word salad (also called schizophasia, or incoherence in Andreasen's terms) is a jumble of words and phrases with no logical or grammatical connection, so that nothing can be understood: "Tree when blue the spoon running government sad of the Tuesday." DSM-5-TR notes that speech this disorganised resembles the speech of receptive aphasia; a neurological examination helps tell them apart. A neologism is a new word coined by the patient, or an ordinary word used in a private, idiosyncratic sense that only he understands: "The neighbours are sending glorbination through the wall to stop my thoughts." A related error, which Andreasen called a word approximation, builds a new expression from ordinary words ("I keep the time-shoe on my wrist" for a watch). In clang association words are chosen for their sound rather than their meaning, so that speech moves by rhymes and puns: "I am fine, wine, mine, divine, the line is mine, shall we dine?" Clanging is commonest in mania and also occurs in schizophrenia. Not every disorder of form is a matter of too much or too strange. Andreasen drew a sharp line between poverty of speech (Section 2.4), in which the patient says very little, and poverty of content of speech , in which the amount of speech is adequate but it conveys little information, because it is vague, over-abstract, over-concrete, repetitive or stereotyped: Clinician: "What are your plans for the future?" Patient: "The future is the future. Life has its things, and the things of life are what they are, so one has to think about the things that come, and the things will come." Two further terms complete the list. Over-inclusion , a term associated with the American psychiatrist and psychologist Norman Cameron, is a widening of the boundaries of concepts so that ideas and objects that are not closely connected are grouped together and irrelevant details are included in thinking. And thinking may be concrete , tied to the literal and the immediate and unable to deal in abstractions, which is tested by asking the meaning of proverbs (Section 2.6). My chappals are from Bata" Tangentiality Oblique answer that never returns "Hospitals are crowded... the British had clocks" Circumstantiality Long detour of detail, but reaches the point "... and that was the week I stopped sleeping" Word salad No connection even within sentences "Tree when blue the spoon running" Neologism Invented word or private meaning "They send glorbination through the wall" Clang association Words linked by sound, not meaning "Fine, wine, mine, divine" Poverty of content Enough words, little information "The future is the future, life has its things" Key study: Andreasen's thought, language and communication disorders (1979) For most of the twentieth century, clinicians assumed that formal thought disorder was the hallmark of schizophrenia, but they could not agree on what its terms meant, and "loose associations" was applied to almost any speech that puzzled the listener. Nancy Andreasen set out to fix the vocabulary. In two papers published in 1979 she gave each kind of thought, language and communication disorder a precise definition with examples, showed that trained raters could use the definitions reliably, and then rated the speech of 113 patients with mania, depression and schizophrenia. The result upset the old assumption. Formal thought disorder turned out to be common in mania as well as in schizophrenia: "positive" forms such as derailment, tangentiality, incoherence, illogicality and loss of goal were found about equally often in both, so that, as Andreasen put it, associative loosening "can no longer be considered pathognomonic of schizophrenia". Pressure of speech, distractible speech, clanging and circumstantiality pointed more towards mania, while the "negative" group, poverty of speech and poverty of content of speech, was more characteristic of schizophrenia; telling the positive from the negative forms often allowed the two diagnoses to be separated. Some celebrated forms, such as neologisms and blocking, turned out to be so rare that they added little to diagnosis. The definitions became the Scale for the Assessment of Thought, Language and Communication (TLC), and the lesson stuck: formal thought disorder is a sign to be described precisely, not proof of any one diagnosis. Exam trap Circumstantiality reaches the goal after a detour; tangentiality never does. Flight of ideas (mania) has understandable links; loosening of associations or derailment (Bleuler's term and Andreasen's preferred one) does not. Poverty of speech is too few words; poverty of content is enough words saying almost nothing. A neologism is a single new word; word salad is a stream of real words with no connection. Clang associations follow sound (rhymes and puns). Bleuler's four As are associations, affect, ambivalence and autism; hallucinations and delusions were, for him, accessory symptoms, not fundamental ones. Disorders of content I: delusions Karl Jaspers called the delusion "the basic characteristic of madness", and it is the most important disturbance of thought content. A delusion is a false, firmly held belief that is not amenable to change in the light of conflicting evidence or reasoned argument, and that is out of keeping with the person's educational, cultural and social background. DSM-5-TR puts the core of it in one line: delusions are "fixed beliefs that are not amenable to change in light of conflicting evidence". Each part of the definition does work. "Firmly held" separates a delusion from a passing suspicion. "Not amenable to change" is the clinical test: the clinician gently offers an alternative explanation ("Could there be any other reason the neighbour looked at you?") and sees whether the belief moves. "Out of keeping with the background" excludes beliefs that the person's community shares. Jaspers described three external characteristics of delusions: an extraordinary conviction , a subjective certainty that nothing can shake; imperviousness to other experiences and to compelling counter-argument; and an impossibility or falsity of content. He also saw that falsity is not the essence. A man with delusional jealousy may, by chance, have a wife who really is unfaithful; his belief is still delusional, because of the way he reached it (from the colour of a scooter parked outside, say) and the way he holds it. What makes a belief delusional is less what is believed than how it arose and how it is held. That point leads to Jaspers' most influential distinction. A secondary delusion (Jaspers called it a delusion-like idea) can be understood as arising from something else in the patient's mental state: a depressed man who believes he has ruined his family, a woman who hears voices threatening her and concludes that she is being persecuted, a manic patient who feels so powerful that he decides he is a prophet. A primary delusion cannot be traced psychologically to any other experience; it arises directly and is, in Jaspers' sense, ununderstandable. Primary delusional experience takes several forms. In delusional mood (Wahnstimmung) the patient feels that something strange and sinister is going on around him, that the world has subtly changed, without knowing what: "Something is happening in the village. Everyone is behaving differently. I don't know what it is, but it is about me." The relief when a full delusion crystallises out of this uneasy mood can be striking. In delusional perception a normal perception is suddenly given a delusional meaning, with no understandable link between the two: "I saw the neighbour's dog lift its front paw, and at that moment I knew that I had been chosen to save India." The perception (a dog lifting its paw) is real and accurately perceived; the meaning is delusional; and the two are joined by nothing the listener can follow. Delusional perception is one of Schneider's first-rank symptoms (below); delusional mood is not. An autochthonous delusion (a sudden delusional idea) arrives fully formed, out of the blue, without any perception to trigger it, and a delusional memory gives a remembered event a new delusional significance ("Now I understand why the teacher gave me that pen in Class 5; it was a sign I was royal"). Several other descriptions are added in the record. Delusions are called bizarre delusions when they are clearly implausible, not understandable to people of the same culture and not derived from ordinary life experience (DSM-5-TR's example is the belief that an outside force has removed one's internal organs and replaced them with someone else's without leaving a scar), and non-bizarre when they could conceivably happen (being followed by the police). They are mood-congruent when their content fits the mood (guilt, poverty, disease and death in depression; power and special identity in mania) and mood-incongruent when it does not. They may be systematised , forming one logically elaborated system that the patient can defend in detail, or unsystematised and fragmentary. And they may be shared: a belief that passes from one person to a close companion who lives with him is the shared delusion that Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret called folie à deux in 1877. Delusions are classified by content, and Table 2.10 lists the types examiners ask about, with the patient's words for each. Persecutory delusions , the belief that one is being deliberately harmed, harassed, interfered with, plotted against or mistreated, are the most common of all. A delusion of reference is the belief that ordinary events, remarks or objects carry a special personal meaning, and it must be distinguished from ideas of reference , the same kind of thought held without delusional conviction: the self-conscious student who feels that people laughing in the canteen might be laughing at him, but accepts that they probably are not. Ideas of reference occur in social anxiety, in paranoid and schizotypal personality and in ordinary embarrassment; delusions of reference occur in psychosis. A grandiose delusion is a belief in one's exceptional powers, wealth, identity or mission, and a delusion of control is the belief that one's will or actions are directed by an outside force (it overlaps with the passivity experiences described below). The eponyms are favourites with examiners. A nihilistic delusion , in its fullest form Cotard syndrome , was described by the French neurologist Jules Cotard in 1880: the patient believes that he is dead, that his organs have rotted or that he or the world does not exist; it occurs in very severe depression, often in older people. Delusional infestation, the belief that one's skin or body is infested with insects or parasites, is called Ekbom syndrome after the Swedish neurologist Karl-Axel Ekbom, who described it in 1938 (do not confuse it with restless legs syndrome, which also carries Ekbom's name). Delusional jealousy , the belief that one's partner is unfaithful, is called Othello syndrome after Shakespeare's tragic hero; it is dangerous, because the patient searches, interrogates and may attack the partner. Erotomania , the belief that another person, usually of higher social status and often a stranger or a celebrity, is secretly in love with the patient, is named de Clérambault syndrome after the French psychiatrist Gaëtan Gatian de Clérambault. In Capgras syndrome , described by Joseph Capgras and Jean Reboul-Lachaux in 1923, a familiar person (usually a spouse or parent) is believed to have been replaced by an identical impostor; in Fregoli syndrome , described by Paul Courbon and Gabriel Fail in 1927 and named after an Italian actor famous for his quick changes of costume, strangers are believed to be one familiar person, usually a persecutor, in disguise. Capgras says the familiar is a stranger; Fregoli says the strangers are a familiar. How does a clinician record a delusion? Never by arguing with it, which only hardens it and destroys rapport. He asks for the belief in the patient's words, then for the evidence ("How did you come to know this?"), tests the conviction ("Is there any chance you could be mistaken?"), and asks what the patient has done or plans to do about it, because a man convinced that his neighbour is poisoning him may decide to act first. The record reads something like: "Delusion of persecution: believes that his neighbours are poisoning the family well to take his land; first noticed 'a bitter taste' two months ago; held with full conviction; not shaken by the negative water test; has stopped drinking water at home and has threatened the neighbour." Indian context Belief in black magic, the evil eye (drishti or nazar), spirit possession and the effects of planets is widespread in India, and DSM-5-TR itself warns that such beliefs "may be viewed as bizarre and possibly delusional in some cultural contexts but be generally accepted in others." A belief is not a delusion simply because the clinician does not share it. Ask whether the family and community hold the same belief and hold it in the same way. A woman who thinks a jealous relative has cast the evil eye on her child, ties a black thread and visits the temple, is within her culture. A woman who is certain that her neighbour sends spirits through the television every night to stop her heart, and who is more convinced than anyone around her and cannot be reassured by the priest, has gone beyond it. Exam trap Being "deliberately interfered with, discriminated against, plotted against, threatened or otherwise mistreated" is a delusion of persecution , not reference (special personal meaning in events), control (outside force directing one's actions) or grandiosity. Othello syndrome is delusional jealousy (infidelity); Ekbom is infestation; de Clérambault is erotomania; Couvade syndrome is not a delusion at all, but pregnancy-like symptoms (nausea, weight gain, abdominal pain) in an expectant father. Capgras : a familiar person replaced by an impostor; Fregoli : strangers are a familiar person in disguise; Cotard : one is dead or does not exist. Ideas of reference lack delusional conviction; delusions of reference do not. Delusional perception is a first-rank symptom; delusional mood is not. Disorders of content II: overvalued ideas, obsessions, phobias and preoccupations Not every abnormal belief is a delusion. An overvalued idea , a term introduced by the German neuropsychiatrist Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905), is a solitary, understandable belief that the person holds with intense emotional investment and that comes to dominate his life and actions far beyond what its truth or importance would warrant. It is not as fixed as a delusion, it is comprehensible given the person's background and personality, and he identifies with it and defends it rather than experiencing it as alien. The young woman with anorexia nervosa who says, "I know I am not fat by other people's standards, but if I go above 38 kilos I will be disgusting, and nothing matters more than that", is describing an overvalued idea. So are the conviction of a man with body dysmorphic concerns that his nose is grotesque, many cases of morbid jealousy that stop short of delusion, and the consuming sense of injustice that drives some people from court to court for decades. An obsession (from the Latin for "to besiege") is a recurrent, persistent thought, image, impulse or urge that intrudes into the mind against the person's will, that he recognises as the product of his own mind, that he usually finds senseless, excessive or repugnant, and that he tries to resist or neutralise. Obsessions are ego-dystonic : experienced as alien to the person's values and wishes, unlike the overvalued idea, which is ego-syntonic, in keeping with the person's sense of himself. They take several forms: obsessional thoughts, doubts ("Did I lock the door?"), images, impulses, fears and endless ruminations on unanswerable questions. A young mother says: "When I hold a knife in the kitchen, the thought comes that I might stab my baby. I would never do it. I know it is my own mind, it is my own stupid thought, but it comes again and again and I cannot push it away. Now I don't go into the kitchen." The obsession is often followed by a compulsion , a repetitive behaviour or mental act (washing, checking, counting, praying a set number of times) that the person feels driven to perform to reduce the anxiety or to prevent a feared event; compulsions are observed as behaviour and recorded in Section 2.4 as well. Notice how firmly the mother insists that the thought is her own. That is exactly what separates an obsession from thought insertion (next subsection), in which the patient insists that the thought is not his own. A phobia is a persistent, excessive and irrational fear of a specific object, activity or situation, out of proportion to any real danger, that leads to avoidance; adults usually recognise that the fear is excessive. "I know the lift is perfectly safe, but I would rather climb eleven floors than get into it." It is recorded under thought content because what the patient fears and avoids is part of what occupies his mind; the phobic disorders are in the Psychiatric Disorders book and their treatment in Chapter 4. The rest of the content of thought is recorded as preoccupations : the themes the patient's thinking keeps returning to. In depression they are the depressive cognitions of worthlessness, hopelessness, helplessness and guilt (the negative cognitive triad of Chapter 5); excessive or inappropriate guilt is one of the symptoms of a depressive episode, and when it is out of all proportion and unshakeable it becomes a delusion of guilt. Other preoccupations concern illness (hypochondriacal ideas), the precipitating event, money, religion or philosophy. One more term belongs here. Magical thinking is the belief that one's thoughts, words or actions can cause or prevent events in ways that defy ordinary cause and effect: "If I tap the door four times before I leave, my father will not have an accident." It is normal in young children, common in obsessive-compulsive disorder, and one of the criteria of schizotypal personality disorder, where it appears alongside ideas of reference. Practices that a whole culture shares, such as wearing a lucky thread before an examination, are not counted as magical thinking in the clinical sense. Finally, every MSE records suicidal and homicidal ideation under thought content, whether or not the patient seems depressed. The clinician asks, step by step as Section 2.2 described, about passive death wishes ("I wish I would not wake up"), active thoughts of ending one's life, plans, intent, preparations and past attempts, and about any thoughts of harming others, and records the answers in the patient's words. Ravi said, "Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me. I have not thought how. I would not do that to my mother." What the clinician does with such answers, the weighing of risk and protective factors, is the subject of Section 2.7. Table 2.11 Telling apart a delusion, an overvalued idea and an obsession. Disorders of possession: thought alienation, passivity and the first-rank symptoms You do not normally wonder whether your thoughts are your own. The sense that thoughts belong to the person thinking them, and are under his control, is so basic that it is noticed only when it fails. In thought alienation the patient experiences his thoughts as under the control of an outside agency, or feels that others are taking part in his thinking. It has three classic forms. In thought insertion the patient experiences thoughts that are not his own being put into his mind from outside: "These are not my thoughts. They are the thoughts of the man next door. He puts them into my head with a ray through the window." In thought withdrawal he experiences his thoughts being taken out of his mind by an outside agency, and the mind is left empty: "My thoughts are sucked out by the satellite. That is why my mind suddenly goes blank when I talk to you." In thought broadcasting (thought diffusion) he experiences his thoughts as escaping from his mind so that other people know them, or as being broadcast to everyone: "Everyone on the bus knows what I am thinking. My thoughts go out of my head like a radio." Closely related are the passivity phenomena (made experiences), in which the patient experiences his feelings, impulses, actions or bodily sensations as imposed or controlled by an outside agency. In made feelings an emotion is experienced as not his own: "I am not angry. The anger is put into me by the computer at the police station." In made impulses the drive to act comes from outside, though he carries out the act. In made volitional acts the action itself is controlled: "My hand picks up the glass, but it is the swami who moves it. I just watch." And in somatic passivity he is the passive recipient of bodily sensations imposed from outside: "They are sending electric currents into my stomach from the tower." Two further points about this heading. First, British texts, Fish's among them, also list obsessions under disorders of possession, because the obsessional patient feels that his thinking has escaped his control, even though, unlike the patient with thought insertion, he knows the thought is his own; American texts put obsessions under content. Second, thought echo (hearing one's own thoughts spoken aloud) sounds as if it belongs here, but it is a perception, recorded under perception (next subsection). These experiences have a special place in the history of psychiatry because of Kurt Schneider (1887 to 1967), a German psychiatrist at Heidelberg. Schneider was looking for symptoms that could be identified reliably in an interview and that would point to schizophrenia. He picked out a group which, when present without any organic brain disease, he regarded as strongly suggestive of schizophrenia, and called them first-rank symptoms ; the list is best known in English from the translation of his Clinical Psychopathology (1959). As usually taught, it has eleven items, set out in Table 2.12. (Some books split or merge them slightly differently.) Table 2.12 Schneider's first-rank symptoms, grouped by MSE heading.
