Delusional perception The first-rank symptoms were enormously influential, partly because they are easy to rate reliably, and they shaped the ICD-10 criteria for schizophrenia. Later research, however, showed that they are neither necessary nor specific: many people with schizophrenia never have them, and they also occur in mania and in other psychoses, and DSM-5-TR notes that experiences closely resembling them are reported in dissociative identity disorder. DSM-IV still gave them special weight (one symptom was enough for criterion A if the voices kept up a running commentary or conversed with each other, or if the delusions were bizarre); DSM-5 (2013) removed that special weight. They remain essential knowledge for the MSE, because they tell the clinician what to ask about and how to name what he hears. Exam trap The first-rank symptoms are thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting, made feelings, impulses and acts, somatic passivity, delusional perception and three kinds of auditory hallucination (audible thoughts, voices arguing or discussing, running commentary). They are not : avolition and flat affect (negative symptoms), memory deficits and disorientation (cognitive impairments, which point to organic disease and which Schneider's rule actually excluded), catatonic excitement (a motor sign), depersonalisation (end of this section), second-person voices, or delusional mood. Thought broadcasting (others know my thoughts) is not thought echo (I hear my thoughts aloud) and not ideas of reference (others are talking about me). Disorders of perception Perception is the process of becoming aware of what is presented through the senses. Its disturbances fall into two families. In a sensory distortion a real object is perceived, but perceived as changed: in intensity (sounds unbearably loud, hyperacusis; the world dulled and colourless in depression), in quality (everything tinged yellow, xanthopsia, as in digoxin toxicity; or red, erythropsia) or in size and shape (objects appearing smaller, micropsia, or larger, macropsia, as in temporal lobe epilepsy, migraine and some drug states). In a sensory deception something new is perceived, which may or may not be triggered by a real stimulus: illusions and hallucinations. Figure 2.5 lays out the family tree. Disorders of perception Sensory distortions a real object, changed in intensity, quality or size Sensory deceptions a new perception, with or without a real stimulus Illusion real stimulus, misperceived Hallucination no stimulus; outer space; feels real completion, affect, pareidolia pseudohallucination: in inner space, or known to be unreal hyperacusis, xanthopsia, micropsia, macropsia Figure 2.5 The classification of disorders of perception. The first question is whether a real object is being perceived differently (a distortion) or something new is being perceived (a deception); among deceptions, the next question is whether there is a real stimulus behind it (an illusion) or none (a hallucination). An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus. The French psychiatrist Jean-Étienne Dominique Esquirol (1772 to 1840) was the first to separate it clearly, in the early nineteenth century, from a hallucination, which has no external object at all. Descriptive psychopathology recognises three kinds. Completion illusions depend on inattention: you read a misprinted word as the correct one, or hear your name in a hubbub. Affect illusions arise from a strong emotion: in a dark, frightening ward, a patient says, "The drip stand turned into a man standing over my bed"; on a village path at night, a rope becomes a snake. Pareidolic illusions are vivid images that the mind makes out of vague stimuli, such as faces in clouds, animals in the cracks of a wall or Ganesha in the shape of a coconut; they persist even when the person attends closely, and they are entirely normal. Illusions are common when perception is degraded (darkness, fatigue, fear) and increase greatly in delirium. A hallucination is a perception-like experience that occurs without an external stimulus. DSM-5-TR describes hallucinations as "vivid and clear, with the full force and impact of normal perceptions, and not under voluntary control". Three features separate them from imagination: they are experienced as coming from outside, in external objective space; they have the substantial, real quality of normal perceptions; and the person cannot summon or dismiss them at will. Jaspers added that they occur alongside real perceptions, not instead of them: the patient hears the voice and the clinician at the same time. Hallucinations are classified first by sensory modality. Auditory hallucinations are the commonest in schizophrenia and related disorders. They may be elementary (bangs, whistles, music) or complex (voices). Voices are described by person. Second-person voices speak to the patient ("You are useless. You should die."), and are common in severe depression, where their content is mood-congruent. Third-person voices speak about the patient ("He is a fool. Look, now he is getting up."), and when they argue or discuss him, or keep up a running commentary on what he is doing, they are first-rank symptoms. In audible thoughts (thought echo) the patient hears his own thoughts spoken aloud, as he thinks them or just after. A command hallucination is a voice that tells the patient to do something, and the clinician must always ask what it commands and whether he obeys, because commands to harm oneself or others raise risk (Section 2.7). Visual hallucinations may be elementary (flashes of light) or complex (people, animals, scenes). They are less common in schizophrenia than auditory ones and should always raise the possibility of an organic cause: delirium (including alcohol withdrawal delirium, with its frightening animals and insects and its tiny Lilliputian people), drug intoxication, epilepsy, some dementias and eye disease. Olfactory and gustatory hallucinations (smells and tastes, often together: burning rubber, rotting flesh, a metallic taste) suggest temporal lobe epilepsy, but they also occur in severe depression ("I can smell my body rotting") and in schizophrenia, where the "taste of poison" in food may feed a persecutory delusion. Tactile (haptic) hallucinations are false sensations of touch on or just under the skin. Formication , the sensation of insects crawling on or under the skin, is typical of cocaine use and alcohol withdrawal. Somatic (visceral or coenaesthetic) hallucinations are false sensations inside the body ("My liver is being twisted"), and kinaesthetic hallucinations are false sensations of movement ("My bed is rising off the floor"). When the patient attributes the bodily sensation to an outside agency, it is somatic passivity, a first-rank symptom. Several special varieties are named for the circumstances in which they occur, and they are collected in Table 2.13. A functional hallucination is triggered by a real stimulus in the same modality and is perceived together with it: a woman hears voices only when the ceiling fan is running, and hears them inside its whirr. A reflex hallucination is triggered by a stimulus in a different modality: a man feels a stab of pain in his head every time a door slams. An extracampine hallucination is experienced outside the limits of the sensory field: seeing someone standing behind one's back, or hearing voices from Delhi while sitting in Mysuru. In autoscopy the person sees himself, as a double. Hypnagogic hallucinations occur while falling asleep and hypnopompic hallucinations while waking up: hearing one's name called, seeing a figure at the foot of the bed. They are common in healthy people, and DSM-5-TR treats them as within the range of normal experience; they are also frequent in narcolepsy. Finally, the Swiss naturalist Charles Bonnet (1720 to 1793) described in 1760 the vivid visual hallucinations (people, patterns, buildings) of his grandfather, who was going blind from cataracts and knew perfectly well that the visions were not real. Charles Bonnet syndrome , complex visual hallucinations with preserved insight in a person with visual loss, is common in older people with eye disease, and recognising it spares them an unnecessary diagnosis of psychosis. That leaves the most confusing term in the subject. A pseudohallucination is, roughly, a perception-like experience that falls short of a true hallucination, and the confusion comes from the fact that the term is used in two different senses. In the European tradition of the Russian psychiatrist Victor Kandinsky (1849 to 1889), who described pseudohallucinations in the 1880s partly from his own psychotic illness (the word itself is usually credited to the German psychiatrist Friedrich Wilhelm Hagen, in 1868), and of Jaspers, a pseudohallucination is experienced in inner, subjective space ("in my head", "in my mind's eye") rather than in the outside world; it is vivid and involuntary like a perception but lacks the substantial quality of one. A widow who hears her husband's voice calling her, inside her head, in the weeks after his death is having a pseudohallucination in this sense. In the other, more British and American sense, a pseudohallucination is an experience located in outer space but recognised by the person as unreal, so that insight is preserved. In either sense pseudohallucinations are common in grief, trauma, severe stress and personality disorders as well as in psychosis, and the clinician should say which sense he means. Asking about hallucinations takes tact, because many patients fear being called mad. Barlow and Durand suggest a normalising introduction: "Let me ask you a couple of routine questions that we ask everybody. Do you ever see things or maybe hear things when you know there is nothing there?" If the answer is yes, the clinician records the modality, the content in the patient's words, whether a voice speaks to him or about him, where it seems to come from, how clear, how frequent and at what times (only when falling asleep?), what the patient does in response, and whether he believes it is real. Exam trap An illusion misperceives a real stimulus; a hallucination has no stimulus; a delusional perception perceives a real stimulus accurately but gives it a delusional meaning (so it is a disorder of content, not of perception). A functional hallucination is triggered in the same modality and heard alongside the trigger; a reflex hallucination crosses modalities. Hypnagogic is falling asleep, hypnopompic is waking (remember "pomp" as the fanfare at the start of the day); both are normal. Formication is tactile (cocaine, alcohol withdrawal). Lilliputian hallucinations (tiny people) point to delirium. Visual hallucinations suggest an organic cause until proved otherwise. Depersonalisation and derealisation The last items under perception describe a change not in what is perceived but in how real it feels. In depersonalisation the person feels unreal, detached, or like an outside observer of his own thoughts, feelings, body or actions; he feels that he is no longer his normal, natural self. In derealisation it is the surroundings that feel unreal: dreamlike, foggy, lifeless, flat, like a stage set or a painting. The word depersonalisation was brought into use in 1898 by the French philosopher Ludovic Dugas. Patients struggle to describe these experiences and nearly always use the words "as if": "I feel as if I am not really here, as if I am watching myself in a film. I know I am me, but it does not feel like me." (depersonalisation) "Mysuru looks like a painting, as if there is a glass wall between me and everything." (derealisation) The "as if" is the key to recording them. Throughout the experience the person knows that he is real and that the world is real; DSM-5-TR's phrase is that "reality testing remains intact". That separates depersonalisation from the nihilistic delusion of Cotard syndrome, in which the patient believes, without any "as if", that he is actually dead. Depersonalisation and derealisation are common and often brief in healthy people who are exhausted, sleep-deprived or frightened; they are frequent during panic attacks, in depression and anxiety, after trauma, in temporal lobe epilepsy and with cannabis and other drugs; and when they are persistent and distressing in their own right, they form depersonalisation-derealisation disorder (Psychiatric Disorders book). Two neighbouring experiences are sometimes recorded here as well: déjà vu , the feeling that a new situation has been experienced before, and jamais vu , the feeling that a familiar situation has never been experienced; both are disturbances of recognition memory, normal when occasional and frequent in temporal lobe epilepsy. Exam trap A change in awareness of one's own identity, the feeling of no longer being one's normal, natural self, is depersonalisation ; the feeling that the outside world is unreal is derealisation . Neither is stress or depression, although both can accompany them. In both, reality testing is intact (the "as if" quality), which separates them from a delusion. And depersonalisation is not one of Schneider's first-rank symptoms, which makes it the favourite "all except" option. The second half of Ravi's MSE Here is how the thought and perception headings of Ravi's MSE were written. Notice that the most important findings are negative ones, carefully asked about and recorded. Ravi's MSE (thought and perception) Thought. Stream: retarded; replies slow and brief; no thought block. Form: no formal thought disorder; relevant, coherent and goal-directed. Content: preoccupied with his examination failure and with being a burden: "I am useless. They spent my mother's gold on me and I gave them nothing back." Feelings of worthlessness, guilt and hopelessness ("Nothing will change"); the guilt is related to real events and he accepts, with some reluctance, that his parents do not blame him, so it is not held with delusional conviction. Passive death wishes ("Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me"); denies any plan or intent, cites his mother as a reason to live. No homicidal ideas. No delusions, overvalued ideas, obsessions or phobias. Possession: no thought alienation or passivity experiences. Perception. No hallucinations in any modality; no illusions; occasional feeling that "things seem far away" in the early mornings, recognised as "just my tiredness" (mild derealisation, insight preserved). Two headings remain: whether Ravi's cognition is intact (his complaint that "nothing goes into my head" makes it essential to test), and whether he understands that he is ill. Those are the subject of Section 2.6, which also shows how the whole examination is written up, and his passive death wishes are weighed in the risk assessment of Section 2.7. Almost all of that came from watching and listening. The last part of the mental status examination is different in kind: the clinician now asks the client to do things. Tell me today's date. Repeat these numbers after me. Take seven away from a hundred. Remember these three words; I will ask you for them again in a few minutes. What do people mean when they say this proverb? For the first time in the interview the client is being tested, and many clients notice the change. Some feel insulted ("Do you think I am mad?"), some become anxious, and a few, who have been chatting fluently for half an hour, suddenly cannot say what month it is. That last group is the reason the cognitive examination exists. Why test at all, if the client has been talking sensibly? Because conversation hides a great deal. A sociable retired schoolteacher in the early stage of dementia can talk about cricket for an hour on well-worn phrases and still not know the year. A man recovering from a head injury, or an older woman in a delirium caused by a urinary infection, may answer social questions politely while being unable to hold a thought for ten seconds. The cognitive examination is the clinician's quick check that the machinery behind the conversation, alertness, attention, memory and reasoning, is working. When it is not, the whole meaning of the rest of the MSE changes: hallucinations in a clouded, disoriented patient point towards a medical cause, not a primary psychosis. Why cognition is examined in a fixed order The cognitive functions are traditionally examined, and written up, in a fixed sequence: consciousness, orientation, attention and concentration, memory, intelligence and general information, and abstract thinking, with judgement and insight closing the examination. The order is not a matter of habit. Each function depends on the ones before it. A person who is drowsy cannot attend; a person who cannot attend cannot register new information, and so cannot later recall it, and will therefore appear disoriented, because knowing today's date depends on having registered it this morning; and a person who cannot hold a question in mind cannot be expected to interpret a proverb. Figure 2.6 shows this hierarchy. The practical rule that follows from it is simple and examinable: test from the bottom up, and interpret every higher failure in the light of the lower ones. A poor score on the recall of three words means "memory impairment" only if the client was alert and attentive when the words were given. Judgement and insight Intelligence, information, abstract thinking Orientation and memory Attention and concentration Consciousness (level of alertness) Examine in this order, from the base up A failure low down makes every test above it hard to interpret Figure 2.6 The cognitive functions as a hierarchy. Each level rests on the ones below it, so the examination starts with consciousness and climbs. Notice that judgement and insight sit at the top: they depend on everything underneath. Two more principles govern the bedside examination. The first is preparation. Clients do better, and feel less humiliated, if the clinician introduces the tests honestly: "I am going to ask some questions that we ask everyone, to check memory and concentration. Some are easy and some are quite hard, so don't worry if you can't do them all." The second is calibration. Every result must be read against the person's education, occupation, language and culture, which is why Section 2.3 insisted that education be recorded in the identifying data. Failing to subtract sevens means one thing in a chartered accountant and something quite different in a woman who left school in the second standard to look after her siblings. Finally, remember what these tests are. They are bedside tests: quick, free, done with nothing but a pencil and a watch, and crude. They screen; they do not measure. When the bedside examination suggests a problem, the clinician refers the client for formal neuropsychological assessment, whose instruments (the Wechsler scales, the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction, the NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery and many others) are taught in the Assessment book. Older case notes, and many Indian case records, group consciousness and orientation (sometimes with attention and memory) under the single heading sensorium , and write "sensorium clear" when they are intact. Exam trap The cognitive part of the MSE begins with consciousness , not with orientation or memory, because every later test assumes an alert patient. A patient who fails a recall test while drowsy or inattentive has not shown a memory deficit; he has shown that the lower levels failed. And do not confuse the bedside cognitive examination, which is part of the MSE, with formal neuropsychological testing, which is a separate assessment done with standardised tests. Consciousness and its levels In the MSE, consciousness means the level of alertness or wakefulness: the degree to which the person is awake and aware of himself and his surroundings. (The deeper question of what consciousness is belongs to General Psychology.) Most clients in an outpatient clinic are fully alert, and the clinician simply writes "conscious and alert". The headings exist for the patients who are not, and they are found most often in emergency departments, medical wards and old-age homes, where a psychologist is asked to see someone who is "confused". Impairment of consciousness is a continuum, and Table 2.14 marks the usual points along it. The mildest and the most easily missed is clouding of consciousness : the person is awake and may talk, but thinking is slowed and muddled, attention drifts, perception is inaccurate (shadows become figures, the drip stand becomes a man), and memory for the period is patchy. Clouding is the hallmark of delirium , an acute confusional state caused by a medical illness, a drug or its withdrawal, in which the level of consciousness typically fluctuates through the day and worsens in the evening and at night, a pattern nurses call "sundowning". (Delirium itself is taught in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) A clinician who sees a confused patient once, at ten in the morning, may find him lucid and miss the delirium entirely; the night nurse's report is part of the assessment. Beyond clouding lies drowsiness (somnolence, sometimes called lethargy), in which the person falls asleep unless stimulated but can be roused by voice; then stupor , in which only vigorous or painful stimulation produces a brief response; and finally coma , in which the person cannot be roused at all. Some texts insert obtundation, a reduced alertness with slowed responses to stimulation, between drowsiness and stupor. At the opposite end from clouding is hypervigilance, an abnormally heightened alertness seen in anxiety, stimulant intoxication, alcohol withdrawal and paranoid states. The GCS adds the scores for three responses: eye opening (1 to 4), the best verbal response (1 to 5) and the best motor response (1 to 6). The total therefore runs from 3, a patient who shows no response of any kind, to 15, a fully alert and oriented one; a score of 8 or less is generally taken to mean coma. You will not be asked to use the GCS in a psychology clinic, but you will read it in every head-injury file you are sent. One word in this list causes trouble. In neurology, stupor is a level of consciousness. In psychiatry the same word is also used for a state of mutism and akinesia (the person neither speaks nor moves, and may not eat or drink) in which consciousness is often fully preserved. This is seen in catatonic stupor, in severe depressive stupor and in dissociative stupor. Such patients may later recall everything that was said at the bedside, which is why nobody should ever discuss a stuporous patient carelessly in his presence. How do you tell the two kinds apart at the bedside? The eyes help: a patient in a psychiatric stupor often keeps his eyes open and follows movement, or resists attempts to open his eyelids, and his reflexes and pupils are normal. Whatever the level, record it in plain words ("drowsy, rouses to his name, falls asleep mid-sentence"), and then read every later finding in its light. A drowsy patient's poor memory says nothing about dementia. Exam trap The lowest possible Glasgow Coma Scale score is 3 , not 0, and the highest is 15 (eyes 4, verbal 5, motor 6); 8 or below is taken as coma. Clouding of consciousness is the mildest impairment and the core of delirium, and it fluctuates . Stupor has two meanings: a deep level of impaired consciousness in neurology, and mutism with immobility, often with clear consciousness, in catatonic, depressive and dissociative states. If an option says a stuporous patient "cannot be aware of his surroundings", be suspicious. Orientation to time, place and person In the MSE, orientation is the person's awareness of himself in relation to time, place and other people: knowing when it is, where he is and who he and the people around him are. Its absence, disorientation , is one of the most reliable signs that something is wrong with the brain rather than with the mind alone, because orientation is preserved in most functional psychiatric disorders, even severe ones. A man with florid schizophrenia who believes that the television is broadcasting his thoughts will usually still tell you, correctly, that it is a Tuesday morning in the outpatient department of the district hospital. Each sphere is tested with simple questions. For time , the clinician asks the day of the week, the date, the month, the year and the approximate time of day ("Is it morning, afternoon or evening?"), and, for an inpatient, how long he has been in hospital. For place , he asks where the patient is now, what kind of place it is ("What sort of building is this?") and which town or city it is in. For person , he asks the patient to identify the people around him (his relative, the nurse, "Who do you think I am?") and, last, to state his own name and age. The questions are only half the test. The other half is judging whether an error matters. Patients in hospital, where every day is the same, often get the date wrong by a day or two, and this is not disorientation. Many rural Indians, farmers and older women in particular, do not follow the calendar of months and dates at all but mark time by the agricultural season, the lunar calendar and the festivals; for them the right questions are "Which season is it?", "Which festival went by most recently?" and "Is it morning or evening?" A clinician who scores such a person "disoriented to time" because she cannot name the date has tested her schooling, not her brain. Orientation is lost in a characteristic order: time first, then place, then person , and the patient's own identity last of all. Why this order? Because the spheres differ in how much continuous new learning they demand. The date changes every day and must be updated constantly, so it is the first thing to go when attention and recent memory fail; one's location changes less often; and the identity of familiar people, and of oneself, is overlearned over a lifetime and is the most resistant. As a delirium clears or a patient emerges from the confusion that follows a head injury, orientation usually returns in the reverse order, person first and time last. Figure 2.7 sets this out. Lost in this order (delirium, dementia, head injury) Time Place Person Day, date, month, year, time of day "Where are we now?" Which building, which town "Who is this?" "Who am I?" Own name, last of all Usually recovered in the reverse order as the confusion clears Own identity lost, time and place intact: think of a dissociative cause Figure 2.7 The order of loss of orientation. Time, which needs constant updating, goes first; the overlearned identity of familiar people and of oneself goes last, and returns first. Notice the box at the bottom: a pattern that breaks the order is itself a clue. The order gives the clinician a diagnostic clue. Disorientation that follows it, time before place before person, is the pattern of organic conditions: delirium, dementia, intoxication and head injury. A patient who has forgotten who he is while knowing perfectly well the date and the name of the hospital has broken the order, and that pattern suggests a dissociative condition such as dissociative amnesia or fugue rather than brain disease (these disorders are taught in the Psychiatric Disorders book). A second curiosity is double orientation , seen in some patients with chronic schizophrenia: the patient states correctly that he is in the psychiatric ward of the district hospital and, in the same breath, that the ward is a palace in which he is being crowned. The real and the delusional orientation run side by side, something the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) called "double bookkeeping". Finally, apparent disorientation in a severely depressed or acutely psychotic patient is often not disorientation at all but a failure of attention or cooperation: he did not answer because he did not attend, or did not care to. The written entry is brief: "Oriented to time, place and person" (many clinicians write "oriented in all three spheres"), or, when there is a deficit, the exact errors: "Gave the year as 2019 and said the hospital was his office; recognised his wife." Exam trap Orientation is lost time, then place, then person , and recovered in the reverse order. Loss of personal identity with intact orientation for time and place points to a dissociative cause, not dementia. Orientation is usually preserved in functional disorders such as schizophrenia and depression, so marked disorientation should make you think of delirium or another organic condition. And orientation is a cognitive function in its own right: it is not insight, which is the patient's awareness of being ill (Section 2.6.9). Attention and concentration The words are often used together, but they name two different things. In clinical usage, attention is the ability to direct the mind to a stimulus or task, to turn towards it and take it in, while concentration is the ability to sustain that focus over time, against distraction and fatigue. Indian case records capture the difference in a standard phrase: "attention is easily aroused and sustained". A patient may show one problem without the other. A man in a manic episode turns instantly to every sound in the corridor (his attention is easily aroused, too easily) but cannot keep it on anything (it is not sustained); this is distractibility . A depressed woman may attend to a question but lose the thread halfway through a long task. Inattention, the inability to direct and hold attention at all, is the cardinal feature of delirium, and in DSM-5-TR a disturbance of attention and awareness is the first criterion for it. Much of the evidence comes from the interview itself: whether the client follows questions, loses the thread, needs questions repeated or is pulled away by noises. The bedside tests then put a number on it. The digit span test asks the client to repeat a string of digits. The clinician reads them at about one per second, in an even voice, without grouping them as one groups a telephone number, starting with three digits and adding one each time until the client fails twice at the same length. Then the client is asked to repeat new strings backwards. Most adults of average education repeat six or seven digits forwards and four or five backwards, and backwards is usually one or two less than forwards; a forward span below five is usually abnormal. Digits forward depends mainly on attention and the immediate registration of information; digits backward also requires holding and manipulating the digits, a working-memory task. This is why some textbooks list digit span under attention and others under immediate memory: it measures the point at which the two meet. The test of serial sevens asks the client to take 7 away from 100 and keep taking 7 from each answer: 93, 86, 79, 72, 65. The clinician records the answers, the errors and the time taken. One slip followed by correct subtraction from the wrong number (93, 85, 78, 71) counts as a single error, because the test is of sustained concentration, not of arithmetic; even healthy people make an occasional slip, so the pattern matters more than a single mistake. Because serial sevens depends on arithmetic, it is unfair to people with little schooling. The alternatives are serial threes (take 3 from 20, and keep going), counting backwards from 20 to 1, saying the days of the week backwards , saying the months of the year backwards , or spelling a five-letter word such as WORLD backwards. The clinician chooses the hardest task that the client's education makes fair; months backwards, for example, assumes that the client knows the months in order forwards. A simple test of vigilance asks the client to tap the table every time he hears the letter A in a long string of letters read aloud; missed A's and taps on other letters are counted. How a person fails is as informative as whether he fails. The depressed patient tends to do the tasks slowly, with effort and complaint ("I can't, my head doesn't work") but often accurately in the end. The manic patient starts quickly and then abandons the task for something more interesting. The anxious patient makes errors he would not make at home, and improves when reassured. The delirious patient cannot keep the instruction in mind long enough to begin. These patterns matter because poor performance on these tests is not specific to any one condition: it tells you that attention is impaired, not why. Exam trap Attention is aroused; concentration is sustained. Digit span tests attention and immediate memory (registration), not long-term memory and not intelligence. Serial sevens (100, 93, 86, 79, 72, 65) tests concentration; for a person with little schooling use serial threes, counting backwards, or days or months backwards. The ability to do serial subtraction is a test of concentration: it has nothing to do with insight, which is a distractor in questions about what "insight" means. Easy distractibility is the attentional sign of mania ; inattention is the core of delirium . Memory: immediate, recent and remote Clinicians divide memory, for bedside purposes, by how long ago the information was learned. The divisions are practical rather than theoretical, and they do not map neatly onto the stores of cognitive psychology (General Psychology): what the clinician calls "recent memory" is mostly what a cognitive psychologist would call long-term memory for recent events. The first division, immediate memory (immediate retention and recall, or registration), is the ability to take in information and reproduce it within seconds. It is tested with the digit span, or by asking the client to repeat three unrelated words straight away (for example, "mango, chair, blue") until he has them all. If he cannot register the words, there is no point asking for them later: the problem lies in attention, not in memory proper. The second, recent memory , is memory for events of the last few minutes, hours and days. The standard test is delayed recall: after about five minutes filled with other tasks, the client is asked for the three words again, with a category cue ("one was a fruit") if he cannot recall them unaided, and then, if needed, a choice ("was it apple, mango or banana?"). Recognition with cues but not free recall suggests a retrieval problem; failure even with choices suggests that the words were never stored. Recent memory is also tested with questions about the last day or two: what he ate for breakfast, how he travelled to the clinic, who visited him yesterday. The answers must be checked against an informant or the ward staff, because a fluent answer can be invented. Some Indian formats add a separate heading, recent past memory , for events of the past few months (the last festival, a recent family wedding, news of the past weeks). The third, remote memory , is memory for events of years ago: personal history (where he went to school, the year of his marriage, his children's names and ages) and public events that a person of his background would know. Again, answers must be verifiable: the clinician who asks the year of a man's marriage must know it from his wife. The three are lost unequally. In dementia, in the amnesia that follows head injury, and in many other brain diseases, recent memories are lost before remote ones: the grandfather who cannot remember that his son visited this morning can describe in detail the day Indira Gandhi visited his village decades ago. This gradient was described by the French psychologist Théodule-Armand Ribot (1839 to 1916) in Les maladies de la mémoire (1881), and it is still called Ribot's law : the newest memories, least consolidated, are the most vulnerable, and the oldest, most rehearsed, the most resistant. (Families often take preserved remote memory as proof that "his memory is fine"; it is not.) Two further phenomena belong to this heading. The first is confabulation : the filling of gaps in memory with false memories that the patient produces fluently and believes. Asked what he did yesterday, an inpatient with severe amnesia may describe a trip to the market and a meeting with friends that never happened. Confabulation is not lying, because there is no intent to deceive (Section 2.3 contrasted it with malingering), and it is classically seen in the amnesic syndrome described by the Russian psychiatrist Sergei Sergeievich Korsakoff (1854 to 1900) in 1887, which results from thiamine deficiency, most often in chronic heavy drinking (the Psychiatric Disorders book). The second is the difference between complaining of poor memory and having it. Depressed people often complain bitterly that "nothing stays in my head", yet perform reasonably when tested; people with early dementia often deny or minimise memory problems that their families describe and the tests confirm. When depression in an older adult produces a picture that looks like dementia, it is called pseudodementia , a term popularised by the psychiatrist Leslie Kiloh in a paper of 1961, although others had used it before him (today it is often called the dementia syndrome of depression). Clinical link Is this older person depressed or dementing? At the bedside, a few contrasts help. The depressed patient tends to have a fairly clear onset, often after a loss; complains of memory loss in detail; gives up quickly with "I don't know" answers; and has low mood that came first. The patient with dementia usually has a gradual onset that the family cannot date; minimises or is unaware of the problem; tries hard and gives near-misses or confabulated answers; and has deficits that are consistent across tests. None of these contrasts is decisive (depression and dementia often coexist, and late-life depression can be an early sign of dementia), so the answer comes from treatment, follow-up and formal testing. But the distinction matters, because the depression is treatable. Exam trap Immediate memory is registration within seconds (digit span, repeating three words at once); recent memory is minutes to days (three words after five minutes, yesterday's events); remote memory is years (personal and public past). By Ribot's law recent memories are lost before remote ones. Confabulation fills memory gaps without intent to deceive (Korsakoff syndrome); malingering is deliberate. Pseudodementia (Kiloh, 1961) is depression that looks like dementia, typically with "don't know" answers and complaints that exceed the measured deficit. Intelligence and general information The MSE does not measure intelligence; it makes a rough clinical estimate of whether the person's intellectual functioning is in keeping with his education and background, and whether it appears to have declined. The estimate rests on several sources. The first is the interview itself: vocabulary, the complexity of the person's sentences, how well he understands questions and how organised his account was. The second is general information , the person's fund of knowledge, tested with questions pitched at what someone of his background would know: the name of the Prime Minister and of the Chief Minister, the capital of the state, a recent event in the news, the winner of a recent cricket series, the price of a kilo of rice. The third is calculation , tested with simple, practical sums ("If you buy two kilos of tomatoes at 30 rupees a kilo and pay with a 100-rupee note, how much change will you get?"). The fourth is comprehension , the ability to understand a short story or a practical situation. The interpretation, again, is everything. A farmer who left school at ten may not know the name of the state's capital and may still calculate the price of a cartload of sugarcane in his head faster than the clinician can on a phone. A failure matters when it falls clearly below what the person's education and occupation predict, because then it suggests either lifelong intellectual disability (when the history shows that he was always so) or deterioration (when the history shows that he used to do better). The written entry reads, for example, "intelligence appears average, consistent with educational and occupational background". When a numerical estimate is needed, the clinician refers for formal testing with an intelligence scale (the Wechsler scales, the Bhatia Battery, the Binet-Kamat test and others, taught in the Assessment book). Abstract thinking: proverbs and similarities In the MSE sense, abstract thinking is the ability to move beyond the particular and literal to the general: to grasp categories, concepts, metaphors and the principle behind a concrete example. Its loss, concrete thinking , is thinking tied to the literal, immediate and physical features of things. The German neurologist Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965), working with soldiers who had suffered brain injuries in the First World War, described the loss of the "abstract attitude" as a basic effect of brain damage, and with Martin Scheerer published a set of tests of abstract and concrete behaviour in 1941. The bedside examination uses two tasks. Proverb interpretation asks the client what a familiar proverb means. A Kannada-speaking client might be asked about haasige iddashtu kaalu chaachu ("stretch your legs only as far as your bed goes"), a Hindi speaker about its twin jitni chadar ho, utne hi pair phailao , and an English speaker about "People who live in glass houses should not throw stones". An abstract answer captures the principle ("live within your means"; "don't criticise others for faults you have yourself"). A concrete answer stays with the objects ("if your legs go off the bed they will touch the cold floor"; "the glass will break"). Proverbs work only if they are familiar, so the clinician uses proverbs from the client's own language and asks first whether he has heard the proverb before. (A standardised version, the Gorham Proverbs Test of 1956, belongs to the Assessment book.) Similarities ask what two things have in common: an orange and a banana, a table and a chair, a dog and a lion, a poem and a statue. Answers fall into three levels. The abstract answer names the category ("both are fruits"; "both are furniture"). The functional answer names a use or action ("you can eat both"; "you use both in a dining room"), a partly abstract level. The concrete answer names a physical feature ("both have skins"; "both have four legs"), or the client simply insists that they are different ("an orange is round and a banana is long"). Differences can be asked too: what is the difference between a lie and a mistake? (The abstract answer turns on intention.) Similarities are easier than proverbs and depend less on culture, so they are the better test for a client with little schooling. Concrete thinking is found in organic brain disease (especially frontal lobe damage and dementia), in intellectual disability, in some patients with schizophrenia, and in young children, for whom it is normal (Jean Piaget's concrete operational stage is in the Developmental Psychology book). Psychiatric texts describe two further abnormalities. In over-abstraction the answer goes too far, generalising far beyond relevance ("an orange and a banana are both manifestations of the cosmic energy"), and in bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretation the answer reflects the patient's thought disorder or delusions ("glass houses means that the government is watching through my windows"); both are seen in schizophrenia and point back to the thought disorder of Section 2.5. Table 2.15 gathers the bedside tests of this section in one place, with a rough guide to what a healthy adult of average education does. Table 2.15 The bedside tests of the cognitive functions, in the order they are examined. Function Bedside test Healthy adult (rough guide) Consciousness Observation; GCS if impaired Alert; GCS 15 Orientation Time, place and person questions Correct, apart from small slips of date Attention Digit span forwards and backwards About 6 to 7 forwards, 4 to 5 backwards Concentration Serial sevens; serial threes; days or months backwards Completed, with at most an occasional slip Immediate memory Repeat three words at once All three registered Recent memory Three words after five minutes; events of the last day All three; events verified Remote memory Verifiable personal and public past Accurate Intelligence General information, calculation, comprehension In keeping with education Abstract thinking Proverbs; similarities and differences Abstract or category answers Exam trap "An orange and a banana are both fruits" is abstract ; "you can eat both" is functional ; "both have skins" is concrete . Proverb interpretation is culture-bound: a concrete answer to an unfamiliar proverb, or from a person with little schooling, is not by itself a sign of illness, which is why similarities are the fairer test. Concrete thinking is normal in young children and abnormal in adults with organic brain disease, intellectual disability or schizophrenia; over-abstraction and bizarre interpretations are the signs that point to schizophrenic thought disorder. Judgement: personal, social and test In the MSE, judgement is the ability to assess a situation correctly, weigh the likely consequences of different courses of action and act appropriately. It is the cognitive function closest to everyday life, and the one whose impairment most often brings a patient to hospital: a man in a manic episode who resigns from a secure job to start five businesses at once, an older woman with dementia who gives her savings to a stranger at the door, a young man who drives home drunk. Clinicians assess it in three ways, summarised in Table 2.16. Personal judgement concerns the person's own life: whether his plans, expectations and decisions about his health, work, money and relationships are realistic. It is assessed by asking about his plans ("What will you do when you leave the hospital?", "How will you manage the loan?") and by comparing what he says with what the history shows he has actually done. Social judgement concerns his conduct with other people: whether he behaves appropriately in the interview, on the ward and at home, and whether he can anticipate how others will react to him. It is assessed by observation (an overfamiliar remark to a stranger, undressing in a public place, shouting in a temple) and from the informants. Finally, test judgement asks how the person would act in a standard hypothetical situation: "What would you do if you found a sealed, stamped and addressed envelope lying on the road?" (post it), "What would you do if you saw smoke and fire in a crowded cinema hall?" (alert the staff and the people near you and leave calmly, rather than shout "fire" and start a stampede), "What would you do if you smelled gas when you entered your kitchen?" (turn off the cylinder, open the windows and not light anything). Table 2.16 The three kinds of judgement assessed in the MSE. Kind Question it answers How it is assessed Personal judgement Are his plans and decisions about his own life realistic? Questions about plans; comparison with what the history shows he has done Social judgement Does he behave appropriately with other people? Observation in the interview and on the ward; informants' reports Test judgement What would he do in a standard hypothetical situation? Problems such as the found envelope, the fire in the cinema, the smell of gas The three are not equally informative, and this is the single most important point about judgement. Test judgement measures whether the person knows what a sensible person would do; it does not measure whether he does it. A man in the middle of a manic episode will usually tell you, correctly and with some impatience, that he would post the envelope, and then go home and spend the family's savings on a car. A patient with frontal lobe damage may give textbook answers to every hypothetical problem while his life falls apart through impulsive decisions. Personal and social judgement, drawn from the history and from behaviour, therefore carry much more weight than test judgement, and an entry that reads only "judgement intact" on the strength of the envelope question tells the reader almost nothing. Judgement is impaired in mania, in acute psychosis (where decisions follow from delusions), in dementia, in frontal lobe disease, in intoxication and in intellectual disability. In depression it is more often distorted than lost: a hopeless person may decide, with what seems to him clear logic, to abandon his studies or resign from his job, and the clinician's advice to postpone major decisions until the depression lifts is a judgement made on his behalf. Exam trap The three kinds are personal (own plans and life decisions), social (conduct with others) and test (hypothetical situations such as the found envelope or the fire in a cinema). Intact test judgement does not mean intact judgement : a manic or frontal patient can answer the envelope question correctly and still behave recklessly, so personal and social judgement from the history and behaviour matter more. Do not confuse judgement (deciding and acting appropriately) with insight (awareness of one's own illness), although the two often fail together. Insight and its six grades The last heading of the MSE asks a question that sounds simple and is not: does the patient know that he is ill? In the MSE, insight is the patient's awareness that he has an illness, his understanding of its nature and causes, and his acceptance that he needs treatment. The classic definition was given in 1934 by Aubrey Lewis (1900 to 1975), the Australian-born psychiatrist who later led the Institute of Psychiatry in London: insight is "a correct attitude to a morbid change in oneself". Each word of the definition does work. "Correct" means that the patient's view matches reality; "morbid change" means that what must be recognised is a change from his usual self, the kind of change the case history was designed to document; and "in oneself" places the change inside the person, not in the neighbours, the government or the evil eye. Insight is assessed by a short sequence of questions, asked without argument: "Do you think anything is wrong with you?" "What do you think it is?" "What has caused it?" "Do you think you need treatment? What kind?" "Will you take it?" The answers are then graded. The six grades most often taught, set out in Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry and in most Indian MSE formats, are shown in Table 2.17 with the kind of statement a patient at each grade might make. Table 2.17 The six grades of insight, with typical statements. Grade Definition A patient might say 1 Complete denial of illness "Nothing is wrong with me. My family brought me here for nothing." 2 Slight awareness of being sick and needing help, while denying it at the same time "Maybe I need a tonic for sleep, but I am not ill." 3 Awareness of being sick, but blaming it on others, on external events or on physical factors "I am like this because my neighbours did black magic", or "It is all the gas in my stomach." 4 Awareness that the illness is due to something unknown in oneself "Something has gone wrong inside my mind. I don't know what." 5 Intellectual insight: admits the illness and that symptoms come from his own irrational feelings or disturbances, but does not apply this knowledge to future experience "The voices are part of my illness and the tablets help", yet he stops the tablets as soon as he feels better. 6 True emotional insight: emotional awareness of his own motives and feelings and those of important people in his life, leading to basic changes in behaviour "When the old suspicion starts, I now tell my wife and see the doctor before it takes hold." The step that students find hardest is the one from grade 5 to grade 6. What is called intellectual insight is knowledge: the patient can say, correctly, that he has an illness and that his symptoms are part of it, but the knowledge does not change what he does. By contrast, true emotional insight is knowledge that has been felt and used: it reaches his feelings, his understanding of himself and the people around him, and his behaviour. The distinction comes from the psychotherapeutic tradition (in psychodynamic therapy, Chapter 3, intellectual insight without emotional insight is a familiar form of resistance), and it explains a common clinical paradox: a patient who can lecture you on his diagnosis and still relapse every year because he stops treatment. Modern research treats insight as a set of dimensions rather than a single ladder. In an influential paper of 1990, the British psychiatrist Anthony David proposed three: recognising that one has a mental illness, accepting the need for treatment (and adhering to it), and being able to relabel unusual mental events, such as hallucinations and delusions, as abnormal. A patient can have one without the others: a woman may take her tablets faithfully "because my husband insists" while denying that anything is wrong, and a man may accept that he is ill while insisting that his voices are real. Rating scales built on this approach, such as the Scale to Assess Unawareness of Mental Disorder of Xavier Amador and colleagues (1993), belong to the Assessment book. Key study: lack of insight in the International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (WHO, 1973) In the late 1960s the World Health Organization ran the International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia, in which psychiatrists in nine centres (Aarhus, Agra, Cali, Ibadan, London, Moscow, Prague, Taipei and Washington) examined 1,202 patients with the Present State Examination that you met in Section 2.1. The researchers wanted to know which symptoms of schizophrenia were common to every culture. The answer surprised many people. The single most frequent finding was not hallucinations or delusions but lack of insight, present in about 97 percent of the patients diagnosed with schizophrenia. The finding has two lessons for the MSE. Poor insight is not a rare complication of psychosis but nearly its rule, so the clinician must expect it and plan engagement around it. And because Agra was one of the nine centres, the result holds for Indian patients too. Why does insight matter so much? Because it predicts behaviour. Poor insight is one of the strongest predictors of non-adherence to treatment, of relapse and of compulsory admission, and in risk assessment (Section 2.7) lack of insight is an item on the best-known violence risk scheme. Yet the relationship is not simple. In schizophrenia, patients who gain insight are, on average, more likely to become depressed and to think of suicide, because to see clearly that one has a serious, long-term illness is painful; this is sometimes called the insight paradox, and it is a reason to watch for depression as insight improves. At the neurological end, unawareness of a deficit can be a direct effect of brain damage: the French neurologist Joseph Babinski (1857 to 1932) coined the word anosognosia in 1914 for the failure of some patients with right-hemisphere strokes to recognise that the left side of the body is paralysed. Some researchers, Amador among them, argue that much of the poor insight of schizophrenia is closer to anosognosia than to psychological denial. Indian context Insight must be judged against the patient's culture. Many Indian families explain illness in terms of karma, planetary influences, the evil eye, spirit possession or sorcery (often called maata or banamathi ), and Section 2.2 showed why the clinician should ask about this explanatory model rather than dismiss it. Holding a belief that is shared by one's family and community is not, by itself, poor insight. What the clinician grades is narrower: does the patient recognise that a change has taken place in himself , and will he accept help for it? A woman who says, "My mother-in-law thinks it is a spirit, and perhaps it is, but I know I have not been myself and the tablets help me sleep" has more insight than her words about spirits suggest. Many clients hold a medical and a spiritual explanation side by side, and use the doctor and the temple together. Exam trap In the MSE, insight is the patient's awareness and understanding of his own illness . It is not orientation to time, place and person, not the level of consciousness, not immediate retention and recall, not the ability to do serial subtraction and not the presence of hallucinations: those are all separate MSE headings, and they are the usual distractors. Know the six grades: 1 complete denial; 2 slight awareness while denying; 3 aware but blames external or physical factors ; 4 aware that the cause is something unknown in himself ; 5 intellectual insight; 6 true emotional insight, which changes behaviour. Do not confuse the MSE's insight with Wolfgang Köhler's "insight learning" in chimpanzees (General Psychology). Bedside screening: the MMSE and its relatives The bedside examination described so far is flexible: the clinician chooses the questions and judges the answers. For some purposes, following a patient's cognition over months, comparing patients across clinics or deciding quickly who needs a full assessment, a standard, scored version is more useful. The best known is the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), published in 1975 by Marshal F. Folstein , Susan Folstein and Paul McHugh under the title "'Mini-mental state': a practical method for grading the cognitive state of patients for the clinician". They wanted something a busy doctor could give in five to ten minutes, and that is what it remains. Table 2.18 shows how its 30 points are distributed; notice how many of the tasks are the ones you have just met. Table 2.18 The structure of the Mini-Mental State Examination (Folstein, Folstein and McHugh, 1975). Domain Task Points Orientation to time Year, season, date, day, month 5 Orientation to place State, county (district in India), town, hospital, floor 5 Registration Repeat three named objects 3 Attention and calculation Serial sevens (five subtractions), or WORLD spelled backwards 5 Recall The three objects, a few minutes later 3 Language Name two objects (2); repeat a phrase (1); three-stage command (3); read and obey "Close your eyes" (1); write a sentence (1) 8 Visuospatial construction Copy two intersecting pentagons 1 Total 30 A score of 23 or less is commonly taken to suggest cognitive impairment, with 24 to 30 regarded as normal, although clinicians adjust the cut-off for age and especially for education. That adjustment is the MMSE's great weakness in India. Several items (writing a sentence, reading a command, serial sevens) assume literacy and schooling, so an illiterate but cognitively healthy villager may score in the "impaired" range, while a retired professor in the early stages of dementia may still score 29. For this reason Mary Ganguli and her colleagues developed the Hindi Mental State Examination (HMSE, 1995) for a largely illiterate rural elderly population near Ballabgarh in Haryana, replacing the literacy-dependent items with tasks that do not require schooling. The MMSE is also insensitive to mild impairment and to problems of executive (frontal) function, and it says nothing about the cause of a low score. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), published by Ziad Nasreddine and colleagues in 2005, was designed to fill that gap: it is also scored out of 30, but adds tasks of executive function (a short trail-making task, drawing a clock, copying a cube, verbal fluency), uses a harder memory test, takes a cut-off of 26 and is more sensitive to mild cognitive impairment. Keep these instruments in proportion. They are screening tests: a low score says "look further", never "this is dementia". The diagnosis comes from the history, the full examination, investigations and formal neuropsychological assessment, and the tests themselves, their norms and their psychometric properties are taught in the Assessment book. Exam trap The MMSE (Folstein, Folstein and McHugh, 1975 ) is a 30-point cognitive screening test ; the MSE is the clinician's whole description of the mental state. They are not the same thing, and the MMSE is not a diagnostic interview (the SCID is, Section 2.1). The usual cut-off is 23 or below ; the MMSE is education-sensitive and insensitive to mild and frontal impairment. The MoCA (Nasreddine, 2005) is more sensitive to mild cognitive impairment, cut-off 26. The HMSE (Ganguli, 1995) is the Hindi adaptation for illiterate rural elderly people. Writing the MSE: a model you can copy An MSE that stays in the clinician's head is of no use to anyone. It has to be written so that a colleague who has never met the patient can picture him, compare him with how he will be next week, and see how the clinician reached the conclusions. A few rules make the difference between a useful MSE and a list of jargon. Describe, then label. Write what you saw and heard, with the patient's own words in quotation marks, and add the technical term afterwards. "Persecutory delusion" alone is an opinion; "believes firmly that his neighbours have fitted a device in his phone to record his thoughts, and was not shaken when shown that the phone was ordinary (persecutory delusion)" is evidence. Record the present, not the past. The MSE is the photograph, not the film. "Has not slept well for three months" belongs to the history; "looks tired and yawned repeatedly" belongs to the MSE. Write every heading, including the normal ones, and the important negatives: "no suicidal ideation", "no hallucinations elicited". An absent heading leaves the reader unsure whether the function was normal or never examined. Record the conditions: the date and time, the setting, the language used, who was present, how long the interview lasted and how cooperative the patient was, since all of these affect the findings. Close with a short summary and a statement of risk. The summary pulls out the significant findings in three or four lines; the risk statement (Section 2.7) records what was asked about harm to self and others and what was found.
