Examined in the outpatient department on 12 March at 11 a.m., in Kannada, for about 45 minutes; his brother was present for the first ten minutes. General appearance and behaviour. A well-built man who looks his stated age, wearing a new, brightly coloured shirt, three gold chains and dark glasses, which he kept on indoors until asked to remove them; hair freshly dyed; hygiene adequate. Eye contact excessive. Overfamiliar and jocular, calling the examiner "boss", and briefly irritable when interrupted. Rapport established easily but difficult to sustain. Psychomotor activity: increased; got up from his chair four times, walked to the window and handled the objects on the desk; no abnormal involuntary movements. Speech: spontaneous; rate and volume increased; pressured and difficult to interrupt; reaction time shortened (began answering before questions were finished); relevant and coherent at first, less goal-directed as the interview went on; frequent rhymes and puns. Mood: subjectively, "I have never felt better in my life, I am on top of the world." Affect: elated, with irritability when contradicted; labile (tearful for a few seconds when speaking of his late father, laughing again within a minute); reactive; congruent with the content of his thought. Thought. Stream and form: pressure of thought with flight of ideas; a sample: "I will buy ten autos, ten autos, ten toes, my toes are faster than Usain Bolt, bolt the door, the door to success is open." Content: a grandiose delusion that the Chief Minister has personally chosen him to run all the transport in Mysuru, held with full conviction and not shaken when his brother pointed out that he has never met the Chief Minister; no persecutory ideas; denies suicidal ideation; no homicidal ideation, but said of his brother, who has taken away his ATM card, "I will teach him a lesson"; no obsessions. Possession of thought: no thought insertion, withdrawal or broadcasting. Perception: denies hallucinations; none inferred from his behaviour; no illusions, depersonalisation or derealisation. Cognitive functions. Conscious and alert. Oriented to time, place and person. Attention easily aroused but not sustained; distracted by traffic noise and by objects on the desk. Digit span 6 forwards and 4 backwards; abandoned serial sevens after 86 ("I don't need mathematics, I will have accountants"); months backwards with two errors from distraction. Immediate memory: registered three words at the first attempt. Recent memory: recalled 3 of 3 at five minutes; described the morning's journey correctly. Remote memory intact (gave the year of his marriage and his children's ages, confirmed by his wife). Intelligence: average, consistent with his education to the tenth standard; general information adequate (named the Prime Minister and the Chief Minister, and the price of petrol). Abstract thinking: explained haasige iddashtu kaalu chaachu as "live within your means", then added, laughing, "but my bed has no end"; similarities abstract. Judgement: personal judgement impaired (plans to borrow fifteen lakh rupees to buy ten auto-rickshaws and sees no difficulty in repaying it); social judgement impaired (overfamiliar with the women at the registration counter, on his brother's report and as observed); test judgement intact. Insight: grade 1, complete denial: "Nothing is wrong with me. My brother is jealous; I came only because my wife was crying." Summary and risk. A 34-year-old man with increased psychomotor activity, pressured speech, elated and labile affect, flight of ideas and a grandiose delusion, with distractible attention, intact orientation and memory, impaired personal and social judgement and no insight. No suicidal ideation; risk of financial harm to himself and his family; verbal threat towards his brother, with no history of violence, requiring assessment (Section 2.7). Notice three things about the model. Every abnormal finding is backed by an example or a quotation; the cognitive section separates a problem of attention (he gave up serial sevens because he was distracted) from problems of memory and orientation (both intact), which is exactly the pattern expected in mania; and the judgement entry shows intact test judgement sitting beside impaired personal and social judgement, the trap from Section 2.6.8 in a real patient. What the MSE does not do is give a diagnosis. That comes in the formulation (Section 2.9), which joins the photograph to the film. What did the same headings show for Ravi? His cognitive examination was close to normal, which is itself informative. He was alert and fully oriented; his digit span was 6 forwards and 4 backwards; he completed serial sevens slowly and with visible effort, making two slips that he corrected himself; he recalled 3 of 3 words at five minutes, although he insisted beforehand that he would not remember any. His complaint that "nothing goes into my head" was therefore far worse than his measured performance, the pattern of depression described in Section 2.6.5. His intelligence was above average and his abstraction intact; his social and test judgement were intact, but his personal judgement was coloured by hopelessness ("There is no point in applying again"). His insight was grade 3: he agreed that he could not sleep or study and accepted help for his sleep, but blamed everything on the examination and his father and said that "no tablet can change my result". And the MSE recorded one more finding, under thought content, that the clinician could not leave there: a passive wish to be dead, and the sentence his mother had already reported, "everyone would be better off without me". What a clinician does with that sentence is the subject of the next section. 2.7 Risk Assessment: Suicide and Violence Lower yield · not asked yet "Everyone would be better off without me." Ravi said it to his mother a week before he came to the clinic, and he said something like it again in the interview. What should the clinician do with that sentence? Two reactions are common in trainees, and both are wrong. One is to panic: to stop the assessment, telephone the family and arrange an admission on the strength of a single sentence. The other is to let it pass, because Ravi is polite, has no plan and "doesn't seem the type". The right response lies between them, and it is a skill: a calm, systematic inquiry into whether this person is likely to harm himself, or anyone else, in the near future, and what can be done to make that less likely. That inquiry is risk assessment . Risk assessment is not a separate test bolted onto the end of the interview. It runs through everything you have read in this chapter: the history (previous attempts, family suicides, substance use, past violence, Section 2.3), the mental state (hopelessness, delusions, command hallucinations, insight, Sections 2.5 and 2.6) and the formulation (Section 2.9). It also needs an honest starting point. No clinician, and no scale, can predict whether a particular person will die by suicide or commit a violent act. What a clinician can do is identify the people and the moments at which risk is raised, understand why, and act on the factors that can be changed. Prevention at the level of services and populations (means restriction, helplines, gatekeeper training, safety planning) is taught in Section 9.7, and dialectical behaviour therapy for chronic self-harm in Section 5.8. This section is about the assessment of one person in one room. Asking about suicide: the words and the ladder First, the vocabulary, because exam questions and case notes depend on it. The term suicidal ideation means thoughts of ending one's life. It may be passive (a wish to be dead, to not wake up, to be killed in an accident, without any thought of acting) or active (thoughts of killing oneself). By contrast, suicidal intent is the strength of the person's wish to die and of his expectation that he will act. A suicide plan specifies the method, the place and the time. Preparatory acts are steps taken to carry the plan out: buying tablets, collecting pesticide, writing a note or a will, giving away belongings, saying goodbyes. Rehearsal is a practice run, either in imagination or in action: standing at the edge of the terrace, holding the tablets, tying the rope. A suicide attempt is a self-injurious act carried out with at least some intent to die; it is interrupted when someone else stops it and aborted when the person stops himself before harm is done. The broader term self-harm , the one used in British and Indian guidelines, covers any intentional self-poisoning or self-injury, whatever its motive, while non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is deliberate damage to one's own body, such as cutting or burning, without any intent to die, usually to relieve unbearable tension or to punish oneself. (DSM-5-TR codes current and past suicidal behaviour and NSSI among the conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention, and proposes a disorder of each for further study; these belong to the Psychiatric Disorders book.) Second, the principle. You ask, directly and in plain words. Section 2.2 introduced the fear that underlies most avoidance, the belief that asking about suicide puts the idea into someone's head, and the evidence that it does not. The study that settled the question for many clinicians is worth knowing in detail. Key study: does asking about suicide plant the idea? (Gould and colleagues, 2005) Madelyn Gould and her colleagues at Columbia University tested the fear directly. In six high schools in New York State, between 2002 and 2004, 2,342 students taking part in a screening programme were randomly assigned, class by class, to complete one of two versions of the screening questionnaires: one that included questions about suicidal thoughts and behaviour, and one identical except that those questions were left out. Two days later all the students were asked about distress and suicidal ideation. If asking plants the idea, the students who had been asked should have reported more suicidal thinking. They did not: the two groups did not differ. The students at highest risk (those who were depressed, using substances or had attempted suicide before) were not harmed either: if anything, the depressed students who had been asked were less distressed, and the previous attempters who had been asked less suicidal, than comparable high-risk students who had not. Later systematic reviews (Dazzi and colleagues, 2014, Section 2.2) reached the same conclusion for adults and adolescents. Asking is safe; not asking leaves risk undiscovered. Third, the method. The inquiry climbs a ladder, one step at a time, from the general to the specific, as Figure 2.8 shows. It starts with a normalising lead-in that gives permission to answer honestly: "When people are as low as you have been, they sometimes feel that life is not worth living. Have you felt like that?" A "yes" leads to the next rung: thoughts of ending life, then intent, then plan and means, then preparation and rehearsal; and, whatever the answers, the clinician asks about any past attempt. Use clear words such as "kill yourself" or "end your life", not euphemisms like "do something silly", which allow both of you to misunderstand. In Kannada, Hindi or any other language, learn the plain local phrase and use it. And see the client alone for part of the interview: an adolescent will not tell you about last week's tablets with her father in the room. 1 Passive ideation "Do you feel life is not worth living?" 2 Active ideation "Have you thought of ending your life?" 3 Intent "Do you think you might act on them?" 4 Plan and means "Have you thought how? Is it at hand?" 5 Preparation and rehearsal "Have you got things ready, or practised?" 6 Past attempts (always ask) "Have you ever tried? What happened?" Each step up raises the risk Climb one step at a time; a "yes" leads to the next question Figure 2.8 The ladder of questions in a suicide risk assessment. Each rung is more specific and, when answered "yes", marks higher risk. Notice that the top rung, past attempts, is asked of everyone, whatever the answers below it. Each rung has its own follow-up questions. For ideation : how often the thoughts come, how long they last, how intense they are, whether he can push them away, and what stops him from acting on them (his children, his religion, fear of pain, the thought of his mother finding him). For intent : "How likely do you think it is that you will act on these thoughts?" and "What do you expect would happen?" For the plan : the method, the place and the time, and whether the plan includes avoiding discovery. For the means : whether the method is available, a question with special force in India, where pesticides stored in a farmhouse, a stock of tablets, a rope, a high terrace or a railway line near the house may be within easy reach. For preparation and rehearsal : whether he has bought or saved anything, written a note, settled debts, given away possessions or "practised". Rehearsal matters because each practice run makes the act less frightening and more possible, an idea developed by the interpersonal theory in Section 2.7.2. A past attempt is explored in detail, because it is the best guide to what the person might do again. The clinician asks what happened, step by step, and listens for the signs of high intent that Aaron Beck and his colleagues built into the Suicide Intent Scale (1974): was the person alone, was the act timed so that discovery was unlikely, did he take precautions against being found, did he leave a note or make final arrangements, did he tell anyone beforehand, and did he believe that the method would kill him? The clinician adds one more question of his own: is he now sorry or relieved to have survived? Notice that the last questions concern belief, not the medical facts. The lethality of an act, its medical danger, is not the same as intent. A 15-year-old girl who swallows five paracetamol tablets believing they will kill her has shown high intent with low lethality; a man who swallows a cupful of a highly toxic pesticide in a fit of anger at his wife, meaning only to frighten her, has shown low intent with very high lethality. Both are serious, for different reasons, and many people are wrong about how dangerous a method is. (Beck's Suicide Intent Scale, his Scale for Suicide Ideation and the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale are taught in the Assessment book.) Exam trap Asking directly about suicide does not increase suicidal thinking (Gould and colleagues, 2005; Dazzi and colleagues, 2014); it is the standard of care. The steps run ideation (passive, then active), intent, plan, means, preparation and rehearsal , with past attempts asked about in every case. Lethality (medical danger) is not intent (the wish and expectation of dying). Self-harm covers all intentional self-poisoning and self-injury whatever the motive; non-suicidal self-injury has no intent to die; an interrupted attempt is stopped by someone else, an aborted one by the person himself. Risk factors, warning signs and protective factors The answers to the ladder of questions are weighed against what is known, from studies of large populations, about who dies by suicide. A risk factor is a characteristic that is associated with a higher probability of suicide across a population. A protective factor is one associated with a lower probability. Table 2.20 sets out the main ones, and a few deserve comment. Table 2.20 The main risk and protective factors for suicide. Domain Risk factors Protective factors Clinical Depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, substance use (especially alcohol), personality disorder; insomnia, agitation Effective treatment, adherence and a good therapeutic alliance History Previous attempt (the strongest single predictor); family history of suicide; childhood abuse Past crises survived with help Psychological Hopelessness; perceived burdensomeness; impulsivity; shame and humiliation Reasons for living; hope and future plans; problem-solving skills Social Living alone; widowed, separated or divorced; isolation; recent loss or conflict Family support; responsibility for children; community and religious ties, including moral objection to suicide Situational Access to lethal means; recent discharge from a psychiatric ward; debt, job loss, chronic painful illness Restricted access to means; easy access to care Demographic Male sex (for death by suicide); age bands that differ by country None in particular A previous suicide attempt is the strongest single predictor of eventual suicide: in follow-up studies of people treated after self-harm, roughly 1 to 2 percent die by suicide within a year, a risk many times that of the general population, and the risk remains raised for years. Mental disorder is present in the great majority of suicides in Western psychological autopsy studies, around 90 percent, with depression the commonest; studies in China have found a lower proportion and Indian studies give mixed figures, and in both countries acute interpersonal and financial crises, and impulsive acts with highly lethal poisons, play a larger part. Hopelessness , the expectation that the future holds nothing good and that nothing can change it, is the psychological factor with the strongest evidence. In a ten-year follow-up of patients who had been admitted to hospital with suicidal ideation, Beck and his colleagues (1985) found that, of all the measures taken on admission, only the Beck Hopelessness Scale (Chapter 5) and the pessimism item of the Beck Depression Inventory predicted who would later die by suicide; hopelessness mattered more than how depressed the patient was. Sex works in opposite directions for different outcomes: in almost every country men die by suicide more often than women, while women report more suicidal ideation and make more attempts, a pattern called the gender paradox of suicide. Even here India is unusual: Indian women have some of the highest suicide rates of women anywhere in the world. Why do some people with these risk factors die while most do not? Two theories are worth knowing, one old and one new. The French sociologist Émile Durkheim (1858 to 1917), in Le Suicide (1897), argued that suicide rates reflect how well a society integrates and regulates its members, and described four types: egoistic suicide, from too little integration (the isolated person with no ties); altruistic suicide, from too much (the person who dies for the group); anomic suicide, from too little regulation, when sudden change, such as a financial collapse or the loss of a high-status job, leaves people without norms; and fatalistic suicide, from too much regulation, when the future is blocked by oppressive control. (Durkheim's sociology is taught more fully in the Social Psychology book.) The newer theory is the interpersonal theory of suicide of the American psychologist Thomas E. Joiner , set out in Why People Die by Suicide (2005) and refined with Kimberly Van Orden and colleagues (2010). Joiner asked why so few of the people who want to die actually kill themselves, and answered that suicide requires two separate things. The desire for death arises when two painful states occur together: perceived burdensomeness , the belief that one's existence is a burden on the people one loves, so that they would be better off without one, and thwarted belongingness , the feeling of being alienated and cut off from others. The capability for suicide, which Joiner called acquired capability , is the lowered fear of death and raised tolerance of pain that people acquire through repeated exposure to painful and frightening experiences: previous attempts, self-injury, rehearsal, violence. Only when desire and capability are present together does a lethal attempt become likely. Listen to Ravi again with the theory in mind: "everyone would be better off without me" is perceived burdensomeness in its purest form, and a young man who has stopped going home at weekends and barely leaves his rented room is losing his sense of belonging. The theory also explains why rehearsal and previous attempts are so ominous: they build capability. Risk factors describe who is at risk over months and years. By contrast, warning signs describe who may be at risk now, in the coming hours or days. A working group of the American Association of Suicidology condensed them into the mnemonic IS PATH WARM: I deation, S ubstance abuse; P urposelessness, A nxiety, T rapped, H opelessness; W ithdrawal, A nger, R ecklessness, M ood change. Some warning signs are behaviours that family members notice before clinicians do: talking or writing about death, searching for methods, giving away prized possessions, saying goodbye, and a sudden, unexplained calm in a person who has been deeply depressed, which may mean that a decision has been made. Protective factors are the other side of the balance. Marsha M. Linehan (1943 to 2026), the creator of dialectical behaviour therapy, and her colleagues built the Reasons for Living Inventory (1983) on the observation that what keeps many suicidal people alive is not the absence of pain but the presence of reasons: responsibility to family and children, fear of the act, moral or religious objection, plans for the future and belief in one's ability to cope. In India, family ties and religious belief are often powerful protective factors, although the family can also be the source of the crisis, as Ravi's is. Two cautions apply. Protective factors do not cancel risk factors arithmetically: a man with a loving wife is still at high risk if he has a rope in his room and a plan for tonight. And a protective factor can disappear overnight, with a quarrel, a bereavement or a failed examination. Finally, the factors differ in whether they can change. The static risk factors are fixed, or change only in one direction: sex, age, a history of previous attempts, a family history of suicide, childhood abuse. They set the person's baseline level of risk. The dynamic risk factors can change, and can be changed: hopelessness, the severity of depression, insomnia, agitation, alcohol use, isolation, access to means. They determine the person's current level of risk, and they are the targets of every intervention. The distinction, as you will see in Section 2.7.5, is equally central to the assessment of violence. Indian context The National Crime Records Bureau records more than 1.7 lakh suicides a year in India (Section 9.7 gives the figures). Most occur between the ages of 18 and 45, so the Western picture of suicide as chiefly a problem of older men does not fit. Family problems and illness are the two commonest reasons recorded, and hanging and poisoning (much of it with pesticides) are the commonest methods. Groups that appear repeatedly in the records include daily-wage earners, housewives, farmers and agricultural labourers, and students, among whom examination results and coaching-centre pressure are recurring triggers, exactly Ravi's situation. Because many suicides in India follow an acute crisis with a highly lethal poison close at hand, asking about access to means is not a formality. Exam trap The strongest single predictor of suicide is a previous attempt ; the strongest psychological predictor is hopelessness (Beck and colleagues, 1985), more than the severity of depression. Men die by suicide more often, women attempt more often (the gender paradox ). Joiner's interpersonal theory (2005): desire = perceived burdensomeness + thwarted belongingness ; capability = acquired capability (habituation to pain and fear). Durkheim (1897): egoistic, altruistic, anomic, fatalistic. Risk factors are long-term and population-based; warning signs (IS PATH WARM) are near-term. Static factors cannot be changed; dynamic factors can, and they are what treatment targets. The SAD PERSONS mnemonic and its limits Faced with a long list of risk factors, busy doctors wanted something they could remember in an emergency department at three in the morning. In 1983 William Patterson and his colleagues Henry Dohn, Julian Bird and Gary Patterson, writing in the journal Psychosomatics , offered one. The SAD PERSONS scale turns ten risk factors into an acronym, scores one point for each factor present and links the total to a recommended action (Table 2.21). It was devised as a teaching aid, to help medical students and non-psychiatrists remember what to ask, and in Patterson's own report medical students who had been taught it were better than untaught students at judging a low-risk and a high-risk patient correctly and recommending what should be done, as rated by three experienced psychiatrists. Table 2.21 The SAD PERSONS scale (Patterson, Dohn, Bird and Patterson, 1983). One point for each factor present. Letter Risk factor S Sex: male A Age: under 19 or over 45 D Depression P Previous attempt E Ethanol (alcohol) abuse R Rational thinking loss (psychosis, confusion) S Social supports lacking O Organised plan N No spouse (single, widowed, separated or divorced) S Sickness (chronic, debilitating illness) Suggested action 0 to 2: send home with follow-up; 3 to 4: close follow-up, consider admission; 5 to 6: strongly consider admission; 7 to 10: admit, involuntarily if necessary Five years later Hockberger and Rothstein (1988) produced a modified SAD PERSONS scale for emergency physicians, which gives two points instead of one to four items that seemed to matter more (depression or hopelessness, rational thinking loss, an organised or serious attempt, and a stated intent to repeat it) and changes several others. Both versions are still widely taught, and as a checklist they are useful: a clinician who runs through the letters will not forget to ask about alcohol or a previous attempt. As a way of deciding what to do with a patient, however, the scale has been heavily criticised, and an examiner who asks you to "use and criticise" it expects you to know why. First, it weights every item equally, so that being over 45 counts as much as having an organised plan, although the evidence says that plans, previous attempts and hopelessness matter far more. Second, it leaves out factors with strong evidence: hopelessness (in the original version), access to lethal means, recent discharge from hospital, impulsivity, a family history of suicide, childhood abuse and every protective factor. Third, its demographic items come from Western data and travel badly. In India, where most suicides occur between 18 and 45 and young women are at high risk, a 25-year-old married woman scores no points for sex, age or marital status. Fourth, most of its items are static, so the score barely changes as the patient improves or deteriorates. Fifth, and most important, when it has been tested as a predictor it has failed. In a study of 4,019 consecutive referrals to the emergency psychiatric services of the two largest hospitals in Manitoba, Canada, both in Winnipeg, James Bolton and his colleagues (2012) found that the scale predicted later suicide attempts no better than chance and, at its usual high-risk cut-off, missed about four in five of the patients who went on to make an attempt, and a systematic review by Warden and colleagues (2014) found that none of the studies that tested it showed that it predicted suicidal behaviour accurately, and concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support its use in assessing or predicting suicidal behaviour. Behind these particular faults lies a problem that no scale can solve: suicide is rare. Even in a group at raised risk, only a small proportion of people die by suicide in any given year, and when an outcome is rare, any test, however good, produces many more false alarms than true alarms. A false positive is a person whom the test flags as high risk who would not have died; a false negative is a person whom it calls low risk who does. The proportion of an outcome in the population being tested is its base rate . A worked example shows the arithmetic. Suppose a risk scale, far better than any that exists, correctly flags 80 percent of the people who will die by suicide (its sensitivity) and correctly clears 80 percent of those who will not (its specificity), and suppose it is used on 1,000 patients of whom 10 (1 percent) will die by suicide within a year. It catches 8 of the 10 and misses 2. But it also flags 20 percent of the 990 who would have lived, which is 198 people. Of the 206 patients labelled "high risk", only 8, fewer than 4 percent, would have died. If the label decides admission, the ward fills with people who were never going to die, and 2 of the 10 who were are sent home with a "low risk" note in the file. Key study: Pokorny's attempt to predict suicide (1983) The American psychiatrist Alex Pokorny asked the obvious question: if we know the risk factors, can we use them to pick out, in advance, the patients who will die? He assessed about 4,800 consecutive patients admitted to the psychiatric service of a Veterans Administration hospital in Houston, Texas, using the best risk factors and scales of the day, and then followed them for about five years. Sixty-seven of them died by suicide. His prediction did identify 35 of those 67 people, about half. It also identified 1,206 people who did not die by suicide: for every person correctly flagged, there were about 35 false positives, and the 32 people it missed included some who had seemed to be at low risk. Pokorny concluded that the prediction of suicide in individual patients was not feasible with the tools available. Four decades later a meta-analysis of 365 studies covering 50 years of research (Franklin and colleagues, 2017) reached essentially the same conclusion: known risk factors predict suicidal thoughts and behaviour only slightly better than chance, and prediction had not improved over the half-century. The lesson has been taken into clinical guidance. The 2022 guideline on self-harm of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in England advises clinicians not to use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, and not to use a global classification of patients into low, medium or high risk to decide who should be offered treatment or who should be discharged. Instead it asks for a thorough psychosocial assessment of each person's needs and of the factors that can be changed. That does not make risk assessment pointless; it changes its purpose, from prediction to understanding and management. Exam trap SAD PERSONS was published by Patterson and colleagues in 1983 as a teaching mnemonic for ten risk factors (Sex, Age, Depression, Previous attempt, Ethanol, Rational thinking loss, Social supports lacking, Organised plan, No spouse, Sickness), one point each; the modified version (Hockberger and Rothstein, 1988) double-weights four items. Its main limits: equal weights, missing factors (hopelessness, means, protective factors), Western demographics, static items and poor predictive validity . Prediction fails mainly because of the low base rate , which guarantees many false positives (Pokorny, 1983: 35 of 67 suicides identified, with 1,206 false positives). Use the mnemonic as a checklist, never as a score that decides admission or discharge. From prediction to formulation: Ravi's risk assessment If the score cannot decide, what does? The clinician's job is to build a risk formulation : a short, reasoned account of this person's risk that pulls together the static and dynamic factors, the warning signs, the answers to the ladder of questions and the protective factors, and explains them. A good risk formulation answers five questions. How high is this person's risk compared with other people (his chronic, baseline risk, set mostly by static factors)? How high is it now compared with his own usual level (his acute risk, set mostly by dynamic factors and warning signs)? Anthony Pisani and his colleagues (2016) call these two judgements risk status and risk state . Why is the risk raised now? What could make it rise suddenly? And what can be done, today, to bring it down? Notice that the last three questions are about understanding and action, not prediction: they are the 5 Ps of case formulation (Section 2.9) applied to one outcome. Here is how the clinician worked through it with Ravi. On the ladder, Ravi described daily passive thoughts that he would be better off dead and, on direct questioning, occasional thoughts over the past fortnight of "just ending it" by drinking the pesticide kept in the shed at his parents' farm. He said he had no intention of acting, because "it would kill my mother", had made no plan beyond that passing thought, had done nothing to prepare and had never rehearsed. He had never harmed himself; the episode at 17 involved no self-harm. Static factors : male; a possible previous depressive episode (the month of untreated sadness at 17); a family history of depression (his maternal uncle); no previous attempt; no family history of suicide. Dynamic factors : a moderately severe depressive episode with insomnia and weight loss; hopelessness ("there is no point in applying again"); perceived burdensomeness ("better off without me") and guilt about the pledged gold; withdrawal from his family (he has stopped going home and barely leaves the shared room he rents in Mysuru); access to a highly lethal method whenever he visits the farm. Warning signs : hopelessness, withdrawal, feeling trapped; no sudden calm, no farewells, no giving away of possessions. Protective factors : his strong bond with his mother, who has been staying with him for the past ten days, and his explicit reason for living ("it would kill my mother"); his religious faith; no alcohol or drug use; a good, if new, relationship with the clinician; and his willingness to come back. The formulation that followed was written in plain sentences. Ravi's baseline risk is modestly raised by his sex, a possible earlier depressive episode (so that his depression may prove to be recurrent) and his family history. His current risk is raised above his own usual level by a depressive episode with hopelessness and a strong sense of being a burden, but he has active ideation without intent, plan, preparation or rehearsal, and real protective factors, so the risk at present is not imminent. It could rise quickly with a further humiliation (another result, an angry scene with his father), with alcohol, or if he were alone at the farm with the pesticide while feeling trapped. The plan follows from the formulation and targets the dynamic factors: treatment of the depression; a collaborative safety plan written in his own words (the Stanley and Brown method taught in Section 9.7); with his agreement, a conversation with his mother about locking the pesticide away and about the warning signs to watch for; a follow-up appointment within a week, with the risk reviewed at every visit; and a crisis number he could ring. Notice what the plan does not contain: a no-suicide contract, which has no evidence behind it (Section 9.7), or an admission justified only by a score. For a patient at high and imminent risk, someone with intent, a plan and the means at hand, the response is proportionately stronger: he is not left alone, the means are removed, the family is involved and an urgent psychiatric assessment, often an admission, is arranged. And whatever the level, the clinician documents what was asked, what the patient said, the reasoning and the plan. A clear note is both good care and the clinician's best protection if things go wrong. One more question arises when risk is high: can the clinician tell the family without the patient's consent? Confidentiality is the rule, but protecting a person from serious and imminent harm is a recognised exception in every professional code and in Indian law; the rules and their limits are set out in Chapter 1. In practice the clinician tries first to obtain the client's agreement, as with Ravi, and explains honestly that safety comes before secrecy. Indian context For most of its history Indian law treated a suicide attempt as a crime, under section 309 of the Indian Penal Code. Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 changed this: notwithstanding section 309, a person who attempts suicide is presumed, unless the contrary is proved, to have severe stress and is not to be tried or punished, and the government has a duty to provide that person with care, treatment and rehabilitation to reduce the risk of another attempt. (The fuller legal story, including the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita that replaced the Penal Code in 2024, is in Section 9.7 and Chapter 1.) For the assessing clinician the change matters in a practical way. Fear of the police once kept many families from bringing a person to hospital after an attempt, and kept many patients from admitting what they had done. Telling a frightened patient that a suicide attempt is now treated as a sign of distress needing care, not as an offence, is often what makes an honest account possible. Exam trap The modern aim of suicide risk assessment is formulation and management , not prediction. Chronic (baseline) risk is set largely by static factors; acute risk by dynamic factors and warning signs (Pisani's risk status and risk state). Management targets dynamic factors. A safety plan (Stanley and Brown) is recommended; a no-suicide contract is not. Under section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 , a person who attempts suicide is presumed to have severe stress and is not to be tried or punished, and the government must provide care, treatment and rehabilitation. Assessing the risk of violence The second half of risk assessment asks whether the person may harm someone else. Mr Manjunath's MSE in Section 2.6.11 ended with a verbal threat against his brother; the same question arises with a man who hears voices telling him that his neighbour is poisoning him, a husband convinced that his wife is unfaithful, a young man brought in drunk after a fight. Before looking at how the assessment is done, it helps to clear away a myth that distorts it. The myth is that mental illness makes people dangerous. The great majority of people with mental illness are never violent, and people with severe mental illness are far more likely to be the victims of violence than its perpetrators. There is a modest association between some disorders and violence, but most of it is accounted for by other factors, above all substance use. The clearest evidence came from the MacArthur Violence Risk Assessment Study, led by Henry Steadman and John Monahan, which followed 1,136 patients for a year after their discharge from acute psychiatric wards in three American cities and, at one of the sites (Pittsburgh), compared them with people living in the same neighbourhoods (Steadman and colleagues, 1998). Discharged patients who did not misuse alcohol or drugs were no more violent than their neighbours who did not; substance misuse raised the rate of violence in both groups, and raised it more in the patients. In a Swedish national study, Seena Fazel and Martin Grann (2006) estimated that only about 5 percent of violent crime could be attributed to people with severe mental illness. Within that picture, some factors do raise risk, and they are what the clinician asks about. The most powerful by far is the oldest rule in the field: the best predictor of future violence is past violence , especially if it was recent, frequent, serious or unprovoked. Others are being young and male, substance misuse, antisocial personality traits and psychopathy, a history of childhood abuse or of witnessing violence, poor adherence to treatment and lack of insight. Among symptoms, attention has fallen on what Bruce Link and Ann Stueve (1994) called threat/control-override symptoms : the belief that one is being threatened or persecuted by others combined with the experience that one's mind is being controlled by outside forces, which together seem to override the usual restraints against violence. (Later analyses of the MacArthur data found the link between delusions and violence weaker than expected, so the evidence is mixed.) Command hallucinations instructing harm, persecutory delusions accompanied by anger, and morbid (delusional) jealousy, a well-known danger to the spouse, are each asked about specifically. Intoxication, withdrawal states, delirium, the irritability of mania and the agitation of dementia account for much of the short-term violence seen on wards and in emergency departments. Key study: the Baxstrom patients and the limits of clinical prediction (1966 to 1981) In 1966, in Baxstrom v. Herold , the United States Supreme Court ruled that Johnnie Baxstrom, a prisoner kept in a New York hospital for the criminally insane after his sentence had ended, had been detained without the legal protections given to other people facing civil commitment. As a result nearly a thousand patients who had been held in secure hospitals, because clinicians had judged them too dangerous for ordinary ones, were transferred to civil hospitals or released. Henry Steadman and Joseph Cocozza followed them up (their book Careers of the Criminally Insane appeared in 1974). In the first four years after the transfers only a minority, about one in five, were assaultive in the civil hospitals or the community, and by 1970 only about 3 percent had been returned to secure hospitals. Most of the people predicted to be dangerous were not. Reviewing this and similar studies, John Monahan concluded in The Clinical Prediction of Violent Behavior (1981) that psychiatrists and psychologists were accurate in no more than one out of three predictions of violence over several years, even in institutionalised populations with a history of violence. His review launched the search for better methods that produced the instruments described next. Three broad approaches to violence risk assessment have grown out of that research, and Table 2.22 compares them. The first, unstructured clinical judgement , is what clinicians did before the research: weighing whatever seemed relevant, with no fixed list and no rules. It is flexible, but it is unreliable and, as Monahan showed, inaccurate over the long term. The second, actuarial risk assessment , combines a fixed set of factors by a statistical formula derived from follow-up studies, in the way insurance companies calculate premiums. The best known, the Violence Risk Appraisal Guide (VRAG) of Grant Harris, Marnie Rice and Vernon Quinsey (1993), scores twelve mostly historical items, of which the Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R) score carries the most weight. Actuarial tools are reliable and outperform unaided judgement, but they rely mainly on static factors, ignore anything not in the formula and say little about what to do. The third, structured professional judgement (SPJ), is the compromise now preferred in most services: the clinician rates every item on a fixed, evidence-based list, including dynamic factors, and then uses professional judgement to reach a final risk formulation and, above all, a management plan. But the clinical interview asks the same questions, directly and without embarrassment, just as it does for suicide. "Have you had thoughts of hurting anyone? Who? Have you thought about how? Do you have a weapon, or access to one? What is the most violent thing you have ever done? When did you last hit someone? Had you been drinking?" The answers about past violence are explored like a past suicide attempt: the victim, the circumstances, the trigger, the injuries, the consequences, and how the person feels about it now. Informants and records matter even more than usual, because people minimise their own violence. The result is formulated in the same way as suicide risk, with static and dynamic factors, triggers and protective factors, and a plan that targets what can change. For Mr Manjunath the static factors were few (no past violence, no substance use), while the dynamic ones, the irritability of mania, poor insight and a quarrel over money with the brother who had taken his card, were all treatable; the plan was treatment of the mania, a calmer arrangement over the family's finances, and a review of the threat at every contact. When a client makes a credible threat against an identifiable person, the clinician also faces the legal and ethical duty to protect that person, the subject of the Tarasoff rulings of 1974 and 1976 discussed in Chapter 1. Clinical link Assessing an agitated patient safely begins before you enter the room: read the file, tell a colleague where you are, and use a room in which you have a clear path to the door without blocking the patient's own way out (a patient who feels trapped is more likely to lash out). Remove objects that could be thrown, know where the alarm is, and do not interview a threatening patient alone. Watch for the signs of escalation: pacing, clenched fists, a rising voice, swearing, staring, moving into your space, threats and banging objects (short checklists such as the Brøset Violence Checklist rate six such behaviours on wards: confusion, irritability, boisterousness, verbal threats, physical threats and attacks on objects). The skills of de-escalation are the interviewing skills of Section 2.2 under pressure: a calm, low voice; standing or sitting at more than arm's length and at an angle rather than face to face; acknowledging the feeling ("I can see you are very angry about being brought here"); not arguing with delusions; offering choices and something to drink; and ending the interview, without heroics, if the situation keeps escalating.
