The formulation proper is written as a short narrative in which the factors are connected by "because", "so" and "which": the connections are the explanation. Here is how the 5 Ps read when they are written up. Ravi's 5 Ps, written as a formulation Ravi is a 24-year-old man who presents with a three-month history of low mood, loss of interest, early morning waking, weight loss, guilt, hopelessness and withdrawal, with daily thoughts that he would be better off dead and occasional thoughts of suicide, without intent or plan. He may have been vulnerable to depression because of a family history of the illness, a perfectionistic and self-critical personality, and a childhood in which his worth in the family seemed to depend on his examination results; he had a brief depressive reaction to an academic setback at 17. The present episode was precipitated by his third failure in the bank examination, made more painful by his cousin's success in the same week and by his father's comparisons. It is maintained by a cycle in which he escapes shame by withdrawing to his room and his phone, which brings short-term relief but removes him from study, cricket, family and friends, worsens his sleep and gives him more time to ruminate on having failed his parents; his father's continued criticism and the family's debt keep the cycle supplied. In his favour are a warm and engaged mother, his intelligence and conscientiousness, a good record of study and work, his faith, the absence of substance use, his recovery from the earlier episode and his willingness to come for help. Exam trap Predisposing = why this person (long-standing vulnerability). Precipitating = why now (the recent trigger). Perpetuating = why it continues (maintaining factors, the main target of treatment). Protective = what helps (strengths and supports). Presenting = the problem itself. A stem describing "factors that maintain the problem" wants perpetuating ; one describing "a stressful event shortly before onset" wants precipitating . Do not confuse perpetuating (operating now) with predisposing (a vulnerability from the past): both are "causes", but only the first is the main target of treatment. The biopsychosocial formulation The 5 Ps organise the factors in time: long ago, recently, now. A second question is at what level each factor operates. The answer comes from the biopsychosocial model (its place among the models of psychopathology is covered in Chapter 1, and Section 9.1 applies it to physical illness) that the American psychiatrist George L. Engel (1913 to 1999) proposed in a 1977 paper in Science , "The need for a new medical model": biological, psychological and social systems are nested inside one another, so that illness is never only a matter of the body, or only of the mind, or only of circumstances, and a change at one level ripples into the others. Applied to formulation, the model becomes a simple and powerful device. Cross the four explanatory Ps with the three levels and you get a grid of twelve cells, each a question: what are the biological predisposing factors? the psychological precipitants? the social perpetuating factors? A biopsychosocial formulation is an explanation of the client's difficulties that fills in that grid and then shows how the levels interact. Table 2.29 is Ravi's. Table 2.29 Ravi's biopsychosocial formulation grid. Factor Biological Psychological Social Predisposing Depression in maternal uncle (genetic loading) Perfectionism, self-criticism; depressive month at 17 Worth measured by marks; father's comparisons Precipitating None found yet: check thyroid and haemoglobin The meaning of the failure: "I have failed them" Third failure; cousin selected the same week Perpetuating Broken sleep, poor appetite, weight loss Avoidance, rumination, hopelessness Father's criticism; debt on pledged gold; living away from home Protective Good physical health; no alcohol or tobacco Intelligent, conscientious; earlier episode recovered Warm mother; sister; faith; supportive roommate The grid earns its place in three ways. First, it exposes gaps. The empty-looking cell for biological precipitants is not a statement that there are none; it is a reminder to check, because tiredness and weight loss in a young man can come from hypothyroidism, anaemia or an infection as easily as from depression (Section 2.3 flagged this). A grid that is full in the psychological column and empty in the other two usually means the clinician has looked only where his training points. Second, it shows how the levels feed each other, which is what turns a list into an explanation. Ravi's broken sleep (biological) worsens his concentration and mood (psychological), which makes study impossible, which makes the next examination less likely to go well (social), which confirms his belief that he is a failure (psychological), which keeps him awake at 3 a.m. (biological). Draw that circle for the client and he sees, perhaps for the first time, that his depression is not simply a weakness of character. Third, every cell suggests an intervention at its own level. At the biological level: investigations, a review by a psychiatrist to consider an antidepressant (the severity, the biological symptoms and the thoughts of death all point that way), and a regular sleep routine. At the psychological level: the cognitive-behavioural work described in the next subsection. At the social level: a family session in which the father's comparisons can be discussed without blame, a conversation about the debt, a reconsideration of whether the bank examination is the only route to a respectable job, and a plan for Ravi to spend more time with his roommate and less alone. The biopsychosocial model has its critics. The American psychiatrist S. Nassir Ghaemi, in The Rise and Fall of the Biopsychosocial Model (2010), argued that in practice it has often become a vague eclecticism that licenses a clinician to mention everything and commit to nothing, without any principle for deciding which level matters most in a given case. The criticism is fair of bad formulations, and it points to the answer: a good biopsychosocial formulation does not merely list factors at three levels but says which ones carry most weight in this person and how they interact. Indian context In Indian formulations the social column is usually the richest, and the most often neglected by trainees taught from Western textbooks. It includes the structure of the family (joint or nuclear, who decides), the family's honour ( maryade , in Kannada) and the shame attached to failure, unemployment and mental illness, the pressure of competitive examinations and the coaching economy that has grown around them, debt, migration from village to town, marriage expectations, caste and gender, and the family's explanatory model, including any faith healer or temple already consulted. These are not background details. For many clients they are the precipitating and perpetuating factors. Exam trap The biopsychosocial model is George Engel's (1977, Science ). It is not Adolf Meyer's psychobiology (Section 2.3), although Meyer's idea of the whole person in his life circumstances anticipated it. A biopsychosocial formulation crosses the predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors with the biological, psychological and social levels. Its main criticism (Ghaemi) is that it can become an unprincipled eclectic list . The cognitive-behavioural formulation The 5 Ps and the biopsychosocial grid are frameworks: they tell you where to look, but not what mechanism links the factors. A cognitive-behavioural formulation supplies a mechanism, taken from cognitive and learning theory. Its pioneer as a formal method was the American psychologist Jacqueline B. Persons , whose Cognitive Therapy in Practice: A Case Formulation Approach (1989) argued that the therapist should treat each case as a hypothesis about the psychological mechanisms producing the client's problems, derive the treatment plan from that hypothesis, and test it as therapy proceeds, revising it when the client does not improve. Persons' formulation lists the problems, proposes the mechanisms (the beliefs and behaviours that produce them), identifies the precipitants and the origins of the mechanisms, and builds the treatment plan from them. Two decades later Willem Kuyken , Christine A. Padesky and Robert Dudley, in Collaborative Case Conceptualization (2009), described formulation with the image of a crucible , a vessel in which the client's experience and the clinician's theory and research are combined and transformed, with collaborative empiricism (Section 5.4) providing the heat. They made three principles central. The formulation is built at increasing levels as therapy proceeds: first a descriptive level (the problems in cognitive-behavioural terms), then a cross-sectional explanatory level (the triggers and maintaining cycles of the problems now), then, if needed, a longitudinal explanatory level (the predisposing and protective factors in the client's history). It is built collaboratively , with the client as co-author. And it incorporates strengths , not just deficits, because strengths are what the client will use to recover. At the cross-sectional level, the simplest tool is the five-part model that Padesky and Kathleen Mooney described in 1990, sometimes called the "hot cross bun" because of the shape in which it is drawn: the environment or situation, and four interacting parts of the person's response to it (thoughts, emotions, physical reactions and behaviours), each affecting the others. Ravi's version is quickly drawn. Situation: he opens his exam guide. Thought: "What's the point? I'll fail again." Emotion: hopelessness. Body: heaviness, fatigue. Behaviour: he shuts the book and lies down. And the behaviour feeds back: another day without study makes failure more likely and gives the thought fresh evidence. Notice that this cycle and the SORKC analysis of Figure 2.9 describe the same evenings from two angles, one emphasising the belief and the other the reinforcement. A good cognitive-behavioural formulation uses both. For the longitudinal level, the standard tool is the cognitive conceptualisation diagram (CCD) of Judith S. Beck , Aaron Beck's daughter, set out in Cognitive Therapy: Basics and Beyond (1995; later editions are titled Cognitive Behavior Therapy: Basics and Beyond ). It is built on Aaron Beck's three levels of cognition, which Section 5.3 and Figure 5.3 have already taught: core beliefs, intermediate beliefs (attitudes, rules and assumptions) and automatic thoughts. What the diagram adds is a way of tying these to one particular person's history and to his typical problem situations, on a single page. Its lower half is cross-sectional. For three typical situations in which the client became upset, it records the situation, the automatic thought, the meaning of the automatic thought to the client (often found by the downward arrow technique of Section 5.4), the emotion and the behaviour. Its upper half is longitudinal. It records the relevant childhood data (the experiences that help explain how the core belief arose), the core belief itself, the conditional assumptions, beliefs or rules that grew from it, and the compensatory strategies , the behaviours the client developed to cope with the core belief and to keep it from being activated. The diagram is filled in by working upwards from the situations and asking, at each step, what belief would make sense of the thought. Figure 2.11 is Ravi's. Childhood data "The bright one": praised for marks, rarely for himself; always measured against his cousin; father's pride felt conditional Core belief "I am a failure." "I am worth only what I achieve." Assumptions, rules If I succeed, I am worth something; if I fail, I have failed my family. Rule: I must never let my parents down. Compensatory strategies Overwork; hide weaknesses; never ask for help; avoid being judged Situation Father phones, mentions the cousin's bank job Opens the bank exam guide at his desk Cousin's photo in the family WhatsApp group Automatic thought "He's ashamed of me." "I wasted their money." "What's the point? I'll fail again." "Everyone is laughing at me." Meaning of thought I am a failure and a burden I can never succeed, however hard I try I have shamed my family Emotion, behaviour Shame; ends the call, skips dinner Hopeless; shuts the book, lies in bed Shame, sadness; leaves the group, goes silent Figure 2.11 Ravi's cognitive conceptualisation diagram, in the format of Judith Beck. The top four rows are longitudinal (how the core belief arose and how he learned to live with it); the three columns are cross-sectional (how it shows itself in today's situations). Notice that the same core belief makes sense of three quite different automatic thoughts. Read the diagram from the top and Ravi's story acquires a mechanism. A boy whose family's pride rested on his marks came to believe that his worth lay in achievement; in Judith Beck's three families of negative core beliefs (Section 5.3) "I am a failure" is a helpless belief. For years his compensatory strategy, relentless hard work, kept that belief quiet, because it worked: he was the topper. The bank examinations are the first challenge that hard work has failed to overcome again and again (the setback at 17 was a single result), and three failures have broken the strategy and activated the belief. Now every situation that touches achievement or family (a phone call, a book, a photograph) produces an automatic thought that confirms it. This explains, in cognitive terms, both why Ravi was vulnerable and why the illness began when it did; the 5 Ps said the same thing in a less specific language. The formulation then writes the treatment plan. Because Ravi is depressed, withdrawn and short of energy, the first step is behavioural: graded activity scheduling to restore reinforcement, using the activity record he has already kept. Next come thought records and behavioural experiments directed at the automatic thoughts and at the rule "I must never let my parents down" (what happens, for instance, if he tells his father plainly how he is feeling?). Work on the core belief itself, with a positive data log of evidence that his worth does not rest on results, comes last (Section 5.4). And the formulation predicts the obstacles: a perfectionist may treat homework as another examination to pass or fail, and a young man who believes he must never disappoint may hide his setbacks from the therapist. Forewarned, the therapist praises effort rather than results and asks regularly what has not gone well. Exam trap The cognitive conceptualisation diagram is Judith S. Beck's (1995), built on Aaron Beck's cognitive model. Its parts, from the top: relevant childhood data, core beliefs, conditional assumptions or rules, compensatory strategies; then, for each typical situation, the automatic thought, its meaning, the emotion and the behaviour. Compensatory strategies are behaviours (overworking, avoiding, seeking approval), not beliefs. Persons (1989) founded the case formulation approach to cognitive therapy; Kuyken, Padesky and Dudley (2009) gave the crucible metaphor and the three levels (descriptive, cross-sectional, longitudinal). The five-part ("hot cross bun") model is Padesky and Mooney (1990) . The psychodynamic formulation The cognitive-behavioural formulation explains Ravi's depression through his beliefs and the behaviour that maintains them. A psychodynamic clinician listening to the same story hears something else: a son who has never been able to be angry with his father. A psychodynamic formulation explains the client's present difficulties in terms of enduring, largely unconscious patterns (conflicts between wishes and fears, the defences used against them, and internalised templates of self and others) that took shape in development and are now being repeated in his current life, and it predicts how those patterns will appear in the relationship with the therapist. The classic structure comes from a 1987 paper in the American Journal of Psychiatry by the psychiatrists Samuel Perry, Arnold Cooper and Robert Michels, "The psychodynamic formulation: its purpose, structure, and clinical application". They proposed that a written formulation should be brief (about 500 to 750 words) and should have four parts. A summary statement that describes the patient and the presenting problem and places the problem in the context of his life. A description of the nondynamic factors that contribute to the problem: genetic, constitutional, medical and traumatic influences. Perry and his colleagues insisted that the presence of such factors does not make psychodynamic understanding irrelevant, and that a psychodynamic formulation that ignores them is a poor one. A psychodynamic explanation of the central conflicts : what they are, how they developed and how they are repeated in the patient's current life and relationships. A prognostic assessment of how these conflicts are likely to show themselves in treatment, as transference and resistance, and what this implies for the choice and conduct of therapy. A more recent teaching scheme, from Deborah Cabaniss and her colleagues at Columbia University ( Psychodynamic Formulation , 2013), reduces the task to three verbs. Describe the problems and the patterns (in the person's sense of self, relationships, characteristic ways of adapting and defending, thinking and working). Review the developmental history. Link the two, using one or more organising ideas: trauma, early difficulties, conflict and defence, relationships with others, the development of the self, or attachment. The ingredients of the explanation come from the theories of Chapter 3. The clinician identifies the central conflict , usually a wish that is opposed by a fear (of punishment, of loss of love, of guilt) and kept out of awareness; the principal defences (Chapter 3 and the Personality book); the object relations , meaning the internal templates of self and other that the person brings to every relationship; the way he regulates self-esteem ; and his ego strengths , such as the capacity to tolerate painful feelings, to reflect on himself (psychological mindedness) and to form a working relationship, which decide whether exploratory therapy is suitable. Several brief psychodynamic therapies have turned this kind of formulation into structured tools, notably David Malan's triangles of conflict and of person and Lester Luborsky's core conflictual relationship theme (CCRT), with its three components of the wish, the response of the other and the response of the self; they are taught with the brief therapies in Section 3.6. Ravi: a psychodynamic formulation (abridged) Summary. Ravi, 24, the eldest son of a farming family, presents with a three-month depression that followed his third failure in the bank examinations and his cousin's success. Nondynamic factors. A family history of depression and the biological features of his illness suggest a constitutional vulnerability and call for a medical review alongside psychotherapy. Central conflict. Ravi has longed all his life to be valued by his father for himself, and has learned that his father's regard is given for achievement. His wish to be loved unconditionally is opposed by the fear that, if he fails, he will lose that love altogether. Alongside the longing there is anger at a father who compares and belittles him, but for a dutiful eldest son in a family that depends on him this anger is unthinkable. It is kept out of awareness and turned against himself, as self-reproach ("I have wasted their money"), an idea that goes back to Freud's "Mourning and Melancholia" (1917). His father's critical voice has become an internal critic that now attacks him from within. The same template, a judging authority and a self that falls short, has organised his relationships with teachers, coaching-centre instructors and his cousin, and his withdrawal protects him from a confrontation he both wants and fears. In Luborsky's terms: the wish, to be valued as he is; the expected response of the other, to be compared and found wanting; the response of the self, to withdraw, hide his anger and feel worthless. Prognosis in treatment. Ravi will probably begin as an ideal patient: punctual, polite and eager to please. He is likely to hear the therapist's comments as grades, to hide setbacks, to feel that a cancelled session means he has disappointed, and to comply without changing. The therapist may feel pulled to push him, as his father does, or to rescue him, as his mother does. His conscientiousness, his capacity for a warm relationship and his ability to reflect suggest he could use a time-limited exploratory therapy focused on his conditional sense of worth and his unspoken anger. Exam trap Perry, Cooper and Michels (1987) gave the psychodynamic formulation four parts: a summary statement , the nondynamic factors , the psychodynamic explanation of central conflicts and the prognostic assessment (how the conflicts will show up in treatment as transference and resistance). A psychodynamic formulation does not ignore biology. The CCRT (wish, response of other, response of self) is Luborsky's ; the triangles of conflict and of person are Malan's . Cabaniss's scheme is describe, review, link . One client, four stories You have now read four formulations of the same young man, built from exactly the same facts. Put them side by side, as Table 2.30 does, and notice what changes and what does not. Table 2.30 Ravi seen through four lenses. Lens Central question Ravi's story in one sentence Treatment that follows 5 Ps Why this person, why now, why still, what helps? A vulnerable perfectionist, triggered by a humiliating failure, kept down by withdrawal and criticism, held up by his mother and his faith Target the perpetuating factors; build on the protective ones Biopsychosocial At which levels do the causes act, and how do they interact? Genes, sleep, beliefs, family pressure and debt feeding one another in a circle Investigations and psychiatric review; psychological therapy; family session and practical help Cognitive-behavioural Which beliefs and behaviours produce and maintain the problem? "I am worth only what I achieve", activated by failure and confirmed every day by avoidance Behavioural activation, thought records, experiments, then core belief work Psychodynamic Which unconscious conflict is being repeated? A son who cannot be angry with a father whose love seems conditional, turning the anger on himself Time-limited exploratory therapy; attention to the transference Three lessons follow. First, the same fact changes its meaning with the lens . The father's comparisons are a precipitating and perpetuating factor in the 5 Ps, a social stressor in the biopsychosocial grid, the activator of a core belief in the cognitive formulation and the current edition of a lifelong relational conflict in the psychodynamic one. None of these readings is false; each picks out a different aspect of the fact and connects it to a different mechanism. Second, the lenses are not equally specific . The 5 Ps and the biopsychosocial grid are frameworks without a theory of their own: they organise the factors and leave open how they are connected. The cognitive-behavioural and psychodynamic formulations are theories: they say what the mechanism is. In practice clinicians often use a framework to collect and organise the information and a theory to explain it, and many write an integrative formulation that does both. Third, a formulation is chosen, not discovered , and the choice should be justified by evidence and by the client. A theory with good evidence for this kind of problem (cognitive-behavioural therapy has a strong evidence base for depression, Section 5.11), a client who finds the account convincing and useful, and a treatment that the service can actually provide are all good reasons for preferring one formulation. The worst reason is that it is the only lens the clinician knows. Notice, finally, what all four formulations share: they explain, they are individual, they are tentative, and they lead to action. That is what distinguishes every one of them from a diagnosis. Diagnosis versus formulation Ravi's provisional diagnosis is a depressive episode, possibly recurrent. That single phrase does a great deal. It places him in a category that research has studied for a century, so it tells the clinician what course to expect, what treatments have been shown to work for people in that category, what risks to watch, and what to write on an insurance claim, a medical certificate or a research form. It lets a psychiatrist in Mysuru and a psychologist in Delhi know at once roughly what they are dealing with. These are the purposes of diagnosis , the assignment of a person's presenting problems to a category of a standard classification such as DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 (Section 2.10). What the diagnosis cannot do is explain Ravi. Two people with the same diagnosis may have become depressed for entirely different reasons and stay depressed through entirely different processes; one may need help mostly with a grief, the other with a marriage, a third with a thyroid. A diagnosis describes what Ravi has in common with other people; a formulation explains what is particular to him. Table 2.31 sets out the contrast. Table 2.31 Diagnosis and formulation compared. Feature Diagnosis Formulation Main purpose To classify the problem in a standard system To explain the problem in this person and guide treatment Approach Nomothetic (what he shares with others) Idiographic (what is particular to him) Form A label, usually categorical A narrative or diagram, a hypothesis Content Symptoms, duration, exclusions Causes, precipitants, maintaining and protective factors Role of theory Largely atheoretical about causes (DSM since 1980) Explicitly theory-informed Who decides The clinician, against the manual's criteria The clinician and the client together Stability Fixed until criteria change Revised as therapy proceeds Strengths Communication, research, epidemiology, services Individual treatment planning; meaning for the client The two are complementary rather than rivals in most clinical practice. The diagnosis tells you which body of evidence applies; the formulation tells you how to apply it to this person and what to do when the standard treatment does not fit. A clinician who has only a diagnosis treats a category; one who has only a formulation may miss what research knows about people like the client, including the risks. Some psychologists go further. Kanfer and Saslow in 1965 offered behavioural analysis as an "alternative to diagnostic classification" (Section 2.8), and in Britain a vocal group of clinical psychologists has argued that formulation should replace psychiatric diagnosis altogether, on the grounds that diagnostic categories lack validity, encourage the belief that distress is a disease located inside the individual, and stigmatise. Its most developed statement is the Power Threat Meaning Framework (2018) of Lucy Johnstone and Mary Boyle, which asks not "What is wrong with you?" but "What has happened to you?", and organises explanations around the operation of power, the threats it poses and the meanings people make of them. The argument about labelling, and Rosenhan's pseudopatients, are taken up in Section 2.10. Formulation has its own weakness, and an honest clinician should know it. Its reliability is modest. When several clinicians formulate the same case, they agree reasonably well on the descriptive level (what the problems are) but much less on the inferential level (which beliefs, conflicts or processes lie underneath). Peter Bieling and Willem Kuyken reviewed the evidence in 2003 under a pointed title, "Is cognitive case formulation science or science fiction?", and concluded that the descriptive level was on firm ground but the deeper inferences needed much more research. Evidence that formulation-driven treatment produces better outcomes than standard protocols is also limited. These are reasons to hold a formulation lightly, as a hypothesis, which is exactly what the definition asks. Exam trap "A formulation differs from a diagnosis in that it primarily aims to ..." Answer: provide a hypothesis about the cause, precipitants and maintaining factors of an individual's difficulties . The distractors each describe something else: classifying symptoms in a nosological system is diagnosis; determining prognosis and course is a use of diagnosis (and of formulation, but not its primary aim); ruling out organic causes is part of differential diagnosis. Diagnosis is nomothetic and categorical; formulation is idiographic , explanatory, collaborative and revisable. The Power Threat Meaning Framework (2018) is Johnstone and Boyle's alternative to diagnosis. Differential diagnosis as a process Before a formulation can be trusted, the clinician must be reasonably sure what he is formulating. Depressed mood, tiredness and weight loss can come from a depressive disorder, from bipolar disorder in its depressed phase, from an underactive thyroid, from a medicine, from alcohol, from early dementia in an older person, or from an ordinary and proportionate reaction to a hard year. Differential diagnosis is the systematic process of distinguishing among the conditions that could account for the same presenting features: the clinician lists the plausible explanations, then gathers evidence for and against each until the most likely one remains. The word "process" matters. Differential diagnosis is not a list written at the end of the case record; it begins in the first minutes of the interview and drives everything that follows. Sullivan's "detailed inquiry" (Section 2.1) is the stage at which the interviewer tests the hypotheses he has formed. The negative history of Section 2.3 ("no elated periods, no head injury, no alcohol") is differential diagnosis written down: each negative is an alternative considered and set aside. A clinician who decides on the diagnosis in the first five minutes and then asks only questions that confirm it has committed premature closure (Section 2.2), and he is in the company of the admitting psychiatrists who met Rosenhan's pseudopatients. Is there a right order in which to consider the possibilities? Broadly, yes: rule out the causes that are most dangerous to miss and most specifically treatable first. The psychiatrist Michael B. First, in the DSM-5 Handbook of Differential Diagnosis (2014), set out six steps that make the logic explicit. Rule out malingering and factitious disorder : is the person feigning or producing the symptoms (Section 2.3)? Rule out a substance as the cause: a drug of abuse, a prescribed medicine or a toxin. Rule out a general medical condition as the cause: thyroid disease, anaemia, a brain tumour, epilepsy, an infection. Determine the specific primary mental disorder or disorders. Distinguish an adjustment disorder , or a residual "other specified" or "unspecified" category, from these specific disorders. Establish the boundary with no mental disorder : are the symptoms severe and impairing enough to count as a disorder at all, or are they within the range of ordinary distress? Indian case conferences follow the same logic in an older, hierarchical form: organic causes first, then substance use, then psychotic disorders, then mood disorders, then anxiety and related disorders, then personality disorders. A higher category, if present, usually explains the symptoms of a lower one, so it is considered first. This is the hierarchical principle of diagnosis usually traced to Karl Jaspers's General Psychopathology (1913; Section 2.4), and the same order is built into the blocks of the ICD-10 chapter on mental disorders that most Indian hospitals still use (F0 organic, F1 substance use, F2 psychotic, F3 mood, F4 neurotic and stress-related, F6 personality). It is not a law: modern classifications allow two diagnoses at once (comorbidity, Section 2.10) where each is independently present. Push Ravi through the steps. There is no hint of feigning and no obvious external gain. He takes no alcohol, tobacco or drugs, and the only medicines he has had are the vitamins his general practitioner prescribed, so a substance cause is unlikely. A medical cause has not yet been excluded, which is why thyroid function and haemoglobin are being checked. Among the primary disorders, the history describes the picture of a depressive episode; the month of low mood at 17 raises the question of whether this is in fact a second, recurrent episode, which a more detailed history of that month will answer. Bipolar disorder must be kept in mind, because a first depression in a young man is sometimes the first episode of a bipolar illness; the history found no periods of elated mood, and the family will be asked again. Adjustment disorder fits the clear stressor, but it is a residual category, used only when the criteria for a specific disorder such as a depressive episode are not met. And the severity of his symptoms, the biological features, the impairment and the thoughts of death place him well beyond the boundary of ordinary disappointment. The case record therefore reads: provisional diagnosis, depressive episode, possibly recurrent (recurrent depressive disorder if the month at 17 proves to have been a depressive episode); differential diagnoses, depressive disorder due to a medical condition (pending investigations) and bipolar disorder (to be monitored). (The criteria themselves belong to the Psychiatric Disorders book; how the classifications are organised is the subject of Section 2.10.) Clinicians' errors in differential diagnosis are mostly errors of reasoning rather than of knowledge: anchoring on the first impression, seeking only confirming evidence, judging by the vivid recent case, and diagnostic overshadowing , a term introduced by Steven Reiss and his colleagues in 1982 for the tendency to attribute a person's new symptoms to a condition already known (his intellectual disability, his schizophrenia) and so to miss a second, treatable problem. A person with schizophrenia who becomes withdrawn may be depressed, or hypothyroid, or in pain. Exam trap Differential diagnosis is a process of generating and testing alternative explanations, not a label. Organic (medical) and substance causes are ruled out first. First's (2014) six steps run: malingering and factitious disorder; substance; medical condition; primary disorder; adjustment and residual categories; boundary with no disorder. Adjustment disorder is diagnosed only when the criteria for a more specific disorder are not met. Diagnostic overshadowing (Reiss and colleagues, 1982) is attributing new symptoms to an existing diagnosis. Writing the clinical report Everything in this chapter ends up in writing. A clinical report (in psychology, often called the psychological or assessment report) is the written account of an assessment, its findings, the formulation and the recommendations, addressed to a particular reader in answer to a particular question. That last phrase is the key to writing a good one. A report is not a record of everything the clinician did; it is an answer. A psychiatrist who asks "Is there evidence of psychosis?", a school that asks "Why is this child failing?", a court that asks "Is this man fit to stand trial?" and a client who asks "What is wrong with me, and what can I do?" each need a different document from the same assessment. The headings vary between settings, but most reports follow the order in Table 2.32. Table 2.32 The usual headings of a clinical (psychological) report. Heading What it contains Identifying information Name, age, sex, education, occupation, dates of assessment, referred by Reason for referral The referral question, stated precisely Sources of information and procedures Interviews, informants, records, tests and observations used, with dates Relevant background A summary of the history, selected for relevance to the question Behavioural observations Appearance, behaviour, rapport and test-taking attitude; the MSE Results and interpretation Findings organised by theme, with their meaning Summary and formulation The integrated explanation Diagnosis Provisional and differential diagnoses Recommendations Specific, feasible next steps, each linked to the findings Signature Name, qualification, registration number, date A handful of principles separate a useful report from a long one. Answer the referral question , early and plainly. If the question cannot be answered, say why. Integrate rather than list. Organise the results by theme (mood, cognition, relationships, risk), drawing on every source, instead of reporting one test after another. A report that says "On test A he scored ... On test B he scored ..." has left the hardest part of the work to the reader. Separate observation from inference. "He wept twice while describing his father" is an observation; "he is grieving the relationship he wished he had" is an inference, and should be marked as one ("this suggests ..."). Write for the reader. Use plain language, define the technical terms you cannot avoid, and keep it as short as the question allows. Be specific to this person. Avoid statements that would be true of almost anyone. Include strengths and limitations : what the client does well, and what limits confidence in the findings (language, fatigue, tests without Indian norms, an uncooperative informant). Make recommendations specific and feasible : "weekly cognitive-behavioural therapy for 12 to 16 sessions, beginning with activity scheduling; thyroid function and haemoglobin; a family session" rather than "therapy is recommended". Remember who may read it. Under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (Section 25), a person with mental illness has the right to access his basic medical records; the professional in charge may withhold specific information only if disclosing it would cause him serious mental harm or would be likely to harm others, and must then tell him that he can apply to the Mental Health Review Board for its release. Write every report as though the client will read it, because he may. The fifth principle has a name. In a classroom demonstration published in 1949, the psychologist Bertram R. Forer (1914 to 2000) gave his students a personality test and, a week later, a "personalised" interpretation of their results. Every student in fact received the same paragraph, assembled largely from a newsstand astrology book ("You have a great need for other people to like and admire you ... At times you are extroverted, affable, sociable, while at other times you are introverted, wary, reserved"). Asked to rate how well it described them on a scale from 0 (poor) to 5 (perfect), the 39 students gave it an average of 4.26. In 1956 Paul Everett Meehl (1920 to 2003) named the tendency to accept vague, universally applicable descriptions as accurate personal ones the Barnum effect , after the American showman P. T. Barnum, whose circus was said to have "a little something for everybody". It is also called the Forer effect. Statements of this kind make a report feel accurate to its reader and tell him nothing; the cure is to say only what distinguishes this person from others. From Ravi's report: summary and recommendations Ravi, 24, came with his mother; the questions for assessment were the nature of his low mood and the treatment he needs. Assessment over two sessions (interviews with Ravi and his mother, mental status examination, risk assessment, a week of self-monitoring and a role play) indicates a depressive episode of three months' duration, without psychotic features, with daily passive death wishes and occasional thoughts of suicide but no intent, plan or preparation; the risk is raised but not imminent (Section 2.7). His difficulties are best understood as the activation, by his third examination failure and his cousin's success, of a long-standing belief that his worth depends on achievement; they are maintained by withdrawal, rumination, poor sleep and continuing family criticism. Strengths include his mother's support, his intelligence and conscientiousness, his faith, and his recovery from an earlier, briefer episode. Recommendations: (1) psychiatric review to consider antidepressant medication; (2) thyroid function and haemoglobin; (3) weekly cognitive-behavioural therapy, beginning with behavioural activation; (4) a family session with both parents; (5) a written safety plan, with the pesticide at the family farm locked away, and risk reviewed at every session. Exam trap The Barnum effect (named by Meehl , 1956; demonstrated by Forer , 1949, hence also the Forer effect) is the acceptance of vague, generally true statements as accurate descriptions of oneself. A report should answer the referral question , integrate findings by theme rather than test by test, separate data from inference and give specific recommendations. Under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 , Section 25 gives the right of access to basic medical records. Giving feedback to the client and the family The last step of assessment is the one most often skimped: telling the client what was found. For much of the twentieth century psychological test results were treated as the property of the professional, written up for the referring doctor and never discussed with the person tested. That attitude is no longer defensible, ethically or legally. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 gives a person with mental illness, and his nominated representative, a right to information (Section 22) about the nature of his illness and the proposed treatment plan, in a language and form he can understand, and a right to confidentiality (Section 23) about his mental health and treatment. (The Act itself is taught in Chapter 1.) But the strongest argument for good feedback is clinical: done well, feedback is itself a treatment. Key study: feedback as an intervention (Finn and Tonsager, 1992) Does simply hearing the results of an assessment help? Stephen E. Finn and Mary Tonsager studied university students who were on the waiting list of a counselling centre. All completed the MMPI-2 personality inventory. One group then received a collaborative feedback session in which the results were discussed with them in relation to their own questions; the control group received equal attention from an examiner but no feedback on their results. Compared with the controls, the students who received feedback showed a decline in symptomatic distress and a rise in self-esteem, both immediately and at follow-up about two weeks later, and they felt more hopeful about their problems. The study helped launch Finn's therapeutic assessment , a collaborative model in which the client helps frame the questions the assessment will try to answer and the findings are worked through together, so that the assessment becomes a brief intervention in its own right. How should feedback be given? Finn suggested that findings be thought of in three levels and presented in order. Level 1 information confirms what the client already thinks about himself ("You are a very conscientious person who sets high standards"); it is easily accepted and builds trust. Level 2 information modifies or extends his self-view in ways he can accept with a little reflection ("Those high standards may also be making it hard for you to start anything you might not do perfectly"). Level 3 information is so discrepant from his self-view that he is likely to reject it or be distressed by it ("Part of you may be very angry with your father"); it is offered tentatively, only when trust is established, and sometimes not at all in the first session. Beginning with Level 3 information is the commonest way to lose a client. Around that ordering, a few practical rules apply in any setting. Prepare. Decide in advance on the three or four main messages, the words you will use and what you will leave for later. Start with the client's questions. Ask what he understands so far and what he most wants to know. Use plain language and his own words , in his own language. "Depression" may need explaining as an illness of mood, sleep, energy and thinking, not a weakness or "madness"; his own idiom ("tension", "my mind is not working") is a good bridge (Section 2.2). Share the formulation, not just the label. Draw the vicious circle of Figure 2.9 or the five-part model on a sheet of paper and ask, "Does this fit your experience? What would you change?" A formulation the client has corrected is one he owns. Name the diagnosis honestly , explain what it means and what it does not mean, and say what can be done. Hope is a clinical intervention, not a courtesy. Check understanding by asking the client to explain the main points back in his own words (sometimes called the teach-back method), allow time for feeling, and give a short written summary to take home. Feedback to the family. In India the family is usually waiting outside, and often expects to hear the findings before the patient does. The clinician's first duty is to the client: with an adult, what is shared with the family is decided with him beforehand, within the limits of confidentiality, except where there is a serious risk to his life or to others (Section 2.7). In practice most clients want their families involved, and a joint session is often the most useful hour of the whole assessment. Its aims are to give the family a shared, blame-free understanding of the problem, to correct harmful beliefs (that he is lazy, that he is possessed, that a marriage will cure him, that medicines for the mind cause addiction), to give each member something specific to do, and to agree on what to do in a crisis. Ravi's family session shows how much skill this takes. His father arrived defensive, sure that he was about to be blamed. The clinician began with what everyone agreed on (Level 1): that Ravi is a hard-working son who has always tried to make his parents proud, and that the family has sacrificed a great deal for his education. She then drew the circle of failure, withdrawal, poor sleep and self-blame, and asked the father where he thought the comparisons with the cousin fitted into it. He was silent for a while, and then said that his own father used to compare him with his elder brother. No one had to tell him to stop; the family agreed instead on a plan: no talk of examinations at meals for a month, a weekly call in which Ravi's mother would also take part, help with activity scheduling from his sister, the pesticide at the farm kept locked away (as agreed in the risk assessment), and a list of the warning signs that should bring them back to the clinic at once. The temple vow was not discouraged. It was part of the family's hope, and the clinician treated it as an ally. Clinical link In a feedback session with a family, frame criticism as worry. "You are frightened for his future, and the comparisons come from that fear" is something a father can hear; "Your criticism is making him worse" usually is not. The goal is not to find the person to blame but to help every member of the family step out of the cycle that is keeping the problem going. Families who feel blamed stop coming; families who feel understood become the most powerful protective factor in the formulation. Exam trap Collaborative feedback can itself reduce distress and raise self-esteem: Finn and Tonsager (1992) , the origin of therapeutic assessment . Present findings from Level 1 (consistent with the client's self-view) through Level 2 to Level 3 (discrepant), not the other way round. Under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 , Section 22 is the right to information , Section 23 the right to confidentiality and Section 25 access to medical records . Family members hear what the adult client has agreed they should hear, except where safety requires otherwise. Ravi's assessment is complete. A frightened mother's complaint that her son "barely leaves his room" has become a history, a picture of his present mental state, an estimate of risk, a functional analysis, a formulation seen through four lenses, a provisional diagnosis with its alternatives, a written report and a plan the family has helped to make. One question remains, the one with which this chapter began: what does it mean to put a person into a diagnostic category, and how far can such categories be trusted? That is the subject of the final section. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Partial-interval recording tends to the true occurrence of a behaviour, and whole-interval recording tends to it. A gradual, unnoticed change in the way an observer applies the behavioural definitions over time is observer . In the 5 Ps, the factors that answer "why now?" are factors, and those that answer "why does it continue?" are factors. Beck; core, (10) Barnum (Forer). 2.10 Classification as a Clinical Tool Lower yield · 2 Qs Section 2.9 drew a line between two ways of summing up a client. A formulation is a story about one person: why this problem, in this person, now. A diagnosis is a name taken from a shared list. This last section is about the shared list. It does not teach the disorders themselves; their symptoms, criteria and causes fill the Psychiatric Disorders book. It asks what the list is for, how its two great versions (the American DSM and the international ICD) are built, how anyone can tell whether two clinicians using the list really agree, and what a label does to the person who receives it. That last question brings us back to the eight pseudopatients who opened the chapter. Why clinicians classify Imagine a clinic with no shared names for anything. One psychologist writes that Ravi is "low and stuck", a second that he has "nervous weakness", a third that he is "going through a phase". None of them is exactly wrong, but their notes cannot be compared, counted, researched or acted on by anyone else. Classification is the sorting of things into groups according to the features they share. A classification of diseases or disorders is called a nosology (from the Greek nosos , disease), and the set of names it uses is its nomenclature . Diagnosis is the act of deciding which group in the nosology an individual's problems belong to. Biologists classify insects and geologists classify rocks for the same reason clinicians classify disorders: without agreed groups, knowledge cannot accumulate. Clinicians classify for at least six reasons, and each reason is also a test that a good classification must pass. Communication. A diagnosis compresses a great deal of information into a few words. "Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic" tells a colleague in Delhi or Toronto a lot before she has met the patient. DSM-5-TR names this as the "clear virtue" of its criteria: they create "a common language for communication between clinicians". Prediction. A sound category tells you what usually happens next: the likely course, the risk of relapse and the outcome with and without treatment. Treatment selection. Most treatments have been tested on diagnostic groups, so the diagnosis points the clinician to the relevant evidence: exposure for a specific phobia, a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder. Research. Studies of causes and treatments need groups of people who have the same condition. The US-UK Diagnostic Project in Section 2.1 showed what happens when two cities use the same word for different patients. Administration. Hospitals count admissions, governments plan services, insurers pay claims, and courts and disability boards make decisions, and all of them work through diagnostic codes. Understanding. Grouping people who share a pattern is the first step towards finding its cause. General paresis, a common cause of madness in nineteenth-century asylums, was first described as a clinical group and only later traced to syphilis. All six jobs depend on a prior decision: what counts as a disorder at all? DSM-5-TR defines a mental disorder as a syndrome marked by clinically significant disturbance in a person's cognition, emotion regulation or behaviour that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological or developmental processes underlying mental functioning, and that is usually associated with significant distress or disability. Two exclusions follow, and both matter for this section. An expectable or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss, such as grief after a death, is not a mental disorder. And socially deviant behaviour (the manual's examples are political, religious and sexual) and conflicts between the individual and society are not mental disorders unless they arise from a dysfunction in the individual. The manual then adds a sentence that students often miss: a diagnosis is not the same thing as a need for treatment. Whether treatment is needed depends on severity, distress, disability, risk and the balance of benefits and harms. Exam trap A nosology is the classification system itself; its nomenclature is the list of names; taxonomy is the general science of classifying. A diagnosis classifies the problem , not the person, and it is descriptive: a DSM diagnosis says what is present, not why. The individual explanation, the hypothesis about cause, precipitants and maintaining factors, is the formulation (Section 2.9). Finally, under DSM-5-TR a diagnosis does not by itself mean that treatment is needed, and distress or disability is "usually", not always, present. Categories, dimensions and prototypes There are two basic ways to sort people's problems, and you use both every day. You can put them in boxes ("she has a fever or she does not") or place them on a scale ("her temperature is 38.4 degrees"). The same choice runs through psychiatric classification. The categorical approach treats each disorder as a distinct class that a person either has or does not have. Its pure form, the classical categorical approach, goes back to Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926), the German psychiatrist who, in the closing years of the nineteenth century, separated dementia praecox (later renamed schizophrenia) from manic-depressive insanity by their course and outcome. Kraepelin believed that each disorder had its own underlying brain pathology, as an infection does. If that were true, every member of a category would share the same essential features, a single set of criteria would fit everyone, and knowing the diagnosis would tell you the cause. That is how a physician thinks about appendicitis. Few mental disorders behave this way. Most arise from interacting biological, psychological and social causes, the same symptom (poor sleep, poor concentration) turns up in many disorders, and the borders between categories are blurred. The dimensional approach instead rates each person on one or more continuous attributes. Barlow and Durand's example is a patient rated, on scales of 1 to 10, as severely anxious (10), moderately depressed (5) and mildly manic (2): a profile of 10, 5, 2 rather than a single name. Dimensions suit problems that are distributed continuously in the population, as anxiety, low mood and most personality traits are. DSM-5-TR's own introduction sums up the trade-off fairly. Dimensional systems increase reliability and carry more information, because they record problems that fall below a categorical threshold. But numbers are less familiar and vivid than names, nobody yet agrees on which dimensions to use, and a clinician who has to decide whether to treat still needs a cut-off point, which quietly brings back a category. Between the two lies the prototypical approach , which is what DSM and ICD actually use. A prototype lists the essential features of a category together with other features that are common but not required, and a person qualifies by matching enough of the list. Criteria of this "any five of nine" kind are called polythetic ; criteria that every member must meet in full are called monothetic. The DSM-5-TR major depressive episode is the standard example: at least five of nine symptoms over the same two weeks, at least one of which must be depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure. Two people can both meet the criteria while sharing only one symptom. The prototype is honest about the state of knowledge and easy to use, but it pays a price: fuzzy edges between categories, great variety within a single diagnosis (heterogeneity), many patients who fall just short of every category and end up with an "other specified" or "unspecified" diagnosis, and high comorbidity , the presence of two or more disorders in the same person at the same time. Modern manuals have therefore moved towards hybrids. DSM-5 (2013) kept its categories but added dimensional severity ratings, cross-cutting symptom measures that rate problems such as anxiety, low mood and poor sleep across all diagnoses, and, in its Section III, an Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders built on levels of personality functioning and pathological traits. The personality disorder criteria in the main body of the manual are still the categorical ones carried over from DSM-IV-TR. ICD-11 went further. It replaced the list of separate personality disorder types with a single diagnosis of personality disorder graded mild, moderate or severe, to which the clinician may add trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition and anankastia) and a borderline pattern. Fully dimensional research systems, such as the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP), have been proposed as replacements for categories altogether. Comorbidity means two or more disorders in one person, not two symptoms of one disorder. "Five of nine symptoms" is polythetic; "all of the following" is monothetic. From DSM-I to DSM-5-TR: a short history Classifications of madness are as old as medicine, but official, shared ones are young. The World Health Organization (WHO) added a section on mental disorders to the sixth revision of its International Classification of Diseases (ICD-6) in 1948. In 1952 the American Psychiatric Association published the first Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-I), the first official manual of mental disorders to include a glossary describing each category. Its language came from Adolf Meyer, whom you met in Section 2.3: disorders were "reactions" of the personality to biological, psychological and social factors. DSM-II (1968) was based on the mental disorders section of ICD-8, and both went into effect in the same year (the World Health Assembly had approved ICD-8 in 1966). It dropped most of the "reactions" but was full of psychoanalytic terms, above all "neurosis". Neither manual gave rules for deciding when a patient had a disorder. The glossary sketched a typical case, and each clinician decided how close was close enough. You already know what happened next. Section 2.1 described Beck's 1962 finding that pairs of psychiatrists agreed on the specific diagnosis only about half the time, the US-UK Diagnostic Project showing that New York and London used "schizophrenia" for different patients, and the analysis showing that criterion variance (different rules for turning information into a diagnosis) was the largest source of disagreement. Rosenhan's 1973 paper landed in the middle of this crisis of confidence. The remedy came largely from Washington University in St. Louis, where Eli Robins (1921 to 1994) and Samuel B. Guze (1923 to 2000) argued that a psychiatric diagnosis is a scientific claim and should be tested like one. In 1972 John Feighner, Robins, Guze and their colleagues published explicit diagnostic criteria for research use (the Feighner criteria), and Spitzer, Jean Endicott and Robins developed them into the Research Diagnostic Criteria (RDC) a few years later. DSM-III (1980), produced under Spitzer's direction, carried these ideas into everyday practice, and it is the most important edition in the series. Three changes stand out. First, it was descriptive and tried to be atheoretical: disorders were defined by what could be observed and reported, not by presumed psychoanalytic or biological causes, so "neurosis" disappeared as an organising idea and the phobias, for example, moved into a new group of anxiety disorders. Second, every disorder had explicit diagnostic criteria, specific enough for their reliability and validity to be studied. Field trials of reliability, a DSM-III innovation, became a fixture of every later edition. Third, it introduced the multiaxial system , which recorded each patient on five axes so that the clinician considered the whole person and not only the disorder. In their DSM-IV form the axes were: Axis I: clinical disorders (the main psychiatric syndromes). Axis II: personality disorders and mental retardation (now called intellectual disability). Axis III: general medical conditions. Axis IV: psychosocial and environmental problems. Axis V: the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF), a single 100-point rating of overall functioning. DSM-III-R (1987) corrected inconsistencies found in DSM-III. DSM-IV (1994) was the product of six years of work by more than 1,000 people, built on systematic literature reviews, reanalyses of existing data and field trials, and coordinated closely with ICD-10. (Sources give different years for ICD-10 because several dates attach to it. The World Health Assembly approved ICD-10 in 1990; its mental disorders chapter appeared with clinical guidelines in 1992, the year DSM-5-TR gives, and with research criteria in 1993; member countries began using it from 1994.) It also abandoned the old split between "organic" and "functional" disorders. DSM-IV-TR (2000) was a text revision: it updated the descriptive text and left the criteria virtually unchanged. DSM-5 (2013), whose task force was chaired by David Kupfer with Darrel Regier as vice-chair, made three structural changes worth knowing. It switched from Roman to Arabic numerals so that later updates could be issued as 5.1, 5.2 and so on. It abolished the multiaxial system: the former Axis I, II and III diagnoses are now listed together, psychosocial problems are recorded with codes from a chapter of "other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention", and the GAF was replaced by the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS). And it ordered its chapters along the life span, from neurodevelopmental disorders at the start to neurocognitive disorders near the end. DSM-5-TR, published in March 2022, is the first published revision of DSM-5. It updated the text of nearly every disorder, clarified the criteria of more than 70, and added one new diagnosis, prolonged grief disorder, together with symptom codes for recording suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury. The text revisions (DSM-IV-TR, DSM-5-TR) are not new editions. The history of the manuals is also a history of what counts as a disorder, and nothing shows this more sharply than the case of homosexuality. Classifying a behaviour or identity as a mental disorder is called pathologisation , and removing it from the classification is depathologisation . DSM-I placed homosexuality among the "sociopathic personality disturbances", and DSM-II listed it as a sexual deviation. In December 1973, after sustained protest by gay activists and research such as the 1957 finding of the American psychologist Evelyn Hooker (1907 to 1996) that expert judges could not tell the projective test records of gay and heterosexual men apart, the American Psychiatric Association's Board of Trustees voted to remove homosexuality as such from the manual. A narrower category for people distressed by their orientation survived, as "sexual orientation disturbance" and then "ego-dystonic homosexuality" in DSM-III, until DSM-III-R dropped it in 1987. The WHO removed homosexuality from the ICD with ICD-10, which the World Health Assembly approved in 1990. (In India, the Supreme Court decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India in 2018.) The same reasoning has since reached gender identity. DSM-5 replaced "gender identity disorder" with gender dysphoria, which places the clinical problem in the distress rather than in the identity, and ICD-11 moved gender incongruence out of the mental disorders chapter altogether. Notice the DSM-5-TR definition of disorder at work here: deviance from social norms is not, by itself, a disorder. Exam trap Learn the DSM years as one string: 1952, 1968, 1980, 1987, 1994, 2000, 2013, 2022 (I, II, III, III-R, IV, IV-TR, 5, 5-TR). Explicit criteria and the multiaxial system arrived with DSM-III (1980) , not DSM-IV; DSM-5 removed the axes. DSM comes from the American Psychiatric Association, not the American Psychological Association. "Pathologisation and depathologisation of homosexuality" means its classification as a mental disorder and the removal of that classification ; it does not mean changing orientation (that is so-called conversion therapy) or coming out. The APA vote was in 1973, but a residual category lasted until DSM-III-R (1987). DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 side by side Two classifications are in use today, and a clinical psychologist in India needs to know both. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) is published by one national professional body, the American Psychiatric Association, and its current version is DSM-5-TR (2022). The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is published by the WHO, covers every disease and health condition from cholera to fractures, and is the international standard that member countries use to record and report health statistics. Its eleventh revision, ICD-11, was adopted by the 72nd World Health Assembly in May 2019 and came into effect on 1 January 2022, although each country decides when to make the switch from ICD-10. Even the United States still codes with ICD-10-CM, its clinical modification of ICD-10. The two systems were developed in close contact, and DSM-5-TR reports that they are now closer than at any time since DSM-II and ICD-8: their chapters are organised in much the same way, and most disorders carry the same names. The differences that remain come mostly from their different jobs. DSM is written for clinicians and researchers and gives explicit polythetic criteria with symptom counts and minimum durations. ICD has to work in every member country, often in busy general clinics without a specialist, so its mental disorders chapter is accompanied by the WHO's Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements, which set out the essential features of each disorder in prose, avoid precise counts and cut-offs where the evidence does not support them, and leave more room for clinical judgement and cultural variation. ICD-11 also has a few categories of its own, among them complex post-traumatic stress disorder, gaming disorder and body integrity dysphoria, and it treats an acute stress reaction as a normal response to an extreme event rather than a disorder, coding it (QE84) outside the mental disorders chapter, in chapter 24, factors influencing health status or contact with health services. Finally, the codes. A DSM-5-TR code is not DSM's own: the manual borrows ICD-10-CM codes (F32.1, for example), because that is the official coding system in the United States. Indian context Indian practice runs on both manuals at once. Government hospitals and national health statistics code with the ICD, still mostly ICD-10, with the move to ICD-11 gradual; many Indian case-record formats and psychiatry teaching programmes grew up around the ICD-10 "blue book" ( Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Guidelines , 1992). Research journals, most textbooks and entrance examinations lean on DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR. The law points to the ICD: under Section 3 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Chapter 1), mental illness is to be determined according to nationally or internationally accepted medical standards, including the latest edition of the WHO's International Classification of Diseases, as notified by the central government. The same diagnosis also opens the door to disability certification (Section 9.9). Exam trap ICD-11 has two dates: adopted in May 2019 by the 72nd World Health Assembly, in effect from 1 January 2022 . If an option says "ICD-11, 2022", read it as the date it came into force. DSM-5-TR is also 2022 (March), and DSM-5 is 2013. ICD-10 (1992) put mental disorders in chapter V with codes beginning with F; ICD-11 puts them in chapter 06 with codes beginning with 6. DSM-5-TR has no codes of its own: it uses ICD-10-CM codes. And the ICD covers all of medicine; the DSM covers only mental disorders. Reliability of diagnosis and Cohen's kappa A classification is useful only if different clinicians, applying it to the same person, reach the same answer. This is the reliability of diagnosis, and in practice it means one of two things. Inter-rater reliability is agreement between two or more clinicians who judge the same information: two psychologists watch the same recorded interview, or one interviews while the other observes, and each records a diagnosis without consulting the other. Test-retest reliability is agreement between two assessments of the same person made at different times, usually by two clinicians who interview separately within a short interval. The second is the harder test. On top of the raters' own disagreements it adds the other sources of variance named in Section 2.1: the patient may tell the second interviewer a different story, or may genuinely have changed. Test-retest designs rest on an assumption that examiners like to probe. They make sense only when the thing being measured ought to stay the same over the interval. A stable trait, such as intelligence or a personality characteristic, should give similar results a few weeks apart, so a low test-retest figure means a poor measure. A rapidly changing state, such as today's mood or the anxiety someone feels in the waiting room, is expected to change, so low test-retest agreement there says nothing against the measure. Diagnoses are meant to describe conditions that last for weeks or months, which is why diagnostic field trials can use two interviews up to two weeks apart. How should agreement be measured? The obvious answer, the percentage of cases on which two clinicians agree, is misleading, because some agreement happens by pure chance. Two clinicians who each tossed a coin to decide "depressed" or "not depressed" would agree about half the time while knowing nothing about the patients. In 1960 the American psychologist and statistician Jacob Cohen (1923 to 1998) published a solution in the journal Educational and Psychological Measurement : a coefficient that measures how far the observed agreement exceeds the agreement chance alone would produce. Cohen's kappa (κ) is calculated as κ = (p o - p e ) / (1 - p e ) where p o is the observed proportion of agreement and p e is the proportion of agreement expected by chance, worked out from how often each rater uses each category. The top of the fraction is the agreement achieved beyond chance; the bottom is the largest amount of agreement beyond chance that was possible. Kappa is therefore 1 when agreement is perfect, 0 when agreement is no better than chance, and negative when the raters agree less often than chance would predict. Kappa only clicks when you calculate one, so push a case through it. Two trainee clinical psychologists at a Mysuru outpatient clinic independently watch the same 100 recorded intake interviews, and for each client each decides whether a depressive disorder is present. Higher raw agreement, lower kappa. When almost everyone is a "no", agreeing on "no" is easy and earns little credit, while the few disagreements on the rare "yes" cases weigh heavily. Kappa therefore depends on the base rate (the prevalence) of the condition in the sample. A diagnosis can look unreliable in a general clinic, where it is rare, and reliable in a specialist clinic, where it is common, without anything about the clinicians having changed. Three relatives of Cohen's kappa are worth recognising. Weighted kappa (Cohen, 1968) is used for ordered categories such as mild, moderate and severe, and gives partial credit for near misses. Fleiss' kappa, after the statistician Joseph Fleiss (1971), extends the idea to more than two raters. And the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) measures agreement on continuous ratings such as severity scores; the DSM-5 field trials used an intraclass form of kappa for diagnoses and the ICC for severity ratings. What counts as a "good" kappa? There is no law of nature here, only conventions, and Table 2.35 gives the two you are most likely to meet. The bands proposed by J. Richard Landis and Gary Koch (1977) are the most widely quoted. Joseph Fleiss offered a simpler set (above 0.75 excellent, 0.40 to 0.75 fair to good, below 0.40 poor).
