The DSM-5 field trials ran at 11 North American academic medical centres between December 2010 and October 2011 and used a deliberately demanding test-retest design: each patient was interviewed by two clinicians, separately and within two weeks, each blind to the other's diagnosis, using an ordinary clinical interview rather than a structured protocol. Post-traumatic stress disorder reached a kappa of 0.67 and autism spectrum disorder 0.69, and schizophrenia reached 0.46. But two of the commonest diagnoses in everyday practice did poorly: major depressive disorder 0.28 and generalised anxiety disorder 0.20 (Regier and colleagues, 2013). The task force argued that earlier field trials had used easier designs and had produced inflated figures; critics replied that relabelling a kappa of 0.28 as "questionable" rather than "fair" or "poor" lowered the bar. Either way, the lesson for practice is the one Section 2.1 drew: unstructured interviews let disagreement in, and research studies keep kappa high by using semi-structured interviews such as the SCID. Reliability is not the whole story, however. For decades the first-rank symptoms described by Kurt Schneider (thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting, voices commenting on the patient, and other passivity experiences, taught in Section 2.5) were valued because clinicians could agree on whether they were present. But they also occur in mania and other conditions, so agreeing that they were present did not make them specific to schizophrenia, and DSM-5 dropped the special diagnostic weight DSM-IV had given them. Agreement, in other words, does not guarantee truth. That is the question of validity. Exam trap Kappa is a measure of agreement corrected for chance on categorical judgements, introduced by Jacob Cohen in 1960 (the same Cohen as Cohen's d). It runs from below 0 to +1; 0 means chance-level agreement, not "no diagnoses". Percentage agreement overstates reliability, especially for rare conditions. Do not confuse kappa with Cronbach's alpha (internal consistency of a test's items) or with Pearson's r (association: two raters who always differ by the same amount correlate perfectly yet never agree). Cohen's kappa is for two raters; Fleiss' kappa for more. Test-retest reliability is the right check for stable traits , not for rapidly changing states. And remember the pattern from the DSM-5 field trials: PTSD and autism high, schizophrenia middling, major depression and generalised anxiety low. Validity and utility of a diagnosis A diagnosis is reliable if clinicians agree on it. It has diagnostic validity if it is true, in the sense that the category picks out a real and distinct condition with its own features, causes, course and response to treatment. The two are linked in one direction only. A diagnosis that clinicians cannot agree on cannot be valid, because it is not picking out anything consistently, so reliability is necessary for validity. But it is not sufficient. Barlow and Durand give the cleanest example: if the only criterion for depression were hearing the patient say "I feel depressed" at some point in the interview, clinicians could agree perfectly, yet the category would be close to useless, because many people with other disorders, or with none, say that now and then. A system that chases reliability by narrowing its criteria to whatever is easy to agree on can lose validity in the process. This is the classification-level version of the trade-off between structured and unstructured interviews that you met in Section 2.1. How would you show that a diagnosis is valid? In 1970 Robins and Guze answered with a five-phase method, using schizophrenia as their example: clinical description, laboratory studies, delimitation from other disorders, follow-up studies showing a characteristic course, and family studies showing that the disorder runs in families. A decade later Kenneth S. Kendler (1980) sorted such evidence by its timing into antecedent validators (familial aggregation, premorbid personality, precipitating factors), concurrent validators (psychological test findings, biological markers) and predictive validators (stability of the diagnosis over time, rates of relapse and recovery, response to treatment). When DSM-5 was prepared, each proposed change had to be supported by evidence organised around exactly these three kinds of validator. Textbooks also speak of construct validity (the criteria hang together and differ from those of other categories), predictive or criterion validity (the diagnosis forecasts course and treatment response) and content validity (the criteria capture what experts mean by the disorder). By these standards most psychiatric diagnoses are only partly validated. Few have a laboratory test; the heterogeneity and comorbidity described earlier suggest that some boundaries are not where nature put them; and genetic studies find many of the same risk factors shared across several disorders. That is why the British psychiatrist Robert Evan Kendell (1935 to 2002) and Assen Jablensky (2003) urged clinicians to separate validity from clinical utility , the usefulness of a category for communication, prediction and choosing treatment. Most DSM and ICD categories, they argued, have not been shown to be discrete entities separated by natural boundaries, yet many of them are highly useful. The danger lies in forgetting the difference. Reification is treating a convenient grouping of observations as if it were a thing: saying that a man hears voices "because he has schizophrenia", when "schizophrenia" was only the name given to his hearing voices and the rest. One research response is to step outside the categories altogether: the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC), a framework of the United States National Institute of Mental Health, studies dimensions of functioning such as threat, reward and cognitive control from genes and circuits up to behaviour, without starting from DSM diagnoses. It is a research framework, not a manual for the clinic. Exam trap Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity: a diagnosis can be reliable and invalid, but it cannot be valid and unreliable. Reliability asks "do we agree?"; validity asks "is what we agree on real and meaningful?". The five-phase validation method (clinical description, laboratory studies, delimitation, follow-up, family studies) is Robins and Guze (1970) ; antecedent, concurrent and predictive validators are Kendler (1980) ; utility versus validity is Kendell and Jablensky (2003) . RDoC belongs to the US National Institute of Mental Health and is not a diagnostic manual. The costs of labelling: Rosenhan and after A diagnosis does more than describe. Once written, it travels: into the case file, the insurance form, the family's conversations and the client's picture of himself. It shapes what the next clinician expects to see and what the neighbours say. This is the problem of labelling , the process by which a diagnostic name, once applied, changes how others perceive and treat a person and how the person sees himself. The study that made labelling famous is the one that opened this chapter. Key study: Rosenhan, "On being sane in insane places" (Science, 1973) The question. Can psychiatric staff tell the sane from the insane, and what does a label do once it has been applied? The method. As the chapter opening described, eight sane people, Rosenhan among them, sought admission to 12 hospitals in five states, each reporting the same unclear voice saying "empty", "hollow" and "thud", and then behaved normally. Methodologically it was a field study using disguised participant observation. The results. All were admitted, all but one with a diagnosis of schizophrenia; they stayed 7 to 52 days (an average of 19) and were discharged with schizophrenia "in remission". Staff read ordinary behaviour through the label. Contact was minimal: when a pseudopatient courteously asked a staff member a question, psychiatrists moved on with head averted 71 percent of the time, and nurses and attendants 88 percent of the time, and daily contact with psychiatrists, psychologists and physicians averaged under seven minutes. The pseudopatients were handed nearly 2,100 pills, almost all of which they pocketed or flushed away. The follow-up. The staff of a research and teaching hospital who had heard of the findings doubted that such errors could happen in their hospital. Rosenhan told them that during the next three months one or more pseudopatients would try to gain admission, and every staff member rated each new patient on the likelihood of being an impostor. Of 193 patients judged, 41 were confidently identified as pseudopatients by at least one staff member, 23 were suspected by at least one psychiatrist, and 19 by a psychiatrist and one other staff member. Rosenhan had sent no one. The conclusion he drew was that diagnoses depend on the setting and on the label more than on the patient, and that a label, once applied, is "sticky" and colours everything the person does afterwards. The paper caused an uproar, and the most influential reply came from Robert Spitzer, who by then was chairing the task force preparing DSM-III. In a 1975 critique in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology , Spitzer argued that the study showed something quite different from what Rosenhan claimed. A diagnosis rests largely on what the patient reports, and a patient who lies convincingly can fool any diagnostician in any branch of medicine. He quoted an analogy from the psychiatrist Seymour S. Kety (1915 to 2000): if Kety drank a quart of blood, hid the fact and arrived at an emergency room vomiting blood, the staff would diagnose and treat a bleeding peptic ulcer, and nobody would conclude from this that medicine cannot diagnose ulcers. A person who asks to be admitted because he is hearing voices is reasonably treated as psychotic until there is evidence otherwise. Spitzer also turned the discharge diagnosis around. In the hospital records he checked, "schizophrenia, in remission" was a rare discharge diagnosis, so its use for the pseudopatients suggested that the staff had in fact noticed that they showed no symptoms. And the follow-up, he argued, showed only that staff warned to expect impostors became readier to suspect one; since no impostor came, nobody could say how accurate they were. For decades the argument rested there: a famous finding and a famous rebuttal. Then the journalist Susannah Cahalan , whose own autoimmune brain inflammation had at first been mistaken for a psychiatric illness (she told that story in Brain on Fire , 2012), went looking for the pseudopatients. Her book The Great Pretender (2019) reported serious problems. Working through Rosenhan's private papers, she could trace only one of the other seven pseudopatients in the paper, a graduate student, plus one further volunteer, Harry Lando, who had found his hospital stay a positive experience and whose data had been left out. Rosenhan's own hospital record (he was admitted to Haverford State Hospital in Pennsylvania under the name "David Lurie") described a man who said he had been putting copper over his ears to keep the voices out and wanted admission because the hospital would be "better insulated": far more than the single unclear voice reported in Science . Cahalan raised the possibility that some of the pseudopatients never existed. In 2023 the historian of psychiatry Andrew Scull, writing in History of Psychiatry , called the study a "successful scientific fraud". Rosenhan died in 2012 and cannot answer, but a classic study whose data cannot be checked can no longer carry the weight it once did. Does the collapse of Rosenhan's study mean that labels are harmless? No. The effect he claimed has been shown in better-controlled work. In 1974 Ellen J. Langer (born 1947) and Robert Abelson showed clinicians the same videotape of a young man talking about his past jobs. Half were told he was a "job applicant" and half that he was a "patient". Psychoanalytically oriented clinicians described the "patient" as considerably more disturbed than the identical "job applicant", whereas behaviourally trained clinicians, whose training directed them to the observable behaviour, rated him much the same under both labels. The label changed what some trained observers saw. A related bias is diagnostic overshadowing , a term introduced by Steven Reiss and his colleagues in 1982 after they found that clinicians were less likely to recognise emotional problems in a person labelled as having intellectual disability: the existing label explained everything away. Today the term is used most often for physical illness missed in people who carry a psychiatric diagnosis, whose chest pain or breathlessness is put down to "anxiety" or "his illness". Sociologists had argued for some time that labels do more than bias observers: they help to create the behaviour they name. Edwin M. Lemert (1912 to 1996), in Social Pathology (1951), distinguished primary deviance, the original rule-breaking, which may be brief and have many causes, from secondary deviance , which develops after a person has been publicly labelled and begins to organise his life and identity around the label. Thomas J. Scheff (1929 to 2025) applied the idea to mental illness in Being Mentally Ill: A Sociological Theory (1966), the classic statement of labelling theory . Scheff called the symptoms of mental illness residual rule-breaking : violations of rules so taken for granted that they have no other name, such as talking to no one or staring fixedly into space. Most residual rule-breaking, he argued, is common, passes unnoticed and fades. But when it is noticed and officially labelled, typically in a crisis, the person is cast in the stereotyped role of "mental patient" that everyone learns in childhood; he is rewarded for playing the role and punished for trying to leave it, and the label becomes the main cause of a lasting career of mental illness. Erving Goffman (1922 to 1982) described that career from the inside in Asylums (1961), based on fieldwork at a large mental hospital in Washington, D.C. A total institution , in which every part of life is lived in one place under one authority, strips the newcomer of his former identity through a series of "mortifications of the self". The psychiatrist Thomas Stephen Szasz (1920 to 2012) went furthest in The Myth of Mental Illness (1961), arguing that "mental illness" is a metaphor for problems in living and that psychiatric labels serve social control. Labelling theory was a valuable corrective, but it overstated its case. The sociologist Walter Gove (1970) reviewed the evidence and concluded that most people are labelled because they are already seriously disturbed, that families usually resist the label for a long time before seeking help, and that treatment more often helps than entrenches illness; labelling could not explain why the rule-breaking began. Bruce Link and his colleagues (1989) proposed a more defensible modified labelling theory. Everyone grows up absorbing the culture's beliefs that psychiatric patients are dangerous and incompetent and will be rejected. When a person is later diagnosed, those beliefs suddenly apply to him. Expecting rejection, he may keep his treatment secret, withdraw from friends or stop applying for jobs, and these ways of coping themselves narrow his life. Labelling, on this view, does not cause the illness; it adds a second burden to it. That second burden is stigma . Goffman, in Stigma (1963), defined it as an attribute that is deeply discrediting, one that reduces a person in others' eyes "from a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one". Barlow and Durand, following Stephen Hinshaw, describe it as a combination of negative stereotypes, prejudices and attitudes that reduces the life chances of the devalued group. Patrick Corrigan's research distinguishes public stigma, the prejudice and discrimination of the community, from self-stigma , in which the person comes to agree with the stereotype and applies it to himself, losing self-esteem and showing what Corrigan called the "why try" effect: "Why try for that job? Someone like me won't get it." History also shows labels used deliberately as weapons. In 1851 the American physician Samuel Cartwright described "drapetomania", a supposed disease that made enslaved people run away, and in the Soviet Union political dissidents were confined in psychiatric hospitals under diagnoses such as "sluggish schizophrenia". The DSM-5-TR rule that political, religious or sexual deviance is not in itself a disorder is meant to guard against exactly such abuses. None of this means that clinicians should stop diagnosing. A label can also bring relief ("so this has a name, and I am not simply weak"), entry to treatment, insurance cover, leave from work, disability benefits and legal protection, and it connects the clinician to the evidence on what helps. Reviewing the labelling research, John Ruscio (2004) concluded that harm is not an automatic consequence of diagnosis; it depends a great deal on how the diagnosis is used and conveyed. Three habits reduce the cost. Use person-first language ("a man with schizophrenia", not "a schizophrenic"), because a disorder is something a person has, not what he is. Treat every diagnosis as a working hypothesis, open to revision when the evidence changes, which is exactly the habit the pseudopatients' clinicians lacked. And pair the diagnosis with a formulation (Section 2.9) that describes the person's story, context and strengths, not only his category. Clinical link Giving a diagnosis is a skill in its own right. When the clinician tells Ravi and his mother that he has depression, she explains what the word means and what it does not mean (common, treatable, not "madness" and not weakness of character), links it to their own words ("what doctors call depression is the heaviness and the 3 a.m. waking you described"), asks what they now understand and what they fear (a "mental case" label, gossip in the village, his sister's marriage), and moves straight to the formulation and the plan. A label delivered this way opens a door; the same label written on a form and handed over in silence can close one. Indian context In India the cost of a psychiatric label often falls on the whole family. Families conceal illness to protect the marriage prospects of the patient and of his siblings, and a diagnosis disclosed at the wrong moment can end an engagement. Indian law tries to limit the damage. Section 3 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Chapter 1) provides that mental illness must not be determined on the basis of a person's political, economic or social status, membership of a cultural, racial or religious group, or non-conformity with the moral, social, cultural, work or political values or religious beliefs of the community; that past treatment or hospitalisation does not by itself justify any present or future determination of mental illness; and that a determination of mental illness does not by itself mean that the person is of unsound mind unless a competent court has declared so. Read the clause on past treatment (section 3(4)) against Rosenhan's "schizophrenia, in remission": the Act rules out exactly the sticky label he described. Exam trap Rosenhan , "On being sane in insane places", Science , 1973 : eight pseudopatients, 12 hospitals, a disguised participant observation design; in the follow-up, 41 of 193 genuine patients were confidently judged impostors although none had been sent. The best-known critique is Spitzer (1975) ; the "quart of blood" analogy he quoted is Kety's . The later doubts are Cahalan's The Great Pretender (2019) and Scull's 2023 charge of fraud. The case of Rosenhan's pseudopatients, revisited Go back to the admissions office in Pennsylvania where this chapter began, and to the question it left open: was the problem the label, or the way the information behind the label was gathered and interpreted? Section 2.10.7 showed that the study itself can no longer settle the matter. Robert Spitzer replied in 1975 that a patient who lies convincingly can fool a diagnostician in any branch of medicine, and that the rare discharge diagnosis "schizophrenia, in remission" suggests the staff had in fact noticed that the pseudopatients showed no symptoms. In The Great Pretender (2019) Susannah Cahalan could trace only one of the other seven pseudopatients, found a volunteer whose data had been left out, and found that Rosenhan's own hospital record described far more than the single unclear voice reported in Science . A classic study whose data cannot be checked cannot carry the weight it once did. Its warning survives anyway, because a label can change what trained observers see (Langer and Abelson, 1974), and because every tool in this chapter exists to stop a clinician from hearing one symptom, reaching for one label and reading everything afterwards through it. Run the chapter's tools over a man who says a voice is saying "thud" and the difference is plain. The case history (Section 2.3) would ask when he was last completely well and find a lone symptom with no course and no previous episode behind it, and a premorbid personality that matched the man in the chair. The MSE (Sections 2.4 to 2.6) would describe rather than diagnose: ordinary appearance, speech, affect and cognition, with one isolated perceptual complaint recorded in his own words. Explicit criteria and a semi-structured interview such as the SCID would narrow criterion and information variance (Section 2.1), and kappa would measure how far two clinicians agreed beyond chance (Section 2.10). First's steps of differential diagnosis (Section 2.9) begin by asking whether the person is feigning his symptoms, which is exactly what the pseudopatients were doing. The psychiatrist who saw "oral-acquisitive" illness in a queue outside the cafeteria broke the report writer's rule of separating observation from inference, and Kent and colleagues (1974) showed that expectation distorts global impressions more than specific behaviour codes (Section 2.8). Above all, a formulation treats every conclusion, a diagnosis included, as a hypothesis to be revised. Ravi's record says "a depressive episode, possibly recurrent" and keeps the question of the month at 17 open on purpose; the pseudopatients' clinicians closed theirs at the first symptom. Chapter summary 2.1 The Clinical Interview: Purposes, Types and Structure. The interview is the core tool of clinical assessment. Interviews differ first by purpose (intake, case history, diagnostic, mental status, crisis and termination), and Harry Stack Sullivan (1954), who saw the clinician as a participant observer, divided them into formal inception, reconnaissance, detailed inquiry and termination. They differ second by structure. Unstructured interviews are flexible but unreliable: in 1962 Aaron Beck's group found psychiatrists agreeing on the specific diagnosis only about half the time, and Spitzer, Endicott and Robins (1975) named five sources of disagreement, of which criterion variance was the largest. The SCID-5 (First, Williams, Karg and Spitzer), Wing's Present State Examination, the WHO's SCAN and the K-SADS are semi-structured; the DIS and CIDI are fully structured. Structure buys reliability but not validity, so practice blends an open start with a semi-structured check. 2.2 The Craft of Interviewing. Allen Ivey's microcounselling (from 1968) broke interviewing into teachable microskills, and Carl Rogers's person-centred tradition runs through them. Rapport rests on attending behaviour, which Gerard Egan summarised as SOLER (1975). Open questions ("Tell me about ...") generate the story and closed questions pin down details, combined in the funnel technique. Minimal encouragers (furthering) keep the client talking; paraphrasing restates content in new words; reflection of feeling, the signature technique of client-centred therapy, names the emotion; summarising draws the threads together. Clarification, gentle confrontation of discrepancies, sparing interpretation and silence follow, and Egan separated primary from advanced empathy. Common errors include leading, double-barrelled and "why" questions and Thorndike's halo effect (1920). Children, older adults, resistant and suicidal clients need adapted methods, and culture enters through Kleinman's explanatory model (1980), idioms of distress and trained interpreters. 2.3 The Case History. The case history is the longitudinal story of the person and the illness, an approach owed most to Adolf Meyer's psychobiology. It follows a standard order: identifying data; the informants and the reliability of their accounts; chief complaints in the patient's own words, with duration; the history of present illness, with onset (abrupt, acute, subacute or insidious), course, progress, precipitating factors and treatment; past psychiatric and medical history; family history, drawn as a genogram of at least three generations (popularised by Murray Bowen) and distinct from Hartman's ecomap and Moreno's sociogram; personal history, from birth and development through education, occupation and sexual and marital life to substance use and forensic history; and premorbid personality, the person before the illness. The history of Ravi, a 24-year-old in a shared rented room in Mysuru whose mother is staying with him, already suggests a depressive episode, possibly recurrent. 2.4 The Mental Status Examination I: Appearance, Behaviour, Speech, Mood and Affect. The mental status examination is a cross-sectional photograph beside the history's film: a description, not a diagnosis, in the vocabulary of Karl Jaspers' General Psychopathology (1913), which taught that form matters more than content. Appearance and behaviour come first, hallucinatory behaviour included and everything read against culture, then attitude to the examiner and eye contact. Psychomotor activity covers agitation, retardation and catatonia, which Kahlbaum described in 1874 and DSM-5-TR treats as twelve signs, three needed, no longer tied to schizophrenia. Speech is recorded for rate, quantity, volume, reaction time, articulation and coherence; pressure of speech is not flight of ideas. Mood is what the patient reports and affect what the clinician observes, restricted, blunted or flat in increasing severity, labile or inappropriate. Anhedonia (Ribot, 1896) and alexithymia (Sifneos, 1973) complete the vocabulary. 2.5 The Mental Status Examination II: Thought and Perception. Thought is known only through speech, as Nancy Andreasen stressed. British texts use four headings: stream (flight of ideas, retardation, thought block, perseveration), form (Bleuler's loosening of associations, derailment, tangentiality, circumstantiality, which reaches its goal, word salad, neologisms), content and possession; American texts merge stream and form as thought process. Delusions, Jaspers' "basic characteristic of madness", are held with extraordinary conviction, impervious to argument and false; they may be primary or secondary and are named by theme, from persecution and reference to Capgras and Cotard. Wernicke's overvalued ideas are understandable, and obsessions are recognised as one's own. Thought insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting and the passivity experiences belong to Kurt Schneider's eleven first-rank symptoms. Perception covers illusions (first separated from hallucinations by Esquirol), hallucinations by modality, special varieties, pseudohallucinations, and depersonalisation and derealisation. 2.6 The Mental Status Examination III: Cognition, Judgement, Insight and the Written MSE. Cognition is examined in a fixed order because each function rests on those below it: consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale 3 to 15); orientation, lost in the order time, place, person, which points to organic causes; attention and concentration (digit span, serial sevens or serial threes); memory, immediate, recent and remote, with Ribot's law, Korsakoff's confabulation and depressive pseudodementia; intelligence; abstraction (proverbs and the fairer similarities); and judgement, personal, social and test. Insight, "a correct attitude to a morbid change in oneself" (Aubrey Lewis, 1934), runs in six grades from complete denial to true emotional insight, and its lack was the commonest finding in the WHO's International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia. The MMSE (Folstein, Folstein and McHugh, 1975) is a 30-point screen, not the MSE, which is written by describing first and labelling afterwards. 2.7 Risk Assessment: Suicide and Violence. Asking directly about suicide does not plant the idea (Gould and colleagues, 2005); the questions climb a ladder from passive ideation through intent, plan, means and preparation, and past attempts are always explored. A previous attempt is the strongest single predictor and hopelessness the strongest psychological one. Durkheim (1897) described four types of suicide, Joiner's interpersonal theory (2005) explains who acts on the wish to die, and Linehan's Reasons for Living Inventory (1983) measures protection. The SAD PERSONS mnemonic (Patterson and colleagues, 1983) is a checklist, not a score: its weights are equal, its items mostly static, and Pokorny (1983) showed that the low base rate defeats prediction. Modern practice formulates risk, targets dynamic factors and writes a safety plan. For violence, past violence predicts best, most people with mental illness are not violent, and structured professional judgement (the HCR-20) joins actuarial tools. 2.8 Behavioural Assessment. Behavioural assessment treats a response as a sample of behaviour, not a sign of an underlying trait (Goldfried and Kent, 1972), backed by Walter Mischel's (1968) evidence that behaviour varies with the situation. Its core is functional analysis, Skinner's term, built on operant conditioning: antecedent, behaviour and consequence, extended by Kanfer and Saslow (1965) into excesses, deficits and assets and later into SORKC. Ravi's withdrawal is maintained by negative reinforcement, and Mowrer's neurotic paradox explains why short-term relief outweighs long-term cost. The behavioural interview defines target behaviours that pass Lindsley's dead man test. Self-monitoring is reactive, usually therapeutically. Observation is naturalistic, analogue (Lang and Lazovik's behavioural avoidance test, 1963) or participant; it is recorded by event, duration, latency, interval or momentary time sampling, and checked by inter-observer agreement against reactivity, observer drift and expectancy bias. Role play and Lang's three response systems complete it. 2.9 Case Formulation. A case formulation is, in Tracy Eells's (1997) definition, a hypothesis about the causes, precipitants and maintaining influences of a person's problems, and treatment follows from it. The 5 Ps ask what the problem is (presenting), why this person (predisposing), why now (precipitating), why it continues (perpetuating, the main target of treatment) and what helps (protective). George Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) crosses these with biological, psychological and social levels. The cognitive-behavioural formulation, pioneered by Jacqueline Persons (1989), uses Padesky and Mooney's five-part model and Judith Beck's cognitive conceptualisation diagram (1995); the psychodynamic formulation follows the four parts of Perry, Cooper and Michels (1987). Diagnosis is nomothetic and categorical, formulation idiographic and explanatory. Differential diagnosis rules out malingering, substances and medical causes first. Reports answer the referral question and avoid the Barnum effect (Meehl, 1956), and feedback can itself help (Finn and Tonsager, 1992). 2.10 Classification as a Clinical Tool. Clinicians classify to communicate, predict, choose treatment, do research, administer services and understand causes. DSM and ICD are categorical systems with polythetic, prototypical criteria and some dimensional additions. DSM-III (1980), produced under Spitzer and growing out of the Feighner criteria, brought explicit criteria and the multiaxial system, which DSM-5 (2013) removed; homosexuality was voted out in 1973. DSM-5-TR (2022, American Psychiatric Association) and ICD-11 (adopted May 2019, in effect 1 January 2022, chapter 06) are now closely aligned. Cohen's kappa (1960) corrects agreement for chance; in the DSM-5 field trials major depression reached only 0.28. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity, and utility differs from validity (Kendell and Jablensky, 2003). Rosenhan's 1973 study, challenged by Spitzer and Cahalan, proves less than once thought, but labelling theory (Lemert, Scheff, Goffman) and stigma still argue for person-first language. stigma, self-stigma, person-first language From the past papers A structured interview commonly used in clinical psychology is: (IHBAS 2025) (a) MMSE (b) SCID (c) WAIS (d) TAT Answer: (b) SCID. The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM walks the clinician through the diagnostic criteria module by module (strictly it is semi-structured, because it needs clinical judgement). The MMSE is a 30-point cognitive screening test, not a diagnostic interview and not the MSE; the WAIS is an intelligence scale and the TAT a projective technique. The Vineland-3, K-SADS, ADI-R, and ADOS-2 are best classified as: (practice mock) (a) EEG paradigms (b) Personality projective techniques (c) Self-report cognitive tests (d) Structured / semi-structured interviews and observation instruments used in developmental and psychiatric assessment (Vineland-3 adaptive, K-SADS childhood psychiatric, ADI-R + ADOS-2 autism) Answer: (d). The K-SADS is a semi-structured interview of parent and child, the ADI-R a caregiver interview for autism, the ADOS-2 a standardised play-based observation and the Vineland-3 an adaptive-behaviour interview with a caregiver. None records brain activity, none is projective, and none is a self-report test. Which of the following techniques is a client centred therapist most likely to use? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Analysis (b) Giving advice (c) Reflection (d) Aversive conditioning Answer: (c) Reflection. Reflection of feeling is the signature technique of client-centred therapy: Rogers held that accurately reflecting the client's inner experience let the client hear himself and grow. Analysis belongs to psychoanalysis, giving advice is a directive move Rogers deliberately avoided, and aversive conditioning belongs to behaviour therapy. Leaning forward, saying umm, nodding, are examples of which one of the following interview techniques? (RML 2020) (a) Paraphrasing (b) Prompting (c) Furthering (d) Checking Answer: (c) Furthering. These minimal encouragers, called furthering responses in social-work interviewing texts, keep the client talking without changing the subject. Paraphrasing restates content in new words, prompting is a specific cue that steers the client to a topic, and checking asks the client to confirm the interviewer's understanding. 'Tell me about' is an example of: (RML 2020) (a) an open-ended question (b) a close-ended question (c) an ethnographic interviewing technique (d) theory-guided inquiry Answer: (a) An open-ended question. It leaves the content and length of the answer entirely to the client. Spradley's ethnographic "grand tour" questions ("Tell me about a typical day") use the same move, but the question is still open; theory-guided inquiry describes where questions come from, not whether they are open or closed. When a counsellor repeats what the client says, but uses words that are different than what the client used, the counsellor is using what skill? (RML 2021) (a) Paraphrasing (b) Questioning (c) Empathy (d) Nonverbal communication Answer: (a) Paraphrasing. Paraphrasing (restatement, reflection of content) feeds back the essence of what was said in the interviewer's own words; repeating it word for word is parroting. Questioning asks for new information, empathy is the broader capacity that a paraphrase is one way of showing, and nonverbal communication is posture, gesture and tone. Anhedonia, a core feature of major depression, is defined as: (practice mock) (a) Excessive guilt (b) Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in nearly all activities (c) Psychomotor agitation (d) Difficulty concentrating Answer: (b). Ribot's term (1896) means the loss of the capacity to experience pleasure. Excessive guilt is a disturbance of thought content, psychomotor agitation a motor sign and difficulty concentrating a cognitive symptom; all four can occur in the same depressive episode, which is why they make tempting distractors. Circumstantiality is a disorder of: (Recall set) (a) Possession of thought (b) Content of thought (c) Form of thought (thought process) (d) Perception Answer: (c) Form of thought. The circumstantial patient takes a long detour through needless detail but reaches the point, a disturbance of how ideas are organised. It says nothing about what he believes (content), his thoughts feel his own (possession), and nothing is misperceived. British texts following Fish file it under stream; choose stream only when form is not offered. First-rank symptoms of schizophrenia (Schneider) most prominently include: (practice mock) (a) Avolition and flat affect (b) Memory deficits and disorientation to person (c) Thought insertion, thought withdrawal, thought broadcasting, made feelings/impulses, somatic passivity, third-person auditory hallucinations (d) Catatonic excitement Answer: (c). Schneider's list centres on thought alienation, passivity experiences, delusional perception and three kinds of auditory hallucination. Avolition and flat affect are negative symptoms, memory deficits and disorientation are cognitive impairments that point to organic disease (which Schneider's rule excluded), and catatonic excitement is a motor sign. In the Mental Status Examination (MSE), 'insight' refers to: (practice mock) (a) The client's orientation to time, place, and person (b) The client's ability to do serial subtraction (c) The client's awareness and understanding of their own illness (d) The presence of hallucinations Answer: (c). Insight is "a correct attitude to a morbid change in oneself" (Aubrey Lewis, 1934), graded from complete denial to true emotional insight. Orientation is a separate cognitive heading, serial subtraction tests concentration, and hallucinations are recorded under perception. What is assessed in the Insight category of the cognitive assessment? (practice mock) (a) Orientation to time, place, and person (b) Level of consciousness (c) Degree of awareness regarding one's illness (d) Immediate retention and recall Answer: (c). The distractors are the other cognitive headings, in the order they are examined: consciousness comes first because every later test assumes an alert patient, orientation next, and immediate retention and recall is registration within seconds, tested with the digit span. Insight closes the examination. Functional analysis is a therapy based on: (RML 2022) (a) Classical conditioning (b) Humanistic principles (c) Operant conditioning (d) Psychodynamic principles Answer: (c) Operant conditioning. Functional analysis examines the antecedents, the behaviour and above all the consequences that maintain it, Skinner's three-term contingency. Classical conditioning can explain how a fear was acquired but not what keeps a behaviour going; humanistic and psychodynamic principles have nothing to do with the ABC. In the context of psychopathology, a "formulation" differs from a "diagnosis" in that a formulation primarily aims to: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Classify the client's symptoms according to a standardized nosological system like DSM-5. (b) Provide a hypothesis about the cause, precipitants, and maintaining factors of an individual's difficulties. (c) Determine the prognosis and likely course of the disorder over time. (d) Rule out organic causes for the presenting psychological symptoms. Answer: (b). This is Eells's (1997) definition of a case formulation. Classifying symptoms in a nosological system is diagnosis; prognosis and course are a use of diagnosis (and of formulation, but not its primary aim); ruling out organic causes is part of differential diagnosis. Test-retest reliability is most appropriate for: (practice mock) (a) Measures of rapidly changing state (b) Stable trait measures (c) Single-item measures only (d) Open-ended interviews only Answer: (b) Stable trait measures. A test-retest design makes sense only when the thing measured ought to stay the same over the interval, as intelligence or a personality characteristic should. A state such as today's mood is expected to change, so low agreement there says nothing against the measure; the other two options are arbitrary restrictions. What do researchers mean by pathologization and depathologization of homosexuality? (practice mock) (a) None of the above (b) The classification of homosexuality as a mental disorder and the removal of this classification (c) The changing of sexual orientation from homosexual to heterosexual (d) The process of coming out as a gay or lesbian individual Answer: (b). The American Psychiatric Association's Board of Trustees voted in December 1973 to remove homosexuality as such from DSM, a residual category lasted until DSM-III-R (1987), and the WHO removed it with ICD-10. Changing orientation is so-called conversion therapy, and coming out has nothing to do with classification. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first.
