Exam trap YAVIS (young, attractive, verbal, intelligent, successful) is William Schofield's acronym (1964), not Freud's; Freud's own warning was about patients near or above fifty. Eysenck's 44 per cent for psychoanalysis counted dropouts as failures, which is one of the standard objections to his review. The "symptom substitution" that analysts predicted when symptoms are treated directly was largely not found (Section 3.2 and Chapter 4). And the historian who found the Bellevue records on Anna O. is Henri Ellenberger (1972), not Ernest Jones, whose 1953 biography of Freud first made her real name public. The Menninger project: forty-two lives in treatment If case histories cannot settle the question, what can? The first serious attempt to study psychoanalytic treatment systematically, with records kept and predictions made by people other than the treating analyst, began in 1954 at the Menninger Foundation in Topeka, Kansas, then one of the great centres of American psychiatry. Its principal investigator was Robert Wallerstein (1921 to 2014), a psychiatrist and analyst who later became president of the International Psychoanalytical Association. The final report, Forty-two Lives in Treatment: A Study of Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy , appeared in 1986, more than thirty years after the first patient was enrolled. Key study: The Menninger Psychotherapy Research Project (1954 to 1982) The question. What changes take place in psychoanalysis and in psychoanalytic psychotherapy, and which features of the patient, the therapist and the treatment account for them? The method. Forty-two adults, most of them seriously disturbed and many of whom had travelled to Topeka from across the United States and abroad, were followed through their treatment: roughly half in classical psychoanalysis and half in psychoanalytic psychotherapy that mixed expressive (interpretive) and supportive techniques. Researchers who were not treating them made detailed predictions at the outset about how each patient would respond and why, gathered case records and clinical ratings during treatment, and reassessed the patients at termination and again at follow-up some years later; Wallerstein kept track of many of them for decades. The result. Three findings surprised the investigators. First, the treatments were less distinct than intended: the analyses contained supportive elements, and the psychotherapies contained more support than planned. Second, the supportive elements did far more of the work than anyone had predicted, and the changes they produced were often as stable and as deep ("structural", in analytic language) as the changes reached through interpretation and insight. Third, many patients changed through what Wallerstein called a "transference cure": in his words, the patient in effect says, I make the agreed-upon changes for you, the therapist, in order to earn and keep your support, your esteem and your love. Proportionally, psychoanalysis did no better than psychotherapy, and several of the sickest patients, placed in full analysis in the hope that only analysis could reach them, did worse than predicted; Wallerstein recorded the failure of these "heroic indications" for analysis. The criticism. There was no randomisation and no untreated comparison group, the sample was small and unusual, and outcome was judged by clinical ratings rather than standard measures. The project could describe change in great depth, but it could not show that the treatment, rather than time, had caused it. The Menninger findings cut against the central assumption of classical technique (Section 3.2): that lasting change comes through insight, while support merely props the patient up. If encouragement, advice, strengthened defences and the wish to please the therapist could produce durable change, the line between "deep" and "superficial" treatment was not where analysts had drawn it. Wallerstein concluded that supportive techniques deserved far more respect, one reason supportive psychotherapy (Section 3.10) is now taught as a treatment in its own right. And the transference cure , change made for the sake of the relationship with the therapist rather than through insight, is a psychoanalytic name for what Chapter 8 calls common factors: improvement carried by the relationship and the patient's attachment to the helper. The same data were also read another way. Otto Kernberg (Section 3.4), who led the project's quantitative analysis (reported in 1972), concluded that patients with weak egos did best in a skilled, expressive psychotherapy that worked on the transference in the here and now, the reading that later grew into transference-focused psychotherapy. One project thus yielded two lessons, Wallerstein's (support does more than analysts believed) and Kernberg's (the most disturbed patients need a structured, transference-focused therapy), and both reappear in the borderline trials below. Exam trap The Menninger Psychotherapy Research Project (Topeka, 1954 to 1982) is Robert Wallerstein's; its book is Forty-two Lives in Treatment (1986), and 42 is the number of patients. Its famous finding is that supportive elements did much of the work and produced change as durable as insight did, often through a "transference cure". It was a naturalistic study, not a randomised controlled trial. Do not confuse it with Eysenck's 1952 review (a reanalysis of published figures), Smith and Glass's 1977 meta-analysis (Section 8.2) or the NIMH depression trial of CBT, interpersonal psychotherapy and imipramine (Section 8.8). Short-term psychodynamic therapy: the meta-analyses Since the 1990s the question has been asked through randomised controlled trials and meta-analyses, the methods of Chapter 8 (Sections 8.2 and 8.7). An effect size expresses the difference between a treated group and a comparison group in standard deviation units; by Jacob Cohen's rule of thumb 0.2 is small, 0.5 moderate and 0.8 large, and Smith, Glass and Miller (1980) put the average effect of psychotherapy of all kinds, against no treatment, at 0.85. To judge psychodynamic therapy you need one further distinction, because nearly every quarrel below turns on it. A between-group effect size compares patients who received the therapy with patients randomly assigned to something else (a waiting list, usual care or another therapy) at the same point in time. A within-group effect size , also called a pre-post effect size, compares the same patients before and after treatment. The second is almost always larger, because it also counts everything that would have improved the patients anyway: the passage of time, spontaneous remission, the tendency of people who seek help at their worst to drift back towards their usual level (regression to the mean), and the hope that comes with starting any treatment. A within-group effect of 1.4 tells you nothing about whether the therapy beats an alternative; a between-group effect of 1.4 would be remarkable. Short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy (STPP), the time-limited family described in Section 3.6, was the first to be tested in numbers. In 2004 the German psychotherapy researcher Falk Leichsenring , with Sven Rabung and Eric Leibing, pooled 17 high-quality randomised trials of STPP (an average of 21 sessions) in the Archives of General Psychiatry . Compared with control conditions, the effect on the patients' target problems was 1.17; within the treated groups, the pre-post effect was 1.39 at the end of therapy and 1.57 at follow-up an average of 13 months later. Two years later came a review for the Cochrane Library, the database of systematic reviews that medicine treats as its most rigorous summary of evidence. Its lead author was the Canadian psychiatrist Allan Abbass of Dalhousie University in Halifax, a leading researcher in Davanloo's intensive short-term dynamic psychotherapy (Section 3.6). Abbass and his colleagues (2006) pooled 23 randomised trials with 1,431 patients who had common mental disorders (non-psychotic depression, anxiety and somatoform disorders, often mixed with personality problems) and who received under 40 hours of STPP, compared with waiting-list, minimal-treatment or usual-care controls. The effect size for general symptom improvement was 0.97, rising to 1.51 at follow-up more than nine months after treatment. The effects for anxiety (1.08, rising to 1.35) and somatic symptoms (0.81, rising to 2.21) were also large; the effect on depressive symptoms was more modest (0.59, rising to 0.98). The reviewers attached two warnings themselves. The trials were few, of variable quality and very different from one another; and most compared STPP with waiting lists, minimal treatment or usual care, which shows that it beats little or nothing, not that it matches the best alternative. The 2014 Cochrane update (Abbass with Steve Kisely, Joel Town, Leichsenring and others: 33 studies, 2,173 participants) reached the same conclusion with the same caution: gains over controls in the short and medium term that generally appeared to grow in the long term. A review by Abbass, Kisely and Kurt Kroenke (2009) found STPP helpful for somatic symptom conditions as well, often with a fall in the patients' use of health care. Remember Before any effect size impresses you, ask two questions. Compared with what? (A waiting list is an easy opponent; an established therapy is a hard one.) And measured how? (A pre-post change within one group includes natural recovery.) Cohen's benchmarks are 0.2 small, 0.5 moderate, 0.8 large. Long-term therapy and the quarrel over 1.8 Short-term therapy is the easy case. The harder question, and the one that matters for psychoanalysis proper, is whether long, open-ended treatment adds anything. In 2008 Leichsenring and Rabung published "Effectiveness of long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy" in the Journal of the American Medical Association ( JAMA ). They defined long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy (LTPP) as psychodynamic therapy lasting at least a year or 50 sessions, and they asked about "complex" mental disorders (personality disorders, chronic disorders and multiple co-occurring disorders), for which short treatments most often fail. Pooling 23 studies with 1,053 patients (11 randomised trials and 12 observational studies), they reported that in the controlled comparisons LTPP was significantly better than shorter psychotherapies in overall effectiveness, target problems and personality functioning. The headline figure was a between-group effect size of 1.8 for overall effectiveness: after LTPP, the authors wrote, patients with complex disorders were on average better off than 96 per cent of the patients in the comparison groups. The number 1.8 caused a storm. An effect that size is far larger than almost anything else in the psychotherapy literature, and critics, among them Brett Thombs and Aaron Beck (Chapter 5), soon argued that it was an artefact. It had not been calculated as a direct difference between randomised groups. Instead the pre-post effects of the LTPP arms had been compared with the pre-post effects of the comparison arms, treating treatment conditions rather than studies as the units of analysis, which throws away the protection that randomisation provides. The comparison treatments were also often short, weak or not genuine psychotherapies, so "better than shorter therapy" partly meant "better than a smaller dose of something lesser". Even Shedler, who cited the result in 2010, added a footnote warning that the atypical method might have inflated it. Leichsenring and Rabung responded to the methodological point and in 2011 published an update in the British Journal of Psychiatry , computing proper between-group effect sizes from ten controlled studies with 971 patients (all but one of them randomised trials). LTPP still came out ahead of less intensive psychotherapies for complex disorders, but the advantage was now moderate, from 0.44 to 0.68 depending on the outcome. In 2012 Smit and colleagues (among them the meta-researcher John Ioannidis and the schema therapy researcher Arnoud Arntz) analysed eleven trials in Clinical Psychology Review , using recovery as the main outcome, and found no difference between LTPP and the control treatments: the evidence, they concluded, was "limited and at best conflicting". Leichsenring's group replied that many of Smit's controls were themselves long-term therapies, so the finding showed that LTPP equals other long treatments, not that length adds nothing. The honest summary is that long-term psychodynamic therapy has some controlled support for complex and chronic problems, from a small number of trials, with effects whose true size is still argued over. Two trials show what long treatment can and cannot do. In the Helsinki Psychotherapy Study (Paul Knekt and colleagues, 2008), 326 outpatients with depressive or anxiety disorders were randomly assigned to up to three years of long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, to short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy or to solution-focused therapy (Chapter 6): the short therapies were ahead in the first year, the groups were level in the second, and the long-term group was ahead at three years. In the Tavistock Adult Depression Study in London (Peter Fonagy and colleagues, 2015), 129 patients whose depression had failed at least two treatments received usual care with or without 18 months of weekly psychoanalytic psychotherapy; the difference in full remission was small at the end of treatment but widened over the next two years. Gains that keep growing after therapy has stopped, sometimes called the sleeper effect , are the most distinctive claim made for psychodynamic treatment; the rising follow-up figures of Leichsenring (2004) and Abbass (2006) above are examples. Defenders explain it by the theory: a patient whose inner capacities have changed goes on using them. Critics point to duller explanations: the patients who stay in follow-up are not a random sample, chronic conditions fluctuate, and further treatment muddies the comparison (in the ten-year Helsinki follow-up the long-term advantage had shrunk, possibly because more short-term patients had gone on to other therapy). The effect is plausible and repeatedly reported, but it rests on fewer and smaller studies than its fame suggests. Exam trap Leichsenring and Rabung's JAMA meta-analysis (2008) is about long-term therapy (at least a year or 50 sessions) for complex disorders; its famous figure is an effect size of 1.8 ("better off than 96 per cent"), and its weakness is the method that produced it, corrected to a moderate effect in the 2011 update. Abbass and colleagues' Cochrane review (2006, updated 2014) is about short-term therapy (under 40 hours) for common mental disorders; its famous figure is 0.97 for general symptoms, rising to 1.51 at follow-up. Do not swap the two, and do not treat a pre-post effect size as evidence that a therapy beats anything. Shedler's case for the defence The paper that carried these findings to a wide audience was Shedler's review "The efficacy of psychodynamic psychotherapy", published in 2010 in American Psychologist , the flagship journal of the American Psychological Association. Its abstract made three claims. First, effect sizes for psychodynamic therapy "are as large as those reported for other therapies that have been actively promoted as 'empirically supported' and 'evidence based'". Second, patients who receive psychodynamic therapy maintain their gains and appear to continue to improve after treatment ends. Third, non-psychodynamic therapies may be effective partly because their more skilled practitioners use techniques long central to psychodynamic practice. The common impression that psychodynamic approaches lack empirical support, he added, might reflect "selective dissemination of research findings", fed by a lingering distaste in the mental health professions for past psychoanalytic arrogance and authority. To make the first claim concrete, Shedler set the psychodynamic figures beside reference points from other treatments, and Figure 3.14 plots a selection of them. Psychotherapy in general, in Smith, Glass and Miller's 1980 meta-analysis, had an effect size of 0.85. CBT for depression, panic disorder and generalised anxiety disorder, in a 2006 meta-analysis by Haby and colleagues, had 0.68. Antidepressant medication, in Erick Turner and colleagues' 2008 analysis of all the trials submitted to the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA), published and unpublished, had 0.31. The replies came quickly, several of them in the same journal in 2011, among them one by Joye Anestis, Michael Anestis and Scott Lilienfeld. The critics' four main points are worth being able to state. Like was not compared with like. Pre-post effects, effects against waiting lists and one atypical calculation sat beside reference figures from other kinds of comparison, exactly the mixture that Figure 3.14 displays. The evidence base was small. Shedler himself conceded that some of his most striking findings rested on only two studies and that there are far more outcome studies of CBT. Many psychodynamic trials were small, used weak controls, mixed diagnoses and were run by researchers committed to the therapy (the allegiance effect of Section 8.6). The process evidence for the third claim, described below, was correlational. Shedler answered that his critics held psychodynamic research to a stricter standard than the treatments they favoured. The fair verdict sits between them: short-term psychodynamic therapy clearly beats no treatment or minimal treatment for common mental disorders, with effects in the same broad range as other psychotherapies, but the comparisons that made the paper famous were less secure than they looked. Exam trap Shedler's "The efficacy of psychodynamic psychotherapy" appeared in American Psychologist in 2010 . Its three claims: effect sizes as large as those of "empirically supported" therapies; gains maintained and growing after treatment; other therapies work partly through psychodynamic techniques. Its reference numbers: 0.85 for psychotherapy in general (Smith, Glass and Miller, 1980), 0.68 for CBT (Haby and colleagues, 2006), 0.31 for antidepressants (Turner and colleagues, 2008), 0.97 for STPP (Abbass and colleagues, 2006). Do not confuse this review with Smith and Glass's 1977 meta-analysis or Eysenck's 1952 review (Chapter 8), and do not confuse Shedler's review with the Shedler-Westen Assessment Procedure, a personality assessment instrument (Assessment book). Borderline personality disorder: MBT and TFP on trial The strongest single body of evidence for modern psychodynamic treatment concerns borderline personality disorder, the pattern of unstable relationships, identity and emotion, with impulsivity and frequent self-harm, that classical analysis had found so hard to help (the disorder itself belongs to the Psychiatric Disorders book). Two psychodynamic treatments built for it have been tested in randomised trials. Mentalisation-based treatment (MBT), Anthony Bateman and Peter Fonagy's therapy for strengthening the patient's capacity to understand behaviour in terms of mental states, is taught in Section 3.5; transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP), Kernberg's treatment, in Section 3.4. Here the only question is how well they work. MBT's trials are told as a Key study in Section 3.5: the small day-hospital trial (1999), its eight-year follow-up (2008) and the outpatient trial (2009) against structured clinical management, a well-organised, supportive, generic treatment. Read as evaluation, those trials have two weaknesses: they were run by the treatment's developers, and the comparison treatment in the first trial was weak. Independent replications have been more mixed; a Danish trial reported in 2013, for example, found intensive MBT better than a less intensive supportive group therapy on only one main outcome, global functioning. TFP's main trials you have already met. In Clarkin and colleagues' New York trial of 2007 (Key study, Section 3.4), TFP, dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) and supportive psychodynamic therapy all helped, with TFP changing the most domains and alone increasing reflective function; in Giesen-Bloo and colleagues' Dutch trial of 2006, schema therapy did better than TFP. A third trial adds an important piece. In 2010, in the British Journal of Psychiatry , a German and Austrian team led by Stephan Doering randomly assigned 104 women with borderline personality disorder to a year of TFP or to treatment by experienced community psychotherapists. Far fewer patients dropped out of TFP (about 39 per cent against 67 per cent), fewer attempted suicide, and TFP did better on borderline symptoms, psychosocial functioning, personality organisation and psychiatric admissions, although depression and anxiety improved equally in both groups. Three lessons follow, and they echo the Menninger project. Specialised psychodynamic treatments for borderline personality disorder work, and some benefits last for years. They are not clearly better than the other specialised treatments, DBT (Section 5.8) and schema therapy (Section 5.7); the 2020 Cochrane review of psychological therapies for the disorder found that disorder-specific psychotherapies reduce its severity compared with usual treatment, with DBT and MBT the most studied, but judged much of the evidence to be of low certainty. And well-structured generic or supportive care does surprisingly well, which suggests that what the successful treatments share (a clear structure, a coherent model, a consistent team and steady attention to the relationship) matters as much as what divides them. Exam trap MBT is Bateman and Fonagy's: the day-hospital trial (1999), the eight-year follow-up (2008: 13 per cent against 87 per cent still meeting criteria) and the outpatient trial against structured clinical management (2009), not against DBT. TFP is Kernberg's: Clarkin and colleagues (2007, against DBT and supportive therapy) and Doering and colleagues (2010, against community psychotherapists). In Giesen-Bloo's 2006 trial it was schema therapy (Jeffrey Young) that beat TFP. DBT is Marsha Linehan's and is a cognitive-behavioural therapy, not a psychodynamic one. Psychodynamic therapy versus CBT The comparison everyone wants is the head-to-head race with CBT, the most researched psychotherapy in the world (Section 5.11 surveys its evidence). Once you separate the disorders, the results form a clear pattern. For depression the two have repeatedly come out roughly level. In Amsterdam, Ellen Driessen and colleagues ( American Journal of Psychiatry , 2013) randomly assigned 341 outpatients with major depression to 16 sessions of CBT or of short-term psychodynamic supportive therapy, and found no significant differences on any outcome. The sobering detail is that only about 23 per cent of patients were in remission at the end of treatment, a reminder that sixteen sessions are not enough for many clinic patients, whatever the brand. In an American community mental health setting, Mary Beth Connolly Gibbons and colleagues ( JAMA Psychiatry , 2016) randomly assigned 237 outpatients and found dynamic psychotherapy no worse (statistically noninferior) than cognitive therapy when both were delivered by community clinicians. For social anxiety disorder, the largest trial of psychodynamic therapy ever run, led by Leichsenring at several German centres and published in 2013, randomly assigned 495 patients to manualised CBT (209), manualised psychodynamic therapy (207) or a waiting list (79). Both therapies beat the waiting list. At the end of treatment CBT was ahead on remission (36 per cent against 26 per cent, with 9 per cent on the waiting list) but not significantly on response (60 against 52 per cent). By the two-year follow-up the remission rates of the two therapies had converged at about 40 per cent. Notice who ran the trial: a team led by psychodynamic researchers that reported a CBT advantage plainly, the kind of result that builds trust in a research programme. For panic disorder, Barbara Milrod's panic-focused psychodynamic psychotherapy beat applied relaxation in a small New York trial (2007: 49 patients; response 73 per cent against 39 per cent), although in a larger two-site trial (2016, 201 patients) CBT gave the more consistent results across the two sites. The meta-analyses tell the same story at a larger scale. David Tolin ( Clinical Psychology Review , 2010) found CBT modestly superior to psychodynamic therapy (an effect size of about 0.28) for anxiety and depressive disorders, though not to interpersonal or supportive therapy, and a reanalysis by Baardseth and colleagues (2013) disputed even that advantage. The most careful test so far, by Christiane Steinert, Thomas Munder, Sven Rabung, Jürgen Hoyer and Leichsenring ( American Journal of Psychiatry , 2017), tested formal equivalence rather than merely the absence of a significant difference. Across 23 randomised trials with 2,751 patients, comparing psychodynamic therapy with established treatments (mostly CBT) for mood, anxiety, eating, personality and substance use disorders and PTSD, psychodynamic therapy was equivalent in efficacy at the end of treatment and at follow-up; to reduce allegiance bias the team deliberately included researchers from both camps. Where does CBT keep a clear lead? Mainly where exposure is the active ingredient and psychodynamic therapy has hardly been tested: obsessive-compulsive disorder, specific phobias and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), for which exposure-based treatments (Chapter 4), trauma-focused CBT and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) remain first-line because they have by far the most trials. Psychodynamic therapy is widely used with trauma survivors, including survivors of sexual assault, but it is not a first-line treatment for PTSD (Section 5.11 has the trap). In schizophrenia, the Boston Psychotherapy Study (John Gunderson and colleagues, 1984) found exploratory, insight-oriented psychotherapy no better overall than reality-adaptive supportive therapy, which had the edge in practical adaptation. And for a short-lived reaction to a stressor, such as an adjustment disorder or an acute crisis, crisis intervention and supportive therapy (Section 3.10 and Chapter 9) are the treatments of choice. The treatment of choice for an adjustment disorder is crisis intervention , not psychoanalytic psychotherapy, group therapy or CBT, because the problem is a time-limited reaction to a stressor. A depressed man whose marital discord is maintaining the depression benefits more from marital and couple therapy (Chapter 7) than from individual psychodynamic therapy, CBT or supportive therapy: match the treatment to the problem that keeps the disorder going. And for survivors of sexual assault the evidence-based core is trauma-focused CBT and EMDR; interpersonal psychotherapy, built for depression (Section 3.7), is the expected answer to "not commonly used". A practice question keys "psychodynamic psychotherapy, trauma-focused CBT and EMDR" as the most effective set: choose it, because it is the only option that contains both guideline treatments, but know that psychodynamic therapy itself is not a first-line treatment for PTSD. Remember too that pharmacotherapy is a treatment but not a psychotherapy. What survives: the distinctive features of psychodynamic process If brand names race to a dead heat, perhaps the useful question is not which therapy wins but what happens inside the sessions that help. In 2000 two American psychologists, Blagys and Mark Hilsenroth , searched the research literature for studies that had compared recordings and transcripts of actual sessions of manualised short-term psychodynamic-interpersonal therapy with sessions of manualised CBT, and asked which therapist activities reliably told the two apart. They found seven, published in Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice as "Distinctive features of short-term psychodynamic-interpersonal psychotherapy" (Table 3.30). Two years later, in Clinical Psychology Review ("Distinctive activities of cognitive-behavioral therapy"), they did the same for CBT and found six distinctive activities of its own: assigning homework and between-session activities, directing the session's activity, teaching skills for coping with symptoms, emphasising the patient's future experiences, giving information about the treatment, the disorder or the symptoms, and an intrapersonal, cognitive focus on thoughts and beliefs. These lists matter because they describe each therapy by what the therapist actually does rather than by its theory, which gives researchers something they can rate in a recording and relate to outcome. The American psychologist Enrico Jones built the Psychotherapy Process Q-set, 100 items that trained raters use to describe a recorded session. With Stacy Ablon (1998) he had expert psychodynamic and cognitive-behavioural therapists describe an ideal session of each kind, built prototypes from their ratings, and measured how closely real sessions from archived trials resembled each prototype, whatever therapy the therapists believed they were delivering. Adherence to the psychodynamic prototype predicted good outcome in both psychodynamic and cognitive therapy; adherence to the CBT prototype showed little relation to outcome in either. Louis Castonguay and colleagues (1996), studying 30 depressed clients in Beck's cognitive therapy (with or without medication), found that the working alliance and the patient's depth of emotional "experiencing" predicted improvement, while the therapist's focus on the impact of distorted thoughts on the depressive symptoms predicted poorer outcome, apparently because some therapists pushed the cognitive model rigidly when the alliance was strained. Do not over-read these findings, and do not let an interviewer catch you doing so. They are correlational: therapists who explore feelings and patterns may simply have patients who are easier to work with. Other studies, by Robert DeRubeis and his colleagues among others, have found that competent use of cognitive techniques predicts improvement in CBT. And the brand labels are leaky: when Ablon and Jones (2002) rated transcripts from the NIMH depression trial, the CBT and interpersonal therapy sessions overlapped so much that the premise of two distinct treatments seemed doubtful. The defensible conclusion is the cautious form of Shedler's third claim: skilled therapists of every school do some of what psychodynamic therapists do, and the processes psychodynamic theory describes are among the ingredients of good therapy in general. The working alliance itself, now the most researched common factor (Section 8.5), began as a psychoanalytic idea (Section 3.3). Psychodynamic ideas have also survived by being absorbed into other therapies, often without their label. Aaron Beck trained as a psychoanalyst before he built cognitive therapy (Chapter 5); schema therapy and cognitive analytic therapy (Section 5.7) reach back into childhood and work through the therapeutic relationship; and the case formulations of Chapter 2 routinely ask the psychodynamic questions of what the patient avoids, what keeps repeating and where it began. Exam trap Blagys and Hilsenroth (2000) listed seven distinctive activities of psychodynamic-interpersonal therapy; their 2002 review listed six for CBT. In an option list, assigning homework, setting the session agenda, teaching coping skills, giving information and focusing on the future are CBT; exploring avoidance, focusing on emotion, linking past and present, and exploring the therapy relationship, wishes and dreams are psychodynamic. The process-outcome findings that favour psychodynamic features are correlational, and other studies find that CBT techniques predict outcome too. Psychodynamic thinking in Indian training and practice Psychoanalysis came to India early, through Girindrasekhar Bose and the Indian Psychoanalytical Society he founded in Calcutta in 1922 (Section 3.2), but it never became the dominant clinical practice that it was for a time in the United States. Indian clinical psychology grew up largely in psychiatric hospitals and medical colleges, where the demand was for brief, practical treatments for very large numbers of patients, and its research base, as Section 5.11 and Chapter 9 describe, lies overwhelmingly in behavioural, cognitive and community-delivered interventions. Randomised trials of psychodynamic therapy in India are few. Yet psychodynamic thinking runs through Indian training. Clinical psychology syllabi teach psychodynamic theory and therapy alongside behavioural, cognitive, humanistic and systemic approaches, and trainees learn to write psychodynamic formulations, to recognise defences and transference, and to use supervision to examine their countertransference, even when the treatment they finally offer is eclectic. In everyday practice psychodynamic ideas usually appear in modified form: weekly or less frequent sessions, a shorter and more focused course, a more active and supportive therapist, and the family drawn into the work rather than kept outside it. Long-term, open-ended psychoanalytic psychotherapy is available mainly in private practice in the larger cities, to the minority who can afford it. Indian clinicians have also asked whether the theory itself travels. The psychoanalyst Sudhir Kakar (born 1938), in The Inner World: A Psycho-analytic Study of Childhood and Society in India (1978), argued that Indian childhood, with its long and intense closeness between mother and child and its embedding in the extended family, produces a self organised more around relationships and the family's expectations than around separateness. The American psychoanalyst Alan Roland, who worked with patients in India and Japan, called this a "familial self" ( In Search of Self in India and Japan , 1988), in contrast to the "individualised self" that Western therapy assumes and tries to strengthen. If separation-individuation (Mahler, Section 3.4) and autonomy are the unspoken goals of Western psychodynamic therapy, an Indian therapist may need to redefine success as a better-negotiated interdependence. In the same spirit Jaswant Singh Neki's guru-chela (teacher-disciple) paradigm of 1973 (Section 3.10) asks the therapist to be an authoritative, caring guide rather than the neutral, opaque listener of Section 3.2; the debate about the dependence it permits, and the related ideas of Surya and Jayaram, return in Section 8.11. Clinical link Meera, a 31-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, has had two episodes of moderate depression. In assessment a pattern stands out: she gives endlessly to her in-laws and colleagues, says nothing, and then feels crushed and worthless when her efforts go unnoticed, much as she once tried to win a distant, critical father's approval. What does the evidence let her clinician offer? For depression of this severity, a focused short-term psychodynamic therapy organised around that repeated relationship pattern (Luborsky's core conflictual relationship theme, Section 3.6), CBT and interpersonal psychotherapy (role disputes, Section 3.7) have broadly similar evidence, so Meera's own preference and the formulation can guide the choice. The evidence also says what not to promise: a cure through insight alone, or a guarantee that sixteen sessions will be enough. Her clinician rates her depression every few sessions and changes course, adding medication or another approach, if she is not improving. Weighing it up Put the pieces together and the verdict is more interesting than either side allows. As a scientific theory, classical psychoanalysis earned its critics: its clinical evidence was contaminated by suggestion, its founding case was not the cure it was claimed to be, and its institutions were slow to test their claims. As a family of treatments, psychodynamic therapy has done far better than that history predicted. What it has not shown is that its own theory of change, insight into unconscious conflict, is the reason it works. From the Menninger project onwards, support, the relationship and the patient's attachment to the therapist have done much of the work, and the dodo bird verdict of Section 8.3, that very different bona fide therapies tend to produce similar results, applies here as much as anywhere. Psychodynamic therapy's most lasting contributions may be the ones every therapist now uses: attention to emotion and avoidance, to repeated patterns and their history, and above all to the relationship in the room. Remember A thirty-second answer to "Does psychodynamic therapy work?": Yes, better than no treatment and, for depression and several anxiety disorders, about as well as CBT in the best trials (Steinert and colleagues, 2017); specialised forms such as MBT and TFP help in borderline personality disorder. The evidence base is smaller and weaker than CBT's, the claims for long-term therapy (Leichsenring and Rabung, 2008) are disputed, and exposure-based treatments remain first choice for PTSD, OCD and phobias. As for why it works, the Menninger project and the process studies suggest that support and the relationship matter as much as insight. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The case of Anna O., revisited Go back to the sickroom in Vienna, and to Bertha Pappenheim pushing away the glass of water she longed for. You can now name everything that happened on the evening she drank again. Her angry account of the companion's dog drinking from a glass was an abreaction, the reliving of a blocked memory with its full feeling, and the relief that followed was catharsis (Section 3.1). The trance in which she talked was hypnosis, and the procedure was Breuer's cathartic method. Freud's reasons for giving that method up are already visible in the story: such cures seemed to depend on the patient's attachment to her physician, and they went round the patient's resistance instead of through it. By replacing hypnosis with free association, and by learning from Dora that the patient's feelings for the analyst were the heart of the work rather than an interruption of it, Freud turned the talking cure into psychoanalysis. Out of that change grew almost every therapy in this chapter, from Klein's play technique and Kohut's selfobject transferences to Malan's triangles, Klerman and Weissman's interpersonal psychotherapy and Berne's ego states. Was she cured by talking? The question the chapter opened with has a plain answer: no. Henri Ellenberger's search of the Bellevue sanatorium records (1972) showed that she was admitted at Kreuzlingen in July 1882, within weeks of the end of Breuer's treatment, still ill and dependent on the morphine she had been given for facial pain. During the next decade she was institutionalised several times with severe returns of her symptoms before a slow recovery began. She then became a pioneering social worker and a campaigner against the sexual exploitation of women and the traffic in women forced into prostitution; she founded a league of Jewish women in 1904 and a home for unmarried mothers in 1907, and after her death in 1936 West Germany honoured her with a commemorative postage stamp. That is the instructive fact. The first case ever offered as evidence for the talking cure left out its ending, and no one can now say how much of a recovery that took years owed anything to the talking. Section 3.11 drew the lesson the field took most of a century to learn: case histories written by the treating clinician cannot show that a therapy works, but controlled comparisons can. They show that psychodynamic therapy does help, about as much as other therapies for depression and several anxiety disorders, while the Menninger project and the process studies suggest that support and the relationship carry as much of the change as insight does. Bertha Pappenheim's real story fits that verdict better than Breuer's version of it ever did. Chapter summary 3.1 From Hypnosis to the Talking Cure. Psychodynamic therapies assume that symptoms come from mental forces in conflict, often outside awareness. Their roots lie in Franz Anton Mesmer's animal magnetism, whose effects a French royal commission (1784) traced to belief, and in James Braid's "hypnotism" (1843). Charcot at the Salpêtrière held that only hysterics could be deeply hypnotised; Bernheim's Nancy school answered that hypnosis is normal suggestibility. Josef Breuer's treatment of Anna O. (Bertha Pappenheim) produced the "talking cure", her own phrase, and the cathartic method of Studies on Hysteria (1895): abreaction relives a repressed memory with its emotion, and catharsis is the release that follows. Pierre Janet explained hysteria by dissociation, a weakness of integration; Freud by repression, an active, motivated exclusion from awareness, which is why repression is the psychodynamic answer for dissociative symptoms. Freud then abandoned hypnosis and the pressure technique for free association. 3.2 Classical Psychoanalysis as a Treatment. Freud's aims were to make the unconscious conscious ("Where id was, there ego shall be") and to turn hysterical misery into common unhappiness, through insight and structural change. The patient lies on a couch with the analyst out of sight, in modern classical analysis four or five times a week, and every analyst first undergoes a training analysis. The fundamental rule asks the patient to say whatever comes to mind (free association), while the analyst keeps evenly suspended attention, neutrality and abstinence. Dreams are the "royal road" to the unconscious: the dream-work turns latent into manifest content. Resistance is analysed rather than overpowered, and Freud classified five kinds (1926). Greenson's sequence runs confrontation, clarification, interpretation; Strachey's mutative interpretations address the live transference; working through repeats insight until change lasts. Libido, cathexis, fixation, sublimation and the defence mechanisms complete the analyst's vocabulary. 3.3 Transference, Countertransference and the Alliance. Transference is the patient's unconscious redirection onto the therapist of feelings and expectations that belonged to figures from the past. Freud learned its importance when Dora broke off treatment (published 1905), and came to see it as both the strongest resistance and the only place where the old conflict can be changed. It may be positive, negative or erotic, and in full analysis the illness is re-staged as a transference neurosis. Countertransference, named by Freud in 1910, is the therapist's emotional reaction arising from his own unresolved conflicts; Winnicott (1949) and Heimann (1950) turned it into an instrument, which Racker refined, and negative countertransference shows as irritation, boredom or punitive remarks. Zetzel, Greenson and Bordin (goals, tasks, bond; 1979) described the working alliance, and Greenson the real relationship. Boundary crossings differ from violations, and managing transference is the hallmark of psychodynamic models. 3.4 Ego Psychology and Object Relations. Freud's structural model of 1923 opened two roads. Anna Freud's The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936) made the defences the analyst's business and added identification with the aggressor; Heinz Hartmann, the father of ego psychology, described the conflict-free ego sphere (1939), and the assessment of ego strength came to guide the choice of treatment. Erik Erikson coined the identity crisis. Object relations are internalised representations of self and others and the relationships between them; Fairbairn held that libido is object-seeking. Melanie Klein's play technique led to the paranoid-schizoid position, with splitting and projective identification, and the depressive position, with guilt and reparation; splitting is her answer for paranoia. Winnicott described the good-enough mother, the holding environment, the transitional object and the false self. Mahler traced separation-individuation and linked schizophrenia to the autistic phase, and Kernberg described borderline personality organisation and transference-focused psychotherapy. 3.5 Self Psychology, Relational Analysis, Attachment and Mentalisation. Heinz Kohut's self psychology treats narcissistic disorders as a deficit: the self needs selfobjects for mirroring, idealisation and twinship, and when these fail it fragments, empties and rages. A client who feels "empty" and "no one" reflects a failure of parental mirroring and idealising. In the mirror, idealising and twinship transferences the therapist serves as the missing selfobject, and empathy (vicarious introspection), optimal frustration and transmuting internalisation build structure. Greenberg and Mitchell's relational psychoanalysis and Stolorow's intersubjectivity make therapy a two-person psychology. John Bowlby's attachment theory gave the therapist five tasks, beginning with a secure base, and Mary Main's Adult Attachment Interview scores the coherence of a narrative. Peter Fonagy's reflective function grew into mentalisation, and Bateman and Fonagy's mentalisation-based treatment for borderline personality disorder uses a not-knowing stance, differing from Kernberg's TFP as deficit differs from conflict. 3.6 Brief Psychodynamic Psychotherapies. Ferenczi's active technique, Rank's fixed end date and Alexander and French's corrective emotional experience (1946) prepared the way for brief dynamic work, which shares selection, a focus, a time limit, an active therapist, early transference work and attention to ending. David Malan's Tavistock focal therapy rests on the triangle of conflict (defence, anxiety, hidden feeling) and the triangle of person (other, therapist, past). Peter Sifneos's short-term anxiety-provoking psychotherapy has the strictest selection criteria and an Oedipal focus, and he coined alexithymia. Habib Davanloo's ISTDP uses pressure, challenge and the head-on collision with resistance. James Mann's time-limited psychotherapy lasts exactly twelve sessions around a central issue. Lester Luborsky's supportive-expressive therapy works on the core conflictual relationship theme (wish, response of other, response of self), and Strupp and Binder's time-limited dynamic psychotherapy on the four-part cyclical maladaptive pattern. 3.7 Interpersonal Psychotherapy. Gerald Klerman and Myrna Weissman built interpersonal psychotherapy (manual 1984) to be tested like a drug: a time-limited, manualised treatment, originally for major depression, that links symptoms to a current interpersonal problem. Its roots are Adolf Meyer, Harry Stack Sullivan, John Bowlby and research on life events. In the initial phase of a 12 to 16 session course the therapist diagnoses the depression, grants Talcott Parsons's sick role and takes an interpersonal inventory. The four problem areas are grief, interpersonal role disputes (at renegotiation, impasse or dissolution), role transitions and interpersonal deficits. Communication analysis is the signature technique, and the transference is not interpreted. The evidence includes the NIMH collaborative trial (1989), Cuijpers's meta-analyses, which put IPT roughly level with other psychotherapies, and Bolton's group IPT trial in Uganda (2003); adaptations include IPT-A, maintenance IPT and Ellen Frank's interpersonal and social rhythm therapy for bipolar disorder. 3.8 The Early Dissenters as Therapists. Carl Gustav Jung's analytical psychology, after his break with Freud in 1913, aims at individuation through the personal and collective unconscious, complexes and archetypes (persona, shadow, anima, animus, Self). Jung sat face to face, described four stages (confession, elucidation, education, transformation) and used the word association test, amplification and active imagination. Alfred Adler's individual psychology rests on organ inferiority, the inferiority complex, striving for superiority, fictional finalism, the style of life and social interest. Dreikurs's four phases run from relationship to reorientation, with lifestyle assessment (family constellation, birth order, early recollections), encouragement, acting as if, spitting in the client's soup and Mosak's push-button technique; analysing the transference is not Adlerian. Karen Horney described basic anxiety, ten neurotic needs, three neurotic trends, the tyranny of the should and self-analysis, and Harry Stack Sullivan the participant observer, selective inattention and parataxic distortion. 3.9 Transactional Analysis. Eric Berne's transactional analysis ( Games People Play , 1964) grew from Paul Federn's ego states. Structural analysis divides the personality into Parent (copied from parent figures), Adult (present reality) and Child (replayed from childhood), with Controlling and Nurturing Parent, Free and Adapted Child, the Little Professor and Dusay's egogram; contamination and exclusion disturb the boundaries. Transactions are complementary, crossed or ulterior, and three rules of communication govern them. A stroke is a unit of recognition; Steiner described the stroke economy, and time is structured from withdrawal to intimacy. Games are repeated ulterior transactions with a payoff, played out on Karpman's drama triangle of Persecutor, Rescuer and Victim. Scripts pass down through counterinjunctions, injunctions (the Gouldings' twelve) and Kahler's drivers. Berne described four life positions, which Thomas Harris popularised in I'm OK, You're OK (1967); therapy uses contracts, permission and redecision. 3.10 Supportive Psychotherapy, Hypnotherapy and Narcoanalysis. Supportive psychotherapy uses direct measures to relieve symptoms and to maintain, restore or improve self-esteem, ego function and adaptive skills (Pinsker and colleagues); Wolberg sorted therapies into supportive, re-educative and reconstructive. It suits crises, weak ego strength, chronic illness and busy clinics, and it is the first response in crisis management. Its techniques include ventilation, reassurance, guidance, suggestion, persuasion, environmental manipulation and externalisation of interests, and Gabbard places every intervention on an expressive-supportive continuum; Neki's guru-chela paradigm fits it to Indian expectations. Hypnosis is focused attention with an enhanced response to suggestion. It helps surgical pain and irritable bowel syndrome, Hilgard explained it by neodissociation, and it raises confidence in recall but not accuracy. Narcoanalysis, the amytal interview, yields no truth, and Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) barred its involuntary use in India. 3.11 Does Psychodynamic Therapy Work? Karl Popper called psychoanalysis unfalsifiable; Adolf Grünbaum (1984) replied that it is testable but that its clinical data are contaminated by suggestion and Freud's tally argument fails. Eysenck's 1952 review put psychoanalysis below no formal therapy, and Ellenberger (1972) showed that Anna O. had not been cured. Wallerstein's Menninger project found that supportive elements did much of the work, often through a transference cure. Meta-analyses by Leichsenring (2004) and Abbass (Cochrane, 2006) show short-term psychodynamic therapy beating control conditions; Leichsenring and Rabung's effect size of 1.8 for long-term therapy (2008) shrank to a moderate one in 2011, and Shedler (2010) defended the field. MBT and TFP help in borderline personality disorder, psychodynamic therapy roughly equals CBT for depression, and exposure-based treatments still lead for PTSD, OCD and phobias. argument, transference cure, between-group effect size, within-group effect size, short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, sleeper effect From the past papers In view of most psychodynamic theorists, dissociative symptoms are produced by which of the following? (RML 2022) (a) Repression (b) Ego state (c) Conflict (d) Gender identity issue Answer: (a) Repression. Freud held that unbearable ideas are actively pushed out of awareness and kept out, and most psychodynamic writers followed him rather than Janet, for whom dissociation was a weakness of integration. "Ego states" is Federn's and Berne's idea, not a cause of dissociation; conflict is what every defence responds to, while repression is the specific mechanism; gender identity has nothing to do with it. Psychodynamic therapists believe that disorder stems from: (Amity 2023) (a) Disturbed thought patterns (b) Emotional trauma experienced in childhood (c) A failure to live up to one's full potential (d) Inappropriate learning patterns Answer: (b) Emotional trauma experienced in childhood. The psychodynamic answer always points to unresolved unconscious conflict and emotional experience from childhood. Disturbed thinking is the cognitive answer, unfulfilled potential the humanistic one and faulty learning the behavioural one. In psychodynamic therapy, analysis of resistance is where: (RML 2021) (a) The client is asked to talk about anything that comes to mind (b) The client transfers their feelings towards significant others onto the therapist (c) The client obstructs the analysis and the therapist explores reasons for this (d) The therapist interprets the dreams of the client Answer: (c). Freud's crucial shift was to treat the patient's obstruction of the work as material to be understood, not overpowered. Option (a) is free association, (b) is transference and (d) is dream analysis: the four options are the four classic techniques, and only (c) is resistance. In psychoanalytic theory, what term describes the mental representation of psychic energy being invested or attached to a particular object, person, or idea? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Libido (b) Cathexis (c) Fixation (d) Sublimation Answer: (b) Cathexis. Cathexis (Strachey's word for Freud's Besetzung ) is where the energy is placed. Libido is the energy itself, fixation is energy stuck at an earlier psychosexual stage, and sublimation is energy redirected to a socially valued aim. In the psychodynamic framework, which concept refers to the defense mechanism where an individual unconsciously attributes their own unacceptable thoughts or feelings to someone else, thereby avoiding direct confrontation with those feelings? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Rationalization (b) Projection (c) Displacement (d) Sublimation Answer: (b) Projection. Projection places one's own unacceptable feeling in someone else, as when a hostile patient is sure the therapist dislikes him. Displacement keeps the feeling as one's own but changes its target, rationalisation offers a respectable excuse, and sublimation redirects a drive into a valued activity. 'Counter transference' in psychotherapy refers to (JEMAS 2025) (a) therapists' emotional reactions to the client based on the therapists' own unresolved conflict (b) client's projection onto the therapist (c) client's resistance to therapy (d) behavioral reinforcement techniques Answer: (a). Freud named countertransference in 1910 as the analyst's unconscious reactions to the patient, arising from the analyst's own unresolved conflicts; Heimann (1950) later made it a tool. The client's projection onto the therapist is transference, obstruction of the work is resistance, and reinforcement belongs to behaviour therapy. The process in which therapist expressed his negative feelings towards patients is termed as: (IHBAS 2024) (a) Negative Transference (b) Counter transference (c) Positive transference (d) Negative counter transference Answer: (d) Negative countertransference. Direction decides the term: therapist to patient is countertransference, and irritation, boredom, dislike or punitive remarks make it negative. Negative transference is the patient's hostility towards the therapist, positive transference the patient's affection, and plain "countertransference" is true but less exact than the keyed answer. A working relationship has all of the following characteristics EXCEPT: (RML 2020) (a) Observable ability of the worker and the client to work together (b) A committed belief in the helping relationship (c) A psychodynamic theory base (d) A contract to work together realistically and collaboratively Answer: (c) A psychodynamic theory base. The working alliance began as a psychoanalytic idea (Zetzel, Greenson), but Bordin (1979) made it pantheoretical: agreement on goals and tasks plus an emotional bond. A working relationship is defined by its features, the other three options, not by any theory. Managing transference and countertransference is critical in which of the following theory-based models of therapy? (RML 2020) (a) behaviour modification (b) cognitive-behavioural therapy (c) psychodynamic models of therapy (d) solution focused models of therapy Answer: (c) Psychodynamic models of therapy. Every therapist has a relationship with the client, but only psychodynamic models make the analysis of transference and countertransference the central route to change. Behaviour modification works on contingencies, CBT on thoughts and behaviour, and solution-focused therapy on exceptions and future goals. Who gave the important concept of 'identity crisis' in adolescents? (RML 2024) (a) Bowlby (b) Melanie Klein (c) Eric Erikson (d) Eric Berne Answer: (c) Erik Erikson. Erikson, an ego psychologist and student of Anna Freud, coined the identity crisis for the adolescent struggle of identity versus role confusion ( Childhood and Society , 1950). Bowlby is attachment, Klein the two positions, and Berne transactional analysis; Berne is a tempting distractor only because Erikson was one of his analysts. The concept of "object relations" in psychoanalytic theory refers to: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) The relationship between the id, ego, and superego (b) The internalized mental representations of self and others and the relationship between them (c) The use of defense mechanisms to protect the ego from anxiety (d) The stage of psychosexual development focused on the genitals Answer: (b). The "object" is almost always a person, and object relations are the inner images of self and others, built from early experience, that shape later relationships. Option (a) is Freud's structural model, (c) is the defences of ego psychology, and (d) is the genital stage. In paranoia, the ego's defense mechanism as given by Melaine Klein is seen as: (RML 2024) (a) Reaction formation (b) Splitting (c) Suppression (d) Projection Answer: (b) Splitting. For Melanie Klein paranoia revives the paranoid-schizoid position, whose defence is splitting the world into wholly good and wholly bad. Projection is the tempting wrong answer because it is Freud's classical account of paranoia (the Schreber case, 1911); reaction formation and suppression are not Kleinian answers. Schizophrenia corresponds to the autistic phase of development and the person fails to develop an adequate and stable symbiosis, was the developmental theory of schizophrenia given by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Ping-Nie Pao (b) Sylvano Arieti (c) Margaret Mahler (d) Edith Jacobson Answer: (c) Margaret Mahler. The "autistic" and "symbiotic" phases are Mahler's forerunners of separation-individuation, and her theory of psychosis grew from them. Silvano Arieti described palaeologic thinking, Pao the "organismic panic" and Jacobson psychosis as a fusion of self and object representations. A client tells you that they are "no one" and feels "empty inside." They report chronic fears of abandonment and have a history of intense, unstable relationships. According to psychoanalytic object relations theory, this pathology of the self is most likely a result of: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Fixation at the oral stage of psychosexual development (b) A failure in parental mirroring and idealizing, leading to a fragmented self (c) Unresolved Oedipal complex and castration anxiety (d) Harsh superego demands leading to constant guilt Answer: (b). Emptiness, a fragmented self and failed mirroring and idealising are Kohut's self psychology, which many textbooks group loosely with object relations. Oral fixation is classical drive theory, the Oedipal option is the classical account of neurosis, and harsh superego guilt is Freud's "Guilty Man", exactly what Kohut said these patients were not. Who developed the technique of Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT)? (RML 2022) (a) L. Benjamin (b) Peter Fonagy and A. Bateman (c) Otto F. Kernberg (d) G.L. Klerman and M. M. Weissman Answer: (d) Klerman and Weissman. Gerald Klerman and Myrna Weissman built IPT in the 1970s and published its manual in 1984. Lorna Smith Benjamin created the Structural Analysis of Social Behavior and interpersonal reconstructive therapy, Fonagy and Bateman mentalisation-based treatment, and Kernberg transference-focused psychotherapy. Interpersonal Therapy (IPT) does NOT typically include which of the following techniques or focus areas? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Role playing and role reversal techniques (b) Grief and bereavement work (c) Role conflict resolution (d) Role transition support Answer: (a). Grief, role disputes (also called role conflicts) and role transitions are three of IPT's four problem areas, and role reversal belongs to Moreno's psychodrama. Accept the key, but know that IPT does use role playing as a behaviour change technique to rehearse a difficult conversation; what it never uses is free association, dream analysis or transference interpretation. A male adult with Depressive Disorder and marital discord would benefit more from: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Psychodynamic psychotherapy (b) Cognitive behavior therapy (c) Marital & couple therapy (d) Supportive therapy Answer: (c) Marital and couple therapy. Match the intervention to what keeps the problem going: when the marriage is maintaining the depression and both partners will attend, couple therapy is the better choice. Individual psychodynamic, cognitive-behavioural or supportive therapy leaves the maintaining factor untouched; IPT with a role-dispute focus is the alternative when only the patient attends. The concept of the "collective unconscious" was given by: (RML 2024) (a) Sigmund Freud (b) Alfred Adler (c) Carl Jung (d) Karen Horney Answer: (c) Carl Jung. Jung's collective unconscious is an inherited layer shared by all humans and made up of archetypes. Freud's unconscious is personal and repressed, Adler's psychology centres on inferiority and social interest, and Horney's on basic anxiety and neurotic needs. 'Animus is the unconscious, masculine side of a woman's female persona' was given by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Alfred Adler (b) Anna Freud (c) Carl Jung (d) Victor Emil Frankl Answer: (c) Carl Jung. The animus is Jung's archetype of the unconscious masculine side of a woman, and the anima the unconscious feminine side of a man. Anna Freud is known for the defences, Viktor Frankl for logotherapy and the will to meaning, and Adler for individual psychology. The concept of inferiority complex and superiority drive was given by: (RML 2024) (a) Carl Jung (b) Victor Frankl (c) Alfred Adler (d) Erik Erikson Answer: (c) Alfred Adler. For Adler normal inferiority feelings drive the lifelong striving for superiority, and overwhelming ones harden into an inferiority complex, sometimes covered by a superiority complex. Jung gave the collective unconscious, Frankl paradoxical intention in logotherapy and Erikson the psychosocial stages. The concept of 'Organ Inferiority' was given by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Harry Stack Sullivan (b) M. Klein (c) Anna Freud (d) Alfred Adler Answer: (d) Alfred Adler. In Study of Organ Inferiority (1907) Adler argued that a constitutionally weak organ produces inferiority feelings that the person strives to make up for, sometimes overcompensating. Sullivan is interpersonal psychiatry, Klein the paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions, and Anna Freud the defences. Which of the following technique or techniques would not typically be included within the repertoire of an Adlerian counsellor? (RML 2022) (a) Acting "as if" (b) Push button (c) Encouragement (d) Analysis of transference Answer: (d) Analysis of transference. Acting "as if" (after Vaihinger), Mosak's push-button technique and encouragement, which Adlerians regard as their most important ingredient, are all Adlerian. Adlerians comment on the relationship but do not foster a transference neurosis or analyse the transference as a repetition of childhood. In Transactional Analysis, which "ego state" is characterized by behaviors, thoughts, and feelings copied from parents or parental figures? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Adult (b) Child (c) Parent (d) Persona Answer: (c) Parent. In Berne's structural analysis the Parent is a recording of real parent figures, the Adult deals with present reality and the Child replays the person's own childhood. "Persona" is Jung's archetype of the social mask, not a TA ego state. The concepts of injunctions, counterinjunctions, and games are fundamental components of which psychological theory? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Gestalt therapy (b) Transactional Analysis (c) Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (d) Person-Centered therapy Answer: (b) Transactional analysis. Counterinjunctions and injunctions are the parental messages of Steiner's script matrix (the Gouldings listed twelve injunctions), and games are Berne's. Gestalt speaks of unfinished business and the empty chair, REBT of irrational beliefs and "musts", person-centred therapy of conditions of worth; the Gouldings borrowed Gestalt techniques, but the injunction is TA's. Which therapy is mostly needed in 'Crisis Management'? (IHBAS 2020) (a) Cognitive behavior therapy (b) Acceptance & commitment therapy (c) Expressive therapy (d) Supportive therapy Answer: (d) Supportive therapy. In a crisis ventilation, realistic reassurance, guidance and environmental manipulation come first, to restore the person's equilibrium. Expressive therapy, whether insight-oriented or arts-based, is not the first response to an acute crisis, and CBT and acceptance and commitment therapy come later if they are needed. Weightage. 90 of the 422 questions mapped in this book (21.3%) test this chapter, 52 of them from real past papers. 6 of its 11 sections are High yield. In the early 1920s, in a playroom of the Heckscher Foundation for Children in New York City, a little boy called Peter sat in a high chair eating food he liked. Peter was two years and ten months old, and terrified of rabbits. He was also afraid of white rats (at the first sight of one he had screamed and fallen flat on his back in a paroxysm of fear), and the fear had spread to a fur coat, a fur rug, feathers and cotton wool, but the rabbit frightened him most of all. On the far side of the room, inside a wire cage, sat a rabbit. The young psychologist watching him was Mary Cover Jones , a graduate student who had heard John Broadus Watson lecture about Little Albert, the infant in whom Watson and Rosalie Rayner had deliberately created a fear of a white rat in 1920. Jones asked the obvious next question. If a fear can be learned, can it be unlearned? Her first approach was social. She let Peter play with three other children who happily handled the rabbit, and his fear began to fade. Then Peter caught scarlet fever and spent two months in hospital; on his way home a large dog jumped at him, and his fears came flooding back. So Jones tried something more precise. Each day, while Peter was eating, the caged rabbit was brought a little closer: never so close that Peter stopped eating, always just close enough that he noticed it. Over the following weeks the cage crept from the far wall to the edge of the table. Then the rabbit was let out. By the end of the treatment Peter let it nibble his fingers, and his fear of the other furry objects had also faded. Jones published the case in 1924. For almost thirty years hardly anyone took any notice. Psychoanalysis ruled the clinic, and a child eating crackers next to a rabbit did not look like psychotherapy. Yet everything in this chapter is already present in that playroom: a fear treated as learned behaviour rather than as a sign of hidden conflict; a response incompatible with fear (eating) paired with the feared object; a graded approach, one small step at a time; and other children serving as models. Keep Peter in mind. When we return to him at the end of the chapter you will be able to name every technique Jones used, and you will see why the man who later turned her method into a therapy called her the mother of behaviour therapy. 4.1 Where Behaviour Therapy Came From and What It Assumes Medium yield · 2 Qs behaviour therapy is the application of experimentally established principles of learning (classical conditioning, operant conditioning and observational learning) to the assessment and treatment of psychological problems. Notice the two halves of that definition. The techniques come from the learning laboratory, and the therapy itself is run like an experiment: define the problem behaviour, measure it, change something, and measure it again. Before we look at the techniques, you need to know how this way of thinking reached the clinic, because the history explains both its strengths and its blind spots. (The learning principles themselves, Pavlov's dogs, Thorndike's cats and Skinner's box, are taught in the General Psychology book; here we take them as known and ask what clinicians did with them.) Learning theory in search of a clinic The idea that disorders are learned is older than behaviour therapy. In 1920 Watson and Rayner showed that a fear could be conditioned in an infant, and in 1924 Jones showed that one could be removed. In 1938 Orval Hobart Mowrer and his wife Willie Mae Mowrer built a bed-wetting alarm on conditioning principles (Section 4.4), and in 1932 Knight Dunlap described how a bad habit might be broken by practising it deliberately (Section 4.9). In 1950 John Dollard and Neal Miller even translated the whole of psychoanalysis into the language of learning theory in Personality and Psychotherapy . But none of this became a movement. Through the 1940s the clinic belonged to psychoanalysis, the learning laboratory belonged to experimental psychologists, and the two hardly spoke. The spur: Eysenck's 1952 challenge What changed? One provocative paper did a great deal. In 1952 Hans Jürgen Eysenck (1916 to 1997), a German-born psychologist working at the Maudsley Hospital in London, published "The effects of psychotherapy: an evaluation." Eysenck compared published improvement rates for neurotic patients given psychoanalysis or eclectic psychotherapy with rates for similar patients who received only custodial care or ordinary medical attention. Roughly two-thirds of neurotic patients, he concluded, improved within about two years whether or not they had psychotherapy; this improvement without treatment he called spontaneous remission . If talk therapy did no better than the passage of time, what was it for? The paper was methodologically weak (the groups were not comparable, and "improvement" meant different things in different studies), and later meta-analyses overturned its conclusion. The details of that debate belong to Chapter 8. What matters here is its effect. Eysenck had demanded evidence, and he had an alternative ready: a therapy derived from learning theory, aimed at the symptom, and testable. In 1959 he published "Learning theory and behaviour therapy," and in 1960 an edited book, Behaviour Therapy and the Neuroses . His most quoted line states the new creed bluntly: there is no neurosis underlying the symptom, but merely the symptom itself; get rid of the symptom and you have eliminated the neurosis. Three roots: Johannesburg, London and the United States Behaviour therapy had not one birthplace but three, which grew up almost independently in the 1950s and merged in the 1960s (Figure 4.1 and Table 4.1). South Africa. In Johannesburg, the psychiatrist Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997) grew dissatisfied with psychoanalysis while serving as an army doctor in the Second World War. His experiments on fear in cats (Section 4.2) led to the principle of reciprocal inhibition and to the technique of systematic desensitisation, published in his landmark book Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958). Around him gathered younger South Africans, notably Arnold Allan Lazarus (1932 to 2013) and Stanley Rachman . Lazarus used the term "behaviour therapy" in a 1958 article in the South African Medical Journal , one of its first appearances in print. In 1960 Wolpe and Rachman published a scathing learning-theory critique of Freud's case of Little Hans, arguing that the boy's fear of horses was better explained by conditioning (he had seen a horse fall in the street) than by castration anxiety. Wolpe later moved to the United States, where he worked at Temple University in Philadelphia. London. At the Institute of Psychiatry and the Maudsley Hospital, Eysenck supplied the theory and the polemics, while Monte Bernard Shapiro , head of clinical psychology training, supplied the method. Shapiro insisted that each patient be treated as a single-case experiment: measure the problem, form a hypothesis about what maintains it, intervene, and measure again. Rachman joined the Maudsley group, and in 1963 Eysenck founded the journal Behaviour Research and Therapy , the first journal devoted to the field. The United States. Here the root was operant. Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990) had shown that behaviour is shaped by its consequences. In 1953 Skinner, Ogden Lindsley and Harry C. Solomon , studying the operant behaviour of psychotic patients at Metropolitan State Hospital in Waltham, Massachusetts, used the phrase "behavior therapy" in a research report, the earliest known use. Through the late 1950s and 1960s Skinner's students carried operant methods onto hospital wards, into schools and into homes for children with intellectual disability. This American strand usually called itself behaviour modification , and later applied behaviour analysis (ABA): the use of operant principles, with careful measurement, to change socially important behaviour. The Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis began in 1968, the same year in which Donald Baer , Montrose Wolf and Todd Risley defined the field's seven dimensions (applied, behavioural, analytic, technological, conceptually systematic, effective and showing generality). The Association for Advancement of Behavior Therapy, today the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies, was founded in 1966.
