In Section 4.2 it was the response that Wolpe set against anxiety at every rung of the hierarchy, and in Section 4.3 the dismantling studies showed that exposure works perfectly well without it. You might conclude that relaxation is a pleasant extra that behaviour therapy could do without. It is not. For a large group of problems the trouble is not a fear of one particular thing but a body that is too often, and for too long, too aroused: the tension headache that builds through a working day, the jaw clenched over a pile of answer scripts, the shoulders that creep up towards the ears while a person worries, the hands that turn white and numb in an air-conditioned office. For these the goal is not to face a feared stimulus but to learn a skill, the skill of switching arousal off at will. This section describes the main ways of teaching that skill, from Jacobson's progressive relaxation to Öst's applied relaxation, and then biofeedback, which uses instruments to make the body's hidden signals visible so that they can be brought under control. Section 9.4 describes how these methods are used in health settings; here the emphasis is on where each method came from, how it is taught and how well it works. Progressive muscle relaxation: Jacobson's method and its abbreviations Edmund Jacobson (1888 to 1983) was a Chicago physician and physiologist who began studying muscular tension as a graduate student at Harvard in the first decade of the twentieth century. One of his early observations was that people who were tense startled much more violently at a sudden noise than people who were relaxed. Over the next twenty years, first at Harvard and then in Chicago, he built that observation into a theory and a treatment. Anxiety, he argued, is not only a state of mind; it is also a pattern of contraction in the skeletal muscles, and the two are so tightly bound that a person whose muscles are completely relaxed cannot at the same time feel anxious. His premise is often paraphrased as "an anxious mind cannot exist in a relaxed body." He set out the method in Progressive Relaxation (1929; enlarged second edition 1938) and for general readers in You Must Relax (1934). progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) is a technique in which a person learns to relax deeply by tensing and then releasing one muscle group after another, attending closely to the contrast between the sensations of tension and of letting go. The word "progressive" has three meanings, all of which Jacobson intended: the training progresses from one muscle group to the next, the relaxation itself progresses to deeper and deeper levels, and the skill progresses from the couch to everyday life. Jacobson's own method was slow and exacting. The patient lay on a couch and, for one muscle group at a time, produced a slight contraction (bending the hand back at the wrist, for example) in order to learn to recognise the faint sensation of tension, which Jacobson called the control sensation. Then the patient simply stopped contracting. Jacobson insisted that relaxation is not something one does but the absence of doing: trying hard to relax is itself a form of tension. Each group might take several hour-long sessions, and a full course ran to dozens of sessions over months. He also taught differential relaxation , keeping tense only the muscles a task needs (the fingers that write, the eyes that read) and relaxing all the rest, so that a person could stay relaxed while driving, typing or talking. In the 1930s Jacobson recorded the tiny electrical potentials of muscles with sensitive instruments and showed that merely imagining lifting the right arm produced measurable activity in the muscles of that arm. That work makes him one of the ancestors of the electromyographic biofeedback described later in this section. No busy clinic could spend fifty sessions on relaxation, and the method survived because it was cut down. Wolpe compressed it into about six sessions for systematic desensitisation (Section 4.2). In 1973 Douglas A. Bernstein and Thomas D. Borkovec published Progressive Relaxation Training: A Manual for the Helping Professions , and their abbreviated version is the one most clinicians now teach. Unlike Jacobson, they used a strong, deliberate tension, because a beginner notices the contrast more easily when the tension is obvious. The client focuses on one muscle group, tenses it on the therapist's signal for about 5 to 7 seconds, releases it all at once on the cue word "relax," and attends to the spreading feeling of relaxation for 30 to 40 seconds; each group is usually done twice. Training begins with 16 muscle groups (hands and forearms, upper arms, forehead, cheeks and nose, jaw, neck, chest and shoulders, abdomen, thighs, calves and feet, right and left separately). As skill grows the groups are combined, first into 7 and then into 4. Then the tensing is dropped altogether: in relaxation by recall the client simply remembers the feeling of release in each group, then recall is combined with slow counting from one to ten, and finally counting alone is enough to produce relaxation. Clients practise for 15 to 20 minutes once or twice a day, and the practice matters: people who practise at home improve more than those who do not. Consider Farida, a 38-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru who has had a tension-type headache most afternoons for two years. The pain starts as a band across her forehead and tightens round to the back of her neck. Her physician has found no medical cause. In the first session of PMR she discovers something that surprises her: when she is asked to release her jaw, it drops a full centimetre, because she had been clenching it without knowing. Over three weeks she works through the 16 groups, then the 7 and the 4; by the eighth week she can relax in about two minutes by counting slowly to ten, and she has learned to catch the tight jaw and raised shoulders while correcting notebooks, and to let them go. Her headache diary shows the afternoon headaches falling from five days a week to one. Notice that the decisive step was not the deep relaxation lying down but the transfer of the skill to the classroom, a point Öst would later make the centre of his method. Progressive relaxation has good evidence for tension-type headache, for insomnia (Section 4.9) and, as part of applied relaxation, for generalised anxiety; it lowers blood pressure modestly and helps with chemotherapy nausea and chronic pain (Section 9.4). It has one paradoxical side effect that every therapist should know about. In 1983 Frederick J. Heide and Borkovec gave chronically tense adults one session of progressive relaxation and one of mantra meditation; about 31 percent reported that the relaxation session made them more tense, and about 54 percent said the same of meditation. This relaxation-induced anxiety seems most likely in people who fear losing control or who are alarmed by unfamiliar bodily sensations (heaviness, tingling, a slowing heart). The remedy is to warn clients in advance that such sensations are harmless, let them keep their eyes open and stay in control of the pace, and treat the sensations as information rather than danger. Exam trap "Progressive deep relaxation" is Edmund Jacobson's technique (RML 2022), not Wolpe's, Skinner's or Pavlov's. Wolpe borrowed and shortened it for systematic desensitisation; Bernstein and Borkovec (1973) wrote the abbreviated manual. For the date, Progressive Relaxation appeared in 1929 and its enlarged second edition in 1938 ; either may be quoted. Notes that give "1920" (Psycho Didi, for example) are pointing loosely to the 1920s, the decade in which Jacobson worked the method out and first published it; no book of his appeared in 1920. Beware of the other Jacobsons: Edith Jacobson was a psychoanalyst of object relations (Chapter 3), Neil Jacobson developed behavioural activation (Section 4.9) and integrative couple therapy (Chapter 7), and Lenore Jacobson co-authored the Pygmalion study of teacher expectancy with Robert Rosenthal (Social book). Autogenic training: relaxation by self-suggestion Progressive relaxation reaches the mind through the muscles. Autogenic training takes the opposite road. Its founder, the Berlin psychiatrist Johannes Heinrich Schultz (1884 to 1970), had worked with the brain researcher Oskar Vogt , who studied hypnosis in the 1890s and noticed that some of his patients could put themselves, briefly and on their own, into a restful hypnotic-like state and came out of it refreshed. Schultz noticed something else: hypnotised people very often reported two sensations, heaviness and a pleasant warmth in the limbs. He asked whether a person could produce those sensations, and the deep rest that went with them, without a hypnotist at all, simply by attending to them. He presented his answer to colleagues in Berlin in the 1920s and published it in 1932 as Das autogene Training . The German physician Wolfgang Luthe (1922 to 1985), who trained with Schultz and later worked in Montreal, brought the method to the English-speaking world and with Schultz wrote the multi-volume Autogenic Therapy (from 1969). autogenic training (autogenic means "self-generated") is a method of deep relaxation in which a person silently repeats a fixed series of verbal formulae describing sensations of heaviness, warmth and calm in the body, and attends to those sensations until they arise of their own accord. The attitude Schultz demanded is passive concentration : a casual, effortless attention to the formula and to the part of the body it names, without trying to make anything happen and without caring whether it does. The moment the trainee strains to make the arm feel heavy, the effort itself produces tension, which is the same point Jacobson made about trying to relax. The trainee sits or lies in one of three positions: lying flat, reclining in an armchair, or the so-called coachman's posture, sitting on a stool slumped forward with the head hanging and the forearms resting on the thighs, like a cab driver dozing on his seat. Eyes closed, he repeats the formula for the current exercise several times, interspersed with the calming phrase "I am completely calm." There are six standard exercises, always learned in the same order (Table 4.18). Each is practised for a few minutes, two or three times a day, and a new exercise is added only when the previous one comes easily, typically after a week or two, so that the whole sequence takes some weeks to a few months to master. Every practice ends with a deliberate "taking back" (cancellation): the trainee flexes the arms vigorously, breathes deeply and opens his eyes, so that he does not walk away groggy. During training people sometimes notice brief twitches, tingling, images or surges of feeling, which Schultz and Luthe called autogenic discharges and regarded as harmless. Table 4.18 The six standard exercises of Schultz's autogenic training, in the order in which they are learned. Exercise Typical formula (repeated silently) Bodily target 1. Heaviness "My right arm is heavy," then both arms, then the legs Relaxation of the skeletal muscles 2. Warmth "My right arm is warm," spreading to all the limbs Widening of the blood vessels in the limbs 3. Heart "My heartbeat is calm and regular" Heart rate and rhythm 4. Breathing "My breathing is calm" (or "It breathes me") Slow, effortless respiration 5. Solar plexus "My solar plexus is warm" Warmth in the upper abdomen; the digestive organs 6. Forehead "My forehead is pleasantly cool" A cool, clear head Look at the right-hand column of Table 4.18 and you will see the logic. Heaviness is what relaxed muscles feel like; warmth is what dilated blood vessels feel like, which happens when sympathetic activity falls; the heart and breathing exercises address the two rhythms most disturbed by anxiety. Autogenic training is therefore aimed squarely at the autonomic nervous system, through suggestion, which is why it is so closely related to self-hypnosis. Trainers usually leave out or soften the heart exercise for people with heart disease or with a fear centred on the heart, and the method is not taught during an acute psychotic episode. After the standard exercises, advanced trainees may go on to meditative exercises (holding a colour or an image in mind) and to short personal resolutions ("Examinations are unimportant; I stay calm"). Autogenic training has always been more popular in Germany and the rest of continental Europe than in Britain, America or India. A meta-analysis of 60 controlled outcome studies by Friedhelm Stetter and Sirko Kupper (2002) found medium-sized benefits over control conditions for tension headache and migraine, mild hypertension, anxiety, mild depression and sleep problems, among others; but when autogenic training was compared head to head with other psychological treatments it was usually no better and sometimes slightly worse. Its formulae also found a second life in biofeedback: the Menninger Foundation's treatment of migraine, described later in this section, combined autogenic phrases about warm hands with an instrument that showed the patient her finger temperature. Exam trap Autogenic training is Johannes Heinrich Schultz's (1932) and works by self-suggestion (passive concentration on formulae of heaviness and warmth); progressive muscle relaxation is Jacobson's and works by tensing and releasing muscles. The first autogenic exercise is heaviness, the second warmth. Some revision notes describe PMR as "bottom up" (body to mind) and autogenic training as "top down" (mind to body). Do not confuse J. H. Schultz with Duane P. Schultz and Sydney Ellen Schultz, the authors of a well-known history of psychology textbook, or with William Schutz, who devised the FIRO theory of interpersonal needs and ran encounter groups (group therapies, Chapter 7). Breathing retraining and the relaxation response Try this for one minute: breathe quickly and deeply through your mouth, as if you had just run for a bus. Most people soon feel light-headed and dizzy, notice tingling in the fingers or round the mouth, feel short of breath despite breathing hard, and sense their heart racing. Some feel strangely unreal. Breathing more than the body needs, called hyperventilation , washes carbon dioxide out of the blood faster than the body produces it, the blood becomes slightly more alkaline, and the resulting sensations are almost exactly the symptoms of a panic attack. In the 1980s several researchers, among them the American psychologist Ronald Ley, argued that chronic over-breathing plays a causal part in many panic attacks; if so, teaching people to breathe slowly should prevent them. Key study: Clark, Salkovskis and Chalkley's respiratory control (1985) Question. Can panic attacks be reduced by treating the breathing that seems to drive them? Method. At Oxford, David M. Clark , Paul M. Salkovskis and Anne Chalkley treated 18 patients with frequent panic attacks in three steps: a brief bout of deliberate over-breathing in the clinic, which brought on a mild attack; an explanation of how over-breathing produces exactly these sensations, so that the patient could reattribute his attacks to breathing rather than to a heart attack or madness; and training in slow, controlled breathing. Result. Within two weeks panic attacks were much less frequent, and fear in a behavioural test had fallen, even though the patients had not been exposed to the situations they feared; further gains appeared at follow-up, though by then other treatments had been added. Conclusion. Respiratory control, together with a new explanation of the symptoms, can reduce panic. Criticism. There was no control group, and the treatment contained two ingredients, breathing and reattribution. Clark himself came to believe that the reattribution, the change in what the patient thought the sensations meant, was the more important of the two, and that idea grew into his cognitive model of panic (Section 5.6). breathing retraining is the teaching of slow, regular, abdominal (diaphragmatic) breathing as a way to correct over-breathing and to calm arousal quickly. The client sits upright with one hand on the chest and one on the abdomen, breathes in through the nose so that the lower hand rises while the upper hand stays almost still, and slows the rhythm to about 8 to 10 breaths a minute, with an out-breath slightly longer than the in-breath and a short pause before the next breath. Some programmes pace the breathing with a recorded count or a phone app. In Foa's prolonged exposure for post-traumatic stress (Section 4.3) the client silently says a calming word such as "calm" on each out-breath. As with any relaxation skill, it is practised for ten minutes or so twice a day while calm before it is used when anxious. Breathing retraining feels natural and clients like it, but the evidence has turned out to be weaker than its popularity. In 2000 Norman B. Schmidt and his colleagues randomly assigned 77 patients with panic disorder to cognitive behavioural treatment with breathing retraining, the same treatment without it, or a waiting list. Breathing retraining added nothing, and some of the data suggested that patients who received it did slightly worse. The likely reason takes you back to Section 4.3. A patient who believes "I survived that attack only because I controlled my breathing" is using the breathing as a safety behaviour , and so never learns that the sensations were harmless all along. Modern panic treatment therefore relies more on interoceptive exposure, deliberately bringing on the sensations, than on techniques to make them go away, and uses breathing, if at all, as a temporary coping skill early in treatment rather than as an escape. A more technical descendant, capnometry-assisted respiratory training, developed by Alicia Meuret and her colleagues in the 2000s, uses a sensor that shows the patient the carbon dioxide level in his exhaled breath and teaches him to raise it; it is, in effect, a form of biofeedback, and in trials it has done about as well as cognitive training for panic. Indian context Regulated breathing has a far longer history in India than in behaviour therapy. Pranayama , the breath control of yoga, includes slow, alternate-nostril breathing that closely resembles breathing retraining, and many Indian clients already know it; building on a practice the client trusts often improves adherence. Not every yogic breathing method is slow, however. In 2000 a team at NIMHANS, Bengaluru (N. Janakiramaiah, B. N. Gangadhar and colleagues) randomly assigned 45 inpatients with melancholic depression to Sudarshan Kriya Yoga, a practice built on rhythmic, partly rapid breathing, or to electroconvulsive therapy or the antidepressant imipramine. All three groups improved; remission rates at four weeks were 93 percent with ECT, 73 percent with imipramine and 67 percent with the yoga, so the yoga was inferior to ECT but similar to the drug, in a trial that could not be blinded. While psychologists were refining relaxation techniques, a cardiologist arrived at the same destination from a different direction. In the late 1960s practitioners of Transcendental Meditation, a mantra-based meditation popularised by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, approached Herbert Benson (1935 to 2022) at Harvard Medical School and offered to show that they could lower their blood pressure. With the physiologist Robert Keith Wallace, Benson recorded meditators' physiology and found that oxygen consumption, heart rate and breathing rate fell during meditation, a state of wakeful low metabolism. Benson's next step was the important one. He argued that there was nothing unique about Transcendental Meditation, or indeed about any one tradition: prayer, meditation, autogenic training and progressive relaxation all trigger the same innate reaction, which he called the relaxation response , a coordinated fall in sympathetic nervous activity that is the physiological opposite of the fight-or-flight response described early in the twentieth century by the physiologist Walter Bradford Cannon . He set this out in The Relaxation Response (1975). Section 9.4 lists the four elements that Benson said elicit the response: a quiet environment, a mental device (a word, sound or phrase repeated silently, or the breath), a passive attitude towards distracting thoughts, and a comfortable position. His own procedure is simple enough to teach in one session. Sit quietly with eyes closed, relax the muscles from the feet upwards, breathe through the nose, and on each out-breath silently say "one." When thoughts intrude, do not fight them; return to the word. Continue for 10 to 20 minutes, once or twice a day. Later Benson encouraged people to choose a word or short prayer from their own faith (a "faith factor" in his phrase), so that an Indian client might use "Om," "Ram" or a line of a prayer, which makes the method easy to fit to a client's culture. Mindfulness meditation, which is often confused with relaxation, has a different aim: noticing experience without judging it, whether or not one becomes calm (Section 5.9). Exam trap The relaxation response is Herbert Benson's term (1975); the fight-or-flight response it opposes is Walter Cannon's ; the general adaptation syndrome (alarm, resistance, exhaustion) is Hans Selye's description of the stress response and is not a relaxation technique at all. Transcendental Meditation was Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's, not Benson's: Benson's point was that its benefits did not depend on its mantra or its tradition. And remember the hyperventilation logic: over-breathing produces panic-like sensations (which is why interoceptive exposure uses it deliberately), whereas slow breathing retraining aims to prevent them. Applied relaxation: relaxation as a portable coping skill Every method so far has one practical weakness. Relaxation is learned lying down, with eyes closed, in a quiet room, over twenty minutes. Anxiety, however, strikes at bus stops, in meetings and in examination halls, and nobody can lie down in an examination hall and tense sixteen muscle groups. In the early 1970s two American psychologists reframed relaxation as an active coping skill rather than a passive state: Marvin R. Goldfried (1971) recast systematic desensitisation as training in self-control, teaching clients to relax away anxiety as it arose during imagined scenes, and Richard Suinn and Frank Richardson (1971) described anxiety management training on the same principle. The most complete version came from Sweden. applied relaxation is Lars-Göran Öst's (1987) method of training a person, step by step, to relax within 20 to 30 seconds in any everyday situation and to apply that skill at the first signs of anxiety. Öst, whom you met in Section 4.3 as the author of the one-session treatment for phobias, described it in "Applied relaxation: description of a coping technique and review of controlled studies," published in Behaviour Research and Therapy in 1987. The method usually takes about 10 to 12 weekly sessions, with home practice twice a day, and moves through a fixed sequence of stages, each one shorter and more portable than the one before (Figure 4.11). Self-observation. Before learning to relax, the client keeps a diary of anxiety episodes and learns to spot his own early warning signs: a tight throat, cold hands, a particular worrying thought. Relaxation is useful only if it is applied early, before anxiety has taken hold. Tension-release relaxation. The client learns progressive relaxation in the Bernstein and Borkovec style, tensing and releasing the muscle groups; a session takes 15 to 20 minutes. Release-only relaxation. The tensing is dropped and the client relaxes each group directly, which halves the time to about 5 to 7 minutes. Cue-controlled relaxation. The client pairs relaxation with his breathing, thinking "inhale" on the in-breath and "relax" on the out-breath while letting tension go, so that the word itself becomes a conditioned cue for relaxing (hence the name cue-controlled relaxation ); relaxation now takes 2 to 3 minutes. Differential relaxation. Using Jacobson's idea, the client learns to relax the muscles he does not need while sitting, writing, telephoning and walking, so that relaxation no longer requires lying still. Rapid relaxation. The goal of the training, rapid relaxation , is relaxing in 20 to 30 seconds, practised 15 to 20 times a day in natural settings. Everyday events are used as reminders (a glance at the watch, a coloured sticker on the phone, entering a room): the client takes one to three slow breaths, thinks "relax" on each out-breath, scans the body for tension and lets it go. Application training. Finally the client practises the skill under real stress: the therapist deliberately provokes anxiety (by hyperventilation, by frightening film clips, by role-played confrontations, or by brief exposure to the feared situation), and the client relaxes it away. A maintenance programme follows: rapid relaxation daily and a full body scan once or twice a week. Goal: relax in 20 to 30 seconds, anywhere Stage 1 Tension- release 15 to 20 min Stage 2 Release- only 5 to 7 min Stage 3 Cue- controlled 2 to 3 min Stage 4 Differential relaxation while active Stage 5 Rapid relaxation 20 to 30 s Stage 6 Application training under stress About 10 to 12 weekly sessions; each stage shortens the time needed to relax Figure 4.11 The stages of Öst's applied relaxation (1987), after an initial period of self-observation. Each step up makes relaxation quicker and more portable, until the client can relax in 20 to 30 seconds and apply the skill in the situations that make him anxious. Let us push a case through. Anjali, a 34-year-old bank officer in Mysuru, has worried excessively about almost everything (her health, her son's marks, her mother-in-law's moods, mistakes at work) for most of her adult life; she sleeps poorly and has constant aches in her neck and shoulders. Her diary in the first week shows that her earliest sign is not a thought at all but a tightening across her shoulders, followed by shallow breathing, usually within a minute of a message arriving on her phone. She learns tension-release relaxation in two weeks, release-only in two more, and cue-controlled relaxation by the sixth week. She puts a small green sticker on the back of her phone, and every time she picks it up she takes a slow breath, thinks "relax" and drops her shoulders: rapid relaxation, perhaps thirty times a day. In the application sessions the therapist asks her to imagine her manager calling her in about an error, and later to rehearse a difficult conversation with her mother-in-law, while she relaxes away the rising tension. By the twelfth week she still worries, but the worries no longer run on unchecked for hours, and the neck pain has eased. Öst's 1987 review of 18 controlled studies found applied relaxation clearly better than no treatment or attention placebo, and as effective as the other behavioural methods with which it had been compared, across panic, phobias, generalised anxiety and several pain conditions. For generalised anxiety disorder, Öst and Elisabeth Breitholtz (2000) found applied relaxation about as effective as cognitive therapy, and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in England recommends it as an alternative to cognitive behaviour therapy for that disorder. For panic disorder the record is mixed: in a well-known trial by Clark and his colleagues (1994), cognitive therapy did better than applied relaxation (Section 5.6). Within applied relaxation, cue-controlled relaxation links a cue word ("relax") to the out-breath; rapid relaxation is the 20 to 30 second version triggered by everyday reminders; differential relaxation (a term that goes back to Jacobson) relaxes the muscles not needed for the current activity. The defining feature of applied relaxation is that the skill is applied at the early signs of anxiety in real situations, not merely practised once a day; a question that offers "a relaxation exercise practised once a day" as a treatment for a habit is describing neither applied relaxation nor habit reversal (Section 4.9). Biofeedback: making the body's signals visible Can you lower your skin temperature by two degrees? Slow your heart by ten beats a minute? Relax one muscle in your forehead while keeping the one beside it tense? Most people would say no, and the reason is not that the body cannot do these things but that we receive almost no information about them. You cannot learn to throw darts blindfolded, because you never find out where the dart landed. biofeedback removes the blindfold. It is a procedure in which an instrument measures a bodily process that a person cannot normally sense (muscle tension, skin temperature, sweat gland activity, heart rhythm, brain waves) and feeds it back to him, moment by moment, as a tone, a light or a moving line on a screen, so that he can learn to control it. Section 9.4 introduced the technique; here we look at how it works and where it came from. Figure 4.12 shows the loop. A sensor picks up the physiological signal, a computer amplifies and processes it, and a display turns it into something the person can see or hear. The person tries a strategy (imagining warmth in the hands, letting the jaw go slack, slowing the breath) and watches what happens. Any change in the desired direction is signalled at once, so the feedback serves two functions: it is information (it tells him which strategies work) and it is reinforcement (a falling tone or a rising line is a small reward for each success). Biofeedback is therefore an application of operant conditioning. The therapist shapes the response by setting an easy target at first and raising it as the client succeeds, exactly as in shaping (Section 4.5), and then fades the feedback, so that the client learns to produce the change without the machine, in the places where he needs it. 1 Body process muscle tension, skin temperature, heart rate 2 Sensor and computer electrodes or thermistor detect and amplify 3 Feedback display tone, light or graph changes at once 4 The person notices the signal and tries a strategy measured fed back seen or heard adjusts Each change in the right direction is signalled at once: information plus reinforcement (operant learning) Later the display is faded so that control carries over to daily life Figure 4.12 The biofeedback loop. An instrument turns a bodily process the person cannot feel into a signal he can see or hear; because success is signalled immediately, the signal both informs and reinforces, and control is shaped step by step before the feedback is faded. The idea is older than the word. In 1948 the Los Angeles gynaecologist Arnold Henry Kegel (1894 to 1981) published his exercises for women whose pelvic floor muscles had been weakened by childbirth, leaving them unable to hold their urine when they coughed or laughed. The difficulty was that most women cannot find these muscles by feel, so Kegel gave them a perineometer, an air-filled chamber placed in the vagina and connected to a pressure gauge. As the woman squeezed the right muscles she watched the needle rise, and she could track her strength as it grew week by week. The perineometer made an invisible muscle visible, which makes Kegel's method an early form of biofeedback. In 1963 the anatomist John V. Basmajian showed in Science that people listening to the amplified electrical activity of their own muscles could learn to fire a single motor unit (one nerve cell and the muscle fibres it controls) while keeping its neighbours silent, and some became skilled enough to tap out drum rolls with one unit. Around the same time Joe Kamiya , working first at the University of Chicago, rang a bell at intervals and asked volunteers to guess whether their brains were producing alpha waves, the 8 to 12 cycles a second rhythm of relaxed wakefulness. With feedback they learned first to recognise the state and then to produce it at will, and the "alpha craze" of the late 1960s followed. But the experiments that convinced the scientific world that internal organs could be trained came from an animal laboratory. Key study: Miller's visceral learning, and its failure to replicate (1967 to 1986) Question. For decades learning theorists had divided responses into two kinds: skeletal, "voluntary" responses, which could be shaped by their consequences (operant conditioning), and visceral, "involuntary" responses of the heart, gut and glands controlled by the autonomic nervous system, which could only be classically conditioned. Whenever a person seemed to change his heart rate for a reward, critics argued that he had done it indirectly, by tensing muscles or changing his breathing. Could autonomic responses be operantly conditioned directly? Method. Neal Elgar Miller (1909 to 2002), the American psychologist who had earlier written Personality and Psychotherapy with Dollard (Section 4.1), and his colleague Leo DiCara paralysed rats with curare, a drug that blocks the junction between nerve and skeletal muscle, and kept them alive on artificial respiration. A paralysed rat cannot use its muscles or its breathing to influence its heart. Because it cannot eat either, the reward was a brief electrical stimulation of a pleasure centre in the brain, delivered whenever the heart rate shifted slightly in the required direction, with the criterion raised step by step. Result. Rats rewarded for speeding up learned to speed up their hearts, and rats rewarded for slowing down learned to slow them. Over the next few years Miller's laboratory reported operant control of blood pressure, intestinal contractions, urine formation and even the blood flow in one ear but not the other, and Miller summarised the work in "Learning of visceral and glandular responses" in Science in 1969. Conclusion. The autonomic nervous system appeared to be open to operant conditioning after all, which suggested that people might learn to control their own blood pressure, heart rhythm and gut, and clinical biofeedback grew rapidly on that promise. Criticism. The effects grew smaller in each new series of experiments and then vanished. Miller himself, with Barry R. Dworkin , spent years trying to reproduce them, and in 1986 they reported that in experiments on more than 2,500 rats the original findings could not be replicated; the visceral learning of curarised rats remains unproven. Miller published the failure himself, a model of scientific honesty. By then, however, human biofeedback had its own evidence, and in people whose muscles and breathing work normally it does not matter clinically whether the control is direct or "mediated": a lowered blood pressure is lowered whichever route the body took. The name "biofeedback" came into use at the end of the 1960s, and the Biofeedback Research Society was founded in 1969 (it later became the Association for Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback). Through the 1970s biofeedback was hailed as a way to cure almost anything psychosomatic, which was more than it could deliver. The next subsection sorts out what it actually does well. Exam trap "The technique based on the idea that the autonomic nervous system can come under voluntary control through operant conditioning" is biofeedback (JEMAS 2025), and the name linked to that idea is Neal Miller . The distractors come from other chapters: hypnosis works by suggestion in a state of focused attention (it was Charcot's and Freud's starting point, Chapter 3), sublimation is the Freudian defence mechanism that channels unacceptable impulses into socially valued activity (Chapter 3), and systematic desensitisation is classical counterconditioning (Section 4.2). Kegel's perineometer (1948) was an early form of biofeedback (NIMHANS 2026 recall), not aversion therapy, a token economy or desensitisation. In one line: biofeedback means learning to control a physiological process using real-time feedback from an instrument (MET mock), not dream interpretation, full-intensity exposure or medication. The forms of biofeedback and what they treat Each form of biofeedback is named after the signal it measures, and each signal suits particular problems (Table 4.20). electromyographic biofeedback (EMG biofeedback) records the electrical activity of contracting muscles through electrodes on the skin, usually over the frontalis muscle of the forehead or the trapezius of the neck and shoulders, and feeds back a tone that falls as the muscle relaxes. Its flagship use is tension-type headache. In 1973 Thomas Budzynski, Johann Stoyva and their colleagues at the University of Colorado reported a controlled trial in which patients given frontalis EMG feedback had fewer headaches than those given false feedback or no treatment, and later meta-analyses have confirmed a moderate to large benefit. EMG feedback is also used for clenching and grinding of the teeth, jaw pain and chronic back pain, and in the opposite direction, to strengthen weak muscles after a stroke or nerve injury, where the patient learns to increase rather than decrease the signal. The same principle, applied to the pelvic floor, is the modern descendant of Kegel's perineometer, and pelvic floor biofeedback for some forms of incontinence and for constipation caused by poorly coordinated straining is among the best-supported uses of biofeedback. thermal biofeedback (temperature biofeedback) uses a small temperature sensor, a thermistor, taped to a finger. Finger temperature reflects blood flow in the skin: when sympathetic arousal falls, the small blood vessels widen and the hand warms. At the Menninger Foundation in Topeka, Kansas, the research team of Joseph Sargent, Elmer Green and Dale Walters combined finger-temperature feedback with autogenic phrases ("my hands are warm and heavy") in a package they called autogenic feedback training, and in 1972 and 1973 reported that most of their migraine patients improved; according to the Greens' own account, the idea came from a volunteer whose migraine eased during a session in which her hand temperature rose sharply. Hand warming became the standard biofeedback treatment for migraine, and an often-cited meta-analysis by Kenneth Holroyd and Donald Penzien (1990) found relaxation combined with thermal biofeedback roughly as effective in preventing migraine as the drug propranolol. Thermal feedback was also the obvious choice for Raynaud's phenomenon, in which the fingers turn white and painful in the cold because their blood vessels clamp down. Early small studies were encouraging, but the large Raynaud's Treatment Study (2000), which randomly assigned 313 patients to sustained-release nifedipine, placebo, temperature biofeedback or a control form of biofeedback, found that temperature biofeedback reduced attacks no more than the control feedback did, whereas nifedipine reduced them by about two-thirds compared with placebo. (Some critics argued that the control biofeedback, which trained forehead relaxation, was not truly inactive.) electrodermal biofeedback feeds back skin conductance, the ease with which a tiny electric current passes across the skin of the fingers or palm, once called the galvanic skin response (GSR). Conductance rises as the sweat glands, controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, become active, so it is a sensitive index of arousal; the client learns to bring it down, and it is used mainly in anxiety and stress management. (The same measure is one channel of the polygraph, the so-called lie detector.) heart rate variability biofeedback (HRV biofeedback) works with a rhythm everyone has but few notice: the heart speeds up slightly with each in-breath and slows with each out-breath. When a person breathes slowly, at about six breaths a minute (the "resonance frequency" for most adults), these swings become very large and regular. Paul M. Lehrer and Evgeny Vaschillo developed a protocol around 2000 in which the client watches his heart rate rise and fall on a screen and adjusts his breathing to maximise the swing. It is used for anxiety, depression and asthma; a 2017 meta-analysis of some two dozen studies found sizeable reductions in self-reported stress and anxiety, although many of the studies were small. Notice how close this is to breathing retraining: here the instrument tells the client whether his slow breathing is doing what it should. neurofeedback (EEG biofeedback) feeds back the electrical rhythms of the brain recorded from the scalp. Its clinical history began with an accident. In the late 1960s M. Barry Sterman , at the University of California, Los Angeles, had trained cats to produce the sensorimotor rhythm (SMR), a 12 to 15 cycles a second rhythm over the motor areas of the cortex. In a separate project testing the toxicity of a rocket fuel for the American space programme, the cats that had happened to receive SMR training turned out to be unusually resistant to the seizures the fuel caused. Sterman went on to train people with epilepsy, and in 1976 Joel F. Lubar and Margaret Shouse reported SMR training in a hyperactive child. Later protocols for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) trained children to reduce slow theta activity (about 4 to 8 cycles a second) and increase faster beta activity, on the theory that inattentive brains produce too much slow activity. The evidence divides sharply according to who rates the outcome. In unblinded studies parents, who know their child is in treatment, report clear improvement. But when the European ADHD Guidelines Group, led by Samuele Cortese, analysed 13 randomised trials with 520 children in 2016, the effects were not significant on ratings made by people who probably did not know which treatment the child had received, nor in trials with sham feedback. Neurofeedback for ADHD is therefore not an established treatment; medication and behavioural parent training remain the first-line options (Section 4.10 describes parent training). Form What is measured What the client learns Main uses (strength of evidence) EMG (electromyographic) Electrical activity of muscles To relax a tense muscle, or to activate a weak one Tension-type headache (good); jaw and back pain; stroke rehabilitation; pelvic floor problems (good) Thermal (skin temperature) Finger temperature, reflecting skin blood flow To warm the hands by lowering sympathetic arousal Migraine (good, with relaxation); Raynaud's (disappointing in the largest trial) Electrodermal (GSR, skin conductance) Sweat gland activity To lower general arousal Anxiety and stress (moderate) Heart rate variability Beat-to-beat change in heart rate To breathe at about six breaths a minute, maximising the rhythm Anxiety, stress, asthma (promising) EEG neurofeedback Brain rhythms (alpha, SMR, theta, beta) To increase or decrease particular rhythms Epilepsy (some support); ADHD (weak in blinded trials) Why does biofeedback work when it works? The obvious answer is that the client learns to change the physiological process, and the change relieves the symptom: lower forehead tension, fewer headaches. A pair of ingenious studies suggested that the obvious answer is at best incomplete. Key study: Andrasik and Holroyd's misleading feedback (1980) Question. Does EMG biofeedback relieve tension headache because patients learn to relax their forehead muscles? Method. Frank Andrasik and Kenneth A. Holroyd gave tension headache sufferers frontalis EMG biofeedback, and told all of them that they were learning to reduce muscle tension. In fact the feedback was arranged so that one group was rewarded for decreasing forehead tension, a second for keeping it unchanged and a third for increasing it. A fourth group only recorded their headaches. Result. All three biofeedback groups improved, by about the same amount and more than the monitoring group, although only the first had actually learned to lower its muscle tension. Conclusion. The headache relief did not depend on learning the specific physiological skill. In a follow-up study (1984) Holroyd and his colleagues manipulated what patients believed about their success, and found that patients led to think they were very successful improved more, whatever their muscles had actually done. Improvement seemed to come from cognitive changes: a growing sense of control over the headaches (self-efficacy, Section 4.7) and changes in how patients noticed and coped with the early signs of stress. Criticism. The findings apply to tension headache. Where the target is a specific, unfelt skill (contracting the right pelvic floor muscle, firing a weak muscle after a stroke) the physiological learning clearly does matter. Put these findings together and a balanced verdict emerges. For headache and for general arousal, biofeedback works about as well as relaxation training, partly through the same routes (lowered arousal and a sense of control), and relaxation is cheaper. Biofeedback earns its extra cost in three situations: when the target is a specific process the person cannot feel at all (single muscles, the pelvic floor, the carbon dioxide level of the breath), when a client does not respond to relaxation alone, and when a client is sceptical of "psychological" treatment but finds a measured signal on a screen convincing. Modern equipment has also become cheap; sensors that link to a mobile phone now measure heart rate variability and skin conductance for a small fraction of what a laboratory instrument once cost. Clinical link A biofeedback display is a powerful teaching aid even when it is not the treatment. Many clients in Indian general hospital clinics present their distress as bodily complaints (headache, "gas," weakness, palpitations) and reject any suggestion that stress is involved. Attach a skin conductance or EMG sensor, ask the client to sit quietly, then ask about the worrying situation at home, and the line on the screen climbs within seconds; ask him to breathe slowly and it falls. The link between mind and body, which no amount of explanation had established, is now something he has seen for himself, and the rest of the treatment becomes far easier to accept. Exam trap Match each form to its classic use: EMG biofeedback to tension-type headache (and muscle re-education); thermal biofeedback to migraine and Raynaud's; electrodermal (GSR) to general arousal and anxiety; EEG neurofeedback to epilepsy and ADHD. EMG biofeedback is not a treatment for a bipolar depressive episode, acute psychosis or antisocial personality disorder (PYQ mock). Neal Miller's dramatic curarised-rat results failed to replicate (Dworkin and Miller, 1986), yet biofeedback in people survived on its own evidence. And biofeedback is not superior to relaxation for most stress-related conditions; its specific value lies where the target process cannot be felt without an instrument. 4.9 Habit Change and Self-Management Medium yield · 3 Qs Relaxation and biofeedback still depend on a teacher, and often on an instrument. The methods in this section move the therapist further out of the picture. A nail-biter learns to catch his own hand on its way to his mouth; a depressed woman plans her own week; a student reorganises his own desk; an insomniac changes what he does with his own bed. In each case the client is taught to act as his own behaviour therapist, observing his behaviour, changing its antecedents and arranging its consequences, an approach that behaviour therapists call self-management. The section begins with the most structured of these methods, habit reversal, looks at two older techniques (negative practice and thought stopping) that turned out less well, and then follows self-management into three areas where it is now central: self-control, depression and sleep. Habit reversal training Everyone has a nervous habit or two: biting the nails during a tense cricket match, twisting a lock of hair while reading, cracking the knuckles, chewing the inside of the cheek. Most are harmless. For some people the habit becomes severe enough to damage the body or to embarrass them into hiding: bleeding fingertips, a bald patch hidden under a dupatta, a jaw sore from grinding. In 1973 Nathan H. Azrin (1930 to 2013), already known for the token economy (Section 4.5) and for overcorrection (Section 4.6), and his colleague R. Gregory Nunn asked why such habits persist when the person wants to stop them. Their answer had four parts. Nervous habits occur largely outside awareness : the hand is in the hair before the person knows it. They are the end of a chain of movements strengthened by thousands of repetitions, so that the habit runs off automatically once the first link begins. They are tolerated by other people, who rarely comment. And the person has no competing response , nothing ready to do instead. A treatment, they argued, should attack each of these in turn. Key study: Azrin and Nunn's habit reversal (1973) Question. Can nervous habits and tics be eliminated quickly by teaching people to notice them and to do something incompatible instead? Method. Azrin and Nunn treated 12 clients, adults and children, with habits that included nail-biting, thumb-sucking, lip-biting and tics, in a single counselling session of about two hours, followed by brief telephone contact. Each learned to describe and detect his habit, to anticipate it, to practise a competing response and to enlist the support of his family. They published the results as "Habit-reversal: a method of eliminating nervous habits and tics" in Behaviour Research and Therapy . Result. By the clients' own records the habits fell by about 95 percent after the first day and by about 99 percent after three weeks, and the gains held over the months of follow-up. Conclusion. A brief, structured training in awareness and competing responses could virtually eliminate long-standing habits. Criticism. The sample was small, the data were self-reports and there was no control group, so the near-total success was surely an overestimate. Later controlled trials confirmed that habit reversal works, although the effects are smaller than in that first report. habit reversal training (HRT) is a multi-component behavioural treatment for repetitive habits and tics in which the client learns to become aware of each occurrence of the habit and of the urge that precedes it, and then to perform a competing response that is physically incompatible with the habit, supported by procedures that build motivation and carry the skill into everyday life. Azrin and Nunn's original package had about a dozen procedures, grouped under four headings (Table 4.21). awareness training comes first, because a person cannot interrupt a habit he does not notice. In response description the client describes the habit in detail, often while performing it in front of a mirror. In response detection the therapist points out every occurrence during the session until the client is catching each one himself. The early warning procedure teaches him to detect the very first movement or sensation of the chain (a hand drifting upwards, an itch on the scalp), and situation awareness training identifies the places, times, people and activities in which the habit is most likely. The second component, and the active ingredient, is competing response training. A competing response is a behaviour that is physically incompatible with the habit, which the client performs as soon as he notices the habit or the urge to do it, and holds for about a minute or until the urge has passed (Azrin and Nunn originally asked for three minutes). A good competing response meets several conditions: it makes the habit impossible at that moment; it can be held for a minute or more; it is socially inconspicuous, so that it can be done in a classroom or on a bus without anyone noticing; it can be combined with ordinary activities; and it usually involves a mild isometric tensing of the muscles opposite to those the habit uses, which also sharpens awareness. For hair-pulling or nail-biting the client might clench his fists, grip a pen or press his palms flat on his thighs. For a head-jerking tic he gently tenses his neck muscles with the chin slightly lowered; for an eye-blinking tic he makes slow, deliberate, soft blinks; for throat-clearing or a vocal tic he breathes slowly and rhythmically through the nose with the mouth closed. The third component, habit control motivation, keeps the client using the competing response after the novelty wears off. In the habit inconvenience review he lists every embarrassment, cost and restriction the habit has caused. Family members are recruited for social support: they praise each use of the competing response and, by agreement, give a gentle prompt when they see the habit. In public display the client deliberately shows others the evidence of improvement, such as growing nails. The fourth component, generalisation training, uses symbolic rehearsal: the client imagines himself in each high-risk situation, noticing the first sign of the habit and performing the competing response, so that the skill transfers beyond the clinic. The original package also included relaxation training and self-recording. In 1998 Raymond Miltenberger, Wayne Fuqua and Douglas Woods reviewed the research and found that a simplified version with only three parts (awareness training, competing response training and social support) works about as well as the full package, and that simplified form is what most clinicians use today.
