(The disorder, trichotillomania, is described in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) When she describes the sequence in front of a mirror she is startled by how long it is: her hand rises to her scalp, searches for a coarse hair, twirls it, pulls it out, rolls it between her fingers and sometimes brings the root to her lips. Her record shows about fifteen pulling episodes a day, almost all while reading in bed or talking on the phone. She chooses a competing response she can use anywhere, gripping a pen firmly in the hand that pulls, and practises it in the session. She stops reading in bed. Her roommate, briefed with Priya's permission, says "hands" gently when she sees the hand rising and praises her when she uses the pen. After four weeks the record shows two episodes a day, and the hair is beginning to grow back. Habit reversal is the behavioural treatment of first choice for tics, trichotillomania, skin-picking, nail-biting and thumb-sucking, and it has been used for teeth-grinding and other repetitive behaviours. A close relative treats stuttering. In 1974 Azrin and Nunn described regulated breathing , in which the person who stutters learns to stop speaking at the first sign of a stutter, breathe out and then in, pause to plan the phrase, and begin speaking on the out-breath; the breathing pattern acts as the competing response. Exam trap Habit reversal training is primarily a treatment for tics and other repetitive habits (Real PYQ 2025). Stuttering is a tempting option because Azrin and Nunn did adapt the method for it (regulated breathing, 1974), but it is not HRT's main use. Obsessive-compulsive behaviours are treated by exposure and response prevention (Section 4.3), because compulsions are performed to neutralise anxiety, not out of habit; aggressive behaviour is managed with the operant methods of Sections 4.5 and 4.6. A good competing response is physically incompatible with the habit, inconspicuous and held for about a minute or until the urge passes (NIMHANS 2026 recall). The distractors describe other techniques: "an unpleasant consequence each time the habit occurs" is punishment or aversion; "the habit itself, performed deliberately and repeatedly until fatigue sets in" is negative practice (below); "a relaxation exercise practised once a day" is ordinary relaxation training. Tics, premonitory urges and CBIT Tics are sudden, rapid, repetitive movements or sounds (blinking, grimacing, shoulder-shrugging, sniffing, throat-clearing), and Tourette's disorder is the combination of several motor tics and at least one vocal tic lasting more than a year (the disorders themselves are described in the Psychiatric Disorders book). For most of the twentieth century tics were treated as purely neurological and therefore beyond the reach of psychology. Two observations changed that view. First, most people with tics, when asked carefully, describe a premonitory urge : an uncomfortable sensation (an itch, pressure or tension in the part of the body that is about to tic) which builds up and is relieved for a while by the tic. Second, tics are strongly affected by the situation: they increase with stress, tiredness, excitement and boredom, and when parents or teachers comment on them or tell the child to stop. The first observation gives a behavioural model of tics that you have met before. If a tic relieves an aversive urge, then the tic is negatively reinforced by that relief, just as a compulsion is negatively reinforced by the relief of anxiety (Figure 4.4). The competing response then does for the tic what response prevention does for the ritual: it blocks the response while the urge rises, peaks and fades on its own, so the person learns that the urge is tolerable and passes without a tic. It is not surprising, then, that a Dutch trial in 2004 (Cara Verdellen and colleagues) found exposure to the urge with prevention of the tic roughly as effective as habit reversal. Clinicians long worried that suppressing tics would cause a rebound burst afterwards; experiments by Douglas Woods, Michael Himle and their colleagues in the 2000s found no such rebound. The second observation, that tics vary with their antecedents and consequences, led to a function-based component. The Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics (CBIT) is a manualised treatment that combines habit reversal (awareness training and competing response training) with function-based interventions (identifying the situations and reactions that make tics worse and changing them), relaxation training, psychoeducation about tics for the child and family, and a reward programme for practice. It usually takes eight sessions over ten weeks. Key study: CBIT for children with Tourette's disorder (Piacentini and colleagues, 2010) Question. Does a behavioural treatment reduce tics in children better than a credible supportive treatment? Method. John Piacentini and a team of American researchers that included Douglas Woods, Lawrence Scahill, Sabine Wilhelm , Alan Peterson and John Walkup randomly assigned 126 children aged 9 to 17 with Tourette's or chronic tic disorder to eight sessions over ten weeks of either CBIT or supportive therapy with education about tics. Tic severity was rated by clinicians who did not know which treatment the child had received. Result. About 52.5 percent of the children given CBIT were rated much or very much improved, compared with 18.5 percent of those given supportive therapy, and most of the CBIT responders reassessed six months later had kept their gains. Very few children's tics worsened. Conclusion. A behavioural treatment produced improvements comparable to those reported for medication, without its side effects. A companion trial in adults led by Wilhelm (2012) found 38 percent much improved with CBIT against about 6 percent with supportive therapy. Criticism. About a third of the children were also taking stable doses of medication for their tics, and about half did not respond; CBIT reduces tics rather than curing them. On the strength of these trials, clinical guidelines in Europe and North America now recommend habit reversal or CBIT as the first treatment to try when tics are troublesome enough to need treatment, before medication. For an Indian family whose child's blinking and grunting have drawn ridicule at school, and who have been told that "nothing can be done except tablets," this is important news. Exam trap CBIT stands for Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics ; its core is habit reversal, to which it adds function-based interventions, relaxation and psychoeducation. Tell a tic from a compulsion: a tic relieves a sensory premonitory urge and is treated with habit reversal or CBIT, whereas a compulsion neutralises an obsessional fear and is treated with exposure and response prevention. And do not assume that tic suppression causes a rebound: the rebound effect belongs to the suppression of thoughts (Wegner, later in this section), not of tics. Massed or negative practice Habit reversal is not the first behavioural attack on habits. Forty years earlier, the American psychologist Knight Dunlap (1875 to 1949) of Johns Hopkins University proposed something that sounds like nonsense: to break a habit, practise it. Edward Thorndike's law of exercise held that repeating a response strengthens it, and Dunlap called this the alpha hypothesis. In a 1928 paper in Science , "A revision of the fundamental law of habit formation," and in his 1932 book Habits: Their Making and Unmaking , he proposed a beta hypothesis: under the right conditions, deliberate repetition of a response, made with full awareness and with the intention of getting rid of it, weakens it. His favourite example came from his own typewriter. He kept typing "hte" for "the," so he sat down and deliberately typed "hte" many times, attending to it as a mistake, and the error disappeared. He applied the same idea to stammering, thumb-sucking, nail-biting and tics, and called it negative practice. negative practice (also called massed practice when it is carried out in long, concentrated sessions) is the deliberate, repeated performance of an unwanted habit or tic, usually for a set period such as several minutes at a time, in order to weaken it. The best-known theory of why it should work came from Aubrey J. Yates , who in 1958 treated a young woman with four distinct tics by having her perform each tic voluntarily, as fast and as often as she could, for long periods. Yates drew on Clark Leonard Hull 's learning theory. Every repetition of a response builds up reactive inhibition, a fatigue-like state that makes the response harder to perform. When the person finally stops and rests, the reduction in fatigue rewards the act of not ticcing, so that a habit of not performing the tic (conditioned inhibition, in Hull's terms) is gradually learned. Yates's patient improved, though not completely. The method has been used for tics, nail-biting, hair-pulling and stuttering, and occasionally for typing and spelling errors, but its results were modest and often short-lived. When Azrin, Nunn and Frantz-Renshaw compared it directly with habit reversal in 1980, in 22 people with tics, habit reversal reduced the tics by more than 90 percent and massed practice by only about a third; a parallel comparison for nail-biting also favoured habit reversal. Negative practice is now rarely used. It is worth knowing chiefly because examiners place it beside three techniques that look similar. Satiation (Section 4.6) presents a reinforcer in such abundance that it loses its value; negative practice repeats a response, not a reinforcer. Rapid smoking , in which the smoker puffs every few seconds until he feels sick, is closer to aversion therapy (Section 4.4). And paradoxical intention (Section 4.10) asks a person to intend or wish for the very symptom he fears, with humour, in order to dissolve anticipatory anxiety; it works on the fear of the symptom rather than on fatigue of the response. Exam trap Negative (massed) practice is Knight Dunlap's (1928; Habits: Their Making and Unmaking , 1932), with a Hullian rationale supplied by Aubrey Yates (1958). "An intervention in which the person deliberately does, or wishes for, the very opposite of the therapeutic goal in order to reach that goal" is paradoxical intention (Viktor Frankl; NIMHANS 2026 recall), not negative practice: negative practice repeats a habit to exhaust it, and has no "wishing" in it. Dereflection is Frankl's other logotherapy technique, which turns the person's attention away from himself (Chapter 6), and reciprocal inhibition is Wolpe's principle behind desensitisation (Section 4.2). If a habit reversal question offers "performing the habit deliberately and repeatedly until fatigue sets in" as the competing response, that option is negative practice. Thought stopping, and why it is now discouraged What can a behaviour therapist do about a thought? The earliest answer was to treat it like any other unwanted response and suppress it. thought stopping is a technique in which an unwanted, recurring thought is interrupted by a sudden command, "Stop!", first shouted by the therapist and then said by the client himself, aloud and later silently, usually followed by a deliberate switch to a pleasant or neutral thought. It was described in 1928 by J. A. Bain in a self-help book, Thought Control in Everyday Life ; adapted for obsessional thinking in the 1950s by J. G. Taylor; and made widely known by Wolpe, who included it with Lazarus in Behavior Therapy Techniques (1966). The standard procedure runs like this. The client closes his eyes and deliberately brings the unwanted thought to mind, raising a finger when it is clearly present. The therapist suddenly shouts "Stop!", sometimes banging the desk at the same time. Startled, the client usually finds that the thought has gone, and the demonstration is repeated several times. Then the client shouts "Stop!" himself, then says it in a normal voice, then whispers it, and finally says it silently, so that he can use it anywhere. Some therapists added a sharp snap of a rubber band worn on the wrist, and many added a substitute thought, a pleasant scene or a reassuring statement. The rationale varied with the theorist: the shout was a mildly aversive stimulus that punished the thought, or a distraction, or an interruption that broke an otherwise automatic chain of thoughts. It was used for obsessional ruminations, jealousy, worry, self-critical thoughts and cravings. Thought stopping is simple, quick and intuitively appealing, which explains its long popularity in counselling manuals. The evidence never supported it. In a small controlled trial at the Maudsley in 1973, Richard Stern, Maurice Lipsedge and Isaac Marks found that thought stopping produced little improvement in patients with obsessional ruminations. The deeper problem was explained by the "white bear" experiment of Daniel M. Wegner and his colleagues in 1987, told as a key study in Section 5.9: students told not to think of a white bear kept thinking of it, and when the ban was lifted they thought of it more often than students who had never tried to suppress it. Deliberately pushing a thought out of mind tends to produce a rebound effect , a later increase in the very thought that was suppressed, and Wegner's later ironic process theory explains why suppression fails most under stress or mental load, which is exactly when people with obsessions try hardest. For obsessions there is a further cost. In the cognitive model of obsessive-compulsive disorder (Section 5.6), intrusive thoughts become obsessions because they are treated as dangerous and in need of control, and every attempt to suppress or neutralise them confirms that belief. Thought stopping teaches the client that the thought is dangerous and must be stopped, and the silent "Stop!" easily becomes one more covert ritual of the kind that defeats exposure and response prevention (Section 4.3). Today, therefore, most clinicians teach the opposite. Obsessional thoughts are treated by exposure to them, through written scripts and recordings, with prevention of neutralising (Section 4.3); worries are handled by postponing them to a set worry period, a stimulus control technique described by Borkovec and colleagues in 1983 and later built into metacognitive therapy (Section 5.10); and acceptance and commitment therapy teaches clients to notice thoughts without fighting them (Section 5.9). A few clinicians still defend a brief "stop" as a cue to interrupt ruminative brooding and turn to an activity, which is close to the way behavioural activation treats rumination (below), but not as a way of getting rid of obsessions. Clinical link A devout 24-year-old man in Mysuru is tormented by obscene images of a deity that intrude during prayer. Each time, he silently says "Rama, Rama" and taps his cheek, and a counsellor has taught him to shout "Stop!" in his mind as well. The images are now more frequent than ever. Seen through this section, every one of these responses is a neutraliser that tells him the thought is dangerous. Treatment reverses the strategy: he writes the feared image into a short script, listens to it repeatedly without praying it away, and learns, often with relief, that such intrusions are common in people of deep faith precisely because they find them so repugnant. Exam trap Thought stopping: Bain (1928) first described it, Taylor adapted it for obsessions and Wolpe (with Lazarus) popularised it. Do not confuse J. A. Bain with Alexander Bain, the nineteenth-century Scottish philosopher of associationism. Thought stopping is a form of thought suppression , and suppression produces a rebound (Wegner, 1987, the white bear study); this is why it is now discouraged, especially for obsessions. It is not the same as cognitive restructuring (which examines the evidence for a thought, Chapter 5), Meichenbaum's self-instructional training (which guides action with self-statements, Chapter 5) or defusion (which changes one's relationship to a thought without trying to remove it, Section 5.9). Self-monitoring, self-reinforcement and self-control Section 2.8 taught self-monitoring as a method of assessment: the client records his own behaviour, thoughts or feelings as they occur, and the record is prone both to inaccuracy and to reactivity, the change that recording itself produces. Section 4.1 noted that reactivity is a nuisance for measurement but a gift for treatment. Here we use the gift. self-monitoring , used as a treatment, is the deliberate recording by the client of a target behaviour in order to change it, arranged so as to make the reactive effect as large as possible. A neat early demonstration came from an American junior high school. In 1971 Marcia Broden, R. Vance Hall and Brenda Mitts gave an eighth-grade girl who rarely studied in her history class a stack of slips on which to mark, at intervals during the lesson, whether she had been studying. Her study behaviour rose as soon as the slips were introduced, fell when they were withdrawn and rose again when they were reinstated, the reversal design of applied behaviour analysis showing that the recording itself was responsible; once her teacher began praising her studying, the slips could be dropped without loss. In a second experiment an eighth-grade boy who constantly talked out of turn in his mathematics class recorded his talk-outs, and they fell. Today self-monitoring is the first component of most self-management programmes. A food record is one of the most consistent predictors of success in behavioural weight-loss programmes, smokers count cigarettes, drinkers keep a drinks diary, and a person who pulls her hair keeps a tally on a counter. The findings summarised in Section 2.8 tell the therapist how to make it work: record each instance immediately, record the urge before acting on it rather than the act afterwards, use an obtrusive device (a wrist counter is a constant reminder), set a goal, graph the results and look at the record in every session. And remember its limitation: reactive effects alone are often short-lived, which is why self-monitoring usually opens a treatment rather than being the whole of it. Self-monitoring is the first step of self-control, and behaviour therapists had to explain how a person can control his own behaviour at all. Skinner offered a behavioural answer in Science and Human Behavior (1953). In self-control, he said, one response (the controlling response) alters the variables of which another response (the controlled response) is a function. A person who sets the alarm clock across the room so that he must get up to switch it off, or who leaves his credit card at home before visiting a shopping mall, is not exercising a mysterious willpower; he is arranging his own environment so that the behaviour he wants becomes more likely. The Greek hero Odysseus, who had himself tied to the mast so that he could hear the Sirens without steering towards them, is the classic example. In 1965 Israel Goldiamond applied the idea to a student who could not study at his desk. Goldiamond told him to use the desk only for studying; whenever he caught himself daydreaming, he was to get up and daydream somewhere else. Gradually the desk became a cue for studying and nothing else, and his studying increased. Remember that desk: Bootzin applied the same logic to the bed (below). Frederick Kanfer, whom you met in Section 4.1 as co-author of the SORKC model, gave self-control its best-known psychological model in the early 1970s (Kanfer, 1970; Kanfer and Paul Karoly, 1972). In Kanfer's model of self-regulation , when a person's routine behaviour is disrupted or he decides to change it, he moves through three stages in a feedback loop. In self-monitoring he observes what he is doing. In self-evaluation he compares his performance with a standard or goal. In self-reinforcement he rewards himself (with praise, a treat or a privilege) when he meets the standard and criticises or punishes himself when he does not. Therapy can target any stage: teaching accurate monitoring, setting realistic standards, and arranging reasonable rewards. In 1977 Lynn P. Rehm turned Kanfer's model into a theory and a therapy for depression. Depressed people, he argued, monitor selectively (noticing failures and ignoring successes, and attending to immediate rather than long-term outcomes), evaluate themselves against perfectionist standards, and give themselves little reward and much punishment; his self-control therapy trains each of the three stages in turn. In Behavioral Self-Control (1974) Carl E. Thoresen and Michael J. Mahoney argued that self-control is not a trait one has or lacks but a set of skills that can be taught, and they sorted the skills into two families. Environmental planning changes the antecedents before the behaviour occurs: not keeping sweets in the house, studying in the library rather than the hostel room, deleting the gaming application during examinations. Behavioural programming arranges consequences after it: self-reward, self-punishment and self-contracts. Self-reinforcement raised an awkward question. If the reward is freely available to the person who sets it, why would he ever withhold it from himself? Research by Bandura and others (Section 4.7) showed that people do hold themselves to standards, but self-rewards work best when they are backed by other people, for example through a deposit contract in which a friend holds a sum of money and returns it in instalments for each week the target is met. Consider Arvind, a 22-year-old preparing in Mysuru for a postgraduate entrance examination, who sits at his books for nine hours a day and studies for perhaps two. His plan follows Kanfer's three stages and Thoresen and Mahoney's two families. He self-monitors with a log of 30-minute blocks, marking each as studied or lost. He plans his environment: his phone stays in another room during study blocks, and his desk is used for nothing but study (Goldiamond's rule). He evaluates himself against a modest standard, four focused hours a day in the first week, rising by half an hour a week. And he reinforces himself: he watches the highlights of the day's cricket match only after the day's target is met, which uses the Premack principle (Section 4.5), and his roommate holds back two thousand rupees, returning five hundred for each week in which the log shows the target met. Within a month the log shows five hours of real study a day, out of fewer hours at the desk. Exam trap Kanfer's model of self-regulation has three stages in a fixed order: self-monitoring, self-evaluation, self-reinforcement . Behavioral Self-Control (1974) is Thoresen and Mahoney's . Self-control therapy for depression is Rehm's (1977), built on Kanfer. When recording a behaviour changes it, the term is reactivity (Amity 2023), and it is reactivity that makes self-monitoring therapeutic; shaping, chaining and applied behaviour analysis are not the answer. Skinner's account of self-control distinguishes the controlling response from the controlled response. Behavioural activation for depression Behavioural activation applies self-management to depression. Its theory is told in full in Section 5.10, so a summary is enough here. In 1974 Peter M. Lewinsohn proposed that depression results from a low rate of response-contingent positive reinforcement , rewards that follow from one's own actions, which can fall because the environment offers few rewards, because the person lacks the skills to obtain them, or because few events are rewarding for him. Low mood then lowers activity, which lowers reinforcement further, and withdrawal is negatively reinforced because it brings short-term relief from effort, sadness and social demands. In their component analysis of 1996 Neil S. Jacobson (1949 to 1999) and his colleagues found that the behavioural component of Beck's cognitive therapy did as well on its own as the full package (Section 5.11). Christopher R. Martell , Michael Addis and Jacobson then set out the modern treatment in Depression in Context (2001), and in the Seattle trial led by Sona Dimidjian (2006), behavioural activation on its own did as well as antidepressant medication, and better than cognitive therapy, for the more severely depressed patients. Behavioural activation's place among the third-wave therapies, its acronyms for avoidance and India's Healthy Activity Program are in Section 5.10. behavioural activation (BA) is a structured behavioural treatment for depression in which the client systematically increases his engagement in rewarding and meaningful activities and reduces avoidance and withdrawal, acting according to a plan rather than according to his mood. Its central instruction reverses the depressed person's natural rule. He waits to feel better before he does things; BA asks him to do things in order to feel better, working "from the outside in." A behaviour therapist delivers it in a sequence of steps. Rationale. The therapist explains the cycle of low mood, withdrawal and lost reward, and the plan to reverse it, so that the client sees activity as treatment rather than as a demand. Activity monitoring. For a week the client records what he does each hour, with a mood rating from 0 to 10 (and often ratings of mastery and pleasure), using the methods of Section 2.8. The record shows which activities lift mood and which, like lying in bed or scrolling the phone, deepen it. Values and goals. Client and therapist identify what matters to him in each area of life (family, friends, work or study, health, faith, leisure) and choose activities that serve those values, not merely activities that are pleasant. Graded task assignment. Activities are broken into small steps and arranged from easiest to hardest, so that the client begins with something he can almost certainly do; this is shaping (Section 4.5) applied to a whole life. Activity scheduling. Each activity is written into a timetable with a day, time, place and duration ("Tuesday, 5 p.m., walk to the vegetable market, 20 minutes"), because a specific plan is far more likely to be carried out than a good intention. Tackling avoidance and rumination. When a planned activity is skipped, client and therapist analyse what happened (the trigger, the feeling, the avoidance and its short-term pay-off) and plan an alternative. Rumination is treated as a behaviour, an avoidant one, and the urge to brood becomes a cue to turn to the next scheduled activity. Review and reinforcement. Each session reviews the schedule, praises what was done, solves problems with what was not, and gradually hands planning over to the client. Mrs Lakshmi, a 52-year-old homemaker in Mysuru, became depressed after her only daughter married and moved to Bengaluru. Her husband works long hours, and she has stopped going to her Thursday bhajan group, stopped cooking anything but the simplest meals and stopped visiting her sister; most afternoons she lies down with the television on. Her activity record shows a mood of 2 or 3 for most of the day, rising to 6 on the two occasions when her neighbour dropped in and on the one evening she walked to the market. The plan begins there: a daily 20-minute walk to the market at five o'clock in the first week; two telephone calls to her sister in the second; the bhajan group again in the third, with the neighbour accompanying her the first time; and in the fifth week, teaching Carnatic music to the neighbour's daughter once a week, an activity that gives her a sense of mastery as well as pleasure. Her mood ratings rise week by week, and the activities, once restarted, are kept going by their own natural rewards, the conversation, the music, the company, which is the real aim of BA: to reconnect the client with reinforcers in his own life rather than to supply artificial ones. Exam trap Behavioural activation is best described as encouraging clients to engage in meaningful activities to counteract depression (JEMAS 2025). Analysing early childhood experiences is the psychodynamic approach (Chapter 3), relaxation training for anxiety belongs to Section 4.8, and hypnosis for symptom relief has nothing to do with it. The theory behind BA is Lewinsohn's low rate of response-contingent positive reinforcement; the evidence that it can stand alone comes from Jacobson's 1996 component analysis and Dimidjian's 2006 Seattle trial; the modern manual is Martell, Addis and Jacobson (2001). BA schedules activities to restore reward and reduce avoidance; it does not challenge the content of thoughts. The behavioural treatment of insomnia Insomnia might seem an odd problem for behaviour therapy. Sleep is not something a person does; it is something that happens to him, and the harder he tries, the less it happens. Yet the most effective treatments for chronic insomnia are behavioural, and they work by changing what the person does around sleep rather than by making him sleep. Section 9.4 lists the components of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), gives the rules of stimulus control and works through a sleep restriction schedule for Ms Kavya. This subsection explains the learning theory behind those components and the model that ties them together. Why does insomnia become chronic? In 1987 Arthur J. Spielman and his colleagues proposed what is now called the 3P model of insomnia (Figure 4.13). Predisposing factors make a person vulnerable: a tendency to physiological and mental hyperarousal, a worrying temperament, a family history of poor sleep. Alone they rarely cause insomnia. Precipitating factors push the person over the threshold: examinations, a bereavement, a new baby, an illness, a move to night shifts. Most people sleep normally again once the precipitant passes. In some, however, perpetuating factors take over: the things the person does and believes in order to cope with the bad nights. He goes to bed earlier to "catch up," lies in bed for hours trying to sleep, naps in the afternoon, drinks more coffee to get through the day, watches the clock, and starts to dread bedtime. These habits and beliefs keep the insomnia going long after the original stress has gone. The model's practical message is that treatment of chronic insomnia should target the perpetuating factors, which are learned behaviours and beliefs, and that is exactly what behaviour therapy is equipped to change. Predisposing traits stay constant; a precipitating stressor pushes the total above the insomnia threshold (the horizontal line across the bars); as the stressor fades, perpetuating habits and beliefs grow and keep the total above the threshold. Behavioural treatment targets the perpetuating factors. The first behavioural treatment aimed at those habits came from Richard R. Bootzin in 1972. stimulus control therapy for insomnia is a set of rules that limit what is done in bed and in the bedroom so that the bed becomes once again a reliable cue for falling asleep quickly. Bootzin's analysis was operant. For a good sleeper, the bed, the bedroom and the usual bedtime are discriminative stimuli for sleep: lie down and sleep follows. For a poor sleeper the same stimuli have become cues for everything except sleep: watching television, answering messages, planning tomorrow, worrying about money, and above all lying awake in frustration. Through classical conditioning, too, the bed becomes a conditioned stimulus for arousal, which is why many insomniacs feel drowsy in front of the television and wide awake the moment their head touches the pillow, and why they often sleep better in a hotel or at a relative's house. The rules (go to bed only when sleepy; use the bed only for sleep and sex; if not asleep within about 20 minutes, get up and go to another room until sleepy again; get up at the same time every morning; no daytime naps) are Goldiamond's study desk applied to the bed. Each rule either strengthens the bed's link with sleep or stops new pairings of bed and wakefulness, so that the conditioned arousal can extinguish. The fixed rising time anchors the body clock, and the ban on naps preserves the pressure to sleep at night. The second technique attacks a different perpetuating habit: spending too long in bed. Spielman, Paul Saskin and Michael Thorpy introduced sleep restriction therapy in 1987. They treated 35 people who had had insomnia for an average of 15 years by first restricting the time they were allowed to spend in bed to roughly the time they actually slept, then extending it in small steps as their sleep efficiency (total sleep time as a percentage of time in bed) improved. After eight weeks the patients fell asleep faster, woke less, slept more efficiently and rated their insomnia as much improved, and the improvements were still present in the 23 patients reassessed an average of 36 weeks later. Two processes explain the effect. The mild sleep loss of the first weeks builds up the homeostatic drive to sleep (the pressure for sleep that accumulates with time awake; the physiology of sleep is in the Physiological Psychology book), so that sleep comes faster and is deeper and less broken. And because the person no longer lies awake for hours, the bed stops being paired with wakefulness, which is stimulus control by another route. Sleep restriction makes people sleepy during the first weeks, so it is used with care, or not at all, in people with bipolar disorder (in whom sleep loss can trigger mania), epilepsy, or jobs that require them to drive or operate machinery. Two further components complete the behavioural picture. sleep hygiene education, whose modern list of rules is usually credited to the sleep researcher Peter J. Hauri (1977), covers caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, heavy meals, exercise, light, noise and a regular schedule; it is sensible advice, but on its own it does little for chronic insomnia (the exam trap in Section 9.4). Relaxation training (Section 4.8) lowers the physiological arousal that keeps the poor sleeper awake. A third technique, paradoxical intention, in which the person lies in bed and tries to stay awake so that the anxious effort to sleep disappears, is Frankl's method applied to sleep and is described in Section 4.10. Combined with cognitive therapy for beliefs such as "If I don't get eight hours I won't be able to function," these components make up CBT-I, which major guidelines, including the American College of Physicians in 2016, recommend as the first treatment for chronic insomnia in adults, ahead of sleeping tablets. The 3P model's factors are predisposing, precipitating and perpetuating, and treatment targets the perpetuating ones. Sleep hygiene alone is not an adequate treatment for chronic insomnia. The therapist trains relaxation, arranges exposure, delivers reinforcement or teaches a competing response, and the client practises. This last technique section stretches that picture in two directions. It begins with the strangest instruction a behaviour therapist ever gives, an instruction to try to make the problem worse, and asks why such an instruction should work and what the evidence says. It then leaves the consulting room altogether for the homes and classrooms where children's problem behaviour actually happens. There the therapist rarely treats the child directly. Instead she teaches the adults who control the child's everyday antecedents and consequences, the parents and the teachers, to become the agents of change. In 1969 Roland Tharp and Ralph Wetzel called this arrangement the triadic model : a consultant (the psychologist) works through a mediator (the parent or teacher) to change the behaviour of a target (the child). Gerald Patterson's parent training and the classroom methods that came out of the applied behaviour analysis laboratories of the 1960s are the triadic model at its most successful. Paradoxical intention as a behavioural technique You met paradoxical intention in Section 6.5 as one of the two techniques of logotherapy. Its founder, the Viennese psychiatrist Viktor Emil Frankl (1905 to 1997), noticed that many anxious patients are caught in a vicious circle of anticipatory anxiety: a person blushes, sweats or lies awake once, fears that it will happen again, and the fear itself brings on the very thing he fears (Figure 6.4). Here is the definition again, because examiners lift it almost word for word. paradoxical intention is a technique in which the client is instructed to intend, wish for or deliberately try to produce the very symptom or outcome he fears, so that the anticipatory anxiety that keeps the symptom going is removed. Frankl described it in print in 1939 and gave his best-known English account in 1960. For him it worked through self-detachment and humour, capacities of the human spirit, and it belonged to a philosophy of meaning. Behaviour therapists had no use for the philosophy. What caught their attention was that the technique was brief, that it could be written down as a precise instruction, that it seemed to work on exactly the problems in which effort and self-watching make matters worse, and that it could therefore be put to the test. Why should trying to produce a symptom make it go away? Look first at the symptoms Frankl chose. Falling asleep, passing urine, sexual arousal, a dry forehead and an unflushed face are all governed largely by the autonomic nervous system, and fluent speech, though under voluntary control, behaves in much the same way when a stammerer is anxious. They share a cruel property: none of them can be produced by an act of will, and the harder you try, the more the effort itself (arousal, muscle tension, anxious monitoring) gets in the way. A man who lies in bed straining to fall asleep is doing the one thing most likely to keep him awake. Behaviour therapists describe this as performance anxiety : anxiety about one's ability to carry out an act, which disrupts the very act it is about. Paradoxical intention reverses the demand. If the man's task is now to stay awake, he cannot fail at falling asleep; the effort and the fear of failure lose their object, arousal falls, and sleep, which never needed his help, arrives by itself. Three familiar learning processes probably help as well. The client stops avoiding the feared symptom and in effect exposes himself to it, which allows habituation and extinction (Section 4.3). He discovers that the feared consequence does not follow (he stays in the meeting while trying to sweat buckets, and nothing terrible happens), which disconfirms his prediction in the way the inhibitory learning model recommends. And he gives up the self-monitoring that kept his attention locked on the symptom. On this account paradoxical intention is not a mysterious reversal of human nature; it is a clever way of removing the effort and avoidance that maintain a problem, packaged in an instruction that sounds absurd and is therefore memorable. The behaviour therapist who did most to test the technique was L. Michael Ascher , a psychologist in the department of psychiatry at Temple University in Philadelphia, where Wolpe also worked. From the late 1970s Ascher and his colleagues applied paradoxical intention to three problems in which performance anxiety is central. The first was sleep-onset insomnia. Ascher and Jay Efran (1978) took clients whose sleep had not improved after weeks of a standard behavioural programme and simply changed the instruction: instead of trying to relax themselves to sleep, they were to lie in bed and try to stay awake. Their time to fall asleep dropped sharply within a few weeks. The second was psychogenic urinary retention (sometimes called paruresis or "shy bladder"), the inability to urinate in a public toilet when other people might be near. In 1979 Ascher reported clients who had not responded to other behavioural methods and who were now told to go into the toilet, take up the usual position and go through all the motions of urinating, but on no account to let any urine pass. Freed from the demand to perform, they improved. The third was the travel restriction of agoraphobia, in which clients were asked to go out and deliberately try to bring on the panic they dreaded, and found that panic does not come on demand. Key study: Turner and Ascher's insomnia trial (1979) Question. Is paradoxical intention a genuine treatment for insomnia or only an intriguing trick, and how does it compare with established behavioural methods? Method. Ralph M. Turner and Ascher randomly assigned adults with chronic sleep-onset insomnia to one of five conditions: progressive relaxation (Section 4.8), stimulus control (Section 4.9), paradoxical intention, a placebo procedure presented as a credible treatment, or a waiting list. Sleep was measured with nightly sleep diaries, including the time taken to fall asleep. Result. All three active treatments improved sleep significantly more than the placebo and the waiting list, and they did not differ significantly from one another. Conclusion. In a controlled comparison, paradoxical intention was as effective as the two best-established behavioural treatments of its day. Criticism. The outcomes were self-reported and the follow-up short, and later studies found the response to paradoxical intention more variable from client to client than the response to stimulus control. Later research confirmed the picture and refined it. In Glasgow, Colin Espie and William Lindsay (1985) described six insomniac clients treated with paradoxical intention whose responses varied widely from one client to the next, and in a controlled trial in 1989 Espie and his colleagues compared stimulus control, paradoxical intention and progressive relaxation with a placebo and with no treatment for chronic sleep-onset insomnia. Only the active treatments produced significant improvement, but they helped in different ways (stimulus control, for example, improved the sleep pattern itself, whereas relaxation mainly improved how well patients felt they had slept), and the gains held at a follow-up 17 months later. In 2003 Niall Broomfield and Espie showed what the technique changes: clients given paradoxical intention reported much less sleep effort and much less anxiety about their sleep performance than untreated clients, exactly as the behavioural account predicts. Sleep-medicine reviews of the 2000s therefore listed paradoxical intention among the effective single-component treatments for insomnia, but with weaker support than stimulus control, sleep restriction or the full cognitive behavioural package for insomnia (Section 4.9). Let us push one case through. Siddharth, aged 24, has spent two years in a rented room in Delhi's Mukherjee Nagar preparing for the civil services examination. For eight months he has taken an hour or more to fall asleep. He goes to bed at eleven determined to get seven hours, checks his phone at 11.20, 11.45 and 12.10, and calculates how few hours remain before the next morning's mock test. His two-week sleep diary shows an average of 80 minutes to fall asleep. The therapist first explains the circle: his wish to sleep is so strong that it keeps him alert, and sleep, like digestion, works best when nobody is supervising it. Then she gives the instruction, word for word: "Tonight, go to bed at your usual time, switch off the light and leave the phone in the other room. Lie in your usual position with your eyes open. Your task is to stay awake for as long as you can. Do not read, do not get up and do not do anything active to keep yourself awake; just lie there quietly and try not to fall asleep. Keep filling in the diary." Siddharth protests that he wants to sleep, not to stay awake, and the therapist agrees: that is exactly the problem. On the second night he reports, laughing, that he "failed" within about half an hour; by the end of the second week his diary average is 25 minutes. Had paradoxical intention not helped within two or three weeks, the plan was to move to stimulus control and sleep restriction, the first-line behavioural methods. Notice how many different instructions a therapist could have given Siddharth, each resting on a different principle. Examiners love to describe one of them and offer the others as options, so Table 4.24 sets them side by side. Table 4.24 Four instructions for a man who cannot fall asleep. Technique Associated with The instruction How it is thought to work Paradoxical intention Frankl; tested by Turner and Ascher (1979) "Lie in bed in the dark and try to stay awake as long as you can" Removes sleep effort and performance anxiety Stimulus control Richard Bootzin (1972) "Go to bed only when sleepy; if not asleep within about 15 to 20 minutes, get up and return only when sleepy; use the bed only for sleep" Re-establishes the bed as a cue for sleep (operant stimulus control) Sleep restriction Arthur Spielman (1987) "Spend in bed only as many hours as you actually sleep, then lengthen the time gradually" Builds sleep pressure and consolidates sleep Dereflection Frankl "Stop watching your sleep; turn your attention to something else worth attending to" Ends hyper-reflection, the anxious self-observation Clinical link Offer paradoxical intention with a clear rationale, a straight face and the client's agreement. Explaining why the instruction may help keeps the technique within the rules of informed consent and turns it into an experiment that client and therapist run together. It is unsuitable when the "symptom" is itself dangerous (self-harm, binge drinking, panic while driving) and, as logotherapists warn (Section 6.5), for severely depressed or suicidal clients. It works best for problems driven by anticipatory and performance anxiety: sleep-onset insomnia, shy bladder, blushing and sweating, stammering in feared situations and anxiety about sexual performance. Exam trap "The person deliberately does, or wishes for, the very opposite of the therapeutic goal in order to reach that goal" is paradoxical intention (NIMHANS 2026 recall). The distractors are close relatives. Dereflection (also Frankl) turns attention away from the self; it does not ask for the symptom. Negative practice (Dunlap) repeats a voluntary habit deliberately until it is weakened (Section 4.9, and below). Reciprocal inhibition (Wolpe) pairs the feared stimulus with an incompatible response such as relaxation. And the insomniac told to lie in the dark and try hard to stay awake is receiving paradoxical intention (NIMHANS 2026 recall), not stimulus control (getting out of bed when not sleepy), not sleep restriction (cutting time in bed) and not dereflection. Paradox elsewhere: negative practice and strategic directives Paradoxical intention is not the only treatment that tells a client to do the very thing he wants to stop. At least three other traditions use a paradox of some kind, and the differences between them, set out in Table 4.25, are a favourite source of exam options. The oldest is Adlerian. Alfred Adler "prescribed the symptom", and his follower Rudolf Dreikurs called the same move "antisuggestion" (Section 3.8): a child who sucks his thumb is told to suck it more often, so that the behaviour loses its purpose and its appeal. Frankl, who began his career in Adler's circle in Vienna, gave the idea its best-known form. The second tradition is behavioural, and it is easily confused with paradoxical intention because it also asks the client to perform the problem on purpose. negative practice (also called massed practice) is the deliberate, repeated performance of an unwanted voluntary habit, many times in quick succession, until fatigue sets in and the habit weakens. Knight Dunlap described it in 1928 and, most fully, in his 1932 book, using examples such as the typist who keeps typing "hte" for "the" and is told to type "hte" deliberately, again and again. In 1958 the Maudsley psychologist Aubrey J. Yates used massed practice of a woman's tics, asking her to produce them voluntarily for long periods, and her involuntary tics declined. The usual explanation is Clark Hull's: massed repetition builds up fatigue (reactive inhibition), resting is reinforcing, and the organism learns a habit of not making the response (conditioned inhibition). Section 4.9 shows why habit reversal, which trains a competing response instead, has largely replaced it. The contrast with paradoxical intention is sharp. Negative practice works on voluntary motor habits and requires the client to perform them, many times; paradoxical intention works on involuntary, anxiety-driven functions such as sleep and urination, and its success usually shows itself in the client's failure to produce the symptom at all. The third tradition comes from family therapy. Strategic therapists such as Jay Haley and Cloe Madanes, the brief therapists of the Mental Research Institute in Palo Alto and the Milan group led by Mara Selvini Palazzoli used paradoxical directives : instructions that prescribe the symptom (a quarrelling couple is told to argue every evening at eight o'clock for exactly twenty minutes), that restrain change ("go slowly; perhaps your family is not ready to change yet") or that describe the symptom as serving the family well (the Milan school's positive connotation). These directives are aimed at the pattern of interaction in a family system rather than at one person's anxiety, and they are often given without the rationale being explained. Some are compliance-based: if the couple obeys and quarrels on schedule, the quarrel has become voluntary and loses its force. Others are defiance-based: if the client resists the therapist's advice to stay the same, he must change to do so, and the therapist wins either way, a manoeuvre strategic therapists called a therapeutic double bind. Chapter 7 teaches strategic and Milan therapy properly; here the point is the contrast. A behaviour therapist gives paradoxical intention openly, as a reasoned instruction based on a learning account of performance anxiety, and measures what happens; a strategic therapist may give a paradox precisely because the family would resist a straightforward request. Does paradox work, whatever its form? In 1987 Varda Shoham-Salomon and Robert Rosenthal combined the controlled studies in a meta-analysis and found that paradoxical interventions, taken together, were clearly better than no treatment and roughly as effective as other psychological treatments. The method is a tool, not a school, and its value depends on fitting it to problems in which effort, avoidance or resistance is the thing keeping the problem alive. Massed or negative practice is Knight Dunlap's (1928; book 1932), applied to tics by Yates (1958); it targets voluntary habits, whereas paradoxical intention targets anxiety-driven involuntary functions. Patterson and the coercive family Why do some children become steadily more defiant and aggressive, while their brothers and sisters, raised in the same house, do not? In the middle of the 1960s Gerald R. Patterson (1926 to 2016), a psychologist in Eugene, Oregon, decided to stop asking parents about their children and go and watch. Trained observers visited the homes of boys referred by schools and courts for aggression and stealing, usually in the hour before dinner when everyone was tired and hungry, and recorded every exchange between family members in a detailed behavioural code, every few seconds. They did the same in the homes of ordinary families for comparison. Patterson and Elizabeth Gullion turned the early lessons into a programmed book for parents, Living with Children (1968); in 1977 Patterson, John Reid and their colleagues founded the Oregon Social Learning Center (OSLC), which became the leading centre for research on family processes and antisocial behaviour; and in 1982 Patterson gathered the theory into Coercive Family Process . What the observers saw was not a household of cruel parents and wicked children. It was a household in which both sides had been trained, by each other, to behave badly. Patterson called the process coercion : the use of aversive behaviour (whining, shouting, hitting, threatening) by one person to make another person stop doing something. Its commonest form is the coercive cycle , shown in Figure 4.14. David Barlow and Mark Durand give the classic example in their textbook of abnormal psychology. A boy's parents ask him to make his bed, and he refuses. One parent yells; the boy yells back and becomes abusive. At some point the exchange becomes so unpleasant that the parent stops and walks away. The fight is over, calm is restored, and the bed is not made. 1. Parent makes a demand "TV off now, start your homework" 2. Child escalates whines, argues, screams 3. Parent gives in "All right, do it later" 4. Child stops screaming calm returns, TV stays on next time The coercive cycle Child learns: escalating makes demands disappear (step 2 to 3) negative reinforcement of the child Parent learns: giving in stops the screaming (step 3 to 4) negative reinforcement of the parent Figure 4.14 Patterson's coercive cycle. Each partner's behaviour is negatively reinforced by the other's: the child's escalation is rewarded by the withdrawal of the demand, and the parent's giving in is rewarded by the end of the screaming. Because the parent gives in only some of the time, the child's escalation is reinforced on an intermittent schedule and becomes very persistent. Look carefully at who is being reinforced. The child's escalation (step 2) is followed by the removal of an aversive demand (step 3), so the escalation is negatively reinforced, and next time he will escalate sooner and harder. The parent's giving in (step 3) is followed by the end of the child's aversive screaming (step 4), so the giving in is negatively reinforced too, and next time the parent will give in sooner. Both partners, in other words, are caught in what is often called a reinforcement trap : a pattern in which the short-term relief each one gets strengthens the behaviour that makes the long-term problem worse. As Barlow and Durand put it, the child learns to keep fighting and not give up, and the parent learns that the only way to "win" is to withdraw all demands. Three refinements make the theory more powerful. First, parents do not give in every time. Sometimes they hold firm, sometimes they collapse, and so the child's coercion is reinforced on an intermittent schedule, which, as you know from the General Psychology book, produces behaviour that is extremely resistant to extinction. Second, the cycle escalates. When a parent does try to hold firm, the child raises the intensity, and the parent may in turn raise his own, until an explosive episode of shouting or hitting finally stops the child. That explosion is itself negatively reinforced (it worked), and it gives the child a vivid model of aggression. Patterson's observers saw this alternation of ineffective scolding (he called it nattering) and occasional explosive punishment again and again in the families of aggressive boys. Third, the same families tended to ignore the child's good behaviour and to attend, angrily, to his bad behaviour, so that deviance earned positive reinforcement in the form of attention while compliance earned nothing. The coercive child does not stay at home. In 1989 Patterson, Barbara DeBaryshe and Elizabeth Ramsey described a developmental sequence that has become a standard account of how early conduct problems grow into delinquency: harsh, inconsistent discipline and poor monitoring at home produce a child skilled in coercion; at school his coercion brings academic failure and rejection by ordinary peers; rejected, he drifts in late childhood and early adolescence into a group of deviant peers, who reinforce rule-breaking; and by adolescence the risk of delinquency is high. (Conduct disorder itself is described in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) The clinical message is optimistic. If the problem was taught in the family by ordinary learning processes, it can be untaught in the family by the same processes, and the people best placed to do the teaching are the parents. Exam trap The coercive cycle runs on negative reinforcement , on both sides: the child's escalation is reinforced by the removal of the demand, and the parent's giving in by the removal of the tantrum. Do not call the parent's giving in "positive reinforcement of the parent", and do not call the child's tantrum "punishment". The option "impact of parenting on behavioural problems in young children" describes Patterson's coercion research; it is not a definition of the Premack principle , which is a technique of behaviour modification often used with children (high-probability behaviour reinforces low-probability behaviour, Section 4.5; IHBAS 2020). Parent management training parent management training (PMT, also called behavioural parent training) is a treatment in which parents are taught, by instruction, modelling, role-play and supervised practice at home, to change the antecedents and consequences of their child's behaviour, so that prosocial behaviour is reinforced and problem behaviour no longer pays. It grew out of Patterson's work at Oregon and was described in detail by Alan E. Kazdin of Yale University, whose own programme for children with conduct problems combined it with problem-solving skills training for the child. Kazdin summarised its defining features in a way worth remembering. Treatment is conducted mainly with the parents, and the therapist rarely works directly with the child. Parents are taught to identify, define and observe the problem behaviour in new ways. They are taught specific procedures based on social learning principles, above all positive reinforcement, mild punishment such as time-out and loss of privileges, and negotiation and contracting. Sessions give parents the chance to see the techniques modelled, to rehearse them in role-play and to review how they went at home. And progress is checked against data, not impressions. A typical programme runs for a dozen or more weekly sessions and builds the skills in a deliberate order, shown in Table 4.26. It begins with tracking , because parents who are worn out by a difficult child usually report that he is "always" naughty, and a week of counting shows when, where and how often the behaviour actually happens (it is also the baseline, Section 4.1). It moves at once to the positive side: attending to the child and praising good behaviour, which many parents of difficult children have almost stopped doing. Only when praise and a simple reward chart are in place does it add discipline, and the discipline it teaches is mild, brief and predictable: planned ignoring of minor attention-seeking, a few minutes of time-out for aggression or defiance, and loss of a privilege for breaking an agreed rule. With older children it adds supervision (knowing where the child is, with whom, and when he will be home) and family problem-solving and contracts. Table 4.26 The skills taught in parent management training. Skill What the parent does Learning principle Pinpointing and tracking Defines one behaviour precisely and counts it every day Measurement and baseline (Section 4.1) Attending and praise Gives warm, specific attention to good behaviour: "catch the child being good" Positive reinforcement Point or sticker chart Child earns points for target behaviours, exchanged for privileges Token reinforcement; Premack principle (Section 4.5) Clear commands Gives one specific instruction at a time, as a statement, not a question, and waits Antecedent control Planned ignoring Withdraws attention from minor attention-seeking misbehaviour such as whining Extinction (Section 4.6) Time-out Removes the child for a few minutes to a dull spot after aggression or defiance Negative punishment (Section 4.6) Loss of privileges Removes a privilege or points after a rule is broken Response cost (Section 4.6) Monitoring and problem solving Supervises an older child's whereabouts; negotiates rules and contracts Antecedent control; contingency contracting Notice what is missing from the table. PMT does not teach parents to use negative reinforcement ; on the contrary, its whole design is an escape from the negative reinforcement trap of Figure 4.14. The parent stops withdrawing demands when the child screams, and so stops negatively reinforcing the screaming; the parent learns to tolerate the extinction burst that follows (Section 4.6), and so stops being negatively reinforced for giving in. Notice too that "ignoring" in PMT means ignoring minor behaviour that is maintained by attention. It is useless for behaviour that is maintained by escape, and dangerous for behaviour that could hurt someone. Let us return to Arjun, the seven-year-old whose homework tantrums you analysed in Table 4.2. The functional analysis showed that his tantrums were maintained by escape from maths: each tantrum ended the demand. His mother, Kavitha, adds that he also whines and tugs at her whenever she is on the phone, and that his grandmother, who lives with them in Mysuru, often quietens him with a sweet. The two behaviours have different functions, so they get different treatment. In the first two sessions Kavitha tracks both and learns to give ten minutes a day of "special time", in which Arjun chooses a game and she simply watches, describes and praises. Then a chart goes up on the fridge: each ten-minute block of homework finished earns a star, and five stars on a weekday earn the choice of Sunday activity, usually cricket in the park with his father; cartoons come only after homework, which is the Premack principle at work. For the homework tantrums Kavitha learns escape extinction: she gives one clear instruction ("Write these five sums now"), keeps the work in place however loudly he screams, and calmly guides him back to the table; Arjun is given a card he can hold up once a session to ask for a five-minute break, an acceptable way of getting what the tantrum used to get. For the whining on the phone she learns planned ignoring, together with praise as soon as he plays quietly. Throwing a book earns three minutes of time-out on a chair in the hall. The therapist warns the family about the extinction burst, and it comes on the fourth evening: the longest tantrum Arjun has ever had, which Kavitha survives only because she knew it was coming. The grandmother's sweets are the other hurdle. Rather than arguing with her, the therapist gives her a job: she is the one who puts the stars on the chart and praises him for them, so her affection now follows good behaviour instead of tantrums. By the sixth week the tantrums have fallen from about eight a week to one or two, and homework that used to take two stormy hours takes forty minutes. Nothing here required insight into Arjun's unconscious. It required the adults who control his consequences to change them, consistently. The evidence for PMT is among the strongest for any psychological treatment of children. Controlled trials show reductions in oppositional and aggressive behaviour at home and often at school, and Patterson's group reported that untreated brothers and sisters of the referred child improved as well, because the parents' new skills spread to the whole household. Several limits are equally clear. PMT works best with younger children, up to about the end of primary school; adolescents need adapted programmes that bring in peers and school (Chapter 7 describes functional family therapy and multisystemic therapy). Families under heavy strain, with poverty, parental depression, marital conflict or a single parent without support, drop out more often and gain less, which led Kazdin to add attention to the parents' own stress and to the alliance between therapist and parent. In the United Kingdom, guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends group parent training programmes for children aged about 3 to 11 with conduct problems. Patterson's programme had many descendants. A parallel line began with Constance Hanf at the University of Oregon Medical School in the late 1960s, whose two-stage model first taught mothers to follow the child's lead in play (the "child's game") and then to give clear commands and use time-out (the "parent's game"); it shaped Rex Forehand and Robert McMahon's Helping the Noncompliant Child (1981) and Russell Barkley 's Defiant Children (1987). Three descendants appear in examinations by name (Table 4.27), and you need only their outlines here (Chapter 10 returns to them in child clinical work). Programme Developer Hallmark Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT) Sheila Eyberg (from the 1970s, building on Hanf) Two phases: child-directed interaction, using the PRIDE skills (praise, reflect, imitate, describe, enjoy), then parent-directed interaction with clear commands and time-out; the therapist coaches the parent live from behind a one-way mirror through an earpiece; for children of about 2 to 7 The Incredible Years Carolyn Webster-Stratton (University of Washington, Seattle, from the early 1980s) Group programme built on videotape modelling: parents watch and discuss short filmed scenes of parents handling everyday situations; linked teacher and child (Dinosaur School) programmes Triple P (Positive Parenting Program) Matthew R. In a joint or extended family a grandparent, an aunt or an older cousin may control as many of the child's consequences as the parents do, and one adult who gives in can keep the coercive cycle alive for everyone. Mothers often attend alone because fathers cannot leave work, so practical plans (a phone call with the father, a Sunday session) matter. Threats ("the police will take you away"), shaming in front of relatives and physical punishment are still common, and many parents need to see a gentler method work before they will give up the slipper. Rewards should fit the household: extra time on the phone, choosing the Sunday breakfast, an outing with a favourite uncle. The principles do not change; the people and the reinforcers do. Exam trap "Which is not a part of parent management training?" Negative reinforcement (IHBAS 2020). Attending to positive behaviour, rewarding positive behaviour and ignoring undesirable behaviour are all core PMT skills; negative reinforcement is the trap PMT teaches parents to get out of. A related item (Amity 2023): a parent who deliberately ignores a child's temper tantrums to discourage them is using extinction , not operant escape or operant avoidance; the old key answer "operant escape" was wrong and has been corrected to extinction, and the full trap is in Section 4.6 under extinction. If anyone in that scene is learning by escape, it is the parent who gives in to stop the noise, not the parent who ignores it. Behaviour in the classroom A classroom is a small society with one adult, many children and a great many consequences, most of them delivered without anyone noticing. When the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis began in 1968, a large share of its first studies came from classrooms, and the most influential came from the group of Wesley C. Becker at the University of Illinois. Their first discovery was uncomfortable for teachers. In one study the observers asked a teacher to stop praising a class that had been behaving reasonably well; disruptive behaviour rose. When she was then asked to increase her disapproving comments ("Sit down!", "Stop talking!"), disruptive behaviour rose further. In a related study in classrooms of young children, the more often the teachers told children to sit down, the more often the children stood up; when the teachers instead praised children who were sitting and working, standing fell. The explanation is the same as in Patterson's homes. A reprimand is attention, and for many children attention is a powerful positive reinforcer, so a teacher who notices children mainly when they misbehave is reinforcing misbehaviour. Yet the teacher is herself reinforced for reprimanding, because the child usually stops for a moment, and that brief relief negatively reinforces the reprimand. Becker and his colleagues called this the criticism trap : the teacher's criticism works in the short run, which keeps her criticising, and backfires in the long run, which keeps the children misbehaving. The way out was tested directly. Key study: Madsen, Becker and Thomas, "Rules, praise and ignoring" (1968) Question. Which of a teacher's everyday tools actually control classroom behaviour: stating rules, ignoring misbehaviour or praising good behaviour? Method. Charles Madsen , Becker and Don Thomas worked in two primary-school classrooms, observing three children (two in one class, one in the other) whose behaviour was a problem. Observers recorded inappropriate behaviour at short intervals while the teachers introduced the three tools one after another: rules alone (stated and reviewed several times a day), then rules plus ignoring of inappropriate behaviour, then rules plus ignoring plus praise for appropriate behaviour. In one class the teacher then briefly returned to her old ways, and finally reinstated the full package. Result. Rules alone made little difference. Adding the ignoring of misbehaviour produced no clear improvement either. Only when praise for appropriate behaviour was added did inappropriate behaviour fall substantially; in the class with the reversal it rose again when the teacher returned to her old ways and fell when the package returned. Conclusion. Praise for appropriate behaviour is the active ingredient; ignoring works only when it is paired with reinforcement of the alternative. Criticism. The study involved three children in two classrooms, and ignoring cannot work when classmates, not the teacher, supply the attention that maintains the misbehaviour. From this and later work came the basic package of praise and ignore : a few clear rules, stated positively and displayed ("Raise your hand to speak", not "Don't shout out"); frequent, specific and immediate praise for children who follow them ("Meena, you put your hand up and waited; thank you"); planned ignoring of minor attention-seeking misbehaviour; and firm, brief action for anything dangerous. Teachers are often advised to aim for several positive comments for every negative one. Even reprimands can be made less reinforcing: in 1970 K. Daniel O'Leary and his colleagues found that soft reprimands, audible only to the child concerned, reduced disruptive behaviour more than loud reprimands delivered in front of the whole class. Praise and ignoring have a weakness, however, which the Key study's criticism points to. In many classrooms the most powerful reinforcer for clowning is not the teacher's attention but the laughter of classmates, and no amount of teacher ignoring can extinguish that. The solution was to make the classmates part of the contingency. A group contingency is an arrangement in which reinforcement depends on the behaviour of a group, or of particular members of it. Behaviour analysts distinguish three kinds: in an independent group contingency every child earns the same reward by meeting the criterion individually; in a dependent group contingency the whole class earns a reward according to the behaviour of one child or a few; and in an interdependent group contingency the reward depends on the performance of the group (or a team) as a whole. The most famous interdependent contingency is a game. Key study: the Good Behaviour Game (Barrish, Saunders and Wolf, 1969) Question. Can a classroom's own competitive spirit be harnessed to reduce disruption, without tokens or prizes bought from outside? Method. Harriet H. Barrish , Muriel Saunders and Montrose Wolf worked in a fourth-grade class in Kansas that included several children described as problem pupils. After observers had recorded baseline rates of two behaviours, talking out without permission and leaving one's seat, the teacher divided the class into two teams and announced a game. Every time any member of a team talked out or left his seat, a mark went up against that team on the blackboard. The team with fewer marks at the end of the period won, and both teams could win if each stayed under an agreed number of marks. Winners earned everyday privileges such as wearing victory tags, being first in line for lunch and extra free time. The game was introduced first in the maths period and later in the reading period, and was withdrawn and reinstated, so that each period served as a control for the other. Result. Talking out and out-of-seat behaviour fell sharply whenever, and only when, the game was in force. Conclusion. An interdependent group contingency using privileges the school already had produced large, reliable reductions in disruption. Criticism. One class, one teacher and a short study; and a team contingency can invite peer pressure on the child who keeps losing the game for his team, which the teacher must watch for (one remedy is to let a persistent offender form a "team" of his own). The Good Behaviour Game became one of the most thoroughly tested interventions in education. From 1985 the psychiatrist and prevention researcher Sheppard G. Kellam and his colleagues ran a randomised field trial in first-grade classrooms in Baltimore, in which some classes played the game and others did not. The children were followed into adulthood. Among boys who had been highly aggressive in first grade, those who had played the game had lower rates of drug and alcohol use disorders, regular smoking and antisocial personality disorder as young adults than comparable boys from ordinary classrooms. Results of this kind led the prevention scientist Dennis Embry to call the game a "behavioural vaccine": a cheap, simple procedure that, given early, protects against later problems. Three further tools complete the classroom kit, and Table 4.28 brings the whole kit together. A classroom token economy applies the principles of Ayllon and Azrin's ward programmes (Section 4.5) to a class: children earn points, stamps or stickers for specified behaviours, and exchange them for back-up reinforcers such as privileges, small items or free time. In 1967 O'Leary and Becker introduced such a system into a class of disruptive nine-year-olds; disruptive behaviour fell sharply, and the teacher was then able to stretch the interval between exchanges and rely increasingly on praise. Tokens are meant to be faded, because the aim is behaviour maintained by the ordinary rewards of school. Critics have argued that tangible rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation: in a well-known 1973 study by Mark Lepper , David Greene and Richard Nisbett, preschool children who had been promised a certificate for drawing with felt-tip pens later chose to draw less in free time than children who had not. The later meta-analytic debate suggests that the danger is real mainly when expected, tangible rewards are given for activities the child already enjoys. For behaviour the child does not yet perform, or for dull but necessary tasks, rewards combined with praise and then faded do little harm. The second tool is response cost in the classroom : the child begins the period with a set number of points (five stars on a card taped to his desk, say) and loses one for each agreed rule-break, keeping what remains for a reward. It is the classroom form of the response cost described in Section 4.6 (a negative punishment), and it is often combined with points earned for good behaviour. It has been used particularly with inattentive and hyperactive children, who respond well to frequent, immediate consequences. Two rules keep it fair: the child should never fall below zero, and he should be able to earn points back by behaving well. The third tool links school to home. A daily report card (DRC, also called a home-school note) lists three to five target behaviours for one child, each defined precisely ("Completes the written work in the maths period", "Follows the teacher's instructions with no more than one reminder"). The teacher marks each target yes or no, period by period, the child carries the card home, and the parents provide a reward that evening when an agreed number of targets has been met. The DRC exploits the fact that parents usually have much more powerful reinforcers than teachers do, and it keeps the two sets of adults talking. William Pelham and his colleagues made it a central part of the behavioural treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and it formed part of the behavioural arm of the large American multimodal treatment study of ADHD (Chapter 10).
