Tool What the teacher does Principle Associated with Rules, praise and ignoring Posts a few positive rules, praises children who follow them, ignores minor misbehaviour Positive reinforcement plus extinction Madsen, Becker and Thomas (1968) Soft reprimands Corrects privately and quietly rather than publicly Reduces the attention value of correction O'Leary and colleagues (1970) Good Behaviour Game Each rule-break puts a mark against the team; teams under the limit win privileges Interdependent group contingency Barrish, Saunders and Wolf (1969); Kellam's Baltimore trials Classroom token economy Children earn points exchangeable for privileges; exchanges are gradually spaced out Token (secondary) reinforcement O'Leary and Becker (1967) Classroom response cost Child starts with points and loses one per rule-break Negative punishment Widely used for inattentive, hyperactive children Daily report card Teacher rates a few targets each period; parents reward at home Home-based reinforcement Pelham and colleagues (ADHD) Let us put the kit to work in an Indian classroom. Mrs Shobha teaches Class 4 in a government primary school in Mysuru. She has 46 children, one blackboard and a voice that is giving out by lunchtime. A trainee clinical psychologist from a nearby college spends two Kannada periods counting: in each 40-minute period there are about 50 call-outs and 30 instances of children leaving their seats, and Mrs Shobha reprimands about 25 times and praises about 3. That last pair of numbers is the criticism trap in plain figures. Together they draw up four rules, written in Kannada and English on a chart beside the blackboard: raise your hand to speak; stay in your seat during work time; keep your hands and feet to yourself; listen when someone is speaking. Mrs Shobha sets herself a target of at least four specific praises for every reprimand, and keeps a tally with a pebble moved from one pocket to the other. Then the class plays the Good Behaviour Game. The two rows by the windows become team Kaveri and the two rows by the door team Kabini. Each call-out or seat-leaving by a team member earns a tally mark under the team's name, and any team with five marks or fewer at the end of the period wins: its members line up first for the mid-day meal, choose the song for the afternoon prayer and get five extra minutes in the games period. Within a week the children are policing their own rows, cheerfully. One boy, Mohan, keeps collecting marks against Kaveri, and the trainee suspects attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and arranges an assessment (Assessment book). Meanwhile Mohan gets his own small team (so that his team-mates do not suffer for him) and a daily report card pasted into his school diary, which Indian parents are already used to signing: three targets, a tick or a cross for each period, and twenty minutes of cricket with his older brother after school on days with at least two ticks out of three. After three weeks the counts are about 12 call-outs and 8 seat-leavings a period, and Mrs Shobha is praising more than twenty times a period and reprimanding about five. To make the gains last, the game is then played on unannounced days and in unannounced periods, so that the children cannot predict when it will count, and praise carries more of the load. Indian context Section 17 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment of children in school. Many teachers were trained to rely on the cane and on public shaming, and a ban alone does not tell them what to do instead. Behavioural classroom management supplies the answer: clear rules, generous praise, group games and home-school notes are cheap, need no equipment, work in large classes and can be taught to teachers in a few workshops. For a clinical psychologist, consulting with a school is often the most efficient way to help many children at once. Exam trap The Good Behaviour Game is Barrish, Saunders and Wolf (1969) , an interdependent group contingency (team-based); it is not Ayllon and Azrin's token economy (1968), which was built for hospital wards. In the classic classroom studies, ignoring alone failed ; praise for appropriate behaviour was the active ingredient. A teacher whose frequent "Sit down!" makes children stand more often is caught in the criticism trap : her attention positively reinforces the misbehaviour, and the child's brief compliance negatively reinforces her criticism. A daily report card is a home-school contingency; classroom response cost, like time-out, is negative punishment , not negative reinforcement. 4.11 Evaluating Behaviour Therapy Lower yield · not asked yet In 1952 Eysenck demanded that psychotherapy prove itself, and he offered behaviour therapy as the treatment that would. That was a bold move, because it invited everyone to judge behaviour therapy by the same standard. More than seventy years later we can do exactly that. This final section asks four questions. What does behaviour therapy do best? Did the symptom substitution its critics predicted ever appear? Where are its limits? And are its methods, especially the aversive ones and the deliberate control of other people's behaviour, ethical? The tools for weighing therapy research (randomised controlled trials, meta-analysis, the criteria for calling a treatment empirically supported, the debate over common factors) are taught in Chapter 8; here we use their results. What behaviour therapy does best No school of therapy has been tested more often. As Richard Sharf observes, behaviour therapy's effectiveness has been studied with more populations and more disorders than that of any other approach, partly because its founders built measurement into the treatment itself. When a task force of the American Psychological Association's Division of Clinical Psychology published its first list of empirically validated treatments in 1995, the large majority of the well-established entries were behavioural or cognitive behavioural. Broad comparisons tell a more modest story: when Smith and Glass pooled 375 controlled studies in 1977, the different families of therapy differed little once the studies were made comparable (Chapter 8). The two findings are not in conflict. Across the general run of outpatient complaints, most well-conducted therapies help to a similar degree; for particular, well-defined problems, behavioural methods are often clearly the best available. An early head-to-head trial showed both sides of this picture. Key study: Sloane and colleagues, psychotherapy versus behaviour therapy (1975) Question. When experienced practitioners of each approach treat ordinary outpatients, does behaviour therapy do better than psychodynamic psychotherapy? Method. R. Bruce Sloane and his colleagues at Temple University randomly assigned 94 outpatients, most with moderately severe anxiety problems or personality difficulties, to about four months of behaviour therapy, short-term analytically oriented psychotherapy or a waiting list with minimal contact. The therapists were experienced and respected in their own approach. Independent assessors who did not know the treatment rated the patients' main target symptoms and general adjustment. Result. At four months both treated groups had improved significantly more than the waiting list on their target symptoms, and they did not differ much from each other; behaviour therapy showed some advantage on overall adjustment. By the one-year follow-up the differences had largely disappeared. Unexpectedly, the behaviour therapists were rated at least as warm, empathic and genuine as the psychotherapists, and patients in both groups named much the same things as most helpful, including the therapist's personality and being able to talk to an understanding person. Conclusion. Behaviour therapy was at least as effective as psychotherapy for general outpatient problems, and the relationship mattered in both. Criticism. The treatments were brief, the sample mixed, and a waiting list cannot be kept untreated for a year. Where, then, is behaviour therapy at its strongest? Table 4.29 lists the main areas, with the section of this chapter in which each treatment is taught. Running through them is one pattern. Behaviour therapy does best when the problem is a specific, observable behaviour or response, when something identifiable in the present (an avoidance, a ritual, a reinforcer, a missing skill) keeps it going, and when the people around the client can change that something. Anxiety disorders fit this description almost perfectly, which is why exposure in one form or another is part of every evidence-based psychological treatment for phobias, panic disorder, social anxiety, post-traumatic stress and obsessive-compulsive disorder. For OCD, Sharf's summary of the research puts improvement with exposure and response prevention at 60 to 75 percent of patients, although only about a quarter are entirely free of symptoms at the end of treatment: a large effect, but not a cure for everyone. Childhood problems fit the pattern too, because children live inside contingencies that adults control. The bell and pad remains the most effective single treatment for bed-wetting, applied behaviour analysis is the best-supported psychological approach to autism (the Lovaas programme's 1987 report that 47 percent of intensively treated children reached normal intellectual and educational functioning, against 2 percent of controls, is examined critically in Section 4.6), habit reversal is the leading behavioural treatment for tics, and parent management training is among the best-supported treatments for disruptive behaviour. In adults, stimulus control and sleep restriction form the core of the first-line psychological treatment for insomnia, contingency management produces some of the largest effects in the treatment of drug use, and behavioural activation, once dismissed as a mere component of cognitive therapy, matched antidepressant medication for more severely depressed patients in a 2006 trial led by Sona Dimidjian . In India the Healthy Activity Program, a brief form of behavioural activation delivered by lay counsellors in Goa, showed in 2017 that the approach can be taken to people who will never see a clinical psychologist (Chapter 9). And in conditions such as depression, where several bona fide therapies have been compared directly, the differences between behavioural and other well-conducted treatments are usually small. Exam trap Match the problem to the behavioural treatment with the strongest record. OCD: exposure and response prevention (IHBAS 2020; RML 2024), not systematic desensitisation alone. Tics: habit reversal training (Real PYQ 2025); habit reversal has also been adapted for stuttering, but the keyed "primary" use is tics, and it is not the treatment of obsessive-compulsive rituals or aggression. Autism: the Lovaas programme (RML 2022), not aphasia, depression or alcoholism. Depression: behavioural activation , which encourages clients to engage in rewarding, meaningful activity (JEMAS 2025), not childhood analysis, relaxation or hypnosis. And the front-line treatment for schizophrenia is antipsychotic medication (RML 2021); social skills training, stress management training and CBT are valuable additions, not the front line. The symptom substitution debate Of all the predictions made about behaviour therapy, the most confident came from its psychoanalytic critics. If a phobia, a tic or a bed-wetting habit is only the visible expression of an unconscious conflict (Section 3.2), then removing it directly is like plugging one hole in a leaking pipe: the pressure is still there and must find another way out. symptom substitution is the psychodynamic prediction that if a symptom is removed without the underlying conflict being resolved, the conflict will re-emerge in the form of a new, perhaps worse, symptom. The prediction followed naturally from Freud's hydraulic model of psychic energy, and it was the analysts' main objection to every technique in this chapter. Desensitising a phobia, on this view, was at best cosmetic and at worst dangerous, because it removed the patient's defence without touching the conflict it defended against. Behaviour therapists answered in two ways. The first was Eysenck's flat denial, quoted in Section 4.1: there is no neurosis underlying the symptom, but merely the symptom itself, so getting rid of the symptom eliminates the neurosis. The second was subtler. In 1958 Yates pointed out in a paper on symptoms and symptom substitution that learning theory could itself predict the appearance of a new response in some circumstances. Clark Hull had described a habit-family hierarchy : an animal that has learned several ways of reaching a goal uses the strongest, and if that one is blocked, the next strongest appears. If a behaviour therapist suppressed one response while the drive and the reinforcer behind it remained, a different response serving the same purpose might well take its place. Whether new symptoms appear was therefore an empirical question, and its answer would not automatically confirm either theory. So the behaviour therapists went and looked. The answer, study after study, was that symptom substitution rarely happened. In Gordon Paul's comparison of desensitisation and insight therapy (Section 4.2), the students whose public-speaking anxiety had been desensitised were followed up two years later (Paul reported the follow-up in 1967): their gains had held, there was no sign of substitute symptoms, and if anything some improvement had spread to other anxieties. The bed-wetting alarm offered an especially clean test, because enuresis was a favourite example of a symptom with a hidden emotional meaning, and analysts warned that a child made dry by conditioning would become anxious or disturbed in some other way. When the psychologist Bruce Baker compared children treated with the bell and pad with untreated children in 1969, those who became dry showed no new problems, and on measures of adjustment they seemed, if anything, happier and more confident than before. In 1982 Alan Kazdin reviewed the whole literature for the Psychological Bulletin . His conclusions have been the standard answer ever since. Evidence for symptom substitution is weak. When behaviours that were not treated change after treatment, they change for the better much more often than for the worse, a process he described as response covariation: treating one problem tends to send ripples of improvement through others, as when a child who stops wetting the bed starts going on school trips. And the hypothesis, as the analysts stated it, could hardly be tested at all, because it specified neither what the new symptom would be nor when it would appear; any new difficulty, years later, could be counted as a substitute, and its absence explained as "not yet". Figure 4.15 sets the two predictions beside what the evidence showed. Psychodynamic prediction Learning-theory prediction Unconscious conflict is never resolved Symptom A is removed by behaviour therapy Pressure finds a new outlet: symptom B appears Problem kept going by present triggers and consequences Triggers and consequences are changed; behaviour changes No new symptom; other areas often improve as well What the evidence shows Substitution rarely appears (Paul 1967; Baker 1969; Kazdin's 1982 review). Improvements in untreated problems are more common than new problems. A new problem that does appear usually serves the old behaviour's function, so functional analysis, not a search for hidden conflict, prevents it. Figure 4.15 The symptom substitution debate. The psychodynamic model predicts that removing a symptom without resolving the conflict produces a new symptom; the learning model predicts that changing the conditions that maintain a problem removes it. The evidence largely supports the learning model, with one important qualification shown in the bottom box. That qualification matters, and it is where the behaviourists' own logic did the most useful work. Sometimes a new problem really does appear. A boy whose head-banging is suppressed by a reprimand begins to bite his hand instead; a woman who stops checking the gas tap starts asking her husband whether it is off. Behaviour therapists explain such cases without any appeal to unconscious conflict. Behaviours that produce the same consequence form a response class , a set of different behaviours that serve the same function for the person. If the head-banging served to escape from difficult tasks (the kind of function Iwata's experimental analysis identified, Section 4.1), suppressing it while leaving the escape contingency intact simply makes room for another member of the response class. Reassurance-seeking is a member of the same response class as checking, which is exactly why exposure and response prevention blocks both (Section 4.3). The remedy is therefore not to dig for a hidden conflict but to ask what the behaviour was for, and to teach an acceptable alternative that serves the same function, as functional communication training, a form of differential reinforcement of alternative behaviour (Section 4.6), does. In this sense the symptom substitution debate ended with a draw that both sides could learn from: the analysts were right that a symptom often "means" something, and the behaviourists were right that what it means can be found in its present consequences. Exam trap Symptom substitution is a psychoanalytic prediction about what happens when symptoms are treated directly; it is not a behavioural technique, and it is not the defence mechanism of substitution or displacement. If it appears as an option for "practising relaxation while visualising situations of increasing intensity" (RML 2020), reject it: that is systematic desensitisation. The key names: Yates (1958) argued that learning theory could itself predict new responses through the habit-family hierarchy; Kazdin (1982) reviewed the evidence and found substitution rare and positive side effects (response covariation) more common. A truly new problem after treatment is best explained by a shared function (a response class), and prevented by functional analysis. The limits: generalisation, maintenance and the cognitive critique If symptom substitution was the critics' wrong prediction, generalisation was behaviour therapy's real weak point, and behaviour therapists were the first to say so. A change produced in one setting does not automatically appear in others. generalisation in this applied sense is the appearance of a treated behaviour change in settings, with people and in behaviours other than those in which it was trained; maintenance is its persistence over time after the treatment contingencies have been withdrawn. A token economy that transforms behaviour on a hospital ward may have little effect once the patient goes home, because home has no tokens. A child taught to greet people in the clinic may not greet anyone at school. In a follow-up published in 1973, Lovaas and his colleagues found that autistic children who had been discharged to institutions lost much of what they had gained, whereas children whose parents had been trained to carry on the treatment kept their gains and in some cases improved further. The lesson was that the natural environment has to be part of the treatment. In 1977 Trevor Stokes and Donald Baer reviewed the applied literature and found that the commonest "technique" for producing generalisation was what they called train and hope : teach the behaviour in one setting and hope that it spreads. They described better strategies, and their list is still the backbone of good practice. Teach behaviours that the natural environment will go on reinforcing (praise from classmates, for example), so that the new behaviour is "trapped" by ordinary consequences. Train with several different examples, people and settings rather than one. Train loosely, varying the conditions, so that the behaviour does not become tied to a single cue. Make the contingencies indiscriminable, by moving from continuous to intermittent and delayed reinforcement, so that the client cannot tell when reinforcement has stopped. Include stimuli from the real setting in training (the teacher comes to the clinic, or training moves to the classroom). And teach the client to manage his own behaviour (Section 4.9), because a client who carries the contingencies with him takes them everywhere. Mrs Shobha's unannounced games and Arjun's grandmother putting the stars on the chart are both examples. Maintenance raises a related problem. Several of the successes in this chapter are followed by a predictable proportion of relapses: fears return after exposure (spontaneous recovery, renewal and reinstatement, Section 4.3), some children start wetting again after the bell and pad, and many people treated for addictive behaviour relapse within months. Behaviour therapy's answers are practical rather than theoretical. Overlearning continues treatment beyond the first success; booster sessions are planned in advance; reinforcement is thinned gradually instead of being stopped; and in the addictions the cognitive behavioural method of relapse prevention teaches the client to anticipate high-risk situations and to treat a single lapse as a mistake to learn from rather than a collapse (Section 9.9). The deepest criticism concerned the theory. Behaviour therapy had advertised itself as applied learning theory, and in 1965 the psychologists Louis Breger and James McGaugh argued in the Psychological Bulletin that this was largely a figure of speech: the "learning theory" invoked in the clinic was a loose borrowing of terms from animal laboratories, the laboratory principles themselves were disputed, and the techniques could not be derived from them in any strict sense. Some of the evidence in this chapter supports them. Systematic desensitisation works, but not because of reciprocal inhibition (Section 4.2); paradoxical intention works, but its learning account was written after the fact. Noam Chomsky 's famous 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior had already argued that human language, and much else, cannot be explained by a history of reinforcement alone. And as early as 1967 Gordon Paul had reframed the whole outcome question in a sentence still quoted in every research methods course: what treatment, by whom, is most effective for this individual with that specific problem, and under which set of circumstances? (Chapter 8.) The criticism that changed the field, however, was cognitive. Behaviour therapists themselves noticed that their clients' expectations, interpretations and self-statements kept getting in the way of, or doing the work of, the conditioning procedures. Albert Bandura showed that people learn by watching, without being reinforced themselves, and in 1977 he argued that all effective treatments may work by raising self-efficacy (Section 4.7 and Section 5.1). Arnold Lazarus, one of the founders, broadened his practice into "broad-spectrum" behaviour therapy in Behavior Therapy and Beyond (1971) and later into multimodal therapy (Chapter 5). Thoughts began to be treated as covert behaviours that could be conditioned, as in covert sensitisation (Section 4.4), and in the 1970s Michael Mahoney and Donald Meichenbaum announced the merger of cognition and behaviour modification. The result was cognitive behaviour therapy, the story of Section 5.1. It is worth noticing what did not happen. Behavioural techniques were not abandoned; they were absorbed. Exposure, activity scheduling, reinforcement, behavioural experiments and skills training are the working parts of almost every cognitive behavioural treatment, and the third-wave therapies of the 1990s (behavioural activation, acceptance and commitment therapy, dialectical behaviour therapy) brought radical behavioural ideas back to the centre. A last criticism, that behaviour therapy is mechanical and cold, has fared worst of all. The Temple study found behaviour therapists at least as warm and empathic as psychotherapists, and every technique in this chapter depends on a client willing to do frightening or tedious things because he trusts the person asking him to. Exposure without a working alliance is a recipe for drop-out. Exam trap "Train and hope" is the problem Stokes and Baer (1977) named, not their recommended strategy. Generalisation is spread across settings, people and behaviours; maintenance is persistence over time; do not swap them. The famous question "What treatment, by whom, is most effective for this individual with that specific problem, and under which set of circumstances?" is Gordon Paul's (1967). Self-efficacy (1977) is Bandura's , not Skinner's or Wolpe's, and it is the bridge from behaviour therapy to CBT (Section 5.1). The ethics of aversive methods and of control Every therapy raises ethical questions, but behaviour therapy raises some of them in an unusually sharp form, for three reasons (the first two are stressed by Richard Sharf). First, the public has long believed that behaviour modification is something done to people against their will. Second, behaviour therapy is used with a wider range of people than any other approach, including infants, people with severe intellectual disability, autistic children and severely psychotic patients, many of whom cannot give informed consent; for them it is often the only suitable psychological treatment, and the therapist must decide on behalf of someone who cannot fully decide for himself. Third, behaviour therapy works by deliberately arranging consequences, sometimes unpleasant ones, in settings such as hospitals, residential schools and prisons where the client has little power. The ethical safeguards that grew up around it address each of these points. The first safeguard is informed consent : agreement to a specific intervention, given voluntarily by a person who is competent to decide, after he has been told in a language and manner he understands what the procedure involves, its likely benefits and risks, and the alternatives, including the alternative of no treatment, and who knows that he may withdraw. Consent matters for every technique in this chapter (Section 4.3 showed why flooding is offered as a choice, never imposed), but it is essential for aversive methods. Where a client cannot consent, behaviour therapists seek partial consent where possible (a patient with schizophrenia who agrees to a programme during a period of lucidity), the consent of a parent or guardian, and in institutions the approval of an ethics or human rights committee that reviews the programme independently. The second safeguard is the least restrictive alternative : the principle that a client should receive care and treatment in the least confining and least intrusive way that can achieve the goal. It came into mental health law through American court decisions of the 1960s and early 1970s, beginning with Lake v. Cameron (1966), which required courts to consider less restrictive alternatives to committing a person to hospital, and it was written into the standards for institutions by Wyatt v. Stickney (decided 1971; standards ordered 1972), the Alabama case that set minimum standards for state institutions and declared that residents had a right to the least restrictive conditions necessary to achieve the purpose of their habilitation or treatment. Applied to behaviour change, it produces a ladder of procedures (Figure 4.16; compare the four-level version in Figure 4.9, Section 4.6). Reinforcement-based methods come first; extinction, response cost and time-out come next; overcorrection and other mildly aversive consequences come later; and aversive stimulation such as electric shock sits at the top, where it is rarely if ever justified. A therapist may move up a rung only when the methods below have been tried properly and have failed, and each rung requires more safeguards: written consent, committee review, careful data, and a time limit after which the programme must be reviewed. The same case had a direct effect on token economies: the minimum standards it set turned many basic amenities (a comfortable bed, adequate meals, privacy, one's own clothes) into rights, which could no longer be used as reinforcers that a patient had to earn. Modern positive behaviour support aims to solve almost every problem on the bottom two rungs, guided by a functional analysis. The least restrictive principle has a rival, and the tension between them is real. In 1988 a task force of the Association for Behavior Analysis, whose report was written by Ron Van Houten and his colleagues, published a statement on the right to effective treatment , arguing that clients are entitled to the most effective treatment procedures available, not merely the least intrusive ones. Imagine a girl with severe intellectual disability whose head-hitting has detached a retina. A slow reinforcement programme that takes months to work is less restrictive, but it may cost her the other eye. Some behaviour analysts argued that, in such rare cases, a brief, well-monitored aversive procedure that works quickly is the more ethical choice. From the late 1980s the positive behaviour support movement answered that the dilemma is usually false: when a thorough functional analysis (Section 4.1) identifies what the behaviour is for, and the child is taught another way of getting it, aversive procedures are almost never necessary. That view has largely prevailed. In 2020 the United States Food and Drug Administration banned electrical stimulation devices used to reduce self-injurious or aggressive behaviour, a ban aimed chiefly at one residential school in Massachusetts that had used contingent skin shock for decades; the ban has since been fought over in the courts. The darkest chapter in the history of aversive methods was their use to change sexual orientation, described in Section 4.4. From the 1950s into the 1970s many people, most of them gay men, were given electric shocks or nausea-inducing drugs while looking at pictures of people of their own sex. Three ethical lessons came out of it. First, consent given under the pressure of stigma, family shame and criminal law is not free consent, however willingly the form is signed. Second, the goal itself was defined by social prejudice rather than by any harm to the client. Third, the methods did not do what was claimed: at best they suppressed arousal for a while, and they left many people depressed and ashamed. In 1973 the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from its diagnostic manual, and in his presidential address to the Association for Advancement of Behavior Therapy, published in 1976, Gerald C. Davison argued that behaviour therapists should stop offering sexual orientation change programmes altogether, even to clients who ask for them, because offering them confirms the prejudice that homosexuality is a disorder. In India the Supreme Court decriminalised consensual same-sex relations in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), the Indian Psychiatric Society, which had stated in 2014 that there is no evidence that homosexuality is a mental illness, reaffirmed that position the same year, and after a 2021 order of the Madras High Court the National Medical Commission declared conversion therapy to be professional misconduct in 2022. Behaviour therapists did not leave these questions to their critics. In 1977 the Association for Advancement of Behavior Therapy published "Ethical issues for human services", a set of questions that any therapist, of any school, can ask before starting treatment. Paraphrased, they are: Have the goals of treatment been adequately considered, and has the client taken part in choosing them? Has the choice of treatment methods been adequately considered, including less intrusive alternatives? Is the client's participation voluntary? When another person or agency (a parent, a court, an institution) has arranged the therapy, have the interests of the client been sufficiently considered? Has the adequacy of the treatment been evaluated, with data? Has the confidentiality of the treatment relationship been protected? Does the therapist refer the client to another therapist when necessary? Is the therapist qualified to provide the treatment? Behind the particular questions about aversive methods lies a larger one: should psychologists be in the business of controlling human behaviour at all? The question was argued most famously by Skinner and Carl Ransom Rogers (1902 to 1987) at a symposium at the American Psychological Association's convention in 1956, published in Science the same year under the title "Some issues concerning the control of human behavior". Skinner's position was that behaviour is always controlled, by parents, teachers, employers, governments and advertisers, whether we admit it or not. Refusing to plan that control does not abolish it; it merely leaves it to accident and to people with worse motives. A science of behaviour, he argued, as he had imagined in his utopian novel Walden Two (1948), could design a culture in which people behave well because good behaviour is reinforced. Rogers granted the growing power of the behavioural sciences but asked two questions Skinner could not answer from inside his science. Who chooses the goals, given that the choice of goals is a matter of values that science itself cannot settle? And who controls the controllers? Rogers proposed instead that science could be used to free people: his own research suggested that when a therapist provides certain conditions, clients become more self-directing, more open and more responsible, and less in need of control. Neither man converted the other, and they argued again at greater length in 1962. But the debate had a postscript that delighted behaviourists. In 1966 Charles B. Truax analysed recordings of one of Rogers's own therapy cases and found that Rogers did not respond to everything his client said with equal warmth: he gave more empathy and acceptance to some kinds of statement than to others, and those kinds of statement became more frequent as therapy went on. Even the most non-directive therapist, it seemed, was reinforcing selectively. The fair conclusion is not that all therapy is manipulation, but that all therapy involves influence, and the ethical question is whether the influence is open, agreed and in the client's interest. Skinner himself pointed out that the controlled person exerts countercontrol over the controller: clients drop out, complain, refuse and vote. He developed his views further in Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971), which was a best-seller and an object of fierce attack. The public image of behaviour therapy was shaped less by these arguments than by a novel. In Anthony Burgess's A Clockwork Orange (1962), filmed by Stanley Kubrick in 1971, the violent young Alex is "cured" by the Ludovico Technique: he is injected with a drug that makes him violently sick and, with his eyes held open, forced to watch films of brutality, until the mere thought of violence nauseates him (and, by an accident of the soundtrack, so does Beethoven's Ninth Symphony). In technical terms this is aversion therapy, a form of classical conditioning (Section 4.4), not operant behaviour modification. The prison chaplain's objection is the moral of the book: goodness that is not chosen is not goodness, and a person who can no longer choose has stopped being fully a person. The image fixed behaviour therapy in the public mind as brainwashing, and a few coercive American prison programmes of the early 1970s, which called themselves behaviour modification and were stopped after public protest and lawsuits, did nothing to dispel it. Yet the reality was close to the opposite. Aversive procedures were always a small and shrinking part of behaviour therapy. Most of the methods in this chapter rely on reinforcement and exposure, chosen with the client, and behaviour therapy's habit of writing down its goals, describing its procedures exactly and recording what happens makes it more open to scrutiny, and so to correction, than almost any other form of treatment. Indian context The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Chapter 1) turns many of these principles into law. It defines informed consent as consent for a specific intervention, given without force, undue influence, fraud, threat, mistake or misrepresentation, after the person has been told the risks, benefits and alternatives in a language and manner he understands; it deems a person to have capacity to make his own treatment decisions if he has the ability to understand the relevant information, to appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision, or to communicate it (Section 4; the Act joins the three abilities with "or"), and it allows advance directives (Section 5). Section 20 gives every person with mental illness the right to live with dignity and to protection from cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and lists among the rights of people in mental health establishments adequate food, privacy, proper clothing and facilities for leisure and recreation, so none of these can be turned into a reward to be earned in a token economy. Section 95 prohibits chaining "in any manner or form whatsoever", and Section 97 forbids seclusion and solitary confinement outright and allows physical restraint only when it is the only means of preventing imminent harm, never as a punishment or deterrent, which leaves no room for a locked, seclusionary "time-out" used as a behavioural consequence on an Indian ward. The Act also defines the least restrictive alternative (Section 2) and makes it a condition of supported (involuntary) admission that hospital care be the least restrictive option available (Sections 89 and 90). The Act defines a clinical psychologist as a mental health professional with a qualification recognised by the Rehabilitation Council of India, and the RCI's registration and code of ethics (Chapter 1) bind every practising clinical psychologist to these standards. Exam trap The least restrictive alternative came from American mental health law ( Lake v. Cameron , 1966) and was written into the standards for institutions by Wyatt v. Stickney (1971 to 1972) ; the right to effective treatment statement is Van Houten and colleagues (1988) . The Skinner and Rogers debate on the control of human behaviour was a 1956 APA symposium published in Science ; Walden Two is 1948 and Beyond Freedom and Dignity 1971, both Skinner's. The Ludovico Technique in A Clockwork Orange is aversion therapy (drug-induced nausea paired with images of violence: classical conditioning), not token economy, shaping or systematic desensitisation. Davison (1976) argued against offering sexual orientation change, and India decriminalised same-sex relations in 2018 ( Navtej Singh Johar ). Behaviour therapy in the balance How, then, should we judge behaviour therapy? It helps to separate three verdicts, because the approach won one argument, lost another and changed the rules of a third. On the evidence, behaviour therapy won. Eysenck asked whether psychotherapy could show that it did better than the passage of time, and behaviour therapists answered with the first psychological treatments that could be shown, in controlled trials, to beat placebo and alternative treatments for specific problems: exposure for phobias and panic, exposure and response prevention for obsessive-compulsive disorder, the bell and pad for bed-wetting, parent management training for defiant children, habit reversal for tics, applied behaviour analysis for autism. These methods have not been superseded. They have been absorbed, and they are the working parts of most of the evidence-based treatments in the chapters that follow. On the theory, behaviour therapy lost several battles. Reciprocal inhibition was not the reason desensitisation worked. "Learning theory" in the clinic was often a vocabulary rather than a derivation, as Breger and McGaugh complained. Human beings turned out to learn by watching and to be changed by what they expect and believe, so that cognition had to be readmitted, and the merger produced cognitive behaviour therapy. Even the symptom substitution debate, which behaviour therapists won on the facts, ended with them conceding that a symptom has a function, and that its function, not its form, is what treatment must address. On values, behaviour therapy changed the profession, and that may be its largest legacy. It insisted that a problem be defined so clearly that two observers could agree on it, that it be measured before treatment and during it, that treatment be described exactly enough for someone else to repeat it, and that a method which does not work be dropped, however elegant its theory. That discipline is now expected of every clinical psychologist, whatever his orientation, and it is the core of the scientist-practitioner identity described in Chapter 1. The ethical debates that behaviour therapy provoked, about aversive methods, about consent and about who controls whom, produced safeguards (the least restrictive alternative, the right to effective treatment, explicit questions about goals and methods) that now protect clients of every kind of therapy. Its weaknesses are just as clear. Changes made in one setting do not travel to others unless they are deliberately taught to; problems without a clear behavioural target slip through its fingers; and, as Rogers warned, a technology of change says nothing by itself about which changes are worth making or who should decide. The best behaviour therapists answer these questions with the client, not for him. Behaviour therapy's great contribution was a single, practical question: what is keeping this problem going now, and what would change it? It is one of the most useful questions in clinical psychology. The cognitive therapists of Chapter 5 kept it, and added a second: what does the person make of what is happening to him? Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Frankl's technique in which the client deliberately tries to produce the symptom he fears is called intention. In Turner and Ascher's 1979 trial, paradoxical intention for insomnia was as effective as progressive relaxation and control. Deliberately repeating a voluntary habit, over and over, until fatigue weakens it is Dunlap's method of practice. Patterson's account of how parents and children train each other to use aversive behaviour is called theory. In the coercive cycle, both the child's escalation and the parent's giving in are maintained by reinforcement. Parent-Child Interaction Therapy, with its child-directed and parent-directed phases, was developed by Sheila . A teacher whose frequent "Sit down!" makes children stand up more often is caught in the trap. The Good Behaviour Game (Barrish, Saunders and Wolf, 1969) is an example of an group contingency. The psychoanalytic prediction that a symptom removed without resolving its conflict will be replaced by a new one is called symptom . The principle, written into the standards for American institutions by Wyatt v. Stickney (1972), that treatment should be no more intrusive than necessary is the least alternative. Answers: (1) paradoxical, (2) stimulus, (3) negative (or massed), (4) coercion, (5) negative, (6) Eyberg, (7) criticism, (8) interdependent, (9) substitution, (10) restrictive. The case of Peter and the rabbit, revisited Go back to the playroom of the Heckscher Foundation and to Peter, two years and ten months old, eating at his high chair while a caged rabbit crept a little closer each day. You can now name everything Jones did. Her first method, letting Peter play beside three children who handled the rabbit happily, was live modelling (Section 4.7). Her second, feeding him while the rabbit came closer, was counterconditioning (Section 4.2): eating was the response incompatible with fear, the kind of response Wolpe would later call antagonistic to anxiety, and Wolpe's shocked cats recovered in just the same way, fed first in a room unlike the laboratory and then in rooms more and more like the cage. Keeping the rabbit close enough to be noticed but never so close that Peter stopped eating was a graded hierarchy climbed in vivo, with each step taken only when the last was calm, which is the logic of systematic desensitisation. No wonder Wolpe called Jones the mother of behaviour therapy. The way Peter's fear had spread from a rat to a fur coat, feathers and cotton wool was stimulus generalisation, and the way his recovery spread to the same objects shows that treatment can generalise too. Even the setback fits the chapter: when a large dog jumped at him on his way home from hospital and his fears came flooding back, that was reinstatement, the return of an extinguished fear that the inhibitory learning model predicts (Section 4.3). The rest of the chapter shows how far that playroom reached. Jones treated a fear as learned behaviour, watched what Peter actually did, and changed the conditions that kept the fear alive instead of searching for a hidden conflict; these are the assumptions set out in Section 4.1. Exposure, aversive methods, reinforcement programmes, modelling, relaxation, habit reversal and parent training each elaborate one of her moves, and the psychoanalytic prediction about cases like Peter's, symptom substitution, turned out to be rarely true (Section 4.11). What behaviour therapy added to her insight was careful measurement, controlled trials and an ethic of consent and the least restrictive alternative. What it learned along the way, from Bandura above all, was that what people expect and believe matters as well as what happens to them, and that lesson is where Chapter 5 begins. Chapter summary 4.1 Where Behaviour Therapy Came From and What It Assumes. Behaviour therapy applies experimentally established principles of learning to psychological problems. Its forerunners were Watson and Rayner (1920), Jones (1924), the Mowrers' bed-wetting alarm (1938) and Dunlap's work on habits, but the spur was Eysenck's 1952 claim that about two-thirds of neurotic patients improved within two years with or without psychotherapy (spontaneous remission). It grew from three roots: Wolpe, Lazarus and Rachman in South Africa; Eysenck and Monte Shapiro at the Maudsley; and Skinner's operant tradition in the United States, which became applied behaviour analysis. It treats the problem behaviour as the disorder, explained by learning models such as Mowrer's two-factor theory, refined by Seligman's preparedness and Rachman's three pathways to fear. Every case begins with a functional analysis (the ABC model, Kanfer and Saslow's SORKC, Iwata's experimental functional analysis), a target behaviour and a baseline. 4.2 Counterconditioning and Systematic Desensitisation. Counterconditioning attaches a new response, incompatible with the old one, to the same stimulus, as when Jones fed Peter while the rabbit came closer. Wolpe produced anxiety in cats with shock alone, removed it by feeding them in steps, and stated the principle of reciprocal inhibition: a response antagonistic to anxiety, evoked in the presence of anxiety-provoking stimuli, weakens their bond with anxiety. His systematic desensitisation (1958) has three steps: relaxation training, an anxiety hierarchy rated on the 0 to 100 subjective units of distress scale (SUDS), and desensitisation proper, moving up only when an item evokes no anxiety. It can be done in vitro (imagined) or in vivo, and emotive imagery (Lazarus and Abramovitz, 1962) adapts it for children. Paul (1966) showed that it works, but dismantling studies pointed to exposure, not relaxation, as the active ingredient. 4.3 Exposure Therapies: Flooding, Implosion and Response Prevention. Exposure therapy is repeated or continuous confrontation with a feared object, situation, thought, memory or bodily sensation, without escape or avoidance, until the fear declines. It varies in intensity (graded or intense), medium (imaginal or in vivo) and duration; special forms are interoceptive exposure in Barlow and Craske's panic control treatment, virtual reality exposure (Rothbaum, 1995) and Öst's one-session treatment for specific phobias (1989). Four accounts explain why it works: habituation, extinction, Foa and Kozak's emotional processing theory (1986) and the inhibitory learning model, which advises dropping safety behaviours. Flooding (Malleson, 1959) starts at full intensity with no hierarchy and no relaxation; Stampfl and Levis's implosive therapy (1967) is imaginal, exaggerated and psychodynamic. Exposure and response prevention, introduced by Victor Meyer (1966) and refined by Foa, is the first-line psychological treatment for OCD, and Foa's prolonged exposure treats PTSD. 4.4 Aversive Methods, the Bell and Pad, and EMDR. Aversion therapy pairs an attractive but unwanted stimulus with an unpleasant one by classical conditioning: chemical aversion with emetine for alcoholism (Voegtlin and Lemere) or electrical aversion, which works poorly for drinking because, as Garcia and Koelling (1966) showed, tastes are linked readily to illness but not to shock. Aversion therapy for homosexuality, abandoned by its pioneer Kurt Freund and opposed by Davison (1974), is now condemned. Cautela's covert sensitisation (1966, 1967) pairs the behaviour with an imagined aversive consequence. The Mowrers' bell and pad (1938) treats bedwetting by classical conditioning, or by avoidance in Lovibond's account (1964), and is a first-line treatment beside desmopressin. Francine Shapiro's EMDR (noticed 1987, first study 1989) is a guideline-recommended treatment for PTSD, but dismantling studies suggest that its eye movements add little to exposure (McNally: what is new is not effective). 4.5 Operant Techniques That Build Behaviour. Reinforcement increases the behaviour it follows: positive reinforcement adds a stimulus and negative reinforcement removes one. Reinforcers are primary, secondary or generalised, and work best when immediate, contingent and consistent, with the schedule thinned later. Shaping reinforces successive approximations (Isaacs, Thomas and Goldiamond, 1960); chaining links the steps of a task analysis forwards, backwards or as a total task; prompts help a response occur and are then faded, as in Terrace's errorless learning (1963). The Premack principle (1959) uses a more probable behaviour to reinforce a less probable one. Ayllon and Azrin's token economy (from 1961) pays generalised reinforcers exchangeable for backup reinforcers, and Paul and Lentz (1977) found a social learning programme superior to milieu therapy. Contingency management (Higgins; Petry) rewards verified abstinence. Stimulus control and programmed generalisation, not what Stokes and Baer (1977) called train and hope, make change last. 4.6 Operant Techniques That Reduce Behaviour, and Applied Behaviour Analysis. Punishment weakens behaviour: positive punishment adds something unpleasant and negative punishment removes something pleasant, whereas escape and avoidance are negative reinforcement. Extinction withholds the reinforcer that maintains a behaviour (planned ignoring, escape extinction, Rincover's sensory extinction) and brings an extinction burst, a gradual decline and spontaneous recovery. Differential reinforcement (DRO, DRI, DRA, DRL) includes Carr and Durand's functional communication training (1985). Time-out and response cost are negative punishment, and Foxx and Azrin's overcorrection (1972) is restitutional or positive practice. Punishment's side effects make the least restrictive alternative the governing rule; Ayllon's towel hoarder illustrates satiation. Baer, Wolf and Risley (1968) defined applied behaviour analysis by seven dimensions, and Lovaas's Young Autism Project (1987) reported 47 percent of intensively treated children reaching normal functioning, against 2 percent of controls, a claim critics disputed. 4.7 Modelling, Rehearsal, Assertiveness and Social Skills. Bandura made observation central to learning: a model produces observational learning, inhibitory and disinhibitory, and response facilitation effects, helped by vicarious reinforcement, and Meichenbaum (1971) found coping models better than mastery models. Modelling may be live (Bandura, Grusec and Menlove, 1967), symbolic (Melamed and Siegel's Ethan Has an Operation , 1975), participant, covert (Cautela) or self-modelling (Dowrick). In Bandura, Blanchard and Ritter's study (1969) participant modelling beat symbolic modelling and desensitisation for snake phobia, which Bandura explained by self-efficacy (1977). Behavioural rehearsal practises new behaviour in role play (Wolpe and Lazarus, 1966). Assertiveness training runs from Salter (1949) through Wolpe (1958) and Lazarus to Alberti and Emmons (1970), who separated passive, assertive and aggressive behaviour; Manuel Smith (1975) named the broken record and fogging. Social skills training rests on Argyle's social skill model (1967) and, for schizophrenia, on Liberman's UCLA modules. 4.8 Relaxation and Biofeedback. Edmund Jacobson's progressive muscle relaxation (1929; 1938) teaches deep relaxation by tensing and releasing muscle groups; Bernstein and Borkovec (1973) wrote the abbreviated version most clinicians use, and some clients experience relaxation-induced anxiety. Johannes Heinrich Schultz's autogenic training (1932) uses passive concentration on six formulae: heaviness, warmth, heart, breathing, solar plexus and a cool forehead. Breathing retraining corrects hyperventilation (Clark, Salkovskis and Chalkley, 1985), though Schmidt (2000) found that it added nothing to CBT for panic. Benson's relaxation response (1975) is the opposite of Cannon's fight-or-flight response. Öst's applied relaxation (1987) trains clients to relax within 20 to 30 seconds and apply the skill at the first signs of anxiety. Biofeedback, foreshadowed by Kegel's perineometer (1948) and by Neal Miller's curarised rats (later unreplicated), feeds back muscle tension (EMG, for tension-type headache), skin temperature (migraine), skin conductance, heart rate variability or brain rhythms (neurofeedback). 4.9 Habit Change and Self-Management. Azrin and Nunn's habit reversal training (1973) combines awareness training, a competing response that is physically incompatible with the habit and held for about a minute, habit control motivation and generalisation training; it is the first behavioural treatment for tics, hair-pulling and nail-biting, and regulated breathing (1974) adapts it for stuttering. CBIT adds function-based interventions (Piacentini and colleagues, 2010). Dunlap's negative or massed practice (1928, 1932), given a Hullian rationale by Yates (1958), and thought stopping, now discouraged because suppression produces a rebound (Wegner, 1987), are older methods. Self-monitoring uses reactivity, and Kanfer's self-regulation runs from self-monitoring to self-evaluation to self-reinforcement. Behavioural activation, from Lewinsohn's low response-contingent positive reinforcement (1974) to Martell, Addis and Jacobson (2001), schedules rewarding activity for depression. For insomnia, Spielman's 3P model (1987) targets perpetuating factors with Bootzin's stimulus control (1972) and sleep restriction. 4.10 Paradoxical Intention, Parents and Classrooms. In Tharp and Wetzel's triadic model (1969) a consultant works through a parent or teacher to change a child's behaviour. Frankl's paradoxical intention (1939) asks the client to wish for or try to produce the feared symptom, removing anticipatory and performance anxiety; Turner and Ascher (1979) tested it for insomnia. It differs from Dunlap's negative practice and from the paradoxical directives of strategic family therapy. Patterson's coercion theory shows how the coercive cycle negatively reinforces both child and parent, and his Oregon work led to parent management training (praise, point charts, planned ignoring, time-out, response cost) and to descendants such as Eyberg's PCIT, Webster-Stratton's Incredible Years and Sanders's Triple P. Becker's classroom group described the criticism trap and showed praise to be the active ingredient (Madsen, Becker and Thomas, 1968); the Good Behaviour Game (1969), token systems and daily report cards complete the kit. 4.11 Evaluating Behaviour Therapy. Behaviour therapy has been tested more than any other school: most well-established entries on the first list of empirically validated treatments (1995) were behavioural or cognitive behavioural, and Sloane and colleagues (1975) found it at least as effective as psychotherapy for outpatients. It is strongest for phobias, panic, OCD, PTSD, enuresis, autism, tics, disruptive behaviour, insomnia and depression, and it does not replace antipsychotic medication in schizophrenia. The psychoanalytic prediction of symptom substitution rarely came true (Baker, 1969; Kazdin, 1982), though a shared response class can explain new problems. Its real weak points were generalisation and maintenance (train and hope) and its theory (Breger and McGaugh, 1965; Bandura's self-efficacy). Aversive methods are governed by informed consent, the least restrictive alternative (Wyatt v.
