consent, right to effective treatment From the past papers Behavioural therapies applying learning principles to: (RML 2020) (a) identify and treat the underlying causes of dysfunction (b) improve learning and insight (c) eliminate the unwanted behaviour (d) improve communication and social sensitivity Answer: (c) Eliminate the unwanted behaviour. Behaviour therapy applies learning principles to remove problem behaviour and build adaptive behaviour, treating the behaviour itself as the problem. Identifying and treating underlying causes is the psychodynamic aim, improving learning and insight describes the insight therapies, and improving communication and social sensitivity describes encounter and communication groups. The process of recording a behaviour causes the behaviour to change, even before any treatment is implemented. This is known as: (Amity 2023) (a) Reactivity (b) Shaping (c) Applied Behaviour Analysis (d) Chaining Answer: (a) Reactivity. Observing or recording a behaviour alters the behaviour itself, which is why a baseline can shift and why self-monitoring works as a treatment. Shaping and chaining are procedures for building behaviour, and applied behaviour analysis is a whole discipline, not an effect of recording. Counter conditioning is an exposure therapy technique that involves: (RML 2022) (a) Learning that one negative event may be linked to another (b) Exposing the client to the feared stimulus (c) Learning that an event or situation is no longer threatening (d) Helping the client to see that their behaviour is counterproductive Answer: (c) Learning that an event or situation is no longer threatening. Counterconditioning attaches a new, calm response to the feared stimulus, as when Peter ate while the rabbit came closer, so the situation stops signalling threat. Exposure (b) is part of it but describes every exposure therapy and leaves out the incompatible response; (a) is how a fear is acquired in the first place; (d) is an insight or motivational aim. The behavioural technique for reducing anxiety in which patients practice relaxation while visualizing provoking situations of increasing intensity refers: (RML 2020) (a) Symptom substitution (b) Flooding (c) Systematic desensitization (d) Token economy Answer: (c) Systematic desensitization. Relaxation paired with imagined scenes of increasing intensity is Wolpe's systematic desensitisation. Flooding starts at full intensity with no relaxation, a token economy is operant, and symptom substitution is not a technique at all but the psychoanalytic prediction that a symptom removed without resolving its conflict will be replaced by another. Subjective unit of distress (SUD) is mostly used under: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Exposure & response prevention (b) Multi-model therapy (c) Mindfulness-based stress management (d) Systematic desensitization Answer: (d) Systematic desensitization. Wolpe introduced the 0 to 100 SUDS scale to rate the items of the anxiety hierarchy in systematic desensitisation. Modern exposure therapies, ERP included, also use SUDS ratings, which makes (a) tempting, but the scale was built for desensitisation; multimodal therapy is Arnold Lazarus's BASIC ID approach and mindfulness-based stress reduction is Kabat-Zinn's. A client with a phobia of heights (acrophobia) is encouraged by their therapist to stand on a balcony for an extended period without any gradual exposure or relaxation techniques until their anxiety subsides. This intervention is an example of: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Systematic Desensitization (b) Flooding (c) Modeling (d) Cognitive Restructuring Answer: (b) Flooding. Prolonged exposure to the most feared situation at full intensity, with escape prevented and no hierarchy or relaxation, until the anxiety subsides, is flooding. Systematic desensitisation climbs a hierarchy while relaxed, modelling is learning by watching someone else, and cognitive restructuring changes beliefs rather than exposing the client to anything. Exposure and response prevention procedure is based on behaviour therapy principal of : (IHBAS 2024) (a) Counter conditioning (b) Habituation and extinction (c) Reciprocal inhibition (d) Graded exposure Answer: (b) Habituation and extinction. In ERP the anxiety provoked by an obsessional trigger is allowed to fall by itself while the rituals are blocked, so the method rests on habituation and extinction. No incompatible response such as relaxation is trained, so counterconditioning and reciprocal inhibition are wrong, and graded exposure is the format of ERP hierarchies, not their principle. Which behavioral technique involves imagining a scene where an undesirable behavior is paired with an unpleasant consequence to reduce the behavior? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Flooding (b) Implosion (c) Covert sensitization (d) Systematic desensitization Answer: (c) Covert sensitization. Cautela's covert sensitisation pairs an imagined unwanted behaviour with an imagined aversive consequence, to create an aversion. Flooding, implosion and systematic desensitisation are exposure methods that remove a fear; implosion is also imaginal and unpleasant, which makes it the tempting option, but it aims to extinguish a fear, not to build an aversion. Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) is sometimes used to treat PTSD. This technique involves: (RML 2021) (a) The administration of an antidepressant. (b) The client focusing on the memory, emotions and thoughts of the traumatic events while engaging in therapist-guided eye movements (c) Training the client in relaxation techniques. (d) The client being asked to relieve the traumatic event in their imagination Answer: (b) Focusing on the traumatic memory while making therapist-guided eye movements. In EMDR the client holds the traumatic memory, with its emotions and thoughts, in mind while following the therapist's fingers back and forth, Francine Shapiro's bilateral stimulation. Reliving the event in imagination, (d), is the imaginal exposure of Foa's prolonged exposure; EMDR involves no antidepressant, and relaxation training alone is not EMDR. In operant conditioning, the process of reinforcing successive approximations of a desired behavior until the target behavior is achieved is known as: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Chaining (b) Shaping (c) Fading (d) Prompting Answer: (b) Shaping. Reinforcing responses that resemble the target more and more closely, until the target itself appears, is shaping. Chaining links a sequence of separate steps, prompting adds a cue before or during the response, and fading gradually removes that cue. According to the Premack Principle, a high-probability behavior (for example, playing video games) can be used to: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Reinforce a low-probability behavior (for example, completing homework). (b) Punish a low-probability behavior. (c) Reinforce another high-probability behavior. (d) Extinguish a maladaptive behavior. Answer: (a) Reinforce a low-probability behaviour. David Premack's principle (1959) says that a more probable behaviour reinforces a less probable one when access to it is made contingent on the less probable one: video games only after homework. It is a principle of reinforcement, not of punishment or extinction, and the reversed or same-level pairings are the standard bait. Proponent of the Token Economy as a psychosocial therapeutic technique: (Amity 2023) (a) B.F. Skinner (b) Pavlov (c) Ayllon and Azrin (d) None Answer: (c) Ayllon and Azrin. The printed key gives (a) B. F. Skinner, and that key is wrong when Ayllon and Azrin are offered: Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin developed the token economy as a therapeutic technique at Anna State Hospital from 1961 and described it in their 1968 book. Skinner supplied the operant principles behind it, and Pavlov's work is classical conditioning. Which of the following is not a treatment developed from classical conditioning principles? (RML 2022) (a) Flooding (b) Token economies (c) Systematic desensitisation (d) Aversion therapies Answer: (b) Token economies. A token economy is operant: tokens are secondary (generalised) reinforcers earned for target behaviours and exchanged for backup reinforcers. Flooding, systematic desensitisation and aversion therapy all change what a stimulus elicits, which is classical conditioning. A parent deliberately ignores a child's temper tantrums in an attempt to discourage them. The parent's strategy is in accordance with: (Amity 2023) (a) Negative reinforcement (b) Extinction (c) Operant escape (d) Operant avoidance Answer: (b) Extinction. The printed key gives (c) operant escape, and it is wrong; the site has corrected it to extinction. The tantrums were maintained by attention, and withholding that attention weakens them. Operant escape and operant avoidance are both forms of negative reinforcement, which strengthens behaviour, so neither they nor (a) can be a way of discouraging tantrums. A therapist uses "time-out" to manage a child's aggressive outbursts. Time-out is technically classified as a form of: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Positive Punishment (b) Negative Reinforcement (c) Negative Punishment (d) Positive Reinforcement Answer: (c) Negative Punishment. Time-out removes access to play and attention (something pleasant is taken away) and makes the outbursts less frequent, which is negative punishment. Positive punishment adds something unpleasant, and either kind of reinforcement would make the outbursts more frequent. The behavioral technique that involves removing a desirable stimulus following an undesirable behavior in order to reduce the frequency of that behavior is called: (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Negative reinforcement (b) Response cost (c) Positive punishment (d) Extinction Answer: (b) Response cost. Losing a reinforcer the person already has, contingent on a problem behaviour, is response cost, a form of negative punishment. Negative reinforcement increases behaviour, positive punishment adds an unpleasant stimulus, and extinction stops delivering the reinforcer that used to follow the behaviour rather than taking away something already held. A child with autism is taught to request a "break" using a picture card instead of engaging in a tantrum. This intervention is a key component of: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) (b) Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) (c) Play Therapy (d) Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy Answer: (b) Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA). Teaching a communicative response that earns the same reinforcer as the tantrum (here, a break) is functional communication training (Carr and Durand, 1985), a form of differential reinforcement of alternative behaviour and a core ABA procedure. CBT, play therapy and psychoanalytic psychotherapy do not work by reinforcing a replacement behaviour. Over-correction is a behavioural technique to manage: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Bed wetting in children (b) Repetitive aggressive behaviour in autistic children (c) Temper tantrum in children (d) Alienation in adolescent Answer: (b) Repetitive aggressive behaviour in autistic children. Foxx and Azrin developed overcorrection (1972, 1973) for aggressive, disruptive and self-stimulatory behaviour in people with intellectual disability and autism. Bedwetting is treated mainly with the bell and pad (Azrin's dry-bed training borrowed overcorrection components, which makes (a) tempting), ordinary temper tantrums with extinction and time-out, and adolescent alienation is not a target behaviour. The "Lovaas programme" utilises behaviour modification techniques for the treatment of : (RML 2022) (a) Autism (b) Aphasia (c) Acute depression (d) Alcoholism Answer: (a) Autism. Ole Ivar Lovaas's Young Autism Project at UCLA gave young children with autism intensive behavioural teaching, mainly discrete trial training at about 40 hours a week, and reported in 1987 that 47 percent reached normal functioning against 2 percent of controls. Aphasia is a language disorder after brain injury, depression is treated behaviourally with behavioural activation, and alcoholism was the target of aversion therapy. In behaviour therapy, the patient is taught the methods of progressive deep relaxation based on the work of : (RML 2022) (a) Wolpe (b) Skinner (c) Jacobson (d) Ivan Pavlov Answer: (c) Jacobson. Edmund Jacobson developed progressive muscle relaxation ( Progressive Relaxation , 1929; second edition 1938). Wolpe borrowed and shortened it as the first step of systematic desensitisation, which makes (a) the tempting wrong answer; Skinner and Pavlov had no part in it. The technique that is based on the idea that the autonomic nervous system can come under voluntary control through operant conditioning is known as (JEMAS 2025) (a) Biofeedback. (b) Hypnosis. (c) Sublimation. (d) Systematic desensitization. Answer: (a) Biofeedback. The claim that autonomic responses can be operantly conditioned, linked to Neal Miller, underlies biofeedback, in which an instrument feeds back a bodily process so that the person can learn to control it. Hypnosis works by suggestion, sublimation is a Freudian defence mechanism, and systematic desensitisation is classical counterconditioning. Habit reversal training (HRT) is primarily used as a behavioral intervention to reduce which type of repetitive behavior? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Tics (b) Stuttering (c) Obsessive-compulsive behaviors (d) Aggressive behaviors Answer: (a) Tics. Azrin and Nunn's habit reversal training (1973) is primarily a treatment for tics and other repetitive habits such as hair-pulling and nail-biting. Stuttering tempts because they adapted the method for it (regulated breathing, 1974), but that is not its main use; compulsions are treated with exposure and response prevention, and aggression with operant methods. Which of the following best describes "behavioural activation" in psychotherapy? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Encouraging clients to engage in meaningful activities to counteract depression (b) Analysing early childhood experiences (c) Relaxation training for anxiety (d) Hypnosis for symptom relief Answer: (a) Encouraging clients to engage in meaningful activities to counteract depression. Behavioural activation schedules rewarding and meaningful activity to restore response-contingent positive reinforcement and reduce avoidance (Lewinsohn's theory; Martell, Addis and Jacobson's manual). Analysing childhood is psychodynamic, relaxation training belongs to the treatment of anxiety, and hypnosis plays no part in it. An intervention in which the person deliberately does, or wishes for, the very opposite of the therapeutic goal in order to reach that goal is: (NIMHANS 2026 recall) (a) Paradoxical intention (b) Dereflection (c) Negative practice (d) Reciprocal inhibition Answer: (a) Paradoxical intention. Viktor Frankl's paradoxical intention asks the client to intend or wish for the feared symptom, which removes the anticipatory anxiety that keeps it going. Dereflection, Frankl's other technique, turns attention away from the self; negative practice repeats a voluntary habit to weaken it; reciprocal inhibition is Wolpe's principle of pairing an incompatible response with the feared stimulus. Which of the following is not a part of Parent Management Training? (IHBAS 2020) (a) Attending positive behaviour (b) Rewarding positive behaviour (c) Ignoring undesirable behaviour (d) Negative reinforcement Answer: (d) Negative reinforcement. Parent management training teaches parents to attend to and reward positive behaviour and to ignore minor misbehaviour. Negative reinforcement, as when a parent gives in to end a tantrum and the child learns that screaming removes demands, is the coercive trap the training is designed to break, so it is the odd one out. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997) developed systematic desensitisation ( Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition , 1958), used mainly for phobias: relaxation training, an anxiety hierarchy, then desensitisation proper, in which the relaxed client imagines (or meets) each item from least to most feared, moving up only when calm. Not Rogers, Bandura, Freud, Skinner, Pavlov or Beck, and cognitive restructuring is not one of its steps. asked 14 times EMDR was developed by Francine Shapiro (effect noticed 1987, first study 1989) for post-traumatic stress disorder : the client holds the traumatic memory, with its emotions and thoughts, in mind while following therapist-guided eye movements (bilateral stimulation). Not Foa, Linehan, Beck, van der Kolk or Ogden, and not for phobia, OCD or eating disorders. asked 7 times Exposure and response prevention (introduced by Victor Meyer, 1966; operationalised by Edna Foa) is the first-line psychological treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder , and it rests on habituation and extinction , not counterconditioning or reciprocal inhibition. asked 7 times Systematic desensitisation rests on Wolpe's principle of reciprocal inhibition : a response incompatible with anxiety (deep relaxation), evoked in the presence of the feared stimulus, weakens the bond between the stimulus and anxiety. Not operant extinction, the law of effect, habituation alone or two-factor theory. asked 7 times Shaping is the reinforcement of successive approximations to a target behaviour, so that simple responses are reinforced in sequence until the complex one appears; chaining links steps, prompting adds a cue and fading removes it. asked 5 times The token economy is operant : tokens are secondary (generalised) reinforcers exchanged for backup reinforcers. In "which is NOT from classical conditioning?" it is the odd one out, because aversion therapy (pairing an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus), flooding and systematic desensitisation are classical. asked 6 times The Premack principle (David Premack, 1959): a high-probability behaviour reinforces a low-probability one (video games allowed only after homework); a technique of behaviour modification used especially with children, and never the reverse. asked 5 times Flooding is prolonged exposure to the most feared stimulus at full intensity, with escape prevented and no hierarchy and no relaxation, until the anxiety subsides (the acrophobic kept on a balcony); it can be in vivo or imaginal. asked 4 times Extinction is the weakening of a behaviour when the reinforcer that maintained it no longer follows: deliberately ignoring tantrums (the Amity 2023 key "operant escape" is wrong), "habit weakening through the elimination of any reward", "a previously reinforced behaviour fades". asked 3 times Biofeedback rests on the idea, linked to Neal Miller , that autonomic processes can be brought under voluntary control by operant conditioning: the client controls a physiological process using real-time feedback from an instrument. Kegel's perineometer (1948) was an early form, and EMG biofeedback is the classic treatment for tension-type headache. asked 4 times The token economy as a therapeutic technique was developed by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin (Anna State Hospital, from 1961; book 1968) for chronic psychiatric inpatients. Skinner supplied the principles; the Amity 2023 key that gives Skinner is wrong when Ayllon and Azrin are offered. asked 3 times The 0 to 100 subjective units of distress scale (SUDS) is Wolpe's rating for the items of the hierarchy in systematic desensitisation ; not the Fear Survey Schedule, the STAI or the Hamilton scale. asked twice Behaviour analysis (applied behaviour analysis) is based on operant conditioning ; its seven dimensions were set out by Baer, Wolf and Risley (1968). asked twice Habit reversal training (Azrin and Nunn, 1973) is primarily for tics and other repetitive habits; its competing response is physically incompatible with the habit, inconspicuous and held for about a minute or until the urge passes. asked twice Paradoxical intention (Viktor Frankl): the person deliberately does or wishes for the very thing he fears, as when an insomniac is told to lie in the dark and try to stay awake; not dereflection, negative practice, stimulus control or sleep restriction. asked twice Time-out (from positive reinforcement) is negative punishment : it removes access to reinforcement and so reduces the behaviour; it is not positive punishment or negative reinforcement. asked twice Behavioural activation encourages depressed clients to engage in rewarding, meaningful activities (Lewinsohn's theory, 1974; Martell, Addis and Jacobson, 2001). asked once Covert sensitisation (Joseph Cautela, 1966 and 1967): the client imagines the unwanted behaviour followed by an unpleasant consequence, to reduce it; not flooding, implosion or desensitisation. asked once Response cost is the removal of a reinforcer the person already has after an undesirable behaviour, to reduce it; a form of negative punishment. asked once Counterconditioning (Mary Cover Jones, 1924) attaches a new, incompatible response to a feared stimulus, so the client learns that the situation is no longer threatening. asked once Progressive (deep) muscle relaxation is Edmund Jacobson 's ( Progressive Relaxation , 1929; second edition 1938), not Wolpe's, Skinner's or Pavlov's. asked once The Lovaas programme (Ole Ivar Lovaas, UCLA) treats autism with intensive discrete trial training; his 1987 report claimed normal functioning in 47 percent of treated children against 2 percent of controls. asked once Teaching a child with autism to ask for a break with a picture card instead of having a tantrum is functional communication training (Carr and Durand, 1985), a core procedure of applied behaviour analysis . asked once Reactivity : recording a behaviour changes it, even before treatment begins; it is what makes self-monitoring therapeutic. asked once Overcorrection (Foxx and Azrin, 1972) manages repetitive aggressive, disruptive or self-stimulatory behaviour in autistic children and others with developmental disability; its forms are restitutional and positive practice. asked once Negative reinforcement is not part of parent management training: parents are taught to attend to and reward good behaviour and to ignore minor misbehaviour. asked once Habituation in exposure therapy is the reduction in anxiety through repeated encounter with the feared stimulus; an increase in fear is sensitisation. asked once Behavioural therapies apply learning principles to eliminate the unwanted behaviour (and build adaptive behaviour), not to treat underlying causes or to build insight. asked once The front-line treatment for schizophrenia is antipsychotic medication ; belief: the cognitive turn in therapy : explain the shared assumptions of the cognitive-behavioural therapies, their roots, and the idea of three "waves". 5.2 Albert Ellis and rational emotive behaviour therapy : apply the ABC model and its extension to D, E and F, name the core irrational beliefs, and describe REBT's techniques and its critics. 5.3 Aaron Beck's cognitive model : describe the cognitive triad, the three levels of cognition and every major cognitive distortion, with an example of each. 5.4 Cognitive therapy in practice : describe collaborative empiricism, Socratic questioning, the structure of a session and Beck's main techniques, and contrast Beck with Ellis. 5.5 Coping skills, problem solving and personal constructs : describe Meichenbaum's two methods, problem-solving therapy, Lazarus's multimodal therapy and Kelly's fixed-role therapy. 5.6 Disorder-specific cognitive models: panic, social anxiety, trauma and psychosis : explain how CBT is tailored to particular disorders, including the role of safety behaviours. 5.7 Going deeper: schema therapy and cognitive analytic therapy : explain early maladaptive schemas, schema modes and limited reparenting, and the main features of Ryle's therapy. 5.8 The third wave I: dialectical behaviour therapy : describe Linehan's biosocial theory, the dialectic of acceptance and change, the four modes and the four skills modules. 5.9 The third wave II: acceptance and commitment therapy and the mindfulness-based therapies : explain relational frame theory, the hexaflex, MBSR and MBCT. 5.10 The third wave III: compassion, metacognition, the therapeutic relationship and activation : describe compassion-focused therapy, metacognitive therapy, functional analytic psychotherapy and behavioural activation. 5.11 How well does CBT work? : summarise the evidence for CBT, its limitations, and computerised and internet-delivered CBT. Weightage. 71 of the 422 questions mapped in this book (16.8%) test this chapter, 25 of them from real past papers. 5 of its 11 sections are High yield. In the late 1950s Aaron Beck was a young psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia and, like most ambitious American psychiatrists of his generation, a fully trained psychoanalyst. His patients lay on the couch and free-associated: they said whatever came into their minds, and he listened for the hidden wishes and conflicts that psychoanalytic theory told him were there. One day a patient was doing exactly what the method asked of him. He was angrily criticising his analyst. When the outburst ran down, Beck asked him what he was feeling. "I feel very guilty," the patient said. That answer did not fit. A man who has just vented his anger should, by the theory Beck had been taught, feel relieved, not guilty. So Beck asked a further question, and the patient explained. While he had been voicing his anger, a second stream of thoughts had been running alongside it, thoughts he had not mentioned because he had barely noticed them himself: "I said the wrong thing... I shouldn't have said that... He won't like me... I'm bad." It was this quiet, rapid, self-critical commentary, and not the anger, that was producing the guilt. Beck began asking his other patients about thoughts of this kind, and nearly all of them had them. The thoughts were fast, they felt completely believable, they arrived without being summoned, and they were followed by feelings the patients were very much aware of. Beck called them automatic thoughts. At about the same time he was running studies that were meant to confirm the psychoanalytic account of depression as anger turned inward against the self. He studied the dreams of depressed patients, expecting to find disguised hostility, and found instead dreams full of loss, defeat and rejection: the same themes his patients voiced when they were awake. In laboratory tasks, depressed patients who were given an experience of success did not sabotage themselves, as a "need to suffer" would predict; their mood and their performance improved. The evidence was pointing somewhere new. Depressed people were not secretly seeking suffering; they were thinking about themselves, their world and their future in a consistently negative and distorted way. Out of that second stream of thought grew cognitive therapy, and out of cognitive therapy grew the large family of treatments now called cognitive-behavioural therapy, the most researched form of psychotherapy in the world. Keep Beck's guilty patient in mind. You will meet him again at the end of this chapter, after you have seen what became of his second stream. 5.1 From behaviour to belief: the cognitive turn in therapy Medium yield · 3 Qs Imagine two students who both score 48 out of 90 on a mock entrance test. The first feels disappointed, studies the questions she got wrong, and books another mock for the weekend. The second feels crushed, tells himself he was never good enough for a clinical programme, and stops opening his books. The event was the same; the reactions were opposite. What made the difference? Not the score, but what each student made of it. That simple observation is the foundation of every therapy in this chapter. cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) is best understood as a family name rather than a single treatment. It covers dozens of therapies that share three propositions, set out by the Canadian psychologist Keith S. Dobson : that cognitive activity affects behaviour and emotion; that cognitive activity can be monitored and altered; and that desired changes in behaviour and emotion can be brought about by changing cognition. The first proposition is often called the cognitive mediation hypothesis: between the event and the reaction stands an interpretation, and the interpretation, not the event alone, shapes how we feel and what we do. Notice that the claim is that thinking mediates , not that thinking is all there is. Biology, learning history and real circumstances matter too; CBT simply chooses thought and behaviour as the most accessible levers for change. Ancient and modern roots The idea is very old. The Greek Stoic philosopher Epictetus (about 50 to 135 CE), a freed slave, taught, in the Enchiridion (the handbook of his sayings compiled by his pupil Arrian), that "men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them." Albert Ellis quoted this line so often that it became the motto of his therapy. Indian and Buddhist traditions said something similar many centuries earlier: the opening verses of the Dhammapada teach that what we are is shaped by our thoughts, and Buddhist meditation was, among other things, a training in watching thoughts arise and pass without being swept away by them. As you will see later in the chapter, this second idea (watching thoughts rather than arguing with them) returns in the third wave. Within modern psychology, several people prepared the ground. Alfred Adler (1870 to 1937) argued that people act on a "private logic" and that neurosis rests on "basic mistakes" in a person's beliefs about self and life. Karen Horney (1885 to 1952) wrote of the "tyranny of the shoulds" (in Neurosis and Human Growth , 1950), the inner dictates that drive neurotic people to impossible standards; Ellis's "musts" are close cousins. George Alexander Kelly (1905 to 1967) published The Psychology of Personal Constructs in 1955, describing every person as a scientist who builds and tests theories about the world (you will meet his fixed-role therapy in Section 5.5). And in academic psychology, the "cognitive revolution" of the 1950s and 1960s made it respectable again to study what goes on inside the head. Why behaviour therapy turned cognitive By the 1960s, behaviour therapy (Chapter 4) had shown that conditioning-based methods could treat phobias and many habits. But it struggled with problems that seemed to live in thought itself: depression, obsessional rumination, worry, self-criticism. Behaviour therapists began to treat thoughts as "covert behaviours" that could be learned and unlearned, and during the 1970s a series of books announced the merger: Michael Mahoney 's Cognition and Behavior Modification (1974) and Donald Meichenbaum's Cognitive-Behavior Modification (1977) gave the hybrid its name. The most influential bridge came from Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021). In 1977 he proposed the concept of self-efficacy : a person's belief in his or her capacity to organise and carry out the actions needed to manage a particular situation. Self-efficacy is not skill; it is confidence in one's skill, and it is specific to a task (you can feel highly efficacious at cricket and hopeless at statistics). Bandura identified four sources of self-efficacy: mastery experiences (actually succeeding), vicarious experiences (watching someone like you succeed), verbal persuasion (being told you can), and physiological and emotional states (reading a calm body as a sign of competence). His bold claim was that all forms of psychological treatment, whatever their theory, work largely by raising self-efficacy. That is why self-efficacy is so often described as a cognitive-behavioural explanation of how people change. Compare this with Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990), whose radical behaviourism explained behaviour entirely by its consequences and treated inner "beliefs" as unnecessary explanations. Exam trap "Which theorist developed self-efficacy, used as a cognitive-behavioural explanation of how people change?" The answer is Albert Bandura (1977), not Beck or Ellis, who built therapies around beliefs, and certainly not Skinner, who rejected cognitive explanations. A related one-liner: pharmacotherapy (treatment with medicines) is not a psychotherapy; cognitive, behavioural and psychodynamic therapies all are, because they work through a psychological relationship and psychological techniques. Three waves In 2004 the American psychologist Steven C. Hayes described the history of the field as three waves, and the metaphor stuck. The first wave was behaviour therapy (1950s onward: Wolpe, Eysenck, Skinner and Lazarus), which applied learning principles directly to observable behaviour. The second wave was cognitive therapy (from the mid-1950s with Ellis, and the 1960s and 1970s with Beck and Meichenbaum), which argued that changing the content of thoughts (from irrational or distorted to rational or realistic) would change emotion and behaviour. The third wave (from the 1990s: dialectical behaviour therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy and others) shifted the target from the content of thoughts to a person's relationship with them: noticing thoughts, accepting feelings, and acting on values even while unpleasant thoughts and feelings are present. Figure 5.1 shows the timeline. Notice that each wave added to the field rather than replacing what came before; all three are practised today, often in the same clinic. First wave: behaviour therapy (1950s on) Learning principles: Wolpe, Eysenck, Skinner, Lazarus Second wave: cognitive therapies (1955 on) Change the content of thoughts: Ellis, Beck, Meichenbaum Third wave (1990s on) DBT 1993, ACT 1999, MBCT 2002 1950 1960 1970 1980 1990 2000 2010 Figure 5.1 The three waves of behavioural and cognitive therapy. Each bar starts at the wave's approximate origin and runs to the present, because no wave replaced the one before it. Steven Hayes named the "third wave" in 2004. All CBTs, whatever their wave, share a recognisable style. They are usually time-limited (often 8 to 20 sessions), focused on present problems rather than the distant past, structured, collaborative, educational (clients learn a model of their problem), and they rely on homework : the real work happens between sessions. They also measure: symptoms are rated at the start and tracked throughout, which is one reason CBT has accumulated more research than any other therapy. Exam trap "Third-wave CBT includes all EXCEPT..." The third wave includes acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT), mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT), compassion-focused therapy, metacognitive therapy and functional analytic psychotherapy. Psychoanalysis belongs to none of the waves; it is a separate, older psychodynamic tradition (Chapter 3). REBT and Beck's cognitive therapy are second wave; systematic desensitisation and token economies are first wave. 5.2 Albert Ellis and rational emotive behaviour therapy High yield · 14 Qs As a young man in New York, Albert Ellis (1913 to 2007) was painfully shy with women. So he set himself an assignment. Over one month in the Bronx Botanical Garden he sat down beside about a hundred women, one after another, and made himself start a conversation within a minute. Almost none of the conversations led anywhere (the one woman who agreed to a date did not turn up), but something more important happened: his fear of rejection faded, because he had proved to himself that rejection was unpleasant but not terrible. Ellis later said he had invented his therapy on himself before he ever practised it on anyone else. The episode already contains its main ingredients: a belief ("being rejected would be awful"), a deliberate behavioural experiment against that belief, and a new conclusion ("I don't like rejection, but I can stand it"). Ellis earned his doctorate in clinical psychology at Columbia University in 1947 and practised psychoanalysis from about 1947 to 1953. He grew frustrated. Patients gained insight, he said, but rarely got better; knowing why you are disturbed did not stop you disturbing yourself. Returning to the philosophy he had read since his teens (the Stoics above all), he began in the mid-1950s to practise a far more active approach. He first called it rational therapy , presenting it at the American Psychological Association convention in 1956; the approach is usually dated to 1955. Because critics heard "rational" as "unemotional", he renamed it rational-emotive therapy (RET) in 1961, and in 1993 he renamed it again as rational emotive behaviour therapy (REBT), to acknowledge how much behavioural homework it had always used. In 1959 he founded the Institute for Rational Living in New York (later the Albert Ellis Institute), and his 1962 book Reason and Emotion in Psychotherapy became the classic statement of the approach. Because it predates Beck's work, REBT is often called the first cognitive-behavioural therapy. The ABC model The heart of REBT is the ABC model . A is the activating event (or adversity): something that happens, or that a person notices, remembers or anticipates. C is the consequence : the emotional and behavioural reaction. Common sense assumes that A causes C ("the exam result made me depressed"). Ellis's central claim is that A contributes to C but does not cause it directly; the main cause is B , the beliefs the person holds about A. Return to the two students who scored 48 out of 90. Same A. The first believes, "I really wanted a better score, and it's disappointing, but one mock doesn't decide my future." Her C is disappointment and more study. The second believes, "I absolutely must score well, and since I didn't, I'm a failure who will never make it." His C is depression and avoidance. Different B, different C. Figure 5.2 lays out the full model. Ellis distinguished two kinds of belief. A rational belief is flexible and phrased as a preference ("I want to pass, but there is no law of the universe that says I must"). It is consistent with reality, it follows logically, and it helps the person reach his or her goals. An irrational belief is rigid and absolute ("I must pass"). It is inconsistent with reality (nothing guarantees that one must pass), illogical (a strong wish does not create a necessity) and self-defeating. Rational beliefs produce healthy emotions even when events are bad; irrational beliefs produce disturbance. Common-sense view: A causes C A: Activating event Scored 48 of 90 on a mock test B: Belief "I must do well; I am a total failure" C: Consequence Depression; stops studying D: Disputing the belief Logical: does it follow? Empirical: where is the proof? Pragmatic: does it help me? E: Effective belief "I'd prefer to pass; I can stand failing" F: sadness, not despair Ellis's chain Common sense Figure 5.2 The ABC model of rational emotive behaviour therapy, extended to D (disputing), E (an effective new belief or philosophy) and F (new feelings and behaviours). The curved arrow across the top is the common-sense view that events cause feelings directly; Ellis's chain runs through the belief. Exam trap In Ellis's model, A = activating event , B = belief about the event , C = consequence of the belief (emotional and behavioural). Wrong options to watch for: "B = behaviour", "B = baseline", "B = bias", "B = biological predisposition", "B = beliefs about oneself" (too narrow: the belief is about the event), "C = critical analysis", "A = anticipatory event", "A = antecedent", and invented strings such as "attention, bonding, change" or "affect, behaviour, coping". "Affect, behaviour, cognition" is a real ABC, but a different one: the three components of an attitude in social psychology (Social book). The behavioural "ABC" of antecedent, behaviour, consequence is a different model altogether: it is the functional analysis of the behaviour therapists (Chapter 4), in which C means the reinforcing or punishing outcome of a behaviour. Same letters, different meanings. The irrational beliefs What makes a belief irrational? Ellis's answer narrowed over the years to four processes. The first and most basic is demandingness : turning preferences into absolute "musts", "shoulds", "oughts" and "have-tos". Ellis, who loved provocative language, called this musturbation (you will also see it spelled "musterbation"). From a demand, three other irrational conclusions tend to follow when the demand is not met. awfulising (or awfulizing, close to what Beck calls catastrophising) is rating an event as "awful", that is, more than 100 percent bad, the worst thing that could happen. low frustration tolerance is the belief that one cannot stand discomfort or frustration ("I can't bear it"; Ellis's joke name was "I-can't-stand-it-itis"). And global rating of self, others or life is judging a whole person by a single act ("I failed, so I am a failure"; "he lied, so he is a rotten person"). Global rating of the self is also called self-downing; of others, damnation. Table 5.1 sets each of the four beside its rational alternative. Table 5.1 Ellis's four irrational processes and their rational alternatives. Irrational belief Typical words Rational alternative Typical words Demandingness (musturbation) "I must", "you should", "it has to" Flexible preference "I'd like to, but I don't have to" Awfulising "It's awful, terrible, the end" Evaluating badness realistically "It's bad, but not the worst" Low frustration tolerance "I can't stand it" High frustration tolerance "I don't like it, but I can bear it" Global rating of self or others "I'm worthless", "he's rotten" Unconditional acceptance "I'm a fallible human who failed at this" Ellis grouped the endless variety of musts into three major musts , one each about the self, other people and the world. The first is "I must do well and win the approval of others, or else I am no good": it underlies anxiety, depression, shame and guilt. The second is "Other people must treat me kindly and fairly, or else they are rotten and deserve to be punished": it underlies anger, rage and violence. The third is "The conditions under which I live must give me what I want, quickly and easily, or else life is awful and I can't stand it": it underlies self-pity, procrastination and addictions. In Reason and Emotion in Psychotherapy (1962) he had listed his "irrational ideas" at greater length (eleven in the version most often quoted; some sources count twelve), among them the ideas that one must be loved and approved of by virtually everyone, that one must be thoroughly competent and achieving in every respect to be worthwhile, that some people are wicked and should be severely blamed and punished, that unhappiness is caused by outside events and cannot be controlled, and that one's past must go on determining one's present. Ellis also described two kinds of anxiety. Ego anxiety arises when one's sense of worth is threatened ("I must perform well or I am worthless"). Discomfort anxiety arises when one's comfort is threatened ("I must not feel uncomfortable"). And he pointed out that people frequently disturb themselves about their disturbance. A student who is anxious before a viva and then tells herself "I mustn't be anxious; it's terrible that I'm anxious" has added a second layer of anxiety to the first. This secondary disturbance (anxiety about anxiety, depression about depression, shame about being depressed) is often tackled first in REBT, because it keeps the primary problem going. Healthy and unhealthy negative emotions A common misunderstanding is that REBT tries to make people calm or cheerful about bad events. It does not. Ellis drew a sharp line between an unhealthy negative emotion , which comes from an irrational belief and blocks a person's goals, and a healthy negative emotion , which comes from a rational belief about the same bad event and helps the person respond to it. If you fail an exam you care about, feeling nothing would be odd; feeling sad and concerned is healthy. Table 5.2 sets out the usual pairs. Table 5.2 Unhealthy and healthy negative emotions in REBT (each pair concerns the same kind of event). Unhealthy (from a must) Healthy (from a preference) Typical event Anxiety Concern A threat or danger Depression Sadness A loss or failure Unhealthy anger (rage) Healthy anger (annoyance) Being frustrated or wronged Guilt Remorse Breaking one's own moral code Shame Disappointment or regret Something "shameful" being revealed Hurt Sorrow Being treated badly by someone close Unhealthy jealousy Healthy concern for the relationship A threat to a relationship D, E and F: disputing and its results Identifying the irrational belief is only the start. The active ingredient of REBT is disputing (D): challenging the irrational belief until the client no longer believes it. Disputing has been described as three steps: detecting the irrational belief, discriminating it from rational beliefs, and debating it. Three kinds of argument are used, and exam papers like to ask for them: Logical disputes ask whether the belief follows from the facts or from the person's wishes. "You would very much like to pass. How does it follow that you must pass?" Empirical disputes ask for evidence. "Where is the evidence that you are a total failure? Have you failed at everything you have ever tried?" Pragmatic (or functional) disputes ask whether the belief helps. "Where does believing 'I must pass or I'm worthless' get you? Does it help you study, or does it keep you away from your books?" Some writers add philosophical disputes ("Even if you fail this exam, can you still find meaning and satisfaction in your life?"). Ellis delivered disputes in several styles: short didactic explanations, Socratic questions, humour and exaggeration (he wrote comic "rational songs" for clients to sing), metaphors and occasional self-disclosure. When disputing succeeds, the client arrives at E , an effective new philosophy (also described as an effective new belief, or simply the new effect): a rational belief that can be used again in future. The result is F , new healthier feelings and behaviours (sadness instead of depression, renewed study instead of avoidance). Some versions of the model also add G , the person's goals, at the very beginning (the "GABCDE" model), because whether a belief is self-defeating can only be judged against what the person is trying to achieve. Ellis also distinguished two levels of change. The inelegant solution relieves the immediate symptom (the client stops being anxious about this particular exam). The elegant solution is a deep philosophical shift: the client gives up demandingness in general and accepts self, others and life unconditionally, so that future adversities disturb him far less. REBT aims for the elegant solution where it can. Exam trap "In the A-B-C-D-E model, D refers to..." Disputing (of irrational beliefs). Not desensitisation (Wolpe's technique, Chapter 4), not "discuss", not "drama". E is the effective new philosophy (some books write "effect" or "effective new belief"), and F is new feelings . Also remember the order of names: rational therapy (about 1955 to 1956), rational-emotive therapy (1961), rational emotive behaviour therapy (1993). Unconditional acceptance If global rating is the poison, unconditional acceptance is the antidote. Ellis urged clients toward unconditional self-acceptance (USA): accepting oneself as a fallible human being whose acts can be rated as good or bad, but whose whole self cannot be given a single rating. "I behaved badly" is a rational evaluation of an act; "I am bad" is an irrational evaluation of a person. He extended the same idea to unconditional other-acceptance (people who act badly are fallible humans, not rotten people) and unconditional life-acceptance (life contains real adversity and is still worth living). The idea resembles Carl Rogers's unconditional positive regard (Chapter 6), but the two men used it differently. Rogers believed the therapist's warmth and acceptance were themselves curative; Ellis accepted his clients fully but thought warmth was neither necessary nor sufficient, and warned that too much of it could feed a client's dire need for approval. His style was famously blunt. Techniques: cognitive, emotive and behavioural REBT is deliberately multimodal, combining three kinds of technique. The cognitive techniques include disputing, REBT self-help forms on which clients write out their own A, B, C, D and E, rational coping statements, reading (bibliotherapy), and listing the real costs and benefits of a habit. Ellis also insisted on precise language: "I can't speak in a group" becomes "I haven't yet spoken in a group and I'm afraid to." The emotive techniques work on beliefs through feeling and vivid experience. In rational emotive imagery , a technique developed by the psychiatrist Maxie C. Maultsby Jr. and adopted by Ellis, the client vividly imagines the activating event, lets himself feel the unhealthy emotion fully, then changes the feeling to its healthy counterpart (from depression to sadness, say), and finally notices what he said to himself to make the change; that new self-statement is the rational belief, discovered from the inside. In a shame-attacking exercise , the client deliberately does something harmless but "shameful" in public, so as to feel the shame, survive it, and learn that other people's disapproval is unpleasant rather than unbearable. Ellis's own favourite example was calling out the names of the stations aloud in a New York subway train. A Mysuru student might ask loudly at a chai stall for "one tea without tea", or wear mismatched slippers to class. Forceful self-statements and role-play are also used. The behavioural techniques include homework (almost every session ends with an assignment), in vivo exposure, "stay in there" exercises (remaining in an uncomfortable situation to build frustration tolerance), skills training, and self-management with rewards and penalties (the client allows himself a favourite activity only after doing the dreaded task, and imposes a penalty if he avoids it). Ellis's own month in the Bronx Botanical Garden was, in effect, a homework assignment of this kind. Clinical link REBT does not say that activating events are unimportant. When the A is real and ongoing (domestic violence, harassment, caste discrimination, poverty), the first job is safety and practical help, and the belief work comes alongside it. An REBT therapist would never tell an abused woman that her distress is "only her beliefs". What REBT targets is the extra, self-made layer of disturbance (self-blame, "I can't survive this") that stops people acting on their situation. Evaluating REBT REBT's strengths are its clarity, brevity and teachability. The ABC model can be explained in one session, used in groups, in schools and in workplaces, and practised as self-help; Ellis's books sold millions of copies. It has been applied to anxiety, depression, anger, addictions, sexual problems and performance anxiety. Its evidence base, though, is thinner and older than Beck's. Many early studies were small and methodologically weak. A meta-analysis by Lyons and Woods (1991) of some 70 outcome studies found REBT more effective than no treatment and placebo conditions, and later trials (for example, by Daniel David and colleagues in Romania in 2008) found REBT broadly comparable with Beck's cognitive therapy and with antidepressant medication for major depression. The criticisms are worth knowing because they turn up as exam options. First, REBT can be direct and confrontational , and a client may experience vigorous disputing as intimidating, invalidating or humiliating, especially early in therapy or if he is fragile. Second, the therapist's idea of what is "rational" may carry the therapist's own values; in cultures where duty to family is a moral ideal, a blanket attack on "shoulds" can feel like an attack on the client's ethics. Third, its philosophical claims (for example, that demandingness is the core of all disturbance) are hard to test. Notice what is not a fair criticism: REBT does not focus on sexuality (that is a criticism of Freud), and it does have evidence for depression. Indian context Many Indian clients carry a powerful version of Ellis's first must, often voiced as "log kya kahenge?" ("what will people say?"). Indian therapists using REBT usually dispute the absolutist form of the belief ("everyone must approve of me or I am nothing") rather than the value of family and community itself, and they work gently, since a frontal attack on a client's sense of duty tends to end the therapy rather than the belief. Exam trap Any stem mentioning musts , musturbation , awfulising , irrational beliefs , disputing or shame attacking points to Albert Ellis and REBT , not to Beck's cognitive therapy, DBT, or William Glasser's reality therapy (Chapter 6). "Rational Emotive Therapy was given by..." Ellis, not Freud, not William James (a founder of functionalism and of the James-Lange theory of emotion), and not Aaron Beck. Ellis was influenced by Adler and the Stoics, but REBT is his own. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first.
