Answers: (1) mediation, (2) Epictetus, (3) self-efficacy, (4) 1993, (5) beliefs, (6) musturbation (demandingness), (7) empirical, (8) shame-attacking, (9) depression. 5.3 Aaron Beck's cognitive model High yield · 12 Qs Ellis reached his therapy through philosophy and through his own shyness. The man you met in the opening pages reached his through data. Aaron Temkin Beck (1921 to 2021) grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, studied English and political science at Brown University and qualified in medicine at Yale in 1946. Like Ellis, he had treated himself before he treated anyone else: a dangerous infection in childhood had left him with a fear of blood and surgery, and during his medical training he overcame it by exposing himself gradually to the sights and sounds of the operating theatre until the fear faded. He trained in psychiatry, joined the University of Pennsylvania in 1954, and graduated from the Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute in 1956. In other words, he set out to prove psychoanalysis, not to replace it. The research described in the opening story changed his mind. His dream studies and his success experiments did not support the idea that depressed people secretly need to suffer, and his patients' "second stream" of thought explained their feelings better than any hidden wish. Beck published his new account in two papers called "Thinking and Depression" (1963 and 1964), then in the book Depression: Clinical, Experimental, and Theoretical Aspects (1967). In Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders (1976) he extended the model to anxiety, phobias and other conditions, and in Cognitive Therapy of Depression (1979), written with A. John Rush, Brian Shaw and Gary Emery, he set out the treatment session by session. That 1979 book was one of the first psychotherapy manuals, and manuals made controlled trials possible. Beck kept working almost to the end of a very long life; with his daughter, the psychologist Judith S. Beck , he founded the Beck Institute for Cognitive Behavior Therapy near Philadelphia in 1994, and he received the Lasker Award, one of medicine's highest honours, in 2006. Key study: cognitive therapy versus imipramine (Rush, Beck, Kovacs and Hollon, 1977) Could a talking treatment match a drug for depression? In 1977 A. John Rush, Beck, Maria Kovacs and Steven Hollon randomly assigned 41 depressed outpatients to about 12 weeks of either cognitive therapy or the tricyclic antidepressant imipramine. Both groups improved, but the cognitive therapy group improved more, and far fewer of them dropped out. It was the first trial in which any psychotherapy had beaten an antidepressant, and it launched a generation of research. Critics noted that the drug dose had been tapered before the final assessment, and later, larger trials usually found cognitive therapy and medication roughly equal during treatment. The lasting finding, as you will see in Section 5.11, was a different one: cognitive therapy protects against relapse after treatment ends. Automatic thoughts Beck's starting point was the second stream itself. automatic thoughts are the quick, evaluative thoughts or images that pop into the mind in a situation, without deliberate reasoning, and shape how a person feels and acts. Beck compared them with Freud's "preconscious": not hidden by repression, but so habitual that people notice the feeling and miss the thought that produced it. Automatic thoughts have a recognisable signature. They are specific and brief, often telegraphic (a single word such as "Idiot!" or a fleeting picture of being laughed at). They feel completely plausible, so they are accepted without question. They are idiosyncratic: two people in the same situation have different ones. And they are hard to switch off. The automatic thought that carries the most emotion is often called the hot thought . Return to the student who scored 48 out of 90 in Section 5.1. A cognitive therapist would not ask him what he believes about life in general. She would ask a much simpler question: "When you saw the score, what went through your mind?" The answer ("I'll never get into a clinical programme; everyone else is better than me") is the automatic thought, and it is the first thing cognitive therapy learns to catch. Notice the difference from Ellis. Ellis went straight for the deep philosophical "must"; Beck starts with the concrete thought in the concrete situation and works downward. The cognitive triad What do depressed people's automatic thoughts have in common? Beck's answer, first set out in 1967, is the most examined idea in this chapter. The cognitive triad is the pattern of negative thinking about three things: the self , the world (or ongoing experience) and the future . A negative view of the self : the person sees himself as defective, inadequate, worthless or unlovable, and attributes unpleasant experiences to these supposed defects ("I failed because I'm stupid"). A negative view of the world , or of current experience: the world seems to make impossible demands, to block every goal and to offer only defeat and deprivation ("Nothing ever works out for me; everyone is against me"). A negative view of the future : present hardships are expected to continue indefinitely ("It will always be like this; things will never get better"). This is the root of hopelessness. Beck argued that the other symptoms of depression follow from the triad. If you expect every effort to fail, it makes sense to stop trying, and the result looks like a loss of motivation or "paralysis of the will". If the future is hopeless, death can begin to look like the only escape, which is why Beck regarded hopelessness, rather than sadness, as the key to suicide. If you believe you cannot cope, you lean on others, and the result is increased dependency. Depression, on this view, is not primarily a disorder of mood. It is a disorder of thinking whose mood is the natural consequence. Exam trap The cognitive triad is negative views of self, world (experience) and future . It is not "past, present and future" (the past is not one of the three), not "self, others and environment", not "self, mother and father", not "mood, behaviour and somatic state", not "body, mind and spirit", and not "id, ego and superego" (Freud's structural model, Chapter 3). Nor is it "thoughts, feelings and behaviours", the three linked parts of the general CBT model. When a stem asks what maintains depression in Beck's model, the answer is the triad and the distortions that feed it; repressed sexual conflict is Freud's account, a "deficiency of reinforcement" is Peter Lewinsohn's behavioural account (Section 5.10), and insecure attachment is John Bowlby's (Developmental book). And if a stem describes "the pattern of negative thoughts about self, world and future", the name is the cognitive triad , not automatic thoughts, cognitive distortions or dysfunctional assumptions, which are the other parts of the model described next. Three levels of cognition Why do some people react to a poor mark with the triad and others with mild disappointment? Beck's answer was that automatic thoughts grow out of deeper and more lasting structures. His daughter Judith Beck later organised these into three levels, set out in her textbook Cognitive Therapy: Basics and Beyond (1995). Figure 5.3 shows how they fit together. At the deepest level are core beliefs : global, rigid, absolute beliefs about oneself, other people and the world, usually formed in childhood ("I am incompetent", "I am unlovable", "People can't be trusted"). Beck often used the word schema (plural schemas or schemata) for the mental structure that holds a core belief and filters incoming information: a schema works like a pair of tinted glasses, so that information that fits it is noticed and remembered and information that does not fit is ignored or explained away. Judith Beck grouped negative core beliefs about the self into three families: helpless beliefs ("I'm weak, I'm a failure"), unlovable beliefs ("I'm unwanted, I'll be rejected") and worthless beliefs ("I'm bad, I don't deserve to live"). At the middle level are intermediate beliefs : the attitudes, rules and assumptions that grow out of a core belief and tell the person how to live with it. Consider a student whose core belief is "I am incompetent". An attitude might be "It's terrible to be seen as stupid." A rule might be "I must top every test." An assumption , usually in if-then form, might be "If I study harder than everyone else, I can hide my incompetence; if I don't, everyone will see it." These conditional rules are also called dysfunctional assumptions , and they can be measured with the Dysfunctional Attitude Scale (Arlene Weissman and Beck, 1978). They are often the source of compensatory strategies : the student copes by overworking, which works until the day it doesn't. At the surface level are the automatic thoughts. When a situation touches the rule (a mock score of 48), the core belief is activated and the automatic thoughts follow ("I'm useless; I'll never get in"), and these in turn produce the person's reactions: an emotion (despair), a behaviour (closing the books) and a physiological response (heaviness, fatigue). Deepest level: formed in childhood Core beliefs (schemas) "I am incompetent" Middle level: conditional rules Intermediate beliefs (rules, assumptions) "If I don't top every test, I'm a failure" Situation Mock test score: 48 out of 90 Automatic thoughts "I'm useless." "I'll never get in." Emotion: despair Behaviour: gives up Body: tired, heavy Surface level: the situation triggers automatic thoughts, which drive the reactions Figure 5.3 Beck's cognitive model, as organised by Judith Beck. A core belief formed early in life gives rise to conditional rules; when a situation touches those rules, automatic thoughts appear and drive emotion, behaviour and bodily reactions. Therapy starts at the surface and works downward. The model is a diathesis-stress model. A dysfunctional schema can lie dormant for years, like a landmine, until a matching stress steps on it. Beck (1983) suggested that people differ in which landmines they carry. A sociotropic person invests his worth in being liked and close to others, so he is most vulnerable to rejection or loss; an autonomous person invests his worth in achievement and independence, so he is most vulnerable to failure or loss of control. The same broken engagement may devastate the first and barely touch the second, while a failed examination does the reverse. Notice the practical consequence: when the depression lifts, the schema does not simply vanish. It goes quiet and can be reawakened by the next matching stress, or even by an ordinary low mood. That observation would later become the starting point for mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (Section 5.9). The cognitive distortions If schemas are tinted glasses, how exactly do they bend what a person sees? Beck noticed that depressed patients made the same errors of reasoning again and again, and he called them cognitive distortions (also cognitive errors or thinking errors): systematic, biased ways of processing information that turn ordinary events into evidence for the negative schema. In 1979 Beck listed six: arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralisation, magnification and minimisation, personalisation, and absolutistic dichotomous thinking. The psychiatrist David D. Burns , who had trained with Beck in Philadelphia, rewrote the list in plain language for his best-selling self-help book Feeling Good (1980) and added several more; later writers added others still. Table 5.3 lists them all, each with an example, and the paragraphs that follow it separate the pairs that examiners like to confuse. Table 5.3 The cognitive distortions, with an example of each. The first six are Beck's original list; the rest come mainly from Burns (1980) and later writers. Distortion What the person does Example Arbitrary inference Draws a conclusion with no evidence, or against the evidence A friend passes without greeting: "He doesn't like me any more" Selective abstraction (mental filter, selective attention) Picks out one detail, ignores the rest and judges the whole by it A teacher sees two bored students in a class of forty: "My class doesn't like me" Overgeneralisation Draws a broad rule from one or a few incidents and applies it everywhere "I failed statistics, so I'll fail at everything" Magnification and minimisation Blows up faults and shrinks strengths One stumble "ruined" the seminar; the praise "meant nothing" Personalisation Takes responsibility for, or takes personally, events that have little to do with oneself "The guests left early because I'm boring" Dichotomous (all-or-nothing) thinking Sees only two extreme categories "If I don't get the first rank, I've failed" Catastrophising Expects the worst possible outcome "If I fail this exam, my whole life is ruined" Disqualifying the positive Insists that good experiences "don't count" "They only praised my answer to be polite" Mind reading Assumes he knows what others are thinking "The examiner thinks I'm stupid" Fortune telling Predicts that things will turn out badly "I'll freeze in the interview" Emotional reasoning Takes a feeling as proof of a fact "I feel like a failure, so I must be one" Should statements Drives himself or others with rigid "shoulds" and "musts" "I should never make a mistake" Labelling Attaches a global label instead of describing an act "I'm a loser", rather than "I made a mistake" arbitrary inference is jumping to a conclusion that the evidence does not support. In a classic example, a patient sees a friend in the street who fails to acknowledge him, and concludes that the friend no longer likes him. Perhaps the friend did not see him, or was preoccupied, or was short-sighted; nothing in the situation points to dislike, yet the conclusion feels certain. Burns later split arbitrary inference into two narrower kinds of "jumping to conclusions": mind reading (concluding what someone else thinks, without checking) and fortune telling (predicting a bad outcome as if it were already fact). When an option offers "arbitrary inference" and no narrower name, that is the one to choose. selective abstraction is focusing on a detail taken out of context, ignoring other, more important features of the situation, and judging the whole experience by that one fragment. Burns called it the mental filter , and some Indian textbooks and papers call it selective attention . A teacher lecturing to forty students notices two who look bored and concludes that his class is not liked by the students: thirty-eight attentive faces have been filtered out. A cricketer who scored a century but dropped one catch, and spends the night replaying the catch, is doing the same thing. Its close cousin is disqualifying the positive : the filtered-out good news is noticed, but then dismissed as a fluke or as politeness. overgeneralisation is different. Here the person takes one or a few events and turns them into a general rule that is then applied across the board, to related and unrelated situations alike: "I couldn't answer one question in the viva, so I'll never be good at interviews," or "Ravi let me down, so nobody can be trusted." The signal words are "always", "never", "everyone" and "nothing". So the difference between the two is the direction of the error. Selective abstraction narrows the view within a situation (one detail stands for the whole). Overgeneralisation spreads a conclusion across situations (one event stands for all events). labelling is overgeneralisation applied to a whole person: instead of "I made a mistake", "I'm a failure"; instead of "she was late", "she's useless". You met its REBT twin, global rating, in Section 5.2. magnification and minimisation is an error of size: one's mistakes, other people's strengths and the importance of bad events are enlarged, while one's own strengths and good events are shrunk. Burns compared it to looking through binoculars, the right way round at one's faults and the wrong way round at one's virtues. catastrophising is the extreme form of magnification applied to the future: worrying that the worst will happen and that it will be unbearable when it does ("If my heart races in the exam hall, I'll pass out, fail, and my family will never forgive me"). It is common in every anxiety disorder, and Beck's term overlaps closely with Ellis's awfulising. Some lists treat catastrophising as a kind of magnification, others as a kind of fortune telling; either way, its defining mark is the expectation of the worst. personalisation is relating external events to oneself when there is no basis for doing so: taking things personally, or taking responsibility for events one did not cause. A mother whose son fails his board examination thinks, "It's my fault; I'm a bad mother," though the boy barely studied. A man who thinks "it always rains when I plan a picnic" has personalised the weather. dichotomous thinking (all-or-nothing or black-and-white thinking) sorts every experience into one of two extreme categories, perfect or worthless, success or failure, saint or sinner, with nothing in between. It is the distortion behind perfectionism, and you will meet it again in borderline personality disorder (Section 5.8), where other people are experienced as wholly good or wholly bad. The remaining three are easily recognised once named. emotional reasoning treats a feeling as evidence ("I feel guilty, so I must have done something wrong"; "I feel anxious on aeroplanes, so flying must be dangerous"). should statements are rigid rules aimed at oneself (producing guilt) or at others (producing anger and resentment); they are cognitive therapy's version (the name is Burns's) of Ellis's musts and Karen Horney's "tyranny of the shoulds". Labelling, already described, completes the list. Exam trap Three classic stems. (1) "A patient sees a friend in the street who fails to acknowledge him; he thinks his friend does not like him any more." This is arbitrary inference : a conclusion without evidence. It is not selective abstraction (no detail is being picked out of a larger picture), not personalisation (he is not blaming himself for an event he did not cause) and not magnification (nothing is being blown up in size). (2) "A teacher sees two students bored and feels his class is not liked by all the students." This is selective abstraction , which the paper called selective attention . A good student may be tempted by overgeneralisation , because the teacher moves from two students to "all the students"; but overgeneralisation means carrying a conclusion from one situation to other, unrelated situations, whereas the teacher has filtered one detail out of a single situation and ignored the rest of it. (3) "Catastrophic thinking describes..." worrying that the worst will always happen . Categorising all experiences as either extremely positive or extremely negative is dichotomous thinking; focusing on negative events while ignoring positive ones is the mental filter (selective abstraction); taking things very personally is personalisation. Exam trap "Catastrophic thinking" belongs to the cognitive model of anxiety, not to the diagnostic criteria of schizophrenia. If a question asks which of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech and catastrophic thinking is not an ICD or DSM criterion for schizophrenia, the answer is catastrophic thinking (the criteria themselves are covered in the Disorders book). 5.4 Cognitive therapy in practice High yield · 12 Qs Suppose the student with the 48 out of 90 decides to see a cognitive therapist. What will actually happen in the room? The short answer is that he will be treated as a scientist with a hypothesis. His automatic thoughts and beliefs will not be interpreted, as a psychoanalyst would interpret them, and they will not be argued down, as Ellis might argue them down. They will be examined, the way a researcher examines a claim: what is the evidence, how else could the data be explained, and what experiment would settle the matter? This section describes the method, the techniques that carry it out, and the way it differs from REBT. Collaborative empiricism Beck called the working relationship collaborative empiricism . "Collaborative" means that therapist and client work as a team, a pair of co-investigators who set goals and agendas together and share responsibility for the work. "Empiricism" means that the client's beliefs are treated as hypotheses to be tested against evidence, not as facts to be accepted and not as errors to be corrected by authority. The core activity of the therapy is therefore making objective assessments of beliefs : gathering data from the client's own life, weighing it, and running real-world tests. A depressed client who says "I can't do anything right" is not told he is wrong; he and the therapist go looking for evidence, and the client draws the conclusion himself. The relationship matters more in Beck's therapy than it did in Ellis's. Beck and his co-authors wrote in 1979 that warmth, accurate empathy and genuineness, the qualities Carl Rogers had emphasised (Chapter 6), were necessary for cognitive therapy but not sufficient: a good relationship is the ground on which the techniques work, not the treatment itself. The therapist is also openly educational. In the first sessions the client learns the cognitive model, using examples from his own week, because the long-term aim is for him to become his own therapist. Notice what is absent. There is no couch, no free association (saying whatever comes to mind so that the analyst can detect unconscious material), no dream analysis , no interpretation of transference and no attempt to uncover repressed childhood memories. Those are the tools of psychoanalysis (Chapter 3). Nor does the therapist administer medication; a cognitive therapist may work alongside a psychiatrist who prescribes, but prescribing is no part of cognitive therapy. Exam trap "Which of the following is NOT a fundamental concept of cognitive therapy: collaborative empiricism, Socratic dialogue, free association, guided discovery?" Free association , which is psychoanalytic. The other three are the core of Beck's method. Similarly, "Which method is used in Beck's cognitive therapy for depression?" is answered by making objective assessments of beliefs , not by encouraging dream analysis or free association (Freud) and not by administering psychoactive medication (pharmacotherapy, which is not a psychotherapy at all). Socratic questioning and guided discovery How does a therapist help a client test a belief without simply telling him it is wrong? By asking questions. The Greek philosopher Socrates (about 470 to 399 BCE) taught not by lecturing but by asking a series of questions that led the other person to examine his own assumptions and discover their weaknesses for himself. Beck borrowed the method. Socratic questioning (or Socratic dialogue) is the use of carefully chosen, open-ended questions to help the client examine his own thoughts, notice evidence he has overlooked, consider other explanations and reach a more balanced conclusion of his own. guided discovery is the broader process the questions serve: the therapist guides, but the client discovers. The American psychologist Christine A. Padesky , in a well-known 1993 address titled "Socratic Questioning: Changing Minds or Guiding Discovery?", gave the definition that examiners now quote. Socratic questioning, she said, asks the client questions which he has the knowledge to answer and which draw his attention to information that is relevant to the issue but outside his current focus. In the words of one past paper, it is a form of dialogue that helps a person discover and attend to previously overlooked information and that guides the discovery of the individual rather than interpretation from the therapist . Padesky argued that the aim is not to change the client's mind for him (the therapist does not know the answer in advance) but to guide a genuine discovery, and she described four steps: informational questions, empathic listening, summarising, and synthesising questions that ask the client to apply what he has found to his original belief. Three questions do much of the work, and together they are sometimes called the three-question technique: What is the evidence for this thought? How else could you look at the situation? If it were true, what would it mean, and how would you cope? Here is how it sounds. Kavya, a first-year MA student, has been asked to present a case at a departmental seminar. Therapist: You said that when your supervisor frowned during your presentation, you thought, "She thinks I'm hopeless." How much did you believe that at the time? Kavya: Completely. Ninety percent. Therapist: What did you see that fitted the thought? Kavya: The frown. And she wrote something down. Therapist: Anything that didn't quite fit? Kavya: Well... afterwards she asked me to send her my slides. And she frowns when she concentrates; she frowned all through Arjun's talk too. Therapist: So, putting all of that together, what do you make of the frown now? Kavya: Maybe she was thinking hard about the case. Maybe forty percent that she thought it was bad. The therapist never said "You're wrong" or "That's mind reading." Every piece of new evidence came from Kavya's own memory, and so did the new conclusion. That is the difference between guided discovery and persuasion. Exam trap Socratic questioning is the therapist guiding the client to discover his own maladaptive thoughts and generate alternatives through open-ended questions. It is not the therapist interpreting unconscious conflicts, not the therapist giving direct advice or telling the client what to think, not direct confrontation of beliefs, not free association while the therapist listens passively, and not hypnotic suggestion. In the long "definition" options, check two details: the information is previously overlooked (not "previously attended"), and the discovery belongs to the individual (not to the therapist), "rather than interpretation from the therapist". Two relatives cause confusion. Viktor Frankl's logotherapy also uses a Socratic dialogue, but to help the client find meaning; logotherapy is an existential therapy (Chapter 6), not a "cognitive therapy emphasising irrational beliefs" (that description fits REBT). And Ellis's disputing can be Socratic in form but is far more persuasive and didactic. The structure of a session and the course of therapy Cognitive therapy is the most structured of the talking therapies. A typical course for depression runs 12 to 20 weekly sessions of about 50 minutes, often followed by a few "booster" sessions spaced weeks or months apart. The early sessions assess the problem, build the relationship, set goals, teach the cognitive model and build a case conceptualisation (the therapist's working map of how the client's core beliefs, rules, automatic thoughts and behaviours fit together; Judith Beck's cognitive conceptualisation diagram is a one-page version, and formulation in general is described in Chapter 2). Termination is planned from the first session. Each session follows a recognisable order, which Judith Beck set out as follows: Mood check , usually with a brief questionnaire such as the Beck Depression Inventory, plus a quick update on the week (and on medication, if any). Bridge from the previous session: what the client learned last time and what he remembers of it. Agenda setting : client and therapist agree on the two or three problems the session will tackle. Homework review : what the client tried, what happened and what he concluded. Discussion of agenda items , using the techniques described below, with frequent summaries. New homework , agreed together and arising directly from the session's work. Final summary and feedback : the client summarises the main points and says what was helpful or unhelpful, including anything the therapist said that upset him. The structure is not bureaucracy. Depressed people find it hard to concentrate and easy to feel overwhelmed, and a predictable structure makes the hour productive. Asking for feedback at the end protects the alliance, and homework carries the work into the 167 hours of the week that the client spends outside the room. Progress is measured throughout, usually with Beck's own scales, which are described fully in the Assessment book. The Beck Depression Inventory (BDI, 1961; revised as the BDI-II in 1996) has 21 items, each with four statements of increasing severity. The Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI, 1988) also has 21 items. The Beck Hopelessness Scale (BHS, 1974) has 20 true-or-false items about the future. All three are self-report measures: the client reads the items and rates himself. They contrast with clinician-rated (observer-rated) scales such as the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (1960) and the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (1959) of the British psychiatrist Max Hamilton (1912 to 1988), which a trained clinician completes after an interview. Exam trap "Which is a clinician-rated questionnaire: BDI, BAI, Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, both BAI and Hamilton?" Only the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale . The BDI and BAI are self-report, so "both" is wrong. A useful memory hook: Beck's scales are filled in by the patient; Hamilton's by the clinician. Clinical link Beck's emphasis on the future part of the triad had a practical payoff. In a ten-year follow-up of patients hospitalised with suicidal thoughts, Beck and his colleagues (1985) found that hopelessness, measured with the BHS, predicted who would later die by suicide better than the severity of depression did. Hopelessness is therefore something a cognitive therapist asks about directly and early. In any risk assessment, risk is judged highest when several markers converge: frequent suicidal ideas, a specific plan, a highly lethal method, previous attempts and a family history of suicide (suicide risk assessment and crisis work are covered in Chapter 9). Working with automatic thoughts The first skill clients learn is to catch automatic thoughts. Because people notice their feelings more than their thoughts, the therapist uses the feeling as the signal. Whenever the client's mood shifts in the session (his face falls, his voice tightens), the therapist asks the key question of cognitive therapy: "What was going through your mind just then?" Between sessions the client does the same thing on paper. The paper is the dysfunctional thought record (DTR), introduced by Beck and his colleagues in 1979 as the "Daily Record of Dysfunctional Thoughts". It is a sheet of columns. The client writes down the situation (what happened, where, when), the emotion and its intensity (0 to 100), the automatic thought and how strongly he believed it (0 to 100 percent), then, with practice, a rational (or balanced) response and finally the outcome , re-rating the original belief and emotion. Later versions, such as the seven-column record in Dennis Greenberger and Christine Padesky's self-help book Mind Over Mood (1995), split the middle into "evidence for the hot thought" and "evidence against it". Its purpose, in a phrase examiners use, is to identify, examine and restructure automatic negative thoughts . Table 5.4 shows a completed example. Belief 40%; despair 45; revised the weak subject for an hour Exam trap A thought record is used to identify, examine and restructure automatic negative thoughts . It is not used to record dreams for symbolic interpretation (psychoanalysis), not to measure galvanic skin response (the change in the skin's electrical conductance with arousal, used in biofeedback and lie detection), and not to track medication side effects. Once a thought is on paper, several techniques help the client examine it. Examining the evidence lists the facts for and against the thought, separating facts from interpretations. Generating alternative explanations asks what else could account for the event (the friend who did not greet you may not have seen you). The double-standard technique asks what the client would say to a close friend in the same situation, since most people are far kinder to friends than to themselves. Identifying the distortion by name ("That sounds like fortune telling") gives the client a quick way to step back. And two techniques have names of their own. decatastrophising , sometimes called the "what if" technique, is used when the client fears an outcome. The therapist asks, in effect: What is the worst that could realistically happen? How likely is it? What is the best that could happen, and the most likely? And if the worst did happen, how would you cope, and would it still matter in five years? Asked properly, the questions shrink a catastrophe to a problem. A student terrified of failing the entrance examination may discover that the worst realistic outcome is a year's delay and a second attempt, which is painful but survivable. reattribution is used when the client takes too much of the blame for an event. The therapist helps him list everyone and everything that contributed and assign each a fair share, often by drawing a responsibility pie . A man who blames himself entirely for his son's failing marks may end up with slices for the son's own effort, a change of school, a long illness, a strict new teacher and, yes, a modest slice for himself. Reattribution targets personalisation; it does not try to make the client blameless, only fairly blamed. For dichotomous thinking, the continuum technique replaces the two boxes with a line from 0 to 100. A perfectionist who thinks she is "a complete failure" is asked who would sit at 0 (someone who never tried at all?) and who at 100, and then where she herself belongs. She rarely puts herself at 0. Finally, balanced responses that work are often written on small coping cards that the client carries and reads when the old thought returns. Behavioural techniques in cognitive therapy Cognitive therapy is not only talk. Beck used behavioural methods from the start, especially with severely depressed patients who were too slowed down to do much thinking work. The difference from pure behaviour therapy (Chapter 4) is the purpose: in cognitive therapy, behaviour change is used above all to produce evidence that tests a belief. activity scheduling begins with monitoring: the client records what he does each hour for a week. Each activity is then rated for mastery (the sense of accomplishment, 0 to 10) and pleasure (enjoyment, 0 to 10). The record usually shows two things the depressed client did not believe: that he does do things, and that some activities lift his mood more than others. The next step is to plan the coming week, scheduling more of the activities that bring mastery or pleasure. A client who believes "I can't do anything" and "nothing helps" now holds a sheet of paper that says otherwise. graded task assignment breaks a daunting task into small, manageable steps, arranged from easiest to hardest, so that the client succeeds early and often. A student who cannot face "revising for the exam" may start with "open the clinical psychology notes and read one page", then "read one section and do five questions", and so on. Each completed step is evidence against "I can't", and the growing sense of mastery is exactly what Bandura called a mastery experience (Section 5.1). behavioural experiments are planned activities designed to test a specific belief in real life. The client states the prediction and how strongly he believes it ("If I ask a question in class, people will laugh at me: 80 percent"), designs a test, carries it out, records what actually happened, and re-rates the belief. Behavioural experiments are often more powerful than any amount of discussion, because the new evidence is lived rather than argued. They differ from exposure (Chapter 4) in their rationale: exposure aims mainly at fear reduction through repeated contact, whereas an experiment aims at disconfirming a prediction, and a single well-designed experiment can be enough. Role-play (rehearsing a difficult conversation in the session) and cognitive rehearsal (imagining each step of a task in detail before doing it, so that obstacles can be anticipated) complete the behavioural toolkit. Reaching the deeper beliefs Automatic thoughts are the way in, but lasting change usually requires work on the intermediate and core beliefs underneath. The standard way down is the downward arrow technique , described by David Burns (1980), who called it the vertical arrow technique. Instead of disputing an automatic thought, the therapist provisionally accepts it and asks, again and again: "Suppose that were true. What would it mean to you? Why would that be so upsetting?" Each answer is written below the last, with an arrow pointing down, until the client reaches a belief that cannot be pushed further. That is usually the core belief. Push Kavya's thought through it: "She thinks my presentation was poor." And if she did, what would that mean? "That she'll think I'm not good enough for clinical work." And if she thought that? "That she'd be right. I'm not good enough." And if you're not good enough? "Then I'm a fraud. Sooner or later everyone will find out I'm incompetent." Four steps have taken her from a frown at a seminar to "I am incompetent": a helpless core belief, and the real target of therapy. Exam trap The downward arrow technique is used to uncover the underlying core belief by repeatedly asking "If that were true, what would it mean?" It is not used to identify behavioural antecedents (that is functional analysis, Chapter 4), not to rate symptom intensity from 0 to 10 (that is the SUDS, subjective units of distress, used in exposure), and not to construct an exposure hierarchy (Wolpe's systematic desensitisation, Chapter 4). Core beliefs change slowly, because the schema filters out disconfirming evidence. Therapists therefore work on them deliberately over many weeks. With a positive data log , the client records every day the small pieces of evidence that do not fit the old belief, which the schema would otherwise let slip. With a historical test of the schema , he reviews his life period by period, looking for evidence for and against "I am incompetent" at each age. He may be asked to act "as if" he held a new, more balanced belief, and to see what happens. Beck and his colleagues described three degrees of success. The fullest is schema restructuring , in which the old belief is replaced. More common is schema modification , in which it is softened and made more flexible. The most limited is schema reinterpretation , in which the belief stays but the person learns to live with it in a less harmful way (a perfectionist who keeps her standards but finds a job, such as quality inspection, where they are an asset). Beck and Ellis compared You are now in a position to compare the two founders, and examiners love the comparison. Begin with what they share. Both Beck and Ellis hold that emotional disturbance arises largely from the way people think about events, rather than from the events themselves; both trace the idea to the Stoics; both are active, directive, present-focused and brief; both use homework and behavioural assignments; and both are therefore counted as founders of the cognitive, or cognitive-behavioural, tradition. Neither holds that behaviour is controlled only by reinforcement (Skinner), that unconscious sexual drives determine behaviour (Freud), or that the therapeutic relationship alone produces change (Rogers). The differences are of emphasis, but they are real. Ellis, a psychologist with a philosopher's temperament, believed that one root process, demandingness, underlies nearly all disturbance, and he set out to persuade clients out of it, vigorously and sometimes bluntly. Beck, a psychiatrist with a researcher's temperament, believed that each disorder has its own characteristic content (loss in depression, danger in anxiety; Section 5.6) and set out to help clients test their thoughts like hypotheses. Ellis calls the problematic beliefs irrational : absolutist and illogical. Beck calls them distorted or dysfunctional : inaccurate and unhelpful. In a published exchange, Padesky and Beck (2003) described the difference as one between science and philosophy: cognitive therapy tests beliefs empirically, whereas REBT disputes them philosophically. Cognitive (cognitive-behavioural) therapy , not psychodynamic, humanistic or family systems therapy. Then watch the distinguishing words. "Irrational belief", "must", "disputing", "awfulising" point to Ellis ; "automatic thought", "cognitive triad", "distortion", "collaborative empiricism", "Socratic questioning", "thought record" point to Beck . Beck's therapy was developed primarily for depression , and only later extended to anxiety disorders, personality disorders, substance use, OCD and schizophrenia. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. Focusing on one negative detail and ignoring the rest of the situation is selective , also called the mental filter. But think of a person who is not so much mistaken as unequipped. A child who rushes every sum and makes careless errors does not hold an irrational belief about arithmetic; he has never learned to slow himself down. A woman whose husband has lost his job, whose mother-in-law is ill and whose loan instalments are due is not distorting anything; she has more problems than she knows how to handle. For people like these, a second group of cognitive-behavioural therapists asked a more practical question. What skills does this person lack, and how can they be taught? Keith Dobson, whose definition of CBT you met in Section 5.1, follows Michael Mahoney and Diane Arnkoff (1978) in sorting the cognitive-behavioural therapies into three families. The cognitive restructuring therapies (Ellis's REBT and Beck's cognitive therapy) replace faulty beliefs with better ones. The coping skills therapies (Donald Meichenbaum's self-instructional training and stress inoculation training) teach people what to do and say to themselves in a difficult situation. The problem-solving therapies (D'Zurilla and Goldfried's problem-solving therapy) teach a general method for working through problems of living. This section covers the second and third families, then two approaches that fit no family neatly: Arnold Lazarus's multimodal therapy, which sets out to leave no part of a person's life unexamined, and George Kelly's much older fixed-role therapy, which asks a client to spend two weeks living as somebody else. Meichenbaum and self-instructional training In the 1960s a graduate student at the University of Illinois named Donald Meichenbaum (born 1940) was running an operant conditioning study with hospitalised patients with schizophrenia. He reinforced them for "healthy talk": coherent, relevant answers in an interview. The method worked. But, as Meichenbaum later told the story, something in the follow-up interviews caught his attention. Some of the patients were quietly repeating the experimenter's instruction to themselves: "Give healthy talk; be coherent and relevant." The reinforcement had come from outside, but these patients had turned it into an instruction that came from inside, and they seemed to do best. What if, Meichenbaum wondered, people could be taught directly what to say to themselves? The idea had a respectable pedigree. The Soviet psychologists Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky (1896 to 1934) and Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977) had described how children gain voluntary control over their behaviour through speech: first the speech of adults directs the child ("Put the red block on top"), then the child directs himself aloud, as any four-year-old building a tower does, and finally the speech goes underground as silent inner speech . Meichenbaum reasoned that in impulsive children this inner guide had never properly formed, and that it could be built deliberately. The result was self-instructional training : a method in which a therapist models a task while talking himself through it aloud, and the client then learns, in stages, to guide his own performance first with overt and finally with covert self-instructions. Key study: teaching impulsive children to talk to themselves (Meichenbaum and Goodman, 1971) Question. Can impulsive children learn to slow down and work carefully by being taught what to say to themselves? Method. Donald Meichenbaum and Joseph Goodman worked with second-grade children who had been placed in a special class because of hyperactivity and poor self-control. Some of the children received a few short sessions of self-instructional training on tasks such as copying line patterns and colouring figures within boundaries; others spent the same time on the same tasks without the self-instructions, or were simply assessed. Result. The trained children improved more than the controls on tests of planning and impulsivity, including the Porteus Maze and Jerome Kagan's Matching Familiar Figures Test, on which they began to take longer before answering (a sign of reflection rather than impulsive guessing), and the gains were still present a month later. Conclusion. Self-talk can be taught, and taught self-talk can regulate behaviour. Criticism. The samples were small, and the gains on laboratory tasks did not show up clearly in the children's classroom behaviour. Generalisation from the training task to everyday life has remained the method's weak point, which is why later versions train self-instructions across many different tasks and settings. Meichenbaum and Goodman's training ran through five steps, and examiners like to ask for them in order: Cognitive modelling. The adult performs the task while talking to himself aloud, and the child watches and listens. Overt external guidance. The child performs the same task while the adult speaks the instructions aloud. Overt self-guidance. The child performs the task while speaking the instructions aloud to himself. Faded overt self-guidance. The child whispers the instructions while performing the task. Covert self-instruction. The child performs the task while guiding himself with silent inner speech. Notice that the five steps recreate, in a few sessions, Vygotsky and Luria's sequence from the speech of others, to one's own speech aloud, to inner speech. The content of the self-talk matters as much as its form. Meichenbaum's model monologue for a line-copying task ran roughly: "Okay, what is it I have to do? Copy the picture. Go slowly and be careful. Draw the line down, good; now to the right. I'm doing fine so far. Oops, I was supposed to go down. That's okay; just erase it carefully. Finished. I did it." Inside that small speech are five skills: defining the problem , focusing attention and guiding the response , self-reinforcement ("good, I'm doing fine"), coping with errors ("that's okay") and self-evaluation at the end. The error-coping step was deliberate. Meichenbaum found that a coping model , who makes mistakes and talks himself through them, teaches more than a mastery model , who performs flawlessly; his 1971 study of modelling found that coping models reduced avoidance more than mastery models did. A model who never stumbles shows the learner what success looks like, but not what to do on the way there when things go wrong. Push a case through the method. Rohan, eight, at a school in Mysuru, races through his arithmetic worksheets, makes careless errors and crumples the page. His therapist works the first sum aloud ("What do I have to do? Add these. Slowly. First the ones: six and seven, thirteen; write three, carry one..."). Rohan does the next sum while she says the words, then says them himself aloud, then in a whisper, then silently. She has already modelled what to do with a mistake: "Oops. That's okay. I can rub it out and go slowly." Because self-talk learned on one worksheet tends to stay on that worksheet, the same instructions are then practised on reading, a board game and getting ready for school. Self-instructional training was soon applied to test-anxious students (Meichenbaum, 1972), to patients with schizophrenia, whom Meichenbaum and Roy Cameron (1973) trained to instruct themselves to "be relevant and coherent", and to anger, pain and attention problems. Meichenbaum, who spent most of his career at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, drew the work together in Cognitive-Behavior Modification: An Integrative Approach (1977), the book that, as Section 5.1 noted, helped give the field its name. Its message was that what people say to themselves, their internal dialogue , is a behaviour that can be observed, modelled, rehearsed and changed. Exam trap Meichenbaum developed two methods, and some books abbreviate both as "SIT". Self-instructional training (Meichenbaum and Goodman, 1971) teaches a person what to say to himself to guide a task; it began with impulsive children. Stress inoculation training (described next) is a broader three-phase package for coping with stress. The five steps of self-instructional training run from the adult's speech to the child's own overt , then whispered , then covert speech: cognitive modelling, overt external guidance, overt self-guidance, faded overt self-guidance, covert self-instruction. The theory behind it, the internalisation of speech, comes from Vygotsky and Luria , not Piaget. And self-instruction is not "positive thinking" or thought stopping (Section 4.9): the statements guide action and cope with errors rather than praising oneself or blocking thoughts. Stress inoculation training How does a vaccine work? It exposes the body to a weakened form of a disease, a dose too small to make you ill but large enough to make the immune system build defences, so that the real disease is resisted when it comes. In the 1970s Meichenbaum borrowed the metaphor for psychology. (The American psychologist Irving Janis had earlier written of the "emotional inoculation" of surgical patients who were prepared in advance for the discomforts of their operations.) stress inoculation training (SIT) is a structured, three-phase cognitive-behavioural programme in which a person first learns to understand his stress, then acquires and rehearses a set of coping skills, and finally applies them to gradually increasing, manageable doses of the real stressor, so as to build resistance to future stress. Meichenbaum set it out fully in his book Stress Inoculation Training (1985). SIT rests on a particular view of stress. Following the American psychologist Richard Stanley Lazarus (1922 to 2002), whose transactional model is described in Section 9.3, Meichenbaum treats stress as a transaction between person and situation: we feel stressed when we appraise the demands of a situation as exceeding our resources for coping. Change the appraisal, or strengthen the resources, and the stress changes too. That is why SIT is a package rather than a single technique. Figure 5.4 shows its three phases. Stress inoculation training (Meichenbaum) 1. Conceptualisation (education) Build the alliance Self-monitoring diary Teach how appraisals shape stress Split stressors into changeable and fixed 2. Skills acquisition and rehearsal Relaxation, breathing Coping self-statements Cognitive restructuring Problem solving Rehearse in imagery and in role play 3. Application and follow-through Imagined exposure Graded real-life practice Relapse prevention Credit own efforts Booster sessions Setback: return to rehearsal, then try again phases in order return after a setback (relapse prevention) Figure 5.4 The three phases of stress inoculation training. Each phase builds on the one before; the return loop beneath the boxes shows that a setback in the real world is treated as information, sending the client back to rehearse rather than as proof of failure. Phase 1: conceptualisation. The first phase is educational and collaborative. The therapist builds a relationship, gathers a detailed picture of the stress (often with a stress diary) and helps the client reconceptualise it: stress stops being a mysterious, overwhelming force and becomes a sequence of reactions that can be anticipated and a set of problems that can be worked on. A key step is to break a global stressor ("my job is killing me") into parts and sort them into those that can be changed (unrealistic deadlines, answering emails at midnight) and those that cannot (the company's restructuring). Changeable parts call for problem-focused coping , acting on the situation; unchangeable ones call for emotion-focused coping , managing one's reactions. Both terms come from Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman. Phase 2: skills acquisition and rehearsal. In the second phase the client learns and practises the coping skills his particular stress requires. Typical skills include relaxation and slow breathing (Section 4.8), cognitive restructuring of stress-producing thoughts, problem solving (described below), assertiveness, and the use of coping self-statements : brief, task-focused instructions a person gives himself at each stage of a stressful encounter, developed from self-instructional training. Meichenbaum divided a stressful encounter into four stages and suggested statements for each (Table 5.6). The skills are rehearsed first in the safety of the session, in imagery and in role play. Table 5.6 Meichenbaum's four stages of a stressful encounter, with coping self-statements a candidate might use before and during an admission interview. Stage Purpose of the self-statements Example self-statements Preparing for a stressor Plan, and replace worry with a task "What exactly will they ask? I have prepared the main topics. Worrying won't help; planning will." Confronting and handling the stressor Stay focused on the task in front of you "One question at a time. Breathe slowly. I can ask them to repeat a question." Coping with the feeling of being overwhelmed Label the arousal and keep going "My heart is racing; that's expected. Pause, breathe out. I don't have to be perfect, just keep going." Reinforcing self-statements Credit oneself afterwards, whatever the result "I got through it. It was easier than I feared, and I handled it better than last time." Phase 3: application and follow-through. The skills are now tried against the real thing in gradually increasing doses: this is the inoculation proper. The client imagines coping, then role-plays it, then meets the stressor in real life in graded steps. Because setbacks are certain, relapse prevention (G. Alan Marlatt and Judith Gordon's approach from the addictions field; Chapter 9) is built in: the client plans for high-risk situations and treats a lapse as a signal to use his skills, not as proof of failure. Crediting improvement to his own efforts raises his self-efficacy (Section 5.1), and follow-up and booster sessions complete the programme. Because it is a framework rather than a fixed protocol, SIT has been applied very widely. Raymond W. Novaco adapted it for anger in 1975, rewriting the four stages as preparing for a provocation, meeting it, coping with arousal and reflecting afterwards. It has been used to prepare patients for surgery, to treat test anxiety and chronic pain, to support carers, and to prepare soldiers, police officers, nurses and athletes for high-stress work before the stress arrives (prevention as well as treatment); in the late 1970s and 1980s it was among the first structured treatments offered to survivors of rape. A meta-analysis of 37 studies by Saunders, Driskell, Johnston and Salas (1996) found that it reduced performance anxiety and state anxiety and improved performance under stress. Key study: stress inoculation versus prolonged exposure after rape (Foa, Rothbaum, Riggs and Murdock, 1991) Which helps survivors of rape with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) more: learning to cope with the fear, or confronting the memory? Edna B. Foa and her colleagues in Philadelphia randomly assigned 45 women to nine sessions of stress inoculation training, prolonged exposure (repeatedly reliving the assault in imagination, Section 4.3), supportive counselling or a waiting list. At the end of treatment SIT had produced the largest improvement; at follow-up some three months later prolonged exposure had pulled ahead. Results like these explain why exposure-based and cognitive trauma therapies (Section 5.6) became the first-line treatments for PTSD, while SIT's coping skills survive as components inside them. Exam trap The three phases of stress inoculation training, in order, are conceptualisation (education), skills acquisition and rehearsal , and application and follow-through . A distractor may offer "relaxation, desensitisation, flooding" or Selye's "alarm, resistance, exhaustion" (the general adaptation syndrome, a description of the stress response, not a therapy). The metaphor is vaccination : small, manageable doses of stress, after skills have been learned. SIT is therefore not flooding, which begins at the top of the fear hierarchy (Section 4.3). Above all, do not confuse the two Lazaruses. Richard Lazarus gave SIT its theory of stress (appraisal and coping); Arnold Lazarus created multimodal therapy (described below). Problem-solving therapy Many people who seek help are not distorted thinkers; they are overwhelmed by debts, a failing marriage, a sick parent. In 1971 Thomas J. D'Zurilla and Marvin R. Goldfried , at the State University of New York at Stony Brook, published "Problem solving and behavior modification" in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology . Much abnormal behaviour, they argued, is better understood as ineffective behaviour, the result of failing to solve the problems life presents, and teaching a general problem-solving strategy might help people with problems they had not yet met. That is the basis of problem-solving therapy (PST): a cognitive-behavioural treatment that trains clients in a systematic method for identifying problems, generating and choosing among solutions and carrying them out, so as to reduce distress and improve functioning. A problem , in this approach, is any situation that demands a response for which no effective response is immediately apparent; a solution is a coping response that changes the situation, one's emotional reaction to it, or both. D'Zurilla and Goldfried's original model had five stages: a general orientation to problems; problem definition and formulation; generation of alternatives; decision making; and verification. Over the following decades D'Zurilla worked with Arthur M. Nezu and Christine Maguth Nezu , who tested the therapy with depressed adults and refined the model. In its mature form it separates two partly independent processes. The first is problem orientation : a person's general attitude to problems and to his own ability to solve them. A positive orientation sees a problem as a challenge, believes it can be solved, trusts one's ability and accepts that solving it takes time and effort. A negative orientation sees problems as threats, doubts one's ability and reacts with frustration. A negative orientation is strongly associated with depression, anxiety and suicidal thinking, so modern PST begins here: before a client can solve problems, he must stop treating every problem as a catastrophe and himself as helpless. The second process is the person's problem-solving style . The effective style is rational problem solving , which is deliberate and systematic and uses four skills (the remaining four stages of the original model). Two styles are ineffective: the impulsive or careless style, which grabs the first solution that comes to mind, and the avoidant style, which procrastinates, waits for the problem to go away or hands it to someone else. The four skills are taught as steps: Problem definition and formulation. Gather the facts, separate them from assumptions, state the problem concretely and set a realistic goal. "My life is a mess" cannot be solved; "I have no free time on weekday evenings" can. Generation of alternative solutions. Produce as many possible solutions as possible, using the rules of brainstorming , popularised by the American advertising executive Alex Osborn and adapted by D'Zurilla and Nezu: the quantity principle (the more ideas, the more good ones), the deferment-of-judgement principle (no criticism while ideas are being produced) and the variety principle (ideas of many different kinds, not twenty versions of one). Decision making. Weigh the likely consequences of each option, short term and long term, for oneself and for others, and choose the best one or a combination. Solution implementation and verification. Carry the solution out, monitor what happens and compare the result with the goal. If it matches, the client rewards himself; if it does not, he returns to an earlier step. Here is the method at work. Lakshmi, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, has become low and tearful: her husband lost his job three months ago, her mother-in-law has had a stroke and needs help each evening, and the family is behind on a loan. Her therapist first works on orientation (problems are a normal part of life and can be tackled one at a time; feeling overwhelmed is a signal to start, not a sign of weakness). Lakshmi chooses one problem, no time in the evenings to prepare her lessons, and defines the goal concretely: "two free hours on at least four evenings a week". She brainstorms without judging (her husband could take over the evening care while he is between jobs; she could prepare lessons in the school's free period; a paid attendant; help from her sister-in-law; a transfer nearer home), weighs the options and chooses the first two together. Two weeks later three evenings are free, so she returns to her list for the fourth. Nothing in this work disputes a belief or names a distortion; her mood lifts because her life is becoming manageable, and because she is regaining the sense that she can manage it. The evidence for PST is solid, particularly for depression. Nezu (1986) found it more effective than a waiting list and than a less structured problem-focused therapy. In Oxford, Laurence Mynors-Wallis and his colleagues (1995) found six sessions of PST, delivered in primary care by a psychiatrist and trained general practitioners, as effective for major depression as the antidepressant amitriptyline and more effective than a placebo pill. Because its steps are simple, PST also travels well. In Zimbabwe the Friendship Bench programme led by the psychiatrist Dixon Chibanda trained lay health workers, many of them older women, to deliver it on benches outside clinics, and a randomised trial published in 2016 found that it reduced depressive symptoms more than enhanced usual care. Problem solving also appears inside many other treatments: stress inoculation training, behavioural family management for schizophrenia (Section 7.2) and dialectical behaviour therapy (Section 5.8). Indian context India has far too few clinical psychologists for its population, so interventions that trained lay counsellors can deliver matter a great deal, and problem solving is one of the main candidates. The Goa-based organisation Sangath, in its PRIDE programme for adolescents, has developed and tested a brief problem-solving intervention delivered by lay counsellors to students in low-income urban schools in New Delhi. Exam trap Problem-solving therapy was introduced by D'Zurilla and Goldfried (1971) and developed with Arthur and Christine Nezu . Its two components are problem orientation (attitude) and problem-solving style or skills ; the rational style has four steps: definition and formulation, generation of alternatives, decision making, implementation and verification. In brainstorming, judgement is deferred , not exercised. Do not confuse PST with solution-focused brief therapy (Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg, Section 6.8), which deliberately spends little time analysing the problem and instead builds on exceptions, using devices such as the miracle question. A third relative, George Spivack and Myrna Shure's interpersonal cognitive problem-solving programme for children ("I Can Problem Solve"), teaches young children to think of alternative solutions and consequences in conflicts with others. Arnold Lazarus and multimodal therapy You met Arnold Allan Lazarus (1932 to 2013) in Chapter 4 as one of Joseph Wolpe's students in Johannesburg and one of the first people to use the term "behaviour therapy" in print (1958). After moving to the United States, where he spent most of his career at Rutgers University, Lazarus did something therapists rarely do: he followed up his own clients. Many who had done well with behaviour therapy had relapsed, and he concluded that the reason was narrowness: a treatment that dealt with a client's avoidance but not his self-critical thoughts, or his anxiety but not his marriage, left gaps through which the problem could return. He argued for a "broad-spectrum" behaviour therapy in Behavior Therapy and Beyond (1971), and turned it into a system in Multimodal Behavior Therapy (1976) and The Practice of Multimodal Therapy (1981). multimodal therapy is a systematic, comprehensive approach in which the therapist assesses a client's problems across seven interacting modalities of personality and then selects, for each problem in each modality, the techniques with the best evidence, whatever their theoretical origin. The seven modalities form the acronym BASIC ID (often written BASIC I.D.): B, behaviour : observable acts, habits and reactions, including doing too much or too little of something. A, affect : emotions and moods, such as anxiety, anger, guilt and depression. S, sensation : what is seen, heard, touched, tasted and smelled, including unpleasant bodily sensations such as tension, pain, dizziness and palpitations. I, imagery : mental pictures, fantasies, dreams and memories, including one's self-image and body image. C, cognition : thoughts, beliefs, values, attitudes and self-statements. I, interpersonal relationships : how the person relates to family, friends, colleagues and partners. D, drugs and biology : physical health, sleep, diet, exercise, substance use and medication. Lazarus used "D" rather than "B" so that the acronym would read as "basic identity", but he stressed that the category covers the whole biological side of the person, of which drugs are only one part. Notice that affect is the one modality that cannot be changed directly. Nobody can simply decide to feel less anxious; but one can change the behaviours, sensations, images, thoughts, relationships and biology that produce the anxiety. Table 5.7 shows how a multimodal therapist would map one client. Table 5.7 A modality profile for Farhan, a 29-year-old bank officer in Hyderabad with anxiety and low mood since his promotion to branch manager, with the techniques a multimodal therapist might choose. Modality Farhan's problems Possible techniques Behaviour Avoids speaking in regional meetings; works until 10 pm Graded exposure, behavioural rehearsal, time management Affect Anxiety, irritability, guilt about neglecting his family Addressed through the other six modalities Sensation Chest tightness, palpitations, tension headaches Relaxation training, slow breathing Imagery Pictures himself freezing in front of the regional manager Coping imagery; rehearsing success in imagination Cognition "I'm not up to this job"; "a manager must never make mistakes" Cognitive restructuring, disputing demands Interpersonal Snaps at his wife; has stopped meeting friends Assertiveness training, a joint session with his wife Drugs and biology Six cups of coffee a day, poor sleep, no exercise Cut caffeine, sleep routine, daily walk, medical check-up Lazarus added several devices for using the BASIC ID. The modality profile is the list in Table 5.7, drawn up with the client; any item on it can be expanded into a second-order BASIC ID of its own. A structural profile asks the client to rate how much he relies on each modality (some people are "thinkers", others "feelers", others react first through the body or the imagination). tracking means following the firing order , the sequence in which the modalities are set off when a problem occurs. Farhan's anxiety starts with a sensation (his heart skips), then a cognition ("I'm going to lose it in the meeting"), an image (himself stammering), the affect (panic) and finally a behaviour (he leaves), so a technique aimed at the first link, such as slow breathing, may work best. bridging means meeting the client in his preferred modality before moving him to a more productive one: with a client who talks only in thoughts, the therapist works with thoughts for a while before asking, "And as you think that, what do you notice in your body?" Lazarus called himself an "authentic chameleon", changing his style to suit each client while remaining genuine. Multimodal therapy is the best-known example of technical eclecticism , a term Lazarus introduced in 1967: borrowing techniques from any school when evidence shows they work, without adopting that school's theory . Lazarus would borrow the empty chair from Gestalt therapy (Section 6.3) without accepting Gestalt theory; his own theory remained social and cognitive learning theory, much influenced by Bandura. He was critical of theoretical integration , which tries to blend the theories themselves (as Paul Wachtel combined psychodynamic and behavioural ideas), warning that mixing incompatible theories breeds confusion. The wider psychotherapy integration movement, in which Lazarus was a founding figure, is described in Section 8.11. Multimodal therapy's strengths are thoroughness and flexibility: a multimodal assessment rarely misses a problem, and treatment is tailored to the person rather than to the diagnosis. The weakness is the other side of the coin. Because every treatment is different, multimodal therapy is hard to test as such in a controlled trial, and its evidence rests largely on the evidence for the techniques it borrows. Exam trap BASIC ID = B ehaviour, A ffect, S ensation, I magery, C ognition, I nterpersonal relationships, D rugs and biology. Common wrong expansions: S as "self" or "social", the first I as "insight", D as "defences", "dreams" or "desensitisation". Multimodal therapy belongs to Arnold Lazarus , not to Richard Lazarus (stress and appraisal), not to Wolpe (systematic desensitisation and SUDS) and not to Jon Kabat-Zinn (mindfulness-based stress reduction, Section 5.9). Technical eclecticism borrows techniques but not theories; theoretical integration combines theories. One last trap: the American "Multimodal Treatment Study of Children with ADHD" (the MTA study of the 1990s) compared medication and behavioural treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and has nothing to do with Lazarus. George Kelly and fixed-role therapy The oldest approach in this section is also the most unusual. George Kelly, whom you met in Section 5.1, trained in physiological psychology but began his career at Fort Hays Kansas State College during the depression of the 1930s, when there was no money for laboratory research. So he set up travelling clinics for schools across rural Kansas and taught himself therapy, largely by assuming that each client was as much a scientist as himself. He later taught at Ohio State University for nineteen years (he replaced Carl Rogers there), published the two volumes of The Psychology of Personal Constructs in 1955, and died in 1967, shortly after moving to Brandeis University. His personality theory belongs to the Personality book; what matters here is the therapy it produced. Kelly's starting point was the person as a scientist, who makes sense of the world by building theories and testing them against experience. The units of these theories are personal constructs : bipolar dimensions, such as kind versus selfish or clever versus dull, through which a person interprets events and predicts what will happen next. His fundamental postulate states that "a person's processes are psychologically channelized by the ways in which he anticipates events". Because constructs are tools rather than truths, Kelly insisted on constructive alternativism : any event can be construed in more than one way, so people are prisoners not of their circumstances but only of their current interpretations. Psychological trouble arises when a person keeps using a construct system that keeps failing to predict events, instead of revising it. How do you find out what a person's constructs are? Kelly's answer was disarmingly simple: "If you don't know what is going on in a person's mind, ask him; he may tell you!" Besides this credulous attitude to the client's own account, he used the Role Construct Repertory Test (the Rep test, described in the Assessment book) and the self-characterisation sketch , in which the client writes about himself in the third person: "I want you to write a character sketch of [client's name] just as if he were the principal character in a play. Write it as it might be written by a friend who knew him very intimately and very sympathetically, perhaps better than anyone ever really could know him." The self-characterisation is the first step of fixed-role therapy : Kelly's method in which the therapist writes a sketch of a new, fictional character, built around constructs different from the client's own, and the client lives as that character for about two weeks, in order to discover that he is free to construe himself, and to act, differently. Kelly is said to have taken the idea from watching a friend who acted in a college play and gradually began to behave offstage like the character he played onstage (Kelly himself had coached drama at a junior college in Iowa). The procedure has four steps. The self-characterisation. The client writes his sketch, and the therapist studies it for the constructs that are trapping him. The fixed-role sketch. The therapist (Kelly often worked with a panel of colleagues) writes a sketch of a new character with a new name. The sketch is not an ideal self and not simply the client's opposite. Turning a shy man into a bold one would only move him from one end of the same construct to the other, a shift that personal construct therapists call "slot rattling". Instead the sketch introduces a new theme, a different dimension along which the character makes sense of people. The acceptance check. The client reads the sketch and is asked whether this sounds like a person he would like to know and could imagine being. If not, it is revised. The enactment. For about two weeks the client is asked to act, think and talk as the character would, as though his old self had gone on holiday. He meets the therapist frequently, often several times a week, to rehearse scenes with his employer, friends and family and to review what happened. At the end the role is dropped, and the client decides what, if anything, to keep. The genius of the method lies in the word "role". Because the client is only playing a part, a failure belongs to the character, not to him, so he can risk behaviour his anxiety would otherwise forbid; and because the experiment is real, other people's responses are real data. Suresh, a 24-year-old engineering graduate in Chennai, describes himself as "a quiet, dutiful boy who never troubles anybody", and his central construct, "troubling others versus being good", keeps him silent and lonely. His therapist does not write him a bold, assertive character, which would only flip the construct. She writes "Vikram", a man fascinated by what makes other people tick, who asks questions out of curiosity and listens to the answers. As Vikram, Suresh asks a colleague how she chose engineering and the tea-stall owner about his village, and he discovers that people enjoy being asked. The aim was never to turn Suresh into Vikram, but to show him that the person he took himself to be was a construction, and constructions can be revised. Fixed-role therapy has little controlled evidence and is rarely practised in its original form, but its influence is large. Kelly anticipated the central claim of cognitive therapy, his constructs closely resemble Beck's schemas, and his client-as-scientist leads straight to collaborative empiricism and behavioural experiments (Section 5.4). His constructivism also inspired later therapies, among them the personal construct psychotherapy of Fay Fransella and Robert Neimeyer, Michael Mahoney's constructive psychotherapy and, indirectly, narrative therapy (Section 6.8).
