George Kelly , as part of his personal construct theory (1955). Not Aaron Beck or Albert Ellis, and not Fritz Perls, whose Gestalt therapy uses the empty chair and other awareness experiments (Section 6.3). Two near neighbours cause confusion. Jacob Moreno's psychodrama (Section 7.11) also uses role-playing, but in a group, on a stage, usually to re-enact scenes from the protagonist's own life. Alfred Adler's acting "as if" asks a client to behave for a week as if he were the person he would like to be; Kelly's fixed role is a fully scripted, invented character with a new name, deliberately not an ideal self. And the Rep test and self-characterisation sketch are Kelly's assessment tools, not separate therapies. 5.6 Disorder-specific cognitive models: panic, social anxiety, trauma and psychosis High yield · 7 Qs Section 5.4 noted a deep difference between Beck and Ellis: Ellis traced almost all disturbance to one process, demandingness, whereas Beck believed that each disorder has its own characteristic content. Beck's idea proved one of the most productive in the history of psychotherapy. From the 1980s it led a group of researchers, most of them at the University of Oxford, to build a precise cognitive model for each anxiety disorder, test it in the laboratory, and design a therapy aimed at exactly the processes the model said were keeping the disorder alive. This section shows how, using four examples: panic, social anxiety, trauma and psychosis. Cognitive specificity and the logic of disorder-specific models In Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders (1976), Beck proposed the cognitive specificity hypothesis (or content-specificity hypothesis): each emotional disorder is marked by its own typical theme of thought. Depression is about loss and failure, anxiety about danger, hypomania about gain. Table 5.9 gives Beck's "cognitive profiles". When Beck and his colleagues (1987) gave patients a checklist of thoughts, depressed patients reported more thoughts of loss and failure and anxious patients more thoughts of danger; the separation is not perfect, since many patients are both anxious and depressed, but it is real. Table 5.9 Beck's cognitive profiles: the characteristic theme of thought in each condition, according to the cognitive specificity hypothesis (the conditions themselves are described in the Psychiatric Disorders book). Condition Characteristic theme of thought Depression Loss, failure and defeat; negative views of self, world and future Hypomania Gain; an inflated view of self and future Anxiety Physical or psychological danger Panic disorder Catastrophic interpretation of bodily or mental experiences Phobia Danger in specific, avoidable situations Paranoid states Other people are biased against me or mean me harm Obsessions and compulsions Repeated doubts and warnings about safety; rituals to ward off the threat Suicidal behaviour Hopelessness, with poor problem solving Anorexia nervosa Fear of being fat Hypochondriasis (health anxiety) Having a serious illness that doctors have missed Knowing the theme is not enough to treat the disorder, however. Early cognitive therapies for anxiety applied Beck's general method and got moderate results. The Oxford group, led by David M. Clark and Paul M. Salkovskis and later joined by Anke Ehlers , Adrian Wells (whose metacognitive therapy is in Section 5.10) and others, asked a sharper question. A man has had three hundred panic attacks; in every one of them he was sure he was about to have a heart attack, and he has never had one. Why has being wrong three hundred times not corrected his belief? Something must be stopping the evidence from getting in. That question gives disorder-specific models their shape. Each model identifies the key appraisal (the specific catastrophe feared: a heart attack in panic, humiliation in social anxiety, current danger in PTSD), then the maintaining processes that stop the appraisal from being disconfirmed, and then designs a therapy, usually built on behavioural experiments, to reverse each maintaining process in turn. Notice the emphasis on maintenance rather than origin. How a disorder began matters, but the past cannot be changed, whereas the vicious circles that keep it going today can be broken. The maintaining process found in almost every model is the subject of the next subsection. Safety behaviours: why fears survive There is an old joke that CBT trainers like to tell. A man on a train keeps snapping his fingers. Asked why, he says, "To keep the tigers away." "But there are no tigers on this train." "Exactly. It works." The joke captures the central idea of Salkovskis's influential 1991 paper on the maintenance of anxiety. safety behaviours (or safety-seeking behaviours) are actions a person takes in, or in anticipation of, a feared situation in order to prevent the feared catastrophe. A man who fears fainting sits down or grips something solid when dizzy; a woman who fears heart failure carries her medicines everywhere and keeps near the exit; a student who fears sounding stupid rehearses every sentence before speaking and avoids eye contact. Safety behaviours are not the same as avoidance. The avoider stays away from the situation altogether; the person using safety behaviours enters it, but with protection. That is exactly why they are so insidious. They keep anxiety alive in three ways: They prevent disconfirmation. When the catastrophe does not happen, the person credits the safety behaviour rather than the harmlessness of the situation: "I didn't faint, but only because I held on to the trolley." Each "narrow escape" strengthens the belief instead of weakening it. This is the misattribution in the tiger joke. They can produce the very symptoms that are feared. Gripping a trolley tightly makes the arms shake; holding a glass with rigid fingers to stop it trembling makes it tremble; breathing deeply to "get enough air" leads to over-breathing, which produces dizziness and tingling. They can make the feared outcome more likely. The student who avoids eye contact and rehearses his sentences comes across as cold and distracted, so the other students respond less warmly, which he takes as proof that they dislike him. Safety behaviours also keep attention fixed on the threat, since a person cannot protect himself from a danger without monitoring it. And what counts as a safety behaviour depends on its function , not its form. Slow breathing used as a general way of calming down is a coping skill; slow breathing used in the belief that it is the only thing standing between the person and a heart attack is a safety behaviour. Key study: dropping safety behaviours (Salkovskis, Clark, Hackmann, Wells and Gelder, 1999) If safety behaviours prevent disconfirmation, exposure should work better when they are dropped. Salkovskis and his colleagues gave patients with panic disorder and agoraphobia brief exposure to feared situations such as shops and crowded streets. One group received the standard rationale of the time (stay until the anxiety fades); the other was told to treat the situation as a test of whether the catastrophe would really happen, and to drop its safety behaviours (stop holding on, walk without a companion, stand rather than sit). With the same amount of exposure, the second group showed much greater reductions in anxiety and in belief in the feared catastrophe. Wells, Clark, Salkovskis and colleagues (1995) found the same in social phobia after a single session. Stanley Rachman and his colleagues (2008) later argued that judicious safety behaviours can help a frightened client to start exposure at all, but for lasting change the protection has to go. Exam trap "A client engages in safety behaviours, such as gripping a shopping cart tightly when feeling dizzy in a store. In CBT for panic disorder, the therapist would likely..." work with the client to gradually drop these behaviours to test catastrophic beliefs (Real PYQ 2024). Not prescribe them to prevent fainting: the behaviour is what keeps the belief alive, and people having a panic attack almost never faint (see below). Not use them as a measure of insight: they are a maintaining process to be changed, not an index to be scored. And not explore the childhood origins of the need for safety, which is a psychodynamic aim; CBT works on what maintains the problem now. Remember also that safety behaviours differ from avoidance : the person is in the feared situation, but protected. Panic: Clark's catastrophic misinterpretation model Ramesh, a 38-year-old software engineer in Hyderabad, has been rushed to emergency departments four times in six months with a racing heart and the certainty that he was dying. Each time the electrocardiogram was normal. He no longer takes the metro, goes to the supermarket only with his wife, and grips the trolley with both hands when he feels light-headed. He has panic disorder (recurrent, unexpected panic attacks with persistent worry about further attacks) and is developing agoraphobia: fear and avoidance of places such as crowds, shops and public transport, from which escape might be difficult or help unavailable if panic struck (both are described in the Psychiatric Disorders book). Why does a man with a healthy heart keep believing it is failing? In 1986 David Clark published a short paper, "A cognitive approach to panic", in the journal Behaviour Research and Therapy . Its central claim fits in one sentence: panic attacks result from the catastrophic misinterpretation of certain bodily sensations, that is, perceiving harmless sensations, mostly the ordinary sensations of anxiety, as signs of an immediate disaster. Palpitations are read as an impending heart attack, breathlessness as suffocation, dizziness as fainting or a stroke, and feelings of unreality (derealisation) or of being detached from oneself (depersonalisation) as the onset of madness or loss of control. Figure 5.5 shows how such a misinterpretation produces a vicious circle. Trigger crowded mall, or a skipped heartbeat Perceived threat "Something is wrong" Apprehension anxiety, fear Body sensations pounding heart, dizzy Catastrophic misinterpretation "My heart is failing" the vicious circle Safety behaviours grip the trolley, sit down, flee: so the belief is never disproved Selective attention to the body scanning makes sensations seem stronger and more alarming Figure 5.5 Clark's (1986) cognitive model of panic. A trigger is perceived as a threat; the resulting apprehension produces bodily sensations; the sensations are misinterpreted as a catastrophe, which increases the threat, and the circle spirals into a panic attack within seconds. The two boxes at the bottom show what keeps the misinterpretation alive between attacks. Follow Ramesh round the circle. In a crowded mall (an external trigger) he feels slightly apprehensive, and apprehension, like any anxiety, speeds up his heart and breathing. He notices his heart pounding and thinks, "My heart is going to fail." The threat now seems far greater, so his anxiety rises, his heart pounds harder and the interpretation seems confirmed; within a minute he is in a full panic attack. The trigger can also be internal: a skipped heartbeat, the light-headedness of standing up quickly, too much coffee, even a thought. That explains attacks that seem to come "out of the blue" (the trigger was a small sensation, misread before the person was aware of noticing it), and it explains attacks that wake people from sleep. Between attacks, two processes keep the misinterpretation alive. The first is selective attention to the body : having been frightened by his heart, Ramesh monitors it constantly, and anyone who monitors his own heartbeat notices changes that others never register. The second is safety behaviours: each time the heart attack does not happen, he credits the trolley, his wife or his quick exit. Clark's model sits beside two related ideas. In 1978 Alan Goldstein and Dianne Chambless described agoraphobia as, at heart, a fear of fear : a learned fear of the bodily sensations of anxiety. In 1985 Steven Reiss and Richard J. McNally introduced anxiety sensitivity , a lasting tendency to believe that the sensations of anxiety are harmful; people who score high on the Anxiety Sensitivity Index are more likely to develop panic attacks later. Anxiety sensitivity is the trait; catastrophic misinterpretation is what happens in the moment. David H. Barlow and Michelle Craske's panic control treatment, with its interoceptive exposure (Section 4.3), attacks the same circle from the behavioural side. Key study: the illusion of control (Sanderson, Rapee and Barlow, 1989) If panic depends on how sensations are interpreted, then changing the interpretation should change the panic, even when the sensations stay the same. William Sanderson, Ronald Rapee and David Barlow asked patients with panic disorder to breathe air enriched with 5.5 percent carbon dioxide, which reliably produces breathlessness, a racing heart and dizziness. All the patients were told that when a light came on they could reduce the carbon dioxide by turning a dial. For half of them the light came on; for the other half it never did. In fact the dial did nothing at all. The physical dose was identical, yet the patients who had no "control" reported more panic symptoms, more catastrophic thoughts and far more panic attacks than those who believed they could control the gas (the figures usually quoted are about 80 percent against about 20 percent, in groups of only ten patients each). The perception of control, a purely cognitive variable, made the difference between panicking and not panicking. Clark's cognitive therapy for panic disorder , developed with Salkovskis and colleagues, follows directly from the model. It usually takes about 12 sessions, and it has four parts. Building the vicious circle. A recent attack is reviewed in slow motion ("What did you notice first? What went through your mind? What happened to the sensation then?") and the client's own version of Figure 5.5 is drawn. Seeing the circle on paper often reduces fear by itself. Verbal reattribution. The evidence is examined. Ramesh's heart has been tested four times; his attacks come when he is sitting still but never when he climbs the stairs, though a weak heart would be most likely to fail under exertion; and the sensations fade when he is distracted. Information helps too: fainting is caused by a sudden drop in blood pressure, whereas panic raises blood pressure, so a panicking person is one of the people least likely to faint (the exception is blood-injection-injury phobia, in which a drop in blood pressure really can cause fainting). Behavioural experiments. The client deliberately produces the feared sensations to discover their harmless cause: over-breathing for a minute or two, focusing on the body, even reading word pairs such as "palpitations: dying", which can bring on a mild attack in the clinic and shows him how powerful his interpretations are. Then, in the feared situations, he drops his safety behaviours : Ramesh lets go of the trolley when he feels dizzy, walks briskly round the shop instead, and does not collapse. Relapse prevention : planning how to respond to future sensations and setbacks. The therapy works remarkably well. In a trial by Clark and his colleagues (1994), patients with panic disorder were randomly assigned to cognitive therapy, to applied relaxation (Lars-Göran Öst's method; Section 4.8), to the antidepressant imipramine or to a waiting list. At three months, when cognitive therapy ended, 86 percent of the cognitive therapy patients were free of panic (counting drop-outs as failures; close to 90 percent of those who completed it), compared with roughly half of those in the other two active treatments. Imipramine caught up while patients were still taking it, but at follow-up fifteen months after the start cognitive therapy was again ahead (76 percent panic-free, against under 50 percent for the others). Exam trap The cognitive model of panic belongs to David M. Clark (1986) : panic is the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations . Do not confuse it with Barlow and Craske's panic control treatment (interoceptive exposure; Section 4.3), with Reiss and McNally's anxiety sensitivity (a lasting trait) or with Goldstein and Chambless's fear of fear . Treatment drops safety behaviours rather than prescribing them. And agoraphobia, when asked about, is fear of public or hard-to-escape places (crowds, shops, public transport, being outside the home alone), because escape might be difficult or help unavailable if panic struck. Nervousness in a lift is claustrophobia and fear of tall trees or buildings is a specific phobia (both are phobias of particular situations or objects), and hearing voices is a psychotic symptom, not a phobia at all. Social anxiety: the Clark and Wells model Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) is an intense, persistent fear of situations in which one might be scrutinised and judged, such as speaking in a group, eating in front of others or meeting strangers (the disorder itself is in the Psychiatric Disorders book). It poses a puzzle like the one in panic. A socially anxious person meets other people every day, and all that exposure should, by the logic of Chapter 4, extinguish the fear. Why doesn't it? In 1995 David Clark and Adrian Wells answered with what has become the standard model. Entering a social situation activates three kinds of long-standing belief: excessively high standards ("I must always sound fluent and intelligent"; "I must never show anxiety"), conditional beliefs ("If I blush, people will think I'm weird") and unconditional negative beliefs about the self ("I'm boring", "I'm odd"). These make the situation look dangerous, and the moment social danger is perceived, attention turns inward. Figure 5.6 shows what happens next. Social situation a question in a seminar Activates beliefs and assumptions "I must sound fluent and clever" "If they see I'm nervous, I'm finished" Perceived social danger Processing of self as a social object (self-focus, felt image) Safety behaviours rehearse sentences, avoid eye contact Somatic and cognitive symptoms blush, shake, go blank Anticipatory and post-event processing worrying beforehand; the "post-mortem" afterwards Figure 5.6 A simplified version of Clark and Wells's (1995) cognitive model of social anxiety. The engine of the model is the centre box: once social danger is perceived, attention turns inward and the person judges how he looks from his own feelings. The paired arrows show that safety behaviours and symptoms both feed, and are fed by, this self-focused processing. The centre of the model is processing of the self as a social object . The person shifts into self-focused attention , monitoring his own sensations, thoughts and behaviour at the expense of the conversation, and he uses this internal information to judge how he looks. He feels hot, so he "sees" himself bright red; he feels shaky, so he imagines his hands visibly trembling. Many socially anxious people report a vivid image of themselves as seen from outside (an observer perspective ), and Ann Hackmann, Clark and Freda McManus (2000) found that such images are often linked to early memories of humiliation. The image feels like the truth, but it is built from feelings, not facts: emotional reasoning (Section 5.3) turned on the self. Three other processes lock the circle. Safety behaviours (rehearsing sentences, speaking little, avoiding eye contact, holding a cup with both hands, covering a blush) prevent disconfirmation, increase self-focus and make the person seem aloof, so that others respond coolly and appear to confirm his fears. The symptoms of anxiety (blushing, trembling, the mind going blank) become further evidence of danger. And the processing extends in time: in anticipatory processing the person rehearses beforehand everything that might go wrong, and in post-event processing , the "post-mortem", he replays the encounter afterwards through his anxious feelings, so that even a conversation that went well is remembered as a failure. Here is the answer to the puzzle: socially anxious people meet others daily, but with attention turned inward and behaviour protected, they never collect the evidence that they were doing better than they thought. Ronald M. Rapee and Richard G. Heimberg (1997) proposed a similar model, stressing the person's mental representation of how he appears to an audience. Clark's cognitive therapy for social anxiety disorder targets each of these processes, over about 14 sessions: An individual version of the model , drawn from a recent social situation. A self-focus and safety behaviours experiment. Ananya, a 23-year-old trainee chartered accountant in Kolkata, has two short conversations with a stranger, once using her safety behaviours and focusing on herself, and once dropping them and attending to the other person. In the second she feels less anxious, believes she looks less anxious and, by the stranger's account, seems warmer: her "protection" was making things worse. Video feedback. Ananya predicts in detail how she will look on the recording ("bright red, voice shaking"), then watches it as if she were watching a stranger. Most clients look far less anxious than they felt, which corrects the observer image directly. Training in external attention , so that the client listens and responds instead of monitoring herself. Behavioural experiments in real situations, including deliberate small "mistakes" (a long pause, spilling a little water) to test whether rejection really follows. Work on anticipatory and post-event processing , and imagery rescripting of the early memories that feed the self-image. The results are among the best for any anxiety disorder. Clark and his colleagues found the therapy more effective than fluoxetine combined with self-exposure (2003) and than exposure combined with applied relaxation (2006); in the 2006 trial 84 percent of the cognitive therapy patients no longer met the diagnostic criteria for social phobia at the end of treatment, against 42 percent of those given exposure and applied relaxation, and the difference held a year later. A trial by Ulrich Stangier, Clark and colleagues (2011) found it more effective than interpersonal psychotherapy, a network meta-analysis by Evan Mayo-Wilson and colleagues (2014) found individual CBT the most effective psychological treatment for social anxiety in adults, and the British National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends individual CBT based on the Clark and Wells or the Heimberg model as the first-line treatment. Heimberg's own approach, cognitive-behavioural group therapy , treats about six clients together, combining exposure to simulated feared situations (a mock interview, a party conversation) with cognitive restructuring before and after, and homework; the group provides a ready-made audience. Earlier treatments relied on exposure alone, or on social skills training (Section 4.7), on the assumption that socially anxious people lack conversational skills. Most, it turned out, have adequate skills that anxiety and safety behaviours stop them using, so skills training is now kept for genuine deficits. A complete CBT package for social anxiety may therefore contain all three elements: exposure, social skills retraining where needed, and cognitive restructuring. Exam trap "Successful CBT treatments of social phobia include elements of exposure therapy, social skills retraining and cognitive restructuring" calls for all of the above (IHBAS 2020). The model to name is Clark and Wells (1995) ; its distinctive ideas are self-focused attention , the observer-perspective self-image , safety behaviours and anticipatory and post-event processing . Its distinctive technique is video feedback . Heimberg's version is the group treatment. Do not credit Clark and Wells to Beck, and do not confuse Adrian Wells's work here with his later metacognitive therapy for worry (Section 5.10). Trauma: cognitive models of post-traumatic stress Most people who live through a terrible event (a road accident, an assault, a flood, a bomb blast) have intrusive memories, nightmares and jumpiness for some weeks, and most of them recover. A minority develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), in which re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal persist for months or years (the disorder itself is in the Psychiatric Disorders book). What keeps them ill? Anke Ehlers and David Clark's answer (2000) begins with a paradox: PTSD is an anxiety-related disorder, and anxiety concerns future threat, yet the trauma is in the past. PTSD becomes persistent, they proposed, when the trauma is processed in a way that produces a sense of serious current threat . Two things create it. The first is excessively negative appraisals of the trauma or its consequences: "Nowhere is safe"; "It was my fault"; "I'm going mad, because I can't stop the flashbacks"; "My life is ruined." The second is the nature of the trauma memory : poorly elaborated and poorly integrated into ordinary autobiographical memory, stored as vivid sensory fragments without the context of time, place and outcome ("and then the ambulance came, and I survived"). Such a memory is easily triggered by cues that merely resemble the trauma (a smell, a sound) and is re-experienced with a sense of "nowness", as though the event were happening again. The disorder is maintained by the person's ways of coping (suppressing thoughts of the trauma, ruminating, avoiding reminders, staying on guard, drinking and other safety behaviours), each of which stops the memory from being elaborated and the appraisals from being corrected. The resulting cognitive therapy for PTSD has one aim for each part of the model. It changes the negative appraisals with Socratic questioning and behavioural experiments. It makes the memory less intrusive by using brief imaginal reliving to find the hot spots (the moments of greatest distress and their meanings) and then updating each with what the person now knows ("At that moment I thought I would die; I know now that I survived and the driver was arrested"), together with discrimination of triggers ("then" versus "now") and sometimes a visit to the site. And it removes the maintaining strategies, asking the client to drop safety behaviours, stop suppressing and ruminating, and reclaim the parts of life he has given up. Key study: early cognitive therapy after road accidents (Ehlers and colleagues, 2003) Can cognitive therapy given soon after a trauma stop PTSD from becoming chronic? Ehlers and her colleagues randomly assigned people who had developed PTSD within six months of a road accident to up to 12 weekly sessions of cognitive therapy, to a detailed cognitive-behavioural self-help booklet, or to repeated assessments only. At follow-up only 11 percent of the cognitive therapy group still had PTSD, against 61 percent of the self-help group and 55 percent of those only assessed: good information on paper did no better than nothing. By contrast, putting every survivor through a single "debriefing" session soon after a trauma has been found unhelpful and sometimes harmful (Section 9.7). An older and equally successful approach was developed in the late 1980s by Patricia A. Resick and her colleagues in St Louis, first for survivors of rape. cognitive processing therapy (CPT) is a 12-session cognitive therapy for PTSD that focuses on how the trauma has changed the survivor's beliefs. When a trauma conflicts with prior beliefs, the conflict can be resolved in three ways (the terms are borrowed from Piaget). In assimilation the person alters his memory of the event to fit his old beliefs: someone who believes the world is just concludes, "It must have been my fault." In over-accommodation he changes his beliefs too far: "No one can be trusted"; "I am never safe." In accommodation , the healthy outcome, he changes them just enough: "Some people are dangerous, and I can be careful whom I trust." The beliefs that block recovery are called stuck points , and CPT looks for them in five areas: safety, trust, power and control, esteem, and intimacy. Therapy begins with an impact statement , a short essay on why the client thinks the trauma happened and how it has changed her beliefs about herself, other people and the world. She then works through a series of worksheets (linking events, thoughts and feelings; challenging questions; patterns of problematic thinking; challenging beliefs) to examine her stuck points Socratically. A detailed written account of the trauma was part of the original therapy, but Resick and her colleagues (2008) found that CPT works about as well without it, and it is now optional. Meera, assaulted by a colleague after agreeing to stay late at the office, holds the stuck points "It happened because I stayed late" (assimilation) and "No man can be trusted" (over-accommodation), and arrives at "He chose to assault me; staying late is not an invitation" and "Some men are dangerous, and I can let trust build slowly." Compared with prolonged exposure for survivors of rape (Resick and colleagues, 2002), CPT was similarly and highly effective, with somewhat greater reductions in guilt. Children need a different approach, with the parent in the room. trauma-focused cognitive-behavioural therapy (TF-CBT), developed in the 1990s by Judith A. Cohen , Anthony P. Mannarino and Esther Deblinger , first for sexually abused children, is now the best-supported treatment for traumatised children and adolescents. It usually runs for 12 to 16 sessions, with parallel sessions for a caregiver who is not the abuser, and its components are remembered by the acronym PRACTICE: p sychoeducation and p arenting skills, r elaxation, a ffective expression and modulation, c ognitive coping, t rauma narrative and processing, i n vivo mastery of trauma reminders, c onjoint child-parent sessions and e nhancing future safety. The early components build coping skills. The centrepiece is the trauma narrative , in which the child gradually tells, writes or draws the story of what happened, so that the memory loses its power and distorted beliefs ("it was my fault") can be corrected, before sharing it with the parent in a joint session. Cohen and her colleagues (2004) found TF-CBT more effective than child-centred therapy for sexually abused children. Two other trauma treatments are described in Chapter 4: Edna Foa's prolonged exposure (Section 4.3) and Francine Shapiro 's eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR), in which the trauma is recalled while the eyes follow the therapist's moving finger, a method whose mechanism is still disputed (Section 4.4). Table 5.10 compares the main trauma therapies. The guidelines of the World Health Organization (2013) and NICE (2018) recommend trauma-focused CBT (used there as a family name covering prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy for PTSD and similar treatments) and EMDR as first-line psychological treatments for PTSD in adults, and TF-CBT for children. Therapy Developer Core idea Main methods Prolonged exposure Edna Foa and colleagues (late 1980s) Avoidance keeps the fear alive; the memory must be emotionally processed Repeated imaginal revisiting; in vivo exposure to safe reminders Cognitive processing therapy Patricia Resick and colleagues (late 1980s) Trauma leaves "stuck" beliefs (assimilated or over-accommodated) Impact statement; worksheets challenging stuck points; optional written account Cognitive therapy for PTSD Anke Ehlers and David Clark (model 2000) A sense of current threat from negative appraisals and a disjointed memory Updating hot spots; discriminating triggers; dropping safety behaviours Trauma-focused CBT for children Cohen, Mannarino and Deblinger (1990s) Skills first, then gradual exposure through a narrative, with the parent PRACTICE components; trauma narrative; joint sessions EMDR Francine Shapiro (1989) Recalling the memory with bilateral eye movements (mechanism disputed) Standard eight-phase protocol (Section 4.4) Exam trap Match the trauma therapy to its developer: prolonged exposure is Foa's , cognitive processing therapy is Resick's , cognitive therapy for PTSD is Ehlers and Clark's , TF-CBT for children is Cohen, Mannarino and Deblinger's , and EMDR is Francine Shapiro's (not Linehan's, Beck's or Foa's). Foa's name also goes with exposure and response prevention for OCD (Section 4.3); Joseph LeDoux, sometimes offered as a distractor there, is a neuroscientist who mapped the brain's fear circuits, not a therapist. In TF-CBT, the trauma narrative is the core component, preceded by coping skills; so when a question asks for the main goal of TF-CBT, choose the option about the trauma narrative and desensitising traumatic memories . Teaching coping skills is the preparation for the narrative, not its goal; "closure" is too vague to be the goal of any one therapy; and an option about "emotion regulation and mindfulness" describes DBT (Section 5.8) more than TF-CBT. Questions on survivors of sexual assault sometimes key "psychodynamic psychotherapy, TF-CBT and EMDR" as the most effective set; choose it because it is the only option that contains both TF-CBT and EMDR, which are the guideline treatments, but know that psychodynamic therapy is not itself a first-line treatment for PTSD. Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT: Gerald Klerman and Myrna Weissman's brief therapy for depression, built around four problem areas, grief, role disputes, role transitions and interpersonal deficits; Section 3.7) is not a standard trauma treatment (though one trial, by John Markowitz and colleagues in 2015, found it roughly as effective as prolonged exposure), so it is the expected answer to "which is NOT commonly used". Psychosis: cognitive behavioural therapy for delusions and voices For most of the twentieth century psychotherapists left delusions and hallucinations alone. The psychiatrist and philosopher Karl Jaspers had called primary delusions "un-understandable", and clinical folklore held that arguing with a delusion was pointless or dangerous. Yet in 1952, as a young psychiatrist years before he broke with psychoanalysis, Aaron Beck published a case report describing how he had helped a man with a long-standing persecutory delusion to examine, piece by piece, the evidence that he was being followed, and the belief weakened. The modern revival came from Britain in the late 1980s and 1990s, from David Kingdon and Douglas Turkington ( Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy of Schizophrenia , 1994), Philippa Garety , Elizabeth Kuipers and David Fowler, Max Birchwood and Paul Chadwick , and Nicholas Tarrier . cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp) applies the cognitive model to psychotic experiences. It aims not to argue a person out of his delusions or voices but to reduce the distress and disability they cause, by helping him understand them and test the beliefs he holds about them. CBTp rests on two ideas. The first is the continuum view : psychotic experiences differ in degree, not in kind, from ordinary ones. Many people hear a voice at some point without becoming ill, suspicious thoughts are common, and anyone deprived of sleep, isolated or held hostage can begin to hallucinate. Kingdon and Turkington built this into a normalising rationale , explaining early in therapy that the client's experiences are understandable reactions to stress, isolation and sleeplessness to which anyone is vulnerable, which reduces fear and the sense of being uniquely abnormal. The second idea is that distress depends on appraisal . Chadwick and Birchwood (1994) found that what made voices distressing was less what they said than what the hearer believed about their identity, power and intent: voices believed to be all-powerful and malevolent were feared, resisted and often obeyed, while the same words from a voice believed to be weak were far less frightening. This is Ellis's ABC applied to voices (A, the voice; B, beliefs about it; C, distress and the urge to comply), and it makes the beliefs, not the voice, the first target. Garety, Kuipers, Fowler, Freeman and Bebbington (2001) combined these ideas in a cognitive model of the positive symptoms. In vulnerable people, stress triggers anomalous experiences (heightened perceptions, thoughts that seem to come from outside, events that feel strangely significant). The person searches for an explanation, and anxiety, low self-esteem and biases in reasoning push him towards a threatening, external one, especially the jumping-to-conclusions bias . In the "beads task" (Huq, Garety and Hemsley, 1988), beads are drawn one at a time from one of two jars with opposite proportions of two colours, and people with delusions typically decide which jar they come from after only one or two beads. Once formed, the belief is maintained like any anxious belief: by selective attention, by worry and, as Daniel Freeman and his colleagues have shown, by safety behaviours. A man who believes his neighbours plan to attack him stays indoors and avoids eye contact, and credits these precautions for his survival, just as Ramesh credits the trolley. CBTp is usually delivered one to one, in at least 16 sessions and often over many months, and it moves slowly. Its main steps are: Engagement : building trust with a person who may suspect everyone, often starting with what he wants to change (sleep, fear, isolation) rather than with the symptoms. Normalising and collaborative formulation : a shared account of how the experiences arose and what keeps them going. Gentle examination of beliefs : Socratic exploration of the evidence for a delusion and of other possible explanations, without confrontation, often beginning with peripheral questions rather than the central belief. Behavioural experiments , such as recording the room on a phone during a voice-hearing episode to see whether the voice is captured, or dropping a safety behaviour to see whether the feared attack follows. Coping strategy enhancement (Tarrier's term): strengthening strategies the client already uses with some success, such as humming, music, talking to someone or going for a walk. Relapse prevention : recognising early warning signs (sleeplessness, irritability, growing suspicion) and planning a response. How well does it work? NICE recommends that CBTp be offered to everyone with psychosis or schizophrenia, alongside family intervention (Section 7.2). Meta-analyses, such as that of Til Wykes and her colleagues (2008), find real but modest effects on positive symptoms, smaller in the most rigorous trials with blinded assessors. The COMMAND trial led by Birchwood (2014) found that cognitive therapy reduced harmful compliance with command hallucinations, voices that order the hearer to harm himself or others. Above all, CBTp is an addition to medication, not a replacement for it; a realistic success is that the person still hears voices but is no longer terrified or ruled by them. Exam trap "The front-line treatment for schizophrenia is..." antipsychotic medication (RML 2021). CBT for psychosis, social skills training (Section 4.7 and Chapter 9), stress management and family psychoeducation (Section 7.2) are valuable adjuncts that reduce distress, improve functioning and prevent relapse, but none of them replaces medication in acute schizophrenia. Note what CBTp aims at: distress and disability , through the person's beliefs about his experiences, not a head-on argument with the delusion. The ABC analysis of voices is Chadwick and Birchwood's; the jumping-to-conclusions bias and the beads task come from Garety's group; the normalising rationale is Kingdon and Turkington's; coping strategy enhancement is Tarrier's. Indian context Many Indian families first explain voices and strange beliefs as possession, black magic or the evil eye, and consult a faith healer or visit a temple or dargah before, or alongside, a psychiatrist. A cognitive therapist need not demolish that explanatory model in order to help: exploring what the client and family believe and fear, and offering the stress-vulnerability and normalising accounts as additional ways of making sense of the experience, keeps the family engaged. In neighbouring Pakistan, Farooq Naeem and his colleagues have culturally adapted CBT for psychosis for South Asian clients, involving family members closely and working respectfully with beliefs about jinn and magic. The wider family of disorder-specific models Panic, social anxiety, trauma and psychosis are only the best-known examples. The same method (find the key appraisal, find what maintains it, reverse each maintaining process) has produced a model for almost every common disorder. For obsessive-compulsive disorder, Salkovskis (1985) argued that intrusive thoughts are nearly universal and become obsessions only when they are appraised as meaning that one is responsible for causing or preventing harm; checking, washing, neutralising and reassurance seeking then work as safety behaviours. That is one reason the behavioural treatment of OCD, exposure and response prevention (introduced by Victor Meyer in 1966 and turned into a standard treatment above all by Edna Foa; Section 4.3), works: blocking the ritual lets the person discover that the feared harm does not follow. For health anxiety, Salkovskis and Hilary Warwick (1986) described the misreading of harmless bodily signs as serious illness, kept alive by body checking and reassurance seeking. For eating disorders, Christopher G. Fairburn and his colleagues (2003) proposed a transdiagnostic model whose core is the overevaluation of shape and weight, which drives strict dieting, which in turn invites binge eating; his enhanced CBT (CBT-E) followed in 2008. Generalised anxiety disorder has several models, including Adrian Wells's metacognitive account of "worry about worry" (Section 5.10). Table 5.11 brings the models together. Table 5.11 The main disorder-specific cognitive models: what the person fears, and what keeps the fear alive. Disorder Model Key appraisal Main maintaining processes Panic disorder Clark (1986) Bodily sensations mean an immediate catastrophe Safety behaviours; attention to the body; avoidance Social anxiety disorder Clark and Wells (1995) Others will see my flaws and reject me Self-focused attention; observer image; safety behaviours; post-mortems Post-traumatic stress disorder Ehlers and Clark (2000) Serious threat now, though the trauma is past Disjointed memory; suppression, rumination, avoidance Obsessive-compulsive disorder Salkovskis (1985) This thought means I am responsible for harm Neutralising, checking, reassurance seeking Health anxiety Salkovskis and Warwick (1986) This bodily sign means a serious illness Body checking; reassurance seeking; searching for symptoms Eating disorders Fairburn and colleagues (2003) My worth depends on my shape and weight Strict dieting; binge-purge cycles; body checking Psychosis Garety and colleagues (2001) Anomalous experiences are external and threatening Reasoning biases; worry; safety behaviours The disorder-specific approach has a cost: a separate model and protocol for each disorder, although real clients often have several. Partly for this reason, transdiagnostic treatments target processes shared across disorders; the best known is the Unified Protocol of Barlow and his colleagues (2011), which treats anxiety and depression together. The two approaches are less opposed than they look. Both rest on Beck's insight that what we make of events shapes what we feel, and both intervene at the maintaining processes, above all avoidance and safety seeking. The next section turns to clients for whom even the best of these models is not enough: people whose difficulties lie in long-standing, rigid patterns of personality. Yet therapists at Beck's centre in Philadelphia kept meeting a different kind of client. She did her thought records faithfully for a fortnight, then missed three sessions in a row. She could list the evidence against "I am unlovable" and then say quietly, "I know all that. I just don't feel it." Her difficulty was not an episode of illness but the shape of her whole life, above all of her relationships, including the one with her therapist. Clients like her were often diagnosed with a personality disorder (described in the Psychiatric Disorders book), and short-term cognitive therapy failed them more often than anyone else. Beck's own answer was Cognitive Therapy of Personality Disorders (1990), written with Arthur Freeman and colleagues, which described the typical core beliefs of each personality disorder (the avoidant person's "If people knew the real me, they would reject me"). Two other therapists went further and built new therapies, one from inside the cognitive tradition, the other by translating psychoanalysis into the collaborative language of cognitive therapy. Both "go deeper" than standard CBT in the same sense: they work on patterns laid down in childhood and repeated in adult relationships. Why standard cognitive therapy struggles with personality problems Jeffrey E. Young trained with Aaron Beck at the Center for Cognitive Therapy at the University of Pennsylvania, and he was struck by how often the clients who failed in standard cognitive therapy were the ones with lifelong, characterological problems. In Cognitive Therapy for Personality Disorders: A Schema-Focused Approach (1990) he set out what he first called schema-focused cognitive therapy, now simply schema therapy . Its fullest statement is Schema Therapy: A Practitioner's Guide (2003), written with Janet Klosko and Marjorie Weishaar; Young and Klosko had already written a popular self-help version, Reinventing Your Life , in 1993. Young's diagnosis of the problem tells you what schema therapy adds. Standard cognitive therapy, he pointed out, quietly assumes that clients can, after brief training, report their thoughts and feelings; that they have specific problems to work on and will do homework; that they can form a collaborative relationship within a few sessions, so that the relationship itself need not be a focus; and that their beliefs will yield to evidence, logic, experiments and practice. Clients with personality disorders break nearly every one of these assumptions. Their problems are vague and pervasive ("my whole life doesn't work"). They avoid painful thoughts and feelings, so they cannot report what they will not let themselves notice. Their beliefs feel like the truth about who they are, so evidence slides off them. And the relationship with the therapist is often not the background to the problem but the problem itself, re-enacted in the room through mistrust, clinging, compliance or hostility. The client who says "I know it, but I don't feel it" states the central difficulty. Cognitive therapy is good at changing intellectual conviction (what the client knows in her head) and much less good at changing emotional conviction (what she feels in her gut). Schema therapy therefore adds methods aimed at the gut: imagery, chair dialogues and an unusually warm, active therapy relationship. It is an integrative therapy, combining cognitive-behavioural methods with ideas from attachment theory, Gestalt therapy, object relations theory and constructivism, around one goal: helping clients get their core emotional needs met by healing the schemas that formed when those needs went unmet in childhood. Exam trap "Schema therapy was developed by..." Jeffrey Young , not Aaron Beck (although Young trained with Beck and the therapy grew out of Beck's), not Marsha Linehan (DBT, Section 5.8) and not Steven Hayes (ACT, Section 5.9). "Schema therapy was originally designed for patients who..." had failed to respond to standard CBT, particularly those with personality disorders . It was not designed for patients hospitalised with acute psychosis (who need medication and the CBT for psychosis of Section 5.6), not for simple specific phobias (exposure therapy works well for them, Chapter 4), and not as a brief solution-focused intervention (solution-focused brief therapy is de Shazer and Berg's, Chapter 6). Schema therapy is long, often a year or more. Early maladaptive schemas You met Beck's use of the word schema in Section 5.3: the mental structure that holds a core belief and filters incoming information, like a pair of tinted glasses. Young's concept is larger. He defined an early maladaptive schema as a broad, pervasive theme or pattern, made up of memories, emotions, thoughts and bodily sensations, about oneself and one's relationships with others, developed during childhood or adolescence, elaborated throughout life, and dysfunctional to a significant degree. Notice four things in that definition. An early maladaptive schema is more than a belief: it includes memories, feelings and body sensations, which is why it can be "known" to be false and still be felt as true. It is about relationships , not just about the self. It begins early . And it is self-perpetuating : a schema fights for its own survival, because however painful it is, it is familiar, and people are drawn back to the situations that trigger it. Where do such schemas come from? Young's answer begins with needs. Every child, he proposed, has five core emotional needs : secure attachment to others (safety, stability, nurturance and acceptance); autonomy, competence and a sense of identity; freedom to express valid needs and emotions; spontaneity and play; and realistic limits and self-control. Schemas form when these needs are not met, through four kinds of early experience: toxic frustration of needs , too little of a good thing (cold or absent parents breed emotional deprivation); traumatisation or victimisation (abuse, humiliation or bullying breed mistrust and defectiveness); too much of a good thing (an overprotected child may grow up dependent, an overindulged one entitled); and selective internalisation or identification with a significant other (the child absorbs a parent's pessimism, harsh standards or fear of the world). Temperament matters too: an anxious, sensitive child and a robust one can grow up in the same family with different schemas, a point you will meet again in Linehan's biosocial theory (Section 5.8). In the 2003 version of the model Young listed 18 early maladaptive schemas, grouped into five schema domains , one for each unmet need (earlier versions listed fewer). Table 5.12 sets them out. Know the numbers (18 schemas, five domains), the names of the domains and the commonest schemas, described below the table. Disconnection and rejection Secure attachment: safety, stability, nurturance, acceptance Abandonment/instability; mistrust/abuse; emotional deprivation; defectiveness/shame; social isolation/alienation 2. Impaired autonomy and performance Autonomy, competence, a sense of identity Dependence/incompetence; vulnerability to harm or illness; enmeshment/undeveloped self; failure 3. Abandonment/instability is the expectation that the people one is close to will leave, die or prove unreliable. Mistrust/abuse is the expectation that others will hurt, humiliate or exploit one. Emotional deprivation is the expectation that one's need for nurturance, empathy and protection will never be met. Defectiveness/shame is the feeling of being inwardly bad or unlovable, so that one would be rejected if truly known. Among the others, subjugation is surrendering control to others, suppressing one's needs to avoid anger or abandonment; self-sacrifice is meeting others' needs at one's own expense; unrelenting standards is the belief that one must meet very high internal standards to avoid criticism; and entitlement/grandiosity is the belief that one is special and above the rules. Schemas are assessed through the client's history, imagery of childhood scenes and the Young Schema Questionnaire (Assessment book). Push a case through the model. Meera is 29, a software engineer in Bengaluru. Her father was warm and playful one week and absent, drinking, the next; her mother, overwhelmed, told her that a good daughter does not make demands. At work Meera is excellent. In love she is in torment. She is drawn, again and again, to men who are charming and unavailable, and when a boyfriend does not answer a message for an hour she is flooded with panic and certain that he has gone for good. Standard cognitive therapy taught her to write, "He is probably in a meeting; he replied within two hours every other time." She believed the balanced response at 80 percent and still felt the panic at 90. A schema therapist would see two early maladaptive schemas at work, abandonment/instability (from the unpredictable father) and subjugation (from "good daughters do not make demands"), and would set out to work on them where they live: in memory, emotion and relationships, not only in thought. Exam trap Know the numbers: Young described 18 early maladaptive schemas in five domains (disconnection and rejection; impaired autonomy and performance; impaired limits; other-directedness; overvigilance and inhibition). Do not confuse an early maladaptive schema with Beck's core belief or with Beck's three families of core beliefs (helpless, unlovable, worthless; Section 5.3). Beck's schema is mainly cognitive; Young's includes memories, emotions and bodily sensations, is rooted in an unmet childhood need, and is about relationships with others as much as about the self. Coping styles: how schemas keep themselves alive A schema by itself does not make a person act. What a person does when a schema is triggered is governed by his schema coping style . Faced with the pain of an activated schema, people respond in one of three ways, which map neatly onto the three basic animal responses to threat. In schema surrender (the freeze response) the person gives in to the schema and behaves as if it were true, choosing partners and situations that confirm it. In schema avoidance (the flight response) the person arranges life so that the schema is never triggered, avoiding situations, closeness and even thoughts and feelings that might activate it, often with the help of alcohol, overwork or compulsive busyness. In schema overcompensation (the fight response) the person behaves as if the opposite of the schema were true, fighting it so hard that he goes too far the other way. Table 5.13 shows all three applied to a single schema. Table 5.13 The three schema coping styles, illustrated with the defectiveness/shame schema ("I am flawed and unlovable"). Coping style Threat response What the person does Example Surrender Freeze Gives in and acts as if the schema were true Chooses critical partners; accepts put-downs without protest Avoidance Flight Keeps the schema from being triggered Avoids closeness; never lets anyone know him well; drinks to numb shame Overcompensation Fight Acts as if the opposite were true Acts superior; criticises others before they can criticise him The cruelty of coping styles is that each one, in the long run, keeps the schema alive. Meera, with her abandonment schema, could surrender (cling to unreliable men and accept being left as her fate), avoid (refuse all close relationships and live for her work), or overcompensate (end every relationship herself, at the first sign of distance, so that no one can leave her first). Whichever she chooses, she never collects the evidence that a reliable person might stay. Young called this process schema perpetuation and described three ways it happens: through the cognitive distortions you met in Section 5.3 (selective abstraction notices every late reply and filters out every loyal act), through self-defeating life patterns (the choice of partners and jobs), and through the coping styles themselves. schema chemistry is the intense attraction people often feel towards partners who trigger their core schemas: the unavailable man feels exciting to Meera, and the kind, steady one feels dull, because the first one feels like home. The opposite of perpetuation is schema healing , the goal of the therapy: weakening the schema's memories, emotional charge, bodily sensations and beliefs, and replacing maladaptive coping styles with behaviour that actually meets the person's needs. Exam trap The three schema coping styles are surrender, avoidance and overcompensation (freeze, flight and fight). Overcompensation is the one students miss, because it can look healthy: the confident, high-achieving, dominating person who never shows weakness may be fighting a defectiveness or failure schema. The test is rigidity and cost. Healthy confidence can bend; overcompensation cannot, and it usually damages relationships. Schema modes Working schema by schema went well with moderate problems. With severely disturbed clients, especially those with borderline and narcissistic personality disorders, it ran into trouble: they often had a dozen schemas active at once, and they shifted, sometimes within minutes, from one intense state to another: tearful and childlike, then furious, then cold and empty, then savagely self-critical. To describe these shifts, Young introduced the concept of schema modes : the moment-to-moment emotional states and coping responses, adaptive and maladaptive, that a person experiences. A mode is the set of schemas and coping responses that is active in a person right now . The distinction is simple and examinable: a schema is a trait , an enduring pattern; a mode is a state , the part of the self that is in charge at this moment. Everyone has modes, but in a healthy person the shifts are smooth and a sensible adult part stays in charge; in severe personality disorders the modes are extreme and walled off from one another. Young described ten modes in four groups. The child modes are innate and universal: the Vulnerable Child (lonely, frightened, carrying the core schemas), the Angry Child (enraged that core needs are not met), the Impulsive or Undisciplined Child (acting on desires without regard to limits) and the Happy Child (content because needs are met). The dysfunctional coping modes correspond to the three coping styles: the Compliant Surrenderer, the Detached Protector (who shuts off needs and feelings, leaving the person numb and empty) and the Overcompensator. The dysfunctional parent modes are internalised versions of the parents at their worst: the Punitive Parent, who punishes the child for having needs or making mistakes, and the Demanding Parent, who pushes ceaselessly for higher standards. Finally, the Healthy Adult nurtures the Vulnerable Child, sets limits on the Angry and Impulsive Child and stands up to the parent modes; it is the mode therapy sets out to strengthen. Later research by the Dutch group around Arnoud Arntz , using the Schema Mode Inventory, extended the list, but the ten-mode version is the one taught. Young's model of borderline personality disorder uses just five modes, shown in Figure 5.7: the Abandoned or Abused Child, the Angry or Impulsive Child, the Punitive Parent, the Detached Protector and a weak Healthy Adult. Imagine Sana, 24, with a borderline pattern, in a single session. She begins flat and distant: "I'm fine. Nothing really matters." (Detached Protector.) The therapist mentions that she will be on leave next month. Sana goes quiet, then tearful: "Everyone leaves." (Abandoned Child.) Within minutes she is shouting: "You're like all the others; you never cared." (Angry Child.) That night she cuts her arm while a voice in her head says, "You're disgusting. You deserve this." (Punitive Parent.) To an onlooker this is the instability of borderline personality disorder; to a schema therapist it is a sequence of mode flips , each of which can be named and worked with. Abandoned or abused child Lonely, frightened, worthless Therapist: protects, comforts Angry or impulsive child Rage, impulsive acts Therapist: sets limits, hears need Healthy adult Weak or absent in BPD Therapist models it at first Punitive parent Self-hatred, self-punishment Therapist: defeats, banishes it Detached protector Numb, empty, cut off Therapist: gently bypasses it punishes, blames flips to rage shuts feelings off Figure 5.7 Young's schema mode model of borderline personality disorder. The arrows show one common sequence of mode flips; the last line in each box gives the therapist's task for that mode. The Healthy Adult is weak at the start, so the therapist plays that role until the client can take it over. Each mode calls for a different response. The therapist bypasses the Detached Protector gently, without attacking it, because it once protected a child who had no other way to survive; she protects and comforts the Abandoned Child; she sets limits on the Angry Child while validating the need underneath the anger; and she fights and banishes the Punitive Parent, the one mode with which there is no negotiation. Throughout, she acts as the Healthy Adult the client does not yet have, so that the client can gradually take that role over for herself. Exam trap A schema is an enduring trait-like pattern; a mode is the state that is active at the moment. Young's dysfunctional parent modes are the Punitive Parent and the Demanding Parent ; the healthy, nurturing role belongs to the Healthy Adult mode. Some books write "Critical Parent" or "Nurturing Parent", but those are the ego-state names of Eric Berne's transactional analysis, a different therapy. And the five-mode model of borderline personality disorder is Young's, not Linehan's: DBT does not use modes. Limited reparenting and the techniques of change Schema therapy runs in two phases. In the assessment and education phase the therapist and client identify the schemas, coping styles and modes, trace them back to their childhood origins, and link them to the client's present problems. In the change phase the therapist uses four groups of techniques: the therapy relationship itself, experiential techniques, cognitive techniques and behavioural pattern-breaking. The relationship comes first, and it is where schema therapy differs most from Beck's. You saw in Section 5.4 that Beck regarded warmth and empathy as necessary but not sufficient: the ground on which the techniques work. In schema therapy the relationship is itself an active ingredient, through limited reparenting . Within the bounds of a professional relationship, the therapist partly meets the core emotional needs that the client's parents did not meet: she offers warmth, safety, stability, praise, validation of feelings and encouragement of autonomy, and also the firm, kind limits that an impulsive child needs. With borderline personality disorder the reparenting goes further: some contact between sessions, or a card or recorded message to hold on to when the Abandoned Child is frightened. The word limited matters: the therapist is not the client's parent and stays within professional ethics (Chapter 1). The partner of limited reparenting is empathic confrontation (or empathic reality testing): the therapist shows that she understands why the schema developed and why it feels true, and at the same time confronts the client, clearly and repeatedly, with the need to change the behaviour that keeps it alive. With Meera: "When you were small, your father really did disappear without warning, and you learned to be ready for everyone to leave. That made sense then. And I notice that when your boyfriend is a little late in replying, you end the relationship before he can. That protects you from being left, and it also keeps you alone. Shall we look at that together?" Empathy without confrontation lets the schema stay in charge; confrontation without empathy feels like one more critical parent. The experiential techniques aim at the gut, where the schema's emotional conviction lives. The best known is imagery rescripting , set out for work with childhood memories by Arnoud Arntz and Anoek Weertman (1999) and now central to schema therapy. The client closes her eyes and goes back, in imagery, to a childhood scene in which a core need was not met: little Meera waiting by the window for a father who did not come home. Once the scene is vivid and the feeling is present, the therapist enters the image (or the client's adult self does), and the scene is changed: the adult comforts the child, tells her that it is not her fault, and perhaps speaks firmly to the father. Nothing changes the historical facts, but the emotional meaning of the memory changes, and with it the intensity of the schema. The second experiential method is chair work , borrowed from Fritz Perls's Gestalt therapy (Chapter 6). The client sits in one chair and speaks as her schema ("You'll always be left; you're too much trouble") and then moves to another chair and answers it from her Healthy Adult; or the Punitive Parent is placed in an empty chair and the client, with the therapist's help, tells it to leave. Clients may also write letters, which are not sent, to the parents who hurt them. The cognitive techniques are the familiar tools of Sections 5.3 and 5.4 turned on the schema: reviewing the evidence for and against the schema across the whole of the client's life, reattributing childhood events ("I was not left because I was too much trouble; my father had a drinking problem"), writing dialogues between the "schema side" and the "healthy side", keeping a schema diary, and carrying schema flashcards , coping cards that the client reads when a schema is triggered. Finally, behavioural pattern-breaking , usually the longest phase, replaces schema-driven coping with healthier choices: Meera practises asking for reassurance instead of ending relationships, notices schema chemistry when she meets an unavailable man, and deliberately gives a steady man more than one evening. Key study: schema therapy versus transference-focused psychotherapy (Giesen-Bloo and colleagues, 2006) Could schema therapy hold its own against a respected psychodynamic treatment for borderline personality disorder? Josephine Giesen-Bloo, Arnoud Arntz and their colleagues in the Netherlands randomly assigned outpatients with borderline personality disorder to three years of either schema therapy or Otto Kernberg's transference-focused psychotherapy (Chapter 3), both delivered twice a week. Both groups improved, but by the end of the three years about 46 percent of the schema therapy patients had recovered, against about 24 percent of the transference-focused patients, and fewer schema therapy patients dropped out. Critics pointed out that the transference-focused arm may not have been delivered as skilfully as its developers would wish, and that a trial run by the developers of one treatment risks allegiance effects (Chapter 8). Later trials of group and individual schema therapy have also been encouraging, and schema therapy is now counted among the evidence-based treatments for borderline personality disorder. Clinical link Schema therapy is now used well beyond borderline personality disorder: for other personality disorders, chronic and recurrent depression, eating disorders, couples, and offenders with personality disorders in forensic hospitals. A clinician meeting a client with a long history of failed short treatments, and relationships that keep collapsing in the same way, should think of it. It is demanding to deliver: limited reparenting asks the therapist to care openly and to hold firm limits at the same time, and good supervision is essential. Exam trap An option reading " schema analysis, mode work, limited reparenting " describes schema therapy. It is the classic distractor when the question asks for DBT's skills modules (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness; Section 5.8). The empty chair technique is used in schema therapy but belongs to Gestalt therapy ; if asked which therapy "focuses on" the empty chair, answer Gestalt. Cognitive analytic therapy Schema therapy started from cognitive therapy and reached towards childhood and relationships. The second therapy in this section travelled the other way. Anthony Ryle (1927 to 2016), a nephew of the Oxford philosopher Gilbert Ryle, spent years as a general practitioner in London and then as head of a university student health service before becoming a consultant psychotherapist at St Thomas' Hospital in London. Two things troubled him: long-term psychoanalytic therapy could be offered to very few patients in Britain's National Health Service, and its ideas were rarely put in a form that patients could understand and researchers could test. Ryle had already used George Kelly's repertory grid, a method of mapping a person's personal constructs (Kelly appears in Sections 5.1 and 5.5), to measure how patients changed in therapy. Through the 1980s he built a brief, structured, collaborative therapy that put psychoanalytic insights into cognitive terms, and in 1990 he published Cognitive-Analytic Therapy: Active Participation in Change . cognitive analytic therapy (CAT) integrates three sources: cognitive psychology and Kelly's personal construct theory; psychoanalytic object relations theory (Chapter 3); and, from the 1990s, the ideas of the Russian psychologist Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky (1896 to 1934; Section 5.5) and the Russian literary theorist Mikhail Mikhailovich Bakhtin (1895 to 1975), introduced into CAT by the Finnish psychologist Mikael Leiman. "Analytic" in the name means psychoanalytic, not statistical. Ryle's first model was the procedural sequence model . Any purposeful action, he argued, runs through a repeated sequence: we perceive a situation and an aim, appraise it, predict what will happen, act, and evaluate the result, confirming or revising the aim or the means. Neurotic problems persist because certain problem procedures are not revised even when they repeatedly fail. Ryle then joined this to object relations theory. The procedures that matter most are learned in early relationships, and they come in pairs. A child who grows up with a critical, contemptuous parent does not learn only how to be a crushed, humiliated child; he learns the whole relationship , both its poles. These internalised pairs are reciprocal roles , written as a pair linked by an arrow: "critical, contemptuous" to "crushed, worthless". As an adult, the person can play either pole: he may provoke criticism from others, treat a junior colleague with contempt, or, most often, play both roles inside his own head, criticising himself in his father's voice. This self-to-self relationship is CAT's translation of the internalised critic. Problem procedures take three typical forms, which Ryle called traps, dilemmas and snags. Table 5.14 defines them. Early in therapy clients are given a questionnaire called the Psychotherapy File, which describes common traps, dilemmas and snags in everyday language, and many clients recognise themselves at once. Table 5.14 The three kinds of problem procedure in cognitive analytic therapy. Procedure What it is Example Trap A vicious circle: a negative belief leads to action that produces consequences confirming the belief "Feeling worthless, I try to please everyone; I am used and ignored, which proves I am worthless" Dilemma A false choice between two extremes, phrased "either... or" or "if... then", when other options exist "Either I keep my feelings bottled up, or I make a terrible mess"; "Either I'm a doormat or a bully" Snag Abandoning a reasonable goal because of others' imagined reactions or a sense of not deserving it "I'd like a good job, but I'd feel guilty that my sister has none, so I sabotage my interviews" CAT is time-limited, usually 16 sessions (eight for milder problems, and often 24 for borderline personality disorder), and it moves through three phases often summarised as the three Rs: reformulation, recognition and revision. In the reformulation phase (roughly the first four sessions) the therapist takes a careful history, agrees with the client on a short list of target problems and the procedures that maintain them, and then writes the reformulation letter , which she reads aloud to the client, usually around the fourth session. The letter tells the client's story back to her with compassion: what happened to her, how her ways of coping made sense as survival strategies at the time, how the same procedures now cause her problems, and how they are likely to show up in the therapy itself. Clients are often deeply moved by it. The prose letter is followed by a sequential diagrammatic reformulation (SDR), a diagram that places the core reciprocal roles at the centre and traces each problem procedure as a loop that leads back to the same pain. Figure 5.8 shows a simple one. Core reciprocal role Critical, contemptuous Crushed, worthless (core pain) Placation trap Try to please everyone Own needs ignored; resentment, guilt Dilemma Perfect or useless Overwork, fall short, attack myself Exit Notice, name, ask for help Problem procedure Exit: a new procedure Figure 5.8 A simple sequential diagrammatic reformulation. At the centre is the core reciprocal role, learned with a critical parent; each loop of plain black arrows is a problem procedure that starts from the core pain and ends back in it. The two arrows leading down to the Exit box (named in the legend) are the "exits" that client and therapist work out in the revision phase. In the recognition phase the client learns to spot her procedures as they happen, often by carrying a copy of the diagram and noting each day when the trap or dilemma appeared. In the revision phase client and therapist work out "exits", new procedures drawn onto the diagram as ways out of each loop. Here the analytic side of CAT comes into its own. Because reciprocal roles are relationships, they will be enacted with the therapist: a client whose core role is "critical, contemptuous to crushed, worthless" may feel criticised by the therapist's every question, or may provoke criticism, and the therapist will feel the pull to reciprocate. Instead of interpreting this transference in the psychoanalytic manner (Chapter 3), the CAT therapist points to the diagram: "I think this is the trap happening between us right now." Ryle drew here on Vygotsky's idea that new mental capacities are first exercised jointly with a more skilled helper, using shared tools and signs, and only later internalised (the zone of proximal development, described in the Developmental book): the letters and diagrams are tools the client first uses with the therapist and then carries inside herself. Ending is planned from the start and worked on openly, because for many clients an ending is itself a trigger for their core roles (abandonment, rejection). In the last session therapist and client exchange goodbye letters , each summarising honestly what has changed, what has not, and what remains to be done, and a follow-up meeting is held a few months later. For borderline personality disorder Ryle developed the multiple self-states model (1997), which describes the disorder as switching between a small number of partly dissociated self-states, each organised around its own reciprocal role, with a weakened capacity to reflect on the switches; the diagram maps the states and the switches between them (compare the schema modes of Figure 5.7). The evidence base for CAT is smaller than that for CBT, DBT or schema therapy. Its best-known trial, by Andrew Chanen and colleagues in Melbourne (2008), treated adolescents with borderline features and found CAT at least as effective as good clinical care, with faster improvement. CAT is widely used in the United Kingdom. Exam trap Cognitive analytic therapy is Anthony Ryle's , published in book form in 1990. Its signatures are reciprocal roles , traps, dilemmas and snags , the reformulation letter , the sequential diagrammatic reformulation and goodbye letters , in a course of about 16 sessions. "Analytic" means psychoanalytic object relations. Do not confuse CAT with Eric Berne's transactional analysis (parent, adult and child ego states), with Kelly's fixed-role therapy (Section 5.5), or with Lazarus's multimodal therapy (Section 5.5). A dilemma in CAT is a false either-or choice; a snag is a goal abandoned because of guilt or others' imagined reactions; a trap is a self-confirming vicious circle. The deeper therapies compared Schema therapy and CAT arrived at similar places from opposite directions. Both treat the problems of a personality disorder as learned patterns of relating, laid down when childhood needs went unmet; both expect those patterns to appear in the therapy relationship and use that as an opportunity; and both describe the rapid shifts of borderline personality disorder as movements between distinct states (modes in one, self-states in the other).
