(Some reviews list schema therapy among the third-wave therapies, but most textbooks treat it as an integrative extension of Beck's work.) The next section turns to a therapy born in the same clinical territory, the chronically suicidal client with borderline personality disorder, which took a different route: instead of only changing what the client thinks, it set out to balance change with acceptance. 5.8 The third wave I: dialectical behaviour therapy High yield · 13 Qs In 1961 a 17-year-old girl from Tulsa, Oklahoma, was admitted to the Institute of Living, a psychiatric hospital in Hartford, Connecticut. She burned her wrists with cigarettes, cut her arms and legs, and banged her head against the walls, and she spent long stretches of her stay locked alone in a seclusion room. She was diagnosed with schizophrenia and given the treatments of the day, strong tranquillising drugs and repeated electroconvulsive therapy. None of it helped. When she was discharged, more than two years later in 1963, her discharge summary recorded that for much of her stay she had been one of the most disturbed patients in the hospital. Before she left she made a private vow: that she would get herself out of hell, and that when she was out she would come back and get others out too. For almost fifty years she told hardly anyone. Then, in June 2011, she stood up in front of an audience at the same hospital and told the whole story, and the New York Times carried it around the world. By then she was one of the most influential clinical psychologists alive, and the treatment she had built for people very like her younger self was being used on every continent. She said she now believed she would have been diagnosed not with schizophrenia but with borderline personality disorder. Her name was Marsha M. Linehan (1943 to 2026), and her treatment is dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). Why a new therapy was needed Linehan took her PhD at Loyola University Chicago in 1971 and in 1977 joined the University of Washington in Seattle, where she set out to treat the clients most therapists avoided: chronically suicidal women who harmed themselves again and again, many of whom met the criteria for borderline personality disorder. She began with the best-tested tool she had, standard behaviour therapy (Chapter 4): define the problem behaviours, analyse what maintains them, teach new skills and change the contingencies. It failed, and the way it failed was instructive. When Linehan pushed for change, her clients heard criticism: to a woman who already felt that she was the problem, every request to monitor her behaviour and practise skills said "you are doing it wrong". She became angry, withdrew or stopped coming. When Linehan switched to warm acceptance and support, in the manner of client-centred therapy (Chapter 6), clients felt that nobody was taking their unbearable misery seriously or helping them change a life that was not worth living. Meanwhile weekly crises swallowed the sessions, and the therapists were exhausted. Neither change alone nor acceptance alone worked. The way out was to do both at once, and to make the tension between them the engine of the therapy. For acceptance Linehan turned to Zen, which she had practised herself (including at Shasta Abbey, a Zen monastery in California, and with the German Zen teacher Willigis Jäger), and translated its mindful awareness and radical acceptance into behavioural skills without religious content. To hold acceptance and change together she borrowed a philosophical framework, dialectics. In 1993 she published the treatment in two manuals, Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment of Borderline Personality Disorder and the Skills Training Manual for Treating Borderline Personality Disorder (revised as the DBT Skills Training Manual in 2015). DBT was the first third-wave therapy (Section 5.1) to gain wide acceptance, yet it remains at heart cognitive-behavioural: change still comes through behavioural analysis, skills training, exposure and contingency management, always balanced with acceptance. Key study: the first DBT trial (Linehan, Armstrong, Suarez, Allmon and Heard, 1991) Could any outpatient treatment reduce repeated self-harm in chronically suicidal women with borderline personality disorder, a group that most trials had excluded? Linehan and her colleagues randomly assigned a small sample of such women (about 45; reports of the trial give slightly different totals) to one year of DBT or to treatment as usual in the community. Over the year, the DBT group made fewer and less medically serious acts of self-harm (then called parasuicide), spent far fewer days as psychiatric inpatients, and were much more likely to stay in therapy: only about one in six dropped out of individual therapy, against about half of the comparison clients. The trial had limits. It was small, it compared DBT with a loosely defined "usual" treatment rather than with another structured therapy, and the two groups did not differ in depression, hopelessness or suicidal thinking. But it was the first randomised trial to show that a psychological treatment could reduce self-harm in this population, and it put DBT on the map. Exam trap DBT was developed by Marsha Linehan primarily for borderline personality disorder with chronic suicidality (her first clients were chronically suicidal, self-harming women). It was not designed for schizophrenia, acute and transient psychotic disorder, specific phobias, panic disorder, OCD, anxiety disorders in general, autism, ADHD or anorexia nervosa. Adapted versions are now used for some of these and for PTSD and substance use (see the end of this section), so read the stem: "originally designed for" or "primarily indicated for" means borderline personality disorder. The other names in such questions belong elsewhere: Aaron Beck (cognitive therapy), Albert Bandura (self-efficacy), Virginia Satir (family therapy, Chapter 7). The biosocial theory Every therapy rests on a theory of what has gone wrong. Linehan's is the biosocial theory of borderline personality disorder, and its central claim is simple to state: borderline personality disorder is primarily a disorder of the emotion regulation system. It arises from a transaction , over many years, between a child who is biologically vulnerable to intense emotion and an environment that invalidates her emotional experience. (The diagnostic criteria for the disorder are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) Linehan first regrouped the diagnostic criteria into five areas of dysregulation (Table 5.16), and each skills module was later built to repair one of them. The disorder, on this view, is not simply moodiness but a pervasive difficulty in managing emotion that spills over into relationships, behaviour, thinking and the sense of self. Table 5.16 Linehan's five areas of dysregulation in borderline personality disorder and the skills module that mainly targets each. Area of dysregulation What it looks like Main skills module Emotional Rapid, intense mood shifts; intense anger Emotion regulation Interpersonal Chaotic, intense relationships; frantic efforts to avoid abandonment Interpersonal effectiveness Behavioural Impulsive acts, self-harm, suicide attempts Distress tolerance Self Unstable identity; chronic emptiness Core mindfulness Cognitive Brief stress-related paranoid thinking or dissociation Core mindfulness (grounding in the present) The biological half of the theory is emotional vulnerability , which has three parts: high sensitivity (a low threshold, so that small events such as a delayed reply or a slightly cool tone set off an emotion others would hardly notice); high reactivity (once triggered, the emotion is extremely intense, narrowing attention and disorganising thought and action); and a slow return to baseline (the emotion lasts, so the next trigger arrives before the last has faded, and emotions pile up). Linehan's own image is famous: people with the disorder are like patients with third-degree burns over most of their bodies; they have, so to speak, no emotional skin, and the slightest touch causes immense suffering. The vulnerability is a matter of temperament, partly inherited, not of character or will. The social half is the invalidating environment : a family or setting that responds to a child's communication of her private experience (feelings, thoughts, sensations) in ways that are erratic, inappropriate or extreme, telling her in effect that her experience is wrong or unimportant. It has three features. It dismisses or punishes emotional expression ("Stop crying or I'll give you something to cry about"; "You're not hurt, you're just tired"). It intermittently reinforces emotional escalation : ordinary distress is ignored but extreme distress finally gets attention, so the child learns that only extremes work, and intermittent reinforcement (Chapter 4) makes the lesson hard to unlearn. And it oversimplifies the ease of solving problems ("If you really wanted to, you'd just stop"), so the child never learns the patient skills real problems need, and blames herself for failing. Linehan described chaotic families (parents preoccupied with their own troubles), perfect families (parents who cannot tolerate negative emotion) and typical families (in cultures that prize self-control and achievement). Abuse is a severe form of invalidation, but it is not required: a poor fit between a highly sensitive child and calm, well-meaning parents can be enough. Such a child does not learn to label her emotions, to trust them as valid responses, or to tolerate and soothe distress. She learns instead to invalidate herself as her environment did, and to swing between suppressing emotion and showing it in extreme form. The result is emotion dysregulation : a pervasive inability to modulate emotion, to stay organised under strong feeling and to act for long-term goals rather than short-term relief. Many dramatic behaviours of the disorder are attempts to regulate unbearable emotion. Self-harm often brings rapid relief, so it is negatively reinforced (Chapter 4) every time it works. To the client, cutting is a solution; to the therapist, it is a problem behaviour to be replaced by better solutions. That double view runs through the whole of DBT. The word transaction is the key, and Figure 5.9 shows why. Biology and environment do not simply add together; each changes the other over time. A highly reactive child is hard to parent; exhausted parents become more dismissive; their invalidation makes her more dysregulated; her escalating behaviour provokes still more invalidation. The theory is therefore a no-blame theory, and families are treated as partners rather than culprits. Sheila Crowell, Theodore Beauchaine and Linehan (2009) later added early impulsivity to emotional sensitivity as an inherited trait. Biological side Emotional vulnerability High sensitivity Intense reactions Slow return to baseline Social side Invalidating environment Feelings dismissed Emotions punished Problems made to look easy each shapes the other over years Pervasive emotion dysregulation the core of the disorder Borderline behaviours Self-harm, suicidal acts, impulsivity Unstable relationships, identity provokes more invalidation Figure 5.9 Linehan's biosocial theory. A biologically sensitive child and an invalidating environment shape each other over years (the paired arrows), producing pervasive emotion dysregulation and the behaviours of the disorder. The arrow labelled "provokes more invalidation" closes the loop: the behaviours provoke more invalidation, which is why the theory is called transactional. The theory also explains three dialectical dilemmas , in which the client swings between opposite extremes, one shaped mainly by biology and the other by environment: emotional vulnerability (feeling overwhelmed) versus self-invalidation (telling herself her feelings are stupid); active passivity (helplessly waiting for others to solve her problems) versus apparent competence (seeming far more capable than she is, so that others expect too much); and unrelenting crises versus inhibited grieving (avoiding the painful emotions of loss and trauma, whose avoidance keeps the crises coming). The therapist helps her find the middle path in each pair, which leads to the idea at the centre of DBT. Indian context Invalidation does not require cruelty. In many Indian homes it arrives in loving, ordinary sentences: "Don't cry, people will see", "What is there to be sad about? You have everything", "Just adjust", "Log kya kahenge?" For most children these do no harm. For a highly sensitive child they can add up to a daily experience of having her feelings declared wrong. A clinician adapting DBT for an Indian family can therefore teach parents to validate, much as the adolescent version of DBT brings parents into the skills group (described at the end of this section), and can present emotion regulation as serving family harmony as well as personal well-being, which makes the skills easier for the whole family to accept. Exam trap Borderline personality disorder is characterised primarily by emotional instability and impulsivity : a pervasive pattern of instability in relationships, self-image and emotion, with marked impulsivity (ICD-10 called it emotionally unstable personality disorder, with impulsive and borderline types). The distractors describe other personality disorders: detachment and restricted emotion (schizoid), eccentric beliefs and odd speech (schizotypal), pervasive grandiosity and lack of empathy (narcissistic), obsessive perfectionism (obsessive-compulsive) and suspicious, paranoid ideation (paranoid). The defence mechanism most characteristic of the disorder is splitting , the defence Otto Kernberg placed at the centre of his account of it (Chapter 3), not repression, sublimation or rationalisation. In Linehan's theory the core problem is emotion dysregulation , arising from the transaction of emotional vulnerability with an invalidating environment . Dialectics: acceptance and change What makes DBT "dialectical"? dialectics , a way of thinking developed by the German philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770 to 1831) and later by Karl Marx, holds that reality is made of opposing forces. A position (popularly called the thesis, though Hegel rarely used the word) contains its opposite (the antithesis), and their tension is resolved not by one side defeating the other but by a synthesis that keeps what is true in both; the synthesis then meets its own opposite, so change never stops. Linehan drew three working principles from this: interrelatedness and wholeness (behaviour must be understood within the client's whole system of relationships and history), polarity (every position contains its opposite, and truth is found by looking at both) and continuous change . The central dialectic of DBT is between acceptance and change . The therapist accepts the client completely as she is and pushes steadily for change: "You are doing the best you can, and you need to do better." Too much acceptance abandons the client to an unbearable life; too much change makes the therapist one more invalidating voice. Think of a seesaw: when the client moves to one extreme, the therapist moves to the other, and both slowly work towards the middle. Dialectical thinking is also something the client is taught, because it is the antidote to one of the most destructive thinking habits of the disorder. You met dichotomous (all-or-nothing) thinking in Section 5.3. In borderline personality disorder it extends to people, who are experienced as wholly good or wholly bad, idealised one week and devalued the next. Psychodynamic writers call this splitting : the failure to hold good and bad images of the same person (or of oneself) together, a concept Melanie Klein introduced and Otto Kernberg made central to his account of the disorder (Chapter 3). DBT does not interpret splitting; it teaches the client to replace "either-or" with "both-and". "My mother loves me and she hurt me." "I am angry with my therapist and I still want to come back next week." "I have made progress and I still have a long way to go." On the acceptance side the core strategy is validation : communicating to the client that her responses make sense and are understandable in her current situation or in the light of her history. Validation is not the same as agreement or praise. The DBT rule is to validate the valid: the therapist validates the pain, the wish for relief and the fact that self-harm "works" in the short term, without validating self-harm as a wise choice. Linehan described six levels of validation, each deeper than the last: Listening and observing : full, alert attention to what the client says and feels. Accurate reflection : saying back, without judgement, what the client has communicated. Articulating the unverbalised : putting into words feelings or thoughts the client has not expressed ("I wonder if you felt humiliated as well as angry"). Validating in terms of past learning or biology : "Given what happened every time you cried as a child, it makes sense that you hide your feelings." Validating in terms of the present context : "Anyone would feel hurt if a friend forgot their birthday"; the response is normal, not just understandable given a disordered past. Radical genuineness : treating the client as an equal and a capable person, not a fragile patient. On the change side the core strategy is problem solving, beginning with behavioural chain analysis : a moment-by-moment reconstruction of one episode of problem behaviour, link by link. The chain runs from vulnerability factors (poor sleep, illness, alcohol, an earlier quarrel) to the prompting event , through every link of thought, emotion, sensation and action, to the problem behaviour and its short- and long-term consequences , which show what is reinforcing it. Solution analysis then asks at which links a skill could have been used. Clients learn that every crisis can be taken apart, and that each link is a place where a different choice can be made. Other change strategies come straight from behaviour therapy and CBT: skills training, contingency management (the therapist's warmth is used as a reinforcer, and care is taken not to reward self-harm with extra attention), exposure to avoided emotions, and cognitive modification. Two further pairs keep the balance. In style, the therapist moves between reciprocal communication (warm, responsive, genuine) and irreverent communication (matter-of-fact, offbeat, used to jolt a client out of a rigid position). Linehan's best-known example: a client announces, "I'm going to kill myself," and the therapist replies, "But I thought you'd agreed not to drop out of therapy." The reply is not callous; it treats the client as capable and refuses the familiar crisis script. The therapist also uses dialectical strategies such as playing devil's advocate (arguing against change so that the client argues for it), metaphor, and "making lemonade out of lemons". Behind all of this sit Linehan's assumptions about clients: they are doing the best they can; they want to improve; they need to do better and try harder; they may not have caused all their problems but must solve them anyway; and they cannot fail in DBT (if a client does not improve, the treatment has failed). Exam trap "DBT's core mindfulness skills are primarily derived from..." Zen Buddhism (with some Western contemplative practice). Not Stoicism (the root of Ellis's REBT, Section 5.2), not psychoanalysis and not existentialism (Chapter 6). "DBT blends CBT with..." mindfulness and acceptance practices drawn from Zen, held together by dialectical philosophy ; not psychoanalytic free association, not pharmacological augmentation, and not Bowen's family systems theory (Chapter 7). The "dialectic" is above all the balance of acceptance and change . Note also that validation in DBT means validating what is valid, not approving every behaviour. The structure of DBT: functions, modes and stages Standard DBT is a whole treatment programme, built to serve five functions : to enhance capabilities (teach the skills the client lacks); to improve motivation to use them; to ensure generalisation , so that skills learned in a clinic are used at home at midnight; to structure the environment so that it reinforces progress rather than crisis; and to enhance the therapists' capabilities and motivation , because chronically suicidal clients burn therapists out. Each function is carried by a mode of treatment, and standard DBT has four (Table 5.17). Table 5.17 The four modes of standard dialectical behaviour therapy and the function each serves. Mode Typical format Main function Individual psychotherapy Weekly, about an hour, with the primary therapist Motivation: works through the target hierarchy; chain analyses Group skills training Weekly, about two and a half hours, for about a year Capability: teaches the four skills modules Telephone coaching Brief calls between sessions, as needed Generalisation: using skills in real crises Therapist consultation team Weekly meeting of the DBT therapists Keeps therapists skilled, motivated and dialectical In individual therapy client and primary therapist work on her targets with chain analyses and the full range of strategies. Each session begins with the diary card , on which she has recorded every day her urges to self-harm or die, any self-harm, drug or alcohol use, her strongest emotions and the skills she used; the card sets the agenda. Group skills training runs more like a class than a therapy group, with handouts and homework, and is usually led by someone other than the individual therapist; a full cycle of the modules takes about six months, so clients usually go through it twice in a year. telephone coaching lets the client call between sessions for brief, practical help in using a skill before she acts on an urge; it is not long telephone therapy. Under the 24-hour rule , a client who has harmed herself may not call for coaching for the next 24 hours (medical emergencies apart), so that contact reinforces reaching out before self-harm, not after it. The consultation team , a weekly meeting of all the programme's DBT therapists, is often called therapy for the therapists: members apply DBT to one another, catch colleagues who have become rigid or burnt out, and agree, among other things, to accept that they are fallible. Linehan insisted that a therapist without a team is not doing DBT. Medication, case management and hospital admission are treated as ancillary. A pretreatment stage of orientation and commitment comes first. The client learns the biosocial theory and the structure of DBT, and she and the therapist agree to work together for a set period (usually a year), to attend, and to work on reducing suicidal and self-harming behaviour. Commitment is sought with named strategies such as weighing pros and cons, the foot-in-the-door and devil's advocate. One rule is famous: a client who misses four consecutive weeks of scheduled skills training or individual therapy is out of the programme for the rest of the contract, though she may apply to return. Treatment then proceeds in stages , defined by how severe the client's problems are. In Stage 1 the aim is to move from severe behavioural dyscontrol to behavioural control, and the work is organised by a strict target hierarchy : Life-threatening behaviours : suicide attempts, suicidal threats and urges, non-suicidal self-injury and behaviour that endangers others. If any occurred during the week, they come first in the session, every time. Therapy-interfering behaviours : anything, by the client or the therapist , that gets in the way of therapy, such as missed sessions, undone homework, hostility, or a therapist who is unreliable or rigid. Quality-of-life-interfering behaviours : substance misuse, high-risk sexual behaviour, problems with money, housing or work, and co-occurring disorders such as depression or eating disorders. Increasing behavioural skills : acquiring and strengthening the skills that will replace the problem behaviours. In Stage 2 the aim is to move from "quiet desperation" to full emotional experiencing, which usually means treating post-traumatic stress and the painful emotions that the client has avoided, often with exposure-based methods. In Stage 3 the aim is ordinary happiness and unhappiness: building self-respect, solving the ordinary problems of living and pursuing personal goals. Linehan later added a Stage 4 , moving from a sense of incompleteness towards a capacity for sustained joy and freedom. The stages explain the phrase that Linehan uses for DBT's ultimate goal: not just staying alive, but building a life worth living . Exam trap The four modes of standard DBT are individual psychotherapy, group skills training, telephone coaching (consultation) and the therapist consultation team . "Family genogram construction" is not one of them; the genogram belongs to Murray Bowen's family systems therapy (Chapter 7). A second trap: some textbooks and coaching notes list DBT's "stages" as (1) life-threatening behaviours, (2) therapy-interfering behaviours, (3) quality of life, (4) skills or growth. That list is really the target hierarchy within Stage 1 . Linehan's stages are pretreatment, then Stage 1 (behavioural control), Stage 2 (emotional experiencing, often trauma work), Stage 3 (ordinary happiness and unhappiness) and Stage 4 (capacity for joy). If a question asks what comes first in a DBT session, the answer is life-threatening behaviour. The four skills modules DBT's skills are its best-known export; many clinics that do not offer full DBT run DBT skills groups. Linehan organised them into four modules, and the dialectic of acceptance and change is built into the very arrangement. Two modules are acceptance skills: core mindfulness and distress tolerance. Two are change skills: emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness. Mindfulness is the "core" because every other skill depends on it, and it is revisited for a week or two at the start of each other module. Table 5.18 summarises the four. Table 5.18 The four skills modules of DBT (mainly from Linehan's 1993 manual, with skills added in the 2015 edition). Module Type Aim Sample skills Core mindfulness Acceptance Be aware of the present moment without judging it Wise mind; "what" skills (observe, describe, participate); "how" skills (non-judgementally, one-mindfully, effectively) Distress tolerance Acceptance Survive a crisis without making it worse; accept what cannot be changed STOP; TIP; distraction (ACCEPTS); self-soothing; IMPROVE the moment; pros and cons; radical acceptance Emotion regulation Change Understand, name and change emotions; reduce vulnerability Check the facts; opposite action; problem solving; PLEASE; building positive experiences Interpersonal effectiveness Change Ask for what one wants, say no, and keep relationships and self-respect DEAR MAN; GIVE; FAST core mindfulness skills are psychological and behavioural versions of Zen meditation practice, taught without religious content. They start from three states of mind. In emotion mind thinking and behaviour are controlled by the current emotion, and facts are bent to fit the feeling. In reasonable mind the person is cool and logical but cut off from feeling. wise mind is the integration of the two, to which it adds intuitive knowing: the quiet sense of what is true and what is needed. Clients reach wise mind through two sets of skills. The three "what" skills say what to do: observe (notice an experience, without words), describe (put words to it: "tightness in my chest", "the thought that she hates me") and participate (throw oneself fully into the activity of the moment). The three "how" skills say how to do it: non-judgementally (describing facts without labelling them good or bad), one-mindfully (one thing at a time, with full attention) and effectively (doing what works, rather than what is "right" or "fair"). Notice the link to the biosocial theory: a client invalidated for years has learned to judge her feelings harshly, and the non-judgemental stance teaches her to observe them instead. (Mindfulness in the wider sense, and the mindfulness-based therapies, are the subject of Section 5.9.) distress tolerance skills are for the moments when emotion is at its peak and nothing can be changed right now: getting through a crisis without making it worse, above all without self-harm. The crisis survival skills include STOP (stop, take a step back, observe, proceed mindfully); TIP, added in 2015, which changes body chemistry fast (cold t emperature, such as holding the face in cold water, which triggers the dive reflex and slows the heart; i ntense exercise; p aced breathing; p aired muscle relaxation); distraction, remembered as "wise mind ACCEPTS" (activities, contributing, comparisons, opposite emotions, pushing away, thoughts, sensations); self-soothing through the five senses; "IMPROVE the moment" (imagery, meaning, prayer, relaxation, one thing in the moment, a brief vacation, encouragement); and weighing the pros and cons of acting on the urge. Distress tolerance also contains the reality acceptance skills , which go to the heart of DBT. radical acceptance is complete acceptance, with mind, body and heart, of facts that cannot be changed, such as a past trauma or a relationship that has ended. It is not approval and not resignation; it is the end of fighting reality. In Linehan's formula, pain is part of life, but pain plus non-acceptance equals suffering. Related skills are turning the mind (choosing acceptance again each time the mind drifts back to "this should not have happened") and willingness (doing what the situation needs, as opposed to wilfulness , refusing to tolerate the moment). Emotion regulation skills are for changing emotions that can and should be changed. Clients first learn what emotions are for (they communicate to others, motivate action and signal that something matters), how they unfold (prompting event, interpretation, body changes, action urge, expression, after-effects) and how to name them accurately. They then learn to change them. Check the facts asks whether the emotion and its intensity fit the actual situation. When they do not, opposite action means deliberately acting opposite to the emotion's action urge: approaching what one unjustifiably fears, staying engaged instead of hiding when shame is not warranted, and, with unjustified anger, gently avoiding the person or doing something a little kind rather than attacking. When the emotion does fit the facts, problem solving changes the situation causing it. Finally, clients reduce their vulnerability to emotion mind by building positive experiences and mastery, coping ahead with difficult situations, and caring for the body with the PLEASE skills: treat p hysica l illness, balance e ating, a void mood-altering substances, balance s leep and get e xercise. Because emotional vulnerability is biological, looking after the body counts as a real regulation skill. Interpersonal effectiveness skills are for asking for what one wants, refusing unreasonable requests and handling conflict, while protecting both the relationship and one's self-respect. Linehan distinguishes three goals, which the client learns to rank in each situation: objectives effectiveness (getting what one wants), relationship effectiveness and self-respect effectiveness. Each has its own acronym. DEAR MAN , for getting what one wants, stands for d escribe the situation, e xpress feelings, a ssert (ask or say no clearly), r einforce (explain what the other person gains), stay m indful (keep to the point, like a "broken record"), a ppear confident and n egotiate. GIVE, for keeping the relationship, means be g entle, act i nterested, v alidate and use an e asy manner. FAST, for keeping self-respect, means be f air, no excessive a pologies, s tick to one's values and be t ruthful. The 2015 manual added "walking the middle path" skills (dialectics, validation and behaviour change), first developed for adolescents and their families. Watch the skills work together in one night. Priya is 22, a final-year BA student in Pune, eight months into DBT. At 11 p.m. her mother says sharply that she is "wasting her life like always". Her diary card already shows poor sleep and a missed lunch that day (vulnerability factors). Shame and rage surge to 90 out of 100, with the old urge to cut. She uses STOP; then TIP, splashing cold water on her face until her heart slows; then distraction, a playlist and a text to a friend. When the urge has dropped to 40, she calls her therapist for two minutes of coaching. The next morning she uses DEAR MAN with her mother: "Last night you said I was wasting my life (describe). I felt hurt and very angry (express). I'd like you to tell me when you are worried, instead of calling me names (assert). Then I can actually tell you what's going on with my studies (reinforce)." In her next session a chain analysis of the night finds the link where the missed lunch and poor sleep made everything harder, and that week's homework is the PLEASE skills. Her diary card shows no self-harm that week, the first such week in a month. Exam trap The four DBT skills modules are mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness . Any option that includes cognitive restructuring or relaxation as a module is wrong (relaxation appears only inside TIP, and Beck-style cognitive restructuring is not a DBT module). "Distress tolerance is a major treatment modality in which therapy?" DBT , not behaviour therapy, CBT in general or psychodynamic therapy. An ACT question may offer "mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness, problem-solving, behavioural activation" as a distractor for the hexaflex; the first four are DBT modules, the list as a whole is nobody's model, and the hexaflex is described in Section 5.9. Mindfulness and distress tolerance are the acceptance modules; emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness are the change modules. Evidence, adaptations and DBT among the treatments for borderline personality disorder DBT has more randomised trials behind it than any other psychotherapy for borderline personality disorder. After 1991 the critical question was whether it worked for specific reasons or simply because it was an organised, enthusiastic treatment. Key study: DBT versus treatment by community experts (Linehan and colleagues, 2006) Linehan's group recruited 101 women with borderline personality disorder and recent suicidal or self-injurious behaviour, and randomly assigned them to a year of DBT or of therapy with community therapists who had been nominated by local mental health leaders as experts with difficult clients. The comparison therapists were experienced, believed in their own methods and received supervision, which controlled for therapist enthusiasm and attention. Over the treatment year and a further year of follow-up, about 23 percent of the DBT clients made a suicide attempt, against about 46 percent of the expert-treated clients; the DBT group also needed fewer hospital admissions for suicidal thinking, made fewer emergency visits, and dropped out of therapy less often. Both groups improved in depression and suicidal thinking. The conclusion: DBT's advantage was specific to suicidal behaviour and to keeping clients in treatment, and it could not be explained by general therapist expertise alone. Not every trial has favoured DBT. In 2009 Shelley McMain and colleagues in Toronto assigned 180 people with borderline personality disorder to a year of DBT or of general psychiatric management, a structured but less intensive approach developed by John Gunderson. Both groups improved substantially, with no differences in suicidal behaviour, self-harm or other outcomes. The lesson is not that DBT is weak but that any well-organised, committed treatment does far better than the disorganised care these clients usually receive (Chapter 8 develops this theme). Cochrane reviews published in 2012 and 2020 found DBT the most-studied psychotherapy for the disorder, with benefits for self-harm and overall severity, but judged the certainty of the evidence low because many trials were small. In Britain, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommended in 2009 that a comprehensive DBT programme be considered for women with borderline personality disorder for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority. And the skills appear to be an active ingredient: Andrada Neacsiu, Shireen Rizvi and Linehan (2010) found that clients' increasing use of skills partly accounted for their reductions in suicide attempts and depression and their better control of anger. DBT has spread through adaptation. DBT for adolescents (Alec Miller, Jill Rathus and Linehan, 2007) is shorter, brings parents into a multifamily skills group and adds the "walking the middle path" module; a multisite trial by Elizabeth McCauley and colleagues (2018) found that it reduced suicide attempts and self-harm in suicidal adolescents during treatment more than supportive therapy did. There are versions for substance use (aiming at "dialectical abstinence": total commitment to abstinence together with a non-judgemental plan for recovering quickly from a lapse), for binge eating and bulimia , and for PTSD , where Melanie Harned's DBT prolonged exposure protocol adds Edna Foa's prolonged exposure (Chapter 4) once behavioural control is achieved, Linehan's Stage 2 made concrete. Thomas Lynch's radically open DBT turns the model around for people who are over-controlled rather than under-controlled (chronic depression, anorexia nervosa), teaching openness rather than restraint. DBT is one of several evidence-based treatments for borderline personality disorder, and examiners like to match them to their developers. Table 5.19 brings together those from this chapter and Chapter 3. Table 5.19 The main psychological treatments for borderline personality disorder. Treatment Developer Tradition Core idea Dialectical behaviour therapy Marsha Linehan Cognitive-behavioural, third wave Skills plus validation; balance acceptance and change Mentalisation-based treatment Anthony Bateman and Peter Fonagy Psychodynamic, attachment Strengthen the capacity to understand one's own and others' minds Transference-focused psychotherapy Otto Kernberg and colleagues Psychodynamic, object relations Integrate split images of self and others through the transference Schema therapy Jeffrey Young Integrative cognitive Heal early maladaptive schemas; mode work; limited reparenting Cognitive analytic therapy Anthony Ryle Integrative cognitive and analytic Reformulate reciprocal roles and self-states General psychiatric management John Gunderson Generalist psychiatric Good case management, psychoeducation, realistic goals DBT has real limitations. It is intensive and expensive: a full programme needs a trained team, weekly individual and group sessions for a year, telephone availability and a consultation team, which few public services anywhere can provide, least of all in low-resource settings. Most trials involved women in high-income countries, and less is known about men, other cultures and how much of the package is needed; stand-alone skills groups are increasingly used as a lighter alternative. And the effects, while real, are moderate: many clients who no longer harm themselves still struggle with emptiness, loneliness and work, which is why Linehan's later stages, and the goal of a life worth living, matter so much. Clinical link Even if you never work in a full DBT programme, three of its ideas will change how you work with any client in crisis. First, validate before you try to change anything: a client who feels understood can listen; one who feels judged cannot. Second, treat self-harm as a behaviour with functions to be analysed, not as manipulation or "attention-seeking", a phrase DBT therapists avoid because it invalidates real distress and blocks curiosity about what the behaviour is doing for the person. Third, look after yourself and use your team: Linehan built the consultation team into the treatment because working with chronic suicidality is hard, and burnt-out therapists become rigid and invalidating without noticing. Exam trap DBT is a third-wave cognitive-behavioural therapy, along with ACT and MBCT (Section 5.9); psychoanalysis is not. Keep the BPD treatments apart: dialectical behaviour therapy is Linehan's; mentalisation-based treatment is Bateman and Fonagy's; transference-focused psychotherapy is Kernberg's; schema therapy is Young's; cognitive analytic therapy is Ryle's. Know the dates: DBT's first trial was published in 1991 , and its two manuals in 1993 . And remember that DBT's exposure work for trauma is borrowed from Foa's prolonged exposure (Chapter 4), not from Francine Shapiro's EMDR. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Jeffrey Young grouped his 18 early maladaptive schemas into five schema . The schema coping style in which a person acts as if the opposite of the schema were true is called schema . In schema therapy, a moment-to-moment state such as the Detached Protector or the Punitive Parent is called a schema . Partly meeting a client's unmet childhood needs, within the bounds of a professional relationship, is called reparenting. In cognitive analytic therapy, a false "either... or" choice between two extremes is called a . Around the fourth session of cognitive analytic therapy, the therapist reads aloud a letter. Linehan's biosocial theory holds that borderline personality disorder arises from the transaction between emotional vulnerability and an environment. The core mindfulness skills of DBT are drawn mainly from Buddhism. In DBT, the integration of emotion mind and reasonable mind is called mind. DEAR MAN, GIVE and FAST belong to the DBT skills module called effectiveness. Answers: (1) domains, (2) overcompensation, (3) mode, (4) limited, (5) dilemma, (6) reformulation, (7) invalidating, (8) Zen, (9) wise, (10) interpersonal. 5.9 The third wave II: acceptance and commitment therapy and the mindfulness-based therapies Medium yield · 5 Qs In 1978 a young assistant professor at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro was arguing a point in a faculty meeting when his heart began to pound, his throat tightened, and he found that he could not finish his sentence. It was his first panic attack. Over the next few years the panic spread, as panic does: to lectures, to telephone calls, to lifts, to restaurants, until there were whole parts of his life he could no longer enter. The irony was painful. He was a behaviour therapist who knew every technique for reducing anxiety, he tried them all, and the harder he fought the fear the more of his life it took. Then one night, a few years in, he woke in the grip of one of the worst attacks he had ever had. Lying on the carpet of his flat, he made a decision that felt more like surrender than strategy. He would stop running from his own experience. Whatever his mind and body served up, he would let it be there, and he would still move towards the life he wanted. The man on the carpet was Steven C. Hayes (born 1948), whom you met in Section 5.1 as the psychologist who named the third wave. His panic did not vanish that night, but his war with it ended, and out of that decision, and out of two decades of laboratory research on how human language works, grew acceptance and commitment therapy. Section 5.8 showed how Marsha Linehan brought acceptance into behaviour therapy for clients overwhelmed by emotion. This section follows the two other main roads into the third wave: Hayes's therapy, built on a behavioural theory of language, and the mindfulness-based programmes of Jon Kabat-Zinn and of Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale, built on meditation. Their starting points were very different, but they arrived at the idea that Section 5.1 promised: you can change your relationship with a thought without changing the thought itself. Steven Hayes and the origins of ACT Hayes had trained as a behaviour analyst in the tradition of B. F. Skinner, and his early research concerned rules . Animals learn from the consequences of what they do; human beings can also learn from verbal rules ("study hard and you will get in"), which lets us avoid dangers we have never met. But behaviour analysts found in the laboratory that people following a rule become strangely insensitive to what is actually happening, and go on obeying the rule after the real consequences have changed. A depressed client who lives by "I must never let anyone see that I'm struggling" may go on hiding long after hiding has cost him his friends. In the early 1980s Hayes and his student Robert D. Zettle turned these ideas into a treatment, which they first called comprehensive distancing , and Zettle compared it with Beck's cognitive therapy for depression in small studies during that decade. The approach was rethought over the following years and emerged, renamed, in the 1999 book Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: An Experiential Approach to Behavior Change , by Hayes, Kirk D. Strosahl and Kelly G. Wilson . By then Hayes had moved to the University of Nevada, Reno, which became the centre of the movement. acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) is a behaviour therapy that combines acceptance and mindfulness processes with commitment and behaviour-change processes in order to increase a person's psychological flexibility: the capacity to stay in contact with the present moment, unwanted thoughts and feelings included, and to act in the service of chosen values. The name is pronounced as the single word "act", not as three letters, and the choice is deliberate, because the therapy is about action. Hayes's own short summary is the acronym itself: A ccept your reactions and be present, C hoose a valued direction, and T ake action. Notice the family tree. ACT is a behaviour therapy, a grandchild of Skinner's radical behaviourism, even though it speaks of values, meaning and the self in a way that can sound humanistic or even spiritual. Its philosophy of science is called functional contextualism , and two ideas define it. First, the thing to be studied is always an act in its context: a thought, a feeling or a behaviour cannot be understood apart from the situation and the history in which it occurs. Second, the test of an idea is not whether it is "true" in the abstract but whether it works in achieving a stated goal; ACT therapists call this its workability . Here ACT parts company with Beck. Beck's cognitive therapy asks of a thought, "Is it accurate? What is the evidence?" ACT asks, "If you hold on to this thought and let it steer you, does that work? Does it take you towards the life you want?" A thought can be perfectly true ("I might stammer in my viva") and still be unworkable, if it keeps you away from the viva altogether. Put another way, second-wave therapy tries to change the form of a thought (its content) or its frequency . ACT leaves the form alone and changes the thought's function , the effect it has on what the person does, by changing the context in which it occurs. "I can't cope, so stay home" stops being a command once it is experienced as "there's my mind telling me I can't cope again", and the person is free to go out anyway. Exam trap "Acceptance and commitment therapy was developed by..." Steven Hayes and colleagues (Kirk Strosahl and Kelly Wilson; the key book is from 1999). Not Marsha Linehan, who developed DBT (Section 5.8); not Aaron Beck or Albert Ellis, the second-wave founders. ACT is a third-wave behaviour therapy rooted in Skinner's radical behaviourism and in functional contextualism, not a psychoanalytic or humanistic therapy, however much it talks about values. Its earlier name was comprehensive distancing. Relational frame theory: why language makes us suffer Here is the puzzle that drove Hayes's research. A dog that is safe, fed and warm is, as far as anyone can tell, at peace. A human being who is safe, fed and warm can be in agony. She can sit in a comfortable hall at a family wedding and be overwhelmed by grief because the song reminds her of her late father; she can lie awake in a soft bed, tormented by a future that has not happened. Why are human beings the only animals that suffer in this way? Hayes's answer is language, and his account of how language works is relational frame theory (RFT), set out in full in 2001 by Hayes, Dermot Barnes-Holmes and Bryan Roche in Relational Frame Theory: A Post-Skinnerian Account of Human Language and Cognition . The theory grew out of a striking discovery by the American behaviour analyst Murray Sidman (1923 to 2019). In 1971 Sidman worked with a young man with severe intellectual disability who could match spoken words to pictures but could not read. Sidman taught him one new thing: to match spoken words to printed words. Without any further teaching, the young man could now match printed words to pictures, which is reading with understanding. Relations he had never been taught had appeared by themselves. Sidman called the phenomenon stimulus equivalence . Nothing in classical or operant conditioning predicted it, and attempts to demonstrate it convincingly in non-human animals have largely failed. RFT generalises Sidman's finding. Its central claim is that the core of human language and thought is derived relational responding . From early childhood we learn to relate things to one another not only by their physical properties but by social convention, and once we have learned a relation in one direction we derive others that were never taught. A small child offered a choice between five one-rupee coins and a single hundred-rupee note will take the coins, because five things are more than one thing. An older child takes the note, because she has learned a relation ("worth more than") that has nothing to do with size or number. RFT calls such learned patterns of relating relational frames , and three properties define them: Mutual entailment. If A is related to B, a relation from B back to A is derived. Teach a child that the English word "dog" goes with the Hindi word "kutta", and she will, untaught, say "dog" when asked what "kutta" means. Teach her that A is bigger than B, and she knows without being told that B is smaller than A. Combinatorial entailment. If A is related to B and B is related to C, a relation between A and C is derived. If Rahul is taller than Sita and Sita is taller than Ravi, nobody needs to tell you that Rahul is taller than Ravi. Transformation of stimulus functions. The psychological effects of one thing are transferred to the things it is related to. A child bitten by a dog may come to fear not only dogs but the word "dog", the word "kutta" and a picture in a storybook, none of which ever bit anyone. Humans learn many families of frames: coordination (same as), distinction (different from), opposition (opposite of), comparison (more than, better than), hierarchy (part of, a kind of), temporal frames (before, after), causal frames (if, then) and deictic frames (I and you, here and there, now and then), which underlie perspective taking and, as you will see, the sense of self. Now look at what this machinery does to suffering. Because of the transformation of functions, a word, a memory or an image can carry much of the pain of the event it is related to, so the past can be brought into the present at any moment. Because of comparison frames, we can rank ourselves against anyone ("my cousin got into NIMHANS; I am the failure of the family") and against ideals no one could meet. Because of temporal and causal frames, we can live through disasters that have not happened and may never happen. And because language gives us problem solving, we develop a rule that serves us brilliantly in the world outside the skin: if something is unpleasant, work out how to get rid of it, and get rid of it . That rule fixes a leaking tap or a weak exam strategy. Applied to the world inside the skin, to anxiety, grief, unwanted memories and painful thoughts, it backfires, because a private experience is not a leaking tap. The very thought "I must stop feeling anxious" is related to anxiety, and so it brings anxiety with it. From this analysis come the two central ideas of ACT's account of psychological problems. The first is cognitive fusion : the state in which a person's behaviour is dominated by the literal content of his thoughts, so that he responds to words as if they were the things they describe. Fused with the thought "I'm worthless", a person does not experience himself as having a thought about worthlessness; he simply is worthless, and he acts accordingly. In a phrase from the ACT literature, he looks at the world from his thoughts instead of looking at them. The second is experiential avoidance , defined by Hayes and his colleagues in 1996 as the unwillingness to remain in contact with particular private experiences (bodily sensations, emotions, thoughts, memories and urges), together with attempts to change their form or frequency or to escape the situations that bring them on, even when those attempts cause harm. Drinking to blunt grief, avoiding the metro because of panic, pushing intrusive thoughts away, seeking reassurance again and again, sleeping through the afternoon to escape low mood: each brings short-term relief, and each, practised for months, makes the person's life smaller. ACT's slogan for this is blunt: control is the problem, not the solution. Key study: "Don't think of a white bear" (Wegner, Schneider, Carter and White, 1987) In 1863 the Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky challenged his readers to try not to think of a polar bear, predicting that "the cursed thing will come to mind every minute." More than a century later the social psychologist Daniel M. Wegner (1948 to 2013) and his colleagues at Trinity University in Texas put the challenge to the test. Students sat alone and spoke their thoughts aloud for five minutes. Those told to try not to think of a white bear, and to ring a bell whenever they did, rang it on average more than once a minute. Then everyone was invited to think freely about white bears. The students who had first suppressed the thought now thought about the bear more often than students who had been allowed to think about it from the start: a rebound effect . Deliberate suppression, in other words, not only fails but can backfire. Later reviews found the rebound real but smaller and less consistent than this first study suggested. The experiment became a cornerstone of the third wave's case against fighting one's own thoughts. Exam trap Relational frame theory (Hayes, Barnes-Holmes and Roche, 2001) is the theory of language and cognition on which ACT is built. It has nothing to do with REBT despite the shared letter R, and it is not George Kelly's personal construct theory (Section 5.5). DBT and ACT both use acceptance, but RFT belongs to ACT alone. Keep the problem terms and process terms apart: fusion and experiential avoidance are the problems; defusion and acceptance are the remedies. The word is defusion (taking the fuse out), not "diffusion", and it has nothing to do with Erikson's identity diffusion (Developmental book). Psychological flexibility and the hexaflex If fusion and avoidance make people rigid, the aim of therapy is the opposite: psychological flexibility . Hayes and his colleagues define it as the ability to contact the present moment fully, as a conscious human being and without needless defence, and on that basis to persist in or change one's behaviour in the service of chosen values. Read the definition twice and notice what is missing: there is nothing in it about feeling better, thinking positively or getting rid of symptoms. A flexible person may still have panic attacks, or a voice in his head that calls him a failure. What has changed is that these experiences no longer decide what he does. Psychological flexibility is built from six core processes, which ACT therapists draw as the six corners of a hexagon called the hexaflex (Figure 5.10). Each process has an opposite, a pattern of psychological inflexibility, and every process is linked to every other, so that work on one tends to strengthen the rest. The easiest way to understand them is to follow a client through them. Imran is a 27-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru who has had panic attacks for two years. He has stopped taking the metro, turned down a promotion because it meant presenting to clients, keeps a water bottle and his phone in his hand "just in case", and has not visited his mother, who is in hospital across the city, because the journey means a crowded bus. He has tried breathing exercises, herbal remedies, two glasses of whisky every night, hours of searching his symptoms online, and a strict rule never to go anywhere he cannot leave quickly. The ACT therapist begins not with a process but with creative hopelessness . Instead of offering one more technique for controlling panic, she helps Imran list everything he has tried, and then asks of each strategy: How did it work in the short term? How has it worked in the long term? What has it cost you? The answer is painfully clear. Each strategy brought a little relief and a little more shrinking of his life. What is hopeless is not Imran but the agenda of controlling anxiety, and seeing that clearly makes room for something new. The therapist may offer the metaphor of a Chinese finger trap, the woven tube that tightens the harder you pull your fingers out of it and loosens only when you push them in. acceptance , also called willingness, is the alternative. It means actively and openly making room for unwanted thoughts, feelings and sensations, without unnecessary attempts to change their form or frequency. Acceptance is not resignation, not liking, and not grimly putting up with something while waiting for it to go away. Imran might be asked to notice the sensations of panic in his chest as a curious scientist would, describing their size, shape, temperature and movement, and to breathe around them and allow them to be there. ACT draws a useful distinction between clean pain , the natural discomfort that life brings (anxiety before a presentation, grief after a death), and dirty pain , the extra suffering we create by struggling against the clean pain (panic about the anxiety, shame about the panic, a life organised around avoiding both). Acceptance cannot remove the first; it can dissolve much of the second. Its opposite pole on the hexaflex is experiential avoidance. cognitive defusion means stepping back from thoughts so that they are seen for what they are: words and pictures passing through the mind, not commands or truths. Its opposite is fusion. Defusion does not test whether a thought is true. Imran's thought "I'm going to collapse" is not weighed against the evidence, as it would be in Beck's therapy; instead he learns to notice it. He may add a prefix ("I'm having the thought that I'm going to collapse"), thank his mind for the thought ("Thanks, mind, very helpful"), name the story ("Ah, the 'I'll collapse on the bus' story again"), or imagine placing each thought on a leaf and watching it float away down a stream. One of the oldest defusion exercises goes back to the structuralist psychologist Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927), who noted in 1916 that a word repeated aloud quickly loses its meaning. Say "milk" aloud fifty times and it becomes a strange sound; say "I'm weak, I'm weak, I'm weak" fifty times and the same thing happens. The thought is still there, but its grip on behaviour, its function in ACT language, has loosened. contact with the present moment is flexible, non-judgemental attention to what is happening here and now, outside and inside the skin. Its opposite is attention captured by the remembered past and the imagined future: rumination about what went wrong, worry about what might. ACT uses short mindfulness exercises to build it (noticing five things you can see and five you can hear, following the breath, eating a meal with full attention), but in ACT mindfulness is a set of processes, not a meditation programme. self-as-context is the hardest process to explain and perhaps the most important. ACT distinguishes three senses of self. The conceptualised self , or self-as-content , is the story we tell about who we are: "I'm an anxious person", "I'm the weak one in my family", even "I'm the topper". Fusion with this story is a form of inflexibility, because we then defend the story at any cost, and it is the opposite pole of this process. The self-as-process is ongoing awareness of experience as it happens ("right now I'm feeling anxious"). Self-as-context , also called the observing self, is the perspective from which all of this is noticed: the "I" that was there when you were five, is here now and will be there tomorrow, whatever thoughts and feelings pass through. RFT traces it to deictic frames (I, here and now, as distinct from you, there and then). The classic image is the chessboard metaphor . Your thoughts and feelings are the black and white pieces, locked in war, and you have been trying to be a white piece and defeat the black ones. But you are not a piece. You are the board, which holds every piece, is in contact with all of them, and is not harmed by the battle. A gentler version says that you are the sky and thoughts and feelings are the weather. values , in ACT, are freely chosen directions for living, the qualities a person wants his actions to have: being a caring son, a curious learner, a reliable friend. A value is not a goal. A goal can be completed and ticked off (visiting his mother on Sunday); a value can never be finished, only lived, like travelling west by compass, which never brings you to a place called "West". Values work proceeds through questions such as "What do you want your life to stand for?" or "At your eightieth birthday, what would you hope the people you love would say about you?" The opposite pole is a life without clear values, steered by avoidance, by other people's approval or by the rules of the mind. ACT adds that pain and values are two sides of one coin: we hurt where we care. Imran's anxiety about the hospital visit is intense precisely because he loves his mother. committed action , finally, is building larger and larger patterns of effective action linked to those values, step by step, and returning to them after every slip. Its opposite is inaction, impulsivity or persistent avoidance. Here ACT shows its behaviour-therapy roots, using goal setting, skills training and exposure; but exposure is framed differently. Its purpose is not to make the fear go down but to practise willingness in the service of something that matters. Imran's first committed action might be two stops on the metro with his hands free of the water bottle, carrying his fear with him; his larger one is the bus ride to his mother's bedside. ACT's passengers on the bus metaphor captures the stance. Imran is the driver; his thoughts, memories and sensations are noisy, frightening passengers who threaten him whenever he turns towards where he wants to go. They can shout, but they cannot take the wheel, and for all their noise they have never actually been able to hurt him. The Australian ACT trainer Russ Harris summarises them as open up (acceptance and defusion), be present (contact with the present moment and self-as-context) and do what matters (values and committed action). Learn it as three pairs: open up, be present, do what matters. The favourite distractors are other famous lists. Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness are DBT's four skills modules (Section 5.8), sometimes padded with problem solving and behavioural activation (Section 5.10). Cognitive restructuring, exposure, relaxation, homework, role-play and contingency management (rewarding target behaviours) are the standard tools of first- and second-wave CBT (Chapter 4 and Section 5.4). Free association, dream analysis, transference, working through, interpretation and abstinence (the analyst's rule of not gratifying the patient's wishes) are psychoanalytic (Chapter 3). Lists of neurotransmitter systems, DSM clusters or mental faculties are pure filler. Two spellings matter: self-as- context is the healthy process and self-as-content the problem; and it is defusion , not diffusion. Exam trap "ACT aims primarily to increase..." psychological flexibility through six core processes . Not symptom elimination: symptoms often do fall in ACT, but as a by-product, and making them the target would feed the very agenda of control that ACT sets out to drop. Not insight into childhood conflicts (psychodynamic therapy, Chapter 3). Not cognitive disputation of irrational beliefs (Ellis's REBT, Section 5.2); ACT deliberately does not argue with the content of thoughts. ACT in practice: evidence and critics An ACT session looks quite unlike a cognitive therapy session. There are few worksheets and little disputing; there are many metaphors, paradoxes and experiential exercises. The reason follows from RFT. If language is what entangles people, then more argument, which is more language, is likely to entangle them further. A metaphor such as the chessboard does not argue; it lets the client see his situation from a new angle. Courses of ACT range from a single workshop to sixteen or more sessions, and it is delivered individually, in groups and through self-help books. Because its target, flexibility, is the same whatever the diagnosis, ACT is a transdiagnostic therapy: one model is applied across depression, anxiety, psychosis, addiction, chronic pain and workplace stress. Key study: four sessions of ACT for psychosis (Bach and Hayes, 2002) Could a brief, acceptance-based therapy help people with hallucinations and delusions? Patricia Bach and Steven Hayes randomly assigned 80 psychiatric inpatients with positive psychotic symptoms either to their usual treatment or to usual treatment plus just four individual sessions of ACT. The sessions taught patients to notice their voices and unusual beliefs as experiences, without either arguing with them or obeying them, and to act on their own values. Over the next four months the ACT group was rehospitalised at about half the rate of the comparison group. The most interesting finding was this: the ACT patients were more willing to report their symptoms, but they believed them less. The symptoms had not disappeared; their power over behaviour had shrunk, which is exactly what defusion predicts. The trial was small and the follow-up short, and a later replication by Brandon Gaudiano and James Herbert (2006) found smaller effects, but it showed that acceptance could be offered even to people with psychosis. ACT now has hundreds of randomised trials. The Society of Clinical Psychology (Division 12 of the American Psychological Association) lists it as having strong research support for chronic pain, and modest support for depression, mixed anxiety problems, obsessive-compulsive disorder and psychosis. Meta-analyses, such as one by A-Tjak and colleagues in 2015, find ACT clearly better than waiting lists, placebo conditions and treatment as usual, and roughly as effective as established CBT, though not clearly better. Critics have raised three objections. First, in 2008 the Swedish psychologist Lars-Göran Öst reviewed the trials of the third-wave therapies and concluded that their methods were, on average, less rigorous than those of CBT trials from the same period, and that none of the third-wave therapies yet met the formal criteria for an empirically supported treatment. The trials have since improved. Second, Stefan G. Hofmann and Gordon Asmundson (2008) asked whether the third wave was a "new wave or old hat", pointing out that cognitive therapy had always contained acceptance-like elements: Beck himself had described distancing , learning to regard one's thoughts as hypotheses rather than facts, in 1976. On this view ACT is a valuable member of the CBT family, not a revolution against it. Third, relational frame theory is complex, is not accepted by all behaviour analysts, and the link between the laboratory theory and the metaphors used in the clinic is looser than ACT's advocates sometimes suggest.
