In ACT, acceptance applies to private experiences that cannot be removed by deliberate effort (a memory, a surge of fear, grief); it never means accepting situations that can and should be changed. With a woman in an abusive marriage, a student facing ragging or a labourer cheated of wages, an ACT therapist helps the client make room for fear and shame precisely so that she can act: seek safety, complain, or leave. Willingness to feel is what makes committed action possible. What is mindfulness? The word "mindfulness" has now appeared in this chapter several times. It is time to define it properly, because the next two therapies are built on it. The most quoted definition comes from Jon Kabat-Zinn, whose work is described next: mindfulness is "paying attention in a particular way: on purpose, in the present moment, and non-judgementally" (1994). In 2004 a group of researchers led by Scott Bishop proposed a two-part working definition for science. The first part is the self-regulation of attention , so that attention is kept on immediate experience (the breath, a sound, a sensation, a thought as it arises). The second is a particular orientation towards that experience, marked by curiosity, openness and acceptance. The practice is ancient. The Pali word sati , usually translated as mindfulness, means awareness or remembering (remembering to come back to the present), and training in it has been part of Buddhist practice for some 2,500 years, especially in the vipassana ("insight") meditation of the Theravada tradition and in Zen. The clinical programmes deliberately teach it in a secular form, without religious belief, so that anyone can practise it. It helps to know what mindfulness is not. It is not relaxation: a mindful person may become calmer, but the instruction is to notice whatever is present, including tension, rather than to produce a relaxed state. It is not emptying the mind: the mind will wander, again and again, and the practice consists precisely in noticing that it has wandered and bringing it back, kindly and without self-criticism. It is not positive thinking, and it is not an escape from difficulty; if anything, it is a way of turning towards difficulty with steadier attention. How often does the mind wander? In a 2010 study, Matthew A. Killingsworth and Daniel T. Gilbert of Harvard used a smartphone application to ask about 2,250 adults, at random moments, what they were doing and what they were thinking about. Their minds were wandering in nearly half of the samples, and people were generally less happy when their minds wandered than when they attended to what they were doing: "A wandering mind is an unhappy mind," as the paper's title put it. Mindfulness can be practised formally , in set periods of meditation, or informally , by bringing full attention to ordinary activities such as walking, eating or washing dishes. Notice that you have now met it in three different roles. In DBT it is a set of skills, the first of the four skills modules (Section 5.8). In ACT it is a set of four processes within the hexaflex, practised mainly through brief exercises and metaphors. In the mindfulness-based programmes that follow, formal meditation practice is the heart of the treatment itself. Indian context Many Indian clients already know a version of these practices. Vipassana is taught across India in ten-day silent residential courses, most widely through the centres founded by S. N. Goenka (1924 to 2013), the best known of them at Igatpuri in Maharashtra, and in the 1990s Kiran Bedi, then in charge of Delhi's Tihar Jail, introduced vipassana courses for prisoners. The mindful movement used in MBSR is drawn from hatha yoga. Familiarity helps, but it can also mislead: a client may expect a religious practice, or a technique for blanking the mind. A clinician should explain that clinical mindfulness is secular, that it is about noticing rather than stopping thoughts, and that it is offered as a skill, not as a belief. Exam trap Mindfulness is attention to the present moment, on purpose and non-judgementally (Kabat-Zinn). It is not relaxation, not suppression of thoughts and not positive thinking. If a question asks from which tradition DBT's core mindfulness skills are derived, the answer is Zen Buddhism (Section 5.8), not Stoicism (the root of Ellis's and Beck's cognitive idea), psychoanalysis or existentialism. MBSR draws on both Zen and vipassana, and on hatha yoga. Jon Kabat-Zinn and mindfulness-based stress reduction Jon Kabat-Zinn (born 1944) did not set out to be a psychologist. He earned a doctorate in molecular biology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1971, in the laboratory of the Nobel laureate Salvador Luria, and had begun meditating as a student, learning from Zen teachers and later from teachers of vipassana. In 1979, during a meditation retreat, an idea came to him, he later said, in a flash lasting only seconds: he could take the essence of these practices, without the Buddhist framework, to the patients whom hospital medicine had failed to help, people living with chronic pain, heart disease, cancer and the stress of long illness. That same year he founded the Stress Reduction Clinic at the University of Massachusetts Medical School in Worcester. His programme, first called the Stress Reduction and Relaxation Program, became known as mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR). His 1990 book about it, Full Catastrophe Living , took its title from a line in Zorba the Greek , in which Zorba sums up his life as "wife, children, house, everything: the full catastrophe". The point of the title is that the programme is not an escape from life's troubles but a way of living fully in the middle of them. MBSR is an eight-week group course, with classes that can include thirty or more people with a wide range of problems. Participants meet weekly for about two and a half hours, attend one all-day silent session late in the course, and are asked to practise at home for about 45 minutes a day, six days a week, using guided recordings. Four formal practices form its core: The body scan : lying down, the participant moves attention slowly through the body from the toes to the top of the head, noticing each sensation, including pain, without trying to change it. Sitting meditation : attention to the breath, widening later to sounds, thoughts and feelings, returning gently to the breath whenever the mind wanders. Mindful movement : gentle hatha yoga postures, done with attention to the body's sensations and limits rather than to achievement. Walking meditation : walking slowly and attending to each step. The first class famously begins with the raisin exercise . Each participant is given a raisin and asked to examine it as if he had never seen one before: its weight, its wrinkles, the light on its surface, its smell, the faint sound it makes when rolled between the fingers, and finally its taste, chewed slowly. Most people discover how much of ordinary life, eating included, they live on "automatic pilot". Alongside the formal practice, participants practise informally, bringing the same attention to brushing their teeth, drinking their morning chai or waiting at a traffic signal. What does MBSR achieve? In his first published study (1982), Kabat-Zinn followed 51 patients with chronic pain through the programme; many reported large reductions in pain and in mood disturbance, though the study had no control group. In a later trial (1998), patients with the skin disease psoriasis who listened to guided meditation while receiving ultraviolet light treatment cleared their skin significantly faster than patients who received the light treatment alone, an early hint that a mental practice could influence a bodily process. Large reviews have since given a more sober verdict. A meta-analysis of 47 trials by Madhav Goyal and colleagues (2014) found that mindfulness meditation programmes produce small to moderate improvements in anxiety, depression and pain, of about the size seen with antidepressant medication in primary care, but are not better than other active treatments such as exercise. MBSR is best understood as a broad programme for stress, pain and illness, not as a treatment for a particular psychiatric disorder. For a disorder-focused version, the next step was needed. Exam trap MBSR : Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979 , University of Massachusetts Medical School, an eight-week group course for stress, chronic pain and illness. MBCT : Segal, Williams and Teasdale, 2002 , MBSR combined with elements of cognitive therapy to prevent depressive relapse. Do not confuse mindfulness with the relaxation response of the Harvard cardiologist Herbert Benson (1935 to 2022), described in 1975, which aims at physiological relaxation and grew out of research on Transcendental Meditation, a mantra-based technique of concentration. Mindfulness trains open, non-judgemental awareness; relaxation is at most a side effect. Segal, Williams and Teasdale: mindfulness-based cognitive therapy Section 5.3 ended with a warning: when depression lifts, the negative schema does not vanish; it goes quiet and can be reawakened. That warning has numbers attached. Commonly cited estimates are that about half of the people who recover from a first episode of major depression will have another, that the risk rises to about 70 percent after two episodes, and to about 90 percent after three. Antidepressant medication protects against relapse only for as long as it is taken. Cognitive therapy has a lasting protective effect (Section 5.11), but it needs a trained therapist for every client. Could a cheaper, group-based programme be taught to people while they were well, to stop the next episode before it began? That was the question put in the early 1990s, through a research network on depression funded by the MacArthur Foundation in the United States, to three cognitive psychologists: Zindel V. Segal in Toronto, J. Mark G. Williams in Wales (later at Oxford) and John D. Teasdale in Cambridge. Teasdale had already proposed the theory they would build on. His differential activation hypothesis (1988) holds that during an episode of depression, sad mood becomes strongly associated with a particular pattern of negative thinking: global, hopeless and self-critical. After recovery, a small dip in mood (a bad day, a sharp word from a colleague) can reactivate the whole pattern, and the reactivated thinking deepens the mood, which feeds more negative thinking. The ease with which this happens is called cognitive reactivity , and each episode strengthens the association, which is one reason the risk climbs with every episode. What turns a passing sadness into relapse is not the sadness itself but rumination : repetitive, analytical brooding on the mood, its causes and its meaning ("Why am I like this? What is wrong with me? Why can't I snap out of it?"). The three researchers first planned a kind of "attentional control training", a slimmed-down maintenance version of cognitive therapy. Then they visited Kabat-Zinn's clinic in Massachusetts, and what they saw changed the plan. The MBSR instructors were not trying to fix their participants' problems; they practised alongside them and taught a different way of being with difficulty. Segal, Williams and Teasdale came to describe two modes of mind . In the doing mode (or "driven-doing" mode), the mind notices a gap between how things are and how it wants them to be, and works to close the gap. Doing mode is excellent for building a bridge or finishing a syllabus. Applied to a sad mood, it becomes rumination: the mind keeps asking why the gap exists and how to close it, and in doing so keeps the mood alive. In the being mode , the mind allows things to be as they are for the moment, attends to experience directly rather than through concepts, and treats thoughts as passing events. The new therapy would train people to recognise when they had slipped into driven-doing, and to shift deliberately into being. The key skill has a name. decentering is the ability to observe one's thoughts and feelings as temporary events in the mind, rather than as facts or as accurate reflections of oneself. The phrase MBCT participants learn is "thoughts are not facts", which is also the title of one of its sessions. The old thought "I'm a failure" may still appear when the mood dips; a person who can decentre sees it as a familiar visitor, a sign that the old pattern has been touched, and not as the truth about her life. Teasdale called the capacity metacognitive awareness , and his research found that it predicts lower relapse. Figure 5.11 shows the relapse cycle and where MBCT breaks it. 1. Mild sad mood a bad day, a small loss 2. Old patterns wake "I'm a failure again" 3. Rumination "Why am I like this?" 4. Mood deepens risk of a new episode Each turn of the cycle strengthens the link, so risk rises with every episode MBCT steps in: see the thought as a passing mental event; breathing space; move from doing to being mode the relapse cycle where MBCT breaks the cycle Figure 5.11 The relapse cycle described by Teasdale's differential activation hypothesis. In a person who has recovered from depression, an ordinary dip in mood reawakens old negative thinking, rumination deepens the mood, and the cycle can spiral into a new episode. MBCT does not argue with the reawakened thoughts; it teaches the person to notice them as mental events and step out of rumination, at the point marked by the arrow from the MBCT box (named in the legend). The result was mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT), set out in 2002 in Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Depression: A New Approach to Preventing Relapse . MBCT is an eight-week group programme, usually for up to about twelve people, meeting weekly for about two hours, with daily home practice. It keeps the core of MBSR (the raisin exercise, the body scan, sitting meditation and mindful movement) and adds elements of cognitive therapy: teaching about depression and how relapse happens, exercises on the links between thoughts and feelings, lists of activities that bring mastery and pleasure (Section 5.4), and the drawing up of a relapse signature (the person's own early warning signs) and an action plan. What it does not borrow from cognitive therapy is the challenging of thought content. In the first edition of the manual, the eight sessions were: Automatic pilot. Dealing with barriers. Mindfulness of the breath. Staying present. Allowing, or letting be. Thoughts are not facts. How can I best take care of myself? Using what has been learned to deal with future moods. Two exercises show how MBCT works. The first is the signature practice of the programme, the three-minute breathing space , a mini-meditation in three steps that can be used anywhere, especially when mood starts to dip. First, awareness : stop, and acknowledge what is here right now (thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations) without changing it. Second, gathering : narrow attention to the breath in the belly for a minute. Third, expanding : widen attention to the whole body, its posture and the space around it. Teachers describe its shape as an hourglass: wide, narrow, wide again. It is not a way of escaping the mood; it is a way of stepping out of automatic pilot, so that the next step is chosen rather than driven. The second is an exercise from an early session, and you have met its situation before. Participants are asked to imagine walking down a street and seeing someone they know on the other side. They smile and wave; the other person does not respond and walks on. What went through your mind, and what did you feel? Some participants think "She's ignoring me; she must be upset with me" and feel hurt; others think "She didn't see me" and feel nothing much; some think "She's probably preoccupied; I hope she's all right." In Section 5.3 this was the textbook case of arbitrary inference, and a cognitive therapist would go on to examine the evidence. MBCT draws a different lesson. The same event produces different thoughts in different people, and in the same person in different moods (participants in a low mood find themselves far more likely to think "she's ignoring me"). Thoughts, in other words, are interpretations shaped by mood, events in the mind rather than readings of reality. Once that is seen, there is no need to argue with them. Key study: MBCT halves relapse in recurrent depression (Teasdale, Segal, Williams and colleagues, 2000) The first trial of MBCT was run at three sites, in Cambridge, Bangor and Toronto. The researchers recruited 145 people who had recovered from recurrent major depression and were no longer taking antidepressants, and randomly assigned them to treatment as usual or to treatment as usual plus the eight-week MBCT programme. They then followed them for 60 weeks. For participants who had had three or more previous episodes (about three-quarters of the sample), MBCT almost halved the relapse rate: 37 percent relapsed, against 66 percent of those receiving usual care. Surprisingly, for participants with only two previous episodes MBCT made no difference. A replication by Ma and Teasdale (2004) found the same pattern (36 percent against 78 percent). The explanation offered was that in people with many past episodes, relapse is set off less by major life events and more by the autonomous, self-perpetuating cycle of mood and rumination that MBCT targets. Later trials led by Willem Kuyken found MBCT about as protective as continuing maintenance antidepressant medication, and a 2016 pooled analysis of nine trials found that it reduced the risk of relapse over 60 weeks by roughly a third compared with treatments that did not include it. On the strength of this evidence, Britain's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends MBCT for people who are currently well but have a history of recurrent depression, originally those with three or more episodes. Notice who MBCT is for . It is a relapse-prevention programme, taught to people when they are in remission , not a treatment for an acute episode. A person in the depths of depression usually cannot concentrate well enough to meditate, and the programme was never designed for that state. It is not a treatment for acute psychosis (meditation can be destabilising in that state), it does not replace drug treatment for bipolar disorder (mood stabilisers remain the mainstay there), and it is not an exposure treatment for specific phobias (exposure is behaviour therapy, Chapter 4). Its developers are Segal, Williams and Teasdale (2002), not Kabat-Zinn, whose MBSR it adapts. Watch the look-alike abbreviations: MBSR (Kabat-Zinn), MBCT (Segal, Williams and Teasdale), MBT (mentalisation-based treatment, a psychodynamic therapy for borderline personality disorder by Anthony Bateman and Peter Fonagy), and MCT (metacognitive therapy, Adrian Wells, Section 5.10). The mechanism is decentering , not disputing. Clinical link Mindfulness is not harmless for everyone. Intensive meditation can occasionally bring up traumatic memories, dissociation, panic or, rarely, psychotic symptoms. MBCT teachers therefore interview every candidate before the course, usually defer people who are acutely depressed or actively suicidal, take special care with people who have a history of trauma or psychosis, and tell participants that they may step out of any practice at any time. Teachers are also expected to have a personal meditation practice of their own, because the programme is taught from the inside rather than read from a manual. 5.10 The third wave III: compassion, metacognition, the therapeutic relationship and activation Lower yield · not asked yet Return to the student with the mock score of 48 out of 90, who has followed us through this chapter, and imagine four different endings to his story. In the first, he has learned with a thought record that "I'm useless" is a distortion, and still says, "I know it isn't true, but I feel it." In the second, what keeps him awake is not any one worry but his worry about how much he worries. In the third, the problem he brings to therapy shows up in the therapy itself: he never disagrees with his therapist and never asks for anything, just as he never does with anyone else. In the fourth, he has simply stopped doing almost everything, and no amount of talking seems to reach him. Each of these problems gave rise to a third-wave therapy of its own: compassion-focused therapy, metacognitive therapy, functional analytic psychotherapy and behavioural activation. They are smaller families than ACT or DBT, but each is tied to a single founder and a single big idea, which is exactly how examiners like to ask about them. Compassion-focused therapy: when logic is not enough The British clinical psychologist Paul Gilbert (born 1951), working with depressed patients in the National Health Service in Derby, kept hearing the same sentence from people who were doing well in cognitive therapy on paper. They could fill in a thought record, find the evidence against "I'm a failure" and write a sensible balanced alternative. Then they would say: "I can see the logic, but I don't feel any different." Gilbert noticed something about how they said their alternative thoughts to themselves. They often used a cold, flat or impatient inner voice ("Oh, come on, there's evidence you're not a failure, stop being so pathetic"), the same voice they used to attack themselves. The content of the thought had changed; its emotional tone had not. And the patients who said this most were those high in shame and self-criticism , very often people who had grown up with abuse, neglect, bullying or constant criticism, and who had little experience of being soothed by anyone, themselves included. Why should a warm inner voice matter more than a correct argument? Gilbert's answer came from evolutionary psychology and the neuroscience of emotion. Human beings, he argued, have a "tricky brain". Our "old brain" contains emotional and motivational systems that evolved long ago to deal with threats and rewards; our "new brain" adds imagination, language, self-monitoring and rumination. The combination means that we can switch on our threat system with our own thoughts, attacking ourselves as if we were our own predator, and a self-critical thought ("you pathetic idiot") is processed by the body much as an attack from outside would be. None of this is anyone's fault: we did not choose our evolved brains, nor the families and circumstances that shaped them. But, in Gilbert's often-repeated phrase, it is not our fault, but it is our responsibility : once we understand how our minds work, we can choose to train them. Hearing this is itself a relief to people drowning in shame. compassion-focused therapy (CFT) is an integrative therapy, developed by Gilbert from the 1990s onwards and set out in The Compassionate Mind (2009) and Compassion Focused Therapy (2010), that helps people high in shame and self-criticism to develop compassion for themselves and others, so that they can feel safe and soothed and not merely think differently. Gilbert defines compassion as "a sensitivity to suffering in self and others, with a commitment to try to alleviate and prevent it". The definition has two parts: the courage to turn towards suffering rather than away from it, and the wisdom to do something helpful about it. Compassion in this sense is not softness, self-pity or letting oneself off the hook; Gilbert likes to compare it with the courage of a firefighter walking into a burning building. In 2006 he founded the Compassionate Mind Foundation, a charity that trains therapists in the approach. Three emotion-regulation systems and compassionate mind training At the centre of CFT is a simple model of emotion, usually drawn as three circles (Figure 5.12). Gilbert proposed that human emotions are organised by three interacting emotion-regulation systems , each with its own evolutionary job: The threat and self-protection system detects danger and drives us to protect ourselves. Its emotions are anxiety, anger and disgust, and its behaviours are fight, flight, freezing and submission. It is fast and works on the principle "better safe than sorry", so it readily fires at false alarms. The drive, excitement and resource-seeking system motivates us to pursue the things we need and want: food, status, achievement, success. Its feelings are wanting, excitement and the pleasure of getting. The soothing, contentment and safeness system operates when we are neither threatened nor striving. Its feelings are calm, contentment, safeness and connection, and it is switched on above all by kindness and care, in the way an infant is calmed by a parent's voice and touch. Gilbert linked the systems loosely with different brain chemistry (stress hormones for threat, dopamine for drive, oxytocin and endorphins for soothing), a simplification he himself acknowledges. The clinical point is about balance. In people high in shame and self-criticism the threat system is overactive, the drive system is often recruited into its service ("I must achieve or I'll be rejected"), and the soothing system is underdeveloped, because it was rarely switched on in childhood. Such a person can work hard and succeed and still never feel safe. Threat system detect and protect anxiety, anger, disgust fight, flight, freeze fuelled by self-attack Drive system seek and achieve wanting, excitement pleasure of getting goals, status, success Soothing system rest and connect calm, contentment safeness, being cared for grown by kindness In shame and harsh self-criticism, threat is overactive and soothing is weak. CFT trains the soothing system so it can calm threat and balance drive. Figure 5.12 Paul Gilbert's three emotion-regulation systems, the basis of compassion-focused therapy. The arrows show the soothing system calming the threat system and balancing the drive system. In people high in shame and self-criticism the threat system dominates and soothing is underdeveloped, so CFT sets out to strengthen it. The aim of CFT is therefore to build up the soothing system, so that it can calm the threat system and balance the drive system. Its methods are called compassionate mind training (CMT). They begin with the body: soothing rhythm breathing , slowing the breath to a gentle, steady rhythm, together with a friendly facial expression and a warm tone of voice. They use imagery: a safe place ; an imagined ideal compassionate other who is wise, strong and warm and wholly on one's side; and, most important, the compassionate self , which the client practises being much as an actor practises a role, imagining himself with those same qualities. They include compassionate letter writing , in which the client writes to himself about a difficulty in the voice of the compassionate self. And they include chair work, in which the client gives voice to the inner critic and then answers it from the compassionate self. Gilbert describes three flows of compassion : from oneself to others, from others to oneself, and from oneself to oneself. People high in self-criticism often find the second and third the hardest, and Gilbert and his colleagues (2011) developed scales to measure these fears of compassion ("If I'm kind to myself I'll become lazy"; "I don't deserve kindness"; "If I let my guard down, I'll fall apart"). Consider Priya, a 30-year-old chartered accountant in Pune, whose inner critic speaks in a voice she recognises as her father's: "You're pathetic. Anyone else would have finished by now." Cognitive therapy helped her see that the criticism was distorted, but she still felt it. Her CFT therapist begins by asking what the critic is for : what does it fear would happen if it stopped? Priya's answer ("I'd become lazy and everyone would see I'm not good enough") reveals the critic as a threat-system safety strategy, an anxious attempt to protect her from rejection. The therapist then teaches her to tell shame-based self-attack , which looks backwards, punishes and frightens (like a bullying teacher), from compassionate self-correction , which looks forwards, encourages and focuses on growth (like a good coach). Over the following weeks Priya practises soothing rhythm breathing, builds an image of her compassionate self, and writes letters to herself about the mistakes at work that used to keep her awake. The critic does not vanish, but it no longer has the last word. CFT is often confused with a related idea. The American psychologist Kristin Neff introduced the concept of self-compassion in 2003, together with a Self-Compassion Scale to measure it. She described it as three components, each with an opposite: self-kindness rather than self-judgement, common humanity (seeing one's suffering as part of the shared human condition) rather than isolation, and mindfulness rather than over-identification with painful thoughts. Neff's work began as a research construct and a basis for self-help programmes; Gilbert's is a therapy built on an evolutionary model. The evidence for CFT itself is promising but still thin: early reviews found benefits, particularly for people high in self-criticism, but few large, rigorous trials. Exam trap Compassion-focused therapy and compassionate mind training: Paul Gilbert . Its three systems are threat, drive and soothing . Do not confuse them with three other famous trios: the three response systems of fear (verbal or cognitive, physiological and behavioural) described by Peter J. Lang in 1968; DBT's three states of mind (reasonable mind, emotion mind and wise mind; Section 5.8); or Neff's three components of self-compassion (self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness). And do not confuse the two Gilberts: Paul Gilbert of CFT is a British clinical psychologist; Daniel Gilbert, of the mind-wandering study in Section 5.9, is a Harvard social psychologist who studies happiness and how people predict their feelings. Adrian Wells and metacognitive therapy Nearly everyone has had the thought "What if I have cancer?" or "Maybe I'm a failure." Most people have it, shrug and move on; a few go on to develop an anxiety disorder or depression. Beck's explanation of the difference lay in the content of the thought and the beliefs behind it. The British clinical psychologist Adrian Wells , of the University of Manchester, proposed a different answer. What matters, he argued, is not what a person thinks but how he responds to his thinking: whether a passing thought is left alone, or seized on and turned into hours of worry and brooding. With Gerald Matthews he set out the theory in 1994 as the self-regulatory executive function (S-REF) model, and in 2009 he described the treatment in Metacognitive Therapy for Anxiety and Depression . Metacognition means thinking about thinking: the knowledge, beliefs and processes by which we monitor, interpret and control our own thoughts (the term was introduced into developmental psychology by John H. Flavell in the 1970s; Developmental book). metacognitive therapy (MCT) is a treatment that aims to change these metacognitive beliefs and processes rather than the content of the client's thoughts. Its central concept is the cognitive attentional syndrome (CAS), a style of thinking that Wells believes is common to most psychological disorders. It has three parts: Perseverative thinking : worry (repetitive "what if" thinking about the future) and rumination (repetitive "why" thinking about the past and one's moods). Threat monitoring : attention locked on to possible danger, such as a health-anxious person scanning his body for symptoms or a socially anxious person monitoring how she comes across. Unhelpful coping behaviours : thought suppression, avoidance, reassurance seeking, checking and the use of alcohol or drugs, all of which keep the problem going. The CAS, in turn, is driven by two kinds of metacognitive belief. Positive metacognitive beliefs hold that the CAS is useful: "Worrying helps me prepare for the worst", "If I analyse why I feel low, I'll find the answer", "Staying alert to danger keeps me safe". These set the process going. Negative metacognitive beliefs hold that thinking is uncontrollable or dangerous: "My worrying is out of control", "Worrying this much will give me a heart attack or make me go mad". These make the person feel trapped, and anxious about the thinking itself. Wells's model of generalised anxiety disorder (1995) shows the two working together (the disorder itself is described in the Disorders book). Lakshmi, a 45-year-old teacher in Chennai, has a son who rides a motorbike to college. Her Type 1 worry is about the outside world: "What if he has an accident? What if he is lying on the road and nobody helps him?" She believes that worrying keeps him safe (a positive belief), so she worries. Then comes Type 2 worry , worry about worry, or meta-worry : "I can't stop this; it's going to damage my heart; I'm going mad." Type 2 worry is what turns a mother's ordinary concern into a disorder. A cognitive therapist might examine the evidence about the risk of road accidents. A metacognitive therapist does not discuss the motorbike at all; she targets Lakshmi's beliefs about worrying. "What would happen if you stopped worrying?" Typical techniques Examining the evidence, decatastrophising Worry postponement, detached mindfulness, attention training Aim A more realistic appraisal of risk Less worry of any content; flexible attention MCT's techniques follow from the model. In worry postponement , Lakshmi is asked, whenever a worry is triggered, to notice it and put off engaging with it until a fixed fifteen-minute "worry time" in the evening; many clients find, when the time comes, that they no longer need it, which is direct evidence against the belief that worry is uncontrollable. The therapist also runs experiments in the session ("Try as hard as you can to worry yourself into a heart attack, right now") to disconfirm the belief that worry is dangerous, and examines the positive beliefs (has worrying ever actually kept her son safe?). Two attentional techniques are distinctive. detached mindfulness , a term coined by Wells and Matthews, means being aware of a thought as an event in the mind while neither engaging with it (no analysing, arguing or worrying) nor trying to push it away, like watching a train pass through a station without getting on board. It is practised with brief exercises such as the tiger task : imagine a tiger and simply watch what it does, without trying to make it do anything. It is not meditation, involves no focus on the breath, and takes minutes rather than weeks. The attention training technique (ATT; Wells, 1990) is a twelve-minute listening exercise. The client hears several sounds at once (a ticking clock, traffic, a voice, a tapping) coming from different places, and practises first focusing on one sound at a time, then switching rapidly between them, and finally spreading attention across all of them together. Its purpose is to strengthen flexible control of attention and to loosen the grip of self-focused attention. It is not distraction: thoughts and feelings are allowed to stay in the background, like more noise. Trials, many of them from Wells's own group, report large effects in generalised anxiety disorder, depression, post-traumatic stress and obsessive-compulsive disorder, and a 2018 meta-analysis found MCT more effective than waiting lists and, in head-to-head comparisons, somewhat more effective than CBT. The trials are few and small, however, and independent replication is still needed before strong conclusions can be drawn. Exam trap Metacognitive therapy: Adrian Wells . Its core concept is the cognitive attentional syndrome (worry and rumination, threat monitoring and unhelpful coping), driven by positive and negative metacognitive beliefs ; Type 2 worry is worry about worry. MCT changes how a person relates to thinking, not what he thinks, so it is not Beck's content-focused therapy, and its detached mindfulness is not the meditation of MBCT. Beware the double acronym: metacognitive training (also abbreviated MCT), developed by Steffen Moritz and Todd S. Woodward (2007), is a group programme for people with psychosis that teaches them to recognise cognitive biases such as jumping to conclusions. Same letters, different treatment. Functional analytic psychotherapy: the relationship as the laboratory Most therapy is talk about behaviour that happened somewhere else: the argument at home last week, the panic in the metro on Monday. Behaviourists know that change is fastest when a behaviour is reinforced immediately, as it happens. So what if the client's problem could be caught happening right there in the room? In the 1980s two psychologists in Seattle, Robert J. Kohlenberg and Mavis Tsai , noticed that a few of their behaviour therapy clients improved far more than the techniques used could explain, and that these were the clients with whom an intense and genuine relationship had formed. They explained the observation in strictly behavioural terms in Functional Analytic Psychotherapy: Creating Intense and Curative Therapeutic Relationships (1991). functional analytic psychotherapy (FAP) is a behaviour therapy, grounded in Skinner's radical behaviourism, that uses the therapeutic relationship as a live social environment in which the client's interpersonal problems actually occur, so that the therapist can notice, evoke and naturally reinforce improvements at the moment they happen. Its central concept is that of clinically relevant behaviours (CRBs), of which there are three kinds: CRB1 : occurrences of the client's problem in the session itself. A client who complains that nobody gets close to him keeps the therapist at a distance with jokes, changes the subject whenever feelings arise, or arrives late. CRB2 : improvements occurring in the session. The same client says, for the first time, "That hurt when you said it." CRB3 : the client's own interpretations of his behaviour and its causes. "I notice I go quiet whenever I feel criticised, just as I did with my father." The therapist's work is summarised in five rules . Rule 1: watch for CRBs. Rule 2: evoke CRBs, by creating situations in therapy that call for the client's problem behaviours and their improvements. Rule 3: reinforce CRB2s naturally. Rule 4: notice the effect of your own behaviour on the client, to check that what you intended as reinforcement actually works as reinforcement. Rule 5: offer functional interpretations and help the client to generalise what he has learned to his life outside. "Naturally" in Rule 3 is the key word. Behaviour analysts distinguish arbitrary reinforcement (a token, a sweet, "good job") from natural reinforcement , the consequence the behaviour would earn in ordinary life. When a client who never asks for anything finally asks to change his appointment time, the natural reinforcer is that the therapist genuinely changes it and is visibly glad to; praise for "being assertive" would be arbitrary, and it would not carry over to his marriage. Tsai and her colleagues later summarised the therapist's stance in three words: awareness, courage and love . Sameer, a 32-year-old bank officer in Lucknow, comes to therapy because he cannot tell his wife or his manager what he wants. In the session he agrees with everything and ends every other sentence with "whatever you think is best, ma'am." A FAP therapist sees this as CRB1 (Rule 1) and gently evokes the alternative (Rule 2): "I've noticed you've agreed with everything I've suggested. Is there anything about how we work that you'd like to be different?" After a long pause Sameer says that the Saturday appointment is hard for him. The therapist thanks him warmly and moves the appointment (Rule 3), watches whether he speaks up more in the following weeks (Rule 4), and helps him see the link between what happened in the room and what happens at home (Rule 5). FAP's evidence is modest: mostly case studies and small trials, and its use as an enhancement of other therapies, such as FAP-enhanced cognitive therapy for depression (Kohlenberg and colleagues, 2002). Because it encourages an intense relationship, it places great weight on the therapist's self-awareness, on clear ethical boundaries and on supervision. Exam trap Functional analytic psychotherapy: Robert Kohlenberg and Mavis Tsai (1991). Its terms are CRB1 (the problem in the session), CRB2 (improvement in the session) and CRB3 (the client's own functional interpretations), and its method is natural reinforcement of improvements within the relationship. Its interest in what happens between client and therapist resembles the psychodynamic idea of transference (Chapter 3), but FAP explains it by reinforcement, not by unconscious repetition. Nor does FAP claim that the relationship alone produces change, which is closer to Carl Rogers's position (Chapter 6); for FAP the relationship is the setting in which reinforcement shapes new behaviour. And do not confuse FAP with functional analysis , the antecedent-behaviour-consequence assessment of behaviour therapy (Chapter 4), which FAP uses but which is not itself a therapy. Behavioural activation: back to behaviour Behavioural activation is the oldest idea in this section and, in a sense, the newest therapy. Its roots lie in two behavioural accounts of depression from the early 1970s. In 1973 Charles B. Ferster (1922 to 1981), who had worked with Skinner on schedules of reinforcement, described depression as a reduced frequency of positively reinforced behaviour combined with an increase in avoidance and escape. In 1974 Peter M. Lewinsohn , at the University of Oregon, gave the idea its best-known form. Depression, he proposed, results from a low rate of response-contingent positive reinforcement (RCPR): rewards that follow from one's own actions, such as a friend's laugh at your joke or the satisfaction of finishing a chapter. RCPR can be low for three reasons: because few events are potentially rewarding for the person, because the environment offers few rewards (after a bereavement, a job loss or a move to a strange city), or because the person lacks the skills, social skills especially, to obtain the rewards that are available. Low mood then lowers activity, which lowers reinforcement further, in a downward spiral. Lewinsohn's group developed the Pleasant Events Schedule, a long list of activities that people rate for how often they do them and how much they enjoy them, and in 1984 a structured, classroom-style Coping with Depression Course . Beck took the same methods into cognitive therapy (Section 5.4), but with a different purpose: there, activity scheduling and graded tasks served chiefly to produce evidence against beliefs such as "I can't do anything." Was the cognitive work actually necessary? In the 1990s Neil S. Jacobson (1949 to 1999) and his colleagues at the University of Washington in Seattle set out to find out. Their component analysis (1996), told in full in Section 5.11 (Table 5.26), gave 150 depressed outpatients behavioural activation alone, behavioural activation plus work on automatic thoughts, or the full cognitive therapy package, and all three did equally well, with no difference in relapse two years later. If activation alone did as well as the full package, perhaps it deserved to be a therapy in its own right. Jacobson died in 1999, but his colleagues carried the idea forward. The result is behavioural activation (BA): a structured, brief treatment for depression that aims to increase contact with sources of reward and to reduce avoidance and withdrawal, by scheduling and gradually increasing valued and rewarding activities, guided by a functional analysis of what the person's behaviour is doing for him. The modern version was set out by Christopher R. Martell , Michael E. Addis and Jacobson in Depression in Context: Strategies for Guided Action (2001). It works from the outside in : the client acts according to a plan rather than according to his mood, instead of waiting until he feels like it. Avoidance is analysed with two acronyms. In a TRAP , a t rigger (a quarrel at work) produces a r esponse (feeling low and tired), which leads to an a voidance p attern (going to bed at six and skipping dinner with friends) that brings relief now and deeper depression later. The client learns to get back on TRAC : the same t rigger and r esponse, followed by a lternative c oping (a short walk and the dinner, even though he does not feel like it). Rumination itself is treated as a behaviour, an avoidant one, to be noticed and replaced with action. A related short form, the brief behavioural activation treatment for depression of Carl Lejuez, Derek Hopko and colleagues (2001), builds the activity plan directly from the client's values, much as ACT does. Does it work? In a large Seattle trial led by Sona Dimidjian (2006), 241 adults with major depression were randomly assigned to BA, cognitive therapy, antidepressant medication or placebo pills. Among the more severely depressed patients, BA did as well as medication and better than cognitive therapy. And a large English trial, COBRA (Section 5.11), found that junior mental health workers could deliver BA as effectively as qualified therapists delivered CBT, and more cheaply. Because it is simple to teach, BA has become one of the most important tools for taking psychological treatment beyond specialist clinics. Indian context India has very few clinical psychologists for its population, and one answer is task sharing : training lay counsellors to deliver simple, structured psychological treatments under supervision. The best-known Indian example is the Healthy Activity Program (HAP), a brief treatment for depression built on behavioural activation, developed by the Goa-based organisation Sangath with Vikram Patel and colleagues (Section 5.11). In the PREMIUM trial in primary health care in Goa, published in 2017, lay counsellors delivering HAP to adults with moderately severe to severe depression achieved better outcomes than enhanced usual care, at low cost. It is a powerful demonstration that behavioural activation can travel. Why is behavioural activation counted as third wave, when its techniques are older than Beck's therapy? Hayes included it because of its contextual stance: it asks what a behaviour does for the person in his context (its function) rather than what his thoughts contain, and it deliberately makes no attempt to change thoughts at all. Exam trap Depression maintained by "a deficiency of reinforcement in the environment" is Peter Lewinsohn's behavioural account (1974), stated as a low rate of response-contingent positive reinforcement. It is not Beck's cognitive triad (Section 5.3), not Freud's repressed conflicts and not Bowlby's insecure attachment; Martin Seligman's learned helplessness is yet another account (Disorders book). Activity scheduling inside Beck's therapy is used to test beliefs; behavioural activation as a stand-alone therapy (Jacobson, Martell and Addis) aims to restore reward and reduce avoidance, and does not target thoughts. Do not confuse it with the behavioural activation system (BAS) of Jeffrey Gray's reinforcement sensitivity theory, a brain system for sensitivity to reward (Personality and Physiological books). The third wave in perspective Step back and look at the whole family, from DBT in Section 5.8 to behavioural activation (Table 5.24). Its members differ in their founders, their theories and their favourite techniques, but several threads run through them. They pay more attention to a person's relationship with thoughts and feelings than to their content. They make wide use of acceptance and mindfulness . They ask what a behaviour or a thought does (its function in context) rather than whether it is true. They give a central place to values and to a meaningful life, not only to reducing symptoms. Several of them (DBT, FAP and CFT) put the therapeutic relationship itself near the centre of change. And most are transdiagnostic , applying one model across many disorders. You met the sceptics in Section 5.9: Öst on the quality of the early trials, and Hofmann and Asmundson on the overlap with cognitive therapy. Look back across this chapter and you can see their point. Beck's "distancing" is close to MBCT's decentering; Beck's activity scheduling is the seed of behavioural activation; exposure runs through ACT's committed action; and Ellis's unconditional self-acceptance anticipates CFT. Interestingly, Hayes himself, together with Hofmann, has since moved away from talk of waves and named packages, arguing instead for process-based therapy : identifying the specific, evidence-based processes of change (such as decentering, flexibility or reappraisal) that matter for a particular person, whichever school they come from. Perhaps the most lasting contribution of the third wave is that it changed the questions therapists ask. Alongside "Is this thought true?" they now also ask "What is this thought doing to you, and what do you want your life to be about?" Whether the third wave works as well as its advocates claim is part of the larger question taken up in Section 5.11. Exam trap "Third-wave CBT includes all EXCEPT..." The third wave includes DBT, ACT, MBCT (and MBSR, from which it grew), CFT, MCT, FAP and behavioural activation. Psychoanalysis is not a wave of CBT at all (Chapter 3). REBT and Beck's cognitive therapy are second wave; systematic desensitisation, token economies and contingency management are first wave (Chapter 4). Medium yield · 2 Qs Back in Section 5.1 you read that CBT is the most researched form of psychotherapy in the world. You have now met most of the family, from Ellis's disputing to Linehan's skills groups. So ask the question that a sceptical patient, a hospital administrator or an interview panel will ask you: does it actually work, for whom, compared with what, and why? This section surveys the big reviews and the trials that pitted CBT against medication, describes the advantage that shows itself only after treatment ends, asks which ingredients do the work, and follows CBT into whole health systems, in England and in India, including by computer and smartphone. The criticisms come too, because a clinician who can only praise a treatment does not yet understand it. The evidence base: what the reviews say Why is there so much research on CBT in particular? Partly because of the features you met in Section 5.1. CBT is brief, so a trial can finish in months rather than years. It is manualised: since Beck's 1979 book, therapists in a trial can be trained to deliver the same treatment, and recordings of their sessions can be rated to check that they did. And it measures: a therapy that rates symptoms every week produces outcome data as a by-product. A therapy that is brief, standardised and measured is easy to test (Chapter 8 explains how trials, meta-analyses and effect sizes work). That cuts both ways: it explains why CBT has more evidence than any other therapy, and why critics warn that more evidence is not the same as a better treatment. By the early 2000s there were so many trials, and so many meta-analyses of those trials, that researchers began to write reviews of the meta-analyses themselves. The most cited is by Andrew C. Butler , Jason Chapman, Evan Forman and Aaron Beck (2006), who gathered 16 methodologically rigorous meta-analyses covering several hundred studies. Their conclusions are worth knowing almost word for word. CBT produced large effects for unipolar depression, generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder with or without agoraphobia, social phobia, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and depressive and anxiety disorders in childhood. It produced moderate effects for marital distress, anger, childhood somatic disorders and chronic pain. It was somewhat superior to antidepressants for adult depression, and about as effective as behaviour therapy for adult depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). For bulimia nervosa and schizophrenia the effects were large but uncontrolled , that is, measured from before to after treatment without a comparison group, which always flatters a treatment. Six years later Stefan G. Hofmann (Section 5.9) and his colleagues (2012) reviewed 269 meta-analyses and reached a similar verdict: the support was strongest for the anxiety disorders, somatoform disorders, bulimia, anger control problems and general stress. Guideline bodies have drawn the practical conclusion. The World Health Organization (WHO) and England's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) , which writes the treatment guidelines for the National Health Service (NHS), recommend CBT, or a therapy built on it, as a first-line psychological treatment for most of the common mental disorders. Table 5.25 brings the picture together, problem by problem. Read it with two cautions. "Strong evidence" means that CBT clearly beats waiting lists and placebo conditions and usually matches the best alternatives; it does not mean that every patient recovers. And for some disorders CBT is an addition to medication, not a replacement for it. The clearest case is schizophrenia, where antipsychotic medication is the front-line treatment and CBT for psychosis (Section 5.6) is added to reduce distress, persisting symptoms and the risk of relapse. Bipolar disorder, where CBT supports mood stabilisers, is another. Table 5.25 Where CBT stands: the evidence, problem by problem. CBT , not humanistic therapy (which works through the relationship and the client's own growth, Chapter 6), psychoanalysis (which works through unconscious conflict and insight, Chapter 3) or play therapy (which helps young children express and work through their difficulties in play, Chapter 10). In a reading-comprehension stem that says CBT "rests on the premise that distorted thinking patterns sustain emotional distress" and that trials "support its effectiveness across a range of disorders", the central idea is that CBT works by changing the distorted thoughts that maintain distress . The bait is the overstatement "CBT cures every psychological disorder": no therapy does, and the passage never says so. Similarly, the front-line treatment for schizophrenia is antipsychotic medication ; CBT, social skills training and stress management are added to it, not used instead of it. For survivors of sexual assault and other trauma, the treatments with the strongest evidence are trauma-focused CBT (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy and cognitive therapy for PTSD, Section 5.6) and EMDR (Francine Shapiro's method, Chapter 4), recommended first-line by the WHO (2013) and NICE (2018). A practice mock keys "psychodynamic psychotherapy, trauma-focused CBT and EMDR" as the most effective set: choose it, as the only option containing both evidence-based treatments, but know that psychodynamic therapy is not a first-line treatment for PTSD. Asked which is not commonly used for survivors, the expected answer is interpersonal psychotherapy , which was built for depression (Section 3.7). CBT against medication: the landmark trials Section 5.3 told the story of the first head-to-head trial: in 1977 Rush, Beck, Kovacs and Hollon found that cognitive therapy beat the antidepressant imipramine. A single small trial run by the therapy's own inventors could not settle the matter. In the 1980s the United States National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) set out to settle it properly in its Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program (TDCRP), the largest and most carefully controlled psychotherapy trial yet attempted. Key study: the NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program (Elkin and colleagues, 1989) The question. Under the most careful conditions anyone had yet arranged, how do two short psychotherapies compare with an antidepressant? The method. At three university sites (Pittsburgh, George Washington University and Oklahoma), about 250 outpatients with major depression were randomly assigned to 16 weeks of one of four treatments: CBT; interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT, Klerman and Weissman's therapy of grief, role disputes, role transitions and interpersonal deficits, Section 3.7); imipramine plus clinical management; or a placebo pill plus clinical management. "Clinical management" meant brief weekly meetings with a psychiatrist who offered support and encouragement, so the placebo group was in fact receiving a minimal supportive therapy. Therapists followed manuals and were trained and supervised, the treatment sites were independent of the therapies' developers, and the study was coordinated at the NIMH by Irene Elkin . Chapter 8 (Section 8.8) treats it as a landmark of research design. The results. All four groups improved, and the overall differences were small. The treatments fell into a consistent order (imipramine best, placebo worst, the two psychotherapies in between and closer to imipramine), but for the less severely depressed there were no significant differences at all, placebo included. Among the more severely depressed, imipramine did clearly better than placebo, IPT showed some evidence of effectiveness, and CBT did not do significantly better than placebo. At an 18-month follow-up, relapse was common in every condition and the treatments did not differ significantly. The criticism. CBT's supporters replied that the trial's cognitive therapists were less experienced than those at Beck's centre and that CBT fared better at some sites than at others: the trial had tested CBT as delivered, not CBT at its best. The severe-depression finding was taken seriously; for some years American practice guidelines advised that severely depressed patients needed medication. Robert J. DeRubeis and his colleagues (1999) challenged that advice with a "mega-analysis", pooling the raw data on severely depressed patients from four randomised trials, the TDCRP among them. Across the four, CBT did as well as medication. A major test came from a trial run jointly at the University of Pennsylvania and Vanderbilt University (DeRubeis, Steven D. Hollon and colleagues, 2005). About 240 moderately to severely depressed outpatients received 16 weeks of cognitive therapy, the antidepressant paroxetine, or (for the first eight weeks) a placebo pill. Both active treatments beat placebo, and by 16 weeks cognitive therapy had matched medication where the therapists were experienced (where they were less so, it lagged). The accepted conclusion: in the acute treatment of depression, well-delivered CBT and antidepressants are about equally effective, and combining them adds a modest further benefit, especially in severe and chronic depression. Anxiety showed the same pattern, with a twist. In a multisite trial of panic disorder, David Barlow, Jack Gorman, Katherine Shear and Scott Woods (2000) compared CBT, imipramine, their combination and placebo conditions. CBT and imipramine both beat placebo and did about equally well, and the combination added little. But six months after treatment stopped, the patients who had received CBT without the drug had kept their gains better than those who had been on imipramine. Adolescents are a partial exception. In the Treatment for Adolescents with Depression Study (TADS, 2004), 12 weeks of fluoxetine plus CBT helped about 71 percent of depressed teenagers, fluoxetine alone about 61 percent, CBT alone about 43 percent and placebo about 35 percent; CBT alone caught up with the other active treatments only by 36 weeks. A rough summary of four decades: medication often works a little faster, and CBT tends to last. Exam trap The NIMH TDCRP compared exactly four conditions: CBT, interpersonal psychotherapy, imipramine plus clinical management and placebo plus clinical management . It did not include psychoanalysis, behaviour therapy or fluoxetine, and it was coordinated by Irene Elkin, not by Beck. Its headline was rough equivalence, with imipramine best for the severely depressed; it did not show CBT beating medication. The trial in which cognitive therapy beat imipramine was the earlier, smaller one by Rush, Beck, Kovacs and Hollon (1977), and the trial that restored CBT's standing for moderate to severe depression was DeRubeis, Hollon and colleagues (2005). The enduring effect: CBT and relapse If CBT and medication are roughly equal while treatment lasts, what is the special case for CBT? It lies in what happens after treatment ends. Depression tends to come back. A relapse is the return of symptoms soon after improvement, within the same episode; a recurrence is a new episode after a period of full recovery. Antidepressants protect against relapse, but mainly for as long as they are taken: as many as half of patients who stop their medication within the first few months of recovering relapse. CBT behaves differently. Its protection outlasts the treatment, and this is called the enduring effect of CBT. An early summary came from a meta-analysis of cognitive therapy for depression by Gloaguen, Cottraux, Cucherat and Blackburn (1998): in the studies that followed patients up after treatment, relapse after cognitive therapy was roughly half as common as after antidepressants. The clearest evidence came from the follow-up phase of the Pennsylvania and Vanderbilt trial (Hollon and colleagues, 2005). Patients who had responded to medication were either kept on it or switched, without knowing it, to a placebo pill; patients who had responded to cognitive therapy simply stopped, with up to three booster sessions allowed during the year. Figure 5.13 shows what happened over the next twelve months. In the second year, when all treatment had stopped, the difference grew: about 17 percent of the former cognitive therapy patients had a recurrence, against about 54 percent of those who had stayed on medication through the first year. 0 25 50 75 100 Relapsed within 12 months (%) 31% 47% 76% Prior cognitive therapy (stopped) Medication continued Medication replaced by placebo Figure 5.13 Relapse in the year after successful treatment of depression (Hollon and colleagues, 2005; percentages rounded). Patients whose medication was quietly replaced by placebo relapsed most often; patients who had stopped cognitive therapy did at least as well as those who stayed on their medication. This is the enduring effect. A related strategy treats the two approaches as relay runners rather than rivals. In sequential treatment , developed by the Italian psychiatrist Giovanni A. Fava and his colleagues, patients who have recovered on antidepressants receive a course of CBT aimed at their residual symptoms while the medication is slowly withdrawn. Six years later, about 40 percent of the CBT group had suffered a recurrence, against about 90 percent of a comparison group given standard clinical management (Fava and colleagues, 2004). Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT, Section 5.9) was designed from the start for the same purpose: preventing relapse in people with recurrent depression. Why should a course of talking last when a course of tablets does not? Three explanations are offered, and they are not exclusive. The first is skills : the patient leaves with a toolkit (catching automatic thoughts, scheduling activity, testing predictions) and keeps using it; Strunk, DeRubeis and colleagues (2007) found that patients who had acquired more cognitive therapy skills were less likely to relapse. The second is schema change : if therapy has softened the core belief (Section 5.4), the next stress finds less to trigger. The third is a changed relationship to thoughts : patients learn to see a negative thought as an event in the mind rather than a fact, which is the idea MBCT builds on. Clinical link Meena, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, has recovered from her second depressive episode on sertraline and asks whether she must take it for ever. The evidence lets you give her a real choice rather than a verdict. Staying on medication protects her while she takes it; a course of CBT, or adding CBT before the medication is tapered with her psychiatrist, offers protection that should outlast the sessions. Whichever she chooses, a written relapse prevention plan (her personal early warning signs, the skills that helped, and whom to contact) and a few booster sessions are good practice. Exam trap CBT's distinctive advantage over antidepressants in depression is lower relapse after treatment ends (the enduring effect), not a faster response (medication is usually as fast or faster) and not a much larger effect during treatment. "Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy was developed primarily to..." prevent relapse in recurrent major depression ; not to treat acute psychosis, replace medication in bipolar disorder or treat phobias by exposure (Section 5.9). Which ingredients matter? Dismantling CBT A full course of cognitive therapy contains many things: a warm relationship, a convincing rationale, activity scheduling, thought records, behavioural experiments and work on core beliefs. When the package works, which parts are doing the work? The research tool for answering is the dismantling study , also called a component analysis: the full treatment is compared with versions from which one or more components have been removed. If a stripped-down version does as well as the whole, the missing parts were not needed, at least for that problem and those patients. Its mirror image is the additive (or constructive) design, which starts with a basic treatment and adds a component to see whether outcomes improve. The best-known dismantling study of CBT was run on Beck's cognitive therapy itself. Key study: Jacobson's component analysis of cognitive therapy for depression (1996) Neil S. Jacobson (1949 to 1999; Section 5.10) of the University of Washington in Seattle was a behaviourist who suspected that the behavioural part of cognitive therapy did most of the work. With Keith Dobson (Section 5.1) and six other colleagues he randomly assigned 150 outpatients with major depression to the three conditions in Table 5.26, for up to 20 sessions. The same four experienced cognitive therapists delivered all three treatments, and because they believed in the full package, any bias should have favoured it. The result: there was no evidence that full cognitive therapy did better than either component, either at the end of treatment or at six-month follow-up. Behavioural activation alone even changed negative thinking and attributional style as much as the full therapy did. A two-year follow-up (Gortner, Gollan, Dobson and Jacobson, 1998) found no difference in relapse. The criticism: one trial of 150 patients cannot detect small differences, and asking cognitive therapists to hold back their usual methods is not the same as testing behavioural activation delivered by enthusiasts. Condition What it contained Outcome Behavioural activation (BA) Activity monitoring and scheduling, mastery and pleasure ratings, graded tasks; no direct work on thoughts As good as full cognitive therapy BA plus automatic thoughts BA, plus identifying, testing and modifying automatic thoughts As good as full cognitive therapy Full cognitive therapy Both of the above, plus identifying and modifying core schemas No better than either component The finding had large consequences. Behavioural activation was developed into a therapy in its own right (Section 5.10 describes it, and the later Seattle trial that compared it with cognitive therapy and medication). In England, the COBRA trial (Cost and Outcome of Behavioural Activation; David Richards and colleagues, 2016) found that behavioural activation delivered by junior mental health workers with no professional psychotherapy training was no less effective than CBT delivered by qualified therapists, and was cheaper. If the simplest component works, it can be taught to people who are not psychologists, an idea you will meet again in Goa. Jacobson's study also opened a wider argument about how CBT works. Richard Longmore and Michael Worrell (2007) asked, in the title of their review, "Do we need to challenge thoughts in cognitive behavior therapy?", and concluded that there was little evidence that cognitive techniques add to behavioural ones, or that changes in thinking cause the changes in symptoms. Defenders such as Hofmann (2008) replied that cognitive change can be produced by behavioural methods too (a behavioural experiment is a way of changing a belief), so a behavioural component working well does not show that cognition is unimportant. Timing is part of the puzzle. Stephen Ilardi and Edward Craighead (1994) pointed out that much of the improvement in CBT for depression happens in the first few weeks, before the main cognitive techniques have been introduced, which suggests that hope, structure and the relationship do a good deal of the early work. Tony Tang and Robert DeRubeis (1999) then described sudden gains : large, stable drops in symptoms between one session and the next, usually following a session in which the client's thinking had changed substantially; patients who had them did better at the end of treatment and at follow-up. The fair summary is that CBT clearly works, but exactly why is still argued. In the anxiety disorders exposure is the strongest single ingredient (Chapter 4), though cognitive methods add to it for some problems, such as generalised anxiety disorder (Butler, Fennell, Robson and Gelder, 1991). Exam trap Jacobson and colleagues (1996) ran a dismantling (component) study , and found that behavioural activation alone did as well as full cognitive therapy ; it did not show cognitive restructuring or schema work to be the essential ingredient. A dismantling study removes components from a full package; an additive design adds them to a basic one. Do not confuse three Jacobsons: Neil Jacobson (behavioural activation; the reliable change index with Truax, 1991, Chapter 8), Edmund Jacobson (progressive muscle relaxation; book 1929, revised 1938; Chapter 4) and Lenore Jacobson ( Pygmalion in the Classroom , with Robert Rosenthal, 1968). And "sudden gains" are large improvements between consecutive sessions, not the spontaneous remission that Eysenck wrote about (Chapter 8). Stepped care: NICE and IAPT Suppose CBT works. A health system still faces a problem of arithmetic: there are far more people with depression and anxiety than there are trained therapists, and a full course of individual CBT costs many hours of a scarce professional's time. One answer is stepped care . As Peter Bower and Simon Gilbody (2005) described it, stepped care rests on two principles. The first is that the treatment offered first should be the least restrictive one (least intensive, least costly and least burdensome for the patient) that is still likely to bring real benefit. The second is that the system is self-correcting : everyone's progress is monitored, and a person who is not improving is "stepped up" to a more intensive treatment. The alternative, sometimes called stratified or matched care, assigns each person to a level of treatment at the start according to the severity of the problem. NICE's guideline for depression in adults (2009) set out the best-known version, in four steps (Figure 5.14). Step 1 is recognition, assessment, education and active monitoring. Step 2 offers low-intensity interventions for persistent mild to moderate symptoms: guided self-help (a self-help programme based on CBT, in a book or online, with a few brief contacts with a practitioner who supports and encourages rather than delivers therapy), computerised CBT and structured group physical activity. Step 3 offers high-intensity interventions for moderate to severe depression or for people who did not improve at step 2: individual CBT, interpersonal psychotherapy, behavioural activation or behavioural couples therapy, often with medication. Step 4 is specialist and multi-professional care for severe, complex or high-risk cases, including inpatient and crisis care.
