Each step is more intensive, more costly and more specialist than the one below; the long diagonal arrow ("step up") shows that people move up only when regular measurement shows they are not improving enough. England then built a national service around this model. In 2006 the economist Richard Layard (born 1934) of the London School of Economics, working with the clinical psychologist David M. Clark, whose cognitive model of panic you met in Section 5.6, published The Depression Report . Its argument was economic as much as clinical: depression and anxiety were among the biggest causes of incapacity and lost work in Britain, the therapies NICE recommended were barely available, and a course of therapy would largely pay for itself if it helped people return to work. After pilot services in Doncaster and Newham, the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme was launched in October 2008. A new workforce of psychological wellbeing practitioners was trained to deliver low-intensity CBT-based help, much of it by telephone; trained CBT therapists delivered the high-intensity step, later joined by therapists in IPT, couples therapy and counselling for depression. Every patient completed two brief questionnaires at every session (the Patient Health Questionnaire, PHQ-9, for depression and the Generalised Anxiety Disorder scale, GAD-7, for anxiety; Assessment book), so that almost every person treated had a recorded outcome, and each service's results were published. The programme set a national target that 50 percent of those completing treatment should "recover", meaning that their scores moved from the clinical to the non-clinical range. Recovery rates rose from under 40 percent in the first years to about 50 percent, and in January 2023 the service was renamed NHS Talking Therapies, for anxiety and depression . Its critics point out that recovery is judged by two short questionnaires, that many people who are referred never start or drop out early, that recovery is less likely in deprived areas, and that the pressure of targets falls heavily on a stretched workforce. Even so, IAPT showed that CBT could be delivered, and its results measured, for hundreds of thousands of people a year. Exam trap Stepped care starts with the least intensive treatment likely to work and steps up only when monitoring shows too little improvement. It does not start everyone at the most intensive level, and it does not mean "medication first". Guided self-help and computerised CBT are low-intensity (step 2); individual CBT, IPT, behavioural activation and couples therapy are high-intensity (step 3). IAPT is an English (NHS) programme, launched in 2008 and renamed NHS Talking Therapies in 2023; NICE is a guideline body, not a therapy. CBT in India and other low-resource settings England's problem of arithmetic is India's, multiplied many times over. The National Mental Health Survey of 2015 to 2016, carried out by the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru, found that for most mental disorders well over half of the people affected were receiving no treatment at all. This difference between the number of people who need care and the number who receive it is called the treatment gap , and India has far too few clinical psychologists to close it by training more of them, however fast. Two ideas have changed what CBT looks like in such settings: adapting the therapy to the culture, and handing parts of it to people who are not mental health professionals. cultural adaptation is the systematic modification of an evidence-based treatment so that it fits the language, beliefs and circumstances of the people receiving it, while keeping its active ingredients. The best-known framework, from Guillermo Bernal , Janet Bonilla and Carmen Bellido (1995), names eight dimensions a therapist can adapt: language, persons (the match between client and therapist), metaphors, content (cultural knowledge and values), concepts (explaining the problem and the treatment in terms that make sense locally), goals, methods and context. Meta-analyses have found culturally adapted therapies modestly more effective than the same therapies delivered unchanged. Indian context Indian clinicians who adapt CBT typically involve the family, since decisions about work, marriage and treatment are rarely made alone; use local idioms of distress ("tension", "weakness", "my mind is not working") and take bodily complaints seriously as the way distress is first presented; treat beliefs about karma, fate and God as resources to work with rather than distortions to dispute; replace written thought records with pictures, stories, proverbs and spoken homework for clients with little schooling; and accept a more directive, teacherly role, which many clients expect (J. S. Neki's guru-chela relationship, Chapter 6). A "should" that expresses family duty is treated as a value, not as musturbation (Section 5.2). The second idea is task sharing (older writings say task shifting): giving defined parts of care to non-specialists, such as community health workers, nurses or trained members of the community, who are trained and supervised by specialists. The Indian psychiatrist Vikram Patel (born 1964), co-founder in 1996 of the Goa-based research organisation Sangath and author of the manual Where There Is No Psychiatrist (2003), became its leading advocate, and the World Health Organization's Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP, launched in 2008) built it into global policy. The early evidence came from South Asia. In rural Rawalpindi in Pakistan, Atif Rahman and colleagues (2008) trained government Lady Health Workers to weave CBT techniques into their routine home visits to depressed pregnant women and new mothers (the Thinking Healthy Programme). Six months after the birth, 23 percent of mothers in the intervention areas met criteria for major depression, against 53 percent in the control areas. In Goa, the MANAS trial (Patel and colleagues, 2010) placed lay health counsellors in primary care clinics to deliver psychoeducation and interpersonal therapy within a stepped-care team; it improved recovery in government clinics, though not in private ones. Key study: the Healthy Activity Program trial in Goa (PREMIUM; Patel and colleagues, 2017) The question. Can a person with no mental health training, after a structured course and with regular supervision, treat severe depression? PREMIUM (the Programme for Effective Mental Health Interventions in Under-resourced Health Systems) developed two brief treatments for lay counsellors in Goa: the Healthy Activity Program (HAP) for depression, and Counselling for Alcohol Problems , based on motivational interviewing, for harmful drinking. HAP was built on behavioural activation, with added problem solving and help in reactivating the client's social network, in six to eight sessions over up to three months. The counsellors were local people with at least a high-school education and no professional mental health training. The method. Adults with moderately severe to severe depression (a PHQ-9 score above 14) attending ten primary health centres were randomly assigned to enhanced usual care alone or enhanced usual care plus HAP. The result. At three months, 64 percent of the HAP group were in remission against 39 percent of the usual-care group, HAP was judged cost-effective, and the advantage was still present at twelve months. The limits. A trial with careful supervision is not yet a public programme; keeping quality high when such treatments are scaled up across a state is the next, harder test. Similar results have come from Africa: in Zimbabwe's Friendship Bench trial (Dixon Chibanda and colleagues, 2016), older women from the community delivered problem-solving therapy on wooden benches in clinic grounds. Notice the thread that runs back to Jacobson's dismantling study: because behavioural activation proved enough on its own, and is far easier to teach than schema work, it was the natural treatment to hand to a lay counsellor in Goa. Exam trap Keep the programmes apart. The Healthy Activity Program (PREMIUM, Goa, 2017) treats moderately severe to severe depression, is based on behavioural activation and is delivered by lay counsellors in primary care; its sister treatment, Counselling for Alcohol Problems , targets harmful drinking. MANAS (Goa, 2010) used lay health counsellors for common mental disorders. The Thinking Healthy Programme (Pakistan, 2008) treated perinatal depression through Lady Health Workers. The Friendship Bench (Zimbabwe, 2016) used problem-solving therapy. Task sharing means specialists train and supervise non-specialists, not that specialists disappear; cultural adaptation changes the packaging of a therapy, not its active ingredients. Criticisms and limitations None of this makes CBT a cure-all, and its strongest supporters say so. The first limitation is simple: many patients do not get better . In trials for depression roughly half of patients respond well, fewer reach full remission, many keep residual symptoms, and relapse is common even after CBT; IAPT's recovery rate of about 50 percent means that half of those who complete treatment do not recover by its own measure. The second is the gap between efficacy and effectiveness (Section 8.7): trial patients are often selected to exclude severe comorbidity, suicidality and substance misuse, and are treated by well-supervised therapists; the patients in a district hospital clinic are not. The third limitation concerns the evidence itself. Pim Cuijpers and his colleagues (2010) showed that the effects of psychotherapy for depression shrink considerably when only high-quality trials are counted, and that unpublished negative studies inflate the averages. Trials that compare CBT with a waiting list, rather than with a credible alternative, flatter it further. Tom Johnsen and Oddgeir Friborg (2015) went further: in 70 trials of CBT for depression published between 1977 and 2014, they reported that the effects had declined steadily over time. That claim was itself disputed; a reanalysis by Ioana Cristea and colleagues (2017) concluded that the apparent fall was most likely spurious. The debate is a good reminder that the numbers in this section are estimates, not constants. The fourth limitation is that CBT is not clearly superior to other well-delivered therapies. When it is compared with interpersonal psychotherapy, behavioural activation or good short-term psychodynamic therapy, differences are usually small, which is the "dodo bird" finding discussed in Section 8.3, and researchers' allegiance to their own therapy predicts part of the result (Section 8.6). Falk Leichsenring and Christiane Steinert (2017) therefore questioned whether CBT deserves to be called the "gold standard" of psychotherapy and argued for plurality in treatment and research; Daniel David, Ioana Cristea and Stefan Hofmann (2018) replied that it does, because it has the largest evidence base and the best-specified theory of change. For the clinician the point is that more evidence for one therapy is not, by itself, evidence against the others. The fifth group of criticisms is about depth. Psychodynamic and humanistic critics argue that CBT treats symptoms rather than causes, neglects childhood experience, emotion and the therapeutic relationship, and can become a mechanical exercise in filling in forms. The British psychiatrist and psychotherapist Jeremy Holmes put the case in a 2002 paper in the British Medical Journal pointedly titled "All you need is cognitive behaviour therapy?". CBT's own development is partly an answer: schema therapy and cognitive analytic therapy (Section 5.7) reach back into childhood and the relationship, and the third wave (Sections 5.8 to 5.10) turned towards acceptance, emotion and values. The sixth is social and cultural. CBT locates the problem in the person's thinking, and when the activating event is poverty, caste discrimination or violence at home, a therapy that examines only the client's beliefs can seem to blame the victim (Section 5.2's clinical link makes the same point about REBT). CBT also assumes literacy, homework and some capacity to observe one's own thoughts, and on its own it does not suit acute mania or psychosis, severe cognitive impairment, or a person in immediate danger. Exam trap Know which criticisms are fair. Fair: CBT does not help everyone; trial results overstate routine results; it is not clearly superior to other bona fide therapies; why it works is unresolved; it may neglect the past, emotion, the relationship and social causes; it demands literacy and homework. Unfair: that CBT "has no evidence", that it "has not been shown to help depression", that it focuses on sexuality (a criticism of Freud), or that it works only for mild problems (well-delivered CBT matched medication in moderate to severe depression). "Most researched" does not mean "proven best". Digital CBT: computers, the internet and apps If CBT is structured, educational and built on homework, can much of it be delivered without a therapist in the room? computerised CBT (cCBT) is a structured CBT programme delivered by computer, first on CD-ROM and later online, in which the software provides the psychoeducation, exercises and homework that a therapist would otherwise give. The best-known British example, Beating the Blues , takes the user through eight weekly interactive sessions; in general practice it did better than usual care for depression and anxiety (Judith Proudfoot and colleagues, 2004). FearFighter , an exposure-based programme for panic and phobia, grew out of Isaac Marks's work in London. In 2006, having declined to recommend computerised CBT in 2002, NICE recommended Beating the Blues for mild to moderate depression and FearFighter for panic and phobia, but not for severe depression. internet-delivered CBT (iCBT) is CBT delivered through a website or app, usually as a series of modules completed over several weeks. It comes in two forms. In guided iCBT a therapist or trained supporter reviews the client's homework and sends brief written messages, often for only a few minutes per client per week; in unguided iCBT the client works alone. The Swedish psychologist Gerhard Andersson and his colleagues built much of the evidence for the guided form. In Australia, MoodGYM , launched free online in 2001 by Helen Christensen and Kathleen Griffiths at the Australian National University, reduced depressive symptoms in a community trial (2004). The most striking result came from a meta-analysis by Andersson, Cuijpers, Carlbring, Riper and Hedman (2014): across 13 trials that compared the two directly, guided iCBT and face-to-face CBT produced equivalent effects. Guidance matters, though. Meta-analyses (for example Richards and Richardson, 2012) find that supported programmes produce larger effects and fewer dropouts than unsupported ones. Dropout is the central weakness of digital help. The Internet researcher Gunther Eysenbach (2005) named it the law of attrition : in trials of online health programmes, a large proportion of users stop using the programme before the end, so attrition must be expected and measured rather than treated as an accident. The REEACT trial (Simon Gilbody and colleagues, 2015) showed what this means in practice. Nearly 700 depressed patients from general practices across England were offered usual care, usual care plus Beating the Blues , or usual care plus MoodGYM , with weekly encouraging telephone calls from non-clinicians. Neither programme did better than usual care, mainly because few patients used them much. Computerised CBT works when people use it, and people use it more when a human being is involved. Smartphone apps are the newest form. Thousands of mental health apps exist, and only a small fraction has ever been tested. A 2017 meta-analysis of randomised trials of smartphone interventions for depressive symptoms (Joseph Firth and colleagues) found a small to moderate benefit, smaller when apps were compared with active control conditions. Chatbots that hold CBT-style text conversations, some developed in India, are being evaluated, and internet-delivered CBT for insomnia has produced clear improvements in sleep (Ritterband and colleagues, 2009). The risks are real: privacy and the sale of users' data, apps that cannot recognise a suicidal crisis, and marketing that runs well ahead of evidence. Table 5.27 summarises the forms. Clinical link A digital programme is a treatment, so it needs an assessment first. Before recommending an app or an online course to a client, a clinician should screen for suicide risk and severity (digital self-help belongs at step 2, not step 4), check that the client can read the language and has private access to a phone, agree how progress will be reviewed, and make sure the client knows whom to call in a crisis. The case of Beck's guilty patient, revisited Go back to the young psychoanalyst in Philadelphia and the patient on his couch who had just vented his anger at his analyst and felt, of all things, guilty. You can now name everything that was happening in that hour. The quiet commentary running beside the anger ("I said the wrong thing... I shouldn't have said that... He won't like me... I'm bad") was a string of automatic thoughts, and the guilt followed the thoughts rather than the outburst, exactly as the cognitive mediation hypothesis of Section 5.1 says. Each thought carries a distortion from Table 5.3: "I shouldn't have said that" is a should statement, "He won't like me" is an arbitrary inference about what another person will think, and "I'm bad" is labelling. Ellis would have heard a demand in the first and, in the last, the global rating of the self that REBT disputes. And "I'm bad" already sits near the bottom of the downward arrow: a core belief of the worthless kind, the deepest of the three levels of Figure 5.3. Beck did not interpret the guilt as anger turned inward. He asked what had been going through the patient's mind, and that simple question became the centre of cognitive therapy, of collaborative empiricism and of the thought record. The rest of the chapter shows how many ways there now are of answering that second stream. A cognitive therapist would treat "He won't like me" as a prediction and test it with a behavioural experiment. A schema therapist might hear in "I'm bad" the voice of a Punitive Parent mode. An ACT therapist would help the patient notice "I'm having the thought that I'm bad" and act on his values anyway; an MBCT teacher would help him see it as a passing event in the mind, not a fact; a compassion-focused therapist would ask whether the voice that says it sounds like a bullying teacher or a good coach. The second wave changes what a thought says and the third changes what a thought does, but both rest on Beck's discovery that the stream is there to be caught. Section 5.11 showed where that discovery led: to the most researched psychotherapy in the world, about as effective as medication for depression while treatment lasts and more protective after it ends, though still not a cure for everyone. Chapter summary 5.1 From behaviour to belief: the cognitive turn in therapy. Cognitive-behavioural therapy is a family of treatments that share Keith Dobson's three propositions: cognitive activity affects behaviour and emotion, it can be monitored and altered, and changing it changes behaviour and emotion. The first is the cognitive mediation hypothesis. The idea goes back to Epictetus ("men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them") and to Buddhist teaching, and was prepared in modern psychology by Adler's "basic mistakes", Horney's "tyranny of the shoulds" and Kelly's personal constructs (1955). Behaviour therapy turned cognitive in the 1970s, and Bandura's self-efficacy (1977) became a bridge between the two. Steven Hayes (2004) described three waves: behaviour therapy, cognitive therapy, and a third wave that changes a person's relationship with thoughts rather than their content. All CBTs are brief, structured, collaborative, present-focused, homework-based and measured; psychoanalysis belongs to none of the waves. 5.2 Albert Ellis and rational emotive behaviour therapy. Albert Ellis (1913 to 2007) left psychoanalysis to found rational therapy (about 1955), renamed rational-emotive therapy in 1961 and rational emotive behaviour therapy (REBT) in 1993; it is often called the first CBT. In the ABC model an activating event (A) does not cause the emotional and behavioural consequence (C) directly; the person's beliefs (B) about it do. Irrational beliefs are rigid demands (musturbation), from which awfulising, low frustration tolerance and global rating follow, and Ellis grouped them into three major musts about the self, others and the world. Unhealthy negative emotions (anxiety, depression) differ from healthy ones (concern, sadness). Disputing (D), logical, empirical or pragmatic, leads to an effective new philosophy (E) and new feelings (F). REBT aims at unconditional self-acceptance, uses cognitive, emotive and behavioural techniques (rational emotive imagery, shame attacking, homework), and is criticised as confrontational, with thinner evidence than Beck's. 5.3 Aaron Beck's cognitive model. Aaron Beck (1921 to 2021), a psychoanalytically trained psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania, found that his depressed patients' dreams and laboratory behaviour did not fit the theory of anger turned inward, and built a cognitive model instead (1963 to 1967; Cognitive Therapy of Depression , 1979). Automatic thoughts are quick, plausible, evaluative thoughts that drive emotion. In depression they share the cognitive triad, negative views of the self, the world and the future, and Beck saw hopelessness as the key to suicide. Judith Beck organised cognition into three levels: core beliefs (held in schemas), intermediate beliefs (attitudes, rules and assumptions) and automatic thoughts, in a diathesis-stress model. Cognitive distortions turn events into evidence for the schema: Beck's six (arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralisation, magnification and minimisation, personalisation, dichotomous thinking) and Burns's additions, including mind reading, fortune telling, catastrophising, emotional reasoning, should statements and labelling. 5.4 Cognitive therapy in practice. Cognitive therapy rests on collaborative empiricism: therapist and client work as co-investigators who treat beliefs as hypotheses and make objective assessments of them. Socratic questioning and guided discovery help the client notice previously overlooked information and reach his own conclusions (Padesky, 1993); free association, dream analysis and medication play no part. A typical course for depression runs 12 to 20 sessions with a set structure (mood check, bridge, agenda, homework review, discussion, new homework, summary and feedback), and progress is tracked with Beck's self-report scales (BDI, BAI, BHS), unlike the clinician-rated Hamilton scales. The main techniques are the dysfunctional thought record, decatastrophising, reattribution, activity scheduling with mastery and pleasure ratings, graded task assignment, behavioural experiments and the downward arrow to core beliefs. Beck and Ellis share the view that disturbance comes from thinking rather than events; Ellis disputes irrational beliefs, whereas Beck tests distorted ones. 5.5 Coping skills, problem solving and personal constructs. Some clients lack skills rather than hold false beliefs. Donald Meichenbaum's self-instructional training (with Goodman, 1971), built on Vygotsky and Luria's account of inner speech, teaches impulsive children to guide themselves in five steps, from cognitive modelling to covert self-instruction. His stress inoculation training has three phases (conceptualisation, skills acquisition and rehearsal, application and follow-through), uses coping self-statements and rests on Richard Lazarus's transactional view of stress. D'Zurilla and Goldfried's problem-solving therapy (1971), developed with the Nezus, combines a positive problem orientation with rational problem-solving skills. Arnold Lazarus's multimodal therapy assesses seven modalities, the BASIC ID, and borrows techniques by technical eclecticism. George Kelly's fixed-role therapy (1955) asks a client to live as an invented character for about two weeks, following from his view of the person as a scientist and his constructive alternativism. 5.6 Disorder-specific cognitive models: panic, social anxiety, trauma and psychosis. Beck's cognitive specificity hypothesis holds that each disorder has its own theme of thought. The Oxford group (Clark, Salkovskis, Ehlers, Wells) built models naming each disorder's key appraisal and the processes that maintain it, above all safety behaviours, which prevent disconfirmation and are dropped in therapy. Clark (1986) explained panic as the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations. Clark and Wells (1995) explained social anxiety through self-focused attention, an observer-perspective self-image, safety behaviours and anticipatory and post-event processing; complete treatment combines exposure, cognitive restructuring and social skills work. Ehlers and Clark (2000) explained PTSD as a sense of current threat; Resick's cognitive processing therapy targets stuck points, and the TF-CBT of Cohen, Mannarino and Deblinger centres on a trauma narrative. CBT for psychosis normalises experiences and targets beliefs about them, as an adjunct to antipsychotic medication. 5.7 Going deeper: schema therapy and cognitive analytic therapy. Clients with personality disorders break the assumptions of short-term cognitive therapy. Jeffrey Young's schema therapy (1990; set out fully with Klosko and Weishaar in 2003), designed for those who did not respond to standard CBT, describes 18 early maladaptive schemas in five domains, each rooted in an unmet core emotional need. Schemas are kept alive by three coping styles (surrender, avoidance, overcompensation) and by schema chemistry; schema modes are moment-to-moment states such as the Vulnerable Child, the Detached Protector, the Punitive Parent and the Healthy Adult. Change comes through limited reparenting, empathic confrontation, imagery rescripting, chair work and behavioural pattern-breaking, and the Giesen-Bloo trial (2006) favoured it over transference-focused psychotherapy. Anthony Ryle's cognitive analytic therapy (1990) recasts object relations as reciprocal roles and problem procedures (traps, dilemmas, snags), worked on in about 16 sessions through a reformulation letter, a sequential diagrammatic reformulation and goodbye letters. 5.8 The third wave I: dialectical behaviour therapy. Marsha Linehan (1943 to 2026), once a severely disturbed inpatient herself, built dialectical behaviour therapy (manuals 1993) for chronically suicidal women with borderline personality disorder after standard behaviour therapy failed them. Her biosocial theory explains the disorder as emotion dysregulation arising from the transaction of emotional vulnerability (high sensitivity, high reactivity, slow return to baseline) with an invalidating environment. Dialectics balances acceptance, through validation and skills drawn from Zen, with change, through behavioural chain analysis, skills training and contingency management. Standard DBT has four modes: individual therapy guided by a diary card, group skills training, telephone coaching and a therapist consultation team; Stage 1 follows a target hierarchy headed by life-threatening behaviour. The four skills modules are core mindfulness and distress tolerance (acceptance) and emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness (change). Trials from 1991 onwards show fewer suicide attempts and better retention, though well-organised alternatives can do as well. 5.9 The third wave II: acceptance and commitment therapy and the mindfulness-based therapies. Steven Hayes, with Kirk Strosahl and Kelly Wilson (1999), developed acceptance and commitment therapy, a behaviour therapy grounded in functional contextualism and in relational frame theory (2001), which traces human suffering to derived relational responding and the transformation of stimulus functions. ACT's problems are cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance; its aim is psychological flexibility, built through the six processes of the hexaflex: acceptance, cognitive defusion, contact with the present moment, self-as-context, values and committed action. Mindfulness is paying attention on purpose, in the present moment and non-judgementally. Jon Kabat-Zinn founded mindfulness-based stress reduction in 1979, an eight-week course for stress, pain and illness. Segal, Williams and Teasdale (2002) combined it with cognitive therapy in MBCT, based on the differential activation hypothesis; its key skill is decentering, and in people with three or more past episodes it almost halved relapse into depression. 5.10 The third wave III: compassion, metacognition, the therapeutic relationship and activation. Four smaller third-wave therapies each have one founder and one big idea. Paul Gilbert's compassion-focused therapy, for people high in shame and self-criticism, rests on three emotion-regulation systems (threat, drive and soothing) and uses compassionate mind training to strengthen soothing; Kristin Neff's self-compassion is a related research construct. Adrian Wells's metacognitive therapy targets the cognitive attentional syndrome (worry and rumination, threat monitoring, unhelpful coping) and the positive and negative metacognitive beliefs that drive it, using detached mindfulness and the attention training technique. Kohlenberg and Tsai's functional analytic psychotherapy (1991) naturally reinforces clinically relevant behaviours as they occur in the therapy relationship. Behavioural activation grew from Lewinsohn's account of low response-contingent positive reinforcement and Jacobson's component analysis, and was set out by Martell, Addis and Jacobson (2001). The third wave shares attention to function, acceptance and values, and is moving towards process-based therapy. 5.11 How well does CBT work? CBT is the most researched therapy because it is brief, manualised and measured. Butler and colleagues (2006) found large effects for depression, generalised anxiety, panic, social phobia, PTSD and childhood disorders. In the NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program (Elkin, 1989) CBT, interpersonal psychotherapy and imipramine differed little, but DeRubeis, Hollon and colleagues (2005) showed well-delivered cognitive therapy matching medication in moderate to severe depression. CBT's distinctive advantage is its enduring effect, less relapse after treatment ends, and Jacobson's dismantling study (1996) found behavioural activation alone as effective as the full package. Stepped care offers the least intensive effective help first, as in England's IAPT (2008), now NHS Talking Therapies; task sharing and cultural adaptation carry CBT to low-resource settings, as in Goa's Healthy Activity Program. Limitations include non-response, inflated trial effects and no clear superiority over other therapies. Guided internet CBT rivals face-to-face therapy, but attrition is high. attrition, digital divide From the past papers "Third-wave CBT" includes all EXCEPT: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (b) Dialectical Behavior Therapy (c) Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (d) Psychoanalysis Answer: (d) Psychoanalysis. ACT, DBT and MBCT are the best-known third-wave therapies, which change a person's relationship with thoughts rather than their content. Psychoanalysis is an older psychodynamic tradition and belongs to none of the three waves of behavioural and cognitive therapy. Which of the following is not a form of psychotherapy used to treat psychological disorders? (RML 2020) (a) Cognitive therapy (b) Pharmacotherapy (c) Behavioural therapy (d) Psychodynamic therapy Answer: (b) Pharmacotherapy. Treatment with medicines is not a psychotherapy. Cognitive, behavioural and psychodynamic therapies all are, because they work through a psychological relationship and psychological techniques. Rational Emotive Therapy is given by: (JEMAS 2025) (a) Albert Ellis (b) Sigmund Freud (c) William James (d) Aaron Beck Answer: (a) Albert Ellis. Ellis founded rational therapy in the mid-1950s and renamed it rational-emotive therapy in 1961. Beck is the tempting wrong answer, but he founded cognitive therapy; Freud founded psychoanalysis, and William James was a founder of functionalism. REBT was developed by: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Aaron Beck (b) Albert Ellis (c) Carl Rogers (d) Adler Answer: (b) Albert Ellis. Ellis renamed his therapy rational emotive behaviour therapy in 1993. Beck's therapy is cognitive therapy, Rogers's is client-centred therapy, and Adler influenced Ellis without founding REBT. Within the cognitive approach, the ABC model describes: (RML 2021) (a) A = activating event; B = beliefs about oneself; C = consequences of the beliefs about oneself (b) A = activating events; B = beliefs about the events; C = consequences of the beliefs about the event (c) A = activating event; B = beliefs about the events; C = critical analysis of the beliefs about the event (d) A = anticipatory event; B = beliefs about the event; D = consequences of the beliefs about the event Answer: (b). In Ellis's model the beliefs (B) are about the activating event (A), and the consequences (C) follow from those beliefs. Option (a) narrows the belief to the self, (c) turns C into "critical analysis" and (d) invents an "anticipatory" event and a misplaced D. A therapist focuses on helping a client identify and challenge irrational beliefs, such as "I absolutely must be approved by everyone" (musterbation). This therapist is most likely practicing: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Beck's Cognitive Therapy (b) Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) (c) Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) (d) Reality Therapy Answer: (b) REBT. "Irrational beliefs", absolute "musts" and Ellis's own word musturbation are the signature of REBT. Beck speaks of automatic thoughts and distortions, DBT of acceptance and skills, and William Glasser's reality therapy (Chapter 6) is a different approach altogether. In the A-B-C-D-E model of cognitive behaviour therapy (RET), "D" refers to: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Drama (b) Desensitization (c) Discuss (d) Disputing Answer: (d) Disputing. D is the logical, empirical and pragmatic challenging of irrational beliefs, which leads to E, an effective new philosophy. Desensitisation is Wolpe's behavioural technique, the tempting look-alike; "drama" and "discuss" are filler. A criticism of the REBT cognitive approach to understanding mental-health problems is that: (RML 2021) (a) There is too much of a focus on sexuality (b) It can be direct and confrontational and so might be seen as intimidatory by the client (c) It has not been shown to be successful at helping individuals with depression (d) It is not relevant in the 21st century Answer: (b). Vigorous disputing can feel intimidating or humiliating, especially to a fragile client early in therapy. The focus on sexuality is a criticism of Freud, REBT does have evidence for depression, and (d) is an opinion, not a criticism made in the literature. A patient sees a friend in the street who fails to acknowledge him; he thinks his friend does not like him anymore. He has the following type of cognitive error: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Selective abstraction (b) Arbitrary inference (c) Personalization (d) Magnification Answer: (b) Arbitrary inference. He draws a conclusion for which there is no evidence: the friend may simply not have seen him. No detail is being picked out of a larger picture (selective abstraction), he is not blaming himself for an event he did not cause (personalisation), and nothing is being blown up in size (magnification). A teacher in his class sees two students bored and feels his class is not liked by all the students. This is which type of cognitive error? (RML 2024) (a) Arbitrary inference (b) Selective attention (c) Over generalization (d) Magnification Answer: (b) Selective attention , that is, selective abstraction or the mental filter: one detail (two bored faces) is taken out of context and all the attentive faces are ignored. Overgeneralisation tempts because he moves to "all the students", but it means carrying a conclusion from one situation to other, unrelated situations. Catastrophic thinking is common to several anxiety disorders. The term describes: (RML 2021) (a) Categorising all experiences as either extremely positive or extremely negative (b) Focusing on negative events and ignoring positive ones (c) Worrying that the worst will always happen (d) Taking things very personally Answer: (c). Catastrophising is the expectation of the worst possible outcome. Option (a) is dichotomous thinking, (b) is the mental filter (selective abstraction) and (d) is personalisation. Which of the following are not included in the ICD criteria for schizophrenia? (RML 2021) (a) Delusions (b) Catastrophic thinking (c) Disorganised speech (d) Hallucinations Answer: (b) Catastrophic thinking. It is a cognitive distortion found in anxiety, described in Beck's model, not a symptom of psychosis. Delusions, hallucinations and disorganised speech are core features of schizophrenia (Psychiatric Disorders book). Which of the following is NOT included as one of the fundamental concepts in cognitive therapy? (RML 2022) (a) Collaborative empiricism (b) Socratic dialogue (c) Free association (d) Guided discovery Answer: (c) Free association. Saying whatever comes to mind so that the analyst can detect unconscious material is a psychoanalytic method. Collaborative empiricism, Socratic dialogue and guided discovery are the core of Beck's method. Which of the following methods is used in Beck's cognitive therapy for depression? (RML 2025) (a) Encouraging dream analysis (b) Making objective assessments of beliefs (c) Administering psychoactive medication (d) Practicing free association Answer: (b). In collaborative empiricism beliefs are treated as hypotheses and weighed against evidence from the client's own life. Dream analysis and free association are Freud's tools, and medication is pharmacotherapy, not cognitive therapy. What is Socratic questioning? (RML 2022) (a) A form of dialogue that helps a person to discover and attend to previously overlooked information and to guide the discovery of the therapist rather than interpretation from the individual (b) A form of dialogue that helps a person to discover and attend to previously attended information and to guide the discovery of the individual rather than interpretation from the therapist (c) A form of dialogue that helps a person to discover and attend to previously overlooked information and to guide the discovery of the individual rather than interpretation from the therapist (d) A form of dialogue that helps a person to discover and attend to previously attended information and to guide the discovery of the therapist rather than interpretation from the individual Answer: (c). Two details decide it: the information is previously overlooked , and the discovery belongs to the individual rather than to interpretation from the therapist (Padesky's definition). Each of the other options reverses one or both of these details. Socratic questioning, a core technique in Cognitive Therapy, involves: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) The therapist interpreting the client's unconscious conflicts (b) The therapist guiding the client to discover their own maladaptive thoughts and generate alternative perspectives through guided discovery (c) The therapist providing direct advice and solutions to the client's problems (d) The client engaging in free association while the therapist listens passively Answer: (b). The therapist asks open-ended questions and the client does the discovering. Interpreting unconscious conflict and free association are psychoanalytic, and giving direct advice is exactly what Socratic questioning avoids. Which of the following is a clinician-rated questionnaire? (RML 2022) (a) Beck Depression Inventory (b) Beck Anxiety Inventory (c) Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (d) Both b and c Answer: (c) Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. Max Hamilton's scales are completed by a trained clinician after an interview. The BDI and BAI are self-report inventories filled in by the patient, which is why "both b and c" is wrong. Fixed role therapy, which encouraged clients to practice new roles and relationships, was developed by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) George Kelly (b) Aaron Beck (c) Albert Ellis (d) Fritz Perls Answer: (a) George Kelly , as part of his personal construct theory (1955): the client lives for about two weeks as an invented character from a fixed-role sketch. Perls tempts because Gestalt therapy uses the empty chair and other experiments, but fixed-role therapy is Kelly's. A client engages in safety behaviors, such as gripping a shopping cart tightly when feeling dizzy in a store. In CBT for panic disorder, the therapist would likely: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Prescribe these behaviors to prevent fainting (b) Use these behaviors as a measure of the client's insight (c) Work with the client to gradually drop these behaviors to test catastrophic beliefs (d) Explore the childhood origins of the need for safety Answer: (c). Safety behaviours stop the catastrophe from being disconfirmed, so dropping them is the test (Salkovskis; Clark). Prescribing them would keep the belief alive, and panicking people almost never faint; exploring childhood origins is a psychodynamic aim, not CBT's. It is considered that successful CBT treatments of social phobia include elements of the following: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Exposure therapy (b) Social skills retraining (c) Cognitive restructuring (d) All of above Answer: (d) All of the above. A complete CBT package for social anxiety combines exposure, cognitive restructuring and social skills work where real deficits exist. Choosing any single element misses the point that each targets a different maintaining process. The front-line treatment for schizophrenia is: (RML 2021) (a) Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) (b) Stress management training (c) Antipsychotic medication (d) Social skills training Answer: (c) Antipsychotic medication. CBT for psychosis, stress management and social skills training are valuable adjuncts that reduce distress and disability, but none replaces medication in schizophrenia. Dialectical Behaviour Therapy is indicated for the treatment of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Anxiety Disorders (b) Borderline Personality Disorder (c) Acute and Transient Psychotic Disorder (d) Post-traumatic Stress Disorder Answer: (b) Borderline personality disorder. Linehan built DBT for chronically suicidal women with the disorder. Adapted versions now exist for PTSD and other problems, which makes (d) tempting, but the primary indication remains borderline personality disorder. In Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), the "core mindfulness" skills are primarily derived from which tradition? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Stoicism (b) Zen Buddhism (c) Psychoanalysis (d) Existentialism Answer: (b) Zen Buddhism. Linehan, herself a Zen practitioner, translated Zen practice into secular behavioural skills. Stoicism is the root of Ellis's REBT, the usual trap, and psychoanalysis and existentialism are not its sources. Distress tolerance is a major treatment modality in which of the following therapy? (RML 2024) (a) Behaviour therapy (b) Dialectical Behaviour therapy (c) Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (d) Psychodynamic therapy Answer: (b) DBT. Distress tolerance is one of DBT's four skills modules, an acceptance module alongside core mindfulness. It is not a component of standard behaviour therapy, Beck-style CBT or psychodynamic therapy. Which therapy focuses on changing maladaptive thought patterns? (IHBAS 2025) (a) Humanistic therapy (b) Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) (c) Psychoanalysis (d) Play therapy Answer: (b) CBT. Changing distorted or maladaptive thinking is CBT's defining aim. Humanistic therapy works through the relationship and the client's growth, psychoanalysis through unconscious conflict and insight, and play therapy through children's play. B is not "behaviour", "baseline" or "biological predisposition", and the behavioural antecedent-behaviour-consequence model is a different ABC. asked 8 times Aaron Beck 's cognitive triad in depression is a negative view of the self, the world (experience) and the future ; Weightage. 55 of the 422 questions mapped in this book (13.0%) test this chapter, 24 of them from real past papers. 4 of its 10 sections are High yield. In 1964 a young woman known to the world only as Gloria walked into a small film studio in California to do something no client had done before. She had agreed to talk about the most private worry in her life, on camera, to three of the most famous psychotherapists in America, one after the other. The project was the idea of the psychologist Everett Shostrom , who wanted students to see, rather than merely read about, how the great schools of therapy actually differed. The three therapists were Carl Rogers, the founder of client-centred therapy; Fritz Perls, the founder of Gestalt therapy; and Albert Ellis , the founder of rational emotive therapy. The result, released in 1965 as Three Approaches to Psychotherapy , became one of the most widely shown teaching films in the history of psychotherapy. Generations of students know it simply as "the Gloria films". Gloria was recently divorced and had a nine-year-old daughter, Pammy. Since the divorce she had begun to see men, and when Pammy asked her whether she had been with anyone since Daddy, Gloria had lied. Now she felt guilty and confused. Would the truth harm her child? Would the lie? She wanted, very simply, to be told what to do. Rogers did not tell her. He leaned towards her, listened, and kept putting into words what she seemed to be feeling, including her half-spoken sense that she already knew what she wanted to do. As the half hour went on, Gloria spoke more slowly and more honestly, and near the end she said she wished her own father could have talked to her the way Rogers was talking to her. "You look to me like a pretty nice daughter," Rogers replied. Perls behaved almost like her opponent. He pointed out that she was smiling and fidgeting while she claimed to be frightened, and told her, in effect, that she was a phony. Gloria grew angry and fought back, and Perls seemed pleased: for a moment, he thought, she had stopped performing and was really present. Ellis, the third, argued briskly with the beliefs he thought were making her miserable (his approach belongs to Chapter 5). Three experts, one client, one problem, three utterly different conversations. Which of them helped? Gloria kept in touch with Rogers by letter for years afterwards, and the films have been argued over ever since. Keep Gloria in mind as you read this chapter, because the questions she raises run through all of it. Must a helper give advice, or can people find their own answers? Is a warm, accepting relationship enough to change someone, or must the helper sometimes frustrate, confront or direct? What would a therapist who believes that life is a search for meaning have said to her, and what would the newer brief therapies, which might have asked Gloria to imagine that a miracle had happened overnight, have added? We will come back to her at the end. 6.1 The Third Force: What These Therapies Share Medium yield · 3 Qs By the middle of the twentieth century two great systems dominated psychotherapy. The first was psychoanalysis (Chapter 3), which pictured the person as driven by unconscious sexual and aggressive wishes laid down in early childhood, and which cast the therapist as an expert who interprets what the patient cannot see. The second was behaviourism (Chapter 4), which pictured the person as the sum of his or her conditioning, and which cast the therapist as a technician who rearranges stimuli and reinforcers. Both systems were powerful. Both, to a growing number of psychologists in the 1950s, left something out: the person as he or she actually lives, choosing, valuing, hoping, and asking what life is for. The American psychologist Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970) gave the new movement its name. Psychoanalysis was the first force in psychology and behaviourism the second; the movement that put human growth, freedom and experience at the centre was the third force . It became organised in the early 1960s, when the Journal of Humanistic Psychology (1961) and the Association for Humanistic Psychology were founded, and Maslow and Carl Rogers were its two best-known figures. Humanistic psychology can be defined as the approach that studies the whole person from the person's own point of view and assumes that people have an inborn potential for growth that flourishes under the right conditions. Maslow's own contributions (the hierarchy of needs, self-actualisation and peak experiences) belong to the Personality book; Maslow was a theorist rather than a therapist. It was Rogers who turned humanistic ideas into a therapy, and we meet him in Section 6.2. Six shared assumptions The therapies in this chapter differ a great deal, as Gloria discovered, but most of them rest on a common set of assumptions. It is worth learning them as a list, because examiners like to ask which statement is "not associated with the humanistic perspective". Phenomenology. The phenomenological approach holds that what matters is the world as the person perceives and experiences it, the person's internal frame of reference , rather than an outside expert's classification of it. Two students failing the same examination live in two different worlds. Growth. Human beings have an inborn tendency to grow, to develop their capacities and to move toward health. Problems arise when this tendency is blocked, not because people are basically bad or merely conditioned. Freedom and responsibility. People are not simply pushed by the past or pulled by reinforcers; within limits they choose, and they are responsible for their choices. Holism. The person is an organised whole (body, feeling, thought and relationships together) and cannot be understood by dissecting symptoms. The present. The focus is on the here and now of experience rather than on reconstructing childhood. The relationship. Change happens through an authentic, respectful human relationship, not through the expert application of technique. Diagnosis and testing are usually played down or rejected. Within this family three branches can be told apart. The humanistic branch (Rogers and Maslow) is optimistic and growth-centred. The existential branch (Binswanger, Boss, May, Frankl and Yalom) shares the respect for experience and freedom but is more sober, because it insists that the person must face the hard limits of life: death, isolation, the burden of freedom and the absence of any ready-made meaning. The difference was real. In 1982 Rollo May published an open letter to Rogers arguing that Rogers's trusting view of human nature left no room for the human capacity for evil. The experiential branch (Gestalt therapy, Gendlin's focusing and Greenberg's emotion-focused therapy) emphasises the moment-by-moment experiencing of bodily sensation and emotion in the session itself. Researchers today group the person-centred, Gestalt, focusing, emotion-focused and existential therapies together as the humanistic-experiential psychotherapies . Robert Elliott, Leslie Greenberg and their colleagues, who have reviewed the research on them, describe their general aim as helping clients to develop a more fluid and integrated way of organising the self, by attending to and making sense of present experience, especially emotion. Compare that aim with the aims of the other families: psychodynamic therapy seeks to understand and resolve deep-seated unconscious conflicts, behaviour therapy seeks to change maladaptive behaviours, and interpersonal and social skills approaches seek to develop interpersonal skills. Each aim is worthy, but only the first is the signature of the humanistic-experiential tradition. These assumptions also produce a distinctive account of how psychological problems arise, sometimes called the humanistic-existential model of abnormal behaviour. Distress comes from blocked growth (Rogers's incongruence), from living inauthentically and avoiding responsibility (the existentialists), or from a loss of meaning (Frankl). This is quite different from the diathesis-stress model, in which a biological or psychological vulnerability is triggered by stress, and from the sociocultural and cognitive models, which locate the causes of disorder in social and cultural conditions and in faulty thinking respectively (all three are taught in Chapter 1). The chapter ends with a group of newer, briefer approaches: narrative therapy, solution-focused brief therapy and motivational interviewing. They were born in the 1970s and 1980s, they keep the humanistic respect for the client as the expert on his or her own life, but they are briefer, more future-focused and more deliberately strategic. Finally, Section 6.10 turns to the helping skills (listening, reflecting, challenging) that every counsellor and clinician uses, whatever the school. Table 6.1 sets the three forces side by side.
