The "third force" is humanistic psychology. The label "fourth force" has been claimed twice: Maslow and Anthony Sutich used it for transpersonal psychology in the late 1960s, and Paul Pedersen later used it for multiculturalism in counselling. If a question lists "availability of reinforcement" among features of the humanistic view, that is the odd one out: reinforcement is a behavioural idea. And if a question asks which model says that a biological predisposition is set off by stress, the answer is the diathesis-stress model, not the humanistic-existential model. 6.2 Carl Rogers and Person-Centred Therapy High yield · 18 Qs No psychotherapist of the twentieth century did more to change how ordinary helpers listen than Carl Ransom Rogers (1902 to 1987). His approach is the most frequently examined topic in this chapter, so we take it slowly: first the man, then the theory of personality, then the conditions he believed were enough to produce change, then what his therapy looks like in practice, then the research it inspired. From Rochester to La Jolla Rogers was born in 1902 in Oak Park, a suburb of Chicago, the fourth of six children in a prosperous, loving and strictly religious Protestant family in which dancing, cards and the theatre were forbidden. He went to the University of Wisconsin to study agriculture, switched toward the ministry, and in 1922 travelled to China for an international Christian student conference, an experience that loosened his family's fundamentalism. He studied at Union Theological Seminary in New York, crossed the road to Teachers College, Columbia University, and took his PhD in clinical and educational psychology in 1931. For twelve years (1928 to 1940) Rogers worked at the child study department of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children in Rochester, New York, seeing delinquent and deprived children. There he met the ideas of Otto Rank , a former member of Freud's inner circle, mainly through Rank's student, the social worker Jessie Taft . Rank saw the client, not the therapist, as the creative force in therapy. Rogers later told a story about how this lesson came home to him. He had been working, with no success, with the mother of a badly behaved boy, patiently trying to help her see that her early rejection of the child lay behind his behaviour. Eventually they both gave up. As she reached the door she turned and asked whether he ever took adults for counselling. When he said yes, she sat down again and poured out her despair about her marriage, and real help began. Rogers concluded that "it is the client who knows what hurts, what directions to go, what problems are crucial." In 1940 Rogers moved to Ohio State University, and in December of that year a lecture at the University of Minnesota made him realise that his ideas were genuinely new. His book Counseling and Psychotherapy (1942) described what he called non-directive therapy , in which the counsellor does not advise, interpret or steer, but follows the client. The book included the case of "Herbert Bryan", the first complete course of psychotherapy ever published from sound recordings. In 1945 Rogers moved to the University of Chicago, where he directed the counselling centre, and in 1951 he published Client-Centered Therapy , which renamed the approach client-centred therapy and added a full theory of personality. He was president of the American Psychological Association in 1947. In 1957 he moved to the University of Wisconsin, where he published his most famous paper (on the necessary and sufficient conditions for change), led a large and troubled study of therapy with hospitalised schizophrenia patients, and wrote the best-selling On Becoming a Person (1961). In 1963 Rogers left university life for La Jolla, California, where he joined the Western Behavioral Sciences Institute and then helped to found the Center for Studies of the Person (1968). His interests widened from individual therapy to encounter groups, education ( Freedom to Learn , 1969), marriage, and the reduction of political conflict; he ran workshops for Catholics and Protestants from Northern Ireland and for black and white South Africans. As the approach spread beyond the consulting room it became known as the person-centred approach . Rogers died in February 1987. So Rogers's therapy carried three names over time, and examiners use all three: non-directive (from 1942), client-centred (from 1951) and person-centred (from the 1970s). Rogers also chose the word "client" deliberately. A patient is sick and passive and receives treatment; a client actively and voluntarily seeks a service and keeps responsibility for his or her own life. The theory: the actualising tendency, the self and conditions of worth Rogers's theory begins with a single motive. He described the actualising tendency as the inherent tendency of every organism to develop all its capacities in ways that maintain or enhance it. He liked to recall the potatoes stored in the basement of his boyhood home: in the dark, far from any window, they still sent pale sprouts reaching toward the faint light. Life, Rogers thought, presses toward growth even in the worst conditions. A related idea is the organismic valuing process : the infant's built-in way of judging experiences by whether they enhance the organism. The hungry baby values food and rejects it when full; the baby enjoys being held and protests at pain. The infant, in other words, trusts its own experience. As the child grows, part of its experience becomes differentiated as the self-concept : the organised, consistent picture a person holds of "I" and "me", together with the values attached to it. Rogers also spoke of the ideal self , the self a person would most like to be. Along with the self comes a powerful need for positive regard, that is, for warmth, love and acceptance from the important people in one's life, and later a need for positive self-regard. Here the trouble starts. Parents, teachers and others rarely give their regard unconditionally. "We love you when you come first in class." "Good boys do not cry." "Girls from our family become doctors." Because the child needs regard so badly, it begins to value its own experiences not by whether they enhance it but by whether they earn approval. Rogers called these internalised rules conditions of worth : the conditions under which a person feels worthy of love and of self-respect. The child takes in, or introjects, other people's values and treats them as its own. Once a self-concept has been built around conditions of worth, some of the person's real experiences will not fit it. Rogers called this mismatch between the self-concept and actual experience incongruence . Consider Ananya, a student in Mysuru, who grew up hearing that she would be "the doctor of the family". Her self-concept is "I am a future doctor and a good daughter". Her actual experience is that she is bored in anatomy and comes alive only when she draws. Experiences that threaten the self-concept are sensed as threats even before they are fully conscious (Rogers borrowed the term "subception" for this), and they produce anxiety. The person defends against them in two ways: by distortion ("I am just tired this term") and by denial (simply not admitting the pleasure of drawing to awareness). The greater the incongruence, the more vulnerable the person; if a large incongruence is suddenly forced into awareness, the self-structure can break down into disorganised behaviour. Figure 6.1 shows the idea, and its second panel shows the direction therapy is meant to take. Incongruence (before therapy) Greater congruence (after therapy) Self- concept Experience overlap = congruence (small) much experience denied or distorted congruence Self- concept Experience experience admitted to awareness and the self-concept enlarged to fit it Figure 6.1 Rogers's model of incongruence. Each pair of circles shows the self-concept and the person's actual experience; their overlap is the area of congruence. Therapy aims to enlarge the overlap by letting denied and distorted experience into awareness. Notice what this theory implies for therapy. If psychological distress comes from conditions of worth, then the cure is a relationship in which there are no conditions of worth: a relationship in which the client is accepted whatever he or she feels, so that denied experience can safely be admitted to awareness and the self-concept can be revised to include it. That is exactly what Rogers set out to describe. Exam trap "A split between the organismic valuing process and a self-concept burdened by conditions of worth, producing tension and confusion" is incongruence . Conflict is a general term with no special place in Rogers's theory. Introjection is how conditions of worth get in (and is also a Gestalt and psychoanalytic term), but the resulting split is incongruence. The actualising tendency is the growth force that incongruence obstructs. Do not confuse Rogers's actualising tendency, which belongs to every organism, with Maslow's self-actualisation , the top of his need hierarchy; Rogers also used "self-actualising tendency" for the part of the actualising tendency expressed through the self. The six necessary and sufficient conditions (1957) In 1957 Rogers published a short paper in the Journal of Consulting Psychology with a breathtakingly bold title: "The necessary and sufficient conditions of therapeutic personality change." He claimed that if six conditions exist and continue over a period of time, constructive personality change will follow, and that nothing else is needed. The six necessary and sufficient conditions are these: Two persons are in psychological contact: each makes some perceived difference to the other. The first, the client, is in a state of incongruence, being vulnerable or anxious. The second, the therapist, is congruent, or integrated, in the relationship. The therapist experiences unconditional positive regard for the client. The therapist experiences an empathic understanding of the client's internal frame of reference and tries to communicate this to the client. The client perceives, at least to a minimal degree, the therapist's empathy and unconditional positive regard. Conditions 3, 4 and 5 are what the therapist must provide, and they have become famous as the three core conditions . Congruence (also called genuineness, realness or authenticity) means that in the relationship the therapist is what he or she actually is: inner experience, awareness and what is communicated match, with no professional façade. Unconditional positive regard (also called acceptance, prizing, or warmth) means a warm, non-judgemental valuing of the client as a person, without conditions. The term itself was coined by Rogers's student Stanley Standal in 1954. Accurate empathic understanding means, in Rogers's own words, sensing "the client's private world as if it were your own, but without ever losing the 'as if' quality", and communicating that understanding. In later writings Rogers called congruence the most basic of the three. Table 6.2 sets out what each condition is, and what it is not. Two words in the title deserve attention. Necessary means that without these conditions no constructive change occurs. Sufficient means that nothing more is required: not a diagnosis, not a special technique, not insight into childhood, not even professional training. Rogers also said the conditions were the same for every kind of client and every kind of therapy, which was a direct challenge to every other school. Table 6.2 Rogers's three core conditions: what they are and what they are not. Core condition Other names What it means What it is not Congruence Genuineness, realness, authenticity, transparency The therapist's feelings, awareness and words match; no façade Telling the client everything one feels; playing the role of "doctor" Unconditional positive regard Acceptance, prizing, warmth, non-possessive warmth Valuing the person without conditions of worth Approving of every behaviour; praise; reassurance Accurate empathic understanding Empathy, empathic understanding Sensing the client's world "as if" it were one's own, and saying so Sympathy (feeling sorry for); identifying with the client; interpreting Exam trap The core conditions are empathy, unconditional positive regard and congruence , so "all of the above" is right when all three are listed. Every other trio in the options belongs elsewhere: interpretation, transference and free association are psychoanalytic (Chapter 3); reinforcement, shaping and modelling are behavioural (Chapter 4); disputation, homework and cognitive restructuring are cognitive-behavioural (Chapter 5); confrontation and paradoxical intention belong to other schools in this chapter. Do not confuse the six conditions with the three core conditions: psychological contact, client incongruence and the client's perception of the therapist's attitudes are conditions, but not therapist-provided core conditions. Also note what is not a Rogerian concept. The therapeutic or working alliance, as defined by Edward Bordin in 1979 (agreement on goals and tasks, plus an emotional bond), grew out of psychodynamic thinking and is a pan-theoretical idea (Chapter 8). Person-centred therapists prefer to speak of the relationship itself, the "real relationship", and the core conditions. Psychoanalysis (where the working alliance was born, Section 3.3), cognitive-behaviour therapy and interpersonal psychotherapy (Klerman and Weissman, Section 3.7) all use the term freely. So person-centred therapy is the approach least likely to use the term "therapeutic alliance", and Bordin's alliance is the option that is not a key concept of client-centred therapy, whereas conditions of worth, unconditional positive regard and the actualising tendency all are. What a person-centred therapist actually does If the conditions are what matter, what does the therapist actually say? Mostly, the therapist listens and responds to the client's feelings and meanings from within the client's frame of reference. The best-known response is reflection of feeling : putting into words the feeling that the client is expressing, often more clearly than the client has said it, and offering it back for the client to check. Related responses include simple acceptance ("Mm-hm", "I see"), restatement of content, clarification and summarising. Questions are used sparingly. Interpretation, advice, reassurance, persuasion, diagnosis, psychological testing, history-taking and homework are all absent, because each of them puts the therapist's frame of reference in charge. So are the analyst's search for unconscious desires (Chapter 3) and the behaviour therapist's methods, such as aversive conditioning, in which an unwanted behaviour is paired with an unpleasant stimulus, and strict programmes of behaviour modification (Chapter 4). A worked example shows the difference. A student says: "My parents keep asking about my marks. I am not even sure why I am doing this course any more." Here are four possible replies. Advice: "You should sit down with your parents and tell them how you feel." This directs the client and assumes the counsellor knows best. Analysis or interpretation: "Perhaps you are still angry with your father for choosing your stream." This imports the counsellor's theory. Reassurance: "Do not worry, everybody feels like that in second year." This dismisses the feeling. Reflection: "There is pressure from outside about marks, and underneath it a deeper doubt, whether this course is really yours at all." This stays with the client's own meaning and invites the client to go further. Only the last is person-centred. In the 1940s Rogers's main opponent was the directive, trait-and-factor counselling of E. G. Williamson at the University of Minnesota, in which the counsellor diagnosed and advised; the contrast between "directive" and "non-directive" counselling was the great debate of the decade. Later, Rogers grew unhappy that reflection had become a mechanical technique, parodied as "parroting". In 1986 he suggested calling such responses "testing understandings" or "checking perceptions", because their purpose is to check whether the therapist has really understood. Indian context In 1973 the Indian psychiatrist J. S. Neki argued in a well-known paper that many Indian clients expect a guru-chela (teacher and disciple) relationship: an active, benevolent, somewhat directive helper. To such a client, pure non-directiveness can feel like indifference. Indian clinicians therefore often combine person-centred listening and acceptance with more structure and guidance than Rogers would have offered, while keeping the decision with the client and the family. Where therapy leads: process, the fully functioning person and the nineteen propositions By listening to hundreds of recorded sessions, Rogers described in 1958 how clients change as therapy proceeds. He pictured a continuum running from fixity to fluidity . At the fixed end the client talks about externals, is remote from feelings, sees problems as outside the self and construes experience rigidly. At the fluid end feelings are experienced immediately and richly, in the moment, the self is trusted, and experience is construed tentatively and openly. With his colleague R. A. Rablen he turned this into a seven-stage Process Scale for rating recordings. Hold on to the word fluid : it is exactly the word modern reviewers use for the goal of humanistic-experiential therapy. The endpoint of this process is what Rogers called the fully functioning person , an ideal toward which people move rather than a state they reach. Rogers described five characteristics: Openness to experience: no need for defensive distortion or denial; every feeling can be admitted to awareness. Existential living: living fully in each moment, letting the self emerge from experience rather than forcing experience into a fixed self. Organismic trusting: trusting one's own total reaction to a situation as a guide to what to do. Experiential freedom: a felt sense of free choice and responsibility for one's life. Creativity: adapting and producing new solutions rather than conforming. "The good life," Rogers wrote, "is a process, not a state of being. It is a direction, not a destination." The formal theory behind all this was set out in 1951 as nineteen propositions. You do not need to memorise all nineteen, but you should recognise their main themes: every person lives in a continually changing world of experience of which he or she is the centre (the phenomenal field); the organism reacts to this field as it is perceived, so perception is, for the individual, reality; the organism has one basic tendency, to actualise, maintain and enhance itself; behaviour is best understood from the person's internal frame of reference; part of the perceptual field gradually becomes differentiated as the self; experiences inconsistent with the self are denied or distorted; maladjustment exists when significant experiences are denied to awareness, and adjustment when all experiences can be assimilated into a consistent self; and, under conditions of complete absence of threat to the self, inconsistent experiences can be examined and the self revised. The last of these is the theoretical heart of the therapy. Research and evaluation Rogers was the first therapist to bring therapy itself under scientific scrutiny. In an era when the only record of a session was the therapist's later notes, he recorded sessions (with clients' permission) so that researchers could study what actually happened, calling the recordings a microscope for examining "the molecules of personality change". His group also needed a way to measure the self-concept, and they found it in a technique devised by the British psychologist William Stephenson . Key study: the Q-sort and the self-ideal gap (Chicago, early 1950s) Question. If Rogers was right, successful therapy should bring the perceived self closer to the ideal self. Could this be measured? Method. The Q-sort , introduced by Stephenson in his book The Study of Behavior (1953), gives the person a large set of cards (around 100) carrying self-descriptive statements such as "I am a submissive person" or "I feel insecure within myself". The person sorts them into about nine piles, from "most like me" to "least like me", with a fixed number of cards in each pile so that the sort forms a forced, roughly normal distribution. The client sorts once to describe "myself as I am" and again to describe "the person I would most like to be", and the two sorts are correlated. Because Q-methodology correlates one person's sorts rather than many people's scores, it captures within-person (idiographic) structure. Results. In the case of "Mrs Oak", the correlation between self and ideal rose from about .36 before therapy to about .79 at follow-up after therapy. In the larger study by John Butler and Gerard Haigh, reported in Rogers and Rosalind Dymond's Psychotherapy and Personality Change (1954), the average self-ideal correlation of 25 clients was close to zero before therapy and rose to about +.3 after therapy, while a comparison group not seeking therapy started higher and did not change. Clients who waited 60 days before starting therapy showed little change while waiting. Criticism. A smaller self-ideal gap could reflect a lowering of ideals, or simply learning what a "healthy" sort looks like; all the data were self-reports; and the samples were small. In 1967 Charles Truax and Robert Carkhuff developed rating scales for accurate empathy, non-possessive warmth and genuineness, and reported that clients whose therapists offered high levels improved more. Later reviews found the relationship real but weaker than these early claims. The most ambitious study, the Wisconsin project on 28 hospitalised patients with schizophrenia (published in 1967), was a disappointment: patients who received high levels of the conditions did better than those who received low levels, but they did little better than untreated controls. One lasting by-product was Eugene Gendlin's discovery that the clients who benefit are those who can attend to their inner experiencing (Section 6.7). Modern meta-analyses show that therapist empathy, positive regard and genuineness each correlate modestly but reliably with outcome, with correlations in the region of .2 to .3, across all kinds of therapy (Chapter 8). A British trial in general practice, published by Ward, King and colleagues in 2000, found that non-directive counselling and cognitive-behaviour therapy for depression were equally effective after four months and both better than usual care by the general practitioner, although the differences had disappeared by twelve months. So the core conditions are clearly facilitative . Whether they are necessary is doubtful (people improve in behaviour therapy with technically skilled but not especially warm therapists), and whether they are sufficient for every problem is more doubtful still: a severe obsessive-compulsive disorder or a specific phobia usually needs exposure as well. Other criticisms are that Rogers's concepts are hard to measure, that the theory is optimistic to the point of naivety (May's objection), that it reflects an individualistic Western culture, and that non-directiveness can leave some clients floundering. On the other side of the ledger, Rogers made the relationship a respectable research topic, pioneered process research, and gave the whole helping world its basic listening skills, including the foundations of motivational interviewing (Section 6.9). Exam trap The Q-sort was devised by William Stephenson (1953); Rogers's Chicago group made it famous by using it to measure the gap between self and ideal self, which is why some questions credit "Stephenson and Rogers". Its defining feature is that one person sorts statements into a forced, roughly normal distribution , so it captures variation within a person rather than differences between people. It was not designed to replace the MMPI or any other inventory, and it is not a diagnostic test. Do not mix up the three scales of this section either: Rogers and Rablen's Process Scale rates fixity versus fluidity in recorded sessions, the Q-sort measures the self-concept, and Truax and Carkhuff's scales rate the therapist's empathy, warmth and genuineness. Encounter groups In the 1960s Rogers became one of the leaders of the human potential movement, whose favourite instrument was the encounter group. An encounter group is a small, relatively unstructured group, typically meeting intensively over a weekend or longer, whose purpose is personal growth, greater self-awareness and more honest relationships, achieved through open self-disclosure, here-and-now expression of feelings and frank feedback from other members. Its members are usually ordinary people seeking growth rather than patients seeking treatment, and its aim is neither diagnosis nor team building. Encounter groups grew partly out of the T-groups (training groups) begun by Kurt Lewin and his colleagues in the late 1940s at the National Training Laboratories in Bethel, Maine, whose aim was to teach people about group dynamics and leadership (Chapter 7). Centres such as the Esalen Institute at Big Sur, California, founded in 1962, made such groups famous. Rogers described his own version, the "basic encounter group", in Carl Rogers on Encounter Groups (1970) and called the intensive group experience perhaps the most significant social invention of the century. He described a typical sequence of about fifteen process patterns, which begins with milling around and resistance to personal expression, moves through the expression of negative feelings, the expression of personally meaningful material, the cracking of façades, feedback and confrontation, and reaches "the basic encounter", in which members meet one another more directly than in ordinary life, followed by expressions of closeness and changes in behaviour. Were encounter groups helpful? The best study, Encounter Groups: First Facts (1973) by Morton Lieberman, Irvin Yalom and Matthew Miles, assigned about 200 Stanford students to 18 groups representing 10 different approaches. About a third of participants benefited, a similar proportion were unchanged, and about 8 percent were "casualties" who suffered lasting harm. The casualties came mostly from groups run by aggressive, charismatic, confrontational leaders; the best results came from leaders who were caring and who helped members make sense of what was happening to them. Exam trap The principal role of an encounter group is to encourage personal growth and self-change through self-disclosure and interaction. Simply "interacting socially", "team building" and "aiding the therapist in diagnosis" are the bait. Keep the group formats apart: encounter groups (Rogers, personal growth), T-groups (Lewin, learning group dynamics and interpersonal skills), psychodrama (Jacob Moreno, acting out one's life on a stage) and the therapeutic community (Maxwell Jones, a whole hospital ward run democratically as a treatment). The last three are taught in Chapters 7 and 9. 6.3 Gestalt Therapy High yield · 10 Qs Go back to the second of the Gloria films. Rogers had followed Gloria wherever she went; the bearded man in his early seventies who interviewed her next seemed almost to go out of his way to unsettle her. Within minutes he was commenting on her smile, her fidgeting hands and the way she held her body, and when she said she was frightened of him he told her she was not frightened at all, merely playing at it. Why would a therapist deliberately frustrate a frightened client? Because, in his view, Gloria's trouble was not a lack of acceptance but a lack of awareness . She was, he thought, playing the helpless little girl so that someone else would do her work for her, and the cure was to frustrate that game skilfully until she discovered the support she already had inside herself. The man was Fritz Perls, and his therapy is the subject of this section. Gestalt therapy shares the humanistic faith in growth and the existential stress on freedom and responsibility, but its method is quite different from Rogers's. Where the person-centred therapist offers conditions and waits, the Gestalt therapist is active, inventive and sometimes provocative, and works through what the client is doing, feeling and sensing in the room, right now. Fritz Perls and the making of Gestalt therapy Fritz Perls (Friedrich Salomon Perls, 1893 to 1970) was born in Berlin, the youngest of three children of a middle-class Jewish family. He was a rebellious pupil who failed a school year twice, served as a medic in the First World War, and qualified in medicine in 1920. In 1926 he became an assistant to the neurologist Kurt Goldstein at an institute for brain-injured soldiers in Frankfurt. Goldstein, who studied his patients through the lens of Gestalt psychology, taught that the organism functions as a whole and strives to actualise itself, and that what a person perceives as figure against ground tells you how that person is organising his world. In Frankfurt Perls also met Laura Perls (born Lore Posner, 1905 to 1990), a student of Gestalt psychology who became his wife and his lifelong intellectual partner. Perls trained as a psychoanalyst in Vienna and Berlin. He was analysed first by Karen Horney (the neo-Freudian whose theory of personality you meet in the Personality book) and later by Wilhelm Reich, whose attention to posture, voice and "character armour" (chronic muscular tension that holds feelings back) shaped Perls's lifelong habit of watching the body rather than listening only to words. When the Nazis came to power the Perlses fled, and in 1934 they settled in Johannesburg, where Perls founded the South African Institute for Psychoanalysis in 1935. There he read Holism and Evolution (1926) by the South African statesman Jan Smuts, the book that coined the word "holism". In 1936 he travelled to the International Psychoanalytic Congress at Marienbad with a paper on "oral resistances" that was coolly received, and his brief visit to Freud in Vienna the same year lasted only a few minutes and left him feeling snubbed. Perls was moving away from psychoanalysis. The break appeared in his first book, Ego, Hunger and Aggression , written in South Africa and first published in Durban in 1942 (a London edition followed in 1947), with several chapters written by Laura, who was not credited. Its central metaphor is eating. A healthy person bites off experience, chews it and digests it, keeping what nourishes and rejecting what does not; a disturbed person either refuses to bite at all or swallows other people's ideas whole, without chewing. Perls called his method at this stage "concentration therapy". In 1946 the Perlses moved to New York, where they joined forces with Paul Goodman (1911 to 1972), a writer and social critic. The founding text, Gestalt Therapy: Excitement and Growth in the Human Personality (1951), was written by Perls, Ralph Hefferline (a Columbia University psychologist who contributed a set of awareness exercises) and Goodman (who wrote most of the theory). In 1952 Fritz, Laura and Goodman set up the New York Institute for Gestalt Therapy, which Laura went on to lead for decades. Perls himself was restless. He travelled, founded training groups in several cities, and from 1964 to 1969 lived as resident teacher at the Esalen Institute at Big Sur, California, the centre of the human potential movement you met in Section 6.2. His weekend demonstration workshops there, recorded in Gestalt Therapy Verbatim (1969), made him famous. In 1969 he moved to Cowichan Lake on Vancouver Island, Canada, to start a Gestalt community, and he died in Chicago in March 1970. Gestalt therapy is therefore a blend. From psychoanalysis it kept the interest in conflict and resistance (but not the unconscious as a hidden storehouse to be interpreted). From Reich it took the body. From Goldstein, Smuts and Gestalt psychology it took holism and the language of figure and ground. From the philosopher Salomo Friedlaender it took the idea that life is organised in polarities balanced around a creative middle point. From existentialism and phenomenology it took the here and now and the stress on responsibility; from Zen Buddhism, the value of simple, non-judging awareness; and from Jacob Moreno's psychodrama (Chapter 7), the practice of acting things out rather than talking about them. Exam trap Gestalt therapy is not Gestalt psychology. Gestalt psychology was the German school of perception founded by Max Wertheimer (with Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka) around 1912; it studied how we perceive organised wholes, and it is taught in the General Psychology book. Gestalt therapy is Perls's psychotherapy of the 1940s and 1950s. The Gestalt psychologists themselves rejected the connection: Mary Henle, one of their students, concluded in 1978 that Perls had borrowed the vocabulary without the substance. Gestalt therapy was founded by Fritz Perls with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman ; the 1951 book is by Perls, Hefferline and Goodman. Karen Horney was one of Perls's analysts, not a Gestalt therapist and not the founder of logotherapy. Core ideas: wholes, figure and ground, the here and now The German word Gestalt has no exact English equivalent; it means a form, shape or configuration, an organised whole that is more than the sum of its parts. Gestalt therapy can be defined as an experiential and existential therapy that aims at growth and integration through moment-to-moment awareness of what one is feeling, sensing and doing, and how, in the here and now. Its view of the healthy person rests on organismic self-regulation : left to itself, the organism attends to its most pressing need, meets it, and moves on. Perls described this process in the language of perception. At any moment one need stands out as the figure while everything else recedes into the ground . Imagine a student in a Mysuru examination hall. For an hour the question paper is the figure. Then thirst grows until it becomes the figure, the paper fades into the ground, the student asks for water and drinks, and with the need satisfied, thirst recedes and the paper returns. Each such episode is a gestalt that forms and closes. Later Gestalt therapists, notably Joseph Zinker in Creative Process in Gestalt Therapy (1977), drew the episode as a cycle of experience, shown in Figure 6.2: a sensation arises, becomes awareness, mobilises energy, leads to action, makes contact with the environment, and ends in satisfied withdrawal, ready for the next figure. The cycle of experience (after Zinker, 1977) Sensation Awareness Mobilisation of energy Action Contact Withdrawal A need becomes figure, is met through contact, and recedes into ground Cycle interrupted: unfinished business Figure 6.2 The Gestalt cycle of experience. A healthy need runs the whole cycle and closes; when the cycle is blocked (here, energy is mobilised but never turned into action), the gestalt stays open as unfinished business. What happens when a gestalt cannot close? A son who never told his dying father that he loved him, a woman who swallowed her anger at a humiliation years ago, a girl who was never allowed to grieve: in each case a need was mobilised and then blocked. The incomplete gestalt does not fade. It remains as unfinished business , unexpressed feelings (resentment, grief, guilt, longing) that press for completion and intrude on the present as preoccupation, tension, repeated quarrels or bodily symptoms. Perls thought resentment the most common and most troublesome kind. Much of Gestalt therapy consists of bringing unfinished business into the present so that it can at last be finished. Notice the phrase "into the present". Gestalt therapy is radically a therapy of the here and now . Perls taught that the past exists only as memory and the future only as anticipation, both of them experienced now; therefore the past is worked with only as it lives in the client today. He even defined anxiety as "the gap between the now and the then": the stage fright of a person rehearsing a future he cannot yet control. For the same reason the Gestalt therapist asks what and how rather than why . "Why do you feel angry with your mother?" invites explanations, theories and excuses, which Perls regarded as a way of talking about life instead of living it. "What are you doing with your hands as you speak of her? How do you feel as you do it?" brings the client back to experience. "Lose your mind and come to your senses" was one of Perls's slogans. The goal is awareness : full contact with what one is sensing, feeling, wanting and doing. "Awareness per se, by and of itself, can be curative," Perls wrote, because an organism that is fully aware will regulate itself. He distinguished three zones of awareness: the inner zone (bodily sensations and feelings), the outer zone (the world as seen, heard and touched) and the middle zone of fantasy (thinking, planning, remembering, imagining), in which neurotic people spend far too much of their time. With awareness comes responsibility, which Perls liked to spell "response-ability": the ability to respond, and the ownership of one's own feelings and actions. Clients are therefore taught to say "I won't" instead of "I can't", and "I choose to" instead of "I have to". Maturity, in Perls's phrase, is "the transcendence from environmental support to self-support". The neurotic person manipulates the environment for support, by playing helpless, confused or charming, and the therapist's job is to frustrate these manoeuvres warmly but firmly until the client finds his own feet. That is what Perls was doing with Gloria. How does change happen? Arnold Beisser stated what he called the paradoxical theory of change in 1970: "change occurs when one becomes what he is, not when he tries to become what he is not." A client who fights his sadness stays stuck in the fight; one who fully experiences and owns the sadness finds that it moves. The therapist therefore does not push the client toward a goal but helps him become more fully what he already is. Perls also pictured the neurotic personality as five layers that must be peeled away on the road to authentic living. The phony (or cliché) layer is made of stereotyped, inauthentic games ("How are you?" "Fine!"). The phobic layer is the avoidance of the pain of seeing ourselves as we are. At the impasse the external supports have been removed but internal support has not yet been found, and the person feels stuck, empty and dead; Perls regarded it as the decisive point of therapy. At the implosive layer the person feels the energy that has been held back, turned in upon itself, and in the explosive layer it is released into authentic experience, which Perls said takes four forms: grief, anger, joy and orgasm. Contact and its disturbances Growth, for the Gestalt therapist, happens at the contact boundary , the meeting point between the person and the environment, where the person both connects with and stays separate from what is not himself. "Contact is the lifeblood of growth," wrote Erving and Miriam Polster in Gestalt Therapy Integrated (1973). Good contact means meeting other people and things vividly while keeping one's own identity. Problems arise when a person habitually interrupts contact in one of several characteristic ways, the contact boundary disturbances . Perls, Hefferline and Goodman (1951) described five, ending with egotism; the Polsters' list of five, the one most textbooks use, keeps introjection, projection, retroflection and confluence, drops egotism and adds deflection. Table 6.3 sets out all six. Table 6.3 The contact boundary disturbances of Gestalt therapy. Disturbance What the person does Everyday example Introjection Swallows other people's values and rules whole, without chewing them over "A good daughter-in-law never disagrees", held as an unquestioned personal rule Projection Disowns a part of himself by attributing it to the environment Blaming the professor for failing an examination one did not study for Retroflection Does to himself what he wants to do to others, or does for himself what he wants others to do for him Biting one's nails instead of expressing anger; "I will manage on my own" Deflection Turns aside from direct contact Joking, vagueness, over-politeness, talking about someone instead of to them Confluence Lets the boundary between self and other dissolve; a high need for acceptance and liking leads to enmeshment "We always feel exactly the same about everything" Egotism Watches and controls himself instead of engaging spontaneously Judging every sentence as one speaks it Each disturbance is easiest to remember as a direction of traffic across the boundary. In introjection something from outside comes in without being digested: Perls's eating metaphor again. Children inevitably introject their parents' values, and some introjection is harmless, but an adult whose "shoulds" are all borrowed lives by rules he has never examined; introjects are the raw material of the top dog you will meet shortly. In projection traffic flows the other way: something inside is placed outside. The person who cannot own his hostility experiences everyone else as hostile; the student who did not prepare sees an unfair examiner. In retroflection the energy that should go out turns back on the self, so that anger becomes self-blame, tension or self-harm, and the wish to be cared for becomes grim self-sufficiency. In deflection the person avoids the impact of contact by blunting it, with humour, abstraction, generalities or a change of subject. In confluence there is no boundary at all: the person merges with others, needs them to agree, and cannot tell where his feelings end and theirs begin. In egotism (a special Gestalt meaning of the word) the person stands outside his own experience, monitoring it, so that nothing is risked and nothing is fully lived. None of these is pathological in itself. Healthy confluence is part of empathy and of intimacy; healthy retroflection is self-control; healthy introjection lets a child learn. The question the Gestalt therapist asks is whether the person is aware of using the style and whether it lets present needs be met. Notice also the overlap with psychoanalytic vocabulary. In psychoanalysis projection and introjection are defence mechanisms of the ego (taught with the other defences in the Personality book); in Gestalt therapy they are styles of contact. The words are the same, but the frame is different. Exam trap "A high need for acceptance and liking, resulting in enmeshment" is confluence , not projection, introjection or retroflection. "Swallowing whole" is introjection; "doing to oneself what one wants to do to others" is retroflection; "turning aside with jokes or vagueness" is deflection. The Polsters' standard five are introjection, projection, retroflection, deflection and confluence; egotism belongs to the original 1951 list. A related stem from the Personality syllabus asks for "any distorting or selective effect of a person's inner world on his perception or conception of the outer world". RML 2024 keyed denial , but that wording is the broad, classic definition of projection (the idea behind projective tests). Denial refuses to admit one particular painful fact; it does not colour perception in general. If the stem reappears, projection is the defensible answer. The techniques: experiments in awareness Gestalt therapists do not call their methods techniques so much as experiments : something the client is invited to try, here and now, to discover what happens. Some are simple. The therapist may ask "What are you aware of now?", or invite the client to begin a string of sentences with "Now I am aware that...", following his attention from moment to moment (the awareness continuum). The therapist reports observations rather than interpretations: "I notice that your voice drops when you mention your brother." When a client shows a small gesture, he may be asked to exaggerate it (a clenched fist made tighter and tighter, until the client says "I want to hit something"). Reversal asks a soft-spoken client to try speaking loudly, or a relentlessly cheerful one to voice a complaint, so that the disowned pole of a polarity comes into awareness. Asked to stay with a feeling rather than escape it, the client learns that the feeling can be lived through. The therapist may ask "May I feed you a sentence?" and offer a statement for the client to try on ("I am angry with you"), to see whether it fits. Language receives close attention, because the way we speak reveals how we disown experience. A client who says "It is frightening" is asked to say "I am frightened"; "You feel lonely in this city" becomes "I feel lonely"; "I can't tell him" becomes "I won't tell him"; "I need to" becomes "I want to"; "I have to" becomes "I choose to". A question that is really a statement ("Don't you think I should leave the course?") is turned into the statement it conceals ("I want to leave the course"). "But" may be replaced by "and", so that two feelings are allowed to stand side by side. In group work a client may be asked to make the rounds , saying a sentence such as "I am afraid you will laugh at me" to each member in turn and adding "and I take responsibility for it" to statements of feeling. The most famous experiment of all is the empty chair technique . The client imagines a person (often someone dead, absent or impossible to confront) sitting in an empty chair and speaks to that person directly, in the present tense. He may then move to the other chair and answer as the other person. Because the client speaks to rather than about , feelings that have been held for years come into the room. Consider a worked example. Meera, aged twenty-eight, was working in Bengaluru when her father collapsed in Mysuru; he died before she could reach home, and two years later she still cannot enter his room. Talking about her grief has changed nothing. Her Gestalt therapist places an empty chair in front of her and asks her to see her father in it. Hesitantly at first, then in a flood, Meera tells him that she is sorry she was not there, that she was angry he never told anyone he was ill, and that she loves him. Invited to sit in his chair and answer as him, she hears herself say, in his voice, "You did not fail me. I was proud of you." Back in her own chair she says goodbye. The unfinished business has been finished, not by insight but by completing in the present the act that the past interrupted. The two-chair technique uses the same method for conflicts inside the person. Each side of an inner split is given its own chair, and the client moves between them, speaking for each side in turn. Perls's favourite split was between the top dog and the underdog . The top dog is the righteous, demanding, perfectionist voice ("You should have cleared the examination last year; you are lazy; you are wasting your parents' money"). The underdog is the apologetic, helpless, wheedling voice ("I am trying my best; I will start properly tomorrow"). The top dog commands and the underdog promises, but the underdog usually wins, by stalling and sabotage. Dialogue between them, with the client fully inhabiting each side, tends to soften the critic and lead to an integration that neither side could reach alone. The same format is used for a dialogue between two parts of the body (one hand against the other), between the client and a symptom ("Be your headache: what do you say to Ravi?"), or between the client and a parent who lives on as an introject. In his workshops Perls used the hot seat . One volunteer at a time took the chair beside Perls and worked with him on an issue, usually with the empty chair facing them, while the rest of the group watched; the others learned by identifying with the person at work. The format suited demonstrations, and it is one reason Gestalt therapy became known as a dramatic, leader-centred method. Dreams receive special treatment. Freud had called the dream the royal road to the unconscious; Perls called it "the royal road to integration". He did not interpret dreams. Instead, every person and every object in a dream was treated as a projection of a disowned part of the dreamer, and the client was asked to tell the dream in the present tense and then to become each element in turn, speaking as it ("I am the locked door. I keep everyone out. Nobody gets in to hurt me"). When the dreamer finds that he is also the door, he reowns a part of himself. Gestalt therapists also give homework, asking clients to carry the experiments into daily life. Perls summed up his individualism in the "Gestalt prayer", printed in Gestalt Therapy Verbatim (1969): I do my thing and you do your thing. I am not in this world to live up to your expectations, and you are not in this world to live up to mine. You are you, and I am I, and if by chance we find each other, it's beautiful. If not, it can't be helped. The prayer captured the spirit of the 1960s, and it also captured the criticism that would follow. In 1972 Walter Tubbs published a reply, "Beyond Perls", warning that if each of us simply does his own thing, we risk losing each other and ourselves. Exam trap The empty chair belongs to Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) ; it is the single most examined fact in this section. It is not person-centred therapy (reflection), psychoanalysis (free association, interpretation), CBT or REBT (disputing beliefs), dialectical behaviour therapy (skills training) or Bowen's family systems therapy (the genogram, Chapter 7). Emotion-focused therapy (Section 6.7), schema therapy and psychodrama later borrowed chair work, but the hallmark is Gestalt. Keep the chairs apart: the empty chair is for unfinished business with another person; the two-chair dialogue is for a split within the self; the hot seat is the workshop chair beside the leader. Top dog and underdog are Gestalt terms, not the Parent and Child ego states of Eric Berne's transactional analysis. Evaluation For many years Gestalt therapy had almost no research behind it; Perls thought that experiments in awareness, not statistics, were the proper test of his ideas. The research that does exist came mainly from Leslie Greenberg and his colleagues, who took the chair techniques into the laboratory. In a series of studies from the late 1970s onward, Greenberg showed that when a client voiced a "split" (two sides of the self in conflict), a two-chair dialogue at that moment led to deeper experiencing and more resolution of the conflict than empathic reflection alone. The empty chair received the same treatment. Key study: resolving unfinished business with the empty chair (Paivio and Greenberg, 1995) Question. Does empty-chair work actually resolve long-standing unfinished business with a significant other? Method. Sandra Paivio and Leslie Greenberg, in Toronto, randomly assigned adults troubled by unresolved feelings toward someone important in their lives (most often a parent who had neglected or abused them) either to twelve weeks of experiential therapy built around empty-chair dialogue or to a psychoeducational group about the same issues. Results. The experiential clients improved more on general symptoms, interpersonal problems and the resolution of their unfinished business, and the gains held at follow-up. Conclusion. Chair work can be a specific, effective intervention when it is used with the right problem at the right moment. Criticism. The trial was small, the comparison group was a less intensive treatment, and the therapists were committed to the method. Broader reviews of the humanistic-experiential family by Robert Elliott, Greenberg and their colleagues have found large improvements from pre-treatment to post-treatment, and roughly equal effectiveness when these therapies are compared head to head with others; the small advantage sometimes found for CBT tends to shrink once the researchers' own allegiance is taken into account (Chapter 8). The criticisms are as well known as the techniques. Classical Gestalt therapy depended heavily on the personality of Perls himself, and in the hands of imitators it could become confrontational and even harmful; you saw in Section 6.2 that Lieberman, Yalom and Miles found the most casualties in encounter groups led by aggressive, charismatic leaders. Its contempt for "thinking" and explanation could be anti-intellectual, and its individualism (the Gestalt prayer) sat uneasily with clients whose lives are built around families and communities, as most lives in India are. Modern Gestalt therapy has moved a long way from the Esalen stage. Relational or dialogic Gestalt therapists such as Gary Yontef and Lynne Jacobs, drawing on Martin Buber's idea of the I-Thou relationship (Section 6.4), stress a warm, respectful, collaborative relationship, and the chair techniques live on in emotion-focused therapy and schema therapy. Clinical link Chair work is powerful, which is exactly why it needs care. A grieving or guilt-ridden client can be helped enormously by an empty-chair goodbye, but a client with psychosis, severe dissociation or a fragile sense of self may be overwhelmed or confused by speaking to an imagined person, and a trauma survivor pushed too quickly to confront an abuser in the chair may be retraumatised. Experienced therapists wait for a clear marker (unfinished business, a self-critical split), explain the experiment, ask permission, and make sure the client leaves the session grounded.
