The therapies in this section and the next go to the source. Existential therapy is less a set of methods than a way of looking at human life and its troubles. It asks what it means to be a person who knows that he will die, who must choose without any guarantee of being right, who can never fully share his inner life with another, and who lives in a universe that does not hand him a ready-made purpose. Its first practitioners were European psychiatrists, trained in psychoanalysis, who found that Freud's biological drives explained too little about the anguished, confused, choosing people in front of them. Existential therapy can be defined as a philosophically based approach that helps clients face the inescapable conditions of human existence (the existential givens , such as death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness) and live more authentically, with awareness, choice and responsibility. Like Gestalt therapy it values the present and experience; like Rogers it values the relationship; but its mood is more sober. Anxiety, for the existentialist, is not a symptom to be removed but a normal part of being human, and sometimes a teacher. The philosophers of existence You cannot understand existential therapy without a few philosophers, because its vocabulary comes straight from them. Table 6.4 lists the ones that therapists cite most often and the single idea each lent to therapy. Table 6.4 The philosophical roots of existential therapy. Thinker Dates Key work Idea taken into therapy Søren Kierkegaard (Danish) 1813 to 1855 The Concept of Anxiety (1844) Anxiety is "the dizziness of freedom"; becoming a self means choosing Friedrich Nietzsche (German) 1844 to 1900 Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883 to 1885) Create your own values; "he who has a why to live can bear almost any how" (from Twilight of the Idols , 1889) Edmund Husserl (German) 1859 to 1938 Ideas (1913) Phenomenology: describe experience as it appears, bracketing assumptions Martin Heidegger (German) 1889 to 1976 Being and Time (1927) Dasein, being-in-the-world, thrownness, authenticity, being-towards-death Martin Buber (Austrian-Israeli) 1878 to 1965 I and Thou (1923) The I-Thou meeting of persons versus the I-It use of objects Jean-Paul Sartre (French) 1905 to 1980 Being and Nothingness (1943) Existence precedes essence; we are "condemned to be free"; bad faith Paul Tillich (German-American) 1886 to 1965 The Courage to Be (1952) Courage is affirming oneself in spite of anxiety about non-being Two of these thinkers matter most for the examination. Martin Heidegger (1889 to 1976) described human existence as Dasein , a German word meaning literally "being there". His point was that a person is never a mind sitting inside a body looking out at a separate world; to exist as a human is always already to be in a world, involved with things, people and projects. He wrote the phrase as being-in-the-world, with hyphens, to stress that it is a single, indivisible whole. We are "thrown" into a world we did not choose (a family, a body, a time and place); we tend to live inauthentically, doing what "one" does, absorbed in the anonymous crowd that Heidegger called das Man (the "they"); and we become authentic when we face our own finitude, our being-towards-death, and choose our own way. Jean-Paul Sartre (1905 to 1980) put the existentialist creed into a slogan in a famous lecture of 1945: "existence precedes essence". A paper knife is designed for a purpose before it exists; a human being exists first and must then define himself through choices. We are "condemned to be free", and when we pretend otherwise ("I had no choice; that is just how I am") we are in what Sartre called bad faith . Daseinsanalysis: Binswanger and Boss The first psychiatrists to apply Heidegger to their patients were two Swiss. Ludwig Binswanger (1881 to 1966) directed the Bellevue sanatorium at Kreuzlingen, on the Swiss shore of Lake Constance, which his family had run for generations. He was a lifelong friend of Freud, and their friendship survived his growing disagreement with Freud's biological theory. From the late 1920s Binswanger turned to Heidegger and developed what he called Daseinsanalysis ( Daseinsanalyse ): the attempt to understand a patient's whole way of being-in-the-world, and especially his world-design , the overall pattern through which his world is disclosed to him and which limits what he can experience. His most famous case was Ellen West, a young woman tormented by a dread of becoming fat and a craving for food (today we would speak of an eating disorder), who took her own life in 1921; Binswanger's long analysis of her existence, published in 1944, became a classic of existential psychiatry. Binswanger described three simultaneous modes in which every person is in the world, and these are the most examined terms in this section. The Umwelt ("world around") is the biological and physical world: the body, its drives and needs, and the natural environment into which we are thrown and which we share with animals; its time is clock time. The Mitwelt ("with-world") is the world of relationships with other people, in which, as Rollo May put it, "in the encounter both persons are changed". The Eigenwelt ("own world") is the person's relationship with himself: self-awareness, the sense of "for me" that colours every experience. These are not three places but three aspects of a single existence. When you eat a meal with your family you are in the Umwelt (the body being fed), the Mitwelt (the conversation and the bonds at the table) and the Eigenwelt (your awareness of what this meal means to you) all at once. Binswanger and May argued that psychoanalysis and behaviourism dealt mainly with the Umwelt and neglected the other two, especially the Eigenwelt. Much later the British existential therapist Emmy van Deurzen added a fourth dimension, the Überwelt ("over-world"), a person's relationship with beliefs, values and the spiritual or ideal world. Medard Boss (1903 to 1990), a Zurich psychiatrist, had a brief analysis with Freud in Vienna as a young man and trained further as an analyst before coming under Heidegger's influence. The two became close friends, and from 1959 to 1969 Heidegger travelled regularly to Boss's home at Zollikon, near Zurich, to teach philosophy to psychiatrists and trainees (the Zollikon seminars). In Psychoanalysis and Daseinsanalysis (English edition 1963) Boss kept the practice of psychoanalysis, the couch and free association, while discarding Freud's theory of drives and energies. He asked what possibilities of existence a patient had closed off: in what ways he was open or closed to others (the spatiality of existence), how he lived his time (temporality), how his mood attuned him to some things and blinded him to others, and how his inevitable guilt (every choice forecloses other possibilities) and his mortality shaped his life. Boss treated dreams phenomenologically: a dream was not a disguised wish to be decoded but a way the dreamer's existence showed itself, to be explored just as it appeared. Exam trap Dasein ("being there", being-in-the-world) is Heidegger's term and belongs to existential psychology , not to behavioural, cognitive or psychoanalytic psychology. Its three modes are Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt (biological world, social world, own world), with van Deurzen's Überwelt as a later fourth. The other trios offered in such questions belong elsewhere: id, ego and superego are Freud's structural model; conscious, preconscious and unconscious are Freud's topographical model; sensorimotor, preoperational and concrete operational are Piaget's stages (Developmental book). Do not confuse Binswanger and Boss's Daseinsanalysis with Frankl's Existenzanalyse , the German name for logotherapy (Section 6.5). Rollo May and existential anxiety It was an American, Rollo May (1909 to 1994), who brought these European ideas to the English-speaking world. May was born in Ohio, studied with Alfred Adler in Vienna in the early 1930s, and then studied theology at Union Theological Seminary in New York, where the theologian Paul Tillich became his friend and mentor. In his early thirties he contracted tuberculosis and spent many months in a sanatorium, uncertain whether he would live. There he noticed that the patients who passively accepted their condition seemed to decline, while those who fought it did better, and he began to think about anxiety from the inside. His doctoral dissertation, published as The Meaning of Anxiety (1950), was among the first clinical psychology doctorates awarded by Columbia University. With Ernest Angel and Henri Ellenberger he edited Existence (1958), which translated Binswanger, Minkowski and other European existential psychiatrists for American readers and effectively launched existential psychology in the United States. His later books, Love and Will (1969), The Courage to Create (1975) and Freedom and Destiny (1981), reached a wide public. For May, anxiety is "the apprehension cued off by a threat to some value which the individual holds essential to his existence as a personality". At bottom it is the awareness that we could cease to be, and the awareness that we are free. May, and later May and Yalom together, distinguished two kinds. Normal anxiety is proportionate to the threat, does not require repression, and can be faced and used creatively; the anxiety of a student before a decisive examination, or of anyone choosing a career or a partner, is of this kind. Neurotic anxiety is out of proportion to the situation, involves repression and other defences, and is destructive rather than constructive, paralysing the person instead of mobilising him. Existential anxiety is the normal anxiety that comes with the givens of existence: death, freedom, choice and the possibility of meaninglessness. Its companion is existential guilt , the guilt we incur not by breaking rules but by failing to live up to our own possibilities. The existential therapist does not try to abolish normal anxiety; he helps the client find the courage to live with it. May also wrote about the daimonic , any natural function (sex, anger, the craving for power) that can either drive creativity or, if denied, take over the whole person destructively. This concept was at the heart of his 1982 open letter to Rogers, mentioned in Section 6.1: a therapy that sees only the actualising tendency, May argued, cannot account for human evil. The American blend of European existentialism with humanistic warmth, associated with May and with James Bugental (1915 to 2008), author of The Search for Authenticity (1965), is called existential-humanistic therapy . Bugental emphasised the therapist's presence , full attention to the client's subjective, moment-to-moment experience, and the client's search for authenticity. Irvin Yalom's four ultimate concerns The clearest map of the existential territory was drawn by Irvin Yalom (born 1931), an American psychiatrist and long-time professor at Stanford University. Yalom is famous in two fields. In group therapy his The Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy (first published in 1970) set out the therapeutic factors, eleven in the form you will study in Chapter 7. In individual therapy his Existential Psychotherapy (1980) became the standard textbook, and his books of case stories, beginning with Love's Executioner (1989), made existential therapy readable for the general public. Yalom argued that four ultimate concerns lie beneath much human distress. Each is an existential conflict between something we wish for and a hard fact of existence: Death. We wish to go on being, and we know that we will die. Death anxiety is the most basic anxiety, and much psychopathology can be understood as a clumsy defence against it. Freedom. In the existential sense, freedom means the absence of any external structure: we are the authors of our own lives, choices and meanings, with no ground beneath us. Freedom brings responsibility , and with it the dread of having to choose and the temptation to avoid choosing. Isolation. However close we become to others, an unbridgeable gap remains: we enter and leave existence alone, and no one can live our life for us. Meaninglessness. We are meaning-seeking creatures thrown into a universe that has no built-in meaning. If we must die, construct our own world and remain ultimately alone, what meaning does life have? A useful mnemonic is "Death Frees Isolated Minds": death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness. Table 6.5 shows how Yalom tied each concern to characteristic defences and to the work of therapy. Table 6.5 Yalom's four ultimate concerns (1980). Ultimate concern The conflict Typical defences or problems What therapy works toward Death Wish to continue versus awareness of inevitable death Specialness ("death is for others"; workaholism, heroics); the ultimate rescuer ("someone will always save me") Facing death so that it awakens fuller living Freedom Wish for ground and structure versus groundlessness Avoiding responsibility: blaming others, playing the victim, compulsivity; inability to wish, will or decide Owning responsibility; wishing, willing and deciding Isolation Wish for contact versus ultimate aloneness Fusion with others; using people as objects to avoid aloneness Accepting aloneness and relating to others as ends, not means Meaninglessness Need for meaning versus a universe without given meaning Emptiness, boredom, aimless activity, nihilism Engagement in life, from which meaning follows Two ideas from the table deserve a word more. Yalom described two great defences against death anxiety. Specialness is the deep, irrational belief that the ordinary laws of mortality do not apply to me, which can show itself in driven achievement, reckless heroics or narcissism. The ultimate rescuer is the belief that some person or power will always step in to save me, which can show itself in clinging dependence. Yalom also distinguished three kinds of isolation: interpersonal isolation (distance from other people, the ordinary loneliness of the friendless), intrapersonal isolation (being cut off from parts of oneself, through defences) and existential isolation (the unbridgeable gulf between oneself and any other being, which no relationship can abolish). Yalom's convictions were shaped by years of work with groups of people dying of cancer. Again and again he saw that confronting death, far from crushing people, often woke them up: they dropped trivial concerns, said what they had never said, and lived their remaining time more fully. He called this an "awakening experience" and summed it up in a much-quoted line: "Although the physicality of death destroys us, the idea of death saves us." On meaninglessness, Yalom agreed with Frankl (Section 6.5) that meaning cannot be pursued head-on; it ensues from engagement , wholehearted involvement in love, work, creation and the welfare of others. Exam trap Yalom's four ultimate concerns are death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness . The distractors are invented sets ("past, present, future and eternity"; "love, work, play and transcendence"; "birth, life, death and rebirth"). Do not confuse the four ultimate concerns ( Existential Psychotherapy , 1980) with Yalom's eleven therapeutic factors of group therapy (from his group therapy textbook, first published in 1970), such as instillation of hope and universality (Chapter 7); "existential factors" is one of those eleven, which is a common source of mix-ups. Existential therapy in practice, and its evaluation What does an existential therapist actually do? There is no manual, and existential therapists distrust technique, which they fear turns the client into an object (an "It" in Buber's language) to be fixed. The work is carried by the relationship, an encounter between two people, and by a steady focus on the client's freedom, choices and responsibility. Yalom's own formula was that "it's the relationship that heals". In practice this means several things. The therapist attends to the here and now of the relationship itself, asking, for example, how the client is relating to the therapist right now, because the way he avoids or engages here mirrors the way he lives. The therapist uses the phenomenological method , which the British existential therapist Ernesto Spinelli summarised as three rules: bracket your assumptions (the epoché ), describe rather than explain, and treat every element of the client's account as potentially equally important rather than deciding in advance what matters. The therapist notices, and gently challenges, the ways in which the client disowns responsibility ("My wife makes me angry"; "I can't help it; that is my nature"). And the therapist does not shrink from the big themes: death, loss, guilt, aloneness and purpose are welcome topics, not distractions from the "real" work. Britain developed its own school. Ronald David Laing (1927 to 1989), a Scottish psychiatrist, used existential phenomenology to make sense of schizophrenia in The Divided Self (1960), describing the "ontological insecurity" of a person who cannot take his own existence and identity for granted; his later experiment at Kingsley Hall in London (1965) made him a hero of the anti-psychiatry movement. Emmy van Deurzen founded the Society for Existential Analysis in London in 1988 and built a systematic existential approach around the four dimensions of existence. How well does it work? Existential therapy has generated far less controlled research than CBT, partly by choice. The best evidence concerns the meaning-centred therapies descended from Frankl: in a 2015 meta-analysis, Joël Vos, Mick Cooper and Meghan Craig found that structured, meaning-centred existential therapies improved clients' sense of meaning in life considerably and reduced psychopathology moderately, with the clearest results among people with serious physical illness such as cancer. The criticisms are familiar. The approach is vague and hard to teach; it suits reflective, verbal, well-educated clients better than others; and its stress on lonely individual choice reflects European philosophy more than collectivist cultures. Its defenders reply that its themes run through every therapy: you will find them in Yalom's group factors, in the values work of acceptance and commitment therapy (Chapter 5) and in palliative care. Clinical link Existential themes come to the clinic uninvited: a young man after a heart attack, a woman whose husband has died, a student who has failed the entrance examination for the third time and asks what the point of anything is. A clinician need not be an existential therapist to listen for them. Questions such as "What has this illness made you think about?" or "What matters most to you now?" open the door, and the existential stance (do not rush to reassure; stay with the client in the hard question) is especially valuable in oncology, palliative care, bereavement and suicide prevention (Chapter 9). Exam trap Keep the founders straight. Binswanger and Boss : Daseinsanalysis. Rollo May : existential anxiety, The Meaning of Anxiety (1950), Existence (1958), the daimonic. Yalom : the four ultimate concerns. Bugental : existential-humanistic therapy and presence. Laing : ontological insecurity. Frankl : logotherapy (next section). And keep the families apart: Maslow and Rogers are humanistic ; the existentialists see anxiety as a normal and inescapable part of existence, whereas for Rogers anxiety signals incongruence. 6.5 Viktor Frankl and Logotherapy High yield · 7 Qs In October 1944 a train carrying some fifteen hundred prisoners from the Theresienstadt ghetto pulled into the station at Auschwitz. The prisoners were made to file past an SS officer who looked each one over and, with a lazy movement of his forefinger, pointed to the right or to the left. Nobody knew what the gesture meant. One of the prisoners, a thirty-nine-year-old Viennese psychiatrist, straightened his back under a heavy rucksack so that he would look fit for work, and the officer, after a moment's hesitation, turned him by the shoulders to the right. That evening he learned the meaning of the finger game. For about nine out of every ten people on his transport, the left had meant the gas chambers within hours. Within a day he had lost his clothes, his hair, his name (he was now prisoner number 119104) and the possession he valued most, the manuscript of his first book, which he had hidden in his coat. The prisoner was Viktor Frankl, and the question that the following months forced upon him is the question of this section: when everything has been taken from a person, what is left, and what keeps that person alive? His answer became the best known and the most structured of the existential therapies introduced in Section 6.4, with its own vocabulary of the will to meaning, the existential vacuum, noogenic neurosis, paradoxical intention and dereflection. From Vienna to the camps Viktor Emil Frankl (1905 to 1997) was born in Vienna on 26 March 1905, the second of three children of a Jewish civil servant. He was a precocious schoolboy with a passion for psychology. While still at school he began a correspondence with Sigmund Freud, and Freud passed one of the young man's short papers to the International Journal of Psychoanalysis , which published it in 1924. Frankl then moved into the circle of Alfred Adler, the founder of individual psychology (Section 3.8), but he did not stay there long either. His insistence that people need meaning, and not only a sense of belonging and mastery, put him at odds with Adlerian orthodoxy, and in 1927 he was expelled from Adler's society. By then he was already using the word logotherapy in lectures for the approach he was developing. As a medical student Frankl organised free counselling centres for young people at the time of year when school reports were issued and student suicides peaked. He qualified in medicine at the University of Vienna in 1930, and from 1933 to 1937 he was in charge of the pavilion for suicidal women at the psychiatric hospital Am Steinhof, where he saw thousands of them. It is not hard to see where his lifelong preoccupation with meaning came from. After Germany annexed Austria in 1938, Jewish doctors were allowed to treat only Jewish patients. From 1940 Frankl headed the neurology department of the Rothschild Hospital, the only hospital in Vienna that still admitted Jews, and there he risked his life by writing false diagnoses so that mentally ill patients would not be handed over to the Nazi "euthanasia" programme, which was killing psychiatric patients. When an American visa finally came through, he let it lapse rather than leave his elderly parents to face deportation alone. In December 1941 he married Tilly Grosser, a nurse at the hospital. In September 1942 Frankl, his wife and his parents were deported to Theresienstadt, where his father died. In October 1944 he and Tilly were sent on to Auschwitz. His mother was murdered in the gas chambers there, his brother also perished in Auschwitz, and Tilly died in Bergen-Belsen. Frankl himself spent only a few days at Auschwitz before being moved to Kaufering and then Türkheim, subcamps of Dachau in Bavaria, where he worked as a labourer and later volunteered as a doctor among prisoners dying of typhus. He was liberated by American troops in April 1945, himself recovering from typhus, after nearly three years in four camps. He learned only after his return to Vienna that his wife, his mother and his brother were dead. Exam trap Logotherapy was founded by Viktor Frankl , not by Irvin Yalom (the four ultimate concerns), Rollo May (existential anxiety) or Karen Horney (a neo-Freudian, and one of Perls's analysts). Question papers often spell him "Victor"; it is the same man. Because Frankl was for a time a member of Adler's circle, his name turns up as a distractor in questions about Adler: the inferiority complex and the striving for superiority belong to Alfred Adler , not to Frankl, Jung or Erikson. What the camps taught Back in Vienna in 1945, Frankl dictated in nine days a short book about what he had lived through. It appeared in German in 1946 as Ein Psycholog erlebt das Konzentrationslager ("A psychologist experiences the concentration camp"). The English translation came out in 1959 as From Death-Camp to Existentialism , and from 1962, in a revised and enlarged edition whose second part summarises logotherapy (headed "Basic Concepts of Logotherapy" in the 1960s editions and "Logotherapy in a Nutshell" in later ones), it carried the title by which millions know it: Man's Search for Meaning . It has sold more than ten million copies. In 1946 he also published the book whose manuscript had been taken from him at Auschwitz and which he had reconstructed in shorthand on scraps of paper while ill with typhus: Ärztliche Seelsorge (in English, The Doctor and the Soul , 1955), the first systematic account of logotherapy. From 1946 to 1971 he headed the neurology department of the Vienna Polyclinic; he remarried in 1947, lectured all over the world and died in Vienna on 2 September 1997. Man's Search for Meaning is not a history of the camps but a psychologist's account of how ordinary prisoners lived inside them. Frankl described three phases in a prisoner's psychological reaction: shock on admission, mixed with the "delusion of reprieve" (the condemned man's belief that he will be spared at the last minute); then apathy, an emotional death that blunted feeling and so protected the prisoner from the daily horror; and, after liberation, depersonalisation (the world felt unreal and joy would not come), with bitterness and disillusionment for many. Within that general picture Frankl noticed something that the theories he had been taught did not predict. Hunger, cold and brutality stripped prisoners down to their most basic needs, just as a drive theory would expect, and yet people did not all become alike. Some behaved like beasts; others walked through the huts comforting others and gave away their last piece of bread. What distinguished those who held on? Frankl's answer was that they had something to live for. When two prisoners told him that they expected nothing more from life, he turned the question round and asked what life might still expect from them . One had a child waiting for him in another country; the other, a scientist, had a series of books still to finish. Each realised that he was irreplaceable to someone or something, and found a reason to go on. Frankl liked to quote Nietzsche (Table 6.4): "He who has a why to live can bear with almost any how ." The reverse was also true. The chief doctor of one camp told Frankl that in the week between Christmas 1944 and New Year 1945 the death rate rose beyond anything seen before, although work, food and weather had not changed. The doctor's explanation, which Frankl shared, was psychological: many prisoners had lived on the naive hope that they would be home by Christmas, and when the hope collapsed, their resistance collapsed with it. Even humour served survival: Frankl and a friend on his work gang promised each other to invent one funny story every day about life after liberation. From these observations came the most quoted sentence of the book: "Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way." The camp could take away almost every outer freedom, but it could not decide what stand a prisoner would take toward what was happening to him. On a freezing march before dawn, the image of his wife's face (he did not know that she was already dead) made the suffering bearable, and he grasped, he wrote, that "love is the ultimate and the highest goal to which man can aspire". These observations, not abstract philosophy, are what logotherapy was built from. Exam trap Dates for Man's Search for Meaning differ between sources because the book has three birthdays: the German original (1946), the first English translation (1959, as From Death-Camp to Existentialism ) and the present English title (from the revised edition of 1962; American textbooks often cite the 1963 paperback or the 1984 and 1992 editions). For the book's first publication, 1946 is the answer. The line "He who has a why to live can bear with almost any how" is Frankl quoting Nietzsche , not a sentence Frankl coined. The "last of the human freedoms" is the freedom to choose one's attitude , which is the root of Frankl's attitudinal values. The will to meaning and the paths to meaning The word logotherapy comes from the Greek logos , which Frankl translated as "meaning" (it can also mean word or reason), so logotherapy is therapy through meaning: an existential therapy that helps a person find and fulfil the meaning of his or her life. In German Frankl also called it Existenzanalyse , existential analysis. It rests on three linked assumptions. Freedom of will : within the limits of biology and circumstance, a person is free to take a stand toward his conditions. The will to meaning : the search for meaning is the deepest human motive. Meaning in life : life has meaning under all circumstances, even the most miserable. The middle assumption is the heart of the theory. The will to meaning is Frankl's name for the basic striving of human beings to find and fulfil meaning and purpose in their lives. Frankl liked to place it in the history of his own city. Vienna had already given psychotherapy two great schools. Freud's psychoanalysis, in Frankl's summary, pictured people as driven by a will to pleasure (the pleasure principle), and Adler's individual psychology pictured them as driven by a will to power (the striving for superiority that compensates for feelings of inferiority). Logotherapy, which became known as the Third Viennese School of Psychotherapy , put the will to meaning first. For Frankl the other two strivings were real but secondary. Pleasure is a by-product of fulfilling a meaning, and power is a means to an end; people chase pleasure and power most frantically when their will to meaning has been frustrated. Table 6.6 sets out the comparison. Table 6.6 The three Viennese schools of psychotherapy, as Frankl described them. School Founder Basic human striving What therapy does Psychoanalysis (first) Sigmund Freud Will to pleasure (the pleasure principle) Makes unconscious conflict conscious Individual psychology (second) Alfred Adler Will to power (striving for superiority to overcome inferiority) Corrects the mistaken style of life and builds social interest Logotherapy (third) Viktor Frankl Will to meaning Helps the person discover meaning and accept responsibility A drive pushes a person from behind, demanding discharge; a meaning pulls a person from ahead, toward something to be done or someone to be loved, and leaves him free to answer or not. Frankl rejected the reductionist habit of saying that ideals are "nothing but" sublimated drives or defences, and he called logotherapy a height psychology , a complement to the depth psychology of Freud and Adler: depth psychology looks down into instincts and conflicts, height psychology looks up toward values and meanings. Behind this lies Frankl's picture of the person. A human being, he argued, exists in three dimensions at once: the somatic (the body), the psychic (the mind in the ordinary psychological sense: feelings, drives, habits and memories) and the noetic dimension (from the Greek noos , mind or spirit), the specifically human dimension of meaning, values, conscience, freedom and responsibility. Frankl used the German word geistig , "spiritual", for this dimension, but he insisted that it is not a religious term; an atheist has a noetic dimension as surely as a believer. Animals share our bodies and much of our psychology, but only human beings can ask whether what they are doing is worth doing. The noetic dimension shows itself in two capacities: self-detachment , the capacity to step back from oneself, to observe one's own moods and symptoms from outside and even to laugh at them, as Frankl and his friend did with their daily story; and self-transcendence , the capacity to reach beyond oneself toward a meaning to fulfil or a person to love. Each of Frankl's two best-known techniques recruits one of them. Self-transcendence is also why Frankl disagreed with the humanistic psychologists of Section 6.1 about self-actualisation. Maslow and Rogers treated self-actualisation as a goal. Frankl argued that it cannot be aimed at directly. "Being human," he wrote, "always points, and is directed, to something, or someone, other than oneself." He compared a person to the eye, which sees the world only so long as it does not see itself; when it begins to see something of itself, such as the cloud of a cataract, something is wrong. In the same way, self-actualisation and happiness arrive only as side-effects of self-transcendence. "Happiness must ensue," Frankl wrote; it cannot be pursued, because the more one aims at it the more one misses it. Hold on to that idea, because it is the key to dereflection. Meaning, for Frankl, is discovered rather than invented. Sartre (Section 6.4) taught that we must create our own values in an empty universe; Frankl held that a meaning is already present in each situation, waiting to be found, unique to the particular person and the particular moment (he spoke of the "meaning of the moment"), and that conscience is the organ that detects it. He reversed the usual question: it is not we who should ask what the meaning of life is, but life that asks us, and we answer by being responsible. Freedom without responsibility, he warned, degenerates into arbitrariness; he once proposed that the Statue of Liberty on America's east coast be balanced by a Statue of Responsibility on the west. Where can meaning be found? Frankl named three main avenues, often drawn as a triangle (Table 6.7). The first is creative values , realised through what we give to the world: creating a work or doing a deed. The second is experiential values , realised through what we receive from the world: goodness, truth or beauty in nature, art or culture, and above all the encounter with another human being in his or her uniqueness, which is to say, love. The third is attitudinal values , realised through the stand we take toward a fate we cannot change, unavoidable suffering. Frankl regarded the third as the highest, because it remains open when the other two are closed: a paralysed patient who can no longer work can still choose how to bear his condition. Notice the word unavoidable . Frankl was emphatic that to suffer unnecessarily, when the suffering could be removed, is not heroic but masochistic; suffering that can be cured should be cured. Table 6.7 Frankl's three paths to meaning. Kind of value How meaning is found Example Creative values Through what we give to the world: creating a work or doing a deed Frankl rebuilding his lost manuscript on scraps of paper; a teacher who stays on in a village school Experiential values Through what we receive from the world: beauty, truth, nature, art, and above all love of another person Frankl's image of his wife on the march; a sunset over the Chamundi Hills shared with a friend Attitudinal values Through the stand we take toward suffering that cannot be avoided A man with terminal cancer who decides to spend his last months making peace with his estranged brother Frankl called pain, guilt and death the tragic triad of human existence. His stance toward it, which he called "tragic optimism", was that a person can say yes to life in spite of all three: by turning suffering into an achievement, guilt into an opportunity to change for the better, and the transitoriness of life into an incentive to act responsibly now. Exam trap The will to meaning is the central concept of logotherapy . The tempting wrong options each belong to someone else. Rational emotive behaviour therapy is Albert Ellis's therapy of irrational beliefs (Section 5.2). Existential-humanistic therapy (Rollo May and James Bugental, Section 6.4) shares Frankl's concerns but is built on presence and authenticity, not on the will to meaning. Acceptance and commitment therapy (Steven Hayes, Section 5.9) does work with values, but it grows out of behaviour analysis and relational frame theory. For the three Viennese schools remember the triad pleasure (Freud), power (Adler), meaning (Frankl) . And Frankl, unlike Maslow, held that self-actualisation cannot be pursued directly: it is a by-product of self-transcendence . Existential frustration, the existential vacuum and noogenic neurosis What happens when the will to meaning is blocked? Frankl called the experience existential frustration , the frustration of the will to meaning. It is not in itself an illness. A woman who wonders whether her life has been worthwhile, or a young man who despairs of finding a purpose after failing to get into the course he wanted, is showing a distinctly human concern, and Frankl warned doctors against burying such a concern under a diagnosis and a tranquilliser. "A man's concern, even his despair, over the worthwhileness of life is an existential distress but by no means a mental disease," he wrote. When existential frustration hardens into a lasting state, the result is the existential vacuum : a pervasive feeling of inner emptiness and meaninglessness, of having nothing worth living for. Frankl thought it the characteristic complaint of the twentieth century, and he offered a historical explanation. Unlike an animal, a human being is not told by instinct what he must do, and, unlike his ancestors, he is no longer told by tradition what he ought to do. Often he does not even know what he wishes to do. So he does what other people do, which Frankl called conformism, or he does what other people wish him to do, which Frankl called totalitarianism. The vacuum shows itself mainly as boredom. Frankl described a Sunday neurosis , the depression that afflicts people who become aware of the emptiness of their lives when the rush of the busy week is over, and he saw the same pattern in the crisis of retirement and in the despondency of the young unemployed, many of whom, he noticed in the 1930s, suffered less from poverty than from the feeling of being useless. Consider a worked example. Suresh, a bank manager in Mysuru, retires at sixty after thirty-five years of rising at six. Within six months he is sleeping late, snapping at his wife and spending his evenings in front of the television. "There is nothing wrong with me," he tells the psychologist his daughter has persuaded him to see. "I just do not see the point of getting up." Nothing in his body or his childhood has changed; what has gone is the structure of tasks and people that gave his days their meaning. A logotherapist would not search his past for a conflict. She would ask what in his life still needs him, and might discover that the neighbourhood's schoolchildren have nobody to help them with mathematics, a task that draws on all of Suresh's old skills. The vacuum does not stay empty for long. Frankl argued that it is often filled with substitutes: the will to power in its crudest form, the will to money; or the will to pleasure, in sexual compensation and the pursuit of thrills. In his later writing he named a mass neurotic triad of depression, aggression and addiction, three social problems that he believed were fed in large part by the existential vacuum. Addiction counsellors will recognise the young man who drinks to fill evenings that have nothing else in them. Only some people in an existential vacuum become ill. When existential frustration does produce neurotic symptoms (anxiety, depression, obsessions, insomnia), Frankl spoke of a noogenic neurosis : a neurosis that originates in the noetic dimension, out of existential problems such as the frustration of the will to meaning or a conflict between values, rather than out of conflicts between drives and instincts. The word is built from noos (mind or spirit) and -genic (originating in). Frankl contrasted it with two other origins of neurotic symptoms, shown in Figure 6.3. A psychogenic neurosis, the neurosis of classical psychotherapy, arises in the psychic dimension, from psychological conflicts, traumas and faulty learning. A somatogenic disturbance arises in the body; an overactive thyroid gland, for example, can produce anxiety. The symptoms may look alike. What differs is their source, and therefore what will help. For noogenic neurosis Frankl regarded logotherapy as the specific treatment, because the problem itself is a problem of meaning. For psychogenic neuroses he offered logotherapy as a non-specific treatment: a set of techniques, paradoxical intention and dereflection, that can relieve symptoms whatever their origin, alongside other methods. Somatogenic conditions need medical treatment first. Figure 6.3 Frankl's three dimensions of the person and the three origins of neurotic symptoms. Similar symptoms can arise in any dimension; logotherapy proper is the specific treatment for the noogenic kind, while its techniques can help whatever the origin. Frankl also took issue with the idea, popular in the psychology of his day, that a healthy organism seeks a state of equilibrium free of tension. "What man actually needs," he wrote, "is not a tensionless state but rather the striving and struggling for a worthwhile goal." He called the healthy tension between what one is and what one ought to become noodynamics , and he compared it to an architect's trick: to strengthen a decrepit arch, you increase the load on it, because the load binds its parts more firmly together. Key study: putting the existential vacuum to the test (Crumbaugh and Maholick, 1964) Question. Is Frankl's existential vacuum a real, measurable condition, and is lack of meaning related to psychological disturbance? Method. The American psychologists James Crumbaugh and Leonard Maholick built the Purpose in Life Test (PIL) directly from Frankl's writings, and reported it in a paper whose title announced its aim: "An experimental study in existentialism: the psychometric approach to Frankl's concept of noogenic neurosis". Its scored part has 20 items, each rated on a seven-point scale between two anchors (for example, "In life I have: no goals or aims at all" at one end and "very clear goals and aims" at the other), giving totals from 20 to 140. They gave it to groups of non-patients and psychiatric patients. Results. On average the non-patient groups reported more purpose than the patients. Conclusion. A sense of meaning can be measured, and its absence goes with distress, as Frankl claimed. Criticism. PIL scores correlate strongly with measures of depression and general well-being, so the test may partly measure low mood rather than a separate noogenic condition; it is a self-report; and correlational data cannot show whether meaninglessness causes disturbance or disturbance drains life of meaning. (The PIL itself belongs to the Assessment book.) Exam trap Noogenic neurosis (or noogenic anxiety) is Frankl's concept, so it is described under the existential school . It is not humanistic in the narrow sense of Rogers and Maslow, not Gestalt, and not psychodynamic (the psychodynamic neurosis is what Frankl called psychogenic ). Do not misread it as neurogenic (arising in the nervous system) or iatrogenic (caused by treatment). The existential vacuum is Frankl's term; Yalom's nearest equivalent is meaninglessness , one of his four ultimate concerns. And if asked what logotherapy is "best described as", the answer is an existential therapy emphasising the search for meaning , not a behaviour therapy using token reinforcement (Section 4.5), a psychodynamic therapy of unconscious conflict (Chapter 3) or a cognitive therapy of irrational beliefs (Ellis, Section 5.2). Paradoxical intention and dereflection For all its philosophy, logotherapy became famous among clinicians for two short, practical techniques. Frankl developed both to deal with a mechanism he saw again and again in anxious patients. A person has an unpleasant experience: he blushes while giving a talk, sweats when shaking hands, or lies awake the night before an examination. The next time a similar situation approaches, he fears that it will happen again. Frankl called this fear anticipatory anxiety , and he pointed out its cruel property: it tends to produce exactly what it fears. The fear of blushing makes the face burn; the fear of sleeplessness keeps the mind alert. Each recurrence confirms the fear and strengthens it, and a vicious circle is set up (Figure 6.4). Fear, as Frankl put it, "brings to pass what one is afraid of". Two kinds of misdirected effort keep the circle turning. The first, hyper-intention , is trying too hard to bring about something that can come only as a by-product: the insomniac who tries to fall asleep, the man who tries to prove his sexual potency, the candidate who tries to be relaxed at an interview. The harder they try, the more surely they fail, because sleep, sexual pleasure and ease are like happiness; they ensue, and cannot be commanded. The second, hyper-reflection , is excessive attention to oneself: anxious self-observation, watching one's own body, feelings or performance for the first sign of trouble. Patients' own responses make matters worse, Frankl added: the phobic patient runs from the fear and avoids whatever triggers it (flight from fear), the obsessive-compulsive patient fights against his obsessions, which only gives them more force, and the patient with a sexual neurosis fights for pleasure, which drives it away. Symptom appears (sweating, blushing, no sleep) Anticipatory anxiety fear that it will happen again Watching and trying hyper-reflection, hyper-intention Fear brings about what one fears Paradoxical intention wish for it, with humour Dereflection turn attention outward keeps the circle going breaks the circle Figure 6.4 The vicious circle of anticipatory anxiety, and where Frankl's two techniques break it. Paradoxical intention attacks the fear by replacing it with a humorous wish for the symptom; dereflection attacks the anxious self-watching and straining by turning attention away from the self. Frankl's first technique, paradoxical intention , invites the patient to intend, or to wish for, the very thing he fears, deliberately, in an exaggerated form and with humour, so that the anticipatory anxiety is replaced by a paradoxical wish and the vicious circle is broken. Frankl had been using the method in Vienna long before the war, and his best-known English account of it appeared in the American Journal of Psychotherapy in 1960. His most quoted case is a young doctor for whom the mere expectation of sweating was enough to make him sweat. Frankl advised him, the next time he feared an outbreak, to resolve deliberately to show people how much he could sweat. A week later the doctor reported that whenever he met someone who set off his fear, he had said to himself, "I only sweated out a quart before, but now I'm going to pour at least ten quarts!" After suffering from the phobia for four years, he was free of it within a week of a single session. A colleague in the speech and throat department of the Vienna Polyclinic told Frankl of a lifelong stammerer whose one fluent moment had come when he tried to stammer: at twelve, caught stealing a ride on a tram, he had tried to stammer to win the conductor's pity, and could not. Frankl's student Elisabeth Lukas described a woman with a mirror compulsion who ran to a mirror up to twenty times a day to check that her hair was perfectly in place. The patient resisted every paradoxical suggestion until Lukas offered to join her in a game of "hair rumpling". The two women messed up their hair as wildly as they could and ran hand in hand around the block, trying to show every passer-by how dishevelled they were. Nobody paid them the slightest attention. The patient learned to tell herself, "Let my hair stand on end; let it be a mess!", and after eight weeks the compulsion had gone. The therapist took the symptom seriously enough to share the joke, and the humour let the patient stand back from the symptom instead of being swallowed by it. Why should such an odd instruction work? Frankl's explanation was that paradoxical intention mobilises self-detachment , and especially humour. A person cannot be terrified of blushing and, at the same moment, cheerfully trying to blush as red as a tomato. The paradoxical wish also turns the mechanism of hyper-intention against itself: if trying hard for something makes it fail, then trying hard for the symptom makes the symptom fail. A behaviour therapist would add that the patient stops avoiding the feared situation and so receives exposure to it (Section 4.3). Frankl used paradoxical intention mainly for anticipatory anxiety, phobias, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, blushing, sweating, stammering and sleep-onset insomnia (the insomniac is told to try to stay awake for as long as possible). It needs a patient who trusts the therapist and can find some humour in his plight. Logotherapists warn that it must never be used with severely depressed or suicidal patients, for whom an instruction to wish for the worst could be dangerous. Section 4.10 shows how behaviour therapists later put paradoxical intention to the test in controlled trials. The companion technique, dereflection , is aimed at hyper-reflection and hyper-intention. The patient is helped to stop watching himself and to stop straining for the effect, and to turn his attention outward, to another person or to a meaningful task, so that the disturbed function can recover by itself. Paradoxical intention says "try to make it happen"; dereflection says "stop attending to it, and attend to something worth attending to". Frankl's best-known case was a young woman who came to him because she could not reach orgasm. She had been sexually abused by her father in childhood, but Frankl traced her difficulty less to the abuse itself than to what she had made of it: having read popular psychoanalytic books, she lived in fearful expectation that the experience would one day take its toll, and in bed with her partner she watched herself anxiously for the damage to show. She was trying hard for orgasm (hyper-intention) and observing herself throughout (hyper-reflection). Frankl told her that he could not begin treatment for a couple of months, and asked her, in the meantime, not to concern herself with whether she was capable of orgasm but to give her attention to her partner. She came back within days rather than months, having experienced orgasm for the first time. The same principle helps a man with erectile difficulties who monitors every moment of lovemaking, and Frankl sometimes removed the demand altogether by having the couple agree that intercourse was, for the time being, off the agenda. William Masters and Virginia Johnson arrived at a similar idea in their sex therapy of 1970. They called anxious self-monitoring during sex "spectatoring" and treated it with sensate focus , a graded programme of non-demand touching exercises during which intercourse is at first banned (Section 7.9). Dereflection is not only a sex technique, however. The man preoccupied with his palpitations, the student who lies awake listening to her own breathing, the chronically ill patient whose whole day revolves around his symptoms: each is helped by being turned away from the self and toward something worth attending to, which is self-transcendence put to clinical use.
