Attend to your partner, not to your own performance Exam trap A stem about a person who stops watching himself and turns his attention outward (from his own sexual performance to his partner, for example) describes dereflection , the remedy for hyper-reflection . Paradoxical intention is the remedy for anticipatory anxiety : the patient wishes for the feared symptom. Sensate focus is Masters and Johnson's structured programme of touching exercises (Section 7.9), built on a similar insight but not Frankl's technique. Socratic dialogue is logotherapy's questioning method for finding meaning, not a symptom technique. Three more "paradoxes" are often confused with Frankl's. Beisser's paradoxical theory of change belongs to Gestalt therapy (Section 6.3). Prescribing the symptom as a strategic directive belongs to Haley and the Mental Research Institute (Section 7.5), and Adler and Dreikurs used a similar move earlier (Section 3.8). Knight Dunlap's negative practice , the deliberate repetition of a habit such as a tic, is a behavioural technique (Section 4.9). Finally, "confrontation, paradoxical intention and prescription" is a mixed bag of directive techniques, not Rogers's core conditions. Socratic dialogue, attitude modulation and evaluation Paradoxical intention and dereflection deal with symptoms. The heart of logotherapy, for noogenic problems, is a conversation about meaning, and its main tool is the Socratic dialogue : a series of questions, in the manner of the Greek philosopher Socrates, that help the client to discover for himself meanings and values that he already half knows but has lost sight of. The logotherapist does not hand out meanings. Frankl was firm that meaning cannot be given, only found, and he said that the therapist's role is that of an eye specialist rather than a painter: a painter shows us the world as he sees it, whereas an eye specialist helps us to see the world as it really is. Frankl's own most famous example is short enough to give whole. An elderly general practitioner came to him, severely depressed two years after the death of the wife he had loved above everything. Frankl offered no comfort. Instead he asked what would have happened if the doctor had died first and his wife had had to survive him. "Oh," said the doctor, "for her this would have been terrible; how she would have suffered!" Frankl replied that she had been spared this suffering, and that it was he who had spared her, at the price of surviving and mourning her himself. The man said nothing, shook Frankl's hand and quietly left the office. His fate had not changed, but its meaning had: his grief had become the price of a sacrifice made for her. The case also illustrates attitude modulation , in which the therapist helps a client replace an attitude toward an unchangeable situation that makes it unbearable with one that makes it bearable and even meaningful; it is attitudinal values put into practice. Logotherapists also invite clients to look at their lives from the perspective of the end, and Frankl's maxim for this was a thought experiment: "Live as if you were living already for the second time and as if you had acted the first time as wrongly as you are about to act now." Compare the Socratic questioning of Beck's cognitive therapy (Section 5.4). Beck's questions test whether a belief is true; the logotherapist's questions look for what is still worth living for. In practice logotherapy is usually brief and active, often a matter of weeks or a few months, and it looks forward rather than back. Frankl called it less retrospective and less introspective than psychoanalysis, and enjoyed telling how an American doctor once asked him to define the difference in a single sentence. Frankl asked the doctor first to define psychoanalysis. "In psychoanalysis," came the reply, "the patient must lie down on a couch and tell you things which sometimes are very disagreeable to tell." To which Frankl answered that in logotherapy the patient may remain sitting erect, but he must hear things which sometimes are very disagreeable to hear. How should logotherapy be judged? Its reach is enormous, and the meaning-centred therapies descended from Frankl have the best research record of all the existential approaches, as the 2015 meta-analysis by Vos, Cooper and Craig showed (Section 6.4); the meaning-centred psychotherapy that William Breitbart developed for people with advanced cancer is described in Chapter 9. Paradoxical intention has been tested more rigorously than the rest of logotherapy, mostly by behaviour therapists, with encouraging results for sleep-onset insomnia and some anxiety problems (Section 4.10). The criticisms are just as clear. Some existential therapists, Yalom among them, felt that Frankl leaned on technique at the expense of the relationship and of the client's own slow search for meaning, and critics have found his manner authoritarian and moralising: a doctor telling patients what is worth living for, despite his own warnings against doing so. The spiritual flavour of his language (in The Unconscious God he argued for a "spiritual unconscious" in every person) attracted clergy but made secular readers uneasy, even though Frankl insisted that the noetic dimension is not religious. And the central theory is hard to test. The will to meaning and noogenic neurosis are plausible ideas, but it is difficult to show that a noogenic neurosis is a different condition from an ordinary depression, as the criticism of the Purpose in Life Test showed. Clinical link In a palliative care unit in Bengaluru, a retired schoolteacher with advanced cancer tells the psychologist that he is "just waiting". A meaning-centred conversation might ask what he would like his grandchildren to remember about how he faced this time; he decides to record the stories of his village childhood for them, a creative value, and to stop hiding his illness from his wife, an attitudinal one. Three cautions apply. A client who is acutely suicidal needs a risk assessment and a safety plan first (Chapter 9), not a discussion of meaning. The clinician must not supply a meaning of her own. And many Indian clients already draw meaning from dharma, karma, seva or devotion; the logotherapeutic stance is to work within the client's own framework, helping him find what it asks of him now, rather than replacing it. 6.6 Reality Therapy and Choice Theory Medium yield · 2 Qs Frankl taught that even in a concentration camp a person keeps the freedom to choose his attitude. In the same years an American psychiatrist was pushing the idea of choice in a more down-to-earth direction. In 1956 he became consulting psychiatrist at the Ventura School for Girls, a California state institution for delinquent adolescent girls. Many of the girls had already been through probation officers, counsellors and psychiatrists, and many could explain fluently why they behaved as they did: the broken home, the drunken father, the rough neighbourhood. The psychiatrist was not much interested in the explanations. His approach was to become warmly and personally involved with the girls, and then to ask them, again and again, what they were doing now, whether it was getting them what they wanted, and what they were going to do instead. He accepted no excuses, he did not punish, and he did not give up. Staff who had at first resisted his ideas about discipline came to find them helpful, and he reported that fewer girls returned to the institution after release. The psychiatrist was William Glasser, and in 1965 he described his approach in a book whose title gave it its name: Reality Therapy . William Glasser and the making of reality therapy William Glasser (1925 to 2013) was born in Cleveland, Ohio, on 11 May 1925. He took a degree in chemical engineering at the age of nineteen, then a master's degree in clinical psychology, and then a medical degree from Case Western Reserve University, which he completed at twenty-eight. He trained in psychiatry at the Veterans Administration Center in Los Angeles and the University of California at Los Angeles, and became a certified psychiatrist in 1961. His residency was a training in psychoanalysis, and it left him dissatisfied. Psychoanalysis, as he saw it, taught patients to look into the past for someone to blame, and it seemed to make little difference to how they actually behaved. In the third year of his residency he confided these doubts to his clinical supervisor, the psychiatrist G. L. Harrington . Harrington, who had come to question psychoanalytic practice himself, was sympathetic, and he served as Glasser's mentor for the next seven years; Glasser acknowledged him as a major influence on reality therapy. Glasser's first book, Mental Health or Mental Illness? (1961), already posed in its title a question that would run through his whole career. He coined the term reality therapy in 1962 and set out the approach in Reality Therapy: A New Approach to Psychiatry (1965). In 1967 he founded the Institute for Reality Therapy in Los Angeles (later renamed the William Glasser Institute), which trains and certifies practitioners. He carried his ideas into education with Schools Without Failure (1969), into social criticism with The Identity Society (1972) and into self-help with Positive Addiction (1976). His first wife, Naomi Glasser, edited the first casebook of the approach and gave it a title that captures it in three words: What Are You Doing? (1980). Glasser died in Los Angeles in 2013. Glasser's reality therapy can be defined as a brief, active, present-focused counselling approach in which a warm, involved therapist helps clients to evaluate their current behaviour and to choose more responsible and effective ways of meeting their basic needs. Responsibility was the key word from the start. Glasser defined it in 1965 as "the ability to fulfil one's needs, and to do so in a way that does not deprive others of the ability to fulfil their needs", and his early approach is often summarised as the "three Rs": reality, responsibility, and right (the client judges for himself whether what he is doing is right). The word "reality" in the name does not mean that the therapist decides what is real and lectures the client about it. It means that the client is helped to face the real consequences of what he is doing, and to stop hiding from them behind excuses, symptoms or the past. In 1965 Glasser described only two basic needs: the need to love and be loved, and the need to feel worthwhile to oneself and to others. The fuller theory came later. For fifteen years reality therapy was a practice with little formal theory behind it. Then in 1977 Glasser read Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973) by the American control-systems engineer William T. Powers . Powers argued that living organisms do not simply respond to stimuli; they act to control their perceptions, keeping what they perceive close to what they want, much as a thermostat switches the heating on and off to hold the perceived temperature at its setting. Glasser adapted the idea as control theory in Stations of the Mind (1981) and the more popular Control Theory (1985). People kept misreading "control" as controlling others, and his version had in any case moved a long way from Powers's, so Glasser renamed it choice theory and set it out in Choice Theory: A New Psychology of Personal Freedom (1998). Choice theory is Glasser's explanation of why people behave as they do; reality therapy is the method of counselling built on it. The method itself was systematised by Robert E. Wubbolding , for many years director of training of the William Glasser Institute, whose WDEP system you will meet below. Exam trap Spell and place the name. William Glasser (reality therapy) is not Barney Glaser , who with Anselm Strauss founded grounded theory in qualitative research in 1967 (Research Methodology book). Keep Glasser's dates in order: the term reality therapy (1962), the book Reality Therapy (1965), control theory (the 1980s) and the name choice theory (the book of 1998). Some revision notes list "1965: Glasser, choice theory"; the 1965 book was Reality Therapy . Reality therapy is also different from reality orientation , a technique for disoriented older people with dementia (Chapter 10), and from reality testing , the psychoanalytic ego function of telling inner from outer reality, which fails in psychosis. The WDEP system was developed by Robert Wubbolding from Glasser's work, not by Glasser himself. Choice theory: five basic needs and the quality world Choice theory begins, as Rogers's and Frankl's theories do, with motivation. Glasser held that all human behaviour is driven by five basic needs , which are built into our genes: survival, love and belonging, power, freedom and fun (Table 6.9). Survival covers the physical needs for food, water, shelter, health, safety and sex. Love and belonging covers friendship, family, intimacy and cooperation; it can be met by people, and to a lesser extent even by pets. Power in Glasser's sense is not domination but achievement, competence, recognition and self-worth, the sense of being listened to and of counting for something, so that it is often written "power or achievement". Freedom covers independence and choice: how we live, whom we spend time with, what we say, read and believe. Fun covers enjoyment, play and laughter, and Glasser called it the genetic reward for learning, the reason children and adults alike enjoy whatever stretches them. Table 6.9 Glasser's five basic needs. Need What it covers A sign that it is being met Survival Food, water, shelter, health, safety, sex Eating and sleeping well; a secure income Love and belonging Friendship, family, intimacy, cooperation; the most important need in practice Someone to share lunch, worries and festivals with Power (achievement) Competence, achievement, recognition, self-worth, being listened to Clearing an examination; being respected at work Freedom Independence, autonomy, choice of how to live and what to believe Choosing one's own course, friends or faith Fun Enjoyment, play, laughter and learning A cricket match with friends; learning a new skill Two features of the needs are worth knowing. First, Glasser regarded love and belonging as the most important need in practice, because it is the one most often frustrated in people who seek help. In his view almost all long-lasting psychological problems are, at bottom, relationship problems, and an unhappy client nearly always lacks at least one satisfying relationship. Second, the needs are not arranged in a fixed hierarchy as Maslow's are. Their strength differs from person to person (one person has a strong need for freedom, another a strong need for power), and they often conflict. The need for power in a marriage can wreck the need for love; Glasser believed that power struggles, more than any shortage of love, destroy marriages. A need for freedom so strong that it keeps everyone at a distance leaves a person lonely. Needs are general; what we actually want is specific. From birth onward, Glasser said, each of us builds a quality world , a personal album of "pictures" of the particular people, things, activities, ideas and beliefs that we have found satisfy our needs best: this friend, that career, a new cricket bat, the belief that hard work pays. The most important pictures are of people. The quality world is unique to each person, it need not be sensible (a man with a drinking problem keeps a picture of the evening drink as the best way to relax, and a girl with anorexia a picture of herself as fat), and it can change, slowly, as one picture is replaced by another that satisfies the same need. Alongside it each of us carries a perceived world, the world as we experience it through our senses and our habits of interpretation. At what Glasser called the comparing place , the brain constantly weighs what we perceive we are getting against the pictures in the quality world. When the two match, we feel pleasure; when they do not, a frustration signal arises, and we choose a behaviour to close the gap. This is Powers's thermostat in human form. It also explains why, in choice theory, "Face reality!" is a suspect demand: none of us has access to reality itself, only to our perceptions of it, so "Face reality" usually means "See it my way". From this model Glasser drew a social message. If behaviour is generated from inside, by the gap between what we want and what we perceive, then nobody can make another person do anything. The only behaviour we can control is our own, and all we can give another person is information. Glasser called the opposite belief, that we can and should control others with rewards and punishments, external control psychology , and he blamed it for much of the unhappiness in families, schools and workplaces. In his later writing he contrasted seven "deadly habits" that destroy relationships (criticising, blaming, complaining, nagging, threatening, punishing, and bribing or rewarding to control) with seven "caring habits" that build them (supporting, encouraging, listening, accepting, trusting, respecting and negotiating differences). Anyone who has watched an anxious parent try to make a teenager study will recognise the first list. Exam trap Glasser's five basic needs are survival, love and belonging, power (achievement), freedom and fun . When a question asks which option is one of them, the distractors are borrowed from other theorists: self-actualisation is the top of Maslow's hierarchy (and close to Rogers's actualising tendency), the collective unconscious is Carl Jung's (Section 3.8 and the Personality book), and unconditional positive regard is one of Rogers's core conditions (Section 6.2). Watch also for Maslow's own levels, safety and esteem, slipped in as distractors: Glasser's survival need is the nearest he comes to Maslow's physiological and safety needs, and Glasser's needs are not arranged in a hierarchy. The 1965 version of reality therapy named only two needs (to love and be loved, and to feel worthwhile); the five came with control theory in the 1980s. Total behaviour: why Glasser said "depressing" Choice theory's most provocative claim concerns what we usually call symptoms. Glasser argued that all behaviour is total behaviour , made up of four components that always occur together: acting (what we do), thinking (voluntary and involuntary thoughts, including daydreams), feeling (pleasant or painful emotions) and physiology (the bodily processes that go with them, such as sweating, a racing heart or a headache). We have direct control only over acting and thinking; feeling and physiology follow them. Glasser's image for this was a car (Figure 6.5). The five basic needs are the engine; our wants, the pictures in the quality world, do the steering; acting and thinking are the front wheels, which we can turn; feeling and physiology are the back wheels, which go wherever the front wheels take them. We cannot make ourselves feel happy by willing it, any more than we can steer a car by its back wheels, but we can change what we are doing and thinking, and our feelings and physiology will follow. Glasser's car: total behaviour Engine: the five basic needs Steering: your wants Feeling (back wheel) Acting (front wheel) Physiology (back wheel) Thinking (front wheel) direction of travel Acting and thinking steer; feeling and physiology follow. Figure 6.5 Glasser's car model of total behaviour, seen from above. The needs supply the power and the wants steer, but only the front wheels (acting and thinking) can be turned directly; the back wheels (feeling and physiology) follow wherever the front wheels go. If total behaviour is chosen, so, in part, is misery. Glasser therefore turned the adjectives of distress into verbs. A person is not "depressed" but "depressing"; not "angry" but "angering"; he does not have a headache, he is "headaching". The point was not to insult sufferers but to remind them that some part of their misery lies in what they are doing now, and can therefore change. Sadness may come unbidden after a loss, Glasser granted; but when it continues month after month, the person is choosing, without realising it, to go on depressing. Why would anyone choose pain? Glasser gave four reasons. Depressing keeps anger under control, and is far safer than angering, which can lead to violence and prison. Depressing is a way of asking for help ("Depressing is a way we ask for help without begging," he wrote). It excuses us from doing something more effective but more frightening, such as looking for a new job after being dismissed. And it gives us power over others, who must comfort us, look after us and do things for us. Glasser went further and regarded even hallucinations and delusions as creative, if desperate, behaviours. He rejected the idea of mental illness for everything except clear brain disease, and he was a fierce critic of psychiatric medication; one of his last books was titled Warning: Psychiatry Can Be Hazardous to Your Mental Health (2003). Clinical link The language of choice is powerful and double-edged. For a student who "cannot" start studying, or a man who "cannot help" shouting at his wife, the question "What are you choosing to do, and is it working?" can be liberating. For a woman in a severe depressive episode, a man hearing voices or a patient with bipolar disorder, being told that he or she is "choosing" the symptoms can deepen guilt and shame and delay effective treatment, including medication (the disorders and their treatment belong to the Disorders book). Most clinicians who draw on reality therapy keep its useful core, the focus on what the client can do today, and leave aside Glasser's rejection of diagnosis and drugs. In Indian families, too, a young client's quality world often holds his parents' pictures as well as his own, so plans usually have to be negotiated with the family rather than made by the individual alone. Doing reality therapy: involvement and the WDEP system Reality therapy is less a collection of techniques than a cycle of counselling: a friendly, involved relationship, inside which a few procedures are repeated until the client's behaviour changes. It begins with involvement . Glasser thought the distant, neutral analyst the worst possible model for his clients, who were usually short of satisfying relationships to begin with. The reality therapist is warm, personal, optimistic and honest. She uses "I" and "me", discloses something of herself when it helps, and is willing to talk about almost anything the client cares about, from cricket to cooking, because the relationship itself begins to meet the client's need for belonging. She is herself, not a screen for the client's transference, and she does not let the past or feelings become the main topic. Feelings are listened to, but the focus moves steadily toward what the client is doing. Glasser's early writings set out the procedure as a series of steps, usually taught as eight: Make friends: become personally involved with the client. Focus on present behaviour: ask "What are you doing now?" rather than "Why?" or "How do you feel?" Ask the client to evaluate that behaviour: is it helping? Help the client make a plan to do better. Get a commitment to the plan, spoken or written. Accept no excuses when a plan is not carried out; make a new plan instead. Do not punish or criticise, but do not protect the client from the reasonable consequences of what he does. Never give up. Wubbolding later reorganised these procedures into the WDEP system , the form in which reality therapy is now taught. Each letter stands for a cluster of questions and interventions. W is for wants , together with needs and perceptions: the counsellor explores what the client wants, what he "really" wants, what he wants from the people around him and how he sees his situation; behind the wants lie the needs. D is for direction and doing : where is the client's life heading, and what exactly is he doing now? The counsellor asks for specifics: what happened, who was there, what you did next, what you did yesterday from the moment you woke up. E is for evaluation , which Wubbolding regarded as the heart of the method. The client is asked to judge his own behaviour, and the questions are characteristic: "Is what you are doing helping you or hurting you?" "Is it getting you what you want?" "Are you breaking the rules?" "Are your wants realistic?" "Does it help you to look at it that way?" It is the client, not the counsellor, who makes the value judgement. P is for planning : once the client has decided that something must change, he and the counsellor make a plan. Wubbolding summed up a good plan in an acronym, usually given as SAMIC3 ("SAMIC cubed", because three of its letters are C): simple, attainable, measurable, immediate, controlled by the planner (it does not depend on someone else), committed to, and consistently (in some versions, continuously) carried out. A good plan is also positive, a matter of doing something rather than merely stopping something: "I will phone Priya on Saturday" beats "I will stop sitting alone". A worked example shows the system in motion. Rohan, a nineteen-year-old commerce student in Mysuru, is brought by his parents because he is failing his examinations. He plays online games until three in the morning, misses his morning classes and has stopped speaking to his father except to shout. His father, for his part, criticises, threatens to stop his pocket money and compares him with a cousin who is studying engineering. A reality therapist would spend much of the first session simply getting to know Rohan, his games, his friends and what he is good at, and only then begin the WDEP cycle (Table 6.10). Table 6.10 The WDEP system applied to Rohan. Step What the counsellor explores Typical question What Rohan says or does W: wants Wants, needs and perceptions; the quality world "If things were going the way you wanted, what would be different?" "I want to pass, and I want my father to trust me again." D: direction and doing What he is actually doing now, in detail "Take me through yesterday, from waking up to going to sleep." Woke at noon, missed class, gamed until 3 a.m., shouted at his father at dinner E: evaluation His own judgement of whether it works "Is what you are doing getting you what you want?" "No. It is making everything worse." P: planning A simple, immediate plan he controls, and a commitment "What will you do differently tomorrow night?" Phone left in the hall at midnight on Monday, Wednesday and Friday; 9 a.m. class on those days; written down and signed At the next session the therapist would not ask why the plan had or had not been carried out, because, as Wubbolding put it, asking "Why?" invites excuses. If Rohan had kept the plan, she would praise him and help him build on it. If he had not, she would accept no excuses, impose no punishment and help him make a smaller plan that he could keep. She might also invite his father to a session to talk about the deadly habits and what might replace them. Notice how different this is from Rogers. Had Glasser interviewed Gloria, in the films described at the start of this chapter, he would not have reflected her feelings about the lie she told her daughter, and he would certainly not have asked why she told it. He would have asked what she wanted for herself and for Pammy, what she was actually doing about it, and whether that was working. Reality therapists use a handful of further strategies: skilful questioning; being positive (meeting a complaint by asking what the client will do about it); using the client's own metaphors; humour, since fun is a basic need and a shared joke equalises power; confrontation, which in reality therapy simply means declining to accept excuses, without arguing or criticising; and, sparingly, paradoxical instructions of the kind you met in Section 6.5. Glasser's Positive Addiction (1976) added one more idea. A positive addiction is a strengthening habit, such as running or meditation, which the person comes to need and which, Glasser believed, gives easy access to strength and creativity. To qualify, he said, the activity should be non-competitive, done alone without much mental effort, of some physical, mental or spiritual value to the person, and done without self-criticism. Exam trap WDEP stands for wants, direction and doing, evaluation, planning ; it is Robert Wubbolding's formulation of Glasser's method. The E is the client's self-evaluation , not the therapist's verdict, and the P is a plan that is simple, attainable, measurable, immediate and within the client's control. Reality therapy asks "what" rather than "why", because "why" invites excuses; it uses consequences and praise but never punishment or criticism. "No excuses" does not mean "no feelings": feelings are heard, but change is sought through doing and thinking, the front wheels of the car. Schools, prisons and the evidence Reality therapy spread fast because it was easy to explain, brief and hopeful, and because it was built for the people whom other therapies found hardest to reach. Glasser carried it into schools. In Schools Without Failure (1969) and The Identity Society (1972) he argued that children who experience repeated failure, and who lack warm involvement with adults, develop a failure identity , a lonely, self-defeating picture of themselves that leads to delinquency or withdrawal, whereas involvement and experiences of success build a success identity . In The Quality School (1990), drawing on the American quality-management expert W. Edwards Deming, he contrasted boss management, which coerces with rewards and punishments, with lead management, which persuades, involves and lets students evaluate their own work. The approach is also widely used in prisons and juvenile justice, in addiction services and in marriage counselling, and South Korea in particular has a large reality therapy movement. Glasser's own favourite evidence came from the early years. Key study: Harrington's ward at the Los Angeles veterans hospital (1960s) Question. Could an active, involved, responsibility-centred approach help even chronic, long-hospitalised psychotic patients? Method. In 1962 Glasser's mentor G. L. Harrington took charge of a ward at the Veterans Administration neuropsychiatric hospital in West Los Angeles that housed more than 210 chronic, regressed patients. They had been confined for an average of seventeen years and had received custodial care but almost no therapy, and about two a year were discharged. Harrington reorganised the ward around warm involvement, rising expectations and increasing responsibility for one's own behaviour. Results. As Glasser and Leonard Zunin later reported, 45 patients were discharged in the first year, 85 in the second and 90 in the third. Conclusion. Glasser took the results as evidence that people labelled hopelessly ill can learn to behave responsibly when someone becomes involved with them and expects it of them. Criticism. There was no control ward; the figures were reported by the approach's own advocates; discharge is not the same as recovery, and there was no systematic follow-up; and the change coincided with the spread of antipsychotic drugs and the movement to discharge long-stay patients into the community (Chapter 9), which emptied wards across the United States in the same years. Beyond such reports, the research base is thin. Glasser was more interested in practice than in experiments, certified reality therapists are not trained in research, and most studies are small, often doctoral dissertations or articles in the approach's own International Journal of Reality Therapy . The best-known synthesis is a meta-analysis by Kim and Hwang (2006) of 43 Korean studies of group reality therapy in schools and colleges, which found that participants gained more in self-esteem and in an internal locus of control than members of control groups. Small trials have also reported benefits with male perpetrators of domestic violence, bullied children and students addicted to the internet. There is nothing like the body of randomised trials behind CBT, and reality therapy is not among the treatments that clinical guidelines recommend for particular disorders. The criticisms are serious. Glasser's rejection of mental illness and his hostility to medication run against strong evidence that conditions such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and severe depression have biological components and respond to medication. By deliberately setting aside the unconscious, the past, dreams and transference, reality therapy may miss what keeps some problems going, and its insistence on individual choice can slide into blaming people for the effects of poverty, abuse, caste or discrimination, which they did not choose. Critics have also worried that "responsible" and "realistic" may come to mean whatever the therapist, the school or the prison finds acceptable, a real danger in institutions where the counsellor also holds power over the client. And the approach can look deceptively simple; Glasser himself insisted that it takes years of training to do well. Its strengths are just as real. It is clear, brief and teachable. It gives hope and a sense of agency to clients who have been told that they are helpless. It works in settings (classrooms, juvenile homes, prisons, de-addiction centres) where long insight-oriented therapy is impossible. And its four questions ("What do you want? What are you doing? Is it working? What will you do instead?") are so useful that counsellors of every school borrow them. Its spirit is close to Frankl's, with whom Glasser shared the conviction that people are responsible for their choices, and its warm involvement owes something to Rogers; Table 6.11 compares the three. Motivational interviewing, in Section 6.9, takes a different route to change, drawing out the client's own reasons rather than asking for a plan and a commitment straight away. Both left questions behind. If the core conditions are what heal, why do some clients of the same warm, accurate therapist change while others, just as well treated, do not? If emotion is so central to change, how exactly does an emotion change, and can a therapist guide that process without becoming the expert who directs it? And must therapy always start from what is wrong with a person, or could it start from what is right? This section follows three answers. The first came from Eugene Gendlin, a philosopher in Rogers's own team, who found the answer inside the client's body. The second came from Leslie Greenberg, who joined Rogers's relationship to Perls's chair work and turned the result into a researched therapy of emotion. The third, which turns from suffering to strengths, came from the positive psychology of Martin Seligman and Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi and, quite separately and earlier, from the Iranian-German psychiatrist Nossrat Peseschkian. Eugene Gendlin and the felt sense Eugene Gendlin (1926 to 2017) was born in Vienna and was still a boy when his family fled the Nazis in 1938 and made their way to the United States. He became a philosopher, not a psychologist, and his lifelong question was a philosopher's one: how do words come out of what we feel? When we finally say something that is exactly right, what is it right to ? While he was a graduate student in philosophy at the University of Chicago in the early 1950s, he joined Carl Rogers's counselling centre, trained as a counsellor and became one of Rogers's closest research colleagues. His doctorate in philosophy (1958) and his book Experiencing and the Creation of Meaning (1962) dealt with how felt experience comes to be symbolised in words. He was one of the leaders of the Wisconsin study of therapy with hospitalised schizophrenia patients that you met in Section 6.2, whose report he edited with Rogers, Donald Kiesler and Charles Truax in 1967, and he taught for many years at the University of Chicago. The research that made Gendlin's name began with a puzzle that every therapist recognises. The Chicago counselling centre was full of tape recordings, and its therapists were carefully trained in the core conditions. Yet some clients changed and others, seen by the same therapists, did not. What made the difference? Key study: who succeeds in therapy? (Gendlin and colleagues, Chicago and Wisconsin, 1950s and 1960s) Question. If the therapist's conditions are much the same, what distinguishes the clients who change from those who do not? Method. Gendlin and his colleagues, among them Marjorie Klein, Philippa Mathieu and Donald Kiesler, listened to recorded segments of sessions and rated them, without knowing the outcome, on what became the Experiencing Scale : a seven-stage scale of how far a client's talk refers to, and works from, his or her own inner felt experience. At the low stages the client narrates events or describes other people impersonally; in the middle stages he describes his feelings; at the high stages he speaks from a directly felt inner sense, tentatively and searchingly, so that new meanings emerge from it and lead on to further steps. Results. The clients' level of experiencing, measurable even in early sessions, predicted who would succeed. Successful clients, at some point in a session, slowed down, groped for words and checked what they said against something they could feel but could not yet say ("It's not exactly anger... it's more like... yes, like being left out"). Unsuccessful clients talked fluently about events, or analysed themselves from the outside, and stayed the same however long therapy went on. What clients talked about, and even the therapist's technique, mattered less than how they talked. Conclusion. The client's way of processing his own experience is a major ingredient of change. Criticism. The findings are correlational: high experiencing might simply mark clients who were healthier or more psychologically minded to begin with. Later studies have, however, found that deeper experiencing in sessions predicts better outcome in several therapies, including cognitive therapy for depression and emotion-focused therapy. The finding raised a hopeful question. If the successful clients were doing something, could the others be taught to do it? To answer, Gendlin first had to describe exactly what the successful clients were attending to, and his name for it is the most examined term in this subsection. A felt sense is a bodily felt, at first unclear and wordless sense of a whole situation or problem: not a thought, and not yet an emotion, but the body's sense of "all of that" about something. Here is an everyday version. You leave your hostel for the examination hall and, halfway down the road, you have the uneasy sense that you have forgotten something. You cannot say what it is, yet the sense is perfectly definite: it is not a vague worry, it is that something. You check. Pen? No, the unease stays. Watch? Still there. Hall ticket! And the body lets go with a small "yes, that's it". The unease was a felt sense. The release when the right word arrived is what Gendlin called a felt shift : a bodily easing which tells you that something has moved and that a real step of change has happened. A felt sense is broader than an emotion. Anger at your brother is an emotion; the felt sense is "the whole thing about my brother", which holds the anger and also some guilt, an old rivalry, affection and something you do not yet understand. It is usually felt in the middle of the body (the throat, chest or stomach), and it always contains more than you can say. Gendlin called the continuous, bodily felt flow of experience experiencing , and he argued, in a paper called "A theory of personality change" (1964), that therapy works when experiencing that has been frozen into rigid, repeating patterns is "carried forward": when words, images or actions are found that fit it, so that it moves on. Notice the overlap with Rogers's process continuum from fixity to fluidity (Section 6.2). Gendlin was giving that continuum a mechanism. The six steps of focusing Gendlin found that the ability to attend to a felt sense could indeed be taught, and in 1978 he published a short self-help book, Focusing , which went on to sell widely around the world. Focusing is the method of turning attention inward, in a friendly and unhurried way, to the bodily felt sense of a problem, and letting words and steps of change come from it. Gendlin taught it in six "movements", shown in Figure 6.6, while insisting that they are scaffolding for beginners rather than a rigid procedure. Clearing a space. The person sits quietly, attends to the middle of the body and asks, "What stands between me and feeling fine right now?" As each concern comes up, he does not go into it but acknowledges it and imagines setting it down a little distance away, like a parcel placed on a bench. Felt sense. He chooses one concern and, instead of thinking about it, lets himself feel the whole of it in the body: the unclear, murky sense of "all of that". Handle. He lets a word, phrase or image come from the felt sense itself ("heavy", "jumpy", "like a closed fist"), a handle by which to hold it. Resonating. He goes back and forth between the handle and the felt sense, checking whether the word really fits and letting either change until it does. A good fit brings a small felt shift. Asking. He asks the felt sense an open question ("What is it about this whole thing that makes it so heavy?" "What does it need?") and waits, without supplying an answer from the head, until something comes with a felt shift. Receiving. He welcomes whatever came, without arguing with it or rushing to act on it, and lets it settle, knowing that he can return to it. Gendlin's six focusing movements (1978) 1 Clearing a space set each worry down 2 Felt sense sense the whole of it 3 Handle a word or image comes 4 Resonating check the word's fit 5 Asking ask it, then wait 6 Receiving welcome what came repeat Steps 3 to 5 may cycle several times until the words fit. A fit is marked by a felt shift: the body eases, "yes, that's it". Figure 6.6 Gendlin's six focusing movements. The arrow marked "repeat" shows that handle, resonating and asking (shaded alike) often cycle several times; the sign that a step is right is a felt shift in the body, not a clever idea. Consider a worked example. Priya, a twenty-four-year-old nursing student in Mysuru, tells her counsellor that she feels "something heavy" whenever she thinks about going home for Diwali, though her family is loving and nothing is wrong. Thinking about it has got her nowhere. Her counsellor invites her to pause, close her eyes if she likes, and first set aside the other things that are pressing on her: the ward examination, a quarrel with a roommate, money (clearing a space). Then she lets herself sense the whole of "going home". After a silence she says it is a tight band across her chest (felt sense). Asked whether there is a word for it, she tries "heavy", shakes her head, and then says "like holding my breath" (handle). She checks it: "Yes... holding my breath until they say it's all right" (resonating, with a small easing). Her counsellor asks gently what it is about going home that is so "holding my breath". She waits, and what comes is not an idea but a recognition, with tears and a long breath out: "I have not told them that I want to work in Bengaluru, not near home" (asking, and a clear felt shift). She sits with it for a while (receiving). Focusing has not told Priya what to do. It has done something earlier and harder: it has turned a vague, heavy dread into a clear, speakable problem that she can now work on. Gendlin later described how any therapist can use the method in Focusing-Oriented Psychotherapy (1996). The therapist listens in a way that leaves room, slows the client down at promising moments ("Can you sense, in your body, the whole of that?" "Is there a word that fits it?"), and treats the felt sense, rather than any theory, as the final judge of whether a step is right. Focusing was also designed to be done without a therapist at all. Gendlin and his colleagues taught it to ordinary people, who practise in pairs, taking turns to focus and to listen, and The Focusing Institute, which he founded with colleagues, spread it internationally. Later teachers, notably Ann Weiser Cornell and Barbara McGavin with their "inner relationship focusing", developed the method further. Within psychotherapy, Gendlin's influence runs straight into emotion-focused therapy, which uses focusing as one of its standard tasks. Exam trap Focusing and the felt sense belong to Eugene Gendlin , a colleague of Rogers, not to Perls, Greenberg or Frankl. The felt sense is a bodily, pre-verbal sense of a whole situation; it is not an emotion and not a thought. The felt shift is the bodily release when the right symbol is found. Keep two process measures apart: Gendlin's Experiencing Scale rates how deeply the client works from inner experience, whereas Rogers and Rablen's Process Scale (Section 6.2) rates movement from fixity to fluidity. And do not confuse Gendlin's focusing with focusing , the second of the four processes of motivational interviewing (Section 6.9), or with mindfulness (Chapter 5), which cultivates non-judging awareness of whatever arises rather than inviting the felt sense of one particular problem to speak. Leslie Greenberg and emotion-focused therapy The second answer came from Toronto. Leslie Greenberg (born 1945), a South African-born psychologist who trained first as an engineer, took his doctorate at York University in Toronto, where his teacher was Laura Rice , a client-centred therapist who had worked with Rogers in Chicago. He also trained in Gestalt therapy. Greenberg was, by temperament, an engineer of process. He wanted to know not just whether therapy worked but how, step by step, a client moves from being stuck to being unstuck in a particular kind of moment. With Rice he developed task analysis , the intensive study of recorded "change events" in order to build a model of how clients resolve one specific kind of problem, which they set out in Patterns of Change (1984). You have already met some of the results in Section 6.3: the studies showing that two-chair dialogue at a moment of inner conflict leads to deeper experiencing and better resolution than reflection alone. Out of this work grew a therapy. Greenberg, Rice and Robert Elliott described it in Facilitating Emotional Change (1993) as process-experiential therapy, and in the early 2000s it took its present name, set out in Greenberg's Emotion-Focused Therapy: Coaching Clients to Work Through Their Feelings (2002) and in Learning Emotion-Focused Therapy (2004) by Elliott, Jeanne Watson, Rhonda Goldman and Greenberg. Emotion-focused therapy (EFT) can be defined as a humanistic-experiential therapy that combines the person-centred relationship with active experiential tasks, derived from Gestalt therapy and from focusing, in order to help clients become aware of, accept, make sense of, regulate and transform their emotions. In a phrase, it is Rogers's relationship plus Perls's experiments plus Gendlin's attention to the body, all guided by a research-based theory of emotion. (In the 1980s Greenberg also worked with Susan Johnson on an emotionally focused therapy for couples; Johnson's attachment-based development of it is taught in Section 7.8.) The theory starts from a claim that may surprise you: emotions are not the enemy. Greenberg, drawing on modern emotion research, sees emotion as an evolved, rapid appraisal system that tells us that something important to our wellbeing is happening and prepares us to act. Fear says "danger: escape". Sadness says "loss: reach out for comfort, or withdraw to recover". Anger says "violation: assert yourself, set a boundary". Psychological problems arise, in this view, not because people have too much emotion but because they avoid their emotions, misread them, or are governed by old emotional responses that no longer fit their lives. Emotional responses are produced by emotion schemes : internal organisations of past emotional experience, combining bodily sensations, feelings, memories, meanings and action tendencies, which are activated automatically and largely outside words. Greenberg spells the word "schemes" on purpose, to set them apart from the more verbal, belief-like schemas of cognitive therapy (Chapter 5). The most useful practical tool in the theory is a classification of emotional responses into four kinds, set out in Table 6.12. A therapist who can tell them apart knows what to do with each. Table 6.12 Greenberg's four kinds of emotional response. Kind of emotion What it is Example What the therapist does Primary adaptive The first, direct response to a situation; carries useful information and a healthy action tendency Sadness at a loss; anger at being treated unjustly Helps the client reach it fully and use it as a guide Primary maladaptive Also a first, direct response, but an old, familiar one, learned in past (often traumatic) experience, that no longer helps Core shame ("I am worthless"); fear of closeness learned through abuse Helps the client arrive at it, then transform it with an adaptive emotion Secondary reactive A reaction to a prior emotion or thought, which hides the primary feeling Anger that covers hurt; hopelessness that covers anger Explores beneath it to reach the primary emotion Instrumental An emotion expressed, deliberately or by habit, in order to influence others Tears to win sympathy; anger to dominate Explores its interpersonal purpose A worked example makes the distinctions concrete. Ravi, a forty-year-old bank manager in Pune, comes to therapy because he keeps exploding at his fifteen-year-old son over marks, and then hates himself for it. His rage is real, but it is a secondary emotion : a reaction that covers something else. As the therapist follows him slowly through the last outburst ("What happened inside you just before you shouted?"), Ravi reaches a sinking, shrinking feeling in his stomach and the words "I am a failure, and everyone can see it". This is a primary maladaptive emotion , a core shame laid down when his own father mocked him in front of relatives for his school results; it is old, familiar, and it does him no good. A primary adaptive emotion , by contrast, is one that fits the present situation and points somewhere useful. The therapist does not argue Ravi out of his shame, as a cognitive therapist might dispute a belief. Instead, having helped him stay with it long enough to arrive at it, she helps him reach the healthier feelings that the shame has been blocking: anger at having been humiliated as a child ("It was not fair; I was a boy who was trying") and grief for the encouragement he never had. As these adaptive emotions are felt and expressed, often in an empty-chair dialogue with the remembered father, the shame begins to lose its grip, and Ravi finds he can sit beside his son's report card without exploding. The fourth kind, instrumental emotion , is expressed in order to influence others (the tears that win sympathy, the anger that wins arguments), and with it the therapist explores what the emotion is for rather than deepening it. Greenberg summarised how emotions change in six principles. Awareness comes first: the client must notice and name what he feels, and Greenberg liked to say that you cannot leave a place until you have arrived at it. Expression means overcoming avoidance and letting the feeling be felt and voiced in the session. Regulation means helping clients who are overwhelmed (by panic, rage or despair) gain enough distance to soothe themselves, through breathing, self-soothing and the calm presence of the therapist. Reflection means making sense of the experience in words and building a new account of it. Transformation is the heart of the method: a maladaptive emotion is changed not by reasoning but by activating a different, adaptive emotion alongside it. Greenberg quoted the seventeenth-century philosopher Baruch Spinoza, who wrote that an emotion can be restrained or removed only by an opposed and stronger emotion; his own slogan is "changing emotion with emotion". Finally, corrective emotional experience means that new lived experiences, above all being met with acceptance where contempt was expected, change old feelings in a way that insight alone cannot. Where does that leave the relationship? EFT keeps Rogers's core conditions as its foundation, and its therapists spend much of their time in empathic exploration of the client's experience. But the stance differs from classical client-centred therapy in one important way. The EFT therapist is process-guiding : she follows the client's lead about what matters, but actively guides how the client works with it, suggesting at the right moment that he focus inward, or speak to the critic in the other chair. Greenberg describes this as a dialectic of following and leading. It is gentler and less confrontational than Gestalt therapy in Perls's hands, and more directive than Rogers. Exam trap Four look-alikes. Emotion-focused therapy (EFT) for individuals is Leslie Greenberg's (earlier called process-experiential therapy). Emotionally focused couple therapy is chiefly Susan Johnson's, based on attachment theory (Section 7.8), although Greenberg and Johnson first wrote it up together in 1988. Emotion-focused coping , managing one's feelings about a stressor rather than changing the stressor itself (problem-focused coping), comes from Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman's theory of stress (General Psychology book) and is not a therapy. Emotional intelligence was named by Peter Salovey and John Mayer (1990) and popularised by Daniel Goleman (1995), whose original five domains are knowing one's own emotions, managing emotions, motivating oneself, recognising emotions in others and handling relationships (General Psychology book); the same five were later relabelled self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills, and that later list is the usual distractor when an item asks for Goleman's original wording. Within EFT itself, anger that covers hurt is a secondary emotion, and old core shame is primary maladaptive . Markers, tasks and the evidence What makes EFT distinctive in practice is its system of markers and tasks, the direct product of Rice and Greenberg's task analysis. A marker is something the client says or does in the session that signals that he is in a particular kind of problem state and is ready to work on it now. Each marker calls for a particular task , a structured piece of experiential work with known steps toward resolution. The therapist does not plan the session in advance. She listens for markers and offers the matching task when one appears. Table 6.13 lists the main pairs. Table 6.13 The main markers and tasks of emotion-focused therapy. Marker (what the client shows) Example Task Problematic reaction point: a puzzling reaction to a specific situation "I don't know why I burst into tears when the conductor shouted at me" Systematic evocative unfolding (Laura Rice) Unclear felt sense "There's something about this job that I can't put my finger on" Experiential focusing (Gendlin) Self-evaluative split: one part of the self criticises another "I'm so stupid; I should have finished this months ago" Two-chair dialogue Self-interruptive split: one part blocks the expression of feeling "I feel the tears coming and then I just shut down" Two-chair enactment Unfinished business: lingering bad feelings toward a significant other "I've never forgiven my father for the way he treated my mother" Empty-chair work Vulnerability: deep shame, fragility or despair "I feel I'm falling apart; I can't bear anyone seeing me like this" Empathic affirmation Three of these tasks you know from Gestalt therapy, now tamed and studied. In two-chair dialogue for a self-critical split, the critic (Perls's top dog) speaks from one chair, and the "experiencing self" that it attacks responds from the other. Greenberg's research showed what resolution looks like: the experiencing self moves from collapse to an assertion of its needs ("I need you to stop; I need some support"), and the critic softens from contempt into something closer to concern or even compassion. In two-chair enactment for self-interruption, the client plays the part of himself that shuts feeling down ("Stop crying, don't be weak"), so that he discovers how he does it and can choose otherwise. Empty-chair work for unfinished business follows the pattern of Paivio and Greenberg's 1995 study (Section 6.3). The other tasks come from Rogers's tradition. In systematic evocative unfolding , devised by Laura Rice, the therapist helps the client re-enter, slowly and vividly, the scene of a puzzling over-reaction until the hidden meaning of the trigger emerges: the conductor's shout, it turns out, was the voice of every adult who had ever shamed her in public. Focusing is Gendlin's method applied to an unclear felt sense. And for moments of acute vulnerability there is no technique at all. The therapist offers empathic affirmation , a quiet, accepting presence that lets the client touch bottom and begin, by himself, to rise. Look back at the aim that Section 6.1 gave for the whole humanistic-experiential family: to help clients develop a more fluid and integrated way of organising the self. EFT puts that aim into practice almost literally. Two-chair work integrates the warring parts of a split self; transformation integrates old emotions with new ones; reflection integrates feeling with meaning. Rogers's "fluidity" has become a set of tasks that can be taught, observed and tested. Key study: the York depression studies (Toronto, 1990s and 2000s) Question. Do EFT's active tasks add anything to Rogers's relationship conditions, or are the conditions enough, as Rogers claimed? Method. In the first York study, published in 1998, Greenberg and Jeanne Watson randomly assigned adults with major depression to about 16 to 20 weekly sessions of either client-centred therapy (empathy, acceptance and genuineness only) or process-experiential therapy (the same relationship plus markers and tasks such as chair work and focusing). Results. Both groups improved substantially and were similar on depression by the end, but the process-experiential group changed faster, was ahead by mid-treatment, and had improved more on self-esteem and interpersonal problems by the end. A second York study, by Rhonda Goldman, Greenberg and Lynne Angus (first reported in 2000 and published in full in 2006), found a clearer advantage for EFT on depressive symptoms, and a follow-up 18 months later (Ellison and colleagues, 2009) found that the EFT clients had fared better over time. A separate Toronto trial led by Watson (2003) compared process-experiential therapy with cognitive-behaviour therapy over 16 sessions in 66 depressed clients: both helped equally with depression and self-esteem, and the process-experiential clients reported fewer interpersonal problems. Conclusion. The core conditions are a strong base, but specific experiential tasks seem to add speed and depth, which is a partial answer to Rogers's claim that the conditions are sufficient (Section 6.2). Criticism. The trials were modest in size, and most were run by EFT's own developers, so researcher allegiance (Chapter 8) cannot be ruled out. Exam trap Match the marker to the task. A self-critical split calls for the two-chair dialogue; unfinished business with another person calls for the empty chair ; an unclear felt sense calls for focusing ; a puzzling over-reaction calls for systematic evocative unfolding ; vulnerability calls for empathic affirmation , not a technique. EFT is process-guiding (it guides how the client works, not what he should conclude), so it is wrong to call it either "non-directive" or "confrontational". If a question asks for the general aim of the humanistic-experiential therapies, the answer is to promote a fluid and integrative self-organisation (Section 6.1), not to resolve deep-seated conflicts (psychodynamic), change maladaptive behaviours (behavioural) or develop interpersonal skills. Martin Seligman, positive psychology and positive psychotherapy All the therapies you have met so far, however hopeful, begin with a problem: incongruence, unfinished business, a maladaptive emotion. In the late 1990s a movement began which asked whether psychology had become too good at studying what goes wrong with people and too poor at studying what goes right. Its founder tells the story of how the idea came to him. Martin E. P. Seligman (born 1942), of the University of Pennsylvania, had recently been elected president of the American Psychological Association when he was weeding his garden with his five-year-old daughter, Nikki. He was trying to get the job done; she was throwing weeds into the air and dancing, and he shouted at her. She walked away, came back and said: "Daddy, do you remember before my fifth birthday? From when I was three until when I was five, I was a whiner. I whined every day. On my fifth birthday, I decided I wasn't going to whine anymore. That was the hardest thing I've ever done. And if I can stop whining, you can stop being such a grouch." Seligman realised that raising Nikki was not about correcting her whining; she had done that herself. It was about recognising and nurturing the strength she had just shown. And he wondered whether psychology, too, had lost its way. Seligman was an unlikely prophet of happiness. He was famous for discovering learned helplessness : in experiments with Steven Maier in the late 1960s, dogs that had received shocks they could not escape later failed to escape shocks that they easily could, and the finding became a model of depression (taught in the Psychiatric Disorders book). He went on to study the explanatory style that protects people against helplessness and wrote Learned Optimism (1990). In his presidential address of 1998 he argued that since the Second World War psychology had become a science of healing damage, shaped by the funding of bodies such as the Veterans Administration and the National Institute of Mental Health, which paid psychologists to treat mental illness, and that it had neglected its two other missions: making the lives of ordinary people more fulfilling, and identifying and nurturing high talent. With Csikszentmihalyi he edited a special issue of the American Psychologist in January 2000 that launched the field. Positive psychology is the scientific study of positive experiences, of positive individual traits such as strengths and virtues, and of the institutions that enable them: in its slogan, building what is strong as well as fixing what is wrong. What, then, is a good life, and can it be studied? Seligman's first answer, in Authentic Happiness (2002), was that there are three routes to it: the pleasant life (positive emotion about the past, present and future), the engaged life (using one's strengths to become absorbed in work, love and play, in the state of flow described below) and the meaningful life (using one's strengths in the service of something larger than oneself). In Flourish (2011) he widened this into a theory of wellbeing with five elements, remembered by the acronym PERMA : positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishment. With Christopher Peterson (1950 to 2012) he also produced Character Strengths and Virtues (2004), the Values in Action (VIA) classification, which its authors offered as a "manual of the sanities" to stand beside the DSM. It describes 24 character strengths grouped under six virtues found across cultures and religious traditions: wisdom and knowledge, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence. A person's top few strengths, the ones that feel most authentically his own and most energising to use, are his signature strengths . These ideas soon became a therapy. In 2006 Seligman, Tayyab Rashid and Acacia Parks published a paper titled "Positive psychotherapy" in the American Psychologist . Positive psychotherapy , in their sense, is a treatment for depression and other problems that works directly to build positive emotion, engagement and meaning alongside attention to symptoms, on the premise that depression is not only the presence of sadness but also the absence of these positive states. A course runs over about fourteen sessions (fewer in groups), and each session introduces an exercise that is practised as homework. The best known are these: Signature strengths. The client writes a story of "you at your best", identifies his signature strengths, and uses one of them in a new way every day. Three good things. Each night the client writes down three things that went well that day and why they happened, a "blessings journal". The gratitude visit. The client writes a letter of thanks to someone who was important to him but was never properly thanked, and then delivers it and reads it aloud in person. Forgiveness. The client writes, but need not send, a letter that lets go of anger toward someone who hurt him. Active-constructive responding. When someone shares good news, the client responds with enthusiastic interest and questions, rather than a passive "nice" or a deflating comment. Savouring and legacy. The client deliberately prolongs his enjoyment of ordinary pleasures, and writes how he would like to be remembered. Key study: testing happiness exercises on the internet (Seligman, Steen, Park and Peterson, 2005) Question. Do simple positive psychology exercises make people happier and less depressed, and for how long? Method. Several hundred adults who visited a website were randomly assigned to do one exercise for one week: the gratitude visit, three good things, "you at your best", identifying signature strengths, using signature strengths in a new way, or a placebo exercise (writing each night about early memories). Happiness and depressive symptoms were measured before, straight after, and one week, one month, three months and six months later. Results. The gratitude visit produced the largest early gains, but they lasted only about a month and had gone by the three-month follow-up. Three good things and using signature strengths in a new way produced gains that appeared more slowly but lasted for six months. The placebo and the remaining exercises produced only brief effects. Participants who went on doing their exercise of their own accord did best. Conclusion. Brief, specific exercises can produce lasting changes in wellbeing, especially if they are kept up. Criticism. The participants were self-selected visitors to a positive psychology website, many dropped out, and the researchers had devised the exercises themselves. Seligman, Rashid and Parks reported in 2006 that group positive psychotherapy reduced depressive symptoms in mildly to moderately depressed university students for a year afterwards, and that individual positive psychotherapy produced more remission in clients with major depression at a university counselling centre than treatment as usual, with or without antidepressant medication. These were small pilot trials. Larger reviews are more sober. A meta-analysis by Nancy Sin and Sonja Lyubomirsky (2009) found that positive psychology interventions moderately increase wellbeing and reduce depressive symptoms, and a stricter meta-analysis by Linda Bolier and colleagues (2013) confirmed that the effects are real but small. Critics have also pointed to a "tyranny of positive thinking" that can make suffering people feel they are failing at happiness, to the Western, individualist picture of the good life built into some exercises, and to the field's occasional overreach. A much-publicised claim by Barbara Fredrickson and Marcial Losada (2005), that flourishing requires a ratio of positive to negative emotions of 2.9013, was shown in 2013 by Nicholas Brown, Alan Sokal and Harris Friedman to rest on misapplied mathematics, and the mathematical part of the paper was formally withdrawn. Clinical link Positive interventions are adjuncts, not replacements. A severely depressed client asked to list "three good things" may find none and conclude that he is failing even at therapy; a recently bereaved client handed a gratitude exercise may feel that his grief is being brushed aside. Clinicians therefore acknowledge the suffering first (the groundwork of Section 6.2), time the exercises carefully and adapt them to the client's world. A gratitude letter to a teacher, a grandparent or an elder sibling, or a strengths conversation that includes what the family is proud of, often fits an Indian client better than a solitary journal. Exam trap Positive psychology was launched by Martin Seligman during his APA presidency (1998), with Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi as co-founder (the special issue of 2000). The phrase itself is older: Abraham Maslow used it as the title of the last chapter of Motivation and Personality (1954), "Toward a positive psychology", so "Maslow used the term first; Seligman founded the field" is the safe formula. Seligman is also the name behind learned helplessness (with Maier), learned optimism , PERMA and, with Peterson, the VIA classification of 24 strengths under six virtues . He did not introduce the concept of flow. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi and flow Seligman's "engaged life" rests on the work of his co-founder. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021; the name is pronounced roughly "me-high cheek-sent-me-high") was born to a Hungarian family in Fiume, then part of Italy and now Rijeka in Croatia. As a boy during the Second World War he watched capable adults lose their homes, their work and their composure, and he began to wonder what makes a life worth living. He moved to the United States in the 1950s, took his doctorate at the University of Chicago and spent most of his career there, later moving to Claremont Graduate University in California. His central discovery began with painters. Studying artists for his doctoral research in the 1960s, he noticed that they would work at a canvas for hours, oblivious to hunger, fatigue and discomfort, utterly absorbed, and yet would lose interest in the painting almost as soon as it was finished. The reward was obviously not the product; it was the activity itself. He went on to interview rock climbers, chess players, dancers, surgeons and composers, and was struck that they described their best moments with the same image, of being carried along effortlessly by a current. He called the state flow : a state of complete absorption in a challenging activity, in which action and awareness merge, attention is wholly focused, self-consciousness disappears, the sense of time is altered and the activity becomes rewarding in itself. He described it first in Beyond Boredom and Anxiety (1975), and for a general audience in Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990). Flow has three conditions and several characteristic features. The conditions are clear goals, immediate feedback about how one is doing, and a balance between the perceived challenge of the task and one's skills, with both stretched. The features are the merging of action and awareness, complete concentration on the task, a sense of control, the loss of self-consciousness, the transformation of time (hours pass like minutes, or a split second stretches out) and an autotelic quality, from the Greek auto (self) and telos (goal): the activity is done for its own sake. A batsman "in the zone", a sitar player lost in a raga, a surgeon midway through a difficult operation and a student wholly absorbed in a hard problem are all in flow. The balance of challenge and skill is easiest to see in a picture. Csikszentmihalyi's own example was a boy learning tennis, and Figure 6.7 follows its logic. At first (A1) the learner can do little, and simply getting the ball over the net is a just-right challenge: she is in flow. With practice her skill grows, and getting the ball over the net becomes dull (A2, boredom). Or she is matched too soon against a far stronger player and is overwhelmed (A3, anxiety). Neither state is pleasant, and both push her back toward the channel: from boredom she seeks a harder challenge, and from anxiety she builds her skill. Either way she reaches A4, flow again at a more complex level. Flow, in other words, is not only enjoyable; it is a ladder of growth, because staying in it demands ever-increasing skill. Later versions of the model, developed with the Italian researchers Fausto Massimini and Massimo Carli, added that flow occurs when both challenge and skill are above the person's own average level, and that when both are low the result is not flow but apathy.
