Figure 6.7 The flow channel. Flow lies along the diagonal where challenge matches skill; challenge above skill produces anxiety, and skill above challenge produces boredom. The path from A1 to A4 shows why staying in flow forces a person to keep growing. To study flow in everyday life, Csikszentmihalyi and Reed Larson developed the experience sampling method . Participants carry a pager (today, a phone) that signals at random moments, about eight times a day for a week, and each time they note what they are doing, with whom, and how they feel. The method produced a famous paradox. In a study with Judith LeFevre (1989), working adults reported flow far more often at work than in their leisure time, which was dominated by passive activities such as watching television, and yet at work they said that they wished they were somewhere else. People, it seems, do not always know what makes them feel most alive. Flow matters clinically in several ways. It is the "engagement" of Seligman's PERMA and of positive psychotherapy. Depressed clients rarely experience it, and behavioural activation (Chapter 4) works partly by scheduling activities that offer a just-manageable challenge. Occupational and rehabilitation programmes (Chapter 9) aim to restore it. And flow has a darker side: the absorbing, finely graded challenges of gambling machines and video games are designed to produce something very like it, which helps to explain why they are so hard to stop. Exam trap Flow was introduced by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (RML 2023 asked exactly this). Each distractor is famous for something nearby. Maslow described peak experiences : brief, intense, often unexpected moments of awe, ecstasy and unity, more common in self-actualising people. Flow, by contrast, is a sustained state of effortful absorption in a challenging task, often recognised as enjoyable only afterwards. Rogers described the fully functioning person (Section 6.2), and Frankl the will to meaning (Section 6.5). The conditions of flow are clear goals, immediate feedback and a balance of challenge and skill: challenge above skill gives anxiety, skill above challenge gives boredom, and both low gives apathy. Nossrat Peseschkian's positive psychotherapy Examiners sometimes ask about "positive psychotherapy" in a way that has nothing to do with Seligman, because a quite different therapy with the same name is some three decades older. Nossrat Peseschkian (1933 to 2010) was born in Kashan, Iran, went to Germany in the 1950s to study medicine, and trained there in neurology, psychiatry and psychotherapy. Working in Wiesbaden from the late 1960s, and struck by how differently his Iranian and German patients thought about illness, family, time and politeness, he developed a transcultural, resource-oriented therapy, which he set out in Positive Psychotherapie (1977; English translation, Positive Psychotherapy , 1987). The word "positive" is the first trap. Peseschkian did not mean positive thinking. He took it from the Latin positum , "the given" or "the factual": a positive approach looks at the whole of what is actually there, which includes the person's capacities as well as his disorder. Every person, in his view, has two basic capacities, the capacity to know and the capacity to love, which unfold into actual capacities . The primary capacities belong to the capacity to love and concern emotional relationships: love, patience, time, trust, contact, hope and faith. The secondary capacities belong to the capacity to know and concern the norms of social life: punctuality, orderliness, cleanliness, politeness, honesty, thrift, diligence, reliability and justice. Conflicts, he argued, come less often from single dramatic traumas than from repeated small frictions over these everyday capacities (the husband who is always late, the daughter-in-law who keeps the kitchen differently, the son who is "lazy") which pile up until they produce symptoms. Anyone who has lived in a large joint family will recognise the idea. Three tools follow from this. The first is the positive interpretation of symptoms. Instead of treating a symptom only as a defect, the therapist offers a reinterpretation that names the capacity hidden in it. Depression, in one of Peseschkian's best-known examples, can be understood as the ability to react to conflicts with deep emotionality. The aim is not to deny the suffering but to widen the frame, so that the client and the family can see the person and not just the disorder. The second tool is the use of stories, fables, proverbs and humour as mediators, drawn especially from Persian and other Eastern traditions. His book Oriental Stories as Tools in Psychotherapy is subtitled The Merchant and the Parrot , after a tale by the thirteenth-century Persian poet Rumi. In it, a merchant about to travel to India asks his caged parrot what he should bring back. The parrot asks only that he tell the free parrots of India about its captivity. When the merchant does so, one wild parrot drops from the tree as if dead; when he reports this at home, his own parrot drops too, the grieving merchant throws it out of the cage, and it flies away. It had received a message about how to free itself. Stories like this let a client hear a new idea without feeling attacked. The third tool is the balance model , Peseschkian's map of the four areas of life through which people experience and handle conflict: the body (health, the senses, sleep, food, appearance), achievement (work, study, career), contact (relationships with partner, family, friends and community) and the future (fantasy, meaning, religion and spirituality). In health, energy is shared among all four. Under stress people tend to flee into one or two of them: into work, into illness and the body, into socialising, or into fantasy and daydreams. Therapy looks at which areas the client has neglected and helps to restore the balance. Peseschkian added that cultures differ in which areas they emphasise, so that a therapist from one culture can easily misread a client from another. Treatment follows five stages, and the logic of each is worth knowing. In observation and distancing , the client (often with the family) describes the conflict concretely: who annoys whom, about what, and when. In taking inventory , therapist and client map the actual capacities involved, with the help of a structured questionnaire. In situational encouragement , the client learns to notice and reinforce the good qualities of the person he is in conflict with, instead of only the faults. In verbalisation , the parties learn to talk about the conflict openly and step by step. In broadening of goals , the client looks beyond the symptom to new aims in all four areas of life. The method rests on three principles: hope (the positive interpretation), balance (the four areas) and consultation (the client and family as active self-helpers, guided through the five stages). Its evidence comes mainly from naturalistic studies in German-speaking countries; controlled trials are few. Table 6.14 sets the two positive psychotherapies side by side. Peseschkian's positive interpretation of a symptom resembles, but is not the same as, the reframing of strategic therapy and the positive connotation of the Milan school (Chapter 7), which are family-systems interventions aimed at the function a symptom serves in the family. 6.8 Narrative and Solution-Focused Brief Therapy Medium yield · 2 Qs Every therapy in this chapter so far assumes that there is something true inside the client waiting to be found: an actualising tendency, a felt sense, a primary emotion, a meaning. In the 1980s two small groups of family therapists, on opposite sides of the world, began from a different assumption. There is no single true story of a life, they said. There are many possible stories, made in language and in relationships, and some of them help people to live better than others. In Adelaide in South Australia and Auckland in New Zealand, Michael White and David Epston built narrative therapy , which helps people re-author the stories by which they understand themselves. In Milwaukee, Wisconsin, Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg built solution-focused brief therapy , which hardly bothers with the problem's story at all and goes straight to building the solution. Both grew out of family therapy, and their family applications are taught in Section 7.7, together with the brief strategic therapy of the Mental Research Institute from which they partly descend. Here we study them as approaches to individual clients, because they share, in a new form, the humanistic conviction that the client is the expert on his or her own life. The postmodern turn: problems as stories Both therapies belong to what is called the postmodern, or social constructionist, movement in therapy. Social constructionism is the view that what we take to be reality, including our identities and our problems, is not simply discovered but is constructed through language and social interaction, within a particular culture and history. "Depressed", "lazy", "a good son", "a failure": none of these is a fact found inside a person, like a blood group. Each is a description, made by people talking to one another, which then shapes how the person is treated and how he sees himself. The idea is a cousin of constructivism, the view of George Kelly (Section 5.5) that each individual builds personal constructs to make sense of the world. The difference is one of emphasis. Constructivism stresses the individual mind as a builder of meaning; social constructionism stresses the shared, cultural and linguistic processes through which meanings are built and imposed. Three consequences follow for therapy. First, the therapist is not an expert on the truth about the client. Harlene Anderson and Harold Goolishian, family therapists in Galveston, Texas, called this the "not-knowing" stance in a 1992 paper titled "The client is the expert". Second, a diagnosis is itself a story, often a powerful one that can shrink a person's identity to a label. Third, change happens through conversation: new ways of talking make new ways of living possible. Both therapies also drew on the earlier brief therapy movement: on the anthropologist Gregory Bateson's idea that information is "news of difference", on the Mental Research Institute's observation that people's attempted solutions often keep their problems going (Chapter 7), and on the American psychiatrist and hypnotherapist Milton Erickson (1901 to 1980), who was famous for utilising whatever the client brought, including his symptoms and his own language, and for orienting clients toward a future in which the problem had been solved. Michael White, David Epston and the stories people live by Michael White (1948 to 2008) began his working life in Adelaide as an electrical and mechanical draughtsman, then retrained as a social worker, and worked at the Dulwich Centre in Adelaide, which became the hub of narrative therapy worldwide. David Epston , a family therapist with a background in anthropology who worked in Auckland, met White in the early 1980s, and the two found that they had been arriving at similar ideas from different directions. Their joint book, first published in Adelaide in 1989 as Literate Means to Therapeutic Ends and in the United States in 1990 as Narrative Means to Therapeutic Ends , launched the approach. White's later Maps of Narrative Practice (2007) set out its methods in detail. Narrative therapy can be defined as an approach that helps people separate their lives and identities from the problems that trouble them, and re-author the stories by which they understand themselves, so that these stories include their own skills, values and preferred ways of living. Its starting point is that people make sense of their lives by linking events together in sequence across time according to a plot: as a story. Such a story is always selective. Out of the countless things that happen to us, we select those that fit the dominant plot and leave out the rest. A person who comes to therapy usually brings a problem-saturated story : a dominant account of his life in which the problem colours everything, so that every event seems to confirm it and everything that does not fit is overlooked. Problem-saturated stories produce what White called thin conclusions about identity ("I am weak", "she is a manipulator", "he is an alcoholic"). White borrowed from the anthropologist Clifford Geertz the contrast between thin descriptions , which reduce a person to a label, and thick descriptions , which are rich, many-stranded and full of context. Where do problem-saturated stories come from? White was strongly influenced by the French philosopher Michel Foucault (1926 to 1984), who studied how the knowledge of experts and institutions (medicine, psychiatry, schools, prisons) defines what counts as normal and, in doing so, exercises power over people, who learn to watch and judge themselves by those standards. Dominant cultural stories about success, gender, beauty, family duty and mental illness can recruit people into seeing themselves as failures. A young woman who starves herself is, in this view, not simply "an anorexic"; she is a person who has been recruited by powerful cultural ideas about thinness and female self-control. Narrative therapy is therefore unusually political. It invites clients to notice and question (to deconstruct ) the cultural stories that support their problems. From the American psychologist Jerome Bruner (1915 to 2016) White took the idea that stories have two landscapes, which you will meet in the re-authoring conversations below. The therapist's stance follows from all this. The narrative therapist is curious, asks far more questions than she makes statements, and treats the client as the expert on his own life. White described the ideal position as "decentred but influential": the client's knowledge and preferences are at the centre, while the therapist influences the direction of the conversation through the questions she chooses to ask. The approach is summed up in its best-known slogan: the person is not the problem; the problem is the problem . Exam trap "Self story", "re-authoring" or "re-storying" a life narrative points to narrative therapy (Michael White and David Epston, 1980s; Narrative Means to Therapeutic Ends , 1990). The distractors in the 2025 paper each work on something else: CBT changes thoughts and behaviours; psychodynamic therapy works with unconscious conflict and transference (although some analysts, such as Donald Spence, have written about "narrative truth"); Gestalt therapy works on here-and-now awareness. Three other near neighbours: George Kelly's fixed-role therapy (1955) is constructivist (Section 5.5); narrative exposure therapy is a trauma treatment in which survivors build a chronological account of their lives so that traumatic memories can be processed, which makes it an exposure method rather than narrative therapy; and Dan McAdams's life-story model of identity belongs to the Personality book. Externalising the problem The best-known practice of narrative therapy is externalising : speaking about the problem as an entity separate from the person, with its own intentions and tactics, so that the person can stand back from it, examine its influence and decide how to respond to it. The shift is made in language. "Arjun is lazy" becomes "the Worry has been keeping Arjun in bed in the mornings". "She is an anorexic" becomes "Anorexia has been telling her that she must not eat". "We are a fighting family" becomes "the Arguments have been taking over our evenings". Clients are invited to give the problem their own, experience-near name, and the name can be playful, especially with children. Once the problem is outside the person, the person is no longer under attack, blame and shame fall away, and family members who were blaming one another can join forces against a common opponent. Key study: Nick and Sneaky Poo (Michael White, 1984) Problem. Nick, aged six, was brought to White by his parents, Sue and Ron, with a long history of soiling. Hardly a day passed without an "accident", many treatments had failed, and the soiling had become a source of shame and conflict for the whole family. Sue doubted that she was a good mother, Ron was too embarrassed to talk about it with anyone and felt isolated, and Nick had come to be seen, and to see himself, as a dirty, naughty boy. Method. White did not ask why Nick soiled. Instead, he and the family gave the problem a name, "Sneaky Poo", and he asked two sets of questions, which he called relative influence questioning . The first set mapped the influence of the problem on the family: how had Sneaky Poo made Nick's life miserable, kept him from friends, driven Sue to despair and cut Ron off from other people? The second set mapped the influence of the family on the problem: had there been times when Nick had not let Sneaky Poo "outwit" him? Times when Sue had refused to let it make her miserable? It turned out that there had. Result. These overlooked moments became the start of a new story, of a boy and a family who could beat Sneaky Poo. Encouraged not to let Sneaky Poo get the better of him, Nick began to win; within weeks the accidents had become rare, and at follow-up the family reported that Nick had triumphed and that each of them felt more capable. Conclusion. When the problem rather than the child becomes the target, a family can unite against it, and its own competence becomes visible. Criticism. This is a single case reported by its own therapist; it illustrates the method rather than proving that it works. In Maps of Narrative Practice White set out the steps of an externalising conversation as a "statement of position map". The therapist helps the person (1) negotiate a particular, experience-near name for the problem; (2) map its effects across the areas of his life, such as home, school or work, friendships, health and hopes for the future; (3) evaluate those effects ("Is this okay with you? Are you for it, against it, or somewhere in between?"); and (4) justify that evaluation ("Why is it not okay? What does that tell me about what matters to you?"). The last two steps matter more than they look. The therapist does not assume that the person is against the problem; she asks, and the person's own reasons for opposing it become the seeds of a new story. Consider how this might go with Arjun, a seventeen-year-old Class 12 student in Mysuru whose parents bring him because, they say, he has become lazy: he has stopped going to his coaching classes, sleeps late and did badly in the last test. Arjun agrees that he is "useless". Asked what he would call the thing that has been happening to him, he eventually says "the Worry". The therapist asks how the Worry operates. It turns out that it whispers, the moment he opens a book, that he will fail anyway and shame the family, so he might as well not try; it keeps him in bed; it has pushed his friends away; it has started quarrels at the dinner table. Is this okay with him? "No." Why not? "Because I actually used to like maths. And because Amma looks so tired." Notice what has happened. Arjun has moved from being the problem ("I am useless") to being someone who is being pushed around by a problem that he has his own reasons to resist. His parents, listening, have moved from criticising him to wondering with him how to deal with the Worry. Externalising is never used to excuse harmful behaviour. Narrative therapists working with men who are violent do not externalise the violence itself, for which the man remains responsible; they externalise the beliefs and habits that support it ("the idea that a husband has the right to control his wife"), so that he can examine and reject them. Exam trap Externalising the problem is a narrative therapy technique (White and Epston): the person is not the problem; the problem is the problem. Do not confuse it with externalising disorders (conduct problems, oppositional behaviour, ADHD), the grouping in child psychopathology that is contrasted with internalising disorders such as anxiety and depression (Psychiatric Disorders book), or with projection , the defence of attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to others (Section 6.3 and the Personality book). Externalising is a deliberate, shared way of talking; projection is an unconscious defence. Relative influence questioning asks about the influence of the problem on the person and of the person on the problem. Unique outcomes, re-authoring and the audience Once the problem has been externalised, the therapist listens for the moments that the problem-saturated story leaves out. White called them unique outcomes , a term he borrowed from the sociologist Erving Goffman: events, thoughts, feelings or actions that contradict the dominant story and could not have been predicted from it. Narrative therapists also call them "sparkling moments". In Nick's family they were the times when Nick had not let Sneaky Poo outwit him. For Arjun they come out slowly. Last week he spent an evening teaching his younger cousin algebra, and enjoyed it. On Sunday he finished a whole chapter before the Worry noticed. Once he told the Worry "not now" and went to class anyway. And he has started asking his favourite teacher for help. On their own, such moments are easily dismissed ("that was nothing"). The work of therapy is to link them together into a new story. That work is done in re-authoring conversations, in which the therapist helps the client connect unique outcomes into an alternative, preferred story of his life and identity. White, following Bruner, described every story as having two landscapes. The landscape of action is the sequence of events: what happened, when and where, who was there and what led up to it ("How did you manage to finish that chapter? What did you do first? Who noticed?"). The landscape of identity (which White first called the landscape of consciousness) is what those events say about the person's values, hopes, intentions and commitments ("What does it say about you that you spent your evening helping your cousin? What were you standing for when you told the Worry 'not now'?"). The therapist zigzags between the two landscapes, so that each new event acquires meaning and each new meaning calls up further events from the past. Gradually a thin description ("lazy, useless") gives way to a thick one ("someone who loves learning when he is not being judged, who cares about his family, and who has started to stand up to the Worry"). Narrative therapists also make sure that the new story has an audience, because identities are sustained socially, not privately. In re-membering conversations , a term taken from the anthropologist Barbara Myerhoff, the client reviews the "membership" of his life, giving more weight to the voices that support his preferred identity and less to those that do not ("Who in your life would be least surprised to hear that you taught your cousin algebra?" "My grandfather. He always said I explained things well"). In definitional ceremonies , also named after Myerhoff, the client tells his story to outsider witnesses : people invited to listen (family members, friends, or others who have faced similar problems) who then retell what caught their attention, what image of the person it evoked, what it touched in their own lives and where it has moved them, before the client in turn responds to their retelling. And the new story is written down. Epston became known for therapeutic letters, sent after sessions, which summarise the client's own words and the unique outcomes; clients reread them for years, and in one small survey clients rated a single letter as worth several sessions of face-to-face therapy. Certificates (for a child who has "beaten" Temper), declarations and "leagues" of people fighting the same problem, such as the anti-anorexia leagues that Epston and his colleagues helped to start, serve the same purpose. Exam trap Unique outcomes (narrative therapy) and exceptions (solution-focused therapy, below) both mean times when the problem did not have its way, and examiners swap them. The difference is in their use: a unique outcome is the entry point to a new story about identity , whereas an exception is studied as a practical blueprint ("do more of what works"). Re-authoring belongs to narrative therapy; reframing belongs to strategic and family therapy (Chapter 7); imagery rescripting belongs to cognitive and schema therapy (Chapter 5). The landscapes of action and identity come from Jerome Bruner, "unique outcome" from Erving Goffman, "thick description" from Clifford Geertz, and re-membering, definitional ceremonies and outsider witnesses from Barbara Myerhoff. Steve de Shazer, Insoo Kim Berg and the solution-focused stance Steve de Shazer (1940 to 2005) was a Milwaukee-born social worker who had trained first as a classical musician and played jazz saxophone. Insoo Kim Berg (1934 to 2007; some sources give her year of birth as 1937) was born in Korea, studied pharmacy in Seoul, came to the United States in 1957 to continue her studies, and turned to social work and family therapy. Both were influenced by the brief therapy of the Mental Research Institute in Palo Alto, especially by John Weakland, and by Milton Erickson. They married, and in 1978, with a group of colleagues, they founded the Brief Family Therapy Center in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where solution-focused brief therapy was developed over the following decade, largely by watching sessions through a one-way mirror and asking what had happened just before clients began to improve. What they found reversed a long tradition. Therapists had always assumed that to solve a problem you must first understand it: its causes, its history, its function. The Milwaukee team noticed that the solutions their clients found often bore no obvious relation to the problems, and that clients improved when the conversation turned to times when things were better and to what they wanted instead. De Shazer put it in a metaphor in Keys to Solution in Brief Therapy (1985). A client's complaint is like a lock on a door. The therapist does not need to study the lock in detail, only to find a key that fits, and some "skeleton keys" fit a great many locks. Solution-focused brief therapy (SFBT) can be defined as a brief, future-oriented, goal-directed approach that helps clients construct solutions by describing the future they prefer and by finding and building on exceptions and existing resources, rather than by analysing the problem. Courses of therapy are short, often only a handful of sessions, and a single session is sometimes enough. Remember The central philosophy of SFBT is three rules. If it isn't broken, don't fix it. Once you know what works, do more of it. If it doesn't work, don't do it again; do something different. Add to these the assumptions that change is constant and inevitable, that small changes lead to larger ones, that no problem happens all the time, that the client is the expert on his own life and goals, and that the future is created and negotiable rather than fixed by the past. In practice this means a deliberate shift from problem talk to solution talk . The therapist listens respectfully to the complaint, but she spends most of the session asking what the client wants, what is already working and what the next small step would be. Goals matter a great deal, and solution-focused therapists help clients shape well-formed goals: goals that are important to the client; small, concrete and described in behaviour that others could see; stated as the presence of something rather than the absence of something ("We will be talking at dinner" rather than "We won't fight"); seen as the start of something rather than the end of it; and realistic. Change may even be under way before the first session. Michele Weiner-Davis, de Shazer and Wallace Gingerich reported in 1987 that about two-thirds of clients, when asked what changes they had noticed since they called to make the appointment, described some pre-session change , and solution-focused therapists often begin by asking about it and building on it. The Milwaukee team noticed, too, that clients arrive in different relationships to change, and de Shazer (1988) described three. In a visitor relationship the client has no complaint of his own: he has been sent by a court, a school or a worried family, and has simply come to visit. The therapist compliments him for coming, explores what he might want (perhaps only "to get them off my back") and gives no task. In a complainant relationship the client describes a problem but sees the solution as lying with someone else ("My son must change"), or does not yet see himself as able to act; the therapist compliments him and may suggest an observation task, such as noticing the times when things go a little better. In a customer relationship the client sees himself as part of the solution and is ready to act, and now behavioural tasks fit. These labels describe the relationship at a given moment, not a fixed trait of the client, and the relationship can shift within a single session. (The parallel with the stages of change of the transtheoretical model, Section 6.9, is close but not exact.) Exam trap SFBT was founded by Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg at the Brief Family Therapy Center, Milwaukee (1978). It is not the brief therapy of the Mental Research Institute in Palo Alto (Paul Watzlawick, John Weakland, Richard Fisch), which is problem-focused: it asks which attempted solution is keeping the problem going and prescribes something different (Chapter 7). The contrast is neat: the MRI looks at what is not working and stops it; SFBT looks at what is working and does more of it. Nor is SFBT one of the brief psychodynamic therapies of Malan, Sifneos, Davanloo and Mann (Chapter 3). Bill O'Hanlon's solution-oriented therapy is a close cousin. Visitor, complainant and customer describe relationships , not types of client. The solution-focused questions Solution-focused therapy is conducted almost entirely through questions, and examiners love them. The most famous is the miracle question , which de Shazer published in Clues: Investigating Solutions in Brief Therapy (1988). According to the story told at the Milwaukee centre, it was born when an overwhelmed client told Berg that perhaps only a miracle would help, and Berg took her at her word. In its standard form it runs like this: Suppose that one night, while you are asleep, a miracle happens and the problems we have been talking about disappear. Because you were asleep, you do not know that the miracle has happened. When you wake up, what will be the first signs for you that a miracle has happened? The question is asked slowly, and the answer is followed up in detail. "What else would be different? What would you be doing instead? Who would be the first to notice? What would your mother see you doing that would tell her?" The miracle question does three things at once. It moves the conversation out of the problem and into a preferred future. It produces goals, described in concrete, observable behaviour, often small and surprisingly ordinary ("I would get up when the alarm rings and make tea"). And it builds hope, because the client finds himself describing a life that he can almost see. If a client answers with a fantasy ("I would win the lottery"), the therapist accepts it lightly and asks what difference that would make, or asks the question again in a more modest form. Exception questions ask about times when the problem was absent, less severe or better handled, and about what was different then: "Tell me about a recent time when the arguments did not happen. What was different? What did you do?" They often follow the miracle question directly: "When has a small piece of this miracle already happened?" Exceptions show the client that the problem does not happen all the time and that he already knows part of the solution. The therapist distinguishes deliberate exceptions, which the client brought about and can repeat ("I went for a walk first"), from spontaneous ones, which simply happened. For spontaneous exceptions the client may be asked to predict each night whether the next day will be a better one, and then to notice what made the difference. Scaling questions ask the client to rate something on a scale, usually from 0 to 10, and then use the number as a lever: "On a scale where 10 is the day after the miracle and 0 is the worst things have ever been, where are you today?" Whatever the answer, the next questions are about progress and small steps, not about the gap. "Three. What puts you at three and not at zero?" (which draws out resources and exceptions). "What will be happening when you are at four?" (which defines the next small step). "What would your best friend notice you doing differently at four?" The same device can scale confidence ("How confident are you, from 0 to 10, that you can do this?") and willingness to work. Sometimes a client is so hopeless that he can find no exceptions and cannot imagine a miracle. Then the therapist uses coping questions , which turn attention to how the client has survived: "With everything that has been happening, how have you managed to keep going? How do you get yourself out of bed in the morning? How come things are not even worse?" The question takes the client's distress seriously while quietly uncovering strengths, and Berg showed how much a single coping question can do. A young mother from a harsh family background was asked how she had worked out that she wanted to be a different kind of mother to her baby than her own mother had been to her. Nobody had taught her, she said; she had watched other people, read magazines and thought about it all the time. The worker's reply, "You are a very thoughtful person", was a compliment built entirely from the client's own evidence. Compliments, in fact, are a technique in their own right. Solution-focused therapists give direct compliments, based on what the client has actually done ("You came today even though you had a night shift"); indirect compliments, through questions that imply a strength ("How did you manage to do that?" "What would your sister say you are good at?"); and invitations to self-compliment , in which the client is asked to describe his own successes. Toward the end of a first session the therapist may set the formula first session task , which de Shazer described in 1985: "Between now and next time we meet, I would like you to observe, so that you can describe to me next time, what happens in your life (or family, or marriage) that you want to continue to have happen." Notice the wording. It asks not whether something good happens but what happens, which presupposes that it will. Many solution-focused therapists also take a short break near the end of each session, often to consult colleagues behind the one-way mirror, and then deliver a brief message in three parts: compliments, a bridging statement that links them to the client's goals, and a task. Later sessions open not with "How have you been?" but with "What is better?", and the therapist follows each improvement through four steps that Peter De Jong and Berg summarised as EARS: elicit the improvement, amplify it with detailed questions, reinforce it with compliments, and start again with "What else is better?" Lakshmi, a thirty-eight-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, has felt low and irritable since she was transferred to a new school, and she says that she dreads every morning. Asked what she has noticed since she phoned for the appointment, she mentions that on Saturday she did not feel so bad (pre-session change). Asked the miracle question, she says that the first sign would be waking before the alarm, making coffee for her husband instead of snapping at him, and walking into the staff room and saying good morning to the other teachers. What else? Her daughter would see her laughing at dinner. Asked when a small part of this has already happened, she remembers that on Thursdays, when she teaches her favourite Class 8 section, she arrives early and chats with the head of department (an exception). On a scale where 10 is the morning after the miracle, she puts herself at 3; asked what keeps her at 3 and not at 0, she names her students and her daughter. At 4, she says, she would greet one colleague every day. The therapist compliments her on how carefully she has kept teaching well through a hard year, and suggests that until the next session she notice what happens on the better days that she wants to continue to have happen. Nothing about the history of her low mood has been discussed, yet she leaves with a clear, small, achievable step and the sense that she has already begun. Exam trap The miracle question is the signature of solution-focused brief therapy (de Shazer and Berg), not of psychoanalysis, Gestalt therapy or classical CBT. It has two ancestors that examiners occasionally use as bait: Alfred Adler's "The Question" ("What would you do if you were well?"), which Adler used mainly to judge what purpose a symptom served (Chapter 3), and Milton Erickson's "crystal ball" technique, in which a hypnotised client imagined a future in which the problem had been solved. Keep the SFBT questions apart: exception questions look back at times when the problem was absent; the miracle question looks forward; scaling measures progress, with 10 as the goal (unlike Wolpe's subjective units of distress in Chapter 4, where 100 is maximum distress); coping questions are for the hopeless client. Compliments are a deliberate technique, not mere politeness. Stories and solutions compared, and the evidence Narrative therapy and SFBT are often taught together, and they share a great deal: a social constructionist philosophy, respect for the client's expertise, a refusal to pathologise, close attention to language, and a search for the times when the problem does not have its way. But they are not the same therapy, as Table 6.16 shows. Narrative therapy is interested in the problem (its history, its tactics, its effects and the cultural ideas that support it) and it is deeply interested in identity and meaning. SFBT is minimalist and pragmatic. It deliberately spends as little time as possible on the problem, does not ask what the problem means, and judges success by whether the client is doing more of what works. SFBT has the larger body of research. In 2000 Wallace Gingerich and Sheri Eisengart reviewed fifteen controlled outcome studies and found preliminary support for the approach, strongest in the five best-controlled trials. A meta-analysis by Johnny Kim (2008) found effects that were small but positive, clearest for internalising problems such as depression and anxiety. A later review by Gingerich and Lance Peterson (2013) of 43 controlled studies found that about three-quarters reported significant benefits, and several suggested that SFBT reached outcomes comparable to other treatments in fewer sessions. Narrative therapy has a thinner evidence base: mainly case studies, qualitative research and small trials, for example with depressed adults and with children and families, which are encouraging but not conclusive. Some narrative practitioners have been reluctant to measure outcomes with standardised scales, which, they argue, embody the very expert knowledge that the approach questions. Critics of SFBT call it "problem-phobic": a client who is pushed into solution talk before he feels heard may feel dismissed, and Eve Lipchik, one of the founding members of the Milwaukee team, herself argued for giving emotion and the therapeutic relationship more room. Its brevity and simplicity can look superficial, it says little about why problems arise, and it is not on its own a treatment for severe mental illness. Critics of narrative therapy point to its vagueness, to political commitments that not every client shares, and to its weak evidence base. Defenders of both reply that they are respectful, strengths-based, collaborative and brief; that they travel well across cultures because they work with the client's own language and meanings; and that they are especially useful in schools, in community and social work, and wherever a clinician has only one or two contacts with a client. Both have been widely taken up in family work (Section 7.7), and methods descended from narrative practice, such as the Tree of Life exercise, which invites people to describe their roots, skills, hopes and relationships through the parts of a tree, have been used with communities affected by poverty, conflict and illness in many countries. Clinical link A solution-focused stance never replaces a risk assessment. Lakshmi's low mood, or a client's remark that "only a miracle can help", must still prompt careful questions about hopelessness and suicidal thinking (Chapter 2); coping questions can then be used within that assessment ("What has stopped you from acting on these thoughts?"). In the same way, narrative externalising should never separate a person from responsibility for violence or abuse. Used with these cautions, both approaches suit the brief, often single, contacts of busy outpatient clinics, school counselling and crisis work, and both suit clients who resist being labelled.
