Or she is a young woman with diabetes who knows that she should walk every evening and does not. The therapies in this chapter so far assume a client who has come for help. What do you do with a person who has come, or been brought, but is not at all sure that he wants to change? For most of the twentieth century the answer in the addictions field was blunt: break down his denial. Motivational interviewing began as a deliberate rejection of that answer, and the transtheoretical model, which grew up beside it, gave clinicians a map of where such a person stands on the road to change. From confrontation to conversation In the 1960s and 1970s American alcohol treatment was dominated by a confrontational style. Problem drinkers were assumed to share a characteristic defence called denial, and the counsellor's job (the counsellor was often a recovering alcoholic) was to attack it until the client admitted that he was an alcoholic. In some therapeutic communities for drug users, such as Synanon in California, sessions of harsh group attack were a central ritual. If the client argued back, that only proved how deep his denial went. William R. Miller , a young psychologist at the University of New Mexico, began to doubt all this. In a trial of behaviour therapy for problem drinkers that he published with two colleagues in 1980, the different behavioural methods made little difference to outcome, but something the researchers had not set out to study made a great deal. Each counsellor's accurate empathy had been rated during treatment, and those ratings predicted how much the counsellor's clients were drinking six months later, accounting for about two thirds of the variation in outcome. The way the counsellor listened seemed to matter more than the technique the counsellor delivered. In 1982 Miller spent a sabbatical at the Hjellestad Clinic near Bergen, in Norway, where a group of young psychologists asked him to show them how he worked. They role-played their own clients, Miller responded, and they kept stopping him to ask why he had said what he said. For the first time he had to put into words rules he had been following without ever stating them, and he wrote them up as "Motivational interviewing with problem drinkers", published in Behavioural Psychotherapy in 1983. Stephen Rollnick , a clinical psychologist working in Wales, had meanwhile begun to use and teach the approach in Britain. The two met in Australia in 1989, and their book Motivational Interviewing: Preparing People to Change Addictive Behavior appeared in 1991. The second edition (2002) widened the scope beyond addiction; the third, subtitled Helping People Change (2013), rebuilt the method around four processes and introduced most of the terms examiners now use; a fourth followed in 2023. So the approach has two founding dates: 1983 for Miller's first paper and 1991 for the first book with Rollnick. In the 2013 edition Miller and Rollnick defined motivational interviewing (MI), in everyday language, as "a collaborative conversation style for strengthening a person's own motivation and commitment to change". An earlier definition (Rollnick and Miller, 1995) put the paradox at its heart more sharply: a directive, client-centred counselling style for eliciting behaviour change by helping clients to explore and resolve ambivalence. At the heart of both definitions is ambivalence , feeling two ways about the same thing at the same time: "I want to stop drinking, and I don't want to stop drinking." Miller and Rollnick insisted that it is neither pathology nor denial but the normal state of a person considering a change, and the place where people get stuck. Listen to an ambivalent man thinking aloud and you hear him argue with himself: "I should cut down, my liver test was bad ... but it's the only way I relax ... but my daughter's wedding is next year ... but everyone in the office drinks." Now notice what happens when a helper takes one side of that argument. If the helper argues for change ("You must stop; your liver is in danger"), the client voices the other side ("My uncle drank all his life"). Because people tend to become more convinced of what they hear themselves say (an idea Miller and Rollnick drew from Daryl Bem's self-perception theory, taught in the Social Psychology book), the helper's well-meant arguments end up strengthening the case for not changing. Miller and Rollnick called the helper's urge to fix, warn and persuade the righting reflex . Learning MI begins with learning to resist it. The word directive is what separates MI from Rogers. A person-centred therapist follows the client wherever he goes, with no preference for one outcome over another (Section 6.2). An MI practitioner has a direction, toward a particular change such as drinking less or taking medicines regularly. He uses Rogers's warmth and listening skills, but reflects selectively, giving more attention to the client's arguments for change than to his arguments against it, and asks questions whose likely answers are reasons for change. Miller and Rollnick called this a guiding style, halfway between directing (telling people what to do) and following (simply going where they go): the style of a mountain guide, who neither drags the climber up the slope nor sits waiting at the bottom. Selective reflection used with respect helps a person hear his own reasons; used without respect, it would be manipulation. That is why MI's attitude, its spirit, matters as much as its skills. Key study: the more the counsellor confronted, the more the client drank (Miller, Benefield and Tonigan, 1993) Question. Is a problem drinker's "denial" a trait he brings with him, or is it partly produced by the way the helper talks? Method. William Miller, Gary Benefield and Scott Tonigan, in New Mexico, offered 42 problem drinkers a "Drinker's Check-up": an assessment followed by a session of personal feedback about the results. Drinkers were randomly assigned to receive the feedback from counsellors using a directive, confrontational style or from counsellors using a client-centred, motivational style, or to a waiting-list control. The sessions were recorded and coded. Results. Both check-ups reduced drinking compared with waiting (overall by more than half within six weeks, a gain maintained at one year), and the two styles did not differ significantly in their overall effect on drinking. But the confrontational style provoked much more resistance in the session (arguing, interrupting, denying that there was a problem), and resistance predicted poorer outcomes. Most strikingly, a single counsellor behaviour predicted drinking a year later: the more the counsellor confronted, the more the client drank. Conclusion. Resistance is not simply a property of the client; it is a signal about the interaction, and the counsellor's style can raise or lower it. Criticism. The sample was small, the outcome measures relied largely on what the drinkers reported, and a research version of confrontation may not match what happens in real treatment programmes. Exam trap Motivational interviewing was developed by William Miller and Stephen Rollnick : Miller's first paper appeared in 1983 and their first book in 1991. The distractors are real names from neighbouring topics. Prochaska and DiClemente created the transtheoretical (stages of change) model, taught later in this section, which is often paired with MI but is a different thing. Albert Bandura gave MI the concept of self-efficacy but did not create MI. G. Alan Marlatt (with Judith Gordon) developed relapse prevention (1985; Section 9.9). Beck (cognitive therapy), Wolpe (systematic desensitisation) and Jung (analytical psychology) have nothing to do with it. And remember where MI was born: in the treatment of problem drinking. The spirit of motivational interviewing Practitioners who learned MI's techniques without its underlying attitude, Miller and Rollnick found, produced something that looked like MI and did not work. So they described the attitude itself, which they called the spirit of motivational interviewing . In the 2002 edition it had three elements, each defined against its opposite: collaboration rather than confrontation, evocation rather than education, and autonomy rather than authority. In 2013 it became four elements, which trainers remember by the acronym PACE (Table 6.17). Partnership. MI is done "for and with" a person, not "on" or "to" him: a collaboration between two experts, the clinician who knows about alcohol and livers and the client who knows about his own life, values and reasons. Miller and Rollnick compared it to dancing rather than wrestling. Acceptance. This element comes almost straight from Rogers and has four parts: absolute worth (Rogers's unconditional positive regard), accurate empathy , autonomy support (honouring the person's irrevocable right to choose his own course, including the choice not to change) and affirmation (seeking out and acknowledging strengths and efforts). Acceptance is not approval: you can accept a man fully without approving of his drinking. Compassion. Added in 2013, compassion means actively promoting the other person's welfare. It is the safeguard that stops MI skills being used to sell a product or to steer someone into a change that serves the helper rather than the client. Evocation. People already have within them much of the motivation and many of the resources they need; the clinician's task is to draw these out, not to install them. This principle of evocation is what most clearly distinguishes MI from advice-giving. Table 6.17 The spirit of motivational interviewing. Element (2013) Nearest 2002 element What the clinician does What it rejects Partnership Collaboration Works with the client as the expert on his own life The expert who prescribes; confrontation Acceptance Autonomy (in part) Prizes the person, empathises, respects his choices, affirms strengths Judging, shaming, labelling ("You are an alcoholic") Compassion None (new in 2013) Puts the client's welfare first Using the skills for the helper's own agenda Evocation Evocation Draws out the client's own reasons and resources Installing motivation by lecturing and warning Exam trap The 2013 spirit of MI is partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation (PACE). The 2002 spirit was collaboration, evocation and autonomy , so a question asking for three elements wants the older set. Any option containing confrontation, persuasion or authority is wrong, because those are exactly what the spirit rejects: "presence, affirmation, confrontation, empathy" is the classic bait. Do not confuse the spirit (the attitude) with the four processes (engaging, focusing, evoking, planning), the core skills (OARS) or the older principles (express empathy, develop discrepancy, roll with resistance, support self-efficacy). A different PACE (playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, empathy) belongs to Daniel Hughes's attachment-focused work with children, not to MI. The four processes and the core skills In 2013 Miller and Rollnick described four processes. Engaging is establishing a helpful connection and a working relationship; a client who feels judged in the first ten minutes may never come back. Focusing is agreeing on a specific direction, the change to be discussed; in a health setting there may be several candidates (drinking, smoking, diet, medicines), and the two choose together. (This focusing has nothing to do with Gendlin's focusing, Section 6.7.) Evoking is drawing out the client's own motivations for change; it is the heart of MI and what makes it different from other approaches. Planning is developing commitment and a concrete plan of action, when, and only when, the client is ready. The processes are sequential but recursive, like a staircase on which each step rests on the one below and on which you sometimes step back down: if a client turns defensive during planning, the wise move is to return to engaging. Evoking without engaging feels like pressure, and planning without evoking produces a plan the client will not follow. Within every process the practitioner relies on four communication skills, remembered as OARS . You met most of them as interviewing skills in Chapter 2 (Section 2.2); in MI they are used with a strategic purpose. Open questions invite the client to think and talk ("What concerns you about your drinking?") rather than answer yes or no. The most useful are evocative questions whose natural answer is a reason for change. An affirmation is a genuine statement recognising the client's strengths, efforts or values: "You care a great deal about being a good father." It is about the client, not about the counsellor's approval; "I'm proud of you" quietly casts the counsellor as judge. Reflections are the core skill. A reflection is a statement, not a question; the voice goes down at the end ("You're worried about your liver"). A simple reflection repeats or rephrases what the client said. A complex reflection adds meaning or emphasis: it guesses at what the client means but has not said, names a feeling, or "continues the paragraph" by voicing the client's likely next sentence. Skilled practitioners offer at least two reflections for every question. Summaries pull together several things the client has said. A collecting summary gathers his statements about change and hands them back, like flowers gathered into a bouquet; linking and transitional summaries connect themes and move the conversation on. The third edition added a fifth skill, informing and advising , on one condition: ask permission first. The recommended format is elicit-provide-elicit : elicit what the person already knows or wants to know ("What do you know about how alcohol affects the liver?"), provide information briefly and neutrally, then elicit his reaction ("What do you make of that?"). Information handed over this way is heard as information; the same facts delivered as a lecture are heard as an attack. A worked example shows the skills in action. Ramesh, a 46-year-old bank clerk in Mysuru, has been sent by his physician after a blood test showed raised liver enzymes. His wife sits in the waiting room. Counsellor: "Dr Rao asked you to come and see me. What would you like us to talk about today?" (Open question.) Ramesh: "Honestly, I came because my wife made me. Everyone is making a big issue out of a few drinks." Counsellor: "It feels as if everyone has ganged up on you." (Complex reflection of feeling; the counsellor does not argue.) Ramesh: "Exactly. I work hard all day. Two or three pegs in the evening is how I relax." Counsellor: "The evening drink is the one part of the day that is just for you. And at the same time, you agreed to come here today." (Double-sided reflection, explained below.) Ramesh: "Well ... the liver report did worry me. My father had liver trouble. He died at fifty-eight. I don't want my children going through what we went through." Counsellor: "Your children matter enormously to you." (Affirmation and complex reflection.) Ramesh: "Yes. Maybe I could stop on weekdays. I don't know if I can, though." Counsellor: "Let me see if I have this right. You came because your wife insisted, and it feels as if people are making too much of it. A drink helps you unwind. At the same time the liver report worried you, you remember your father, and you don't want that for your children. You're even wondering about stopping on weekdays, though you're not sure you could. What else?" (Collecting summary.) The counsellor never argued, warned, labelled Ramesh an alcoholic or told him what to do. Every reason for change in that conversation came out of Ramesh's own mouth. Before 2013 the method was taught through general principles rather than processes, and these still appear in exam questions. The 1991 book listed five: express empathy, develop discrepancy, avoid argumentation, roll with resistance and support self-efficacy; the 2002 edition folded avoiding argumentation into rolling with resistance, leaving four. In developing discrepancy the practitioner helps the client see the gap between his present behaviour and his own important goals and values ("You want to be well for your daughter's wedding, and you're drinking more than you'd like"); motivation grows as the gap becomes vivid, provided the client also believes change is possible. The principle of rolling with resistance means not opposing the client's arguments against change but responding in ways that let him reconsider (the next subsection shows how). Supporting self-efficacy , a concept taken from Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021), means building the client's belief in his own ability to carry out the change; a client who sees the danger but believes he cannot change falls back on excuses. For busy health settings, Rollnick, Miller and Christopher Butler (2008) condensed the principles into RULE: resist the righting reflex, understand the patient's own motivations, listen with empathy and empower the patient. Miller and Rollnick (2002) also named the commonest traps a helper falls into: the question-answer trap (a string of closed questions that makes the client passive), the confrontation-denial trap (taking sides), the expert trap, the labelling trap, the premature focus trap and the blaming trap. Exam trap OARS stands for open questions, affirmations, reflections (reflective listening) and summaries . The R is never reframing, rewards or responsibility, and the S is never support, suggestion or sanctions; "outcomes, assessment, rewards, sanctions" and "openness, acceptance, responsibility, support" are invented sets. The skills (OARS, plus informing with permission) are used across all four processes; the processes are engaging, focusing, evoking and planning , in that order. If an older question asks for the principles, they are express empathy, develop discrepancy, roll with resistance and support self-efficacy (with "avoid argumentation" as a fifth in 1991). In MI a reflection is a statement, not a question. Change talk, sustain talk and discord The single most important thing an MI practitioner listens for is a particular kind of speech. The client's change talk is any speech that favours movement toward change ("I'd like to cut down", "My children need a healthy father"); his sustain talk is the opposite, his own arguments for keeping things as they are ("I need a drink to sleep"). Both come out of ambivalence, often in the same breath. In the evoking process the practitioner draws out change talk, responds to it so that the client says more, and responds to sustain talk without strengthening it, because the balance between the two in a session predicts what the client will do afterwards. Miller and Rollnick, working with the psycholinguist Paul Amrhein, divided change talk into two kinds, remembered as DARN-CAT. Preparatory change talk expresses the motivation that comes before a decision: D esire ("I want to ..."), A bility ("I could ..."), R easons ("I would feel better if ...") and N eed ("I have to ..."). Mobilising change talk signals movement toward action: C ommitment ("I will ..."), A ctivation ("I'm ready to ...") and T aking steps ("This week I didn't buy a bottle"). Each kind has a mirror image in sustain talk, as Table 6.18 shows. Table 6.18 Change talk (DARN-CAT) and its mirror image in sustain talk, from the case of Ramesh. Kind Letter Change talk Sustain talk Preparatory Desire "I want to be healthy for my children." "I don't want to give it up." Preparatory Ability "I could probably stop on weekdays." "I couldn't sleep without it." Preparatory Reasons "If I stopped, I'd save money and sleep better." "It's the only way I unwind." Preparatory Need "I have to do something about my liver." "My levels are only a bit high; I don't need to stop." Mobilising Commitment "I will stop drinking on weekdays from Monday." "I'm not going to stop." Mobilising Activation "I'm ready to give it a try." "I'm not ready to do anything yet." Mobilising Taking steps "I told my colleagues I won't join them on Fridays." "I've bought a case for the wedding." Key study: the language of commitment (Amrhein, Miller and colleagues, 2003) Question. Does what clients say during an MI session predict what they do afterwards? Method. Paul Amrhein, William Miller and their colleagues analysed video recordings of MI sessions with 84 drug users, coding every client statement about change for its type (desire, ability, reasons, need, readiness, commitment) and its strength, minute by minute through the session, and related the patterns to drug use over the following year. Results. Desire, ability, reasons and need did not predict outcome directly. What predicted outcome was the strength of commitment language, especially toward the end of the session; desire, ability, reasons and need, in turn, predicted how strong commitment became. The researchers also noticed that some clients' commitment language fell away at the very end of the session, at the point where the protocol required the counsellor to complete a change plan, and these clients did worse. Conclusion. Preparatory change talk builds toward commitment, and commitment talk predicts change; pushing a plan on a client who is not yet ready can undo the good work of the session. Criticism. The findings are correlational: commitment talk may simply reveal motivation that already existed, rather than create it. The simplest way to evoke change talk is to ask for it with evocative questions shaped around DARN: "What would you like to be different?" "If you did decide to cut down, how might you go about it?" "What are the three best reasons for making this change?" A widely used tool is the importance ruler , a 0 to 10 scale on which the client rates how important the change is to him, often paired with a confidence ruler for how confident he is that he could make it. Suppose Ramesh rates importance at 4. The counsellor does not ask "Why only 4?", which invites sustain talk, but "Why 4 and not 1?", whose answer is change talk ("Because of the liver report and my children"), and then "What would it take to move you from 4 to 6?" (The rulers resemble the scaling questions of solution-focused therapy, Section 6.8, but here they evoke reasons for change.) Other strategies are querying extremes ("What is the worst that could happen if you carried on as you are?"), looking back to life before the problem, looking forward to life after the change, and exploring the client's values to find what the behaviour conflicts with. When change talk appears, the practitioner responds with EARS: asking the client to elaborate , affirming , reflecting and summarising , so that he hears his own reasons again. One caution concerns the decisional balance , the familiar exercise of listing the pros and cons of changing and of not changing, which comes from Irving Janis and Leon Mann's work on decision making and is part of the transtheoretical model (later in this section). Because it asks the client to argue both sides equally, it draws out sustain talk as well as change talk. Miller and Rollnick therefore advised against using it routinely when the aim is to help someone move toward change, and kept it mainly for situations in which the counsellor deliberately wants to stay neutral, such as helping a woman decide whether to continue a pregnancy. What became of the old idea of resistance? In 2013 Miller and Rollnick dropped the word, because it seemed to blame the client, and replaced it with two ideas. Sustain talk, as you have seen, concerns the target behaviour and is the normal voice of ambivalence. The second idea, discord , concerns the relationship: arguing, interrupting, discounting or ignoring the counsellor. It is a signal that the counsellor has done something (pushed, lectured, labelled) that the client experiences as a threat to his freedom. Both are met by "rolling with" them rather than opposing them, with responses worth knowing by name: A simple reflection of the sustain talk, which often lets the client hear it and soften it himself. An amplified reflection , which reflects the statement in a slightly exaggerated form, without a trace of sarcasm. Ramesh: "My drinking doesn't affect anyone." Counsellor: "Nobody at all is affected by it." Ramesh, usually: "Well, my wife does get upset." A double-sided reflection , which reflects both sides of the ambivalence: "On the one hand a drink helps you relax, and on the other hand you're worried about your liver." The change side goes second, because people respond to what they hear last. Emphasising autonomy ("It really is your decision; nobody can make it for you"), since people defend their freedom less when it is acknowledged. Reframing , which offers a new meaning ("My wife nags me" becomes "She seems to care a great deal about what happens to you"), and agreeing with a twist , agreement followed by a reframe. Shifting focus away from a stuck point, and coming alongside , siding with the sustain talk ("Maybe drinking is so important to you that it's worth the risk to your liver"), which often prompts the client to take up the other side himself. Exam trap DARN (desire, ability, reasons, need) is preparatory change talk; CAT (commitment, activation, taking steps) is mobilising change talk. Commitment language is the best predictor of change (Amrhein and colleagues, 2003). Sustain talk is the client's own speech in favour of the status quo; discord is friction in the relationship. These two replaced the older term "resistance" in 2013, so "rolling with resistance" in an older question corresponds to responding to sustain talk and discord without opposing them. An amplified reflection must never be sarcastic, and in a double-sided reflection the change side comes last. A full pros-and-cons decisional balance is a transtheoretical model tool that MI now uses with caution. Where motivational interviewing is used, and how well it works MI's most established uses remain in the addictions where it was born: alcohol, illicit drugs and, more recently, tobacco. From there it spread to almost every situation in which a person's own behaviour affects his health: diet and physical activity, diabetes self-care, medication adherence (in HIV, hypertension and severe mental illness), safer sex, gambling, people with both a mental illness and a substance problem, and offenders. It is also used as a short prelude to other treatments, to build the motivation a client needs to tolerate them; a few sessions of MI before cognitive-behaviour therapy for generalised anxiety, for example, have been found to improve outcomes for some clients. One adaptation has its own name: motivational enhancement therapy (MET), which combines the MI style with structured, personalised feedback from an assessment (how much the person drinks compared with others of the same age and sex, what his test results show), in a small number of sessions. It was developed for Project MATCH, the largest psychotherapy trial ever conducted in the alcohol field (1997), in which four sessions of MET produced outcomes broadly similar to twelve sessions of cognitive-behavioural coping skills therapy and twelve of twelve-step facilitation (Section 8.8). MI also shaped the brief interventions of a few minutes to an hour, given in primary care or emergency departments to people drinking at risky levels, whose effective ingredients were summarised in the early 1990s as FRAMES: F eedback of personal risk, emphasis on the client's R esponsibility, clear A dvice to change, a M enu of options, an E mpathic style and support for S elf-efficacy. Does it work? The first major meta-analysis, by Brian Burke, Hal Arkowitz and Marisa Menchola in 2003, pooled 30 controlled trials of adaptations of MI. MI was as effective as other active treatments, and better than no treatment or placebo, for problems involving alcohol, drugs, and diet and exercise (including trials with obese women with Type 2 diabetes), but the trials then available did not support its efficacy for smoking or HIV-risk behaviour (Section 9.4). A review of 72 trials by Jennifer Hettema, Julie Steele and Miller (2005) found that effects varied enormously from one study, site and counsellor to another, so the quality of delivery matters, and that effects were larger with clients from ethnic minority groups. A meta-analysis of 119 studies by Brad Lundahl and colleagues (2010) found a small but reliable advantage over no treatment or weak comparisons, and results comparable to other active treatments. MI is not a treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder, which needs exposure and response prevention (Chapter 4), nor a primary treatment for personality disorders or bipolar disorder, though MI-style conversations are used to support medication adherence in all of these. In 2009, worried by misunderstandings, Miller and Rollnick published "Ten things that motivational interviewing is not": it is not based on the transtheoretical model, not a way of tricking people, not a technique, not the decisional balance, not dependent on assessment feedback, not a form of cognitive-behaviour therapy, not just client-centred counselling, not easy, not what most practitioners were already doing, and not a panacea. Clinical link In India the person with a drinking problem is very often brought by the family, and at home the family has usually tried every version of the righting reflex already: pleading, scolding, hiding the money, taking vows at the temple. The MI stance (respect, curiosity, the client's own reasons) can feel surprising to such a client, and that surprise is often where engagement begins. Families can be helped too. Miller, Robert Meyers and Scott Tonigan (1999) compared three ways of helping family members of drinkers who refused treatment. With Community Reinforcement and Family Training (CRAFT), which teaches relatives to reward sober behaviour, let natural consequences happen and invite the drinker into treatment at a good moment, 64 percent of the drinkers entered treatment; with a confrontational family "intervention" the figure was 30 percent, and with referral to Al-Anon, a self-help group for families, 13 percent. Gentle, well-timed invitations worked better than ambushes. Exam trap "Motivational interviewing is used in the management of" has the keyed answer substance abuse (IHBAS 2020), because that is where MI was developed and where its evidence is strongest. "Non-compliance to treatment" is tempting, and MI is indeed used to improve adherence, but it is a later extension; anxious-avoidant personality disorder and bipolar disorder are not its targets. For Burke, Arkowitz and Menchola (2003) , the problems studied were alcohol, drugs, diet and exercise (diabetes-related trials included), smoking and HIV risk (studied but not supported); obsessive-compulsive disorder was not among them (RML 2022). Note the third author's name, Menchola, often misspelt in papers. The transtheoretical model: stages and processes of change At about the same time, another American psychologist was asking a different question: not how a helper should talk, but how people change at all, with or without a helper. James O. Prochaska , at the University of Rhode Island, had published Systems of Psychotherapy: A Transtheoretical Analysis in 1979, a comparison of the leading schools of therapy, and concluded that beneath their different theories they relied on a small number of common processes of change. Because the framework cut across all the theories, he called it transtheoretical. With Carlo C. DiClemente he then turned to the people who change most often without any therapy at all: smokers who quit on their own. Key study: how smokers change on their own (Prochaska and DiClemente, 1983) Question. Do people who stop smoking by themselves use the same processes as people in therapy, and do they use them all at once or at different times? Method. Prochaska and DiClemente gave questionnaires to several hundred smokers and former smokers who were at different points in changing, from those not yet thinking about quitting, through those thinking about it and those who had recently quit, to those who had stayed quit and those who had relapsed, and asked how often they used each of ten processes of change. Results. The use of the processes varied systematically with the person's position: people thinking about quitting relied most on becoming aware of the problem and re-evaluating themselves, while people who had recently quit relied on the behavioural processes, such as rewarding themselves, substituting other behaviours and seeking support. Conclusion. Change is not a single event but a movement through stages, and different processes help at different stages. Criticism. The study was cross-sectional (it compared different people rather than following the same people through time), relied on self-report and was limited to smoking. From that beginning grew the transtheoretical model (TTM), also called the stages of change model, which Prochaska, DiClemente and later John C. Norcross elaborated over the following decades and popularised in Changing for Good (1994). It has four parts: the stages of change (when people change), the processes of change (how they change), the decisional balance and self-efficacy (what moves them), and the levels of change (what is to be changed). The stages are the part everyone remembers. The commonly taught version has five, with a sixth added later, each defined by the person's intentions and behaviour over a fixed period (Table 6.19 and Figure 6.9). Table 6.19 The stages of change (transtheoretical model), with what the clinician might hear and what helps. Stage Definition What you might hear What helps most Precontemplation No intention of changing in the next six months "I don't have a problem. My grandfather chewed tobacco till ninety." Engaging, respectful listening, information offered with permission; raising doubt, not arguing Contemplation Intends to change within six months; ambivalent "I know I should quit. But not just now." Evoking change talk, exploring ambivalence, developing discrepancy Preparation Intends to act within the next month; has taken some steps "I've told my wife I'm quitting on the first of the month." Planning, choosing among options, strengthening commitment Action Has changed the behaviour within the last six months "I haven't smoked for five weeks." Behavioural skills, stimulus control, rewards, support Maintenance Has sustained the change for more than six months "It's been a year. I still get urges at weddings." Relapse prevention, coping with high-risk situations Termination No temptation and complete confidence (added later) "I never even think about it now." Nothing further; few people with addictions reach it In precontemplation the person does not intend to change in the next six months. He may be unaware of the problem, demoralised by failed attempts or simply unpersuaded, and precontemplation is not the same as denial. DiClemente later described four kinds of precontemplator, the "four Rs": the reluctant , held back by lack of information or inertia; the rebellious , heavily invested in the behaviour and in making their own decisions; the resigned , who have given up hope; and the rationalising , who have every answer about why it is not a problem. None of them is helped by a lecture. In contemplation the person is seriously thinking about changing within six months but has not committed; this is ambivalence in its purest form, and some smokers in Prochaska's studies stayed there for years (chronic contemplation, or behavioural procrastination). In preparation the person intends to act within the next month and has taken small steps, such as telling his family, buying nicotine gum or (in the definition used for smokers) making at least one quit attempt of a day or more in the past year. In older versions of the model, including the "wheel of change" that Miller and Rollnick printed in 1991, this stage was called determination . In the action stage the person has visibly changed the behaviour within the past six months, to a criterion that experts agree reduces risk: for smoking, total abstinence, not merely cutting down. Action is the busiest stage, and the one that traditional treatment programmes assumed everyone was in. In maintenance the change has lasted more than six months (up to about five years) and the person works to prevent relapse; temptation is lower and confidence higher than in action, but the risk remains. Later versions added termination , in which the person feels no temptation in any situation and has complete confidence that he will not return to the old behaviour. Only a minority of people with addictions reach it, and for many problems maintenance is lifelong. The stages of change (transtheoretical model) Pre- contemplation not considering Contemplation ambivalent, weighing it up Preparation intends soon, first steps Action changing behaviour now Maintenance sustaining the change Termination sixth stage, added later Relapse (curved line): most people recycle and climb again Figure 6.9 The stages of change. People climb from precontemplation toward maintenance, but relapse (from action or maintenance) is the rule rather than the exception; most relapsers return to contemplation or preparation rather than to the bottom step, which is why Prochaska, DiClemente and Norcross (1992) drew the model as a spiral. Where is relapse? Some early versions drew it as a stage of its own, and some textbooks still list it. In the modern model relapse is an event, a return from action or maintenance to an earlier stage, and Prochaska, DiClemente and Norcross (1992) found it to be the rule rather than the exception: most people who quit smoking relapse several times before they succeed. But relapse rarely sends a person back to the beginning. In their data on smokers, only about 15 percent of those who relapsed went all the way back to precontemplation; about 85 percent recycled to contemplation or preparation and tried again, usually having learned something. Hence the spiral model of change, in which a person can circle back without losing all the ground he has gained. The second part of the model is the ten processes of change , the covert and overt activities people use to move through the stages (Table 6.20). Five are experiential (they work through thinking and feeling) and five are behavioural (they work through doing), and they work best when matched to the stage. Consciousness raising, dramatic relief and environmental re-evaluation help people move from precontemplation to contemplation; self-re-evaluation helps them move from contemplation to preparation; self-liberation (choosing and committing) carries them into action; and reinforcement management, helping relationships, counterconditioning and stimulus control sustain action and maintenance. Teaching a precontemplator how to avoid cues to smoke is like teaching someone to swim who has no intention of entering the water. Five men attend the tobacco cessation clinic of a district hospital on the same morning. Mahesh, a farmer who chews gutka, came only because his son insisted: a precontemplator, he needs engagement, a question about what he knows of gutka and mouth cancer, and an offer, with permission, to look together at the white patch inside his cheek (consciousness raising). Imran, a tailor, knows bidis are ruining his chest but cannot imagine his workday without them: a contemplator, he needs his ambivalence explored and his reasons evoked, perhaps through how his breathlessness affects his work and his children (self-re-evaluation, environmental re-evaluation). Suresh has decided to quit on his daughter's birthday next week and has told his family: in preparation, he needs a concrete plan, a choice among options such as nicotine replacement, and a firmer commitment (self-liberation). Joseph stopped a month ago and is struggling with cravings after meals: in action, he needs behavioural tools, such as removing lighters, a walk after dinner, rewards and a friend who has also quit (stimulus control, counterconditioning, reinforcement management, helping relationships). Ravi has not smoked for eighteen months but dreads a wedding season full of old smoking companions: in maintenance, he needs relapse prevention planning (Section 9.9). Five men, one behaviour, five different conversations. What drives movement between stages? Prochaska borrowed the decisional balance from Irving Janis (1918 to 1990) and Leon Mann, whose 1977 book on decision making described how people weigh the gains and losses of a choice. In the TTM the pros of changing rise and the cons fall as people move through the stages, usually crossing over between contemplation and action. Across twelve problem behaviours Prochaska (1994) found that moving from precontemplation to action involved a rise in the pros of about one standard deviation but a fall in the cons of only about half a standard deviation (his "strong" and "weak" principles of progress): raising the benefits of change does more than attacking its costs. Alongside the decisional balance runs self-efficacy in Bandura's sense: confidence that one can keep the change in tempting situations rises across the stages, while temptation falls. The fourth part, the levels of change , describes what is being changed. Prochaska and Norcross distinguished five increasingly deep and interrelated levels: symptoms or situational problems, maladaptive cognitions, current interpersonal conflicts, family or systems conflicts, and intrapersonal conflicts. Different schools suit different levels (behaviour therapy for symptoms, cognitive therapy for maladaptive thoughts, family therapy for family conflicts, and psychodynamic, Gestalt or existential therapy for intrapersonal conflicts), and transtheoretical therapists usually start at the most concrete level, the symptom, and go deeper only when needed. With "Mrs C", a mother with severe compulsive hand-washing, the therapist worked at all five: her washing, her thoughts about dirt, her relationships with her children, her own mother's rules about cleanliness, and her overcontrol of feelings. How do MI and the TTM fit together? They grew up together in the 1980s among people who knew one another, and they complement each other neatly. The TTM tells the clinician where the client is and what kind of help is likely to be useful; MI tells the clinician how to talk with an ambivalent client, which describes most clients in precontemplation and contemplation. MI is therefore often called the method of choice for the early stages, and the action-oriented therapies (behaviour therapy, relapse prevention) for the later ones. But, as you saw, Miller and Rollnick insisted that MI is not based on the TTM; the two are separate ideas that happen to fit. The TTM has been enormously popular in smoking cessation, alcohol treatment, exercise promotion and HIV prevention, because it is intuitive and frees clinicians from expecting every client to be ready for action. Its critics are equally vocal. In a widely read editorial in 2005 the British psychologist Robert West argued that it was time to put the model to rest. The boundaries between stages are arbitrary (why six months and not five?), the stages may not be truly distinct, and many smokers report moving from not thinking about quitting to quitting within a single day. Most important, systematic reviews of smoking cessation, such as that by Robert Riemsma and colleagues in 2003, found little evidence that interventions tailored to a person's stage work better than interventions that are not. The model survives as a useful clinical map, but not as a law of change. Exam trap The stages, in order, are precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance , with termination as a later sixth stage; Indian exam notes often list all six. "Determination" is the older name for preparation, and relapse is now treated as an event and a return to an earlier stage rather than a stage of its own. Know the time frames: no intention within six months (precontemplation), intention within six months (contemplation), within the next month (preparation), changed for less than six months (action), more than six months (maintenance). The model is Prochaska and DiClemente's (1983) , not Miller and Rollnick's. Recognise models by their constructs: "precontemplation" and "processes of change" mean the transtheoretical model ; "perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers" mean the health belief model ; "attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control" mean the theory of planned behaviour ; and "self-efficacy, outcome expectancies, observational learning" mean social cognitive theory (all compared in Section 9.2). 6.10 Counselling and the Helping Skills Lower yield · 1 Q Motivational interviewing taught a hard lesson: the same assessment and the same advice, delivered with more or less confrontation, can leave one client drinking less and another drinking more. If that is true, then the skills of listening and responding are not a pleasant extra laid on top of "real" treatment. They are the working tools of every helper, whether the helper is a psychoanalyst, a behaviour therapist, a school counsellor or a nurse in a primary health centre. This last section of the chapter turns from schools of therapy to those tools. It asks first what counselling is and how it differs from psychotherapy, and then looks at the three best-known attempts to turn helping into a set of teachable skills: Allen Ivey's microskills hierarchy, Robert Carkhuff's helping model and Gerard Egan's skilled helper. The individual skills themselves (attending and SOLER, open and closed questions, minimal encouragers, paraphrasing, reflection of feeling, summarising, and primary and advanced empathy) were taught in Chapter 2 (Section 2.2), and this section builds on them rather than repeating them. What counselling is Few words in the helping professions are used as loosely as "counselling". A friend gives "counselling" over tea; a bank offers "debt counselling"; and in India the word is stretched further still, because the "counselling" for medical and engineering admissions is a process of allotting seats, not a helping conversation at all. In its professional sense the word means something much more specific. In 2010 a group of American counselling organisations agreed on a consensus definition: "Counseling is a professional relationship that empowers diverse individuals, families, and groups to accomplish mental health, wellness, education, and career goals." Put more fully, counselling is a professional helping relationship in which a trained person uses psychological knowledge and communication skills to help people understand themselves and their situation, resolve problems of living, make decisions and grow, usually with people whose everyday functioning is basically intact. Counselling has a different family tree from clinical psychology. Clinical psychology grew out of mental testing and the psychiatric clinic (Chapter 1); counselling grew out of the guidance movement, the giving of information and advice to help people make educational and vocational choices. Its founder is usually taken to be Frank Parsons (1854 to 1908), a Boston social reformer who opened the Vocation Bureau in 1908 to help young people choose work. In his book Choosing a Vocation , published in 1909, the year after his death, Parsons set out three steps: a clear understanding of oneself (one's aptitudes, abilities, interests and limitations), a knowledge of the requirements and prospects of different kinds of work, and "true reasoning" on the relations between the two. This matching of person to job became known as the trait-and-factor approach, and Parsons is remembered as the father of vocational guidance. In the 1930s Edmund Griffith Williamson (1900 to 1979) at the University of Minnesota turned trait-and-factor guidance into a full directive counselling method, in which the counsellor analysed test data, diagnosed the problem and advised the student; his How to Counsel Students appeared in 1939. You met the other side of the story in Section 6.2: Rogers's Counseling and Psychotherapy (1942) challenged Williamson's directive method and turned counselling from advice-giving into a therapeutic relationship. After the Second World War the need to help returning soldiers find work and adjust to civilian life created a large demand for counsellors, and at a conference at Northwestern University in 1951 American psychologists adopted the title counselling psychologist for the new specialty. (How counselling psychology and clinical psychology differ as professions is discussed in Chapter 1; the areas of counselling, such as school, career, marital and grief counselling, and the theories of career counselling, are taught in Chapter 10.) Counselling versus psychotherapy Is counselling simply a lighter form of psychotherapy, or the same thing under another name? Examiners like the question because there is a traditional answer and a modern one, and you need both. The traditional answer draws a set of contrasts between guidance, counselling and psychotherapy, summarised in Table 6.21. Counselling, on this view, serves people who are basically well but face problems of living: a decision, a transition, a relationship difficulty, stress, grief. It works mainly with conscious material and present concerns, aims at problem solving, adjustment, prevention and growth, tends to be shorter, and takes place in schools, colleges, workplaces and community settings. Psychotherapy serves people with psychological disorders or long-standing personality problems, works with the past as well as the present and with what lies outside awareness, aims at symptom relief and deeper change in personality, tends to be longer, and takes place in hospitals, clinics and private practice. Guidance sits at the other end of the line from psychotherapy: it is the most information-centred and the least concerned with feelings. Table 6.21 Guidance, counselling and psychotherapy: the traditional contrasts (all of them differences of degree). Feature Guidance Counselling Psychotherapy Typical client Student or job-seeker needing information Basically well person facing a problem of living Person with a disorder or long-standing personality problem Typical concern Choosing a course, career or college Decisions, adjustment, relationships, stress, grief Depression, anxiety disorders, trauma, personality disorders Aim An informed choice Problem solving, coping, prevention, growth Symptom relief and deeper personality change Focus Facts about the person and the options Conscious, present, everyday experience Present and past, including what lies outside awareness Length One or a few meetings Usually short to medium Often longer Usual setting Schools, colleges, career centres Schools, workplaces, community and health settings Hospitals, clinics, private practice The modern answer is that these are differences of degree, not of kind. One influential American textbook, Therapeutic Psychology (first published in 1960) by Lawrence Brammer and Everett Shostrom (the same Shostrom who later made the Gloria films), treated counselling and psychotherapy as overlapping regions of a single continuum rather than as separate activities. Rogers had already refused to separate them: the title of his 1942 book put the two words side by side, and he used them interchangeably for the rest of his life. Later writers such as C. H. Patterson argued that there is no essential difference between the two in theory, relationship or method, only in the severity of the client's difficulties and the setting. The practical reality bears this out. A counsellor in a de-addiction centre works with people who have a diagnosable disorder; a psychotherapist may spend a session helping a client decide which job to take; and both rely on exactly the same listening skills. The fairest summary is that counselling tends to be shorter, more present-focused, more concerned with development and prevention, and offered to a wider range of people, while psychotherapy tends to be longer, deeper and more concerned with disorder; but the two overlap so much that a sharp line cannot be drawn. Egan, as you will see, avoided the problem by speaking simply of "helping". One further distinction matters in practice: counselling is not advice. Advice tells a person what to do; guidance supplies information so that a person can choose; counselling helps the person work out for himself what he wants and how to get it. A counsellor may give information, and sometimes advice, but the decision stays with the client. Exam trap If asked how counselling differs from psychotherapy, the expected contrasts are: counselling deals with relatively normal people, conscious material, present and developmental problems, and is shorter and more educational or preventive; psychotherapy deals with more disturbed people, deeper and unconscious material, and longer-term personality change. But textbooks agree that the difference is one of degree, not kind , and many (following Rogers) use the terms interchangeably. Guidance is the most directive and information-centred of the three; its founder is Frank Parsons (Vocation Bureau, Boston, 1908; Choosing a Vocation , 1909), the father of vocational guidance. Williamson's directive trait-and-factor counselling is the "Minnesota" approach that Rogers opposed. In Indian usage, admission "counselling" means seat allotment, which has nothing to do with the profession. Allen Ivey and the microskills hierarchy In the early 1960s counsellors were trained largely by apprenticeship. A trainee read about theory, watched an experienced counsellor, tried a few interviews and received feedback such as "You need to be more empathic." But what does a trainee actually do to be more empathic? Allen E. Ivey , then at Colorado State University, set out with his colleagues to answer that question. They borrowed an idea from teacher training, the "microteaching" developed by Dwight Allen and his colleagues at Stanford University, in which a complex performance was broken into small skills that could be practised one at a time. Ivey's group first described the result, microcounselling , in 1968, and Ivey's book Microcounseling followed in 1971. The method rests on a simple idea: an interview is made of small, observable, teachable units of behaviour, which Ivey called microskills, such as attending, asking an open question or reflecting a feeling. Each skill is defined, shown and practised separately, in a format called microtraining. The trainee records a short baseline interview, reads a brief description of one skill, watches video recordings of the skill used well and badly, practises it in a short role-played interview, watches his own recording to see whether he used the skill and what effect it had on the client, and practises again. Because each skill is concrete, its effect can be seen: when a trainee uses more open questions, the client talks more; when he paraphrases accurately, the client goes further into the topic. Research in the following decades showed that the skills could be learned quickly and that they transferred across professions (doctors, nurses, managers, police officers and teachers) and across cultures. The approach was later developed in Ivey's textbook Intentional Interviewing and Counseling , written with Mary Bradford Ivey and later Carlos Zalaquett. That title points to Ivey's central idea, intentionality : the ability to choose, from a range of possible responses, the one most likely to help this client at this moment, and to change course when a response does not work. As Ivey put it, an intentional counsellor always has more than one possible response available. A trainee who knows only one move, however good, will use it whether it fits or not. Ivey later widened the idea to cultural intentionality : the ability to respond in ways that fit the client's culture, so that eye contact, physical distance, directness and the role of the family are adjusted to the person in front of you. (Recall the note in Section 2.2 that SOLER's direct eye contact can be uncomfortable for many Indian clients.) Ivey arranged the microskills in a microskills hierarchy , usually drawn as a pyramid (Figure 6.10). The details have changed a little from edition to edition, but the logic has not: simpler skills at the bottom support more complex ones above. At the foundation are ethics, multicultural competence and an emphasis on wellness and the client's strengths. Above them come the skills of listening: attending behaviour (culturally appropriate eye contact, vocal qualities, verbal tracking and body language), open and closed questions, client observation (noticing nonverbal behaviour, discrepancies and the client's characteristic words), encouraging, paraphrasing and summarising, and reflection of feeling. Together these form the basic listening sequence , which Ivey found to be the core of effective interviews in almost every helping profession; a doctor taking a history, a manager hearing a complaint and a counsellor in a first session all draw out the story with it. Ivey's microskills hierarchy (simplified) Ethics, multicultural competence and wellness Attending behaviour Open and closed questions Client observation Encouraging, paraphrasing, summarising Reflection of feeling Five-stage interview structure Confrontation Focusing Reflection of meaning Influencing skills and strategies Skill integration Personal style and theory Basic listening sequence Challenging and influencing Foundation Figure 6.10 Ivey's microskills hierarchy, simplified. Each skill rests on those below it: the attending and listening skills of the basic listening sequence come first, then the structure of the interview, then the challenging and influencing skills, and finally the integration of all of them into a personal style. The order varies slightly between editions. Above the basic listening sequence sits the five-stage interview structure , a map of a well-formed session that Ivey's recent editions call empathic relationship (building rapport and structuring), story and strengths (drawing out the client's concerns and resources), goals (agreeing what the client wants), restory (exploring alternatives and new ways of seeing the problem) and action (generalising the learning to daily life). Older editions used other labels for the same five steps. Higher in the pyramid are the skills that do more than reflect. Confrontation , which Ivey also called supportive challenge, means listening for and pointing out discrepancies and conflicts (between words and actions, between two statements, between the client's goals and his behaviour) within a supportive relationship. Ivey proposed a Client Change Scale for judging whether a confrontation has worked, according to how the client responds: with denial (level 1), partial examination (level 2), acceptance and recognition but no change (level 3), the creation of a new solution (level 4) or transcendence, a new and larger way of understanding the problem (level 5). Focusing , in Ivey's sense, means deliberately choosing where the conversation directs its attention. Ivey listed seven possible foci: the client, the main theme or problem, other people, the family, mutuality (the "we" of the helping relationship), the interviewer, and the cultural or environmental context. Consider Arjun, 22, whose father expects him to take over the family sweet shop in Mysuru while Arjun wants to study for an MA in psychology. The counsellor can focus on Arjun ("What do you want?"), on the problem ("Let's look at the options in front of you"), on others ("What does your father hope for?"), on the family ("How have such decisions been made in your family before?"), on mutuality ("We can work on this together over the next few weeks"), on the interviewer ("I faced a similar choice once"), or on the context ("In many Indian families the eldest son is expected to carry on the business; how does that expectation affect you?"). Each focus opens a different conversation, and the intentional counsellor shifts among them deliberately. (Ivey's focusing is unrelated to Gendlin's focusing, the attention to a bodily felt sense described in Section 6.7.) The skill of reflection of meaning goes beneath feelings to the values, purposes and meanings that give an experience its significance: "Behind the argument about the shop, it sounds as if the real question is whether you can be a good son and still live your own life." It is the microskill closest to the existential therapies, and to Frankl's search for meaning (Section 6.5). Interpretation and reframing, which offer the client a new frame of reference, sit close beside it. Above these come the influencing skills, in which the counsellor actively contributes: logical consequences (helping the client foresee what will follow from a choice), self-disclosure, feedback, information and psychoeducation, and directives (instructions to do something, such as a relaxation exercise, a Gestalt empty-chair experiment or a homework task). At the top of the pyramid stand skill integration, the ability to put all the skills together in a full interview, and the counsellor's own personal style and theory: Ivey's point is that a mature helper, whatever school he belongs to, should be able to name the skills he is using and say why. Exam trap Microcounselling and the microskills hierarchy are Allen Ivey's (first described in 1968; Microcounseling , 1971), not Egan's or Carkhuff's. Microteaching (Dwight Allen, Stanford) was its inspiration, not its name. The base of the hierarchy is ethics and multicultural competence, with attending behaviour as the first skill; the basic listening sequence is attending, questions, observation, encouraging, paraphrasing, summarising and reflection of feeling. Intentionality means having more than one response available and choosing deliberately. SOLER , by contrast, is Egan's acronym for physical attending (Section 2.2). And do not confuse Ivey's focusing (choosing the focus of the conversation) with Gendlin's focusing (Section 6.7) or with the focusing process of motivational interviewing (Section 6.9). Robert Carkhuff and the human resource development model You met Robert R. Carkhuff in Section 6.2 as Charles Truax's partner in measuring Rogers's core conditions. In Toward Effective Counseling and Psychotherapy (1967) Truax and Carkhuff developed rating scales for accurate empathy, non-possessive warmth and genuineness, and in Beyond Counseling and Therapy (1967), written with Bernard Berenson, and the two volumes of Helping and Human Relations (1969), Carkhuff took the work further in two directions. He refined the scales, and he turned them into a training programme and a model of the whole helping process. Carkhuff's scales rate a helper's response on five levels. The best known is the scale of empathic understanding. At levels 1 and 2 the response is subtractive : it ignores, distorts or noticeably weakens the feeling the client has expressed. At level 3 the response is an interchangeable response : it expresses essentially the same feeling and meaning as the client, adding nothing and taking nothing away, so that the client's statement and the helper's could be exchanged. Carkhuff called level 3 the minimally facilitative level. At levels 4 and 5 the response is additive : it expresses feelings and meanings a little deeper than the client has been able to express, which is roughly what Egan later called advanced empathy. Table 6.22 shows the five levels applied to a single statement. Carkhuff built similar five-level scales for respect, genuineness, concreteness (specificity), self-disclosure, confrontation and immediacy, and grouped them into the facilitative conditions (empathy, respect and concreteness), which help the client explore, and the action-oriented conditions (genuineness, confrontation, immediacy and self-disclosure), which help the client act. Table 6.22 Carkhuff's five levels of empathy applied to one statement. A student says: "I studied for months and I still failed the entrance exam. My parents haven't said a word to me since." Level What the response does Example 1 Ignores the feeling or detracts from it (subtractive) "Lots of people fail. Have you thought about a coaching class?" 2 Responds, but noticeably weakens the feeling (subtractive) "You're a bit disappointed with the result." 3 Interchangeable: the same feeling and meaning, nothing added or lost "You feel crushed because months of work came to nothing, and your parents' silence makes it worse." 4 Additive: voices a feeling or meaning the client implied "You feel crushed, and perhaps frightened that their silence means they have given up on you." 5 Significantly additive: deeper feeling and a direction, offered when trust allows "Underneath the hurt you want to know they still believe in you, so that you can find the will to try again." Two findings made Carkhuff's work influential far beyond the counselling room. The first was that helping can be, in his phrase, "for better or for worse". Clients of helpers who functioned at high levels of the facilitative conditions improved; clients of helpers who functioned at low levels did no better than untreated people, and sometimes deteriorated (the "deterioration effect" discussed in Chapter 8). Professional credentials, Carkhuff found, did not guarantee high functioning: many trained professionals responded at levels below 3. The second finding followed from the first. In a review published in 1968 Carkhuff reported that lay helpers (hospital attendants, volunteers, parents) given brief, systematic training in these skills could function at levels comparable to professionals, and could achieve comparable results with clients. That finding laid part of the foundation for training paraprofessional and lay counsellors, a strategy that matters greatly in countries with too few mental health professionals (Section 9.6). Carkhuff's model of the helping process, which he called the human resource development model (HRD), and which he set out for a wide readership in The Art of Helping (first published in the early 1970s and revised many times), describes four sets of helper skills, each of which produces a client process. In the pre-helping phase the helper attends (physically and psychologically), and the client becomes involved in the helping process. In phase 1 the helper responds to the client's feelings and meanings with interchangeable responses, and the client explores where he is now ("Where am I?"). In phase 2 the helper personalises , helping the client to own his part in the problem and to see the goal implied by it, and the client comes to understand where he is in relation to where he wants to be ("Where do I want to be?"). In phase 3 the helper initiates , helping the client to define goals and develop step-by-step programmes, and the client acts ("How do I get there?"). The results of action feed back into renewed exploration, so the cycle can begin again. Carkhuff gave trainees simple formats for each phase. A responding statement takes the form "You feel [feeling] because [reason]." A personalised statement takes the client's part in the problem and the goal into account: "You feel [feeling] because you cannot [the client's own deficit], and you want to [goal]." "You feel angry because your manager passed you over" is a response; "You feel disappointed in yourself because you haven't been able to speak up for your work, and you want to learn how" is personalising. Exam trap On Carkhuff's five-level scales, level 3 is the interchangeable , minimally facilitative response; levels 1 and 2 are subtractive , levels 4 and 5 additive . Do not reverse the scale: higher is better. Carkhuff's helping model runs attending, responding, personalising, initiating (helper) and involvement, exploration, understanding, action (client). The empathy, warmth and genuineness rating scales of 1967 are Truax and Carkhuff's ; Rogers proposed the conditions, but he did not build these scales. Carkhuff's "helping is for better or for worse" and the effectiveness of trained lay helpers are his two most cited findings. Gerard Egan and the skilled helper The most widely used helping model in counselling courses around the world is the work of Gerard Egan , a psychologist at Loyola University of Chicago, whose The Skilled Helper was first published in 1975 and has been revised in many editions since (the recent ones with Robert Reese). Egan built on Carkhuff's model and on Rogers's core conditions, and added the structure of practical problem solving. He called the result the skilled helper model , or in its later subtitle a problem-management and opportunity-development approach to helping. Its assumptions are pragmatic. Helping, for Egan, is not about curing illness but about helping clients manage the problems of living more effectively and develop opportunities they have left unused, and in the process become better at helping themselves. Success is judged by outcomes in the client's life, not by insight in the session. The model is deliberately open: Egan presented it as a framework into which techniques from many schools can be fitted. The model has three stages, each with three tasks, and an action arrow that runs beneath all of them (Figure 6.11). Stage I asks "What is going on?" and builds a picture of the client's current situation, the current picture. Its tasks are to help clients tell their stories (I-A); to help them become aware of blind spots and develop new perspectives, getting to what Egan calls the real story (I-B); and to help them choose the issues that will make the most difference, the issues with the greatest leverage (I-C). Stage II asks "What do I want instead?" and builds the preferred picture. Its tasks are to help clients explore possibilities for a better future (II-A), to choose realistic and challenging goals from among them (II-B), and to find the incentives that will sustain commitment, which Egan put as the question "What am I willing to pay for what I want?" (II-C). Stage III asks "How do I get what I need or want?" and plans the way forward. Its tasks are to help clients brainstorm possible strategies (III-A), choose the strategies that best fit their resources and circumstances (III-B), and turn them into a plan with steps in sequence (III-C). The action arrow stands for implementation: clients can begin acting from the first session, and the stages are not a rigid sequence. A helper may move back and forth among them as the story changes. Stage III The way forward How do I get there? I-A Help clients tell their stories I-B Blind spots and new perspectives I-C Choose issues that make a difference II-A Possibilities: what would be better? II-B Goals: choose what to aim for II-C Commitment: what am I willing to pay? Each stage asks one question and has three tasks; the action band at the bottom shows that clients can start acting at any point, so the stages are a map rather than a strict sequence. Two families of skills carry the model. The communication skills are used throughout: attending (Egan's SOLER, Section 2.2), active listening, basic empathy, probing (prompts and questions that help the client fill in the story) and summarising. The challenging skills help clients see what they have not seen. They include advanced empathy (voicing what the client has only hinted at, the themes running through several stories, or the implications he has not drawn), information-sharing, helper self-disclosure, suggestions, confrontation, and immediacy , which Egan described as "you-me talk": discussing what is happening in the helping relationship itself, either in the relationship as a whole ("I notice we keep returning to your manager and never to you") or in the present moment ("You seem annoyed with me right now; can we talk about that?"). Challenge in Egan's model has a precise purpose, to help clients notice their blind spots, the things about themselves, their situation or their behaviour that they fail to see, avoid or misread. And it has a precise condition: the right to challenge must be earned by first understanding. In the early editions of The Skilled Helper the three stages were called exploration, new understanding and action, and the challenging skills, advanced empathy among them, belonged to the second stage, after the client's story had been heard with basic empathy. That is why advanced empathy is regarded as inappropriate in an initial session, while basic (primary) empathy is appropriate from the first minute. Egan also wrote frankly about what he called the shadow side of helping, the things that go wrong and that textbooks rarely discuss: helpers who are tired, judgemental or more interested in their own theory than in the client, and clients who hold back. He distinguished reluctance , a client's hesitancy to engage in change, often born of fear, shame or ambivalence, from resistance , the client's push-back against feeling coerced, and argued (much as Miller and Rollnick later did) that both are normal and should be worked with, not blamed. A worked example takes one client through the model. Kavya, 24, a software engineer in Bengaluru, comes to a counsellor saying that she cannot sleep and wants to resign. In Stage I the counsellor listens with basic empathy and probes gently, and the story emerges: long hours, a critical manager, loneliness in a city far from her family in Kerala. Kavya calls herself "bad at the job", yet she mentions that her ratings are good and that she never refuses extra work. Once trust is established, the counsellor offers a challenge (advanced empathy and a gentle confrontation): "You describe yourself as bad at the job, and at the same time you're the one the team turns to when something urgent comes up. I wonder whether the real difficulty is less the job than how hard it is for you to say no." Kavya is quiet, then agrees. The issue with the most leverage is not the job itself but her difficulty setting limits. In Stage II they explore what a better working life would look like, and Kavya chooses a goal: to leave the office by seven on at least four evenings a week and to refuse weekend work except in emergencies. Asked what she is willing to pay for it, she admits that she fears her manager's disapproval, and decides the risk is worth her health. In Stage III they brainstorm strategies (talking to her manager, asking to move teams, finding a mentor, practising assertive replies, rebuilding a social life through a dance class) and choose the two that fit best: a conversation with her manager, prepared through role-play, and practice in saying no to small requests first. The action arrow begins that week: she declines one weekend request and reports back in the next session. She did not, in the end, resign. Exam trap "Which kind of empathy is inappropriate in an initial counselling session?" The answer is advanced empathy (RML 2022). It goes beyond what the client has said, so it depends on trust and on knowing the client well; offered too early it sounds presumptuous and intrusive. Primary (basic) empathy , which reflects what the client has openly expressed, is appropriate from the first minute, so "both" is wrong. Culturally sensitive empathy , understanding the client within his cultural world (Ivey's cultural intentionality), is always appropriate. Egan's stages are current picture, preferred picture and the way forward (in early editions exploration, new understanding and action), plus the action arrow; SOLER is Egan's; and advanced empathy corresponds roughly to Carkhuff's additive levels 4 and 5. Bringing the helping models together Set the models side by side and a striking convergence appears. Ivey, Carkhuff and Egan all begin with attending and listening, move through a phase in which the client comes to understand the problem in a new way, and end with action. A later model, by the American counselling psychologist Clara E. Hill , makes the pattern explicit. In Helping Skills: Facilitating Exploration, Insight, and Action (1999, with Karen O'Brien) Hill described three stages: exploration, which draws on the client-centred tradition (attending, listening, reflection of feelings); insight, which draws on the psychodynamic tradition (challenge, interpretation, immediacy); and action, which draws on the behavioural tradition (information, goal setting, homework). The helping models, in other words, are a practical integration of the three great families of therapy you have studied in Chapters 3 to 6. Partly because these skills are the common ground beneath every therapy: whatever technique a clinician uses, it is delivered through a relationship, and the research on common factors (Chapter 8) suggests that the relationship carries a good share of the benefit. And partly because clinical psychologists in India increasingly train and supervise others. Carkhuff's discovery that systematically trained lay helpers could help as well as professionals is the logic behind the lay counsellor programmes described in Chapter 9, in which community health workers and lay counsellors, trained in a structured set of listening and problem-solving skills and supervised by specialists, deliver psychological treatments to people who would otherwise receive none. Clinical link Interviewers for clinical psychology programmes often ask candidates to "show" a skill, for example by responding to a statement as a counsellor would. The models in this section give you a ready answer. Begin with an interchangeable response (Carkhuff's level 3: "You feel ... because ..."), add an open question to invite more of the story, and hold back advanced empathy and challenge until you have earned them. If you are asked what you would do with a client who is not ready to change, describe the stage of change you think the client is in and how you would use motivational interviewing to engage him rather than argue.
