The case of Gloria, revisited You can now see why the Gloria films have been argued over for so long: each of the three conversations was a faithful demonstration of a theory. Rogers did not tell Gloria what to do because, on his theory, she already knew. Her guilt about the lie she had told Pammy pointed to a gap between the self she felt she ought to be and what she was actually experiencing, the incongruence of Section 6.2, and the remedy was a relationship without conditions of worth: congruence, unconditional positive regard and accurate empathy, carried by reflection of feeling. Her wish that her own father could have talked to her that way is exactly the kind of moment the core conditions are meant to produce. Perls worked on something else, awareness in the here and now. When he pointed to her smile and her fidgeting hands, he was refusing to support what he saw as a game of the helpless little girl, frustrating her bid for outside support until she found support in herself; when she grew angry and fought back, she was, for him, at last really present (Section 6.3). Ellis's brisk argument with her beliefs belongs to Chapter 5. The rest of the chapter adds voices that were not in the studio. A logotherapist would have asked what her situation was asking of her, and what she wanted to stand for as a mother (Section 6.5). Glasser would have asked what she wanted for herself and for Pammy, what she was actually doing about it, and whether it was working (Section 6.6). A solution-focused therapist might have asked the miracle question, and then when a small piece of that miracle had already happened (Section 6.8). A motivational interviewer would have heard her ambivalence ("Would the truth harm her child? Would the lie?"), reflected both sides and left the decision with her (Section 6.9), and the helping-skills models of Section 6.10 would have described much of what Rogers did as basic empathy offered from the first minute, with challenge held back until trust had been earned. Which of the three helped most is a question the films cannot settle. The research in this chapter suggests a quieter answer: the warmth, genuineness and empathy that Rogers showed are reliably, if modestly, linked to good outcomes in every kind of therapy, while specific methods (chair work, focusing, the miracle question, evoking change talk) can add speed and depth for particular problems. Gloria, who kept writing to Rogers for years afterwards, had found what every school in this chapter values in its own way: a helper who treated her as the expert on her own life. Chapter summary 6.1 The Third Force: What These Therapies Share. Abraham Maslow called humanistic psychology the third force, after psychoanalysis and behaviourism; it became organised in the early 1960s, with Maslow and Carl Rogers as its best-known figures. The therapies of this chapter share six assumptions: phenomenology (the client's internal frame of reference), an inborn tendency to grow, freedom and responsibility, holism, a focus on the here and now, and change through an authentic relationship rather than technique. The humanistic branch (Rogers, Maslow) is optimistic; the existential branch (Binswanger, Boss, May, Frankl, Yalom) is more sober about death, isolation, freedom and meaninglessness; the experiential branch (Gestalt, focusing, emotion-focused therapy) works with moment-by-moment experiencing. The general aim of the humanistic-experiential psychotherapies is a more fluid and integrated organisation of the self, and their account of distress (blocked growth, inauthenticity, lost meaning) differs from the diathesis-stress model. 6.2 Carl Rogers and Person-Centred Therapy. Carl Rogers (1902 to 1987) called his approach non-directive (1942), then client-centred (1951) and later person-centred. His theory starts from the actualising tendency and the organismic valuing process; the need for positive regard leads the child to introject conditions of worth, and the resulting mismatch between self-concept and experience is incongruence, defended by distortion and denial. In 1957 he named six necessary and sufficient conditions, three of which (congruence, unconditional positive regard and accurate empathic understanding) are the core conditions the therapist provides. The signature response is reflection of feeling; advice, interpretation and diagnosis are absent. Clients move from fixity to fluidity toward the fully functioning person. Stephenson's Q-sort measured the self-ideal gap, Truax and Carkhuff rated the conditions, and research finds them facilitative but probably not sufficient. Rogers's encounter groups aimed at personal growth through self-disclosure and interaction. 6.3 Gestalt Therapy. Gestalt therapy was founded by Fritz Perls (1893 to 1970) with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman; the founding book (1951) is by Perls, Hefferline and Goodman, and the therapy is not Gestalt psychology. Drawing on Goldstein, Reich, Smuts, existentialism and Zen, it aims at awareness in the here and now, asks what and how rather than why, and treats responsibility as response-ability. Needs form as figure against ground and complete a cycle of experience; blocked needs remain as unfinished business. Beisser's paradoxical theory of change holds that change occurs when one becomes what one is. The contact boundary disturbances are introjection, projection, retroflection, deflection, confluence and egotism. The experiments include the empty chair for unfinished business, the two-chair dialogue between top dog and underdog, the hot seat, and dream work in which every element is a projection of the dreamer. Paivio and Greenberg (1995) supported empty-chair work. 6.4 Existential Therapy. Existential therapy helps clients face the existential givens (death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness) and live with awareness, choice and responsibility. Its vocabulary comes from philosophers such as Kierkegaard, Heidegger, Buber and Sartre: Heidegger's Dasein, or being-in-the-world, and Sartre's "existence precedes essence" and bad faith. Ludwig Binswanger and Medard Boss founded Daseinsanalysis; Binswanger described three modes of being-in-the-world, the Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt, to which Emmy van Deurzen later added the Überwelt. Rollo May brought existential psychology to America (The Meaning of Anxiety, 1950; Existence, 1958) and distinguished normal from neurotic anxiety; with James Bugental he is linked to existential-humanistic therapy. Irvin Yalom's Existential Psychotherapy (1980) named four ultimate concerns: death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness. Practice rests on the relationship and the phenomenological method rather than technique, and the meaning-centred therapies have the best evidence. 6.5 Viktor Frankl and Logotherapy. Viktor Frankl (1905 to 1997) survived four camps, among them Auschwitz, and in Man's Search for Meaning (German original 1946) described the last of the human freedoms, the freedom to choose one's attitude. Logotherapy, the Third Viennese School after Freud's will to pleasure and Adler's will to power, holds that the will to meaning is the primary human motive and that meaning is found through creative, experiential and attitudinal values. The person has somatic, psychic and noetic dimensions, with the capacities of self-detachment and self-transcendence. Frustrated meaning brings existential frustration, the existential vacuum (with its Sunday neurosis) and noogenic neurosis, which Crumbaugh and Maholick's Purpose in Life Test (1964) set out to measure. Paradoxical intention, wishing for the feared symptom with humour, breaks the circle of anticipatory anxiety; dereflection, turning attention outward, cures hyper-reflection; Socratic dialogue and attitude modulation help clients find meaning. 6.6 Reality Therapy and Choice Theory. William Glasser (1925 to 2013), mentored by G. L. Harrington and tested at the Ventura School for Girls, coined the term reality therapy in 1962 and published Reality Therapy in 1965: a brief, present-focused approach in which a warm, involved therapist helps clients evaluate their behaviour and choose responsible ways of meeting their needs, accepting no excuses. Building on William Powers's control-systems theory, Glasser's control theory became choice theory (1998): five basic needs (survival, love and belonging, power or achievement, freedom and fun), a quality world of wanted pictures, the comparing place, and total behaviour (acting, thinking, feeling, physiology), pictured as a car steered by its front wheels, hence "depressing". Robert Wubbolding systematised the method as WDEP: wants, direction and doing, evaluation by the client, and planning. The evidence is thin, and the rejection of mental illness is its main weakness. 6.7 Focusing, Emotion-Focused Therapy and Positive Psychotherapy. Eugene Gendlin found that successful clients speak from inner experiencing (the Experiencing Scale) and named the bodily, wordless felt sense and the felt shift; Focusing (1978) teaches six steps: clearing a space, felt sense, handle, resonating, asking and receiving. Leslie Greenberg, with Laura Rice and Robert Elliott, developed process-experiential, later emotion-focused, therapy: emotion schemes; primary adaptive, primary maladaptive, secondary and instrumental emotions; changing emotion with emotion; and markers matched to tasks such as two-chair dialogue, empty-chair work and focusing, supported by the York depression studies. Martin Seligman launched positive psychology in 1998 (PERMA, the VIA strengths) and, with Rashid and Parks, positive psychotherapy (2006). Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi named flow, absorption when challenge matches skill. Nossrat Peseschkian's older positive psychotherapy (1977) works with positum, the balance model and stories. 6.8 Narrative and Solution-Focused Brief Therapy. Both approaches are social constructionist: problems and identities are built in language, and the client is the expert. Michael White and David Epston (Narrative Means to Therapeutic Ends, 1990), drawing on Foucault and Bruner, help clients move from a problem-saturated story to a preferred one. Externalising separates the person from the problem ("the person is not the problem; the problem is the problem"), as in the case of Sneaky Poo, and relative influence questions, unique outcomes, re-authoring across the landscapes of action and identity, outsider witnesses and therapeutic letters build the new story. Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg developed solution-focused brief therapy at Milwaukee's Brief Family Therapy Center (1978) on the rule "do more of what works", using the miracle, exception, scaling and coping questions, compliments and the formula first session task. SFBT has a larger evidence base than narrative therapy. 6.9 Motivational Interviewing and the Stages of Change. Motivational interviewing was developed by William Miller (first paper, 1983) and Stephen Rollnick (joint book, 1991) in the treatment of problem drinking, as a guiding style that resolves ambivalence and resists the righting reflex. Its spirit is partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation (PACE, 2013); its processes are engaging, focusing, evoking and planning; its core skills are OARS. The older principles were express empathy, develop discrepancy, roll with resistance and support self-efficacy. Change talk (preparatory DARN, mobilising CAT) predicts change, commitment language most of all, and resistance was renamed sustain talk and discord in 2013. Burke, Arkowitz and Menchola (2003) supported MI for alcohol, drugs, and diet and exercise. Prochaska and DiClemente's transtheoretical model (1983) adds the stages of change (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance, termination), ten processes of change, decisional balance and levels of change, with relapse as recycling in a spiral. 6.10 Counselling and the Helping Skills. Counselling is a professional helping relationship, usually with people whose functioning is basically intact; it grew from Frank Parsons's vocational guidance (Vocation Bureau, 1908) and Williamson's directive trait-and-factor method, which Rogers opposed. Traditionally counselling is shorter, present-focused and developmental, and psychotherapy longer, deeper and concerned with disorder, but the difference is one of degree, not kind. Allen Ivey's microcounselling (1968) teaches one skill at a time through a microskills hierarchy, from attending and the basic listening sequence to influencing skills, guided by intentionality. Robert Carkhuff's five-level scales make level 3 the interchangeable response, and his human resource development model runs attending, responding, personalising and initiating; trained lay helpers can match professionals. Gerard Egan's skilled helper (1975) has three stages (current picture, preferred picture, way forward) plus action, with advanced empathy kept for after trust is earned. A general aim of humanistic-experiential psychotherapy is: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Promote fluid and integrative self-organization (b) To understand and resolve deep seated psychological conflicts (c) To change maladaptive behaviours (d) To develop interpersonal skills Answer: (a) Promote fluid and integrative self-organization. Robert Elliott, Leslie Greenberg and their colleagues describe the shared aim of the person-centred, Gestalt, focusing, emotion-focused and existential therapies as a more fluid and integrated way of organising the self, reached by attending to present experience, especially emotion. Resolving deep-seated conflicts is the psychodynamic aim, changing maladaptive behaviours the behavioural aim, and developing interpersonal skills the aim of interpersonal and social skills approaches. Which of the following techniques is a client centred therapist most likely to use? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Analysis (b) Giving advice (c) Reflection (d) Aversive conditioning Answer: (c) Reflection. Reflection of feeling puts into words the feeling the client is expressing and offers it back to be checked, so the client's frame of reference stays in charge. Analysis (interpretation) imports the therapist's theory, advice directs the client, and aversive conditioning, pairing an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus, is a behaviour therapy method. Which of the following might be considered as the central tenets of Client-Centered Therapy: (RML 2021) (a) Empathy (b) Unconditional positive regard (c) Congruence (d) All of the above Answer: (d) All of the above. These are Rogers's three core conditions, the therapist-provided conditions 3, 4 and 5 of his six necessary and sufficient conditions (1957). Choosing any one of them alone misses the point that the three work together. What is the critical feature of Carl Rogers' client-centred therapy? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Analysing unconscious desires (b) Therapist providing unconditional positive regard (c) Implementing strict behaviour modifications (d) Using aversive stimuli Answer: (b) Therapist providing unconditional positive regard. Warm valuing of the client without conditions is the direct remedy for the conditions of worth that, in Rogers's theory, produce incongruence. Analysing unconscious desires is psychoanalytic, and strict behaviour modification and aversive stimuli are behavioural methods with no place in person-centred work. A split between the organismic valuing process and a self-concept burdened by conditions of worth which results in feelings of tension and confusion: (Amity 2023) (a) Conflict (b) Incongruence (c) Introjection (d) Actualizing tendency Answer: (b) Incongruence. Incongruence is Rogers's term for the mismatch between the self-concept and actual experience. Introjection is how conditions of worth are taken in, not the split that results; the actualising tendency is the growth force that incongruence obstructs; and "conflict" is a general word with no special place in Rogers's theory. Which of the following is NOT a key concept in Carl Rogers' Client-Centered Therapy? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Conditions of Worth (b) Unconditional Positive Regard (c) Actualizing Tendency (d) The Therapeutic Alliance (as defined by Bordin) Answer: (d) The Therapeutic Alliance (as defined by Bordin). Edward Bordin's working alliance (1979: agreement on goals and tasks plus an emotional bond) grew out of psychodynamic thinking and is a pan-theoretical idea. Conditions of worth, unconditional positive regard and the actualising tendency are all central to Rogers's theory. Which therapeutic approach would be LEAST likely to use the term "therapeutic alliance," preferring instead to focus on the "real relationship" and the therapist's unconditional positive regard? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Psychoanalysis (b) Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (c) Person-Centered Therapy (d) Interpersonal Therapy Answer: (c) Person-Centered Therapy. Person-centred therapists speak of the relationship itself and the core conditions. Psychoanalysis, where the working alliance was born, cognitive-behaviour therapy and interpersonal psychotherapy (Klerman and Weissman) all use the term freely. What is the principal role of an "encounter group"? (RML 2022) (a) Enables individuals to interact with others in a social setting (b) Encourages team building (c) Aids the therapist in diagnosis (d) Encourages therapy and self-growth through disclosure and interaction Answer: (d) Encourages therapy and self-growth through disclosure and interaction. An encounter group, such as Rogers's basic encounter group, is a small, intensive, relatively unstructured group of people seeking personal growth through open self-disclosure, here-and-now feeling and frank feedback. Mere social interaction and team building miss that aim, and encounter groups are not a diagnostic aid. Which therapy focuses on "empty chair technique"? (IHBAS 2025) (a) CBT (b) Gestalt therapy (c) Psychoanalysis (d) DBT Answer: (b) Gestalt therapy. Speaking directly to an imagined person in an empty chair, usually to finish unfinished business, is the hallmark of Fritz Perls's Gestalt therapy. CBT disputes beliefs, psychoanalysis uses free association and interpretation, and DBT teaches skills; emotion-focused therapy later borrowed chair work, but the technique is Gestalt. Any distorting or selective effect of a person's inner world on his perception or conception of the outer world is termed: (RML 2024) (a) Projection (b) Introjection (c) Empathy (d) Denial Answer: (a) Projection; the paper's key, (d) Denial, is wrong. The stem is the broad, classic definition of projection, the idea behind projective tests. Denial refuses to admit one particular painful fact and does not colour perception in general. Introjection is swallowing other people's values whole, and empathy is sensing another person's world as if it were one's own. The concept of "Dasein," which refers to human existence as "being-in-the-world," is primarily associated with which school of psychology? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Behavioral psychology (b) Existential psychology (c) Cognitive psychology (d) Psychoanalytic psychology Answer: (b) Existential psychology. Dasein ("being there") is Martin Heidegger's term in Being and Time (1927), carried into therapy by Binswanger and Boss as Daseinsanalysis. It has no place in behavioural or cognitive theory, and although Boss kept the analytic couch, he discarded Freud's drive theory. In existential psychology, Dasein encompasses three fundamental psychological dimensions of human existence. Which of the following correctly identifies these three modes of being-in-the-world? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Id, Ego, and Superego (b) Umwelt, Mitwelt, and Eigenwelt (c) Conscious, Preconscious, and Unconscious (d) Sensorimotor, Preoperational, and Concrete Operational Answer: (b) Umwelt, Mitwelt, and Eigenwelt. Binswanger's three modes are the biological and physical world, the world of relationships with others and the person's relationship with himself. Id, ego and superego are Freud's structural model, conscious, preconscious and unconscious his topographical model, and the last option lists Piaget's stages. Viktor Frankl's concept of the "will to meaning," the fundamental motivational force in humans to find purpose in life, is central to which therapeutic school? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) (b) Logotherapy (c) Existential-Humanistic Therapy (d) Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) Answer: (b) Logotherapy. Frankl's Third Viennese School puts the will to meaning first, after Freud's will to pleasure and Adler's will to power. REBT is Ellis's therapy of irrational beliefs, existential-humanistic therapy (May, Bugental) is built on presence and authenticity, and ACT works with values but grows out of behaviour analysis. Noogenic anxiety is described under: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Humanistic School (b) Gestalt school (c) Existential school (d) Psychodynamic school Answer: (c) Existential school. Noogenic neurosis (or anxiety) is Frankl's term for symptoms that arise in the noetic dimension, from frustrated meaning or a conflict of values, and logotherapy is an existential therapy. It is not humanistic in the narrow sense of Rogers and Maslow, not Gestalt, and not psychodynamic; the psychodynamic kind is what Frankl called psychogenic. Frankl's technique for 'hyper-reflection', in which a person stops watching himself and turns his attention outward, for example from his own sexual performance to his partner, is: (NIMHANS 2026 recall) (a) Paradoxical intention (b) Sensate focus (c) Dereflection (d) Socratic dialogue Answer: (c) Dereflection. Dereflection counters hyper-reflection and hyper-intention by turning attention away from the self, as in Frankl's case of the woman who attended to her partner instead of watching herself. Paradoxical intention targets anticipatory anxiety by wishing for the symptom, sensate focus is Masters and Johnson's programme of touching exercises, and Socratic dialogue is logotherapy's questioning method for finding meaning. In Reality Therapy, developed by William Glasser, which of the following is considered one of the five basic genetic needs? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Self-actualization (b) Power or Achievement (c) Collective Unconscious (d) Unconditional positive regard Answer: (b) Power or Achievement. Glasser's five needs are survival, love and belonging, power (achievement, competence, recognition), freedom and fun. Self-actualisation is Maslow's, the collective unconscious is Jung's, and unconditional positive regard is one of Rogers's core conditions. Who introduced the concept of "flow" in psychology? (RML 2023) (a) Carl Rogers (b) Abraham Maslow (c) Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (d) Viktor Frankl Answer: (c) Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi. He described flow, complete absorption in a task whose challenge matches one's skill, in Beyond Boredom and Anxiety (1975). Maslow described the briefer peak experience, Rogers the fully functioning person and Frankl the will to meaning. The concept of "self story" or helping clients re-author their life narratives is most closely associated with which therapeutic approach? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (b) Narrative Therapy (c) Psychodynamic Therapy (d) Gestalt Therapy Answer: (b) Narrative Therapy. Michael White and David Epston help clients move from a problem-saturated story to a preferred one through externalising, unique outcomes and re-authoring conversations. CBT changes thoughts and behaviours, psychodynamic therapy works with unconscious conflict and transference, and Gestalt therapy with here-and-now awareness. Motivational interviewing is used in the management of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Non-compliance to treatment (b) Substance abuse (c) Anxious-avoidant personality disorder (d) Bipolar disorder Answer: (b) Substance abuse. Motivational interviewing was born in the treatment of problem drinking, and its evidence is strongest for alcohol and drug problems. It is also used to improve adherence, which makes (a) tempting, but that is a later extension; personality disorders and bipolar disorder are not its targets. Which of the following is NOT listed by Burke, Arkowitz and Mechola (2003) as being treatable with motivational interviewing: (RML 2022) (a) Substance-related disorders (b) Smoking cessation (c) Diabetes mellitus (d) Obsessive-compulsive disorder Answer: (d) Obsessive-compulsive disorder. The 2003 meta-analysis of 30 trials covered alcohol, drugs, diet and exercise (including trials with obese women with Type 2 diabetes), smoking and HIV-risk behaviour; smoking was studied, although the trials then available did not support MI for it. Obsessive-compulsive disorder was not among the problems at all; it needs exposure and response prevention. The third author is Marisa Menchola. Which kind of empathy is considered inappropriate for an initial counselling interview or session? (RML 2022) (a) Advanced empathy (b) Primary empathy (c) Both a and b (d) Culturally sensitive empathy Answer: (a) Advanced empathy. Advanced empathy voices what the client has only hinted at, so it depends on trust and on knowing the client; offered too early it sounds presumptuous, which is why Egan placed it among the challenging skills that come after the story has been heard. Primary (basic) empathy is appropriate from the first minute, so (c) is wrong, and culturally sensitive empathy is always appropriate. In the early 1950s a British-born anthropologist named Gregory Bateson (1904 to 1980) was working at the Veterans Administration hospital in Palo Alto, California. Bateson had made his name far from any hospital: he had lived among the Iatmul people of New Guinea and, with his wife Margaret Mead, had photographed and filmed village life in Bali. What fascinated him was a puzzle about communication. Every message, he noticed, carries a second message about how the first one is to be taken. A friend who says "I'll kill you" with a grin is not making a threat; a parent who says "Go to bed" is also saying "I am in charge here". In 1952 Bateson started a research project on these layers of communication, and over the next two years he was joined by Jay Haley, a young student of communication, John Weakland, a chemical engineer turned anthropologist, and the psychiatrist Don Jackson. They listened to the talk of patients with schizophrenia, and then they began to watch those patients with their families. One scene from their notes became the most famous anecdote in the history of family therapy. A young man who had fairly well recovered from an acute schizophrenic episode was visited in hospital by his mother. He was glad to see her and impulsively put his arm around her shoulders, whereupon she stiffened. He withdrew his arm, and she asked, "Don't you love me any more?" He blushed, and she said, "Dear, you must not be so easily embarrassed and afraid of your feelings." The young man could stay with her only a few minutes more. After she left, he assaulted an aide and was put in the tubs (the continuous baths then used to calm disturbed patients). Look at the young man's position. If he moves towards his mother, her body tells him he is unwelcome. If he moves away, her words accuse him of not loving her. If he shows confusion, he is told that his feelings are the problem. Every move is wrong, he cannot point out the contradiction (she is his mother, and he is the patient), and he cannot walk away. In 1956 Bateson, Jackson, Haley and Weakland published a paper called "Toward a theory of schizophrenia" in which they argued that a child who grows up inside such no-win situations, over and over, might learn the confused, metaphorical, guarded style of communication that we call schizophrenic. They called the trap a double bind. The idea was bold, and it was mostly wrong as an account of what causes schizophrenia. But notice what it did. It moved the illness, at least in part, out of the young man's head and into the space between him and his mother. That move, from the individual to the relationship, is the foundation of everything in this chapter: family therapy, which treats the family as a living system; couples therapy, which treats the relationship between two partners; and group therapy, which uses a room full of strangers as a laboratory for relationships. Remember the young man and his mother; you will return to them at the end of the chapter, and you will see what became of the idea that began with them. 7.1 The Family as a System Lower yield · 1 Q For the first half of the twentieth century, psychotherapy meant a private conversation between two people: one patient and one therapist, behind a closed door. The patient's family was, if anything, an obstacle. Psychoanalysts in particular kept relatives at arm's length, because contact with them was thought to contaminate the transference (the patient's feelings about the analyst). Yet clinicians kept noticing things that the one-to-one model could not explain. A young woman who recovered well in hospital relapsed within weeks of going home. A boy's tantrums stopped, and his father promptly became depressed. A couple's quarrels vanished whenever their daughter refused to eat, and returned when she began eating again. It was as if the problem did not belong to one person at all, but moved around the family like water finding its level. This section explains the ideas that let therapists take that observation seriously. From the consulting room to the family Family therapy had several roots. The first was the child guidance clinic. From the 1920s, clinics in the United States and Britain treated troubled children with a division of labour: a psychiatrist saw the child, and a social worker saw the mother, usually separately and often with the unspoken assumption that the mother was the cause of the trouble. The second root was marriage counselling. The first marriage counselling centres opened in the 1930s, in Los Angeles under Paul Popenoe and in New York under Abraham and Hannah Stone, and at first each partner was usually seen by a different counsellor. Only in the 1950s did conjoint therapy , in which both partners (or all family members) are seen together by the same therapist, become common. The third root was a handful of psychiatrists who simply started inviting the whole family in. In 1949 the British psychiatrist John Bowlby (1907 to 1990), better known for attachment theory, described holding a joint meeting with a troubled adolescent and his parents at the Tavistock Clinic in London. In 1951 the American psychologist John Elderkin Bell (1913 to 1995) began treating whole families as groups at Clark University in Massachusetts. And in New York the child psychiatrist and psychoanalyst Nathan Ackerman (1908 to 1971) began, in the 1940s and 1950s, to see entire families for both diagnosis and treatment, watching how they sat, who spoke for whom and who fell silent. Ackerman's book The Psychodynamics of Family Life (1958) and his warm, provocative style earned him the title "grandfather of family therapy", although he never wrote down a method that others could follow step by step. The fourth and most important root was research on schizophrenia. During the 1950s at least four research teams, working independently, studied the families of patients with schizophrenia: Bateson's group in Palo Alto, Murray Bowen's at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), Theodore Lidz's at Yale and Lyman Wynne's, also at NIMH. You will meet each of them in Section 7.2. By 1962 the new field had its own journal, Family Process , founded by Ackerman and Don Jackson with Jay Haley as its first editor. It helps to separate two terms at the start. Family therapy is any psychotherapeutic treatment of a family aimed at better psychological functioning; a psychoanalyst, a behaviour therapist or a person-centred counsellor can all do family therapy in their own style. Family systems therapy is the narrower family of approaches that treat the family as a system: they concentrate on the interactions between members, not the personalities of individuals, and they try to change the pattern rather than any one person. Most of this chapter is about family systems therapy, and to understand it you need to borrow some ideas from biology and engineering. General systems theory and cybernetics The key idea came from the Austrian biologist Ludwig von Bertalanffy (1901 to 1972). From the late 1930s onwards, and most fully in his book General System Theory (1968), von Bertalanffy argued that living things cannot be understood by taking them apart and studying the pieces one at a time. A cell, an organ, an organism, a family and a society are all systems: sets of parts in continuous interaction, organised so that the whole behaves in ways that no single part can explain. His general systems theory proposed a set of principles that apply to every system, whatever it is made of. Four of them matter for families. Wholeness. The whole is more than the sum of its parts. You can interview a mother, a father and a son separately and still know nothing about what happens when the three of them sit down to dinner, because the family has properties (its rules, its alliances, its typical arguments) that exist only between people. Interdependence. A change in any part changes the whole. When the eldest daughter leaves for college in Bengaluru, the whole household reorganises: the younger son gets her room, the mother loses her ally, the parents find themselves alone together at dinner. Open systems. A closed system exchanges nothing with its surroundings and runs down; an open system , like every living thing and every family, constantly exchanges energy and information with its environment (school, work, relatives, neighbours, the media) and can grow more complex over time. Equifinality. In an open system the same end state can be reached from different starting points and by different routes. Two families can arrive at the same problem (a teenager who will not go to school) by completely different histories, which is why systems therapists care more about the pattern that maintains a problem today than about how it began. Systems are also nested in a hierarchy. Each family is part of a larger system (a neighbourhood, a caste or community, a town, a culture), and each member is a smaller system of organs and cells. A systems therapist always asks at which level a problem is best understood. The second borrowed idea was cybernetics , the science of self-regulating systems and of communication and control in machines and animals, named by the American mathematician Norbert Wiener (1894 to 1964) in his book Cybernetics (1948). Wiener had worked during the Second World War on anti-aircraft fire control: aiming a gun at a moving plane by feeding information about the plane's course back into the aiming system, so that the aim was corrected continuously. The central concept is feedback : information about the output of a system that is fed back into the system and changes what it does next. Bateson attended the famous Macy conferences in New York at which Wiener and others developed these ideas, and he carried them straight into the study of families. Feedback and homeostasis Think of the thermostat on an air conditioner set to 24 degrees. When the room warms above 24, the thermostat switches the compressor on; when the room cools below 24, it switches it off. The room temperature wobbles but stays close to the set point. A system that holds itself steady in this way shows homeostasis , a term the physiologist Walter Cannon had used for the body's regulation of temperature and blood sugar. In 1957 Don Jackson (1920 to 1968) published a paper on "the question of family homeostasis", arguing that families too have set points. Each family has unwritten family rules about who may say what to whom, how close people may be, how anger is expressed and who makes decisions, and when a member breaks a rule the others act, often without realising it, to restore the old balance. Two kinds of feedback do the work. Negative feedback reduces deviation and restores the previous state; it is the thermostat switching the compressor off. Positive feedback amplifies deviation and pushes the system further from where it was, as when a microphone held near a loudspeaker produces an ever louder howl. Here is the trap that every examiner sets: in systems language, "negative" and "positive" have nothing to do with bad and good. Suppose sixteen-year-old Priya comes home at midnight. If her father sits her down, listens and they agree on a curfew, the family returns to its usual pattern: that is negative feedback, and here it is helpful. If her father shouts, she stays out later, he shouts louder and she stops coming home at all, the deviation is being amplified: that is positive feedback, and here it is destructive. But positive feedback can also be the only route to healthy change, as when a family that has always avoided conflict is finally pushed into the open argument it needed. Later writers gave the two tendencies names. Morphostasis is a system's tendency to keep its structure stable; morphogenesis is its capacity to change its structure and grow. A healthy family needs both: enough stability to give its members a secure base, and enough flexibility to reorganise when a baby is born, a grandparent moves in or a child grows up. Many family problems arise when a family clings to morphostasis at a moment when life demands morphogenesis, for example by treating a seventeen-year-old exactly as it treated him at seven. Exam trap Therapists who describe the family as a system with homeostasis, boundaries and feedback loops are applying general systems theory (Ludwig von Bertalanffy), together with Norbert Wiener's cybernetics. The distractors are operant conditioning (Skinner's learning theory, which explains behaviour by its consequences for one organism), psychosexual stage theory (Freud's account of individual development) and the medical model (which locates the illness inside one patient, the opposite of systems thinking). And remember: negative feedback restores the old balance, positive feedback amplifies change; neither word means good or bad. Circular causality and the identified patient Ordinary explanations are linear: A causes B. The husband drinks because his wife nags; the wife nags because her husband drinks. Each partner offers a perfectly sensible linear story in which the other is to blame. The systems therapist hears both stories and concludes that each is half of a circle. In circular causality each person's behaviour is at once a cause and an effect of the others' behaviour, so the question "who started it?" has no useful answer (Figure 7.1). The more she nags, the more he withdraws; the more he withdraws, the more she nags. The therapist's target is the loop itself, not either person. Linear view: each partner's story Wife's account He withdraws so I nag Husband's account She nags so I withdraw Each blames the other and asks "who started it?" Circular view: the loop Wife nags more Husband withdraws more Each act is both cause and effect No starting point: treat the pattern Figure 7.1 Linear and circular causality. Each partner punctuates the sequence so that the other started it; the systems therapist sees a single loop and blames no one. Why does each partner see only half the circle? The answer came from Paul Watzlawick (1921 to 2007), Janet Beavin Bavelas and Don Jackson in Pragmatics of Human Communication (1967), a book that set out five axioms of communication drawn from the Palo Alto work. Three of them are worth knowing by heart. First, "one cannot not communicate": silence, turning away and refusing to answer are all messages. Second, every communication has a content aspect (what is said) and a relationship aspect (what the message implies about the relationship between the speakers); Bateson called these the report and the command. Third, the nature of a relationship depends on the partners' punctuation of the sequence of events: each divides the endless circle at a different point, so that his own behaviour appears as a reaction and the other's as the cause. ("I withdraw because you nag." "I nag because you withdraw.") The remaining two axioms distinguish digital (verbal) from analogic (non-verbal) communication, and symmetrical interaction, in which partners mirror each other (insult for insult, boast for boast), from complementary interaction, in which one partner's behaviour fits the other's (one leads, one follows). Bateson had described both patterns as early as 1936, in his book Naven about the Iatmul, under the name schismogenesis: the way symmetrical rivalry or complementary dominance can escalate until a relationship splits. Circular thinking transforms how the family's problem member is seen. The person whom the family brings for treatment ("our son is the problem; please fix him") is called the identified patient (IP). To a systems therapist the identified patient is the symptom-bearer: the visible sign that the system is under strain, rather than the cause of the strain. Often the symptom even serves a function for the system. A twelve-year-old's stomach aches may keep his quarrelling parents united in worry about him; if the stomach aches stopped, the parents might have to face their marriage. Treating only the boy, the systems therapist predicts, will fail, or will succeed only for the symptom to reappear in someone else. An early and influential description of this process came from the sociologists Ezra Vogel (1930 to 2020) and Norman Bell in their 1960 paper "The emotionally disturbed child as the family scapegoat". In families they studied, the parents' unresolved tensions were displaced onto one child, who was chosen for some characteristic that already set him apart (he resembled a disliked relative, he was slower, or the child was a girl when a boy was wanted). The scapegoat carried the family's conflicts; by blaming and worrying about him, the parents could avoid confronting each other, and the family held together at his expense. Scapegoating is a classic example of a symptom that stabilises a system. Finally, circular thinking shifts attention from content to process . The content of a family argument is what it is about (money, homework, the mother-in-law). The process is how it unfolds: who speaks first, who interrupts, who sides with whom, who goes silent, how it ends. Family systems therapists watch the process, because the same process tends to repeat whatever the content, and changing it changes many arguments at once. Exam trap The identified patient is the family member presented as the problem; systems therapists see that person as the symptom-bearer of a troubled system, not its cause. The scapegoat (Vogel and Bell, 1960) is a child onto whom parental conflict is displaced. Do not confuse circular causality (a systems idea about mutual cause and effect) with circular questioning (a Milan interviewing technique, Section 7.5). Subsystems, boundaries and triangles Three more structural words appear in every school of family therapy, so it is worth meeting them here before each school gives them its own twist. A subsystem is a smaller unit within the family that carries out particular functions: the spousal (husband and wife) subsystem, the parental subsystem (whoever raises the children, which in an Indian joint family may include a grandmother), the sibling subsystem, and each individual. A two-person unit is a dyad ; a three-person unit is a triad . A boundary , in the family therapist's sense, is the set of invisible rules that defines who participates in a subsystem and how: whether the children may interrupt the parents' discussions about money, whether a grandmother may overrule the mother about bedtime, whether a teenager's diary is private. Boundaries can be too loose, too tight or about right, and Salvador Minuchin built a whole therapy around them (Section 7.4). The third word is the triangle. Two-person relationships are unstable under stress. When a husband and wife are anxious with each other, one of them is likely to pull in a third person (a child, a parent, a friend, a lover, even a therapist) to absorb the tension: the wife complains to her son about his father, or the husband spends his evenings with his mother. This drawing-in of a third person to manage the tension between two is triangulation , and Murray Bowen made it central to his theory (Section 7.3). A coalition is an alliance of two members against a third; when it crosses generations (a mother and son allied against the father) it undermines the parental hierarchy and is a classic target of both structural and strategic therapists. The family life cycle Families are not only structures; they move through time. Just as an individual passes through developmental stages, a family passes through a sequence of stages, each of which demands that it reorganise. The sociologist Evelyn Duvall described an eight-stage family life cycle in 1957, but the version family therapists use comes from two Bowen-trained therapists in New York, Betty Carter (1929 to 2012) and Monica McGoldrick (born 1943), in their book The Family Life Cycle (1980) and its later editions, The Changing Family Life Cycle (1989) and The Expanded Family Life Cycle (1999). Carter and McGoldrick described six stages of the middle-class American family life cycle, each with a key emotional task, summarised in Table 7.1. Their central claim is that symptoms cluster at the transitions between stages, when the old rules no longer fit and the new ones have not yet been worked out. A young adult develops panic attacks in the month before leaving home; a mother becomes depressed when her last child leaves; a man starts drinking in the year after he retires. Table 7.1 Carter and McGoldrick's family life cycle and the key emotional task of each stage (stage names as in the later editions of their book). Stage Key emotional task Typical changes required 1 Leaving home: single young adults Accepting emotional and financial responsibility for oneself Separating from the family of origin; work; close peer relationships 2 Joining of families through marriage: the new couple Commitment to a new system Forming the marital system; realigning ties with both extended families and friends 3 Families with young children Accepting new members into the system Making room for children; sharing child care, money and housework; grandparent roles 4 Families with adolescents Making boundaries more flexible for children's independence and grandparents' frailty Letting adolescents move in and out; refocusing on mid-life marriage and careers 5 Launching children and moving on Accepting many exits from and entries into the family Renegotiating the couple as a dyad; adult-to-adult relations with grown children; in-laws and grandchildren; dealing with the death of parents 6 Families in later life Accepting the shift of generational roles Coping with physical decline, retirement, loss of spouse and peers; making room for the wisdom of the elderly Carter and McGoldrick added a useful distinction between two kinds of stress. Horizontal stressors move forward through time: the predictable transitions of the life cycle and unpredictable events such as an accident, a job loss or an early death. Vertical stressors come down the generations: patterns of relating, family secrets, legacies, expectations and anxieties that are passed from grandparents to parents to children. When a horizontal stressor (a daughter's marriage) lands on a family already loaded with a vertical one (three generations in which daughters who marry are cut off from their mothers), the strain can be enormous. Jay Haley, whose strategic therapy you will meet in Section 7.5, organised much of his work around the same idea: in Uncommon Therapy (1973) he presented the hypnotherapist Milton Erickson's cases as interventions at stuck points in the family life cycle, and in Leaving Home (1980) he focused on the young adult who cannot launch. Indian context Carter and McGoldrick's stages describe the middle-class American nuclear family, and they need translation in India. In many Indian families "leaving home" never happens in the American sense; a son may live with his parents all his life, and the key task of young adulthood is to take on adult responsibility within the family rather than outside it. "The joining of families through marriage" is literal: in an arranged marriage two families are joined, and the new couple often lives inside the husband's parental household, so the first task is not forming a couple alone but fitting a daughter-in-law into an existing system with its own hierarchy. Several Indian family therapists have proposed modified stages that give weight to the joint family, to the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law relationship and to the care of elderly parents by grown sons. The principle survives translation: symptoms cluster at transitions, and the therapist's first question is "what change is this family going through right now?" Clinical link A therapist who does not understand a family's culture will misread it. Closeness that looks like intrusion by one culture's standards (a mother who still feeds her adult son, a family that makes every decision together, a daughter-in-law who defers to her mother-in-law) may be ordinary, supportive and expected in another. Poor awareness of a family's culture and customary practices leads to wrong assessments and misinterpretations : normal behaviour is labelled pathological, the family feels judged, and the therapeutic alliance suffers. This is why Monica McGoldrick and her colleagues edited Ethnicity and Family Therapy (1982) and why cultural humility is now part of every family therapy training. 7.2 Families and Schizophrenia: From Blame to Expressed Emotion High yield · 8 Qs The first serious family research asked the most painful question a family can be asked: did you cause your child's illness? Between the late 1940s and the early 1960s several brilliant clinicians answered, in effect, yes. Their theories have not survived as accounts of what causes schizophrenia, and they did real harm to a generation of parents who were told, or who quietly assumed, that their mistakes had produced a devastating disorder. Yet the same line of research, once it changed its question from "what causes schizophrenia?" to "what makes a person with schizophrenia relapse?", produced one of the best-replicated findings in clinical psychology and one of its most useful treatments. This section tells that story from blame to help. (The disorder itself, its symptoms and its biological causes, is covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) The schizophrenogenic mother Frieda Fromm-Reichmann (1889 to 1957) was a German-born psychoanalyst who worked at Chestnut Lodge, a private hospital near Washington, and who was famous for treating patients with schizophrenia by intensive psychotherapy at a time when most psychiatrists thought them unreachable. (One of her patients, Joanne Greenberg, later wrote a novel about her treatment, I Never Promised You a Rose Garden .) In a 1948 paper Fromm-Reichmann wrote that the schizophrenic patient was "painfully distrustful and resentful of other people, due to the severe early warp and rejection he encountered in important people of his infancy and childhood, as a rule, mainly in a schizophrenogenic mother." The phrase schizophrenogenic mother (literally, the schizophrenia-producing mother) came to mean a mother who was cold, dominating, rejecting and at the same time overprotective, insecure and anxious. The idea spread rapidly, because it fitted the psychoanalytic assumption that severe disorders begin in the earliest relationships. It collapsed because no one could ever show that mothers of people with schizophrenia were different, in these ways, from other mothers before their children became ill. Any differences that were observed could equally be effects of living with a severely ill child rather than causes. Meanwhile twin and adoption studies were building the case for a strong genetic contribution. Today the schizophrenogenic mother is regarded as discredited, and the episode is taught as a warning: a theory that blames families without evidence adds guilt to grief. A parallel theory blamed the "refrigerator mother" for autism, an idea associated with Leo Kanner's early descriptions of the parents of autistic children and popularised by Bruno Bettelheim's book The Empty Fortress (1967); it too has been abandoned. Bateson's double bind Bateson's group approached the same question from communication theory rather than psychoanalysis. Their 1956 paper defined a double bind as a situation with the following ingredients: Two or more persons, one of whom is the "victim" and another (usually a parent, often the mother) on whom the victim depends. Repeated experience, so that the double bind becomes a habitual expectation rather than a single traumatic event. A primary negative injunction, such as "Do not do that, or I will punish you." A secondary injunction that conflicts with the first at a more abstract level, usually conveyed non-verbally by posture, tone or gesture ("Do not see this as punishment"; "Do not question my love"). A tertiary negative injunction that prohibits the victim from escaping the field: he cannot leave the relationship, and he cannot comment on the contradiction. Eventually the complete set of ingredients is no longer needed; almost any part of the pattern is enough to trigger panic or rage in the victim. Apply this to the opening story. The mother's stiffening body says "Do not come close"; her words say "You should come close, and if you do not, you do not love me"; her final remark says "Do not notice the contradiction; the problem is your feelings". The son depends on her, he is in hospital, and he cannot say "Mother, you stiffened when I hugged you." Bateson's group used the episode as an illustration of the symptomatic double bind, the double bind as a supposed cause of schizophrenic symptoms, and suggested that a child raised on such messages would learn never to trust the literal meaning of any message and to speak in the guarded, metaphorical way that looked like schizophrenic thought disorder. The theory drew on the philosophers Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead's theory of logical types: a message about a message (a metacommunication) belongs to a higher logical level than the message itself, and confusion arises when the two levels contradict each other. How did the theory fare? As a cause of schizophrenia, badly. Research teams could not reliably identify double binds, could not show that they were more common in families of people with schizophrenia than in other families, and could not show that they came before rather than after the illness. Double binds, it turned out, occur in all families, and in classrooms and offices too ("Be spontaneous!" is a double bind). But the concept was enormously fertile for therapy. It taught therapists to listen for the relationship message underneath the content, it led directly to the idea that therapists could use paradox to break such binds (the "therapeutic double bind" of the strategic therapists, Section 7.5), and the Palo Alto circle that produced it went on to shape the Mental Research Institute (founded by Don Jackson in 1959), the strategic school and the whole communications approach to family therapy. Exam trap "One parent conveys two conflicting messages to the child at the same time" is double bind communication , proposed by Gregory Bateson and colleagues (Don Jackson, Jay Haley, John Weakland) in 1956 as an early family-communication theory of schizophrenia (not of phobias, depression or autism). The bait options are deliberately vague ("faulty communication") or belong elsewhere ("social skills deficits", "conflict resolution"). The mother-and-son hospital story illustrates the symptomatic double bind , not a "cybernetic system" or "homeostatic system" (general systems ideas, Section 7.1) or an "incongruent family dyad" (incongruence is Satir's and Rogers's word, Section 7.6). First-rank symptoms are Kurt Schneider's, not Bateson's; dementia praecox is Emil Kraepelin's; Aaron Beck is cognitive therapy (Chapter 5). An option printed as "Wayne" in such questions is almost certainly Lyman Wynne , the researcher of pseudomutuality (below), who has nothing to do with first-rank symptoms either. Marital schism, marital skew and pseudomutuality At Yale, the psychiatrist Theodore Lidz (1910 to 2001) and his colleagues studied the families of hospitalised young people with schizophrenia in great depth, and in 1957 (Lidz, Cornelison, Fleck and Terry) described two kinds of disturbed marriage. In marital schism the parents are in chronic open conflict, each preoccupied with his or her own problems, each undermining the worth of the other and competing for the children's sympathy and loyalty. The child is caught: pleasing one parent means betraying the other, and a father who despises the mother may fear that the child will turn out like her. In marital skew there is little open conflict, because one parent's serious disturbance dominates the home while the other parent passively accepts it and pretends that everything is normal. The children are left to make sense of a reality that the family officially denies. At NIMH, Lyman Wynne (1923 to 2007) and his colleagues (Wynne, Ryckoff, Day and Hirsch, 1958) described pseudomutuality : a family facade of harmony, closeness and agreement that hides emotional distance and, more importantly, leaves no room for any member to develop a separate identity. Divergence is felt as a threat to the whole family, so it is never allowed to surface. Wynne pictured the boundary of such a family as a rubber fence : it stretches to include whatever fits the family's picture of itself and snaps back to exclude whatever does not, so the child can neither leave nor be fully known. Its mirror image, pseudohostility , is a surface of constant bickering that hides the same underlying fusion. Wynne later worked with the psychologist Margaret Thaler Singer (1921 to 2003) on communication deviance , a measurable tendency of parents to communicate in vague, fragmented or confusing ways, which proved one of the more durable findings of this era. Partly because they were built on small numbers of families seen after the illness had begun, with no comparison groups and no way of separating cause from effect. Partly because they ignored genetics. And the most convincing modern evidence suggests that family environment matters in a different way: in the Finnish adoptive family study led by Pekka Tienari, children who were adopted away from mothers with schizophrenia were at raised risk of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders mainly when they were raised in adoptive families rated as disturbed. Genetic vulnerability and family environment interacted; neither alone told the story. That conclusion fits the diathesis-stress model taught in Chapter 1, and it prepares the ground for the research that did survive. Expressed emotion The research that survived began in London, with a simple observation by the sociologist George Brown (1930 to 2026). In 1959 he followed men with schizophrenia who had been discharged from hospital and found, contrary to what anyone expected, that those who went home to live with their parents or wives relapsed more often than those who went to live in lodgings or with brothers and sisters. Something about close family life seemed to be risky. With colleagues, Brown developed a long, semi-structured interview with a key relative, the Camberwell Family Interview (CFI; Brown and Rutter, 1966), named after the district of south London where the research was done. The relative is interviewed alone, usually soon after the patient's admission, about the past few months at home; the interview is audio-recorded, and trained raters code not only what the relative says but how it is said: tone of voice, speed, emphasis. From these ratings came the construct of expressed emotion (EE): the emotional climate of a home as revealed by the attitudes that a key relative expresses about the patient. In the definitive form of the index, developed by Brown, James Birley and John Wing (1923 to 2010) in 1972, a home is rated high in EE on the basis of three components: Critical comments : statements that clearly express dislike or disapproval of something the patient does, judged by content or by tone ("He just lies in bed all day; he is plain lazy"). Hostility : criticism generalised from what the patient does to who the patient is, or outright rejection ("He has always been a selfish person; I wish he had never come back"). Emotional over-involvement (EOI): exaggerated, intrusive, self-sacrificing or overprotective concern, dramatic distress, and an inability to let the patient do anything alone ("I haven't left the house since he got ill; I sleep in his room"). The CFI also rates warmth and positive remarks , but these are not part of the high-EE index. In Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff's version, a relative is rated high in EE if he or she makes six or more critical comments in the interview, shows any hostility, or shows marked emotional over-involvement. Brown, Birley and Wing (1972) confirmed that patients returning to high-EE homes were far more likely to relapse within nine months than those returning to low-EE homes. Then came the study that made the finding famous. Key study: Vaughn and Leff (1976) Question. Does the expressed emotion of relatives predict relapse in schizophrenia, and can anything protect a patient living in a high-EE home? Method. Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff (1938 to 2021), working at the Institute of Psychiatry in London, used a shortened Camberwell Family Interview to rate the relatives of patients with schizophrenia admitted to hospital, and then followed the patients for nine months after discharge, recording whether they relapsed, whether they took maintenance antipsychotic medication, and how many hours a week they spent in face-to-face contact with their relatives. They also studied a group of patients with depression. Results. About half of the patients who returned to high-EE homes relapsed, compared with roughly one in eight of those in low-EE homes. Within high-EE homes two factors were protective: regular medication, and less than 35 hours a week of face-to-face contact with the high-EE relative. Patients who had neither protection did worst of all; nearly all of them relapsed (Figure 7.2). Depressed patients were also sensitive to criticism, relapsing at even lower levels of critical comments. Conclusion. The emotional climate at home predicts relapse in schizophrenia independently of medication, and its effect can be buffered by medication and by reduced contact. Criticism. The study was correlational: high EE might partly reflect a more severely ill or more difficult patient. Later work showed that the influence runs in both directions. Relapse within 9 months of discharge (%) 0 25 50 75 100 13 15 42 53 92 Low EE (all) High EE low contact, drug High EE low contact, no drug High EE high contact, drug High EE high contact, no drug Figure 7.2 Expressed emotion and relapse in schizophrenia (approximate nine-month figures from the London studies of Brown and of Vaughn and Leff). "High contact" means 35 or more hours a week face to face with the relative; "drug" means regular maintenance medication. Notice that in high-EE homes, medication and reduced contact each protect, and together they bring risk down to the low-EE level. The finding has been replicated around the world. A meta-analysis by Ronald Butzlaff and Jill Hooley (1998), pooling 27 studies, confirmed that high EE is a robust predictor of relapse in schizophrenia, and showed something unexpected: EE predicts relapse even more strongly in mood disorders and eating disorders. Hooley's own research explained part of the mechanism. High-EE relatives, especially critical ones, tend to believe that the patient's symptoms are under the patient's control ("he could get up if he wanted to"), whereas low-EE relatives see the same behaviour as part of the illness. Criticism follows from blame. The relationship is also bidirectional: patients who are more disturbed or more irritating provoke more criticism, and criticism in turn raises stress and the risk of relapse. EE has even been measured in hospital staff, with similar effects. Three things about EE are tested again and again. First, high EE predicts relapse , not the onset of schizophrenia, not negative symptoms and not violence. Second, the three components are critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement; warmth is rated but is not one of them. Third, because high EE is a stressor that acts through contact, one of the simplest ways to manage it, when the emotional climate cannot be changed quickly, is to reduce the hours of face-to-face contact : a day-care centre, a sheltered job, a club, separate meal times or a hostel place for part of the week. Indian context India has played an important part in EE research. In the 1980s Narendra Nath Wig, Julian Leff and colleagues measured EE among the relatives of patients with schizophrenia in and around Chandigarh as part of the World Health Organization's work on the outcome of schizophrenia. Indian relatives, and rural relatives in particular, showed much lower rates of high EE than British or Anglo-American relatives (Janis Jenkins and Marvin Karno's 1992 review compared Indian, Mexican-American, British and Anglo-American samples, with Indian families lowest). Where EE was high, it still predicted relapse. This may be one reason why the WHO studies found a better course of schizophrenia in developing countries. But be careful in applying the ratings: an Indian mother who feeds her ill son by hand and accompanies him everywhere may look "over-involved" by a London scoring manual and be entirely ordinary and supportive in her own culture. Family psychoeducation If the emotional climate at home predicts relapse, can changing it prevent relapse? From the late 1970s several groups set out to find out, and the answer was a clear yes. The resulting treatments are known together as family psychoeducation or family intervention for psychosis: structured work with the patient's relatives that combines education about the illness with training in coping, communication and problem solving. Notice the change of attitude. The family is no longer the cause to be treated but an ally to be informed and supported; the first message of every programme is that the family did not cause the illness. Leff and his colleagues ran the first controlled trial in London (Leff, Kuipers, Berkowitz, Eberlein-Vries and Sturgeon, 1982). Patients living in high-EE homes were all kept on medication; half of the families also received education sessions at home, a fortnightly relatives' group in which low-EE relatives modelled calmer ways of coping, and family sessions aimed at lowering criticism and reducing contact. At nine months about 9 percent of the patients in the intervention group had relapsed, against about half of the controls. In California, Ian Falloon and his colleagues developed behavioural family management , a home-based programme that teaches the whole family, patient included, about schizophrenia and its treatment, and then trains communication skills (expressing positive feelings, making positive requests, expressing negative feelings constructively, active listening) and a six-step method of structured problem solving. In their 1982 trial relapse over nine months was about 6 percent with family management against about 44 percent with individual management. At Pittsburgh, Carol Anderson , David Reiss and Gerard Hogarty (1935 to 2006), in the programme described in their book Schizophrenia and the Family (1986), began with a one-day "survival skills workshop" for families, teaching them about schizophrenia, its course, its biology and its treatment, followed by regular family sessions lasting a year or more; and William McFarlane developed multiple-family groups in which several families learn together and support one another. The programmes differ in style, but they share a set of ingredients: Education about the illness, its treatment and its course, given in plain language, with the explicit message that the family is not to blame. Support for regular medication and for recognising the early warning signs of relapse, with a written plan for what to do when they appear. Communication training, especially in expressing negative feelings and requests without criticism or hostility. Structured problem solving for the practical stresses of daily life. Reducing face-to-face contact where the climate remains tense, and helping relatives look after their own health and social lives, which lowers over-involvement. A long enough course (guidelines such as those of the UK's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence ask for at least ten planned sessions over three months to a year) and, where possible, the patient's own participation. Systematic reviews, including those of the Cochrane Collaboration, have confirmed that family intervention reduces relapse and readmission and improves adherence to medication, and clinical guidelines in many countries recommend it for every family in close contact with a person with schizophrenia. The benefits fade if the intervention stops early, which is why it is usually offered as a long-term part of care (Chapter 9 places it within psychosocial rehabilitation). Indian context Indian psychiatry involved families long before Western family therapy did. In the 1950s Dr Vidya Sagar at the Amritsar Mental Hospital invited the relatives of patients to live in tents on the hospital grounds and share in their care, learning about the illness through group meetings; the family members became co-therapists. Because most Indian patients with severe mental illness live with their families, and because families provide most of the care in a country with very few professionals, psychoeducation for caregivers is one of the most practical interventions an Indian clinical psychologist can offer. Exam trap Expressed emotion means a family environment with emotionally loaded communication patterns of a critical, hostile or over-involved nature ; it is not the patient's difficulty in talking about feelings, not a family full of positive comments, and not a lack of emotion. High EE predicts relapse of psychotic illness , not onset, negative symptoms or violence, and "poor treatment outcome" is too vague to be the best answer. Its three components are critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement; warmth and positive regard are not among them. Reducing contact hours is a strategy for managing high EE, not for interpersonal violence, parasuicide risk or stubbornness in children. Names to match: George Brown (the original London research), Brown, Birley and Wing (1972), Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff (1976, the 35-hour finding), the Camberwell Family Interview. Clinical link EE research gives you a ready-made formulation for a family visit. Listen for criticism ("he is lazy"), hostility ("he has always been like this"), and over-involvement ("I cannot leave him for a minute"). Then ask what the relative believes about the cause of the behaviour; criticism usually rests on the belief that the patient could control it. Explaining negative symptoms as part of the illness, not laziness, is often the single most effective thing you can do for a critical relative. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks.
