In one room an energetic man with an Argentinian accent is on his feet, moving a mother's chair away from her daughter, telling a father to take charge, joking with a teenager one minute and challenging her the next. You will meet him in Section 7.4. In the other room a quiet man from Tennessee sits very still. He asks a wife, in a level voice, "What is your theory about why your husband goes silent when you raise the subject of his mother?" When the husband begins to answer his wife angrily, the therapist turns to him and asks him to speak to the therapist instead. Nobody cries, nobody shouts, and the session looks almost boring. Yet the quiet man believed that what he was doing went deeper than anything happening next door, because he was not trying to rearrange the family in front of him. He was trying to help each person become, slowly, more of a self. His name was Murray Bowen, and of all the founders of family therapy he was the one most interested in theory. This section explains that theory, the calm style of therapy that grew from it, and its most famous tool, the genogram. Murray Bowen and the family as an emotional unit Murray Bowen (1913 to 1990) was born in the small town of Waverly, Tennessee, took his medical degree at the University of Tennessee in 1937 and served as an army doctor during the Second World War, where his interest moved from surgery to psychiatry. From 1946 to 1954 he trained and worked at the Menninger Clinic in Topeka, Kansas, then the leading psychoanalytic hospital in the United States, and there he became fascinated by the intense, symbiotic attachment between some mothers and their children with schizophrenia. In 1954 he moved to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) near Washington, and set up one of the strangest research projects in the history of psychiatry. Whole families were admitted to a research ward and lived there for months at a time alongside their young adult son or daughter with schizophrenia: at first mothers with their children, later fathers and brothers and sisters as well. Bowen and his staff could watch, day and night, what no clinician seeing a patient for fifty minutes a week could ever see. What they saw changed Bowen's thinking. The intensity he had noticed between mother and child was not a two-person affair; the father was part of it, usually by keeping his distance, and the whole family behaved like a single emotional organism. When one member became anxious, the anxiety passed through the others like a current. Bowen first called this stuck-together quality the undifferentiated family ego mass , a phrase he later dropped. He also noticed that the same processes, in milder form, could be seen in ordinary families, including his own. In 1959 he moved to Georgetown University in Washington, where he worked for the rest of his life and where his Georgetown Family Center later became the Bowen Center for the Study of the Family. His two main books are Family Therapy in Clinical Practice (1978), a collection of his papers, and Family Evaluation (1988), written with his colleague Michael Kerr . One episode shows what kind of man he was. In 1967 the psychologist James Framo (1922 to 2001) organised a national conference in Philadelphia to bring family researchers and family therapists together. Bowen was expected to present an update on his NIMH research. Instead he stood up and described, in detail, his own efforts over several years to change his position in his own family of origin back in Tennessee: the visits home, the letters he wrote to stir up old triangles, the way he stayed calm when his relatives reacted. The audience was stunned. A senior psychiatrist had made his own family the case study, and the message was clear: a therapist cannot help a family become less fused than he is himself. When Framo published the conference papers in 1972, Bowen's paper appeared under the name "Anonymous". From then on, working on one's own family became the heart of Bowenian training. Bowen built his theory on a few assumptions. Every family is an emotional system , and the emotional system, which humans share with other animals, runs much of our behaviour automatically. Against it stands the intellectual system , the capacity to think, reason and choose. Each family also balances two life forces, a pull towards togetherness (closeness, approval, being one of us) and a pull towards individuality (being a separate person directed by one's own goals). When chronic anxiety , the sustained, background tension of a family under strain, rises, togetherness takes over, people react rather than think, and the family's automatic emotional patterns come to the surface. Out of these assumptions Bowen developed eight interlocking concepts, which the rest of this section takes one at a time. The first six had been set out by the mid-1960s (in a 1966 paper); emotional cutoff and societal regression were added in 1975. Because the theory traces how these patterns pass from grandparents to parents to children, Bowen's approach is also called multigenerational , intergenerational or transgenerational family therapy, and Bowenians often describe their work as family-of-origin therapy. Exam trap Bowen's family systems theory is not the same as Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory (Section 7.1). Bowen insisted that his theory grew out of his own observations of families and from biology, not from von Bertalanffy, and the two terms are a favourite pair of distractors. When an option says "transgenerational", "intergenerational" or "multigenerational" family therapy, think first of Bowen (Ivan Boszormenyi-Nagy's contextual therapy, Section 7.6, is the other transgenerational school). The "undifferentiated family ego mass" is Bowen's early term; "pseudomutuality" and the "rubber fence" are Lyman Wynne's (Section 7.2). Differentiation of self The cornerstone of Bowen's theory is differentiation of self : the degree to which a person can separate thinking from feeling, and can remain a distinct self while staying emotionally connected to the people who matter. The definition has two halves, and you need both. The first half is intrapsychic , inside the person: can she notice her feelings, and yet choose to be guided by considered thought rather than be swept along by them? The second half is interpersonal , between people: can she hold her own views in a close relationship, without either giving them up to keep the peace or attacking and running away to protect them? The opposite of differentiation is fusion , in which thinking and feeling are merged inside the person and selves are merged between people, so that one person's mood instantly becomes another's. A worked example makes the idea concrete. Meera, twenty-seven, is a software engineer in Bengaluru. Every Sunday her mother phones from Mysuru, and every Sunday the call ends in the same place: why is Meera not yet married, when all her cousins are? Consider three ways Meera might respond. She gives in. She agrees to meet the prospective grooms her mother has lined up, though she has no wish to marry this year, because she cannot bear her mother's disappointment. Her decision is driven by her mother's feelings, not by her own thinking. She explodes. She shouts that her mother is backward and controlling, hangs up, and stops taking the calls. This looks like independence, but it is just as driven by emotion as giving in; the mother's anxiety still decides what Meera does, only in reverse. She stays in contact and states her position calmly: "I know you worry about me, Amma. I have thought about it, and I am not ready to marry this year. I would still like to talk every Sunday." When her mother cries, Meera does not shout and does not give in; she listens, says she understands, and holds her ground. Only the third response is differentiated. Notice that differentiation is not about the content of the decision (Meera could equally have decided, after real thought, that she did want to marry) but about how the decision is made and how she stays in the relationship while making it. A calm statement of one's own beliefs and intentions, made without attacking or demanding that others change, is what Bowen called taking an I-position . Bowen distinguished two kinds of self. The solid self is made of beliefs and principles that a person has arrived at by careful thought; it is not negotiable in relationships, and it does not change because someone is pleased or annoyed. The pseudo-self is made of positions borrowed from others or adopted under emotional pressure, to win approval or to oppose someone; it can be traded away in a relationship and it shifts with the emotional weather. The rebel who reflexively opposes his parents is, on this view, as poorly differentiated as the son who obeys them in everything; both are reacting, not choosing. Bowen also separated a person's basic level of differentiation, which is fairly fixed by the end of adolescence and changes only through long, deliberate effort, from the functional level, which rises and falls with anxiety and with relationships. In a marriage one partner may appear highly competent and the other helpless, because one has "borrowed" self from the other: the overfunctioning wife who runs everything and the underfunctioning husband who cannot decide anything are a reciprocal pair, and each keeps the other in place. To convey how differentiation varies across people, Bowen described a theoretical scale of differentiation running from 0 to 100, divided into four broad quarters. It was a way of thinking, not a test with norms, and in later years he preferred describing people's functioning to giving them numbers. At the bottom of the scale, people live almost entirely in a world of feelings; they cannot distinguish feeling from fact, they spend their energy seeking love and approval or reacting against its absence, and under stress they are prone to severe and lasting problems. In the lower middle range people can think, but their thinking is easily captured by the emotional system; they are highly sensitive to approval, they say "I feel" when they mean "I think", and much of their self is pseudo-self. Higher up the scale people can hold a thought-out position under moderate stress, can be close without being fused and can disagree without cutting off. Bowen believed that people functioning above about 60 are a small minority of any society, and that the top of the scale is a theoretical ideal. Later researchers built questionnaires to measure the idea; the best known, the Differentiation of Self Inventory of Elizabeth Skowron and Myrna Friedlander (1998), has four subscales: emotional reactivity, I-position, emotional cutoff and fusion with others. Studies with it have generally found that lower differentiation goes with more anxiety, more psychological symptoms and more marital distress, which is broadly what Bowen predicted. Indian context Is differentiation just Western individualism in disguise? Many critics have asked this, and the question matters in India. The psychoanalyst Alan Roland , comparing patients in India, Japan and the United States in In Search of Self in India and Japan (1988), described the Indian "familial self": a self experienced through close, hierarchical family ties rather than in separation from them. Bowen himself insisted that differentiation is not the same as independence or distance; the person who moves far away and stops calling is, in his terms, poorly differentiated. Read this way, the concept travels well. An Indian son who lives with his parents all his life can be highly differentiated if he can disagree with his father calmly, keep his own counsel and still be a warm and dutiful son; a young woman who leaves for Canada after a bitter quarrel and never speaks to her family again is not. Exam trap Differentiation of self (Bowen) means separating thinking from feeling and keeping a self within close relationships. It does not mean distance, independence or rebellion; the emotionally cut-off person is poorly differentiated. Do not confuse it with Margaret Mahler's separation-individuation (the infant's psychological birth, Section 3.4), with Minuchin's enmeshment (a property of family boundaries, Section 7.4) or with Wynne's pseudomutuality (Section 7.2). Fusion , solid self , pseudo-self and the I-position are all Bowen's words. Triangles and the nuclear family emotional process Section 7.1 introduced triangulation: the drawing in of a third person to absorb the tension between two. For Bowen this was not an occasional event but a law of emotional systems. A two-person relationship is stable only while it is calm. As anxiety rises, the more uncomfortable partner pulls in a third person, and the tension spreads across three relationships instead of being trapped in one. The triangle is therefore the smallest stable relationship system, and Bowen thought of families as networks of interlocking triangles : when one triangle can no longer hold the tension, it spills into the next, drawing in grandparents, in-laws, teachers, friends and, very often, the therapist. Bowen added a subtle point about positions in a triangle. In calm periods there are two comfortable insiders and one uncomfortable outsider, and the outsider works to get closer to one of the others. When tension is high, the positions reverse: the outside position becomes the desirable one, and each person tries to get out and leave the other two to fight. Consider Arjun and Meera, now married with a ten-year-old son, Kabir. When Arjun starts staying late at the office, Meera, lonely and anxious, begins to confide her worries to Kabir. Kabir, flattered and burdened, becomes his mother's companion; Arjun, already uncomfortable, becomes the outsider. When Kabir starts having stomach aches on school mornings, both parents turn their worry towards him, and for a while they argue much less. The triangle has stabilised the marriage, at Kabir's expense. If Meera's mother now phones daily to criticise Arjun's long hours, a second, interlocking triangle (Meera, her mother, Arjun) begins to carry part of the load. Triangles are not bad in themselves; every family has them, and once formed they persist. The problem is a triangle that becomes rigid, so that the same third person, usually a child, always carries the tension. The way out is detriangulation : a person caught in a triangle stays in emotional contact with both others while refusing to take sides, to carry messages or to become the go-between. If Kabir's grandmother, instead of passing on Meera's complaints to Arjun, says "That sounds like something you two need to talk about", she has detriangled herself. Bowen's third concept describes how the anxiety of a single generation is expressed within the household. He originally called it the nuclear family emotional system; the Bowen Center now speaks of the nuclear family emotional process . Bowen observed that people tend to marry partners at about their own level of differentiation, so two poorly differentiated people form a highly fused couple, and the fusion has to go somewhere. It is absorbed in four basic patterns: Marital conflict. Each spouse externalises anxiety into the marriage; they blame each other, try to control each other and resist being controlled. Dysfunction in one spouse. One spouse pressures and the other yields; the yielding, underfunctioning partner absorbs the anxiety and may develop a physical illness, depression or a drinking problem. Impairment of one or more children. The parents focus their anxiety on a child, who becomes the symptom-bearer (the family projection process, explained next). Emotional distance. Partners distance from each other to lower the intensity, at the risk of becoming isolated; distance usually accompanies the other three patterns. The more undifferentiated the couple and the higher the anxiety, the more intense the patterns. One of Bowen's students, Thomas Fogarty , described a familiar version of the distance pattern: the pursuer , who seeks closeness and talk when anxious, and the distancer , who seeks space, each driving the other further into his or her own move. Fogarty's advice to pursuers was blunt: never pursue a distancer. Stop chasing, attend to your own life, and the distancer, no longer fleeing, often comes closer. Exam trap Keep the triangles apart. Bowen's triangle is the basic unit of any emotional system, in which a third person is drawn in to lower anxiety between two. Minuchin's triangulation is narrower: a rigid pattern in which each parent demands that the child side with him or her against the other (Section 7.4). Jay Haley's perverse triangle is a cross-generational coalition that is denied (Section 7.5). Stephen Karpman's drama triangle of persecutor, rescuer and victim comes from transactional analysis (Section 3.9). The four patterns of the nuclear family emotional process are marital conflict, dysfunction in a spouse, impairment of a child and emotional distance. Projection, transmission and cutoff across generations The family projection process is the main route by which parents pass their own lack of differentiation to a child. The Bowen Center describes it in three steps: the parent focuses on a child out of fear that something is wrong with the child; the parent interprets the child's behaviour as confirming the fear; and the parent treats the child as if something really is wrong. The child, who is genuinely attentive to the parent's anxiety, gradually develops the problem that was feared. The child chosen is usually the one most emotionally attached to the parents: it may be the eldest son, the only daughter, a child born at a time of family crisis, or a child with a real illness. In Arjun and Meera's family it is Kabir. Meera's fear that he is fragile leads her to check on him constantly, she reads every quiet afternoon as a sign of trouble, and she keeps him home at the first stomach ache; Kabir learns that his body is the thing everyone watches. What the child inherits is less a specific symptom than a set of sensitivities: a heightened need for attention and approval, difficulty with expectations, a tendency to blame himself or others, and a feeling of being responsible for his parents' happiness. Siblings who are less caught in the projection grow up more mature, which is why Bowen expected brothers and sisters raised in the same home to differ in differentiation. Extend the projection process across many generations and you have the multigenerational transmission process . In each generation, the child who is most involved in the projection emerges slightly less differentiated than his parents, while a sibling who is less involved emerges slightly more differentiated. Each of these children then marries someone at about the same level and repeats the process with the next generation. Over several generations, Bowen argued, one line of descent moves towards greater differentiation and stability, and another towards lower differentiation, more anxiety and more severe problems. In his early NIMH years Bowen even suggested that schizophrenia might be the product of several generations of declining differentiation, an idea no one now accepts as a cause of the disorder (Section 7.2 told what became of such theories). But the broader point survives: patterns of relating, and not only genes, are handed down, and you cannot understand the anxiety in a nuclear family without looking at the generations above it. That is why Bowen therapists always want to know about the grandparents. How do people cope with unresolved fusion with their parents? Very often, Bowen saw, by cutting themselves off. Emotional cutoff is the reduction or elimination of emotional contact with one's family of origin in order to manage unresolved attachment. It can be physical, as when a son moves to another city or country and rarely visits, or purely emotional, as when a daughter lives in the same house but keeps every conversation polite, brief and away from anything that matters. Cutoff feels like freedom, but Bowen's central claim is that it solves nothing: the unresolved attachment travels with the person and resurfaces in new relationships, which tend to become intense and fused, because the cut-off person asks a spouse or a child to supply everything the original family no longer can. The more a family relies on cutoff, the more vulnerable its members are to problems. Picture a man who left his parents' home in Kanpur after a quarrel about his marriage and has not spoken to his father in seven years. He tells you he is "completely free of all that". Then you notice how desperately he needs his wife never to disagree with him. The seventh concept, sibling position , Bowen borrowed from the Austrian-born psychologist Walter Toman (1920 to 2003), whose book Family Constellation (1961) proposed that a person's position among brothers and sisters shapes lasting characteristics: eldest children tend to take responsibility and lead, youngest children tend to follow and to expect others to take charge, and so on for the other positions, with differences according to the sex of the siblings. Toman's duplication theorem held that new relationships, including marriage, go most smoothly when they repeat the relationships of childhood. An elder brother of a younger sister who marries a younger sister of an elder brother fits his early pattern exactly; two eldest children who marry may compete over who is in charge (a rank conflict); a brother who grew up only with brothers, married to a sister who grew up only with sisters, may find the other sex unfamiliar (a sex conflict). Bowen used Toman's work, but he cared less about the literal birth order than about functional position . A first-born son who is the target of his parents' projection may function more like a helpless youngest child, while a second daughter steps into the role of the responsible eldest. Knowing the sibling positions of both spouses helps a Bowenian therapist predict how they will share power and which child is most likely to be drawn into the projection process. The eighth concept, societal regression (the Bowen Center calls it the societal emotional process), extends the theory from families to whole societies. Bowen argued that a society under sustained chronic anxiety, from pressures such as rapid population growth, dwindling natural resources, economic strain or social upheaval, behaves like an anxious family: togetherness overwhelms individuality, decisions are made to relieve the anxiety of the moment rather than on principle, quick fixes replace long-term thinking, and people emphasise their rights more than their responsibilities. Bowen pointed to the way American society handled juvenile delinquency in the 1960s and 1970s as an example. Societies, like families, pass through progressive and regressive periods. The bait options belong elsewhere: narrative externalisation is Michael White and David Epston's (Section 6.8), strategic paradox and prescribing the symptom belong to Haley and the Milan and MRI teams (Section 7.5), and exception questions belong to solution-focused brief therapy (Section 6.8). Sibling position comes from Walter Toman , not from Alfred Adler, although Adler also wrote about birth order (Section 3.8). Emotional cutoff is a sign of low differentiation, not high. Therapy as coaching: the calm, detriangled therapist Bowen's therapy follows directly from his theory, and it has two goals: to lower the anxiety in the system enough for symptoms to settle, and, more ambitiously, to raise each person's basic level of differentiation. Symptom relief alone he regarded as a modest achievement, because a family that is just as fused as before will produce a new symptom at the next crisis. Who comes to therapy? Bowen rarely saw the symptomatic child. He preferred to work with the two parents, on the view that the child's problem was part of their emotional process, and very often with just one person, the most motivated and best differentiated member of the family. This sounds odd for a family therapist, but it follows from systems thinking: if one person in a triangle changes his own part, calmly and persistently, the other two must change in response. Family therapy, for Bowen, was defined by how the therapist thinks about the problem, not by how many people are in the room. The therapist's own position is the most important tool. A family in distress will try, without knowing it, to pull the therapist into its triangles: a wife wants the therapist to agree that her husband is cold, a husband wants the therapist to see that his wife is unreasonable. Bowen's answer was to stay emotionally in contact with both while remaining outside their emotional field: calm, curious, neutral and low-key. He believed that if a couple can remain in contact with a third person who is not reacting to them, the fusion between them gradually loosens. To keep the emotional temperature down he usually had the spouses talk to him, not to each other; while one spoke, the other listened, and each heard the partner's thinking without having to defend against it. He asked process questions , questions about how the pattern works that invite thought rather than feeling: "What happens between you two when Kabir has a stomach ache?" "Who in your family worried most, when you were a child?" "What do you think you contribute to the distance?" He saw himself as a coach , in his own word: like a sports coach on the touchline, he helped clients understand their families and plan their own moves, but it was the client, not the coach, who went onto the field. Several methods grew out of this stance. The therapist models and encourages the I-position . Clients are helped to design relationship experiments , deliberate changes in their own part of a pattern (a pursuer stops pursuing, a peacemaker stops carrying messages) and to observe what the system does in reply. Some Bowenians use displacement stories , films or stories about other families, so that a family can see its own process with less defensiveness. Above all, clients are coached to go home again: to visit the family of origin, to reopen contact with relatives they have cut off, to build a person-to-person relationship with each parent (talking one to one about each other's lives, rather than about third people), and to detriangle from old family triangles while staying in contact. Bowen warned that a differentiating move provokes a predictable reaction from the family: first "you are wrong", then "change back", and then "if you do not, here are the consequences". The person who expects this reaction, stays calm through it and neither attacks nor gives in usually finds that the family settles at a new level. Return to Arjun, Meera and Kabir. A Bowenian therapist sees the parents, not Kabir. She draws a genogram with them (the next subsection) and finds that Meera's father was also a distant man who worked late, and that Meera, as an eldest daughter, was her own anxious mother's confidante. She asks Meera what she notices about the similarity, and asks Arjun what he does when Meera is anxious. Over some months she coaches Meera to take her worries about the marriage to Arjun rather than to Kabir, and to visit her mother and talk about her own childhood instead of about Arjun's faults. She coaches Arjun to stay in the room when Meera is upset rather than retreating to his laptop. Nobody works directly on Kabir's stomach aches. As his parents become a little less reactive and a little more of a couple, he is released from the triangle, and the aches fade. Bowen's ideas were carried forward by a group of gifted students. Philip Guerin and Thomas Fogarty developed practical methods for working with triangles. Betty Carter and Monica McGoldrick, whom you met in Section 7.1, brought Bowenian thinking to the family life cycle and to the genogram. The rabbi and family therapist Edwin Friedman (1932 to 1996) applied the theory to churches and synagogues in Generation to Generation (1985), and the psychologist Harriet Lerner (born 1944) made it famous with general readers in The Dance of Anger (1985). As for evidence, Bowen theory has inspired a large correlational literature on differentiation but few controlled trials of Bowenian therapy, so its effectiveness rests more on clinical tradition than on outcome research. Critics have also argued that its prizing of reason over emotion and of the autonomous self reflects Western, middle-class and stereotypically masculine values, a criticism that feminist family therapists pressed hard (Section 7.7 takes up gender and culture). Clinical link Process questions are one of the most portable skills in this chapter. When a family meeting in an Indian clinic becomes heated, with a mother and grandmother talking over each other about a teenager, you do not need to win the argument or take a side. Slow things down, ask each person to speak to you, and ask questions about the pattern: "When Rahul refuses to eat, what does his mother do? And then what does his grandmother do? And then?" Thinking about a pattern lowers reactivity, and a calm, non-reactive clinician in the room is itself an intervention. Exam trap The calm, neutral coach who stays out of the family's triangles is Bowen. The active, directive stage director who joins the family and then rearranges it is Minuchin (Section 7.4). The therapist who gives directives and paradoxical tasks is Haley (Section 7.5). The playful, deliberately "crazy" therapist who uses his own spontaneity is Carl Whitaker (Section 7.6). Bowen often saw only the parents or a single family member; that is still family therapy in his sense. The genogram: drawing and reading one Bowen called it the family diagram. His students made it famous as the genogram : a diagram of a family across at least three generations that records who is in the family, the main facts about each person and, in its fullest form, the emotional relationships between them. Section 2.3 introduced the genogram as part of the case history and drew a simple one (Figure 2.2). Here you will meet it as a therapeutic tool, the way Bowenians use it. Its symbols were standardised by Monica McGoldrick and Randy Gerson in Genograms in Family Assessment (1985), and later editions, retitled Genograms: Assessment and Intervention , remain the standard reference. McGoldrick and Gerson describe building a genogram in three layers: mapping the family structure, recording information about each member, and drawing in the relationships. The structural symbols are the ones you met in Section 2.3. A square is a male and a circle a female, with the current age written inside; the index person (the identified patient) has a double outline. A cross inside a symbol marks a death, usually with the year and the age at death. A horizontal line joins a married couple, with the year of marriage written on it; a dashed line marks a couple living together without marriage; one slash across the line means separation and two slashes mean divorce. Children hang from the couple's line in birth order, eldest on the left. A shaded symbol marks a condition such as depression or alcohol misuse, explained in a key, and the members of the current household may be enclosed by a dotted line. The third layer is what makes a genogram Bowenian. Relationship lines between symbols show the quality of each important relationship: two parallel lines for a close relationship, three for a fused one, a dotted line for a distant one, a zigzag for conflict , three lines with a zigzag for a relationship that is fused and conflictual at once, and a line broken by a gap between two short bars for a cutoff . With these lines in place, triangles, cutoffs and repeating patterns literally become visible. How do you draw one with a family? Start with the household and the presenting problem, then move up to each parent's family of origin, and keep going until you have three generations. Ask about the nodal events , the births, deaths, marriages, separations, migrations, illnesses and job losses, and get their dates. Then ask the relationship questions: Who was close to whom? Who does not speak to whom? Who did your mother turn to when she was worried? Many therapists draw the genogram on a whiteboard with the family, over the first two or three sessions, because the drawing is itself a conversation; families often discover links they had never put together. Reading a genogram is a skill. McGoldrick and Gerson suggest looking at the family's structure (who lives in the household, the sibling constellation), at life cycle fit (unusual ages or timing, such as a very late marriage or a child born just after a death), at patterns repeating across generations (in functioning, in relationships and in structure), at the coincidence of life events with symptoms, at relational patterns and triangles, and at balance and imbalance in the family. Apply these to Figure 7.3. Rohan stopped going to school within weeks of the death of his grandfather, Dada, in 2025, a coincidence of dates that invites questions about grief in a household where, it turns out, no one has mentioned Dada since the funeral. Rohan is fused with his mother Lata and distant from his father Suresh, and Suresh was equally distant from his own father: a pattern repeating across generations. Lata is in open conflict with her mother-in-law, who lives with the family, and has cut off her only brother, Vinod, after a quarrel over their father's property, so the person she turns to for closeness is her son. Her own father drank heavily, which may help explain why she learned to watch the men in her life anxiously. The triangle of Lata, Suresh and Rohan, interlocking with the triangle of Lata, Dadi and Suresh, now looks like the obvious place to begin, and Rohan's school refusal looks less like a problem inside one boy and more like a sign of a family under strain at a moment of loss. Exam trap The genogram belongs to Murray Bowen's family systems therapy, with standard symbols from McGoldrick and Gerson (1985) ; it is not a part of dialectical behaviour therapy (Chapter 5) or a projective test. Squares are males, circles are females, a double outline marks the index person, a cross marks a death, and relationship lines show closeness, fusion, distance, conflict and cutoff. Keep it apart from Minuchin's structural map , which shows the family's present organisation (boundaries, coalitions) rather than its history across generations (Section 7.4), and from Virginia Satir's family sculpting , in which members are physically posed to show relationships (Section 7.6). The genogram, the ecomap and the sociogram The genogram has two relatives that are easily confused with it, and both appeared briefly in Section 2.3. The first is the ecomap , developed in 1975 by the social worker Ann Hartman at the University of Michigan to help child welfare workers see families in their surroundings, and published in her 1978 paper "Diagrammatic assessment of family relationships". Where the genogram maps a family across time, the ecomap maps it across space: the household is drawn as a circle in the centre, and around it are circles for every system the family deals with, such as the school, the workplace, the temple, the extended family, the clinic, the tuition centre, the welfare office or the courts. Lines between the household and each circle show the quality of the connection: a heavy line for a strong, supportive link, a dashed line for a weak or tenuous one, and a hatched line for a stressful one, with arrows to show the direction in which energy, money or help flows. At a glance the ecomap shows where a family draws its support, where it is drained and how isolated it is. It is widely used in social work and community mental health for assessment and for planning which outside links to strengthen. The second relative is the sociogram. It comes not from family therapy but from group psychology: the psychiatrist Jacob Levy Moreno, founder of psychodrama and of sociometry (the measurement of attractions and rejections within groups), introduced it in Who Shall Survive? (1934). Members of a group are asked sociometric questions such as "Whom would you choose to sit beside?" or "Whom would you most like to work with?", and their answers are drawn as circles joined by arrows. The diagram reveals who is a star (chosen by many), who is an isolate (chosen by none), which pairs choose each other, and where cliques, chains and rejections lie. Because it shows the actual lines of attraction, communication and avoidance in a group, both those people would admit to and those they would not, the sociogram captures a group's implicit and explicit interaction patterns. The answer is a sociogram (Moreno), because only the sociogram maps the interactions among the members of a group. A genogram maps a family across generations, an ecomap (Hartman) maps a family's links to outside systems, and a cognitive map is Edward Tolman's term for an animal's mental representation of a maze, which has nothing to do with groups or families. The key word that decides the question is "group". 7.4 Minuchin's Structural Family Therapy Medium yield · 5 Qs Bowen asked families to think. Salvador Minuchin asked them to act. Where Bowen sat still and kept the emotional temperature low, Minuchin got up, moved chairs, interrupted, told a mother to stop answering for her son and a father to make his daughter sit down, then praised them both for doing it. Where Bowen looked back across three generations, Minuchin looked at the family in front of him, here and now, and asked one question: how is this family organised, and how does that organisation keep the problem alive? His answer, structural family therapy, became for a time the most widely practised model of family therapy in the world, and its vocabulary of boundaries, enmeshment and disengagement is now part of everyday clinical language. This section explains the ideas and the techniques, and Section 7.1's brief introduction to subsystems and boundaries is where it begins. Salvador Minuchin: from Wiltwyck to Philadelphia Salvador Minuchin (1921 to 2017) was born in San Salvador, a small town in the province of Entre Ríos in Argentina, into a family of Russian-Jewish immigrants. He qualified in medicine in Argentina, served as a doctor in the Israeli army during the war of 1948, and then went to New York, where he trained in child psychiatry under Nathan Ackerman, the "grandfather of family therapy" you met in Section 7.1. He returned to Israel to work with displaced Jewish children, and in 1954 came back to New York to train in psychoanalysis at the William Alanson White Institute, the centre of Harry Stack Sullivan's interpersonal psychoanalysis (Chapter 3). The turning point came at the Wiltwyck School for Boys , a residential school in New York State for boys from the poorest neighbourhoods of New York City, most of them African American or Puerto Rican and most of them in trouble with the law. Working there as a psychiatrist in the late 1950s and early 1960s, Minuchin found that the talking therapies he had been trained in, designed for verbal, reflective, middle-class adults, did not reach these boys or their families. The families were not interested in insight; they were overwhelmed by poverty and by crises, they communicated through action more than words, and they were often organised in ways that the psychoanalytic textbooks did not describe. With colleagues including Braulio Montalvo , Minuchin began seeing whole families, built a one-way mirror so that colleagues could watch and consult, and invented concrete, active techniques: splitting the family into subgroups so that the parents could watch their children from behind the mirror, giving tasks to be done in the session, and changing who talked to whom. The project produced Families of the Slums (1967), written with Montalvo, Bernard Guerney, Bernice Rosman and Florence Schumer, which first described the two styles of family organisation that structural therapy is known for: the enmeshed family and the disengaged family. In 1965 Minuchin became director of the Philadelphia Child Guidance Clinic , then a small clinic in a poor, largely African American neighbourhood. Over the next decade he turned it into one of the most famous family therapy centres in the world. Jay Haley, the strategic therapist you will meet in Section 7.5, joined him there in 1967, and the two learned a great deal from each other. Together they trained members of the local Black community, people with no formal qualifications in psychology, as family therapists, on the belief that they would join poor families better than middle-class professionals could. In Philadelphia Minuchin wrote Families and Family Therapy (1974), the book that set out structural theory and became one of the most widely read books in the field; with Rosman and the paediatrician Lester Baker he wrote Psychosomatic Families: Anorexia Nervosa in Context (1978); and with H. Charles Fishman he wrote Family Therapy Techniques (1981), a detailed manual of the methods. In 1981 he moved to New York and founded Family Studies, Inc., later renamed the Minuchin Center for the Family. In his later years he returned to his first concern, poor families and the social services that deal with them, in books such as Working with Families of the Poor (1998), written with his wife, the developmental psychologist Patricia Minuchin, and Jorge Colapinto. He died in Florida in 2017, aged 96. The central idea of structural family therapy can be put in a sentence. A family's symptoms are maintained by the way the family is currently organised, so if the therapist changes the organisation, the symptom loses its function and fades. The therapist does not need to uncover the origins of the problem or give the family insight into it. He needs to see the structure, join the family, and then act, in the session, to change who relates to whom and how. Family structure, subsystems and hierarchy Minuchin defined family structure as the invisible set of functional demands that organises the ways in which family members interact. You cannot see a family's structure directly, any more than you can see the grammar of a language; you infer it from the patterns that repeat. If, every evening, the mother asks the son to do his homework, the son ignores her, the mother complains to the grandmother, and the grandmother tells the son he may finish it in the morning, then that sequence, repeated a hundred times, tells you who holds authority in the household, who is allied with whom and where the parent is weak. Minuchin said such patterns are maintained by two kinds of constraint. The generic constraints are the universal rules of family organisation, above all that there should be a power hierarchy in which parents and children have different levels of authority. The idiosyncratic constraints are the particular expectations of one family, built up over years of negotiation and accommodation until no one remembers where they came from ("Father is never disturbed after dinner"; "Big sister always takes the little one to school"). The family carries out its work through subsystems (Section 7.1), formed by generation, by sex, by interest or by function. Minuchin gave each of the main subsystems a job. The spouse subsystem exists to meet the couple's needs for each other; it requires complementarity and mutual accommodation, and it needs a boundary that protects it from intrusion by children, in-laws and work, because a couple who never has time or space alone stops being a couple and becomes only a pair of parents. The parental subsystem is the family's executive: it nurtures, guides and controls the children, and it may include a grandparent, an aunt or an older child as well as the parents. The sibling subsystem is a child's first peer group, where children learn to negotiate, cooperate, compete, make friends and handle rivalry. Each person belongs to several subsystems at once and plays a different role in each: the same woman is a wife, a mother, a daughter-in-law and an elder sister, and she must behave differently in each role. For Minuchin, a well-functioning family has a clear hierarchy : the parents are in charge, they exercise their authority together, and older children have more responsibilities and privileges than younger ones. Many problems arise when the hierarchy is confused or inverted: a child who rules the household by tantrums, parents who undercut each other's decisions, a grandmother who overrules the mother in front of the children, or a child who has been elevated into a parent's confidant. Minuchin used the term parental child for a child who has been given parental authority, typically an eldest daughter in a large family or a single-parent household who looks after the younger children. This can work well when the authority is clearly delegated, limited and backed by the parent. It becomes a problem when the child carries responsibilities beyond her age, is given authority the parent does not support, or is cut off from her own childhood and peers. (Ivan Boszormenyi-Nagy's related idea of parentification is explained in Section 7.6.) Minuchin also stressed that a normal family is not a family without stress. Every family meets stress: from one member's contact with the outside world (a father loses his job), from the whole family's contact with it (a move to a new city), from developmental transitions (a child reaches adolescence, a grandparent comes to live with the family) and from particular problems (a child with a disability). A functional family responds by adjusting its structure: rules are renegotiated, boundaries loosen or tighten, roles shift. A dysfunctional family responds by holding the old structure even more rigidly, and the symptom appears at the point where the structure fails to adapt. This is the structural version of Section 7.1's lesson that symptoms cluster at life cycle transitions. Exam trap Structural family therapy is Salvador Minuchin's , and it focuses primarily on subsystems, boundaries (clear, diffuse, rigid) and hierarchy in the family's present organisation. The distractors each belong to another school: "multigenerational transmission of anxiety" is Bowen (Section 7.3), "cognitive distortions in family members" is cognitive therapy (Chapter 5), and "paradoxical injunctions" belong to the strategic and Milan therapists (Section 7.5). In the "who founded which school" questions: structural is Minuchin, multigenerational or intergenerational is Bowen, strategic is Jay Haley (with Cloe Madanes), and experiential is Virginia Satir and Carl Whitaker (Section 7.6). Boundaries: clear, diffuse and rigid Section 7.1 defined a boundary as the invisible rules that define who participates in a subsystem and how. Minuchin made the boundary his central concept. Its function is to protect the differentiation of each subsystem, so that the couple can be a couple, the parents can be parents and the children can be children, while still allowing contact and support to pass between them. Boundaries can be placed on a continuum (Table 7.5). At one end are rigid boundaries , which are overly restrictive and permit little contact between subsystems. At the other end are diffuse boundaries , which are blurred and permeable, so that members intrude freely into each other's business. In the middle lies the normal range of clear boundaries , which are firm enough to protect each subsystem's work and privacy and flexible enough to allow closeness, support and change. A family organised around diffuse boundaries shows enmeshment . Its members are highly involved in each other's lives; they speak for each other, finish each other's sentences, know each other's every mood and treat any disagreement as disloyalty. The gain is a strong sense of belonging and mutual support. The cost is autonomy. Children in enmeshed families are slow to develop independent competence, because parents step in before they can struggle, and stress in one member reverberates instantly through all the others: when the daughter has a bad day at school, the mother cannot sleep and the father is irritable. Consider thirteen-year-old Kavya Iyer of Chennai. Her mother, Shalini, still sleeps in Kavya's room "because she has nightmares", answers every question addressed to Kavya, and checks her school bag, her phone and her diary. When Kavya is upset, Shalini is upset; when Kavya refuses to go to school, Shalini takes leave from work to stay home with her. A family organised around rigid boundaries shows disengagement . Members function independently, go their own ways and rarely ask each other for help. The gain is autonomy; the cost is a lack of warmth, loyalty and support. In a disengaged family only a very high level of stress in one member brings a response from the others, so problems can go unnoticed for a long time: a son's depression comes to the parents' attention only when the school phones to say he has stopped attending. Kavya's father, Prakash, an engineer who leaves home at seven and returns at ten, is disengaged from the household. He knows little about his children's daily lives and is called in only as the "final authority" when Shalini cannot cope, at which point he shouts, and then withdraws again. Notice two things about the Iyer family, because they hold for most families Minuchin described. First, enmeshment and disengagement are styles of transaction , not diagnoses. Most families have both enmeshed and disengaged subsystems, and the common pattern of an enmeshed mother and child with a disengaged, peripheral father is a classic example of both in one household. Second, only the extremes signal trouble. A mother may be closely involved with an infant, appropriately, and a father may be busy at work, appropriately; the question is whether the arrangement still fits the family's stage of life and allows each member to develop. Shalini's closeness would be ordinary with a three-year-old; with a thirteen-year-old who now refuses school, it no longer fits. Table 7.5 Minuchin's continuum of boundaries. Boundary Family style What you see Gain and cost Rigid Disengagement Little contact or interest; members go their own way; help comes only in a crisis Autonomy, at the cost of warmth, loyalty and support Clear Normal range Firm but flexible rules; closeness with privacy; parents in charge together Belonging and autonomy, adjusted to the life stage Diffuse Enmeshment Over-involvement; members speak for each other; distress spreads instantly Belonging and support, at the cost of autonomy and competence Indian context An Indian family in which a grandmother helps raise the children, a mother feeds her ten-year-old by hand, everyone shares a room and decisions are taken together can look "enmeshed" to a therapist trained on Western textbooks. It may be nothing of the kind. Minuchin himself insisted that a family must be judged against the norms of its own culture and its own stage of life. The structural questions that travel across cultures are not "how close are they?" but "is the hierarchy clear, so that the children know who is in charge?", "does the couple have any space of its own?" and "does the arrangement allow each child to grow in competence for his or her age?" In a joint family the most common structural problem is not closeness as such but a confused hierarchy, as when a mother-in-law and a daughter-in-law give the children contradictory instructions and the children learn to play one against the other. As Section 7.1 warned, a therapist who misreads the culture will make wrong assessments and lose the family. Exam trap Enmeshment (Minuchin) means diffuse boundaries with over-involvement, intrusion and loss of individual autonomy. Disengagement means rigid boundaries with little emotional contact. Clear boundaries are the healthy middle, so "healthy reciprocal closeness" describes clear boundaries, not enmeshment. "Pathological scapegoating of a single member" is Vogel and Bell's scapegoat (Section 7.1), and "a complete lack of communication" is not the definition of either style. Do not mix up the authors of similar-sounding ideas: enmeshment is Minuchin's, fusion and the undifferentiated family ego mass are Bowen's (Section 7.3), and pseudomutuality and the rubber fence are Wynne's (Section 7.2). Alignments, coalitions and detouring Boundaries tell you how close or far apart the parts of a family are. To describe who sides with whom, Minuchin used three further terms. An alignment is the joining or opposing of family members in carrying out any activity: the mother and daughter who always agree about what to cook, the father and son who always side together on cricket. Power is each member's relative influence on what happens. A coalition is an alignment of two members against a third. Coalitions between members of the same generation are ordinary (two brothers who gang up on their sister for a week); the dangerous kind is the cross-generational coalition , a stable alliance between a parent and a child, or a grandparent and a grandchild, against the other parent, because it destroys the parental hierarchy. Jay Haley's "perverse triangle" (Section 7.5) describes the same pattern from the strategic side. In Families and Family Therapy Minuchin described three rigid triads in which children are used to manage the conflict between their parents: Triangulation. Each parent demands that the child side with him or her against the other, so that whenever the child sides with one parent he is automatically attacking the other. The child is paralysed, because every move is disloyal to someone. (Notice that this is a narrower meaning than Bowen's triangle, Section 7.3.) Stable coalition. One parent and the child form a fixed alliance against the other parent, who is pushed to the outside. Detouring . The parents submerge their conflict by uniting around the child. In detouring-attacking they define the child as bad and unite to control him ("our son is the problem; if he behaved we would be fine"). In detouring-supportive they define the child as sick or fragile and unite to protect him. Either way the child's problem holds the marriage together, which is why Minuchin expected a marital conflict to surface as soon as the child improved. In the Iyer family, Shalini and Kavya form a stable coalition from which Prakash is excluded, while the paternal grandmother, Kamala, who lives with them, regularly sides with Kavya against her daughter-in-law ("Let the child rest; you push her too hard"). There are two coalitions crossing generations, and a mother who is undermined from both sides. Structural maps To keep track of all this, Minuchin drew a structural map : a quick, simple diagram of the family's organisation as the therapist sees it in the session. A structural map is not a family tree; it shows the present, not the past. Members are placed so that the generations are at different levels, with the parental subsystem above the children, and lines show the boundaries between subsystems and the relationships between members. Minuchin's conventions, set out in Families and Family Therapy , are reproduced in most textbooks: a dashed line for a clear boundary, a dotted line for a diffuse boundary and a solid line for a rigid boundary; a double line for affiliation and a triple line for overinvolvement; a line crossed by two short bars for conflict; a bracket to mark a coalition; and an arrow to show detouring. The map is a working hypothesis, drawn early in therapy, tested in the session and redrawn as the family changes. It also gives the therapist a target: a second map of how the family would be organised if it worked well. The goal map shows the parents leading together, with clear boundaries around the grandmother, the parents and the children. Read the two maps in Figure 7.5 from left to right and you have the whole plan of therapy. The therapist must bring Prakash in from behind his rigid boundary, put him alongside Shalini as a parental team, move Kavya out of the parental level and back among the children with her brother Arun, loosen the fusion between mother and daughter into a clear boundary that leaves Kavya room to grow, and help the grandmother, Kamala, keep an honoured place in the family without overruling the parents. The next two subsections describe how a structural therapist does it. Exam trap Bowen's genogram maps a family's history across three generations; Minuchin's structural map maps its present organisation (subsystems, boundaries, coalitions). In the structural map a dotted line is a diffuse boundary (enmeshment), a solid line is a rigid boundary (disengagement) and a dashed line is a clear boundary; do not carry over the genogram's conventions, in which a dotted line means a distant relationship. Minuchin's triangulation (each parent demands that the child take his or her side) is one of three rigid triads; the other two are the stable coalition and detouring , which can be attacking (the "bad" child) or supportive (the "sick" child). Psychosomatic families and the lunch session Minuchin's most famous research began with a medical puzzle. At the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia there were children with diabetes whose blood sugar went out of control again and again, landing them in hospital with ketoacidosis (a dangerous build-up of acids in the blood), even though they took their insulin and followed their diets. In hospital they stabilised quickly; at home they crashed. Lester Baker, the paediatrician in charge, wondered whether something in the family was involved, and he and Minuchin set out to find out. Key study: the family and the diabetic child (Philadelphia, 1970s) Question. Can family conflict produce measurable physiological changes in a child with "brittle" diabetes? Method. Minuchin, Baker and their colleagues measured free fatty acids (FFA) in the blood, a chemical index of emotional arousal that, in a diabetic child, is one of the steps on the road to ketoacidosis. The parents were interviewed about stressful family issues while the child watched from behind a one-way mirror; then the child was brought into the room and drawn into the discussion. Results. The children's FFA levels rose as they watched their parents in conflict. In the families of the "psychosomatic" diabetic children, when the child entered the room and became involved, the child's FFA kept rising while the parents' FFA fell. The parents' stress had, quite literally, been passed through the child. Conclusion. A child's involvement in parental conflict can have physical consequences, and the child's symptom can relieve the parents. Criticism. The studies were small, and an association in a laboratory session does not show that family conflict causes the illness; the findings fitted the team's model rather than testing it against alternatives. From this work and from families of children with severe asthma and anorexia nervosa, the Philadelphia team proposed a model of the psychosomatic family (Minuchin, Baker, Rosman, Liebman, Milman and Todd, 1975). Three conditions, each necessary but none sufficient alone, were thought to combine to produce and maintain severe psychosomatic symptoms in a child: a physiological vulnerability, the child's involvement in parental conflict, and a family organisation that encourages somatising. That organisation had four characteristics: Enmeshment : diffuse boundaries, so that members are intensely involved in each other's lives and bodies. Overprotectiveness : a high degree of concern for each other's welfare, which retards the child's autonomy and competence. Rigidity : a commitment to keeping things as they are, so that the family cannot adapt at transitions such as adolescence. Lack of conflict resolution : conflict is avoided, denied or detoured, never settled. The sick child's symptom, on this view, protected the family from its unresolved conflicts, typically through detouring. For anorexia nervosa the team devised a dramatic technique, the family lunch session , described by Bernice Rosman, Minuchin and Ronald Liebman in 1975. Early in treatment, often in the first or second session, the therapist has lunch with the whole family, food included, and the parents are asked to get their daughter to eat. In one version each parent tries in turn while the other stays out of the way, and the therapist watches how each one fails and how the other undermines the attempt; then the two are asked to do it together. The lunch is not really about the food. It is an enactment (the next subsection) designed to bring the family's structure into the room, to strengthen the parents as a team that can take charge, to move the conflict out of the daughter's body and into the open between family members, and to redefine the problem from an illness that happens to the girl into a struggle in which she is an active participant. Minuchin and his colleagues often relabelled the anorexic girl as "stubborn" rather than "sick", because a family can do something about stubbornness, whereas sickness belongs to the doctors. In Psychosomatic Families (1978) Minuchin, Rosman and Baker reported a successful outcome at follow-up for about 86 percent of the 53 anorexic patients they had treated, a remarkable figure for a disorder with a reputation for chronicity and death. But the series had no control group, the treatment combined family therapy with a behavioural programme in hospital, and the patients were mostly young adolescents with a short history of illness, the group most likely to do well. Later research did not find a single "psychosomatic" or "anorexic" family type, and the idea that families cause eating disorders is now rejected. What survived was the practice of involving the family and putting the parents in charge of refeeding. In 1987 Gerald Russell, Christopher Dare, Ivan Eisler and colleagues at the Maudsley Hospital in London showed in a controlled trial that family therapy did better than individual therapy for adolescents whose illness had begun early and was of short duration, and the family-based treatment that grew from their work is now the first-line treatment for adolescent anorexia (Section 7.7 returns to the evidence; the disorder itself is in the Psychiatric Disorders book). Exam trap The psychosomatic family (Minuchin, Rosman and Baker) is defined by enmeshment, overprotectiveness, rigidity and lack of conflict resolution , plus the child's involvement in parental conflict. It is not the same as high expressed emotion (critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement), which is a predictor of relapse measured with the Camberwell Family Interview (Section 7.2). The lunch session belongs to structural therapy for anorexia nervosa, not to Bowen, and its real aim is to strengthen the parental subsystem and bring the conflict into the open, not merely to get the patient to eat. Joining and accommodation Minuchin's therapy moves in two broad phases. First the therapist joins the family; then he restructures it. Joining comes first because no family will accept being challenged by a stranger. Joining is the therapist's entry into the family system: making contact with each member, showing that he understands and respects them, and earning the authority to lead. Minuchin called it the glue that holds the therapeutic system together. A structural therapist joins the family as its leader, but a leader who first adapts himself to the family's ways, and the process of adapting is called accommodation . Minuchin described three accommodation techniques. Maintenance : deliberately supporting the family's existing structure at the start, so that the family feels respected rather than threatened. In the Iyer family the therapist might greet the grandmother first, as the eldest, and acknowledge how much Shalini does for Kavya. Tracking : following the content of what the family says, the way a needle follows the groove of a record, with clarifying questions, encouragement and repetition, without challenging; and picking up the family's own words, themes and metaphors to use later. If Shalini says "In our house nobody keeps secrets", the therapist notes the phrase, because it will be useful when he wants to talk about privacy. Mimesis : adopting the family's style, tempo, language and mood: speaking slowly with a slow, careful family, joking with a family that jokes, using the family's own expressions, sharing something of the therapist's own life ("I have a daughter too, and she also hates mornings"). Minuchin and Fishman also described the therapist joining from different distances: a close position , affiliating warmly with family members; a median position , listening neutrally and tracking; and a disengaged position , acting as an expert director who stands back from the family and gives instructions. A skilled therapist moves between them as the session requires. Clinical link Joining is not a preliminary to be hurried through; families drop out of therapy when it fails. In Indian settings joining usually means respecting the family's hierarchy before trying to change it: greeting the elders first, addressing the father as the head of the family if that is how the family sees itself, accepting tea, and using the family's language and idiom. A therapist who challenges a grandmother's authority in the first ten minutes will not see the family again; a therapist who has first earned her trust can later ask her to let the mother decide. Enactment, unbalancing and boundary making: restructuring the family Once joined, the therapist sets out to change the structure, and the techniques that do this are known together as restructuring . They share one principle: change happens in the session, through action, not through talk about events at home. In Family Therapy Techniques (1981) Minuchin and Fishman grouped them under three strategies: challenging the symptom, challenging the family structure and challenging the family's view of reality. Table 7.6 summarises the main techniques. The signature technique is enactment : the therapist asks family members to deal with each other, in the session, about the problem, instead of describing it to the therapist. "Mrs Iyer, you have told me Kavya will not go to bed on time. Talk to her about it now, and see if you can agree on a time." Minuchin and Fishman described an enactment in three movements. The therapist observes the family's spontaneous transactions and decides which area to highlight; he then elicits a transaction, directing members to talk to each other about it; and finally he steps in to suggest or demand a different way of transacting ("Mr Iyer, your wife needs your help; do not let Kavya walk away"). Enactment does two things. It gives the therapist direct evidence of the structure (who interrupts, who rescues, who gives up), so that the structural map can be tested. And it gives the family the experience of doing something differently, which, Minuchin believed, changes people more than any amount of explanation. While the family enacts, the therapist resists being pulled in; if Kavya turns to him for support, he points her back to her parents. Messages must not only be given; they must be heard. Minuchin used the word intensity for the means of making a structural message register with a family whose rules filter out anything new: repeating the same message many times, repeating it across different contents (homework, bedtime, food, phone use all turn out to be the same struggle), prolonging an interaction past the point where the family usually stops, changing the physical distance between members, and refusing to accept the family's pull to return to the old pattern. Boundary making creates, strengthens or loosens boundaries. A structural therapist may rearrange the seating, moving Kavya away from her mother and seating the parents side by side; block interruptions ("Shalini, let Kavya answer for herself"); insist that members speak for themselves; hold part of a session with the parents alone, sending the children out to establish that some business belongs to the couple; or give homework that redraws the lines, such as the parents going out alone once a week while the grandmother looks after the children, Kavya moving back to her own room, or Prakash taking over the bedtime routine. For a disengaged pair the work runs the other way: the therapist increases contact, asking Prakash and Kavya to plan something together. Unbalancing changes the hierarchy within a subsystem by the therapist's own deliberate partiality. Instead of remaining neutral, the therapist temporarily affiliates with one member to give that person more power, ignores another member to reduce his or her influence, or enters a coalition with some members against another. In the Iyer family the therapist backs Prakash every time he tries to set a limit, even when he does it clumsily, and ignores Kavya's attempts to draw him into her alliance with her mother. Unbalancing feels unfair, and it is meant to: it breaks a stalemate that fair treatment would leave in place, and the therapist balances it out over the course of therapy. Reframing (defined formally with the MRI in Section 7.5) challenges the family's view of reality by offering a new, systemic definition of the problem that makes change possible. The family arrives with its own frame ("Kavya is sick"; "Kavya is lazy") and the therapist offers another ("Kavya is fighting a battle that belongs to the grown-ups"; "your daughter is stubborn, and she is winning, because you two keep disagreeing about what to do"). The new frame shifts the problem from inside one person to the relationships around her, and points to what the family can do. Closely related is complementarity : helping members see that their behaviour is part of a larger whole, that the mother's over-involvement and the father's absence fit together like the two halves of one pattern, so that neither is simply the villain or the victim. Structural therapists also point out the family's strengths , because a family is more willing to change when it feels competent. Table 7.6 The main techniques of structural family therapy, illustrated with the Iyer family. Technique What the therapist does Example Joining (maintenance, tracking, mimesis) Enters the system by respecting and adapting to its style Greets the grandmother first; uses the family's phrase "no secrets" Enactment Has members deal with the problem in the session "Talk to Kavya about bedtime now" Intensity Repeats and prolongs messages until they register Keeps the parents negotiating past the usual breaking point Boundary making Creates or redraws boundaries between subsystems Moves Kavya's chair; sees the parents alone Unbalancing Sides temporarily with one member to shift power Backs every limit Prakash sets Reframing and complementarity Offers a systemic definition; shows how behaviours fit together "She is stubborn, not sick"; mother's closeness and father's absence fit together Restructuring The umbrella aim: a new organisation in which the symptom has no function Parents lead together; Kavya returns to school Here, in brief, is how the Iyer family might move through therapy. In the first session the therapist joins each member and tracks the story of Kavya's school refusal. When Kavya interrupts her father for the third time, he asks Prakash and Shalini to decide together, there and then, what time Kavya will leave for school tomorrow (an enactment). Shalini keeps turning to Kavya to ask her opinion; the therapist blocks this, moves Kavya to sit beside her brother, and backs Prakash when he speaks up (boundary making and unbalancing). He reframes the problem: Kavya is not ill but loyal, staying at home to keep her mother company, and only her parents together can release her. Homework puts Prakash in charge of the morning routine for a week and sends the couple out alone on Sunday evening. Over the following sessions the grandmother is thanked for her years of help and invited to support the parents' decisions rather than overrule them. As the parental team grows stronger and the mother-daughter boundary clearer, Kavya goes back to school, and, as Minuchin would have predicted, the strains in the marriage, long hidden behind Kavya, come into view and become the next focus. Exam trap The core sequence of structural therapy is joining, then restructuring . Mimesis (copying the family's style), tracking (following its content and metaphors) and maintenance (supporting its structure) are joining techniques. Enactment (acting out the problem in the session), boundary making , unbalancing (temporarily siding with one member) and reframing are restructuring techniques. Paradoxical directives and prescribing the symptom are strategic (Section 7.5), and circular questioning is Milan (Section 7.5); reframing is shared by structural, strategic and MRI therapists, so a question about reframing alone does not identify Minuchin. Bowen and Minuchin compared Bowen and Minuchin are the two pillars of classical family therapy, and they are easily confused. Both were psychiatrists trained in psychoanalysis who broke away from it, both treated the family as a system, and both cared about boundaries between selves and between generations. But they differed on almost everything else, as Table 7.7 shows. Bowen looked at the past and at three generations; Minuchin at the present and the household. Bowen's therapist was a calm coach who stayed outside the family's emotional field; Minuchin's was an active director who joined the family and then pushed it to change. Bowen worked on the differentiation of individuals, often seeing one person; Minuchin worked on the organisation of the whole family, and wanted everyone in the room. Table 7.7 Bowen's family systems therapy and Minuchin's structural family therapy. Feature Bowen Minuchin Time focus Past and present; three or more generations Present; the current household Key concepts Differentiation, triangles, projection, transmission, cutoff Structure, subsystems, hierarchy, boundaries, enmeshment and disengagement Unhealthy pattern Fusion and chronic anxiety Diffuse or rigid boundaries; confused hierarchy; cross-generational coalitions Therapist's stance Calm, neutral, detriangled coach Active leader who joins, then challenges and directs Who attends Often the parents or one motivated person The whole family, with subsystems seen separately at times Signature tools Genogram, process questions, I-position, coaching visits home Structural map, joining, enactment, unbalancing, boundary making Main goal Higher differentiation of self; lower anxiety A reorganised family in which the symptom has no function Structural therapy has had a long afterlife. Its ideas run through brief strategic family therapy, developed by José Szapocznik in Miami for Hispanic adolescents with drug problems, through multisystemic therapy and functional family therapy (Section 7.7), and through the family-based treatment of adolescent anorexia. It has also drawn sharp criticism. Some critics found the therapist's power and manipulation troubling, and asked whose idea of a "normal" family the goal map expressed. Feminist family therapists pointed out that strengthening the parental hierarchy could mean strengthening a dominant father, and that the enmeshed mother and the peripheral father were too easily read as the mother's fault (Section 7.7 takes up gender and culture). And from the 1980s the postmodern therapists rejected the idea that a family has an objective structure for an expert to diagnose at all. That last point also tells you which kind of theory a statement about reality belongs to. The statement "individuals, families and entire cultures are given a different level of power as creators of their realities" expresses social constructionism, the view that reality is constructed through language and shared stories, and it describes narrative therapy (Section 6.8 and Section 7.7). Structural and transgenerational therapies are the opposite kind of theory: they assume that a family really has a structure (Minuchin) or a multigenerational emotional process (Bowen) that a trained observer can map and change. Strategic therapy (Section 7.5) likewise treats the therapist as the expert who designs the intervention. Exam trap Statements about people as creators of their own realities , about the power of dominant stories, or about re-authoring lives point to narrative therapy (Michael White and David Epston), not to structural therapy (Minuchin's real family structure), transgenerational theory (Bowen's emotional processes across generations) or strategic therapy (Haley's expert directives). Structural therapy is the answer when the stem mentions subsystems, boundaries, hierarchy, enmeshment, disengagement, joining or enactment ; Bowen is the answer when it mentions differentiation, triangles, emotional cutoff, multigenerational transmission or the genogram .
