The therapists in this section have a more modest and, in a way, more radical aim. They want to solve the problem the family came with, as quickly as possible, and they are not much interested in why it began. All of them grew from a single root, the Bateson project in Palo Alto that gave us the double bind (Section 7.2) and the axioms of communication in Pragmatics of Human Communication (Section 7.1). From that root grew three branches: the strategic therapy of Jay Haley and Cloe Madanes, eventually based in Washington; the brief therapy of the Mental Research Institute (MRI) in Palo Alto; and the systemic therapy of a team of four psychiatrists in Milan, Italy. The three branches look different on the surface, but they share five convictions, and if you hold on to these you will rarely mix them up with the other schools. First, the presenting problem is to be taken seriously in its own right; it is not merely the surface sign of a deeper disorder that must be dug out. Second, problems are kept alive by what people are doing now, in the present pattern of interaction, so history and insight are unnecessary for change. Third, the therapist, not the family, is responsible for planning how change will happen. Fourth, change can be fast, often within ten sessions. Fifth, because families often resist direct advice, indirect methods, including the deliberately paradoxical, are sometimes the most effective ones. You have already met the individual version of paradox in Section 4.10 (behaviour therapy's paradoxical intention, tested on insomnia) and in Section 6.5 (Viktor Frankl's logotherapy). This section teaches the systemic version, in which the target is not one person's anxiety but the job a symptom is doing for a family. From Palo Alto to strategic therapy: Haley and Erickson In 1959 the psychiatrist Don Jackson (1920 to 1968), a member of Bateson's team, founded the Mental Research Institute (MRI) in Palo Alto, together with the psychiatrist Jules Riskin and the social worker Virginia Satir, whose own therapy you will meet in Section 7.6. For a few years Bateson's research project and the new institute ran side by side, sharing people and ideas, until the project ended in 1962 and Bateson turned to the communication of dolphins. The MRI went on to become the most influential training and research centre of the early family therapy movement. The most restless mind in the Palo Alto group belonged to Jay Haley (1923 to 2007). Haley had trained not as a clinician but in theatre and communication, and he came to the project as a young man fascinated by the ways people use communication to control one another. Through the project he and John Weakland began, in the 1950s, to make repeated visits to the psychiatrist and hypnotherapist Milton Erickson (1901 to 1980) in Phoenix, Arizona. (Section 3.10 introduced Erickson's indirect, permissive style of hypnosis, and Section 6.8 traced his influence on solution-focused therapy.) What struck Haley was that Erickson cured people in a handful of sessions without ever interpreting anything. He accepted whatever the patient brought, including the resistance, and used it. Haley spent years studying Erickson's cases and in Uncommon Therapy (1973) he extracted the principles behind them, among them encouraging resistance (asking a reluctant patient to hold back even more, so that holding back becomes cooperation), providing a worse alternative (so that the desired change looks like the easier choice), communicating in metaphor, encouraging a relapse (so that a relapse, if it comes, is under the therapist's direction), seeding ideas early that would be used later, amplifying a small deviation once it appeared, and avoiding self-exploration. In the same book Haley gave the new approach its name. Therapy can be called strategic therapy , he wrote, if the clinician initiates what happens during therapy and designs a particular approach for each problem. Notice how much this definition leaves out. It says nothing about a theory of personality, nothing about the past, nothing about insight or growth. What makes a therapy strategic is that the therapist takes charge: she sets a clear goal, plans how to reach it, and accepts responsibility for whether it is reached. Haley's career then took him through two other centres of family therapy. In 1967 he left the MRI to join Salvador Minuchin and Braulio Montalvo at the Philadelphia Child Guidance Clinic, where he absorbed Minuchin's concern with family structure and hierarchy (Section 7.4); his own work became a blend of Erickson's strategy and Minuchin's structure. And in 1976 he and his then wife, the Argentine-born psychologist Cloe Madanes, founded the Family Therapy Institute of Washington, DC, which trained strategic therapists for the next two decades. This is why textbooks sometimes speak of the "Washington school" of strategic therapy, to distinguish Haley and Madanes from the Palo Alto brief therapists described in Section 7.5.5, who used many of the same techniques but did not share Haley's interest in hierarchy. Exam trap Strategic family therapy is Jay Haley and Cloe Madanes ; structural is Salvador Minuchin; multigenerational or Bowen family systems is Murray Bowen; experiential is Virginia Satir and Carl Whitaker (Section 7.6). Haley worked with Minuchin in Philadelphia, but he is never the answer to "structural family therapy". Milton Erickson (1901 to 1980), the hypnotherapist who inspired Haley and the brief therapists, is not Erik Erikson , the psychoanalyst of the eight psychosocial stages. The MRI was founded by Don Jackson in 1959, not by Bateson, though it grew out of Bateson's project. Haley's problem-solving therapy: power, hierarchy and the first interview Haley's starting point was the Palo Alto idea that every message has a content (report) aspect and a relationship (command) aspect (Section 7.1). When a mother says to her son, "Your room is a mess," she is reporting on the room and also telling him to clean it; if he leaves it as it is, the two of them are in a quiet struggle over who defines their relationship. In Strategies of Psychotherapy (1963) Haley argued that much human behaviour, including much psychopathology, is best understood as a struggle of this kind. A symptom, on this view, is a way of controlling a relationship while denying that one is doing so. A wife who has panic attacks whenever her husband plans to go out with his friends gains enormous influence over his evenings, yet she never asks him to stay; the panic does the asking, and she can say, truthfully, that she cannot help it. Symptoms are powerful precisely because they are defined as involuntary. From Minuchin, Haley took the idea of hierarchy : a well-functioning family has an organisation in which the parents are in charge of the children and the generations are clearly marked. Trouble arises when the hierarchy is confused, and Haley singled out one pattern as especially damaging. In a 1967 paper on pathological systems he described the perverse triangle : two people of different generations (a mother and her son, a grandmother and her grandson) form a coalition against a third person of the same generation as one of them (the father, the mother), and the coalition is denied. The boy who shouts at his father and is quietly defended by his mother is caught in such a triangle; so is the young wife whose mother-in-law sides openly with her son against her. Section 7.1 introduced coalitions and triangles in general; Haley's addition was that a cross-generational coalition that cannot be acknowledged is the most common structure behind a child's symptoms. Haley thought in triads rather than individuals or dyads. A child's problem behaviour usually involves at least two adults: one parent who is over-involved with the child and another who is peripheral. Therapy therefore cannot work by persuading the child alone; it must change the sequence of behaviour among all three. Change the sequence, and the symptom loses its job. Haley set out his method most clearly in Problem-Solving Therapy (1976), which opens with the sentence: "If therapy is to end properly, it must begin properly." By "properly" he meant negotiating a solvable problem and discovering the social situation that makes the problem necessary. He divided the first interview into five stages, summarised in Table 7.8. They give a strategic therapist's first session its recognisable shape, and they are worth knowing because examiners occasionally list them. Table 7.8 The five stages of Haley's first interview ( Problem-Solving Therapy , 1976). Stage What the therapist does Why 1 Social stage Greets every member, helps each feel at ease, notices where they sit and who speaks for whom The family's organisation shows before anyone mentions the problem 2 Problem stage Asks each member for his or her view of the problem, often starting with the adult who seems least involved; offers no interpretations Every member's view counts, and no one feels blamed 3 Interaction stage Asks members to talk to one another about the problem, in the room The therapist sees the sequence, the coalitions and the hierarchy in action 4 Goal-setting stage Defines the problem in concrete, solvable terms ("Manav will go to school four days a week") A clear goal makes progress measurable 5 Task-setting stage Ends the session with a directive to be carried out at home Therapy happens between sessions; whether the task is done is itself information Two features of the method distinguish it from almost everything you met in Chapters 3 and 6. The therapist decides on the goal, after hearing the family, and the goal is concrete: not "better communication" but "father and son will spend an hour together each Sunday without the mother present". And the therapist does not offer insight. Haley argued that pointing out to people why they behave as they do usually makes them defensive, and that people change first and understand later, if at all. Exam trap For Haley a symptom is a strategy for controlling a relationship while denying the control ("I cannot help it"), not an unconscious compromise (Freud) or a learned habit (behaviour therapy). The perverse triangle (Haley, 1967) is a denied cross-generational coalition . Haley's interaction stage , in which members talk to each other in the session, looks like Minuchin's enactment (Section 7.4); if the option says "enactment", think Minuchin. Strategic goals are set by the therapist and are concrete ; insight is not a goal. Directives: straightforward, paradoxical and ordeal The core technique of strategic therapy is the directive : an instruction from the therapist about what family members are to do, in the session or at home. Directives are to strategic therapy what interpretations are to psychoanalysis, the main vehicle of change. Haley (1976) gave three reasons for relying on them. First, a task changes the way people behave, and therefore the sequence that maintains the problem. Second, because the therapist designs the task and asks for a report, she becomes an important person in the family's week, and her influence grows. Third, whether or not the task is done, and how, gives the therapist information about the family that no amount of talk would reveal. Directives come in two broad kinds. A straightforward directive is an instruction the therapist expects the family to follow. Sometimes it is plain advice, but advice rarely works on its own, because the family has usually been given it already. More often a straightforward directive is designed to alter a sequence. A peripheral father might be asked to take his daughter on an outing that the over-involved mother has no interest in, so that father and daughter spend time together without the mother stepping in. A couple who meet only to quarrel might be sent back to a place where they were happy when they first met. Haley insisted that directives be precise (who does what, when, for how long), easy enough to complete, suited to the abilities of every member including the children, and preceded by a careful look at what the family has already tried, so that the therapist does not prescribe a failed solution all over again. Some directives are metaphorical : the family is asked to solve a small problem that has the same shape as a larger one they cannot discuss. A mother and her grown daughter who are too entangled to talk about the daughter leaving home might be set the task of separating their bank accounts; settling who pays which bills becomes a rehearsal, in miniature, for the larger separation. A paradoxical directive is an instruction to keep or even increase the very behaviour the family wants to change, given in such a way that the family benefits whether it obeys or rebels. It is reserved for families that have resisted straightforward tasks. The family therapist Peggy Papp of the Ackerman Institute in New York described three steps in a systemic paradox. The therapist first redefines the symptom as serving a positive purpose for the family (anger is described as caring, a child's misbehaviour as a way of keeping the parents united). She then prescribes the symptom: since it does so much good, the family should continue it, often on a schedule. Finally, when the family begins to improve, she restrains change, warning them not to change too fast, because they would lose what the symptom provides. This last move is called restraining , and in its mildest form ("go slowly; your family may not be ready to change yet") it is used by almost every strategic and brief therapist. Push a case through to see how the three steps work. Ten-year-old Kiran, the only son of a busy couple in Bengaluru, has had stomach aches every school night for four months. Doctors find nothing. Each evening at about seven, Kiran doubles over; his mother rushes to him, phones his father, and the father, who otherwise works until ten, comes home early. That evening the parents sit together by Kiran's bed, worried about him and, for once, not quarrelling with each other. After a careful first interview, the therapist sees the sequence: the aches bring father home and give the parents something to share other than their disagreements. She tells the family, with complete seriousness, that Kiran's stomach is doing an important job for them: it brings his father home and keeps his parents close ( redefining ). So, she says, until the family finds another way to do that job, Kiran should have his stomach ache every evening at exactly seven o'clock, and both parents must sit with him and comfort him for fifteen minutes, which means that father must be home by seven ( prescribing ). When, two weeks later, the family reports that the aches are fewer and that Kiran has been "forgetting" his seven o'clock appointment, she frowns and warns them not to improve too quickly: what would happen to the parents' evenings if Kiran's stomach stopped needing them ( restraining )? In the next sessions the parents, now at home in the evenings for their own reasons, work directly on their quarrels with the therapist. Why should such an instruction work? Haley's answer was relational rather than individual. A symptom is powerful because it is involuntary; it controls others while the person disowns responsibility. Once the symptom is performed on the therapist's instructions, it is no longer involuntary, and it no longer controls anyone. If Kiran has his ache on schedule, he is obeying the therapist; if he does not, he has given up the ache; either way the old sequence is broken. Section 4.10 described the two forms this takes, compliance-based paradox (the family obeys and the symptom becomes voluntary) and defiance-based paradox (the family rebels against the therapist by getting better), and the "therapeutic double bind" in which the therapist wins either way; it also reported Shoham-Salomon and Rosenthal's 1987 meta-analysis showing that paradoxical interventions are roughly as effective as other psychological treatments. The important contrast is with Frankl. In logotherapy, paradoxical intention is given openly to one person, to defuse his own anticipatory anxiety (Section 6.5). The strategic prescription is aimed at the function a symptom serves in a family, and it is often given without explaining the reasoning, because a family that understood the reasoning would simply resist it in a new way. The third kind of directive is the most memorable. In Ordeal Therapy (1984), Haley described a technique he had learnt from watching Erickson. Its principle is simple: if you make it more difficult for a person to have a symptom than to give it up, the person will give up the symptom. In ordeal therapy the client agrees, in advance, that every time the symptom occurs he will carry out a task that is harder than the symptom itself. The ordeal has to meet strict conditions. It must cause at least as much discomfort as the symptom; it must be good for the person, or at least harmless (exercise, study, housework, a donation to a cause); it must be something he can actually do and cannot legitimately object to; it must be precisely defined; and it must be performed every time, without exception, until the symptom disappears. Because the ordeal is unpleasant, the therapist first asks for a commitment: the client must want to get over the problem badly enough to promise to do whatever is asked. A typical ordeal for insomnia, of the kind Erickson used, requires the client to get out of bed whenever he is not asleep within a set time and spend the night on some useful but dull chore, such as polishing the floors. A typical Indian version might be given to Tanvi, a seventeen-year-old preparing for her medical entrance examination, who bites her nails until they bleed: every time she bites them, she must get up and solve ten extra physics problems from the chapter she finds most boring. The ordeal is good for her (she needs the practice anyway), it is more tiresome than the habit, and she cannot reasonably refuse it. Clinical link Strategic directives raise real ethical questions, because some are given without telling the family the reasoning. Modern strategic therapists answer them in three ways. They never prescribe a dangerous symptom (self-harm, violence, drinking, driving while panicking; see also the warning in Section 4.10). They frame a paradox in terms that are true and respectful ("the aches are doing an important job") rather than sarcastic. And they treat paradox as a minority tool for stuck families, not as the first move. Haley's own defence was that every therapist influences clients; the honest question is not whether to influence but whether to plan the influence carefully and take responsibility for it. Exam trap " Paradoxical injunctions ", " paradoxical directives ", " strategic paradox " and " prescribing the symptom " in a family therapy question point to the strategic and systemic therapists (Haley, Madanes, the MRI, the Milan team), not to Bowen's differentiation, Minuchin's boundaries or narrative externalisation. " Paradoxical intention " belongs to Frankl (Section 6.5). Papp's three steps are redefine, prescribe, restrain . Ordeal therapy is Haley's (1984, from Erickson): a beneficial task the client performs every time the symptom occurs. It is not aversion therapy (Section 4.4), which pairs the unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus such as a nausea-inducing drug or a shock. Cloe Madanes: protection, pretending and incongruous hierarchies Cloe Madanes (born 1940) studied psychology in her native Buenos Aires, moved to the United States, and from 1976 directed the Washington institute together with Haley. In Strategic Family Therapy (1981) and Behind the One-Way Mirror (1984) she gave strategic therapy a gentler, more playful face. Where Haley emphasised power, Madanes emphasised the love and protectiveness that symptoms often express. Madanes saw a symptom as a metaphor . A child's "My stomach hurts" carries an explicit message (pain in the stomach) and an implicit one (perhaps "I am worried about Mother", or "Something in this house hurts"). Often, she argued, a child's symptom is an attempt to help a parent: a boy who misbehaves gives his depressed mother something to be angry about, and anger pulls her out of her depression for a while; a girl who refuses to go to school stays at home to keep an eye on a mother she fears may harm herself. The child is protecting the parent, without either of them knowing it. This protection creates a peculiar organisation that Madanes called an incongruous hierarchy . Officially the parents are in charge and the child is beneath them. But through the symptom the child controls the parents: they rearrange their days around his aches, his fears, his refusals. The child is at once inferior (as a child) and superior (as the one whose symptom governs the household), and the two hierarchies contradict each other. Strategic therapy aims to restore a congruous hierarchy, with the parents openly in charge and the child free to be a child. Madanes's signature contribution was a technique that uses play instead of defiance. In a 1980 paper, "Protection, paradox and pretending", and in her 1981 book, she described the pretend technique : the therapist asks the child to pretend to have the symptom, and asks the parents to pretend to help him, or asks a parent to pretend to have a problem so that the child can pretend to help. Three things happen at once. A symptom that is pretended cannot also be real, so the real one starts to look silly. The child's wish to help or protect the parent is acted out in play, so the real symptom is no longer needed to do the job. And because the parents direct the game, the hierarchy is quietly put right. Applied to Kiran, the therapist might ask him to put on his best fake stomach ache at the dinner table, while his father plays the doctor and his mother plays the worried nurse, and ask the family to repeat the game every evening for a week. Families usually end up laughing, which is part of the point: it is hard to take an ache seriously after you have staged it twice as comedy. Key study: Madanes's boy who set fires (1981) The problem. A mother of five consulted Madanes because her ten-year-old son was setting fires. The father had just left the family, sent no money and moved to another city; the mother, who had come from Puerto Rico and spoke no English, was overwhelmed and would not leave the boy alone for a minute. The observation. In the first interview the therapist gave the boy matches, asked him to light one and asked the mother to do whatever she did at home when she caught him. The mother took the match and burned him with it. Madanes's hypothesis was that the fire-setting was helping the mother: by giving her someone to blame and punish, the boy made her angry instead of depressed, and anger kept her going. The intervention. The therapist taught the boy to light matches safely and to put them out properly. She then asked the mother to light some paper in an ashtray and pretend to burn herself, while the boy rescued her by putting out the fire with water; the other children could watch but not join in. The mother was to repeat this game with him every evening for a week. The result. The boy stopped setting fires after this session. He was still special in the family, but now as an expert on fires who helped his mother, not as a threat; and when he lit fires under her direction he was once more beneath her in the hierarchy. Criticism. This is a single uncontrolled case, reported by the therapist, and it shows the strengths and limits of the strategic literature: vivid, clever and persuasive case reports, with few controlled trials behind them. In later work, especially Sex, Love and Violence (1990), Madanes applied strategic methods to violence and sexual abuse in families, and sorted family problems according to four underlying intentions: the wish to dominate and control, the wish to be loved, the wish to love and protect others, and the wish to repent and forgive. The therapist's task, she suggested, is to move a family from the first of these towards the others. Exam trap The pretend technique is Cloe Madanes 's (1980, 1981): the child pretends to have the symptom and the parents pretend to help. Do not confuse it with Moreno's role reversal and doubling in psychodrama (Section 7.11), George Kelly's fixed-role therapy (Section 5.5), Adler's " acting as if " (Section 3.8) or the Gestalt empty chair (Section 6.3). Incongruous hierarchy (the child is both beneath and above the parents) is also Madanes's term. Ordeal therapy is Haley's. The MRI brief therapy model: when the solution becomes the problem Haley's departure did not end the MRI's interest in rapid change. In 1965 the psychiatrist Richard Fisch (1926 to 2011) sent Don Jackson a memo proposing a project in short-term therapy, and with Jackson's backing he, John Weakland (1919 to 1995), Paul Watzlawick (Section 7.1) and Arthur Bodin set up the MRI's Brief Therapy Center . Weakland had been the first recruit to Bateson's project; a chemical engineer by training, he had turned to anthropology after meeting Bateson. The centre met one day a week, saw whatever cases came to it, and set itself a strict rule: treatment would last a maximum of ten sessions . The team worked in pairs, one therapist in the room and the others watching through a one-way mirror, and every case was discussed before and after each session. Key study: Brief therapy, focused problem resolution (Weakland, Fisch, Watzlawick and Bodin, 1974) Question. Can a wide range of problems be resolved in no more than ten sessions by focusing only on the presenting complaint and on what keeps it going? Method. Over about six years the Brief Therapy Center, working one day a week, treated 97 cases of every kind that came to it, in which 236 individuals were seen. Treatment was limited to a maximum of ten sessions, and outcome was judged at follow-up by whether the main complaint had been resolved. Result. Treatment was judged a significant success in about three-quarters of the cases: 40 percent were rated successes (the main complaint resolved), another 32 percent were significantly improved, and 28 percent were failures. Conclusion. Many problems are maintained by current interaction and can be resolved quickly when that interaction is changed. Criticism. There was no control group, the cases were not randomly allocated, and the outcome was assessed by the treating team itself, so the study is better seen as an encouraging demonstration than as proof. The theory behind the centre was set out in Change: Principles of Problem Formation and Problem Resolution (1974) by Watzlawick, Weakland and Fisch, and the practice in The Tactics of Change: Doing Therapy Briefly (1982) by Fisch, Weakland and Lynn Segal . Its central idea fits in one sentence: the attempted solution becomes the problem . Life is full of ordinary difficulties (a child's tantrums, a bad night's sleep, a teenager's moodiness, a quarrel between newlyweds). Most of them pass. A difficulty becomes a "problem" in the clinical sense when people respond to it with an attempted solution that makes it worse, and then, because the difficulty is worse, apply more of the same solution, which makes it worse still. The authors called one of their chapters "More of the same, or: when the solution becomes the problem". The therapist's job is to identify the attempted solution and stop it. Figure 7.6 shows the loop. 1 A difficulty Varun feels low 2 Attempted solution parents cheer him up vicious circle more of the same 3 The problem grows he withdraws further 4 MRI intervention Block the attempted solution; prescribe its opposite: "It is natural to feel low after a blow; take your time" Expected result: the circle breaks First-order change: more effort within the same loop. Second-order change: the attempted solution itself is replaced. Figure 7.6 The MRI model of how problems are maintained. An ordinary difficulty is met with an attempted solution that makes it worse, and the worsening is met with more of the same. The brief therapist does not explore causes; she blocks the attempted solution, often by prescribing its opposite. Take the example in the figure. After failing his twelfth-standard board examination, Varun is miserable. His parents, frightened, try to cheer him up: they list his good qualities, tell him that failure means nothing, plan outings, and urge him to look on the bright side. Every cheerful remark tells Varun that his sadness is unacceptable and that no one understands how bad he feels, so he withdraws to his room; his parents, more frightened, cheer harder. The MRI therapist would not explore Varun's childhood or his parents' marriage. She would ask the parents exactly what they have tried, and then ask them to do something that runs against all of it: to tell Varun, in their own words, that anyone would feel low after such a blow, that they do not expect him to feel better soon, and that he should take as long as he needs. Brief therapists call such a reversal a "180-degree turn". Freed from the demand to cheer up, Varun often begins to talk. The book Change also gave family therapy one of its most quoted distinctions. First-order change is change within a system that itself stays the same: the members try harder, or try a variation of the same thing, but the rules of the system are untouched. Second-order change is a change of the system itself, a change in the rules that govern it; the authors called it "change of change". Two of their illustrations are worth remembering. A person having a nightmare can do many things inside the dream: run, hide, scream, fight. All of these are first-order changes, and none of them ends the nightmare. The only way out is to wake up, which is a change of a different order. Similarly, in a car you can press the accelerator harder (first-order change, more of the same), or you can change gear (second-order change, a different way of producing speed). Families stuck in a problem are usually making first-order changes: the parents of a defiant teenager first scold, then scold louder, then scold and punish, and the pattern of escalation stays exactly the same. Second-order change often looks illogical or paradoxical from inside the system, which is why it so often has to come from outside, from the therapist. Watzlawick, Weakland and Fisch described three ways in which an ordinary difficulty gets mishandled until it becomes a problem. Action may be needed but not taken, because the difficulty is denied ("there is nothing wrong with our marriage"); they called this the terrible simplification . Action may be taken when it should not be, in pursuit of an impossible ideal (the couple who must never disagree, the parents who expect a teenager to be always cheerful); they called this the utopia syndrome . And action may be taken at the wrong level, as when a first-order solution is applied to a problem that needs second-order change, or when someone demands a behaviour that can only happen spontaneously: "Be spontaneous!", "I want you to want to help me", "Stop being so self-conscious". These are the paradoxes , and they are the everyday cousins of Bateson's double bind (Section 7.2). In The Tactics of Change Fisch, Weakland and Segal listed five attempted solutions that they met again and again, each with its typical reversal (Table 7.9). Notice how many of them involve trying to force something that cannot be forced. Table 7.9 Five common attempted solutions and the MRI reversal of each (after Fisch, Weakland and Segal, 1982). Attempted solution Example Typical MRI reversal Trying to force something that can only happen spontaneously Straining to fall asleep, to feel sexually aroused, to stop a tremor Stop trying; even try to produce the opposite Trying to master a feared event by postponing it A student avoids the library until she feels "ready"; a man avoids speaking until he is sure he will not stammer Approach the feared event while deliberately performing imperfectly Trying to reach agreement through opposition Parents argue a rebellious son out of his views; spouses lecture each other Take a one-down position: agree, ask for advice, admit helplessness Trying to get compliance through voluntarism "I should not have to ask; you should want to help" Ask directly and plainly, even arbitrarily Confirming the accuser's suspicions by defending oneself A husband protests his fidelity to a jealous wife, which convinces her he is hiding something Stop defending; agree with the accusation or jam the accusation game MRI brief therapy follows a regular sequence. The therapist first defines the problem in concrete behavioural terms: who does what, to whom, when, and why it is a problem now. She then investigates the attempted solutions in great detail, because they are the target. Next she agrees on a minimal, concrete goal ("What would be the first small sign that things were getting better?"); brief therapists believe that a small change in the right place can spread through the system. She then designs an intervention that blocks the attempted solution, usually by prescribing something that runs against it, and phrases it in the client's own language and in a way that fits the client's position , that is, his values and his view of the problem. Throughout, she restrains change ("go slowly"), and she ends treatment as soon as the goal is reached. The MRI team did not insist on seeing the whole family. They worked with whoever was most concerned about the problem and most willing to do something, sometimes a single parent or spouse. In one series of cases, Lynn Segal worked only with the wives of men who had had heart attacks and refused to change their diet or exercise. The wives' attempted solution was to nag and argue; one wife was asked instead to tell her husband to live the rest of his life exactly as he pleased, however short it might be, and to start, in his presence, going over life insurance and plans for the estate. Within weeks the husband began his rehabilitation exercises. The most widely borrowed MRI technique is reframing . To reframe, in the words of Change , is to change the conceptual or emotional setting in which a situation is experienced, placing it in another frame that fits the facts of the situation equally well or even better, and thereby changing its entire meaning. The facts do not change; their meaning does, and with it the behaviour that follows. The authors' favourite illustration came from Mark Twain: Tom Sawyer, ordered to whitewash a fence as a punishment, reframes the chore as a rare privilege, and his friends end up paying him for the chance to do it. In a family, a teenager's "disobedience" might be reframed as "growing independence that frightens everyone", a mother's "nagging" as "worry about how much she cares", a husband's silence as "his way of avoiding a fight he does not want to have with you". A good reframe must fit the facts and the family's own values, or it will be rejected. A simpler cousin, relabelling , changes only the adjective (from "stubborn" to "determined"). Reframing is now used across family therapy, by structural therapists (Section 7.4), by motivational interviewers (Section 6.9) and many others, but it entered the field through the MRI. Exam trap First-order change is change within an unchanged system (more of the same); second-order change is change of the system's rules ("change of change"); both terms come from Change (1974) by Watzlawick, Weakland and Fisch , not from Pragmatics of Human Communication (1967) by Watzlawick, Beavin and Jackson, the source of "one cannot not communicate" (Section 7.1). "Second-order" conditioning is Pavlov's, and has nothing to do with family therapy. MRI brief therapy is problem-focused and limited to ten sessions : it asks which attempted solution keeps the problem going and stops it. Solution-focused brief therapy (de Shazer and Berg, Milwaukee; Section 6.8) asks what is already working and does more of it. Reframing entered family therapy through the MRI and the strategic therapists. The Milan systemic school The third branch grew far from California. Mara Selvini Palazzoli (1916 to 1999) was a Milanese psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who had spent years treating young women with anorexia nervosa in individual psychoanalytic therapy, with results that frustrated her. In 1967 she founded a centre for the study of the family in Milan, at first with a psychoanalytic orientation. In 1971 she and three colleagues, the psychiatrists Luigi Boscolo (1932 to 2015), Gianfranco Cecchin (1932 to 2004) and Giuliana Prata , broke with the psychoanalytic approach, adopted the ideas of Bateson and the MRI, and formed the team that became known as the Milan associates . Their therapy is called Milan systemic therapy . They described their early work with families of patients with anorexia and schizophrenia in Paradox and Counterparadox (published in Italian in 1975 and in English in 1978). The Milan team worked as a team in the most literal sense. A male and female pair of therapists conducted the interview while the other two watched through a one-way mirror, and every session had the same five-part structure, shown in Figure 7.7. The team also made a discovery about timing. At first they saw families weekly, but they found that their interventions needed time to work through the family, so they spaced sessions about a month apart and offered about ten sessions in all. Because the total number of sessions was small but the treatment lasted most of a year, the approach came to be called "long brief therapy". One Milan session (sessions about a month apart) family absent family present family absent family present family absent 1 Pre-session Team meets before the family comes; forms a hypothesis 2 Session Therapist interviews the family; team watches via the mirror 3 Intersession Therapist leaves to confer with the team behind mirror 4 Intervention Therapist returns with a positive connotation or a ritual 5 Post-session Team discusses the family's reaction and plans the next session about one month later: the next session Figure 7.7 The five-part structure of a Milan session. The family is present only for the interview and the intervention; the hypothesis and the intervention are built by the whole team, two of whom watch through the one-way mirror. The line running back from the post-session to the pre-session shows the month-long gap before the next session. What did the team see in these families? The Milan associates described rigid "games" in which every member was caught, and above all a paradox: the family came asking for the identified patient to be changed, while behaving in every way to keep the family exactly as it was. Their answer was a counterparadox : instead of pushing for change, which the family would resist, the team told the family not to change, at least for now. To make this credible, they first had to describe the family's pattern in a way that no one could object to, and for this they invented the technique for which they are best known. Positive connotation is the team's practice of describing the symptom, and the behaviour of every member of the family around it, as positively motivated, usually as serving to preserve the family's cohesion and stability. Two features distinguish it from an ordinary compliment or a reframe. It is applied to the whole system , never to one person: if the symptom is praised but the parents are not, the parents become the villains. And it connotes positively the family's tendency to stay the same , which is exactly what allows the team then to prescribe no change. Consider the Sharma family in Delhi, whose seventeen-year-old daughter Neha has been starving herself. The father is silent and works long hours; the mother watches every mouthful Neha eats; the paternal grandmother, who lives with them, cooks rich food and complains that no one eats it. At the end of the second session the therapist returns from the team with a written message. The team, she says, is impressed by how much each member is sacrificing for the family. Neha, by not eating, keeps her mother busy and close to her at a time when the mother might otherwise feel lonely; the mother, by watching Neha, gives the father the quiet he needs after work; the father, by staying silent, avoids disagreeing with his own mother, whose cooking holds the family's traditions together; and the grandmother, by cooking, reminds everyone that the family is still one family. Because each member is doing so much to keep the family together, the team advises that no one should change anything until the next meeting in a month's time. No one has been blamed; everyone has been put on the same level; and the family has been given the problem of what to do with a symptom that is now described as an act of family loyalty. The Milan team's other main intervention was the family ritual : a prescribed action or series of actions, with exact details of time, place, participants and words, designed to change the family's rules without discussing them. A ritual is not explained; it is performed. The best known is the ritual of odd and even days, published by the team in 1978. On odd days of the week (Monday, Wednesday and Friday) the father alone is in charge of the children, and the mother is to behave as if she were not there; on even days (Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday) the mother alone is in charge; on Sundays everyone behaves spontaneously; and each parent keeps a written record of any breach by the other. Applied to parents who undermine each other, the ritual makes the hidden competition between them visible and unworkable, and it gives the children one clear authority at a time. Exam trap The Milan associates are Mara Selvini Palazzoli, Luigi Boscolo, Gianfranco Cecchin and Giuliana Prata (team formed in 1971); their classic book is Paradox and Counterparadox (1975, English 1978). Positive connotation (Milan) describes the behaviour of every member and the family's wish to stay the same as positively motivated; reframing (MRI, Haley) gives any behaviour a new, more useful meaning; relabelling changes a single label. Do not confuse the Milan team with the MRI (Palo Alto), the Philadelphia Child Guidance Clinic (Minuchin) or the Milwaukee Brief Family Therapy Center (de Shazer and Berg). Hypothesising, circularity and neutrality In 1980 the four associates published a short paper in Family Process that became one of the most cited in the history of family therapy: "Hypothesizing, circularity, neutrality: three guidelines for the conductor of the session". By then they were relying less on dramatic prescriptions and more on the interview itself, and the paper explains how they conducted it. Hypothesising is the formulation, by the team before each session, of a hypothesis about how the family is organised around the problem, based on what the team already knows. A Milan hypothesis has to be systemic : it must include every member of the family and explain what function the symptom serves in the family's relationships. It is neither true nor false, only more or less useful, and it guides the questions the therapist asks; as the answers come in, it is confirmed, revised or abandoned, and a new hypothesis is formed. For the Sharma family a first hypothesis might be: "Since the grandmother moved in, the father has been caught between loyalty to his mother and loyalty to his wife; Neha's not eating gives everyone something to worry about other than that divided loyalty." The therapist will then ask questions designed to test it. Circularity is the therapist's capacity to conduct the interview on the basis of the feedback the family gives in response to the questions she asks about relationships, and therefore about difference and change. Each answer shapes the next question. The interviewing method that puts circularity into practice is circular questioning , developed especially by Boscolo and Cecchin: questions that ask family members about the relationships and differences between other members, rather than about their own feelings or about one person's symptom. Bateson had defined information as "a difference that makes a difference", and the Milan team built their questions to bring differences into view. The most characteristic form is the triadic question, in which one member is asked to comment on the relationship between two others in their presence, a kind of respectful gossip. Its effect is striking. Family members hear, often for the first time, how others see their relationships; the interview itself becomes the intervention; and the family begins to see the problem as a pattern among people rather than a defect in one of them. Table 7.10 gives the main types, applied to the Sharma family. Table 7.10 Types of circular question, with examples from one family. Type What it asks about Example Triadic One member's view of the relationship between two others "Kunal, when Neha refuses dinner, what does your father do? And what does your mother do then?" Difference Differences between people or relationships "Who is closer to Neha, your mother or your grandmother?" Ranking An ordering of members on one dimension "Who is most worried about Neha's eating? Who is next? Who is least?" Before and after Change in relationships over time "Did your parents argue more before your grandmother came to live with you, or after?" Hypothetical or future What would happen if things were different "If Neha went to college in Pune next year, which of your parents would miss her more? What would happen between them?" Neutrality , the third guideline, was defined not as an inner attitude but as an effect. A therapist is neutral if, at the end of the session, no member of the family can say that she has sided with anyone; she may ally with one member and then another, but the net result is that she is allied with no one, and also with no particular outcome, including change itself. Neutrality protects the therapist from being drawn into the family's coalitions and keeps her curious about everyone's part in the pattern. In 1987 Cecchin revisited the idea in a paper subtitled "an invitation to curiosity", arguing that neutrality is best understood as a stance of curiosity about the many possible explanations of a family's behaviour. The Canadian psychiatrist Karl Tomm of Calgary, who did much to spread the Milan approach in North America, later classified a therapist's questions into four kinds according to their purpose: lineal (investigating, "What is the problem?"), circular (exploring patterns, "Who notices when...?"), strategic (leading the family towards a change the therapist has in mind) and reflexive (inviting the family to reflect and generate new options themselves). Exam trap The three Milan guidelines are hypothesising, circularity and neutrality (Selvini Palazzoli, Boscolo, Cecchin and Prata, 1980). Circular questioning (Milan, especially Boscolo and Cecchin) is an interviewing technique; circular causality (Section 7.1) is a systems idea about mutual cause and effect. Milan neutrality means siding with no one in effect; it is not Nagy's multidirected partiality (siding with everyone in turn, out of concern for fairness; Section 7.6) and not Rogers's unconditional positive regard (Section 6.2). A Milan hypothesis is judged by usefulness , not truth. After the split: the invariant prescription and the legacy of Milan Around 1980 the Milan team divided into two pairs. Boscolo and Cecchin turned to training and founded what became the Milan Centre for Family Therapy. Influenced by constructivism and by the idea of second-order cybernetics , which holds that the observer is always part of the system being observed, they gave up most of the dramatic prescriptions and treated the circular interview itself as the main intervention; their approach is set out in Milan Systemic Family Therapy (1987) by Boscolo, Cecchin, Lynn Hoffman and Peggy Penn. Their work fed directly into the postmodern and narrative approaches of the 1980s and 1990s (Sections 6.8 and 7.7), and into the reflecting team developed by the Norwegian psychiatrist Tom Andersen in the mid-1980s (first used in 1985 and published in 1987), in which the team behind the mirror changes places with the family and discusses its impressions openly while the family listens. Selvini Palazzoli and Prata turned to research and went the other way, towards a single standard intervention. From the late 1970s they experimented with giving the same prescription to every family, whatever its problem, and this invariant prescription became the focus of Selvini Palazzoli's later work, reported with new colleagues in Family Games (1989). The parents are seen alone and told to keep everything said in the session secret from the rest of the family. Then, on several occasions before the next session, they are to disappear from home together without warning, leaving only a note ("We shall not be in tonight"), go somewhere they will not be recognised, and, when the children ask where they have been, reply only that it concerns the two of them. Each parent secretly writes down how each child reacts, and the notes are read out at the next session. In one reported case, a couple with three adolescent daughters, one of whom had attempted suicide, carried out the prescription after the fifth session; at the next meeting a month later the identified patient had improved, and after three more sessions with the parents alone relationships across the family were better. The aim is to draw a firm boundary around the parental couple and to break up the hidden cross-generational alliances and "dirty games" in which the children, especially the symptomatic one, have become entangled.
