Feature Strategic (Haley, Madanes) MRI brief therapy Milan systemic Base Washington (earlier Palo Alto, Philadelphia) Palo Alto Milan, Italy Key people Jay Haley, Cloe Madanes Watzlawick, Weakland, Fisch Selvini Palazzoli, Boscolo, Cecchin, Prata Why problems persist Symptoms control relationships; confused or incongruous hierarchy Attempted solutions that become the problem Family games that the symptom preserves Signature methods Directives, paradox, ordeals, pretend techniques Blocking attempted solutions, reframing, "go slow" Positive connotation, rituals, circular questioning, invariant prescription Length Short; as many sessions as needed Ten sessions at most About ten sessions, a month apart Who attends Usually the family Whoever is most concerned The family; later often the parents alone How should these therapies be judged? Their strengths are clear. They are brief, practical and focused on what families come for; they produced some of the most inventive techniques in all of psychotherapy; and they gave the field the team behind the one-way mirror, still standard in family therapy training. Their weaknesses are equally clear. The early literature consists mostly of vivid case reports by the therapists themselves, with few controlled trials. Directives given without explanation, and therapists who conceal their reasoning, sit uneasily with modern standards of informed consent and collaboration. And from the late 1970s feminist family therapists argued that the language of circularity and neutrality can disguise real differences of power: calling a husband's violence and a wife's fear "parts of a circular pattern" risks blaming the victim (Section 7.7 takes up the gender critique). The strategic tradition survives today mainly in evidence-based descendants, such as brief strategic family therapy for adolescent drug use, which Section 7.7 describes, and in the techniques of reframing, restraining and circular questioning, which have been absorbed by almost every school. Indian context Many Indian families arrive at a clinic expecting an expert to tell them what to do, and a therapist who only reflects feelings or asks open questions may seem unhelpful. Concrete directives framed in the family's own values ("for your son's sake, the two of you must decide together") often fit this expectation well, as do positive connotations that honour sacrifice and family loyalty, which are already prized. But the joint family needs care: an invariant prescription that sends the parents out of the house in secret may simply hand the children to a grandmother, and a directive that ignores the elders' place in the hierarchy will not be followed. Exam trap The invariant prescription (the parents' secret disappearances) is Selvini Palazzoli and Prata 's, from the period after the Milan team split; Boscolo and Cecchin took the circular interview and second-order cybernetics in another direction. The reflecting team is Tom Andersen's. In any list asking which school a technique belongs to: directives and ordeals, Haley; pretending, Madanes; attempted solutions and first-order and second-order change, the MRI; positive connotation, rituals, circular questioning and neutrality, Milan. 7.6 Experiential and Contextual Family Therapies Lower yield · not asked yet The strategic and brief therapists of Section 7.5 had little patience with feelings. Haley thought that insight was unnecessary and that talk about emotions was usually a way of avoiding change; the MRI asked only what people were doing to keep a problem alive. At the same time, and sometimes in the same buildings, another group of family therapists took almost the opposite view. For them a symptom was not a move in a power struggle but a sign that growth had been blocked. The therapist's main tool was not a clever directive but her own presence: her warmth, her spontaneity, her willingness to show what she felt. And the aim was not the removal of a symptom but a family in which every member could feel what he felt, say it, and be heard. These experiential family therapies drew on the humanistic and existential therapies of Chapter 6, especially Carl Rogers's emphasis on genuineness and congruence (Section 6.2) and the Gestalt therapists' insistence on immediate experience in the here and now (Section 6.3). Their two great figures were Virginia Satir and Carl Whitaker. The section ends with a third approach that fits neither the strategic nor the experiential mould. Ivan Boszormenyi-Nagy came from psychoanalysis, and his contextual therapy looks across generations, as Bowen's does (Section 7.3). But like Satir and Whitaker he refused to treat a family as a machine to be adjusted, and he asked a question no other school had asked: in this family, what is fair? Virginia Satir: self-worth and the family Virginia Satir (1916 to 1988) grew up on a farm near Neillsville, Wisconsin, trained first as a teacher and then as a social worker, and in 1951, in private practice in Chicago, saw her first family. As she later told the story, she had been treating a young woman diagnosed with schizophrenia, and when the young woman began to improve, her mother reacted with alarm; Satir invited the mother in, then the father, then the brother, and found that she could understand the young woman's difficulties only by watching all of them together. In 1959 she moved to California and joined Don Jackson and Jules Riskin in founding the MRI (Section 7.5), and from 1962 she directed its first formal training programme in family therapy. Her first book, Conjoint Family Therapy (1964), was for many years one of the most widely read introductions to the field; Peoplemaking (1972), written for ordinary families rather than professionals, became a best seller and was revised as The New Peoplemaking (1988). In 1977 she founded the Avanta Network to carry on her training work, and her approach was set out systematically after her death in The Satir Model (1991) by Satir, John Banmen, Jane Gerber and Maria Gomori. Satir began her career at the MRI, and she never lost the Palo Alto interest in communication; some textbooks classify her with the communications therapists for this reason. But her heart was humanistic. The single idea at the centre of her work was self-worth (she also called it self-esteem): the feelings and ideas a person has about himself. In Peoplemaking she called it "the pot", after the big black iron pot that stood on the back porch of her childhood farm and was used at different times for making soap, for cooking stew and for storing manure: what matters about a pot, as about a person, is what it is filled with and how full it is. Families she worked with took up the phrase, saying they felt "high pot" or "low pot", and she argued that the most important thing a family does is to fill, or drain, its members' pots. In Conjoint Family Therapy she traced how low self-worth travels through a family. Two people with low self-worth, each hoping the other will supply what he or she lacks, marry; each is disappointed; and the child is drawn into the gap, expected to make the parents feel worthwhile. The identified patient (Section 7.1), she wrote, is the member most obviously affected by the pain of the parents' relationship, and his symptom is a signal of that pain. In Peoplemaking Satir described four aspects of family life that every therapist should look at: the members' self-worth ; their communication , the ways they work out meaning with one another; the rules they use for how they should feel and act; and their link to society , the way they relate to people and institutions outside the family. In troubled families, she wrote, self-worth is low, communication is indirect, vague and dishonest, the rules are rigid, inhuman and never discussed, and the link to society is fearful, placating or blaming. In nurturing families self-worth is high, communication is direct, clear, specific and honest, the rules are flexible, human and open to change, and the link to society is open and hopeful. The test of a family rule, for Satir, was whether it allowed what she called the "freedom to comment": whether a member could say what he saw and felt, including something about the rules themselves. She summarised what healthy families give their members as five freedoms: the freedom to see and hear what is here, instead of what should be or will be; to say what one feels and thinks, instead of what one should; to feel what one feels, instead of what one ought; to ask for what one wants, instead of always waiting for permission; and to take risks on one's own behalf, instead of always choosing to be secure. Satir's mature model, which she called the human validation process model , rests on these ideas. Every person is born with the potential for growth; the first and most important learning takes place in the primary triad of father, mother and child, where a child learns whether he is worth something, how to communicate and how to survive; and therapy aims to raise self-worth and open the way for growth, not to cure a disease. She contrasted this growth or "seed" model with what she called the threat-and-reward model, a hierarchical way of thinking in which people are judged by whether they obey, someone is always to blame, and change is something done to people by those in charge. Exam trap Virginia Satir is an experiential (sometimes called humanistic or communications) family therapist. She was a co-founder of the MRI (1959) with Don Jackson and Jules Riskin, but she is not the answer to "brief strategic therapy" or "first-order and second-order change". Her central concept is self-worth (self-esteem; "the pot"); her books are Conjoint Family Therapy ( 1964 ) and Peoplemaking ( 1972 ); her model is the human validation process model . "Differentiation of self" is Bowen's (Section 7.3), not Satir's. The five communication stances Satir is examined above all for one idea: the ways people communicate when they are under stress and their self-worth feels threatened. In Peoplemaking she described four incongruent ways of communicating, later called survival stances , and a fifth, healthy way, and she gave each a physical posture so that families could see and feel what they were doing. In her later model each stance is defined by which of three elements a person leaves out of the communication: the self (my own feelings and needs), the other (your feelings and needs) and the context (the situation, the task, the facts). Table 7.12 sets them out. Placating . The placater ignores the self. He agrees, apologises, pleases and takes the blame, whatever he really feels: "Whatever you want is fine with me; it was all my fault." Inside, Satir wrote, the placater feels like nothing, worthless without the other's approval. Blaming . The blamer ignores the other. He finds fault, accuses, bosses and attacks: "You never do anything right; what is wrong with you?" Inside he feels lonely and unsuccessful, and the attack keeps others from seeing it. Super-reasonable , which Satir also called computing . The super-reasonable person ignores both self and other and attends only to the context: he is correct, logical, unemotional and abstract, like a computer or a dictionary ("If one examines the situation objectively, it is clear that adolescents of this age are prone to irregular sleep"). Inside he feels vulnerable, and the calm shields him from feeling anything. Irrelevant , also called distracting . The distracter ignores self, other and context altogether. Whatever he says or does has nothing to do with what anyone else is saying or doing: he changes the subject, makes a joke, fidgets, starts to tidy the room. Inside he feels that nobody cares and that there is no place for him. Congruent communication , also called levelling . The congruent communicator attends to self, other and context together. Words, face, body and voice match one another and match what the person feels: "I am hurt and angry that you shouted at me in front of the children. I want us to talk about it tonight." Satir saw congruence as the goal of therapy and the hallmark of high self-worth. Table 7.12 Satir's five communication stances. Stance Leaves out Typical words Satir's posture Placating Self "Whatever you want; it is all my fault" Kneeling, one hand raised, pleading Blaming Other "You never do anything right" Standing over others, finger pointing Super-reasonable (computing) Self and other "Research shows that at this age..." Rigid, still, expressionless Irrelevant (distracting) Self, other and context Changes the subject, jokes, fidgets Off balance, in constant motion Congruent (levelling) Nothing "I feel hurt when you shout; I want us to talk" Balanced; words, body and tone match Watch the stances at work in one family. The Iyers of Mysuru have come because their nineteen-year-old daughter Lakshmi has stopped eating properly and cries at night. In the first session it emerges that she wants to change her degree course from engineering to psychology. Her father, red in the face, says that she has never finished anything she started and that she is throwing away everything he worked for (blaming). Her mother says quickly that it is all her own fault for not guiding Lakshmi better, that her husband is right, and that Lakshmi will of course do whatever he wants (placating). Lakshmi's elder brother explains, in a level voice, that placement figures for engineering graduates are higher than for psychology graduates and that the family should look at the data (super-reasonable). The twelve-year-old sister asks whether anyone has seen her cricket bat (irrelevant). No one in the room has said what he or she actually feels. A Satir therapist would not argue about degree courses. She would make warm contact with each person, help each to notice the stance he takes under stress, and coach each towards a congruent statement: the father's fear that his daughter's future is not secure, the mother's fear of conflict, the brother's discomfort with emotion, the sister's distress whenever voices are raised, and Lakshmi's own wish to be taken seriously. The stances are Satir's version of an idea that runs through this chapter. When a person's words say one thing while his face, tone or body says another, he is sending what Satir called a double-level message , a message that is incongruent . The mother who says "I'm not upset" through clenched teeth is incongruent; so is Bateson's mother in the hospital, whose words invited an embrace that her body refused (Section 7.2). Satir's congruence is close to Rogers's, but not identical: for Rogers, congruence is a quality of the therapist, a match between inner experience and outward expression that the therapist brings to the relationship (Section 6.2); for Satir it is a way of communicating that the whole family can learn. Exam trap Satir's five stances are placating, blaming, super-reasonable (computing), irrelevant (distracting) and congruent (levelling) . Learn both names for the third and fourth: computing is the super-reasonable stance, distracting is the irrelevant one, and levelling is congruence. The four incongruent stances are survival stances, each leaving out self, other or context. An option that speaks of an " incongruent " family pattern points to Satir; Bateson's mother-and-son story is still the double bind (Section 7.2). Do not confuse the stances with Eric Berne's Parent, Adult and Child ego states (Section 3.9) or with the cognitive distortions of Beck (Chapter 5). Satir's techniques: sculpting, family reconstruction and the life chronology Satir's sessions were warm, active and often physical. She shook every family member's hand, children first as often as adults, got down to the eye level of small children, used touch and humour freely, and modelled congruence in everything she said. She wanted families to experience a different way of being together in the session, not to talk about one. Several of her techniques have become standard equipment for family therapists. The family life chronology is a structured history of the family's development, gathered with the whole family present: how the parents met, what each brought from his or her own family, what they expected of marriage and of parenthood, how each child arrived, and how the children see their parents and the family's life. Satir used it to show the family, early in therapy, that its present difficulties had a history that made sense, and to find the hopes and disappointments beneath the complaints. Family sculpting is a technique in which one member, the sculptor, arranges the others in space, placing their bodies and directing their postures and facial expressions, so that the arrangement shows how he or she experiences the family's relationships. The technique was developed in the late 1960s and early 1970s at the Boston Family Institute by David Kantor and Fred and Bunny Duhl, who described it in 1973, and Peggy Papp used a version she called family choreography; but it was Satir who made it famous, often combining it with her communication stances so that each member took up the posture of his or her own stance. The rules are simple. Closeness and distance stand for emotional closeness and distance; height stands for power (a father standing on a chair, a mother kneeling); the direction people face shows where their attention goes; and hands, arms and glances show alliances. When the sculpture is finished, each member, still in position, says how it feels to stand there; then the sculptor may be asked to make a second sculpture, showing the family as he or she would like it to be, and the family is asked what it would take to move from one to the other. Imagine that the Iyers' twelve-year-old is asked to sculpt her family. She places her father standing on a chair, pointing down at Lakshmi, who is kneeling with her head bowed. She puts her mother beside the father, holding his arm but leaning towards Lakshmi with one hand outstretched. She puts her brother some distance away, facing a wall, and herself at the edge of the room with her hands over her ears. No one has used a word, and yet everything the family has been unable to say is in the room. Sculpting is especially useful with children, with members who are not fluent talkers, and with families in which some members, such as a young daughter-in-law in a joint family, cannot easily criticise others aloud. Family reconstruction , which Satir developed and used mainly in training groups and workshops, takes sculpting further back in time. One person, the star (sometimes called the explorer), works with a guide (Satir herself, or a trained leader) to re-enact the history of his or her family over three generations. Before the event the star prepares a family map of the three generations, a family life chronology and a "wheel of influence" showing the important people in his or her life. Group members are then chosen to play the star's parents, grandparents and other relatives, and key scenes are brought to life: how the parents met, what their own childhoods were like, the star's birth, the crises that shaped the family. The purpose is threefold: to help the star see where his or her ways of feeling and coping were learnt, to see the parents as people with their own histories rather than only as parents, and to free the star to make new choices. Family reconstruction resembles psychodrama, which Section 7.11 describes, and it also draws on the guided fantasy and role-play of the human potential movement. Satir used other structured exercises too. In a parts party , group members play the different inner parts of one person (her generosity, her jealousy, her sense of humour, her anger), the parts are allowed to interact and quarrel at a "party", and the person is helped to accept and integrate them. In a temperature reading , a family or a group regularly shares appreciations, new information, puzzles, complaints with recommendations, and hopes and wishes, a way of keeping communication open. And in her later model she used the image of an iceberg : visible behaviour is only the tip, beneath which lie coping stances, feelings, feelings about feelings, perceptions, expectations, yearnings and, at the base, the self. Clinical link Satir's methods have rarely been tested in controlled trials, but they live on in training and in practice. A short family sculpture is one of the fastest ways to assess a family's alliances without asking anyone to accuse anyone else, and asking each member "What do you feel, standing there?" turns assessment into intervention. Teaching the stances to a couple in conflict ("When you placate, he hears nothing about you; when you blame, she hears nothing about her") gives them a shared, non-blaming language for their quarrels. Emotionally focused couple therapy (Section 7.8) carries the experiential emphasis on primary emotion into work with couples. Exam trap Family sculpting , the family life chronology , family reconstruction , the parts party and the temperature reading are Satir's (sculpting was developed with Kantor and the Duhls, and Papp used it as "choreography"). The genogram is Bowen's three-generation diagram (Section 7.3); the family map of boundaries and subsystems is Minuchin's (Section 7.4); the sociogram is Moreno's map of group relationships (Section 7.11). A Satir-style re-enactment is not a psychodrama, although the two are close relatives. Carl Whitaker's symbolic-experiential therapy If Satir was family therapy's warmest presence, Carl Whitaker (1912 to 1995) was its most irreverent. He qualified in medicine at Syracuse University in 1936 and trained in obstetrics and gynaecology before turning, in 1938, to work in a psychiatric hospital, where he became interested in schizophrenia. During the Second World War he counselled workers at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, the secret site of the atomic bomb project, and it was there that he began working with a second therapist in the room. From 1946 he chaired the department of psychiatry at Emory University in Atlanta, where he and his colleagues treated patients with schizophrenia and, increasingly, their families; he described this early work with Thomas Malone in The Roots of Psychotherapy (1953). From 1965 until he retired in 1982 he was a professor of psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin Medical School in Madison. His best-known book, The Family Crucible (1978), written with his co-therapist Augustus Napier , tells the story of one family's therapy in the form of a novel; Dancing with the Family (1988), with William Bumberry, describes his symbolic-experiential approach in his later years. Whitaker called his approach symbolic-experiential family therapy . "Experiential" meant that families change through emotional experience in the session, not through understanding or instruction. "Symbolic" meant that the therapist works with the family's inner world: the private meanings, impulses, fantasies and unspoken rules that lie beneath its words, which Whitaker believed were more powerful than anything said aloud. He distrusted theory. In a 1976 paper on the hindrance of theory in clinical work he argued that theory lets the therapist hide behind technique instead of meeting the family as a person; his own "method" was to use himself, his free associations, his boredom, his irritation, his playfulness, and to let the family affect him as much as he affected it. He spoke openly of using his countertransference, and he insisted that a good therapy changes the therapist too. The goal was growth: a family whose members had both a stronger sense of belonging and greater freedom to be separate, and in which each member could be more spontaneous, more playful and, in Whitaker's word, more "crazy", by which he meant creative rather than disturbed. Symptoms, he suggested, were often failed efforts to grow. Whitaker almost always worked with a co-therapist, and he made co-therapy , two therapists working together with the same family, a hallmark of experiential work. He gave several reasons. A family is a powerful system that can absorb a lone therapist, drawing him into its coalitions and its way of seeing things; a partner can pull him out. With two therapists, one can move in close, become involved, even act "crazy", while the other stays outside and keeps the session safe. And the two therapists model a relationship in which people can disagree, take turns at leading and following, and stay connected, which is exactly what many families cannot do. Napier and Whitaker described therapy as a contest with two sides. In the battle for structure , which the therapist must win, the family is required to accept the therapist's terms for therapy: who will attend, when and how. Whitaker would not begin until the whole family came, often including grandparents and other important figures, and he would refuse to see a family that insisted on sending only the "sick" child. In the battle for initiative , which the family must win, the family must take responsibility for its own life and for whether and how it changes. The therapist will not push, persuade or rescue, and a family that waits for the therapist to tell it what to do finds itself facing silence. A therapist who loses the first battle cannot help the family; a therapist who wins the second has taken over a responsibility that belongs to the family. Key study: The Family Crucible (Napier and Whitaker, 1978) The Brice family came to Napier and Whitaker because of their sixteen-year-old daughter Claudia, whose angry battles with her mother and late nights out had become unmanageable. The parents, David and Carolyn, expected the therapists to fix Claudia. The therapists insisted that the whole family attend, including the younger children, and won the battle for structure. Over the following months the focus moved, as it so often does in family therapy, from Claudia to the tension in her parents' marriage, which Claudia's fights with her mother had both expressed and concealed. Along the way the therapists kept nudging the parents, David especially, away from a calm, rational and authoritarian stance and towards saying what they actually felt, so that the content of the quarrels gave way to the experience beneath them. The book shows the method at its best (spontaneous, intuitive, deeply involved) and its limits: it is a single family described by its own therapists, and it would be hard to teach anyone to do what Whitaker did. Whitaker and his colleague David Keith (1981) described three phases of therapy. The beginning is the battle for structure and initiative. In the middle phase the therapists work actively and emotionally, bringing in extended family, confronting, exaggerating and playing. In the ending phase the family and the therapists separate, with some sadness and anxiety on both sides, and the family leaves with the initiative fully its own. Among the moves Whitaker and Keith listed were redefining symptoms as efforts for growth, offering fantasy alternatives to real-life stress, augmenting the despair of a family member so that the family has to respond to it, affective confrontation, and insisting that children be treated as children rather than as their parents' peers. Whitaker's most distinctive move was what he called the psychotherapy of the absurd , described in a 1975 paper in Family Process . The therapist takes a family's complaint or rigid belief and, instead of disputing it, pushes it further and further until its absurdity becomes obvious. Suppose a father says, in front of his family, "This boy will be the death of me." A Whitaker-style reply might be: "How long do you think you have? Should we start planning the funeral? Who will look after your wife when you are gone, the boy?" The family laughs, the father finds himself defending his own survival, and the deadly seriousness of the complaint is loosened. Absurdity of this kind is related to the strategic therapists' paradox (Section 7.5), but its purpose is different: it is not a calculated manoeuvre to block a sequence but a spontaneous, playful way of making an experience vivid and widening the family's tolerance for anxiety and for each other. Exam trap Carl Whitaker is symbolic-experiential family therapy: co-therapy , the battle for structure (the therapist must win) and the battle for initiative (the family must win), the psychotherapy of the absurd (1975), anti-theory, the therapist's own spontaneity and countertransference, and The Family Crucible (1978, with Augustus Napier). "Experiential family therapy" in an option list means Satir and Whitaker ; "strategic" means Haley and Madanes; "structural" means Minuchin; "multigenerational" means Bowen. Joining is Minuchin's term (Section 7.4), not Whitaker's. Ivan Boszormenyi-Nagy's contextual therapy Ivan Boszormenyi-Nagy (1920 to 2007) was born in Budapest, trained in psychiatry in Hungary and emigrated to the United States in 1950. He was a psychoanalytically trained psychiatrist who worked with patients with schizophrenia, and from 1957 he worked at the Eastern Pennsylvania Psychiatric Institute in Philadelphia, first leading research on schizophrenia and then directing its department of family psychiatry, one of the early centres of family research. With the psychologist James Framo he edited Intensive Family Therapy (1965), one of the first textbooks of the field. His own approach was set out in Invisible Loyalties: Reciprocity in Intergenerational Family Therapy (1973), written with the social worker Geraldine Spark , and later in Between Give and Take (1986), written with Barbara Krasner , and Foundations of Contextual Therapy (1987). He called it contextual therapy , because a person can be understood only in the context of his relationships, and those relationships stretch across generations and carry obligations. Boszormenyi-Nagy described four dimensions of what he called relational reality, each of which a therapist should keep in view. The first is facts : the given circumstances of a life, such as genetic inheritance, illness, adoption, migration, poverty, a death or a divorce. The second is individual psychology : each person's needs, motives, fantasies and defences, the territory of psychoanalysis. The third is systemic transactions : the patterns of power, alliance, rules and communication that the other schools of family therapy study. The fourth, and for him the most important and most neglected, is relational ethics : the balance of fairness, trust and give-and-take between family members over time. He later added a fifth, ontic dimension, concerned with the way persons come into being through their relationships. Contextual therapy did not reject the other three dimensions; it insisted that no family can be understood, or helped, if the fourth is ignored. To describe relational ethics Boszormenyi-Nagy used the language of accounting. Every family keeps an invisible ledger , a multigenerational account of merits and debts: what each member has given to the others, what each has received, and therefore who owes what to whom. A person earns merit by giving due care and consideration to others; he incurs indebtedness by receiving. Some debts are built into existence. Parents owe their children care simply because they brought them into the world, and children owe their parents a basic loyalty and, later, consideration in return for life and care. When the ledger is roughly balanced over time, relationships are trustworthy. When it is badly out of balance, someone is always owed and someone always owing, and trust breaks down. The merit a person has earned is his entitlement : an ethical credit that gives him freedom and a sense of worth. Entitlement earned by giving fairly is constructive; it is the reason a person who has cared well for an ageing parent can feel at peace. But entitlement can also be earned by being wronged, and this is where the trouble starts. A child who was exploited, neglected or made to carry burdens beyond his age acquires destructive entitlement : he is genuinely owed, but the people who owe him cannot or will not pay, and so he feels justified in taking from others, often from people who never harmed him, such as a spouse or his own children. Boszormenyi-Nagy called the result the revolving slate : the injustice suffered in one generation is passed on to an innocent party in the next, who acquires destructive entitlement in turn, and so on down the generations (Figure 7.8). The revolving slate across three generations Generation 1 Sunita's parents Sunita, the eldest, raised her siblings; her giving was never seen or repaid debt passed on Generation 2 Sunita (mother) She feels owed (destructive entitlement) and collects care and loyalty from Nandini debt passed on Generation 3 Nandini (daughter) Nandini is parentified and caught in split loyalty between her mother and her husband Therapy: credit Sunita's unrepaid giving (multidirected partiality) and help her exonerate her own parents, so that the slate stops with her generation. Figure 7.8 Boszormenyi-Nagy's revolving slate. Giving that is never acknowledged or repaid in one generation becomes destructive entitlement in the next, which is collected from someone who did no harm. The contextual therapist stops the slate by crediting the unrepaid giving rather than by blaming anyone. The concept that gave Boszormenyi-Nagy's book its title is loyalty . In his sense, loyalty is not a feeling but a structure: a preferential commitment to one's family of origin, rooted in the ledger, that binds members to each other across generations. Much of it is hidden. An invisible loyalty is an unacknowledged obligation to the family of origin that shapes a person's behaviour without his knowing it, often at the cost of his present relationships. A young woman repeatedly sabotages her own promotions, out of loyalty to a mother who was never allowed to succeed; a son cannot commit himself to his wife, because to put her first would feel like abandoning a lonely father; a couple quarrel endlessly about money, each loyal to the rules of a different family. What looks like a symptom, or like plain bad behaviour, may be an act of loyalty, and it cannot be given up until the loyalty is recognised. Two more of Boszormenyi-Nagy's concepts appear often in examinations. Split loyalty describes the position of a child whose parents have made loyalty to one of them a betrayal of the other, as commonly happens in bitter marriages and divorces: whatever the child does for one parent is an injury to the other, and the child is forced into an impossible choice that Boszormenyi-Nagy regarded as one of the most damaging situations a child can face. Parentification , a term he and Spark made widely known, is the process by which a child is placed in the role of parent to his own parent or siblings, giving care, comfort or management far beyond his years. Some parentification is ordinary, and even a source of constructive entitlement; but when the child's giving is unacknowledged and unrepaid, it becomes the raw material of destructive entitlement and the revolving slate. Every person also inherits a legacy : the expectations that arise simply from being born into a particular family, such as caring for one's parents, continuing a family's work or making good its losses. What does the contextual therapist do? Her central method is multidirected partiality : she sides with each member of the family in turn, crediting each person's contributions and acknowledging each person's injuries, including those of members who are absent, dead or not yet born. This is quite different from Milan neutrality (Section 7.5). The Milan therapist ensures that she is allied with no one; the contextual therapist is allied, actively and openly, with everyone, and she also holds each member accountable for the consequences of his actions for the others. Her aims are to rebalance the ledger, to restore trustworthiness, and to help members re-engage with one another in fairer ways, a process Boszormenyi-Nagy called rejunction. One of the most powerful steps on the way is exoneration : lifting the burden of blame from a parent by coming to understand the parent's own history of unfair treatment and the constraints under which he or she acted. Exoneration is not the same as forgiveness, which implies that a wrong has been excused; it is a recognition that the parent, too, was owed and unpaid, and it frees the adult child from the need to keep collecting. Push a case through. Sunita, aged 48, comes to a clinic in Pune with depression. She is the eldest of five children; when her mother fell ill, Sunita, then twelve, left school to raise her siblings and run the house, and no one ever thanked her. Now she demands constant attention from her married daughter Nandini, who telephones three times a day, visits every evening and is quarrelling with her husband because of it. A strategic therapist might look for the sequence that keeps the quarrels going; a contextual therapist looks at the ledger. She credits Sunita's childhood giving, explicitly and repeatedly, in Nandini's presence: "You gave your whole childhood to your family, and no one has ever said so." She credits Nandini's loyalty to her mother, and acknowledges the cost to Nandini's marriage and to the husband, who is also entitled to consideration. She helps Sunita see her own parents' situation (a sick mother, a poor and overwhelmed father) so that she can begin to exonerate them, and she helps Nandini find ways of giving to her mother that are fair to her husband too. The goal is not to cut Nandini off from her mother but to stop the slate from revolving onto a third generation. Contextual therapy has a close relative in the family-of-origin therapy of James Framo, who worked with Boszormenyi-Nagy in Philadelphia. Framo held that adults' marital difficulties are often attempts to repair, through the spouse, relationships left unfinished with their own parents, and he invited adult clients to bring their parents and siblings to one or two long sessions to address those relationships directly. Bowen's coaching of clients to return to their families of origin (Section 7.3) is a third member of the same transgenerational family. Indian context Indian clients often already speak the language of the ledger. Classical Hindu thought holds that every person is born owing debts ( rina ), among them a debt to one's ancestors ( pitri rina ), and many families talk openly about what parents have given, what children owe and what a son, a daughter or a daughter-in-law has or has not "done for" the family. Contextual therapy gives this vocabulary a therapeutic use: crediting giving that has gone unacknowledged (very often a woman's caregiving), and helping an adult son or daughter meet real obligations to ageing parents without passing the cost on to a spouse or to the next generation. It also guards against a risk in the opposite direction, that a Western-trained therapist dismisses filial obligation as "enmeshment" when, by the family's own ethics, it is simply fairness. Exam trap Contextual therapy is Ivan Boszormenyi-Nagy 's; Invisible Loyalties ( 1973 ) was written with Geraldine Spark . Its vocabulary is ethical and intergenerational: relational ethics , the ledger of merit and indebtedness, entitlement (constructive and destructive), the revolving slate , invisible loyalties , split loyalty , parentification , legacy , exoneration and the therapist's multidirected partiality . It is a transgenerational (intergenerational) therapy, like Bowen's and Framo's. "Emotional cutoff" and "multigenerational transmission" are Bowen's terms (Section 7.3), not Nagy's; and multidirected partiality (siding with everyone) is not Milan neutrality (siding with no one). The schools of family therapy side by side You have now met most of the schools of family therapy, and examiners love to test them as matching questions: a name, a technique or a key word, and four schools to choose from. Table 7.13 gathers them in one place, with pointers to the sections where each is taught. In practice the boundaries have blurred. Most family therapists today are integrative, borrowing the genogram from Bowen, joining and enactment from Minuchin, reframing from the MRI, circular questions from Milan, sculpting from Satir and multidirected partiality from Boszormenyi-Nagy, and choosing among evidence-based programmes for particular problems (Section 7.7). Bowen, Minuchin, Haley, the Milan team and Satir rarely tested their methods in controlled trials, and each was confident that a skilled therapist could see the family's pattern more clearly than the family could. From the 1970s that confidence came under attack from two opposite directions. Behaviour therapists asked for data: define the problem behaviour, count it, change its consequences and show that it changed. Postmodern therapists asked a more unsettling question: what gives the therapist the right to decide what the family's "real" pattern is? Out of both challenges, and out of a new demand from courts and health services for proof that treatment works, came the family programmes that are funded today. This section follows those three developments and then turns to the questions about gender, power and culture that every family therapist now has to answer. Behavioural family therapy: the family as an exchange of reinforcers Behavioural family therapy applies the principles of learning (operant conditioning, social learning and, later, cognitive change) to the interactions between family members. It has two roots. The first is Oregon, where Gerald R. Patterson (1926 to 2016) and his colleagues sent observers into the homes of aggressive boys and described the coercive cycle, in which a child's escalation and a parent's giving in negatively reinforce each other; Patterson's parent management training taught parents to break the cycle. Chapter 4 (Section 4.10) tells that story in full, together with the skills of parent training, so here you need only its lesson for family therapy: a child's problem behaviour is kept going by what the other members of the family do, and the people best placed to change it are those same family members. The second root is the work of Richard B. Stuart , who in 1969 published "Operant-interpersonal treatment for marital discord". Stuart's starting point was that partners in a distressed marriage each want something from the other and each withholds it until the other gives first. His treatment made the exchange explicit: each partner's most wanted change was tied to the other's, and both were rewarded for delivering. He soon took the same logic to the families of delinquent adolescents, where parents and teenagers negotiated written contracts that traded privileges for responsibilities (Section 4.5 defines the contingency contract; couples work is taken up in Section 7.8). In 1970 the psychiatrist Robert Paul Liberman published "Behavioral approaches to family and couple therapy", arguing that many symptoms are maintained by the attention that relatives give them, and that the family therapist's job is to help relatives move their attention from maladaptive to adaptive behaviour. Behind these methods lies a view of family life borrowed from social psychology. In social exchange theory , set out for small groups by John Thibaut and Harold Kelley in The Social Psychology of Groups (1959), people stay in a relationship to the extent that its rewards outweigh its costs, compared with the alternatives open to them. Family members are constantly exchanging rewards (praise, help, affection, company) and costs (criticism, nagging, sulking, refusals). The exchanges tend toward reciprocity : people return the kind of behaviour they receive, kindness for kindness and insult for insult. Observational studies found that distressed families exchange fewer pleasant behaviours and more aversive ones than contented families, and that in distressed families an aversive act is more likely to be answered at once with another. To a behavioural family therapist, then, a troubled family is one whose members have drifted into a low rate of mutual reward and a high rate of mutual punishment. Treatment therefore begins with a functional analysis of family interaction : a precise description of the target behaviours of each member, what comes before them, what follows them, and who reinforces whom. It is the ABC analysis of Chapter 4 stretched across several people, so that the consequence of one person's act is the antecedent of the next person's. Consider the family of Aditya, a fifteen-year-old in Bengaluru whose parents say he is "addicted to his phone" and "disrespectful". A week of recording shows that the trouble comes almost every evening at the same point (Figure 7.9). His mother tells him to put the phone away and start his homework; Aditya argues and shouts; his father, tired after work and wanting peace, says "Leave him, he is tired"; Aditya keeps the phone and the shouting stops; his mother goes quiet, angry with her husband. Every step is being reinforced. Aditya's arguing pays, because the demand disappears. His father's rescue pays, because the noise stops at once. And his mother's requests are punished, because she is overruled in front of her son. The consequence of each person's behaviour is the antecedent for the next person's, so three people are reinforcing one another's part in the problem. Changing Aditya alone would not work while his father's rescue still pays. Notice what this analysis reveals and what an individual analysis of Aditya would miss. Early behaviour therapists were criticised by systems therapists for thinking in straight lines (the parent's behaviour shapes the child's) and for working with one dyad at a time, usually mother and child. A parent-training plan given to Aditya's mother alone would fail, because his father's rescue would keep reinforcing the arguing. Behavioural family therapists absorbed the criticism. The plan for Aditya's family starts with the parents: they meet without him, agree on a rule about the phone and homework, and agree that neither will overrule the other in front of him, which is a structural therapist's goal (Section 7.4) reached by behavioural means. Only then is the rule put to Aditya, with a contract that makes the evening phone time something he earns. Remember The parenting that behavioural programmes try to build is what the developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind called authoritative : high warmth and responsiveness combined with firm, consistent and reasoned control that supports the child's growing autonomy. Her authoritarian style is high in demands and low in warmth (obedience without explanation), and her permissive style is warm with few demands; Eleanor Maccoby and John Martin (1983) added a fourth, uninvolved or neglectful parenting, low on both. The styles themselves belong to the Developmental book. Exam trap Behavioural family therapy grew from Gerald Patterson (Oregon, the coercive cycle, parent management training), Richard Stuart (contingency contracting with couples from 1969 and with delinquents' families) and Robert Liberman (1970). Its theory of relationships is social exchange theory (Thibaut and Kelley, 1959): rewards against costs, with reciprocity of positive and negative behaviour. The coercive cycle runs on negative reinforcement for both child and parent (Section 4.10). Do not confuse a behavioural functional analysis (antecedents and consequences of behaviour) with functional family therapy , a separate programme met later in this section. Contracts, communication training and problem solving Three tools do most of the work in behavioural family therapy, and they are summarised in Table 7.14. The first is the contract. Family therapists distinguish two kinds. In a quid pro quo contract one person's change is made conditional on another's: "If Aditya is off the phone by eight on school nights, he may take the scooter on Saturday afternoon"; "If his father stops overruling his mother, she will stop complaining to her own sister about him." (The Latin phrase, "something for something", had entered family therapy earlier, through Don Jackson's 1965 paper "Family rules: marital quid pro quo", which used it to describe the unspoken bargain at the heart of every marriage; the behaviourists made the bargain explicit and wrote it down.) Quid pro quo contracts have a weakness: each person can wait for the other to go first, and when one fails, the other's obligation collapses too. In a good faith contract (also called a parallel contract) each person agrees to change independently and earns his or her own reward, so one person's lapse does not cancel the other's commitment. Aditya earns his data top-up by finishing homework; his father earns an evening out of his choice by not intervening for a week. The second tool is communication training . You met its content in Section 7.2: Ian Falloon's behavioural family management taught families of people with schizophrenia to express positive feelings, make positive requests, express negative feelings constructively and listen actively. What makes it behavioural is the method of teaching. The therapist explains the skill, models it, asks family members to rehearse it on a real issue in the session, gives immediate and specific feedback, and sets homework. A mother who says "You never listen, you are just like your father" is helped to say "I feel worried when you are on the phone at midnight; I would like you to hand it to me at eleven." The second statement names a feeling, a behaviour and a request, and it leaves out the blame and the comparison that would start the next round of shouting. The third tool is problem-solving training . Falloon's families learned a six-step method that is still the standard: (1) pinpoint the problem or goal as precisely as possible; (2) list every possible solution without judging any of them; (3) go through the likely advantages and disadvantages of each; (4) agree on the best solution or combination; (5) plan exactly how to carry it out, who does what and when; and (6) review the result at the next meeting and praise every effort. Families are encouraged to hold a short weekly family meeting for the purpose, with one member chairing and another writing down what was agreed. Working with parents and teenagers, Arthur Robin and Sharon Foster combined problem solving and communication training with the cognitive restructuring of extreme beliefs in Negotiating Parent-Adolescent Conflict (1989). A father who believes "if I let her go to the college festival she will ruin her life" (ruination), or a daughter who believes "I should be allowed to decide everything myself" (autonomy), will not solve problems well until those beliefs are softened. The addition of thoughts to behaviour produced cognitive-behavioural family therapy , developed by Norman Epstein, Frank Dattilio and others, which works with the shared assumptions, or family schemas, through which members interpret one another's actions. Its weakness, in its critics' eyes, was that it treated a family as a set of individual learners rather than a system with loyalties and alliances; a contract will not hold while a grandmother quietly sides with the child against his mother. The programmes that later proved most effective joined behavioural methods to a systemic understanding of why families resist change. Exam trap In a quid pro quo contract each change depends on the other's ("you do this, I do that"); in a good faith or parallel contract each person changes independently for his own reward. The six problem-solving steps (pinpoint, brainstorm, evaluate, choose, plan, review) and the four communication skills belong to Ian Falloon's behavioural family management (Section 7.2). Problem-solving communication training for parent and adolescent conflict is Robin and Foster's (1989). Behavioural family therapy teaches skills by instruction, modelling, rehearsal, feedback and homework; it does not use paradoxical directives, which belong to the strategic school (Section 7.5). The postmodern turn: from expert to collaborator At the same time as behaviourists were demanding more precision, a different group of family therapists began to doubt that precision about families was possible at all. Their doubts came from philosophy, and you met the core of them in Section 6.8. The first generation of family therapists were, in the language of philosophers, modernists: they believed that a family has a real structure or pattern that an expert observer can discover and then correct. The structural therapist maps the family's real boundaries; the strategic therapist designs a directive that the family need not understand; the Milan team forms hypotheses behind a one-way mirror and delivers its verdict. In each case the therapist knows something about the family that the family does not. The first crack came from within cybernetics itself. The Austrian-born physicist Heinz von Foerster (1911 to 2002) called for a "cybernetics of cybernetics", now usually called second-order cybernetics : the study of systems that includes the observer as part of what is observed. A therapist cannot stand outside a family and describe it neutrally, like an engineer inspecting a thermostat; the moment she walks in she becomes part of a new system, and her description of the family says as much about her own theories as about the family. The Chilean biologist Humberto Maturana (1928 to 2021) added that a living system can be disturbed from outside but never instructed to change in a particular way, and the family therapist Lynn Hoffman , in a 1985 essay titled "Beyond power and control: toward a 'second order' family systems therapy", urged colleagues to stop trying to control families and to work with them instead. The second influence was social constructionism , the view that what people take to be reality, including their problems and identities, is built in language and in relationships within a culture (Section 6.8 contrasts it with George Kelly's constructivism, which stresses the individual mind). The American social psychologist Kenneth Gergen did much to bring it into psychology with his 1985 article "The social constructionist movement in modern psychology". For family therapists the consequences were radical. A diagnosis such as "enmeshed family" or "schizophrenogenic mother" stops being a discovery and becomes one more story, often a harmful one, told by an expert. The therapist's task changes from finding the truth about a family to helping its members create new and more useful meanings together. Table 7.15 sets the two generations side by side. Social constructionism (Gergen: meanings are built socially, in language and culture) is not the same as constructivism (George Kelly, Humberto Maturana, Ernst von Glasersfeld: each mind or organism builds its own reality). Postmodern family therapy grew out of both. Conversations and reflections: Anderson, Goolishian and Andersen The clearest statement of the postmodern position in family therapy came from Galveston, Texas. Harold Goolishian (1924 to 1991), known to everyone as Harry, had worked since the 1950s at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston, and with Harlene Anderson and others he founded the Galveston Family Institute (later the Houston Galveston Institute). Working with families that had defeated every other treatment, they grew suspicious of the field's confident theories, and in 1988 they set out an alternative in a Family Process paper titled "Human systems as linguistic systems". Its central claim reversed one of the oldest ideas in family therapy. The system that matters in therapy, they argued, is not the family defined by its roles and structure; it is the group of people who are "in language" about a problem: the family, but also the teacher who sent the complaint, the probation officer, the psychiatrist, the worried uncle, and the therapist. The family does not create the problem; the problem creates this system. They called it a problem-organising, problem-dis-solving system, and the idea is usually referred to as the problem-determined system . Problems, on this view, are not solved so much as dissolved, when the people talking about them come to new understandings in which the problem no longer exists in the same form. From this followed the therapist's stance. In their 1992 chapter "The client is the expert" Anderson and Goolishian described the not-knowing stance : the therapist approaches every family with genuine curiosity, assumes that she does not already know what their words mean or what their situation is like, and lets her questions arise from what has just been said rather than from a theory. The therapist is an expert in creating a space for dialogue, not an expert on the content of the family's life. The result is the collaborative language systems approach , which Anderson later called simply collaborative therapy. A session looks like an unusually respectful conversation: there are no directives, no hidden hypotheses and no interpretations delivered from above, and the therapist is as willing to be changed by the conversation as the family is. A second innovation came from the far north of Norway. Tom Andersen (1936 to 2007) was a psychiatrist who became professor of social psychiatry at the University of Tromsø. In 1985 he and his colleagues were working in the Milan style, with a team behind a one-way mirror that conferred in private and then sent the family its conclusions. Andersen grew uncomfortable with the arrangement, which made the team's thinking invisible and its conclusions sound like verdicts. One day the team simply asked the family whether they would like to listen to the team's discussion. The result, which Andersen described in a 1987 Family Process paper and in his book The Reflecting Team (1991), is now used all over the world. In the reflecting team the roles of watcher and watched are reversed (Figure 7.10). First the interviewer talks with the family while the team watches from behind the mirror. Then, with the family's permission, the lights and sound are switched, and the family and interviewer watch and listen while the team members talk among themselves about what they heard. Finally the family and interviewer talk about what struck them in the team's conversation. The cycle may be repeated once or several times in a session. The reflections follow strict rules. Team members speak tentatively ("I wondered whether...", "Perhaps..."), talk to one another rather than lecturing the family, comment only on what was actually said in the room, offer several possibilities rather than one verdict, and avoid criticism. Andersen held that new ideas help a stuck system only when they are "appropriately unusual": too familiar and they make no difference, too strange and the family closes up. 1 Interview 2 Reflection 3 Response Family and interviewer talk Family and interviewer listen Family responds to the reflections one-way mirror one-way mirror one-way mirror Team listens Team talks together Team listens Team watches through the mirror in silence Lights and sound switched: tentative, many-sided ideas Family says what struck them; they have the last word Arrows show which way the talk flows. Unlike a Milan team, which confers privately and sends a message, the reflecting team thinks aloud in front of the family, and the family has the last word on which ideas are useful. Andersen's ideas travelled furthest in Finland, where from the 1980s Jaakko Seikkula and his colleagues in Western Lapland developed open dialogue : in a psychiatric crisis, especially a first episode of psychosis, a team meets the person together with his family and social network within a day, usually at home, and every discussion and treatment decision takes place in that network meeting. Its reported outcomes are striking but come mainly from naturalistic follow-up studies rather than randomised trials. Exam trap Two similar names, two different contributions. Harlene Anderson (with Harry Goolishian, Galveston) gave us the collaborative language systems approach , the problem-determined system and the not-knowing stance . Tom Andersen (Tromsø, Norway) gave us the reflecting team . Not-knowing (genuine curiosity, the client as expert) is not the Milan team's neutrality (not siding with any member or any one view, Section 7.5), and a reflecting team, which talks openly in front of the family, is not the Milan team, which confers in private and delivers a message or prescription. Narrative and solution-focused work with whole families Narrative therapy and solution-focused brief therapy were both born in family therapy, although Chapter 6 (Section 6.8) taught them as approaches to individual clients. That section explained the techniques: externalising the problem, relative influence questions, unique outcomes, re-authoring and outsider witnesses in narrative therapy; the miracle, exception, scaling and coping questions, compliments and the formula first session task in solution-focused therapy. Here the question is what changes when these methods are used with a whole family in the room. Narrative family therapy , developed by Michael White (1948 to 2008) in Adelaide and David Epston in Auckland, treats a family as a group of people who live by stories: stories about who each of them is, what the family is like and what has gone wrong. Those stories are not invented privately. They are shaped by the dominant stories of the surrounding culture (about what a good son, a good mother or a successful family should be), and following the philosopher Michel Foucault, White argued that these cultural stories carry power: they decide whose account of a family counts and which members are judged as failures. Narrative therapy therefore gives individuals, families and whole cultures an active part as the creators of their realities, with different degrees of power to author or impose a story, and it invites families to examine where their problem-saturated stories came from. This is the point of contrast with the earlier schools. A Bowenian, structural or strategic therapist looks for something wrong in the family's emotional process, structure or hierarchy; a narrative therapist rejects the idea that the symptom serves a function for the family, and sees the family as a group that the problem has recruited and divided. The family version of externalising makes this concrete. Imagine a joint family in Mysuru: nine-year-old Ishaan, his parents and his paternal grandmother, who come because Ishaan has violent tantrums and everyone blames someone. The father blames the grandmother for spoiling him, the grandmother blames the mother for working, and the mother blames herself. The therapist invites the family to name the problem, and Ishaan calls it "the Volcano". She then asks relative influence questions of every member in turn. How does the Volcano get Ishaan into trouble at school? What has it done to the father's evenings, to the grandmother's sleep, to the mother's confidence? Then the second set: has anyone ever stopped the Volcano from erupting? The grandmother remembers that it calms when she tells him a story; the mother remembers a Sunday when Ishaan warned her that it was coming and went to his room. Each of these unique outcomes is now a family achievement, and each member hears the others describe it. The blame that was flowing between the adults is redirected at a shared opponent, and the family leaves with a plan to "outwit the Volcano together" and a letter from the therapist summarising what each of them said. Family members also serve as audience and outsider witnesses for one another's preferred stories, which is easier to arrange in a family session than in individual work. Solution-focused family therapy grew up at the Brief Family Therapy Center in Milwaukee, founded in 1978 by Steve de Shazer (1940 to 2005) and Insoo Kim Berg (1934 to 2007) as a family therapy centre. With several people present, the standard questions take on new uses. The miracle question is asked of each member, and the therapist listens for overlap ("So all three of you would notice that the morning starts without shouting"). Relationship questions ask people to describe change through someone else's eyes: "What would your mother notice you doing differently the day after the miracle?" "If I asked your grandmother what is better this week, what would she say?" They bring the other members' perspectives into every answer, rather as the Milan school's circular questions do (Section 7.5). Scaling questions can be put to every member ("Where would each of you put the family today, from 0 to 10?"), and differences between the numbers become something to explore rather than argue about. Because family members often stand in different relationships to change, the therapist may treat a reluctant teenager as a visitor and his worried mother as a customer, complimenting each for coming. Berg carried the approach into home-based child welfare work in her book Family Based Services (1994), and in Western Australia Andrew Turnell and Steve Edwards built on it in Signs of Safety , an approach to child protection casework that asks families and workers to map dangers and existing safety together and to scale how safe the child is ( Signs of Safety , 1999). Exam trap "Individuals, families and entire cultures are given a different level of power as creators of their realities" describes narrative therapy (White and Epston): social constructionist, attentive to how dominant cultural stories carry power, and committed to letting people author their own stories. The distractors are modernist schools in which the therapist is the expert on what is wrong: transgenerational therapy (Bowen: differentiation passed down the generations, Section 7.3), strategic therapy (Haley: directives aimed at the family's hierarchy and its problem sequence, Section 7.5) and structural therapy (Minuchin: boundaries and subsystems, Section 7.4). Relationship questions ("What would your mother notice?") are solution-focused; circular questions are Milan's. Programmes for troubled adolescents: FFT, MST, MDFT and BSFT By the 1980s one group of young people had become a test case for every kind of psychological treatment: adolescents who were stealing, fighting, using drugs and appearing in juvenile courts. Individual counselling, residential institutions and detention had poor results, and parent training, which works well with younger children (Section 4.10), was not enough on its own for teenagers whose lives were organised around deviant peers. Four family programmes rose to the challenge. Each combines systemic ideas with behavioural methods, each is written down in a manual with training and supervision to keep therapists faithful to it, and each was tested in randomised trials (Table 7.16). Functional family therapy (FFT) was developed from 1969 at the University of Utah by James Alexander and Bruce Parsons . Its name reflects its central idea: a young person's problem behaviour is functional, in the sense that it serves a purpose in the family's relationships. Running away and staying out late may regulate distance from a parent; a dramatic crisis may draw a distant parent closer. FFT therapists do not try to change these relational functions of closeness and distance, which they regard as neither good nor bad; they help the family find less destructive behaviours that achieve the same ends. The work runs through three phases, usually in about twelve to fourteen sessions over three to five months. In engagement and motivation, the therapist uses reattribution and reframing (Section 7.5) to reduce blame and negativity and to build a shared, family-focused definition of the problem ("Everyone in this family is exhausted and frightened"). In behaviour change, the therapist teaches communication, parenting skills, contracts and problem solving, fitted to the family's relational functions. In generalisation, the family learns to extend its gains to the school, the court and the neighbourhood and to plan for relapse. Key study: Alexander and Parsons (1973) and the siblings Question. Can a short behavioural-systems family treatment reduce reoffending among delinquent adolescents? Method. Eighty-six families of young people referred to a juvenile court in Utah for status offences (offences such as truancy, running away and being "ungovernable", which are offences only because of the young person's age) were randomly assigned to FFT, to client-centred family groups, to psychodynamic family therapy or to no treatment. The therapists were graduate students supervised by the developers. Results. FFT families showed more improvement in their observed interaction, and FFT adolescents committed fewer further status offences than those in the three comparison conditions, although there was no significant difference in criminal offences. In a follow-up three years later, Klein, Alexander and Parsons (1977) found that the younger brothers and sisters of FFT adolescents had appeared in court less often than the siblings in the other groups. Conclusion. Changing the family's interaction helped the referred child and, apparently, prevented problems in children who had never been treated. Criticism. The young people were relatively minor offenders, and a much later trial in routine services (Sexton and Turner, 2010, with 917 families of young offenders in 14 counties) found the same 22 percent felony reoffending rate a year after FFT and after ordinary probation, except that the young people whose therapists followed the model closely did significantly better. Multisystemic therapy (MST) was developed by Scott Henggeler and his colleagues, including Charles Borduin, and is now based at the Medical University of South Carolina. Its theory comes from the developmental psychologist Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917 to 2005), whose social-ecological model ( The Ecology of Human Development , 1979) pictured a child at the centre of nested systems: family, peers, school and neighbourhood, within a wider society. Serious antisocial behaviour, in this view, has many causes spread across all these systems, so treatment must reach all of them (Figure 7.11). MST is delivered at home and in the community by a small team of master's-level therapists, each with only four to six families, on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, for three to five months (about 60 hours of contact). The parents are the main agents of change, and the therapist works with them on monitoring, discipline and warmth, and on the school, the peer group and the family's supports. Nine treatment principles guide the work; among them, the therapist must find the "fit" between the problem and its systemic context, build on strengths, focus on present, action-oriented and well-defined goals, and, unusually, accept that the team, not the family, is responsible for engagement and outcome. Neighbourhood School Peers Family Young person What MST works on Young person: skills, anger, drug use Family: monitoring, discipline, warmth, parents' stress Peers: less time with deviant peers, more with others School: attendance, homework, parent-teacher contact Neighbourhood: relatives, neighbours, activities, supports Delivered at home, team on call 24 hours a day Figure 7.11 The social-ecological model behind multisystemic therapy. Following Bronfenbrenner, the young person is nested inside family, peer, school and neighbourhood systems, and MST intervenes in all of them, using the parents as the main agents of change. MST's best-known trial, the Missouri Delinquency Project (Borduin and colleagues, 1995), randomly assigned 176 serious juvenile offenders, who had averaged almost four felony arrests each, to MST or to individual therapy. Four years later the MST group had been rearrested less often, including for violent crimes, and a follow-up when the participants were on average 37 years old (Sawyer and Borduin, 2011) still found felony reoffending of 34.8 percent after MST against 54.8 percent after individual therapy. Independent researchers have been less impressed. A Cochrane review by Julia Littell and colleagues (2005) pointed out that most trials had been run by the developers and concluded that the evidence that MST beats other services was inconclusive. In England, the large START trial (Peter Fonagy and colleagues, 2018) assigned 684 families to MST or to good usual services and found no difference in the main outcome, out-of-home placement at 18 months (13 percent against 11 percent). Multidimensional family therapy (MDFT), developed from the 1980s by Howard Liddle at the University of Miami, targets adolescent drug use and the delinquency that goes with it. The therapist works in four interlinked domains at once: the adolescent (seen alone as well as with the family), the parents (as adults with their own stresses and as caregivers), the family's interactions, and the systems outside the family, such as the school, the peer group and the juvenile justice system. In a 2001 trial with 182 adolescents using cannabis and alcohol, MDFT produced more improvement than adolescent group therapy or a multifamily educational programme, and its advantage in school performance and family functioning was still present a year later. Brief strategic family therapy (BSFT) began in 1972 at the Spanish Family Guidance Center in Miami, which José Szapocznik and his colleagues set up to understand drug use among Cuban adolescents. They found families locked in a struggle with a cultural flavour: the children were becoming American faster than their parents, and parents and children had become adversaries over values. BSFT, a brief treatment lasting a few months, combines Minuchin's joining and restructuring (Section 7.4) with Haley's strategic focus on the interactions that maintain the problem (Section 7.5). Its team made two original contributions. In one-person family therapy they showed that the family system could be changed by working through one member when the others would not attend, with results comparable to conjoint therapy. And in a 1988 trial with 108 families, a deliberate "strategic structural systems engagement" procedure, which treated the family's refusal to come as the first interactional pattern to be changed, brought 93 percent of families into treatment, against 42 percent with ordinary engagement.
