The Maudsley approach to adolescent anorexia Anorexia nervosa has a special place in family therapy. Minuchin's work on "psychosomatic families", with its famous family lunch session, made it a showcase for structural therapy (Section 7.4), but his claims rested on uncontrolled case series and on the assumption that the family's structure kept the illness going. (The disorder itself is described in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) The approach that now dominates treatment came from the Maudsley Hospital in London. There the psychiatrist Gerald Russell (1928 to 2018), who described bulimia nervosa in 1979, worked with the family therapists Christopher Dare and Ivan Eisler and the psychiatrist George Szmukler on the first controlled trial of family therapy for anorexia nervosa. In that trial (Russell, Szmukler, Dare and Eisler, 1987) 80 patients, 57 with anorexia nervosa and 23 with bulimia nervosa, first had their weight restored in a specialist inpatient unit and were then randomly assigned to a year of family therapy or of individual supportive therapy. Family therapy was more effective for patients whose illness had begun before the age of 19 and had not become chronic; for older patients, individual therapy looked tentatively better. The advantage for the young patients was still visible at a five-year follow-up. A later trial by Eisler and colleagues (2000) compared conjoint family therapy, with everyone in the room, against separated family therapy, in which the therapist saw the parents and the adolescent separately. The two did equally well overall, but where mothers were highly critical of the patient, separated therapy worked better: expressed emotion (Section 7.2) at work again. The Maudsley method was written into a manual by James Lock and Daniel le Grange , with Stewart Agras and Dare, in Treatment Manual for Anorexia Nervosa: A Family-Based Approach (2001), and it is now called family-based treatment (FBT). Its principles break with the older schools. The therapist is agnostic about the cause of the illness and tells the parents plainly that they did not cause it. The illness is separated from the young person, borrowing the narrative idea of externalising: it is the anorexia, not the daughter, that refuses food. And the parents, rather than the hospital, are put in charge of refeeding, much as a nursing team would be, while the therapist acts as a consultant to them. Treatment runs in three phases, typically over about twenty sessions in six to twelve months. In phase one (weight restoration) the parents take full control of eating; in the second session the family brings a meal, and the therapist helps the parents persuade their child to eat a little more than she intended. In phase two, as weight returns, control over eating is handed back to the adolescent step by step. In phase three the work turns to ordinary adolescent issues, such as independence, friendships and school, and to ending therapy. In a trial at Stanford and Chicago (Lock and colleagues, 2010) with 121 adolescents aged 12 to 18, FBT and an individual adolescent-focused therapy did equally well at the end of treatment, but FBT produced significantly more full remissions at the six-month and one-year follow-ups. Guidelines in several countries now put family therapy first for young people with anorexia. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in Britain (2017), for example, advises considering anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy before any other psychological treatment for children and young people, with individual cognitive behavioural therapy or adolescent-focused psychotherapy as the alternatives when family therapy is unsuitable. Exam trap The Maudsley approach is family-based treatment for adolescent anorexia: first trial by Russell, Szmukler, Dare and Eisler (1987) , manual by Lock and le Grange (2001) . It works best for younger patients with a short illness . Do not confuse its family meal (which helps parents take charge of refeeding, with no assumption that the family caused the illness) with Minuchin's lunch session (which used the meal to expose and restructure the family's enmeshed patterns, Section 7.4). And keep the Maudsley Hospital's other famous names apart: Hans Eysenck and the behaviour therapists of Chapter 4 worked there too. What the outcome research shows After half a century of trials, what can be said about family therapy as a whole? In 1995, in a special issue of the Journal of Marital and Family Therapy , William Pinsof and Lyman Wynne (the author of pseudomutuality, Section 7.2) reviewed the field and concluded that marital and family therapy works: it is better than no treatment and, for several problems, it does better than individual treatment, but there was little evidence that any one school outperforms the others. William Shadish and Scott Baldwin (2003), pulling together twenty meta-analyses, reached similar conclusions: couple and family interventions are effective, their effects shrink a little at follow-up but remain significant, differences between kinds of family therapy are small, and about 40 to 50 percent of those treated show clinically significant change. When Baldwin, Shadish and colleagues (2012) pooled 24 trials of BSFT, FFT, MDFT and MST for adolescent delinquency and drug use, the four programmes together did better than usual treatment and better than alternative therapies, but by a modest margin (standardised effect sizes of about 0.2 to 0.3), and there was not enough evidence to say which of the four was best. Reviews by the Irish psychologist Alan Carr (2009, updated several times since) list the problems for which systemic interventions have the strongest support: conduct problems and drug misuse in young people, adolescent anorexia, and, among adults, schizophrenia (family psychoeducation, Section 7.2), alcohol problems and relationship distress (couple therapy, Section 7.8). Three lessons stand out. First, the strongest evidence belongs to manualised programmes aimed at particular problems, not to the classic schools, partly because the schools were simply never tested in the same way. Second, effects tend to shrink when a programme leaves its developers' hands and is compared with good usual services, as the MST and FFT stories show, and a therapist's fidelity to the model makes a large difference. Third, the ideas of the classic schools have not disappeared; they live on inside the programmes, in BSFT's joining and restructuring, FFT's reframing, FBT's externalising and the attention every programme pays to engagement. Chapter 8 takes up the general questions of how therapies are tested and why different therapies so often perform alike. Exam trap If asked which family intervention has the best evidence: for adolescent anorexia , family-based treatment (Maudsley); for conduct problems in young children , parent management training (Section 4.10); for serious adolescent offending , MST or FFT; for adolescent drug use , MDFT, BSFT or MST; for relapse prevention in schizophrenia , family psychoeducation (Section 7.2), not any therapy based on the double bind. Overall, family therapy beats no treatment, but no single school has been shown to beat the others. Gender, power and violence: the feminist critique In 1978 the American psychologist Rachel Hare-Mustin published "A feminist approach to family therapy" in Family Process . Family therapists, she pointed out, prided themselves on understanding the social context of behaviour, yet they had never examined the consequences of a traditional socialisation that mainly disadvantages women, and much of their practice reinforced stereotyped sex roles without question. She showed how a gender-aware therapist could change sexist patterns through the therapy contract, the sharing of family tasks, communication, generational boundaries, relabelling, modelling and the alliances the therapist forms. A year earlier, in 1977, four family therapists, Marianne Walters , Betty Carter, Peggy Papp and Olga Silverstein , had formed the Women's Project in Family Therapy, which ran workshops across the United States and published The Invisible Web: Gender Patterns in Family Relationships (1988). Through the 1980s a series of papers, among them Virginia Goldner 's "Feminism and family therapy" (1985), turned these concerns into a broad critique of family systems theory itself, and gave rise to feminist family therapy . The critique had four main targets. The first was circular causality and neutrality . If every behaviour in a family is both cause and effect (Section 7.1), and the therapist must side with no one, then a husband who hits his wife and the wife who is hit are equally "part of the pattern". Michele Bograd 's 1984 critique of family systems approaches to wife battering argued that this language hides who is doing what to whom and can end by blaming the victim. The second target was the hidden assumption that partners have equal power, when in most families men controlled more of the money, the decisions and the physical force. The third was mother-blaming . The classic systemic picture of the over-involved mother and the peripheral father, from the schizophrenogenic mother (Section 7.2) to the enmeshed mother of structural therapy (Section 7.4), located the pathology in mothers, without asking why mothers were so involved (society had handed them all the child care) or why fathers were absent (work and custom kept them out). The fourth was technique: interventions that restore a father's "executive" position, or a paradoxical task that asks a woman to clean the kitchen again and again, can reinforce the very roles that keep her unhappy. Hare-Mustin later (1987) gave the field a useful pair of terms: an alpha bias exaggerates the differences between men and women, as she argued psychodynamic theories did, while a beta bias ignores real differences, as systemic theories did when they treated husband and wife as interchangeable parts of a system (with Jeanne Marecek she developed the idea in "The meaning of difference", 1988). The critique changed practice, above all where there is violence. A family or couple session can be dangerous for a woman who may be punished at home for what she says in the room, so therapists now screen each partner separately for violence before any joint work, and where there is ongoing, serious violence they treat safety as the first priority and do not begin conjoint couple therapy. The person who uses violence is held responsible for it; it is not treated as one more circular pattern. Some teams, such as the Gender and Violence Project of Goldner and her colleagues at the Ackerman Institute in New York ("Love and violence", 1990), developed conjoint work for couples who wished to stay together, but only under strict conditions of safety and accountability. Suspected abuse of a child overrides the usual rules of confidentiality: in India the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 makes reporting of sexual offences against children compulsory, and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 gives women civil remedies against abuse at home (Chapter 1 covers the law). Exam trap The feminist critique of family therapy began with Rachel Hare-Mustin (1978) and the Women's Project in Family Therapy (Walters, Carter, Papp and Silverstein, 1977; The Invisible Web , 1988). Its main targets were neutrality and circular causality in cases of violence, unequal power , mother-blaming and techniques that reinforce sex roles. Alpha bias exaggerates gender differences; beta bias ignores them. Betty Carter appears twice in this chapter: as co-author of the family life cycle (Section 7.1) and as a founder of the Women's Project. Culture, and family work in India Gender was the first difference the field learned to take seriously; culture was the second. Every school of family therapy carries cultural assumptions: that a healthy young adult leaves home, that parents should form a strong couple separate from their own parents, that feelings should be expressed openly, that children should become autonomous. Section 7.1 showed how Carter and McGoldrick's life cycle has to be translated for an Indian family, and how a therapist who does not understand a family's culture and customary practices will make wrong assessments and misinterpret normal behaviour as pathology. Cultural competence is the remedy: awareness of one's own cultural assumptions, knowledge of the family's culture, and skill in adapting methods so that they fit. BSFT, which began by noticing the clash of values between Cuban parents and their Americanising children, is one example of a programme built around culture rather than adapted to it afterwards. Another is the idea that interdependence is not automatically enmeshment: a mother who still decides what her twenty-year-old son eats may be over-involved, or she may be doing what every mother in her community does, and only the family's own norms can say which. Indian families raise these questions in a sharp form. The traditional ideal is the joint family , in which three or four generations (grandparents, their sons, the sons' wives and children, and often unmarried aunts and uncles) live in one household under one authority, and Indian families have generally been patriarchal, patrilineal and patrilocal, with the bride moving into her husband's family home. Even where households have become nuclear, decisions about illness, treatment, marriage and money are often taken by the wider family, so the person who brings a patient to a clinic may not be the person who decides whether treatment continues. The Indian family therapist therefore asks early who holds authority (an elder brother, a grandfather, a mother-in-law), invites them respectfully, and joins with the hierarchy rather than challenging it head on, while protecting the less powerful members, who are often daughters-in-law and young women. Separate sessions may be needed, because a daughter-in-law may not be able to speak freely in front of her mother-in-law. Many Indian families also expect the therapist to be an active, directive expert; the psychiatrist Jaswant Singh Neki argued in 1973 that the guru and disciple (guru-chela) relationship offers a culturally familiar model for therapy, which is one reason why a purely not-knowing stance may need adapting here. India also has its own tradition of involving families in care, which began before Western family therapy reached the country. In the 1950s (1957 is the year most Indian reviews give, though some accounts say 1950) Vidya Sagar , superintendent of the Amritsar Mental Hospital, allowed relatives to stay with patients in tents pitched on the hospital grounds and to take part in their care (Section 7.2). The idea of the family ward followed: family wards were set up at the Christian Medical College, Vellore, where descriptive reports appeared from 1967, and at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) in Bangalore, where a family psychiatric ward and a Family Psychiatric Centre were described by R. S. Bhatti, N. Janakiramaiah and S. M. Channabasavanna in Family Process in 1980. To this day a relative commonly stays on the ward as the patient's attendant in many Indian hospitals, which gives the clinician daily access to the family. Indian research has followed the same direction. Studies of expressed emotion in Chandigarh found lower levels of high EE than in Britain (Section 7.2). In Bangalore, S. Pai and R. L. Kapur developed an interview schedule for measuring the burden that a psychiatric patient places on the family (1981), and then showed (1983) that first-episode patients with schizophrenia treated at home by a visiting nurse trained in counselling did better after six months, clinically and socially and with a lighter burden on the family, than patients admitted to a mental hospital and followed up as outpatients. At the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research in Chandigarh, a randomised trial by Kulhara and colleagues (2009) gave 76 patients with schizophrenia and their caregivers either monthly psychoeducation sessions for nine months or routine outpatient care, and found the psychoeducation group better on psychopathology, disability, caregiver support and satisfaction. At the Schizophrenia Research Foundation in Chennai, R. Thara and her colleagues found that families preferred flexible, informal education tailored to their needs over a structured research programme, and attended it better (2005). Clinical link For an Indian clinical psychologist the practical conclusions are clear. Most people with severe mental illness live with their families, who provide most of their care, so family work is not an optional extra. Begin with psychoeducation and the reduction of blame, because many families have been told, by relatives or even by professionals, that they caused the illness or that it is the result of fate or black magic. Use the family's own language and explanations as a starting point rather than an obstacle. Ask about caregiver burden, because exhausted caregivers become critical caregivers. And remember the rules of this section: screen for violence separately, protect the less powerful members, and never mistake a culture's ordinary closeness for pathology. Exam trap The consequence of poor awareness of a family's culture and familial practices is wrong assessments and misinterpretations , not accurate understanding, better communication or a stronger alliance. Indian firsts to keep straight: relatives staying with patients in tents at Amritsar (Vidya Sagar, 1950s, usually dated 1957); family wards at CMC Vellore (reports from 1967) and NIMHANS (Bhatti and colleagues, Family Process , 1980); the Chandigarh expressed emotion studies (Wig, Leff and colleagues, Section 7.2); the family burden interview schedule of Pai and Kapur (Bangalore, 1981). The theory that relationships last when their rewards outweigh their costs, set out by Thibaut and Kelley in 1959, is social theory. A contract in which each person changes independently and earns his own reward, rather than trading changes, is a contract. Heinz von Foerster's "cybernetics of cybernetics", in which the observer is part of the observed system, is called cybernetics. Harlene Anderson and Harry Goolishian's stance of genuine curiosity, with the client as the expert, is the stance. Answers: (1) exchange, (2) good faith (parallel), (3) second-order, (4) not-knowing, (5) reflecting, (6) relationship, (7) Parsons, (8) social-ecological, (9) parents, (10) beta. 7.8 Couples Therapy Lower yield · 1 Q Vikram and Ritika have been married for six years. Theirs was an arranged marriage: their parents met first, the two of them met three times, and the wedding followed within the year. They live with Vikram's parents in a flat in Pune, with their five-year-old son. Ritika asked for the appointment, and she does most of the talking. "He comes home, eats, and sits with his phone. When I try to talk to him, he gets up and leaves the room. I am alone in a house full of people." Vikram, when he is finally asked, speaks quietly. "Whatever I do, it is wrong. She starts complaining the moment I walk in. So I keep quiet. If I say nothing, at least there is no fight." You have met this couple before, in a different form: they are the nagging wife and the withdrawing husband of Figure 7.1, each telling a linear story in which the other started it. Seventy years ago Vikram and Ritika might have been seen separately, each by a different counsellor, and given advice about the duties of a husband and a wife. Today a couples therapist would see them together and could draw on at least four well-researched maps of their problem. A behaviour therapist would see two people who have stopped rewarding each other and never learned to solve problems together. An integrative behaviour therapist would add that some of their differences will never change and must be accepted. An emotionally focused therapist would see two frightened people caught in a cycle that protects each of them from the hurt underneath. A cognitive-behavioural therapist would ask what each believes the other's behaviour means. And John Gottman, the researcher who spent four decades filming couples, would listen to the first three minutes of their argument and look for contempt. This section follows these maps in turn, then asks what the evidence says and how couples therapy has to bend to fit an Indian marriage. From marriage counselling to couples therapy Section 7.1 described the first marriage counselling centres of the 1930s. For their first few decades they offered what Alan Gurman and Peter Fraenkel, in their 2002 history of the field, call atheoretical marriage counselling: practical advice and education about the values and obligations of married life, given by people trained in many fields, usually to each partner separately. A second strand ran alongside it. Some psychoanalysts began, cautiously, to experiment with treating both spouses, at first each in a separate analysis. Then, from the 1960s, the new family therapists swallowed the field. To Don Jackson, Virginia Satir, Jay Haley and Murray Bowen, a marriage was simply one more family subsystem, to be understood with the ideas of homeostasis, triangles and communication that you met in Section 7.1 (their schools are taught in Sections 7.3 to 7.6). Gurman and Fraenkel describe family therapy as having not merely absorbed marriage counselling but "engulfed, consumed and devoured" it. Only from the mid-1980s did couple therapy re-emerge as a field in its own right, with its own theories, its own treatment manuals and its own randomised trials, and that is the period this section is mostly about. The name changed along the way. "Marital therapy" and "marriage counselling" assumed a husband and a wife; "couple therapy" or couples therapy (both forms are used) covers any two partners in a committed relationship, married or not, of the same sex or different sexes. It can be defined as psychotherapy in which the two partners are seen together, with the relationship itself as the focus of treatment. Three formats are worth distinguishing, because they turn up as options in questions. In conjoint therapy (Section 7.1) both partners attend the same sessions with the same therapist; this is the standard format today. In concurrent therapy one therapist sees each partner separately. In collaborative therapy each partner has a different therapist, and the two therapists consult each other. Why treat the relationship at all? Because relationship distress is common, and it is bad for people. Distressed partners are more likely to be depressed or anxious and to drink heavily, and their children are more likely to have emotional and behavioural problems. The link with depression is strong enough that couples therapy is a recognised treatment for depression when the marriage is in trouble (Section 7.8.7). Couples therapy is not, however, for every couple. A careful therapist sees each partner alone at least once during assessment and asks, in that private meeting, about violence, fear and coercion. Where one partner is afraid of the other, joint sessions can put her in danger (what she says in the room may be punished at home), and the first task is safety, not communication training. An affair that is still going on in secret, or a partner who has already decided to leave and wants the therapist to break the news, are other common reasons why conjoint therapy cannot start, or must start differently. Assessment usually combines joint and individual interviews, a watched discussion of a real disagreement, and questionnaires such as Graham Spanier's Dyadic Adjustment Scale (1976), which most of the trials in this section use as their outcome measure (the questionnaires themselves belong to the Assessment book). Exam trap Conjoint means both partners together with one therapist; concurrent means one therapist seeing each partner separately; collaborative means two therapists, one for each partner, who confer. "Couple therapy", "couples therapy" and the older "marital therapy" name the same field. Before conjoint work begins, each partner should be screened alone for intimate partner violence; couples therapy is not the first treatment when one partner fears the other. Traditional behavioural couple therapy Behaviour therapists came to marriage in the late 1960s, carrying two ideas. The first was the social learning principle you met in Chapter 4: behaviour that is rewarded becomes more frequent, behaviour that is punished or ignored becomes less frequent, and people learn new skills by watching and practising. The second came from social psychology. In The Social Psychology of Groups (1959), John Thibaut (1917 to 1986) and Harold Kelley (1921 to 2003) had proposed social exchange theory (Section 7.7): people stay in relationships to the extent that the rewards outweigh the costs, compared with what they believe they could get elsewhere. Put the two ideas together and you have a behavioural account of a failing marriage. Satisfied couples give each other many rewards (affection, help, interest, praise) and few punishments. Distressed couples give fewer rewards and more punishments, and they show negative reciprocity : a hostile remark from one is swiftly returned by the other. Worse, distressed partners try to change each other by aversive control, nagging, threatening, sulking and withdrawing until the other gives in. Each surrender rewards the coercion, so both partners learn to coerce more; the Oregon psychologist Gerald Patterson described the same coercive process between parents and aggressive children (Section 7.7). The behavioural therapist's job follows from the analysis: increase the rewards, reduce the punishments, and teach the skills that distressed couples lack. One of the pioneers was the American therapist Richard B. Stuart , whom you met in Section 7.7. In 1969 he reported what he called the operant-interpersonal treatment of four distressed couples: each partner named the specific behaviours he or she wanted more of from the other, and the couple agreed in writing to exchange them. Stuart's later book Helping Couples Change (1980) gave the field one of its best-known exercises, caring days . Each partner writes a list of small, specific, positive actions that would make him or her feel cared for ("Ask about my day before you pick up your phone"; "Bring me tea on Sunday morning"), and each then performs several of the other's items every day, whatever the other does. Stuart's instruction was, in effect, to act as if you cared. The point is not the tea. Distressed couples have stopped noticing anything good about each other, and a daily stream of small, visible positives breaks the deadlock in which each waits for the other to change first. Agreements between partners were usually written down as contracts, and two kinds were used (Section 7.7 introduced both for families; the general rules for behavioural contracts are in Section 4.5). In a quid pro quo contract (Latin for "something for something") each partner's change is made conditional on the other's: "If Vikram greets me without his phone in his hand, I will not raise complaints until after dinner." The phrase came from Don Jackson, whose 1965 paper on the "marital quid pro quo" described the unspoken bargains that every marriage runs on; the behaviourists simply made the bargain explicit. Quid pro quo contracts have a weakness, however: if one partner fails, the other is released, and distressed couples are experts at waiting for the other to fail first. In a good faith contract , proposed in 1973 by Robert Weiss, Hyman Hops and Gerald Patterson of the Oregon Marital Studies Program, each partner's change is independent of the other's and is rewarded separately, often by a privilege the person chooses, so that one partner's lapse does not cancel the other's effort. The approach was systematised by Neil S. Jacobson (1949 to 1999), whose component analysis of cognitive therapy for depression you met in Chapter 5, and Gayla Margolin , in Marital Therapy: Strategies Based on Social Learning and Behavior Exchange Principles (1979). Their manual defined what is now called traditional behavioural couple therapy (TBCT; also called behavioural marital therapy or behavioural couples therapy), and it rests on three components. Behaviour exchange . Each partner identifies behaviours that please the other, the couple keeps track of how often they happen, and each deliberately increases them, through caring days and similar exercises. The aim is quick relief: a rise in daily positives that makes the harder work possible. Communication training . The couple learn speaker and listener skills. The speaker talks about his or her own feelings and a specific behaviour, using an "I" statement ("I feel hurt when you look at your phone while I am talking") rather than an attack on the other's character ("You never care about anyone but yourself"). The listener paraphrases what he heard and checks that he has understood before replying. The therapist teaches these skills as any behaviour therapist teaches a skill: instruction, modelling, rehearsal in the session, feedback and homework (behaviour rehearsal is described in Section 4.7). Problem-solving training . The couple learn to solve one problem at a time, in two separate phases. In the definition phase they begin with something positive, describe the problem in specific behavioural terms, say how it makes them feel, admit their own part in it and keep it brief. Only then, in the solution phase, do they brainstorm solutions without criticising any, weigh them, agree on a specific change, write it down and set a time to review it. Push Vikram and Ritika through this. In the first weeks each writes a caring-days list: Ritika asks for fifteen minutes of tea together on the balcony after dinner, and Vikram asks to be greeted without a complaint when he walks in. They practise in the session. Ritika says, "I feel lonely in the evenings when you go to your phone," and Vikram, instead of defending himself, says back what he heard. Then they tackle a real problem, the Sunday visits to Vikram's sister that Ritika dreads. They define it, brainstorm, and agree to visit on alternate Sundays and to spend the others as a family of three. For many couples this is enough, and the change can be quick. TBCT became the most thoroughly researched of all couple therapies. A meta-analysis by William Shadish and Scott Baldwin (2005) pooled 30 randomised trials and found behavioural marital therapy clearly better than no treatment, with a moderate effect size (d of about 0.59). But Jacobson, to his great credit, looked harder at his own results. In a 1984 reanalysis of outcome data from several trials, he and his colleagues asked not whether couples improved on average but how many actually ended up in the range of happy, non-distressed couples. The answer was sobering. About half of the couples improved, but only about a third moved into the non-distressed range, and in later follow-ups roughly a third of the couples who had improved relapsed within two years. A study from Texas sharpened the worry. Key study: behavioural versus insight-oriented marital therapy (Snyder, Wills and Grady-Fletcher, 1991) Question. Does a behavioural or an insight-oriented couple therapy produce more lasting change? Method. At Texas A&M University, Douglas Snyder and Robert Wills (1989) had randomly assigned distressed couples to behavioural marital therapy, to insight-oriented marital therapy (IOMT), or to a waiting list. IOMT, Snyder's own approach, helps each partner understand how feelings, expectations and defences learned in earlier relationships, especially with parents, are being replayed in the marriage (the psychodynamic ideas behind it are in Chapter 3). In 1991 Snyder, Wills and Grady-Fletcher obtained four-year follow-up data on 59 of the treated couples. Results. At the end of therapy and six months later the two treatments had done equally well. At four years, 38 percent of the couples who had received behavioural therapy had divorced, compared with 3 percent of those who had received insight-oriented therapy. Conclusion. Skills training may produce change that fades, whereas working through each partner's emotional history may produce change that lasts. Criticism. Jacobson replied that the insight-oriented therapy in the study included many behavioural techniques, that the behavioural therapy was a narrow version, and that the investigators were committed to IOMT. It was a single trial, and no later study has reproduced so large a difference. Together with the reanalyses, however, it convinced Jacobson that something was missing from TBCT. Exam trap Jacobson and Margolin (1979) wrote the manual of traditional behavioural couple therapy; Jacobson and Christensen (1996) wrote integrative behavioural couple therapy. TBCT's three components are behaviour exchange, communication training and problem-solving training , and its theory is social learning plus social exchange (Thibaut and Kelley), not attachment (that is emotionally focused therapy). Caring days are Richard Stuart's. A quid pro quo contract makes each partner's change conditional on the other's (the phrase "marital quid pro quo" is Don Jackson's, 1965); a good faith contract rewards each partner's change independently (Weiss, Hops and Patterson, 1973). Insight-oriented marital therapy is Douglas Snyder's. Integrative behavioural couple therapy Jacobson went back to his failures and asked who they were. TBCT, he found, worked best for couples who were younger, less distressed, still emotionally engaged with each other and broadly agreed about how a marriage should be run. It worked worst for couples divided by deep differences of temperament or values: one who needs closeness and one who needs space, one who plans and one who improvises, one who spends and one who saves. For such couples, teaching both partners to negotiate change was rather like teaching two people to negotiate a change in their height. Worse, the push for change was itself part of the problem. Each partner's efforts to make the other change led the other to dig in, and each round of pressure and resistance drove the two further apart. Jacobson's answer, developed with the psychologist Andrew Christensen of the University of California, Los Angeles, was integrative behavioural couple therapy (IBCT), set out in their book Integrative Couple Therapy: Promoting Acceptance and Change (1996). It is "integrative" because it integrates two goals. Change is still sought where change is possible, using the behaviour exchange and the communication and problem-solving training of TBCT. But IBCT adds, and usually puts first, acceptance : letting go of the struggle to change a partner's unwanted behaviour and coming to experience that behaviour differently, as understandable, tolerable, or even as part of what one loves in the partner, so that it stops being a battleground. Acceptance is not resignation, and it never means putting up with abuse. It means that a partner's quietness, say, stops being evidence that he does not care and becomes simply the way he is. And acceptance has a paradoxical result that IBCT therapists see again and again: when the pressure to change stops, partners often change. IBCT begins with a formulation of the couple's problem, which in the original version had three parts. The theme is the central difference that the couple's conflicts keep returning to, such as closeness and distance, or control and responsibility. The polarisation process is the way each partner's efforts to change the other push both to more extreme positions: the more Ritika pursues closeness, the more Vikram protects his space, and the more he withdraws, the more urgently she pursues. The mutual trap is the stuck and hopeless place this leaves them in, each feeling unable to give way without losing something essential. (In later writing Christensen and his colleagues organised the formulation as a DEEP analysis: the partners' Differences, their Emotional sensitivities, the External stressors on them, and their Patterns of communication.) The formulation is shared with the couple at a feedback session and becomes the backbone of the therapy. Three groups of techniques then build acceptance. Empathic joining . The therapist helps each partner voice the soft emotions (hurt, fear, sadness, loneliness) that lie beneath the hard ones (anger, blame, contempt) that the other usually sees. When Ritika stops saying "You don't care" and says "In the evenings I feel invisible," Vikram can respond with sympathy instead of self-defence. The problem is reframed as a painful difference from which both partners suffer, not a fault in one of them. Unified detachment . The partners are helped to step back and describe their pattern together, calmly and without blame, as if they were watching another couple: what sets it off, who does what next, how it ends. They often give it a name and are encouraged to find it a little funny; Vikram and Ritika call theirs "the phone and the complaint". The problem becomes an "it" that they face together rather than something one does to the other, much as narrative therapists externalise a problem (Sections 6.8 and 7.7). Tolerance building . For behaviour that probably will not change, the therapist helps the partners become less upset by it. The methods include pointing out the positive side of the negative behaviour (Vikram's calm silence, which maddens Ritika in an argument, is the same steadiness she relied on when her father was in hospital); rehearsing the troublesome behaviour in the session until its sting fades; asking a partner to fake the behaviour at home now and then, when he does not really feel it, and to tell the other afterwards, so that both can observe the reaction without the usual heat; and encouraging self-care, so that each partner can meet some needs in other ways when the other cannot meet them. Key study: traditional versus integrative behavioural couple therapy (Christensen and colleagues, 2004 to 2010) Question. Does adding acceptance to behavioural couple therapy help seriously distressed couples more than change-focused TBCT? Method. The trial began under Jacobson and Christensen; after Jacobson's sudden death in 1999, Christensen carried it through. At the University of California, Los Angeles, and the University of Washington in Seattle, 134 seriously and chronically distressed married couples were randomly assigned to about eight months of either TBCT or IBCT and were then followed for five years. Results. The two therapies took different paths. TBCT couples improved faster at first and then levelled off; IBCT couples improved steadily throughout. By the end of treatment 71 percent of IBCT couples and 59 percent of TBCT couples were reliably improved or recovered on the Dyadic Adjustment Scale. Through the two-year follow-up IBCT kept a statistically significant advantage in relationship satisfaction, although the proportions of couples clinically improved were similar (69 against 60 percent). By five years the two had converged: about half of the couples in each group (50 and 46 percent) were still clinically improved, and about a quarter in each (26 and 28 percent) had separated or divorced. Conclusion. Both therapies helped even very distressed couples substantially; the advantage of IBCT was real but modest, and it faded over time without further treatment. Criticism. There was no untreated control group, so the trial compares two active treatments; all the couples were married Americans; and the investigators included the developers of IBCT. IBCT has since been rolled out across the United States Department of Veterans Affairs, and an online self-help programme based on it, OurRelationship, has been tested in a national trial. It is often grouped with the third-wave behaviour therapies of Chapter 5, because like them it adds acceptance to the traditional behavioural goal of change. Exam trap IBCT is Andrew Christensen and Neil Jacobson's (1996), and its signature idea is acceptance , built through empathic joining (expressing the soft emotions beneath the hard ones), unified detachment (describing the pattern together, without blame, as an "it") and tolerance building (becoming less reactive to behaviour that will not change), combined with TBCT's change techniques. Acceptance in IBCT means giving up the struggle to change the partner; it is not resignation and not tolerance of abuse. Do not confuse it with acceptance in Steven Hayes's acceptance and commitment therapy (Section 5.9), which is acceptance of one's own thoughts and feelings. Emotionally focused couple therapy While Jacobson was rethinking behaviour therapy in Seattle, a different answer was taking shape in Canada. In the early 1980s Susan Johnson (1947 to 2024), known to everyone as Sue Johnson, was a doctoral student at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, and her supervisor was Leslie Greenberg (born 1945), whose emotion-focused therapy for individuals you met in Section 6.7. Together they built a couple therapy out of the humanistic and experiential tradition: Rogers's empathy, the Gestalt therapists' attention to emotion in the present moment, and the systems therapists' attention to circular interaction. In their first trial, Johnson and Greenberg (1985) compared this experiential treatment with a behavioural problem-solving treatment for distressed couples, and the experiential treatment produced the greater gains. They described the method in Emotionally Focused Therapy for Couples (1988). Johnson then took the approach in her own direction, at the University of Ottawa, by grounding it in attachment theory. John Bowlby (Sections 3.5.5 and 7.1) had argued that infants are born with an attachment system that keeps them close to a caregiver who offers safety, and that separation from that figure triggers a predictable sequence of protest, despair and finally detachment. In 1987 the American social psychologists Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver proposed that adult romantic love is an attachment process too. Johnson drew the clinical conclusion. In emotionally focused couple therapy (EFT, sometimes written EFCT), partners are understood as each other's attachment figures, and relationship distress is understood as separation distress: the panic and protest that arise when a person can no longer count on the partner to be there. The fights are not, at bottom, about the dishes or the in-laws or the phone. They are about one question, which Johnson put in plain words: "Are you there for me?" Her books, beginning with The Practice of Emotionally Focused Marital Therapy: Creating Connection (1996) and including the popular Hold Me Tight (2008), spread the approach worldwide. A secure bond, she wrote, needs a partner who is accessible (can I reach you?), responsive (will you respond to me emotionally?) and engaged (will you value me and stay close?), which she abbreviated as A.R.E. Where behaviour therapists saw skill deficits, Johnson saw emotion organising behaviour. When the bond feels threatened, each partner reacts in the way that his or her attachment history has made automatic, and the two reactions lock together into a negative interaction cycle that runs on its own. The commonest is the pursue-withdraw cycle : one partner, anxious about the connection, protests, criticises and pursues; the other, feeling attacked and afraid of failing, defends, goes quiet and withdraws, which makes the first pursue harder still. Researchers had already documented the same pattern under the name demand-withdraw . In a 1990 study of 31 couples, Andrew Christensen and Christopher Heavey found that the wife-demand, husband-withdraw sequence was more common than the reverse, but only when the couple was discussing a change the wife wanted; when they discussed a change the husband wanted, the difference disappeared. The pattern, in other words, belongs to the situation as much as to gender. The two other cycles are attack-attack, in which both partners criticise and blame, and withdraw-withdraw, in which both have given up and the relationship goes cold. In Hold Me Tight Johnson gave the three cycles memorable names: Find the Bad Guy (attack-attack), the Protest Polka (pursue-withdraw) and Freeze and Flee (withdraw-withdraw). The key to changing the cycle lies underneath it. What each partner shows the other is a secondary, reactive emotion (anger, irritation, coldness). What each actually feels, and hides, is a primary and more vulnerable emotion (fear of being abandoned, shame at being inadequate), bound up with an unmet attachment need. Greenberg's distinction between primary and secondary emotions (Section 6.7) is used directly. Figure 7.12 shows the cycle in which Vikram and Ritika are caught. On the surface: secondary, reactive emotions and moves Ritika pursues criticises, complains, follows him from room to room Vikram withdraws goes quiet, defends himself, picks up his phone, leaves pressure distance covers covers The cycle is the enemy (not either partner) Fear and loneliness "Do I matter to you? Are you there for me?" Shame, fear of failing "I can never get it right. Silence keeps the peace." Underneath: primary emotions and attachment needs, reached and shared in therapy Figure 7.12 The pursue-withdraw cycle as an emotionally focused therapist maps it. Each partner's visible move (top) provokes the other's, so the loop runs by itself; the vertical lines labelled "covers" show that each move covers a more vulnerable primary emotion (bottom). Therapy names the cycle as the common enemy and helps each partner reveal what lies underneath. The EFT therapist works on two levels at once. Within each partner, she tracks and deepens emotion: she reflects and validates, asks evocative questions ("What happens inside you when her voice rises?"), heightens a key phrase by repeating it slowly, and offers empathic conjectures that put words to what has not yet been said ("Maybe part of you is saying, 'I will never be good enough for her'?"). Between the partners, she tracks and names the cycle and reframes the problem: the enemy is the cycle, not the partner. Then she restructures the interaction directly through enactments , asking one partner to turn and tell the other, here and now, what he has just discovered ("Can you tell Ritika, now, what you just told me about always feeling that you fail?"). Change happens not because the couple has learned a skill but because they have had a new emotional experience of each other in the room. The process unfolds in three stages and nine steps, summarised in Table 7.17. Stage 2 contains the two change events that Johnson's research singled out as the heart of the therapy. In withdrawer re-engagement the withdrawn partner comes out of hiding and states his own fears and needs. In blamer softening the previously critical partner, now able to trust that the other is reachable, asks for comfort and closeness from a position of vulnerability, and the other responds. Couples who complete a softening tend to do well. Johnson and her colleagues also described the attachment injury (Johnson, Makinen and Millikin, 2001): a betrayal or abandonment at a moment of urgent need, such as an affair, or a partner's absence during a miscarriage or a parent's death, which becomes an impasse because the injured partner returns to it whenever closeness is attempted. In their model of resolution, the injured partner describes the hurt and its impact, the other acknowledges it and expresses remorse, and the injured partner then asks for, and receives, the comfort that was missing at the time. Table 7.17 The three stages and nine steps of emotionally focused couple therapy (after Sue Johnson). Stage Steps What happens with Vikram and Ritika 1 Cycle de-escalation (1) Build the alliance and assess the conflicts in attachment terms; (2) identify the negative cycle; (3) reach the unacknowledged emotions beneath each partner's position; (4) reframe the problem as the cycle and the underlying needs They learn to see "the phone and the complaint" as a cycle that grips them both, driven by her fear and his shame 2 Restructuring interactional positions (5) Help each partner own disowned needs and fears; (6) help each accept the other's experience; (7) help each express needs directly, creating new bonding events (withdrawer re-engagement, then blamer softening) Vikram tells Ritika he goes silent because he feels he can never please her; Ritika, softer, asks him to hold her when she feels alone 3 Consolidation (8) Find new solutions to old practical problems; (9) consolidate the new positions and the new, secure cycle With the bond safer, they solve the Sunday-visit problem easily and build rituals of connection EFT has a solid, if smaller, evidence base. A 1999 meta-analysis of the early trials by Johnson, John Hunsley, Greenberg and Schindler reported a large effect, and Johnson has cited recovery from distress in about 70 percent of treated couples, though the trials were few, small and run by the therapy's developers. A larger meta-analysis by Rathgeber and colleagues at the University of Münster (2019) pooled 33 randomised trials with 2,730 participants. At the end of treatment both emotionally focused therapy (effect size g of 0.73) and behavioural couple therapy (g of 0.53) produced medium effects on relationship satisfaction, the difference between them was not significant, and the gains shrank over follow-up. The authors warned that publication bias may have inflated both. Exam trap Emotionally focused couple therapy is Sue Johnson's , first developed with Leslie Greenberg (Johnson and Greenberg, 1985; Greenberg and Johnson, 1988), and it rests on attachment theory (Bowlby; Hazan and Shaver, 1987): distress is separation distress, not a skill deficit. Do not confuse it with Greenberg's emotion-focused therapy for individuals (Section 6.7) or with emotion-focused coping (a stress concept). The pursue-withdraw cycle is the same pattern as the demand-withdraw pattern studied by Christensen and Heavey (1990). The two key change events, withdrawer re-engagement and blamer softening , both come in Stage 2. A.R.E. stands for accessible, responsive and engaged. Cognitive-behavioural couple therapy Behavioural couple therapy treated what partners do; the cognitive revolution of Chapter 5 asked what they think about what the other does. The same act can mean very different things. When Vikram picks up his phone, Ritika could think "He is exhausted after work" or "He avoids me because I bore him", and only the second makes her angry. Donald H. Baucom and Norman B. Epstein brought this idea into couple therapy in Cognitive-Behavioral Marital Therapy (1990) and later broadened it in Enhanced Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Couples (2002). Cognitive-behavioural couple therapy (CBCT) keeps the behaviour exchange and the communication and problem-solving training of TBCT and adds the identification and testing of five kinds of relationship cognition that Baucom, Epstein and their colleagues described: Selective attention : what each partner notices and what he or she misses (Ritika notices every evening on the phone and none of the mornings he makes her tea). Attributions : explanations of why the partner behaved as he or she did. Expectancies : predictions about what will happen ("If I bring it up, he'll walk out"). Assumptions : beliefs about how partners and relationships actually are ("Men don't talk about feelings"). Standards : beliefs about how they should be ("If he really loved me, he would know what I need without my telling him"). Attributions have been studied most. In a 1990 review, Thomas Bradbury and Frank Fincham showed that distressed spouses make distress-maintaining attributions : the partner's negative behaviour is put down to causes that are internal to him, stable, global and intentional ("He ignores me because he is selfish; he has always been like that; it's how he treats everyone"), while his positive behaviour is put down to external, temporary and specific causes ("He was nice today only because his mother was watching"). Happy couples do the reverse, giving each other the benefit of the doubt. Distress-maintaining attributions keep a relationship miserable whatever the partner actually does, because good behaviour is discounted and bad behaviour confirms the case. CBCT therapists teach partners to catch such thoughts and test them with the methods of Chapter 5: Socratic questions, looking for alternative explanations and examining the evidence, and, for rigid standards, the kind of challenge to "musts" that Albert Ellis taught. Aaron Beck brought the same thinking to a popular audience in Love Is Never Enough (1988). In trials, CBCT works about as well as TBCT; adding cognitive restructuring changes how partners think, but it has not reliably improved the overall outcome. Exam trap Cognitive-behavioural couple therapy is Baucom and Epstein's (1990); Aaron Beck's couples book is Love Is Never Enough (1988). Distressed couples explain the partner's bad behaviour as internal, stable, global and intentional, and the partner's good behaviour as external, unstable and specific (Bradbury and Fincham, 1990). "Standards" are beliefs about how a relationship should be; "assumptions" are beliefs about how it is . Gottman's research on what predicts divorce The therapies so far began with a theory and then tested it. John Mordecai Gottman (born 1942), who studied mathematics before he turned to psychology, began at the other end. He set out to watch, measure and follow up large numbers of ordinary couples, to find out what actually distinguishes relationships that last from relationships that break. With his long-time collaborator, the psychophysiologist Robert Levenson , he developed a laboratory procedure that became famous. A couple arrived after being apart for at least eight hours. They first talked about the events of their day; then they spent 15 minutes trying to resolve a continuing disagreement; then they talked about something pleasant. Throughout, video cameras recorded their faces and bodies, and sensors recorded heart rate, skin conductance, blood flow and even how much each partner fidgeted in the chair. Afterwards each partner watched the video alone and turned a rating dial to show how he or she had felt, moment by moment. Trained coders then scored every second of the interaction for specific emotions (interest, affection, humour, anger, sadness, whining, contempt and others) using Gottman's Specific Affect Coding System. At the University of Washington in Seattle, Gottman later added a studio apartment, which reporters nicknamed the Love Lab , where couples spent a day living as normally as they could while the cameras ran. And then came the crucial step: the researchers followed the couples for years to see which stayed together and which divorced. What they found overturned several common beliefs. Anger on its own did not predict divorce; plenty of stable, satisfied couples argued loudly. Nor did the sheer number of arguments. What mattered was the balance between positive and negative behaviour during conflict, and certain particular kinds of negativity. The five to one ratio. In What Predicts Divorce? (1994) and its popular companion Why Marriages Succeed or Fail (1994), Gottman reported that stable couples showed at least about five positive interactions (interest, affection, humour, agreement, empathy) for every negative one while they were discussing a conflict, whereas couples heading for divorce showed a ratio of about one to one or worse. He found that stable couples came in three styles: validating couples, who listen and compromise calmly; volatile couples, who argue passionately but also laugh and love passionately; and conflict-avoiding couples, who agree to disagree and rarely confront each other. Each style can work, as long as the ratio holds. The two unstable types, hostile and hostile-detached couples, fall below it. The four horsemen. Four kinds of negativity predicted divorce so strongly that Gottman named them, after the riders who bring the end of the world in the Book of Revelation, the four horsemen : criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Criticism , in Gottman's sense, is an attack on the partner's character, usually with "always" or "never" ("You never think of anyone but yourself"); it differs from a complaint , which is about a specific behaviour ("I was upset that you didn't call to say you'd be late"), and complaints are healthy. Contempt speaks from a position of superiority: sarcasm, mockery, name-calling, hostile humour, sneering, rolling the eyes. Its facial sign is a one-sided tightening of the lip corner. Contempt was the single strongest predictor of divorce in Gottman's research, because it tells the partner that he or she is beneath respect. Defensiveness is self-protection by counter-attack or by playing the innocent victim ("Yes, but you..."), which is really a way of blaming the partner. Stonewalling is the listener's withdrawal from the interaction: he stops responding, looks away, and sits like a stone wall. It tends to arrive later in a relationship's decline, often as a response to being overwhelmed, and in Gottman's samples of married couples the stonewaller was most often the husband. Gottman also described an antidote for each horseman, as Table 7.18 shows. Table 7.18 Gottman's four horsemen and their antidotes. Horseman What it is Example Antidote Criticism An attack on the partner's character, not a complaint about a behaviour "You never listen. You only care about your phone." Gentle start-up: describe the situation and your feeling, and ask for what you need Contempt (strongest predictor) Disrespect from a position of superiority: sarcasm, mockery, eye-rolling "Oh, the great man is too tired to speak to his wife." Build a culture of appreciation and respect; express fondness and admiration Defensiveness Excuses, counter-attack, innocent victimhood; blaming the partner "It's not my fault. You start complaining the moment I walk in." Take responsibility, even for part of the problem Stonewalling Withdrawing from the interaction; shutting down and not responding Vikram says nothing, picks up his phone and leaves the room Physiological self-soothing: take a break of at least 20 minutes, then return Harsh start-up. Gottman noticed that a conflict discussion tends to end the way it begins. A harsh start-up opens with criticism or contempt; a soft or gentle start-up opens with a complaint stated without blame. The key study below showed how much the opening matters. Key study: the first three minutes (Carrère and Gottman, 1999) Question. Can the way a marital conflict discussion begins predict divorce? Method. Sybil Carrère and John Gottman videotaped 124 newlywed couples in Seattle during a 15-minute discussion of a continuing disagreement, coded the emotions shown with the Specific Affect Coding System, and divided each discussion into five three-minute segments. They then followed the couples for six years. Results. The balance of positive and negative emotion in the first three minutes alone, for both husbands and wives, predicted which couples would divorce over the six years. For wives, the first three minutes predicted as well as the remaining twelve. Conclusion. A harsh start-up sets the course of the whole conversation, and repeated over thousands of conversations, the course of the marriage. Criticism. Like most divorce-prediction studies, it fitted statistical models to couples whose outcomes were already known, which inflates apparent accuracy (see below). Flooding. When a conflict turns hostile, a partner may experience flooding , becoming so physiologically aroused (Gottman's marker was a heart rate climbing above about 100 beats a minute, with a surge of stress hormones) that he can no longer listen, think or respond with humour, and feels only the urge to fight or flee. Flooding is what usually lies behind stonewalling. Its remedy is not to push on but to stop: Gottman advised a break of at least 20 minutes spent doing something calming, rather than rehearsing grievances, before returning to the discussion. Repair attempts and bids. Stable couples are not couples who never slip; they are couples who recover. A repair attempt is any statement or action, silly or serious, that stops negativity from escalating: "Can we start again?", a joke, a touch on the arm, "I'm sorry, that came out wrong." In stable couples repair attempts are made and, crucially, accepted. Gottman also studied the small moments of everyday life. A bid is any attempt by one partner to get the other's attention, interest or affection ("Look at that bird"; "Guess who called today"). The other can turn toward the bid (respond with interest), turn away (ignore it) or turn against it (respond with irritation). In Gottman's six-year follow-up of newlywed couples, those who stayed married had turned toward each other's bids about 86 percent of the time, and those who divorced only about 33 percent of the time. Perpetual problems and accepting influence. Gottman reported that most couples' conflicts (69 percent, in his estimate) are perpetual problems, rooted in lasting differences of personality or values, which never get solved. Happy couples do not solve them either; they keep talking about them with humour and affection instead of becoming gridlocked, a conclusion strikingly close to IBCT's acceptance. And in a study of newlyweds he found that husbands who accepted influence from their wives, letting their wives' views shape decisions rather than resisting them, were less likely to divorce. Gottman and his wife, the clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman , turned these findings into Gottman Method Couples Therapy, and in 1996 they founded the Gottman Institute in Seattle to train therapists. Its model of a healthy relationship is the Sound Relationship House , shown in Figure 7.13 and popularised in The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work (1999, with Nan Silver). The house has seven floors and two load-bearing walls. The ground floor is love maps : detailed knowledge of the partner's inner world, his worries, hopes, friends and daily stresses. Above it come sharing fondness and admiration (the antidote to contempt), turning towards instead of away (responding to bids), and the positive perspective, in which a store of goodwill leads each partner to read the other's neutral or ambiguous acts charitably (Robert Weiss had called this positive sentiment override ). Only then comes managing conflict, which means not solving every problem but using gentle start-up, repair, self-soothing and compromise, and living with perpetual problems through dialogue. The top floors are making life dreams come true (Gottman found that gridlocked conflicts often hide an unspoken dream) and creating shared meaning through rituals, roles, goals and symbols. The walls holding the house up are trust and commitment . 7 Create shared meaning Trust wall Commitment wall 6 Make life dreams come true 5 Manage conflict 4 The positive perspective 3 Turn towards instead of away 2 Share fondness and admiration 1 Build love maps Friendship floors Figure 7.13 Gottman's Sound Relationship House. Notice that friendship (the three lowest floors) is the foundation on which conflict management rests, and that the whole house is held up by the two walls of trust and commitment. How good is the research? Its observational detail is unmatched, and many of its findings, especially the corrosive effect of contempt and the importance of positive interaction, have held up. But the most famous claim, that Gottman can predict divorce with over 90 percent accuracy, needs care. In 2001 Richard Heyman and Amy Smith Slep pointed out that these accuracy figures came from fitting a statistical model to couples whose outcomes were already known. A model built and tested on the same small sample always looks better than it is; true prediction requires cross-validation, applying the model to a new sample, and that had not been done. The research is also correlational: contempt predicts divorce, but that does not prove that teaching couples to avoid contempt will prevent it. Gottman Method Couples Therapy itself has fewer randomised trials behind it than behavioural or emotionally focused couple therapy. Exam trap The four horsemen are criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling , and contempt is the strongest single predictor of divorce. "Anger", "complaint" and "conflict" are not horsemen: anger and complaints occur in happy marriages too. The 5 to 1 ratio of positive to negative interactions refers to behaviour during conflict in stable couples. Flooding (overwhelming physiological arousal) usually precedes stonewalling, and its antidote is self-soothing during a break. The Sound Relationship House has seven floors, from love maps at the bottom to shared meaning at the top, and two walls, trust and commitment . The research came from John Gottman and Robert Levenson; the therapy and the Gottman Institute (1996) are John and Julie Schwartz Gottman's. The evidence, and couples therapy in India Taken together, the trials give a consistent picture. Couples therapy works for relationship distress, with moderate effects; the main research-based approaches (behavioural, integrative behavioural, cognitive-behavioural and emotionally focused) produce broadly similar results when they are compared directly; many couples improve without becoming fully happy; and gains tend to fade over the years after therapy ends unless they are maintained. Table 7.19 sets the approaches side by side. Table 7.19 The main approaches to couples therapy compared. The best evidence concerns depression. Steven Beach and K. Daniel O'Leary argued that marital discord often precedes and maintains depression, especially in women, by removing support and adding daily criticism and conflict; if so, treating the marriage should treat the depression. In 1990 O'Leary and Beach randomly assigned 36 maritally discordant couples in which the wife was depressed to behavioural marital therapy, individual cognitive therapy for the wife, or a waiting list. Both therapies reduced depression substantially, but only marital therapy also improved marital satisfaction, and the difference held at one-year follow-up. A year later, Jacobson and his colleagues (1991) found the same pattern from the other side: for depressed wives in distressed marriages, behavioural marital therapy relieved depression as well as cognitive therapy did and was the only treatment that significantly improved the relationship, whereas for depressed wives in non-distressed marriages cognitive therapy worked better. The lesson is a matching rule: when marital discord is a central part of what keeps a depression going, couples therapy is the treatment of choice. The same logic underlies behavioural couples therapy for alcohol and drug problems, developed by Timothy O'Farrell and William Fals-Stewart, in which the partner joins a daily recovery contract; it has produced better abstinence and relationship outcomes, and less partner violence, than individual treatment alone. Exam trap "A male adult with depressive disorder and marital discord would benefit more from" marital and couple therapy (IHBAS 2020). Cognitive behaviour therapy is a good treatment for depression, but on its own it leaves the discord, the factor maintaining the depression, untouched; psychodynamic psychotherapy (Chapter 3) and supportive therapy (Section 3.10) share that limitation, because both treat the depressed individual rather than the relationship. The trials (O'Leary and Beach, 1990; Jacobson and colleagues, 1991) studied depressed wives, but the matching principle is the same for a depressed husband: when the relationship maintains the depression, treat the relationship. Indian context Couples therapy in India has to work with a different kind of marriage. Most marriages are still arranged, so partners may begin married life almost as strangers, and a marriage joins two families rather than two individuals. Many couples live in joint families, as Vikram and Ritika do, and the problem they bring is often about a mother-in-law, money sent to the husband's parents, or who decides how the child is raised. The in-laws may literally be in the room: parents sometimes bring a couple to therapy or insist on attending. A therapist cannot simply shut them out, because they may hold real power over the problem, but she must protect the couple's own subsystem (Minuchin's boundary between the spouses and the older generation, Section 7.4), seeing the couple alone for at least part of the work. Goals may differ too: harmony in the household and keeping the family together may matter more to a couple than individual romantic fulfilment, and a therapist who imposes other goals will lose them. Indian law builds counselling into marital disputes: the Family Courts Act, 1984 provides for counsellors attached to family courts and requires the court, in the first instance, to try to bring the parties to a settlement. Within psychiatry, the Family Psychiatry Centre at NIMHANS in Bengaluru pioneered family and marital therapy in Indian clinical settings. Couples often arrive indirectly: through a child's problem, through a gynaecologist or a sex clinic (Section 7.9), or after a complaint of dowry harassment or domestic violence, in which case safety and the law, including the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, come before any joint work. Clinical link In an interview you may be asked which couples therapy you would choose. A good answer starts from the formulation rather than the brand name. If the couple are fairly well connected but stuck on practical problems, behavioural skills training is quick and effective. If each is trying to change a partner who cannot or will not change, acceptance work (IBCT) is the core. If the fights are fuelled by hurt, fear and a sense that the partner is not there, emotionally focused work on the cycle is the natural fit. Whatever you choose, listen for Gottman's horsemen, especially contempt, and always screen each partner alone for violence before you begin. 7.9 Sex Therapy Lower yield · not asked yet In 1957 a gynaecologist at Washington University in St Louis, William Howell Masters (1915 to 2001), took on a research assistant. Virginia Eshelman Johnson (1925 to 2013) had no university degree, but she had a gift for putting people at ease, and Masters needed exactly that, because he intended to do something no scientist had done systematically before: to observe and measure what the human body does during sex, in a laboratory. Over the next eight years the two of them recorded the responses of several hundred volunteers. Their first book, Human Sexual Response (1966), was written in deliberately dry medical prose and became a bestseller anyway. Their second, Human Sexual Inadequacy (1970), turned the laboratory findings into a treatment, and within a decade it had changed how sexual problems were treated around the world. Before them, sexual problems were treated, when they were treated at all, in one of two ways. Psychoanalysts saw a man's impotence or a woman's "frigidity" (an old word, now rejected) as the surface sign of a deep unconscious conflict, to be explored over years of analysis. Behaviour therapists of the 1950s and 1960s had begun to treat sexual anxieties with desensitisation; Joseph Wolpe used sexual arousal itself as one of the responses that inhibit anxiety (Section 4.2). And Alfred Kinsey's surveys of 1948 and 1953 had shown how varied ordinary sexual behaviour is. Masters and Johnson's contribution was a brief, direct, couple-based therapy aimed at the anxiety and ignorance that keep most sexual problems going. In this book sex therapy means psychological treatment for problems of sexual function or satisfaction, usually brief, usually with the couple, and built around structured homework. This section describes Masters and Johnson's model and programme, the techniques that grew from them, the revisions of Helen Singer Kaplan, the PLISSIT model that tells any clinician how far to go, and the shape sex therapy takes in India. (The sexual dysfunctions themselves, their criteria and their causes, belong to the Psychiatric Disorders book; here they are named only as the targets of each technique.) The sexual response cycle Key study: Human Sexual Response (Masters and Johnson, 1966) Question. What actually happens in the human body during sexual arousal and orgasm? Method. From 1957 to 1965 Masters and Johnson recruited volunteers in St Louis and observed and measured them in the laboratory during masturbation and intercourse, recording heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, muscle tension and the changes in the genitals, including, by means of a camera inside a transparent artificial penis, changes inside the vagina. They observed 382 women and 312 men and estimated, conservatively, that they had recorded 10,000 complete cycles of sexual response. Results. Despite the obvious anatomical differences, men and women passed through the same sequence of four phases, driven by the same two physiological processes. Conclusion. Sexual response is an orderly physiological sequence that can be described, and when it goes wrong, retrained. Criticism. The volunteers were self-selected and, by design, people who could respond reliably under observation in a laboratory, and the pilot work had used sex workers; how far the findings generalise is uncertain. Critics such as the psychologist Leonore Tiefer later argued that by presenting genital physiology as a universal sequence, the model left out desire, meaning and the relationship, and set a single performance standard against which many people would then judge themselves. The two physiological processes are worth naming. Vasocongestion is the swelling of tissues as blood flows into them faster than it flows out; it produces erection of the penis, swelling of the clitoris and labia and lubrication of the vagina. Myotonia is the rise in muscle tension throughout the body, which peaks in the involuntary contractions of orgasm. Masters and Johnson divided the sexual response cycle into four phases (Figure 7.14). Excitement. Arousal begins in response to physical or psychological stimulation. In men the penis becomes erect; in women the vagina lubricates (fluid seeps through the engorged vaginal walls), the clitoris and labia swell and the inner part of the vagina lengthens and widens. In both sexes the nipples may become erect, and heart rate and blood pressure rise. Plateau. Arousal levels off at a high level, for anything from seconds to many minutes. In women the outer third of the vagina swells to form what Masters and Johnson called the orgasmic platform, and the clitoris draws back under its hood; in men the testes rise and enlarge, and a few drops of fluid may appear at the tip of the penis. Orgasm. The shortest phase: a series of rhythmic contractions of the pelvic muscles, at first at intervals of about 0.8 seconds in both sexes, with peak heart rate and breathing and an intense release of tension. In men orgasm is accompanied by ejaculation. Resolution. The body returns to its unaroused state. Men enter a refractory period , during which further erection or orgasm is not possible; it lasts minutes in young men and can stretch to hours or longer with age. Women have no refractory period and, if stimulation continues, may return to orgasm. Masters and Johnson described one pattern for men and three for women. In pattern A a woman may have repeated orgasms, returning to orgasm from the plateau level without dropping back; in pattern B she has a long plateau without orgasm and a slow resolution; in pattern C she rises rapidly through excitement to an intense orgasm and resolves quickly. Figure 7.14 also previews a later revision, Helen Singer Kaplan's three-phase model, which you will meet in Section 7.9.5.
