Masters and Johnson's four phases begin with excitement; men have a single pattern followed by a refractory period, whereas a woman in pattern A can return to orgasm from plateau-level arousal. Kaplan's later model adds desire before arousal and merges excitement and plateau. Exam trap Masters and Johnson's four phases, in order, are excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution ; there is no desire phase in their model. Desire was added by Helen Singer Kaplan , whose triphasic model is desire, excitement and orgasm . The two physiological processes are vasocongestion (blood engorgement) and myotonia (muscle tension). The refractory period belongs to the male resolution phase. Human Sexual Response (1966) is the physiology book; Human Sexual Inadequacy (1970) is the therapy book. Masters and Johnson's therapy programme The treatment described in Human Sexual Inadequacy rested on a handful of principles that were radical in 1970 and are now so standard that they are easy to overlook. The couple is the patient. Masters and Johnson held that in a sexual problem there is no such thing as an uninvolved partner. Whatever the origin of a man's erectile difficulty, his partner is part of the pattern that keeps it going, and both must take part in treatment. They treated the relationship, not one person's body. A dual-sex therapy team. Every couple was treated by a dual-sex therapy team , a male and a female co-therapist working together (Masters and Johnson were the original pair). Each partner then had a therapist of the same sex who could understand his or her experience and, when needed, interpret it to the other; neither partner faced two therapists of the opposite sex; and the therapists modelled open communication between a man and a woman. A rapid, intensive format. Couples came to St Louis, often from far away, and stayed for two weeks of daily sessions, free of work, children and relatives. The first days were given to detailed histories, each partner interviewed first by the same-sex therapist and then by the other, and to a medical examination. Then, at a round-table meeting, the four of them reviewed what the therapists had understood about the problem, and the homework began. Education. A great deal of time went to plain information about anatomy and sexual response, and to dismantling myths: that a man must always be ready for sex, that a woman's arousal should follow the same course and timing as a man's, that intercourse is the only "real" sex. Removing performance anxiety. Most important of all, they identified the immediate cause that keeps most sexual dysfunctions going: performance anxiety , the fear of failing sexually, which itself makes failure more likely. With it goes spectatoring : during sex, the anxious person mentally steps outside and watches himself or herself like a spectator ("Is it working? Is it going to fail again?"), monitoring and judging instead of feeling. Spectatoring kills arousal, failure confirms the fear, and the cycle tightens with every attempt. Viktor Frankl had described the same trap as hyper-reflection (Section 6.5). The results Masters and Johnson reported were remarkable. Across more than 790 people treated in their programme they reported, characteristically, failure rates rather than success rates, and overall about four in five responded within the two weeks. Almost all the men treated for premature ejaculation recovered, whereas lifelong erectile problems were the hardest, with success closer to 60 percent. Specialist clinics modelled on St Louis opened across the United States and then around the world. Later research was less kind. In 1980 Bernie Zilbergeld and Michael Evans argued, in an article pointedly titled "The inadequacy of Masters and Johnson", that the book never clearly defined success or failure and that its couples were highly selected. Clinics elsewhere, using similar methods, never matched the St Louis figures, perhaps partly because couples who had taken two weeks off and travelled to St Louis were exceptionally motivated. Several structural features of the programme also turned out to be unnecessary: one therapist proved as effective as two (LoPiccolo, Heiman, Hogan and Roberts, 1985), and weekly sessions as effective as daily ones (Heiman and LoPiccolo, 1983). What survived were the core ideas: treat the couple, educate, remove the demand to perform, and retrain the response step by step. Two parts of the Masters and Johnson record are now remembered as warnings. For some single men who had no partner they arranged partner surrogates , women who were not therapists and who took part in the exercises with the client; the practice drew fierce ethical criticism and remains controversial. And from 1968 to 1977 their institute ran a programme to "convert" gay men and lesbians to heterosexuality, reported in Homosexuality in Perspective (1979). Its claimed success was doubted even by people close to the institute, and conversion efforts of every kind are now condemned by professional bodies as ineffective and harmful (Section 4.4 tells this history for aversion therapy). Clinical link In sex therapy every touching exercise is done by the partners, in private, at home. The therapist talks, educates and assigns tasks, and never touches or watches. This is not prudishness but the most basic rule of professional boundaries. A boundary crossing is a minor departure from the usual frame that may even help the client (a brief self-disclosure, a session held somewhere other than the office); a boundary violation is a departure that exploits or harms the client to meet the therapist's needs, and a romantic or sexual relationship with a current client is the textbook example, forbidden by every professional code (ethics is covered in Chapter 1). Clients who talk about sex in therapy are unusually exposed, which is why the rule matters most here. Sensate focus The centrepiece of the programme was sensate focus : a graded series of touching exercises, done by the couple at home, in which the demand to perform is removed and attention is turned to sensation. It begins with a ban. In the first stages intercourse, and at first even touching of the breasts and genitals, is forbidden. The ban sounds odd, but it is the active ingredient. A man cannot fail to have an erection when an erection is not required, and a woman cannot fail to reach orgasm when orgasm is not on the agenda. With failure impossible, performance anxiety has nothing to feed on, and the spectator has nothing to watch. Because nothing is demanded of the person being touched, the exercises are often called non-demand pleasuring . The stages are summarised in Table 7.20; books number them slightly differently, and the first two are often called sensate focus I and II. Table 7.20 The stages of sensate focus. Stage What the couple does Rules Purpose 1 Non-genital touching Partners take turns touching, stroking and massaging each other's body, except the breasts and genitals; the receiver attends to sensations and later guides the giver's hand Intercourse and genital touching banned; no demand for arousal Remove performance anxiety; rediscover sensual pleasure; learn to communicate likes 2 Genital touching Touching now includes the breasts and genitals, still taking turns Still no intercourse and no goal of orgasm; erection or lubrication may come and go Arousal without demand; learning that arousal fades and returns 3 Non-demand intercourse Usually with the woman on top, the penis is inserted slowly and held still (containment); gentle movement is added gradually Either partner may stop and return to touching at any point Intercourse without pressure, built up in small steps 4 Full intercourse Intercourse with continued pleasuring Attention stays on sensation, not performance Carry the gains into ordinary sexual life Why does it work? First, it is in vivo desensitisation of sexual anxiety (Section 4.2), with a hierarchy that climbs from non-genital touching to intercourse and with pleasure itself as the response that competes with anxiety. Second, it redirects attention from self-monitoring to sensation, which is the cure for spectatoring and close to Frankl's dereflection (Section 6.5). Third, it forces communication. Partners have to say what they like, often for the first time, and in "hand-riding" the receiver lays a hand over the giver's to show the pressure and pace he or she enjoys, so that the message can be given without words. Fourth, it is diagnostic. Couples who "forget" the homework, break the ban, or quarrel before every exercise reveal the fears or relationship conflicts that the sexual problem may be protecting, and these then become the material of therapy. Push a case through it. Siddharth, 29, and Pooja, 25, married eight months ago in an arranged marriage and live with Siddharth's parents and grandmother in Lucknow. Intercourse has never succeeded. On the wedding night Siddharth, anxious and exhausted after days of ceremonies, lost his erection; since then he lies awake before every attempt wondering whether it will happen again, and it does. Pooja received no sex education, has heard frightening stories about pain, and has come to dread the attempts herself. Relatives have begun asking about a grandchild. After a medical check, the therapist teaches them about the sexual response and talks frankly about the myths they carry (that the first night must succeed, that a "real man" is always ready). Then she bans intercourse completely and prescribes stage 1 exercises three times a week. The first problem is practical: privacy in a crowded flat. The couple agree to use the hours when Siddharth's parents take his grandmother to the temple on Sunday mornings, and to close the bedroom door without apology. Within three weeks Siddharth reports, almost embarrassed, that he had firm erections during the exercises; because nothing was expected, nothing failed. They move through the stages over two months, with Pooja in control of every step of penetration (the dilator work described in Section 7.9.4 helped her), and they consummate the marriage without the drama they had both feared. Exam trap Sensate focus is Masters and Johnson's (1970), not Kaplan's, Frankl's or Wolpe's, although it resembles desensitisation and dereflection. Its active ingredient is the ban on intercourse , which removes the demand to perform. The order is non-genital touching, then genital touching, then non-demand intercourse, then full intercourse. It targets performance anxiety and spectatoring (anxious self-monitoring during sex). The other hallmarks of the Masters and Johnson programme are the couple as the patient , the dual-sex therapy team and the two-week daily format . Techniques for specific problems Sensate focus is the common base of sex therapy. On top of it, therapists add techniques aimed at particular problems. Premature (early) ejaculation. The oldest behavioural technique came from the American urologist James Semans , who in 1956 published "Premature ejaculation: a new approach". In the stop-start technique the partner stimulates the man's penis until he feels that ejaculation is approaching, and he signals her to stop. They wait until the sensation subsides, then begin again, repeating the cycle several times before he allows himself to ejaculate. Over weeks the man learns to recognise the sensations that come before the point of no return and gains control over them, and the exercise then moves to intercourse, first without movement and then with it. Masters and Johnson modified the method into the squeeze technique . Instead of simply stopping, the partner firmly squeezes the penis for a few seconds just below the head, with her thumb on the underside and two fingers on the upper side; the urge to ejaculate passes and the erection partly subsides, and after a short pause stimulation resumes. A later variant, the basal squeeze, applies pressure at the base of the penis so that it can be used during intercourse. Helen Singer Kaplan preferred the simpler stop-start method, and many therapists now use it in place of the squeeze. Both work well at first, with 60 to 90 percent of men improving, but the gains often fade, to about a quarter after three years or more, and medication that delays ejaculation is now often combined with them. Kegel exercises. The pelvic floor exercises published in 1948 by the gynaecologist Arnold Kegel (Section 4.8.5 describes his perineometer, an early form of biofeedback) train voluntary control of the pubococcygeus muscle, the sling of muscle around the vagina and urethra. Kegel exercises consist of repeatedly contracting and relaxing this muscle, which a person can locate by stopping the flow of urine midstream. In sex therapy they are used to increase a woman's awareness of genital sensation in orgasm problems, to show a woman with vaginismus that she can deliberately tighten and, more importantly, relax the muscles around the vagina, and in men as part of training in ejaculatory control. Vaginal dilators for vaginismus. In vaginismus, now part of genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder in DSM-5, involuntary tightening of the muscles around the vagina and fear of pain make penetration difficult or impossible. Treatment is graded exposure under the woman's own control. After education, relaxation and Kegel training, she inserts a series of vaginal dilators (smooth cylinders of graduated sizes), or her own fingers, starting with the smallest, at her own pace and only when relaxed, leaving each in place until the discomfort fades. Later her partner inserts them under her guidance, and finally, with the woman on top and in charge, the penis. All this happens within the sensate focus programme, so that arousal is maintained, and because the fear is sometimes linked to earlier sexual abuse, the therapist watches for distress and goes slowly. Success rates are high: in the studies reviewed by Barlow and Durand, 80 to 100 percent of women overcome the problem, often within a short time. Directed masturbation for lifelong orgasm problems. For a woman who has never had an orgasm, Joseph LoPiccolo and W. Charles Lobitz (1972) developed directed masturbation , a graded programme in which she first learns about her own body alone and then brings what she has learned into the relationship. The steps move from looking at her body and genitals with a mirror, through exploring by touch to find the areas that give pleasure, to focused self-stimulation for longer and more intense periods, with fantasy, erotic material or a vibrator where needed. Then her partner watches, then he stimulates her as she has shown him, and finally the stimulation is combined with intercourse. The programme was set out for women themselves in Becoming Orgasmic (1976) by Julia Heiman, Leslie LoPiccolo and Joseph LoPiccolo, and Lonnie Barbach ran similar groups for "pre-orgasmic" women. It is among the most successful of all sex therapy techniques, with 70 to 90 percent of women benefiting. To carry the gains into intercourse, therapists use what is called the bridge manoeuvre , usually credited to Kaplan: the clitoris is stimulated manually during intercourse until the woman is close to orgasm, and the manual stimulation is withdrawn earlier and earlier, so that intercourse itself increasingly carries her the rest of the way. Medication. Since sildenafil (Viagra) was approved for erectile dysfunction in the United States in 1998, drug treatment has transformed the management of erectile problems, and sex therapy now increasingly works alongside medicine rather than instead of it. A tablet can restore an erection; it cannot remove performance anxiety, teach a couple to talk or repair a relationship, which is why combined treatment often does best. (The drugs, and the physical causes of dysfunction, belong to the Psychiatric Disorders book.) Exam trap The stop-start technique is James Semans's (1956); the squeeze technique is Masters and Johnson's modification of it. Be careful: some textbooks, Barlow and Durand among them, describe "a procedure developed by Semans (1956), sometimes called the squeeze technique", so an item may credit Semans with the squeeze. If both names appear as separate options, pair stop-start with Semans and squeeze with Masters and Johnson. Both treat premature ejaculation . Directed masturbation (LoPiccolo and Lobitz, 1972) treats lifelong female orgasm problems; vaginal dilators treat vaginismus; Kegel exercises (1948) train the pubococcygeus muscle; the bridge manoeuvre is usually credited to Kaplan. Helen Singer Kaplan and the new sex therapy The most influential revision of Masters and Johnson came from New York. Helen Singer Kaplan (1929 to 1995) was born in Vienna, trained both as a psychologist and as a psychiatrist, and built her career in New York. At Cornell's medical college and the Payne Whitney Clinic she founded the first clinic for sexual disorders at an American medical school. In The New Sex Therapy (1974) she argued that Masters and Johnson's behavioural tasks and psychoanalytic understanding were not rivals but partners. Kaplan distinguished two levels of cause. The immediate causes of a sexual dysfunction are what is happening in the bedroom now: performance anxiety, spectatoring, a partner's demands, poor communication, ignorance of effective technique. The deeper or remote causes are conflicts within the person (guilt about sex, fear of intimacy, conflicts left over from childhood) and conflicts in the relationship (anger, power struggles, mistrust). Her treatment, known as brief sex therapy or psychosexual therapy, worked on both levels. The couple carried out prescribed sexual tasks at home, sensate focus and the specific techniques, and came to weekly outpatient sessions, usually with a single therapist rather than a dual-sex team, while carrying on their ordinary lives. In the sessions the therapist reviewed the tasks, and when a couple avoided them or reacted to them with anxiety or anger, she used psychodynamic exploration to understand the resistance before returning to the tasks. Her principle was to use the least intensive intervention that worked: behavioural tasks first, and psychodynamic work only to the depth needed to get past an obstacle. Many couples needed only the tasks; some had to work through deep material before the tasks would work at all. Kaplan's second great contribution concerned desire. In practice she kept meeting patients whose problem was not erection, lubrication or orgasm but a lack of interest in sex altogether, and they did not fit Masters and Johnson's model, which began with excitement. In Disorders of Sexual Desire (1979) she proposed a triphasic model of sexual response: desire, excitement and orgasm, three phases that are related but can be disturbed independently, so that each has its own family of dysfunctions. She thus added desire before arousal and treated plateau and resolution as parts of the other phases rather than as phases of their own. She also found desire problems the hardest to treat, often rooted in deeper conflict or depression. Her model shaped psychiatric classification: from DSM-III (1980) onwards the sexual dysfunctions were organised by phase of the response cycle, beginning with desire, and later editions described the cycle as desire, excitement, orgasm and resolution, joining Kaplan's first phase to Masters and Johnson's last. Feature Masters and Johnson Helen Singer Kaplan Key books Human Sexual Response (1966); Human Sexual Inadequacy (1970) The New Sex Therapy (1974); Disorders of Sexual Desire (1979) Model of response Four phases: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution Three phases: desire, excitement, orgasm Causes addressed Immediate: performance anxiety, spectatoring, ignorance, poor communication Immediate causes plus deeper intrapsychic and relationship causes Therapists Dual-sex co-therapy team Usually a single therapist Format Daily sessions for two weeks, away from home Weekly outpatient sessions; the couple stays in ordinary life Methods Education, sensate focus, squeeze technique, dilators Behavioural tasks plus psychodynamic work on resistance; stop-start technique Later researchers questioned whether any single linear sequence fits everyone. In 2000 the physician Rosemary Basson of the University of British Columbia proposed a circular model of women's sexual response, especially in long-term relationships. Many women, she argued, do not begin with spontaneous desire. They start from sexual neutrality, choose to engage for reasons of intimacy and closeness, and experience desire responsively, once arousal has begun; a satisfying experience then strengthens the motivation for the next time. Her purpose was partly to stop clinicians from diagnosing a dysfunction when a woman's response is simply different from the traditional sequence. Exam trap Kaplan's triphasic model has desire, excitement and orgasm (no plateau, no resolution); Masters and Johnson's has excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution (no desire). The DSM sequence of desire, excitement, orgasm and resolution combines the two. Kaplan's brief sex therapy combines behavioural tasks with psychodynamic exploration of resistance, usually with one therapist and weekly sessions; Masters and Johnson's was a behavioural and educational programme with a dual-sex team over two weeks. The New Sex Therapy (1974) is Kaplan's. The circular model built around responsive desire is Rosemary Basson's (2000). Annon's PLISSIT model Most people with sexual worries never see a sex therapist. They mention the worry, often in passing, to a general practitioner, a gynaecologist, a nurse, a counsellor or a psychologist who is seeing them for something else. How far should that professional go? In 1976 the American psychologist Jack S. Annon proposed an answer in the form of a graded model named after the initials of its four levels: the PLISSIT model , for Permission, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions and Intensive Therapy. Permission. By a calm, non-judgmental attitude and by what he says, the professional conveys that the client's thoughts, feelings, fantasies and behaviours are normal and acceptable (provided they harm no one), and that talking about sex here is allowed. For a student who is ashamed that he masturbates and fears that he is damaging himself, hearing a doctor say quietly that masturbation is a normal behaviour of most men and women may be all that he needs. Permission can also be permission not to do something: a woman does not have to want sex as often as a magazine says she should. Limited Information. The professional gives specific facts directly relevant to the concern, not a lecture: that masturbation does not cause weakness or impotence, that nocturnal emissions are normal, that penis size has little to do with a partner's satisfaction, that erections become slower with age, or that a particular medicine can affect sexual function. Specific Suggestions. After taking a brief sexual history, the professional gives specific suggestions aimed at the particular problem: sensate focus exercises, the stop-start technique, a change of position, a lubricant, setting aside unhurried time for intimacy. This level needs training in sex therapy. Intensive Therapy. When the first three levels have not helped, or the problem is bound up with deeper individual or relationship difficulties (trauma, serious conflict, depression, a complex dysfunction), the client is referred for intensive treatment by a specialist, which may be sex therapy, couples therapy, individual psychotherapy or medical care. The model works like a funnel. Most people's needs are met at the first two levels, fewer need the third, and only a minority need the fourth; each level requires more knowledge, skill and time than the one before, so that every professional can work at the level of his or her competence and refer onwards beyond it. Its great virtue is that it makes sexual health part of ordinary care, rather than something only specialists may mention. In the 2000s Bridget Taylor and Sally Davis proposed an extended version, the Ex-PLISSIT model, for use with people living with illness or disability: permission-giving is placed at the core of every level rather than only at the start, and the professional reviews and reflects on each conversation. Table 7.22 summarises the original model. Table 7.22 Annon's PLISSIT model (1976). Level What the professional does Example Who can offer it P: Permission Conveys that the client's feelings and behaviour are normal and that sex can be discussed "Many people worry about this; it is a normal thing to ask about." Any health professional LI: Limited Information Gives brief, specific facts relevant to the concern Explaining that nocturnal emissions do not cause weakness Any trained professional SS: Specific Suggestions Takes a sexual history and gives targeted behavioural suggestions Prescribing sensate focus or the stop-start technique A professional trained in sex therapy IT: Intensive Therapy Refers for specialist treatment of complex or deep-rooted problems Referral for sex, couples or individual therapy A specialist Exam trap PLISSIT is Jack Annon's (1976), and its levels, in order, are Permission, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions and Intensive Therapy . "IT" is Intensive Therapy, not "integrated treatment" or "individual therapy"; "LI" is limited information, not a full course of sex education. The levels are graded: most clients need only the first two, each level needs more expertise, and Intensive Therapy usually means referral. Do not mix it up with Kaplan's triphasic model or Masters and Johnson's four phases, which are models of the sexual response, not of how far a clinician should intervene. Sex therapy in India Sex therapy in India meets a particular landscape of beliefs. The best known is captured by dhat syndrome , a term introduced by the Indian psychiatrist Narendra Nath Wig in 1960 for the common presentation of young men who attribute weakness, fatigue, poor concentration, aches, worries about sexual performance and low mood to the loss of semen, which they believe they see as a whitish discharge in the urine or lose through masturbation or nocturnal emissions ("nightfall"). The belief draws on a popular reading of Ayurveda, in which semen ( shukra ) is the last and most concentrated of the seven dhatus , the essential bodily substances distilled from food through blood, flesh, fat, bone and marrow, so that losing it seems to drain the body's strength. DSM-5-TR lists dhat syndrome in its glossary of cultural concepts of distress and describes it not as a discrete disorder but as a cultural explanation of distress; it notes estimates that 64 percent of men attending psychiatric clinics in India for sexual complaints present in this way, and that comparable worries about white vaginal discharge occur among women. The people who present with dhat often have treatable depression or anxiety, which a clinician who simply says "there is nothing wrong with you" will miss. (Chapter 2 discusses idioms of distress and explanatory models; the syndrome itself belongs to the Psychiatric Disorders book.) Dhat is one member of a wider family of sexual myths that Indian clinicians meet every week: that masturbation causes weakness, impotence or a bent penis; that a man's sexual power is fixed in quantity and can be used up; that a small penis cannot satisfy a woman; that a bride must bleed on the wedding night. Many men first take these fears to self-styled sexologists who advertise on walls, in newspapers and online, promising cures for "night discharge" and "weakness", and who sell remedies that reinforce the very beliefs causing the distress. Many marriages are arranged and many couples marry with little accurate sex education, so clinics regularly see couples whose marriage remains unconsummated months or years after the wedding, usually because of a combination of the husband's performance anxiety and the wife's fear of pain or vaginismus, as with Siddharth and Pooja. The standard programme of education, sensate focus and graded dilators works well for them. Practical adaptations matter: privacy for homework in a joint family, the involvement of the extended family's expectations about children, and the fact that women are less likely to raise sexual concerns directly, often presenting instead to a gynaecologist with pain or a "white discharge". Clinical link PLISSIT fits the Indian sexual health clinic almost perfectly. A 22-year-old man arrives convinced that years of masturbation have drained his semen and caused his fatigue. Permission : take the worry seriously, listen to his explanation without ridicule, and say that masturbation is a normal behaviour. Limited information : explain, with a simple diagram, what semen is, that the body goes on producing it, that the whitish discharge he sees is usually harmless, and that his tiredness has other causes worth exploring. Many men need nothing more. If he also has depressive symptoms, treat or refer for them; if he has a specific problem such as early ejaculation, move to specific suggestions such as the stop-start technique; and if the anxiety is part of a wider disorder or a troubled marriage, refer for intensive therapy . Eight chairs stand in a circle. In them sit a retired bank manager who has not left his flat for a year except to come here, a college student who cuts her arms, a young father who flies into rages at work, a widow who cannot stop crying, a software engineer who has never had a friend he trusts, and three others. Two psychologists sit among them, not at the front. For the first ten minutes nobody says anything that matters. Then the student mentions, almost in passing, that she has not told anyone about her arms, and the widow says quietly, "I thought I was the only one who hides things." Something shifts in the room. The families and couples of Sections 7.1 to 7.9 were groups that existed before the therapist arrived and would go on existing after the therapist left. A therapy group is different. Its members are strangers, brought together for the sole purpose of helping one another change, and the relationships they form inside the room are the main instrument of that change. Group psychotherapy is the treatment of psychological problems in which a small number of selected people meet regularly with one or two trained therapists, and in which the interactions among the members, not only the interventions of the therapist, are used to bring about change. Notice the distinction hidden in that definition. A lecture to thirty patients is therapy in a group; group psychotherapy proper is therapy through a group. This section traces how clinicians discovered the difference, explains Irvin Yalom's account of why groups help, and then turns to the practical questions every group leader must answer: who should be in the group, how it should be run, how groups develop and what to do with members who make the work difficult. From tuberculosis classes to the Second World War The story usually begins in Boston in July 1905. Joseph Hersey Pratt (1872 to 1956) was a physician, trained under William Osler at Johns Hopkins, who was troubled by the fate of poor patients with tuberculosis. The standard treatment was months of rest, fresh air and good food in a sanatorium, which the poor of Boston's tenements could not afford. With money and meeting space provided by Emmanuel Church and its rector Elwood Worcester, Pratt gathered these patients into weekly meetings that he called "classes". He taught them the rules of home treatment, checked the diaries in which they recorded their weight, temperature and hours spent resting outdoors, and asked members who were improving to describe how they had done it. Pratt called his approach the class method , or home sanatorium treatment. What struck him over the following years was that his lectures were not the most powerful part of the treatment. The patients' encouragement of one another, the hope they drew from seeing others recover, and the sense of belonging to a class with a shared purpose seemed to matter as much as the medical instruction. Pratt preferred the word class to group, and his meetings were more education than psychotherapy, but he had stumbled on three of the therapeutic factors you will meet below: hope, universality and the sharing of information. Through the 1920s and 1930s a scattering of psychiatrists in the United States borrowed the idea for their own patients. In Washington, Edward Lazell gave lectures to groups of patients with schizophrenia at St Elizabeths Hospital. L. Cody Marsh, a minister turned psychiatrist, ran lectures, classes and group activities for hospitalised patients under a memorable motto: "By the crowd they have been broken; by the crowd they shall be healed." The American psychoanalyst Trigant Burrow (1875 to 1950) went further and, from the mid-1920s, analysed people together in groups rather than alone, describing what he called the group method of analysis; he believed that much individual disturbance reflected the distortions of society, and later renamed his approach phyloanalysis. In New York hospitals in the 1930s, Louis Wender and Paul Schilder (1886 to 1940) ran psychoanalytically oriented groups for inpatients and outpatients, interpreting the members' feelings towards one another as transference. Two men who disliked each other intensely gave the new field its names and its institutions. Jacob Levy Moreno (1889 to 1974), the Viennese psychiatrist who invented psychodrama (Section 7.11), claimed to have coined the terms group therapy and group psychotherapy, and in 1932 he presented his work on group psychotherapy to the American Psychiatric Association in Philadelphia. In 1942 he founded the society now called the American Society of Group Psychotherapy and Psychodrama. Samuel Richard Slavson (1890 to 1981), an engineer and educator turned therapist, began working in 1934 with groups of disturbed children at the Jewish Board of Guardians in New York. Finding that troubled children would not sit and talk, he gave them a room with tools, games and materials and a permissive adult, and let them work, play and quarrel together; he called this activity group therapy . In 1943 Slavson founded the American Group Therapy Association (the association's own emblem says 1942, so both years appear in books), later renamed the American Group Psychotherapy Association, which remains the main professional body for group therapists in the United States. What turned these scattered experiments into a profession was the Second World War. The armies of Britain and the United States suffered enormous numbers of psychiatric casualties, soldiers with what was then called war neurosis or battle exhaustion, and there were far too few psychiatrists to treat them one at a time. Group treatment began as a necessity and was soon recognised as a method in its own right. The most famous experiments took place at Northfield Military Hospital, a converted mental hospital at Northfield in Birmingham, England, which became a military psychiatric hospital in 1942. In the first Northfield experiment (1942 to 1943), the psychoanalysts Wilfred Bion and John Rickman ran the hospital's training wing as a group that was expected to take responsibility for its own discipline and morale; the army, alarmed by the apparent disorder, closed the experiment after about six weeks. The second Northfield experiment, which followed, was led by S. H. Foulkes with Tom Main and Harold Bridger, and it went further: the whole hospital was treated as a community in which every activity could be therapeutic. Main gave that idea a name, the therapeutic community, which Section 7.11 takes up. Figure 7.15 sets out the milestones of the whole group movement, including the methods taught in the next section. Notice how many beginnings cluster in the 1930s and 1940s. Exam trap Match each pioneer to the right first. Joseph Pratt (Boston, 1905) ran the first deliberate therapeutic groups, classes for poor patients with tuberculosis , and is often called the father of group therapy in American textbooks. Jacob Moreno coined the term group psychotherapy (presented to the American Psychiatric Association in 1932) and founded psychodrama. Samuel Slavson devised activity group therapy for children (1934) and founded the American Group Psychotherapy Association (1943; sometimes dated 1942). Trigant Burrow analysed patients in groups in the 1920s. S. H. Foulkes founded British group analysis . Irvin Yalom came much later (1970); he systematised group therapy but did not found it. Bion and Foulkes: the group as a whole Two of the Northfield psychoanalysts went on to build theories that treat the group itself, not just the individuals in it, as the thing to be understood. Wilfred Bion (1897 to 1979) you have met in Chapter 3 as the Kleinian analyst who described the mother as a container for her infant's unbearable feelings. After the war he ran small groups at the Tavistock Clinic in London, and the papers he wrote about them in the late 1940s were collected in Experiences in Groups (1961). Bion's groups were deliberately unstructured. He sat with them, refused to lead in the ordinary way, and commented only on what the group as a whole seemed to be doing. What he saw was that every group functions on two levels at once. On the first level is the work group : the group that meets to do its real task (to understand itself, to make a decision, to treat patients, to plan a festival), works rationally and cooperatively, puts up with frustration and learns from experience. On the second level, operating outside awareness, the group behaves as if it had come together for an entirely different purpose. Bion called these shared unconscious fantasies basic assumptions , and he described three of them. Dependency. The group behaves as if it has met to be looked after by a leader who knows everything and will provide all the answers. Members sit back, wait for the therapist to speak and treat each of the therapist's remarks as wisdom; when the leader fails to rescue them, they feel cheated and look for someone else to depend on. Fight-flight. The group behaves as if it has met to fight or to run away from an enemy, and it follows whoever offers to lead the fight or the escape. Fight shows itself as quarrelling, attacks on an outsider or on one member; flight shows itself as changing the subject, joking, lateness, absence and endless talk about matters outside the room. Pairing. The group behaves as if it has met so that two of its members will produce something (an idea, a plan, a new leader, almost a messiah) that will save it. The atmosphere is hopeful, and the group watches with interest as two members talk to each other. The hope must stay in the future; if the saviour actually arrived, the hope would die. Imagine the staff of a psychiatric ward in Mysuru holding a meeting to plan a new rehabilitation programme. In dependency, everyone waits for the head of department to announce what will happen. In fight-flight, the meeting becomes a complaint session about the hospital administration, and the actual plan is never discussed. In pairing, two enthusiastic junior doctors start sketching a scheme while everyone else watches hopefully and does nothing. In each case the basic assumption serves to relieve the group's anxiety, and in each case it stops the work group from working. Bion's ideas became the foundation of the Tavistock tradition of group relations training and of much organisational consulting, and his style of commenting on the group as a whole ("the group seems to be waiting for me to tell it what to do") remains a recognisable school of group therapy. S. H. Foulkes (born Siegmund Heinrich Fuchs; 1898 to 1976) was a German psychoanalyst who left Frankfurt for England in 1933 after the Nazis came to power. He ran his first therapy groups at Exeter, worked at Northfield during the war, founded the Group Analytic Society in London in 1952 and inspired the Institute of Group Analysis, set up in 1971 to train practitioners. His method, group analysis , is a psychoanalytic group therapy that he summed up as psychotherapy by the group, of the group, including its conductor. Several of its terms are worth knowing. Foulkes called the therapist the conductor rather than the leader, because the therapist's job is to help the group communicate, not to direct it, much as a conductor helps an orchestra to play. Members are encouraged to say whatever comes to mind in a free-floating discussion , the group's equivalent of free association (Section 3.2.3). Over time the group builds up its matrix , the shared web of communication and relationship within which every member's contribution takes on meaning; Foulkes pictured each individual as a nodal point in this network. Members see aspects of themselves reflected in others ( mirroring ) and are stirred by others' material that touches their own ( resonance ). Group-analytic groups are usually of seven or eight members, meet once or twice a week for ninety minutes, run for years and take in new members as others leave. Exam trap Bion's three basic assumptions are dependency, fight-flight and pairing . The work group is not a fourth basic assumption; it is the rational, task-oriented level that the basic assumptions interfere with. Do not give the basic assumptions to Foulkes, whose terms are the conductor , the matrix , mirroring and resonance, and whose method is called group analysis . And keep group analysis (Foulkes) apart from Maxwell Jones's therapeutic community (Section 7.11), a pairing examiners like to offer as distractors for each other. Yalom's eleven therapeutic factors Bion and Foulkes explained what groups are like. The question a practising clinician most wants answered is a different one: when group therapy works, what is it that does the work? The most influential answer came from Irvin Yalom (born 1931), the Stanford psychiatrist whose existential psychotherapy you met in Section 6.4. In 1970 he published The Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy , which became the standard textbook of the field and has gone through many editions, the later ones written with the Canadian psychiatrist Molyn Leszcz. Earlier writers had tried to list the mechanisms of group therapy (in 1955 Raymond Corsini and Bina Rosenberg had distilled nine, including acceptance, universalisation, ventilation and spectator therapy), but Yalom's list, drawn from clinical observation, patients' own accounts and research, is the one every exam asks about. He first called them curative factors and later therapeutic factors , and in their standard form there are eleven. Instillation of hope . Members see others who have improved, and they come to believe that the group can help them too. Hope keeps people coming long enough for the other factors to work, and leaders build it deliberately, by preparing members before the group begins and by pointing out progress when it happens. In an open group, a member who has been there for a year and is doing better is living proof for the newcomer. Universality . Members discover that they are not alone: that others have the same fears, secrets, impulses and miseries. Many people arrive convinced that they are uniquely wretched, and the relief of hearing someone else say the unsayable is enormous. Yalom sometimes asked members to write down anonymously the secret they would least like to share; the commonest, by far, was a deep conviction of being inadequate, of being a fraud who would one day be found out. This is the factor the widow in the opening scene experienced. Imparting information . This includes didactic instruction by the therapist (about the nature of an illness, its treatment, how anxiety works) and direct advice from members. It is central in psychoeducational groups and in groups for a shared problem (Section 7.10.9). In interactional groups advice itself rarely helps much, but the act of giving it shows care and interest, and early meetings are full of it. Altruism . Members help one another, and being useful to someone else raises the helper's self-esteem. Demoralised patients often believe they have nothing to offer anyone; discovering that their words have helped another person can be the most powerful experience of the group. Group therapy is one of the few treatments in which the patient is also a healer. Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group . The group resembles a family in many ways, with authority figures (the therapists, sometimes a man and a woman) and siblings (the other members) who compete for attention. Members tend to relive their early family relationships within it, and the difference is that the old patterns can now be noticed, explored and ended differently. A man who was always overshadowed by a brilliant older brother may find himself bitterly resenting the most articulate member; this time, instead of withdrawing, he can say so and see what happens. Development of socialising techniques . Members learn basic social skills, either directly (in a social skills group, by role play and practice) or indirectly, through honest feedback that is rarely available in ordinary life: "When you look at the floor while you talk, I feel you don't want me to answer." Imitative behaviour . Members model themselves on the therapist and on other members, trying out ways of speaking or of handling feelings that they have watched work for someone else. A member may also benefit from watching another member with a similar problem being helped, which earlier writers called spectator therapy. This is observational learning in Albert Bandura's sense (Chapter 4). Interpersonal learning . Yalom regarded this as the most powerful and most distinctive factor of interactional groups, and Section 7.10.4 explains it fully. In brief, members display their typical ways of relating to others inside the group, receive feedback about the effect they have, and learn to relate differently. It builds on Harry Stack Sullivan's interpersonal theory (Section 3.8.7): we come to know ourselves through our relationships, and our distortions of other people can be corrected only by checking them against others' perceptions. Group cohesiveness . This is the members' sense of belonging, of being accepted and valued, of "we-ness"; it is the attraction the group holds for its members. Yalom saw cohesiveness as the group equivalent of the therapeutic relationship in individual therapy, and as the condition that makes the other factors possible: people take risks, disclose and hear hard feedback only in a group they trust. Cohesive groups have better attendance and fewer dropouts, and research has repeatedly found a modest but reliable link between cohesion and outcome. Catharsis . Members express strong feelings, positive and negative, that they have held back, often for years, and feel relief. But Yalom was emphatic that catharsis is not enough on its own: the release of emotion helps only when it happens within a supportive group and is followed by some understanding of what it means. Shouting in a room full of strangers changes nothing by itself. Existential factors . Members come to recognise that life is sometimes unfair, that there is no escape from some of life's pain and from death, that however close they are to others they must face life alone, and that they are ultimately responsible for the way they live it, however much help they receive. Yalom found that patients often rated these items highly, to his surprise, and they are the bridge to his later existential psychotherapy. Table 7.23 condenses the list, with the kind of sentence a member might say for each. It helps to see that the factors are not all of the same kind. Some are conditions for change (cohesiveness, hope), some are mechanisms of change (interpersonal learning, imitative behaviour) and some are themselves changes (relief through catharsis, a new sense of responsibility). Their importance also shifts with the type of group and with time: hope, universality and information matter most in the early weeks and in short, structured groups, while interpersonal learning and cohesiveness matter most in long-term interactional groups. Which of the therapeutic factors do patients themselves think helped them? Method. Yalom, with James Tinklenberg and Marshall Gilula, studied twenty successful patients who had completed long-term outpatient group therapy (on average about sixteen months) for neurotic and characterological problems. Each sorted sixty statements, five for each of twelve categories, from "most helpful to me" to "least helpful to me". (The twelve categories split interpersonal learning into input, learning from feedback, and output, learning to relate, and included self-understanding, which is why some books list twelve factors.) Results. The categories ranked highest were interpersonal learning through feedback (input), catharsis, cohesiveness and self-understanding; the lowest were family re-enactment, guidance and identification (imitation). Conclusion. Long-term outpatients credit their improvement above all to honest feedback, emotional expression within a cohesive group and new understanding of themselves. Criticism. The patients were few, all successful and all reporting retrospectively; the questionnaire contained more interpersonal items than others; and later studies show that rankings depend on the group. Inpatients and members of brief groups rate instillation of hope, universality and existential factors more highly, and members of self-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous stress hope, universality and altruism. Exam trap "The realisation that one is not alone in one's suffering" is universality . Do not confuse it with instillation of hope (seeing that others have improved), altruism (being helped by helping) or catharsis (expressing pent-up feeling). Curative factors and therapeutic factors are the same list under its older and newer names. Yalom's eleven group factors are not his four ultimate concerns of existential psychotherapy (death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness, 1980; Section 6.4.4); the only overlap is that "existential factors" is one of the eleven. Options such as free association and interpretation (psychoanalysis, Chapter 3), token reinforcement and shaping (behaviour therapy, Chapter 4) or schema reconstruction and mode work (schema therapy, Section 5.7) are never Yalom's factors. The group as a social microcosm: the here-and-now Why should a group of strangers, who will never meet outside the room, be a good place to change how one relates to the people who matter? Yalom's answer is that a therapy group becomes, given time and freedom, a social microcosm : a miniature version of each member's social world. Members do not describe their interpersonal problems so much as act them out, in front of witnesses. Mahesh, who complains that nobody at home ever listens to him, talks over everyone in the group and turns every topic back to himself. Lata, who feels exploited by her family, rushes to comfort every member who is upset and never once asks for anything for herself. Anil, who cannot understand why his colleagues avoid him, makes sarcastic jokes whenever anyone in the group becomes serious. Within a few weeks the group has a front-row view of the very patterns that bring each member to therapy. This makes possible the sequence of interpersonal learning . A member displays a characteristic pattern; other members react to it and, if the group's norms allow, say how it affects them; with the leader's help, the member comes to see the pattern, its effect on others and his or her own part in it; the member then tries out a different way of behaving in the relative safety of the group; and the new behaviour gradually carries over to relationships outside. In Sullivan's language, members correct their parataxic distortions (seeing others through the lens of earlier relationships) by consensual validation , checking their perceptions against those of several other people. Each time a member takes a risk and the expected disaster does not follow, he or she has the kind of corrective emotional experience that Franz Alexander described for individual therapy (Section 3.6.2). For the social microcosm to do its work, the group must attend to the here-and-now : what is happening in the room, at this moment, between these people, rather than the there-and-then of members' past lives and outside relationships. Yalom described the here-and-now as working in two tiers. The first tier is experiencing : the leader steers members towards their immediate feelings about one another, about the leader and about the group ("How are you feeling towards Lata right now?"). The second tier is process illumination : the group steps back and examines what has just happened, why it happened and what it means, in what Yalom called a self-reflective loop. Both tiers are needed. Experiencing without illumination is an emotional event that teaches nothing, the trap of many encounter groups (Section 7.11.6); illumination without experiencing is an intellectual discussion with no feeling in it. The word process here carries the meaning that Section 7.1 gave it for families. The content of a group discussion is what it is about (a member's divorce, a quarrel with the boss); the process is how it unfolds: who speaks, who interrupts, who rescues whom, who goes quiet and why the group keeps changing the subject whenever someone begins to cry. The leader's most characteristic intervention is a process comment that turns attention from content to process: "I notice that each time Shabnam starts talking about her mother, someone makes a joke. I wonder what that is about." Leaders also learn to bring outside material into the room. When a member says that his boss makes him feel invisible, the leader might ask, "Is there anyone here who makes you feel a little like that?" The here-and-now does not forbid talk of the past or of outside life; it uses that talk as a bridge back to the present, where change can be observed and practised. Exam trap Yalom's emphasis on the here-and-now means using the members' immediate interactions in the group, the social microcosm , as the engine of change: working with interpersonal patterns as they appear in the session and then illuminating them (experiencing, then process illumination). It does not mean avoiding all discussion of outside life (outside material is used as a bridge to the present), replacing individual therapy permanently, bypassing group dynamics (they are the whole point), discussing only events outside the group, limiting the group to didactic teaching, or disputing irrational beliefs (Albert Ellis's REBT, Section 5.2). Gestalt therapy also speaks of the here and now (Section 6.3), but there it means one person's present awareness; Yalom's here-and-now is interpersonal. The leader's tasks If the members do much of the healing, what does the leader do? Yalom described three basic tasks. The first is the creation and maintenance of the group . The leader is the group's gatekeeper: he or she selects and prepares the members, fixes the time, place and length of meetings, keeps the membership stable, works to prevent dropouts, and deals with anything that threatens the group's survival, such as persistent lateness, members meeting secretly outside the group, or one member being driven out as a scapegoat. The second task is culture building . A group's most powerful influences on its members are its norms , the unwritten rules about what is done and not done, and once norms form they are hard to change. The leader tries to shape norms that serve therapy: that members speak honestly about their feelings, including feelings about one another; that they stay with the here-and-now; that they accept one another without judging; that the members, not just the leader, are the main source of help; and that the group itself is valued. Leaders build norms in two roles at once: as a technical expert , who explains and reinforces the rules, and as a model-setting participant , who demonstrates by example the honesty, attentiveness and non-defensive acceptance of feedback that they hope members will adopt. A degree of therapist transparency , judicious disclosure of the leader's own here-and-now reactions ("I find myself feeling shut out when the group jokes like this"), is one of the most effective ways to model these norms. The third task, already described, is activation and illumination of the here-and-now . Many groups are led by two therapists, an arrangement called co-therapy (Section 7.6 described it in family work). Co-therapists can support each other, notice more, cover for each other's absences and model a respectful relationship in which disagreement is safe; a male and female pair can evoke parental feelings that feed the corrective recapitulation of the family. The risks are rivalry between the leaders, competition for the group's affection and members playing one leader off against the other, which is why co-therapists need time together after each session to talk through what happened. The best evidence about what effective leaders actually do came from a study you met in Section 6.2.7: Encounter Groups: First Facts (1973) by Morton Lieberman , Irvin Yalom and Matthew Miles , who followed Stanford students through encounter groups of many different schools. Observers rated the leaders' behaviour, and four basic leader functions emerged. Emotional stimulation means challenging, confronting, revealing one's own feelings and pushing members to express theirs. Caring means offering support, warmth, protection and acceptance. Meaning attribution means explaining, clarifying and interpreting, giving members a framework for understanding what is happening to them. Executive function means setting limits, rules and goals and managing time and procedure. The most effective leaders were high in caring and in meaning attribution and moderate in emotional stimulation and executive function. Leaders very high in emotional stimulation, the charismatic, aggressive "energisers", produced the most casualties, and leaders with too little executive function ran chaotic groups. Notice what this says about catharsis: members who had intense emotional experiences without any framework for understanding them did not change, which is exactly why Yalom insisted that experiencing must be followed by illumination. Clinical link Confidentiality is harder to promise in a group. You, the professional, are bound by your code of ethics and the law (Chapter 1); the other members are not bound in the same way, and you cannot guarantee what they will do. In the pre-group interview, explain this honestly, make "what is said here stays here" a firm group rule, agree how members will handle chance meetings outside, and ask them to report any outside contact with one another to the group. In smaller Indian towns, where members may know each other's families, these conversations matter even more. Composition, selection and preparation A group can be no better than its membership, and most of a leader's decisions about membership are made before the first meeting. For a heterogeneous outpatient interactional group, Yalom's advice was that selection is mainly a matter of exclusion. People are unlikely to benefit, and may disrupt the group, if they cannot take part in its primary task: those who are acutely psychotic, actively misusing alcohol or drugs, in an acute suicidal crisis, severely cognitively impaired, intensely paranoid or antisocial. Many such people do well in specialised groups designed for them; what they need is a different group, not no group. Good candidates are motivated, have problems that are at least partly interpersonal (loneliness, shyness, difficulty with intimacy or anger) and can both give and receive feedback. The best single predictor of staying and benefiting is the member's attraction to the group. Leaders also avoid creating a lone group deviant , a member who differs sharply from everyone else (the only older person, the only member with a psychotic illness), because such members are the most likely to drop out. The first design decision is the mix of members. A homogeneous group brings together people with the same problem or situation: a group for bereaved spouses, for women with breast cancer, for adolescents with eating disorders, for men with alcohol dependence. Homogeneous groups become cohesive quickly, offer immediate universality and support, attend well and suit brief, focused work, but they can stay superficial and offer less interpersonal learning. A heterogeneous group mixes people with different problems, backgrounds and interpersonal styles, as in the Bengaluru group at the start of this section. Heterogeneity makes for a richer social microcosm, more friction and more to learn, but cohesion takes longer. Yalom's rule of thumb was to seek heterogeneity in members' conflict areas and ways of coping and homogeneity in their degree of vulnerability, so that no member is far more fragile than the rest. The second decision is whether membership will change. A closed group starts with a fixed set of members who begin and end together, usually for a fixed number of sessions, as in a twelve-session cognitive behavioural group; it develops cohesion steadily and passes through its stages together, but it shrinks as members drop out. An open group admits new members as places become free, so its membership changes continually, as in an inpatient ward group, a self-help meeting or a long-term outpatient group (when members join only occasionally, such groups are sometimes called slow-open). Open groups offer continuity and let newcomers learn from veterans, but each arrival and departure disturbs the group. Table 7.24 summarises these choices together with size and frequency. Decision Option one Option two Usual guidance Mix of members Homogeneous: same problem; quick cohesion and support Heterogeneous: varied problems and styles; more interpersonal learning Mix conflict areas, match vulnerability Membership over time Closed: fixed members, fixed length Open: members join and leave Closed for brief structured groups; open for wards and long-term groups Size Small: fewer than five, little interaction Large: more than ten, too little time each Seven or eight is ideal; five to ten works Frequency and length Outpatient: weekly, 75 to 90 minutes Inpatient: often daily, shorter sessions Brief groups run for weeks; interactional groups for a year or more Finally, members need pre-group preparation . Dropouts are common in the first dozen meetings, and the commonest reasons are that members did not understand what the group was for, were frightened by its early awkwardness, or felt like outsiders. In one or more individual meetings before the group begins, the leader explains how the group works and why talking about relationships in the room helps, warns that the first weeks often feel frustrating and pointless, sets out the rules on attendance, confidentiality and outside contact, agrees each member's goals, and corrects common misconceptions (that group therapy is second-rate treatment for those who cannot get individual therapy, or that members will be forced to reveal everything). Research has consistently found that such preparation reduces dropout and speeds the group's engagement. Exam trap A closed group has fixed membership from start to finish; an open group takes in new members as others leave. Homogeneous means the members share a problem or characteristic; heterogeneous means they differ. Do not reverse the advantages: homogeneous groups gel faster and give more support; heterogeneous groups give more interpersonal learning. The ideal size of an interactional group is about seven or eight . Stages of group development Groups change as they grow older, and they change in roughly predictable ways. The most widely taught description came in 1965 from the American educational psychologist Bruce Tuckman , who reviewed some fifty studies of small groups of many kinds (therapy groups, training groups, laboratory groups and natural work groups) in a paper in the Psychological Bulletin called "Developmental sequence in small groups". Tuckman looked at two strands of development at once, the relationships among members and the way they tackle the group's task, and he named four stages with a rhyme that has made them famous. Forming . Members are polite, anxious and uncertain. They test what behaviour is acceptable, look to the leader for direction and depend on the leader for structure. The unspoken questions are "What are we here for?" and "Is it safe?" Storming . Conflict breaks out: members resist the task, compete for influence, form factions and, very often, turn against the leader, who has failed to provide the answers they wanted. Norming . The group pulls together. Members accept one another, develop shared norms and roles, and begin to express personal opinions and feelings openly. A sense of cohesion appears. Performing . The relationships the group has built become a tool for its task. Roles are flexible, energy goes into the work, and in a therapy group, members do the real work of insight and change. In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Conover Jensen reviewed the research that had appeared since, in "Stages of small-group development revisited", and added a fifth stage. Adjourning is the ending of the group: completing the task, reviewing what has been achieved and dealing with the separation, with the mixture of pride, sadness and loss that endings bring. Some writers call it mourning. Yalom, writing about therapy groups, described a similar sequence in three stages. In the initial stage of orientation, hesitant participation and search for meaning, members wonder how the group will help them, depend heavily on the leader, give one another advice and look for similarities. In the second stage of conflict, dominance and rebellion , members struggle for control and status, criticise one another and almost always attack the leader, who has not turned out to be the all-knowing figure they hoped for. In the third stage, the development of cohesiveness , members grow close, trust one another and disclose more; at first the new closeness may suppress negative feelings, and only a mature group can hold both affection and criticism. Later comes termination , which the leader treats as an important piece of work in its own right: facing the end of the group is a small rehearsal for the losses and endings of life. A third model, from the American psychologist William Schutz (1925 to 2002), derived the sequence from his FIRO theory (Fundamental Interpersonal Relations Orientation, 1958) of three interpersonal needs: groups deal first with inclusion (am I in or out?), then with control (who has power?) and then with affection (how close will we be?). Tuckman's five stages (top) line up with Yalom's account of therapy groups and with Schutz's sequence of inclusion, control and affection. Notice that every model puts a period of conflict before real cohesion; in practice the stages blur, and groups slip back when members join or leave. Two practical lessons follow. First, conflict is a normal and necessary stage, not a sign that the group is failing; a group that never storms seldom becomes truly cohesive, and a leader who smothers every disagreement keeps the group stuck at forming. Second, the leader's job changes with the stage: providing structure, safety and hope early on, tolerating and helping the group understand its attacks on the leader in the storming phase, supporting the new norms, stepping back when the group performs, and helping it to face its ending. Bion's basic assumptions, by contrast, are not stages at all: a group can slip into dependency or fight-flight at any point in its life. Exam trap The order is forming, storming, norming, performing (Bruce Tuckman, 1965 ), with adjourning added in 1977 by Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen . Norming comes before performing; storming is the conflict stage. The stages are Tuckman's, not Yalom's; Yalom's own three stages are orientation, conflict and cohesiveness. Inclusion, control and affection are Schutz's (FIRO). Problem members Every group therapist meets members whose behaviour seems to block the group's work. Yalom's advice about all of them is the same in principle: the problem member is also a group problem, the behaviour is a here-and-now display of the member's interpersonal pattern, and the aim is to understand it, not to silence or expel the member. Three types are classic. The monopoliser (or monopolist) talks compulsively, fills every silence, interrupts, and turns every topic back to his or her own concerns. Monopolising is usually driven by anxiety: silence feels unbearable, and talking keeps the anxiety at bay. At first the other members are relieved that someone is talking and that they need not; later they grow resentful, but they say nothing and quietly collude. A leader who simply cuts the monopoliser off, or who lets the group gang up on him, creates a scapegoat (Section 7.1.4). The more useful move is to ask the group about its part: "The group seems to let Mahesh carry the conversation every week. I wonder what it gets out of that, and what it costs?" The monopoliser can then hear, with support, how the behaviour affects others. The silent member rarely speaks. Silence may reflect shyness, fear of exposure or of losing control, contempt for the group, or simply a person who learns by watching (and members can benefit from imitative behaviour and spectator learning without saying much). But a member who stays silent for months cannot get feedback or practise new behaviour, and the group begins to wonder what he or she is thinking. The leader invites participation gently, often by noticing non-verbal reactions ("You looked moved when Asha was speaking"), never forces disclosure, and treats the silence itself as here-and-now behaviour that can be understood. The help-rejecting complainer is a term coined in 1952 by the American psychiatrist Jerome Frank (1909 to 2005) and his colleagues for a member who constantly asks the group for help and then rejects every piece of help offered. Every suggestion is met with "Yes, but...": he has already tried it, it would never work in his case, his situation is worse than anyone's. Eric Berne later described the same pattern as the game "Why don't you, yes but" (Section 3.9.5). Beneath it lies a painful combination of dependency and mistrust, and often hostility towards anyone in authority; the complainer needs help desperately and cannot bear to be helped. The group's usual response, ever more advice followed by exasperation, only feeds the pattern. The leader stops offering solutions, acknowledges how hard the member's situation is, and helps the group talk about the feelings that the complainer stirs in them, so that the pattern itself becomes the subject of the work.
