Exam trap The help-rejecting complainer (Jerome Frank and colleagues, 1952) asks for help and rejects it all; the monopoliser dominates the talking. Berne's "Why don't you, yes but" is the transactional analysis name for the same help-rejecting pattern. In each case the leader treats the problem as the group's business, not as one member's fault. Cognitive behavioural and psychoeducational groups, and the evidence Not every group is an interactional group in Yalom's style. The Association for Specialists in Group Work in the United States distinguishes four types: task groups (committees and work teams, aimed at getting a job done), psychoeducational groups (structured groups that teach information and skills, often to people who are well but facing a problem or risk), counselling groups (for everyday personal and interpersonal problems) and psychotherapy groups (for more serious and lasting psychological problems). Psychoeducational groups are the descendants of Pratt's classes. Examples include the relatives' groups of family psychoeducation for schizophrenia (Section 7.2.5), stress management and diabetes education groups (Chapter 9), and Peter Lewinsohn's Coping with Depression course, which taught people with depression in a classroom format, with a textbook and homework. Cognitive behavioural groups apply the methods of Chapters 4 and 5 in a group. They are structured and time-limited, follow an agenda, teach skills, set homework, and are usually closed and homogeneous; the leader is more teacher and coach than process commentator. The group adds things individual therapy cannot: universality and hope from others with the same problem, models to imitate, partners for practice and an audience that makes exposure real. In Richard Heimberg's cognitive behavioural group therapy for social anxiety, developed in the 1980s, members enact feared situations (giving a speech, starting a conversation) with other members playing the audience, then examine the anxious predictions that the exposure tested. Dialectical behaviour therapy teaches its skills in weekly groups (Section 5.8), social skills training is usually done in groups (Sections 4.7 and 9.8), and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy is delivered to classes of a dozen or so (Section 5.9). In these groups the information, hope, universality and cohesiveness factors do most of the work; interpersonal learning in the here-and-now is less emphasised. Is group therapy as good as individual therapy, or merely cheaper? A 1998 meta-analysis by Chris McRoberts, Gary Burlingame and Matthew Hoag found no overall difference in outcome between group and individual formats, and later reviews by Burlingame and colleagues have reached the same broad conclusion for many conditions, including depression, social anxiety, panic disorder, eating disorders and substance misuse. Groups treat several people for the time of one therapist, and some members prefer them. Cohesion and the quality of preparation predict outcome, and dropout is the format's chief weakness. Group therapy is not second-best treatment; for problems rooted in relationships it may be the treatment of choice. Indian context Wilfred Bion, the theorist of basic assumptions, was born in Mathura in 1897 and spent his early childhood in India before being sent to school in England. Group methods are now a routine part of Indian inpatient wards and de-addiction programmes, and they need some adaptation. Members may expect the leader to give advice and direction like a guru, which can stall the here-and-now and tempt the group into Bion's dependency assumption (the guru-chela model of the Indian therapeutic relationship is discussed in Section 8.11). Groups are often conducted in a mix of languages, relatives may expect to attend, and members may be reluctant to criticise an older member openly. A leader who explains the method carefully in the pre-group interview, and who models respectful honesty, usually finds that the therapeutic factors travel well. 7.11 Psychodrama, Encounter Groups, Self-Help and Therapeutic Communities Medium yield · 5 Qs The groups of Section 7.10 mostly sit in a circle and talk. This section is about groups that do something else. Some act out their members' lives on a stage. Some meet to learn how groups themselves work, or to grow as people rather than to recover from illness. Some have no professional in the room at all. And some are not a meeting but a whole hospital, in which every conversation in the corridor is part of the treatment. Each of these grew from a particular person and a particular moment: a Viennese doctor watching children play make-believe in a park, a German refugee social scientist running a workshop in Connecticut, two drinkers talking through a night in Akron, Ohio, and a British psychiatrist who found that his patients learned more from one another than from his lectures. Together they make up much of what clinical psychology inherited from the twentieth century's discovery of the group. Jacob Levy Moreno and the theatre of spontaneity Jacob Levy Moreno, whom you met in Section 7.10.1 as the man who named group psychotherapy, was born in Bucharest in 1889 and grew up in Vienna, where he qualified in medicine in 1917. Even as a student he was drawn to action rather than talk. He liked to tell how he would join the children in Vienna's public gardens and invent stories with them that they then acted out, and how he organised groups of women working as prostitutes in the Spittelberg district to meet and discuss their common problems, an early example of the self-help group. He also liked to tell of a meeting in 1912, after one of Sigmund Freud's lectures, at which he said to Freud: "I start where you leave off. You meet people in the artificial setting of your office. I meet them on the street and in their homes... You analyse their dreams. I try to give them the courage to dream again." Moreno was a showman and an inventor of his own legend, so such stories are best read as statements of his philosophy, but the philosophy is clear: people are healed by acting spontaneously in the presence of others, not by lying on a couch. In 1921 Moreno opened the Stegreiftheater , the Theatre of Spontaneity, in Vienna (its first public performance was in April 1921; from 1922 the company played in a rented room of its own, so some books give 1922). Its actors had no scripts. They improvised plays from suggestions shouted by the audience or from the day's newspaper headlines. The episode that Moreno later told as the birth of psychodrama concerned one of his actresses, Barbara, who was admired for playing sweet, gentle heroines. Her husband George came to Moreno in distress: at home, he said, the gentle Barbara was a shrew who flew into rages and abused him. Moreno began casting her in coarse, violent roles: a streetwalker, a woman who fights in the gutter. She played them with gusto, and George reported that her outbursts at home grew fewer. Before long Moreno had the couple act scenes from their own marriage on stage, with the audience watching, and the marriage improved further. Whether or not it happened exactly so, the story contains every ingredient of psychodrama: real life brought onto a stage, enacted rather than described, before a group that is moved by it. Moreno emigrated to the United States in 1925. In New York he developed both psychodrama and sociometry (Section 7.11.4), and in 1936 he opened a sanatorium at Beacon, a town on the Hudson River north of New York City, with a purpose-built therapeutic theatre: a round stage on three levels, with a balcony above it. With his wife, Zerka Toeman Moreno (1917 to 2016), who refined and taught the method for decades after his death, he trained psychodramatists from all over the world. Moreno died at Beacon in 1974. The five elements and three phases of psychodrama Psychodrama is a group method in which one member enacts scenes from his or her life, past, present, feared or wished-for, on a stage, with other members playing the other people in those scenes, under the guidance of a trained director, in order to explore and change the way he or she feels and acts. Moreno described five instruments that every psychodrama needs. The protagonist. The protagonist is the member whose life is being enacted in this session. Moreno chose the word from Greek drama: the first actor, around whom the play turns. The director. The director is the trained therapist who guides the enactment. Moreno described the director as at once a producer (who stages the scenes), a therapist (who keeps the protagonist safe and moving towards change) and an analyst (who makes sense of what is revealed). The auxiliary egos. Auxiliary egos , often simply called auxiliaries, are the group members (or trained staff) who play the other people in the protagonist's world: a father, a boss, a dead child, even a part of the protagonist's own self. They take their cues from the protagonist and the director. The audience. The other members watch, and they are not passive. They support the protagonist, are moved by recognising their own lives in the drama, and may be drawn in as auxiliaries. The stage. The stage is the space in which the action happens, a raised platform at Beacon but often just a cleared area of a room. It marks the boundary between talking about life and living it, and it allows what Moreno called surplus reality : scenes that never happened and never could, such as a conversation with someone who has died. A session moves through three phases. In the warm-up , the director uses exercises, movement and sharing to build trust and spontaneity in the group, and a protagonist emerges, either by volunteering or by the group's choice. In the action phase, the protagonist, guided by the director, sets the scene (the room, the furniture, the time of day), chooses auxiliaries and enacts the story, typically moving from a scene in the present towards an earlier, more central one, reaching an emotional peak, and then trying out a new way of responding. In the sharing phase, the protagonist rejoins the group, and members tell what the drama touched in their own lives. Sharing is personal: members do not analyse, interpret or advise, because a protagonist who has just exposed so much needs to hear "this is my story too", not a verdict. Training groups sometimes add a fourth phase, processing, in which the director's technique is discussed. Follow a session to see how the parts fit. Divya, a twenty-six-year-old engineer in Pune, volunteers in the warm-up. Her father died suddenly a year ago, two weeks after an angry phone call in which she told him she was leaving her government job to join a start-up. In the action phase the director asks her to set the scene of that call: her hostel room, the phone, the evening. A member she chooses plays her father. She speaks to him, stiffly at first. The director then asks her to set up a scene that never happened: her father, sitting in a chair, one last time. Now the director brings in the techniques of the next subsection, and the scene ends with Divya, in tears, saying what she never said. In the sharing, a man in the group speaks of the brother he never forgave, and a woman of her own father's silence. Divya leaves feeling not exposed but accompanied. Techniques, spontaneity and catharsis Psychodramatists use a large repertoire of techniques, but six are examined again and again (Table 7.26). In role reversal , the protagonist and an auxiliary swap places: Divya sits in her father's chair and speaks as him, while the auxiliary plays Divya. Role reversal lets the protagonist see the situation from the other person's side, often producing sudden empathy ("As him, I can feel how frightened he was for me"); it lets the protagonist see herself as others see her; and it shows the auxiliary how the absent person really speaks, so that the auxiliary can play the part more truly. Moreno regarded it as the heart of the method. In doubling , an auxiliary stands beside or slightly behind the protagonist, adopts her posture and voices the thoughts and feelings she is not expressing ("I'm so afraid you died ashamed of me"); the protagonist accepts, corrects or rejects what the double says, and the double helps her reach and own what lies beneath her words. In mirroring , the protagonist steps out of the scene and watches while an auxiliary replays her behaviour, her slumped shoulders and flat voice, as if in a mirror; it is used when a protagonist cannot see what she is doing or is too overwhelmed to go on, and it must be done with care so that it does not become mockery. In the soliloquy , the protagonist speaks her private thoughts aloud, alone, often while walking slowly around the stage before entering a scene or after leaving one. The empty chair places an absent person (or a part of the self) in a chair to be addressed; psychodrama shares this device with Gestalt therapy, which made it famous (Section 6.3). In future projection , the protagonist enacts a scene from the future, a feared confrontation, a job interview, the conversation in which she tells her mother she is marrying outside the community, both to rehearse it and to discover what she hopes and fears. Behaviour therapists later developed much the same idea as behaviour rehearsal (Section 4.7.3). Table 7.26 Six core techniques of psychodrama. Technique What happens Main purpose Role reversal Protagonist plays the other person; an auxiliary plays the protagonist Empathy for the other; seeing oneself from outside Doubling An auxiliary beside the protagonist voices unspoken thoughts and feelings Reaching and owning what lies beneath the words Mirroring Protagonist watches an auxiliary replay her behaviour Self-observation when the protagonist cannot see herself Soliloquy Protagonist speaks private thoughts aloud, alone Bringing hidden thoughts into the open Empty chair Protagonist addresses an absent person placed in a chair Unfinished business with someone absent or dead Future projection Protagonist enacts a scene that has not yet happened Rehearsal; clarifying hopes and fears Behind the techniques lie three of Moreno's ideas. The first is spontaneity , which he defined as an adequate response to a new situation or a new response to an old one. Psychological problems, in his view, are failures of spontaneity: we respond to today's situations with yesterday's rigid scripts, which he called cultural conserves. The warm-up exists to raise spontaneity, and the action phase gives it room. The second is catharsis. Aristotle had used the word for the purging of pity and fear in the audience of a tragedy, and Breuer and Freud for the release of strangulated emotion by remembering (Section 3.1.2). Moreno argued that the deepest catharsis comes to the actor, through action, and he spoke of a catharsis of integration : not merely an emotional discharge but a new pulling together of the person, which is why every enactment ends with new behaviour and with sharing. The third is tele , Moreno's word for the two-way flow of feeling between people, the immediate sense of attraction, repulsion or indifference that each person has towards another. Unlike transference, which is one-way and distorted, tele is mutual and accurate, and Moreno thought it was the glue of every group. Tele is what sociometry measures. Does psychodrama work? The research is thinner than for most methods in this book. A 2003 meta-analysis by David Kipper and Timothy Ritchie of 25 experimental studies found large average effects, with role reversal and doubling the most effective techniques, but most of the studies were small and poorly controlled. Psychodrama is better regarded as a powerful method with a modest evidence base, and its greatest influence has been indirect: role play, behaviour rehearsal, the empty chair, the here-and-now and the idea of the group as audience have passed into almost every other therapy. Exam trap The five elements of psychodrama are the protagonist (whose life is enacted), the director (the therapist), the auxiliary egos (members who play roles), the audience and the stage ; its three phases are warm-up, action and sharing . Role reversal (swapping parts), doubling (voicing the inner self beside the protagonist) and mirroring (watching oneself replayed) are Moreno's. Do not give role reversal to interpersonal psychotherapy (Section 3.7), Kelly's fixed-role therapy (Section 5.5) or Adler's acting "as if" (Section 3.8). The empty chair is best known as Fritz Perls's Gestalt technique (Section 6.3), and behaviour rehearsal belongs to the behaviour therapists (Section 4.7). In the sharing phase members share their own experience; they do not interpret. Sociometry and the sociogram Moreno's second great invention was a way of measuring the invisible structure of a group. Sociometry (from the Latin socius , companion, and metrum , measure) is the study and measurement of the patterns of choice, attraction and rejection among the members of a group. Its basic tool is the sociometric test : each member is asked, on a stated criterion that matters to the group (whom would you like to share a room with, work on a project with, sit next to in class?), to name a first, second and third choice, and sometimes the people he or she would not choose. The answers can be set out in a table, the sociomatrix, or drawn as a diagram, the sociogram. Key study: the runaways of Hudson (Moreno, 1934) Question. In the early 1930s the New York State Training School for Girls at Hudson, an institution for delinquent adolescent girls who lived in separate cottages, suffered a sudden epidemic of runaways. Why were girls running away, and why in clusters? Method. Moreno and his colleague Helen Hall Jennings asked every girl whom she would like to live with and work with, and mapped the choices and rejections across the whole school. Results. The runaways were not random. They followed the channels of attraction in the school's network of choices, spreading along chains of friendship much as an infection spreads. When girls were reassigned to cottages on the basis of mutual choices, the runaways fell sharply. Conclusion. A group's hidden network of attraction and rejection shapes its members' behaviour, and it can be measured and deliberately rearranged. Moreno reported the work in Who Shall Survive? (1934). Criticism. Choices change over time and depend on the criterion asked, the work was not a controlled experiment, and rearranging people's lives by their choices raises its own questions. But Moreno's diagrams are now recognised as among the first drawings of social networks, the ancestors of modern network science. A sociogram draws each member as a circle (often a circle for girls and a triangle for boys in school studies) and each choice as an arrow from the chooser to the chosen, with different lines for rejection. Several patterns can be read straight off it. A star receives many choices. An isolate neither chooses nor is chosen. A neglectee chooses others but receives few choices, and a rejectee receives many rejections. A mutual choice (a pair) links two people who chose each other, and pairs can join into chains, triangles and closed cliques; a cleavage is a gap between subgroups that choose only within themselves. Ravi Asha Imran Nisha Joseph Preeti Sunil Farah Key one-way choice mutual choice rejection Ravi: the star, chosen by five Farah: an isolate, no ties at all Mutual pairs: Asha and Joseph, Ravi and Nisha Joseph rejects Preeti Figure 7.17 A sociogram of an eight-member group. Arrows run from the chooser to the person chosen; heavy lines join mutual choices; the one arrow drawn in the key's rejection style (Joseph to Preeti) is a rejection. Notice how quickly the diagram shows what an observer might take weeks to see: a star at the centre, a clique around him, and a member (Farah) whom nobody chooses and who chooses nobody. Sociograms are used by teachers to find isolated or rejected children, by group therapists to understand the subgroups forming in their groups, and by organisations to understand who really talks to whom. In psychodrama groups the same idea is used in action: members may be asked to stand near the person they would choose for a scene, so that the group's choices become visible in the room. Three other diagrams are easily confused with the sociogram, and Section 7.3 teaches two of them. The genogram is a family tree of at least three generations, with standard symbols for people, relationships and events, popularised by Murray Bowen; the ecomap , devised by Ann Hartman, shows a family's links with the outside systems around it (school, work, relatives, health services). The sociogram, by contrast, maps the choices and communication within a group. A cognitive map is something else again: Edward Tolman's term for a rat's mental representation of a maze (General Psychology book). Moreno also distinguished psychodrama from sociodrama , a group method in which the group as a whole is the protagonist and the roles enacted are collective rather than personal: not Divya and her father, but "a father" and "a daughter" in a changing society. Sociodrama explores the shared social roles, conflicts and prejudices of a group: a new daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law, a police officer and a protester, a landlord and a tenant from a community that has faced discrimination. It is used in education, community work, the training of teachers and police, and the reduction of conflict between groups. Exam trap The tool that "captures implicit and explicit group communication and interaction patterns" is the sociogram (Jacob Moreno, sociometry, Who Shall Survive? , 1934). The genogram is a multigenerational family tree (Bowen), the ecomap shows a family's ties to outside systems (Hartman), and a cognitive map is Tolman's mental map of a maze. In a sociogram the star receives many choices and the isolate gives and receives none. Psychodrama enacts one person's life; sociodrama enacts collective social roles, with the group as protagonist. Kurt Lewin and the T-group The second stream of the group movement came not from a clinic but from social science. Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947) was a German psychologist who emigrated to the United States in 1933, developed field theory (behaviour as a function of the person and the environment, taught in the General and Social Psychology books) and, more than anyone, founded the study of group dynamics , the forces that shape how groups form, decide, lead and change. In 1945 he set up the Research Center for Group Dynamics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. His earlier experiments with Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White on autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire leadership in boys' clubs belong to social psychology; here what matters is an accident in the summer of 1946. That summer the Connecticut State Interracial Commission asked Lewin to run a two-week workshop in New Britain, Connecticut, to train community leaders, teachers and social workers to deal with racial and religious tensions. Lewin and his colleagues, among them Leland Bradford , Kenneth Benne and Ronald Lippitt , divided the participants into small discussion groups and placed research observers in each group to record what happened. Every evening the staff met to discuss the observers' notes. A few participants asked whether they could sit in on these staff meetings, and Lewin agreed. The result astonished everyone. When an observer described a participant's behaviour that day, the participant would often object ("That isn't what I meant at all"), others would join in, and the evening sessions became the most intense and valuable learning of the whole workshop. Within days, nearly all the participants were attending. Lewin and his colleagues realised that people learn powerfully about themselves and about groups when they receive direct feedback on their behaviour in a group, here and now, and examine it together. Lewin died in February 1947, but that summer Bradford, Benne and Lippitt ran the first session of what became the National Training Laboratories (NTL) at Bethel, Maine. Its central method was the T-group (training group): a small, unstructured group of about a dozen people with a trainer, whose task is to study its own behaviour as it happens. With no agenda, the group must create its own structure, and in doing so its members learn how groups work, how leadership and decisions emerge, and how their own behaviour affects others. The method was called the laboratory method because the group is its own laboratory; its core tools are the here-and-now, feedback and what Lewin called unfreezing, loosening people's habitual ways of seeing and acting so that change becomes possible. Through the 1950s and 1960s T-groups spread into business, government, the churches and education, and the approach came to be known as sensitivity training : training in awareness of one's own feelings, of others' reactions and of group processes. Critics pointed out that its effects on behaviour back at work were often small, and that employees sent compulsorily by their companies could be harmed by intense confrontation. It is worth being clear about what a T-group is: an educational group for people who are not patients, aimed at learning about groups and interpersonal skills, not a treatment for disorder. Encounter groups and the human potential movement By the 1960s the T-group had a more emotional descendant. Section 6.2.7 described the encounter group : a small, relatively unstructured group, often meeting intensively over a weekend, whose purpose is personal growth, self-awareness and more honest relationships through open self-disclosure, the here-and-now expression of feelings and frank feedback. It also described Carl Ransom Rogers 's version, the basic encounter group, which he wrote about in Carl Rogers on Encounter Groups (1970). Encounter groups were the favourite instrument of the human potential movement , a loose movement of the 1960s and 1970s built on humanistic psychology's belief that ordinary, healthy people have great untapped capacities for feeling, creativity, intimacy and growth. Its centre was the Esalen Institute at Big Sur in California, founded in 1962, where Fritz Perls ran Gestalt workshops (Section 6.3) and William Schutz, whom you met in Section 7.10.7, led "open encounter" groups that added physical exercises, touch and non-verbal games, described in his book Joy (1967). Some groups ran as marathons lasting a day or more without a break, on the theory that fatigue would wear down defences. Moreno, characteristically, claimed priority: he had used the word encounter (Begegnung) in his Viennese writings long before. The difference between a T-group and an encounter group is mainly one of aim. The T-group studies the group in order to learn about groups, leadership and organisations; the encounter group uses the group in order to change the individual, with much more emphasis on emotional expression and intimacy. Both differ from a therapy group in that their members are not patients and are not selected or prepared for treatment. That difference proved important. Section 6.2.7 described how Morton Lieberman, Irvin Yalom and Matthew Miles (1973) found that about a third of the students in their encounter groups benefited, a similar proportion were unchanged, and about 8 percent became casualties who suffered lasting psychological harm, mostly in groups run by aggressive, charismatic leaders who pushed for emotional intensity and attacked members' defences. Section 7.10.5 drew the lesson for leaders: high caring and meaning attribution help, unrestrained emotional stimulation harms. Encounter groups faded in the late 1970s, but their legacy survives in the here-and-now focus of interpersonal group therapy, in team-building and leadership training, and in the many personal growth workshops still offered today. Self-help and mutual-aid groups In May 1935 a New York stockbroker named William Griffith Wilson (1895 to 1971), known to millions since as Bill W., was alone in a hotel in Akron, Ohio. A business deal he had come to close had collapsed, and he was desperate for a drink. Wilson's drinking had already wrecked his career, and he had been sober only since the previous December, after a spiritual experience during his last stay in a New York hospital for alcoholics, inspired by an old drinking friend who had stopped drinking through the Oxford Group, an evangelical Christian movement. Wilson had discovered that his own sobriety seemed to depend on trying to help other drinkers. So instead of going to the hotel bar, he telephoned around until he was put in touch with an alcoholic surgeon, Robert Holbrook Smith (1879 to 1950), Dr Bob. The two men talked for hours, one drunk to another. Smith took his last drink on 10 June 1935, the date that Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) celebrates as its founding. Within four years there were about a hundred sober members in three groups, and in 1939 they published their basic text, Alcoholics Anonymous , known as the Big Book, from which the fellowship took its name. AA now meets in about 180 countries. The Big Book set out the twelve steps , the programme of personal recovery that each member works through. In paraphrase, the member admits being powerless over alcohol and that life has become unmanageable (the first step reads "We admitted we were powerless over alcohol, that our lives had become unmanageable"); comes to believe that a Power greater than oneself can restore sanity, and decides to turn one's will and life over to God "as we understood Him"; makes a searching moral inventory of oneself, admits one's wrongs to God, to oneself and to another person, and asks for one's defects to be removed; lists the people one has harmed and makes amends to them wherever possible; continues the self-inventory, prays and meditates; and, having had a spiritual awakening, carries the message to other alcoholics. The last step is Wilson's discovery in Akron made into a rule: helping others keeps one sober. By 1946 Wilson had also summarised the twelve traditions , which were adopted at AA's first international convention in Cleveland in 1950. Where the steps guide the individual, the traditions guide the groups: the only requirement for membership is a desire to stop drinking; each group is self-supporting through members' own contributions and refuses outside money; AA stays forever non-professional, has no opinion on outside issues, does not promote itself, and holds anonymity to be its spiritual foundation. A newcomer is encouraged to find a sponsor , an experienced member with stable sobriety who guides him through the steps and can be telephoned at any hour when the urge to drink strikes. Meetings are open (anyone may attend) or closed (only for those who want to stop drinking), and members are encouraged to take recovery "one day at a time". AA became the model for a whole family of self-help groups , also called mutual-aid or mutual-help groups: voluntary groups of people who share a problem or situation, run by the members themselves rather than by professionals, usually free of charge, in which members help one another to cope or recover. Al-Anon was founded in 1951 by Lois Wilson, Bill's wife, and her friend Anne B., for the families and friends of alcoholics, and Alateen followed for teenagers. Narcotics Anonymous (NA), adapting the twelve steps to drug addiction, began in California in 1953. Gamblers Anonymous and Overeaters Anonymous applied them to other problems. Not all mutual-aid groups follow the twelve steps: Recovery, Inc., founded in Chicago in 1937 by the psychiatrist Abraham Low (1891 to 1954), taught former psychiatric patients a self-help method of controlling their reactions; SMART Recovery (1994) offers a secular, cognitive behavioural alternative for addiction; and there are now groups for carers of people with dementia, for parents of children with autism, for people who hear voices and for almost every illness and loss. How does a mutual-aid group differ from a therapy group? Table 7.28 compares them. Two ideas explain why mutual aid can help. The sociologist Thomasina Borkman (1976) pointed out that self-help groups run on experiential knowledge , the truth learned by living through a problem, which members trust in a way they may not trust professional knowledge; the old-timer who says "I sat where you are sitting" carries an authority no doctor can. And the sociologist Frank Riessman (1965) described the helper therapy principle : those who help are helped, because helping raises self-esteem, makes the helper rehearse the lessons he is teaching and gives him a valued role. This is Yalom's altruism in another vocabulary. Of Yalom's factors, AA mobilises especially instillation of hope (the speaker with twenty years' sobriety), universality, altruism, imparting information and imitative behaviour; interpersonal learning in the here-and-now plays little part, because meetings discourage members from commenting on one another's contributions ("cross-talk"). For decades the honest answer was "probably, for those who stay", because people choose whether to attend, and those who choose AA may differ from those who do not. Two kinds of evidence changed the picture. In Project MATCH (Chapter 9), a manualised twelve-step facilitation therapy, which encourages active involvement in AA, did as well as cognitive behavioural and motivational treatments. And in 2020 a Cochrane review settled much of the debate. Key study: the Cochrane review of AA (Kelly, Humphreys and Ferri, 2020) Question. Do Alcoholics Anonymous and clinical interventions that promote AA (twelve-step facilitation) help people with alcohol use disorder? Method. John Kelly, Keith Humphreys and Marica Ferri pooled 27 studies with more than 10,000 participants, including randomised trials, comparing AA and twelve-step facilitation with other established treatments such as cognitive behaviour therapy. Results. Manualised AA and twelve-step facilitation interventions were more effective than the other treatments in producing continuous abstinence, and about as effective on other drinking outcomes such as the intensity of drinking; they also tended to reduce health-care costs. Conclusion. Encouraging patients to engage with AA is an effective, low-cost part of treatment for alcohol use disorder. Criticism. Many studies came from the United States, the evidence for drinking outcomes other than abstinence was less certain, and the review tested professionally delivered facilitation as much as AA itself. Research on mechanisms suggests that AA works largely by changing members' social networks towards sober friends and by building their confidence and coping, not only through its spiritual content. AA has its critics. Its spiritual language deters some people, its emphasis on powerlessness sits awkwardly with the self-efficacy that cognitive behavioural therapists try to build, it insists on total abstinence, and court-mandated attendance strains its voluntary spirit. Clinicians therefore offer it as one option among several and help each person find the group that suits them. Indian context AA reached India in 1957, when its message was carried to a schoolteacher in Bombay, and the city had the country's first and, for some years, largest group; meetings are now held in many Indian cities and languages. Some Indian programmes have blended the twelve steps with local traditions, as the Kripa Foundation in Mumbai did with yoga and meditation (Section 9.9.7). Because most Indian patients with alcohol dependence live with their families, Al-Anon and family groups, and family involvement in treatment generally, are particularly useful here. Clinical link Simply telling a patient "go to AA" achieves little. Twelve-step facilitation works because the clinician explains what meetings are like, suggests trying several different groups before deciding, links the patient with a member who can take him to his first meeting, encourages him to find a sponsor, and asks about his experience at the next session. Offer Al-Anon to the spouse, whatever the drinker decides. The same principles apply to referral to any mutual-aid group. Exam trap Alcoholics Anonymous was founded in 1935 in Akron, Ohio , by Bill Wilson (a stockbroker) and Dr Bob Smith (a surgeon); the Big Book appeared in 1939. The twelve steps guide the individual member; the twelve traditions guide the groups. Al-Anon (1951) is for families and friends of alcoholics, Alateen for their teenage children, Narcotics Anonymous (1953) for drug addiction. A self-help group is led by its members, not by professionals. The helper therapy principle (Riessman) is the mutual-aid version of Yalom's altruism. Milieu therapy and the therapeutic community The last idea of this chapter enlarges the group to the size of a whole institution. Its ancestor is the moral treatment of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries (Chapter 1), when reformers such as Philippe Pinel in Paris and William Tuke at the York Retreat (1796) argued that a humane, ordered, respectful environment could itself restore the insane. By the twentieth century, though, the great mental hospitals had become custodial warehouses, and the hospital environment was more likely to cause disability than cure it (Chapter 9 describes what Erving Goffman called the total institution). The Second World War brought the idea back. You have already met Northfield (Section 7.10.1), where the second experiment turned a whole military hospital into a community in which soldiers took responsibility for its life and work. In 1946 one of the Northfield psychiatrists, Tom Main (1911 to 1990), described the hospital as a therapeutic institution in a paper of that title, and coined the term therapeutic community for an institution organised so that the whole community, staff and patients together, and the relationships and daily life within it, become the means of treatment. Main later directed the Cassel Hospital near London for thirty years. The name most closely linked with the therapeutic community, however, is that of Maxwell Jones (1907 to 1990), a psychiatrist born in South Africa and trained in Edinburgh. During the war Jones ran a unit at Mill Hill in London for soldiers with "effort syndrome", palpitations, breathlessness and exhaustion with no heart disease to explain them. He began by giving groups of patients lectures on the physiology of their symptoms, and noticed that the discussions that followed, and the patients' explanations to one another, did more good than his lectures. After the war he treated returned prisoners of war, and in 1947 he took charge of the Industrial Neurosis Unit at Belmont Hospital in Surrey, later renamed the Henderson Hospital. Its patients were chronically unemployed men and women with what would now be called personality disorders, people whom ordinary psychiatric wards could not help. Jones described the work in Social Psychiatry (1952), published in the United States as The Therapeutic Community . Life at the Henderson was organised around a daily community meeting of all patients and all staff, in which anything that had happened in the community could be raised and examined. Staff did not wear uniforms, and the usual hierarchy of doctor, nurse and patient was deliberately flattened; patients sat on committees, shared the running of the unit and, at the Henderson, had a large say in decisions about admissions and discharges. Every incident, an argument in the kitchen, a broken rule, a resident who did not get up, became what Jones called a living-learning situation: something to be talked about openly by the community, so that the person involved could see how his behaviour affected others and try something different. Treatment relied on the community, not on medication or individual therapy. In the 1950s the anthropologist Robert Rapoport and his team spent several years studying the Henderson, and in Community as Doctor (1960) they distilled its ideology into four principles that are still quoted as the definition of a democratic therapeutic community. Democratisation : every member of the community, patient or staff, has an equal right to share in decisions about the community's life. Permissiveness : members tolerate a wide range of behaviour, including disturbing behaviour, so that it can be expressed and examined rather than simply suppressed or punished. Communalism : life is shared, with open communication, shared tasks and facilities, close relationships and a free flow of information; everything is everybody's business. Reality confrontation : members are continually shown, by the reactions of the others, how their behaviour is actually seen and what effect it has. Rapoport also noticed tensions between these ideals and the practical need to rehabilitate people for life outside, a reminder that a therapeutic community is always a balance. Jones went on in the 1960s to turn a whole mental hospital, Dingleton Hospital at Melrose in Scotland, into an open-door therapeutic community, and later took his ideas to North America. Democratic therapeutic communities spread to prisons (Grendon prison in England has run as one since 1962) and to services for people with personality disorders; the Henderson itself closed in 2008. Their research base is encouraging but methodologically weak, because residents choose to come and randomised trials are hard to run. Milieu therapy is the broader idea of which the therapeutic community is one form: the deliberate use of the whole environment of a ward or residential unit (its routines, activities, staff attitudes, relationships and rules) as a treatment. The term is usually traced to Bruno Bettelheim and Emmy Sylvester, who wrote in 1948 about the therapeutic milieu of the Orthogenic School for disturbed children in Chicago, and its forerunners include Harry Stack Sullivan's specially staffed ward at Sheppard Pratt (Section 3.8.7). In 1978 the American psychiatrist John Gunderson described five therapeutic functions that a milieu can serve, and argued that different patients need different mixtures of them: containment (physical safety and limits, vital in acute crisis), support (comfort and reassurance), structure (a predictable timetable and clear expectations), involvement (active participation in the community, central for people with personality disorders) and validation (respect for each person's individuality). Milieu therapy did not always win when tested: in Gordon Paul and Robert Lentz's long comparison for severely disabled long-stay patients (1977), a social learning programme built on a token economy did better than milieu therapy (Sections 4.5 and 9.8.7). One more distinction completes the picture. The concept-based or hierarchical therapeutic communities for drug addiction, which began with Synanon in California in 1958 and continued in Daytop Village in New York and many others, borrowed the name but not the democracy. They are run on a strict ladder of jobs and privileges, with senior residents in recovery as role models and confrontational encounter groups as a central ritual; Section 9.9.7 teaches them. Maxwell Jones's therapeutic community is democratic and flattened; the addiction therapeutic community is hierarchical and structured. Both use the community as the agent of change, in opposite ways. Exam trap The modality "pioneered by Maxwell Jones " and marked by democratic involvement of staff and patients in decisions and daily life is the therapeutic community . The distractors: encounter groups are Rogers's personal growth groups; group analysis is Foulkes's psychoanalytic group therapy; milieu therapy is the broader idea of a therapeutic ward environment (Bettelheim; Gunderson's five functions), of which the therapeutic community is one specific, democratic form, so when Maxwell Jones is named, choose therapeutic community. The token economy is Ayllon and Azrin's (Chapter 4), aversion therapy is a behaviour therapy and EMDR is Francine Shapiro's trauma treatment (both in Section 4.4), psychodrama to Moreno, logotherapy to Viktor Frankl (Section 6.5) and solution-focused brief therapy to de Shazer and Berg (Section 6.8). The case of the young man and his mother, revisited Go back to the hospital visit that opened this chapter. As an explanation of schizophrenia, the double bind failed: research teams could not reliably identify double binds, could not show that they were more common in the families of people with schizophrenia, and could not show that they came before the illness rather than after it (Section 7.2). Today the young man's illness would be understood through the interaction of genetic vulnerability and environment, the diathesis-stress model of Chapter 1, and nobody would tell his mother that she had caused it. Yet the scene still teaches. Bateson's group used it to illustrate the symptomatic double bind: her stiffening body said "do not come close", her words said "you should come close, or you do not love me", and her last remark forbade him to notice the contradiction, while he could neither leave nor comment. Virginia Satir would call such a message incongruent, a double-level message in which words and body disagree (Section 7.6). And the members of the Palo Alto group who recorded the scene went on to shape the Mental Research Institute that Don Jackson founded in 1959, Jay Haley's strategic therapy and the MRI's brief therapy (Section 7.5), all of which listen for the relationship message underneath the content. What would a clinician do for this family now? The question that survived is not "what caused his illness?" but "what will make him relapse?". A researcher interviewing his mother with the Camberwell Family Interview would listen for critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement, because Vaughn and Leff (1976) showed that high expressed emotion predicts relapse, and that regular medication and less than 35 hours a week of face-to-face contact protect against it. The treatment would be family psychoeducation: telling the mother plainly that the family did not cause the illness, teaching both of them about schizophrenia and its early warning signs, practising how to express feelings and requests without criticism, and solving the practical problems of daily life together. In hospital he might join a ward group, where he could discover that he is not the only one (Yalom's universality), or live on a ward run as a therapeutic community (Sections 7.10 and 7.11). The move Bateson made with this scene, from the inside of one person's head to the space between people, is the foundation on which every therapy in this chapter, from Bowen's coaching to a couples session to a room of eight strangers, still builds. Chapter summary 7.1 The Family as a System. Family therapy grew from child guidance clinics, marriage counselling, pioneers who saw whole families (John Bowlby in 1949, John Elderkin Bell in 1951 and Nathan Ackerman, the "grandfather of family therapy") and, above all, 1950s research on the families of patients with schizophrenia. Its ideas came from Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory (wholeness, interdependence, open systems, equifinality) and Norbert Wiener's cybernetics (1948). Don Jackson's family homeostasis (1957) is kept by family rules; negative feedback restores the old balance and positive feedback amplifies change, and neither word means good or bad. In circular causality each person's behaviour is both cause and effect, and each partner punctuates the sequence differently. The identified patient is the symptom-bearer, sometimes a scapegoat (Vogel and Bell, 1960). Subsystems, boundaries and triangulation recur in every school, and in Carter and McGoldrick's family life cycle (1980) symptoms cluster at transitions. 7.2 Families and Schizophrenia: From Blame to Expressed Emotion. Early theories blamed families: Frieda Fromm-Reichmann's schizophrenogenic mother (1948), the double bind of Bateson, Jackson, Haley and Weakland (1956), Theodore Lidz's marital schism and marital skew (1957) and Lyman Wynne's pseudomutuality and rubber fence (1958). None survived as a cause of schizophrenia, although the double bind was seminal for the communication and strategic therapies. What survived was expressed emotion: George Brown's London research, the Camberwell Family Interview and the index of Brown, Birley and Wing (1972), whose three components are critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement (warmth is not one). Vaughn and Leff (1976) showed that high EE predicts relapse, not onset, and that medication and under 35 hours a week of face-to-face contact protect. Family psychoeducation (Leff, Falloon's behavioural family management, Anderson and Hogarty) educates without blame, trains communication and problem solving, and reduces relapse. 7.3 Bowen's Family Systems Theory. Murray Bowen (1913 to 1990) watched whole families living on an NIMH research ward and saw the family as an emotional unit driven by chronic anxiety. His eight concepts are differentiation of self (separating thinking from feeling while keeping a self in close relationships; fusion is its opposite), triangles, the nuclear family emotional process, the family projection process, the multigenerational transmission process, emotional cutoff, sibling position (from Walter Toman) and societal regression. Differentiation is not distance: the cut-off person is poorly differentiated. The Bowenian therapist is a calm, detriangled coach who asks process questions, often sees one motivated member and coaches clients to go home to their families of origin. The genogram, with symbols standardised by McGoldrick and Gerson (1985), maps three generations; Ann Hartman's ecomap maps a family's outside links, and Moreno's sociogram maps choices within a group. 7.4 Minuchin's Structural Family Therapy. Salvador Minuchin (1921 to 2017) developed structural family therapy at the Wiltwyck School ( Families of the Slums , 1967) and the Philadelphia Child Guidance Clinic ( Families and Family Therapy , 1974). Symptoms are maintained by the family's present structure: its subsystems, its hierarchy and its boundaries. Diffuse boundaries produce enmeshment, over-involvement with loss of autonomy; rigid boundaries produce disengagement; clear boundaries are the healthy middle. Cross-generational coalitions, triangulation and detouring use a child to manage the parents' conflict, and the structural map shows the present organisation. The psychosomatic family (enmeshment, overprotectiveness, rigidity and lack of conflict resolution) and the family lunch session came from work with diabetic and anorexic children. Therapy first joins (maintenance, tracking, mimesis) and then restructures through enactment, intensity, boundary making, unbalancing and reframing. Bowen looks across generations as a calm coach; Minuchin looks at the present household as an active director. 7.5 Strategic, Brief and Systemic Therapies: Haley, the MRI and Milan. Three branches grew from the Bateson project. Jay Haley named strategic therapy in Uncommon Therapy (1973), drawn from Milton Erickson's cases: the therapist takes charge, sets concrete goals and gives directives, straightforward, paradoxical (Peggy Papp's redefine, prescribe, restrain) or ordeals. For Haley a symptom controls a relationship while denying it, and the perverse triangle is a denied cross-generational coalition; Cloe Madanes added incongruous hierarchies and the pretend technique. The MRI Brief Therapy Center limited treatment to ten sessions and held that the attempted solution becomes the problem; Change (1974) distinguished first-order from second-order change and brought reframing into the field. The Milan team (Selvini Palazzoli, Boscolo, Cecchin and Prata) used positive connotation, rituals and counterparadox, then the guidelines of hypothesising, circularity and neutrality (1980), with circular questioning; Selvini Palazzoli and Prata later developed the invariant prescription. 7.6 Experiential and Contextual Family Therapies. Experiential family therapists put feeling and the therapist's own presence at the centre. Virginia Satir (1916 to 1988), a co-founder of the MRI, wrote Conjoint Family Therapy (1964) and Peoplemaking (1972); her central idea is self-worth, "the pot". Under stress people take incongruent survival stances: placating (leaving out the self), blaming (the other), super-reasonable or computing (self and other) and irrelevant or distracting (all three), as against congruent communication, or levelling. Her techniques include the family life chronology, family sculpting and family reconstruction. Carl Whitaker's symbolic-experiential therapy relied on co-therapy, the battle for structure and the battle for initiative, and the psychotherapy of the absurd ( The Family Crucible , 1978, with Augustus Napier). Ivan Boszormenyi-Nagy's contextual therapy ( Invisible Loyalties , 1973, with Geraldine Spark) studies relational ethics: the ledger, entitlement, the revolving slate, invisible and split loyalties and parentification, met by multidirected partiality and exoneration. 7.7 Behavioural, Postmodern and Evidence-Based Family Work. Behavioural family therapy grew from Gerald Patterson's coercive cycle and parent training, Richard Stuart's contracts (1969) and Robert Liberman (1970), on Thibaut and Kelley's social exchange theory; its tools are functional analysis of family interaction, quid pro quo and good faith contracts, communication training and six-step problem solving. The postmodern turn (second-order cybernetics, social constructionism) made the therapist a collaborator: Anderson and Goolishian's not-knowing stance, Tom Andersen's reflecting team and Seikkula's open dialogue. Narrative family therapy (White and Epston) treats people as creators of their realities and externalises the problem; solution-focused work adds relationship questions. Evidence-based programmes include FFT (Alexander and Parsons), MST (Henggeler, after Bronfenbrenner), MDFT (Liddle), BSFT (Szapocznik) and the Maudsley family-based treatment for adolescent anorexia. Hare-Mustin's feminist critique (1978) challenged neutrality and mother-blaming, and Indian joint families demand cultural competence. 7.8 Couples Therapy. Couples therapy treats the relationship, usually conjointly, after each partner has been screened alone for violence. Traditional behavioural couple therapy (Jacobson and Margolin, 1979), built on social learning and social exchange, combines behaviour exchange (Stuart's caring days), communication training and problem solving. Integrative behavioural couple therapy (Christensen and Jacobson, 1996) adds acceptance through empathic joining, unified detachment and tolerance building. Sue Johnson's emotionally focused couple therapy, developed with Leslie Greenberg and grounded in attachment theory, treats distress as separation distress, tracks the pursue-withdraw cycle and moves through three stages and nine steps, with withdrawer re-engagement and blamer softening. Baucom and Epstein added cognition. John Gottman's research found the five-to-one ratio and the four horsemen, criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling, with contempt the strongest predictor of divorce, and built the Sound Relationship House. When marital discord maintains depression, couples therapy is the treatment of choice. 7.9 Sex Therapy. William Masters and Virginia Johnson described the sexual response cycle in Human Sexual Response (1966): excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution, driven by vasocongestion and myotonia, with a male refractory period. Human Sexual Inadequacy (1970) set out their therapy: the couple as the patient, a dual-sex therapy team, two weeks of daily sessions, education and the removal of performance anxiety and spectatoring. Sensate focus moves from non-genital to genital touching and then to intercourse, which is banned at first. James Semans's stop-start technique (1956) and Masters and Johnson's squeeze technique treat premature ejaculation; vaginal dilators treat vaginismus and directed masturbation lifelong orgasm problems. Helen Singer Kaplan's brief sex therapy ( The New Sex Therapy , 1974) combined tasks with psychodynamic work, and her triphasic model added desire. Jack Annon's PLISSIT model (1976) grades intervention from Permission to Intensive Therapy. Indian practice must address dhat syndrome and sexual myths. 7.10 Group Psychotherapy. Group psychotherapy is therapy through a group. Joseph Pratt's tuberculosis classes (Boston, 1905), Moreno's naming of group psychotherapy (1932), Slavson's activity group therapy and the wartime Northfield experiments made it a profession. Bion described the work group and three basic assumptions (dependency, fight-flight and pairing); Foulkes founded group analysis, with its conductor and matrix. Irvin Yalom (1970) listed eleven therapeutic factors, from instillation of hope and universality to group cohesiveness, catharsis and existential factors, and treated the group as a social microcosm worked in the here-and-now through experiencing and process illumination. Leaders create the group, build its culture and illuminate process; Lieberman, Yalom and Miles found caring and meaning attribution most helpful. Groups may be homogeneous or heterogeneous, open or closed, ideally of seven or eight. Tuckman's stages are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning; problem members include the monopoliser and the help-rejecting complainer. 7.11 Psychodrama, Encounter Groups, Self-Help and Therapeutic Communities. Jacob Levy Moreno's psychodrama, born in his Theatre of Spontaneity (Vienna, 1921), has five elements (protagonist, director, auxiliary egos, audience and stage) and three phases (warm-up, action and sharing); its techniques include role reversal, doubling, mirroring, soliloquy and future projection, resting on spontaneity, catharsis and tele. His sociometry and sociogram ( Who Shall Survive? , 1934) map a group's choices, with stars and isolates. Kurt Lewin's 1946 workshop produced the T-group and sensitivity training; encounter groups (Rogers and the human potential movement) aim at personal growth through disclosure and interaction. Alcoholics Anonymous (Bill Wilson and Dr Bob Smith, 1935) gave the twelve steps and twelve traditions and became the model for self-help groups. Milieu therapy uses the whole ward environment as treatment; the therapeutic community, named by Tom Main (1946) and pioneered by Maxwell Jones, rests on democratisation, permissiveness, communalism and reality confrontation. draw on: (practice mock) (a) Operant conditioning (b) Psychosexual stage theory (c) The medical model (d) General Systems Theory (von Bertalanffy) applied to families Answer: (d) General Systems Theory (von Bertalanffy) applied to families. Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory, together with Norbert Wiener's cybernetics, gave family therapy its ideas of wholeness, homeostasis, feedback and boundaries. Operant conditioning explains one organism's behaviour by its consequences, psychosexual stage theory is Freud's account of individual development, and the medical model locates the illness inside one patient, the opposite of systems thinking. One parent conveys two conflicting messages to the child at the same time is called : (IHBAS 2024) (a) Faulty communication (b) Social skills deficits (c) Double bind communication (d) Conflict resolution Answer: (c) Double bind communication. The double bind (Bateson, Jackson, Haley and Weakland, 1956) is a repeated contradiction between two levels of message, usually words against tone or body, from a person the child depends on, with no escape and no permission to comment. "Faulty communication" is too vague to be the named concept, and social skills deficits and conflict resolution have nothing to do with it. Gregory Bateson describes a classic example of the interaction between a mother and her son who had fairly well recovered from an acute schizophrenic episode. Bateson described this interaction as follows: '[The son] was glad to see her [his mother] and impulsively put his arm around her shoulders, whereupon she stiffened. He withdrew his arm and she asked, Don't you love me anymore? He then blushed, and she said, Dear, you must not be so easily embarrassed and afraid of your feelings. The patient was able to stay with her only a few minutes more, and following her departure, he assaulted an aide and was put in the isolation room.' Bateson used this interaction to illustrate which ONE of the following concepts? (RML 2021) (a) The cybernetic system (b) The homeostatic system (c) The incongruent family dyad (d) The symptomatic double bind Answer: (d) The symptomatic double bind. Bateson's group used this visit to show the double bind as a supposed cause of schizophrenic symptoms: the mother's stiffening body says "do not come close", her words say "you should", and her last remark forbids her son to notice the contradiction. Cybernetic and homeostatic systems are general systems ideas, not this pattern, and "incongruent" is Satir's and Rogers's word. In the context of schizophrenia, the term expressed emotion (EE) refers to: (RML 2021) (a) An individual with schizophrenia who has difficulty talking about their feelings. (b) A family environment where overwhelmingly positive comments are made. (c) A lack of emotion displayed in a family. (d) A family environment where there are emotionally loaded communication patterns of a hostile nature. Answer: (d) A family environment where there are emotionally loaded communication patterns of a hostile nature. Expressed emotion is the emotional climate of a home as revealed by a key relative's attitudes to the patient, rated with the Camberwell Family Interview for critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement. It is not the patient's own difficulty in talking about feelings, not a home full of positive comments (warmth is rated but is not part of the high-EE index) and not an absence of emotion. Expressed Emotion (EE) is a significant predictor of relapse in schizophrenia. Which of the following is NOT one of the three core dimensions of high Expressed Emotion? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Hostility (b) Critical Comments (c) Emotional Over-involvement (d) Warmth and Positive Regard Answer: (d) Warmth and Positive Regard. In the index of Brown, Birley and Wing (1972) a home is rated high in EE on critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement. The Camberwell Family Interview also rates warmth and positive remarks, but these are not part of the high-EE index. High EE (Expressed Emotion) is known to cause: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Poor treatment outcome (b) Relapse of psychotic illness (c) Negative symptoms of schizophrenia (d) Violent behavior in schizophrenic patients Answer: (b) Relapse of psychotic illness. In Vaughn and Leff's study (1976) about half of the patients who returned to high-EE homes relapsed within nine months, against roughly one in eight of those in low-EE homes. High EE predicts relapse, not the onset of the illness, negative symptoms or violence, and "poor treatment outcome" is too vague to be the best answer. Reducing contact hours is one of the important strategies in the management of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Interpersonal violence (b) Para suicidal risk (c) Expressed emotion (d) Stubbornness in children Answer: (c) Expressed emotion. Vaughn and Leff (1976) found that in high-EE homes less than 35 hours a week of face-to-face contact with the relative protected against relapse, so a day-care centre, a sheltered job or separate meal times are used when the emotional climate cannot be changed quickly. Reducing contact hours is not the strategy for interpersonal violence, parasuicidal risk or stubbornness in children. Bowen family systems therapy emphasises: (practice mock) (a) Narrative externalisation (b) Strategic paradox and prescribing the symptom (c) Differentiation of self, triangulation, and multigenerational transmission (d) Solution-focused exception questions Answer: (c) Differentiation of self, triangulation, and multigenerational transmission. These are three of Murray Bowen's eight interlocking concepts. Externalisation belongs to White and Epston's narrative therapy, paradox and prescribing the symptom to Haley, the MRI and the Milan team, and exception questions to de Shazer and Berg's solution-focused therapy. Which one of the following captures implicit and explicit group communication and interaction patterns? (RML 2020) (a) A genogram (b) A cognitive map (c) An ecomap (d) A sociogram Answer: (d) A sociogram. Jacob Moreno's sociogram ( Who Shall Survive? , 1934) draws the choices and rejections among the members of a group, showing stars, isolates, pairs and cliques. A genogram maps a family across three generations (Bowen; McGoldrick and Gerson), an ecomap maps a family's links to outside systems (Ann Hartman) and a cognitive map is Edward Tolman's mental map of a maze; the word that decides the question is "group". Minuchin's structural family therapy focuses primarily on: (practice mock) (a) Multigenerational transmission of anxiety (b) Subsystems, boundaries (rigid, clear, diffuse), and hierarchies within the family (c) Cognitive distortions in family members (d) Paradoxical injunctions Answer: (b) Subsystems, boundaries (rigid, clear, diffuse), and hierarchies within the family. For Minuchin, symptoms are maintained by the family's present organisation, so the therapist maps and changes its subsystems, boundaries and hierarchy. Multigenerational transmission is Bowen's, cognitive distortions belong to cognitive therapy, and paradoxical injunctions to the strategic and Milan therapists. In Minuchin's structural family therapy, enmeshment refers to: (practice mock) (a) Diffuse interpersonal boundaries with over-involvement, intrusion, and loss of autonomy among family members (b) Strategic paradoxical interventions (c) Rigid boundaries with disengagement (d) A complete lack of communication between family members Answer: (a) Diffuse interpersonal boundaries with over-involvement, intrusion, and loss of autonomy among family members. Diffuse boundaries produce enmeshment, in which members speak for one another and distress spreads instantly; rigid boundaries produce disengagement, which is option (c). Paradoxical interventions are strategic, and "a complete lack of communication" defines neither style. Consider this statement: 'Individuals, families, and entire cultures are given a different level of power as creators of their realities.' This statement BEST describes which ONE of the following family therapies? (RML 2021) (a) Transgenerational theory (b) Strategic family therapy (c) Structural family therapy (d) Narrative therapy Answer: (d) Narrative therapy. Narrative therapy (Michael White and David Epston) is social constructionist: it treats individuals, families and cultures as creators of their realities, with different degrees of power to author or impose a story. Transgenerational (Bowen), strategic (Haley) and structural (Minuchin) therapies are modernist schools in which the expert maps a real emotional process, hierarchy or structure. What is a potential consequence of poor awareness of the culture and prevalent familial practices in family therapy? (practice mock) (a) Wrong assessments and misinterpretations (b) Accurate understanding of the family's dynamics (c) Effective communication with the family (d) Development of a strong therapeutic alliance Answer: (a) Wrong assessments and misinterpretations. A therapist who does not know a family's culture may label ordinary closeness, such as a mother who still feeds her adult son or a daughter-in-law who defers to her mother-in-law, as pathology, and the family feels judged. The other three options are what good cultural awareness produces, not poor awareness. A male adult with Depressive Disorder and marital discord would benefit more from: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Psychodynamic psychotherapy (b) Cognitive behavior therapy (c) Marital & couple therapy (d) Supportive therapy Answer: (c) Marital & couple therapy. When marital discord maintains a depression, treating the relationship treats the depression: O'Leary and Beach (1990) and Jacobson and colleagues (1991) found that behavioural marital therapy relieved depression as well as cognitive therapy and was the only treatment that also improved the marriage. Cognitive behaviour therapy, psychodynamic psychotherapy and supportive therapy treat the depressed individual and leave the discord untouched. The therapeutic factor in group therapy described by Yalom as 'the realisation that one is not alone in their suffering' is: (practice mock) (a) Catharsis (b) Universality (c) Altruism (d) Instillation of hope Answer: (b) Universality. Universality is discovering that others share one's fears, secrets and miseries. Instillation of hope is seeing others improve, altruism is being helped by helping, and catharsis is expressing feelings that have been held back. Yalom's therapeutic factors in group therapy include: (practice mock) (a) Free association and interpretation (b) Universality, instillation of hope, altruism, corrective recapitulation, cohesiveness (and others) (c) Token reinforcement and shaping (d) Schema reconstruction and mode work Answer: (b) Universality, instillation of hope, altruism, corrective recapitulation, cohesiveness (and others). Yalom's eleven factors (1970) are instillation of hope, universality, imparting information, altruism, corrective recapitulation of the primary family group, development of socialising techniques, imitative behaviour, interpersonal learning, group cohesiveness, catharsis and existential factors. Free association and interpretation are psychoanalytic, token reinforcement and shaping are behavioural, and schema reconstruction and mode work belong to schema therapy. Yalom's 'here-and-now' focus in group therapy refers to: (practice mock) (a) Discussing only events outside the group session (b) Strictly limiting the group to didactic content (c) Working with interpersonal patterns as they appear in the group session itself, then illuminating those patterns (d) Cognitive disputation of irrational beliefs Answer: (c) Working with interpersonal patterns as they appear in the group session itself, then illuminating those patterns. The group becomes a social microcosm in which members act out their interpersonal patterns, and the leader works in two tiers, experiencing and then process illumination. Discussing only outside events and limiting the group to teaching are the opposite of the here-and-now, and disputing irrational beliefs is Albert Ellis's REBT. What is the principal role of an "encounter group"? (RML 2022) (a) Enables individuals to interact with others in a social setting (b) Encourages team building (c) Aids the therapist in diagnosis (d) Encourages therapy and self-growth through disclosure and interaction Answer: (d) Encourages therapy and self-growth through disclosure and interaction. Encounter groups, Carl Rogers's basic encounter group and the favourite instrument of the human potential movement, aim at personal growth, self-awareness and more honest relationships through self-disclosure, here-and-now feeling and frank feedback. Social interaction is too weak an aim, team building describes organisational training, and diagnosis is no part of the method. Which of the following therapeutic modalities was pioneered by Maxwell Jones and is characterized by the democratic involvement of all community members (staff and patients) in decision-making and daily activities to promote rehabilitation? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Encounter Groups (b) Therapeutic Community (c) Group Analysis (d) Milieu Therapy Answer: (b) Therapeutic Community. Maxwell Jones's democratic therapeutic community (Belmont, later the Henderson Hospital, from 1947) flattened the hierarchy and made the daily community meeting and every incident part of treatment; Rapoport summed up its principles as democratisation, permissiveness, communalism and reality confrontation. Encounter groups are Rogers's personal growth groups, group analysis is S. H. Foulkes's, and milieu therapy is the broader idea of a therapeutic ward environment, of which the therapeutic community is one democratic form. works, describe Eysenck's 1952 review and its claim of spontaneous remission, and list the methodological replies to it. 8.2 Meta-Analysis: Measuring How Much Therapy Helps : explain how a
