One of its best-known chapters describes the Balaji temple at Mehandipur in Rajasthan, where pilgrims who believe themselves troubled by spirits come for healing, and where the temple works like a court in which the afflicting spirit is summoned and tried. Kakar interpreted possession and its cure psychologically while insisting that healing cannot be separated from its cultural setting. The lesson for a clinical psychologist is double. Traditional healing can relieve distress because it carries Frank's common factors, which is why many Indian families consult a temple, a dargah or a healer before a clinic. But common factors do not make every practice safe or sufficient for severe mental illness: Section 9.6 tells how 28 chained patients died in a fire at a faith-healing home in Erwadi, Tamil Nadu, in 2001. Section 8.11 discusses how therapy can be adapted to Indian clients. Frank's argument also explains a finding that will return in Section 8.11. If a therapy's explanation must fit the client's world view, then therapies adapted to the client's culture should work better. A 2011 meta-analysis by Benish, Quintana and Wampold found exactly that: for ethnic and racial minority clients, culturally adapted psychotherapies were modestly more effective than the same bona fide therapies unadapted ( d = 0.32), and the one kind of adaptation that accounted for the advantage was adapting the explanation of the illness to the cultural group's own beliefs (its "myth", in Frank's sense). Lambert's pie: four sources of change Frank described the common factors; Michael Lambert tried to weigh them. In 1992, in the Handbook of Psychotherapy Integration edited by John Norcross and Marvin Goldfried, Lambert (whom you met in Section 8.1 as the reviewer of spontaneous remission and in Section 8.2 as the keeper of the running total of how much therapy helps) turned to a different question: how much of clients' improvement could be credited to each of four sources. His answers, drawn as a pie chart in Figure 8.3, became among the most reproduced numbers in counselling and clinical training. Client and extratherapeutic factors, about 40 percent. Everything about the client and his life outside therapy that aids recovery whether or not he is in therapy. These extratherapeutic factors include the severity and duration of the problem, motivation, inner strengths, supportive family and friends, and chance events such as a new job or the end of examinations. Spontaneous remission and regression to the mean (Section 8.1) belong in this slice. Common factors, about 30 percent. The relationship variables found in therapies of every school: empathy, warmth, acceptance, encouragement to take risks, the therapeutic alliance. Lambert called this slice "common factors"; later writers usually call it "relationship factors". Expectancy (placebo), about 15 percent. The improvement that comes from the client's knowledge that he is being helped, his hope, and his belief in the rationale and power of the treatment. Techniques, about 15 percent. The model-specific procedures unique to particular therapies: exposure, interpretation, disputing, systematic desensitisation, hypnosis, biofeedback. Client factors 40% Relationship 30% Expectancy 15% Technique 15% Client and extratherapeutic: 40% strengths, motivation, support, chance events, natural recovery Relationship (common) factors: 30% empathy, warmth, acceptance, encouragement, the alliance Expectancy (placebo): 15% hope, belief in the rationale and in the treatment's power Model-specific techniques: 15% exposure, interpretation, disputing, desensitisation Figure 8.3 Lambert's (1992) estimates of the percentage of client improvement attributable to four groups of factors. These are rough estimates from his review of the research, not measured results; read the chart for its order (client first, technique last), not for its exact numbers. Push Ravi from Section 8.1 through the pie. His examinations ended, his family rallied and his panic was at its worst when he came for help: all of that is the 40 percent slice. A psychologist who listened without judging and whom he trusted supplied the 30 percent. Learning that panic is a surge of adrenaline and not a heart attack, and believing that the treatment would work, gave him the expectancy slice. The interoceptive exposure exercises were the technique. The pie does not say that technique was unimportant for him; Section 8.3 showed that for panic it matters a good deal. It says that technique was one source of change among several. Now the caveats, which matter as much as the numbers. Lambert himself said that the percentages were "not derived from a strict statistical analysis"; they were his judgement of what the research of the day suggested. They describe shares of improvement, not measured proportions of variance, and the categories overlap (a warm relationship raises expectancy, a credible technique strengthens the relationship). Other researchers, using other methods, have produced quite different numbers. The estimates spread widely after Asay and Lambert restated them in The Heart and Soul of Change (1999), a book edited by Mark Hubble, Barry Duncan and Scott Miller that argued for building practice around common factors, and the pie is now often quoted as if it were a measured result. It is not. Its lasting message is the ranking: the client brings the largest share of change, the relationship comes next, and the techniques that fill most textbooks (including Chapters 3 to 7 of this one) come last, level with hope. Exam trap Lambert (1992): client and extratherapeutic factors 40 , relationship (common) factors 30 , expectancy or placebo 15 , techniques 15 percent. The largest slice is the client , not the relationship; technique and expectancy are equal. The figures are Lambert's rough estimates, not results of a meta-analysis, and they are not Frank's or Wampold's. Do not confuse Lambert's four factors with Frank's four features . Placebo, expectancy and remoralisation Two of Lambert's slices, expectancy and part of the relationship, overlap with what medicine calls the placebo. A placebo (Latin for "I shall please") is a treatment with no active ingredient for the condition treated, such as a sugar pill or a sham procedure; the placebo effect is the improvement that follows because the patient believes he is being treated. In 1955 the Harvard anaesthetist Henry K. Beecher (1904 to 1976) published "The powerful placebo", estimating that about a third of patients in the trials he reviewed (35 percent) improved on placebo alone. Later research has been more cautious. In 2001 Asbjørn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gøtzsche reviewed 130 trials that compared a placebo with no treatment at all and found little evidence of powerful effects in general, but possible small benefits for subjective outcomes such as pain. Much of what looks like a placebo response in a trial is the improvement that would have happened anyway: Eysenck's spontaneous remission and the regression to the mean of Section 8.1. The psychologist who has done most to explain how expectations heal is Irving Kirsch (born 1943). His response expectancy theory (1985) holds that expecting a particular experience, such as less pain or less anxiety, can directly produce it, like a self-fulfilling prophecy. Kirsch then turned the idea on antidepressants. In 1998, with Guy Sapirstein, he meta-analysed 19 double-blind trials with 2,318 patients and concluded that about 75 percent of the response to the drugs was duplicated by placebo; in 2008, using the trial data submitted to the United States Food and Drug Administration, he and his colleagues found the difference between drug and placebo small except in very severe depression. These conclusions are contested, and drugs belong to the psychiatrists; the point here is how much of any healing, chemical or psychological, is carried by expectation. Key study: Kaptchuk and colleagues, the components of the placebo effect (2008) Question: Can the placebo effect be separated into parts, and how much does the relationship with the practitioner add? Method: Ted J. Kaptchuk of Harvard Medical School and his colleagues (Kirsch was one of the authors) randomly assigned 262 adults with irritable bowel syndrome to a waiting list; to sham acupuncture with a practitioner who kept conversation to a minimum ("limited"); or to the same sham acupuncture with an "augmented" relationship, in which the practitioner asked about the symptoms and their meaning with warmth, attention, active listening and confidence. Result: After three weeks, adequate relief of symptoms was reported by 28 percent on the waiting list, 44 percent in the limited group and 62 percent in the augmented group. Conclusion: Non-specific effects can be clinically significant, and "the patient-practitioner relationship is the most robust component". Criticism: Irritable bowel syndrome has subjective outcomes that respond well to expectation, so the size of the effect may not carry over to every condition. Kaptchuk's trial shows the problem with the idea of a placebo in psychotherapy. A drug placebo is the real treatment minus its chemical. But what is psychotherapy minus its active ingredient? A "placebo" therapy (the placebo-attention control described in Section 8.7) is a series of meetings with a caring professional who listens and offers some explanation, which is to say it contains most of the common factors by design. In 2003 Baskin, Tierney, Minami and Wampold showed what follows. When the placebo control was structurally equivalent to the real therapy (the same number and length of sessions, equally trained therapists, the same format, clients free to talk about their problems), active treatments were barely better than it; only placebos that were structurally weaker produced large differences. Within psychotherapy itself, a 2011 meta-analysis led by Michael Constantino found a small but reliable relationship between clients' expectations of improvement and their outcomes ( d about 0.24). Frank's remoralisation was put into a testable form in 1993 by Kenneth Howard and his colleagues, whose dose-effect research appears in Section 8.9. Their phase model describes three phases of change in sequence: remoralisation , an early improvement in subjective well-being, often within the first few sessions; remediation , the relief of symptoms; and rehabilitation , the slower change in long-standing patterns of living and working. In a large sample of outpatients, improvement in well-being came first and was, in their words, "a probabilistically necessary condition" for symptomatic improvement, which in turn preceded improvement in life functioning. This may be one reason why so much change in CBT for depression happens before the main cognitive techniques have been taught (Section 5.11). Exam trap Keep four "improvements without the technique" apart: spontaneous remission (improvement without treatment), regression to the mean (extreme scores drift back), the placebo effect (improvement because the person believes he is treated) and remoralisation (restored hope, Frank). The phase model order is remoralisation, remediation, rehabilitation (Howard and colleagues, 1993). Response expectancy is Kirsch's theory; "The powerful placebo" (1955) is Beecher's. Do not mix them with Victor Vroom's expectancy theory of work motivation (1964), in which motivation is highest when a person believes effort leads to performance, performance leads to outcomes, and the outcomes are valued (valence). Wampold's contextual model Frank's ideas were given their most rigorous modern form by Bruce Wampold, whose meta-analysis you met in Section 8.3. In The Great Psychotherapy Debate: Models, Methods, and Findings (2001), and in a second edition written in 2015 with Zac E. Imel , Wampold argued that the field was really choosing between two models of how psychotherapy works, and that the evidence could decide between them. The first is what Wampold called the medical model of psychotherapy. The name does not mean that therapy is biological; it means that therapy is understood on the analogy of a drug. The model has five components: the client has a disorder, problem or complaint; there is a psychological explanation of it; there is a mechanism of change; the therapy has specific ingredients that act on that mechanism; and the specific ingredients are what produce the benefit (specificity). Cognitive therapy for depression fits the model well: the disorder is depression, the explanation is distorted thinking, the mechanism is cognitive change, and the specific ingredients are the techniques for testing thoughts. The second is the contextual model , built on Frank. It treats psychotherapy as a special case of a social healing practice, which benefits clients through capacities that human beings, the most social of species, have evolved for helping one another. Before anything else, an initial therapeutic relationship must form: within the first meeting the client decides whether this stranger is trustworthy, competent and willing to understand him, judging partly from the therapist's manner, dress and room. (More clients drop out after the first session than at any other point, Section 8.10.) Once that bond exists, therapy works through three pathways, shown in Figure 8.4. The real relationship. The real relationship , in the definition of Charles J. Gelso , is "the personal relationship between therapist and patient marked by the extent to which each is genuine with the other and perceives/experiences the other in ways that befit the other" (Section 3.3 traced the idea from Greenson to Gelso and Carter's tripartite model). Therapy is an unusual relationship: it is confidential, and the client can disclose shameful things without losing the bond. For a lonely or isolated client, simply having a genuine human connection with an empathic person is health-promoting. Expectations. Clients arrive with their own explanation of their distress, a "folk psychology" shaped by their culture, which usually offers no way out ("I am weak", "it is my fate"). Therapy provides an adaptive explanation that comes with something to do, and when the client accepts it, he comes to expect that by carrying out the tasks of therapy he will be able to cope. This is Frank's mastery, Bandura's self-efficacy and Kirsch's response expectancy at work. It requires agreement on the goals and tasks of therapy, two components of the alliance (Section 8.5). Specific ingredients that promote healthy actions. Every cogent therapy has specific ingredients, and they matter, but not, in this model, because each repairs one particular deficit. They matter because they get the client to do something healthy: think about the world less rigidly (CBT), improve relationships (interpersonal and dynamic therapies), accept himself (acceptance and self-compassion therapies), express difficult emotions (emotion-focused therapy) or take another person's perspective (mentalisation-based therapy). Initial therapeutic relationship first bond and trust 1. The real relationship genuine human connection 2. Expectations an explanation the client accepts, and hope 3. Specific ingredients that prompt healthy actions Benefits less distress, better living Agreement on goals and tasks (the alliance, Section 8.5) is needed for pathways 2 and 3 Figure 8.4 Wampold's contextual model. Once an initial therapeutic relationship has formed, psychotherapy produces benefits through three pathways: the real relationship, expectations created by an accepted explanation, and specific ingredients that lead the client to act in healthier ways. The value of setting the two models side by side is that they make different predictions, and Wampold and Imel gathered meta-analytic evidence on each. Incidental Yes About 0.24 On this scorecard the contextual model wins most rounds, and that is how Wampold answered Donald Klein (Section 8.3). Psychotherapy is not "merely a placebo", because a placebo is designed to lack a cogent explanation and healthy actions, whereas a real therapy delivers both through a real relationship; that structurally equivalent placebos do almost as well shows only that they are almost therapy. Wampold's 2007 paper put the conclusion in its title: psychotherapy is "the humanistic (and effective) treatment". The scorecard needs two warnings, though. First, most of the common-factor numbers come from correlational studies, in which the alliance or empathy is measured and then correlated with outcome, whereas most of the specific-factor numbers come from experiments that manipulate a component. A correlation can run the wrong way: clients who are already improving may rate the alliance more highly. Wampold argued that the best longitudinal studies show the alliance predicting later change even after earlier improvement is controlled, and Section 8.5 examines that argument; but the two kinds of number are not quite like with like. Second, the scorecard averages across problems, so it says nothing against the disorder-specific findings of Section 8.3. Exposure for OCD is not refuted by a meta-analysis of depression. Specific-effects researchers would add that the contextual model, like the dodo verdict, is most persuasive where the specific techniques for a disorder have least to offer. Exam trap Wampold's contextual model ( The Great Psychotherapy Debate , 2001; second edition 2015 with Zac Imel) has an initial therapeutic relationship followed by three pathways : (1) the real relationship , (2) expectations created by an explanation the client accepts, and (3) specific ingredients that promote healthy actions. His medical model is a model of how therapy works (disorder, explanation, mechanism, specific ingredients, specificity), not the biomedical model of mental illness. The real relationship (genuineness and realistic perception) is not the same as the working alliance (agreement on goals and tasks plus a bond, Section 8.5). What common factors mean for practice It is easy to hear "common factors" as "the vague, nice things therapists do alongside the real work". The research of this section says the opposite: these are among the most powerful things a therapist does, and they can be learned, practised and monitored. Translated into practice, the evidence suggests six habits. Build the bond first. The client decides early whether to come back, so the first session is spent listening, understanding and showing competence, not rushing to technique. Give an explanation the client can accept. A good rationale is plausible, fits the client's culture and points to something he can do. If it clashes with his world view, it will not create hope, however true it is. Remoralise honestly. Hope is therapeutic, but it must be realistic: the evidence (Section 8.2) allows you to say that therapy gives good odds, not a guarantee. Choose procedures that get the client acting, and use specific techniques where they matter. For OCD, phobias, panic and childhood conduct problems the specific techniques of Section 8.3 are not optional extras. Recruit the 40 percent. Family, friends, work, faith and the client's own strengths do more of the healing than any technique, so therapy should mobilise them. Monitor and adjust. Because therapists differ and alliances break down, check progress and the relationship session by session (Sections 8.5, 8.6 and 8.9). Common factors also provide one of the routes to combining therapies, the common-factors approach to integration described in Section 8.11. And they carry a danger worth naming. "All therapies work through common factors" can become an excuse for never learning the specific treatments that some disorders need, which is exactly what Rachman and Wilson warned against. The mature position holds both ideas at once: the relationship is the vehicle, and the technique is part of what the vehicle carries. The next two sections look more closely at the two biggest common factors, the alliance itself (Section 8.5) and the therapist who forms it (Section 8.6). Clinical link Geeta, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, has been low and tearful since her mother's death a year ago, and her mother-in-law believes she has been affected by nazar (the evil eye). A common-factors reading of her first session would be this. Meet her with warmth and full attention, and let the family see that you take the problem seriously (relationship and setting). Offer an explanation she and her family can accept, for example that grief and exhaustion have drained her, and that she has withdrawn from the things that used to restore her, without ridiculing the family's beliefs (rationale). Agree on one small, concrete step, such as resuming her evening walk with a friend, and review it next week (ritual, healthy action and a chance for mastery). Whatever specific therapy follows, you have begun to remoralise her. Exam trap Match the name to the common-factors idea. Rosenzweig (1936) : three implicit common factors, the dodo epigraph. Of all the shared ingredients, the one that has been studied most is the relationship between the client and the therapist. Every clinician knows this from experience. Picture Rekha, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Bengaluru with depression, referred for cognitive behaviour therapy. Suppose she sees one therapist, does her homework, feels understood and recovers in twelve sessions. Suppose that in a parallel world she sees a second therapist, equally well trained and following the same manual, and leaves after three sessions saying, "She doesn't really get what my life is like." The manual is identical in both worlds. The relationship is not. Turning that ordinary observation into science required three steps: a definition of the relationship that did not belong to any one school, a way of measuring it, and studies that tested whether it predicts outcome. This section follows those steps for the therapeutic alliance, and then asks the same questions about the older relationship variables, Carl Rogers' core conditions, and about the newer idea of the real relationship. From friendly transference to the helping alliance The idea is older than the word. Sigmund Freud noticed early that his patients' cooperation depended on their feelings towards him. In "The dynamics of transference" (1912) he separated the troublesome forms of transference, erotic and hostile, from the patient's friendly and affectionate feelings towards the analyst, which could be admitted to consciousness and which he treated as the vehicle of success in analysis; later analysts called these feelings the "unobjectionable positive transference". In "On beginning the treatment" (1913) he wrote that the first aim of analysis is to attach the patient to the treatment and to the person of the doctor, which takes time, a serious interest in the patient and sympathetic understanding. Freud was saying, in other words, that nothing technical can happen until a working tie exists. Section 3.3 tells the psychoanalytic story that followed. Richard Sterba (1934) described the split between the patient's experiencing ego and the observing ego that allies itself with the analyst. Elizabeth R. Zetzel coined the term therapeutic alliance in 1956 for the patient's capacity to use the healthy part of the ego to join the analyst in the work. Ralph R. Greenson (1911 to 1979) named the working alliance in 1965: the relatively rational, non-neurotic rapport that lets a patient keep working even when the transference is stormy. All of these were defined against transference. The alliance was the realistic, conscious part of the relationship; the transference was the distorted, unconscious part. The first researcher to make the idea measurable was Lester Luborsky, whom you met in Section 8.1 as one of Eysenck's first critics. Working at the University of Pennsylvania, Luborsky (1976) read transcripts of psychodynamic therapy and counted the signs that patient and therapist were working well together. He proposed the helping alliance , which develops in two phases. In the Type 1 alliance, typical of the early sessions, the patient experiences the therapist as warm, supportive and a potent source of help. In the Type 2 alliance, which develops later, the patient comes to feel that the two of them are working together in a joint struggle against what is impeding the patient, and invests in the process of therapy itself. Although Luborsky's thinking was psychodynamic, nothing in his definition required a psychodynamic therapy, and his group's Penn Helping Alliance scales were the first of the modern alliance measures. Exam trap Match the term to its author. Freud (1912): friendly, affectionate ("unobjectionable") positive transference. Zetzel (1956): coined "therapeutic alliance". Greenson (1965): named the "working alliance" (and later the "real relationship", Section 8.5.7). Luborsky (1976): the "helping alliance", Type 1 (therapist experienced as supportive) and Type 2 (working together in a joint struggle). Bordin (1979): the pantheoretical working alliance of goals, tasks and bond. "Alliance", "working alliance", "helping alliance" and "therapeutic alliance" are used almost interchangeably in modern research. Bordin's working alliance: goals, tasks and bond The decisive step came from a counselling psychologist rather than an analyst. Edward S. Bordin (died 1992), who directed the counselling centre at the University of Michigan for more than thirty years, published "The generalizability of the psychoanalytic concept of the working alliance" in the journal Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice in 1979. His argument was that the working alliance between the person who seeks change and the person who offers to be a change agent is one of the keys, perhaps the key, to change in every kind of therapy, and that it can be described without any reference to the unconscious. Bordin defined the working alliance as a collaborative stance made of three components (Figure 8.5). Agreement on goals. Client and therapist agree about what the therapy is for: which problems are to change and what a good outcome would look like. Agreement on tasks. They agree about the activities of therapy, that is, what each of them will do in and between sessions to reach the goals (free association, keeping thought records, exposure exercises, role-plays, talking about the past or practising new behaviour). Each must see the tasks as relevant and feel able to carry them out. The bond. There is a personal attachment between them, made of mutual trust, liking, respect and confidence, strong enough to carry the client through the difficult parts of the work. Goals Agreement on what therapy should change WAI Goal subscale Tasks Agreement on the activities that will reach the goals WAI Task subscale Bond Mutual trust, liking, respect and confidence WAI Bond subscale Working alliance Bordin (1979) Figure 8.5 Bordin's pantheoretical working alliance. Two of the three components are agreements (about goals and about tasks) and one is an emotional bond; the Working Alliance Inventory (Section 8.5.3) has a 12-item subscale for each. Two further ideas in Bordin's paper are worth knowing. First, different therapies make different demands on the alliance. Psychoanalysis asks the patient to tolerate frustration, silence and painful interpretations, so it needs a deep bond; behaviour therapy asks the client to carry out exposure tasks that are frightening, so agreement on tasks matters most. The strength of an alliance therefore depends on the fit between what a particular therapy requires and what a particular client and therapist can offer. Second, Bordin later argued that strains in the alliance are inevitable and that the cycle of strain and repair is itself one of the ways in which clients change, an idea that Safran and Muran developed into a research programme (Section 8.5.5). A worked example shows why the three components have to be assessed separately. Arjun, a 26-year-old software engineer in Hyderabad, has obsessive-compulsive disorder with fears of contamination (the disorder itself is described in the Disorders book). He likes his therapist from the first session: she is warm, she listens, and she does not laugh at his fears. The bond is strong. But Arjun's goal is "to stop the thoughts completely", whereas his therapist's goal is to help him tolerate the thoughts without washing. And the central task of the treatment, exposure and response prevention (Chapter 4), strikes him as absurd and dangerous: why would anyone touch a dustbin on purpose? With a strong bond but weak agreement on goals and tasks, the alliance as a whole is fragile, and Arjun is at risk of politely dropping out. The repair is not more warmth. It is a frank conversation about what he wants, a revised goal they can both accept (fewer hours lost to washing, rather than no thoughts at all), and a rationale for exposure that makes sense to him, the "rationale" that Jerome Frank counted among the common factors (Section 8.4). Because Bordin's alliance is defined by these features rather than by any theory, it is often taught in social work and counselling as the working relationship , and an older formulation lists its characteristics as a realistic, collaborative contract to work together, an observable ability of the worker and the client to work together, and a committed belief in the helping relationship. What it does not need is a psychodynamic theory base. Its origins are psychoanalytic, but its modern form is pantheoretical : it applies equally to a cognitive therapist, a family therapist and a counsellor in a college. Fittingly, it was its school-free definition that made it the most researched relationship variable in psychotherapy. Exam trap Bordin's three components are goals, tasks and bond , two agreements and one emotional tie. Do not substitute Rogers' trio (empathy, unconditional positive regard, congruence) or the psychodynamic pair (transference, countertransference). Three questions are built on this: (1) the "working alliance" is the collaborative relationship and bond between clinician and client, focused on the tasks and goals of therapy or assessment, not a score on an outcome measure, not agreement between two clinicians on a diagnosis, and not the client's ability to do homework alone; (2) a working relationship has all of a realistic collaborative contract, an observable ability to work together and a committed belief in helping, but not a psychodynamic theory base ; (3) Bordin's alliance is not a key concept of Rogers' client-centred therapy (conditions of worth, unconditional positive regard and the actualising tendency are), and person-centred therapy is the approach least likely to use the term, preferring to speak of the real relationship and the core conditions (Sections 6.2 and 8.5.7). Measuring the alliance A concept becomes a research variable only when it can be measured reliably. The measure that made Bordin's alliance the centre of process-outcome research was the Working Alliance Inventory (WAI), published in 1989 by Adam O. Horvath and Leslie S. Greenberg . The WAI turns Bordin's definition directly into items: 36 statements, each rated on a seven-point scale, divided into three subscales of 12 items each, one for goals, one for tasks and one for the bond. A client completes items of the kind "My therapist and I agree about the things I will need to do in therapy to help improve my situation" or "I believe my therapist likes me". There are parallel forms for the therapist, who rates the same relationship from the other chair, and for trained observers, who rate recordings of sessions. Thirty-six items is a lot to ask of a client after every session, so short versions followed. Terence Tracey and Anna Kokotovic (1989) used factor analysis to pick four items per subscale, producing the 12-item WAI short form (WAI-S). Robert Hatcher and J. Arthur Gillaspy (2006) re-examined the items and produced the 12-item revised short form (WAI-SR), rated on a five-point scale, which is now one of the most widely used client measures. In the 2018 meta-analysis described below, about seven in ten of the new studies used an inventory based on WAI items. The WAI was not the only measure. Luborsky's group at Pennsylvania developed the Penn Helping Alliance scales, including the Helping Alliance Questionnaire (HAq) and its 1996 revision, the HAq-II. Charles Marmar, Louise Gaston and their colleagues in California developed the California Psychotherapy Alliance Scales (CALPAS), which include the patient's working capacity and commitment as well as the therapist's understanding and involvement. Hans Strupp's group at Vanderbilt University developed observer scales for rating alliance-related behaviour in recorded sessions. Table 8.7 sets out the main instruments. When Hatcher and Barends (1996) analysed the WAI, the CALPAS and the HAq together, the theme they had in common was a "confident collaborative relationship", which is a good one-line definition of the alliance to carry into an interview. Whose rating counts? The alliance belongs to a relationship, so client, therapist and observer each see part of it, and their ratings agree only moderately. Therapists tend to rate the alliance lower than clients do, particularly early in therapy, and they are not especially good at knowing how their clients see it. The early meta-analyses found that client and observer ratings predicted outcome a little better than therapist ratings; in the 2018 meta-analysis the differences were small (clients about .25, observers and therapists about .22). The practical lesson is that if you want to know how the alliance stands, ask the client, preferably on a short questionnaire that makes it easy to be honest. Exam trap The Working Alliance Inventory is by Horvath and Greenberg (1989) , not by Bordin, who supplied the theory. It has 36 items and three subscales (Goal, Task, Bond) ; the short forms have 12. The Helping Alliance Questionnaire belongs to Luborsky . Do not confuse alliance measures with the measures of Rogers' conditions (Truax and Carkhuff's rating scales, the Barrett-Lennard Relationship Inventory, Section 8.5.6) or with Stephenson's Q-sort, which measures the self-concept (Section 6.2). What the alliance predicts Once there were measures, the question could be put directly: do clients with stronger alliances do better? Because the alliance cannot be assigned at random, the answer has to come from correlations between alliance scores, usually collected early in therapy, and outcome scores at the end. Hundreds of such studies now exist, and they have been combined in a series of meta-analyses (the method is explained in Section 8.2). Key study: the alliance meta-analyses, from Horvath and Symonds (1991) to Flückiger and colleagues (2018) Question: Across all forms of therapy, how strongly does the alliance predict outcome? Method: Horvath and Dianne Symonds (1991) combined the 24 studies then available, based on 20 data sets (published in the Journal of Counseling Psychology ); later reviews added studies as they appeared, ending with Christoph Flückiger, A. C. Del Re, Bruce Wampold and Horvath (2018), who analysed 295 independent studies covering more than 30,000 patients, published between 1978 and 2017. Result: The correlation has stayed remarkably stable: r = .26 in 1991, .22 across 79 studies (Martin, Garske and Davis, 2000), .28 across 190 studies (Horvath and colleagues, 2011) and .278 in 2018 (equivalent to d of about 0.58). Only 2 percent of the 295 correlations were negative. The figure for internet-based therapy was almost identical (r = .275). Conclusion: The alliance is a moderate, robust predictor of outcome across therapies, measures, raters, disorders and countries. Criticism: The studies are correlational, so they cannot by themselves show that the alliance causes improvement. What does a correlation of about .28 mean? Squared, it says that the alliance accounts for roughly 8 percent of the variance in outcome, which sounds modest. A more intuitive translation is the binomial effect size display devised by Robert Rosenthal (Section 8.2) and Donald Rubin in 1982, which turns a correlation into a difference in success rates: the success rate in the "high" group is 50 plus half the correlation (expressed as a percentage), and in the "low" group 50 minus half. For r = .28 this gives 50 + 14 = 64 percent against 50 minus 14 = 36 percent. In plain words, if you imagine clients split into those with stronger and weaker alliances, about 64 percent of the first group would have a good outcome against about 36 percent of the second. That is a large practical difference, and it is larger than the typical difference between two bona fide treatments (Section 8.3). The association is also remarkably even across schools. In the 2018 meta-analysis the adjusted correlations were about .20 for cognitive behaviour therapy, .24 for psychodynamic therapy, .26 for humanistic therapy and .28 for interpersonal therapy, and the differences between them were not significant. The alliance is not a humanistic luxury that matters only in "talking" therapies; it predicts outcome in the most structured, technique-driven treatments as well. Timing matters in two ways. First, the alliance measured early, in the first five sessions, already predicts outcome (r about .22 in 2018), which is why clinicians are urged to build it from the first contact and to watch it closely in the first few weeks, when most dropouts happen. Second, alliances measured late in therapy correlate a little more strongly with outcome (about .30), partly because they are measured closer in time to the outcome itself. The alliance also predicts whether clients stay: weaker alliances go with dropout (Section 8.10). Does the alliance cause improvement, or does improvement cause a good alliance? The second possibility is real. In 1990 Robert DeRubeis and Mary Feeley found, in cognitive therapy for depression, that early symptom change predicted later ratings of the alliance more clearly than early alliance predicted later change: clients who feel better start to like their therapist. If that were the whole story, the alliance would be an epiphenomenon , a by-product of improvement rather than a cause of it. Two kinds of evidence argue against that conclusion. In 66 studies that reported both raw correlations and partial correlations controlling for intake severity and early improvement, the association barely shrank (from about .25 to .22). And session-by-session studies have found that an improvement in the alliance in one session predicts a reduction in symptoms by the next, even within the same client. The careful conclusion of Flückiger and colleagues is that the alliance is a moderate causal facilitative factor for outcome, while admitting that an experiment is impossible: nobody can ethically randomise clients to a deliberately poor alliance. Exam trap The alliance-outcome correlation is about r = .28 (Flückiger and colleagues, 2018; 295 studies; more than 30,000 patients), a moderate effect that explains about 8 percent of outcome variance; the first meta-analysis was Horvath and Symonds (1991) , r = .26. It holds about equally for CBT, psychodynamic, humanistic and interpersonal therapy and for internet therapy. An option saying the alliance matters "only in psychodynamic or humanistic therapy" is wrong. The early alliance (sessions 1 to 5) already predicts outcome. A correlation is not proof of causation: DeRubeis and Feeley (1990) showed early improvement can strengthen the alliance. Alliance ruptures and their repair If the alliance matters this much, what happens when it goes wrong? The most systematic answer comes from Jeremy D. Safran (1952 to 2018) and J. Christopher Muran , who ran the Brief Psychotherapy Research Program at Beth Israel Medical Center in New York. Their book Negotiating the Therapeutic Alliance: A Relational Treatment Guide (2000) is the standard text. They defined an alliance rupture as a deterioration in the alliance, shown by disagreement between client and therapist about the goals of treatment, a lack of collaboration on its tasks, or a strain in the emotional bond: Bordin's three components, seen from the side of failure. Ruptures are not rare accidents. They range from a moment of tension that passes in seconds to a breakdown that ends therapy, and nearly every course of therapy contains some. Safran and Muran adopted a distinction first drawn by Harper in 1989 between two broad kinds of rupture, which you can remember by the direction in which the client moves (Figure 8.6). A withdrawal rupture is one in which the client moves away from the therapist or the work. The markers include going silent or giving minimal answers, talking in vague or abstract terms, abruptly shifting the topic, telling a painful story with no feeling (a split between content and affect), denying a feeling that is plainly present, sinking into self-criticism and hopelessness that shuts the therapist out, and, most deceptively, being overly compliant: agreeing with everything, deferring and appeasing. A confrontation rupture is one in which the client moves against the therapist or the work. The markers include complaining about the therapist, about the activities of therapy (the homework, the exercises), about the lack of progress or about the arrangements (fees, timings), rejecting the therapist's interventions, defending oneself against perceived criticism, and trying to control the session or pressuring the therapist for a quick fix. Withdrawal ruptures are the more common and the easier to miss, because a withdrawn client may look like a cooperative one. Confrontation ruptures are more uncomfortable for the therapist, and in a study using Safran and Muran's observer measure, the Rupture Resolution Rating System (3RS), confrontation markers in early sessions of cognitive behaviour therapy predicted dropout (Catherine Eubanks and colleagues, 2019). Withdrawal rupture the client moves away Goes silent, gives minimal answers Over-agrees, defers, appeases Shifts topic, talks in abstractions Confrontation rupture the client moves against Complains about you or the therapy Rejects the task or the homework Pushes for a quick fix 1 Notice the rupture marker 2 Step back and talk about it 3 Explore what the client felt 4 Reach the underlying need Resolution: the alliance is restored, often stronger than before Withdrawal path ends in the client asserting a need ("I wanted to say no") Confrontation path ends in the hurt or disappointment beneath the anger Figure 8.6 Alliance ruptures and their repair, after Safran and Muran. Both kinds of rupture are worked through the same broad sequence, but they end in different places: withdrawn clients learn to say what they need, and confronting clients get underneath their anger to the vulnerability it protects. How is a rupture repaired? Safran and Muran distinguish two families of strategy. Immediate (or direct) strategies get the work back on track without making the rupture itself the topic: the therapist clarifies a misunderstanding, explains the rationale for a task again, or changes a task or goal that is not working. Expressive (or exploratory) strategies make the rupture the focus: the therapist invites the client to talk about what has just happened between them. The key skill here is metacommunication , communicating about the communication: "I notice that when I suggested the exposure exercise you went quiet and then said 'okay, fine'. I wonder whether something about what I said didn't sit right with you?" Metacommunication lets both people step out of the interaction they are caught in, which Safran and Muran called "disembedding", and look at it together. It works only if the therapist is genuinely curious and non-defensive and is willing to acknowledge his or her own part in the rupture. Using the task-analytic method (studying many recorded resolution events to build and then test a model), Safran and Muran described in 1996 the typical course of a successful resolution: the therapist notices the rupture marker; steps back and draws attention to what is happening between them; explores with the client what the client experienced; explores what made it hard for the client to express this directly (the avoidance); and finally helps the client reach the wish or need underneath. The two kinds of rupture end in different places. A withdrawn client moves from vague, qualified statements towards clear self-assertion ("I didn't want to do that exercise, and I didn't feel I could say so"). A confronting client moves from anger and blame towards the disappointment and vulnerability underneath ("I felt you weren't really listening, and I'm afraid nobody can help me"). In both cases the repaired alliance is often stronger than before, and the client has had a corrective experience of a relationship in which conflict did not lead to rejection. The evidence is encouraging but smaller than for the alliance itself. A meta-analysis by Safran, Muran and Catherine Eubanks-Carter in 2011 found only three studies relating rupture repair to outcome (r = .24). The update by Eubanks, Muran and Safran in 2018 found 11 studies with 1,314 patients, and a moderate association between rupture resolution and good outcome (r = .29). A second meta-analysis in the same paper looked at whether training therapists in rupture resolution improved their clients' outcomes and found no significant effect (r = .11, six studies), so the skill matters but is not easily taught in a short course. Safran and Muran also built a treatment around these ideas, brief relational therapy, which puts the negotiation of the here-and-now relationship at the centre of the work. Indian context Withdrawal ruptures can be especially hard to see in Indian settings. A client who has grown up to respect elders, doctors and teachers may never say "I disagree" to a therapist, particularly an older or senior one. Disagreement shows up instead as a polite "ji, haan, I'll try", homework not done, a family function that suddenly clashes with the next appointment, or simply not coming back. It helps to invite disagreement openly ("Many people find this exercise strange; tell me honestly what you think of it") and to ask about the relationship at the end of each session, so that the client has a permitted way to say no. Exam trap Ruptures and repair are the work of Safran and Muran ( Negotiating the Therapeutic Alliance , 2000). Do not confuse this with Safran and Segal's earlier book on interpersonal process in cognitive therapy (1990). Withdrawal = moving away (silence, minimal response, topic shifts, abstract talk, and over-compliance ); confrontation = moving against (complaints, rejecting tasks, pressure). An "excessively agreeable" client is showing a withdrawal rupture, not a strong alliance. Metacommunication is talking about what is happening between therapist and client. Rupture repair correlates with outcome at about r = .29 (Eubanks, Muran and Safran, 2018). Rogers' core conditions as evidence Long before the alliance was measured, Carl Rogers had made the boldest claim ever offered about the therapy relationship. Section 6.2 sets out his 1957 hypothesis that six conditions are necessary and sufficient for constructive personality change, and explains the three that the therapist provides, the core conditions : accurate empathic understanding, unconditional positive regard and congruence. Do not re-learn the definitions here. What concerns this chapter is that Rogers' claim was a scientific hypothesis, and one that could be tested: if the conditions matter, clients whose therapists offer more of them should improve more. Section 6.2 also describes the early Chicago studies with the Q-sort and the disappointing Wisconsin project with hospitalised patients; this section follows the evidence from there. The first systematic tests used rating scales. Charles B. Truax and Robert R. Carkhuff built scales on which trained judges rated short segments of recorded sessions for accurate empathy, non-possessive warmth (their term for unconditional positive regard) and genuineness, and their book Toward Effective Counseling and Psychotherapy (1967) reported that clients whose therapists offered high levels of these conditions improved more, while those whose therapists offered low levels could actually deteriorate. Carkhuff went on to build a training programme in "human relations" skills on these scales. A second tradition measured the conditions as the client perceives them. Rogers' student Godfrey T. Barrett-Lennard (1962) developed the Barrett-Lennard Relationship Inventory , a questionnaire on which the client rates the therapist's level of regard, empathic understanding, unconditionality of regard and congruence. Rogers himself had said that the conditions work only if the client perceives them (his sixth condition), so client-perceived measures are closest to his theory. Truax also produced an awkward finding for the non-directive ideal. Analysing recordings of Rogers' own sessions in 1966, he found that Rogers responded with more empathy and warmth to some kinds of client statements than to others, and that the client statements he favoured became more frequent over the course of therapy. Even the most non-directive therapist, it seemed, was selectively reinforcing his client (Chapter 4 explains reinforcement). The early claims did not survive closer scrutiny intact. In 1977 Kevin Mitchell, Jerold Bozarth and Conrad Krauft reappraised the studies and concluded that the relation between the conditions and outcome was much weaker and less consistent than Truax and Carkhuff had said; in 1978 Michael Lambert, Stephen DeJulio and David Stein reached a similar verdict in the Psychological Bulletin , pointing to unreliable ratings and small samples. For a while it looked as though the core conditions might be one of psychotherapy's comfortable myths. The modern meta-analyses, prepared for the APA task force described in Section 8.5.8 and published in 2018, restored them, though at a realistic size (Table 8.8). Robert Elliott, Arthur Bohart, Jeanne Watson and David Murphy combined 82 samples with 6,138 clients and found that empathy is a moderately strong predictor of outcome (r = .28), holding across theoretical orientations and presenting problems. Importantly, empathy as perceived by the client, or rated by observers or therapists, predicted outcome better than tests of the therapist's "empathic accuracy" in guessing exactly what the client felt: what heals is feeling understood, not being read correctly. Barry Farber and his colleagues at Teachers College, Columbia University, combined 64 studies of positive regard and found a small positive association with outcome (an effect size of 0.28, expressed as Hedges' g , which is a standardised mean difference rather than a correlation). Gregory Kolden and colleagues combined 21 studies with 1,192 patients and found that congruence or genuineness correlated .23 with outcome.
