The evidence supports a more modest statement: they are facilitative . They predict outcome in every kind of therapy, not just person-centred therapy, and the effects are as large as those of most technical factors. But they are not strictly necessary, since people improve with self-help books and therapist-free internet programmes, and with technically skilled therapists who are not especially warm; and they are probably not sufficient for every problem, since a severe obsessive-compulsive disorder or a specific phobia usually needs exposure as well. There is a measurement problem, too. Empathy, positive regard and the alliance bond overlap heavily, and a client who rates the therapist as empathic is often also a client who is improving, so the same chicken-and-egg question that dogs the alliance applies here. The fair conclusion is that Rogers was right that the relationship matters in every therapy and wrong that nothing else does. Exam trap Truax and Carkhuff (1967) rated accurate empathy, non-possessive warmth and genuineness from recordings; the Barrett-Lennard Relationship Inventory (1962) measures the conditions as the client perceives them . The modern verdict (2018): empathy r = .28, positive regard g = .28, congruence r = .23, so the conditions are facilitative across all therapies but not shown to be either necessary or sufficient. Client-perceived empathy predicts outcome better than "empathic accuracy". The conditions themselves are taught in Section 6.2. The real relationship The third strand of the relationship is the one that person-centred therapists care most about. Greenson coined the term real relationship in psychoanalysis for the genuine, undistorted, person-to-person bond between analyst and patient (Section 3.3). It was brought into modern research by the counselling psychologist Charles J. Gelso of the University of Maryland, who with Jean Carter proposed in 1985 that every therapeutic relationship, in every school, contains three parts: a working alliance, a transference configuration and a real relationship (the tripartite model drawn in Figure 3.2). Gelso defines the real relationship as the personal relationship between client and therapist marked by the extent to which each is genuine with the other and perceives and experiences the other realistically , that is, as the person he or she actually is rather than through the lens of transference. A real relationship has two dimensions: its magnitude (how much genuineness and realism there is) and its valence (how positive the feelings are). It is different from the alliance: the alliance is about working together on a task, whereas the real relationship is about who the two people are to each other. A client can have a good working alliance with a therapist he does not much like as a person, and can like a therapist as a person while disagreeing with what she asks him to do. Gelso and his colleagues developed the Real Relationship Inventory, with client and therapist forms, and a meta-analysis by Gelso, Dennis Kivlighan and Rayna Markin in 2018 combined 16 studies with 1,502 patients and found a moderate association with outcome (r = .38), whether the client or the therapist rated the real relationship. This is the largest correlation in Table 8.8, but it rests on far fewer studies than the alliance, so it should be read with caution. Exam trap The real relationship was named by Greenson in psychoanalysis; Gelso (with Carter, 1985) made it a research variable present in every therapy. It is defined by genuineness and realism , and differs from the working alliance (collaboration on goals and tasks) and from transference (distortion carried over from the past). Because person-centred therapists prefer the language of the real relationship and the core conditions, person-centred therapy is the keyed answer to "which approach is least likely to use the term therapeutic alliance?" Clinical link The research on relationships has a practical message for a trainee: monitor the relationship as deliberately as you monitor symptoms. A two-minute question at the end of a session ("How was today for you? Was there anything I said that didn't fit, or anything we should do differently?") catches withdrawal ruptures that would otherwise end in silent dropout, and a short client-rated alliance scale such as the WAI-SR in the first few sessions tells you whether goals and tasks are really shared. Interviewers at clinical programmes often ask "What makes therapy work?"; an answer that names Bordin's three components, the r of about .28, and rupture repair shows you know the evidence, not just the slogans. The APA task forces on evidence-based relationships In the 1990s the American Psychological Association's Division 12 (Clinical Psychology) began publishing lists of "empirically validated" (later "empirically supported") treatments, defined by manuals and randomised trials (the Chambless criteria, Section 8.8). Many researchers felt that the lists treated therapy as if it were a drug delivered by interchangeable technicians, and ignored the relationship through which every treatment is delivered. In response, Division 29 (Psychotherapy) set up a Task Force on Empirically Supported Therapy Relationships, chaired by John C. Norcross (born 1957), which reported in 2001 and published its evidence in the book Psychotherapy Relationships That Work (2002). It judged the alliance, cohesion in group therapy, empathy, and goal consensus and collaboration to be demonstrably effective, and several other elements (among them positive regard, congruence and feedback) to be promising. Two further task forces followed. The second, an interdivisional task force of Divisions 12 and 29, reported in 2011. The third, the Interdivisional APA Task Force on Evidence-Based Relationships and Responsiveness, published 16 new meta-analyses in a special issue of the journal Psychotherapy in 2018 and a two-volume third edition of the book in 2019, edited by Norcross with Michael Lambert and with Bruce Wampold. Its expert panels judged each relationship element on the strength of the evidence, in three categories. Demonstrably effective (nine elements): the alliance in individual adult psychotherapy, the alliance in child and adolescent therapy, the alliance in couple and family therapy, collaboration, goal consensus, cohesion in group therapy, empathy, positive regard and affirmation, and collecting and delivering client feedback. Probably effective (seven elements): congruence or genuineness, the real relationship, emotional expression, cultivating positive expectations, promoting treatment credibility, managing countertransference, and repairing alliance ruptures. Promising but insufficient research to judge (one element): self-disclosure and immediacy (Section 8.10). The task forces also asked a second question: which client characteristics should a therapist adapt to? The 2011 task force judged adapting therapy to the client's reactance or resistance level, preferences, culture, and religion and spirituality to be demonstrably effective, and adapting to the client's stage of change and coping style to be probably effective. These are the client variables of Section 8.6. The task forces' central conclusion was that the therapy relationship makes substantial and consistent contributions to outcome independent of the specific type of treatment, and that it accounts for why clients improve, or fail to improve, at least as much as the particular treatment method does. Notice how carefully that is worded. The task forces did not claim that technique is irrelevant, and the evidence is correlational. In real therapy the two are inseparable: a client does her exposure homework partly because she trusts the therapist who set it, and she trusts the therapist partly because the homework is working. The modern consensus is "relationship and technique", not "relationship versus technique". Exam trap Two different APA task forces are easily confused. The Division 12 task force (Chambless, 1995 and 1998) listed empirically supported treatments (Section 8.8). The Division 29 task force chaired by Norcross (2001; book 2002; later editions 2011 and 2019) listed evidence-based therapy relationships . In 2019, empathy and positive regard were "demonstrably effective", congruence and rupture repair "probably effective", and self-disclosure and immediacy only "promising". 8.6 Therapist Effects, Allegiance Effects and Client Variables Medium yield · 3 Qs Recall the two uniformity myths that Donald Kiesler attacked in 1966 (Section 8.1): the assumption that the therapists in a study are interchangeable, and the assumption that its patients are alike. Recall too Gordon Paul's question of 1967: what treatment, by whom , is most effective for this individual ? Section 8.5 looked at the relationship between therapist and client. This section takes the two people one at a time. First the therapist: how much does it matter which therapist you see, and what makes one therapist better than another? Then a third person who is usually invisible, the researcher who designs the study, and whose loyalties turn out to predict its results. Finally the client: who benefits from therapy, and why do clients so often appear to improve more than they really have? Therapist effects: some therapists are better than others Key study: Ricks and the "supershrink" (1974) Question: Do different therapists in the same clinic produce different outcomes? Method: David F. Ricks followed up, into adulthood, seriously disturbed adolescents who had been treated at the same clinic by two different therapists. Result: Of the 15 adolescents treated by one therapist, 4 (27 percent) went on to develop schizophrenia as adults; of the 13 treated by the other, 11 (85 percent) did. The adolescents had a nickname for the first therapist, "supershrink". This therapist put more effort into the most disturbed cases, supported the young people's autonomy, made use of resources outside therapy and built better relationships with their parents; the other therapist became depressed and had little energy for the most difficult cases. Conclusion: The therapist can matter enormously, especially with the most severely disturbed clients. Criticism: Two therapists and small, non-random samples; a vivid case study rather than a test. For decades after Ricks, outcome research behaved as though his finding did not exist. Trials compared treatments and treated the therapists who delivered them as interchangeable. A therapist effect is the proportion of the variation in clients' outcomes that is due to which therapist they saw, over and above the treatment and the clients' own characteristics. Measuring it requires care, because clients are nested within therapists: the clients of one therapist share something, namely that therapist. The right tool is a multilevel (hierarchical linear) model, which separates the variance in outcome into a between-therapist part and a within-therapist part; the therapist effect is the between-therapist share (statistically, an intraclass correlation). For the results to generalise to therapists in general, the therapists in a study must be treated as a random sample from the population of therapists. The statistics belong to the Research Methodology book; the idea is what matters here. The first quantitative summary, by Paul Crits-Christoph and colleagues in 1991, found that across 27 treatment groups therapists accounted for an average of 8.6 percent of the variance in outcome, with a range from 0 to almost half. The most thorough modern review, by Scott A. Baldwin and Zac E. Imel in 2013, examined 46 studies using random-effects models and put the therapist effect at about 5 percent overall: about 3 percent in efficacy trials and about 7 percent in naturalistic studies of routine practice. Trials shrink therapist effects because they select therapists carefully, train them, supervise them, check their adherence to a manual and exclude the most complicated clients (Section 8.7). On average, the most effective therapists in these studies were about twice as effective as the least effective. An update by Robert Johns, Michael Barkham and colleagues in 2019 again found a weighted average of about 5 percent, ranging from almost nothing to 29 percent in different settings, and noted that therapist effects grow with the severity of the clients' problems, exactly as Ricks had observed. Five percent sounds small until you compare it with the alternative. When bona fide treatments are compared with one another, the differences between them typically account for around 1 percent of the variance or less (Section 8.3). When Dong-Min Kim, Bruce Wampold and Daniel Bolt (2006) re-analysed the psychotherapy conditions of the NIMH depression trial (Section 8.8) with therapists treated as random, they estimated that about 8 percent of the variance in outcome was due to the therapists and none of it to which of the two psychotherapies was delivered, although a re-analysis of the same data by Irene Elkin and colleagues, making different analytic decisions, found no significant therapist effects, and the dispute has not been settled. The same logic applies to medication. McKay, Imel and Wampold (2006) re-analysed the medication arms of that trial, in which psychiatrists gave either imipramine or a placebo with clinical management, and found that the psychiatrist accounted for more of the variance in depression scores (about 9 percent on the Beck Depression Inventory) than the drug did (about 3 percent). Routine practice shows the spread most vividly. In "Waiting for supershrink" (2003), Okiishi, Lambert and their colleagues analysed 1,841 clients seen by 91 therapists over two and a half years at a university counselling centre, where clients filled in a symptom questionnaire every session. The clients of the most effective therapists improved about ten times faster than the average for the centre; the clients of the least effective therapists, on average, got worse. The therapists' sex, level and type of training, and theoretical orientation (cognitive behavioural, humanistic or psychodynamic) explained very little of this difference. Exam trap Therapist effects are about 5 percent of outcome variance on average (Baldwin and Imel, 2013), smaller in trials (about 3 percent) than in routine practice (about 7 percent), and typically larger than the differences between bona fide treatments . The word "supershrink" comes from Ricks (1974) ; Okiishi and colleagues (2003) titled their counselling-centre study "Waiting for supershrink". The assumption that therapists are interchangeable is Kiesler's therapist uniformity myth (1966). Do not confuse the therapist effect (which therapist) with the allegiance effect (the researcher's loyalty, Section 8.6.3). What makes an effective therapist? If some therapists are reliably better than others, the obvious question is what the better ones have. The surprising answer is that most of the things a clinic records about its therapists do not predict their effectiveness. Smith, Glass and Miller (1980) had already found little relation between therapist experience and outcome (Section 8.2), and later research has kept confirming it. The most direct test was a longitudinal study by Simon Goldberg, Tony Rousmaniere, Scott Miller, Bruce Wampold and colleagues (2016), which followed 170 therapists treating 6,591 patients for up to 18 years. On average, the therapists' outcomes did not improve with experience; if anything they declined very slightly as the years and the cases accumulated, although fewer of their clients dropped out early. Profession, level of training, gender and theoretical orientation have likewise shown little consistent relation to outcome, as the Okiishi study found. Even therapists' ratings of their own social skills do not predict their results. What does predict them is what therapists actually do with difficult people. Key study: facilitative interpersonal skills (Anderson, Ogles, Patterson, Lambert and Vermeersch, 2009) Question: Why do therapists in the same counselling centre differ in their results? Method: Timothy Anderson and colleagues studied 25 therapists who had treated 1,141 clients, whose progress had been tracked session by session. Each therapist watched eight brief video scenes of interpersonally difficult moments in therapy, re-enacted by actors from real session transcripts, and spoke a response to each as if in session. Trained judges rated the recorded responses on facilitative interpersonal skills : verbal fluency, emotional expression, persuasiveness, hopefulness, warmth, empathy, the capacity to form an alliance bond, and keeping a focus on the problem. The therapists also rated their own social skills, and their age, sex, training and orientation were recorded. Result: Facilitative interpersonal skills predicted how fast the therapists' clients improved; self-rated social skills, orientation and training did not, and the small advantage of older therapists disappeared once interpersonal skill was taken into account. Conclusion: Part of what separates more effective therapists is their ability to respond well in interpersonally challenging moments. Criticism: One centre, 25 therapists, and a correlational design; later work by Anderson's group has found similar results with trainee therapists. This finding fits several others. Baldwin, Wampold and Imel (2007) studied 331 patients seen by 80 therapists and separated the alliance into two parts: differences between therapists in the alliances they typically formed, and differences between the patients of the same therapist. Only the therapist part predicted outcome. In other words, the alliance-outcome correlation of Section 8.5.4 is driven largely by the fact that some therapists are better at forming alliances with all kinds of clients. Hans Strupp's group at Vanderbilt found the other side of the coin: when therapists responded to difficult clients with subtly hostile, controlling or dismissive communication, outcomes were worse. Good therapists are not people who never have hard moments; they are people who handle hard moments without becoming defensive, which is the skill of rupture repair (Section 8.5.5). If experience alone does not make therapists better, can anything? The most promising candidates are routine outcome monitoring (feedback from clients' session-by-session scores, Section 8.9) combined with deliberate practice , the effortful, repeated rehearsal of specific skills just beyond one's current level, with expert feedback, borrowed from research on expertise in music, chess and sport. In an agency in Calgary that built feedback, consultation and deliberate practice into its routine, Goldberg and colleagues (2016) found that outcomes improved slightly but steadily year on year across 153 therapists and 5,128 patients, and that individual therapists improved within their own caseloads. Supervision and training are taken up in Section 8.12. Clinical link For a trainee this research is both humbling and hopeful. Years in practice will not by themselves make you better, and neither will your choice of school. What you can work on are the skills in Anderson's list: speaking clearly and warmly, conveying hope without false promises, staying empathic and focused when a client is angry or silent, and noticing and repairing ruptures. Record your sessions (with consent), watch the difficult moments with your supervisor, and track your clients' outcomes with a standard measure instead of trusting your impression of how they are doing. Exam trap What does not reliably predict a therapist's effectiveness: years of experience (Goldberg and colleagues, 2016, found a tiny decline), theoretical orientation , training level, profession, gender, self-rated social skill. What does : facilitative interpersonal skills measured on a performance task (Anderson and colleagues, 2009), the ability to form alliances across many clients (Baldwin, Wampold and Imel, 2007), and handling difficult moments without hostility. An option claiming "more experienced therapists get better outcomes" is the bait. The researcher allegiance effect There is a third person in every outcome study: the researcher. The researcher allegiance effect is the tendency for the treatment favoured by the investigators (the one they developed, practise, train others in or have written in support of) to come out ahead in their comparative studies. It is different from therapist allegiance, the therapist's own belief in the treatment he or she delivers, which is usually counted among the common factors (Section 8.4). Researcher allegiance is about whose study it is. Key study: Luborsky and colleagues, "The researcher's own therapy allegiances: a 'wild card' in comparisons of treatment efficacy" (1999) Question: When two therapies are compared, does the researchers' allegiance predict which one wins? Method: Lester Luborsky, Louis Diguer, Robert Rosenthal and colleagues examined 29 comparative studies of psychotherapies, after eight earlier reviews had hinted at an allegiance trend. They rated allegiance in three ways: from the published paper itself (the usual "reprint" method, judging which treatment the authors favoured from how they wrote about it), from ratings by colleagues who knew the researchers, and from the researchers' own self-ratings. Result: Each measure of allegiance correlated significantly with the outcome differences between the treatments, and together the three measures explained 69 percent of the variance in which treatment did better. Conclusion: Allegiance is a "wild card" that can distort comparisons of treatment efficacy and must be controlled. Criticism: A correlation cannot show whether allegiance biases results or whether researchers become loyal to treatments that genuinely work better. Later work confirmed the finding on a larger scale. In 2013 Thomas Munder and colleagues combined 30 meta-analyses that had estimated the allegiance-outcome association and found a mean correlation of about .26, robust across treatments, populations and ways of measuring allegiance. With a nice irony, they also found that the association was stronger in meta-analyses whose authors believed in the allegiance hypothesis: allegiance to the idea of allegiance. How can allegiance produce its effect? Several routes are possible, and none requires dishonesty. The favoured treatment is often delivered by the investigators' own well-trained, enthusiastic therapists, while the comparison is delivered by therapists with less training or less conviction. The comparison treatment may be a weakened version (sometimes called an "intent-to-fail" condition) rather than the treatment as its own advocates would deliver it. Researchers may choose outcome measures that suit their treatment, or report the measures on which it did best. And their expectations may be conveyed, without anyone meaning it, to therapists, clients and assessors, the experimenter expectancy effect that Robert Rosenthal documented in the 1960s. Yet an allegiance association is not automatically a bias, as Leykin and DeRubeis cautioned in 2009: researchers may also come to favour treatments that have genuinely worked in their hands, so the arrow can point both ways. The remedies follow from the routes. Comparative trials should include investigators allied to each treatment (an "adversarial collaboration"), use therapists who are expert in and committed to each treatment, check that each is delivered competently, use outcome assessors who do not know which treatment a client received (Section 8.7), and register their outcome measures in advance. Because allegiance effects are large enough to account for many of the apparent differences between treatments, they are one of the strongest arguments for the dodo bird verdict (Section 8.3). Exam trap The researcher allegiance effect (Luborsky and colleagues, 1999, "a wild card"; 29 studies; allegiance explained 69 percent of the variance in outcome differences) is about the investigator's loyalty, not the client's expectation (expectancy or placebo, Section 8.4), not the therapist's skill (therapist effects), and not cues in the research setting (demand characteristics, Section 8.6.6). The usual way of rating it is the "reprint method", judging allegiance from the published paper. Client variables: who benefits from therapy? Whatever the therapist and the researcher bring, it is the client who does the changing. Arthur C. Bohart and Karen Tallman made this the theme of their book How Clients Make Therapy Work (1999): clients are active self-healers who use whatever the therapist offers, sometimes in ways the therapist never intended. Lambert's estimates, which put client and extratherapeutic factors at the top of the list of what produces change, are discussed in Section 8.4. Here the question is which characteristics of the client predict a good outcome. Two terms help. The prognosis of a problem is the forecast of its likely course and outcome: whether, how far and how fast the person is likely to recover, or to relapse or become chronic. It is different from diagnosis (identifying the condition) and from aetiology (its causes). A prognostic variable predicts outcome whatever treatment is given (for example, more severe and long-standing problems tend to have a poorer prognosis in any therapy). A prescriptive variable , also called a moderator, predicts which treatment will work better for whom (for example, a client's reactance, below). Prognostic variables tell you who will find therapy harder; prescriptive variables tell you what to do about it. The most famous statement about client variables is less a finding than an accusation. In 1964 William Schofield , a psychologist at the University of Minnesota, published Psychotherapy: The Purchase of Friendship . He argued that psychotherapists, consciously or not, prefer clients who are YAVIS : young, attractive, verbal, intelligent and successful. Such clients resemble therapists themselves, are rewarding to work with, talk easily about their feelings and make the therapist feel competent, and so they are the ones most often accepted for therapy and given the most time and effort, often at the expense of people with much greater need. Schofield's point was critical: the "YAVIS syndrome" describes a bias in who receives psychotherapy, not a law about who can benefit from it. His Minnesota colleague Paul Everett Meehl (1920 to 2003) took it up in his essay "Why I do not attend case conferences" (1973), noting that poorer patients were more likely to be given medication, electroconvulsive therapy or supportive therapy, and better-off patients the intensive psychotherapy that therapists themselves found most interesting. The mocking opposite of YAVIS that appears in some textbooks and exam notes is HOUND (homely, old, unsuccessful, nonverbal and dumb); its origin is obscure, and it is not Schofield's. Does YAVIS predict outcome? Only weakly. Once people are actually in therapy, demographic characteristics such as age, sex, ethnicity and social class are poor predictors of how much they improve, although they predict who is offered therapy and who drops out. The client variables that do predict outcome are psychological, and the strongest of them have been the subject of their own meta-analyses (Table 8.9). Readiness to change. The further along the stages of change a client is at the start (from precontemplation through contemplation and preparation to action, Section 6.9), the better the outcome; a meta-analysis by Paul Krebs, John Norcross and colleagues (2018) of 76 studies and 25,917 patients found a moderate effect ( d = 0.41). Expectations. An outcome expectation is the client's belief about whether therapy will help; a role expectation is the client's belief about what will happen in therapy and what client and therapist will each do. Clients with more optimistic early outcome expectations do better: r = .18 across 81 samples and 12,722 patients (Michael Constantino and colleagues, 2018). Clients whose role expectations clash with what actually happens (a client who expects a doctor to give advice and medicine, and meets a therapist who mostly listens) are more likely to drop out. Albert Bandura's (1977) distinction is useful here. An outcome expectation is a belief that a course of action will lead to a result; a self-efficacy expectation is the person's belief in his or her own capability to organise and carry out the actions needed to reach a specific goal. Self-efficacy is specific to a task, unlike global self-esteem or self-worth; it is not a belief that outcomes depend on fate or chance (that is an external locus of control); and it has nothing to do with Alfred Adler's striving to overcome inferiority. Bandura argued that all therapies work in part by raising self-efficacy. Severity, chronicity and complexity. Clients with more severe, long-standing or complicated problems, including those with coexisting personality disorders, tend to need more sessions and are less likely to reach full recovery, even though, starting from further back, they may show large absolute changes. Social support. Clients with supportive relationships outside therapy tend to do better, partly because the support itself helps and partly because it makes the alliance easier to form. Attachment style. In a meta-analysis of 36 studies with 3,158 patients, Kenneth Levy and colleagues (2018) found that clients securely attached before treatment had better outcomes than insecurely attached clients, and that gains in attachment security during therapy went with better outcomes. Psychological mindedness and motivation. The classic selection criteria for psychodynamic therapy (Section 3.6), the capacity to think about one's own feelings and motives and the wish to change rather than merely to feel better, predict who engages in insight-oriented work. Preferences and reactance. These are prescriptive variables. When clients receive the kind of therapy they prefer, they are less likely to drop out (odds ratio 1.79) and do somewhat better ( d = 0.28), according to a meta-analysis of 53 studies by Joshua Swift and colleagues (2018). The term reactance means a person's tendency to resist being controlled or directed; highly reactant clients do much better with a non-directive, reflective therapist than with a directive one ( d = 0.79 in a meta-analysis of 13 studies by Larry Beutler and colleagues, 2018), and the reverse is somewhat true for clients low in reactance. Client variable Finding What it means in practice YAVIS characteristics (Schofield, 1964) Predict who therapists prefer and accept, more than how much clients improve Watch your own biases about whom you take on Readiness (stage of change) Further along the stages, better outcome ( d = 0.41; 76 studies) Match the intervention to the stage (Section 6.9) Outcome expectations Optimism predicts outcome (r = .18; 81 samples) Offer a credible rationale and realistic hope Role expectations Mismatch predicts dropout Explain early what therapy involves Severity, chronicity, personality disorder Slower progress, less full recovery Plan for longer or more intensive help Attachment security Secure attachment predicts better outcome (36 studies) Give extra attention to the relationship Preferences Accommodation: fewer dropouts (odds ratio 1.79), better outcome ( d = 0.28) Ask what the client wants Reactance High reactance does better with non-directive work ( d = 0.79) Be less directive with reactant clients Exam trap Schofield's (1964) YAVIS (young, attractive, verbal, intelligent, successful) describes patient characteristics , the clients therapists prefer, so it is not a therapy technique, not a psychiatric illness and not a set of therapist qualities, even though it is called a "syndrome". The book is Psychotherapy: The Purchase of Friendship . YAVIS is about therapists' bias in selecting clients, not proof that YAVIS clients benefit more. Prognosis means the likely course and outcome of a disorder, not its history, its immediate symptoms or its diagnostic criteria. Self-efficacy (Bandura) is belief in one's capability to carry out the actions needed for a specific goal, not self-worth, not fate or chance, and not Adler's striving against inferiority. Matching clients to treatments Paul's question implies that the best treatment depends on the client, and the obvious research strategy is to look for interactions: client characteristics that make one treatment work better than another. Educational psychologists had already named this idea. Lee Cronbach and Richard Snow (1977) called it the aptitude-treatment interaction : a method of teaching that suits one kind of student may not suit another, so the right question is not "which method is best?" but "which method is best for which student?" Applied to therapy, the "aptitudes" are client variables of the prescriptive kind described above. The most developed matching scheme is systematic treatment selection , proposed by Larry E. Beutler and John Clarkin in 1990. Beutler argued that therapists should select and adjust their interventions according to a few client dimensions that research had shown to matter, among them functional impairment, subjective distress, reactance and coping style. Coping style is the client's habitual way of handling distress: externalising clients act out, blame others and seek stimulation, while internalising clients withdraw, blame themselves and ruminate. The predicted matches are that externalising clients do better with symptom-focused, skill-building interventions and internalising clients with insight-oriented and interpersonal work, and that, as above, highly reactant clients do better with less directive approaches. The 2011 APA task force rated adaptation to reactance as demonstrably effective and adaptation to coping style as probably effective (Section 8.5.8). Large-scale tests of matching have been sobering. The biggest of them, Project MATCH, randomised more than 1,700 people with alcohol problems to three different treatments specifically to test a series of predicted client-treatment matches, and found very few (Section 8.8). The lesson most researchers have drawn is not that client differences are unimportant, but that matching probably works less by assigning clients to one of a few fixed treatment packages and more by responsiveness : a skilled therapist adjusting what he or she does, moment by moment and session by session, to the person in the room. Newer statistical approaches try to combine many client variables into a single prediction of which treatment would suit a particular person best, but these are still being tested. Exam trap An aptitude-treatment interaction is a client characteristic that changes which treatment works best (a prescriptive variable), not a characteristic that predicts a good outcome in any treatment (a prognostic variable). Systematic treatment selection is Beutler 's (with Clarkin, 1990), built on coping style (externalising versus internalising), reactance, distress and impairment. Project MATCH, the largest matching trial, found few of its predicted matches. Why clients look better than they are: the hello-goodbye effect and other artefacts Much of the evidence a practising clinician sees is a comparison of a client's scores at the start and the end of therapy, with no comparison group. Such pre-post change is easy to collect and easy to over-read, because several processes can make clients look better at the end even if therapy has done less than it seems. Section 8.1 introduced two of them, spontaneous remission and regression to the mean. This subsection adds the others and shows how each one inflates change. The first was described in 1948 by Starke Rosecrans Hathaway (1903 to 1984), the Minnesota psychologist best known as co-author of the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (the test itself belongs to the Assessment book). Writing about non-directive counselling in the Journal of Clinical Psychology , he described what is now called the hello-goodbye effect : clients tend to exaggerate their distress when they arrive and to exaggerate their improvement when they leave. At the "hello", a client has every reason to overstate how bad things are: to justify asking for help, to be taken seriously, to be sure of being accepted for treatment, or simply because people seek help at their worst moment and describe it vividly. At the "goodbye", the pressures run the other way: to thank a therapist who has been kind, to justify the time, money and effort spent, to avoid disappointing someone, and to convince oneself that the decision to end is right. Neither exaggeration need be deliberate. Together they inflate the difference between intake and termination scores, so that the apparent change is larger than the real change (Figure 8.7). Distress score (higher is worse) 40 30 20 10 0 Hello: overstates distress Goodbye: overstates gains Intake End of therapy Reported by the client True level Reported change: 22 points True change: 10 points Inflation: 12 points Control groups and blind assessors reveal the gap Figure 8.7 The hello-goodbye effect in a worked example. The client's true distress falls from 30 to 20, but she reports 36 at intake and 14 at the end, so her questionnaires show a 22-point improvement when the real improvement is 10 points. The line for what the client reports starts above the line for her true level and finishes below it. Work through the figure. A client's true distress on a 40-point scale is 30 when she starts and 20 when she finishes, a real improvement of 10 points. But at intake she rates herself at 36, and at the end at 14. The questionnaire therefore shows an improvement of 22 points, more than double the true change. If a clinic adds up such scores across hundreds of clients and reports the average pre-post change as evidence that its service works, the hello-goodbye effect alone can make a modest service look excellent. It also distorts the reliable change index (Section 8.9), which assumes that any change larger than measurement error is real. The second artefact is regression to the mean, introduced in Section 8.1. Because people come for help when they are at their worst, and because any single measurement contains some random error, a group selected for high scores at intake will on average score lower at the next measurement even if nothing happens to them. Suppose a counselling service accepts only students scoring 20 or more on a depression inventory. Some of them scored that high partly because they were having a particularly bad week; at the next testing their bad weeks will mostly be over, and the group average will fall without any help at all. Regression and the hello-goodbye effect both work in the same direction, but they are different things: regression is a statistical property of selection and measurement error, whereas the hello-goodbye effect is a motivated bias in how clients report. The third is demand characteristics , a term introduced by Martin Theodore Orne (1927 to 2000) in a famous 1962 paper in the American Psychologist . Orne showed that research participants are not passive: they look for cues to what the study is about and what the researcher hopes for, and many try to be "good subjects" who help to confirm the hypothesis. A therapy client filling in a questionnaire at the end of treatment, often in the therapist's room or handed to the therapist afterwards, knows exactly which answers the therapist hopes for. Demand characteristics overlap with the goodbye half of the hello-goodbye effect, but they are a property of the situation (the cues), whereas the hello-goodbye effect is a pattern in the client's self-presentation at the two ends of therapy. The fourth is placebo responding: real improvement produced by the expectation of help rather than by the specific ingredients of the treatment. Placebo and expectancy are discussed as common factors in Section 8.4, and placebo control groups in Section 8.7. Here the point is only that expectancy alone produces substantial change. In a well-known meta-analysis of antidepressant trials, Irving Kirsch and Guy Sapirstein (1998) estimated that about three-quarters of the improvement seen in patients taking the drug was also seen in patients taking placebo. A pre-post comparison in a single treated group cannot separate placebo responding from the effect of the treatment. Table 8.10 Processes that inflate pre-post change, and how research controls them. Process What happens How it is controlled Spontaneous remission (Section 8.1) Problems ease with time, life events and support An untreated or waiting-list comparison group Regression to the mean (Section 8.1) Extreme intake scores drift back towards average Comparison group selected the same way; several baseline measurements Hello-goodbye effect (Hathaway, 1948) Clients overstate distress at intake and gains at the end Independent assessors, collateral reports, behavioural measures, follow-up Demand characteristics (Orne, 1962) Clients respond to cues about what is hoped for Assessors who do not know the treatment; measures collected away from the therapist Placebo responding (Section 8.4) Expectation of help produces real improvement Placebo or attention control group (Section 8.7) The remedies, as Table 8.10 shows, are the ordinary tools of good outcome research: a comparison group that shares everything except the treatment, assessors who do not know which treatment the client received, measures that do not depend only on the client's self-report (behavioural counts, reports from family members, observer ratings), more than one baseline measurement, and follow-up after the goodbye pressures have faded. Section 8.7 describes how a randomised controlled trial builds these safeguards in. Exam trap The hello-goodbye effect (Hathaway, 1948) is the tendency of clients to exaggerate distress at intake ("hello") and exaggerate improvement at termination ("goodbye"), which inflates pre-post change . Do not confuse it with regression to the mean (a statistical drift of extreme scores towards the average), with demand characteristics (Orne, 1962: cues in the research situation that tell participants what is expected), with spontaneous remission (real improvement without treatment) or with the placebo effect (real improvement caused by expectation). Only the hello-goodbye effect and demand characteristics are biases in reporting; the others produce change that is real but not due to the treatment. Client factors in Indian settings Most of the research in this section comes from Europe and North America, from individual clients who refer themselves. Indian clinics differ in ways that change how client variables work, and you should be able to discuss three of them: the family, the route to help and stigma. The first is the family. In most Indian clinics the client does not come alone. A parent, spouse or sibling usually accompanies the client, gives much of the history, takes part in decisions about treatment and may expect to sit in on sessions. Families are a resource; Section 7.1 describes how Vidya Sagar at the Amritsar Mental Hospital in the 1950s involved relatives in care, and Section 7.2 describes the lower rates of high expressed emotion found among relatives in Chandigarh. But the family also changes Bordin's alliance. There may be several sets of goals in the room (a father who wants his son to return to his engineering course, a son who wants to change his course, a mother who wants the son married), so goal consensus has to be negotiated with the family as well as with the client, and confidentiality has to be agreed openly at the start. A therapist unaware of a family's culture and customary practices is likely to make wrong assessments and misinterpret behaviour: an adult son who consults his parents about his career, or a young wife who defers to her mother-in-law, may be behaving normally for that family, not showing "enmeshment" or a dependent personality. The second is the route to help. Many Indian clients reach a psychologist late, after consulting general physicians for bodily complaints and faith healers, temples or dargahs for help that carries no psychiatric label, and they often describe distress in bodily terms such as "weakness", "tension" or "gas" (Section 9.6). They frequently arrive with role expectations formed by medical consultations: a brief visit, a diagnosis, advice and a prescription. A client who expects an active, benevolent guide (the guru-chela relationship described by J. S. Neki, Section 8.11) and meets a silent, reflective therapist may decide that nothing is being done and not return. Explaining early what therapy involves, and offering more structure than a Western manual might, protects both the alliance and attendance. The third is stigma. Fear of being labelled "mental" keeps many people from seeking help at all, and is one reason why the treatment gap in India is so large (between about 70 and 92 percent for different disorders in the National Mental Health Survey, Section 9.6). Families worry, in particular, about the effect of a psychiatric label on the marriage prospects of the client and of the client's siblings, and may ask for discretion about records and certificates. Stigma also shapes the hello and the goodbye: some clients minimise their distress at intake because admitting it is shameful, and some families declare a client "fine now" and stop treatment as soon as the most visible symptoms ease. Finally, Schofield's YAVIS bias has an Indian form. Psychotherapy in India is often delivered in English, in cities, to educated and articulate clients who resemble their therapists, while a rural, older, less educated client who speaks only Kannada, Tamil or Hindi may be offered medication and advice instead. Offering therapy in the client's own language and idiom is one of the simplest ways of correcting the bias; cultural adaptation of therapy is the subject of Section 8.11. Exam trap Poor awareness of a family's culture and customary practices leads to wrong assessments and misinterpretations , pathologising behaviour that is normal for that family; it does not produce an accurate understanding of the family's dynamics, effective communication or a strong alliance. In Indian settings, remember three client factors: family involvement (several sets of goals, negotiated confidentiality), the route to help (general physicians and faith healers first, bodily idioms of distress, medical role expectations) and stigma (label avoidance, marriage concerns, a treatment gap of about 70 to 92 percent).
