Lakshmi, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, lives with her husband, two children and her parents-in-law, and has been depressed for eight months. Research : for moderate depression in adults, CBT, behavioural activation and IPT all have strong support (Chapter 5 and Section 3.7), and so do antidepressants. Patient characteristics, culture and preferences : Lakshmi does not want medication, partly because her mother-in-law disapproves of "English medicine for the mind"; she has little private time for written homework; and her depression began when her husband's job took him to another city during the week, leaving her alone with heavy household duties. Clinical expertise : her psychologist recognises that the onset is a role transition (one of IPT's four problem areas), that behavioural activation can be done with very little writing, and that a joint session with her husband may be needed if any plan is to stick. The evidence-based decision might be IPT focused on the role transition, with activity scheduling and one or two family sessions, and weekly monitoring with a depression questionnaire. A different woman with the same diagnosis might receive a different treatment, and both decisions could be equally evidence-based. Exam trap The APA (policy 2005, report 2006) defines evidence-based practice in psychology as the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture and preferences : three components, not "RCT evidence only" and not "the therapist's experience". Its root is Sackett's evidence-based medicine : "the conscientious, explicit, and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients" (1996), later "the integration of best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values" (2000). The term evidence-based medicine was coined by Guyatt (1991). An EST is a treatment; EBPP is a process of decision-making. Clinical practice guidelines and the hierarchy of evidence No clinician can read every trial, so the evidence is usually digested for them. A clinical practice guideline is a set of systematically developed recommendations, based on a review of the evidence, that helps clinicians and patients decide on appropriate care for a specific condition. Unlike an EST list, which is organised by treatment, a guideline is organised by problem: it starts from depression or psychosis and recommends what to offer, to whom and in what order. The most influential guideline body in mental health is England's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). It was set up in 1999 as the National Institute for Clinical Excellence, became the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence in 2005, and took its present name in 2013. For each condition NICE convenes a committee of clinicians, researchers and people with experience of the condition, which commissions systematic reviews of the evidence and analyses of cost-effectiveness and then issues recommendations for the National Health Service. NICE guidelines helped make CBT, behavioural activation, IPT and family intervention standard offers in England, and shaped the stepped-care psychological therapy services England built (Section 5.11). They are also notable for what they advise against, such as single-session psychological debriefing after trauma (Section 9.7). The American Psychological Association began issuing clinical practice guidelines of its own later, for post-traumatic stress disorder in 2017 and for depression in 2019, and the World Health Organization's mhGAP programme provides guidance for non-specialist health workers in low- and middle-income countries. Every guideline must decide how much weight to give each kind of study, and for questions about whether a treatment works the usual answer is a hierarchy of evidence : a ranking of study designs by how well they protect against bias. One of the first formal hierarchies was published in 1979 by the Canadian Task Force on the Periodic Health Examination, and many versions have followed. Figure 8.10 shows a typical one. At the top sit systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials. A systematic review answers a stated question by searching for all the relevant studies with an explicit, reproducible method, appraising their quality and synthesising their results, often with a meta-analysis (Section 8.2); the reviews of the Cochrane Collaboration are the best-known examples. Below them come individual randomised controlled trials; then controlled studies without randomisation (quasi-experiments, in which, for example, one clinic offers the new treatment and a similar clinic does not); then observational studies; then case series and case studies; and at the bottom, expert opinion and clinical experience unsupported by systematic data. Some versions, meant for decisions about a single patient, put at the very top an "n-of-1" trial, a randomised single-case experiment run on the patient in question. 1 2 3 4 5 6 Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs Randomised controlled trials Controlled studies without randomisation Cohort and case-control studies Case series and case studies Expert opinion and clinical experience Higher levels give more protection against bias in judging whether a treatment works Figure 8.10 A typical hierarchy of evidence for questions about the effects of treatment. Designs nearer the top do more to rule out the rival explanations of Section 8.1; the hierarchy is a rough guide, and a badly run study at a high level can be worth less than a careful one below it. The two observational designs in the middle of the pyramid are favourites of examiners, and the Research Methodology book teaches them fully; here is what you need. In a cohort study the researcher identifies people who have and have not been exposed to something (a childhood adversity, a new community programme) and follows them forward in time (which is why it is also called a prospective study), comparing how often the outcome develops in each group. The result is naturally expressed as a risk ratio, read exactly as in Section 8.7: a risk ratio of 1.0 means the outcome was equally common in exposed and unexposed people. In a case-control study the researcher works backwards. She starts with people who already have the outcome (the cases) and comparable people who do not (the controls), and looks back for differences in their past exposures; the result is expressed as an odds ratio. Because it does not have to wait for a rare outcome to develop, the case-control design is the most feasible way to study a rare disorder and its possible past causes, such as a rare dissociative disorder and childhood trauma; a prospective cohort would have to follow thousands of people for years to collect a handful of cases, and an RCT is impossible, because nobody can be randomly assigned to a childhood trauma. Its classic demonstration was Richard Doll and Bradford Hill's 1950 study linking smoking to lung cancer, the same Bradford Hill who had designed the streptomycin trial. A third observational design, the cross-sectional study , measures exposure and outcome at a single point in time in one sample, like a snapshot; a national survey of how many people have a disorder and what goes with it, such as India's National Mental Health Survey (Section 9.6), is the usual example. It is quick and good for estimating how common a condition is, but it cannot show which came first, and to find enough people with a rare disorder it would need an enormous sample. None of these designs involves random assignment, so none can rule out confounding as an RCT can, which is why they sit below trials in the hierarchy. Two cautions keep the pyramid in its place. First, it is a hierarchy for questions about the effects of treatment. For other questions the best design differs: for prognosis, the likely course of a disorder, a long-term cohort study is usually best, and for understanding what treatment is like from the client's side, qualitative research is. Second, design is not everything. A small, badly run RCT with heavy dropout can be less trustworthy than a large, careful cohort study. Modern guideline bodies, NICE and the World Health Organization among them, therefore rate the whole body of evidence on each question rather than ranking single studies by design alone, using the GRADE system (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation). In GRADE, evidence from randomised trials starts as high quality and is downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency between studies, indirectness (the studies did not quite test the question being asked), imprecision and publication bias; evidence from observational studies starts as low quality and can be upgraded, for instance when an effect is very large. The final rating (high, moderate, low or very low) tells the reader how confident to be. Indian context In India the main source of guidelines for mental disorders is the Indian Psychiatric Society, which publishes clinical practice guidelines in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry ; they cover psychological treatments as well as medication, as in its 2020 guidelines on supportive psychotherapy (Section 3.10). Much of the evidence behind any Indian guideline still comes from trials run in Europe and North America, on clients who differ from Indian clients in language, family structure and expectations of a healer (Section 8.11). That is why Indian trials such as MANAS and PREMIUM in Goa (Sections 5.11 and 9.6) matter so much, and why the Clinical Trials Registry of India (Section 8.7) asks Indian researchers to register their trials before they begin. Exam trap At the top of the usual hierarchy of evidence are systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs , then single RCTs, non-randomised controlled studies, cohort and case-control studies, case series and case studies, and expert opinion at the bottom. For a rare outcome and past exposures the most feasible design is the case-control study ; a cohort study follows exposed and unexposed people forward; a cross-sectional study takes one snapshot and cannot show which came first; an RCT cannot randomise people to a past exposure. A risk ratio or odds ratio of 1.0 means no association. NICE (1999) is England's guideline body, not a therapy and not an Indian institution. Every one of those answers is a statement about groups: the average treated client, the mean of the experimental condition, the effect size across a hundred studies. A clinician sitting with one client needs answers of a different kind. How many sessions will this person probably need? Has she really changed, or has her questionnaire score simply wobbled? Is she now within the range of ordinary, untroubled people, or merely a little less unwell? And is there any chance that therapy is making her worse? This section takes those questions in turn: the amount of therapy (the dose), the meaning of change for an individual (clinical significance), and the minority who deteriorate. The dose-effect relationship Suppose a large hospital in Bengaluru has to decide how many sessions of psychotherapy to offer each outpatient. Offer too few, and many people leave before they have been helped; offer too many, and the waiting list stretches to months. "How much therapy is enough?" is therefore a practical and financial question as well as a scientific one. In the United States of the 1980s, where insurance companies were beginning to cap the number of sessions they would pay for, it had become urgent. The first systematic answer came from Kenneth I. Howard of Northwestern University and his colleagues Kopta, Merton Krause and David E. Orlinsky , in a 1986 paper in American Psychologist titled "The dose-effect relationship in psychotherapy". They borrowed their method from pharmacology. When a new drug is tested, different patients receive different doses, and the percentage who respond is plotted against the dose; the result is a dose-response curve. Howard's team treated one session of psychotherapy as one dose and measurable improvement as the response. They gathered 15 sets of data, covering 2,431 patients, in which both the number of sessions each patient had attended and whether that patient had improved were known. They then fitted a curve with probit analysis , a technique from drug research that relates the probability of a response to the logarithm of the dose. The relationship they described, between the number of sessions and the probability of improvement, is called the dose-effect relationship (or dose-response relationship). The results, drawn in Figure 8.11, became some of the most quoted numbers in psychotherapy research. Between 10 and 18 percent of patients had already improved before the first session, probably because deciding to seek help, booking an appointment and expecting it mobilises hope. About 30 percent had improved after 2 sessions, 53 percent after 8, 74 percent after 26 (six months of weekly sessions) and about 83 percent after 52 (a year). The rounded version, which is the one you should remember, is that about half of patients are measurably improved by 8 sessions and about three-quarters by 26 . 0 25 50 75 100 0 10 20 30 40 50 60 Number of weekly sessions attended (52 is about one year) Patients measurably improved (%) 2 sessions: 30% 8 sessions: 53% 26 sessions: 74% 52 sessions: 83% Each extra session adds less: a negatively accelerated curve Figure 8.11 The dose-effect relationship (Howard, Kopta, Krause and Orlinsky, 1986). The dots are the reported percentages of patients improved after 2, 8, 26 and 52 sessions; the curve is a probit (log-dose) curve fitted through them. Notice how steeply it rises over the first eight sessions and how slowly it climbs after twenty-six. Before the first session, 10 to 18 percent had already improved. Look at the shape of the curve. It rises steeply over the first few sessions and then flattens, so that each additional session produces less extra improvement than the one before. A curve of this shape is called negatively accelerated , and it expresses a law of diminishing returns: going from 0 to 8 sessions helps about half of all patients, while going from 26 to 52 sessions, which doubles the cost, adds only about another tenth. The curve also never reaches 100 percent. Some patients do not improve however long they attend. Patients were not all alike. Those with depression or anxiety improved sooner than those the authors classed as borderline or psychotic, who needed many more sessions for the same chance of improvement. Kopta, Howard and their colleagues pursued this in 1994 with 854 outpatients who completed symptom checklists during treatment. Sixty-two symptoms fell into three classes with different speeds: acute distress and chronic distress symptoms (anxiety, low mood and their relatives) responded within weeks to months, while characterological symptoms, the long-standing problems of trust, anger and relationships that belong to personality, responded much more slowly. A typical outpatient, they calculated, needed about a year of therapy for a 75 percent chance of symptomatic recovery. The dose-effect method also gave a neat answer to Eysenck. In 1991 McNeilly and Howard applied the same probit analysis to Eysenck's own figures (Section 8.1) and showed that psychotherapy produced in about 15 sessions the amount of improvement that spontaneous remission took two years to produce. Therapy, on this reading, does not so much change where patients end up as how quickly they get there, and for a person who is suffering, speed matters. The 1986 study had limits that its authors acknowledged. Improvement was judged mostly by clinicians at the end of treatment or from case records, rather than by standardised questionnaires; "improved" meant any measurable improvement, not recovery; and the improvement at each session number was estimated statistically from pre-treatment and post-treatment data rather than observed session by session. When later researchers measured patients before every session and used the stricter standard of recovery explained below, the numbers grew. Michael Lambert's group at Brigham Young University followed about 6,000 patients in ordinary American services, from employee assistance programmes to community mental health centres, who completed the Outcome Questionnaire-45 before each session. Across their studies, the session by which half the patients had recovered ranged from the 11th to the 21st, and the session by which three-quarters had recovered from the 25th to the 45th. A review by Nathan Hansen, Lambert and Evan Forman (2002) concluded that about 13 to 18 sessions are needed for half of patients to recover. Yet in routine care the same patients attended, on average, fewer than five sessions, and only about a fifth to a third recovered. Many people in ordinary clinics, in other words, receive less therapy than the research says they need. Key study: Howard, Kopta, Krause and Orlinsky, "The dose-effect relationship in psychotherapy" (1986) Question: How many sessions of psychotherapy are needed for patients to improve? Method: A probit analysis, borrowed from drug research, of 15 data sets covering 2,431 patients, treating each session as a dose and measured improvement as the response. Result: 10 to 18 percent improved before the first session, about 30 percent by session 2, 53 percent by session 8, 74 percent by session 26 and 83 percent by session 52. The curve was negatively accelerated, and depressed and anxious patients responded faster than borderline or psychotic ones. Conclusion: Most of the benefit comes early, but a substantial minority need much longer treatment. Criticism: Improvement was crudely defined and mostly rated by clinicians, session-by-session change was estimated rather than observed, and pooling patients who stopped at different times may itself produce the curve's shape (see the good-enough level, below). Exam trap Eight sessions, about 50 percent; twenty-six sessions, about 75 percent (and about 83 percent by one year). The authors are Howard, Kopta, Krause and Orlinsky (1986, American Psychologist ). The "dose" is a session and the "response" is improvement. The curve is negatively accelerated (steep early gains, diminishing returns), not a straight line. Do not confuse these figures for any improvement with the later figures for recovery (about 13 to 18 sessions for half of patients, Hansen, Lambert and Forman, 2002). Three phases of change: remoralisation, remediation, rehabilitation If improvement comes in a curve, does everything improve at the same rate? Clinicians had long noticed that it does not. A client often says after the first or second session that she feels lighter and more hopeful, although her symptoms are much as before; weeks later the symptoms ease; only after months does her life (work, marriage, friendships) really change. Jerome Frank, whose common-factors model you met in Section 8.4, had argued that people come to therapy not only with symptoms but demoralised : feeling helpless, hopeless and unable to cope, and that every therapy first restores morale (his 1974 paper was titled "Psychotherapy: the restoration of morale"). In 1993 Howard, Robert Lueger, Michael Maling and Zoran Martinovich turned these observations into the phase model of psychotherapy outcome. It proposes three phases, each defined by what improves, and claims that they occur in a fixed order: Remoralisation is the improvement of subjective well-being : hope returns, the client feels understood and less overwhelmed. It happens fastest, often within the first few sessions, and corresponds to Frank's restoration of morale. Remediation is the reduction of symptoms : the anxiety, low mood, panic or obsessions that brought the client to therapy. It takes weeks to months, and it is the target of most specific techniques. Rehabilitation is the improvement of life functioning : returning to work, repairing relationships, changing the long-standing habits and patterns that keep problems going. It is the slowest phase and may take many months. Howard's team tested the model with a large sample of outpatients who rated their well-being, symptoms and life functioning before therapy and after sessions 2, 4 and 17. The averages moved in the predicted order: well-being first, symptoms next, functioning last. More strikingly, when each patient was classified as improved or not improved on each variable, improvement in well-being came before, and was what the authors called a "probabilistically necessary condition" for, improvement in symptoms; and improvement in symptoms came before, and was probabilistically necessary for, improvement in functioning. In plain words, patients seldom improved in their symptoms without first feeling better, and seldom functioned better in life without first improving in their symptoms. Table 8.16 summarises the model. Table 8.16 The phase model of psychotherapy outcome (Howard, Lueger, Maling and Martinovich, 1993). Phase What improves Typical timing What helps most 1. Remoralisation Subjective well-being, hope First few sessions Being heard, a credible plan, the alliance 2. Remediation Symptoms Weeks to months Specific techniques aimed at the symptoms 3. Rehabilitation Life functioning, long-standing patterns Many months Longer work on relationships, habits and roles The model has three practical uses. First, it tells you what to measure and when: a questionnaire on symptoms given after two sessions may show little change, while a well-being measure already shows a lot. Second, it explains Kopta's finding that distress symptoms respond quickly and characterological problems slowly, and it fits the dose-effect curve, whose steep early rise is largely remoralisation. Third, it warns against stopping too soon. A client who feels much better after three sessions has usually been remoralised, not cured. Clinical link Sunita, a 41-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, comes for help with depression after her husband's death. After the second session she tells you that for the first time someone has understood her, and she is sleeping a little better. Her brother, who brings her, asks whether she is now cured. The phase model gives you an honest answer: she has been remoralised, which is real and important, but her low mood and poor concentration (remediation) have not yet shifted, and returning to her classroom and her own social life (rehabilitation) will take longer. Explaining this to the family is one of the best protections against premature dropout (Section 8.10). Exam trap The order is remoralisation, remediation, rehabilitation (well-being, then symptoms, then functioning), proposed by Howard and colleagues in 1993 . Remoralisation is about feeling better and hopeful , not about symptom relief; rehabilitation here means restored life functioning , not the rehabilitation services of Chapter 9. Do not mix up three different sequences: the phases of change within therapy (this model), the stages of therapy (beginning, middle, end; Section 8.10) and Prochaska's stages of change (precontemplation to maintenance; Section 6.9). Dose-effect or good-enough level? There is a hidden assumption in the dose-effect curve. It is drawn by pooling patients, and the patients who contribute to the point at session 26 are only those who were still attending at session 26. Is the curve, then, a picture of what happens inside each patient, with every person's gains slowing down as therapy goes on? Or is it a picture of who is left? A British group led by Michael Barkham, with William Stiles and colleagues, tested the question in 2006 with 1,868 clients seen in routine primary care services. Each client attended between 1 and 12 sessions, ended therapy by plan rather than by dropping out, and completed the Clinical Outcomes in Routine Evaluation Outcome Measure (CORE-OM) at the start and the end. If each client's improvement grew with each session, the clients who had attended more sessions should have shown higher rates of reliable and clinically significant improvement. They showed the opposite. Among clients who began above the clinical cut-off, the rate of reliable and clinically significant improvement was 88 percent for those who attended one session and fell steadily to 62 percent for those who attended twelve. Barkham's explanation is the good-enough level (GEL) model. Clients and therapists do not stop at a fixed number of sessions; they stop, responsively, when the client has improved enough to manage, a level that differs from person to person. Clients who change quickly reach their good-enough level early and leave; clients who change slowly stay longer. Seen this way, the flattening of the aggregate curve partly reflects the progressive departure of the people who had already improved, not a slowing of change within each person. In 2009 Scott Baldwin and his colleagues confirmed the prediction with 4,676 patients in individual therapy: patients who received small total doses changed relatively fast, while those who received large doses changed more slowly. The two models are not enemies. Both agree that some people improve in a few sessions and others need many. What the good-enough level model adds is that there is no single right dose. A rule that every client gets six sessions will be too long for some and far too short for others, which is why the modern answer to "How much therapy is enough?" is "Measure each client's progress and decide together" (routine outcome monitoring, below). Exam trap The good-enough level model (Barkham and colleagues, 2006; Baldwin and colleagues, 2009) does not say that therapy fails or that more sessions are harmful. It says that clients tend to stop when they have improved enough , so those who attend longest are mainly the slow responders, and the dose-effect curve partly reflects who is left in treatment. Its practical message: no uniform session limit fits everyone. Statistical significance versus clinical significance Imagine a trial in which 2,000 adults with depression are randomly assigned to a new therapy or to a waiting list. At the end, the treated group's average score on a depression questionnaire is 26 and the waiting-list group's is 28. With so many participants, this two-point difference is statistically significant: the probability of getting a difference so large by chance alone, if the therapy did nothing, is well under 5 percent ( p < .05). The authors announce that the therapy works. But a score of 26 on most depression questionnaires still means moderate to severe depression. Has the therapy made a difference that any patient, or any patient's family, would notice? The example shows the gap between two ideas. Statistical significance tells you only that a difference between groups is unlikely to be due to chance; with a large enough sample, even a trivial difference becomes significant, and with a small sample, an important one may not. Effect sizes (Section 8.2) improve matters by telling you how large the difference is, in standard deviation units, but they are still group averages. Clinical significance asks a different question: does the change make a real, practical difference to the life of the individual client, judged by standards that clients, families and clinicians would recognise? Alan E. Kazdin (born 1945) described it as the practical or applied importance of a treatment's effect. Researchers have operationalised clinical significance in several ways: Return to normal functioning. Does the client end treatment within the range of people who do not have the problem? This is the approach of Jacobson and Truax and of normative comparisons, both explained below. Reliable change. Is the client's change larger than the error of the measuring instrument, so that we can believe it is real? No longer meeting diagnostic criteria, or reaching a predefined level of functioning, quality of life or symptom freedom. Social validity. Do the people who matter in the client's life judge the change to be important? Kazdin in 1977 and Montrose Wolf in 1978, both working in applied behaviour analysis, argued that a treatment's goals, methods and results should be judged acceptable and worthwhile by the client and by those around him, a test called social validity (or social validation). A boy's tantrums falling from ten a day to eight is a reliable change; whether his teacher now finds him manageable in class is the socially valid question. Notice how these echo Strupp and Hadley's tripartite model (Section 8.1): the client's view, society's view and the professional's view of what counts as better. Exam trap Statistical significance concerns the probability that a group difference arose by chance, and depends heavily on sample size. Clinical significance concerns whether the change matters in the client's everyday life. An effect size is a third thing: the size of a group difference in standard deviation units. A result can be statistically significant and clinically trivial. Social validity (Kazdin, 1977; Wolf, 1978) asks whether others in the client's life judge the change important. Jacobson and Truax: the reliable change index The most widely used method for judging clinical significance came from Neil S. Jacobson (1949 to 1999), a psychologist at the University of Washington in Seattle who is also remembered for behavioural activation and couple therapy (Chapter 5 and Chapter 7). His own research on couple therapy showed the problem plainly: treatment reliably raised couples' average satisfaction, yet many treated couples were still distressed at the end of it. In 1984, with William Follette and Dirk Revenstorf, he proposed that clinically significant change should mean the extent to which therapy moves someone outside the range of the dysfunctional population or into the range of the functional population. In 1991, with Paula Truax , he published the paper that turned this idea into arithmetic: "Clinical significance: a statistical approach to defining meaningful change in psychotherapy research", in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology . Their method asks two questions about each client: is the change real, and where did the client end up? The first question is answered by the reliable change index, the second by a cut-off point. Why do we need to ask whether a change is real? Because every test score contains error. If Meera scores 32 on a depression questionnaire today, she might score 29 or 35 next week without any real change in her depression, simply because of her mood that morning, how she read an item or the time of day. So when her score falls by 5 points after therapy, we cannot be sure the change is anything more than this ordinary wobble. The reliable change index (RCI, written RC by Jacobson and Truax) measures how large a client's change is compared with the change that measurement error alone could produce: RC = (x 2 minus x 1 ) ÷ S diff Here x 1 is the client's score before treatment and x 2 the score after it. The denominator, S diff , is the standard error of difference : the spread of the difference scores we would expect if the client had not changed at all. It is calculated in two steps from two numbers you can find in a test manual, the standard deviation of the scores of a clinical (pretreatment) group, s 1 , and the test-retest reliability of the measure, r xx : S E = s 1 × √(1 minus r xx ) and then S diff = √(2 × S E 2 ) S E is the standard error of measurement , the typical size of the error in a single score (the Research Methodology book explains it fully). The second step multiplies it by the square root of 2 because a change score is built from two scores, each with its own error; this form of the denominator was an amendment suggested by Christensen and Mendoza in 1986. Finally, the rule: if the RCI is larger than 1.96 (ignoring its sign), a change that large would occur by measurement error alone less than 5 percent of the time ( p < .05), so we call the change reliable . A worked example. Meera is a 29-year-old software tester in Bengaluru who comes for help with depression. Her clinic uses a depression questionnaire on which higher scores mean more symptoms. The manual reports that people attending clinics for depression average 30 with a standard deviation of 7, that people in the community without depression average 10 with a standard deviation of 4, and that the test-retest reliability is 0.84. Meera scores 32 at her first session and 17 at her last. Standard error of measurement. S E = 7 × √(1 minus 0.84) = 7 × √0.16 = 7 × 0.4 = 2.8. Standard error of difference. S diff = √(2 × 2.8 2 ) = √(2 × 7.84) = √15.68 = 3.96. Reliable change index. RC = (17 minus 32) ÷ 3.96 = -15 ÷ 3.96 = -3.79. Interpretation. The sign is negative because her score fell, and on this questionnaire a fall means improvement. Ignoring the sign, 3.79 is larger than 1.96, so Meera's improvement is reliable : it is very unlikely to be measurement error. A useful shortcut follows. Multiply 1.96 by S diff : 1.96 × 3.96 = 7.76. On this questionnaire, therefore, any change of 8 points or more is reliable, and a clinic can work this out once and apply it to every client. Notice also what the formula does with a poor test. If the reliability were only 0.64, S E would be 7 × 0.6 = 4.2, S diff would be 5.94, and a client would need to change by nearly 12 points before we could trust the change. The less reliable the measure, the more change it takes to rise above the noise. Exam trap The RCI answers "Is the change bigger than measurement error?" , not "Is the client now normal?" It is the client's change score divided by the standard error of difference , and the critical value is 1.96 ( p < .05). The formula uses the measure's test-retest reliability and the standard deviation of a clinical or normal group. Lower reliability means a larger S diff and a larger change needed. The method is Jacobson and Truax (1991), building on Jacobson, Follette and Revenstorf (1984); do not confuse Neil Jacobson with Edmund Jacobson of progressive muscle relaxation. Cut-off points a, b and c, and the four outcome categories Reliable change tells us that a client has changed, not where she has arrived. Harish, another client at the same clinic, falls from 35 to 24. That is an 11-point change, reliable by the shortcut above, yet a score of 24 is still well inside the range of clinic attenders. To capture where a client ends up, Jacobson and Truax defined three possible cut-off points between the dysfunctional and the functional populations. On our questionnaire, where lower scores are better, they work out as follows. Cut-off a : the client's score after therapy should fall outside the range of the dysfunctional population , defined as two standard deviations beyond the dysfunctional mean in the direction of functioning. Here a = 30 minus (2 × 7) = 16. It needs only the clinical group's data, so it is the only cut-off available when no norms for well people exist. Cut-off b : the score should fall within the range of the functional population , defined as within two standard deviations of the functional mean. Here b = 10 + (2 × 4) = 18. It needs norms for well people. Cut-off c : the score should place the client closer to the mean of the functional population than to the mean of the dysfunctional population , the point beyond which a score is more likely to come from the functional group. When the two standard deviations are equal, c is simply halfway between the means. When they differ, each mean is weighted by the other group's standard deviation: c = (s functional × M dysfunctional + s dysfunctional × M functional ) ÷ (s functional + s dysfunctional ) Here c = (4 × 30 + 7 × 10) ÷ (4 + 7) = 190 ÷ 11 = 17.3. a = 16 c = 17.3 b = 18 Functional group (mean 10, SD 4) Dysfunctional group (mean 30, SD 7) 0 10 20 30 40 Score on the depression questionnaire (higher means more symptoms) Number of people Meera: 32 before therapy, 17 after Figure 8.12 Jacobson and Truax's three cut-off points for the worked example. Cut-off a lies two standard deviations beyond the dysfunctional mean, b lies two standard deviations from the functional mean, and c is the point at which a score becomes more likely to belong to the functional group. Because the two distributions overlap, a is the strictest and b the most lenient. Meera's final score of 17 passes c and b but not a. Figure 8.12 shows the three cut-offs against the two populations, and it shows why the choice matters. With overlapping distributions, as here, a is the strictest and b the most lenient. Meera's final score of 17 is below c (17.3) and below b (18), but not below a (16), so whether she counts as recovered depends on which cut-off the clinic has chosen. Jacobson and Truax called c the least arbitrary of the three and gave practical advice: when norms for well people are available, b or c is usually preferable to a; when the two distributions overlap, choose c; when they do not overlap, choose b; when no norms exist, a is the only option. Putting the two criteria together gives the four outcome categories that Jacobson and Truax used, and that most outcome studies now report alongside effect sizes: Recovered: the change is reliable in the direction of improvement and the client has crossed the cut-off into the functional range. Improved: the change is reliable in the direction of improvement, but the client has not crossed the cut-off. Unchanged: the change is not reliable (the RCI lies between -1.96 and +1.96), whatever the final score. Deteriorated: the change is reliable in the direction of worsening. Table 8.17 applies the rules, using cut-off c, to five clients at Meera's clinic. Two of them deserve a second look. Fatima's score fell by 6 points; her family may be pleased, but 6 points is within the range of measurement error on this questionnaire, so she is classed as unchanged. Kavya began only a little above the cut-off and ended comfortably below it, yet her change is also 6 points and not reliable. She has not "recovered" in Jacobson and Truax's sense, because a client who starts near the border can cross it through measurement error alone. That is exactly why they insisted on both criteria.
