For Lambert's Outcome Questionnaire-45, described below, a change of 14 points is reliable and the cut-off between the dysfunctional and functional ranges falls between 63 and 64: a client is classed as recovered when his score has improved by at least 14 points and ends below 64, and as deteriorated when it has worsened by at least 14 points. Exam trap Recovered needs both reliable improvement and crossing the cut-off; improved is reliable change without crossing; unchanged is change that is not reliable, even if the client crosses the cut-off; deteriorated is reliable worsening. The cut-offs: a = two SDs beyond the dysfunctional mean (no norms needed); b = within two SDs of the functional mean; c = closer to the functional than to the dysfunctional mean (the least arbitrary, preferred when distributions overlap). Normative comparisons and the limits of clinical significance The Jacobson and Truax method classifies individuals. Philip C. Kendall of Temple University, with Marrs-Garcia, Nath and Sheldrick, proposed in 1999 a complementary method for whole groups, called normative comparison . The question is whether the treated group, after therapy, is statistically indistinguishable from a normative group of people without the problem: for example, whether children treated for anxiety end up with scores like those of their non-anxious classmates. The difficulty is that an ordinary significance test cannot answer it, because failing to find a difference does not prove that two groups are the same (a small study fails to find most differences). Kendall's procedure therefore uses equivalence testing : the researcher decides in advance how close the two means must be to count as equivalent, and then tests whether the treated group's mean falls within that range of the normative mean. Clinical significance has its own limitations, and you should be able to state them. Both methods need good norms, which many measures, and many Indian populations, lack. A return to the normal range is a fair goal for depression or panic, but an unrealistic one for chronic schizophrenia, dementia or intellectual disability, where a meaningful outcome may be greater independence rather than "normality" (Chapter 9). A single questionnaire captures only one slice of a person's life, usually the slice a client can report about himself. And the cut-offs, for all their arithmetic, rest on a convention (two standard deviations, the halfway point) rather than on what a client or family would call recovery. Exam trap Normative comparisons (Kendall and colleagues, 1999) work at the group level and use equivalence testing to ask whether treated clients have become indistinguishable from a normal sample. The Jacobson and Truax RCI and cut-offs work at the individual level. Both are ways of assessing clinical significance; neither is the same as statistical significance. When therapy harms: deterioration and negative effects Section 8.1 recorded Allen Bergin's warning of 1966. Re-reading the controlled studies of the 1950s and early 1960s, Bergin noticed that at the end of treatment the treated groups were often more spread out than the control groups: some treated clients had improved a great deal, but others had got worse. An average improvement could hide real harm to a minority. Bergin called this the deterioration effect , and his 1966 paper, "Some implications of psychotherapy research for therapeutic practice", argued that psychotherapy can make people better or worse adjusted than comparable people who receive no treatment. In 1977 Hans Strupp, Suzanne Hadley and Beverly Gomes-Schwartz devoted a book to the subject, Psychotherapy for Better or Worse: The Problem of Negative Effects , and the term negative effects has been used ever since for any harm that follows therapy. How common is deterioration? The estimates have been remarkably stable. Reviews by Lambert and others put the proportion of adult clients who are worse at the end of therapy at about 5 to 10 percent , with figures nearer 10 or even 15 percent in substance misuse treatment. When 12 leading outcome researchers from several countries were surveyed in 2003, they agreed strongly with the statement that approximately 10 percent of clients get worse as a result of therapy. In Smith, Glass and Miller's meta-analysis (Section 8.2), about 9 percent of the effect sizes were negative. These figures need careful reading, and Scott O. Lilienfeld (1960 to 2020) of Emory University pointed out why in 2007. A client who is worse at the end of therapy has not necessarily been made worse by it: some would have deteriorated anyway, and to blame the therapy is to commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy ("after this, therefore because of this"). On the other hand, the figures also miss harm: a client who improved a little, but would have improved more without therapy, has been harmed by having his natural recovery slowed. The only clean evidence that a therapy causes harm comes from comparing randomly assigned treated and untreated groups. Why do some clients get worse? Research points to five overlapping sources: The client and his circumstances. Severe, chronic or complex problems, marked interpersonal difficulties, low motivation, and crises outside therapy (a bereavement, a job loss) all raise the risk. A poor fit. A mismatch between client and therapist, or between the client and the method, such as a fiercely confrontational approach with a fragile client, or a highly structured protocol with someone who needs above all to be heard. The relationship. Therapist coldness, hostility, criticism or lack of empathy, and alliance ruptures that are never repaired (Section 8.5), together with negative countertransference that the therapist acts out rather than understands (Section 3.3). Boundary violations are the extreme case (Chapter 1). Harmful or misapplied techniques. Pushing a traumatised client to relive the event before she is stable enough, encouraging catharsis that inflames rather than relieves distress, or using suggestive memory techniques. Iatrogenic effects. An iatrogenic effect (from the Greek iatros , physician) is a problem created by the treatment itself, such as false memories produced by "recovered memory" techniques, or delinquent behaviour learned from fellow members of a delinquency-prevention group. The most sobering demonstration of iatrogenic harm in the whole literature comes not from a psychotherapy clinic but from a well-meant programme for boys. Key study: the Cambridge-Somerville Youth Study and McCord's 30-year follow-up (1978) Question: Can friendly, long-term counselling and support prevent delinquency in boys at risk? Method: In a programme begun in 1935 by the Boston physician Richard Cabot, boys from crowded industrial areas of Cambridge and Somerville, Massachusetts, were matched in pairs and one boy of each pair was assigned to treatment by the toss of a coin. From 1939, for about five years, treated boys received visits from counsellors (on average twice a month), tutoring for over half, medical or psychiatric attention for over a hundred, summer camps for a quarter, and links with the Boy Scouts and the YMCA. In 1975 and 1976 Joan McCord (1930 to 2004) traced 480 (95 percent) of the 506 men from the 253 pairs. Result: Two-thirds of the treated men said the programme had helped them. The objective records said otherwise. Treated men who had criminal records were more likely to have committed more than one crime (78 against 67 percent); more treated men showed signs of alcoholism (17 against 7 percent), more had stress-related diseases, more of those hospitalised received severe diagnoses, those who had died had died younger, and fewer held white-collar or professional jobs. Conclusion: A caring, intensive intervention had done measurable long-term harm. Criticism: The mechanisms are uncertain. McCord suggested conflict between the counsellors' values and those of the boys' families, dependence on outside help that later disappeared, expectations raised and then disappointed, and boys coming to see themselves as people who needed help; later writers also pointed to the summer camps, where at-risk boys spent weeks in one another's company. Random assignment, however, rules out the usual explanation that the treated boys were different to begin with. The study holds two lessons for therapy. First, clients' own satisfaction is not proof of benefit: the men who had been harmed believed they had been helped. Second, putting at-risk young people together can backfire. Thomas Dishion, Joan McCord and François Poulin brought this second lesson up to date in 1999 in a paper titled "When interventions harm", showing that adolescents in peer-group interventions for antisocial behaviour could teach one another antisocial behaviour, a process called deviancy training . A parallel warning came from group work: Irvin Yalom and Morton Lieberman's 1971 study of "casualties" of encounter groups at Stanford found that some members were harmed by intense, confrontational groups, and that the leaders were poor at recognising which members had been harmed. In 2007 Lilienfeld drew the evidence together in a paper titled "Psychological treatments that cause harm", in Perspectives on Psychological Science . Taking the medical maxim primum non nocere ("first, do no harm") as his starting point, he argued that the field had spent far more energy listing treatments that work than listing treatments that hurt, and he offered a provisional list of potentially harmful therapies (PHTs), graded by the strength of the evidence (Table 8.18). Level I treatments are "probably harmful for some individuals"; Level II treatments are "possibly harmful for some individuals". Table 8.18 Lilienfeld's provisional list of potentially harmful therapies (2007). Level I: probably harmful for some individuals; Level II: possibly harmful for some individuals. Level Treatment Potential harm Main evidence I Critical incident stress debriefing Higher risk of post-traumatic stress symptoms Randomised trials I Scared Straight programmes More conduct problems and offending Randomised trials I Facilitated communication False accusations of abuse against family members Replicated case reports I Attachment therapies (for example, rebirthing) Death and serious injury to children Replicated case reports I Recovered-memory techniques False memories of trauma Replicated case reports I Therapy oriented to dissociative identity disorder Creation of "alter" personalities Replicated case reports I Grief counselling for normal bereavement More depressive symptoms Meta-analysis I Expressive-experiential therapies Worsening of painful emotions Randomised trials I Boot camps for conduct disorder More conduct problems Meta-analysis I DARE drug-prevention programmes More use of alcohol and other substances Randomised trials II Peer-group interventions for conduct disorder More conduct problems (deviancy training) Quasi-experiments II Relaxation for panic-prone patients Panic attacks induced by relaxation Single-case designs Two entries on the list are examined most often. Critical incident stress debriefing (CISD), a single group session held within a few days of a trauma in which survivors are encouraged to recount the event and express their feelings, was tested in randomised trials that found it no better than nothing and, in two trials, linked with worse outcomes months or years later; Section 9.7 tells that story in full. Scared Straight programmes, which began in New Jersey in the 1970s and became famous through a widely seen television documentary, take young offenders or at-risk teenagers into prisons, where inmates describe the brutal realities of prison life in the hope of frightening them out of crime. A randomised trial of the original New Jersey programme in 1982 found that participants were arrested more often than controls, and in 2003 Anthony Petrosino and his colleagues pooled seven randomised and controlled studies and found that such programmes raised the odds of later offending by a ratio of about 1.6 to 1.7. Fear, it turned out, did not deter; if anything, it backfired. Lilienfeld drew a further lesson from the list: because some treatments are clearly harmful, the strong form of the dodo bird verdict, that all therapies are equally effective (Section 8.3), cannot be true. Exam trap Bergin (1966) named the deterioration effect after noticing increased variance in treated groups; about 5 to 10 percent of adult clients are worse at the end of therapy. Lilienfeld (2007) listed potentially harmful therapies ; critical incident stress debriefing and Scared Straight are Level I ("probably harmful") on the strength of randomised trials. Iatrogenic means caused by the treatment itself. The Cambridge-Somerville study (follow-up by Joan McCord , 1978) found long-term harm despite clients believing they had been helped. Routine outcome monitoring and feedback If 5 to 10 percent of clients deteriorate, the obvious remedy is for therapists to notice it early and change course. The trouble is that therapists are poor at noticing. In a study published in 2005, Hannan, Lambert and their colleagues asked the therapists at a university counselling centre to predict which of their 550 clients would be worse off at the end of therapy. Forty clients actually deteriorated. The therapists predicted that 3 would, and only 1 of those 3 did. A simple statistical method, based on clients' weekly questionnaire scores compared with the expected course of recovery, identified every one of the 40 by the end of treatment and 85 percent of them by the third session. Therapists are also optimistic about themselves. When Walfish, Lambert and colleagues asked mental health professionals in 2012 to rate their own skill against their peers, a quarter placed themselves at the 90th percentile and not one rated himself or herself below average; on average they overestimated how many of their clients improved and underestimated how many deteriorated. The fix is routine outcome monitoring (ROM): measuring every client's progress with a brief standard questionnaire at every session (or at regular intervals) and using the results to guide treatment. Its best-known tool is the Outcome Questionnaire-45 (OQ-45), developed by Michael Lambert and his colleagues in the 1990s. It has 45 items, takes 5 to 10 minutes and gives a total score with three subscales: symptom distress (mainly depression and anxiety), interpersonal relations, and social role functioning (problems at work, at college or at home). As noted above, a 14-point change is reliable and the clinical cut-off lies at 63/64. Lambert's system does more than measure. Using data from thousands of clients, it charts the expected recovery curve for a client with any given starting score, and before each session it compares the client's actual score with that expectation and sends the therapist a coloured signal: white when the client is functioning like a non-patient and ending can be considered, green when progress is as expected, yellow when the client is doing less well than expected, and red when the client is at serious risk of treatment failure. Clients with yellow or red signals are called not-on-track cases. For them the therapist can also use clinical support tools: a structured checklist that prompts the therapist to examine the alliance, the client's motivation, social support and the need for referral or medication. Key study: Lambert's feedback trials (2001 onwards) Question: Does telling therapists, session by session, how their clients are progressing improve outcomes? Method: Five studies in routine care, mostly at a university counselling centre, in which clients completed the OQ-45 before every session and were assigned (randomly, in all but one study) either to have their progress fed back to the therapist or to treatment as usual. The same therapists saw clients in both conditions. Result: For not-on-track clients, 20 percent of those whose therapists received no feedback had deteriorated by the end, compared with 15 percent when therapists received feedback and 8 percent when they received feedback and used the clinical support tools. Reliable or clinically significant improvement rose from 22 percent to 33 percent and 45 percent. On-track clients were affected little. A combined re-analysis of six studies with 6,151 clients by Shimokawa, Lambert and Smart (2010) confirmed the benefit. Conclusion: Simple feedback roughly halves deterioration among the clients at greatest risk. Criticism: Most studies came from one research group and one type of setting; later trials elsewhere have found smaller benefits. Other systems work on the same principle. In Britain, the CORE-OM, the measure used in Barkham's good-enough level study, is widely used in routine services. Barry Duncan and Scott Miller's Partners for Change Outcome Management System uses two four-item scales, the Outcome Rating Scale for progress and the Session Rating Scale for the client's view of each session and of the alliance, chosen for being quick enough to use in every session. The measures themselves are described in the Assessment book; what matters here is the logic. Routine outcome monitoring turns the clinician from someone who hopes therapy is working into someone who checks, and it is the practical answer to both of this section's big questions: how much therapy a particular client needs, and whether that client is getting worse. Clinical link You do not need special software to monitor outcome. In an Indian outpatient department, a free and brief symptom measure such as the PHQ-9 for depression, completed in the waiting area before each session and plotted on a simple graph in the file, lets you see at a glance whether a client is on track. Share the graph with the client: "Your score has not moved in four sessions; let us think together about what needs to change." Clients are rarely offended by being asked; they are often relieved that someone is checking. Exam trap The OQ-45 is Michael Lambert's measure: 45 items, three subscales (symptom distress, interpersonal relations, social role), a reliable change of 14 points and a cut-off of 63/64. "Not-on-track" clients are those with yellow or red signals. Therapists predict deterioration very poorly (Hannan and colleagues, 2005: 3 predicted, 40 actual, 1 correct), which is the main argument for routine outcome monitoring. 8.10 Inside the Therapy Room: Process Research, the Course of Therapy and Its Ending Lower yield · not asked yet Section 8.1 drew a line between two kinds of research: outcome research, which asks whether and how much clients change, and process research, which asks what happens in the sessions and how it produces the change. Everything in Section 8.9 was about outcome. This section goes inside the therapy room. It begins with how researchers study what happens in sessions, then follows a course of therapy from its first meeting to its last, including the endings nobody planned, and finishes with four practical decisions every clinician makes: whether to talk about oneself, whether to set homework, how often and for how long to meet, and what to write down afterwards. Process research and the link between process and outcome Outcome research treats therapy as a closed box: clients go in, their scores change, and the question is how much. Process research opens the box. Its raw material is what therapist and client actually say, do and experience during sessions: the therapist's questions, reflections and interpretations, the depth of the client's feeling, the quality of the relationship, the moments that the client later remembers as turning points. Some process research simply describes these events (How often do cognitive therapists interpret? What does a rupture in the alliance look like?). Process-outcome research goes further and links them to change, asking whether more of a particular event, or a better quality of relationship, predicts a better outcome. Most of what Section 8.5 reports about the alliance is process-outcome research. The field became possible only when sessions could be recorded. Until the 1940s the only record of a session was the therapist's later memory of it. Carl Rogers and his colleagues began recording sessions, with their clients' permission, and published the first complete recorded course of psychotherapy, the case of "Herbert Bryan", in 1942 (Section 6.2). For the first time, researchers could study what therapists actually did rather than what they said they did, and they quickly found that the two were not always the same. By the 1980s there were so many process-outcome studies that they needed a map. David Orlinsky and Kenneth Howard supplied one in 1987, which they called the generic model of psychotherapy because it applies to every school. It describes the process of any therapy under six headings: The therapeutic contract , the formal side of therapy: what business these two people have with each other, and on what terms. Therapeutic operations : what therapist and client do, including the techniques. The therapeutic bond : the relationship, including the working alliance. Self-relatedness : how open or defensive each participant is. In-session impacts : the immediate effects of a session, such as relief, insight or new hope. Temporal patterns : how all of these unfold across sessions and across the whole course of therapy. When Orlinsky, Klaus Grawe and Barbara Parks used this framework to review the evidence in 1994, the most consistent process predictors of good outcome lay in the bond and in the client's own contribution, notably the client's openness and active participation, rather than in any particular technique. That finding fed directly into the common-factors argument of Section 8.4. Process-outcome research has a trap that took years to recognise. In 1989 William B. Stiles and David Shapiro criticised what they called the "drug metaphor" in process research: the assumption that the ingredients of therapy act like doses of a drug, so that if an ingredient helps, more of it should go with better outcomes. Therapy does not work like that, because therapists are responsive. They adjust what they do, moment by moment, to the person in front of them. A therapist offers more reassurance to a client who is struggling, more interpretations to a client who seems stuck, and more time on homework with a client who has not done it. As a result, an ingredient may be used most with the clients who are doing worst, and so correlate weakly or even negatively with outcome although it helps. Stiles, Lisa Honos-Webb and Michael Surko (1998) called this the problem of responsiveness . Its lesson is that a correlation between how often something happens in therapy and how well clients do cannot, on its own, tell us whether that thing helps. You have already met one consequence: the good-enough level of Section 8.9, where the "dose" of therapy itself responds to how quickly the client changes. Process research has also shown that change is often uneven. Stephen Ilardi and Edward Craighead argued in 1994 that in cognitive behaviour therapy for depression much of the improvement comes in the first four weeks, before the specific cognitive techniques have been delivered in any real quantity, which they took as evidence for common factors. The most influential reply came from a study of sudden jumps in improvement. Key study: Tang and DeRubeis, sudden gains in cognitive therapy for depression (1999) Question: Does improvement in cognitive behaviour therapy for depression happen gradually, or in jumps, and if in jumps, what precedes them? Method: Tony Z. Tang and Robert J. DeRubeis at the University of Pennsylvania examined session-by-session Beck Depression Inventory scores of depressed patients in cognitive behaviour therapy, and coded recordings of the sessions just before large improvements and of comparison sessions. Result: Many patients showed a sudden gain , a large improvement within a single interval between two sessions, averaging 11 points on the Beck Depression Inventory and accounting for about half of those patients' total improvement. Patients who had sudden gains were less depressed at the end of treatment and remained so 18 months later. The sessions before a gain contained substantial cognitive change; comparison sessions contained little. The alliance improved after the gain. Conclusion: For these patients recovery followed a three-stage sequence: preparation, a critical session with a sudden gain, and an "upward spiral". Criticism: Not all patients show sudden gains, the study was correlational, and later research has found sudden gains in therapies that do not target cognitions. Exam trap Process research studies what happens in sessions; outcome research studies the change that results; process-outcome research links the two. The generic model (Orlinsky and Howard, 1987) has six aspects, beginning with the therapeutic contract and ending with temporal patterns. The drug metaphor critique and the responsiveness problem belong to Stiles (with Shapiro, 1989; with Honos-Webb and Surko, 1998). Sudden gains are Tang and DeRubeis (1999) : about 11 points on the Beck Depression Inventory, about half of total improvement. What process researchers measure Every process study must answer three questions before it can begin. Whose view? The client, the therapist and an outside observer listening to a recording each see something different, and they often disagree. In one study of brief therapy by Stiles, Shapiro and Firth-Cozens (1990), clients' own ratings of how good their sessions had been did not predict their improvement, while one therapist's ratings did and the other's did not. Which unit? A single speaking turn, an episode of a few minutes, a whole session or the entire course of therapy. Which aspect? The therapist's techniques, the client's experiencing, the relationship or the impact of the session. Table 8.19 lists the measures you are most likely to meet, several of which appear in other chapters. Table 8.19 Some widely used process measures. Measure Origin What it rates Rated by Recorded and transcribed sessions Carl Rogers's group, from the early 1940s Everything said, for later coding Researchers Response category systems (verbal response modes) Clara Hill; William Stiles The type of each statement: question, reflection, interpretation, advice, self-disclosure Observers Session Evaluation Questionnaire William Stiles (1980) Depth and smoothness of a session Client and therapist Working Alliance Inventory Adam Horvath and Leslie Greenberg (Section 8.5) Agreement on goals and tasks; the bond Client, therapist or observer Experiencing Scale Klein, Mathieu, Gendlin and Kiesler (Section 6.7) How deeply the client speaks from inner experience (seven stages) Observers Process Scale Rogers and Rablen (Section 6.2) Movement from fixity to fluidity Observers Helpful Aspects of Therapy form Susan Llewelyn, Robert Elliott and colleagues (1988) The most helpful (or hindering) event in a session, in the client's words Client The Session Evaluation Questionnaire , devised by Stiles in 1980, is a good example of how a process measure works. After each session the client (and, separately, the therapist) rates the session on pairs of opposite adjectives, such as deep or shallow, valuable or worthless, and relaxed or tense. The ratings form two dimensions: depth (how powerful and valuable the session felt) and smoothness (how comfortable, safe and easy it felt). The two are not the same, and the difference teaches something about therapy: a session in which a client finally faces a painful memory may feel deep but anything but smooth. Another family of measures classifies what therapists say. In a response category system , such as Clara E. Hill 's category system for counsellor responses or Stiles's verbal response modes, trained judges listen to a recording and code each therapist statement as one of a small number of types: a question, a restatement, a reflection of feeling, an interpretation, advice, information, self-disclosure and so on. With such codes a researcher can show, for example, how differently a psychodynamic and a cognitive therapist talk, or which kinds of response tend to be followed by deeper client experiencing. A different strategy, the events paradigm , picks out particular kinds of moments in therapy (a rupture, an insight, a client's harsh self-criticism) and studies them intensively. In task analysis , developed by Laura Rice and Leslie Greenberg in their 1984 book Patterns of Change , the researcher collects many recorded examples of one kind of event, compares those in which the client resolved the problem with those in which the client did not, and builds a step-by-step model of the route to resolution. Several of the tasks of emotion-focused therapy, including the two-chair dialogue for a split within the self, were refined in this way (Section 6.7). Finally, qualitative methods have added the client's own account of what helped. In Clara Hill's consensual qualitative research, a small team of judges reads interviews with clients or therapists and reaches agreement, by discussion, about the themes they contain. Exam trap Match each measure to its owner. Session Evaluation Questionnaire : Stiles (1980), depth and smoothness. Experiencing Scale : depth of the client's experiencing (Gendlin's group). Process Scale : fixity to fluidity (Rogers and Rablen). Working Alliance Inventory : Horvath and Greenberg. Task analysis : Rice and Greenberg (1984). The first published complete recorded therapy was Rogers's case of Herbert Bryan (1942). The course of therapy: beginning, middle and end Whatever its school, a course of therapy has a beginning, a middle and an end, and each stage has its own tasks (Figure 8.13). The idea is old and appears in many forms in this book: Harry Stack Sullivan divided even a single interview into stages (Section 2.1), Gerard Egan's skilled helper model moves through three stages (Section 6.10), interpersonal psychotherapy has initial, intermediate and termination phases (Section 3.7), and cognitive therapy has its own session structure and course (Section 5.4). What follows is the generic version that applies to all of them. Beginning Middle End After Sessions 1 to 3 Most of therapy Final sessions Weeks to months Assessment Formulation Contract, goals Role induction Alliance and hope Core techniques Working through Homework Repair ruptures Monitor progress Raise it early Review gains Relapse plan Feelings about it Taper sessions Follow-up visit Booster sessions Door left open Time in therapy Termination is planned from the first session; dropout can happen at any point. Figure 8.13 The stages of a course of therapy and the main tasks of each. Notice that the ending is prepared long before the last session, and that the work continues after it through follow-up and booster sessions. The beginning. The beginning stage usually covers the first one to three sessions, though with complex problems it may take longer. It has five tasks. The first is assessment and formulation : understanding the problem, the person and the context, including risk (Chapter 2), and deciding whether psychotherapy is the right help at all or whether a referral, for medication or to another service, is needed. The second is agreeing a contract. The third is preparing the client for therapy. The fourth is building the alliance (Section 8.5), and the fifth, which runs through all the others, is instilling hope: the remoralisation of Section 8.9. The therapeutic contract is the explicit agreement, spoken or written, about how client and therapist will work together. It has a practical part: how often and how long sessions will be, roughly how many there will be, fees, what happens about missed or late appointments, how to make contact between sessions, and the limits of confidentiality (whose rules are set out in Chapter 1). It also has a therapeutic part: the goals, the methods, what each person is responsible for and how progress will be reviewed. A contract protects both parties, makes expectations explicit and turns therapy into a joint project rather than something done to the client. It is the first element of Orlinsky and Howard's generic model, and when the contract states the likely length of therapy, the ending has been planned from the first session. Clients often arrive with little idea of what therapy involves. Many expect something like a medical consultation: describe the problem, receive advice or a prescription, and leave. In the early 1960s Jerome Frank's group at Johns Hopkins University tested whether preparing patients would help. Rudolf Hoehn-Saric, Frank and their colleagues (1964) gave some outpatients a role induction interview before therapy began. It explained what psychotherapy is, what patient and therapist would each do, that the patient should talk freely about feelings, and that progress would have ups and downs, including moments of frustration with the therapist. Compared with unprepared patients, the prepared patients behaved more as therapy requires and, on several measures, improved more. Role induction (also called pretherapy preparation or socialisation to therapy) is now a standard part of the beginning stage; in cognitive therapy it takes the form of teaching the cognitive model in the first session (Section 5.4). The middle. The middle stage is where most of the remediation of Section 8.9 happens and where each school's main techniques are used: exposure, cognitive restructuring, interpretation, empathic exploration, family tasks. Psychodynamic therapists call much of this working through , the repeated re-examination of the same conflict in new contexts until insight turns into change (Section 3.2), and every school has an equivalent: practising, generalising and applying the new skill to one situation after another. The middle stage is rarely smooth. There are plateaus when nothing seems to move, setbacks after a life event, the return of ambivalence (Section 6.9) and ruptures in the alliance that must be noticed and repaired (Section 8.5). Two habits protect it: reviewing progress regularly against the goals in the contract, ideally with a measure (routine outcome monitoring, Section 8.9), and revising the formulation when the client does not change as it predicted. The end and after. The final stage, termination, is the subject of the next subsection. After it come follow-up and booster sessions, which keep the gains in place. Do not confuse these stages of therapy with the stages of change of James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente's transtheoretical model (Section 6.9): precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance. The stages of therapy describe the treatment; the stages of change describe the client's readiness to change, which may be quite different from what the therapist assumes. A young man in precontemplation, brought to therapy by his parents, is in the beginning stage of therapy but is not ready for the action-oriented techniques of the middle stage, and mismatches like this are a common road to dropout. In a culturally diverse sample of adolescents admitted to inpatient substance-abuse treatment, for example, those in precontemplation dropped out significantly more often than those in the contemplation, preparation or action stages (Callaghan and colleagues, 2005). Exam trap Keep four sequences apart: the stages of therapy (beginning, middle, end), Howard's phases of change (remoralisation, remediation, rehabilitation), Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change (precontemplation to maintenance) and Egan's three stages of the skilled helper. A question about the features of a working relationship (an observable ability to work together, a committed belief in the helping relationship, a realistic and collaborative contract) will often slip in "a psychodynamic theory base" as the odd one out: the working relationship, like Bordin's alliance, belongs to no single theory. Role induction was tested by Hoehn-Saric, Frank and colleagues (1964). Ending well: termination Termination is the planned process of bringing therapy to a close. It is a phase rather than an event, and some writers prefer to call it consolidation, because its purpose is to make the gains last. Endings come in three kinds. A planned or mutual termination is agreed by client and therapist because the goals have been met or the agreed number of sessions is complete. A client-initiated ending happens when the client stops before the therapist thinks the work is done; this includes premature dropout (next subsection), but not every client-initiated ending is premature, since some clients stop because they have reached their good-enough level. A therapist-initiated or forced ending happens when the therapist moves, falls ill or retires, when a trainee's placement ends, when a session limit set by a service or an insurer is reached, or when the therapist judges that therapy is not helping. How do you know it is time to end? The usual criteria are that the goals agreed in the contract have been met; that symptoms have fallen into the normal or a manageable range (the clinical significance criteria of Section 8.9 are a formal version of this test); that the client has the skills to cope with setbacks without the therapist; that the gains have held over several sessions, including some spaced further apart; and that further sessions are bringing diminishing returns. There is also an ending for the opposite reason. If a client is not benefiting, or is being harmed, continuing is not kindness. Professional codes require a therapist to end therapy, or to refer the client elsewhere, when the client no longer needs it, is unlikely to benefit from it or is being harmed by it (Chapter 1). How should therapy end? In 2017 John Norcross and three colleagues asked 65 experts from many theoretical traditions how often they carried out each of 80 possible tasks when ending a successful therapy. There was far more agreement across schools than difference, and the tasks fell into eight groups that make a good checklist for any ending: Talking through the client's, and the therapist's, feelings about ending. Discussing how the client will function and cope in the future. Helping the client use the new skills beyond therapy. Framing personal development as something never finished. Anticipating continued growth and generalisation after therapy. Preparing explicitly for the ending, well before the last session. Reflecting on the client's gains and consolidating them. Expressing pride in the client's progress and in the relationship. In practice this means raising the ending several sessions before it happens; often tapering the sessions from weekly to fortnightly to monthly, so that the client tests his independence while support is still available; reviewing progress together, if possible with the scores collected along the way; attributing the change to the client's own effort, which protects his confidence; and agreeing a written relapse prevention plan that lists the early warning signs, the coping steps that worked and whom to contact if problems return (relapse prevention is taught in Section 9.9). What do clients feel at the end? The classical view, from psychoanalysis, treats termination as a loss. Ending a close relationship revives earlier separations, so the patient may grieve, become angry or suffer a return of the original symptoms as the last session approaches, and analysing these reactions is part of the work. Freud's late doubts about whether an analysis can ever be complete appear in Section 3.2, and James Mann built his 12-session therapy around the meaning of the ending (Section 3.6). Research on shorter therapies paints a gentler picture. Reviewing it in 1993, Stephen M. Quintana found that the prediction that termination is inherently a crisis for clients had not been confirmed: most clients in planned endings experience it as a positive transition, with pride and a sense of accomplishment mixed with some sadness and some anxiety about managing alone. Quintana proposed replacing the metaphor of termination as loss with that of termination as transformation : the client leaves changed, taking the relationship with him as part of a new view of himself. Loss still matters for some clients, particularly those whose lives have been marked by abandonment, and after long, intensive therapies. Therapists have feelings too: pride, sadness, relief and sometimes doubt about whether they did enough, and trainees whose placements force an ending often feel guilty about leaving. The work does not stop at the last session. A follow-up appointment a month or three months later lets client and therapist check that the gains have held and tells the client that the door remains open. Booster sessions , planned in advance and spaced weeks or months apart, are a standard part of behavioural and cognitive treatments (Chapter 4 and Section 5.4) and help to prevent relapse in recurrent conditions such as depression. Indian context In Indian practice, therapy often ends by default rather than by plan. A family that brought a son for "exam fear" may stop coming as soon as the fear lifts, which is often after remoralisation and before the work is consolidated. A grateful client may wish to keep visiting, as one might keep visiting a respected elder or teacher (the guru-chela relationship is discussed in Section 8.11), and may bring sweets or an invitation to a wedding at the last session. Discussing the likely length of therapy with the family at the start, explaining why the last few sessions matter, and thinking in advance about gifts and invitations (Section 3.3 on boundaries; Chapter 1 on ethics) prevent most of these difficulties. Exam trap Termination is a planned phase , prepared from the first session, not an event at the last one. Endings may be planned (mutual), client-initiated or therapist-initiated (forced) . Classical theory sees termination as loss ; Quintana (1993) proposed termination as transformation , since research did not confirm that ending is a crisis for most clients. Norcross and colleagues (2017) found eight groups of termination tasks shared across schools. Booster sessions come after the regular sessions end. Premature dropout Not every therapy reaches a planned ending. Premature termination , or dropout, is a unilateral ending by the client before the goals of therapy have been reached. It is hard to define precisely, and researchers have used several definitions: the therapist's judgement that the client left too early, failure to return after a missed session, attending fewer than a set number of sessions, or not completing a manualised treatment. The rate found in a study depends heavily on which definition it uses. The first large review, by Michael Wierzbicki and Glenn Pekarik in 1993, pooled 125 studies and found an average dropout rate of about 47 percent: nearly half of all clients. They also found that dropout was more likely among clients from ethnic minorities, with less education and with lower incomes. Two decades later Joshua K. Swift and Roger Greenberg (2012) repeated the exercise on a far larger scale, with 669 studies and 83,834 clients, and found a lower weighted average of 19.7 percent, about one client in five. Dropout varied with the client's diagnosis and age, the therapist's experience, the setting, the definition of dropout and whether the study was an efficacy trial or an effectiveness study (Section 8.7). It was highest among younger clients, clients with personality disorders or eating disorders, and clients seen by trainees. It did not differ between theoretical orientations or between individual and group formats. Why do clients drop out? The reasons overlap with the causes of deterioration (Section 8.9) and with the client variables of Section 8.6. Some leave because they are dissatisfied: the alliance never formed, the therapist seemed not to understand, or the method made no sense to them. Some leave because their expectations did not match the therapy, expecting advice or medicine and receiving questions, or expecting three sessions and being offered twenty. Some leave for practical reasons: fees, travel, time off work, child care, a family that disapproves. Some leave because they were never ready to change (the precontemplators above). And some, it should be remembered, leave because they feel better, which is why not every dropout is a failure. The research suggests several ways to keep clients in therapy: Prepare them. Role induction at the start (above) explains what will happen, how long it is likely to take and that progress is uneven. Ask what they want, and accommodate it where possible. In a 2018 meta-analysis of 53 studies with over 16,000 clients, Swift and his colleagues found that clients who received a treatment they preferred were less likely to drop out (odds ratio 1.79) and had somewhat better outcomes ( d = 0.28). Build the alliance early and ask for feedback on each session, so that dissatisfaction is voiced in the room rather than expressed by not returning (Section 8.5). Monitor progress so that clients who are not on track are noticed before they disappear (Section 8.9). Work with ambivalence using motivational interviewing when readiness is low (Section 6.9). Remove practical barriers : short waiting times, reminders, flexible hours, sessions by telephone or video, and a phone call after a missed appointment. Exam trap Dropout rates: about 47 percent in Wierzbicki and Pekarik (1993) , about 20 percent (19.7) in Swift and Greenberg (2012) . Higher dropout goes with younger clients, personality and eating disorders and trainee therapists; theoretical orientation makes no difference. The hello-goodbye effect , in which clients exaggerate their distress at the start and their improvement at the end, is a different idea (Section 8.6). Therapist self-disclosure Halfway through her fourth session, a client asks her therapist, "Have you ever lost someone close to you?" What should the therapist say? The question goes to one of the oldest disagreements between the schools of therapy. Therapist self-disclosure is any statement in which the therapist reveals something personal about himself or herself: a fact, a feeling or an experience from outside the therapy. Clara Hill, who with Sarah Knox has done most of the research on the subject, classifies disclosures by content. A disclosure may concern facts (credentials, training, whether the therapist is married or has children), feelings ("When my father was ill, I felt guilty too"), insight ("I realised that my own perfectionism came from wanting my teachers' approval") or strategies ("What helped me was making a list each morning"). Researchers also separate two kinds of statement. A self-disclosing statement reveals something about the therapist's life outside the session. A self-involving statement , also called immediacy , expresses the therapist's present reaction to the client or to the relationship: "I feel moved as you tell me this", or "I notice that I feel pushed away when you laugh about what happened". Finally, some disclosure is unavoidable. A therapist's name, accent, wedding ring, age, pregnancy, the pictures in the consulting room or a chance meeting at a temple all tell the client something, and in India a surname can reveal region, religion or caste before a word has been spoken. Almost all therapists disclose something at some time: surveys reviewed by Jennifer Henretty and Heidi Levitt in 2010 found that over 90 percent do, although disclosures make up only a small fraction of what therapists say. The schools differ sharply in how they regard it. Classical psychoanalysis discourages it. Freud advised in 1912 that "the doctor should be opaque to his patients and, like a mirror, should show them nothing but what is shown to him". The analyst's anonymity lets the transference develop and be analysed without contamination; disclosure gratifies the patient's wishes (against the rule of abstinence, Section 3.2), shifts the focus to the analyst and may burden the patient. Later relational and intersubjective analysts allow judicious disclosure, especially of the analyst's own reactions in the room (Section 3.5). Humanistic therapists are far more open. For Carl Rogers, congruence or genuineness means being a real person rather than a professional facade (Section 6.2). Sidney M. Jourard (1926 to 1974) argued in The Transparent Self (1964) that honest self-disclosure is a mark of psychological health and that disclosure invites disclosure in return, which he called the dyadic effect . Existential and Gestalt therapists use the here-and-now relationship directly. Even so, Rogers did not mean that therapists should tell clients everything they feel; congruence means sharing persistent feelings that are relevant to the relationship. Feminist and multicultural therapists use disclosure to reduce the power difference between therapist and client and to show shared experience, which can build trust across cultural lines. Cognitive and behavioural therapists use it pragmatically, as a coping model ("I used to get anxious before presentations; here is what I did") or to normalise a reaction. Albert Ellis was famous for disclosing his own past shyness (Section 5.2). Addiction counsellors who are themselves in recovery often disclose their history as part of the treatment's ethos. What does the evidence show? In 2014 Henretty, Levitt and their colleagues pooled 53 experimental and quasi-experimental studies comparing counsellor self-disclosure with non-disclosure. Overall, disclosure had a favourable effect: clients viewed disclosing counsellors more positively and said they would be more willing to open up to them, and disclosures that revealed similarity between counsellor and client were especially helpful. In 2018 Hill, Knox and Pinto-Coelho reviewed 21 studies of real therapy and found that self-disclosure and immediacy were most often followed by a stronger relationship, improved functioning, new insight and a sense that the session had helped. The research and clinical experience agree on when disclosure helps and when it harms (Table 8.20). Table 8.20 When therapist self-disclosure tends to help and when it tends to harm. Tends to help when it is Tends to harm when it is Infrequent and brief Frequent or long For the client's benefit: to normalise, validate, model coping, offer a new view or strengthen the alliance For the therapist's benefit: to be liked, to unburden, to fill a silence About past experiences the therapist has resolved About current, unresolved problems Relevant to the client's concern, and followed by a return of focus to the client A shift of focus to the therapist that the client must manage Revealing similarity, in a strong alliance Intimate (sexual or financial) or blurring the professional boundary A short, honest answer to a culturally ordinary question Used with clients whose boundaries or sense of self are fragile, where it may confuse Back to the client who asked about loss. A rigid refusal ("We are here to talk about you") can feel like a slap, and in an Indian setting, where questions such as "Are you married?" or "Do you have children?" are ordinary courtesy, it can damage the alliance before it has formed. A brief, honest answer followed by a return to the client usually works better: "Yes, I lost my mother some years ago. I wonder whether you are asking if I can understand what you are going through?" Exam trap Freud's "opaque ... like a mirror" (1912) is the classical case against disclosure; Jourard's The Transparent Self (1964) and the dyadic effect (disclosure begets disclosure) are the humanistic case for it. A self-involving statement (immediacy) concerns the therapist's here-and-now reaction to the client; a self-disclosing statement concerns the therapist's life outside. Hill's four content types: facts, feelings, insight, strategies. Disclosure is a boundary crossing , not in itself a boundary violation (Section 3.3). Homework A client spends perhaps one hour a week with a therapist and the other 167 hours living his life (Section 5.4). Homework , or between-session assignments, is any planned task the client carries out between sessions to practise, test or apply what has been learned in them. It is central in cognitive and behavioural therapies (thought records, behavioural experiments, activity scheduling, exposure practice, relaxation practice, the diary cards of dialectical behaviour therapy), common in family and couple therapy (Chapter 7), solution-focused therapy (Section 6.8) and interpersonal therapy, and used occasionally even by Gestalt therapists, who set experiments to try during the week. Classical psychodynamic therapy is the main exception. Why should homework help? Several reasons work together. Practice strengthens new skills and makes them automatic. Carrying them out in real life helps them generalise beyond the consulting room. Self-monitoring collects data that cannot be gathered in the session. Behavioural experiments test beliefs where they matter. Doing the work oneself builds self-efficacy, because the client can attribute the change to his own effort. And homework gives continuity between sessions and rehearses the independence the client will need after termination. Key study: Kazantzis, Deane and Ronan's meta-analysis of homework (2000) Question: Does homework improve the outcome of cognitive and behavioural therapy, and do clients who do more of it improve more? Method: Nikolaos Kazantzis , Frank Deane and Kevin Ronan pooled 27 studies with 1,702 clients, in Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice . Result: Studies comparing therapy with and without homework gave a weighted mean effect size of r = .36 in favour of homework; the relation between how much homework clients completed (compliance) and their outcome gave r = .22. Conclusion: Assigning homework improves outcome, and clients who do more of it tend to do better. Criticism: Compliance findings are correlational: clients who are already improving may find homework easier, which is the responsiveness problem again. Later meta-analyses broadly agree: Brent Mausbach and colleagues (2010) found r = .26 for compliance across 23 studies, and Kazantzis and colleagues (2016) showed that the quality of homework (how skilfully it is done) predicts outcome as well as its quantity. The commonest problem with homework is that clients do not do it. They may not understand the task or its purpose, find it too hard, forget, fear doing it badly (perfectionists treat it as another examination, Section 2.9), lack the time or privacy, or feel that the therapist does not really care whether it is done. Experienced therapists improve homework compliance in several ways. They design the task together with the client and explain its rationale. They make it specific (what, when, where and how often) and small enough to succeed. They start it in the session and write it down. They ask "What might get in the way?" and plan for it, and they ask how confident the client feels about doing it, simplifying the task if the answer is lukewarm. Above all, they review it at the start of the next session, every time; a therapist who forgets to ask teaches the client that homework does not matter. Partial completion is praised, and non-completion is treated as useful information rather than failure. In India the word itself can be a problem, carrying memories of school, tuition and scolding; calling the task "practice", an "experiment" or a "between-session task" often helps. Exam trap The homework meta-analyses are by Kazantzis and colleagues: r = .36 for assigning homework and r = .22 for compliance (2000); Mausbach and colleagues found r = .26 for compliance (2010). Homework review comes near the start of a cognitive therapy session, after the mood check, bridge and agenda (Section 5.4), and new homework is set near the end. Homework is used across many therapies, not only CBT, but rarely in classical psychoanalysis. How often, how long, and what to write down Frequency. Freud saw his patients six days a week, and classical psychoanalysis still meets four or five times a week (Section 3.2). Most modern therapies meet weekly, often tapering to fortnightly or monthly towards the end. Is weekly the right rhythm? A 2013 meta-regression by Pim Cuijpers and colleagues of 70 trials of psychotherapy for adult depression, with 5,403 patients, found only a small association between the total number of sessions and the effect size, and none with total contact time or the duration of therapy once other features of the studies were taken into account. The number of sessions per week , however, was strongly associated with outcome: moving from one to two sessions a week, with the total number of sessions held constant, raised the effect size by about 0.45. In 2015 David Erekson, Lambert and Dennis Eggett examined 21,488 clients of a university counselling centre, tracked with the OQ-45 over 17 years, and found that clients who attended weekly reached clinically significant change faster than those who attended fortnightly, although the total amount of change was similar. A Dutch trial that randomly assigned 200 depressed patients to cognitive behaviour therapy or interpersonal psychotherapy, once or twice a week, found twice-weekly sessions more effective on average (Sanne Bruijniks and colleagues, 2020), though a later analysis of the same trial suggested that some patients did better with weekly sessions. The practical lesson is to concentrate sessions early, when the client is most distressed and most at risk of dropping out, and to space them out later. Length. The conventional session is the "fifty-minute hour", which leaves the therapist a few minutes for notes before the next client. But there is nothing sacred about it. Brief sessions of 20 to 30 minutes are common in primary care and with children; family and couple sessions often run longer; prolonged exposure for post-traumatic stress disorder usually uses 90-minute sessions so that anxiety has time to fall; and some treatments are deliberately massed into a single long meeting. In 1989 Lars-Göran Öst described a one-session treatment for specific phobias, combining exposure and modelling, that averaged 2.1 hours; at follow-up after an average of four years, 90 percent of his first 20 patients were much improved or completely recovered. What matters as much as the length is its predictability: the same time, the same place and a clear start and finish are part of the frame that makes therapy feel safe (Section 3.3). Notes. Every session ends with a record. Notes preserve continuity when memory fades, communicate with colleagues, supervisors and anyone who later takes over the case, protect client and therapist if a complaint or a court case arises, allow audit and research, and are increasingly open to the client himself. A good note records the date and attendance; the client's state and any change in mental status; the risk assessment and any action taken; the main themes and interventions; the client's response; homework and outcome scores; contacts with family or other professionals; and the plan for next time. It is signed and dated. Several formats help. The best known is the SOAP note , borrowed from Lawrence Weed's problem-oriented medical record of the late 1960s: Subjective (what the client reports), Objective (what the clinician observes, including test scores and mental status), Assessment (the clinician's interpretation and judgement of progress) and Plan (what happens next). The DAP note (data, assessment, plan) merges the first two headings. Clinicians also distinguish progress notes , the official, concise and factual record kept in the case file, from process notes , the therapist's private and more detailed reflections on what happened in a session, including hypotheses and his own reactions, which are often written for supervision (Section 8.12). In some countries the law gives such private notes extra protection. The principles of note-keeping are simple. Write on the same day. Describe behaviour rather than attach labels: "shouted, walked out ten minutes early, returned and apologised" says more, and more fairly, than "hostile". Be concise and avoid jargon. Never alter a note after the event; add a dated addition instead. Store notes securely. And write every note as though the client, a supervisor and a judge will one day read it, because any of them may. The legal and ethical rules on records, confidentiality and clients' access to their files are set out in Chapter 1. Clinical link Interviewers sometimes ask a trainee, "What would you write after a session?" A clear answer uses a structure: "A SOAP note. Subjective: what he told me, in his words where it matters. Objective: what I saw and his questionnaire score. Assessment: my judgement of progress and risk. Plan: the homework, the next appointment and anything I need to discuss in supervision." Add that you would document any risk assessment carefully and keep personal reflections for supervision separate from the case record. Exam trap Cuijpers and colleagues (2013): the number of sessions per week predicted outcome much more strongly than the total number of sessions. The sections since have answered it piece by piece, and two of the answers have awkward consequences for the way therapy is organised. If bona fide therapies built on rival theories produce broadly similar results (Section 8.3), and if much of what heals is shared by all of them (Section 8.4), why should a therapist stay loyal to one school? And if every therapy grew up in a particular place (Vienna, London, the universities of North America), does it travel unchanged to a joint family in Mandya or a slum resettlement colony in Delhi? This section takes up both questions: first the movement to combine therapies, called psychotherapy integration, and then the adaptation of therapy to culture, ending with the answers Indian clinicians have given since the 1960s. Why therapists began to combine therapies For the first half of the twentieth century a psychotherapist was usually trained inside one school and stayed there. Schools had their own journals, institutes and heroes, and moving between them was treated almost as disloyalty. Then the schools multiplied. In 2001 Raymond Corsini summarised 69 new and innovative therapies, and by 2008 the count stood at more than 400. Most had little research behind them, but their number alone made the old question "Which school is right?" look less and less answerable. What therapists actually do turned out to be different from what the textbooks implied. When James Prochaska and John Norcross combined several American surveys of more than 1,500 psychologists, counsellors, psychiatrists and social workers in 2010, the most common answer to "What is your primary theoretical orientation?" among clinical psychologists was not psychoanalytic, behavioural or cognitive but eclectic or integrative , at about 29 percent. Cognitive therapy was a close second at about 28 percent, psychodynamic therapy was chosen by about 12 percent and behaviour therapy by about 10 percent. Even therapists who name a single orientation usually borrow techniques from others. In practice, combining therapies is the rule rather than the exception. Why did this happen? John C. Norcross, the most prolific chronicler of the movement, lists a set of reasons that are worth knowing because each connects to an earlier section of this chapter. There were too many therapies for any one to claim the whole truth. No single theory proved adequate for every client and every problem. The outcome research of Sections 8.2 and 8.3 showed that rival therapies produced similar results, which weakened the case for loyalty to any one of them. The search for common factors (Section 8.4) suggested that therapies share their most important ingredients. Treatment manuals (Section 8.7) let therapists see in detail what other schools actually did in the room. Insurers and health services pushed for brief, problem-focused treatment, which encouraged therapists to use whatever worked fastest. And by the 1980s there was a professional network to support the work: the Society for the Exploration of Psychotherapy Integration (SEPI), whose founders included the cognitive-behaviourist Marvin R. Goldfried and the psychoanalyst Paul L. Wachtel , and from 1991 its Journal of Psychotherapy Integration . The field's standard reference, the Handbook of Psychotherapy Integration edited by Norcross and Goldfried, appeared in 1992. The idea itself is older than the movement. In 1950 two Yale psychologists, John Dollard (1900 to 1980) and Neal E. Miller (1909 to 2002), published Personality and Psychotherapy , which translated the central ideas of psychoanalysis (conflict, repression, transference) into the language of learning theory (drive, cue, response and reinforcement). A neurotic conflict, for Dollard and Miller, was an approach-avoidance conflict that had been learned, and repression was a learned avoidance of thinking certain thoughts because thinking them had been followed by anxiety. The book showed that two theories which looked incompatible could be made to speak to each other, and it remained a point of reference for every later attempt. Two words need to be kept apart. Eclecticism (from a Greek word meaning "to select") means choosing what seems to work from several sources without necessarily joining their theories together. Psychotherapy integration is the broader effort to combine therapies into a coherent whole, at the level of techniques, theories or shared principles. Integration is the umbrella term today, and most writers treat systematic eclecticism as one form of it. What both camps reject is the unsystematic mixing of whatever a therapist happens to like, with no rationale for when or why each technique is used; critics call this syncretism, and it is the caricature of eclecticism that gave the word a bad name. Exam trap In the large American surveys the single most common orientation among clinical psychologists is eclectic or integrative (about 29 percent, Prochaska and Norcross, 2010), with cognitive a close second; it is not psychoanalysis. An early landmark of integration is Dollard and Miller's Personality and Psychotherapy (1950), which joined psychoanalysis and learning theory. Eclecticism selects; integration combines into a whole; unsystematic mixing is syncretism. The four routes to integration Integration can be attempted at different levels. In 1989 Hal Arkowitz described three strands in the movement: technical eclecticism, theoretical integration and the common factors approach. In 1992 Stanley B. Messer named a fourth, assimilative integration. These four routes are now the standard classification, and Table 8.21 sets them side by side before we take each in turn. Table 8.21 The four routes to psychotherapy integration. Route What is combined Best-known examples Strength Weakness Technical eclecticism Techniques, chosen by evidence and by client characteristics; theories are not merged Lazarus's multimodal therapy (BASIC I.D.); Beutler's systematic treatment selection Practical, flexible, tied to evidence Can lack a unifying account of why change happens Theoretical integration Two or more theories, fused into a new framework Wachtel's cyclical psychodynamics; Prochaska and DiClemente's transtheoretical approach; Ryle's cognitive analytic therapy Conceptual depth and coherence Hard to reconcile rival assumptions; hard to test Common factors integration The ingredients all therapies share Frank's shared features of healing; Goldfried's change principles Rests on the outcome evidence of Sections 8.3 and 8.4 Can be vague about what to do next Assimilative integration One home theory, plus techniques imported from others Messer; Stricker and Gold's assimilative psychodynamic therapy Keeps a stable framework while gaining flexibility Imports may be distorted by the home theory Technical eclecticism. The first route borrows techniques but not theories. The term technical eclecticism was introduced in 1967 by Arnold Allan Lazarus (1932 to 2013), whose multimodal therapy you met in Section 5.5. Lazarus assessed every client across seven modalities, the BASIC I.D. (Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal relationships, Drugs and biology), and then chose, problem by problem, whichever technique had the best evidence, whatever school it came from. He could use the Gestalt empty chair without accepting Gestalt theory; his own guiding framework remained social and cognitive learning theory. Lazarus was openly suspicious of the second route, warning that blending incompatible theories produces confusion rather than insight. A second technical eclectic, Larry E. Beutler, tried to make the choice of technique more systematic. In Systematic Treatment Selection (1990), written with John Clarkin, he argued that the question is not which therapy is best but which features of treatment fit which features of the client. Systematic treatment selection matches treatment to a handful of client dimensions. Greater functional impairment calls for more intensive treatment. Coping style matters: clients with an externalising style (who act out, blame others and avoid inner experience) tend to do better with symptom-focused, skill-building methods, while clients with an internalising style (self-critical, withdrawn, inclined to blame themselves) tend to do better with insight-oriented and interpersonal work. The client's level of reactance , the tendency to resist being directed, decides how directive the therapist should be: a highly reactant client who bristles at instructions does better with a non-directive, self-paced approach, while a client low in reactance accepts and benefits from direct guidance. Subjective distress is managed so that it stays in a workable middle range: support for clients overwhelmed by it, and raised arousal for clients too comfortable to work. The reactance finding is the best supported; a 2011 meta-analysis of 12 studies by Beutler and colleagues found a large advantage (an effect size of about 0.8) when the directiveness of therapy was matched to the client's level of resistance. Theoretical integration. The second route goes deeper and tries to join the theories themselves. Theoretical integration combines the concepts of two or more theories into a new framework that is meant to be better than either parent. Its best-known example is Paul Wachtel's cyclical psychodynamics , set out in Psychoanalysis and Behavior Therapy: Toward an Integration (1977). Wachtel was trained as a psychoanalyst, but he became dissatisfied with what he called the "woolly mammoth" view of the unconscious, the idea that childhood wishes and fears are preserved unchanged, like a mammoth frozen in ice, and simply play themselves out in adult life. In his view the past persists because the present keeps recreating it. Inner conflicts shape how a person behaves; that behaviour draws predictable reactions from other people; and those reactions confirm and strengthen the original conflict. The other people become, in Wachtel's word, accomplices in keeping the pattern alive. Because the problem runs in a circle, it can be attacked at any point on the circle: through insight into the conflict, through behavioural methods such as exposure and assertion training that change what the person does, and through the changed responses of others that follow. A worked example shows the circle. Shalini, a 30-year-old schoolteacher in Mysuru, grew up feeling that her love was welcome only when she pleased everyone. Married into a joint family, she agrees to every request from her in-laws, says nothing when she is overloaded, and seethes inside. Because she never objects, her in-laws reasonably assume she is content and ask for more; their extra demands feed her resentment and her secret conviction that her own wishes do not count, which makes her even less able to speak. A purely psychoanalytic therapist might work only on the childhood conflict; a purely behavioural one might teach assertion without asking why it feels so dangerous. Wachtel would do both, and would expect that the first small act of assertion, by changing how the in-laws respond, would itself loosen the old conviction. The second classic example of theoretical integration is the transtheoretical approach of James O. Prochaska and Carlo C. DiClemente , set out in their 1984 book The Transtheoretical Approach: Crossing Traditional Boundaries of Therapy . Section 6.9 described its stages of change. What makes it integrative is that it assigns the contributions of the rival schools to different moments of change. The stages say when change happens; the processes of change say how, and they were drawn from many schools (consciousness raising from the insight therapies, counterconditioning and stimulus control from behaviour therapy, the helping relationship from Rogers); and the levels of change say what is to be changed, from symptoms and situations, through maladaptive cognitions, current interpersonal conflicts and family or systems conflicts, to intrapersonal conflicts. Insight-oriented processes are most useful in the early stages and action-oriented ones in the later stages, so the approach tells the therapist not which school is right but when each school is useful. A third example, Anthony Ryle's cognitive analytic therapy, which joins cognitive psychology and personal construct theory to psychoanalytic object relations theory, was described in Section 5.7. Common factors integration. The third route builds therapy around what the schools already share. Common factors integration starts from the evidence of Sections 8.3 and 8.4: if Jerome Frank was right that every healing practice works through a confiding relationship, a healing setting, a credible rationale and a ritual, then a therapist should deliberately strengthen those ingredients whatever techniques she uses. In 1980 Goldfried proposed looking for principles of change at a level of abstraction between theory and technique, the level at which the schools agree, and named two candidates: providing the client with new corrective experiences, and giving direct feedback that helps the client see himself more accurately. Later writers built whole approaches on this footing, most visibly The Heart and Soul of Change (edited by Mark Hubble, Barry Duncan and Scott Miller, 1999), which urged therapists to organise their work around the client's resources, the alliance and hope, and to check progress with the client session by session (Section 8.9). Assimilative integration. The fourth route is the one most practising therapists actually follow. Assimilative integration keeps a single home theory and imports techniques from other approaches into it. Messer's important point was that an imported technique does not arrive unchanged: it takes on the meaning of its new home. When a psychodynamic therapist uses the Gestalt empty chair, the exercise becomes a way of bringing an internalised parent into the room and exploring the client's relationship with that figure, not a Gestalt experiment in awareness. George Stricker and Jerry Gold described an assimilative psychodynamic psychotherapy that adds behavioural, cognitive and experiential techniques to a psychodynamic framework, and Louis Castonguay's integrative cognitive therapy for depression adds humanistic and interpersonal methods for repairing alliance ruptures (Section 8.5) to a cognitive therapy base. In surveys of integrative therapists, assimilative integration is among the most commonly endorsed forms. Figure 8.14 shows how the four routes differ in what they do with theory and with technique. Notice that only theoretical integration changes the theory itself; technical eclecticism and assimilative integration both keep one theory and differ in whether imported techniques are reinterpreted. Return to Shalini to see the four routes side by side. A technical eclectic would map her problems across the BASIC I.D. and choose assertion training for her silence, relaxation for her headaches and cognitive work on "my wishes do not count", without worrying about where each technique came from. Wachtel, as you saw, would work the whole circle from conflict to behaviour to the in-laws' responses. A common factors therapist would concentrate on a strong alliance, a rationale that makes sense to Shalini and her husband, and the hope that change is possible, and would let the techniques follow. A psychodynamic therapist working assimilatively would keep the focus on the repeated relationship pattern and the feelings it stirs in the therapy, and might borrow a behavioural role-play of saying no to her mother-in-law, treating it as a way of living through the old fear in a safer relationship. Is integration better than pure-form therapy? The honest answer is that "integration" is not one treatment and cannot be tested as one. Some integrative therapies have good trial evidence (cognitive analytic therapy, dialectical behaviour therapy, which joins behaviour therapy to Zen acceptance, Section 5.8, and the systematic matching of directiveness to reactance), while the everyday eclecticism of many practitioners has never been tested at all. Integration also asks a great deal of training: a therapist who combines four schools must understand each of them well enough to know what she is borrowing. Exam trap Match the name to the route.
