Wachtel : theoretical integration, cyclical psychodynamics, psychoanalysis plus behaviour therapy (1977). Prochaska and DiClemente : the transtheoretical approach, also theoretical integration (stages, processes, levels). Frank and Goldfried : common factors. Messer : assimilative integration (1992). Arkowitz (1989) named the first three strands; Messer added the fourth. Do not confuse Arnold Lazarus with Richard Lazarus, whose appraisal theory of stress belongs to the General book. Culture and the therapy room: adapting the treatment Every therapy in this book carries assumptions from the culture that produced it. Most of them assume that the client is an individual who makes his own decisions; that talking about feelings to a stranger is healthy; that the therapist and client meet as near equals; that the hour is fifty minutes and the client comes alone; that what is said is confidential to the client; and that insight, independence and self-expression are signs of health. None of these is a law of nature. In 1962 the American counselling psychologist C. Gilbert Wrenn warned against the culturally encapsulated counsellor , one who takes the assumptions of his own culture to be universal, ignores cultural variation among clients, and substitutes a stereotype for the real person in front of him. Cross-cultural psychology gives a useful pair of terms for this problem. They were coined in 1954 by the linguist Kenneth L. Pike , who borrowed them from the words phonetic (sounds described by universal criteria) and phonemic (sounds as they matter inside one language). An etic approach describes behaviour with concepts assumed to apply in every culture; an emic approach describes behaviour from inside a culture, in the terms its own members use. Much of the history of cross-cultural therapy is the discovery that concepts assumed to be etic (the value of autonomy, the meaning of dependence, the right to confidentiality) are in fact the emic concepts of Western middle-class culture. Ignoring culture leads, first of all, to wrong assessments. Picture a family therapist, trained abroad, who sees a family from rural Karnataka. The married son consults his mother before every decision, the young wife says almost nothing in front of her in-laws, and the parents expect to attend every session. A therapist who does not know how such households usually work may record "enmeshment", label the son dependent and the wife depressed or resistant, and push the son to "separate" from his parents, when what she is seeing is a normal pattern of roles in that family's culture. The result is a wrong assessment and a misinterpretation of culturally ordinary behaviour as pathology, and very likely a ruptured alliance and a family that does not return. The same mistake can run the other way, when real distress is dismissed as "just their culture". Dropout is the visible cost: in a study of community mental health services in Seattle, Stanley Sue found in 1977 that about half of ethnic minority clients did not return after the first session, compared with about 30 percent of white clients. The remedy most researched is cultural adaptation , the systematic modification of an evidence-based treatment so that it fits the language, values and circumstances of the people receiving it while keeping its active ingredients. Section 5.11 introduced the best-known framework, the ecological validity framework of Guillermo Bernal , Janet Bonilla and Carmen Bellido (1995), with its eight dimensions that can be adapted: language, persons, metaphors, content, concepts, goals, methods and context. A second distinction, from the public health researcher Ken Resnicow and his colleagues (1999), sorts adaptations by depth. Surface structure adaptation matches what is visible: the language of the materials, the names, foods, places and examples used, the ethnicity of the therapist or the pictures on a leaflet. It makes a treatment acceptable and familiar. Deep structure adaptation builds in the cultural, social, historical and religious forces that shape how people understand the problem and its cure: beliefs about the causes of illness, family roles and obligations, ideas of fate and duty, stigma, and the place of elders and healers. It is what gives the treatment its impact. Apply the distinction to cognitive behaviour therapy for depression in a district town in Karnataka. Surface adaptation would translate the worksheets into Kannada, use local proverbs and examples from village life, and replace written thought records with pictures for clients who cannot read. Deep adaptation would go further: it would explain depression in a way that fits local beliefs about "tension" and weakness, set goals in terms of the client's duties to the family as well as his own wishes, involve the family in planning activities, and treat beliefs about karma as part of the client's world to be worked with rather than as distortions to be disputed. Adaptation of an imported treatment ("top-down") is not the only way. Some cultures built their own therapies from the bottom up, starting from local traditions of healing. Japan offers the best-known examples. Morita therapy, originated by the psychiatrist Shoma Morita (1874 to 1938) early in the twentieth century, treats anxious self-preoccupation through a period of isolated bed rest followed by graded, purposeful work, teaching the patient to accept feelings as they are and to act constructively regardless; Naikan therapy, developed by Ishin Yoshimoto in the 1940s from a Buddhist practice of self-examination, has clients reflect systematically on what others have given them, what they have given in return, and the trouble they have caused. Both rest on cultural ideals of acceptance and obligation to others, and both have been exported to the West in adapted form. Does cultural adaptation make therapy work better? Several meta-analyses agree that it does, though by a modest amount. The evidence is summarised in the Key study box. Two findings stand out. Adaptations help most when a treatment is designed for one specific cultural group rather than for a mixed one, and when it is delivered in the client's own language. And the most important single adaptation seems to be the one Jerome Frank would have predicted (Section 8.4): changing the explanation of the illness and its cure so that it makes sense within the client's own worldview. Key study: Does adapting therapy to culture help? (2006 to 2018) Question: Are culturally adapted treatments more effective than standard ones for clients from ethnic and cultural minority groups? Method: Successive meta-analyses. Griner and Timothy Smith (2006) pooled 76 studies; Smith, Melanie Domenech Rodríguez and Bernal (2011) pooled 65; Benish, Quintana and Bruce Wampold (2011) included only direct comparisons of an adapted therapy with the same kind of bona fide therapy unadapted; Gordon Nagayama Hall and colleagues (2016) pooled 78 studies. Results: Griner and Smith found an average effect size of d = 0.45 for adapted interventions, with interventions targeted at one cultural group about four times as effective as those for mixed groups, and those delivered in the client's own language (where it was not English) about twice as effective. Benish and colleagues found adapted therapy better than unadapted bona fide therapy by d = 0.32, and the only adaptation that predicted this advantage was adapting the illness myth , the explanation of the problem and its cure. Hall and colleagues found an effect of 0.52 in favour of adapted over unadapted versions of the same intervention. Conclusion: Culturally adapted treatments do somewhat better, and the explanation offered to the client matters most. Criticism: A 2018 update of 99 studies found the average effect shrank from about 0.50 to about 0.35 once publication bias was allowed for, and many studies compared adapted treatment with no treatment rather than with the unadapted version. There is a real tension here, sometimes called fidelity versus fit. A treatment adapted too freely may lose the very ingredients that made it work in trials; a treatment delivered with perfect fidelity to a manual written for another culture may never be accepted by the people it is meant to help. The working rule most researchers accept is that adaptation should change the packaging, the language, examples, explanations, goals and delivery, while protecting the active ingredients that the evidence identifies. Exam trap If a question asks what follows from poor awareness of a family's culture and customary practices, the answer is wrong assessments and misinterpretations (culturally normal behaviour read as pathology), not accurate understanding, effective communication or a strong alliance. Bernal, Bonilla and Bellido (1995) gave the ecological validity framework with eight dimensions; Resnicow (1999) gave surface versus deep structure ; Wrenn (1962) gave the culturally encapsulated counsellor ; Pike (1954) gave emic and etic . Adapted treatments do somewhat better (roughly d = 0.3 to 0.5), most when targeted at one group, in the client's language, and with an adapted illness explanation. The culturally competent therapist Adapting a treatment manual is one level of the answer. The other is the therapist. The person most associated with this second level is Derald Wing Sue (born 1942), a Chinese American psychologist whose book Counseling the Culturally Different (1981) became a standard text. In a 1982 position paper Sue and his colleagues proposed that cross-cultural counselling competence has three components, and in 1992, with Patricia Arredondo and Roderick McDavis, he expanded them into a set of multicultural counselling competencies that professional bodies adopted. The three components are the heart of what is now called multicultural competence . Awareness (beliefs and attitudes): the therapist is aware of her own cultural background, values and biases, and of how they shape her view of what is normal, healthy and desirable. Knowledge : the therapist understands the worldview, history, values and circumstances of the client's cultural group, including experiences of discrimination and the ways that group usually seeks help. Skills : the therapist can choose and adapt intervention strategies, and ways of communicating, that suit the client's culture, and can work with family members, interpreters and traditional healers when that helps. Sue's model told therapists what to know; Stanley Sue, a fellow Chinese American psychologist (and Derald's brother), asked what actually happens in the room that makes culture matter. With Nolan Zane he argued in 1987 that knowledge of a culture and culture-specific techniques matter only because they affect two more immediate processes. The first is credibility , the client's perception that the therapist is trustworthy and effective. Ascribed credibility is given by the client's culture because of the therapist's position: age, gender, profession, status. Achieved credibility is earned by what the therapist does: a formulation that makes sense to the client, goals the client shares, methods that seem likely to work. The second is gift-giving : the client's sense of receiving something of value early in treatment, such as relief from anxiety, a clear explanation, reassurance that the problem is understandable, a useful skill or renewed hope. A first session that sends the client home with nothing but questions is a poor start for a client who expected help. In 1998 Stanley Sue added three characteristics of a culturally competent therapist: scientific mindedness (forming hypotheses about clients of other cultures and testing them, rather than jumping to conclusions); dynamic sizing (knowing when to generalise from what is known about a group and when to treat the person as an individual who may not fit it); and culture-specific expertise . More recently many writers have preferred the idea of cultural humility (Joshua Hook and colleagues, 2013): an interpersonal stance that is open and curious about the client's cultural identity, aware of the limits of one's own understanding, and committed to lifelong self-examination, rather than a claim to have "mastered" another culture. Derald Wing Sue and colleagues also drew attention in 2007 to racial microaggressions, the brief, everyday slights, often unintended, that communicate disrespect to members of minority groups and can quietly damage an alliance. Does therapist competence of this kind matter for outcome? A 2018 meta-analysis of 15 studies gave a striking answer that depends on who does the rating. When clients rated their therapists' cultural competence, those ratings correlated about 0.38 with treatment outcomes; when therapists rated their own competence, the correlation was close to zero (about 0.06). Therapists, in other words, are poor judges of their own cultural competence, which is one more reason to ask clients how the therapy is going (Section 8.9). Clinical link A 26-year-old psychologist meets a retired headmaster of 64 who has been brought by his son for depression after his wife's death. Ascribed credibility is not on her side: she is young, female and the age of his granddaughter. She can earn it. She addresses him respectfully, asks about his career, explains his sleeplessness and loss of appetite as an understandable response to grief that also has a treatable side, and ends the first session with one concrete step (a morning walk with his old colleagues) and a clear plan. The explanation and the first step are Sue and Zane's gift; his return the next week is the achieved credibility. Exam trap D. W. Sue's three components of multicultural competence are awareness (of one's own values and biases), knowledge (of the client's worldview) and skills (culturally appropriate interventions). Sue and Zane (1987) gave credibility (ascribed versus achieved) and gift-giving . Stanley Sue (1998) gave scientific mindedness, dynamic sizing and culture-specific expertise. Client ratings of therapist cultural competence predict outcome; therapist self-ratings do not. Psychotherapy in India In 1964 (some later reviews give 1968) the Indian Journal of Psychiatry printed a short paper that had been read at a conference of Indian psychiatrists. Its authors, N. C. Surya and S. S. Jayaram , began by pointing at the programme in their hands: "The paucity of papers submitted on psychotherapy at this Conference gives some food for thought." Western psychiatrists, they observed, seemed keener on the theory and practice of psychotherapy in the Indian setting than Indian psychiatrists were. Their paper, "Some basic considerations in the practice of psychotherapy in the Indian setting", was short, but it set the agenda for the debate that followed, and the journal reprinted it in 1996. Surya and Jayaram made five arguments. The first was about language. The Indian psychiatrist, they wrote, had learned his medicine and psychiatry in a language and in conceptual frameworks foreign to the milieu of his birth; for him the English words of psychiatry often had only a "desiccated, cognitive significance" and a prestige value, and for his patients they had little meaning at all, even when the patients understood English. Words carry motivation and feeling as well as information, and a therapy conducted in borrowed words would be weak. The second was about what the Indian patient expects, which they traced to upbringing in a joint family. Compared with his Western counterpart, they wrote, the Indian patient is "more ready to expect and accept dependency relationships; more ready to accept overt situational support, less ready to seek intrapsychic explanations; more insistent and importunate with regard to personal needs and time; more ready to discard ego-bounds and involve the therapist in direct role relationship; and finally his ideal or idealised support is the good joint-family elder." A therapist who did not consciously understand and fulfil that role, they warned, would fail. Their third point was that Indian patients of every class orient themselves by concepts such as karma and dharma and by traditional figures, rather than by Western ideas of conscience or superego. The fourth was the most provocative: the Western ideal of mental health implies the search for intrapsychic integration, a single consistent self, whereas the implied Indian ideal allows a degree of separation between thinking, feeling and acting, so that "rigid, mutually exclusive consistencies" are a product of Western thought. The fifth used a story. In the legend of Savitri, whose husband Satyavan is fated to die, Savitri walks alongside Yama, the lord of death, wins his friendship by walking seven steps with him, and, when he offers her a boon, asks to be the mother of a hundred sons by Satyavan; Yama grants it, and only then discovers that he must return Satyavan's life to keep his word. For Surya and Jayaram the legend contained two principles of therapy in the Indian setting: first walk alongside the patient, and then work through an implied goal, an acceptable overt aim whose fulfilment requires a necessary but unwelcome intermediate step. They ended by asking psychiatrists to take religion and faith seriously as part of how people make sense of the world, not to dismiss them. In 1973 Jaswant Singh Neki , whom you met in Section 3.10, offered a positive model in the American Journal of Orthopsychiatry : "Guru-chela relationship: the possibility of a therapeutic paradigm" (1973). The guru-chela relationship (teacher and disciple) is a voluntary relationship in which a person seeking change accepts the guidance of a master who has gone further along the same path. The guru is active, benevolent and directive; he takes responsibility for leading the disciple, helps directly with decisions where needed, and acts as a model; the chela accepts guidance and, for a time, depends on him. The goal is not lifelong obedience but the disciple's growth towards self-mastery. Neki argued that this, rather than the neutral, egalitarian, interpretive stance of Western psychotherapy, was the relationship many Indian patients were looking for. The heart of Neki's argument was about dependence. In two papers of 1976 in the British Journal of Medical Psychology , "An examination of the cultural relativism of dependence as a dynamic of social and therapeutic relationships", he argued that Western developmental theory treats dependence as immaturity to be outgrown and, in therapy, as something to be interpreted and resolved, whereas in Indian family life dependence is expected, accepted and answered by dependability: the child and the young adult depend, and the elders make themselves dependable. What is a symptom in one culture is a norm in another. A therapist who confronts dependence too early, or treats it as pathology, will lose the client; a therapist who accepts it and works through it gradually, as the guru does, may lead the client to a mature interdependence. Neki also proposed an Indian ideal of mental health, sahaja (1975), a natural state marked by illumination, equipoise, spontaneity, freedom and harmony, and in a 1992 editorial he argued that Western notions of confidentiality and privacy have no ready equivalents in Indian languages and can seem to cut a person off from an interdependent family, so that a few sessions with the family alongside individual therapy usually help. Not everyone accepted the paradigm. Neki returned to it in a 1974 reappraisal, and critics objected that it could foster lasting dependency, since the guru takes total responsibility for leading the disciple. Later Indian writers welcomed its cultural fit but warned that it can become an excuse for paternalism, a therapist who simply tells clients what to do. In 1982 V. K. Varma , in a review titled "Present state of psychotherapy in India", listed seven features of Indian clients that he thought made Western therapy hard to apply: dependence or interdependence; lack of psychological sophistication; social distance between doctor and patient; religious belief in rebirth and fatalism; guilt attributed to misdeeds in a past life; problems with confidentiality; and reluctance to take personal responsibility for decisions. A survey of 32 Fellows of the Indian Psychiatric Society by Varma and Ghosh (1976) had already found that most of them practised short-term supportive therapy. Other Indian clinicians disagreed with the pessimists. K. Nagaraja Rao practised existential psychotherapy and argued that the critics were judging all Western therapy by psychoanalysis, and that existential philosophy is close to Indian thought; C. Shamasundar held that psychotherapy can be conducted effectively with Indian patients. A 2010 review of the Indian Journal of Psychiatry by L. S. S. Manickam, of JSS Medical College, Mysuru, added a further caution: with globalisation, rising education, greater awareness of human rights and the spread of electronic media even in rural areas, it is a fair question whether these generalisations about "the Indian patient" still hold today. Three practical themes run through this literature and through Indian clinics today. The first is family involvement . Families usually accompany the client, decisions about treatment, work and marriage are often family decisions, and an inpatient may have a relative staying with him on the ward. Indian therapists therefore meet families early, agree with the client what will and will not be shared with them, use family members as allies in homework and relapse prevention, and remember that the family's view of the problem may differ from the client's. The second is the expectation of direction . Many clients expect advice, a clear plan and sometimes a prescription, and experience pure non-directive listening as indifference (Section 6.2). Indian clinicians usually respond by being directive about the structure of therapy (what we will do, how often, what to practise) while keeping decisions about the client's life collaborative, which is close to what Sue and Zane called giving a gift without taking over. The third is religion and idiom : beliefs about karma, fate and God are treated as resources to work with, and local idioms of distress are respected (Section 5.11). Indian clinicians have also drawn directly on Indian traditions. The ancient medical text the Charaka Samhita classifies treatment into three kinds: daivavyapashraya (spiritual or divine therapy), yuktivyapashraya (rational therapy with medicines and diet) and sattvavajaya (literally "conquest of the mind"), a psychological therapy that restrains the mind from harmful objects and is often described as Ayurveda's psychotherapy. In Bombay, N. S. Vahia and his colleagues built a psychophysiologic therapy on the concepts of Patanjali's yoga, reporting it in the British Journal of Psychiatry in 1966 and the American Journal of Psychotherapy in 1973 as a new approach to neurotic and psychosomatic disorders; a 1977 comparison found it more helpful than drug treatment for stress-related neurotic disorders, and Vahia's work is often credited with opening yoga to psychiatric research in India. The meditation that underlies mindfulness-based therapies (Section 5.9) has Indian Buddhist roots in vipassana, and the modern use of yoga and meditation in Indian clinical settings is described in Chapter 10. Indian stories have served as therapy texts too. The Bhagavad Gita is, in form, a counselling dialogue: on the battlefield of Kurukshetra the warrior Arjuna, overwhelmed by grief, guilt and physical symptoms of anxiety at the prospect of fighting his own kin, lays down his bow and asks Krishna for help ("I am your disciple; guide me", in the second chapter), and at the end of the eighteenth chapter declares that his delusion is gone, his doubts have vanished and he will act as Krishna directs. The psychiatrist M. S. Reddy (2012) read the dialogue as a model of crisis counselling within a guru-shishya relationship, and Dilip Jeste and Ipsit Vahia (2008) compared its account of wisdom with modern psychological definitions. Its central teaching of action without attachment to its fruits (chapter 2, verse 47) is often compared with the acceptance and values-based action of acceptance and commitment therapy (Section 5.9). N. N. Wig of the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, described in 2004 what he called the Hanuman complex : in the Ramayana, Hanuman lost the knowledge of his own power to fly because of a childhood curse by sages, and regained it only when Jambavan reminded him of it during the search for Sita. Wig used the story with patients who had forgotten their own strengths, and with trainees, to show that a therapist's task is often to remind clients of capacities they already have. The psychoanalyst Sudhir Kakar's argument that the Indian self is organised around family relationships, and Alan Roland's "familial self", were described in Section 3.11. Neki's (1973, American Journal of Orthopsychiatry ); dependence is accepted and worked through, not interpreted away. The 1964 paper on psychotherapy in the Indian setting (dependency, situational support, the joint-family elder, karma and dharma, the Savitri legend) is Surya and Jayaram's , not Neki's. Sahaja (1975) and the cultural relativism of dependence (1976) are Neki's; the Hanuman complex is Wig's (2004); Patanjali-based psychophysiologic therapy is Vahia's; sattvavajaya is the psychological therapy of the Charaka Samhita ; The Inner World (1978) is Kakar's. 8.12 Becoming a Therapist: Training, Supervision, the Wounded Healer and Self-Care Lower yield · not asked yet Section 8.6 showed that therapists differ: some, treating comparable clients with the same method, get consistently better results than others. That finding turns the spotlight from the therapy to the person who delivers it, and raises the questions with which this chapter ends. How is a therapist made? How does a beginner learn to do something as subtle as building an alliance or noticing her own countertransference? Who watches over her work while she learns? And what do years of listening to suffering do to the listener? This section follows a therapist from training through supervision to the hazards of the work and the ways of surviving it. Training models in brief Two American conferences set the pattern for training clinical psychologists, and Chapter 1 tells their story in full. At the Boulder conference of 1949 the profession adopted the scientist-practitioner model : a clinical psychologist should be trained as both a researcher and a clinician, earning a research doctorate (the PhD) and bringing scientific thinking to practice. At the Vail conference of 1973 a second route was endorsed, the practitioner-scholar model , which places practice first, treats the clinician as an informed consumer of research rather than necessarily a producer of it, and leads to the professional Doctor of Psychology (PsyD) degree. A third, the clinical science model, later pushed in the opposite direction, emphasising research training above all. In India the route to practice is a professional qualification in clinical psychology recognised by the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI), for decades the two-year M.Phil and now the newer RCI-approved programmes, followed by registration with the RCI; Chapter 1 sets out the courses and the registration rules. Whatever the model, the core of training is the same: coursework, then clinical work with real clients under close supervision, with the trainee's independence growing as her competence does. Experience alone is not enough. In a 2016 study, Simon Goldberg and his colleagues followed 170 therapists in one university counselling service over several years and found that their clients' outcomes did not improve as the therapists gained experience; on average they declined slightly. What seems to improve therapists is not the passage of time but feedback on their outcomes and deliberate practice of the skills they lack (Sections 8.6 and 8.9). The most important vehicle of that feedback during training is supervision, so much so that supervision is often called the signature teaching method of the mental health professions. Exam trap Boulder (1949) : scientist-practitioner model, PhD. Vail (1973) : practitioner-scholar model, PsyD. Do not swap the conferences or the degrees. The clinical science model is a later, more research-centred position. Clinical experience by itself does not reliably improve a therapist's outcomes; feedback and deliberate practice do. What clinical supervision is and what it is for The most widely quoted definition comes from Janine M. Bernard and Rodney K. Goodyear , whose Fundamentals of Clinical Supervision (first published in 1992) is the standard text. Clinical supervision , in their definition, is an intervention provided by a more senior member of a profession to a more junior member or members of that same profession. The relationship is evaluative and hierarchical, it extends over time, and it has three simultaneous purposes: enhancing the professional functioning of the junior person; monitoring the quality of the services offered to the clients she sees; and acting as a gatekeeper for those who wish to enter the profession. That third purpose, gatekeeping , is the uncomfortable one: a supervisor must sometimes decide that a trainee is not yet safe to practise, and say so. The definition separates supervision from three activities it resembles. It is not consultation , which takes place between professionals who may be equals, is voluntary and leaves responsibility for the client with the person seeking advice, who is free to reject it (Section 9.6 describes Caplan's types of mental health consultation); a supervisor, by contrast, shares responsibility for the supervisee's clients and evaluates her. It is not teaching in a classroom, because it is tied to particular clients and particular sessions. And it is not therapy for the supervisee: a supervisor may explore the trainee's feelings about a client, but only insofar as they affect the work. If a trainee's personal difficulties go deeper, the supervisor's job is to recommend that she seek therapy of her own, not to provide it, because combining the roles of evaluator and therapist creates a dual relationship (Chapter 1). What does supervision actually do? The classic answer comes from social work. In Supervision in Social Work (1976), Alfred Kadushin named three functions: administrative , educational and supportive . A decade later the British counselling writer Brigid Proctor (1986) described the same three under different names, normative , formative and restorative , and both sets of terms appear in exam questions. Table 8.23 lines them up. Table 8.23 The three functions of supervision. Kadushin (1976) Proctor (1986) What it covers Example Administrative Normative Standards, ethics, agency rules, protecting clients, accountability Checking a risk assessment, case notes and consent Educational Formative Knowledge, skills, understanding and professional growth Teaching formulation; reviewing a recording together Supportive Restorative Helping the supervisee cope with the emotional demands of the work Debriefing after a client's suicide attempt Supervision happens in several formats: individually, in groups, in peer groups without a designated senior, and in triads. It draws on several kinds of information about the trainee's sessions: her own account (self-report), process notes written soon after the session, audio or video recordings, and direct observation. Self-report is the most common and the least reliable, because trainees cannot report what they did not notice. Like therapy, supervision depends on its relationship. In 1983 Edward Bordin applied his model of the working alliance (Section 8.5) to supervision: the supervisory working alliance consists of agreement on the goals of supervision, agreement on its tasks, and an emotional bond of trust between supervisor and supervisee. Trainees who distrust their supervisors hide their mistakes, which is exactly what supervision exists to prevent. Indian writers have been frank about the gaps. Manickam's 2010 review (Section 8.11) noted that young therapists in India are often given too little supervision, that the multilingual mix of patients, trainees and supervisors makes supervision harder, and that audio recording of sessions, though professionals react positively to it, is not widely used in training and is not mandatory. In a study at a general hospital psychiatry unit, Tharyan (2000) showed that group supervision of psychotherapy was feasible and acceptable to trainees, though not a substitute for individual supervision. Exam trap Supervision is evaluative, hierarchical and ongoing , with three purposes: developing the supervisee, protecting clients and gatekeeping the profession (Bernard and Goodyear). Consultation is between peers, voluntary and non-evaluative, and the consultee keeps responsibility. Kadushin's functions are administrative, educational, supportive ; Proctor's are normative, formative, restorative . Supervision is not personal therapy for the trainee. Models of supervision Bernard and Goodyear sort the many models of supervision into three families. Psychotherapy-based models supervise in the language of a particular therapy. Developmental models describe how trainees change over time and what they need at each point. Process models (also called social role models) describe what the supervisor does in a session, whatever the therapy being supervised. Psychotherapy-based models. The oldest supervision is psychoanalytic, and its classic text is The Teaching and Learning of Psychotherapy (1958) by Rudolf Ekstein and Robert S. Wallerstein . They pictured the training situation as a "clinical rhombus" of four people (patient, therapist, supervisor and the administrator of the clinic) and distinguished learning problems , difficulties in the trainee's work with patients that arise from her own blind spots, from problems about learning , difficulties that show up in the relationship with the supervisor. Psychodynamic supervisors pay close attention to transference and countertransference (Section 3.3) in both relationships. Person-centred supervisors offer the trainee the same core conditions she is meant to offer clients (Section 6.2), trusting her to grow in a climate of empathy and acceptance. Cognitive-behavioural supervision is structured like a CBT session, with an agenda, a review of homework, a focus on specific skills, role-play and rehearsal, and rating of competence on instruments such as the Cognitive Therapy Scale (Jeffrey Young and Aaron Beck, 1980). The strength of these models is consistency between what is taught and how it is taught; the weakness is that they say little about how supervision should change as the trainee develops, or what to do when supervisor and supervisee come from different schools. Developmental models. These answer the question the first family leaves open. An early version, by Carol Loganbill, Emily Hardy and Ursula Delworth (1982), described trainees moving through stagnation, confusion and integration. The best-known and best-researched is the integrated developmental model (IDM) of Cal D. Stoltenberg , which grew from his counsellor complexity model of 1981 and was set out with Delworth in Supervising Counselors and Therapists: A Developmental Approach (1987) and later with Brian McNeill (1998). The IDM tracks three overriding structures in the trainee: self and other awareness (how far she is focused on herself or on the client, both in thought and in feeling), motivation , and autonomy (how dependent she is on the supervisor). These are assessed in eight domains of practice: intervention skills, assessment techniques, interpersonal assessment, client conceptualisation, individual differences, theoretical orientation, treatment plans and goals, and professional ethics. A trainee moves through three levels, and a fourth integrated level, as Table 8.24 and Figure 8.15 show. Table 8.24 The levels of Stoltenberg's integrated developmental model. Each step is a level of development, assessed separately in each domain of practice, so a trainee can be at Level 2 in assessment and still at Level 1 in, say, family work. As the supervisee climbs, the supervisor gives less structure and more autonomy. Two features of the IDM are worth noticing. First, development is domain-specific: a trainee who interviews confidently may still be a beginner at formulating a case or at working with a family. Second, Level 2 is the turbulent one, often compared to adolescence. Having discovered the client, the trainee can be swept into the client's feelings, may resent supervision as interference and may swing between "I am useless" and "I know what I am doing". A supervisor who keeps treating a Level 2 trainee like a beginner provokes rebellion; one who withdraws too soon leaves her to flounder. Research supports the broad idea that trainees' needs change with experience, but the evidence for distinct, invariant stages is weaker. Process models. The best known is the discrimination model of Janine Bernard (1979), so called because the supervisor must discriminate, moment by moment, which role to take and what to focus on. Bernard described three roles. As teacher , the supervisor instructs, demonstrates, models and evaluates. As counsellor , she helps the supervisee explore her own thoughts and feelings about the work, without becoming her therapist. As consultant , she acts as a resource for a supervisee who is trusted to lead, offering ideas and alternatives. She also described three foci. Intervention skills (in Bernard's original wording, process skills) are what the trainee observably does in the session: her questions, reflections and techniques. Conceptualisation skills are how she understands the client: seeing themes, making sense of what the client says and choosing goals. Personalisation skills are how the trainee's own person enters the work: her style, culture, feelings and countertransference, and her comfort with the client's emotions and with being challenged. Three roles by three foci gives nine possible choices, set out in Table 8.25. Later writers added professional behaviour (punctuality, record keeping, ethics) as a fourth focus. Table 8.25 Bernard's discrimination model (1979): three roles by three foci, with an example of what the supervisor might do in each cell. Focus Teacher Counsellor Consultant Intervention Demonstrates how to ask about suicidal thoughts, then role-plays it Explores what made the trainee freeze when the client began to cry Lists with the trainee the techniques she might try next session Conceptualisation Explains how to link the client's history and symptoms in a formulation Explores why the trainee keeps describing the client as "manipulative" Discusses two formulations the trainee has drafted and lets her choose Personalisation Teaches about countertransference and cultural bias Helps her notice her anger at a client who reminds her of her father Asks how she would like to handle a client's personal questions A worked example shows the model in motion. Divya, a first-year trainee at a hospital in Mysuru, brings a recording of her third session with a 40-year-old man with alcohol dependence. In the first ten minutes of supervision, her supervisor acts as teacher with an intervention focus, showing her how to respond to his "I can stop any time" with a reflection rather than an argument (Section 6.9). Then Divya admits that she cannot stand him; he talks down to her. The supervisor shifts to counsellor with a personalisation focus, helping her see that he sounds like a dismissive uncle, without turning the hour into therapy about her family. Finally, as consultant with a conceptualisation focus, she asks Divya how she now understands his contempt, and Divya suggests it may protect him from shame. The skill being modelled is the discrimination itself: choosing the role and focus the moment needs, rather than defaulting to the one the supervisor prefers. A second process model, from Britain, is the seven-eyed model of Peter Hawkins and Robin Shohet (first set out in Supervision in the Helping Professions , 1989). It names seven things a supervisor can attend to: the client; the supervisee's interventions; the relationship between client and supervisee; the supervisee herself; the supervisory relationship (where parallel process appears, below); the supervisor's own reactions; and the wider context of organisation, profession and culture. Exam trap Bernard's discrimination model (1979) has three roles (teacher, counsellor, consultant) and three foci (intervention or process, conceptualisation, personalisation): nine cells. It is a process model, not a developmental one. The integrated developmental model is Stoltenberg's (with Delworth, 1987): three structures (self and other awareness, motivation, autonomy), eight domains, Levels 1, 2, 3 and 3i. Loganbill, Hardy and Delworth (1982) gave stagnation, confusion, integration. Ekstein and Wallerstein (1958) are the psychoanalytic classics. The seven-eyed model is Hawkins and Shohet's. Parallel process and live supervision Supervisors have long noticed something uncanny. A trainee whose client keeps saying "I don't know, you tell me what to do" arrives at supervision and, without realising it, keeps saying to the supervisor, "I don't know what to do with him; just tell me." The supervisor then feels the same pull to rescue that the trainee felt in the session. The pattern of one relationship has been re-enacted in the other. This is parallel process . It was first described in 1955 by the American psychoanalyst Harold F. Searles , who called it the reflection process, and was developed by Ekstein and Wallerstein in 1958; the name parallel process has been standard ever since. Psychodynamic writers explain it through identification: the trainee unconsciously takes on the client's way of relating and plays it out with the supervisor, often because it is the part of the case she has not yet understood. The process also runs the other way. A supervisor who is harsh and critical may find the trainee becoming harsh and critical with her clients; a supervisor who listens patiently teaches patience by example. Figure 8.16 shows both directions. Upward: the client's pattern is re-enacted in supervision Client "Tell me what to do" Trainee therapist "Tell me what to do" Supervisor feels pull to rescue therapy supervision Downward: the supervisor's way of relating is passed on to the client Figure 8.16 Parallel process. The upper arrow ("Upward") shows a pattern from the therapy (here helpless dependence) reappearing between trainee and supervisor; the lower arrow ("Downward") shows the supervisor's own style being carried into the trainee's work with the client. Naming the parallel in supervision turns it from a re-enactment into information about the case. The usefulness of the idea is practical. When a supervisor notices that she feels with the trainee what the trainee seems to feel with the client, she can say so, explore what it reveals about the case, and model a different response, for example helping the trainee think rather than giving her an answer, which the trainee can then offer the client. The evidence for parallel process consists mostly of case reports and a small number of studies, so it is best treated as a useful hypothesis about a particular supervision rather than a law that always operates. Most supervision relies on what the trainee remembers. Live supervision removes that filter: the supervisor observes the session as it happens and can intervene during it. It grew up in family therapy (Chapter 7), and the family therapist Braulio Montalvo , a colleague of Salvador Minuchin, described its methods in a 1973 paper. The supervisor or team sits behind a one-way mirror and communicates by telephoning into the room, through a small earphone worn by the therapist (the "bug in the ear"), by knocking and walking in, or by calling the therapist out for a consultation break, as the Milan team did. In the reflecting team devised by the Norwegian psychiatrist Tom Andersen (1987), the observers change places with the family and discuss their impressions openly while the family listens. Live supervision protects clients and gives the trainee help at the moment it is needed; its costs are time, staff and the risk that the trainee comes to depend on the voice from behind the mirror. Between self-report and live observation lie recordings. A particularly well-developed method for using them is interpersonal process recall (IPR), developed by Norman Kagan at Michigan State University from the 1960s. Trainee and supervisor (in Kagan's term, the "inquirer") replay a recorded session; the trainee stops the recording whenever she remembers a thought or feeling she had at that moment but did not express, and the inquirer asks open, non-judgemental questions ("What were you feeling just then? What did you want to say?"). The method makes the trainee, not the supervisor, the expert on her own experience, and it is especially good at bringing personalisation issues to light. Exam trap Parallel process is the re-enactment in supervision of a pattern from the therapy (or the reverse); Searles (1955) called it the reflection process , and Ekstein and Wallerstein (1958) developed it. It is not countertransference itself (the therapist's reaction to the client, Section 3.3), though countertransference is often how it shows up. Live supervision (one-way mirror, phone-in, bug in the ear, consultation break) comes from family therapy ; Montalvo (1973) described it; the reflecting team is Tom Andersen's. Interpersonal process recall is Kagan's . The wounded healer Why do people become therapists? One old answer is that many of them have suffered first. Carl Gustav Jung (1875 to 1961), as Section 3.8 described, called the analyst a wounded healer , and drew the image from Greek myth. The centaur Chiron, the wise teacher of medicine who raised the healer-god Asclepius, was wounded by one of Heracles' poisoned arrows; being immortal he could not die, and his wound never healed, yet he remained the great teacher of the healing arts. For Jung the doctor is effective only when he himself is affected by the patient; "only the wounded physician heals", and an analyst who hides behind his professional role like a suit of armour has no effect. It was this conviction that led Jung's Zurich school to insist that every analyst must first be analysed (the training analysis of Section 3.2). The phrase reached a wider audience through the Dutch priest Henri Nouwen's book The Wounded Healer (1972), written for clergy, which argued that a helper's own acknowledged suffering can become a source of compassion for others. How wounded are therapists in fact? In 1994 Kenneth S. Pope and Barbara Tabachnick mailed a survey to 800 American psychologists, and nearly 60 percent replied. About 84 percent had been in therapy themselves. Sixty-one percent reported at least one episode of clinical depression, 29 percent had felt suicidal, and almost 4 percent had made at least one suicide attempt. Norcross's review of 25 years of research on the psychotherapist's own psychotherapy (2005) drew the same broad picture: most mental health professionals have had personal therapy, most found it helpful, and many say it taught them lasting lessons about what it is like to be a client, such as the importance of warmth, of being heard and of the therapist's patience. The wound cuts both ways. A review by Zerubavel and Wright (2012) listed the benefits a therapist's own struggles can bring: deeper empathy, the ability to offer realistic hope, humility, and a feel for the client's side of the room. It also listed the dangers: a recovery that is not yet stable, difficulty managing countertransference (for example over-identifying with clients whose stories resemble one's own), greater vulnerability to compassion fatigue (below), and in the worst case impairment. Because the profession rarely talks about its own wounds, the authors argued, therapists who struggle tend to hide it and seek help too late. The point of the wounded healer is therefore not that a wound is an asset in itself, but that a wound which has been acknowledged and is being healed can become one. Should therapists be required to have therapy themselves? Psychoanalytic training has required it for about a century, and some counselling bodies require a set number of hours of personal therapy during training. The case for it is strong on grounds of self-knowledge, of experiencing the client's role and of the therapist's own well-being. The evidence that a therapist's personal therapy directly improves her clients' outcomes, however, is surprisingly thin and inconsistent, so most training programmes in clinical psychology recommend it rather than require it. Whether and how a therapist should mention her own experiences to a client is a separate question, the question of self-disclosure (Section 8.10). Exam trap The wounded healer is Jung's archetype (from the myths of Chiron and Asclepius), not Freud's, Rogers' or Adler's; Henri Nouwen's book of that title (1972) popularised it for clergy. Pope and Tabachnick (1994): about 84 percent of psychologists had been in therapy and 61 percent reported clinical depression. The idea is not that unhealed wounds help, but that acknowledged, healing ones can. When helping hurts the helper: burnout, compassion fatigue and vicarious traumatisation In the early 1970s Herbert J. Freudenberger (1926 to 1999), a psychoanalyst in private practice in New York, spent his evenings volunteering at a free clinic for young drug users in the East Village. After months of full days at his practice and long nights at the clinic, he noticed that he and his fellow volunteers, idealistic people who had come to help, were becoming exhausted, irritable, cynical and detached from the very clients they had come to serve. He borrowed a word already used on the street for the burnt-out state of chronic drug users and, in a 1974 paper in the Journal of Social Issues titled "Staff burn-out", described the condition in helpers. Burnout is a state of physical and emotional exhaustion, with negative attitudes towards one's work and the people one serves, that develops from prolonged, unrelieved stress at work. Freudenberger named burnout; Christina Maslach (born 1946) measured it. A social psychologist at the University of California, Berkeley, she had been interviewing nurses, social workers, lawyers and other human service workers about how they coped with emotionally demanding work, and found them describing the same pattern. With Susan E. Jackson she published the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) in 1981. The original Human Services Survey has 22 items, each rated for how often the feeling occurs, from 0 (never) to 6 (every day), and it measures three dimensions. Emotional exhaustion : feeling emotionally drained and used up by one's work, with nothing left to give (nine items). It is the central, most widely reported dimension. Depersonalisation : a detached, callous and impersonal response to the people one serves, treating clients as objects or "cases" rather than as people (five items). It is the helper's way of protecting herself from further emotional demands. Reduced personal accomplishment : a decline in one's feelings of competence and achievement at work, a sense that one is no longer making a difference (eight items, scored so that low accomplishment indicates burnout). The three subscales are scored separately, and burnout is indicated by high emotional exhaustion, high depersonalisation and low personal accomplishment. Later versions extended the inventory to teachers (the Educators Survey) and to all occupations (the General Survey, whose dimensions are named exhaustion, cynicism and professional efficacy). With Michael Leiter, in The Truth About Burnout (1997), Maslach argued that burnout is above all a problem of the job rather than of the person: it arises from a mismatch between the worker and six areas of working life, namely workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Its positive opposite is engagement: energy, involvement and a sense of efficacy. Jerry Edelwich and Archie Brodsky (1980) described the slide into burnout in four stages: enthusiasm, stagnation, frustration and apathy. Is burnout a mental disorder? The World Health Organization's ICD-11 answers no. It lists burn-out (code QD85) as an occupational phenomenon in the chapter on factors influencing health status or contact with health services, defines it by three dimensions that echo Maslach's (energy depletion or exhaustion; increased mental distance from one's job, or negativism and cynicism about it; and reduced professional efficacy), and restricts it to the occupational context. That last point distinguishes it from depression, which spreads to every area of life; the disorder itself belongs to the Psychiatric Disorders book. Therapists face the general hazards of any helping job, high caseloads, little control, paperwork and isolation, and some special ones: clients who are suicidal, hostile or not improving, the one-way intimacy of the work, and the need to hold strong feelings without discharging them. A second set of hazards comes specifically from working with trauma. In 1992 the nurse Carla Joinson used the term compassion fatigue for a loss of the ability to nurture that she observed in nurses, and in 1995 the traumatologist Charles R. Figley developed it in Compassion Fatigue: Coping with Secondary Traumatic Stress Disorder in Those Who Treat the Traumatized . Figley equated compassion fatigue with secondary traumatic stress : the stress that results from helping, or wanting to help, a traumatised person, with symptoms that mirror post-traumatic stress disorder (intrusive images of the client's trauma, avoidance of reminders, numbing and hyperarousal) and that can come on suddenly. It is often described as the cost of caring. Its counterpart is compassion satisfaction , the pleasure and meaning that come from helping well, and the Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL) developed by Beth Hudnall Stamm measures compassion satisfaction, burnout and secondary traumatic stress together. A third concept came from therapists who worked with survivors of trauma. In 1990 I. Lisa McCann and Laurie Anne Pearlman published "Vicarious traumatization: a framework for understanding the psychological effects of working with victims" in the Journal of Traumatic Stress . Vicarious traumatisation is a cumulative transformation of the therapist's inner experience that results from empathic engagement with clients' traumatic material. Drawing on their constructivist self-development theory, McCann and Pearlman argued that hearing story after story of cruelty gradually alters the therapist's own beliefs, or schemas, about the world and other people, especially in the areas of safety, trust, esteem, intimacy and control. A therapist may begin to see danger everywhere, distrust ordinary kindness, or feel her own family is never safe. Unlike compassion fatigue, which can strike after a single harrowing case, vicarious traumatisation builds up over many clients and is, to some degree, an expected consequence of the work. Pearlman and Karen Saakvitne (1995) also drew a distinction that examiners like. Countertransference (Section 3.3) is a reaction to a particular client, shaped in part by the therapist's own history, and it arises within one relationship; vicarious traumatisation accumulates across all the therapist's trauma work, whoever the client. The two interact: a therapist whose own history resembles her clients' is more vulnerable to both. Writers on therapist stress sometimes speak loosely of "countertransference fatigue" for the wearing effect of strong reactions to particular clients that are never noticed or worked through; the phrase is descriptive rather than a formal construct with its own measure, and the cure is the same as for countertransference generally: noticing, understanding and supervision. Self-care and prevention If the work can harm the worker, looking after oneself is not a luxury but part of professional competence. The APA Ethics Code makes the point directly: under its standard on personal problems and conflicts (2.06), psychologists refrain from starting work when they know or should know that their personal problems are likely to prevent them from performing competently, and when they become aware of such problems they take appropriate measures, such as obtaining consultation or assistance and deciding whether to limit, suspend or end their work (Chapter 1 covers the codes, including the RCI's). Writers on the topic distinguish distress , which every therapist feels at times, from impairment , in which distress has begun to reduce the quality of care. Self-care is the set of deliberate practices by which a therapist keeps distress from becoming impairment. The best-known practical guide is Leaving It at the Office: A Guide to Psychotherapist Self-Care by Norcross and James D. Guy (2007; a second edition with Gary VandenBos appeared in 2018). Its recommendations sound simple and are hard to keep: value the person of the therapist as much as the technique; refocus on the rewards of the work; recognise its hazards; attend to the body through sleep, exercise and food; nurture relationships outside work; set boundaries on hours, availability and caseload; restructure unhelpful beliefs such as "I must save every client"; keep healthy escapes; seek personal therapy when needed; and cultivate a sense of meaning in the work. Many Indian therapists add the practices of their own tradition (yoga, meditation and prayer) and the support of family, which can protect against the isolation that private practice especially brings. Because burnout is largely a problem of the job, prevention also has to happen at the level of the organisation. Reasonable caseloads, a mix of trauma and non-trauma work for those who see survivors, regular supervision whose restorative function is taken seriously, peer consultation groups, and a culture in which admitting strain is safe all reduce risk. Group discussion of difficult cases has a long history in medicine too: from the 1950s the Hungarian-born psychoanalyst Michael Balint ran groups in London in which general practitioners discussed their relationships with difficult patients, and Balint groups still meet today. Trauma-informed organisations (Section 9.7) build staff care into their design. Measures such as the MBI and the ProQOL can be used to monitor staff, though they are screening tools, not diagnoses. In Indian public hospitals, where a clinical psychologist may see dozens of patients a day and trainees work long hours, the organisational side of prevention is often the weakest, and the stigma of a mental health professional seeking help for herself remains a barrier. Clinical link Ananya, a 28-year-old psychologist at a one stop centre for women affected by violence in Bengaluru, notices over six months that she dreads Mondays, sleeps badly, has stopped seeing friends and has begun to think of her clients as "the cases". She checks the locks at night several times, though nothing has happened to her. In supervision she and her supervisor sort out the strands: exhaustion and depersonalisation (burnout), intrusive images from one client's account of an assault (compassion fatigue), and a new conviction that no man can be trusted (vicarious traumatisation). The plan works at both levels: a capped caseload with fewer acute trauma referrals, fortnightly restorative supervision, a return to her evening yoga class and her friends, and a few sessions of personal therapy. Six months later she still finds the work hard, and she is still doing it well. Exam trap Self-care is an ethical obligation tied to competence (APA standard 2.06 on personal problems and conflicts), not an optional extra. Distress is normal; impairment is distress that reduces the quality of care. Leaving It at the Office (2007) is Norcross and Guy's. Burnout is prevented at two levels, the individual and the organisation, and Maslach's research says the organisation matters most. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The case of Eysenck's two-thirds, revisited Eysenck asked a fair question in 1952, and you can now see why his answer did not survive. His two-thirds came from comparing groups that were not alike: insurance claimants with jobs to return to against patients who had sought psychoanalysis, "untreated" patients who were in fact seeing their family doctors, and dropouts from analysis counted as failures (Section 8.1). Better baselines put spontaneous remission nearer 30 percent (Bergin) or at a median of 43 percent (Lambert), and once Gene Glass had invented meta-analysis the whole literature could be weighed at once: the typical treated client was better off than 75 percent of untreated people in Smith and Glass's analysis (1977) and than about 80 percent in Smith, Glass and Miller's (1980). Even Eysenck's own figures, run through the dose-effect method by McNeilly and Howard (1991), showed psychotherapy producing in about 15 sessions the improvement that spontaneous remission took two years to bring (Section 8.9). Therapy, on that reading, changes less where people end up than how quickly they get there, and for someone who is suffering, speed matters. Now go back to Ravi, the engineering student in Mysuru whose panic attacks eased after ten sessions. Eysenck would have asked whether he would have got better anyway, and part of the answer is yes: the end of his examinations, his family's support and the fact that he came for help at his worst all belong to the 40 percent slice that Lambert credited to client and extratherapeutic factors (Section 8.4). But the chapter also tells you what else was at work, and how to check it. For panic disorder, cognitive therapy with interoceptive exposure beats credible alternatives (Section 8.3); it works better through a strong alliance of agreed goals, agreed tasks and a bond (Section 8.5), and in the hands of a psychologist who handles difficult moments well (Section 8.6); and whether Ravi has really recovered, rather than simply saying a grateful goodbye, is a question for the reliable change index and a cut-off score (Section 8.9). The answer to Eysenck, in other words, is not that time does nothing. It is that a good therapist, using a well-chosen treatment and checking progress session by session, gives a person like Ravi better odds, sooner, than waiting would. Chapter summary 8.1 Eysenck's Challenge: Does Psychotherapy Work at All? Outcome research asks whether clients improve; process research asks what happens in sessions. Improvement after therapy is not proof, because spontaneous remission, regression to the mean, life events, support and expectancy produce change, and Strupp and Hadley's tripartite model (1977) adds that society, the client and the professional judge outcome differently. Hans Eysenck's 1952 review set about 44 percent improvement with psychoanalysis and 64 percent with eclectic therapy against Denker's and Landis's untreated baselines, and concluded that about two-thirds of neurotic patients improve within two years with or without psychotherapy. Rosenzweig and Luborsky (1954) replied first; critics showed the groups were not comparable, the criteria differed, the "untreated" were treated and dropouts counted as failures. Bergin (1971) put remission near 30 percent and Lambert (1976) at a median of 43. Kiesler's uniformity myths and Paul's 1967 question set the new agenda. 8.2 Meta-Analysis: Measuring How Much Therapy Helps. Box-score reviews counted wins and ties, ignoring effect size and precision. Gene Glass coined meta-analysis in 1976 for the statistical combination of many studies, using the effect size: the difference between treated and control means divided by the standard deviation, judged against Jacob Cohen's benchmarks of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. Smith and Glass (1977), with 375 studies, found an average effect size of 0.68, the typical client better off than 75 percent of untreated people; Smith, Glass and Miller (1980), with 475 studies, found 0.85 (80 percent) and little difference between kinds of therapy. Eysenck called it "an exercise in mega-silliness". The criticisms are garbage in, garbage out, apples and oranges, Rosenthal's file-drawer problem and non-independence, and re-analyses confirmed the effect. Lambert's summaries put the average effect near 0.8, with most gains maintained and a minority getting worse. 8.3 The Dodo Bird Verdict and the Specific-Effects Debate. Saul Rosenzweig (1936) took the Dodo's "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes" from Lewis Carroll to argue that therapies work through implicit common factors rather than specific techniques. Luborsky, Singer and Luborsky (1975) found a tie score and popularised the label dodo bird verdict. Wampold and colleagues (1997), using 277 direct comparisons of bona fide therapies, put the upper bound of their difference at about 0.2, against 0.82 for therapy versus no treatment. Specific-effects researchers (Rachman and Wilson) point to ERP for obsessive-compulsive disorder (Lindsay and colleagues; Foa and colleagues), Clark's cognitive therapy for panic, behavioural methods for children and Tolin's CBT meta-analysis. Critics (Chambless, Beutler) cite averaging across disorders, similar treatments, diluted outcomes, low power and allegiance, while dismantling studies find little. The verdict is roughly right for many common problems and wrong for some. 8.4 Common Factors: Frank, Lambert's Pie and Wampold's Contextual Model. Jerome Frank's Persuasion and Healing (1961) compared psychotherapy with religious healing, thought reform and placebo: clients come demoralised, and every therapy remoralises them through four shared features, an emotionally charged confiding relationship, a healing setting, a rationale or myth, and a ritual or procedure. Michael Lambert (1992) estimated that client and extratherapeutic factors account for about 40 percent of improvement, relationship factors 30, expectancy 15 and techniques 15, rough judgements rather than measured results. Beecher's "The powerful placebo" (1955), Kirsch's response expectancy theory and Kaptchuk's sham acupuncture trial show how much expectation and the relationship carry; Howard's phase model runs remoralisation, remediation, rehabilitation. Bruce Wampold set a medical model of therapy against a contextual model in which an initial relationship works through the real relationship, expectations and healthy actions; the evidence favours the contextual model on most counts. 8.5 The Therapeutic Alliance and the Core Conditions. The alliance grew from Freud's friendly transference, Zetzel's therapeutic alliance (1956), Greenson's working alliance (1965) and Luborsky's helping alliance (1976). Edward Bordin (1979) made it pantheoretical: agreement on goals, agreement on tasks and a bond. Horvath and Greenberg's Working Alliance Inventory (1989) has 36 items in three subscales, with 12-item short forms. Meta-analyses from Horvath and Symonds (1991) to Flückiger and colleagues (2018, 295 studies) put the alliance-outcome correlation at about .28, similar across therapies but correlational. Safran and Muran described withdrawal and confrontation ruptures, repaired through metacommunication. Truax and Carkhuff's rating scales and the Barrett-Lennard Relationship Inventory tested Rogers' core conditions, which the 2018 meta-analyses found facilitative (empathy r = .28) but not shown to be necessary or sufficient. Gelso's real relationship differs from the alliance, and Norcross's Division 29 task force and its successors listed evidence-based relationship elements. 8.6 Therapist Effects, Allegiance Effects and Client Variables. Ricks's "supershrink" (1974) showed that therapists differ, and multilevel studies put therapist effects at about 5 percent of outcome variance (Baldwin and Imel, 2013), more than the differences between treatments. Experience, training and orientation predict little; facilitative interpersonal skills and the ability to form alliances predict more, and deliberate practice may help. The researcher allegiance effect (Luborsky and colleagues, 1999) explained 69 percent of the variance in outcome differences. Prognostic variables predict outcome in any treatment and prescriptive variables, such as reactance, predict which treatment suits whom. Schofield's YAVIS (1964) describes the clients therapists prefer, not those who benefit most; readiness, expectations, self-efficacy, severity, attachment and preferences matter more. Hathaway's hello-goodbye effect (1948), regression to the mean, Orne's demand characteristics and placebo responding inflate pre-post change. In India the family, the route to help and stigma shape client factors. 8.7 Testing a Treatment: Efficacy, Effectiveness and the Randomised Controlled Trial. Efficacy asks whether a treatment can work under ideal conditions and prizes internal validity; effectiveness asks whether it works in ordinary practice and prizes external validity, as in Seligman's Consumer Reports survey (1995). Analogue research uses non-clinical participants, as in Gordon Paul's 1966 experiment; case studies and single-case designs come earlier. The randomised controlled trial, which dates from Bradford Hill's streptomycin trial of 1948, needs registration, inclusion and exclusion criteria, randomisation, allocation concealment, blind assessment, intention-to-treat analysis and enough power, and reports effect sizes, risk ratios and numbers needed to treat. The control condition (no treatment, waiting list, attention-placebo, treatment as usual, an active treatment, dismantling or additive designs) decides what is ruled out. Manuals, adherence and competence define fidelity, CONSORT governs reporting, and practical trials, benchmarking and practice-based evidence carry trials into clinics. 8.8 Landmark Trials, Empirically Supported Treatments and Evidence-Based Practice. The NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program (Elkin and colleagues, 1989) assigned 250 outpatients to CBT, IPT, imipramine or placebo, each pill with clinical management, for 16 weeks: the psychotherapies roughly equalled each other and imipramine, differences appeared only among the more severely depressed, and few stayed well over 18 months. Project MATCH (1997) tested the matching hypothesis in 1,726 clients with alcohol problems and found few matches; four sessions of motivational enhancement therapy did about as well as twelve of the other treatments. The Division 12 Task Force chaired by Chambless (1995, 1998) defined well-established and probably efficacious treatments, criticised by Seligman, Wampold, Westen and Garfield. Evidence-based practice in psychology (APA, 2006), built on Sackett's evidence-based medicine, integrates the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture and preferences. 8.9 How Much Therapy, How Much Change: Dose, Clinical Significance and Deterioration. Howard, Kopta, Krause and Orlinsky (1986) applied probit analysis to 2,431 patients and found a negatively accelerated dose-effect curve: about half improved by 8 sessions and three-quarters by 26. Howard's phase model runs remoralisation, remediation, rehabilitation, and Barkham's good-enough level model explains part of the curve by clients leaving once improved enough. Clinical significance asks whether change matters in a client's life, not whether it is statistically significant. Jacobson and Truax (1991) divide the change score by the standard error of difference: a reliable change index beyond 1.96 is reliable, and cut-offs a, b and c classify clients as recovered, improved, unchanged or deteriorated; Kendall's normative comparisons assess groups. Bergin's deterioration effect touches about 5 to 10 percent, Lilienfeld (2007) listed potentially harmful therapies, McCord's Cambridge-Somerville follow-up showed harm, and Lambert's OQ-45 feedback reduces deterioration. 8.10 Inside the Therapy Room: Process Research, the Course of Therapy and Its Ending. Process research studies what happens in sessions and process-outcome research links it to change. Rogers's recordings made the field possible; Orlinsky and Howard's generic model (1987) runs from the therapeutic contract to temporal patterns; Stiles warned that responsiveness defeats the drug metaphor; Tang and DeRubeis (1999) described sudden gains. Measures include Stiles's Session Evaluation Questionnaire, response category systems and task analysis. Therapy has a beginning (assessment, contract, role induction, alliance, hope), a middle and an end. Termination is a planned phase, which Quintana (1993) recast as transformation rather than loss. Dropout averaged about 47 percent in Wierzbicki and Pekarik (1993) and about 20 percent in Swift and Greenberg (2012). Self-disclosure divides the schools, from Freud's mirror to Jourard's transparent self; homework improves outcome (Kazantzis and colleagues, 2000); frequency, session length and SOAP notes complete it. 8.11 Combining and Adapting Therapies: Integration, Culture and Therapy in India. Eclectic or integrative is the commonest orientation among clinical psychologists, and Dollard and Miller (1950) were an early landmark. Integration has four routes: technical eclecticism (Lazarus, 1967; multimodal therapy; Beutler's systematic treatment selection), theoretical integration (Wachtel's cyclical psychodynamics; Prochaska and DiClemente's transtheoretical approach), common factors integration (Frank, Goldfried) and assimilative integration (Messer, 1992). Wrenn warned against the culturally encapsulated counsellor, and Pike's emic and etic name the problem. Cultural adaptation (Bernal's eight dimensions; Resnicow's surface and deep structure) helps modestly, most when the illness explanation is adapted. Derald Wing Sue's awareness, knowledge and skills, Sue and Zane's credibility and gift-giving, and cultural humility describe the competent therapist. In India, Surya and Jayaram (1964) described the dependent, support-seeking patient, Neki proposed the guru-chela paradigm (1973) and sahaja, Varma listed obstacles, Vahia built yoga-based therapy and Wig described the Hanuman complex. 8.12 Becoming a Therapist: Training, Supervision, the Wounded Healer and Self-Care. Boulder (1949) set the scientist-practitioner model and Vail (1973) the practitioner-scholar model; experience alone does not improve outcomes. Bernard and Goodyear define clinical supervision as evaluative, hierarchical and ongoing, with gatekeeping among its purposes; Kadushin's administrative, educational and supportive functions match Proctor's normative, formative and restorative ones. Models are psychotherapy-based (Ekstein and Wallerstein), developmental (Stoltenberg's integrated developmental model, Levels 1 to 3i) or process models (Bernard's discrimination model of three roles by three foci). Parallel process (Searles), live supervision (Montalvo) and Kagan's interpersonal process recall add tools. Jung's wounded healer draws on Chiron, and Pope and Tabachnick found that most psychologists had had therapy. Freudenberger named burnout and Maslach measured it (emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, reduced accomplishment); Figley's compassion fatigue and McCann and Pearlman's vicarious traumatisation complete the hazards, and self-care is an ethical duty.
