personal accomplishment, compassion fatigue, secondary traumatic stress, compassion satisfaction, vicarious traumatisation, self-care From the past papers According to the "Dodo Bird Verdict," what is the primary factor responsible for equivalent outcomes across different therapeutic modalities? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) The specific techniques used by the therapist (b) Common factors such as the therapeutic alliance and empathy (c) The theoretical orientation of the clinician (d) The specific diagnosis of the patient Answer: (b) Common factors such as the therapeutic alliance and empathy. Saul Rosenzweig (1936) borrowed the Dodo's "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes" to argue that different therapies succeed through what they share, and Luborsky, Singer and Luborsky (1975) credited their tie score to the shared components, "especially the helping relationship with a therapist". The specific technique, the clinician's theoretical orientation and the patient's diagnosis are exactly what the verdict says matter least. ERP is a form of therapy used for: (RML 2024) (a) Personality disorders (b) Depression (c) Schizophrenia (d) Obsessive-compulsive disorder Answer: (d) Obsessive-compulsive disorder. In exposure and response prevention the client faces the feared situation while giving up the ritual that normally follows, and it is the clearest specific effect in the literature: Lindsay, Crino and Andrews (1997) found OCD symptoms fell with ERP but not with anxiety management, and Foa and colleagues (2005) found 62 percent responders against 8 percent on placebo. It is not the treatment of choice for depression, schizophrenia or personality disorders. 'Healing and Persuasion' is the work of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Alfred Pritz (b) Jerome Frank (c) Charles Winnicot (d) Jeff Klerman Answer: (b) Jerome Frank. The book is Persuasion and Healing: A Comparative Study of Psychotherapy (1961), with the title reversed in the question; Frank argued that demoralised clients are remoralised by four shared features, a confiding relationship, a healing setting, a rationale or myth and a ritual. Alfred Pritz is an Austrian psychoanalyst linked to the Sigmund Freud Private University and the World Council for Psychotherapy, "Charles Winnicot" garbles Donald Woods Winnicott, and "Jeff Klerman" garbles Gerald Klerman, co-developer of interpersonal psychotherapy. In Expectancy Theory, motivation is highest when an individual believes: (1) effort leads to performance, (2) performance leads to outcomes, and (3) outcomes are: (RML 2025) (a) Uncertain (b) Valuable (c) Difficult (d) Negative Answer: (b) Valuable. In Victor Vroom's expectancy theory of work motivation (1964) the third belief is valence: the outcome must be valued, and uncertain, difficult or negative outcomes are not what motivates. Keep it apart from Irving Kirsch's response expectancy theory and from the client's expectancy of help, which are common factors in therapy (Section 8.4). A working relationship has all of the following characteristics EXCEPT: (RML 2020) (a) Observable ability of the worker and the client to work together (b) A committed belief in the helping relationship (c) A psychodynamic theory base (d) A contract to work together realistically and collaboratively Answer: (c) A psychodynamic theory base. The working relationship is the social-work and counselling name for Bordin's working alliance, which is pantheoretical: its origins are psychoanalytic, but it is defined by agreement on goals, agreement on tasks and a bond, so it belongs to no single theory. The other three options are its listed characteristics. The concept of the "working alliance" in therapeutic assessment refers to the: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Client's score on a measure of therapeutic outcome. (b) Collaborative relationship and bond between the clinician and client, focused on the tasks and goals of assessment/therapy. (c) Agreement between two different clinicians on the client's diagnosis. (d) Client's ability to work independently on therapeutic homework. Answer: (b) Collaborative relationship and bond between the clinician and client, focused on the tasks and goals of assessment/therapy. Edward Bordin (1979) defined the working alliance as agreement on goals, agreement on tasks and a personal bond, the three subscales of Horvath and Greenberg's Working Alliance Inventory (1989). An outcome score is what the alliance predicts (r about .28), agreement between two clinicians concerns the diagnosis rather than the relationship with the client, and independent homework is a separate topic (Section 8.10). Which of the following is NOT a key concept in Carl Rogers' Client-Centered Therapy? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Conditions of Worth (b) Unconditional Positive Regard (c) Actualizing Tendency (d) The Therapeutic Alliance (as defined by Bordin) Answer: (d) The Therapeutic Alliance (as defined by Bordin). Bordin's alliance of goals, tasks and bond grew out of the psychoanalytic line of Zetzel and Greenson and was generalised by a counselling psychologist in 1979; it is not Rogers's vocabulary. Conditions of worth, unconditional positive regard and the actualising tendency are central to Rogers's theory (Section 6.2). Which therapeutic approach would be LEAST likely to use the term "therapeutic alliance," preferring instead to focus on the "real relationship" and the therapist's unconditional positive regard? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Psychoanalysis (b) Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (c) Person-Centered Therapy (d) Interpersonal Therapy Answer: (c) Person-Centered Therapy. Person-centred therapists prefer the language of the core conditions and the genuine, person-to-person real relationship. Psychoanalysis gave the alliance its names (Zetzel, 1956; Greenson, 1965), and alliance research spans CBT and interpersonal therapy, where the alliance predicts outcome about as strongly as anywhere else. Schofield's (1964) 'YAVIS Syndrome' describes: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Therapy technique (b) Psychiatric Illness (c) Therapist's Qualities (d) Patient's Characteristics Answer: (d) Patient's Characteristics. In Psychotherapy: The Purchase of Friendship (1964) William Schofield argued that therapists prefer clients who are young, attractive, verbal, intelligent and successful. Despite the word "syndrome" it is not an illness, it describes clients rather than therapists or techniques, and it is a bias in who receives therapy, not proof that such clients benefit more. Which of the following best defines "prognosis"? (IHBAS 2025) (a) History of the illness (b) Likely outcome or course of the disorder (c) Immediate symptoms (d) Diagnostic criteria Answer: (b) Likely outcome or course of the disorder. Prognosis is the forecast of whether, how far and how fast a person is likely to recover, relapse or become chronic. The history, the immediate symptoms and the diagnostic criteria are what assessment and diagnosis work from; a prognostic variable, such as severity, predicts outcome whatever treatment is given. All of the following are the characteristics of efficacy studies EXCEPT (RML 2020) (a) Therapist actions are controlled by a protocol or treatment manual (b) Therapist flexibility is encouraged (c) The treatment is applied to a homogenous client population (d) The research design relies on random selection and random assignment to a treatment or control condition Answer: (b) Therapist flexibility is encouraged. Efficacy studies test a treatment under ideal, controlled conditions, so a manual, a homogeneous single-diagnosis sample and random assignment protect internal validity; flexibility belongs to ordinary practice and to effectiveness research. Option (d) is loosely worded, because efficacy trials randomly assign volunteers but almost never achieve random selection, yet the intended exception is (b). Analogue research involves: (RML 2022) (a) Undertaking research to determine the efficacy of treatments and interventions (b) Undertaking research to compare the effectiveness of two different types of treatment (c) Undertaking research on clinical populations (d) Undertaking research on healthy, non-clinical populations Answer: (d) Undertaking research on healthy, non-clinical populations. Analogue research studies treatment under conditions that only resemble clinical practice, most often with non-clinical volunteers such as Lang and Lazovik's snake-fearful students (1963) or Paul's speech-anxious students (1966). Efficacy research uses real patients under controlled conditions, comparing two treatments is a comparative outcome study, and research on clinical populations is the opposite of analogue research. A recent study showed that viral medications might be useful in fighting certain bacterial infections. Participants with gastrointestinal issues were assigned to either a placebo or viral medication for the first four weeks of the study, followed by an additional four weeks on the other treatment. Their symptoms showed significantly more improvement from the viral medication than the placebo. What type of study is this, and what is the explanatory variable? (RML 2021) (a) An observational study where symptom improvement is the explanatory variable (b) An observational study where the type of treatment (viral or placebo) is the explanatory variable (c) An experiment where symptoms improvement is the explanatory variable (d) An experiment where the type of treatment (viral or placebo) is the explanatory variable Answer: (d) An experiment where the type of treatment (viral or placebo) is the explanatory variable. The researchers, not the participants, decided who received what, in a crossover design in which each participant had both conditions in turn, so the study is an experiment and the assigned treatment is the explanatory (independent) variable. Symptom improvement is the response (dependent) variable, which rules out (a) and (c), and an observational study assigns nothing. In a cohort study investigating the association between a new psychological intervention and relapse rates in schizophrenia, the risk ratio is calculated as 1.0. This finding indicates that: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) The incidence of relapse in the exposed group is double that of the unexposed group. (b) The intervention has a significant protective effect against relapse. (c) There is no difference in the risk of relapse between the intervention and control groups. (d) The odds of exposure are equal in both the relapse and non-relapse groups. Answer: (c) There is no difference in the risk of relapse between the intervention and control groups. A risk ratio divides the proportion of one group who relapse by the proportion of the other, so 1.0 means the risk is the same in both. Double the incidence would give 2.0 and a protective effect a ratio below 1.0 (0.5 halves the risk), while (d) describes the odds ratio of a case-control study, not the risk ratio of a cohort study. To investigate a rare psychological outcome (for example, a specific dissociative disorder) and its potential past exposures (for example, childhood trauma), which of the following epidemiological study designs would be the MOST feasible and appropriate? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Prospective Cohort Study (b) Cross-Sectional Study (c) Case-Control Study (d) Randomized Controlled Trial Answer: (c) Case-Control Study. Starting from people who already have the rare outcome and comparable controls, and looking back at their past exposures, avoids waiting for a rare disorder to develop; Doll and Bradford Hill used the design to link smoking with lung cancer (1950). A prospective cohort would have to follow thousands of people for years, a cross-sectional snapshot cannot show which came first, and nobody can be randomly assigned to childhood trauma. The working alliance as defined by Edward Bordin (1979) is the collaborative relationship and bond between clinician and client: agreement on goals, agreement on tasks and a bond . It is pantheoretical, so a working relationship needs a realistic collaborative contract, an observable ability to work together and a committed belief in helping, but not a psychodynamic theory base . asked 4 times Bordin's therapeutic alliance is not a key concept of Rogers's client-centred therapy (conditions of worth, unconditional positive regard and the actualising tendency are), and person-centred therapy is the approach least likely to use the term, preferring the real relationship and the core conditions. asked twice The dodo bird verdict holds that different bona fide psychotherapies produce roughly equivalent outcomes , explained by common factors such as the alliance, empathy and hope. Therapist flexibility belongs to effectiveness research in ordinary practice, whose classic example is Seligman's Consumer Reports survey (1995). asked once Analogue research studies treatment under conditions that only resemble clinical practice, most often with healthy, non-clinical participants such as volunteer students with mild fears; it buys control at the price of external validity. asked once Exposure and response prevention is the treatment of choice for obsessive-compulsive disorder and the clearest specific effect: it beat anxiety management (Lindsay, Crino and Andrews, 1997) and placebo (Foa and colleagues, 2005: 62 against 8 percent responders). asked once Prognosis is the forecast of a disorder's likely course and outcome (recovery, relapse or chronicity), not its history, its immediate symptoms or its diagnostic criteria. asked once For a rare outcome and past exposures (a rare dissociative disorder and childhood trauma) the most feasible design is the case-control study , which starts from cases and controls and looks back; a cohort follows people forward, a cross-sectional study cannot show which came first, and nobody can be randomised to a past exposure. asked once When the researcher assigns the conditions, as in a crossover design where each participant receives both in random order, the study is an experiment , the assigned treatment is the explanatory (independent) variable and the outcome is the response (dependent) variable. asked once In Victor Vroom's expectancy theory of work motivation (1964), motivation is highest when effort is believed to lead to performance, performance to outcomes, and the outcomes are valued (valence); it is not Kirsch's response expectancy theory. asked once Hans Eysenck (1952) claimed that about two-thirds of neurotic patients improve within two years with or without psychotherapy ( spontaneous remission ). Weightage. 19 of the 422 questions mapped in this book (4.5%) test this chapter, 16 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 9 sections is High yield. On the night of Saturday 28 November 1942, the Thanksgiving weekend, the Cocoanut Grove was the busiest nightclub in Boston. About a thousand people, more than twice the club's legal capacity, were packed into its rooms: soldiers and sailors on leave, young couples, families out to celebrate. A little after ten o'clock a flame appeared among the artificial palm trees and cloth hangings of the basement bar. Within minutes, fire and poisonous smoke had swept through the whole building. The main entrance was a single revolving door, and it jammed as the crowd pressed against it. Other doors were locked, hidden behind curtains, or opened inwards against the crush. By morning 492 people were dead. It remains one of the deadliest fires in American history. The burned and the dying were carried to the city's hospitals, Massachusetts General among them. A psychiatrist on that hospital's staff, Erich Lindemann, began to sit with the survivors and with the families of the dead. He went on interviewing bereaved people for months, and in 1944 he published what he had seen in a paper called "Symptomatology and management of acute grief", based on 101 bereaved people. Grief, he wrote, is not a vague sadness. It is a definite syndrome, with bodily distress that comes in waves (tightness in the throat, choking, sighing, an empty feeling in the stomach, exhaustion), preoccupation with the image of the dead person, guilt, irritability towards others, and a loss of the ordinary patterns of daily life. With help, most of the bereaved worked their way through this "grief work" in a matter of weeks; eight to ten interviews over four to six weeks were ordinarily enough. Some did not. Their grief was delayed or distorted, and it surfaced months later as physical illness, agitation, hostility or depression. Lindemann drew a bold conclusion. If the normal course of a reaction to a terrible event could be described, then the people who were going wrong could be spotted early, and a few well-timed conversations might stop a temporary crisis from hardening into a lasting disorder. In 1948 he set up one of the first community mental health projects, the Wellesley Human Relations Service near Boston, and he was later joined in this work by a younger psychiatrist, Gerald Caplan. Out of their collaboration came crisis theory, the language of prevention in mental health, and much of the thinking behind the community mental health centres that the United States began to build after 1963. Notice where this story travels. A disaster in a nightclub led a psychiatrist out of his consulting room, onto the hospital wards, into the homes of the bereaved and finally into a whole town. That journey is the subject of this chapter. Clinical psychology is not only the fifty-minute psychotherapy hour. It is also helping a newly diagnosed diabetic take her medicine, helping a bus driver stop smoking, talking to a suicidal student on a helpline at two in the morning, training village health workers to deliver counselling, and helping a man with schizophrenia keep a job. Remember the Cocoanut Grove; you will return to it at the end of the chapter. 9.1 Health Psychology and Behavioural Medicine Medium yield · 2 Qs A century ago most people in India died of infections: plague, cholera, smallpox, tuberculosis, malaria. Today about six in every ten deaths in the country are caused by non-communicable diseases such as heart disease, stroke, chronic lung disease, cancer and diabetes. Think about what causes those diseases. Tobacco, alcohol, too much food of the wrong kind, too little movement, unmanaged stress, and medicines that are prescribed but never taken. Every one of those causes is a behaviour. That simple observation is the reason health psychology exists: if the great killers of our time are partly behavioural, then the science of behaviour must have something to say about preventing and treating them. Health as more than the absence of disease For most of the twentieth century medicine worked within the biomedical model : the view that every illness is fully explained by a biological fault (a germ, a lesion, a chemical imbalance), that mind and body are separate, and that health is simply the absence of disease. The World Health Organization (WHO) challenged that view in its constitution (adopted in 1946 and in force from 1948), which defined health as "a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity". Critics have pointed out that "complete" well-being is a standard almost nobody meets, but the definition did its job: it made well-being, not just disease, the business of health care. Psychologists then set about measuring well-being. The best-known measure comes from Edward Diener (1946 to 2021), who in 1984 defined subjective well-being as having three components: a cognitive judgement of life satisfaction (how well your life measures up to your own standards), the frequent presence of positive affect, and the relative absence of negative affect. This is often called Diener's tripartite model. A different approach came from the medical sociologist Aaron Antonovsky (1923 to 1994). Instead of asking what makes people ill (pathogenesis), Antonovsky in 1979 asked what keeps people well, which he called salutogenesis . His answer was a sense of coherence , a general feeling that life is comprehensible (it makes sense), manageable (I have the resources to meet its demands) and meaningful (it is worth engaging with). People high in sense of coherence stay healthier under stress. The related idea of hardiness, and the theories of stress and coping themselves, are taught in the General Psychology book. Exam trap Diener's three components of subjective well-being are life satisfaction (the cognitive part), positive affect and low negative affect . Distractors replace "life satisfaction" with "physical wellness", "spiritual wellness" or "social wellness"; none of those is in the model. Do not confuse it with Carol D. Ryff 's six-dimension model of psychological well-being (autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations, purpose in life, self-acceptance). Defining the field: health psychology, behavioural medicine and behavioural health Three overlapping labels appeared in the late 1970s, and examiners love to ask how they differ. The first is behavioural medicine. The term seems to have been used first in 1973, in the title of a book on biofeedback edited by Lee Birk . The field was formally defined at the Yale Conference on Behavioral Medicine in 1977, and the definition published by Gary E. Schwartz and Stephen M. Weiss in 1978 is the standard one: behavioural medicine is "the interdisciplinary field concerned with the development and integration of behavioural and biomedical science knowledge and techniques relevant to health and illness, and the application of this knowledge and these techniques to prevention, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation". The key word is interdisciplinary. Physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, sociologists and psychologists all belong to behavioural medicine; no single discipline owns it. The second label is health psychology, and it belongs to psychology alone. The American Psychological Association created its Division of Health Psychology (Division 38) in 1978, and its first president, Joseph D. Matarazzo , wrote the definition that every textbook quotes. In 1980 he defined health psychology as "the aggregate of the specific educational, scientific, and professional contributions of the discipline of psychology to the promotion and maintenance of health, the prevention and treatment of illness, and the identification of etiologic and diagnostic correlates of health, illness, and related dysfunction"; in 1982 he added "the analysis and improvement of the health care system and health policy formation". Read the definition slowly and you will see four targets: promoting health, preventing and treating illness, finding the psychological causes and correlates of disease, and improving the health-care system itself. The third label, behavioural health , was proposed by Matarazzo in the same 1980 paper for the part of the enterprise that deals with keeping currently healthy people healthy: prevention, health promotion and the maintenance of good habits. Two older terms complete the family. Psychosomatic medicine , the psychoanalytically flavoured study of how emotions cause bodily disease, came first (you will meet it in Section 9.3). Clinical health psychology is the applied, patient-facing branch of health psychology: the psychologist on the cardiac ward, in the pain clinic or in the diabetes outpatient department. Table 9.1 sets the terms side by side. Table 9.1 The family of fields that link behaviour and physical health. Field Origin Discipline Centre of gravity Psychosomatic medicine 1930s to 1950s (Dunbar, Alexander) Psychiatry, psychoanalysis Emotional conflicts as causes of specific bodily diseases Behavioural medicine Yale Conference 1977; Schwartz and Weiss 1978 Interdisciplinary Integrating behavioural and biomedical techniques for prevention, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation Health psychology APA Division 38, 1978; Matarazzo 1980 Psychology Psychology's whole contribution: promotion, prevention, treatment, causes, health-care system Behavioural health Matarazzo 1980 Interdisciplinary Keeping healthy people healthy Clinical health psychology 1980s onwards Psychology Assessment and treatment of patients with physical illness Exam trap The standard contrast is: health psychology is a branch of psychology with a strong emphasis on health promotion and prevention as well as treatment, whereas behavioural medicine is an interdisciplinary field that integrates behavioural and biomedical knowledge and interventions. Distractors such as "health psychology only uses medication", "health psychology is purely neurological" or "behavioural medicine does not consider behaviour" are nonsense and are there to be eliminated. Matarazzo's 1980 definition, Division 38 (not Division 12, which is clinical psychology), 1978. The biopsychosocial model at the bedside The theoretical engine of health psychology is the biopsychosocial model proposed by the American psychiatrist George L. Engel (1913 to 1999) in a 1977 paper in Science , "The need for a new medical model". Its history and its place among models of psychopathology are covered in Chapter 1; here the point is how it changes what happens to a patient with a physical illness. Engel argued that biological, psychological and social systems are nested inside one another, so a change at any level ripples into the others. A disease is something the body has; an illness is something a person experiences, inside a family and a society. Push a case through the model and its value becomes obvious. Mr Raghavendra, a 52-year-old bank manager in Mysuru, is admitted with a heart attack. The biomedical account is complete in its own terms: a coronary artery blocked by atherosclerotic plaque, high cholesterol, a father who died of the same disease at 60. But look at the psychological level. He is impatient and quick to anger, he has been sleeping five hours a night, and since the heart attack he has become quietly hopeless, convinced that he is now an invalid. And the social level: his branch is short-staffed, the family's evening meal is fried snacks with tea, his colleagues smoke together at lunch, and the statin he has been prescribed costs money he resents spending. Each level suggests its own intervention: medication and perhaps a stent (biological), treatment of his post-heart-attack depression and help with anger (psychological), and work with his family on diet and with his employer on hours (social). Depression after a heart attack is not a side issue: it roughly doubles to triples the risk of dying in the following year, as you will see in Section 9.3. A purely biomedical treatment would have missed half of what will decide whether he lives. Illness behaviour and the sick role Two people notice the same chest pain. One ignores it for a week; the other is in the emergency department within the hour. The difference is not in their arteries but in their illness behaviour , a term introduced by the American medical sociologist David Mechanic in 1962 to describe "the ways in which given symptoms may be differentially perceived, evaluated, and acted (or not acted) upon by different kinds of persons". Mechanic listed the factors that decide what a person does with a symptom: how visible and recognisable it is, how serious it seems, how much it disrupts work and family life, how often and how persistently it appears, the person's tolerance for it, what they know and believe about it, their need to deny it, competing needs (a daily-wage labourer cannot easily take a day off to see a doctor), other possible explanations for it ("it's just gas"), and how available and affordable treatment is. Four years later, Stanislav V. Kasl and Sidney Cobb (1966) separated three kinds of behaviour: health behaviour , which is what a healthy person does to stay well (exercise, vaccination); illness behaviour, which is what a person with symptoms does to find out what is wrong; and sick-role behaviour, which is what a diagnosed person does to get better. Much of what happens between noticing a symptom and seeing a professional happens inside the family. The sociologist Eliot Freidson called this the lay referral system : the chain of relatives, neighbours and friends who are consulted first, and who often suggest home remedies, a pharmacist, an astrologer, a temple or a faith healer long before a doctor or a psychologist. In India, where pathways to mental health care very often pass through traditional and religious healers first, understanding the lay referral system is a practical clinical skill, not a sociological curiosity. Once a person is accepted as ill, society gives them a temporary role. The American sociologist Talcott Parsons (1902 to 1979) described this sick role in his book The Social System (1951). Parsons saw illness as a kind of socially permitted deviance, and the sick role as the set of rules that keeps the deviance from spreading. It carries two rights and two obligations: The sick person is exempted from normal social roles and duties (no work, no school, no cooking), in proportion to how ill they are. The sick person is not held responsible for being ill and cannot be expected to get better simply by an act of will. The sick person must regard being ill as undesirable and must want to get well. The sick person must seek technically competent help (in Parsons's day, a physician) and cooperate with it. The model has been criticised from several directions. It fits short, acute illnesses (a fever, a broken leg) much better than chronic illnesses such as diabetes or schizophrenia, from which the person never fully "returns" to normal roles. It assumes that everyone can reach a doctor. And it fails badly for stigmatised conditions: people with HIV, alcohol dependence or mental illness are often blamed for their illness, which is precisely the right the sick role is supposed to grant. Still, the idea that being sick is a social role, with secondary benefits as well as costs, remains indispensable. When a person's way of perceiving, evaluating and acting on their own health is persistently out of proportion to the medical findings, the Australian psychiatrist Issy Pilowsky (1969) spoke of abnormal illness behaviour . The concept covers the person who keeps seeking investigations after repeated reassurance, but also the person who denies a serious illness and refuses treatment. The specific disorders in this territory (illness anxiety disorder, somatic symptom disorder, conversion disorder, factitious disorder) are described in the Psychiatric Disorders book, but the sick role gives you the cleanest way to tell three of them apart. Exam trap The sick role is the key to separating three presentations. In malingering the symptoms are produced deliberately for an external incentive (money, avoiding duty or prosecution, drugs). In factitious disorder (including factitious disorder imposed on another, once called Munchausen by proxy) the symptoms are also produced deliberately, but there is no obvious external incentive : the motive is to occupy the sick role itself. In conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) the symptoms are not intentionally produced at all. Distractors such as "presence of dissociation", "onset only in adolescence" or "comorbid substance use" do not separate them. 9.2 Why People Do or Do Not Protect Their Health Medium yield · 2 Qs Here is a puzzle that health workers meet every day. A free vaccination camp is announced in a village; half the families stay away. A man is told that he has high blood pressure and is given tablets that cost almost nothing; a year later he is taking them on perhaps half the days. Everyone knows that tobacco kills, yet roughly 28.6 percent of Indian adults used some form of tobacco in the second Global Adult Tobacco Survey (2016 to 2017). Knowledge clearly is not enough. Something stands between knowing and doing, and the models of health behaviour are attempts to say what it is. Each one is a theory about which beliefs matter. As you read, notice that the models borrow from one another; by the end of the section you should be able to recognise any of them from a list of its constructs, which is exactly how the examiners test them. The health belief model The oldest and most famous model was born of a practical failure. In the early 1950s the United States Public Health Service sent mobile X-ray vans into city neighbourhoods to screen for tuberculosis, free of charge, and very few people came. A group of social psychologists in the service, among them Godfrey M. Hochbaum , Irwin M. Rosenstock and Stephen S. Kegeles , set out to find out why. Key study: Hochbaum and the tuberculosis X-rays (1958) Hochbaum interviewed more than a thousand adults in three American cities about their beliefs concerning tuberculosis and then checked who had actually gone for a voluntary chest X-ray. Two beliefs stood out. People who believed that they personally could have tuberculosis without knowing it (perceived susceptibility) and who believed that early detection would make a difference (perceived benefits) were far more likely to have been screened: about four in five of those who held both beliefs had had an X-ray, against about one in five of those who held neither. The conclusion was that health actions depend less on the objective facts of a disease than on a person's beliefs about it. The criticism, which applies to the whole model that grew from this study, is that the data were correlational and the beliefs were measured after the behaviour. Rosenstock formalised these ideas in 1966 and 1974 as the health belief model , and Marshall H. Becker extended it to explain how well patients follow medical advice. In its mature form the model says that the likelihood of a health action depends on six beliefs (Figure 9.1): Perceived susceptibility : my own estimate of how likely I am to get the disease ("diabetes runs in my family; I could get it"). Perceived severity : how serious I believe the disease and its consequences would be, medically and socially ("I would lose my legs; I could not work"). Perceived benefits : my belief that the recommended action would actually reduce the threat ("walking every day really does prevent diabetes"). Perceived barriers : the costs I see in the action: money, time, pain, embarrassment, side effects, inconvenience ("I have no time to walk; the road has no footpath"). Cues to action : the trigger that tips a ready person into acting: a symptom, a relative's illness, a doctor's advice, a reminder SMS, a television campaign. Self-efficacy : my confidence that I can carry out the action. This was added in 1988 by Rosenstock, Victor J. Strecher and Becker, borrowing Albert Bandura's concept (next subsection), because the original model could not explain why people who believed in the benefits of quitting smoking still did not try. Susceptibility and severity together make up the perceived threat ; benefits minus barriers is, in effect, a cost-benefit judgement about the action. Demographic and psychological variables (age, gender, education, personality, knowledge) are treated as modifying factors that act on these beliefs. Modifying factors age, sex, education, knowledge, personality Perceived susceptibility Perceived severity Perceived benefits Perceived barriers Cues to action symptom, advice, media, a relative's illness Perceived threat Benefits minus barriers Self-efficacy (added in 1988) Likelihood of taking the health action Figure 9.1 The health belief model. Susceptibility and severity combine into perceived threat; benefits are weighed against barriers; a cue to action and the person's self-efficacy then decide whether the action is taken. The health belief model is simple, intuitive and still widely used to design campaigns. Its weaknesses are just as clear. It says nothing about how the beliefs combine (should threat and cost-benefit be added or multiplied?), it ignores social pressure, emotion and habit, and in reviews its constructs predict behaviour only weakly, with barriers usually the strongest single predictor and severity the weakest. Social cognitive theory and self-efficacy Several models in this section lean on the work of Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021). In social cognitive theory (set out in full in 1986), Bandura argued that behaviour, personal factors and the environment influence one another (reciprocal determinism), that people learn by observing others, and that two kinds of expectation steer action: outcome expectancies (will this behaviour lead to that result?) and self-efficacy (can I perform the behaviour?), a concept he introduced in 1977. Self-efficacy turns out to be one of the most powerful predictors of whether a person starts and keeps up a health behaviour, which is why later models kept adding it. Social cognitive theory has a broader scope than health, and its learning principles are covered in the General and Personality books; for this chapter, remember it as the source of self-efficacy. The theories of reasoned action and planned behaviour A second family of models came from social psychology's long struggle to explain why attitudes predict behaviour so poorly. Martin Fishbein (1936 to 2009) and Icek Ajzen (born 1942) proposed the theory of reasoned action in their 1975 book Belief, Attitude, Intention, and Behavior . Its central claim is that the immediate cause of a deliberate behaviour is the person's behavioural intention , and that intention has two sources: The attitude toward the behaviour : my overall evaluation of doing it, built from my beliefs about its outcomes ("if I eat less rice I will lose weight") weighted by how much I value those outcomes ("losing weight matters to me"). The subjective norm : the social pressure I perceive, built from my beliefs about what important people want me to do ("my wife and my doctor think I should cut down") weighted by my motivation to comply with them. The theory worked well for behaviours under full voluntary control but poorly for behaviours that need skill, resources or other people's cooperation. Wanting to quit smoking is not the same as being able to. Ajzen therefore added a third determinant in 1985 (the classic statement is his 1991 paper) and renamed the model the theory of planned behaviour . The new element is perceived behavioural control : how easy or difficult I think the behaviour will be for me. Perceived behavioural control does two things (Figure 9.2). It feeds intention like the other two components, and it can also predict behaviour directly, because people who feel in control are often actually in control. Attitude toward the behaviour Subjective norm what important others want Perceived behavioural control (added 1985) Intention Behaviour path through intention direct path, control to behaviour top two boxes alone = theory of reasoned action (1975) Figure 9.2 The theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen). Remove the third box and its two arrows and you have the earlier theory of reasoned action (Fishbein and Ajzen, 1975). The theory of planned behaviour is one of the best-supported models in social and health psychology: across many studies intention predicts a substantial share of behaviour, and attitude, norm and control predict a larger share of intention. Its great weakness is the intention-behaviour gap . Many people who sincerely intend to exercise, take their tablets or use condoms do not, and the model, which stops at intention, cannot say why. The stage models below were built to fill that gap. Exam trap The theory of planned behaviour has three determinants of intention: attitude , subjective norm and perceived behavioural control . Some papers (for example RML 2023) key the answer as "attitude, subjective norms and self-efficacy". Accept it: Ajzen himself said perceived behavioural control is closely compatible with Bandura's self-efficacy, and options listing genetics, personality, social support or health literacy are plainly wrong. But in your own answers write "perceived behavioural control", and remember that the theory of reasoned action (Fishbein and Ajzen, 1975) has only the first two. The theory of planned behaviour belongs to Ajzen alone. Protection motivation theory Public health campaigns often try to frighten people: cigarette packets in India carry graphic pictures of mouth cancer over most of their surface. Do fear appeals work? Ronald W. Rogers addressed exactly that question with protection motivation theory , first proposed in 1975 as a theory of fear appeals and revised in 1983. Rogers argued that a threatening message sets off two appraisals: Threat appraisal : how severe the danger is, how vulnerable I am to it, set against the rewards of carrying on with the risky behaviour (the pleasure of the cigarette, the relief of stress). Coping appraisal : whether the recommended action works ( response efficacy ), whether I can do it (self-efficacy), set against the costs of doing it (response costs). The outcome of the two appraisals is protection motivation , which functions like an intention to act. The model's practical lesson is important: fear alone backfires. A high threat with low coping appraisal produces denial, avoidance and fatalism ("everyone dies of something"). Frightening messages work only when they also tell people what to do and convince them that they can do it. Notice the overlap with the health belief model (vulnerability and severity are susceptibility and severity under new names) and with social cognitive theory (self-efficacy). Stage models: the transtheoretical model and the health action process approach All the models so far are continuum models: they place everyone on one scale of likelihood to act. Stage models argue instead that people pass through qualitatively different phases, and that each phase needs a different kind of help. The best known is the transtheoretical model of James O. Prochaska and Carlo C. DiClemente (1983), with its stages of precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance; it is taught in full alongside motivational interviewing in Chapter 6, and it is the model most often used in smoking and alcohol programmes. A more recent stage model was designed to explain the intention-behaviour gap directly. The German psychologist Ralf Schwarzer proposed the health action process approach (HAPA) in 1992. It divides change into two phases. In the motivational phase a person forms an intention, driven by risk perception, outcome expectancies and action self-efficacy (much as the earlier models describe). In the volitional phase the person must turn the intention into action and keep it going, and here three new ingredients matter: planning (action planning, which spells out when, where and how: "I will walk from 6 to 6.30 every morning on Chamundi Hill road"; and coping planning, which anticipates obstacles: "if it rains I will walk in the corridor"), maintenance self-efficacy (confidence that I can keep going when it gets boring or difficult) and recovery self-efficacy (confidence that I can get back on track after a lapse). The emphasis on planning and on different kinds of self-efficacy at different phases is HAPA's distinctive contribution. Table 9.2 brings the models together. Adherence and compliance All the models above apply to one behaviour that matters more than almost any other in medicine: doing what the doctor recommended. The older term compliance was defined by the Canadian physician R. Brian Haynes (1979) as "the extent to which a person's behaviour (in terms of taking medications, following diets, or executing lifestyle changes) coincides with medical or health advice". The word was gradually replaced by adherence , because "compliance" suggests an obedient patient and a commanding doctor, whereas adherence implies that the patient has agreed to the plan. A further step is concordance , a term promoted in Britain in the late 1990s for a negotiated agreement between patient and clinician in which the patient's beliefs are treated as legitimate. How big is the problem? A WHO report on adherence to long-term therapies (2003) concluded that in developed countries only about 50 percent of patients with chronic illnesses take their treatment as prescribed, and the figure is lower in poorer countries. Non-adherence comes in two forms. Unintentional non-adherence happens when people forget, misunderstand the instructions, cannot afford the drug or cannot manage a complicated regimen. Intentional non-adherence happens when people decide not to follow the advice: because the side effects are unpleasant, because they feel better and see no reason to continue (a common story with antihypertensives, which treat a condition that has no symptoms), or because they hold beliefs about the medicine ("English medicines are too heating"; "I will become addicted to these tablets"). The British psychologist Philip Ley showed in the 1970s and 1980s that many patients forget a large part of what they are told within minutes of leaving the consulting room, and that they remember best what they are told first. His cognitive hypothesis model proposed that adherence depends on the patient's understanding of the advice, memory for it and satisfaction with the consultation. The practical techniques for raising adherence follow almost directly from that model and from the theories above: Give the most important instruction first, use simple words, be specific ("one tablet after breakfast and one after dinner", not "twice a day"), repeat it, and give it in writing or as pictures for patients who cannot read. Simplify the regimen: fewer doses, combination tablets, timing linked to daily routines such as meals or prayer times. Use reminders and cues: pill boxes with compartments, mobile phone alarms, SMS reminders, blister calendars. Involve the family, who in India often hold the medicines and decide on spending. Elicit and address the patient's beliefs and fears about the illness and the medicine, using the language of the health belief model (benefits, barriers) and, where the person is ambivalent, motivational interviewing. Use behavioural methods: self-monitoring charts, behavioural contracts and reinforcement for attendance and adherence (Chapter 4). Reduce cost and distance: free medicines at primary health centres, home delivery, directly observed therapy (as in tuberculosis programmes). Exam trap "Compliance" means two different things in two different books. In health psychology it is following medical advice (now usually called adherence). In social psychology, compliance is going along with a direct request from another person, which is different from conformity (changing behaviour to match group pressure without being asked) and obedience (following an order from an authority). If a question says "In social psychology", the answer is the request-based meaning. The patient-practitioner relationship The most important single influence on adherence is the quality of the relationship between the patient and the clinician. In 1956 the psychiatrists Thomas S. Szasz and Marc H. Hollender described three models of that relationship, each appropriate in a different situation: Activity-passivity : the clinician acts on a patient who cannot participate, as with an unconscious patient in the emergency room. The prototype is a parent and an infant. Guidance-cooperation : the clinician advises and the patient follows, as in an acute infection. The prototype is a parent and an adolescent. Mutual participation : clinician and patient share decisions as near-equals, the model best suited to chronic illnesses that the patient must manage every day (diabetes, hypertension, asthma). The prototype is two adults. Later research contrasted a doctor-centred style (closed questions, focus on the disease, the doctor controls the agenda) with a patient-centred communication style (open questions, interest in the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations, shared decision making). Patient-centred consultations produce more satisfied patients, better recall of information and better adherence. Common barriers include medical jargon, rushed consultations (a few minutes per patient in a crowded government outpatient department), differences in language and social class, and the clinician's failure to ask what the patient believes is wrong. When the patient feels heard, the barriers in the health belief model shrink. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Answers: (1) health, (2) interdisciplinary, (3) sick, (4) threat, (5) control, (6) coping, (7) volitional, (8) satisfaction, (9) participation. 9.3 Stress and Physical Illness High yield · 4 Qs The models in Section 9.2 explain how beliefs lead to behaviours that make people ill. But there is a second, more direct route from mind to body. Emotions are bodily events: fear speeds the heart, anger raises blood pressure, prolonged distress floods the body with cortisol. If such states are frequent and long-lasting, can they by themselves damage organs? That question has driven a century of research, from psychoanalytic speculation to modern immunology. Stress in brief The theory of stress is taught in the General Psychology book; what you need here is the vocabulary that health psychology borrows from it. A stressor is an event or situation that makes demands on a person; the stress response is the physiological and psychological reaction to it. Stressors are usually classified by their time course. An acute stressor is short-lived, has a clear beginning and end, and is usually over in minutes or hours: a pop quiz, a job interview, a near-miss on the Ring Road. A chronic stressor persists for months or years and often has no clear end: caring for a parent with dementia, a long-running marital conflict, poverty, living with HIV or with cancer. In their influential 2004 review of about 300 studies, Suzanne Segerstrom and Gregory Miller used a finer taxonomy (acute time-limited stressors such as a laboratory speech task, brief naturalistic stressors such as examinations, stressful event sequences such as bereavement, chronic stressors, and distant stressors such as childhood abuse) and found that the body's response depends heavily on duration: brief stressors tend to mobilise parts of the immune system, while chronic stressors suppress it. The classic physiological account is the general adaptation syndrome of the Austrian-Canadian endocrinologist Hans Selye (1907 to 1982), first described in 1936 and popularised in The Stress of Life (1956). Selye found that rats exposed to very different noxious agents (cold, injury, toxins) showed the same nonspecific response in three stages: alarm (the sympathetic fight-or-flight reaction and the release of adrenal hormones), resistance (the body adapts and copes at a raised level of arousal) and exhaustion (resources run out; illness and, in Selye's rats, enlarged adrenals, shrunken thymus and bleeding stomach ulcers follow). The other classic approach measures stress by counting life changes. Thomas H. Holmes and Richard H. Rahe (1967) built the Social Readjustment Rating Scale, 43 life events weighted in life change units (death of a spouse 100, marriage 50, a minor violation of the law 11); higher totals predicted later illness, though only weakly. In 1981 Allen Kanner, Richard Lazarus and their colleagues showed that minor daily hassles predicted psychological symptoms better than major life events did, and a 1982 follow-up by Anita DeLongis and colleagues found the same for physical health. Lazarus's transactional model of appraisal and coping, which underlies most modern stress management, is in the General book. Exam trap A pop quiz is the textbook acute stressor (brief, time-limited). HIV disease, colon cancer and marital discord are chronic . "Alarm, resistance, exhaustion" is Selye's general adaptation syndrome ; life events theory is Holmes and Rahe; the health belief model and protection motivation theory are models of health behaviour , not of stress. Psychosomatic medicine and Alexander's "holy seven" The first systematic attempt to link emotions to bodily disease came from psychoanalysis. In 1935 the American psychiatrist Helen Flanders Dunbar (1902 to 1959) published Emotions and Bodily Changes , and she went on to propose personality profiles for patients with particular diseases (a "coronary personality", for example). The most influential figure, however, was the Hungarian-born psychoanalyst Franz Alexander (1891 to 1964) of the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis, whose book Psychosomatic Medicine appeared in 1950. Alexander proposed a specificity hypothesis : each disease arises from a specific unconscious emotional conflict acting on an organ that is constitutionally vulnerable. Frustrated longings to be cared for and fed were linked to peptic ulcer; chronically suppressed hostility to essential hypertension; and a repressed wish to cry out for the mother, coupled with fear of separation from her, to bronchial asthma. Alexander and his colleagues concentrated on seven conditions, which became known as the holy seven (sometimes the "Chicago seven") of the psychophysiological disorders , also called psychosomatic disorders: physical diseases with real tissue damage in which emotional factors were thought to play a major causal role. Its evidence came from psychoanalytic interviews with patients who already had the disease, so there was no way to tell whether the "conflict" caused the illness or the illness produced the emotions. The decisive blow came in the early 1980s, when the Australian physicians Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that most peptic ulcers are caused by a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori , and are cured by antibiotics; they received the Nobel Prize in 2005. Yet the broader idea, that psychological factors influence the onset and course of physical disease, has only grown stronger. What changed is that no one now thinks of a few diseases as "psychosomatic" and the rest as purely physical. As Barlow and Durand put it, biological, psychological and social factors are implicated in every disorder, mental and physical. The diagnostic manuals tracked this shift: the "psychophysiologic disorders" of DSM-I and DSM-II became "psychological factors affecting physical condition" in DSM-III and, in DSM-5, "psychological factors affecting other medical conditions" (the details are in the Psychiatric Disorders book). Exam trap Learn the seven exactly: peptic ulcer, essential hypertension, bronchial asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, neurodermatitis, thyrotoxicosis. Diabetes, coronary heart disease, migraine and irritable bowel syndrome are often called psychosomatic in loose usage, but they are not in Alexander's list. The specificity hypothesis is Alexander's (1950); personality profiles are Dunbar's . Coronary heart disease: Type A, hostility and Type D In the 1950s two San Francisco cardiologists, Meyer Friedman (1910 to 2001) and Ray H. Rosenman (1920 to 2013), had their waiting-room chairs reupholstered. The upholsterer remarked that the chairs were worn out in an odd way: only along the front edge of the seat, as if their patients spent the whole wait perched, ready to spring up. Friedman later said that he did not appreciate the remark at the time, but that it captured exactly what he and Rosenman went on to describe in 1959: a Type A behaviour pattern , made up of a chronic sense of time urgency and impatience, intense competitiveness and achievement striving, and easily aroused hostility and aggressiveness. People with the opposite, relaxed and unhurried pattern were labelled Type B. Notice that Friedman and Rosenman called it a behaviour pattern , a way of reacting to challenges, rather than a fixed personality type. Key study: the Western Collaborative Group Study (1960 to 1969) Did Type A behaviour actually predict heart disease, or did heart patients simply look hurried? To find out, Rosenman and Friedman classified 3,154 healthy men aged 39 to 59 as Type A or Type B using a structured interview, and then followed them for about eight and a half years. The Type A men were about twice as likely to develop coronary heart disease as the Type B men, even after the standard risk factors (smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure) were taken into account. The Framingham Heart Study found a similar result in men and women. For a time, Type A behaviour was accepted as an independent risk factor. Then came the criticism: several large later studies, including the Multiple Risk Factor Intervention Trial in the 1980s, found no relationship at all. Why did the global Type A pattern stop predicting heart disease? The answer that emerged was that Type A is a bundle, and only one part of it is toxic. When researchers took the pattern apart, time urgency and achievement striving predicted heart disease much less consistently; the component that carried most of the risk was hostility , especially cynical hostility (a mistrustful, contemptuous view of other people) combined with frequent anger. In a famous study, John Barefoot, Grant Dahlstrom and Redford B. Williams (1983) found that physicians who had scored high on the Cook-Medley Hostility scale of the MMPI while in medical school had several times the rate of coronary heart disease, and a much higher death rate, over the next 25 years. Anger causes surges of blood pressure and heart rate, promotes inflammation and clotting, and goes with smoking, drinking and poor social support. Treatment confirms the link: in the Recurrent Coronary Prevention Project (Friedman and colleagues, 1986), heart-attack survivors who received group counselling to reduce Type A behaviour, especially anger and impatience, had substantially fewer second heart attacks than those who received cardiac counselling alone. A third construct came from the Belgian psychologist Johan Denollet in the 1990s. The Type D personality ("distressed") combines high negative affectivity (worry, gloom, irritability) with high social inhibition (keeping those feelings to oneself), and in Denollet's studies it predicted a poorer outcome in people who already had heart disease. Beyond these patterns, depression is now one of the best-established psychological risk factors: in Nancy Frasure-Smith's studies in Montreal, heart-attack patients who were depressed were about three times as likely to die in the following year as those who were not, whatever the severity of their heart disease.
