Strictly on the evidence, however, hostility is the component of Type A that is most directly linked to coronary disease, which is why the global Type A pattern stopped predicting heart disease once hostility was separated out. Know both facts: if the question asks for the behaviour pattern or personality type, answer Type A; if it asks for the specific toxic component , answer hostility. Type B is protective, and self-efficacy is a belief about one's ability, not a coronary risk factor. Cancer and the Type C debate If personality could cause heart disease, could it cause cancer? In 1979 Steven Greer and his colleagues at King's College Hospital in London reported that women with early breast cancer who reacted with "fighting spirit" or denial were more likely to be alive and free of recurrence five years later than women who reacted with stoic acceptance or helplessness. In the 1980s the American psychologist Lydia Temoshok popularised the Type C personality : a cooperative, patient, unassertive person who suppresses anger and other negative emotions and complies with authority, said to be prone to cancer and to faster cancer progression. The evidence did not hold up well. A much larger study of breast cancer patients by Maggie Watson and colleagues (1999) found that fighting spirit made no difference to survival, though helplessness and hopelessness predicted a modestly worse outcome, and later systematic reviews concluded that coping style has little or no reliable effect on cancer survival. The point matters clinically. Telling patients that a positive attitude will cure them sets them up to blame themselves when the cancer progresses; Jimmie C. Holland (1928 to 2017), the founder of modern psycho-oncology , called this "the tyranny of positive thinking". Key study: Spiegel's support groups for metastatic breast cancer (1989) David Spiegel and his colleagues at Stanford randomly assigned 86 women with metastatic breast cancer to routine care or to routine care plus a weekly supportive-expressive group for a year, where they talked openly about their fears and death, supported one another and learned self-hypnosis for pain. The group members had less distress and pain, and, to everyone's surprise, a follow-up ten years later showed that they had lived on average about twice as long (roughly 37 months against 19). The finding was a sensation. But larger replications, including a Canadian trial of 235 women (Goodwin and colleagues, 2001) and Spiegel's own later study (2007), found that the groups improved mood and pain but did not lengthen survival. The safe conclusion is that psychological interventions reliably improve quality of life in cancer, not life span. Where psychology clearly helps in cancer is with distress, pain, fatigue, insomnia and the side effects of treatment. A classic example is anticipatory nausea : after a few cycles of chemotherapy, a quarter or more of patients begin to feel sick, or even vomit, at the sight of the hospital, the nurse or the smell of the ward, before any drug is given. This is classical conditioning, with the hospital cues as conditioned stimuli, and it responds well to relaxation training and systematic desensitisation (Chapter 4). HIV and AIDS Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, which leads without treatment to acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), is the clearest case of an illness whose spread is entirely behavioural: unprotected sex, shared needles, and transmission from mother to child. Until effective combination antiretroviral therapy arrived in the mid-1990s, behaviour change was the main weapon, and health psychology built specific models for it. The AIDS risk reduction model of Joseph Catania, Susan Kegeles and Thomas Coates (1990) describes three stages: labelling one's behaviour as risky, committing to change it, and enacting the change (which depends on skills such as negotiating condom use). The information-motivation-behavioural skills model of Jeffrey and William Fisher (1992) argues that all three ingredients in its name are needed; information alone changes little. Antiretroviral therapy (ART), available free in India's public programme since 2004, has turned HIV into a manageable chronic illness, which has moved psychology's role to new places. Testing is preceded and followed by counselling (pre-test and post-test counselling at Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres under the National AIDS Control Organisation, set up in 1992). Disclosure of status to partners and family is a delicate counselling task. Adherence must be very high, because missed doses allow resistant virus to emerge. Depression is common and worsens adherence. And stigma remains severe enough that India passed the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act in 2017 to prohibit discrimination in employment, education and health care. Psychological interventions such as Michael Antoni's cognitive-behavioural stress management reduce distress and improve adherence. The neurocognitive effects of HIV are described in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Diabetes Diabetes mellitus is a disorder of blood sugar regulation. In Type 1 diabetes , an autoimmune process destroys the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas, usually in childhood, and the person needs insulin for life. In Type 2 diabetes , which accounts for about nine in ten cases, the body's cells become resistant to insulin and the pancreas eventually cannot keep up. Genes contribute (South Asians develop Type 2 diabetes at lower body weights and younger ages than Europeans, partly because they carry more fat around the abdomen), but the factors most strongly associated with developing it are a poor diet and a sedentary lifestyle, acting largely through obesity. The ICMR-INDIAB survey reported in 2023 that more than 10 crore Indians have diabetes. Key study: the Diabetes Prevention Program (2002) If lifestyle causes Type 2 diabetes, changing lifestyle should prevent it. The Diabetes Prevention Program in the United States randomly assigned 3,234 overweight adults with raised blood sugar to a placebo, to the drug metformin, or to an intensive lifestyle programme aiming at 7 percent weight loss and 150 minutes of brisk walking a week, delivered with behavioural techniques (self-monitoring, goal setting, problem solving). Over about three years the lifestyle programme reduced the incidence of diabetes by 58 percent, against 31 percent for metformin. Behaviour change beat the drug. Similar trials in Finland, China and India (the Indian Diabetes Prevention Programme in Chennai) reached the same conclusion. Once diabetes develops, it is almost entirely self-managed. The patient, not the doctor, must monitor blood glucose, take tablets or inject insulin, control diet, exercise and care for the feet, every day for life. Not surprisingly, adherence is a constant problem, depression is about twice as common as in the general population and worsens glucose control, and many patients experience "diabetes distress", the frustration and burnout of relentless self-management. Stress also raises blood glucose directly through cortisol and adrenaline. Psychological care therefore includes diabetes self-management education, motivational interviewing, problem solving, treatment of depression, and work with the family, who in Indian homes usually cook the meals. Exam trap "Most strongly associated with Type 2 diabetes" is keyed as poor diet and sedentary lifestyle . Genetics is a real risk factor (and a tempting option), but lifestyle factors are the strongest and most modifiable contributors in exam terms. Psychological stress and environmental toxins play smaller roles. Do not confuse with Type 1, which is autoimmune. Chronic pain Acute pain follows an injury and fades as the tissue heals. Chronic pain persists beyond the normal time of healing, usually defined as longer than three months, and often bears little relation to any remaining tissue damage. Low back pain, headache, arthritis and fibromyalgia are the commonest forms. The severity of the damage is a poor predictor of how disabled a person with chronic pain becomes; anxiety, depression, beliefs about the pain, social reinforcement and compensation claims predict disability better. The physiological basis for that observation is the gate control theory proposed by Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall in 1965 (taught in the Physiological Psychology book): a "gate" in the spinal cord, which descending signals from the brain can open or close, means that attention, emotion and expectation genuinely change how much pain reaches awareness. The American psychologist Wilbert E. Fordyce , working at the University of Washington in Seattle, transformed pain treatment with his book Behavioral Methods for Chronic Pain and Illness (1976). Fordyce distinguished pain (the sensation), suffering (the emotional response) and pain behaviours : the observable things people in pain do, such as grimacing, limping, groaning, lying down, complaining, asking for medicine and staying away from work. Pain behaviours, he argued, are operants. They are reinforced by attention and sympathy from the family, by rest, by medication and by escape from unpleasant duties, and so they can persist long after the injury has healed. His operant approach to pain therefore changes the consequences: the family and staff are taught to give attention to "well behaviours" (walking, working, cheerful talk) and to withdraw it from pain behaviours; activity is increased by gradually rising quotas rather than "until it hurts"; and medication is given on a fixed time schedule rather than when the patient complains (pain-contingent medication rewards complaint). The goal is to reduce disability, not necessarily the sensation. The cognitive-behavioural approach to pain , developed by Dennis Turk, Donald Meichenbaum and others in the late 1970s and 1980s, adds the patient's thoughts. Patients learn that pain is influenced by attention and mood, are taught coping skills (relaxation, distraction, pacing, problem solving) and learn to challenge pain catastrophising ("this pain means my spine is crumbling; it will only get worse"). Catastrophising feeds the fear-avoidance cycle described by Johan Vlaeyen and Steven Linton (2000): fear of pain leads to avoidance of movement, which leads to deconditioning, disability and depression, which make pain worse. Acceptance and commitment therapy (Chapter 5) offers a third route, helping patients pursue valued activities while accepting some pain. These treatments are usually delivered in multidisciplinary pain clinics , a model pioneered in the United States by the anaesthesiologist John J. Bonica (1917 to 1994), who brought physicians, psychologists, physiotherapists and others into one team; Fordyce worked in Bonica's Seattle programme. Clinical link A useful question for any patient with chronic pain is "What would you be doing if the pain were gone?" The answer reveals the life the pain has taken away and becomes the treatment target. Rehabilitation aims to give that life back, even if some pain remains. Psychoneuroimmunology For most of the twentieth century the immune system was thought to operate on its own, untouched by the brain. That belief was overturned by a laboratory accident. Key study: Ader and Cohen's conditioned immunosuppression (1975) The psychologist Robert Ader (1932 to 2011) at the University of Rochester was studying taste aversion. Rats drank saccharin-flavoured water and were then injected with cyclophosphamide, a drug that causes nausea. Later, when the rats were given saccharin water alone, an unexpected number of them died. Ader realised that cyclophosphamide is also an immunosuppressant, and reasoned that the rats might have learned to suppress their own immune systems in response to the taste. With the immunologist Nicholas Cohen he tested this directly: rats conditioned in this way and later given saccharin alone produced fewer antibodies to an injected antigen than control rats. The immune system could be classically conditioned, so it had to be connected to the brain. Ader named the new field psychoneuroimmunology and edited the first book under that title in 1981. Research in humans soon followed. Janice K. Kiecolt-Glaser and her husband, the immunologist Ronald Glaser , showed in the 1980s that the activity of natural killer cells in medical students fell during examinations, and in 1995 that a small standard wound on the arm took about nine days (24 percent) longer to heal in women caring for a relative with dementia than in matched controls. In 1991 Sheldon Cohen , David Tyrrell and Andrew Smith gave nasal drops containing common cold viruses to 394 healthy volunteers who had first completed stress questionnaires, and then kept them in quarantine: the higher the stress score, the more likely a person was to become infected and develop a cold, in a dose-response fashion. The pathways run through the two stress systems you will meet in the Physiological book, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (cortisol suppresses many immune functions) and the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary system, and through behaviour, because stressed people sleep, eat and exercise worse and smoke and drink more. Psychological interventions can push in the other direction: in the expressive writing studies of James Pennebaker in the late 1980s, students who wrote about their deepest feelings concerning a trauma for a few days made fewer visits to the health centre and showed better immune responses than students who wrote about trivial topics. Exam trap Psychoneuroimmunology began with Ader and Cohen (1975) , conditioned immunosuppression in rats using saccharin and cyclophosphamide. The term is Ader's. Do not attribute it to Selye (general adaptation syndrome) or to Cannon (fight or flight). Acute stress can briefly enhance some immune responses; it is chronic stress that suppresses immunity. 9.4 Behavioural Medicine Techniques and Lifestyle Change Medium yield · 3 Qs Knowing that stress and behaviour cause illness is only half of the story; the other half is what a psychologist can actually do about it. This section looks at the main tools of behavioural medicine. Many of them were developed in behaviour therapy and cognitive therapy, and their mechanics are taught in Chapters 4 and 5; here the emphasis is on how they are applied to physical health. Biofeedback and relaxation Biofeedback is a procedure in which a bodily process that a person cannot normally sense (muscle tension, skin temperature, heart rate, brain waves) is measured by an instrument and fed back as a tone, a light or a graph on a screen, so that the person can learn to control it. Its scientific origin lies in experiments by the American psychologist Neal E. Miller (1909 to 2002) in the late 1960s, which appeared to show that rats paralysed with curare could learn, by operant conditioning, to raise or lower their heart rate and blood pressure. Miller himself later found that the dramatic animal results could not be replicated, but by then clinical biofeedback had taken off. The main types are electromyographic (EMG) biofeedback of muscle tension, used for tension headache and for retraining muscles after stroke; thermal biofeedback of finger temperature (learning to warm the hands), used for migraine and for Raynaud's disease; electrodermal biofeedback of skin conductance, used for anxiety; heart rate variability biofeedback; and EEG biofeedback or neurofeedback, used with debated results for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Biofeedback works well for some conditions, but for many others it does no better than simple relaxation training, which is cheaper. Relaxation is the most widely used technique in behavioural medicine. The main methods are Edmund Jacobson's progressive muscle relaxation (alternately tensing and releasing muscle groups), Johannes Schultz's autogenic training (self-suggestions of heaviness and warmth), slow diaphragmatic breathing, guided imagery, meditation, and yoga with pranayama, which has a long history in Indian clinical settings. The cardiologist Herbert Benson (1975) argued that all of these share a common relaxation response , the physiological opposite of the fight-or-flight response, which can be elicited by a quiet setting, a mental focus (a word or the breath), a passive attitude and a comfortable position. Relaxation lowers arousal, reduces blood pressure modestly, helps with headache, insomnia and pain, and is a component of almost every stress management package. The techniques are described step by step in Chapter 4, and mindfulness-based stress reduction in Chapter 5. Stress management Stress management is not a single technique but a package that teaches people to recognise and reduce their stress. A typical programme for, say, a group of software engineers in Bengaluru would run for six to eight weekly sessions and combine: education about the stress response and its effects on health; self-monitoring with a stress diary to identify triggers; relaxation and breathing training; cognitive restructuring of stress-producing thoughts ("if this release is late, I am finished"); problem-solving and time-management skills; assertiveness training for handling unreasonable demands; and advice on exercise, sleep and social support. The best-known structured version is Donald Meichenbaum's stress inoculation training (1985), with its three phases of conceptualisation, skills acquisition and rehearsal, and application and follow-through; it is taught in Chapter 5. Insomnia: cognitive behavioural therapy and sleep hygiene Chronic insomnia (difficulty falling or staying asleep on at least three nights a week for three months, with daytime impairment) is common, and sleeping pills lose effectiveness and carry risks. The first-line treatment recommended by major guidelines is cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), a package of four or five components. Stimulus control , introduced by Richard Bootzin in 1972, aims to make the bed a strong cue for sleep again. Go to bed only when sleepy; use the bed only for sleep and sex (no phone, television or work in bed); if you cannot sleep within about 20 minutes, get up, go to another room and return only when sleepy; get up at the same time every morning; avoid daytime naps. Sleep restriction , introduced by Arthur Spielman and colleagues in 1987, limits the time in bed to the time actually spent asleep, which builds up sleep pressure and consolidates sleep. The window is then widened in small steps as sleep efficiency improves. Cognitive therapy targets beliefs that keep insomnia going, such as "I must get eight hours or I will not be able to function" and catastrophic worry about the effects of a bad night. Relaxation training reduces the physiological arousal that keeps people awake. Sleep hygiene education covers lifestyle and environment: avoid caffeine after midday and nicotine and alcohol in the evening, avoid heavy meals and vigorous exercise close to bedtime, keep the bedroom dark, quiet and cool, reduce screen use before bed, and keep a regular schedule. A worked example shows how sleep restriction works. Ms Kavya spends nine hours in bed (from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.) but, by her sleep diary, sleeps only about six of them. Her sleep efficiency (total sleep time divided by time in bed, times 100) is 6 ÷ 9 × 100, or about 67 percent. The therapist prescribes a six-hour window, say midnight to 6 a.m., with a fixed rising time. For the first week she is sleepy, but she falls asleep faster and wakes less. When her sleep efficiency rises above about 85 to 90 percent for a week, the window is extended by 15 to 30 minutes, and so on until she is sleeping well and feels rested. The time in bed is never cut to less than about five hours. Exam trap Sleep hygiene is not the same as CBT-I. On its own, sleep hygiene education is not an effective treatment for chronic insomnia; the most active components of CBT-I are stimulus control (Bootzin) and sleep restriction (Spielman). "Use the bed only for sleep and sex" and "get up if you cannot sleep" are stimulus control rules, not sleep hygiene rules. Smoking cessation Tobacco is the largest preventable cause of death in the world, and in India it comes in many forms: cigarettes and bidis, and smokeless products such as gutka, khaini and zarda, which are used by more Indians than smoked tobacco. Most tobacco users want to quit and many try, but nicotine dependence makes success difficult; without help, only a small percentage of quit attempts succeed for a year. Effective help combines behavioural support with medication. On the medication side, nicotine replacement therapy (patches, gum, lozenges), bupropion and varenicline roughly double quit rates. On the behavioural side, the core techniques are setting a quit date, self-monitoring of smoking triggers, removing tobacco from the home and workplace, planning for high-risk situations, coping with cravings (delay, distract, deep breathing, drink water), enlisting social support, and relapse prevention (Section 9.9). Even very brief advice from a doctor helps. In a classic 1979 study in London general practices, Michael Russell and colleagues showed that a few minutes of firm advice to stop, with a leaflet and a warning of follow-up, produced a small but real increase in the number of patients who quit; across millions of consultations, a small effect becomes a large public-health gain. Clinical guidelines now teach the five As for every consultation: Ask about tobacco use, Advise quitting clearly and personally, Assess willingness to quit, Assist the attempt (counselling and medication), and Arrange follow-up. For those not yet willing, the five Rs are used to build motivation: relevance, risks, rewards, roadblocks and repetition. India supports quitting through tobacco control law (the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act, COTPA, 2003), large pictorial warnings, a national tobacco quitline and an SMS-based cessation programme. Alcohol: screening, the AUDIT and brief interventions Most people whose drinking harms their health are not alcohol dependent; they are hazardous drinkers (their drinking pattern raises the risk of harm) or harmful drinkers (harm has already occurred). They will never walk into a de-addiction centre, but they visit doctors for other reasons, and that is where they can be found. The standard screening instrument is the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT), developed by a World Health Organization collaborative project across six countries and published in 1989, with its validation study by John B. Saunders , Thomas F. Babor and colleagues in 1993. It has 10 items covering three domains: hazardous use (items 1 to 3: frequency, typical quantity, frequency of heavy drinking), dependence symptoms (items 4 to 6) and harmful use (items 7 to 10, including guilt, blackouts, injury and others' concern). Each item scores 0 to 4, for a total of 0 to 40, and a score of 8 or more usually indicates hazardous or harmful use. The first three items alone form the short AUDIT-C. The WHO manual links scores to four risk zones (Table 9.5). An older and shorter screen is the four-question CAGE (Ewing, 1984): have you felt you should Cut down, have people Annoyed you by criticising your drinking, have you felt Guilty about drinking, have you ever had an Eye-opener drink in the morning? Two or more "yes" answers suggest a problem. Table 9.5 AUDIT scores and the matching intervention (WHO guidance). Zone AUDIT score Risk level Intervention I 0 to 7 Low risk Alcohol education II 8 to 15 Hazardous use Simple advice III 16 to 19 Harmful use Simple advice plus brief counselling and monitoring IV 20 to 40 Possible dependence Referral to a specialist for diagnosis and treatment A positive screen is followed by a brief intervention : one to four short sessions, often of five to fifteen minutes, delivered by a doctor, nurse or counsellor. The whole sequence is known as screening, brief intervention and referral to treatment (SBIRT). The active ingredients of brief interventions were summarised by William Miller and his colleagues in the acronym FRAMES : Feedback of personal risk (your AUDIT score, your liver tests), Responsibility for change resting with the person, clear Advice to cut down, a Menu of options for doing so, an Empathic style, and support for Self-efficacy . Many controlled trials in primary care show that brief interventions reduce drinking in hazardous and harmful drinkers; they are not a substitute for specialist treatment of dependence. Obesity, weight management and exercise Obesity is usually defined by the body mass index (BMI), weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres. Because South Asians carry more body fat and metabolic risk at a given BMI, Indian consensus guidelines (2009) use lower cut-offs than the international ones: 23 to 24.9 for overweight and 25 or above for obesity, against 25 and 30 internationally. Obesity is multiply determined, by genes, the biology of appetite (the hypothalamic mechanisms are in the Physiological book), cheap calorie-dense food, sedentary work and screens, sleep loss, stress and medications. Binge-eating disorder, which is common among people seeking weight-loss treatment, is described in the Psychiatric Disorders book. Behavioural weight management grew out of Richard Stuart's 1967 report on the behavioural control of overeating and now has a standard set of components: self-monitoring of food intake, activity and weight (the single most powerful technique); stimulus control (eat only at the table, keep tempting foods out of the house, use smaller plates, never eat while watching television); slowing the rate of eating; realistic goal setting (losing 5 to 10 percent of body weight, which already improves blood pressure and blood sugar); reinforcement for changes in behaviour rather than for kilograms lost; cognitive restructuring of all-or-nothing thinking ("I ate one sweet, so the diet is ruined"); problem solving; and family involvement. Such programmes typically produce weight losses of about 5 to 10 percent in six months. The hard problem is maintenance: most people regain much of the weight within a few years unless contact, self-monitoring and physical activity continue. Physical activity protects against heart disease, diabetes, some cancers, depression and cognitive decline. The World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines recommend that adults do at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking) or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days. Starting is easy; continuing is hard, and a commonly cited estimate is that about half of the people who begin an exercise programme drop out within six months. Adherence is improved by choosing enjoyable and convenient activities, exercising with others, setting specific plans (the action and coping planning of HAPA), self-monitoring with a pedometer or phone, and building self-efficacy through early success. Motivational interviewing as a health tool Almost every lifestyle change above runs into the same obstacle: ambivalence. The smoker wants to quit and wants to smoke. Motivational interviewing , developed by William Miller and Stephen Rollnick and taught in full in Chapter 6, is a collaborative, person-centred but goal-directed style of conversation for resolving that ambivalence. Its spirit is summarised as partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation (drawing the person's own reasons for change out of them, rather than installing the clinician's). It was created in the addictions field, as a deliberate alternative to the confrontational style of older alcohol treatment, and it has since spread to almost every area of health behaviour. How far has it spread, and does it work? In 2003 Brian Burke, Hal Arkowitz and Marisa Menchola published the first major meta-analysis of controlled trials of adaptations of motivational interviewing. Pooling 30 trials, they found that motivational interviewing was as effective as other active treatments, and better than no treatment or placebo, for problems involving alcohol , drugs and diet and exercise (the diet-and-exercise trials included work with obese women with Type 2 diabetes); the results did not support its efficacy for smoking or for HIV-risk behaviour. Later meta-analyses have added medication adherence and other health behaviours. Obsessive-compulsive disorder, by contrast, is treated with exposure and response prevention (Chapter 4), not with motivational interviewing as a primary treatment. Exam trap Three motivational interviewing questions recur. (1) Where it was developed and is mainly used: substance abuse (IHBAS 2020). It is also used to improve treatment adherence, so "non-compliance to treatment" is a tempting option, but the original and best-established application is addiction; it is not a treatment for anxious-avoidant personality disorder or bipolar disorder as such. (2) Burke, Arkowitz and Menchola (2003) : alcohol, drugs, diet and exercise (diabetes-related trials included) were studied, smoking was studied but not supported, and OCD was not among the problems (RML 2022). (3) The spirit : partnership, acceptance, compassion, evocation, the wording of the 2013 third edition, which is what papers key. In the fourth edition (2023) Miller and Rollnick widened evocation into empowerment , and "evoking" lives on as one of MI's four processes (engaging, focusing, evoking, planning); if an option lists either version of the four, it is the MI spirit. "Confrontation, persuasion, expert authority" is exactly what motivational interviewing rejects; "free association, transference, abstinence" is psychoanalysis; "shaping, contingency management" is operant behaviour therapy. Hypertension, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, HIV infection, chronic pain and many cancers are rarely cured; they are managed, often for decades. Modern medicine has become so good at keeping people alive that the typical patient of the twenty-first century is not someone who will be cured next week or dead next week, but someone who will live with an illness for the rest of their life. That changes the psychological task. Living with a chronic illness means adjusting to a new body, a new identity and an uncertain future. When the illness finally cannot be held back, the task changes again: to dying as well as possible and, for the family left behind, to grieving. This section follows that arc, from diagnosis to bereavement. Living with chronic illness A chronic illness is a long-lasting condition, usually defined as one that persists for three months or more, that can be controlled but not cured. Think of what it asks of a person. Mrs Shobha, a 46-year-old schoolteacher in Mandya, is told that she has rheumatoid arthritis. Her hands are painful and stiff every morning, she needs tablets every day and an injection every week, her blood must be tested every month, and nobody can tell her whether she will still be able to teach in five years' time. She was the person who looked after everyone else; now she needs help to open a jar. None of this is a psychiatric disorder. It is the ordinary, heavy psychological work of being chronically ill. The American psychologist Rudolf H. Moos and his colleague Vivien Tsu (1977) described the diagnosis of a serious physical illness as a crisis in exactly the sense you will meet in Section 9.7: a turning point that overwhelms a person's usual ways of coping. They listed seven adaptive tasks that a seriously ill person faces. Three are specific to illness: The patient must deal with pain, incapacity and the other symptoms of the illness. The patient must deal with the hospital environment and the special procedures of treatment, from injections to scans to surgery. The patient must develop and keep adequate relationships with the doctors, nurses and other staff. Four are general tasks that any major life crisis brings: The patient must preserve a reasonable emotional balance, managing anxiety, anger and sadness. The patient must preserve a satisfactory self-image and a sense of competence and mastery. The patient must sustain relationships with family and friends. The patient must prepare for an uncertain future. The list is useful because it turns a vague impression ("she is not coping well") into specific targets. Mrs Shobha may be managing her pain well but quietly withdrawing from her friends because she is ashamed of her swollen fingers, and that is where a psychologist can help. How a person copes depends heavily on what they believe the illness is. Howard Leventhal and his colleagues (from 1980) proposed the common-sense model of illness , also called the self-regulation model. Faced with symptoms or a diagnosis, people build their own lay theory of the illness, an illness representation , and then choose coping actions that make sense within it. Research has found five dimensions in these representations: Identity : the label and the symptoms that go with it ("I have sugar; it makes me tired and thirsty"). Cause : what brought it on ("tension at work", "eating too many sweets", "karma", "the evil eye"). Timeline : whether it is acute, chronic or cyclical ("it will go once the tension is over"). Consequences : what it will do to the person's life ("I will lose my legs like my uncle did"). Cure or control : whether it can be cured or controlled, and by whom ("only insulin can control it now; nothing I do matters"). The model explains many puzzling cases of non-adherence. A man who holds an acute, symptom-driven timeline for his hypertension ("the pressure comes when I am tense") takes his tablets only on days when he feels tense, which is exactly the wrong way to treat a condition that has no symptoms. Illness representations are measured with the Illness Perception Questionnaire (John Weinman and colleagues, 1996), and, as the next study shows, they can be changed. Key study: changing illness perceptions after a heart attack (2002) Keith Petrie, John Weinman and their colleagues in Auckland, New Zealand, randomly assigned 65 patients admitted with a first heart attack either to usual care or to usual care plus three short sessions with a psychologist while they were in hospital. The sessions targeted the patients' own illness perceptions: what had caused the heart attack (many blamed stress alone and ignored smoking or diet), how long it would affect them and how much they could control it, and each patient left with a written plan for recovery. Compared with the controls, the intervention patients developed more positive views of their illness, felt better prepared to leave hospital, returned to work sooner and reported fewer angina symptoms at follow-up. The criticism is that the sample was small and the follow-up short. The lesson is still striking: three conversations about a patient's beliefs changed what happened to him after discharge. Is it always better to face an illness squarely? Not necessarily. Denial sounds unhealthy, but it can protect people during the acute phase. In a well-known study of heart patients, Jerome Levine and his colleagues (1987) found that patients high in denial spent fewer days in intensive care and showed fewer signs of cardiac dysfunction while in hospital; in the year after discharge, however, the same patients followed medical advice less well and were rehospitalised more often. Denial helps in the first few days and hurts in the long run. More generally, chronic illness needs both of the kinds of coping that Lazarus and Folkman distinguished (their theory is in the General book): problem-focused coping for the parts of the illness that can be controlled (diet, exercise, medicines, appointments) and emotion-focused coping , including acceptance, for the parts that cannot (the diagnosis itself, an uncertain prognosis). Some people do more than cope; they find something of value in the illness. The American social psychologist Shelley E. Taylor interviewed women with breast cancer and in 1983 proposed a theory of cognitive adaptation . People adjust to threatening events, she argued, through three themes. They search for meaning (why did it happen, and what does it mean for my life now?), try to regain a sense of mastery over the illness and over life in general, and restore their self-esteem , often by comparing themselves with others who are worse off. Taylor's striking observation was that many of the beliefs that helped were not strictly accurate: women who believed that they could control their cancer adjusted better, even when the belief had little medical basis. She called these beliefs positive illusions . Related to this is post-traumatic growth , a term introduced in the mid-1990s by Richard G. Tedeschi and Lawrence G. Calhoun for the positive changes some people report after a major life crisis, including serious illness: closer relationships, new possibilities and priorities, a sense of personal strength, a greater appreciation of life and spiritual change. Not everyone adapts. Depression is two to three times more common in people with chronic illness than in the general population, and it worsens the illness, mostly by eroding self-care: depressed diabetics check their sugar less often, and depressed heart patients skip their walks and their tablets. Screening for depression is therefore part of good chronic care. The family carries much of the load. In India, where hospitals expect a relative to stay with the patient and where most care after discharge happens at home, the burden on family carers, usually women, is heavy, and their own health suffers. Helping the carer is helping the patient. The most widely copied psychological programme for chronic illness was developed by Kate Lorig at Stanford University. Her Chronic Disease Self-Management Program, which grew out of an earlier programme for arthritis, runs for six weekly sessions of about two and a half hours and is led by trained lay people who themselves live with a chronic illness. It teaches action planning, problem solving, the management of symptoms, communication with doctors and the proper use of medicines, and its explicit aim is to raise self-efficacy (Section 9.2). Participants report better health behaviours and more confidence, and they spend fewer days in hospital. Notice the theme that runs through this whole section and the next: the patient, not the professional, does most of the work, so the professional's job is to build the patient's capacity. Exam trap Keep three frameworks apart. Moos and Tsu (1977) listed seven adaptive tasks of physical illness, three illness-related and four general. Leventhal's common-sense model describes illness representations : identity, cause, timeline, consequences, cure or control. Taylor's cognitive adaptation theory (1983) has three themes, meaning, mastery and self-enhancement, sustained by positive illusions. Post-traumatic growth is Tedeschi and Calhoun 's term, not Taylor's. Dying and palliative care For most of human history people died at home, surrounded by their families. In the twentieth century, in the richer countries, dying moved into hospitals, and death became something that doctors felt they had failed at and families did not discuss. Two American sociologists, Barney G. Glaser and Anselm L. Strauss , spent several years observing dying patients and the people around them in hospitals in the San Francisco area, and in Awareness of Dying (1965) they described four awareness contexts , defined by who knows what about the patient's approaching death: In closed awareness , the staff and the family know that the patient is dying, but the patient does not. In suspected awareness , the patient suspects and tries to confirm or disprove the suspicion, while the others try to keep the secret. In mutual pretence , everyone knows, including the patient, but everyone acts as if they did not. In open awareness , everyone knows and acknowledges it, so the dying person can talk about death and plan for it. If closed awareness sounds old-fashioned, it is not. In India it is common for a family to ask the doctor not to tell the patient that he has cancer, a practice clinicians call collusion . The family's motive is love, but the cost can be high: the patient cannot say goodbye, settle his affairs or make choices about his own care. The person who did most to break the silence around dying was the Swiss-born American psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross (1926 to 2004). In the mid-1960s, at the University of Chicago, she began a seminar in which she interviewed dying patients, with their permission, in front of medical and theology students, simply asking them what it was like. Her book On Death and Dying (1969), drawn from interviews with about 200 patients, proposed that people who learn that they are dying tend to pass through five stages. The study of death and dying, which her book helped to make respectable, is called thanatology . Follow Mrs Lakshmi, a 52-year-old woman with advanced cancer, through the five stages of dying : Denial (and isolation): "No, not me. The reports must have been mixed up." Denial cushions the shock and is, Kübler-Ross argued, usually temporary. Anger : "Why me? I never smoked; I did everything right." The anger is often displaced onto the doctors, the nurses or the family. Bargaining : "God, let me live until my daughter's wedding in March, and I will walk up the hill to Tirupati." It is an attempt to postpone the inevitable through a deal, often a secret one with God. Depression : "What is the use of anything now?" Kübler-Ross separated reactive depression (sadness over what has already been lost: the job, the hair, the role in the family) from preparatory depression (grieving in advance for the losses to come). Acceptance : "I am tired; I am ready." This is not a happy stage, she wrote, but one almost empty of feeling, as if the struggle were over. Kübler-Ross herself said that the stages could overlap, that not everyone passes through all of them, and that hope persists through every stage. Her readers were less careful. The stages hardened into a fixed sequence that nurses and relatives expected patients to follow, so that a dying man who stayed angry was said to be "stuck", and a woman who never accepted death was felt to have failed. The research does not support a fixed sequence. The model came from clinical impressions rather than systematic measurement; people move back and forth between the reactions, many never show some of them, and the reactions differ with personality, age, culture and the illness itself. Its lasting value is moral rather than scientific: it taught a generation of clinicians to sit down and listen to dying people. The American thanatologist Charles Corr (1992) offered a task-based alternative in which the dying person works on four areas of need (physical, psychological, social and spiritual) at their own pace and in their own order, which fits the evidence better. While Kübler-Ross was listening to dying patients in Chicago, a British nurse who had become a medical social worker and then a doctor, Cicely Saunders (1918 to 2005), was changing how they were cared for. In 1967 she opened St Christopher's Hospice in south London, the first modern hospice, which combined expert control of pain and other symptoms with research and teaching. Saunders introduced the concept of total pain : the suffering of a dying person has physical, psychological, social and spiritual components, and all four must be treated. She also showed that morphine given regularly, by the clock and in adequate doses, controls cancer pain without the addiction and stupor that doctors feared, a close parallel to the time-contingent medication of Fordyce's operant approach in Section 9.3. The movement she started is now called palliative care . The World Health Organization (2002) defines it as an approach that improves the quality of life of patients and their families facing the problems associated with life-threatening illness, through the prevention and relief of suffering by early identification, assessment and treatment of pain and other problems, physical, psychosocial and spiritual. Three features of the definition matter for psychologists. The unit of care is the patient and the family , including support for the family in bereavement. The aim is quality of life, not length of life. And palliative care is not only for the last days: it can begin at diagnosis, alongside treatment aimed at cure or control. Hospice care is the part of palliative care given in the final phase of life, in a hospice or at home. Key study: early palliative care in lung cancer (2010) Does it matter when palliative care begins? Jennifer Temel and her colleagues in Boston randomly assigned 151 patients with newly diagnosed metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer to standard cancer care or to standard care plus early, regular visits from a palliative care team. The early palliative care group had a better quality of life and fewer depressive symptoms, chose less aggressive treatment at the end of life and, unexpectedly, lived longer (a median of 11.6 months against 8.9). The survival finding came from a single trial and needs replication, but the main lesson is now widely accepted: palliative care belongs early in a serious illness, not only at the very end. What does a psychologist do in palliative care? Assessment comes first, because sadness is normal in dying and depression is not, and the two need to be told apart (a useful clue: the dying person who is sad can still enjoy a visit from the grandchildren; the depressed one cannot). A related state, demoralisation , a loss of hope and meaning with a feeling of being trapped, is common and responds to meaning-focused work. Brief psychotherapies have been designed for the dying. In dignity therapy , developed by the Canadian psychiatrist Harvey Max Chochinov (2005), the patient is interviewed about the things that matter most to them, what they are proudest of and what they want their family to know and remember, and the edited transcript becomes a document they can leave behind. Meaning-centred psychotherapy, developed by William Breitbart, helps patients draw on sources of meaning in the spirit of Frankl's logotherapy (Chapter 6). The psychologist also helps with communication. Breaking bad news well is a skill, and one widely taught protocol, SPIKES (Walter Baile, Robert Buckman and colleagues, 2000), sets out six steps: S etting up the interview; assessing the patient's P erception of the situation; obtaining the patient's I nvitation (how much does the patient want to know?); giving K nowledge in small, clear pieces; responding to the patient's E motions with empathy; and agreeing a S trategy, with a summary. Indian context Most Indians who need palliative care never receive it. Two obstacles stand out. The first is access to opioids: for decades the strict licensing rules under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act 1985 made morphine almost unobtainable in most hospitals, until a 2014 amendment created a simpler category of "essential narcotic drugs". The second is that hospital-based care cannot reach people dying at home in villages. Kerala showed an alternative: a community-based model, the Neighbourhood Network in Palliative Care, in which trained local volunteers find bedridden patients in their own area and support them at home, backed by doctors and nurses. In 2008 Kerala became the first Indian state to adopt a palliative care policy, and a large share of the country's palliative care services are still found there. Exam trap Kübler-Ross's five stages, in order: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance (DABDA), from On Death and Dying ( 1969 ). They describe dying patients facing their own death; they were later applied, much less successfully, to the bereaved. They are neither a fixed nor a universal sequence. The founder of the modern hospice movement is Cicely Saunders (St Christopher's Hospice, 1967 ), whose concept is total pain . "Awareness contexts" are Glaser and Strauss (1965). Dignity therapy is Chochinov's. Grief, mourning and the models that describe them When death comes, the focus of care moves to the people who are left. Three words are used carefully in this field. Bereavement is the objective situation of having lost someone significant through death. Grief is the emotional, cognitive, physical and behavioural response to that loss: the sorrow and yearning, the disbelief, anger and guilt, the sleeplessness and the tight throat that you read about in the chapter's opening story. Mourning is the process by which people adapt to the loss, including the public expressions of grief shaped by culture and religion: the cremation and the immersion of the ashes, the rites of the days after a death (about thirteen days in many Hindu families), the annual shraddha, the prayers for the dead in Muslim and Christian homes. Grief can begin even before a death. Erich Lindemann (1900 to 1974), whose study of the Cocoanut Grove bereaved opened this chapter, noticed it in the wives of soldiers who had gone to war and named it anticipatory grief : grieving in advance for a loss that is expected, as families of people with dementia or advanced cancer often do. The first modern theory of grief came from Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939). In "Mourning and Melancholia" (written in 1915 and published in 1917), he argued that in mourning the bereaved person must gradually withdraw the emotional energy (libido) invested in the dead person, memory by memory, a painful process that takes time; when "the work of mourning is completed the ego becomes free and uninhibited again" and can invest in new relationships. Freud also drew a distinction that clinicians still use. "In mourning it is the world which has become poor and empty; in melancholia it is the ego itself": the depressed person, unlike the grieving one, loses self-esteem and is full of self-reproach. Lindemann's account of grief work (1944) continued the same idea. The bereaved, he wrote, must emancipate themselves from their bondage to the deceased, readjust to an environment in which the deceased is missing, and form new relationships. The assumption that grief must be "worked through" by confronting the loss, and that avoiding it stores up trouble for later, is known as the grief work hypothesis . As you will see, it has been seriously questioned. Attachment theory gave grief a biological meaning. John Bowlby (1907 to 1990) saw grief as a form of separation distress: the attachment system, built to keep us close to the people we depend on, goes on searching for a person who will never return. Working with Colin Murray Parkes , whose studies of London widows were published in Bereavement (1972), Bowlby described four phases of grief , set out most fully in Loss (1980), the third volume of Attachment and Loss : numbing , a period of shock and disbelief lasting from a few hours to about a week; yearning and searching , with pining, restlessness, anger and preoccupation with the dead person; disorganisation and despair , when the reality of the loss sinks in and the person feels apathetic and aimless; and reorganisation , when the person builds a new life and a new identity. Parkes found that widows often had a vivid sense of their dead husband's presence in the first months, an experience that is common in grief and not a sign of psychosis. Many people also apply Kübler-Ross's five stages to the bereaved, a use she herself encouraged in her last book, On Grief and Grieving (2005, with David Kessler). The best test came from the Yale Bereavement Study, in which Paul Maciejewski, Holly G. Prigerson and their colleagues (2007) assessed 233 people at different points up to two years after a death from natural causes. Disbelief, yearning, anger and depression did peak roughly in that order over the first six months, which gives the stage idea some support. But the most frequently reported reaction, from the very first month, was not denial but acceptance , and the strongest negative feeling throughout was yearning , not anger or depression. The stages are better thought of as overlapping reactions than as steps on a ladder. A different kind of model came from the American psychologist J. William Worden , whose Grief Counseling and Grief Therapy first appeared in 1982 and has been revised several times since. Worden objected that stages and phases make the mourner passive, someone to whom grief simply happens. He described instead four tasks of mourning , things the bereaved person has to do, which can be revisited and worked on in any order. In their current wording they are: To accept the reality of the loss , intellectually and emotionally: the person really is dead and will not return. Seeing the body and taking part in the funeral rites help with this task. To process the pain of grief , rather than avoiding or numbing it with alcohol, constant busyness or a hasty move to another city. To adjust to a world without the deceased . This includes external adjustments (learning to manage the money, to cook, to raise the children alone), internal adjustments ("Who am I now, if I am no longer a wife?") and spiritual adjustments ("What do I now believe about the world, and about God?"). To find an enduring connection with the deceased while embarking on a new life . In the first edition this task was to withdraw emotional energy from the deceased and reinvest it in another relationship, which was Freud's idea; Worden changed it as evidence grew that healthy mourners keep a bond with the dead. Worden also listed the mediators of mourning that make grief easier or harder: who the person who died was (a child, a spouse, a parent); the nature of the attachment (how strong, how secure, how ambivalent); how the person died (suddenly, violently, by suicide, after a long illness); the mourner's history of losses and mental health; the mourner's personality; the social support available; and other stresses happening at the same time. And he drew a line that matters for the next subsection: grief counselling helps people with normal, uncomplicated grief to work through the tasks, whereas grief therapy is for people whose grief has become complicated. The Dutch psychologists Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut (1999) noticed that the grief work hypothesis captured only half of what bereaved people actually do. In their dual process model , bereaved people face two kinds of stressor (Figure 9.3). Loss-oriented coping deals with the loss itself: crying, looking at photographs, yearning, ruminating about the death, the grief work of the older models. Restoration-oriented coping deals with the secondary consequences of the death: learning to do the things the dead person used to do, taking on new roles and a new identity, building new relationships, and also taking time off from grief through distraction. The heart of the model is oscillation : healthy grieving moves back and forth between confronting the loss and turning away from it, sometimes many times a day. A widow who weeps over her husband's photograph in the morning and goes to the bank in the afternoon to transfer the accounts is not in denial in the afternoon; she is doing what grief requires. Problems arise when a person is stuck at one pole, grieving all the time with no restoration (chronic grief), or keeping so busy that the loss is never faced (avoided grief). Everyday life experience Loss-oriented grief work intrusion of grief yearning, looking at photos breaking or relocating bonds avoiding restoration tasks Restoration-oriented attending to life changes doing new things distraction, time off grief new roles and identity new relationships oscillation Healthy grief moves back and forth between the two orientations Figure 9.3 The dual process model of coping with bereavement (Stroebe and Schut, 1999). Neither box alone is healthy grieving: adjustment comes from oscillating between confronting the loss and attending to the life that has to go on. Worden's revised fourth task and the dual process model both reflect a shift that took place in the 1990s. In Continuing Bonds (1996), Dennis Klass , Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman challenged the Freudian assumption that healthy grief ends by "letting go". Bereaved people, they showed, commonly keep an inner relationship with the dead: they talk to them, consult them in their minds before decisions, keep their belongings and feel watched over by them. These continuing bonds are usually healthy. In much of the world this was never news. An Indian family that garlands a parent's photograph, lights a lamp before it, performs the annual rites for the ancestors and tells the grandchildren what their grandfather would have said is maintaining a continuing bond, and nobody would think it pathological. The grief work hypothesis was challenged from another direction as well. In "The myths of coping with loss" (1989), Camille B. Wortman and Roxane Cohen Silver examined the evidence for several beliefs widely held by professionals: that intense distress after a loss is inevitable; that its absence is a sign of trouble (the person is "in denial" and will break down later); that the loss must be worked through; and that recovery should be complete within a year or so. None, they concluded, was well supported. In 2002 George A. Bonanno and his colleagues studied older married people from before a spouse's death to 18 months after it and identified distinct trajectories of grief. The most common, shown by about half of the bereaved, was resilience : some sadness and disruption, but stable, healthy functioning throughout. Others showed recovery (marked distress that eased over a year or two) or chronic grief (distress that stayed high), while delayed grief , the outcome that the grief work hypothesis predicted for people who did not grieve openly, was rare. Resilience, Bonanno argued (2004), is the norm, not a sign of denial. Finally, not every grief is permitted. Kenneth J. Doka (1989) coined the term disenfranchised grief for grief that is not openly acknowledged, socially sanctioned or publicly mourned. It arises when the relationship is not recognised (a lover in a secret affair, a same-sex partner, a former spouse), when the loss is not recognised (a miscarriage, an abortion, the death of a pet, the "living loss" of a parent with dementia), when the griever is not recognised (a young child or a person with intellectual disability, who is assumed not to understand), or when the death itself is stigmatised (suicide, AIDS, a drug overdose). Disenfranchised mourners lack the rituals and support that help other mourners, and their grief is more likely to become complicated. Table 9.6 brings the models of grief together.
