"Mourning and Melancholia" (1917) is Freud's, and the term anticipatory grief goes back to Lindemann (1944). Complicated grief and bereavement care If most grief is normal and most bereaved people are resilient, who needs help? Lindemann already knew that some people's grief went wrong. He described morbid grief reactions of two kinds: delayed grief, postponed for weeks, months or even years, and distorted grief, in which grief appears in disguised forms such as overactivity without any sense of loss, the symptoms of the dead person's last illness, physical disease, furious hostility against particular people, or agitated depression. Over the following decades the problem acquired many names (pathological, abnormal, chronic, traumatic and complicated grief ), and it was only in the twenty-first century that it was defined precisely. The research of Prigerson and of M. Katherine Shear showed that a minority of bereaved people, roughly one in ten after a death from natural causes and more after a violent death, develop a distinct syndrome. Its core is persistent, intense yearning or longing for the dead person, or preoccupation with them, together with symptoms such as disbelief, intense emotional pain, a feeling that part of oneself has died, avoidance of reminders, numbness, loneliness and a sense that life is meaningless, all lasting well beyond the period that the person's culture would expect and seriously impairing their life. It responds poorly to the standard treatments for depression, and it is not the same thing as either depression or post-traumatic stress disorder. The diagnostic systems now recognise it as prolonged grief disorder : ICD-11 (adopted in 2019) includes prolonged grief disorder, requiring that the grief persist for an atypically long period, at least six months after the loss, and clearly exceed the norms of the person's culture. DSM-5 (2013) was more cautious. It placed a similar condition, persistent complex bereavement disorder , in Section III, "Conditions for Further Study", alongside other proposals such as non-suicidal self-injury (repeatedly cutting, burning, scratching or otherwise deliberately injuring one's own body without any intent to die, usually to relieve tension or distress), internet gaming disorder (persistent, impairing loss of control over gaming) and attenuated psychosis syndrome (mild, subthreshold psychotic symptoms in a person at raised risk of psychosis). A Section III condition is a proposed criteria set offered to encourage research, not an official diagnosis. DSM-5-TR (2022) moved it into the main text as an official diagnosis, renamed prolonged grief disorder , in the chapter on trauma- and stressor-related disorders. The death must have occurred at least 12 months earlier (at least 6 months for children and adolescents), with intense yearning or preoccupation and at least three of eight further symptoms present nearly every day for at least the last month. The full criteria, and the differences from major depression and post-traumatic stress disorder, belong to the Psychiatric Disorders book. What matters here is what to do about it. Here the evidence gives a clear and perhaps surprising answer: offering counselling to everyone who is bereaved does little good. In a meta-analysis of 61 controlled studies, Joseph Currier, Robert Neimeyer and Jeffrey Berman (2008) found that universal interventions, offered to anyone who had lost someone, had no reliable effect, whereas interventions offered to people who were already struggling, especially those with complicated grief, did help. Some early bereavement interventions may even get in the way of natural recovery, just as psychological debriefing does after trauma (Section 9.7). The practical model that follows is a stepped one, set out for example in British guidance on supportive and palliative care for adults with cancer (2004): All bereaved people should receive information about grief and about the support that is available; most will cope with the help of their family, friends and community. Some will benefit from a more formal opportunity to talk about their loss, through trained volunteers, self-help groups, faith communities or bereavement services. A few, those with complicated or prolonged grief, depression or post-traumatic stress, need specialist mental health intervention. For that last group, specific treatments work. Shear and her colleagues developed complicated grief treatment , a 16-session therapy that combines elements of interpersonal psychotherapy and cognitive behavioural therapy. It works on both orientations of the dual process model: loss-focused work, including "imaginal revisiting" (telling the story of the death in detail, with exposure to its most painful moments) and imaginal conversations with the dead person; and restoration-focused work on personal goals and relationships. In a randomised trial published in 2005, 51 percent of patients responded to complicated grief treatment, against 28 percent of those given standard interpersonal psychotherapy. Interpersonal psychotherapy itself (Chapter 3) counts grief as one of its four problem areas, alongside interpersonal role disputes, role transitions and interpersonal deficits, and cognitive-behavioural treatments for prolonged grief also have good support. Specialist grief therapy of this kind is normally conducted one to one, because it must be paced to the individual's distress; groups, especially groups for people bereaved by suicide, are a valuable complement that reduces isolation and stigma. One more distinction matters after disasters. When a death is sudden, violent or witnessed (a fire, a road accident, a murder, a suicide), the bereaved may develop traumatic grief , in which the symptoms of grief are entangled with those of trauma: intrusive images of how the person died, nightmares, avoidance of reminders of the death, hypervigilance. Traumatic grief needs attention to both the trauma and the loss. But the word "may" is important. Most people bereaved in a disaster grieve normally and recover with ordinary support; Lindemann himself, whose 101 bereaved included Cocoanut Grove families, found that an uncomplicated grief reaction could ordinarily be settled in four to six weeks with eight to ten interviews. Exam trap RML 2020 asked which approach to bereavement after a crisis should not be adopted. Three options are sound: bereavement is a normal process that will usually run its course; complicated grieving requires intervention; and bereavement counselling, when it is needed, is best conducted one to one. The false one is that crisis-related bereavement should always be considered traumatic grief: most people bereaved in a crisis grieve normally, and treating all of them as traumatised wastes help and may hinder recovery. "Always" and "never" are warning words in such options. Also: persistent complex bereavement disorder was a DSM-5 Section III proposal (2013); in DSM-5-TR (2022) it became the official prolonged grief disorder (12 months; 6 months in children), while ICD-11 requires 6 months. Non-suicidal self-injury remains a Section III proposal (RML 2022). Exam trap A 2025 paper asked what interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT, Gerald Klerman and Myrna Weissman) does not typically include, offering grief and bereavement work, role conflict resolution, role transition support, and "role playing and role reversal techniques"; the key is the last. The first three are IPT's own problem areas (grief, interpersonal role disputes, role transitions; the fourth is interpersonal deficits), so the answer follows by elimination. Role reversal , in which the client acts the part of the other person, belongs to Jacob Levy Moreno's psychodrama (Chapter 7) and to Gestalt-style enactment. Do not overlearn the key, though: IPT manuals do list brief role play, rehearsing a difficult conversation with the therapist, among IPT's behaviour change techniques. What IPT lacks is psychodrama's staged enactment and role reversal. Clinical link Telling grief from depression is a daily clinical task. In grief the painful feelings come in waves, or "pangs", triggered by reminders of the dead person, and they are mixed with warm memories and even humour; self-esteem is preserved, and thoughts of death are usually about joining the person who died. In depression the low mood and loss of pleasure are pervasive, and there are feelings of worthlessness and self-loathing: Freud's contrast between the world becoming empty and the self becoming empty. DSM-5 removed the old "bereavement exclusion", so major depression can be diagnosed after a loss when its full criteria are met (details in the Psychiatric Disorders book). 9.6 Community Mental Health Lower yield · 1 Q Everything in this chapter so far has been about one person at a time: one woman with rheumatoid arthritis, one smoker, one widow. Now do some arithmetic. India has well under one psychiatrist for every lakh of its people, far fewer clinical psychologists, and most of both work in cities. Suppose every one of them saw patients for fifty hours a week, fifty weeks a year. They would still reach only a small fraction of the people who, according to the National Mental Health Survey, need care. No amount of skill in the consulting room can close a gap of that size. The American psychologist George W. Albee (1921 to 2006) liked to put the point in the language of public health: no mass disorder afflicting humankind has ever been eliminated by treating affected individuals one at a time. Cholera was beaten by clean water and sewers, not by more doctors. Community mental health is the attempt to think about mental illness in the same way, at the level of whole populations, and to move care out of the institution and into the places where people live. This section follows that idea from its history to its four big strategies: prevention, consultation, empowerment and the sharing of tasks with non-specialists, and finally to the obstacle that runs through all of them, stigma. From the asylum to the community The nineteenth century answered the problem of severe mental illness with the asylum. The reformers who built the first ones, whose moral treatment is described in Chapter 1, meant them to be small, humane retreats. They did not stay small. By the middle of the twentieth century the state mental hospitals of the United States held about 559,000 patients (the peak, reached in 1955), many of them for decades, on wards of a hundred beds or more. Britain's county asylums and India's old mental hospitals at Ranchi, Agra and elsewhere ran on the same custodial lines: patients were kept, fed and controlled, and very few went home. After the Second World War a series of critics argued that the institution itself produced some of the disability it was supposed to treat. The British psychiatrist Russell Barton described in 1959 an "institutional neurosis" of apathy, submissiveness, lack of initiative and loss of interest in the future, which he blamed not on the illness but on enforced idleness, loss of contact with the outside world and the authoritarian attitudes of staff. Two years later the Canadian-born sociologist Erving Goffman (1922 to 1982), who had spent a year doing fieldwork at St Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, published Asylums (1961). Goffman described the mental hospital as a total institution : a place, like a prison, a monastery or an army barracks, where large numbers of people sleep, work and spend their leisure in the same place, under one authority, on a fixed timetable, cut off from the wider society. On admission, he argued, the patient undergoes a "mortification of the self": personal clothes and possessions are taken away, privacy disappears and every action is supervised, until the person has learned to be the patient the institution expects. The most careful evidence came from John Wing and George Brown, whose Institutionalism and Schizophrenia (1970) followed patients in three English mental hospitals through the 1960s. The poorer the social environment of a hospital (fewer personal possessions, less contact with the outside, more hours spent doing nothing), the more its patients showed the negative symptoms of schizophrenia: social withdrawal, flat affect and poverty of speech. As the environments improved, so did the patients. Several forces then came together. The first was pharmacological. Chlorpromazine, the first antipsychotic drug, was introduced into psychiatry in Paris in 1952 by Jean Delay and Pierre Deniker and reached American hospitals in 1954; for the first time many people with psychotic illness could be helped enough to leave hospital (the drugs themselves belong to the Physiological and Disorders books). The second was the experience of the war. Military psychiatrists had found that soldiers with combat stress recovered best when they were treated quickly and close to their units rather than sent to distant hospitals, and the sheer number of psychiatric casualties had made mental health a public concern. The third was money and conscience: the hospitals were expensive, and their conditions had become a scandal. In the United States the National Mental Health Act of 1946 led to the creation of the National Institute of Mental Health, and a Joint Commission on Mental Illness and Health recommended in its report Action for Mental Health (1961) that the huge state hospitals be replaced by smaller services based in the community. The decisive step was taken by John F. Kennedy (1917 to 1963), whose sister Rosemary had an intellectual disability and had been left severely impaired by a lobotomy in 1941. On 5 February 1963 Kennedy sent Congress a special message on mental illness and mental retardation, promising that "reliance on the cold mercy of custodial isolation will be supplanted by the open warmth of community concern and capability". On 31 October 1963, a few weeks before his assassination, he signed the Mental Retardation Facilities and Community Mental Health Centers Construction Act, usually called the Community Mental Health Centers Act. This launched the community mental health movement as national policy. The Act funded the building of community mental health centres , each responsible for a defined geographical catchment area of roughly 75,000 to 200,000 people, and each expected to provide five essential services: Inpatient care, for short admissions close to the patient's home. Outpatient care, for individuals, groups and families. Partial hospitalisation, in the form of day care (and night care for people who could work during the day). Emergency services, available twenty-four hours a day. Consultation and education for the community's other agencies: schools, courts, police, clergy and family doctors. Notice the last item. The centres were meant not only to treat but to prevent, and to work through other people as well as directly with patients. Those two ideas, prevention and consultation, are the subjects of the next two subsections, and both came largely from Gerald Caplan. The policy that went with the centres was deinstitutionalisation : the systematic discharge of long-stay patients from mental hospitals into the community, together with the shrinking or closure of the hospitals themselves. In numbers it succeeded. The resident population of American state hospitals fell by about three quarters over the next three decades. In human terms the results were mixed, and the movement learned several hard lessons: The money did not follow the patients. Far fewer centres were built than had been planned, and many of those that opened drifted towards treating less disabled and more rewarding clients, leaving the discharged long-stay patients with little support. Many discharged patients relapsed, were readmitted, were discharged again and were readmitted again, a cycle known as the revolving door phenomenon. Some ended up homeless. Barlow and Durand note that about 30 percent of homeless people in the United States have a severe mental illness, although the rise in homelessness in the 1980s also had economic causes, such as unemployment and a shortage of cheap housing. Others simply moved from one institution to another: to nursing homes, boarding homes and, increasingly, jails and prisons. This is transinstitutionalisation , and the drift of untreated people into the criminal justice system is called criminalisation. Much of the burden of care moved, unpaid and unsupported, onto families. Barlow and Durand's verdict is that deinstitutionalisation is largely considered a failure: not because care in the community was a bad idea, but because the community services needed to make it work were never adequately provided. The lesson, repeated in country after country, is that closing beds is easy and building community services is hard, and that doing the first without the second harms the very people it was meant to free. Other countries ran the same experiment in their own ways. The most radical was Italy. The psychiatrist Franco Basaglia (1924 to 1980) unlocked the wards of the asylum at Gorizia in the 1960s and later dismantled the asylum at Trieste, replacing it with community mental health centres open twenty-four hours a day. His campaign led to Law 180 of 1978, often called the Basaglia Law, which stopped new admissions to Italy's psychiatric hospitals and moved inpatient care into small units in general hospitals. Trieste's network of community centres is still held up by the World Health Organization as a model of community care. India's story is different, because India never had the enormous asylum population that the West had to empty. Its problem was too little care of any kind. A handful of old mental hospitals, many in poor condition (a National Human Rights Commission review at the end of the 1990s described overcrowding, locked cells and neglect), coexisted with vast rural areas that had no mental health service at all. Families, temples, dargahs and faith healers filled the gap, sometimes with terrible results. On 6 August 2001, twenty-eight people with mental illness who were chained at a faith-healing home in Erwadi, in Tamil Nadu, burned to death when a fire broke out, because no one could free them in time. The Supreme Court took up the matter on its own motion, and the tragedy became a turning point in the regulation of such places. India's answer to the shortage of specialists was to put mental health into primary care. In the 1970s pilot projects at Raipur Rani in Haryana (run from the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, as one centre of a WHO study in several developing countries) and at Sakalwara near Bengaluru (run by NIMHANS) showed that doctors and health workers in primary health centres could be trained to recognise and treat common and severe mental disorders. That work fed into the National Mental Health Programme (1982) and the District Mental Health Programme (1996), which was modelled on a pilot in Bellary district of Karnataka. The details of these programmes, of the National Mental Health Survey (2015 to 2016) and of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, which gives every person a right to access mental health care and a right to live in the community, are set out in Chapter 1. Exam trap The Community Mental Health Centers Act was signed by Kennedy in 1963 ; its centres had five essential services (inpatient, outpatient, partial hospitalisation, 24-hour emergency, and consultation and education). Deinstitutionalisation is the discharge of hospital patients into the community; transinstitutionalisation is their movement into other institutions (nursing homes, jails) instead; the revolving door is repeated discharge and readmission. Goffman wrote Asylums ( 1961 , the total institution) and Stigma ( 1963 ); do not swap them. Italy's Law 180 (1978) is the Basaglia law. Prevention: from three levels to three targets Public health measures disease in two ways, and you need both terms before prevention makes sense. Incidence is the number of new cases of a disorder that arise in a population during a given period, usually a year. Prevalence is the total number of cases, old and new, present in the population at a given time. Picture a bathtub. Incidence is the water flowing in from the tap; prevalence is the water in the tub. You can lower the level in the tub by turning down the tap (fewer new cases) or by opening the drain (shorter illnesses, through earlier and better treatment). In the 1950s two American professors of preventive medicine, Hugh R. Leavell and E. Gurney Clark , organised the work of public health into "levels of prevention" that ran from health promotion and specific protection (immunisation is the classic example) through early diagnosis and prompt treatment to the limitation of disability and rehabilitation, grouped into primary, secondary and tertiary prevention. Gerald Caplan (1917 to 2008), the psychiatrist whom you met in the chapter's opening story working with Erich Lindemann, carried the scheme into mental health in Principles of Preventive Psychiatry (1964), the book that made prevention part of the everyday vocabulary of psychiatry and psychology. Caplan's three levels are defined by what they reduce (Table 9.7): Primary prevention aims to reduce the incidence of a disorder: to stop new cases arising at all, by counteracting harmful circumstances before they have had a chance to produce illness. Caplan argued that people need a steady flow of three kinds of "supplies" to stay mentally healthy: physical supplies (food, shelter, sensory stimulation, protection from injury), psychosocial supplies (love, recognition and interaction with the significant people in one's life) and sociocultural supplies (the customs, values and social structures that give a person a place in society). Primary prevention protects those supplies and helps people through the crises that threaten them, which is why crisis intervention (Section 9.7) began as a preventive strategy. Secondary prevention aims to reduce the prevalence of a disorder by shortening its duration, through early case finding, screening, prompt diagnosis and effective treatment. Tertiary prevention aims to reduce the disability that an established disorder leaves behind, and the risk of relapse, through rehabilitation (Sections 9.8 and 9.9). Level Aim Who receives it Mental health examples Physical health examples Primary Lower incidence (fewer new cases) People who do not have the disorder Parenting programmes, life-skills education, iodised salt and rubella vaccination (against intellectual disability), crisis help Vaccination, helmets, clean water Secondary Lower prevalence by shortening duration People with an early or undetected disorder Screening for postnatal depression, early intervention in psychosis, newborn screening for phenylketonuria Cancer screening, blood pressure checks Tertiary Less disability and relapse People with an established disorder Psychosocial and vocational rehabilitation, relapse prevention Cardiac rehabilitation, physiotherapy after a stroke Apply the scheme and most exam questions on it answer themselves. Promoting vaccination to prevent a disease is primary prevention, because it acts on healthy people before the disease exists. Treating a diagnosed illness is secondary prevention (or simply treatment). Rehabilitation after an injury, or surgery to limit the damage of a chronic disease, deals with a condition that is already established, which is tertiary territory. Newborn screening for phenylketonuria is a neat secondary-prevention example from mental health: the metabolic disorder is detected in the first days of life, before any damage is done, and a special diet prevents the intellectual disability that would otherwise follow. Public health textbooks add a further level, primordial prevention , a term introduced by the WHO cardiologist Tomas Strasser in 1978, which goes back one step more and tries to stop the risk factors themselves from appearing in a population: keeping children from ever starting to use tobacco, or building towns in which walking to school is safe. Caplan's scheme had a weakness that critics soon pointed out. Only primary prevention is prevention in the everyday sense. Secondary prevention is really early treatment, and tertiary prevention is rehabilitation; calling them prevention stretches the word until almost everything a mental health service does counts as preventive. In 1983 the American public health physician Robert S. Gordon proposed a different classification, based not on the stage of the disorder but on who receives the intervention. This matters, he argued, because every intervention has costs and risks, and those must be weighed against the risk of the disorder in the people who receive it. In the United States the Institute of Medicine (IOM) adopted Gordon's terms in its 1994 report Reducing Risks for Mental Disorders , edited by Patricia Mrazek and Robert Haggerty, and reserved the word prevention for interventions delivered before a disorder begins: Universal prevention is aimed at a whole population, or a whole group such as every child in a school, chosen without regard to individual risk. It must therefore be cheap, safe and acceptable to everyone. Examples are school-based life-skills education (the World Health Organization's programme lists ten core life skills: decision making, problem solving, creative thinking, critical thinking, effective communication, interpersonal relationship skills, self-awareness, empathy, coping with emotions and coping with stress), anti-bullying programmes and laws restricting access to lethal pesticides. Selective prevention is aimed at subgroups whose risk is higher than average because of a known biological, psychological or social risk factor, although the individuals in them show no symptoms: children of parents with depression or alcohol dependence, bereaved children, refugees, or young first-time mothers living in poverty who receive regular home visits from a nurse. Indicated prevention is aimed at high-risk individuals who already show minimal but detectable signs or symptoms foreshadowing a disorder, but who do not yet meet diagnostic criteria. Brief cognitive behavioural programmes for adolescents with mild depressive symptoms are one example; monitoring and support for young people at "clinical high risk" of psychosis, whose attenuated symptoms DSM-5 placed as a proposal in its Section III (attenuated psychosis syndrome), are another. The IOM report placed prevention at the start of a wider mental health intervention spectrum , followed by treatment (case identification and standard treatment for known disorders) and maintenance (support for long-term treatment and aftercare, including rehabilitation). Figure 9.4 shows how the old and new vocabularies line up. Roughly, Caplan's primary prevention became the three IOM types of prevention, his secondary prevention became treatment, and his tertiary prevention became maintenance.
