Caplan's primary prevention corresponds to the three IOM types of prevention, all delivered before a disorder begins; his secondary and tertiary prevention correspond to the IOM's treatment and maintenance. Prevention aims to reduce disorder. A related but distinct goal is mental health promotion , which aims to increase positive mental health in everyone, whether or not they are at risk. The World Health Organization (2004) defines mental health as "a state of well-being in which the individual realizes his or her own abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and fruitfully, and is able to make a contribution to his or her community", and promotion works on the conditions that make this possible: secure early childhoods, good schools, decent work, safe neighbourhoods, social inclusion. Albee summarised the logic of both prevention and promotion in a well-known formula. The incidence of disorder, he wrote, rises with organic factors and stress (and, in later versions, exploitation), and falls with coping skills, self-esteem and support groups. A preventive programme can therefore work on either side of the fraction: reduce the stresses and injustices in the numerator, or strengthen the competence and support in the denominator. Why spend money on everyone when only a few will ever become ill? The British epidemiologist Geoffrey Rose (1926 to 1993) answered with the prevention paradox (1981): a preventive measure that brings large benefits to the community offers little to each participating individual. Because most people are at modest risk, the many people at small risk produce more cases of a disease than the few at high risk, so shifting the whole population a little towards safety prevents more cases than treating the high-risk minority intensively. The paradox has a cost. The benefit to any one person of a universal programme is so small that its effects are hard to detect, and universal programmes in mental health often show small effects or none; Barlow and Durand note, for example, that school curricula on suicide aimed at all students have generally not been shown to work, whereas programmes targeted at people at risk do better (Section 9.7). Good prevention planning combines both: universal measures that are cheap and safe, and selective and indicated measures for those who need more. Exam trap Primary prevention acts before a disorder exists and lowers incidence : promoting vaccination is the classic answer (JEMAS 2025). Secondary prevention is early detection and treatment and lowers prevalence ; treating a diagnosed illness belongs here. Tertiary prevention is rehabilitation and limiting disability; rehabilitation after injury belongs here. The three-level scheme comes from public health ( Leavell and Clark ) and was brought into psychiatry by Caplan (1964) . Universal, selective, indicated is Gordon (1983) , adopted by the IOM (1994) ; indicated prevention is for people with early symptoms who do not yet meet criteria, so it is still prevention, not treatment. Incidence counts new cases; prevalence counts all existing cases. Mental health consultation In 1949, a few years before he joined Lindemann in Boston, Caplan was working in Jerusalem, where a small team of mental health workers was responsible for many thousands of immigrant children living in residential institutions. Children were referred faster than they could possibly be seen. Caplan noticed something about the referrals: often the problem lay less in the child than in the way the institution's caretakers understood the child. So instead of treating children, his team began to discuss them with the caretakers. Each such discussion helped not only that child but every child the caretaker would look after in the future. Out of this experience came mental health consultation , which Caplan described fully in The Theory and Practice of Mental Health Consultation (1970). Caplan defined consultation as an interaction between two professionals: the consultant , a specialist, and the consultee , a professional in another field (a teacher, a nurse, a general practitioner, a police officer, a priest) who asks for help with a current work problem that the consultee has decided lies within the consultant's competence. Several features set it apart from other kinds of professional help: The relationship is coordinate, not hierarchical. The consultant has no administrative authority over the consultee, and the consultee is free to accept or reject the consultant's suggestions. Professional responsibility for the client stays with the consultee. The consultant does not take over the case. The focus is the work problem, not the consultee's personal life. If the consultee's own feelings are getting in the way, the consultant works on them indirectly, through discussion of the case, and does not turn the meeting into psychotherapy. The aim is twofold: to help with the current case and to increase the consultee's ability to handle similar cases in the future without help. Because one consultee may deal with hundreds of clients, consultation multiplies the reach of a scarce specialist, which is why Caplan saw it as a tool of primary prevention. These features distinguish consultation from supervision , in which a senior member of the same profession has authority over the supervisee, evaluates his work and shares responsibility for his cases; from psychotherapy , whose subject is the client's own problems; from education , which follows a curriculum rather than the consultee's current problem; and from collaboration , in which the specialist joins the team and shares responsibility for the outcome, a model that Caplan and Ruth B. Caplan described in 1993 as an alternative for settings such as hospitals and schools where a mental health specialist works on site. Caplan divided consultation into four types (Table 9.8), according to whether the focus is a particular case or an administrative programme, and whether the main target is the client (or programme) or the consultee. Follow one school through all four. Ms Rekha teaches Class 6 in a government school in Mysuru. One of her pupils, eleven-year-old Divya, has become silent, tearful and inattentive since her father died three months ago, and Ms Rekha is convinced that the girl will fail her examinations and drop out. She asks the psychologist who visits the school every fortnight for help. In client-centred case consultation , the psychologist assesses Divya herself, perhaps with an interview and a few tests, and gives the teacher an expert opinion and specific recommendations for managing her. The main goal is to help this child; anything the teacher learns is a bonus. In consultee-centred case consultation , the focus moves to the teacher's difficulty in handling the case. Caplan listed four reasons why a consultee may struggle: lack of knowledge (Ms Rekha does not know how grief shows itself in children), lack of skill (she knows but does not know how to talk with a grieving child), lack of self-confidence (she is newly appointed and doubts herself) and lack of professional objectivity , when the consultee's own feelings or experiences distort her view of the client. The main goal is to improve the consultee's work with this and future cases. In programme-centred administrative consultation , the headmaster asks the psychologist to help design a school programme for children who have been bereaved or are in distress: how to identify them, what the teachers should do, when to refer. The focus is the programme. In consultee-centred administrative consultation , the focus is the difficulties that the administrators themselves have in running the school's programmes: poor communication between staff and management, weak leadership, conflict between departments. The consultant works with the organisation's people rather than on a specific plan. Caplan's most original idea concerns the fourth reason for difficulty, lack of objectivity, and especially the form he called theme interference . Suppose Ms Rekha lost her own father as a child and grew up being told that a fatherless girl would never amount to anything. That unresolved theme now takes the form of a hidden syllogism: an "initial category" (a girl whose father has died) leads to an "inevitable outcome" (she will fail). Divya fits the category, so the teacher sees the outcome as certain and, without meaning to, gives up on her. Caplan's advice was not to interpret the teacher's past to her, which would turn consultation into therapy and offend her, but to reduce the theme interference indirectly: by examining Divya's case carefully with the teacher until it becomes clear that, for this girl, the outcome is not inevitable at all. The teacher's fear is disconfirmed in the case, and her objectivity returns. Table 9.8 Caplan's four types of mental health consultation (1970). Type Focus Main goal Example in a school Client-centred case A particular client Expert assessment and advice for that client Psychologist assesses the grieving pupil and advises the teacher Consultee-centred case The consultee's handling of a case Remedy the consultee's lack of knowledge, skill, confidence or objectivity Psychologist helps the teacher whose fears about the pupil are distorting her view Programme-centred administrative A programme or policy Help plan or improve the programme Designing a school programme for distressed children Consultee-centred administrative The administrators' own difficulties Improve their functioning as planners and leaders Working on communication and leadership problems among the school's staff Caplan's model is psychodynamic in flavour, and other approaches followed. In behavioural consultation , set out by John Bergan in 1977 and widely used by school psychologists, the consultant guides the teacher through four stages, problem identification, problem analysis, plan implementation and problem evaluation, using the methods of applied behaviour analysis (Chapter 4). In process consultation , described by the organisational psychologist Edgar Schein in 1969, the consultant helps an organisation to see and improve its own processes (communication, decision making, roles) rather than supplying an expert answer. In general hospitals, consultation-liaison work brings psychologists and psychiatrists onto medical wards to advise on patients' psychological problems, the hospital face of the health psychology described in Sections 9.1 to 9.5. Exam trap Caplan's four types, in order: client-centred case , consultee-centred case , programme-centred administrative and consultee-centred administrative . The consultee-centred case type is the most characteristically Caplanian, with its four "lacks" (knowledge, skill, self-confidence, objectivity) and theme interference . In consultation the consultee keeps responsibility for the client and is free to reject the advice; a question that gives the consultant authority over the consultee is describing supervision. Caplan's 1964 book is on prevention; his 1970 book is on consultation. Community psychology and empowerment The new community mental health centres needed psychologists, and in May 1965 a group of American psychologists met at Swampscott, Massachusetts, for a conference on how to train them. They came away dissatisfied with the idea that psychologists should simply do traditional clinical work in a new building. They wanted a new field, which they named community psychology : the study of how individuals are shaped by, and can shape, their social systems, with the community rather than the individual as the main level of analysis and intervention. The Swampscott participants described the community psychologist as a "participant-conceptualiser", someone who works inside the community and also studies it. The field's core values are still those set out in its early years: prevention rather than treatment; strengths and competence rather than deficits; an ecological view of people in their settings; respect for diversity; collaboration with communities rather than doing things to them; citizen participation; and social justice. The ecological view came largely from James G. Kelly , who in 1966 borrowed four principles from biology to describe how human settings work. Interdependence : a change in one part of a social system (a new principal, a factory closure) ripples through all the others. Cycling of resources : every setting has resources (people's talents, time, money, goodwill) that can be identified and used. Adaptation : people adapt to the demands of their settings, and settings change people. Succession : settings change over time, so an intervention must fit the history of the place. A second key idea came from Seymour B. Sarason (1919 to 2010), who in 1974 argued that the psychological sense of community , the feeling of belonging to a network of mutual support that one can depend on, should be the central concept of the field. David W. McMillan and David M. Chavis (1986) later broke the sense of community into four elements: membership (the feeling of belonging), influence (mattering to the group, and the group mattering to you), integration and fulfilment of needs (being rewarded by membership) and shared emotional connection (a shared history, places and experiences). Community psychology also asked uncomfortable questions about where problems are located. In Blaming the Victim (1971) the psychologist William Ryan showed how social problems such as poverty, poor schooling and ill health are routinely explained by the supposed defects of the people who suffer from them (their attitudes, their culture, their families) rather than by the conditions that produce them. This kind of victim blaming leads naturally to programmes that try to fix individuals and leave the conditions alone. A clinical psychologist who treats one farmer's depression after crop failure, while ignoring the debt trap that is producing depression in the whole village, is in danger of doing exactly this. The most influential answer came from Julian Rappaport . In a 1981 paper titled "In praise of paradox: A social policy of empowerment over prevention", Rappaport argued that even prevention could be paternalistic: experts decide what people need and deliver it to them, treating them like children. The opposite, an advocacy model that defends people's rights, treats them as citizens but may leave their needs unmet. Rappaport's resolution of this paradox was empowerment , which he later (1987) defined as "a process: the mechanism by which people, organizations, and communities gain mastery over their affairs". Empowerment treats people as complete human beings with both rights and needs, and as the experts on their own lives. The professional's role changes from expert provider to collaborator and resource. Marc A. Zimmerman (1995) separated three components of psychological empowerment: an intrapersonal component (perceived control and self-efficacy in a domain of life), an interactional component (a critical understanding of one's social environment, the resources available and how to use them) and a behavioural component (actually taking part in actions that change one's situation, such as joining an organisation). Empowerment has roots outside psychology too. The Brazilian educator Paulo Freire (1921 to 1997), in Pedagogy of the Oppressed (written in Portuguese in 1968, first published in English in 1970), described conscientisation: the process by which poor and oppressed people, through dialogue, come to understand the social causes of their situation and to act on them. In mental health, empowerment takes several concrete forms. Self-help and mutual-help groups, from Alcoholics Anonymous (founded in 1935) to groups of people who hear voices and associations of family carers, let people with an experience help one another without professional control. The user and survivor movement demands a say in how services are run. Peer support workers, themselves in recovery, are employed in services. And law can empower: the advance directives and nominated representatives of India's Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Chapter 1) are attempts to keep decisions in the hands of the person with the illness, even when they are unwell. Exam trap Empowerment is Rappaport 's (1981, "empowerment over prevention"; defined in 1987), not Caplan's. Community psychology was named at the Swampscott Conference (1965) . The psychological sense of community is Sarason 's concept (1974); its four elements (membership, influence, integration and fulfilment of needs, shared emotional connection) are McMillan and Chavis (1986). Blaming the victim is William Ryan (1971). Kelly's ecological principles are interdependence, cycling of resources, adaptation and succession. Task-shifting and lay counsellors The treatment gap is the proportion of people with a disorder who need treatment but do not receive it. In a much-cited review of studies from many countries, Robert Kohn, Shekhar Saxena, Itzhak Levav and Benedetto Saraceno (2004) found that the gap was large everywhere and largest in low-income countries; in India the National Mental Health Survey (Chapter 1) put it at between about 70 and 92 percent for different disorders. The obvious solution, training more specialists, would take generations. As early as 1975 a WHO expert committee recommended that basic mental health care be integrated into primary health care and delivered by non-specialist health workers, and the Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978, with its call for primary health care for all, strengthened the case. The Indian pilot projects of the 1970s described in Section 9.6.1 were early tests of the idea. The strategy now has a name. Task-shifting , defined in WHO guidelines of 2008, is the rational redistribution of tasks from highly qualified health workers to workers with shorter training, so that scarce specialists are used where only they can help. Because the specialists do not disappear but move into training and supervising the non-specialists, many writers now prefer the term task-sharing . In the same year the WHO launched its Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP), and its Intervention Guide (2010) gave non-specialist health workers simple protocols for the priority conditions: depression, psychosis, epilepsy, dementia, alcohol and drug use, child and adolescent disorders, and self-harm and suicide. The most important question was whether people with no formal mental health training could deliver psychological treatments, not just medicines. A series of trials, several of them in India, answered it. The central figure is the Indian psychiatrist Vikram Patel (born 1964). In 1996 he co-founded Sangath, a non-governmental organisation in Goa, and his manual Where There Is No Psychiatrist (2003) was written for community health workers. With colleagues at Sangath he designed brief psychological treatments that could be delivered by a lay health counsellor : a local person, often a woman with a school or college education, selected for her interpersonal skills, trained for a few weeks and closely supervised. Key study: the MANAS trial in Goa (2010) Could lay counsellors improve the outcome of common mental disorders (depression and anxiety) in ordinary primary care? Patel and his colleagues added a lay health counsellor to 12 of 24 primary care clinics in Goa, half of them government health centres and half private general practices; the other 12 gave enhanced usual care, and 2,796 adult patients with common mental disorders took part. (MANAS, from the Konkani for "project to promote mental health", also means "mind".) The counsellors screened patients, gave psychoeducation, delivered a brief psychological treatment based on interpersonal psychotherapy, supported adherence to antidepressants prescribed by the clinic doctor and referred severe cases to a visiting specialist, a model of collaborative stepped care. In the government health centres the results were striking: at six months about two thirds of the intervention patients had recovered, against about two fifths of those in enhanced usual care, and suicide attempts and plans were also reduced. In the private clinics there was no benefit, probably because their patients did well even with usual care. The conclusion was that lay counsellors could deliver effective care where public services are thinnest; the criticism was that the treatment was a package, so it was hard to know which ingredient did the work. The next step was to test specific, manualised psychological treatments. In the PREMIUM programme Sangath developed two such treatments and tested them in Goa, with results published in 2017. The Healthy Activity Program , a brief form of behavioural activation (Chapter 4) delivered by lay counsellors in six to eight sessions, produced significantly more remission from moderately severe to severe depression than enhanced usual care. Counselling for Alcohol Problems , a brief treatment built on motivational interviewing (Chapter 6), was tested in men with harmful drinking and also improved outcomes. The PRIDE programme (PRemIum for aDolEscents) carried the approach into secondary schools in New Delhi and Goa. Its first step, a brief problem-solving intervention delivered by lay counsellors with the help of printed booklets, reduced the severity of psychosocial problems among distressed students in a randomised trial published in 2020. Patel summed up the lessons of this work in the acronym SUNDAR (Hindi for "beautiful"): Simplify the message (avoid jargon), UNpack the treatment into simple components, Deliver it where people are (at home, in the community), use Affordable and available human resources (lay health workers), and Reallocate specialists to training and supervision. Key study: the Friendship Bench in Zimbabwe (2016) In the early 2000s Dixon Chibanda was one of only a handful of psychiatrists in Zimbabwe, a country of more than twelve million people. After one of his patients, who could not afford the bus fare to his hospital, took her own life, he began to look for a way to bring help to people where they lived. In 2006 he trained older women who already worked as community health volunteers in Harare (the "grandmothers") to deliver a simple form of problem-solving therapy, on wooden benches placed in the grounds of primary care clinics. The therapy used Shona ideas: people describe kufungisisa , "thinking too much", and the sessions move through kuvhura pfungwa (opening up the mind), kusimudzira (uplifting) and kusimbisa (strengthening). In a cluster randomised trial in 24 clinics, published in JAMA in 2016, 573 adults with common mental disorders received either six sessions on the Friendship Bench or enhanced usual care. After six months the Friendship Bench group had markedly fewer symptoms of common mental disorders, including depression. The model has since spread to other countries, and it is the best-known example of how lay workers, embedded in their own culture and supervised by professionals, can close part of the treatment gap. A third landmark came from Pakistan. In the Thinking Healthy Programme , Atif Rahman and his colleagues (2008) trained lady health workers, the government's village-based community health workers, to deliver a cognitive behavioural intervention for depressed pregnant women and new mothers in rural Rawalpindi, woven into their routine home visits. Six months after the birth, 23 percent of the mothers in the intervention group were depressed, against 53 percent in the control group. WHO later adopted the programme as one of its scalable psychological interventions. Why do these programmes work, and where do they fail? The successful ones share several ingredients. The counsellors are carefully selected for warmth and good judgement, not just qualifications. The treatments are short, structured and built on a few common elements of evidence-based therapy (psychoeducation, behavioural activation, problem solving, motivational interviewing). Training is competence-based, and supervision, usually in peer groups led by a specialist, never stops. There is a clear stepped-care pathway, so that people who do not improve, or who are at risk of suicide, are referred up to specialists. The difficulties are equally clear: supervision is expensive and easily cut when money is short, counsellors leave, quality drifts when a trial becomes a routine programme, and lay counsellors cannot manage severe or complicated illness. Task-sharing extends specialist care; it does not replace it. Indian context India already has a huge non-specialist health workforce. The Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), village women appointed under the National Rural Health Mission (2005), are increasingly trained to identify common and severe mental disorders and to refer and follow up patients, and the Health and Wellness Centres of the Ayushman Bharat scheme (2018) include mental health in the services they provide. Community programmes such as Atmiyata in Gujarat's Mehsana district train village volunteers to offer basic counselling and to link distressed people to welfare benefits and to care. Tele-MANAS, the national tele-mental health helpline launched in 2022, adds a telephone layer to the same stepped system (Section 9.7). Exam trap Match the programme to its place and person. The Friendship Bench : Zimbabwe, Dixon Chibanda , grandmothers delivering problem-solving therapy (trial 2016). MANAS : Goa, Vikram Patel , lay counsellors in primary care (2010). PREMIUM : Goa, the Healthy Activity Program for depression and Counselling for Alcohol Problems (2017). PRIDE : adolescents in schools in Delhi and Goa. Thinking Healthy : Pakistan, Atif Rahman , perinatal depression (2008). mhGAP is the WHO's programme (2008). "Task-sharing" is now preferred to "task-shifting" because specialists stay involved as trainers and supervisors. Stigma and anti-stigma work Imagine two job applicants with the same qualifications. One mentions that he had typhoid last year; the other mentions that he spent a month in hospital with depression. Most people know at once which one is less likely to get the job, and that knowledge is the subject of this subsection. Goffman, whose Asylums you met in Section 9.6.1, followed it with Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity (1963). Stigma , in Goffman's words, is "an attribute that is deeply discrediting", which reduces the bearer "from a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one". He described three kinds: abominations of the body (physical deformities), blemishes of individual character (among which he listed mental disorder, imprisonment, addiction and unemployment) and tribal stigma (of race, nation or religion). He also noticed that stigma spreads to the people around the stigmatised person, which he called courtesy stigma and which is now often called associative or family stigma. In India it is the reason a family may hide a son's schizophrenia for fear that his sisters will not find husbands. Later researchers took stigma apart. The sociologists Bruce G. Link and Jo C. Phelan (2001) described it as the coming together of several components: people label a human difference ("mentally ill"); the label is linked to negative stereotypes ("dangerous", "unpredictable", "weak"); the labelled people are separated into a "them" distinct from "us"; they suffer status loss and discrimination ; and the whole process depends on unequal power , because only groups with social, economic and political power can make their labels stick. The British psychiatrist Graham Thornicroft offered a simpler three-part scheme that is useful for planning interventions: stigma involves problems of knowledge (ignorance), problems of attitudes (prejudice) and problems of behaviour (discrimination). Each needs a different remedy: information for ignorance, contact and persuasion for prejudice, and law and policy for discrimination. The American psychologist Patrick W. Corrigan distinguished the levels at which stigma operates: Public stigma is the prejudice and discrimination of the general population towards people with mental illness: the landlord who will not rent, the employer who will not hire, the neighbour who keeps her children away. Self-stigma occurs when people with mental illness turn the public stereotypes on themselves. Corrigan described it as a progression: the person becomes aware of the stereotype, agrees with it, applies it to himself ("I am mentally ill, so I must be weak and incompetent") and suffers the harm of lowered self-esteem and self-efficacy. The result is what Corrigan called the "why try" effect: "Why try to get a job? Someone like me could not hold one." Structural stigma lies in the rules, policies and practices of institutions: lower spending on mental than on physical health, insurance that excludes mental illness, laws that bar people with mental illness from certain roles. Stigma matters clinically because it keeps people away from care. Label avoidance , the decision not to seek treatment so as not to be labelled, is one of the main reasons for the treatment gap described in Section 9.6.5. In many Indian families the first help sought is from a faith healer or a temple, partly because such help carries no psychiatric label, and illnesses are often described in bodily terms ("weakness", "tension", "gas") that are less shameful than "mental". What reduces stigma? Corrigan and David Penn (1999) grouped anti-stigma strategies into three kinds (Table 9.9). Protest objects to stigmatising images, for example in films and newspapers. It can stop a particular offensive advertisement, but as a way of changing attitudes it tends to fail and may even backfire, because telling people not to think something can make the thought stronger. Education replaces myths with facts (most people with mental illness are not violent; mental illnesses are common and treatable). Contact brings members of the public into direct interaction with people who have lived experience of mental illness, ideally as equals, telling their own stories of illness and recovery. In a meta-analysis of outcome studies from many countries, Corrigan and his colleagues (2012) found that both education and contact reduced stigma, but that contact was the more effective for adults, whereas education did better with adolescents. Social psychology explains why contact works: the contact hypothesis (taught in the Social book) predicts that personal acquaintance under favourable conditions breaks down stereotypes better than any amount of information. Table 9.9 Three strategies against stigma (Corrigan and Penn, 1999). Strategy What it does Example Evidence Protest Objects to stigmatising messages Complaining about a film that shows a "psycho killer" May stop a message; weak or rebound effect on attitudes Education Replaces myths with facts School talks, leaflets, media campaigns Modest, short-term change; works better for adolescents Contact Personal interaction with people with lived experience A person in recovery speaking to police or medical students Most effective for adults Large campaigns have combined all three. The World Psychiatric Association's "Open the Doors" programme against the stigma of schizophrenia (from 1996) ran in many countries. England's Time to Change campaign (2009 to 2021), built around social contact, was followed by modest but measurable improvements in public attitudes. In India the Live Love Laugh Foundation, set up by the actor Deepika Padukone in 2015 after she spoke publicly about her own depression, is the best-known effort, and the public disclosures of well-known people have done much to make talking about mental illness acceptable. Several other measures help: responsible media reporting (using "a person with schizophrenia" rather than "a schizophrenic", and never using psychiatric words as insults), training for health workers, police and teachers, and legal protection against discrimination, such as the rights to equality and confidentiality in the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Chapter 1). The most powerful single influence may be the quality of mental health care itself: when people see others getting better in ordinary clinics close to home, mental illness begins to look like any other illness. Exam trap Goffman's Stigma (1963) : "deeply discrediting" attribute, "spoiled identity", three types (abominations of the body, blemishes of character, tribal stigma) and courtesy stigma (stigma of the family and associates). Link and Phelan (2001) : labelling, stereotyping, separation, status loss and discrimination, power. Thornicroft : ignorance, prejudice, discrimination. Self-stigma (internalised) is not the same as public stigma ; the "why try" effect is self-stigma. Of the three strategies, contact works best for adults, education for adolescents, and protest can backfire. 9.7 Crisis Intervention Medium yield · 3 Qs It is two in the morning in a college hostel in Mysuru. Arjun, a twenty-year-old engineering student, has just seen his results: he has failed three of his six papers. A week ago the girl he hoped to marry told him it was over. His father, a bus conductor who borrowed money to pay the fees, telephones every evening to ask how the studies are going. Arjun has not slept properly for days, he has told nobody, and tonight he has sent his closest friend a message that says only "I can't do this any more. Sorry for everything." Nothing in his history suggests a psychiatric disorder; until a month ago he was a cheerful, ordinary student. What he is in now is a crisis, and what happens in the next few hours and weeks may decide whether he comes out of it stronger, the same, or not at all. This section is about what a crisis is and what helpers can do in one, from a single conversation with a frightened student to the care of a whole town after a disaster. What a crisis is Crisis theory began with the observations described in this chapter's opening story. Lindemann (1944) noticed that the survivors and the bereaved of the Cocoanut Grove fire went through a recognisable sequence of reactions, that most came through it within weeks, and that those who were going wrong could be helped by a few well-timed conversations. Caplan, working with Lindemann on the Wellesley project and at Harvard, turned these observations into crisis theory . He started from the idea of homeostasis. Each of us normally lives in a state of emotional equilibrium, kept steady by habitual ways of solving problems. In his best-known definition (1961), "people are in a state of crisis when they face an obstacle to important life goals that is, for a time, insurmountable through the utilization of customary methods of problem solving". A period of disorganisation and upset follows, in which the person tries many solutions that do not work, and eventually some kind of adaptation is reached, which may or may not be in the person's best interests. Four features of a crisis follow from this definition, and they shape everything that crisis workers do: A crisis is the person's reaction to an event, not the event itself. The same failed examination is a disappointment for one student and a crisis for another; what decides the matter is how the event is perceived and what coping resources are available. A crisis is not an illness. Healthy, well-adjusted people have crises, and the reactions in a crisis (anxiety, confusion, sleeplessness, tearfulness, a narrowing of attention onto the problem) are normal responses to an abnormal load. A crisis is self-limiting. Caplan observed that the acute state usually resolves within about four to six weeks, one way or another, because nobody can stay in such disequilibrium for long. A crisis is a turning point. The person may emerge with better coping than before, with the same coping, or with worse: a lasting disorder, a damaging habit such as heavy drinking, a broken relationship or a suicide attempt. And because old habits have failed and defences are loosened, people in crisis are unusually open to help. The social worker Lydia Rapoport put this in a sentence that crisis workers still learn: "a little help, rationally directed and purposefully focused at a strategic time, is more effective than more extensive help given at a period of less emotional accessibility". Caplan (1964) described four phases through which a crisis develops. In the first, the stressor raises the person's tension, and he tries his habitual ways of solving problems. In the second, those ways fail; tension rises further, and the person feels upset, ineffective and disorganised, and tries one thing after another. In the third, the rising tension mobilises emergency resources: the person may find a new way of solving the problem, redefine it, ask for help or give up an unattainable goal, and many crises are resolved here. If they are not, the fourth phase arrives: tension reaches a breaking point and there is major disorganisation, with severe distress and sometimes a psychiatric disorder or self-harm. Arjun, sending his message at two in the morning, is somewhere between the third and fourth phases. Why does one person tip into crisis when another, facing the same event, does not? The American nurses Donna C. Aguilera and Janice M. Messick , in their textbook Crisis Intervention: Theory and Methodology , gave the most widely taught answer. A stressful event upsets equilibrium and creates a need to restore it. Whether equilibrium is restored depends on three balancing factors : a realistic perception of the event , adequate situational support (people who can be relied on to help) and adequate coping mechanisms (ways of reducing tension that have worked before). If all three are present, the problem is solved and there is no crisis; if one or more is missing, disequilibrium continues and a crisis follows (Figure 9.5). The model tells the crisis worker exactly where to look. Arjun perceives his results as the end of his life (a distorted perception, since supplementary examinations exist), he has told no one (no situational support), and his usual way of coping, working harder, is no longer available. All three balancing factors are missing. Stressful event Disequilibrium need to restore balance Balancing factors present One or more factors absent Realistic perception of the event Adequate situational support Adequate coping mechanisms Distorted perception of the event Inadequate situational support Inadequate coping mechanisms Problem resolved Problem unresolved Equilibrium regained no crisis Disequilibrium continues crisis Figure 9.5 Aguilera and Messick's balancing factors. The event is the same on both sides; what differs is perception, support and coping, which are therefore the three targets of crisis intervention. The family sociologist Reuben Hill (1958) had proposed the same logic for families in his ABC-X model : A, the stressor event, interacting with B, the family's resources for meeting it, and C, the meaning the family gives to the event, produces X, the crisis. In both models the event alone never explains the crisis. Textbooks often add that the Chinese word for crisis combines the characters for "danger" and "opportunity"; linguists point out that this is a popular misreading of the second character, but the idea it is used to illustrate, that a crisis is a turning point and not only a catastrophe, is sound. Three neighbouring terms need to be kept apart. A psychiatric emergency is a situation that demands immediate action to prevent death or serious harm: an overdose, a violent patient, a person standing on a bridge. Some crises are emergencies; most are not. Stress is a continuing demand that the person may be coping with, well or badly; a crisis is the acute point at which coping breaks down. A traumatic event involves actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence; it may cause a crisis, but many crises (a failed examination, a broken engagement, a child leaving home) involve no trauma at all. And recall from Section 9.5 that Moos and Tsu (1977) described the diagnosis of a serious physical illness as a crisis in exactly this sense, which is why their adaptive tasks read like a list of balancing factors. Exam trap Lindemann (1944) made the founding observations on grief after the Cocoanut Grove fire; Caplan (1961, 1964) built crisis theory, with its homeostatic view, four phases and the rule that a crisis resolves within about four to six weeks . A crisis is defined by the person's perception and coping , not by the size of the event, and it is not a mental illness . The three balancing factors (perception, situational support, coping mechanisms) are Aguilera and Messick 's; the ABC-X model of family crisis is Reuben Hill 's. Kinds of crisis Caplan distinguished two broad kinds. A developmental crisis (also called a maturational or normative crisis) arises at the predictable transitions of the life cycle, when old ways of living no longer fit the new stage: starting school, puberty, leaving home for a hostel, marriage (for many Indian brides, moving into a husband's joint family), the birth of the first child, children leaving home, retirement. Developmental crises are the ones that Erik H. Erikson (1902 to 1994) placed at the heart of his psychosocial stages (Chapter 3). A situational crisis (Caplan's accidental crisis) is triggered by sudden, unexpected and usually unwanted events: a road accident, a sudden death, the loss of a job, a failed examination, a diagnosis of cancer, a rape, a divorce, a house fire. The American counsellors Richard K. James and Burl E. Gilliland , whose textbook Crisis Intervention Strategies is widely used, added two more (Table 9.10). Table 9.10 Four kinds of crisis (Caplan; James and Gilliland). Kind Arises from Predictable? Examples Developmental (maturational) Normal transitions of the life cycle Yes Leaving home, marriage, first child, retirement Situational (accidental) Sudden, unexpected events No Accident, sudden death, job loss, assault, failing an examination Existential Inner conflict over purpose, freedom, responsibility and meaning Often gradual Realising at fifty that one's life's work was meaningless; loss of faith Ecosystemic (environmental) Natural or human-made disaster affecting a whole community No Flood, cyclone, earthquake, epidemic, war, industrial disaster A finer classification, ordered by how much psychopathology is involved, was proposed by Bruce A. Baldwin in 1978. His six classes run from the least to the most severe: Dispositional crises : problems of a practical kind, such as a lack of information or of a service, which need information, advice or referral. Crises of anticipated life transitions : normal, expected changes over which the person may have little control, such as a planned move or retirement. Crises resulting from traumatic stress : sudden, unexpected events imposed from outside, such as an assault or the sudden death of a spouse. Maturational or developmental crises : struggles over recurring developmental issues such as dependence, intimacy, identity or power, which keep coming back at new life stages. Crises reflecting psychopathology : crises in which an existing disorder (a personality disorder, a psychosis) has precipitated the crisis or greatly complicates its resolution. Psychiatric emergencies : crises in which general functioning is severely impaired and the person is dangerous to self or others, such as an acute psychosis, a serious suicide attempt or a drug overdose. A different distinction, common in the crisis literature and in examination questions, concerns the scale of the precipitating event. Large-scale events affect whole communities at once: natural disasters (floods, cyclones, earthquakes, tornadoes, tsunamis), industrial disasters such as the Bhopal gas leak of 1984, terrorist attacks, war and epidemics. They call for the community-wide response described in Section 9.7.5. Small-scale events strike one person or one family, though they can be just as devastating for those involved: violent events (child abuse, domestic violence, crime), crises triggered by psychopathology (a suicide attempt, a drug overdose) and personal catastrophes (a road accident, a life-threatening illness). Most of a clinical psychologist's crisis work deals with small-scale events. Exam trap RML 2020 asked which is not a small-scale crisis event. Child abuse, domestic abuse and crime; a suicide attempt or overdose; a car accident or life-threatening illness are all small-scale (individual or family) events. A tornado or flood is a large-scale , community-wide event (an ecosystemic crisis), so it is the exception. Also: a developmental crisis is predictable (marriage, retirement); a situational crisis is unexpected (an accident). Baldwin's six classes end with psychiatric emergencies , the most severe. The goals and steps of crisis intervention Crisis intervention is brief, active, present-focused help for a person in crisis, aimed at resolving the immediate crisis and restoring at least the level of functioning that existed before it. Aguilera and Messick set out its goals in two tiers. The minimum goal is the psychological resolution of the immediate crisis and a return to the pre-crisis level of functioning. The maximum goal is improvement beyond the pre-crisis level, so that the person leaves the crisis with new coping skills and is better prepared for the next one. Crisis intervention is not a short version of psychotherapy. Its principles are distinctive: Immediacy. Help is given at once, ideally within hours, because the period of openness that Rapoport described is short. Crisis services therefore work by telephone, drop-in and home visit rather than by appointment next month. Brevity. Crisis intervention usually takes one to six contacts within about six weeks, matching Caplan's time course. Focus. The work concentrates on the precipitating event and the present problem ("why now?"), not on personality or childhood. Activity. The worker is active and, when necessary, directive: asking questions, giving information and advice, contacting other people, making arrangements. Safety first. Risk to life is assessed at the start and throughout. Support and self-reliance. The worker mobilises the person's own network and resources, and does things with the person rather than for him wherever possible, so that he regains a sense of control. Hope. The worker conveys a realistic expectation that the crisis will pass and the person will cope. Military psychiatry, which has handled acute combat reactions since the First World War, summarises the same ideas as proximity (help close to where the person is), immediacy and expectancy (the expectation of recovery and return). Several step-by-step models put these principles into practice. The most widely used is the seven-stage crisis intervention model of the American social work professor Albert R. Roberts , first set out in 1991 and refined in his Crisis Intervention Handbook . Table 9.11 lists its stages and follows Arjun through them. Roberts stressed that the stages often overlap, and that the first two (assessment and rapport) usually happen together. Table 9.11 Roberts's seven-stage model of crisis intervention, applied to Arjun. Stage Task In Arjun's case 1 Plan and conduct a thorough biopsychosocial assessment, including lethality and imminent danger The counsellor asks directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and means; Arjun admits to saving up sleeping tablets 2 Make psychological contact and rapidly establish rapport Respect and a calm, non-judgemental tone: "You did the right thing by messaging your friend" 3 Identify the major problems, including the precipitating event Results, the break-up and fear of his father's reaction; the results were the last straw 4 Encourage the exploration of feelings and emotions Active listening and validation of his shame and exhaustion; he weeps about letting his father down 5 Generate and explore alternatives and coping strategies Supplementary examinations; speaking to his father with the counsellor's help; friends who helped before 6 Restore functioning through an action plan Tablets handed to the warden; a friend stays the night; he calls his father the next evening; he meets his professor 7 Plan follow-up and booster sessions A meeting in two days, then weekly for a month; screening for depression; referral if needed James and Gilliland's six-step model organises the same work differently. The first three steps are mainly listening : defining the problem from the client's point of view, ensuring the client's safety, and providing support. The last three are mainly acting : examining alternatives, making plans and obtaining the client's commitment to them. Assessment is not a step but runs through the whole process. James and Gilliland also describe how directive the worker should be: nondirective when the client is able to act for himself, collaborative when he is partly able, and directive (taking charge for a while) when he is immobilised by the crisis. Arjun at two in the morning needs a directive worker; Arjun three days later, rested and talking to his father, needs a collaborative one. Which kind of therapy best fits this work? Insight-oriented therapies that explore defences and the past, and structured therapies that need weeks of homework, are poorly suited to the acute phase. What a person in crisis needs first is support: the techniques of supportive psychotherapy (taught in Section 3.10). The worker allows ventilation of feelings, offers realistic reassurance , gives information and guidance , uses environmental manipulation (arranging leave from college, a safe place to stay, a call to the family), strengthens the person's existing defences and coping rather than challenging them, and helps with practical problem solving. Cognitive behavioural techniques have a place once the person is stable, for example to challenge "I am a complete failure", and longer therapy may follow if a disorder emerges. The same is true of acceptance and commitment therapy (Chapter 5), which builds psychological flexibility over many sessions, and of the expressive therapies (art, music, dance and movement, and drama therapy), which use creative activity as a channel for feelings that are hard to put into words: both can help in the weeks after a crisis, but neither is the first response to it. But in the crisis itself, support comes first. Because it is built for a short, normal reaction to an identifiable stressor, crisis intervention is the classic treatment of choice for adjustment disorders , which by definition arise within three months of a stressor and usually settle within six months once the stressor or its consequences end (the diagnosis is described in the Psychiatric Disorders book). It is also used for acute stress reactions, for people who have just attempted suicide, for victims of violence and for families facing a sudden illness or death. It is delivered in many settings: telephone helplines, walk-in crisis centres, emergency departments, mobile crisis teams that visit people at home, the crisis resolution and home treatment teams that offer an alternative to admission in Britain, and crisis houses where a person can stay for a few days. Clinical link In India the family is usually part of the crisis and part of its solution. Arjun's greatest fear is his father's disappointment, but his father, told gently and with the counsellor present, is far more likely to say "come home for a few days" than "you have disgraced us". Bringing the family in early, with the client's agreement, turns the person most feared into the most important source of situational support. Exam trap "Which therapy is mostly needed in crisis management?" The answer is supportive therapy (IHBAS 2020): ventilation, reassurance, guidance and environmental manipulation. CBT, acceptance and commitment therapy and expressive therapies may help later, but they are not the core of the acute phase. "The treatment of choice for adjustment disorder" is crisis intervention (RML 2024), not psychoanalytic or group psychotherapy; brief problem-focused therapies are also used, but crisis intervention is the classic answer. In Roberts's seven stages , assessment including lethality comes first and follow-up comes last. Suicide prevention Every year, according to the World Health Organization, more than 700,000 people die by suicide, and for every death there are many more attempts. In India the National Crime Records Bureau recorded 1,70,924 suicides in 2022 and 1,71,418 in 2023, the highest numbers in its records, and suicide is among the leading causes of death of young Indians. How to assess an individual's risk (the risk and protective factors, the SAD PERSONS mnemonic and the reasons why no checklist predicts suicide well) is taught in Section 2.7. This subsection is about prevention, both for the individual in front of you and for the population. Organised suicide prevention began with two initiatives of the 1950s. In London in 1953 the Anglican priest Chad Varah (1911 to 2007) advertised a telephone number that people thinking of suicide could ring, and so founded the Samaritans, whose trained volunteers offer confidential, non-judgemental listening ("befriending"). In 1958 the psychologists Edwin S. Shneidman (1918 to 2009) and Norman L. Farberow founded the Los Angeles Suicide Prevention Center, the model for crisis centres across the United States. Shneidman went on to found the field he called suicidology, developed, with his colleagues, the psychological autopsy (a reconstruction of the state of mind of a person who has died by suicide, from interviews with relatives and records) and described the central experience of the suicidal person as "psychache", unbearable psychological pain. In India, Lakshmi Vijayakumar founded Sneha in Chennai in 1986, a volunteer befriending service on the Samaritans model. The levels of prevention from Section 9.6.2 organise the modern evidence neatly. The WHO's guide to national suicide prevention, LIVE LIFE (2021), recommends four key interventions: limiting access to the means of suicide, working with the media for responsible reporting, fostering socio-emotional life skills in adolescents, and early identification, assessment, management and follow-up of anyone affected by suicidal behaviour. The first three are universal; the last is selective and indicated. Means restriction. The most consistently effective single measure is means restriction : reducing access to the methods people use to kill themselves. It works because many suicidal crises are brief and the person is ambivalent; if the most lethal method is not at hand during the worst hours, the crisis often passes, and most people do not simply substitute another method. The classic evidence comes from Britain. Until the late 1950s, domestic cooking gas, made from coal, contained a high proportion of carbon monoxide, and putting one's head in the gas oven was the commonest method of suicide. As coal gas was replaced by non-toxic natural gas during the 1960s, the psychiatrist Norman Kreitman showed in 1976, suicides by gas almost disappeared and the total suicide rate in England and Wales fell by about a third, with no matching rise in other methods. Sri Lanka, where pesticide poisoning was the commonest method, banned the most toxic pesticides in the 1990s; its suicide rate roughly halved over the following decade. In India, where pesticides and hanging account for much of the toll, the equivalents are removing the most hazardous pesticides from sale, locked storage of pesticides on farms, smaller pack sizes for dangerous medicines and barriers at bridges, railway lines and tall buildings. Key study: Seiden's Golden Gate Bridge follow-up (1978) A common objection to means restriction is that a person determined to die will find another way. The psychologist Richard H. Seiden tested this with the most dramatic means available. San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge was then described as the world's most popular site for suicide, and between 1937 and 1971 police, bridge workers and passers-by had restrained 515 people who were about to jump. Seiden traced what had happened to them, through death records, on average more than two decades later. If the determination hypothesis were true, most would have gone on to kill themselves somewhere else. In fact about 94 percent were still alive or had died of natural causes; only about 5 percent had gone on to die by suicide. The conclusion is that suicidal behaviour is often crisis-bound: get a person through the crisis, and the wish to die frequently passes. The study is still the standard answer to the objection, and it helped the argument for building a safety net under the bridge, a project finally completed in the 2020s. The media. In 1974 the sociologist David P. Phillips showed that suicides in the United States and Britain rose in the month after a suicide was reported on the front pages of newspapers, and rose more the more publicity it received. He named this imitative effect the Werther effect , after the hero of Goethe's novel The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774), which was blamed for a wave of copycat suicides among young men in Europe. The opposite has also been shown: stories of people who were suicidal but found a way through their crisis appear to reduce suicides, the Papageno effect (named by Thomas Niederkrotenthaler and colleagues in 2010, after the character in Mozart's The Magic Flute who is talked out of suicide). The WHO's guidelines for journalists, adopted in India by the Press Council, follow directly: do not describe the method or the location in detail, do not use sensational headlines or present suicide as a solution to a problem, do not repeat a story prominently, and do include information about where to get help. Schools and gatekeepers. School curricula about suicide aimed at all students have a mixed record, but well-designed programmes that teach young people about mental health and coping can work: in a large European trial (2015), schools that ran the Youth Aware of Mental Health programme had about half as many new suicide attempts over the following year as control schools. A related selective strategy is gatekeeper training : teaching people who are in regular contact with those at risk (teachers, hostel wardens, police, pharmacists, priests, ASHAs) to recognise warning signs, ask about suicide directly and help the person to care. One widely used format, QPR, devised by the American psychologist Paul Quinnett in 1995, teaches three steps: Question, Persuade, Refer. Gatekeeper training works best as part of a whole-system effort. The United States Air Force programme, launched in the late 1990s, combined training of commanders and staff, reduced stigma for seeking help and changed policies, and was followed by a reduction of about a third in suicides. A systematic review of suicide prevention strategies by John Mann and colleagues (2005) concluded that the two approaches with the clearest evidence were training doctors to recognise and treat depression, and means restriction. Helplines. Telephone and online crisis lines are the most visible form of suicide prevention. They are hard to evaluate, because callers are anonymous, but studies of callers in the United States have found that their distress and suicidal feelings fall during the course of the call. Barlow and Durand add an important caution: volunteers on helplines must be backed up by mental health professionals who can respond to callers at serious risk. India's national helpline, Tele-MANAS (14416), described in the Indian context box below, is designed to do exactly that by linking callers to counsellors and, when needed, to specialist services. People who have already attempted suicide. A previous suicide attempt is the strongest single predictor of eventual suicide, and the weeks after an attempt, and after discharge from a psychiatric admission, are the period of highest risk. This is where indicated prevention matters most. A study by Jason Luoma and colleagues (2002) found that about 45 percent of people who died by suicide had been in contact with a primary care doctor in the month before their death, so these contacts are opportunities that are often missed. The interventions with good evidence are these: The safety planning intervention of Barbara Stanley and Gregory K. Brown (2012), a brief collaborative exercise, often completed in a single session, in which the clinician and the patient write a personalised, step-by-step plan for the patient to follow when suicidal feelings return (Table 9.12). In a large study in the emergency departments of United States veterans' hospitals (Stanley and colleagues, 2018), patients who received a safety plan plus follow-up telephone calls showed substantially less suicidal behaviour over the next six months than those who received usual care (about 3 percent against about 5 percent, a reduction of nearly half). Brief contact and follow-up. In a famous study the psychiatrist Jerome A. Motto sent short, personal, caring letters several times a year for five years to people who had been admitted to hospital in a depressed or suicidal state and had then refused further treatment; in the first two years after discharge they had a significantly lower suicide rate than a comparable group who received no letters. These caring contacts cost almost nothing. Specific psychological treatments. Ten sessions of cognitive therapy for recent suicide attempters, developed by Gregory Brown, Aaron Beck and their colleagues (2005), cut the rate of repeat attempts by about half over the following eighteen months. Dialectical behaviour therapy (Chapter 5) reduces self-harm in people with borderline personality disorder. Lithium in mood disorders and clozapine in schizophrenia also reduce suicide (the Psychiatric Disorders book). Table 9.12 The six steps of a Stanley and Brown safety plan, written in the patient's own words. Step Content Arjun's plan 1 Warning signs that a crisis may be developing Lying awake after midnight; thinking "I have ruined everything" 2 Internal coping strategies (things to do alone) Go for a walk round the campus; listen to music; a cold-water wash 3 People and social settings that provide distraction Go to the common room; sit at the tea stall near the gate 4 People whom I can ask for help His room-mate; his elder cousin in Bengaluru 5 Professionals and agencies to contact in a crisis College counsellor; Tele-MANAS 14416; the nearest emergency department 6 Making the environment safe Tablets given to the warden; no alcohol in the room Notice what the safety plan is not. For many years clinicians asked suicidal patients to sign a no-suicide contract , a promise not to harm themselves (or to call before doing so). There is no evidence that such contracts prevent suicide; they may reassure the clinician more than they protect the patient, and a patient who refuses to sign may simply stop telling the truth. The safety plan replaces a promise not to do something with a plan of what to do instead. Finally, suicide prevention continues after a death. Shneidman coined the term postvention for the support offered to people bereaved by suicide, whose grief is often complicated by guilt, anger and stigma (the disenfranchised grief of Section 9.5), and for the steps a school or college takes after a suicide to reduce the risk of further, imitative suicides. Remember Four myths about suicide. (1) "Asking about suicide puts the idea into someone's head": it does not, and many people feel relief at being asked (Section 2.2). (2) "People who talk about suicide do not do it": most people who die by suicide have given some warning. (3) "Someone who has decided will not be stopped": most suicidal people are ambivalent, and most who survive a crisis do not later die by suicide (Seiden). (4) "When a severely depressed person suddenly improves, the danger is over": risk can rise as energy returns, and it is highest in the weeks after discharge from hospital. Indian context Until 2017, attempting suicide was an offence under Section 309 of the Indian Penal Code. Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Chapter 1) now presumes, unless the contrary is proved, that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress and shall not be tried or punished, and it places a duty on the government to provide that person with care, treatment and rehabilitation; the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which replaced the Indian Penal Code on 1 July 2024, does not carry over the general offence of attempting suicide. In November 2022 India released its first National Suicide Prevention Strategy, which aims to reduce suicide mortality by 10 percent by 2030, and in October 2022 the government launched Tele-MANAS, a free, round-the-clock national tele-mental health service (14416 or 1-800-891-4416) that connects callers to trained counsellors in their own language and, when needed, to specialists. Exam trap The best-supported population measure is means restriction (the British coal gas story, Sri Lanka's pesticide bans); Seiden's Golden Gate study shows most people restrained from suicide do not later die by it. The Werther effect is imitative suicide after publicised suicides (Phillips, 1974); the Papageno effect is the protective effect of stories of coping. The safety plan is Stanley and Brown 's; a no-suicide contract has no evidence behind it. QPR (Question, Persuade, Refer) is gatekeeper training. The Samaritans were founded by Chad Varah (1953); the Los Angeles Suicide Prevention Center by Shneidman and Farberow (1958); postvention and the psychological autopsy are Shneidman's. Psychological first aid and disaster mental health When a cyclone, an earthquake or a flood strikes, thousands of people are in crisis at once, and the methods of the counselling room cannot reach them. The first thing to understand about disasters is that most of the reactions that follow them are normal. Fear, grief, sleeplessness, irritability, startle and intrusive memories are common in the first days and weeks, and for most people they fade with time, safety and the support of family and community. As Section 9.5 showed for bereavement, resilience is the usual outcome; only a minority go on to develop post-traumatic stress disorder, depression or problem drinking. Disaster workers often describe a typical sequence in a community's response: a heroic phase of rescue in the first hours and days, a "honeymoon" phase of solidarity and outside help, a phase of disillusionment when the help is withdrawn and the bureaucracy of compensation begins, and a long phase of reconstruction. Psychological needs change with each. The Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC), which coordinates the humanitarian agencies of the United Nations and others, set out the now-standard framework in its Guidelines on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Emergency Settings (2007). Support is arranged as a pyramid of four layers (Figure 9.6). Everyone needs the bottom layer, and progressively fewer people need each layer above it. The pyramid carries a lesson that surprises many psychologists: the most important mental health interventions after a disaster are not psychological at all. Safety, shelter, food, water, information about missing relatives, and the chance to carry out funeral rites and to resume daily routines do more for most people's mental health than any counsellor. 4 Specialised services 3 Focused, non- specialised supports 2 Community and family supports 1 Basic services and security What each layer provides clinical care by psychiatrists and psychologists for severe disorders psychological first aid and basic care by trained, supervised workers reviving family and community networks, rituals, self-help groups, safe spaces shelter, food, water, health care and security, delivered with dignity Figure 9.6 The IASC intervention pyramid (2007). Every affected person needs the base; each higher layer is needed by fewer people. Psychological first aid sits in layer 3, and specialist treatment only at the top. In the hours and days after a disaster, the recommended psychological response for distressed people is psychological first aid (PFA). The WHO, the War Trauma Foundation and World Vision International published Psychological First Aid: Guide for Field Workers in 2011, defining PFA as a humane, supportive response to a fellow human being who is suffering and who may need support. Its action principles are usually summarised as look, listen and link , preceded by prepare : Prepare : learn about the crisis event, the services and supports available, and the safety and security concerns before going in. Look : check for safety; check for people with obvious urgent basic needs (the injured, the lost child); check for people with serious distress reactions. Listen : approach people who may need support; ask about their needs and concerns; listen to them and help them feel calm. Link : help people meet basic needs and reach services; help them cope with practical problems; give accurate information; connect them with loved ones and social support. The guide is just as clear about what PFA is not . It is not something only professionals can do; it is not professional counselling; it is not psychological debriefing; it does not require a detailed discussion of the event; and it does not involve pressing people to analyse what happened or to talk about their feelings if they do not wish to. A volunteer from the village, a teacher or a police officer can learn PFA in a day. Its principles rest on a review by Stevan E. Hobfoll and a panel of trauma experts (2007), who identified five essential elements of immediate and mid-term intervention after mass trauma, each supported by research: promoting a sense of safety , calming , a sense of self-efficacy and community efficacy , connectedness and hope . An American version, the Psychological First Aid Field Operations Guide (2006) of the National Child Traumatic Stress Network and the National Center for PTSD, sets out eight core actions in the same spirit: contact and engagement, safety and comfort, stabilisation, information gathering on current needs, practical assistance, connection with social supports, information on coping, and linkage with collaborative services. Indian context India meets disasters often: the Bhopal gas leak (1984), the Odisha super cyclone (1999), the Gujarat earthquake (2001), the Indian Ocean tsunami (2004), the Kerala floods (2018) and the COVID-19 pandemic. Indian teams, NIMHANS prominent among them, have trained community-level workers in "psychosocial care" after many of these events, and the National Disaster Management Authority issued guidelines on psychosocial support and mental health services in disasters in 2009, built on the same principles: normalise reactions, restore routines and community rituals, train local helpers, and refer the few who need specialist care. Exam trap Psychological first aid (WHO, War Trauma Foundation and World Vision, 2011 ): look, listen, link (with prepare). It is given by non-specialists, does not require people to recount the event, and is not debriefing or counselling . Hobfoll's five elements (2007): safety, calming, efficacy, connectedness, hope. The IASC pyramid (2007), from bottom to top: basic services and security, community and family supports, focused non-specialised supports, specialised services. Psychological debriefing: a cautionary tale For about twenty years from the early 1980s, the standard response to a traumatic event in much of the Western world was psychological debriefing. Its best-known form, critical incident stress debriefing (CISD), was developed by Jeffrey T. Mitchell , a former firefighter and paramedic, and described in 1983. It was designed for emergency workers (firefighters, ambulance crews, police) after a distressing incident: a single structured group meeting, usually held within a few days of the event and lasting a few hours, led by a mental health professional with trained peers. It moves through seven phases: introduction (purpose, rules and confidentiality), fact (what happened, from each person's point of view), thought (each person's first thoughts during the incident), reaction (the worst part of it for them, and the feelings it aroused), symptom (the physical and psychological reactions they have had since), teaching (education about normal stress reactions and ways of coping) and re-entry (questions, summing up and referral). CISD later became one part of a wider package, critical incident stress management (CISM), developed by Mitchell and George Everly, which also includes training before incidents, brief "defusing" sessions, individual crisis support, family support and follow-up. The logic seemed obvious: talk about the event early, express the emotions, learn that your reactions are normal, and you will be less likely to develop post-traumatic stress disorder. Debriefing spread from emergency services to the survivors of accidents, robberies, shootings and disasters, often offered to individuals who had been directly harmed, and in some organisations attendance was compulsory. Participants usually said they found it helpful. Then the randomised trials arrived. Key study: Bisson's debriefing trial with burn victims (1997) Jonathan I. Bisson and his colleagues in Cardiff randomly assigned adults admitted to hospital with burns either to a single debriefing session, held individually or with a partner within about the first three weeks after the injury, or to no intervention. They then followed them up. At three months the two groups did not differ. At thirteen months, 26 percent of the debriefed patients had post-traumatic stress disorder, against 9 percent of those who had not been debriefed. Critics pointed out that the groups were not perfectly matched at the start, so the size of the harm is uncertain. But the trial showed, at the very least, that debriefing had not prevented PTSD, and it raised the possibility that it could make things worse. Other trials told the same story. In a study of road accident survivors in Oxford, Richard Mayou, Anke Ehlers and Mark Hobbs (2000) found that three years later the patients who had been debriefed had a worse outcome than those who had not, especially those who had been most distressed at the start. A Cochrane systematic review by Suzanna Rose, Jonathan Bisson, Rachel Churchill and Simon Wessely (2002) concluded that single-session individual debriefing did not reduce distress or prevent PTSD, and that compulsory debriefing of trauma victims should cease. A meta-analysis by Arnold van Emmerik and his colleagues in The Lancet in the same year found that CISD did not improve on natural recovery. Guidelines followed. Britain's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, 2005, reaffirmed in 2018) advised against offering psychologically focused debriefing to prevent or treat PTSD, and the WHO (2013) recommended that psychological debriefing should not be used for people exposed to a traumatic event in the previous month. Why might a procedure that feels helpful fail, or even harm? Several explanations have been offered. Debriefing asks people to relive the most frightening moments of an event in vivid detail while they are still highly aroused, which may strengthen the traumatic memory; but it does so in a single session, far too short for the habituation and reprocessing that real exposure therapy provides over many sessions. It may teach people to expect symptoms and to read normal reactions as signs of disorder. It may interfere with natural recovery, replacing the support of family, friends and colleagues with a single professional encounter. And because it is offered to everyone, though most people recover without help, it cannot improve on natural recovery for the majority, and it may disrupt it for some. The story is a lesson in why clinical psychology insists on controlled trials: an intervention that was plausible, popular and sincerely delivered turned out not to work. What should be done instead? In the first days, psychological first aid and practical help. Then watchful waiting , now usually called active monitoring: keeping in touch with people who were exposed, and checking again after about a month, because most reactions fade by then. Those who still have marked symptoms, or who develop acute stress disorder or PTSD, are offered trauma-focused psychological treatment , such as trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR), over several sessions (Chapters 4 and 5). Such targeted early treatment works. Barlow and Durand describe a trial by Ehlers and her colleagues (2003) of people who had been in frightening road accidents and were clearly at risk: after up to twelve weekly sessions of cognitive therapy only 11 percent developed PTSD, compared with 61 percent of those given a detailed self-help booklet and 55 percent of those who were simply assessed repeatedly. The difference between debriefing and these treatments is not that one talks about the trauma and the others do not; it is who receives the help (everyone, or only those who need it), when, and how much.
