Do not confuse it with psychological first aid , which is recommended and does not ask people to recount the event, or with the "debriefing" of research participants after a study (the Research Methods book), which is an ethical duty and has nothing to do with trauma. Trauma-informed care Debriefing taught clinicians to be careful about treating trauma too eagerly. A different line of research taught them that they were usually not thinking about trauma enough. The turning point was a study that began in an obesity clinic. Key study: the Adverse Childhood Experiences study (1998) In the 1980s Vincent J. Felitti , a physician running a weight-loss programme for the health organisation Kaiser Permanente in San Diego, was puzzled that some of his most successful patients dropped out just as they were losing weight fastest. Interviewing them, he found that many had been sexually abused as children, and that their weight protected them in ways they could not give up. With Robert F. Anda of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, he designed a much larger study. Adult members of the health plan who came for routine medical examinations in the mid-1990s were asked about seven categories of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs): psychological, physical and sexual abuse, and growing up with a household member who misused alcohol or drugs, was mentally ill, was imprisoned, or treated the mother violently. The first report, in 1998, covered 9,508 respondents. More than half reported at least one category, and about one in sixteen reported four or more. The relationship with adult health was graded, like a dose and its response: compared with people who had none, those with four or more categories had four to twelve times the risk of alcoholism, drug abuse, depression and suicide attempts, and higher rates of smoking, severe obesity, heart disease, lung disease and cancer. The criticisms are that the sample was mostly white, middle-class and insured, and that the childhood experiences were reported retrospectively. Even so, the study showed that childhood adversity is common, cumulative and one of the most powerful influences on adult health. If a large share of the people who come to health and social services have histories of trauma, the services themselves need to change. Trauma-informed care is an approach to organising a whole service, not a particular therapy, on the assumption that many of its clients (and staff) have experienced trauma. Its pioneers in mental health, Maxine Harris and Roger D. Fallot (2001), argued that services designed without this awareness often re-enact the dynamics of the original abuse: a woman who was held down as a child is held down again in physical restraint; a man who was powerless is again given no say. The question at the heart of trauma-informed care shifts from "What is wrong with you?" to "What happened to you?" The most widely used definition comes from the United States Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA, 2014). SAMHSA describes trauma in terms of three Es (an event or circumstances, the individual's experience of it, and its lasting adverse effects ) and says that a trauma-informed programme follows four Rs: it realises the widespread impact of trauma and understands paths to recovery; it recognises the signs and symptoms of trauma in clients, families and staff; it responds by fully integrating knowledge about trauma into its policies, procedures and practices; and it seeks actively to resist re-traumatisation . SAMHSA lists six key principles: Safety : physical and emotional safety for clients and staff, in the setting and in every interaction. Trustworthiness and transparency : decisions are explained and made openly, and promises are kept. Peer support : people with their own lived experience of trauma are part of the service. Collaboration and mutuality : power differences between staff and clients are reduced, and decisions are shared. Empowerment, voice and choice : clients' strengths are built on and they are given real choices. Cultural, historical and gender issues : the service recognises and responds to cultural, historical and gender-based trauma and avoids stereotypes. In practice, trauma-informed care changes many small things. Staff ask about trauma routinely and sensitively, but do not press for details. Procedures that involve touch, undressing or restraint are explained before they happen and kept to a minimum; women who have been sexually assaulted can ask to be examined by a woman. Clients are given choices wherever possible, routines are predictable, and seclusion and restraint are reduced. In India, the Mental Healthcare Act 2017's ban on chaining and its strict limits on physical restraint, the child-friendly procedures of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act 2012 and the One Stop Centres for women affected by violence (from 2015) all move in this direction. The approach also cares for staff, because people who work every day with traumatised clients are at risk of secondary traumatic stress and burnout. It is important to keep two terms apart. Trauma-informed care is a framework for a whole organisation and applies to every client, whatever their diagnosis. Trauma-focused (or trauma-specific) treatment, such as trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, prolonged exposure or EMDR, is a therapy for individuals who have a trauma-related disorder. A good service needs both. Exam trap Trauma-informed care is an organisational framework , not a therapy; trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are treatments . He lives with his parents in a small house in Hassan, and he was first admitted to hospital with schizophrenia at 22, in the final year of an engineering diploma. For the past three years a monthly depot injection has kept the voices quiet and the frightening ideas away. By every psychiatric measure he is better. Yet he has not worked for twelve years. He spends most of the day on a mat in front of the television, his school friends have married and moved away, his mother handles his money, and when relatives visit he stays in the back room. His father, recently retired, asks the question that families everywhere ask: "The voices have stopped. Why is he still like this?" The honest answer is that medicine treats illness, and what Mr Prakash now lives with is mostly something else: a disability. Twelve years of illness have taken away his skills, his confidence, his friendships, his place in the family and his place in the town, and the injection cannot give those back. Helping people like him rebuild a life, in the community rather than in a hospital, is the work of psychosocial rehabilitation. It grew up alongside the community mental health movement (Section 9.6), which emptied the large mental hospitals and then had to answer the obvious next question: where would the people who left them live, what would they do all day, and who would help them? From symptoms to functioning: what rehabilitation is Rehabilitation is meant for people whose illness is long-lasting and disabling, a group described as having severe mental illness (older writing says "chronic mental illness" or "serious and persistent mental illness"). Service planners have defined the group, since the early 1980s, by three Ds: a diagnosis of a major mental disorder (most often schizophrenia or another psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe recurrent depression), a long duration of illness or treatment, usually two years or more, and significant disability in everyday life. The disorders themselves are described in the Psychiatric Disorders book. What matters here is the third D. Two people with the same diagnosis and the same symptom score can live very different lives, and it is the life, not the symptom score, that rehabilitation sets out to change. The clearest statement of the idea comes from the American psychologist William A. Anthony and his colleagues at the Center for Psychiatric Rehabilitation, which he founded at Boston University in 1979. Psychiatric rehabilitation (today usually called psychosocial rehabilitation; the two terms mean the same thing) aims, in their definition, to help people with psychiatric disabilities increase their ability to function, so that they are successful and satisfied in the environment of their choice, with the least amount of ongoing professional help. Read that slowly and every phrase carries weight. The target is functioning , not symptoms. Success is judged in a particular environment (a hostel, a job, a family home, a college) that the person chooses . And the professional's aim is to become steadily less necessary. Anthony's group pointed out that there are only two ways to improve a person's functioning in an environment. The first is to develop the person's skills : teach Mr Prakash to travel alone by bus, to cook a simple meal, to keep a conversation going, to manage his own money. The second is to develop environmental supports : change the setting so that the person can succeed with the skills he already has. His mother might be helped to give him his own pocket money and let him make small mistakes with it; an employer might allow him a later start because his medicine makes him slow in the morning; a neighbour might be asked to take him along to the temple committee. Every rehabilitation plan is some mixture of the two. To build such a plan, the clinician starts not with a diagnostic assessment (what is wrong with him?) but with a functional assessment : what does this person want to do, in which setting, what can he already do there, and what skills or supports are missing? The principles that follow from this way of thinking are now accepted across the field: The person's own goals set the agenda. A plan built around the clinician's goals ("he should attend the day centre") rarely survives contact with a person who wants something else ("I want to earn money"). Hope is a treatment ingredient, not a decoration. People do not work at rebuilding a life they believe is already finished. Skills are taught, and supports arranged, in the real setting where they will be used, because skills learned in a hospital often fail to transfer to a home or a workplace. Rehabilitation builds on strengths (what the person still does well, enjoys and values) rather than cataloguing deficits. The family and the person are partners in planning, and the help continues for as long as it is needed; severe mental illness is rarely a problem that is solved once. A shared language for describing disability came from the World Health Organization. Its International Classification of Impairments, Disabilities and Handicaps (ICIDH, 1980) separated three levels: an impairment is a loss or abnormality of a psychological or bodily function (hallucinations, poor attention); a disability is the resulting restriction in the ability to perform an activity (being unable to concentrate long enough to read a newspaper); and a handicap is the social disadvantage that follows (losing a job, being left out of family decisions). The scheme was criticised for implying a one-way chain and for locating the whole problem inside the person, so in 2001 the WHO replaced it with the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF). The ICF keeps three levels but renames them in neutral terms (Figure 9.7): body functions and structures , where problems are called impairments; activities , where problems are called activity limitations ; and participation in life situations, where problems are called participation restrictions . It then adds contextual factors , both environmental (family attitudes, stigma, services, laws, the physical setting) and personal (age, gender, education, coping style), and it draws every arrow in both directions. In the ICF, disability is not something a person has; it is the outcome of an interaction between a health condition and a context. Health condition disorder or disease Body functions and structures problem: impairment Activities problem: activity limitation Participation problem: participation restriction Contextual factors Environmental factors family, stigma, services, laws Personal factors age, gender, coping style Figure 9.7 The WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF, 2001). Every arrow runs both ways: disability is the product of an interaction between a health condition, what the person can do and take part in, and the context around them. Push Mr Prakash through Figure 9.7 and the plan almost writes itself. His impairments are residual negative symptoms (little drive, flat expression), slowed thinking and the sedation from his medication. His activity limitations are that he cannot manage money, travel alone or hold a conversation with strangers. His participation restrictions are that he has no job, no friends and no role in family decisions. And his contextual factors pull in both directions: an overprotective but devoted mother, a town where everyone knows he was "in the mental hospital", no rehabilitation service within 40 kilometres, and, on the personal side, a good memory for engineering and a lifelong love of cricket. The psychiatrist works mainly on the impairments; the rehabilitation team works on the other three boxes. In the language of prevention that Section 9.6 introduces, rehabilitation is tertiary prevention : it does not stop a disorder from occurring (primary prevention) or catch it early (secondary prevention), but reduces the disability that an established disorder leaves behind. Exam trap Know both WHO schemes. The ICIDH (1980) used impairment, disability and handicap ; the ICF (2001) uses impairment (body functions and structures), activity limitation and participation restriction , plus environmental and personal contextual factors. "Handicap" is not an ICF term. Rehabilitation is tertiary prevention, so "providing rehabilitation after injury" is never the answer to a question asking for an example of primary prevention (immunisation, health education). And rehabilitation targets functioning ; reducing symptoms with medication is treatment, not rehabilitation. Recovery as the guiding vision For most of the twentieth century, psychiatry expected very little of people like Mr Prakash. Emil Kraepelin had defined dementia praecox by its deteriorating course, and the textbooks taught that schizophrenia, once established, led downhill. Rehabilitation was therefore about "maintenance": keeping a chronic patient stable and occupied. Two kinds of evidence overturned that pessimism, and they changed the goal of the whole enterprise. Key study: the Vermont longitudinal study (1987) In the late 1950s, 269 of the most severely and chronically ill patients on the back wards of Vermont State Hospital, people whom everyone had given up on, took part in an unusually thorough rehabilitation programme and were then discharged into the community with continuing support: help with housing, work and daily life. Some twenty to twenty-five years later the psychologist Courtenay M. Harding and her colleagues traced almost all of them and interviewed the survivors. The result, published in 1987, astonished the field: between one-half and two-thirds of these "hopeless" patients had improved considerably or recovered, most were living in the community, and many needed no medication at all. A follow-up comparison with matched patients from the neighbouring state of Maine, which had offered ordinary aftercare without the rehabilitation programme, found that the Vermont group were more productive, had fewer symptoms and were better adjusted to community life. The conclusion was twofold: the long-term course of schizophrenia is far more varied and hopeful than Kraepelin believed, and what services do makes a difference to it. The criticism is that the study was not randomised and the diagnoses were made by the standards of the 1950s, so later investigators re-diagnosed the cases by modern criteria; the main finding held. International research pointed the same way. The World Health Organization's International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (reported in 1973) and its Determinants of Outcome of Severe Mental Disorders study (reported in 1992) found, to general surprise, that people with schizophrenia in the developing countries, including those at the Indian centres in Agra and Chandigarh, tended to have a better course over two to five years than those in Europe and North America. The finding has been argued about ever since, and the explanations offered (close family involvement, less rigid expectations about work, less stigma, a higher share of acute-onset illness) remain debated. But for Indian clinicians it carries a practical message: the family and the community, not just the clinic, are where outcomes are decided. The second kind of evidence came from the people with the illness themselves. In the 1980s and 1990s, former patients organised, wrote and spoke publicly about their experience. The American psychologist Patricia E. Deegan , who had been diagnosed with schizophrenia as a teenager, wrote in 1988 that recovery is not the same as being cured or returning to the person one was before; it is a process of discovering a new sense of self and purpose within and beyond the limits of the disability. In 1993 Anthony turned the idea into policy. In a paper subtitled "the guiding vision of the mental health service system in the 1990s", he described recovery as a deeply personal, unique process of changing one's attitudes, values, feelings, goals, skills and roles: a way of living a satisfying, hopeful and contributing life even with the limitations caused by illness. Notice that there are now two meanings of the word. Clinical recovery is the professional's meaning: symptoms remit and functioning returns to a normal range, judged by rating scales. Personal recovery is the person's meaning: living a meaningful life, as judged by the person, whether or not symptoms persist. Mr Prakash may never be clinically recovered and still achieve a great deal of personal recovery. A systematic review led by Mary Leamy and Mike Slade (2011) found that the personal accounts share five processes, remembered as CHIME : C onnectedness (relationships and belonging), H ope and optimism about the future, I dentity (rebuilding a positive sense of self beyond "patient"), M eaning in life, and E mpowerment (personal responsibility, control over one's life, a focus on strengths). Recovery-oriented services try to support all five, which is why the rest of this section keeps returning to choice, work, housing and belonging rather than to symptoms alone. Exam trap Recovery does not mean cure. In the recovery model it means living a satisfying, hopeful and contributing life even with continuing symptoms (Anthony, 1993). Distinguish clinical recovery (symptom remission, judged by professionals) from personal recovery (meaning and control, judged by the person). CHIME = connectedness, hope, identity, meaning, empowerment. Patricia Deegan (1988) wrote from lived experience; William Anthony (Boston University) gave the definition used in policy. The Vermont study (Harding, 1987) is the classic evidence that long-term outcome in schizophrenia is often good. Where to live and where to spend the day A person leaving a long hospital stay, or a person like Mr Prakash who has never left home, needs two things before anything else: somewhere to live and something to do with the day. Rehabilitation services grew up around those two needs, and they are easiest to understand if you keep them apart. Start with the day. A day hospital (also called partial hospitalisation) provides active psychiatric treatment during the day, with the patient going home each evening. It is an alternative to inpatient admission for people who are acutely ill but have a safe home, and an early step down after discharge. The first day hospitals appeared in Moscow in the 1930s and in Montreal and London soon after the Second World War. A day care centre is different in purpose: it offers longer-term rehabilitation to people whose acute illness has settled but who are disabled, through a structured daily programme of occupational therapy, social skills groups, recreation, vocational training, psychoeducation and simply the company of others. In India many teaching hospitals, the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru among them, run day care centres where people with severe mental illness spend the day in occupational therapy, vocational training and group activities. A third, looser form is the drop-in centre , which people visit when they wish for a cup of tea, company and informal support. Now the place to live. In the countries that closed their mental hospitals, a range of residential options appeared, differing in how much supervision they provide: A halfway house is a transitional residence, halfway between hospital and independent life. A small group of residents live together with staff on hand, follow house rules, share the cooking and cleaning, and work on daily living skills, with the expectation that they will move on, usually within months to a year or two. Halfway houses are also widely used for people recovering from alcohol and drug dependence (Section 9.9). Long-stay residences, group homes and hostels offer permanent, supervised accommodation for people who are unlikely to manage alone, sometimes with staff present around the clock. In supported housing , the person lives in an ordinary flat or house, alone or with flatmates of their choosing, and the support comes to them through visiting staff, as much or as little as is needed at the time. In family foster care (boarding out), a person with mental illness lives as a lodger with a family who are paid and supported to look after them. The oldest example of the last option in the world is a small town in Belgium. In Geel, east of Antwerp, people with mental illness have lived as boarders in ordinary family homes for some seven hundred years. The custom began with the pilgrims who came to the shrine of St Dymphna, a seventh-century Irish princess who, according to legend, fled to Geel and was killed there by her father, and who became the patron saint of the mentally ill. When the church could not house all the pilgrims, local families took them in, and the practice became a tradition that continues, on a smaller scale, today. Geel is the standard reply to anyone who claims that people with severe mental illness cannot live among ordinary families. In the 1970s and 1980s these options were usually arranged as a linear continuum (Figure 9.8): a person was expected to move from hospital to a halfway house to a group home to supported housing and finally to independence, earning each step by showing readiness for it. The same "train then place" logic shaped vocational services. Critics in the 1990s pointed out the flaws. Every move meant leaving friends and staff and starting again; many people stalled on a middle rung for years; and the skills learned in one setting often did not carry over to the next. The newer approach reverses the order: help the person into the setting they want first, and then provide support there. Its boldest form is Housing First , begun by the psychologist Sam Tsemberis at Pathways to Housing in New York in 1992 for homeless people with severe mental illness. Instead of requiring sobriety or treatment before housing, it offers an ordinary flat immediately, with an assertive support team (see below) that the person can use as they choose. Housing First programmes have kept most of their tenants stably housed, a result that the "earn your housing" model rarely achieved. Where to live Hospital ward Long-stay or group home Halfway house Supported housing Own home or family less supervision, more independence Where to spend the day Day care centre Sheltered workshop Transitional employment Supported employment Competitive job Train then place: climb one rung at a time, proving readiness at each step. Place then train (Housing First, IPS): go straight to the right-hand box, with support. Figure 9.8 The linear continuum of rehabilitation services. The older model moved people rightwards step by step; the newer place-then-train approaches put people into ordinary housing and ordinary jobs first and bring the support to them. India's situation is different again, and it is worth being clear about why. Here the great majority of people with severe mental illness live with their families, who provide the housing, the supervision and much of the rehabilitation without any formal service at all. The gaps are at the two ends: people with no family, or whose families have abandoned them, and families who are exhausted. For the first group, India has relied on non-governmental organisations. The Banyan, founded in Chennai in 1993 by Vandana Gopikumar and Vaishnavi Jayakumar to care for homeless women with mental illness found on the streets, went on to develop community-based group homes for people who could not return to their families. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Chapter 1) now turns such services into legal duties: section 18, the right to access mental healthcare, lists halfway homes, sheltered accommodation and supported accommodation among the services the government must provide, and section 19 gives every person with mental illness the right to community living , that is, the right to live in, be part of and not be segregated from society. Exam trap A day hospital gives active treatment by day as an alternative to admission; a day care centre gives longer-term rehabilitation and structured activity. A halfway house is a transitional residence between hospital and independent living (time-limited, with skills training); a sheltered workshop is a place of protected work , not a place to live. Geel (Belgium) is the classic example of family foster care. Housing First (Tsemberis, 1992) gives housing without preconditions; it is the housing version of "place then train". Work: from sheltered workshops to supported employment Ask people with severe mental illness what they want, and a large proportion say the same thing: a job. Work gives a day its structure, provides money and therefore choice, brings ordinary social contact, and answers the question that strangers always ask ("What do you do?") with something other than "I am a patient". In surveys most people with severe mental illness say they would like to work, yet only a small minority are in paid employment. Closing that gap is the task of vocational rehabilitation , and its history is a story of a field slowly discovering that its first methods were holding people back. The traditional approach was "train then place". The person first received a vocational assessment and prevocational training in work habits (punctuality, grooming, following instructions, tolerating a full day), often through occupational therapy. The next step was a sheltered workshop : a protected workplace, run by a hospital or charity, where people with disabilities do simple paid work (making paper bags, envelopes, candles or incense sticks, assembling components on contract) at their own pace, usually for a small piece-rate wage, among others with disabilities. Sheltered workshops give structure, a small income and a sense of contributing, and many Indian hospitals still run them. Their weakness is that they were meant as a step towards open employment and rarely led there: people stayed in them for years. A middle path was developed by the Clubhouse movement (Section 9.8.7). In transitional employment , the clubhouse negotiates real jobs with ordinary employers, part-time and for a fixed period (typically six to nine months), and places members in them one after another. If a member falls ill, a staff member or another member covers the shift, so the employer is guaranteed that the work gets done. Transitional employment gives people a real job on their record and a chance to test themselves, without the pressure of having to find and keep the job alone. The decisive shift came with supported employment , which turned the old sequence around into "place then train": help the person find a real job in the open labour market as quickly as possible, and then train and support them on the job. The best-defined version is Individual Placement and Support (IPS), developed in the early 1990s by Deborah R. Becker and Robert E. Drake at Dartmouth in New Hampshire. IPS rests on eight principles: Zero exclusion : everyone who wants to work is eligible, whatever their diagnosis, symptoms, substance use or work history. Wanting to work is the only criterion. Competitive employment is the goal: ordinary jobs, at ordinary wages, that anyone could apply for, not jobs set aside for people with disabilities. Rapid job search : contact with employers starts within about a month, without lengthy prevocational training. Integration with mental health treatment : the employment specialist is a member of the clinical team, so work and treatment plans fit together. Attention to the person's preferences about the type of job, the hours and whether to disclose the illness to the employer. Time-unlimited, individualised support after the person starts work, for as long as it helps. Benefits counselling , so the person knows how earning will affect any pension or allowance. Systematic job development : specialists build relationships with local employers, learning what they need. Key study: IPS across Europe, the EQOLISE trial (2007) IPS had done well in American trials, but would it work in countries with different labour markets and welfare systems? Tom Burns and his colleagues randomly assigned 312 people with severe mental illness in six European cities, from London to Sofia, either to IPS or to the best vocational rehabilitation service available locally, usually a train-then-place programme. Over 18 months, 55 percent of the IPS group worked for at least one day in an open-market job, against 28 percent of the comparison group; the IPS group also worked more hours, were less likely to drop out of the service and were less likely to be readmitted to hospital. Supported employment did not make people ill; if anything, the reverse. The criticism is that many jobs were short and part-time, and the effect varied with local unemployment. IPS is now the best-evidenced form of vocational rehabilitation for severe mental illness. Apply this to Mr Prakash. A train-then-place service would start him in the day care centre's candle unit and review his "readiness" in six months. An IPS specialist would ask what work he wants (he says he would like to do something with electronics, as he once studied), help him decide what to tell an employer, and within weeks approach a mobile phone repair shop in Hassan town whose owner needs an assistant for afternoons. The specialist would keep visiting, helping Mr Prakash with the bus journey at first, with the owner's instructions and with his anxiety on a bad day. The same logic underlies supported education , which helps people with severe mental illness enter and stay in college or vocational courses. Exam trap Sheltered workshops and prevocational training are train then place ; supported employment and IPS are place then train . IPS was developed by Becker and Drake and its signature principles are zero exclusion , competitive employment , rapid job search and time-unlimited support . Transitional employment , with time-limited part-time placements guaranteed by the clubhouse, belongs to the Clubhouse model . Supported employment does not raise relapse rates. Assertive community treatment Everything so far assumes that the person will turn up: at the day centre, at the job interview, at the clinic. Many of the most severely ill people do not. They miss appointments, stop their medicine, relapse, are readmitted, discharged, and the cycle starts again, a pattern clinicians call the revolving door . In the early 1970s three clinicians in Wisconsin decided that if these patients would not come to the services, the services would go to them. Key study: Stein and Test's Training in Community Living (1972 to 1980) At Mendota State Hospital in Madison, Wisconsin, Leonard I. Stein and Mary Ann Test , working with Arnold Marx, noticed that patients who had learned to manage on the ward lost those skills within weeks of discharge. Their solution was radical: they moved the staff of an inpatient ward out into the community. In the trial they reported in 1980, 130 patients who were seeking admission were randomly assigned either to usual care (a short admission followed by referral to aftercare) or to the Training in Community Living programme, in which the team helped each person find housing, taught daily living skills in the person's own home and neighbourhood, helped them find work or sheltered employment, made sure they took their medicine, supported their families and was available around the clock. Over 14 months the programme's patients spent far less time in hospital, more time in employment, had fewer symptoms and were more satisfied with their lives; an economic analysis found that the programme cost somewhat more than usual care but that its benefits, including patients' earnings, outweighed the extra cost. Then came the lesson that shaped everything afterwards. When the programme ended and the patients were transferred to ordinary services, many of the gains faded. Support for severe mental illness, Stein and Test concluded, must be continuous, not time-limited. The model they built became known as assertive community treatment (ACT), sometimes described as a "hospital without walls". Its defining features are these: A multidisciplinary team (psychiatrist, nurses, social workers, psychologists, vocational and substance-use specialists, and often a peer worker with lived experience) shares one caseload , so every client knows several staff and no one is lost when a staff member is on leave. The staff-to-client ratio is low, about one to ten. Services are delivered in vivo , in the person's home, street and workplace, rather than in an office; most contacts happen in the community. The team is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week , and handles crises itself. Outreach is assertive : if a client misses an appointment, the team goes to find them, persistently and respectfully. The team provides most services directly (medication, help with housing, money, shopping, work, family and substance use) rather than referring the person elsewhere. Support is time-unlimited . ACT has been tested in many trials. Reviews have consistently found that, compared with standard care, it reduces time spent in hospital, improves housing stability and keeps people in contact with services, and that clients like it; its effects on symptoms and on social functioning are smaller. The benefits depend on fidelity , how faithfully a team follows the model, which can be measured with fidelity scales such as the Dartmouth Assertive Community Treatment Scale. They also depend on what ACT is compared with. In London, where ordinary community mental health teams already visited patients at home, trials such as REACT (Helen Killaspy and colleagues, 2006) found that ACT engaged people better and satisfied them more but did not reduce hospital use. Because ACT is expensive, it is now targeted at the people who need it most: those caught in the revolving door, people who are homeless, and people with both severe mental illness and substance use problems. A Dutch adaptation, flexible ACT, switches individual clients between ordinary case management and intensive shared-caseload care as their needs change. Exam trap ACT was developed by Stein and Test (with Marx) in Madison, Wisconsin , in the 1970s (the Training in Community Living programme, reported 1980). Its signatures are a shared team caseload , a ratio of about 1:10 , in vivo services, 24-hour availability, assertive outreach , direct service provision and time-unlimited support. Its best-established effect is less time in hospital . Do not confuse it with acceptance and commitment therapy (Chapter 5), which shares the abbreviation, or with brokerage case management, in which one worker links the client to other agencies instead of treating them. Case management When the American mental hospitals emptied in the 1960s and 1970s, the people who left found themselves dealing with a dozen separate agencies: one for medication, one for housing, one for welfare benefits, one for work, one for emergencies, each with its own forms, rules and waiting lists. Many fell through the gaps. In 1977 the National Institute of Mental Health launched its Community Support Program to stitch these services together, and the stitch it chose was the case manager. Case management is a way of coordinating services for a person with complex, long-term needs, so that one worker or one team takes responsibility for seeing that the person gets the right help from all the agencies involved, and keeps getting it. Its roots lie in the social casework of the American social worker Mary Ellen Richmond (1861 to 1928), whose Social Diagnosis (1917) taught that a client's difficulties must be understood and addressed in the context of their whole social situation. Whatever the model, case management is usually said to involve five core functions. The case manager assesses the person's needs and strengths across every area of life; plans services with the person; links them to the services and resources they need (a psychiatrist, a disability pension, a hostel place, a job programme); monitors whether the services are actually delivered and are helping; and advocates for the person when an agency refuses, delays or treats them unfairly. The models differ in how much of the help the case manager gives personally, how large the caseload is, and, more subtly, in where they place the power between worker and client. Model Associated with Signature features Evidence Broker (brokerage) Early US community support services, 1970s Assess, refer and link; little direct help; large caseloads; office-based Weak: more contact with services, little else Clinical case management Joel Kanter, 1989 The worker is also a clinician: the relationship itself is therapeutic; links and treats Plausible; less tested as a distinct model Strengths model Charles Rapp, University of Kansas, 1980s Client directs; focus on strengths; community seen as a source of resources; outreach Promising, mostly smaller studies Rehabilitation model Anthony and colleagues, Boston Client-chosen goals; skills and supports for a chosen environment Overlaps with psychiatric rehabilitation Intensive case management 1980s onwards Small individual caseloads (fewer than about 20); more direct help Fewer hospital days where baseline use is high Assertive community treatment Stein and Test, 1970s Team with shared caseload, 1:10, in vivo, 24-hour, time-unlimited Strongest: less hospital use, stable housing The broker model is the simplest: the case manager is a kind of travel agent who books the services and leaves the person to use them. Dissatisfaction with it pushed the field in two directions. The American social worker Joel S. Kanter argued in 1989 for clinical case management , in which the case manager is a trained clinician who also offers psychotherapeutic help, uses the relationship as a vehicle of change, and attends to the person's inner world as well as their practical needs. At the University of Kansas, Charles A. Rapp and his colleagues developed the strengths model , which deliberately turns away from deficits: the client, not the worker, directs the process; the worker helps the person identify their talents, interests and aspirations; the relationship is primary; contact happens in the community; and the community is regarded not as an obstacle but as an oasis of resources (a neighbour, a temple, a tea-shop owner, a cricket club). Intensive case management cut caseloads to allow more direct help, and ACT went further still, replacing the individual case manager with a team. Social work texts also describe models in terms of the relationship between worker and client, and one examination question has asked about the task or role performance model . This model applies structure-function theory (the structural functionalism of the sociologist Talcott Parsons, whose sick role you met in Section 9.1) at the level of the organisation. The agency is a structure with functions; the case manager occupies a formal role within it; and the client is expected to perform assigned tasks, such as attending appointments, taking medicine and applying for jobs. The worker therefore holds and uses real authority : to provide, deny or withdraw services depending on whether the client complies with the tasks. Because the worker controls resources that belong to the agency and the public, the case manager carries a fiduciary obligation (to use those resources responsibly, like a trustee) as well as a humanitarian obligation to the client's welfare. The contrasting empowerment or advocacy models reject this hierarchy. In them the worker sides with the client against the barriers the client faces, shares power and decisions with them and treats them as a partner or consumer: the worker forms what is sometimes called a power alliance with the client. Holding the two side by side makes the exam question easy. Authority, compliance, organisational roles and fiduciary duty describe the task or role performance model; a power alliance does not. What should case management achieve? Not a cure. Case management is for people whose conditions are by definition long-term, and its desired outcomes are about living with the condition as well as possible: continuity of care (no one falling through the gaps between agencies), access to services and entitlements, community tenure (more time living in the community and less in hospital), skill training and acquisition , environmental accommodations (changes in the person's surroundings, such as a modified job, a supportive landlord or a family that has learned to lower its criticism, that let them function despite the condition), empowerment and a better quality of life . The treatment of the primary condition is the business of medicine and psychotherapy, and case management coordinates it; it does not claim to cure it. The evidence is sobering for the simpler models. A Cochrane review by Max Marshall and his colleagues (1998) found that standard case management kept more people in contact with services but, if anything, increased hospital admissions (probably because case managers spotted relapses and arranged admission sooner), with no clear gains in symptoms, social functioning or quality of life. ACT and well-run intensive case management did better on hospital use and housing. The lesson is that coordination alone is not enough: people with severe mental illness need someone who coordinates and helps directly, continuously, where they live. Exam trap Two RML 2020 questions. (1) The task or role performance model rests on structure-function theory at the organisational level, on the worker's authority to provide, deny or withdraw services according to the client's compliance with assigned tasks, and on the case manager's fiduciary and humanitarian obligations. "Workers form a power alliance with the client" is the EXCEPTION: power-sharing belongs to the empowerment or advocacy models. (2) The desired outcomes of case management include environmental accommodations , skill training and acquisition and empowerment ; " cure of a primary condition " is the EXCEPTION. Also know the five functions (assess, plan, link, monitor, advocate) and that the strengths model is Rapp's and clinical case management is Kanter's. Skills, families, clubhouses and peers Housing, work and coordinated care are the scaffolding of rehabilitation. Inside it, several specific interventions work on the person's skills and relationships. Most of them are taught in detail in other chapters, so here the emphasis is on how they fit together for severe mental illness. The first systematic psychological treatment for long-stay patients was the token economy , an operant programme in which patients earn tokens (exchangeable for privileges, snacks or outings) for self-care, work and social behaviour. It was developed at Anna State Hospital in Illinois by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan H. Azrin , whose book The Token Economy appeared in 1968; the method is explained in Chapter 4. Its most rigorous test was a study by Gordon Lee Paul and Robert J. Lentz (1977), who spent more than four years comparing three regimes for severely disabled long-stay patients at a mental health centre in Illinois: a social learning programme built on a token economy, milieu therapy (a therapeutic-community style of ward organised around group responsibility and expectations), and routine hospital care. The social learning programme was the clear winner. Its patients gained most in self-care, social and vocational skills, and far more of them were discharged and stayed in the community. Paul and Lentz showed that even very disabled people can learn the skills they need to live outside hospital. Token economies have since faded from use, partly because of concerns about coercion and the difficulty of keeping gains when the tokens stop, and partly because the long-stay wards they were designed for have closed. Social skills training took the learning approach into the community. The American psychiatrist Robert Paul Liberman and his colleagues at the University of California, Los Angeles, packaged it from the 1980s into structured modules, the Social and Independent Living Skills programme, on topics such as medication management, symptom management (recognising one's personal warning signs of relapse and making an emergency plan), basic conversation, recreation and leisure, and avoiding alcohol and street drugs. Each skill is broken into small steps and taught by instruction, modelling, role play, feedback and homework in real settings, the techniques described in Chapter 4. Reviews find large gains on tests of the skills taught, smaller gains in everyday community functioning and only modest effects on relapse; the persistent problem is getting skills learned in a group room to appear in a bank or a bus queue. Many people with schizophrenia also have lasting difficulties with attention, memory, processing speed and planning, and these predict everyday functioning better than hallucinations do. Two opposite strategies have been developed, and they foreshadow the distinction that Section 9.9 develops for brain injury. Cognitive remediation tries to improve the cognitive functions themselves through graded practice, usually on computerised exercises; meta-analyses, notably by Til Wykes and colleagues (2011), find moderate improvements in cognition, with gains in everyday functioning mainly when remediation is combined with other rehabilitation such as supported employment. Cognitive adaptation training , developed by Dawn I. Velligan and colleagues in Texas, does the reverse: it leaves the cognitive deficits alone and changes the person's surroundings to bypass them, with signs, checklists, alarms, labelled cupboards and pill containers placed where they will be seen. The first is a restorative approach and the second a compensatory one. The family is the setting where most rehabilitation actually happens, especially in India. Research on expressed emotion (criticism, hostility and emotional over-involvement in the family) showed that it predicts relapse, and family psychoeducation , which teaches families about the illness, its treatment and how to solve problems and communicate calmly, substantially reduces relapse rates. That story, from George Brown's studies to the modern programmes, is told in Chapter 7. Two related packages are often listed among the evidence-based practices for severe mental illness: illness management and recovery , which teaches people themselves to manage their condition (understanding the illness, using medication effectively, recognising early warning signs, coping with persistent symptoms, building social support) and to pursue personal recovery goals; and integrated dual-disorders treatment , in which the same team treats both the mental illness and a co-existing substance use problem rather than sending the person between two services that each blame the other. Not all rehabilitation is done by professionals. In the 1940s a group of former patients of Rockland State Hospital in New York began meeting to support one another and called themselves WANA, for "We Are Not Alone". In 1948, with help from volunteers, they acquired a house on West 47th Street in Manhattan with a fountain in its garden, and named it Fountain House. Under the social worker John H. Beard , who became its director in 1955, Fountain House developed what is now called the Clubhouse model . Its principles are unusual. The people who attend are members , not patients or clients, and membership is voluntary and for life. The clubhouse is run through a work-ordered day : members and staff work side by side in units that keep the clubhouse going (the kitchen, the office, reception, the snack bar, the newsletter), and the number of staff is deliberately kept too small to run the house without the members, so that every member is genuinely needed. Through transitional employment (Section 9.8.4) the clubhouse opens doors to ordinary jobs, and it also supports members in housing, education and social life. There are now hundreds of clubhouses in many countries, working to shared international standards. Members' experience of being wanted, rather than treated, is the heart of the model, though research on its outcomes is harder to interpret because the people who choose to join may differ from those who do not. The same insight lies behind peer support : people who have lived through severe mental illness and recovery are trained and employed to support others, in clubhouses, ACT teams, hospitals and self-help groups. A peer worker can say "I have been where you are" with an authority no professional has, and is living evidence of recovery. Table 9.15 brings the components of psychosocial rehabilitation together. Clinical link A clinical psychologist in a rehabilitation team does more than test and counsel. Typical tasks are functional assessment, setting goals with the person in their own words, running social skills and illness management groups, family psychoeducation, cognitive remediation, training lay and peer workers, and evaluating whether the programme actually changes lives. The most useful interview question is the simplest: "If things were going well for you a year from now, what would you be doing?" Exam trap Token economies were developed for psychiatric inpatients by Ayllon and Azrin (1968) and rest on operant conditioning (secondary reinforcers), not classical conditioning. Paul and Lentz (1977) showed that a social learning (token) programme beat both milieu therapy and routine care. The UCLA skills modules are Liberman 's. The Clubhouse began at Fountain House , New York, in 1948 , and its people are members , not patients. Do not confuse the Clubhouse with Maxwell Jones's therapeutic community (Chapter 7), which is a hospital ward run democratically. 9.9 Neuropsychological and Addiction Rehabilitation, and Disability Certification Lower yield · 1 Q On a wet evening in July, Kiran, a 24-year-old software tester, was riding pillion without a helmet on the Bengaluru to Mysuru highway when the motorcycle skidded. He spent eleven days unconscious in a neurosurgical intensive care unit. Four months later he walks almost normally and talks fluently, and a stranger meeting him for five minutes would notice nothing. His family notices everything. He asks his mother the same question five times in an hour. He cannot follow the plot of a television serial. He starts making tea and leaves the gas on. He snaps at his younger sister over nothing and then forgets that he did. And he insists, with complete sincerity, that he is ready to go back to work next Monday. Kiran's case opens the three topics of this final section. The first is how psychologists help people whose brains have been damaged. The second takes the same rehabilitation logic into addiction, where the problem is not a lost skill but a habit that keeps returning. The third is the legal machinery, disability certification, through which people like Kiran, Mr Prakash in Section 9.8 and a man recovering from alcohol dependence can claim the support the law promises them. What brain-injury rehabilitation tries to do Brain injury comes from many causes: traumatic brain injury (in India most often from road traffic crashes, frequently young men on two-wheelers), stroke, brain tumours and their surgery, encephalitis, and lack of oxygen after cardiac arrest or near-drowning. After the acute phase, most people improve for months on their own, fastest in the first six months, as swelling settles and the brain reorganises. Neuropsychological rehabilitation is what is added to that natural recovery: the planned effort to reduce the cognitive, emotional, behavioural and social consequences of brain injury and to help the person and family live as well as possible with whatever remains. The narrower term cognitive rehabilitation refers to the part that addresses thinking (attention, memory, language, perception, executive functions). The British clinical psychologist Barbara A. Wilson (born 1941), the most influential figure in the modern field, defines it broadly as any intervention that helps people with brain injury, and their families, to live with, manage, bypass, reduce or come to terms with the deficits the injury has caused. Notice that "reduce" is only one verb among five. Modern neuropsychological rehabilitation was born in two world wars, which produced large numbers of young men with penetrating head wounds who survived and needed to work. During the First World War, the German neurologist Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965) set up an institute in Frankfurt in 1916 for research on the consequences of brain injury, which combined assessment, retraining and sheltered workshops for injured soldiers. Goldstein noticed that his patients lost the abstract attitude (the ability to think in categories, shift between ideas and consider the merely possible) and were left with a concrete one, and he described the catastrophic reaction : the sudden distress, agitation or tears of a brain-injured person confronted with a task they can no longer perform. A good rehabilitation programme, he taught, arranges the environment so that such failures are avoided. During the Second World War, the Soviet neuropsychologist Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977) ran a rehabilitation hospital for wounded soldiers. In Restoration of Function after Brain Injury (1948 in Russian; English translation 1963), he argued that complex psychological functions such as reading, writing or walking are not stored in one spot but produced by functional systems : chains of brain areas working together, each contributing one link. When one link is destroyed, the function can sometimes be rebuilt by recruiting a different chain, using the intact links in a new way. Luria called this functional reorganisation , and it is the theoretical ancestor of every compensatory technique you will meet below. Key study: Luria's "man with a shattered world" In 1943 a young Soviet officer, Lev Zasetsky, was shot in the head during the fighting near Smolensk. The bullet damaged the left parieto-occipital region of his brain. He lost half his field of vision, could not read, could not find words, could not tell left from right and could not hold a sentence in his mind long enough to understand it. Luria worked with him for some twenty-five years. Zasetsky's breakthrough came when Luria encouraged him to write without stopping to think about the letters: although he could not spell letter by letter, he could write fluently if he wrote quickly without lifting the pen, using the intact motor "melody" of writing that he had learned as a child. Over a quarter of a century he wrote a diary of about 3,000 pages, struggling sometimes for a whole day over a single paragraph. Luria published it with his own commentary as The Man with a Shattered World (1972). The case shows functional reorganisation in action: a damaged route to a function was bypassed by an intact one. It also shows the limits. Zasetsky never recovered the ability to read with ease, and his world stayed shattered. In Britain the same war produced the Edinburgh brain injury unit, where the psychologist Oliver Louis Zangwill (1913 to 1987) worked with injured servicemen. In a paper published in 1947 he distinguished three approaches to retraining, and his classification is still the starting point of the field. Compensation means reorganising psychological function to minimise or get round a disability (for example, a man who can no longer remember appointments learns to rely on a notebook). Substitution means building up an entirely new method of response to replace one that has been irreparably damaged (for example, a person who cannot read by sight learns Braille, or a person with severe aphasia learns to communicate with gestures and a picture board). Direct retraining means training the damaged function itself, by practice, in the hope that it will improve. These three collapse into the two approaches that modern rehabilitation contrasts: restoring the function, or compensating for its loss. Exam trap Zangwill (1947) named three approaches: compensation, substitution and direct retraining . Luria ( Restoration of Function after Brain Injury , 1948; English 1963) gave the theory of functional systems and functional reorganisation , and wrote The Man with a Shattered World (1972) about Zasetsky. The catastrophic reaction and the loss of the abstract attitude are Goldstein 's. Cognitive rehabilitation is only one part of neuropsychological rehabilitation, which also covers emotion, behaviour, family and work. Restorative and compensatory approaches Every decision in cognitive rehabilitation sits somewhere between two strategies. The restorative approach (also called the remedial or retraining approach, and its drills cognitive retraining) aims to repair the damaged function itself, on the assumption that the brain is plastic and that repeated, graded exercise will strengthen the weakened networks, much as physiotherapy strengthens a weak muscle. The compensatory approach accepts that the function may not come back and teaches the person other ways of achieving the same goal, using intact abilities, strategies, external aids or a changed environment. Neither is always right. The choice depends on how severe the impairment is, how long ago the injury happened, how aware the person is of the problem and, above all, what the person is trying to do in daily life. The best-known restorative programme for attention came from the American speech-language pathologist McKay Moore Sohlberg and the neuropsychologist Catherine A. Mateer . Their attention process training (APT), first evaluated in 1987, rests on a clinical model in which attention is a hierarchy of five levels, each building on the one below: Focused attention : responding at all to specific visual, auditory or touch stimuli, the level that returns first after coma. Sustained attention : keeping a consistent response going over a continuous activity (vigilance), including holding information in mind while working on it. Selective attention : maintaining a response in the face of distraction, such as listening for target words while a radio plays in the background. Alternating attention : shifting the focus flexibly between tasks with different demands, such as switching back and forth between adding and subtracting. Divided attention : responding to two tasks at the same time, such as sorting cards while listening for a target word. Patients work through graded exercises at each level, moving up as they succeed. Attention training of this kind produces gains, especially when it is linked to everyday activities and combined with strategy training, but the gains on the exercises do not always show up in daily life. That last caution applies to the restorative approach in general, and it has been tested on a large scale. In 2010 the British neuroscientist Adrian M. Owen and his colleagues, working with a BBC science programme, had 11,430 healthy viewers practise online tasks of reasoning, memory, planning and attention for six weeks. The participants improved steadily on the tasks they practised, but there was no transfer to untrained tasks, even ones that were closely related. Commercial "brain training" games make people better at the games. For people with brain injury, the lesson is that drill should target, or closely resemble, the real activity the person needs. The clearest success of the restorative approach is in movement rather than thought. The American behavioural neuroscientist Edward Taub , working with monkeys whose sensory nerves to one arm had been cut, observed that they stopped using the arm even when it could move: every failed attempt was punished and using the good arm was rewarded, a pattern he called learned non-use . He reasoned that many stroke patients do the same. In constraint-induced movement therapy , the unaffected arm is restrained in a mitt or sling for most waking hours over about two weeks while the patient practises intensively with the affected arm, using shaping (Chapter 4) to reward small improvements. In the EXCITE trial (Steven Wolf and colleagues, 2006), stroke patients given this therapy three to nine months after their stroke regained significantly more arm function than controls, and the gains lasted at least a year. Here practice really did restore function, and brain imaging showed reorganisation of the motor cortex. For memory, the evidence points the other way: in people with significant memory impairment, practice at remembering (memorising lists, playing memory games) does little to improve memory itself. Rehabilitation therefore relies mainly on compensation, of three kinds: Internal strategies are mental techniques that make the most of the memory that remains: visual imagery (linking a name to a picture), first-letter mnemonics, chunking, and study methods such as PQRST (Preview, Question, Read, State, Test) for remembering written material. They require effort and some remaining memory, so they suit people with mild impairments. External memory aids move the remembering outside the head: diaries and memory notebooks, wall calendars and whiteboards, alarms, pill organisers, and today the smartphone, with its calendar reminders, notes, photographs and location tracking. They are the most useful tools for people with moderate to severe impairment, but the person has to be taught to use them, which is harder than it sounds when the problem is memory. Environmental modification changes the surroundings so less memory is needed: labels on cupboards and doors, a fixed place for keys, a written daily routine on the fridge, a quieter room for work, a family that gives one instruction at a time. A neat demonstration of external aids was NeuroPage, a simple paging system that sent timed reminders ("Take your tablets now"; "Feed the dog") to people with memory and planning problems. In a randomised trial by Wilson and her colleagues (2001), the 143 participants, most with brain injury, carried out far more of their target everyday tasks while using the pager than during the baseline period, and for many the improvement persisted after the pager was returned. Today the same principle runs on every phone. Executive problems (difficulty planning, organising, starting, monitoring and stopping) can also be helped with strategies. In goal management training , developed by the psychologist Ian H. Robertson in the 1990s and tested by Brian Levine and colleagues in 2000, people learn to interrupt automatic behaviour and run through a fixed sequence for any task: stop and ask "What am I doing?"; define the main goal; list the steps; learn the steps; and, while carrying them out, check "Am I doing what I planned?" For Kiran, that sequence written on a card beside the gas stove might prevent the forgotten kettle. Table 9.16 summarises the two approaches.
