Systematic reviews of the evidence by Keith Cicerone and colleagues for the American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine (first published in 2000 and updated several times since) have become the standard guide. In broad outline, they support attention training after traumatic brain injury, memory strategy training for people with mild memory problems and external aids for those with severe problems, training in metacognitive strategies for executive problems, visual scanning training for neglect after right-hemisphere stroke, and language therapy for aphasia after left-hemisphere stroke, and they support comprehensive holistic programmes (Section 9.9.4) for people with complex needs. Most real programmes mix restorative and compensatory methods. Exam trap Restorative = repair the function (direct retraining, drill, attention process training, constraint-induced movement therapy). Compensatory = bypass the deficit (external aids, internal strategies, environmental change). A memory notebook, a smartphone alarm or NeuroPage is compensatory, never restorative. Attention process training is Sohlberg and Mateer 's, with five levels: focused, sustained, selective, alternating, divided . Learned non-use and constraint-induced movement therapy are Taub 's. Goal management training (Robertson) targets executive dysfunction. Owen's 2010 study is the standard evidence that brain training does not transfer. Teaching people who cannot remember: errorless learning and its relatives There is a hidden trap in the way most of us learn. We guess, make mistakes, are corrected and try again. This works because explicit memory lets us remember that the first guess was wrong. Now imagine someone with severe amnesia, like Kiran at his worst. He still has implicit memory : skills and habits strengthen with repetition even when he cannot recall the learning episode. So every time he guesses wrongly, the wrong answer is strengthened implicitly, and he has no explicit memory to tell him it was the mistake. Trial and error, for him, means practising errors. The solution came from an unexpected source. In 1963 the American psychologist Herbert S. Terrace showed that pigeons could learn a difficult colour discrimination without ever pecking the wrong key, if the incorrect stimulus was introduced so faintly and briefly at first that they never responded to it, and was then gradually strengthened. He called this errorless discrimination learning, and it was applied in the 1960s and 1970s to teaching people with intellectual disability. Thirty years later two British psychologists asked whether it could help people with amnesia. Key study: Baddeley and Wilson on errorless learning in amnesia (1994) Alan D. Baddeley and Barbara Wilson taught lists of five-letter words to 16 people with severe amnesia and to young and elderly control participants, in two conditions. In the errorful condition, participants were given the first two letters and invited to guess (for example, "I am thinking of a five-letter word beginning with QU; can you guess what it is?"), so they usually produced several wrong words before being told the right one. In the errorless condition they were simply told the word ("The word beginning with QU is QUOTE") and wrote it down, so they never made a mistake. When memory was later tested by giving the first two letters, the amnesic participants performed much better on the words they had learned errorlessly, and every one of the 16 amnesic patients showed the advantage. The explanation offered was that amnesic patients learn by implicit memory, which cannot separate correct responses from errors; only explicit memory can weed out a mistake. Wilson and her colleagues went on, in the same year, to apply the method to practical goals in single patients: learning the names of therapists, programming an electronic memory aid, recognising pictures of people. The criticism is that errorless learning helps most with specific facts and routines and with severe impairment; it produces rather rigid learning that may not generalise to new situations. In practice, errorless learning means arranging teaching so that the person is prevented from making errors while learning: no guessing is allowed, the correct answer or action is supplied or modelled from the start, tasks are broken into small steps, and help is withdrawn only gradually as success is secure. It is usually combined with two related techniques: The method of vanishing cues , introduced by Elizabeth L. Glisky , Daniel Schacter and Endel Tulving in 1986 to teach amnesic patients the vocabulary needed to use a computer. The person is given a definition and the whole word; on later trials letters are removed one at a time from the end ("SAV_", "SA__") until the person can produce the word from the definition alone. If the person cannot answer, a letter is added back. Spaced retrieval , in which the person recalls a piece of information at gradually lengthening intervals (after 15 seconds, 30 seconds, a minute, two minutes and so on), with the interval shortened again after any failure. It has been used widely with people with dementia to teach a single useful fact, such as "My room is the one with the blue door". Apply them to Kiran. To teach him to check the calendar on his phone, the therapist does not ask "What should you do when you wake up?" and wait for a wrong answer. She says "When you wake up, open the calendar. Watch me," shows him, has him do it with her hand guiding his, then asks him to show her after half a minute, then after two minutes, then after five, then the next morning, prompting immediately if he hesitates so that he never practises the wrong move. Exam trap Errorless learning means preventing errors during learning, because people with amnesia learn implicitly and cannot use the memory of an error to correct it. It comes from Terrace 's errorless discrimination learning in pigeons ( 1963 ) and was applied to amnesia by Baddeley and Wilson (1994) . It is not "learning from mistakes", not shaping by reinforcing successive approximations, and not trial and error. The method of vanishing cues is Glisky, Schacter and Tulving (1986) ; spaced retrieval lengthens the gap between successful recalls. Holistic rehabilitation and the problem of awareness Remember that Kiran believes he can return to work next week. That belief may be the biggest obstacle in his rehabilitation, because a person who sees no problem has no reason to use a strategy or a memory aid. Lack of awareness of one's own deficits after brain injury is called anosognosia , a term coined by the French neurologist Joseph Babinski in 1914 for stroke patients who denied that they were paralysed. It is not the same as psychological denial: it is a deficit of self-monitoring caused by the injury itself, typically involving the right hemisphere or the frontal lobes. Bruce Crosson and colleagues (1989) distinguished three levels of awareness, arranged as a pyramid. Intellectual awareness is knowing that a function is impaired ("my memory is poor since the accident"). Emergent awareness is recognising a problem at the moment it happens ("I have just lost track of this conversation"). Anticipatory awareness is foreseeing that a problem will arise and acting in advance ("I will forget the appointment, so I will set an alarm now"). Each level depends on the one below it, and compensatory strategies need the top one. Brain injury also changes emotion and personality. Depression and anxiety are common in the year after injury; irritability, impulsivity, apathy and loss of social sensitivity, typical of frontal damage, are often harder on families than any cognitive problem. Relatives describe living with a stranger in a familiar body, and the burden on carers is heavy. These problems cannot be separated from the cognitive ones, which is why the most respected programmes treat the whole person. Holistic neuropsychological rehabilitation was developed in the 1970s and 1980s, especially by Yehuda Ben-Yishay at the Rusk Institute of New York University, who began a day programme for brain-injured adults in 1978, and by George P. Prigatano , whose Neuropsychological Rehabilitation after Brain Injury (1986) put awareness, emotion and motivation at the centre of the work. In Britain Barbara Wilson founded the Oliver Zangwill Centre for Neuropsychological Rehabilitation at Ely in 1996, named after Zangwill. Holistic programmes share several features: an intensive programme of several months, usually as a day patient; a combination of group and individual work; a therapeutic milieu in which patients and staff form a community; explicit work on awareness and acceptance, often by having patients predict their own performance and then compare the prediction with the result; training in compensatory strategies; psychological therapy for mood and identity; involvement of families; and planned return to work or other meaningful activity. Goals are set with the patient in everyday terms and progress is often measured with goal attainment scaling , devised by Thomas Kiresuk and Robert Sherman in 1968, in which each personal goal is given a five-point scale from much less than expected (minus 2) to much more than expected (plus 2), with 0 as the expected outcome. Reviews have found that holistic programmes improve community participation, productivity and self-efficacy, and they are recommended for people with complex needs after traumatic brain injury. Clinical link Assessment comes before rehabilitation: a neuropsychological evaluation maps strengths and weaknesses (the tests and batteries are in the Assessment book, and neuropsychology as a specialty is described in Chapter 10). But a test profile is not a plan. A good rehabilitation goal for Kiran is not "improve memory score by 10 points" but "Kiran will use his phone calendar to attend all his physiotherapy appointments for four weeks without reminders from his mother". Goals of this kind are specific, measurable, agreed with the person and tied to everyday life. Exam trap Anosognosia (Babinski, 1914) is unawareness of deficit caused by the brain injury itself, not psychological denial. Crosson's three levels of awareness are intellectual, emergent and anticipatory . Holistic programmes are linked to Ben-Yishay (Rusk Institute, New York), Prigatano (1986) and the Oliver Zangwill Centre (Wilson, 1996). Goal attainment scaling (Kiresuk and Sherman, 1968) rates each personal goal from minus 2 to plus 2. Rehabilitation in addiction: from detoxification to aftercare Rehabilitation after brain injury rebuilds lost abilities. Rehabilitation in addiction has a different problem. A man who has stopped drinking for three weeks in a de-addiction ward has not lost a skill; he has lost a habit, temporarily, and almost everything in his life (his friends, his evening routine, the stresses that drinking used to numb, the shop on his way home) is pulling it back. Most people treated for alcohol or drug dependence relapse at least once, most often within the first few months. Addiction rehabilitation is therefore organised less around getting people off a substance than around keeping them off it. The disorders themselves, and the pharmacology, are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book; here the focus is the sequence of psychological care. The first step, for people who are physically dependent, is detoxification : the medically supervised management of withdrawal. For alcohol this usually means a reducing course of a long-acting benzodiazepine such as chlordiazepoxide over about a week, with thiamine to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy; for opioids it means a tapering dose of buprenorphine or methadone, or clonidine to ease the symptoms. Detoxification makes stopping safe and bearable, but on its own it does almost nothing to prevent relapse. It is the doorway to treatment, not treatment itself, and a programme that discharges people after detoxification has simply arranged their next admission. After detoxification, rehabilitation usually moves through overlapping phases. Engagement and motivation come first, because ambivalence is the rule: motivational interviewing, born in the addictions field, is the main tool (Chapter 6; its use in health care is described in Section 9.4). Active treatment then teaches the person to live without the substance, using several evidence-based approaches: Cognitive-behavioural coping skills training teaches the person to recognise triggers, refuse offers, manage cravings and negative moods, and solve the problems that used to lead to use. Contingency management gives tangible rewards, such as vouchers, for verified abstinence (for example, drug-free urine samples); it is one of the most effective methods for stimulant use and is described in Chapter 4. The community reinforcement approach , introduced by George Hunt and Nathan Azrin in 1973, rearranges the person's everyday life (work, family, recreation, social life) so that sober living is more rewarding than drinking. Its family version, community reinforcement and family training, teaches relatives how to encourage a reluctant drinker into treatment. Family and couples therapy , and twelve-step facilitation, which encourages active involvement in Alcoholics Anonymous or Narcotics Anonymous (mutual-help groups are described in Chapter 7). Medication to support abstinence : disulfiram (which makes drinking unpleasant), naltrexone and acamprosate (which reduce craving), and for opioid dependence long-term opioid substitution with methadone or buprenorphine, which is a harm-reduction strategy as much as a treatment. Finally come relapse prevention (the next subsection) and aftercare : continuing outpatient contact, mutual-help groups, and sometimes a sober-living halfway house, for months or years. Does it matter which active treatment is chosen? Key study: Project MATCH (1997) By the late 1980s it seemed obvious that different alcoholics needed different treatments, and that matching clients to treatments by their characteristics would improve results. The United States National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism funded the largest psychotherapy trial ever conducted for alcohol problems to find out. The Project MATCH Research Group randomly assigned 1,726 people with alcohol problems, in an outpatient arm and an aftercare arm, to one of three twelve-week individual treatments: cognitive-behavioural coping skills therapy (twelve sessions), motivational enhancement therapy (only four sessions) and twelve-step facilitation (twelve sessions). Drinking fell sharply and similarly in all three groups and stayed down over the follow-up. And most of the predicted matching effects did not appear: client characteristics did little to predict who did best with which treatment, with a few exceptions (for example, clients high in anger did better with motivational enhancement). The conclusion was that well-delivered structured treatments work about equally well, so a four-session motivational treatment can be as effective as twelve sessions of other therapy. The criticism is that all the participants were volunteers who received unusually good care, there was no untreated control group, and matching might still matter for people with more severe or complex problems. Indian context The national survey Magnitude of Substance Use in India (2019), carried out by the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre of AIIMS for the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, found that about 14.6 percent of Indians aged 10 to 75 used alcohol, about 2.8 percent cannabis and about 2.1 percent opioids, and that only a small fraction of those dependent had ever received treatment. Treatment is offered by government centres such as the NIMHANS Centre for Addiction Medicine and the AIIMS centre, by Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts funded by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, by non-governmental organisations, and by many private "rehab centres", some of which have been exposed for locking up and beating residents. Because the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 includes mental conditions associated with the use of alcohol and drugs within mental illness, people in such centres are entitled to the Act's protections, including its prohibition of chaining. Exam trap Detoxification is not treatment ; it manages withdrawal and on its own does not prevent relapse. Motivational interviewing was developed for, and is mainly used in, substance use (Miller and Rollnick). Project MATCH (1997) found that cognitive-behavioural coping skills therapy, motivational enhancement therapy and twelve-step facilitation worked about equally , and that matching clients to treatments added little. The community reinforcement approach is Hunt and Azrin (1973) ; disulfiram is aversive, while naltrexone and acamprosate reduce craving. Relapse prevention Earlier treatment models looked at relapse in one of two ways. In the disease model, relapse proved that the person was powerless over the substance, and a single drink was the first step of an inevitable slide. In ordinary moral thinking, relapse proved weak will. The American psychologist G. Alan Marlatt (1941 to 2011) of the University of Washington in Seattle proposed a third view: relapse is the result of a failure of coping, learned and therefore preventable, and it is a process that unfolds over time rather than a sudden event. With Judith R. Gordon , he set out the cognitive-behavioural model and its treatment in Relapse Prevention: Maintenance Strategies in the Treatment of Addictive Behaviors (1985). Relapse prevention is the resulting self-management programme for maintaining change, designed for alcohol and drugs but applied since to smoking, gambling, overeating and many other habits. The model starts with a distinction that changes how both clients and clinicians think. A lapse is a single slip: one drink, one cigarette, one bet. A relapse is a return to the old pattern of use. A lapse is common and need not lead to relapse; what happens next depends on how the person interprets and handles it. Marlatt sometimes spoke of a lapse as a fork in the road, one path leading back to the old pattern and the other, a "prolapse", back towards the goal. Where do lapses happen? Marlatt and his colleagues asked people who had relapsed to describe in detail the situation in which they first used again. In an analysis of 311 initial relapse episodes, reported by Cummings, Gordon and Marlatt in 1980, among people with problems with alcohol, smoking, heroin, gambling and overeating, three kinds of high-risk situation accounted for nearly three-quarters of the episodes. The commonest were negative emotional states such as anger, anxiety, boredom, frustration and depression (about 35 percent), followed by social pressure , direct or indirect, to use (about 20 percent) and interpersonal conflict , such as an argument with a spouse or employer (about 16 percent). Marlatt grouped the high-risk situations into intrapersonal determinants (negative emotional states, negative physical states, positive emotional states, testing personal control, urges and temptations) and interpersonal determinants (interpersonal conflict, social pressure, positive emotional states with others, such as a celebration). The heart of the model is what happens in the high-risk situation (Figure 9.9). If the person has an effective coping response (leaving, refusing, phoning a sponsor, using a relaxation skill), the situation passes, the person's self-efficacy (Bandura's concept, Section 9.2) rises, and the probability of relapse falls; each success makes the next one easier. If the person has no coping response, or uses it badly, self-efficacy falls, and if they also hold positive outcome expectancies for the substance ("one drink will calm me down"; "I deserve this"), an initial use, the lapse, becomes likely. Then a second process takes over. Marlatt called it the abstinence violation effect , and it has two parts. The first is cognitive dissonance : the lapse clashes with the person's new self-image as an abstainer, and the discomfort is often resolved by abandoning the self-image ("I am an addict after all"). The second is a self-attribution of the lapse to internal, stable and global causes, such as a lack of willpower or a disease that cannot be controlled, rather than to a specific, changeable situation. The result is guilt, a sense of having lost control, and the classic thought "I have blown it now, so I might as well finish the bottle". The more intense the abstinence violation effect, the more likely a lapse is to become a relapse. Dieters know the same pattern from Section 9.4: "I ate one sweet, so the diet is ruined". Figure 9.9 Marlatt and Gordon's (1985) cognitive-behavioural model of relapse. The upper path shows how coping builds self-efficacy; the lower path shows how a missing coping response, positive expectancies about the substance and the abstinence violation effect turn a single lapse into a relapse. Marlatt added a further insight: many high-risk situations are not stumbled into by accident. People set them up, without admitting it to themselves, through a chain of covert antecedents . It often begins with lifestyle imbalance , a life with too many "shoulds" (obligations, pressures) and too few "wants" (pleasures, rest). Imbalance breeds a desire for indulgence ("I deserve a reward"), which feeds urges and cravings, which are supported by rationalisation and denial . The person then makes a series of apparently irrelevant decisions (later called seemingly irrelevant decisions): small choices that each look innocent but together lead straight into the high-risk situation. A worked example shows the whole chain. Ramesh, a 41-year-old bus conductor in Mysuru, has been sober for four months after treatment for alcohol dependence. His wife's family are pressing him over a property dispute, and he has been working double shifts to pay the loan (lifestyle imbalance). On Saturday he tells himself he has earned a relaxing evening (desire for indulgence). He decides to attend an old friend's son's wedding reception "just to show his face" (an apparently irrelevant decision), takes the long route home past the arrack shop "to avoid traffic" (another), and arrives with Rs 500 in his pocket because the shops might be open late (another). At the reception, his friends press a glass on him (social pressure, a high-risk situation) and he has no prepared way of refusing. He drinks one glass (the lapse). On the way home he thinks, "Four months wasted; I am a hopeless drunkard; my father was the same" (the abstinence violation effect, with an internal, stable, global attribution), and he stops at the arrack shop. Relapse prevention would have offered him a way out at every step: rebalancing his week, recognising "just showing my face" as a decision that leads somewhere, rehearsing a refusal ("No thanks, I have the early shift"), carrying a reminder card for the moment after a lapse ("One drink is a slip, not a failure; call my sponsor; leave now"), and reframing any lapse as a specific mistake in a specific situation from which he can learn. The techniques of relapse prevention fall into two groups. Specific intervention strategies deal with the immediate chain: self-monitoring to identify personal high-risk situations; coping skills training for them, including drink and drug refusal, assertiveness, relaxation and problem solving; enhancing self-efficacy through graded success; challenging positive outcome expectancies by recalling the full sequence of effects ("one drink calms me" versus the hangover, the fight, the lost wages); a decisional balance of the short- and long-term pros and cons of using; and lapse management, including a written plan and the cognitive restructuring of the abstinence violation effect. Global self-control strategies address the covert antecedents: restoring lifestyle balance, building "positive addictions" such as exercise or meditation, learning to recognise apparently irrelevant decisions, and coping with urges. Marlatt's best-known urge technique is urge surfing : instead of fighting a craving or giving in to it, the person observes it like a wave that rises, peaks and subsides on its own, riding it out without acting on it. Does it work? A meta-analysis of 26 studies by Jennifer Irvin and her colleagues (1999) found that relapse prevention was generally effective, particularly for alcohol problems, and was more effective in improving psychosocial adjustment than in reducing substance use itself. In 2004 Katie Witkiewitz and Marlatt revised the model into a dynamic one, in which risk factors interact and small changes can tip a person suddenly into relapse, rather than a fixed sequence of steps. And Marlatt's interest in Buddhist meditation led his group, with Sarah Bowen and Neha Chawla, to develop mindfulness-based relapse prevention , which combines relapse prevention skills with mindfulness practice in the manner of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (Chapter 5); a 2014 trial found it better than standard relapse prevention at reducing heavy drinking and drug use a year later. Exam trap Relapse prevention is Marlatt and Gordon (1985) , not Prochaska and DiClemente (stages of change) and not Miller and Rollnick (motivational interviewing). A lapse is a single slip; a relapse is a return to the old pattern. The abstinence violation effect has two parts, cognitive dissonance and an internal, stable, global self-attribution ("I have no willpower"); it turns lapses into relapses. The commonest high-risk situation is negative emotional states (about 35 percent), then social pressure and interpersonal conflict. Apparently irrelevant decisions and lifestyle imbalance are covert antecedents. Urge surfing is Marlatt's. A lapse increases relapse risk only when it is interpreted catastrophically. Therapeutic communities for addiction For people whose whole way of life is organised around drugs (whose friends use, who have no job, who may have been in prison, whose families have given up), a weekly outpatient session cannot compete with the street. The therapeutic community for addiction takes the person out of that world altogether, into a residential community where recovery is the purpose of daily life and other residents are the main agents of change. The first was Synanon, founded in Santa Monica, California, in 1958 by Charles E. Dederich (1913 to 1997), a former alcoholic who had been through Alcoholics Anonymous. Dederich ran it without professionals: residents lived together, worked to keep the house going and confronted one another's excuses in intense group sessions known as "the game". Synanon's later history is a warning. In the 1970s it turned into an authoritarian cult under Dederich's control, and it was eventually dissolved after criminal convictions of its leaders and the loss of its tax exemption. But its methods were adopted, and moderated, by programmes such as Daytop Village (New York, 1963) and Phoenix House (New York, 1967), which brought in professional staff, and they spread through the world. The American psychologist George De Leon , the leading researcher on these programmes, summarised their principle as "community as method": the community itself, its structure, relationships and daily routines, is the treatment. A traditional drug-free therapeutic community of this kind (sometimes called a concept-based or hierarchical therapeutic community) has recognisable features: A long residential stay, traditionally twelve to twenty-four months, now often shorter, moving through phases of induction, primary treatment and re-entry into the outside community. A strict structure of house rules (no drugs, no violence, no threats of violence) and a hierarchy of jobs , from cleaning to running departments, through which residents rise as they show responsibility, earning privileges and losing them for breaking rules. Peers as change agents : senior residents and staff who are themselves in recovery act as role models, and residents are expected to hold one another accountable ("acting as if" they already hold the values of recovery). Groups, including encounter groups in which residents confront one another's behaviour, alongside groups for support, education and skills. Work as therapy, with every resident contributing to running the community. A view of addiction as a disorder of the whole person, so the goal is a change of lifestyle and identity, not only abstinence. The therapeutic community for addiction should not be confused with the older therapeutic community of psychiatry, developed by Maxwell Jones in British hospitals in the 1940s and 1950s and described in Chapter 7. Jones's community was democratic : staff and patients shared decisions in daily community meetings, roles were flattened, and the community was used to understand behaviour in the here and now. The addiction therapeutic community is hierarchical and highly structured, with privileges earned by moving up a ladder of responsibility. Both use the community as the agent of change, but in opposite ways. What is the evidence? People who complete therapeutic community programmes do well, with large reductions in drug use and crime and better employment, and the longer they stay the better they do. The difficulty is that many residents leave early, often within the first few weeks, and comparisons with other forms of residential treatment show less clear advantages. The most convincing evidence comes from therapeutic communities in prisons, which reduce reoffending and return to drug use, especially when residents go on to community aftercare after release. In India, the residential model was developed by organisations such as the T. T. Ranganathan Clinical Research Foundation (TTK Hospital) in Chennai, founded in 1980, which built family involvement into its programme, and the Kripa Foundation in Mumbai, founded in 1981 by the priest Joseph Pereira, which combined the twelve-step programme of Alcoholics Anonymous with yoga and meditation. Exam trap The therapeutic community "pioneered by Maxwell Jones and characterised by the democratic involvement of staff and patients in decisions" is the psychiatric therapeutic community (Chapter 7). The addiction therapeutic community began with Synanon (Dederich, 1958) and is hierarchical , peer-led and long-term ("community as method", De Leon). Milieu therapy is the broader idea of using the whole ward environment therapeutically. Encounter groups belong to the humanistic group movement, though the addiction therapeutic community borrowed its confrontational style. Disability certification in India Kiran's family is told that he may be entitled to a disability certificate. Why would anyone want a certificate saying they are disabled? Because in Indian law almost every entitlement for people with disabilities, from a reserved government post to a railway concession, flows from a single document: a certificate, issued by a designated medical authority, stating the specified disability and its extent as a percentage. Disability certification is where the clinical psychologist's assessments turn into legal rights. The legal framework is the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (RPWD Act), which replaced the Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 and is taught in Chapter 1. Three points from it matter here. First, the Act lists 21 specified disabilities , including mental illness, intellectual disability, specific learning disabilities, autism spectrum disorder and chronic neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's disease. Second, a person with benchmark disability is one with not less than 40 percent of a specified disability, as certified, and most of the Act's special entitlements are reserved for this group. Third, the Act requires the government to notify official guidelines for assessing each disability; these were issued in 2018 and replaced by revised guidelines notified in March 2024, and certifying authorities must use them. The process is straightforward in outline. The person or family applies, since 2021 online through the national Unique Disability ID (UDID) portal, which issues both the certificate and a single identity card valid throughout India. The applicant is assessed by a designated medical authority, usually a board of specialists at a government district or teaching hospital, using the notified method for that disability. The certificate states the disability and its percentage and says whether it is permanent or temporary; a temporary certificate, common for children and for conditions that may change, must be renewed after reassessment. A person who disagrees with the decision can appeal to an appellate authority designated by the state government. Each disability has its own assessment method, and four of them are the clinical psychologist's daily business. For mental illness , the tool is the Indian Disability Evaluation and Assessment Scale (IDEAS), developed by the Rehabilitation Committee of the Indian Psychiatric Society and adopted by the government for certification in 2002 (in guidelines notified by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment that February). Using an interview with the person and the family, a psychiatrist rates disability in four areas, each from 0 (no disability) to 4 (profound disability): self-care (hygiene, dressing, eating); interpersonal activities (social relationships); communication and understanding ; and work (employment, housework or study, whichever applies). A fifth score, from 1 to 4, reflects the duration of illness, longer illness scoring higher (less than two years scores 1, two to five years 2, six to ten years 3 and more than ten years 4). The total, from 0 to 20, is the global disability score, and it is converted into a grade and a percentage (Table 9.17). Duration also limits what can be certified. Under the 2024 guidelines a permanent certificate for mental illness requires at least two years of illness; for a shorter illness the board normally issues a certificate valid only for a limited time, so that the temporary disability of an acute episode is not certified as lasting, and a person who has not yet received adequate treatment is also given only a time-limited certificate. IDEAS is used only for mental illness: intellectual disability, autism and specific learning disabilities have their own methods. Table 9.17 Converting the IDEAS global disability score into a disability grade. Global score (0 to 20) Disability grade Percentage 0 No disability 0 percent 1 to 6 Mild Less than 40 percent 7 to 13 Moderate 40 to 70 percent 14 to 19 Severe 71 to 99 percent 20 Profound 100 percent Look at what the table means for Mr Prakash in Section 9.8. If he scores 2 for self-care, 3 for interpersonal activities, 2 for communication, 4 for work and 4 for duration, his global score is 15: severe disability, above the 40 percent benchmark. A score of 6 or less, however much the person suffers, falls below the benchmark and brings few legal entitlements. The COPSI trial described in Section 9.8 used IDEAS scores as one of its outcome measures, which shows that the same scale serves both certification and research. For autism spectrum disorder , the official tool is the Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (ISAA), developed at the National Institute for the Mentally Handicapped in Secunderabad (now the National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities). Its 40 items cover six domains: social relationship and reciprocity; emotional responsiveness; speech, language and communication; behaviour patterns; sensory aspects; and cognitive component. Each item is rated from 1 (rarely) to 5 (always), using observation, an interview with the parents and the clinician's own testing, so totals run from 40 to 200. A total below 70 indicates no autism; 70 to 106 indicates mild autism, 107 to 153 moderate autism and above 153 severe autism, and each band is linked to a range of disability percentages. Under the 2024 guidelines the diagnosis itself is first established with the AIIMS-modified INCLEN diagnostic tool for autism, and ISAA is then used to calculate the disability of children aged six and over: mild autism counts as 40 to 59 percent, moderate as 60 to 79 percent and severe as 80 percent or more. A child under six is given 60 to 79 percent (moderate autism) on a temporary certificate and reassessed between the ages of six and seven. ISAA should not be confused with the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), developed in the United States by Eric Schopler and colleagues (1980), a widely used rating scale of autism severity that is not the Indian certification instrument. For intellectual disability , a clinical psychologist on the board measures intelligence and adaptive (social) functioning with standardised tests adapted for Indian children and adults (the tests are described in the Assessment book), and the level of intellectual disability fixes the percentage (under the 2024 guidelines the level is read from the social quotient on the Vineland Social Maturity Scale); a child under five is certified as having global developmental delay rather than intellectual disability. For specific learning disabilities , the guidelines require that the child be at least 8 years old, because before that age reading, writing and arithmetic are too new to judge, and the assessment compares the child's attainment with what is expected for their age and schooling after ruling out poor teaching, sensory impairment and intellectual disability. In the 2024 version, teachers screen children at eight years or in Class III, whichever comes first, and the diagnosis requires an IQ of 85 or more together with attainment at least three standard deviations below the child's current class on the NIMHANS battery for specific learning disability (or a score below 40 percent on the Grade Level Assessment Device). Table 9.18 brings the methods together. Internationally, the WHO's own measure of disability, the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0, 2010), built on the ICF of Figure 9.7, rates six domains (understanding and communicating, getting around, self-care, getting along with people, life activities, and participation in society) and appears in DSM-5 as a recommended measure. For persons with benchmark disabilities, the RPWD Act reserves not less than 4 percent of vacancies in government establishments, of which one percentage point is shared among autism, intellectual disability, specific learning disability, mental illness and multiple disabilities; it reserves not less than 5 percent of seats in government and government-aided institutions of higher education; and it gives every child with a benchmark disability the right to free education from 6 to 18 years. Certificates also open the way to disability pensions, travel concessions, tax deductions and many state schemes. For people with autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability and multiple disabilities, the National Trust Act 1999 (Chapter 1) adds a system of legal guardianship through local level committees; it does not cover mental illness, for which the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 provides nominated representatives instead. The clinical psychologist faces real dilemmas here. Under-certifying denies people their rights; over-certifying, or certifying during a temporary crisis, can attach a permanent label to a recoverable condition. Many families of people with mental illness refuse to apply at all, because a certificate stating "mental illness, 50 percent" feels like an announcement to the world, and the stigma described in Section 9.6 weighs more than the benefits. Explaining honestly what a certificate will and will not do is part of the work. Finally, it helps to know which part of the government does what, because examiners like to ask. Disability and rehabilitation in India come under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment , through its Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. That ministry administers the RPWD Act, the National Trust and the national institutes for the various disabilities, and the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI), which began as a registered society in 1986 and became a statutory body under the RCI Act 1992 (in force from 1993). The RCI regulates the training of rehabilitation professionals, including clinical psychologists, and maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register in which they must be registered to practise (Chapter 1). Mental health services, by contrast, come under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare , which administers the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, the National Mental Health Programme and NIMHANS. A clinical psychologist in India therefore works under two ministries at once: registered by a council of the social justice ministry, and practising within a health system run by the health ministry. Exam trap The Indian tool for assessing and certifying disability in autism is ISAA , the Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism. Some IHBAS papers (2020 and 2024) key the answer as CARS (the Childhood Autism Rating Scale); CARS is an American rating scale (Schopler and colleagues, 1980), not the Indian certification instrument, so the fact to know is ISAA. The catch is the examiners: IHBAS keyed CARS both times it asked, in 2020 ("The instrument used for the assessment of disability in autism is") and in 2024 ("Name of the Indian tool to assess the severity and disability of children with autism", where ISAA was one of the options). So in an IHBAS paper expect CARS to be the marked answer; in any other paper choose ISAA. IDEAS is for mental illness only, not intellectual disability. Benchmark disability = at least 40 percent . Specific learning disabilities are not certified before age 8 . The RCI is under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment , not the Ministry of Health; the National Trust covers autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability and multiple disabilities, but not mental illness. The case of the Cocoanut Grove fire, revisited Go back to Massachusetts General Hospital in the winter of 1942, where Erich Lindemann sat with the survivors and the bereaved of the Cocoanut Grove. You can now name almost everything he saw. The waves of bodily distress, the sighing and the exhaustion are grief as the whole body lives it, the meeting point of emotion and physiology that Section 9.3 explored. His "grief work" carried forward the idea of Freud's "Mourning and Melancholia" that a loss must be worked through, an idea later questioned by Wortman and Silver's "myths of coping with loss" and by Bonanno's finding that resilience is the commonest outcome; today it survives inside Stroebe and Schut's dual process model, in which healthy mourners oscillate between confronting the loss and rebuilding their lives. His delayed and distorted grief reactions are the complicated grief that Prigerson and Shear studied and that ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR now call prolonged grief disorder. And his practical finding, that most of the bereaved came through with a few interviews while a minority went wrong, is what the modern evidence on bereavement care and on psychological debriefing confirms: help offered to everyone does little, while help aimed at the people who are struggling does a great deal. Lindemann's bolder conclusion was that a few well-timed conversations at a turning point could stop a temporary crisis from hardening into a lasting disorder. Gerald Caplan, who joined him on the Wellesley project, turned that conclusion into crisis theory (a crisis is the person's reaction rather than the event, it is not an illness, it resolves within about four to six weeks, and it is a time when people are unusually open to help), into the three levels of prevention of Principles of Preventive Psychiatry (1964) and into mental health consultation (1970). The same thinking stood behind the Community Mental Health Centers Act that Kennedy signed in 1963, whose centres were meant to prevent and consult as well as to treat. When a counsellor in Mysuru sits with a student like Arjun at two in the morning, assesses lethality, mobilises his perception, support and coping and plans follow-up, she is using tools whose history begins on those hospital wards. A nightclub fire led a psychiatrist out of the consulting room and into a whole town; this chapter has followed the same road, from one patient's beliefs about illness to the communities, crisis services and rehabilitation teams that carry clinical psychology beyond the fifty-minute hour. Chapter summary 9.1 Health Psychology and Behavioural Medicine. Most deaths in India now come from non-communicable diseases whose causes are largely behavioural, which gives psychology a direct role in physical health. The biomedical model gave way to the WHO's definition of health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, to Diener's subjective well-being (life satisfaction, positive affect, low negative affect) and to Antonovsky's salutogenesis and sense of coherence. Behavioural medicine, defined by Schwartz and Weiss (1978) after the Yale Conference of 1977, is interdisciplinary; health psychology, defined by Matarazzo (1980), is psychology's own contribution to promotion, prevention, treatment, causes and the health-care system. Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) shapes care at the bedside. Mechanic described illness behaviour (1962), Freidson the lay referral system, Parsons (1951) the sick role with its two rights and two obligations, and Pilowsky abnormal illness behaviour; the sick role separates malingering, factitious disorder and conversion. 9.2 Why People Do or Do Not Protect Their Health. Knowledge alone does not produce health behaviour; each model names the beliefs that fill the gap. The health belief model, born of Hochbaum's tuberculosis X-ray study, rests on perceived susceptibility and severity (together, threat), benefits, barriers, cues to action and, from 1988, Bandura's self-efficacy. Fishbein and Ajzen's theory of reasoned action (1975) makes intention the immediate cause of behaviour, fed by attitude and subjective norm; Ajzen's theory of planned behaviour adds perceived behavioural control. Rogers's protection motivation theory (1975) sets threat appraisal against coping appraisal, so fear works only with a credible way out. Stage models, Prochaska and DiClemente's transtheoretical model and Schwarzer's health action process approach (1992), tackle the intention-behaviour gap. Only about half of chronically ill patients adhere; clear instructions, simpler regimens and patient-centred communication help, and Szasz and Hollender's mutual participation suits chronic illness. 9.3 Stress and Physical Illness. Stressors are acute (a pop quiz) or chronic (HIV, caring for a parent with dementia). Selye's general adaptation syndrome runs through alarm, resistance and exhaustion, and Holmes and Rahe (1967) measured stress by life change. Dunbar and Alexander founded psychosomatic medicine, and Alexander's specificity hypothesis tied the holy seven (peptic ulcer, essential hypertension, bronchial asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, neurodermatitis, thyrotoxicosis) to specific unconscious conflicts; it did not survive. Friedman and Rosenman's Type A pattern doubled coronary risk in the Western Collaborative Group Study, but hostility proved its toxic component; Type D and depression also worsen outcome. Type C and fighting spirit do not reliably affect cancer survival. HIV, Type 2 diabetes (most strongly linked to poor diet and inactivity) and chronic pain (Fordyce's operant approach, cognitive-behavioural treatment, Bonica's pain clinics) are behavioural problems too, and Ader and Cohen (1975) founded psychoneuroimmunology. 9.4 Behavioural Medicine Techniques and Lifestyle Change. Biofeedback, which grew from Neal Miller's experiments, feeds back muscle tension, skin temperature or heart rate so that they can be controlled, though for many conditions it does no better than relaxation, whose common element Benson called the relaxation response. Stress management packages combine education, relaxation, cognitive restructuring and skills. CBT for insomnia rests on Bootzin's stimulus control and Spielman's sleep restriction; sleep hygiene alone is not an effective treatment. Smoking cessation combines medication with behavioural support and the five As. The 10-item AUDIT screens drinking (8 or more suggests hazardous or harmful use), and positive screens lead to brief interventions built on FRAMES. Weight management relies on self-monitoring and stimulus control. Motivational interviewing (Miller and Rollnick) began in addiction work; Burke, Arkowitz and Menchola (2003) supported it for alcohol, drugs, and diet and exercise, but not for smoking. 9.5 Chronic Illness, Dying and Grief. Chronic illness is managed rather than cured. Moos and Tsu (1977) listed seven adaptive tasks, Leventhal's common-sense model describes illness representations (identity, cause, timeline, consequences, cure or control), Taylor's cognitive adaptation theory (1983) stresses meaning, mastery and self-esteem, and Tedeschi and Calhoun named post-traumatic growth. Glaser and Strauss (1965) described awareness contexts; Kübler-Ross (1969) proposed five stages of dying (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) that are not a fixed sequence; Cicely Saunders opened St Christopher's Hospice (1967) and introduced total pain, and palliative care belongs early. Grief has been described as grief work (Freud, Lindemann), phases (Bowlby and Parkes), tasks (Worden), oscillation (Stroebe and Schut's dual process model), continuing bonds and trajectories in which resilience is commonest (Bonanno). Doka named disenfranchised grief. A minority develop prolonged grief disorder, and help works best when targeted at them. 9.6 Community Mental Health. Albee argued that no mass disorder has been eliminated by treating individuals one at a time. Critiques of the asylum (Barton's institutional neurosis, Goffman's total institution), chlorpromazine and the cost of the hospitals led to Kennedy's Community Mental Health Centers Act of 1963 and to deinstitutionalisation, with its revolving door and transinstitutionalisation; Basaglia's Law 180 (1978) ended new admissions to Italy's asylums. Caplan (1964) brought Leavell and Clark's primary, secondary and tertiary prevention into psychiatry; Gordon (1983) and the IOM (1994) introduced universal, selective and indicated prevention, and Rose described the prevention paradox. Caplan's consultation (1970) has four types, theme interference arising in consultee-centred case consultation. Community psychology (Swampscott, 1965) and Rappaport's empowerment shift power towards communities. Task-sharing with lay counsellors (Patel's MANAS, Chibanda's Friendship Bench, Rahman's Thinking Healthy) narrows the treatment gap, and stigma (Goffman, Link and Phelan, Corrigan) is reduced most by contact. 9.7 Crisis Intervention. Crisis theory grew from Lindemann's Cocoanut Grove observations and Caplan's work: a crisis is a reaction to an obstacle that customary coping cannot overcome, not an illness, self-limiting within about four to six weeks and a turning point, and Aguilera and Messick's balancing factors (perception, support, coping) decide whether it occurs. Crises are developmental, situational, existential or ecosystemic, and small-scale (abuse, accidents, overdoses) or large-scale (floods, earthquakes). Crisis intervention is immediate, brief, focused and active; Roberts's seven stages begin with lethality assessment and end with follow-up, supportive therapy is its core, and it is the classic treatment for adjustment disorder. Suicide prevention relies on means restriction, responsible reporting (the Werther and Papageno effects), gatekeeper training, helplines and Stanley and Brown's safety plan. After disasters, WHO psychological first aid (look, listen, link) is recommended, Mitchell's critical incident stress debriefing is not, and trauma-informed care reshapes services. 9.8 Psychosocial Rehabilitation of Severe Mental Illness. Rehabilitation targets functioning, not symptoms. Anthony's psychiatric rehabilitation builds skills and supports for a setting the person chooses, and the WHO's ICF (2001) replaced impairment, disability and handicap with impairment, activity limitation and participation restriction. The Vermont study (Harding, 1987) and Deegan's account made recovery, a satisfying life with or without symptoms (CHIME), the guiding vision. Day hospitals treat, day care centres rehabilitate, halfway houses are transitional residences, and Housing First offers homes without preconditions. Sheltered workshops train then place; Becker and Drake's Individual Placement and Support places then trains and has the best evidence. Stein and Test's assertive community treatment reduces time in hospital. Case management assesses, plans, links, monitors and advocates, and its outcomes never include cure. Token economies (Ayllon and Azrin), social skills training (Liberman), family psychoeducation, the Clubhouse model (Fountain House, 1948) and peer support complete the picture. 9.9 Neuropsychological and Addiction Rehabilitation, and Disability Certification. Neuropsychological rehabilitation grew from Goldstein's and Luria's wartime work and from Zangwill's compensation, substitution and direct retraining (1947). Restorative methods (Sohlberg and Mateer's attention process training, Taub's constraint-induced movement therapy) repair function; compensatory methods (external memory aids, goal management training) bypass it, and errorless learning (Baddeley and Wilson, 1994) suits amnesia. Holistic programmes add work on awareness and emotion. In addiction, detoxification is only the doorway, and Project MATCH found three structured treatments roughly equal. Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention (1985) separates a lapse from a relapse, maps high-risk situations and targets the abstinence violation effect. Therapeutic communities for addiction (Synanon, 1958) are hierarchical, unlike Maxwell Jones's democratic ward. Under the RPWD Act 2016 benchmark disability is at least 40 percent; IDEAS certifies mental illness, ISAA autism, and the RCI sits under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. relapse prevention, therapeutic community, benchmark disability, Indian Disability Evaluation and Assessment Scale, Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism From the past papers Health psychology differs from behavioural medicine primarily in that (JEMAS 2025) (a) Health psychology focuses on health promotion and prevention; behavioural medicine integrates behavioural and biomedical interventions (b) Health psychology only uses medication (c) Behavioural medicine does not consider behaviour (d) Health psychology is purely neurological Answer: (a). Behavioural medicine (Yale Conference 1977; Schwartz and Weiss, 1978) is an interdisciplinary field that integrates behavioural and biomedical knowledge and techniques, while health psychology (Matarazzo, 1980) is psychology's own contribution, with a strong emphasis on promotion and prevention. The other three options are false on their face: psychologists do not treat with medication, behaviour is in the very name of behavioural medicine, and health psychology is not a branch of neurology. Which model explains health behaviour by focussing on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Health Belief Model (b) Theory of Planned Behaviour (c) Social Cognitive Theory (d) Transtheoretical Model Answer: (a) Health Belief Model. Susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers are the signature constructs of the model built by Hochbaum, Rosenstock and Kegeles from the tuberculosis screening failures of the 1950s. The theory of planned behaviour uses attitude, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control; social cognitive theory centres on self-efficacy and outcome expectancies; the transtheoretical model describes stages of change from precontemplation to maintenance. According to the Theory of Planned Behavior, which of the following factors influences an individual's intention to engage in health behaviors? (RML 2023) (a) Attitude, subjective norms and self-efficacy (b) Genetics, personality traits and socio-economic status (c) Cultural beliefs, social support and health literacy (d) Physical environment, emotional intelligence and coping strategies Answer: (a), as keyed. Ajzen's three determinants of intention are attitude toward the behaviour, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control; the paper writes "self-efficacy" for the third, which Ajzen himself regarded as closely compatible with Bandura's concept, so the key can be accepted. In your own answers write "perceived behavioural control". None of the variables in (b), (c) or (d) is a construct of the theory. In social psychology, what is the difference between conformity and compliance? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Conformity involves a change in behaviour due to social pressure, while compliance involves following direct requests (b) Compliance involves peer pressure, while conformity does not (c) Both terms refer to obedience (d) Conformity is always involuntary, while compliance is voluntary Answer: (a). In social psychology, compliance is going along with a direct request, conformity is changing behaviour to match group pressure without being asked, and obedience is following an order from an authority, so (c) merges three different things and (b) reverses the facts. Do not carry over the health psychology meaning of compliance (following medical advice, now usually called adherence) when a question says "in social psychology". Which of the following would be considered an acute stressor? (RML 2024) (a) A pop quiz (b) HIV disease (c) Marital discord (d) Colon cancer Answer: (a) A pop quiz. An acute stressor is short-lived, with a clear beginning and end, usually over in minutes or hours. HIV disease, colon cancer and a long-running marital conflict persist for months or years with no clear end, which makes them chronic stressors. Alarm, resistance and exhaustion describe three stages represented in which model of stress? (RML 2020) (a) Life events theory (b) Protection motivation theory (c) Selye's general adaptation syndrome (d) Health belief model Answer: (c) Selye's general adaptation syndrome. Hans Selye described the same nonspecific three-stage response in rats exposed to very different noxious agents. Life events theory is Holmes and Rahe's counting of life change units (1967), and protection motivation theory and the health belief model are models of health behaviour, not of stress. Which of the following factors is most directly linked to a higher risk for coronary heart disease? (RML 2024) (a) Type A personality (b) Type B personality (c) Hostility (d) Self-efficacy Answer: (a) Type A personality, as keyed. This is the classic textbook answer: in the Western Collaborative Group Study, Friedman and Rosenman's Type A men had about twice the coronary risk of Type B men. Strictly, hostility is the component of Type A that carries most of the risk, so choose hostility if a question asks for the toxic component. Type B is the low-risk pattern, and self-efficacy is a belief about one's ability, not a coronary risk factor. Which of the following factors is most strongly associated with the development of Type 2 diabetes? (RML 2023) (a) Genetics (b) Poor diet and sedentary lifestyle (c) Psychological stress (d) Exposure to environmental toxins Answer: (b) Poor diet and sedentary lifestyle. These act largely through obesity, and the Diabetes Prevention Program showed that changing them cut the incidence of diabetes by 58 percent. Genes are a real and tempting contributor (South Asians develop the disease at lower body weights), but lifestyle is the strongest and most modifiable factor; stress and toxins play smaller roles. Which of the following is NOT listed by Burke, Arkowitz and Menchola (2003) as being treatable with motivational interviewing? (RML 2022) (a) Substance-related disorders (b) Smoking cessation (c) Diabetes mellitus (d) Obsessive-compulsive disorder Answer: (d) Obsessive-compulsive disorder. (The paper misspells the third author as "Mechola".) Their meta-analysis of 30 trials covered alcohol, drugs, diet and exercise (including work with obese women with Type 2 diabetes) and smoking, though for smoking the results did not support efficacy. OCD was not among the problems studied; it is treated with exposure and response prevention. Motivational interviewing is used in the management of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Non-compliance to treatment (b) Substance abuse (c) Anxious-avoidant personality disorder (d) Bipolar disorder Answer: (b) Substance abuse. Miller and Rollnick created motivational interviewing in the addictions field, as an alternative to the confrontational style of older alcohol treatment, and substance use remains its original and best-established use. It is also used to improve adherence, which makes (a) tempting, but it is not a treatment for anxious-avoidant personality disorder or bipolar disorder as such. When crisis results in bereavement, all of the following approaches to bereavement should be considered EXCEPT: (RML 2020) (a) Bereavement is a normal process that will run its course (b) Complicated grieving requires intervention (c) Bereavement counselling, when needed, is best conducted one-by-one (d) Crisis related bereavement should always be considered traumatic grief Answer: (d). Most people bereaved in a crisis grieve normally and recover with ordinary support, so treating all of them as traumatised wastes help and may hinder recovery; "always" is the warning word. The other three are sound: grief usually runs its course, complicated grief responds to targeted treatment such as Shear's complicated grief treatment, and specialist grief work is paced to the individual, one to one. Which of the following is a proposed criterion set in the current DSM that involves cutting, burning, or otherwise intentionally hurting one's own body without the intent to kill oneself? (RML 2022) (a) Internet gaming disorder (b) Attenuated psychosis syndrome (c) Persistent complex bereavement (d) Non-suicidal self-injury Answer: (d) Non-suicidal self-injury. It is a Section III proposal: deliberate self-injury without intent to die, usually to relieve tension or distress. The other three were also Section III proposals in DSM-5 but describe different problems: impairing loss of control over gaming, mild subthreshold psychotic symptoms, and prolonged grief (which DSM-5-TR made an official diagnosis, prolonged grief disorder, in 2022). Interpersonal Therapy (IPT) does NOT typically include which of the following techniques or focus areas? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Role playing and role reversal techniques (b) Grief and bereavement work (c) Role conflict resolution (d) Role transition support Answer: (a), as keyed. Grief, interpersonal role disputes and role transitions are three of IPT's four problem areas (the fourth is interpersonal deficits), so the answer follows by elimination. Role reversal belongs to Moreno's psychodrama and Gestalt-style enactment. Do not overlearn the key: IPT manuals do list brief role play, rehearsing a difficult conversation, among their techniques; what IPT lacks is staged enactment and role reversal. Which of the following is an example of primary prevention in health psychology? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Promoting vaccination to prevent disease (b) Treating a diagnosed illness (c) Providing rehabilitation after injury (d) Surgery for chronic disease Answer: (a). Primary prevention acts on healthy people before a disorder exists and lowers its incidence (Leavell and Clark's scheme, brought into psychiatry by Caplan in 1964). Treating a diagnosed illness is secondary prevention, or simply treatment; rehabilitation after injury and surgery to limit the damage of a chronic disease deal with an established condition, which is tertiary prevention. There are small-scale events that can perpetuate a 'crisis'. All of the following are such events EXCEPT: (RML 2020) (a) tornado or flood (b) violent events such as child abuse, domestic abuse, crime (c) psychopathology that triggers a crisis, such as a suicide attempt or drug overdose (d) car accident, life-threatening illness Answer: (a) tornado or flood. Small-scale events strike one person or one family: violence, crises triggered by psychopathology and personal catastrophes such as accidents and serious illness. A tornado or flood affects a whole community at once, so it is a large-scale event (an ecosystemic crisis in James and Gilliland's terms) that calls for a community-wide disaster response. The treatment of choice for Adjustment disorder is: (RML 2024) (a) Psychoanalytic psychotherapy (b) Group psychotherapy (c) Cognitive behaviour therapy (d) Crisis intervention Answer: (d) Crisis intervention. Adjustment disorder arises within three months of an identifiable stressor and usually settles within six months, and crisis intervention is built for exactly this kind of short reaction to an identifiable stressor. Psychoanalytic and group psychotherapy are long and not focused on the precipitating event; brief problem-focused and cognitive behavioural therapies are also used, but crisis intervention is the classic answer. Which therapy is mostly needed in 'Crisis Management'? (IHBAS 2020) (a) Cognitive behavior therapy (b) Acceptance and commitment therapy (c) Expressive therapy (d) Supportive therapy Answer: (d) Supportive therapy. In the acute phase a person in crisis needs ventilation, realistic reassurance, information and guidance, environmental manipulation and support for existing coping, which are the techniques of supportive psychotherapy. CBT is useful once the person is stable, acceptance and commitment therapy builds flexibility over many sessions, and expressive therapies (art, music, dance and movement, drama) may help in the following weeks, but none is the first response. The task or role performance model of case management is based on all of the following premises EXCEPT: (RML 2020) (a) It is consistent with structure-function theory applied at the organisational level (b) Workers are expected to use their authority to provide, deny, or withdraw services based on a client's compliance with assigned tasks (c) Workers are expected to form a power alliance with the client (d) Case managers have both a fiduciary and a humanitarian obligation to clients Answer: (c). The task or role performance model applies structure-function theory (the structural functionalism of Talcott Parsons) to the agency, gives the worker real authority to provide, deny or withdraw services according to the client's compliance with tasks, and binds the case manager to fiduciary and humanitarian duties. Forming a power alliance with the client is the mark of the empowerment or advocacy models, which reject that hierarchy. The desired outcomes of case management consist of all of the following EXCEPT: (RML 2020) (a) Cure of a primary condition (b) Environmental accommodations (c) Skill training and acquisitions (d) Empowerment Answer: (a) Cure of a primary condition. Case management serves people with long-term conditions and aims at living with them as well as possible: continuity of care, access to services, community tenure, skill training, environmental accommodations, empowerment and quality of life. Treating the primary condition is the business of medicine and psychotherapy, which case management coordinates but does not claim to cure. Rosenstock, Strecher and Becker added it to the health belief model in 1988; it is part of coping appraisal in protection motivation theory and close to Ajzen's perceived behavioural control. It is a belief, not a coronary risk factor. asked 3 times The health belief model (Hochbaum, Rosenstock and Kegeles, 1950s; Rosenstock 1966, 1974): perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers, plus cues to action and (1988) self-efficacy; susceptibility plus severity is the perceived threat. It is a model of health behaviour, not of stress. asked 2 times The theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen, 1985; classic paper 1991): intention depends on attitude toward the behaviour, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control (keyed once as "self-efficacy"), and control can also predict behaviour directly. The theory of reasoned action (Fishbein and Ajzen, 1975) has only attitude and subjective norm. asked 2 times Motivational interviewing (William Miller and Stephen Rollnick) was created in the addictions field, and substance abuse is its classic use. The boy was called Dibs, and he was five years old. For almost two years he had attended a small private school on the Upper East Side of New York, and in all that time his teachers had never managed a conversation with him. Each morning he stood whimpering at the classroom door until someone led him in. Then he crept slowly around the edges of the room, keeping away from the other children; he hid, rocked himself, sucked his thumb, or lay rigid on the floor. When it was time to go home he crouched in a corner and hit out at anyone who tried to put on his hat and coat, and on some days his mother sent the family chauffeur, who simply carried him out to the car. His teachers could not decide what was wrong with him. Some days they thought he was mentally retarded, as the phrase then went. On other days they suspected that he was unusually bright, and one of them was half sure that he could read. They wondered whether he was autistic, or only very unhappy. The school psychologist and the paediatrician had each tried to test him, and he had refused to cooperate with either. The staff were close to asking his parents to take him away. Before they did, they invited a clinical psychologist, Virginia Axline, to come and observe him. Dibs came from a wealthy and highly educated family, and his parents had already reached their own verdict: he was probably mentally defective, and nothing much could be done. His mother, whom the teachers found cold and difficult, agreed to bring him to Axline's playroom once a week. Only later, in her own conversations with Axline, did the rest of the story come out. The pregnancy had never been planned. When the child seemed backward, the parents had been ashamed of him and had cut him off from the world. A neurologist had found nothing wrong with him. A psychiatrist had told them that the problem was theirs, that Dibs was an emotionally deprived child, which they could not bear to hear. And his mother, desperate to prove that he could learn, had tested and drilled him constantly without ever quite getting close to him. In the playroom Axline did something that nobody in Dibs's life had done: she let him lead. She did not quiz him, ask him to perform or tell him what to play. She watched, she put into words the feelings that his play seemed to carry, and she waited. Week by week Dibs began to talk, and the playroom filled with his inner life. He locked the doll family inside the dollhouse, then staged a fire from which the little boy doll rescued them. He sucked on a baby's feeding bottle and asked for help with his hat and shoes, as if trying out what it would be like to be little and looked after; then he read hard words aloud, painted with real skill and mended broken toys. His teachers reported that he was changing at school too. A week after the sessions ended, Dibs was given the Stanford-Binet intelligence test. His IQ was 168, far into the gifted range, and his reading was years ahead of his age. Axline told the story in Dibs in Search of Self (1964). Years later, she wrote, a friend who taught at a school for gifted boys showed her a letter that Dibs, by then fifteen, had written for the school newspaper in defence of a friend. Notice three things about Dibs, because they are true of almost every child a clinical psychologist meets. He did not refer himself: the adults around him decided that something was wrong, disagreed about what it was, and brought him. He could not explain his trouble in words; he showed it, and worked it through, in play. And his difficulty did not live inside him alone. It lived in a family and in a school, and the adults who referred him were part of the problem as well as part of the solution. This chapter is about clinical work with people who do not fit the picture of the standard adult client who walks in alone, describes a problem and asks for help: children and adolescents, older adults with failing memories and the exhausted relatives who care for them, people who seek counselling for the ordinary crises of school, work and marriage, people caught up in the legal system, and people helped through art, music, movement or a screen. Remember Dibs; you will return to him at the end of the chapter. 10.1 Children as Clients Medium yield · 3 Qs Clinical psychology was born with a child client. The first psychological clinic, which Lightner Witmer opened at the University of Pennsylvania in 1896, saw children who were struggling at school (Section 1.4). Yet for most of the twentieth century the talking therapies were designed for adults and then cut down to child size, as if a child were simply a small adult with a small vocabulary. The modern view is that working with a child is a different job, not a smaller one. It begins with a different kind of referral, uses different methods of assessment, needs different arrangements for consent and confidentiality, and rests on a different kind of knowledge: knowledge of how children normally develop. Child clinical psychology (also called clinical child and adolescent psychology) is the branch of clinical psychology that assesses, treats and tries to prevent psychological problems in children and adolescents, always in the context of their development, their families and their schools. This section takes its distinctive features one at a time and ends with how child mental health care is organised in India. Why a child is not a small adult Start with the most obvious difference. Adults usually refer themselves, or at least agree to come. Children almost never do. A child arrives because a parent, a teacher, a paediatrician or, occasionally, a court has decided that something is wrong. This has three consequences. First, the reason for referral tells you about the referrer as well as about the child. The same restless eight-year-old may be "naughty" to a strict teacher with forty-five pupils, "just a boy" to an indulgent grandmother and "hyperactive" to a parent who has been reading about attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) on the internet. Second, children are referred mostly for problems that bother adults. Disruptive, aggressive, defiant and overactive behaviour, which clinicians call externalising problems because the trouble is directed outwards at other people, gets a child noticed quickly. Anxiety, sadness, worry and withdrawal, the internalising problems , are directed inwards; they disturb nobody else and are easily missed, so the quiet, frightened child in the back row is under-referred while the child who throws chalk is referred at once. (This is one reason why boys outnumber girls in child clinics before puberty.) Third, the child may not believe there is any problem at all, or may believe that the problem is that the adults are angry with him. Motivation for change, which adult therapies largely take for granted, has to be built. The second difference is that what counts as a problem depends on age. A three-year-old who wets the bed, is terrified of the dark, throws tantrums when frustrated and talks to an imaginary friend is behaving quite normally; a ten-year-old who does all four is not. Children's fears follow a predictable sequence (strangers and separation in infancy; animals, the dark and imaginary creatures in the preschool years; injury, school and the judgement of other children later), and most of them fade without any treatment at all. So the first question a child clinician asks is not "Is this behaviour abnormal?" but "Is it abnormal for a child of this age and developmental level, in this family and this culture?" Answering it needs a working knowledge of normal development, which is taught in the Developmental book. It also needs humility, because development is a moving target: a problem may disappear, change its form or grow worse as the child moves into a new phase of life. Third, children have limited means of telling you what is wrong. A young child may have few words for feelings beyond "good", "bad" and "angry", may not be able to say when something started, and cannot step back and reflect on her own thoughts in the way that adult talking therapies require; in Jean Piaget's terms, a child below about seven is still in the preoperational stage, thinking concretely and from her own point of view. Children are also suggestible. They tend to give the answer they think the adult wants, especially in reply to a leading question, and they may agree to things they do not understand simply to please. This is why child clinicians work through play, drawing, puppets and stories, why they speak in short, concrete sentences, and why cognitive behavioural therapy for children has to be made visual and practical (Section 10.3). Fourth, a child lives inside systems that he cannot change. An adult who is miserable at work can look for another job; a child who is bullied at school or frightened at home cannot move out. His behaviour is shaped from hour to hour by the people around him, so the most powerful interventions often work through those people: parents are trained (Section 4.10 and Section 10.3), teachers adjust their classrooms, and sometimes the whole family is seen together (Chapter 7). Many child clinicians spend more time with the adults than with the child. The parents' own difficulties, a mother's depression, a father's drinking, a marriage at war, are often part of the picture and must be noticed and addressed, even though the parents did not come to be treated. This raises an ethical question that adult work rarely meets: who exactly is the client? The usual answer is that the child is the client and the parents are partners in the work, but the clinician has to keep asking whose interests a particular decision serves. Finally, there is a hopeful side to all this. Because children are still developing, help given early can change the direction of a life rather than repair damage already done. Treating a frightened, withdrawn five-year-old may prevent a depressed and isolated adolescence. That is why child work is so closely bound up with prevention (Section 9.6), and why the developmental view in the next subsection matters so much. Table 10.1 gathers the differences together.
