Answers: (1) accommodation, (2) FEAR, (3) narrative, (4) attribution, (5) Sanders, (6) reinforcement, (7) power (or strength), (8) control, (9) positive, (10) community. 10.5 Autism, Intellectual Disability and Learning Disability High yield · 8 Qs Walk into the child clinic of any large Indian hospital on a weekday morning and three groups of children will account for a large part of the queue: children with autism, children with intellectual disability, and children of ordinary intelligence who cannot learn to read, write or calculate as their classmates do. All three are neurodevelopmental conditions. They begin in the developmental period, they are rooted in the way the brain develops, and none of them is cured. That last fact changes what "treatment" means. The aim is not to remove a disease but to teach the skills the child has not acquired, to reduce the behaviour that stands in the way of learning, to change the environment so that the child can take part in it, and to support the family over many years. The criteria, causes and course of these conditions are described in the Psychiatric Disorders book, and their assessment in the Assessment book (with the Indian certification scales in Section 9.9). This section is about what clinicians do. Keep one fact from the Disorders book in mind as you read: DSM-5 requires two domains for autism, persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction, and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests. Almost every intervention you are about to meet targets one or both of them. Exam trap The DSM-5 questions on autism (the full criteria are in the Disorders book). What a diagnosis requires is persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts (criterion A), together with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities (criterion B), present from the early developmental period (JEMAS 2025). Delayed speech alone, intellectual disability and hyperactivity-impulsivity are not required, and an IQ below 70 is not a core symptom (IHBAS 2024): DSM-5 records intellectual and language impairment as specifiers ("with or without accompanying intellectual impairment", "with or without accompanying language impairment"). Even so, intellectual disability and language disorder are frequently associated with autism, and ADHD is among the commonest co-occurring conditions; DSM-5, unlike DSM-IV, allows autism and ADHD to be diagnosed together. Hence language development is compromised most commonly in autism , not in ADHD or specific learning disability (JEMAS 2025), and no eye contact, delayed language and repetitive movements together point to autism spectrum disorder (IHBAS 2025). Autism, ADHD, intellectual disability and specific learning disorder are all neurodevelopmental disorders; OCD, borderline personality disorder and generalised anxiety disorder are not (IHBAS 2024). From Kanner to the refrigerator mother: how autism was discovered In October 1938 a lawyer from the small town of Forest, Mississippi, brought his five-year-old son Donald to the child psychiatry clinic of the Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. Donald seemed happiest when he was left alone. He did not look up when his father came home, he paid no attention to other children, and he spent hours spinning blocks, pans and lids. He repeated words and phrases he had heard, often long after he had heard them, and flew into a rage if anything in his routine was changed. Yet he could recite long passages and lists from memory. The psychiatrist who saw him was Leo Kanner (1894 to 1981), an Austrian-born physician who had come to the United States in 1924 and had written the first English-language textbook of child psychiatry, Child Psychiatry (1935). Over the next few years Kanner collected ten more children who resembled Donald. Key study: Kanner's eleven children (1943) Question. Did these children, until then labelled feeble-minded, schizophrenic or deaf, share a single condition of their own? Method. Kanner described in detail eight boys and three girls whom he had seen at Johns Hopkins, drawing on his own observation and on long histories from their parents. Result. In "Autistic disturbances of affective contact", published in the journal Nervous Child in 1943, he identified two cardinal features present from early life: an "extreme autistic aloneness", a powerful desire to be left alone and an inability to relate in the ordinary way to people, and "an anxiously obsessive desire for the maintenance of sameness". Around them clustered other features: delayed or unusual language, with echolalia (repeating others' words), reversal of pronouns ("you want a biscuit" meaning "I want a biscuit") and very literal use of words; fascination with objects rather than people; and islands of excellent rote memory. Conclusion. Kanner argued that this was a distinct syndrome, an inborn inability to form the usual affective contact with people, which, from 1944, he called early infantile autism . Criticism. The sample was small and highly selected, mostly children of educated, professional parents. Kanner's remarks about those parents, whom he described as intellectual, serious and undemonstrative, seeded a disastrous theory of cause, as you will see next. A year later, in wartime Vienna, the paediatrician Hans Asperger (1906 to 1980), who had not read Kanner's paper, described four boys whom he called "autistic psychopaths". They spoke fluently, sometimes in an adult, pedantic way, but their conversation was one-sided; they had intense, narrow interests, poor understanding of other people, odd eye contact and clumsy movement. Asperger's 1944 paper, written in German, was hardly known in the English-speaking world until the British psychiatrist Lorna Wing (1928 to 2014) drew attention to it in 1981 and proposed the name "Asperger's syndrome". Asperger's disorder entered DSM-IV in 1994; DSM-5 (2013) folded it, together with autistic disorder and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified, into a single autism spectrum disorder. In 2018 the historian Herwig Czech published evidence that Asperger had cooperated with the Nazi regime's programme for "euthanasia" of disabled children, referring some children to the Am Spiegelgrund clinic in Vienna where children were killed (some later scholars dispute that he knowingly took part in the killings), and many clinicians now avoid his name as a label. Two older names sometimes appear in the options. The word "autism" itself was coined by the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler in 1911 for the withdrawal into an inner world that he saw in schizophrenia, one of his "four As" (the Disorders book). And in 1925, in Moscow, the child psychiatrist Grunya Sukhareva had described six boys with very similar features, a paper that became widely known only recently. Wing also did something of great practical importance. In 1979, with Judith Gould, she surveyed all the children with special needs in the London borough of Camberwell and found that the children with autistic features shared a triad of impairments : in social interaction, in communication, and in imagination (with rigid, repetitive behaviour in its place). The triad shaped DSM-IV's three criteria; DSM-5 merged social interaction and communication into one domain, leaving the two you met at the start of this section. Now to the theory of cause that shaped treatment for twenty years. In 1949 Kanner wrote that the children he saw had been "kept neatly in refrigerators which did not defrost", and out of remarks like this grew the refrigerator mother hypothesis: that autism is a child's withdrawal from a cold, rejecting mother. Its loudest champion was the Austrian-born psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim (1903 to 1990), who ran the Orthogenic School in Chicago. In The Empty Fortress (1967) he compared children with autism to prisoners in concentration camps, who had withdrawn from an environment they experienced as deadly, and he treated them by separating them from their parents. Psychodynamic treatments aimed at building the child's ego did not help, and the theory caused a generation of parents, mothers above all, to feel guilty for their children's disability. The counter-attack came from research and from parents. Bernard Rimland (1928 to 2006), a research psychologist whose own son had autism, argued in Infantile Autism (1964) that the condition is biological, and helped found the Autism Society of America in 1965. Eric Schopler, whom you will meet in a moment, showed that parents of children with autism did not differ from other parents and could be their children's best teachers. In 1977 Susan Folstein and Michael Rutter reported a much higher concordance for autism in identical than in fraternal twins, the first strong evidence of its heritability. By the 1980s the blaming of parents had been abandoned, and the questions became practical ones: what can these children learn, and how should they be taught? Exam trap "Infantile autism was first described by..." Leo Kanner , in 1943 (IHBAS 2020 and IHBAS 2025). Hans Asperger (1944) described the verbally fluent form, now inside autism spectrum disorder. Eugen Bleuler (1911) coined the word autism, but as a symptom of schizophrenia, not as a childhood syndrome. Kurt Schneider is known for the first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia; Norman Cameron for over-inclusive thinking in schizophrenia; Kurt Goldstein for the loss of the abstract attitude (concrete thinking) after brain injury; and "Jasper" in the IHBAS 2020 options most likely means Karl Jaspers , the founder of phenomenological psychopathology ( General Psychopathology , 1913). Lovaas treated autism; he did not describe it. Bettelheim blamed "refrigerator" parents; Rimland (1964) argued for a biological cause. And the double-bind theory (Gregory Bateson and colleagues, 1956) was a family theory of schizophrenia , not of autism (Chapter 7). The behavioural foundation: early intensive teaching and functional communication Section 4.6 told the story of Ole Ivar Lovaas at the University of California, Los Angeles: his 1987 report that 9 of 19 children who received about 40 hours a week of one-to-one behavioural teaching before the age of four reached normal functioning, against 1 of 40 controls, and the criticism that cut that claim down. What survives is early intensive behavioural intervention (EIBI), built on discrete trial training, which helps many children a great deal and cures none. The same section introduced functional communication training, devised by Edward Carr and V. Mark Durand in 1985, in which a child whose tantrums are maintained by escape from difficult tasks is taught to ask for a break or for help instead. Rather than retell those stories, this subsection adds the idea that turned them into everyday clinical practice. The idea is that problem behaviour is communication. A child with little or no speech who bangs his head, bites or screams is usually doing so because the behaviour works: it gets him something or gets him out of something. Behaviour analysts sort the possible functions into four. Attention : the behaviour brings adults running. Escape : it ends or postpones a demand, a noise or a crowded room. Tangible : it produces a toy, a food or an activity. Sensory (or automatic): the behaviour is reinforcing in itself, as rocking or flicking fingers in front of the eyes may be. To identify the function, clinicians use direct observation of antecedents and consequences (the ABC chart of Section 2.8), interviews and rating scales such as the Motivation Assessment Scale (Durand and Daniel Crimmins, 1988), and sometimes a formal functional analysis in which the suspected consequences are arranged one at a time under controlled conditions. Once the function is known, the replacement response must meet two tests. It must be functionally equivalent , producing the same reinforcer as the problem behaviour; and it must be more efficient , easier and faster, so that the child has no reason to go back to screaming. A child who escapes by biting will not give up biting for a "break" card that is honoured only after five minutes of argument. When functional communication training is combined with making demands easier, with extinction of the old route to the reinforcer, and with lots of reinforcement for everything else, severe behaviour often falls dramatically. Punishment-based procedures such as overcorrection (Section 4.6) are now reserved for dangerous behaviour that has not responded to these positive methods, under supervision. This combination is the core of the positive behaviour support approach you met in Section 4.6, and it is the first thing a clinician should reach for when a child with autism or intellectual disability is referred for "aggression". Aarav, the boy from Bengaluru whose functional communication training you followed in Section 4.6, is now four and a half. His head-banging is rare, he uses his "break" and "top please" cards many times a day, and he has a few dozen words. His parents want him to join an ordinary preschool next year, to talk more, to cope with the barber and the doctor, and to play with his cousins. The interventions in the rest of this section are the tools his team now draws on. Exam trap "A child with autism is taught to request a 'break' using a picture card instead of engaging in a tantrum. This intervention is a key component of..." applied behaviour analysis (Real PYQ 2024). The specific technique is functional communication training (Carr and Durand, 1985), a form of differential reinforcement of alternative behaviour. It is not CBT (which needs the verbal reasoning many such children lack), not play therapy and not psychoanalytic psychotherapy. The "Lovaas programme" uses behaviour modification for autism (RML 2022). Overcorrection is keyed for repetitive aggressive behaviour in autistic children (IHBAS 2020; Section 4.6). The four functions of problem behaviour are attention, escape, tangible and sensory . Structured teaching: TEACCH While Lovaas was building his programme in California, a very different one was taking shape on the other side of the United States. Eric Schopler (1927 to 2006) was born in Fürth, Germany, and came to the United States as a refugee child. He trained in clinical psychology and joined the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1964, where he and the psychiatrist Robert Reichler ran a research project on children with autism. Two of their findings went against the received wisdom of the time. First, parents were not the cause of the problem; working alongside the therapists, they were the most effective teachers their children had. Second, the children understood what they saw far better than what they heard. In 1971 the project became TEACCH , short for Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication Handicapped Children, and in 1972 its methods were extended across North Carolina's schools and clinics as a statewide programme. Gary Mesibov, who later directed it, and Schopler set out its methods in a series of books. TEACCH starts from a different question from Lovaas. Lovaas asked how to change the child so that he would fit the world; TEACCH asks, in addition, how to change the world so that it makes sense to the child. Its writers speak of a "culture of autism": a way of thinking that is strong on visual processing, rote memory and attention to detail, and weak on understanding language, time, sequence and other people's intentions. Instead of fighting this style, TEACCH builds on it. The programme serves people of all ages, from diagnosis to adulthood, and treats parents as co-therapists. Its central method is structured teaching , which has four components. Physical structure. The classroom or home is divided into clearly marked areas, each for one purpose (a work table, a play corner, a snack area, a quiet place to calm down), with visual boundaries such as shelves or coloured tape and as few distractions as possible, so that the place itself tells the child what happens there. Visual schedules. The sequence of the day is shown in a form the child can understand: real objects for a child at an early level (a cup means snack), then photographs, line drawings or written words. The child checks the schedule at each transition, which makes the day predictable and transitions less frightening. Work systems. Each work session is organised so that it answers four questions without words: What work am I to do? How much? How will I know when I have finished? What comes next? Typically, tasks are placed in trays on the left, the child does each one and puts it in a "finished" basket on the right, and a picture at the end shows the reward or the next activity. Visual structure of tasks. Each task carries its own visual instructions (a picture of the completed product, materials arranged in order, the relevant part highlighted), so the child can work independently instead of waiting for an adult's prompt. Independence is the point. A child who has learned to follow a schedule and a work system can work alone in a classroom, and later at a job, in a way a child who depends on an adult's spoken prompts cannot. For Aarav, the team builds a picture schedule for the mornings (toilet, bath, breakfast, shoes, school van) and a simple work system for his puzzles and matching tasks; tantrums at transitions fall as soon as he can see what is coming. How good is the evidence? Reviews describe TEACCH's results as positive but modest: gains in some skills, such as social behaviour and fine motor skills, and reductions in parents' stress, with inconsistent effects on communication and daily living skills. It has fewer randomised trials than the behavioural and naturalistic programmes, but its visual supports have been absorbed into almost every autism programme in the world, including those that call themselves ABA. Exam trap TEACCH = Eric Schopler , University of North Carolina (1971; statewide from 1972), structured teaching with physical structure, visual schedules, work systems and visual task organisation. Do not attribute it to Lovaas (UCLA, discrete trials) or to Bondy and Frost (PECS). Schopler was also one of Lovaas's sharpest critics (Section 4.6), and the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) is his group's assessment tool, which is not the Indian certification instrument (ISAA; Section 9.9). IHBAS 2024 nevertheless keyed CARS as "the Indian tool to assess the severity and disability of children with autism"; the correct fact is ISAA, and Section 9.9 explains how to handle that key. The paper's other two options are not autism tools at all: the Children's Global Assessment Scale (CGAS) is a single rating, from 1 to 100, of a child's overall functioning, and the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) is Achenbach's broad parent-report checklist of behavioural and emotional problems (Section 10.1). Expand the acronym correctly: Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication Handicapped Children. Communication without speech: PECS and augmentative communication Perhaps a quarter to a third of children with autism, in different estimates, never develop enough speech to meet their daily needs. For them, clinicians use augmentative and alternative communication (AAC): any method that supplements or replaces speech. Unaided AAC uses only the body (gestures, signs). Aided AAC uses something outside the body: a board or book of pictures, a speech-generating device, or an app on a tablet that "speaks" a word when its picture is touched. Parents often fear that a picture system will stop their child from ever talking. The research says the opposite: reviews have found no evidence that AAC inhibits speech, and some evidence that it helps speech emerge. The best-known aided system began with a practical frustration. In 1985 Andrew Bondy , a psychologist, and Lori Frost , a speech and language therapist, were working in the Delaware Autistic Program in the United States. They noticed that children who had been taught to point to pictures or to label them on request still did not initiate communication: they waited for an adult to ask. So they designed the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS), in which, from the first day, the child goes up to another person and hands over a picture in exchange for what he wants. In behavioural terms the child is taught a request (Skinner called it a mand ) that is reinforced by the very thing requested; in everyday terms, the child learns that communication is something you do to another person and that it pays. PECS is taught in six phases (Figure 10.7), each mastered before the next. Phase 1, how to communicate. The child sees something he wants (a biscuit) and is physically guided to pick up its picture and put it in the adult's hand, and gets the biscuit at once. Two adults are used: the communicative partner in front, who holds the biscuit, and a physical prompter behind the child, who guides his hand and fades the help as quickly as possible. No spoken prompts ("What do you want?") are used, so that the child initiates. Phase 2, distance and persistence. The child learns to fetch the picture from a communication book and to travel to a partner who is across the room, or a different person, or in a different place, and to persist until he is noticed. Phase 3, picture discrimination. The child learns to choose the right picture from two and then from many, so that "biscuit" brings a biscuit and "ball" brings a ball. Phase 4, sentence structure. The child builds a sentence on a strip, an "I want" card followed by the picture, and hands over the strip. The adult reads it aloud and pauses before giving the item, which often draws out the child's own speech. Attributes (big, red, two) are added later. Phase 5, answering a direct question. The child learns to answer "What do you want?" with the sentence strip. Phase 6, commenting. The child learns to answer "What do you see?", "What do you hear?" and "What is it?" ("I see a bus"), and to comment spontaneously, which shares an experience rather than asking for a thing. Phases 1 to 5: requesting Phase 6: commenting Move up one phase at a time Phase 1: How to communicate Hand over one picture, receive the item Phase 2: Distance and persistence Seek out a listener in any setting Phase 3: Picture discrimination Choose the right picture from several Phase 4: Sentence structure Build "I want" + picture on a strip Phase 5: Answering a question "What do you want?" "I want juice." Phase 6: Commenting "What do you see?" "I see a bus." Figure 10.7 The six phases of the Picture Exchange Communication System (Bondy and Frost, 1985). Notice that the child learns to initiate a request first and to comment last, and that a spoken question is not introduced until Phase 5. The evidence for PECS is good for what it was designed to do. Meta-analyses find that it reliably teaches children to request, often within weeks; the evidence is weaker for maintenance over time, for generalisation to new people and settings, and for the later phases, and it is best seen as a first communication system that may later be replaced by speech or by a more flexible device. For Aarav, whose few words are not enough to ask for most things, PECS begins at Phase 1 with his favourite foods and toys; within two months he is carrying his book to his grandmother in the kitchen, and the delay built into Phase 4 brings out "want" and "juice" in his own voice. Exam trap PECS = Andrew (Andy) Bondy and Lori Frost , Delaware, 1985 , six phases : (1) how to communicate (the physical exchange), (2) distance and persistence, (3) picture discrimination, (4) sentence structure ("I want" strip), (5) answering "What do you want?", (6) commenting. It teaches requesting first and commenting last, and the child initiates without a spoken prompt in Phase 1. PECS does not stop children from learning to speak. Do not confuse it with social stories (Carol Gray, next subsection) or with facilitated communication (discredited, as you will see shortly), in which another person holds the child's hand while he types. Teaching social understanding: social stories and social skills training Imagine trying to get through a wedding, a birthday party or a haircut if nobody had ever explained to you what happens there, why people do what they do, and what is expected of you, and if you could not pick these things up by watching. That is the position of many children with autism, and it is the problem that Carol Gray , an American teacher of children with autism in Jenison, Michigan, set out to solve at the start of the 1990s (1991 is the year usually cited; Gray's own account dates her first stories to 1990). A social story is a short, individualised story, written from the child's point of view and often illustrated, that describes a particular situation, the cues that matter in it, what other people are thinking and feeling, and what the child might do. It is read with the child before the situation, often for several days. Gray specified the kinds of sentences a story should contain: descriptive sentences, which state the facts (where, who, what happens, why); perspective sentences, which describe other people's thoughts and feelings; directive sentences, which suggest a response, gently ("I will try to..."); affirmative sentences, which state a shared value or a rule; cooperative sentences, which say what others will do to help; and control sentences, which the child writes himself to remember the strategy. Her rule is that a story should describe much more than it directs: two to five descriptive, perspective, cooperative or affirmative sentences for every directive or control sentence. Here is the story Aarav's mother writes for his first visit to the barber. "Sometimes my hair grows long. Amma takes me to the barber shop to cut it. The barber has a big chair and a pair of scissors. The scissors make a snip-snip sound. Many children feel a little worried at the barber. That is okay. The barber wants my hair to look nice. I will try to sit still in the big chair. Amma will hold my hand and sing my song. When the haircut is finished, I can play with my top." Count the sentences: one directive ("I will try to sit still") among nine others, comfortably inside Gray's ratio. Social stories are cheap, safe and easy for parents and teachers to write, and they are used everywhere. The research evidence, however, is limited: reviews find inconsistent and generally modest effects, and because stories are usually combined with other methods it is hard to say how much of the change they produce. They are best treated as one helpful ingredient, not a treatment. For verbally fluent older children and adolescents, the main approach is social skills training in small groups, using instruction, modelling, role-play, feedback and homework in real settings (the general method is described in Section 4.7). Video modelling , in which the child watches a short film of someone (sometimes himself, edited to show success) performing a skill such as greeting or taking turns, exploits the visual strengths TEACCH builds on. Peer-mediated interventions train typically developing classmates to invite, prompt and respond to the child with autism, which takes the teaching into the playground where it is needed. Learning through play: naturalistic and developmental approaches Discrete trial training at a table is efficient, but, as Section 4.6 noted, skills learned there often stay there. From the 1980s onwards, two groups of researchers moved the teaching onto the floor. Behaviour analysts began to teach during play and daily routines, following the child's interests and using natural consequences; developmental psychologists began to build programmes around the social and emotional milestones that children with autism miss, such as joint attention (looking back and forth between an adult and an object to share interest in it), imitation and pretend play. The two streams met in what are now called naturalistic developmental behavioural interventions. Three of them appear in examinations. The first, pivotal response treatment (PRT), was developed by Robert L. Koegel (who had worked with Lovaas) and Lynn Kern Koegel , from a "natural language paradigm" for teaching speech that they described in 1987. Its premise is that a few pivotal areas, once improved, produce widespread gains in many untaught behaviours. The pivotal areas are motivation (the most important), responding to multiple cues (attending to more than one feature of a situation, which children with autism often fail to do), self-management and self-initiation of social interaction. To raise motivation, PRT lets the child choose the toy or activity, varies the tasks, intersperses easy, already-mastered tasks among new ones, reinforces reasonable attempts and not only perfect responses, and uses natural reinforcers : when the child says "ball", he gets the ball, not a sweet. A 2020 meta-analysis of randomised trials found a benefit for expressive language, and possibly for social interaction, while rating the quality of the evidence as low. The second, the Early Start Denver Model (ESDM), was developed by Sally J. Rogers and Geraldine Dawson for toddlers aged about 12 to 48 months. It grew from a play-based preschool programme that Rogers and her colleagues began in Denver in the 1980s, and it adds techniques from PRT. Teaching takes place inside "joint activity routines", playful exchanges such as blowing bubbles or singing action songs, in which the adult follows the child's interest, keeps positive emotion high, and works through a developmental curriculum of imitation, joint attention, communication, play and social skills, using behavioural principles (prompting, shaping, reinforcement) to teach each step. Parents are coached to use the same routines at home. Key study: Dawson's randomised trial of the Early Start Denver Model (2010) Question. Can an intensive, play-based, developmental and behavioural programme begun in toddlerhood improve the outcome of autism, tested in a properly randomised trial? Method. Geraldine Dawson, Sally Rogers and their colleagues randomly assigned 48 children diagnosed with autism at 18 to 30 months of age either to ESDM or to the intervention ordinarily available in their community, for two years. The ESDM children received a mean of about 15 hours a week of therapy from trained therapists at home, and their parents reported using ESDM strategies for about 16 hours a week more. Result. Over two years the ESDM group's mean composite cognitive score rose by 17.6 points, against 7.0 points in the comparison group; adaptive behaviour improved more; and seven ESDM children (30 percent), against one comparison child (5 percent), moved from a diagnosis of autistic disorder to the milder pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified. Conclusion. Intensive early intervention that combines developmental and behavioural methods can improve intellectual and adaptive outcomes in toddlers with autism. Criticism. The sample was small and from one research centre, and the comparison group received much less intervention. A larger, three-site trial published in 2019 replicated the advantage for language only, with no significant differences in developmental quotient, autism severity or adaptive behaviour, and a brief parent-delivered version tested in 2012 did no better than community care. The third approach comes from outside behaviour analysis altogether. The American child psychiatrist Stanley Greenspan (1941 to 2010), working with the psychologist Serena Wieder , built the DIR/Floortime model. DIR stands for Developmental, Individual-difference, Relationship-based: it describes the child's level on a ladder of "functional emotional" capacities (from shared attention and engagement, through two-way gestural communication and problem-solving, to the use of ideas in pretend play and logical, emotional thinking), the child's individual differences in sensory processing and motor planning, and the relationships through which development happens. Floortime is the method: the adult literally gets down on the floor, follows the child's lead, joins whatever he is doing (even lining up cars) and playfully extends it, so that the child must respond, "opening and closing circles of communication" that grow longer over time. The evidence for DIR/Floortime is thinner than for ESDM or PRT, consisting of a few small trials. A related, more tightly researched programme, JASPER (developed by Connie Kasari and her colleagues), targets joint attention, symbolic play, engagement and regulation directly. What do these approaches mean in a country with very few autism specialists? Their common thread is that the most important "therapists" are the people who spend the most time with the child. In the Preschool Autism Communication Trial (PACT), published in 2010 by Jonathan Green and colleagues in the United Kingdom, parents of 152 children aged two to four were filmed playing with their children and coached, using the videos, to notice and respond to their child's communication. Parent-child interaction improved, and a follow-up published in 2016 found a modest reduction in the children's autism symptoms about six years later. Indian context The PACT approach was adapted for South Asia as PASS (Parent-mediated intervention for Autism Spectrum disorders in South Asia) by Atif Rahman, Gauri Divan of the Goa-based organisation Sangath, and their colleagues. Non-specialist health workers, not autism professionals, delivered 12 sessions of video-feedback coaching to the parents of children with autism aged two to nine in Goa (India) and Rawalpindi (Pakistan). In a randomised trial of 65 children, published in The Lancet Psychiatry (2016), PASS improved the quality of parent-child interaction compared with usual treatment, and 81 percent of families completed the programme. It is an example of the task-shifting you met in Section 9.6: a treatment designed for a rich country, carried by ordinary health workers to families who would otherwise receive nothing. What does not work: the lesson of facilitated communication Parents of a child with a lifelong condition are understandably vulnerable to anyone who promises a cure, and the history of autism is crowded with treatments that were sold before they were tested. Clinicians need to know them, both to advise families and to understand why evidence matters. Key study: Testing facilitated communication (1993) Question. In 1977 the Australian special educator Rosemary Crossley began to support the hands of people with severe disabilities as they pointed at letters, and in 1990 the American education professor Douglas Biklen introduced the method, called facilitated communication , to the United States. Through a "facilitator" steadying their hand or arm over a keyboard, young people who had never spoken appeared to type poems, essays and conversations, and some typed accusations that their parents had sexually abused them. Were the messages really theirs? Method. At the O. D. Heck Developmental Center in New York, Douglas Wheeler and his colleagues (1993) tested clients with autism together with their usual facilitators. Client and facilitator sat on either side of a screen and were each shown a picture; sometimes the pictures were the same, sometimes different, and neither could see the other's. Result. The clients typed correct answers only when the facilitator had seen the same picture; when the pictures differed, the typed answer named the picture the facilitator had seen. Conclusion. The facilitators, sincerely and without realising it, were producing the messages, through the ideomotor effect (the tiny, unconscious muscle movements that also move a Ouija board). By the mid-2000s dozens of controlled studies had reached the same conclusion, and in 1994 the American Psychological Association resolved that facilitated communication had no scientifically demonstrated support. Criticism. Supporters argued that testing made the clients anxious, but no controlled test has ever shown authorship by the disabled person. Meanwhile families had been torn apart by abuse allegations that came from the facilitator's keystrokes. Facilitated communication is the field's great cautionary tale, and its lesson reaches far beyond autism: the sincerity of practitioners and the delight of families are not evidence, and a claim that can be tested by a simple control must be tested. Other unsupported or harmful treatments are worth naming. Sensory integration therapy , developed by the American occupational therapist A. Jean Ayres (1920 to 1988), uses swings, brushing, weighted vests and similar activities on the theory that problems in processing sensory input underlie the child's difficulties; reviews have found little evidence that it changes behaviour or learning, although simply accommodating real sensitivities (ear defenders in a noisy hall) is sensible. Special diets such as gluten-free and casein-free diets have no consistent support in controlled trials. Chelation , which removes heavy metals from the blood, is dangerous and has caused deaths. The fear that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine causes autism came from a 1998 paper by Andrew Wakefield that was retracted in 2010; large population studies, including those from Denmark, have found no link, and refusing vaccination puts children at real risk. Medicines have a limited but genuine place. No drug treats the core social and communication features of autism. Two antipsychotics, risperidone and aripiprazole, were approved in the United States (in 2006 and 2009) for the severe irritability, aggression and self-injury that some children show, and stimulants can help co-occurring ADHD. They are adjuncts to teaching, not substitutes for it. Table 10.12 brings the interventions of this section together. Table 10.12 The main interventions for autism compared. Risperidone and aripiprazole treat irritability and aggression, not the core features. Psychoanalytic treatment based on the refrigerator-mother theory did not help. Intellectual disability: training, education and support In January 1800 a boy of about twelve, naked and scarred, came out of the woods near the village of Saint-Sernin in the Aveyron region of southern France. He did not speak, ate like an animal and seemed indifferent to heat and cold. He was taken to the National Institute for Deaf-Mutes in Paris, where the great psychiatrist Philippe Pinel examined him and pronounced him an incurable "idiot". A young physician at the institute, Jean Marc Gaspard Itard (1774 to 1838), disagreed. He believed the boy's state was the product of isolation, and for five years he tried to educate "Victor", training his senses, his attention and his social responses with an ingenuity that anticipated many modern methods. Victor learned to recognise some written words, to understand simple requests and to show affection, but he never learned to speak more than a word or two, and Itard, in his reports of 1801 and 1806, counted the project a failure. His student Edouard Seguin (1812 to 1880) drew the opposite lesson: if systematic training could achieve that much, children with intellectual disability could be taught. Seguin's "physiological method" of graded sensory, motor and practical training, set out in his treatise of 1846 and taken to the United States after he emigrated, became the basis of special education, and Maria Montessori (1870 to 1952) adapted his materials, first for children with intellectual disability in Rome and then for all children. From the start, the answer to intellectual disability was education, not cure. The definition of intellectual disability (significant limitations in both intellectual functioning, roughly two standard deviations below the mean, and adaptive behaviour, beginning in the developmental period) and its levels belong to the Disorders and Assessment books. Two ideas from the field's history, however, govern how clinicians work. The first is normalisation , formulated in Scandinavia by Bengt Nirje (1969) and spread in North America by Wolf Wolfensberger (1972): people with intellectual disability should have patterns of daily life as close as possible to those of everyone else, living in ordinary homes, going to school, working and having relationships, rather than spending their lives in institutions. The second is the shift from asking what is wrong with the person to asking what support he needs. In 1992 the American Association on Mental Retardation (now the American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities, AAIDD) described levels of support : intermittent (help as needed, at times of transition or crisis), limited (consistent help for a limited time, such as job training), extensive (regular, long-term help in some settings, such as daily support at home) and pervasive (constant, high-intensity help across all settings). DSM-5 similarly grades severity by adaptive functioning rather than by IQ. Adaptive skills training. The core clinical work is teaching the conceptual, social and practical skills of daily life. DSM-5's three domains give a useful map: conceptual skills (language, reading, money, time), social skills (friendships, judgement, safety with strangers) and practical skills (self-care, cooking, travel, work). The method is the behavioural one taught in Chapter 4. The clinician assesses what the person can already do, chooses functional goals with the family (skills that will be used every day and will make life more independent), breaks each skill into its steps by task analysis, teaches the chain forwards or, often, backwards (Section 4.5), prompts and fades the prompts, reinforces, and teaches in the real settings where the skill is needed so that it generalises. Brushing the teeth may have a dozen steps; buying milk at the corner shop may have twenty. Toilet training by Azrin and Foxx's rapid method (1971) and the reduction of challenging behaviour by functional assessment and positive behaviour support were described in Section 4.6. Two clinical cautions. People with intellectual disability have higher rates of mental illness than the general population, but their depression, anxiety or psychosis is easily missed, because changes in behaviour are put down to the disability itself. In 1982 Steven Reiss and his colleagues called this diagnostic overshadowing . A young man with moderate intellectual disability who stops eating and sleeping and begins hitting himself may be depressed, in pain or being mistreated, not simply "behaving badly". The second caution is about abuse: children and adults with disabilities are more often abused than others and are less able to report it, which is why the POCSO Act treats taking advantage of a child's disability as an aggravating factor (Section 10.6). Teaching body safety, the difference between private and public, and whom to tell is part of adaptive skills training. Education. Three models have succeeded one another. In special schools , children with disabilities are taught separately by trained special educators, with small classes and adapted curricula. In integrated education , they attend an ordinary school, often in a separate resource room or special class, and are expected to fit in. In inclusive education , the ordinary school and classroom change to fit the child: curriculum, teaching methods, assessment and the physical environment are adapted so that children with and without disabilities learn together. Inclusion became international policy with UNESCO's Salamanca Statement (1994), and India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (Chapter 1) defines inclusive education in exactly these terms and directs the government to work towards it in every school it funds or recognises. The usual instrument is an individualised education programme (IEP), a written plan for each child that records the present level of performance, annual goals broken into short-term objectives, the teaching methods and supports to be used, who is responsible, and when progress will be reviewed. In early childhood, home-based programmes such as the Portage Guide to Early Education, a developmental checklist and home-teaching method from Portage, Wisconsin, that has been widely adapted in India, teach parents to be the child's first teachers. Vocational training and work. For adolescents and adults the goal shifts to work. Training begins with prevocational skills (getting to work on time, following instructions, staying on task, working alongside others) and moves to specific trades. Some people work in a sheltered workshop , a protected setting where they do simple paid work, and others, with the help of a job coach, in supported employment in ordinary jobs; the evidence and the debate between "train then place" and "place then train" were covered in Section 9.8. Kabir is sixteen and has moderate intellectual disability. He lives with his parents and grandmother in Hyderabad and attends a special school. He can dress, bathe and eat on his own, reads a few words, and can count to twenty; he is cheerful and loves cricket and Telugu film songs. His parents' questions are about the future: what will he do, and who will look after him when they are gone? The clinical psychologist assesses his adaptive behaviour and helps the school write goals for his last two years. A task analysis of making tea and of travelling by bus to his aunt's house turns these into teachable chains, practised with his father in the real kitchen and on the real bus. In the school's vocational unit he learns to pack and label paper bags, and later he begins a supported job, with a job coach, stacking shelves in a supermarket. His parents are helped with their own grief, which often returns at each stage of life (Simon Olshansky, writing about parents of children with intellectual disability in 1962, called it "chronic sorrow"), and with long-term planning, including legal guardianship once Kabir turns eighteen. That last point brings in Indian law. Under the National Trust Act 1999 (taught with the RPwD Act in Chapter 1), a Local Level Committee in each district can appoint a legal guardian for an adult with autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability or multiple disabilities. The National Trust also runs schemes for these four groups, among them Disha (early intervention and school readiness for children up to ten), Vikaas (day care for older children and adults), Samarth (respite and residential care), Gharaunda (group homes for adults) and Niramaya (health insurance). Indian context India's national institute for intellectual disability is the National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities (NIEPID) in Secunderabad, under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. It was registered in 1984 as the National Institute for the Mentally Handicapped (NIMH; not to be confused with the American National Institute of Mental Health) and has regional centres at Noida, Kolkata and Mumbai. It trains special educators and rehabilitation professionals, runs model special-education, early-intervention and vocational services, has trained tens of thousands of parents, and develops Indian tools and teaching materials (ISAA, the Indian autism scale of Section 9.9, was developed there). Special educators and rehabilitation professionals in India are trained in courses recognised by the Rehabilitation Council of India. Exam trap "Which disabilities are explicitly covered under the National Trust Act (1999)?" The Act's full name gives the answer: the National Trust for the Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act. So "both autism and intellectual disability" is correct (Real PYQ 2024); specific learning disability and mental illness are not covered (they are among the 21 specified disabilities of the RPwD Act 2016). Conversely, ADHD is not one of the RPwD Act's 21 specified disabilities, although intellectual disability, specific learning disabilities and autism spectrum disorder are (Recall set). For certification, autism uses ISAA , not CARS (Section 9.9). The old DSM-IV-TR IQ criterion for mental retardation was about two standard deviations below the mean (RML 2021), but under DSM-5 an IQ score alone never makes the diagnosis: adaptive deficits are required and set the severity. Normalisation = Nirje and Wolfensberger; levels of support = intermittent, limited, extensive, pervasive; diagnostic overshadowing = Reiss. Specific learning disability: remediation and accommodation Sneha is nine and in Class IV at an English-medium school in Mysuru. In class discussions she is quick and funny, and she can explain the water cycle better than most of her friends. But she reads aloud haltingly, guessing at words from their first letter, confuses b and d, spells "because" as "bikos", and takes twice as long as anyone else to copy from the board. Her teacher's report says "careless and lazy; can do better if she tries". After assessment (Section 9.9 explains why specific learning disability is not certified before the age of eight, and the Assessment book describes the tests), she is found to have average intelligence and a specific learning disability in reading and spelling, the condition usually called dyslexia. What now? There are two broad strategies, and good practice uses both. The first, remediation , means teaching the deficient skill directly, intensively and systematically, to close the gap as far as possible. The second, accommodation , means changing the conditions of learning and examination so that the disability does not hide what the child knows: extra time, a reader or a scribe, oral rather than written answers, audiobooks, reduced copying, typed rather than handwritten work. To these the older student adds compensatory strategies of his own, such as spell-checkers and text-to-speech software. Remediation matters most in the early school years, while the brain's reading networks are still being built; accommodation becomes more important as the demands of school outrun what remediation can achieve. Accommodation without remediation leaves a child dependent on help he may not always get; remediation without accommodation leaves a bright child failing examinations that test his reading speed rather than his knowledge. What works in remediation. For reading, the strongest evidence supports teaching that is explicit, systematic, intensive and given in small groups or one to one. It usually starts with phonological awareness , the ability to hear and manipulate the sound structure of words: rhyme, then syllables, then individual phonemes (blending "c-a-t" into "cat", splitting "ship" into "sh-i-p", deleting or swapping sounds). It then teaches systematic phonics (the links between letters and sounds, in a planned order), followed by fluency through repeated reading of the same passage, and comprehension strategies such as predicting and summarising. Barlow and Durand describe two broad kinds of educational help, specific skills instruction (vocabulary, finding the main idea, finding facts) and strategy instruction (decision making and critical thinking), and highlight Direct Instruction , a programme originated by the American educator Siegfried Engelmann that uses scripted lessons, small groups formed by progress, and teaching to mastery. Imaging studies have shown that successful remediation changes the activity of the left-hemisphere reading areas, so it is more than a trick for getting round the problem. Multisensory methods. Two classic methods, much used by Indian special educators, rest on the idea that learning is stronger when several senses are linked at once. In the 1920s the American neuropsychiatrist Samuel Torrey Orton (1879 to 1948) studied children who could not learn to read and called their difficulty "strephosymbolia" (twisted symbols), believing it arose from incomplete dominance of one cerebral hemisphere. With the educator and psychologist Anna Gillingham (1878 to 1963), who published a teaching manual with Bessie Stillman in 1936 (some sources give 1935), he developed the Orton-Gillingham approach : letters and sounds are taught explicitly, in a structured, sequential and cumulative order, and each is learned through several channels at once, the child seeing the letter, saying its sound, hearing it and tracing or writing it. At the University of California, Los Angeles, the psychologist Grace Maxwell Fernald (1879 to 1950), who had opened a clinic school for remedial teaching there in 1921, developed the Fernald method , described in Remedial Techniques in Basic School Subjects (1943). It is often called the VAKT method, for visual, auditory, kinaesthetic and tactile. The child chooses a word he wants to learn; the teacher writes it in large letters; the child traces it with a finger while saying each part aloud, again and again, until he can write it from memory; the words are then used in the child's own sentences and stories, and the tracing is gradually dropped as the child learns to recognise words by sight. Both methods are widely recommended and intuitively appealing, but neither has much rigorous research behind it: reviews in the United States have found few studies of Orton-Gillingham that meet modern standards. Their active ingredient is probably the explicit, systematic phonics they contain. Writing and mathematics are remediated on the same principles. A child with difficulty in written expression is taught to plan with graphic organisers and to type, and may dictate answers. A child with difficulty in arithmetic is taught number sense and moves through a concrete-representational-abstract sequence: objects first (beads, matchsticks), then pictures and number lines, and only then written numbers and symbols. Response to intervention. For decades a child was diagnosed with a learning disability when there was a large discrepancy between IQ and achievement. Critics called this a "wait to fail" model: because the gap takes years to grow large, children were identified only in the middle school years, long after early help would have worked best. In 2004 the reauthorised Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in the United States allowed schools to use response to intervention (RTI) instead. Every child receives good, evidence-based teaching and is screened (Tier 1); children who lag behind receive extra small-group teaching with frequent checks of progress (Tier 2); and those who still do not respond receive intensive individual help and a full evaluation for specific learning disability (Tier 3), as Figure 10.8 shows. The child's failure to respond to good teaching becomes part of the evidence for the diagnosis, and help begins before the child has failed. Formal RTI is rare in Indian schools, but the 2024 Indian guidelines, which ask teachers to screen children at eight years or in Class III (Section 9.9), move in the same direction. Tier 3 a few Tier 2 some pupils Tier 1 all pupils Tier 3: intensive help One-to-one or very small group; children who still do not respond are evaluated for SLD Tier 2: targeted help Extra small-group teaching for children who lag behind, with progress checked every few weeks Tier 1: good teaching for all Evidence-based class teaching and screening of every child; most need nothing more Figure 10.8 Response to intervention. Help grows more intensive, and fewer children need it, as you move up the pyramid; a child's failure to respond at Tiers 2 and 3 becomes part of the evidence for a specific learning disability (SLD). Accommodations in India. The RPwD Act 2016 directs the government and local authorities to modify the curriculum and examination system for students with disabilities, naming in particular extra time for completing the examination paper, the facility of a scribe or amanuensis, and exemption from second and third language courses. School boards, including the CBSE and many state boards, grant such concessions to students with a disability certificate for specific learning disability, and the details (how much extra time, which language is exempted, whether a reader is allowed) differ from board to board. Sneha's plan therefore has three parts: four sessions a week of small-group phonological and phonics teaching with a special educator, using multisensory letter work; extra time and reduced copying in class, with a disability certificate to secure examination concessions later; and work with her parents and teacher. That last part may matter most. Children with specific learning disability are often called lazy or stupid for years before anyone identifies the problem, and many lose confidence, avoid school and become anxious or depressed. Explaining to Sneha, her parents and her teacher that her difficulty is specific, real and treatable, and that it has nothing to do with intelligence or effort, is itself an intervention. If she also had ADHD, as many children with learning disability do, its treatment (Section 10.4) would be added. Exam trap Remediation teaches the weak skill directly; accommodation changes the conditions (extra time, scribe, reader, language exemption) without teaching the skill; good practice uses both. Orton-Gillingham (Samuel Orton and Anna Gillingham) is a structured, sequential, multisensory phonics approach; the Fernald method (Grace Fernald, 1943) is the VAKT tracing method, visual, auditory, kinaesthetic and tactile. Response to intervention replaces the "wait to fail" IQ-achievement discrepancy with three tiers of increasingly intensive teaching. The RPwD Act names extra time, a scribe and exemption from second and third languages . Specific learning disability requires normal intelligence; if a child's difficulties are explained by intellectual disability, the diagnosis is intellectual disability, not SLD. 10.6 Child Abuse, Child Protection and Adolescents Medium yield · 2 Qs Most of the children in this chapter are brought to the clinic by adults who love them and want help. This section begins with children who are harmed by the very adults who should protect them, and it ends with the adolescents who are often reluctant to come at all. The two belong together for a practical reason. A clinical psychologist is frequently one of the few adults outside the family to whom a child or a teenager speaks privately, and what is said in that room can create a legal duty to act. To do this work well you need three things: knowledge of what abuse is and how it shows itself, the skill to listen to a child without contaminating what the child says, and an exact grasp of what Indian law, above all the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012, requires of you. The discovery of child abuse Children have been beaten, starved, exploited and sexually used throughout history, but as a medical and psychological problem child abuse was discovered surprisingly late. In 1946 the American paediatric radiologist John Caffey drew attention to infants who had both chronic subdural haematomas (bleeding between the brain and its outer covering) and fractures of the long bones of the arms and legs, with no disease to explain either. He was puzzled, and cautious. Doctors of his generation, faced with a toddler with a broken arm and a parent who said he had fallen off the bed, treated the arm and accepted the story, or looked for some rare bone disease. It took a paediatrician willing to say the unthinkable to change that. Key study: Kempe and the battered-child syndrome (1962) Question. Why did some young children arrive at hospital again and again with fractures, bruises and brain injuries that no illness could account for? Method. C. Henry Kempe (1922 to 1984), a German-born paediatrician who chaired the department of paediatrics at the University of Colorado, brought together the evidence from his own department and from enquiries to hospitals and law officers across the United States. His co-authors were the psychiatrist Brandt Steele, the radiologist Frederic Silverman, William Droegemueller and the paediatrician Henry Silver. Result. In "The battered-child syndrome", published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in 1962, they described a recognisable clinical picture: a child, usually under three, with fractures at different stages of healing, subdural haematoma, soft-tissue swelling and bruises, often poor hygiene and failure to thrive, and a history from the parents that did not fit the injuries. Many of these children died or were left with permanent brain damage. Conclusion. The injuries had been inflicted by parents or other carers, and physicians had a duty not merely to treat them but to recognise them for what they were and to report them. Impact and criticism. The deliberately striking label made abuse visible: by the end of the 1960s every American state had passed a law requiring doctors to report suspected abuse. Kempe went on to found a national centre for the prevention and treatment of child abuse and neglect in Denver (1972), to help found the International Society for the Prevention of Child Abuse and Neglect (1977), and to edit The Battered Child (1968) with Ray Helfer. The focus on visible injury, however, meant that sexual abuse, emotional abuse and neglect were recognised only later. Today the World Health Organization defines child maltreatment as the abuse and neglect that occurs to children under 18 years of age, including "all types of physical and/or emotional ill-treatment, sexual abuse, neglect, negligence and commercial or other exploitation, which results in actual or potential harm to the child's health, survival, development or dignity in the context of a relationship of responsibility, trust or power". Notice the last phrase: what makes harm maltreatment is that it comes from someone the child should be able to trust. The WHO estimates that one in five women and one in seven men report having been sexually abused as children. In India, the Ministry of Women and Child Development's Study on Child Abuse: India 2007 , which surveyed 12,447 children in 13 states, found that 53.22 percent reported having faced one or more forms of sexual abuse, that boys were affected as well as girls, that most abuse happened within the family and was committed by people the children knew and trusted, and that most children had told nobody. The forms of maltreatment Maltreatment is usually divided into four forms, with exploitation (child labour, trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation) often added as a fifth. They frequently occur together: a child who is beaten is usually also emotionally abused, and a neglected child is more vulnerable to sexual abuse. Table 10.13 sets them out. The first form, physical abuse , is the non-accidental use of force that injures or endangers a child: hitting, kicking, burning, biting, throwing, poisoning or shaking. Shaking an infant can tear the veins that bridge the surface of the brain and cause bleeding and lasting brain damage without a mark on the skin; this is now called abusive head trauma (formerly shaken baby syndrome). A rarer and stranger form was described in 1977 by the British paediatrician Roy Meadow, who called it Munchausen syndrome by proxy: a carer, usually the mother, fabricates or induces illness in a child (inventing symptoms, falsifying samples, poisoning or suffocating the child) and presents the child repeatedly for medical care. In DSM-5 the carer's condition is called factitious disorder imposed on another, and child-protection services speak of fabricated or induced illness. Where the line between discipline and physical abuse falls is partly cultural, and many Indian parents and teachers still regard beating as ordinary discipline. The law has moved, however: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment of children in schools. The second, child sexual abuse , is the involvement of a child in sexual activity that he or she does not fully understand, cannot give informed consent to, or is not developmentally prepared for. It includes contact abuse (touching, penetration) and non-contact abuse (exposing oneself, showing a child pornography, making a child undress or pose, sexual talk, and the same acts online). Most abusers are known to the child, and many prepare the ground by grooming : winning the trust of the child and the family, singling the child out with attention and gifts, gradually crossing small boundaries so that each step seems normal, isolating the child and insisting on secrecy. Grooming explains why so many children do not resist or tell, and why the abuse is so often discovered late. The third, emotional abuse (psychological abuse), is a persistent pattern of behaviour that tells a child he is worthless, unloved, unwanted or in danger. In The Psychologically Battered Child (1986) James Garbarino and his colleagues described five forms: rejecting (belittling, shaming, refusing to acknowledge the child's worth), isolating (cutting the child off from friends and normal social experience), terrorising (threatening the child with violence or abandonment), ignoring (being psychologically unavailable and unresponsive) and corrupting (encouraging antisocial or criminal behaviour). Exposing a child to violence between parents is now treated as emotional abuse too. Emotional abuse is probably the most common form and the least often reported, because it leaves no physical marks. The fourth, neglect , is the persistent failure of a carer to meet a child's basic physical, medical, educational, emotional or supervisory needs, when the carer is able to meet them or to obtain help in meeting them. That last condition matters in a country with much poverty. A family that cannot afford food or medicine is a family in need of support, not necessarily a neglectful one; neglect is a failure of care, not a lack of money. Neglect is usually divided into the categories in Table 10.14, and it is the form of maltreatment most often reported to child-protection services in many countries.
