The answer is: a great deal, but not the same thing to every child. Section 9.7 described the Adverse Childhood Experiences study, in which the number of categories of abuse and household dysfunction a person had experienced in childhood predicted adult depression, substance misuse, suicide attempts and physical disease in a graded, dose-response way. In infancy, maltreatment is strongly associated with disorganised attachment, in which the child, frightened of the very person who should be his source of comfort, shows contradictory, freezing or apprehensive behaviour on reunion (the fourth category, added by Mary Main and Judith Solomon, Section 3.5; the attachment classifications are taught in the Developmental book). Even in the absence of blows, severe emotional deprivation is damaging: René Spitz's descriptions of "hospitalism" (1945) and anaclitic depression (1946) in infants who were fed and kept clean in institutions but rarely held or played with (Chapter 3) are early evidence of what emotional neglect does. Yet many maltreated children grow up without disorder. The protective factors of Section 10.1, above all a stable relationship with at least one caring adult, help explain why, and they are what intervention tries to supply. Exam trap "All of the following are categories of child neglect EXCEPT..." The answer is use of licensed day care (RML 2020): arranging care by a licensed, responsible provider is a way of meeting the child's need for supervision, not a failure to meet it. Health (medical) neglect, physical neglect (nutrition, housing, clothing) and supervisory neglect are all genuine categories, as are educational and emotional neglect. Do not confuse neglect with poverty. Kempe described the battered-child syndrome in 1962 ; Caffey (1946) noticed the fractures and haematomas before him; Meadow (1977) described Munchausen syndrome by proxy, now factitious disorder imposed on another , whose motive is the sick role and not external gain (Section 9.1). Recognising abuse and responding to a disclosure Clinicians, teachers and school counsellors rarely see abuse happen. They see its traces, and the signs in Table 10.13 are only signs. A child may be withdrawn because of bullying, a bruise may come from a cricket ball, and sexualised play may have been learned from a film. No single sign proves abuse, and some abused children show no signs at all. The clinician's task is therefore not to investigate and decide whether abuse occurred, which is the job of the police and the courts, but to recognise when there is reason to suspect it, to keep the child safe, and to report. Concern should rise when an explanation does not fit the injury or the child's stage of development (a baby who cannot yet crawl does not bruise himself), when injuries are on protected areas such as the ears, neck, buttocks or inner thighs, when marks have the shape of a hand, a belt or a cigarette, when the carer delayed seeking help, and when a child's behaviour changes suddenly: new fearfulness, regression (bed-wetting in a child who was dry), refusal to go home or to a particular place, self-harm or running away. Often the first sign is something the child says, and it rarely comes as a clear, complete account. In 1983 the American psychiatrist Roland Summit described a pattern he called the child sexual abuse accommodation syndrome , with five elements: secrecy (the abuser insists on it, with threats or bribes), helplessness (a child cannot resist an adult in authority), entrapment and accommodation (unable to escape, the child adapts, sometimes blaming himself), delayed, conflicted and unconvincing disclosure , and retraction (once disclosure brings chaos to the family, the child often takes it back). Summit's purpose was to explain why genuinely abused children often delay telling, tell only part of the story, or retract, so that professionals would not dismiss them. It is not a diagnostic test: the same behaviour occurs in children who have not been abused, and courts have rightly refused to treat the "syndrome" as proof that abuse happened. Its lesson for the clinician is simply that a hesitant, partial or withdrawn disclosure is not evidence that the child is lying. Pooja is fourteen and in Class IX in Nagpur. She has been referred to the school counsellor, a clinical psychologist, because her marks have fallen and she has started missing her evening tuition classes. In the third session, after a long silence, she says that her tuition teacher "does things" when the other students have left, and that he told her nobody would believe her. Then she begs: "Promise you won't tell my parents. Papa will stop my studies." What should the counsellor do? Stay calm and listen. Shock, anger or disbelief on the adult's face teaches the child to stop talking. Take her seriously and tell her she has done the right thing by telling, and that what happened is not her fault. Do not promise secrecy. Explain honestly, in words she can understand, that this is something you must tell people whose job is to keep her safe, that you will tell her what happens next, and that you will stay with her through it. Ask only enough to understand whether she is safe now, using open prompts ("Tell me more about that"). Do not question her in detail, ask leading questions or ask her to repeat the story; the formal interview belongs to trained investigators, and every extra conversation risks changing her account, as the next subsection shows. Write down, as soon as possible, exactly what she said in her own words, with the date and time, and what prompted it. Report, as the POCSO Act requires (described below), and make sure she is safe now: she should not go back to that tuition class. Never confront the alleged abuser yourself. Clinical link Every clinician who works with children should have a sentence ready for the moment a child asks for a promise of secrecy. One that works: "I can keep most things private, but if you tell me that someone is hurting you, I will have to tell people whose job is to make it stop. I will tell you before I do it, and I will help you through it." Saying this early, as part of explaining confidentiality (see later in this section), means that a child who discloses later does so knowing what will happen, and the clinician is never forced to choose between breaking a promise and breaking the law. Interviewing children: the science of suggestibility In the 1980s a series of criminal trials in the United States turned on the testimony of very young children who, after many interviews by social workers, therapists, parents and police, described bizarre abuse at their day-care centres. Several convictions were later overturned, and when the interview recordings were examined, the questioning was found to be heavily suggestive: interviewers had asked the same leading questions again and again, praised children for "disclosing", told them that other children had already told, and used anatomically detailed dolls. These cases raised an urgent scientific question: how far can a young child's report of events be trusted, and what makes it go wrong? The researchers who did most to answer it were the developmental psychologist Stephen J. Ceci (born 1950) of Cornell University and Maggie Bruck , whose 1993 review in the Psychological Bulletin , "Suggestibility of the child witness: a historical review and synthesis", and 1995 book, Jeopardy in the Courtroom , are still the starting point. In this context, suggestibility is the degree to which a person's memory and report of events can be altered by information, expectations and pressures introduced after the event. Key study: The Sam Stone study (Leichtman and Ceci, 1995) Question. How do stereotypes and suggestive questions affect what preschool children report about an event? Method. A stranger called Sam Stone visited a day-care classroom of children aged three to six for about two minutes. He said hello, walked round the room and left, without touching or harming anything. In the stereotype condition, children had been told stories before the visit, over several weeks, about how clumsy Sam was and how he broke things. In the suggestion condition, they were interviewed four times after the visit with questions that falsely implied that Sam had ripped a book and soiled a teddy bear. A third group got both, and a control group got neither. Some weeks later a new interviewer asked each child what had happened. Result. In the control condition, only about 10 percent of the three- and four-year-olds claimed that Sam had done anything to the book or the bear, and about 5 percent claimed to have seen it. In the combined stereotype and suggestion condition, 72 percent of the three- and four-year-olds claimed one or both misdeeds, 44 percent said they had seen him do it, and 21 percent still insisted they had seen it when gently challenged. Many embellished their accounts with vivid, invented detail. Five- and six-year-olds were misled less often. Conclusion. Young children's free, unprompted recall was accurate, though sparse; it was the combination of prior expectation and repeated suggestive questioning that produced false reports, and false reports could be detailed and confidently held. Criticism. A two-minute visit and a torn book are far from the experience of abuse, and studies of genuinely stressful events find children often more resistant to suggestion. The study does not show that children's accounts of abuse are false; it shows how interviewers can make them unreliable. Other experiments point the same way. In Ceci's "mousetrap" studies, preschool children were asked once a week for ten weeks to "think very hard" about whether certain events had happened to them, some real and some invented (one was getting a finger caught in a mousetrap and going to hospital); in one study 58 percent eventually described at least one invented event as real, often in convincing detail. In a study by Bruck, Ceci and their colleagues (1995), three-year-old children were asked to show, with an anatomically detailed doll, where a doctor had touched them during a routine medical check-up; many who had had a genital examination did not show it, and some who had not showed the doctor touching or inserting fingers into the doll's genitals. Anatomical dolls are therefore not a reliable way to establish what happened to a young child. What does good interviewing look like? The best-researched answer is the investigative interview protocol developed by Michael Lamb, Yael Orbach and their colleagues at the United States National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, known as the NICHD protocol . It builds rapport, explains ground rules (it is fine to say "I don't know" or "I don't understand", and to correct the interviewer), and has the child practise giving a narrative about a neutral event such as a festival or a birthday. It then moves to the topic with an open prompt ("Tell me why you came to talk to me today") and relies as far as possible on open-ended invitations . Figure 10.9 ranks the types of question. The more open the question, the more accurate the answer; the more the question contains its own answer, the more it risks shaping what the child says. Good practice also means interviewing the child as few times as possible, recording the interview (the POCSO Act asks for audio-video recording wherever possible), and keeping the interviewer free of assumptions about what happened. Section 2.2 defined the leading question; this is where it does the most damage. Question type (safest at the top) Example Open-ended invitation "Tell me everything that happened." Cued invitation "You said he came in. Tell me more about that." Directive (wh-) question "Where were you when that happened?" Option-posing question "Was it in the bedroom or the kitchen?" Suggestive (leading) "He touched you there, didn't he?" Figure 10.9 Types of question in an interview with a child, ranked from the safest (top) to the riskiest (bottom). Interviewers start at the top, move down only when they must, and return to open invitations after every focused answer; suggestive questions are never used. Exam trap Children are most suggestible in the preschool years, and suggestibility is produced by the interviewer : leading questions, repeated interviews, stereotypes planted beforehand, praise for "disclosing" and anatomical dolls. A child's free recall is the most accurate part of the account. The Sam Stone study is Leichtman and Ceci (1995) ; the classic review is Ceci and Bruck (1993) . Summit's accommodation syndrome explains delayed disclosure and retraction but cannot prove that abuse occurred. In the hierarchy of questions, open-ended invitations come first and suggestive questions never. The POCSO Act 2012 Before 2012, Indian law on the sexual abuse of children was scattered and incomplete. The Indian Penal Code's offence of rape protected only women and girls, sexual abuse of boys had to be squeezed into the offence of "unnatural offences", and much non-penetrative abuse was covered only by the vague offence of insulting or outraging a woman's modesty. The trial process, in which a child might have to describe the abuse repeatedly, in open court, in front of the accused, under hostile cross-examination, was itself a second trauma. The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012 (POCSO) was passed to remedy both problems. It received the President's assent on 19 June 2012 and came into force on 14 November 2012, India's Children's Day. The Act's foundations are simple to state. A "child" is any person below the age of eighteen years (section 2(1)(d)). The Act is gender-neutral: both the child and the offender may be of any gender. It defines five groups of offences, each with its punishment: penetrative sexual assault (sections 3 and 4); aggravated penetrative sexual assault (sections 5 and 6); sexual assault, meaning sexual touching without penetration (sections 7 and 8); aggravated sexual assault (sections 9 and 10); and sexual harassment, which includes sexual remarks, gestures, showing pornography and stalking a child, including online (sections 11 and 12). Using a child for pornographic purposes, and storing such material, are offences under sections 13 to 15. An offence is "aggravated" when the offender is in a position of trust or authority (a police officer, a member of the armed forces, a public servant, a member of the staff of a school, hospital, religious or other institution, or a relative or member of the household), when it is committed by a gang, with a weapon, repeatedly, or causes serious injury, or when the child is below twelve years or has a mental or physical disability that the offender takes advantage of. For the clinician, the most important part of the Act is Chapter V, on reporting. Under section 19(1) , any person (including the child) who has an apprehension that an offence under the Act is likely to be committed, or has knowledge that one has been committed, shall provide that information to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or to the local police. This is mandatory reporting , and it is universal: there is no exception for doctors, psychologists or counsellors, and no exception because the information was given in confidence or because the family does not want the matter reported. The police must record the report in writing and read it back to the informant, and within 24 hours must report the matter to the Child Welfare Committee and the Special Court (section 19(6)). A person who reports in good faith incurs no civil or criminal liability (section 19(7)). Under section 20 , personnel of the media, hotels, lodges, hospitals, clubs, studios and photographic facilities who come across sexually exploitative material involving a child must report it. The penalty for silence is in section 21 . Any person who fails to report an offence as required by section 19(1) or section 20, or who (as a police officer) fails to record it, can be punished with imprisonment of up to six months , or a fine, or both (section 21(1)). A person in charge of a company or institution who fails to report an offence committed by a subordinate under his or her control can be punished with imprisonment of up to one year and a fine (section 21(2)): a principal who quietly transfers a teacher accused of abuse, instead of reporting him, commits this offence. A child is never punished for failing to report (section 21(3)). To protect against misuse, section 22 punishes a false complaint made solely to humiliate, extort, threaten or defame, but a child who makes a false complaint is not punished. The rest of the Act makes the legal process gentler for the child. The child's statement is to be recorded at the child's home or a place of the child's choice, as far as practicable by a woman police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector, who is not in uniform; the child must never come into contact with the accused and must not be kept in a police station at night (section 24). The statement is recorded in the presence of a parent or another person the child trusts, with an interpreter or a special educator if needed, and wherever possible by audio-video means (section 26). A girl is medically examined by a woman doctor (section 27). Each district has a designated Special Court (section 28), which presumes that the accused committed the offence unless the contrary is proved (section 29). In court, questions are put to the child through the judge, frequent breaks are allowed, the child is not called repeatedly, aggressive questioning and character assassination are forbidden, and the child's identity is never disclosed (section 33). The child's evidence must be recorded within 30 days of the Special Court taking cognisance of the offence, and the trial completed as far as possible within one year (section 35). The child must not be exposed to the accused while testifying, through screens, one-way mirrors or video links (section 36), and trials are held in camera , closed to the public (section 37). Section 39 asks the states to frame guidelines for professionals with knowledge of psychology, social work, mental health and child development to assist the child before and during the trial, which is where clinical psychologists enter the process as supporters. The Act was amended in 2019 (in force from 16 August 2019) to increase punishments: the minimum sentence for penetrative sexual assault was raised from seven to ten years, and to twenty years if the child is under sixteen; aggravated penetrative sexual assault now carries a minimum of twenty years, which may extend to imprisonment for the rest of the offender's natural life, or death; and child pornography was defined and the offence of storing such material was widened. Section 19 imposes the duty to report on any person , to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police ; section 21 punishes failure to report ( up to six months , or fine, or both; up to one year and fine for the person in charge of an institution); a child is exempt. Do not confuse POCSO with the Juvenile Justice Act 2015, which deals with children in need of care and protection and children in conflict with the law (Section 10.9). Helping abused children and their families The first priority after abuse is the child's safety: medical care, protection from further contact with the abuser and, where the family cannot protect the child, the Child Welfare Committee constituted under the Juvenile Justice Act (Section 10.9). Only then does treatment begin, and not every abused child needs formal therapy. Many do well with support, monitoring and a parent who believes them. For children with post-traumatic stress symptoms, depression or behavioural problems, the first-line treatment is trauma-focused cognitive-behavioural therapy (TF-CBT), developed by Judith Cohen, Anthony Mannarino and Esther Deblinger and first tested with sexually abused children. Section 10.3 described its components and its evidence; here, note that it includes a non-offending parent in every phase, because how that parent responds to the disclosure is one of the strongest influences on the child's recovery. A mother who believes her daughter, protects her and stays calm does more for her than any therapist; a mother who doubts her, or blames her for "bringing shame on the family", can undo months of treatment. Work with the non-offending parent's own shock, guilt and divided loyalties (when the abuser is her husband or brother) is therefore part of the treatment, not an extra. David Finkelhor and Angela Browne (1985) offered a useful map of what sexual abuse does, which tells the therapist what needs repairing. They described four traumagenic dynamics : traumatic sexualisation (the child's sexuality is shaped in developmentally inappropriate and confusing ways), betrayal (the discovery that someone trusted caused harm, or that a parent failed to protect), stigmatisation (shame, guilt and the sense of being "spoiled", which in India is often reinforced by talk of family honour) and powerlessness (the repeated experience of having one's will and body overridden). A twelve-year-old who now distrusts every adult needs help with betrayal; one who believes she is "dirty" needs help with stigmatisation. For physical abuse and neglect, the focus moves to the parents. Behavioural parent training (Sections 4.10 and 10.3) teaches alternatives to harsh punishment, and adaptations of parent-child interaction therapy for physically abusive parents have reduced repeat abuse: in a trial by Mark Chaffin and his colleagues (2004), about one in five parents who received PCIT were re-reported for physical abuse over the following years, against about one in two who received a standard community parenting group. Treatment for neglect usually has to address the parent's own depression, substance use or isolation, and the family's practical needs, at the same time. Prevention is better still. Home-visiting programmes, in which nurses visit young, poor, first-time mothers from pregnancy to the child's second birthday, have been tested in randomised trials by David Olds and his colleagues in the United States, beginning in Elmira, New York, in the late 1970s; the 15-year follow-up found fewer verified reports of child abuse and neglect in the visited families. School programmes on personal safety (often called "good touch, bad touch" in India) teach children the correct names for their body parts, that they may say no to unwanted touch even from adults they know, that secrets about touching should not be kept, and whom to tell. They increase children's knowledge and their willingness to tell, though whether they prevent abuse itself is harder to show. Working with abuse also takes a toll on the professional, and the vicarious traumatisation described in Chapter 8 and the self-care it calls for apply with special force here. Working with adolescents Adolescence was long described as a time of inevitable turmoil. The American psychologist G. Stanley Hall, in his two-volume Adolescence (1904), called it a period of "storm and stress", and psychoanalysts such as Anna Freud and Peter Blos argued that healthy development required the adolescent to detach emotionally from the parents. Research since the 1970s has revised both ideas. Most adolescents get on reasonably well with their parents, and serious turmoil is a sign that something is wrong, not a normal stage to be waited out. Autonomy develops best not by cutting ties but within a continuing, warm relationship in which parents gradually hand over responsibility; continued interdependence with parents, far from being immature, is healthy. Nor is detachment simply moved earlier, into middle childhood, or handed over to friends: peers do matter more in adolescence, above all in everyday matters such as dress, music and leisure, but they add to the parents' influence rather than replacing it, and parents remain the main influence on values and on long-term plans such as education and career. Families also differ in what they hope for from their adolescents, which is one more reason to ask rather than assume. Erik Erikson's account of identity versus role confusion, and James Marcia's identity statuses, are taught in the Developmental book. Why do adolescents take more risks than children or adults, driving fast, experimenting with alcohol and drugs, having unprotected sex? The developmental psychologist Laurence Steinberg has proposed a dual systems model: a socioemotional, reward-seeking brain system becomes much more active around puberty, while the cognitive control system that restrains impulses matures slowly, into the early or middle twenties. In between lies a period of heightened sensitivity to reward, especially in the presence of peers. In one well-known experiment (Margo Gardner and Steinberg, 2005), adolescents playing a video driving game took more risks when friends were watching, while adults did not. Adolescents are not ignorant of risk; they know the facts about smoking or drink-driving as well as adults do. That is why lectures and scare tactics achieve little, and why approaches that build autonomy, competence and good relationships work better. Engaging an adolescent is a skill of its own. Adolescents rarely refer themselves. They are brought by parents or sent by schools, often for problems the adult has defined ("he is always on his phone"; "she is rude"), and they may arrive suspicious that the psychologist is an agent of the parents. Experienced clinicians do several things. They explain confidentiality and its limits clearly at the start, to the adolescent and the parents together (see the next subsection), and they see the adolescent alone for at least part of every session. They are genuine, curious and non-judgemental, neither another parent nor a pretend friend who uses the adolescent's slang, and they show respect by asking the adolescent's view of the problem before anyone else's. They negotiate goals the adolescent actually wants ("getting my parents off my back" is a legitimate starting point), and they use motivational interviewing (Section 6.9) to work with ambivalence instead of arguing with it. They start with safe topics and interests (music, cricket, games, friends) before the difficult ones, and they offer choices and flexible formats: walking while talking, drawing, writing, or short check-ins between sessions where the setting allows. They involve parents in ways the adolescent agrees to, usually by sharing general progress and coaching the parents, rather than reporting what the adolescent has said. A structured way to cover the ground is the HEADSS assessment , a psychosocial interview for adolescents set out by John M. Goldenring and Eric Cohen in 1988: H ome, E ducation and employment, A ctivities (and peers), D rugs, S exuality and S uicide and depression. An expanded version, HEEADSSS (Goldenring and David Rosen, 2004), adds E ating and S afety (including violence, bullying and online risks). The order is deliberate: it moves from the least to the most sensitive topics, so that trust is built before the hardest questions are asked. Pooja, a few weeks after the report to the police, illustrates how these skills come together. She is angry with the counsellor for "telling" and refuses to talk. The counsellor does not defend herself; she acknowledges that it felt like a betrayal, explains again why she had to act, and asks what Pooja would like from their meetings now. Pooja wants two things: to stop the nightmares and to make her father let her continue her studies. The counsellor agrees to both goals, begins TF-CBT's skills phase for the nightmares, and holds a joint session in which Pooja, not the counsellor, tells her parents what she needs from them. Consent and confidentiality with minors Who decides about the treatment of a child or an adolescent? In Indian law a person attains majority at eighteen (the Indian Majority Act 1875), and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 defines a minor as a person who has not completed eighteen years (section 2(t)). For a minor, the legal guardian acts as the nominated representative (section 15), and a minor may be admitted to a mental health establishment only on the nominated representative's application, after two independent examinations (by two psychiatrists, or a psychiatrist together with a mental health professional or medical practitioner) find that admission is in the minor's best interests and that community alternatives have failed or are unsuitable (section 87). The guardian or an attendant must stay with the minor throughout, a female attendant must stay with a minor girl if the nominated representative is male, treatment is given with the informed consent of the nominated representative, and the Mental Health Review Board must be informed within 72 hours (Chapter 1 teaches the Act; electroconvulsive therapy for minors is prohibited except with the guardian's consent and the Board's prior permission). In outpatient work the same principle applies: the parent or guardian gives legal consent and the child gives assent, a principle introduced in Sections 1.8 and 10.1. Confidentiality is harder. Legally, parents may be entitled to know what happens in their child's treatment; clinically, an adolescent who believes everything will be repeated to his parents will tell the therapist nothing that matters. The usual solution is an explicit agreement made at the first meeting, with the adolescent and the parents present. What the adolescent says will be kept private; the parents will be told about general progress and about anything the adolescent agrees to share; and there are exceptions, which are named in advance. The exceptions are serious risk to the adolescent's own life or safety (a suicidal plan, for example), serious risk to others, abuse (which the POCSO Act and child-protection duties require to be reported), and orders of a court. The clinician also promises that, if an exception arises, he or she will tell the adolescent first and involve the adolescent in how the information is shared. Between the clear cases lie grey ones: occasional drinking, a first cigarette, superficial self-harm without suicidal intent, a romantic relationship. Here clinicians weigh the seriousness and immediacy of the risk, the adolescent's maturity and the likely effect of disclosure, and they consult a supervisor. Indian parents, often used to being told everything by teachers and doctors, may need the reasons for this arrangement explained with care: a private space is what allows their child to talk. Exam trap In India the age of majority and of consent to treatment is 18 ; below it the parent or guardian consents and the child assents . Under the MHCA 2017 the legal guardian is a minor's nominated representative (section 15) and minors are admitted only under section 87 . Confidentiality with adolescents is confidentiality with stated exceptions (serious risk to self or others, abuse, court orders), agreed at the outset, with a promise to tell the adolescent before disclosing. Mandatory reporting under POCSO overrides any promise of secrecy. The view that healthy adolescence requires detachment from parents (Anna Freud, Blos) has given way to the finding that continued interdependence is healthy (RML 2022). LGBTQ adolescents and affirmative therapy A seventeen-year-old boy is brought by his parents after they found messages between him and another boy on his phone. They want him "treated" before his cousins find out. He sits silently, looking at the floor. What should the psychologist do? Section 4.4 told the history of attempts to "cure" homosexuality by aversion and the reasons the profession now condemns them: homosexuality is not a disorder (it was removed from DSM in 1973 and from the ICD with ICD-10), change efforts do not work, and they cause harm. In India, the Supreme Court decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), recognised transgender people as a third gender in National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014), and Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019. In 2021 the Madras High Court, in S. Sushma v. Commissioner of Police , directed action against conversion therapy, and in 2022 the National Medical Commission declared conversion therapy to be professional misconduct. Any attempt to change a person's sexual orientation or gender identity is called conversion therapy (also reparative therapy, or sexual orientation change efforts), and offering it is unethical. So the psychologist will not try to change the boy's orientation. The question is what to offer instead. The answer starts with understanding why LGBTQ adolescents have higher rates of depression, anxiety, substance use and suicide attempts than their peers. The minority stress model , set out by the American public-health researcher Ilan H. Meyer in the Psychological Bulletin in 2003, explains it as the result not of sexual orientation itself but of the chronic stress of belonging to a stigmatised minority. Meyer distinguished distal stressors, external events of prejudice, discrimination, rejection and violence, from proximal stressors, which work from inside: the expectation of rejection and constant vigilance against it, the strain of concealing one's identity, and internalised homophobia , the turning of society's negative attitudes against oneself. Family reactions matter enormously. Caitlin Ryan and her colleagues (2009) found that young lesbian, gay and bisexual adults who had experienced high levels of family rejection as adolescents were several times more likely to have attempted suicide and to report depression than those whose families had been accepting. What the psychologist offers instead is affirmative therapy (LGBTQ-affirmative or gay-affirmative therapy). It is not a separate school of therapy but a stance that can be taken within any approach, CBT, person-centred or family therapy. It treats lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and other sexual and gender-minority identities as normal and valid variations, and it directs therapy at the stresses the client faces rather than at the identity itself. In practice it involves the following. The therapist examines his or her own attitudes and assumptions first, and learns about the client's communities. The therapist does not presume heterosexuality, uses inclusive language ("Is there someone you are close to?") and the name and pronouns the client prefers, and does not treat the client's identity as the cause of every problem. Therapy addresses minority stress directly: internalised shame, fear of discovery, bullying at school, family conflict and isolation. Coming out is supported at the client's own pace and with attention to safety. An adolescent who depends on his family for food, shelter and education may reasonably decide not to come out yet, and the therapist respects that judgement. Families are helped to move from rejection towards acceptance, which, as Ryan's research shows, is protective; parents' grief and fears ("Who will marry him? What will people say?") are heard and answered with accurate information. The client is connected with supportive peers, groups and resources. For the seventeen-year-old, this means seeing him alone, telling him plainly that nothing is wrong with him and that the psychologist will not try to change who he is, asking what he wants, and screening for depression and suicidal thoughts. With his agreement, it means meeting the parents to hear their fears and to give them the facts: that his orientation is not an illness, that attempts to change it fail and harm, and that their acceptance is the strongest protection he has. For gender-diverse adolescents, psychosocial support follows the same principles, while decisions about medical treatment for minors are complex, remain debated internationally, and require careful specialist assessment. Exam trap "Affirmative therapy is specifically designed to support..." LGBTQ+ individuals (NIMHANS mock), not elderly clients with cognitive decline (validation therapy and cognitive stimulation, Section 10.7), anxious clients or children with developmental delays. Do not confuse it with affirmations , the A of OARS in motivational interviewing (Section 6.9), or with the affirmative sentences of Carol Gray's social stories (Section 10.5). The minority stress model is Ilan Meyer 's (2003): distal stressors (prejudice events) and proximal stressors (expected rejection, concealment, internalised homophobia). Age was one of his limits. "Near or above the fifties," he said, "the elasticity of the mental processes, on which the treatment depends, is as a rule lacking; old people are no longer educable." Freud was 48 when he said it, and he went on writing and treating patients until he died at 83. For half a century his pessimism set the tone: older people were thought too rigid to change, too close to death to be worth the investment, and their sadness and forgetfulness were put down to "just old age". Every part of that view has turned out to be wrong. Older adults benefit from psychological treatment about as much as younger adults do, and there are now far more of them. According to the India Ageing Report 2023 of the United Nations Population Fund and the International Institute for Population Sciences, India had about 149 million people aged 60 and over in 2022, 10.5 percent of the population, and the share is projected to double to 20.8 percent (about 347 million people) by 2050; by about 2046 the country will have more older people than children under 15. This section is about what a psychologist does for them: the field of geropsychology, dementia care and support for the family, the psychosocial therapies built for confused older people, late-life depression, and the assessment of capacity and the problem of elder abuse. Geropsychology: the field and the older client Three words are easily confused. The first, gerontology , is the scientific study of ageing in all its aspects, biological, psychological and social; the word was coined in 1903 by the Russian-born biologist Élie Metchnikoff (1845 to 1916). The second, geriatrics , is the branch of medicine concerned with the health care of older people; the term was introduced in 1909 by the Vienna-born American physician Ignatz Leo Nascher (1863 to 1944). The third, geropsychology , is the application of psychology to older adults: understanding them, assessing them and helping them and their families. Professional geropsychology took shape as a specialty only recently. In 2006 a national conference held in Colorado Springs set out the competencies a psychologist needs for work with older adults, published in 2009 by Bob Knight and colleagues as the Pikes Peak model of geropsychology training, and in 2010 the American Psychological Association recognised professional geropsychology as a specialty in professional psychology. Who counts as old? In Indian law a senior citizen is anyone aged 60 or more (you will meet the 2007 Act that says so in Section 10.7.6), but a sixty-year-old schoolteacher and a ninety-year-old widow confined to bed have little in common. The American psychologist Bernice Neugarten (1916 to 2001) drew a distinction in the 1970s between the young-old , active, healthy and often still working, and the old-old , among whom frailty and dependence are common; later writers added the oldest-old , usually those over 85. A practical rule follows: older adults differ from one another more than any younger age group does, so the label "elderly" tells you very little about the person in front of you. What gets in the way of good care is often not the client's age but the clinician's attitudes. In 1969 the American psychiatrist Robert Neil Butler (1927 to 2010) coined the word ageism for the systematic stereotyping of, and discrimination against, people because they are old, a prejudice he compared to racism and sexism. Butler went on to win the Pulitzer Prize in 1976 for Why Survive? Being Old in America (1975) and to serve as the founding director of the American National Institute on Aging (1975 to 1982). Ageism in the clinic has a recognisable sound: "What do you expect at your age?", the depressed seventy-five-year-old who is told that low mood is natural after retirement, the condescending, sing-song "elderspeak" that treats an older person like a child (Section 2.2), and the quiet assumption, Freud's assumption, that psychotherapy is wasted on the old. The result is therapeutic nihilism : treatable conditions such as depression, anxiety, alcohol misuse and the confusion caused by medicines go untreated because nobody expected anything better. The clinician therefore has to keep normal ageing and disorder apart. Normal ageing brings slower processing, some difficulty in learning and recalling new information quickly, and poorer performance on timed tasks, while vocabulary, general knowledge and well-practised skills hold up well (the developmental changes themselves are taught in the Developmental Psychology book). Dementia is not normal ageing: it is a progressive disorder that erodes memory, reasoning and the ability to manage daily life, and its types and criteria belong to the Psychiatric Disorders book, as screening tests such as the Mini-Mental State Examination belong to the Assessment book. The trickiest boundary is the one you met in Section 2.6: depression in an older person can produce poor concentration and complaints of forgetfulness that look like dementia, the picture called pseudodementia, and the two conditions also occur together. How is the work different? Much less than Freud supposed, and in predictable ways. The American geropsychologist Bob G. Knight , whose Psychotherapy with Older Adults first appeared in 1986, argued that older clients are not a different species: they are more mature in some respects, they belong to a cohort that grew up with different values and expectations (many of today's older Indians grew up in joint families, with arranged marriages and little talk of feelings), and they face specific challenges such as chronic illness, disability and the death of a spouse and friends. Therapy is adapted to those facts rather than to "age" as such. In practice that means attending to hearing and vision (Section 2.2), a slower pace and sometimes shorter sessions, written summaries and memory aids, close liaison with the physician because most older clients have several illnesses and take several medicines (polypharmacy), and, with the client's consent, involving the family. The settings are varied too: memory clinics, geriatric wards, primary care, day-care centres, old age homes and, very often, the client's own home. Erik Erikson's last psychosocial stage, integrity versus despair, gives a useful frame for this work and is taught in the Developmental Psychology book; the rest of this section turns to the clinical tasks themselves. Exam trap Gerontology (Metchnikoff, 1903) is the scientific study of ageing; geriatrics (Nascher, 1909) is the medical care of older people; geropsychology is psychology applied to older adults. Ageism was coined by Robert Butler in 1969, not by Erikson, who gave us integrity versus despair. Depression, anxiety and confusion are not normal parts of ageing; an option such as "depression is an expected consequence of old age" is a distractor. In India a senior citizen is a person of 60 or more . Dementia care and the family caregiver No psychological treatment can halt the brain changes of Alzheimer's disease or the other dementias, and the drugs available slow the decline only modestly. So what is a psychologist for? David Barlow and Mark Durand, in their textbook of abnormal psychology, put the goals of care plainly: to prevent what can be prevented (strokes, alcohol damage), to delay the onset of the worst symptoms so that the person has more years of good life, and to help the person and the family cope with the decline that remains. The last of these is where most psychological work lies, and it is aimed as much at the family as at the patient. In India, as in most low- and middle-income countries, almost all dementia care is given at home by relatives, most of them women: wives, daughters and daughters-in-law, many of them unpaid, untrained and unsupported. The cost of that care to the carer has a name. In 1966 the psychiatric researchers Hoenig and Hamilton, studying the families of psychiatric patients living at home, distinguished two kinds of caregiver burden . What they called objective burden is the observable disruption that caring causes: lost income and working hours, money spent, broken sleep, abandoned social life, a household reorganised around the patient. By contrast, subjective burden is how much the carer feels burdened. The two are only loosely related, and it is subjective burden that is most closely linked to the carer's own depression. The best-known measure of burden comes from Steven H. Zarit and his colleagues Reever and Bach-Peterson, who in 1980 published "Relatives of the impaired elderly: correlates of feelings of burden" in The Gerontologist . They interviewed the main carers of older people with dementia and built a burden interview asking how far caring had affected the carer's health, finances, social life and relationship with the patient. Their most quoted finding was a surprise: the severity of the patient's memory loss and behaviour problems was not closely related to how burdened the carer felt, whereas the support the carer received, in particular how often other family members visited, was. Burden, in other words, depends as much on the carer's circumstances as on the illness, which is good news, because circumstances can be changed. A later 22-item version, the Zarit Burden Interview , is now the standard measure of caregiver burden worldwide, including in Indian research. A broader account came in 1990 from the sociologist Leonard Pearlin and his colleagues, whose stress process model of caregiving separates the primary stressors that come directly from the illness (the patient's care needs, memory loss, behaviour problems), the secondary stressors that spread from them (conflict with siblings over who should help, strain at work, the carer's sense of being trapped in the role and of losing herself), the mediators that soften the impact (coping skills and social support) and the outcomes (depression, anxiety, poorer physical health). The outcomes are real. Carers of people with dementia have high rates of depression and anxiety, and you saw in Section 9.3 that women caring for a relative with dementia healed a small standard wound about nine days more slowly than matched controls. The American caregivers' handbook by Nancy Mace and Peter Rabins, first published in 1981, captured the experience in its title: The 36-Hour Day . Caregiver interventions follow directly from the stress process model. First, psychoeducation gives the family information about the illness, its likely course, what the behaviour means and what to expect next, and about legal, financial and practical matters; early in the illness, families need little else. Skills training teaches carers to manage behaviour problems and to communicate with a person whose memory is failing (Section 10.7.4). Counselling and cognitive-behavioural methods address the carer's own guilt, grief, anger and depression; dementia is a "living loss" whose grief begins long before death (the anticipatory and disenfranchised grief of Section 9.5). Support groups reduce isolation, and respite care (day-care centres, a paid attendant for some hours a week, short residential stays) gives the carer time off. Reviews find that single components help a little and multicomponent programmes, tailored to the family, help most. Key study: counselling the spouse keeps the patient at home (Mittelman and colleagues, 2006) Question: Can supporting the carer change what happens to the patient? Method: At New York University, Mary S. Mittelman and her colleagues randomly assigned spouses caring for a husband or wife with Alzheimer's disease either to usual care or to an enhanced programme: individual and family counselling sessions in the first months, a weekly support group, and counselling by telephone whenever a crisis arose, for as long as the carer needed it. They followed the couples for years and recorded when the patients entered nursing homes. Result: Patients whose spouses received the programme had a 28 percent lower rate of nursing-home placement; the difference in predicted median time to placement was 557 days, about a year and a half more at home. Improvements in the carers' satisfaction with social support, in their reactions to the patients' behaviour problems and in their depression accounted for about 61 percent of the effect. Conclusion: Helping the carer helps the patient. Criticism: The sample was of spouse carers in New York, a population with resources few Indian families have, which is why the Goa trial in the next box matters. Indian context In focus groups in Goa, Vikram Patel and Martin Prince (2001) found that dementia was widely regarded as a normal part of ageing, not as an illness needing care, and that both dementia and late-life depression were blamed on neglect by the children; they also found family care less reliable than the image of the devoted Indian joint family suggests, and sometimes conditional on inheriting the parent's property. Building on this, Amit Dias, Vikram Patel and their colleagues in the 10/66 Dementia Research Group ran a randomised trial in two talukas of Goa (published in 2008). Local community workers called home care advisors, supervised by a counsellor and a psychiatrist, visited families at home and gave them information about dementia, guidance on managing behaviour problems and, where needed, a psychiatric assessment and medication. Among 81 families, the programme significantly improved the carers' mental health and reduced their distress over the patient's behaviour; the fall in burden scores was smaller and not statistically significant. The lesson echoes the lay counsellor programmes of Section 9.6: low-cost, locally available people can deliver real help. One more idea changed how dementia care is thought about. The British social psychologist Tom Kitwood (1937 to 1998), in Dementia Reconsidered: The Person Comes First (1997), argued that much of the decline seen in people with dementia comes not from the brain disease alone but from how other people treat them, which he called malignant social psychology : talking over their heads, infantilising them, labelling them, ignoring their wishes, hurrying them, outpacing them. Its antidote is person-centred dementia care , which aims to preserve the person's personhood , their standing as a person with a history, preferences and relationships, through recognition, respect and inclusion. With Kathleen Bredin, Kitwood developed dementia care mapping , a structured observation method in which a trained observer records, minute by minute, what happens to residents in a care setting and how it affects their well-being. Person-centred care is now the stated philosophy of dementia services in many countries. Exam trap The Zarit Burden Interview (Zarit, Reever and Bach-Peterson, 1980) measures the caregiver's burden; it is not a measure of the patient's dementia. Objective burden is the observable disruption (money, time, health, routine); subjective burden is the felt strain, and it is the one most closely linked to carer depression. Zarit's surprising finding was that burden was tied less to the severity of the patient's impairment than to the support the carer received. Person-centred dementia care and malignant social psychology are Kitwood's; do not attribute them to Rogers, though the spirit is similar. Reality orientation, reminiscence, validation and cognitive stimulation Imagine an 81-year-old woman, Mrs Venkatesan, who lives with her son and daughter-in-law in Mysuru and has had Alzheimer's disease for five years. Every evening at about five o'clock she packs a cloth bag and goes to the front door, insisting that she must go home because her mother is waiting with dinner. Her mother died more than forty years ago. What should her daughter-in-law say? The four psychosocial approaches in this subsection give four different answers, and the difference between them lies in one question: whose reality should the helper work in? Figure 10.10 arranges them on that dimension, and Table 10.16 compares them. Orient the person to our present Enter the person's own world Focus shifts from facts towards feelings Reality orientation Folsom, from 1958 Repeats the date, place and names Boards, clocks Focus: facts Cognitive stimulation Spector, 2003 14 themed group sessions Opinions, not facts Focus: thinking Reminiscence and life review Butler, 1963 Photos, songs, objects, stories Whole-life review Focus: the past Validation therapy Feil, 1963 to 1980 Accepts the person's reality Answers the feeling Focus: emotions Figure 10.10 Four psychosocial approaches to dementia care, arranged by whose reality the helper works in. Reality orientation brings the person back to the shared present; validation therapy goes into the person's own world; cognitive stimulation and reminiscence sit between them. Reality orientation. The oldest of the four began in 1958 as a pilot rehabilitation programme on one ward of the Winter Veterans Administration Hospital in Topeka, Kansas, led by the American psychiatrist James C. Folsom . Its first patients were severely disturbed war veterans, not people with dementia; only later was it applied to confused older patients, and Taulbee and Folsom described it for geriatric patients in 1966. (Some accounts date the start to 1959.) The method of reality orientation rests on the idea that confusion is made worse by a lack of information and that repeated presentation of the basic facts of time, place and person will help the person understand their surroundings and regain a sense of control. It has two forms. In 24-hour or informal reality orientation, every member of staff, at every contact, restates the facts ("Good morning, Mr Rao. It's Monday, and I'm Asha, your nurse. Breakfast is in ten minutes"), and the environment is filled with cues: large clocks and calendars, signs on doors, and the reality orientation board giving the day, date, weather and the next meal. In classroom reality orientation, small groups meet for a short daily session to rehearse orientation information. Reviews, including one by Aimee Spector and colleagues for the Cochrane Collaboration (2000), found some benefit for cognition and behaviour, but the approach drew heavy criticism: applied mechanically, it becomes a quiz the person keeps failing, and it can be cruel. Told every evening that her mother died forty years ago, Mrs Venkatesan would grieve afresh each time and become more agitated, not less. Reminiscence and life review. Until the 1960s, an old person's habit of talking about the past was usually treated as a symptom: living in the past, a sign of failing memory or of senility. Butler turned that view on its head. Key study: Butler and the life review (1963) In "The life review: an interpretation of reminiscence in the aged", published in the journal Psychiatry in 1963, Robert Butler drew on his psychiatric work with older people to argue that reminiscence is not a sign of decline but a normal, indeed universal, developmental process. As people become aware that death is approaching, he proposed, past experiences return progressively to consciousness, and especially unresolved conflicts , which can then be surveyed, re-evaluated and integrated. He called this the life review . Its outcome can be good or bad. Successfully completed, it can bring candour, serenity, acceptance of one's life and something like wisdom; where the past is full of guilt and failure that cannot be reconciled, it can bring anxiety, despair and depression, and in extreme cases suicide. The paper's impact was to make reminiscence something to encourage and work with rather than to correct, and it launched the reminiscence and life review therapies. Its criticism is the usual one for clinical theorising: Butler's claim that the process is universal was based on clinical observation, and later research found that only some kinds of reminiscence are good for people (next paragraph). Two therapies grew from Butler's idea, and examiners expect you to tell them apart. The first, reminiscence therapy , uses the recall of past events, usually pleasant ones, to give pleasure, prompt communication and build social contact and self-esteem. It is often done in groups and uses triggers: old photographs and wedding albums, film songs from the person's youth, household objects, smells and tastes, stories of festivals and of the places they grew up. Because memories from long ago survive in dementia far better than recent ones, reminiscence is one of the few activities in which a person with moderate dementia can be the expert, and a "life story book" put together with the family gives staff something to talk about with the person. The second, life review therapy , is more structured and more evaluative. Usually individual, it moves through the whole of life in order, from childhood to the present, and deliberately includes the painful parts, aiming at integration and acceptance; it is used mainly with older people who are depressed or facing death (dignity therapy, Section 9.5, is a close relative). Research by the Canadian psychologist Paul Wong and Lisa Watt (1991) showed why the distinction matters. Comparing older people who were ageing well with those who were not, they found that successful agers engaged more in integrative reminiscence (accepting the past and finding meaning in it) and instrumental reminiscence (recalling how past problems were solved), and less in obsessive reminiscence, the bitter, ruminative replaying of guilt and failure. Their other types (transmissive, passing on lessons to the young; narrative, simple storytelling; and escapist, glorifying the past to escape the present) were less clearly related to adjustment. The evidence for the therapies is respectable: a meta-analysis by Ernst Bohlmeijer, Filip Smit and Pim Cuijpers (2003) found a large effect of reminiscence and life review on depressive symptoms in older people (an effect size of 0.84), larger in people who were already depressed (1.23) than in others (0.37). Validation therapy. Naomi Feil (1932 to 2023) grew up in the Montefiore Home for the Aged in Cleveland, Ohio, where her parents worked, and returned to work there as a social worker after training at Columbia University. Running groups for very old, severely disoriented residents, she found that reality orientation made them withdraw or become angry, and between 1963 and 1980 she developed an alternative, set out in Validation: The Feil Method (1982) and The Validation Breakthrough (1993). Her validation therapy starts from the opposite premise to reality orientation: the helper accepts the reality and personal truth of the confused person's experience instead of correcting it, on the assumption that behind the confused words and behaviour lies a real feeling, an unmet need or an unfinished task from earlier life. Building on Erikson, Feil argued that very old disoriented people are struggling to resolve unfinished business before death, in a final stage of life beyond Erikson's eight that she called the stage of resolution (the person who cannot resolve the past withdraws further and further inward, towards vegetation), and she described four stages of increasing disorientation (later renamed the four phases of resolution): malorientation (the person is oriented but expresses old conflicts in disguised ways, often blaming others), time confusion (losing track of time and of present reality), repetitive motion (repeated movements and sounds replace words) and vegetation (withdrawal into almost total inactivity). Her techniques are concrete: centring yourself before the contact; asking non-threatening factual questions (who, what, where, when, how) but never "why", which demands an insight the person no longer has; rephrasing the person's words; asking about the extreme ("What is the worst thing about it?"); reminiscing; close, genuine eye contact; a clear, low, warm tone of voice; mirroring the person's movements; linking the behaviour to an unmet need such as love, usefulness or safety; touch; and music. Faced with Mrs Venkatesan at the door, a validating daughter-in-law might say: "You want to go to your mother. Tell me about her. What would she cook for you in the evening?" Mrs Venkatesan talks about her mother's rasam and the house in Thanjavur, the urgency drains away, and after a few minutes she agrees to help set out the plates. Nobody has told her a lie, and nobody has told her a painful truth she will forget within the hour. Validation is popular with staff, who report that it makes their work more satisfying, but its evidence is thin. A Cochrane review by Neal and Barton Wright (2003) found too few good trials to say whether it improves behaviour or mood in people with dementia. The ethical question it raises is still debated: when a person with dementia asks for a dead mother, is it ever right to say "She'll be here soon"? Validation itself does not require deception, only that the helper respond to the feeling rather than to the facts. Cognitive stimulation therapy. The approach with the strongest evidence was built partly out of the wreckage of reality orientation. Aimee Spector and her colleagues in London reviewed the earlier research, kept what seemed to work, discarded the mechanical quizzing, and designed a group programme they called cognitive stimulation therapy (CST): enjoyable, themed activities that engage thinking, memory, language and concentration in a social setting, without demanding that the person get facts right. Key study: Spector and the cognitive stimulation trial (2003) Method: Aimee Spector , Martin Orrell, Bob Woods and their colleagues ran a single-blind, multi-centre randomised controlled trial with 201 older people with dementia living in care homes and attending day centres in Britain; 115 received CST and 86 continued with their usual activities. CST groups of about five to eight people met for 14 sessions of 45 minutes, twice a week for seven weeks. Each session had a theme (among them childhood, food, current affairs, faces and scenes, word games, using money and a team quiz), began with a warm-up and a group song, and followed principles such as asking for opinions rather than facts, using all the senses, and using reminiscence as an aid to the here and now. Result: Compared with the controls, the CST group improved significantly on the Mini-Mental State Examination, on the cognitive scale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-Cog) and on a quality-of-life scale. Six people needed to be treated for one to gain four or more points on the ADAS-Cog. Conclusion: The benefits compared favourably with those of the anti-dementia drugs. Since then: In 2006 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in England recommended cognitive stimulation for people with mild to moderate dementia, and CST has been adapted for use in many countries, with longer-term (maintenance) and individual, carer-delivered versions. Do not confuse cognitive stimulation with two neighbours. Cognitive training is guided practice on standard tasks aimed at a particular function, such as memory drills; cognitive rehabilitation sets individual goals in the person's everyday life and works towards them with compensatory aids and techniques such as errorless learning (Section 9.9). The distinction was drawn by Linda Clare and Bob Woods in 2004. Simple compensatory aids belong here too: the American speech scientist Michelle Bourgeois showed in 1992 that a "memory wallet" of cards carrying sentences and pictures ("My husband John and I have three children") helped people with Alzheimer's disease hold better conversations.
