Validation therapy is Naomi Feil's ; it is not the validation strategies of Linehan's DBT (Section 5.8), although both mean accepting the person's experience as real. The life review is Robert Butler's (1963); reminiscence therapy is the looser, usually group, pleasant-memory form, while life review therapy is structured, individual and evaluative. Of the four approaches, cognitive stimulation therapy (Spector, 2003) has the best evidence. Agitation, wandering and other behaviour that challenges For most families the hardest part of dementia is not the memory loss but the behaviour: agitation and restlessness, shouting, aggression during bathing, wandering, sleeplessness and night-time confusion, suspiciousness and accusations of theft, apathy, and disinhibited sexual or social behaviour. Since a consensus conference of the International Psychogeriatric Association in 1996 these have been grouped as the behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD). Almost everyone with dementia shows some of them at some stage, and they are the commonest reason a family gives up home care. The psychologist's first rule is that the behaviour has a cause, and the first causes to look for are physical. A person who cannot say "my tooth hurts", "I am constipated" or "I need the toilet" may show it by shouting or hitting out. Pain, infections (especially of the urinary tract), dehydration, side effects of medicines, a lost hearing aid or spectacles, and above all delirium , a sudden, fluctuating confusion caused by physical illness, must be ruled out before anything else. The second rule is that the behaviour usually serves a purpose. The gerontologist Jiska Cohen-Mansfield's unmet needs model treats much agitation as the person's attempt to meet a need (for comfort, company, activity, rest, the toilet) or to communicate it when words have gone. The tool for finding the need is the functional analysis you learned in Section 2.8: an ABC chart recording the antecedents (time of day, place, who was present, what was being asked), the behaviour itself, and its consequences (what happened next, what the person got or escaped). Mrs Venkatesan's family kept an ABC chart for two weeks. The pattern was clear. The packing and pleading came between five and seven in the evening, after a long afternoon nap, in a dimly lit room with the television news turned up loud, while her daughter-in-law was busy in the kitchen; the consequence was usually an argument in which she was told the facts, after which she became tearful and sometimes slapped whoever stood in the doorway. This is the late-day worsening often called "sundowning". The plan that followed changed the antecedents and the consequences. Her afternoon nap was shortened, the lights went on at half past four and the television was turned down; at five her son took her for a walk on the terrace, and afterwards she was given the task of folding the dried clothes, a job she had done all her life, with a cup of tea and a snack. When she still asked for her mother, the family used the validating response from Section 10.7.3 and then gently redirected her. Within three weeks the evening episodes fell from almost every day to about twice a week, and the slapping stopped. Most behavioural strategies fall into a few families. Environmental changes reduce noise and crowding, improve lighting in the evening, mark the toilet door with a picture, and make walking safe by giving the person a secure route, a garden or a terrace rather than locking them in a room. Routine and simplification keep the day predictable and break tasks into single steps with one instruction at a time ("Put your arm in here"), so that bathing and dressing do not become battles. Meaningful activity , music, exercise and contact prevent the boredom and loneliness behind much restlessness; in trials led by the American psychologist Linda Teri, exercise for the patient combined with training for the carer in managing behaviour problems improved both physical health and depression in people with Alzheimer's disease. Communication matters most: carers learn to approach from the front, speak calmly, avoid arguing and correcting, acknowledge the feeling, and distract and redirect. Barlow and Durand note that teaching communication skills in ways similar to programmes for people with autism, in which a person learns an acceptable way of signalling a need instead of a disruptive one (the functional communication training of Section 10.5), may help reduce aggression in dementia too. Wandering needs special care: tying a person to a chair or bed, or sedating them, adds injury, distress and loss of dignity to the risks it is meant to prevent, while identity bracelets, door alarms and electronic location devices protect safety, though tracking technology raises its own questions of privacy. Medication is a last resort, not a first one. Antipsychotic drugs are often given for agitation in dementia, but their benefit is modest and their risks are serious: in 2005 the United States Food and Drug Administration warned that the newer antipsychotics increase the risk of death in older people with dementia-related psychosis, a warning later extended to the older drugs. Guidelines everywhere now recommend that non-drug approaches be tried first, which is precisely the psychologist's territory. Exam trap When a person with dementia suddenly becomes agitated or aggressive, the first step is to look for a physical cause , above all pain, infection, medication effects and delirium , not to start a behaviour programme or a sedative. The behavioural approach rests on an ABC functional analysis ; restraint and sedation are not the preferred answers to wandering. "Sundowning" is the late-afternoon and evening worsening of confusion and agitation. BPSD is the umbrella term for these behavioural and psychological symptoms. Late-life depression Mr Dutta is 72, a retired railway engineer who lives alone in a flat in Kolkata. His wife died eighteen months ago; his only son works in Bengaluru and phones on Sundays. He goes to his doctor complaining of poor sleep, aches in his back and knees, no appetite and, most of all, his memory: "It is going. I forget why I came into a room." He no longer goes to the evening adda with his old colleagues, and when asked about it he says, "What is the use? My work is done." His doctor's first thought is that this is what happens when a man of 72 loses his wife. It is not. Depression is not a normal part of ageing. Major depression is in fact no more common among healthy older people living in the community than among younger adults, but depressive symptoms are common among older people who are medically ill, disabled, bereaved, isolated or living in institutions, and they are under-recognised for three reasons. Older people are less likely to describe themselves as "depressed" and more likely to present with bodily complaints, sleep problems, fatigue, anxiety and worry about memory, as Mr Dutta does. Their symptoms overlap with those of physical illness. And clinicians, like Mr Dutta's doctor, too often take sadness in old age for granted. The memory complaint needs particular care: a depressed person usually complains loudly of memory loss, gives up easily on memory tests ("I don't know") and has a clearly datable onset, while a person with early dementia more often minimises problems that the family describes. This is the pseudodementia picture of Section 2.6, and the two conditions also occur together, since late-life depression can be an early sign of dementia. The stakes are high. In many countries the highest suicide rates are found among older men, especially those who are widowed, living alone, physically ill and depressed, which describes Mr Dutta exactly; his risk must be asked about directly (Sections 2.7 and 9.7). The good news is that the psychological treatments you studied in earlier chapters work in late life, usually with modest adaptations: a slower pace, written summaries and homework reminders, attention to hearing and vision, and coordination with the physician. Cognitive behaviour therapy (Chapter 5), problem-solving therapy (Section 5.5), behavioural activation, interpersonal psychotherapy (Section 3.7), whose problem areas of grief and role transition fit late life especially well, and reminiscence and life review (Section 10.7.3) all have controlled trials in older adults. The most instructive single study concerns not the treatment of an episode but the prevention of the next one. Key study: maintenance therapy for depression after 60 (Reynolds and colleagues, 1999) Question: Older people who recover from depression often relapse. What keeps them well? Method: At the University of Pittsburgh, Charles Reynolds, Ellen Frank and their colleagues treated 187 patients older than 59 (average age 67) who had recurrent major depression with the antidepressant nortriptyline plus interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT). The 107 who recovered fully were randomly assigned to one of four maintenance conditions for up to three years: monthly IPT with nortriptyline, monthly IPT with a placebo pill, nortriptyline in a medication clinic, or placebo in a medication clinic. Result: Over three years, depression recurred in 20 percent of those given combined IPT and nortriptyline, 43 percent of those on nortriptyline alone, 64 percent of those on IPT with placebo, and 90 percent of those on placebo. Conclusion: All three active treatments beat placebo, and the combination was best. Why it matters: Monthly psychotherapy on its own protected a substantial number of older patients, and adding it to medication gave the best protection of all. The other lesson of late-life depression research is about where treatment happens. Most depressed older people never see a mental health professional; they see a primary care doctor, as Mr Dutta did. Two large American trials tested collaborative care , in which a depression care manager (usually a nurse, social worker or psychologist) works alongside the primary care doctor under the supervision of a psychiatrist. In the IMPACT trial (Improving Mood, Promoting Access to Collaborative Treatment), published by Jürgen Unützer and colleagues in 2002, 1,801 patients aged 60 or over with major depression or dysthymia in 18 primary care clinics were randomly assigned to usual care or to up to a year with a care manager, who offered education, followed the patient's progress, supported the doctor's prescribing, or delivered a brief psychotherapy, problem-solving treatment in primary care. At twelve months 45 percent of the care-managed patients had halved their depressive symptoms, against 19 percent with usual care. In PROSPECT (the Prevention of Suicide in Primary Care Elderly: Collaborative Trial), published by Martha Bruce and colleagues in 2004, the target was suicide risk itself. Among 598 depressed older patients in 20 practices, those whose care followed guidelines with the help of a care manager lost their suicidal ideation faster: at four months the proportion reporting it fell by 12.9 percentage points, against 3.0 points with usual care. The message for a country with very few geriatric psychiatrists and psychologists is the one you met in Section 9.6: a well-supported non-specialist, with specialist backing, can deliver much of what depressed older people need. For Mr Dutta, the psychologist to whom his doctor refers him starts with a careful assessment (a depression screening scale designed for older people, a cognitive screen, a review of his medicines with the doctor, and direct questions about suicide), which shows a moderate depressive episode with intact cognition and passive thoughts that life is not worth living, without plans. Treatment combines three of the threads of this section. Behavioural activation rebuilds his days: a morning walk to the lake, a return to the adda twice a week, helping the para committee plan its Durga Puja. Interpersonal work focuses on his unfinished grief for his wife (Section 9.5) and on the role transition from engineer and husband to a man living alone. And a life review, which he turns into a handwritten memoir of his years building railway bridges, to be posted to his grandson in Bengaluru, helps him find again the sense that his life has counted for something. The memory complaints fade as the depression lifts. Exam trap Late-life depression is not normal ageing and responds to psychotherapy. It often presents with somatic and memory complaints rather than stated sadness; when it mimics dementia it is called pseudodementia . In Reynolds's 1999 maintenance trial, combined IPT and nortriptyline gave the lowest recurrence (20 percent against 90 percent on placebo). IMPACT (Unützer, 2002) and PROSPECT (Bruce, 2004) are trials of collaborative care in primary care ; PROSPECT's special target was suicidal ideation. Older men who are widowed, alone and ill are the highest-risk group for suicide. Capacity, elder abuse and the law As Mrs Venkatesan's dementia advances, her elder son asks her to sign a gift deed transferring the family house to him "to avoid problems later". Her younger son objects, and the family's doctor asks the psychologist a question that comes up again and again with older clients: does she have the capacity to make this decision? In clinical terms, decision-making capacity is a person's ability to make a particular decision for himself or herself. Clinicians assess capacity; competence , strictly, is a legal status that only a court can decide, though the words are often used interchangeably. Four principles guide the assessment. Capacity is presumed : the burden lies on showing that a person lacks it, not on the person to prove they have it. Capacity is decision-specific : Mrs Venkatesan may be perfectly able to decide what to wear, what to eat and that she wants to keep living with her family, and yet unable to make a complex decision about property. Capacity is time-specific : it can fluctuate, with delirium, with the time of day, with medication, so it is assessed for this decision at this time, and reassessed if things change. And an unwise decision is not proof of incapacity : people with full capacity make choices others think foolish, and the question is how the person decides, not what they decide. What exactly is assessed? In an influential 1988 paper in the New England Journal of Medicine , the American psychiatrist Paul S. Appelbaum and the psychologist Thomas Grisso set out the four abilities that the legal standards for consent to treatment require: the ability to communicate a choice , to understand the relevant information , to appreciate the situation and its consequences for oneself, and to reason about the options, weighing risks and benefits. They later built a structured interview around these abilities, the MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool for Treatment (a test described in the Assessment book). England's Mental Capacity Act 2005 uses a closely similar functional test: a person lacks capacity for a decision if, because of an impairment of the mind or brain, he cannot understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it, or communicate his decision. Indian law takes the same approach for mental health decisions. Section 4 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (taught in full in Chapter 1) says that every person, including a person with mental illness, shall be deemed to have capacity to make decisions about his mental healthcare or treatment if he is able to understand the information relevant to the decision, to appreciate any reasonably foreseeable consequence of a decision or of a lack of decision, and to communicate the decision by speech, expression, gesture or any other means. (The Act's own wording links the three abilities with "or"; in practice clinicians assess all three.) The information must be given in simple language the person understands, or in sign language or with visual aids, and a decision that others think inappropriate or wrong does not by itself mean that the person lacks capacity. The same Act lets a person make an advance directive and appoint a nominated representative for the time when he may lose capacity (Chapter 1). Decisions about property and wills fall under other laws; the Indian Succession Act 1925, for example, allows any person of sound mind who is not a minor to make a will, and clinicians asked to judge a will-maker's capacity still use the questions of the old English case Banks v Goodfellow (1870), which asks whether the person understands that he is making a will and what it does, knows the extent of his property, and can bring to mind the people who might expect to benefit. The psychologist's job is to give the person every chance to show capacity: to choose the best time of day, to explain the decision simply, with written notes, to treat anything reversible first, and to test understanding in the person's own words ("Tell me what this paper will do"). Seen at eleven in the morning, her best time, Mrs Venkatesan could say that the house was "for my sons", but could not explain that the deed would transfer ownership now, could not remember from one minute to the next what had been explained, and could not weigh the consequences for her younger son or for herself. The psychologist concluded that she lacked capacity for this decision at this time , while she retained it for many everyday decisions, and wrote the opinion in exactly those terms. The episode also raised a further concern, which leads to the last topic of this section. The World Health Organization, following the Toronto Declaration of 2002, defines elder abuse as a single or repeated act, or lack of appropriate action, occurring within any relationship where there is an expectation of trust, which causes harm or distress to an older person. The key phrase is "expectation of trust": the abusers are usually not strangers but sons, daughters, daughters-in-law, spouses and paid carers. In a 2017 meta-analysis of 52 studies from 28 countries, Yongjie Yon and colleagues estimated that about one in six older people living in the community (15.7 percent) had experienced some form of abuse in the past year, roughly 141 million people worldwide. Barlow and Durand note that withholding food or medication and physical abuse are most common among carers of older people with cognitive deficits, which is one more reason to support carers before their strain turns into harm. Warning signs include unexplained injuries, weight loss and poor hygiene, fear or silence in the carer's presence, a carer who will not leave the clinician alone with the patient, missing money and sudden changes to a will or property. The clinician's response begins with interviewing the older person alone (Section 2.2), documenting carefully, assessing safety and capacity, and linking the person with help: social services, the police where a crime has been committed, the Maintenance Tribunal under the 2007 Act, and the national helpline for senior citizens, Elderline (14567), launched by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on 1 October 2021, the International Day of Older Persons. A capable older person's wishes must be respected even when they are frustrating; many abused parents refuse to act against a son. And because much abuse grows out of caregiver strain, helping the carer is often part of protecting the victim. Indian context The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 (assented to on 29 December 2007) defines a senior citizen as an Indian aged 60 or above. It obliges children and grandchildren to maintain parents and grandparents who cannot maintain themselves (a childless senior citizen can claim from relatives who will inherit his property), sets up Maintenance Tribunals that must decide applications within 90 days, and fixes the maximum maintenance allowance at Rs 10,000 a month. Under section 23, a transfer of property made on condition that the transferee will provide for the senior citizen can be declared void if that condition is not kept. Under section 24, abandoning a senior citizen is an offence punishable with imprisonment of up to three months, a fine of up to Rs 5,000, or both. State governments may set up old age homes, at least one in each district, for indigent senior citizens. The National Policy on Older Persons dates from 1999, and the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE), launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2010 to 2011, aims to bring preventive, curative and rehabilitative services for older people to every level of the health system, from sub-centres to district hospitals with dedicated geriatric wards and regional geriatric centres in medical colleges. Behind these laws lies social change: smaller families, the migration of adult children to cities and abroad, more older women living as widows because women live longer, and the slow loosening of the joint family that once took care of old age for granted. Exam trap Capacity is presumed , decision-specific and time-specific , and an unwise decision is not incapacity . Clinicians assess capacity; competence in the strict sense is a legal finding. Appelbaum and Grisso's four abilities are communicating a choice, understanding, appreciation and reasoning . Section 4 of the MHCA 2017 asks about three: understand the relevant information, appreciate foreseeable consequences, and communicate the decision. In elder abuse, psychological abuse is the commonest form and the abusers are usually family members. The 2007 Act: age 60 , Tribunal decision within 90 days , maximum Rs 10,000 a month, abandonment punishable under section 24 . 10.8 Counselling Medium yield · 3 Qs You already know a good deal about counselling. Section 6.10 defined it, traced its roots to Frank Parsons and the guidance movement, set out the traditional contrasts between guidance, counselling and psychotherapy (Table 6.21) and the modern view that they differ in degree rather than kind, and described the three great helping-skills models of Allen Ivey, Robert Carkhuff and Gerard Egan. Section 2.2 taught the individual skills: attending and SOLER, questions, minimal encouragers, paraphrasing, reflection of feeling, summarising, confrontation and empathy. This section completes the picture from the side of practice. It begins with the guidance programme from which counselling grew, and within which much counselling in Indian schools and colleges still happens; it then compares the three classic approaches to counselling, follows the counselling process from the first meeting to follow-up with the skills at work inside it, surveys the main areas in which counsellors work, and ends with the theories that guide career counselling. Guidance and the guidance programme Think of a Class 10 student in a government school in Mandya who has to choose between the science, commerce and arts streams. What she needs is partly information (Where does each stream lead? What marks do the courses need? What do the jobs at the end of them actually involve?), partly knowledge of herself (What am I good at? What do I enjoy?), and partly a conversation in which she can weigh the two against her worry about what her parents expect. A school guidance programme exists to provide all three. Guidance, as Section 6.10 explained, is the process of helping people understand themselves and their opportunities so that they can make wise choices and adjustments. It is traditionally divided into three kinds: educational guidance (choosing subjects, streams and institutions, study habits, learning difficulties), vocational or career guidance (choosing, preparing for and entering an occupation) and personal-social guidance (relationships, adjustment, health and emotional problems). An organised guidance programme is usually described as a set of guidance services , each of which does a different job (Table 10.18). The orientation service helps newcomers settle into a new school or college. The appraisal or individual inventory service collects, organises and interprets information about each student, from tests, records, observations and interviews, so that the student and the counsellor have an accurate picture to work with. The information service supplies educational, occupational and personal-social information: what courses exist, what jobs require, where to find help. The counselling service offers individual and group counselling. The placement service helps the student into the next step, an educational placement in the right course or stream or a vocational placement in a job, apprenticeship or internship. The follow-up service keeps track of former students to see how they are faring and whether the programme helped them, and research and evaluation studies the programme itself so that it can be improved. Table 10.18 The services of a school or college guidance programme. Service What it does Example Orientation Helps newcomers adjust to a new institution A first-week programme for Class 11 entrants Appraisal (individual inventory) Collects and interprets information about each student Aptitude and interest testing, cumulative records Information Provides educational, occupational and personal-social information A careers corner, talks by professionals Counselling Helps the student understand, decide and adjust Individual sessions on choosing a stream Placement Places students in courses, jobs or internships Stream allocation, campus recruitment Follow-up Tracks how students fare after placement A check six months into the new course Research and evaluation Studies whether the programme works A survey of former students Which of these services matters most? Writers on guidance have long answered: counselling. The reason is clear when you look at what the others do. Appraisal and information gather facts; placement and follow-up act on a decision once it has been made. It is in counselling that the student brings knowledge of herself together with knowledge of the world, works through her doubts and her family's expectations, and actually makes the choice. That is why the counselling service is called the heart (or the hub) of the guidance programme. A school with an excellent battery of tests and a well-stocked careers library but no counselling has a filing cabinet, not a guidance programme. Guidance workers collect their information with two families of tools. The testing techniques are the standardised tests of intelligence, aptitude, achievement, interests and personality, described in the Assessment book. Of these, the aptitude test deserves a definition here because it is so often confused with its neighbours: it measures a person's potential to acquire, with training, a particular skill or body of knowledge (mechanical, clerical, numerical, verbal, spatial), and so predicts future success; an achievement test measures what has already been learned, and an intelligence test measures general ability. The non-testing techniques include observation, questionnaires, rating scales, autobiographies, sociometry, the interview, the anecdotal record, the cumulative record and the case study. The interview , a purposeful face-to-face conversation, is used in guidance to gather facts, to give information and, above all, to counsel: the counselling interview is the vehicle through which counselling is done. The cumulative record is a longitudinal file kept by the school for each student over many years, recording identifying data and family background, attendance, marks year by year, test results, health, co-curricular activities, teachers' ratings of personal qualities and their remarks; it moves with the student from class to class and school to school, so that it gives a picture of development rather than a single snapshot. An anecdotal record is a brief, dated, factual description of one specific incident of a student's behaviour, written by a teacher who saw it, with any interpretation kept separate; many such anecdotes, often filed in the cumulative record, reveal patterns that a single observation cannot. The case study is the most comprehensive technique of all: an in-depth study of one individual that draws on every other source, used for students with serious or puzzling difficulties. Indian context Organised vocational guidance in India began before independence, with bureaus such as the Batliboi Vocational Guidance Bureau set up in Bombay in 1941. After independence the Secondary Education Commission (1952 to 1953, chaired by A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar) recommended guidance services in secondary schools, and in 1954 the Government of India set up the Central Bureau of Educational and Vocational Guidance, later merged into the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT), which still trains teacher-counsellors through its Diploma Course in Guidance and Counselling. Three recent steps matter for a clinician. The Central Board of Secondary Education's affiliation bye-laws of 2018 require every affiliated secondary and senior secondary school to appoint a counsellor and wellness teacher (part-time in small schools). In 2020 the Ministry of Education launched Manodarpan , its psychosocial support programme and helpline for students (Section 10.3). And on 25 July 2025, in Sukdeb Saha v. State of Andhra Pradesh , a case arising from a student's death, the Supreme Court issued interim guidelines on student mental health, including that every educational institution with 100 or more enrolled students must appoint at least one qualified counsellor, psychologist or social worker trained in child and adolescent mental health, and that smaller institutions must set up referral links with outside professionals. Exam trap "Which technique or process involved in guidance is called the heart of the guidance programme?" (RML 2022) The phrase belongs to counselling : the counselling service is the heart of guidance, because it is where the student uses all the information to decide. The paper's options were case study, interview, cumulative record and aptitude test, and its key gave aptitude test . That key is doubtful. An aptitude test is only one tool of the appraisal service; the cumulative record is the main record of that service; the case study is the most comprehensive technique; and the interview , as the counselling interview, is the core tool of counselling itself, which makes it the most defensible of the four. If "counselling" appears among the options, choose it; if it does not, the interview is the best answer. Keep the definitions apart too: an aptitude test predicts potential with training, an achievement test measures what has been learned, and an anecdotal record describes one incident while a cumulative record covers years. Directive, non-directive and eclectic counselling In the middle of the twentieth century counsellors argued about who should lead the interview, the counsellor or the client. Three answers emerged, and they remain a staple of Indian guidance and counselling syllabi. Directive counselling , also called counsellor-centred counselling or the Minnesota point of view, is Edmund Williamson's trait-and-factor method, which you met in Section 6.10. The counsellor is the expert. He gathers and interprets the facts, works out what is wrong, and tells the client what he thinks should be done, relying on the client's reason rather than his feelings. Williamson set the work out in six steps. Analysis collects data about the student from tests, records, interviews and other sources. Synthesis organises the data to show the student's strengths, weaknesses and characteristic patterns. Diagnosis identifies the problem and its causes. Prognosis predicts how the problem is likely to develop, or how the student is likely to fare on each of the paths open to him. Counselling (or treatment) helps the student understand the findings and act on them, often by advising him directly. And follow-up checks how things have gone and whether the problem has returned. The method is quick and suits problems that turn on information, such as choosing a course; its weaknesses are that it makes the client dependent, neglects feelings, and puts the decision in the counsellor's hands. Non-directive counselling , also called client-centred counselling, is Carl Rogers's answer, launched in Counseling and Psychotherapy (1942) as an explicit challenge to Williamson and taught fully in Section 6.2. The client leads. The counsellor does not diagnose or advise but provides the conditions of empathy, unconditional positive regard and genuineness and reflects the client's feelings, trusting that a person who feels understood will find his own direction. It respects autonomy and builds self-reliance; its critics say it is slow, depends on clients who are verbally fluent and fairly mature, and suits problems that need information or quick decisions poorly. A third position, eclectic counselling , took the view that both are right some of the time. Its best-known advocate was the American psychiatrist and psychologist Frederick C. Thorne (1909 to 1978), founder of the Journal of Clinical Psychology , whose Principles of Personality Counseling (1950) argued that the counsellor should select whatever methods, directive or non-directive, best fit the particular client, problem and stage of counselling. In practice an eclectic counsellor often begins non-directively, letting the client tell his story and express his feelings, and becomes more directive when information, interpretation or a plan is needed. The danger, as Section 8.11 explained in discussing technical eclecticism and integration, is that choice without a guiding theory becomes a grab-bag. Table 10.19 compares the three. Table 10.19 Directive, non-directive and eclectic counselling. Feature Directive Non-directive Eclectic Main figure E. G. Williamson (1939) Carl Rogers (1942) Frederick Thorne (1950) Centre Counsellor-centred Client-centred Varies with the client and stage Who decides Counsellor advises Client decides Shared, as the case requires Emphasis Intellect, facts, diagnosis Feelings, the relationship, growth Both, chosen deliberately Typical method Six steps from analysis to follow-up Reflection and the core conditions Non-directive start, directive when needed Main criticism Dependence; neglects emotion Slow; needs a fluent, mature client Can lack a unifying theory Clinical link Many Indian clients arrive expecting a directive expert ("Madam, you tell me what I should do"), and a counsellor who only reflects feelings may seem evasive or unhelpful. Jaswant Singh Neki's proposal of the guru-chela relationship as a therapeutic model (Section 3.10), and the discussion of therapy in India in Section 8.11, describe this expectation. The skilled response is usually eclectic: begin by listening, so the client feels understood; give information and clear structure where they are needed; and still leave the decision with the client, because a decision someone else made for you is easily abandoned. Exam trap Williamson's six steps run analysis, synthesis, diagnosis, prognosis, counselling, follow-up ; questions often swap synthesis and diagnosis or leave out prognosis. Directive counselling is counsellor-centred (Williamson, Minnesota); non-directive is client-centred (Rogers); eclectic counselling is associated with Frederick Thorne . Parsons founded vocational guidance but did not write the six steps. The counselling process and its skills Whatever the approach, counselling moves through a recognisable sequence. One widely used description, from the American counsellor educators Harold L. Hackney and Sherry Cormier in their textbook The Professional Counselor: A Process Guide to Helping , has five stages: rapport and relationship building, assessment or problem definition, goal setting, initiating interventions, and termination and follow-up. Other models cut the same journey differently (Egan's three stages and Ivey's five-stage interview in Section 6.10, Carkhuff's attending, responding, personalising and initiating), but the arc is the same: build a relationship, understand the problem, decide what the client wants, help him get there, and end well. Before the first stage comes the intake: the referral, the first contact, and the informed consent that tells the client what counselling involves and where its confidentiality ends (Chapter 1). In the relationship stage the counsellor's aim is trust and a working alliance (Section 8.5). The skills are attending, minimal encouragers, open questions and primary empathy, and one more that beginners forget, structuring : explaining briefly what counselling is, how long sessions last, what the counsellor will and will not do, and the limits of confidentiality. In the assessment stage the counsellor helps the client tell the whole story and understand it in context: what the problem is, when and where it happens, how often, with whom, what the client has tried and what strengths he has. Questions, clarification, paraphrasing, reflection of feeling and summarising carry this stage; in guidance settings, tests and records add to it. In the goal-setting stage the problem is turned into goals that are specific, observable, realistic and the client's own. Hackney and Cormier distinguish process goals , the conditions the counsellor works to create (a safe, accepting relationship), from outcome goals , the changes the client wants in his life. In the intervention stage the counsellor draws on whatever methods fit the client and the goal: problem solving and decision making, cognitive techniques, information giving, role-play and assertiveness training, relaxation; here too the challenging skills come in, confrontation, immediacy, advanced empathy and self-disclosure (Section 6.10). In the last stage, termination is planned rather than allowed to happen: progress is reviewed, the client says what he has learned and how he will handle setbacks, sessions may be spaced out, and a follow-up contact weeks or months later checks that the gains have held (the ending of therapy is discussed in Section 8.10). Referral belongs here too: when a problem is beyond the counsellor's training or setting, such as psychosis, severe depression or high suicide risk, the counsellor's job is to refer the client to a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist and to make sure the referral is completed. Watch the skills at work with one client. Neelam, 19, a second-year BSc student at a college in Mysuru, comes to the college counselling cell. She says: "My parents have fixed my engagement for next March. Everyone at home is so happy. I don't know why I can't sleep." Table 10.20 shows how a counsellor might respond with each skill, and what each response does. Table 10.20 One client statement, many skills. Neelam: "My parents have fixed my engagement for next March. Everyone at home is so happy. I don't know why I can't sleep." Skill What it does Example response Minimal encourager Invites more without directing "Mm-hm. Go on." Closed question Pins down a fact "When did the sleeplessness start?" Open question Invites the story "What has it been like for you since the engagement was fixed?" Paraphrase Restates the content briefly, in the counsellor's own words "So the engagement is set for March, the family is delighted, and since then your sleep has gone." Reflection of feeling Names the emotion, stated or implied "You sound confused, perhaps a little frightened, as if you're not allowed to feel anything but happy." Clarification Makes a vague message clear "When you say it's all decided, do you mean the date, or the marriage itself?" Summary Draws the threads of a longer stretch together "Today you've told me about the engagement, your wish to finish your degree and how hard it is to say so at home." Confrontation Points out a discrepancy, supportively "You've said you're happy about it, and three times you've said you wish you could finish your degree first." Immediacy Talks about what is happening between you now "I notice you look away each time your father comes up. What's happening for you right now?" Advanced empathy Voices what the client has only hinted at (later, once trust exists) "I wonder whether part of you fears that if you speak up, you'll lose your family's approval." Look closely at the paraphrase, because it is the skill examiners ask about most. It restates the content of what Neelam said, the facts of her situation, in the counsellor's own, different words, and usually more briefly. It does not add an interpretation, does not ask anything, and does not name a feeling; it simply shows that she has been heard accurately and gives her the chance to correct the counsellor. Repeating her exact words ("Your parents have fixed your engagement for next March") would be parroting, which sounds mechanical. The reflection of feeling goes one level deeper, to the emotion beneath the content, and a summary does for a whole stretch of conversation what a paraphrase does for a single statement. In Neelam's case the process ran its full course. Over the first two sessions the relationship and the story emerged: she liked the young man her parents had chosen but wanted to finish her degree before the wedding, and she had never in her life disagreed with her father. Her goals, in her own words, were "to know what I actually want" and "to tell Amma without a fight". The interventions were a simple decision balance of the costs and benefits of each option, and two sessions of role-play in which she practised what she would say to her mother, with the counsellor playing first her mother and then her father. She chose to enlist an aunt she trusted. Her family agreed to hold the wedding after her final examinations. Termination came after six sessions, with a review of what she had learned about speaking up, and at a follow-up meeting at the end of the semester she was sleeping well. Nothing in the counselling told Neelam to reject an arranged marriage; it helped her find, and say, what she wanted within the family she valued. Exam trap "When a counsellor repeats what the client says, but uses words that are different from those the client used, the counsellor is using what skill?" (RML 2021). The answer is paraphrasing (restatement, or reflection of content). Questioning asks for information rather than restating it. Empathy is the broader capacity to understand the client's world from inside and communicate that understanding; reflection of feeling is its main vehicle, and a paraphrase can express empathy, but "repeating what the client said in different words" defines the paraphrase. Nonverbal communication is posture, eye contact, tone and gesture, the territory of attending behaviour and SOLER. And keep the three reflecting skills apart: paraphrase = content , reflection = feeling , summary = many statements drawn together. The main areas of counselling Counselling has spread into almost every setting where people face problems of living. The skills are the same everywhere; what changes is the population, the typical concerns and the knowledge the counsellor needs. Table 10.21 gives an overview, and the paragraphs that follow pick out what each area adds. School counselling is developmental, preventive and remedial at once: it helps every student with the normal tasks of growing up (study skills, choosing a stream, friendships, puberty), runs prevention programmes (on bullying, exam stress, substance use, online safety), and helps individual students in difficulty, working closely with teachers and parents. The school counsellor is often the first to notice a learning difficulty (Section 10.5), abuse (Section 10.6) or the warning signs of suicide, and school-based programmes are described in Section 10.3. College and university counselling deals with the transition to independent life, homesickness, examination and performance pressure, relationships, sexuality, identity and, increasingly, suicide prevention; the Supreme Court's 2025 guidelines described in Section 10.8.1 have made it a legal obligation for larger institutions. Career counselling is the subject of the next subsection. Marital and premarital counselling helps couples with conflict, communication, infidelity, sexual problems, in-laws and decisions about separation; couples therapy is taught in Section 7.8, which also describes the counsellors attached to India's family courts, and sex therapy in Section 7.9. Premarital counselling is preventive: structured programmes teach couples who are about to marry to communicate, solve problems and handle conflict, and some use questionnaires that help each partner see where their expectations differ (Howard Markman and Scott Stanley's PREP programme and David Olson's PREPARE inventory are well-known American examples). Family counselling is covered in Chapter 7. Rehabilitation counselling helps people with physical, sensory, intellectual and psychiatric disabilities to reach their personal, vocational and independent-living goals: adjusting to a disability, planning a return to work, using vocational training and supported employment, and claiming the benefits of disability certification. Its methods are described in Sections 9.8 and 9.9, and the rights it rests on (the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016) in Chapter 1. HIV counselling is the clearest example of counselling built into a medical procedure. Section 9.3 explained that in India testing at the Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres of the National AIDS Control Organisation is preceded and followed by counselling. Pre-test counselling (or, in the World Health Organization's newer guidance, brief pre-test information) explains what HIV is and how it is transmitted, what the test involves, what a positive, negative or indeterminate result would mean, and the window period , the weeks after infection during which a test can still be negative; it assesses the person's risk and obtains informed consent. Post-test counselling depends on the result. After a negative result it reinforces risk reduction and advises a repeat test if the person may still be in the window period. After a positive result the counsellor gives the result clearly and simply, allows time for the shock, deals with immediate fears (Will I die? Who must I tell? Will I lose my job?), plans disclosure to a partner, and, most importantly, links the person straight to treatment. The World Health Organization's 2015 guidelines sum up the ethics of testing as the five Cs : consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct test results, and connection to prevention, treatment and care. De-addiction counselling rests on motivational interviewing and the stages of change (Section 6.9) and on relapse prevention and aftercare (Section 9.9), with the family drawn in wherever possible; in India it is delivered in de-addiction centres, hospitals and community programmes such as the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (launched in 2020). Grief counselling draws on the models of grief in Section 9.5; J. William Worden, in Grief Counseling and Grief Therapy (1982), distinguished grief counselling , which helps people through normal grief, from grief therapy , which treats complicated grief. Crisis counselling is described in Section 9.7, and the counselling of older adults and their families in Section 10.7. Two smaller areas complete the list. Genetic counselling helps families understand the risk of an inherited condition, such as thalassaemia or Down syndrome, and the choices open to them. Health counselling supports people with chronic illness and lifestyle change, the territory of Chapter 9. Workplace counselling deals with work stress, burnout (Section 8.12), conflict with colleagues and managers, career transitions, and personal problems that spill into work. Much of it is delivered through employee assistance programmes (EAPs), which grew out of the occupational alcoholism programmes that American companies began in the 1940s and broadened, from the 1970s, to cover any personal problem that affects work. A typical EAP offers employees and their families free, confidential, short-term counselling and referral, and advises managers on how to handle a troubled employee; many large Indian companies, especially in information technology, now provide one. Workplace counselling is not the same as the branch of psychology that studies work itself. The branch called industrial-organisational psychology applies psychological principles and research to the workplace in order to optimise human behaviour there, improving both organisational effectiveness and employees' well-being. Its industrial side deals with fitting people to jobs (job analysis, selection and testing, training, performance appraisal, ergonomics); its organisational side deals with motivation, job satisfaction, leadership, teams and organisational change. Its founder is usually taken to be the German-American psychologist Hugo Münsterberg (1863 to 1916), whom you will meet again in Section 10.9 as a pioneer of forensic psychology, and whose Psychology and Industrial Efficiency appeared in English in 1913, and the Hawthorne studies you met in Section 2.8 are part of its history. Career counselling and the theories of career development Sameer is 17 and in Class 12 at a school in Lucknow, studying physics, chemistry and mathematics and attending an engineering entrance coaching class every evening because his father, an engineer himself, has always said that Sameer will be one too. His marks are falling, and after failing two mock tests he is sent to the school counsellor. He comes alive only when he talks about the things he does outside class: he captains the debating team, acts in the school's plays, designs the posters for the annual fest and organised it last year. What should a career counsellor do with him? Each of the theories in this subsection gives part of the answer, and Table 10.22 compares them. The trait-and-factor tradition. The oldest answer is Frank Parsons's (Section 6.10): understand the person, understand the world of work, and use "true reasoning" to match the two. Parsons's Choosing a Vocation (1909) made him the father of vocational guidance, and Williamson turned his approach into directive counselling. The approach survives in every aptitude test and interest inventory, but on its own it is static. It assumes that each person has one right job, that people and jobs stay the same, and that the choice is made once, in adolescence; it says nothing about development, about chance, or about the family that, in India, so often makes the decision. Holland's theory of vocational personalities and work environments. The most influential modern version of matching comes from John L. Holland (1919 to 2008) of Johns Hopkins University, who first set out his theory in "A theory of vocational choice" in the Journal of Counseling Psychology in 1959 and developed it in Making Vocational Choices (1973, revised 1985 and 1997). Holland made four assumptions: that most people can be described as resembling one or more of six personality types; that there are six matching kinds of work environment; that people search for environments that let them use their skills and abilities, express their attitudes and values and take on agreeable problems and roles; and that behaviour is determined by the interaction between personality and environment. The six types, known by their initials as RIASEC , are: Realistic (the doers): prefer practical work with tools, machines, plants and animals; mechanics, farmers, electricians, civil engineers. Investigative (the thinkers): prefer observing, analysing and solving intellectual problems; scientists, researchers, doctors. Artistic (the creators): prefer unstructured, expressive, original work; artists, writers, designers, actors, musicians. Social (the helpers): prefer informing, training, caring for and healing others; teachers, counsellors, nurses, social workers. Enterprising (the persuaders): prefer leading, persuading and managing others for organisational or economic goals; managers, lawyers, salespeople, politicians. Conventional (the organisers): prefer ordered, systematic work with data and records; accountants, bank clerks, office administrators. A person is described by a Holland code of the two or three types he most resembles, in order: a counsellor might be SAE, an accountant CEI. Holland's types are arranged on a Holland's hexagon , first drawn in a 1969 research report by Holland and his colleagues, in which the distance between two types reflects how different they are (Figure 10.11). Adjacent types, such as Realistic and Investigative, have much in common; opposite types, Realistic and Social, Investigative and Enterprising, Artistic and Conventional, have least. Four concepts follow. Congruence is the degree of fit between a person's type and the environment (a Social person in a Social job); it predicts satisfaction, stability and achievement. Consistency is how close together on the hexagon the first two letters of a person's code lie; an RI code is consistent, an RS code is not. Differentiation is how clearly a profile is defined, one or two high peaks against a flat profile in which everything scores about the same. Identity is the clarity and stability of a person's goals, interests and talents. Holland also designed a self-scored interest inventory, the Self-Directed Search, and his six types are used in other interest inventories (the inventories are described in the Assessment book). Realistic (R) tools, machines Investigative (I) ideas, science Artistic (A) art, music, writing Social (S) helping, teaching Enterprising (E) leading, selling Conventional (C) data, records, order Adjacent: most alike Opposite: least alike Figure 10.11 Holland's hexagon. The six RIASEC types sit at the corners in a fixed order; the black outer edges join neighbouring, similar types, and the three lines that cross the centre join opposite, least similar types (Realistic and Social, Investigative and Enterprising, Artistic and Conventional). Applied to Sameer, an interest inventory gives a code of EAS: Enterprising, Artistic and Social, with low scores on Realistic and Investigative. Engineering is largely a Realistic and Investigative environment, on the far side of the hexagon from his code, so his congruence with it is poor, which helps to explain why the coaching class feels like a cage. His profile is well differentiated; his first two letters, E and A, are not neighbours on the hexagon but alternate corners with S between them, which Holland would call moderately consistent; and the code points towards environments such as law, management, journalism, advertising and design. Holland's theory has strong research support and is easy to use, but it is still a matching theory: it describes where a person might fit, not how he gets there, and it says little about the family, social class and gender pressures that narrow choices before any test is taken. Super's life-span, life-space theory. The developmental answer comes from Donald E. Super (1910 to 1994) of Teachers College, Columbia University, whose "A theory of vocational development" (his presidential address to the American Psychological Association's Division of Counseling and Guidance, published in 1953) and The Psychology of Careers (1957) turned career choice from a single event into a lifelong process. Super's central proposition was that in choosing an occupation a person is implementing a self-concept : his picture of his own abilities, interests, values and personality, which develops through childhood play, school, part-time work and the reactions of others, and which keeps changing, so that career choice and adjustment are continuous. Careers unfold through a maxicycle of five life stages (Figure 10.12): growth (birth to about 14), when the self-concept and attitudes to work form through fantasy, play and interests; exploration (about 15 to 24), when the young person tries out roles in school, leisure and part-time work and moves through the developmental tasks of crystallising a vocational preference, specifying it and implementing it; establishment (about 25 to 44), when he secures a place in a field, stabilises and consolidates it and advances; maintenance (about 45 to 64), when he holds on to what he has achieved, updates his skills and innovates; and decline or disengagement (65 onwards), when work slows down and retirement brings new roles. The ages are flexible, and Super stressed that people recycle through smaller versions of exploration and establishment (minicycles) whenever they change jobs, lose one, migrate or return to study. Super's life stages (the maxicycle) Ages are approximate; people recycle through stages at transitions Growth birth to 14 Self-concept forms; fantasy and interests Exploration 15 to 24 Crystallise, specify and implement a choice Establishment 25 to 44 Stabilise, consolidate, advance Maintenance 45 to 64 Hold on, update skills, innovate Disengagement 65 onwards Slow down, retire, take up new roles Life span (approximate ages in years) Figure 10.12 Super's five life stages of career development. Involvement in work rises through exploration to a plateau in establishment and maintenance and falls in disengagement; the developmental tasks of crystallising, specifying and implementing a choice belong to exploration, and stabilising and consolidating to establishment. Two further ideas complete Super's theory. The first, career maturity (Super's term was vocational maturity), is a person's readiness to make the career decisions expected at his stage: planfulness, exploration, knowledge of occupations and decision-making skill. It is measured against age-mates, not against adults, and for adults Super and later writers preferred the term career adaptability , the readiness to cope with changing work and working conditions. The life-space half of the theory recognises that work is only one of the roles a person plays. In a 1980 paper Super presented the life-career rainbow , in which the outer arcs show the life stages and the inner bands show how much of a person's time and emotional involvement goes into each of nine major roles over the life span (child, student, leisurite, citizen, worker, spouse, homemaker, parent and pensioner), played in four principal "theatres": the home, the community, the school and the workplace. Sameer, in Super's terms, is in the exploration stage but has not explored at all: his preference was specified for him by his father before he ever crystallised one of his own, which is a problem of career maturity, not of ability. Counselling therefore starts with exploration: shadowing a lawyer and a design studio for a day, talking to people in the fields his code points to, and reflecting on what his theatre and debating say about his self-concept. Ginzberg's developmental theory. Super's was not the first developmental theory. In Occupational Choice: An Approach to a General Theory (1951) the Columbia economist Eli Ginzberg (1911 to 2002) and his colleagues, the psychiatrist Sol Ginsburg, the sociologist Sidney Axelrad and the psychologist John Herma, proposed that occupational choice develops through three periods. In the fantasy period (up to about 11) children choose freely and playfully, without regard to ability or reality ("I will be a pilot"). In the tentative period (about 11 to 17) choices are based first on interests , then on capacities , then on values , ending in a transition substage in which the young person begins to face reality. In the realistic period (about 17 to the early twenties) the person moves through exploration , crystallisation and specification of a choice. Ginzberg first described the process as largely irreversible and as a compromise between wishes and possibilities; in a restatement in 1972 he concluded that occupational choice is a lifelong process of decision making and that "optimisation" describes it better than compromise. Super built his own theory partly as a reply, adding the self-concept and extending the stages across the whole of working life. Krumboltz's social learning theory and planned happenstance. John D. Krumboltz of Stanford University applied Albert Bandura's social learning theory to careers. In "A social learning theory of career selection" (1976, with Anita Mitchell and G. Brian Jones) he identified four kinds of influence on career decisions: genetic endowment and special abilities (sex, physical characteristics, talents such as musical or athletic ability); environmental conditions and events (the job market, family resources, social and educational policies, natural events, largely outside the person's control); learning experiences , both instrumental (being reinforced or punished for an activity) and associative (observing others and pairing an occupation with positive or negative images, as Sameer has done with his engineer father and with an admired theatre teacher); and task approach skills , such as setting goals, gathering information and making decisions. Out of these come the person's beliefs about himself and about the world of work, and the actions he takes. Two decades later, in "Planned happenstance: constructing unexpected career opportunities" (1999), Kathleen Mitchell, Al Levin and Krumboltz added that unplanned events are inevitable and often decisive in careers, and that counselling should teach people to create and use them rather than fear them. They named five skills that turn chance into opportunity: curiosity , persistence , flexibility , optimism and risk taking . Krumboltz later combined the two ideas as the happenstance learning theory (2009). For Sameer, a chance invitation to a workshop by a visiting advertising agency could be just such an event, if he is curious enough to go. Other theories in brief. The American psychologist Anne Roe (1904 to 1991), in The Psychology of Occupations (1956), proposed that early parent-child relations (emotionally concentrated, avoiding or accepting) shape whether a person becomes oriented towards people or away from them, and so towards occupational groups such as service and business contact or technology and science. Linda S. Gottfredson 's theory of circumscription and compromise (1981) describes how children, from an early age, rule out occupations they see as wrong for their sex and then for their social class and ability, and later compromise among what is left; it explains why some options never even reach a career counsellor. And social cognitive career theory , proposed in 1994 by Robert Lent, Steven Brown and Gail Hackett, builds on Bandura's later social cognitive theory: career interests, choices and performance grow from self-efficacy beliefs ("Can I do this?"), outcome expectations ("What will happen if I do?") and personal goals, all shaped by the person's background and by the support and barriers around him. In an outpatient clinic the psychologist asks, "What is wrong, and how can I help?" In a forensic assessment the questions come from the law, and they are strange ones for a clinician. Can this man understand the charge against him? On the night of the killing, did he know that what he was doing was wrong? Which parent should a six-year-old live with? Is this seventeen-year-old mature enough to be tried as an adult? Will this prisoner offend again if he is released? The person in front of you may not want to be seen, may have every reason to exaggerate or to conceal, and will not be helped, in the ordinary sense, by what you write, because your report goes to a judge. This section follows clinical psychology into the legal system, from the first question a criminal court asks (is the accused fit to be tried?) to the last (what will stop him offending again?), and then into the family court, the juvenile justice system and the prison. What forensic psychology is, and the roles it gives a clinician The word forensic comes from the Latin forum , the public square of ancient Rome in which trials were held; anything forensic belongs to the courts. In the sense used in this book, forensic psychology is the application of psychological science and practice to questions that arise in the law and the legal system. A narrow definition confines it to clinical work for the courts: assessments of fitness to stand trial, criminal responsibility, risk and child custody, and the testimony that goes with them. A broad definition takes in everything psychology does where it meets the law, including research on eyewitness memory and juries, the investigation of crime, the treatment of offenders and the support of victims. Forensic clinical psychology is the clinical core of that wider field, and it is what an Indian clinical psychologist is most likely to be asked to do. The field is older than many people think. In 1908 Hugo Münsterberg (1863 to 1916), the German experimental psychologist whom William James had brought to Harvard, published On the Witness Stand , a book of essays arguing that the courts ignored what the laboratory already knew about the unreliability of perception and memory, the effects of suggestion and the detection of deception. The lawyers were not impressed. In 1909 the American legal scholar John Henry Wigmore replied with a satirical account of an imaginary trial in which Münsterberg was sued for libelling the legal profession and lost, because psychology could not yet produce the precise, tested findings he had claimed for it. The exchange set the terms of a debate that still runs: when is psychological knowledge good enough to be heard in court? American courts gave two famous answers. In Frye v. United States (1923) a court refused to admit the results of a systolic blood pressure "lie detector" test devised by the psychologist William Moulton Marston , ruling that a scientific technique must have gained general acceptance in its field before it could be used as evidence. This Frye standard governed American courts for seventy years, until Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals (1993) made the trial judge the gatekeeper who must decide whether the evidence is scientifically valid: whether the method has been tested, peer-reviewed and has a known error rate. Meanwhile, in Jenkins v. United States (1962), a federal appeals court held that a properly qualified psychologist could give expert opinion on mental disease, which until then had been treated as the psychiatrist's preserve. (India's own encounter with scientific lie detection, the Supreme Court's 2010 ruling in Selvi v. State of Karnataka on narcoanalysis, the polygraph and brain-mapping, is told in Section 3.10.) The American Psychology-Law Society, founded in the late 1960s, later merged with the Psychology and Law division of the American Psychological Association (APA) and is now its Division 41; in 2001 the APA recognised forensic psychology as a specialty, and its Specialty Guidelines for Forensic Psychology (2013) now set out the standards of practice. Within this field a clinician can play five roles. As an evaluator , the psychologist assesses a person to answer a legal question and writes a report: fitness to stand trial, mental state at the time of an offence, risk of violence, parenting capacity, the psychological damage claimed in a compensation case. As an expert witness , the psychologist testifies in court. An ordinary witness may describe only what he or she saw and heard; an expert witness may give opinions, because the court accepts that the expert has specialised knowledge the judge lacks. The court decides whether to admit the testimony, the other side cross-examines it, and the expert's duty is to the court, not to the side that pays the fee. The public's suspicion that experts are "hired guns" whose opinions suit whoever engaged them is the reason that duty matters. As a consultant , the psychologist advises lawyers or the police. As a treating clinician , the psychologist works in a prison, a forensic psychiatric ward, a juvenile home or a probation service. And as a researcher , the psychologist studies the questions the law depends on. The consulting role includes two investigative tools that appear as distractors in exam questions about offender treatment. In offender profiling , investigators attempt to infer the likely characteristics of an unknown offender (age, background, lifestyle, where he lives) from the way a crime was committed. It was developed in the 1970s by the Behavioral Science Unit of the American Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and in Britain from the 1980s by David Canter , who called his more statistical approach investigative psychology. The cognitive interview , developed in the mid-1980s by Ronald P. Fisher and R. Edward Geiselman , is a way of questioning cooperative witnesses that uses principles of memory to help them recall more without increasing errors. Its four original instructions are to reinstate mentally the context of the event (where you were, what you felt), to report everything, however trivial it seems, to recall the events in different orders (for example backwards), and to recall them from a different perspective (as another witness would have seen them). Both tools belong to the investigation of crime; neither is a treatment for offenders. The hardest lesson of forensic work is that the forensic role and the therapeutic role are different jobs. Stuart A. Greenberg and Daniel W. Shuman argued in 1997 that there is an "irreconcilable conflict" between them, and Table 10.23 shows why. The therapist's client is the patient; the forensic evaluator's client is the court or the lawyer who asked the question. The therapist is supportive and accepts the patient's account as the patient's truth; the evaluator is neutral and must test that account against records and informants, because the examinee may have strong reasons to distort it. The therapist promises confidentiality within its usual limits (Chapter 1); the evaluator must tell the examinee at the start that what is said will go into a report that may be read in open court and may be used against him. A therapist who agrees to give expert evidence about his own patient betrays one role or the other: either he advocates for the patient and stops being impartial, or he becomes the patient's judge and destroys the therapy. The rule that follows is simple: do not act as both treating therapist and forensic evaluator for the same person. Many forensic psychologists hold that the expert should describe the person's mental state and explain how it bears on the legal test, and leave the legal conclusion to the judge, whose job it is. After the Hinckley verdict (Section 10.9.3) the American federal rules of evidence went further and barred experts from stating whether a defendant had the mental state that the crime requires. Hugo Münsterberg wrote On the Witness Stand (1908). APA Division 41 is the American Psychology-Law Society (Division 12 is clinical psychology). Offender profiling and the cognitive interview (Fisher and Geiselman) are investigative tools, not offender treatments. Never be both the therapist and the forensic evaluator of the same person. Fitness to stand trial Before anyone can be tried, the law requires that he be able to take part in his own trial. A trial is a contest: the accused must understand what he is charged with, follow the evidence, tell his lawyer what really happened, decide whether to plead guilty and give evidence if he chooses. A person who cannot do these things is not really being tried at all; he is being processed. The question of competence to stand trial (in British and Indian usage, fitness to plead or fitness to stand trial) therefore comes first, and it concerns the person's mental state now , at the time of the proceedings. The standard test comes from the United States Supreme Court's decision in Dusky v. United States (1960). Milton Dusky had been tried for kidnapping although there were doubts about his mental state, and the Court held that it was not enough for the trial judge to find that he was oriented in time and place and had some recollection of events. The test, the Court said, is whether the defendant has "sufficient present ability to consult with his lawyer with a reasonable degree of rational understanding" and "a rational as well as factual understanding of the proceedings against him". Read it slowly and you will find three abilities. Factual understanding means knowing the charge, the possible penalties and the roles of the judge, the prosecutor and one's own lawyer. Rational understanding means that this knowledge is not distorted by illness: a man who can name the judge's role but believes the trial is a test sent by God to prove his divinity has factual but not rational understanding. The ability to consult means being able to communicate with one's lawyer, follow the evidence and help with the defence. Three features of competence surprise students. First, the threshold is low: a diagnosis of schizophrenia or intellectual disability does not make a person unfit, and most people with mental illness are fit to be tried. Second, competence is not about guilt or about the time of the offence; a person may have been floridly psychotic when he committed the act and be perfectly fit by the time of trial, or the reverse. Third, the usual outcome of a finding of unfitness is treatment, with the aim of restoration of competence , after which the trial goes ahead. Because treatment can drag on, the Supreme Court ruled in Jackson v. Indiana (1972) that a person found unfit cannot be held indefinitely: after a reasonable period he must either be restored to competence, committed under the ordinary civil law, or released. Structured instruments for assessing competence, such as the MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool for Criminal Adjudication, are described in the Assessment book. Indian law handles the same problem in the chapter of the criminal procedure code titled "Provisions as to accused persons of unsound mind". This was Chapter XXV of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 (sections 328 to 339); since 1 July 2024 it has been Chapter XXVII of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), sections 367 to 378, which replaced the Code. Section 367 of the BNSS (formerly section 328) covers a Magistrate holding an inquiry, and section 368 (formerly section 329) covers a trial before a Magistrate or a Court of Session. The steps are worth knowing in order: If the Magistrate has reason to believe that the accused is of unsound mind and consequently incapable of making his defence, the accused is examined by the civil surgeon of the district or another medical officer named by the State Government. If the civil surgeon finds unsoundness of mind, the accused is referred to a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist of a government hospital or government medical college for care, treatment and prognosis, who informs the Magistrate whether the accused is suffering from unsoundness of mind or intellectual disability. The accused may appeal against that finding to a Medical Board made up of the head of psychiatry at the nearest government hospital and a member of the psychiatry faculty of the nearest government medical college. The Magistrate then decides whether the condition makes the accused incapable of making (in a trial, entering) his defence. If it does, the court looks at the prosecution's evidence. If there is no prima facie case, the accused is discharged; if there is, the proceedings are postponed for the period of treatment that the psychiatrist or clinical psychologist considers necessary. Where the incapacity is due to intellectual disability, the Magistrate orders the inquiry closed (in a trial, the court does not hold the trial) and deals with the accused under section 369. In every case the person is then dealt with under section 369 (formerly section 330). It provides for release on bail where in-patient treatment is not needed and a relative or friend undertakes to obtain regular out-patient psychiatric treatment and to prevent harm; otherwise for the accused to be kept where regular psychiatric treatment can be provided; and, in some cases, for transfer to a residential facility for persons with unsoundness of mind or intellectual disability. When the person becomes fit again, the inquiry or trial resumes. Indian context Notice that Indian criminal procedure names the clinical psychologist, alongside the psychiatrist, as the professional to whom an accused of unsound mind is referred for treatment and prognosis. The words were added to the old Code by the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act 2008 and carried into the BNSS. A clinical psychologist working in a government hospital in India can therefore expect to be asked by a court whether an accused person is of unsound mind or has an intellectual disability, and whether he can follow his trial. The report should answer the Dusky -type questions in plain words (what the person knows about the charge, the court and the possible outcomes; whether illness distorts that knowledge; whether he can instruct his lawyer) and give an opinion on whether and how soon treatment could restore fitness. Push a case through these provisions. Raghav, a 29-year-old daily-wage worker in Bengaluru with a ten-year history of schizophrenia, stopped his medication, became convinced that his neighbour was poisoning the family's water tank, and struck the neighbour on the head with an iron rod, seriously injuring him. When he was produced before the Magistrate, Raghav spoke about radio signals and laughed when asked whether he understood the charge. The civil surgeon referred him to the clinical psychologist and psychiatrist at the district hospital. The psychologist found that Raghav knew he was in a court and that the man in the black robe was "the judge", but believed that the trial was a staged drama arranged by his neighbour's political party and that his lawyer was part of the plot; he refused to speak to the lawyer at all. He had some factual understanding, but neither rational understanding nor the ability to consult. The Magistrate recorded that Raghav was incapable of making his defence and postponed the proceedings. After eight weeks of antipsychotic treatment Raghav could describe the charge, accepted his lawyer and discussed what had happened, and the proceedings resumed. Whether he can be held responsible for the assault is a different question, about a different moment, which you will return to in Section 10.9.4. Table 10.24 sets the two questions side by side.
