The insanity defence, from M'Naghten to Hinckley The criminal law punishes people who choose to do wrong. Two things must therefore be proved: the actus reus , the guilty act, and the mens rea , the guilty mind (intention, knowledge or recklessness). A driver who kills a pedestrian who steps without warning in front of her car has caused a death but has no guilty mind, and is not a murderer. The insanity defence extends the same logic to people whose mental disorder at the time of the act was so severe that blaming them makes no sense. It is a legal concept, not a medical one: the question is never simply whether the accused had a mental illness, but whether the illness took away the particular capacities that the law's test names. The tests have changed over 180 years, and the changes form one of the most examined stories in this book (Table 10.25 and Figure 10.13). The story begins in London. On 20 January 1843 Daniel M'Naghten , a woodturner from Glasgow who believed that the Tory party was persecuting him and following him wherever he went, shot Edward Drummond, the private secretary of the Prime Minister, Sir Robert Peel, in the mistaken belief that Drummond was Peel. Drummond died five days later. At his trial in March 1843 medical witnesses described M'Naghten's delusions, and he was found not guilty on the ground of insanity. The verdict caused an uproar. Queen Victoria, who had herself survived three attempts on her life in the previous three years, wrote to the Prime Minister about it, and the House of Lords put a series of questions on the law of insanity to a panel of judges led by Sir Nicolas Conyngham Tindal, Chief Justice of the Common Pleas. The judges' answers became the M'Naghten rules . Their core reads: "it must be clearly proved that, at the time of the committing of the act, the party accused was labouring under such a defect of reason, from disease of the mind, as not to know the nature and quality of the act he was doing; or if he did know it, that he did not know he was doing what was wrong". M'Naghten himself spent the rest of his life in hospital, at Bethlem and then at the new Broadmoor asylum, where he died in 1865. The M'Naghten test has two limbs, and both concern knowledge. A person is excused if, because of disease of the mind, he did not know the nature and quality of his act (the classic textbook example is the man who strangles his wife believing that he is squeezing a lemon) or, if he did know what he was doing, did not know that it was wrong. The test is purely cognitive. The judges also answered a question about delusions: a person who acts under a delusion is to be judged as if the facts in his delusion were true. If he believed that a man was about to kill him and killed in what he thought was self-defence, he is excused; if he believed that the man had insulted him and killed in revenge, he is punishable, because revenge would be a crime even if the insult were real. Critics soon argued that knowing is not the whole of the mind. A person may know perfectly well that an act is wrong and yet, because of mental illness, be unable to stop himself. The irresistible impulse test , adopted by the Alabama Supreme Court in Parsons v. State (1887; some sources give 1886) and in several other American states, added a volitional limb: the accused is excused if mental disease had so destroyed his power to choose that he could not avoid the act, even though he knew it was wrong. Courts sometimes put the question as the "policeman at the elbow" test: would he have done it even with a policeman standing at his elbow? The objection is obvious and has never been answered: nobody, psychologist or judge, can tell an impulse that could not be resisted from one that was simply not resisted. In 1954 Judge David L. Bazelon (1909 to 1993) of the federal Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia tried a radically broader approach in Durham v. United States . Under the Durham rule an accused "is not criminally responsible if his unlawful act was the product of mental disease or mental defect". Mental health professionals welcomed it at first, because it let them describe the whole person to the jury rather than squeezing him into the narrow questions of knowledge and control. It soon became clear, however, that clinicians could not reliably say whether a crime was the "product" of an illness, that the experts were in effect deciding the verdict, and that the result depended on whatever the latest diagnostic manual counted as a disease. The rule was abandoned in the District of Columbia in 1972, in United States v. Brawner , in favour of the test described next. That test was drafted by the American Law Institute (ALI), a body of judges, lawyers and law professors, for its Model Penal Code of 1962. The ALI test reads: "A person is not responsible for criminal conduct if at the time of such conduct as a result of mental disease or defect he lacks substantial capacity either to appreciate the criminality (wrongfulness) of his conduct or to conform his conduct to the requirements of law". Three words carry the weight. "Substantial" means that a total loss of capacity is not required. "Appreciate" is broader than M'Naghten's "know": it includes an emotional grasp of what one is doing, not just an intellectual one. And "conform" brings back the volitional limb of the irresistible impulse test. A second clause excludes any abnormality "manifested only by repeated criminal or otherwise antisocial conduct", so that a history of offending cannot by itself prove the illness that excuses it; the clause was aimed at psychopathy. By the 1970s the ALI test was used in most federal courts and many states. Then came the case that changed everything. On 30 March 1981, outside the Washington Hilton Hotel, John W. Hinckley Jr. fired six shots at President Ronald Reagan. He wounded the President, his press secretary James Brady (who was left permanently disabled), a police officer and a Secret Service agent. Hinckley had become obsessed with the actress Jodie Foster after watching the film Taxi Driver , and said that he had tried to kill the President to impress her. At his trial in 1982, under the ALI test and a rule that required the prosecution to prove his sanity beyond reasonable doubt, the jury found him not guilty by reason of insanity on all thirteen charges. He was sent to St Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, where he stayed until 2016, when he was released to live with his mother under conditions; the last conditions were lifted in June 2022. The public reaction was fury, and the law moved fast. About three-quarters of the American states tightened their insanity rules. Congress passed the Insanity Defense Reform Act of 1984 (IDRA) for the federal courts, which returned to a M'Naghten-like test: the accused is excused only if, "as a result of a severe mental disease or defect", he "was unable to appreciate the nature and quality or the wrongfulness of his acts". The volitional limb was dropped, the illness had to be severe, the burden of proof was moved to the defence, which must now prove insanity by clear and convincing evidence, and experts were barred from stating the ultimate conclusion. Some states went further. Michigan had already introduced, in 1975, an alternative verdict of guilty but mentally ill (GBMI), under which the accused is convicted and sentenced like any other offender, with treatment to be provided while he is in custody; several states followed after Hinckley. Research found that people given a GBMI verdict were more likely to be imprisoned, and received longer sentences, than defendants who pleaded insanity, and were no more likely to receive treatment than other mentally ill prisoners. Idaho, Kansas, Montana and Utah abolished the insanity defence as a separate defence altogether, and in Kahler v. Kansas (2020) the Supreme Court held that a state does not violate due process by refusing to excuse a defendant on the ground that mental illness left him unable to tell that his act was morally wrong (Kansas still lets evidence of illness show that the accused lacked the intent the crime requires). A related idea, diminished capacity , works differently. It does not excuse the accused completely; it allows evidence of mental abnormality to show that he did not form the specific intent a particular crime requires, so that he is convicted of a lesser offence (manslaughter rather than murder, for example). The American tests broadened from knowledge (M'Naghten) to control (irresistible impulse, ALI) and causation (Durham), then narrowed again after the Hinckley verdict; Indian law has kept the M'Naghten formula since 1860. Behind the outrage lay a set of beliefs about the insanity defence that turn out to be false, and the research that tested them is a model of how psychology can correct the law's assumptions. Key study: the myths of the insanity defence (Silver, Cirincione and Steadman, 1994) Eric Silver, Carmen Cirincione and Henry Steadman compared what the American public believed about the insanity defence with what actually happened in a large sample of American cases. The public estimated that 37 percent of felony indictments ended in an insanity plea; the true figure was 0.9 percent, fewer than one in a hundred. The public thought that 44 percent of insanity pleas succeeded; the true figure was 26 percent. The public believed that a quarter of those acquitted were simply set free; in fact about 85 percent were sent to a mental hospital. And the public guessed that acquittees were confined for about 22 months, when the average was about 32 months for all crimes and about 76 months for murder. The conclusion: the insanity defence is rarely used, usually fails, and when it succeeds it often leads to longer confinement than a prison sentence would have. The limitation is that the data are American, but the pattern has been found repeatedly: being found not guilty by reason of insanity is not "getting away with it". Exam trap Match each test to its key word. M'Naghten (1843) : know the nature and quality of the act, or that it was wrong (cognitive). Irresistible impulse (1887) : could not control (volitional). Durham (1954) : act was the product of mental disease. ALI (1962) : lacks substantial capacity to appreciate wrongfulness or to conform . IDRA (1984) : back to cognitive only, after Hinckley. Hinckley was acquitted under the ALI test, not M'Naghten. Guilty but mentally ill is a verdict of guilt, not an acquittal. Insanity is a legal , not a medical, concept. M'Naghten shot Drummond , Peel's secretary, not Peel. Unsoundness of mind in Indian law India's rule is older than every American test except M'Naghten itself. The Indian Penal Code (IPC), drafted by the first Law Commission under Thomas Babington Macaulay (1800 to 1859) and enacted in 1860, wrote the M'Naghten rules into its chapter of general exceptions, seventeen years after the House of Lords had framed them. Since 1 July 2024 the IPC has been replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), and the old section 84 is now section 22 , under the same heading, "Act of a person of unsound mind", with unchanged words: "Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law." Take the section phrase by phrase. "Unsoundness of mind" is the law's term, not a diagnosis; it can cover psychosis, severe intellectual disability, delirium and other conditions, and the law does not list them. "At the time of doing it" fixes the moment that matters: not the accused's state at trial, and not his history in general, though both are evidence of it. "Incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law" is the M'Naghten test, with the addition of the words "contrary to law". The test is cognitive. There is no volitional limb, so an irresistible impulse is not a defence in India, and there is no general partial defence of diminished responsibility. Three principles from the case law guide how the section is applied. First, the courts are concerned with legal insanity , not medical insanity : not every person with a mental illness is exempt, but only one whose illness made him incapable of the knowledge the section describes at the time of the act. Second, the burden of proof. In Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakker v. State of Gujarat (decided on 19 March 1964), in which a man had killed his wife, inflicting many wounds, and pleaded insanity, the Supreme Court explained that the prosecution's general burden of proving the offence never shifts, but because the law presumes that the accused does not fall within an exception, he must establish his unsoundness of mind; he need not do so beyond reasonable doubt, because the burden on him is no higher than that resting on a party to civil proceedings (a preponderance of probabilities). The Court added that even if he fails to establish the defence, evidence about his mental state may still raise a reasonable doubt about whether he had the intention the offence requires, and then he is entitled to be acquitted. (Dahyabhai himself did not succeed: his conviction for murder and life sentence were upheld.) Third, the courts look closely at the accused's behaviour before, during and after the act: motive, preparation, concealment, flight and what he said afterwards. A man who hides the weapon and runs away is usually taken to have known that what he did was wrong or illegal. What happens after an acquittal on this ground is also set out in the BNSS. The court's finding must state specifically whether the accused committed the act (section 373, formerly section 334 of the Code), and a person who did commit it is then detained in safe custody or handed over to a relative or friend who gives security that he will be looked after and prevented from harming himself or others (section 374, formerly section 335). Detention in a mental health establishment follows the rules under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017. For people with mental illness who are already in prison, whether awaiting trial or convicted, section 103 of the Mental Healthcare Act provides that an order admitting such a prisoner for treatment is met by transfer to the psychiatric ward of the prison's medical wing or, where the prison has no such ward, by transfer to a mental health establishment with the prior permission of the Mental Health Review Board; the prison's medical officer must send the Board a quarterly report, and every State and Union Territory must set up a mental health establishment in the medical wing of at least one prison. Mental illness that develops after conviction can matter even at the final stage: in Accused X v. State of Maharashtra (decided on 12 April 2019) the Supreme Court held that severe post-conviction mental illness is a mitigating factor that an appellate court must weigh before confirming a death sentence, and commuted to imprisonment for the rest of his life the death sentence of a prisoner found to have developed severe mental illness during his long years on death row. Return to Raghav. Once fit, he pleaded unsoundness of mind under section 22. The question now was his state of mind on the morning of the assault, and it had to be reconstructed after the event, which is the hardest task in forensic assessment. The psychologist read the hospital records of his earlier admissions, interviewed his mother and two neighbours about the days before the assault, obtained the police account of what he said when arrested ("I had to stop him before he poisoned my mother"), and assessed his current mental state and his effort and honesty on testing. The picture was of a relapse of schizophrenia over three weeks, with a fixed persecutory delusion. Raghav knew that he was hitting a man with a rod, so he knew the nature of the act. The contested question was whether he was capable of knowing that it was wrong or contrary to law. The M'Naghten judges' answer on delusions suggests one way to think about it: if Raghav truly believed that his mother was about to be killed, then on the facts as he believed them he was defending her. The psychologist's report described the illness, the delusion and its timing, and his behaviour (he did not run, hide the rod or deny the act); the legal conclusion was left to the court. Clinical link A mental state at the time of the offence assessment rests on many sources, not on one interview: the account of the accused (taken more than once, to check consistency), informants, police and witness statements, medical and prison records, the timeline of symptoms before and after the act, and tests of symptom validity. Be honest about its limits: you are reconstructing a past state of mind, and your opinion is an inference. Write for a judge, not for a colleague: define terms, separate what you observed from what you were told and from what you infer, and explain how the clinical findings bear on each element of the legal test without claiming to decide it. Exam trap Section 84 IPC is now section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (in force 1 July 2024), with the same words. It follows the M'Naghten rules: it is cognitive, uses the phrase unsoundness of mind (not "insanity"), refers to the time of the act, and adds "or contrary to law". It has no irresistible impulse limb and India has no general diminished responsibility defence. The court applies legal , not medical, insanity; the accused bears the burden of establishing it ( Dahyabhai , 1964), but not beyond reasonable doubt: a preponderance of probabilities, as in a civil case, is enough. The Code of Criminal Procedure is now the BNSS , and the Indian Evidence Act is now the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023, both also from 1 July 2024. Risk assessment, malingering and testimony Courts, parole boards and forensic hospitals constantly ask about the future: is this person likely to be violent again? Section 2.7 has already taught the core of violence risk assessment: the MacArthur study, Monahan's finding that unaided long-term clinical predictions were right at most one time in three, the three approaches of unstructured judgement, actuarial tools such as the VRAG and structured professional judgement with the HCR-20, and the rule that past violence is the best single predictor of future violence. Here three forensic additions are needed. The first is the history of the argument. In 1954 Paul Everett Meehl (1920 to 2003) published Clinical versus Statistical Prediction , in which he reviewed about twenty studies that had pitted clinicians' judgements against simple statistical formulas for predicting outcomes such as success on parole or response to treatment. In almost every study the formula did as well as or better than the clinician. Later reviews of many more studies have found the same: actuarial prediction , combining a fixed set of factors by an explicit rule, is rarely beaten by clinical prediction , the clinician's informal weighing of the same information. Forensic risk assessment grew directly out of Meehl's challenge, and structured professional judgement is the field's attempt to keep the reliability of the formula while allowing the clinician to plan how the risk will be managed. The second addition is a group of specialised tools. The best known of them measures psychopathy , a personality pattern of callousness, lack of remorse, superficial charm, manipulation and impulsive, antisocial behaviour: it is the Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R) of the Canadian psychologist Robert D. Hare , a 20-item rating made from an interview and file review. High PCL-R scores predict violent reoffending, which is why the PCL-R carries great weight in the VRAG, but the label is powerful and easily misused, especially with adolescents, whose personalities are still forming. For sexual offending, actuarial scales such as the Static-99 are used, alongside assessment of the dynamic factors that treatment can change. The instruments themselves belong to the Assessment book. Third, modern practice speaks of risk formulation rather than prediction: instead of a yes-or-no verdict, the report states how likely harm is, of what kind, against whom, in what circumstances, how soon, and, above all, what would reduce it. Every forensic evaluation must also consider malingering : the intentional production of false or grossly exaggerated physical or psychological symptoms, motivated by an external incentive such as avoiding prosecution or punishment, obtaining compensation, avoiding military duty or obtaining drugs. Malingering is not a mental disorder; the DSM lists it among other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention. In the clinic it is rare, but in forensic settings, where so much depends on the findings, it must always be considered, and evaluators look for symptoms that are improbable, rare, inconsistent with each other or with observed behaviour, or that appear only when the person is being observed. The structured interviews and symptom validity tests used to detect it are described in the Assessment book. Remember the distinction drawn in Section 9.1: in malingering the motive is an external incentive; in factitious disorder, including factitious disorder imposed on another, the person deliberately produces symptoms without any obvious external reward, in order to occupy the sick role. Finally, the psychologist must be able to explain all this in court. A good forensic report answers the question that was asked, in plain language; separates the facts observed from the information reported by others and from the expert's inferences; states the methods used and their limits; and considers alternative explanations. Under cross-examination the expert's best protection is to have stayed within what the evidence supports. Research on eyewitness memory, the other great contribution of psychology to the courtroom (including Elizabeth Loftus's work on misleading post-event information), is taught in the General Psychology book, and the suggestibility of child witnesses is discussed in Section 10.6. Exam trap Meehl (1954) showed that statistical (actuarial) prediction equals or beats clinical prediction. The PCL-R is Robert Hare 's; the HCR-20 is a structured professional judgement scheme (Section 2.7); the VRAG is actuarial. Malingering = deliberate symptoms for an external incentive, and it is not a mental disorder; factitious disorder = deliberate symptoms with no obvious external reward, to occupy the sick role. A nurse who secretly injects patients with insulin to cause emergencies, for the satisfaction of the attention, shows factitious disorder imposed on another, not malingering (there is no external gain), not conversion disorder (in which symptoms are not produced deliberately, and are the person's own), and not, on this evidence alone, antisocial personality disorder (a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of others' rights since the age of fifteen; the disorders themselves are in the Psychiatric Disorders book). Child custody evaluations When parents separate and cannot agree about where their children will live, a family court must decide, and it may ask a psychologist to help. The legal standard almost everywhere is the best interests of the child : the court's decision must be governed by what is best for the child's welfare, not by the rights or wishes of either parent. Earlier doctrines treated children as the father's property, and later the "tender years" doctrine presumed that young children belonged with their mothers; the best-interests standard replaced both with a question about the particular child. In Indian law, the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and, for Hindus, the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956 govern custody. Section 6(a) of the 1956 Act provides that the custody of a minor who has not completed five years of age shall ordinarily be with the mother, and section 13 makes the welfare of the minor the paramount consideration, so that the welfare of the child overrides even the presumption about young children. The Family Courts Act 1984 allows family courts to use counsellors to help families settle such disputes. The APA's Guidelines for Child Custody Evaluations in Family Law Proceedings (first issued in 1994 for divorce proceedings and revised under the present title in 2010) describe how the work should be done. The child's psychological best interests and well-being are paramount; the evaluator is impartial and must not be the therapist of the child or of either parent; and the evaluation focuses on three things: the parenting attributes of each parent, the psychological needs of the child, and the fit between them. In practice the evaluator interviews each parent about the child's history and their own; observes each parent with the child, often at home; interviews the child in a way that suits his or her age, without forcing the child to choose between parents; gathers information from teachers, doctors and relatives; reviews records; and, where it helps answer a specific question, tests the parents. Particular weight is given to allegations of abuse or domestic violence, to the continuity of the child's attachments, schooling and friendships, to keeping siblings together, and to each parent's willingness to support the child's relationship with the other. Consider a case. Farida, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Hyderabad, separated from her husband after eight years of marriage. Each sought custody of their six-year-old son, and the husband alleged that Farida's treatment for depression made her unfit to care for him. The evaluator found that Farida's depression had been treated and was in remission, that she had been the boy's main caregiver since birth, that the boy was securely attached to both parents but turned to his mother when distressed, and that his school reports were good. The father was a warm and involved parent too, but his long working hours meant that the boy would in practice be cared for by his grandparents. The recommendation was that the boy live with Farida, with generous regular time with his father, and that both parents attend sessions with the court's counsellor to agree on how they would make decisions together. Notice what the evaluator did not do: treat a psychiatric history as proof of unfitness. The question is always how a parent actually functions as a parent. Custody disputes also produce claims that one parent has turned the child against the other. The American psychiatrist Richard A. Gardner (1931 to 2003) proposed a "parental alienation syndrome" in 1985, but it is not recognised as a disorder in the DSM and has been strongly criticised for lacking scientific support and for being used to discredit children's and mothers' reports of abuse. A careful evaluator asks why a child resists contact, which may be alienation, may be the child's own reaction to a parent's behaviour, or may be both. Exam trap The custody standard is the best interests (welfare) of the child , not the rights of the parents. Under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956, section 6(a) says a child under five shall ordinarily be in the mother's custody, but section 13 makes the child's welfare paramount . The custody evaluator must not also be the family's therapist. "Parental alienation syndrome" (Gardner, 1985) is not a DSM diagnosis. Juvenile justice Children who break the law have been treated differently from adults since the first juvenile court opened in Chicago in 1899, on the principle that a child who offends needs care and correction rather than punishment. Clinical psychology was there almost from the start: in 1909 the psychiatrist William Healy (1869 to 1963) set up the Juvenile Psychopathic Institute in Chicago to study the young people who came before the court, one of the roots of the child guidance movement described in Section 10.1. India's present law is the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015 , which replaced the Act of 2000 (itself the successor of the Juvenile Justice Act 1986). Its background is the gang rape and murder of a young woman on a bus in Delhi in December 2012. One of the accused was a few months short of eighteen; as a juvenile, he was sentenced in August 2013 to three years in a reform home, the most the law then allowed, and the public outrage that followed led to the new Act, which received the President's assent on 31 December 2015 and came into force on 15 January 2016. Its key ideas are these (Figure 10.14 traces the path of a case): A child is a person who has not completed eighteen years of age. The Act deals with two kinds of children: a child in conflict with law , who is alleged or found to have committed an offence while under eighteen, and a child in need of care and protection , for example a child who is homeless, abused, exploited, working illegally or at risk of child marriage. The first comes before a Juvenile Justice Board , the second before a Child Welfare Committee in each district. The Juvenile Justice Board (section 4) consists of a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class with at least three years' experience and two social workers, at least one of them a woman. A social worker may qualify by seven years of work in children's health, education or welfare, or as a practising professional with a degree in child psychology, psychiatry, sociology or law. Offences are graded by punishment: petty offences (maximum punishment up to three years), serious offences (three to seven years) and heinous offences , those with a minimum punishment of seven years' imprisonment or more. (An amendment in 2021 widened the serious category.) For a child aged sixteen or above who is alleged to have committed a heinous offence, the Board conducts a preliminary assessment under section 15 of the child's mental and physical capacity to commit the offence, ability to understand its consequences, and the circumstances in which it was allegedly committed. The Board may take the assistance of experienced psychologists, psycho-social workers or other experts. An explanation in the section says that the assessment is not a trial. It must be completed within three months. If the Board decides that the child need not be tried as an adult, it holds the inquiry itself and may pass the orders listed in section 18: advice or admonition with counselling for the child and parents, group counselling, community service, a fine, probation for up to three years, or a stay of up to three years in a special home , together with directions to attend school, vocational training, a therapeutic centre or a de-addiction programme. If the Board decides that there is a need for trial as an adult, it transfers the case to the Children's Court (section 18(3)). That court may itself decide either way (section 19). A child found guilty is kept in a place of safety until the age of twenty-one, with education, skill training, counselling, behaviour modification and psychiatric support; at twenty-one the court reviews whether the young person has reformed and may release him on conditions or send him to jail for the rest of the term (section 20). No child may be sentenced to death or to life imprisonment without the possibility of release (section 21). While an inquiry is pending, a child is kept in an observation home , not in a police lock-up or jail. The psychologist's work is concentrated in the preliminary assessment, which decides which branch the case follows. Why should a seventeen-year-old be treated differently from an eighteen-year-old at all? Developmental science gives the answer (taught in the Developmental book). The prefrontal systems that support planning, impulse control and the weighing of long-term consequences go on maturing into the early twenties, while sensitivity to reward and to the presence of peers peaks in mid-adolescence, a pattern described in the dual systems model of Laurence Steinberg (Section 10.6). Adolescents therefore take more risks, especially in groups, and most of them grow out of offending as they mature. Arguments of this kind were accepted by the United States Supreme Court in Roper v. Simmons (2005), which abolished the death penalty for crimes committed under eighteen. The preliminary assessment puts the psychologist in a difficult position, because "capacity to commit" an offence has no agreed clinical meaning; almost any physically healthy sixteen-year-old is physically capable of committing a crime. In Barun Chandra Thakur v. Master Bholu (2022), a case arising from the killing of a seven-year-old schoolboy in Gurugram, the Supreme Court held that the assessment calls for a holistic evaluation; that the child's mental capacity to commit the offence and his ability to understand its consequences are different questions, which the Board and the court below had wrongly treated as one; that a Board with no member who is a practising professional with a degree in child psychology or child psychiatry must take the help of experienced psychologists, psycho-social workers or other experts (the "may" in section 15 operates as "must"); and it left it open to the Central Government and the national and state commissions for protection of child rights to issue guidelines for the assessment. Consider how it is done. Tushar, aged seventeen, was arrested in Pune after a fight between two groups of boys; he was alleged to have stabbed a boy from the other group, who died. The psychologist assessing him for the Board interviewed Tushar on three occasions, assessed his intellectual functioning (in the borderline range), screened for mental disorder (he met criteria for conduct disorder and was using cannabis daily), took a developmental history from his mother (his father had left when he was four; he had dropped out of school in the ninth standard), and spoke with his former teacher. On the question of understanding consequences, Tushar knew that a stab wound could kill and that stabbing someone was a serious crime, but his account showed how strongly he had been carried along by older boys in the group. The report described these findings, their bearing on each element of section 15, and the treatment and educational needs that would apply whichever way the Board decided. The interventions for conduct problems, including multisystemic therapy, are described in Section 10.4; the protection of children who are themselves victims, under the POCSO Act 2012, is covered in Section 10.6. Exam trap Under the Juvenile Justice Act 2015 (in force 15 January 2016 ), only a child aged 16 to 18 accused of a heinous offence (minimum punishment of seven years or more ) can be considered for trial as an adult, and only after the Board's preliminary assessment under section 15 of mental and physical capacity, ability to understand the consequences and the circumstances; experienced psychologists may assist, and the assessment is not a trial. The Board , not the psychologist, decides. No child may be given death or life imprisonment without release (section 21). A child in conflict with law goes to the Juvenile Justice Board ; a child in need of care and protection to the Child Welfare Committee . Observation home = during inquiry; special home = after a finding; place of safety = a secure facility for older children, including those tried as adults (never a police lock-up or jail). Correctional psychology and offender rehabilitation The term correctional psychology refers to the practice of psychology in prisons, probation services and other parts of the criminal justice system that hold or supervise offenders. A prison psychologist screens new prisoners for mental illness, intellectual disability and suicide risk (suicide is far more common in prison than outside, especially in the first days of custody); manages crises; treats mental illness and substance use; runs programmes aimed at offending itself; assesses risk for parole and release; trains staff; and does research. Behind all of this lies a question that the field once answered with despair: can anything be done to make offenders less likely to offend again? Key study: Martinson and "nothing works" (1974) In the late 1960s the State of New York commissioned a review of every evaluation of offender rehabilitation it could find. Douglas Lipton , Robert Martinson (1927 to 1979) and Judith Wilks examined 231 studies published between 1945 and 1967, covering education, vocational training, counselling, psychotherapy, changes to the institutional environment, medical treatment and supervision in the community. The state was slow to release the report, and in 1974 Martinson published its conclusions on his own in an article in The Public Interest titled "What works? Questions and answers about prison reform". His verdict was that, with few and isolated exceptions, the rehabilitative efforts reported so far had had no appreciable effect on reoffending. The message was soon shortened to "nothing works", and it suited both those who wanted harsher punishment and those who distrusted coerced treatment. The full report appeared as a book in 1975. Critics pointed out that many of the studies were too weak to detect any effect, and that some programmes had worked. In 1979 Martinson himself published a revision, "New findings, new views", conceding that some programmes did reduce reoffending; he died later that year. The lesson for clinicians is that a negative verdict based on poor studies is as dangerous as a positive one. The revival began in Canada. In 1979 Paul Gendreau and Robert Ross answered Martinson with a review of successful programmes pointedly titled "Effective correctional treatment: bibliotherapy for cynics". In 1990 Donald A. Andrews and his colleagues, among them James Bonta , Robert Hoge, Gendreau and Francis Cullen, published a meta-analysis titled "Does correctional treatment work?" that produced 154 effect sizes (phi coefficients) from studies of juvenile and adult offenders. Criminal sanctions without rehabilitative services did not reduce reoffending (mean phi of minus 0.07); nor did services that ignored the principles of effective rehabilitation (minus 0.06). But "appropriate" treatment, which followed those principles, clearly reduced reoffending (mean phi of 0.30, against 0.13 for services of unspecified type). And the setting mattered: appropriate treatment worked in diversion, community and residential programmes alike, but its effects were weaker in residential settings than in the community. The principles became the risk-need-responsivity model (RNR), first set out by Andrews, Bonta and Hoge in 1990 and developed in Andrews and Bonta's textbook The Psychology of Criminal Conduct . It has three principles (Table 10.26). The risk principle says that the intensity of treatment should match the offender's risk of reoffending: intensive services for high-risk offenders, minimal ones for low-risk offenders. Intensive programmes for low-risk offenders can actually make them worse, by mixing them with high-risk offenders and pulling them away from the jobs, families and friends that were keeping them out of trouble. The need principle says that treatment should target criminogenic needs , the dynamic (changeable) risk factors that are directly linked to offending, rather than problems that do not drive offending, such as low self-esteem, anxiety or vague emotional distress. The responsivity principle says that treatment should be delivered in the way offenders learn best: in general, with structured cognitive-behavioural and social learning methods (general responsivity), and in particular, tailored to the person's motivation, ability, learning style, gender and culture (specific responsivity). Andrews and Bonta identified eight major risk and need factors, the "central eight". The first four, the "big four", are the strongest predictors: A history of antisocial behaviour (the only static factor of the eight: it cannot be changed, only taken into account). An antisocial personality pattern (impulsivity, restless aggression, callousness, a taste for risk). Antisocial cognition: attitudes, values, beliefs and rationalisations that support crime ("he deserved it", "everyone takes bribes"). Antisocial associates: friends and companions who offend, and isolation from those who do not. The remaining four: family or marital problems, problems at school or work, lack of rewarding prosocial leisure activities, and substance misuse. Table 10.26 The risk-need-responsivity model of offender rehabilitation (Andrews, Bonta and colleagues). Principle What it says In practice Risk Match the intensity of treatment to the risk of reoffending Assess risk first; concentrate resources on higher-risk offenders; do not over-treat the low-risk Need Target criminogenic (dynamic) needs Work on antisocial attitudes, associates, substance use, employment, family; not on self-esteem alone Responsivity (general) Use methods offenders learn from Structured cognitive-behavioural and social learning programmes Responsivity (specific) Fit the programme to the person Adjust for motivation, ability, literacy, gender, culture, mental health Put the research together and you get a description of what successful rehabilitation programmes look like. They are community-based where possible, because offending happens in the community and new skills must be practised where the temptations are. They are cognitive-behavioural and skills-based , teaching problem-solving, self-control, anger management and prosocial thinking, as in the Reasoning and Rehabilitation programme of Robert Ross and Elizabeth Fabiano (1985). They target criminogenic needs and concentrate on higher-risk offenders. They are structured, delivered as designed by trained staff who model prosocial behaviour and combine warmth with firm, fair limits, and they are followed by aftercare. For young offenders, interventions that work with the family and the neighbourhood, such as multisystemic therapy (Section 10.4), have the strongest evidence. What does not work is just as instructive: punishment and deterrence alone, military-style boot camps and "Scared Straight" programmes, in which delinquent youths visit prisons to be frightened by inmates. A Cochrane review by Anthony Petrosino and colleagues found that Scared Straight programmes actually increased later offending compared with doing nothing. The RNR model has been criticised for concentrating on deficits and risks. The Good Lives Model of the New Zealand psychologist Tony Ward (2002) argues that offenders, like everyone else, seek basic human goods (relationships, competence, autonomy, meaning, pleasure) and that offending is often a harmful way of pursuing them; rehabilitation should therefore help offenders build a way of life that meets those needs without harming others. Most programmes now combine the two: RNR tells you whom to treat and what to target, and the Good Lives Model helps with motivation and the shape of a life after release. A wider movement, therapeutic jurisprudence , associated with the American law professors David Wexler and Bruce Winick , asks how the law itself can be applied in ways that help rather than harm the people it touches; drug courts and mental health courts, which supervise treatment instead of imposing ordinary sentences, are its best-known products. Indian context Indian prisons hold far more undertrial prisoners than convicts, so correctional work in India often means caring for people who have not yet been tried. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (section 103) provides for prisoners with mental illness to be treated in the psychiatric ward of the prison's medical wing or, with the Mental Health Review Board's permission, in a mental health establishment, and requires every State and Union Territory to set up a mental health establishment in at least one prison. India also gave the world a well-known correctional experiment: from 1993, when Kiran Bedi was Inspector General of Prisons, Delhi's Tihar Jail offered ten-day courses of Vipassana meditation in the tradition taught by S. N. Goenka, including one course for about a thousand prisoners, an experiment made famous by the 1997 documentary Doing Time, Doing Vipassana . The courses were welcomed by many prisoners and staff, but controlled evidence about their effect on reoffending is thin, which is exactly the question the RNR research teaches you to ask. The criminal justice system also has to care for those whom offenders harm. The word victimology is usually credited to the lawyer Benjamin Mendelsohn in the 1940s, and the criminologist Hans von Hentig 's The Criminal and His Victim (1948) began the systematic study of victims. Early victimology asked how victims contributed to crimes against them (victim precipitation), an approach later criticised as victim-blaming. Today victimology is the study of victims and their needs: the psychological effects of crime, secondary victimisation (the further harm caused by insensitive police, hospital and court procedures), victim support, compensation, and restorative justice, which brings victims and offenders together, when both agree, to repair the harm. The child-friendly procedures that the POCSO Act requires for child victims (Section 10.6) are an example of victimology in law. Exam trap Asked for "the qualities of successful rehabilitation programmes to treat offenders" (RML 2020), choose being community-based . Cognitive interviews and offender profiling are investigative tools used to solve crimes (Section 10.9.1), not features of treatment, and a focus on the relationship with parents is not a defining principle of effective programmes (family problems are only one of the central eight, and family-based work matters mainly for juveniles). Martinson (1974) = "nothing works"; Andrews and colleagues (1990) and the RNR model = "what works". Risk = who to treat, need = what to treat, responsivity = how to treat. Self-esteem is a non-criminogenic need. Scared Straight increases offending. Neighbouring specialties: neuropsychology and rehabilitation psychology Two other specialties often work alongside forensic and clinical psychologists. The first, clinical neuropsychology , is the assessment and treatment of people whose behaviour or cognition is affected by brain injury or disease: head injury, stroke, epilepsy, dementia, tumours and the effects of alcohol and toxins. The clinical neuropsychologist measures memory, attention, language, perception and executive functions with standardised batteries, describes the pattern of strengths and deficits, relates it to what is known about brain-behaviour relationships, and advises on diagnosis, capacity, return to work and rehabilitation. In forensic settings neuropsychologists assess people claiming compensation after head injuries, which is why tests of effort and symptom validity are a routine part of their work. The tests and batteries belong to the Assessment book and the underlying brain science to the Physiological book. The second, rehabilitation psychology , helps people with chronic illness, injury or disability achieve the greatest possible independence and participation; its methods, including the restorative and compensatory approaches to cognitive rehabilitation after brain injury, are described in Section 9.9. Exam trap Do not confuse the specialties by setting. Forensic psychology answers legal questions; correctional psychology works with offenders in custody or under supervision; clinical neuropsychology assesses brain-behaviour relationships; rehabilitation psychology maximises function after illness or disability; industrial-organisational psychology deals with the workplace; counselling psychology with the normal-range problems of living (Section 10.8). A neuropsychologist may work in a court, and a forensic psychologist in a prison, but the specialty is defined by the kind of question it answers. 10.10 Creative, Adjunct and Digital Therapies Lower yield · 1 Q Almost every therapy in this book works through words. The client talks, the therapist listens, and change happens in conversation. But some experiences have no words yet: the terror of a child who was abused before she could speak, the grief of a woman who cannot say her dead son's name, the inner world of a man with chronic schizophrenia who has long since stopped trying to explain himself. Other clients have words but cannot use them with a stranger in an office. For them, clinicians have borrowed from the arts (painting, music, dance, drama, literature), from the bond between people and animals, from India's own traditions of yoga and meditation, and, most recently, from the smartphone. These approaches are usually called adjunct therapies , because in most clinical settings they are added to, not substituted for, the main treatment. The creative ones are often grouped as the arts therapies or expressive therapies; in several countries art, music, drama and dance movement therapy are separate professions with their own postgraduate training. This section describes each of them, what they claim, and what the evidence does and does not show, and ends with the promise and the ethical risks of digital mental health. Art therapy: Naumburg, Kramer and the image In art therapy the client makes images (drawings, paintings, sculptures, collages) in the presence of a trained art therapist, and the making of the image and the relationship around it are the means of change. The term was coined in 1942 by the British artist Adrian Hill (1895 to 1977), who discovered the value of drawing and painting while recovering from tuberculosis in a sanatorium and went on to teach art to other patients; he described the work in Art Versus Illness (1945), praising its power of "completely engrossing the mind (as well as the fingers)". In the United States, two women gave the field its two great theories, and they disagreed. Margaret Naumburg (1890 to 1983), a New York educator who in 1914 had founded the progressive school later renamed the Walden School, worked from 1941 to 1947 at the New York State Psychiatric Institute, using art with disturbed children and adults. She called her approach dynamically oriented art therapy and grounded it in psychoanalysis. For Naumburg, spontaneous art is symbolic speech : the unconscious, which censors words, expresses itself more freely in images. The client is encouraged to draw spontaneously and then to free-associate to the picture; the therapist withholds interpretation so that the client can discover its meaning, and the images become a bridge to talking, to insight and to the transference. Art here is a tool in therapy, a royal road to the unconscious alongside dreams. Edith Kramer (1916 to 2014), a painter born in Vienna who had studied as a girl with the Bauhaus artist Friedl Dicker-Brandeis, worked for seven years with delinquent and disturbed boys aged eight to thirteen at the Wiltwyck School for Boys in New York, and described the work in Art Therapy in a Children's Community (1958) and Art as Therapy with Children (1971). Kramer argued that the healing lies in the creative process itself. Drawing on Freud's concept of sublimation, the transformation of primitive impulses into socially valued activity, she held that when a child turns rage or fear into a well-made picture, the act of giving it form contains and transforms the feeling. Interpretation is less important than helping the child make good art, and the therapist acts as a "third hand", helping the child's own artistic process (mixing a colour, steadying a clay figure) without taking it over. Kramer called this art as therapy , against Naumburg's art in therapy , and the two phrases still mark the main division in the field. The British Association of Art Therapists was founded in 1964 and the American Art Therapy Association in 1969. See how a session works. Leela, a 41-year-old woman in Kochi, had not spoken about the death of her teenage son in a road accident for a year; in her sessions with a clinical psychologist she answered questions politely but said nothing about him. She agreed to join an art therapy group on the ward. In her third session she painted a closed door, black, with a small yellow shape at its foot. Asked about it, she said only that the yellow was his school shoe, which she had never put away. Over the following weeks the paintings changed, the door half open, a figure beside it, and in the sixth session she began to talk, for the first time, about the morning he left the house. A Naumburg-style therapist would emphasise the symbolic meaning of the door and the shoe and Leela's associations to them; a Kramer-style therapist would emphasise that the act of painting allowed her to give form to what she could not yet say. In practice most art therapists do both. Art therapy is used with children (for whom it overlaps with the play therapies of Section 10.2, especially sandplay), with survivors of trauma and abuse, with people with psychosis, in dementia care and in palliative care. Its evidence base, however, is small. The most important test is described below. Do not confuse art therapy with projective drawing tests such as the House-Tree-Person or the Draw-a-Person, which use drawings to assess personality and are described in the Assessment book; art therapists generally avoid reading fixed meanings into features of a drawing. Key study: the MATISSE trial of group art therapy in schizophrenia (Crawford and colleagues, 2012) Small studies had suggested that art therapy helps people with schizophrenia, especially with negative symptoms, and British guidance on psychosis had encouraged it. Mike Crawford and colleagues tested it properly. At 15 sites across the United Kingdom, 417 adults with schizophrenia were randomly assigned to twelve months of weekly 90-minute group art therapy plus standard care, twelve months of weekly activity groups (games, outings and other activities with no art materials) plus standard care, or standard care alone. Raters who did not know the group assignment measured global functioning and symptoms two years after randomisation. There were no differences: art therapy did no better than activity groups or standard care on functioning, symptoms or social functioning, and attendance at both kinds of group was low (almost 40 percent of those offered art therapy never attended a session). A 2019 meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (Laws and Conway) later found a small to moderate effect of art therapies on negative symptoms, but only in the lower-quality trials; it did not appear in trials whose raters were blind. The conclusion is not that art therapy is useless for everyone, but that its claims for schizophrenia have not survived a large, well-controlled test. Exam trap Adrian Hill coined "art therapy" (1942). Margaret Naumburg : psychoanalytic, art as symbolic speech , free association to the image, art in therapy ; often called the mother of American art therapy. Edith Kramer : art as therapy , healing through the creative process and sublimation , the therapist's "third hand". Do not swap them. Projective drawings (House-Tree-Person, Draw-a-Person) are assessment tools, not art therapy. Music therapy By music therapy clinicians mean the use of music and musical activity, within a therapeutic relationship with a trained music therapist, to reach clinical goals: expressing feelings, building communication and social interaction, reducing anxiety, improving mood, or maintaining memory and movement. It takes two main forms. In active music therapy the client makes music: improvising on drums, xylophones or piano with the therapist, singing, writing songs. In receptive music therapy the client listens to live or recorded music, chosen and used by the therapist, and responds to it with relaxation, imagery, movement or discussion. Music as medicine is ancient, but music therapy as a profession grew from the work of musicians in American veterans' hospitals during and after the two world wars. The first university degree programmes in music therapy opened in 1944 (Michigan State College was among them), the National Association for Music Therapy was formed in 1950, and the American Music Therapy Association was created by merger in 1998. Two approaches are often named. In the 1950s and 1960s the American composer and pianist Paul Nordoff (1909 to 1977) and the British special educator Clive Robbins (1927 to 2011) developed creative music therapy (now called Nordoff-Robbins music therapy), in which the therapist improvises at the piano with a child with autism, intellectual disability or other disabilities, meeting and extending whatever sound or rhythm the child produces, on the view that a "music child" capable of responding lies within every child. In the 1970s the American music therapist Helen Lindquist Bonny (1921 to 2010) developed Guided Imagery and Music , a receptive method in which a relaxed client listens to sequences of classical music and describes the images, memories and feelings that arise, with the therapist as guide. Music therapy should be distinguished from music medicine, in which doctors or nurses play recorded music to patients, for example to reduce anxiety before surgery, without a music therapist or a therapeutic relationship. The evidence for music therapy proper is among the best of the arts therapies. A Cochrane review in 2017 (Aalbers and colleagues) found moderate-quality evidence that music therapy added to usual care produces short-term improvements in depressive symptoms, anxiety and functioning in people with depression. Another Cochrane review in 2017 (Geretsegger and colleagues) found that music therapy added to standard care improves global state, mental state including negative symptoms, social functioning and quality of life in schizophrenia, with effects that depend on the number of sessions and on the quality of the therapy, and the 2022 Cochrane review of music therapy for autistic people (Geretsegger and colleagues) found moderate-certainty evidence that it probably increases the chance of global improvement and likely reduces overall autism severity and improves quality of life, though with no clear effect on social interaction or verbal and non-verbal communication. India has its own tradition, often called raga chikitsa , which holds that particular ragas heal particular ailments; it is culturally meaningful to many clients, but its specific claims have not been tested in rigorous trials. Music is also widely used in dementia care, alongside the approaches described in Section 10.7. Exam trap Active music therapy = the client makes music (improvisation, singing, song-writing). Receptive music therapy = the client listens and responds. Nordoff-Robbins = improvisational, with children with disabilities and autism; Guided Imagery and Music = receptive, Helen Bonny . Music therapy needs a trained therapist and a relationship; playing background music in a ward is music medicine, not music therapy. Dance and movement therapy As its name suggests, dance movement therapy uses movement and dance, within a therapeutic relationship, to further the emotional, cognitive, social and physical integration of the person. Its starting point is that body and mind are one: posture, gesture and movement express feeling, often more truthfully than words, and changing how one moves can change how one feels and relates. Its founder in the United States was Marian Chace (1896 to 1970), a dancer trained at the Denishawn school of Ruth St Denis and Ted Shawn, who noticed that some of the pupils in her dance classes came less for technique than for the feelings that dancing released. From the early 1940s she worked with psychiatric patients at St Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, many of them withdrawn, mute or severely disturbed, and found that patients who could not be reached in conversation would join a circle of movement. Four ideas sum up her method: body action (helping the patient to move, loosen tension and become aware of the body), symbolism (movement as a way of expressing and working through feelings and memories), the therapeutic movement relationship (the therapist joins and reflects the patient's movements, establishing contact through movement), and rhythmic group activity (shared rhythm organises behaviour and creates a sense of belonging). In 1966 she helped found the American Dance Therapy Association and became its first president. A second tradition, authentic movement , grew from the work of Mary Starks Whitehouse (1911 to 1979), who called her approach "movement in depth" and drew on Carl Jung's active imagination; her student Janet Adler later developed it into the mover and witness form. The mover, eyes closed, follows inner impulses to move, while a witness watches without judgement, and the two then speak about what was experienced and seen. Many dance movement therapists also use the system of movement analysis developed by the dance theorist Rudolf Laban to describe qualities of movement such as weight, time, space and flow. The approach suits people for whom words are hard: children with autism, survivors of trauma, people with chronic psychosis, older adults with dementia, and patients with medical illness. Indian practitioners have adapted classical and folk dance forms to the same ends. The evidence remains limited. A Cochrane review of dance movement therapy for depression (Bonnie Meekums, Vicky Karkou and Andrea Nelson, 2015) found only three small trials with 147 participants and concluded that the low-quality evidence did not allow any firm conclusion about its effectiveness. Exam trap Dance/movement therapy is Marian Chace 's (St Elizabeths Hospital; first president of the American Dance Therapy Association, founded 1966 ). Authentic movement is Mary Whitehouse's, influenced by Jung. Do not credit dance therapy to Moreno (psychodrama) or to Naumburg (art therapy). Drama therapy and how it differs from psychodrama The term drama therapy (in British spelling, dramatherapy) means the intentional use of drama and theatre processes, such as role-play, improvisation, storytelling, puppetry, masks, enactment of myths and scripted scenes, to achieve therapeutic goals. It is easy to confuse with psychodrama, which Section 7.11 described: Jacob Levy Moreno's group method in which a protagonist enacts scenes from his or her own life, with auxiliary egos, a director, role reversal and doubling. The two share a belief that acting can heal, but they come from different roots and work differently. Psychodrama was invented by one man, a psychiatrist, and goes straight to the protagonist's real life. Drama therapy grew in Britain and North America from theatre, drama in education and remedial drama, and it often works through fiction and metaphor: a client may play a character in a story, speak through a puppet or a mask, or re-enact a myth, and discover his own life in it at a safer distance. The British drama educator Peter Slade is usually credited with first using the word "dramatherapy", in the 1930s, and the British Association of Dramatherapists was founded in 1977, with Sue Jennings among its founder members. Three ideas from drama therapy are worth knowing. Jennings described a developmental sequence of dramatic play, embodiment, projection and role : infants first explore the world through the body, then project their feelings onto objects and toys, and finally take on roles, and drama therapy can work at whichever stage a client needs. The American drama therapist Robert Landy built a role method on the idea that personality is a system of roles (the victim, the hero, the helper, the critic) and that therapy helps a person discover, play and balance them; he also stressed aesthetic distance , the point at which a person can feel strongly while still being able to reflect, which drama therapy tries to find by moving the client closer to or further from personal material. Renée Emunah proposed an integrative model in five phases, moving from dramatic play through scene work and role play to a culminating enactment of personal material and finally a closing dramatic ritual. Drama therapy is used in schools, in work with children and adolescents, in psychiatric and forensic hospitals, and with people with learning disabilities; its evidence comes mostly from small studies. Exam trap Psychodrama (Moreno, Section 7.11) enacts the protagonist's own life directly, with a director, auxiliaries, role reversal and doubling. Drama therapy is a separate profession that often works through fiction, story, role and metaphor at a safe distance (Jennings, Landy, Emunah). Some revision lists write "Drama therapy: Moreno"; if the options include psychodrama, Moreno belongs with psychodrama, and if a question pairs "drama therapy" with Moreno and offers no drama therapist (Slade, Jennings, Landy, Emunah), the setter means psychodrama. Sociodrama (also Moreno's) enacts the shared problems of a group or community. Bibliotherapy and expressive writing The term bibliotherapy means the use of reading material, chosen for its relevance to the reader's situation, to help with emotional or behavioural problems. The idea that books heal is very old. The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus recorded that the royal library of the Egyptian pharaoh Ramses II bore over its entrance the words "healing place of the soul", and Benjamin Rush recommended reading for patients in American hospitals in the early nineteenth century. The word itself was coined by the American essayist and minister Samuel McChord Crothers (1857 to 1927) in an article titled "A Literary Clinic", published in the Atlantic Monthly in September 1916. There are two kinds. Affective (or creative) bibliotherapy uses fiction, poetry and biography. The reader is thought to move through three stages: identification with a character whose situation resembles his own, catharsis as he lives through the character's feelings, and insight as he sees his own situation in a new light. A teenager reading a novel about a boy whose parents divorce, or an Indian reader who finds Arjuna's despair on the battlefield in the Bhagavad Gita uncannily like his own (Section 8.11), is using literature this way. Cognitive (self-help) bibliotherapy uses structured self-help books that teach the methods of a therapy, usually CBT, step by step, such as David Burns's Feeling Good (1980) for depression or the behavioural programme Control Your Depression by Peter Lewinsohn and colleagues. Bibliotherapy can also be clinical, used by therapists as part of treatment, or developmental, used by teachers, librarians and parents to help ordinary children through ordinary difficulties such as starting school, a new sibling or a death in the family. Self-help bibliotherapy has a respectable evidence base. In a series of studies at the University of Alabama, Forrest Scogin and his colleagues showed that mildly and moderately depressed older adults who read Feeling Good or Control Your Depression improved more than those waiting for treatment (1989), and that most kept their gains two years later (1990); with depressed adults recruited from the community, minimal-contact cognitive bibliotherapy was clearly better than a waiting list, with gains maintained at three months and reductions in dysfunctional attitudes and negative automatic thoughts (Jamison and Scogin, 1995). Self-help works best for mild to moderate problems, for motivated readers, and when someone checks in on progress; this is guided self-help, the printed ancestor of the guided internet CBT described in Section 5.11.8. In Britain, Books on Prescription schemes allow a general practitioner to "prescribe" an evidence-based self-help book, which the patient borrows from the public library. Writing can heal as well as reading. In 1986 James W. Pennebaker and Sandra Beall asked college students to write for fifteen minutes on four consecutive days, either about the most traumatic or upsetting experiences of their lives, with their deepest thoughts and feelings, or about trivial topics. Those who wrote about both the facts of their traumas and their feelings were more upset immediately after writing, but made fewer visits to the university health centre in the following months. This expressive writing paradigm has since been tested in hundreds of studies, with small but reliable benefits; journaling, letter-writing (including unsent letters to someone who has died) and poetry therapy are its clinical relatives. Exam trap Samuel Crothers coined "bibliotherapy" ( 1916 , "A Literary Clinic"). The three stages of affective bibliotherapy are identification, catharsis and insight . Self-help (cognitive) bibliotherapy, for example with Feeling Good , is effective for mild to moderate depression , especially when guided. Expressive writing about trauma is Pennebaker 's (with Beall, 1986). Animal-assisted and horticultural therapy In the 1950s the American child psychologist Boris M. Levinson (1907 to 1984) had an unexpected session. A withdrawn child came to his office while Levinson's dog, Jingles, happened to be there; the child, who had barely spoken in therapy, began to talk to the dog, and then, through the dog, to Levinson. Levinson began to use Jingles deliberately as what he called a "co-therapist", and presented the idea at an American Psychological Association meeting and in a paper, "The dog as a 'co-therapist'", published in Mental Hygiene in 1962. Many in his audience laughed, but Levinson persisted, coined the term "pet therapy" in 1964, and set out his methods in Pet-Oriented Child Psychotherapy (1969). He was not entirely the first: the York Retreat, founded in 1796, is said to have kept small animals for its patients, and Sigmund Freud often had his chow Jofi in the room during sessions. But Levinson made the animal a deliberate part of therapy and gave the field its research agenda. Today a distinction is drawn between animal-assisted activities , informal visits by animals and their handlers to hospitals, old-age homes or schools for comfort and recreation, and animal-assisted therapy , a goal-directed intervention in which a specially trained animal is part of a treatment plan delivered by a professional, with goals set and progress recorded. Dogs are most common, but horses are used in equine-assisted therapy (and in hippotherapy, a physiotherapy in which the horse's movement is used to improve posture and balance). Animals seem to help in several ways: they are non-judgemental, they make contact easier (a "social lubricant" between client and therapist), touching and stroking them can lower arousal, and caring for an animal gives a sense of competence and responsibility. The evidence, however, consists mostly of small studies, often without adequate control groups, and the benefits may owe much to novelty and enthusiasm. There are practical risks too: allergies, bites, infections passed from animals, the welfare of the animal itself, and clients who are afraid of animals or, as many people in India are, wary of dogs for reasons of culture, religion or fear of street dogs and rabies. In much the same spirit, horticultural therapy uses gardening and plant-based activities, guided by a trained practitioner, to improve physical and mental well-being. Benjamin Rush is often quoted as having observed that the patients in his hospital who worked in its gardens recovered better than those who did not, and many asylums of the nineteenth century had farms and gardens worked by patients, an idea that survives in the occupational and vocational rehabilitation of Section 9.8. Gardening combines physical activity, structure, a sense of achievement and contact with nature, and is widely used in psychiatric rehabilitation, dementia care and work with people with intellectual disability.
