Yoga and meditation in Indian clinical settings For many Indian clients, yoga is not an exotic import but something their grandparents did every morning, and that familiarity is part of its clinical value. Classical yoga is set out in the Yoga Sutras attributed to Patanjali, compiled perhaps two thousand years ago (the dating is uncertain). Its second sutra defines yoga as chitta vritti nirodha , the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind, and its eight limbs ( ashtanga ) lay out a path from ethics to absorption: yama (restraints, such as non-violence and truthfulness), niyama (observances, such as cleanliness and contentment), asana (posture), pranayama (regulation of the breath), pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses from their objects), dharana (concentration), dhyana (meditation) and samadhi (absorption). What is used in clinics is mostly the middle of this list: postures, breathing practices, relaxation in the corpse posture ( shavasana ) and simple meditation, taught in a structured module and then practised at home. India's leading centre for testing yoga as a treatment is NIMHANS in Bengaluru, where the NIMHANS Integrated Centre for Yoga offers yoga therapy as an add-on to psychiatric treatment and a Department of Integrative Medicine studies it, often with researchers from yoga institutions such as Swami Vivekananda Yoga Anusandhana Samsthana (S-VYASA). You have already met the first landmark trial in Section 4.8.3: in 2000, N. Janakiramaiah, B. N. Gangadhar and colleagues found Sudarshan Kriya Yoga, a rhythmic breathing practice, about as effective as imipramine (though less effective than ECT) for melancholic depression, in a trial that could not be blinded. Research on schizophrenia followed. Key study: yoga as an add-on treatment for schizophrenia (NIMHANS, 2007 and 2012) G. Duraiswamy, Jagadisha Thirthalli, H. R. Nagendra and B. N. Gangadhar randomly assigned 61 moderately ill patients with schizophrenia, all continuing their antipsychotic medication, to four months of yoga therapy or of physical exercise, the exercise acting as a control for activity, attention and contact. A rater who did not know the groups assessed them before and after. Of the 41 who completed the trial, those in the yoga group had significantly less psychopathology and better social and occupational functioning and quality of life than those in the exercise group (2007). A larger trial by Shivarama Varambally and colleagues (2012) randomised 119 outpatients to yoga, exercise or a waiting list, with a month of supervised training followed by three months of home practice. Only the yoga group showed significant reductions in negative symptoms, and about 35 percent of the yoga group improved, against fewer than 10 percent in the other groups. The authors themselves noted the limits: the effects were modest, many patients dropped out, and home practice could not be checked. The conclusion is that yoga is a promising complement to medication, especially for negative symptoms, not a replacement for it. For depression, a meta-analysis by Holger Cramer and colleagues (2013) of twelve randomised trials with 619 participants found moderate evidence that yoga reduces the severity of depression in the short term compared with usual care, and limited evidence of benefit compared with relaxation and aerobic exercise. But only three of the trials were at low risk of bias, too few trials followed patients up for any long-term effect to be pooled, and none reported safety data. Read all this evidence carefully, because enthusiasm often runs ahead of it. What the trials show is that yoga, added to standard treatment, produces short-term improvements in symptoms and functioning in several disorders. What they do not show is that yoga can replace medication or psychotherapy, that its effects last, or that they are due to anything specific to yoga rather than to activity, relaxation, expectation and the group. The trials cannot be blinded, many are small, and many are run by researchers committed to yoga, an allegiance effect of the kind described in Section 8.6. Meditation has followed a similar path. The mindfulness-based therapies of Section 5.9 grew from Buddhist meditation, much of it originating in India; Herbert Benson's relaxation response (Sections 4.8.3 and 9.4.1) was first studied in practitioners of Transcendental Meditation, a mantra technique popularised by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi; and Vipassana, an Indian Buddhist insight meditation taught in ten-day silent courses, has been offered in prisons (Section 10.9.8). Meditation is generally safe, but case reports describe anxiety, depersonalisation and, rarely, psychotic episodes during intensive retreats in vulnerable people, so a history of psychosis or recent trauma calls for caution and supervision. The older Indian attempts to build psychotherapy on yoga, such as N. S. Vahia's psychophysiologic therapy in Bombay, are described in Section 8.11. Indian context: how Indian psychology differs from Western psychology "Indian psychology" does not mean psychology as practised in India; it is an approach that draws its ideas and methods from Indian philosophical, spiritual and religious traditions (the Upanishads, Samkhya, yoga, Buddhism) and restates them in terms that can be studied and applied. In 2002 more than 150 psychologists meeting in Pondicherry issued a Manifesto for Indian Psychology, which criticised mainstream psychology in India as largely a Western import that ignored India's own psychological traditions, and The Handbook of Indian Psychology (2008), edited by K. Ramakrishna Rao, Anand C. Paranjpe and Ajit K. Dalal, set out the field. Compared with mainstream Western psychology, which grew from Wundt's laboratory and tends to be empirical, analytic, materialist and centred on the separate individual, Indian psychology is holistic (body, mind and spirit as one system), consciousness-centred and spiritual (its aim is self-realisation and the transformation of the person, not only the relief of symptoms), it accepts first-person, experiential and contemplative methods alongside experiment, and it sees the self as embedded in family and community relationships (Sections 3.11 and 8.11). Its proponents present it as complementary to Western psychology, not a replacement. So when asked how Indian psychology differs from Western psychology, the answer is that it emphasises holistic and spiritual approaches, including community dynamics . It does not rely solely on ancient texts without modern relevance (it seeks to test and apply them); Western psychology does not focus entirely on spirituality and community (that reverses the contrast); and the two do not emphasise individualism equally. Exam trap Patanjali's eight limbs, in order: yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi . Pranayama = breath control; pratyahara = withdrawal of the senses; dharana = concentration; dhyana = meditation. The NIMHANS yoga trials show yoga as an add-on (with medication) that helps symptoms and functioning in the short term, especially negative symptoms in schizophrenia; they do not show that yoga replaces medication. Sudarshan Kriya Yoga for depression: Janakiramaiah, Gangadhar and colleagues, 2000. Telepsychology and digital mental health The newest adjunct is not an art but a technology. The term telepsychology covers the provision of psychological services by telecommunication: telephone, video, text and email. Its history is longer than the smartphone's. In 1959 the Nebraska Psychiatric Institute began to use two-way closed-circuit television for teaching, and by 1964 a television link connected it to Norfolk State Hospital, elsewhere in the state, for consultations and group therapy. For half a century telepsychology remained a niche, used for remote areas and the housebound. Then the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 moved much of the world's psychotherapy online in a matter of weeks. In India, the Telemedicine Practice Guidelines of 25 March 2020, issued for registered medical practitioners, gave remote consultation a legal footing, and Telepsychiatry Operational Guidelines prepared by the Indian Psychiatric Society and the Telemedicine Society of India with NIMHANS followed in May 2020. Reviews of psychotherapy by videoconference have generally found outcomes and therapeutic alliance broadly comparable with face-to-face therapy for depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress, though most clients and therapists still report that something of the room is lost. India's national tele-mental health service, Tele-MANAS (14416), launched in October 2022, extends this to the whole country by telephone (Sections 5.11.8 and 9.7; the national programmes are described in Chapter 1). The phrase digital mental health covers the broader family of interventions delivered through digital technology, with or without a clinician. Section 5.11.8 described its best-tested member, internet-delivered CBT, and the finding that guided internet CBT can match face-to-face CBT while unguided programmes lose many of their users (Eysenbach's law of attrition). Beyond these structured programmes lie thousands of smartphone apps for mood tracking, psychoeducation, CBT exercises, mindfulness and peer support, most of which have never been tested. Phones can also collect data: brief questionnaires several times a day in the person's ordinary life ( ecological momentary assessment ), and passive data from the phone's own sensors, such as movement, sleep, typing and calls, which some researchers hope can detect relapse early, an idea called digital phenotyping. Virtual reality exposure, the immersive form of digital therapy, was described in Section 4.3. The most dramatic development is the chatbot. The first was ELIZA , written at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the mid-1960s by the computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum (1923 to 2008). Its best-known script, DOCTOR, imitated a Rogerian psychotherapist by turning the user's statements back into open questions ("I am unhappy." "Why do you say you are unhappy?"), with no understanding at all. Weizenbaum was disturbed by how readily people confided in it (his own secretary is said to have asked him to leave the room so that she could talk to ELIZA in private), and in Computer Power and Human Reason (1976) he argued that machines should never replace human judgement in matters of care. The tendency to attribute understanding and feeling to a program that has none is now called the ELIZA effect. Key study: Woebot, a CBT chatbot (Fitzpatrick, Darcy and Vierhile, 2017) Kathleen Kara Fitzpatrick and colleagues at Stanford tested whether a fully automated conversational agent could deliver CBT. Seventy students aged 18 to 28 with self-reported symptoms of depression and anxiety were randomly assigned either to two weeks of daily text conversations with Woebot, which delivered CBT-based self-help (mood checks, identifying thinking errors, short lessons), or to an information-only control: an e-book on depression in college students from the American National Institute of Mental Health. After two to three weeks, the Woebot group showed a significant fall in depressive symptoms on the PHQ-9 and the control group did not; anxiety fell in both groups. Users said they valued the bot's "empathy" and check-ins. Notice the limits: a tiny sample of students, two weeks, self-report measures, no blinding, a weak control condition, and a declared conflict of interest, since the second author had founded the company that built Woebot. The study shows that a chatbot can be acceptable and helpful in the short term, not that it can treat clinical depression. Since the early 2020s, chatbots built on large language models, which generate fluent, apparently understanding replies to anything a user types, have been used by very large numbers of people as informal confidants and "therapists", mostly outside any health service. They are available at three in the morning, never tired and never judgemental, and some users find them genuinely helpful. They also raise the problems Weizenbaum foresaw, in sharper form: they can produce confident but wrong or harmful advice, they cannot reliably recognise or respond to a suicidal crisis, they may encourage dependence on a relationship with a machine, and they are owned by companies whose interests are not the user's. Return to Leela. After discharge she returned to a village two hours from the nearest clinic. Her psychologist arranged monthly video sessions, and between them Leela used a free CBT-based app to record her mood and practise behavioural activation, which the psychologist reviewed at each session: a guided, blended arrangement in the middle of Figure 10.15. The psychologist also agreed with her, at the first video session, where she would be during sessions, who else was in the house, which phone number to call if the connection failed, and what to do, and whom to call, if she ever felt unsafe. That last conversation is the subject of the final subsection. Exam trap ELIZA (Joseph Weizenbaum , MIT, mid-1960s) imitated a Rogerian therapist; the ELIZA effect is attributing understanding to a program. Woebot (2017) reduced depressive symptoms in students over two weeks compared with an e-book, but the trial was small, short and run by the company's founder among others. Guided digital help beats unguided (Section 5.11.8). Tele-MANAS = 14416 , launched October 2022. The ethics of digital mental health The general ethics of teletherapy (consent, confidentiality, competence and jurisdiction) are set out with the rest of professional ethics in Chapter 1. Digital mental health adds problems of its own, which Table 10.28 summarises. The first is privacy and data . A therapy session in a room leaves no record except the therapist's notes; a session through an app or a platform may leave recordings, transcripts, location data and usage logs on servers owned by a company, sometimes in another country, and some mental health apps have been found sharing users' data with advertisers. In India the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for consent to, and the handling of, personal data, but a clinician must still know what a platform does with the data before recommending it. The second is confidentiality at the client's end : in a crowded home with one shared phone, a family member may be listening, so the clinician must agree where the client will be and how to signal if someone enters. The third is emergencies . A therapist in a room can call for help; a therapist on a video call to a suicidal client in another town may not even know where the client is. Good practice is to record the client's location at every session, keep a local emergency contact and the nearest services on file, and agree a crisis plan at the start. Automated tools are weakest exactly here, which is why every responsible app and chatbot directs users in crisis to human help. The fourth is competence and jurisdiction . In the United States a psychologist is licensed by a state and may generally treat only clients located in states where he is licensed, a problem that interstate agreements such as PSYPACT were created to ease; in India a clinical psychologist's practice rests on registration with the Rehabilitation Council of India, and a client abroad may be subject to that country's law. Clinicians who work online also need the technical competence to choose secure platforms and to manage a session when the connection fails. The fifth is evidence . Most mental health apps have never been tested, marketing claims run far ahead of data, and published trials are often run by the products' developers, as in the Woebot study. The sixth is equity : the digital divide (Section 5.11.8) means that the people with least access to clinics, older, poorer, rural and female users, are often also the least likely to have their own smartphone, data and privacy, so digital services can widen the very gaps they are meant to close. The seventh is automation and accountability : when a chatbot gives harmful advice, nobody is professionally responsible in the way a therapist is, and users may not even realise that no human being is involved. The principle that ties these together is the one with which this chapter began, with children who cannot refer themselves: the more vulnerable the client, the more the clinician must think about who is protecting them. The case of Dibs, revisited Go back to the playroom where Virginia Axline let a five-year-old lead. You can now see how typical of child work almost everything in Dibs's story was. He did not refer himself: the adults around him decided that something was wrong and could not agree on what it was. His teachers thought him retarded on some days and unusually bright on others, his parents had decided that he was defective, and a psychiatrist had told them that the problem was theirs. That disagreement is the informant problem that Achenbach, McConaughy and Howell measured (Section 10.1): each adult saw a different slice of a child whose behaviour changed with the setting, and the school psychologist and the paediatrician could not test a child who would not cooperate with strangers. Tested a week after his sessions ended, he scored 168 on the Stanford-Binet, a reminder that no single test, informant or setting is ever enough. The method that reached him was non-directive play therapy (Section 10.2), Carl Rogers's client-centred approach applied to a child through Axline's eight principles of warmth, acceptance, permissiveness, reflection of feeling, respect for the child's own capacity, following his lead, not hurrying and keeping only the limits that anchor therapy to reality. When Dibs locked the doll family in the house and staged a fire, Axline named what he showed instead of interpreting it as Melanie Klein would have done, and he went on to stage his own rescue. The chapter has also shown the limits of the story. Dibs is a case study, with one child, one therapist and no comparison group, and Bratton's meta-analysis and the trials of Sections 10.3 to 10.5 suggest that play therapy suits emotional and relationship difficulties, while specific problems such as anxiety, defiance, ADHD and autism respond better to structured treatments delivered through parents and schools. His parents, who drilled and tested him without ever quite getting close to him, were part of the problem as well as part of the solution, which is the insight behind filial therapy, parent training and family work. And the three things you were asked to notice at the start hold for every client in this chapter: the woman with dementia whose family brings her, the student whose career his father has chosen, the accused whom a court sends, the grieving mother who could paint her loss before she could speak of it. None of them is the standard adult who walks in alone and asks for help, and with each the clinician has to ask who made the referral, what language the client can use, and which family, school, court or community the problem lives in. As Section 10.10 ended by saying, the more vulnerable the client, the more the clinician must think about who is protecting them. Chapter summary 10.1 Children as Clients. Children are referred by adults, mostly for externalising problems, while internalising problems are under-referred; abnormality is judged against age norms, and a child talks through play and lives inside systems he cannot change. Developmental psychopathology (Sroufe and Rutter, 1984) studies normal and abnormal development together: homotypic and heterotypic continuity, equifinality and multifinality, Rutter's cumulative risk from the Isle of Wight studies, Werner and Smith's resilience on Kauai and Sameroff's transactional model. Thomas and Chess's New York Longitudinal Study (1956) described easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up children and goodness of fit. Informants agree poorly (about 0.60, 0.28 and 0.22 in Achenbach, McConaughy and Howell, 1987), so assessment is multi-informant because symptoms vary across contexts. Parents consent and children assent, and confidentiality yields to risk and to POCSO. India's first child guidance clinic opened in Bombay in 1937, and RBSK (2013) screens for the four Ds. 10.2 Play Therapy. Play is the child's natural medium: Piaget's symbolic play, Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, and play's powers of communication, release, mastery (Freud's fort-da game), safe distance and rehearsal. Hug-Hellmuth (1920) first used play in child analysis. Anna Freud (1927) began with a preparatory phase, worked with parents and doubted that children form a full transference neurosis, while Klein treated play as free association and interpreted deeply from the first session. Levy's release therapy (1938), Hambidge's structured play therapy and the relationship therapy of Taft, Allen and Moustakas led to Axline's non-directive play therapy (1947) and its eight principles. Landreth's child-centred play therapy added the ACT model of limit setting, the Guerneys' filial therapy (1964) trains parents, Lowenfeld's World Technique (1929) became Kalff's Jungian sandplay, and Jernberg's Theraplay is adult-led. Bratton's 2005 meta-analysis found an average effect of 0.80, largest when parents delivered the sessions. 10.3 Cognitive Behavioural, Parent and School Interventions. CBT for children is rebuilt, not merely simplified: it is more behavioural the younger the child, concrete and visual, uses coping modelling, and brings in parents as consultants, collaborators or co-clients, because family accommodation keeps anxiety going. Kendall's Coping Cat (16 sessions, the FEAR plan, graded exposure in the second half) treats childhood anxiety, and in CAMS (2008) CBT plus sertraline beat either alone. Trauma-focused CBT (Cohen, Mannarino and Deblinger) builds a trauma narrative with a non-offending caregiver. Dodge's hostile attribution bias underlies Kazdin's problem-solving skills training and Lochman's Coping Power. Barkley's Defiant Children and Sanders's five-level Triple P extend parent training, which removes negative reinforcement rather than using it; helicopter parenting has many causes. Schools offer three tiers of support (Horner and Sugai), social and emotional learning and the Olweus programme, and India adds RKSK, Manodarpan and the Happiness Curriculum. 10.4 Treating Common Childhood and Adolescent Problems. Nocturnal enuresis is treated first with the urine alarm and overlearning, with retention control, dry-bed (Azrin) and full-spectrum home (Houts) training as packages; retentive encopresis needs the bowel cleared and scheduled toileting with rewards. Safety signals and accommodation keep anxiety alive. Berg separated school refusal (anxious, at home with the parents' knowledge) from truancy, and Kearney and Silverman's four functions of school refusal behaviour, two negatively and two positively reinforced, guide a quick, graded return; selective mutism yields to stimulus fading. In the MTA study (1999) medication management beat behavioural treatment for core ADHD symptoms, the combination helped other outcomes, and the differences had gone by three years. Conduct problems call for parent training, then child skills training and, in adolescence, multisystemic therapy, avoiding deviancy training. Adolescent depression responds to CBT and IPT-A, and repeated self-harm to safety planning, DBT-A and MBT-A. 10.5 Autism, Intellectual Disability and Learning Disability. Kanner first described early infantile autism in 1943 and Asperger the verbally fluent form in 1944; Bettelheim's refrigerator mother gave way to Rimland's biological view. Behavioural work is the foundation: early intensive behavioural intervention and functional communication training, after problem behaviour has been analysed for attention, escape, tangible or sensory functions. Schopler's TEACCH (1971) uses structured teaching, Bondy and Frost's PECS (1985) runs in six phases from requesting to commenting, Gray's social stories describe more than they direct, and pivotal response treatment, the Early Start Denver Model and DIR/Floortime teach through play; PACT and PASS coach parents. Facilitated communication was discredited in 1993. Intellectual disability, from Itard and Seguin onwards, is met with normalisation, levels of support, adaptive skills training and the National Trust's schemes; specific learning disability with remediation (phonological awareness, Orton-Gillingham, Fernald's VAKT method, response to intervention) together with accommodation. 10.6 Child Abuse, Child Protection and Adolescents. Kempe's battered-child syndrome (1962) made abuse visible. Maltreatment is physical, sexual or emotional abuse or neglect, and neglect is a failure of care, not poverty. A disclosure calls for calm listening, no promise of secrecy, a few open questions, exact notes and a report; Summit's accommodation syndrome explains delayed and retracted disclosure but proves nothing. Ceci and Bruck's research, including the Sam Stone study, showed how stereotypes and repeated leading questions create false reports, so the NICHD protocol relies on open invitations. The POCSO Act 2012 covers everyone under 18, is gender-neutral, makes reporting mandatory under section 19 and punishes failure to report under section 21. TF-CBT with a non-offending parent is first-line. Adolescents need engagement, the HEADSS interview and confidentiality with stated exceptions; continued interdependence with parents is healthy; and affirmative therapy addresses Meyer's minority stress, while conversion therapy is unethical. 10.7 Working with Older Adults. Freud thought old people no longer educable, but they benefit from therapy about as much as younger adults. Gerontology (Metchnikoff, 1903), geriatrics (Nascher, 1909) and geropsychology differ, and Butler coined ageism (1969). Caregiver burden, objective and subjective, is measured with the Zarit Burden Interview; counselling the spouse delayed nursing-home placement (Mittelman, 2006), and Kitwood's person-centred care replaced malignant social psychology. Folsom's reality orientation restates time, place and person; Butler's life review (1963) gave rise to reminiscence and life review therapy; Feil's validation therapy accepts the person's reality; Spector's cognitive stimulation therapy (2003) has the best evidence. Behaviour that challenges is analysed for physical causes and unmet needs. Late-life depression is not normal ageing and responds to IPT, CBT and collaborative care (IMPACT, PROSPECT). Capacity is presumed and decision-specific, elder abuse is mostly psychological and committed by family, and the 2007 Act protects senior citizens. 10.8 Counselling. Guidance helps people understand themselves and their opportunities; it is educational, vocational or personal-social. Its services are orientation, appraisal, information, counselling, placement and follow-up, and the counselling service is the heart of the guidance programme; aptitude tests predict potential, records document students, and the counselling interview is the vehicle of counselling. Williamson's directive counselling runs from analysis to follow-up, Rogers's non-directive counselling lets the client lead, and Thorne's eclectic counselling chooses between them. Hackney and Cormier's five stages run from rapport to termination and follow-up; a paraphrase restates content in the counsellor's own words, a reflection names the feeling and a summary draws threads together. Counselling spans schools, colleges, marriage, rehabilitation, HIV testing (the five Cs), de-addiction, grief and the workplace (EAPs), which is not industrial-organisational psychology. Career theories include Parsons's matching, Holland's RIASEC hexagon, Super's life-span, life-space theory, Ginzberg's three periods and Krumboltz's planned happenstance. 10.9 Forensic Clinical Psychology. Forensic psychology applies psychology to legal questions. A clinician may be an evaluator, expert witness, consultant, treating clinician or researcher, but never both therapist and evaluator for one person. Fitness to stand trial concerns the present (Dusky, 1960; BNSS sections 367 to 369 in India). Insanity concerns the moment of the act: M'Naghten (1843) is cognitive, the irresistible impulse test volitional, Durham (1954) a product test and ALI (1962) a substantial-capacity test, and the Insanity Defense Reform Act (1984) followed Hinckley; India's section 22 of the BNS, formerly section 84 IPC, follows M'Naghten. Actuarial prediction equals or beats clinical prediction (Meehl), and malingering needs an external incentive. Custody follows the child's best interests. The Juvenile Justice Act 2015 allows a preliminary assessment of 16 to 18 year olds accused of heinous offences, and Martinson's "nothing works" gave way to Andrews and Bonta's risk-need-responsivity model. 10.10 Creative, Adjunct and Digital Therapies. Adjunct therapies add to the main treatment. Adrian Hill coined art therapy (1942); Naumburg saw art as symbolic speech within therapy and Kramer saw art as therapy through sublimation, and the MATISSE trial found no benefit in schizophrenia. Music therapy is active or receptive (Nordoff-Robbins; Bonny's Guided Imagery and Music), Marian Chace founded dance movement therapy, and drama therapy works through fiction and role at a safe distance, unlike Moreno's psychodrama. Crothers coined bibliotherapy (1916); guided self-help reading helps mild to moderate depression, and Pennebaker's expressive writing brings small benefits. Levinson's dog Jingles began animal-assisted therapy. Patanjali's eight limbs underlie yoga, which the NIMHANS trials show to be a promising add-on, especially for negative symptoms, and Indian psychology is holistic and spiritual. Telepsychology, internet CBT, apps and chatbots, from Weizenbaum's ELIZA to Woebot, raise questions of privacy, emergencies, jurisdiction, evidence and equity. assessment From the past papers When diagnosing developmental disorders, multi-information assessment is recommended because (JEMAS 2025) (a) parents tend to over report problems (b) teachers provide no relevant information (c) symptoms may vary across contexts (d) only clinical observation is not sufficient Answer: (c) symptoms may vary across contexts. A child's behaviour depends on the setting and on who is with him (situational specificity), which is why Achenbach, McConaughy and Howell (1987) found agreement of only about 0.28 between informants who see the child in different settings, and concluded that each informant adds valid information. Parents under-report some problems as well as over-reporting others, teachers are often the best judges of attention, learning and peer behaviour, and "clinical observation is not sufficient" is a consequence of the real reason, since the clinic is just one more context. Helicopter Parenting is the result of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Parental anxiety (b) Parental unfulfilled wishes (c) Parents' personality traits (d) All of above Answer: (d) All of above. Helicopter parenting, named from the teenager in Haim Ginott's Between Parent and Teenager (1969) whose mother "hovers over me like a helicopter", is an over-involved, over-protective style with no single cause. Parental anxiety, wishes the parents live out through the child, traits such as perfectionism and a need for control, and a competitive education system all feed it, so no single option is complete. Which of the following is not a part of Parent Management Training? (IHBAS 2020) (a) Attending positive behaviour (b) Rewarding positive behaviour (c) Ignoring undesirable behaviour (d) Negative reinforcement Answer: (d) Negative reinforcement. Attending to and rewarding positive behaviour, and planned ignoring of minor misbehaviour (extinction), are core skills of every parent training programme from Patterson's onwards. Negative reinforcement is the trap the training exists to remove: in the coercive cycle the parent withdraws a demand when the child screams, which reinforces the screaming, and the parent's giving in is itself reinforced when the screaming stops. A parent deliberately ignores a child's temper tantrums in an attempt to discourage them. The parent's strategy is in accordance with: (Amity 2023) (a) Negative reinforcement (b) Extinction (c) Operant escape (d) Operant avoidance Answer: (b) Extinction. The paper's key, (c) operant escape, is wrong. Ignoring withholds the attention that has been reinforcing the tantrums, which is extinction; parent training teaches parents to sit out the extinction burst that comes first. Escape describes behaviour that ends something unpleasant that is already present, which is what a parent who gives in to stop the noise is doing; avoidance prevents an aversive event from starting; and negative reinforcement strengthens a behaviour rather than discouraging it. Which parenting style is characterized by the combination of giving emotional support, setting clear boundaries, and maintaining accountability for children's behavior? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Authoritarian parenting (b) Authoritative parenting (c) Permissive parenting (d) Neglectful parenting Answer: (b) Authoritative parenting. Diana Baumrind's authoritative parent is warm and responsive and at the same time firm, consistent and willing to explain the rules, which is the parent that behavioural parent training sets out to create. Authoritarian parenting is strict and cold, permissive parenting warm with few rules, and neglectful parenting is the uninvolved style (the styles themselves are taught in the Developmental book). A stimulus that is constantly present, or paired with, the absence of a noxious stimulus may become a: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Safety signal (b) Avoidance cue (c) Relief stimulus (d) Readiness prompt Answer: (a) Safety signal. A stimulus consistently present with the absence of something feared comes to reduce fear, as a mother does for a child with separation anxiety, which is why safety signals are gradually faded in exposure therapy. An avoidance cue (warning signal) predicts that the aversive event is coming, relief is the pleasant drop in fear when an aversive event ends, and "readiness prompt" is not a learning-theory term at all. "Escape learning" differs from "avoidance learning" in that, in escape learning, the behavior: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Prevents the onset of an aversive stimulus (b) Terminates an aversive stimulus that is already present (c) Is maintained by positive reinforcement (d) Is under the control of a discriminative stimulus Answer: (b). In escape learning the behaviour ends an aversive situation that is already present; in avoidance learning, option (a), it prevents the aversive situation from beginning. Both are maintained by negative reinforcement, not positive, which is why the two school refusal functions of avoiding distressing school stimuli and escaping evaluative situations sit on the negative-reinforcement side of Kearney's model; option (d) does not distinguish the two at all. According to DSM-5, which of the following is required for a diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Delayed speech alone (b) Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction across multiple contexts (c) Intellectual disability only (d) Hyperactivity and impulsivity Answer: (b). DSM-5 requires persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts together with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, present from the early developmental period. Language and intellectual impairment are recorded as specifiers, not requirements, and hyperactivity-impulsivity belongs to ADHD, which DSM-5 allows to be diagnosed alongside autism (the full criteria are in the Psychiatric Disorders book). Infantile Autism was first described by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Leo Kanner (b) Cameron (c) Goldstein (d) Jasper Answer: (a) Leo Kanner. Kanner's 1943 paper "Autistic disturbances of affective contact" described eleven children at Johns Hopkins with extreme autistic aloneness and an anxiously obsessive desire for sameness, and from 1944 he called the syndrome early infantile autism. Norman Cameron is known for over-inclusive thinking in schizophrenia, Kurt Goldstein for the loss of the abstract attitude after brain injury, and "Jasper" most likely means Karl Jaspers, the founder of phenomenological psychopathology. Infantile autism was first described by : (IHBAS 2025) (a) Hans Asperger (b) Leo Kanner (c) Eugen Bleuler (d) Kurt Schneider Answer: (b) Leo Kanner , in 1943. Hans Asperger described the verbally fluent form a year later (1944), in a German paper that Lorna Wing brought to English readers in 1981. Eugen Bleuler coined the word autism in 1911, but for the withdrawal into an inner world that he saw in schizophrenia, and Kurt Schneider is known for the first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia. The "Lovaas programme" utilises behaviour modification techniques for the treatment of : (RML 2022) (a) Autism (b) Aphasia (c) Acute depression (d) Alcoholism Answer: (a) Autism. Ole Ivar Lovaas's programme at UCLA gave young children with autism about 40 hours a week of one-to-one discrete trial teaching, and his 1987 report claimed normal functioning in 9 of 19 children against 1 of 40 controls. Later work cut that claim down, but early intensive behavioural intervention helps many children; Lovaas treated autism, he did not describe it, and his programme has nothing to do with aphasia, depression or alcoholism. A child with autism is taught to request a "break" using a picture card instead of engaging in a tantrum. This intervention is a key component of: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) (b) Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) (c) Play Therapy (d) Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy Answer: (b) Applied Behavior Analysis. The technique is functional communication training (Carr and Durand, 1985), a form of differential reinforcement of alternative behaviour: the child learns a communicative response that is functionally equivalent to the tantrum (it gets him out of the task) and more efficient. CBT needs verbal reasoning that many such children lack, and neither play therapy nor psychoanalytic psychotherapy teaches a replacement behaviour. Over-correction is a behavioural technique to manage: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Bed wetting in children (b) Repetitive aggressive behaviour in autistic children (c) Temper tantrum in children (d) Alienation in adolescent Answer: (b). Overcorrection (Section 4.6) is a punishment-based procedure keyed for repetitive aggressive or disruptive behaviour in autism and intellectual disability, and it is now reserved for dangerous behaviour that has not responded to positive methods. Dry-bed training for bedwetting contains positive practice, a form of overcorrection, which makes (a) tempting, but bedwetting is treated with the urine alarm; tantrums are handled with planned ignoring and time-out; and alienation is not a behaviour overcorrection targets. Name of the Indian tool to assess the severity and disability of children with autism : (IHBAS 2024) (a) CGAS (b) Childhood Autism Rating Scale (c) CBCL (d) ISAA Answer: (d) ISAA. The paper's key, (b) the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, is wrong. The Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism, developed at the National Institute for the Mentally Handicapped in Secunderabad (now NIEPID), is the Indian instrument used to certify the severity and disability of autism; CARS is the American rating scale of Schopler's group. Section 9.9 explains how to handle this key in an IHBAS paper. CGAS is a single 1 to 100 rating of a child's overall functioning and the CBCL is Achenbach's parent-report problem checklist; neither is an autism tool. Which of the following disabilities is explicitly covered under the scope of The National Trust Act (1999) in India for the welfare of persons with the disability? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Autism Spectrum Disorder (b) Specific Learning Disability (c) Intellectual Disability (Mental Retardation) (d) Both (a) and (c) Answer: (d) Both (a) and (c). The Act's full name gives the answer: the National Trust for the Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act. Specific learning disability and mental illness are among the 21 specified disabilities of the RPwD Act 2016 but are not covered by the National Trust. Which of the following is NOT listed as a specified disability under the RPwD Act, 2016? (Recall set) (a) Specific learning disabilities (b) Intellectual disability (c) Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (d) Autism spectrum disorder Answer: (c) ADHD. Intellectual disability, specific learning disabilities and autism spectrum disorder are all among the Act's 21 specified disabilities; ADHD is not, however common it is in child clinics. Do not let the neurodevelopmental grouping of DSM-5, which includes all four, mislead you about the Act's list. Psychologists and psychiatrists have often viewed adolescence as a time when the healthy trajectory of development involves detachment from the parents. Today, however, there is a greater awareness that: (RML 2022) (a) it can be healthy for interdependence to continue (b) detachment typically occurs earlier, in middle childhood (c) the peer group is more important than parents (d) all parents have the same goal for their adolescent child Answer: (a). The view of G. Stanley Hall's "storm and stress", and of Anna Freud and Peter Blos, that healthy adolescents must detach from their parents has given way to the finding that autonomy grows best within a continuing, warm relationship. Detachment has not simply moved into middle childhood; peers gain influence in everyday matters but add to the parents' influence rather than replacing it; and families differ in what they hope for from their adolescents. Which of the following technique/process involved in guidance is called "the heart of the guidance programme"? (RML 2022) (a) Case Study (b) Interview (c) Cumulative record (d) Aptitude test Answer: (b) Interview. The paper's key, (d) aptitude test, is wrong. The phrase belongs to counselling: the counselling service is the heart of the guidance programme, because it is where the student brings knowledge of herself and of the world together and makes the choice. Counselling is not among these options, and the interview, as the counselling interview, is the vehicle through which counselling is done, so it is the most defensible answer. An aptitude test is only one tool of the appraisal service, the cumulative record is that service's main record, and the case study is the most comprehensive technique; if "counselling" is offered, choose it. When a counsellor repeats what the client says, but uses words that are different than what the client used, the counsellor is using what skill? (RML 2021) (a) Paraphrasing (b) Questioning (c) Empathy (d) Nonverbal communication Answer: (a) Paraphrasing. A paraphrase restates the content of what the client said in the counsellor's own, different words, usually more briefly, without adding an interpretation, a question or a feeling; repeating the client's exact words would be parroting. Questioning asks for information, empathy is the broader capacity whose main vehicle is reflection of feeling, and nonverbal communication is posture, eye contact and tone (SOLER). Paraphrase is content, reflection is feeling, summary is many statements drawn together. Which branch of psychology is concerned with optimising human behaviour in workplaces? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Counselling psychology (b) Industrial-organizational psychology (c) Forensic psychology (d) Developmental psychology Answer: (b) Industrial-organisational psychology. It applies psychology to the workplace, from job analysis, selection, training and ergonomics on its industrial side to motivation, leadership and teams on its organisational side, and Hugo Münsterberg is usually taken as its founder. Counselling psychology helps individuals with problems of living, at work through employee assistance programmes, but does not study the organisation; forensic psychology applies psychology to the law; developmental psychology studies change across the life span. The qualities of successful rehabilitation programs to treat offenders include (RML 2020) (a) Cognitive interviews (b) Offender profiling (c) Being community-based (d) Focus on relationship with parents Answer: (c) Being community-based. Programmes that reduce reoffending are community-based where possible, cognitive-behavioural and skills-based, target criminogenic needs and concentrate on higher-risk offenders, as Andrews and Bonta's risk-need-responsivity model requires. The cognitive interview (Fisher and Geiselman) and offender profiling are investigative tools for solving crimes, not treatments, and family problems are only one of the central eight risk factors, so a focus on the relationship with parents is not a defining quality. How does Indian psychology differ from Western psychology? (RML 2025) (a) It solely relies on ancient texts without modern relevance (b) Western psychology focuses entirely on spirituality and community (c) Indian psychology emphasizes holistic and spiritual approaches including community dynamics (d) Both emphasize individualism equally Answer: (c). Indian psychology draws on Indian philosophical and spiritual traditions (the Upanishads, Samkhya, yoga, Buddhism) and is holistic, consciousness-centred and spiritual, with a self embedded in family and community, as the Pondicherry Manifesto of 2002 argued. It seeks to test and apply its ancient sources rather than rely on them alone, option (b) reverses the contrast, and mainstream Western psychology is the more individual-centred of the two. negatives to judge a diagnosis. 1.7 The DSM from DSM-I to DSM-5-TR, and the Multiaxial System : trace the DSM edition by edition and say what each changed and why, record a diagnosis on the five DSM-IV-TR axes, and explain why DSM-5 abolished them. 1.8 Inside DSM-5-TR: Sections, Specifiers, Conditions for Further Study and Z Codes : find your way around DSM-5-TR's three sections and twenty Chapter 6 groupings with their codes, list what changed between them, and compare the ICD with the DSM. 1.10 Culture and Diagnosis: Culture-Bound Syndromes and Cultural Concepts of Distress : explain how culture shapes distress, trace the move from culture-bound syndromes to cultural concepts of distress, use the Cultural Formulation Interview, and identify the main cultural syndromes, especially those of India, by region and core feature. Weightage. 30 of the 411 questions mapped in this book (7.3%) test this chapter, 18 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 10 sections is High yield. In the last days of October 1967 a strange fear spread through Singapore. Swine fever, a disease of pigs, had broken out on the island's farms that July, and the government had vaccinated the herds. Now a rumour was passing from mouth to mouth: eating pork from a pig that had been given the injection could make a man's penis shrink. On 29 October the newspapers reported the fear, and within days men began to arrive at the emergency departments of the city's hospitals in a state of terror. Most of them were ethnic Chinese. Each was sure that his penis was retracting into his abdomen, and that when it had disappeared completely he would die. Many came holding on to it with their fingers; others had tied it with string or rubber bands, or gripped it with clamps, clothes pegs or chopsticks, so that it could not slip away. At the height of the panic, in the first week of November, a single hospital was receiving dozens of these men a day. The first official reassurance did not help. On 3 November the Ministry of National Development announced that pork from the government abattoir was perfectly safe and told the public to ignore the rumours. It did nothing to calm the city (some accounts say it made the panic worse), and pork sales, already low, collapsed as families and diners refused to buy the meat. The next day the Singapore Medical Association, through a panel of doctors led by the physician Gwee Ah Leng, declared that neither swine fever nor the vaccine nor the meat of vaccinated pigs could harm anyone, and at a televised press conference it told the city that the cause was fear and rumour. Over the following days the Ministry of Health repeated the message in the newspapers and on television. The effect was swift. At Singapore General Hospital the number of cases seen in a day fell from 38 on 5 November to 17 two days later, and within a month the epidemic was over and pork was back on the table. Gwee's team, who published their survey in 1969 under the collective name of the Koro Study Team, counted more than 450 cases in the hospitals alone, almost all of them men. Nobody knows how many more went only to private doctors or to practitioners of Chinese medicine. The condition had a name and a history. The men called it suo yang (in Cantonese, shook yong ), the "shrinking of the yang", the male principle, and it is described in Chinese medical books of the Qing dynasty. Doctors knew it by a word from the Malay and Indonesian world, koro , whose origin is disputed. Nor was it confined to Chinese men. From late June to mid-September 1982, through the monsoon months, a koro epidemic swept through four districts of lower Assam. Psychiatrists at Gauhati Medical College, D. Dutta, H. R. Phookan and P. D. Das, studied 83 of the people affected. Most were men under 30 from Hindu Assamese families, but 19 were women. Here too, hearing about a case or seeing one was often enough to set off an attack, and here too the epidemic ended, with no deaths, after the public was reassured through the mass media. Stories like these force three questions on anyone who studies mental disorder, and this chapter is built around them. First, were these hundreds of frightened people mentally ill? Their belief was shared by their neighbours and printed in their newspapers, it made sense within their own medical tradition, and in almost every case the terror was gone within hours or a few days. If a disorder is something that has gone wrong inside a person, what exactly had gone wrong? Second, what caused it: a rumour, a culture's ideas about vital essences and the genitals, ordinary anxiety catching fire in a crowded city, or some vulnerability in the particular men and women who fell ill while their neighbours did not? Third, what should it be called, and who decides: a "culture-bound syndrome", an attack of anxiety, mass hysteria or, as DSM-5-TR now suggests, an example of an "other specified" obsessive-compulsive and related disorder? Section 1.1 takes up the first question, Section 1.3 the second and Section 1.10 the third. Remember the men of Singapore; you will return to them at the end of the chapter. 1.1 What Counts as Abnormal, and What Counts as Normal Medium yield · 4 Qs A physician who suspects diabetes sends a sample of blood to the laboratory and gets a number back. Even that number has to be interpreted: the level at which blood sugar counts as diabetic was fixed by expert committees weighing the risks of blindness, kidney failure and heart disease, and it has been revised more than once. A psychologist who suspects depression does not even have the number. There is no blood test for depression, no scan that confirms obsessive-compulsive disorder, no laboratory value that separates a worried mind from a disordered one. The line between normal and abnormal has to be drawn by people, using criteria they can defend in front of a patient, a family, a colleague and, sometimes, a court. This section sets out those criteria and puts them to work (1.1.2), examines the official definitions of a mental disorder that grew out of them (1.1.3), turns the question round to ask what "normal" itself means (1.1.4), and ends with the idea that normal and abnormal are two ends of a continuum (1.1.5). Why the question comes first Every chapter that follows describes disorders: what schizophrenia looks like from the inside, how a panic attack unfolds, how anorexia nervosa takes hold of a teenager. Each of those descriptions rests on a decision that has been made before the first symptom is listed, the decision that a particular pattern of experience and behaviour lies on the far side of a line. It is tempting to treat that decision as a technicality. It is not, because a great deal hangs on it. Where the line falls decides who is offered treatment and who is told to go home and rest. It decides who may be admitted to a psychiatric hospital without full consent under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, and who keeps the right to refuse (Book 2, Section 1.10.7). It decides who receives a disability certificate, with the concessions and reservations that come with it (Book 2, Section 9.9). And it decides who carries a label that may follow them into marriage negotiations, job interviews and insurance offices (Section 1.6.8). How, then, is the line drawn? Look closely at any serious attempt and you will find two kinds of judgement mixed together. One is a judgement of fact: is something inside the person failing to work as it should, a memory that no longer holds, a mood that no longer lifts, a perception that reports voices when nobody is speaking? The other is a judgement of value: does that failure harm the person or the people around them, and harm by whose standards? Medicine faces the same mixture. The blood-sugar line for diabetes rests on facts about damaged eyes and kidneys, but the decision about how much risk is too much is a value judgement. Psychopathology has the harder task, because it usually has no measurement to start from, and because harm is judged against what a family, a community and a culture expect of a person at a particular age and in a particular role. The men of Singapore in the chapter opening show how stubborn the mixture can be. The facts were not in doubt: their terror was real and their belief about their bodies was false. Whether those facts added up to a disorder depended on values, on what counts as an expectable reaction in a city where almost everyone had heard the rumour and many believed it. Keep that difficulty in mind through the rest of this section. (Two terms used throughout this book, psychopathology and abnormal psychology, are defined in Section 1.2.1.) The criteria of abnormality in brief Over the last century psychologists and psychiatrists have proposed a handful of criteria for drawing the line. Book 2, Sections 1.6.1 to 1.6.5, examines each of them at length, with its history and its classic failures. What follows is a compact reminder, because every later chapter of this book leans on these ideas, and then a worked application, because the criteria only make sense when you push real people through them. The statistical criterion equates abnormal with unusual. Behaviour is abnormal if it deviates from typical behavioural patterns, that is, if it is rare in the population. For anything that can be measured on a scale and that spreads out in the bell-shaped normal distribution, the criterion becomes a simple rule: choose a cut-off, often two standard deviations from the mean, and call everything beyond it abnormal (Book 2, Figure 1.9, draws the rule for intelligence). Its attractions are objectivity and simplicity. Its flaws are just as plain. It cannot tell admirable rarity from harmful rarity, so the perfect pitch of a gifted singer is as "abnormal" as a severe intellectual disability. It misses disorders that are common: depressive and anxiety disorders are among the most frequent conditions in every population that has been surveyed (Section 1.2.6), and being common makes them no less disabling. And its cut-off is arbitrary, a choice made by people rather than a boundary found in nature. The social-norm criterion calls behaviour abnormal when it violates a society's norms: its explicit norms, the laws and written rules, and its implicit norms, the unwritten expectations about how close to stand to a stranger, how loudly to speak in a temple and what to wear to a funeral. Its strength is that it judges behaviour in context. Its weakness is cultural relativity : norms differ from one community to the next and change from one decade to the next. Thirty years ago a man walking along a Mumbai pavement, laughing and arguing with nobody, would have drawn anxious looks; today passers-by assume he is wearing a wireless earphone. Worse, norms can be enforced in the name of medicine. The American physician Samuel Cartwright invented a disease called "drapetomania" in 1851 to explain why enslaved people ran away; Soviet psychiatrists diagnosed political dissidents with "sluggish schizophrenia"; and homosexuality stayed in the American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual until the association's board of trustees voted to remove it in December 1973 (Book 2, Section 1.6.2, tells these stories). Two further criteria look at consequences rather than appearances. On the maladaptiveness or dysfunction criterion, behaviour is abnormal when it interferes with the person's ability to manage daily life: to study or work, to look after themselves and to keep relationships going. On the personal distress criterion, behaviour is abnormal when it causes the person suffering: anxiety, sadness, guilt, mental pain. Both capture something important, and both fail in a revealing way. Some people who are plainly disordered are not distressed at all. A woman in a manic episode may feel better than she has ever felt while she spends her family's savings, and a man with a long record of cruelty and fraud may feel no remorse whatever; the people around them do the suffering. In the other direction, distress is often perfectly healthy. Grief after a death, fear before a viva and anger at an injustice all hurt, and none of them is a disorder (Book 2, Section 1.6.3). Marie Jahoda (1907 to 2001) turned the whole problem upside down in 1958 by defining positive mental health instead, through six criteria (positive attitudes towards the self, growth and self-actualisation, integration of the personality, autonomy, accurate perception of reality, and environmental mastery), so that on her ideal mental health criterion abnormality is a falling short of that ideal, a bar so high that few people clear it (Book 2, Section 1.6.4). Because each criterion fails when used alone, textbooks combine them. The most widely taught combination is the four Ds of the American psychologist Ronald J. Comer . Deviance means thoughts, feelings and behaviour that differ markedly from a society's ideas of proper functioning, and it takes in both statistical rarity and the breaking of norms. Distress means that the experience is unpleasant and upsetting to the person. Dysfunction means that it interferes with the ability to conduct daily life in a constructive way. Danger means that it puts the person or others at risk. Many teachers add a fifth D, duration , because a pattern that persists is treated differently from a passing reaction, and you will find minimum durations written into most diagnostic criteria, from two weeks for a major depressive episode to six months for generalised anxiety disorder. Danger is the least common of the four. Most people with a mental disorder, including most people with a psychosis, are a danger to nobody, and the belief that they are violent is one of the oldest sources of stigma. The clinician must still ask about danger every time, because when it is present it decides what happens next (Book 2, Section 1.6.5). None of these criteria settles a case on its own. The way to see why is to watch them at work on three people. Aarti is 28 and works as a software engineer in Pune. She lives alone, and every night before bed she checks that the front door is locked, that the gas knob on the stove is turned off and that the geyser switch is down. She does not check once. She touches the lock and pulls the handle, walks away, comes back and checks again, and if she loses count she starts from the beginning. The routine takes about two hours. "I can see that the knob is off," she says, "but I do not feel that it is off." For two years she has slept about five hours a night, she now reaches the office an hour late on most days, and last month her manager gave her a written warning. She is ashamed and has told nobody. Her colleagues see a capable, slightly tired engineer. Sameer is 19 and lives in Kolkata. He is one of the strongest junior chess players in the country and spends eight or nine hours a day on chess: playing online, studying openings, replaying the games of the great masters in his head on the metro. His aunts complain that this is "not normal" for a boy of his age. Sameer is cheerful, has a close circle of friends from his chess club, passes his college examinations after some last-minute cramming, and cannot imagine a better life. Leela is 58 and lives in a village in Kerala. Twelve days ago her husband of 35 years died suddenly of a heart attack. Since then she has wept every day, eaten little, slept badly and dreamt of him almost every night. She has not left the house; relatives cook for her and sit with her, as her community expects them to during the days of mourning. When her daughter told the visiting doctor that her mother had said "I wish I had gone with him", the doctor asked Leela gently whether she had thought of ending her life. She looked shocked. "Never. Who would watch my grandchildren grow up?" Now run each of them through the four Ds. Aarti shows distress (shame, frustration, tears at two in the morning) and dysfunction (lost sleep, late arrival, a written warning). Danger is absent. Deviance is the interesting one. Nothing she does breaks a norm, since everybody checks a lock, and nobody sees her do it; only the amount is unusual, and only she knows the amount. A clinician does not need visible deviance to take her seriously, and if she sought help the question would be whether her checking meets the criteria for obsessive-compulsive disorder (Section 6.5). The lesson is that many serious disorders are private, invisible to the people who work beside the sufferer every day. Sameer is the reverse. He is deviant in the statistical sense, far out in the tail of any distribution of chess skill or hours of practice, but he shows no distress, no dysfunction and no danger. He is the statistical criterion's classic false alarm: rare talent, not disorder. His aunts' complaint is a judgement about norms, and a weak one, since devoting oneself to a demanding skill breaks no rule of their society. Leela shows intense distress, and perhaps dysfunction in the narrow sense that she has stopped her usual work. But her withdrawal is exactly what her community expects of a new widow. The roles she has dropped are the ones that custom suspends during mourning, and the role of mourner she fills completely. She is not deviant; if anything, it would be deviant for her not to grieve. The doctor was right to ask about suicide, and her answer settles that question: no danger. She is the textbook case of distress without disorder, the expectable response to a loss that the official definitions explicitly exclude (Section 1.1.3). If, many months from now, her longing were still so intense that she could not take up her life again, the question would change (Section 7.4.3 teaches prolonged grief disorder, and Section 5.2.4 the boundary between grief and depression). Figure 1.1 places the three of them on a map of the four Ds. Notice that the person who most needs help, Aarti, sits where two circles overlap, outside the circle of deviance altogether. A clinician who looked only for unusual or rule-breaking behaviour would never find her. No single criterion is enough on its own. In practice a criterion is often recognised from a single phrase rather than from a whole case, and several of the phrases sound alike. The distractors are all real features of disorder, which is what makes them tempting. "Experiencing intense anxiety" is a symptom and belongs to distress; "loss of contact with reality" describes psychosis, and was once the everyday and legal meaning of "insanity"; "withdrawal and depression" are symptoms. None of them says anything about rarity. Exam trap The aspect of abnormality that "includes unhappiness" is distress : deviance is about being different from others, distress about the person's own suffering. When a stem speaks of "society's explicit and implicit norms", the answer is deviance , not dysfunction or distress. Deviance covers both kinds of difference, statistical rarity and norm-breaking, so a question about "the D that includes statistical and social abnormality" also wants deviance. The four Ds are deviance, distress, dysfunction and danger; "delusion", "disability", "diagnosis", "dependence" and "drug use" are invented Ds. If a fifth D is offered, it is duration. Clinical link Ask whose distress brought the person to the clinic. In Indian outpatient departments it is often the family's: parents bring a son who "talks too much and has stopped sleeping" and who insists that nothing is wrong with him. The four Ds explain why such a referral must be taken seriously even when the person denies any problem, since mania and psychosis can bring dysfunction and danger without personal distress. The opposite mistake is just as common. People like Aarti, whose disorder is private and shameful, may wait years before telling anyone, so a clinician who sees them for something else should ask directly about time-consuming habits, worries and rituals. What a mental disorder is: the official definitions The four Ds tell a clinician what to look for. They do not say what a mental disorder is. That question was taken up in the 1990s by a philosopher of psychiatry and by the committees that write the official manuals, and their answers now stand at the front of DSM-5-TR and ICD-11. The most influential analysis came from Jerome C. Wakefield , an American professor of social work and philosopher of psychiatry, in a 1992 paper in American Psychologist . A mental disorder, he argued, is a harmful dysfunction , and the two words do different jobs. Dysfunction is the factual part: some mental mechanism is failing to perform the function that evolution designed it to perform. Harmful is the value part: the failure must damage the person, judged by the standards of their culture. Both are needed. Leela's grief is harm without dysfunction, because the mechanism that makes us mourn is doing exactly what it evolved to do. On Wakefield's analysis Aarti shows both: the inner signal that tells a person a job is finished seems to fail her, and the failure costs her sleep and perhaps her job. Book 2, Section 1.6.6, sets out the account and its main weakness, which is that we rarely know for certain what any mental mechanism was designed to do. DSM-5-TR (2022) begins its discussion of key concepts with a definition that keeps the wording of DSM-5 (2013). In plain words, a mental disorder is a syndrome, a cluster of features that go together, marked by a clinically significant disturbance in a person's cognition, emotion regulation or behaviour that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological or developmental processes underlying mental functioning. Such disorders are usually, though not always, accompanied by significant distress or disability in social, occupational or other important activities. Two things are then excluded. An expectable or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss, such as the death of a loved one, is not a mental disorder. Nor is socially deviant behaviour, whether political, religious or sexual, or a conflict that lies mainly between the individual and society, unless the deviance or conflict results from a dysfunction in the individual. Read the definition again with Section 1.1.2 in mind and you can see where each piece came from: Wakefield's dysfunction, Comer's distress and dysfunction, and two exclusion clauses, one to keep ordinary grief out and one to stop the social-norm criterion being turned against rebels, believers and minorities. The paragraph that follows the definition in the manual is quoted far less often, and it matters just as much. It makes four points. First, a diagnosis should have clinical utility : it should help the clinician to predict the course, to plan treatment and to anticipate the outcome. A label that does none of these things is not worth giving. Second, a diagnosis is not the same as a need for treatment. Whether to treat is a separate decision, which weighs how severe the symptoms are, how salient they are (suicidal thoughts outweigh most other symptoms), how much mental pain and disability they cause, the risks and benefits of the treatments on offer, and other factors such as psychiatric symptoms that complicate a physical illness. Third, the logic runs the other way as well: a person whose symptoms fall short of the full criteria may still clearly need care, and the manual warns that missing symptoms should not be used as a reason to deny someone appropriate help. Fourth, the definition was written for clinical, public health and research purposes. A court deciding criminal responsibility, a board deciding disability compensation or a judge deciding competency needs more information than a diagnosis can supply (the manual's Cautionary Statement for Forensic Use is described in Section 1.8.1). The manual is also candid about the weak point in all of this. Under the heading of the clinical significance criterion it admits that, in the absence of clear biological markers or useful measures of severity for many disorders, it has not been possible to separate normal from pathological expressions of a symptom completely. Sadness, worry and suspicion all appear in diagnostic criteria, yet in their milder forms they are part of everyone's life. The manual's solution is a general requirement attached to most disorders, usually worded "the disturbance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning". It describes deciding whether this is met as an inherently difficult clinical judgement, and it advises that information from family members and other informants is often needed. In effect, the distress and dysfunction of the four Ds have been written into the criteria themselves. The World Health Organization's ICD-11, adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2019 and in effect from 1 January 2022, describes the conditions in its Chapter 6, "Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders", in almost the same terms. They are syndromes marked by a clinically significant disturbance in a person's cognition, emotional regulation or behaviour that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological or developmental processes that underlie mental and behavioural functioning, and they are usually associated with distress or impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning. The overlap with DSM-5-TR is no accident; the two organisations worked to bring their systems closer together (Section 1.9). Notice that ICD-11 names more areas of life in which impairment may show, including the family and education, and that it handles the border with normality disorder by disorder in its clinical guidelines rather than through exclusion clauses attached to the general definition. Textbooks condense the official wording into working definitions. The best known belongs to David H. Barlow and V. Mark Durand , whose textbook of abnormal psychology defines a psychological disorder by three components that must be present together: a psychological dysfunction , meaning a breakdown in cognitive, emotional or behavioural functioning; personal distress or impairment; and a response that is atypical or not culturally expected. Each component is insufficient alone. A dysfunction that causes no distress or impairment may be a harmless quirk; distress alone may be grief; and an atypical response may be talent or eccentricity, as Sameer's is. Apply the third component to the opening of this chapter and you see at once why koro is a hard case: in Singapore in November 1967, terror about pork and the genitals was, for a few weeks, exactly what a man in that city might be expected to feel. Indian law needs a definition for a different purpose: to decide when the state may limit a person's choices and when special protections apply. It therefore draws the line in a different place. Section 2(1)(s) of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 defines mental illness as "a substantial disorder of thinking, mood, perception, orientation or memory that grossly impairs judgment, behaviour, capacity to recognise reality or ability to meet the ordinary demands of life". The definition includes mental conditions associated with the abuse of alcohol and drugs, and it excludes mental retardation (the Act's term), which it describes as a condition of arrested or incomplete development of mind, specially characterised by subnormality of intelligence. Section 3(3) adds an Indian version of DSM's second exclusion clause: mental illness shall not be determined on the basis of a person's political, economic or social status, membership of a cultural, racial or religious group, or non-conformity with the moral, social, cultural, work or political values or religious beliefs prevailing in their community. The words "substantial" and "grossly" matter, because they set the legal bar well above the clinical one. Aarti has a condition that a clinician might well diagnose, yet it would be a stretch to call her checking a substantial disorder that grossly impairs her judgement or her capacity to recognise reality. The Act's definition is built for decisions about capacity, rights and admission, and its high threshold stops people being brought under those provisions lightly (Book 2, Section 1.10.3).
