Four ways of being normal: Offer and Sabshin Every definition so far is a definition of abnormality. Its mirror image is more awkward: what, exactly, is normal? It sounds as if the answer should be easy, the absence of abnormality, but two American psychiatrists showed in the 1960s that the word "normal" is used in at least four different senses, and that clinicians slide from one to another without noticing. Daniel Offer (1929 to 2013) spent his career studying ordinary teenagers, an unusual subject for a psychiatrist trained to treat illness. Melvin Sabshin (1925 to 2011) later served for almost a quarter of a century, from 1974 to 1997, as medical director of the American Psychiatric Association. Together they pointed out that psychiatrists are trained to recognise the abnormal and are therefore poorly equipped to recognise the normal: the training that sharpens one skill dulls the other. In Normality: Theoretical and Clinical Concepts of Mental Health (New York: Basic Books, 1966) they reviewed what the behavioural and social sciences had meant by normality and found four "functional perspectives", each with its own definition, which they argued complement one another. Normality as health is the traditional medical and psychiatric view. Behaviour is normal when no manifest psychopathology is present, when the person is free of grossly observable signs and symptoms. On this view normality covers most of human behaviour and abnormality is the small remainder, and health means a reasonable rather than an optimal level of functioning. Offer and Sabshin illustrated it with a simple definition from the psychiatric literature of their day: a healthy person is someone reasonably free of undue pain, discomfort and disability. It is the view of the general practitioner who examines you, finds nothing wrong and sends you home: you are "normal" because no disease has been found, not because you are flourishing. Normality as utopia is its opposite. Here normality is an ideal, a harmonious and optimal blending of the parts of the mental apparatus that culminates in optimal functioning. This is the sense psychoanalysts use when they describe the ideal person or the goal of a completed analysis, and Offer and Sabshin traced it to Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939), who wrote in his 1937 essay "Analysis terminable and interminable" that a normal ego, like normality in general, is "an ideal fiction". The same ideal appears among therapists of quite different schools, Carl Rogers (1902 to 1987) among them, and Jahoda's positive mental health and Abraham Maslow 's (1908 to 1970) self-actualising person are its close cousins. Its weaknesses are that few people ever reach it and that the ideal itself shifts with the culture and the century: the self-reliant individualist admired in one society is the selfish son in another. Normality as average borrows the mathematics of the bell-shaped curve. The middle range is normal and both extremes are deviant, so the unusually well-adjusted person is as far from normal as the unusually disturbed one. This is the logic of the statistical criterion of Section 1.1.2, and it is the perspective behind every test norm, an IQ of 100 or a personality score near the mean. Offer used it in the study for which he is best remembered. Key study: Offer's modal adolescents (from the early 1960s) In the mid-twentieth century it was widely believed, especially among psychoanalysts, that turmoil is a normal and even necessary part of adolescence. Offer wanted to know what typical teenagers were actually like. He gave a specially constructed Self-Image Questionnaire to the boys entering two high schools in middle-class suburbs of Chicago, and selected as "modal" those whose scores fell within one standard deviation of the mean on almost all of its scales. This was normality as average put into practice: the method deliberately removed both the disturbed teenager and the one who functioned at a superior level. The 73 modal boys were then interviewed and followed for eight years, through high school and beyond. They had almost no history of gross psychopathology, had mastered earlier developmental tasks without serious setbacks, coped reasonably well with anxiety, shame, guilt and anger, and related well both to friends and to adults. Some had experimented with minor delinquency in their early teens and then left it behind. What the researchers did not find was serious "adolescent turmoil". The study's limits are the limits of its perspective. It described only what was average in one group, middle-class suburban American boys of one era, and "average" is not the same as "healthy"; a definition that labels the superior teenager deviant has an obvious blind spot. But the project showed that normality could be studied rather than assumed, and it challenged the belief that storm and stress are an inevitable part of growing up. Normality as process insists that normality cannot be judged from a single snapshot. Normal behaviour is the end result of interacting systems that change over time, so change across time is part of the definition. Offer and Sabshin pointed to Erik Erikson 's (1902 to 1994) developmental stages and to general system theory as examples of this way of thinking, and as their example of process research they chose the work of Futterman, Hoffman and their colleagues at the University of Illinois, who followed parents of children with leukaemia from diagnosis onwards and asked how their ways of coping changed as the illness ran its course. The practical consequence is that the same behaviour can be normal at one age and abnormal at another. An imaginary friend at four, intense self-consciousness at fifteen and slower recall of names at seventy-five are all expected; none of them is expected at forty. Some later accounts of the scheme add a fifth view, normality as transactional systems, in which normality is defined within an ongoing relationship, between a parent and a child for instance, each partner helping to define what is normal for the other. Offer and Sabshin returned to the theme in an edited collection, The Diversity of Normal Behavior (1991). Figure 1.2 draws the four original perspectives. Health is the absence of manifest symptoms, a reasonable rather than an optimal state; utopia is an ideal that few people reach; average is the middle of the bell curve, with both tails deviant; process treats normality as something that changes across the life span, so the stepped line of what counts as normal shifts at each stage. Indian MPhil teaching and psychiatry notes often present a slightly different list, the "models of normality". Each model names a different yardstick. The subjective model uses the person's own experience: you are normal if you feel no distress, suffer no disability and seek no help. The medical or health model uses the clinician's examination: you are normal if no psychiatric disorder or psychopathology can be found. The ideal or utopian model uses an image of optimal functioning, the statistical model uses the average, and the social-norm model uses the standards of the community, so that you are normal if your behaviour is socially acceptable. Three of these map straight onto Offer and Sabshin (ideal onto utopia, statistical onto average, medical onto health), and the social-norm model is the criterion of Section 1.1.2 turned into a definition of normality. The subjective model is normality as health seen from the patient's side of the desk, close to that simple definition of the healthy person as reasonably free of pain, discomfort and disability. The two health models can disagree, and the disagreement matters clinically. A man in a manic episode feels wonderful and asks for no help, so on the subjective model he is normal; the clinician who finds a manic syndrome disagrees. A conscientious student who comes to the college counselling centre with ordinary examination nerves is seeking help, so on the subjective model she is not normal; a careful assessment finds no disorder at all. People who lack insight, and people who seek help readily, are exactly where a purely subjective yardstick goes wrong. Table 1.3 brings the views together. "Optimal functioning" is the ideal or utopian model; "absence of any psychiatric disorder or psychopathology" is the medical or health model, judged by the clinician; "socially acceptable behaviour" is the social-norm model. If a question asks instead for Offer and Sabshin's four perspectives, the answer is health, utopia, average and process; "subjective" and "social norm" are not among their four. Normal and abnormal as a continuum The criteria and definitions in this section can leave the impression that people fall into two boxes, the normal and the disordered. Most of the evidence points the other way. Almost every symptom in this book is continuous with ordinary experience. Everyone feels low after a setback, worries before an important event, wonders now and then whether colleagues are talking about them, and holds a belief or two that others find odd. Many people in the general population report experiences that resemble hallucinations, such as hearing their name called when nobody has spoken (Chapter 2 describes them). Barlow and Durand put the point plainly: most psychological disorders are "simply extreme expressions of otherwise normal emotions, behaviors, and cognitive processes". The Indian notes that many students learn from say the same thing in a single line: abnormality depends on the intensity and frequency of behaviour. What turns an ordinary experience into a symptom? Four things, which the criteria in later chapters measure again and again. Intensity : how strong is it? Frequency : how often does it come? Duration : how long has it lasted? Impairment : what has it cost? Worry becomes part of generalised anxiety disorder only when it is excessive, occurs on more days than not and has lasted at least six months. Low mood becomes part of a major depressive episode only when it, or a loss of interest and pleasure, has been present for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, together with other symptoms. Aarti's checking differs from yours or mine not in kind (we all check a lock now and then) but in amount and in cost. Figure 1.3 draws the idea. Each experience runs from left to right along the same scale, and the clinical significance criterion of Section 1.1.3 marks the point at which a clinician begins to speak of disorder. ordinary experience disorder Worry Low mood Suspicion Checking nerves before an examination sadness after a setback wariness of a stranger checking the lock once more worry most days for months weeks of low mood, joyless a fixed belief of persecution two hours of checking a night vertical line: threshold of clinical significance, distress or impairment What moves an experience to the right: intensity frequency duration impairment Figure 1.3 Normal and abnormal as one continuum. The same experience, from exam nerves to months of worry, lies on a single scale; there is no natural break, so the manuals place a threshold where intensity, frequency, duration and impairment make the experience clinically significant. Exactly where the threshold belongs is a live argument, and grief is its best-known battleground. DSM-IV told clinicians not to diagnose a major depressive episode in the first two months after a death unless certain severe features were present, a rule known as the bereavement exclusion. DSM-5 (2013) removed the exclusion and replaced it with explanatory notes to help clinicians tell grief from depression (Section 5.2.4), and DSM-5-TR (2022) went further by adding a new diagnosis, prolonged grief disorder, for grief that remains intense and disabling long after a loss (Section 7.4.3). Supporters saw both changes as recognising real suffering; critics saw a universal human experience being turned into a diagnosis. Normality also depends on who you are. It depends on developmental stage: a three-year-old's tantrum on the floor of a sweet shop is ordinary, and the same tantrum at twenty-three is not, which is Offer and Sabshin's normality as process at work. It depends on sex and gender, because societies expect different emotional displays from women and men; a man who weeps openly at his desk may be judged more harshly than a woman who does the same, and a clinician must not mistake a breach of a gender expectation for a symptom. And it depends on culture, which shapes not only what is expected of a person but how distress itself is felt and expressed, the subject of Section 1.10. The continuum has a danger built into it. If there is no natural break between ordinary unhappiness and disorder, then every revision of a manual can move the line, and critics argue that it usually moves in one direction. The most prominent of them is Allen Frances (born 1942), the psychiatrist who chaired the task force that produced DSM-IV. In Saving Normal (2013) he argued that DSM-5 would medicalise ordinary life, turning everyday grief, the overeating of a world full of tempting food and other common experiences into mental disorders, so that more people would be labelled and more would be given medicines they did not need; his name for the process was diagnostic inflation . The manuals' main defence is the clinical significance criterion: an experience counts as a symptom of disorder only when it causes clinically significant distress or impairment. Whether that defence holds depends on how carefully clinicians apply it, one patient at a time. Clinical link When a family asks "Is this normal?", four questions do most of the work: how intense is it, how often does it happen, how long has it lasted, and what has it cost? Add a fifth: what is expected of a person of this age, this gender and this community? Remember too the DSM-5-TR point from Section 1.1.3, that need for care and diagnosis are separate questions. Leela has no disorder, but a widow who lives alone may still benefit from a follow-up visit, from practical help and from someone who checks, in a few months, that her grief is easing. Exam trap The bereavement exclusion was removed in DSM-5 (2013) ; prolonged grief disorder was added in DSM-5-TR (2022) , not in DSM-5. The general definition of a mental disorder still excludes an expectable response to the death of a loved one. What changed is that bereavement no longer automatically rules out a diagnosis of major depression when the full criteria for it are met. Critics, labels and culture Some critics reject the enterprise itself rather than the position of the line. The psychiatrist Thomas Szasz (1920 to 2012) argued in The Myth of Mental Illness (1961) that, apart from demonstrable disease of the brain, mental illness is a metaphor for problems in living , and that medical labels disguise moral and social judgements. David L. Rosenhan 's 1973 study, in which people with no psychiatric history were admitted to psychiatric hospitals as pseudopatients and diagnosed with schizophrenia, was taken for decades as proof that a label changes what clinicians see; the journalist Susannah Cahalan 's The Great Pretender (2019) has since raised serious doubts about how the study was carried out. These critiques, and the labelling theory that grew up beside them, are told in full in Book 2, Sections 1.6.7 and 2.10.7, and are not retold here. This chapter returns to what a diagnostic label costs, and what it gives, in Section 1.6.8. Culture has run through every part of this section: whose norms, whose expectations of a woman or a man, whose idea of a proper response to a death. Section 1.10 takes it up directly, with the cultural concepts of distress, the Cultural Formulation Interview and the syndromes themselves. For now, carry one conclusion forward. Whether a person is disordered cannot be read off them the way a blood group can be typed; it is decided, and the decision blends evidence about what is failing with judgements about what matters. The rest of this chapter is about making that decision well: first by naming carefully what we see (Section 1.2), then by asking why it happens (Sections 1.3 to 1.5), and finally by sorting it into the categories of the DSM and the ICD (Sections 1.6 to 1.9). "The course is episodic, with full recovery between episodes in most cases." "The prognosis is guarded." "The 12-month prevalence is about 1 percent, and comorbidity with depression is the rule." Each of these sentences is packed with technical words, and each word has a precise meaning that examiners test directly. A student who half-knows them reads every later chapter through a fog. This section is therefore the glossary for the rest of the book. It defines the words that clinicians use to describe a disorder (what it looks like, how it starts, how it unfolds and how it ends) and the words that epidemiologists use to count it (how many people have it, how many new cases appear each year, and how often it comes in company with other disorders). Section 1.1 asked where the line between normal and abnormal should be drawn; this section gives you the language for describing what lies on the far side of the line. Describing, explaining, treating Start with the name of the field. The word psychopathology means the scientific study of mental disorders: their nature, their causes, how they develop and change over time, and how they can be treated. The word joins the Greek psyche (mind) and pathos (suffering) to logos (study), so it means, literally, the study of the mind's sufferings. Clinicians also use the word more loosely, for the abnormal experiences and behaviour themselves. When a report ends "no evidence of psychopathology", it means that the examiner found no symptoms, not that no science was done. The term abnormal psychology names the branch of psychology that studies abnormal behaviour and experience, and in practice the two terms overlap so much that most textbooks treat them as synonyms; the difference is one of flavour. "Abnormal psychology" is the name of the undergraduate course and of the textbooks that psychology departments use, while "psychopathology" is the word preferred in psychiatry and in clinical reports. Indian revision notes such as Psycho Didi's put the difference neatly: abnormality is atypicality in general, and psychopathology is its medical angle, with its concern for aetiology, diagnosis and prognosis. What does the science of psychopathology actually do? David H. Barlow and V. Mark Durand, whose Abnormal Psychology: An Integrative Approach is one of the most widely used textbooks in the field, divide the work into three tasks. The first is clinical description , which they define as the unique combination of behaviours, thoughts and feelings that make up a specific disorder. A good clinical description says what makes the disorder different from ordinary experience and from neighbouring disorders, and it also gathers the facts about who gets it, when it starts and how it runs. The second task is aetiology , the study of causes: why the disorder begins, at the biological, psychological and social levels (Section 1.3 is about the language of cause). The third is treatment and outcome: what helps, and what becomes of people with and without help. The three are linked. A treatment that works can hint at a cause, although, as Barlow and Durand warn, the hint can mislead: a headache that lifts after an aspirin was not caused by a shortage of aspirin. Description is the oldest of the three tasks and, in psychiatry, still the foundation of the others, because most mental disorders are still identified by what they look like rather than by what causes them. The careful, disciplined description of abnormal experiences, as the patient lives them, is called descriptive psychopathology , and its founding text is General Psychopathology (1913), by the German psychiatrist and philosopher Karl Jaspers (1883 to 1969). Jaspers taught clinicians to separate the form of an experience (is it a hallucination, a delusion, an obsession?) from its content (what the voice says, what the delusion is about), and Chapter 2 is built on his method. Two more words complete the picture. A nosology is a system for classifying diseases (the word also names the science of doing so), and nomenclature is the agreed set of names that a classification uses; DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 are both nosologies, and each provides a nomenclature (Book 2, Section 2.10.1 explains why clinicians classify at all, and Sections 1.6 to 1.9 of this chapter take the classifications apart). Symptom, sign, syndrome, disorder, disease Meet Pooja, who will help us through the rest of this section. She is 31, a mathematics teacher from Nagpur, married, with a son of six. Four months ago her husband was transferred to Pune, and she gave up her job to move with him into a flat in a city where she knows nobody. When she comes to the outpatient clinic, she says that for about two months she has felt "empty, as if someone switched off the lights inside". Nothing gives her pleasure, not even her son. She wakes at four every morning and cannot fall asleep again, she has no appetite, she is tired all day, she cannot follow the plot of a television serial, and she feels that she has become "a useless burden on everyone". Once or twice she has thought that it would not matter if she did not wake up, though she has made no plan. While she talks, the psychologist notices other things. Her speech is slow, with long pauses before each answer. She looks at the floor, her eyes fill with tears twice, and the clinic's scale shows that she weighs four kilograms less than at her last medical check-up. Pooja's first list is made of symptoms, and her second of signs. A symptom is a subjective experience that the person reports and that the clinician can know only by asking: low mood, loss of pleasure, early waking, guilt, poor concentration, thoughts of death. A sign is an objective feature that the clinician observes or measures: slowed speech, tearfulness, poor eye contact, loss of weight. Some features can be both, as when a man complains of shaking hands and the doctor also sees the tremor. Psychiatry leans more heavily on symptoms than the rest of medicine does, which is one reason the interview matters so much in this field. The difference has a practical edge: a symptom can be concealed or exaggerated, while a sign is open to anyone who looks. Signs and symptoms that tend to occur together and suggest a common underlying condition make up a syndrome , from the Greek for "running together". Pooja's low mood, loss of interest, sleep and appetite changes, fatigue, guilt, poor concentration and slowing hang together as the depressive syndrome, and the same cluster has been recognised for centuries. Whether the syndrome counts as a mental disorder depends on whether it meets the definition given in Section 1.1.3 (clinically significant disturbance, reflecting a dysfunction, usually with distress or impairment); Pooja's does, and she would be diagnosed with major depressive disorder, recurrent episode, for reasons that will become clear below. DSM chose the word "disorder" deliberately, because it makes no claim about cause. A disease , in strict medical usage, is a condition whose pathology and cause are known: general paresis, the dementia and paralysis caused by syphilis of the brain (Book 2, Section 1.3.6), Huntington's disease, caused by a single abnormal gene, or Alzheimer's disease, with its plaques and tangles. Most psychiatric conditions are not yet diseases in this sense. A third word, illness , is sometimes used for the person's own experience of being unwell. The psychiatrist and anthropologist Arthur Kleinman , writing with Leon Eisenberg and Byron Good in 1978 (Section 1.10.1 introduces all three), made the distinction famous: the doctor diagnoses and treats a disease, but the patient suffers an illness, which includes what the problem means to her, to her family and to her culture. Pooja's illness includes her conviction that she is failing as a wife and mother, and that meaning matters as much to her recovery as her sleep does. One more word explains why psychiatric diagnosis works the way it does. A sign is pathognomonic when it is found in one condition only, so that seeing it settles the diagnosis; the small white Koplik spots inside the cheek in measles are the textbook medical example. Psychiatry has almost no pathognomonic signs. Even the first-rank symptoms of the German psychiatrist Kurt Schneider (1887 to 1967), which were once treated as nearly decisive for schizophrenia, turned out to occur in mania and other psychoses too (Section 4.1.6). Because no single feature settles a psychiatric diagnosis, the diagnostic manuals define disorders by syndromes: a required number of features from a list, lasting a required time, causing a required degree of trouble. Chapter 2 adds two further distinctions that you will need there (primary versus secondary symptoms, and the form versus the content of a symptom). Exam trap A symptom is reported by the patient (subjective); a sign is observed by the clinician (objective). A syndrome is a cluster of signs and symptoms that go together; it says nothing about cause. A disease has a known pathology or cause, which is why the manuals speak of disorders . Pathognomonic means "diagnostic of one condition only", and options claiming that a psychiatric symptom is pathognomonic are almost always wrong. Onset The first thing a clinician wants to know about a new problem is how it began. The onset is the beginning of a disorder, described by when it happened and how fast it developed. Barlow and Durand give the two basic patterns. An acute onset is sudden: the person passes from well to clearly ill in hours or days. An insidious onset is gradual: the disorder creeps in over months or years, so that the family can often say only that "he slowly changed". Delirium is the model of an acute onset; DSM-5-TR states that it develops over a short period, usually hours to a few days. Brief psychotic disorder usually begins abruptly too; its ICD-10 counterpart, acute and transient psychotic disorder, requires an acute onset by definition, and when the episode follows events that would be markedly stressful to almost anyone, DSM-5-TR adds the specifier "with marked stressors", the condition once called brief reactive psychosis. At the other extreme, the neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease requires, as one of its criteria, an insidious onset and gradual progression, and DSM-5-TR says that most people with schizophrenia show a slow and gradual development of social withdrawal, emotional change and cognitive change before the first psychotic symptoms, although the onset may be abrupt. Pooja's depression sits in between, as many depressions do: it came on over about six weeks, which a clinician would call gradual but not insidious in the sense of the slow decline of years. Two refinements are worth knowing. First, some classifications put numbers on these words. ICD-10, for its group of acute and transient psychotic disorders, defines an acute onset as a change from a non-psychotic to a clearly psychotic state within two weeks or less, and records an abrupt onset, within 48 hours or less, separately (Section 4.5.1). Second, the word "acute" is also used for duration rather than onset, which can trap the unwary. DSM-5-TR specifies delirium as acute when it lasts a few hours or days and persistent when it lasts weeks or months, and it specifies hypersomnolence disorder as acute (less than one month), subacute (one to three months) or persistent (more than three months). Read the stem carefully to see whether "acute" is describing how the problem began or how long it has lasted. The age at onset is the second descriptor, and it differs greatly from disorder to disorder. Taking the figures in DSM-5-TR, specific phobias usually begin in childhood, with a mean age at onset of about 10; social anxiety disorder has a median onset of 13 in the United States; obsessive-compulsive disorder has a mean onset of 19.5; schizophrenia peaks in the early to mid-20s in men and the late 20s in women; and generalised anxiety disorder begins later than the other anxiety disorders, with a mean onset of 35 in North America. Taken together, mental disorders are mostly disorders of the young. In the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, a large American survey that you will meet in Section 1.2.6, half of all lifetime cases of mental disorder had begun by the age of 14 and three-quarters by the age of 24. That one finding explains why prevention and early intervention services aim at schools and colleges. Three related terms describe the period around the onset. The prodrome (from the Greek prodromos , running before) is the period of early, non-specific change that comes before the full syndrome: in schizophrenia, months of withdrawal, falling marks, neglect of hygiene and odd ideas before any voice is heard (Section 4.6.4 follows one young man through it). A person's premorbid functioning is how well the person managed at work, study and relationships before the illness, and premorbid personality is what the person was like before it; both are taken in the case history (Book 2, Section 2.3) and both carry prognostic weight, as Section 1.2.5 shows. Finally, a precipitating event is a stressor that comes shortly before the onset and appears to trigger it. Pooja's move to Pune, the loss of her job and her sudden isolation are candidate precipitants. Notice the word "appears": a stressor before an onset is not proof of cause, as Section 1.3.3 explains. Exam trap Insidious onset means gradual , developing slowly over months or years. It does not mean dangerous, sly, hidden or deliberately concealed, which is what the everyday word suggests. Acute onset means sudden. Watch for the second meaning of "acute": short duration, as in acute versus persistent delirium. The prodrome comes before the full disorder; the residual phase (Section 1.2.4) comes after it. Course Once a disorder has begun, it unfolds in a pattern over time, and that pattern is its course . Barlow and Durand describe three basic patterns. A chronic course is one in which the disorder tends to last a long time, sometimes a lifetime; much schizophrenia follows such a course. An episodic course is one in which the person is likely to recover within a few months, only to suffer a recurrence later, a pattern that may repeat throughout life; the mood disorders are the classic example. A time-limited course is one in which the disorder improves, even without treatment, in a relatively short period. Brief psychotic disorder is time-limited by definition: DSM-5-TR requires that an episode last at least one day but less than one month, with an eventual full return to the person's previous level of functioning. Adjustment disorder is another, because by definition it must resolve within six months of the end of the stressor or its consequences. Real disorders add some variations to Barlow's three. A waxing and waning course (also called fluctuating) is continuous but uneven: the disorder never fully lifts, yet it is better in some months and worse in others. DSM-5-TR uses these very words for generalised anxiety disorder, whose symptoms "tend to be chronic and wax and wane across the life span", and for untreated obsessive-compulsive disorder, whose course is usually chronic with waxing and waning symptoms (Sections 6.4 and 6.5). A progressive course , also called deteriorating, is one in which the person steadily gets worse; it is the course of the neurodegenerative neurocognitive disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease, while vascular neurocognitive disorder often declines in steps, each step following a fresh stroke. Two further words describe episodes. A single episode is the only one the person has had; a recurrent disorder has had two or more. DSM-5-TR codes major depressive disorder differently for a single episode and for a recurrent one, and Pooja's diagnosis is recurrent because she had an earlier episode at 22, after failing to win a government teaching post. That episode lasted about seven months and ended with a full recovery, after which she was well for nine years. Figure 1.4 draws the five commonest shapes on the same time scale. Look at the difference between the second and third panels: both are episodic, but in the third the person never quite returns to her old self between episodes. That leftover, below the level needed for a diagnosis but above normal, is called residual symptoms, and in schizophrenia the period after an active episode, when such symptoms linger, is called the residual phase (Section 4.6.4). Whether recovery between episodes is full or partial matters a great deal, because people with residual symptoms relapse sooner. Four more words describe what happens to an episode once treatment begins, and they are easy to muddle. A remission is a period in which the symptoms have fallen to a minimal level, so that the person is, for practical purposes, well again. A recovery is a remission that has lasted long enough (usually several months) for the episode to be considered over. A relapse is the return of the full syndrome during remission, before recovery, so it is the same episode coming back. A recurrence is a new episode after recovery. The distinction decides how long treatment continues, and Section 5.7.1 teaches all of these terms, with response, in the setting where they were defined, the treatment of depression. Course is not only a description. It was the main tool that the German psychiatrist Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926) used, at the end of the nineteenth century, to divide the psychoses into a deteriorating dementia praecox and an episodic manic-depressive insanity, and Section 1.6.2 tells how course became the basis of modern classification. DSM-5-TR still builds course into its diagnoses through specifiers: after a year of illness, for example, schizophrenia can be specified as first episode or multiple episodes, each currently in acute episode, in partial remission or in full remission, or as continuous (Section 4.4.2). Exam trap Barlow's three courses: chronic (lasts a long time, sometimes a lifetime: schizophrenia), episodic (recovery within months, then recurrence: the mood disorders) and time-limited (improves without treatment in a relatively short time). Do not confuse acute , which describes onset, with episodic , which describes course. Relapse is the same episode returning before recovery; recurrence is a new episode after recovery. A disorder that is better and worse but never gone is waxing and waning , not episodic. Prognosis and outcome Onset and course describe what has happened so far. The clinician's next question looks ahead. The prognosis is the anticipated course and likely outcome of a disorder: a forecast of whether, how fully and how soon the person will recover, and of how likely the disorder is to return or to become chronic. The word comes from the Greek for "knowing beforehand". Barlow and Durand give the two phrases you will hear on every ward: "the prognosis is good", meaning that the person will probably recover, and "the prognosis is guarded", meaning that the probable outcome does not look good. Clinicians also speak of a fair or poor prognosis. A prognosis can be stated for a disorder in general ("untreated obsessive-compulsive disorder has a poor prognosis") or for one person at one moment ("Pooja's prognosis for this episode is good"). The easiest way to keep prognosis apart from its neighbours is to think about time. The history of an illness looks backwards: it is the account, taken from the patient and the family, of how the problem began and developed up to today (Book 2, Section 2.3 teaches how to take it). The presenting symptoms are the complaints of the present moment, the reasons the person has come now. The diagnosis identifies and names the condition, and it is reached by applying diagnostic criteria , the rules a classification sets out for deciding whether a disorder is present. Aetiology asks what caused it. Only prognosis looks forward. In one sentence: history and aetiology deal with the past, the presenting symptoms and diagnosis with the present, and prognosis with the future. How can anyone forecast the future of a mental disorder? By studying large numbers of people over time and noting which features, present early, predict a better or worse course. Such features are called prognostic factors , and they should be kept apart from risk factors. A risk factor predicts who will develop a disorder in the first place; a prognostic factor predicts what will happen to someone who already has it. DSM-5-TR puts both under the single heading "Risk and Prognostic Factors" and adds a subsection on course modifiers, the factors that make the course worse or better. The best-studied set belongs to schizophrenia, and Section 4.6.7 teaches it in full. In outline, the outlook is better when the onset is acute rather than insidious, late rather than early, and follows a clear precipitating stressor; when the person functioned well before the illness; when mood symptoms and positive symptoms are prominent and negative symptoms are not; when the person is a woman, is married, and has relatives with mood disorder rather than schizophrenia; when the psychosis is treated quickly; and when the family atmosphere is calm and supportive. The logic is worth seeing. Good premorbid functioning means there is a life to return to, and an acute onset after a stress suggests an episode laid over a fairly intact brain, while an insidious, early onset with negative symptoms suggests a long-standing developmental problem. Now apply the idea to Pooja. In favour of a good outcome for this episode are her full recovery last time, her good functioning for nine years in between, an identifiable precipitant, no alcohol or drug use, a supportive husband, and the fact that she has come for help within weeks rather than years. Against her is the fact that this is her second episode: in major depressive disorder, every episode makes another more likely, so her long-term prognosis, the risk of further recurrences, is more guarded (Sections 5.5.6 and 5.7 explain why and what can be done). Her passing thoughts of death also belong in the prognosis, because the risk of suicide is part of any forecast in depression (Section 5.8). Prognoses differ widely across disorders. Brief psychotic disorder has a favourable outcome for most people, although DSM-5-TR notes that more than half later relapse. Adjustment disorder, by definition, resolves within six months of the end of its stressor. Untreated obsessive-compulsive disorder, by contrast, usually runs a chronic course, and DSM-5-TR cites a remission rate of only about 20 percent among adults re-examined 40 years later. Prognosis is the forecast; outcome is what actually happens. Researchers distinguish two kinds. A symptomatic remission means that the symptoms have gone or fallen to a minimal level. A functional recovery means that the person is back at work or study, in their relationships and in their ordinary roles. The two often part company. A man with schizophrenia may lose his voices on medication yet remain unable to hold a job because of the cognitive and negative symptoms that medication helps least, and a woman whose depression has lifted may take months to regain her old confidence at work. Service users have added a third meaning: personal recovery, living a satisfying and hopeful life with or without continuing symptoms. Clinical link Families nearly always ask, "Will she become normal again?" A good answer gives the forecast as odds, not destiny, and names the factors that can still be changed. For Pooja: "Most people recover from an episode like this one, as you did last time. Because this is the second episode, we will plan to keep treatment going after you are well, and we will agree on the early signs that should bring you back." For a young man after a first psychotic episode the modifiable factors are the ones in Section 4.6.7: taking treatment, avoiding cannabis, and a calm home. A prognosis delivered this way gives everyone a job to do. Exam trap "Which of the following best defines prognosis?" The answer is the likely outcome or course of the disorder , a forecast. The distractors each name something else: the history of the illness is the account of its past; the immediate symptoms are the presenting complaints; the diagnostic criteria are the rules for making the diagnosis. Also not prognosis: diagnosis (naming the condition) and aetiology (its cause). A prognostic factor predicts course in someone already ill; a risk factor predicts who becomes ill. How common? Prevalence, incidence and the burden of disorder So far the words have described a disorder in one person. The next set describes it in a population, and they belong to epidemiology , the study of how disorders are distributed in populations and of the factors that determine that distribution (the word comes from the Greek epi , upon, and demos , the people). Epidemiology asks two kinds of question. Descriptive questions ask how many people have a disorder, and who, where and when. Analytic questions ask why: which exposures raise or lower the risk. The answers matter to three different people. A health planner needs them to decide how many beds, clinics and psychologists a district needs. A researcher uses them to find causes, because a disorder that is commoner in one place, period or group may point to something operating there. And a patient's relative, asking "What are the chances that my son will get it too?", is asking an epidemiological question. The most basic count is prevalence : the proportion of a population that has the disorder. It counts existing cases, new and old together, and it is usually given as a percentage or as so many per 1,000. Because "has the disorder" needs a time frame, there are three kinds. The point prevalence is the proportion who have the disorder at a single point in time, such as the day of the survey. The period prevalence is the proportion who have it at any time during a stated period, and the period used most often is 12 months; DSM-5-TR says that its Prevalence sections most often give 12-month figures, although point prevalence is given for some disorders. The lifetime prevalence is the proportion who have had the disorder at any time in their lives up to the survey, including people who have long since recovered. Imagine a survey of 1,000 adults in which 30 are depressed on the day of the interview, 70 have been depressed at some time in the past year, and 160 have been depressed at some time in their lives. The point prevalence is 3 percent, the 12-month prevalence 7 percent and the lifetime prevalence 16 percent. Notice the built-in rule: in any one survey, lifetime prevalence can never be smaller than 12-month prevalence, and 12-month prevalence can never be smaller than point prevalence, because each count includes the one before it. Lifetime prevalence has a weakness. It depends on how old the people surveyed are, because a 20-year-old has lived through only a fraction of the years in which most disorders begin, and on memory, because people forget or play down episodes from long ago. Epidemiologists therefore also calculate the lifetime morbid risk : the projected proportion of people who will have developed the disorder by a given age, if they live that long, with an allowance made for the years of risk that the younger members of the sample have still to live. DSM-5-TR gives a lifetime morbid risk of 9.0 percent for generalised anxiety disorder in the United States. In the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, described below, the lifetime prevalence of any mental disorder was 46.4 percent, and the projected risk of having had one by the age of 75 was 50.8 percent. Prevalence counts the people who are ill. The incidence counts the people who become ill: the number of new cases arising in a population at risk during a stated period, usually expressed as a rate, such as so many new cases per 100,000 people per year. The words "at risk" matter. People who already have the disorder cannot become new cases, so they are left out of the denominator. The careful reviews of the Australian epidemiologist John McGrath and his colleagues put the median incidence of schizophrenia at about 15 new cases per 100,000 people per year (Section 4.6.1). Incidence is the figure a researcher wants when hunting for causes, because a change in incidence means that the forces that start the disorder have changed; prevalence is the figure a planner wants, because it says how many people need care now. How are the two related? The easiest way to see it is the bathtub in Figure 1.5. New cases flow in from the tap: that is incidence. The water in the tub is everyone who has the disorder at the moment: that is prevalence. Water leaves through two drains, recovery and death (and, in a district survey, people moving away). The level in the tub depends not only on how fast the tap runs but on how fast the drains empty it. When a population is in a steady state and the disorder is not too common, prevalence is roughly equal to incidence multiplied by the average duration of the disorder. A chronic disorder therefore has a high prevalence compared with its incidence, and a brief one has a low prevalence even if it strikes often. Tap: incidence new cases flow in each year Water level = prevalence everyone who has the disorder now Drain: recovery Drain: death A brief disorder drains fast, so the level stays low. A chronic disorder drains slowly, so the level stays high. Prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by average duration. Figure 1.5 The bathtub model of prevalence and incidence. The tap (incidence) adds new cases, the water level (prevalence) is all current cases, and the drains (recovery and death) remove them. A long-lasting disorder keeps the level high even when the tap runs slowly. Push a number through the tub. Take an imaginary district, Sundarpur, with one million adults. If schizophrenia arises there at about 15 new cases per 100,000 a year, the tap adds about 150 new cases each year. A systematic review of the world literature by Sukanta Saha , McGrath and their colleagues (2005) put the median point prevalence of schizophrenia at 4.6 per 1,000, which in Sundarpur means about 4,600 people living with the illness on any given day. Divide the level by the inflow and you get about 30 years: on average, a case of schizophrenia stays in the tub for decades, which is exactly what a chronic disorder means. Now imagine a different disorder with the same incidence that lasted, on average, one month. The same 150 cases a year would produce a point prevalence of only about 12 people. Same tap, different drains, a very different level. The tub also explains a paradox that puzzles students. A better treatment that keeps people with a chronic illness alive longer, without curing them, slows the death drain and so raises prevalence, even though nothing has got worse; a treatment that speeds recovery lowers it. Barlow and Durand list two more descriptors that every clinical description includes. The sex ratio is the proportion of cases in men and in women. DSM-5-TR reports that women have roughly twice the rate of major depressive disorder that men do, especially between menarche and menopause, and that women and girls are at least twice as likely as men and boys to have generalised anxiety disorder, while substance use disorders run the other way. The second descriptor, age at onset, was covered in Section 1.2.3. Epidemiologists also need words for the strength of a link between an exposure and a disorder. A risk factor is any characteristic or exposure associated with a higher probability of developing a disorder. Its strength is often expressed as the relative risk , the risk of the disorder in people who were exposed divided by the risk in people who were not. If 10 percent of people who lost a parent in childhood become depressed by 30, against 5 percent of everyone else, the relative risk is 2: the exposed group carries twice the risk. Case-control studies, which start from people who already have the disorder and look back at their exposures, report instead an odds ratio , which approximates the relative risk when the disorder is rare. The arithmetic of both belongs to the Research Methodology book. The point to hold on to here is that a risk factor is a statistical association, not necessarily a cause, and Section 1.3.3 explains why. Where do the famous figures come from? Three generations of large surveys, each made possible by structured interviews that trained lay interviewers could give to thousands of people in their homes (the interviews themselves belong to the Assessment book). The first was the American Epidemiologic Catchment Area study of the early 1980s, which interviewed about 20,000 adults at five sites in the United States and was reported in a 1991 book edited by Lee N. Robins and Darrel A. Regier . The second was the National Comorbidity Survey , the first to give a structured psychiatric interview to a national probability sample of Americans (aged 15 to 54). In 1994 Ronald C. Kessler and his colleagues reported that nearly 50 percent of the respondents had had at least one DSM-III-R disorder in their lifetime and close to 30 percent in the past year. The repeat survey, the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, interviewed 9,282 adults between 2001 and 2003; published in 2005, it put the lifetime prevalence of any DSM-IV disorder at 46.4 percent and the 12-month prevalence at 26.2 percent, with anxiety disorders the commonest group (28.8 percent lifetime). The third generation is the World Health Organization's World Mental Health Survey Initiative, which has given the same interview in many countries so that their rates can be compared. Indian context India's own count is the National Mental Health Survey 2015 to 2016 , carried out by NIMHANS in 12 states (Book 2, Section 1.10.11 describes how it was done). Excluding tobacco use disorder, it found that 10.6 percent of adults had a current mental disorder and 13.7 percent had had one at some time in their lives: current versus lifetime prevalence, the distinction this subsection has just taught. Its most sobering figure was the treatment gap , the proportion of affected people receiving no treatment, which ran from 70.4 percent for bipolar disorder to 86.3 percent for alcohol use disorder, and reached 91.8 percent for tobacco use (hence the survey's summary range of "70 to 92 percent"). Do not compare its lifetime figure directly with the American 46.4 percent: the surveys used different interviews, counted different disorders and asked about different spans of memory. Two last terms measure the weight that disorders place on a population rather than their numbers (Table 1.4 then collects every term of this subsection). The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) is one year of healthy life lost, counted by adding the years of life lost to early death to the years lived with disability. The years lived with disability (YLDs) count time spent in ill health, weighted by how severe the condition is. Because most mental disorders disable far more often than they kill directly, their burden lies mainly in the YLDs. In the Global Burden of Disease study's analysis for 2019, mental disorders accounted for 125.3 million DALYs and 14.6 percent of all the world's YLDs, and they remained among the ten leading causes of burden worldwide. The World Health Organization's World Mental Health Report of 2022 put the human scale plainly: in 2019 nearly a billion people, including 14 percent of the world's adolescents, were living with a mental disorder. Comorbidity Gaurav is 28 and works as an accountant for a firm in Hyderabad. His wife brought him to the clinic after he missed a second audit deadline. From about the age of 13 he dreaded being looked at: when he had to read aloud in class he blushed, his voice shook and his mind went blank, and he invented stomach aches to avoid school functions. In college he made a discovery. Two beers before a party made him, as he puts it, "normal for one evening". After he joined the firm he began to drink before client meetings and office celebrations, then most evenings at home, alone. He now needs far more than he used to for the same effect, his hands shake on Monday mornings, and his attempts to cut down have failed. For the past two months he has also felt hopeless and flat, and he wakes at three in the morning. The clinician's working list has three entries: social anxiety disorder, alcohol use disorder, and a depressive syndrome whose nature is still uncertain. If the low mood clears within about a month of stopping drinking, it was probably alcohol-induced; if it persists well beyond that, DSM-5-TR's guidance points to an independent depressive disorder (Chapter 10 explains the rule). Gaurav illustrates comorbidity : the co-occurrence of two or more differently defined disorders in the same person. The disorders may be present together now, which is concurrent comorbidity (Gaurav's social anxiety and his alcohol use disorder), or at different times over the person's life, which is lifetime comorbidity (his social anxiety began fifteen years before his drinking became a disorder). Comorbidity is about one person carrying more than one diagnosis; it has nothing to do with how common a disorder is in the population, and nothing to do with how much a person suffers. The word was coined not in psychiatry but in general medicine. In 1970 the American physician and epidemiologist Alvan R. Feinstein , in a paper in the Journal of Chronic Diseases on the classification of "co-morbidity" in chronic disease, defined it as any additional co-existing ailment in a patient with a particular index disease. His concern was statistical. A trial that compares two treatments for, say, diabetes will mislead if one group happens to have more heart disease than the other, because the extra illness alters the course, the choice of treatment and the outcome. Psychiatry took up the word in the 1980s and 1990s, once the manuals began to allow people to carry more than one diagnosis at a time (the hierarchy and exclusion rules that once prevented this are taught in Section 1.6.5), and it found that in mental disorders co-occurrence is not the exception but the rule. DSM-5-TR itself lists "high rates of comorbidity among disorders" first among the structural problems of a purely categorical system. Key study: the National Comorbidity Survey (Kessler and colleagues, 1994) The survey that gave comorbidity its public name was designed, as its title says, to study it. Kessler's team interviewed a national probability sample of Americans aged 15 to 54 with a structured diagnostic interview given by lay interviewers. Beyond the headline prevalence figures, the most striking finding concerned concentration. More than half of all the lifetime disorders found occurred in the 14 percent of the population who had a history of three or more disorders, and this highly comorbid group also included the vast majority of the people with severe disorders. Mental illness, in other words, was not spread thinly across the population; much of it was piled up in about one person in seven (the 14 percent). Even in this group, fewer than half had ever received specialist mental health treatment. The replication survey (2005) found the same pattern a decade later: of the people with a disorder in the past year, 55 percent had one diagnosis, 22 percent had two and 23 percent had three or more. Some pairings are so common that every chapter of this book will mention them. Depression goes with the anxiety disorders so often that some researchers wonder whether they are separate disorders at all (Section 6.1.7 gives the figures). Substance use disorders go with post-traumatic stress disorder, with depression, and with antisocial personality disorder. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder goes with oppositional and conduct problems in children. Eating disorders go with depression and anxiety. And mental disorders go with physical illness: depression is more common after a heart attack and in diabetes, and it worsens the outcome of both. Services in India, as elsewhere, use a special phrase for one of these pairings. The phrase dual diagnosis means a mental disorder together with a substance use disorder, and such patients have long tended to fall between two services, with psychiatric wards reluctant to manage their drinking and de-addiction centres reluctant to manage their psychosis or depression. Why do disorders keep company? There are at least five reasons, and in any one person several may be at work. Shared causes. The same genes can raise the risk of several disorders, a phenomenon called pleiotropy (Section 1.4.6), and the same temperament, especially neuroticism, the tendency to react to life with anxiety and low mood, predisposes to both anxiety and depression. One disorder leading to another. Gaurav drank to quieten his social fear. DSM-5-TR notes that social anxiety disorder usually begins before the disorders that accompany it, that people may use substances as self-medication for social fears, and that the isolation of social anxiety may in time lead to depression. The causal arrow can also run the other way, as when heavy drinking produces low mood. Overlapping criteria. Poor sleep, poor concentration, restlessness and fatigue appear in the criteria for major depressive disorder, generalised anxiety disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, so one set of complaints can count towards several diagnoses at once. An artefact of classification. If a single continuous problem, such as a general tendency to distress, is cut up into many narrow categories, one person will inevitably meet several of them. This is one argument for dimensional classification (Section 1.6.4). Referral bias. People with two disorders are more likely to seek or be sent for treatment than people with one, so clinic samples overstate how often disorders occur together. The American statistician Joseph Berkson showed in 1946, in a paper on the limits of analysing hospital data, that studying only hospital patients can create an apparent association between two conditions that does not exist in the general population. The distortion is now called Berkson's bias, and it is one reason why community surveys such as the National Comorbidity Survey were needed. Why does comorbidity matter? Because it changes almost everything about a case. People with comorbid disorders are usually more severely ill, more impaired and at higher risk of suicide than people with one disorder, and their prognosis is worse, exactly as Feinstein argued for physical illness. Treatment has to be planned for the combination: treating Gaurav's depression while ignoring his drinking, or his drinking while ignoring the social fear that drives it, is likely to fail, and integrated treatment of both is preferred. Research is affected too, since a trial that admits only "pure" cases studies people unlike most of those seen in clinics. A clinician who finds one disorder should therefore always ask about the commonest companions, and should take a time line, as Gaurav's clinician did, to see which disorder came first. Reading a disorder's description You now have the vocabulary, and the best way to see it at work is to open DSM-5-TR at any disorder. After the diagnostic criteria comes a text that describes the disorder under a fixed set of headings, and almost every word taught in this section has a heading of its own. Table 1.6 lists them in the manual's order with what each tells you. When a section has little information to give, the manual simply leaves it out, so not every disorder has every heading. The disorder chapters of this book follow roughly the same order: what the disorder looks like, how it is diagnosed, who develops it and what becomes of them, what causes it, how it is told apart from its neighbours, and how it is treated. Once the headings are familiar, a new disorder is no longer a page of unfamiliar facts but a set of answers to questions you already know how to ask. This section turns to the second of the field's three tasks, explaining it. Why did Pooja become depressed after moving to Pune when her husband, who made the same move, did not? Why did Gaurav's shyness become a disorder and then pull two more disorders in behind it? Every school of psychology has offered its own answer, and for most of the twentieth century the schools argued as rivals. The modern view is that each caught part of the truth, and that disorders arise from many causes acting together. This section first shows what that claim means in a single case, then recaps the classic models briefly (Book 2 teaches them one by one), then gives you the precise vocabulary of causation, and finally explains the two frameworks that tie the causes together, the diathesis-stress model and the biopsychosocial model. Together they are the scaffolding on which every "causes" section in Chapters 3 to 11 is built. One cause or many For most of history, explanations of abnormal behaviour have been one-dimensional. Barlow and Durand describe three great traditions, each of which looked for the cause: the supernatural tradition (demons, spirits, the stars, divine punishment), the biological tradition (a disease of the body or brain) and the psychological tradition (something gone wrong in the mind, in upbringing or in learning). They call any explanation that traces a disorder to a single cause a one-dimensional model , or linear model. A linear model might hold that a phobia or schizophrenia is caused by a chemical imbalance in the brain, or that it is caused by growing up surrounded by overwhelming family conflict. Such explanations are attractive because they are simple, and because a single cause suggests a single cure. They are almost always wrong. The alternative is a multidimensional integrative model , which treats the causes of a disorder as a system. A system has many inputs, but once an input becomes part of the system it can no longer be considered on its own, because every part affects every other part through feedback loops. Barlow and Durand call this way of thinking systemic: any single influence on a disorder, whether a gene, a belief or a family argument, has to be understood in the context of all the others, biological and behavioural, cognitive and emotional, social and cultural, and the person's stage of development. The best way to understand the idea is to watch it work. Irfan is 20, in the final year of a commerce degree at a college in Delhi. One afternoon in May, standing in a packed bus in the heat, he suddenly felt his heart pounding so hard that he thought it would burst. He could not breathe, his hands tingled, and he was certain he was dying, as his father's elder brother had died of a heart attack at 52 only four months earlier. He got off at the next stop and took an auto-rickshaw to a hospital. The electrocardiogram was normal. In the next three months he had five more attacks and two more normal electrocardiograms. He now checks his pulse many times a day, avoids buses and the metro, and has asked his mother to come with him to the college for his examinations. He has been drinking three or four cans of an energy drink a day to stay awake for revision. The diagnosis is panic disorder (Section 6.2). What caused it? Look at it strand by strand, as Figure 1.6 does. Biological influences. Irfan's mother is a lifelong worrier, and DSM-5-TR notes that the children of parents with anxiety and depressive disorders are at greater risk of panic disorder. He may have inherited a nervous system that sounds the alarm easily. The caffeine in his energy drinks, on top of the heat and the crush, pushed his heart rate up on the day of the first attack. Behavioural influences. The first attack happened on a bus, and buses now trigger fear by classical conditioning. His own racing heart has become a conditioned signal too, so that a flight of stairs can set off an attack. Every time he avoids a bus his anxiety falls, and that relief rewards the avoidance and keeps the fear alive. Emotional influences. Irfan now fears the fear itself. He lives in a state of anxious apprehension about the next attack, which keeps his body on alert and makes the next attack more likely. Cognitive influences. The key event in each attack is a thought: a racing heart is read as "I am having a heart attack". That catastrophic misinterpretation turns an ordinary bodily sensation into terror (Section 6.8.5 tells the cognitive theory of panic). Social and cultural influences. His uncle's sudden death made heart disease the obvious meaning of a pounding heart, and DSM-5-TR notes that most people with panic disorder report identifiable stressors, including illness or death in the family, in the months before their first attack. His family's alarm, the rushed trips to hospital and his mother's escort to college all confirm that he is in danger. The final-year examinations add strain. Developmental influences. The timing is typical. Panic disorder most often begins in early adulthood (DSM-5-TR gives a median age at onset of 20 to 24 in the United States), and Irfan's came at a point of transition, at the end of college and the start of adult responsibility. No single strand explains Irfan's disorder. His brother, with the same parents, uncle and bus routes, has no panic attacks. Thousands of people drink energy drinks without panicking, and many young men lose uncles to heart disease without developing a disorder. A pounding heart after a fast run means nothing at all to a cricketer, because he reads it as exertion. What made the disorder was the combination: a sensitive alarm, a frightening meaning, a conditioned cue, an emotional state of dread and a family that, out of love, kept confirming the danger. Notice also the feedback loops. Fear raises the heart rate, which confirms the catastrophic thought, which raises the fear; avoidance lowers anxiety today and raises it tomorrow. Once a loop like this is running, the original cause hardly matters, which is why treatment can work even when the cause is unknown. Multidimensional: causes interact Irfan, 20 panic disorder Biological Anxious temperament like his mother's; energy drinks Social and cultural Uncle's sudden death from a heart attack; exam strain Cognitive Racing heart read as "I am having a heart attack" Behavioural Attack on a crowded bus; now avoids buses and metro Emotional Fear of fear: dread of the next attack Developmental First attack at 19, in the final year of college Figure 1.6 A multidimensional account of Irfan's panic disorder. Each of the six influences acts on the disorder, and the disorder acts back on each of them (paired arrows). The influences also act on one another: the frightening thought feeds the dread, and the family's alarm feeds the avoidance. No box on its own explains the disorder. Remember A one-dimensional (linear) model traces a disorder to a single cause, such as "a chemical imbalance" or "family conflict". A multidimensional integrative model treats causes as a system with feedback, so that biological, behavioural, emotional, cognitive, social and cultural, and developmental influences can be understood only in relation to one another. The classic models at a glance Before the integrative view, each major school offered its own model of psychopathology: a set of assumptions about what goes wrong in a disorder and therefore what should be done about it. Each model is a lens that brings one level of the person into sharp focus and blurs the rest. Table 1.7 sets them side by side. Book 2, Sections 1.7.1 to 1.7.8 teach each one fully, with its history, its key concepts and its evidence; here the point is the comparison, because examination questions ask you to match a model to the cause it blames, and the wrong options are always the causes blamed by the other models. Read across a row and you can see why each mattered: each cause implied a treatment, and most of the treatments in Book 2 began as the practical arm of one of these models. The modern view keeps every one of the levels and stops treating them as rivals, which is where Sections 1.3.4 and 1.3.5 lead. Remember The therapies that grew from each model (psychoanalysis and its descendants, behaviour therapy, cognitive therapy, client-centred and existential therapy, family therapy) are taught in Book 2, Chapters 3 to 7. This book names the treatment and its evidence for each disorder and points there. Exam trap "Psychodynamic therapists believe that disorder stems from" emotional trauma experienced in childhood (unresolved, unconscious conflict from early life). The other options are other models' answers: disturbed thought patterns is the cognitive model; a failure to live up to one's full potential is the humanistic model; inappropriate learning patterns is the behavioural model. In the same way, a statement that disorders arise when "a biological predisposition is set off by a stressful situation" is not humanistic-existential, sociocultural or cognitive: it is the diathesis-stress model (Section 1.3.4). The language of cause Clinicians and researchers who argue about causes need precise words, and the words come mostly from medicine and philosophy. Aetiology , defined in Section 1.2.1, is the cause or set of causes of a disorder, and also the study of them. The most basic distinction is between three kinds of cause. A necessary cause must be present for the disorder to occur: without it, there is no disorder. The spirochaete Treponema pallidum is a necessary cause of general paresis, since nobody develops general paresis without syphilis (Book 2, Section 1.3.6). In psychiatry, exposure to a traumatic event is a necessary cause of post-traumatic stress disorder by definition, because the diagnosis cannot be made without one (Section 7.2). A sufficient cause guarantees the disorder: if it is present, the disorder follows. Sufficient causes are rare in psychiatry. One of the few clear examples is genetic: DSM-5-TR states that a repeat length of 40 or more in the huntingtin gene is invariably associated with Huntington's disease. Notice that the two ideas are independent. Syphilis is necessary for general paresis but not sufficient, because only a minority of people with untreated syphilis ever develop it; the Huntington's mutation is sufficient, given a long enough life. Most causes in psychiatry are neither. A contributory cause raises the probability of a disorder without being either necessary or sufficient. Childhood adversity is a contributory cause of depression: many people who suffered it never become depressed, and many depressed people never suffered it, yet it clearly increases the risk. Causes also differ in their distance from the outcome. A distal cause is remote, in time or in the chain of events: genes, a difficult birth, the loss of a parent in childhood. A proximal cause is close at hand, the immediate trigger: last month's humiliation, a week without sleep, the move to a strange city. Distal causes usually act through proximal ones. Pooja's mother's history of depression is part of the distal story; her lonely months in Pune are part of the proximal one. A warning belongs here, because it is the commonest error in reasoning about mental disorders. A risk factor, as Section 1.2.6 defined it, is a characteristic associated with a higher probability of developing a disorder, and an association is not yet a cause. There are three other ways the association can arise. The disorder may cause the supposed risk factor, which is reverse causation: schizophrenia is commoner in the poorest parts of cities partly because the illness itself pushes people down the social ladder (the social drift explanation of Book 2, Section 1.7.7). A third factor may cause both, which is confounding: if heavy cannabis users are also more often poor, traumatised or genetically vulnerable, those shared factors may explain part of the link between cannabis and psychosis, which is why researchers work so hard to control for them (Section 4.7.8). Or the association may be chance or an artefact of how the sample was chosen, like the referral bias of Section 1.2.7. A treatment effect can mislead in the same way. That a drug relieves a disorder does not show that the disorder was caused by a lack of that drug, any more than a headache is caused by a lack of aspirin. Clinicians who explain a particular person's problem use a related set of words, the four Ps of case formulation, which Book 2, Section 2.9.2 teaches as the 5 Ps (adding the presenting problem). The predisposing factors are the long-standing vulnerabilities that explain why this person was at risk; precipitating factors are the recent events that explain why the problem began now; perpetuating factors are the processes that keep it going; and protective factors are the strengths that reduce the risk or help recovery. DSM-5-TR uses the same four words in its own introduction, saying that diagnosis requires clinical training to recognise when the combination of predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors has produced a psychopathological condition. For Pooja: a family history of depression and a self-critical style (predisposing), the move and the loss of her job (precipitating), her isolation and her habit of lying in bed brooding (perpetuating), and a loving husband and a good recovery last time (protective). Causes also loop back on themselves. In reciprocal causation (bidirectional causation), the cause and the effect influence each other. Stress can cause depression, but depression can also cause stress. In 1991 the American psychologist Constance Hammen followed women with unipolar depression for a year and compared them with women who had bipolar disorder, chronic medical illness or no illness. The women with depression met more stressful events than the healthy women, significantly more interpersonal stress than everyone else, and tended to have more dependent events, the kind that a person's own behaviour helps to bring about (a quarrel, a broken friendship), as opposed to independent events such as a relative's death. Hammen called this stress generation : through their symptoms, behaviour and circumstances, depressed people create some of the stress that then keeps them depressed. Gaurav's drinking, which wrecked his audits and so gave him new reasons to drink, is the same kind of loop. Table 1.8 collects the whole vocabulary of causation. The last pair of terms comes from developmental psychopathology , the study of how disorders arise and change across the lifespan (the Developmental book has more). The term equifinality names the principle that many different pathways can lead to the same outcome. Barlow and Durand compare it to fever, which can have many causes. A delusional syndrome may be part of schizophrenia or the result of amphetamine use; delirium may follow surgery in an older person or come from thiamine deficiency or kidney disease. Depression may be reached through a loss, through hypothyroidism (Section 5.3.4) or through heavy genetic loading with very little stress at all. Its partner, multifinality , is the reverse principle: the same starting point can lead to many different outcomes. Children who suffer maltreatment may grow up to develop depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, a personality disorder or a substance use disorder, and some, the resilient ones of Section 1.3.6, develop no disorder at all. The two terms were set side by side in a short, much-cited paper by Dante Cicchetti and Fred A. Rogosch in Development and Psychopathology in 1996. Their practical message is humbling. Knowing someone's disorder does not tell you the path that led to it, and knowing someone's history does not tell you where it will lead. Table 1.8 The vocabulary of causation.
