Multifinality : one starting point, many outcomes. Do not swap them. The diathesis-stress model Return to Pooja and her husband. They made the same move, lost the same friends and faced the same strange city, and only Pooja became depressed. The single-cause models cannot explain that, but the most widely used framework in psychopathology can. The diathesis-stress model holds that a disorder develops when a predisposition is set off by a stressor. The diathesis (from the Greek for disposition or arrangement) is the vulnerability, which may be genetic, biological or psychological. The stress is the environmental event or circumstance that triggers it. Neither alone usually produces the disorder: a vulnerable person who meets little stress may never fall ill, and most people who meet hardship cope. The two also trade off, so that the more vulnerable a person is, the less stress it takes to tip them over. The model goes under other names, the stress-vulnerability model and the vulnerability-stress model , and they are the same idea. Its history belongs to schizophrenia research. In 1962 the American psychologist Paul Everett Meehl (1920 to 2003) proposed that what is inherited is not schizophrenia but a subtle neural defect he called schizotaxia, which becomes clinical schizophrenia only in some people, under adverse experience; and in 1977 Joseph Zubin (1900 to 1990) and Bonnie Spring recast the idea as a vulnerability model in which an episode occurs whenever stress exceeds a threshold set by the person's vulnerability. Book 2, Section 1.7.10 tells both stories and draws Zubin and Spring's threshold as its Figure 1.11, and Book 1, Section 11.9.8 introduces the model. Four further points turn this summary into a working tool. First, consider the range of things that can serve as a diathesis. A diathesis may be genetic, as in Pooja's family history (her mother was treated for depression after a miscarriage). It may be biological without being genetic: an obstetric complication or prenatal infection that disturbs brain development (Section 4.7.6), or an inborn temperament such as behavioural inhibition, the shy, easily alarmed style that Jerome Kagan (1929 to 2021) found in some infants (Section 6.7.2). It may be psychological: a dormant negative schema ("I am worthless unless I succeed"), a pessimistic attributional style that explains bad events as permanent and personal, or the anxiety sensitivity that made Irfan's heartbeat so frightening (Sections 5.6.4, 5.6.5 and 6.8.5). Pooja's lifelong belief that she must never fail is a diathesis of this kind. And it may be social. George W. Brown and Tirril Harris 's study of women in Camberwell, London (1978), found that a severe event was far more likely to lead to depression in women with certain vulnerability factors, such as having no confiding relationship or no employment outside the home (Section 5.6.8). Since the move, Pooja has no job, although she does have a confiding husband. Second, consider the range of things that count as stress. Acute life events are the most studied: a death, a separation, a job loss, a move, each of which Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe weighted on their Social Readjustment Rating Scale of 1967 (Book 1, Section 11.9.1). Chronic strain is the long-running difficulty, such as bad housing, a sick child or an alcoholic husband; Brown and Harris counted as major difficulties only problems that had lasted at least two years. Daily hassles are the small, repeated irritations of ordinary life (the crowded commute, the quarrelling neighbours), which Allen D. Kanner , Richard S. Lazarus (1922 to 2002) and their colleagues argued in 1981 predict psychological symptoms at least as well as major events. Trauma is the extreme end: events that threaten death, serious injury or sexual violence (Section 7.2). And not all stressors are unpleasant. In bipolar disorder, a promotion or a new romance, a goal-attainment event, can set off mania (Section 5.6.9). Third, the model comes in more than one version, and the difference matters to researchers. In an additive version the two simply add up, so that a large enough dose of either can push a person over the threshold: even someone with very little vulnerability may break down under an extreme stress, and a highly vulnerable person may need almost none. Zubin and Spring's picture, in which everyone has some degree of vulnerability and the two trade off along a threshold curve, works this way. In an interactive version stress has an effect only, or mainly, in people who carry the diathesis: for those without it, the risk barely rises however much stress they meet, while for those with it, the risk climbs steeply with each stressor. The famous gene-environment studies of the early 2000s were tests of an interactive model (Section 1.5.1). The American psychologists Scott M. Monroe and Anne D. Simons , reviewing the life-stress research in Psychological Bulletin in 1991, added two further cautions. Researchers must be precise about which kinds of stress are supposed to interact with which diatheses, and they must remember that the diathesis can itself shape the stress a person meets. A self-critical, irritable or impulsive person does not meet a random sample of life events. Hammen's stress generation (Section 1.3.3) and gene-environment correlation (Section 1.5.2) are two forms of this point. Fourth, the balance between diathesis and stress can change over a person's life. Clinicians have long noticed that first episodes of depression often follow a major blow, while later episodes need less and less provocation. The American psychiatrist Robert M. Post explained this in 1992 with the idea of kindling, borrowed from epilepsy research: each episode leaves a lasting trace that lowers the threshold for the next, a process also called stress sensitisation (Section 5.5.6). Pooja fits the pattern. Her first episode followed a severe disappointment, the loss of the government post she had worked for; her second has followed a stress that is real but smaller. In diathesis-stress terms, her first episode has become part of her diathesis. Finally, the model has a version at the level of genes. When a particular gene raises the risk of a disorder only in people exposed to a particular environment, the result is called gene-environment interaction, and it is the diathesis-stress model written in molecular terms (Book 2, Section 1.7.10 tells the Dunedin study of 2003 that made the idea famous, and Section 1.5.1 of this chapter teaches the concept and its troubled history). Two other names sometimes appear beside diathesis-stress in examination options. The neurodevelopmental model is a real but narrower theory, proposed for schizophrenia in 1987 by Daniel Weinberger and, separately, by Robin Murray and Shôn Lewis: that the disorder begins with a disturbance of early brain development that stays silent until adolescence (Sections 1.5.4 and 4.7.6). "Clinical-reductionist model" and "syndrome-sign model" are not established models at all; each borrows a real word (reductionism, syndrome, sign) to sound plausible (Book 2, Table 1.16). How does this book use the model? Each disorder chapter teaches the biological causes first and the psychological and social causes second, and then puts them together in a diathesis-stress form: the vulnerability-stress account of schizophrenia (Section 4.9.5), the integration of the causes of depression (Section 5.6.10), David Barlow's triple vulnerability theory of anxiety (Section 6.8.11), and the before, during and after risk factors for post-traumatic stress disorder (Section 7.3.4). Table 1.9 gives a preview. Notice that even the most heritable disorders have stressors in the table. Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder carry the heaviest genetic loading in psychiatry, yet life events, sleep loss, cannabis and a critical family still time their episodes; Section 1.5.6 takes up a past-paper question built on the opposite claim. The answer every time is the diathesis-stress model . Every wrong option names a single factor: genetic factors only, environmental factors only, neurobiological abnormalities only, purely biological causes, learned experiences alone, stress alone regardless of constitution, genetics alone, unconscious conflicts only, supernatural influences. The neurodevelopmental model is real but is a narrower theory of how schizophrenia begins; "clinical-reductionist" and "syndrome-sign" are not models. The diathesis is the vulnerability and the stress is the trigger, not the reverse, and the diathesis need not be genetic. The biopsychosocial model The diathesis-stress model says how causes combine. A broader framework says which kinds of cause a clinician must look for. In 1977 the American internist and psychiatrist George Libman Engel (1913 to 1999), of the University of Rochester, published in Science a paper titled "The need for a new medical model: A challenge for biomedicine". The dominant biomedical model, he argued, explains illness entirely through measurable biological variables, which makes it reductionist, and it separates the body from the mind, which makes it dualist. He proposed instead the biopsychosocial model : illness, physical or mental, always results from interacting biological, psychological and social factors, which form linked levels of one system, so that a change at any level spreads to the others. Book 2, Section 1.7.9 tells the story of the paper and of the patient Engel used to show what the biomedical model misses. What a clinician needs from this chapter is how the model is used. The model becomes a working tool when its three levels are crossed with the four Ps of Section 1.3.3, giving a grid of twelve questions: what are the biological predisposing factors, the psychological precipitants, the social perpetuating factors, and so on. Consider Bhavna. She is 19, from Nashik, a first-year arts student living in a college hostel in Mumbai. For six months, about three times a week, she has eaten very large amounts of food in secret (a packet of biscuits, two plates of leftover rice, a bag of chips, all within an hour) with a feeling that she cannot stop, and then made herself vomit. Between binges she skips breakfast and lunch. Her weight is in the healthy range, but she weighs herself several times a day and feels that her worth depends on the number. Her roommate found her vomiting and brought her to the college counsellor. The diagnosis is bulimia nervosa (Chapter 8). Table 1.10 is her formulation grid. It stops the clinician from missing a level: a counsellor focused on Bhavna's self-esteem might forget to check her potassium, and a physician focused on her potassium might never ask about the teasing or the aunt's remark (in much of India "you have become healthy" is a polite way of saying "you have put on weight", which is exactly how Bhavna heard it). It also shows how the levels interact. Dieting is a behaviour with a social origin, but the hunger it produces is biological, and the binge that hunger drives produces the shame that drives the next diet. DSM-5-TR notes that binge eating frequently begins during or after a diet, and Bhavna's did. Finally, it points to treatment, because perpetuating and protective factors are the ones that can still be changed: regular meals to break the cycle of fasting and bingeing, a medical check, cognitive behaviour therapy aimed at the eating disorder (Book 2, Chapter 5; Chapter 8 gives the evidence), and the help of her roommate and her parents. The biopsychosocial model has become the official philosophy of modern psychiatry and clinical psychology, and it has its critics. The psychiatrist S. Nassir Ghaemi argued in The Rise and Fall of the Biopsychosocial Model (2010) that it is so broad that it predicts nothing: it tells the clinician to consider everything but gives no rule for deciding which level matters most in a given case, and so it can be used to justify almost any treatment. That criticism points to the right relationship between the two models of this section. The biopsychosocial model is a framework, a reminder of what must not be left out. The diathesis-stress model is a more specific mechanism that operates inside the framework, saying how a vulnerability at one level and a trigger at another combine to produce a disorder. Exam trap The biopsychosocial model is George L. Engel's , published in Science in 1977 as an alternative to the biomedical model. The distractors are all famous for something else: Emil Kraepelin classified the psychoses by their course, separating dementia praecox from manic-depressive insanity (Section 1.6.2); Aaron T. Beck built the cognitive model and the cognitive triad of depression (Book 2, Section 5.3); Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) coined the word schizophrenia (Section 4.1.4). Do not confuse the biopsychosocial model (which levels) with the diathesis-stress model (how vulnerability and trigger combine). Vulnerability, resilience and protective factors The diathesis-stress model has a gap. Two people with the same vulnerability may meet the same stress and still end up differently, and the difference lies in a third ingredient. Protective factors , introduced with the four Ps in Section 1.3.3, are characteristics of the person or the environment that lower the probability of a disorder in someone who is at risk; they are not merely the absence of risk, but something that works against it. In 1984 Keith H. Nuechterlein and Michael E. Dawson built them into a vulnerability-stress model of schizophrenic episodes, alongside personal vulnerabilities and environmental stressors (Book 2, Section 1.7.11). Their partner concept is resilience , positive adaptation in spite of significant adversity. Its classic demonstration is the study that Emmy Werner (1929 to 2017) and Ruth Smith began on the Hawaiian island of Kauai, following every child born there in 1955 into adulthood: about one in three of the children at highest risk grew into competent, caring adults, protected by ordinary things such as an easy temperament, at least one stable relationship with a caring adult and a sense of purpose. Ann Masten later summed up the field by calling resilience "ordinary magic", and Jay Belsky and Michael Pluess 's differential susceptibility hypothesis added a twist: some of the traits counted as vulnerabilities are better seen as sensitivity to the environment, making the same child do worst in a harsh home and best in a kind one (Book 2, Section 1.7.11 tells all three stories). How genes help to choose the environments people meet, gene-environment correlation, is the subject of Section 1.5.2. Clinical link Put the four people of this section side by side and you have the clinician's whole task. For each, the predisposing factors (Pooja's family history, Gaurav's shyness since 13, Irfan's anxious temperament, Bhavna's perfectionism) explain but cannot be undone, and the precipitants are already in the past. Treatment acts on what keeps the disorder going and on what protects against it: Pooja's isolation and brooding, Gaurav's drinking, Irfan's avoidance and catastrophic thoughts, Bhavna's cycle of fasting and bingeing, and on the other side a husband, a wife, a mother and a roommate. Engel. 1.4 Genes and Mental Disorder: Family, Twin, Adoption and Molecular Studies Lower yield · 1 Q Rakesh is 29, an accounts officer in a cooperative bank in Kanpur, and he lives in the house his grandfather built: his parents, his father's two brothers, their wives and children and his grandmother, fourteen people and one kitchen. Three years ago his elder brother, then 31, stopped sleeping, talked without pause about a business scheme, spent two lakh rupees of the family's savings in a single week and was admitted to hospital in a manic state. The diagnosis was bipolar I disorder, and on lithium he has been well since. Now Rakesh's own marriage is being arranged, and over tea the young woman's father asked the question that is asked in every psychiatric outpatient department in India: "Is it hereditary?" Behind that polite question are three harder ones. Will Rakesh himself fall ill? Will his children? And when an illness does run through a family, is it the genes the family shares, or the house, the worries, the habits and the ways of reacting to trouble that it shares? This section explains how researchers answer those questions. It is a section about methods : how family, twin and adoption studies estimate how much genes matter, what the much-misread numbers called concordance and heritability really mean, and how molecular genetics hunts for the genes themselves. The findings for particular disorders are taught in their own chapters (schizophrenia in Section 4.7, the mood disorders in Section 5.5.1, the anxiety disorders and OCD in Section 6.7.1); here they appear as examples of the methods at work. Genes, genotype and phenotype Start with the vocabulary, because every later idea depends on it. Almost every cell in your body carries, in its nucleus, 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs, one member of each pair inherited from your mother and one from your father. A chromosome is a single, enormously long molecule of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) wound around supporting proteins. A gene is a stretch of that DNA that carries the instructions for building a particular protein (or for regulating other genes), and your complete set of genes, more than 20,000 of them, is your genome . Because chromosomes come in pairs, you carry two copies of most genes, and the copies need not be identical. The alternative versions of a gene are called alleles . A dominant gene is an allele that shows its effect even when only one copy is present; a recessive gene shows its effect only when both copies are of that kind. Brown eyes are dominant over blue: a child who inherits one "brown" allele and one "blue" allele has brown eyes, and blue eyes appear only when both alleles are "blue". When a trait depends on a single gene of this kind, the laws Gregor Mendel worked out with pea plants in the nineteenth century let you predict how many children of a given couple will show it. Two more words are needed. Your genotype is your genetic make-up: the particular alleles you carry. Your phenotype is what can be observed: your height, the colour of your eyes, your temperament, your blood pressure, and, if you develop one, a psychiatric disorder. The phenotype is never simply the genotype printed out. It is what the genotype produces in interaction with everything that happens to the person, from the womb onwards. Two people with the same genotype (identical twins) can have different phenotypes, and, as you will see, one twin may develop depression while the other does not. A handful of conditions with psychiatric features do follow Mendel's rules, and they are worth knowing because they show what a single-gene, or Mendelian , disorder looks like. Huntington's disease is caused by a single dominant gene on chromosome 4: every child of an affected parent has a 50 percent chance of inheriting it, and almost everyone who inherits it develops, usually in middle life, the characteristic movements, together with depression, irritability, sometimes psychosis, and finally dementia (Chapter 10). Phenylketonuria is recessive: a child must inherit the faulty allele from both parents, and without a special diet the result is intellectual disability (Chapter 3). Fragile X syndrome , carried on the X chromosome, is the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability (Chapter 3). In conditions like these, one gene of large effect is enough. The common psychiatric disorders are not like this at all. They are polygenic : influenced by many genes, each contributing only a tiny effect, all of which may in turn be influenced by the environment. DSM-5-TR puts it precisely for schizophrenia: "Liability is conferred by a spectrum of risk alleles, common and rare, with each allele contributing only a small fraction to the total population variance." For bipolar disorder it says that the mechanism of heritability "is not Mendelian" and involves multiple genes of small effect. There is no "schizophrenia gene" and no "depression gene", just as there is no single gene for height. This is why the question Rakesh's future father-in-law asked has no yes-or-no answer. But how can hundreds of tiny genetic nudges produce an illness that a person either has or does not have? The answer is the liability-threshold model , which the Scottish geneticist Douglas Scott Falconer (1913 to 2004) put into its standard quantitative form in 1965, building on earlier ideas of a "threshold" for congenital malformations. Imagine adding up, for each person, every influence that pushes towards a particular disorder: every risk allele, every complication at birth, every severe loss, every night without sleep. The total is the person's liability , and like height or blood pressure it varies continuously across the population, with most people in the middle and few at the extremes, in the shape of a bell curve. The disorder appears only in people whose liability passes a threshold . Now consider the first-degree relatives of someone who has the disorder. They share some of that person's risk alleles (and some of his environment), so their whole curve of liability is shifted towards the threshold, and a larger share of them lies beyond it. Figure 1.7 draws the idea. In the general population 1 percent cross the threshold; shift the relatives' curve by a little less than one standard deviation and about 8 percent of them cross it, which is roughly the risk DSM-5-TR gives for the first-degree relatives of a person with bipolar disorder (5 to 10 percent). The curve labelled "general population" shows how liability to a disorder is spread across everyone; the curve labelled "first-degree relatives" is the same curve for the relatives of an affected person, shifted towards the threshold because they share some of the risk. Only people beyond the threshold have the disorder: a thin tail of the population (1 percent, the small shaded area under the general-population curve) but a much larger share of relatives (about 8 percent, the whole shaded area under the relatives' curve). The height of each curve shows how many people have that level of liability. The figures are illustrative. The model explains four facts that would otherwise be puzzling. First, most people with a polygenic disorder have no affected parent: the risk alleles are individually common and are carried, in smaller doses, by many people who stay well, so two unaffected parents can pass on a heavy load. Second, risk falls smoothly, not in Mendelian steps, as the relationship becomes more distant, because more distant relatives share fewer of the alleles. Third, relatives of severely ill people, or of families with several affected members, are at higher risk than relatives of a single mild case, because such families carry more liability. Fourth, an identical twin of an affected person can stay well, because genes are only part of the liability. The American psychologist Irving Gottesman (1930 to 2016) and the British psychiatric geneticist James Shields (1918 to 1978) applied the model to schizophrenia in 1967 (Section 4.7.2), and it is now the standard way of thinking about almost every disorder in this book. How, then, do researchers find out how much of the liability comes from genes, and which genes they are? The psychiatric geneticist Kenneth S. Kendler described the field in 2005 as a sequence of four research strategies, which Barlow and Durand use to organise their account (Table 1.11). The first two use statistics on relatives and need no DNA at all; the last two work with DNA itself. The rest of this section follows the table from top to bottom. (Book 1, Section 9.7, applies the same family, twin and adoption designs to intelligence.) Huntington's disease (dominant), phenylketonuria (recessive) and fragile X syndrome (X-linked) are single-gene conditions; schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression are polygenic , with no single causal gene. In the liability-threshold model it is liability that is continuous; the disorder appears only beyond the threshold. Family studies The oldest and simplest question is whether a disorder runs in families. A family study begins with an affected person, called the proband (or index case), and counts how often the disorder appears among his relatives, compared with the relatives of unaffected control probands or with the rate in the general population. Relatives are grouped by how many genes they share with the proband on average. First-degree relatives (parents, brothers and sisters, and children) share about half. Second-degree relatives (grandparents, grandchildren, uncles and aunts, nephews and nieces, and half-siblings) share about a quarter. Third-degree relatives such as first cousins share about an eighth. If genes matter, the disorder should be commonest in first-degree relatives, less common in second-degree relatives, and less common again, though still above the population rate, in more distant ones. The tendency of a disorder to cluster in families is called familial aggregation . Counting is harder than it sounds. A 20-year-old brother who is well today may fall ill at 30, so a raw count of affected relatives underestimates their lifetime risk. Researchers therefore calculate the morbid risk : the proportion of relatives expected to develop the disorder if they all lived through the whole age of risk, with younger relatives counted as only part of a person according to how much of the risk period they have already passed. They must also decide how to find out who is ill. In the family study method every available relative is interviewed directly, ideally by an interviewer who does not know whether that person is related to a patient or to a control. In the cheaper family history method the proband, or one well-informed relative, is asked about everyone else. The family history method misses a good deal, especially milder illness and illness that families keep quiet about, so it underestimates familial rates. The results are clear for many disorders. Against a general-population risk of about 1 percent, the first-degree relatives of a person with bipolar disorder have a risk of 5 to 10 percent (DSM-5-TR). The first-degree relatives of a person with major depressive disorder have two to four times the general population's risk, and the relative risk is higher still when the proband's depression began early or keeps recurring. Alcohol use disorder is three to four times commoner in close relatives of affected people, and the rate climbs with the number of affected relatives, with closeness of relationship and with the severity of their problems. Barlow and Durand report that familial aggregation for blood-injection-injury phobia, the phobia in which people faint at the sight of blood or a needle, is as high as 60 percent: six in every ten first-degree relatives share the reaction to some degree, one of the highest rates for any psychological disorder. For schizophrenia, the pooled figures compiled by Irving Gottesman show risk rising steadily with genetic closeness, from 1 percent in the general population to about 9 percent in siblings and about 48 percent in identical twins (Section 4.7.1 gives the whole gradient). Return to Rakesh. As the brother of a man with bipolar I disorder he is a first-degree relative, and his lifetime risk of bipolar disorder is somewhere around 5 to 10 percent, against 1 percent in the population. That is a large relative increase, five to ten times the usual risk, but a modest absolute one: of every hundred men in his position, about ninety or more will never develop the illness. His future children would be second-degree relatives of his brother, with a smaller increase still. Notice that these are averages for people in his position; they say nothing certain about Rakesh himself, and he has already lived through some of the years in which bipolar disorder usually begins. Now notice the weakness of every family study. Rakesh's family shares far more than genes. Fourteen people share one kitchen, one television, one set of money worries, the same neighbourhood, the same water tank and the grandmother's firm ideas about how to react to illness. Barlow and Durand give the example of a mother who developed a strong reaction to blood after witnessing a serious accident as a girl; her children watch her turn pale and faint every time someone cuts a finger, learn the same reaction, and pass it on to their own children. Nothing genetic need be involved. Hepatitis A can run through a household that shares a contaminated water tank, and speaking Bhojpuri runs in families too; nobody calls either of them genetic. "Familial" means only that a disorder clusters in families. To separate genes from the shared household, researchers need families in which genes and environment come apart, and nature supplies two kinds: twins and adopted children. Exam trap Familial aggregation alone cannot separate genes from environment, because families share homes as well as genes. A family study begins from the proband . First-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) share about 50 percent of their genes; second-degree relatives (grandparents, uncles, aunts, nephews, nieces, half-siblings) about 25 percent. A relative risk of five to ten times can still mean that 90 percent or more of relatives stay well. Twin studies Meenal and Divya are identical twins, now 27, who grew up in the same two-room flat in Nashik, went to the same school, wore the same uniforms and were, as their mother likes to say, "never apart for a single night until college". Meenal teaches mathematics in a girls' school; Divya is a pharmacist. At 22, in the year after their father died, Meenal had a major depressive episode, and at 25 she had another. Divya grieved for her father too, but she has never been depressed. Here are two women with the same genes and, by any ordinary measure, the same upbringing, and only one of them has the disorder. Twin studies are built on pairs like this. Twins come in two kinds. Monozygotic (MZ) twins , identical twins, develop from a single fertilised egg that splits in two, so they carry virtually the same genes. Dizygotic (DZ) twins , fraternal twins, develop from two eggs fertilised by two sperm, so they share on average about half of the genes that vary between people, exactly as ordinary brothers and sisters do; they may be of the same sex or of different sexes. Both kinds share a womb, a birthday and usually a home. The logic of the twin method follows. If MZ pairs resemble each other in a trait more than DZ pairs do, the extra resemblance is attributed to their extra genetic similarity, because (the method assumes) their environments are equally similar. For a disorder, which a person either has or does not have, resemblance is measured as concordance : the rate at which both members of a twin pair have the disorder. A pair in which both are affected is concordant; a pair like Meenal and Divya, in which one is affected and the other is not, is discordant. There are two ways of calculating the rate. Pairwise concordance is the proportion of pairs, among all pairs with at least one affected twin, in which both twins are affected. Probandwise concordance is the proportion of affected twins whose co-twin is also affected, counting a pair twice when both twins were independently found by the researchers; it gives higher figures and is the one that can be compared with the risks of other relatives. Section 4.7.2 works through both with schizophrenia's numbers. The essential result is always the comparison: Kendler and his colleagues (1991) found, among more than 2,000 female twins they interviewed, that both twins had bulimia nervosa in 23 percent of MZ pairs but in only 9 percent of DZ pairs (Barlow and Durand's figures), so genes matter, but most MZ co-twins of women with bulimia did not have it. For traits that vary continuously, such as height or a score on a scale of anxiety, resemblance is measured as a correlation. The behaviour geneticist Robert Plomin pointed out that the correlation for height is about 0.90 between MZ twins and about 0.45 both between DZ twins and between other first-degree relatives. From two such correlations Falconer derived a simple estimate of heritability , the proportion of the variation in a trait within a population that is associated with genetic differences between its members. Falconer's formula doubles the difference between the MZ and DZ correlations: h 2 = 2 × (r MZ minus r DZ ). The reasoning is that MZ twins share all their varying genes and DZ twins half, so the difference between their correlations reflects half the genetic effect. Push the height figures through it: 2 × (0.90 minus 0.45) = 2 × 0.45 = 0.90. About 90 percent of the variation in height in such populations is associated with genetic variation, and about 10 percent with environment. (Book 1, Section 9.7.3, applies the same formula to IQ.) For disorders, which are yes-or-no, Falconer's 1965 paper also showed how to turn the rates of illness among relatives into a correlation in the underlying liability, so the same reasoning can be applied. Modern twin studies go one step further and divide all the variation in a trait into three parts, known by their initials as the ACE model . A is additive genetic influence , the summed effects of many genes. C is the shared environment (or common environment): everything that makes twins reared together alike, such as the family's income, the neighbourhood, the school and the parents' general style. E is the non-shared environment : everything that makes members of the same family different, such as different friends, a different teacher, an accident, an illness, a different position in the womb, and also, unavoidably, errors of measurement. The three parts can be estimated from MZ and DZ correlations. On the height figures, the shared environment comes out at about zero (C = 2 × 0.45 minus 0.90 = 0) and the non-shared environment at about 0.10 (E = 1 minus 0.90). A real psychiatric example shows the typical pattern. In a study of more than 31,000 Swedish twins published in 2006, Cynthia Bulik and her colleagues estimated the heritability of narrowly defined anorexia nervosa at 0.56, the shared environment at only 0.05 and the non-shared environment at 0.38. Again and again, for disorder after disorder, twin studies find substantial A, substantial E and little C. The experiences that matter most seem to be the ones that siblings do not share. That is the most surprising lesson twin research has taught psychiatry. The twin method rests on the equal environments assumption : that MZ twins are treated no more alike than DZ twins in ways that matter for the trait. Critics point out that identical twins are sometimes dressed alike and even given rhyming names, are more often mistaken for each other, and influence each other more than fraternal twins do, so part of their greater resemblance could be environmental. Meenal and Divya were dressed alike until the age of ten. Two answers have been developed. One is to study identical twins reared apart, who share genes but not homes (Book 1, Section 9.7.1, tells the Minnesota study). The other is to combine twin and adoption methods, which is the subject of the next subsection. Twins have also allowed one of the most elegant tests in psychiatric genetics. If an identical twin stays well while her co-twin develops schizophrenia, has she escaped the genes, or merely failed to express them? Gottesman and the Danish psychiatrist Aksel Bertelsen answered by following up the children of Danish twin pairs discordant for schizophrenia, a design built on the earlier work of Margit Fischer. In 1989 they reported that the children of the healthy identical co-twins had about the same risk of schizophrenia and related disorders as the children of the affected twins, about 17 percent in each group (Section 4.7.2 gives the figures). The healthy twin carried, and passed on, the same genetic liability; it simply had not been expressed in her. This is called the offspring-of-discordant-twins design, and its message is the message of the whole section: a genotype is a liability, not a destiny. Even identical twins are not perfectly identical. Barlow and Durand note that chemical markers on the DNA, called epigenetic markers, begin to differ between MZ twins even in the womb, which explains some of the subtle differences between them; how such marks work is taught in Section 1.5.3. Between that, the non-shared environment and chance, it is no surprise that MZ concordance for every psychiatric disorder ever studied is well below 100 percent. Exam trap Concordance is the rate at which both twins are affected; heritability is a population statistic estimated from the comparison of MZ and DZ resemblance. They are different numbers: schizophrenia's heritability is about 80 percent but its MZ concordance only about 33 to 48 percent. An MZ concordance below 100 percent is proof that something other than DNA sequence contributes. DZ twins share about half their varying genes, like ordinary siblings, not a quarter. In the ACE model, C is the environment twins share and E the environment that makes them different. Adoption studies Twin studies cannot escape the suspicion that identical twins share a more similar environment. Adoption breaks the link between genes and upbringing completely, because a child adopted in infancy receives genes from one family and rearing from another. Barlow and Durand give the simplest version. Suppose a young man has a disorder, and researchers discover that his brother was adopted as a baby and brought up in a different home. They examine the brother. If enough such pairs are found, and the adopted-away brothers have the disorder more often than chance would predict, genes are probably at work, since the brothers shared genes but not homes. Researchers have built four more systematic designs on this idea (Figure 1.8). The adoptee study (also called the adopted-away offspring design) starts from parents who have the disorder and follows up their children who were adopted away early in life, comparing them with control adoptees whose biological parents were well. The classic example is the study by the American psychiatrist Leonard Heston , published in 1966, of children born to mothers with schizophrenia in an Oregon state hospital and removed from them within days of birth: schizophrenia appeared among these children, raised by others, but not among the controls (Section 4.7.3 tells the study with its numbers). The same design has been used for alcohol: DSM-5-TR reports a three- to fourfold increase in the risk of alcohol use disorder in the children of affected parents, even when the children were given up for adoption at birth and raised by adoptive parents who did not have the disorder. The adoptees' family study works in the opposite direction. It starts from adoptees who have developed the disorder and examines both sets of their relatives: the biological relatives, who gave them their genes, and the adoptive relatives, who raised them. If genes matter, the disorder should be concentrated among the biological relatives. The definitive studies were done in Denmark, whose national registers of adoptions and psychiatric admissions made it possible to trace every adoptee and every relative, by the American team of Seymour Kety (1915 to 2000), David Rosenthal and Paul Wender , with the Danish psychiatrist Fini Schulsinger; the team began reporting in 1968. Schizophrenia and milder related conditions were concentrated among the biological relatives of adoptees with schizophrenia, while the adoptive relatives did not differ from those of controls (Section 4.7.3). The same design was used for bipolar disorder by Julien Mendlewicz and John Rainer, who reported in 1977 that mood disorders were far commoner among the biological parents of adoptees with bipolar disorder than among the parents who had raised them (Section 5.5.1). The cross-fostering design asks the most pointed question of all: what happens to a child with no genetic risk who is raised by an ill parent? Wender and his colleagues found, among Danish adoptees, children whose biological parents were well but one of whose adoptive parents later developed schizophrenia, and compared them with adoptees who had an ill biological parent and well adoptive parents. In their 1974 report, psychopathology was commoner among the adopted-away children of ill biological parents, but there was no such increase among the cross-fostered children. Being raised by a parent with schizophrenia did not, on its own, produce schizophrenia. The fourth design adds what the Danish studies left out, a direct look at the adoptive home. In the Finnish Adoptive Family Study of Schizophrenia, Pekka Tienari and his colleagues traced children of mothers with schizophrenia who had been adopted away and compared them with control adoptees, but they also visited and rated the functioning of every adoptive family. The children at high genetic risk did worst when they were placed in disturbed adoptive families and much better in healthy ones, while for children at low genetic risk the adoptive family made little difference. That result is not simply "genes" or "environment"; it is the two working together, and it is taught as gene-environment interaction in Section 1.5.1 (with the details in Section 4.7.3). 1. Adoption studies have their own weaknesses, and examiners like to ask about them. The first is selective placement : agencies often try to match a child to adoptive parents who resemble the biological parents in background or education, which partly reunites genes and environment. The second is the prenatal environment. An adopted child spent nine months in the biological mother's womb, sharing her nutrition, her stress hormones, her infections and perhaps her alcohol, all of which are environmental influences that an adoption study wrongly counts as genetic. The third is late adoption: a child who lived with the biological parent for months or years before placement has shared that parent's environment too. The fourth is that adoptive families are screened by agencies, so they are, on average, more stable and better off than other families; the range of rearing environments is narrowed, and the effect of environment is underestimated. Finally, the parents who give up children for adoption, and the children themselves, may differ from other people in ways that limit how far the results apply to everyone else. Such studies need national registers of adoptions and of hospital admissions, which is why almost all of them come from Scandinavia and the United States. Exam trap Match the design to its starting point. Adoptee study : start from ill biological parents and follow their adopted-away children (Heston, Oregon, 1966). Adoptees' family study : start from ill adoptees and compare biological with adoptive relatives (Kety, Rosenthal and Wender, Denmark, from 1968). Cross-fostering : children of healthy parents raised by an ill adoptive parent (Wender and colleagues, 1974: no increase). Tienari (Finland) rated the adoptive families and found gene-environment interaction. The main weaknesses are selective placement, the shared prenatal environment, late adoption and screened adoptive homes. Heritability: what the number means Family, twin and adoption studies come together in a single number, heritability, and Book 1, Section 9.7.3, explains carefully what it is and what it is not. In brief: heritability (h 2 ) is the proportion of the variation in a trait, within a particular population at a particular time, that is associated with genetic variation in that population. It describes differences among people, not the make-up of any one person. It is not fixed: it changes when the range of environments changes. And a highly heritable trait can still be changed by the environment, as height (which has risen over generations with better nutrition) and phenylketonuria (whose effects a diet prevents) both show. Hold those three points in mind, because every one of them is violated daily in conversations about mental illness. The first is that every disorder in the table is partly heritable, and none is wholly genetic. Even at the top, where bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, autism and ADHD carry heritabilities of 70 to 90 percent, the concordance of identical twins is far below 100 percent: DSM-5-TR itself says of bipolar disorder that monozygotic concordance of 40 to 70 percent indicates that "much risk is left unexplained by genes alone". The second is that a high heritability is perfectly compatible with a modest concordance. The two numbers measure different things: heritability is about the share of variation in liability that tracks genetic differences, while concordance is about how often a co-twin actually crosses the threshold. The third is that for the common disorders in the lower half of the table, depression, generalised anxiety and the phobias, more than half of the variation lies with the environment, and the twin studies say it is mostly the non-shared environment. The fourth is that heritability depends on exposure. Alcohol use disorder has a heritability of 40 to 60 percent, yet nobody develops it without drinking; in a community where nobody drank, its heritability could not even be estimated. Heritability is always a statement about a particular population living in a particular range of environments, which is also why figures from Scandinavian, American and Australian twin registers cannot simply be assumed to hold in Kanpur or Nashik. Whether these figures mean that some disorders are "caused by biology" and have "little to no" psychosocial cause, as one examination question claims for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, is taken up in Section 1.5.6, once gene-environment interplay has been explained. Clinical link When Rakesh asks "Will I get it?", the answer comes from empiric risk figures for relatives (about 5 to 10 percent for the sibling of a person with bipolar disorder), not from heritability. Telling a family that bipolar disorder is "90 percent genetic" invites them to hear "a 90 percent chance", which is false and frightening. Good genetic counselling gives the absolute risk, explains that most relatives never fall ill, describes the early warning signs (in bipolar disorder, reduced need for sleep and rising energy), and points to what is changeable: regular sleep, avoiding cannabis and other drugs, and early help. Exam trap A heritability of 80 percent does not mean that 80 percent of a person's illness comes from genes, nor an 80 percent chance of illness in a relative. Heritability belongs to a population, changes with the environment, and says nothing about whether a disorder can be treated. The most heritable disorders (bipolar disorder about 90 percent in some studies, schizophrenia about 80) still have MZ concordance far below 100 percent. Major depression is moderately heritable, about 40 percent. Finding the genes: linkage, association and genome-wide studies Family, twin and adoption studies can tell you that genes matter and roughly how much, but not which genes, or where they lie. Finding them needed new tools, and the first was genetic linkage analysis . Its principle is simple. Genes that lie close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, because the shuffling of chromosomes that happens when eggs and sperm are made rarely separates near neighbours. So researchers choose genetic markers , stretches of DNA whose position on a chromosome is already known and which vary between people, and trace them through a family with many affected members. If one version of a marker travels with the disorder, turning up in the affected members far more often than chance allows, a gene for the disorder probably lies near that marker. The strength of the evidence is expressed as a LOD score (the logarithm of the odds that the marker and the disorder are linked); a score of 3 or more, odds of a thousand to one in favour, is the traditional threshold. Linkage was a triumph for single-gene diseases: in 1983 the gene for Huntington's disease was located on chromosome 4 in this way, with the help of a huge Venezuelan family. For the psychiatric disorders, linkage produced one of the most instructive disappointments in the history of the field. In 1987 Janice A. Egeland and her colleagues reported in Nature on a large Old Order Amish family in Pennsylvania. The Amish suited the method perfectly: large families, careful genealogies, little migration, and little alcohol or drug use to blur diagnosis. Two markers at the tip of the short arm of chromosome 11, the gene for insulin and a known cancer gene, appeared to travel with bipolar disorder through the pedigree, and the authors concluded that a dominant gene conferring a strong predisposition to manic-depressive illness lay there. Two years later John Kelsoe and colleagues, including Egeland herself, re-analysed the family. Several new members had been added to the pedigree and the clinical status of two members had changed; with those changes, and with a larger extension of the pedigree, the linkage disappeared and could be excluded. Barlow and Durand draw the lesson: the failure to replicate casts doubt on any claim that a single gene is responsible for such complex disorders, so be wary the next time a newspaper reports that "the gene" for a disorder has been found. Linkage works well for genes of large effect, and the psychiatric disorders turned out not to have many. The second tool, the association study , is better at finding genes of small effect. Instead of following markers through families, it compares a large group of people with the disorder with a group without it: if a particular allele is significantly commoner among the cases, the allele, or a gene very close to it, is assumed to be involved. For two decades association studies were mostly candidate gene studies. Researchers chose a gene whose function seemed relevant (a dopamine receptor gene for schizophrenia, the serotonin transporter gene for depression, the gene for the enzyme that breaks down dopamine) and tested it in a few hundred people. Hundreds of positive findings were published, and almost none survived when much larger samples were examined. Section 1.5.1 tells the most famous case, the serotonin transporter gene in depression, and Section 4.7.4 the candidate genes of schizophrenia. The breakthrough was the genome-wide association study (GWAS) . The commonest form of genetic variation is the single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) , a single position in the DNA where people differ by one "letter" (one base). A GWAS measures hundreds of thousands to millions of SNPs spread across the entire genome in every participant, without any prior guess about which genes matter, and compares cases with controls at every one of them. Because so many comparisons are made, chance "hits" are inevitable, so a very strict criterion of genome-wide significance is used, conventionally a probability below 5 × 10 -8 (five in a hundred million), roughly the ordinary 0.05 divided by a million tests. Effects so small can be detected only in enormous samples, tens or hundreds of thousands of people, which no single research group can collect. Hence the international consortia, above all the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, whose schizophrenia analyses have identified hundreds of associated loci (Section 4.7.4 gives the counts and what the genes do). For other disorders DSM-5-TR notes, for example, that large GWAS have identified a number of loci for ADHD, and that there is no single gene for it. The genome-wide era brought a surprise that matters for classification. The same variants turn up in more than one disorder. DSM-5-TR says that the risk alleles identified for schizophrenia "are also associated with other mental disorders, including bipolar disorder, depression, and autism spectrum disorder." One gene influencing several apparently different traits is called pleiotropy . In 2013 the Cross-Disorder Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium analysed 33,332 cases and 27,888 controls of European ancestry with five disorders, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder and schizophrenia, and found four loci with effects across disorders, among them variants in two genes for subunits of L-type calcium channels (CACNA1C and CACNB2). Shared genes are one reason why disorders co-occur so often (comorbidity, Section 1.2.7), and they challenge the assumption that the categories of the manuals are separate natural kinds (Section 1.6.4). Common SNPs of tiny effect are not the whole story. There are also rare variants of large effect. Copy number variants (CNVs) are stretches of DNA that are deleted or duplicated; the best known, the 22q11.2 deletion, carries a greatly raised risk of psychosis (Section 4.7.4). Some variants are de novo mutations , new changes present in the child but in neither parent; they become more frequent with the father's age. For autism, DSM-5-TR reports that as many as 15 percent of cases appear to be associated with a known genetic mutation, with different de novo copy number variants or mutations in different families. And yet a gap remains, known as missing heritability . Twin studies put the heritability of schizophrenia at about 80 percent, but in 2014 the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium found that all the common variants it could score together explained only about 7 percent of the variation in liability, and the genome-wide significant loci about half of that. Where is the rest? Probably in thousands of further variants too weak to detect yet, in rare variants that SNP chips do not capture, in interactions among genes and between genes and environments, and partly, perhaps, in twin estimates that run a little high. The gap shrinks as samples grow, but it is the reason no genetic test can yet tell a person whether he will develop a common psychiatric disorder. Exam trap Linkage analysis traces markers of known position through families and finds genes of large effect; association studies compare cases with controls and find genes of small effect; a GWAS is an association study across the whole genome, with significance set at 5 × 10 -8 . The Amish chromosome 11 linkage for bipolar disorder (Egeland, 1987) collapsed on re-analysis (Kelsoe, 1989). Pleiotropy : one gene, several disorders. Missing heritability: found variants explain far less than twin studies estimate. Polygenic risk scores If a disorder depends on thousands of variants of tiny effect, no single one is worth testing. But they can be added up. A polygenic risk score is a weighted sum of a person's risk alleles across thousands or even millions of variants: for each SNP, the number of risk alleles the person carries (none, one or two) is multiplied by the size of that allele's effect as estimated in a GWAS, and the products are summed. Scores calculated this way are spread across the population in a bell curve, just as the liability-threshold model predicts. People in the top tenth of the distribution have a clearly higher average risk than people in the bottom tenth. Polygenic risk scores have become one of the most useful tools in psychiatric research. They allow researchers to compare groups (are scores for schizophrenia raised in people with bipolar disorder? they are), to test whether the genetic risk of one disorder overlaps with another or with a trait such as educational attainment, and to ask whether genetic risk and an environmental exposure combine (Section 1.5.1). The 2013 cross-disorder study used them to show genetic overlap especially among the disorders that begin in adulthood. What they cannot do, at least not yet, is tell an individual whether he will fall ill. A score that explains about 7 percent of the variation in liability to schizophrenia leaves 93 percent unexplained; most people with a high score never develop the disorder, and many people who develop it have ordinary scores (Sections 4.7.4 and 5.5.1). There is a second limitation, and it matters directly for Indian readers. Scores are only as good as the GWAS from which their weights come, and those studies have been done overwhelmingly in people of European ancestry: in 2019 Alicia Martin and her colleagues reported that about 79 percent of all GWAS participants were of European descent, although Europeans make up about 16 percent of the world's population. When they applied European-derived scores to people of other ancestries in the UK Biobank, prediction accuracy for the 17 body-measurement and blood-test traits they studied (not psychiatric disorders) fell, by 1.7-fold on average in South Asians and 4.9-fold in Africans. Until large genetic studies are done in South Asian populations, a polygenic score calculated for Rakesh would be even less informative than one calculated for a European. The ethical questions arrive before the science is ready. Commercial companies already offer polygenic scores directly to the public and even to couples choosing among embryos, practices most psychiatric geneticists regard as premature. Scores could be misused by insurers and employers, and in a country where marriages are still often arranged with horoscopes and family histories in hand, a "genetic score" could easily become one more reason to reject a bride or a groom, or one more source of stigma for a family already affected. Remember A polygenic risk score adds up thousands of small genetic effects, each weighted by its GWAS effect size. It is a research tool for groups, not a diagnostic test for individuals: for schizophrenia it explains only about 7 percent of the variation in liability (2014), and it predicts less well in people of non-European ancestry, including South Asians, because most GWAS samples are European. There is no genetic test that can diagnose or predict schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or depression in an individual. Endophenotypes: the links between genes and symptoms Consider how long the road is from a gene to a symptom. A variant in a stretch of DNA alters, very slightly, how much of some protein a neuron makes. That changes, very slightly, how certain synapses form during development, which changes how a circuit in the prefrontal cortex handles information, which makes it harder to hold a thought in mind for a few seconds, which, together with a hundred other influences, years later and under stress, may contribute to disorganised thinking or a delusion. Every step of that road is shaped by other genes and by experience. And the diagnosis at the end of the road is itself a mixture: two people with schizophrenia may share hardly a symptom. No wonder the search for a single "schizophrenia gene" failed. What if researchers stopped looking for the genes of the diagnosis, and looked instead for the genes of something nearer to the DNA? That something is an endophenotype : a measurable, heritable characteristic, which may be neurophysiological, biochemical, endocrine, neuroanatomical, cognitive or neuropsychological, that lies on the pathway between the genotype and the disorder, closer to the genes than the symptoms are. The prefix "endo" means within: an endophenotype is an internal phenotype, invisible to the naked eye, that has to be measured with an instrument or a test. Because it sits nearer the genes, it should be influenced by fewer of them, and so their effects should be easier to find. Barlow and Durand define endophenotypes as "the genetic mechanisms that ultimately contribute to the underlying problems causing the symptoms and difficulties experienced by people with psychological disorders". Their example makes the idea concrete: in schizophrenia, researchers are not looking for a "schizophrenia gene" (a genotype); they are searching for the gene or genes responsible for the working memory problems characteristic of people with the disorder (an endophenotype), and for the genes behind its other problems. The word has an unexpected history. It was coined in 1966 by two geneticists, Bernard John and Kenneth R. Lewis , who were trying to explain the geographical distribution of grasshoppers: the insects' distribution, they argued, depended less on their visible features than on an internal, microscopic one, the structure of their chromosomes, which they called the endophenotype. Irving Gottesman and James Shields, the London psychiatric geneticist who maintained the Maudsley Hospital twin register, borrowed the term for psychiatry in the early 1970s, in their work on the genetics of schizophrenia. Three decades later Gottesman and the younger American researcher Todd Gould revived and popularised it, in 2003, in a paper in the American Journal of Psychiatry on "the endophenotype concept in psychiatry". They also set out criteria that a good endophenotype should meet: It is associated with the illness in the population: people with the disorder show it more often than people without. It is heritable. It is largely state-independent: it is present whether or not the illness is active at the time, so it is not simply a symptom or a side effect of being ill or of treatment. Within families, the endophenotype and the illness co-segregate, that is, they tend to be inherited together. It is found in the unaffected relatives of affected people at a higher rate than in the general population, which shows that it reflects the genetic liability rather than the illness itself. The best-studied candidates come from schizophrenia, and Section 4.7.5 teaches them with their history. The oldest is smooth-pursuit eye movement dysfunction : asked to follow a swinging pendulum with their eyes, many people with schizophrenia, and many of their unaffected relatives, cannot keep their gaze gliding smoothly and fall back on jerky catch-up movements. P50 sensory gating is the failure to damp down the brain's electrical response to the second of two identical clicks; prepulse inhibition is the normal reduction of a startle blink when a weak sound comes just before a loud one, which is weaker in schizophrenia; and working memory deficits appear, in milder form, in relatives too. Other disorders have candidates of their own. In ADHD, Barlow and Durand describe research suggesting that poor inhibitory control, the ability to stop a response when signalled to, is common both in children with the disorder and in their unaffected siblings and parents, and may be a marker of the genetic liability (Goos and colleagues, 2009). For alcohol use disorder, DSM-5-TR describes "intermediate characteristics (or phenotypes)" that alter risk, among them a low level of response to alcohol, which goes with a high risk of the disorder, and the alcohol-related flushing reaction commoner in people of Asian descent, which goes with a low one. In antisocial personality disorder, Barlow and Durand note, researchers look for genes behind specific traits such as fearlessness and impulsivity rather than for genes of the disorder as a whole (Chapter 11). Two related terms are easily confused with endophenotypes. A biomarker is any measurable biological indicator of a disorder, and biomarkers come in two kinds. A state marker is present only while the person is ill and disappears on recovery, as raised cortisol may in a depressive episode; a trait marker is present whether the person is ill or well. Endophenotypes are trait markers that are also heritable and run in families. None of the candidates is specific enough to diagnose anyone; their value is as research tools that cut a heterogeneous diagnosis into pieces closer to biology, an approach that also underlies the Research Domain Criteria (Section 1.6.4; Book 2, Section 2.10.6). Table 1.13 sets the endophenotype beside the three other terms that examiners offer as distractors, so that you can see why each is wrong. Not phenotypes (the observable symptoms and disorder), not genotypes (the genetic make-up), not molecular genetics (a research method). The term came from insect genetics (John and Lewis, 1966), entered psychiatry with Gottesman and Shields in the early 1970s, and was revived by Gottesman and Gould in 2003. Smooth-pursuit eye movement dysfunction is the classic example. 1.5 Genes Meet the World: Interaction, Correlation, Epigenetics and the Brain Lower yield · 1 Q Go back to Meenal and Divya, the identical twins of Section 1.4.3. They carry the same genes, they grew up in the same flat, and only one of them has had a depressive illness. Section 1.4 established two facts that seem to pull in opposite directions: almost every psychiatric disorder is substantially heritable, and no disorder is wholly genetic. This section shows how the two facts fit together. Genes and environments do not simply add their effects like two weights on one side of a scale. A gene can change how strongly a person reacts to an experience (gene-environment interaction). Genes can change which experiences a person meets in the first place (gene-environment correlation). And experiences can change which genes are switched on (epigenetics). After those three ideas, the section maps what is known about the brain's chemistry, hormones and structure across the disorders, sweeps through the environmental risks from the womb to the city, and ends with a question that examiners like to set: are some disorders simply biological? Gene-environment interaction A gene-environment interaction (often written G × E) exists when the effect of a genotype depends on the environment, or, saying the same thing the other way round, when the effect of an environment depends on the genotype. The word "interaction" is meant in its statistical sense: the effect is not genes plus environment but something more like genes times environment. The simplest example is phenylketonuria. The faulty genotype does harm only in an environment that contains the amino acid phenylalanine; on a low-phenylalanine diet it does almost none, and phenylalanine, harmless to everybody else, is damaging only to people with the genotype. Neither the gene nor the diet alone predicts the outcome; the combination does. This is the diathesis-stress model of Section 1.3.4 written at the level of genes: the gene is the diathesis, the environment is the stress, and illness requires both. Key study: Caspi, Moffitt and the MAOA gene (2002) Question. Children who are maltreated are at higher risk of becoming violent and antisocial adults, but most of them do not. Why? Avshalom Caspi , Terrie Moffitt and their colleagues asked whether a gene could protect some children. Method. They used the Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study, a cohort of 1,037 children born in Dunedin, New Zealand, in the early 1970s and assessed at regular intervals from the age of 3 into adulthood. Between the ages of 3 and 11, 8 percent of the children had experienced "severe" maltreatment, 28 percent "probable" maltreatment and 64 percent none. The gene they chose codes for monoamine oxidase A (MAOA), an enzyme that breaks down the neurotransmitters serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine; a common variant in the gene's promoter makes it work at low or at high activity. Because the gene lies on the X chromosome, males carry only one copy, so the analysis was done in the boys. Antisocial outcomes were measured four ways: conduct disorder in adolescence, convictions for violent crime, a personality disposition towards violence, and symptoms of antisocial personality disorder reported by people who knew the men well. Result. The genotype on its own predicted nothing, and maltreatment on its own predicted antisocial behaviour; but the effect of maltreatment was much stronger in boys with the low-activity genotype than in boys with the high-activity genotype. Men who combined low MAOA activity with maltreatment made up only 12 percent of the male cohort but accounted for 44 percent of its convictions for violent crime, and 85 percent of the severely maltreated boys with the low-activity genotype developed some form of antisocial behaviour. The maltreated and non-maltreated groups did not differ in genotype, so the gene was not causing the maltreatment. Conclusion. Genotype can moderate a child's sensitivity to an environmental insult; a gene can protect as well as endanger. Criticism. The authors themselves warned that the finding needed replication before anyone spoke of clinical use. Individual replications were mixed, but meta-analyses ( Julia Kim-Cohen and colleagues, 2006; Amy Byrd and Stephen Manuck, 2014, pooling 20 male cohorts) supported the interaction in males, which makes it one of the more durable gene-environment findings. A year later the same Dunedin team published an even more famous result, on depression. Book 2, Section 1.7.10, tells it with its numbers: people with one or two short versions of the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR) seemed to become depressed after stressful life events and childhood maltreatment far more often than people with two long versions. The paper became one of the most cited in psychiatry, and then it fell apart. A meta-analysis of 14 studies by Neil Risch and his colleagues in 2009 found no evidence of the interaction. In 2019 Richard Border and his colleagues tested the 18 candidate genes for depression that had each been studied ten or more times, in samples of between about 62,000 and 443,000 people, and found no clear evidence for any of them, alone or in interaction with childhood abuse or socioeconomic adversity; most of the published candidate-gene findings, they concluded, were probably false positives (Section 5.5.1). The lesson is not that gene-environment interaction is a myth. It is that a single common variant of tiny effect cannot be studied reliably in a few hundred people, however tidy the result looks. The principle survives, now tested with polygenic scores in large samples, even where the particular gene did not. Two other interactions recur in this book. In 2005 Caspi and colleagues reported from the Dunedin cohort that adolescent cannabis use raised the risk of adult psychosis mainly in people carrying one version of a common variant of the COMT gene, which codes for an enzyme that breaks down dopamine; later studies have been less consistent (Section 4.7.8). And the Finnish adoption study of Pekka Tienari, met in Section 1.4.4, is an interaction study in all but name. Children of mothers with schizophrenia who were adopted into disturbed, poorly functioning families developed schizophrenia-spectrum disorders far more often than those adopted into healthy families, while for children of healthy mothers the quality of the adoptive family made little difference (Section 4.7.3). The genetic risk mattered chiefly in a harmful environment; the harmful environment mattered chiefly for the genetically vulnerable. One twist on the idea deserves a line. Jay Belsky and Michael Pluess's differential susceptibility hypothesis (Book 2, Section 1.7.11) suggests that some "vulnerability" genes are really sensitivity genes: their carriers do worse than others in bad environments and better than others in good ones. Exam trap Gene-environment interaction : the effect of a gene depends on the environment (and the reverse). Caspi and colleagues 2002 : the MAOA gene, childhood maltreatment and antisocial behaviour in Dunedin boys (low-activity MAOA plus maltreatment = most risk); Caspi and colleagues 2003 : the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR), stress and depression, not replicated (Risch 2009; Border 2019). Do not swap the genes or the outcomes. Tienari's Finnish adoption study is also an interaction: genetic risk plus a disturbed adoptive family. Gene-environment correlation Interaction assumes that genes and environments are dealt out independently and then meet. Often they are not independent at all. In gene-environment correlation (rGE), a person's genes influence the environments he is exposed to. Book 2, Section 1.7.11, teaches the three kinds that Robert Plomin, John DeFries and John Loehlin distinguished in 1977 (Book 1, Section 9.7.4, gives Sandra Scarr and Kathleen McCartney's 1983 version), so a fresh example of each is enough here. In passive gene-environment correlation , parents give a child both genes and a home that reflect the same tendencies: a girl whose mother has an anxiety disorder may inherit an anxious temperament and also grow up watching her mother check the locks, avoid crowds and warn of dangers, so that genes and upbringing push the same way. In evocative gene-environment correlation (also called reactive), a child's inherited characteristics draw particular responses from other people: a restless, impulsive, easily frustrated boy is shouted at and punished more by parents and teachers than his calmer brother. In active gene-environment correlation , people seek out environments that suit their dispositions: a thrill-seeking adolescent chooses risky friends, fast vehicles and drugs. Passive correlation matters most in early childhood; active correlation grows as young people gain control over their own lives. Barlow and Durand call the same idea the reciprocal gene-environment model , and their example is worth retelling because it shows how a genetic vulnerability can manufacture its own trigger. Imagine a person with an inherited tendency to faint at the sight of blood, who also has an inherited impulsive temperament. Always rushing, careless of physical safety, she has more minor accidents than other people, and so she sees blood more often, and each fright strengthens the phobia. A person with neither tendency rarely meets the trigger at all. The genes, in other words, help to create the very environmental risk that then sets off the genetic vulnerability. Salim shows the same pattern in an Indian setting. He is 24 and works as a food-delivery rider in Hyderabad, and he has always been the boy who climbed highest, rode fastest and answered back first; his father, he says, was "exactly the same at my age". In two years he has had three road accidents, lost two jobs after quarrels with supervisors, broken an engagement and been in a fight outside a tea stall that ended at a police station. He comes to the clinic, at his mother's insistence, because he is drinking every night and cannot sleep. A life-events checklist shows a heavy burden of stress, and a diathesis-stress account might say that stress has tipped a vulnerable young man into a disorder. But look at the events. Almost all of them are what researchers call dependent events, ones his own behaviour helped to produce; only one, his grandfather's death, was independent of him. His temperament, partly inherited, is generating his stressors. How large is this effect? Kenneth Kendler and his colleagues asked 2,315 pairs of twins from the Virginia Twin Registry about the stressful events of the past year and reported in 1993 that, for total life events, genetic factors and the family environment each accounted for about 20 percent of the variation. The kind of event mattered. For "network" events, which happen to people in one's social circle (a relative's illness, say), twin resemblance came entirely from the family environment; for "personal" events, which happen directly to the respondent (being robbed, losing a job, a quarrel), most of the twin resemblance was genetic. In 2007 Kendler and Baker reviewed 55 independent studies of the heritability of environments that matter to psychiatry: stressful life events, parenting, the family environment, social support, peer relationships and marital quality. The weighted average heritability was 27 percent, with most measures between 15 and 35 percent; it was smaller but still present (14 percent) when the environment was rated by direct observation rather than by the person, so it reflects actual behaviour and not only perception. Barlow and Durand add a striking example from Matt McGue and David Lykken (1992): the probability that you will divorce roughly doubles if your fraternal twin has divorced, and rises about sixfold if your identical twin has. Nobody inherits a gene for divorce; people inherit traits, such as being impulsive, short-tempered or drawn to incompatible partners, that make a divorce more likely. Gene-environment correlation has two practical consequences. For research, it means that an "environmental" risk factor may carry genetic information. If harsh parenting goes with conduct problems in children, the harshness may be causing the problems, or the parents and children may share genes that produce both, or the children's difficult temperament may be provoking the harshness. Only genetically informative designs (adoption studies, twin studies, studies of the children of twins) can tell these apart, which is one reason Caspi's team checked that genotype did not predict maltreatment. For the clinician, it means something hopeful. If a temperament keeps steering a person into harmful situations, then helping him to recognise and change those choices (a different job, a safer route, different friends, learning to walk away from a quarrel) cuts the chain that links his genes to his stressors. Genetic influence on an environment does not make the environment unchangeable. Table 1.14 sets interaction and the three kinds of correlation side by side.
