Epigenetics: experience written on the genome Nearly every cell in your body carries the same DNA, yet a neuron and a liver cell could hardly be more different. The difference lies in which genes each cell actually uses. Genes can be switched on or off, turned up or down, without any change in the DNA sequence itself, and the study of these changes is epigenetics . The prefix "epi" means on or around, and the name fits: the changes are made by chemical material sitting on or around the genome, collectively called the epigenome . Two mechanisms are best understood. In DNA methylation , small chemical tags called methyl groups are attached to the DNA, often in the region at the start of a gene that controls its activity (the promoter), and heavy methylation there usually silences the gene. In histone modification , chemical changes are made to the histones, the proteins around which DNA is wound like thread on a spool; some changes loosen the winding so that a gene can be read, others tighten it so that it cannot. A useful analogy is a play. The DNA sequence is the script, identical in every copy; the epigenome is the director's pencil marks, which decide which lines are spoken loudly, which softly and which are cut. What made epigenetics revolutionary for psychopathology is the discovery that experience, especially early experience, can make those pencil marks. Key study: Meaney's mothers and their pups (1999 to 2005) Question. Some rat mothers spend a great deal of time licking and grooming their pups and nursing them in a protective, arched-back posture; others do much less. Their offspring differ too: the pups of attentive mothers grow up less fearful and better able to tolerate stress. Is that inherited through the mothers' genes or through their mothering? Method. The neuroscientist Michael Meaney and his colleagues at McGill University in Montreal used cross-fostering : newborn pups of one mother are given to another mother to rear (Figure 1.9). Darlene Francis, Josie Diorio, Dong Liu and Meaney (1999) took newborn pups of fearful, easily stressed mothers and placed them with calm, attentive mothers, while other pups stayed with their own mothers. Result. Pups born to easily stressed mothers but reared by calm ones grew up calm, and, as mothers themselves, they were calm and attentive with their own pups. The style of mothering was passed down the generations independently of the genes. Cameron and colleagues (2005), as Barlow and Durand report, showed that the maternal care had lastingly altered the pups' hormonal response to stress by affecting gene expression, but only if the care was given in the pups' first week of life; after that it no longer mattered. Ian Weaver and colleagues (2004) found the mechanism: pups of high-licking mothers had different DNA methylation at the promoter of the glucocorticoid receptor gene in the hippocampus, the receptor that lets the brain switch off the stress response. The differences emerged over the first week of life, were reversed by cross-fostering and persisted into adulthood, and a drug that altered histone chemistry, infused into the brain, removed them. Conclusion. Early experience can set the epigenetic state of a stress-related gene, and that state is potentially reversible. Criticism. These are rats; human brains cannot be sampled in the same way, and how far the mechanism carries over to people is still being worked out. Read the bottom row: the adults' calmness follows the mother who reared them, not the mother who bore them. Primates show the same thing. The American primatologist Stephen Suomi used cross-fostering with rhesus monkeys and reported in 1999 that genetically reactive, emotional infants reared by calm mothers for their first six months behaved in later life as if they had never been reactive at all; and when they became mothers, they too were calm and supportive with their young. The early environment had overridden, and even reversed across a generation, an inherited tendency. A third study made the point from the opposite direction. John Crabbe , Douglas Wahlsten and Bruce Dudek (1999) tested several genetically distinct strains of mice (Barlow and Durand simplify them to three types) at the same time in three laboratories, at their three universities, and went to extraordinary lengths to make the conditions identical: the same sawdust bedding changed on the same day of the week, the same gloves, even the same kind of pen for marking tails. If genes alone determined behaviour, each strain should have behaved identically at all three sites. On some tests it did; on others it did not, and for some tests even the size of the differences between strains depended on which laboratory did the testing. Small, uncontrolled differences in environment still mattered. The neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky drew the conclusion that Barlow and Durand quote: genetic influences "are often a lot less powerful than is commonly believed". Is there human evidence? Experiments are impossible, but history has provided some terrible natural ones. In the winter of 1944 to 1945, a German blockade of the western Netherlands caused a sharp, time-limited famine, the Dutch Hunger Winter, in which average daily rations fell below about 4,200 kilojoules, roughly 1,000 kilocalories. Because the famine began and ended abruptly and the Dutch kept excellent records, researchers could identify exactly who had been conceived or carried during it. Ezra Susser and Shang Lin reported in 1992 that people whose first trimester in the womb fell during the severe famine had a raised risk of later being admitted to hospital with schizophrenia: about twice the usual risk in women (a relative risk of about 2.2), though not in men; a more precise study in 1996 found that people conceived at the height of the famine, men and women alike, had double the risk (a relative risk of 2.0). Was the famine written on their genes? In 2008 Bastiaan Heijmans and colleagues compared people who had been exposed to the famine around the time of conception with their own unexposed brothers and sisters of the same sex. Six decades later, the exposed siblings had less methylation of IGF2, a gene involved in growth: the first direct evidence that early-life conditions can cause epigenetic changes in humans that persist throughout life. (IGF2 is not a gene for schizophrenia; the study showed that the mechanism exists in people.) The closest human parallel to Meaney's rats came from his own institute. Patrick McGowan , Meaney and their colleagues examined brain tissue from the hippocampus of people who had died by suicide, some with and some without a history of childhood abuse, and of control subjects. Published in 2009, the study found that the suicide victims who had been abused in childhood had increased methylation of the promoter of the glucocorticoid receptor gene and lower expression of the receptor: the same gene, the same direction of change and the same brain region as in the poorly mothered rat pups. DSM-5-TR now mentions epigenetic factors among the influences on susceptibility to PTSD, and Section 5.5.1 notes several epigenetic mechanisms that have been implicated in depression. Three cautions keep the excitement in proportion. First, almost all the human evidence is correlational, and the methylation measured in blood or saliva, which is all that can be sampled in living people, may not match what is happening in the brain. Second, the transmission across generations in Meaney's and Suomi's animals ran through behaviour : calm mothers raised calm daughters who became calm mothers. Whether epigenetic marks themselves pass from human parents to grandchildren through eggs and sperm is far less certain than some popular accounts suggest. Third, epigenetic marks are not destiny either; in the rats they were reversible. What epigenetics does settle is a question of logic. Heritability estimates assume that the contributions of genes and environment can be separated and added up. If experience alters the activity of genes, the separation is artificial. Barlow and Durand draw the conclusion: it is probably too simplistic to say that the genetic contribution to a personality trait or a psychological disorder is about 50 percent; a heritable contribution can be spoken of only in the context of the individual's past and present environment. The differences between identical twins such as Meenal and Divya, which begin in the womb and widen with every year of separate experience, are part of the same story. Exam trap Epigenetics changes whether and how much a gene is expressed , not the DNA sequence ; the main mechanisms are DNA methylation (usually silencing) and histone modification . Meaney's rats: pups of fearful mothers cross-fostered to calm mothers grew up calm (Francis and colleagues, 1999), the effect needed the first week of life (Cameron, 2005), and it worked through methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene (Weaver, 2004). Suomi: rhesus monkeys. Crabbe: identical mice in three laboratories. Human evidence: the Dutch Hunger Winter (Susser; Heijmans) and McGowan's suicide victims abused in childhood. The brain: messengers, hormones and structures Genes and experiences can only cause a disorder by changing the brain, and the biological chapters of this book each describe what has been found in the brains of people with particular disorders. This subsection is a map of those findings, not a lesson in neuroscience: how neurons communicate, how drugs act at the synapse and how the brain is imaged belong to the Physiological Psychology book, and the disorder-specific details to Sections 4.8, 5.5 and 6.7. Neurons communicate by releasing chemical messengers, neurotransmitters , across the tiny gap of the synapse, where they act on receptors on the next neuron and are then broken down or taken back up into the neuron that released them (reuptake). Antipsychotics block dopamine receptors, so schizophrenia must involve too much dopamine; antidepressants raise serotonin and noradrenaline, so depression must involve too little (Section 5.5.2 tells the monoamine story). Reasoning from what a treatment does to what caused the illness has a Latin name, ex juvantibus reasoning , and it is risky. A headache is not caused by a lack of aspirin; paracetamol relieves a fever without telling you whether the cause is malaria or influenza. The monoamine hypothesis of depression shows the danger: antidepressants change serotonin within hours but take weeks to help, and a 2022 umbrella review led by Joanna Moncrieff found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin (Book 2, Section 1.7.2). The popular phrase "a chemical imbalance" claims far more than the evidence shows. A drug's effect tells you something about the brain systems that can relieve a disorder, not necessarily about the systems that caused it. Hormones form the second strand. The body's main stress system is the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis : in response to stress the hypothalamus signals the pituitary gland, which signals the adrenal glands to release the stress hormone cortisol, and cortisol in turn feeds back on the brain, through glucocorticoid receptors like those Meaney studied, to switch the response off. Chronic stress and severe depression are often accompanied by an overactive axis (Book 1, Section 11.8.4; Section 5.5.3). The thyroid is the other gland every clinician must remember, because thyroid disease mimics psychiatric disorder: an underactive thyroid produces slowness, fatigue, low mood and weight gain that look like depression, and an overactive one produces tremor, palpitations and restlessness that look like anxiety. That is why a careful clinician checks thyroid function before diagnosing either (Sections 5.3.4 and 6.1.8). Structure and function make the third strand, and here a sentence each is enough, with the full stories in their chapters. Many people with schizophrenia have enlarged lateral ventricles, the fluid-filled spaces of the brain, and reduced grey matter (Section 4.7.7). In the anxiety disorders, an overactive amygdala, the brain's alarm centre, appears to be poorly regulated by the prefrontal cortex (Section 6.7.4). In OCD, attention centres on a loop running from the orbitofrontal cortex through the striatum and thalamus and back, the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit (Section 6.7.6). In long-standing recurrent depression, the hippocampus, which is rich in glucocorticoid receptors and sensitive to prolonged stress, is often smaller (Sections 5.5.4 and 5.5.7). These findings come from four main imaging methods: computed tomography (CT), which builds pictures of brain structure from X-rays; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which gives far more detailed pictures of structure using magnetic fields; positron emission tomography (PET), which uses radioactive tracers to show metabolism or receptors at work; and functional MRI (fMRI), which tracks changes in blood oxygen as a sign of which regions are active during a task (the Assessment and Physiological Psychology books explain the methods). One theory ties genes, the early environment and the brain together for schizophrenia. The neurodevelopmental model , proposed in 1987 by Daniel Weinberger and, independently, by Robin Murray and Shôn Lewis , holds that the disorder begins with a disturbance of brain development before or around birth, produced by risk genes, prenatal infection or malnutrition, or complications of delivery. The disturbance stays silent through childhood, apart from subtle differences, and declares itself only in adolescence or early adulthood, when the maturing brain, pruning its synapses and completing the wiring of the prefrontal cortex, comes to depend on the very circuits that were built wrongly (Section 4.7.6). It is a narrower theory than the diathesis-stress model, a theory of when and how the vulnerability arises, and the two are compatible (Section 1.3.4; Book 2, Table 1.16). It should not be confused with the neurodevelopmental disorders , such as autism and intellectual developmental disorder, which form their own DSM-5-TR chapter (Chapter 3). A newer strand of research looks at inflammation: a subset of people with depression show raised inflammatory markers in the blood (Section 5.5.8). Finally, the warning that applies to every finding in this subsection: correlation is not cause. A brain difference found in people with a disorder may be a cause of the disorder, but it may equally be a consequence of the illness, of years of stress, poverty or poor sleep, of alcohol or cannabis, or of the medication used to treat it. The best studies examine people at their first episode, before treatment, or follow children at high risk before anyone falls ill, precisely to untangle these possibilities. Exam trap A drug's effect does not prove a disorder's cause ( ex juvantibus reasoning): headache is not a lack of aspirin, and depression has not been shown to be a lack of serotonin. GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter (benzodiazepines), glutamate the main excitatory one (NMDA receptors, ketamine); antipsychotics block D2 dopamine receptors; acetylcholine is the transmitter of Alzheimer's disease (cholinesterase inhibitors). The neurodevelopmental model (Weinberger; Murray and Lewis, 1987) is a theory of schizophrenia, not the DSM chapter of neurodevelopmental disorders. The environment: from the womb to the city In psychiatric research "environment" means far more than upbringing. It means everything that is not written in the DNA sequence, and it begins before birth. This subsection sweeps through the environmental risks that recur in the disorder chapters, a sentence or three on each, so that you recognise them when they appear; each is taught in full where it matters most. Before and around birth. For schizophrenia, DSM-5-TR names pregnancy and birth complications with hypoxia (a shortage of oxygen) and greater paternal age as risk factors, and links other prenatal and perinatal adversities, among them maternal stress, infection, malnutrition and maternal diabetes, with the disorder; then it adds at once that the vast majority of offspring with these risk factors do not develop schizophrenia. The Dutch Hunger Winter (Section 1.5.3) is the best-studied example of prenatal malnutrition. For autism spectrum disorder, DSM-5-TR lists advanced parental age, extreme prematurity and exposure in the womb to certain drugs, such as the anticonvulsant valproic acid. Alcohol drunk in pregnancy can damage the developing brain; DSM-5-TR proposes a "neurobehavioural disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure" as a condition for further study (Section 1.8.6; Chapter 3). Notice that every one of these influences is biological and every one is environmental. Childhood adversity. The largest single demonstration of how early adversity echoes through adult life is the Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) study of Vincent Felitti , Robert Anda and their colleagues, published in 1998. They mailed a questionnaire to 13,494 adults who had had a standard medical check-up at Kaiser Permanente, a large health organisation in San Diego, and 9,508 replied. It asked about seven categories of adverse experience in childhood: psychological, physical or sexual abuse; violence against the mother; and living with household members who were substance abusers, mentally ill or suicidal, or ever imprisoned. More than half of the respondents reported at least one category. The striking finding was a graded , dose-response relationship: the more categories a person had experienced, the higher the risk of every adult health problem studied. People with four or more categories, compared with those with none, had four to twelve times the risk of alcoholism, drug abuse, depression and suicide attempts, and higher rates of heart disease, cancer, chronic lung disease and liver disease. The same adversity led to many different outcomes, which is multifinality (Section 1.3.3), and the adversities clustered: a child who suffered one usually suffered several. Trauma, life events and chronic difficulties. Exposure to a traumatic event is a necessary cause of PTSD by definition (Section 1.3.3; Chapter 7). Severe life events, especially losses, and chronic difficulties such as a bad marriage or poverty precede many depressive episodes, as George Brown and Tirril Harris showed in their Camberwell study (Section 5.6.8; Book 1, Section 11.9.1, for Holmes and Rahe's life-event scale). Remember from Section 1.5.2 that many such events are partly produced by the person's own temperament. Drugs. Heavy cannabis use in adolescence raises the risk of a later psychotic disorder, especially with high-potency forms and early, frequent use (Section 4.7.8). Alcohol and other drugs both cause and complicate many disorders (Chapter 10). The city, migration and social defeat. People who are born or brought up in cities, and migrants and their children, have higher rates of schizophrenia than people raised in the countryside or in their own country of origin; one explanation, the social defeat hypothesis, proposes that the chronic experience of being an outsider and of being excluded sensitises the brain's stress and dopamine systems (Sections 4.6.3 and 4.9.6). Poverty. Serious mental illness is commoner among the poor, and two explanations compete: social causation (the stresses of poverty cause illness) and social drift (illness drives people down the social ladder). Both operate, to different degrees in different disorders (Book 2, Section 1.7.7). Gender. Women have about twice the rate of depression that men have, especially between menarche and menopause, and DSM-5-TR notes that women are disproportionately affected by major risk factors for depression across the lifespan, including interpersonal trauma; differences in rumination and in social roles add to the gap (Section 5.6.6). Discrimination. DSM-5-TR states that there is evidence that racism can worsen many psychiatric disorders and contribute to poor outcomes, and that racial biases can affect diagnostic assessment. In India the same questions arise about caste, which DSM-5-TR lists among the aspects of cultural identity that a clinician should explore (Section 1.10.3). Set against all these risks are the protective factors and the capacity for resilience described in Section 1.3.6: a stable relationship with at least one caring adult, an easy temperament, problem-solving ability and a sense of purpose. They are environmental too, and they are where much of prevention begins. Clinical link This list is also an assessment checklist. A complete history asks about the pregnancy and birth (complications, maternal alcohol or drug use), early development, adversity and abuse in childhood, trauma, substance use, migration, poverty, discrimination and the supports a person has. Asking about adverse childhood experiences is not prying: it identifies people at raised risk, explains symptoms that otherwise seem to come from nowhere, and guides treatment, since the same depression may need a different plan in someone who was abused as a child (Book 2, Section 2.3, on the case history). How biological is a disorder? It is often said that bipolar disorder and schizophrenia are "biological illnesses", with little or no psychological or social cause, whereas a disorder such as bulimia nervosa is "psychological" or "cultural". After Sections 1.4 and 1.5 you can test that claim properly. Part of it is right, and part of it is wrong, and the way it is wrong is the most important idea in this chapter. Start with what is right. Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia are the two most heritable of the major adult disorders in Table 1.12: around 90 percent in some twin studies of bipolar disorder and about 80 percent for schizophrenia. DSM-5-TR says plainly that genetic processes "strongly affect predisposition to bipolar disorder". Both disorders respond more clearly to medication than to any other treatment: lithium and the other mood stabilisers prevent relapses of bipolar disorder (Section 5.7.5), antipsychotic drugs reduce the positive symptoms of schizophrenia and prevent relapse (Section 4.10), and in both disorders psychological treatment alone is not enough. Brain differences are well documented, especially in schizophrenia (Section 4.7.7). Bulimia nervosa looks different. DSM-5-TR lists the internalisation of a thin body ideal as a risk factor, and childhood sexual or physical abuse as another; binge eating frequently begins during or after an episode of dieting to lose weight; and the disorder is closely tied to the cultural pressure on young women to be thin (Chapter 8). On a forced choice between these three, the first two are the disorders with the strongest evidence of biological causation. Now look at what is wrong, and begin with the bulimia comparison. Bulimia nervosa is not "non-biological" either: both twins are affected in 23 percent of identical pairs but only 9 percent of fraternal pairs, and the consensus of twin studies puts genes at about half of the causal equation for the eating disorders. The difference between the disorders is one of degree, not of kind. More important is what is wrong about bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. The claim that there is "little to no" evidence of psychosocial causation is simply false. Consider bipolar disorder first. If genes were everything, an identical twin of a person with bipolar disorder would always have it; in fact monozygotic concordance is only 40 to 70 percent, which, in DSM-5-TR's words, indicates that "much risk is left unexplained by genes alone". The timing of episodes is strongly influenced by events. Sleep loss can precipitate mania; so can life events, and so, remarkably, can success: in Sheri Johnson's studies, goal attainment events, such as a promotion, an acceptance letter or falling in love, were followed by rises in manic symptoms (Section 5.6.9). Rakesh's brother is a case in point. Looking back, the family recalled that his manic episode had begun after a month in which he slept four hours a night, working late to set up the business, and his psychiatrist's plan for preventing the next one combines lithium with a regular sleep routine and a family that knows the warning signs. Schizophrenia tells the same story. Identical twins of people with schizophrenia develop it only about 33 to 48 percent of the time (Section 4.7.2). In the families of people who have recovered from an episode, high expressed emotion, a climate of criticism, hostility and emotional over-involvement, predicts relapse, and family interventions that reduce it lower relapse rates (Section 4.9.4; Book 2, Sections 7.2.4 and 7.2.5). Being conceived during a famine doubled the risk (Section 1.5.3). Growing up in a city, migrating, heavy adolescent cannabis use and childhood adversity all raise it (Sections 4.6.3, 4.7.8 and 4.9.6). Tienari's Finnish adoptees at high genetic risk developed schizophrenia-spectrum disorders mainly when they were raised in disturbed families (Section 1.5.1). Every one of those findings is psychosocial or environmental evidence about the most "biological" disorder in the book. The resolution is the one this section has been building towards. Genes set the diathesis; the environment, from the womb onwards, decides whether the diathesis is expressed, when the illness begins, how severe it is and how often it returns. The two kinds of cause are not rivals competing for a fixed share of the explanation, because they act through each other: genes alter sensitivity to experience (interaction), shape the experiences a person meets (correlation), and are themselves switched on and off by experience (epigenetics). Asking whether a disorder is "biological or psychosocial" is a little like asking whether the area of a rectangle comes from its length or its width. Remember Four clarifications to carry into every chapter. Biological is not the same as genetic : prenatal infection, famine, a head injury and heavy cannabis use are biological and environmental at once. Genetic is not the same as unchangeable : phenylketonuria is almost entirely genetic and almost entirely preventable by diet (Book 1, Section 9.7.3). A drug response does not prove a biological cause : headache is not a lack of aspirin (Section 1.5.4). Psychological causes and treatments act through the brain too : in Lewis Baxter's 1992 study, people with OCD who improved with behaviour therapy showed the same change in the activity of the caudate nucleus as those who improved with fluoxetine (Section 6.7.6). Exam trap Asked (RML 2020) which illness has "considerable evidence that it is caused by biological factors and little to no evidence that it is caused by psychosocial factors", with the options bipolar disorder, bulimia nervosa, schizophrenia, and "(a) and (c)", choose (a) and (c) : bipolar disorder and schizophrenia have the highest heritabilities and the clearest response to drugs, while bulimia nervosa is the most strongly shaped by culture and dieting. But know that the premise is false. Identical-twin concordance is only 40 to 70 percent for bipolar disorder and about 33 to 48 percent for schizophrenia; sleep loss, life events and goal attainment trigger manic episodes; expressed emotion, prenatal famine, urban upbringing, migration, cannabis and childhood adversity all affect schizophrenia; and bulimia nervosa is itself about half heritable. Before lunch a single junior doctor may see forty new patients: a farmer's wife who has stopped eating and cannot stop crying, a college student who hears his dead father's voice, a shopkeeper who washes his hands fifty times a day, a retired teacher who keeps getting lost on the way home from the market, a young man who has not slept for four nights and has spent his family's savings on a car he cannot drive. To help any of them she must do three things quickly. She must decide what kind of problem each person has, she must write it down in words that the next doctor, the pharmacist and the hospital's records office will all understand, and she must choose a treatment that has worked for other people with the same kind of problem. All three depend on one act: sorting the people in front of her into groups. Sections 1.1 to 1.5 asked what a disorder is and what causes one. This section asks how disorders should be sorted. Should they be grouped by what you can see and hear, or by what caused them? Should a person be put in a box or placed on a scale? When two diagnoses seem to fit, which one wins? How can you tell whether a way of sorting is any good, and what happens when it sorts a person wrongly? Finally, what does the label cost the person who receives it? Sections 1.7 to 1.9 then follow the two great classifications in use today, the American Psychiatric Association's DSM and the World Health Organization's ICD, edition by edition. Why classify Consider Harish, a 35-year-old bank clerk from Lucknow. In ten years he has been admitted to hospital three times, each time after a week or two of racing thoughts, sleeplessness, grand plans and reckless spending, and each admission was followed by months of heavy, slowed-down depression. His old discharge slips describe him in three different ways: "nervous exhaustion", "acute psychosis" and "depression with excitement". Each phrase captures something, but none of them tells a new doctor what to expect next, which medicine has the best evidence, or which research applies to him, and none could be counted by the hospital's records office. Written instead as "bipolar I disorder", the same history tells every reader that further episodes are likely, that a mood stabiliser such as lithium is the usual first choice (Section 5.7.5), and that a large body of research on people like him is relevant. That is what classification buys. The vocabulary is worth having straight. A nosology (from the Greek nosos , disease) is a classification of diseases or disorders; its nomenclature is its agreed list of names; taxonomy is the general science of classifying anything, from beetles to rocks, and the word is borrowed from biology. A diagnosis is the act of deciding which category of a nosology a particular person's problems belong to, and also the name that results. Clinicians classify for six overlapping reasons: to communicate, to predict the course, to choose a treatment, to make research possible, to run health services (records, insurance, certificates and the courts all work through diagnostic codes), and, in the long run, to understand causes, because grouping people who share a pattern is the first step towards finding out why they share it. Book 2, Section 2.10.1 takes each purpose in turn. Two cautions belong at the very start. First, a diagnosis classifies a problem, not a person. Harish has bipolar disorder; he is not "a bipolar", any more than a man with diabetes is "a diabetic" in any sense that matters about him. Writing and speaking this way is called person-first language , and it is now the expected style in case notes, reports and research papers. Second, the DSM and the ICD are not tests, therapies or rating scales. They are classification and diagnostic systems : nosologies that list the disorders, define them and give each a code. That single fact is the whole answer to a recurring easy question that Section 1.9.7 takes up when it compares the two systems. Early classifications: from Hippocrates to Kraepelin The urge to sort madness into kinds is as old as medicine. The Greek physician Hippocrates (about 460 to 377 BCE) divided mental disorders into three broad groups: mania , states of excitement and overactivity; melancholia , states of sadness and despondency; and phrenitis , an acute feverish confusion that we would now call delirium. The word hysteria , from the Greek for womb, also comes from the Hippocratic tradition, along with the mistaken idea that a wandering womb caused the symptoms (Section 7.1.1 follows the word through history). Notice what kind of scheme this was. Hippocrates explained disorder by the balance of the four humours, but he sorted his patients by what they looked like. Book 2, Section 1.2.2 tells his story. India has its own early nosology. The Charaka Samhita , the classical Ayurvedic text, describes five types of unmada , the Ayurvedic term for insanity: three arising from a disturbance of a single dosha ( vataja , pittaja and kaphaja ), a fourth from the disturbance of all three together ( sannipatika ), and a fifth, agantuja , from causes that come from outside the body, among which the classical texts include possessing spirits. This scheme is interesting for a reason that the next subsection will make clear: it sorts disorders by their supposed cause , not by their appearance. It is an aetiological classification two thousand years before the word existed (Book 2, Section 1.2.3). The modern story begins in the asylums of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, where for the first time large numbers of disturbed people lived under medical observation for years. The French physician Philippe Pinel (1745 to 1826), remembered above all for striking the chains off patients in Paris (Book 2, Section 1.3.1), also simplified the bewildering lists of his predecessors. In his treatise on mental alienation of 1801 he recognised only a handful of kinds: melancholia, mania (with and without delirium), dementia (in his sense, a breakdown of coherent thinking, not the memory loss of old age) and idiocy. In Germany, Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum (1828 to 1899) described catatonia in 1874 and his younger colleague Ewald Hecker (1843 to 1909) described hebephrenia in 1871, and Kahlbaum insisted that a disease should be recognised by its whole course and not by a snapshot of its symptoms (Section 4.1.2). That insistence found its master in Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926). The asylum doctors of his day noticed that the same symptoms, excitement or delusions or despair, appeared in patients whose futures turned out to be completely different. Kraepelin therefore classified descriptively , by the pattern of symptoms, but above all by course and outcome : how the illness began, how it unfolded over the years and how it ended. Following his patients for years, he drew the great line of modern psychiatry. On one side he placed dementia praecox , an illness beginning early in life and moving towards lasting deterioration; on the other, manic-depressive insanity , an illness of episodes from which the patient recovered in between. By the sixth edition of his textbook (1899) the division was complete. The split of the major psychoses into these two families is called the Kraepelinian dichotomy , and it still shapes the DSM and the ICD, which keep schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in separate chapters. Kraepelin also believed that each disease he described would turn out to have its own brain pathology, as general paresis had turned out to have syphilis; the very name dementia praecox (early dementia) carried that belief. His story, including the way he worked, is told in Book 2, Section 1.3.7 and in Section 4.1.3 of this book; dementia praecox was renamed schizophrenia by Eugen Bleuler in 1908 (Section 4.1.4). Kraepelin's ideas had a second life in the United States half a century after his death. In 1978 the American psychiatrist Gerald L. Klerman (1928 to 1992) coined the term neo-Kraepelinian for a group of psychiatrists, centred on Washington University in St Louis, who held that psychiatry is a branch of medicine, that mental disorders are discrete conditions rather than points on a vague continuum of maladjustment, and that diagnosis should be made by explicit, testable rules. Their research criteria became the backbone of DSM-III in 1980 (Section 1.7.3). Exam trap Kraepelin is the name for classification by course and outcome and for the split between dementia praecox and manic-depressive insanity. Pinel is the name for humane reform (and a simple four-part scheme); Bleuler is the name for the word schizophrenia (1908). Dementia praecox is schizophrenia , not Alzheimer's disease or any dementia of old age, even though the word "dementia" is in it. Hippocrates' phrenitis was a feverish delirium, not schizophrenia. And Charaka's five types of unmada are classified by cause (the doshas and external agents), which makes them an early aetiological scheme. Syndromal and aetiological approaches Neelam is a 42-year-old schoolteacher in Pune. For four months she has felt low and heavy, has lost interest in her pupils, sleeps ten hours and wakes unrefreshed, has gained six kilograms, and cannot follow the plot of a television serial. Described by what anyone can observe and what she reports, this is a depressive syndrome, and it would comfortably meet the criteria for a major depressive episode. Then a routine blood test comes back: her thyroid gland is badly underactive. Now the same picture has a cause, and the cause changes everything. Her diagnosis becomes a depressive disorder due to another medical condition (hypothyroidism), and the first treatment is not an antidepressant but thyroid hormone. Neelam's case contains the whole argument of this subsection in miniature, because there are two fundamentally different ways of deciding what to call her. The first is the syndromal approach , also called the descriptive approach. A syndrome (from the Greek for "running together") is a cluster of signs and symptoms that tend to occur together and to follow a recognisable course (Section 1.2.2 defines symptom, sign and syndrome). The syndromal approach defines each category by such a cluster, whatever its cause: if the right symptoms are present for the right length of time and cause enough distress or impairment, the category applies. The second is the aetiological approach : categories are defined by their cause (their aetiology), so that everyone whose illness has the same cause belongs to the same category, whatever their symptoms look like. For the rest of medicine the aetiological approach is the ideal, and two stories show why. The first is general paresis (Book 2, Section 1.3.6). Asylum doctors first recognised it in the 1820s as a syndrome: grandiose delusions, a slow collapse of intellect, slurred speech and paralysis, then death within a few years. Once the syphilis spirochaete was found in the brains of paretic patients in 1913, the category was redefined by its cause. Today neurosyphilis is diagnosed by blood and spinal-fluid tests, includes patients with no grandiosity at all, and is treated with penicillin. The second is tuberculosis. For centuries "consumption" was a syndrome: cough, fever, night sweats and wasting. After the German physician Robert Koch (1843 to 1910) identified the tubercle bacillus in 1882, tuberculosis became a cause-defined disease. The new category lumped together illnesses that look nothing like consumption, such as tuberculosis of the spine, the lymph glands and the brain, and it split off coughing, wasting illnesses with other causes, such as lung cancer. That is the power of an aetiological classification: it sorts by what actually happened in the body, so it predicts course and points straight to treatment. The two labels you are most likely to meet for these approaches are "syndromal" and "historical". The second is not a term the DSM or ICD use, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising. In some Indian study materials and mock papers the cause-based approach is called the historical approach. They do not explain the label, but the most sensible reading is that the cause-based approach is the older ideal: it is how Charaka sorted unmada, how nineteenth-century psychiatrists hoped to sort every form of madness once general paresis had shown the way, and how medicine still sorts diseases whenever their cause is known. Read "historical" in this context as "the older, aetiological, cause-based approach", and the contrast is simple: the syndromal approach rests on clinical signs and symptoms, the historical approach on known aetiology. Why, then, are the DSM and ICD mainly syndromal? Because for most mental disorders the ideal is out of reach. Sections 1.3 to 1.5 showed that the causes of most disorders are unknown, or are many small causes acting together (dozens or hundreds of genes of small effect, early adversity, stress, the city, the family) with none of them necessary or sufficient. The same cause can lead to several different disorders: childhood maltreatment raises the risk of depression, posttraumatic stress disorder, substance use disorders and personality disorders. And the same disorder can be reached by different routes in different people. A classification built on causes would have to be built on theories of cause, and history shows what happens then. The "neuroses" of DSM-I and DSM-II were defined partly by a psychoanalytic theory of unconscious conflict, so clinicians who did not share the theory could not apply the categories consistently. DSM-III's answer in 1980 was to describe disorders by what can be observed and reported and to stay as neutral as possible about cause (Section 1.7.3). ICD-10 took the same descriptive line. Aetiology has not vanished, however. It returns wherever a cause is secure enough to rely on, so the modern manuals are really hybrids: syndromal at their core, aetiological at their edges. You will meet the aetiological edges in five places. Disorders due to another medical condition. Neelam's diagnosis is one; anxiety disorder due to hyperthyroidism and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition are others. The cause is part of the name. Substance/medication-induced disorders. An alcohol-induced depressive disorder or a psychotic disorder induced by a stimulant is defined by its cause (Chapter 10). The organic block of ICD-10 and the secondary syndromes of ICD-11. ICD-10 groups delirium, dementia and other conditions with a demonstrable brain cause in its first block, F00 to F09; ICD-11 has a grouping of secondary mental or behavioural syndromes caused by a medical condition (Sections 1.9.4 and 1.9.5). The trauma- and stressor-related disorders. Posttraumatic stress disorder cannot be diagnosed without exposure to a traumatic event, and adjustment disorder requires an identifiable stressor (Sections 7.2 and 7.4). Even here the event is necessary but not sufficient: most people exposed to trauma never develop the disorder. The neurocognitive disorders. Major and mild neurocognitive disorder are first diagnosed as syndromes and then subtyped by aetiology: due to Alzheimer's disease, vascular, with Lewy bodies, due to traumatic brain injury, and so on (Chapter 10). Three older divisions of disorder belong to the same debate and are worth one sentence each, because the terms are still in common use. The division between organic disorders (caused by a demonstrable physical disease of the brain or body) and functional disorders (no such cause found, also called "psychogenic") was used in the DSM up to DSM-III-R; DSM-IV dropped it in 1994 because it wrongly implied that "functional" disorders have no biology and that "organic" ones have no psychology, and replaced it with "due to a general medical condition", "substance-induced" and "primary" (DSM-5 later changed "primary" to "independent"). The division between psychosis and neurosis is taught in Section 6.1.3. The division of depression into endogenous (arising from within) and reactive (a response to events) is taught in Section 5.1.5. Table 1.16 brings the two main approaches together. Option sets love to swap the two, so read every word. "The syndromal approach is not used in psychiatry" is the reverse of the truth: it is the approach the DSM and ICD mainly use. And neither approach belongs only to medical or only to psychiatric illness: medicine uses both (migraine and irritable bowel syndrome are still syndromal categories), and so does psychiatry (Neelam's depressive disorder due to hypothyroidism is aetiological). Finally, "organic versus functional" was dropped by DSM-IV, not by DSM-5. Categories, dimensions and prototypes Sorting by symptoms still leaves a second choice: boxes or scales. In categorical classification a person either has a disorder or does not, as a woman either is or is not pregnant. In its classical form, which goes back to Kraepelin, every member of a category shares the same defining features and, it is hoped, the same cause. In dimensional classification each person is placed on one or more continuous scales, as blood pressure and height are measured, so that a patient might be described as very anxious, moderately low in mood and only slightly suspicious. Between them sits prototypical classification , which is what the DSM and ICD actually do: a category is described by a typical case, and a person qualifies by matching enough of its features. Criteria of the "any five of these nine" kind are called polythetic criteria ; criteria that require every listed feature are called monothetic criteria . The standard example is the major depressive episode, which needs at least five of nine symptoms over the same two weeks, one of them depressed mood or loss of interest. The consequence is startling when you first work it out. One man may have depressed mood, weight loss, broken sleep, slowed movements and exhaustion; another may have depressed mood, loss of interest, crushing guilt, poor concentration and thoughts of death. They share a single criterion, yet both have the same diagnosis. Even within one criterion the features can be opposites, since "insomnia or hypersomnia" and "weight loss or gain" each count once. Book 2, Section 2.10.2 compares the three approaches in its Table 2.33, and Book 1, Section 8.2.3 explains the psychology of prototypes. The categorical approach dominates because clinicians must make yes-or-no decisions (treat or not, admit or not, certify or not) and because names are easier to communicate than profiles of numbers. But DSM-5-TR is unusually frank about the costs. In the chapter that introduces its dimensional measures it lists six problems with categorical diagnosis, and each deserves a sentence of explanation. No zones of rarity. If disorders were natural kinds, there should be gaps, "zones of rarity", between them and between each disorder and health, where few people fall, as there are between measles and chickenpox. The British psychiatrist Robert Evan Kendell (1935 to 2002) made this the test of a valid category. For most mental disorders the gaps are not there: depression shades into ordinary sadness and into generalised anxiety. The need for intermediate categories. Schizoaffective disorder exists because many patients fall between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (Section 4.5.3); a classification that needs bridges between its boxes is admitting that the boxes overlap. High rates of comorbidity. Many people meet the criteria for two, three or more disorders at once (Section 1.2.7), which is what you would expect if the categories were slices of a few underlying dimensions. Frequent use of "other specified" and "unspecified" diagnoses. Large numbers of patients fit no category well and end up in the residual ones (Section 1.8.4). Few unique antecedent validators. The categories have not led to distinctive causes. Genes, brain findings and childhood risks turn out to be shared across many disorders (Section 1.4.6). Lack of treatment specificity. The same treatments work across categories: a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor helps depression, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, generalised anxiety disorder and bulimia nervosa. DSM-5 (2013) therefore added dimensional elements to a categorical frame. Some categories became spectrum disorders, the clearest case being autism spectrum disorder, which absorbed several separate DSM-IV diagnoses (Section 1.7.6), and the schizophrenia spectrum chapter, which runs from schizotypal personality disorder to schizophrenia. Many disorders gained severity ratings (mild, moderate, severe), and Section III added cross-cutting symptom measures that rate problems such as anxiety, depression and poor sleep in every patient whatever the diagnosis (Section 1.8.5), and an alternative, trait-based model of personality disorder (Chapter 11). The core, however, is still a list of categories. Is that core real? Can one ever find out whether a condition is truly a category or truly a dimension? The American psychologist Paul Everett Meehl (1920 to 2003), whose theory of schizotaxia you met in Section 1.3.4, believed that one could, and with his colleagues he developed a family of statistical procedures called taxometrics . A taxon is a natural category: a group whose members really differ in kind from everyone else, so that their scores on several indicators are related within the whole sample only because the sample is a mixture of two latent groups. Taxometric procedures (with names such as MAXCOV and MAMBAC) look for the statistical fingerprints of such a hidden mixture. The results, pooled by the Melbourne psychologist Nick Haslam and his colleagues, are clear. A 2012 review of 177 articles and 311 findings estimated that only about 14 percent of findings were truly taxonic once weaker methods were allowed for, with little convincing evidence of taxa for mood, anxiety, eating or externalising problems or for most personality disorders, and more promising evidence for schizotypy, substance use disorders and autism. A 2020 meta-analysis of 317 findings found dimensional results outnumbering taxonic ones by about five to one, with alcohol use disorder, intermittent explosive disorder, problem gambling, autism, suicide risk and paedophilia as the most plausible candidate taxa. For most of psychopathology, in other words, the categories are cut-points placed on continua, which is exactly what Section 1.1.5 argued about the line between normal and abnormal. If the underlying structure is dimensional, what are the dimensions? Two research programmes have tried to answer from the data upwards rather than from expert committees downwards. The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP), set out by Roman Kotov and a large consortium of colleagues in 2017, groups individual signs and symptoms into narrow components and traits, these into syndromes, syndromes into subfactors, subfactors into broad spectra and spectra into superspectra, all according to which problems actually co-occur. Its six spectra so far are internalising, thought disorder, disinhibited externalising, antagonistic externalising, detachment and somatoform. In HiTOP, comorbidity stops being a nuisance and becomes information: depression and generalised anxiety co-occur because they are neighbouring parts of the internalising spectrum. At the very top of such a hierarchy sits the p factor . In 2014 Avshalom Caspi and his colleagues analysed 20 years of mental health data, from adolescence to midlife, in the Dunedin cohort in New Zealand. Three broad factors (internalising, externalising and thought disorder) explained the pattern of disorders well, but a single general factor of psychopathology explained it even better. They named it p , by analogy with g , the general factor of intelligence, and found that people higher on p had more impairment in life, more affected relatives, harder childhoods and more signs of compromised brain function early in life. Neither HiTOP nor the p factor is an official manual; they are research frameworks, like the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) of the United States National Institute of Mental Health, which studies dimensions of functioning from genes and circuits up to behaviour (Book 2, Section 2.10.6). Exam trap DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR are categorical systems with polythetic (prototypical) criteria and some dimensional additions (spectra, severity ratings, cross-cutting measures, the Section III personality model). They are not dimensional systems. "Five of nine symptoms" is polythetic ; "all of the following" is monothetic . A taxon is a natural category, and taxometrics (Meehl) tests for one; most findings favour dimensions. The p factor is Caspi and colleagues (2014), named by analogy with Spearman's g ; HiTOP is Kotov and colleagues (2017); RDoC belongs to the US National Institute of Mental Health. None of the three is a diagnostic manual. Hierarchy, exclusion and the "better explained" rule Tanvir is a 30-year-old tailor from Bhopal with a ten-year history of schizophrenia. During his present relapse he hears voices commenting on him and is sure that his neighbours are poisoning his water. He is also tense and fearful most of the day, sleeps badly, has lost interest in his work and says he feels "finished". Counted mechanically against the criteria, his symptoms might seem to justify four diagnoses: schizophrenia, a generalised anxiety disorder, insomnia disorder and a depressive episode. No experienced clinician would write all four. The anxiety, the sleeplessness and the low mood are understood as part of the psychotic relapse, and they are expected to lift as the psychosis is treated. The rule being applied here is one of the oldest in clinical psychiatry. The diagnostic hierarchy arranges disorders in an order of precedence. In its classical form the order is: organic states (brain disease, delirium, dementia, intoxication) at the top; then the psychoses such as schizophrenia; then the mood (affective) disorders; then the neurotic disorders, such as anxiety; and personality disorders at the bottom. A condition higher in the order can produce the symptoms of conditions below it, but not the other way round. A brain tumour or a delirium can produce delusions, low mood and anxiety; schizophrenia can produce low mood and anxiety; depression can produce anxiety; but an anxiety disorder does not produce delusions. So when a higher condition is present, it is diagnosed, and the lower symptoms are treated as part of it rather than given names of their own. There is a practical logic as well. The higher conditions are usually the more urgent and the more specifically treatable, so they must be looked for first: missing a brain tumour in a man with "anxiety" costs far more than missing his anxiety. The principle is usually traced to Karl Jaspers (1883 to 1969), whose General Psychopathology (1913) you will meet in Chapter 2. In Britain the psychologist Graham Foulds tested it with questionnaires. The Delusions-Symptoms-States Inventory, which he devised with his colleague Bedford, lists his levels in its very name, from delusions at the top, through neurotic symptoms, down to states of anxiety and depression at the bottom. Foulds and Bedford (1975) reported that the symptoms of about 93 percent of 480 psychiatric patients fitted the predicted pattern: people with symptoms at a higher level nearly always had symptoms at every lower level too. Foulds set out the full model in The Hierarchical Nature of Personal Illness (1976). DSM-III (1980) built the hierarchy into its criteria as exclusion criteria : rules stating that a diagnosis may not be made if the symptoms are due to, or occur only during, another disorder. Many anxiety diagnoses, for example, could not be made if the anxiety arose during a depressive episode or during schizophrenia. The rules soon met an awkward fact. Key study: Do excluded disorders really belong to the dominant ones? (Boyd and colleagues, 1984) The question was whether DSM-III's exclusion rules matched the way symptoms actually cluster in the population. Boyd and his colleagues used the National Institute of Mental Health's Diagnostic Interview Schedule with a community sample of 11,519 adults in the United States and scored every syndrome without applying the exclusion rules. They found that when two disorders were linked by an exclusion rule, having the "dominant" one greatly raised the odds of also having the "excluded" one, as the hierarchy assumed. But they also found a broad tendency for disorders to co-occur in general: having almost any disorder raised the odds of having almost any other, including pairs that DSM-III treated as unrelated. The authors concluded that the assumptions behind the hierarchy should be tested empirically rather than taken on trust. A limitation is that a community survey using a structured interview given by lay interviewers may count mild syndromes that a clinician would not; even so, studies like this one helped persuade the next revision to loosen the rules. DSM-III-R (1987) did loosen them. Many of the hierarchical exclusions were removed, so that, for example, panic disorder and major depression could now be diagnosed together when each met its own criteria. One consequence was a boom in recorded comorbidity, and with it the research on comorbidity described in Section 1.2.7. Some exclusions survived into DSM-IV: generalised anxiety disorder, for instance, could still not be diagnosed if it occurred only during a mood disorder. Today's criteria carry the hierarchy in two standard clauses, and once you know them you will see them at the end of nearly every criteria set in Chapters 3 to 11. "Not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition." This is the old organic tier at the top of the hierarchy. The generalised anxiety disorder criteria even name an example, hyperthyroidism, because an overactive thyroid can produce tremor, palpitations, restlessness and worry that look exactly like an anxiety disorder. "Not better explained by another mental disorder." This replaces many of DSM-III's rigid rules with a clinical judgement. Worry that is only about having panic attacks is better explained by panic disorder (Section 6.2.3); worry that is only about contamination is better explained by obsessive-compulsive disorder; and schizophrenia is diagnosed only after schizoaffective disorder and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features have been ruled out (Section 4.4.2). Notice what the modern rule does and does not forbid. It forbids giving a separate name to symptoms that are simply part of another disorder, as with Tanvir's anxiety during his relapse. It does not forbid two diagnoses when each disorder is independently present. If Tanvir had also had, for years and between his psychotic episodes, intrusive fears of contamination with hours of washing, he could receive a diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder as well, because his schizophrenia would not explain it. The same logic decides the order in which a clinician works through the possibilities, a process called differential diagnosis . The American psychiatrist Michael B. First , the editor of DSM-5-TR, sets it out in six steps: first rule out feigning (malingering or factitious disorder); then rule out a substance or medication as the cause; then rule out another medical condition; only then decide which primary mental disorder or disorders are present; then decide whether an adjustment disorder or an "other specified" or "unspecified" category fits better; and finally decide whether the problem crosses the line into disorder at all (Book 2, Section 2.9.8 walks a case through the steps). The hierarchy and First's steps express one idea: look first for the causes that are most dangerous to miss and most specifically treatable. Neelam's thyroid test in Section 1.6.3 is step three in action. Exam trap The classical hierarchy runs organic, then psychotic, then mood, then neurotic, then personality : a higher condition explains the symptoms of a lower one, never the reverse. DSM-III (1980) enforced it with exclusion criteria; DSM-III-R (1987) relaxed many of them , which is one reason comorbidity rose. Today's two clauses are "not attributable to a substance or another medical condition" (the organic tier) and "not better explained by another mental disorder". The hierarchy does not forbid comorbidity when each disorder is independently present. The definition of comorbidity itself is in Section 1.2.7. Reliability and validity How do you judge whether a way of sorting people is any good? Two questions do most of the work. The first is whether different clinicians, using the same system on the same person, reach the same answer. That is the reliability of a diagnosis. It is tested in two main ways. One is inter-rater reliability : agreement between two or more clinicians who judge the same information, for example two psychologists who each rate the same recorded interview without consulting each other. The other is test-retest reliability : agreement between two separate assessments of the same person a short time apart, usually by different clinicians; it is the harder test, because the patient may tell a different story the second time. Book 2, Section 2.1.3 tells how badly psychiatry did on this test in the 1950s and 1960s: Aaron T. Beck (1921 to 2021) and his colleagues found in 1962 that pairs of experienced psychiatrists agreed on a specific diagnosis only about half the time, the US-UK Diagnostic Project showed that New York and London psychiatrists used "schizophrenia" for different patients, and the largest source of disagreement turned out to be criterion variance, clinicians applying different rules to the same information. Section 1.7.2 shows how that crisis drove the making of DSM-III. Agreement is measured with Cohen's kappa , introduced by the American psychologist Jacob Cohen (1923 to 1998) in 1960. Raw percentage agreement flatters clinicians, because some agreement happens by chance alone, so kappa asks how far the observed agreement rises above chance: kappa = (observed agreement minus chance agreement) divided by (1 minus chance agreement). A kappa of 1 means perfect agreement and 0 means agreement no better than chance. Because chance agreement depends on how common the diagnosis is, kappa is sensitive to the base rate of the condition in the sample. Book 2, Section 2.10.5 works through a calculation step by step and gives the conventions for what counts as a good kappa. The headline from the DSM-5 field trials, which used a demanding design in which two clinicians interviewed each patient separately, is worth remembering: kappa was about 0.67 for posttraumatic stress disorder and 0.46 for schizophrenia, but only 0.28 for major depressive disorder and 0.20 for generalised anxiety disorder (Darrel Regier and colleagues, 2013). Two of the most common diagnoses in everyday practice were among the least reliable. The second question is whether the category is real and useful: does it pick out a condition with its own features, causes, course and response to treatment? That is diagnostic validity . In 1970 Eli Robins and Samuel B. Guze of Washington University proposed that a diagnosis is validated in five phases: clinical description, laboratory studies, delimitation from other disorders, follow-up studies and family studies. In 1980 Kenneth S. Kendler sorted the evidence by timing into antecedent validators (family history, premorbid personality, precipitating factors), concurrent validators (psychological test results, biological markers) and predictive validators (stability of the diagnosis, course, response to treatment). The two qualities are linked in one direction only. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. A diagnosis that clinicians cannot agree on cannot be valid, because it does not consistently pick out anything; but perfect agreement guarantees nothing. Two record clerks who sorted every patient by month of birth would agree perfectly, and their twelve categories would predict nothing about anyone's illness. By these standards most psychiatric categories are only partly validated, which led Kendell and Assen Jablensky in 2003 to urge a distinction between validity and clinical utility , the usefulness of a category for communication, prediction and choosing treatment. Many DSM and ICD categories, they argued, have not been shown to be distinct natural entities separated by zones of rarity, yet they are very useful; the danger lies only in forgetting the difference and treating a useful name as a discovered thing. Book 2, Section 2.10.6 develops the argument. Exam trap Reliability asks "do we agree?"; validity asks "is what we agree on real and meaningful?". A diagnosis can be reliable but invalid , never valid but unreliable. Kappa corrects agreement for chance (Cohen, 1960); 0 means chance-level agreement, not "no diagnoses made". The five phases of validation are Robins and Guze (1970); antecedent, concurrent and predictive validators are Kendler (1980); validity versus utility is Kendell and Jablensky (2003). Low reliability is a different problem from a high false-positive rate, which the next subsection explains. When diagnosis goes wrong: false positives and false negatives Reliability tells you whether clinicians agree with each other. It does not tell you whether they are right. To ask that, you need a standard of truth: some better way of knowing who really has the disorder, such as a careful interview by an experienced clinician, a structured research interview, or the course of the illness over the following years. Once you have such a standard, every diagnostic decision can be placed in one of four boxes, because the person either has the disorder or does not, and the clinician (or the questionnaire, or the screening test) either says so or does not. A true positive is a person who has the disorder and is diagnosed with it: a case correctly found. A false positive is a person who does not have the disorder but is diagnosed with it anyway: a well person labelled disordered. This is over-diagnosis . A false negative is a person who has the disorder but is not diagnosed: a real case missed. This is under-diagnosis . A true negative is a person without the disorder who is correctly cleared. Two summary figures describe how good a test or a set of criteria is, and each is read down one column of the table in Figure 1.10. The first, sensitivity , is the proportion of people who truly have the disorder whom the test correctly identifies: true positives divided by everyone with the disorder. A sensitive test misses few cases. The second, specificity , is the proportion of people who truly do not have the disorder whom the test correctly clears: true negatives divided by everyone without the disorder. A specific test rarely raises a false alarm. A high false-positive rate therefore means low specificity; a high false-negative rate means low sensitivity. Sensitivity and specificity describe the test. But the clinician facing one patient with a positive result wants to know something different: given this result, how likely is it that this person really has the disorder? That is the positive predictive value , the proportion of positive results that are true positives, read across the top row of the table. Its partner, the negative predictive value , is the proportion of negative results that are true negatives. Here is the surprise that every clinician has to learn, often the hard way: the predictive values depend not only on the test but on how common the disorder is in the group being tested, its base rate (the prevalence of Section 1.2.6). Key study: Meehl and Rosen on base rates (1955) The question that Paul Meehl and Albert Rosen asked in the Psychological Bulletin in 1955 sounds simple: when is a psychological test sign or cutting score actually worth using? Their method was logical and arithmetical rather than experimental. They showed, with worked cases, that the usefulness of any sign depends on the antecedent probability (what we now call the base rate) of the condition in the population where it is used. Their result was uncomfortable for clinicians. When a condition is rare, even a sign with good accuracy can produce more wrong decisions than simply predicting, for everyone, the more common outcome, because most of its positive results come from the large group of people who do not have the condition. Their conclusion was that test manuals should report base rates, that a cutting score chosen in one setting may be wrong in another, and that clinicians routinely neglect the base rate when they interpret a test result. The criticism, which they anticipated, is that counting errors is not enough: a missed suicide and a false alarm are not equally bad, so the costs of each kind of error have to be weighed as well. The habit of ignoring base rates is now called base-rate neglect, and it is studied by cognitive psychologists as well as clinicians. Push a case through the arithmetic, because this idea only clicks when you do. A university counselling centre gives a depression questionnaire to all 1,000 first-year students. Suppose the questionnaire has a sensitivity of 90 percent and a specificity of 90 percent, which is good for a short screen, and suppose that 5 percent of the students truly have a depressive disorder. Split the population by the truth. Five percent of 1,000 is 50 students with depression; the other 950 do not have it. Apply the sensitivity to the 50. Ninety percent of 50 is 45 true positives; the remaining 5 are false negatives, students with depression whom the screen misses. Apply the specificity to the 950. Ninety percent of 950 is 855 true negatives; the remaining 10 percent, 95 students, are false positives. Count the positives. The screen flags 45 + 95 = 140 students. Work out the positive predictive value. Only 45 of the 140 flagged students are truly depressed: 45 divided by 140 is about 32 percent. Roughly two out of every three positive results are false alarms. Work out the negative predictive value. Of the 860 students the screen clears, 855 are truly well: about 99.4 percent. Read down a column for sensitivity and specificity, which describe the test; read across a row for the predictive values, which describe what a result means. Notice that the false positives (95) outnumber the true positives (45) even though the screen is right 90 percent of the time in each column. Now notice two things. First, the screen is "90 percent accurate" in both directions, yet most of its positive results are wrong. That is not a flaw in the questionnaire; it is the arithmetic of a rare condition. Because the well students outnumber the depressed ones by 19 to 1, even a small error rate among the well produces a crowd of false positives. Second, the screen makes 100 errors in all (95 false positives and 5 false negatives), so it is right about 900 of the 1,000 students. A counsellor who simply declared every student well, without testing anyone, would be right about 950. This is exactly Meehl and Rosen's point. The screen is still worth using, because it finds 45 of the 50 students who need help, but only if everyone it flags is then properly assessed before anyone is told that they have a disorder.
