Lower the threshold of a questionnaire, or loosen the criteria for a diagnosis, and sensitivity rises: fewer cases are missed, but more well people are caught. Raise the threshold, or tighten the criteria, and specificity rises: fewer false alarms, but more real cases slip through. Loose criteria therefore breed false positives, over-diagnosis and the medicalisation of ordinary unhappiness that Section 1.1.5 warned about. Strict criteria breed false negatives: people with real and treatable disorders who receive no help, which in India adds to the very large treatment gap described in Section 1.2.6. Think back to Harish in Section 1.6.1: his first episode of mania, at 25, was put down to "examination stress" by the family doctor, and the false negative cost him three years without treatment. Which error is worse depends on the setting. A suicide-risk screen in an emergency department should be set to tolerate many false positives, because a false alarm costs a careful conversation and a missed case can cost a life. A decision with heavy consequences for the person, such as an admission without consent under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (Book 2, Section 1.10.7) or a diagnosis that will be disclosed to a prospective employer, should demand high specificity, because the harm of a false positive is serious and hard to undo. That is why good practice runs in two stages: a sensitive, cheap screen that casts a wide net, followed by a careful clinical assessment of everyone it catches. You may also meet the labels Type I and Type II error for these mistakes. They come from statistical hypothesis testing, where the null hypothesis is that nothing is there. If the null hypothesis is "this person has no disorder", then diagnosing a well person rejects a true null hypothesis, a Type I error (a false positive), and missing a real case fails to reject a false null hypothesis, a Type II error (a false negative). The Research Methodology book explains the statistical terms. Clinical link Short screening questionnaires for depression, anxiety and alcohol use are increasingly used in Indian primary health centres and college counselling services (the instruments themselves belong to the Assessment book). The arithmetic of this subsection tells you how to talk to a student who has "screened positive": not "you have depression", but "your answers suggest you may be going through a lot; let us talk about it properly". The screen opens the conversation; it does not make the diagnosis. Exam trap A high false-positive rate means that normal people are diagnosed as disordered . It reflects low specificity and criteria that are too loose , not too strict. "Disordered people go undetected" describes a high false-negative rate (low sensitivity, criteria too strict). "Low reliability" means that raters disagree with each other, which is a different problem: two clinicians can agree perfectly and both be wrong. Sensitivity is read among the truly ill, specificity among the truly well, and the predictive values among the test results; only the predictive values change with the base rate. The costs of a label Every diagnosis is also a label, and a label travels. It goes into the case file and the insurance form, into the family's conversations and the neighbours' gossip, and into the person's own picture of himself. Book 2 tells the story of the critics who made this point famous: the sociologists of labelling, Edwin Lemert, Thomas Scheff and Erving Goffman, the later and more modest modified labelling theory of Bruce Link and his colleagues, Thomas Szasz's attack on the very idea of mental illness, and the pseudopatient study and the doubts that have since engulfed it (Book 2, Sections 1.6.7 and 2.10.7). That story is not retold here. What matters for a student of the disorders is the set of harms and benefits that any label carries, and the habits that keep the harms small. The harms come in three forms. The first, public stigma , is the prejudice and discrimination of the community: the assumption that a person with schizophrenia is dangerous, the landlord who will not rent to him, the family that breaks off a marriage negotiation when it hears of a sister's depression. The second, self-stigma , is what happens when the person comes to believe the stereotype about himself, loses self-esteem and stops trying ("who would give a job to someone like me?"). The third, diagnostic overshadowing , is the clinician's version: once a psychiatric label is on the file, new problems are put down to it. When Tanvir, whose schizophrenia you met in Section 1.6.5, came to the emergency department breathless and feverish, the first doctor wrote "anxious, known psychiatric case"; it took a second doctor and a chest X-ray to find his pneumonia. The term was introduced by Steven Reiss and his colleagues in 1982 for emotional problems missed in people with intellectual disability, and it is now used most often for physical illness missed in people with mental disorders. A label also brings benefits, and a fair account must include them. It can bring relief ("this has a name; I am not simply weak or wicked"), it opens the door to treatment and to the research on what works, and it gives access to sick leave, insurance cover, disability certification (Book 2, Section 9.9) and the protections of the law. Three habits keep the balance on the right side. Use person-first language. Treat every diagnosis as a working hypothesis that can be revised when the evidence changes. And pair the diagnosis with a formulation that describes the person's story, context and strengths (Book 2, Section 2.9), so that the label is never the only thing written about him. Indian context The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 writes three protections against the misuse of labels into its very first rules on diagnosis. Section 3(2) forbids anyone to classify a person as a person with mental illness except for purposes directly related to treatment, or as the Act or another law provides. Section 3(4) says that past treatment or hospitalisation in a mental health establishment, though relevant, does not by itself justify any present or future determination that the person is mentally ill. Section 3(5) says that a determination of mental illness does not by itself mean that the person is of unsound mind, unless a competent court has declared so. In plain words: a diagnosis is for care, an old diagnosis is not a life sentence, and a diagnosis is not a declaration of incompetence. Section 3(1), which ties the determination of mental illness to the ICD, is discussed in Section 1.9.3. Exam trap Public stigma is the community's prejudice; self-stigma is the person applying it to himself; diagnostic overshadowing (Reiss and colleagues, 1982) is a clinician attributing new problems to an existing label. Labelling theory and its critics belong to Book 2 and the Social book; the DSM-5-TR rule that socially deviant behaviour is not in itself a disorder is taught in Section 1.1.3. Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, past treatment alone cannot justify a present determination of mental illness (section 3(4)), and mental illness does not equal unsound mind without a court's declaration (section 3(5)). 1.7 The DSM from DSM-I to DSM-5-TR, and the Multiaxial System Medium yield · 3 Qs Say the full name of the American manual slowly: the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders . Why "statistical"? A book of diagnostic criteria has no obvious need for statistics. The word is a fossil, and like all fossils it records a history. The manual did not grow out of a wish to understand mental disorders; it grew out of a government's wish to count them. This section follows that history from a nineteenth-century census to the edition on the desk of every clinician today, DSM-5-TR. Along the way it teaches the best-known structure the manual ever had, the five axes of DSM-III and DSM-IV, by building a complete five-axis record for a real-sounding patient, and it explains why DSM-5 threw the axes away. The ICD's parallel history is told in Section 1.9, and the inside of today's DSM-5-TR (its sections, chapters, specifiers and codes) in Section 1.8. Before the DSM: counting the insane The first official attempt to collect information about mental illness in the United States was the census of 1840, which recorded the frequency of a single category, "idiocy/insanity", household by household. One category is about the crudest classification imaginable: it lumps together what we would now call intellectual disability, psychosis, dementia and much else. But the census of 1840 is remembered for something worse than crudeness. Key study: The census that found too much madness (Edward Jarvis, 1844) When the 1840 figures were printed, they seemed to show that insanity and idiocy were far more common among free Black Americans in the northern states than among enslaved people in the South. Defenders of slavery seized on the numbers as proof that freedom drove Black people mad; in 1844 the Secretary of State, John C. Calhoun (1782 to 1850), cited the census in a letter to the British government defending slavery. The Massachusetts physician Edward Jarvis (1803 to 1884) went back to the returns town by town. He found that the 133 "coloured" insane recorded for Worcester, Massachusetts, were in fact the white patients of the state hospital, entered in the wrong column, and that towns with no Black inhabitants at all had been credited with insane Black residents. He published his analysis, "Insanity among the coloured population of the free states", in the American Journal of the Medical Sciences in 1844 and concluded that the figures were worthless. An official review nevertheless defended them, and they went on being quoted. Jarvis spent much of the rest of his life campaigning for better statistics (he was president of the American Statistical Association from 1852 until his death) and is remembered as a pioneer of American psychiatric epidemiology. The lesson has not dated: a classification applied carelessly by untrained counters produces numbers, and numbers, once printed, will be used for whatever purpose suits the user. Forty years later, the census of 1880 distinguished seven categories of mental illness: mania, melancholia, monomania, paresis, dementia, dipsomania and epilepsy. Several of the terms need translation. Monomania was a nineteenth-century idea of madness confined to a single subject, a fixed false belief or obsession in an otherwise reasonable mind (Section 4.5.4 meets its descendant, delusional disorder). Paresis was general paresis, the brain syphilis of Section 1.6.3. Dipsomania meant bouts of uncontrollable craving for drink (Chapter 10). Epilepsy was still counted among the mental illnesses. The next step came from the asylum doctors themselves. In 1917 the Committee on Statistics of the American Medico-Psychological Association (the asylum superintendents' professional body), working with the National Committee for Mental Hygiene (founded in 1909; the APA's own history of the DSM calls it the National Commission on Mental Hygiene), drew up a plan for collecting uniform statistics across the country's mental hospitals, and the Bureau of the Census adopted it. It was published in 1918 as the Statistical Manual for the Use of Institutions for the Insane , with 22 diagnostic categories, and it is usually regarded as the first official psychiatric nosology in the United States. It paid more attention to clinical usefulness than the census lists had, but it was still above all a scheme for counting hospital patients. In 1921 the American Medico-Psychological Association changed its name to the American Psychiatric Association (APA), the name that appears on every DSM. Between the wars the APA also worked with the New York Academy of Medicine on a psychiatric nomenclature for the American Medical Association's Standard Classified Nomenclature of Disease, but it too was designed mainly for inpatients with severe psychiatric and neurological disorders. The Second World War exposed the limits of such schemes. The army's psychiatrists found that a nomenclature built for long-stay inpatients had no good place for many of the soldiers they saw. They were dealing with acute breakdowns under combat stress, bodily symptoms with emotional causes, and personality problems that surfaced under military discipline. A committee led by the American psychiatrist William C. Menninger (1899 to 1966) produced a new nomenclature for the army, the War Department Technical Bulletin known as Medical 203 (it is usually dated 1943, although some accounts date its release to 1945); one historian has called it the first psychodynamic nomenclature. The Veterans Administration modified it for its own clinics. These broader wartime systems strongly influenced the sixth revision of the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases, ICD-6, adopted in 1948, the first ICD to contain a section on mental disorders (Section 1.9.1). The APA's Committee on Nomenclature and Statistics then prepared a variant of the ICD-6 section for American use, and published it in 1952 as the first Diagnostic and Statistical Manual . Exam trap The "S" in DSM is for statistical , because American classification began as a way of counting patients: the 1840 census had one category, "idiocy/insanity"; the 1880 census had seven; the 1918 Statistical Manual for the Use of Institutions for the Insane was the first official American nosology. The American Medico-Psychological Association became the American Psychiatric Association in 1921 . The first ICD with a section on mental disorders was ICD-6 (1948) , and DSM-I (1952) began as an American variant of it. The DSM is published by the American Psychiatric Association, not the American Psychological Association. DSM-I (1952) and DSM-II (1968) DSM-I was a slim book, by the usual count 106 categories in about 130 pages. Its claim to a place in history is that it was the first official manual of mental disorders to contain a glossary describing each diagnostic category, so that a clinician could read what "schizophrenic reaction" was supposed to mean instead of guessing. That phrase shows its most distinctive feature: the word reaction ran right through the classification (schizophrenic reaction, depressive reaction, anxiety reaction). The word reflected the influence of the Swiss-born American psychiatrist Adolf Meyer (1866 to 1950), whose psychobiological view held that mental disorders are reactions of the whole personality to psychological, social and biological factors, rather than diseases that strike a person from outside. It was a humane idea and, in the post-war years, a psychoanalytically coloured one. DSM-II, which appeared in 1968, was built on a different decision: to base the American classification on the mental disorders section of the eighth revision of the ICD, ICD-8, for which APA representatives had acted as consultants, and both went into effect in 1968. By the usual count it was slightly longer, 182 categories in 134 pages. It dropped most of the "reactions" but kept the psychoanalytic vocabulary, above all the neuroses (anxiety neurosis, hysterical neurosis, depressive neurosis and others), which were understood as the outward signs of unconscious conflict and the defences against it (Section 6.1.4 follows the neuroses through every edition). The history of homosexuality's place in these manuals, from DSM-I's "sociopathic personality disturbance" to the vote of the APA's trustees in December 1973 that removed it from DSM-II, is told in Book 2, Section 2.10.3. Both manuals shared a weakness that mattered more than any single category: neither gave rules for deciding when a disorder was present. Each glossary entry was a short paragraph sketching a typical case, and each clinician decided how close a patient had to come to the sketch. The result, documented through the 1960s and early 1970s, was a crisis of reliability: the low agreement of experienced psychiatrists, the different meanings of "schizophrenia" in New York and London, and the discovery that most disagreement came from clinicians applying different rules to the same information (Section 1.6.6 and Book 2, Section 2.1.3). The remedy came from the neo-Kraepelinians of Section 1.6.2. In 1972 John Feighner , Eli Robins, Samuel Guze and their colleagues at Washington University published explicit diagnostic criteria for use in research on the main psychiatric disorders, now called the Feighner criteria , and a few years later Robert Spitzer, Jean Endicott and Robins developed them into the Research Diagnostic Criteria. For the first time, a diagnosis could be defined by a rule that two strangers could apply in the same way. The next edition of the DSM would apply that idea to the whole of psychiatry. Exam trap The dates are DSM-I 1952 and DSM-II 1968 ; ICD-6, the first ICD with a section on mental disorders, is 1948 . Some widely circulated Indian notes give DSM-II as 1962 and ICD-6 as 1952, and claim that DSM-5 "introduced Roman numerals". All three are wrong: 1962 is the year of Beck's reliability study, 1952 is DSM-I, and DSM-5 did the opposite, replacing Roman numerals with an Arabic one. DSM-I is the manual of "reactions" (Adolf Meyer); DSM-II kept the neuroses and was based on ICD-8. Neither had explicit criteria. DSM-III (1980): the revolution Work on the third edition began in 1974 under the direction of the American psychiatrist Robert L. Spitzer (1932 to 2015), who had helped write the Research Diagnostic Criteria, and the manual appeared in 1980. Its development, like that of its predecessors, was coordinated with the ICD, this time with ICD-9. (DSM-5-TR says ICD-9 was published in 1975 and implemented in 1978; other sources give 1979. The dates differ because an ICD revision is adopted in one year and comes into use later, a pattern you will meet again in Section 1.9.) DSM-III is the most important edition in the series, and it is worth knowing exactly what it changed. Explicit diagnostic criteria. For almost every disorder the glossary paragraph was replaced by a list of rules: which symptoms must be present, how many, for how long, and what must be ruled out. The Feighner and Research Diagnostic Criteria had done this for a handful of research diagnoses; DSM-III did it for the whole of clinical psychiatry. A descriptive approach neutral about causes. Disorders were defined by what could be observed or reported, not by presumed psychoanalytic or biological causes. The stance was called atheoretical . Its most visible casualty was the neurosis. Phobias, for example, were no longer classed as a "phobic neurosis" defined by unconscious conflict; they were placed in a new, broader group of anxiety disorders defined by their symptoms (Section 6.1.4). The multiaxial system. Each patient was described on five axes, so that the clinician looked beyond the main disorder to the personality, the body, the stresses and the level of functioning (Section 1.7.5). Fuller descriptions. Each disorder came with far more descriptive text than before, covering such matters as its associated features, age at onset, course, prevalence, sex ratio, familial pattern and differential diagnosis. Today's DSM-5-TR text headings (Section 1.2.8) are its descendants. Field trials. Draft criteria were tested in clinical settings before publication to check that clinicians could apply them reliably, a step that DSM-IV and DSM-5 repeated (the text revisions had none). DSM-III also introduced new categories, of which the most consequential was posttraumatic stress disorder, first named in DSM-III in 1980 after years of pressure from clinicians who worked with Vietnam veterans (Section 7.2). The book was much bigger than its predecessors, by the usual count 265 categories in 494 pages. And it spread far beyond the United States. When Maser, Kaelber and Weise surveyed the international use of diagnostic systems in 1991, they found that DSM-III had become popular because of its precise descriptive format, its neutrality about the causes of disorder and its multiaxial view of the whole person, and that more clinicians around the world were using DSM-III-R at the beginning of the 1990s than the ICD, the system designed for international use. The revolution had its critics, and their points are still worth making in an interview. First, an "atheoretical" manual is not free of theory: choosing to define disorders by observable symptoms and to treat them as discrete medical conditions is itself a theoretical choice, the neo-Kraepelinian one, and psychoanalysts protested that it threw away their way of understanding patients. Second, many of the cut-offs were committee decisions. Why five symptoms of nine, or two weeks rather than ten days? Barlow and Durand list "arbitrary decisions on criteria for many disorders" among DSM-III's shortcomings, along with low reliability for some diagnoses even with the new rules. Third, reliability was bought partly at the cost of validity: criteria were written to be easy to agree on, and agreement is not truth (Section 1.6.6). None of this undoes DSM-III's achievement. Before 1980, two psychiatrists could not be sure they meant the same thing by a diagnosis; after 1980 they could at least check. Exam trap DSM-III (1980), directed by Robert L. Spitzer , introduced explicit diagnostic criteria, the "atheoretical" descriptive approach and the multiaxial system ; none of these began with DSM-IV. Posttraumatic stress disorder was first named in DSM-III. "Atheoretical" means neutral about causes , not free of all assumptions. DSM-III's companion ICD was ICD-9, not ICD-10. Spitzer is also the best-known critic of the pseudopatient study (Book 2, Section 2.10.7); do not confuse him with Kraepelin, Kupfer or Frances. DSM-III-R (1987), DSM-IV (1994) and DSM-IV-TR (2000) Experience with DSM-III soon revealed inconsistencies and criteria that did not work as intended, so the APA appointed a work group to revise it, and its corrections were published in 1987 as DSM-III-R (the R stands for "revised"). Three changes matter for this chapter. Many of DSM-III's hierarchical exclusion rules were removed, so that co-occurring disorders could be diagnosed together (Section 1.6.5). DSM-III's category of ego-dystonic homosexuality was dropped (Book 2, Section 2.10.3). And Axis V became the Global Assessment of Functioning scale that Section 1.7.5 explains. By the usual count DSM-III-R had 292 categories in 567 pages. DSM-IV , published in 1994, was the culmination of a six-year effort that involved more than 1,000 people and numerous professional organisations. Its task force, chaired by the American psychiatrist Allen Frances (born 1942), set itself a rule: no change without empirical support, relying as little as possible on expert consensus. Every proposed change therefore went through three stages: systematic reviews of the published literature, reanalyses of large data sets that had been collected for other purposes, and 12 field trials testing the reliability and validity of alternative criteria. The developers worked closely with the WHO team preparing ICD-10 (published in 1992), and the result was increased congruence between the two systems. Five of DSM-IV's changes matter most for this book. The end of "organic" versus "functional". The old split between organically and psychologically based disorders was eliminated, for the reasons given in Section 1.6.3. The clinical significance criterion. To reduce false positives (Section 1.6.7), almost half the criteria sets gained a requirement that the symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning. The clinical significance criterion is still part of most DSM-5-TR criteria sets. New axes. Axis II was restricted to personality disorders and mental retardation (developmental disorders that DSM-III-R had placed on Axis II moved to Axis I), and Axis IV changed from a rating of stress to a list of psychosocial and environmental problems (Section 1.7.5). Culture. Appendix I added an Outline for Cultural Formulation and a Glossary of Culture-Bound Syndromes, the first serious attempt by the manual to deal with culture (Section 1.10.2). Criteria sets for further study. Appendix B collected proposed disorders that were not yet official, the ancestor of DSM-5's conditions for further study (Section 1.8.6). DSM-IV-TR (2000) was a text revision : the descriptive text accompanying each disorder was updated with the research published since 1994, and the diagnostic criteria were left virtually unchanged. Its multiaxial form, which the next subsection teaches, was the version in use around the world for thirteen years, which is why it still dominates older textbooks, case files and question banks. The multiaxial system A diagnosis on its own says very little about a person. "Generalised anxiety disorder" fits a contented retired professor who worries too much about his grandchildren and also a young man who is failing his examinations, sleeping four hours a night, borrowing money and hiding a physical illness. The multiaxial system was designed to stop clinicians from writing the name and moving on. Introduced in DSM-III (1980) and used, with changes, through DSM-III-R, DSM-IV and DSM-IV-TR, it required every patient to be described on five separate axes, each a different domain of information: the clinical disorder, the personality, the body, the circumstances and the overall level of functioning. Its purpose, in a phrase, was to make the clinician look at the whole person. In its final DSM-IV-TR form the axes were these. Axis I: Clinical disorders, and other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention. All the mental disorders except the personality disorders and mental retardation went here: schizophrenia, mood disorders, anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, eating disorders, the childhood disorders and the rest. So did the "other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention", problems such as bereavement or a relational problem that bring someone to a clinician without being disorders, recorded with codes that began with V (the V codes ; DSM-5-TR's equivalents are the Z codes of Section 1.8.7). Axis II: Personality disorders and mental retardation. The ten personality disorders and mental retardation (now called intellectual developmental disorder, Chapter 3) were recorded here. The clinician could also note prominent maladaptive personality features that fell short of a disorder, and habitual defence mechanisms. If there was nothing to record, the entry read "V71.09 No diagnosis on Axis II". Axis III: General medical conditions. Physical illnesses potentially relevant to understanding or managing the person's mental disorder: a thyroid disorder in a depressed patient, epilepsy in a patient with psychosis, diabetes in someone taking a medicine that raises weight. Axis IV: Psychosocial and environmental problems. The stresses and disadvantages that might affect diagnosis, treatment or outcome, generally those of the past year, listed under nine headings: problems with the primary support group (the family), problems related to the social environment, educational problems, occupational problems, housing problems, economic problems, problems with access to health care services, problems related to interaction with the legal system or crime, and other psychosocial and environmental problems. Axis V: Global Assessment of Functioning. A single number from 0 to 100 summarising the clinician's judgement of the person's overall psychological, social and occupational functioning on what the manual called a hypothetical continuum of mental health and illness. The Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) scale deserves a closer look, because it is the part of the system that most needs practice. It descends from a 0 to 100 Health-Sickness Rating Scale published by Lester Luborsky and colleagues in 1962 and from Jean Endicott and colleagues' Global Assessment Scale of 1976; DSM-III-R turned it into Axis V. The scale is divided into bands of ten points, each with an anchor description and examples (Table 1.19). The clinician finds the band that best fits, using one rule that students often miss: symptoms and functioning are judged separately, and if they point to different bands, the final rating always reflects the worse of the two. A man with mild symptoms who has stopped going to work is rated by his work; a woman who still works but has persistent thoughts of suicide is rated by her symptoms. The rating usually describes the present, though it could also be given for the highest level in the past year or at discharge. In DSM-III, Axis IV was a rating of the severity of the psychosocial stressors the person had faced, on a numbered scale, and Axis V was a rating of the highest level of adaptive functioning the person had reached in the past year, on a seven-point scale. Clinicians in the field trials found the stress rating hard to apply, not least because the same event (a divorce, a move, a loss of job) is crushing for one person and a relief for another. DSM-III-R replaced the old Axis V with the GAF, and DSM-IV replaced the stress rating with the list of problems you have just read. Axis II also changed: DSM-III-R had placed the developmental disorders there as well, and DSM-IV moved them to Axis I, leaving only personality disorders and mental retardation. Why give those two a separate axis at all? Because they are lifelong, background conditions, and the designers feared that they would be overlooked whenever a florid Axis I disorder such as a psychotic episode or a severe depression held the clinician's attention. A personality disorder changes how a depression should be treated and how quickly it will lift; mental retardation changes how a psychosis presents and how its treatment must be explained. Separate axes forced the question to be asked. The multiaxial idea was not only American: in 1997 the WHO published a three-axis presentation of ICD-10 for adult psychiatry (clinical diagnoses, disabilities and contextual factors), which Section 1.9 places in the ICD's history. The axes are easiest to understand by filling them in for one person. Meet Dinesh , whom you will follow through the next three sections of this chapter: Section 1.8.3 records his diagnosis in DSM-5-TR, Section 1.9.7 codes it in ICD-10 and ICD-11, and Section 1.10.3 shows his Cultural Formulation Interview. The running case: Dinesh Dinesh is 24 and unmarried, the elder son of a farming family from a village in eastern Uttar Pradesh. He holds a BA degree. For two years he has lived in a rented room in Delhi, preparing for a government recruitment examination; his coaching fees are paid from money his father borrowed. Four months ago his engagement was fixed, and the wedding is planned for after the examination results, about five months away. He comes to the psychiatry outpatient clinic of a Delhi general hospital on referral from a physician whom he has seen three times for "weakness". For about nine months he has worried, on most days, about many things: his health, the examination, the family's debt and the marriage. He cannot switch the worry off. He is restless, tires easily and cannot concentrate ("I read a page and nothing stays"); he is irritable, his neck and shoulders ache, and his sleep is broken. He has had no panic attacks, no obsessions or compulsions and no psychotic symptoms. His mood is "low at times", but he still enjoys watching cricket on his phone and the Sunday meals he shares with his elder cousin, and he has had no thoughts of suicide. He takes no alcohol, tobacco or other drugs. Dinesh has his own explanation. He is sure that his weakness comes from the loss of dhat , a whitish discharge he believes he sees in his urine, and from night emissions, and he fears that he is losing his strength and will not be able to satisfy his wife or father children. He has spent several thousand rupees at a roadside clinic that advertises cures for "gupt rog" (secret diseases) and has taken herbal powders. He has told no one in his family. The physician found a mild iron-deficiency anaemia, for which Dinesh is taking iron tablets; his thyroid function and urine tests were normal. He attends his coaching classes irregularly, failed the preliminary examination three months ago and avoids phone calls from his fiancée's family, but he still cooks, bathes and meets his cousin. He describes himself as conscientious and "a worrier since school". He has no past psychiatric history. A maternal uncle "had nerves"; nothing more is known. Now build his record in the DSM-IV-TR form, one axis at a time, and notice how each axis makes the clinician ask a different question. Axis I: what clinical disorder is present? The clinician works through the criteria for generalised anxiety disorder as DSM-IV-TR wrote them. Dinesh has excessive worry on more days than not for at least six months (nine, in fact) about a number of events and activities, and he finds it hard to control. He has not merely three but all six of the associated symptoms: restlessness, being easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension (the aching neck and shoulders) and disturbed sleep. The worry is not confined to the features of another disorder: it is not only about having panic attacks (he has none), not only about contamination (he has no obsessions), and not only about having a serious illness, since his health is one worry among several. It causes clinically significant distress and impairment. Then come the hierarchy's questions from Section 1.6.5. Is a substance responsible? He uses none. Is a general medical condition responsible? His anaemia may add to his tiredness, but it cannot produce nine months of uncontrollable worry about debt and marriage, and his normal thyroid tests exclude a classic medical mimic of anxiety. Is the anxiety occurring only during a mood disorder, which DSM-IV-TR would have treated as excluding the diagnosis? His mood is low at times, but he still enjoys cricket and his Sunday meals and has no thoughts of suicide, so there is no major depressive episode. The diagnosis is 300.02 generalised anxiety disorder . His belief about dhat is not given a separate diagnosis here; the clinician treats it as his own cultural explanation of his weakness, to be recorded in the cultural formulation (DSM-IV-TR's Appendix I provided an outline for one and listed dhat in its glossary). Section 1.10.3 interviews him about it. Axis II: is there a personality disorder or mental retardation? There is no evidence of either. Dinesh is anxious and conscientious and has been "a worrier since school", but these are traits, not a pervasive, inflexible pattern that has damaged his life since adolescence. The entry is V71.09 no diagnosis on Axis II , with the anxious, conscientious traits noted in words, because they help explain why examination pressure hit him so hard and they will shape how he responds to treatment. Axis III: what physical illness is relevant? Iron-deficiency anaemia . It belongs on the record because it contributes to the tiredness and "weakness" that brought him to a doctor in the first place, and because it had to be considered and treated before his symptoms could be blamed on anxiety alone. Normal test results are not conditions and are not listed. Axis IV: what psychosocial and environmental problems are there? Three of the nine headings apply. Educational problems : he failed the preliminary examination three months ago. Economic problems : the family is in debt for his coaching. Problems with the primary support group : the pressure surrounding the coming marriage, the fiancée's family whose calls he avoids, and a family who do not know what he is going through. Axis V: how well is he functioning overall? Look at symptoms and functioning separately and take the worse. His symptoms are moderate: constant worry with bodily tension and poor sleep, but no suicidal ideation and no symptom that a band in the 40s would require. His functioning shows moderate difficulty: irregular attendance at coaching, a failed examination and avoidance of his future in-laws, yet he still looks after himself, sees his cousin and enjoys his cricket. Both point to the 51 to 60 band, "moderate symptoms or moderate difficulty", and the parts of his life that still work place him towards its upper end. The rating is GAF = 58 (current) . It is not in the 61 to 70 band, because his difficulties are more than "some"; it is not in the 41 to 50 band, because there is no serious symptom such as suicidal thinking and no serious impairment such as being unable to function at all. Notice that only Axis I and Axis II carry psychiatric codes; his belief about dhat is coded on none of the axes. Clinical link The axes have gone from the manual, but the five questions they asked have not gone from good practice. A well-written case summary in any Indian clinic still covers the disorder or disorders, the personality, the physical health, the current stresses and the level of functioning, because each changes the plan. For Dinesh, the anaemia needs treating, the examination and marriage pressures shape what can be done before his results, his conscientiousness will make him a diligent patient, and his functioning tells you how urgent things are. Section 1.8.3 shows how DSM-5-TR records the same information without axes. Exam trap Axis III is general medical conditions. Axis I is clinical disorders (the "clinical psychiatric diagnosis", plus the V codes); Axis II is personality disorders and mental retardation; Axis IV is psychosocial and environmental problems; Axis V is the Global Assessment of Functioning (0 to 100; rate the worse of symptoms and functioning). The axes arrived with DSM-III in 1980 , not with DSM-IV, and lasted through DSM-IV-TR; DSM-5 (2013) abolished them. In DSM-III, Axis IV rated the severity of stressors and Axis V the highest functioning in the past year; the GAF came with DSM-III-R (1987) and the list of problems on Axis IV with DSM-IV (1994). DSM-5 (2013): the axes go The fifth edition took longer to make than any before it. In 1999 the APA began an evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of the DSM, working with the WHO, the World Psychiatric Association and the United States National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH); the first fruit was a 2002 monograph called A Research Agenda for DSM-V , and between 2003 and 2008 thirteen international research planning conferences brought together about 400 participants from 39 countries to review the evidence for both the DSM and the coming ICD-11. In 2006 the APA named David J. Kupfer as chair and Darrel A. Regier as vice-chair of the DSM-5 Task Force, which worked through 13 diagnostic work groups. For the first time, every task force and work group member had to disclose income from industry and keep it under a cap, and draft criteria were posted on a website for public comment before field trials tested them. The manual was published in May 2013. Its name used an Arabic numeral, "5", rather than the Roman "V" of the planning documents, so that later updates could be numbered as software is (5.1, 5.2 and so on); in the event, the next revision was called DSM-5-TR. The most visible structural change was the end of the axes. DSM-5 moved to a non-axial record of diagnosis. Disorders and conditions formerly listed on Axis I (clinical disorders), Axis II (personality disorders and intellectual disability) and Axis III (other medical conditions) are now listed together, without formal differentiation, usually in order of clinical importance. The psychosocial and contextual factors of the old Axis IV are listed alongside them, using the Z codes of the chapter on other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention (Section 1.8.7). The GAF of Axis V was replaced by the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS), a measure of disability based on the WHO's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health and usable across all of medicine; it is printed in Section III of the manual (Section 1.8.5, and the Assessment book for the instrument itself). Three reasons are usually given for the change. First, separating Axis I from Axis II implied that personality disorders differ in kind from other mental disorders, as if they were fixed and untreatable, and research did not support so sharp a line: some personality disorders change considerably over time, while some "Axis I" disorders, such as the chronic depressions, are as enduring as any personality disorder. Second, a separate axis for "general medical conditions" suggested that mental disorders are not medical conditions. DSM-5-TR now says the opposite in so many words: "mental disorder" and "another medical condition" are merely terms of convenience and do not imply any fundamental distinction between them. (This is why DSM-5 replaced the phrase "general medical condition" with "another medical condition".) Third, the GAF was judged conceptually muddled, because one number mixed symptoms, suicide risk and disability, and its reliability in routine practice was questionable. A rating of 45 might mean a man who is suicidal but still at work, or a man with no thoughts of suicide who has lost his job and all his friends, and two clinicians could give the same patient quite different numbers. DSM-5 also rearranged its chapters. They now follow a developmental and lifespan order, beginning with the disorders thought to reflect processes that show themselves early in life (neurodevelopmental disorders, then the schizophrenia spectrum), moving through those that usually begin in adolescence and young adulthood (bipolar, depressive and anxiety disorders) and ending with those of later life (neurocognitive disorders). After the neurodevelopmental disorders, the chapters are grouped broadly into internalising disorders (with prominent anxiety, depressive and somatic symptoms), externalising disorders (with prominent impulsive, disruptive conduct and substance use symptoms), neurocognitive disorders and others, an arrangement meant to encourage research into what neighbouring disorders share. The loudest voice belonged to Allen Frances, who had chaired the DSM-IV task force. In his book Saving Normal (2013) and many articles he argued that DSM-5 would turn ordinary suffering into disorder: temper tantrums into disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, normal grief into major depression once the bereavement exclusion went, and the forgetfulness of old age into mild neurocognitive disorder. These are, in the language of Section 1.6.7, predictions of a rise in false positives. A different criticism came from the research side. On 29 April 2013, a few weeks before publication, the director of the NIMH, Thomas Insel , wrote that the institute would be "re-orienting its research away from DSM categories" towards its Research Domain Criteria (RDoC), because the DSM's categories lacked validity. Within weeks the NIMH and the APA issued a joint statement describing the two as complementary, the DSM for clinical diagnosis today and RDoC for the research that might change it tomorrow (Book 2, Section 2.10.6). Exam trap Compared with DSM-IV-TR, DSM-5 abolished the multiaxial system . It did not add a sixth axis, it did not keep the five axes, and it did not replace diagnoses with ICD codes: it still gives named diagnoses with criteria, and prints ICD-10-CM codes beside them for recording (Section 1.8.3). Former Axes I, II and III are listed together; Axis IV problems become Z codes; the GAF is replaced by the WHODAS. DSM-5 also changed "general medical condition" to "another medical condition", switched to an Arabic numeral, and ordered its chapters along the lifespan. DSM-5-TR (2022): the edition in use Nine years after DSM-5, in March 2022, the APA published DSM-5-TR , the first published revision of DSM-5. Its editor was Michael B. First, who co-chaired the Revision Subcommittee with Philip Wang, and more than 200 experts did most of the work. The manual is the product of three overlapping processes: the original criteria and text written by the DSM-5 Task Force for 2013; the online updates that the APA's DSM Steering Committee had issued since 2013 in response to clinical experience, new research and changes in the United States coding system; and a full rewrite of the descriptive text by the Revision Subcommittee. Four changes define it. Clarified criteria. The criteria sets of more than 70 disorders were modified, mostly for clarity. The conceptual content of the criteria was not changed, which is why criteria that originated in 2013 are still called "DSM-5 criteria". Updated text. The descriptive text of almost every disorder was revised in light of the research since 2013, most extensively the sections on prevalence, risk and prognostic factors, culture-related and sex- and gender-related diagnostic issues, association with suicidal thoughts or behaviour, and comorbidity (Section 1.2.8 explains these headings). One new diagnosis and new codes. Prolonged grief disorder became an official diagnosis in the chapter on trauma- and stressor-related disorders (its history as a condition for further study is told in Section 1.8.6 and the disorder itself in Section 7.4.3), and symptom codes were added for recording suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury (Section 1.8.7). Language and equity. For the first time the whole text was reviewed by a Work Group on Ethnoracial Equity and Inclusion, to give proper attention to risk factors such as the experience of racism and discrimination and to use non-stigmatising language. Some names changed: intellectual disability became intellectual developmental disorder (with "intellectual disability" kept in parentheses), to match ICD-11's "disorders of intellectual development" (Chapter 3), and conversion disorder became functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) , with the two names now in that order (Section 7.7). A residual category, unspecified mood disorder , was added for presentations in which it is hard to choose between an unspecified bipolar and an unspecified depressive disorder, for example in acute agitation. Compare that with the previous text revision. DSM-IV-TR (2000) confined its updates almost entirely to the text and left the criteria virtually unchanged; DSM-5-TR went further, clarifying criteria and adding a disorder. Both, however, are text revisions within an edition, not new editions. There is no DSM-6, and the planning documents of the early 2000s that spoke of "DSM-V" described the manual that was eventually published as DSM-5. Remember The DSM string: 1952, 1968, 1980, 1987, 1994, 2000, 2013, 2022 for DSM-I, DSM-II, DSM-III, DSM-III-R, DSM-IV, DSM-IV-TR, DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR. The turning points are DSM-III (explicit criteria and the five axes) and DSM-5 (axes abolished, Arabic numeral). Book 2, Section 2.10.3 drills the same string. Exam trap Asked which DSM is "currently in use", and offered DSM-IV, DSM-V, DSM-III and DSM-6, choose DSM-V : examiners often write the fifth edition with a Roman numeral, and "DSM-V" means DSM-5. Know, though, that the text now in use is DSM-5-TR (2022) , the text revision of DSM-5, and pick it if it is offered. DSM-IV and DSM-III are superseded, and there is no DSM-6. Do not confuse DSM-5-TR (APA, March 2022) with ICD-11 (WHO, adopted 2019, in effect from 1 January 2022), which happens to share the year (Section 1.9.5). Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. Now open the edition you will actually use. DSM-5-TR runs to more than a thousand pages, and it rewards a reader who knows its geography. A student who starts at page one wades through a long introduction and a classification list dozens of pages long before the first disorder appears. A student who jumps straight to the criteria for generalised anxiety disorder may never notice that half of what is needed to use those criteria properly lives somewhere else: in two pages on specifiers, in a coding rule, in a chapter of problems that are not disorders at all. This section is a guided tour. It shows how the book is built, why its disorder chapters come in the order they do, how a clinician turns a criteria set into a written diagnosis with its subtypes, specifiers and codes, what to do when a patient fits no category exactly, and what lives in the less-read parts of the manual: the rating scales, the alternative model of personality disorder, the proposed conditions for further study and the long list of "other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention". Section 1.9 then does the same for the World Health Organization's classification. Three sections and an appendix Before any numbered section comes the DSM-5-TR Classification , a list of every diagnosis in the manual in chapter order, each with its code and the page on which its criteria begin. Clinicians use it the way a traveller uses the index of a railway timetable: to find the right entry fast and to check a code. Then come three numbered sections and an appendix, stacked as Figure 1.13 shows. Section I, "DSM-5 Basics" , is the instruction booklet, and it has three parts. The Introduction tells how DSM-5 and its text revision were produced, explains the order of the chapters and the effort to harmonise them with ICD-11, and sets out the manual's key ideas: the definition of a mental disorder (Section 1.1.3), the uneasy marriage of categories and dimensions (Section 1.6.4), and the influence of culture, sex and gender on how disorders appear. Use of the Manual is the practical part: how to move from criteria to a diagnosis, what subtypes and specifiers are, when to use the "other specified" and "unspecified" categories, why clinical judgement matters and how to code and record what you have decided. Most of Sections 1.8.3 and 1.8.4 comes from these few pages, which students skip and examiners do not. The section closes with the Cautionary Statement for Forensic Use of DSM-5 . Its message is simple. The manual's definition of mental disorder was written for clinicians, public health workers and researchers, not for the technical needs of courts and lawyers, so a DSM diagnosis does not by itself show that a person meets a legal standard: that he was not criminally responsible for an act, is not competent to make a decision, or is entitled to disability compensation. Those questions need more than a diagnosis, above all evidence about how this person's particular impairments affect the particular abilities the law cares about. The statement adds that the manual is not a treatment guide and should not be used to diagnose by people without clinical training. Indian law draws a similar line between a clinical diagnosis and a legal finding, as Book 2, Section 1.10 explains. Section II, "Diagnostic Criteria and Codes" , is the heart of the book and the only part whose disorders are officially recognised for clinical use. It contains 22 chapters, which Section 1.8.2 takes in order. Every disorder in it appears in the same format: the code and name, the criteria set, and then the descriptive text under standard headings such as Diagnostic Features, Prevalence, Development and Course, Risk and Prognostic Factors, Culture-Related Diagnostic Issues and Differential Diagnosis (Section 1.2.8 explains how to read those headings). Section III, "Emerging Measures and Models" , holds material the American Psychiatric Association considers promising but not yet established enough for routine use. It has four chapters: Assessment Measures , rating scales that add dimensions to the categories; Culture and Psychiatric Diagnosis , with the Cultural Formulation Interview and a glossary of cultural concepts of distress; the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders ; and Conditions for Further Study , proposed disorders with research criteria. The manual is frank about the difference in status. The Section II criteria are described as well established and extensively reviewed; the Section III tools and proposals are those for which more scientific evidence may be needed before they can be widely used in the clinic. Sections 1.8.5 and 1.8.6 explain what each contains. The Appendix lists every diagnosis twice, once alphabetically and once in numerical order of its ICD-10-CM code, and ends with the names of the advisors and contributors and the index. The numerical list is the one to reach for when a referral letter gives you only a code ("F41.1") and you need to know what it means. The twenty disorder chapters and why they come in this order Section II has 22 chapters, but only 20 of them are chapters of mental disorders.
