A psychiatrist armed only with a checklist could have examined each of them, counted racing hearts, sweating and terror, and written "panic attack" on every case sheet. The label would not have been wrong, exactly, but it would have missed almost everything that mattered: why these men, in this city, in these few weeks, all feared the same impossible thing, and why a few public statements from the city's doctors and its Ministry of Health did more to end the epidemic than any medicine. Every diagnosis in this book is made by one person about another, and both of them bring a culture into the room. The patient's culture shapes what he feels, what he calls it, what he thinks caused it and whom he goes to for help; the clinician's culture, including the culture of psychiatry itself, shapes what she notices and what she counts as a symptom. This section asks how much of a disorder is culture, how psychiatry has tried to describe the disorders that seem to belong to one place, and how a clinician in an Indian clinic can make a diagnosis that is accurate without being blind to the person's world. Culture shapes distress Book 2 opened this subject in two places. Its Section 1.6.8 argued that culture shapes the way distress is felt and expressed, not merely the yardstick by which conduct is measured, and it named the three cultural concepts of distress and gave dhat syndrome a brief first look, and its Section 1.7.1 described Arthur Kleinman's idea that every patient brings an explanatory model of the illness (Book 2, Section 2.2.9, adds the skills of interviewing across cultures and through interpreters). Here you need the fuller picture: what psychiatry now means by culture, the ways culture works on every stage of an illness, and the language you will use for the rest of this section. Start with a woman in a clinic. Rekha, 38, a domestic worker in Pune who grew up in a village in Odisha, comes to a municipal health post saying she has "full tension", "gas" in her stomach, "weakness" in her body and a feeling that her "nerves have become weak". Asked what is going on at home, she explains that her son's school fees are due, her employer has cut her hours and she quarrelled with her sister-in-law last week. Her sleep is a little broken, but she still enjoys her evenings with her children, works every day and has no hopelessness. Rekha does not have a mental disorder. She is using the shared words of her community to say that life is pressing on her, much as a Delhi office worker might say "I'm so stressed" or an American student "I'm totally burned out". Words of this kind are called idioms of distress, and their first lesson is that they are a way of communicating, not a symptom count. A clinician who heard "tension, gas, weakness" and reached for a diagnosis would be making a mistake; so would one who heard the same words from a woman with severe depression and sent her home with an antacid. What, then, is culture? The DSM-5-TR chapter "Culture and Psychiatric Diagnosis", in Section III of the manual, defines culture as the systems of knowledge, concepts, values, norms and practices that people learn and pass on across generations. It includes language, religion and spirituality, family structures, the stages of the life cycle, rituals and customs, and ways of understanding health and illness, together with moral, political, economic and legal systems. Three features of the definition matter for diagnosis. First, cultures are open and always changing, and most people today live in several at once: a young woman from a Malayali Christian family studying engineering in Bengaluru draws on her family's tradition, her college's youth culture and the global culture of the internet, and she builds her identity from all of them. Second, much of culture is implicit, background knowledge and assumptions so taken for granted that people find them hard to describe. Third, and following from the first two, DSM-5-TR warns clinicians not to overgeneralise cultural information or to stereotype groups in terms of fixed cultural traits. Knowing that a patient is a Tamil Brahmin, a Punjabi Sikh or a Gond tribal does not tell you what he believes; only he can tell you that. The manual then makes its central claim: all forms of illness and distress, including the DSM disorders themselves, are shaped by cultural contexts. DSM-5-TR defines two related terms. It describes race as "a social, not a biological, construct", a way of dividing humanity by superficial physical traits such as skin colour that have been falsely taken to indicate inborn capacities; the construct matters to psychiatry because racism and discrimination harm mental health, worsen many disorders and bias diagnosis. And it defines ethnicity as a culturally constructed group identity, rooted in a shared history, ancestry, geography, language or religion, which may be claimed by the group or assigned to it by outsiders. In India the same logic applies to caste, religion, region and language, which shape access to care, exposure to discrimination and the way people present their suffering, and DSM-5-TR names caste explicitly among the aspects of identity a cultural assessment should consider (Section 1.10.3). The most influential thinker in this field is Arthur Kleinman (born 1941), an American psychiatrist and medical anthropologist who did his early fieldwork in Taiwan and China. In 1978, with the psychiatrist Leon Eisenberg and the anthropologist Byron Good, he set out the distinction between disease , a malfunction of biological or psychological processes as the practitioner sees it, and illness , the person's own experience of being unwell (Section 1.2.2 uses the distinction). The year before, in a paper on depression and somatisation in Social Science and Medicine (1977), he had named a mistake that cross-cultural psychiatry kept making. The category fallacy is taking a diagnostic category that was developed in one culture and applying it to people of another culture, for whom it does not hang together and whose validity has never been shown there. Imagine an Indian psychiatrist arriving at a London university with a checklist for dhat syndrome. A few students would admit to tiredness and to worry about masturbation, and a "prevalence of dhat" could be calculated to two decimal places; the number would be meaningless, because for those students the idea of strength draining away with semen organises nothing about their distress. Kleinman's point was that Western psychiatrists did exactly this when they went abroad with Western categories. The most famous study of the problem is his own work with patients diagnosed with neurasthenia in Hunan, which is told in Section 5.2.7; there you will also see that critics accused him of committing the very fallacy he had named. How does culture actually reach into a disorder? A useful starting point is the distinction, made by Karl Jaspers early in the twentieth century and taught in Chapter 2, between the form of a symptom and its content . The form (a delusion, a hallucination, an obsession) appears in every society that has been studied; the content is borrowed from the person's world. A persecuted man in a Bihar village fears that a neighbour has used black magic on him, his counterpart in a Mumbai high-rise fears hidden cameras, and a third man in Ohio fears the government; all three have persecutory delusions, but each delusion speaks the idiom of its place. DSM-5-TR notes that ideas which look delusional in one setting, such as the evil eye, illness caused by curses or the influence of spirits, may be commonly held in another; that hearing God's voice can be an ordinary part of religious experience in some communities; and that although auditory hallucinations are more common than visual ones everywhere, the proportion of visual hallucinations is higher in some regions than in others. Obsessions follow the same rule. Barlow and Durand report that obsessions in Saudi Arabia and Egypt centre on religious practice and cleanliness, while contamination themes are especially common in India, yet the forms and proportions of obsessions and compulsions are similar wherever they have been counted (Section 6.5). Culture also decides where people go for help. In much of India the first stop for a troubled mind is not a clinic but a temple, a dargah, a church, a faith healer, an astrologer or an elder, and families often move between these and doctors, or use several at once (Book 2, Section 1.7.1, explains why these pathways make sense from inside the supernatural model). It decides how distress is presented to a doctor. Many Indian and Chinese patients with depression or anxiety lead with their bodies, with pain, burning, heaviness, weakness and "gas", rather than with sadness or fear (Sections 5.2.7 and 7.7 take this up). Barlow and Durand add a warning: researchers long assumed that expressing distress through the body was a feature of non-Western or developing societies, but closer study has shown that it is fairly common, and fairly uniform, throughout the world, and that the old impression may have come from the way the early studies were done. Finally, culture decides what counts as pathological in the first place. A woman whom the goddess "enters" at a village festival, who speaks in the deity's voice and afterwards remembers little, is taking part in an accepted collective practice; DSM-5-TR is explicit that a dissociative trance is a disorder only when it is "not a normal part of a broadly accepted collective cultural or religious practice" (Section 7.6.7 draws the line in detail). Indian context Traditional healing in India is neither all good nor all harmful. Many healers offer meaning, hope, ritual and the support of a community, and families value them for it. But on 6 August 2001, 28 people with mental illness (some reports give 25), kept in chains in a privately run home near the dargah at Erwadi in Tamil Nadu's Ramanathapuram district, died in a fire because they could not escape. The Supreme Court took up the case on its own motion, and the National Human Rights Commission later directed every state to certify that no person with mental illness was kept in chains; the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 now forbids chaining a person with mental illness "in any manner or form whatsoever" (Section 95). The clinician's task, as Section 1.10.6 explains, is to work alongside healers who do no harm and to make sure that no one is denied treatment in their name. Indian patients use a rich vocabulary of distress, and you should learn to hear it. "Tension" is both an idiom and an explanation all over South Asia; DSM-5-TR lists it as the South Asian relative of the Latin American nervios . "Weakness" ( kamzori ), "my nerves are weak", "gas", "heat in the body", "burning in the hands and feet", ghabrahat (an anxious, restless agitation) and "thinking too much" are heard daily in Indian clinics. DSM-5-TR names the Indian idiom ashaktapanna , a feeling of weakness or lost strength, among the neurasthenia-like conditions of many cultures. Among Punjabi migrants in Bedford, England, the anthropologist Inga-Britt Krause described in 1989 the complaint of a "sinking heart", physical sensations in the heart or chest that sufferers attributed to excessive heat, exhaustion, worry or social failure, and she concluded that the Punjabi model corresponded exactly to no Western category, though it came closest to the Western idea of stress. None of these idioms is a diagnosis. Each is an invitation to ask more. Exam trap Keep Kleinman's three ideas apart. The category fallacy (1977) is imposing one culture's diagnostic category on another culture where it lacks coherence. The disease versus illness distinction (Kleinman, Eisenberg and Good, 1978) separates the practitioner's view of a malfunction from the patient's experience. The explanatory model (most fully in his 1980 book) is the patient's own account of what the illness is, what caused it and what should be done. Two more traps: an idiom of distress such as "tension" does not by itself indicate a disorder; and in the form versus content distinction it is the content of a symptom that culture supplies, while the form is broadly universal. From culture-bound syndromes to cultural concepts of distress Long before anyone spoke of cultural concepts, European doctors in the colonies were writing home about disorders they had never seen in Europe: men in Malaya who brooded over an insult and then ran murderously "amok", women in Java who, when startled, imitated every word and gesture around them. Emil Kraepelin, whose classification you met in Section 1.6.2, travelled to Java in 1904 to find out whether the disorders of his Munich clinic existed there too, and his journey is often taken as the start of what he called comparative psychiatry. For half a century afterwards the strange conditions of distant places were filed under headings such as the "exotic psychoses": curiosities from the edge of the map, described by outsiders and rarely understood from inside. The psychiatrist who did most to bring order to them was Pow Meng Yap (1921 to 1971), who arrived in Hong Kong in 1948 as the colony's first qualified psychiatrist. In 1951 he published a survey of "mental diseases peculiar to certain cultures", and over the next twenty years he wrote on latah (1952), on the possession syndrome (1960) and on koro, which in 1965 he called "a culture-bound depersonalization syndrome". In 1967 he proposed a classification of what he named the culture-bound reactive syndromes . His argument had two halves. These conditions, he held, were reactive: psychogenic responses to stress, shaped by local beliefs about the body, the spirits and the social world. And precisely because they were reactions of a familiar kind, they were not new diseases at all but local forms of disorders psychiatry already knew, which should be fitted into the standard classification as variants. Yap died suddenly in November 1971 while attending the World Congress of Psychiatry in Mexico City; his book Comparative Psychiatry: A Theoretical Framework was published after his death, in 1974. The shorter phrase, culture-bound syndrome , is the one that stuck: a recurrent, locally recognised pattern of disturbed behaviour or experience, found in a particular society or region and understood there as an illness or an affliction. By the 1980s the idea had a textbook of its own, The Culture-Bound Syndromes (1985), edited by the psychiatrist Ronald C. Simons and the anthropologist Charles C. Hughes , and in 1994 it entered the official manuals. DSM-IV placed in its Appendix I two new tools, an Outline for Cultural Formulation (Section 1.10.3) and a Glossary of Culture-Bound Syndromes with brief descriptions of 25 conditions, among them amok, ataque de nervios, brain fag, dhat, koro, latah, pibloktoq, susto, taijin kyofusho and zar; DSM-IV-TR (2000) kept both (Section 1.7.4 places the appendix in the history of the DSM). The ICD took a lighter step. ICD-10 itself lists dhat syndrome under F48.8, other specified neurotic disorders, and the ICD-10 Diagnostic Criteria for Research (1993) added an annex on culture-specific disorders that described the best-known conditions and suggested where in Chapter V each might be coded, while warning that these placements were tentative and giving no detailed criteria. The term was useful, because it made generations of trainees aware that culture matters, but it drew four lasting criticisms. First, it was lopsided. The syndromes on every list came from Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Arctic, as if Western psychiatry described nature while everyone else had culture. Yet the West has syndromes of its own: anorexia nervosa, with its pursuit of thinness in societies that idealise slim bodies, has often been called a Western culture-bound syndrome (Chapter 8 weighs the argument), and DSM-5-TR itself now concedes that many DSM diagnoses "started out as cultural syndromes" and became widely accepted because they proved useful in clinics and research. Second, it exaggerated how local these conditions are. When Athula Sumathipala and his colleagues searched the historical literature in 2004, they found the anxiety about semen loss that defines dhat described in nineteenth-century Britain, the United States and Australia, and concluded that dhat "is not as culture-bound as previously thought". Third, it pointed attention at unusual clusters of symptoms when many clinically important cultural differences lie elsewhere, in how people explain and talk about their distress. Fourth, it carried Yap's assumption that each syndrome is really one Western disorder in local dress, waiting to be translated. That assumption rarely holds: a single cultural syndrome may include presentations that DSM would scatter across several disorders, and a single DSM disorder may appear under several local names. DSM-5 (2013) answered these criticisms by retiring the construct. In its place, and retained in DSM-5-TR, are three cultural concepts of distress , which describe the different jobs a cultural term can do: A cultural idiom of distress is a behaviour, word, phrase or way of talking about symptoms, problems or suffering that people of similar cultural background share, used to express or communicate distress. DSM-5-TR's example is saying "I feel so depressed" to express low mood or discouragement that falls short of major depressive disorder. An idiom need not be tied to particular symptoms, syndromes or causes; it may cover everyday worries, problems below the threshold of a disorder or suffering caused by social circumstances, and most cultures have bodily idioms that express a wide range of troubles. A cultural explanation or perceived cause is a label, attribution or feature of an explanatory model that offers a culturally coherent account of why the symptoms, illness or distress happened, such as "stress", spirits, sorcery or a failure to follow prescribed practices. Such explanations are often the backbone of the local classifications that lay people and healers use. A cultural syndrome is a cluster of co-occurring, distinctive symptoms found in a particular cultural group, community or context, such as ataque de nervios . The syndrome may or may not be recognised as an illness locally (it might be described in non-medical terms), but an outside observer can still recognise the pattern. The three are not boxes into which every term must fall exactly once. DSM-5-TR stresses that the same term often serves more than one function, and that usage changes over time. "Depression" is its own example: it names a syndrome (major depressive disorder), it has become an everyday idiom ("I'm so depressed about the result"), and it can be offered as an explanation ("the baby was born with emotional problems because his mother was depressed in pregnancy"). Dhat shows the same movement, as Figure 1.16 shows. Wig named it a syndrome in 1960, Indian patients use it as an explanation for weakness and worry, and it also serves as an idiom for genital infections; DSM-5-TR now describes it as "not a discrete syndrome but rather a cultural explanation of distress". Why did DSM-5's authors think this vocabulary was better? Their own text gives the reasons. The term culture-bound syndrome, they wrote, ignores the fact that clinically important cultural differences often involve explanations or experiences of distress rather than unique symptom clusters, and it overstates how far cultural concepts are restricted to particular places; the new formulation accepts that all forms of distress are locally shaped, the DSM disorders included. DSM-5-TR then lists four features of cultural concepts that every clinician should keep in mind. There is seldom a one-to-one match between a cultural concept and a DSM disorder; the correspondence is more often one-to-many in both directions. Cultural concepts span the whole range of severity, so that a grieving widow with a social predicament and a man with severe psychopathology may use the same idiom or show the same cultural syndrome. The same term often names more than one kind of concept. And like culture and like the DSM itself, cultural concepts change over time. Add a fifth point from the same chapter: cultural concepts of distress are not endorsed uniformly by everyone in a culture, so a clinician must never assume that a Punjabi patient believes in the sinking heart or that every young man from Uttar Pradesh worries about dhat. Knowing these concepts, the manual argues, improves practice in seven ways: it helps clinicians recognise people's concerns and detect disorders, because people often know their own cultural terms better than professional ones; it prevents misdiagnosis, for instance mistaking socially warranted suspicion for paranoia or an unfamiliar presentation for psychosis; it yields clinical information about risk, resilience and outcome; it improves rapport, because "speaking the language of the patient" improves communication, retention and adherence; it improves treatment, since culturally specific catastrophic thoughts can drive a panic attack and must be addressed; it guides clinical research; and it clarifies cultural epidemiology. It also feeds back into classification, because cultural syndromes may point to variants of a disorder that the manual had missed. DSM-5-TR's own example: in a change from DSM-IV, the experience of possession was written into the DSM-5 criteria for dissociative identity disorder (Section 7.6). What happened to the glossary? DSM-5-TR's Section III chapter "Culture and Psychiatric Diagnosis" ends with ten examples of cultural concepts of distress, chosen because they are well studied and illustrate how cultural concepts can affect diagnosis: ataque de nervios , dhat syndrome, hikikomori , khyâl cap , kufungisisa , maladi dyab , nervios , shenjing shuairuo , susto and taijin kyofusho . Each entry ends with two lists: "related conditions in other cultural contexts", and "related conditions in DSM-5-TR", which includes both the disorders that overlap with the concept in their symptoms and the disorders that people commonly attribute to the explanation or express through the idiom. The manual adds that the principles these ten illustrate apply to the countless other cultural concepts found around the world, which is why the older syndromes still appear in textbooks and examination papers (Sections 1.10.4 and 1.10.5). The ICD has moved the same way. ICD-11's clinical descriptions and diagnostic requirements, released by the WHO in 2024, do not keep a list of exotic syndromes; instead, each main disorder carries a section on culture-related features. Exam trap Since DSM-5 (2013) the term culture-bound syndrome has been replaced by cultural concepts of distress , of exactly three kinds: cultural idioms of distress, cultural explanations (perceived causes) and cultural syndromes . The older term came from Pow Meng Yap (culture-bound reactive syndromes, 1967) and the old glossary of 25 conditions sat in DSM-IV's Appendix I ; DSM-5-TR's ten examples sit in the Section III chapter "Culture and Psychiatric Diagnosis", not in Section II. DSM-5-TR calls dhat "not a discrete syndrome but rather a cultural explanation of distress", and stresses that there is "no one-to-one correspondence at the categorical level between DSM disorders and cultural concepts of distress". The cultural formulation and the Cultural Formulation Interview A diagnosis answers the question "what does this person have?" A formulation answers the harder questions "why this person, why now, and what will help?" (Book 2, Section 2.9, teaches formulation as a clinical skill). The cultural formulation is the part of that story that asks how culture enters it: who the person is, how he understands his trouble, what in his world makes it worse or better, and what stands between him and the clinician. DSM-IV's Outline for Cultural Formulation gave clinicians the first framework for this in 1994. DSM-5 expanded the Outline and added an interview to carry it out, and DSM-5-TR updated both. Notice one sentence in the manual's introduction to the Outline: the assessment is useful for every individual, "not only those whose cultural background may be unfamiliar to the clinician". A Hindi-speaking psychiatrist in Delhi interviewing a Hindi-speaking student has as much need of it as a London psychiatrist interviewing a refugee. The Outline asks for a systematic assessment under five headings. Cultural identity of the individual. The clinician describes the person's age, gender and ethnic or racialised background, and the other socially defined characteristics that may shape relationships, access to resources and current predicaments: religion and spirituality, socioeconomic class, caste, where the person and the family were born and grew up, migrant status, occupation and sexual orientation, among others. The clinician notes which aspects of identity the person treats as most important and how they interact (DSM-5-TR uses the word intersectionality), how far a migrant is involved with the culture of origin and the new one, and which languages the person speaks and prefers, since this decides whether an interpreter is needed. Cultural concepts of distress. The idioms, explanations and syndromes through which the person experiences, understands and communicates the problem. The severity and meaning of the distress are judged against the norms of the person's own cultural background, together with which symptoms matter most to the person, how serious the illness seems, how much stigma it carries and what outcome is expected. This heading also covers how the person and the family cope, whom they have consulted and whom they expect to consult, including traditional, alternative and complementary healers as well as professionals. Psychosocial stressors and cultural features of vulnerability and resilience. The key stressors and supports in the person's world: social determinants of mental health such as housing, transport, education and employment; exposure to racism, discrimination and social exclusion (DSM-5-TR calls the last "structural violence"); and the part that religion, family, friends, neighbours, co-workers and online groups play in causing stress or giving support. Functioning, disability and resilience are judged in the light of the person's background. Cultural features of the relationship between the individual and the clinician, treatment team and institution. Differences in background, language, education and social status between the person and the clinician, and how each perceives the other, may make it hard to elicit symptoms, lead to misreading their cultural and clinical significance, and block the trust that accurate assessment needs. Experiences of racism and discrimination in the wider society may follow the person into the consulting room. Overall cultural assessment. The clinician draws the threads together: what the first four headings imply for the differential diagnosis, for other problems that need attention, and for management and treatment. The Outline tells you what to find out; the Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI) tells you how to ask. DSM-5-TR describes it as a set of protocols with three components: the core CFI , 16 questions that can be used for an initial assessment of any individual; an informant version of the core CFI for collateral information; and a set of supplementary modules that expand the evaluation where needed. The core CFI is a brief semistructured interview. It is person-centred: it asks the person for his own views and those of the people around him, rather than assuming what someone of his background must believe, and this is the manual's defence against stereotyping. Because the questions are about personal views, there are no right or wrong answers, and the interviewer says so at the start. The printed form has two columns, instructions for the interviewer on the left and suggested questions on the right, and the questions may be rephrased, followed up or used selectively so that the interview keeps a natural flow. The CFI can be used at any age, in any setting and whatever the backgrounds of patient and clinician; DSM-5-TR points out that people who appear to share a background may still differ in ways that matter for care. It is especially helpful when the clinician and the person differ markedly in cultural, religious or socioeconomic background; when it is unclear whether culturally distinctive symptoms fit the diagnostic criteria; when severity or impairment is hard to judge; when the person's expectations come from other systems of healing; when patient and clinician disagree about the course of care; when the person may mistrust mainstream services because of a collective history of trauma or oppression; and when engagement and adherence are poor. The 16 core questions are grouped into four domains, which run in a natural order from the person's view of the problem to the help he wants now (Figure 1.17). Cultural definition of the problem Perceptions of cause, context and support Self-coping and past help seeking Current help seeking Questions 1 to 3 Questions 4 to 10 Questions 11 to 13 Questions 14 to 16 The problem in own words; how it is told to family; what troubles most Own and others' causes; stresses and supports; role of identity Own coping; healers, doctors and what helped; barriers to help Help wanted now; others' advice; worries about the clinician Informant version: the same domains, asked of a relative or carer Supplementary modules: twelve, to go deeper or to serve special groups Figure 1.17 The core Cultural Formulation Interview. Its 16 questions move through four domains from left to right; the question numbers are worth memorising. Below them sit the two other components of the CFI, the informant version and the supplementary modules. Here is what each domain asks, in paraphrase. The interview opens with a short introduction: the clinician wants to understand the problems that bring the person in, wants to hear his own experience and ideas, and reminds him that there are no right or wrong answers. The first domain, the cultural definition of the problem (questions 1 to 3), asks what brings the person today, how he would describe the problem in his own words (which may differ from the way doctors describe it), how he would describe it to family, friends or others in his community, and what troubles him most about it. The clinician then uses the person's own term, "your weakness" or "your trouble with your son", in every later question. The second domain, cultural perceptions of cause, context and support (questions 4 to 10), asks why the person thinks this is happening and what he thinks the causes are (people often name several: bad events, problems with others, a physical illness, a spiritual reason), and what family, friends and community think the cause is; what kinds of support make the problem better and what stresses, such as money worries or family problems, make it worse; and which aspects of his background or identity matter most to him (his communities, languages, origins, ethnic background, gender, sexual orientation or faith), whether any of them make the problem better or worse, and whether any cause other difficulties, such as problems related to migration or conflict between generations or over gender roles. The third domain, cultural factors affecting self-coping and past help seeking (questions 11 to 13), asks what the person has done on his own to cope, what help, advice or healing he has sought from doctors, helpers or healers of any kind and what was or was not useful, and whether anything, such as money, work or family commitments, stigma, discrimination or services that do not understand his language or background, has kept him from the help he needs. The fourth domain, cultural factors affecting current help seeking (questions 14 to 16), asks what help would be most useful now, what other kinds of help family and friends have suggested, and finally, because doctors and patients sometimes misunderstand each other when they come from different backgrounds or have different expectations, whether the person has been concerned about this and what the clinic can do to give him the care he needs. The informant version asks the same things of someone who knows the person's problems and circumstances well, usually a relative or carer. It can supplement the core CFI or replace it when the person cannot give the information himself, as with young children, people in florid psychosis and people with cognitive impairment. The twelve supplementary modules named in DSM-5-TR go deeper. Eight expand the core domains (explanatory model; level of functioning; social network; psychosocial stressors; religion and spirituality; cultural identity; coping and help seeking; and the clinician-patient relationship), and four serve particular groups (children and adolescents, older adults, immigrants and refugees, and caregivers). DSM-5-TR prints the core CFI and its informant version in Section III; the modules are available online. Key study: Does the CFI work in real clinics? (Lewis-Fernández and colleagues, 2017) Before the CFI went into DSM-5, a 14-question pilot version was field-tested in routine practice at eleven sites in six countries: Canada, India (Pune and New Delhi), Kenya, the Netherlands, Peru and the United States. Roberto Lewis-Fernández and his colleagues had clinicians administer it to diagnostically varied psychiatric outpatients as part of a diagnostic interview; afterwards patients and clinicians were interviewed about the experience and completed rating scales, and the time taken was recorded. Across 318 patients and 75 clinicians, the CFI was rated feasible, acceptable and useful. One finding is worth remembering: clinicians rated its feasibility lower than patients did, but after administering a single CFI their ratings rose significantly and later interviews took less time. These results, with other field-trial data, shaped the final 16-question version. The trial measured how practical and welcome the interview was; it was not designed to show that patients assessed with the CFI receive more accurate diagnoses or recover better, which later research must test. To see the interview at work, return to a young man you have already met. Dinesh, the 24-year-old examination candidate from eastern Uttar Pradesh whose multiaxial record was built in Section 1.7.5, was sent to the psychiatry clinic by a physician he had consulted three times for "weakness". Running case: Dinesh's Cultural Formulation Interview The psychiatrist works through the four domains in Dinesh's own words. Cultural definition of the problem (questions 1 to 3). He calls his trouble kamzori , weakness, and dhat jaana , losing dhat. What worries him most is the marriage: he fears he will not be able to satisfy his wife or father children. Cultural perceptions of cause, context and support (questions 4 to 10). The cause, he says, is dhat lost through "bad habits" in his teens, by which he means masturbation; he grants only partly that the examination and the family's debt "give tension". His support is his elder cousin; his stresses are the debt and the fiancée's family. He identifies himself as the son of a Hindu farming family and the first in his family to try for a government job. Self-coping and past help seeking (questions 11 to 13). He has taken herbal powders, prayed and fasted on Tuesdays, spent several thousand rupees at a roadside clinic advertising cures for gupt rog , "secret diseases", and seen the physician. He has told no one in his family. Current help seeking (questions 14 to 16). He wants "a tonic" to restore his strength, fears that a "mental" label would end the engagement, and would prefer a doctor who speaks his own dialect. Notice what the CFI has added to the diagnosis of generalised anxiety disorder: the meaning he gives his symptoms, the secrecy around them, the stake that makes the label dangerous to him, and the kind of explanation he will accept. Section 1.10.6 shows what the clinician does with it. Clinical link Kleinman's explanatory-model questions, published with Eisenberg and Good in 1978, and the CFI do the same job: what do you call the problem, what do you think caused it, why did it start when it did, what does it do to you, how severe is it, what do you fear most, and what treatment do you hope for? In a crowded Indian outpatient department you may have fifteen minutes, not an hour. Fit the essentials into the first interview: ask what the person calls the problem and what he thinks caused it (questions 1 and 4), ask what the family thinks (question 5), ask whom he has already consulted (question 12), and ask what help he expects and what he fears about coming here (questions 14 and 16). The remaining questions can follow at the next visit or from the informant version with a relative. Use his word for the problem throughout, and see him alone for part of the time, because some answers (about sex, a husband's drinking or thoughts of death) will not be given in front of the family. Exam trap The core CFI has 16 questions in four domains : cultural definition of the problem (1 to 3); cultural perceptions of cause, context and support (4 to 10); cultural factors affecting self-coping and past help seeking (11 to 13); and cultural factors affecting current help seeking (14 to 16). Do not confuse it with the Outline for Cultural Formulation , which has five headings and dates from DSM-IV (1994) ; the CFI arrived with DSM-5 (2013) and lives in Section III. The CFI's three components are the core CFI, the informant version and the supplementary modules. It is meant for every patient, not only immigrants or minorities. Cultural syndromes of the Indian subcontinent For an Indian clinician the cultural concepts of distress are not exotic entries in an appendix; several of them walk into the outpatient department every week. Indian examination papers know this, and the question they set most often is a simple one: which of these syndromes is reported in India, and which is not? This subsection teaches the Indian syndromes one by one, beginning with the most important. Mohan, 20, a commerce student in Rohtak, sits in a skin and sexually transmitted diseases clinic with his eyes on the floor. For a year he has noticed a whitish thread in his urine after straining at stool, and he has night emissions two or three times a month. He feels tired, his face looks "dull" to him, he cannot study as he used to, and he is sure that his body is being drained. A friend told him it was because of masturbation, which he gave up six months ago with great effort, and an advertisement painted on a wall near the bus stand promised a cure. His real fear comes out only when the doctor asks what troubles him most: his marriage is being discussed at home, and he is afraid he will fail as a husband. Physical examination and urine tests are normal. He does not meet the criteria for a depressive or anxiety disorder, a sexual dysfunction or illness anxiety disorder; his functioning is intact apart from his worry. What he has is the most studied cultural concept of distress in South Asia. The name dhat syndrome comes from dhat , the word that Mohan, and many patients and families like his, use for semen. It was named in 1960 by Narendra Nath Wig (1930 to 2018), who in 1963 founded the department of psychiatry at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER) in Chandigarh and later headed psychiatry at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi; the name appeared in his paper on the problems of mental health in India. In 1975 H. K. Malhotra and Wig introduced it to an international readership in the Archives of Sexual Behavior as "a culture-bound sex neurosis of the Orient". DSM-5-TR describes dhat as a term coined in South Asia "little more than half a century ago" to account for common presentations of young men who attributed their various symptoms to semen loss. The symptoms they attribute to it are diverse: anxiety, fatigue, weakness, weight loss, erectile dysfunction, many other bodily complaints and depressed mood. The cardinal feature is anxiety and distress about the loss of dhat in the absence of any identifiable physiological dysfunction. Patients describe dhat as a white discharge they notice on urination or defecation, and sometimes they link it to night emissions or masturbation. Why should losing semen frighten anyone? The answer lies in an old and widely shared idea of the body. In Ayurveda, the Hindu system of medicine, dhatu refers to the seven essential bodily substances whose balance maintains health, and semen is the last of the seven. Patients often explain the danger with a folk arithmetic; in the version that Sumathipala and his colleagues (2004) quote, it takes forty days for forty drops of food to become one drop of blood, and the same ratio holds at each later step, as blood becomes flesh, flesh becomes marrow and marrow at last becomes semen. If semen is the concentrated essence of the whole body, its loss must drain strength, beauty, memory and manhood, and the weakness, the dull face and the poor concentration all make sense. DSM-5-TR adds that such ideas about the harm of semen loss are widespread in the general population, not only among patients, which suggests a cultural disposition to explain health problems in terms of dhat. Research in health care settings has given very different prevalence figures: 64 percent of men attending psychiatric clinics in India for sexual complaints in one study, 30 percent of men attending general medical clinics in Pakistan in another. Dhat is most often identified in young men from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, but middle-aged men may also be affected, and similar worries about white vaginal discharge (leukorrhoea) have been described as a variant in women. The word may also serve as an idiom and causal explanation for sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhoea and chlamydia, without any psychological distress. The concept is found across South Asia, in India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh. The DSM-IV glossary named jiryan in India and sukra prameha in Sri Lanka as similar conditions; DSM-5-TR names koro in Southeast Asia, particularly Singapore, and shen-k'uei , "kidney deficiency", in China as related conditions in other cultures. And as Sumathipala and his colleagues showed (Section 1.10.2), semen-loss anxiety was once common in Western medicine too. What is dhat in DSM-5-TR's terms? Not a disorder, and not even a discrete syndrome: "a cultural explanation of distress". The person who explains his suffering by dhat may have no disorder at all, like Mohan, or he may have one of the disorders DSM-5-TR lists as related: major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, erectile disorder, early (premature) ejaculation, other specified or unspecified sexual dysfunction, or, in a reminder that some of these men simply lack accurate information, educational problems. Management follows from this. Every patient needs a respectful explanation of sexual physiology within his own frame of reference (that night emissions and masturbation are normal and do not drain the body), reassurance based on examination and tests, and the involvement of a trusted relative where he agrees; any depression, anxiety disorder or sexual dysfunction underneath is treated in its own right (Chapter 9 discusses the sexual complaints, and Dinesh's outcome in Section 1.10.6 shows the approach). Mohan, given twenty unhurried minutes and a diagram, went home visibly lighter. The second great Indian syndrome is koro , the acute fear that the genitals are shrinking and retracting into the body and that death will follow. The opening of this chapter told the story of the Singapore epidemic of 1967 and glanced at the Assam epidemic of 1982; here the Indian story is told in full. India has had several koro epidemics, and they form a clear series. A review of the Indian epidemics by Sayanti Ghosh, Arabinda N. Chowdhury and their colleagues (2013) lists the first in North Bengal in 1968, the second in 1982 in West Bengal and Assam, a third small outbreak in a village in South 24 Parganas district of West Bengal in 1988, a fourth in Tripura in 1998, and a fifth in 2010, which began in Assam and spread to labour camps in Mumbai, to West Bengal and to Tripura. In a Mumbai labour camp that October, where most of the men affected were migrants from Odisha and West Bengal, one worker described sitting for three or four hours in a tub of iced water to stop his genitals retracting; in West Bengal, where sitting in cold water up to the neck was the commonest home remedy, the feverish illness that went with the 2010 attacks was nicknamed "disco fever". Key study: The koro epidemic in lower Assam (Dutta, Phookan and Das, 1982) The opening of this chapter summarised this study; here are its details. From late June to the middle of September 1982, a koro epidemic swept through four districts of lower Assam. D. Dutta , H. R. Phookan and P. D. Das of the psychiatry department at Gauhati Medical College surveyed 83 cases, 19 of them women. Most of those affected were young men under 30 from Hindu Assamese middle-class families, and their complaints were mainly genital; attacks usually came at night, indoors. Hearing about koro or seeing a case was an important trigger of an attack. Marriage, education and occupational skill gave no protection, relapses were few, and the epidemic subsided without a single death after massive public reassurance through the mass media. Locally the illness was called jinjinia , Assamese for tingling. At almost the same time P. S. Sachdev and A. Shukla announced an "epidemic koro syndrome in India" in a letter to the Lancet (1982), and Sachdev's later analysis of 31 cases from north-east India found most of them poorly educated, poor and aged 20 to 40, with many women among them and little evidence of premorbid or sexual psychopathology. Ajita Chakraborty , reporting the simultaneous epidemic in West Bengal, tied it to social tensions of the time. Two lessons stand out: koro spreads by rumour and fear, and it is stopped by authoritative information. Indian koro epidemics have differed from the classical Chinese picture in one striking way: many women have been affected, fearing that their breasts or nipples are retracting or, more rarely, the vulva; Psycho Didi's notes record koro in north-east India as "seen in both the sexes", and two of the women in the 2010 West Bengal series described their nipples drawing in. Barlow and Durand note that typical Chinese sufferers feel guilty about masturbation, unsatisfactory intercourse or promiscuity, worries that may focus attention on the genitals and feed the anxiety, much as in the anxiety disorders. In DSM-5-TR, koro appears in three places. In the glossary it is a related condition of dhat. In Section II it is one of the named examples of other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder : an episode of sudden and intense anxiety that the penis in males, or the vulva and nipples in females, will recede into the body, possibly leading to death. And the text on body dysmorphic disorder separates it from that disorder by its focus on death rather than on perceived ugliness (Sections 6.6.3 and 6.6.6). The Assamese name for koro, jinjinia , leads to a different condition with almost the same name. The condition called jhinjhinia ( jhin-jhini , Bengali for tingling and numbness) was described by D. N. Nandi and his colleagues (1992), who traced every victim of an outbreak that struck the village of Arkhali, about 50 kilometres north of Calcutta in North 24 Parganas, in March 1982. A rumour that the disease had broken out in neighbouring villages created an atmosphere of terror. The illness struck suddenly with tingling and numbness in the legs that spread upwards through the body; within seconds the person was seized with horror of impending death and cried for help before becoming speechless and motionless, and would fall to the ground unless "rescued" by a squad of villagers with a local remedy, recovering within half an hour to two hours. Eighteen people fell ill within two months, as many women as men, most of them under 40. The villagers blamed an evil spirit. Because the West Bengal koro epidemic of the same year was also locally called jhin-jhini , the two are easily confused, but Nandi's team insisted that their epidemic was a distinct entity: the victims had no concern at all about their genitals. Today you would recognise it as a form of mass psychogenic illness (Section 7.8.9). Four more syndromes complete the Indian list. The first, suchi-bai , described in Bengal, is an obsessional preoccupation with cleanliness and ritual purity ( suchi means pure); Psycho Didi's notes call it "a condition like obsessional neurosis". It sits at the meeting point of custom and compulsion. Many Hindu households keep purity rules about bathing before cooking, separating clean from polluted spaces and washing after contact with certain people or objects, and following them is not a disorder; when the washing and purifying become excessive, time-consuming and distressing, go beyond what the family's own tradition requires and are resisted or regretted by the person, the presentation should be assessed for obsessive-compulsive disorder (Section 6.5). The second, the possession syndrome of rural India, is a state in which a person is taken over, usually by the spirit of a dead relative or by a local deity, speaks in a changed tone of voice and may even change gender if the possessing spirit is of the opposite sex. Most possession states are part of accepted religious practice and are not disorders; when they are involuntary, distressing, uncontrollable, in conflict with family or community and out of place and time, they fall under ICD-10's trance and possession disorders (F44.3), ICD-11's possession trance disorder or DSM-5-TR's possession-form dissociative identity disorder or other specified dissociative disorder (Section 7.6.7 draws these lines). The third, bhanmati sorcery (also spelt bhanamati ), is a cultural explanation from South India: illness of almost any kind is attributed to sorcery worked by an envious or hostile person. In a clinical study of 209 patients who attended a special clinic in South India, Matcheri S. Keshavan , H. S. Narayanan and B. N. Gangadhar (1989) found that most had somatisation or conversion disorders, though several other psychiatric and medical disorders were also seen; Psycho Didi's notes add dysthymia, anxiety disorders and schizophrenia to the conditions found behind the explanation. The fourth, gilhari syndrome , reported from western Rajasthan, is the belief that a small swelling on the body is moving about under the skin like a squirrel ( gilhari ) or a lizard, travelling from the back towards the neck, where it will block the airway and kill the person unless it is destroyed; medically, the "swelling" is a strong contraction of a group of muscles under severe tension and stress. Two last entries appear in Indian notes. One is suudu , described in Tamil culture (the Tamil word means heat), which presents with severe abdominal pain, dark yellow urine, painful and burning urination, headaches, fatigue, constipation and dry mouth. And mass hysteria , in the old term, describes short-lived epidemics in which hundreds or thousands of people behave in ways they normally would not; the koro and jhin-jhini outbreaks are Indian examples, and the modern concept of mass psychogenic illness is taught in Section 7.8.9. Dhat belongs to the Indian subcontinent (with Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh), not to Malaysia, Latin America or the Arctic, and it was named by N. N. Wig in 1960 . Koro is not only Chinese or Singaporean: Indian epidemics (1982 in Assam and West Bengal, 2010 in several states) affected women as well as men. Do not confuse jinjinia , a local name for koro in Assam, with jhinjhinia , the tingling-and-collapse epidemic of a West Bengal village. Cultural syndromes around the world The world list is long, and memorising it as an alphabet of strange names is the hardest way to learn it. It is easier to sort the syndromes by what they most resemble: the startle and running syndromes, the attacks of panic, anxiety and anger, the syndromes of social fear and withdrawal, the syndromes of weakness, fatigue and "thinking too much", the explanations built on fright, sorcery, the evil eye and spirits, the states of possession, trance and collapse, and the psychosis-like episodes. Keep two cautions in mind as you read. Resemblance is not identity: each syndrome overlaps with several DSM-5-TR disorders and maps onto none of them exactly. And many of these terms are explanations or idioms rather than syndromes, in the vocabulary of Section 1.10.2. The startle and running syndromes. In a Malay village a middle-aged woman is poked in the ribs by a grinning neighbour. She jumps, shrieks a word she would never use in polite company, and then, to the delight of the onlookers, copies every gesture the neighbour makes and obeys whatever she is told to do, until the spell passes and she scolds them all. This is latah , described in Malaysia and Indonesia: an exaggerated, hypersensitive startle to sudden or minimal stimuli, followed by echolalia (repeating the words of others), echopraxia (imitating their movements), automatic obedience to commands and a dissociative or trance-like state, often with the blurting of obscene or sexual words ( coprolalia ). The DSM-IV glossary noted that in Malaysia it is more frequent in middle-aged women. Yap wrote one of the classic papers on it in 1952, and similar startle syndromes have been described in Siberia ( myriachit ), Thailand, among the Ainu of Japan ( imu ) and in the Philippines ( mali-mali ). A second Malay syndrome, amok , gave English the phrase "running amok". It is a dissociative episode in which a period of brooding, often after a perceived slight or insult, is followed by an outburst of violent, aggressive or even homicidal behaviour against people and objects, with persecutory ideas, automatic behaviour, amnesia for the episode and exhaustion afterwards, and then a return to the person's usual state. The DSM-IV glossary described it as seemingly prevalent only among men, and Barlow and Durand agree that most sufferers are male. Similar patterns have been reported from Laos, the Philippines, Polynesia, Papua New Guinea and Puerto Rico ( mal de pelea ), and some episodes occur during a brief psychotic episode or at the start of a chronic psychosis. Barlow and Durand place amok among the "running" syndromes, in which a person in a trance-like state runs or flees for a long time as if driven by a mysterious energy; apart from amok, these are somewhat more common in women. The best-known running syndrome comes from the Arctic. The syndrome called pibloktoq (also written piblokto), or "Arctic hysteria", was described among the Inuit of the Arctic and subarctic, above all the Inughuit of north-west Greenland. After hours or days of withdrawal or mild irritability, the person, often a woman and usually in the long nights of winter, would be seized by an abrupt dissociative episode of extreme excitement lasting up to half an hour: tearing off her clothes, breaking furniture, shouting obscenities, eating faeces, or fleeing from shelter out into the snow and ice. Convulsive seizures and a stupor or coma of up to twelve hours could follow, and afterwards she remembered nothing. Many of the classic accounts came from the Greenland expeditions of the American explorer Robert Peary at the turn of the twentieth century, and that is the problem. The Canadian historian Lyle Dick argued in 1995, in Arctic Anthropology , that pibloktoq may be largely a phantom: the scholarly literature rested on a handful of cases, the word itself could not be found in the Inughuit language, and the episodes may say more about the experience and behaviour of the explorers than about Inuit psychology; some later scholars have read them as responses to colonial violence, including the sexual exploitation of Inuit women. Others have proposed physical causes, among them vitamin A poisoning from eating the livers of Arctic animals. Pibloktoq is now a lesson in method as much as a syndrome: a "cultural syndrome" can be partly a product of the observer's culture. Attacks of panic, anxiety and anger. DSM-5-TR describes ataque de nervios ("attack of nerves") as a syndrome found in Latinx cultural contexts in the Caribbean, Latin America and the United States: intense emotional upset with acute anxiety, anger or grief, uncontrollable screaming and shouting, attacks of crying, trembling, heat in the chest rising into the head and verbal or physical aggression, sometimes with dissociative experiences, seizure-like or fainting episodes or suicidal behaviour. Its general feature is a sense of being out of control, and attacks usually follow a stressful family event, such as news of a death or a conflict with a spouse or children. In US community samples 7 to 15 percent of Latinx adults report an ataque; it is linked with suicidal thoughts and disability even after psychiatric diagnoses are taken into account, yet some ataques, at a funeral for example, are normal expressions of acute grief. It differs from a panic attack in its family trigger, its anger and aggression and its longer duration (Section 6.2). Its cousin nervios ("nerves") is a broader idiom of distress and causal explanation in the same communities, a general state of vulnerability to stress, with headaches and "brain aches", irritability, stomach upsets, poor sleep, nervousness, easy tearfulness, poor concentration, trembling, tingling and dizziness; it spans everything from no disorder at all to presentations resembling depressive, anxiety, dissociative, somatic symptom or psychotic disorders. Its relatives include nevra among Greeks in North America, "nerves" in Appalachia and Newfoundland, and "tension" in South Asia. Among Cambodians, khyâl cap ("wind attacks") combines the symptoms of a panic attack (dizziness, palpitations, breathlessness, cold hands and feet, tinnitus, neck soreness) with the catastrophic belief that khyâl , a wind-like substance, is rising in the body with the blood and may compress the lungs or enter the skull and cause a fatal collapse; attacks are set off by worrying thoughts, standing up, certain smells, crowds or riding in a car, and usually meet the criteria for a panic attack. Related ideas include pen lom in Laos and vata in Sri Lanka. A Vietnamese person who panics after walking into a windy street may attribute the attack to trúng gió ("hit by the wind"); DSM-5-TR uses this example to show that a cultural explanation can turn what looks like an unexpected panic attack into an expected one. The Korean hwa-byung (literally "fire illness", where hwa means fire and, by extension, anger; the DSM-IV glossary translated it "anger syndrome") is attributed to the suppression of anger and presents with insomnia, fatigue, panic, fear of impending death, low mood, indigestion, loss of appetite, breathlessness, palpitations, aches, a sensation of heat and a feeling of a mass in the upper abdomen; it is diagnosed most often in middle-aged women, and DSM-5-TR lists it as a relative of khyâl cap. Social fear and withdrawal. The Japanese taijin kyofusho ("interpersonal fear disorder") is a syndrome of anxiety about and avoidance of social situations because of the thought, feeling or conviction that one's appearance or actions are inadequate or offensive to others. Notice the difference from Western social anxiety, which fears one's own embarrassment: in the "offensive type" the central worry is causing offence to others. DSM-5-TR describes a "sensitive type" and an "offensive type" and variants centred on blushing ( sekimen-kyofu ), an offensive body odour ( jiko-shu-kyofu ), an inappropriate gaze ( jiko-shisen-kyofu ) and a stiff or deformed appearance ( shubo-kyofu ). It is broader than social anxiety disorder, taking in features of body dysmorphic disorder, olfactory reference syndrome and delusional disorder, and a similar syndrome in Korea is called taein kong po (Section 6.3.7). Japan has also given psychiatry the word hikikomori (from Japanese words meaning to pull back and to seclude oneself): protracted, severe social withdrawal, typically in an adolescent or young adult man who does not leave his room in his parents' home and has no face-to-face contact with anyone, often while spending long hours online; a 2010 guideline of Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare requires six months of withdrawal for the diagnosis. It may be "secondary" to an established disorder or "primary", and similar withdrawal has now been reported from many countries, India among them. Weakness, fatigue and thinking too much. The Chinese shenjing shuairuo ("weakness of the nervous system" in Mandarin) joins the concepts of traditional Chinese medicine with the Western idea of neurasthenia. The second revised Chinese Classification of Mental Disorders (CCMD-2-R) defined it by three of five clusters: weakness (mental fatigue), emotions (feeling vexed), excitement (such as increased recollections), nervous pain (headache) and sleep problems. China adopted ICD-10 as its official system in 2011, and ICD-11 no longer contains neurasthenia; the diagnosis has declined sharply, replaced in the cities by idioms of depression and anxiety, though up to 45 percent of medical clinic patients with shenjing shuairuo met the criteria for no DSM-IV disorder at all (Kleinman's famous study of these patients is told in Section 5.2.7). Its close Chinese relative shen-k'uei ("kidney deficiency"; shenkui in mainland China) is marked anxiety or panic with dizziness, backache, fatigue, weakness, insomnia, frequent dreams and sexual complaints such as premature ejaculation and erectile failure, all attributed to excessive loss of semen, the vital essence, through intercourse, masturbation, night emissions or "white turbid urine"; you will recognise it as the Chinese cousin of dhat. The syndrome of brain fag was first described by the psychiatrist Raymond Prince in 1960 in a paper on "the 'brain fag' syndrome in Nigerian students". It is a West African condition of secondary school and university students, mostly young men, who complain that their brains are "fatigued" from study: they cannot concentrate, remember or think, and they report pain, pressure, tightness, heat, burning or crawling sensations in the head and neck and blurred vision. DSM-5-TR treats it as a cultural syndrome built around "thinking too much", attributed to excessive study, which is believed to damage the brain. The term itself is British: it was coined around 1850, in Victorian Britain, for the mental exhaustion of "brainworkers" who studied too hard, and it spread to the British colonies, West Africa among them, while it faded at home. Finally, kufungisisa ("thinking too much" in Shona) is an idiom of distress and a cultural explanation among the Shona of Zimbabwe. As an explanation it is held to cause anxiety, depression and bodily problems ("My heart is painful because I think too much"); as an idiom it signals interpersonal and social difficulties such as marital problems, unemployment or having no money for the children. In one random community sample, two-thirds of the cases identified by a general psychopathology measure included this complaint. "Thinking too much" turns out to be one of the commonest idioms on earth, reported from Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, Latin America and the Middle East, and you will hear it in Indian clinics too. Fright, sorcery, the evil eye and spirits. The Latin American susto ("fright") is a cultural explanation for distress and misfortune in Latinx communities of North, Central and South America: a frightening event makes the soul leave the body, causing unhappiness, sickness and difficulty in carrying out one's social roles. Symptoms can appear days or even years after the fright and include disturbed appetite and sleep, troubled dreams, sadness, low self-worth or a sense of being dirty, interpersonal sensitivity, lack of motivation, aches, cold hands and feet, pallor, headache, stomach ache and diarrhoea; in extreme cases susto is believed to cause death. It is called espanto in the Andes, is not recognised as an illness among Latinx people from the Caribbean, and has three syndromic forms that resemble major depressive disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder and somatic symptom disorder respectively. The phrase mal de ojo , the "evil eye", is the Spanish name for a belief found across the Mediterranean, Latin American and Muslim worlds, and in India as nazar : an envious or admiring gaze causes illness, especially in infants and children, who sleep fitfully, cry without apparent cause and develop diarrhoea, vomiting and fever. In Haitian communities maladi dyab ("devil illness", also called "sent sickness") explains illness of almost any kind, from psychosis and depression to academic failure, as sent by sorcerers at the request of envious enemies; because visible success invites attack, the attractive, the clever and the newly prosperous are thought most at risk. DSM-5-TR warns that this explanation may lead a clinician to misdiagnose delusional disorder or schizophrenia. In the southern United States and the Caribbean, rootwork likewise explains illness as the result of hexing, witchcraft, voodoo or the influence of an evil person ( mal puesto and brujería are Latin American equivalents). How powerful such beliefs can be was the subject of a famous 1942 paper on "voodoo death" by the American physiologist Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945), who suggested that a sentence of death pronounced by a healer could produce an intolerable state of autonomic arousal, made worse when family and friends, assuming the victim already as good as dead, withdrew their support. Among some American Indian groups, ghost sickness is a preoccupation with death and the dead, sometimes linked to witchcraft, with bad dreams, weakness, a sense of danger, loss of appetite, fainting, dizziness, fear, anxiety, hallucinations, confusion, feelings of futility and a sense of suffocation. Possession, trance and collapse. The word zar is the general term in Ethiopia, Somalia, Egypt, Sudan, Iran and other North African and Middle Eastern societies for the experience of being possessed by spirits. Possessed people may have dissociative episodes of shouting, laughing, singing, weeping or hitting the head against a wall, may become apathetic and withdrawn, refusing to eat or work, or may develop a long-term relationship with the spirit; locally such behaviour is not necessarily considered pathological. Korea's shin-byung begins with anxiety and bodily complaints (weakness, dizziness, fear, loss of appetite, insomnia, digestive problems) and ends in dissociation and possession by ancestral spirits. In the southern United States a spell is a trance in which a person "communicates" with dead relatives or spirits; it is not considered a medical event in the folk tradition but may be mistaken for a psychotic episode in a clinic. The episode called falling out (southern United States) or blacking out (the Caribbean) is a sudden collapse, sometimes after dizziness or a "swimming" feeling in the head: the eyes are usually open but the person says he cannot see, and he hears and understands what is going on but feels powerless to move. DSM-5-TR lists falling out and blacking out as relatives of ataque de nervios and warns that these terms must not be confused with the blackouts of alcohol or drug use. India's possession syndrome (Section 1.10.4) belongs to this family. Psychosis-like episodes. The French term bouffée délirante (a "puff" of delirium) names a syndrome described in West Africa and Haiti: a sudden outburst of agitated and aggressive behaviour, marked confusion and psychomotor excitement, sometimes with visual and auditory hallucinations or paranoid ideas; it resembles brief psychotic disorder (Section 4.5.1). A qi-gong psychotic reaction is an acute, time-limited episode of dissociative, paranoid or other psychotic or non-psychotic symptoms after taking part in qi-gong, a Chinese folk practice of exercising one's vital energy; people who become over-involved in the practice are especially vulnerable. Locura , in Latin America, is a severe chronic psychosis attributed to an inherited vulnerability, to the accumulated difficulties of life, or to both. And then there is windigo (also wendigo or witiko), the most famous syndrome that may never have existed. Among the Algonquian-speaking peoples of the Great Lakes region and the northern forests of Canada (the Ojibwe, Cree and Innu among them), the windigo is a cannibal monster, and windigo psychosis was described as an obsessive fear of turning into one, or a craving for human flesh, supposedly brought on in times of famine. In 1982 the anthropologist Lou Marano argued in Current Anthropology , in a paper subtitled "the anatomy of an emic-etic confusion", that there were probably never any windigo psychotics in the behavioural sense: the "psychosis" was an artefact of research that confused what people believed with what people did, and accusations that someone was turning windigo may have served to justify killing a person whom a hungry group saw as a threat to its survival. Windigo was not included in the DSM-IV glossary. Its nearest clinical neighbour is clinical lycanthropy , the delusional belief that one has been transformed into an animal, which is a symptom rather than a cultural syndrome (delusions are taught in Chapter 2). These descriptions also dispose of the wrong options in a favourite question, "What is the characteristic belief associated with koro?" The right answer is the belief that the genitals are retracting into the body and that this may cause death. The belief that the body has been possessed by evil spirits belongs to possession syndrome, zar or shin-byung. The belief that one is being transformed into a mythical creature echoes windigo or clinical lycanthropy. And "a sense of impending doom associated with atmospheric changes" matches no standard syndrome exactly; the nearest are the folk "wind and cold illnesses" of Asian and Latin American traditions, which Psycho Didi's notes describe as a fear of cold and wind with a feeling of weakness and susceptibility to illness, Vietnam's trúng gió (DSM-5-TR itself links trúng gió attacks to fear of "atmospheric wind"), and the wind attacks of khyâl cap.
