Recognised as one's own, felt as senseless, resisted These experiences have a special place in psychiatry because of Kurt Schneider (1887 to 1967), the Heidelberg psychiatrist who chose them, with a few others, as his first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia: experiences that could be identified reliably at a single interview and that, in the absence of organic brain disease, he regarded as strongly suggestive of the illness. The usual list has eleven items: three kinds of voices (audible thoughts or thought echo, voices arguing or discussing the patient in the third person, and voices giving a running commentary); thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting; made feelings, made impulses, made volitional acts and somatic passivity; and delusional perception (Section 2.5.2). Section 4.1.6 tells their history and gives the evidence that they are characteristic of schizophrenia but not specific to it (they also occur in mania and organic psychoses, and DSM-5-TR notes that the intruding identity states of dissociative identity disorder can resemble them); Book 2, Section 2.5.6 shows how to ask about them. What matters for this chapter is the list, and the items that are often mistaken for it. Exam trap Not first-rank: depersonalisation (an "as if" experience with insight, Section 2.10); loosening of associations (Bleuler's fundamental symptom, a sign the listener judges, Section 2.4.4); second-person voices ("You are useless") and hallucinations in senses other than hearing; delusional mood (only delusional perception is first-rank, Section 2.5.2); ideas or delusions of reference (defined by content, Section 2.5.5). An obsession is recognised as one's own thought and resisted; thought insertion is experienced as someone else's thought. Passivity means loss of authorship , not an urge that is merely strong or unwanted. 2.5 Delusions and the Other Disorders of Thought Content High yield · 5 Qs Geeta, the retired nurse from Guntur whose slowed thinking appeared in Section 2.4.2, told the doctor that her family was ruined. "There is no money left. We will have to sell the house and go and live in my brother's back room, and it is my fault, because when I was working I took money from the families of patients." She never had. Her son put her bank passbook on the table, open at a page that showed several lakhs of rupees in savings. She glanced at it and said quietly, "The bank prints those numbers to make me feel better." He had shown her the passbook every evening for a week. Each time the evidence changed nothing, except to widen the circle of the kind deceivers: first the bank, then her son, and by the end of the interview the doctor too. Geeta's belief is a delusion, and Section 2.4 has already shown that the form of thinking can be disordered while its content is ordinary. This section turns to content: what a person thinks, and the ways in which belief itself goes wrong. It starts with the delusion, the most important disorder of content and one of the defining marks of psychosis: what makes a belief delusional, how delusions arise, how they are described and what their themes point to. It then turns to the neighbours with which delusions are confused (the overvalued idea, the obsession, the phobia, the preoccupation and magical thinking) and ends with a table that sets them side by side. What makes a belief a delusion The British definition that Indian teaching follows is a sentence in which every clause does work. A delusion is a false belief, firmly held, not amenable to reason or to contrary evidence, and out of keeping with the person's educational, cultural and social background. DSM-5-TR compresses it into one line: delusions are "fixed beliefs that are not amenable to change in light of conflicting evidence". Take the clauses one at a time. "Firmly held" separates a delusion from a suspicion, a hunch or a passing fear: the person is not wondering, he knows. "Not amenable to reason or contrary evidence" is the clinical test, and Geeta's passbook shows it at work: the evidence did not dent the belief, it was absorbed into it. "Out of keeping with the person's background" excludes beliefs that the person's family, community or religion share, however strange they seem to an outsider. A delusion is idiosyncratic: it belongs to the person, not to his group. And though no definition says so, most delusions are about the person himself. They concern his safety, his worth, his body, his relationships or his destiny, which is one reason they are held with such feeling. Karl Jaspers gave the classic external marks of a delusion in his General Psychopathology of 1913: an extraordinary subjective certainty, an imperviousness to experience and to compelling counter-argument (incorrigibility), and an impossibility or falsity of content. Book 2, Section 2.5.4 and Section 4.2.2 set them out, and the opening of this section has just shown the first two. Barlow and Durand quote his description of delusion as "the basic characteristic of madness". Jaspers' deeper point is the one examiners and interviewers like, because it overturns the obvious answer. Falsity, he argued, is the weakest of the three marks. Consider a cloth merchant in Surat who became convinced that his business partner was stealing from the firm because the partner's new car carried a number plate whose digits added up to thirteen, and because the partner had worn a black shirt on a new-moon day. A year later an audit showed that the partner had in fact been taking money. The merchant's belief turned out to be true, yet it was still a delusion, because of the way he reached it (from number plates and shirts) and the way he held it (with total certainty from the first moment, untouched by the absence of any real evidence at the time). The reverse holds too: a false belief is not necessarily a delusion. A student who believes, from a misprinted notice, that the examination is on Friday holds a false belief, but it gives way at once to the correct notice. What makes a belief delusional is less what is believed than how it arose and how it is held, which is the form-and-content principle of Section 2.1 applied to belief. The definition has hard edges, and a clinician meets them every week. Some beliefs cannot be checked at all: that God speaks to one in prayer, that one was a king in a former birth, that a dead father watches over the family. These are judged not by their truth but by whether the person's group holds them, how they are held and what else is present. Religious and political convictions are held with great certainty by healthy people, but they are shared, learned and open at least to discussion within the group. DSM-5-TR concedes that the line between a delusion and a strongly held idea is "sometimes difficult to determine" and depends partly on the degree of conviction in the face of clear or reasonable contradictory evidence. Conviction can also change over time. At the beginning of an illness, and again during recovery, a delusion may be held with fluctuating conviction ("Sometimes I think it really happened; sometimes I think it was the illness"); this is called a partial delusion , and its appearance during treatment is usually a good sign. Conviction and action can come apart as well: Bleuler's patients who called themselves emperors went on with their ordinary ward work, the "double bookkeeping" that Section 4.2.2 describes, a cousin of the double orientation of Section 2.2. And knowledge can come apart from belief. DSM-5-TR observes that people with delusional disorder may be able to describe, as a fact, that others regard their beliefs as irrational, while being unable to accept it themselves: in its phrase, there may be "factual insight" but no true insight (Section 2.10). Finally, a delusion is not a lie, since the person is not trying to deceive, and it is not a perceptual error, since the senses may be working perfectly. Delusions are one of the marks of psychosis , and this chapter uses that word in a single sense. Psychosis is a loss of contact with reality, or more precisely a gross impairment of reality testing, the ability to tell what goes on in one's own mind from what goes on in the world. It shows itself in delusions, in hallucinations that the person takes to be real, and in grossly disorganised speech or behaviour. DSM-5-TR defines the psychotic disorders by abnormalities in five domains: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking (speech), grossly disorganised or abnormal motor behaviour (including catatonia) and negative symptoms. Psychosis is not a measure of severity: a person with severe depression or crippling panic can be desperately ill without being psychotic, and a person with one encapsulated delusion can be psychotic while holding down a job. The old division between the psychoses and the neuroses, in which preserved insight marked the neuroses, is discussed in Section 6.1.3. Exam trap A false belief that cannot be shaken by reason is a delusion , a disorder of thought content . An illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus and a hallucination is a perception without a stimulus: both are disorders of perception (Section 2.3). A false memory is an error of memory (Section 2.7; Book 1, Section 7.9). "Loss of contact with reality" defines psychosis , not anhedonia (Section 2.8). Falsity is the weakest of Jaspers' three marks; a true belief can still be delusional. How delusions begin: the primary delusions Jaspers' most influential contribution to the study of delusions was a question about origins. Some delusions can be understood as growing out of something else in the person's mental life: a mood, a hallucination, an earlier belief. Others cannot. A primary delusion arises directly, as a new and immediate experience of meaning that cannot be traced, by any psychological route the listener can follow, to anything that came before. Jaspers called the underlying event a primary delusional experience, and he took its ununderstandability as a sign that something new had broken into the person's life (Section 2.1 explains his distinction between understanding and explaining). British texts often call primary delusions autochthonous , from the Greek for "sprung from the soil itself", meaning that they arise from nowhere outside themselves; the same word is also used more narrowly for the sudden delusional idea described below. Section 4.2.2 follows the usual sequence of these experiences in a first episode of schizophrenia and teaches Klaus Conrad's phase model; what follows here is the phenomenology of each form. Delusional mood (in German Wahnstimmung , also called delusional atmosphere) comes first in many patients, and it is not yet a belief at all. The person feels that the world has changed in some subtle, uncanny and usually ominous way, that something is going on and that it concerns him, but he cannot say what. For two weeks before Venkat "knew", he told his brother that the factory "felt wrong". The hooter sounded different. The tea glasses in the canteen seemed to have been set out in a particular order. The trucks in the yard were parked "as if for a reason". "Something is being prepared," he said, "and it is about me, but nobody will tell me what." Delusional mood is usually anxious and perplexed, sometimes strangely exalted, and patients often find it unbearable. When a definite delusion finally crystallises out of it, the relief can be visible, because at last the strangeness has an explanation. Delusional perception ( Wahnwahrnehmung ) is the form that Kurt Schneider placed among his first-rank symptoms, and its structure is precise. Schneider described it as two-membered. The first member is a real perception, correctly perceived: nothing is wrong with the senses. The second is a delusional meaning attached to that perception, usually immediate, momentous and personal, and joined to it by no link that the listener can follow. Venkat's delusion arrived this way. "The foreman put his helmet down on the left side of the table, and I knew that I had been chosen to be killed on Friday." The helmet was there; he saw it accurately; the meaning came at once and with complete certainty; and nothing about a helmet on a table leads, by any ordinary reasoning, to a death sentence. Notice what delusional perception is not. It is not an illusion (the helmet was not misperceived) and not a hallucination (the helmet was real). Nor is it a delusional interpretation of a hallucination, in which a voice that says "Friday" is explained as a threat, because that is a secondary delusion (Section 2.5.3). The sudden delusional idea ( Wahneinfall , also called delusional intuition or delusional notion) arrives fully formed in the mind, like an inspiration, without any perception to trigger it. A second-year engineering student in Warangal was brushing his teeth one morning when he suddenly knew, beyond any doubt, that he was the grandson of a famous freedom fighter, hidden at birth and destined to lead the country. Schneider counted this form among the second-rank symptoms. In delusional memory ( Wahnerinnerung ) the delusion attaches to the past. Either a real memory is suddenly invested with a new delusional significance ("Now I understand why the nurse in the hospital where I was born wrote my name in green ink: I was registered for the experiment even then"), or the person recalls, with delusional content already built in, an event that never happened. The second kind must be told apart from confabulation (Section 2.7): confabulation fills the gaps of an amnesia, while delusional memory occurs with memory otherwise intact, as part of a psychosis. Why is delusional perception first-rank while delusional mood is not? The reason usually given lies in what Schneider was looking for: experiences that could be identified reliably at a single interview and that pointed strongly towards schizophrenia. Delusional perception has a structure that can be checked (a real percept, a sudden meaning, no understandable bridge). Delusional mood has no content yet; it is a diffuse state of unease and perplexity, and a similar uncanny feeling can occur in severe anxiety, in intoxication, in epileptic auras and at the start of a delirium, so it can neither be recognised reliably nor tied to one illness. The sudden delusional idea has a related problem: healthy people also have sudden convictions, and without the two-membered structure it is harder to be sure what has happened. One more distinction catches many students: delusional perception against the delusion of reference. They overlap, because many delusional perceptions are self-referential, but they are defined in different ways. A delusion of reference is defined by its content: the belief that events, remarks, objects or broadcasts refer to oneself (Section 2.5.5). It is often understandable as an outgrowth of an existing fear. A man who already believes that his workmates despise him sees them laughing together and is sure that they are laughing at him. Delusional perception is defined by its form: a particular percept is followed by an abrupt meaning that has no understandable connection with it, whether or not that meaning is about the person. "They laughed because they know my secret" is a delusion of reference; "When the foreman put down his helmet, I knew I would die on Friday" is a delusional perception. When a question asks which is first-rank, the answer is delusional perception; delusions of reference are not. Exam trap The four forms of primary (autochthonous) delusion are delusional mood (Wahnstimmung: something is going on, but what?), delusional perception (Wahnwahrnehmung: a real percept, then an unconnected delusional meaning; two-membered; first-rank ), the sudden delusional idea (Wahneinfall: out of the blue, no percept; second-rank) and delusional memory (Wahnerinnerung). Delusional mood is not first-rank. Delusional perception is defined by form ; a delusion of reference is defined by content . A primary delusion is Jaspers' concept (not Bleuler's or Schneider's), and the phases of trema and apophany are Conrad's. Secondary delusions, and the two roads to a fixed false belief A secondary delusion is one that can be understood as arising from another psychological experience. Jaspers called such beliefs delusion-like ideas, because the listener can follow how the person came to hold them, even though the belief is just as fixed as a primary delusion and must be treated just as seriously. Understandability is about origins, not about strength. The common sources are worth knowing, because each points to a different disorder. A depressed mood produces beliefs that fit it: guilt and sin, poverty and ruin, illness and bodily decay, and at the extreme nihilism. Geeta's certainty that she has ruined the family grows out of a mood in which she already feels worthless and to blame. An elevated mood produces beliefs of power, wealth, talent and mission. Hari, swept along by his elation, announced that God had given him a plan to end unemployment in Andhra Pradesh within forty days. Hallucinations demand an explanation. A woman who hears threatening voices through the wall every night concludes that a gang is planning to kill her; a man with burning sensations in his abdomen decides that he is being operated on while he sleeps. Passivity experiences are explained in the same way: the patient who feels his arm moved from outside infers a machine, a spirit or a satellite, and the explanation is a delusion of control (Section 2.4.7). Other delusions breed new ones. Once a man is sure that his neighbour is poisoning him, the police who refuse to arrest the neighbour must be bribed, and the doctor who finds no poison must be in the plot. This elaboration is how a delusion becomes a system. Cognitive impairment leaves gaps that suspicion fills. An 80-year-old woman with early dementia mislays her gold bangles and concludes that the maid has stolen them; the next week it is the daughter-in-law. Sensory loss and isolation do the same in later life. DSM-5-TR notes that pre-existing cognitive impairment and vision and hearing impairments may increase the risk of psychosis in older people, possibly by lowering the threshold for it. A partially deaf widow living alone hears the muffled voices of her neighbours through the wall and decides that they are plotting to take her flat. A real event can be magnified beyond all proportion: a man passed over for promotion comes to believe that the entire office is conspiring against him, which shades into the overvalued idea of Section 2.5.6. Figure 2.7 draws the two roads. Primary delusions are especially characteristic of schizophrenia; the delusions of mood disorders are usually secondary and fit the mood; and the delusions of organic states are usually secondary to confusion, memory loss or sensory loss. But the roads are tendencies, not laws. Many delusions in schizophrenia are secondary to hallucinations or to earlier delusions, and a patient can travel both roads at once. Primary road (typical of schizophrenia): cannot be traced to anything else Delusional mood "something is going on" Delusional perception, sudden delusional idea or delusional memory Elaboration, systematisation DELUSION fixed, false, not amenable to reason Secondary road (mood, organic and other states): understandable Depressed mood Elevated mood Hallucinations, passivity Memory loss, sensory loss An understandable inference: "I feel worthless, so I must have ruined us" Figure 2.7 The two roads to a fixed false belief. On the primary road a delusional meaning arrives with no understandable link to anything before it; on the secondary road the belief grows out of a mood, a hallucination, a passivity experience or an impairment. Both end in a belief that is equally fixed; what separates them is how it arose, not how firmly it is held. Why do delusions form at all? The full cognitive and biological accounts belong to Section 4.9.2 (and to Section 4.8 for dopamine), but two ideas are worth a paragraph here. Barlow and Durand, following McKay, Langdon and Coltheart (2007), sort the theories into two families. Motivational theories see a delusion as serving a purpose: a story that relieves anxiety or protects self-esteem, as when erotomania supplies love to a lonely life or persecution explains failure without blaming oneself. Deficit theories see the delusion as the product of a fault in perception, reasoning or brain function. Among the faults, the best studied is a reasoning style. In 1988 Huq, Garety and Hemsley gave people a probability task now called the beads task, in which the participant draws beads one at a time from a jar and must decide which of two jars, with opposite proportions of coloured beads, they come from. People with delusions asked for fewer beads before deciding and were more certain of their decision, a pattern now called the jumping-to-conclusions bias. The two-factor theory, which explains the misidentification syndromes by a strange experience plus a failure to reject the belief it suggests, is taught with those syndromes in Section 2.6. Exam trap A primary delusion cannot be traced to any other experience; a secondary delusion (Jaspers' delusion-like idea) can be understood from a mood, a hallucination, a passivity experience, another delusion or an impairment. "Secondary" does not mean "less firmly held" or "less serious". Jaspers' primary and secondary are not Bleuler's fundamental and accessory symptoms (Section 2.1). Delusions in depression and mania are usually secondary and mood-congruent ; primary delusions are especially typical of schizophrenia . The jumping-to-conclusions bias comes from the beads task of Huq, Garety and Hemsley (1988). Describing a delusion Naming a delusion's theme is only the start of describing it. Several further descriptions are recorded, and each tells the clinician something different. The first is organisation. A systematised delusion is a single, logically elaborated belief, or a connected set of beliefs, built around one theme, which the person can defend point by point and from which everything else follows. Unsystematised or fragmentary delusions are multiple, loosely knitted and sometimes contradictory. Systematisation is more typical of delusional disorder and fragmentation of schizophrenia, and DSM-5-TR uses the difference in its differential diagnosis: delusions in schizophrenia show greater disorganisation, while those of delusional disorder show greater conviction, greater extension into the various areas of the person's life and greater pressure (preoccupation and concern). A related term, the encapsulated delusion , describes a delusion that is walled off from the rest of the person's life, so that personality, work and conversation on other subjects remain intact; DSM-5-TR remarks on "the apparent normality" of behaviour and appearance in delusional disorder when the delusional ideas are not being discussed or acted on (Section 4.5.4). The second is fit with mood. A mood-congruent delusion has content consistent with the prevailing mood. DSM-5-TR lists the typical depressive themes as personal inadequacy, guilt, disease, death, nihilism or deserved punishment, and the typical manic themes as grandiosity and invulnerability, which may include suspiciousness about other people's doubts of the person's abilities. A mood-incongruent delusion does not fit: a severely depressed woman who believes that her thoughts are being broadcast through the ceiling fan, or a manic man who believes that his neighbours are poisoning him for no reason connected with his greatness. The distinction enters the psychotic features specifier of the mood disorders (Section 5.3.9). The third is plausibility. A bizarre delusion , in DSM-5-TR's words, is clearly implausible, not understandable to people of the same culture and not derived from ordinary life experience; its example is the belief that an outside force has removed one's internal organs and replaced them with someone else's without leaving a wound or scar. A non-bizarre delusion could happen, at least in principle, as with the belief that one is under police surveillance without convincing evidence. Delusions that express a loss of control over mind or body (thought withdrawal, thought insertion and delusions of control) are generally counted as bizarre. Two cautions follow. "Bizarre" is judged against the person's own culture, so the same belief can be bizarre in one setting and ordinary in another. And bizarre does not mean dangerous: some of the most dangerous delusions, of jealousy or persecution, are entirely plausible. DSM-IV allowed a single bizarre delusion to satisfy the first criterion for schizophrenia, and DSM-5 removed that special weight (Section 4.4.2); DSM-5-TR now offers "with bizarre content" as a specifier for delusional disorder. Delusions may also be shared , passing from one person to a close companion; folie à deux is in the eponym table of Section 2.6 and in Section 4.5.5. The last description is the one that matters most for safety: what the delusion makes the person do. Delusions vary in conviction, in how much of the day they occupy (preoccupation, or pressure), in how far into life they extend, and above all in action. A man convinced that his food is poisoned stops eating at home; a woman sure that her medicines are part of the plot stops taking them; a persecuted man may move house again and again, complain to the police, file cases or, as DSM-5-TR notes of delusional disorder, send hundreds of letters of protest to the government. Some act against the supposed persecutor or rival. DSM-5-TR observes that anger and violent behaviour can occur with the persecutory, jealous and erotomanic types. A delusion that has begun to drive behaviour is a different clinical problem from one that is merely held. Clinical link Never argue with a delusion: it hardens the belief and costs the relationship. Ask for the belief in the person's words, how he came to know it, how sure he is, and, most important, what he has done or plans to do about it. "If the neighbour really is poisoning your tank, what will you do?" is a risk question, not a challenge. Persecutory, jealous and erotomanic delusions that name a particular person need a specific assessment of that person's safety, which Book 2, Section 2.7.5 teaches. Exam trap Systematised delusions (one logical system) are typical of delusional disorder ; multiple, fragmentary ones of schizophrenia. Mood-congruent depressive themes are inadequacy, guilt, disease, death, nihilism and deserved punishment; manic themes are grandiosity and invulnerability. Bizarre means implausible, not understandable to same-culture peers and not drawn from ordinary life; it is not a measure of danger, and loss-of-control delusions count as bizarre. DSM-5 removed the rule that one bizarre delusion was enough for criterion A of schizophrenia. Delusions by theme Delusions are classified by what they are about, and the theme is one of the best single clues to the disorder behind them. Table 2.13 lists the themes with the disorders each points to; the eponymous syndromes of jealousy, love, infestation and misidentification are taught in full in Section 2.6, and the themes as they appear in schizophrenia are in Section 4.2.2, Table 4.5. Schizophrenia (first-rank) Not tied to a mood; bizarre 2.4.7 Persecutory delusions come first because they are the commonest of all. DSM-5-TR defines them as the belief that one is going to be harmed, harassed and so on by an individual, an organisation or another group, and it states plainly that they are the most common delusions. Its description of the persecutory type of delusional disorder spells out the range: the person believes that he is being conspired against, cheated, spied on, followed, poisoned or drugged, maliciously maligned, harassed or obstructed in the pursuit of long-term goals. The persecutor may be a neighbour, a relative, a caste or political group, the police, the government, a company or an unseen force, and the method borrows from the times: poison in the water tank, black magic, mobile towers, hacked phones. Persecutory delusions are found above all in schizophrenia, where they are the most frequent delusion, and in delusional disorder, whose commonest subtype is persecutory. They also occur in mania, in psychotic depression (where the persecution is often felt to be deserved: "They are coming to punish me, and I deserve it"), in delirium and dementia, and in intoxication with stimulants, where Barlow and Durand note that cocaine-induced paranoia is common. Two old words travel with persecution, and examiners use both. "Paranoia" comes from the Greek para (beside) and nous (mind), and in ancient Greek it meant madness in general; it appears in the Greek tragedians and in Plato and Hippocrates in roughly that sense. Physicians revived the word in the eighteenth century, and Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926) gave its narrower modern meaning the classic description: a chronic, systematised delusional state that develops slowly, usually later in life, without hallucinations and without the deterioration of personality seen in dementia praecox. Today that condition is called delusional disorder (Section 4.5.4). In modern clinical English, "paranoid" means persecutory or self-referential: paranoid ideation is suspiciousness and the sense of being persecuted or watched, held short of delusional certainty. Paranoid personality disorder, an enduring pattern of distrust and suspicion without fixed delusions, is taught in Chapter 11, and the paranoid subtype of schizophrenia, which DSM-5 abandoned, in Section 4.4.3. Exam trap A person who believes that others are "out to get" him and that he is being attacked by rays has a persecutory delusion, the hallmark of paranoia and paranoid states; it is not a symptom of depression, dissociative disorder or anxiety disorder as such. Being "deliberately interfered with, discriminated against, plotted against, threatened or otherwise mistreated" is persecution , not reference (special meaning in events), control (outside force directing one's acts) or grandiosity. Persecutory delusions are the most common delusions, and they are most commonly seen in schizophrenia ; they also occur in bipolar disorder, so read "most commonly" as the deciding word. They are not features of OCD or panic disorder. A delusion of reference is the belief that events, objects, gestures, remarks or broadcasts that have nothing to do with the person are directed at him; DSM-5-TR calls these referential delusions and counts them among the common ones. A man watching a cricket match hears the commentator say "a long innings ahead" and knows it is a warning to him; a woman is sure that the songs on the radio are chosen to comment on her life. The same kind of thought held without delusional conviction is an idea of reference , which DSM-5-TR describes, in its account of schizotypal personality disorder, as an incorrect interpretation of casual incidents and external events as having a particular and unusual meaning specifically for the person, and distinguishes from the delusion of reference held with full conviction. Ideas of reference are common in social anxiety, in schizotypal and paranoid personality (Chapter 11) and in ordinary self-consciousness: the student who walks into a silent classroom and wonders, for a moment, whether everyone was talking about him, and then accepts that they probably were not. A grandiose delusion , in DSM-5-TR's words, is the belief that one has exceptional abilities, wealth or fame, and the grandiose type of delusional disorder adds the conviction of having some great but unrecognised talent or insight or of having made an important discovery. Grandiose delusions are the classic mood-congruent delusions of mania; they also occur in schizophrenia and delusional disorder, and historically they were the hallmark of general paresis, the brain syphilis of Book 2, Section 1.3.6. Closely related are religious delusions , in which the content concerns God, gods, saints, sin or a divine mission. Here the clinician must hold two cautions at once. Religious belief is part of ordinary life for most Indians and is not a symptom; yet DSM-5-TR warns that elevated religiosity can itself be a feature of many presentations of psychosis. The question, as always, is form: whether the belief is shared and held in the ordinary way, or is personal, unshakeable and new. Three themes belong to depression. In delusions of guilt and sin the person believes that he has committed a terrible wrong, or that his past failings, often trivial, have caused real disasters, and that he deserves punishment. In delusions of poverty or ruin , like Geeta's, he believes that he and his family are destitute or about to be. And in the nihilistic delusion he believes that he, his body, his mind or the world does not exist, is dead or is decaying: his intestines have rotted, his blood has dried up, his brain is gone, the world has ended. Nihilistic delusions are most typical of severe psychotic depression, especially in older people, where they are mood-congruent; they can also occur in schizophrenia and in organic states. Their most extreme form, in which the person believes that he is dead, is Cotard syndrome, taught in Section 2.6. One wording trap deserves a sentence of its own: DSM-5-TR's own definition, in its chapter on the psychotic disorders, says that nihilistic delusions "involve the conviction that a major catastrophe will occur", a meaning wider than the British one, so read the stem of a question carefully. Exam trap Nihilistic delusions (oneself, one's organs or the world do not exist, are dead or are decaying) are commonly seen in depression , above all severe psychotic depression in older people. They are not features of obsessive-compulsive disorder (obsessions are resisted, not believed) or of somatoform disorder (bodily preoccupation without delusional conviction). They can occur in schizophrenia, but depression is the keyed and the best answer. DSM-5-TR defines them differently, as "the conviction that a major catastrophe will occur". Cotard syndrome (the belief that one is dead) is the extreme form (Section 2.6). Hypochondriacal or somatic delusions are, in DSM-5-TR's words, focused on "preoccupations regarding health and organ function", and the somatic type of delusional disorder covers any central delusion about bodily functions or sensations. In psychotic depression they take mood-congruent forms ("My bowels are blocked with cement; nothing has passed for a month"); in schizophrenia they are often bizarre ("My kidneys have been changed for a goat's"); in delusional disorder they are usually plausible (an infestation, a foul smell, a misshapen feature). They must be kept apart from the health anxiety of illness anxiety disorder (Section 7.7.3), where the fear of disease can be reasoned with at least for a while, and from the conviction of body dysmorphic disorder, which DSM-5-TR grades by insight and diagnoses as body dysmorphic disorder "with absent insight/delusional beliefs" rather than as delusional disorder when conviction is complete (Section 6.6.2). Four further themes have eponyms and are taught in Section 2.6: delusional infestation (Ekbom syndrome), delusional jealousy (Othello syndrome), erotomania (de Clérambault syndrome) and the misidentification delusions (Capgras and Fregoli). Delusions of control , the explanations patients give for the passivity experiences, were taught in Section 2.4.7. Every one of these themes must finally be judged against culture. DSM-5-TR warns that some religious and supernatural beliefs, such as the evil eye, illness caused by curses and the influence of spirits, may look bizarre and possibly delusional in one cultural setting and be generally accepted in another, and that people who have survived torture, political violence or discrimination may report fears that sound persecutory but are realistic fears of recurrence or post-traumatic symptoms. Book 2, Section 2.5.4 and Section 4.2.2 each give an Indian-context box on black magic, the evil eye and spirits; their shared rule is to ask whether the family and community hold the same belief in the same way, and whether the patient's conviction has gone beyond theirs in certainty, elaboration and personal reference. What a culture supplies is the vocabulary of a delusion; what makes it a delusion is still its form. Overvalued ideas Not every abnormal belief is a delusion, and the most important intermediate category has a German name. The overvalued idea ( überwertige Idee ) was introduced by Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905), the German neuropsychiatrist whose name is also on a language area of the brain and on an encephalopathy of thiamine deficiency. He first described it in 1892, in a forensic context, and gave it a fuller account in his Grundriss der Psychiatrie (1900), the date many textbooks cite. An overvalued idea is a solitary, abnormal but understandable belief, charged with intense feeling, that comes to dominate the person's life and actions to a morbid degree. Four features separate it from a delusion. It is understandable in the light of the person's personality, history and values, often as an exaggeration of a value that others share. The person identifies with it and defends it, rather than experiencing it as an alien intrusion. It is held strongly but not with full delusional fixity, so that it can be argued about, even if not easily changed. And it dominates: the idea organises the person's time, choices and relationships far beyond what its truth or importance would justify. In the terms of Section 2.1 it is ego-syntonic. The examples show how varied the category is. A 17-year-old schoolgirl in Bengaluru with anorexia nervosa says: "I know the doctor says I am underweight. But one chapati makes my stomach stick out, and being thin matters more to me than my board exams." The dread of fatness is the overvalued idea of anorexia nervosa (Chapter 8). A young man with body dysmorphic disorder is certain that his nose is crooked and that everyone notices it, though he will concede, when pressed, that the mirror may exaggerate (Section 6.6.2). A retired clerk has spent twenty years fighting a pension dispute through every court and has written to the Prime Minister eleven times; his grievance began with a real injustice, but it has consumed his marriage and his savings. Morbid jealousy that stops short of delusion (Section 2.6), hypochondriacal convictions and single-minded political or religious causes complete the list. In 1984 the British psychiatrist P. J. McKenna reviewed the disorders in which an overvalued idea is the central symptom. He argued that they are well documented but variably recognised, that they share a distinctive phenomenology and develop in similar settings, and that they carry a uniformly poor prognosis. Where does the overvalued idea end and the delusion begin? There is no sharp line. DSM-5-TR's insight specifier for body dysmorphic disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder (good or fair insight, poor insight, absent insight or delusional beliefs) is in effect a ladder across it, and DSM-5-TR also notes that in some cultural groups distress may take the form of overvalued ideas that can look like psychosis but are normative for that group. The practical guide is the one Wernicke gave the idea: an overvalued idea is understandable and not fully fixed; a delusion is neither. Exam trap The overvalued idea is Wernicke's , not Jaspers' or Schneider's. It is a solitary, understandable, emotionally charged belief that dominates the person's life, held strongly but less fixedly than a delusion, and defended rather than resisted (unlike an obsession). The anorexic dread of fatness, the body dysmorphic defect and querulous litigation are the classic examples. Morbid jealousy can be delusional, overvalued or obsessional (Section 2.6). Obsessions, phobias, preoccupations and magical thinking The remaining disorders of content are the ones the person does not believe in the way he believes a delusion, or does not believe at all. The obsession is the most important, and it was met in Section 2.4.7 through Padma's blasphemous thought during her puja. Its classical definition has four parts: an obsession is a recurrent, persistent thought, image, impulse or doubt; the person recognises it as a product of his own mind; he experiences it as intrusive and usually as senseless, excessive or repugnant; and he tries to resist, suppress or neutralise it. DSM-5-TR keeps the core, defining obsessions as recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges or images experienced as intrusive and unwanted, which the person tries to ignore, suppress or neutralise with another thought or action, usually a compulsion. Notice what it left out. DSM-IV had also required that the person recognise the obsessions as a product of his own mind (not imposed from without, as in thought insertion); DSM-5 dropped that clause, and DSM-5-TR's criteria do not contain it. The distinction from thought insertion has not become any less important at the bedside (Section 2.4.7), and ICD-10 still lists recognition of the thoughts as one's own among its tests (Section 6.5.2). Obsessions take several forms: obsessional thoughts and images ("a picture of my baby falling from the balcony"), impulses ("I might shout an obscenity in the temple"), doubts ("Did I switch off the gas?"), fears and obsessional ruminations , prolonged, inconclusive deliberations on questions that cannot be answered ("Why is the sky above and not below?"). Rumination in the looser sense, the brooding of depression over past failures and losses, is different: it is not resisted, it is tied to the low mood and it does not feel senseless to the person. The obsession is ego-dystonic (Section 2.1), and that is precisely what separates it from the delusion and the overvalued idea, which are accepted. What happens when conviction does creep in is captured by DSM-5-TR's rule: if a person with obsessive-compulsive disorder becomes completely convinced that his obsessional beliefs are true, the diagnosis remains obsessive-compulsive disorder, with absent insight or delusional beliefs, rather than delusional disorder. The disorder itself, its insight specifier and its look-alikes are in Sections 6.5.2, 6.5.5 and 6.5.8; compulsions are described with the motor signs in Section 2.9. A phobia , as a symptom, is a persistent, excessive and irrational fear of a specific object, activity or situation, out of proportion to any real danger, that leads to avoidance or to endurance with intense distress; adults usually recognise that the fear is excessive. It is recorded under content because what a person fears and avoids is part of what occupies his mind. "I know the dog next door is chained, but I take the long road round to the bus stop every day." What makes a fear a phobia, and the names of the phobias, are in Sections 6.3.1 and 6.3.5. The rest of thought content is recorded as preoccupations , the themes to which a person's thinking keeps returning without the intrusiveness of an obsession or the fixity of a delusion. In depression they are the depressive cognitions of worthlessness, hopelessness, helplessness and guilt (Chapter 5). Other common preoccupations are hypochondriacal (with health and illness), religious, philosophical (with questions about the meaning of life, seen in healthy people as well as in mild depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder and schizotypal personality) and with the event that precipitated the illness, as in a reactive depression after a business failure. Every examination also records thoughts of death, and here the wording matters. A passive death wish ("I wish I would not wake up") is not the same as suicidal ideation (thoughts of ending one's own life), which in turn is not a plan or an intent; how each is asked about and weighed is in Book 2, Section 2.7, and suicide itself in Section 5.8. Finally, magical thinking is the belief that one's thoughts, words or actions can cause or prevent events in ways that defy ordinary cause and effect. It is normal in young children, and practices that a whole culture shares, such as hanging a lemon and green chillies at a shop door against the evil eye, are not magical thinking in the clinical sense. It is common in obsessive-compulsive disorder, where a ritual is felt to prevent a disaster, and DSM-5-TR lists odd beliefs or magical thinking that influence behaviour and are inconsistent with subcultural norms among the criteria for schizotypal personality disorder, beside ideas of reference (Book 2, Section 2.5.5 gives the clinical recording; Chapter 11 the disorder). Answers: (1) flight of ideas, (2) block; withdrawal, (3) circumstantiality; tangentiality, (4) word salad, (5) Cameron; Goldstein, (6) broadcasting, (7) perception, (8) persecution, (9) depression, (10) overvalued idea. 2.6 The Named Syndromes: Misidentification, Cotard, Othello and the Other Eponyms High yield · 12 Qs Psychiatry inherited from the great nineteenth-century clinics of Paris a habit of putting a person's name on any picture striking enough to be remembered. A woman who insists that her husband is an impostor, a man who says that he has been dead for a month, a husband who searches his wife's clothes every night for proof of an affair, an expectant father who is sick every morning of his wife's pregnancy: each of these has been given an eponym, and the eponyms have become some of the most reliable marks in any psychopathology paper. Why should you learn them as more than a list? There are three good reasons. Each name is a precise shorthand: "Capgras" tells a colleague in one word what would otherwise take a paragraph. Each comes with a history that explains what the first observers thought was going wrong, and in several cases that history turned out to be a clue to the brain. And, most important for answering questions correctly, almost none of them is a diagnosis. Look in DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 for "Capgras syndrome" or "Cotard syndrome" and you will not find a disorder with criteria. These are descriptive syndromes : recognisable clusters of beliefs or experiences that turn up inside many different disorders, among them schizophrenia, delusional disorder, psychotic depression, mania, dementia and brain injury. The practical consequence is a two-step habit. When a stem describes a patient, first name the syndrome (an impostor belief is Capgras), then ask which disorder it is sitting in (a woman with Parkinson's disease and visual hallucinations points to a dementia; a young man with voices and thought insertion points to schizophrenia). The delusional themes in general (persecution, reference, grandiosity, guilt, nihilism, jealousy, love, infestation) were introduced in Section 2.5, and Section 4.5.4 describes the types of delusional disorder; this section is where the named syndromes are taught in full, with who named them, where they occur and how they are explained. Capgras syndrome and the misidentification family Start with the family to which the most famous eponym belongs. In 1981 the Greek psychiatrist George N. Christodoulou , writing with S. Malliara-Loulakaki, grouped a set of strange beliefs under one heading, and the 1986 volume he edited, The Delusional Misidentification Syndromes , made the umbrella term standard. A delusional misidentification syndrome is a delusion in which the identity of a person, a place or an object is believed to have been changed, duplicated or disguised, although the person or place is perceived essentially normally. Christodoulou counted four core members: Capgras syndrome, Fregoli syndrome, intermetamorphosis and the syndrome of subjective doubles. He noticed three things about them. They often occur in the same patient, at the same time or one after another. They share a single theme, the idea of the double (French sosie ). And they divide neatly into two directions. In hypoidentification a well-known person is under-identified: the familiar is declared unfamiliar, which is Capgras. In hyperidentification unknown people are over-identified: the unfamiliar is declared familiar, which is the other three. Because each patient's delusion is usually confined to this one theme, the syndromes are also called monothematic delusions . You met the first patient at the start of this chapter. Madame M. agreed that the men who visited her resembled her husband, offering only trifles as proof that they were not him, and that agreement was the whole puzzle. Joseph Capgras (1873 to 1950) and his intern Jean Reboul-Lachaux called what she showed l'illusion des sosies , the illusion of doubles, in 1923, and in 1929 their colleague Joseph Lévy-Valensi proposed that it be called le syndrome de Capgras . Today Capgras syndrome (or the Capgras delusion) is the delusional belief that a person well known to the patient has been replaced by an impostor who is physically identical, or nearly so. Three features define it. The replaced person is almost always someone emotionally close: a spouse above all, then a parent, a child or a sibling. The patient accepts the physical resemblance; at most she points to trivial differences (a mark, a slightly thinner face) as her proof, and there is no failure to see the face. And the conviction is held with delusional certainty, so that proofs of identity (wedding photographs, shared memories, a scar in the right place) are absorbed into the belief: the impostor has simply studied his part very well. The impostors can multiply, and the same idea can attach to a pet, to a treasured object or to the patient's own home. Here is what the syndrome looks and sounds like. Usha, a 71-year-old retired school principal in Thrissur, has changed over the past year. Her memory and alertness swing from one day to the next, her walk has become slow and shuffling, and for some months she has seen small children playing on the terrace in the evenings, a combination that her neurologist recognises as dementia with Lewy bodies (Chapter 10). One evening she bolts her bedroom door and telephones her son in Bengaluru. "Your father has gone somewhere. This man has his face, his voice, even his spectacles with the broken arm, but he is not your father. Your father would never leave me sitting in the dark." When her husband speaks to her on the telephone from the market the next morning she is warm and relieved; when he walks in through the door an hour later he is the stranger again, and she asks him what he has done with her real husband. Notice what is intact: she sees his face accurately, she names every feature correctly, and she remembers forty-six years of marriage. What has failed is the conclusion she draws from the sight of him. Where does Capgras syndrome occur? In psychiatric practice it is seen most often in schizophrenia and the other psychoses, especially in paranoid presentations, and also in mood disorders with psychotic features. In neurological practice it is a well-recognised feature of dementia with Lewy bodies, Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, and it follows brain injury, stroke and other lesions, typically involving the right hemisphere and the frontal lobes; it has also been reported with migraine, diabetes and hypothyroidism. It may be acute and transient, or chronic. For decades after 1923 the explanations offered were psychoanalytic: the patient was said to resolve unbearable ambivalence towards a loved person by splitting off the hated part and attributing it to an impostor. Attention turned to the brain in the late 1970s and 1980s, when clinicians noticed how often the patients had organic lesions, and Christodoulou's advice still stands: the appearance of a misidentification syndrome should make the clinician look for an organic contribution, even in a patient with an established psychosis. The syndrome matters clinically because of what the patient may do. A person who believes that an impostor has taken over her home, and has perhaps harmed her real husband, is frightened and angry. Patients refuse to eat food the "impostor" prepares, lock him out, demand that the police find the real spouse, and occasionally attack the double; assaults and even killings have been reported, so the safety of the misidentified person is part of every assessment (Book 2, Section 2.7.5 teaches the assessment of the risk of violence). Treatment is the treatment of the underlying condition: an antipsychotic for a psychosis, attention to the delirium or dementia in an older patient, and great caution with antipsychotics in dementia with Lewy bodies, in which severe neuroleptic sensitivity is a recognised feature (Chapter 10). Exam trap A familiar person replaced by an identical impostor is Capgras, whatever the setting (schizophrenia, dementia or brain injury). Strangers who are really one familiar person in disguise is Fregoli. The belief that one is dead or has lost one's organs is Cotard. Delusional infidelity is Othello. Folie à deux is a shared delusion passed from one person to another (Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret, 1877; Section 4.5.5). "One is being persecuted by a secret organisation" is an ordinary persecutory delusion (Section 2.5), and "one's body has been stolen and replaced" is not a named syndrome at all but a bizarre somatic delusion (Section 2.5). In the vignette of an older man with mild cognitive impairment who says his wife of forty years is an identical "duplicate", the answer is still Capgras: the object is a person. Reduplicative paramnesia is the near miss, because it classically duplicates a place ; some authors (Michael Alexander, Donald Stuss and Frank Benson, 1979) have described Capgras as a "reduplication" of a person, which is why the two are confused. Fregoli, intermetamorphosis, subjective doubles and reduplicative paramnesia In 1927 Paul Courbon (1879 to 1958) and Gabriel Fail published a paper whose title linked a music-hall artist to schizophrenia: "Syndrome d'illusion de Frégoli et schizophrénie". Their patient was a 27-year-old woman who believed that two actors she often saw at the theatre were persecuting her, pursuing her closely by taking on the forms of people she knew or met. Courbon and Fail named the picture after Leopoldo Fregoli (1867 to 1936), an Italian actor famous across Europe for quick-change acts in which he played many characters in a single performance, reappearing within seconds in a new costume and a new voice. Fregoli syndrome is the delusional belief that different people the patient meets are in fact one and the same person, usually someone known to the patient, who keeps changing appearance or disguise. Because the person "behind" the disguises is usually a persecutor, the syndrome is nearly always paranoid. A 30-year-old man in Lucknow is sure that the supervisor who dismissed him is following him: he is the sugarcane-juice seller at the corner, the security guard at the mall, the new clerk at the bank, each wearing a different face but betrayed by "the same eyes". Fregoli syndrome is seen in schizophrenia and other psychoses and after brain injury, and it has been reported with levodopa treatment of Parkinson's disease. It is rarer than Capgras. The third member was described by Courbon again, this time with Jean Tusques , in 1932. In intermetamorphosis the patient believes that people around him change into one another, in their external appearance and in their personality, and he may claim to see the transformation happen. One man with Alzheimer's disease took his wife first for his dead mother and later for his sister, and his son for his brother, and the misidentification continued even on the telephone, which showed that it was not a simple failure of seeing. Where Fregoli is a disguise (the same persecutor under different costumes), intermetamorphosis is a real change of identity, of mind as well as face. The fourth core member concerns the self. In 1978, in the American Journal of Psychiatry , Christodoulou described the syndrome of subjective doubles : the delusional belief that one has a double, or several doubles, physically identical to oneself (sometimes with a different character) and leading separate lives. Patients may hold the double responsible for things they are accused of, or fear that the double will take their place with their family. Keep this apart from the autoscopic hallucination of Section 2.3. In autoscopy a person sees an image of himself, a perceptual experience; in the syndrome of subjective doubles he believes, without necessarily seeing anything, that another copy of him exists. The last syndrome in the group is older than the others and concerns places. In 1903 the Prague psychiatrist Arnold Pick (1851 to 1924), best known for the dementia that bears his name, published a paper in Brain called "On reduplicative paramnesia". His patient, a woman with a progressive dementia, insisted that she had been moved from his clinic in the city to another clinic that looked exactly the same but stood in a suburb she knew well; to explain the coincidence she said that Pick and his staff worked in both places. Today reduplicative paramnesia means the delusional belief that a familiar place exists in two or more locations at once, or has been moved to another site. A 58-year-old woman recovering from a right-hemisphere stroke in a large Delhi hospital agrees that it is the same hospital, with the same doctors and the same canteen, "but it has been shifted to Meerut, near my mother's lane; that is why I can hear the trains." For seventy years the condition was a curiosity. Then in 1976 D. Frank Benson , Howard Gardner and J. C. Meadows described three patients who, after severe head injuries, had recovered most of their memory but persistently relocated the hospital to another town, even in the face of compelling evidence; they drew attention to damage in the right hemisphere and the frontal lobes, the same pattern that later work found in Capgras syndrome. The condition is seen after head injury and stroke, with tumours and in dementia. Why did Pick call it a paramnesia , a distortion of memory, rather than a delusion? Because the place is recognised: the patient knows the ward, the faces, the routine. What has gone wrong is the attachment of that familiarity to the right location, a fault in the recognition of the familiar, which is why Section 2.7 places reduplicative paramnesia on the recognition branch of the paramnesias. Modern accounts combine two deficits, much like the two-factor account you will meet below: right-hemisphere damage that disturbs spatial orientation and visual memory, and frontal damage that stops the patient from rejecting the impossible conclusion. Two further pictures are seen mainly in dementia. In mirrored-self misidentification the patient believes that her reflection in a mirror is another person, a stranger, a younger version of herself or a relative, while still recognising other people's reflections; she may talk to the woman in the mirror, offer her tea, or complain that someone is watching her from the bathroom. It is associated with right-hemisphere dysfunction. The phantom boarder belief, that strangers are living in the house, eating the food and moving things, is common in Alzheimer's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. Courbon named two of them: Fregoli with Fail in 1927, intermetamorphosis with Tusques in 1932. Why a face can look right and feel wrong: the Ellis and Young account Return to Usha's question, the one Capgras could not answer: if she sees her husband's face correctly and remembers him perfectly, why does she conclude that he is someone else? The answer that most researchers now accept came from an unexpected direction, the study of a neurological disorder that looks like Capgras turned inside out. In prosopagnosia , after damage to the face-processing regions of the temporal and occipital lobes, a person can see a face clearly, describe its features and tell that it is a face, but cannot recognise whose face it is, even when it belongs to a spouse or a child (the Physiological book teaches the condition itself). In 1984 the American neuropsychologist Russell M. Bauer showed a prosopagnosic patient photographs of familiar people while reading out several names for each and recording his skin conductance, the tiny change in the electrical resistance of the skin that accompanies autonomic arousal. The patient could not say who the people were. Yet his skin conductance rose more when the correct name was read than when a wrong one was. Some part of his brain knew the faces and responded to them emotionally, without his being aware of it. This is called covert recognition , and it implied that recognising a face involves at least two routes: one that delivers the conscious identification ("that is my wife") and another that delivers an automatic, emotional response to a face that matters. In 1990 two British psychologists, Hadyn D. Ellis and Andrew W. Young, put the pieces together in a paper in the British Journal of Psychiatry called "Accounting for delusional misidentifications". They proposed that Capgras syndrome is the mirror image of prosopagnosia. In prosopagnosia the conscious route is broken and the affective route survives, so the face is not recognised but still "feels" familiar to the autonomic nervous system. In Capgras syndrome the conscious route survives and the affective route is broken, so the face is recognised as looking exactly like the husband's while the expected glow of familiarity is missing. Faced with a face that looks right and feels wrong, the patient reaches for the only explanation that fits both facts: this is someone who looks exactly like my husband, an impostor. The account also explains why the impostor is nearly always a person the patient loves. The stronger the emotional response a face normally produces, the more conspicuous its absence. The same paper explained Fregoli syndrome and intermetamorphosis as faults at other stages of the same chain of face processing, in which a sense of familiarity is wrongly attached to strangers. Figure 2.10 shows the two routes and the two opposite breaks. Break 1 = prosopagnosia: no conscious recognition, yet skin conductance still rises to known faces (covert recognition) A familiar face is seen Face is processed and matched Conscious route identity named: "that is my husband" Affective route familiarity is felt (skin conductance rises) 1 2 Combined: looks right, feels right Break 2 = Capgras: conscious recognition intact, but no felt familiarity; the face looks right, feels wrong, "so he is an impostor" Figure 2.10 Two routes from a seen face, after Ellis and Young (1990). Prosopagnosia breaks the conscious route (break 1) but spares the affective one, so the skin still responds to faces the person cannot name; Capgras syndrome breaks the affective route (break 2) but spares the conscious one, so the face is named correctly and yet feels like a stranger's. The two disorders are a double dissociation. Key study: the skin that did not recognise (Ellis, Young, Quayle and de Pauw, 1997) A theory that says Capgras patients lack the autonomic response to familiar faces makes a testable prediction, and in 1997 Ellis, Young and their colleagues A. H. Quayle and K. W. de Pauw tested it in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B . They recorded skin conductance in five people with the Capgras delusion while they looked at photographs of familiar and of unfamiliar faces, and compared them with five healthy middle-aged volunteers and with five psychiatric patients taking similar antipsychotic medication. The healthy and the psychiatric controls responded more strongly to the familiar faces. The Capgras patients did not: their skin made no distinction between faces they knew and faces they had never seen. Their responses to simple tones were normal, so the deficit was not a general flattening of arousal but specific to the personal significance of faces. In the same year William Hirstein and Vilayanur S. Ramachandran described a young man, DS, who developed the delusion after a head injury. His skin conductance responses to photographs of his own parents were no larger than to strangers, and his delusion was tied to the eyes: his parents were impostors when he looked at them, but not when he spoke to them on the telephone, because the route from the voice to the emotions was intact. They proposed a disconnection between the face areas of the temporal lobe and the limbic system, particularly the amygdala. Criticism: the samples are tiny, and the same loss of autonomic response has been found in some patients with frontal damage who never developed a delusion, which is the strongest argument that the odd experience alone is not enough. That last criticism led to the most influential refinement of the theory. If an absent feeling of familiarity were enough to create the belief, everyone with that deficit would have the delusion, and they do not. The Australian cognitive neuropsychologist Max Coltheart , with Robyn Langdon , Martin Davies, Ryan McKay and others, therefore proposed a two-factor theory of monothematic delusions, set out in a series of papers from about 2000 and summarised in a 2011 review. The first factor is a neuropsychological abnormality that produces an anomalous experience and explains the delusion's content: in Capgras, the missing autonomic response to a loved face. The second factor is an impairment in the system that evaluates beliefs, which explains why the bizarre explanation is adopted and kept instead of being rejected, as a healthy person would reject the thought "my husband has been replaced". The second factor has most often been linked to damage in the right frontal lobe, which fits the frequency of right frontal lesions in Capgras syndrome and reduplicative paramnesia. In the terms of Section 2.5, this is a deficit account rather than a motivational one: the delusion is the product of a damaged recognition system plus damaged belief checking, not a defence against unacceptable feelings, although the two kinds of explanation may each fit some patients. Andrew Young and his colleagues went one step further in the 1990s and suggested that the same abnormal experience, a world of faces that has lost its emotional colour, may be interpreted in two opposite ways. A suspicious person who looks outwards for causes concludes that something is wrong with the others: they are impostors (Capgras). A depressed person who looks inwards concludes that something is wrong with himself: perhaps he is dead (Cotard). Whether or not that bridge holds, it leads naturally to the next syndrome. Cotard syndrome: the walking corpse Jules Cotard (1840 to 1889) trained in Paris and worked at the Salpêtrière with Jean-Martin Charcot before spending the last fifteen years of his life in practice at Vanves, near Paris. In 1880, in a lecture to the Société Médico-Psychologique titled "On hypochondriacal delusions in a severe form of anxious melancholia", he described a woman he called Mademoiselle X. She said that she had no brain, no nerves, no chest and no entrails, that she was nothing but skin and bones over a decomposing body. She therefore had no need to eat. She also said that she could not die a natural death and was condemned to exist for ever. Cotard thought that he had found a new and grave form of agitated melancholia, and in 1882 he gave the central symptom the name by which the French still know the syndrome, le délire des négations , the delusion of negation. Cotard syndrome (Cotard's delusion, the "walking corpse" syndrome) is a set of nihilistic delusions centred on the patient's own body and existence: the belief that one is dead, does not exist, is rotting or putrefying, or has lost one's blood, internal organs or soul. The denial may spread outwards to the world (the family no longer exists, the city has been destroyed, there is no God) and, paradoxically, it is often combined with a delusion of immortality : having no body, the patient cannot die and will suffer for ever. Listen to how it sounds in a 66-year-old retired railway clerk in Vijayawada, admitted after three weeks of refusing food: "Why do you give me rice? There is no stomach to put it in. The pipes inside me have closed. I died in the month of Shravan; you are talking to what is left." He is agitated, wrings his hands, and asks the nurses to send him to the burning ghat. Note the logic of the delusion, which is also its danger: a person who believes himself dead sees no reason to eat, drink, take medicines or avoid harm, so starvation, dehydration and suicide are the main risks. How common is each feature, and in which illnesses? The best-known answer is a 1995 statistical analysis by the Cambridge historian of psychiatry Germán E. Berrios and R. Luque of 100 published cases. Depression was reported in 89 per cent; the commonest nihilistic delusions concerned the body (86 per cent) and existence (69 per cent); anxiety (65 per cent), guilt (63 per cent), hypochondriacal delusions (58 per cent) and delusions of immortality (55 per cent) were also frequent; and the likelihood of the syndrome increased with age. A factor analysis divided the cases into three groups: psychotic depression with few nihilistic delusions, a "pure" Cotard type I closer to the delusional disorders than to mood disorder, and a mixed Cotard type II with anxiety, depression and auditory hallucinations. The usual setting, then, is a severe, often agitated psychotic depression in an older person (Section 5.3.9), but the syndrome also occurs in schizophrenia, in bipolar disorder (in adolescents and young adults it has been linked to a later bipolar course) and in neurological illness, including brain injury, epilepsy, stroke and dementia. Treatment follows the setting: an antidepressant combined with an antipsychotic for psychotic depression, and electroconvulsive therapy, which works quickly and is often the treatment of choice when the patient is refusing food or is at high risk of suicide (Section 5.7.7). One distinction must be made at the bedside every time. Many people with depersonalisation say that they feel "as if I were dead", "like a robot", "not really here". That is an experience held as if , with reality testing intact: the person knows that he is alive. The Cotard patient says, without any "as if", that he is dead, and argues the point. The first is depersonalisation (Section 2.10 and Table 7.14); the second is a delusion. Exam trap Cotard syndrome is defined by nihilistic delusions: of being dead, not existing, rotting, or having lost one's organs or blood (Jules Cotard, 1880; délire des négations , 1882). It is not grandiose (special powers or abilities are the grandiose delusions of mania), not persecutory (being followed or monitored), not an impostor belief (that is Capgras) and not a somatic delusion of serious illness such as cancer or AIDS, even though its content concerns the body: the Cotard patient does not believe the organs are diseased but that they are gone or dead. Watch the wording of the classifications too: DSM-5-TR uses "nihilistic delusions" for the conviction that a major catastrophe will occur, so read each stem to see which meaning is being tested. The usual setting is severe psychotic depression in later life, but the syndrome is not confined to it. Othello syndrome and the forms of morbid jealousy In Shakespeare's play the Moorish general Othello is led by his ensign Iago to believe that his faithful wife Desdemona has betrayed him with his lieutenant Cassio, and the "evidence" is a handkerchief planted where he will find it. He smothers her. In 1955 two British psychiatrists, John Todd and Kenneth Dewhurst , borrowed his name for a paper in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease , "The Othello syndrome: a study in the psychopathology of sexual jealousy". Othello syndrome is now used for delusional jealousy : the fixed, false belief that one's spouse or sexual partner is being unfaithful, held without adequate cause and unshaken by evidence. Critics point out that the eponym fits poorly, because Othello was deceived by a skilled manipulator rather than deluded, and because it suggests a single condition where there is really a family. That family is called morbid jealousy (or pathological jealousy), and the first job of the clinician is to decide which member is in front of him. In delusional jealousy the belief has the full character of a delusion: certain, ego-syntonic, not resisted, and often elaborated with care and plausibility. DSM-5-TR's description of delusional disorder, jealous type, catches the reasoning exactly: the belief is arrived at without due cause and rests on incorrect inferences from small bits of "evidence", such as disarrayed clothing, and the person usually confronts the partner and tries to intervene in the imagined infidelity. Delusional jealousy is seen in delusional disorder (Section 4.5.4), in schizophrenia, in organic states such as dementia and brain injury, and with alcohol and stimulants. In overvalued jealousy the idea is understandable and not absurd (perhaps the partner once did have an affair) but it is pursued beyond the bounds of reason and dominates the person's life, though it remains open to some argument. In obsessional jealousy the thoughts "what if she is with someone?" are recognised as excessive and senseless, resisted, ego-dystonic and shameful, and they drive checking and reassurance-seeking; DSM-5-TR lists this non-delusional preoccupation with a partner's perceived infidelity as an example of other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder (Section 6.6.6).
