Naveen, a 45-year-old dealer in tractor spare parts in Hubballi, has been drinking heavily for twelve years. For the last two he has been sure that his wife is meeting the young man who delivers milk. He checks the time she was last seen on WhatsApp against the time she says she slept; he smells her dupatta for a stranger's perfume; he marks the position of the gate latch before he leaves for the shop and phones home four times a day; he has twice come back unannounced at noon. A crumpled bedsheet, a new hair clip, the fact that she smiled at the milkman's mother at the temple, all of it is proof. When she cries and denies it, he says that her tears are the proof of her guilt, and one night, drunk, he held a kitchen knife to her throat and demanded a confession. The behaviour in this vignette is typical: searching the partner's clothes, possessions, phone and correspondence, examining bed linen and underclothes for signs of sexual activity, repeated telephone calls and surprise visits, following, and sometimes hidden recording devices. Naveen's drinking is not a coincidence. Alcohol dependence has the best-known association with morbid jealousy: in two studies of men attending alcohol treatment services, morbid jealousy was present in 27 per cent and 34 per cent. Several mechanisms are suggested. Chronic drinking causes sexual dysfunction, and a man who fails sexually may explain the failure by the partner's infidelity; the drinking estranges the partner, who withdraws, which the drinker reads as evidence; intoxication disinhibits the expression of suspicion and aggression; and alcohol can produce a delusional psychosis of its own. Some authors think alcohol more often aggravates an existing jealousy than creates it, while others, finding that in most of their patients the jealousy began only after the alcohol dependence, give it a causal role. The treatment of the drinking is part of the treatment of the jealousy (Chapter 10). Clinical link Morbid jealousy is one of the most dangerous phenomena in psychiatry, and the danger falls on the partner. In a classic forensic series from a British secure hospital, Mowat in 1966 described 110 morbidly jealous people who had killed or seriously assaulted someone; in 94 the victim was the partner. Every assessment therefore includes a risk assessment for the partner (threats, weapons, previous violence, intoxication, a partner who is planning to leave), and the clinician may have to warn her, involve the police or admit the patient even without his consent when the risk is serious and immediate (Book 2, Section 2.7.5). The partner should be interviewed separately. Treatment depends on the form: an antipsychotic for delusional jealousy, an SSRI with cognitive behavioural work (Book 2) for the obsessional form, treatment of the alcohol dependence when it is present, and in refractory cases the only effective measure may be geographical separation, after which the jealousy often returns if the couple resume living together. Exam trap A fixed belief that the spouse or sexual partner is unfaithful, without evidence, is Othello syndrome (John Todd and Kenneth Dewhurst, 1955), the delusional form of morbid jealousy and the jealous type of delusional disorder. The distractors each name a different syndrome: Ekbom is infestation by parasites (and, separately, restless legs); de Clérambault is erotomania, the belief that someone is secretly in love with the patient; Couvade is pregnancy-like symptoms in an expectant father; Capgras (impostor) and Fregoli (disguised persecutor) are misidentifications. Remember the classic association with alcohol dependence , and that obsessional jealousy, which is resisted and ego-dystonic, is not Othello syndrome. De Clérambault syndrome and Ekbom syndrome If Othello syndrome is the delusion of being betrayed, de Clérambault syndrome is the delusion of being loved. It is named after Gaëtan Gatian de Clérambault (1872 to 1934), the psychiatrist in charge of the special infirmary for the insane attached to the Paris police prefecture, a clinician of unusual gifts who was also an accomplished photographer and an authority on draped costume. In 1921, in Les psychoses passionnelles , he gave the classic account of erotomania : the delusional conviction that another person, usually of higher social status and often a stranger, a public figure or a superior at work, is secretly in love with the patient. Notice the details de Clérambault insisted on. It is the other person who fell in love first and made the first advance; the love cannot be openly declared, for reasons the patient can always supply (the object's marriage, career or family); and the object communicates it by secret signals, so that ideas of reference run through the delusion. Any rejection is explained away as concealment or as a test of the patient's devotion, usually described as the object's "paradoxical conduct". His best-known case, the woman who kept a vigil outside Buckingham Palace for a sign from King George V, is told in Section 4.5.4. De Clérambault described a typical evolution, usually summarised as three phases: a phase of hope , sometimes lasting years, in which the patient waits for and pursues the lover; a phase of spite (in French dépit ), as the lover's failure to respond becomes undeniable; and a phase of rancour ( rancune ), in which love turns to grievance, complaint and sometimes threats. He also distinguished a pure or primary erotomania, beginning suddenly in an otherwise intact person and running a chronic course, from secondary erotomania, which appears within another illness such as schizophrenia or mania. DSM-5-TR's erotomanic type of delusional disorder carries the same core: another person, usually of higher status but sometimes a complete stranger, is in love with the individual, and efforts to contact the object of the delusion are common. Those efforts are where the clinical problems lie: letters, gifts, telephone calls, messages on social media, unannounced visits and stalking, sometimes for years, with distress to the object and legal trouble for the patient. Clinical samples have been predominantly women, while the men who come to attention tend to do so through forensic services, because they are more likely to stalk and to be violent, sometimes towards a perceived rival. Karl-Axel Ekbom (1907 to 1977) was a Swedish neurologist who worked at the Karolinska Institute and then held the chair of neurology at Uppsala. In a paper of 1938 (he had also described cases in 1937) called "Der präsenile Dermatozoenwahn", the presenile delusion of skin parasites, he gave the classic account (the French physician Georges Thibierge had written of "acarophobia" in the 1890s) of what is now called delusional parasitosis (or delusional infestation), and his name came to be attached to it as Ekbom syndrome . It is the fixed belief that one's skin or body is infested by insects, mites, worms or other parasites, when no infestation exists. The belief is usually accompanied by crawling, biting or itching sensations (formication, Section 2.3), and the patient's attempts to get rid of the parasites, with scratching, picking, tweezers, kerosene, harsh disinfectants and repeated washing, damage the skin and create the sores that are then offered as proof. The most famous sign is the matchbox sign (also called the specimen sign): the patient brings "specimens" of the parasites, in practice flakes of skin, scabs, hairs, threads or fluff, wrapped in paper or carried in a matchbox, a pill bottle or, today, a plastic bag or a set of photographs on a phone. It is found in roughly half to four-fifths of patients. The typical patient is a woman, socially isolated, in late middle or old age: the condition is diagnosed about twice as often in women as in men, with an average age in the late fifties. Because she believes her problem is a skin disease, she goes to dermatologists, pest-control firms and general practitioners, often for years, and refuses referral to a psychiatrist. A 63-year-old widow in Kozhikode who lives alone brings a dermatologist a folded newspaper containing fragments of skin and hair, saying that the "white worms" come out at night and that she has had the house fumigated three times. In primary delusional parasitosis the belief is the only psychiatric abnormality, and the diagnosis is delusional disorder, somatic type (Section 4.5.4). In secondary forms it arises in schizophrenia, depression or dementia, from a medical illness (vitamin B 12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, diabetes, kidney or liver disease) or from drugs, above all cocaine and amphetamine, which produce the "cocaine bugs" of formication (Chapter 10). Treatment is a low-dose antipsychotic, and the key skill is engagement: many patients accept treatment only from a dermatologist who takes the skin seriously, examines the specimens and works jointly with a psychiatrist. Exam trap Two eponyms in this subsection carry a second meaning. Ekbom's name is also on restless legs syndrome , which he described in detail in his doctoral thesis of the mid-1940s and which is now called Willis-Ekbom disease : an urge to move the legs at rest, worse in the evening, with unpleasant creeping sensations (Chapter 8). In a delusion question, "Ekbom syndrome" means delusional parasitosis. De Clérambault also described mental automatism (the Kandinsky-Clérambault syndrome), a different set of experiences of thoughts and acts as alien and automatic; in a delusion question, de Clérambault means erotomania . And do not confuse erotomania with Othello syndrome: the first is "someone loves me", the second "my partner betrays me". Couvade syndrome and Diogenes syndrome The last two eponyms in the main table are not delusions at all, which is exactly why examiners use them as distractors. The word couvade comes from the French couver , to brood or hatch, and was adopted in 1865 by the British anthropologist Edward Burnett Tylor for customs, recorded in many societies from South America to Asia, in which the father takes to his bed during or after his wife's labour, imitates the pains of childbirth, fasts or observes taboos, and is treated as if he had given birth. In 1965 the British psychiatrists W. H. Trethowan and M. F. Conlon published a paper in the British Journal of Psychiatry called "The couvade syndrome", describing its modern, unritualised counterpart. In Couvade syndrome (sometimes called sympathetic pregnancy) an expectant father develops pregnancy-like symptoms during his partner's pregnancy: nausea and morning sickness, indigestion and heartburn, abdominal pain or bloating, changes in appetite, weight gain, toothache, backache and disturbed sleep. The symptoms come and go with the pregnancy and usually disappear after the baby is born. The man does not believe that he is pregnant and has no physical disease to explain his symptoms. Proposed explanations include anxiety about the pregnancy and fatherhood, identification with the partner, ambivalence and envy of her capacity to bear a child, and hormonal change: expectant fathers show rises in prolactin and falls in testosterone, and men with more symptoms show larger changes. It is not a DSM-5-TR or ICD diagnosis. Keep it apart from its female counterpart, pseudocyesis , which DSM-5-TR lists as an example of other specified somatic symptom and related disorder: a false belief of being pregnant associated with objective signs and reported symptoms of pregnancy (the abdomen swells, periods stop). In pseudocyesis the woman believes she is pregnant; in Couvade syndrome the man knows perfectly well that his partner is. The final syndrome begins with an image every hospital social worker in India will recognise. A retired professor, a widower of 79, is brought to a Pune emergency department after a neighbour noticed the smell from his flat and found him on the floor, too weak to stand. The flat is waist-deep in newspapers, plastic bags, empty milk packets and rotting food; there is no clean surface and no working tap. He is malnourished and filthy, and he is courteous, articulate and quite unembarrassed. He has refused every offer of help from his nephew for years and asks to be taken home. In 1975 A. N. G. Clark , G. D. Mankikar and Ian Gray described thirty such patients (fourteen men and sixteen women) admitted to hospital with acute illness and extreme self-neglect, in a Lancet paper titled "Diogenes syndrome: a clinical study of gross neglect in old age". All had dirty, untidy homes and a filthy personal appearance about which they showed no shame; some hoarded rubbish ( syllogomania ); all but two lived alone; poverty and bad housing were not the cause; a third had persistently refused help; and their mortality was high. Strikingly, half had no psychiatric disorder and were of higher than average intelligence, and many had led successful professional lives; their personalities tended to be aloof, suspicious, emotionally labile and aggressive. Clark and his colleagues had been anticipated in 1966 by Duncan Macmillan and Patricia Shaw , whose British Medical Journal paper spoke of "senile breakdown in standards of personal and environmental cleanliness". Diogenes syndrome (also called senile squalor syndrome) is therefore the combination of gross self-neglect, domestic squalor, social withdrawal and refusal of help, often with hoarding, usually in older people living alone. About half the patients have a mental disorder, most often a dementia (frontotemporal dementia in particular), frontal lobe damage, alcohol misuse or a psychosis; the other half have no major disorder but a long-standing reclusive, suspicious or paranoid personality, and the syndrome has been read as a late-life reaction to stress in such a personality. The name is a well-known misnomer: the Greek philosopher Diogenes of Sinope, the Cynic who is said to have lived in a large jar in Athens, owned almost nothing, so he hoarded nothing, and he sought company every day in the market place. When hoarding occurs without self-neglect and squalor, and is not caused by a dementia, the diagnosis to consider is hoarding disorder (Section 6.6.4); DSM-5-TR notes that when accumulation follows frontotemporal degeneration or Alzheimer's disease it may come with self-neglect and severe domestic squalor and is not diagnosed as hoarding disorder. The hardest clinical question is usually ethical: whether a competent person has the right to live in squalor, which turns on the assessment of capacity (Book 2, Section 1.10.3). Exam trap Couvade : an expectant father develops pregnancy symptoms; not a delusion, and the man knows he is not pregnant (Trethowan and Conlon, 1965). Pseudocyesis : a woman falsely believes she is pregnant and shows signs of pregnancy. Diogenes : gross self-neglect, squalor and hoarding in the elderly living alone (Clark, Mankikar and Gray, 1975); about half have no psychiatric disorder, so do not assume dementia. Neither Couvade nor Diogenes is a misidentification syndrome or a delusion of infidelity. Reduplicative paramnesia was called a disorder of memory by the man who named it, and the misidentification syndromes as a whole have been described as lying at the far end of a continuum of anomalies of familiarity whose mild, everyday end is déjà vu. Section 2.7 starts from the other end, with what happens when memory itself is lost or distorted. 2.7 Disorders of Memory: Amnesia and the Paramnesias High yield · 5 Qs Everybody forgets. You walk into a room and cannot remember why; you meet a colleague at a wedding and her name has gone; you are sure you locked the scooter and you go back to check. None of that is psychopathology. Ordinary forgetting is selective (we lose the unimportant and the unrehearsed), it is proportionate to how well something was learned and how long ago, it improves with cues, and the person knows that he has forgotten. Forgetting becomes a sign when it breaks those rules: when it is out of proportion to the person's age, attention and the importance of what was lost, when it is a change from his own previous level, when it takes a pattern that ordinary forgetting never takes (a man who cannot remember that his wife died last year, a woman who forgets her own name but not the price of rice), or when what comes back is not a gap but a memory of something that never happened. Descriptive psychopathology sorts the disorders of memory into two great families and one small one. The first family is loss : amnesia in its several forms. The second is distortion : the paramnesias , in which what is remembered, or the feeling that something is remembered, is false. The small family is excess : hypermnesia. Where memory is normally stored, how it is forgotten and what the brain does in amnesia belong to Book 1, Chapter 7, and Book 1, Sections 7.10.1 and 7.10.3 teach the kinds of amnesia and Korsakoff's syndrome with their neurology. How memory is tested at the bedside belongs to Book 2, Section 2.6.5, which you should have in mind before reading on. In brief: immediate memory (registration, tested with digit span or by repeating three words at once) is retention over seconds; recent memory (the three words after about five minutes, the events of yesterday) is retention over minutes to days; remote memory (personal and public events of years ago) is retention over years. By Ribot's law , described by Théodule-Armand Ribot (1839 to 1916) in 1881, recent memories are lost before remote ones in brain disease. And in depression the complaint of poor memory often exceeds the measured deficit, the picture called pseudodementia. This section describes the phenomena those tests uncover. Amnesia: when forgetting becomes a symptom In psychopathology, amnesia is a pathological loss of memory: partial or total, temporary or permanent, out of proportion to ordinary forgetting and, in its pure forms, out of proportion to any other cognitive impairment. It is defined by what is missing from memory, not by how the person behaves, feels or perceives. A man with amnesia may also be agitated, low in mood or misperceiving his surroundings, but those are separate findings recorded under their own headings. The cause may be organic (a head injury, a stroke, a tumour, an infection such as herpes simplex encephalitis, a deficiency such as that of thiamine, a degenerative disease, a drug, a seizure, electroconvulsive therapy) or psychological, as in dissociative amnesia after overwhelming stress. One rule follows from the definition and saves many errors: amnesia is never diagnosed from the patient's word alone. A memory gap must be tested, its edges mapped and its content checked against an informant, because a fluent answer can be invented (as you will see under confabulation) and a claimed loss can be feigned. Exam trap "Amnesia is a clinical condition of..." has one answer: pathological loss of memory . It is not a behavioural disturbance (that would be recorded under appearance and behaviour or under disorders of movement and will, Section 2.9), not depressed affect (a disorder of emotion, Section 2.8) and not impaired perception (illusions and hallucinations, Section 2.3). Depression, delirium and dementia can all cause amnesia, which is exactly why the distractors are tempting; but the word itself names only the memory loss. The forms of amnesia The first and most useful way to describe an amnesia is by time. Fix the moment of onset (the blow to the head, the stroke, the start of the illness) as a point on a line. The first, anterograde amnesia , is the inability to lay down new memories from that point onwards: the person cannot learn the name of his new doctor, forgets within minutes that his daughter visited, reads the same newspaper article three times with fresh interest. The second, retrograde amnesia , is the loss of memories formed before that point. It usually follows Ribot's gradient, the last months or years before the onset being lost while childhood is preserved, and after a head injury it often shrinks during recovery, the older memories returning first, until only a short gap of seconds or minutes before the injury remains, a gap that is usually permanent because those memories were never consolidated. Most organic amnesias combine the two, and the anterograde part is usually the more disabling, because a person who cannot form new memories cannot keep track of his own life. A second description is by extent. A lacunar amnesia (circumscribed amnesia) is a gap, a lacuna, for a defined period, with good memory on either side of it. The commonest causes are a head injury, an epileptic seizure, an episode of delirium, a course of electroconvulsive therapy and heavy drinking. The amnesia of intoxication is the alcoholic blackout , also called a palimpsest (after the old parchments that were scraped clean and written over): the drinker wakes with no memory of how he got home, though he was awake, talking and even driving at the time, because the alcohol prevented the events from being recorded. Blackouts may be complete (en bloc) or patchy, the "greyouts" that drinkers describe, in which islands of memory return with cues. They are an early warning sign of harmful drinking (Chapter 10). Electroconvulsive therapy produces an anterograde difficulty during the course of treatment and a patchy retrograde loss for the period around it; most of this recovers over the following weeks and months, though some gaps for the treatment period can persist (Section 5.7.7). Two time-limited amnesias have names of their own. The first, post-traumatic amnesia (PTA), is the period after a head injury during which the person is awake but unable to lay down continuous memories; he may talk, eat and answer questions, but he is confused and later remembers nothing of the period except perhaps "islands". It ends when continuous day-to-day memory returns, and because its length is closely related to the amount of brain damage, it is one of the best clinical measures of the severity of a head injury: in one widely used scheme, a PTA of under an hour marks a mild injury, one of one to 24 hours a moderate injury and one of more than a day a severe injury. Clinicians track it day by day with brief orientation and memory questionnaires (the Assessment book names them). The second, transient global amnesia , named by the American neurologists C. Miller Fisher and Raymond Adams , whose full description appeared in 1964, is a sudden attack of dense anterograde amnesia, with a patchy loss of the recent past, in a middle-aged or older person, usually in the fifties, sixties or seventies. The attack often follows physical exertion, a plunge into cold water, sexual intercourse or an emotional shock. For a few hours the person is bewildered and asks the same questions over and over ("What day is it? How did we get here?"), forgetting each answer within a minute, yet he keeps his personal identity throughout and can still drive a car or follow a recipe. The attack resolves within 24 hours, leaving a permanent gap for the hours it lasted, and in most people it never recurs. The British neurologists John Hodges and Charles Warlow, in a 1990 study of 153 patients with transient amnesia, separated true transient global amnesia, with its excellent outlook, from attacks that are brief or repeatedly recurrent, which are more often epileptic. The most famous organic amnesia is the one described in 1887 by the Russian psychiatrist Sergei Sergeievich Korsakoff (1854 to 1900) in chronic heavy drinkers. Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine (vitamin B 1 ) deficiency, often after an acute Wernicke encephalopathy, and damages the mammillary bodies and the medial thalamus (Book 1, Section 7.10.3; Chapter 10). DSM-5-TR no longer uses the eponym as a diagnosis: it is recorded as alcohol-induced major neurocognitive disorder, amnestic-confabulatory type . Its text describes the picture exactly: an impairment in recent memory out of proportion to the other neurocognitive symptoms, with prominent amnesia (severe difficulty learning new information, with rapid forgetting) and a tendency to confabulate, although, it adds, confabulation can be seen with any severe loss of recent memory. Immediate memory, measured by digit span, is typically normal, which is one of the clues that the problem is in storing memories, not in attending to them. Finally there is the amnesia that has no lesion. In dissociative amnesia (Section 7.5.5) the person loses autobiographical memories, usually of a traumatic or intensely stressful period, and sometimes of his whole identity, while his ability to learn new information is intact. The organic and the dissociative amnesias fail in almost opposite directions, and Section 7.5.7 sets out the full comparison. Dissociative amnesia : retrograde and autobiographical; new learning intact; the gap is often for a traumatic period, and identity can be the first thing lost; linked in time to severe stress; the memories may return suddenly. The term hypermnesia means an exaggerated degree of retention and recall: memories, usually of the past, return with unusual vividness, clarity and detail. In psychopathology it is described in mania, where a flood of old memories may feed the pressure of speech; under hypnosis, where people recall more (though, as Book 1, Section 7.9 shows, they also recall more that is false, and they are more confident about all of it); in some fevers and near-death states; and in the intrusive memories of trauma, which return with sensory sharpness and can be relived as flashbacks (Section 7.2.4). Experimental psychology uses the word in a narrower sense: the American psychologist Matthew Erdelyi , from the mid-1970s, showed that when people try repeatedly to recall the same material, especially pictures, their total recall can improve from one attempt to the next, a net gain also called hypermnesia. For the examination, the clinical sense is the one to know: "memory of past events with unusual clarity" is hypermnesia. The paramnesias: a map In the paramnesias memory is not lost but falsified. The word covers two quite different kinds of error, and it helps to separate them before meeting the individual phenomena. In a distortion of recall the content of what is remembered is false: the person retrieves a memory of something that did not happen, or did not happen that way, or did not happen to him. In a distortion of recognition the content is not the problem; it is the feeling of familiarity attached to an experience that is wrong. A new situation feels already known (déjà vu), or a known situation feels never seen (jamais vu), or a known place feels as if it were somewhere else (reduplicative paramnesia). Confabulation Ramesh is 52 and has been on the medical ward of a district hospital in Mandya for nine days, admitted confused and unsteady after a long period of heavy drinking and very little eating. His confusion has cleared with intravenous thiamine, and he is friendly, polite and talkative. Asked what he did this morning, he answers at once: "This morning? I went to my godown at six. A lorry of cement came from Tumakuru, three hundred bags, and I had to stand there till the boys unloaded it, otherwise they steal. Then I had idli at Udupi Krishna Bhavan and came here to see you." He has not left the ward. When the house surgeon gently points this out, he smiles and agrees that perhaps it was yesterday, and when she asks him the same question an hour later he describes, with the same easy confidence, a meeting with his bank manager. Some of the pieces are real. He did own a hardware godown, years ago; he used to eat at that hotel. What he cannot do is place them in time, and he does not know that he cannot. That is confabulation : the production of false memories, often detailed, fluent and believable, that fill the gaps in an amnesia, given without any intention to deceive and without awareness that they are false. The standard British definition is the one given in 1972 by N. Berlyne : confabulation is "a falsification of memory occurring in clear consciousness in association with an organically derived amnesia". Each phrase of that definition rules something out. "Falsification of memory" separates it from lying about the present. "In clear consciousness" separates it from the muddled, fluctuating talk of delirium, in which the person is not fully alert at all (Section 2.2). "Organically derived amnesia" ties it to a memory deficit, and separates it from the fantastic stories of psychosis and from pathological lying. Two kinds have been recognised since the German psychiatrist Karl Bonhoeffer (1868 to 1948) studied alcoholic patients in 1901. In momentary confabulation (Bonhoeffer called it the confabulation of embarrassment) the patient, asked a question he cannot answer from memory, fills the gap with a plausible account, usually built from real but misplaced fragments of his own past, as Ramesh did. In fantastic confabulation the patient produces, unprompted, stories that are grandiose, bizarre or impossible: a voyage on a warship, a meeting with a prime minister, a battle won. In 1987 the London neuropsychiatrist Michael D. Kopelman renamed the two as provoked confabulation , which he argued may be a normal response to a faulty memory (healthy people produce similar errors when asked to recall a story after a long delay), and spontaneous confabulation , which he argued results from frontal dysfunction superimposed on an organic amnesia. Spontaneous confabulators sometimes act on their false memories: a retired man gets dressed to go to the office he left years ago, a woman packs to catch a train to a wedding that took place decades before. Where is confabulation seen? Above all in Korsakoff syndrome, especially in its early stage; after rupture of an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery , which damages the basal forebrain and the ventromedial frontal lobes; with other frontal lesions; in Alzheimer's disease and other dementias; and in the denial of disability after right-hemisphere stroke (Section 2.10). How does it arise? The leading account links it to failed source monitoring (Book 1, Section 7.9.4): the patient retrieves real fragments of memory but cannot tell when, where or in what context they occurred, or whether he did something or only thought about it, and his damaged frontal lobes fail to check the result. That is why so many confabulations are true memories in the wrong place. One last point is worth carrying to the ward: a fluent answer to "What did you do yesterday?" proves nothing about memory until someone who was there has confirmed it. Exam trap A Korsakoff patient who gives detailed, believable but false accounts of his past to fill memory gaps, without intending to deceive , is confabulating. It is not lying , because there is no intent to deceive and no awareness of falsity. It is not malingering , the deliberate faking or exaggeration of symptoms for an external gain such as compensation or avoiding duty (Section 7.9.6). It is not confusion or delirium , which are disturbances of consciousness and attention (Section 2.2); Berlyne's definition requires clear consciousness. And it is not the delusional memory of psychosis, in which a memory is given a sudden delusional meaning (Section 2.5). Confabulation is a paramnesia, a distortion of recall. Pseudologia fantastica, retrospective falsification and cryptomnesia If confabulation is the honest error of an amnesic person, pseudologia fantastica (pathological lying, mythomania) is its unsettling cousin: the telling of elaborate, often grandiose stories that mix fact and fantasy, which the teller seems half to believe. It was described in 1891 by the German psychiatrist Anton Delbrück . The stories are usually about the teller himself: a distinguished family, heroic deeds, important connections, dramatic illnesses, a career as a pilot, an army officer or a surgeon. They are plausible enough to be believed for a while, they are told repeatedly and embroidered over the years, and the lying seems to serve the teller's self-image more than any obvious external gain. When the teller is confronted with clear evidence he may drop the story, admit that it was untrue, or simply move on to a new one. Pseudologia fantastica is the second of the four features of Munchausen syndrome (Section 7.9.3), and it is seen in factitious disorder generally and in antisocial, histrionic and narcissistic personality disorders (Chapter 11). Set it beside confabulation and the differences are clear. The pseudologue has no amnesia and his memory tests normally; he retains some awareness that the stories are untrue, enough to drop them under pressure; and the stories are not filling gaps in memory but building a more impressive self. Set it beside ordinary lying and the difference is that ordinary lies serve a clear purpose (to escape punishment, to gain money) and are abandoned once the purpose is served, while pathological lies are excessive, repetitive and out of proportion to any gain, and the teller seems caught up in them. The third distortion of recall happens to everyone a little and to some people a great deal: retrospective falsification , the unconscious distortion of past memories so that they fit the person's present mood, beliefs or circumstances. The depressed woman who says that her childhood was entirely miserable and that her marriage has always been empty, when her sister remembers a happy girl and the photographs show a smiling bride, is not lying; her present mood is selecting and colouring what she can retrieve, the mood-congruent memory of Book 1, Section 7.7.5. The man with a persecutory delusion who reinterprets a quarrel with a neighbour twenty years ago as the first move in the plot is doing the same in the service of a belief. The practical lesson is that a history taken from a patient in the grip of a mood or a delusion must be checked against an informant. Delusional memory, in which a real or false memory is suddenly given delusional significance, is a different phenomenon and belongs to Section 2.5. The larger question of whether whole false memories of events, including childhood abuse, can be created by suggestion is the false memory and recovered memory debate (Book 1, Section 7.9, and Section 7.6.5). The last distortion of recall is a failure to recognise a memory as a memory. In cryptomnesia (hidden memory) something once read, heard or seen is forgotten, then returns without being recognised as a memory, so that the person experiences it as an original idea or creation. The term was used by the Swiss psychologist Théodore Flournoy (1854 to 1920) of the University of Geneva, who spent five years studying a medium he called Hélène Smith and published his account, From India to the Planet Mars , in 1900. Many of the "revelations" she produced in trance, he concluded, were latent memories of things she had once encountered, transformed by imagination. Cryptomnesia is the basis of unconscious plagiarism; Book 1, Section 7.9.4 tells the case of a famous popular song and the laboratory studies that reproduced the effect. Déjà vu and the distortions of recognition Shabnam is 19, a second-year engineering student in Pune. For about a year she has had brief, strange spells. She will be sitting in the canteen, and suddenly the whole scene, the clatter of plates, a friend's sentence, the light on the table, feels as if it has happened before, exactly so, and she has an eerie sense that she knows what will be said next. It lasts less than a minute. Sometimes there is a rising feeling in her stomach and a faint smell of burning rubber that no one else notices, and twice her friends have told her that she stared and smacked her lips for a few seconds and did not answer them. An EEG shows epileptic discharges over the right temporal lobe. Shabnam's spells are the aura and the onset of focal seizures, and the feeling of having lived through the moment before is one of the classic experiences of temporal lobe epilepsy. The everyday form of the experience is déjà vu (French, "already seen"), the illusion of recognition: the strong but false feeling that a new situation has been experienced before, while the person knows perfectly well that it has not. That last part is important: in ordinary déjà vu insight is preserved, and the experience is puzzling precisely because the person can see that the familiarity is wrong. The term was used in 1876 by the French philosopher Émile Boirac . Most people have had the experience. In a 2003 review of more than a century of surveys, the American psychologist Alan S. Brown estimated that about 60 per cent of people have experienced déjà vu (some surveys give about two-thirds); its frequency decreases with age, so that it is commonest in adolescents and young adults; it is associated with stress and fatigue; and, perhaps surprisingly, it is reported more often by people with more education and higher socioeconomic status, and by those who travel often. Brown grouped the explanations into four kinds: dual processing (two normally synchronised processes, such as familiarity and recollection, momentarily out of step), neurological (a small seizure-like discharge or a delay in neural transmission), memory (implicit familiarity from something genuinely similar that is not consciously recalled) and attentional (a scene glimpsed without attention and then perceived again with attention a moment later). The pathological form belongs to epilepsy. The English neurologist John Hughlings Jackson (1835 to 1911), who worked out much of what we know about focal seizures, described the "dreamy state" of temporal lobe seizures, with its intense feelings of reminiscence and unreality, in the 1880s. Déjà vu that is frequent, prolonged, accompanied by other aura symptoms (a rising epigastric feeling, smells, fear), followed by confusion, or witnessed with automatisms should be investigated as possible epilepsy, as Shabnam's was. Déjà vu is also reported in anxiety and depersonalisation, and with some drugs. The other "déjà" experiences are variations on the same theme in other forms. The first is déjà entendu ("already heard"), the illusion of having heard something before: a sentence, a piece of music or a conversation feels as if it had been heard previously when it has not. A more complete form is déjà vécu ("already lived"), in which the whole present moment feels as if it is being relived, often with the sense of knowing what will happen next, as Shabnam felt. In some older people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment the feeling becomes persistent and is believed: they stop watching the news because "this is a repeat", or refuse an appointment because they "have already been". Chris Moulin and his colleagues, who have studied such patients, call this recollective confabulation, because the patient supports the false feeling of familiarity with invented details, and families describe it as persistent déjà vu. Finally, jamais vu ("never seen") is the reverse of déjà vu: a familiar situation, place, person or word suddenly feels strange, new and unfamiliar, although the person knows that it is not. It occurs with fatigue, in temporal lobe epilepsy and in anxiety, and you can produce it in yourself: write a common word over and over and it soon begins to look foreign. In one study by Moulin, about two-thirds of volunteers who wrote the word "door" thirty times in a minute reported this kind of strangeness, some beginning to doubt that it was a real word. Reduplicative paramnesia (Section 2.6) belongs on this branch too: the familiarity of a place is real, but it is attached to the wrong location. Table 2.19 gathers every paramnesia in one place. Memory in the major disorders Each of the phenomena in this section turns up in particular disorders, and the pattern of a memory disturbance is often more useful for diagnosis than its severity. Delirium spoils memory at the first step: a person who cannot attend cannot register, so immediate recall is poor, and afterwards there is a patchy amnesia for the whole episode. Dementia, by contrast, typically begins with a failure to retain new information while immediate memory and remote memories hold up, following Ribot's law. Korsakoff syndrome is the purest amnesia, dense and anterograde, with intact immediate memory and confabulation. Depression produces memory complaints that are greater than the deficit found on testing, with effortful, "I don't know" answers. Dissociative amnesia removes a block of autobiographical memory while sparing new learning; post-traumatic stress disorder floods the person with intrusive memories while leaving gaps for parts of the trauma; and in malingered amnesia the pattern is inconsistent and implausible, and performance on forced-choice memory tests can fall below chance, the level that guessing alone would produce. Answers: (1) Capgras, (2) Fregoli, (3) prosopagnosia, (4) négations (negation), (5) Othello, (6) matchbox (specimen), (7) Diogenes, (8) confabulation, (9) pseudologia fantastica, (10) entendu; jamais. 2.8 Disorders of Emotion: Mood, Affect and Their Vocabulary High yield · 8 Qs Two people wept in the psychiatry outpatient department of a Bengaluru hospital on the same Tuesday morning. Preeti, a 34-year-old schoolteacher, cried quietly as she described the last four months. She woke at four every morning with a weight on her chest; the Carnatic songs she had sung since childhood now meant nothing to her; and when her daughter came first in her class, she had smiled for the photograph and felt, in her words, "nothing, like a wall". Jagdish, a 68-year-old retired railway clerk who had come south to live with his son after a second stroke, cried far more dramatically. Great heaving sobs began when the receptionist wished him good morning and stopped, as abruptly as they had started, half a minute later. "I am not sad, doctor," he said, wiping his face and looking embarrassed. "My grandson is getting married next month. These tears just come. Last week I laughed like this at my cousin's funeral." From the doorway the two scenes look alike: an adult in tears in front of a doctor. Underneath, they are opposites. Preeti's tears expressed a feeling that had soaked into every hour of her day for months. Jagdish's tears expressed nothing that he felt; they were closer to a reflex, released by damage to the brain pathways that normally keep emotional expression in step with emotional experience. To tell the two apart you need a vocabulary that separates what a person feels from what a person shows, a lasting state from a passing one, and a disorder of feeling from a disorder of expression. This section builds that vocabulary. Book 2, Sections 2.4.6 and 2.4.7 show how the clinician asks about mood and records affect at interview; here the aim is to understand each term as a phenomenon, where it came from, and which disorders it points to. Four words: emotion, feeling, mood and affect Everyday English uses "emotion", "feeling", "mood" and "affect" almost interchangeably. Psychology does not, and Book 1, Section 11.1.2 sets out how general psychology separates them. An emotion is a brief, many-sided reaction to a particular event, lasting seconds to minutes: a flash of anger when someone pushes ahead of you in the ration-shop queue, a jolt of fear when a dog lunges at your scooter. A feeling is the experienced side of that reaction, what the anger or the fear is like from the inside. Research psychologists also use "affect" as an umbrella word for every state that feels good or bad, which is why questionnaires speak of "positive affect" and "negative affect". Clinical psychopathology narrows all this into two working terms, and almost everything else in this section hangs on them. Mood is a pervasive and sustained emotional state, lasting days or weeks rather than minutes, that colours how the person sees himself, the world and the future. It is known chiefly from what the person tells you, so it is subjective, and it is judged over a period of time. Affect is the way emotion shows itself, here and now, second by second, carried by the face, the eyes, the voice and its melody (prosody), posture, gesture and tears. It is judged by the clinician, here and now, during the interview. The usual image, which Book 2 uses and Section 5.1.1 repeats, is that mood is the climate and affect the weather. Kerala has a wet climate, yet a particular afternoon in Kochi may be dry and bright; a man whose mood is depressed may laugh at a joke for a few seconds without his mood having lifted at all. Why insist on two words when one would seem to do? Three reasons stand out. First, mood and affect are measured differently and can disagree, and the disagreement is itself a finding. Preeti reported a depressed mood and showed a sad, tearful affect: the two matched. Jagdish reported a contented mood and showed sudden sobbing: his affect was wildly out of keeping with his mood, and that dissociation is the clue to his diagnosis. A young man who insists "I am perfectly fine" while his eyes fill with tears shows a mismatch of the opposite kind. Second, the diagnostic systems define the mood disorders by mood, not affect: a major depressive episode requires depressed mood or loss of interest most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks (Section 5.2.2), and no single tearful moment in a clinic can establish that. Third, several of the most important signs in this section are disorders of affect alone. Blunting, incongruity and pseudobulbar outbursts are things the clinician sees, and the person may feel quite differently inside, as the study of blunting described in Section 4.3.2 showed. When the affect fits the reported mood, the clinician records it as mood-congruent affect : the sad face and slowed voice of a person who also says she feels low. The phrase turns up in examination options, usually as a distractor ("mood-congruent affect in major depressive disorder"), and it simply describes the normal relation between feeling and showing. Do not confuse it with mood-congruent psychotic features, in which the content of a delusion or hallucination matches the mood, as with delusions of guilt and ruin in severe depression (Section 2.5 and Chapter 5). Indian context Few patients say "my mood is depressed". In many North Indian clinics you will hear " man nahi lagta " (my mind does not settle on anything, which often turns out to be loss of interest), " ghabrahat " (a mixture of nervousness, restlessness and a pounding heart) or simply "tension", which can mean worry, sadness, anger or a headache. In every part of the country many people describe distress first through the body: tiredness, burning, a heavy head. Record the person's own words in quotation marks, then ask what they mean. The technical label comes afterwards, and it must describe the phenomenon, not translate the idiom word for word. Exam trap "Our current mood and feelings", meaning the emotion shown at this moment, is best called affect . Mood is the sustained state over days or weeks; an emotion is a brief reaction to a particular event; a feeling is the experienced side of an emotion. Mood is reported (subjective), affect is observed (objective): mood is the climate, affect the weather. In general psychology "affect" is also the umbrella word for all good or bad feeling states (Book 1, Section 11.1.2), so a research question may use it in that wider sense. "Mood-congruent affect" is affect that fits the mood; it is normal, not a sign of disorder. Disorders of mood: quality, reactivity and rhythm The first thing to describe about a mood is its quality, the kind of feeling it is. The commonest abnormal quality is depressed mood : sadness, lowness, gloom or hopelessness, often felt in the body as heaviness or, as Preeti put it, a weight on the chest. Not every low mood is alike. In its specifier for melancholic features DSM-5-TR asks whether the mood has a "distinct quality", a profound despondency, despair or moroseness, or a so-called empty mood, which is experienced as different in kind from the low mood of a nonmelancholic depression, not simply a bigger dose of it. A mood that is simply more severe, longer lasting or without a reason does not count as distinct. People with melancholia often say that it is not like grief at all: grief has an object and comes in waves, whereas this is a flat, grey heaviness that lies over everything. Elevated mood is a mood more cheerful than usual and more cheerful than the person's circumstances justify; its grades are the subject of Section 2.8.3. Expansive mood is a different idea: not how high the mood is but how far it reaches outwards. Niraj Ahuja 's Short Textbook of Psychiatry , a standard Indian text, describes it as an unceasing and unselective enthusiasm for interacting with people and the surroundings, and DSM-5-TR's account of mania speaks of an unlimited and haphazard enthusiasm for interpersonal, sexual or occupational interactions, with the person striking up long conversations with strangers in public. The expansive person shows feeling without restraint and often carries an inflated sense of his own importance. Irritable mood is a readiness to be annoyed and provoked to anger. In mania it often replaces elation, especially when the person's wishes are blocked, and DSM-5-TR then asks for four rather than three of the additional manic symptoms (Section 5.4.1). In children and adolescents an irritable mood can stand in for a depressed one when a major depressive episode is diagnosed, and irritability is common in post-traumatic stress, dementia, withdrawal states and many medical illnesses. Anxious mood is apprehension, a tense expectation that something bad is about to happen, and it is taken up with the other morbid emotional states in Section 2.8.4. Dysphoria (from the Greek for "hard to bear") is an unpleasant mood that is not simply sadness but a mixture of sadness, tension, irritability and discontent. It is the mood of premenstrual dysphoric disorder (Section 5.3.3), of withdrawal from stimulants (DSM-5-TR builds its stimulant withdrawal syndrome on "dysphoric mood"), and of the mixed states in which manic and depressive features combine (Chapter 5). Euthymia is normal mood: neither low nor high, the ordinary middle of the range. It is the right word for a person whose mood shows nothing abnormal, and for a person with bipolar disorder who is well between episodes. It does not mean "happy". An apathetic mood is one in which feeling, interest and concern seem to have drained away (Section 2.8.6). Finally, some people in an acute psychosis or a delirium show perplexity, a puzzled bewilderment, as if the world had suddenly stopped making sense and they were searching for its meaning. A mood has a quality, but it also has a behaviour over time, and two features of that behaviour matter clinically. The first is mood reactivity : does the mood lift, even briefly, when something good happens? Ordinary low moods do. So do many depressions: in depression with atypical features, reactivity is the defining requirement, and the person brightens when a friend visits or good news arrives, only to sink back afterwards (Section 5.3.8). In melancholic depression the mood is unreactive. DSM-5-TR gives a practical guideline: even highly desired events bring no marked brightening, and if the mood lifts at all it reaches perhaps 20 to 40 percent of normal for only minutes at a time. Preeti's smile for the photograph, with "nothing, like a wall" behind it, is exactly this. The second feature is diurnal variation , a regular change in the mood across the twenty-four hours. In melancholia the depression is regularly worse in the morning, and the person often wakes two or more hours early (both appear among the DSM-5-TR melancholic criteria), lies awake in the dark at the lowest point of the day and feels a little better by evening. The opposite rhythm, worsening in the late afternoon and at night, is typical of delirium (the "sundowning" of Section 2.2), and it is one of the clues that an older person's withdrawal on a medical ward is not depression. Two further time words complete the picture. Lability of mood means rapid swings over minutes or hours, which DSM-5-TR describes in mania as an alternation among euphoria, dysphoria and irritability; it is taught with labile affect in Section 2.8.8. Persistence is how long a mood state lasts, and the time rules of the mood disorders depend on it: at least one week for a manic episode, four days for a hypomanic one, two weeks for a major depressive episode and two years for persistent depressive disorder (Chapter 5). The grades of elevated mood: euphoria, elation, exaltation, ecstasy How do you describe a mood that is too high? Indian examiners like a precise answer, and it comes as a ladder of four steps. The clearest way to learn the ladder is to watch someone climb it. Ashok, a 27-year-old engineer with a Pune software firm, had one previous episode of depression in college. In the first week of a new illness his colleagues noticed only that he was in unusually good spirits. He joked through meetings, praised everyone's work, slept five hours instead of seven and said he had never felt better in his life. Nothing in his circumstances had changed. This first step is euphoria : a mild elevation of mood, an exaggerated sense of psychological well-being and happiness that is out of keeping with what is actually happening. It is the mood of hypomania, and on its own it can look like a pleasant personality on a good day. By the second week Ashok's cheerfulness had become infectious and energetic. He laughed loudly, made everyone around him laugh, took on three new projects, started planning a start-up at two in the morning and could not understand why his manager wanted him to slow down. This is elation : a moderate elevation, a feeling of confidence and enjoyment together with increased psychomotor activity. It is the classic mood of mania. A few days later the mood had become something larger. Ashok announced that his software would end poverty in India, that the Prime Minister's office would soon call him, and that ordinary rules about money no longer applied to him; he transferred most of his savings to strangers who had praised his ideas. This is exaltation : intense elation combined with grandiosity, typically with delusions of grandeur, the mood of severe mania. Finally, on the night his family brought him to hospital, he stood motionless on the terrace with his arms raised, tears of joy on his face, saying that he had become one with God and could hear the universe singing, and he barely responded when spoken to. This last step is ecstasy : a feeling of intense rapture or bliss, often with a sense of union with something greater than oneself, seen at the most severe end of mania, in what older texts call delirious or stuporous mania. Where does this ladder come from? It is not in DSM-5-TR, which grades nothing: its criterion for mania speaks of an "abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood" and adds that the mood is often described as euphoric, excessively cheerful, high or "feeling on top of the world". The four-step scale is a teaching device of Indian textbooks built on the older European vocabulary of mood. Ahuja's Short Textbook of Psychiatry sets it out as four stages that the elevated mood can pass through as a manic episode becomes more severe: euphoria (Stage I, usually hypomania), elation (Stage II, classically mania), exaltation (Stage III, severe mania with delusions of grandeur) and ecstasy (Stage IV, typically delirious or stuporous mania). Indian question papers follow it closely, and Figure 2.12 draws it as a stair. Ordinary joy fits the event 1 Euphoria mild hypomania 2 Elation moderate joy + activity mania 3 Exaltation severe + grandiose delusions severe mania 4 Ecstasy most severe rapture, bliss delirious or stuporous mania also mystical states, epilepsy and drugs Increasing severity: judgement and insight fall away Figure 2.12 The four grades of elevated mood as a stair, with ordinary joy at its foot. Each step adds something to the one below: elation adds activity, exaltation adds grandiosity, ecstasy adds rapture with a loss of contact with the surroundings. Put ordinary happiness at the foot of the stair and the meaning of "morbid" becomes clear. When Ashok's sister passed her chartered accountancy examination after three attempts, she was overjoyed: she laughed, phoned everyone she knew and could not sleep that night. Her joy was intense, but it had a cause, it was in proportion to the cause, it faded over a day or two, it did not make her believe she could run the Reserve Bank, and it cost her neither judgement nor money. Each of those five features was missing from Ashok's elevation. Morbid elevated mood is out of proportion or without a cause, persists for days, drives a rise in energy and activity with a reduced need for sleep, and progressively erodes judgement and insight, so that the person feels best precisely when he is most ill. Elevated mood is not confined to mania. Euphoria appears with alcohol, opioids, cannabis and stimulants (DSM-5-TR lists euphoria among the effects of intoxication with several substances), with corticosteroids, and in diseases of the brain. A placid, unconcerned cheerfulness has long been described in advanced multiple sclerosis, and frontal lobe damage produces a euphoria of its own. In 1888 the German physician Moritz Jastrowitz described moria , a childish, silly, euphoric excitement, in patients with frontal tumours, and in 1890 the German neurologist Hermann Oppenheim (1858 to 1919) described Witzelsucht ("joking addiction"), a compulsive habit of making trivial, pointless and often sarcastic jokes and puns, in patients with frontal lobe tumours, linking it especially to the right side. DSM-5-TR still lists facetiousness, disinhibition, euphoria and a lack of judgement or foresight as the picture that frontal lobe injury can produce in personality change due to another medical condition. Ecstasy, for its part, occurs outside illness in religious and mystical experience, and in disease as the ecstatic aura of some temporal lobe seizures and with hallucinogens; the name of the drug MDMA, "ecstasy", borrows the word but is irrelevant to the grading. Exam trap The order from mildest to most severe is euphoria, elation, exaltation, ecstasy . Given i) elation, ii) exaltation, iii) euphoria and iv) ecstasy, the answer is iii, i, ii, iv . Ecstasy is the extreme, not euphoria. Memory hook: eu-phoria "feels good", e- l ation adds l abour (activity), e- x altation adds an e x aggerated self (grandiosity), e- c stasy is the c limax (rapture). The grading comes from Indian and older European teaching; DSM-5-TR speaks only of elevated, expansive or irritable mood. A reduced need for sleep belongs to mania, not to anhedonia or depression. Anxiety, fear and irritability as symptoms Anxiety and fear are taught as disorders in Chapter 6, but as phenomena they belong here, because they appear in almost every psychiatric condition. Fear is the emotional response to a definite threat that is present now: the dog in front of you, the bus that swerves towards you. Anxiety is the response to a threat that is anticipated, uncertain or vague: a diffuse, unpleasant apprehension about what might happen, with bodily arousal (a racing heart, tight muscles, a dry mouth) and a mind that keeps scanning for danger. When anxiety is attached to a particular object or situation, it is situational or phobic; when it is not attached to anything in particular, it is called free-floating anxiety , the restless, pervasive worry about everything and nothing that marks generalised anxiety disorder (Chapter 6). A panic attack is different again: in DSM-5-TR's words an abrupt surge of intense fear or intense discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes, with palpitations, breathlessness, trembling and a fear of dying or losing control (Section 6.2.1). Anxiety as a symptom is just as common outside the anxiety disorders. It accompanies most depressions; it is the emotional core of a persecutory delusion (the man who believes he is being poisoned is, above all, frightened); it marks alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal, hyperthyroidism and stimulant intoxication; and it can be the first sign of a delirium. The anxious affect of a person with generalised anxiety disorder (a strained face, restless hands, a tense voice that keeps returning to "what if") is a good example of a mood-congruent affect, and like the mood-congruent affect of depression it is a distractor in questions about pseudobulbar affect. Irritability, described with the moods in Section 2.8.2, completes the morbid emotional states: it is a lowered threshold for anger, common in mania, in depression among the young, in post-traumatic stress disorder, in dementia and in hypoglycaemia, and it must be judged against the person's usual temperament. Exam trap Distractors in anhedonia questions borrow from this territory. An excessive fear of social situations is social anxiety disorder (Section 6.3.6). A pervasive fear of open spaces is a description of agoraphobia, although DSM-5-TR's agoraphobia is fear of at least two of five kinds of situation, of which open spaces are only one (Section 6.2.6). Neither is anhedonia. Free-floating anxiety is attached to nothing in particular; phobic anxiety is attached to a specific object or situation. Anhedonia: when pleasure goes Of all the changes in emotion that depression brings, the one people find hardest to explain to their families is not sadness but the disappearance of pleasure. Preeti could describe it exactly. Singing had been the centre of her life since she was six; now she sat at the harmonium and felt nothing. Festival preparations, which she used to love, felt like a list of chores. When her daughter won the class prize, she knew she ought to feel proud and could not. The French psychologist Théodule-Armand Ribot (1839 to 1916) gave this loss its name in 1896 (Book 2, Section 2.4.6 records the attribution). He coined anhedonia (Greek an , "without", and hēdonē , "pleasure") as a counterpart to analgesia: as analgesia is insensitivity to pain, anhedonia is insensitivity to pleasure. Today anhedonia means the inability to experience pleasure, or the loss of interest, in activities that were previously enjoyed. Notice the two halves of that definition. One is the loss of liking (the music no longer feels good when it is playing); the other is the loss of wanting (there is no pull towards the harmonium in the first place). DSM-5-TR's second criterion for a major depressive episode joins them: "markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all, or almost all, activities most of the day, nearly every day", as shown either by what the person says or by what others observe. It is one of the two gateway symptoms of the episode, the other being depressed mood, and at least one of the two must be present (Section 5.2.2). DSM-5-TR adds that some diminished interest or pleasure is nearly always present in a depressive episode, that people describe "not caring anymore", and that families notice the abandoned hobby before the patient admits to it. In melancholia the loss is near-complete, not merely a reduction. The two halves of pleasure can come apart, and that separation explains a puzzle about schizophrenia. People with schizophrenia report enjoying a pleasant activity while it is happening about as much as anyone else, yet they seek out such activities far less often. David Gard , Ann Kring and their colleagues (2007) resolved this by distinguishing consummatory pleasure , the enjoyment felt in the moment, from anticipatory pleasure , the pleasure of looking forward to something, which is what motivates us to go and get it. Their patients showed a deficit in anticipatory but not consummatory pleasure. Section 4.3.2 tells that study in full. In severe depression, by contrast, the enjoyment of the moment is usually lost as well, which is part of what makes melancholia so bleak. Where else is anhedonia found? It is one of the five negative symptoms of schizophrenia (Section 4.3.2), and in 1962 the American psychologist Paul Everett Meehl (1920 to 2003) made a constitutional weakness in the capacity for pleasure one of the four core signs of schizotypy (the personality organisation that, in his model, grows out of an inherited neural weakness and can lead on to schizophrenia), alongside cognitive slippage, aversiveness to other people and ambivalence. It is a common and distressing part of withdrawal from stimulants (DSM-5-TR notes that anhedonia and craving are often present although they are not among the criteria) and of the protracted phase of opioid withdrawal, which can last weeks to months. It is reported in Parkinson's disease, alongside the apathy that DSM-5-TR lists among its frequent features, and it appears in the alternative personality model of DSM-5-TR as a trait facet of detachment. Rating scales such as the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale measure it, and they belong to the Assessment book. Two clinical facts give anhedonia its weight. First, DSM-5-TR notes that anhedonia has a particularly strong association with suicidal ideation, so the person who says "nothing gives me any pleasure any more" should always be asked about thoughts of death (Book 2, Section 2.7 and Section 5.8). Second, anhedonia helps to separate a depressive illness from demoralisation, the understandable reaction of a person with a chronic medical illness who feels helpless, incompetent and ready to give up. DSM-5-TR points out that the demoralised person usually still finds pleasure in meaningful activities and can have moments of happiness, whereas anhedonia is typical of a depressive disorder. A man on a dialysis unit who feels hopeless about his kidneys but still lights up when his grandchildren visit is demoralised; the man who feels nothing at all when they arrive may be depressed. Clinical link Families often read anhedonia as ingratitude or laziness ("we took her to the temple festival and she just sat there"). Explaining that the capacity for pleasure has itself been switched off by the illness, and that it usually returns as the depression lifts, relieves guilt on both sides. Ask about it directly and concretely: "What did you used to enjoy? When did you last do it? How did it feel?" A vague "Do you enjoy things?" invites a polite "yes". Exam trap Anhedonia is the inability to experience pleasure or interest in activities once enjoyed (Ribot, 1896). Every other option in the classic questions is a different phenomenon: a reduced need for sleep is a feature of mania (Section 5.4.1); an excessive fear of social situations is social anxiety disorder (6.3.6); a pervasive fear of open spaces is agoraphobia (6.2.6); a loss of contact with reality is psychosis (Section 2.5); a period of abnormally elevated mood is mania or hypomania; excessive guilt belongs to the content of thought (2.5); psychomotor agitation is a motor sign (2.9); difficulty concentrating is a cognitive symptom (2.2). All of these can occur in the same depressive episode, but only one of them is anhedonia. Apathy, alexithymia, ambivalence, shallowness and coldness Several other emotional signs are easily muddled with anhedonia, because each involves something missing. The first is apathy , a lack of feeling, interest and concern, in which the person is not distressed by his own indifference. The American psychiatrist Robert S. Marin argued in 1991 that apathy is, at heart, a loss of motivation, and he separated the symptom from the syndrome: apathy is a symptom when the loss of motivation is explained by something else (a depressed mood, an intellectual impairment, a lowered level of consciousness), and a syndrome when the loss of motivation is primary and cannot be explained that way. DSM-5-TR describes the apathy of neurocognitive disorders in similar terms, as diminished motivation and reduced goal-directed behaviour accompanied by decreased emotional responsiveness, common in Alzheimer's disease and often prominent in frontotemporal degeneration, where "apathy or inertia" is one of the behavioural criteria. Apathy is also found in Parkinson's disease, in severe depression and in chronic schizophrenia. The disorders of will that sit beside it, avolition and abulia, are taught in Section 2.9. The second is alexithymia , a word coined by the Greek-born American psychiatrist Peter Emanuel Sifneos (1920 to 2008) and usually dated to his 1973 paper "The prevalence of 'alexithymic' characteristics in psychosomatic patients" (some sources date the term to 1972). The word is built from Greek roots meaning "no words for feelings". A person with marked alexithymia has difficulty identifying what he feels, difficulty describing it to others and difficulty telling a feeling apart from the bodily sensations that go with it; his thinking is turned outwards, towards concrete facts and events, with a thin inner life of fantasy. Picture a 45-year-old factory supervisor sent by the cardiologist because of chest pain with a normal angiogram. Asked how he felt when his only son left for a job in Dubai, he looks puzzled: "What is there to feel? He has a good job. That week my BP was high and I had acidity." Sifneos first met this style among psychosomatic patients: they would list every ache and pulse rate, yet fall silent when asked what they had felt. Alexithymia is a dimension on which everyone can be placed, not a diagnosis. It is commoner in somatic symptom disorder and the other conditions in which distress is expressed through the body (Section 7.7), in autism spectrum disorder, in some people with post-traumatic stress disorder, and in eating and substance use disorders, but many healthy people score high on it. The questionnaire most often used to rate it, the Toronto Alexithymia Scale, belongs to the Assessment book. One caution matters in India: a person who speaks of distress through the body because that is the respectable language of suffering in his family or community is not necessarily alexithymic, and a questionnaire translated without care can mistake a cultural idiom for a deficit. The third is ambivalence , a word introduced by the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) in a lecture in 1910 and placed in his 1911 monograph among the fundamental symptoms of schizophrenia, the "four As" of Section 4.1.4. Ambivalence is the simultaneous presence of opposite feelings, wishes or ideas towards the same object: loving and hating the same person at the same moment, wanting and not wanting the same thing. Bleuler distinguished three forms: an emotional (affective) ambivalence, as in a husband who both loves and hates his wife; a volitional ambivalence, an inability to decide for or against an action, which shows itself in the catatonic sign of ambitendency (Section 2.9); and an intellectual ambivalence, in which an idea and its contradiction are asserted together, as when a patient insists in one breath that his food is poisoned and that it is perfectly safe. Everyone feels mixed feelings, about leaving home or about a marriage; what Bleuler meant was something stronger, in which the opposite feelings coexist without being weighed, resolved or even noticed as contradictory, and can paralyse action. Freud took the word over for psychoanalysis, where it describes the mixture of love and hostility towards the same person (psychoanalysis is taught in Book 2, Chapter 3). Whether a feeling is accepted as one's own or resisted as alien, its ego-syntonic or ego-dystonic quality, is a different distinction, taught in Section 2.1. Finally, two older descriptive words describe the depth and warmth of feeling. Shallow affect is emotion that is shown on the surface without any sense of depth or conviction behind it: it comes and goes quickly and leaves no mark, so that the observer does not quite believe it. It was a classic feature of the hebephrenic form of schizophrenia, it is close to the "rapidly shifting and shallow expression of emotions" of histrionic personality disorder (Chapter 11), and DSM-5-TR uses "shallow or deficient affect" as one of the features of conduct disorder with limited prosocial emotions, in which emotions seem to be switched on and off or displayed to manipulate others. Emotional coldness is a lack of warmth and tender feeling towards other people. DSM-5-TR includes "emotional coldness, detachment, or flattened affectivity" among the criteria for schizoid personality disorder, and coldness without remorse is part of the callousness of psychopathy (Chapter 11). Exam trap Alexithymia (Sifneos, 1973) is having no words for one's feelings; anhedonia (Ribot, 1896) is having no pleasure. They are not the same, and neither is blunted affect , which is reduced outward expression. Apathy is a lack of feeling, interest and concern, a loss of motivation (Marin, 1991). Ambivalence (Bleuler, one of his four As) means holding contrary feelings about one and the same object at once; its volitional form is ambitendency. Alexithymia is a trait dimension, not a DSM-5-TR diagnosis. Affect and its dimensions Mood is described mainly by its quality and its course. Affect, because it is observed, has to be described along several dimensions at once, much as a doctor describes a pulse by its rate, rhythm, volume and character. Book 2, Section 2.4.7 shows how each dimension is recorded during an interview. Here the aim is to see the dimensions as a system, because examiners test exactly that: which descriptors belong to affect, and which do not. Figure 2.13 sets them out as the spokes of a wheel. Affect observed, moment to moment Quality which emotion? Range how many kinds? Intensity how strong? Reactivity moves with topic? Appropriateness fits the content? Stability steady or abrupt? Communicability can you feel it? Outside the wheel: Mood reported, sustained Persistence how long the state lasts not a dimension of affect Figure 2.13 The dimensions of affect as the spokes of a wheel, each with the question the clinician asks. Persistence sits outside the wheel, beyond the vertical dividing line, because it describes how long a mood lasts, not the outward expression of emotion at this moment. Take the spokes in turn. Quality of affect names the emotion on display: sadness, anxiety, anger, cheerfulness, fear, perplexity, suspicion. Range of affect is how many different emotions appear as the conversation moves; a broad or full range moves naturally from seriousness to worry to amusement. Intensity is how strongly emotion is shown. At one end lies heightened or exaggerated affect, more emotion than the subject warrants; at the other lies a ladder of reduction that Book 2, Section 2.4.7 draws in its Figure 2.3. Restricted affect (also called constricted affect) is a mild reduction in range and intensity; blunted affect is a marked loss of intensity, a face that barely moves and a voice without colour even when the subject matters; flat affect is the end of the ladder, where virtually no emotion can be seen at all. Reactivity (or mobility) is whether the affect moves with the conversation, softening at a painful subject and brightening at a pleasant one; an affect that does not budge, whether the talk turns to a death or a wedding, is fixed or unreactive, as in Preeti's melancholia. Appropriateness (or congruence) asks whether the emotion fits its occasion: the topic of the moment and the setting. Stability is whether the affect changes in step with events or swings abruptly. Communicability is whether the emotion reaches the observer at all: whether you can feel with the patient. Inappropriate affect , also called incongruous affect, is emotion that clashes with what is being said or with where the person is: a young man who smiles broadly while describing how his father beat him, a woman who looks furious while saying that she is perfectly happy. Its place in schizophrenia, and the way ICD-10 groups it with blunting among the negative symptoms, are taught in Section 4.2.5, along with the caution that a person who suddenly laughs may be answering a voice. Indian examinations use two older European words here that DSM-5-TR does not use, so treat them as exam vocabulary, as Book 2 advises. Parathymia is the expression of an emotion opposite to the one the circumstances call for, such as laughing at news of a death; paramimia is a disagreement among the channels of expression themselves, such as a smiling mouth with a tearful voice. Communicability deserves a word of history, because it gave rise to one of the strangest ideas in psychiatry. In 1941 the Dutch psychiatrist Henricus Cornelius Rümke (1893 to 1967) published a paper on "the nuclear symptom of schizophrenia and the 'praecox feeling'". The praecox feeling (from dementia praecox, the old name for schizophrenia) is the examiner's sense, often in the first minutes of an interview, that he cannot make emotional contact with the person in front of him: a peculiar strangeness, as if an invisible pane of glass stood between them. Rümke thought that this intuition captured the core of the illness better than any list of symptoms, though he limited its use to acute phases. Later work found it hard to standardise, and empirical studies gave inconclusive results, so today it is not a diagnostic criterion. It survives as a cue: when you cannot feel your way into a patient's emotional world, look harder for the reason, which may be schizophrenia, but may equally be fear, a language gap, an antipsychotic drug or your own fatigue. That last point applies to blunting too. Antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism, the slowing of severe depression and cultural rules about showing emotion to a stranger can each mimic blunted affect, as Book 2, Section 2.4.7 and Section 4.3.2 explain. A final mismatch is worth one line here: la belle indifférence, an odd calm in a person who has, for example, suddenly lost the use of a leg, long associated with conversion disorder, which DSM-5-TR now says is not specific and should not be used to make the diagnosis (Sections 7.1 and 7.8.7).
