Quality, range and reactivity are dimensions of affect; persistence (how long a state lasts) describes mood. One option is worded "reactivity of mood", which looks as if it too should be excluded. It is a deliberate trap: reactivity is normally listed as a dimension of affect, and the "mood reactivity" of atypical depression (Section 2.8.2) is a different use of the word, so the key, persistence, stands. Restricted, blunted and flat form a ladder of increasing severity; inappropriate is a problem of fit, labile a problem of stability. Lability, emotional incontinence and pseudobulbar affect Return to Jagdish, sobbing at the receptionist's "good morning". His affect was unstable, but in a very particular way, and to understand it you need to place it at the far end of a range of instabilities. Labile affect is affect that lurches from one emotion to another faster and further than the conversation can explain: tears one moment, laughter the next. In lability as usually meant, the person feels each emotion as it comes, even if it comes too fast. Lability is seen in mania (DSM-5-TR's alternation among euphoria, dysphoria and irritability), in delirium, dementia and head injury, in intoxication, and in some personality disorders. Two personality patterns are easily confused with it and are taught in Chapter 11: the affective instability of borderline personality disorder, which DSM-5-TR attributes to a marked reactivity of mood with intense episodes of dysphoria, irritability or anxiety lasting a few hours, and the "rapidly shifting and shallow expression of emotions" of histrionic personality disorder, in which emotion is displayed dramatically and often for an audience. Push lability far enough and control over expression is lost altogether. Older British and Indian textbooks call this emotional incontinence , a loss of control over the expression of emotion and the extreme form of emotional lability, and in British and Indian usage the term is often used for the same phenomenon that neurologists now call pseudobulbar affect (PBA). Other names for it are pathological laughing and crying and involuntary emotional expression disorder. Pseudobulbar affect is a neurological disorder of emotional expression. Its episodes are sudden, brief (seconds to a minute or two), involuntary bursts of crying or laughing that are out of proportion to the felt mood or flatly contrary to it, often set off by trivial or emotionally neutral stimuli (a greeting, a television advertisement, a question about breakfast), ending as abruptly as they began and leaving the person embarrassed. Jagdish's laughter at his cousin's funeral was the classic incongruent episode. Crucially, the mood between and beneath the episodes may be quite normal: Jagdish was looking forward to his grandson's wedding, slept and ate well, and enjoyed his days. Why "pseudobulbar"? The bulb is the old name for the medulla, the lowest part of the brain stem, which contains the motor nuclei for the muscles of the face, tongue, throat and voice. A bulbar palsy is weakness from damage to those nuclei themselves. A pseudobulbar palsy produces similar difficulties (slurred speech, trouble swallowing, a brisk jaw jerk) from damage higher up, to the corticobulbar pathways that carry commands from the cerebral cortex down to the bulb, usually on both sides. The emotional outbursts often accompany that palsy, hence the name. DSM-5-TR mentions a pseudobulbar syndrome as one of the physical signs that point to cerebrovascular disease in vascular neurocognitive disorder, and pseudobulbar signs in progressive supranuclear palsy. Pseudobulbar affect occurs after strokes (especially multiple or bilateral ones), in multiple sclerosis, in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, motor neuron disease, where some series find it in up to half of patients), after traumatic brain injury, and in Alzheimer's disease, other dementias and Parkinson's disease. Key study: Where does the uncontrollable laughter come from? (Wilson, 1924; Parvizi and colleagues, 2001) In 1924 the British neurologist Samuel Alexander Kinnier Wilson (1878 to 1937), whose name is also on Wilson's disease, analysed pathological laughing and crying in a paper in his series "Some problems in neurology". He proposed that the brain stem holds centres that coordinate the facial, vocal and breathing movements of laughing and crying, and that these centres are normally held in check by pathways descending from the cerebral cortex. Damage those corticobulbar pathways on both sides, and the centres are released: they fire in response to stimuli that would never have moved the person before. This "release" or "disinhibition" account explained why the condition travels with pseudobulbar palsy, multiple strokes, ALS and multiple sclerosis, and it remained the accepted view for most of the century. In 2001 Josef Parvizi , Antonio Damasio and their colleagues at the University of Iowa reported a patient whose lesions lay instead in the cerebro-ponto-cerebellar pathways, the routes that carry information from the cortex through the pons to the cerebellum. They proposed that the cerebellum normally adjusts the execution of laughter or crying to the cognitive and social context; deprived of full information about that context, it produces responses that are inadequate and even chaotic. Their paper drew the conclusion that matters most for psychopathology: pathological laughing and crying is a disorder of emotional expression rather than a primary disturbance of feeling, and so is distinct from the mood disorders, in which laughter and crying come with real happiness or sadness. The two accounts may well be complementary, and the evidence for the cerebellar view still rests largely on single cases and small series. Because pseudobulbar affect looks so much like emotion, it is regularly mistaken for something else, and the mistakes lead to the wrong treatment. Its most common mimic is depression. The difference lies in the relation between expression and feeling: in depression the tears match a low mood that is present most of the day and comes with the other symptoms of a depressive episode, whereas in PBA the tears are brief, stereotyped, provoked by trivia and disowned ("these are not my feelings"). The two can coexist, since depression after a stroke is common, so the clinician asks about the mood between the episodes. The labile affect of mania differs because the person feels the shifting emotions and the mood is elevated or irritable, with the other features of mania. Histrionic display differs because the emotions are felt or performed for an effect, shift with the audience and belong to a lifelong pattern of personality, not to a recent brain lesion. Feature Pseudobulbar affect Depression Labile affect of mania Histrionic display Mood underneath Often normal Persistently low Elevated or irritable Variable, often normal Expression and feeling Dissociated: expression not felt Matched Matched but fast-changing Felt or performed for effect Episodes Sudden, seconds to minutes, stereotyped, trivial triggers Tearfulness through the day Rapid swings over minutes to hours Dramatic, shallow, audience-related Setting Stroke, MS, ALS, brain injury, dementia Depressive disorders Bipolar disorder Histrionic personality disorder The first treatment approved for pseudobulbar affect came in October 2010, when the United States Food and Drug Administration approved a capsule combining dextromethorphan (a drug long used as a cough suppressant, which acts on brain glutamate and sigma receptors) with a very low dose of quinidine. The quinidine is there for a pharmacokinetic reason: it blocks the liver enzyme (CYP2D6) that would otherwise break dextromethorphan down within hours, so that useful levels reach the brain. In the pivotal 12-week trial reported by Erik Pioro and colleagues in 2010, 326 patients with ALS or multiple sclerosis and clinically significant PBA were randomised to one of two doses of the combination or to placebo; the daily rate of episodes was about 47 to 49 percent lower on either dose than on placebo, and both doses were well tolerated. Before and alongside it, clinicians have used tricyclic antidepressants and SSRIs off-label, with more limited evidence. Severity can be rated with the Center for Neurologic Study Lability Scale, an instrument for the Assessment book. As important as any drug is the explanation: once Jagdish's family understood that his tears were a short circuit, not grief, they stopped tiptoeing around him, and he stopped avoiding weddings. Two further organic emotional signs complete the picture. The German-American neurologist and psychiatrist Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965), who worked with brain-injured soldiers during and after the First World War, described the catastrophic reaction : a sudden storm of anxiety, distress, tears or anger when a person with brain damage is faced with a task he can no longer perform, as when a man with aphasia is pressed to name objects he cannot name. Ahuja lists it among the additional features of dementia, where an overtaxed patient may fly into a sudden rage. In 1972 the Italian neuropsychologist Guido Gainotti reported that catastrophic reactions were commoner after left-hemisphere lesions, while an "indifference reaction", with unconcern, joking and minimising of the deficit, was commoner after right-hemisphere lesions; DSM-5-TR similarly notes that right hemisphere strokes can bring personality change with neglect and anosognosia (Section 2.10). The practical lesson is that an outburst during cognitive testing may be a sign of the brain disease being tested, not of a difficult personality. Clinical link Before you write "depressed" for a tearful stroke patient, ask three questions. How long does each bout of crying last, and what sets it off? Does the crying match what he feels inside? How is his mood between the bouts? Brief, trivially triggered, disowned outbursts with a reasonable mood in between point to pseudobulbar affect; a persistently low mood with loss of interest points to post-stroke depression; both can be present. The distinction decides whether the family hears "he is grieving" or "his brain's brakes on expression are damaged", and whether the dose of an antidepressant is pushed up needlessly. Exam trap Pseudobulbar affect means short, uncontrollable bursts of laughing or crying that are too big for, or contrary to, what the person feels, occurring in neurological disease: stroke, multiple sclerosis, ALS, brain injury and dementia. It is not the anxious affect of GAD , not the blunted or restricted affect of schizophrenia , not the mood-congruent affect of depression and not the histrionic emotional shifts of a personality disorder. In PBA expression is dissociated from feeling; in all four distractors expression and feeling go together (or, in histrionic display, the emotion is shown for an effect). Treatment: dextromethorphan with quinidine (approved in the United States in 2010), or SSRIs and tricyclics off-label. Labile affect is the wider category; emotional incontinence is its extreme. 2.9 Disorders of Movement and Will Lower yield · 1 Q Stand at the entrance of a busy psychiatric ward for ten minutes and, before anyone has said a word, you will already have seen a great deal of psychopathology. In one corner a woman sits so still that the tea beside her has grown a skin; in another a young man paces the length of the corridor, turns, and paces back, rubbing his hands; an older man by the window raises his right hand to his ear, again and again, in exactly the same way. Most of what this chapter has described so far (hallucinations, delusions, the loss of pleasure, the feeling of unreality) is invisible and has to be inferred from what people say. Movement is the great exception. It can be watched, filmed, timed and agreed upon by two observers, and that makes the motor signs some of the most reliable findings in the whole of psychiatry. This section describes them: the slowing and the agitation of the whole body, the catatonic signs, the other repeated and abnormal movements, and finally the disorders of the will that lies behind movement. Why movement belongs to psychopathology Why should a book about the mind spend so long on the body's movements? Because a voluntary movement is the last link in a chain that begins in the mind. A wish becomes an intention, the intention becomes a decision, and the decision becomes an act. The faculty that turns an intention into action is the will, or volition . Older psychology called the striving, acting side of the mind conation (from the Latin conari , "to try"), and psychiatry textbooks still divide mental life into the classic three domains: cognition (thought), conation (action) and affect (feeling). When this chain is disturbed, the disturbance shows itself in movement: too little of it, too much of it, the wrong kind of it, or movement that seems to have escaped from the person's control. The word psychomotor captures the link: in many mental states the speed of the body rises and falls with the speed of the mind. Before any movement is called psychiatric, however, one question must be asked: could a drug be causing it? Antipsychotic medicines in particular produce four movement disorders that mimic psychopathology, and Book 2, Section 2.4.4 and Section 4.10.4 teach them in the order in which they usually appear. An acute dystonia is a sudden, painful, sustained muscle spasm (the neck twisted, the eyes rolled upwards, the jaw locked) within hours or days of starting the drug. Akathisia, usually within days or weeks, is a torment of restlessness: the person cannot stay seated and keeps shifting his weight from foot to foot. Drug-induced parkinsonism brings tremor, rigidity, slowness and a mask-like face over the first weeks. Tardive dyskinesia appears after months or years as chewing, lip-smacking and tongue-rolling movements that the person cannot stop. Each has a psychiatric double: dystonia can look like catatonic posturing, akathisia like agitation, parkinsonism like retardation or blunted affect, and tardive dyskinesia like grimacing or tics. Keep this list in mind through everything that follows. Psychomotor retardation and psychomotor agitation Preeti, the schoolteacher with melancholic depression of Section 2.8, showed the commonest change of all. Every answer she gave came after a pause of several seconds, as if the question had to travel a long way to reach her. Her voice was low and monotonous, she hardly moved her hands as she spoke, she sat slumped with her eyes on the floor, and when she stood up to leave, the movement seemed to take enormous effort. This is psychomotor retardation : a general slowing of movement, speech and thought, with a long delay before responses, few spontaneous gestures, a soft and unvaried voice, a slow gait and an air of heaviness about everything. From the inside, people describe it as moving through deep water or wet sand, and as thinking with a mind full of glue (the slowing of thought itself is described in Section 2.4). DSM-5-TR is careful about one point. Its criterion for a major depressive episode counts psychomotor agitation or retardation only when it is "observable by others, not merely subjective feelings of restlessness or being slowed down". The reason is reliability: a feeling of being slowed is common in many states, but a slowing that a stranger can see is a firmer sign, and in melancholia DSM-5-TR notes that psychomotor changes are nearly always present and observable by others. Retardation is the motor face of melancholic and bipolar depression, and at its extreme it becomes depressive stupor (Section 2.2). It is also seen in hypothyroidism, in Parkinson's disease and drug-induced parkinsonism (where neurologists call the slowing bradykinesia), with sedative drugs, in the negative syndrome of schizophrenia and in the hypoactive form of delirium (Section 2.2), and every one of these must be considered before the slowing is put down to depression. At the other pole lies psychomotor agitation : restless overactivity that serves no purpose and is pushed along by tension inside. A 70-year-old retired headmaster with agitated depression cannot sit for more than a minute. He wrings his hands, rubs his thighs, picks at the edge of his kurta, gets up, walks to the door, comes back and follows the nurse down the corridor asking, "What will happen to me? What will happen to my family?" The movements achieve nothing and are not meant to; they discharge a tension that he feels as unbearable. Agitation is typical of agitated depression, which is especially common in later life, and it appears in severe anxiety, in delirium and dementia, in stimulant intoxication and in alcohol and sedative withdrawal. Catatonic excitement, one of the catatonic signs below, is a further form, distinguished by being uninfluenced by anything in the surroundings. Agitation has to be told apart from three other kinds of overactivity. The first is akathisia, the drug-induced restlessness above, which the person feels mainly in the legs and describes as an urge to keep moving; raising the dose of the drug that causes it makes it worse, which is why it is so dangerous to mistake it for agitation. The second is the overactivity of mania. When Ashok, the young engineer of Section 2.8.3, was elated, he was constantly on the move, but his activity was purposeful: he was starting projects, making calls, rearranging his flat and inviting the neighbours to a party. It was goal-directed but scattered, shifting with every new thing that caught his attention, so that he started ten tasks and finished none. DSM-5-TR captures both forms in one manic criterion, an "increase in goal-directed activity" or psychomotor agitation, which it glosses as purposeless, non-goal-directed activity. The third is the hyperactivity of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, a developmental pattern of fidgeting, restlessness and difficulty staying seated that dates from childhood and is present across settings, not an episode (Chapter 3). The hyperactive and hypoactive forms of delirium, finally, are the motor faces of a disturbance of consciousness, described in Section 2.2. Exam trap Psychomotor agitation is a motor sign , not a disorder of thought, mood or perception, and in DSM-5-TR it counts only when observable by others . Agitation is purposeless and driven by inner tension; manic overactivity is goal-directed but distractible ; ADHD hyperactivity is a lifelong developmental pattern. Akathisia is a drug side effect that mimics agitation. Retardation also occurs in hypothyroidism and parkinsonism, so slowness alone does not mean depression. Catatonia: the syndrome in brief The most dramatic of all the motor syndromes has a history that Book 2 and Chapter 4 tell in full, so it is recapped here in a paragraph. The German psychiatrist Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum (1828 to 1899) named catatonia in an 1874 monograph that also called it "tension insanity" ( Spannungsirresein ), an illness of the muscles and the will in which stupor, mutism, rigid postures and imitation came and went. Emil Kraepelin then absorbed it into dementia praecox, and generations of students learned it as one variety of schizophrenia until DSM-5 (2013) broke that link. DSM-5-TR recognises catatonia associated with another mental disorder, used as a specifier with psychotic, bipolar, depressive, neurodevelopmental and other disorders; catatonic disorder due to another medical condition; and unspecified catatonia. The rule is three or more of twelve signs. Treatment begins with a benzodiazepine, the lorazepam challenge being both a test and a first dose, and turns to electroconvulsive therapy when benzodiazepines fail or in malignant catatonia. Book 2, Section 2.4.4 (Table 2.5) shows how the signs are elicited at the bedside, Section 4.5.7 (Table 4.21) explains catatonia across the disorders and its treatment, and Figure 4.5 in Section 4.2.6 separates the signs that are most often confused. What does this section add? It treats each sign as a phenomenon in its own right, a thing that can appear outside catatonia, with its own differential diagnosis. DSM-5-TR itself suggests the best way to organise them, by what has happened to movement. Motor activity may be decreased, severely (stupor) or moderately (catalepsy and waxy flexibility). Engagement with the examiner may be decreased, severely (mutism) or moderately (negativism). And motor activity may be excessive and peculiar, either complex (stereotypy) or simple (agitation), including the echoing of speech and movement. The same person can swing between the decreased and the excessive forms, which is one reason the syndrome confuses clinicians. DSM-5-TR also blames teaching for part of the problem: by dwelling on rare and spectacular signs such as waxy flexibility, it has left clinicians less able to recognise catatonia at all. In practice the syndrome is more often a silent patient who stares, resists and will not eat than a statue holding an arm in the air. The American psychiatrists Richard Abrams and Michael Alan Taylor decided to test the habit. Over 14 months they studied every patient admitted to two inpatient units of a municipal hospital who showed one or more of eight catatonic signs: mutism, stereotypy, posturing, catalepsy, automatic obedience, negativism, echolalia or echopraxia, and stupor. Each of the 55 patients they found was then diagnosed with explicit research criteria. Only four met their criteria for schizophrenia. More than two-thirds had a diagnosable affective disorder, usually mania. The motor signs were spread evenly across the diagnostic groups, so that no sign marked any particular illness, and the number and type of signs did not predict the short-term outcome; two-thirds of the whole sample were markedly improved or in remission by discharge. The study had limits: a single sign was enough for entry, and the research criteria of the time defined schizophrenia narrowly. But its message, repeated by later work, was that catatonia is a syndrome that cuts across diagnoses and is especially common in mood disorders. DSM-5-TR reaches the same verdict: although up to 35 percent of people with schizophrenia show catatonia, most people with catatonia have a depressive or bipolar disorder. The catatonic signs as phenomena, and where else they occur Start with the pair that examiners ask about most. Echolalia is the automatic repetition of words or phrases that another person has just spoken; echopraxia is the automatic imitation of another person's movements. Both are echo phenomena: the person's own speech or action has been replaced by a copy of someone else's, without any apparent intention to mock, play or communicate. They are among the twelve catatonic signs, and in a question that asks which syndrome they are "most associated with", catatonia is the answer. Yet they also appear in at least five other settings, and a good clinician knows them all. In autism spectrum disorder, echolalia is part of the repetitive use of speech that DSM-5-TR describes as "the delayed or immediate parroting of heard words": immediate echolalia repeats what has just been said, delayed echolalia reproduces phrases heard hours or days earlier, such as a whole advertisement jingle or a line from a cartoon. In Tourette's disorder echolalia and echopraxia are complex tics, and DSM-5-TR notes that seeing a gesture or hearing a sound in another person may set off a similar tic. In dementia with severe language impairment, DSM-5-TR observes that echolalia and automatic speech typically come before mutism. In the transcortical aphasias, in which the ability to repeat is spared although spontaneous speech, comprehension or both are impaired, a patient may echo the examiner's sentences word for word (the aphasias themselves belong to the Physiological book). And in latah, a cultural syndrome reported from South-East Asia, a sudden startle sets off automatic obedience, echolalia and echopraxia. Echolalia is also a normal, passing stage in toddlers learning to talk, which is one reason it means little on its own in a young child. Mutism is the absence, or near-absence, of speech in a person who is awake. It is taught as a disorder of speech in Section 2.4; as a catatonic sign it is the severe form of decreased engagement, and DSM-5-TR excludes it when a known aphasia explains it. Mutism also occurs in severe depression and depressive stupor, in dissociative states, as selective mutism (speech present in some settings and consistently absent in others, an anxiety disorder of childhood, Section 6.4.8), and in akinetic mutism, a neurological state of absent drive described in Section 2.2. The mute patient's eyes are the first clue: eyes that follow the examiner, resist being opened or fill with tears suggest preserved awareness. Negativism is an apparently motiveless resistance to instructions or to being moved. In passive negativism the person simply fails to do what is asked: told to sit, he stands where he is; offered food, he keeps his mouth closed. In active negativism he does the opposite: asked to open his eyes, he screws them shut; asked to sit, he walks away. The word "motiveless" matters. A frightened patient who refuses tablets because he believes they are poison, or an angry teenager who will not answer his parents, is not negativistic in this sense, because the refusal has an understandable reason. The commonest clinical error runs in the other direction: real catatonic negativism is often misread as deliberate uncooperativeness, and the patient is labelled difficult while he quietly starves. The signs of decreased movement have neighbours that sound alike. Catalepsy, the holding of a posture that someone else has placed, must not be confused with cataplexy , the sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion (a burst of laughter, a surprise) without loss of consciousness, which is a symptom of narcolepsy (Chapter 8): one word holds a posture, the other drops it. Catalepsy can also be produced by suggestion in hypnosis. Posturing, a posture adopted and held by the patient himself, must be told apart from an acute dystonia, which is painful, involuntary and drug-induced. Grimacing has its own doubles: a facial grimace can be a simple motor tic, an orofacial movement of tardive dyskinesia or a catatonic sign, and only the setting and the rest of the picture tell them apart. Stereotypies, mannerisms and the other repeated acts are compared in Section 2.9.6. Two further motor emergencies are recapped in a line each. Malignant catatonia, the lethal catatonia that Karl Stauder described in 1934, is catatonia with high fever, autonomic instability and stupor, which can be fatal without prompt treatment, usually with ECT. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a reaction to antipsychotic drugs with fever, severe rigidity, autonomic instability and abnormal blood tests, and it is widely seen as malignant catatonia provoked by the drug (Section 4.10.5). Both explain why clinicians avoid starting or raising antipsychotics in a patient who is still catatonic. Exam trap Echolalia (repeating others' words) and echopraxia (imitating others' movements) are most associated with catatonia , not with major depressive disorder, panic disorder or specific phobia. Catatonia can complicate depression (major depressive disorder with catatonia), but the echo signs point to the catatonic syndrome, not to depression as such; panic and phobia have no motor echo signs at all. The same phenomena occur outside catatonia in autism (immediate and delayed echolalia), Tourette's disorder (as complex tics), dementia, transcortical aphasia and latah, so read the options. Do not confuse palilalia (repeating one's own words, Section 2.4) with echolalia (repeating someone else's), or catalepsy (holding a placed posture) with cataplexy (sudden loss of tone in narcolepsy). The older signs: a ward round with Nirmala Several catatonic signs that DSM-5-TR does not list survive in British and Indian texts and in rating scales, and examiners still ask about them. They are easiest to understand in a single patient. Nirmala, a 52-year-old woman from a village near Mandya, was admitted to the district hospital two months after her husband died. For six weeks she had been severely depressed, convinced that she had brought ruin on her family; for the last four days she had stopped speaking and eating. On the morning ward round she lay on her back staring at the ceiling, neck rigid, her head lifted clear of the pillow as if an invisible cushion supported it. The nurses had already noticed that she kept this posture for hours, a classic form of posturing known as the "psychological pillow". When the doctor said, "Nirmala-amma, please sit up", she sat up at once; when he said, "Stand", she stood; when he said, almost to himself, "Turn around", she turned, and she kept obeying every instruction mechanically, however pointless. This is automatic obedience : carrying out every command literally, regardless of its sense or consequence. Next he told her clearly, "Do not let me move your arm", and pressed lightly on her elbow with one finger. The arm rose and followed his fingertip wherever it went, like an anglepoise lamp. This is Mitgehen ("going with"), movement in any direction in response to the slightest pressure, even against instructions; it is an extreme form of Mitmachen ("doing with"), in which the examiner can place the body in any position despite being told to resist. The junior doctor then tried to bend her wrist. She resisted, and the harder he pushed the harder she resisted, with a force that exactly matched his; when he stopped, she stopped. This is Gegenhalten ("counter-holding"), opposition to passive movement with a force equal to the force applied. Neurologists call the same phenomenon paratonia and see it in frontal lobe disease and dementia, which is a reminder that several catatonic signs have neurological relatives. The nurse held out a steel tumbler of water. Nirmala's hand moved towards it, stopped halfway, drew back, moved forward again and stopped again, over and over for several minutes, without ever taking it. This is ambitendency , the motor expression of Bleuler's volitional ambivalence (Section 2.8.6): two opposed impulses, to act and not to act, each cancelling the other, so that the movement is begun and withdrawn without any goal-directed act ever being completed. When the doctor's fingers brushed her palm, she gripped them and could not let go, even when asked; this forced grasping is a primitive grasp reflex, normal in infants, which reappears in frontal lobe disease and is included in catatonia rating scales. When the nurse said, "Take your tablets", Nirmala whispered back, "take your tablets", and then shut her eyes tightly when asked to open them: echolalia and active negativism. Her stupor, mutism and refusal of food completed the picture. The diagnosis was major depressive disorder with catatonia. The doctor gave lorazepam 2 mg intravenously. Within the hour Nirmala asked for water and drank two glasses, and by the evening she was speaking in short sentences about her husband. Regular lorazepam was continued, the depression was treated, and electroconvulsive therapy was kept ready in case the response faded, as it is when benzodiazepines are not enough. Severity is often followed with the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale, an instrument described in the Assessment book that includes several of these older signs. Nirmala's story also shows the clinical stakes: a patient who neither eats nor drinks for days is at risk of dehydration, malnutrition, blood clots in the legs and pressure sores, so catatonia is a medical emergency as well as a psychiatric one. Exam trap Know the older signs by what the limb does. Mitmachen : the body can be put in any position despite instructions to resist. Mitgehen : the limb follows the lightest touch in any direction (the anglepoise lamp), an extreme of Mitmachen. Gegenhalten : passive movement is opposed with equal force (paratonia). Waxy flexibility : slight, even resistance as the limb is moved. Catalepsy : a placed posture is then held. Automatic obedience : every command is obeyed literally. Ambitendency : an action is begun and withdrawn repeatedly. The "psychological pillow" is a form of posturing. Of the signs in this box, only waxy flexibility and catalepsy are named among the twelve DSM-5-TR signs (the psychological pillow counts under posturing, which is also one of the twelve). Mannerisms, stereotypies, tics, compulsions and other repeated acts A repeated movement is one of the commonest things a clinician is asked to explain, and five or six quite different phenomena can produce one. The first step is to notice whether the movement has a goal. A mannerism is an odd, stilted or exaggerated version of a normal, goal-directed act, what DSM-5-TR calls an "odd, circumstantial caricature of normal actions". The act still reaches its goal, but in a strange way: a man with chronic schizophrenia who walks to the dining table on his toes with his knees raised high, as if marching in a parade, or who brings every spoonful to his mouth in a slow arc over his head. The everyday sense of the word (a habitual gesture such as twirling a moustache) is not what the psychiatric term means. A stereotypy , by contrast, has no goal at all: it is a repetitive, often rhythmic movement that serves no obvious purpose, such as rocking the body, flapping the hands, banging the head or rubbing the same spot over and over. In catatonia and chronic schizophrenia stereotypies appear as part of the motor syndrome. In autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability they are common, and when they are severe enough to interfere with life or cause self-injury, DSM-5-TR diagnoses stereotypic movement disorder, defined by "repetitive, seemingly driven, and apparently purposeless motor behavior" (Chapter 3). A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic movement or vocalisation, in DSM-5-TR's words. Tics are motor (blinking, grimacing, shrugging) or vocal (sniffing, throat clearing, grunting), and simple or complex; complex tics last longer and can look purposeful, and they include echopraxia, obscene gestures, repeating one's own words (palilalia), repeating another's (echolalia) and, in a minority, uttering obscenities (coprolalia), which DSM-5-TR notes comes out as an abrupt bark or grunt without the melody of ordinary angry speech. What marks a tic most clearly is its relation to the will. Most people with tics feel a premonitory urge, an uncomfortable local sensation before the tic, and can hold the tic back for a while, at the price of mounting tension, followed by relief when it is released. Tics are therefore neither fully voluntary nor fully involuntary, and they wax and wane over time. DSM-5-TR separates them from stereotypies: stereotypies usually begin earlier (often before the age of three), last longer (seconds to minutes), are rhythmic and repetitive in form and place, lack a premonitory urge and stop with distraction, such as hearing one's name called. The tic disorders, including Tourette's disorder (both motor and vocal tics), are taught in Chapter 3. A compulsion is a repeated act, either visible (washing, checking, ordering, touching) or silent (counting, praying, saying words in one's head), that the person feels compelled to carry out because of an obsession or because of strict rules of his own. Its aim is to lower distress or to stop some feared event, yet it has no realistic link with that event or is plainly excessive. That is the substance of DSM-5-TR's definition, and each part of it rules something out. A compulsion is not pleasurable in itself: it relieves distress for a while and then the cycle starts again. It is usually recognised as excessive and resisted, at least early on (the obsession behind it is ego-dystonic, Section 2.1). And it is driven from inside by a thought, not by a sensory urge, although the line can blur: some people with tics feel they must repeat a tic until it feels "just right", and DSM-5-TR concedes that complex tics and compulsions can be hard to tell apart. The disorder is taught in Section 6.5.2. A culturally normal ritual is not a compulsion. A grandmother who performs her morning puja in the same order every day, lighting the lamp, offering flowers and ringing the bell, does so willingly, as part of a shared and meaningful practice, in a time the family expects, and without the dread that something terrible will happen if one step is imperfect. The same sequence becomes a compulsion only when it is driven by an obsessional fear, repeated far beyond custom, distressing, and time-consuming (DSM-5-TR's example is more than one hour a day). Two more kinds of repetition complete the list. Habits are automatic, learned routines with little thought behind them, and the body-focused repetitive behaviours (hair pulling, skin picking, nail biting) are habits that have become harmful, often preceded by tension or boredom and followed by a sense of gratification or relief (Section 6.6.5). Perseveration of action is the continuation of an act after its goal has been reached or after the task has changed: the patient asked to draw a circle and then a square goes on drawing circles, or keeps wiping a plate that is already clean. It suggests a damaged brain, most often frontal damage or dementia; perseveration of speech and thought is described in Section 2.4. Because each repeated act leads to a different treatment. Tics respond to habit reversal training and comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics and, when severe, to medication; compulsions respond to exposure and response prevention and to SSRIs (both psychological treatments are taught in Book 2); stereotypies in autism often need no treatment unless they cause injury; perseveration calls for a neurological workup; and a catatonic stereotypy may vanish with lorazepam. Asking "Do you feel an urge just before it? What would happen if you did not do it?" separates most tics from most compulsions in two questions. Exam trap A mannerism is a goal-directed act done oddly; a stereotypy has no goal at all. A tic is sudden, rapid, non-rhythmic, preceded by an urge and briefly suppressible; a stereotypy is rhythmic, starts earlier and stops with distraction. A compulsion answers an obsession or rigid rule and relieves distress without giving pleasure. Perseveration of action continues an act whose goal is over and points to frontal or organic disease. A culturally prescribed ritual such as a daily puja is not a compulsion unless it is driven by obsessional fear, excessive and distressing. Disorders of will Behind every movement described so far stands the will, and the will can fail in its own right. The commonest failure is avolition , which DSM-5-TR defines as a decrease in motivated, self-initiated, purposeful activities: such a person can spend hours in one chair, uninterested in work, friends or family life. It is one of the five negative symptoms of schizophrenia and the one most closely tied to disability (Section 4.3.2), and a lesser form is common in depression, where it lifts as the mood improves. The neurological counterpart is abulia (Greek a , "without", and boulē , "will"): a marked lack of will and initiative, with slowed responses and little spontaneous speech or movement. Jagdish, the stroke patient of Section 2.8.8, showed it after a further small stroke deep in the brain. He sat in his chair for most of the day, answered questions after a long pause in two or three words, and never started a conversation or an activity. Yet when his son said, "Papa, drink your tea", he drank it, and when he was walked to the garden, he enjoyed it. That responsiveness to prompting is typical: the machinery of action is intact, but the self-starter is broken. Abulia follows damage to the frontal lobes (especially their inner, medial surface) and to the basal ganglia, and DSM-5-TR lists it, with emotional lability, among the features commonly associated with vascular neurocognitive disorder. Its extreme is akinetic mutism, in which a wakeful person with eyes that follow the examiner neither moves nor speaks (Section 2.2). Apathy, avolition and abulia overlap, and examiners like to see that you can separate them. Apathy is a lack of feeling, interest and concern, a disorder of emotion and motivation (Section 2.8.6). Avolition is a lack of self-initiated, goal-directed activity, the psychiatric term used above all for the negative syndrome of schizophrenia. Abulia is the neurological term for a severe loss of will and initiative with slowness and poverty of spontaneous action, lying on a continuum that ends in akinetic mutism. Families often call all three "laziness"; none of them is a choice. Three disorders of will have already appeared among the catatonic signs. Ambitendency is the volitional form of ambivalence, the hand that reaches and withdraws. Negativism is the will turned automatically against every instruction. Automatic obedience is its mirror image, the will surrendered to every instruction. A fourth disorder is the opposite of avolition: an excess of drive. In mania the will seems supercharged, and DSM-5-TR lists an increase in goal-directed activity, socially, at work, at school or sexually, among the criteria, together with excessive involvement in activities with a high potential for painful consequences, such as unrestrained buying sprees, sexual indiscretions or foolish business investments (Section 5.4.1). That last criterion leads to impulsivity , acting on a sudden urge without forethought, reflection or regard for the consequences, and to disinhibition , the loss of the social restraints that normally keep urges and remarks to oneself. Impulsivity is found in mania, ADHD, borderline and antisocial personality disorders, intoxication and the impulse-control disorders (Chapter 11); disinhibition is a hallmark of frontal lobe injury and of the behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia, for which DSM-5-TR lists "behavioral disinhibition" as a criterion. An impulse and a compulsion are opposites, and the contrast is a favourite question. An impulse is acted on readily and is gratifying or pleasurable at the moment it is acted on, even if regretted later; a compulsion is resisted, gives no pleasure, and relieves the distress produced by an obsession. The shoplifter with kleptomania feels a rising tension and then pleasure or relief as he steals; the man with obsessive-compulsive disorder checks the gas tap for the twentieth time with mounting misery. Key study: The patient who copied his doctor (Lhermitte and colleagues, 1986) What happens to the will when the frontal lobes are damaged? The French neurologist François Lhermitte had noticed that some patients with frontal lesions picked up and used everyday objects placed within their reach without being asked, which he called utilisation behaviour. In 1986 he and two colleagues described a further behaviour, imitation behaviour: while the examiner simply sat opposite the patient and made gestures, the patient copied them, although no instruction to imitate had been given. Asked why, patients explained that they thought they had to. In a neuropsychological study of 75 patients (40 with imitation behaviour, 35 with utilisation behaviour) and 50 patients with other diseases as controls, one or both behaviours were present in 96 percent of the 29 patients with focal frontal lesions, and brain scans showed damage to the lower part of the front of one or both frontal lobes. Lhermitte interpreted the behaviours as a release: without frontal inhibition, the brain systems that respond automatically to the physical and social environment take over. In a companion paper he followed two patients into a doctor's office, a lecture room, a car, a garden, an apartment and a gift shop, and found that they behaved as though the environment itself contained an order to respond, which he called the environmental dependency syndrome, a disorder of personal autonomy. The work matters for this section twice over. It shows that echopraxia-like imitation can arise from frontal damage outside catatonia, and it shows what the will normally does: it frees us from having to do whatever our surroundings suggest. A final disorder of will is visible in a person's home rather than in his body. Self-neglect, the failure to wash, eat properly, take medicine or keep one's surroundings habitable, is a behavioural sign that can come from severe depression, avolition in schizophrenia, dementia, alcohol dependence or frontal damage, and in its extreme form in older people living alone it forms the Diogenes syndrome of Section 2.6. How do you know that the thoughts you are thinking as you read this sentence are yours? You did not check. Nobody told you. You simply know, with a certainty so complete that it has never occurred to you to doubt it. The same goes for a handful of other certainties: that you are the one moving your hand when you turn the page, that you are one person and not two, that you are the same person who went to sleep last night, that your thoughts stay inside your own head, that the body in the chair is yours, and that if something went wrong with your mind you would be able to tell. None of these is a perception, a belief or a memory of the kind the earlier sections described. They are the background against which perceiving, believing and remembering take place. In psychopathology, every one of them can fail. This last section of the chapter is about those background certainties. It begins with the self as the person experiences it, using the four characteristics that Karl Jaspers described (Section 2.1 introduced Jaspers and his method), and then turns to the commonest way in which the self and the world lose their felt reality, depersonalisation and derealisation. It moves next to the body as the person experiences it, which can be wrongly felt, wrongly believed about, or simply not noticed. It ends with the two headings that close every mental status examination: insight, the person's knowledge of his own illness, and judgement, his ability to weigh a situation and decide well, which in Indian law leads straight to the question of capacity. The four formal characteristics of self-awareness In General Psychopathology Jaspers distinguished two directions in which awareness can point. Most of the time it points outwards, at objects: the tree I see, the voice I hear, the problem I am working on. Jaspers called this object-consciousness. But every such experience also carries an awareness of the one who is having it, and this he called ego-consciousness , which in plainer English is self-awareness. He described it by four formal characteristics, "formal" in exactly the sense of Section 2.1: they concern the structure of self-experience, not its content. Whether I think of myself as clever or dull, devout or sceptical, a success or a failure, is content. That I experience myself as active, as one, as continuous and as separate from the world is form. Fish's Clinical Psychopathology , the British text on which much Indian teaching is based, sets out the four as follows. Awareness of activity : the awareness that I exist and that I am the one who is thinking, perceiving, feeling and acting. My thoughts arrive with the sense that I am thinking them; my movements arrive with the sense that I am making them. Awareness of unity : the awareness that at any given moment I am one person, not two or more. Awareness of identity : the awareness that I am the same person over time, continuous with the child I was and with the person who went to sleep last night. Awareness of boundaries : the awareness that I am distinct from the outside world and from other people, so that my thoughts and feelings are inside me and theirs are inside them. Healthy people never notice these four, any more than they notice the floor under their feet. That is exactly why the disorders that break them are so hard for patients to put into words and so easy for clinicians to misread. The value of Jaspers' scheme is practical. When a person says something strange about himself, the first question to ask is which of the four has given way, because experiences that sound alike can turn out to belong to different characteristics and therefore to different disorders. Figure 2.15 shows the four with the main experiences that break them, and Table 2.27 adds the settings in which each occurs. 1. Notice that depersonalisation and the passivity experiences both disturb the sense of activity, and that the first-rank symptoms can also be read as failures of the boundary. Activity. The awareness of activity is close to what researchers now call the sense of agency , a link the Heidelberg psychiatrist Thomas Fuchs has drawn explicitly. It can fail in two very different ways. In the first, the person still knows that he is the one acting but no longer feels it: he moves, speaks and thinks as if on automatic pilot, watching himself from a distance. This is depersonalisation, and Fish files it under exactly this heading; it is taught in full in the next subsection. In the second, the person is convinced that the activity is not his at all. These are the passivity experiences of Section 2.4: thought insertion (thoughts placed in the mind by an outside agency), thought withdrawal (thoughts taken out of it), thought broadcasting (thoughts passing out of the mind so that others know them), and the made feelings, made impulses, made actions and somatic passivity, in which emotions, urges, movements or bodily sensations are imposed from outside. It was on Jaspers' account of ego-consciousness that Kurt Schneider later built the German term Ich-Störungen , ego disorders , for these experiences; ICD-10 and DSM-IV treated the same experiences as bizarre delusions of control or passivity. The difference between the two failures is the difference between "it is as if I were a puppet" and "I am a puppet, and I know who pulls the strings". Hold on to it: it is one of the most important lines in the whole chapter. Unity. Disturbances of unity are rarer and harder to pin down. The clearest appears in depersonalisation itself, where, as DSM-5-TR describes, the self can seem split, one part observing and the other taking part; at its extreme this becomes an out-of-body experience, in which the person seems to watch his own body from a point outside it. In schizophrenia some patients describe a doubleness of another kind, living at the same time in the shared everyday world and in a private delusional one. One patient told the Danish psychiatrist Josef Parnas and his colleagues, in a paper published in 2020, "I really feel that I live in two worlds." Eugen Bleuler's name for this was double bookkeeping (Section 2.2 mentions it). Whether it is a true division of the self, or a single consciousness holding two incompatible realities at once, is still argued, and Parnas himself takes the second view. Seeing one's own double, autoscopy, is a perceptual experience and belongs with the special hallucinations of Section 2.3. Identity. The awareness of being the same person over time can be shaken in several ways. In the early phase of schizophrenia some people say that they have changed in some fundamental and indescribable way, that the person they used to be has gone, or that they have been altered from within. In dissociative identity disorder (Section 7.6.1) the break in continuity is more visible: two or more distinct personality states take turns, and the person loses stretches of time that another state lived through. DSM-5-TR describes the disorder in terms of discontinuities in both the sense of self and the sense of agency, so it disturbs activity as well as identity. In possession states (Section 7.6.7) the person's ordinary identity is displaced by that of a deity, a spirit, an ancestor or a demon, who speaks and acts through him. Here culture decides almost everything. A woman through whom the goddess speaks at a village festival, who enters the state at the expected moment, is recognised by her community and returns to herself afterwards, is taking part in a religious practice, and DSM-5-TR excludes from the disorder any possession that is a normal part of a broadly accepted cultural or religious practice. The same experience arriving unbidden, frightening her and disrupting her life, is another matter. Boundaries. The fourth characteristic is the sense of where I end and the world begins. Schneider wrote of the permeability of the ego boundary in schizophrenia, and Figure 4.3 shows how naturally the first-rank symptoms can be read as one boundary giving way at many points: thoughts, feelings and impulses come in from outside, thoughts are pulled out or leak out, and one's own thinking is heard aloud as voices. A subtler boundary disturbance is transitivism , in which the person confuses his own thoughts, feelings or experiences with those of the person he is with, as though they were shared or had changed hands. Loosening of the boundary also has a normal counterpart. The French writer Romain Rolland (1866 to 1944) described to Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) a religious sense of oneness with the universe, an "oceanic feeling", which Freud discussed at the opening of Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), and meditators and mystics in many traditions, Indian ones prominent among them, seek such states on purpose. As with every phenomenon in this chapter, the experience alone does not make a diagnosis: its form, its setting and what it does to the person's life do. Jaspers' scheme has had a vigorous second life. Since the early 2000s a group of phenomenological psychiatrists led by Parnas in Copenhagen, together with the American psychologist Louis Sass , has argued that schizophrenia rests on a subtle, often long-standing disturbance of the most basic sense of being a self, which they call self-disorder or ipseity disturbance (from the Latin ipse , self). The person may feel that his thoughts have become oddly anonymous, that he is not quite present in his own experience, or that the line between himself and other people is uncertain, sometimes well before any voice or delusion appears. To study these experiences Parnas and his colleagues published the Examination of Anomalous Self-Experience (EASE) in 2005, and its five domains read like a modern expansion of Jaspers' list: cognition and the stream of consciousness, self-awareness and presence, bodily experiences, demarcation and transitivism, and existential reorientation. Reviews have found self-disorders to be characteristic of the schizophrenia spectrum, although similar experiences are reported in bipolar disorder and in depersonalisation disorder, so they are a pointer rather than a test. The interview itself belongs to the Assessment book. Table 2.27 Jaspers' four formal characteristics of self-awareness and how they break. Depersonalisation and the passivity experiences both disturb activity, but in depersonalisation the person knows he is acting and only feels as if he is not ("as if a robot"), while in passivity he is convinced that an outside agency is acting through him ("they move me like a robot"). Schneider's ego disorders ( Ich-Störungen ) are the passivity experiences, not depersonalisation. Dissociative identity disorder and possession break identity; the first-rank symptoms are failures of the boundary. And these are disorders of form: "I am a great man" is a delusion of content, not a disorder of self-awareness. Depersonalisation and derealisation: the self and the world grown strange Rahul is 21 and in the final year of a commerce degree in Jaipur. On the afternoon of Holi, after two glasses of bhang thandai at a friend's terrace party, the world changed. "It was as though I was operating my body by remote control, like a drone. My legs were walking and I was watching them do it. My friends were laughing and I laughed too, but the laugh was only on my face. Then I looked down at the street and it had lost its depth. The people and the shops looked cut out of cardboard and pasted one behind the other, and even the gulal on my kurta looked printed on." The intoxication had worn off by the next morning; the strangeness lasted most of a week. Since then it has come back three times, each time for a few hours, twice in a crowded examination hall. "Doctor, I can tell you exactly where I am, who I am and what day it is. I know it is all real. That is what frightens me. I know it, and I cannot feel it." Rahul is describing the two experiences of this subsection. The first, depersonalisation , is a change in the awareness of oneself, so that the self, or some part of it, feels unreal, detached, changed or not one's own; in the phrase that the textbooks repeat, the person feels that he is no longer his "normal, natural self". The second, derealisation , is the same change turned outwards: the surroundings feel unreal, distant, lifeless or strange. The word depersonalisation was introduced in 1898 by the French philosopher and psychologist Ludovic Dugas , who took it from the private journal of the Swiss writer Henri-Frédéric Amiel . The experience itself had been described before him, notably by the Hungarian-born physician Maurice Krishaber in the early 1870s, who included it in what he called a cerebro-cardiac neuropathy and traced it to a disturbance of the senses. What exactly has changed? Patients find this the hardest question in the interview, because ordinary language has no words for an experience that alters not what is perceived but how real it feels. They fall back on comparisons, and almost always on the words "as if". From many such accounts a consistent picture emerges. The person may feel estranged from the self as a whole ("I am nobody"), from his feelings, from his thoughts, from his body or parts of it, or from his own actions. The emotional side is so prominent that DSM-5-TR gives it a name, hypoemotionality : the person knows that he loves his family, or that the news is sad, and simply does not feel it, which is itself acutely distressing. Memories can lose their personal colour, so that the past seems to have happened to somebody else, and time can seem to rush or to stand still. In derealisation the world looks flat, two-dimensional, foggy, too sharp or artificial; objects can seem too near or too far, too large or too small (the micropsia and macropsia of Section 2.3); sounds can seem muffled or too loud. Is this one experience or several? In 2005 Mauricio Sierra and his colleagues at the Institute of Psychiatry in London put the question to the test. They gave the Cambridge Depersonalisation Scale to 138 consecutive patients with depersonalisation disorder and examined which of its items went together. Four factors emerged, which between them accounted for about 73 percent of the variation in the scores: anomalous body experience (the body or its parts feel unreal or not one's own), emotional numbing, anomalous subjective recall (memories and imagination feel unreal or impersonal, with distortions of time), and alienation from surroundings, which is derealisation. Their conclusion was that depersonalisation is a syndrome made of distinct but related symptoms, and DSM-5-TR now describes its symptom factors in much the same terms. Rahul shows three of the four: his body moves "by remote control", his laughter has no feeling behind it, and the street has gone flat. The single most important fact about depersonalisation and derealisation is what does not change. Throughout the experience the person knows that he exists and that the world is real; it only feels otherwise. DSM-5-TR calls this intact reality testing , and it is what the "as if" in the patient's account signals. It explains why depersonalised people so often fear that they are going mad: they are observing their own experience with full critical awareness and cannot make sense of it. It is also the line that separates depersonalisation from psychosis, and the line is easiest to see where the content is most extreme. Compare two people who both use the word "dead". "I feel as if I have died inside. I go about like a ghost, although of course I know I am alive." This is depersonalisation: the "as if" is kept and reality testing is intact. "I am dead. My blood has stopped and my stomach has rotted away; there is no point feeding a corpse." This is a nihilistic delusion, the heart of the Cotard syndrome of severe psychotic depression (Section 2.6; Table 7.14 sets out the look-alikes side by side). The content moves only a short distance between the two statements; the form moves all the way from an altered feeling to a false belief held with conviction. That is Jaspers' distinction between form and content once more, and it is why a careful clinician asks not only what the person feels but what he believes about the feeling. Depersonalisation must also be kept apart from the passivity experiences met under the awareness of activity. Rahul says that he moved "by remote control", and a man with schizophrenia may say that his arm is moved by a remote control in the hands of his neighbours. The image is the same; the form is opposite. Rahul knows that he is the one walking and only feels detached from it; the second man is certain that somebody else is doing it. One is an altered feeling with reality testing intact, the other a delusion of control and a first-rank symptom. Depersonalisation is not a first-rank symptom, however bizarre it sounds. Key study: Freud on the Acropolis (1904, published 1936) In 1904 Sigmund Freud and his younger brother Alexander were on holiday in Trieste when an acquaintance advised them to sail to Athens instead of following their original plan. Both felt oddly gloomy and hesitant about the change, but they went. Standing on the Acropolis, Freud was struck by a surprising thought, which in English translation runs: "So it really does exist, just as we learnt at school!" He had never doubted that the Acropolis existed; the strangeness lay in the feeling that what he was looking at could not quite be real. More than thirty years later, in 1936, he analysed the episode in an open letter for Romain Rolland's seventieth birthday, "A Disturbance of Memory on the Acropolis". He classed the experience as a derealisation and traced it to guilt at having gone further in life than his father, a man without secondary education for whom Athens could have meant little, as though to excel one's father were still forbidden. The case matters for two reasons. It is a careful first-person account of derealisation in a healthy and highly articulate man, with reality testing fully intact. And it shows the difference between the descriptive and the dynamic questions of Section 2.1: the description (what the experience was like) is not in dispute, while the explanation (what it meant) is Freud's own interpretation, which you may or may not accept. Who has these experiences? Almost everyone, briefly. DSM-5-TR estimates that about half of all adults have had at least one episode, and surveys give lifetime figures anywhere from about a quarter to three-quarters of people, depending on how the question is asked. In healthy people the usual triggers are exhaustion, lack of sleep, intense stress and sudden danger; people who have survived a road accident or a fall sometimes say that they watched it as though it were happening to somebody else. In clinical settings depersonalisation is one of the commonest and least specific of all symptoms. It is one of the thirteen listed symptoms of a panic attack (Section 6.2.1). It is frequent in depression and in the anxiety disorders; after trauma, persistent depersonalisation or derealisation defines the dissociative subtype of posttraumatic stress disorder; and it runs through the dissociative disorders. It occurs in the aura and the seizures of temporal lobe epilepsy. It is brought on by cannabis, as in Rahul's case, by hallucinogens and by ketamine. And it can be part of the early, prodromal phase of schizophrenia, before the illness declares itself. Why should one experience turn up in so many conditions? In 1935 the German psychiatrist Wilhelm Mayer-Gross (1889 to 1961), by then working in Britain, proposed in his paper "On depersonalisation" that it is a "preformed functional response" of the brain: a stock reaction that the nervous system can produce in many different states, much as fever is a stock reaction of the body to many different infections. The idea has aged well. It explains why depersonalisation tells you so little about the diagnosis by itself, and why its meaning depends on everything else in the picture: the panic that came first, the low mood around it, the drug, the seizure, or the strange new conviction that follows it. When depersonalisation or derealisation becomes persistent or recurrent, causes distress or impairment, is not the product of a drug or of a medical condition such as epilepsy, and is not better explained by another mental disorder, the diagnosis is depersonalisation/derealisation disorder. That disorder belongs to Chapter 7: Section 7.5.3 gives its criteria and Table 7.14, and Section 7.5.4 its prevalence (about 1 to 2 percent over a month in British surveys), its onset (on average at 16), its causes and the disappointing results of drug treatment. Book 2, Section 2.5.8 shows how to ask about both experiences in a mental status examination. Whether Rahul's recurrences add up to the disorder depends on how distressing and disabling they become; what he needs first is an explanation (the experience has a name, it is common after cannabis, it is not madness and it does not damage the brain) and the advice to keep away from the drug. Exam trap Depersonalisation is the self felt as unreal, detached or changed, no longer one's normal, natural self (papers phrase it as a change in the awareness of one's own identity); derealisation is the surroundings felt as unreal, flat or dreamlike. "Stress" and "depression" are distractors: they can set off both experiences but name neither. In both, reality testing is intact (the "as if"); "I am dead" held as a fact is a nihilistic delusion (Cotard syndrome, Section 2.6). Depersonalisation is not a first-rank symptom and not a passivity experience: "as if a robot" is depersonalisation, "they work me like a robot" is a made action. Déjà vu and jamais vu are disorders of recognition memory, taught in Section 2.7, not forms of derealisation. The word was introduced by Ludovic Dugas in 1898 . The body as experienced: body schema, body image and their disorders Your body is the one part of the world that is also part of you, and you experience it from both sides at once: as an object you can see in a mirror and as the place from which you see. Disorders of body experience are correspondingly varied. Some are failures of perception, some are failures of awareness caused by damage to the brain, and some are beliefs and attitudes about the body that range from an anxious worry to a delusion. Two technical terms keep them apart, and the difference between them organises everything in this subsection. The first is the body schema . In 1911 the London neurologists Henry Head (1861 to 1940) and Gordon Morgan Holmes (1876 to 1965), describing patients with damage to the parietal lobe, proposed that the brain keeps a constantly updated model of the posture and position of the body, against which each new movement and sensation is measured; they called it the postural schema. The schema works below awareness. You do not consciously consult it when you reach for a glass in the dark or duck under a low doorway, yet without it you could do neither. The second term is the body image , given its classic form by the Austrian psychiatrist Paul Ferdinand Schilder (1886 to 1940) in The Image and Appearance of the Human Body (1935): the picture of one's own body that one forms in the mind, the way the body appears to oneself. Schilder, who spent his last years at Bellevue Hospital in New York, insisted that this picture is not only perceptual. It is built from sensation and posture, but also from feeling, attitude, desire and the way other people respond to us, so that a body image can be bent by emotion and by culture as well as by a lesion. Modern research keeps the distinction: the schema is a largely unconscious sensorimotor system that serves action, the image a conscious set of perceptions, attitudes and beliefs about one's body. The most dramatic evidence that the body schema lives in the brain rather than in the limbs is the phantom limb , the vivid sensation that an amputated limb is still present. The French military surgeon Ambroise Paré (about 1510 to 1590) described soldiers who complained of pain in limbs he had removed, and the American physician Silas Weir Mitchell (1829 to 1914), who treated amputees of the American Civil War, gave the experience its name in a magazine article of 1871 and in his book on nerve injuries the following year (some sources date the name to the book). Most amputees go on experiencing the missing limb, and Pinel and Barnes report that about half of all amputees have severe, chronic pain in it; remarkably, about one in five people born without a limb report a phantom too. The phantom usually feels entirely real, so much so that a man may try to step out of bed onto a leg that is not there. It may feel stuck in an awkward or painful position, and over the years it may seem to shrink up towards the stump, a change called telescoping. Notice the form: phantom limb is a perceptual experience, not a belief, because the person knows perfectly well that the limb is gone. Its neural basis, the reorganisation of the somatosensory cortex demonstrated by Vilayanur Ramachandran, and his mirror-box treatment belong to the Physiological book. Sarita is 68, a retired Hindi teacher in Lucknow, admitted to a medical ward with a stroke in the right hemisphere of her brain that has paralysed the left side of her body. On the third day the ward team asks for a psychiatric opinion because, in the resident's words, "she has started talking nonsense". She is alert, oriented and pleasant, and she remembers the doctor's name from the day before. Asked whether anything is wrong with her, she says she has come in "for a little blood pressure". Asked to lift her left arm, she says, "There, I have lifted it," while it lies motionless on the sheet. When the doctor raises the limp left hand into her line of sight and asks whose it is, she glances at it and says, "That is my husband's. He sits here at night and leaves it behind." The nurses add that she eats only from the right half of her thali, and that she has to be turned to see visitors who stand on her left. Sarita is not psychotic in the sense of Chapter 4. She is showing, in one patient, the family of body disorders that can follow damage to the right parietal region. Her unawareness of the paralysis is anosognosia , the word coined in 1914 by the French neurologist Joseph Babinski (1857 to 1932) for exactly this failure to recognise a deficit (Book 2, Section 2.6.9). Her neglect of the left half of her plate and of the left side of space is unilateral neglect , which the Physiological book teaches. Her failure to recognise the left arm as part of her own body is asomatognosia , which Pinel and Barnes describe as usually one-sided and commonly a part of neglect; when it affects a whole half of the body it is also called hemisomatognosia. And her explanation that the arm is her husband's goes one step further. Denying ownership of one's own limb and attributing it to somebody else, with an explanation that resists every correction, is somatoparaphrenia , a term introduced by the Austrian-born neurologist Josef Gerstmann (1887 to 1969) in 1942. It most often concerns the left arm, usually comes with paralysis of that side and often, though not always, with anosognosia. In form it is a true delusion, a fixed false belief, but one built on a neurological deficit. These states often fade over the weeks after a stroke. The psychiatrist's task is to recognise them for what they are, so that Sarita is not given a diagnosis of psychotic illness or an antipsychotic she does not need. Two neighbouring disorders follow damage to the left parietal lobe instead. In autotopagnosia , first described in 1908 by the Prague neuropsychiatrist Arnold Pick (1851 to 1924), the person cannot localise or point to parts of his own body on request ("show me your knee", "touch your left ear"), although he can use them perfectly well. The narrower inability to name, identify or select one's own fingers, finger agnosia , was described by Gerstmann in 1924 and is one of the four elements of Gerstmann syndrome. Their neurology, with the agnosias in general, belongs to the Physiological book; what matters here is that they too are disorders of body experience that a psychiatric interview can stumble upon. The psychiatric disorders of body image are different in kind. The brain's maps of the body are intact; what is disturbed is the body image in Schilder's wider sense, the attitudes, beliefs and feelings about the body. The best studied example is anorexia nervosa (Chapter 8). The German-born American psychiatrist Hilde Bruch (1904 to 1984), writing in 1962 about her own patients with anorexia nervosa, described a disturbance of the body image of delusional proportions and regarded it as an important sign for both diagnosis and outcome. Her observation entered the diagnostic criteria. DSM-5-TR's Criterion C for anorexia nervosa still offers three ways in which the person's relation to her body may be disturbed: in the way body weight or shape is experienced, in the undue influence of weight or shape on her judgement of herself, or in a persistent failure to recognise how serious the low weight is. Some patients feel fat all over; others accept that they are thin but insist that the abdomen, buttocks or thighs are "too fat", and check them constantly by weighing, measuring and looking in mirrors. Key study: does she see herself as fat, or judge herself as fat? If body image has a perceptual part and an attitudinal part, which is disturbed in anorexia nervosa? In 1973 Peter Slade and Gerald Russell asked patients with anorexia nervosa to estimate the widths of parts of their own bodies, and reported that the patients overestimated them, which seemed to show a perceptual distortion: they literally saw themselves as larger than they were. Over the next two decades dozens of studies used size-estimation tasks of this kind, with inconsistent results. In 1997 Thomas F. Cash and his co-author E. A. Deagle combined 66 such studies, published between 1974 and 1993, in a meta-analysis. Attitudinal body dissatisfaction produced substantially larger differences between patients and controls than perceptual inaccuracy did, and only the attitudinal measures distinguished patients with anorexia nervosa from those with bulimia nervosa. They concluded that the size distortion was unlikely to reflect a general sensory or perceptual deficit. The lesson for descriptive psychopathology is that the "distorted body image" of anorexia nervosa is mainly a matter of attitude and evaluation, an overvalued idea about shape and weight (Section 2.5) that is sometimes held with delusional intensity, rather than a hallucination of fatness. It also helps to explain why such patients so often have poor insight into how ill they are. The remaining psychiatric disturbances of body image fit into the families this chapter has already built. In body dysmorphic disorder (Section 6.6.2) the person is preoccupied with one or more perceived defects in appearance that are slight or invisible to others, most often the skin, the hair or the nose. Its variant muscle dysmorphia, the conviction that one's build is too small or insufficiently muscular, occurs almost exclusively in men, according to DSM-5-TR. In koro , which DSM-5-TR describes as a culturally related disorder that usually occurs in epidemics in South-East Asia, the person fears that the penis (in women, the labia, nipples or breasts) is shrinking or retracting into the abdomen, often believing that death will follow; India has had its own outbreaks, among them one in Assam and West Bengal in 1982. Dhat syndrome, the anxious conviction that semen is being lost, often in the urine, and that the loss is draining the body's strength, is the South Asian cultural concept of distress that DSM-5-TR names as a relative of koro; both are taught in Chapter 1. Hypochondriacal concern, in which ordinary bodily sensations are read as signs of serious disease, is the territory of illness anxiety disorder (Section 7.7.3). At the psychotic end lie the somatic delusions of Section 2.5 ("my intestines have turned to stone") and the somatic passivity of Section 2.4 ("they heat my liver with rays"); at the non-psychotic end, the changed, numb or unreal body of depersonalisation. Finally, ICD-11 includes body integrity dysphoria, a persistent desire to have a healthy limb amputated because the body's actual shape feels wrong, which DSM-5 does not include.
