Exam trap The body schema (Head and Holmes, 1911) is the unconscious postural model of the body that serves movement; the body image (Schilder, 1935) is the conscious picture of one's body, with its attitudes and feelings. Phantom limb is a perception, not a belief: the amputee knows the limb is gone. Anosognosia (Babinski, 1914) is unawareness of a deficit; somatoparaphrenia (Gerstmann, 1942) is a delusional disowning of one's own limb; both usually follow right-hemisphere damage and concern the left side. Autotopagnosia (Pick, 1908) and finger agnosia follow left parietal damage. In anorexia nervosa the disturbance is mainly attitudinal , an overvalued idea, more than a perceptual error. Koro is the fear of genital retraction with fear of death and dhat the fear of semen loss; neither is body dysmorphic disorder. Insight: knowing that one is ill Tushar is 38 and runs a garment shop in Surat. His elder brother brings him to the emergency department after a week in which Tushar has slept two or three hours a night, booked a new car, signed for a loan to open three showrooms "before Diwali" and spent an afternoon handing out sarees to strangers outside the shop. Asked why he has come, Tushar laughs. "Ask my brother. He is jealous because business has never been better. I have never felt better in my life." Ten days later, sleeping again and calmer, he says, "I got carried away. It was the heat, and the wedding season, and too much tea." By discharge he can explain to the junior doctor that he has bipolar disorder, that his tablets prevent relapse and that he will need them for years. Three months later he stops them, "because I was perfectly fine", and he is readmitted in the next wedding season. Two years on, it is Tushar himself who telephones the clinic when he notices that he is sleeping less and planning more, and he has agreed with his family that his brother keeps the chequebook during the busy months. Tushar's story is a journey through the grades of insight , the heading that closes the mental status examination. In the MSE, insight means the person's awareness that he is ill, his understanding of the nature and cause of the illness, and his acceptance that he needs treatment. Book 2, Section 2.6.9 teaches it in detail, so only its essentials are recalled here. Aubrey Lewis (1900 to 1975) defined it in 1934 as "a correct attitude to a morbid change in oneself". The British psychiatrist Anthony David proposed in 1990 that it has three overlapping dimensions: recognising that one has a mental illness, accepting treatment, and being able to relabel unusual experiences such as voices and delusions as abnormal. In the WHO International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia, lack of insight was the most frequent symptom of all, found in about 97 percent of patients. Gaining insight in schizophrenia can bring depression with it, the insight paradox. And an explanation of illness shared with one's family and culture is not by itself poor insight. Section 4.2.7 adds the view, which DSM-5-TR takes, that the poor insight of psychosis is a symptom of the illness comparable to anosognosia rather than a way of coping. The six grades taught in most Indian MSE formats are summarised in Table 2.29 and drawn as a ladder in Figure 2.17. The vertical line between grades 5 and 6 separates knowing about the illness from knowledge that changes what the person does; Tushar stood on grade 5 at his first discharge and crossed the line only after a second admission. Put Tushar on the ladder. On the day of admission he was on grade 1, complete denial. Ten days later, blaming the heat, the wedding season and the tea, he was on grade 3: he accepted that something had happened to him but placed its cause outside himself. At discharge he was on grade 5, intellectual insight: he could describe his illness correctly, but the knowledge did not survive the first months of feeling well. Two years later, telephoning the clinic at the first sign and handing over the chequebook, he had reached grade 6, in which knowledge has become a change in conduct. Notice that the step from 5 to 6 is not a step in what he knew. It is a step in what he did with it. Two older ideas sharpen the ladder. Jaspers separated a mere awareness of illness , the feeling of being ill or changed, which need not extend to all the symptoms or to the illness as a whole and involves no correct judgement of its kind or severity, from insight proper, which requires that correct judgement. A depressed man who says, "Something has gone terribly wrong with me; I think God is punishing me," has awareness of illness without insight. Later writers loosened the distinction: in 1992 Ivana Marková and Germán Berrios described insight as a continuum of thinking and feeling, affected by many internal and external variables, which is closer to the way the grades are used today. Lewis made a second point that is easy to forget: insight cannot by itself separate psychosis from neurosis, because it is found, and lost, in both. What Book 2 does not do is follow insight across the disorders, and the pattern is worth learning because it shows what each disorder does to a person's knowledge of himself. Table 2.30 sets it out. Insight is usually absent in acute psychosis: hence the 97 percent of the pilot study. It is usually absent in mania too; DSM-5-TR observes that people in a manic episode often do not perceive that they are ill or in need of treatment and vehemently resist efforts to treat them, and it returns as the episode resolves, as Tushar's did. In depression the picture is mixed. Without psychotic features the depressed person usually knows that he is ill, but his insight is often distorted rather than absent: he may accept the illness and yet regard it as deserved, or as proof that he is beyond help, and the hopelessness is itself a symptom. With psychotic features, when guilt or nihilism has become a delusion, insight is lost. The obsessive-compulsive and related disorders made insight part of the diagnosis itself. DSM-5-TR asks the clinician to specify, for obsessive-compulsive disorder, body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding disorder, whether the person has good or fair insight (recognises that the beliefs behind the symptoms are definitely or probably not true, or may or may not be true), poor insight (thinks they are probably true) or absent insight with delusional beliefs (is completely convinced that they are true). The levels differ between the disorders. In obsessive-compulsive disorder most people have good or fair insight and only a few, 4 percent or fewer, have absent insight; in body dysmorphic disorder insight is on average poor, and a third or more of patients are completely convinced that they are ugly; in hoarding disorder poor insight is common enough that the person may report no distress at all, while the impairment is obvious to everyone else. For obsessive-compulsive disorder DSM-5-TR links poorer insight to a worse long-term outcome, and in all three disorders a person with absent insight is not given an extra diagnosis of a psychotic disorder unless the delusional beliefs extend beyond the disorder's own themes (Section 6.5.5). Insight is often poor in anorexia nervosa, where, in DSM-5-TR's words, individuals frequently either lack insight into or deny the problem, so that information from the family is essential; and it is often reduced in the neurocognitive disorders, where it shades into anosognosia. In the behavioural variant of frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder DSM-5-TR notes that insight is usually impaired, which delays medical consultation and means that the first referral is often to a psychiatrist. At the other end, insight is characteristically preserved in Charles Bonnet syndrome (Section 2.3), where the person knows the images are not real; in depersonalisation, where reality testing is intact by definition; and in most anxiety disorders. A person with a specific phobia usually recognises that his fear is excessive, although DSM-5-TR adds that he tends to overestimate the danger, so the judgement that the fear is out of proportion is finally the clinician's. Preserved insight was for a century the classic mark of the neuroses (Section 6.1.3), with Lewis's caveat that it is a tendency, not a rule. Table 2.30 Insight across the disorders. Insight is best preserved where the symptom is ego-dystonic, felt as intrusive, unwanted and alien to the self (Section 2.1): the obsession the person fights, the panic he dreads, the unreality he cannot bear. It is poorest where the symptom is ego-syntonic, at one with the person's values or with his sense of who he is: the anorexic pursuit of thinness, the personality trait that seems simply "the way I am" (DSM-5-TR notes that personality disorder traits are often ego-syntonic, which is why informants matter), and the elation that feels like the truth at last. Delusions are the extreme case. A belief held as a plain fact about the world is not experienced as a symptom at all, so there is nothing to have insight into until the belief begins to loosen. That is why ego-syntonic problems bring fewer people to treatment of their own accord, and why so many patients with poor insight arrive, as Tushar did, because somebody else brought them. Indian context The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 writes the cultural caution of Book 2, Section 2.6.9 into law. Section 3(3)(b) provides that mental illness shall not be determined on the basis of non-conformity with the moral, social, cultural, work or political values or religious beliefs prevailing in the person's community. For insight this means that a woman who explains her illness, as her family does, by the evil eye, a difficult planetary period or a goddess's displeasure has not thereby shown poor insight. What is graded is whether she recognises a morbid change in herself and will accept help for it. The rule cuts both ways: a belief does not become healthy because its content is religious, if its form is delusional (Section 2.5). Exam trap In the MSE, insight is the client's awareness and understanding of his own illness and of the need for treatment. It is not orientation to time, place and person (Section 2.2), not the ability to do serial subtraction, which tests attention and concentration (Section 2.2), and not the presence of hallucinations, which is a finding under perception (Section 2.3). Know the six grades: 1 complete denial; 2 slight awareness while still denying; 3 aware but blames others, external events or physical factors ; 4 aware that the cause is something unknown in oneself ; 5 intellectual insight , which leaves behaviour unchanged; 6 true emotional insight , which changes it. Insight is usually preserved in Charles Bonnet syndrome, depersonalisation and most anxiety disorders, and usually lost in acute psychosis and mania. And MSE insight is not the insight learning of Wolfgang Köhler (1887 to 1967), the sudden solution his chimpanzees found to problems such as reaching fruit with stacked boxes (Book 1). Judgement, and the capacity to decide Insight is knowledge about oneself; judgement is the ability to weigh a situation, foresee the likely results of acting in different ways, and act sensibly. Book 2, Section 2.6.8 teaches the three kinds that the MSE records: personal judgement (about one's own plans and life), social judgement (about conduct with other people) and test judgement , the answers given to standard hypothetical problems such as a stamped, addressed envelope found on the road or smoke in a crowded cinema hall. Its central warning is that the three can come apart, and that intact test judgement does not mean intact judgement. Tushar shows why. On the day of his admission he was asked what he would do if a caller offered him a prize in return for his bank details, and he answered at once and correctly that he would hang up and tell the bank. The same week he had committed himself to a loan he could never repay. Knowing what a sensible person would do is not the same as doing it. What Book 2 leaves for this chapter is the question of where judgement fails, and here the descriptive vocabulary of the earlier sections explains a great deal. In mania , DSM-5-TR describes how expansive mood, excessive optimism, grandiosity and poor judgement lead to spending sprees, giving away possessions, reckless driving, foolish business investments and sexual indiscretions that are unusual for the person, despite their likely catastrophic consequences, and it adds that the serious consequences of a manic episode, from involuntary admission to legal and financial ruin, often result from poor judgement, loss of insight and hyperactivity together. In acute psychosis the reasoning may be intact while the premise is false: the man who sells his flat at a loss to escape the persecutors who have bugged it is reasoning well from a delusion (Section 2.5). In dementia and frontal lobe disease the machinery of weighing and inhibiting is itself damaged; DSM-5-TR lists poor judgement among the common symptoms of behavioural-variant frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder, alongside disinhibition and socially inappropriate behaviour. In intoxication DSM-5-TR includes impaired judgement among the changes produced by alcohol and many other drugs. In intellectual disability the problem is a limited grasp of risk; DSM-5-TR notes that gullibility and a lack of awareness of risk may leave the person open to exploitation. In depression , finally, judgement is distorted rather than lost: decisions follow a hopeless logic, to give up a course, resign a job or end a marriage, that the person would not endorse once well, which is why clinicians advise depressed patients to delay major decisions until they recover. Judgement and insight matter beyond the MSE because they bear on one of the hardest questions in clinical work: can this person decide for himself? In India the question is now framed by the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, which Book 2, Section 1.10.3 teaches. Its definition of mental illness in section 2(1)(s) is written in the vocabulary of this chapter: a substantial disorder of thinking, mood, perception, orientation or memory that grossly impairs judgement, behaviour, the capacity to recognise reality or the ability to meet the ordinary demands of life. Section 4(1) then states that every person, including a person with mental illness, shall be "deemed to have capacity" to make decisions about his mental healthcare or treatment if he is able to understand the information relevant to the decision, to appreciate any reasonably foreseeable consequence of a decision or of a lack of decision, or to communicate the decision by speech, expression, gesture or any other means. Section 4(2) requires the information to be given in simple language, sign language or visual aids that the person can understand, and section 4(3) adds that a decision others perceive as inappropriate or wrong does not by itself mean that the person lacks decision-making capacity . Read those three abilities as a psychopathologist and you can see which disorders threaten each. Understanding depends on clear consciousness, sustained attention, working memory and language, so it is lost in delirium, advanced dementia and severe intellectual disability (Sections 2.2 and 2.7). Appreciating is where insight and delusion bite: a patient may repeat accurately that people with his illness relapse without treatment and still be unable to accept that this applies to him, because he believes the illness is not his or the medicine is poison. Communicating fails in catatonic stupor (Section 2.9) and in severe aphasia, although the Act's "any other means" matters here: a mute patient who can nod, point or write may still communicate a decision. Notice, too, what the three concepts are not. Insight, judgement and capacity overlap but are not the same thing, as Table 2.31 shows. Capacity under the Act is presumed, is judged for a particular decision at a particular time, and is not cancelled merely because the person's choice seems unwise. Where a person with a severe mental illness cannot make treatment decisions independently and needs very high support from his nominated representative, and certain risks are present, section 89 provides for supported admission for up to thirty days, with safeguards. Is consciousness clear, attention held, memory working and language intact, so that he can understand? And is the question about this treatment, now, or about something else? A report built on those questions is useful to the team, fair to the patient, and consistent with the Act's starting point that capacity is presumed. Exam trap The three kinds of judgement are personal (own plans and decisions), social (conduct with others) and test (hypothetical problems such as the found envelope or the fire in the cinema). Intact test judgement does not mean intact judgement. Judgement fails in mania, acute psychosis, dementia, frontal lobe disease, intoxication and intellectual disability, and is distorted rather than lost in depression. Judgement (deciding and acting well) is not insight (knowing one is ill), and neither is the same as capacity , which the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 presumes (section 4) and judges by the abilities to understand , appreciate and communicate a decision; a decision others think wrong does not by itself show incapacity (section 4(3)). This chapter began with Jaspers' insistence that the clinician first describe exactly what the patient experiences, and it ends with the patient describing himself. Insight is, in a sense, the patient's own descriptive psychopathology: his account of which of his experiences are symptoms, what kind of change has taken place in him, and what should be done about it. Every earlier heading feeds into it. A clouded consciousness cannot survey itself; a hallucination taken as real, a delusion held as fact and an elated mood felt as the truth all close off the view; an obsession resisted, a depersonalisation feared and a phantom limb known to be absent leave it open. That is why the mental status examination ends where it does, and why the vocabulary of this chapter is not a list to be memorised but a set of distinctions to be used: perception or belief, feeling or conviction, "as if" or "it is", form or content. The case of Madame M., revisited Go back to the woman who walked into a Paris police station in June 1918 to report children imprisoned in cellars, and who, by the time Joseph Capgras presented her case in January 1923, held that her husband, her daughter and almost everyone around her had been replaced by doubles. Put the questions of this chapter to her, one function at a time. Was it a disorder of perception? No. She saw the visitor accurately and offered only trifles as proof (a little mark on an ear, a thinner face, a longer moustache), so it was neither an illusion, which misperceives a real stimulus, nor a hallucination, which has no stimulus at all (Section 2.3). Was it a disorder of memory? No: her memory of her husband's face worked, which is why Capgras and Jean Reboul-Lachaux, though they still used the word "illusion", added that it was not an illusion of the senses but "the conclusion of an emotional judgement". What remains is a disorder of belief: a false conviction, held with certainty, that no proof could shift, which is a delusion (Section 2.5.1). Its content was the double; its form was a delusion; and because the familiar was declared unfamiliar, it is the hypoidentification member of Christodoulou's delusional misidentification syndromes, the picture that Joseph Lévy-Valensi named Capgras syndrome in 1929 (Section 2.6.1). The rest of the chapter fills in her picture. Her doubles multiplied, as Section 2.6.1 says impostors can, from her husband and daughter to the concierge, the tenants, the doctors and the nurses, and the title of the 1923 paper placed them inside a chronic systematised delusion, one connected system of belief (Section 2.5.4). She acted on the belief, asking the courts for a divorce from "this double", which is why the safety of the misidentified person is part of every assessment. And where would she stand on the ladder of insight (Section 2.10.4)? She took her trouble to the police and the courts, not to a doctor. What Capgras could not explain, Hadyn Ellis and Andrew Young proposed in 1990: the conscious route that recognises a face had survived and the affective route that makes it feel familiar had failed, so that a face that looked right and felt wrong could only belong to an impostor (Section 2.6.3), and the two-factor theory adds a second fault, in the checking of beliefs, that let the explanation stand. But the explanation came nearly seventy years after the description, and it could come only because Capgras had first written down, in her own words, exactly what she experienced. Describe first, explain afterwards: that is Jaspers' method, and it is the method of every section of this chapter. Chapter summary 2.1 What Descriptive Psychopathology Is: Jaspers, Form and Content. Descriptive psychopathology is the precise description and classification of abnormal experiences, beliefs and behaviour as the person lives them, without a theory of their cause. It grew out of Karl Jaspers' General Psychopathology (1913), written when psychiatry spoke the languages of course (Kraepelin), of the brain (Griesinger's successors) and of hidden meaning (Freud). Jaspers' phenomenology uses neutral, empathic questioning to grasp what an experience is like (static understanding) and how it grows from what went before (genetic understanding); what cannot be understood points to a process. Its central distinction is form, the kind of experience, versus content, what it is about: culture shapes content, form carries the diagnosis. The section also sorts the senses of primary and secondary, sign and symptom, syndrome, pathognomonic, organic and functional, ego-syntonic and ego-dystonic, and descriptive versus dynamic psychopathology. 2.2 Disorders of Consciousness, Attention and Orientation. Consciousness has a level (arousal) and a content. Above normal lies hypervigilance; below it come clouding, the mildest lowering and the core of delirium, then drowsiness, obtundation, stupor and coma, and every other finding is read in the light of the level. Delirium is a disturbance of attention and awareness with an acute onset, a fluctuating course often worse at night, a further cognitive change and a physical cause; its hypoactive form is mistaken for depression. The qualitative changes include the twilight state of epilepsy and Mayer-Gross's oneiroid state. Psychiatric stupor often preserves consciousness, unlike organic stupor, and must be told from akinetic mutism and the locked-in syndrome. Distractibility marks mania and inattention delirium. Orientation is lost for time first, then place, then person; marked disorientation means an organic state, while lost identity with intact time and place points to dissociation. 2.3 Disorders of Perception: Distortions, Illusions and Hallucinations. Sensory distortions change a real perception (hyperacusis, the xanthopsia of digoxin, micropsia); sensory deceptions are new perceptions. An illusion misperceives a real stimulus (completion, affect and pareidolic illusions). A hallucination, which Esquirol first separated from illusion, is a percept without a stimulus, as forceful as a real one and involuntary (Slade and Bentall) and, Jaspers added, located in outer space: a disorder of perception, not of thinking, judgement or intelligence. The pseudohallucination has two meanings. Each sense points somewhere: third-person voices and running commentary to schizophrenia, visual hallucinations to organic states and Lewy body dementia, smells and tastes to temporal lobe epilepsy, formication to cocaine. Special types include functional, reflex, extracampine, autoscopic and Lilliputian hallucinations. Hypnagogic hallucinations are commonest in normal people (37 percent in Ohayon's survey), and Charles Bonnet syndrome is complex visual hallucinations with visual loss and preserved insight. 2.4 Disorders of Thought and Speech: Stream, Form and Possession. Thought is known only through speech, as Andreasen stressed, and the British headings ask four questions: stream (how fast and continuous), form (how ideas are linked), content (what is thought) and possession (whose the thoughts feel). Flight of ideas, a rapid shift between ideas linked by chance, rhyme and clang, marks mania; retardation and poverty of thought mark depression and negative states; thought block is an observed sudden stop; perseveration points to frontal disease. Bleuler's loosening of associations, knight's move thinking and derailment belong to schizophrenia; tangentiality never reaches the goal, while circumstantiality finally does. Word salad is the most severe formal thought disorder. Cameron described overinclusive thinking and Goldstein concrete thinking. Speech disorders, from dysarthria to Ganser's approximate answers, are excluded first. Thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting are disorders of possession and, with made experiences, Schneider's first-rank symptoms. 2.5 Delusions and the Other Disorders of Thought Content. A delusion is a false belief, firmly held, not amenable to reason or contrary evidence and out of keeping with the person's background; of Jaspers' marks (certainty, incorrigibility, impossibility of content) falsity is the weakest. Primary delusions have no understandable origin: delusional mood, delusional perception (first-rank), the sudden delusional idea and delusional memory. Secondary delusions grow out of a mood, a hallucination, a passivity experience, another delusion or an impairment. Delusions are described as systematised or fragmentary, mood-congruent or incongruent, bizarre or non-bizarre, and by what they make the person do. Persecutory delusions are the commonest, above all in schizophrenia and delusional disorder; grandiose delusions mark mania, and guilt, poverty and nihilism severe depression. Wernicke's overvalued idea is understandable and less fixed, the obsession is recognised as one's own and resisted, and phobias, preoccupations and magical thinking complete thought content. 2.6 The Named Syndromes: Misidentification, Cotard, Othello and the Other Eponyms. The eponyms are descriptive syndromes found inside many disorders. Christodoulou grouped the delusional misidentification syndromes: Capgras syndrome (1923, named by Lévy-Valensi in 1929), a familiar person replaced by an identical impostor; Fregoli syndrome (Courbon and Fail, 1927), strangers as one familiar persecutor in disguise; intermetamorphosis; subjective doubles; and Pick's reduplicative paramnesia (1903) for places. Ellis and Young (1990) explained Capgras as the mirror image of prosopagnosia, recognition intact but the affective response lost; Coltheart's two-factor theory adds faulty belief evaluation. Cotard (1880) described nihilistic delusions of being dead or without organs, usually in severe psychotic depression. Othello syndrome (Todd and Dewhurst, 1955) is delusional jealousy, linked to alcohol dependence and dangerous to the partner. De Clérambault described erotomania (1921) and Ekbom delusional parasitosis (1938). Couvade and Diogenes syndromes are not delusions. 2.7 Disorders of Memory: Amnesia and the Paramnesias. Amnesia is a pathological loss of memory: anterograde or retrograde (by Ribot's law, recent before remote), lacunar, post-traumatic or transient global, the organic amnesia of Korsakoff syndrome (1887), and dissociative amnesia, in which identity can be lost first. Hypermnesia is memory too vivid. Paramnesias distort recall or recognition. Confabulation, in Berlyne's definition a falsification of memory in clear consciousness with an organic amnesia, fills gaps without intent to deceive, above all in Korsakoff syndrome; Kopelman's provoked and spontaneous forms renamed Bonhoeffer's two. Pseudologia fantastica (Delbrück, 1891) is lying the teller half believes, retrospective falsification bends the past to the present, and cryptomnesia returns a memory as an original idea. Déjà vu, the illusion of recognition, is common in health and pathological in temporal lobe epilepsy; déjà entendu is the illusion of having heard before, and jamais vu the familiar felt as new. 2.8 Disorders of Emotion: Mood, Affect and Their Vocabulary. Mood is the sustained, reported emotional climate; affect is the immediate, observed weather, so the emotion shown at this moment is affect. Mood is described by quality (depressed, elevated, expansive, irritable, anxious, dysphoric, euthymic), reactivity and diurnal variation, morning worsening marking melancholia. Elevated mood rises from euphoria through elation and exaltation to ecstasy. Anhedonia (Ribot, 1896), the loss of pleasure or interest, is a cardinal symptom of depression and a negative symptom of schizophrenia. Apathy (Marin), alexithymia (Sifneos, 1973) and Bleuler's ambivalence are different things. Affect has the dimensions of quality, range, intensity, reactivity, appropriateness, stability and communicability, while persistence describes mood; restricted, blunted and flat affect form a ladder. Lability, emotional incontinence and pseudobulbar affect, sudden involuntary laughing or crying out of keeping with mood after stroke or in multiple sclerosis, ALS, brain injury and dementia, complete the section. 2.9 Disorders of Movement and Will. Volition turns intention into action; a drug cause is excluded before any movement is called psychiatric. Psychomotor retardation and agitation count in DSM-5-TR only when observable by others, and agitation is not akathisia. Kahlbaum named catatonia in 1874; DSM-5-TR requires three of twelve signs, and Abrams and Taylor (1976) found it commoner in mood disorders than in schizophrenia. Echolalia repeats others' words and echopraxia imitates their movements; Nirmala showed the older signs (automatic obedience, Mitgehen, Gegenhalten, ambitendency) and their response to lorazepam, and catalepsy is not cataplexy. A mannerism is a goal-directed act done oddly, a stereotypy has no goal, a tic is sudden, non-rhythmic and preceded by an urge, and a compulsion answers an obsession. Avolition is a negative symptom, abulia a frontal or basal ganglia loss of will, and Lhermitte's imitation behaviour shows the will released by frontal damage. 2.10 The Self, the Body, Insight and Judgement. Jaspers described four formal characteristics of self-awareness: activity, unity, identity and boundaries. Depersonalisation (the self felt unreal, a word Dugas introduced in 1898) and derealisation (the world felt unreal) keep reality testing intact, and the patient's "as if" separates them from passivity and from Cotard's delusion. The body schema (Head and Holmes, 1911) and body image (Schilder, 1935) frame the phantom limb, anosognosia (Babinski, 1914), somatoparaphrenia (Gerstmann, 1942) and autotopagnosia, while in anorexia nervosa it is mainly attitudinal. Insight in the mental status examination is the person's awareness and understanding of his own illness and need for treatment (Aubrey Lewis, 1934), graded from complete denial to true emotional insight; it is kept where symptoms are ego-dystonic and lost in acute psychosis and mania. Judgement is personal, social or test, and under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 both feed into decision-making capacity. Who's who Table 2.32 The people in this chapter. From the past papers Symptoms where a person believes that other people are out to get them and that he or she is being attacked by rays from outer space. These patients are experiencing: (JEMAS 2025) (a) Depression (b) Paranoia (c) Dissociative disorder (d) Anxiety disorder Answer: (b) Paranoia. The belief that others are plotting against one and attacking one is a persecutory delusion, the hallmark of paranoia and paranoid states (Section 2.5.5). Depression, dissociative disorder and anxiety disorder do not, as such, produce persecutory delusions; when persecution appears in a psychotic depression it is often felt to be deserved. "Hallucination" is a disorder of: (JEMAS 2025) (a) Judgement (b) Perception (c) Intelligence (d) Thinking Answer: (b) Perception. A hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus, so it is a disorder of perception (Section 2.3.3). "Thinking" is the bait: the disorder of belief is the delusion, and judgement and intelligence can be intact, as in the old man with failing sight who knows that the children on his bed are not real. 'Nihilistic delusions' are commonly seen in: (JEMAS 2025) (a) Depression (b) Schizophrenia (c) Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (d) Somatoform disorder Answer: (a) Depression. Nihilistic delusions (that oneself, one's organs or the world do not exist or are dead) belong above all to severe psychotic depression, and Cotard syndrome is their extreme (Sections 2.5.5 and 2.6.4). They can occur in schizophrenia, but depression is the keyed and best answer; obsessions are resisted rather than believed, and somatoform disorder has bodily preoccupation without delusional conviction. A patient presents with a fixed delusional belief that their spouse is being unfaithful, despite having no evidence. This specific form of delusional jealousy is known as: (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Capgras syndrome (b) Othello syndrome (c) Fregoli syndrome (d) De Clérambault's syndrome Answer: (b) Othello syndrome. Othello syndrome (Todd and Dewhurst, 1955) is the delusional form of morbid jealousy (Section 2.6.5). Capgras is a familiar person replaced by an impostor, Fregoli is strangers believed to be one familiar persecutor in disguise, and de Clérambault's is erotomania, the delusion of being loved. Which of the following phenomena is characterized by the "illusion of recognition," where a person feels a new situation has been experienced before? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Jamais vu (b) Pseudologia fantastica (c) Déjà vu (d) Confabulation Answer: (c) Déjà vu. Déjà vu is the illusion of recognition, a distortion of the feeling of familiarity (Section 2.7.7). Jamais vu is its opposite, the familiar felt as unfamiliar, while pseudologia fantastica (Delbrück, 1891) and confabulation are distortions of recall, not of recognition. Cotard syndrome, a rare neuropsychiatric condition, is primarily characterized by which type of delusional belief? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Grandiose delusions of having special powers or abilities (b) Persecutory delusions of being followed or monitored (c) Nihilistic delusions of being dead or not existing (d) Somatic delusions of having a serious medical illness Answer: (c) Nihilistic delusions of being dead or not existing. Jules Cotard (1880) described the délire des négations: the belief that one is dead, does not exist, or has lost one's organs or blood (Section 2.6.4). The somatic option is the near miss, because the Cotard patient believes the organs are gone or dead, not diseased; special powers are grandiose and being followed is persecutory. Delusion of infidelity on part of the sexual partner is known as: (RML 2024) (a) Ekbom's syndrome (b) Othello syndrome (c) de Clérambault's syndrome (d) Couvade syndrome Answer: (b) Othello syndrome. Delusional jealousy is Othello syndrome, classically associated with alcohol dependence (Section 2.6.5). Ekbom syndrome is delusional parasitosis (and, separately, restless legs), de Clérambault's is erotomania, and Couvade syndrome is pregnancy-like symptoms in an expectant father, which is not a delusion at all. Hypnagogic hallucinations most commonly occur in: (RML 2024) (a) Schizophrenia (b) Delirium (c) Drug dependence (d) Normal Answer: (d) Normal. Hallucinations while falling asleep are commonest in healthy people: Ohayon's survey (1996) found them in 37 percent, and DSM-5-TR counts them as normal (Section 2.3.6). Narcolepsy is the disorder that features them; schizophrenia, delirium and drug dependence are wrong because the stem asks where they are most common, not where they can occur. Our current mood and feelings are best described by the term: (RML 2024) (a) Emotion (b) Mood (c) Affect (d) Feeling Answer: (c) Affect. Affect is the immediate, observed expression of emotion here and now, the weather, while mood is the sustained state over days or weeks, the climate (Section 2.8.1). "Mood" is the bait because the word is in the stem; an emotion is a brief reaction to a particular event, and a feeling is the experienced side of an emotion. False belief which cannot be shaken by reason is termed as: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Illusion (b) Delusion (c) Hallucination (d) False memory Answer: (b) Delusion. A delusion is a false belief, firmly held, not amenable to reason or contrary evidence and out of keeping with the person's background: a disorder of thought content (Section 2.5.1). An illusion and a hallucination are disorders of perception, and a false memory is an error of memory. Amnesia is a clinical condition of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Pathological loss of memory (b) Behavioral disturbance (c) Depressed affect (d) Impaired perception Answer: (a) Pathological loss of memory. Amnesia is defined by what is missing from memory (Section 2.7.1). A person with amnesia may also be agitated, low in mood or misperceiving, which is why the distractors tempt, but those belong to behaviour, emotion and perception. Delusional beliefs of an individual that he is being deliberately interfered with, discriminated against, plotted against, threatened, or otherwise mistreated is called delusion of: (IHBAS 2024) (a) Reference (b) Persecution (c) Control (d) Grandiosity Answer: (b) Persecution. Being harmed, plotted against or mistreated is persecution, the commonest of all delusions (Section 2.5.5). Reference is the belief that unrelated events refer to oneself, control the belief that an outside force directs one's acts, and grandiosity the belief in one's exceptional abilities, wealth or fame. Choose the correct arrangement of these stages of elevated mood based upon severity: i) Elation, ii) Exaltation, iii) Euphoria, iv) Ecstasy. (Amity 2023) (a) i, ii, iii and iv (b) iii, i, ii and iv (c) iv, iii, ii and i (d) None of the above Answer: (b) iii, i, ii and iv. From mildest to most severe the ladder is euphoria, elation (which adds activity), exaltation (which adds grandiosity) and ecstasy (which adds rapture) (Section 2.8.3). Option (a) starts with elation and (c) reverses the order; ecstasy, not euphoria, is the extreme. Illusions are: (Amity 2023) (a) Distortions of existing stimuli (b) The same as hallucinations (c) The result of innate mechanisms (d) Not based on external reality Answer: (a) Distortions of existing stimuli. An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus (Section 2.3.2). "Not based on external reality" describes a hallucination, so (b) and (d) are wrong by definition, and (c) is not a definition at all: illusions arise from normal perceptual processes that learning shapes. A patient with Korsakoff's psychosis who fabricates detailed and believable stories about their past to fill memory gaps, without the intention to deceive, is exhibiting: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Confabulation (b) Confusion (c) Delirium (d) Malingering Answer: (a) Confabulation. Confabulation is a falsification of memory in clear consciousness with an organic amnesia (Berlyne, 1972), given without intent to deceive (Section 2.7.5). Confusion and delirium are disturbances of consciousness, which that definition excludes, and malingering is the deliberate faking of symptoms for an external gain. Déjà entendu refers to: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Illusion of having seen something before (b) Memory of past events with clarity (c) Illusion of having heard something previously (d) Repetitive involuntary speech Answer: (c) Illusion of having heard something previously. Entendu means heard (Section 2.7.7). Having seen something before is déjà vu, memory of past events with unusual clarity is hypermnesia, and repetitive involuntary speech is a speech sign such as palilalia or verbigeration. Delusion of persecution is most commonly seen in: (IHBAS 2025) (a) OCD (b) Bipolar disorder (c) Schizophrenia (d) Panic disorder Answer: (c) Schizophrenia. Persecutory delusions are found above all in schizophrenia, where they are the most frequent delusion, and in delusional disorder (Section 2.5.5). They also occur in mania, which makes bipolar disorder tempting, but "most commonly" decides it; they are not features of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) or panic disorder. Circumstantiality is a disorder of: (Recall set) (a) Possession of thought (b) Content of thought (c) Form of thought (thought process) (d) Perception Answer: (c) Form of thought (thought process). Circumstantiality is the gentlest disorder of form: a long, over-detailed route that finally reaches the goal, unlike tangentiality, which never does (Section 2.4.4). It says nothing about what is believed (content), the thoughts feel entirely the person's own (possession), and nothing is misperceived. For two or three years before 1800, woodcutters and peasants in the hills of the Tarn, in the south of France, told stories of a naked boy who lived alone in the forests around the small town of Lacaune. He was glimpsed grubbing for acorns and roots, and when people came near he ran. He was caught at least once, kept for about a week in Lacaune, and escaped back into the woods. Then, in the first days of January 1800 (8 January is the date usually given), he came out of the forest near the village of Saint-Sernin-sur-Rance, in the department of the Aveyron, and was taken in at the house of a dyer. He looked about twelve years old. He did not speak. His body was covered with scars, 23 of them by one count, and one long scar ran across his throat, as if someone had once tried to cut it. The naturalist Pierre-Joseph Bonnaterre, who studied him at Rodez over the following months, found a boy who seemed hardly to feel the cold: when Bonnaterre undressed him and led him out into the snow, he frolicked in it with obvious delight. He rocked back and forth for long periods. Later, in Paris, his teacher noticed something stranger still. A pistol fired close behind his head drew hardly any response, yet the soft crack of a walnut, his favourite food, made him turn at once. News of the "savage of the Aveyron" reached Paris, where scholars were arguing about what a human being would be like if he grew up outside society, and in August 1800 the boy was brought to the capital and placed in the National Institution for Deaf-Mutes, directed by the Abbé Roch-Ambroise Cucurron Sicard. A boy who did not speak, people assumed, must be deaf. Crowds came to stare at him. The most famous physician in France, Philippe Pinel (1745 to 1826), the reformer of the Paris asylums (Book 2, Section 1.3), examined him and compared him with the patients he knew at the hospital of Bicêtre. In a report to the Society of Observers of Man late in 1800 he concluded that the boy was no noble savage whom the forest had made wild. He was an "idiot" from birth, like the children in the Paris hospitals, and he could not profit from instruction. A young physician at the institution, Jean Marc Gaspard Itard (1774 to 1838), took the opposite view. The boy, he argued, had lived in almost complete solitude since early childhood; what looked like idiocy was the result of that isolation, and education could undo it. At the end of 1800 Sicard put Itard in charge of the boy. With the help of his housekeeper, Madame Guérin, Itard took him on, and named him Victor, because of all the sounds the boy heard, the vowel "o" was the one he responded to most. For five years Itard worked with Victor almost every day and wrote down everything he saw. He began with the senses: hot baths of two or three hours a day, after which Victor began, for the first time, to show that he felt the cold; games in which a chestnut was hidden under one of three cups, to hold his attention and train his memory; then matching shapes, colours and, at last, letters cut out of metal. Victor learned to recognise some written words and to set out the metal letters of LAIT to ask for milk, and he came to understand some simple spoken words. He grew attached to Madame Guérin; when her husband died and she wept at the table, Victor quietly cleared away the dead man's place. Itard even tested whether the boy had a sense of justice. After a lesson that Victor had done well, Itard pretended to punish him, dragging him towards the closet where he had been shut up before. Victor resisted furiously and bit him, and Itard took the bite as proof of a moral sense. But Victor never learned to speak. A handful of sounds and words, "lait" (milk) and "Oh Dieu" (oh God) the best known, were almost all the speech he ever produced. Itard described his work in a memoir of 1801, De l'éducation d'un homme sauvage (On the education of a wild man), and in a report of 1806 to the Minister of the Interior, and he judged the experiment a failure. Victor lived on with Madame Guérin in a house in the impasse des Feuillantines in Paris and died there in 1828, when he would have been about forty. Itard's methods outlived him: his pupil Édouard Seguin (1812 to 1880) turned them into the first systematic method for educating children with intellectual disability, and Maria Montessori (1870 to 1952) later built on both (Book 2, Section 10.5.8). In 1970 the director François Truffaut retold the story in his film L'Enfant sauvage (The Wild Child), playing Itard himself. More than two centuries later, nobody knows for certain what was wrong with Victor, and the explanations still on the table are the questions of this chapter. Pinel thought he had been born with an intellectual disability. Itard thought he was a normal child stunted by isolation, a boy in whom the window for learning language had closed before anyone reached him (Book 1, Section 8.8.4 tells the parallel story of Genie). A third answer only became possible after 1943, when autism was first described. Victor rocked, paid little attention to people, showed almost no interest in communicating, ignored a pistol shot and turned to a walnut. The psychologist Uta Frith (born 1941), in her book Autism: Explaining the Enigma (1989), suggested that he may have been autistic, and perhaps abandoned because of it; the French writer Serge Aroles , who went back to the archives, argued that the records point to a moderate degree of autism and that Victor was not a true wild child at all, but an abused boy whose scars came from people rather than from the forest. So: how do we tell a disorder of development from the effects of neglect? How do we tell intellectual disability from autism? And what can education and treatment do for a brain that developed differently from the start? Remember Victor; you will return to him at the end of the chapter. 3.1 Disorders of a Developing Brain: Defining and Classifying the Neurodevelopmental Disorders Medium yield · 2 Qs Spend a morning in the child guidance clinic of a large Indian teaching hospital and watch who comes through the door. A grandmother carries in a three-year-old boy who has never said a word and who spins the wheels of a toy car for as long as anyone lets him. A father brings a ten-year-old whose school has written, for the third year running, that he "cannot sit in his seat". A mother sits with a quiet girl in Class 4 who speaks two languages fluently but still cannot read a simple sentence in either. A teenager is brought because, for years, he has blinked, jerked his head and cleared his throat many times an hour. These children look very different, and yet they belong to one family of conditions. None of them has lost a skill he once had, and none of them fell ill after a period of good health. In each, the brain has developed along an unusual path from the beginning, and the difficulty became visible as the child grew and the world began to ask more of him. That shared idea, a difference in how the developing brain is built, is what the word "neurodevelopmental" means, and this section sets up everything the rest of the chapter needs: what the term includes and excludes, how the classification of childhood disorders reached its present form, where each disorder sits in the two great manuals, why a child can never be assessed from a single source, and how Indian law turns a diagnosis into a certificate. What makes a disorder neurodevelopmental DSM-5-TR opens its first diagnostic chapter with a definition. The neurodevelopmental disorders are a group of conditions with onset in the developmental period , the years from conception through childhood and adolescence in which the brain and its skills are still being built. They typically show themselves early, often before the child starts school, and they are characterised by developmental deficits or differences in brain processes that produce impairments of personal, social, academic or occupational functioning. Each part of that sentence does work. "Onset in the developmental period" separates these disorders from conditions that strike a mature brain. "Deficits or differences in brain processes" says where the trouble lies: not in the child's circumstances, his upbringing or his character, but in the way his brain has come to process language, attention, movement, social information or learning. And "impairments of functioning" says why anyone should care: the difference matters because it makes ordinary life harder at home, at school, with friends and later at work. The family is broad. DSM-5-TR notes that the range of difficulty runs from very specific limitations, such as a problem with learning to read or with the control of executive functions (the processes that plan, organise and hold back behaviour), to global impairments of social skills or of intellectual ability. A child with a specific learning disorder may be bright, sociable and well coordinated and still be unable to decode the words on a page. A child with profound intellectual disability may need help with every activity of the day. Both have a neurodevelopmental disorder, because both differences arose in the developing brain. The next sentence of DSM-5-TR is easy to skim past, but it explains a great deal. These disorders, it says, were once thought to be categorically defined, present or absent like a broken bone. More recent dimensional measurement shows a range of severity, often without a very clear boundary with typical development. Think about attention. Every child is inattentive sometimes; some children are inattentive much of the time; a few are so inattentive that they cannot learn in a classroom. Reading, social understanding, motor coordination and intelligence are the same: each is a continuum on which every child has a place. Where, then, does the disorder begin? DSM-5-TR's answer is that a diagnosis requires the presence of both symptoms and impaired function. A boy who is restless and fidgety but learns well, has friends and is managing at home has a temperament, not a disorder. The same symptoms in a boy who is failing every subject and has been excluded from every game cross the line. You will meet this rule in every criteria set of the chapter, usually as a criterion that the symptoms "interfere with" or "limit" functioning. DSM-5-TR adds two more observations that shape how the disorders are diagnosed. First, some neurodevelopmental disorders are defined by excess and some by deficit, and some by both. In ADHD the overactivity and impulsivity are behaviours that are more frequent or more intense than in other children of the same developmental age and sex; in intellectual disability the core is a failure to reach expected milestones; and autism needs both, since DSM-5-TR diagnoses it only when deficits of social communication are accompanied by excessively repetitive behaviours, restricted interests and insistence on sameness. Second, the disorders show a great deal of co-occurrence : they appear together far more often than chance would predict. Many children with autism spectrum disorder also have intellectual developmental disorder; many children with ADHD also have a specific learning disorder. They also travel with other childhood disorders outside the family: communication disorders and autism with anxiety disorders, ADHD with oppositional defiant disorder, tics with obsessive-compulsive disorder. Why should this be? Partly because the disorders share genes and risk factors such as extreme prematurity, and partly because the developing brain is a connected system, so a difference that starts in one set of circuits seldom stays confined to it. The practical lesson is simple: when you find one neurodevelopmental disorder, look for the others (Figure 3.3 in Section 3.1.6 maps the commonest overlaps). A useful teaching idea helps here, although it is a way of thinking rather than a DSM rule. Development can go wrong in two broad ways. In developmental delay the child travels the usual road but more slowly: he sits, walks, talks, dresses himself and learns his letters in the usual order, only later than his age-mates, and at any moment he resembles a typical younger child. Much intellectual disability looks like this. In developmental deviance the road itself is different: some skills arrive on time or even early, others lag far behind, and some behaviours appear that are not part of typical development at any age. Autism is the clearest example. Consider two four-year-olds. Aarav, born very prematurely, walks steadily, feeds himself, speaks in two- and three-word phrases, plays simple pretend games with his cousins and loves to be chased; in every domain he is where a typical child of about two and a half would be. Myra can finish a fifty-piece jigsaw puzzle faster than her father and has known her numbers to a hundred since she was three, yet she does not answer to her name, rarely looks at faces, repeats whole advertisements word for word and screams if her shoes are not lined up by the door. Aarav is behind; Myra is different. Figure 3.1 draws the contrast. Neither picture is a diagnosis, but the distinction tells a clinician what to look for: an even lag points first towards intellectual disability, an uneven profile with unusual behaviours points towards autism or a specific disorder of one skill. Typical child Delay (Aarav) Uneven profile (Myra) 100 50 0 Level reached, percent of age expectation Motor Puzzles and shapes Language Social contact Schematic: illustrative values, not data Figure 3.1 Delay versus deviance. A delayed child (Aarav) is behind in every domain by roughly the same amount, like a typical younger child; a child with an uneven profile (Myra) is at or above age level in some domains and far behind in others, and also shows behaviours that typical children do not show at any age. With that idea in hand, here is the family as DSM-5-TR arranges it. Each member gets its own section later in the chapter. Intellectual developmental disorders : intellectual developmental disorder (intellectual disability), global developmental delay and unspecified intellectual developmental disorder, in which reasoning, learning and everyday adaptive skills are all below age expectations (Sections 3.2 and 3.3). Communication disorders : language disorder, speech sound disorder, childhood-onset fluency disorder (stuttering) and social (pragmatic) communication disorder, in which the development of language, of speech sounds, of the flow of speech or of the social use of language is impaired (Section 3.4). Autism spectrum disorder : persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction together with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities (Sections 3.5 and 3.6). Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) : impairing levels of inattention and disorganisation, hyperactivity and impulsivity, or both (Sections 3.7 and 3.8). Specific learning disorder : persistent difficulty in learning to read, write or calculate, out of keeping with the child's general ability and schooling (Section 3.9). Motor disorders : developmental coordination disorder, stereotypic movement disorder and the tic disorders, of which Tourette's disorder is the best known (Section 3.10). Other specified and unspecified neurodevelopmental disorder : categories for impairing presentations that do not meet the full criteria for any specific disorder. In other specified neurodevelopmental disorder the clinician records the reason, and DSM-5-TR's own example is "neurodevelopmental disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure", a range of developmental disabilities following exposure to alcohol in the womb (Section 1.8.6 describes the related condition for further study, and Section 3.3.5 teaches fetal alcohol syndrome as a cause). In unspecified neurodevelopmental disorder the clinician does not give the reason, often because there is not yet enough information, as in an emergency department. Three confusions trip up students, and each needs clearing away before you go further. The first is a matter of words. The neurodevelopmental disorders are not the same thing as the neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia, the theory proposed in 1987 by Daniel Weinberger and, separately, by Robin Murray and Shôn Lewis , that schizophrenia begins with a disturbance of early brain development that stays silent until adolescence (Sections 1.5.4 and 4.7.6). The model is a theory about one adult disorder; the neurodevelopmental disorders are a chapter of the manual. The second confusion is with the neurocognitive disorders, such as delirium and the dementias, which DSM-5-TR places at the opposite end of the manual (Chapter 10 of this book). The difference is the difference between never having built a skill and losing one. A neurocognitive disorder is a decline from a level of functioning the person once had; a neurodevelopmental disorder is a failure or difference in development itself. DSM-5-TR is explicit that intellectual developmental disorder is distinct from the neurocognitive disorders, which are characterised by a loss of cognitive functioning. The two can occur together, and then both are diagnosed: a man with Down syndrome who develops Alzheimer's disease in middle age has both, and so does a child whose intellectual disability follows a severe head injury once his abilities have stabilised. This old distinction between a mind that never developed and a mind that was lost goes back to the nineteenth century, and Section 3.2.1 tells its history. The third confusion is the commonest in examinations. Not every disorder that begins in childhood is a neurodevelopmental disorder. DSM-5-TR scatters the disorders of childhood across its chapters according to their nature, not their age of onset. Separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism are anxiety disorders (Sections 6.4.7 and 6.4.8). Reactive attachment disorder and disinhibited social engagement disorder, which follow grossly inadequate care, are trauma- and stressor-related disorders (Section 7.4.5). Enuresis and encopresis are elimination disorders, and pica and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder are feeding and eating disorders (Chapter 8). Oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder are disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders (Chapter 11), and disruptive mood dysregulation disorder is a depressive disorder (Section 5.3.2). Section 3.1.2 and its Table 3.1 show how each of them was moved out of the old childhood section. ADHD itself was a close call: the DSM-5 work groups found evidence that could have placed it among the disruptive behaviour disorders, but the preponderance of evidence from its symptoms, its comorbidity and its risk factors put it here (Section 1.8.2 tells the reasoning). One more frame sits behind the whole chapter. Developmental psychopathology , the study of how disorders arise and change as a person develops, insists that a behaviour can only be judged against what is expected at a particular age: a tantrum at three is ordinary and at thirteen is not, and the same disorder looks different at two, at eight and at twenty-five (Book 2, Section 10.1.2, and the Developmental book). Every criteria set in this chapter is written with that principle in mind, which is why so many of them say "inappropriate for age" or "below age expectations". Exam trap "Which disorder is classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder?" The answer is ADHD . The usual distractors each live in another chapter of DSM-5-TR: obsessive-compulsive disorder in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (Section 6.5), generalised anxiety disorder in the anxiety disorders (Section 6.4) and borderline personality disorder in the personality disorders (Chapter 11). The full neurodevelopmental list is intellectual developmental disorders, communication disorders, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, specific learning disorder and the motor disorders, including tics. Two more traps: separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism begin in childhood but are anxiety disorders, and the neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia is a theory, not a DSM category. From "disorders of childhood" to a neurodevelopmental chapter Psychiatry came to children late. For most of its history the only childhood condition with a long medical literature was what the nineteenth century called idiocy, the condition Pinel saw in Victor (Section 3.2.1 follows its names from Esquirol to DSM-5-TR). The other members of the family were described one at a time, mostly by physicians and educators who worked with children rather than by the authors of classifications. John Langdon Down (1828 to 1896) described the syndrome that bears his name in 1866 (Section 3.3.2). George Frederic Still (1868 to 1941) lectured in 1902 on restless, inattentive children with what he called a "defect of moral control" (Section 3.7). Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911) and Théodore Simon (1873 to 1961) published their intelligence scale in 1905, giving clinicians the first practical way to measure the intellectual side of development (Book 1, Section 9.2.3). Theodor Heller , a special educator in Vienna, described in 1908 children who developed normally and then lost their skills (Section 3.5.2). Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) coined the word "autism" in 1911, but for a symptom of schizophrenia, and it was Leo Kanner (1894 to 1981) in 1943 and Hans Asperger (1906 to 1980) in 1944 who described autism in children (Section 3.5.1). Kanner had already written Child Psychiatry (1935), the first English-language textbook of the subject, and the child guidance clinics of the 1920s and 1930s had begun to treat children as patients in their own right (Book 2, Sections 10.5.1 and 10.1.6). The official manuals took much longer to make room for them, and the story of how they did so explains the shape of the present chapter. Chapter 1 describes each edition of the DSM in general; here we follow only what each did to the disorders of childhood. The first Diagnostic and Statistical Manual , DSM-I (1952), had almost nothing to say about children. It recognised mental deficiency , in familial or hereditary and idiopathic forms graded by IQ into mild, moderate and severe (its "mild" level reached as high as an IQ of 85), with a separate "chronic brain syndrome with mental deficiency" when a brain disease was known. Most other childhood problems were filed as transient "adjustment reactions" of infancy, childhood or adolescence, or as "special symptom reactions" such as a learning disturbance, a speech disturbance, enuresis or sleepwalking. A child of the kind Kanner had described, if diagnosed at all, received "schizophrenic reaction, childhood type". DSM-II (1968) replaced mental deficiency with mental retardation , graded by IQ into five levels from borderline to profound, and created the first group of behaviour disorders meant specifically for the young: "behavior disorders of childhood and adolescence". Its members were the hyperkinetic reaction of childhood (or adolescence), the forerunner of ADHD (Section 3.7), the withdrawing reaction, the overanxious reaction, the runaway reaction, the unsocialized aggressive reaction and the group delinquent reaction. The word "reaction", which DSM-II dropped from most adult diagnoses, survived here, and it reflected a view of the time: a disturbed child was mainly a child reacting to his circumstances. A separate group of "special symptoms" collected speech disturbance, specific learning disturbance, tic, other psychomotor disorders, disorders of sleep, feeding disturbance, enuresis, encopresis and headache. And autism was still not a diagnosis in its own right. DSM-II's "schizophrenia, childhood type" was for schizophrenic symptoms appearing before puberty, which might show themselves, it said, in autistic, atypical and withdrawn behaviour, a failure to develop an identity separate from the mother's, and a general unevenness, gross immaturity and inadequacy of development. The decisive change came with DSM-III (1980), which gave childhood its first full section, "disorders usually first evident in infancy, childhood, or adolescence". The section brought together mental retardation; attention deficit disorder, with or without hyperactivity; conduct disorder; the anxiety disorders of childhood (separation anxiety, avoidant and overanxious disorders); the eating disorders, anorexia nervosa and bulimia included, since they usually began in adolescence; the stereotyped movement disorders, which were then the tic disorders, Tourette's disorder among them; disorders with physical manifestations such as stuttering, enuresis and encopresis; and a new group of pervasive developmental disorders , headed by infantile autism. For the first time the official American manual separated autism from schizophrenia. The specific developmental disorders , of reading, arithmetic, language and articulation, were recorded on Axis II, beside the personality disorders, so that a child's lifelong learning problem would not be forgotten behind his presenting complaint (Section 1.7.5 explains the axes). DSM-III-R (1987) took a step towards the modern idea. It gathered mental retardation, the pervasive developmental disorders (now autistic disorder and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified, PDD-NOS) and the specific developmental disorders under one heading, "developmental disorders", and coded all three on Axis II. Attention deficit disorder became attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. DSM-IV (1994) and its text revision DSM-IV-TR (2000) renamed the section disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence and divided it into ten groups: mental retardation; learning disorders; motor skills disorder; communication disorders; pervasive developmental disorders; attention-deficit and disruptive behavior disorders; feeding and eating disorders of infancy or early childhood; tic disorders; elimination disorders; and "other disorders of infancy, childhood, or adolescence", a mixed group that held separation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, reactive attachment disorder of infancy or early childhood and stereotypic movement disorder. The pervasive developmental disorders grew to five, since Rett's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder and Asperger's disorder joined autistic disorder and PDD-NOS. Only mental retardation was now coded on Axis II, beside the personality disorders; the learning, motor and communication disorders moved to Axis I. DSM-IV itself warned that the section existed for convenience: adults could receive these diagnoses, and children could receive diagnoses from any other part of the manual. That warning points to the weakness of the arrangement. The section grouped disorders by the age at which they were usually first diagnosed, not by what they were. It put autism and intellectual disability, lifelong differences in how the brain is built, beside bedwetting, a fear of leaving mother, a refusal to eat and a habit of stealing cars. DSM-5 (2013) dissolved it. The disorders whose essence is a difference in early brain development were kept together in a new chapter, "Neurodevelopmental Disorders", which became the first chapter of the manual because DSM-5 arranges its chapters along the life span, beginning with the disorders that show themselves earliest (Section 1.8.2). The rest were sent to the chapters that match their nature, as Table 3.1 shows. Inside the new chapter several things changed at once: the four separate pervasive developmental disorders became one autism spectrum disorder, the three learning disorders became one specific learning disorder with specifiers, social (pragmatic) communication disorder was added, transient tic disorder was renamed provisional tic disorder, and mental retardation became intellectual disability, with severity judged by adaptive functioning rather than IQ (Section 3.2.3). DSM-5-TR (2022) made one more change of name. DSM-5 had called the condition "intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder)"; DSM-5-TR reversed the order to intellectual developmental disorder (intellectual disability), to show its relationship with ICD-11's "disorders of intellectual development", and kept "intellectual disability" in brackets because educators, advocacy groups and the public use it. In the United States, Rosa's Law (Public Law 111-256) had already replaced "mental retardation" with "intellectual disability" throughout federal law in 2010. This chapter uses the two terms interchangeably. Exam trap "Disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence" is the DSM-IV and DSM-IV-TR heading (DSM-III said "first evident"), and "pervasive developmental disorders" was their name for the autism group (autistic disorder, Rett's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder, Asperger's disorder and PDD-NOS). ICD-10 keeps both ideas alive in its own blocks (Section 3.1.3). In DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR the heading is neurodevelopmental disorders , and it is not a home for every childhood disorder: separation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, reactive attachment disorder, the elimination disorders, conduct and oppositional defiant disorders and disruptive mood dysregulation disorder all live elsewhere. In DSM-IV-TR only mental retardation was coded on Axis II; in DSM-III it was the specific developmental disorders. Where each disorder lives: DSM-5-TR, ICD-10 and ICD-11 An Indian clinician has to move between three systems. Research papers and most entrance examinations speak the language of DSM-5-TR; hospital records, insurance forms and the law still largely speak WHO's ICD-10; and ICD-11, in force internationally since 2022, is gradually replacing it. Each system places the neurodevelopmental disorders a little differently, and each gives them different codes. Chapter 1 has already laid out the large blocks: ICD-10's Chapter V gives F70 to F79 to mental retardation, F80 to F89 to the disorders of psychological development and F90 to F98 to the behavioural and emotional disorders with onset usually occurring in childhood and adolescence (Section 1.9.4), and ICD-11's Chapter 6 opens with a single grouping of neurodevelopmental disorders, 6A00 to 6A0Z (Section 1.9.5). This subsection goes down to the individual codes, which Chapter 1 does not give. Start with the code numbers printed in DSM-5-TR. The APA does not have codes of its own: DSM-5-TR prints the codes of ICD-10-CM , the clinical modification of ICD-10 used in the United States (Section 1.8.3). They look like WHO ICD-10 codes, and most of them mean the same thing, but not all. Two examples matter for this chapter. F88 does double duty in DSM-5-TR, standing for both global developmental delay and other specified neurodevelopmental disorder, because ICD-10-CM files both under its "other disorders of psychological development"; this is the same borrowing that gives some other conditions in DSM-5-TR their R and Z codes (Section 1.8.7). And F90.0 and F90.1 change meaning between the two systems. In DSM-5-TR they are ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, and ADHD, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation; in the WHO's ICD-10 they are "disturbance of activity and attention" and "hyperkinetic conduct disorder". ICD-10 itself spreads the family across three blocks. The first, F70 to F79, holds mild (F70), moderate (F71), severe (F72) and profound (F73) mental retardation, with F78 for "other" and F79 for "unspecified". A fourth character records how much the person's behaviour is affected: .0 for no or minimal impairment of behaviour, .1 for significant impairment requiring attention or treatment, .8 for other impairments and .9 when none is mentioned. A young man with moderate mental retardation who has begun hitting his carers would therefore be coded F71.1. The second block, F80 to F89, the disorders of psychological development , holds two kinds of condition. The "specific developmental disorders" are those in which one skill lags while development is otherwise normal: of speech and language (F80, from specific speech articulation disorder, F80.0, through expressive and receptive language disorders, F80.1 and F80.2, to acquired aphasia with epilepsy, the Landau-Kleffner syndrome of Section 3.4.2, F80.3), of scholastic skills (F81: specific reading disorder, specific spelling disorder, specific disorder of arithmetical skills and a mixed disorder, with developmental expressive writing disorder among the "other" disorders at F81.8), of motor function (F82), and mixed (F83). Beside them sit the pervasive developmental disorders of F84: childhood autism (F84.0), atypical autism (F84.1), Rett syndrome (F84.2), other childhood disintegrative disorder (F84.3), an ICD oddity with no DSM equivalent called overactive disorder associated with mental retardation and stereotyped movements (F84.4), and Asperger syndrome (F84.5). The third block, F90 to F98, mixes disorders that DSM-5-TR would call neurodevelopmental with others that it would not. It contains the hyperkinetic disorders (F90), ICD-10's narrower cousin of ADHD (Section 3.7 explains the difference), next to the conduct disorders, the emotional disorders of childhood, elective mutism and the attachment disorders; the tic disorders (F95: transient, chronic motor or vocal, and "combined vocal and multiple motor tic disorder [de la Tourette]", F95.2); and, under F98, nonorganic enuresis and encopresis, pica, stereotyped movement disorders (F98.4), stuttering [stammering] (F98.5) and cluttering (F98.6). Attention deficit disorder without hyperactivity has no place in F90 at all: ICD-10 lists it among the "other specified" disorders at F98.8. ICD-11 tidied all of this into one grouping, as DSM-5 did (Section 1.9.6 summarises the change). Its neurodevelopmental disorders are the disorders of intellectual development (6A00, with mild, moderate, severe and profound levels, a "provisional" category for a child under four or a person who cannot be validly assessed, and an unspecified one); developmental speech or language disorders (6A01, divided into developmental speech sound disorder, developmental speech fluency disorder and developmental language disorder, the last with sub-codes for receptive and expressive, mainly expressive, mainly pragmatic and other impairments); autism spectrum disorder (6A02, sub-coded by two questions, whether there is a disorder of intellectual development and how far functional language is impaired, into five codes, 6A02.0 to 6A02.3 and 6A02.5, since the current release has no 6A02.4); developmental learning disorder (6A03, with impairment in reading, in written expression, in mathematics, or of another kind); developmental motor coordination disorder (6A04); attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (6A05, in predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive and combined presentations); and stereotyped movement disorder (6A06, with or without self-injury), with 6A0Y and 6A0Z for other specified and unspecified presentations. Three things lie just outside the grouping. Tourette syndrome (8A05.00) and the other primary tic disorders are classified in the chapter on diseases of the nervous system; Tourette syndrome and the two chronic tic disorders (8A05.01 and 8A05.02) are only cross-listed among the neurodevelopmental disorders, and Tourette syndrome, as Section 6.6 notes, among the obsessive-compulsive or related disorders as well. Rett syndrome is no longer a mental disorder at all but a developmental anomaly (LD90.4). And a secondary neurodevelopmental syndrome (6E60) is recorded when neurodevelopmental features that do not meet any specific disorder are the direct result of another health condition, ICD-11's examples being the autistic-like features of Rett syndrome, the aggression and self-mutilation of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and the abnormal language development of Williams syndrome (Section 3.3.3). Last, DSM-5-TR uses a few kinds of specifier across the whole chapter, so it helps to know them before you meet them disorder by disorder. Severity specifiers exist for intellectual developmental disorder, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, specific learning disorder and stereotypic movement disorder. Specifiers describing the current symptoms exist for ADHD (its presentation), specific learning disorder (the academic domains and subskills affected) and persistent motor or vocal tic disorder (motor tics only or vocal tics only). And autism spectrum disorder and stereotypic movement disorder can both be specified as "associated with a known genetic or other medical condition or environmental factor", which lets the clinician record a cause, such as fragile X syndrome or exposure to valproate in the womb, that may matter for the course and for the family.
