Why several informants: assessing a developing child An adult patient can usually tell you what is wrong. A child often cannot, and even when he can, his behaviour depends heavily on where he is and who is with him. That is why child assessment collects information from several informants, by several methods, about several settings, an approach called multi-informant assessment . Book 2, Section 10.1.4 tells the research behind it: when investigators compared different people's ratings of the same children, agreement between a parent and a teacher turned out to be low, and most of the disagreement was not error but a true picture of a child who behaves differently in different places. Consider Siddharth, aged eight, who sits in a Class 3 section of fifty-two children in a crowded government school in Kanpur. His class teacher writes that he is never in his seat, calls out answers, pushes in the line and loses his books every week. His mother, who works long shifts in a garment unit, sees him mostly when he is tired and asleep. His grandmother, who sits beside him at the kitchen table for his homework, one adult to one child, says he is "a little naughty but sits fine with me". In the clinic, on a quiet morning with one friendly adult and a box of new puzzles, he works steadily for forty minutes. Who is right? All of them. Each has seen a true slice of the boy's life, and only together do the slices show where and when his difficulty appears and what the different settings demand of him. DSM-5-TR itself explains why the clinic is often the worst place to judge. In its text on ADHD it notes that the signs may be minimal or absent when the child is receiving frequent rewards for good behaviour, is under close supervision, is in a new setting, is doing something especially interesting, has constant outside stimulation such as a screen, or is in a one-to-one situation, and it gives the clinician's office as the example. Siddharth in the clinic was all of these at once. A clinician who relied on observation alone would have sent him home with a clean bill of health. The criteria do not merely recommend several sources; for most of the disorders in this chapter they cannot be applied without them. Go through them one by one. ADHD. Several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms must be present in two or more settings , such as home, school or work, with friends or relatives, or in other activities. DSM-5-TR adds that confirming substantial symptoms across settings typically cannot be done accurately without consulting informants who have seen the person in those settings, and that symptoms typically vary with the context even within one setting. When an adult is assessed, his own memory of his childhood is unreliable, so DSM-5-TR advises getting information from others as well. ICD-11 says the same in its own words: the symptoms must be evident across multiple situations or settings, but are likely to vary with the structure and demands of each one. Autism spectrum disorder. The social communication deficits must be present "across multiple contexts", and both groups of criteria may be met "currently or by history". DSM-5-TR explains why history is allowed: symptoms change with development and may be masked by strategies the person has learned, so the parents' account of the toddler years is part of the evidence, although the present picture must still cause significant impairment. Intellectual developmental disorder. The adaptive deficits must limit functioning in one or more activities of daily life "across multiple environments, such as home, school, work, and community". Adaptive functioning is measured with standardised scales completed with knowledgeable informants (a parent or other family member, a teacher, a counsellor or care provider) and with the person himself as far as possible, together with educational, developmental, medical and mental health records. An intelligence test in a clinic room can measure reasoning; only the people who live and work with a child can say whether he can buy vegetables, take a bus or keep a friend. Specific learning disorder. DSM-5-TR states that its four criteria are to be met on a clinical synthesis of the person's developmental, medical, family and educational history, school reports and psychoeducational assessment. No single test score can show that a difficulty has lasted despite targeted help, or that the child was taught adequately in the first place. Communication disorders. Assessment must take account of the child's cultural and language background, especially in bilingual homes, and tests standardised on one group may not give appropriate norms for another. A true language disorder in a bilingual child affects both languages, so both should be assessed. A child who speaks Bhojpuri at home and is taught in English cannot be judged on an English test alone. Behind all of these sources stands one that no rating scale replaces: the developmental history , the clinician's step-by-step account of the child's life from conception to the present. It begins with the pregnancy (illnesses, infections, bleeding, medicines, alcohol and tobacco), moves to the birth (at term or early, the birth weight, whether the baby cried at once or needed oxygen or a stay in the neonatal unit, jaundice, seizures) and then follows the milestones in each domain: when the child first smiled, sat, crawled, walked, babbled, pointed, said words and then phrases, and when he became toilet trained. It asks about illnesses, head injuries and seizures, about hearing and vision, about schooling, and about relatives with similar difficulties or a marriage between relatives. Above all it asks one question that can change the whole diagnosis: has the child ever lost a skill he once had? Such a loss, called regression , is never part of ordinary development, and it sends the clinician looking for autism with regression, for the rare neurological and genetic conditions of Sections 3.3 and 3.5.2, and for epilepsy. Each part of the history maps onto a later section of this chapter: the pregnancy and birth onto the causes of intellectual disability (Section 3.3), the milestones onto the distinction between delay and deviance (Section 3.1.1), and the course over time onto the question of whether a child is catching up or falling further behind. The normal sequence of language milestones is taught in Book 1, Section 8.8.5. Some findings in the history are serious enough that the clinician should not wait and see. Nisha, aged two years and two months, is brought by her parents because she says only "mama" and "dudu". Her grandmother is not worried: "Her father also talked late; she will talk when she is ready." Many late talkers do catch up, but Nisha has no two-word phrases at 24 months, one of the warning signs in Table 3.3, and the right response is a hearing test and a developmental assessment now, not a review in six months. The table collects the best-known warning signs. The first five come from the practice parameter on screening for autism published in 2000 by the American Academy of Neurology and the Child Neurology Society, written by a group led by Pauline Filipek , which called them absolute indications for immediate further evaluation; they flag any developmental disorder, not only autism. Parents rarely remember dates, so anchor each milestone to an event they do remember ("Was she walking at her first birthday? At Diwali that year? When her brother was born?"), and use the immunisation card, birthday photographs and, increasingly, the videos on the family's mobile phone, which can show a toddler's babble, pointing or hand-flapping more reliably than memory. Ask who looks after the child during the day, since that person, often a grandmother, may be the best informant of all, and ask which languages are spoken to the child. Hear the family's reassurances ("boys talk late", "he is just naughty", "she will grow out of it") respectfully, but do not let them override a warning sign. Exam trap "When diagnosing developmental disorders, multi-informant assessment is recommended because..." The answer is that symptoms may vary across contexts : a child's behaviour at home, at school and in the clinic genuinely differs, so each informant sees a valid but partial picture. Reject the other options. "Parents tend to over-report problems" blames one informant, and parents may equally under-report. "Teachers provide no relevant information" is false, since teachers are often the best judges of attention and learning. "Only clinical observation is not sufficient" is true, but it is a consequence of the real reason (behaviour in the clinic is one more context, and often an unrepresentative one), not the reason itself. Remember the criterion that makes the point in a single line: ADHD needs several symptoms in two or more settings . The tools you will meet, one line each The later sections of this chapter mention many tests and scales by name, and examiners like to ask which tool belongs to which disorder. The tests themselves, how they are built, scored and interpreted, belong to the Assessment book, and the intelligence tests are introduced in Book 1 (Sections 9.3.2 to 9.3.6 and 9.8.2). Table 3.4 is therefore a map, not a lesson: one line per tool, grouped by what it is for, with the section of this chapter where it matters. Four groups are worth keeping apart. Developmental schedules for infants and preschool children compare a child's skills with the ages at which typical children achieve them and yield a developmental age and a developmental quotient (DQ, developmental age divided by chronological age, times 100). Intelligence tests yield a mental age or, in their modern form, a deviation IQ. Adaptive behaviour scales, completed with an informant, describe what the person actually does in daily life; the Vineland Social Maturity Scale gives a social age and a social quotient . And the disorder-specific instruments screen for, diagnose or rate the severity of one condition. Two Indian entries deserve a word. The Developmental Screening Test of J. Bharat Raj , published in Mysore (Indian sources give 1977 or 1983), is a quick Indian screen of mental development from birth to fifteen years that gives a developmental age and DQ. The Seguin Form Board , a performance test descended from the form boards Édouard Seguin designed for teaching, asks the child to fit ten shaped blocks into their recesses as fast as possible over three timed trials; the best time is converted into a mental age from Indian norms, and because it needs no language it is still part of many Indian test batteries for young children. Neurodevelopmental disorders in India: numbers, law and certification How many Indian children have a neurodevelopmental disorder? For a long time nobody could say, because most Indian figures came from single clinics, single schools or single districts, each using its own methods. The first large answer, covering several regions with one method, came from a multicentre study published in 2018, and it is worth knowing in detail. Key study: How common are neurodevelopmental disorders in Indian children? (Arora and colleagues, 2018) A national team coordinated by the INCLEN Trust (International Clinical Epidemiology Network) and led by Narendra K. Arora set out to measure the burden in children aged 2 to 9. Using cluster sampling, they assessed 3,964 children, with almost equal numbers of boys and girls, from five deliberately different populations: Palwal in Haryana (north-central, all rural), Kangra in Himachal Pradesh (north), Dhenkanal in Odisha (east), Hyderabad in Telangana (south, all urban) and North Goa (west). Every child was examined for seven conditions (vision impairment, epilepsy, neuromotor impairment including cerebral palsy, hearing impairment, speech and language disorders, autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability), and the 6- to 9-year-olds were also assessed for ADHD and learning disorders. Pooled across the sites, 9.2 percent of children aged 2 to under 6 and 13.6 percent of those aged 6 to 9 had at least one of these conditions, roughly one child in eleven and one in seven. The sites differed widely (from 2.9 to 18.7 percent in the younger group), but there was no significant difference by sex, by rural or urban residence or by religion, and almost one fifth of the affected children had more than one condition. Hearing impairment, intellectual disability, speech and language disorders, epilepsy and learning disorders were the common conditions across the sites, and autism was about as common as in studies from other countries. The risk factors were telling: birth outside a health institution, asphyxia at birth, illness in the newborn period, infections of the brain after birth, stunting, and low birth weight or prematurity. The authors concluded, in their paper in PLOS Medicine , that most of these risks could be modified by public health measures. Two cautions. The sample contained fewer stunted and low-birth-weight children than the national population and 15.6 percent of families refused, so the true burden is probably higher. And the study's list of conditions is wider than the DSM-5-TR chapter, since vision and hearing impairment, epilepsy and cerebral palsy are not mental disorders; its figures measure developmental disability in the broad sense, not the neurodevelopmental disorders of this chapter alone. The finding that so many children had more than one condition is the Indian face of a pattern you met in Section 3.1.1: the neurodevelopmental disorders overlap. Figure 3.3 draws the family as overlapping ovals and numbers the overlaps that matter most clinically. Autism and intellectual disability often occur together; so do ADHD and specific learning disorder; tics are common in children with ADHD; and tics are closely linked with obsessive-compulsive disorder, which sits outside the family altogether. The communication disorders and the motor disorders shade into their neighbours too. The figure is a schematic of which conditions travel together, not a chart of how often; the figures belong to the sections on each disorder. The sizes and overlaps are schematic, not proportional to prevalence. What do Indian clinicians actually see? No survey measures it, but the pattern is familiar in every child clinic. Children arrive late, because relatives reassure the parents that "he will talk when he is ready", that "boys are naughty" or that a dreamy girl is "just quiet". The first person consulted is often a paediatrician, a teacher, an elder in the family or a religious healer, and a referral to a psychologist frequently comes from the school only when marks begin to fall, or when a child cannot keep up in an English-medium classroom. Some families fear that a label will spoil a child's marriage prospects, or a sibling's, and some would rather hear "weakness" or "slow" than a diagnosis. And the causes that weigh more heavily in India than in richer countries (iodine deficiency, asphyxia at birth, infections of the brain, undernutrition and low birth weight) are among the most preventable (Section 3.3 teaches them). The public health system's main tool for finding these children early is the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) of 2013, which screens children for the "four Ds", defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays including disability, and refers them to District Early Intervention Centres (Book 2, Section 10.1.6). Once a disorder is diagnosed, the law decides what the child is entitled to. Book 2 teaches the laws (Section 1.10.9) and the certification procedures (Section 9.9.8) in full; here is what you need for this chapter. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 recognises 21 specified disabilities, and under its heading of intellectual disability it lists specific learning disabilities and autism spectrum disorder; its older predecessor, the Persons with Disabilities Act 1995, had recognised mental retardation but not autism. Most of the Act's entitlements, such as reserved posts, reserved college seats and free education from 6 to 18, go to people with benchmark disability , certified as not less than 40 percent of a specified disability. The National Trust Act 1999 covers exactly four conditions (autism, cerebral palsy, mental retardation and multiple disabilities) and lets a family obtain a legal guardian for an adult who cannot manage his own affairs through a local level committee. The Rehabilitation Council of India, a statutory body since the RCI Act of 1992, registers the professionals, clinical psychologists among them, who carry out the assessments. Certification follows official guidelines notified in 2024, which replaced those of 2018, and applications are now made through the national Unique Disability ID (UDID) portal. Every village has always known a child who learned to walk late, spoke little, could not keep up with the others at school and needed looking after long after his brothers and sisters had grown up and left. What has changed, again and again, is what that child was called, how he was measured, where the line between him and everyone else was drawn, and what was done for him. This section follows those changes and then sets out the modern definition: the three criteria of DSM-5-TR, the reason each is there, the levels of severity, the labels used when a child is too young or too hard to test, and the conditions that can be mistaken for intellectual disability. The causes have a section of their own (Section 3.3). A condition that kept changing its name For most of history the words were blunt. A person who never developed ordinary understanding was an idiot , from the Greek idiōtēs , a private person cut off from public life; a less severely affected person was an imbecile , from the Latin for weak; and in the English-speaking world of the late nineteenth century the mildest group, people who could talk and work but could not manage school or their own affairs, were feeble-minded . These were not insults when they were coined. They were technical terms for three grades, from the most to the least severe, and doctors, judges and teachers used them as calmly as a modern clinician says "moderate" or "mild". The trouble is that every technical term for people with low intelligence has, sooner or later, been taken up as a playground taunt, and once that happens it can no longer be used in a clinic. You will see this cycle repeat itself four or five times in what follows. The first person to define the condition carefully was Jean-Étienne Dominique Esquirol (1772 to 1840), the favourite pupil of Philippe Pinel at the Salpêtrière in Paris. In his treatise Des maladies mentales of 1838, Esquirol complained that earlier writers had confused idiots with demented patients, and he drew the line that this chapter still uses. "Idiocy is not a disease," he wrote, "but a condition in which the intellectual faculties are never manifested; or have never been developed sufficiently to enable the idiot to acquire such an amount of knowledge, as persons of his own age, and placed in similar circumstances with himself, are capable of receiving." By contrast, dementia was the loss of a mind that had once been whole, and he put the difference in an image that examiners still like: "A man in a state of dementia is deprived of advantages which he formerly enjoyed; he was a rich man, who has become poor. The idiot, on the contrary, has always been in a state of want and misery." (The quotations are from the English translation of 1845.) Older nosologists had called the condition amentia , being without a mind, as opposed to dementia, being out of one's mind. Esquirol also split it into two grades, imbecility and idiocy proper, the first attempt at what we now call levels of severity. Read Esquirol's definition again and two things stand out. First, it is developmental: the faculties never developed, so the condition begins with life or in early childhood. That is exactly the difference between the neurodevelopmental disorders of this chapter and the neurocognitive disorders of Chapter 10, in which abilities that were once acquired are lost. Second, it measures the person against "persons of his own age, and placed in similar circumstances", which is the germ of the modern rule that a person's functioning must be compared with that of age-mates from the same culture. What Esquirol lacked was any hope. "We can conceive of no possibility of changing this state," he wrote. His teacher Pinel had reached the same verdict about the wild boy of Aveyron, whom he judged an incurable "idiot" (see the opening of this chapter), and it took Itard's pupil Seguin to show that such children could be taught (Book 2, Section 10.5.8). From the late nineteenth century the vocabulary moved into the law. In Britain the Idiots Act of 1886 separated idiots and imbeciles from lunatics, so that they could be cared for and trained apart from the insane, and the Mental Deficiency Act of 1913 recognised four classes (idiots, imbeciles, feeble-minded persons and "moral imbeciles") and allowed people certified as "mentally defective" to be detained indefinitely in special colonies. The general term on both sides of the Atlantic became mental deficiency , and it was the term of the first DSM in 1952. In the United States, Henry Goddard added the word "moron" in 1910 for the mildest grade and used it in the cause of eugenics (Book 1, Section 9.2.4). From DSM-II (1968) to DSM-IV-TR (2000) the official term was mental retardation , and its definition was written largely by the American Association on Mental Deficiency (AAMD). Two of its revisions show how much the boundary is a decision rather than a discovery. The definition prepared by Rick Heber (1959, revised 1961) required three things for the first time: subaverage general intellectual functioning, impairment in adaptive behaviour (the practical and social skills of everyday life), and onset during the developmental period. Adaptive behaviour was put into the definition precisely so that an IQ score would not decide the matter on its own. But Heber set the intellectual line at one standard deviation below the mean, about IQ 85, with a "borderline" level between one and two standard deviations, so that in principle about one person in six fell below it. In 1973 the revision edited by Herbert Grossman required "significantly subaverage" functioning, two standard deviations below the mean, about IQ 70. Overnight, people with IQs between about 70 and 85 who had been "retarded" under the old definition were no longer retarded at all, although nothing about them had changed. The descendant of Heber's borderline level survives today, outside the disorder, as borderline intellectual functioning (Section 3.2.4). The association's own name records the same history. It was founded in 1876, with Édouard Seguin among its founders, as the Association of Medical Officers of American Institutions for Idiotic and Feeble-minded Persons; it became the American Association for the Study of the Feebleminded in 1906, the AAMD in 1933, the American Association on Mental Retardation in 1987, and the American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD) in 2007. In 2010 the United States passed Rosa's Law (Public Law 111-256), named after Rosa Marcellino, a schoolgirl with Down syndrome in Maryland, which replaced "mental retardation" with "intellectual disability" throughout federal law. DSM-5 (2013) followed with the name intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder), and DSM-5-TR (2022) turned the two round to give intellectual developmental disorder (intellectual disability), so that its name matches ICD-11's disorders of intellectual development . ICD-11 describes these disorders as a "metasyndrome" of the developmental period analogous to dementia in later life, a phrase Esquirol would have understood at once. DSM-5-TR notes that the medical and research literature use both names, while "intellectual disability" is the term of teachers, advocacy groups and the public. This chapter uses the two interchangeably. India travelled the same road. The Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 spoke of "mental retardation"; the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 speaks of "intellectual disability" (Book 2, Section 1.10.9). The Mental Healthcare Act 2017, curiously, still uses the old phrase, but only to exclude it: its definition of mental illness "does not include mental retardation which is a condition of arrested or incomplete development of mind of a person, specially characterised by sub normality of intelligence". Alongside the change of name came a change of grammar. Clinicians now use person-first language , "a person with intellectual disability" rather than "a retarded person" or "a mental retard", because the person is not the condition. Exam trap Esquirol (1838) separated idiocy (the faculties never developed) from dementia (faculties once present, then lost): the rich man become poor is the demented person, not the idiot. Do not confuse Esquirol with Goddard, who coined "moron" (1910), or with Seguin, who taught such children. Heber's 1959 AAMD definition put the line at one SD below the mean (about 85); Grossman's 1973 revision moved it to two SD (about 70). Mind the British usage: in Britain "learning disability" means intellectual disability, whereas "learning difficulty" or "specific learning difficulty" usually means a problem such as dyslexia (Section 3.9). And under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, intellectual disability is not a mental illness. The three criteria, and why each is there DSM-5-TR opens with a one-sentence summary: intellectual developmental disorder is a disorder with onset during the developmental period that includes both intellectual and adaptive functioning deficits in the conceptual, social and practical domains. Then it gives three criteria, and all three must be met. Each closes a door that would otherwise let the wrong people in, or keep the right people out, so it is worth taking them one at a time and asking what each is for. Criterion A: a deficit in intellectual functions. The functions meant are the ones that intelligence tests sample: reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgement, academic learning and learning from experience. The criterion insists that the deficit be confirmed by both clinical assessment and individualised, standardised intelligence testing. Neither is enough alone. A clinician's impression can be fooled by a shy, frightened or unfamiliar child, and a test score can be fooled by a bad day, a strange language or a poorly chosen test. Requiring both is a cross-check. How low is low enough? DSM-5-TR answers in its text rather than in the criterion itself: people with the disorder have scores "approximately two standard deviations or more below the population mean, including a margin for measurement error (generally ± 5 points)". On the tests clinicians use, which are built to have a mean of 100 and a standard deviation (SD) of 15, two SD below the mean is 70, so the zone is 65 to 75 (70 plus or minus 5). Figure 3.4 shows what that means. Because intelligence test scores in the population follow the bell-shaped normal curve, only about 2.3 percent of people score below 70. Why a margin of 5 points? Because no test measures perfectly. Every score is an estimate of a person's true ability, and the standard error of measurement tells you how far the estimate is likely to stray. On a well-built test such as the Wechsler scales it is only 2 or 3 points, but a clinician wants to be fairly sure, so the band within which the true score lies with about 95 percent confidence runs roughly 5 points either side: a score of 70 means that the true score probably lies somewhere between 65 and 75. A child who scores 73 on Monday might score 68 on Friday without any change in his brain. Drawing a hard line at 70 would therefore label one child and not another when the test cannot tell them apart; the margin hands the decision back to criterion B and to clinical judgement. Two standard deviations below the mean is IQ 70; with a margin for measurement error the zone is 65 to 75, and only about 2.3 percent of people score below 70. The ICD-10 IQ bands for the four levels lie beneath the axis; borderline intellectual functioning (DSM-IV-TR's 71 to 84) is not intellectual disability. Not just any test will do. DSM-5-TR asks for tests that are individually administered, psychometrically valid, comprehensive and culturally appropriate, and it spells out what can go wrong. Brief screening tests and group tests can give invalid scores. When a person's subtest scores are wildly uneven (very good at puzzles and very poor at vocabulary, say), the overall IQ averages things that do not belong together and may itself be invalid; a profile of strengths and weaknesses then tells you more than one number. Scores are inflated by practice effects , when a child is retested too soon on the same test and remembers it, and by the Flynn effect , the steady rise in average test performance over the decades, which means that a test with old norms compares today's child with a weaker generation and flatters him. The effect is not trivial at the line: in one study by Kanaya, Scullin and Ceci (2003), the number of people scoring just below 70 tripled when they were given a newly renormed version of the test. Above all, the test must be normed for the person's sociocultural background and native language. A child from a Kannada-medium village school tested in English on a test standardised in America is being tested on his English and his schooling, not on his intelligence, which is why Indian clinicians use Indian adaptations (Book 1, Section 9.3.6; the tests are listed in Table 3.4 of Section 3.1.5). Disorders that affect hearing, vision, movement or language can also pull scores down for reasons that have nothing to do with intellect. And even a valid score is not the whole story. IQ tests sample conceptual reasoning well but sample poorly how a person reasons in real situations and copes with practical tasks. DSM-5-TR gives the example of a person whose IQ is somewhat above the 65 to 75 zone but whose adaptive problems in social judgement are so severe that his everyday functioning is like that of people with much lower scores; it concludes that using IQ tests "as the sole criteria for the diagnosis of an intellectual developmental disorder is insufficient". That sentence is the reason criterion B exists. Criterion B: a deficit in adaptive functioning. By adaptive functioning DSM-5-TR means how well a person meets the community's standards of personal independence and social responsibility, compared with others of the same age and sociocultural background. DSM-5-TR groups it into three domains. The conceptual domain covers memory, language, reading, writing, mathematical reasoning, practical knowledge, problem solving and judgement in new situations. The social domain covers awareness of other people's thoughts, feelings and experiences, empathy, communication, the ability to make friends, and social judgement. The practical domain covers looking after oneself and managing life: personal care, job responsibilities, money, recreation, controlling one's own behaviour, and organising school and work tasks. The deficit must mean a failure to meet developmental and sociocultural standards, and without ongoing support it must limit functioning in one or more activities of daily life, such as communication, social participation and independent living, across several environments: home, school, work and community. The text adds the threshold: criterion B is met when at least one of the three domains is impaired badly enough that ongoing support is needed for the person to perform adequately. It does not require all three. Why insist on adaptive deficits? Because the diagnosis exists to identify people who need help to live, and some people who score below 70 do not. A man who scores 66 because the test was in his second language, or because he never went to school, may run a tea stall, keep accounts in his head, raise a family and be respected in his village; calling him disabled would be a mistake of measurement, not a discovery. Criterion B is also the reason the diagnosis has to be made with the help of people who know the person. Adaptive behaviour is assessed by clinical evaluation together with individualised, culturally appropriate, standardised measures completed with knowledgeable informants (a parent or other family member, a teacher, a carer) and with the person himself as far as possible; in India the Vineland Social Maturity Scale is the usual instrument and the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales its modern successor (Book 1, Section 9.8.2; Table 3.4). DSM-5-TR warns that adaptive functioning is hard to judge in controlled settings such as prisons, where daily life is organised for you, so information about life outside should be sought. Criterion C: onset during the developmental period. Both the intellectual and the adaptive deficits must be present during childhood or adolescence. DSM-IV-TR put a number on it, before age 18; DSM-5-TR does not, and the AAIDD extended its own limit to before age 22 in 2021 (Book 1, Section 9.8.1). The criterion is what keeps the disorder developmental. A 40-year-old engineer whose intellect is devastated by a stroke or by encephalitis has a neurocognitive disorder (Chapter 10), not intellectual disability, however low his scores. The criterion can be met by history: a woman first assessed at 30 can receive the diagnosis if school reports and her family's account show that the difficulties were there in childhood. Push a case through all three. Ishaan is nine and in Class 4 of a Kannada-medium government school near Mandya. His teacher sends him to the district hospital because he "cannot read even simple words and does not follow anything". His mother says he walked at about 18 months, spoke his first words at two and a half, and was dry at night only at five. He can bathe and dress himself, though he needs reminding; he cannot tell the time; he cannot be sent to the shop because he cannot count the change; he plays happily with children of six; and last month he handed over his new bicycle to an older boy who asked for it. On an individually administered Indian adaptation of the Wechsler scale, given in Kannada, his full-scale IQ is 62, with no wild scatter between subtests, and the psychologist's observations agree. On the Vineland Social Maturity Scale, completed with his mother and his teacher, his social quotient is 58. Criterion A is met: a valid, culturally appropriate score in the right zone, confirmed clinically. Criterion B is met: deficits in the conceptual domain (reading, numbers, money, time), the social domain (gullibility, play with younger children) and the practical domain (shopping, needing reminders), at home and at school, needing ongoing support. Criterion C is met: the delays go back to infancy. The diagnosis is intellectual developmental disorder; Section 3.2.3 explains how its severity is graded. Exam trap "The cardinal DSM-IV-TR criterion for mental retardation was an IQ how far below the mean?" Two standard deviations , about 70 on a test with mean 100 and SD 15 (RML 2021). One SD (about 85) was Heber's old 1959 line and now marks the upper edge of borderline intellectual functioning; four SD (about 40) is the boundary between moderate and severe disability in ICD-11; seven SD would be a score of minus 5, which no test can produce. DSM-5-TR keeps the two-SD idea but adds a margin of about 5 points, giving 65 to 75 , and it moves the number out of the criterion into the text. Now take a different young man. Joel is 19 and lives in Kochi. He scraped through school with poor marks and failed his Class 12 examinations twice. On the WAIS-IV, given in Malayalam and English by a careful psychologist, his full-scale IQ is 70. But Joel works in his uncle's bakery, handles the cash counter without mistakes, takes two buses to get there, uses his phone for payments, plays football with his friends and helps look after his grandmother. Does he have intellectual disability? No. His score falls inside the 65 to 75 zone, so criterion A on its own could be satisfied, but criterion B is not: he meets the standards of independence and responsibility expected of a young man of his age and community without ongoing support. A score is not a diagnosis. Exam trap "On the WAIS-IV, an FSIQ of 70 typically corresponds to which classification?" The keyed answer is "borderline intellectual functioning; intellectual disability requires deficits in adaptive functioning" (MET Mock 2), and its point is right : an FSIQ near 70 without adaptive deficits is not intellectual disability. But keep three things apart. (1) On the WAIS-IV, 70 falls in the publisher's band labelled "borderline", 70 to 79 (Book 1, Section 9.3.4). (2) DSM-IV-TR's borderline intellectual functioning was IQ 71 to 84, so 70 is technically just below it. (3) A score of 70 lies inside DSM-5-TR's 65 to 75 zone, so it does not rule out intellectual disability; what decides is criterion B. Reject "average" because the WAIS-IV average band is 90 to 109, two SD higher; "mild intellectual disability solely on score" because no score diagnoses alone; and "profound" because profound lies below 20. How severe: from IQ bands to adaptive functioning Once the diagnosis is made, the next question a parent asks is "how bad is it?", and the honest answer has changed with the manuals. Book 1 (Section 9.8.1, Table 9.13) lists the four traditional levels, mild, moderate, severe and profound, with the IQ ranges that defined them in DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 and the share of cases at each. Here the task is to go further: to see what each level meant in a person's life, why DSM-5 stopped defining the levels by IQ, and what it put in their place. Under the old system the level was read off the IQ. ICD-10, which is still the classification behind most Indian hospital records, gives a band for each and adds a mental age : the age at which an average child performs as the adult does on the tests. An adult with mild disability, in ICD-10's words, has an IQ of about 50 to 69 and a mental age "from 9 to under 12 years"; moderate disability means an IQ of 35 to 49 and an adult mental age of 6 to under 9; severe, 20 to 34 and 3 to under 6; profound, below 20 and below 3. The mental age is a description of test performance, not of the person: a 30-year-old woman with moderate disability is not a child of seven, and she has thirty years of experience, interests, relationships and a body that a seven-year-old does not. Special education attached its own labels to the levels. Children with mild disability were called educable , because they could be expected to learn basic academic skills, and children with moderate disability trainable , because the expectation was self-care and simple work skills rather than academics; older texts called the severe and profound levels "custodial" or "dependent". All of these labels are now obsolete, but they survive in exam questions. What did the levels mean for an adult? DSM-IV-TR's descriptions, summarised in Table 3.6, are the source of most textbook answers. People with mild disability, about 85 percent of all cases, usually look and talk much like other children in the preschool years and are often identified only when school begins to demand reading and arithmetic; by their late teens they can learn academic skills up to roughly the sixth-grade level, and as adults most achieve the social and vocational skills needed to support themselves, with some guidance at times of stress. People with moderate disability, about 10 percent, show obvious delays in the preschool years; they rarely progress beyond the second-grade level in academic subjects, but with teaching they learn to look after their own personal care, travel familiar routes and do unskilled or semi-skilled work under supervision, and most live in the community in supervised or family settings. That is what "partial independence in activities of daily living" means. People with severe disability, about 3 to 4 percent, acquire little or no communicative speech in early childhood; during the school years they may learn to talk, to look after themselves in elementary ways and to recognise a few "survival" words such as their name or a sign on a door, and as adults they can do simple tasks under close supervision. People with profound disability, about 1 to 2 percent, usually have an identifiable neurological or genetic condition, often with sensory and motor impairments, and they need help and supervision in every part of daily life. Its severity levels "are defined on the basis of adaptive functioning, and not IQ scores, because it is adaptive functioning that determines the level of supports required. Moreover, IQ measures are less valid in the lower end of the IQ range." Both reasons repay a moment's thought. The first is practical: a family, a school or a disability board wants to know what help a person needs, and two people with the same IQ can need very different amounts. Imagine two young men who both score 45. One travels to a sheltered workshop by bus, earns a little money packing paper bags and goes to the temple with his friends on Sundays; the other has frequent seizures, does not sleep and strikes out when frustrated, and cannot be left alone. By IQ they are identical; by adaptive functioning they are not, and it is the second description that tells you what to do. The second reason is technical. The commonly used intelligence scales have a floor: their lowest possible scores are around 40, and below that they cannot discriminate at all, so the distinction between severe and profound disability cannot honestly be made with a test score. ICD-11 says so explicitly: severe and profound disorders of intellectual development "are differentiated exclusively on the basis of adaptive behaviour", because standardised tests cannot reliably or validly distinguish among people functioning below about the 0.003rd percentile. DSM-5-TR's severity table describes each level in each of the three domains, and Table 3.7 condenses it. Notice how the descriptions are written. There are no numbers; instead there are pictures of everyday life, from the mildly affected adult who works in a job that does not demand conceptual skills but needs help with banking, health decisions and raising a family, to the profoundly affected person who understands simple gestures, enjoys music and the company of familiar people, and depends on others for every aspect of physical care. That is the picture of the mild level in every domain, so his diagnosis is intellectual developmental disorder, mild. Notice that the level was chosen from his adaptive functioning; his IQ of 62 happens to agree, but it was not the deciding fact. Two other systems grade severity differently, and both are examined. The AAIDD, as DSM-5-TR puts it, uses a classification that is "multidimensional rather than categorical". Instead of a severity label it describes a profile of the supports a person needs, and it grades their intensity as intermittent, limited, extensive or pervasive (Book 2, Section 10.5.8, explains each). So where DSM-5-TR might say "moderate intellectual disability", the AAIDD would describe "a person with intellectual disability who needs limited supports in home living, health and safety, and academic skills". ICD-11, for its part, keeps the four levels and defines them in standard deviations and percentiles: mild disorder of intellectual development lies about two to three SD below the mean (roughly the 0.1st to 2.3rd percentile), moderate about three to four SD below (roughly the 0.003rd to 0.1st percentile), and severe and profound four or more SD below, with severe and profound separated, as you have seen, by adaptive behaviour alone. Because standardised tests are simply not available in much of the world, ICD-11's diagnostic guidelines also supply tables of behavioural indicators, descriptions of what people at each level typically can and cannot do at different ages, which clinicians use when testing is impossible. Exam trap "Individuals who are moderately retarded..." The answer is that they can achieve partial independence in activities of daily living (Amity 2023). "Can become self-supporting adults with appropriate training" describes the mild level ("educable"). "Are generally institutionalised" is wrong for every level today: most people with intellectual disability, including most with severe disability, live with their families or in community settings. "Are usually diagnosed in infancy" fits the severe and profound levels, whose motor, language and social delays show in the first two years (DSM-5-TR); moderate disability usually becomes obvious in the preschool years, and mild disability often only at school. Remember too that in DSM-5 severity is set by adaptive functioning, while the IQ bands are ICD-10's and DSM-IV-TR's. Too young, too hard to test, or not quite: global developmental delay, unspecified intellectual developmental disorder and borderline intellectual functioning The three criteria assume that you can measure intelligence and adaptive behaviour. Sometimes you cannot, either because the child is too young for the tests to mean much, or because a disability gets in the way of testing. And sometimes the measurements come out just above the line. DSM-5-TR has a label for each situation, and examiners love to ask which is which. Aditi is three and lives in Bhopal. She sat alone at 11 months and walked at 26 months; she says "ma" and "pa" but no other words; she does not point at things she wants; she cannot stack three blocks or feed herself with a spoon; and she plays with toys mostly by mouthing and banging them. Her hearing and thyroid tests are normal. On a developmental schedule her developmental quotient (DQ) is about 50 in every area. Does she have intellectual disability? Perhaps, but nobody can yet say so honestly, or say how severe it is. Intelligence tests for children of her age measure mainly sensory, motor and early language skills, and scores in the first years of life predict later IQ only loosely; children who are delayed at three because of prematurity, illness, deprivation or a hearing problem may catch up, while others will turn out to have autism, a language disorder or cerebral palsy rather than, or as well as, intellectual disability. So the clinician gives a provisional label: global developmental delay. The label global developmental delay (F88) is reserved, in DSM-5-TR's words, for individuals under the age of 5 years "when the clinical severity level cannot be reliably assessed during early childhood". It is diagnosed when a child fails to meet expected developmental milestones in several areas of intellectual functioning and cannot undergo systematic assessment of intellectual functioning, including children who are simply too young for standardised testing, and it "requires reassessment after a period of time". The label is a promise to look again, not a verdict. DSM-5-TR adds, carefully, that some children under 5 whose presentation will eventually meet the criteria for intellectual developmental disorder have deficits that meet the criteria for global developmental delay; it does not say all, or even most. It also notes that because early and continuing intervention can improve functioning, it is common practice to delay the diagnosis of intellectual developmental disorder in infants and young children until a course of intervention has been tried. Aditi will be investigated for a cause (Section 3.3), given early stimulation through the district early intervention centre with her mother as her first teacher, and reassessed when she is old enough for standardised testing, at about six. In India the same logic runs through disability certification: a child under five is certified as having global developmental delay rather than intellectual disability (Book 2, Section 9.9.8). The second label is for the opposite problem: a child old enough to test whom no available test can reach. The category of unspecified intellectual developmental disorder (F79) is reserved for individuals over the age of 5 years when assessing the degree of disability "by means of locally available procedures" is difficult or impossible because of associated sensory or physical impairments (blindness, prelingual deafness), locomotor disability, severe problem behaviour or a co-occurring mental disorder. Think of a twelve-year-old with severe cerebral palsy, no speech and poor vision, who cannot hold a pencil or point reliably to a picture. A clinician can see from his history and his everyday functioning that his understanding is very limited, but no Wechsler scale, Binet scale or performance test can be given to him in a way that would mean anything. DSM-5-TR says the category should be used "only in exceptional circumstances", because the first duty is to find a way of assessing (non-verbal tests, tests in sign language, eye-gaze responses, adaptive measures from informants), and it, too, requires reassessment. Notice the phrase "locally available": a child in a district hospital without a psychologist trained in non-verbal testing may need this label when the same child in a national institute would not. ICD-11 merges the two situations into a single code, "disorder of intellectual development, provisional" (6A00.4), used when there is evidence of the disorder but the person is an infant or a child under the age of four , or when a valid assessment is not possible because of sensory or physical impairments, motor or communication impairments, severe problem behaviour or a co-occurring disorder. So DSM-5-TR's line falls at five and ICD-11's at four. The third label is for people who are not quite inside the disorder, and borderline intellectual functioning is not a mental disorder at all. Section 1.8.7 explains its status: it is one of DSM-5-TR's "other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention", coded R41.83, used when a person's borderline intellectual level is itself the focus of attention or affects treatment or prognosis. DSM-IV-TR defined it by an IQ of 71 to 84; DSM-5 dropped the number and asks instead for a careful assessment of intellectual and adaptive functioning and the gap between them. In clinical practice in India the person with borderline intellectual functioning is very often the child whom schools call the slow learner : a boy or girl with an IQ in the 70s or low 80s who is a little behind in every subject, not dramatically behind in one, who learns if taught slowly and repeatedly, and who falls further behind each year as the syllabus speeds up. Such a child does not have intellectual disability, because his adaptive functioning is broadly adequate, and he does not have a specific learning disorder either, because his difficulty is general rather than confined to reading, writing or arithmetic (Section 3.9.6 makes the comparison from the other side; Indian certification of a specific learning disability requires an IQ of 85 or more, Book 2, Section 9.9.8). He falls between the categories, and he needs what neither label supplies: patient teaching at his own pace, a realistic choice of subjects and courses, and protection from being called lazy. The age matters because it stands for testability: below five, severity cannot be reliably measured. The distractors name things both conditions can have: social deficits, language delay and motor impairment all occur in global developmental delay and in intellectual disability, so none of them separates the two. Do not confuse DSM-5-TR's under 5 with ICD-11's under 4 for the provisional category. Exam trap "In which situation would a diagnosis of global developmental delay be inappropriate ?" Answer: the 7-year-old boy with a full-scale IQ of 65 and severe impairment in adaptive functioning (RML 2022). He is over five, he has been tested validly, his score lies in the 65 to 75 zone and his adaptive deficits are established: he meets criteria A, B and C, so the diagnosis is intellectual developmental disorder, and a provisional label would be wrong. Each of the other options describes a situation in which a young child's picture is incomplete, which is exactly what global developmental delay is for: a child too young to show the full picture or to complete the assessments (the textbook case); a child whose test scores point to intellectual disability but whose adaptive skills have not yet been established; and a child whose adaptive functioning points to it but whose cognitive level has not been measured with standardised instruments. In each, the clinician holds back the full diagnosis until reassessment. Who has intellectual disability, and what becomes of them How common is intellectual disability? DSM-5-TR gives an overall figure of about 10 per 1,000 , that is, about 1 percent of the population, but it varies with a country's level of development: about 16 per 1,000 in middle-income countries and about 9 per 1,000 in high-income ones. That difference is itself a clue to the causes. Many causes of intellectual disability are preventable (iodine deficiency, birth asphyxia, infections, malnutrition, lead), and they weigh most heavily where health care is weakest, which is why Section 3.3 spends so long on prevention. DSM-5-TR makes the same point with a striking comparison from Western Australia, where the prevalence among Aboriginal children was 39 per 1,000 against 16 per 1,000 among the more affluent non-Aboriginal children, and it attributes such differences to environmental risks, such as perinatal injury and chronic social deprivation, that travel with poverty and poor access to care. Within the United States, by contrast, prevalence does not vary significantly between ethnoracial groups. Prevalence is also higher in young people than in adults. Part of the reason is that the severe forms shorten life, but a larger part is that mild disability is often most visible at school. A girl who cannot keep up with the syllabus stands out in Class 5; at 25, cooking, caring for children or working on a family farm, she may need some help with money and paperwork but never come near a clinic again. Indian counts show the other side of the problem, which is under-recognition. The Census of 2011 recorded only about 15 lakh people with "mental retardation" among the roughly 2.68 crore people it counted with any disability, far fewer than a prevalence of 1 percent would predict in a country of more than a hundred crore. Census figures depend on families reporting a disability to an enumerator, and DSM-5-TR notes that where intellectual disability is explained as a punishment for the parents' wrongdoing or as a supernatural affliction, shame leads to under-reporting. The best Indian survey of children, the INCLEN study, is described in Section 3.1.6. More males than females are diagnosed, at both the mild level (on average about 1.6 to 1) and the severe level (about 1.2 to 1), although the ratios vary widely between studies. DSM-5-TR offers three possible reasons: genes on the X chromosome (a boy has only one X, so a faulty X-linked gene such as the one behind fragile X syndrome is not masked by a second copy, Section 3.3.3), sex differences in other genetic factors such as particular copy number variants, and a general male vulnerability to brain injury. What is the course? Onset is in the developmental period, but the age and the features at onset depend on the cause and the severity. In the more severe forms, delayed motor, language and social milestones can usually be seen in the first two years; mild disability may not be recognised until school age, when academic learning becomes difficult. When the cause is a genetic syndrome there may be a characteristic appearance, as in Down syndrome, and sometimes a characteristic pattern of behaviour (Section 3.3.1). When the cause is acquired, as after meningitis, encephalitis or a head injury in childhood, the onset may be abrupt, and if the child has lost skills he once had, both intellectual developmental disorder and a neurocognitive disorder may be diagnosed. The disorder is generally non-progressive : the brain does not keep deteriorating. There are exceptions among the genetic conditions. In Rett syndrome (Section 3.5.2) there are periods of worsening followed by stabilisation; in others, such as Sanfilippo syndrome (Section 3.3.4) and Down syndrome, intellectual functioning worsens progressively in varying degrees. In Down syndrome the decline often represents a neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease developing in adult life (Section 3.3.2), and then both diagnoses are given. The disorder is generally lifelong, although its severity level may change over time, and the course is shaped by medical and genetic conditions and by co-occurring problems such as hearing or visual impairment and epilepsy. Here DSM-5-TR strikes a hopeful note. Early and continuing intervention can improve adaptive functioning through childhood and adulthood, and in some cases it improves intellectual functioning so much that the diagnosis no longer fits, which is one more reason for delaying the diagnosis in very young children. For older children and adults the manual draws a careful distinction. If a person's improved adaptive skills reflect stable, generalised new learning, the diagnosis may no longer be appropriate; if the improvement depends on supports and interventions continuing, the diagnosis still stands. A young man who manages his job only because a job coach visits every morning still has intellectual disability; the coach is part of the reason he is doing well. Several features of adult life deserve a clinician's attention. People with intellectual disability have more physical health problems than the general population, obesity among them, and many cannot put into words what they feel, so illnesses go undiagnosed and untreated. Because they are less aware of risk and danger, their rates of accidental injury are raised. A naive trust in others and a tendency to be easily led, called gullibility , is common, and together with a poor sense of risk it exposes them to exploitation, fraud, physical and sexual abuse, unintended involvement in crime and false confessions. These features matter in courts; DSM-5-TR mentions the American "Atkins-type hearings" that follow the Supreme Court's ruling in Atkins v. Virginia (2002) that people with intellectual disability may not be executed. People with intellectual disability can also be distressed by their own limitations, and they are at risk of suicide. The risk is associated with a co-occurring mental disorder, with higher intellectual and adaptive functioning (probably because such people understand their situation and its losses more fully) and with recent stressful events, and because a co-occurring mental disorder may show itself in unusual ways, any change in a person's behaviour should prompt a question about suicidal thoughts. Remember Prevalence about 1 percent (10 per 1,000; 16 in middle-income and 9 in high-income countries); more males (1.6 to 1 mild, 1.2 to 1 severe); severe forms show in the first two years, mild forms at school; generally non-progressive and lifelong, with Rett syndrome, Sanfilippo syndrome and Down syndrome as the exceptions that can worsen; suicide risk is linked to co-occurring mental disorder, recent stressors and, perhaps surprisingly, higher intellectual and adaptive functioning. Co-occurring disorders and the differential diagnosis People with intellectual disability have, on average, more of almost everything else. DSM-5-TR estimates that some co-occurring conditions, mental disorders, cerebral palsy and epilepsy among them, are three to four times commoner than in the general population. The most frequent co-occurring mental and neurodevelopmental disorders it lists are attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder; depressive and bipolar disorders; anxiety disorders; autism spectrum disorder; stereotypic movement disorder, with or without self-injury (Section 3.10.2); impulse-control disorders; and major neurocognitive disorder. Major depressive disorder can occur at every level of severity, even in people who cannot say that they are sad; it then shows itself in withdrawal, loss of interest in favourite activities, tearfulness, poor sleep, weight loss or new aggression. In DSM-5-TR's words, self-injurious behaviour , such as head banging, biting the hands or picking at the skin, "requires prompt diagnostic attention" and may warrant a separate diagnosis of stereotypic movement disorder. People with more severe disability may also show aggression and disruptive behaviour, including harm to others and to property, and it is often the behaviour, rather than the disability, that brings them to a psychiatrist. Recognising these disorders is hard for two reasons. The first is communication: a person with limited speech cannot describe a low mood, a voice, a fear or a toothache, so DSM-5-TR insists that knowledgeable informants are essential for identifying irritability, mood swings, aggression, eating problems and sleep problems. The second is a habit of mind in the people around them. In 1982 Steven Reiss and his colleagues called it diagnostic overshadowing : once a person carries the label of intellectual disability, every new symptom tends to be put down to the disability itself (Book 2, Section 10.5.8). Saanvi is 24, has moderate intellectual disability and lives with her parents in Pune. Over a fortnight she begins to scream at night, to slap the side of her face and to refuse her food. Her family, and at first the doctor at the local clinic, say that "it is her condition; she gets like this". Only when her sister notices a swelling of her cheek is she taken to a dentist, who finds an abscess at the root of a molar. Once the tooth is treated, the screaming and slapping stop. A sudden change in behaviour in a person with intellectual disability is a message, and the clinician's job is to work out what it says: pain, physical illness, side effects of a medicine, abuse, a change of carer or routine, depression, or psychosis. The differential diagnosis begins with a rule that sounds obvious but is often broken: intellectual developmental disorder should be diagnosed whenever criteria A, B and C are met, and it "should not be assumed because of a particular genetic or medical condition". A child with Down syndrome or cerebral palsy must still be assessed; many children with cerebral palsy, for instance, have normal intelligence, and some children with Down syndrome, especially the mosaic form (Section 3.3.2), score well above the usual range. When a genetic syndrome is present it is recorded as a separate, concurrent diagnosis. The main look-alikes then follow, and Table 3.9 sums them up. Major and mild neurocognitive disorders are losses of cognitive functioning; intellectual disability is a failure to develop it (Esquirol's rich man made poor, versus the man who was always poor). The two can coexist: a man with Down syndrome who develops Alzheimer's disease, or a woman with intellectual disability who loses further capacity after a head injury, receives both diagnoses. When a brain injury in childhood leaves a child with stable, non-progressive deficits that meet the criteria, both diagnoses can again be used. Communication disorders and specific learning disorder are confined to one domain (language, speech, reading, writing or mathematics), with no general intellectual and adaptive deficit. A child who cannot read but reasons well, plays cricket strategically and runs errands competently is not intellectually disabled. If someone meets the full criteria for both, both are diagnosed (Sections 3.4 and 3.9). Autism spectrum disorder commonly co-occurs with intellectual disability, and testing a child with autism is difficult: his social and communication difficulties may stop him understanding or complying with test procedures, so a low score may underestimate what he can do. IQ in autism can be unstable in early childhood, and DSM-5-TR asks for reassessment across development (Sections 3.5 and 3.6). Borderline intellectual functioning lies above the intellectual criterion and lacks the degree of adaptive deficit the disorder requires (Section 3.2.4). Sensory impairment : a child with an undetected hearing loss or poor vision may seem slow, inattentive and unresponsive. Hearing and vision should be tested before any judgement about intelligence, and tests chosen to bypass the impaired sense. Severe deprivation and lack of schooling : a child who has been neglected, never taught, or kept out of school may perform at a low level that improves, sometimes dramatically, with care and teaching. The wild boy of Aveyron (the opening of this chapter) is the oldest case on record of the argument over whether a child's state was disability or deprivation; Section 3.3.6 describes deprivation as a cause in its own right. The wrong test : a child tested in a language he does not speak, or against norms from another culture, may score low for reasons that have nothing to do with ability (Section 3.2.2). Intellectual disability and a neurocognitive disorder can both be given (Down syndrome with Alzheimer's disease is the classic example). Intellectual disability, communication disorders and specific learning disorder are not mutually exclusive either. And "behaviour problems are part of her condition" is the error called diagnostic overshadowing (Reiss, 1982), not a diagnosis. Care, support and medicines There is no cure for intellectual disability, but there is a great deal of help, and almost all of it is educational and social rather than medical. Book 2 (Section 10.5.8) teaches the methods in full, so here they are only named, with what the evidence shows. The guiding idea since the 1960s has been normalisation, formulated by Bengt Nirje (1969) and spread by Wolf Wolfensberger (1972): people with intellectual disability should live lives as close as possible to everyone else's, in ordinary homes, schools and workplaces rather than institutions. The core clinical method is adaptive skills training: a skill such as brushing teeth or buying milk is broken down by task analysis, taught step by step by chaining, prompting and fading, and reinforced (Book 2, Sections 4.5.2 to 4.5.4), and challenging behaviour is reduced by first working out what the behaviour achieves for the person, through functional analysis, and then teaching a better way of achieving it, which is the basis of positive behaviour support (Book 2, Sections 2.8.2 and 4.6). Education has moved from special schools through integrated education to inclusive education, international policy since UNESCO's Salamanca Statement of 1994 and Indian law under the RPwD Act 2016, with an individualised education programme for each child. The evidence for this whole approach is consistent on three points. Even people with severe and profound disability can learn useful skills when teaching is systematic. Skills learned in a clinic often do not transfer by themselves, so they must be taught and practised in the real settings where they are needed. And early, sustained, family-centred intervention improves adaptive functioning, which is exactly what DSM-5-TR's account of the course would lead you to expect. Where do medicines fit? The first point is negative and must be made clearly, because families in India are often sold "brain tonics": no medicine improves intellectual functioning itself . The claim has been tested. Piracetam, a supposed cognitive enhancer that was widely given to children with Down syndrome, was tested by Lobaugh and colleagues in Toronto in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial published in 2001: four months of piracetam did not improve cognition or behaviour in children aged about 6 to 13, and seven children had stimulant side effects, among them aggressiveness, agitation, sexual arousal and poor sleep. The only "medical" treatments that prevent intellectual disability work on particular causes before the damage is done: a low-phenylalanine diet for phenylketonuria and thyroxine for congenital hypothyroidism, which Section 3.3.4 describes. The second point is that co-occurring mental and neurological disorders should be treated, and treated with the usual medicines: antidepressants for depression and anxiety (Section 5.7.2), stimulants for ADHD (Section 3.8), antiepileptic drugs for epilepsy, antipsychotics for psychosis (Section 4.10). Three cautions apply. Doses usually start lower and rise more slowly, because people with brain damage are often more sensitive to side effects. Side effects must be watched for actively, because the person may not be able to report a dry mouth, constipation, stiffness, dizziness or a feeling of restlessness, and may show them only as a change in behaviour. And the diagnosis must be real: a medicine given for "depression" that is really toothache, or for "aggression" that is really fear of a new carer, treats nothing. The third point is the controversial one. Antipsychotic drugs, especially risperidone, are widely prescribed to people with intellectual disability who have no psychotic illness at all, to calm aggression, self-injury and other challenging behaviour . Risperidone has good evidence for reducing severe irritability in children with autism (Section 3.6.8), and that evidence is often stretched to cover adults with intellectual disability. The harms are well known: weight gain and metabolic changes leading towards diabetes, sedation, raised prolactin, and extrapyramidal side effects such as stiffness and restlessness (Section 4.10.5). The question is whether the benefits are real. Key study: Tyrer and colleagues' trial of antipsychotics for aggressive challenging behaviour (2008) Question. Do antipsychotics reduce aggression in adults with intellectual disability who are not psychotic? Method. Peter Tyrer and his colleagues randomly assigned 86 such adults, recruited from ten centres in England and Wales and one in Queensland, Australia, to flexible doses of haloperidol (a first-generation antipsychotic, 28 people), risperidone (a second-generation antipsychotic, 29) or placebo (29), and measured aggression, other problem behaviour, quality of life, side effects, carers' burden and costs at 4, 12 and 26 weeks. Result. Aggression fell substantially in all three groups by four weeks, and it fell most in the placebo group: a median fall of 79 percent from baseline with placebo, against 58 percent with risperidone and 65 percent with haloperidol. At no point did the placebo group do worse than either drug group. Conclusion. The authors wrote, in The Lancet , that antipsychotic drugs "should no longer be regarded as an acceptable routine treatment for aggressive challenging behaviour in people with intellectual disability". Criticism. The trial was small, so it could have missed a modest benefit of the drugs, and the large fall in every group shows how much of the improvement in such studies comes from attention, monitoring and the natural ups and downs of behaviour rather than from any drug. That is precisely the lesson: without a placebo group, every one of those falls would have been credited to the medicine. The same worry led to action. In 2015 Public Health England estimated that up to 35,000 adults with a learning disability (the British term for intellectual disability) were being prescribed an antipsychotic, an antidepressant or both without an appropriate clinical reason, and in 2016 NHS England launched STOMP, "stopping over-medication of people with a learning disability, autism or both", with a pledge signed by the professional bodies of psychiatrists, nurses, general practitioners, pharmacists and psychologists. The sensible practice that follows from all this is simple to state. Look first for a cause of the behaviour (pain, illness, a side effect, abuse, a change in routine, a mental disorder) and for what the behaviour achieves; use positive behaviour support and communication training; and if a drug is used for behaviour, use it for a limited time, at the lowest dose, with a clear target, and review it regularly with a plan to withdraw it. Clinical link What does a clinical psychologist actually do for a child like Ishaan in an Indian district early intervention centre or a NIEPID clinic? Assessment comes first: a developmental history, a culturally appropriate intelligence test and an adaptive behaviour scale with the parents and teacher, which together give the diagnosis, the level and, where the family wants it, the disability certificate (Book 2, Section 9.9.8). Then the parents need someone to explain, plainly and kindly, what the diagnosis means and what it does not mean, what is known about the cause (Section 3.3) and what the future may hold, and to listen to their grief, which often returns at each stage of life. Then comes the practical work: a home programme of early stimulation or skills training, advice to the school on placement and on an individualised education programme, screening for co-occurring problems such as epilepsy, hearing loss, ADHD and depression, and information about rights and schemes under the RPwD Act and the National Trust Act (Book 2, Sections 1.10.9 and 10.5.8). Families are also warned, gently, against costly "cures". 3.3 The Causes of Intellectual Disability: Genes, Pregnancy, Birth and Childhood Medium yield · 2 Qs "Why did this happen to our child?" is usually the parents' first question and sometimes their only one. It deserves a careful answer, for three reasons. A cause may be treatable or preventable in the next child; it may predict medical problems that should be looked for, such as heart disease in Down syndrome or obesity in Prader-Willi syndrome; and it may lift a burden of blame that parents, grandparents and neighbours have placed on the mother. Barlow and Durand remark that there are literally hundreds of known causes. This section first shows how they are sorted and how often one is found, then describes the genetic syndromes that every examiner asks about, the inborn errors of metabolism with phenylketonuria as the great success story, the damage done in the womb by alcohol, infections and iodine deficiency, and finally the injuries of birth and childhood, ending with what can be prevented. How causes are sorted The simplest way to sort causes is by when they act, and DSM-5-TR does exactly this. The prenatal causes act before birth: genetic syndromes, whether from a change in the sequence of one or more genes, a copy number variant (a stretch of chromosome deleted or duplicated) or a disorder of a whole chromosome; inborn errors of metabolism; malformations of the brain; maternal disease, including disease of the placenta; and environmental influences such as alcohol, other drugs, toxins and teratogens. The perinatal causes are events around labour and delivery that lead to neonatal encephalopathy , a damaged and malfunctioning brain in the newborn. The postnatal causes act after birth: injury from lack of oxygen and blood supply, traumatic brain injury, infections, demyelinating disorders, seizure disorders such as infantile spasms, severe and chronic social deprivation, and toxic and metabolic syndromes and poisonings such as lead and mercury.
