The case of Victor of Aveyron, revisited Go back to the boy who came out of the forest near Saint-Sernin-sur-Rance in January 1800, and put the questions of this chapter to him one at a time. Was he intellectually disabled, as Pinel judged? DSM-5-TR would ask for three things: a deficit in intellectual functions confirmed by individualised, standardised testing, deficits in adaptive functioning in the conceptual, social and practical domains, and onset in the developmental period (Section 3.2.2). Nobody could test Victor; the scale of Binet and Simon lay more than a century ahead, in 1905 (Section 3.1.2). And even a valid score would not have settled it, because a child who has been neglected or never taught may perform at a low level that improves, sometimes dramatically, with care and teaching (Section 3.2.6). Was he a normal child stunted by isolation, as Itard believed? The English and Romanian Adoptees study (Section 3.3.6) gave the answer Itard lacked: severe early deprivation can produce intellectual impairment that is largely reversible in a loving family, the earlier the better, but children deprived for longer kept a quasi-autistic pattern, disinhibited social behaviour and inattention into adult life. Or was he autistic, as Uta Frith suggested? Read the opening again with criterion B in mind. He rocked for long periods, a stereotyped movement (B1); he seemed hardly to feel the cold and ignored a pistol shot, yet turned at once to the crack of a walnut, the hypo- and hyperreactivity to sensory input that DSM-5 added as B4 (Section 3.5.4); and he paid little attention to people (criterion A, Section 3.5.3). But almost every feature of autism, taken alone, occurs in some other condition, rocking among them as a result of neglect (Section 3.5.7), and criterion C asks about the early developmental period, which nobody saw. That is why the question stays open, as Section 3.5.1 concludes. What Victor's case lacked was not a clever examiner but the tools this chapter describes: a developmental history from the pregnancy onwards, several informants who knew the child in different settings (Section 3.1.4), and individually administered, standardised measures of intelligence and adaptive behaviour (Section 3.2.2). What it did not lack was consequence. Itard's patient, daily teaching passed to his pupil Édouard Seguin, who turned it into the first systematic method for educating children with intellectual disability and was among the founders, in 1876, of the association that became the AAIDD (Section 3.2.1); it was Seguin, not Pinel, who showed that such children could be taught. And Itard returned to this chapter by another door: in 1825 he described the Marquise de Dampierre, whose movements, cries and obscene words made her the first of Gilles de la Tourette's nine patients in 1885 (Section 3.10.5). The doctor who could not teach a wild boy to speak left his mark on two of this chapter's disorders: the education of children with intellectual disability and the first description of Tourette's disorder. Chapter summary 3.1 Disorders of a Developing Brain: Defining and Classifying the Neurodevelopmental Disorders. The neurodevelopmental disorders begin in the developmental period, often before school, and impair personal, social, academic or occupational functioning. They are dimensional, show delay or deviance, and frequently co-occur. They are not the neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia (Weinberger; Murray and Lewis, 1987) or the neurocognitive disorders, and not every childhood disorder belongs: ADHD does, while OCD, generalised anxiety disorder and borderline personality disorder do not. The categories grew from DSM-I's mental deficiency to DSM-5's neurodevelopmental chapter; ICD-10 spreads them over F70 to F79, F80 to F89 and F90 to F98. Because behaviour varies across contexts, children are assessed through several informants and a developmental history. The INCLEN survey (Arora, 2018) found a disorder in 9.2 percent of Indian children aged 2 to under 6 and 13.6 percent aged 6 to 9; the RPwD Act 2016 governs certification. 3.2 Intellectual Developmental Disorder: Definition, Criteria and Severity. Esquirol (1838) called idiocy a condition, not a disease, and the boundary has since moved: Heber (1959) added adaptive behaviour and drew the line one standard deviation below the mean, Grossman (1973) two. DSM-5-TR requires deficits in intellectual functions confirmed by clinical assessment and individualised, standardised testing (about two standard deviations below the mean, 65 to 75 with the margin), deficits in adaptive functioning in the conceptual, social and practical domains, and onset in the developmental period. ICD-10 and DSM-IV-TR graded severity by IQ (mild 50 to 69, "educable"; moderate 35 to 49, "trainable", with partial independence; severe 20 to 34; profound below 20); DSM-5 grades it by adaptive functioning. Global developmental delay is for children under 5, and borderline intellectual functioning is not a disorder. Prevalence is about 1 percent. No medicine improves intellect; in Tyrer's 2008 trial placebo matched antipsychotics. 3.3 The Causes of Intellectual Disability: Genes, Pregnancy, Birth and Childhood. Causes are sorted by when they act and, after Zigler (1967), into organic and cultural-familial groups, a division Reichenberg confirmed in 2016. Down syndrome (Down, 1866), usually trisomy 21 from nondisjunction, was traced to an extra chromosome by Gautier, Lejeune and Turpin in 1959 and brings early Alzheimer's disease. Fragile X syndrome, an expanded CGG repeat in FMR1, is the commonest inherited cause; Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes show genomic imprinting. In phenylketonuria (Følling, 1934) missing phenylalanine hydroxylase leaves phenylalanine unconverted to tyrosine; Bickel's diet and Guthrie's newborn test prevent the damage. Fetal alcohol syndrome (Jones and Smith, 1973) joins a small head, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip and short palpebral fissures. TORCH infections, iodine deficiency, birth asphyxia, meningitis, lead and severe deprivation, measured in the English and Romanian Adoptees study, complete the list. 3.4 Communication Disorders: Language, Speech, Fluency and Social Communication. Speech is the line, language the code and communication its social use; each communication disorder is a fault in one layer. Language disorder is a developmental deficit in vocabulary, sentence structure and discourse, receptive problems carrying the poorer outlook; Landau-Kleffner syndrome (1957) is language lost, not undeveloped. Speech sound disorder affects producing speech sounds. Childhood-onset fluency disorder, stuttering, begins by age 6 in 80 to 90 percent of cases; Wendell Johnson's diagnosogenic theory, tested in Mary Tudor's "Monster Study" (1939), blamed the listener, but stuttering is now seen as a disorder of speech timing and control with a strong genetic contribution. Social (pragmatic) communication disorder, new in DSM-5, is told from autism by the absence of restricted, repetitive behaviour. When a child does not speak, ask where the barrier lies (inherent mutism, selective mutism, autism, learning disorder), and test hearing first. 3.5 Autism Spectrum Disorder I: From Kanner to the Spectrum, and the Diagnosis. Bleuler coined autism in 1911 for a symptom of schizophrenia; Kanner described early infantile autism in eleven children in 1943, Asperger "autistic psychopathy" in 1944, and Sukhareva six similar boys in 1925. Wing and Gould's triad of impairments (1979) made autism a spectrum, while Bettelheim's refrigerator mother was discredited by Rimland, twin studies and studies of parents. DSM-III named infantile autism (1980), and DSM-5 merged autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder (Heller, 1908) and PDD-NOS into one spectrum, leaving out Rett syndrome (Rett, 1966; MECP2, 1999). Criterion A needs all three deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, criterion B two of four restricted, repetitive patterns, sensory reactivity among them; onset is early, and an IQ below 70 is not a criterion. Severity levels 1 to 3 are rated per domain. 3.6 Autism Spectrum Disorder II: Who, Why and What Helps. Recorded prevalence rose to about 1 in 31 American eight-year-olds (2022), mainly through broader criteria, diagnostic substitution (Shattuck, 2006) and recording changes (Hansen, 2015); the well-ascertained sex ratio is about 3 to 1. Intellectual disability and ADHD (28 percent; Lai, 2019) are the commonest companions, and language development is compromised more often in autism than in ADHD or specific learning disorder. Heritability is about 80 percent (Bai, 2019), after Folstein and Rutter's twins (1977); older parents and valproate add risk, while Wakefield's 1998 MMR claim was fraudulent and retracted, and Hviid's 657,461 Danish children showed no link. Theories include theory of mind (the Sally-Anne task of Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith, 1985), poor encoding of social cues, weak central coherence (Frith, 1989), executive dysfunction and the extreme male brain. Behavioural and educational treatment comes first; risperidone and aripiprazole treat severe irritability. 3.7 Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder I: History, Symptoms and Diagnosis. Crichton described a disease of attention in 1798, Hoffmann drew Fidgety Philip in 1845, and Still (1902) a "defect of moral control". Encephalitis lethargica, Bradley's Benzedrine, minimal brain damage and minimal brain dysfunction (1966) followed; DSM-II named the hyperkinetic reaction of childhood, Douglas (1972) moved the emphasis to attention, and DSM-III created attention deficit disorder. DSM-5-TR requires six or more of nine inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (five from age 17) for at least 6 months, several before age 12 (7 in DSM-IV), in two or more settings, with impairment. "Does not seem to listen when spoken to directly" is inattention; talking excessively is hyperactivity. The presentations are combined, predominantly inattentive and predominantly hyperactive/impulsive. ICD-10's hyperkinetic disorder (F90) needs both impaired attention and overactivity, and social withdrawal is not a feature. Oppositional defiant disorder, learning disorder and medical mimics are the main look-alikes. 3.8 Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder II: Course, Causes and Drug Treatment. DSM-5-TR puts ADHD at about 7.2 percent of children and 2.5 percent of adults, twice as common in boys, and the youngest in a class are diagnosed most (Morrow, 2012). Hyperactivity fades but inattention often persists: about 15 percent meet full criteria at 25, about 65 percent counting partial remission (Faraone, 2006), and mortality is about doubled (Dalsgaard, 2015). Heritability is about 74 percent; the catecholamine hypothesis points to dopamine and noradrenaline in frontostriatal circuits, and Shaw (2007) found cortical maturation about three years late. Low birth weight and prematurity are firm risks; sugar is not. Barkley's behavioural inhibition model (1997), Sonuga-Barke's dual pathway and Sergeant's cognitive-energetic model explain the psychology. Methylphenidate (Panizzon, 1944) and the amphetamines block dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake, methylphenidate first in children (Cortese, 2018); atomoxetine, clonidine and guanfacine are the non-stimulants. 3.9 Specific Learning Disorder: Dyslexia, Dysgraphia and Dyscalculia. Kussmaul (1877) named word blindness and Berlin (1887) dyslexia, both acquired; Hinshelwood and Pringle Morgan (1896) described the congenital form, Orton blamed incomplete cerebral dominance, and Kirk coined "learning disabilities" in 1963. DSM-5 merged the learning disorders into one diagnosis: difficulties lasting at least 6 months despite targeted intervention, skills well below age expectation, onset in the school years, and no better explanation by intellectual disability, sensory problems or inadequate teaching. Intelligence is in the normal range; the IQ-achievement discrepancy gave way to response to intervention. Specifiers name impairment in reading (dyslexia), written expression and mathematics (dyscalculia). Prevalence is 5 to 15 percent of schoolchildren. The phonological deficit theory, supported by Bradley and Bryant (1983) and Ramus (2003), explains most dyslexia. ADHD is not a learning disorder, and auditory processing disorder joins them only in educational usage. Treatment is teaching. 3.10 Motor Disorders: Developmental Coordination, Stereotypies, Tics and Tourette's Disorder. Developmental coordination disorder, or dyspraxia, is a developmental failure to acquire coordinated movement, in 5 to 8 percent of children, often with ADHD; it differs from Liepmann's acquired apraxia (1900), Freud's agnosia (1891) and anomia. Stereotypic movement disorder is driven, purposeless repetitive movement. A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic movement or vocalisation, usually preceded by a premonitory urge and briefly suppressible, unlike a seizure, dissociation or Parkinson's tremor. Tourette's disorder needs multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, not necessarily together, for more than 1 year, with onset before 18; provisional tic disorder lasts under a year. Itard described the first case (1825), Gilles de la Tourette nine patients (1885). Tics peak around 10 (Leckman, 1998), coprolalia is a minority symptom, and OCD and ADHD are common companions. A key differentiation between global developmental delay and intellectual disability is (JEMAS 2025) (a) Age of assessment (under 5 years for GDD, 5 years or over for ID). (b) Presence of social deficits. (c) Language delay alone. (d) Motor impairment. Answer: (a) Age of assessment (under 5 years for GDD, 5 years or over for ID). Global developmental delay is reserved for children under 5 whose severity cannot yet be reliably assessed; the age stands for testability (Section 3.2.4). Social deficits, language delay and motor impairment all occur in both conditions, so none of them separates the two. When diagnosing developmental disorders, multi-information assessment is recommended because (JEMAS 2025) (a) parents tend to over report problems. (b) teachers provide no relevant information. (c) symptoms may vary across contexts. (d) only clinical observation is not sufficient. Answer: (c) symptoms may vary across contexts. A child behaves differently at home, at school and in the clinic, so each informant sees a valid but partial picture, which is why ADHD needs symptoms in two or more settings (Section 3.1.4). Parents may under-report as easily as over-report, teachers are often the best judges of attention and learning, and the limits of clinic observation are a consequence of the real reason, not the reason itself. According to DSM-5, which of the following is required for a diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Delayed speech alone (b) Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction across multiple contexts (c) Intellectual disability only (d) Hyperactivity and impulsivity Answer: (b) Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction across multiple contexts. Criterion A requires persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, in all three of its areas, and criterion B adds restricted, repetitive behaviour (Section 3.5.3). Delayed speech alone is neither required nor sufficient, intellectual disability is a specifier, and hyperactivity and impulsivity belong to ADHD. The DSM-5 criteria for specific learning disorder include (JEMAS 2025) (a) Average intellectual functioning with persistent difficulties in academic skills (b) IQ below 50 (c) Only attention deficit (d) Motor coordination deficit only Answer: (a) Average intellectual functioning with persistent difficulties in academic skills. Specific learning disorder is a persistent difficulty in academic skills, lasting at least 6 months despite targeted help, in a person of otherwise normal intellectual functioning (Section 3.9.2). An IQ below 50 means at least moderate intellectual disability, attention deficit alone describes ADHD, and a motor coordination deficit alone describes developmental coordination disorder. Strictly, DSM-5-TR asks only for an IQ above about 70 (plus or minus 5), so "average" is the best option rather than an exact rule. Language development is compromised most commonly in (JEMAS 2025) (a) Attention Deficit-Hyperactivity Disorder. (b) Autism spectrum disorder. (c) Specific learning disability. (d) Childhood onset dissociation. Answer: (b) Autism spectrum disorder. Delayed or absent language is the commonest first concern in autism, it has its own specifier, and language disorder is one of its most frequent companions (Section 3.6.2). Some keys mark specific learning disability, but that disorder impairs written language and number, not the development of spoken language; the language delays of ADHD are not specific to it; and "childhood onset dissociation" is not a diagnostic category. In Phenylketonuria (PKU), the body fails to convert phenylalanine into which substance due to a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Urea (b) Tyrosine (c) Tryptophan (d) Histidine Answer: (b) Tyrosine. Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine into tyrosine, the first step towards L-dopa, dopamine and noradrenaline; in PKU, an autosomal recessive disorder described by Følling in 1934, phenylalanine builds up instead (Section 3.3.4). Urea is the end product of the body's disposal of nitrogen, tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin and histidine of histamine. Research evidence suggests that people with autism spectrum development show deficits in: (RML 2020) (a) Anger management (b) Encoding social cues (c) Deception (d) Memory retrieval Answer: (b) Encoding social cues. Eye-tracking and face-processing studies, such as Klin's 2002 study in which autistic viewers looked far less at the eyes, show that the first step of Crick and Dodge's social information-processing model, encoding the cues, is impaired (Section 3.6.7). Difficulty deceiving is a consequence of the theory of mind difficulty, not the deficit the research names; anger problems are not a core deficit, and memory retrieval is usually intact. The cardinal DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criterion for Mental Retardation is based primarily on an IQ score: (RML 2021) (a) Seven standard deviations below the mean. (b) One standard deviations below the mean. (c) Two standard deviations below the mean. (d) Four standard deviations below the mean Answer: (c) Two standard deviations below the mean. Two standard deviations below the mean is about 70 on a test with mean 100 and SD 15, and DSM-5-TR keeps the idea with a margin of about 5 points, giving 65 to 75 (Section 3.2.2). One SD (about 85) was Heber's old 1959 line, four SD (about 40) marks the boundary between moderate and severe disability in ICD-11, and seven SD would be a score no test can produce. Within attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, which of the following is NOT classified as a problem relating to hyperactivity/impulsivity? (RML 2021) (a) Experiences difficulties in playing quietly. (b) Rather than sitting still, squirms in seat and fidgets. (c) Talks excessively. (d) Doesn't appear to listen when being told something or spoken to Answer: (d) Doesn't appear to listen when being told something or spoken to. Not seeming to listen when spoken to directly is inattention item A1c (Section 3.7.2). Difficulty playing quietly, squirming and fidgeting, and talking excessively are all hyperactivity items; note that talking excessively counts as hyperactivity, not impulsivity. Maya's baby was born with a smaller than average head size, facial malformations, and an intellectual disability. It is likely that Maya _____ during her early pregnancy. (RML 2022) (a) drank too much caffeine (b) drank alcohol (c) smoked marijuana (d) ate fish with mercury in it Answer: (b) drank alcohol. A small head, a characteristic face (smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures) and intellectual disability make up fetal alcohol syndrome, named by Jones and Smith in 1973 (Section 3.3.5). Caffeine and cannabis produce no such malformation syndrome, and methylmercury from contaminated fish damages the fetal brain, as at Minamata, but does not produce the FAS face. In which of the following situations would a diagnosis of "global developmental delay" be inappropriate? (RML 2022) (a) The patient is a child who is too young to fully manifest specific symptoms or to complete requisite assessments. (b) The patient, a 7-year-old boy, has a full-scale IQ of 65 and severe impairment in adaptive functioning. (c) The patient's scores on psychometric tests suggest intellectual disability, but there is insufficient information about the patient's adaptive functional skills. (d) The patient's impaired adaptive functioning suggests intellectual developmental disorder, but there is insufficient information about the level of cognitive impairment measured by standardized instruments. Answer: (b) The patient, a 7-year-old boy, has a full-scale IQ of 65 and severe impairment in adaptive functioning. The 7-year-old is over 5, has been validly tested, scores inside the 65 to 75 zone and has established adaptive deficits, so he meets criteria A, B and C and the diagnosis is intellectual developmental disorder (Section 3.2.4). Each of the other options describes an incomplete picture in a young child (too young to test, adaptive skills not yet established, or cognitive level not yet measured), which is exactly what the provisional label is for. Which of the following best describes a common characteristic of dyslexia? (RML 2025) (a) Difficulty understanding spoken language. (b) Difficulty with reading and decoding words. (c) Difficulty with motor coordination. (d) Difficulty concentrating during lectures. Answer: (b) Difficulty with reading and decoding words. Dyslexia, the pattern DSM-5-TR names under impairment in reading, is inaccurate or slow word recognition, poor decoding and poor spelling, rooted in most cases in a phonological deficit (Sections 3.9.3 and 3.9.5). Difficulty understanding spoken language is language disorder, difficulty with motor coordination is developmental coordination disorder, and difficulty concentrating during lectures suggests ADHD. Which is NOT typically considered a learning difficulty? (RML 2025) (a) Dysgraphia (b) ADHD (c) Dyslexia (d) Auditory processing disorder Answer: (b) ADHD. ADHD harms learning and often co-occurs with a learning disorder, but it is a separate neurodevelopmental disorder of attention and self-control (Section 3.9.6). Dyslexia, dysgraphia and dyscalculia are learning difficulties, and auditory processing disorder is grouped with them in educational usage, although DSM-5-TR does not list it. Hyperkinetic syndrome is characterized by the following except: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Social Withdrawal (b) Over-activity (c) Distractibility (d) Short attention-span Answer: (a) Social Withdrawal. ICD-10's hyperkinetic disorder (F90) requires impaired attention and overactivity, shown by distractibility and a short attention span, and hyperkinetic children are socially disinhibited and intrusive, not withdrawn (Section 3.7.4). They may become isolated because other children reject them, but a child who withdraws points instead to depression, social anxiety disorder or autism. Infantile Autism was first described by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Leo Kanner (b) Cameron (c) Goldstein (d) Jasper Answer: (a) Leo Kanner. Leo Kanner described early infantile autism in eleven children in 1943 (Section 3.5.1). Norman Cameron is known for over-inclusive thinking, Kurt Goldstein for concrete thinking, and "Jasper" stands for Karl Jaspers, the founder of descriptive psychopathology. Which disorder is classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder? (IHBAS 2024) (a) OCD (b) ADHD (c) Borderline personality disorder (d) Generalized Anxiety Disorder Answer: (b) ADHD. ADHD sits in DSM-5-TR's neurodevelopmental chapter with intellectual disability, the communication disorders, autism, specific learning disorder and the motor disorders (Section 3.1.1). OCD belongs to the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, generalised anxiety disorder to the anxiety disorders and borderline personality disorder to the personality disorders. Which is NOT a core symptom to diagnose as autism in children as per DSM-5? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Communication skills (b) Unusual repetitive behavior (c) Social reciprocity (d) I.Q. is below 70 Answer: (d) I.Q. is below 70. Intellectual impairment is a specifier ("with or without accompanying intellectual impairment"), and many autistic people have average or high intelligence (Section 3.5.5). Communication and social reciprocity (criterion A) and unusual repetitive behaviour (criterion B) are the core. A condition characterised by the occurrence of sudden, rapid, purposeless involuntary movement in the body: (Amity 2023) (a) Dissociation (b) Tics (c) Parkinson's Disease (d) Seizures Answer: (b) Tics. A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic movement or vocalisation, usually preceded by a premonitory urge (Section 3.10.3). Seizures are abnormal electrical discharges that cannot be suppressed and often alter awareness, dissociation is a disruption of consciousness, memory or identity rather than a movement, and Parkinson's disease gives a rhythmic resting tremor with slowness and rigidity. Strictly, tics are semi-voluntary rather than fully involuntary. A neurological disorder characterised by impairments in motor performance and coordination is known as: (Amity 2023) (a) Dyspraxia (b) Apraxia (c) Agnosia (d) Anomia Answer: (a) Dyspraxia. Dyspraxia, that is, developmental coordination disorder, is a developmental failure to acquire coordinated movement (Section 3.10.1). Apraxia is the acquired loss of skilled, purposeful movement (Liepmann, 1900), agnosia an acquired failure of recognition (Freud's term, 1891) and anomia an acquired failure of naming. Individuals who are moderately retarded: (Amity 2023) (a) Can achieve partial independence in activities of daily living (b) Can become self-supporting adults with appropriate training (c) Are generally institutionalised (d) Are usually diagnosed in infancy Answer: (a) Can achieve partial independence in activities of daily living. Moderate disability (the old "trainable" level, IQ 35 to 49) allows partial independence in daily living with supervised or supported work (Section 3.2.3). Becoming self-supporting with training describes the mild ("educable") level; most people at every level now live with their families or in the community; and diagnosis in infancy fits the severe and profound levels. Infantile autism was first described by: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Hans Asperger (b) Leo Kanner (c) Eugen Bleuler (d) Kurt Schneider Answer: (b) Leo Kanner. Kanner's 1943 paper "Autistic disturbances of affective contact" first described the condition (Section 3.5.1). Bleuler only coined the word, in 1911, for a symptom of schizophrenia; Asperger described the verbally fluent form a year after Kanner, in 1944; and Schneider is known for the first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia. A child exhibits no eye contact, delayed language, and repetitive movements. These are characteristic of: (IHBAS 2025) (a) ADHD (b) Conduct disorder (c) Autism spectrum disorder (d) Specific learning disorder Answer: (c) Autism spectrum disorder. Absent eye contact and delayed language reflect the social communication deficit, and repetitive movements the restricted, repetitive behaviour: the two domains of autism (Section 3.5.4). ADHD is inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity, conduct disorder a repetitive pattern of violating others' rights and major social rules, and specific learning disorder a difficulty with reading, writing or mathematics; none of them requires both domains. Weightage. 79 of the 411 questions mapped in this book (19.2%) test this chapter, 34 of them from real past papers. 7 of its 10 sections are High yield. On 19 May 1930, in a hospital in Lansing, Michigan, a woman gave birth to four baby girls. They were identical quadruplets: all four had grown from a single fertilised egg that had divided and divided again, so they carried exactly the same genes. Births like that are extraordinarily rare, and this one made the newspapers. As small children the sisters took singing and dancing lessons and appeared together on stage in touring shows, four matching girls who delighted their audiences. Behind the public image the home was a very different place. Later accounts describe a family that was highly controlling and abusive, and parents who did not treat the four alike. One daughter, Hester, was treated as the problem child: her parents described her as a habitual masturbator, and she had more social problems than her sisters as she grew up. The illness came first to Hester, who had severe symptoms by the age of 18. The others broke down one after another in their early twenties, and all four had developed the illness by the age of 24; Myra, the last, was not hospitalised until about six years after Hester's illness had begun. All four were diagnosed with schizophrenia. From 1955 to 1958 a team at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) in the United States, led by David Rosenthal , studied them intensively: their histories, their family, their bodies and their minds. The results filled a book, The Genain Quadruplets (1963), edited by Rosenthal. To protect the family the researchers gave the sisters pseudonyms whose initials spell the name of the institute: Nora, Iris, Myra and Hester. The surname they invented, Genain, comes from Greek words meaning, roughly, "dire birth" or "dreadful gene". Decades later the psychologist Allan F. Mirsky and his colleagues estimated that the chance of identical quadruplets all developing schizophrenia was about one in 1.5 billion. What made the Genains famous was not that all four fell ill but how differently the same illness ran in four people who shared every gene. Hester was the most severely ill: she deteriorated and spent most of her adult life in hospital. Iris spent long, chronic periods in hospital, and her state ranged from severe catatonic withdrawal to spells of marginal adjustment when she was able to leave hospital. Nora was admitted again and again and managed only a marginal life outside. Myra, in contrast, was never readmitted after her first episode; she married and raised a family. When Mirsky's team retested the sisters at the age of 66, in a follow-up published in 2000, their performance on neuropsychological tests had stayed stable or even improved since they were first tested in their twenties. Hold on to that picture: identical genes, one disorder, four different lives. It tells you at once that genes load the dice for schizophrenia but do not decide everything, because even sisters raised in the same house had different experiences, beginning in the womb and continuing in the way their parents treated them. It also tells you something about the concept of schizophrenia itself. The first psychiatrist to define this illness believed that it usually ended in mental ruin, and called it a "dementia". The Genain sisters, like the patients who made later psychiatrists doubt him, show a far more varied disorder. This chapter follows that disorder from the name to the symptoms, the diagnosis, its relatives on the spectrum, its course, its causes and its treatment. Remember the Genain sisters; you will return to them at the end of the chapter. 4.1 From Dementia Praecox to Schizophrenia High yield · 17 Qs There is no blood test for schizophrenia, no brain scan that settles the diagnosis and no single symptom that every patient has. So where did the category come from, and why do the diagnostic manuals draw its boundaries where they do? The honest answer is that schizophrenia is a concept built by clinicians over about a hundred and fifty years. Each builder asked a different question. Emil Kraepelin asked what the illness does over time. Eugen Bleuler asked what its psychological core is. Kurt Schneider asked which symptoms a doctor can recognise reliably at a single interview. The authors of the modern manuals asked how to make two psychiatrists in different cities give the same diagnosis to the same patient. Their answers are layered inside today's criteria like the strata of a rock, and once you can see the layers, the criteria in Section 4.4 stop looking arbitrary. Figure 4.1 sets out the whole story; this section tells it. Era 1: describing the forms (1800s) 1810 Haslam describes James Tilly Matthews and his "Air Loom" 1852 Morel: démence précoce, an early loss of mind 1871 Hecker: hebephrenia, a disorder beginning in youth 1874 Kahlbaum: catatonia, "tension insanity" Era 2: one disease, or a group? (1893 to 1913) 1893 Kraepelin: dementia praecox (4th edition of his textbook) 1899 Kraepelin divides it from manic-depressive insanity 1908 Bleuler coins "schizophrenia" (Berlin lecture) 1911 Bleuler: the group of schizophrenias; the four As 1913 Jaspers: General Psychopathology; primary delusions Era 3: making the diagnosis reliable (1939 to today) 1939 Schneider: first-rank symptoms (English edition 1959) 1972 US-UK Diagnostic Project: the US concept far broader 1980 DSM-III: explicit criteria, 6 months, a narrow concept 1992 ICD-10: first-rank symptoms weighted; 1 month 2013 DSM-5: subtypes and the special weight of FRS dropped 2022 ICD-11 in force: specifiers replace the subtypes Figure 4.1 How the concept of schizophrenia was built. Notice the three eras: first the separate forms were described, then Kraepelin and Bleuler argued over what united them, and finally the twentieth century tried to make the diagnosis reliable, which narrowed it. Before the name: Haslam, Morel and démence précoce People who heard voices, believed strange things and withdrew from the world were described long before anyone gave the condition a name: Ayurvedic texts such as the Charaka Samhita describe unmada , madness, and Greek and Arab physicians wrote about mania and melancholia. The long history of how madness was explained, feared and confined, from the temple to the asylum, is told in Book 2, Section 1.2. For our story, two pieces of that history matter. In 1809 the English apothecary John Haslam (1764 to 1844) of Bethlem Hospital in London described, in Observations on Madness and Melancholy , young patients who changed from promising and vigorous to dull and withdrawn, and in 1810 he published a whole book, Illustrations of Madness , about a single patient, the tea merchant James Tilly Matthews . Matthews believed that a gang of villains hidden nearby worked a machine he called the "Air Loom", whose rays forced thoughts into his head, drew thoughts out of it and moved his body against his will. Keep that description in mind: more than a century later, Kurt Schneider would make exactly these experiences the centre of the diagnosis. At about the same time in Paris, Philippe Pinel (1745 to 1826) was describing similar patients. The first label came from France. Bénédict Augustin Morel (1809 to 1873), a physician who spent his career in French asylums, used the phrase démence précoce ("early" or "premature loss of mind") in passing in his clinical studies of 1852, and more often in his textbook of mental diseases of 1860. He used it for young people, previously bright and lively, who in their teens sank into apathy, lost their intellectual powers and never came back. Notice what Morel meant by it. Démence précoce was not a disease with its own causes and symptoms; it was a description of an end state, the mental ruin that normally came at the end of a long illness, arriving tragically early in life. Morel is remembered for a second, darker idea. In his Treatise on Degenerations (1857) he set out the degeneration theory : the belief that mental illness is the sign of a hereditary taint that grows worse with each generation, so that nervous parents have insane children, whose own children are idiots, until the family line ends in sterility. Degeneration theory was enormously influential in late nineteenth-century psychiatry. It encouraged doctors to look at the whole family and at the course of illness over time, which was useful, but it also bred deep therapeutic pessimism (what could anyone do against a curse of the blood?) and, later, it fed the eugenics movement. Keep both legacies in mind, the attention to course and the pessimism, because they flow directly into Kraepelin. Hecker, Kahlbaum and the clinical method The next step was taken in an asylum at Görlitz, in eastern Germany. Its director, Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum (1828 to 1899), was impatient with the way psychiatrists classified their patients. Grouping illnesses by what they looked like on the day of the examination was, he argued, futile: a patient might be excited one month, sad the next and stuporous the next, and a cross-sectional label would change each time. The proper unit was the whole clinical course : how the illness began, how it unfolded and how it ended. This "clinical method", classifying by course and outcome as well as by symptoms, is the most important idea in this subsection, because it is the method Kraepelin later used to build dementia praecox. Kahlbaum's younger colleague at Görlitz, Ewald Hecker (1843 to 1909), applied the method in 1871 to a group of patients whose illness began around puberty. He named the condition hebephrenia , after Hebe, the Greek goddess of youth. Hecker's patients were silly and giggling, with an emotional tone that did not fit the situation; they rambled, adopted odd mannerisms, behaved in a foolish, childish way and then, often quite quickly, sank into a lasting weak-mindedness. Three years later, in 1874, Kahlbaum published his own monograph, Die Katatonie oder das Spannungsirresein ("Catatonia, or tension insanity"). In catatonia the most striking disturbance is of movement and will: patients who hold strange postures for hours, who let a doctor mould their limbs like wax, who fall mute, resist every instruction or repeat words and phrases over and over, and who may suddenly burst into purposeless excitement. Kahlbaum saw catatonia as a brain disease that passed through stages (phases resembling melancholia and mania, then stupor and confusion) and that typically ended in dementia. Today hebephrenia survives as the hebephrenic subtype of ICD-10 (called the disorganised subtype in DSM-IV), and the individual catatonic signs are described in Section 4.2. Kahlbaum's belief that catatonia is a single disease, however, did not survive: catatonia is now understood as a syndrome that can accompany schizophrenia, mood disorders and many medical illnesses, and DSM-5-TR notes that most cases of catatonia occur in people with depressive or bipolar disorders, not schizophrenia (Section 4.5). Hecker and Kahlbaum also gave psychiatry several other words still in use, among them cyclothymia . Alongside these two forms, many psychiatrists described patients with chronic delusions of persecution or grandeur, the "paranoid" forms. Table 4.1 lists the pieces that were lying on the table, waiting for someone to fit them together. Table 4.1 The nineteenth-century pieces that Kraepelin assembled into dementia praecox. Form Described by The picture What became of it Démence précoce Morel, 1852 and 1860 Bright youngsters sinking early into lasting mental ruin Gave the concept its name and its pessimism Hebephrenia Hecker, 1871 Onset near puberty; silly, incongruous affect; rambling; rapid decline Hebephrenic (ICD-10) or disorganised (DSM-IV) subtype Catatonia Kahlbaum, 1874 Stupor, posturing, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, excitement Catatonic subtype; now a syndrome across disorders Paranoid forms Many authors Chronic delusions of persecution or grandeur Paranoid subtype, the commonest in ICD-10 Exam trap Match the person to the word: Morel , démence précoce (French, 1850s); Hecker , hebephrenia (1871); Kahlbaum , catatonia (1874); Kraepelin , dementia praecox (Latin, 1893 to 1899); Bleuler , schizophrenia (1908 to 1911). A favourite swap is to credit catatonia to Hecker or hebephrenia to Kahlbaum: Kahlbaum was the senior partner and described catatonia; Hecker, his younger colleague, described hebephrenia, and the name comes from Hebe, goddess of youth. Kraepelin: dementia praecox and the great divide The man who fitted the pieces together was Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926), the most influential psychiatrist of his age. Kraepelin had trained in experimental psychology with Wilhelm Wundt in Leipzig (you met Wundt's laboratory in Book 1), and he brought to psychiatry a scientist's taste for counting. As professor at Heidelberg from 1891 and at Munich from 1903, he kept a card for every patient admitted to his clinic. On it he recorded the symptoms at admission and then, often years later, what had become of the patient: recovered, relapsed, or sunk into a permanent defect. Periodically he went through the whole stack and sorted the cards, looking for groups of patients whose illnesses had ended in the same way. His conviction, taken from Kahlbaum, was that a true disease, a "natural disease entity", would reveal itself not in any single symptom but in a shared course and outcome. Like a botanist who classifies a plant by its whole life cycle rather than by the colour of one leaf, Kraepelin classified a psychosis by its whole history. He set out his results in the successive editions of his textbook, Psychiatrie , and the concept grew in steps. In the fourth edition (1893) he used the Latin term dementia praecox , "premature dementia", echoing Morel's French phrase, for one of a small group of "psychic degenerative processes", listed alongside catatonia and a paranoid dementia. In a lecture at Heidelberg in 1898 and in the sixth edition of the textbook (1899) the construction was complete. Hebephrenia, catatonia and the paranoid forms, which earlier authors had treated as separate diseases, now became three forms of a single illness, dementia praecox, because the cards showed that all three tended to begin in youth and to end in the same kind of mental weakening. And the whole territory of the major psychoses was divided into two great groups by their course: Dementia praecox began early, usually in adolescence or young adulthood, ran a chronic course, and ended in a lasting deterioration of personality and intellect, which Kraepelin called "mental weakness". Manic-depressive insanity came in episodes of mania, depression or mixtures of the two, with recovery between episodes and no lasting defect, however many episodes the patient had. It included what we now call bipolar disorder and recurrent major depression. This division is known as the Kraepelinian dichotomy , and Kraepelin's "two clinical types" are among the most examined facts in the whole history of psychiatry. Figure 4.2 shows the two courses he had in mind. Dementia praecox early onset, deteriorating course Manic-depressive insanity episodes, full recovery between them each episode leaves a defect; no return to the healthy level healthy level mania mania healthy depression full recovery between episodes time (years) time (years) Figure 4.2 The Kraepelinian dichotomy (schematic). The thin horizontal line marks the healthy level in both panels. In dementia praecox each episode leaves the person a little further below it; in manic-depressive insanity the swings into mania and depression can be severe, but the person returns to health between them. To feel the force of the idea, imagine two patients whom Kraepelin might have met in a modern Indian hospital. Arun was a quiet, studious boy from a village near Madurai. In the first year of his engineering course in Chennai, when he was 19, his marks fell; he stopped going to classes, stayed in his hostel room for days, and told his roommate that the lecturers were sending him messages through the ceiling fan. He was treated, improved a little and went home, but over the next four years he never returned to his old self. Each relapse left him a little flatter, a little more withdrawn and a little less able to look after himself. Vasanthi, now a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Coimbatore, had her first illness at 26: a few weeks of sleeplessness, ceaseless talk, lavish spending and the conviction that she had been chosen to reform every school in the state. Two years later she had a month-long depression in which she barely ate or spoke. Between and after these episodes she has been entirely herself, teaching, joking with colleagues and running her household. Kraepelin's cards would have placed Arun with dementia praecox and Vasanthi with manic-depressive insanity, and they would have done so on the course, not on any single symptom; both, after all, had held beliefs that were plainly delusional. Kraepelin believed that dementia praecox was a physical disease of the brain, and he speculated that it might be a kind of self-poisoning, a disturbance of the body's metabolism, perhaps connected with the sex glands because it so often began after puberty. He also kept two other conditions apart. Paranoia , in his sense, was a chronic, systematised delusion in a person whose thinking and personality otherwise stayed intact; it is the ancestor of today's delusional disorder (Section 4.5). In his later editions he added paraphrenia , for paranoid psychoses with delusions and hallucinations but little deterioration of the personality. Why both words turned out to be partly wrong. Kraepelin's name makes two claims, and both have weakened. "Praecox" claims that the illness begins early. It usually does, in the late teens and twenties, but by no means always: many people fall ill in their thirties or later, and women show a second peak of onset in midlife (Section 4.6). "Dementia" claims that the illness ends in mental ruin. Kraepelin's own data never fully supported this. In his own later editions he reported that a minority of patients recovered, and in 1920, near the end of his life, he conceded that the outcome was less uniformly grim than he had claimed in the 1890s and that the two great groups could not always be told apart. Modern follow-up studies show the whole range of outcomes, from full recovery to lasting disability (Section 4.6). Nor is the cognitive impairment of schizophrenia a dementia in the modern sense. It is real and it matters (Section 4.3), but much of it is present before the first episode and then stays fairly stable, rather than marching steadily downhill as it does in Alzheimer's disease (Chapter 10). The Genain sisters, whose test scores at 66 were no worse than in their twenties, are a vivid example. What survived. Yet Kraepelin's framework has outlived every objection. His insistence on course survives in DSM-5-TR's rule that six months of illness must pass before the word schizophrenia may be used (Section 4.4). His dichotomy survives in the structure of every modern manual, which places schizophrenia and its relatives in one chapter and the bipolar and depressive disorders in others (Chapter 5). And the awkward patients who straddled his line, with both full mood episodes and schizophrenic symptoms, eventually needed a category of their own, schizoaffective disorder (Section 4.5). One more piece of his legacy carries an irony worth knowing. It was Kraepelin, in the 1910 edition of his textbook, who gave the name "Alzheimer's disease" to the brain disease described by his Munich colleague Alois Alzheimer; yet dementia praecox has nothing to do with Alzheimer's disease. Exam trap Kraepelin's two clinical types were dementia praecox and manic-depressive insanity (manic-depressive illness), separated by course: deteriorating versus episodic with recovery. Not depression and anxiety, not schizophrenia and borderline personality disorder (the borderline concept came decades later), not obsessive-compulsive disorder and bipolar disorder. "Dementia praecox" ("premature dementia") is the ancestor of schizophrenia . It is not Alzheimer's disease, not frontotemporal dementia (Arnold Pick's disease) and not bipolar I disorder, whose ancestor is manic-depressive insanity. On dates, sources differ because the concept grew in steps: the term in the fourth edition (1893), the Heidelberg lecture (1898), the full split in the sixth edition (1899); some Indian notes give 1896, the fifth edition. If asked when Kraepelin separated the two psychoses, answer the sixth edition, 1899. Bleuler and the group of schizophrenias Kraepelin looked at his patients from the outside and across the years. The Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) looked at them from the inside. Before he became, in 1898, professor of psychiatry at the University of Zurich and director of its hospital, the Burghölzli (a post he held until 1927), Bleuler had spent years running the rural asylum at Rheinau, where he came to know his patients unusually well. He talked with them at length, and he was one of the first university psychiatrists to take Sigmund Freud's ideas seriously, hoping that psychoanalysis could make sense of what his patients said and did. Among his assistants at the Burghölzli was Carl Gustav Jung , whose book on the psychology of dementia praecox appeared in 1907. What Bleuler saw did not fit Kraepelin's name. Many of his patients had not fallen ill young, and many did not deteriorate: some improved and lived outside hospital for years, although Bleuler believed that nobody recovered so completely that no trace of the illness remained. If neither "early" nor "dementia" described the illness, what did? Bleuler gave his answer in a lecture in Berlin on 24 April 1908 and in his great monograph of 1911, Dementia Praecox oder Gruppe der Schizophrenien ( Dementia Praecox, or the Group of Schizophrenias ; English translation 1950). He proposed a new name, schizophrenia , from the Greek schizein , to split, and phren , mind; colleagues in Zurich had been using it since 1907. He also pointed out, with practical good sense, that a single word would give an adjective, "schizophrenic", which "dementia praecox" did not. The splitting he meant was a splitting of psychic functions : a loosening of the associative threads that normally bind thinking, feeling and will into one coordinated whole, so that thought goes one way, emotion another and action a third. A patient may describe his mother's death with a smile, or say that he longs to leave the hospital while making no move to go. Bleuler did not mean a split into two or more personalities. That condition, once called multiple personality, is dissociative identity disorder (Chapter 7), and confusing the two is the commonest error about schizophrenia in newspapers, films and everyday speech. Notice too the plural in Bleuler's title. He believed that schizophrenia was not one disease but a group of diseases sharing a common psychological picture, a view that the four different illnesses of the Genain sisters, and the research of Section 4.7, would support. Fundamental and accessory symptoms. Bleuler's most influential move was to rank the symptoms. Fundamental symptoms , he said, were present in every case and at every stage of the illness, though sometimes only faintly; they were what made a case schizophrenia. Accessory symptoms might or might not appear, came and went, and also occurred in other illnesses: hallucinations, delusions, catatonic signs, and acute states of confusion or excitement. This is the reverse of how most people (and many students) picture schizophrenia. The voices and the delusions, the most dramatic features, were to Bleuler secondary, because a fever, a poison or a brain disease could produce them too. The fundamental symptoms were subtler, and textbooks later compressed them into the famous four As (Table 4.2): Associations (loosening of associations). The links between one idea and the next are broken, so that the patient's talk drifts or jumps between ideas with no logical connection. Bleuler regarded this as the central disturbance from which the others followed; today it belongs to formal thought disorder (Section 4.2). Affect (blunted or incongruous affect). Emotional expression is flattened, or it does not fit what the patient is saying or experiencing: laughter while describing a tragedy, indifference to people and things that once mattered. Ambivalence. Opposite feelings, wishes or ideas are held at the same time towards the same object, without being resolved: loving and hating the same person at once, wanting to eat and refusing to eat, believing a statement and its opposite. Bleuler distinguished emotional ambivalence, ambivalence of the will (sometimes called ambitendency) and intellectual ambivalence. He coined the word itself, around 1910, and Sigmund Freud, who borrowed it, called it "Bleuler's happily chosen term". Autism. Withdrawal from shared reality into a private inner world, with thinking that follows wishes and fantasies rather than the logic of the outside world. Bleuler coined this word too. It does not mean the neurodevelopmental condition: Leo Kanner borrowed Bleuler's word in 1943 for the children he described, and autism spectrum disorder is an entirely different disorder (Chapter 3). By 23, Arun spent most of his days at home. Asked by the psychologist how he passed the time, he said: "I sit. The fan turns. Turning is the engine of time, and time is money, and money is in the bank, the river bank, where my grandfather used to fish." Each step follows from a sound or a passing meaning of the last word, not from any plan of what he wanted to say: that is loosening of associations. He smiled faintly as he mentioned that his grandfather had died the year before: incongruous affect. Asked whether he would like to visit his cousins at Pongal, he said, "Yes. No. I want to go, and I must not go, and I want to go," and then sat without moving: ambivalence. His mother said that he spent hours writing numbers in a notebook according to a system he would not explain and no longer seemed to notice whether anyone was in the room: autism in Bleuler's sense. Arun also heard voices, but to Bleuler that would have been an accessory symptom; the diagnosis rested on the four As. Bleuler drew a second, more theoretical distinction, between primary symptoms, the direct product of a disease process in the brain (above all the loosening of associations), and secondary symptoms, the person's psychological reactions to that underlying disturbance, which included much of the content of the delusions and hallucinations. It explains why Bleuler, unlike Kraepelin, believed that what a patient said could be understood and that human contact could help. A broader concept, and where it travelled. Bleuler's schizophrenia was broader than Kraepelin's dementia praecox in two ways. It did not require early onset or deterioration, and because its fundamental symptoms could be faint, it reached far into the mild end of the spectrum. To Kraepelin's hebephrenic, catatonic and paranoid forms Bleuler added a simple form, a slow drift into apathy and withdrawal without florid symptoms (described by Otto Diem in 1903); these four became the classical subtypes, and ICD-10's "simple schizophrenia" descends from it. He also wrote of latent schizophrenia in odd, eccentric people who never became psychotic, and he believed that the illness was far commoner than diagnosed because of these simple and latent forms. Latent schizophrenia is an ancestor of today's schizotypal disorder (Section 4.5 and Chapter 11). Bleuler's broad concept travelled especially well to the United States, where psychoanalysis and the "psychobiology" of the Swiss-born Adolf Meyer (1866 to 1950) dominated psychiatry. Meyer taught that mental disorders were reaction types , the reactions of the whole person to the stresses of his or her life history, rather than disease entities, and the first edition of the DSM (1952) accordingly spoke of "schizophrenic reactions". The consequence, as the last part of this section shows, was that by the 1960s American psychiatrists were calling schizophrenia a great deal that their British colleagues called something else. Bleuler's other legacies are just as visible today: his blunted affect and autistic withdrawal are the ancestors of the negative symptoms (Section 4.3), and his loosening of associations is the core of formal thought disorder (Section 4.2). Exam trap Bleuler's four As are loosening of Associations , blunted or incongruous Affect , Ambivalence and Autism . Auditory hallucinations are not one of them : hallucinations and delusions were Bleuler's accessory symptoms. The look-alike As are distractors: alogia, avolition, anhedonia and asociality are the later negative-symptom list associated with Nancy Andreasen (Section 4.3; her negative-symptom scale also rates attention); apathy, anxiety and anger are not Bleuler's; aphasia is a language disorder caused by brain damage, amnesia is memory loss, anosognosia is unawareness of one's own illness (Section 4.2), and audible thoughts are one of Schneider's first-rank symptoms. Ambivalence was coined by Eugen Bleuler , not Kraepelin and not Freud (who borrowed it). "Richmond Fromm" in one paper is a garbled name: Erich Fromm (1900 to 1980) was a social psychoanalyst, and Frieda Fromm-Reichmann (1889 to 1957) proposed the schizophrenogenic mother (Section 4.9). Ambivalence is Bleulerian, not a negative symptom. And schizophrenia means a split between mental functions, never a split personality. Clinical link Families in India often first meet the word schizophrenia through films and television, where it is used for a "split personality" or for someone who is violent and unpredictable. Both images frighten families and feed stigma. When explaining the diagnosis, it helps to say what Bleuler meant: the person's thinking, feelings and actions have fallen out of step with one another, rather like an orchestra whose players have lost the conductor, and the person has not turned into someone else. Jaspers: understanding, explaining and the primary delusion While Kraepelin counted and Bleuler interpreted, a young psychiatrist at Heidelberg asked a more basic question: how can a doctor know what a patient is actually experiencing? Karl Jaspers (1883 to 1969), who later left psychiatry to become one of the major philosophers of the twentieth century, published Allgemeine Psychopathologie ( General Psychopathology ) in 1913, at about the age of thirty. The book founded phenomenology in psychiatry: the careful description of a patient's experiences as the patient lives them, set down without theory, so that every clinician can recognise the same experience in the same way. Chapter 2 of this book and Book 2, Section 2.5 are built on his method. Jaspers distinguished two ways of knowing another mind. Understanding ( Verstehen ) is grasping, by empathy, how one mental state grows meaningfully out of another: a man who has been cheated becomes suspicious; a mother who has lost her child becomes sad and blames herself. Explaining ( Erklären ) is the natural scientist's way of tracing a mental state to causes outside meaning, such as a tumour or a toxin. Most of what mentally ill people experience can be understood, at least in part. Some of it cannot. A man glances at a row of parked cars and suddenly knows, with complete certainty and no reason he can give, that he has been chosen to save the world. Jaspers called a belief of this kind a primary delusion : a delusion that arises directly, as if out of nowhere, and cannot be traced back to any mood, experience or earlier belief. A secondary delusion , by contrast, is understandable in the light of something else, such as the guilt-laden beliefs of a severely depressed woman, or the persecutory explanation a man builds to account for the voices he hears. For Jaspers this un-understandability marked a process : something new breaking into a person's life and changing it, as opposed to a development of the personality that can be followed step by step. The primary delusion was, for him, close to the heart of schizophrenia. Jaspers also set out the classic marks of a delusion (the extraordinary conviction with which it is held, its imperviousness to argument and experience, and the falsity or impossibility of its content) and the forms that primary delusions take (delusional mood, delusional perception, delusional intuition and delusional memory); these are taught in Section 4.2. What matters for this history is his principle that a symptom is diagnosed by its form , the way it is experienced, rather than by its content. The belief "my neighbours are poisoning me" can be an understandable suspicion in a lonely, quarrelsome old man or a primary delusion in a young man who "knew" it the moment he saw a red flower in a pot; what decides is how the belief arose and how it is held. That principle passed directly to Jaspers's younger Heidelberg colleague, Kurt Schneider. Schneider's first-rank symptoms Kurt Schneider (1887 to 1967) was a German psychiatrist trained in the phenomenological tradition, and with Jaspers he is counted among the founders of the Heidelberg school. From 1931 he directed the clinical work of the research institute in Munich that Kraepelin had founded, and after the Second World War he became professor and dean at Heidelberg. Schneider's problem was a practical one. Kraepelin's criterion, the course, could be known only in hindsight, years after the doctor had to decide what to do. Bleuler's fundamental symptoms were subtle: one psychiatrist's "loosening of associations" or "flattened affect" was another's shyness, eccentricity or poor schooling, so diagnoses built on them varied from doctor to doctor. Schneider wanted a short list of experiences that a clinician could identify with reasonable confidence at a single interview and that, when present in a person with no physical brain disease, would point strongly to schizophrenia. He made no claim that these symptoms explained the illness; he valued them only for diagnosis. He first published the list in 1939. It became known worldwide through his book Klinische Psychopathologie (published under that title from 1950) and its English translation, Clinical Psychopathology (1959). Schneider called them first-rank symptoms (FRS). The phrase means first in rank of diagnostic weight; it does not mean that they appear first in the illness or that they are the commonest symptoms. The list is usually counted as eleven experiences, which fall into four groups (Table 4.3): Three kinds of hallucinatory voices. Audible thoughts (in German Gedankenlautwerden , "thoughts becoming loud"; in French écho de la pensée , thought echo): the patient hears his own thoughts spoken aloud, as he thinks them or just afterwards. Voices arguing or discussing the patient among themselves, referring to him in the third person ("he", "she"). Voices giving a running commentary on the patient's actions or thoughts as they happen. Thought alienation , three experiences in which the patient's own thinking seems to be under outside control: thought insertion (thoughts that are not his own are put into his mind), thought withdrawal (thoughts are taken out of his mind, often felt as a sudden emptying in mid-sentence) and thought broadcasting (his thoughts leave his mind and spread out, so that other people know them). Passivity experiences , also called delusions of control: four experiences in which feelings, drives, actions or the body itself are felt to be controlled by an outside agency. They are made feelings (emotions imposed from outside), made impulses (urges or drives imposed from outside), made volitional acts (actions carried out by the patient's own body but willed by someone else) and somatic passivity (bodily sensations imposed from outside, such as being burned by rays or "electrified"). Delusional perception : a normal perception that suddenly acquires a private, delusional meaning, with no understandable link between the two. It is "two-membered": first the ordinary perception (a red traffic light, a dog lifting its paw, a pen lying on a table), then the unrelated meaning (I have been chosen; the world is about to end). Look at the list as a whole and a single theme appears (Figure 4.3). In almost every first-rank symptom the normal boundary between the self and the outside world has failed. My thoughts, feelings, impulses and actions are felt as not mine, or as no longer private, or as made by someone outside; my own thinking is heard as voices; an ordinary piece of the world speaks to me with a meaning meant for me alone. Psychopathologists call these disturbances of the self, or of the ego boundaries (in German, Ich-Störungen ). Now think back to James Tilly Matthews and his Air Loom: thoughts forced in, thoughts drawn out, a body moved from outside. Haslam had recorded a near-complete set of first-rank symptoms in 1810, a century and more before Schneider gave them their name. Feelings, impulses, acts and thoughts are felt to come in from outside; thoughts are taken out or leak out; the person's own thinking is heard as voices; and a neutral perception carries a meaning aimed at the self. Schneider also gave a second list, of second-rank symptoms , which occur in schizophrenia but carry less diagnostic weight because they are common in other conditions too: other hallucinations (including voices that speak to the patient in the second person, and hallucinations in the other senses), sudden delusional ideas that arise without a perception (sometimes called delusional intuitions), perplexity, depressive or euphoric changes of mood, and feelings of emotional impoverishment, that is, emotional blunting. He was explicit that schizophrenia could be diagnosed without a single first-rank symptom, from the second-rank symptoms and the whole clinical picture, and that first-rank symptoms counted only when no physical illness could explain them. What is not first-rank. For examinations, what is missing from the list matters as much as what is on it. Students tend to assume that anything typical of schizophrenia must be first-rank, and examiners exploit the assumption. None of the following is a first-rank symptom: Loosening of associations and other formal thought disorder. This is Bleuler's fundamental symptom, a feature of the patient's speech judged by the listener, not an experience the patient reports. Ideas and delusions of reference (self-reference): the belief that the news, strangers' remarks or chance events refer to oneself. They are common in schizophrenia, but they are defined by their content . Delusional perception is defined by its form : an ordinary perception followed, without understandable connection, by a sudden new meaning. Second-person voices ("You are dirty") and visual, olfactory, gustatory or tactile hallucinations; smells, tastes and touches in particular should make you look for a physical cause (Section 4.2). Delusions in general , persecutory, grandiose or any other, unless they take one of the forms in the list (passivity or delusional perception). Catatonic signs such as echolalia, echopraxia, stereotyped movements, posturing and catatonic excitement. Negative symptoms such as flat affect, alogia, avolition and anhedonia. Depersonalisation and derealisation : the feeling that one's self or the world is unreal or changed. These are experienced "as if" ("I feel as if I were a robot"), with insight, and they are common in anxiety and dissociative states (Chapter 7). In a passivity experience the patient says, as plain fact, "They are moving my arm." Memory loss and disorientation , which point to delirium, dementia and other organic states (Chapter 10). Obsessional thoughts , which are unwanted and distressing but recognised as products of the patient's own mind (Chapter 6). In thought insertion the thought is experienced as someone else's. Worked example: sorting Arun's experiences At 23, Arun told the psychiatrist seven things. (1) "My thoughts come out of my head and spread through the house; everyone knows what I am thinking." (2) "The man reading the evening news was talking about me." (3) "A voice tells me, 'You are dirty, you are useless.'" (4) "Two voices argue about me: 'He should be punished.' 'No, he is only a boy.'" (5) "I saw a crow land on the gate, and at that moment I knew the government had chosen me." (6) "Sometimes I feel as if the world were made of cardboard." (7) His own speech ran "train, rain, brain, the drain of the brain", rhyme leading meaning. Only (1) thought broadcasting, (4) third-person voices arguing and (5) delusional perception are first-rank. (2) is a delusion of reference, (3) a second-person voice (second-rank), (6) derealisation with an "as if" quality, and (7) a clang association, a form of thought disorder that the interviewer observes. Section 4.4 shows how these symptoms are weighed by ICD-10, which can accept a single clear first-rank symptom lasting a month, and by DSM-5-TR, which counts them like any other delusion or hallucination. Characteristic, but not specific. Schneider's symptoms are strongly associated with schizophrenia, but they are not confined to it. Remember Vasanthi. During her manic episode at 26 she told the doctor that her thoughts were being broadcast on the radio, a textbook first-rank symptom, yet she recovered completely within weeks, and since her later depression she has stayed well on lithium. Her diagnosis is bipolar disorder with psychotic features (Chapter 5), exactly as Kraepelin's course criterion would predict. First-rank symptoms are found in a substantial minority of people with mania, in some with psychotic depression, in drug-induced and other organic psychoses such as temporal lobe epilepsy (which is why Schneider insisted on the absence of physical illness), and, as DSM-5-TR notes, in dissociative identity disorder, where voices of other identity states can resemble voices arguing and intruding thoughts can resemble thought insertion. How good a test are they? A Cochrane review by Karla Soares-Weiser and colleagues (2015) pooled 21 studies with 5,515 participants analysed. Compared with all other diagnoses, the presence of first-rank symptoms had a sensitivity of about 57 percent and a specificity of about 81 percent; compared only with other psychoses, the specificity fell to about 75 percent. Put into words: roughly four in ten people diagnosed with schizophrenia did not show first-rank symptoms when they were assessed, and about one in four people with other psychoses did. A sign found only in one disease is called pathognomonic ; first-rank symptoms are characteristic of schizophrenia but not pathognomonic. That is why DSM-5 stopped giving them special weight, while ICD-10 built them into its first groups of criteria and ICD-11 still lists experiences of influence, passivity or control among its core symptoms (Section 4.4). Exam trap First-rank symptoms were described by Kurt Schneider : not Kraepelin (dementia praecox), not Bleuler (four As), not Karl Jaspers (phenomenology and primary delusions), not Gregory Bateson (the double bind, 1956, Section 4.9) and not "Wayne", a misprint for Lyman Wynne (pseudomutuality, Section 4.9). Not first-rank: depersonalisation, loose associations, delusions of self-reference, catatonic signs (echolalia, stereotyped movements, catatonic excitement), negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, flat affect), olfactory hallucinations and tactile illusions, memory deficits and disorientation. First-rank: audible thoughts, voices arguing or discussing, running commentary, thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting, made feelings, impulses and acts, somatic passivity and delusional perception; so delusions of control, insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting are all correct. Delusional perception is first-rank, but a sudden delusional idea without a perception is second-rank. If an options list offers "auditory hallucination" beside an obvious non-first-rank item such as delusion of self-reference, read the hallucination as standing for Schneider's voices and pick the other item. Strictly, only three forms of voices are first-rank; a simple voice addressing the patient as "you" is second-rank. Finally, FRS are most associated with schizophrenia , not bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder or obsessive-compulsive disorder, but they are not specific to it: they occur in mania too. Clinical link Eliciting first-rank symptoms is a skill taught in Book 2, Section 2.5.6. The key is form, not content. Many patients answer "yes" to a loose question such as "Do thoughts come into your head that are not your own?" when they mean an unwanted worry, a mother's advice that keeps replaying or an obsessional doubt, all of which they recognise as their own thoughts. In India, a patient may also say that someone has done black magic on him or cast the evil eye. That is a culturally shared explanation, not in itself a passivity experience; the clinician has to ask what the patient actually experiences, for example whether his arm moves without his willing it or whether a thought arrives that he knows is someone else's. Possession states are discussed in Chapter 7. From broad to narrow: the modern definition By the 1960s the word schizophrenia meant quite different things in different countries. In the United States, where Bleuler's broad concept, Meyer's reaction types and psychoanalysis held sway, the diagnosis was given to patients with mild, odd or mixed pictures; Paul Hoch and Phillip Polatin even described a "pseudoneurotic schizophrenia" (1949) hidden behind severe neurotic symptoms. In Britain and much of Europe, where Schneider's symptoms were used, the concept was narrower. In Norway, Gabriel Langfeldt had separated "true" or process schizophrenia, with its poor prognosis, from good-prognosis schizophreniform states in studies published in 1937 and 1939, a word you will meet again in Section 4.5. In the Soviet Union, the school of Andrei Snezhnevsky used an extremely broad concept that included "sluggish schizophrenia", a diagnosis notoriously given to political dissidents. Did these differences reflect different patients, or different doctors? Key study: the US-UK Diagnostic Project (1972) Official hospital statistics showed schizophrenia to be far commoner among admissions in New York than in London, and manic-depressive illness far commoner in London. Was the illness really distributed so differently? A joint American and British team led by John E. Cooper , Robert Kendell and Barry Gurland interviewed patients admitted to hospitals in both cities using the same standardised interview, the Present State Examination devised by John Wing (Assessment book), and the same diagnostic rules. When the project team made the diagnoses, the rates of schizophrenia in the two cities were broadly similar. The American excess had been produced by hospital psychiatrists who called schizophrenia many patients whom the project team diagnosed as having mania, depression or a personality disorder. A companion study (Kendell and colleagues, 1971) showed videotaped interviews to audiences of psychiatrists on both sides of the Atlantic; for one patient, about 69 percent of the Americans diagnosed schizophrenia against 2 percent of the British. The conclusion, published in Psychiatric Diagnosis in New York and London (Cooper and colleagues, 1972), was that diagnostic habits, not patients, differed. The WHO International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia, published the following year (Section 4.6), found the same pattern: its Washington and Moscow centres used much broader concepts than the other centres. A diagnosis that depends on which city you are admitted in is of little use for research or treatment, so the response was to write the rules down. In 1972 a group at Washington University in St Louis, with John P. Feighner as first author, published explicit research criteria that, among other things, required at least six months of illness. The Research Diagnostic Criteria of Robert Spitzer and his colleagues followed in 1978, and in 1980 the third edition of the DSM (DSM-III) built explicit criteria into the official manual. DSM-III's schizophrenia was deliberately narrow: it required psychotic symptoms, deterioration from an earlier level of functioning, continuous signs of illness for at least six months and, in that edition only, onset before the age of 45; and it sent patients with full mood episodes to the mood disorders. Look at what the new definition contains, and you can see every builder at once. The six-month rule is Kraepelin's course in miniature. The weight that DSM-III and its successors gave to bizarre delusions and Schneiderian voices is Schneider's. The exclusion of mood disorders is Kraepelin's dichotomy. And Bleuler lives on in the negative symptoms that later editions placed among the core criteria. The story since then is one of refinement rather than revolution, and Section 4.4 tells it in detail. ICD-10 (1992) wrote Schneider's symptoms into its first groups of criteria but required only one month of illness. DSM-5 (2013) abolished the classical subtypes, which were unreliable and told clinicians little about treatment or outcome, and it stopped allowing a single bizarre delusion or Schneiderian voice to satisfy the symptom criterion on its own. ICD-11, in force since 2022, replaced the subtypes with specifiers for the kinds of symptoms present and for the course. The general history of classification, and the statistics of reliability such as kappa, are in Book 2, Section 2.10. The modern concept, then, is narrow where Bleuler's was broad. Psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech) are required; a period of illness long enough to show something of its course is required (one month in ICD, six months in DSM); mood psychoses are excluded; and no single symptom, not even a first-rank one, is enough.
