Feature Type I Type II Characteristic symptoms Positive: delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder Negative: affective flattening, poverty of speech, loss of drive Typical course Acute, episodic Chronic Response to neuroleptics Good Poor Intellectual impairment Absent Sometimes present Outcome Potentially reversible Relatively irreversible, sometimes progressive Proposed basis Neurochemical: more dopamine D2 receptors Structural: cell loss, enlarged ventricles Added by Crow in 1985 Abnormal involuntary movements, cognitive impairment, deterioration Crow's scheme was elegant because it tied each group of symptoms to a different biology and a different response to treatment, and it fitted what clinicians saw: the acute, florid, drug-responsive patient and the chronic, withdrawn, drug-resistant one. But Crow himself recognised its main weakness. Both syndromes often occur in the same patient, sometimes at the same moment, so they are better thought of as two dimensions of pathology within one illness than as two diseases. And the clean links did not all hold up: later studies found the association between enlarged ventricles and negative symptoms inconsistent. Andreasen's positive, negative and mixed schizophrenia. At the University of Iowa, Nancy Andreasen gave the positive-negative distinction its measuring instruments. Her Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS, 1982) and Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS, 1984) are described in the Assessment book. With her colleague Olsen she proposed in 1982 three subtypes: positive schizophrenia, with prominent delusions, hallucinations, positive formal thought disorder and persistently bizarre behaviour; negative schizophrenia, with affective flattening, alogia, avolition, anhedonia and attentional impairment; and mixed schizophrenia, in which both kinds are prominent or neither is. The subtypes differed on premorbid adjustment, cognitive measures, ventricular size and course in hospital. The very need for a "mixed" group, however, showed that many patients do not fit either pole. Key study: Three syndromes, not two (Liddle, 1987) Is two the right number? Peter F. Liddle , in London, examined how symptoms clustered in 40 patients with chronic schizophrenia, chosen because their symptoms were persistent and stable. If the positive-negative model were right, the symptoms should have fallen into two groups. They fell into three. Psychomotor poverty comprised poverty of speech, lack of spontaneous movement and various aspects of blunted affect. Disorganisation comprised inappropriate affect, poverty of content of speech and disturbances of the form of thought. Reality distortion comprised particular types of delusions and hallucinations. The crucial discovery was that thought disorder and inappropriate affect did not go with delusions and hallucinations, even though all are "positive": disorganisation was its own dimension. The syndromes also had different consequences, psychomotor poverty going with poor personal relationships and disorganisation with poor self-care and impersistence at work. In 1992 Liddle, Karl Friston, Christopher Frith and colleagues measured cerebral blood flow with positron emission tomography in 30 patients and found that each syndrome had its own pattern: psychomotor poverty and disorganisation were linked with altered blood flow at different sites in the prefrontal cortex, and reality distortion with the medial temporal lobe. The PANSS and the five factors. In 1987 Stanley Kay, Abraham Fiszbein and Lewis Opler published the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), a 30-item interview-based scale with 7 positive items, 7 negative items and 16 items of general psychopathology. It became the standard outcome measure in drug trials (details are in the Assessment book). When researchers factor-analysed PANSS ratings from large samples, the data were described better by five factors than by the scale's three subscales, and a consensus model (Wallwork and colleagues, 2012) names them: positive, negative, disorganised or concrete, excited, and depressed. Other analyses call the third factor cognitive and the fifth anxiety and depression. The five-factor picture keeps Liddle's three dimensions and adds two that clinicians had always seen: excitement and hostility, and depression and anxiety. First, a better description of each patient: "schizophrenia with prominent negative and cognitive symptoms and little reality distortion" says far more about Meenakshi than "schizophrenia" alone, and it says something quite different from what it says about Suresh at his first admission. Second, a guide to treatment: reality distortion responds best to antipsychotic drugs, while negative and cognitive symptoms need rehabilitation, activity and cognitive remediation as well (Section 4.10). Third, a bridge to biology: the different dimensions seem to involve different brain systems, as Liddle's blood-flow study suggested and as the dopamine pathways of Section 4.8 will show, with too much dopamine in one pathway linked to positive symptoms and too little in another to negative and cognitive ones. Exam trap Crow (1980) : Type I is positive, acute, drug-responsive, without intellectual impairment, with normal brain structure and a dopamine (D2) excess; Type II is negative, chronic, drug-resistant, with intellectual impairment and enlarged ventricles. Do not swap them. Liddle (1987) : reality distortion, disorganisation, psychomotor poverty; "psychomotor poverty" is the negative syndrome, and disorganisation (thought disorder, inappropriate affect) was separated from delusions and hallucinations. About five months ago his parents noticed that he had stopped going to college. He stayed in his room, slept through the day and paced at night, gave up cricket, stopped bathing regularly and answered questions with a shrug. He spent hours with a notebook in which he wrote lists of numbers that he said were "important". Nobody thought of illness; his mother thought he was upset about an examination, and his father thought he was lazy. Then, about six weeks ago, things changed sharply. Ganesh began to say that two men were talking about him from behind the wall ("He is useless. He will be finished by Deepavali"), and that the neighbours had fixed a device inside the ceiling fan that pulled his thoughts out and played them over the loudspeaker of the temple down the road, so that the whole colony knew what he was thinking. He covered the fan with a bedsheet. His speech, when he did talk, drifted from one subject to another so that his brother could not follow it. His family brought him to the outpatient department of the district hospital. Does Ganesh have schizophrenia? You might think that the answer depends only on Ganesh. It does not. It also depends on which diagnostic manual the clinician opens. A psychiatrist using the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) would, on this history, diagnose schizophrenia today. A psychologist using the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) would not, at least not yet. By the end of this section you will be able to say exactly why, and to work through the rules of all three systems that Indian examiners ask about: DSM-5-TR (2022), ICD-10 (1992) and ICD-11 (in force since 2022). You will also learn the other conditions that can look exactly like Ganesh's illness, because the most dangerous mistake in diagnosing schizophrenia is not choosing the wrong subtype; it is missing a treatable medical cause. No single symptom: why schizophrenia is diagnosed by rules Start with an uncomfortable fact. There is no blood test, brain scan or psychological test that diagnoses schizophrenia. DSM-5-TR says so directly: there are currently no radiological, laboratory or psychometric tests for the disorder, and although groups of patients differ from healthy people on brain imaging, eye tracking and electrophysiology, none of these differences can diagnose one person. Nor is there a single symptom that settles it. A symptom that occurs in one disorder and in no other is called pathognomonic (Section 4.1; from the Greek for "judging the disease"), and schizophrenia has none. Thought broadcasting, the symptom that frightens Ganesh most, can occur in mania. Voices can occur in severe depression, in delirium, after a bereavement and in temporal lobe epilepsy. Blunted affect can come from depression or from the antipsychotic drugs themselves. If no one symptom is decisive, how is the diagnosis made? By recognising a pattern: a particular combination of symptoms, lasting a particular length of time, with a particular effect on the person's life, after the other possible causes have been excluded. For most of the twentieth century that pattern lived in the heads of individual psychiatrists, and different heads held different patterns. Section 4.1 told the story of the US-UK Diagnostic Project of the early 1970s, which showed that New York psychiatrists diagnosed schizophrenia far more readily than London psychiatrists did when they watched the same patients. The cure for that unreliability was to write the pattern down as explicit rules that any trained clinician could apply in the same way. Such rules are called operational criteria : each symptom is defined, the number required is stated, and so are the duration and the exclusions. The general story of classification, reliability and the kappa statistic is told in Book 2, Section 2.10; here we apply it to one disorder. The first influential operational criteria for schizophrenia were published in 1972 by a group at Washington University in St Louis (Eli Robins, Samuel Guze and their colleagues), with the psychiatry resident John P. Feighner as first author. The Feighner criteria demanded a chronic illness with at least six months of symptoms without a return to the earlier level of adjustment. That six-month rule entered the official American manual with DSM-III in 1980 and has stayed there ever since. Its purpose was deliberate: by refusing the label to short illnesses, the Americans were narrowing schizophrenia back towards the chronic, deteriorating disorder that Kraepelin had described, and away from the very broad concept that the US-UK Project had exposed. The World Health Organization took a different view: when ICD-10 finally set a duration for schizophrenia in 1992 (ICD-9 had none), it chose one month. Almost every difference between DSM and ICD that you will meet in this section flows from that one disagreement about how long to wait. Notice also that modern criteria are polythetic : they require some number out of a list of features ("two or more of the following five") rather than every feature on the list. A polythetic rule accepts that schizophrenia is a heterogeneous syndrome. Two people can both meet the criteria while sharing none of their symptoms: one may be hallucinating and deluded, the other incoherent in speech and without any drive. That heterogeneity is part of the reason Section 4.3 needed symptom dimensions, and part of the reason DSM-5 eventually gave up on subtypes. Exam trap "Schizophrenia can be confirmed by a CT or MRI scan" and "first-rank symptoms are pathognomonic of schizophrenia" are both false. Brain scans in a first episode are done to exclude other causes (a tumour, a stroke, encephalitis), not to confirm schizophrenia. Kurt Schneider himself called his symptoms "first rank" in importance, not unique to schizophrenia; they occur in mania and in organic psychoses too (Section 4.1). DSM-5-TR schizophrenia, criterion by criterion DSM-5-TR sets out six criteria, A to F. All six must be satisfied. It helps to read them not as a list to memorise but as six questions the clinician asks, each designed to rule something out. Criterion A: are the characteristic symptoms there? Two or more of five symptoms must each be present for a significant portion of time during a one-month period: (1) delusions, (2) hallucinations, (3) disorganised speech (frequent derailment or incoherence), (4) grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, and (5) negative symptoms (diminished emotional expression or avolition). At least one of the two must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech. These five are the symptoms described in Sections 4.2 and 4.3. The period during which Criterion A is met is called the active phase . Why insist that one of the first three be present? Imagine the rule without it. A young man who has become withdrawn, flat and unmotivated (negative symptoms) and who behaves oddly (disorganised behaviour) would qualify. So would many people with severe depression, autism, frontal lobe damage or a chronic institutionalised life. The requirement that at least one symptom be a clear psychotic symptom of thought or perception keeps the diagnosis anchored to psychosis. It was added in DSM-5 (2013); DSM-IV had allowed any two. Two small phrases in Criterion A matter in practice. "A significant portion of time" means the symptoms must be more than fleeting; a single night of hearing a voice does not count. And the month can be shorter "if successfully treated". If Ganesh is started on an antipsychotic and his voices vanish in three weeks, the clinician may still count Criterion A as met if, in her judgement, the symptoms would have persisted for a month without treatment. Without that clause, effective treatment would make the diagnosis impossible. Criterion B: has the person's life fallen apart? For a significant portion of the time since onset, functioning in one or more major areas, such as work, relationships or self-care, must be markedly below the level achieved before onset. When the illness begins in childhood or adolescence, the criterion is met by a failure to reach the expected level; comparing the young person with unaffected brothers and sisters is often the best guide. Criterion B is what makes schizophrenia a disorder of the whole life rather than a set of experiences. It is also a requirement that schizophrenia's closest neighbours lack: schizophreniform disorder, schizoaffective disorder and brief psychotic disorder do not require a decline (Section 4.5). Criterion C: has it lasted six months? Continuous signs of the disturbance must persist for at least six months. That six months must include at least one month of active-phase symptoms (Criterion A), less if successfully treated, and it may include periods of prodromal or residual symptoms. The prodromal phase is the period of gradual change before the psychosis becomes obvious; the residual phase is the period after an active episode settles. During both, the signs of the disturbance may consist only of negative symptoms, or of two or more Criterion A symptoms in a weakened, attenuated form: odd beliefs that are not yet delusions (ideas of reference, magical thinking), unusual perceptual experiences (sensing the presence of an unseen person), speech that is vague but understandable, behaviour that is odd but not grossly disorganised (mumbling in public). Figure 4.7 shows how the six months are counted. The phases themselves, and what happens over the long course of the illness, are described in Section 4.6. ICD-10 and ICD-11: 1 month of active symptoms DSM-5-TR: 6 months of continuous signs Prodromal phase withdrawal, odd beliefs Active phase Criterion A Residual phase negative or attenuated signs the 6 months may include prodromal and residual periods 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 Months from the first noticeable change Figure 4.7 How the duration criteria are counted, for one possible course. ICD-10 and ICD-11 are satisfied once the characteristic symptoms have been present for most of one month; DSM-5-TR waits until the disturbance, counting prodromal and residual periods, has lasted six months. Criterion D: is this really a mood disorder? Psychotic symptoms are common in severe depression and mania, and mood episodes are common in schizophrenia. Criterion D rules out schizoaffective disorder and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features. It is satisfied in one of two ways: either no major depressive or manic episode has occurred at the same time as the active-phase symptoms, or, if mood episodes have occurred during the active phase, they have been present for only a minority of the total duration of the active and residual periods. DSM-5-TR adds that a diagnosis of schizophrenia requires delusions or hallucinations at some time in the absence of a mood episode. How these timing rules separate the three disorders is shown in Figure 4.9 in Section 4.5. Criterion E: is there a physical cause? The disturbance must not be attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (a drug of abuse or a medication) or to another medical condition. You will see in Section 4.4.6 how much clinical work hides behind that one sentence. Criterion F: is this autism or a childhood communication disorder? Children and adults with autism spectrum disorder or a childhood-onset communication disorder may show odd speech, social withdrawal, flat expression and unusual behaviour, which could be misread as disorganised speech and negative symptoms. So if there is such a history, schizophrenia is diagnosed as an additional condition only if prominent delusions or hallucinations, along with the other required symptoms, are also present for at least one month (or less if successfully treated). Autism itself is covered in Chapter 3. Table 4.14 gathers the six criteria and the job each one does. Table 4.14 The DSM-5-TR criteria for schizophrenia, and what each one is there to rule out. The full answer is: at least 6 months of continuous signs of disturbance, of which at least 1 month must be active-phase (Criterion A) symptoms . So "1 month of active phase (6 months total)" is right, and so is "6 months" when the question asks for the total or the "minimum duration of continuous signs". "1 month" alone is the ICD answer, or the DSM active-phase answer, but not the DSM answer to "minimum duration of the disorder". Distractors of 1 week, 2 weeks, 3 months, 12 months and 2 years belong to other disorders: 2 weeks is a major depressive episode, 1 week a manic episode, 2 years persistent depressive disorder. And Criterion C does not require six months of active psychosis. Specifiers, and the subtypes DSM-5 abandoned Once the diagnosis is made, DSM-5-TR asks the clinician to describe it more precisely with specifiers , extra labels that add information without changing the diagnosis. Schizophrenia has three kinds. The course specifiers may be used only after the disorder has lasted a year, because before that the pattern of the illness cannot be known. They are: first episode (currently in acute episode, in partial remission, or in full remission); multiple episodes (currently in acute episode, in partial remission, or in full remission), which requires at least two episodes, that is a first episode, a remission and at least one relapse; continuous, when symptoms meeting the criteria persist for most of the illness with only brief subthreshold periods; and unspecified. An acute episode is a period when the symptom criteria are fulfilled; partial remission is a period of maintained improvement in which the criteria are only partly fulfilled; full remission is a period with no disorder-specific symptoms. The second specifier is with catatonia , used when the criteria for catatonia (three or more of twelve psychomotor signs, Section 4.5.7) are met, and coded with an extra code for catatonia associated with schizophrenia. The third is current severity . Each of the primary symptoms of psychosis (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, abnormal psychomotor behaviour and negative symptoms) is rated for its worst level in the last seven days on a five-point scale from 0 (not present) to 4 (present and severe), using the Clinician-Rated Dimensions of Psychosis Symptom Severity in Section III of the manual, which also rates impaired cognition, depression and mania. The diagnosis can be made without the severity rating; its purpose is to give a dimensional picture alongside the categorical label. What DSM-5-TR does not contain is just as important. From DSM-III to DSM-IV-TR, the American manuals divided schizophrenia into subtypes according to the symptoms that dominated the current picture. DSM-IV (1994) had five: Paranoid type : preoccupation with one or more delusions or frequent auditory hallucinations, with no prominent disorganised speech, disorganised or catatonic behaviour, or flat or inappropriate affect. Often later onset and better preserved functioning. Disorganised type (Hecker's hebephrenia, Section 4.1): disorganised speech, disorganised behaviour and flat or inappropriate affect all prominent. Early, insidious onset and a poor outlook. Catatonic type : a picture dominated by catatonic signs such as immobility, purposeless excitement, extreme negativism or mutism, peculiar voluntary movements, and echolalia or echopraxia. Undifferentiated type : Criterion A met, but not the pattern of the paranoid, disorganised or catatonic types. Residual type : a past active episode, with only negative symptoms or attenuated positive symptoms continuing. DSM-5 (2013) deleted all five. The reasons, set out by the work group, were that the subtypes had limited diagnostic stability, low reliability and poor validity. Patients did not stay in one subtype: a man diagnosed paranoid at 25 might be undifferentiated at 30 and residual at 40, so the label described the moment, not the illness. The subtypes did not predict different responses to treatment or clearly different long-term courses. And in practice the disorganised, catatonic and residual types were rarely used, so most patients ended up paranoid or undifferentiated and the labels carried little information. In their place DSM-5 put the dimensional severity ratings, which describe the same information (how much psychosis, how much disorganisation, how many negative symptoms) without forcing a patient into a box. DSM-5 also removed a rule that gave special weight to certain symptoms. Under DSM-IV, Criterion A needed only one symptom instead of two if the delusions were bizarre or if the hallucinations consisted of a voice keeping up a running commentary on the person's behaviour or thoughts, or two or more voices conversing with each other. Those two kinds of voice are, of course, Schneider's first-rank symptoms (Section 4.1). DSM-5 dropped the exception, for two reasons. Clinicians could not agree reliably on what made a delusion bizarre, and the special voices were shown not to be specific to schizophrenia. Today a bizarre delusion counts like any other delusion, so a person with one bizarre delusion and nothing else does not meet Criterion A; such a person may instead have delusional disorder, which DSM-5 now allows to have bizarre content (Section 4.5.4). Exam trap If an option offers "paranoid schizophrenia" or "disorganised schizophrenia" as a DSM-5 or DSM-5-TR diagnosis, it is wrong: those are DSM-IV subtypes (and paranoid, hebephrenic and others are ICD-10 subtypes). DSM-5 dropped the subtypes because of low reliability, poor validity and instability, not because they were "too rare". DSM-5 also dropped the special weight of bizarre delusions and Schneiderian voices; in DSM-5-TR, two Criterion A symptoms are always needed. Course specifiers are used only after one year of illness. ICD-10 F20: the Schneiderian legacy and the one-month rule The tenth revision of the ICD, whose chapter on mental disorders (chapter V, the F codes) came with a separate volume, Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Guidelines , published in 1992, is still the system on which many Indian hospital records, case-file codes and university syllabuses are built. Its schizophrenia, coded F20 , is organised quite differently from DSM's. Instead of five symptoms of equal weight, ICD-10 lists nine groups of symptoms, labelled (a) to (i), and gives the first four groups more weight than the rest. Table 4.15 sets them out. Table 4.15 The ICD-10 symptom groups for schizophrenia (F20), in plain words. Thought echo and the three kinds of thought alienation, passivity and delusional perception, voices commenting and voices discussing the patient in the third person. Group (d) captures the "impossible" delusion that DSM-IV called bizarre. ICD-10 was, in this sense, the most Schneiderian of the modern manuals, and that is why so many Indian examination questions on first-rank symptoms sit right beside questions on ICD criteria. The rule built on these groups is this. The normal requirement is a minimum of one very clear symptom (and usually two or more if less clear-cut) from any one of groups (a) to (d), or symptoms from at least two of groups (e) to (h) , clearly present for most of the time during a period of one month or more . Read the second half carefully. A person who has only negative symptoms and catatonic behaviour, two groups from (e) to (h), qualifies under ICD-10, which is a looser rule than DSM-5's insistence on one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech. Notice too that group (h) lists "blunting or incongruity of emotional responses" among the negative symptoms; incongruous affect, laughing while describing a death, is placed there by ICD-10, which is why an option such as "incongruity of emotional responses" counts as a negative symptom in questions built on ICD wording (Section 4.3). Three further rules complete the picture. First, the one-month period applies only to the specific symptoms in the table, not to any prodromal phase; a long prodrome does not count towards the month, and its absence does not prevent the diagnosis. Second, a condition that meets the symptom requirements but has lasted less than a month, whether treated or not, is diagnosed in the first instance as acute schizophrenia-like psychotic disorder (F23.2, Section 4.5.2), and reclassified as schizophrenia if the symptoms persist. Third, there are exclusions much like DSM's: schizophrenia should not be diagnosed in the presence of extensive depressive or manic symptoms unless it is clear that the schizophrenic symptoms came before the mood disturbance (if both develop together and are evenly balanced, the diagnosis is schizoaffective disorder, F25), nor in the presence of overt brain disease, nor during drug intoxication or withdrawal. ICD-10 has no criterion of functional decline equivalent to DSM's Criterion B. ICD-10 kept subtypes, and examiners still ask about them. Each is coded by a fourth character, F20.0 to F20.9, and a fifth character can record the course: continuous, episodic with progressive deficit, episodic with stable deficit, episodic remittent, incomplete remission, complete remission, other, or period of observation less than a year. Table 4.16 lists the subtypes. Table 4.16 The ICD-10 subtypes of schizophrenia. Code Subtype What defines it F20.0 Paranoid schizophrenia Relatively stable, often paranoid delusions, usually with hallucinations (especially voices); affect, speech and volition relatively spared. The commonest type in most parts of the world F20.1 Hebephrenic schizophrenia Prominent affective change (shallow, silly, inappropriate mood, giggling, mannerisms, pranks), disorganised thought and rambling speech, fleeting delusions and hallucinations. Onset usually between 15 and 25; poor outlook because negative symptoms develop rapidly F20.2 Catatonic schizophrenia Psychomotor disturbance dominates: stupor, excitement, posturing, negativism, rigidity, waxy flexibility, command automatism. Now rare in industrial countries, still seen elsewhere F20.3 Undifferentiated schizophrenia General criteria met, but no single subtype fits, or features of several without one predominating F20.4 Post-schizophrenic depression A depressive episode (at least 2 weeks) arising within 12 months after a schizophrenic illness, while some schizophrenic symptoms are still present F20.5 Residual schizophrenia A chronic stage after at least one clear psychotic episode: prominent negative symptoms, with florid symptoms minimal for at least a year F20.6 Simple schizophrenia Insidious, progressive development over at least a year of negative symptoms and decline (group (i)) without any history of hallucinations, delusions or other overt psychotic symptoms F20.8 and F20.9 Other; unspecified Residual categories Two of these subtypes deserve a second look, because they are unusual. Simple schizophrenia is the only form of schizophrenia anywhere in modern classification that can be diagnosed without a psychotic symptom ever having occurred: a slow slide into apathy, idleness, aimlessness and social withdrawal over at least a year. ICD-10 itself warns that it is a difficult diagnosis to make with confidence, because the same picture can come from depression, a personality change or a drifting life; it was dropped in ICD-11. Post-schizophrenic depression recognises that a depressive episode commonly follows an acute psychotic episode, often as insight returns, and that this is a period of high suicide risk (Section 4.6). DSM handles the same situation differently: a depressive episode after psychosis is coded as an additional other specified or unspecified depressive disorder rather than as a form of schizophrenia. Exam trap The ICD-10 duration for schizophrenia is 1 month (symptoms present most of the time during a period of one month or more), not 6 months, 3 months or 2 weeks. When an option lists something that is not in any group, such as catastrophic thinking , it is the odd one out: catastrophic thinking is a cognitive distortion from Aaron Beck's cognitive model of anxiety and depression (Book 2, Section 5.3), not a psychotic symptom. Delusions, hallucinations and disorganised speech all appear in the ICD groups. Simple schizophrenia (F20.6) needs one year , and is the subtype with no positive symptoms. ICD-11 6A20: fewer rules, more description The eleventh revision was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2019 and came into effect on 1 January 2022, and its clinical guidance for mental disorders, the Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements , followed. In India this matters legally as well as clinically: Section 3(1) of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 says that mental illness shall be determined in accordance with nationally or internationally accepted medical standards, including the latest edition of the International Classification of Disease of the World Health Organisation, as notified by the Central Government (Book 2, Section 1.10). ICD-11 places schizophrenia in a block called schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders . "Primary" means that the psychosis is not the result of a substance or a medical condition; those secondary psychoses are coded elsewhere. The block contains schizophrenia (6A20), schizoaffective disorder (6A21), schizotypal disorder (6A22), acute and transient psychotic disorder (6A23), delusional disorder (6A24), the symptom specifiers (6A25), and other specified and unspecified categories. You will meet each member in Section 4.5. The ICD-11 description of schizophrenia ( 6A20 ) lists seven kinds of symptom: (a) persistent delusions; (b) persistent hallucinations, most commonly auditory; (c) disorganised thinking or formal thought disorder, such as tangentiality, loose associations, irrelevant speech or neologisms, which in its severe form becomes incoherent "word salad"; (d) experiences of influence, passivity or control, that is the experience that one's feelings, impulses, actions or thoughts are not one's own, are inserted or withdrawn by others, or are broadcast; (e) negative symptoms such as affective flattening, alogia or paucity of speech, avolition, asociality and anhedonia; (f) grossly disorganised behaviour that impedes goal-directed activity; and (g) psychomotor disturbances such as catatonic restlessness or agitation, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, mutism or stupor. The requirement is that at least two of these be present most of the time for a period of one month or more, with at least one from (a) to (d) , and that the symptoms not be a manifestation of another medical condition or of a substance or medication, including withdrawal. Compare this with the two older systems and you can see what the WHO borrowed from each. From ICD-10 it kept the one-month rule and gave passivity experiences their own place among the core symptoms. From DSM-5 it took the idea that two symptoms are needed, with one of them a core psychotic symptom, so that a single first-rank symptom is no longer enough on its own. Like ICD-10, and unlike DSM-5-TR, it does not demand a decline in functioning. Table 4.17 sets the three systems side by side. ICD-11 abolished all the subtypes, simple schizophrenia and post-schizophrenic depression included, and replaced them with two sets of qualifiers. The course is coded in the code itself: first episode (6A20.0), multiple episodes (6A20.1) or continuous (6A20.2), each further described as currently symptomatic, in partial remission or in full remission. The current clinical picture is then described with the symptom specifiers of 6A25, which can be applied to any primary psychotic disorder: positive symptoms (6A25.0), negative symptoms (6A25.1), depressive mood symptoms (6A25.2), manic mood symptoms (6A25.3), psychomotor symptoms (6A25.4) and cognitive symptoms (6A25.5), each rated for severity. Any number may be used together. If the full syndrome of catatonia is present, it is coded separately as catatonia associated with another mental disorder (6A40). The design is plainly dimensional: rather than asking "which kind of schizophrenia is this?", ICD-11 asks "how much of each kind of symptom does this person have now?" Also remember that ICD-11 has no subtypes : "paranoid schizophrenia, ICD-11" does not exist. Schizophreniform disorder as a one-to-six-month category is a DSM diagnosis; ICD calls an illness of that length schizophrenia. What else could it be? The differential diagnosis Criteria D and E, and the exclusions of ICD, are short sentences, but behind them lies the most important clinical work of the first assessment. The differential diagnosis is the list of other conditions that could produce the same picture, each of which has to be considered and, where possible, ruled out. For a first episode of psychosis the list falls into four families: mood disorders, the other psychotic disorders, physical causes (substances and medical illnesses), and non-psychotic conditions that can look psychotic. Mood disorders with psychotic features. A severely depressed woman may hear a voice telling her she is a sinner, and a manic man may believe he has been chosen by God; both are psychotic, and neither has schizophrenia. The rule that separates them is timing: if delusions or hallucinations occur only during a major depressive or manic episode, the diagnosis is depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features, however florid the psychosis. A useful, though not decisive, clue is the content of the psychotic symptoms. In mood-congruent psychotic features the content fits the mood: guilt, deserved punishment, poverty, disease, nihilism ("my intestines have rotted") or death in depression, and inflated worth, power, knowledge or a special relationship with a deity or a famous person in mania. Mood-incongruent features, such as thought insertion or voices commenting in a neutral tone in a depressed patient, raise the possibility of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder but do not settle it. First-rank symptoms are reported in a substantial minority of people with mania, which is why Schneider's symptoms cannot by themselves distinguish the two great psychoses that Kraepelin separated. Depressive and bipolar disorders are taught in Chapter 5. The other psychotic disorders. If the psychosis has lasted less than six months, DSM-5-TR offers brief psychotic disorder or schizophreniform disorder; if a mood episode runs through most of the illness, schizoaffective disorder; if there is a single persistent delusion with little else, delusional disorder. These neighbours, and the rules that divide them, are the subject of Section 4.5. Schizotypal personality disorder lies on the near side of the psychotic threshold: odd beliefs, unusual perceptions and eccentric behaviour that are long-standing traits rather than a change of state (Chapter 11). Substances and medications. Ask every person with a first episode about cannabis, alcohol, stimulants and prescribed drugs, and test the urine. Amphetamines and cocaine can produce a paranoid psychosis within hours or days, cannabis an anxious persecutory state, hallucinogens and phencyclidine vivid perceptual changes, alcohol withdrawal a delirium with visual and tactile hallucinations, and long heavy drinking an auditory hallucinosis in clear consciousness. Corticosteroids, levodopa and other antiparkinsonian drugs, anticholinergic drugs and many others can do the same. The key is the time relationship: substance-induced psychosis begins during or soon after intoxication, withdrawal or a change of medication, and psychotic symptoms that persist for a substantial period, about a month, after the substance is stopped point towards an independent psychotic disorder (Section 4.5.6 and Chapter 10). The two can, of course, coexist; many people with schizophrenia also use cannabis. Medical and neurological illness. DSM-5-TR offers three questions for deciding whether a medical condition is causing psychosis. Biological plausibility : is there an illness that can cause psychosis through a known mechanism? Temporality : did the psychosis begin, worsen or remit along with the illness? Typicality : are there features unusual for a primary psychotic disorder, such as onset in later life, visual or olfactory hallucinations, or a dreamlike quality to the delusions? The causes are many: delirium (marked by clouded and fluctuating consciousness, disorientation and poor attention); epilepsy, especially of the temporal lobe (olfactory hallucinations are a classic clue, and postictal psychosis is the commonest epileptic psychosis); brain tumours, strokes, head injury and multiple sclerosis; infections of the brain, HIV and neurosyphilis; thyroid, parathyroid and adrenal disease; vitamin B12 deficiency; systemic lupus erythematosus; Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, Parkinson's disease and the dementias, especially Lewy body dementia. An important newer cause is anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis , an autoimmune illness described by the neurologist Josep Dalmau and his colleagues in 2007, in which antibodies attack the brain's NMDA glutamate receptors. It typically strikes young women, sometimes in association with an ovarian teratoma; it often begins, sometimes after a flu-like illness, with an acute psychosis and anxiety, and progresses over days to weeks to seizures, abnormal movements, catatonia, autonomic instability and falling consciousness. Recognised early, it responds to immunotherapy and removal of the tumour. It is also a striking piece of evidence for the glutamate hypothesis of Section 4.8. Age matters too: DSM-5-TR estimates that about 60 percent of older individuals with new-onset psychosis have a medical cause. Conditions that can look psychotic. In obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder, insight can be poor or absent, so that the person is completely convinced that the door really is contaminated or that his nose really is deformed; DSM-5-TR then diagnoses obsessive-compulsive or body dysmorphic disorder "with absent insight/delusional beliefs", not a psychotic disorder, because the belief belongs to the obsessive-compulsive picture. In post-traumatic stress disorder, flashbacks can have a hallucinatory quality and hypervigilance can reach paranoid proportions, but the trauma and the reliving symptoms identify the disorder. Autism spectrum disorder was discussed under Criterion F. Dissociative disorders and possession states can produce voices and altered identity (Chapter 7). Finally, culture: beliefs in the evil eye, sorcery, spirit possession or illness caused by curses are widely held in many communities, and hearing the voice of a recently dead parent is common in bereavement. DSM-5-TR stresses that such culturally shared beliefs and experiences are not delusions or hallucinations; the test is whether the person's own cultural group regards the belief or experience as normal. The routine work-up includes a physical and neurological examination, a full blood count, blood sugar, kidney, liver and thyroid function, vitamin B12, tests for HIV and syphilis, a urine drug screen, and usually brain imaging; an EEG, cerebrospinal fluid and autoimmune antibodies are added when the picture is atypical (rapid onset, confusion, seizures, abnormal movements, catatonia, fever). As a psychologist you will often be the person who notices that something does not fit: a patient whose "voices" are accompanied by smells of burning, or whose concentration fluctuates from hour to hour. Saying so is part of the job. Exam trap No single feature proves a medical cause or excludes schizophrenia. Visual hallucinations are not rare in schizophrenia, and olfactory hallucinations are consistent with it; they only raise the index of suspicion. Equally, first-rank symptoms do not exclude mania. The decisive rules are about time : whether psychosis occurs outside mood episodes, and whether it began and ended with a substance or an illness. Ganesh, diagnosed three ways Now return to Ganesh and push his case through all three systems. Begin with the facts the clinician gathered. The work-up found nothing physical: no fever or confusion, a normal neurological examination, normal blood tests, a negative urine drug screen, and a family who were sure he had never used cannabis or alcohol. He had never had a depressive or manic episode; his mood was flat rather than low, and he denied sadness. His symptoms were (1) voices of two men discussing him in the third person, for six weeks, most days; (2) the belief that his thoughts were being pulled out and broadcast over the temple loudspeaker, for the same six weeks; (3) speech that derailed from topic to topic; and (4) for about four months before that, and continuing, withdrawal, loss of drive and a decline in self-care. So his illness has lasted about five months in all, of which about six weeks has been the active phase. ICD-10. Thought withdrawal and thought broadcasting belong to group (a); voices discussing him belong to group (c). One very clear symptom from (a) to (d) would have been enough, and he has two, present most of the time for more than a month. Mood, brain disease and drugs have been excluded. The diagnosis is schizophrenia, F20; because delusions and hallucinations dominate while affect and speech are less affected, the subtype is paranoid schizophrenia, F20.0, with a fifth character of 9 (period of observation less than one year). ICD-11. He has persistent delusions (a), persistent hallucinations (b), disorganised thinking (c), experiences of influence (d) and negative symptoms (e): far more than the two required, for more than a month. The diagnosis is schizophrenia, first episode, currently symptomatic (6A20.00), with symptom specifiers for positive symptoms (severe) and negative symptoms (moderate), and perhaps cognitive symptoms once he has been tested. DSM-5-TR. Criterion A: delusions, hallucinations and disorganised speech, three of the first three, for a significant part of a month. Criterion B: his studies and self-care have collapsed. Criteria D, E and F: no mood episodes, no substance, no medical condition, no history of autism. Criterion C: here is the snag. The question is not how long he has been psychotic, but how long continuous signs of the disturbance have lasted, prodrome included. His withdrawal began about five months ago, so even counting the prodrome the six months are not yet complete. Today Ganesh has had symptoms for less than six months and has not recovered, and his DSM-5-TR diagnosis is schizophreniform disorder (provisional) . If he is still ill a month from now, when the six months are complete, the diagnosis changes to schizophrenia; if he recovers before then, it stays schizophreniform disorder (Section 4.5.1). The clinician's dating of the prodrome therefore matters a great deal: had his parents placed the first change seven months back, the same interview would have produced a DSM diagnosis of schizophrenia today. The course specifiers cannot be applied for another year. Notice what this exercise has taught you. The same young man, on the same day, can have schizophrenia in one manual and a provisional, potentially recoverable disorder in another. The disagreement is not about his symptoms but about time, and it goes all the way back to the different choices the St Louis group (1972) and the WHO (1992) made decades ago. Notice too what all three systems agree on: before any of them can be applied, the clinician must look for a mood disorder, a drug and a disease. In Ganesh's case the agreement on the treatment is complete. Whatever the label, he needs an antipsychotic (Section 4.10), a family who understand what is happening to him (Section 4.9), and a clinician who will keep watching how his illness unfolds. 4.5 The Rest of the Spectrum High yield · 10 Qs Schizophrenia sits at the centre of its chapter in DSM-5-TR, but it is surrounded by neighbours. Some of them have exactly the same symptoms and differ only in how long they last. Some have a narrower set of symptoms: a single fixed delusion, or a disturbance of movement. Some mix psychosis with a mood disorder. And some have the same symptoms but a cause that can be found: a drug, a medication, an inflamed brain. DSM-5-TR says that the chapter is organised along a gradient of psychopathology, and tells the clinician to work along it in order: first consider conditions that fall short of a full psychotic disorder or affect only one domain, then the time-limited conditions, and only then schizophrenia, after excluding the conditions that can give rise to psychosis. This section follows roughly that path, beginning with the disorders defined by the clock. A spectrum organised by time: brief psychotic disorder and schizophreniform disorder Fatima, 26, had been married for eight months and had moved from her parents' home in Lucknow to her husband's joint family in Pune when her father died suddenly of a heart attack. She travelled home for the funeral and came back to Pune a week later. Within three days she was sleeping barely two hours a night. She sat on the floor of the kitchen, frightened and bewildered, asking her mother-in-law where she was. She said she could hear her father calling her name from the terrace, then that the house was full of people who were not really people, then that her in-laws were mixing poison into her tea. One hour she laughed loudly; the next she wept and begged to be taken home. Her husband brought her to a general hospital psychiatry unit on the fifth day of the illness. A physical examination and blood tests found nothing, she had never taken alcohol or drugs, and she had no history of depression or mania. She was given a small dose of an antipsychotic and admitted for ten days. By the end of the third week she was sleeping normally, embarrassed by what she had said, grieving for her father in the ordinary way, and back to her usual self. What does Fatima have? Not schizophrenia: her illness lasted three weeks and left no trace. DSM-5-TR calls it brief psychotic disorder . The criteria are simple. Criterion A requires one or more of four symptoms, delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech (frequent derailment or incoherence), and grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, at least one of which must be one of the first three; a symptom does not count if it is a culturally sanctioned response. Notice that negative symptoms are not on the list: a few weeks of apathy cannot make a brief psychotic disorder. Criterion B is the defining one: an episode lasts at least one day but less than one month , with eventual full return to the premorbid level of functioning . Criterion C excludes depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features, other psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, catatonia, substances and medical conditions. Three specifiers describe the setting. With marked stressor(s) , also called brief reactive psychosis (the name of the disorder in DSM-III), applies when the symptoms occur in response to events that, singly or together, would be markedly stressful to almost anyone in similar circumstances in the person's culture; Fatima's sudden bereavement, so soon after leaving her own family, qualifies. Without marked stressor(s) applies when there is no such event. With peripartum onset applies when the illness begins during pregnancy or within four weeks after delivery; psychosis after childbirth is often an early form of bipolar disorder and is taught in Chapter 5. As with schizophrenia, catatonia and current severity can also be specified. The clinical picture is often dramatic. DSM-5-TR describes emotional turmoil or overwhelming confusion, with rapid shifts from one intense feeling to another, exactly what Fatima's family saw. Although the illness is short, impairment may be severe, and supervision may be needed to keep the person fed, clean and safe from acting on delusions; the risk of suicidal behaviour is raised during the acute episode. Brief psychotic disorder accounts for about 2 to 7 percent of first-onset psychoses. It can begin at any age, with an average onset in the mid-30s, later than schizophrenia. The outlook is mixed. By definition the episode remits within a month, and for most people social functioning and symptoms recover well, but more than half later have a relapse, and in a minority the diagnosis later changes, more often to a schizophrenia spectrum disorder than to a mood disorder. Two other differential points are worth knowing. In some people with personality disorders, borderline personality disorder above all, severe stress can bring brief psychotic experiences lasting hours; these do not usually warrant a separate diagnosis, but if they last at least a day, brief psychotic disorder may be added. And because the symptoms are short-lived and dramatic, factitious disorder and malingering have to be considered when there is a clear gain from appearing ill. Fatima's grief also raises a cultural question. In many cultures it is common for bereaved relatives to hear, see or speak with a recently dead person without any pathology following, and a single experience of hearing her father's voice would have meant nothing. What made Fatima psychotic was the whole picture: perplexity, persecutory delusions, disorganised behaviour and the collapse of her daily functioning. Now stretch the clock. Suppose Fatima's psychosis had not cleared at three weeks but had continued for three months, with voices and delusions and, by the second month, some flatness and withdrawal, and had then lifted completely. That illness meets the symptom criteria of schizophrenia (Criterion A) but not its duration, and DSM-5-TR calls it schizophreniform disorder . The criteria are those of schizophrenia with three differences. The episode, counting prodromal, active and residual phases, lasts at least one month but less than six months . There is no requirement of functional decline. And when the diagnosis must be made before the person has recovered, it is labelled provisional , because no one yet knows whether the illness will stop before six months. Ganesh in Section 4.4.7 is exactly such a case: if he is still ill at six months, his diagnosis becomes schizophrenia. The term goes back to the Norwegian psychiatrist Gabriel Langfeldt (Section 4.1), who in follow-up studies published in 1937 and 1939 divided the patients then called schizophrenic into two groups: a "true" or typical schizophrenia with a poor outcome, and the schizophreniform psychoses , which looked less typical and recovered. The idea was influential, but it had a curious fate. When Norwegian researchers re-examined Langfeldt's own schizophreniform cases fifty years later (Bergem and colleagues, 1990), they found that most of them did not look schizophrenia-like at all and were mainly mood disorders. The modern DSM category keeps Langfeldt's name and his interest in prognosis, but defines the disorder purely by duration. That interest in prognosis survives in a specifier. Schizophreniform disorder is coded with good prognostic features when at least two of the following are present: onset of prominent psychotic symptoms within four weeks of the first noticeable change in behaviour or functioning; confusion or perplexity at the height of the episode; good premorbid social and occupational functioning; and absence of blunted or flat affect. Otherwise it is coded without good prognostic features. Each of these four mirrors one of the classic predictors of a good outcome in schizophrenia itself (Section 4.6): acute onset, a confusional, affect-laden picture, a good life before the illness, and no negative symptoms. The course bears this out only partly. About a third of people first diagnosed with schizophreniform disorder (provisional) recover within six months and keep that diagnosis; most of the remaining two-thirds are eventually diagnosed with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. In the United States and other high-income countries schizophreniform disorder is uncommon, perhaps five times less common than schizophrenia, but in lower-income countries, DSM-5-TR notes, it may be more common, especially the form with good prognostic features, and in some settings may be as common as schizophrenia. That observation will matter when you meet the acute psychoses of the next subsection. Put the three DSM-5-TR disorders side by side and you have the duration ladder of Figure 4.8: the same psychotic symptoms are called brief psychotic disorder if they last a day to under a month, schizophreniform disorder if they last a month to under six months, and schizophrenia if they last six months or more. The ICD rungs are placed differently, which is why the figure shows both systems.
