Exam trap The official key to one IHBAS 2025 question calls psychosis "lasting for at least one month but less than six months" brief psychotic disorder . That is wrong. Brief psychotic disorder ends within a month (at least 1 day, less than 1 month, with full recovery). An illness with schizophrenia's symptoms lasting 1 to under 6 months is schizophreniform disorder . Schizoaffective disorder needs a major mood episode, delusional disorder has only delusions, and schizophrenia needs 6 months in DSM (the stem's wording, "grossly disorganized or abnormal motor behavior", is DSM-5's; under ICD-10 or ICD-11, with their one-month rule, the same illness would be schizophrenia). If you meet that exact question again with schizophreniform disorder absent from the options, know that the key given was brief psychotic disorder; whenever schizophreniform disorder is offered, choose it. Also remember: schizophreniform disorder does not require a decline in functioning, and brief psychotic disorder does not count negative symptoms. Acute and transient psychotic disorders: the ICD view If Fatima had been seen in a hospital that codes with ICD-10, as many Indian hospitals still do, she would not have received a diagnosis of brief psychotic disorder, because ICD-10 has no such category. She would have been given one of the acute and transient psychotic disorders (F23), a group the WHO introduced in 1992 to bring together acute psychoses of this kind, which clinicians in many countries, India among them, see often. The group is built on three key features, which ICD-10 lists in order of priority, and an expectation about recovery. First and most important, acute onset : a change from a state without psychotic features to a clearly abnormal psychotic state within two weeks or less (with "abrupt" onset, within 48 hours or less, recorded separately). Second, the presence of typical syndromes, either a rapidly changing, variable "polymorphic" state or one with typical schizophrenic symptoms. Third, the presence or absence of an associated acute stress, recorded with a fifth character: events that would be stressful to most people in the same culture, such as bereavement, the unexpected loss of a partner or a job, or the psychological trauma of combat, terrorism or torture, occurring within about two weeks before the first psychotic symptoms. Beyond these three, ICD-10 expects early recovery: complete recovery usually occurs within two to three months, often within a few weeks or even days. Organic causes, intoxication and mood episodes are excluded. The polymorphic picture is the heart of the concept. ICD-10 describes hallucinations, delusions and perceptual disturbances that are obvious but markedly variable, changing in type and intensity from day to day or even within a day, with emotional turmoil, intense transient feelings of happiness or ecstasy, or of anxiety and irritability, and often perplexity. Read that description beside Fatima's story and you will see that she fits it closely. The subtypes are shown in Table 4.19. They are separated by two things: whether the picture is polymorphic, schizophrenia-like or predominantly delusional, and how long it may last before the diagnosis must change. Table 4.19 Acute psychoses in ICD-10, ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR. Category Picture If it lasts longer ICD-10 F23.0 acute polymorphic psychotic disorder without symptoms of schizophrenia Variable, rapidly changing delusions, hallucinations and emotional turmoil; includes bouffée délirante and cycloid psychosis without schizophrenic symptoms Beyond 3 months: change the diagnosis (persistent delusional disorder or other psychosis) ICD-10 F23.1 acute polymorphic psychotic disorder with symptoms of schizophrenia Polymorphic picture plus typical schizophrenic symptoms; includes bouffée délirante and cycloid psychosis with schizophrenic symptoms Schizophrenic symptoms beyond 1 month: schizophrenia ICD-10 F23.2 acute schizophrenia-like psychotic disorder Stable schizophrenic symptoms without the polymorphic turmoil Beyond 1 month: schizophrenia ICD-10 F23.3 other acute predominantly delusional psychotic disorder Relatively stable delusions (often persecution or reference) or hallucinations Delusions beyond 3 months: persistent delusional disorder ICD-11 6A23 acute and transient psychotic disorder Onset without prodrome, maximal severity within 2 weeks; rapidly changing symptoms; perplexity; no negative symptoms Episode does not exceed 3 months (usually a few days to 1 month) DSM-5-TR brief psychotic disorder Any of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech or behaviour; full recovery 1 month or more: schizophreniform or another disorder The two polymorphic subtypes gathered up two older European ideas. In France, Valentin Magnan (1835 to 1916) and his followers in the 1880s described bouffée délirante , literally a "puff" or sudden gust of delusion: a delusional state that appears out of a clear sky in a previously well person, with fleeting, many-sided delusions and hallucinations, and clears within weeks or months, which they contrasted with the chronic, systematised delusional illnesses that led to deterioration. In Germany, Karl Kleist introduced the term cycloid psychosis in the 1920s (sources give 1926 or 1928) for phasic illnesses that came and went like manic-depressive illness, often swinging between contrasting poles, and left no defect; Karl Leonhard (1957) described three forms, the anxiety-happiness psychosis, the confusion psychosis and the motility psychosis, disturbing affect, thinking and movement respectively, and held that they belonged neither with schizophrenia nor with manic-depressive illness. Both concepts share what ICD-10 wanted to capture: sudden onset, a polymorphic picture and recovery. ICD-11 kept the category but trimmed it. Acute and transient psychotic disorder (6A23) is now restricted to the polymorphic form: an acute onset of psychotic symptoms that emerge without a prodrome and reach their maximal severity within two weeks; symptoms that may include delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking, perplexity or confusion, and disturbances of affect and mood, sometimes with catatonia-like disturbance; and above all symptoms that change rapidly in nature and intensity from day to day, or even within a single day. Negative symptoms must be absent during the episode. The episode does not exceed three months and most commonly lasts from a few days to a month. Acute presentations with stable schizophrenic symptoms are no longer placed here: the ICD-11 diagnostic guidance says that an illness meeting the requirements for schizophrenia except that it has lasted less than a month, with no previous history of schizophrenia, is coded as other specified primary psychotic disorder (6A2Y), not as acute and transient psychotic disorder, and if it lasts a month it is schizophrenia. The rule also works the other way. A fluctuating, polymorphic episode that has met the symptom requirements of schizophrenia for more than a month, but is still under three months and has no history of schizophrenia behind it, is coded as acute and transient psychotic disorder, not schizophrenia. ICD-11 also codes the course: first episode or multiple episodes, currently symptomatic or in partial or full remission. Key study: Susser and Wanderling's acute remitting psychoses (1994) Were acute, quickly remitting psychoses really commoner in poorer countries, or did psychiatrists there simply label them differently? Ezra Susser and Joseph Wanderling went back to the WHO Determinants of Outcome study (Section 4.6), which had counted every new case of psychosis in defined areas of several countries, and picked out what they called nonaffective acute remitting psychosis: psychosis of acute onset, without mood disorder, that remitted fully. Its incidence in the developing-country setting was about ten times that in the industrialised-country setting, and in men about half that in women, a pattern sharply different from that of schizophrenia, which varied little between settings or sexes. The conclusion was that these psychoses may be a distinct group with causes of their own; other studies have linked them to stress and to fever and infection. The criticism came partly from the same group: when Ramin Mojtabai, Vijoy Varma and Susser (2000) measured how long such psychoses lasted, the commonest duration was two to four months, so that few fitted the ICD-10 time limits, and the criteria have kept being adjusted. Indian context Acute and transient psychoses are a common diagnosis in Indian hospitals, especially among young women, and Indian psychiatrists have contributed much of the research on them. At the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, Das, Malhotra and Basu (1999) found that acute and transient psychotic disorder ran in families differently from schizophrenia, and the same group (2001) tested the stress-vulnerability idea in these disorders. The outcome is usually good, which is one reason why the better outcome of psychosis in India reported by the WHO studies (Section 4.6) has been questioned: part of the difference may reflect more acute, remitting illness rather than better recovery from the same illness. In the clinic, a sudden psychosis after a marriage, a death, an examination or a fever, in someone who was well a fortnight earlier, should make you think first of this category, and also of infection, delirium and drugs. Exam trap Two weeks is the ICD onset window for acute and transient psychotic disorder, not the minimum duration of schizophrenia. ICD-11 allows an acute and transient psychotic disorder to last up to 3 months , longer than DSM's brief psychotic disorder (under 1 month), so the two categories overlap but are not identical. Bouffée délirante is French (Magnan); cycloid psychosis is German (Kleist, Leonhard); both are folded into ICD-10 F23.0 (or F23.1 when schizophrenic symptoms are present). Schizoaffective disorder: when psychosis and mood run together Kraepelin's great division of 1899 separated a deteriorating psychosis (dementia praecox) from an episodic one (manic-depressive insanity). Almost at once clinicians began to meet patients who would not stay on either side of the line. In 1933 the American psychiatrist Jacob Kasanin published a paper called "The acute schizoaffective psychoses", describing a small group of young people whose illnesses began suddenly, often after a stress, with a striking mixture of schizophrenic and emotional symptoms, who had been well adjusted before, and who recovered. The word he coined has lasted, though the concept has changed almost beyond recognition. Kasanin's patients had a good outlook; today's schizoaffective disorder is usually a long illness whose prognosis, DSM-5-TR says, is somewhat better than that of schizophrenia but worse than that of the mood disorders. Bindu is a 31-year-old schoolteacher in Kochi. Her illness began four years ago, when over a few weeks she started to hear a woman's voice calling her a prostitute and became convinced that her colleagues had hidden cameras in the staffroom. Her mood at that time was not unusual. After about a month of this she became manic: she stopped sleeping, spent her salary on gifts for strangers, and announced that she had been chosen to reform the state's education system, while the voice continued. The mania lasted two months; when it settled, the voice and the belief about the cameras lingered for another three weeks before fading. A year later she had a severe depressive episode, during which the same voice told her that she deserved to die. Looking back over the four years, her treating team calculated that she had been in a manic or depressive episode for most of the time she had been ill, and that she had twice had periods of more than two weeks of psychosis with no mood episode at all. Bindu has schizoaffective disorder , and the DSM-5-TR criteria show why. Criterion A requires an uninterrupted period of illness during which a major mood episode, depressive or manic, is present at the same time as Criterion A of schizophrenia. If the mood episode is depressive it must include depressed mood itself; loss of interest or pleasure alone is not enough, because anhedonia is so common in schizophrenia that it would make every patient eligible. Criterion B requires delusions or hallucinations for two weeks or more in the absence of a major mood episode at some point in the lifetime of the illness. Criterion C requires that symptoms meeting criteria for a major mood episode be present for the majority of the total duration of the active and residual portions of the illness. Criterion D excludes substances and medical conditions. Schizophrenia's own Criteria B (functional decline), C (six months) and F (autism) need not be met. Each criterion has a job, and the jobs become clear if you set schizoaffective disorder between its two neighbours, as Figure 4.9 does. Criterion B separates it from a depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features, in which the psychosis appears only inside the mood episodes: a patient who has never been psychotic outside a mood episode cannot have schizoaffective disorder. Criterion C separates it from schizophrenia, in which mood episodes may occur but occupy only a minority of the illness. DSM-5-TR gives two worked examples. In one, a person has two months of hallucinations and persecutory delusions, then four months in which a full major depressive episode and the psychosis run together, then one month of psychosis alone after the depression lifts: seven months in all, with depression present for the majority, so the diagnosis is schizoaffective disorder. In the other, a person with a four-year history of schizophrenia develops depressive and manic episodes that together occupy no more than one year of the four: mood episodes for a minority, so the diagnosis stays schizophrenia. The majority rule was introduced in DSM-5; DSM-IV had asked only that mood symptoms be present for a "substantial" portion of the illness, and the change makes schizoaffective disorder a rarer diagnosis than it used to be. Depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features major mood episode psychosis Psychosis occurs only during the mood episode Schizoaffective disorder (DSM-5-TR) psychosis major mood episode psychosis alone for 2 weeks or more; mood episode for most of the illness Schizophrenia (with a brief mood episode) psychosis mood Mood episodes fill only a minority of the illness time Figure 4.9 Timing decides. The same two ingredients, psychosis and a major mood episode, give three different DSM-5-TR diagnoses depending on whether psychosis ever occurs outside the mood episode (Criterion B of schizoaffective disorder) and how much of the illness the mood episodes occupy (Criterion C). The type is specified by the mood episodes: the bipolar type applies if a manic episode is part of the presentation (major depressive episodes may also occur), as in Bindu's case, and the depressive type if only major depressive episodes occur. Catatonia, course (after one year) and current severity can be specified as in schizophrenia. Because the judgement depends on the proportion of mood to psychosis over the whole course, it needs a long view of the illness, often reconstructed from records and from relatives, and the diagnosis can legitimately change: a person diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder whose later years bring only residual psychosis may be rediagnosed with schizophrenia, and a person first diagnosed with a mood disorder may become schizoaffective when psychosis appears between episodes. Schizoaffective disorder is about a third as common as schizophrenia; a Finnish study estimated a lifetime prevalence of 0.3 percent, higher in women, under the looser DSM-IV criteria. It usually begins in early adulthood. The bipolar type may be commoner in young adults and the depressive type in older adults. The risk of schizoaffective disorder is raised in people who have a first-degree relative with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or schizoaffective disorder itself, and polygenic risk scores for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depression may all be raised, which is exactly what you would expect of a disorder that sits on the boundary. The lifetime risk of suicide in schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder together is about 5 percent, and depressive symptoms raise it. Treatment combines an antipsychotic with treatment of the mood episodes, a mood stabiliser for the bipolar type and an antidepressant where appropriate for the depressive type (Section 4.10 and Chapter 5). The ICD systems draw the boundary in a completely different place, and the difference is a favourite of examiners. ICD-10 (F25) and ICD-11 (6A21) define schizoaffective disorder by the episode , not the lifetime course. In ICD-11 the requirements for schizophrenia must be met at the same time as those for a moderate or severe depressive episode, a manic episode or a mixed episode, with the psychotic and mood symptoms starting simultaneously or within a few days of each other, and lasting at least a month. ICD-10 similarly required definite schizophrenic and definite affective symptoms to be prominent simultaneously, or within a few days, in the same episode, and it had manic, depressive and mixed types; it explicitly excluded people whose schizophrenic and affective symptoms appeared only in different episodes. Consider a young man whose first and only illness begins with mania and thought insertion on the same day and ends with both a month later. ICD-10 calls this schizoaffective disorder, manic type (F25.0); ICD-11, which has no manic or depressive types, codes it as schizoaffective disorder (6A21) provided the full requirements for schizophrenia (two symptoms, at least one of them core, for a month) were met alongside the mania. DSM-5-TR cannot, because he has never had two weeks of psychosis without a mood episode; his DSM diagnosis is bipolar I disorder with mood-incongruent psychotic features. Exam trap DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder = a major mood episode concurrent with Criterion A of schizophrenia, plus at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations without a major mood episode , with mood episodes present for the majority of the illness. The two weeks are of psychosis without mood, not mood without psychosis. Wrong options: "mood symptoms only during acute psychosis" (that describes a mood disorder with psychotic features turned round), "lifetime absence of psychosis", "bipolar features only" (there is also a depressive type). Jacob Kasanin coined the term in 1933. ICD (F25, 6A21) uses the single episode, with onset of both kinds of symptom within a few days of each other. Delusional disorder: one false belief in an otherwise ordinary life Raghav is 56, a retired bank officer in Madurai, and for two years he has been certain that his wife is having an affair with the son-in-law of the family next door. His evidence is a collection of small things: the neighbour's scooter was parked facing their gate; his wife changed the way she tied her hair; there was a crease on her sari after she came back from the temple. He checks her phone each night, times her trips to the market and has twice followed her. When she weeps and denies it, he takes her tears as proof of guilt. Yet in every other way Raghav is unchanged. He keeps the household accounts, attends the meetings of his pensioners' association, talks sensibly about cricket and politics, and has no voices, no disorganisation of speech and no flattening of feeling. He drinks no alcohol, has never been depressed or manic, and his memory is good. He has come to the clinic only because his wife's brother insisted, and what he wants from the doctor is help in making her confess. Raghav has delusional disorder , jealous type. Its DSM-5-TR criteria tell you what it is by telling you what it is not. Criterion A: one or more delusions lasting one month or longer. Criterion B: Criterion A for schizophrenia has never been met; hallucinations, if present, are not prominent and are related to the delusional theme, such as a sensation of insects crawling in someone convinced he is infested. Criterion C: apart from the impact of the delusion and its ramifications, functioning is not markedly impaired and behaviour is not obviously bizarre or odd. Criterion D: if manic or major depressive episodes have occurred, they have been brief relative to the delusional periods. Criterion E: the disturbance is not due to a substance or medical condition and is not better explained by another mental disorder, such as body dysmorphic or obsessive-compulsive disorder. Since DSM-5 the delusion no longer has to be non-bizarre; a specifier, with bizarre content , records a delusion that is clearly implausible, not understandable and not derived from ordinary life experience. As with schizophrenia, course specifiers may be added after a year and severity may be rated. The disorder has a long history under another name. Kraepelin used paranoia (Section 4.1) for an insidiously developing, permanent and unshakeable delusional system, with clear and orderly thinking, willing and acting completely preserved, which he set apart both from dementia praecox and from paraphrenia , his term for patients with delusions and hallucinations whose personality remained relatively intact. Later the British psychiatrist Martin Roth , working in the 1950s, described late paraphrenia, a paranoid psychosis beginning in old age, often in women living alone and in people with impaired hearing. ICD-10 still listed paranoia, paranoid state and late paraphrenia among the inclusion terms of its delusional disorder. The type is named by the theme of the delusion, and Table 4.20 lists the seven. Three of them have eponyms that examiners like. Erotomania is also called de Clérambault's syndrome , after the French psychiatrist Gaëtan Gatian de Clérambault (1872 to 1934), who described it in detail in the 1920s; his best-known patient was a woman convinced that King George V of Britain was in love with her, who waited for hours outside Buckingham Palace and read the movement of a curtain as a signal from him. Pathological jealousy was named the Othello syndrome by the British psychiatrists John Todd and Kenneth Dewhurst in 1955, after Shakespeare's Moor, whose jealousy is built from a handkerchief. And the somatic delusion of being infested by insects or parasites, delusional parasitosis , is also called Ekbom's syndrome after the Swedish neurologist Karl-Axel Ekbom , who described it in 1938; such patients often arrive at a skin clinic, not a psychiatric one, bringing "specimens" of the parasites in a matchbox. Table 4.20 The types of delusional disorder in DSM-5-TR. Type Central theme Notes Erotomanic Another person, usually of higher status (a film star, a politician, a superior at work), is in love with the patient De Clérambault's syndrome; attempts at contact, stalking, legal trouble Grandiose The patient has a great but unrecognised talent or insight, or has made an important discovery May be religious, or a special relationship with a famous person Jealous The spouse or lover is unfaithful, inferred from small bits of "evidence" Othello syndrome; probably commoner in men; confrontation and violence Persecutory Being conspired against, cheated, spied on, followed, poisoned or drugged, maligned, harassed or obstructed The commonest type; resentment, repeated litigation, violence Somatic Bodily functions or sensations: emitting a foul odour, infestation by insects, an internal parasite, a part of the body not working Delusional parasitosis (Ekbom's syndrome) Mixed No single theme predominates Unspecified The dominant belief cannot be determined or is not one of the above For example referential delusions without a persecutory or grandiose element What is it like to talk to someone with delusional disorder? The most striking thing, DSM-5-TR says, is how normal the person seems when the delusion is not being discussed or acted on. Raghav could sit beside you on a bus for an hour without you noticing anything. Some patients have what DSM-5-TR calls factual insight without true insight: Raghav knows perfectly well that his wife's family think he is imagining things, but he cannot accept that they are right. The delusions differ in quality from those of schizophrenia. In schizophrenia they tend to be more disorganised, less internally consistent and less systematised; in delusional disorder they show greater conviction, greater extension into the different areas of the person's life, and greater pressure, meaning preoccupation and concern. Irritable or dysphoric mood is common and is often an understandable reaction to the belief. Anger and violence can occur with the persecutory, jealous and erotomanic types, and persecuted patients may write hundreds of letters to the authorities or bring case after case to court (the litigious or querulous form). Legal difficulties are commonest in the jealous and erotomanic types. Delusional disorder is uncommon. A Finnish study put its lifetime prevalence at about 0.2 percent, with the persecutory type the most frequent. There are no major sex differences overall, though the jealous type is probably commoner in men, and men tend to have more severe symptoms and worse functional outcomes. It may be more common in older people, and global functioning is generally better than in schizophrenia. The diagnosis is generally stable once established, but about a third of people with delusional disorder of one to three months' duration are later diagnosed with schizophrenia, whereas the diagnosis is much less likely to change once the disorder has lasted six to twelve months. It runs in families with schizophrenia and schizotypal personality disorder. The ICD systems demand more time. ICD-10 grouped the persistent delusional disorders under F22: delusional disorder (F22.0) needed delusions present for at least three months, clearly personal rather than shared by the person's subculture, with no more than occasional transitory voices and no history of schizophrenic symptoms; other persistent delusional disorders (F22.8) included delusional dysmorphophobia and the litigious paranoia querulans. ICD-11 delusional disorder (6A24) similarly requires a delusion or set of related delusions typically persisting for at least three months and often much longer, in the absence of a depressive, manic or mixed episode and of the other characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia (persistent hallucinations, negative symptoms, disorganised thinking and experiences of influence, passivity or control), although perceptual disturbances related to the delusional theme are allowed. Apart from actions and attitudes directly related to the delusion, affect, speech and behaviour are typically unaffected. The differential diagnosis follows from the criteria. If other psychotic symptoms appear, think of schizophrenia; if the delusions occur only during mood episodes, of a mood disorder with psychotic features; if they began in later life with memory loss, of a neurocognitive disorder; if with a drug such as cocaine or amphetamine, of substance-induced psychosis. Pathological jealousy in particular is common in alcohol use disorder, so a drinking history is essential. If the fixed belief is about contamination, symmetry or a perceived flaw in appearance, the diagnosis is obsessive-compulsive or body dysmorphic disorder with absent insight. And paranoid personality disorder, a lifelong suspicious and grudging style, falls short of delusion: the person mistrusts everyone but holds no single fixed false belief (Chapter 11). Treatment is difficult chiefly because the patient does not think he is ill. Antipsychotic medication helps some patients, and cognitive behavioural approaches to delusions (Book 2, Section 5.6) can loosen the hold of the belief, but often the realistic goal is to reduce distress, risk and conflict rather than to remove the delusion. Clinical link With a patient like Raghav, do not argue with the delusion and do not pretend to share it. Arguing ends the conversation; agreeing confirms the belief and betrays the spouse. Work instead with what he does accept: his sleeplessness, his anger, the strain at home. Always ask directly about risk. Delusional jealousy can lead to violence against the partner or the imagined rival, and erotomania to stalking; where the risk is serious, the partner's safety comes first, and temporary separation may be needed (Book 2, Section 2.7, on violence risk). Exam trap The belief that a celebrity or person of higher status is secretly in love with the patient is the erotomanic type (de Clérambault's syndrome), not grandiose, persecutory or somatic. Othello syndrome is jealous type; delusional parasitosis (Ekbom's syndrome) is somatic type; the commonest type is persecutory . Do not confuse these with the delusional misidentification syndromes taught in Chapter 2: Capgras (a familiar person replaced by an impostor), Fregoli (strangers are a familiar persecutor in disguise) and Cotard (nihilistic delusions of being dead or having no organs). DSM-5-TR delusional disorder needs only 1 month ; ICD-10 and ICD-11 need about 3 months . Since DSM-5 the delusion may be bizarre. Shared psychotic disorder: folie à deux In 1877 two Paris physicians, Charles Lasègue (1816 to 1883) and Jules Falret (1824 to 1902), published a paper called "La folie à deux ou folie communiquée", the madness of two, or communicated madness. They described something that seemed to contradict everything known about psychosis: a delusion passing from one person to another, as if it were an infection. Their cases followed a pattern that has been confirmed many times since. One partner, the primary (also called the inducer, or the active partner), has a genuine psychotic illness with an established delusion. The other, the secondary (the induced or passive partner), comes to share it. The two have lived together for a long time in close intimacy and are cut off from other people, by language, culture, geography or their own withdrawal, so that the primary's voice is the only one the secondary hears. The primary is usually the more dominant and often the more intelligent; the secondary is more passive, dependent and suggestible. The shared belief is usually persecutory or grandiose, and it is usually plausible rather than fantastic, built on fears or hopes the two already shared. Most pairs are relatives: two sisters, husband and wife, a parent and a child. The most useful observation Lasègue and Falret made was about treatment. When the pair is separated, the secondary partner's belief often fades within weeks, while the primary's does not. Consider a widow in her sixties with a long-standing persecutory delusion that a neighbour is pumping gas into her flat, and her unmarried daughter, who has looked after her for twenty years and has helped her seal the windows with newspaper. When the daughter is admitted to a medical ward with pneumonia and spends three weeks away from her mother, she begins to wonder aloud whether the smell might have come from the drain after all. The mother, meanwhile, is as certain as ever. Separation is therefore both a test and a treatment: it shows who is the primary, and it often frees the secondary. The primary partner needs treatment of her own psychotic disorder; the secondary may need brief support, sometimes a short course of an antipsychotic, and both need help when they are reunited. Later authors divided the phenomenon into forms, which still appear in examinations: Folie imposée , the classic form of Lasègue and Falret: the delusion of a psychotic person is imposed on a previously healthy partner, and the secondary's belief usually disappears on separation. Folie simultanée : two predisposed people, living closely together, develop the same psychosis at about the same time, each triggering the other; there is no clear dominant partner, and separation may help neither. Folie communiquée : the secondary resists for a long time, then adopts the delusion, develops it further, and keeps it even after separation. Folie induite : a person who is already psychotic adds the delusions of another psychotic person to his own, as can happen between two patients in hospital. When three people share the delusion the term is folie à trois, with four folie à quatre, when a whole family is involved folie à famille (also written folie en famille), and with several people folie à plusieurs. The classifications have handled the condition very differently. ICD-10 coded it as induced delusional disorder (F24), with three requirements: two or more people share the same delusion or delusional system and support one another in the belief; they have an unusually close relationship; and there is temporal or other contextual evidence that the delusion was induced in the passive member or members by contact with the active partner. DSM-IV called it shared psychotic disorder . DSM-5 abolished the separate category. If the secondary partner meets the criteria for delusional disorder, that is the diagnosis; if not, the presentation is recorded as other specified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorder, using the example DSM-5-TR names "delusional symptoms in the context of relationship with an individual with prominent delusions", in which the delusional material from the person with a psychotic disorder provides the content of the same delusions held by the other person, who may not otherwise meet criteria for a psychotic disorder. ICD-11 also has no separate code: "induced delusional disorder" is an index term of delusional disorder (6A24), within the block of schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders, and the ICD-11 diagnostic guidance for 6A24 notes that delusional disorder may rarely occur at the same time in two people with a strong emotional or situational link, "often referred to as shared or induced Delusional Disorder or folie à deux", with the delusion often remitting in the less dominant person when the two are separated. Exam trap Folie à deux is the transmission of a delusion from a primary person with an established psychotic disorder to a previously healthier, more passive person in a close and usually isolated relationship . It is not two people having independent psychotic episodes at the same time, not a brief stress psychosis in two relatives, not a belief shared by a whole cultural, religious or subcultural group (that is a shared belief, not a delusion), not group hallucinations in a cult, not mass psychogenic illness, and not schizophrenia passed on genetically. ICD-10 code: F24 induced delusional disorder (F21 is schizotypal disorder, F23 the acute and transient psychoses). In DSM-5-TR it falls under delusional disorder or other specified schizophrenia spectrum disorder; in ICD-11 under delusional disorder (6A24), among the "schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders", not as a separate category and not under schizoaffective or schizotypal disorder; that is why a key of "other primary psychotic disorders (induced delusional disorder)" is accepted. Some textbooks, Barlow and Durand among them, say that DSM-5 added a "shared" specifier to delusional disorder; neither DSM-5 nor DSM-5-TR contains such a specifier. Psychosis with a known cause: substances, medications and medical illness Every disorder so far has been a primary psychosis, one for which no external cause can be found. The last two members of the DSM-5-TR spectrum are the secondary psychoses, in which the cause is known. They matter for two reasons. They are common, and they are often reversible if the cause is found and treated. Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder requires delusions or hallucinations or both (Criterion A), with evidence from the history, examination or laboratory findings that they developed during or soon after intoxication or withdrawal, or after exposure to or withdrawal from a medication, and that the substance can produce such symptoms (Criterion B). Criterion C asks whether an independent psychotic disorder would explain the picture better, and lists the signs that it would: symptoms that began before the substance use; symptoms that persist for a substantial period, about a month, after acute withdrawal or severe intoxication has ended; or a history of recurrent episodes unrelated to substances. The disturbance must not occur only during a delirium (Criterion D) and must cause distress or impairment (Criterion E). The onset is specified as during intoxication, during withdrawal or after medication use. One subtle point: if a person hallucinates but knows that the experience comes from the drug, reality testing is intact, and the diagnosis is not a psychotic disorder but intoxication or withdrawal "with perceptual disturbances". The substances that can produce psychosis during intoxication are alcohol, cannabis, the hallucinogens (including phencyclidine), inhalants, sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics, and stimulants including cocaine; those that can produce it during withdrawal are alcohol and the sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics. Each has its own flavour. Amphetamines and cocaine can bring persecutory delusions within hours, sometimes with the hallucination of insects crawling under the skin (formication), which leads to scratching and excoriations. Cannabis can produce persecutory delusions with marked anxiety, emotional lability and depersonalisation, usually remitting within a day. Alcohol-induced psychosis with hallucinations, the old alcoholic hallucinosis , usually follows prolonged heavy drinking in people with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder, and the hallucinations are generally voices heard in clear consciousness. The list of medications that can cause psychosis is long: corticosteroids, anticholinergic drugs, antiparkinsonian drugs, anticonvulsants, some antimicrobial and cardiovascular drugs, and many others. Between 7 and 25 percent of people presenting with a first episode of psychosis in different settings are reported to have a substance or medication-induced disorder. And the label is not always the end of the story: in a Danish registry study that followed people with substance-induced psychosis for 20 years, about a third were later diagnosed with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder (26 percent) or a bipolar disorder (8 percent), and the rate was highest, 44 percent, for cannabis-induced psychosis. The drugs themselves, their intoxication and withdrawal syndromes, and the evidence linking cannabis to schizophrenia (Section 4.7) are taught in Chapter 10. Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition requires prominent hallucinations or delusions, evidence that they are the direct physiological consequence of another medical condition, and that they are not better explained by another mental disorder, do not occur only during a delirium, and cause distress or impairment. It is specified as with delusions or with hallucinations, depending on which predominates. The three questions of biological plausibility, temporality and typicality, and the list of causes, were given in Section 4.4.6. Two further points complete the picture. The diagnosis is not made if the person keeps reality testing for the hallucinations and understands that they come from the illness, and a psychotic reaction that is a psychological response to a frightening illness, rather than a physiological effect of it, is a brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor. In epilepsy, psychosis may be ictal, postictal or interictal; postictal psychosis is the commonest, seen in about 2 to 7.8 percent of people with epilepsy. Lifetime prevalence of the disorder has been estimated at 0.21 to 0.54 percent in Swedish and Finnish studies, rising in older people, and in late life Alzheimer's disease is commonly accompanied by psychosis and psychosis is a defining feature of Lewy body disease. The ICD names are different but the logic is the same. ICD-10 coded psychotic disorders due to psychoactive substances within the substance block (F10 to F19, with the fourth character .5), and medical causes as organic hallucinosis (F06.0) or organic delusional disorder (F06.2). ICD-11 codes substance-induced psychotic disorders in the chapter on substance use, and psychosis due to a medical condition as secondary psychotic syndrome (6E61). Because the word "primary" in ICD-11's block title means "not secondary to a substance or medical condition", this is the distinction the WHO wants clinicians to make first. Exam trap A psychosis that continues for about a month or more after the drug has been stopped suggests an independent psychotic disorder, not a substance-induced one. Hallucinations that the person recognises as drug-induced are not a psychotic disorder (they are intoxication or withdrawal with perceptual disturbances). Psychosis occurring only during delirium is part of the delirium. And a medical patient whose psychosis is an emotional reaction to the illness has a brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor, not a psychotic disorder due to the medical condition. Catatonia across the disorders When Karl Kahlbaum described catatonia in 1874 (Section 4.1) he regarded it as a disease in its own right, often with a cyclical course that included melancholy and excitement. Kraepelin absorbed it into dementia praecox, and for most of the twentieth century catatonia was taught as a subtype of schizophrenia. The clinical evidence slowly undid this. Catatonia turned out to be common in mood disorders, in medical and neurological illness and in autism, and to respond dramatically to benzodiazepines, which do little for the psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia. DSM-5-TR now states that catatonia occurs in up to 35 percent of people with schizophrenia, but that the majority of catatonia cases involve people with depressive or bipolar disorders; in clinical samples about 9 percent of patients show catatonia. DSM-5 (2013) drew the logical conclusion. It does not treat catatonia as an independent class of disorder but recognises it in three forms: catatonia associated with another mental disorder , which works as a catatonia specifier attached to a neurodevelopmental, psychotic, bipolar, depressive or other mental disorder (schizophrenia with catatonia, major depressive disorder with catatonia); catatonic disorder due to another medical condition ; and unspecified catatonia , used when the underlying condition is unclear, full criteria are not met, or there is not enough information, as in an emergency department. For the first two, the same criterion applies: the clinical picture is dominated by three or more of twelve psychomotor features, listed in Table 4.21. How each sign looks at the bedside, and the related signs such as automatic obedience and Mitgehen, are described in Section 4.2. In catalepsy the examiner puts the arm in a position and the patient leaves it there; in posturing the patient adopts the posture himself; in waxy flexibility the examiner feels a slight, even resistance as he moves the limb, like bending a soft candle. The table also shows why catatonia is so easily missed. Its signs point in opposite directions, from complete stillness to purposeless excitement, and the same person can swing between the two; DSM-5-TR warns that teaching has overemphasised rare, dramatic signs such as waxy flexibility, so that the commoner quiet forms, mutism, negativism and staring, go unrecognised. The consequences of missing it can be grave: a person in catatonic stupor may stop eating and drinking and is at risk of malnutrition, exhaustion, blood clots, pressure ulcers, contractures and high fever. Many medical conditions can cause catatonia: neurological illnesses such as tumours, head injury, stroke and encephalitis (anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis among them), and metabolic disturbances such as hypercalcaemia, hepatic encephalopathy, homocystinuria and diabetic ketoacidosis. Catatonia occurring only during a delirium is not diagnosed separately. In a patient taking an antipsychotic, two medication effects must be considered before the word catatonia is used: acute dystonia, which can produce abnormal postures, and above all neuroleptic malignant syndrome , which can look catatonic but comes with fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and abnormal laboratory findings (Section 4.10). The resemblance is not accidental. In 1934 the German psychiatrist Karl Stauder described malignant catatonia (he called it lethal catatonia), a catatonic state with high fever, autonomic instability and stupor that was often fatal before modern treatment; many authorities regard neuroleptic malignant syndrome as a drug-induced form of malignant catatonia. Because antipsychotics can worsen catatonia or precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome, they are generally held back while catatonia is being treated. The treatment of catatonia is one of the most satisfying in psychiatry. The lorazepam challenge is both a diagnostic test and the first step of treatment: a benzodiazepine, usually lorazepam in a dose of 1 to 2 mg given intravenously or intramuscularly, is followed within minutes to hours by a clear improvement in a majority of patients, and a positive response supports the diagnosis. Regular benzodiazepine treatment is then continued. When benzodiazepines fail, and in malignant catatonia, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is highly effective and can be life-saving (ECT is described in Chapter 5). Severity is rated with instruments such as the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (1996), described in the Assessment book. The underlying disorder, whether depression, mania, schizophrenia or a medical illness, must of course be treated as well. The ICD systems have followed the same path. ICD-10 still had catatonic schizophrenia (F20.2) and an organic catatonic disorder (F06.1). ICD-11 created a separate grouping for catatonia, with catatonia associated with another mental disorder (6A40), catatonia induced by substances or medications, and a secondary catatonia syndrome for medical causes, so that catatonia is no longer tied to schizophrenia in either system. Exam trap In DSM-5, catatonia is a specifier across several disorders (psychotic, bipolar, depressive, neurodevelopmental and others), plus catatonic disorder due to another medical condition and unspecified catatonia. It is not an independent disorder, not a personality disorder, and not a subtype of bipolar disorder or of schizophrenia. Three of twelve signs are needed. Catatonia is more often associated with mood disorders than with schizophrenia. First-line treatment is a benzodiazepine (lorazepam), then ECT; antipsychotics are not the first step. At the edges: attenuated psychosis, the high-risk state and schizotypal disorder Most people who develop schizophrenia pass through a prodrome first (Section 4.6). If that prodrome could be recognised, could treatment begin before the first full episode, and could the episode even be prevented? That question drove one of the most debated proposals in DSM-5. Attenuated psychosis syndrome is described in Section III of DSM-5-TR, among the conditions for further study, which means it is a research proposal, not an official diagnosis. Its proposed criteria are: at least one of attenuated delusions, attenuated hallucinations or attenuated disorganised speech, severe or frequent enough to warrant clinical attention (A); present at least once a week for the past month (B); begun or worsened in the past year (C); distressing and disabling enough to warrant attention (D); not better explained by another disorder, including a mood disorder with psychotic features, or by a substance or medical condition (E); and the criteria for a psychotic disorder never having been met (F). What makes a symptom "attenuated"? It is psychosis-like but below the threshold. The experiences are less severe and more transient, and the person keeps reasonable insight: doubt about the belief can be elicited, and scepticism about the perception can be induced, by a question such as "I see that this is how you experience the world; could there be a different explanation?" A young woman who has begun to feel that strangers on the bus may be watching her, but who can say that it is probably her imagination, has an attenuated persecutory idea; if she becomes certain, the threshold has been crossed. The research findings are sobering in both directions. In help-seeking groups meeting the criteria, the three-year cumulative risk of developing psychosis was up to 22 percent, against 1.54 percent in those who did not meet them, and over ten years the risk of transition was 34.9 percent; most who made the transition developed a schizophrenia spectrum disorder (73 percent), a minority an affective psychosis (11 percent). Overall, DSM-5-TR summarises, about a third develop psychosis, a third remit and a third remain disabled. In other words, the syndrome identifies people at real risk, but most of them will not become psychotic, which is one reason the proposal was kept in Section III: labelling and treating everyone with attenuated symptoms would expose many people to stigma and to medication they would never have needed. In clinical practice the presentation can be recorded in Section II as other specified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorder. The proposal grew out of the clinical high-risk state (also called the ultra-high-risk or at-risk mental state), identified largely at a clinic for young people in Melbourne, Australia, by Patrick McGorry , Alison Yung and their colleagues in the mid-1990s. Their criteria take three routes: attenuated psychotic symptoms; brief limited intermittent psychotic symptoms, that is frank psychotic symptoms that resolve on their own within about a week; and a genetic risk, such as a first-degree relative with psychosis, combined with a recent decline in functioning. Specialised interviews for the high-risk state are described in the Assessment book, and the early intervention services built on this work are outlined in Section 4.10. On the other side of attenuated psychosis lies a stable trait rather than a changing state. Schizotypal personality disorder, a lifelong pattern of social and interpersonal deficits with odd beliefs, unusual perceptions and eccentric behaviour below the psychotic threshold, is listed in the DSM-5-TR psychotic disorders chapter because it belongs to the schizophrenia spectrum, but its criteria are given in the chapter on personality disorders (Chapter 11). The WHO goes further. ICD-10 placed schizotypal disorder (F21) beside schizophrenia, not among the personality disorders, requiring typical features continuously or episodically for at least two years, and ICD-11 keeps it in the schizophrenia block as 6A22. The difference between it and attenuated psychosis syndrome is the difference between a climate and the weather: schizotypy is how the person has always been, attenuated psychosis is a recent change. Finally, DSM-5-TR provides two residual categories. Other specified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorder is used when the clinician wants to record why the criteria are not met, and the manual gives four examples: persistent auditory hallucinations with no other features; persistent delusions with overlapping mood episodes that are too long for delusional disorder; attenuated psychosis syndrome; and delusional symptoms in the partner of a person with prominent delusions, the old folie à deux. Unspecified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorder is used when the reason is not specified or the information is insufficient, as in the emergency room. Three related presentations are taught elsewhere in this book: postpartum psychosis in Chapter 5, possession and trance states and the culture-bound syndromes in Chapter 7, and delirium and the psychoses of dementia in Chapter 10. The first is "Why him?" The second, asked more quietly, is "Will he get better?" The first question is about causes, and Sections 4.7 to 4.9 deal with it. This section answers the questions that come before and after it. Who develops schizophrenia: how many people, at what age, of which sex, in what places and circumstances? And what happens after the illness begins: how does it unfold over months and decades, how many people recover, what predicts a good or a poor course, and why did the World Health Organization find, to everyone's surprise, that patients in Agra and Chandigarh did better than patients in Europe and the United States? These are the facts of epidemiology , the study of how a disorder is distributed in populations, and of prognosis , the expected course and outcome of an illness. They matter in the examination hall, and they matter even more at the bedside, because a family's hope depends on them. How common is schizophrenia? Before counting cases we need three different ways of counting, because examiners like to swap them. Prevalence is the proportion of a population that has the disorder: at one moment (point prevalence), during a stated period such as the past year (12-month prevalence), or at any time in their lives so far (lifetime prevalence). Incidence is the rate at which new cases arise, usually expressed as new cases per 100,000 people per year. The lifetime morbid risk is the probability that a person will develop the disorder if they live through the whole age range in which it usually begins; it is "age-corrected", which means that people who are still young, and so may yet fall ill, are counted in a way that allows for the years of risk they have not lived through. Prevalence tells a health planner how many beds and clinics are needed today; incidence tells a researcher whether a cause is operating more strongly in one place or one period than another; morbid risk is the figure a worried relative is really asking about. The number almost every textbook repeats is that schizophrenia affects about 1 percent of people at some point in their lives. It is a useful round figure and the one most multiple-choice papers expect. The more careful figure in DSM-5-TR (2022) is a lifetime prevalence of approximately 0.3 to 0.7 percent , with a fivefold variation between the nationally representative surveys that were pooled. Barlow and Durand give a range of 0.2 to 1.5 percent and conclude that the disorder will affect about 1 percent of the population. The most careful pooling of the world literature came from the Australian epidemiologist John McGrath and colleagues, who summarised their systematic reviews in 2008: the median incidence was 15.2 new cases per 100,000 people per year (the middle 80 percent of studies lay between 7.7 and 43.0), and the median lifetime morbid risk was 7.2 per 1,000, a little under 1 percent. Notice the size of these numbers. In a district of one million people, about 150 people develop schizophrenia every year, and at any given time several thousand are living with it. Why do the estimates differ so much? Partly because studies define the disorder differently (a narrow definition that requires six months of illness yields fewer cases than one that accepts a single month), partly because some surveys count only people in treatment, and partly because the risk genuinely varies with place and population, as you will see in Section 4.6.3. DSM-5-TR adds a fourth reason: some groups are more likely to be misdiagnosed or overdiagnosed, so a high rate in a minority community may partly reflect the diagnostician rather than the illness. For India, the best figures come from the National Mental Health Survey of 2015 to 2016, carried out by the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS) in 12 states. It found a lifetime prevalence of 1.41 percent and a current prevalence of 0.42 percent for "schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders", a broader group than schizophrenia alone. The same survey found that roughly three in every four people with a current psychotic disorder were receiving no treatment, a figure known as the treatment gap . In a country of more than a billion people, that gap means millions of untreated people, most of them living with their families. Exam trap The round answer for lifetime risk is about 1 percent ; DSM-5-TR's own figure is 0.3 to 0.7 percent . If both appear as options, read the stem: "according to DSM-5-TR" points to 0.3 to 0.7. Do not confuse prevalence (existing cases) with incidence (new cases per year). And do not repeat the old claim that the incidence of schizophrenia is "identical in every culture": the WHO ten-country study found that, with its broad definition of the illness, incidence varied almost threefold between centres (from about 1.5 to 4.2 new cases per 10,000 a year), a statistically significant difference, and later reviews (McGrath and colleagues) found more variation still. Who falls ill: age and sex Schizophrenia is above all a disorder of young adults . DSM-5-TR states that the psychotic features typically emerge between the late teens and the mid-30s and that onset before adolescence is rare. The peak age of onset is the early to mid-20s for men and the late 20s for women. Think about what that timing means. The illness usually strikes just as a person is finishing college, starting a first job, moving away from home or getting married, so it interrupts the very years in which an adult life is built. That is one reason why schizophrenia, though less common than depression, causes such a large share of the world's disability. The age rule has edges worth knowing. Childhood-onset schizophrenia , beginning before about 13 years, is very rare; DSM-5-TR notes that in children delusions and hallucinations are less elaborate, visual hallucinations are commoner, and the disorganised speech and behaviour must not be confused with the far commoner autism spectrum disorder or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (Chapter 3). Childhood-onset cases tend to resemble poor-outcome adult cases, with gradual onset and prominent negative symptoms. At the other end, late-onset schizophrenia , beginning after 40, is overrepresented by women, and is often marked by persecutory delusions and hallucinations with relatively preserved affect and social functioning. An international consensus in 2000 suggested calling onset after 60 "very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis", because at that age a new psychosis is so often linked to brain disease, sensory loss or dementia (Chapter 10) that it may not be the same condition. The sex difference is one of the most consistent findings in psychiatry, and it is more subtle than "men get it more". McGrath's reviews found that the incidence in men is about 1.4 times that in women. Yet over a whole lifetime the prevalence is roughly equal, and a large worldwide study cited in DSM-5-TR found no sex difference in prevalence at all. How can both be true? Because women fall ill later. Barlow and Durand, summarising Assen Jablensky's work, note that new cases are commoner in men until about age 36, after which the balance switches, and women contribute more of the cases that begin in midlife. DSM-5-TR adds that the sex ratio depends on the definition: definitions that emphasise negative symptoms and long duration give higher rates in men, while definitions that admit more mood symptoms and brief illnesses give equal rates. Why should women fall ill later? The leading explanation is the oestrogen hypothesis , associated especially with the German psychiatrist Heinz Häfner and his ABC (Age, Beginning and Course) study in Mannheim. Oestrogen appears to dampen dopamine sensitivity and may protect a vulnerable brain. DSM-5-TR lists the clinical observations that fit: psychotic symptoms worsen in the premenstrual days when oestrogen falls, admissions rise just before and during menstruation, symptoms tend to improve in pregnancy when oestrogen is high and to worsen after delivery when it drops sharply, and the falling oestrogen of the menopause may explain the second peak of onset in women in midlife , around 45 years. The sexes also differ in the shape of the illness. Men, especially those with a long period of untreated psychosis and poor adjustment before the illness, have more negative symptoms, more cognitive impairment and generally worse functional outcomes. Women show more mood-laden symptoms, less disorganisation, fewer negative symptoms and better preserved social functioning, though DSM-5-TR warns that there are frequent exceptions. Exam trap "Schizophrenia is most commonly found in" has the answer young adults , not adolescents (onset before adolescence is rare and the peak is in the 20s), not the middle-aged (only the smaller second peak in women) and not the elderly. Men: early to mid-20s. Women: late 20s, with a second peak around the menopause. Incidence is somewhat higher in men (about 1.4 to 1); lifetime prevalence is roughly equal . Men have the worse outcome. Where and when: place, migration, season and social class If schizophrenia were purely a matter of genes, its rate would be the same in a Danish city and a Danish village. It is not. The most convincing demonstration came from Denmark, which keeps national registers of births, addresses and psychiatric admissions. In 1999 Preben Bo Mortensen and colleagues followed 1.75 million Danes and identified 2,669 cases of schizophrenia. A parent or sibling with schizophrenia raised a person's risk about seven to nine times, which was expected. More surprising, being born in the capital, Copenhagen, rather than in a rural area raised the risk 2.4 times, and the season of birth mattered too: risk was highest for people born in February and March and lowest for those born in August and September. The authors then calculated the population attributable risk , the share of all cases in the population that would disappear if a risk factor were removed. For family history it was 5.5 percent; for urban birth it was 34.6 percent; for season of birth 10.5 percent. A strong but rare risk factor (an affected parent) accounts for few cases in a population; a weak but common one (a city birth) accounts for many. This link between city life and schizophrenia is called urbanicity , and it is stronger the longer a child lives in a city, which suggests that something about urban upbringing, not merely urban birth, is involved. The same logic applies to migration. In their 2005 meta-analysis Elizabeth Cantor-Graae and Jean-Paul Selten found that first-generation migrants had about 2.7 times the risk of the native population, and the children of migrants, the second generation, about 4.5 times. The risk was highest for migrants from countries where most people are Black, living in mainly white European countries; in the United Kingdom, people of African-Caribbean and Black African origin have much higher rates of first-episode schizophrenia than the white population. Because the second generation has the higher risk, the effect cannot simply be that ill people are more likely to emigrate (selective migration). DSM-5-TR adds the ethnic density effect: the rates are highest when members of a minority live in areas with few others of their own background. The proposed reasons are discrimination, social isolation, less support and fewer ordinary explanations available for odd experiences. Selten's idea that the chronic experience of being an outsider, which he calls social defeat, sensitises the brain's dopamine system is taken up in Section 4.9. The season-of-birth effect is small but remarkably consistent. In 1997 E. Fuller Torrey and colleagues reviewed more than 250 studies from 29 Northern and five Southern Hemisphere countries and found a 5 to 8 percent excess of winter and spring births among people who later develop schizophrenia (the same excess appears in bipolar disorder). Statistical artefacts and parents' timing of conception were judged unlikely explanations; seasonal infections, nutrition, light and temperature during pregnancy are the main suspects, and Section 4.7 returns to them. DSM-5-TR adds that the rare deficit form of the illness (Section 4.3) shows a summer excess instead. Finally there is social class, the oldest finding of all. In 1939 the Chicago sociologists Robert Faris and Warren Dunham showed that hospital admissions for schizophrenia were concentrated in the poorest inner-city districts; their study and the general debate it opened are taught in Book 2, Section 1.7. Two explanations compete. The social causation hypothesis says that the stresses of poverty (crowding, violence, poor nutrition, insecurity, discrimination) help to cause the illness. The social drift hypothesis , also called social selection, says that the illness, often during its slow prodrome, pushes people down the social ladder: they fail examinations, lose jobs, cannot pay rent and drift into cheap housing in poor areas. A neat test was devised in England by E. M. Goldberg and S. L. Morrison in 1963. If poverty caused schizophrenia, the patients should have been born into poor families. They looked up the occupations of the patients' fathers at the time of the patients' birth and found that the fathers' social class was distributed much like that of the general population, whereas the patients themselves had slid into the lowest occupational classes. For these patients, at least, the low social class was more a consequence of the illness than its cause. Later work has been more mixed: there is evidence for drift, but also for real effects of social adversity, childhood trauma and neighbourhood deprivation, and DSM-5-TR lists social deprivation, social adversity and adverse childhood experiences among the environmental risk factors. The phases of the illness Schizophrenia rarely arrives out of a clear sky. It usually unfolds through recognisable phases, and the easiest way to learn them is to follow one person through them. Mohan grew up in a small town near Coimbatore, the elder son of a bus conductor. His mother remembers him as a quiet, slightly clumsy boy who walked late, preferred to play alone and was teased at school for being "lost in his own world", though his marks were average and nobody thought he was ill. At 18 he began a commerce degree. In his second year things changed slowly. He stopped playing cricket with his friends, then stopped meeting them at all. He spent whole days in his room, bathed only when his mother insisted, and his marks fell from the sixties to the thirties. He became irritable when questioned and spent hours with a notebook of numbers, explaining that the dates of his examinations "had a pattern meant for him". His parents thought he was lazy, then that he had been affected by the evil eye; they took him to a temple and later to a healer, who tied an amulet on his arm. About fourteen months after the first change, Mohan began to hear two men discussing him from the next house, calling him a coward and commenting on everything he did, and he became convinced that the neighbours were reading his thoughts through their mobile tower. He stopped eating food his mother had not tasted first. When he threw a stone at the neighbour's window, his family brought him to the psychiatric unit of a hospital in Coimbatore. Mohan's story contains all four phases (Figure 4.10). The premorbid phase is the period before any recognisable illness. In many people who later develop schizophrenia it is not entirely normal: the late walking, clumsiness, solitary play and social awkwardness in Mohan's childhood are exactly the subtle motor, cognitive and social signs that cohort studies have found (Section 4.7.6), though they are far too common and too non-specific to predict the illness in any single child. The prodromal phase (from the Greek prodromos , running before) is the period of deterioration before the first frank psychotic symptoms. Barlow and Durand, citing Jablensky, state that up to 85 percent of people who develop schizophrenia go through a prodrome, typically lasting one to two years. In Häfner's ABC study of 232 first-episode patients, 73 percent of illnesses began with a prodromal phase, which lasted on average about five years when dated from the first non-specific sign. The two figures differ because the start of a prodrome can only be reconstructed afterwards, from what the patient and family remember, and different researchers draw the line at different points. The signs are mostly negative and non-specific: social withdrawal, a fall in work or study, neglect of hygiene, loss of interest, initiative and energy, blunted or odd emotional reactions, vague or circumstantial speech, unusual beliefs that stop short of delusion (ideas of reference, magical thinking), unusual perceptual experiences (sensing a presence in an empty room), irritability, depression and anxiety. DSM-III-R (1987) listed nine such prodromal and residual signs, and DSM-5-TR still describes the same picture. Notice how many of them resemble the features of schizotypal personality (Chapter 11), and how easily they are mistaken for adolescent moodiness, laziness or depression. The active phase is the period of florid psychosis: the delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech and behaviour, and catatonic features taught in Section 4.2, which bring the person to attention, often in crisis. DSM-5-TR requires at least one month of these Criterion A symptoms (less if successfully treated), and the six months that schizophrenia requires in DSM-5-TR may include the prodromal and residual periods (Section 4.4). With treatment the active symptoms usually lessen over weeks. The residual phase follows: the florid symptoms have faded, but negative symptoms, cognitive difficulties and attenuated positive symptoms (odd beliefs, mild suspiciousness, occasional voices) may linger. In some people the residual phase is brief and functioning returns almost to its previous level; in others it lasts for decades. Most people then experience relapse , a return of active symptoms after a period of improvement. The commonest triggers are stopping medication, stressful life events, heavy cannabis or alcohol use and a critical, hostile family atmosphere (Section 4.9). Premorbid Active phase Prodromal Residual phase, with relapses Threshold of psychosis subtle motor, cognitive and social signs relapse relapse persistent negative and cognitive symptoms Severe Normal Symptom severity Birth 10 20 30 40 Age in years (schematic) Figure 4.10 The course of schizophrenia, schematic (after Lieberman and colleagues, 2001, as adapted by Barlow and Durand). Subtle signs in childhood give way to a prodromal decline, the active phase crosses the threshold of psychosis, and the residual phase brings relapses, after each of which functioning may settle a little lower. Real courses vary greatly from person to person. Between the first psychotic symptom and the start of proper treatment there is usually a gap. The duration of untreated psychosis (DUP) is defined as the time from the manifestation of the first psychotic symptom to the initiation of adequate treatment. For Mohan it was several months, spent at the temple and the healer's; Barlow and Durand note that in Western samples it typically takes one to two years from the first symptoms to diagnosis and treatment, partly because people hide symptoms as their suspiciousness grows. Does the delay matter? In 2005 Max Marshall and colleagues reviewed 26 cohorts of first-episode patients, 4,490 people in all, and found a modest but convincing association: a longer DUP went with worse total, positive and negative symptoms, worse overall and social functioning, and a lower chance of remission. Crucially, the association was not explained by poor premorbid adjustment, the obvious alternative explanation (people whose illness creeps in slowly might both be recognised late and do badly anyway). Whether untreated psychosis actually damages the brain is still argued, but the practical lesson is accepted everywhere, and it is the basis of the early intervention services described in Section 4.10. Clinical link In India the pathway to care very often passes through temples, dargahs, churches and traditional healers before it reaches a psychiatrist or psychologist, and that pathway lengthens the DUP. A clinical psychologist who meets a family like Mohan's should not ridicule the healer they consulted first; the aim is to add effective treatment to what the family believes, not to win an argument about causes. The young person with only prodromal signs, who is help-seeking but not psychotic, belongs to the clinical high-risk state and attenuated psychosis syndrome described in Section 4.5. Exam trap The phases in order are premorbid, prodromal, active, residual . The prodrome consists mainly of negative and non-specific signs (withdrawal, declining function, odd ideas), not full delusions. DSM-5-TR's six months of illness include the prodromal and residual phases; only one month need be active phase. DUP runs from the first psychotic symptom , not from the first prodromal sign, to adequate treatment. What happens next: course and long-term outcome Emil Kraepelin built his concept of dementia praecox on the belief that the illness ended in mental deterioration (Section 4.1). For half a century, textbooks repeated his pessimism, and families were told to expect a lifetime in hospital. Was he right? The answer came from researchers who did the slow, unglamorous work of following patients for decades. The first great long-term study was carried out by Manfred Bleuler (1903 to 1994), the son of Eugen Bleuler, who directed the same Burghölzli hospital in Zurich where his father had coined the word schizophrenia. He followed 208 patients (100 men and 108 women) admitted in 1942 and 1943 until 1963 to 1965 or until their death, more than 20 years for most of them, and knew many of them and their families personally. His book, published in German in 1972 and in English in 1978 as The Schizophrenic Disorders: Long-term Patient and Family Studies , overturned Kraepelin's picture. Courses were enormously varied: some patients recovered fully and stayed well, many had an undulating course of episodes and remissions, and a minority went on to a severe chronic state. Bleuler also observed that the illness did not, on average, keep getting worse: after the first years it tended to stabilise or even improve. When Swiss researchers re-examined his records in 2003 using modern criteria, about 30 percent of his patients no longer qualified for schizophrenia (most were rediagnosed with schizoaffective disorder), but even among the strictly diagnosed patients, half had an undulating course with remissions and 12 to 15 percent recovered. In Lausanne, Luc Ciompi and Christian Müller traced the lives of patients first admitted decades earlier (published in German in 1976 and summarised in English in 1980). Of 1,642 original patients, 289 survived to be examined after an average of about 37 years. The long-term course was favourable in at least half of them, and outcome depended mainly on the person's premorbid personality, on certain features of the illness, and on the effects of advanced age. Old age, for many, brought a quieting of the illness. A third approach pooled everything. In 1994 James Hegarty and colleagues meta-analysed a century of outcome studies (1895 to 1992): 320 studies with 51,800 subjects. After an average follow-up of 5.6 years, 40.2 percent of patients were considered improved. Outcome was better under broad diagnostic criteria (46.5 percent improved) than narrow ones (27.3 percent), which is exactly what you would expect if broad criteria sweep in good-prognosis brief psychoses. The improvement rate rose after the mid-1950s, the era of antipsychotic drugs (48.5 percent for 1956 to 1985 versus 35.4 percent for 1895 to 1955), and fell again to 36.4 percent in the last decade studied, perhaps because narrower diagnostic concepts returned. Barlow and Durand cite a classic analysis by Joseph Zubin and colleagues (1992) of four course types: about 22 percent of patients had a single episode and recovered without lasting impairment, while the remaining 78 percent had several episodes, with varying degrees of impairment between them. DSM-5-TR reports two more recent meta-analyses. Across 79 studies of first-episode schizophrenia, the pooled remission rate was 56 percent and the pooled recovery rate 30 percent; across 50 studies of broadly defined schizophrenia, the median proportion meeting strict recovery criteria was only 13.5 percent. These numbers look contradictory until you notice that they measure different things. Remission means that symptoms are absent or mild for a sustained period; an international working group led by Nancy Andreasen proposed in 2005 that eight core symptoms rated mild or less for at least six months should define it. Recovery is a higher bar: symptomatic remission plus a return of social and occupational functioning, sustained for at least two years. Many people reach remission; fewer reach recovery in this full sense. Clinicians and exam guides compress all this into a rough rule of thirds : about a third of people recover or nearly recover, about a third improve but have recurrent episodes or residual symptoms, and about a third remain persistently ill and disabled. It is a teaching simplification, not a finding, but it captures the essential truth that Kraepelin missed: schizophrenia is heterogeneous, and deterioration is not inevitable. DSM-5-TR puts the modern view plainly: course and outcome are heterogeneous, prognosis is uncertain at the onset of psychosis, and many people experience periods of remission and even recovery. It adds two useful details: cognitive impairment tends to appear before the first episode and then remain fairly stable, and psychotic experiences tend to lessen in late life.
