"A third recover, a third improve, a third stay ill" is a rough teaching rule. Remission (symptoms mild or absent) is not the same as recovery (symptoms and functioning, sustained). Outcome looks better when the diagnosis is broad, because broad criteria include brief, good-prognosis psychoses. The WHO studies and the Indian evidence In the 1960s nobody knew whether schizophrenia was the same illness everywhere, or even whether psychiatrists in different countries meant the same thing by the word (the US-UK Diagnostic Project described in Section 4.1 was showing at about the same time that they often did not). The World Health Organization (WHO) set out to find out. The International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (IPSS) began in 1966 and published its first report in 1973. It examined 1,202 patients in nine centres: Aarhus (Denmark), Agra (India), Cali (Colombia), Ibadan (Nigeria), London (United Kingdom), Moscow (Soviet Union), Prague (Czechoslovakia), Taipei (Taiwan) and Washington (United States). Every patient was interviewed with the same standardised instrument, the Present State Examination, and classified by the same computer program. The first finding was methodological and reassuring: a similar core syndrome of schizophrenia could be identified in every centre, across very different cultures and languages. The second finding was the surprise. At the two-year follow-up, published in 1979, patients in the centres in developing countries had a considerably better course and outcome than patients in the centres in developed countries. At the five-year follow-up (Julian Leff and colleagues, 1992), covering 807 patients in eight centres, clinical and social outcomes were still significantly better in Agra and Ibadan; in Cali only social outcome was better. Critics pointed out that the IPSS patients were not a representative sample: each centre picked cases from its own hospital, and a hospital in Agra might admit a very different kind of patient from one in Washington. So the WHO ran a second, better-designed study, the Determinants of Outcome of Severe Mental Disorders (DOSMeD), often called the WHO ten-country study, published by Assen Jablensky , Norman Sartorius and colleagues in 1992. It enrolled 1,379 patients at the point of their first contact with any helping agency, including traditional healers, in twelve centres in ten countries, among them Agra and Chandigarh in India, Ibadan and Cali, alongside centres in Europe, the United States and Japan. Starting from first contact avoided the selection bias of the IPSS. Of the 1,078 patients (78 percent) followed for about two years, complete clinical remission was more than twice as common in the developing-country centres (37 percent) as in the developed ones (15.5 percent), although the proportions with a continuous, unremitting illness did not differ significantly. The strongest predictors of outcome were the type of onset (acute onset did better than gradual) and the setting (developing country better than developed). The WHO then traced the surviving cohorts for 15 and 25 years in the International Study of Schizophrenia (Glynn Harrison and colleagues, 2001), whose authors included the Indian investigators K. C. Dube, Savita Malhotra, V. K. Varma and R. Thara: about half of the surviving patients had favourable outcomes, there was marked variation between centres, the pattern of the first two years was the best predictor of the fifteen-year outcome, and even 16 percent of patients whose early illness had never remitted achieved recovery later. Several explanations were proposed, and you should be able to discuss them in an interview. Extended families shared the burden of care and kept the patient within a web of relationships. Relatives in Chandigarh were found to be far less often critical, hostile or over-involved than relatives in London, a finding on expressed emotion taught in Section 4.9. Agricultural and family work allowed a person to return to a useful role at their own pace, without the competitive job interview. Illness was more often explained by external causes (spirits, fate, the evil eye) that did not blame the person. And a larger share of the patients in developing countries had an acute onset, which predicts a good outcome anywhere. The finding became an axiom of international psychiatry, and axioms invite challenge. In 2008 Alex Cohen , Vikram Patel , R. Thara and Oye Gureje published "Questioning an axiom: better prognosis for schizophrenia in the developing world?" They tabulated 23 longitudinal studies from 11 low- and middle-income countries and found that outcomes varied widely, with many poor outcomes, so that the WHO conclusions needed re-examination. They also argued that outcome studies must take account of the high mortality and suicide in poorer settings, since patients who die are not counted among the poor outcomes. Other critics noted that "developing country" lumps together places as different as Agra, Ibadan and Cali, that brief acute psychoses (Section 4.5), which recover by their nature, may have inflated the developing-country samples, and that follow-up was harder in some centres. The fairest summary is that the WHO studies showed that the course of schizophrenia is shaped by its social setting, but that being poor is not in itself protective. India has its own long-term evidence. The Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF) in Chennai, founded in 1984 by the psychiatrist M. Sarada Menon with R. Thara and colleagues, ran the Madras Longitudinal Study , which followed 90 first-episode patients prospectively. At ten years (Thara and colleagues, 1994), 76 could be fully assessed; the pattern of illness was rated good in 67 percent, the commonest pattern was one of recurrent episodes, and positive and negative symptoms had declined steeply. At twenty years (Thara, 2004), complete data were available for 61 patients, while 16 had died and 13 could not be traced. Only 5 had recovered completely and 5 had been continuously ill; most had had several relapses, with or without full remission between them. Yet symptoms and social functioning were much better than in many Western cohorts, and rates of marriage and employment were higher than usually reported. Read the two halves of that result together: the Indian course was better than the Western one, but "better" did not mean benign. Indian context Two Indian cities are written into the history of schizophrenia research. Agra , through its mental hospital, was the Indian centre of the IPSS (1973) and also took part in DOSMeD; Chandigarh , through the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, was a DOSMeD centre and the site of the WHO expressed-emotion study of Indian relatives. Chennai's SCARF produced the Madras Longitudinal Study, one of the few long-term follow-ups of first-episode schizophrenia from a low- or middle-income country. Exam trap IPSS : WHO, report 1973, nine countries, 1,202 patients, Indian centre Agra . DOSMeD : WHO ten-country study, 1992, first-contact cases, twelve centres including Agra and Chandigarh . Both found a better outcome in developing countries, not a better outcome in developed ones and not a lower incidence. The critique "Questioning an axiom" (2008) is by Cohen, Patel, Thara and Gureje. Predicting the outcome If outcomes vary so widely, can a clinician tell at the start which way a particular patient is likely to go? Not with certainty, but decades of follow-up studies have produced a reliable list of prognostic factors , features present early in the illness that predict a better or worse course (Table 4.26). The list is among the most frequently examined in this chapter, and it is easiest to remember if you understand why each factor works. Table 4.26 Prognostic factors in schizophrenia. Factor Better prognosis Worse prognosis Onset Acute (days to weeks) Insidious (months to years) Age at onset Later (late 20s or older) Early (adolescence) Precipitating stressor Clear precipitant present No precipitant Premorbid adjustment Good social, sexual and work history Poor; withdrawn, schizoid or schizotypal traits Symptom picture Mood symptoms (especially depression), positive symptoms, confusion or perplexity Prominent negative symptoms, disorganisation, cognitive impairment Sex and marital status Female; married Male; single, separated, divorced or widowed Family history Of mood disorder Of schizophrenia Duration of untreated psychosis Short Long Early course Remissions in the first two years No remission; many relapses Brain and neurological signs Normal Neurological soft signs, enlarged ventricles Insight and adherence Good Poor; continued substance use Support Good support; low expressed emotion at home Poor support; high expressed emotion Most of the factors fall into three families. The first concerns how much of a person was built before the illness struck : a late onset, good premorbid functioning, marriage and a work history all mean that the person has skills, relationships and roles to return to. The second concerns how much of the illness is a neurodevelopmental deficit and how much an episode : insidious onset, early onset, negative symptoms, cognitive impairment, neurological soft signs and enlarged ventricles all suggest a long-standing brain abnormality of the kind described in Section 4.7, whereas an acute onset after a clear stressor, with mood symptoms and perplexity, suggests an episode laid on top of a fairly intact brain. Prominent mood symptoms and a family history of mood disorder also hint that the illness lies closer to the mood end of the psychotic spectrum, where outcome is better. The third family concerns what happens after onset : a short DUP, good insight, taking medication, avoiding cannabis and living in a calm, supportive home all reduce relapse. Notice that the sex difference in outcome is partly explained by the first two families: men fall ill earlier, before marriage and work are established, and more often with negative symptoms. Now push two cases through the table. You already know Mohan: early onset at 19, insidious prodrome over more than a year, no precipitant, poor premorbid social adjustment, prominent withdrawal and self-neglect, single, male, several months of untreated psychosis. Almost every factor points to a guarded prognosis. Leela, by contrast, is a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Thrissur, married with two children, popular with her colleagues and an active member of her church choir. Ten days after her father died suddenly, in the middle of a bitter property dispute with his brothers, she became frightened and sleepless, then convinced that her uncles had hired men to poison her and her children, and she heard her dead father's voice warning her not to eat. She cried for hours and said she deserved to die for failing him. She was treated within a fortnight. The active symptoms settled over six weeks, and after a few further months of mild suspiciousness and low mood she returned to teaching. Leela has acute onset, late onset, a clear precipitant, good premorbid functioning, marked mood symptoms, a supportive husband and a short DUP: nearly every factor points to a good prognosis. Notice also that her picture, with prominent mood symptoms, sits close to the boundaries with psychotic depression and schizoaffective disorder, which is exactly why Section 4.4 teaches how mood congruence and timing decide the diagnosis. The table cannot tell you that Mohan will do badly or that Leela will stay well. It tells you where the odds lie, and it tells the clinician which modifiable factors (DUP, adherence, cannabis, the family atmosphere) are worth fighting for. Exam trap Good prognosis: acute onset, late onset, clear precipitant , good premorbid functioning, mood symptoms, positive symptoms, female , married , family history of mood disorder, short DUP. Poor prognosis: the reverse, especially insidious onset, early onset and prominent negative symptoms . A family history of schizophrenia is a poor sign; a family history of mood disorder is a good one. Positive symptoms respond better to treatment than negative symptoms, so a mainly positive picture is the better one. Death, disability and daily life Schizophrenia shortens life. The bluntest measure is the standardised mortality ratio , the number of deaths observed in a group divided by the number expected for people of the same age and sex in the general population. McGrath's reviews found a median standardised mortality ratio of 2.6 for all causes of death, meaning that people with schizophrenia die at about two to three times the expected rate, and the gap has widened over recent decades as the general population's health has improved faster than theirs. In 2017 Carsten Hjorthøj and colleagues pooled 11 studies covering up to 247,603 patients and estimated that schizophrenia costs a person, on average, 14.5 years of life (15.9 years for men, 13.6 for women), with an average life expectancy of 64.7 years. Suicide is part of the explanation but not the largest part. DSM-5-TR states that approximately 5 to 6 percent of people with schizophrenia die by suicide, about 20 percent attempt suicide at least once, and many more have serious suicidal thoughts. Older textbooks quoted a lifetime suicide rate of 10 percent; when Brian Palmer and colleagues re-examined the evidence in 2005 they showed that the figure came mainly from studies of chronic patients, and estimated the true lifetime risk at about 4.9 percent , with the deaths concentrated near the onset of the illness. DSM-5-TR lists the risk factors: being a younger man, especially with substance use; depressive symptoms and hopelessness; unemployment; the period just after a psychotic episode or discharge from hospital; many admissions; closeness to the onset of illness; a history of attempts; poor adherence to treatment; and, perhaps surprisingly, higher intelligence and older age at onset, which may give a person a sharper sense of what the illness has taken from them. Some suicidal acts are responses to command hallucinations. The depression that can follow an acute episode (post-psychotic depression, ICD-10's post-schizophrenic depression) is described in Section 4.4, and the assessment of suicide risk is taught in Book 2, Section 2.7. Most of the remaining excess deaths come from ordinary physical illness: cardiovascular disease, diabetes and the metabolic syndrome, respiratory disease and some cancers. DSM-5-TR notes that more than half of people with schizophrenia smoke regularly, that they engage less in health maintenance such as screening and exercise, and that weight gain and metabolic effects of some antipsychotic drugs (Section 4.10) add to the risk. Health services add their own share: a breathless patient with a psychiatric label may be dismissed as anxious, a failure of care called diagnostic overshadowing. The public fear of the "violent schizophrenic" deserves a correction. DSM-5-TR states that the vast majority of people with schizophrenia are not aggressive, and that they are more frequently victimised than people in the general population. Aggression, when it occurs, is commoner in younger men and in those with a history of violence, substance use, impulsivity and poor adherence to treatment, which are the same predictors of violence in anyone. Spontaneous or random assault is uncommon. Disability is the daily face of the illness. DSM-5-TR notes that most people with schizophrenia are employed at a lower level than their parents and that most, particularly men, do not marry or have limited social contacts outside the family. In India the family is the main, and often the only, system of care: parents, spouses and siblings supervise medication, manage crises, find work and pay for treatment, frequently for decades. The resulting caregiver burden is financial (lost earnings, the cost of medicines and travel), practical and emotional, and it is sharpened by stigma , the shame and social exclusion attached to the illness. Families may hide the diagnosis to protect the marriage prospects of the patient's siblings; marriage is sometimes arranged in the hope that it will "cure" the illness, and a woman whose illness is discovered after marriage risks being sent back to her parents. Ageing parents carry a particular fear, voiced in almost every family meeting: "What will happen to him after we are gone?" Psychologists who work in Indian settings spend much of their time with these questions; the rehabilitation services that address them are taught in Book 2, Section 9.8, and the rights that the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 gives to people with mental illness, including the right to community living, in Book 2, Section 1.10. Clinical link When you take a history from a family like Mohan's or Leela's, ask about the carers as well as the patient: who supervises the tablets, who lost a job to stay at home, who in the house is exhausted, and whether anyone is hiding the illness from relatives or prospective in-laws. A caregiver who is supported is less likely to become critical and over-involved, and a calmer home lowers the risk of relapse (Section 4.9). Asking about suicidal thoughts, especially in the first years after diagnosis and after discharge, is never optional. Exam trap Lifetime suicide in schizophrenia: about 5 percent (DSM-5-TR: 5 to 6 percent die by suicide; about 20 percent attempt). The old figure of 10 percent overstates it. Risk is highest early in the illness, in young men , after discharge , and with depression and hopelessness. Life expectancy is reduced by roughly 15 years , mostly through physical illness, not suicide. People with schizophrenia are more often victims than perpetrators of violence. 4.7 Genes, Development and the Brain Lower yield · 1 Q Section 4.6 showed that schizophrenia strikes about one person in a hundred, mostly in early adulthood, more often in cities and among migrants, and with a course that ranges from full recovery to lifelong disability. Now we turn to the first and largest of the causal questions: what in the person's biology makes them vulnerable? The story has three strands, and they turn out to be one story. The first is genetic: schizophrenia runs in families, and twin and adoption studies show that most of that family resemblance comes from shared genes, not shared upbringing. The second is developmental: many of the risk factors act before birth, and the illness seems to be set up years before it appears. The third concerns the brain: people with schizophrenia have, on average, larger ventricles, less grey matter and a prefrontal cortex that does not switch on properly when it is needed. The neurotransmitters that carry this vulnerability into symptoms, dopamine above all, are the subject of Section 4.8; the psychological, family and social stresses that interact with it are the subject of Section 4.9. Does schizophrenia run in families? The first systematic answer came from the German-born psychiatrist Franz Josef Kallmann (1897 to 1965), who in 1938 published a study of the families of more than 1,000 people diagnosed with schizophrenia in a Berlin psychiatric hospital. Two of his observations still guide research. The more severe the parent's illness, the more likely the children were to develop it. And the subtypes of the day did not breed true: a parent with paranoid schizophrenia might have a child with the catatonic form. What runs in families, in other words, is a general vulnerability to schizophrenia, and later research showed that it extends to a broader group of related psychotic and schizotypal conditions, the schizophrenia spectrum . A family study compares the rate of a disorder in the relatives of affected people (the probands) with the rate in the general population or in the relatives of unaffected controls. The definitive summary was compiled by the American psychologist Irving Gottesman (1930 to 2016) in his book Schizophrenia Genesis: The Origins of Madness (1991). Gottesman pooled about 40 family and twin studies conducted in European populations between 1920 and 1987 and calculated the average lifetime morbid risk for each kind of relative. His figures (Figure 4.11) are the most frequently examined numbers in the whole of this chapter, and they are worth learning as a set, because the set tells a story. Risk climbs with the proportion of genes shared with an affected person, but even an identical co-twin falls ill only about half the time. Read the chart from the bottom. In the general population the lifetime risk is 1 percent; for a spouse of a patient, who shares no genes with the patient but often shares a home, it is only 2 percent. Third-degree relatives (first cousins, who share about one-eighth of their genes with the patient) and second-degree relatives (uncles and aunts, nephews and nieces, grandchildren and half siblings, who share about a quarter) carry risks of 2 to 6 percent. First-degree relatives, who share about half their genes, carry 6 to 17 percent: siblings about 9, children of one affected parent about 13, fraternal twins about 17. At the top are the two situations in which a person inherits the largest dose of risk genes: the child of two affected parents (about 46 percent) and the identical twin (about 48 percent). The orderly rise of risk with genetic closeness is the single most striking fact about the figure. Two details repay a second look. Why are parents (6 percent) at lower risk than siblings and children? Because people with schizophrenia have fewer children than other people, partly because the illness begins in early adulthood and impairs relationships, so the parents of patients are a selected group: they were well enough to marry and have children, and some of them would have been excluded from parenthood had they fallen ill early. And why do fraternal twins (17 percent) exceed ordinary siblings (9 percent), when both share half their genes? Because twins also share the womb, the same birth date and an unusually similar upbringing. That gap is a first clue that environment matters, and it is why family studies alone can never settle the question of genes. A family shares its kitchen, its quarrels and its neighbourhood as well as its DNA. There is one more number to keep beside Gottesman's figure. DSM-5-TR points out that, despite the strong genetic contribution, most people who are diagnosed with schizophrenia have no family history of psychosis . The risks to relatives are high relative to 1 percent, but the absolute numbers are small: 91 percent of the siblings of a patient will never develop the illness. A worked example shows how these figures are used in a real conversation. Paul is a 26-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru. His younger brother developed schizophrenia two years ago. Paul's family is now discussing his marriage, and the young woman's parents have asked, politely but directly, whether the illness is hereditary. Paul asks the psychologist three questions. What is his own risk? As a sibling, about 9 percent over a lifetime, against 1 percent in the general population; but since he is already 26 and well, he has lived through much of the peak period of risk for men, so his remaining risk is lower than that lifetime figure. What is the risk for his future children? They would be the nephews and nieces of an affected person, so about 4 percent, which means that about 96 children in 100 in that position never develop the illness. And is there a test? No: there is no genetic test that can predict schizophrenia in an individual, for reasons Section 4.7.4 explains. The psychologist adds one more piece of advice, prompted by something Paul mentions in passing: he smokes cannabis with his friends most weekends. For a man with an affected brother, that is a risk worth removing (Section 4.7.8). Exam trap Gottesman's (1991) figures to memorise: general population 1 , sibling 9 , child of one affected parent 13 , fraternal twin 17 , child of two affected parents 46 , identical twin 48 (so "about 50 percent" is the exam answer). Parents are lower (6 percent) because people with schizophrenia have fewer children. Family studies show that schizophrenia is familial ; they cannot by themselves show that it is genetic . Twin studies: identical genes, different fates Twins offer a natural experiment. Monozygotic (identical) twins develop from a single fertilised egg that splits, so they share essentially all their genes. Dizygotic (fraternal) twins develop from two eggs fertilised by two sperm, so, like ordinary siblings, they share on average half the genes that vary between people. Both kinds of twins share a womb and are usually raised together. If schizophrenia were caused entirely by the family environment, identical and fraternal twins should be equally alike for it. If it were caused entirely by genes, an identical twin of a patient should always be affected. The truth lies between, and the twin method measures where. The key measure is concordance , the extent to which both members of a twin pair have the disorder. There are two ways of calculating it, and they give different numbers. Pairwise concordance is the proportion of twin pairs in which both twins are affected. Probandwise concordance is the proportion of affected twins (probands) whose co-twin is also affected; pairs in which both twins were independently found by the researchers are counted twice. Probandwise figures are higher, and they are the ones that can be compared with the risk for other relatives. Early twin studies, including Kallmann's, reported very high concordance for identical twins, but they relied on unblinded diagnosis, uncertain zygosity and samples drawn from chronic hospital patients. The modern era began in London. James Shields and Irving Gottesman studied every twin admitted to the Maudsley and Bethlem Royal Hospitals over 16 years (from 1948, when the hospital's twin register began, to 1964), reporting first in 1966 and then in their book Schizophrenia and Genetics: A Twin Study Vantage Point (1972). The identical co-twins were affected several times as often as the fraternal co-twins. In 1967 the two men proposed a polygenic theory of schizophrenia: the illness is not caused by one gene but by many, each of small effect, which add up to a person's liability ; only when the total of genetic and environmental liability passes a threshold does the illness appear. This liability-threshold model, borrowed from the British geneticist Douglas Falconer's work of 1965, explains at a stroke why most patients have no affected relative, why risk rises smoothly with genetic closeness, and why identical twins can be discordant. Later studies have refined the numbers. In 2003 Patrick Sullivan, Kenneth Kendler and Michael Neale pooled 12 twin studies and estimated the heritability of liability to schizophrenia at 81 percent, with a further 11 percent of the variation attributable to environment shared by the twins. The most complete modern study used the whole Danish twin register: Rikke Hilker and colleagues in 2018 followed 31,524 twin pairs born between 1951 and 2000 and found a probandwise concordance of 33 percent in identical twins and 7 percent in fraternal twins, with a heritability of 79 percent. Heritability is the most misunderstood number in psychiatry, so be precise about it. It is the proportion of the variation in liability within a particular population that is attributable to genetic differences between people in that population. A heritability of 80 percent does not mean that 80 percent of any one person's illness is caused by genes, and it does not mean that a person with risk genes has an 80 percent chance of falling ill. It is perfectly compatible with an identical co-twin falling ill only about half the time. Indeed, the most important fact in Figure 4.11 is not the 48 percent but the 52 percent: more than half of the identical twins of patients, with the same genome and usually the same upbringing, never develop schizophrenia. Something other than the inherited DNA sequence must decide. You have already met the most famous illustration of this. The Genain quadruplets with whom this chapter opened shared one genome and one disturbed home, and all four developed schizophrenia; yet their age at onset, their symptoms, their hospital stays and their eventual functioning differed widely. Identical genes, it turns out, do not guarantee identical lives. Even identical twins differ in their position in the womb, their blood supply and birth weight, the complications of their delivery, the illnesses of their childhood and the way their parents treat them; behaviour geneticists call these experiences the non-shared environment . Later sections show how such differences may leave marks on the brain itself (Section 4.7.7). Key study: The children of discordant twins (Fischer 1971; Gottesman and Bertelsen 1989) If an identical twin escapes schizophrenia, has she escaped the genes, or merely failed to express them? The Danish psychiatrist Margit Fischer found a way to ask. In 1971 she identified Danish twin pairs in which one twin had schizophrenia and looked at their children. Gottesman and Aksel Bertelsen later followed all those children through the Danish psychiatric register to 1985. The age-corrected risk of schizophrenia and related disorders was 16.8 percent in the children of the affected identical twins and 17.4 percent in the children of their healthy identical co-twins. For fraternal twins the figures were 17.4 percent for children of the affected twin but only 2.1 percent for children of the healthy co-twin. Conclusion: a healthy identical co-twin carries, and passes on, the same risk as her ill sister. A schizophrenia genotype can remain unexpressed unless something, perhaps an environmental stressor, releases it. Criticism: the samples were small, and "related disorders" broadened the outcome. Exam trap "The chance of developing schizophrenia if you have an identical twin with the disorder" is about 50 percent (Gottesman's 48 percent; modern probandwise figures 33 to 50 percent). The tempting 80 percent is the heritability , a different quantity; 10 percent is roughly the risk for a sibling; 1 percent is the general population. Twin concordance is not 100 percent , which is the strongest single proof that environment matters too. Adoption studies: separating genes from upbringing Twin studies have a weakness: identical twins may be treated more alike than fraternal twins, and they share a womb, so a critic can always argue that their greater similarity is partly environmental. Adoption breaks the link completely. A child adopted at birth receives genes from one set of parents and upbringing from another, so the two influences can finally be pulled apart. In the 1960s the idea that schizophrenia was caused by disturbed parenting (the "schizophrenogenic mother" of Section 4.9) was still widely taught, which made the adoption studies a direct test of a popular theory. Key study: Heston's foster children (1966) The American psychiatrist Leonard Heston traced children born between 1915 and 1945 to mothers with schizophrenia who were confined in an Oregon state psychiatric hospital. By hospital policy, every baby was removed from the mother within three days of birth and raised by relatives or in foster or adoptive homes, with no further contact with the mother. Heston compared 47 of these children, now adults, with 50 control adults who had also been separated from their mothers in infancy but whose mothers were not ill. Psychiatrists who did not know which group a person belonged to made the diagnoses. Result: 5 of the 47 children of mothers with schizophrenia had developed schizophrenia, and none of the 50 controls; the age-corrected morbid risk was 16.6 percent , about the same as for children raised by their own ill mothers. About half of the experimental group (26 of 47) showed marked psychosocial disability, and besides schizophrenia they had more sociopathic personality, mental deficiency and neurotic personality disorder, and more criminal convictions, than the controls. Conclusion: being raised by a mother with schizophrenia was not necessary for the risk to be passed on. Criticism: the samples were small, and the children had shared their mothers' wombs and pregnancies, so prenatal influences could not be excluded. The definitive adoption studies were carried out in Denmark, whose national registers of adoptions and psychiatric admissions made it possible to trace every adoptee and every relative. The American team of Seymour Kety (1915 to 2000), David Rosenthal and Paul Wender , working with the Danish psychiatrist Fini Schulsinger, began reporting in 1968. They started from the 5,483 people adopted in Copenhagen and found the adoptees who had later developed schizophrenia; then they examined both sets of relatives of each one, the biological family who had given them genes and the adoptive family who had raised them, and compared them with the relatives of matched control adoptees. Schizophrenia and the milder conditions they called the schizophrenia spectrum (a term this team introduced) were concentrated among the biological relatives of the adoptees with schizophrenia; the adoptive relatives, who had raised them, did not differ from the controls. In the Copenhagen sample, 5.6 percent of the biological relatives of chronically ill adoptees had chronic schizophrenia and a further 14.8 percent had what Eugen Bleuler had called latent schizophrenia. A replication across the rest of Denmark, published in 1994, found that in the combined national sample chronic schizophrenia occurred exclusively in the biological relatives and was ten times commoner than in the biological relatives of controls. The team also used the opposite design, cross-fostering (Wender and colleagues, 1974): children of healthy biological parents who happened to be raised by an adoptive parent who developed schizophrenia did not show the raised risk seen in adoptees whose biological parent was ill. The adoption studies did not end the story of the family environment; they changed it. The largest, the Finnish Adoptive Family Study of Schizophrenia led by Pekka Tienari , searched the records of nearly 20,000 Finnish women hospitalised with schizophrenia or a paranoid psychosis and found about 190 of their children who had been adopted away, then compared them with control adoptees. Unlike the Danish studies, it observed the adoptive families directly and rated how well they functioned. In 2004 Tienari and colleagues reported the long-term results (adoptees were rediagnosed after a median of 12 years, with register follow-up after 21 years). Among adoptees at high genetic risk, the quality of the adoptive family significantly predicted who developed schizophrenia-spectrum disorders: those raised in disturbed adoptive families fared worst, those raised in healthy ones much better. Among adoptees at low genetic risk, the adoptive family made no significant difference. This is a gene-environment interaction : the environment matters, but chiefly for people whose genes make them sensitive to it. It is exactly the pattern that the stress-vulnerability model of Section 4.9 predicts. Table 4.27 compares the three classic designs. From heritability to genes If schizophrenia is about 80 percent heritable, where are the genes? For three decades the search was disappointing. Linkage studies , which track chromosome regions through families with many affected members, pointed to regions on many different chromosomes that rarely replicated. Candidate gene studies tested genes chosen because their function seemed plausible, such as the gene for catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT, an enzyme that breaks down dopamine), neuregulin 1 and dysbindin; each had its moment, and most failed to hold up when much larger samples were examined. One striking exception was a large Scottish family in which a chromosomal translocation disrupting a gene later named DISC1 (Disrupted in Schizophrenia 1) travelled with schizophrenia, depression and bipolar disorder; Pinel describes transgenic mice carrying the defective human gene, which developed a reduced cerebral cortex, enlarged ventricles and behaviour reminiscent of schizophrenia. The failure of the hunt for single "schizophrenia genes" was itself informative. It is just what Gottesman and Shields's polygenic theory predicted. The breakthrough came with the genome-wide association study (GWAS), which scans hundreds of thousands of common genetic variants across the whole genome in very large numbers of cases and controls, looking for variants that are slightly commoner in the cases. In 2014 the Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, an international collaboration, analysed up to 36,989 cases and 113,075 controls and identified 108 genetic loci associated with schizophrenia. The associations were enriched among genes expressed in the brain; they included the gene for the dopamine D2 receptor (the target of every antipsychotic drug, Section 4.8) and several genes involved in glutamate transmission, and, unexpectedly, genes expressed in tissues important for immunity. A larger study in 2022 (Trubetskoy and colleagues, 76,755 cases and 243,649 controls) raised the count to 287 loci, concentrated in genes expressed in excitatory and inhibitory neurons and involved in the organisation and transmission of synapses. Each common variant raises risk only very slightly. Adding up a person's risk variants gives a polygenic risk score , which is useful in research but explains only a modest part of who becomes ill, so it cannot diagnose schizophrenia or predict it in an individual such as Paul. Alongside the many common variants of small effect there are a few rare variants of large effect. The most important are copy number variants (CNVs), stretches of DNA that are deleted or duplicated. The best known is the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (also called velocardiofacial or DiGeorge syndrome), the loss of a small piece of chromosome 22, which causes heart defects, a cleft palate, a characteristic face, learning difficulties and immune problems. About one in four people with this deletion develop schizophrenia, more than twenty times the general population risk, which makes it the strongest single known genetic risk factor; it is still rare, and accounts for only a small fraction of all cases. Other rare deletions and duplications, many of them shared with autism and intellectual disability, add further risk. Some of these variants arise as de novo mutations , new mutations not present in either parent. Because sperm-producing cells keep dividing throughout a man's life, mutations accumulate in older fathers. In 2001 Dolores Malaspina and colleagues followed 87,907 people born in Jerusalem between 1964 and 1976 and found that the risk of schizophrenia rose steadily with the father's age at conception, reaching about 2 times in children of fathers aged 45 to 49 and about 3 times for fathers aged 50 or more, whereas the mother's age had no effect once the father's was allowed for. The most famous single discovery from the genome-wide era explained the strongest association of all, in the major histocompatibility complex, a region of chromosome 6 full of immune genes. In 2016 Aswin Sekar , Steven McCarroll and colleagues showed that the association arises partly from structurally different versions of the genes for complement component 4 (C4), a protein of the immune system. Versions that produce more of the C4A form in the brain carried more risk. C4 was found at neuronal synapses, and in mice it mediated synapse elimination during development. The finding linked a risk gene to a process, excessive pruning of synapses, that may explain why people with schizophrenia have fewer synapses in the cortex (Section 4.7.7). Two further lessons complete the genetic picture. First, the genes are not specific to schizophrenia. DSM-5-TR notes that the risk alleles identified so far are also associated with bipolar disorder, depression and autism spectrum disorder; the boundaries between our diagnostic categories are blurrier in the genome than in the textbook. Second, genes act through, and together with, the environment. Epigenetics , the study of chemical marks such as DNA methylation and histone modification that switch genes on and off without changing the DNA sequence, offers one route: Pinel describes evidence that such marks alter the expression of synaptic genes in prefrontal neurons in schizophrenia, and early adversity may act partly through them. The clearest example of a gene-environment interaction at the level of a single gene came from the Dunedin birth cohort in New Zealand, where in 2005 Avshalom Caspi , Terrie Moffitt and colleagues found that adolescent cannabis use raised the risk of adult psychosis mainly in people who carried the valine version of a common COMT variant, and hardly at all in those with two copies of the methionine version. It was a striking result, though later studies have not consistently replicated it. Exam trap Schizophrenia is polygenic : many common variants of small effect plus a few rare variants of larger effect. There is no single schizophrenia gene and no predictive genetic test. Remember 2014 ( 108 loci , Psychiatric Genomics Consortium) and the 22q11.2 deletion (about one in four develop schizophrenia). Older fathers , not older mothers, raise the risk (de novo mutations). The C4 finding links genes to synaptic pruning . Endophenotypes: markers between genes and symptoms Diagnoses such as schizophrenia are a long way from genes. Between the DNA and the delusion lie many steps of brain development and function, and the symptoms themselves fluctuate with treatment and stress. Gottesman and Shields brought into psychiatry the idea of an endophenotype : a measurable, internal characteristic (neurophysiological, cognitive, neuroanatomical or biochemical) that lies on the path from genes to illness. A good endophenotype is associated with the illness, is heritable, is present whether or not the person is currently ill (it is "state-independent"), and is found more often in the unaffected relatives of patients than in the general population. Because it is closer to the genes, it should be easier to study genetically than the diagnosis itself. Barlow and Durand call the strategy endophenotyping. Three candidates are examined most often. Smooth pursuit eye movement dysfunction is the oldest. Ask a person to keep their head still and follow a swinging pendulum with their eyes: a healthy person's eyes glide smoothly after it, but many people with schizophrenia cannot keep up, so their eyes fall behind and then jump forward in small catch-up movements called saccades, producing a jagged trace. Pinel illustrates the finding with recordings of a healthy participant and three participants with schizophrenia. It was first recorded in 1908 by Allen Diefendorf and Raymond Dodge and was rediscovered by Philip Holzman and his colleagues, who reported in Science in 1973 that a significant number of patients with schizophrenia showed tracking patterns strikingly different from those of healthy people and of other psychiatric patients. The deficit is not explained by medication or institutional life, and it appears in many unaffected relatives of patients, becoming less frequent the more distant the relative. P50 sensory gating measures the brain's ability to filter out repeated, irrelevant input. Two identical clicks are played about half a second apart while the electrical activity of the brain is recorded. In most people the response to the second click, a wave appearing about 50 milliseconds after the sound (the P50), is much smaller than the response to the first: the brain has "gated out" a stimulus it already knows about. In many people with schizophrenia, and in many of their relatives, the second response is barely reduced. Robert Freedman's group in Colorado linked this deficit to the region of chromosome 15 that holds the gene for the alpha-7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, and the finding offers one explanation for why so many patients smoke heavily: nicotine briefly improves the gating. Prepulse inhibition is a related measure: a weak sound (the prepulse) presented a fraction of a second before a loud, startling one normally reduces the startle blink, and this inhibition is weaker in schizophrenia. Working memory and other cognitive deficits (Section 4.3) are also studied as endophenotypes. None of these markers is specific to schizophrenia or sensitive enough to diagnose it; their value is as tools for research. Exam trap An endophenotype is a heritable, state-independent marker that is also found in unaffected relatives ; it is not a symptom and not a diagnostic test. The classic example is smooth pursuit eye movement dysfunction (Holzman, 1973). P50 sensory gating: the response to the second of two clicks fails to shrink. Prepulse inhibition: a weak prepulse fails to reduce the startle response. The neurodevelopmental hypothesis Kraepelin's very name for the illness, dementia praecox, implied a degenerative process, a brain wearing out early as it does in old age. By the 1980s that view was in trouble. Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease leave behind gliosis , scars of glial cells where neurons have died, but the brains of people with schizophrenia examined after death generally showed no gliosis, which suggested that whatever had gone wrong had happened early, before the brain could react in that way. Brain scans showed abnormalities already present at the first episode. And the risk factors that epidemiologists kept finding (season of birth, obstetric complications, prenatal infection) all acted around the time of birth, twenty years before the illness appeared. In 1987 two papers drew these threads together. The American psychiatrist Daniel Weinberger , working at the National Institute of Mental Health, argued in "Implications of normal brain development for the pathogenesis of schizophrenia" that the illness fits neither a degenerative nor a post-traumatic model but a neurodevelopmental hypothesis , in which a fixed "lesion" from early in life interacts with normal brain maturation that occurs much later. The early abnormality, he proposed, stays silent until the brain regions it affects, especially the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and the dopamine systems that innervate them, mature in adolescence and early adulthood. In the same year the British psychiatrists Robin Murray and Shôn Lewis asked in the British Medical Journal , "Is schizophrenia a neurodevelopmental disorder?", and in a companion review concluded that patients more often had a history of obstetric complications, which were associated with enlarged ventricles, especially in patients without a family history. The hypothesis explains the most puzzling fact about schizophrenia, its timing: why should a disorder of genes and pregnancy wait twenty years to show itself? Because the parts of the brain on which the lesion falls are not fully used until then. The evidence for it comes from several directions (Table 4.28 and Figure 4.12). Obstetric complications. In 2002 Mary Cannon, Peter Jones and Robin Murray meta-analysed the prospective population studies and found three groups of complications significantly associated with later schizophrenia: complications of pregnancy (bleeding, diabetes, rhesus incompatibility, pre-eclampsia), abnormal foetal growth and development (low birth weight, congenital malformations, a small head circumference) and complications of delivery (asphyxia, uterine atony, emergency Caesarean section). The common thread is a shortage of oxygen to the foetal brain. The effects are real but modest, with pooled estimates generally below a doubling of risk, and some complications may themselves be consequences of a foetus already developing abnormally. Key study: The Helsinki influenza epidemic (Mednick and colleagues, 1988) In the autumn of 1957 a type A2 influenza epidemic swept through Helsinki. Sarnoff Mednick and his colleagues saw a natural experiment: every child then in the womb had been exposed to the epidemic at a known stage of pregnancy, which could be worked out from the date of birth. They searched the psychiatric hospital records of everyone in greater Helsinki who had been a foetus during the epidemic. Those exposed during the second trimester were at raised risk of being admitted with schizophrenia as adults, in both sexes and independently in several hospitals. The second trimester is the period when neurons are migrating to their places in the developing cortex. Criticism, much of it noted by the authors themselves: there was no direct evidence that the mothers had actually been infected; diagnoses came from hospital records; the follow-up stopped at about 26 years of age; and some later studies replicated the finding while others did not. The authors' own conclusion was that the type of disturbance matters less than its timing in foetal brain development. Famine. In the winter of 1944 to 1945 the German occupation cut off food supplies to the cities of the western Netherlands, and the official rations fell to a few hundred calories a day: the Dutch Hunger Winter. Because the famine began and ended abruptly and the Dutch kept meticulous records, it became another natural experiment. In 1996 Ezra Susser and colleagues found that people conceived at the height of the famine, and so exposed to severe maternal malnutrition in early gestation, had a twofold risk of schizophrenia in adulthood, in both men and women. Pinel notes that the Chinese famine of 1959 to 1961 produced the same result. Season of birth, the father's age and the city. The 5 to 8 percent excess of late winter and spring births (Section 4.6.3) may reflect seasonal infections or nutritional shortages during pregnancy; the father's age effect points to de novo mutations (Section 4.7.4); and urban birth raises the risk by a mechanism not yet known. Marks on the body. People with schizophrenia have more minor physical anomalies , small structural deviations such as a high-arched palate, malformed or low-set ears, widely spaced eyes and unusual skin creases. Because the face and the brain develop from the same embryonic tissue during the first and early second trimesters, these anomalies act as fossils of a disturbance at that time. DSM-5-TR also lists neurological soft signs , subtle impairments of motor coordination, sensory integration and the sequencing of complex movements, left-right confusion and overflow movements, which point to the same early origin. Signs in childhood. If the illness is set up early, children destined to develop it should differ from other children long before any symptom. In a study that is now a classic, Elaine Walker and Richard Lewine (1990) collected home movies made by families of adults with schizophrenia, films that showed the patients and their healthy brothers and sisters from infancy through at least their first five years. Viewers who did not know which child had later fallen ill could nevertheless pick out the preschizophrenic children reliably, although none of them had had any psychiatric disorder in childhood. Later analyses of such films pointed to subtle motor abnormalities and less positive emotional expression. Prospective birth cohorts confirmed the picture without relying on anyone's memory. Peter Jones and colleagues (1994) examined the 5,362 people of the British 1946 birth cohort, all born in one week of March 1946, of whom 30 developed schizophrenia between the ages of 16 and 43. As children, the future patients had learned to walk later (by about 1.2 months on average), had more speech problems, scored lower on educational tests at 8, 11 and 15 years, preferred solitary play at 4 and 6, rated themselves less socially confident at 13 and were rated by teachers as more anxious in social situations at 15. Mohan's childhood in Section 4.6.4 shows the same pattern. But notice the size of the differences: a month's delay in walking, a slight preference for playing alone. These signs are found in thousands of children who never develop schizophrenia, so they are clues to the origin of the illness, not a means of predicting it in a child. Exam trap The neurodevelopmental hypothesis is credited to Daniel Weinberger (1987) and to Robin Murray and Shôn Lewis (1987) . It says the decisive abnormality arises early (before or around birth) and is unmasked by brain maturation in adolescence; it is the opposite of Kraepelin's degenerative idea. The influenza study (Mednick, Helsinki 1957 epidemic) implicates the second trimester ; the Dutch Hunger Winter study implicates famine in early gestation. The brain in schizophrenia Every neurodevelopmental argument leads back to the brain. What, exactly, is different about the brain of a person with schizophrenia? The basic anatomy (the ventricles, the lobes, the hippocampus, the prefrontal cortex) is taught in the Physiological Psychology book; here we need only the findings and what they mean. The most replicated structural finding concerns the lateral ventricles , the fluid-filled cavities deep in each cerebral hemisphere. As early as 1927 German researchers using pneumoencephalography (X-rays taken after replacing cerebrospinal fluid with air) saw enlarged ventricles in some patients. The modern era began in 1976, when Eve Johnstone , Timothy Crow, Christopher Frith and their colleagues at the Clinical Research Centre at Northwick Park in Harrow used the new technique of computerised axial tomography (CT) on 17 long-stay hospital patients with schizophrenia and on age-matched controls in employment. The patients' ventricles were larger, and within the patient group larger ventricles went with greater cognitive impairment. Since then dozens of studies, now using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), have confirmed ventricular enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles. The ventricles themselves are not the problem. Ventricles enlarge when the brain tissue around them is smaller, because it either failed to develop fully or has been lost. Three cautions apply. The enlargement is modest and found on average, not in every patient; it overlaps heavily with healthy people; and it is commoner in men, in patients with negative symptoms and cognitive impairment (the profile of Crow's Type II schizophrenia, Section 4.3), and in those with a poor prognosis. The tissue that is missing is mostly grey matter , the layer of neuronal cell bodies, dendrites and synapses. DSM-5-TR summarises the imaging evidence: reduced overall brain volume, reduced grey matter in a variety of regions such as the prefrontal and temporal cortices, altered white matter connectivity, and an exaggerated reduction of brain volume with age. Within the temporal lobe, the hippocampus and the superior temporal gyrus, which contains auditory cortex and has been linked to the auditory hallucinations of Section 4.2, are especially affected. Pinel lists four conclusions from the meta-analyses: people at genetic risk but not yet ill already show reduced volume in regions such as the hippocampus; extensive changes are already present at the first scan; the changes continue to develop after diagnosis; and different brain areas change at different rates. Part of the later progression may be due to antipsychotic treatment, alcohol, cannabis and poor physical health, which makes it hard to separate the illness from its consequences. The picture that emerges combines early development with later change: a neurodevelopmental illness, not simply a static lesion. Key study: Identical twins discordant for schizophrenia (Suddath and colleagues, 1990) If the brain differences in schizophrenia were wholly genetic, an ill identical twin and the healthy co-twin should have the same brain. Richard Suddath , E. Fuller Torrey, Daniel Weinberger and colleagues at the NIMH scanned 15 pairs of identical twins discordant for schizophrenia with MRI and compared the images blind. In 12 of the 15 pairs, the ill twin could be picked out simply by looking at the size of the fluid spaces in the brain. Measurement showed that the anterior hippocampus was smaller on the left in 14 of the 15 ill twins and on the right in 13, and that the lateral ventricles were larger on the left in 14 and on the right in 13; the third ventricle was larger in 13. Seven pairs of healthy identical twins scanned as controls showed none of these differences. Conclusion: small anterior hippocampi and enlarged ventricles are consistent features of schizophrenia, and since the twins share their genes, their cause is at least partly not genetic . In a follow-up study of discordant twins, the more an ill twin's left hippocampus differed from the healthy co-twin's, the more the ill twin's prefrontal cortex failed to activate during a card-sorting task, linking the temporal and frontal findings into a single network. Structure is only half of the story; the other half is function. In 1974 the Swedish researchers David Ingvar and Göran Franzén , measuring regional cerebral blood flow with a radioactive tracer (xenon-133), reported in The Lancet that patients with chronic schizophrenia lacked the normal pattern in which the frontal regions receive relatively more blood than the rest of the cortex. They called the result hypofrontality , reduced activity of the frontal lobes. A decade later Weinberger, Karen Berman and Ronald Zec (1986) showed that hypofrontality depends on what the brain is asked to do. They measured blood flow in 20 medication-free patients and 25 healthy controls at rest, during a simple number-matching task and during the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, a task in which the person must work out a sorting rule (by colour, shape or number) from feedback and then switch when the rule changes without warning; the test itself belongs to the Assessment book. During the card-sorting test, the controls showed a clear rise in blood flow to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex , the region at the front and side of the frontal lobe that supports working memory and flexible thinking; the patients did not. The difference was specific to that region and that task, and the patients whose prefrontal cortex activated best performed best. Later studies found that some patients show too much prefrontal activity on easier tasks, which suggests that the real problem is inefficiency, a prefrontal cortex that has to work harder to achieve less. Hypofrontality is the brain counterpart of the negative and cognitive symptoms, and Section 4.8 explains how low dopamine activity in the pathway to the prefrontal cortex may produce it. Why should the illness emerge in late adolescence? In 1982 the American psychiatrist Irwin Feinberg pointed out that the brain undergoes a profound reorganisation in adolescence: deep sleep and brain metabolism fall sharply, and the density of cortical synapses declines as unused connections are removed, a process called synaptic pruning . Pruning is normal and useful; it makes the adult brain faster and more efficient. Feinberg asked whether schizophrenia might be caused by a fault in this programmed elimination of synapses, in which too many connections, or the wrong ones, are removed. Post-mortem studies have since found fewer dendritic spines (the tiny protrusions on which synapses form) on prefrontal pyramidal neurons in schizophrenia, and the C4 discovery of 2016 supplied a plausible genetic mechanism for excessive pruning. Feinberg's hypothesis fits the timing of onset, the reduction in grey matter without loss of neurons, and Weinberger's idea of a lesion unmasked by maturation. Hypofrontality (Ingvar and Franzén, 1974) means reduced frontal activity, shown most clearly in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (Weinberger, 1986). The discordant twin MRI study is Suddath (1990) : the ill twin has the smaller hippocampus and larger ventricles. None of these findings is present in every patient, so none can be used to diagnose schizophrenia; DSM-5-TR states that there are no radiological, laboratory or psychometric tests for the disorder. Cannabis, the adolescent brain and the whole picture Of all the environmental risk factors, cannabis matters most to a clinician, because it is the one a young person can change. The question was put to the test in Sweden, where in 1969 and 1970 almost every young man was conscripted into the army and filled in a questionnaire about drug use. In 1987 Sven Andréasson and colleagues linked the questionnaires of 45,570 conscripts to psychiatric admissions over the next 15 years. Men who had used cannabis on more than 50 occasions by the time of conscription had six times the risk of schizophrenia of non-users, and the association persisted after allowing for other psychiatric illness and social background. Critics raised three objections. Perhaps the young men were already in the prodrome and using cannabis to cope (reverse causation or self-medication); perhaps other drugs, not cannabis, were responsible; perhaps a personality trait led both to drug use and to illness. In 2002 Stanley Zammit and colleagues re-analysed the extended cohort of 50,087 conscripts with a longer follow-up. The risk rose in a dose-dependent fashion; it was present in men who had used only cannabis and no other drug; and it remained when the analysis was restricted to men who fell ill more than five years after conscription, too long after for the drug use to have been prodromal. Cannabis is neither necessary nor sufficient for schizophrenia. Most heavy users never become psychotic, and most patients developed the illness without heavy use. But the dose-response relation, the timing and the consistency of the evidence across countries are consistent with a causal contribution, especially for heavy use of high-potency cannabis in adolescence, when the prefrontal cortex is being pruned and remodelled. Its active ingredient, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), increases dopamine release (Section 4.8), and in people who already have schizophrenia continued use predicts more relapses. Caspi's COMT study (Section 4.7.4) suggests that some people are genetically more vulnerable than others, though nobody can yet tell who. The practical advice to Paul in Section 4.7.1 follows directly: his brother's illness puts him at raised genetic risk, and cannabis is the one risk factor he controls. Substance-induced psychotic disorder, in which a drug produces a psychosis that clears when the drug is stopped, is described in Section 4.5 and Chapter 10. Step back now and put the strands together. Schizophrenia is highly heritable, but the heritability is spread across hundreds of common genetic variants of small effect and a few rare ones of large effect, and even an identical genome produces the illness only about half the time. Many of the environmental risks act before birth, during the critical months when the foetal brain is being assembled, and they leave traces in the body, in childhood behaviour and in the brain itself. The vulnerable brain stays largely silent until adolescence, when the pruning and maturation of the prefrontal cortex, together with stresses such as cannabis, city life, migration and adversity, unmask it. Gottesman and Shields's liability threshold, Weinberger's lesion unmasked by maturation and Tienari's sensitive adoptees are three versions of one idea: a genetic and developmental diathesis that becomes an illness only when life adds enough stress. Paul Meehl's term for the inherited neural defect, schizotaxia, and the full stress-vulnerability model of Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring are taught in Section 4.9, and the general diathesis-stress model in Book 2, Section 1.7. How the vulnerable brain actually generates delusions and voices, through dopamine, glutamate and serotonin, is the subject of Section 4.8. Clinical link Families often ask, "Did we cause this?" The genetic and developmental evidence allows a clinician to answer honestly: no parent's behaviour causes schizophrenia, the vulnerability is largely inherited and laid down before birth, and the family's real power lies in what happens next, in getting early treatment, supporting adherence and keeping the home calm. When relatives ask about marriage and children, give the actual figures (Figure 4.11) rather than vague reassurance or alarm, and say plainly that no genetic test can predict the illness in an individual; refer for formal genetic counselling only where a syndrome such as the 22q11.2 deletion is suspected. Exam trap Andréasson and colleagues (1987) : 45,570 Swedish conscripts; heavy cannabis use (more than 50 occasions) carried about six times the risk of schizophrenia. The extended follow-up (Zammit, 2002) showed a dose-response relation that persisted after excluding probable prodromal cases. But a gene does not hear voices, and an enlarged ventricle does not believe that the neighbours are reading its thoughts. Somewhere between the genes and the experience, something must be going wrong in the moment-to-moment chemistry by which neurons talk to one another. What is it? For more than half a century the leading answer has been a single word: dopamine. This section tells how that answer was reached, why it has survived, why it had to be rewritten twice, and why two other transmitters, glutamate and serotonin, now share the stage with it. Notice one unusual feature of the story as you read. The theory was not found by studying the brains of patients. It was worked out backwards, from the drugs that happened to help them. Clues from drugs: how the dopamine hypothesis was born When chlorpromazine was introduced into psychiatry in 1952 (Section 4.10 tells that story), nobody knew how it worked. A second drug soon joined it. Reserpine, the active ingredient of the snakeroot plant Rauwolfia serpentina , also calmed agitated patients and reduced their delusions and hallucinations. Chemically the two drugs had nothing in common, yet clinicians noticed that they shared two odd features. First, neither worked at once: the antipsychotic effect built up over two or three weeks of treatment. Second, at the doses that helped psychosis, both drugs often made patients stiff, slow and tremulous, with a mask-like face and a shuffling walk. They looked, in other words, as if they had Parkinson's disease. That second clue turned out to be the key. In the late 1950s the Swedish pharmacologist Arvid Carlsson (1923 to 2018) showed that dopamine, until then regarded merely as a chemical step on the way to noradrenaline, is a neurotransmitter in its own right, concentrated in the basal ganglia, the deep motor structures of the brain. Reserpine emptied the brain of it, and animals given reserpine lay almost motionless until Carlsson restored their dopamine with its precursor, L-dopa. In 1960 Oleh Hornykiewicz (1926 to 2020) and his colleague Ehringer reported that the striatum (the caudate nucleus and putamen) of people who had died with Parkinson's disease was severely depleted of dopamine. Put these facts together and a chain of reasoning follows. Parkinson's disease is a shortage of dopamine. Antipsychotic drugs produce a Parkinson-like state. So antipsychotic drugs must reduce dopamine function. And if reducing dopamine function relieves psychosis, perhaps psychosis is a state of too much dopamine. Carlsson shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Paul Greengard and Eric Kandel for this line of work. The next step came in 1963, when Carlsson and Margit Lindqvist measured the breakdown products of dopamine in the brains of mice given chlorpromazine or haloperidol. If the drugs simply emptied the brain of dopamine, as reserpine does, the breakdown products should have fallen. Instead they rose, while the level of dopamine itself stayed about the same. Carlsson and Lindqvist proposed an elegant explanation. The drugs sit on the receptors for dopamine without activating them, a receptor blockade , and the neurons that make dopamine, sensing that their message is not getting through, fire harder and release more, which is then broken down. Chlorpromazine thus became the first antipsychotic known to work by blocking receptors. (Pinel calls it the first receptor blocker ever identified, which overstates the case: curare and atropine had long been known to block acetylcholine receptors.) The theory now had a mechanism: antipsychotics work by blocking dopamine receptors. A second line of evidence ran in the opposite direction. If blocking dopamine relieves psychosis, raising dopamine ought to cause it, and it does. In 1958 the British psychiatrist Philip Connell published a monograph, Amphetamine Psychosis , describing 42 people who had become psychotic after taking amphetamine, a drug that floods synapses with dopamine and noradrenaline. Their illness looked like acute paranoid schizophrenia: persecutory delusions, ideas of reference and hallucinated voices, usually in clear consciousness (only three of his patients were disoriented), without the confusion of a delirium, and it usually cleared within a week of stopping the drug. Connell noted that the picture was commonly mistaken for paranoid schizophrenia. This is amphetamine psychosis , and in 1970 Burton Angrist and Samuel Gershon reproduced it under supervision, giving repeated doses of amphetamine to volunteers who had used the drug before until paranoid ideas emerged. Two further observations completed the picture. Small doses of stimulants, too small to affect healthy people, can make the symptoms of a person with schizophrenia worse; and L-dopa, the dopamine precursor used to treat Parkinson's disease, can produce hallucinations and paranoid delusions in some of the patients who take it. What none of these drugs reliably does is relieve negative symptoms. They add positive symptoms; they do not restore lost drive or emotion. Vinod's story shows what this looks like in practice. A 24-year-old who worked night shifts at a call centre in Gurugram, he began buying amphetamine tablets from a colleague to stay awake, and over two months took more and slept less. Then he became certain that his team leader had fitted cameras inside the office lights, and that a white car parked outside his paying-guest accommodation belonged to men sent to follow him. He heard two male voices in the corridor discussing what he was doing ("Now he is checking the window again"). He was fully alert, knew the date and could subtract sevens from a hundred without a slip, and a doctor who saw him without the history might easily have written "paranoid schizophrenia". Within a week of stopping the drug, with a small dose of an antipsychotic and plenty of sleep, the voices had gone and the white car was just a car. The chemistry of his psychosis had been produced, and then reversed, from the outside. From these clues came the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia. In its classic form it is the proposal that the positive symptoms of schizophrenia arise from excessive dopamine activity in the brain, specifically at D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway, and that antipsychotic drugs work by blocking those receptors. The receptor and the pathway named in that sentence are the subjects of the next two subsections. Indian context The snakeroot plant, sarpagandha in Sanskrit and Hindi, had long been used in India to treat mental illness. In 1931 two Calcutta physicians, the Ayurvedic practitioner Gananath Sen and Kartick Chandra Bose, reported in the Indian Medical World on Rauwolfia serpentina as "a new Indian drug for insanity and high blood pressure", recommending it for insanity with violent symptoms. The work was largely ignored until the Bombay cardiologist Rustom Jal Vakil published his experience of it in high blood pressure in 1949 and reserpine was isolated from the plant in the early 1950s; the American psychiatrist Nathan Kline then reported its calming effect in psychiatric patients in 1954. Reserpine is no longer used for psychosis, because the doses needed lower blood pressure dangerously and can cause severe depression, an observation that later fed the monoamine hypothesis of depression (Chapter 5). But it gave the dopamine story its first chemical clue. Exam trap The order matters: the drug came first and the theory afterwards. Chlorpromazine (Delay and Deniker, 1952) was found by clinical observation; the dopamine hypothesis was built in the 1960s and 1970s to explain why it worked. Arvid Carlsson won the Nobel Prize (2000) for showing that dopamine is a neurotransmitter, not for discovering an antipsychotic. Amphetamine psychosis (Connell, 1958) is a paranoid psychosis in clear consciousness , which is exactly why it supports the theory; a confused, disoriented state would point to delirium instead. And the dopamine-raising drugs create or worsen positive symptoms: an option claiming that L-dopa "reliably improves negative symptoms" is wrong. The key evidence: potency and the D2 receptor By the early 1970s the dopamine hypothesis was plausible but unproven. The decisive test needed a new technique. In radioligand binding, a drug is labelled with a radioactive atom and mixed with a preparation of brain membranes; the radioactivity left stuck to the membranes after washing tells you how many receptors the drug has occupied, and adding a second, unlabelled drug shows how strongly that drug competes for the same receptors. With this method two laboratories, working independently, asked the same question in 1976. Ian Creese , David Burt and Solomon Snyder at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, and Philip Seeman and his colleagues in Toronto, measured how strongly each of the antipsychotic drugs then in use competed for dopamine receptors in membranes taken from the striatum, the most dopamine-rich part of the brain, and compared this with how much of each drug doctors needed to give to control psychosis. Key study: Potency and D2 binding (Seeman and colleagues; Creese, Burt and Snyder, 1976) Question. If antipsychotics work by blocking dopamine receptors, does a drug's strength at the receptor predict its strength in the clinic? Method. For each drug the researchers measured the concentration needed to displace radioactively labelled haloperidol from dopamine receptors in striatal membranes, and set it against the drug's average effective daily dose in patients, a measure of its clinical potency . Result. Across drugs whose doses differed a hundredfold or more, from a few milligrams of haloperidol a day to several hundred milligrams of chlorpromazine, the two measures lined up closely (Figure 4.13). Binding to other receptors showed no such orderly relation. Conclusion. The clinical action of antipsychotic drugs is tied to blockade of one particular kind of dopamine receptor, later named the D2 receptor. Criticism. A correlation across drugs shows how the drugs work, not what causes the illness, a point taken up in Section 4.8.4.
