The more tightly a drug binds D2, the smaller the daily dose that controls psychosis: spiperone and haloperidol work in a few milligrams, chlorpromazine and promazine need hundreds. There had been a puzzle on the way, and its solution is worth knowing. Earlier binding studies that used radioactive dopamine itself as the label found that chlorpromazine competed well but that haloperidol, one of the most potent antipsychotics known, seemed to bind only weakly. The answer was that dopamine acts on more than one kind of receptor. In 1979 John Kebabian and Donald Calne divided them into two families: D1 receptors, which stimulate the enzyme adenylate cyclase inside the cell, and D2 receptors, which do not. Chlorpromazine and the other drugs of its chemical class, the phenothiazines, block both; haloperidol and the other butyrophenones block mainly D2. Since both classes treat psychosis, the receptor that matters must be D2. Five dopamine receptors are now known, grouped as D1-like (D1 and D5) and D2-like (D2, D3 and D4), and until 2024 every drug approved for schizophrenia acted at least partly by blocking, or partly blocking, the D2 receptor . Binding studies in animal brain show how the drugs work. Do the brains of patients actually contain too much dopamine, or too many D2 receptors? Post-mortem studies of the 1970s and 1980s found more D2 receptors in the striatum of patients, but nearly all of them had taken antipsychotics for years, and blocking a receptor makes the brain build more of it, so the finding could be an effect of the treatment. Positron emission tomography (PET), which images radioactive tracers in the living brain, offered a way round the problem by scanning patients who had never been treated. The results disagreed. In 1986 Dean Wong and his colleagues at Johns Hopkins reported a large increase in D2 receptors in drug-naive patients; in 1990 Lars Farde and his colleagues at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, using a different tracer, found none. Later pooled analyses settled on a small increase at most. Whatever is wrong, it is not mainly the number of receptors. The more telling result came from a different design. In 1996 Marc Laruelle and his colleagues gave patients a small dose of amphetamine and imaged a radioactive tracer that competes with dopamine for D2 receptors: the more dopamine the amphetamine released, the more tracer was pushed off the receptors. Patients with schizophrenia released markedly more dopamine than healthy people given the same dose, and the more they released, the more their positive symptoms worsened. The excess, in other words, seemed to lie on the presynaptic side, in how much dopamine the neurons release, rather than in the receptors that receive it. Hold on to that idea; it became the basis of the modern version of the theory (Section 4.8.5). Exam trap The original support for the dopamine hypothesis is that the clinical potency of typical antipsychotics correlates with their affinity for D2 receptors (Seeman and colleagues; Creese, Burt and Snyder; both 1976). The primary target of typical antipsychotics is therefore the D2 receptor, not D1, not the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor (the extra target of the atypicals) and not the muscarinic M1 receptor (blocked by some drugs as a side effect, causing dry mouth and constipation). "Potency" means how many milligrams are needed, not how well a drug works: at equivalent doses, high-potency haloperidol and low-potency chlorpromazine are about equally effective. Options such as "all antipsychotics raise serotonin levels" or "twin concordance is 100 percent" are invented distractors. The four dopamine pathways If dopamine were spread evenly through the brain, a drug that blocks D2 receptors would do just one thing. It is not. The cell bodies of dopamine neurons are clustered in a few small groups in the midbrain and hypothalamus, and their long axons run to particular targets, so that dopamine travels along a handful of separate pathways, each with its own job. Four of them matter in psychiatry. Because a typical antipsychotic blocks D2 receptors in all four at once, each pathway explains a different part of what the drug does, for good or ill. Learn them as a set; they are among the most frequently examined facts in this chapter. The mesolimbic pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) of the midbrain (the mesencephalon, hence "meso-") to the nucleus accumbens, which is the ventral part of the striatum, and to other limbic structures such as the amygdala and hippocampus. It is the brain's system for reward and motivation, and more precisely for marking which events in the world matter and deserve attention: the smell of food when you are hungry, the voice of someone you love, the sound of a threat. The same pathway is the target of addictive drugs (Chapter 10). In the classic dopamine hypothesis it is overactive in schizophrenia, and its overactivity produces the positive symptoms. Blocking D2 receptors here is the therapeutic action of every antipsychotic. Because the pathway also carries pleasure and drive, blocking it too heavily can dull them, one source of the secondary negative symptoms described in Section 4.3. The mesocortical pathway also starts in the VTA but projects to the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that holds information in mind, plans, switches between tasks and regulates emotion. In the revised hypothesis (Section 4.8.5) this pathway is underactive in schizophrenia, and the shortfall contributes to the negative and cognitive symptoms: poverty of thought and drive, poor working memory, difficulty planning. Blocking D2 receptors here does not help these symptoms and may make them worse. The nigrostriatal pathway runs from the substantia nigra ("black substance", coloured by the pigment neuromelanin) to the dorsal striatum, the caudate nucleus and putamen ("striatum" means striped body). It is part of the extrapyramidal motor system that starts, smooths and stops voluntary movement, and it is the pathway that degenerates in Parkinson's disease. Blocking D2 receptors here causes the extrapyramidal side effects of antipsychotics: acute dystonia, akathisia and drug-induced parkinsonism within days or weeks and, after months or years of blockade, tardive dyskinesia, thought to arise partly because the long-blocked receptors become supersensitive. Section 4.10 describes these side effects. They are the price of blocking D2 in the wrong place. The tuberoinfundibular pathway runs from the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (in the region called the tuber cinereum) to the median eminence at the top of the infundibulum, the stalk of the pituitary gland. Its dopamine is released into the small blood vessels that carry it to the anterior pituitary, where it continually holds back the release of the hormone prolactin; dopamine is, in effect, the body's prolactin-inhibiting factor. Block D2 receptors here and the brake comes off. Prolactin rises (hyperprolactinaemia), which can cause milk secretion from the breasts (galactorrhoea), missed periods, breast enlargement in men, sexual dysfunction and, over years, loss of bone density. A fifth, smaller projection to the thalamus is sometimes added, but the four above are the ones examiners ask about. Table 4.30 sets them side by side. A drug such as haloperidol is a key that fits D2 locks everywhere. It cannot be sent only to the mesolimbic pathway, so at one and the same dose it treats positive symptoms (mesolimbic), may worsen negative and cognitive ones (mesocortical), causes extrapyramidal side effects (nigrostriatal) and raises prolactin (tuberoinfundibular). Much of the history of antipsychotic drug development, told in Section 4.10, is the search for a way out of that dilemma. Exam trap Match each pathway to its origin, target and consequence. Mesolimbic : VTA to nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum) and limbic structures; reward; overactive in untreated schizophrenia, producing positive symptoms. Mesocortical : VTA to prefrontal cortex (including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex); underactive, producing negative and cognitive symptoms. Nigrostriatal : substantia nigra to caudate and putamen; voluntary movement; D2 blockade here gives the extrapyramidal side effects and parkinsonian rigidity. Tuberoinfundibular : hypothalamus to median eminence and pituitary; D2 blockade raises prolactin. The common baits give the mesolimbic pathway the substantia nigra as its origin, or the caudate and putamen as its target (both are nigrostriatal), or the median eminence (tuberoinfundibular). Notice also that underactivity of the mesocortical pathway causes negative symptoms, whereas D2 blockade there worsens them. What the simple theory could not explain By the late 1970s the dopamine hypothesis looked unassailable. Within a decade it was in trouble, and it is worth seeing exactly why, because the weaknesses shaped every later theory, and because "evaluate the dopamine hypothesis" is a favourite question in interviews. The first problem was timing . An antipsychotic blocks D2 receptors within hours of the first dose, yet textbooks long taught that its antipsychotic effect takes two to six weeks to appear. If excess dopamine causes the symptoms, why does removing its effect take so long? Part of the answer turned out to be that the delay had been exaggerated. In 2003 Ofer Agid , Shitij Kapur and their colleagues pooled 42 drug trials with about 7,450 patients and found that improvement is already clear in the first week and is greater in that week than in any later week; the drugs start working quickly, but beliefs held with total conviction take longer to fade. That pattern, as you will see, fits the modern version of the theory better than the old one. The second problem was non-response . Somewhere between a fifth and a third of people with schizophrenia gain little from typical antipsychotics, even when scans show that their D2 receptors are well blocked. If excess dopamine were the whole story, full blockade should always work. Many of these patients improve on clozapine, which is a relatively weak D2 blocker (Section 4.10). Later PET work deepened the puzzle in an instructive way: in 2012 Arsime Demjaha, Oliver Howes and their colleagues found that patients whose illness had resisted treatment had normal dopamine synthesis, unlike patients who had responded. In some people, it seems, the psychosis is not driven by dopamine, and blocking dopamine achieves little. The third problem was the negative and cognitive symptoms . Blunted affect, avolition, alogia and the deficits of attention and working memory (Section 4.3) are barely touched by D2 blockade and may be worsened by it, and the drugs that raise dopamine do not produce them. A theory of too much dopamine explains half the illness at best. The fourth problem was specificity . Dopamine-raising drugs produce a paranoid hallucinatory state, not the full syndrome of schizophrenia with its thought disorder, negative symptoms and decline in functioning. And D2 blockers relieve psychosis wherever it occurs: in mania, in psychotic depression, in delirium and in dementia. The drugs are anti-psychotic, not anti-schizophrenic. Dopamine seemed to be linked to psychosis as such, rather than to schizophrenia in particular. The fifth problem was the weak direct evidence . Measures of homovanillic acid (HVA), the main breakdown product of dopamine, in cerebrospinal fluid and blood gave inconsistent results; post-mortem increases in D2 receptors were confounded by treatment; and the PET increases in receptors were small. Finally there is a problem of logic that you should be able to state in one sentence: that a drug works by blocking a chemical does not prove that the illness is an excess of that chemical. Aspirin cures a headache, but a headache is not a shortage of aspirin. Table 4.31 brings the case for and against together. Table 4.31 The case for and against the classic dopamine hypothesis. When a question asks for evidence against the dopamine hypothesis, look for the delay in response, the patients who do not respond, clozapine's success despite weak D2 blockade, and the poor effect on negative symptoms. When it asks for the original evidence for it, the best answer is the correlation between clinical potency and D2 binding; amphetamine and L-dopa psychosis and the parkinsonian side effects of antipsychotics are supporting clues. Rewriting the theory: from receptors to salience Faced with these problems, researchers did not abandon dopamine. They asked where, and in which direction, it goes wrong. The first answer came in 1991 from Kenneth Davis , René Kahn, G. Ko and Michael Davidson at Mount Sinai in New York, in a review that has come to be called the revised dopamine hypothesis . Schizophrenia, they argued, involves too little dopamine in one place and too much in another. In the prefrontal cortex, fed by the mesocortical pathway, dopamine activity is low, and this cortical deficit produces the negative and cognitive symptoms; it fits the hypofrontality that brain imaging had found in patients (Section 4.7). In subcortical regions, fed by the mesolimbic pathway, dopamine activity is high, and this produces the positive symptoms. The two faults may even be linked. When Pycock, Kerwin and Carter destroyed the dopamine terminals in the prefrontal cortex of rats in 1980, the rats' subcortical dopamine system became more active, as though the cortex normally holds it in check. Later work refined the cortical half of the story: the cortical shortfall seems to involve D1 receptors, the main dopamine receptors of the prefrontal cortex, more than D2. The second rewriting came from Oliver Howes and Shitij Kapur in a 2009 paper subtitled "version III: the final common pathway". (Version I was the classic receptor hypothesis, version II the revision of Davis and colleagues.) By then a new PET technique had matured. If a person is given a radioactive form of DOPA, the precursor from which neurons make dopamine, the rate at which the striatum takes it up and converts it gives a measure of presynaptic dopamine synthesis capacity : roughly, how much dopamine the nerve terminals are geared to make and release. Study after study found it raised in schizophrenia, and when Howes and his colleagues pooled the PET literature in 2012, the presynaptic abnormality was large and consistent while the change in D2 receptors was small. The excess was also present before the illness began. People at clinical high risk of psychosis (Section 4.5) showed raised synthesis capacity, and it rose further in those who went on to become psychotic. Version III makes four claims, worth knowing in order. First, many different "hits", genetic and environmental (risk genes, obstetric complications, stimulant and cannabis use, childhood adversity, migration and social defeat, stress), interact and converge on one result, dysregulated dopamine. Second, the main site of the fault is presynaptic, in the dopamine synthesis and release of the striatum, not in the D2 receptors. Third, dopamine dysregulation is the final common pathway to psychosis, not to schizophrenia as a whole, which is why the same drugs work for psychosis in other disorders and why the negative and cognitive symptoms need another explanation. Fourth, current antipsychotics act downstream of the fault: they block the receptors that receive the excess dopamine but do nothing to the overproduction itself, so if the drug is stopped the excess is still there and relapse often follows. The person's psychology and culture, finally, decide what the psychosis is about. One detail of the new findings will surprise you if you have learned the four pathways well. The striatal excess is greatest not in the limbic (ventral) striatum, the target of the mesolimbic pathway, but in the associative part of the dorsal striatum, a region closely linked to the prefrontal cortex and supplied largely by dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra. Research has, in other words, moved the site of the fault partly away from the classic mesolimbic pathway. For an examination question about the classic dopamine hypothesis, however, the answer remains mesolimbic excess. How does too much striatal dopamine turn into a delusion? The most influential answer is Kapur's 2003 theory of aberrant salience . Normally, dopamine released in the striatum does not simply carry pleasure; it tags events as salient, as worth noticing and acting on, because they predict something that matters. A hungry person's attention snaps to the smell of food; a parent picks out his own child's cry in a noisy room. Now imagine that dopamine is released chaotically, out of step with events. Ordinary things (a stranger's glance, a number plate, a phrase on the radio, a thought that crosses the mind) suddenly feel charged with significance. This is the strange, uneasy stage that Jaspers called delusional mood and that patients describe as a feeling that something is going on (Section 4.2). The person searches for an explanation, and the delusion is the explanation he arrives at: they are watching me, the radio is sending me messages, I have been chosen. Hallucinations, in Kapur's account, are internal representations, such as inner speech and memories, that acquire the same aberrant salience and are experienced as if they came from outside. The content of the explanation comes from the person's own fears, history and culture, which is why the persecutors of the 1950s worked through radios and those of today work through mobile phones and hidden cameras. The theory also explains how antipsychotics work, and why the effect looks the way it does. By blocking D2 receptors, the drugs dampen salience. They do not erase a delusion; they take the heat out of it. Patients recovering on medication typically say not "I was wrong" but "It doesn't bother me so much now" or "I don't think about it as much", and only later, as new experience accumulates, does the belief itself fade, which is why full recovery takes weeks even though the drug acts in hours. Dampening salience too much has a cost: if rewards also lose their pull, the person may feel flat, slowed and uninterested, a drug-induced cousin of the negative symptoms. And if the drug is stopped, the aberrant salience returns, which is one reason relapse after stopping medication is so common (Section 4.10). "When the brain is under strain, the chemical that marks things as important can start firing at the wrong times, so ordinary things feel loaded with meaning. The tablet turns that volume down and gives your mind a quieter space to make sense of what has happened." Many patients find this less insulting than being told that their beliefs are false, and it also explains why the tablet should not be stopped as soon as the fear has gone: the volume control is still needed. Exam trap Keep the versions apart. The classic hypothesis: hyperactivity of mesolimbic dopamine at D2 receptors produces the positive symptoms. The revised hypothesis (Kenneth Davis and colleagues, 1991 ): subcortical excess for positive symptoms plus prefrontal (mesocortical) deficit for negative and cognitive symptoms. Version III (Howes and Kapur, 2009 ): raised presynaptic dopamine synthesis and release in the striatum, the final common pathway to psychosis . Aberrant salience is Kapur's (2003). An option saying that positive symptoms come from "reduced dopamine in the prefrontal cortex only" describes the negative-symptom half of the revised hypothesis, not the classic account of positive symptoms. The glutamate hypothesis If dopamine explains the positive symptoms but not the rest, what explains the rest? The most important candidate is glutamate, the main excitatory neurotransmitter of the brain, released by most of the pyramidal neurons of the cortex and hippocampus. Glutamate acts on several kinds of receptor, and the one that matters here is the NMDA receptor , named after N-methyl-D-aspartate, a synthetic chemical that activates it selectively. The NMDA receptor is an unusual lock. It opens only when glutamate binds to it, a second chemical (glycine or D-serine) binds to a separate co-agonist site, and the cell membrane is already partly excited, so that a magnesium ion plugging the channel is pushed out. Because it opens only when several signals coincide, it works as a detector of coincidence, and it is central to learning, memory and the fine timing of cortical circuits. The clue, once again, came from a drug. Phencyclidine (PCP) was introduced in the late 1950s as a surgical anaesthetic under the trade name Sernyl. In 1959 Elliot Luby and his colleagues gave small doses to volunteers and reported a state they called "schizophrenomimetic": distortions of body image, disorganised thinking, apathy, negativism and withdrawal, as well as hallucinations and paranoid ideas. Patients waking from PCP anaesthesia were often agitated and psychotic, so the drug was withdrawn from human use, to reappear on the street as "angel dust". Ketamine , a shorter-acting relative developed in the 1960s, produced similar but milder effects. In 1983 pharmacologists showed that PCP and ketamine both block the NMDA receptor, plugging its channel. The decisive argument was made in 1991 by Daniel Javitt and Stephen Zukin . Amphetamine, they pointed out, mimics only the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. PCP mimics the positive symptoms, the negative symptoms, the formal thought disorder and the cognitive deficits, and in people who already have schizophrenia it rekindles their own characteristic symptoms. A drug that blocks NMDA receptors reproduces the whole illness better than any drug that releases dopamine. So perhaps schizophrenia is, at root, a state of reduced NMDA receptor function. This is the glutamate hypothesis , also called the hypothesis of NMDA receptor hypofunction , the phrase John Olney and Nuri Farber used in 1995. Experiments with ketamine soon confirmed the claim under controlled conditions. In 1994 John Krystal and his colleagues at Yale gave healthy volunteers small, sub-anaesthetic infusions of ketamine and recorded suspiciousness, unusual perceptions, conceptual disorganisation, blunted emotion and withdrawal, and poorer performance on tests of attention, memory and frontal-lobe function, all wearing off as the drug cleared. There had been an earlier hint from patients' spinal fluid too: in 1980 Kim, Kornhuber and their colleagues reported low glutamate in the cerebrospinal fluid of people with schizophrenia, although later studies did not consistently confirm it. Nature has supplied a striking test case. In 2007 Josep Dalmau and his colleagues identified anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, an autoimmune illness in which the body makes antibodies against its own NMDA receptors, sometimes triggered by a tumour such as an ovarian teratoma. It mostly affects young women and children, and it very often begins psychiatrically, with anxiety and insomnia followed by delusions, hallucinations, agitation or catatonia, so that many patients are first admitted to psychiatric wards. Only later come seizures, abnormal movements, unstable pulse and blood pressure, and falling consciousness. When the antibodies are removed by immunotherapy, the psychosis usually resolves. Here, then, is a psychosis caused by a known loss of NMDA receptor function, exactly as the glutamate hypothesis predicts, and it is one of the medical mimics that must be considered in a first episode (Section 4.4). Genetics points the same way. Among the 108 regions of the genome linked to schizophrenia in 2014 (Section 4.7) were several genes for glutamate receptors and for the enzyme that makes D-serine, along with the gene for the D2 receptor itself. How could a glutamate fault produce a dopamine excess? The best-supported answer runs through inhibitory neurons. Among the neurons that carry NMDA receptors are fast-firing GABA interneurons , which release gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the brain's main inhibitory transmitter, and keep the cortex and hippocampus in rhythm. These interneurons seem especially sensitive to NMDA receptor blockade. If their NMDA receptors underperform, they fire less; the pyramidal neurons they normally restrain are released from inhibition; and cortical activity becomes noisy and poorly timed, a plausible basis for disorganised thinking and failing working memory. In the hippocampus the same disinhibition makes the region overactive, and work in Anthony Grace's laboratory with animal models showed that an overactive hippocampus, through a relay in the basal ganglia, increases the number of VTA dopamine neurons that are ready to fire. The result is the striatal dopamine excess of version III. In this account glutamate is upstream and dopamine downstream: the glutamate and GABA faults would produce the negative and cognitive symptoms directly and the positive symptoms indirectly, through dopamine. Figure 4.14 draws the chain. NMDA receptor hypofunction (genes, PCP, ketamine) GABA interneurons underactive, so circuits disinhibited Hippocampus overactive; drives VTA dopamine cells Prefrontal circuits weak; low cortical dopamine Stress, cortisol, social defeat (Section 4.9) Striatal dopamine synthesis and release raised Negative and cognitive symptoms Positive symptoms: delusions and hallucinations Aberrant salience: neutral events feel charged with meaning Antipsychotics block D2 receptors at the end of the dopamine chain: they damp salience and positive symptoms, but leave the glutamate and prefrontal faults untouched. Figure 4.14 One way the transmitter theories fit together. A glutamate (NMDA receptor) fault weakens inhibitory GABA interneurons; disordered prefrontal circuits give negative and cognitive symptoms directly, while an overactive hippocampus, helped by stress, drives the striatal dopamine excess that produces aberrant salience and, through the person's attempts to explain it, the positive symptoms. If the glutamate hypothesis is right, drugs that boost NMDA receptor function should help, especially with negative and cognitive symptoms. The idea has been tested many times: with the co-agonists glycine and D-serine, with sarcosine and with drugs that slow the removal of glycine from synapses, and with drugs acting on other glutamate receptors. Small early trials looked promising, but large trials have so far been disappointing, and no glutamate drug is yet in routine use. The hypothesis is strong as an explanation and still weak as a guide to treatment. Exam trap The glutamate hypothesis proposes hypofunction (underactivity) of NMDA receptors, not "glutamate excess at NMDA receptors". Its evidence is that the NMDA receptor antagonists phencyclidine (PCP) and ketamine produce a schizophrenia-like state in healthy people. Learn the contrast with amphetamine: dopamine-releasing drugs mimic mainly positive symptoms, whereas PCP and ketamine mimic positive, negative and cognitive symptoms (Javitt and Zukin, 1991). Pinel's textbook puts the drug models in one line each: LSD-type drugs model the positive symptoms through serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, ketamine-type drugs model the negative symptoms through glutamate receptors. Serotonin, GABA and the other transmitters Serotonin entered the story through another accident. In April 1943 the Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann (1906 to 2008), working at the Sandoz laboratories in Basel, absorbed a trace of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), a compound he had synthesised in 1938, and experienced the first LSD trip: vivid colours, shifting shapes, a distorted sense of time and self. Because LSD was found to block some actions of serotonin in tissues outside the brain, Woolley and Shaw suggested in 1954 that disturbed serotonin might underlie mental disorders such as schizophrenia, and through the 1950s LSD was studied as a model psychosis , a drug-made copy of the illness that could be switched on and off in the laboratory. We now know that LSD, psilocybin (from "magic mushrooms") and mescaline (from the peyote cactus) produce their effects by stimulating the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor. As a model of schizophrenia, LSD is poor. Its hallucinations are mainly visual (colours, patterns, objects that seem to breathe or melt), and it often blends the senses, so that sounds are seen as colours (synaesthesia); the hallucinations of schizophrenia, by contrast, are mainly voices. The LSD user also usually knows that the drug is responsible, whereas insight is typically lost in schizophrenia. Clinicians who knew both conditions rarely confused them, which is a large part of why the serotonin theory of schizophrenia faded in the 1960s. Serotonin returned in a different role, through the atypical antipsychotics. Clozapine and the drugs that followed it block 5-HT2A receptors more strongly than they block D2 receptors, and in 1989 Herbert Meltzer , with Matsubara and Lee, proposed that a high ratio of 5-HT2A to D2 blockade is what makes a drug "atypical": effective against psychosis with few extrapyramidal side effects. The usual explanation is that serotonin, acting through 5-HT2A receptors, puts a brake on dopamine release. Block that brake while also blocking D2, and dopamine release rises a little in the nigrostriatal pathway (fewer extrapyramidal side effects), in the tuberoinfundibular pathway (a smaller rise in prolactin) and perhaps in the mesocortical pathway (possibly a little help for negative and cognitive symptoms), while D2 blockade in the mesolimbic pathway still controls the positive symptoms. Hence the name serotonin-dopamine antagonists for these drugs. The serotonin route can relieve psychosis on its own in at least one setting: pimavanserin, which acts on 5-HT2A receptors without blocking dopamine, was approved in the United States in 2016 for the hallucinations and delusions of Parkinson's disease psychosis. Not everyone accepts Meltzer's explanation. In 2001 Shitij Kapur and Philip Seeman argued that atypicality comes instead from the way a drug holds the D2 receptor: clozapine and quetiapine bind loosely and let go quickly, so that natural surges of dopamine can still get through, and amisulpride behaves as an atypical drug even though it barely touches 5-HT2A receptors. Both mechanisms probably contribute. Note also that blocking 5-HT2A is not what causes the weight gain and metabolic problems of drugs such as olanzapine and clozapine; those are linked more to their blockade of histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2C receptors (Section 4.10). GABA has already appeared in the glutamate story. Its own evidence comes mainly from post-mortem studies of the prefrontal cortex, in which David Lewis and his colleagues found reduced levels of GAD67, an enzyme that makes GABA, in the subgroup of fast-firing interneurons that contain the protein parvalbumin. These interneurons pace the fast gamma rhythms (roughly 30 to 80 cycles a second) that bind neurons together while information is held in mind, and gamma rhythms are weak in schizophrenia, which may help to explain the deficits in working memory. Drugs that enhance GABA, the benzodiazepines, calm agitation and are the first treatment for catatonia (the lorazepam challenge of Section 4.5), but they do not treat the core psychosis. Acetylcholine, finally, has become a treatment target. Some older antipsychotics and clozapine block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, which causes dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision and, in older people, confusion (Section 4.10). Stimulating certain muscarinic receptors in the brain (the M1 and M4 types), by contrast, damps the release of striatal dopamine indirectly. In September 2024 the United States approved xanomeline combined with trospium (xanomeline stimulates these receptors; trospium, which does not enter the brain, blocks the unwanted effects elsewhere in the body), the first modern drug for schizophrenia that does not act directly on D2 receptors. Notice the final common pathway again: even this new drug works, in the end, by reducing striatal dopamine. People with schizophrenia also smoke far more often and more heavily than the general population, and one suggested reason is that nicotine briefly improves attention and sensory gating through nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Where does this leave the chemistry of schizophrenia? No single transmitter explains it. The most defensible picture today is layered. Faults in glutamate signalling and in GABA interneurons disturb the timing of cortical and hippocampal circuits, producing negative and cognitive symptoms directly. These faults, together with stress and the other hits of version III, push striatal dopamine synthesis and release too high, the final common pathway to the positive symptoms. Serotonin and acetylcholine modulate the system and offer further handles for treatment. For an examination question, however, dopamine remains the answer for positive symptoms. Drugs Main action Positive symptoms Negative and cognitive symptoms How like schizophrenia? Amphetamine, cocaine, L-dopa Raise dopamine release or supply Yes: persecutory delusions, voices Few Like acute paranoid schizophrenia, in clear consciousness Phencyclidine (PCP), ketamine Block NMDA glutamate receptors Yes Yes: blunting, withdrawal, thought disorder, poor working memory Closest overall copy LSD, psilocybin, mescaline Stimulate serotonin 5-HT2A receptors Mainly visual hallucinations and illusions Few Poor copy: visual, insight often kept Exam trap The classic dopamine hypothesis says that positive symptoms come from excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathways . Each distractor misplaces a real fact. "Decreased serotonin activity" belongs to the old monoamine theory of depression (Chapter 5). "Excess serotonin at 5-HT2A receptors only" overstates the LSD model; 5-HT2A is the extra target of the atypical drugs, not the cause of schizophrenia. "Decreased GABA activity in the cerebellum" puts a genuine GABA finding in the wrong place (the findings are in the prefrontal cortex; the cerebellum coordinates movement). "Excess acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction" belongs to the synapse between nerve and muscle, the territory of myasthenia gravis and organophosphate poisoning, not to psychosis. Atypical antipsychotics add 5-HT2A blockade to D2 blockade (Meltzer's serotonin-dopamine idea), and the glutamate hypothesis is NMDA hypofunction . 4.9 Psychological, Family and Social Explanations High yield · 9 Qs Genes and neurotransmitters tell you why a person is vulnerable to psychosis and what the brain is doing during it. They do not tell you why the illness began in this person in this year, why it returned after a family quarrel, why the voices say what they say, or why the children of migrants in London and Amsterdam fall ill more often than the people of the countries their parents left. For those questions you need psychology and sociology. This section evaluates five kinds of explanation: the psychodynamic theories, which dominated American psychiatry for half a century and are now mainly of historical interest; the cognitive theories, which explain how particular symptoms arise and persist; the family theories, which first blamed parents and then, with expressed emotion, found something real; the theories of stress and vulnerability, which tie the biological and psychological strands together; and the social theories, from labelling to social defeat. Keep one distinction in mind throughout, because the examiners do. Some of these factors are claimed to cause the illness; others only to shape its course . The evidence treats the two claims very differently. Psychodynamic accounts For the first two-thirds of the twentieth century, especially in the United States, the most prestigious explanations of schizophrenia were psychoanalytic. They are rarely used in practice today, but the papers still ask who proposed which idea, and the theories are worth understanding as serious attempts to make sense of experiences that can seem senseless. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) seldom treated patients with psychosis, and he built his theory largely from a book. In 1903 Daniel Paul Schreber (1842 to 1911), a distinguished German judge who had been appointed presiding judge of a senate of the Saxon court of appeal shortly before his second breakdown, published his Memoirs of My Nervous Illness , a detailed account of his delusions: that God was turning him into a woman by means of "rays" so that he could bear a new race of humans, that his former doctor Paul Flechsig had committed "soul murder" against him, and that the world had come to an end. In 1911 Freud published an analysis of the memoirs, a case of a man he never met. He proposed two ideas. The first concerned the content of paranoia. Schreber's persecutory delusions, Freud argued, were a defence against an unacceptable homosexual wish, transformed in steps: "I (a man) love him" is denied ("I do not love him, I hate him") and then projected ("He hates me"), so that the love returns as persecution. By other transformations the same wish could produce delusions of jealousy, erotomania and grandeur. This part of the theory has found no support and is now of historical interest only. The second idea concerned psychosis in general and has had more influence. In schizophrenia, Freud suggested, the libido (the energy of attachment) is withdrawn from people and things in the outside world and turned back onto the self, a regression to the earliest, narcissistic stage of development. The world, emptied of emotional investment, seems to end; the self, overcharged, swells into grandiosity and hypochondria. The delusions and hallucinations come later, as a crude attempt to reconnect with the world. "The delusional formation, which we take to be the pathological product," Freud wrote, "is in reality an attempt at recovery, a process of reconstruction." In 1924 he put the contrast between the two great classes of illness in a sentence: neurosis is a conflict between the ego and the id, psychosis a conflict between the ego and the external world. And because people with psychosis had withdrawn their libido from others, Freud believed they could not form a transference to the analyst and so could not be analysed. Freud's followers disagreed about that last point and tried to adapt the method. Paul Federn (1871 to 1950), a Viennese analyst whose papers were collected as Ego Psychology and the Psychoses (1952), argued that the basic fault in psychosis is not a withdrawal of libido from objects but a weakening of the ego boundaries, the felt edges of the self that separate what belongs to me (my thoughts, my wishes) from what belongs to the world. When the boundary is weak, inner events are experienced as outer ones: a thought is heard as a voice, a wish is felt as an influence from outside. The idea is a remarkably good description of the passivity experiences and thought alienation that Schneider later ranked first (Section 4.1). Federn concluded, unusually for an analyst, that uncovering hidden conflicts was dangerous for such patients, and that therapy should instead support their defences and strengthen the boundary. In the United States, Harry Stack Sullivan (1892 to 1949) moved the theory from drives to relationships. Working at the Sheppard and Enoch Pratt Hospital near Baltimore in the 1920s, he set up a small ward for young men with schizophrenia, staffed by aides chosen for their warmth and tact, and reported unusually good results. For Sullivan, personality is built out of relationships, and schizophrenia arises when early relationships, above all with the mothering person, are so charged with anxiety that parts of experience cannot be integrated into the self and are dissociated as "not-me". Under later stress, often a crisis of sexuality or failure in adolescence, the dissociated experience breaks through as panic and returns as psychotic symptoms. Because the illness was interpersonal, Sullivan argued, it could be reached through a patient, respectful relationship; his one-genus postulate held that "we are all much more simply human than otherwise". His colleague Frieda Fromm-Reichmann (1889 to 1957) carried the approach into intensive psychotherapy at Chestnut Lodge in Maryland. Her 1948 phrase "schizophrenogenic mother" belongs with the family theories (Section 4.9.3). Silvano Arieti (1914 to 1981), an Italian-born American psychiatrist, is remembered for his account of the logic of schizophrenic thought in Interpretation of Schizophrenia (1955; second edition 1974). Arieti described the thinking of acute psychosis as palaeologic thinking , an older, more primitive logic that follows the von Domarus principle , named after Eilhard von Domarus, who described it in 1944. Ordinary logic treats two things as identical only when the subjects are identical; palaeologic accepts identity on the basis of a shared predicate. Arieti's best-known example is a patient who reasoned: "The Virgin Mary was a virgin; I am a virgin; therefore I am the Virgin Mary." Arieti also saw schizophrenia as the end of a long psychological story: a child who grows up with a damaged, anxious self-image, whose defences hold for years, and who, faced in early adulthood with a crisis that seems to confirm his worst view of himself, abandons ordinary logic for a private one in which the unbearable can be escaped. Several later analysts appear in examination questions mainly as names to be matched with ideas. Margaret Mahler (1897 to 1985), the Hungarian-born child analyst of separation-individuation, proposed that the infant passes from a normal autistic phase in the first weeks, through a normal symbiotic phase in which mother and infant are experienced as one, to gradual separation. In a 1952 paper on childhood psychosis she described two failures: an autistic psychosis, in which the child never emerges from the autistic phase, and a symbiotic psychosis , in which the child cannot move beyond symbiosis to separate. Her developmental view of schizophrenia, as it is usually summarised, is that the person remains at the autistic phase and fails to develop an adequate and stable symbiosis with the mother. (Later infant research, notably Daniel Stern's, cast doubt on whether a normal autistic phase exists at all.) Ping-Nie Pao , in Schizophrenic Disorders (1979), traced the illness to an early disturbance in the mother-infant relationship that leaves the person liable, under later conflict, to organismic panic , an overwhelming anxiety that paralyses the ego; the symptoms are then the best adaptation the person can manage to restore a sense of self. Edith Jacobson (1897 to 1978), author of The Self and the Object World (1964), proposed that psychotic regression dissolves the boundary between the mental images of the self and of other people, so that self and object representations fuse. And Melanie Klein (1882 to 1960) traced psychotic anxieties to the paranoid-schizoid position of the first months of life, in which the infant splits its world into wholly good and wholly persecuting parts. As explanations of cause, badly. None has been supported by evidence that the proposed early experiences come before the illness, and the twin and adoption studies of Section 4.7 show that much of the risk is genetic. As treatments, they were tested and found wanting. In 1968 Philip May reported a trial at Camarillo State Hospital in California in which first-admission patients with schizophrenia were randomly assigned to individual psychotherapy alone, antipsychotic medication alone, psychotherapy with medication, electroconvulsive therapy or milieu care. Psychotherapy alone did no better than milieu care; the two groups that received medication did best; and adding psychotherapy to medication added little. In the Boston Psychotherapy Study of the early 1980s, John Gunderson and his colleagues compared exploratory, insight-oriented psychotherapy with practical, reality-adaptive supportive therapy and found no advantage for the insight-oriented approach. And when Thomas McGlashan followed up the patients who had received intensive psychotherapy at Chestnut Lodge itself, most of those with schizophrenia had done poorly. What survives of the tradition is its humane insistence that psychotic experience has meaning and that the relationship with the patient matters, an insistence that cognitive therapy for psychosis has inherited in a testable form. Exam trap "Schizophrenia corresponds to the autistic phase of development, and the person fails to develop an adequate and stable symbiosis" is Margaret Mahler 's developmental theory (IHBAS 2020). The other names in that question have ideas of their own: Silvano Arieti , palaeologic thinking and the von Domarus principle; Ping-Nie Pao , organismic panic; Edith Jacobson , fusion of self and object representations. Paul Federn is weak ego boundaries, Harry Stack Sullivan interpersonal anxiety, and Freud withdrawal of libido with regression to narcissism, delusions being an attempt at recovery (the Schreber case, 1911). Do not confuse Mahler's "autistic phase" with Bleuler's "autism" (withdrawal into an inner world, one of the four As of Section 4.1) or with autism spectrum disorder (Chapter 3). Cognitive accounts Cognitive psychology asks a narrower but more answerable question than psychoanalysis. Not "what childhood conflict causes schizophrenia?" but "what goes wrong in perception, reasoning and self-monitoring that lets a particular symptom form and persist?" Since the 1980s, British researchers in particular have built a detailed and testable account of the positive symptoms, and it is the scientific basis of cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (Book 2, Section 5.6.6). Here the focus is on the explanations themselves. Consider Gopal. Gopal is a 38-year-old clerk in a cooperative bank in Madurai. Over the past year he has become convinced that a group of colleagues, led by the new branch manager, is collecting evidence to have him dismissed and arrested. The evidence, as he sees it, is everywhere. When a colleague coughed twice as Gopal walked past, it was a signal to the others. When the manager joked at a staff meeting that "some people here are counting more than money", Gopal knew at once that the remark was aimed at him. When his loan files were moved to another desk, it was proof of the conspiracy, not a reorganisation. At night he hears a man's voice saying, "We have all the papers now." Ask Gopal why these things happen and he is never in doubt: other people are doing them to him. Listen first to how quickly Gopal reaches his conclusions. One cough becomes a signal; one joke becomes a threat. In 1988 Huq, Philippa Garety and David Hemsley at the Institute of Psychiatry in London measured this tendency with an elegant experiment, the beads task . The participant is shown two jars of beads, one holding 85 beads of one colour and 15 of another, the other with the proportions reversed. The jars are hidden, beads are drawn one at a time from one of them, and the participant may see as many beads as he likes before deciding which jar they come from. Most healthy people ask for several beads. People with delusions typically decide after one or two. This is the jumping-to-conclusions bias : a habit of gathering too little evidence before accepting a conclusion. It is a bias in data gathering, not an inability to reason with probabilities, and it is found in a large proportion of people with delusions and, more weakly, in their relatives and in healthy people prone to unusual beliefs. A person who jumps to conclusions is more likely to accept the first explanation that occurs to him for a strange experience, and less likely to collect the evidence that might dissolve it. Listen next to how Gopal explains bad events. Every misfortune is caused by someone else, and in particular by other people's intentions towards him. Richard Bentall and his colleagues have studied this as an attributional bias . Healthy people show a mild self-serving bias: they tend to credit themselves for good events and blame circumstances for bad ones. In 1989 Kaney and Bentall found that people with persecutory delusions show an exaggerated externalising bias , blaming bad events on external causes far more than either healthy or depressed people do. Peter Kinderman and Bentall later showed that the bias is, more precisely, a personalising bias : people with persecutory delusions blame other people rather than situations or chance ("the manager moved my files to get me", not "files get moved when a branch reorganises"). Bentall proposed that the style may be defensive, protecting a fragile self-esteem by locating the cause of failure outside the self, at the cost of a world full of persecutors. A rival view, from Daniel Freeman and his colleagues, sees persecutory delusions less as a defence than as a direct expression of anxiety, a threat belief built from worry, low self-esteem and the anomalous experiences of early psychosis. Both camps agree that emotion as well as reasoning drives the delusion. Gopal also misreads other minds. The manager's joke was in fact aimed at an accountant who had miscounted the cash the week before; everyone else in the room understood that, and Gopal did not. The ability to infer what other people believe, intend and mean, including what they mean when they hint or joke, is called theory of mind (Section 4.3 places it under social cognition). In The Cognitive Neuropsychology of Schizophrenia (1992), the British psychologist Christopher Frith proposed that many symptoms of schizophrenia reflect faults in the brain's capacity to represent mental states, its own and other people's. He sorted them into three kinds. A failure to generate willed actions produces the poverty of action and speech of the negative symptoms. A failure to monitor one's own intentions produces passivity experiences and some hallucinations (below). And a failure to infer other people's intentions produces paranoid delusions and delusions of reference: if you cannot tell what others mean, you may assume they mean you harm, or that their words and gestures are about you. Corcoran, Mercer and Frith tested the third claim in 1995 with a hinting task: short stories in which one character drops a hint (a man late for an interview tells his wife, "I want to wear that blue shirt, but it's very creased") and the participant is asked what the character really means. People with schizophrenia, especially those with paranoid or negative symptoms, were poor at taking hints. Frith's second claim explains some of the strangest symptoms of all, thought insertion and the experience of being controlled (Section 4.1). Each time you move, your brain sends a copy of the motor command to the sensory systems, predicting the sensation the movement will produce; when the sensation arrives as predicted, it is muted and labelled as self-caused. This self-monitoring is why you cannot tickle yourself. Frith proposed that in passivity experiences the prediction fails, so that actions and thoughts the person has generated feel as if they come from elsewhere. In 2000 Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Frith and their colleagues tested the idea with a device that stroked the palm, worked either by the participant or by the experimenter. Healthy people rated self-produced touch as much less intense and tickly than touch produced by someone else. Patients with auditory hallucinations or passivity experiences did not: their own touch felt as intense as another person's, just as the theory predicts. A related account explains the voices. Hearing a voice in an empty room is, on this view, a failure of source monitoring (Bentall in 1990 called it a failure of reality discrimination): the person's own inner speech, the silent talking to oneself that everyone does, is produced but not recognised as self-produced, and so is experienced as an external voice. Two lines of evidence support it. People who hallucinate are more likely than others to misattribute their own words or thoughts to an outside source in laboratory memory tasks; and in 1993 Philip McGuire , Shah and Robin Murray showed with brain imaging that Broca's area, the region of the left frontal lobe that produces speech, is active while patients are hearing voices. The voice, in other words, is speech the person is generating without knowing it. Its content is not random either. It usually echoes the person's own fears, guilt and preoccupations, which is why Gopal's voice talks about papers and arrest. Cognitive theory has turned to the negative symptoms as well. Aaron T. Beck (1921 to 2021), whose cognitive therapy is taught in Book 2, and Paul Grant showed in 2009 that people with schizophrenia who hold defeatist beliefs about performance ("If I cannot do something well, there is little point in doing it at all"; "If I fail partly, it is as bad as being a complete failure") show more avolition and social withdrawal, and that these beliefs partly carry the link between cognitive impairment and poor everyday functioning. A person who has failed repeatedly expects to fail again, stops trying and withdraws, and the withdrawal looks like a pure deficit even when part of it is a learned, and therefore changeable, expectation. These findings were drawn together in 2001 by Garety, Elizabeth Kuipers, David Fowler, Daniel Freeman and Paul Bebbington in a cognitive model of positive symptoms , whose use in therapy is described in Book 2, Section 5.6.6. In outline: a biological and psychological vulnerability, triggered by stress, produces anomalous experiences, such as things that seem strangely significant, thoughts that seem alien and perceptions that seem altered. These are, in the language of Section 4.8.5, experiences of aberrant salience. The person then searches for an explanation, and here psychology decides the outcome. Emotion (anxiety, depression, low self-esteem), reasoning biases (jumping to conclusions, an externalising and personalising attributional style, poor theory of mind) and the social context (isolation, adversity, a threatening environment) all push towards an explanation that is external and threatening: someone is doing this to me. Once formed, the belief is kept alive by selective attention to confirming evidence, by worry and by safety behaviours that prevent it from ever being disconfirmed. The model is the meeting point of the biology of Section 4.8 and the psychology of this one. Table 4.35 summarises the cognitive findings. Family theories: from blame to verdict Between the late 1940s and the early 1960s a group of gifted clinicians proposed that schizophrenia is caused by disturbed family relationships. Book 2, Section 7.2 tells their story at length, because the same researchers went on to found family therapy; here you need the theories in outline and, above all, the verdict. Table 4.36 summarises them. The first and most notorious was the schizophrenogenic mother described by Frieda Fromm-Reichmann in 1948: a cold, dominating, rejecting yet overprotective mother whose treatment of the child was said to produce the illness. The second, and the most often examined, was the double bind proposed in 1956 by the anthropologist Gregory Bateson (1904 to 1980) with Don Jackson, Jay Haley and John Weakland in Palo Alto, California. A double bind is a repeated pattern in which a person who depends on someone receives two contradictory messages at different levels (usually a verbal message contradicted by tone, posture or gesture), cannot comment on the contradiction, and cannot leave the relationship, so that every response is wrong. Bateson's own illustration is the one examiners quote. A young man, fairly well recovered from an acute schizophrenic episode, was visited in hospital by his mother. He impulsively put his arm round her shoulders, and she stiffened. He withdrew his arm, and she asked, "Don't you love me any more?" He blushed, and she said, "Dear, you must not be so easily embarrassed and afraid of your feelings." He could stay with her only a few minutes more, and after she left he assaulted an aide and was put in the isolation room. The group offered the episode as an example of the symptomatic double bind , the double bind as a supposed cause of symptoms. At Yale, Theodore Lidz and his colleagues (1957) described two patterns of marriage in the families of young patients: marital schism , in which the parents are in chronic open conflict and compete for the child's loyalty, and marital skew , in which one parent's serious disturbance dominates the family while the other passively accepts it and pretends that all is well. At the National Institute of Mental Health, Lyman Wynne and his colleagues (1958) described pseudomutuality , a façade of family harmony that hides emotional distance and leaves no room for a separate identity, and Wynne later worked with Margaret Singer on communication deviance , a measurable tendency of parents to speak in vague, fragmented or confusing ways that make it hard for a listener to share a focus of attention. R. D. Laing went furthest, describing the "madness" of patients as an intelligible response to impossible family situations (Section 4.9.6).
