The verdict of half a century of research is no. The studies that proposed them were based on small numbers of families, seen after the illness had begun, usually without comparison groups and with no way of telling whether a parent's odd behaviour was a cause of the child's illness, a response to it or a sign of a shared genetic vulnerability. Double binds proved impossible to measure reliably and turned out to occur in all families. Communication deviance did predict later illness in prospective work, most notably in Michael Goldstein's UCLA High-Risk Project, which followed troubled but non-psychotic adolescents for about fifteen years, but the samples were small, and communication deviance is itself commoner in parents who carry some of the genetic liability. The most convincing evidence that family environment matters at all comes from Pekka Tienari's Finnish adoption study (Section 4.7), in which the adopted-away children of mothers with schizophrenia were at raised risk mainly when they grew up in disturbed adoptive families: a gene-environment interaction, not a family cause. The causal theories did real harm by adding guilt to the burden of parents, and they are now taught partly as a warning. But one strand of family research survived, because it changed the question from what causes schizophrenia to what makes it come back. Exam trap The double bind (Gregory Bateson , with Jackson, Haley and Weakland, 1956 ) was an early family-communication theory of the cause of schizophrenia , not of phobias, depression, autism, PTSD or bipolar disorder. The mother who stiffens at her son's embrace and then asks "Don't you love me any more?" illustrates the symptomatic double bind ; "cybernetic system" (a family seen as a self-regulating system steered by feedback loops) and "homeostatic system" (Don Jackson's idea that a family resists change to keep its balance, so that one member's symptom may hold the family steady) are general systems ideas (Book 2, Section 7.1), and incongruence is Satir's and Rogers's word (Book 2, Section 7.6). The double bind is not Kraepelin's, Schneider's or Aaron Beck's. An option printed "Wayne" is almost certainly Lyman Wynne (pseudomutuality), and one printed "Richmond Fromm" is probably a garbled Frieda Fromm-Reichmann (the schizophrenogenic mother); neither proposed first-rank symptoms (Schneider) or coined ambivalence (Bleuler). All of these family causes are now discredited. Expressed emotion and relapse The research that survived began, as Book 2, Section 7.2.4 describes in detail, with an unexpected observation by the London sociologist George Brown. In 1959 he reported that men with schizophrenia discharged from hospital to live with their parents or wives relapsed more often than those discharged to lodgings or to live with brothers and sisters. Something about close family life was risky. To find out what, Brown and his colleagues developed a long, semi-structured, audio-recorded interview with the key relative, the Camberwell Family Interview (named after the district of south London where the research was done), and rated not only what the relative said about the patient but how it was said. From the ratings came the construct of expressed emotion (EE): the emotional climate of a home as revealed by the attitudes a key relative expresses about the patient. A relative is rated high in EE on the basis of three components. Critical comments are remarks that express dislike or disapproval of something the patient does, judged by content or by tone ("She just sits in her room all day; she is plain lazy"). Hostility is criticism generalised from what the patient does to who the patient is, or outright rejection ("She has always been selfish; I wish she would go"). Emotional over-involvement is exaggerated, intrusive or self-sacrificing concern, dramatic distress and an inability to let the patient do anything alone ("I have not slept properly since she fell ill; I check on her every hour"). The interview also rates warmth and positive remarks, but these are not part of the high-EE index. In the version used by Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff, a relative is rated high in EE if he or she makes six or more critical comments, shows any hostility or shows marked over-involvement. The key findings come from three London studies. In 1972 Brown, James Birley and John Wing showed that patients returning to high-EE homes were roughly three to four times as likely to relapse in the nine months after discharge as those returning to low-EE homes. In 1976 Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff replicated the finding and identified two protective factors within high-EE homes: regular maintenance medication, and less than about 35 hours a week of face-to-face contact with the high-EE relative. Patients in high-EE homes with neither protection relapsed almost without exception (about nine in ten in the pooled figures), whereas patients in low-EE homes relapsed at about one in eight; Book 2, Figure 7.2 shows the full pattern. The finding has since been replicated around the world. A meta-analysis of 27 studies by Ronald Butzlaff and Jill Hooley (1998) confirmed that high EE robustly predicts relapse in schizophrenia, and showed that it predicts relapse even more strongly in mood and eating disorders. Three further findings shape how EE is understood today. First, EE predicts relapse , not onset. It is measured in families after the illness has begun, and nothing suggests that low-EE families protect anyone from developing schizophrenia in the first place. Second, the influence runs in both directions. Hooley's work showed that critical relatives tend to believe that the patient could control the symptoms ("she could get up if she wanted to"), while low-EE relatives see the same behaviour as part of the illness; and a more disturbed or more difficult patient provokes more criticism, which in turn raises stress and the risk of relapse. Third, the effect depends on culture. In a study of Mexican-American families in Los Angeles, Steven López and his colleagues (2004) found that family warmth predicted fewer relapses: warmth, though not a high-EE component, can be actively protective. Shabnam's family shows what the components sound like at home. She is 29 and lives in Lucknow with her widowed mother and her elder brother, and she has had two episodes of schizophrenia. Since the second, she spends most of the day in her room, speaks little and has stopped helping in the house. Her brother, who runs the family's shop, says: "There is nothing wrong with her now; the doctor said the voices have gone. She is simply lazy, and she is making fools of us in front of the neighbours." Her mother, by contrast, has given up her own outings to stay at home with Shabnam, sleeps beside her, will not let her go to the market alone and weeps whenever she talks about the future. On the Camberwell Family Interview the brother would score high for critical comments and the mother for emotional over-involvement, and either would make the household high in EE. Shabnam's psychologist does not tell the family that they caused her illness. She explains that the withdrawal is part of the illness, not laziness; she helps the mother to take a few hours a day for herself; she arranges for Shabnam to attend a day centre five mornings a week, which cuts face-to-face contact in a way that suits everyone; and she checks that Shabnam is taking her tablets. These are the elements of family psychoeducation , a treatment shown in controlled trials to reduce relapse, taught in Book 2, Section 7.2.5 and placed among the treatments of schizophrenia in Section 4.10. Indian context Expressed emotion research has an important Indian chapter. As part of the World Health Organization's studies of the outcome of schizophrenia, Narendra Nath Wig , Julian Leff and their colleagues measured EE among the relatives of patients with a first episode of schizophrenia in and around Chandigarh, publishing in 1987 and 1990. The Chandigarh relatives made far fewer critical comments, fewer positive remarks and showed less over-involvement than relatives in Aarhus in Denmark (who closely resembled British relatives), and far fewer of them were rated high in EE than in a London sample. Within Chandigarh, city dwellers scored higher than villagers on every component except over-involvement, and at the one-year re-interview not a single rural relative was rated high in EE. Where EE was high, it still predicted relapse in the first year, and hostility was the component most clearly linked to relapse, over two years as well as one (over two years the overall EE index no longer predicted relapse, but hostility still did). The researchers concluded that much of the better outcome of the Chandigarh patients, compared with a London sample, was due to the lower proportion of high-EE relatives, one of the explanations offered for the better course of schizophrenia in India found by the WHO studies (Section 4.6). Why might Indian relatives be less critical? Suggested reasons include an extended family that spreads the burden and dilutes contact with any one relative, and a tendency to attribute the illness to external causes (fate, stress, spirits, the evil eye) rather than to the patient's character, which, in the light of Hooley's findings, leaves less room for blame. A caution runs the other way: an Indian mother who feeds her ill son and goes everywhere with him may look over-involved on a London scoring manual and be entirely ordinary in her own culture. Exam trap Expressed emotion is a family environment with emotionally loaded communication of a critical, hostile or over-involved kind ; it is not a patient who has difficulty talking about feelings, not a family full of overwhelmingly positive comments and not a lack of emotion in the family. Its three components are critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement ; warmth and positive regard are rated but are not high-EE dimensions . High EE predicts relapse of psychotic illness , not its onset, negative symptoms or violence, and "poor treatment outcome" is too vague to be the best answer. Reducing contact hours (below about 35 a week) is a strategy for managing high EE, not for interpersonal violence, parasuicide risk or stubbornness in children. Names: Brown, Birley and Wing (1972); Vaughn and Leff (1976); the Camberwell Family Interview. Life events, stress and the vulnerability-stress model Expressed emotion is one kind of stress. Do other stresses matter too? The classic study is again from London. In 1968 Brown and Birley studied patients whose first episode or relapse could be dated to within a week, and asked them and their relatives about events in the preceding months, counting only life events that could not have been caused by the illness itself (a death in the family, a burglary, an eviction ordered by a landlord). The events clustered in the three weeks before onset, at a rate well above that of a healthy comparison group over the same period. A World Health Organization study published in 1987 (Day and colleagues) found the same concentration of life events before episodes in centres in several countries. Life events seem to act as triggers, bringing forward an episode in a person who was already vulnerable, rather than as causes of the illness in someone who was not. The design has a weakness you should be able to name: the events are reported after the episode, and memory can be biased by the illness and by the family's search for an explanation. The obvious way to combine vulnerability and stress is the vulnerability-stress model , taught in Book 2, Section 1.7. Its logic goes back to Paul Meehl's 1962 theory of schizotaxia, an inherited defect of neural integration that develops into a schizotypal personality and, under adverse conditions, into schizophrenia, and its best-known form comes from Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring (1977). Each person, they argued, has a threshold of vulnerability, inborn or acquired; an episode occurs when stress pushes the person over that threshold, and it ends when the stress subsides, so that what is permanent is the vulnerability, not the illness. Applied to schizophrenia, the model makes a practical prediction: anything that lowers stress or raises the threshold should reduce relapse, and anything that adds stress should increase it. Keith Nuechterlein and Michael Dawson turned the model into a working map of relapse in 1984, and its later versions underlie much of modern psychosocial care (Figure 4.15). On one side are enduring vulnerability characteristics : in the 1984 version, a reduced capacity to process information, heightened physiological (autonomic) reactivity to stress and limited social competence and coping; later versions add genetic liability and dopamine dysregulation. On another are environmental stressors : a critical or emotionally over-involved relative, stressful life events, an overstimulating social environment. On a third are protective factors , some personal (antipsychotic medication, coping skills) and some environmental (effective family problem solving, supportive services). When stressors outweigh protection in a vulnerable person, transient intermediate states develop: information-processing overload, raised arousal, misreading of social cues. These show as the prodromal signs of relapse (poor sleep, tension, irritability, growing suspicion) and, if nothing intervenes, the psychotic symptoms return. The symptoms then feed back into the environment, because a relapse is itself a stress for the family. raises risk lowers risk feedback from relapse Enduring vulnerability genes, dopamine and processing deficits Stressors high-EE relative, life events, overstimulation Protective factors medication, coping, family problem solving Intermediate states processing overload, high arousal, misread social cues Prodromal signs: poor sleep, tension, suspiciousness Psychotic relapse positive symptoms return feedback: a relapse adds to stress at home Figure 4.15 A vulnerability-stress model of relapse, simplified from Nuechterlein and Dawson (1984). Vulnerability and stressors push towards relapse, protective factors push against it, and a relapse feeds back as fresh stress on the family (the three kinds of line are named in the key). Each treatment of schizophrenia works on one of the boxes. Read the figure and you can see why the treatments of schizophrenia take the shape they do. Medication works on the vulnerability side, damping the dopamine dysregulation. Family psychoeducation lowers EE and improves problem solving. Day centres, supported work and reduced contact hours cut stressors and overstimulation. And teaching patients and families to recognise the early warning signs of relapse catches the prodromal stage, when a temporary increase in medication or support can prevent a full episode. Max Birchwood and his colleagues showed in the late 1980s that most relapses are preceded by days or weeks of such non-psychotic changes, and that each person tends to have a characteristic pattern of them, a "relapse signature". Each treatment plugs a different gap in the same model. How does stress get into the brain? Elaine Walker and Donald Diforio proposed in 1997 a neural diathesis-stress model in which the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is the link. Stress raises cortisol; cortisol increases dopamine activity, especially in the striatum; and people vulnerable to schizophrenia may have a heightened HPA response, while hippocampal abnormalities weaken the brakes on the axis. A stressful home or a run of life events could therefore raise striatal dopamine in exactly the system that Section 4.8 implicated in psychosis. The model also suggests why late adolescence and early adulthood, when cortisol output naturally rises, are the years of greatest risk. Stress at the other end of life, in childhood, fits the same picture. Adverse childhood experiences such as abuse, neglect and bullying are among the best-documented environmental risk factors for psychosis: a meta-analysis by Filippo Varese and colleagues (2012) found that people who had suffered childhood adversity had nearly three times the odds of developing psychosis, and DSM-5-TR notes that the severity of positive and negative symptoms tracks the severity of earlier trauma and neglect. Exam trap A question describing "a predisposition set off by a stressor" is asking for the vulnerability-stress (diathesis-stress) model (Meehl, 1962; Zubin and Spring, 1977), not for a single cause such as "genes only", "family only" or "stress alone". In schizophrenia, stress (life events, high EE) is a trigger of episodes and relapses , not a sufficient cause in a person without vulnerability. Schizotaxia, schizotypy and schizophrenia are Meehl's three terms; schizotypal personality disorder itself is in Chapter 11. Keep the two Brown studies apart: Brown and Birley (1968) is the life events study; Brown, Birley and Wing (1972) is the expressed emotion study. Social explanations: labelling, antipsychiatry, the city and social defeat The last group of explanations looks beyond the family to society. The most radical of them, popular in the 1960s, questioned whether schizophrenia is an illness at all. The psychiatrist Thomas Szasz called mental illness a myth (1961), and the sociologist Thomas Scheff argued in Being Mentally Ill (1966) that much of what is called mental illness is "residual rule-breaking" that becomes a stable career once society labels it, the core of labelling theory ; Rosenhan's pseudopatient study (1973) seemed to dramatise the point. These ideas are evaluated in Book 2, Section 1.6. The Scottish psychiatrist Ronald David Laing (1927 to 1989) argued in The Divided Self (1960) that schizophrenia grows out of a basic "ontological insecurity", a precarious sense of being a real, whole and continuous person, and in Sanity, Madness and the Family (1964, with Aaron Esterson) he presented eleven families of women diagnosed with schizophrenia in which, he claimed, the patient's experiences became intelligible once the family's patterns of communication were understood. Laing saw psychosis as a potentially meaningful journey and, at Kingsley Hall in London from 1965, let people live through it with little or no medication. The loose movement against conventional psychiatry became known as antipsychiatry , a word coined by David Cooper in 1967. Taken as causal theories, these ideas fail on the same evidence that sank the family theories: the genetic findings, the brain changes present at the first episode and the strong effect of antipsychotic drugs are hard to square with an illness that is only a label or only a family's way of talking. But labelling theory contains a truth that has survived. A diagnosis of schizophrenia carries a heavy stigma, and the modified labelling theory developed by Bruce Link and his colleagues from 1989 showed that people who expect to be devalued and rejected once labelled tend to withdraw, conceal their illness and lose social support, which harms its course. Laing's insistence on listening to patients' experience lives on, too, in cognitive therapy and in the service user and survivor movements. The most active social research today is epidemiological, and it asks why schizophrenia is commoner in some social groups than in others. Three findings stand out. The first is urbanicity: being born or brought up in a city is associated with higher risk, in a dose-response fashion (the larger the city and the more years of childhood spent there, the higher the risk). Whether this reflects social causation or social drift, the debate that began with Faris and Dunham's maps of Chicago in 1939, is discussed in Section 4.6 and Book 2, Section 1.7; the fact that the risk attaches to where a person was born and raised, before any illness could cause a downward drift, favours some causal role for the urban environment. The second is migration. A meta-analysis by Elizabeth Cantor-Graae and Jean-Paul Selten (2005) found that first-generation migrants had about 2.7 times the risk of schizophrenia of the native-born population, and the children of migrants about 4.5 times, with the highest figures for migrants from developing countries and from countries where most of the population is black. The third is the ethnic density effect : members of minority groups are at higher risk when they live in neighbourhoods with few people of their own ethnicity, and at lower risk when they live among many, a pattern DSM-5-TR now describes and links to discrimination or fear of it, social isolation, weaker social support and the lack of shared, normalising explanations for unusual experiences. What links cities, migration and minority status? Selten and Cantor-Graae proposed the social defeat hypothesis : the long-term experience of being an outsider, of being excluded, discriminated against or held in a subordinate position, sensitises the brain's mesolimbic dopamine system, as chronic social defeat has been shown to do in animals, and so raises the risk of psychosis. The hypothesis is attractive because it joins the social and the biological in one chain, from humiliation to dopamine to aberrant salience, the chain of Figure 4.14; it would also explain why raised risk has been reported in other groups who often meet exclusion, such as people with hearing impairment and people who were bullied as children. It remains a hypothesis, and the size of the migrant effect must be read with DSM-5-TR's caution that some groups are more likely than others to be misdiagnosed or overdiagnosed with schizophrenia. Exam trap Keep the social theorists and their ideas apart: Thomas Szasz , the myth of mental illness (1961); Thomas Scheff , labelling theory and residual rule-breaking (1966); R. D. Laing , The Divided Self (1960) and schizophrenia as an intelligible response to an unliveable situation; David Cooper , who coined "antipsychiatry" (1967); Faris and Dunham (1939), schizophrenia concentrated in the poor centre of Chicago, the start of the social causation versus social drift debate; Jean-Paul Selten , social defeat. None of these is a sufficient cause of schizophrenia, and no psychological, family or social approach displaces antipsychotic medication as the front-line treatment (Section 4.10); CBT, family psychoeducation, social skills training and stress management are adjuncts. Answers: (1) blocker, (2) D2, (3) mesolimbic, (4) tuberoinfundibular, (5) pathway, (6) NMDA, (7) 5-HT2A, (8) Margaret Mahler, (9) jumping-to-conclusions, (10) emotional over-involvement. 4.10 Treating Schizophrenia: Antipsychotic Drugs and Beyond High yield · 11 Qs Picture a young man brought to a district hospital in Karnataka by his frightened parents late one night. For three months Prabhu, a 19-year-old diploma student, has heard two voices discussing him, has become certain that the neighbours are putting chemicals in the family's water tank, and has stopped going to college. Tonight he locked himself in his room with a kitchen knife, shouting that he would not let them poison him. What should be done for him? Had he arrived in 1930, the honest answer would have been: keep him safe behind a locked door and hope. Today the answer begins with a medicine that, for most people, quietens the voices and loosens the grip of the false beliefs within weeks. It does not end there. The same medicine acts on parts of the brain that have nothing to do with psychosis, and those actions produce side effects that every clinician must recognise on sight. And a medicine alone does not return a person to college, to work or to family life. This section follows the drugs from their accidental discovery to the clinic, explains how they work and how they harm, and then outlines the other physical and psychosocial treatments that complete care. The neurochemistry behind the drugs (the four dopamine pathways, the binding studies and the glutamate and serotonin hypotheses) is explained in Section 4.8; here you will apply it at the bedside. Before 1952, and the accidental discovery of chlorpromazine In the first half of the twentieth century the great mental hospitals of Europe, America and India were filled with people whom Kraepelin would have called cases of dementia praecox, many of whom stayed for decades (the story of the asylums is told in Book 2, Section 1.2). Psychiatry had little to offer them, and the physical treatments it invented in the 1930s were bold, crude and often dangerous. Manfred Sakel (1900 to 1957), a Vienna-trained physician, developed insulin shock treatment from 1927 and began applying it to schizophrenia in Vienna in 1933. In insulin coma therapy the blood sugar was driven down until the patient became comatose, day after day for weeks. Some patients improved, some suffered prolonged coma, brain damage or death, and when a controlled trial was finally run in the 1950s (Ackner, Harris and Oldham, 1957), patients who received the same intensive care but were put into unconsciousness with barbiturates instead of insulin did about as well. A year after Sakel, the Hungarian psychiatrist Ladislas Meduna (1896 to 1964) reasoned, wrongly, that schizophrenia and epilepsy rarely occur in the same person, so that an artificial seizure might drive out psychosis. In January 1934 he began inducing seizures with injections of camphor and then of pentylenetetrazol (Metrazol). In 1938 in Rome, Ugo Cerletti (1877 to 1963) and Lucio Bini (1908 to 1964) produced the seizure more safely with an electric current, and electroconvulsive therapy was born; it survives today, much modified, and is discussed in Section 4.10.8 and in Chapter 5. The most drastic step was surgical. The Portuguese neurologist António Egas Moniz (1874 to 1955) persuaded the neurosurgeon Almeida Lima in 1935 to cut the white matter connecting the prefrontal lobes with the rest of the brain, and Moniz received the Nobel Prize for this prefrontal leucotomy in 1949. Tens of thousands of people with schizophrenia were lobotomised before the operation fell out of use. What replaced all of these was a drug discovered by a surgeon who was not looking for a psychiatric medicine at all. The French firm Rhône-Poulenc had been making antihistamines from a family of chemicals called phenothiazines, and one of them, promethazine, turned out to be strongly sedating. Henri Laborit (1914 to 1995), a French naval surgeon, was searching for ways to protect patients from surgical shock, and he used such drugs in a "lytic cocktail" that put patients into a state he called artificial hibernation. He asked the company for a compound with stronger effects on the brain, and in December 1950 its chemist Paul Charpentier synthesised a new phenothiazine, RP 4560: chlorpromazine . In 1951 Laborit tried it at the Val-de-Grâce military hospital in Paris and noticed something curious. His patients were not asleep, yet before their operations they lay calm and strangely detached, indifferent to what was about to happen to them. He suggested that psychiatrists try it. When a psychiatrist volunteered to take an intravenous dose, she felt the same indifference, but she fainted when she stood up to walk: you will meet that side effect, a fall in blood pressure on standing, in Section 4.10.5. In January 1952 a 24-year-old manic patient in Paris, given chlorpromazine together with other drugs and ECT, settled dramatically and went home three weeks later. The decisive step was taken a few kilometres away at the Sainte-Anne Hospital in Paris. The psychiatrists Jean Delay (1907 to 1987) and Pierre Deniker (1917 to 1998) gave chlorpromazine on its own, in larger doses, to psychotic patients and published their first reports in 1952, describing thirty-eight patients. The effect went beyond sedation. Agitated, shouting patients became calm within days; over the following weeks hallucinations faded and delusions lost their hold; and some withdrawn, mute patients became more active and talkative. Rhône-Poulenc marketed the drug in France late in 1952 as Largactil (from "large activity"). In Montreal Heinz Lehmann (1911 to 1999) confirmed its effects, and by 1954 it was in use in American hospitals under the name Thorazine. Within a few years the populations of mental hospitals in many countries had begun to fall, the beginning of the deinstitutionalisation described in Book 2, Sections 1.2 and 9.8. Delay and Deniker later named the new class of drugs neuroleptic , from Greek words meaning "taking hold of the nerve", because they believed that the stiffness and slowness the drugs produced, so like Parkinson's disease, were part of how they worked. That belief would be overturned by clozapine, but the name stuck. You will also meet the older label major tranquilliser , coined to set these drugs apart from the "minor tranquillisers", the anxiety-relieving drugs such as the benzodiazepines, which have no antipsychotic action. Today the preferred name is antipsychotic drug : a drug that reduces psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions and disorganisation. No Nobel Prize was ever given for chlorpromazine; Laborit, Deniker and Lehmann shared the 1957 Lasker Award for clinical research, together with the Americans Nathan Kline and Robert Noce, who were honoured for their work on reserpine (below). Indian context: sarpagandha, the "medicine for the insane" The second antipsychotic came from India. The root of Rauwolfia serpentina , known as sarpagandha and in parts of north India as pagal-ki-dawa ("medicine for the mad"), had been used for centuries in folk medicine. In 1931 two Calcutta physicians, Gananath Sen and Kartick Chandra Bose , reported its use for "insanity" and high blood pressure, and the Bombay cardiologist Rustom Jal Vakil (1911 to 1974) established it as a treatment for hypertension in 1949, becoming the first Indian to win a Lasker Award. Its active ingredient, reserpine , was isolated in 1952, and in 1954 the American psychiatrist Nathan Kline (1916 to 1983) reported its antipsychotic effect. Reserpine works differently from chlorpromazine: it empties the vesicles in which dopamine and the other monoamines are stored, whereas chlorpromazine blocks the receptors (Section 4.8). Both, tellingly, produced parkinsonian stiffness. Reserpine was abandoned for psychosis because the doses needed caused dangerously low blood pressure and depression. The third landmark came from Belgium. On 11 February 1958, while making variations on the painkiller pethidine, the team of Paul Janssen (1926 to 2003) produced haloperidol , the first of a new chemical class, the butyrophenones. Milligram for milligram it was far more powerful than chlorpromazine, it caused little sedation or fall in blood pressure, and it became the most widely used antipsychotic in the world; it is still on the World Health Organization's list of essential medicines and is still widely injected to calm acutely disturbed psychotic patients. It also caused movement side effects more readily than any of its predecessors, and the long search for a drug that could treat psychosis without them led, as Section 4.10.3 explains, to clozapine. Exam trap Jean Delay and Pierre Deniker (1952) are credited with introducing chlorpromazine into psychiatry; Henri Laborit was the surgeon who first noticed its calming effect; Paul Janssen (1958) made haloperidol; Nathan Kline is linked with reserpine (and with the antidepressant iproniazid); John Cade (1949) introduced lithium for mania (Chapter 5), not chlorpromazine. Neuroleptics are used primarily to treat schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders; they are also used in acute mania (Chapter 5), but they are not the primary treatment for major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders. "Major tranquilliser" means antipsychotic; "minor tranquilliser" means an anxiolytic such as diazepam. How antipsychotic drugs work Dozens of antipsychotic drugs have been marketed since 1952, from many chemical families, and they share only one property: every one of them reduces transmission at the dopamine D2 receptor. Most do it by blocking the receptor (they are D2 antagonists); a few, such as aripiprazole, occupy it and stimulate it only weakly. Section 4.8 tells how this was discovered, from the observation by Arvid Carlsson and Margit Lindqvist in 1963 that chlorpromazine blocks dopamine receptors rather than depleting dopamine, to the binding studies of Philip Seeman and of Ian Creese, David Burt and Solomon Snyder in 1976, which showed that the dose of a drug needed to treat psychosis tracks its affinity for D2 receptors. Here the important consequence is practical. A tablet swallowed by mouth goes everywhere in the brain. It cannot choose to block only the mesolimbic pathway, where excess dopamine activity is thought to drive the positive symptoms. It blocks D2 receptors in all four dopamine pathways at once, and that single fact explains most of what follows (Table 4.40 in Section 4.10.5 lists the consequences). Blockade in the mesolimbic pathway is the treatment. Blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway, which controls movement, produces the extrapyramidal side effects. Blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, which controls the pituitary, raises the hormone prolactin. And blockade in the mesocortical pathway, already underactive in schizophrenia, may deepen apathy and slowness of thought, producing what clinicians call secondary negative symptoms. How much blockade is needed? Since the 1980s this question has been answered directly by positron emission tomography (PET). A patient taking an antipsychotic is injected with a tiny dose of a radioactive tracer, usually raclopride, that sticks to D2 receptors; the fewer receptors are left free for the tracer, the more of them the drug is occupying. The pioneering work was done by the group of Lars Farde at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, and the clearest single study came from Toronto. Key study: Kapur and the therapeutic window (2000) Shitij Kapur, Robert Zipursky and their colleagues randomly assigned 22 patients with a first episode of schizophrenia, under double-blind conditions, to a very low dose of haloperidol, 1 or 2.5 mg a day. After two weeks they measured each patient's striatal D2 receptor occupancy with PET, along with symptoms, movement side effects and prolactin; patients who had not responded were raised to 5 mg and scanned again at four weeks. Occupancy varied widely, from 38 to 87 percent, and it predicted everything. Clinical response became likely once occupancy passed about 65 percent, prolactin rose above about 72 percent, and extrapyramidal side effects appeared above about 78 percent (Figure 4.16). The conclusion is a therapeutic window : block roughly two thirds to three quarters of the D2 receptors and you get the benefit with the fewest movement effects; block more and you buy side effects, not extra benefit. The criticisms are that the sample was small, the study used one drug, and some atypical drugs (clozapine and quetiapine) seem to work at lower occupancies, so occupancy cannot be the whole story. The practical lesson stood: the far higher doses of haloperidol common in the 1970s and 1980s (the treatment-resistant patients in Kane's 1988 trial, Section 4.10.6, were first given an average of 61 mg a day) bought side effects, not benefit, for most patients. 72%: prolactin rises 65%: response becomes likely 78%: movement side effects rise Antipsychotic response unlikely Window EPS likely 0% 20% 40% 60% 80% 100% Striatal D2 receptor occupancy measured by PET Thresholds from Kapur and colleagues (2000), haloperidol in first-episode patients Figure 4.16 The D2 occupancy window. Below about 65 percent occupancy the drug does little for psychosis; above about 78 percent extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) climb steeply, and prolactin rises from about 72 percent. Good prescribing aims for the narrow band between. How quickly do the drugs work? Textbooks long taught that antipsychotics take two or three weeks to act, and the delay was a famous puzzle for the dopamine hypothesis, because the receptors are blocked within hours of the first dose. In 2003 Ofer Agid, Kapur and their colleagues tested the idea by pooling 42 double-blind studies with 7,450 patients. Symptom scores fell by 13.8 percent in the first week, 8.1 percent in the second, 4.2 percent in the third and 4.7 percent in the fourth. The response, in other words, begins in the first week and accumulates, with more improvement in the first fortnight than in the next. What you see on the ward follows a typical order. Sleep, agitation and hostility settle within days. Hallucinations become quieter and less frequent over the following weeks. Delusions usually fade last, and often they do not vanish so much as lose their urgency. A patient may say, "I still think the neighbours did something, but it doesn't bother me now." That observation fits Kapur's aberrant salience account (Section 4.8): the drug dampens the excessive importance that dopamine lends to experiences, but the person still has to rethink the beliefs built on them, which is one reason why psychological help is added. Because the full benefit takes weeks, a fair test of a drug, an adequate trial, means a proper dose taken reliably for about four to six weeks. What do the drugs treat, and how well? Antipsychotics are most effective against positive symptoms and disorganisation and have little effect on negative and cognitive symptoms, which is why so many patients who are free of voices remain unable to work. Barlow and Durand summarise that the first-generation drugs help roughly 60 to 70 percent of the people who take them. Roughly a fifth to a third of patients respond poorly to two or more drugs, the treatment-resistant group described in Section 4.10.6. And as Pinel reminds his readers, the drugs do not cure schizophrenia: they reduce symptoms enough for most people to leave hospital, and the illness tends to return when they are stopped (Section 4.10.7). Finally, two terms that examiners confuse. The potency of an antipsychotic is the number of milligrams needed for an effect, not how well it works. Chlorpromazine is a low-potency antipsychotic , given in hundreds of milligrams a day; haloperidol, fluphenazine and trifluoperazine are high-potency antipsychotics , given in a few milligrams. Clinicians compare doses as chlorpromazine equivalents : about 2 mg of haloperidol does the work of 100 mg of chlorpromazine. At equivalent doses the old drugs are equally effective; what potency predicts is the side-effect profile. High-potency drugs are "clean" D2 blockers, so they cause more movement side effects. Low-potency drugs also block muscarinic acetylcholine, histamine and alpha-adrenergic receptors, so they cause more sedation, dry mouth and dizziness, but fewer movement effects, because their built-in anticholinergic action partly protects the movement system (the reason is explained in Section 4.10.4). Pinel adds one more clue that D2 is the receptor that matters: the phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine bind both D1 and D2 receptors, but haloperidol and the other butyrophenones bind D2 almost alone, and they are just as effective. Exam trap The primary target of typical (first-generation) antipsychotics is the dopamine D2 receptor . Not D1 (phenothiazines bind it, but it does not predict efficacy), not serotonin 5-HT2A (the extra target of the atypicals), and not muscarinic M1 (blocking it causes side effects such as dry mouth, not the antipsychotic effect). Antipsychotics do not work by lowering the amount of dopamine in the brain; they block its receptors (reserpine is the drug that depletes dopamine). And "high potency" means a small dose in milligrams, not a stronger antipsychotic effect. Typical and atypical antipsychotics Antipsychotics are divided into two generations. The first-generation antipsychotics , also called typical or conventional antipsychotics, are the drugs introduced from chlorpromazine in 1952 onwards. They are grouped by chemistry: the phenothiazines (chlorpromazine, thioridazine, trifluoperazine, fluphenazine and perphenazine), the butyrophenones (haloperidol), the thioxanthenes (flupentixol and zuclopenthixol), the diphenylbutylpiperidines (pimozide, and penfluridol, a once-a-week tablet still used in India), and a few others such as loxapine. The second-generation antipsychotics , also called atypical antipsychotics, begin with clozapine and include the drugs introduced from the 1990s onwards: risperidone and its derivative paliperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, ziprasidone, aripiprazole, amisulpride, lurasidone and asenapine among others. Why "atypical"? For two decades after 1952 it was taken for granted that a drug could not relieve psychosis without also causing parkinsonian stiffness; Delay and Deniker had built the idea into the very word neuroleptic, and drug companies screened new compounds by whether they made rats rigid and motionless (catalepsy). Clozapine, synthesised by the Swiss firm Wander in 1958, broke the rule. It relieved psychosis in patients, yet it hardly caused catalepsy in animals or movement side effects in people. It was therefore "atypical", and the original meaning of the word is exactly that: an antipsychotic that causes few extrapyramidal side effects, and little rise in prolactin, at doses that treat psychosis. Later writers added further claims (better effects on negative symptoms, on cognition, on treatment-resistant illness), but strictly only clozapine meets all of them. Three explanations have been offered for why the atypicals cause fewer movement problems, and each fits some drugs better than others. Serotonin and dopamine blockade. Most atypicals block serotonin 5-HT2A receptors more strongly than D2 receptors, the ratio emphasised by Herbert Meltzer (Section 4.8). Serotonin acting at 5-HT2A receptors normally acts as a brake on dopamine release in the striatum and prefrontal cortex. Remove the brake and a little more dopamine reaches the nigrostriatal and mesocortical pathways, offsetting the D2 blockade there: fewer movement effects and, in theory, less worsening of negative symptoms. Drugs such as risperidone and olanzapine are therefore sometimes called serotonin-dopamine antagonists. Loose, brief binding. In 2001 Kapur and Philip Seeman proposed the fast-off hypothesis : what makes a drug atypical is not its serotonin action but that it binds the D2 receptor loosely and lets go quickly, so that the brain's natural bursts of dopamine can still get through. Clozapine and quetiapine behave like this, and PET shows that they work at lower D2 occupancies. Kapur and Seeman also pointed out that a drug loses its atypical character when its D2 occupancy is pushed too high, whatever its serotonin blockade, which is why risperidone at high doses causes movement effects and raises prolactin as a typical drug would. Partial agonism. Aripiprazole binds D2 receptors tightly but, instead of blocking them completely, stimulates them weakly. A partial agonist of this kind behaves as a blocker where dopamine is abundant and as a mild stimulant where dopamine is scarce, which is why aripiprazole is sometimes called a "dopamine system stabiliser". It raises prolactin least of all the antipsychotics and carries a low metabolic risk, but it commonly causes akathisia (Section 4.10.4). Brexpiprazole and cariprazine work in a similar way. Amisulpride is an odd one out: it has no serotonin action at all, but blocks D2 and D3 receptors with some preference for limbic areas, and at low doses it blocks the presynaptic receptors that brake dopamine release, which is why it has been used for predominantly negative symptoms. It raises prolactin strongly. When the atypicals arrived they were promoted as more effective, especially against negative and cognitive symptoms, as well as safer, and by the early 2000s they had largely replaced the older drugs in wealthy countries at many times the price. Then came two large trials run independently of the drug companies. In the American CATIE study (Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness), Jeffrey Lieberman and colleagues in 2005 randomly assigned 1,493 people with chronic schizophrenia at 57 sites to olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, ziprasidone or the old phenothiazine perphenazine, for up to 18 months. Seventy-four percent stopped their assigned drug before the 18 months were up, because it did not work well enough, because of side effects, or for other reasons. Olanzapine kept patients on treatment longest but caused the most weight gain and the largest rises in blood sugar and lipids, and perphenazine, the typical drug, did about as well as quetiapine, risperidone and ziprasidone; it was dropped more often for movement effects. In England the CUtLASS trial (Peter Jones and colleagues, 2006) randomised 227 patients whose medication needed changing to a first- or a second-generation drug other than clozapine and found no advantage for the newer drugs in quality of life over a year; if anything, the trend favoured the old ones, and costs were similar. The fullest comparison is the 2013 network meta-analysis by Stefan Leucht and colleagues, which combined 212 trials with 43,049 participants comparing 15 antipsychotics with placebo and with each other. Every drug beat placebo. The differences in effectiveness were small but consistent: clozapine came first by a clear margin, followed by amisulpride, olanzapine and risperidone, with haloperidol in the middle and chlorpromazine and several newer drugs lower down. The differences in side effects were large. For movement side effects the range ran from clozapine (lowest) to haloperidol (highest); for weight gain, from haloperidol (least) to olanzapine (most); for prolactin, from aripiprazole (least) to paliperidone (most); for sedation, from amisulpride to clozapine. Leucht's group concluded that the split into "first" and "second" generation hides more than it reveals: a clinician should choose a drug by its particular side-effect profile and what matters most to the particular patient. The first atypical is clozapine ; aripiprazole is a partial agonist, not a pure antagonist. If a question says atypicals are "better for negative symptoms", that is the expected textbook answer, but know the evidence: apart from clozapine the advantage is small, and much of it comes from causing less drug-induced slowness. Atypicals are not free of extrapyramidal effects, tardive dyskinesia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and high-dose risperidone behaves much like a typical drug. Extrapyramidal side effects, in the order they appear The pyramidal tracts carry voluntary commands from the motor cortex to the spinal cord. Everything else that shapes movement, above all the circuits of the basal ganglia that start, stop, smooth and scale our actions, was once lumped together as the extrapyramidal system, and the movement disorders caused by antipsychotics are therefore called extrapyramidal side effects (EPS). They arise because the drugs block D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway, which runs from the substantia nigra to the caudate and putamen (Section 4.8). In the striatum, dopamine is normally balanced against acetylcholine released by local interneurons. Block the dopamine and acetylcholine dominates. This balance explains two practical facts at once: anticholinergic drugs such as trihexyphenidyl relieve several of the side effects, and low-potency antipsychotics, which have anticholinergic action built in, cause fewer of them. The four classic extrapyramidal syndromes appear in a regular order, over hours, days, weeks and finally months to years (Figure 4.17; Table 4.39 summarises all four), and that order is the most useful single thing to learn in this section. Acute dystonia. In the emergency room Prabhu was given an injection of haloperidol, then haloperidol tablets. The next afternoon his mother rushed him back. His eyes had rolled upwards so that little but the whites showed, his neck was twisted hard to one side, and his jaw was clenched so tightly that he could barely speak. A neighbour had already suggested that "something" had seized him more strongly. The duty doctor recognised the picture at once, gave an intramuscular injection of an anticholinergic drug, and within twenty minutes the spasms melted away. What Prabhu had was acute dystonia , a sustained, involuntary contraction of muscles that forces the body into abnormal postures. It most often affects the head and neck: an oculogyric crisis (the eyes forced upwards, downwards or sideways for minutes to hours), torticollis (the neck twisted to one side, or bent backwards or forwards), lockjaw, a protruding tongue, grimacing, arching of the back, or a sideways lean of the trunk. Spasm of the muscles of the larynx is rare but can block the airway and is an emergency. DSM-5-TR reports that at least half of affected people develop dystonia within 24 to 48 hours of starting a drug or raising its dose, and about 90 percent within five days. The risk is greatest in children and in adults under 40, in males, with high-potency typical drugs, with injections and in people who have had a dystonic reaction before. Treatment is an anticholinergic (benztropine, procyclidine) or the antihistamine promethazine by injection; with high-potency drugs in young men, many Indian clinicians prevent it by prescribing oral trihexyphenidyl from the first day. Dystonia is painful and terrifying, and a patient who is not warned about it may never trust the medicine again. Clinical link: when a side effect looks like the illness Acute dystonia can be mistaken for catatonic posturing, for a conversion (functional) disorder, for "attention seeking", or, in many Indian families, for possession. Each mistake is dangerous, because it can lead to a higher dose of the very drug that caused the problem. Always ask what medicine was given in the last few days, and remember that the dramatic relief after an injection of an anticholinergic is both the treatment and the confirmation of the diagnosis. DSM-5-TR adds a useful contrast: people with dystonia are distressed and ask for help, whereas people in a retarded catatonic state are usually mute and show no distress. Akathisia. Asha, a 34-year-old schoolteacher from Pune, was admitted with persecutory delusions and started on haloperidol tablets. Ten days later the nursing notes read "agitated, pacing the corridor". She could not sit through the ward round; standing, she shifted her weight from foot to foot. "My legs want to walk by themselves," she said. "Inside I feel I will jump out of my skin." The junior doctor read this as worsening psychosis and raised the dose. Asha became more restless and told her husband that she would rather die than go on feeling like this. The consultant recognised akathisia (Greek for "not sitting"): a subjective feeling of inner restlessness, usually felt in the legs, together with movements that relieve it, such as fidgeting, swinging the legs while seated, rocking from foot to foot, marching on the spot or pacing. DSM-5-TR describes it as typically appearing within four weeks of starting or increasing a drug, often much sooner, more often with high-potency drugs and with rapid dose increases, and persisting for as long as the drug is continued. Reported rates among people taking antipsychotics range widely, from 20 to 75 percent. Akathisia matters for three reasons. It is easily mistaken for the agitation of psychosis, mania or anxiety, and the "treatment" then makes it worse. It is one of the commonest reasons patients stop their medication. And it is associated with dysphoria, irritability, aggression and suicide attempts. Clues that restlessness is akathisia include its onset soon after a dose change, the patient's report that it feels unlike ordinary anxiety, and its worsening when the dose is raised. Management is to lower the dose or switch to a drug less likely to cause it; the beta-blocker propranolol and benzodiazepines are the usual remedies, while anticholinergics help little unless parkinsonism is also present. Asha's dose was reduced and propranolol added, and within a week she could sit and read again. Drug-induced parkinsonism. What DSM-5-TR calls medication-induced parkinsonism reproduces the signs of Parkinson's disease: bradykinesia (slowness, with fewer spontaneous movements; at the extreme, akinesia), rigidity, tremor and an unsteady posture. Watch an affected patient walk into the room. The face is mask-like and blinks rarely, the arms do not swing, the steps are small and shuffling, the posture is stooped, the voice is soft and monotonous, and the handwriting shrinks. Moving the patient's arm feels like bending a lead pipe (constant resistance throughout the movement), or like turning a ratchet (cogwheel rigidity, a tremor superimposed on rigidity). The tremor is a slow resting tremor of about three to six beats a second; when it affects only the lips it is called rabbit syndrome . DSM-5-TR calls medication-induced parkinsonism the second most common cause of parkinsonism after Parkinson's disease itself. With antipsychotics it typically develops two to four weeks after starting, usually by three months, and at least half of outpatients on long-term typical drugs show parkinsonian signs at some point; older people, women and people with cognitive impairment are most at risk. Two features help separate it from Parkinson's disease: it starts on both sides of the body at once, within weeks of a new drug, whereas Parkinson's disease begins on one side and spreads asymmetrically over years, often with loss of smell and acting out of dreams. The greater danger is confusing it with schizophrenia itself. Akinesia and a mask face look exactly like avolition and blunted affect, so a patient may be labelled as having worsening negative symptoms (or depression) when he is in fact over-medicated; reduce the dose and the "negative symptoms" lift. Treatment is to lower the dose or switch to an atypical drug, or to add an anticholinergic (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine, procyclidine) or amantadine. Anticholinergics have costs of their own (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, poorer memory, and euphoria that leads some patients to misuse them), and they worsen tardive dyskinesia, so they should not be continued indefinitely by routine. Tardive dyskinesia. Dinesh, a 52-year-old retired bus conductor from Thrissur, was first diagnosed with schizophrenia at 24 and has received an injection of fluphenazine every three weeks for almost twenty years, with trihexyphenidyl tablets alongside. His daughter brought him to the clinic because his mouth "keeps chewing even when he isn't eating". Sitting quietly, his jaw works from side to side, his lips pucker and smack, his tongue pushes against his cheek and darts out between his lips, and his fingers move as though playing an invisible harmonium. Dinesh himself barely notices the movements; his family is embarrassed by them at weddings. This is tardive dyskinesia ("late abnormal movement"), a syndrome of involuntary, repetitive, purposeless movements that appears after long exposure to dopamine-blocking drugs. The orofacial movements (chewing, lip smacking and pursing, tongue protrusion, grimacing, cheek puffing, blinking) are the commonest; about half of patients also have limb movements, which may be choreiform (quick, jerky and irregular) or athetoid (slow and writhing), and some have rocking of the trunk or irregular breathing. DSM-5-TR requires the movements to have been present for at least four weeks, after at least three months of exposure to the drug (one month in people aged 60 or over); they may appear while the drug is being taken or within four weeks of stopping a tablet (eight weeks for a long-acting injection). Among people on long-term antipsychotic treatment the prevalence is about 20 to 30 percent, and the yearly incidence in younger patients is about 3 to 5 percent. Older people are far more vulnerable, with prevalence figures up to 50 percent. The most consistent risk factors are age and cumulative exposure; others include early extrapyramidal side effects, mood disorders, alcohol use disorder and, possibly, being a woman after the menopause. Second-generation drugs carry a somewhat lower risk, but, DSM-5-TR notes, the difference is not as large as was once believed. Several odd features of tardive dyskinesia point to its likely mechanism. The movements are worse under stress, disappear during sleep and lessen when the person deliberately moves the affected part. Above all, raising the dose of the antipsychotic temporarily suppresses them, while stopping the drug or adding an anticholinergic makes them worse. The leading explanation is dopamine receptor supersensitivity : after years of blockade, striatal neurons respond by making more D2 receptors and becoming hypersensitive to whatever dopamine reaches them, so the motor striatum becomes, in effect, overactive. Extra blockade masks the excess for a while; removing the blockade unmasks it. The hypothesis is not proven, and damage to striatal neurons from oxidative stress has also been proposed, but it explains why the illness looks like the opposite of parkinsonism. Tardive dyskinesia may be irreversible, especially in older people, although many patients improve slowly once the drug is reduced. The best treatment is prevention: use the lowest effective dose, avoid unnecessary long-term use and examine patients regularly, often with the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS, covered in the Assessment book). Once it appears, anticholinergics are stopped, the patient may be switched to clozapine, which carries the lowest risk of any antipsychotic, and a VMAT2 inhibitor may be added. These drugs (valbenazine, the first medicine approved for tardive dyskinesia by the United States Food and Drug Administration in April 2017, deutetrabenazine and the older tetrabenazine) reduce the packaging of dopamine into vesicles, a gentler version of what reserpine does. DSM-5-TR warns that the two kinds of treatment pull in opposite directions: anticholinergics, used for parkinsonism, worsen tardive dyskinesia, and VMAT2 inhibitors, used for tardive dyskinesia, worsen parkinsonism. Late-appearing, persistent forms of dystonia and akathisia also occur, called tardive dystonia and tardive akathisia. Dinesh's trihexyphenidyl was stopped and, as Section 4.10.6 describes, he was later moved to clozapine. Neurologists distinguish a primary movement disorder , in which the disorder arises from the nervous system itself, usually through an inherited or idiopathic degeneration, from a secondary movement disorder , which has an identifiable outside cause such as a drug, a toxin, a stroke or an infection. Parkinson's disease, first described by James Parkinson in An Essay on the Shaking Palsy (1817), is primary: the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra degenerate. Huntington's disease, described by George Huntington in 1872, is primary too: an inherited expansion in the huntingtin gene produces chorea, dementia and psychiatric symptoms. All four extrapyramidal side effects are secondary. Drug-induced parkinsonism is a secondary parkinsonism, imitating Parkinson's disease without being it. Tardive dyskinesia must likewise be told apart from the primary choreas and from other causes of mouth and limb movements that DSM-5-TR lists, including Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, Sydenham's chorea after rheumatic fever, thyroid overactivity, heavy metal poisoning, ill-fitting dentures and the dyskinesias caused by L-dopa. It must also be told apart from spontaneous dyskinesias, which DSM-5-TR says can occur in more than 5 percent of people, more often in the elderly, and which have been described in people with schizophrenia who have never taken an antipsychotic. DSM-5-TR gathers all of these reactions in a chapter of Section II called "Medication-Induced Movement Disorders and Other Adverse Effects of Medication". The chapter lists medication-induced parkinsonism (with antipsychotics and other dopamine receptor blocking agents as the main cause), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, medication-induced acute dystonia, medication-induced acute akathisia, tardive dyskinesia, tardive dystonia and tardive akathisia, medication-induced postural tremor (lithium is the classic cause), other medication-induced movement disorder, antidepressant discontinuation syndrome and other adverse effect of medication. DSM-5-TR is explicit that these are not mental disorders. It includes them because they matter so much in managing medication and in differential diagnosis: telling an anxiety disorder from akathisia, malignant catatonia from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and tardive dyskinesia from chorea. It also notes that the word neuroleptic is becoming outdated, being replaced by "antipsychotic medications and other dopamine receptor blocking agents". That longer phrase is a reminder that the anti-nausea drugs metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, and the antidepressant amoxapine, also block dopamine receptors and can cause the same movement disorders. Exam trap Read the time course in the stem. Years of treatment plus involuntary lip smacking, tongue movements and grimacing is tardive dyskinesia ; a recent start plus subjective inner restlessness and a need to pace is akathisia ; sudden painful spasms within days is acute dystonia ; slowness, stiffness and tremor after some weeks is parkinsonism ; fever, rigidity and confusion is neuroleptic malignant syndrome . Tardive dyskinesia is caused by neuroleptics (antipsychotics), not by antidepressants, anxiolytics or barbiturates. Akathisia and tardive dyskinesia are secondary (drug-induced) movement disorders; Huntington's chorea and Parkinson's disease are primary . Typical drugs cause extrapyramidal effects by blocking nigrostriatal D2 receptors : not by blocking serotonin reuptake (that is what SSRIs do), not by stimulating GABA-A receptors (benzodiazepines), and not by blocking only mesolimbic receptors (a drug that did that would cause no extrapyramidal effects at all). Neuroleptic malignant syndrome and the other adverse effects The rarest serious reaction to an antipsychotic is also the most dangerous. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening reaction in which the brain's control of muscle tone, temperature and the autonomic nervous system breaks down. DSM-5-TR describes its features in detail. The person has usually been given a dopamine blocker within the previous 72 hours. The distinguishing sign is high fever (above 38.0 °C on at least two occasions) with profuse sweating. There is generalised rigidity, "lead pipe" in severe cases, which does not respond to anti-parkinsonian drugs, often with tremor, drooling and difficulty swallowing. The mental state changes, often early, from confusion and delirium to stupor and coma; the person may lie alert but dazed and unresponsive, looking catatonic. The autonomic nervous system becomes unstable, with a racing pulse, high or swinging blood pressure, rapid breathing, pallor and incontinence. In the blood, the muscle enzyme creatine kinase (CK, also called creatine phosphokinase) is raised, commonly to at least four times the normal upper limit, as muscle breaks down, and the white cell count is often high. Four features are easy to remember together: fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and altered consciousness , confirmed by a raised CK. NMS is rare: database studies suggest 0.01 to 0.02 percent of people treated with antipsychotics, although a population study in Hong Kong found 0.11 percent. Some cases begin within 24 hours of the first dose, most within the first week and virtually all within 30 days. The risk is higher with high-potency drugs, injections, rapid dose increases and high total doses, and in patients who are agitated, exhausted, dehydrated or iron deficient; 15 to 20 percent of patients have had an earlier episode. Yet it can follow any antipsychotic at an ordinary dose, including the atypicals, and even anti-nausea drugs such as metoclopramide. Once it is recognised and the drug is stopped, NMS usually resolves, on average in 7 to 10 days and nearly always within 30 days (longer if a depot injection is the cause). Unrecognised, it kills 10 to 20 percent of patients. Treatment is an emergency in a medical ward or intensive care unit: stop the antipsychotic, cool the patient, give fluids and support breathing and circulation, and consider a benzodiazepine, the muscle relaxant dantrolene or the dopamine agonist bromocriptine; electroconvulsive therapy is used for cases that do not resolve. NMS must be told apart from infections of the brain, heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia during anaesthesia, the serotonin syndrome caused by serotonergic drugs, and malignant catatonia, from which it may be clinically indistinguishable. Some investigators regard NMS as a drug-induced form of malignant catatonia (Section 4.5). Remember A patient recently started on haloperidol who becomes feverish, stiff, sweaty and confused, with a fast pulse and a high CK, has neuroleptic malignant syndrome until proved otherwise. Stop the drug and treat it as a medical emergency. Do not mistake the stupor for catatonia and give more antipsychotic. The other side effects follow from the receptors that antipsychotics block besides the nigrostriatal D2 receptor, and Table 4.40 maps them out. Four deserve a closer look. Hyperprolactinaemia. Dopamine released by the tuberoinfundibular neurons of the hypothalamus is the brake on the release of prolactin from the anterior pituitary; it is the "prolactin-inhibiting factor". Block D2 receptors there and prolactin rises: hyperprolactinaemia . In women it causes irregular or absent periods (amenorrhoea), milk secretion from the breasts ( galactorrhoea ) and infertility; in men, breast enlargement (gynaecomastia) and erectile difficulties; in both, loss of sexual desire and, over years, thinning of the bones. Four months after her admission Asha stopped menstruating and noticed milk leaking from her breasts; she was terrified that she was pregnant. Her prolactin level was several times normal. Her psychiatrist switched her to aripiprazole, and her periods returned. The worst offenders are risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride and the typical drugs; aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine raise prolactin least. Because patients are often too embarrassed to mention these effects, a good clinician asks about them directly, since they are a common hidden reason for stopping treatment. Weight gain and the metabolic syndrome. Many antipsychotics increase appetite, largely through blockade of histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2C receptors, and some also impair the body's response to insulin directly. The result can be rapid weight gain, type 2 diabetes, raised triglycerides and cholesterol and high blood pressure: together, the metabolic syndrome . Clozapine and olanzapine are the worst offenders, quetiapine and risperidone come in between, and aripiprazole, ziprasidone, lurasidone and haloperidol carry the least risk. This matters enormously, because people with schizophrenia already die years earlier than the general population, mostly from heart disease (Section 4.6), and because South Asians develop diabetes at lower body weights than Europeans. Good practice is to measure weight, waist, blood pressure, blood sugar and lipids before treatment and regularly afterwards, to advise on diet and exercise from the start, and, when weight climbs, to consider switching drug or adding metformin. Anticholinergic and adrenergic effects. Blockade of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors produces anticholinergic side effects : dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, difficulty passing urine, a fast heart rate and, especially in older people, confusion and poor memory. Chlorpromazine, thioridazine, clozapine and olanzapine have strong anticholinergic actions. Blockade of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in blood vessels causes orthostatic hypotension , a fall in blood pressure on standing that produces dizziness, fainting and falls, the very reaction Laborit's volunteer had in 1951; it is common with chlorpromazine, clozapine and quetiapine and is one reason why doses are increased slowly. Blockade of histamine H1 receptors causes sedation, which is welcome in an acutely disturbed patient and a burden in one who is trying to study or work. The heart and other effects. Some antipsychotics slow the electrical recovery of the heart muscle, seen on the electrocardiogram as QTc prolongation , which can lead to a dangerous irregular rhythm (torsades de pointes) and sudden death. Thioridazine, pimozide, sertindole, ziprasidone and intravenous haloperidol carry the most risk, and an electrocardiogram is advised before using them. Other effects to know are a lowered seizure threshold (especially clozapine and chlorpromazine), sensitivity to sunlight, skin pigmentation and jaundice with chlorpromazine, damage to the retina with high doses of thioridazine, sexual dysfunction with many drugs, and a raised death rate when antipsychotics are given to elderly people with dementia, about which regulators issued warnings in the 2000s. Finally there is the subjective side. When K. Windgassen questioned 61 people with recent-onset schizophrenia in 1992, about half complained of sedation ("I always have to fight to keep my eyes open"), and others described slowed thinking (18 percent), problems with salivation (16 percent) and blurred vision (16 percent).
