And do not confuse neuroleptic malignant syndrome (antipsychotics, rigidity, develops over days) with serotonin syndrome (serotonergic drugs, twitching and overactive reflexes, develops within hours). Clozapine and treatment-resistant schizophrenia For a sizeable minority of patients, roughly one in five to one in three, the voices and delusions persist however carefully the drugs are chosen. Their condition, treatment-resistant schizophrenia , is usually defined as the persistence of significant symptoms despite at least two adequate trials of two different antipsychotics: each given at a proper dose, for an adequate period (about six weeks), with adherence checked, since a drug that is not being swallowed has not failed. For these patients one drug stands apart, and its history is one of the strangest in psychiatry. The drug that defined the word atypical, clozapine , was synthesised in 1958 and came into use in parts of Europe in the early 1970s. In 1975 a cluster of cases of agranulocytosis in Finland, eight of them fatal, led to its withdrawal or severe restriction in many countries. Agranulocytosis is a near-total loss of the neutrophils, the white blood cells that fight bacterial infection; the first signs are usually fever, sore throat and mouth ulcers, and without treatment the person can die of overwhelming infection. Clozapine might have disappeared altogether had a few researchers not continued to study it for patients who had nothing else. Key study: Kane, Honigfeld, Singer and Meltzer (1988) The question was whether clozapine could help people for whom the standard drugs had failed. John Kane , Gilbert Honigfeld , Jack Singer and Herbert Meltzer recruited, at several American centres, patients with DSM-III schizophrenia who had failed to respond to at least three different antipsychotics. To make sure that they really were resistant, every patient first received haloperidol (an average of 61 mg a day) for six weeks; only those still unimproved went on. Then 268 patients were randomly assigned, double-blind, to clozapine (up to 900 mg a day) or chlorpromazine (up to 1,800 mg a day) for six weeks. By criteria fixed in advance, 30 percent of the clozapine group responded, compared with 4 percent of the chlorpromazine group, and clozapine improved negative as well as positive symptoms. No case of agranulocytosis occurred in so short a trial, but the authors argued that the risk meant clozapine should be reserved for treatment-resistant patients. The criticisms are that six weeks is short and that a 30 percent response rate still left most patients unwell; later studies found that more patients respond if clozapine is continued for several months. The result changed practice everywhere. Clozapine was approved in the United States and marketed from February 1990, but only with compulsory blood monitoring, and it has been the treatment of choice for resistant schizophrenia ever since. Every comparison since has confirmed that clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic; it came top for efficacy in Leucht's 2013 network meta-analysis. It also carries the lowest risk of extrapyramidal side effects and tardive dyskinesia of any antipsychotic. And it does something no other antipsychotic has been shown to do. In the International Suicide Prevention Trial (InterSePT), Meltzer and colleagues in 2003 randomised 980 people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder at high risk of suicide to clozapine or olanzapine for two years: suicidal behaviour was significantly lower with clozapine (34 versus 55 suicide attempts). On the strength of these results the United States Food and Drug Administration approved clozapine in December 2002 for reducing suicidal behaviour in schizophrenia, shortly before the trial was published. Large Finnish registry studies have since found the lowest overall death rates among patients taking clozapine. Why, then, is clozapine a third-line drug and not a first-line one? Because of its risks, which every patient and family must understand. The most famous is agranulocytosis. When Jose Alvir , Lieberman and colleagues analysed the first American monitoring data in 1993 (11,555 patients), agranulocytosis had developed in 73, two of whom died; 61 of the 73 cases began within the first three months, and the cumulative risk was 0.8 percent at one year, higher in older people and in women. Because the danger is concentrated early, monitoring is most intensive at the start: a white cell and neutrophil count before treatment, then weekly for the first few months (18 weeks in the United Kingdom, six months in the United States), then less often but for as long as the drug is taken, with the drug stopped at once if the neutrophil count falls below a set threshold. (In June 2025 the United States ended its compulsory national registry for clozapine, but the blood counts are still recommended on the same schedule.) Clinicians sum the rule up as "no blood, no drug". The other risks are these: Inflammation of the heart muscle, myocarditis , can occur, almost always in the first two months, and is signalled by fever, chest pain, breathlessness and a fast pulse. Seizures become more likely at high doses and high blood levels. Drooling, or hypersalivation , especially at night, troubles a large proportion of patients; it is a paradox, since clozapine otherwise has strong anticholinergic actions. Severe constipation is common and can progress to bowel obstruction, which can kill if it is ignored. Sedation, dizziness on standing and a fast heart rate are common at the start, which is why the dose is built up slowly from 12.5 mg over several weeks. Marked weight gain and diabetes are frequent, and some patients develop fever in the first weeks or bedwetting at night. Clinical link: clozapine and cigarettes Tobacco smoke (not nicotine itself) speeds up the liver enzyme CYP1A2, which breaks down clozapine, so smokers have clozapine levels roughly 30 percent lower, sometimes up to 50 percent lower, than non-smokers on the same dose. Because so many people with schizophrenia smoke heavily, this matters in both directions. A patient who stops smoking suddenly, for example on admission to a smoke-free ward, can develop toxic levels with sedation and seizures; one who starts smoking again after discharge may relapse. Blood levels of clozapine should be checked whenever smoking habits change. Dinesh had failed two adequate trials, first of fluphenazine and then of risperidone, before his psychiatrist suggested clozapine, and his family worried about the blood tests. They were reassured that he would have weekly counts at the district hospital and would be told to report any fever or sore throat at once. The dose was built up over a month to 300 mg a day. He drooled onto his pillow at night, needed a daily laxative and put on six kilograms, but by the fourth month the voices that had followed him for twenty-eight years were rare and quiet, and the chewing movements of his tardive dyskinesia were less noticeable. Despite stories like his, clozapine is underused all over the world: many eligible patients never receive it, or receive it only after years of delay, mainly because clinicians overestimate its dangers and dislike the monitoring. Even clozapine is not enough for many resistant patients: George Petrides and colleagues estimate that up to 70 percent of people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia do not respond adequately to it. The next steps are to check that the blood level is adequate, to add a second antipsychotic such as amisulpride or aripiprazole (aripiprazole also helps to limit weight gain), or to add electroconvulsive therapy. In a randomised study published in 2015, Petrides's group gave 39 clozapine-resistant patients either clozapine alone or clozapine plus a course of ECT: half of the ECT group responded and none of the clozapine-alone group did, and 47 percent of those later crossed over to ECT also responded. Figure 4.18 sets out this stepwise approach to drug treatment. 1. Assess: confirm diagnosis, rule out medical and substance causes, baseline tests 2. Start one antipsychotic at the lowest effective dose; explain side effects 3. Adequate trial: about 4 to 6 weeks at a proper dose, with adherence checked 4. Poor response: switch to a different antipsychotic for a second adequate trial 5. Two adequate trials failed: treatment- resistant schizophrenia, so offer clozapine 6. Clozapine not enough: check blood level, then augment (second drug or ECT) Alongside every step psychoeducation, family work, CBT for psychosis, rehabilitation, early intervention (Book 2) If response: maintenance 1 to 2 years or longer; depot if adherence is poor responds Figure 4.18 A stepwise approach to drug treatment in schizophrenia. Clozapine is offered once two adequate trials of other antipsychotics have failed; at any step, a good response leads to maintenance treatment, and psychosocial care runs alongside the drugs throughout. Exam trap Clozapine is the first atypical antipsychotic and the drug of choice for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (after two failed adequate trials). It is reserved because of agranulocytosis , which requires regular blood counts, not because it is weaker; it is in fact the most effective antipsychotic. It causes very few extrapyramidal effects and the least tardive dyskinesia, it reduces suicidal behaviour, and it causes drooling despite its anticholinergic action. Do not confuse clozapine with clomipramine (an antidepressant used in OCD), clonazepam (a benzodiazepine) or clonidine (a blood pressure drug used in opioid withdrawal and ADHD). Staying well: maintenance treatment, adherence and long-acting injections Prabhu's voices faded within a month and he went back to college. Six months later he felt entirely well, he had put on weight, his friends teased him about "mad pills", and he quietly stopped taking them. Four months after that the voices returned, and he was readmitted. His story is the commonest story in the treatment of schizophrenia, and the evidence behind it is unusually clear. Key study: relapse after a first episode (Robinson and colleagues, 1999) Delbert Robinson and colleagues at Hillside Hospital in New York followed 104 patients who had recovered from a first episode of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. Within five years of recovery the cumulative rate of a first relapse was 81.9 percent, and most of those who relapsed went on to relapse again. The strongest single predictor was stopping medication: discontinuing antipsychotic treatment raised the risk of relapse almost fivefold (a hazard ratio of 4.89). Poor adjustment at school and social withdrawal before the illness predicted earlier relapse as well. The conclusion: relapse after a first episode is the rule rather than the exception, and maintenance medication greatly reduces it. The term maintenance treatment means continuing an antipsychotic after the acute episode has resolved, in order to prevent relapse. The strongest evidence for it comes from the 2012 meta-analysis by Leucht and colleagues of 65 randomised trials involving 6,493 patients who had been stabilised on medication and were then either continued on an antipsychotic or switched to placebo. At one year, 27 percent of those continued on medication had relapsed, against 64 percent of those on placebo; only three patients needed to be kept on medication to prevent one relapse. Readmissions were 10 percent against 26 percent, and there was some evidence of better quality of life and fewer aggressive acts. The price was paid in side effects: more weight gain (10 versus 6 percent), more movement disorders (16 versus 9 percent) and more sedation (13 versus 9 percent). How long should maintenance last? Guidelines generally advise at least one to two years after a first episode and longer, often indefinitely, after repeated relapses. The question is not closed. In 2013 Lex Wunderink and colleagues in the Netherlands reported a seven-year follow-up of a trial in which patients who had recovered from a first episode were randomly assigned either to maintenance or to a cautious reduction or discontinuation of their dose. The reduction group had about twice as many relapses early on, but seven years later twice as many of them had recovered (40.4 versus 17.6 percent), the difference lying in everyday functioning rather than in symptoms. The authors themselves warned that the finding needs replication before it changes practice; what it shows is that the lowest effective dose, not simply the most medication, is the goal. None of this helps if the medicine is not taken. Treatment adherence , the extent to which a person takes treatment as agreed with the clinician (the older word "compliance" implied obedience), is poor in schizophrenia, as it is in most long-term illnesses. In CATIE, as you saw, 74 percent of patients had stopped their assigned drug within 18 months, and partial adherence, missing some doses, is even commoner. The reasons are many: side effects such as sedation, weight gain, sexual problems and akathisia; lack of insight, since a person who does not believe he is ill sees no reason to take medicine for it (Section 4.2); feeling well and concluding that the drug is no longer needed; stigma; cost and distance from the clinic; a poor relationship with the prescriber; substance use; and family members who prefer a faith healer or fear that the tablets are addictive. Some patients, like a young man described by Barlow and Durand, "cheek" their tablets, holding them in the mouth until the nurse has gone and then spitting them out. Adherence improves when side effects are asked about and treated, the regimen is simple (one daily dose), decisions are shared, patient and family understand the illness, and a trusted relative helps; psychological approaches to adherence are discussed in Book 2. For patients who repeatedly relapse after stopping tablets, or who prefer not to take a daily pill, there is the long-acting injectable antipsychotic , also called a depot injection . The drug is chemically bound to a fatty acid (as a decanoate, for example) and dissolved in oil, or made into tiny crystals or microspheres, and injected deep into a muscle, from which it is released slowly over weeks. The first-generation depots are fluphenazine decanoate (every two to four weeks), haloperidol decanoate (about every four weeks), and flupentixol and zuclopenthixol decanoate. The second-generation long-acting injections include risperidone microspheres (every two weeks), paliperidone palmitate (monthly, with three-monthly and six-monthly forms), long-acting aripiprazole (monthly) and olanzapine pamoate. Olanzapine pamoate requires the patient to be observed for three hours after each injection because of a rare post-injection delirium and sedation syndrome. Depots have real advantages. Delivery is guaranteed; a missed injection is known at once, so the team can act before a relapse; and the patient is spared the daily reminder of illness. In Leucht's 2012 meta-analysis, depot preparations reduced relapse more than oral drugs did. The disadvantages are pain at the injection site, less flexible dosing, side effects that take weeks to wear off once they appear, and, for some patients, a feeling of being controlled. After his second admission Prabhu chose a monthly injection at the district hospital, where it is free; he has not been readmitted in three years and has finished his diploma. Exam trap A depot is not a different or stronger drug: it is the same antipsychotic in a slow-release form, and its benefit comes from better adherence and the early detection of missed doses. Fluphenazine decanoate and haloperidol decanoate are typical depots; paliperidone palmitate and risperidone microspheres are atypical long-acting injections. Maintenance medication prevents relapse ; it does not cure the illness, and most first-episode patients who stop medication relapse within a few years. Medication and family work reduce relapse in additive ways (Section 4.9 explains expressed emotion). Other physical treatments: ECT and brain stimulation Of the physical treatments of the 1930s, only one survives. In electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), doctors produce a brief, controlled seizure by passing a current through the brain of an anaesthetised patient whose muscles have been relaxed with a drug, usually in a course of six to twelve treatments given two or three times a week. How it is given, how it is thought to work and its main use, in severe depression, are taught in Chapter 5. Meduna's theory that seizures antagonise schizophrenia was wrong, and Barlow and Durand note that the early enthusiasm for ECT in schizophrenia faded once it proved unhelpful for most patients. It keeps a definite place, however, in four situations. The first is catatonia , in which ECT is the treatment of choice if a benzodiazepine (the lorazepam challenge described in Section 4.5) fails, and the emergency treatment for malignant catatonia. The second is severe acute psychosis with dangerous refusal of food and drink, or a violent or suicidal crisis, where a rapid response is needed. The third is schizophrenia with prominent mood symptoms, including schizoaffective disorder. The fourth is treatment resistance, especially as an addition to clozapine, as the Petrides trial in Section 4.10.6 showed. ECT is used more often for schizophrenia in India than in most Western countries. Indian law regulates it closely, as Book 2, Section 1.10 explains. Section 95 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 prohibits ECT without muscle relaxants and anaesthesia (the old "unmodified" ECT) and prohibits ECT for minors, except that a psychiatrist may give it to a minor with the informed consent of the guardian and the prior permission of the Mental Health Review Board. Section 94 forbids the use of ECT as emergency treatment, and Section 96 allows psychosurgery only with the person's informed consent and the Board's approval. Newer forms of brain stimulation are still being tested. The best studied, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), uses a coil held against the scalp to produce rapidly changing magnetic fields that induce small currents in the cortex beneath. Ralph Hoffman and colleagues reported in 2000 that slow, repeated stimulation over the left temporoparietal cortex, an area active during auditory hallucinations, reduced persistent voices in some patients. Later studies confirmed a modest effect, but Barlow and Durand note that it lasts less than a month. Transcranial direct current stimulation, which passes a weak steady current through the scalp, is experimental. Insulin coma therapy and lobotomy are of historical interest only. Psychosocial treatments that complete care Antipsychotic medication is the front-line treatment for schizophrenia: no psychological treatment on its own has been shown to match it in the acute illness, and clinical guidelines everywhere place it first. But medicine reduces symptoms; it does not teach a person how to live with an illness, talk to a stranger, hold a job or rebuild a family's trust. Most patients therefore need psychosocial treatment alongside the drug, and the evidence shows that the combination does better than either alone. These treatments belong to the Clinical Psychology book, which teaches how each is done; what follows is a map of what each offers in schizophrenia and where to find it. Cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp; Book 2, Section 5.6) helps the person examine the evidence for delusional beliefs, reinterpret voices so that they are less frightening and less powerful, cope with distress and plan to prevent relapse. Its effects on positive symptoms are real but modest, larger on distress than on the symptoms themselves, and guidelines such as those of the British National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommend offering it to everyone with schizophrenia, as an addition to medication. Family psychoeducation and family intervention (Book 2, Section 7.2) grew directly out of the expressed emotion research described in Section 4.9. Families learn about the illness, its treatment and the early warning signs of relapse; they practise calmer communication and joint problem solving; critical comments and emotional over-involvement are gently reduced; and, where tension at home is high, the hours of face-to-face contact between patient and relative are reduced, for example through a day centre or a job. Family intervention reduces relapse and readmission, especially when combined with medication. It is the treatment for the family climate that predicts relapse; it was never a treatment for a family that "caused" schizophrenia. Social skills training (Book 2, Section 4.7), developed in particular by Robert Paul Liberman and colleagues, breaks social behaviour (starting a conversation, asking for help, refusing a request, handling a job interview) into small steps that are modelled, rehearsed in role play, corrected with feedback and practised as homework. People do learn the skills that are taught; how well the skills carry over into everyday life is less certain. The token economy (Book 2, Section 4.5), introduced on psychiatric wards by Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin in their book The Token Economy (1968), rewards self-care and constructive activity with tokens exchangeable for privileges. In the best-known comparison, Gordon Paul and Robert Lentz (1977) found that a social learning programme built on these principles helped chronic hospital patients more than milieu therapy or routine care. Token economies are used much less today, as long-stay wards have closed and concerns about coercion have grown. The aim of cognitive remediation is to improve the attention, memory, processing speed and problem solving that antipsychotics leave untouched (Section 4.3), through graded practice exercises, often on a computer, together with teaching strategies. In a 2011 meta-analysis of 40 studies with 2,104 participants, Til Wykes and colleagues found small to moderate, durable gains in cognition and in everyday functioning, with much larger gains in functioning when cognitive remediation was combined with other rehabilitation. The approach called supported employment , especially the Individual Placement and Support model, reverses the old sequence of "train, then place": the person is helped to find an ordinary paid job quickly and then supported in it, and it gets far more people with schizophrenia into work than traditional vocational rehabilitation. The model of assertive community treatment (ACT; Book 2, Section 9.8), pioneered by Leonard Stein and Mary Ann Test in Madison, Wisconsin, and reported in 1980, brings treatment to people who do not come to clinics: a multidisciplinary team with small caseloads visits patients at home and at work, delivers medicine, helps with housing, money and benefits, and is available around the clock. It reduces time spent in hospital for people with severe illness who repeatedly disengage from services. Finally, early intervention services aim to shorten the duration of untreated psychosis (Section 4.6) and to give intensive, hopeful, youth-friendly care in the first years of the illness, when the course is thought to be most open to change. The model was developed in Melbourne in the early 1990s and has spread to many countries. Exam trap The front-line treatment for schizophrenia is antipsychotic medication . CBT, social skills training, family work and stress management (training in relaxation, problem solving and coping with daily stress) are valuable additions , not substitutes. Reducing face-to-face contact hours with a high-EE relative is a strategy for managing expressed emotion , and family intervention reduces relapse , not the onset of the disorder. Token economies are behavioural (operant) treatments for chronic institutionalised patients; social skills training is based on modelling and rehearsal. Treating schizophrenia in India Most people with schizophrenia in India live with their families, and the family is the main provider of care: it notices the illness, chooses where to seek help (very often a temple, dargah or faith healer first), supervises the medicine, absorbs the cost and carries the burden for decades. This is both a strength and a strain. Indian families have been found to show lower expressed emotion than Western ones (Section 4.9), and family involvement may be one reason for the better outcomes in the WHO studies described in Section 4.6. But caregivers, most often mothers and wives, report heavy financial and emotional burden, and services that support them are scarce. Specialist care is concentrated in institutions such as the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru, the Central Institute of Psychiatry in Ranchi and the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences (IHBAS) in Delhi, and in the psychiatry departments of medical colleges. Non-governmental organisations such as the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF) in Chennai, long led by R. Thara, have pioneered community care and research. To reach the districts, the National Mental Health Programme set up the District Mental Health Programme in 1996, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 gave every person a legal right to access mental health care (Book 2, Section 1.10). Section 18 of the Act also requires that all medicines on the government's Essential Drug List be provided free of cost to people with mental illness at government health establishments, from Community Health Centres upwards. In practice, many patients receive inexpensive typical drugs, often haloperidol or trifluoperazine with trihexyphenidyl, or fluphenazine decanoate injections, alongside newer generic atypicals such as risperidone and olanzapine, which are now cheap in India. Can care be delivered where specialists are scarce? The COPSI trial (Community care for People with Schizophrenia in India), led by Sudipto Chatterjee with Vikram Patel, R. Thara, Graham Thornicroft and others and published in 2014, tested this at three sites: Goa, Satara in Maharashtra, and rural Tamil Nadu. It randomly assigned 282 people with schizophrenia either to usual clinic-based care or to clinic care plus collaborative community care delivered by trained lay health workers under specialist supervision, including home visits, adherence support, psychoeducation for the family and help with rehabilitation. After a year the community care group had less disability and slightly fewer symptoms (the symptom difference fell just short of statistical significance), with the clearest benefit at the rural Tamil Nadu site, and the authors concluded that the approach is best used where services are scarce, such as rural areas. The lesson fits the whole of this section. The antipsychotic drug is the foundation of treatment, but recovery from schizophrenia is built by people: families, health workers, employers and the patient, over years. The case of the Genain quadruplets, revisited Go back to the four identical sisters born in Lansing, Michigan, on 19 May 1930, and to the National Institute of Mental Health, where David Rosenthal's team studied them from 1955 to 1958. You can now read their story as this chapter has taught it. Their genes loaded the dice heavily. Gottesman's figures put the risk for the identical twin of a patient at about 48 percent, and twin studies estimate the heritability of liability at around 80 percent, so four sisters who shared one genome and all fell ill (an outcome Mirsky put at about one in 1.5 billion) are what a strongly genetic, polygenic illness can occasionally produce. Yet the same figures say that more than half of identical co-twins never fall ill, and the Genains show why the inherited DNA sequence cannot be the whole story: their age at onset, their symptoms, their hospital stays and their eventual functioning differed widely. Hester, the first to fall ill, severely so by 18, and the sister who had more social problems than the others as she grew up, had the worst course and spent most of her adult life in hospital. Myra, the last to fall ill, was never readmitted after her first episode, and she married and raised a family. Early onset and poor premorbid adjustment on one side, a later onset on the other: these are the poor and good prognostic signs of Table 4.26. And the sisters' test scores at 66, stable or better than in their twenties, answer Kraepelin's word "dementia": the cognitive impairment of schizophrenia is largely present early and then stays fairly stable, rather than marching downhill. What made four lives out of one genome? Section 4.7 gave the answer that behaviour geneticists call the non-shared environment: even identical sisters differ in their position in the womb, their blood supply and birth weight, the complications of their delivery, the illnesses of their childhood and the way their parents treat them, and the neurodevelopmental hypothesis explains how such early differences can lie silent until the maturing brain unmasks them in adolescence and early adulthood. The controlling, abusive home that later accounts describe, and parents who did not treat the four alike, belong to the other side of the vulnerability-stress model of Section 4.9. Family life does not cause schizophrenia (the schizophrenogenic mother and the double bind were rejected as causes), but stress acting on a vulnerable brain can trigger an episode, and a critical, hostile or over-involved family climate, high expressed emotion, predicts relapse. A clinician meeting four such sisters today would start antipsychotic medication early, to shorten the duration of untreated psychosis, and continue it to prevent relapse; would offer clozapine to any sister whose illness resisted two adequate trials of other drugs; and would add family psychoeducation, CBT for psychosis and rehabilitation. Bleuler's plural, the group of schizophrenias, fits the Genains well: one diagnosis, one genome and four different illnesses. That is why this chapter has treated schizophrenia not as a fixed fate but as a vulnerability whose course genes, development, stress and treatment decide together. Chapter summary 4.1 From Dementia Praecox to Schizophrenia. Schizophrenia is a concept built in layers over about a hundred and fifty years. Haslam (1810) recorded in Matthews's "Air Loom" a near-complete set of first-rank symptoms. Morel gave démence précoce (1852) and degeneration theory; Kahlbaum classified by clinical course, Hecker described hebephrenia (1871) and Kahlbaum catatonia (1874). Kraepelin's dementia praecox (1893) absorbed these forms, and in 1899 he split it by course from manic-depressive insanity, the Kraepelinian dichotomy. Bleuler named schizophrenia (1908, 1911), a splitting of psychic functions, not of personality, and ranked fundamental symptoms (the four As: associations, affect, ambivalence, autism) above accessory hallucinations and delusions. Jaspers (1913) founded phenomenology and defined the primary delusion. Schneider's first-rank symptoms (1939) are characteristic but not pathognomonic. The US-UK Diagnostic Project (Cooper, Kendell and Gurland, 1972) exposed American breadth, and the Feighner criteria (1972) and DSM-III (1980) narrowed the concept with a six-month rule. 4.2 Positive Symptoms: Delusions, Hallucinations and Disorganisation. Positive symptoms add something unusual to experience; negative ones take something normal away. Jaspers gave delusions three marks (certainty, incorrigibility, impossibility) and separated ununderstandable primary delusions from secondary ones. Delusional mood (Conrad's trema, 1958) precedes delusional perception (his apophany); Hambrecht and Häfner (1993) confirmed only trema as a common first phase. Persecutory delusions are commonest, held with Bleuler's double bookkeeping, and DSM-5 ended the special weight of bizarre delusions. Auditory hallucinations dominate (about 60 to 80 percent); third-person voices and thought echo are first-rank, second-person voices are not. Kandinsky described pseudohallucinations; Waters (2014) found visual hallucinations in 27 percent and McGrath (2015) psychotic experiences in 5.8 percent of adults; Romme and Escher began the Hearing Voices Movement. Bleuler's loosening, Meehl's cognitive slippage (1962), was defined form by form by Andreasen (1979). Disorganised behaviour, inappropriate affect and catatonia follow; insight has David's three dimensions (1990) and Amador's continuum (1993). 4.3 Negative and Cognitive Symptoms, and the Symptom Dimensions. Negative symptoms, losses of normal function, account for much of schizophrenia's disability; the terms date from Reynolds (around 1861) and Hughlings Jackson. The NIMH-MATRICS consensus (2006) fixed five: blunted affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia and asociality. Berenbaum and Oltmanns (1992) found blunted patients feel but do not express emotion; Gard and Kring (2007) located anhedonia in anticipatory, not consummatory, pleasure. Secondary negative symptoms arise from positive symptoms, depression, antipsychotics and understimulation (Wing and Brown's institutionalism study); Carpenter's deficit syndrome (1988) requires primary ones for 12 months. Cognitive deficits are broad (Heinrichs and Zakzanis, 1998), span Nuechterlein's seven MATRICS domains (2004) and predict functioning better than psychotic symptoms (Green, 1996). Crow (1980) proposed positive Type I and negative Type II syndromes, Andreasen and Olsen (1982) positive, negative and mixed subtypes, Liddle (1987) reality distortion, disorganisation and psychomotor poverty, and PANSS analyses five factors; DSM-5 and ICD-11 rate symptom dimensions. 4.4 Diagnosing Schizophrenia: DSM-5-TR, ICD-10 and ICD-11. With no test or pathognomonic symptom, operational criteria decide; the Feighner criteria (1972) gave DSM-III (1980) its six-month rule. DSM-5-TR Criterion A needs two of five symptoms, at least one being delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech; B, functional decline; C, six months of continuous signs, including at least one month of active phase; D to F exclude mood disorders and substance or medical causes and, after autism, demand prominent delusions or hallucinations. DSM-5 (2013) dropped the unreliable subtypes. ICD-10 F20 needs one very clear symptom from groups (a) to (d), largely Schneider's first-rank symptoms, or two groups from (e) to (h), for one month; its subtypes are paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual, simple and post-schizophrenic depression. ICD-11 6A20 needs two of seven, at least one from (a) to (d), for one month, with course and symptom specifiers, not subtypes; neither ICD requires decline. Mimics include anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (Dalmau, 2007). 4.5 The Rest of the Spectrum. The duration ladder separates brief psychotic disorder (at least 1 day and under 1 month, full recovery), schizophreniform disorder (1 to under 6 months, no decline needed; Langfeldt, 1937 and 1939) and schizophrenia (6 months). ICD's acute and transient psychotic disorders absorbed Magnan's bouffée délirante and Kleist's and Leonhard's (1957) cycloid psychosis. Kasanin coined schizoaffective (1933); DSM-5-TR requires a major mood episode with Criterion A, two weeks of psychosis alone, and mood for most of the illness; ICD uses the single episode. Delusional disorder has seven types, persecutory the commonest; erotomanic is de Clérambault's syndrome, jealous Todd and Dewhurst's Othello syndrome (1955), somatic Ekbom's delusional parasitosis (1938). Lasègue and Falret (1877) described folie à deux, ICD-10's induced delusional disorder. Secondary psychoses have known causes. Catatonia (three of twelve signs; lorazepam, then ECT) is a DSM-5 specifier across disorders. McGorry and Yung's high-risk state led to attenuated psychosis syndrome. 4.6 Who Develops Schizophrenia and What Happens Next. About 1 percent develop schizophrenia (DSM-5-TR: 0.3 to 0.7 percent). Onset peaks in men's early to mid-20s and women's late 20s, with a second female peak around 45; men's incidence is about 1.4 times women's, prevalence roughly equal. Risk rises with urban birth (Mortensen, 1999), migration (Cantor-Graae and Selten, 2005) and winter and spring birth (Torrey, 1997); low social class largely reflects social drift (Goldberg and Morrison, 1963). The phases are premorbid, prodromal, active and residual, and longer untreated psychosis goes with worse outcome (Marshall, 2005). Manfred Bleuler (1972) and Ciompi (1976) overturned Kraepelin's pessimism. The WHO's International Pilot Study (1973) and Determinants of Outcome study (Jablensky and Sartorius, 1992) found better outcomes in developing countries, questioned by Cohen and colleagues (2008); SCARF (Sarada Menon, Thara) ran the Madras Longitudinal Study. Acute, late onset bodes well; life is about 15 years shorter, and 5 to 6 percent die by suicide. 4.7 Genes, Development and the Brain. Kallmann (1938) found that a general vulnerability runs in families. Gottesman's lifetime risks (1991) rise from 1 percent (general population) to about 46 (child of two affected parents) and 48 (identical twin). Shields and Gottesman's polygenic liability-threshold theory (1967) explains why most identical co-twins stay well. Adoption studies (Heston, 1966; Kety, Rosenthal and Wender, from 1968) tied risk to biological, not adoptive, families; Tienari found gene-environment interaction. Genome-wide studies found 108 loci (2014); the 22q11.2 deletion, older fathers (Malaspina) and C4 variants (Sekar and McCarroll, 2016) add risk. Holzman's smooth pursuit eye movement dysfunction (1973) is the classic endophenotype. The neurodevelopmental hypothesis (Weinberger; Murray and Lewis, 1987) holds that an early lesion is unmasked by adolescent maturation; Mednick's second-trimester influenza effect supports it. Johnstone found enlarged ventricles (1976) and Ingvar and Franzén hypofrontality (1974); Feinberg proposed faulty pruning (1982); Andréasson linked heavy cannabis use to sixfold risk (1987). 4.8 Neurochemistry: Dopamine, Glutamate and Serotonin. The dopamine hypothesis began with drugs. Antipsychotics caused parkinsonism; Carlsson showed dopamine is a neurotransmitter, Hornykiewicz found it depleted in Parkinson's disease (1960), and Carlsson and Lindqvist proposed receptor blockade (1963). Amphetamine psychosis (Connell, 1958; Angrist and Gershon, 1970) mimics paranoid schizophrenia. Decisive evidence came in 1976: clinical potency tracks D2 binding (Creese, Burt and Snyder; Seeman). D2 blockade eases positive symptoms (mesolimbic), may worsen negative ones (mesocortical), causes extrapyramidal effects (nigrostriatal) and raises prolactin (tuberoinfundibular). The theory's weaknesses led to Davis's revised hypothesis (1991), prefrontal deficit plus subcortical excess, and Howes and Kapur's version III (2009), presynaptic striatal excess as the final common pathway to psychosis, experienced as aberrant salience (Kapur, 2003). Luby's phencyclidine psychosis (1959) led Javitt and Zukin (1991) to NMDA receptor hypofunction, confirmed with ketamine (Krystal, 1994); Hofmann's LSD is a poor model, and Meltzer (1989) tied atypicality to stronger 5-HT2A than D2 blockade. 4.9 Psychological, Family and Social Explanations. Psychodynamic theories are now historical: Freud (Schreber case, 1911) saw libido withdrawn into the self, Federn weak ego boundaries, Sullivan interpersonal anxiety, Arieti palaeologic thinking and Mahler fixation at the autistic phase without a stable symbiosis. Cognitive accounts explain symptoms: jumping to conclusions on the beads task (Huq, Garety and Hemsley, 1988), Bentall's externalising and personalising attributions, Frith's theory of mind and self-monitoring failures (1992) and Garety and colleagues' cognitive model (2001). Fromm-Reichmann's schizophrenogenic mother, the double bind (Bateson and colleagues, 1956), marital schism and skew (Lidz) and pseudomutuality (Wynne) were rejected as causes. Expressed emotion (critical comments, hostility, emotional over-involvement) predicts relapse, not onset (Brown, Birley and Wing, 1972; Vaughn and Leff, 1976); medication and reducing contact hours (below about 35 a week) protect. In Zubin and Spring's vulnerability-stress model (1977), stress triggers episodes. Labelling (Scheff) and Laing fail as causes; social defeat links exclusion to dopamine. 4.10 Treating Schizophrenia: Antipsychotic Drugs and Beyond. Sakel's insulin coma, Meduna's convulsions, Cerletti and Bini's ECT and Moniz's leucotomy gave way to chlorpromazine, noticed by Laborit, introduced by Delay and Deniker (1952), and to Janssen's haloperidol (1958). Every antipsychotic reduces D2 transmission in all four dopamine pathways; Kapur and Zipursky (2000) found a therapeutic window of occupancy. Atypicals, beginning with clozapine, cause fewer movement but more metabolic effects than typical drugs, though in CATIE (Lieberman, 2005) perphenazine matched most atypicals. The four extrapyramidal effects appear in order: acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, confusion, raised creatine kinase) is an emergency. Clozapine, the most effective drug, is reserved for treatment resistance (Kane and colleagues, 1988) because of agranulocytosis. Stopping medication predicts relapse (Robinson, 1999); hence maintenance and depots. CBT for psychosis, family intervention, social skills training (Liberman), cognitive remediation (Wykes), supported employment and assertive community treatment (Stein and Test) complete care. the past papers The concept of "Dementia Praecox," which translates to "premature dementia," is historically most directly associated with which contemporary diagnostic category? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Alzheimer's Disease (b) Bipolar I Disorder (c) Schizophrenia (d) Frontotemporal Dementia Answer: (c) Schizophrenia. Emil Kraepelin used the term in the fourth edition of his textbook (1893) and in the sixth edition (1899) separated dementia praecox from manic-depressive insanity by course; Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia (1908, 1911). "Dementia" referred to a supposedly deteriorating course, not to a dementia in the modern sense: Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia (Pick's disease) are neurocognitive disorders, and bipolar I disorder descends from the other half of Kraepelin's dichotomy, manic-depressive insanity. The term 'Ambivalence' was coined by: (RML 2024) (a) Kraepelin (b) Eugen Bleuler (c) Richmond Fromm (d) Sigmund Freud Answer: (b) Eugen Bleuler. Ambivalence, opposite feelings, wishes or ideas held towards the same thing at the same time, is one of Bleuler's four As, the fundamental symptoms of his "group of schizophrenias". Freud borrowed the word from Bleuler, and Kraepelin defined dementia praecox by its course, not by this symptom. "Richmond Fromm" is a garbled name: Frieda Fromm-Reichmann proposed the schizophrenogenic mother (1948), and Erich Fromm was a social psychoanalyst. Eugen Bleuler's four A's of schizophrenia include: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Attention, Affect, Ambivalence, Aphasia (b) Affect, Amnesia, Autism, Anxiety (c) Affect, Ambivalence, Autism, Association disturbances (d) Affect, Anhedonia, Autism, Avolition Answer: (c). The four As are loosening of associations, blunted or incongruous affect, ambivalence and autism (withdrawal into an inner world); hallucinations and delusions were only accessory symptoms for Bleuler. Option (d) mixes in anhedonia and avolition, which belong to the later negative-symptom list associated with Nancy Andreasen; attention appears on Andreasen's negative-symptom scale, not Bleuler's list; aphasia, amnesia and anxiety are on no list at all. "First rank symptoms" of schizophrenia given by Schneider include all except (JEMAS 2025) (a) Depersonalization (b) Hallucinatory voice in the form of running commentary (c) Delusional perception (d) Thought broadcasting Answer: (a) Depersonalization. Kurt Schneider's first-rank symptoms are three kinds of voices (audible thoughts, voices arguing or discussing, a running commentary), somatic passivity, thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting, made feelings, impulses and volitional acts, and delusional perception; in almost every one the normal boundary between self and world is breached. Depersonalisation, the feeling that one's self is unreal or changed, is experienced "as if", with insight, and is common in anxiety and dissociative states (Chapter 7). Which of the following is NOT a Schneider's first-rank symptom? (RML 2024) (a) Auditory hallucination (b) Delusional perception (c) Passivity phenomenon (d) Delusion of self-reference Answer: (d) Delusion of self-reference. Delusions of reference, the belief that remarks, broadcasts and ordinary events are aimed at oneself, are common in schizophrenia but are not first-rank. Delusional perception and the passivity (made) experiences are. Strictly, only three forms of auditory hallucination are first-rank (audible thoughts, voices arguing or discussing, and a running commentary), and a voice simply addressing the patient as "you" is second-rank, so read option (a) as standing for Schneider's voices and choose the delusion of self-reference. We know that a distinction is made between positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia. What is the difference between these symptoms? (RML 2020) (a) Negative symptoms indicate the presence of something normal and negative symptoms indicate the absence of something unusual (b) Positive symptoms indicate the presence of something normal, and negative symptoms indicate the absence of something unusual (c) Positive symptoms indicate the presence of something unusual, and negative symptoms indicate the absence of something normal (d) Positive symptoms indicate the absence of something normal, negative symptoms indicate the presence of something unusual Answer: (c). Positive symptoms add something that a healthy mind does not produce, an excess or distortion of normal function: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech and grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour. Negative symptoms take away or reduce something normal: blunted affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia and asociality. Every other option swaps "normal" and "unusual" or presence and absence. Hallucinations most often occur in people suffering from: (Amity 2023) (a) Mania (b) Schizophrenia (c) Depression (d) Personality Disorders Answer: (b) Schizophrenia. Auditory hallucinations alone are found in about 60 to 80 percent of people with a schizophrenia spectrum diagnosis, and hallucinations are central to the picture. Mania and depression with psychotic features produce mood-congruent voices, and in borderline personality disorder brief hallucinations can appear under stress, but in all three they are less frequent and less central. No hallucination is specific to schizophrenia. Negative symptoms of schizophrenia are all except (JEMAS 2025) (a) Marked apathy (b) Paucity of speech (c) Incongruity of emotional responses (d) Delusion Answer: (d) Delusion. A delusion is a positive symptom. The other three options are, almost word for word, ICD-10's description of the negative symptoms of its group (h): "marked apathy, paucity of speech, and blunting or incongruity of emotional responses". Incongruity is the tempting wrong pick, because Liddle grouped inappropriate affect with disorganisation, but ICD-10 counts it among the negative symptoms. Following are negative features of schizophrenia except: (RML 2024) (a) Avolition (b) Alogia (c) Ambivalence (d) Affective blunting Answer: (c) Ambivalence. Ambivalence is one of Bleuler's four As, not a negative symptom. Avolition, alogia and affective blunting are three of the five negative symptoms fixed by the NIMH-MATRICS consensus (2006), with anhedonia and asociality. The trap is the letter A: Bleuler's As (associations, affect, ambivalence, autism) and the negative As are different lists. The ICD-10 duration criterion for schizophrenia requires symptoms to persist for at least: (IHBAS 2025) (a) 6 months (b) 2 weeks (c) 3 months (d) 1 month Answer: (d) 1 month. ICD-10 (F20) requires the symptoms for most of the time during a period of one month or more, and ICD-11 (6A20) keeps the same rule (Real PYQ 2025 asked it for ICD-11). Six months is DSM-5-TR's total, including at least one month of active-phase symptoms; 2 weeks is the ICD onset window of acute and transient psychotic disorder; 3 months is the ICD minimum for delusional disorder. Which of the following are not included in the ICD criteria for Schizophrenia? (RML 2021) (a) Delusions (b) Catastrophic Thinking (c) Disorganised speech (d) Hallucinations Answer: (b) Catastrophic Thinking. Catastrophic thinking is a cognitive distortion from Aaron Beck's cognitive model of anxiety and depression, not a psychotic symptom. Delusions (groups (a), (b) and (d) of ICD-10), hallucinations (groups (c) and (e)) and disorganised speech (group (f): breaks in the train of thought, incoherence, neologisms) are all part of the ICD criteria. The presence of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking, and grossly disorganized or abnormal motor behavior, lasting for at least one month but less than six months, is indicative of: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Schizoaffective Disorder (b) Delusional Disorder (c) Brief Psychotic Disorder (d) Schizophrenia Answer: schizophreniform disorder, which is not among the options; the official key, (c) Brief Psychotic Disorder, is wrong. In DSM-5-TR, brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to the premorbid level; 1 month to less than 6 months is schizophreniform disorder; 6 months or more is schizophrenia (Figure 4.8). Schizoaffective disorder needs a major mood episode, and delusional disorder has delusions without the other symptoms. Under ICD-10 or ICD-11, with their one-month rule, the same illness would be schizophrenia. If you meet this exact question again, know that the key was (c); whenever schizophreniform disorder is offered, choose it. "Folie à deux," or Shared Psychotic Disorder, is characterized by: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Two individuals simultaneously experiencing independent psychotic episodes (b) The transmission of delusional beliefs from one individual to another who are in a close relationship (c) A delusion that is shared by an entire cultural or subcultural group (d) A brief psychotic episode triggered by extreme stress in two closely related people Answer: (b). Lasègue and Falret (1877) described a delusion passing from a primary partner with an established psychotic illness, usually the more dominant, to a more passive, dependent partner in a close and socially isolated relationship; on separation the secondary partner's belief often fades. Two independent psychoses (a) and a brief stress psychosis in two relatives (d) involve no transmission, and a belief shared by a whole cultural group (c) is a shared belief, not a delusion. ICD-10 codes the condition F24, induced delusional disorder. Catatonia is classified in DSM-5 as: (IHBAS 2025) (a) An independent disorder (b) A specifier across several disorders (c) A personality disorder (d) A subtype of bipolar disorder Answer: (b) A specifier across several disorders. Since DSM-5, catatonia (three or more of twelve psychomotor signs) is a specifier added to psychotic, bipolar, depressive, neurodevelopmental and other disorders, alongside catatonic disorder due to another medical condition and unspecified catatonia. It is not an independent disorder, not a personality disorder and not a subtype of bipolar disorder (nor of schizophrenia, whose subtypes DSM-5 dropped); it is in fact more often associated with mood disorders than with schizophrenia. Schizophrenia is most commonly found in: (RML 2022) (a) Adolescents (b) Young Adults (c) The Middle-Aged (d) The Elderly Answer: (b) Young Adults. DSM-5-TR states that psychotic features typically emerge between the late teens and the mid-30s, with the peak onset in the early to mid-20s for men and the late 20s for women. Onset before adolescence is rare, and the middle-aged and elderly account only for a smaller second peak in women around the menopause and for late-onset cases. The chance of developing schizophrenia if you have an identical twin with the disorder is approximately: (RML 2021) (a) 1% (b) 10% (c) 80% (d) 50% Answer: (d) 50%. Irving Gottesman's pooled figures (1991) put the lifetime risk for the identical twin of a patient at about 48 percent, against 17 for a fraternal twin, 9 for a sibling and 1 for the general population. So 1 percent is the population risk and 10 percent roughly a sibling's, while 80 percent is the approximate heritability of liability, not a concordance. Modern register studies give lower concordance (33 percent in Hilker's Danish twins, 2018), but "about 50 percent" is the exam answer. Schizophrenia corresponds to the autistic phase of development and the person fails to develop an adequate and stable symbiosis, was the developmental theory of schizophrenia given by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Ping-Nie Pao (b) Sylvano Arieti (c) Margaret Mahler (d) Edith Jacobson Answer: (c) Margaret Mahler. Mahler, the child analyst of separation-individuation, held that the infant passes from a normal autistic phase through a normal symbiotic phase to separation, and in a 1952 paper she described autistic and symbiotic psychoses of childhood. Silvano Arieti is palaeologic thinking and the von Domarus principle, Ping-Nie Pao organismic panic, and Edith Jacobson the fusion of self and object representations in psychotic regression. Gregory Bateson describes a classic example of the interaction between a mother and her son who had fairly well recovered from an acute schizophrenic episode. Bateson described this interaction as follows: '[The son] was glad to see her [his mother] and impulsively put his arm around her shoulders, whereupon she stiffened. He withdrew his arm and she asked, Don't you love me anymore? He then blushed, and she said, Dear, you must not be so easily embarrassed and afraid of your feelings. The patient was able to stay with her only a few minutes more, and following her departure, he assaulted an aide and was put in the isolation room.' Bateson used this interaction to illustrate which ONE of the following concepts? (RML 2021) (a) The cybernetic system (b) The homeostatic system (c) The incongruent family dyad (d) The symptomatic double bind Answer: (d) The symptomatic double bind. Bateson, Jackson, Haley and Weakland (1956) offered this episode as their example of the double bind as a supposed cause of symptoms: the mother's stiffening and her words contradict each other at two levels, and the son can neither comment on the contradiction nor leave. "Cybernetic system" (a family as a self-regulating system steered by feedback) and "homeostatic system" (Don Jackson's idea that a family resists change to keep its balance) are general systems ideas, and incongruence is Satir's and Rogers's word. The double bind is no longer accepted as a cause of schizophrenia. Expressed Emotion (EE) is a significant predictor of relapse in schizophrenia. Which of the following is NOT one of the three core dimensions of high Expressed Emotion? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Hostility (b) Critical Comments (c) Emotional Over-involvement (d) Warmth and Positive Regard Answer: (d) Warmth and Positive Regard. The Camberwell Family Interview rates critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement, and these three make up high EE. It also rates warmth and positive remarks, but they are not part of the high-EE index; López and colleagues (2004) even found that family warmth predicted fewer relapses in Mexican-American families. High EE (Expressed Emotion) is known to cause: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Poor treatment outcome (b) Relapse of psychotic illness (c) Negative symptoms of schizophrenia (d) Violent behavior in schizophrenic patients Answer: (b) Relapse of psychotic illness. Brown, Birley and Wing (1972) found that patients returning to high-EE homes were roughly three to four times as likely to relapse in the nine months after discharge, Vaughn and Leff (1976) replicated the finding, and Butzlaff and Hooley's meta-analysis (1998) confirmed it. High EE predicts relapse, not the onset of the illness, its negative symptoms or violence, and "poor treatment outcome" is too vague to be the best answer. Reducing contact hours is one of the important strategies in the management of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Interpersonal violence (b) Para suicidal risk (c) Expressed emotion (d) Stubbornness in children Answer: (c) Expressed emotion. Vaughn and Leff (1976) found two protective factors in high-EE homes: regular maintenance medication and less than about 35 hours a week of face-to-face contact with the high-EE relative. Patients with neither protection relapsed almost without exception. Reducing contact hours, together with family psychoeducation, is therefore a way of managing high EE; it is not a standard strategy for violence, parasuicide risk or a stubborn child. The front-line treatment for schizophrenia is: (RML 2021) (a) Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) (b) Stress management training (c) Antipsychotic medication (d) Social skills training Answer: (c) Antipsychotic medication. Since Delay and Deniker introduced chlorpromazine in 1952, antipsychotics (neuroleptics, used primarily for schizophrenia and the other psychotic disorders, as RML 2025 asked) have been the front-line treatment: no psychological treatment on its own matches them in the acute illness, and stopping them is the strongest predictor of relapse after a first episode. CBT for psychosis, social skills training and stress management are valuable additions, not substitutes. A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia has been on antipsychotic medication for years. He presents with repetitive, involuntary, and purposeless movements of his mouth, tongue, and face, including lip-smacking and grimacing. This condition is most likely: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Akathisia (b) Acute Dystonia (c) Tardive Dyskinesia (d) Parkinsonism Answer: (c) Tardive Dyskinesia. Years of treatment plus involuntary chewing, lip smacking, tongue protrusion and grimacing is tardive dyskinesia: it appears after at least 3 months (usually months to years), is the last extrapyramidal effect to appear and the most likely to be irreversible, and is caused by neuroleptics, not by antidepressants, anxiolytics or barbiturates (RML 2022). Akathisia is a subjective restlessness, acute dystonia sudden painful spasms within hours to days, and parkinsonism slowness, rigidity and tremor after a few weeks. A client recently started antipsychotic medication and reports an intense, subjective feeling of inner restlessness and a compelling need to pace or move constantly. This side effect is best described as: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Akathisia (b) Tardive Dyskinesia (c) Dystonia (d) Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Answer: (a) Akathisia. Akathisia is an inner restlessness with an urge to move (pacing, rocking from foot to foot) that begins within hours to about four weeks of starting or raising the dose; lowering the dose, propranolol or a benzodiazepine help. Tardive dyskinesia comes after months or years and is involuntary rather than driven by an urge, dystonia is a painful muscle spasm, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome is the emergency of fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and confusion with a raised creatine kinase. Which movement disorder is a secondary one? (JEMAS 2025) (a) Huntington's chorea (b) Parkinson's (c) Akathisia (d) None of these Answer: (c) Akathisia. A secondary movement disorder has an identifiable outside cause such as a drug, a toxin, a stroke or an infection, and akathisia, like all four extrapyramidal side effects, is caused by antipsychotic drugs. Huntington's disease (described by George Huntington in 1872; an inherited expansion in the huntingtin gene) and Parkinson's disease (James Parkinson, 1817; degeneration of the substantia nigra) are primary movement disorders, so (d) is wrong too. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Positive symptoms are the presence of something unusual (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour); negative symptoms are the absence of something normal: blunted (flat) affect, alogia (poverty of speech), avolition (apathy), anhedonia and asociality (NIMH-MATRICS, 2006). ICD-10 adds "marked apathy, paucity of speech, and blunting or incongruity of emotional responses". In an "all except" list the exception is a positive symptom (delusion, auditory hallucination) or ambivalence, one of Bleuler's four As. asked 8 times Schneider's first-rank symptoms : audible thoughts (thought echo, Gedankenlautwerden), voices arguing or discussing, voices giving a running commentary, somatic passivity, thought insertion, thought withdrawal, thought broadcasting, made feelings, made impulses, made volitional acts, and delusional perception; delusions of control are first-rank. Not first-rank: depersonalisation, loose associations, delusions of self-reference, catatonic signs, negative symptoms, second-person voices. asked 7 times Expressed emotion (George Brown and colleagues; the Camberwell Family Interview) is a family climate of critical comments, hostility and emotional over-involvement ; warmth and positive regard are rated but are not high-EE dimensions. High EE predicts relapse (Brown, Birley and Wing, 1972: about three to four times the risk within nine months), not onset, negative symptoms or violence. Vaughn and Leff (1976): maintenance medication and less than about 35 hours a week of face-to-face contact protect, so reducing contact hours is a way of managing high EE. asked 4 times DSM-5-TR schizophrenia needs at least 6 months of continuous signs of disturbance, including at least 1 month of active-phase (Criterion A) symptoms, or less if successfully treated; prodromal and residual periods count towards the six months. Criterion A is two of five symptoms, at least one of them delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech. asked 7 times Folie à deux (Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret, 1877): a delusion transmitted from a primary partner with an established psychotic disorder, usually the more dominant, to a more passive partner in a close, socially isolated relationship; on separation the secondary partner's belief often fades. ICD-10: F24 induced delusional disorder ; DSM-IV: shared psychotic disorder; DSM-5-TR: delusional disorder or other specified; ICD-11: within delusional disorder (6A24), among the schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders. A belief shared by a whole cultural group is not folie à deux. asked 6 times Dopamine is the transmitter most implicated in the positive symptoms: in the classic hypothesis they arise from hyperactivity of the mesolimbic pathway , which runs from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum) and limbic structures and serves reward. Not serotonin, GABA or acetylcholine. asked 6 times Bleuler's four As (Eugen Bleuler; lecture 1908, monograph 1911): loosening of Associations, blunted or incongruous Affect, Ambivalence and Autism, his fundamental symptoms; hallucinations and delusions were only accessory. Bleuler coined ambivalence (not Kraepelin; Freud borrowed it). Schizophrenia means a splitting of psychic functions, not a split personality. asked 4 times The double bind (Gregory Bateson with Don Jackson, Jay Haley and John Weakland, 1956) was a family-communication theory of the cause of schizophrenia : contradictory messages at two levels from someone one depends on, with no way to comment or escape. The mother who stiffens at her son's embrace and asks "Don't you love me any more?" is the symptomatic double bind . Not a cause today, but seminal for family therapy. asked 4 times Tardive dyskinesia : involuntary chewing, lip smacking, tongue protrusion and grimacing after at least 3 months, usually months to years, of antipsychotic treatment; the last extrapyramidal effect to appear and the most likely to be irreversible; caused by neuroleptics , not antidepressants, anxiolytics or barbiturates; explained by dopamine receptor supersensitivity. asked 4 times The primary target of typical antipsychotics is the D2 receptor (not D1, 5-HT2A or muscarinic M1), and D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway (substantia nigra to caudate and putamen) causes the extrapyramidal side effects; D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway raises prolactin. asked 5 times ICD-10 (F20) and ICD-11 (6A20) require schizophrenia's symptoms for at least 1 month ; the 6-month rule is DSM's. Two weeks is the ICD onset window of acute and transient psychotic disorder; 3 months is the ICD minimum for delusional disorder. asked 3 times Kurt Schneider (1887 to 1967) described the first-rank symptoms (list first published 1939; Clinical Psychopathology , English edition 1959), not Kraepelin, Bleuler, Jaspers, Bateson or Wynne (printed "Wayne"). They are most associated with schizophrenia but are not pathognomonic: they also occur in mania. asked 3 times Emil Kraepelin 's dementia praecox ("premature dementia"; fourth edition, 1893) is the ancestor of schizophrenia, not of Alzheimer's or frontotemporal dementia. In the sixth edition (1899) he separated his two clinical types , dementia praecox and manic-depressive insanity, by course: deteriorating versus episodic with recovery. asked 3 times Akathisia : a subjective inner restlessness with a compelling need to pace, within hours to about four weeks of starting or raising an antipsychotic; lower the dose, add propranolol or a benzodiazepine. Akathisia and tardive dyskinesia are secondary (drug-induced) movement disorders; Huntington's chorea and Parkinson's disease are primary. asked 2 times Antipsychotic medication is the front-line treatment for schizophrenia; CBT, social skills training and stress management are additions, not substitutes. Neuroleptics are used primarily for schizophrenia and the other psychotic disorders (also acute mania), not for depression or anxiety. Chlorpromazine: Jean Delay and Pierre Deniker, 1952. asked 2 times The duration ladder (DSM-5-TR): brief psychotic disorder, at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning; schizophreniform disorder, 1 month to less than 6 months ; schizophrenia, 6 months or more. The IHBAS 2025 key that calls a 1 to 6 month episode "brief psychotic disorder" is wrong (schizophreniform was not offered). asked once For the identical twin of a patient the lifetime risk is about 48 percent ("about 50 percent"); child of two affected parents 46, fraternal twin 17, child of one affected parent 13, sibling 9, general population 1 (Irving Gottesman, 1991). About 80 percent is the heritability, not the concordance. asked once Catastrophic thinking is a cognitive distortion from Beck's model of anxiety and depression and is not in the ICD criteria for schizophrenia; delusions, hallucinations and disorganised speech are. asked once Schizophrenia is most commonly found in young adults : onset between the late teens and the mid-30s, peaking in the early to mid-20s in men and the late 20s in women, with a second female peak around the menopause; incidence about 1.4 times higher in men, lifetime prevalence roughly equal. asked once Margaret Mahler : schizophrenia corresponds to the autistic phase, with failure to develop an adequate and stable symbiosis (symbiotic psychosis). Silvano Arieti: palaeologic thinking and the von Domarus principle; Ping-Nie Pao: organismic panic; Edith Jacobson: fusion of self and object representations. asked once Hallucinations most often occur in schizophrenia ; auditory ones are the commonest kind (about 60 to 80 percent of people with a schizophrenia spectrum diagnosis). Mania, psychotic depression and, briefly under stress, borderline personality disorder can produce them too. asked once In DSM-5, catatonia is a specifier across several disorders (three or more of twelve signs), plus catatonic disorder due to another medical condition and unspecified catatonia; not an independent disorder or a subtype of bipolar disorder. Treat first with lorazepam, then ECT. asked once The mesocortical pathway (ventral tegmental area to prefrontal cortex) is underactive in schizophrenia, linked to negative and cognitive symptoms; the tuberoinfundibular pathway (hypothalamus to median eminence and pituitary) controls prolactin, which rises when its D2 receptors are blocked. asked once The original support for the dopamine hypothesis : the clinical potency of typical antipsychotics correlates with their affinity for D2 receptors (Philip Seeman and colleagues; Ian Creese, David Burt and Solomon Snyder; both 1976). asked once Erotomanic delusional disorder (de Clérambault's syndrome): the belief that a person, often famous or of higher status, is secretly in love with the patient. Jealous type is the Othello syndrome, somatic type includes delusional parasitosis (Ekbom), and persecutory is the commonest type. asked once Schizoaffective disorder (DSM-5-TR): a major mood episode concurrent with Criterion A of schizophrenia, plus at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations without a major mood episode, with mood episodes present for the majority of the illness; bipolar and depressive types; term coined by Jacob Kasanin (1933). asked once
