The case of John Cade and W.B., revisited Go back to the unused pantry at Bundoora, and to W.B., who had been "in a state of chronic manic excitement for five years". You can now name what Cade saw. W.B.'s restless, sleepless, interfering excitement was a manic episode, and in DSM-5-TR terms a single manic episode is enough for a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder (Section 5.4); the two courses of electroconvulsive therapy that settled him for only a few months were the best that psychiatry then had. Cade's chain of reasoning, from a toxin in the urine to uric acid to its soluble lithium salt, was a hunch, and his placid guinea pigs were probably simply sick; yet the salt worked, much as Meduna's mistaken belief that epilepsy and schizophrenia rarely occur together led to the convulsive treatments (Section 5.7). A treatment found by accident, and a theory inferred backwards from it, is the story of the monoamine hypotheses as well (Section 5.5), and how lithium works is still uncertain, though the leading ideas involve second-messenger systems inside neurons. What Cade's patients did show, through the specificity of the effect (the ten manic patients changed, the six with schizophrenia and the three with depression did not), is that mania is at least partly a disorder of the body's chemistry. W.B.'s relapse and death are just as instructive. He stopped his tablets once he felt well, as so many people with bipolar disorder do (Section 5.4), and his son-in-law's letter about the first excitable, argumentative weeks is exactly the early warning that psychoeducation now teaches families to notice (Section 5.7). His vomiting, seizures and semi-coma were lithium toxicity, the price of a narrow therapeutic index at a time when blood levels could not be measured routinely; today 12-hour serum levels, kidney and thyroid tests and warnings about dehydration, low-salt diets and interacting drugs guard against it (Table 5.22). The same physiology, the body handling lithium like sodium, explains why lithium chloride sold as a salt substitute to heart patients on low-salt diets proved so dangerous. Schou's placebo-controlled trial and the prophylaxis studies of Baastrup and Schou (1967 and 1970) turned Cade's observation into the gold-standard mood stabiliser, which also lowers the risk of suicide (Section 5.9). And W.B.'s weeks back at his old firm are a reminder that recovery is measured in work, family and a life, which is why medication for bipolar disorder is now combined with psychoeducation, family-focused therapy and interpersonal and social rhythm therapy. A cheap salt opened the biological study of mood; the people around W.B. show why that study was never the whole story. Chapter summary 5.1 Mood, Mood Episodes and How Mood Disorders Are Classified. Mood is the sustained state a person reports; affect is the moment-to-moment expression the clinician observes. Aretaeus of Cappadocia linked melancholia with mania, and in 1854 Baillarger (folie à double forme) and Jean-Pierre Falret (folie circulaire) described one illness with two poles. Kraepelin separated manic-depressive insanity from dementia praecox (1899); Leonhard split unipolar from bipolar forms (1957), confirmed by Angst and Perris (1966). Diagnosis starts from three episodes: major depressive (five of nine symptoms for 2 weeks, including depressed mood or anhedonia), manic (three of seven DIG FAST symptoms, four if mood is only irritable, for a week, with marked impairment, hospitalisation or psychosis) and hypomanic (4 days, observable, no marked impairment or psychosis). DSM-5 split the mood disorders into bipolar and related and depressive disorders and replaced the mixed episode with a specifier; ICD-10 codes them F30 to F39. 5.2 Major Depressive Disorder. Major depressive disorder needs at least one major depressive episode and no history of mania or hypomania. Its nine symptoms are two core mood symptoms, four bodily ones (appetite or weight, sleep, psychomotor change, fatigue) and three cognitive ones (worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, thoughts of death); phobias, anxiety and pain are associated features. ICD-10 grades episodes mild, moderate or severe and adds the somatic syndrome. DSM-5 removed the bereavement exclusion over the objections of Allen Frances. Seligman called depression the common cold of psychopathology: 12-month prevalence is about 7 percent in the United States, lifetime prevalence about 15 to 20 percent, and India's National Mental Health Survey found 2.7 percent current and 5.2 percent lifetime. Women outnumber men about two to one from puberty. Episodes tend to recur, often present through bodily complaints (Kleinman's neurasthenia patients), and travel with anxiety and substance use. 5.3 The Other Depressive Disorders and the Specifiers. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is depressed mood more days than not for at least 2 years (1 in children), with two of six symptoms and no gap over 2 months: milder than major depression but longer; a major episode on top of it is double depression (Keller and Shapiro, 1982). Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, created in DSM-5 after the rise in paediatric bipolar diagnoses, needs severe outbursts three or more times a week, irritable mood between them, onset before 10 and diagnosis between 6 and 18. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder needs prospective daily ratings over two cycles. Mixed anxiety and depressive disorder is the "hybrid", and Spitz described anaclitic depression (1946). The specifiers cover anxious distress, mixed features, melancholic and atypical features (separated by mood reactivity), psychotic features, catatonia, peripartum onset, seasonal pattern (Rosenthal, 1984) and, for bipolar disorders only, rapid cycling. 5.4 Bipolar and Related Disorders. A manic episode, like Rahul's, joins elevated or irritable mood and increased energy for at least a week with symptoms such as grandiosity and flight of ideas. Hypomania has the same symptoms for at least four days, observable by others, without marked impairment or psychosis. One manic episode establishes bipolar I disorder (12-month prevalence 1.5 percent in the United States in DSM-5-TR; equal sex ratio; mean onset at 22). Bipolar II disorder needs a hypomanic and a major depressive episode and never mania; it is not milder, because its burden is depression. Cyclothymic disorder is at least 2 years of swings that never reach a full episode. Rapid cycling (Dunner and Fieve, 1974) means four or more episodes in 12 months. Depression dominates the long course (Judd, 2002), suicide risk is high, and the illness is often missed, mistaken or stretched. 5.5 Biological Causes. Bipolar disorder has among the highest heritability in psychiatry (about 60 to 85 percent) and major depressive disorder a moderate one (37 percent; Sullivan, Neale and Kendler, 2000); no single gene has been found, and Caspi's 5-HTTLPR gene-by-stress finding (2003) failed to replicate. The monoamine hypotheses were inferred backwards from drugs: reserpine depleted the monoamines, while iproniazid and imipramine (Kuhn, 1957) raised them. Schildkraut's catecholamine hypothesis (1965), Coppen's serotonin hypothesis and Prange's permissive hypothesis (1974) all face the lag between the drugs' synaptic effect and recovery, which the neurotrophic hypothesis (Duman, Heninger and Nestler, 1997) explains through BDNF and the hippocampus. Depression brings an overactive HPA axis with non-suppression on Carroll's dexamethasone suppression test, shortened REM latency (Kupfer), disturbed social rhythms and altered circuits, including Mayberg's area 25. Post's kindling hypothesis (1992) holds that each episode lowers the threshold for the next. 5.6 Psychological and Social Causes. Psychodynamic theories made depression a response to loss: Abraham (1911), Freud's "Mourning and Melancholia" (1917) with introjection and anger turned inward, Klein's depressive position, Bibring's ego helplessness (1953) and Bowlby's attachment and loss. Ferster and Lewinsohn (1974) blamed a low rate of response-contingent positive reinforcement. Seligman and Maier's yoked dogs (1967) showed learned helplessness, which Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale (1978) reformulated around internal, stable and global attributions and Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy (1989) turned into hopelessness theory. Beck's cognitive theory (1967) is a diathesis-stress model built on the negative cognitive triad of self, world and future, latent schemas and distortions. Nolen-Hoeksema's rumination helps explain women's excess, Coyne and Hammen described interpersonal processes, and Brown and Harris (1978) found four vulnerability factors among Camberwell women. Goal attainment events, sleep loss and expressed emotion trigger bipolar episodes. 5.7 Treating Mood Disorders: Drugs, ECT and Other Physical Treatments. Treatment is judged by response, remission, relapse and recurrence (Frank and colleagues, 1991). The antidepressants are the MAOIs (iproniazid first; the cheese reaction), the tricyclics (imipramine; anticholinergic effects, danger in overdose), the SSRIs (fluoxetine, 1987), the SNRIs, the atypicals and ketamine. Mood lifts after two to four weeks, the advantage over placebo is modest but real (Cipriani, 2018), STAR*D showed that many patients need more than one step, and an antidepressant alone can switch a bipolar patient into mania. Lithium, Cade's discovery of 1949, is the gold-standard mood stabiliser for treatment and prophylaxis, with a narrow therapeutic index and an anti-suicidal effect; valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine and the atypical antipsychotics complete the list. Modified ECT (Cerletti and Bini, 1938) serves severe, psychotic or suicidal depression and catatonia; rTMS, deep brain stimulation, light therapy and ketamine are other options, alongside the psychotherapies. 5.8 Suicide I: Definitions, Scale and Risk. Suicidal behaviour runs from ideation through plans and attempts to death; intent is the wish to die and lethality the medical danger of the method. Kreitman coined parasuicide (1969), and DSM-5 made non-suicidal self-injury a condition for further study. WHO's current fact sheet (2023 estimates) gives more than 740,000 deaths a year, most in low- and middle-income countries. India's NCRB recorded 1,70,746 suicides in 2024, a rate of 12.2 per lakh, about three in four of them male, with family problems the leading recorded cause and hanging the commonest method. Women attempt more and men die more: the gender paradox. Western psychological autopsies find a mental disorder in about 90 percent of suicides, Asian studies fewer. A previous attempt is the strongest single predictor, and risk peaks when high lethality, a specific plan, frequent ideation and a family history converge. 5.9 Suicide II: Explanations and Prevention. Durkheim's Le Suicide (1897) explained rates by social integration and regulation, giving egoistic, altruistic, anomic and fatalistic suicide. Freud saw hostility turned inward, Menninger three wishes, and Shneidman, the founder of suicidology, described psychache, the cubic model and the psychological autopsy. Beck and colleagues (1985) showed that hopelessness predicts suicide better than depression, and Baumeister (1990) proposed escape from the self. Ideation-to-action theories separate desire from capability: Joiner's interpersonal theory (2005: perceived burdensomeness, thwarted belongingness, acquired capability), O'Connor's integrated motivational-volitional model and Klonsky and May's three-step theory. Åsberg and colleagues (1976) linked low CSF 5-HIAA to violent attempts, and Mann's stress-diathesis model (1999) joins the strands. Publicised suicides breed imitation (the Werther effect; Phillips, 1974), stories of coping protect (the Papageno effect), and means restriction, treatment, lithium, clozapine, follow-up, India's 2022 strategy and postvention prevent deaths. model, Werther effect, suicide clusters, Papageno effect, means restriction, postvention From the past papers Which disorder is characterised by persistent sadness and loss of interest? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Schizophrenia (b) Depression (c) OCD (d) Bipolar-disorder Answer: (b) Depression. Depressed mood and loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) are the two core symptoms of a major depressive episode, and at least one of them must be among its five or more symptoms. Schizophrenia is defined by psychotic symptoms and OCD by obsessions and compulsions. Bipolar disorder can include depressive episodes, but it is defined by mania or hypomania, so a picture of persistent sadness and lost interest points to depression. Which disorder is characterized by persistent sadness and loss of interest? (IHBAS 2025) (a) Bipolar disorder (b) Major depressive disorder (c) Anxiety disorder (d) OCD Answer: (b) Major depressive disorder. The same question came back a year later with new distractors. The two core symptoms of major depressive disorder are exactly these; the anxiety disorders centre on fear and worry (Chapter 6), OCD on obsessions and compulsions, and bipolar disorder on episodes of elevated mood. Symptoms of major depressive disorder might include: i. specific phobias ii. losing interest or pleasure in things that you usually enjoy iii. changes in appetite iv. an excessively euphoric mood (RML 2020) (a) i & ii (b) iii & iv (c) ii & iii (d) i & iv Answer: (c) ii & iii. Loss of interest or pleasure is a core symptom and a change in appetite or weight is one of the four bodily symptoms of a major depressive episode. Phobias are common in depressed people but are only associated features (specific phobia is an anxiety disorder, Chapter 6), and an excessively euphoric mood belongs to the opposite pole, mania. Which illness is known as the common cold of psychiatry? (RML 2024) (a) Schizophrenia (b) Depression (c) Obsessive-compulsive disorder (d) Hysteria Answer: (b) Depression. Seligman called depression the "common cold of psychopathology" in the 1970s because it is by far the most common of the serious mental disorders (12-month prevalence about 7 percent in the United States, lifetime about 15 to 20 percent). Schizophrenia has a lifetime risk under 1 percent, and neither obsessive-compulsive disorder nor hysteria (the old name for the conversion and dissociative conditions, Chapter 7) carries the phrase. Identify the following statements that least accurately characterizes depression. (JEMAS 2025) (a) Its rate of incidence is widespread and increasing. (b) It is often triggered by a stressful event. (c) Men are more vulnerable to depression than women. (d) Severity of depression is associated with suicide risk. Answer: (c). The reverse is true: from puberty onwards women are about twice as likely as men to be depressed (estimates run from about 1.5 to 3). The other three are accurate. Depression is widespread and has been rising, especially among the young; severe events precede most first episodes, as Brown and Harris showed; and severity is associated with suicide risk, although hopelessness is the stronger predictor. Dysthymic or Persistent depressive disorder (PDD) differs from major depressive disorder (MDD) in the following ways: (RML 2021) (a) Symptoms include hallucinations and delusional thinking. (b) Symptoms only affect women during the winter months. (c) Symptoms are more severe and last longer. (d) Symptoms are less severe but last longer. Answer: (d). Persistent depressive disorder needs depressed mood more days than not for at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children and adolescents) with two of six symptoms: a quieter but more chronic depression than a major episode. Hallucinations and delusions are not part of it, (b) is a garbled version of the seasonal pattern specifier, which is not limited to women, and (c) gets the severity backwards. A 12-year-old boy begins to have new episodes of temper outbursts that are out of proportion to the situation. Which of the following is NOT a diagnostic possibility in this patient? (RML 2022) (a) Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (b) Bipolar Disorder (c) Conduct Disorder (d) Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder Answer: (a) Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder. DMDD requires onset before age 10 (and a first diagnosis between 6 and 18), so outbursts that begin at 12 rule it out. Bipolar disorder remains possible if there are distinct episodes, and conduct disorder and ADHD can also present with temper outbursts (Chapters 3 and 11). Hybrid disorder is: (Amity 2023) (a) Multiple personality disorder (b) Borderline personality disorder (c) Mixed anxiety-depressive disorder (d) Schizoid personality disorder Answer: (c) Mixed anxiety-depressive disorder. It is the "hybrid" of two symptom sets, neither severe enough for a diagnosis on its own: ICD-10 F41.2, ICD-11 mixed depressive and anxiety disorder (placed among the depressive disorders), and absent from DSM-5-TR. Multiple personality disorder is the old name for dissociative identity disorder (Chapter 7), and borderline and schizoid personality disorders belong to Chapter 11. According to the DSM-5-TR, which of the following is NOT a specifier for a manic episode? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) With Mixed Features (b) With Psychotic Features (c) With Anxious Distress (d) With Limited Prosocial Emotions Answer: (d) With limited prosocial emotions. That specifier belongs to conduct disorder (Chapter 11), not to any mood disorder. With mixed features (three or more concurrent depressive symptoms), with psychotic features and with anxious distress are all genuine specifiers of a manic episode. Which of the following best distinguishes psychotic disorders from mood disorders with psychotic features? (IHBAS 2025) (a) Presence of delusions only (b) Mood congruence of psychotic symptoms (c) Duration of depressive episodes (d) Comorbidity with anxiety disorders Answer: (b) Mood congruence of psychotic symptoms. In mood disorders the delusions and hallucinations are usually mood-congruent (guilt, disease and deserved punishment in depression; grandiosity in mania) and occur only during mood episodes. Both kinds of disorder have delusions, so (a) cannot separate them, and the duration of depressive episodes and comorbid anxiety do not discriminate. An affective disorder in which a person swings from one mood extreme to another is classified as: (RML 2020) (a) Manic (b) Depressive (c) Unipolar (d) Bipolar Answer: (d) Bipolar. Since Leonhard's split of 1957, mood disorders are first divided into unipolar (mood moves in one direction only, almost always down) and bipolar (both poles). "Manic" and "depressive" name episodes, not classes of disorder, and unipolar is exactly what the question rules out. Which disorder involves alternating episodes of mania and depression? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Bipolar disorder (b) Major depressive disorder (c) Schizophrenia (d) Generalized anxiety disorder Answer: (a) Bipolar disorder. Alternation between the poles is the classic picture, although strictly one manic episode is enough for bipolar I disorder. Major depressive disorder requires that there has never been a manic or hypomanic episode, and schizophrenia and generalised anxiety disorder are not mood disorders. Within mood disorders, two key symptoms of a manic episode are: (RML 2021) (a) Hallucinations and flight of ideas (b) Distractibility and social phobia. (c) Extremely elevated mood and grandiose ideas. (d) Delusional thinking and intense fear of weight gain. Answer: (c). An abnormally elevated mood is the core of the episode, and grandiosity is the G of DIG FAST. Flight of ideas and distractibility are genuine manic symptoms, but each is paired with something that is not: hallucinations occur only as psychotic features and are not among the seven symptoms, social phobia is an anxiety disorder, and intense fear of weight gain is anorexia nervosa (Chapter 8). Which of the following statements concerning Bipolar disorder is INCORRECT? (RML 2022) (a) Bipolar-I Disorder includes mania (b) Bipolar-II Disorder includes hypomania (c) Bipolar-I Disorder includes hypomania (d) Bipolar-I Disorder includes periods of depression even if these do not reach the threshold for major depressive disorder Answer: (c), as keyed. Bipolar I disorder is defined by mania, and hypomania is the defining episode of bipolar II, so (c) is the statement that misdescribes bipolar I. Read it as a statement about defining features: hypomanic episodes may occur in bipolar I, but they are never what establishes it. Statement (d) is true, because subthreshold depressive periods are allowed in bipolar I. Cyclothymia is best defined as: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Alternating manic and depressive episodes of equal severity (b) A single hypomanic episode without depression (c) Recurrent dysthymic episodes lasting 6 months (d) At least 2 years of fluctuating hypomanic and depressive symptoms not meeting criteria for bipolar disorder Answer: (d). Cyclothymic disorder is at least 2 years (1 year in children and adolescents) of numerous hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet the criteria for a hypomanic, manic or major depressive episode, with no symptom-free stretch longer than 2 months; ICD-10 calls it a persistent instability of mood. Full alternating episodes are bipolar I, a hypomanic episode without a prior depression is recorded as other specified bipolar and related disorder, and dysthymia does not come in 6-month episodes. The "kindling hypothesis" in mood disorders suggests: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Each episode of depression lowers the threshold for future episodes (b) Bipolar disorder is caused solely by genetics (c) Antidepressants permanently cure depression (d) Anxiety and depression are unrelated Answer: (a). Robert Post (1992), borrowing Goddard's kindling of seizures in rats, proposed that each episode leaves a lasting trace that lowers the threshold for the next, so early episodes follow major stress and later ones need little or none and come faster. The other options are simply false: identical twins are concordant for bipolar disorder in only 40 to 70 percent of pairs, depression tends to recur, and anxiety and depression are closely linked. Which medication is considered the gold standard mood stabilizer for the treatment and prophylaxis of bipolar disorder? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Fluoxetine (b) Lithium (c) Haloperidol (d) Lorazepam Answer: (b) Lithium. Since Cade's report of 1949 and the prophylaxis trials of Baastrup and Schou, lithium has been the standard for acute mania and, above all, for preventing new episodes of both poles, and it is the only mood stabiliser with a clear anti-suicidal effect. Fluoxetine is an SSRI antidepressant that can trigger mania, haloperidol an antipsychotic used short term for agitation, and lorazepam a benzodiazepine used as an adjunct; none is a mood stabiliser. Which of the following is NOT typically considered a first-line pharmacological treatment for acute mania in bipolar disorder? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Lithium (b) Valproate (Divalproex) (c) Fluoxetine (d) Atypical antipsychotics (such as Olanzapine, Risperidone) Answer: (c) Fluoxetine. An antidepressant given on its own in bipolar disorder can precipitate a switch into mania or speed up cycling, so it has no place in treating acute mania. Lithium, valproate and the atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole) are all first line; carbamazepine is an alternative. Mode of suicide attempt indicates: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Intentionality (b) Lethality (c) Conviction (d) Survival Answer: (b) Lethality. The method decides how medically dangerous an act is. Intent, the wish to die, is judged from the circumstances and the person's statements rather than from the method, because people often misjudge how dangerous a method is. Conviction is not a standard dimension of suicide assessment, and survival is an outcome, not something the method indicates. Suicidal risk is assessed to be highest when the following criteria are met in comparison to others, the 'time' factor being the same for all: (JEMAS 2025) (a) High lethality, specific plan, frequent suicidal ideas, family history (b) Disrupted biological functioning, no recent attempt, no suicidal ideation (c) Adequate biological functioning, no previous attempt, moderate intent (d) Frequent suicidal ideation, recent suicide attempt, low lethality, absence of family history Answer: (a). Four of the weightiest markers converge in one person. Option (b) offers only non-specific disturbance of sleep and appetite, with no ideation and no attempt; (c) has a single marker; (d) is genuinely worrying, because a recent attempt is a strong risk factor, but low lethality and no family history make it less dangerous than (a). Remember that a previous attempt is the strongest single predictor and hopelessness the strongest psychological one. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Aaron T. Beck 's cognitive theory (1967): depression is maintained by the negative cognitive triad , negative views of the self, the world (ongoing experience) and the future , fed by latent schemas, automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions. That pattern is called the cognitive triad; it is not id, ego and superego, not past, present and future, not self, mother and father, and not thoughts, feelings and behaviours. asked 8 times Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) : depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children and adolescents) , with 2 or more of 6 symptoms and never symptom-free for more than 2 months. Compared with MDD its symptoms are less severe but last longer ; DSM-5 merged dysthymia and chronic major depression into it. asked 7 times Persistent sadness (depressed mood) and loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) are the two core symptoms of major depressive disorder ; appetite or weight change is one of the nine symptoms. Specific phobias (an anxiety disorder) and an excessively euphoric mood (mania) are not. asked 3 times A major depressive episode needs five or more of nine symptoms (depressed mood plus SIG E CAPS) over at least 2 weeks , most of the day, nearly every day, at least one being depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure. One week is the minimum for mania and four days for hypomania. asked 5 times Bipolar I disorder requires at least one manic episode (a week, or any duration if hospitalised); depressive episodes are common but not required, and subthreshold depressive periods are allowed. Bipolar II disorder requires at least one hypomanic and one major depressive episode and never a manic episode; it is not simply milder and needs no psychotic features. DSM-5-TR gives bipolar I a 12-month US prevalence of 1.5 percent and an equal sex ratio. asked 4 times A mood disorder in which a person swings from one mood extreme to the other , or has alternating episodes of mania and depression , is bipolar disorder (Leonhard's unipolar-bipolar split, 1957); unipolar means depression only, and "manic" and "depressive" name episodes. asked 2 times Mania versus hypomania : the same symptoms (three of seven DIG FAST, four if the mood is only irritable); mania lasts at least 1 week and brings marked impairment, hospitalisation or psychotic features ; hypomania lasts at least 4 consecutive days , is observable by others and has none of the three. Psychosis makes any elevated episode manic. asked 3 times Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DSM-5, 2013, after the rise in paediatric bipolar diagnoses): severe temper outbursts three or more times a week with persistently irritable mood between them, for 12 months, in two of three settings; onset before age 10 , first diagnosis between 6 and 18. A new onset at 12 rules DMDD out; bipolar disorder, conduct disorder and ADHD remain possible. asked 2 times Specifiers of a manic episode include with mixed features (three or more concurrent depressive symptoms), with psychotic features and with anxious distress. "With limited prosocial emotions" is a specifier of conduct disorder, not of any mood disorder. asked 2 times Lithium (John Cade, 1949) is the gold-standard mood stabiliser for both the treatment and the prophylaxis of bipolar disorder and the only one with a clear anti-suicidal effect; its therapeutic index is narrow (toxicity usually above about 1.5 mmol/L). Fluoxetine, haloperidol and lorazepam are not mood stabilisers. asked once Fluoxetine (an SSRI) is not a first-line treatment for acute mania and can trigger a switch into mania; the first-line drugs are lithium, valproate and the atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole). Haloperidol and lorazepam are adjuncts. asked once Suicide risk is highest when high lethality, a specific plan, frequent suicidal ideas and a family history converge. Hallucinations are not among the DIG FAST symptoms, social phobia is an anxiety disorder, and intense fear of weight gain is anorexia nervosa. asked once The mode (method) of a suicide attempt indicates its lethality , the medical danger of the act; intent is the wish to die and is judged from circumstances and statements, not from the method. asked once The "hybrid" disorder is mixed anxiety and depressive disorder : ICD-10 F41.2 and ICD-11 mixed depressive and anxiety disorder; it is absent from DSM-5-TR. asked once Cyclothymic disorder : at least 2 years (1 in children) of numerous hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet the criteria for a hypomanic, manic or major depressive episode, never symptom-free for more than 2 months (ICD-10 F34.0: persistent instability of mood). asked once What best distinguishes a primary psychotic disorder from a mood disorder with psychotic features is the mood congruence of the psychotic symptoms, together with their confinement to mood episodes; delusions occur in both. asked once The kindling hypothesis (Robert Post, 1992): each episode lowers the threshold for future episodes , so later episodes need less stress and come faster; it rests on Goddard's kindling of seizures in rats. asked once Anaclitic depression (1946), the withdrawal and decline of infants separated from their caregivers, and hospitalism (1945) were described by René Spitz , not Piaget, Skinner or Eysenck. asked once Seasonal affective disorder (Rosenthal and colleagues, 1984) is coded in DSM-5 as the "with seasonal pattern" specifier of recurrent major depressive disorder or of bipolar I or II disorder, not a separate disorder; it is treated with light therapy. asked once

Classifying the Anxiety Disorders : tell normal fear and anxiety apart from an anxiety disorder, trace the idea of neurosis from Cullen to DSM-5, and compare how DSM-5-TR, ICD-10 and ICD-11 group these disorders and time their symptoms. 6.2 Panic Attacks, Panic Disorder and Agoraphobia : recognise a panic attack and its thirteen symptoms, and diagnose panic disorder and agoraphobia and tell each from its look-alikes. 6.3 Specific Phobia, Social Anxiety Disorder and the Names of the Phobias : describe the five types of specific phobia and the fear of scrutiny in social anxiety disorder, with their course, and decode the Greek names of the phobias. 6.4 Generalised Anxiety Disorder, Separation Anxiety Disorder and Selective Mutism : distinguish the excessive, uncontrollable worry of generalised anxiety disorder from normal worry, and diagnose the two anxiety disorders that usually begin in childhood. 6.5 Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: The Clinical Picture : define obsessions and Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviours : describe body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania and excoriation disorder, and explain why DSM-5 and ICD-11 group them with OCD. 6.7 The Biology of Anxiety and Obsessions : evaluate the genetic, temperamental, neurochemical and brain-circuit evidence on the anxiety disorders and OCD, including Klein's suffocation false alarm theory and In the first days of January 1908, in Vienna, a little boy of four and three-quarters began to be afraid of the street. On 7 January he set off as usual with his nursemaid for the Stadtpark, the city park, and on the way he started to cry and begged to be taken home. The next day his mother took him herself to the gardens of Schönbrunn, where he loved to go. He cried, did not want to leave the house, and was plainly frightened the whole way. On the way back, after much internal struggling, he told her what was wrong: "I was afraid a horse would bite me." That evening he wept again and said, "The horse will come into the room." In the Vienna of 1908 there was no escaping horses. They pulled the buses, the carts and the heavily loaded furniture vans, and the boy, whom the world knows as Little Hans, was most frightened of the bus horses and of horses straining at heavy loads, which he thought might fall down. At its worst he would go no further than the front door of the house. He called his fear "the nonsense". His father, the music critic Max Graf, and his mother were both among the closest followers of Sigmund Freud, and since before Hans turned three the father had been noting down the boy's sayings for Freud. Now he recorded everything Hans said, did and dreamed about horses, and posted the reports to Freud. When Hans noticed him writing and asked why, his father explained that it was going to a Professor who could take away the nonsense. Freud guided the treatment through the father and saw the boy as a patient only once, for a short consultation in his rooms on the afternoon of 30 March 1908. Hearing that Hans was especially bothered by the things horses wear in front of their eyes and by the black round their mouths, Freud asked him, half in jest, whether his horses wore spectacles, whether his father did (the boy said no, against all the evidence), and whether the black round the mouth might be a moustache. Freud had seen in the horse a disguised father. On the way home Hans asked, "Does the Professor talk to God, as he can tell all that beforehand?" Yet Hans had also told his father something much simpler. Out shopping with his mother one day, he had watched a horse pulling a bus fall down in the street and lie there kicking, and he had been terribly frightened. "That was when I got the nonsense," he said, and his mother confirmed that the fear had broken out straight afterwards. Freud published the case in 1909 as "Analysis of a Phobia in a Five-Year-Old Boy". In the same year he published a second famous case, a young man tormented by obsessional fears, known as the Rat Man, whom you will meet in Section 6.8. Half a century later Little Hans became a battleground. In 1960 the behaviour therapists Joseph Wolpe and Stanley Rachman argued that nothing in the father's notes required a hidden fear of the father: a small child had watched a horse collapse in front of him, and the fear of horses that followed was a conditioned fear (Book 2, Section 4.1.3). And the boy himself? In the spring of 1922 a young man introduced himself to Freud as Little Hans, now "a strapping youth of nineteen". He said that he was perfectly well and suffered from no troubles or inhibitions; his parents had divorced and each had married again. When he had read his own case history, he told Freud, it all seemed strange to him: he did not recognise himself and could remember nothing of it. He was Herbert Graf (1903 to 1973), who grew up to become an opera director, for many years at the Metropolitan Opera in New York. Notice how many stories one small boy's fear can tell. For Freud it was a story of unconscious conflict, a forbidden feeling disguised as a horse. For Wolpe and Rachman it was a story of learning, a single terrifying event that left a lasting fear. A clinician today would add a third story: a child with an anxious temperament and a sensitive alarm system, ready to fire at the first real fright. This chapter asks which of these stories fits which disorder: the panic that strikes out of nowhere, the phobia of one thing, the worry about everything, and the obsessions that drive a person to wash until the skin cracks. Remember Hans; you will return to him at the end of the chapter. 6.1 Fear, Anxiety and the Neuroses: Classifying the Anxiety Disorders Lower yield · not asked yet Sit in an examination hall in the ten minutes before the papers are handed out and you can watch anxiety at work: the jiggling knees, the dry mouths, the third trip to the water cooler. Nobody in that hall has a mental disorder because their heart is racing. Yet a few of the people in it will one day sit in a clinician's room because of anxiety: the student who cannot make herself enter the hall at all, the one who has lain awake every night for a year worrying about everything from his marks to his father's blood pressure, the one who panicked once on a crowded bus and has not boarded a bus since. Three questions run through this section and through the whole chapter. What exactly are fear and anxiety? When do they stop being useful and become a disorder? And once they are a disorder, which disorder is it? The answer to the last question has changed several times in two and a half centuries, and that history explains why the disorders of this chapter are grouped as they are today. Fear and anxiety: one alarm, two time frames In everyday speech the two words are used almost interchangeably, but DSM-5-TR draws a clear line between them. It defines fear as the emotional response to real or perceived imminent threat, and anxiety as the anticipation of future threat. Imagine walking down a lane in your neighbourhood when a large dog breaks its chain and runs at you, barking. Your heart pounds, your breathing quickens, blood floods your muscles, and within a second you are running or reaching for a stone. That is fear: in DSM-5-TR's words, a surge of autonomic arousal of the kind needed for fight or flight, thoughts of immediate danger ("it will bite me") and escape behaviour. Now imagine the next morning, as you approach the same lane. No dog is in sight. Yet your shoulders are tight, you scan every gate, you listen for barking, and you think about taking the longer road round. That is anxiety: muscle tension and vigilance in preparation for a danger that has not yet arrived, and cautious or avoidant behaviour. Fear says "danger now"; anxiety says "danger might come". David H. Barlow , whose research and textbook you will meet again and again in this chapter, makes the same distinction in his own words: anxiety is a negative mood state marked by bodily tension and apprehension about the future, whereas fear is an immediate alarm reaction to danger. ICD-11 uses almost the same contrast: fear "represents a reaction to perceived imminent threat in the present", while anxiety "is more future-oriented, referring to perceived anticipated threat". The two states overlap, of course; the anxious walker will be flooded with fear if a gate creaks open. And DSM-5-TR adds a point that matters clinically: the level of fear or anxiety is sometimes reduced by pervasive avoidance. A man who never goes near the lane may report very little fear at all, because the avoidance has done its work. An absence of felt fear is not proof that there is no disorder; sometimes the avoidance is the symptom. The physiology of fear, the emergency reaction that Walter Cannon called fight or flight, and the brain's routes to it are taught in Book 1 (Sections 11.6.1 and 11.8.2); here you need only its shape. Fear is fast, intense and tied to something present. Anxiety is slower, more diffuse and tied to something expected. One particular kind of fear response needs a name of its own, because it turns up in almost every disorder of this chapter: the panic attack, an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that reaches its peak within minutes. Barlow describes it as a false alarm, the full fight-or-flight reaction firing when there is nothing to fight and nothing to flee. Section 6.2 takes it apart symptom by symptom. Neither emotion is a disease. Fear keeps you alive, and anxiety keeps you prepared. Howard Liddell (1949) called anxiety "the shadow of intelligence": the price a species pays for being able to plan for a future in which things might go wrong. Moderate anxiety improves performance; too little leaves you careless, and too much leaves you paralysed. That inverted-U relation between arousal and performance is the Yerkes-Dodson law (Robert Yerkes and John Dodson, 1908), taught with its own exam trap in Book 1, Section 10.3.5. Every clinician meets both ends of the curve: the student who barely studied because she felt no anxiety at all, and the student who knew every answer but could not read the questions because his hands were shaking. Exam trap Fear is the response to real or perceived imminent threat (autonomic surge, thoughts of immediate danger, escape). Anxiety is the anticipation of future threat (muscle tension, vigilance, cautious avoidance). A panic attack is a kind of fear response that occurs at the wrong time. Two distractors to reject: "fear is irrational and anxiety rational" (either can be proportionate or excessive), and "anxiety always has a definite object" (anxiety is often objectless, as in the free-floating anxiety of generalised anxiety disorder, Section 6.4). When anxiety becomes a disorder Fear and anxiety also follow a normal developmental timetable. Around the first birthday most infants show stranger anxiety , wariness and distress at unfamiliar faces, and protest when a parent leaves the room; DSM-5-TR notes that heightened separation anxiety at this age is part of normal development and may signal that a secure attachment is forming. Many young children then pass through phases of fearing the dark, imaginary creatures or animals, and most of these fears fade on their own as the child faces them and grows. (The development of attachment and of children's fears belongs to the Developmental book.) A clinician therefore needs rules for deciding when anxiety has stopped being ordinary. DSM-5-TR gives four tests and two exclusions, and each exists for a reason, so learn the reason with the rule. It is excessive or out of proportion. The fear or anxiety is out of proportion to the actual threat and to the person's sociocultural context. Who decides? The clinician, not the patient, because, as DSM-5-TR puts it, people with anxiety disorders typically overestimate the danger in the situations they fear or avoid. The clinician must also take culture into account: DSM-5-TR's own examples are that a fear of the dark may be reasonable where there is ongoing violence, and that the point at which a fear of insects becomes disproportionate is different where insects are part of the diet. It persists beyond the developmentally appropriate age. A two-year-old who screams when her mother leaves is behaving normally; a ten-year-old who cannot sleep unless his mother is in the room and vomits every school morning is not. It is persistent. The disorders typically last 6 months or more, and this rule separates them from transient fear or anxiety, which is often brought on by stress and passes when the stress does. DSM-5-TR calls the duration "a general guide with allowance for some degree of flexibility", and it is shorter in children for two disorders: 4 weeks for separation anxiety disorder and 1 month for selective mutism. Panic disorder has its own 1-month rule (Section 6.2). It causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning, the "distress" and "dysfunction" of the four Ds (Book 2, Section 1.6.5). The two exclusions apply to every anxiety disorder. The symptoms must not be attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or medication or to another medical condition (the last subsection of this section explains what is diagnosed instead), and they must not be better explained by another mental disorder (each section of this chapter has its own list of look-alikes). Push a case through the tests and they come alive. Ritu, aged 21, is in the final year of a BSc in Pune. In the month before her university examinations she sleeps badly, her stomach churns every morning and she cannot stop picturing what will happen if she fails. Her mother wonders whether she needs a psychiatrist. Does Ritu have an anxiety disorder? Her anxiety is proportionate to a real event that matters to her; it is developmentally ordinary for a student; it began with the examination timetable, and she tells you that last year it disappeared within days of the final paper; and although it is unpleasant, it has made her study more, not less. She fails every test. Now change the facts. Suppose the worry began two years ago and has continued through holidays and good results alike; it ranges from her marks to her father's health to whether the house will be burgled; and she is now too tired and tense to attend half her lectures. The anxiety is out of proportion, persistent and impairing, and Section 6.4 will tell you what to call it. Exam trap Whether a fear is excessive is judged by the clinician , taking cultural context into account, because sufferers overestimate danger. The "6 months" is typical , a general guide, and it is shorter for separation anxiety disorder in the young (4 weeks) and for selective mutism (1 month). Transient, stress-induced anxiety (before an examination, after a quarrel) is not a disorder, however intense it feels. The neuroses, from Cullen to Freud Until 1980 most of the disorders in this chapter shared a different family name: they were neuroses. The word is much older than psychoanalysis, and examiners like to ask who coined it. It was the Scottish physician William Cullen (1710 to 1790), who taught medicine at Glasgow and then Edinburgh. In 1769, in his Synopsis Nosologiae Methodicae (a methodical classification of diseases), Cullen set up a whole class of neurosis (plural neuroses), and in his later textbook, First Lines of the Practice of Physic , he defined it as "all those preternatural affections of sense or motion" that occur without fever as part of the primary disease and that depend not on a local disease of some organ but on "a more general affection of the nervous system". (Sources differ slightly on the date, because Cullen refined the class in later editions and in First Lines ; 1769 is the date usually given for the coinage.) Cullen's neuroses were a huge and mixed class. He divided them into four orders: comata (losses of voluntary movement and of the senses, such as apoplexy and palsy), adynamiae (failures of the vital functions, such as fainting), spasmi (spasms and convulsions without fever) and vesaniae (disorders of judgement, that is, insanity). At first, then, a neurosis was simply a disease of the nerves. Over the following century the class shrank. Each time physicians found a lesion behind one of the "nervous" diseases, that disease passed to neurology or general medicine, and the word neurosis was left with the conditions for which no bodily cause could be found: hysteria, hypochondria, nervous exhaustion, the obsessions and the phobias. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) narrowed the word again and gave it a theory. For Freud a neurosis was a disorder that arose from unconscious conflict, from the anxiety that the conflict produced and from the defences the ego raised against that anxiety. The neurotic patient suffered, sometimes terribly, but kept contact with reality and knew that something was wrong; that is what separated neurosis from psychosis. In January 1895 Freud published a paper with a magnificent title, "On the Grounds for Detaching a Particular Syndrome from Neurasthenia under the Description 'Anxiety Neurosis'". Neurasthenia, "nervous exhaustion", was then the fashionable diagnosis for almost any vague nervous complaint (it is taught in Chapter 7). Freud argued that one group of these patients had something different, an anxiety neurosis , and his description reads like a first draft of two modern disorders. Its "nuclear symptom", he wrote, was anxious expectation : a quantity of anxiety present in a "freely floating" state ( frei flottierend ), ready to attach itself to any idea that came along. That is the ancestor of the free-floating worry of generalised anxiety disorder. But the anxiety could also break into consciousness suddenly, without any train of thought to call it up, as an anxiety attack: palpitations, breathlessness, sweating and the conviction of dying, of a stroke or of going mad, and sometimes only "rudimentary" attacks with one or two of these features. That is the ancestor of the panic attack and of the limited-symptom attack. Freud's theories of where anxiety comes from are taught in Section 6.8; here notice only that the clinical picture was described more than a century ago. Fourteen years later, in the case of Little Hans, Freud gave the phobias a psychoanalytic name of their own. For phobias like Hans's, which he believed were the commonest of all the psychoneuroses and the neuroses of childhood above all, he proposed the term anxiety hysteria : a hysteria whose symptom is anxiety rather than a bodily "conversion" symptom such as a paralysis. The name has outlived the theory in one odd corner. ICD-10 still lists "anxiety hysteria" as an inclusion term under F41.8, other specified anxiety disorders. By the middle of the twentieth century psychiatry divided the mental disorders that had no known organic cause into two great classes, the neuroses and the psychoses, and the line between them was drawn by insight and by contact with reality. The second edition of the American manual, DSM-II (1968), put the idea in a few sentences: anxiety is "the chief characteristic of the neuroses"; the neuroses, unlike the psychoses, show "neither gross distortion or misinterpretation of external reality, nor gross personality disorganization"; and neurotic patients, "however severely handicapped by their symptoms", are not classed as psychotic "because they are aware that their mental functioning is disturbed". Table 6.1 sets out the old contrast. You will still hear clinicians say "neurotic" and "psychotic" in this sense, and Indian examination notes still list the features of neurosis, so the table is worth knowing even though neither manual now uses neurosis as a diagnosis. In the neurosis, insight and reality testing are preserved; that is what made it "not psychotic". From DSM-I to DSM-5-TR: how the anxiety disorders took shape The first American manual, DSM-I (1952), borrowed Adolf Meyer's language of "reactions" (Book 2, Section 2.10.3) and grouped the neuroses as "psychoneurotic disorders": anxiety reaction, dissociative reaction, conversion reaction, phobic reaction, obsessive compulsive reaction and depressive reaction. DSM-II (1968) renamed them "neuroses": anxiety neurosis, hysterical neurosis (with conversion and dissociative types), phobic neurosis, obsessive compulsive neurosis, depressive neurosis, neurasthenic neurosis, depersonalization neurosis and hypochondriacal neurosis. Notice that the list mixes the disorders of this chapter with disorders that now live in Chapters 5 and 7. That mixture was held together by a theory, not by a shared clinical picture. Then came the break. DSM-III (1980), produced under Robert L. Spitzer (1932 to 2015), tried to describe disorders by what could be observed and reported rather than by their presumed causes. The term neurosis was dropped, for two reasons that Barlow gives: it implied a specific but unproven psychoanalytic cause, and it was too vague, applying to almost every non-psychotic disorder. The phobias, instead of being classed under the broad heading of neurosis, were given their own place inside a new, broader group, the anxiety disorders . The old anxiety neurosis was split into two disorders, panic disorder and generalised anxiety disorder (Section 6.2 tells how a drug helped to split them). The old phobic neurosis was divided into agoraphobia (with or without panic attacks), social phobia and simple phobia. Obsessive-compulsive disorder joined the group, and so did a new diagnosis, post-traumatic stress disorder. The rest of the old neuroses were scattered: hysterical neurosis went to the somatoform and dissociative disorders, and depressive neurosis became dysthymic disorder among the mood disorders. DSM-III-R (1987) and DSM-IV (1994) revised the criteria but kept the shape. OCD and PTSD remained anxiety disorders, and DSM-IV added acute stress disorder, PTSD-like symptoms in the first month after a trauma, to the same group. Several disorders that belong to this chapter today lived elsewhere: separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism among the disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence, body dysmorphic disorder among the somatoform disorders, and trichotillomania among the impulse-control disorders. DSM-III-R had also folded most agoraphobia into panic disorder, as "panic disorder with agoraphobia", and DSM-IV kept that arrangement. DSM-5 (2013) broke the group into three neighbouring chapters (Figure 6.2). The first kept the name anxiety disorders . The second, the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders , gathered OCD with body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania and two new diagnoses, hoarding disorder and excoriation (skin-picking) disorder. DSM-5-TR explains the move by "the increasing evidence of these disorders' relatedness to one another in terms of a range of diagnostic validators" and by the clinical usefulness of grouping them. In plain terms, these disorders share repetitive thoughts and driven repetitive behaviours, and they overlap in family history, brain circuitry, course and response to treatment (Sections 6.7 and 6.9). OCD, for example, improves with serotonergic antidepressants and with exposure and response prevention but not with the benzodiazepines that calm many anxious patients. The manual still placed the new chapter immediately after the anxiety disorders, to signal that OCD remains a close neighbour. The third chapter, the trauma- and stressor-related disorders , took PTSD and acute stress disorder (with the adjustment disorders), because these diagnoses require an identifiable stressful event and because anxiety is only one of several responses to trauma, alongside anger, guilt, shame, numbing and dissociation (Chapter 7). Two disorders moved in. Separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism left the childhood section and became anxiety disorders, and DSM-5 made it explicit that separation anxiety disorder can begin in adulthood. Agoraphobia was unhitched from panic disorder and became an independent diagnosis, so that a person who meets both sets of criteria receives both (Section 6.2). And the panic attack became a specifier that can be attached to any disorder ("social anxiety disorder, with panic attacks"; "major depressive disorder, with panic attacks"). DSM-5-TR (2022) kept this arrangement, and with it DSM-5's developmental ordering of the anxiety chapter by typical age at onset: separation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, agoraphobia and generalised anxiety disorder, followed by substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder, anxiety disorder due to another medical condition, and the other specified and unspecified categories. Exam trap In DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR, OCD is not an anxiety disorder : it heads the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. PTSD and acute stress disorder are not anxiety disorders : they are trauma- and stressor-related. Body dysmorphic disorder is an obsessive-compulsive and related disorder, not a somatic symptom, anxiety or personality disorder. Separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism are anxiety disorders , not childhood or communication disorders. A phobia is an anxiety disorder, not a mild stress reaction, a personality disorder or a passing hallucination. And it was DSM-III (1980) , not DSM-5, that dropped the term neurosis. The anxiety disorders at a glance With the history behind you, the modern map is easy to read. DSM-5-TR observes that the anxiety disorders tend to be "highly comorbid with each other", yet they "can be differentiated by close examination of the types of situations that are feared or avoided and the content of the associated thoughts or beliefs". That sentence holds the most useful diagnostic habit in this chapter: ask what the person fears, and what they think will happen. The child who clings at the school gate fears that something terrible will happen to her mother while they are apart. The student who freezes in his viva fears that the examiners will see him tremble and think him a fool. The woman who will not take the metro fears that she will panic and be unable to get out. The man who has worried for years about money, his children's safety and his own health has no single focus at all. Specific phobia is the one exception, and DSM-5-TR says so: in specific phobia "a specific cognition is not featured"; the fear attaches to the dog, the needle or the height itself. Six months is the usual rule, but it is not universal, and the exceptions have reasons. Children's lives change quickly, and a month of refusing school or of silence in the classroom is already costly, so the two childhood disorders run on shorter clocks; the selective mutism rule also excludes the first month of school, when many shy children are briefly silent in a strange new room. Panic disorder is defined not by how long the attacks have gone on but by what they do to the person afterwards: a month or more of worry, or of changed behaviour, after at least one attack. Exam trap Learn the clocks as a set. GAD : more days than not for at least 6 months in adults, not 1, 3 or 12 months. Specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia : typically 6 months , not 1 week, 1 month or 3 months. Panic disorder : 1 month of persistent worry or maladaptive behaviour change after at least one attack. Separation anxiety disorder : 4 weeks in children and adolescents, typically 6 months in adults. Selective mutism : 1 month , not limited to the first month of school. "Typically 6 months" applies to separation anxiety disorder only in adults. The same disorders in ICD-10 and ICD-11 The World Health Organization's classifications tell the same story with a different ending. ICD-10, approved by the World Health Assembly in 1990 and published with its clinical descriptions and diagnostic guidelines for mental disorders in 1992, never gave up the neurotic umbrella. Its block F40 to F48 is called neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders , and its contents are, more or less, everything that was once a neurosis: F40, phobic anxiety disorders , in which anxiety is evoked only, or mainly, in well-defined situations that are not currently dangerous: F40.0 agoraphobia (F40.00 without and F40.01 with panic disorder), F40.1 social phobias and F40.2 specific (isolated) phobias. F41, other anxiety disorders , in which the anxiety is not restricted to any particular situation: F41.0 panic disorder, subtitled "episodic paroxysmal anxiety"; F41.1 generalised anxiety disorder; F41.2 mixed anxiety and depressive disorder (Chapter 5); F41.3 other mixed anxiety disorders; and F41.8 other specified anxiety disorders, which still includes "anxiety hysteria". F42, obsessive-compulsive disorder , with subtypes for predominantly obsessional thoughts or ruminations (F42.0), predominantly compulsive acts (F42.1) and mixed obsessional thoughts and acts (F42.2). F43, reaction to severe stress, and adjustment disorders (acute stress reaction, PTSD and the adjustment disorders) and F44, dissociative [conversion] disorders , both taught in Chapter 7. F45, somatoform disorders , including hypochondriacal disorder (F45.2), under which ICD-10 also files non-delusional dysmorphophobia and nosophobia, the fear of having a disease (Chapter 7 and Section 6.6). F48, other neurotic disorders : neurasthenia (F48.0), depersonalisation-derealisation syndrome (F48.1) and other specified neurotic disorders (F48.8), whose inclusion list names psychasthenia and Dhat syndrome (Chapters 1 and 7). There are no codes F46 or F47; the block simply stops at F48. ICD-10 also settles the relationship between phobia and panic the opposite way round from DSM-IV. "A panic attack occurring in an established phobic situation is regarded as an expression of the severity of the phobia, which should be given diagnostic precedence", and panic disorder is to be the main diagnosis "only in the absence of any of the phobias listed in F40". A woman with agoraphobia who also has panic attacks therefore receives F40.01, agoraphobia with panic disorder, rather than a panic disorder code. ICD-10 adds a second hierarchy: panic disorder should not be the main diagnosis if the person had a depressive disorder when the attacks began, because the attacks are then probably secondary to the depression. The ICD-10 codes also solve a small puzzle in DSM-5-TR. The American manual prints an ICD-10-CM code (the United States' version of ICD-10) beside every diagnosis, and some of these codes betray where a disorder used to live. Separation anxiety disorder carries F93.0, from ICD-10's "emotional disorders with onset specific to childhood". Selective mutism carries F94.0, from the "disorders of social functioning with onset specific to childhood and adolescence", where ICD-10 called it elective mutism. Body dysmorphic disorder carries F45.22, a somatoform code, and trichotillomania F63.3, from ICD-10's "habit and impulse disorders"; Section 6.6 explains both moves. ICD-11, adopted by the World Health Assembly in May 2019 and in effect from 1 January 2022, finally abandoned the neurotic block. Its chapter on mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders contains a grouping of anxiety or fear-related disorders (codes 6B00 to 6B0Z): generalised anxiety disorder (6B00), panic disorder (6B01), agoraphobia (6B02), specific phobia (6B03), social anxiety disorder (6B04), separation anxiety disorder (6B05) and selective mutism (6B06), with other specified (6B0Y) and unspecified (6B0Z) categories. Like DSM-5, ICD-11 moved separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism out of the childhood section and into this grouping. Its definition echoes DSM-5-TR: fear is a reaction to perceived imminent threat in the present, anxiety is more future-oriented, and "a key differentiating feature" among these disorders is their "disorder-specific foci of apprehension". Like DSM-5, too, ICD-11 gives OCD a grouping of its own, the obsessive-compulsive or related disorders (6B20 to 6B2Z), whose membership differs from DSM's in ways that Section 6.6 explains, and it places PTSD among the "disorders specifically associated with stress" (Chapter 7). Anxiety caused by a drug is coded with the drug in the substance section (alcohol-induced anxiety disorder, for example, is 6C40.71), and anxiety caused directly by a medical illness is called secondary anxiety syndrome (6E63). Where the systems still differ is in their clocks. DSM-5-TR counts: 6 months, three of six symptoms, two of five situations. ICD-11 prefers clinical description and flexible language. For generalised anxiety disorder it asks for marked symptoms of anxiety that "persist for at least several months, for more days than not", with no fixed minimum number of accompanying symptoms. ICD-10's guidelines had been looser still, asking for anxiety on most days "for at least several weeks at a time, and usually several months" (Section 6.4 compares the three). So a contamination-washing patient is diagnosed with OCD in every system, never with GAD, illness anxiety or specific phobia, whatever chapter OCD sits in. ICD-11 asks for GAD symptoms over "at least several months" , not a fixed 6 months; one practice key's explanation says ICD-11 "also uses 6 months", which is wrong. The 6-month rule is DSM-5-TR's. And in ICD-10 a phobia takes precedence over panic : panic disorder with agoraphobia is coded as agoraphobia (F40.01). Who develops anxiety disorders? Taken together, the anxiety disorders are among the commonest of all mental disorders, and three facts hold across the group. First, as DSM-5-TR puts it, many of them develop in childhood and tend to persist if not treated; the anxious child is very often the anxious adult who finally asks for help twenty years later. Second, most occur more often in girls and women than in boys and men, at a ratio of roughly two to one. Third, they rarely come alone: comorbidity , the presence of two or more disorders in the same person, is the rule in this chapter rather than the exception. Key study: how often anxiety travels in company (Brown and colleagues, 2001) Timothy A. Brown , Barlow and their colleagues asked a simple question: when a patient arrives at a specialist clinic with one anxiety or mood disorder, how often does he or she have another? They interviewed 1,127 patients at one of Barlow's centres with a semistructured diagnostic interview, using DSM-IV criteria. Of the patients whose principal diagnosis was an anxiety or depressive disorder, 55 percent had at least one additional anxiety or depressive disorder at the time of assessment; counting any time in their lives, the figure rose to 76 percent. By far the commonest additional diagnosis was major depression, which 50 percent had had at some point. Later work showed why this matters: an additional diagnosis of depression or of alcohol or drug abuse makes recovery from an anxiety disorder less likely and relapse more likely (Bruce and colleagues, 2005). The study's limit is its sample: people with several problems are more likely to seek specialist treatment, so a clinic may overstate how often disorders co-occur in the community. Even so, the conclusion has shaped treatment: the "pure" case of a single anxiety disorder is the exception, which is one reason Barlow's group later built a single unified protocol for the emotional disorders (Book 2, Section 5.6.7). Anxiety also keeps company with physical illness. In an important population study, Jitender Sareen and colleagues (2006) found that having any anxiety disorder was uniquely and significantly associated with thyroid disease, respiratory disease, gastrointestinal disease, arthritis, migraine headaches and allergic conditions. The anxiety disorder usually began before the physical disorder, which suggests, without proving, that something about being anxious may contribute to the physical illness; and people with both had more disability and a poorer quality of life than people with the physical disorder alone. DSM-5-TR similarly notes raised rates of anxiety disorders among people with asthma, hypertension, ulcers and arthritis. The link runs in the other direction too, as the last subsection of this section shows: some illnesses produce anxiety directly. Finally, anxiety is not a "minor" problem when it comes to suicide. DSM-5-TR states that people with anxiety may be more likely to have suicidal thoughts, to attempt suicide and to die by suicide than people without anxiety, and it names panic disorder, generalised anxiety disorder and specific phobia as the anxiety disorders most strongly associated with the step from suicidal thoughts to a suicide attempt. A clinician who asks about suicide only in depressed patients will miss some of the people most at risk. Indian context The National Mental Health Survey of India (2015 to 2016) diagnosed its 34,802 adults by ICD-10 criteria, so its anxiety figures are reported under the F40 to F48 heading. The neurotic and stress-related disorders were among the three commonest groups of mental disorder, with substance use and mood disorders, and about 3.5 percent of adults had one at the time of the survey; more than eight in ten of them were receiving no treatment (Book 2, Section 1.10.11). Notice that the survey's heading still carries the word "neurotic": in India you will meet the ICD-10 vocabulary in hospital records, research papers and examination questions for years to come. Many of those untreated people are not hidden; they are sitting in the waiting rooms of general physicians. Shalini, a 38-year-old schoolteacher in Lucknow, has seen four doctors in a year. She describes attacks of thumping in the chest, a burning in the stomach and a heaviness in the head, and she sleeps badly. She has had two ECGs and an echocardiogram, all normal; she takes antacids for "gas" and a tonic for "weakness". Each doctor has told her that her heart is fine, and each reassurance has helped for about a week. Nobody has asked her what goes through her mind during the attacks, or what she has stopped doing because of them. When a clinical psychologist finally asks, the story changes. She lies awake worrying about her son's safety on his motorbike, her husband's job and her own health; she dreads the next attack; and she has stopped going to the market alone in case one strikes there. In Indian primary care anxiety very often arrives like this, described in the language of the body, and many patients expect, and receive, a tonic or an injection rather than a question about worry. The clinician's task is not to dismiss the bodily complaint but to complete the picture: first make sure that the physical causes described next have been considered, then ask about the worry, the attacks and the avoidance. (Shalini's story hints at more than one diagnosis; Sections 6.2 and 6.4 will show you how to sort them out.) Anxiety caused by a substance or an illness, and the leftover categories Before any anxiety disorder in this chapter can be diagnosed, the clinician must ask whether the anxiety is the direct physiological effect of something else: a drug, a medicine, a toxin or a medical illness. If it is, the diagnosis changes, and so does the treatment, because the cure for anxiety caused by an overactive thyroid gland is to treat the thyroid. The diagnosis of substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder is made when panic attacks or anxiety dominate the clinical picture and the history, examination or laboratory findings show both that the symptoms developed during or soon after intoxication with, or withdrawal from, a substance, or after exposure to or withdrawal from a medication, and that the substance is capable of producing them. The symptoms must not be better explained by an independent anxiety disorder, and DSM-5-TR says what would suggest one: anxiety that began before the substance use, anxiety that persists for a substantial period (about 1 month) after acute withdrawal or severe intoxication has ended, or a history of anxiety episodes unrelated to substances. The disturbance must not occur only during a delirium, and it must cause distress or impairment. There is one more condition, and it is the one most often forgotten: this diagnosis is made instead of a diagnosis of intoxication or withdrawal only when the anxiety is predominant and severe enough to need clinical attention in its own right. Shakiness and dread on the second morning without alcohol are usually just part of alcohol withdrawal. The specifiers say when it began: with onset during intoxication, with onset during withdrawal, or with onset after medication use. The name of the disorder begins with the substance, so a clinician records, for example, "caffeine-induced anxiety disorder, with onset during intoxication" or "salbutamol-induced anxiety disorder, with onset after medication use". In the general population it seems rare (DSM-5-TR estimates a 12-month prevalence of about 0.002 percent in the United States), but it is far commoner in clinics. The substances themselves are taught in Chapter 10. A diagnosis of anxiety disorder due to another medical condition (F06.4) is made when panic or anxiety is predominant and there is evidence from the history, examination or laboratory findings that it is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical illness; the illness is named in the diagnosis ("anxiety disorder due to phaeochromocytoma"). DSM-5-TR asks the clinician to weigh three things: a clear time relationship between the onset, worsening or remission of the illness and the anxiety; features that are atypical of an independent anxiety disorder, such as an unusual age at onset or course; and evidence in the literature that the illness can cause anxiety through a known physiological mechanism, as hyperthyroidism does. The anxiety must not be better explained by another mental disorder, above all by adjustment disorder with anxiety , in which the stressor is the illness itself and the person is distressed by its meaning or consequences (Chapter 7). DSM-5-TR gives a useful contrast: in anxiety caused by an illness there is often a prominent physical component, such as shortness of breath, whereas in adjustment disorder the anxiety concerns what the illness means. Nor is it illness anxiety disorder, in which the person worries about having an illness that is not causing the anxiety physiologically (Chapter 7). The course of the anxiety follows the course of the illness. Table 6.4 lists the physical causes DSM-5-TR names. He is 46, a bank cashier in Hyderabad, and has always been the calm one in his family; no one in his family has had an anxiety disorder. Over two months he has become constantly nervous and irritable. His heart races, his hands shake so much that he fumbles the notes he counts, he sweats in air-conditioned rooms, he sleeps badly and, although he is eating more than usual, he has lost five kilograms. He is ashamed, convinced that he is "losing his nerve". Is this generalised anxiety disorder? His physician orders thyroid function tests, which show hyperthyroidism. If the anxiety is prominent enough to need attention in its own right, the diagnosis is anxiety disorder due to hyperthyroidism, and it settles as the thyroid is treated. Change one fact and the diagnosis changes with it. Had the symptoms begun in the week Imran started drinking six tumblers of strong filter coffee a day to get through the annual audit, the diagnosis would be caffeine-induced anxiety disorder; had they begun when he started an inhaler for asthma, it would be medication-induced. Clinical link Clues that anxiety may have a physical cause, from DSM-5-TR: onset at an atypical age (panic attacks beginning after about 45 should raise the question), atypical symptoms (during a "panic attack", vertigo, loss of consciousness, loss of bladder or bowel control, slurred speech or amnesia), no personal or family history of anxiety disorders, and a clear time link with an illness, a new medicine, or a change in the use of a substance. In practice, ask every new anxious patient about tea, coffee, colas and energy drinks, tobacco, alcohol and sedatives (and when the last dose was), cough and cold remedies, asthma inhalers, thyroid tablets and steroids, and check that a physician has examined them. A clinical psychologist does not order the thyroid test, but she should notice when one is needed and refer. The opposite error matters too: anxiety disorders can themselves raise the risk of heart disease, and when an anxious patient has a heart attack, the anxiety disorder is not reclassified as "due to" the heart disease. Two leftover categories complete the chapter's list. The first, other specified anxiety disorder (F41.8), is used when symptoms characteristic of an anxiety disorder predominate and cause distress or impairment but do not meet the full criteria for any anxiety disorder (or for adjustment disorder with anxiety), and the clinician chooses to record why. DSM-5-TR's examples are limited-symptom attacks (panic-like attacks with fewer than four symptoms, Section 6.2); generalised anxiety occurring less often than "more days than not"; khyâl cap, the "wind attacks" described among Cambodians; and ataque de nervios, the "attack of nerves" described among Latin Americans (both cultural concepts are explained in Chapter 1). The second, unspecified anxiety disorder (F41.9), is used when the clinician chooses not to say why the criteria are not met, including when there is too little information for a more specific diagnosis, as in an emergency department. Exam trap Anxiety from caffeine, a decongestant, a bronchodilator or alcohol withdrawal is substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder , but only when the anxiety predominates and needs attention in its own right; otherwise the diagnosis is simply intoxication or withdrawal. Anxiety that is the direct physiological effect of an illness (hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, hypoglycaemia) is anxiety disorder due to another medical condition . Distress about the meaning of an illness (a new diagnosis of cancer) is adjustment disorder with anxiety ; worry about having an illness that one does not have is illness anxiety disorder . Anxiety that persists for about a month after intoxication or withdrawal ends points to an independent anxiety disorder. And panic attacks caused by hyperthyroidism do not make panic disorder: Criterion C of panic disorder excludes them (Section 6.2). Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks.
