Answers: (1) fear, (2) clinician, (3) William Cullen, (4) neurasthenia, (5) DSM-III, (6) trauma- and stressor-related, (7) 4 weeks, (8) neurotic, (9) several months, (10) another medical condition. 6.2 Panic Attacks, Panic Disorder and Agoraphobia Medium yield · 5 Qs Section 6.1 drew a line between fear, the alarm that fires when danger is here now, and anxiety, the apprehension that looks towards a danger that might come. This section is about what happens when the alarm fires and there is no danger at all. The result, a panic attack, is one of the most frightening experiences a healthy body can produce, and the people who have one almost never think of it as a psychological event. They think they are dying. So they go to a hospital, and the first professional they meet is usually a cardiologist or an emergency physician, not a psychologist. We begin with one such person, take the panic attack apart symptom by symptom, and then follow the two disorders that can grow out of repeated attacks: panic disorder, which is a fear of the attacks themselves, and agoraphobia, which is a fear of being caught by them in a place with no way out. The anatomy of a panic attack Deepak was twenty-nine, a software engineer in Bengaluru, and by his own account a calm person. On a Sunday night, a week after his team had shipped a difficult release, he was lying on the sofa watching a film with his wife. Without warning his heart began to pound so hard that he could see his shirt move. Within a minute or two he could not get a full breath; his chest felt tight, his hands and lips tingled, and he was soaked in sweat although the fan was on. The room looked strangely flat and distant, "like a television screen". He was certain he was having a heart attack. "Call an ambulance," he told his wife, "I am going to die." By the time they reached the emergency department of a private hospital, perhaps twenty-five minutes later, the worst was over. His electrocardiogram, blood pressure and cardiac enzymes were normal. The doctor told him it was probably "gas" and stress and sent him home with an antacid. Deepak was relieved, but he was also puzzled and, underneath, frightened: if nothing was wrong with his heart, what had just happened to him? What happened was a panic attack , which DSM-5-TR defines as an abrupt surge of intense fear or intense discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes, during which four or more of a list of thirteen symptoms occur. The word itself is old. The ancient Greeks blamed sudden, groundless terror on the god Pan, who was said to frighten travellers in lonely places with his blood-curdling cries, and "panic" has meant a sudden, overwhelming fear ever since. Each part of the modern definition does a particular job, so it is worth reading it slowly. First, the attack is an abrupt surge . It is not a slow build of worry over an afternoon; it is a sudden jump, a crescendo. Second, it is a surge of fear or discomfort . Most people describe terror, but some, especially older adults, describe the experience as intense discomfort rather than fear, and the definition deliberately includes them. Third, and most important for examinations, the surge reaches its peak within minutes . DSM-5-TR is unusually precise about what this means: the time to peak intensity is "literally only a few minutes". Not a few seconds (a startle at a sudden noise peaks in a fraction of a second and is gone), not half an hour, and certainly not several hours. Notice what the rule measures. It fixes the time to peak , not the length of the whole attack. Deepak's attack peaked within two or three minutes, but he felt shaken for the best part of an hour. Textbooks often say that an attack typically subsides within about ten to thirty minutes, and that is a fair description of many attacks, but it is a description, not a criterion. A panic attack can fade into calm, or it can fade into a state of ongoing anxiety and then peak again. Fourth, the surge can arise from either a calm state or an anxious state. Deepak was relaxed when his attack began, but a student already tense in an examination hall can also have one. DSM-5-TR therefore tells the clinician to time the attack from the moment of the abrupt increase in discomfort, not from the moment the person first began to feel uneasy. This is also what separates a panic attack from ongoing anxiety: the attack is discrete, it peaks within minutes, and it is usually far more intense. Fifth, there must be four or more of the thirteen symptoms. They are easiest to remember in clusters, as Figure 6.4 shows. The heart and chest give palpitations, a pounding heart or a racing pulse, and chest pain or discomfort. Breathing gives sensations of shortness of breath or smothering, and feelings of choking. The general surge of the sympathetic nervous system (the emergency reaction described in Book 1, Section 11.8.2) gives sweating, trembling or shaking, and chills or heat sensations. The gut and the balance system give nausea or abdominal distress, and feeling dizzy, unsteady, light-headed or faint. The skin gives paraesthesias , which simply means numbness or tingling sensations, often in the fingers and around the mouth. Then come three experiences of the mind. Derealisation is a feeling that the world is unreal, as when Deepak's living room looked like a flat screen; depersonalisation is a feeling of being detached from oneself, as if watching oneself from outside or moving like a robot. (These experiences as symptoms are described in Book 2, Section 2.5.8, and depersonalisation/derealisation disorder, where they persist on their own, is taught in Chapter 7.) Last come the two fears: a fear of losing control or "going crazy", and a fear of dying. DSM-5-TR counts eleven of the thirteen symptoms as physical and two as cognitive, and the two cognitive ones are the fear of losing control or going crazy and the fear of dying. (Derealisation and depersonalisation are clearly experiences of the mind rather than the body, but the manual counts them with the eleven.) The phrase "going crazy" is the patients' own colloquial expression, kept because it is what people actually say; it is not meant as a diagnosis or an insult. The fear of dying matters clinically, because people who report it tend to have more severe attacks and more severe panic disorder. Two further rules complete the picture. The first concerns culture. People from different cultures notice and report different sensations during an attack, and DSM-5-TR lists some culture-specific symptoms that may be seen: tinnitus (ringing in the ears), neck soreness, headache, and uncontrollable screaming or crying. These may be part of the experience, but they do not count towards the four required symptoms. The second rule concerns attacks that do not reach four. An attack that meets every other part of the definition but has fewer than four symptoms is called a limited-symptom attack . Limited-symptom attacks are common in people with panic disorder, mixed in among their full attacks, and a history of such "fearful spells" in youth is a risk factor for later full attacks. But they do not, on their own, allow a diagnosis of panic disorder. Any four or more, rising to a peak within a few minutes, make a full attack; the numbering follows DSM-5-TR's list. Is a panic attack really fear, or something else that merely resembles it? David H. Barlow (born 1942), whose Boston clinic has studied panic for decades, argues that it is fear: the same emotion, with the same urge to escape and the same bodily surge, simply firing at the wrong time. In his terms a panic attack is a false alarm . The most direct evidence comes from the rare occasions on which an attack has been caught on a laboratory recorder. Key study: a panic attack on the recorder (Cohen, Barlow and Blanchard, 1985) Barlow's group often recorded the physiology of patients with panic disorder while they sat quietly or practised relaxation. In one such session, reported by A. S. Cohen, Barlow and Edward B. Blanchard in 1985 in a paper on relaxation-associated panic attacks, a patient had an attack in the middle of the recording, unexpectedly from the patient's point of view and from the researchers'. The traces show a sudden, steep rise in heart rate from about the eleventh to the thirteenth minute, together with rises in muscle tension in the forehead (frontalis electromyogram) and in finger temperature. The whole surge rose and subsided within about three minutes. The conclusion: a panic attack is a genuine, measurable autonomic storm, not something the patient imagines, and it can strike while a person is relaxing. DSM-5-TR summarises the wider literature in the same terms: recordings of naturally occurring attacks show abrupt surges of arousal, usually of heart rate, that peak within minutes and subside within minutes, with faster, deeper breathing and a fall in the carbon dioxide level of the blood. The limitation is obvious: a handful of attacks caught by chance in a laboratory cannot tell us how typical they are. Exam trap A panic attack peaks within minutes , literally a few minutes. Distractors offer "a few seconds" (that is a startle), "30 to 60 minutes" and "several hours" (those describe ongoing anxiety or worry). The rule fixes the time to peak , not the total length, so "10 to 30 minutes" is a typical duration, not a criterion. You need four or more of thirteen symptoms; fewer is a limited-symptom attack. The two cognitive symptoms are fear of losing control or going crazy and fear of dying. Headache, tinnitus, neck soreness and screaming or crying do not count. Finally, the defining feature of a panic attack is the abrupt surge with bodily symptoms, not "persistent worry for 6 months" (generalised anxiety disorder), "avoidance of a specific feared object" (specific phobia) or "re-experiencing a traumatic event" (post-traumatic stress disorder). Expected, unexpected and nocturnal attacks, and the panic attack specifier Suppose a woman who is terrified of dogs has a panic attack when a street dog runs at her. Suppose a man has one on a Sunday evening on his sofa. Both are panic attacks by the definition above, but they mean very different things, and the difference is captured by two terms. An expected panic attack is one for which there is an obvious cue or trigger: the dog, the lift for a person afraid of lifts, the stage for a person afraid of public speaking, or a situation in which the person's attacks have usually happened before. An unexpected panic attack is one for which there is no obvious cue or trigger at the time it occurs; it seems to come "out of the blue", while the person is relaxing, shopping, driving on an empty road or emerging from sleep. Deepak's first attack, on the sofa, was unexpected. Who decides which kind an attack was? The clinician does, and DSM-5-TR says how: by careful questioning about the sequence of events before the attack, combined with the person's own judgement of whether it seemed to happen for no reason. The decision is not always easy. People search hard for causes after an attack, and older adults in particular tend to explain an attack afterwards by a stressful situation ("it was the hospital visit"), even when it was unexpected at the time. Culture matters too. A Vietnamese person who panics after walking out into a strong wind may attribute the attack to the wind, because a cultural syndrome called trúng gió ("hit by the wind") links wind exposure with illness; in that person's eyes the attack was expected. The clinician has to find out what the person believes before classifying the attack. The distinction is not a technicality. Expected attacks are found in almost every anxiety disorder; recurrent unexpected attacks are the hallmark of panic disorder. In the United States and Europe about half of people with panic disorder have expected attacks as well as unexpected ones, so the presence of some expected attacks does not rule panic disorder out. One kind of unexpected attack deserves a special name. A nocturnal panic attack is waking from sleep in a state of panic, which is different from waking up normally and then panicking. DSM-5-TR estimates that in the United States between a quarter and a third of people with panic disorder have had at least one; Barlow, citing earlier clinical studies, puts the figure higher, at about 60 percent, and notes that attacks occur more often between about 1.30 and 3.30 in the morning than at any other time. Some patients become afraid to fall asleep. Are they having nightmares? Sleep-laboratory studies say no. Nightmares and other dream activity occur in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which comes mostly later in the night. Nocturnal panic attacks arise in slow-wave (delta) sleep, the deepest stage of non-REM sleep, usually a few hours after the person has fallen asleep, and the patient typically begins to panic as he or she sinks into it. The best current explanation is that the physical sensations of "letting go" as one enters deep sleep are themselves frightening to a person who already fears bodily sensations (the idea of fear of fear, explained below). Because the attacks do not arise in REM sleep, there is no dream to be "repressed", whatever an older style of therapy might assume. Nocturnal panic must also be told from sleep terrors , which occur mostly in children, also in deep sleep: the child screams and may run about but does not fully wake and has no memory of the episode in the morning, whereas the person with nocturnal panic wakes fully and remembers the attack vividly. (Nightmares and sleep terrors are taught in Chapter 8.) Obstructive sleep apnoea, in which breathing stops repeatedly during sleep, can also feel like suffocation, but it has a repeated cycle of waking and falling back to sleep that nocturnal panic lacks. Because panic attacks occur in so many conditions, DSM-5-TR does not treat a panic attack as a disorder at all. It states plainly that a panic attack is not a mental disorder and cannot be coded. Instead, when attacks occur in the course of some other disorder, the clinician adds the panic attack specifier : one writes "post-traumatic stress disorder with panic attacks", "major depressive disorder with panic attacks" or "social anxiety disorder with panic attacks". Attacks can occur with any anxiety disorder, with depressive and bipolar disorders, eating disorders, obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, personality disorders, psychotic disorders and substance use disorders, and with some medical conditions of the heart, lungs, balance system and gut. The specifier is useful because attacks are a marker of severity: in almost every disorder, people who have panic attacks have more severe symptoms, more comorbidity, a poorer response to treatment and a higher rate of suicidal thoughts and attempts. There is one exception to the specifier rule. In panic disorder the attacks are already part of the criteria, so the specifier is not added; "panic disorder with panic attacks" would say the same thing twice. How common are panic attacks? Far more common than panic disorder. In the general population of the United States and Spain, between 9.5 and 11.2 percent of adults have at least one panic attack in a year, and the lifetime figure across nations is 13.2 percent. Attacks are more common in women, are rare before puberty, and have a mean age of onset in the United States of about 22 to 23 years. Compare those figures with the 2 to 3 percent of adults who have panic disorder in a given year (subsection 6.2.5), and the conclusion is clear: most people who have a panic attack never develop the disorder. What separates them? Barlow's answer is that those who do not go on to develop panic disorder put the attack down to the events of the moment (an argument, something they ate, a bad week) and get on with their lives. A real illustration is the American professional golfer Charlie Beljan . In late 2012, on his way to winning his first tournament on the professional tour, he had a panic attack on the course that he took to be a heart attack. With paramedics following him in a golf cart, he staggered from shot to shot, sometimes sitting down on the fairway, finished with his best round of the year and only then went to hospital in an ambulance, where the attack was identified. The attack was terrifying; what it did not do, at least in the account Barlow gives, was turn into a lasting fear of the next attack. That fear is what the next subsection is about. Nocturnal panic arises in slow-wave (non-REM) sleep , so it is not a nightmare , which is a REM-sleep event, and unlike a sleep terror the person wakes fully and remembers it. Panic disorder: how it was born and how it is diagnosed Attacks of sudden terror with a pounding heart and breathlessness were described long before anyone called them panic disorder. Freud's "anxiety neurosis" of 1895 (Section 6.1) already included anxiety attacks with palpitations, disturbed breathing, sweating and trembling, alongside a chronic state of anxious expectation. For most of the twentieth century both kinds of anxiety, the sudden attacks and the steady apprehension, were treated as degrees of one thing. What pulled them apart was, of all things, a drug. Key study: Klein's pharmacological dissection (1959 to 1964) In 1959 the young American psychiatrist Donald F. Klein (1928 to 2019) joined Hillside Hospital in Queens, New York, where he and Max Fink were studying the effects of imipramine, the first of the tricyclic antidepressants. Klein noticed something unexpected in a group of anxious inpatients who were not depressed, patients who would later be called agoraphobic. Imipramine stopped their apparently spontaneous attacks of terror. What it did not quickly remove was the chronic anticipatory anxiety between the attacks, the dread of the next one, or the avoidance that had grown around them; those needed psychological help and encouragement. Klein and Fink published their reaction patterns to imipramine in 1962, and in 1964 Klein described "two drug-responsive anxiety syndromes". His reasoning was bold: if a drug blocks one kind of anxiety but not the other, the two may be different conditions. He called this method pharmacological dissection (sometimes psychopharmacological dissection): using the selective effect of a drug to carve a clinical picture at its joints. The criticism is that a drug's effect is weak evidence about the nature of a disorder (aspirin relieves many different kinds of headache), and later research found that antidepressants such as imipramine also help generalised anxiety, so drug response does not divide the two as cleanly as Klein hoped. But the argument was persuasive at the time, and when DSM-III appeared in 1980 it split the old anxiety neurosis into two disorders: panic disorder, defined by the attacks, and generalised anxiety disorder, defined by chronic apprehension (Section 6.4). Klein later proposed a biological theory of why the alarm misfires, the suffocation false alarm theory, which is taught in Section 6.7. Panic disorder , as DSM-5-TR now defines it, is recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by a lasting fear of further attacks or a lasting change in behaviour because of them. The criteria fall into four groups, and each group exists to rule something out. Criterion A: recurrent unexpected panic attacks. "Recurrent" means more than one. "Unexpected" means at least some of the attacks came with no obvious trigger. Both words matter. A single attack, however terrifying, is not panic disorder; so many people have one isolated attack in their lives that a diagnosis built on one would make a disorder of an ordinary experience. And attacks that only ever come with a trigger point to some other anxiety disorder. DSM-5-TR adds that more than one full-symptom unexpected attack is needed; a person who has only ever had limited-symptom attacks does not qualify. Criterion B: the aftermath. At least one attack must have been followed by a month or more of one or both of two things. The first is persistent concern or worry about having more attacks or about their consequences: that the next one will be a heart attack, that it will make the person lose control or "go crazy", that it will happen in front of colleagues. The second is a significant maladaptive change in behaviour related to the attacks, such as avoiding exercise or unfamiliar situations so as not to bring on an attack. This criterion is the heart of the disorder. Panic disorder is not really a disorder of panic attacks; it is a disorder of what a person comes to feel and do about them. Criterion C: not caused by a substance or a medical condition. Stimulants, caffeine and cannabis, withdrawal from alcohol and other depressants, an overactive thyroid gland and disorders of the heart and lungs can all produce attacks, and in such cases the diagnosis is a substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder or an anxiety disorder due to another medical condition (subsection 6.2.5). Criterion D: not better explained by another mental disorder. If the attacks occur only in feared social situations, the diagnosis is social anxiety disorder; only on meeting a circumscribed phobic object or situation, specific phobia; only in response to obsessions, obsessive-compulsive disorder; only in response to reminders of a trauma, post-traumatic stress disorder; only on separation from attachment figures, separation anxiety disorder. In all these cases the attacks are expected, and the other disorder explains them. If, however, the person also has unexpected attacks and worries about them, panic disorder can be diagnosed as well. Push Deepak through the criteria. Over the next three months he had five more attacks: two at his desk, one on the Metro, one in a traffic jam and one, worst of all, that woke him at two in the morning. At least four were full attacks, and none had an obvious trigger (Criterion A). Since the first attack he had thought about his heart every day; he had seen three cardiologists, had a treadmill test and wore a fitness band to watch his pulse, and he had stopped going to the gym and stopped drinking coffee in case either set off an attack (Criterion B, both halves). His thyroid tests were normal, he used no drugs and drank little (Criterion C). His attacks were not tied to social situations, to any one phobic object, to obsessions or to a trauma (Criterion D). Deepak has panic disorder. Notice that he still travels on the Metro and goes to the office, although with dread; he does not yet avoid two or more of the situations that define agoraphobia. That will matter in subsection 6.2.6. Exam trap "Panic disorder is where ..." The answer is recurrent and unexpected panic attacks (followed by a month of worry or behaviour change). The distractors each describe something else: "an individual experiences a singular panic attack" (one attack is common and is not a disorder); "excessive anxiety and worry about many different aspects of life " (generalised anxiety disorder, Section 6.4); "a fear of panicking in enclosed spaces " (a fear tied to a place: claustrophobia, a situational specific phobia, if it is one kind of place, or agoraphobia if two or more of the five agoraphobic situations are feared). Also remember the duration: the worry after an attack must last 1 month , not 6 months; panic disorder is the one adult anxiety disorder in this section without a "typically 6 months" rule. Fear of fear: anticipatory anxiety, interoceptive avoidance and safety signals Why does one person shrug off a panic attack while another, like Deepak, spends months watching his own pulse? In 1978 two American behaviour therapists, Alan J. Goldstein and Dianne L. Chambless , published "A reanalysis of agoraphobia" in the journal Behavior Therapy . Their central idea was that after a few attacks the person comes to fear not a place, an animal or a situation, but the bodily sensations of anxiety themselves. A slight quickening of the heart, a moment of breathlessness on the stairs, a wave of dizziness on standing up: each becomes a signal that the next attack may be starting, and the signal itself triggers fear. They called this fear of fear . Because the cue for the fear is inside the body, it can never be left at home, and because fear produces the very sensations that are feared, the process can feed on itself. The detailed cognitive account of how this cycle escalates into an attack, David Clark's catastrophic misinterpretation model, is taught in Section 6.8 and, as a treatment, in Book 2, Section 5.6.3; the learning account of how internal sensations come to act as conditioned cues is also Section 6.8's. Fear of fear shows itself in three ways. The first is anticipatory anxiety : the steady, nagging apprehension between attacks about when the next one will come, where it will strike and what it will do. This is Criterion B's "persistent concern or worry", and it is often more disabling than the attacks, which may come once a month while the anticipatory anxiety is there every day. The second is interoceptive avoidance , avoidance of activities that produce internal sensations resembling the beginning of an attack. Barlow's clinic lists the typical ones: running up flights of stairs, getting involved in heated arguments, getting angry, hot and stuffy rooms, cars and shops, saunas and showers with the doors and windows closed, walking in intense heat or very cold weather, sport, aerobics, dancing and hiking, lifting heavy objects, drinking coffee or other caffeinated drinks, eating chocolate or heavy meals, sexual relations, watching horror films or exciting matches, and standing up quickly from a sitting position. Deepak's abandoned gym and his abandoned filter coffee belong here. Psychopathologists now regard this cluster as every bit as important as the more familiar avoidance of places. The third is the use of safety behaviours , small acts meant to prevent a feared catastrophe or to make survival more likely if it comes: sitting near the exit in a cinema or on a bus, holding on to a railing, carrying a water bottle, checking the pulse, sitting down at the first sign of dizziness, keeping a mobile phone charged and a hospital's number ready. Closely related are safety signals , people or objects whose mere presence makes the person feel safe: a trusted companion who "knows what to do", a strip of tablets in the pocket that is never actually taken, the knowledge that a hospital is close by. Barlow notes that anxiety falls when a person is with a "safe" person or in a "safe" place even when that person or place could do nothing useful if disaster struck. The trouble with safety behaviours and signals is that they work too well in the short run. When the feared heart attack does not happen, the person credits the water bottle or the companion rather than learning that the attack was never dangerous, so the fear is preserved (the general idea of safety behaviours is set out in Book 2, Section 5.6.2). Figure 6.5 shows how the three strands can lead from one unexpected attack to agoraphobia. 1 First unexpected panic attack 2 Misread as a catastrophe: heart attack, stroke, going mad 3 Fear of fear: the body's own sensations become the alarm 4 Anticipatory anxiety: "When will the next one come?" more arousal, more attacks Why it spreads each escape brings relief, so the avoidance is negatively reinforced Interoceptive avoidance no running, coffee, saunas, hot rooms Situational avoidance trains, buses, crowds, markets, queues Safety behaviours and signals companion, water, tablet, exit seat 5 Agoraphobia: fear of two or more of the five situations avoided, endured with dread or faced with a companion; at worst, housebound Figure 6.5 From a first unexpected attack to agoraphobia. Fear of the body's own sensations keeps anticipatory anxiety high and makes further attacks more likely (the loop on the left); avoidance of sensations and of places, and reliance on safety signals, bring short-term relief and so spread, until the person fears and avoids the situations that define agoraphobia. Not everyone travels the whole path. Exam trap "Fear of fear" (Goldstein and Chambless, 1978) belongs to panic disorder and agoraphobia . In a question that asks what the sufferer of generalised anxiety disorder experiences, "fear of fear" is a distractor; the answer is continued apprehension about unspecified things (Section 6.4). "Continual flashbacks to past events" is post-traumatic stress disorder (Chapter 7), and "a desire to check that the environment is safe" describes checking compulsions in obsessive-compulsive disorder (Section 6.5). Do not confuse fear of fear, which is fear of the sensations of anxiety, with anticipatory anxiety, which is worry about future attacks: the first drives the second. Who develops panic disorder, how it runs, and what else it might be In any one year about 2 to 3 percent of adults and adolescents in the United States and several European countries have panic disorder. The global lifetime prevalence is estimated at 1.7 percent, and estimates from Asian, African and Latin American countries are lower still, between 0.1 and 0.8 percent. Whether those low figures reflect a real difference or a difference in how people describe and report their distress is not settled; as you will see below, a person who experiences an attack as "heart trouble" may never be counted as a case of panic disorder at all. Women are affected about twice as often as men, and the difference is already visible before the age of 14. Panic disorder itself is rare before 14 (below 0.4 percent), rises through adolescence, perhaps after puberty, and peaks in adulthood; it becomes less common again after middle age, falling to about 1.2 percent of adults over 55 and 0.7 percent over 64, possibly because the autonomic nervous system responds less sharply with age. The median age of onset in the United States is 20 to 24 years, and across nations about 32 years. A small number of cases begin in childhood, often with "fearful spells" that are dated back to childhood only in retrospect, and onset after 55 is unusual. Left untreated, panic disorder usually runs a chronic but waxing and waning course. Some people have bursts of frequent attacks separated by months or years of remission; others have continuous severe symptoms; only a minority recover fully without relapse within a few years. It is rarely alone. In the general population about 80 percent of people with panic disorder have had another mental disorder at some point in their lives, most often another anxiety disorder (agoraphobia above all), major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder or an alcohol use disorder. Depression comes first in about a third of those who have both; in the other two-thirds it begins with or after the panic. Some people drink or take sedatives to control their attacks, which is one route into a substance use disorder (Chapter 10). Panic disorder carries a raised rate of suicidal thoughts and behaviour, even when depression and other risk factors are allowed for; about a quarter of primary-care patients with panic disorder report suicidal thoughts, so the question must always be asked. It also produces the highest number of medical visits of any anxiety disorder, with repeated trips to emergency departments, absence from work and, for some, loss of a job or a course of study. The risk factors (temperament, anxiety sensitivity, parenting, stress, smoking and genes) are taught in Section 6.7, and the psychological theories in Section 6.8. Culture shapes both what people fear during an attack and how they explain it. Among Latin Americans, especially from the Caribbean, ataque de nervios ("attack of nerves") resembles a panic attack, but more often includes uncontrollable shouting or crying, trembling, aggressive or suicidal behaviour and depersonalisation, and it may last longer than the few minutes of a typical panic attack. Among Cambodians, khyâl cap or "wind attacks" combine dizziness, tinnitus and neck soreness. The psychiatrist and anthropologist Devon Hinton and his colleagues showed how such beliefs feed panic among Khmer refugees in the United States: the traditional idea of kyol goeu , "wind overload", in which too much wind or gas in the body may cause blood vessels to burst, becomes the focus of catastrophic thinking during an attack, so that a sore neck or a dizzy spell on standing is read as the start of a fatal rupture. These cultural syndromes are described in Chapter 1. Indian context In India, as in much of Asia, a panic attack is usually experienced and reported as a bodily illness. The person, often in his or her twenties or thirties, arrives at a cardiologist's clinic or an emergency department complaining of a pounding heart, chest pain or breathlessness, or at a physician's with "gas", "acidity" or ghabrahat (a common Hindi word for agitated nervousness). Tests are normal, the patient is reassured or given an antacid or a vitamin injection, and the attacks return. Many patients have seen several doctors and had several electrocardiograms and treadmill tests before anyone mentions anxiety. This is a clinical observation rather than a measured figure, but every Indian clinician recognises it, and it is one reason why panic disorder should be asked about in any young adult with repeated normal cardiac work-ups. Because the symptoms of a panic attack are bodily, the first step in diagnosis is always to rule out a bodily cause (Criterion C). DSM-5-TR lists the medical conditions that can cause attacks or be mistaken for them: an overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism) or parathyroid gland (hyperparathyroidism); phaeochromocytoma, a rare tumour of the adrenal gland that releases bursts of adrenaline; disorders of the vestibular (balance) system; seizure disorders; and heart and lung conditions such as arrhythmias, supraventricular tachycardia, asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Simple tests help: thyroid hormones, serum calcium for the parathyroid, a Holter monitor (a portable 24-hour electrocardiogram) for arrhythmias. Substances are the second check. Intoxication with stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines and plain caffeine) or with cannabis, and withdrawal from alcohol, barbiturates and other depressants, can all set off attacks. Two warning signs suggest a medical or substance cause rather than panic disorder: onset after the age of 45, and atypical symptoms during an attack, such as true vertigo (the room spinning), loss of consciousness, loss of bladder or bowel control, slurred speech or amnesia. A clinician who sees any of them should look harder for another cause. A substance cause does not settle the matter for good, however. If attacks continue long after intoxication or withdrawal has ended, or if they began before the drinking did, panic disorder may be present as well, and many people with panic disorder use alcohol to quieten their attacks. The third check is other mental disorders. In the other anxiety disorders the attacks are expected: cued by social situations in social anxiety disorder, by phobic objects in specific phobia, by worry in generalised anxiety disorder, by separation in separation anxiety disorder. People with illness anxiety disorder (Chapter 7) also worry about their health, but they fear having a disease, and their anxiety is a steady preoccupation rather than a series of attacks; the person with panic disorder fears the attacks and what the attacks might do. Generalised anxiety disorder (Section 6.4) shares the chronic apprehension, but its worry is spread across many everyday matters rather than fixed on the next attack. Finally, panic attacks happen in depression, in psychotic disorders and in personality disorders, and there the specifier, not a second diagnosis, is usually the right label. Clinical link Explaining the diagnosis well is the first treatment. A patient told "it is nothing, only stress" leaves feeling dismissed and, often, still convinced that something has been missed. A patient told "this is a panic attack: your body's emergency alarm going off with no fire. It feels like dying, but it cannot stop your heart, and it can be treated" has been given a reason to stop searching for a heart disease. The psychological treatment with the strongest evidence for panic disorder is cognitive behaviour therapy with interoceptive exposure, in which the patient deliberately brings on the feared sensations (spinning in a chair, breathing through a straw, running on the spot) until they lose their power (Book 2, Sections 5.6.3 and 4.3; breathing retraining is Section 4.8.3). The drugs, including the antidepressants and the benzodiazepines, and the reasons for caution with the latter, are compared in Section 6.9. Agoraphobia: the fear of being trapped In 1871 the Berlin psychiatrist Carl Friedrich Otto Westphal (1833 to 1890), often written Karl Westphal, described three men who were seized by extreme anxiety and dread whenever they had to cross certain open squares and public places of the city. He named their condition agoraphobia , from the Greek agora , the marketplace and place of assembly at the centre of a Greek city, and phobos , fear. Barlow points out that the name fits better than it seems: the agora was a busy, bustling place, and the most stressful places for people with agoraphobia today are its modern equivalents. In India these are the shopping mall, the railway station, the crowded bazaar during a festival, the queue at a bank, the packed suburban train and the bus with its door jammed with commuters. Nandini, thirty-four, lives in Kochi with her husband and two school-age children. Her first panic attack came four years ago on a crowded private bus stuck in traffic; she remembers thinking that if she fainted no one could reach her and the bus could not stop. More attacks followed, in a textile shop during the Onam sales and in the queue at the ration shop. Little by little she gave up the bus, then the market, then the bank. She can still go to the temple on Fridays, but only with her husband, and she stands at the back near the gate. If he is travelling, she does not go out at all; the children buy the vegetables on their way home from school, and the grocer delivers. "It is not the place," she says. "It is that if it happens there, I cannot get out, and nobody will help me. At home, if it comes, I can lie down." Nandini's words contain the essence of the disorder. Agoraphobia is not, as its name suggests, a fear of open spaces. It is a fear of being in situations from which escape might be difficult, or in which help might not be available, if panic-like symptoms or other incapacitating or embarrassing symptoms were to occur. The organising theme is being trapped or helpless. DSM-5-TR's criteria spell this out in groups. Criterion A: the situations. Marked fear or anxiety about two or more of five situations: (1) using public transport (cars, buses, trains, ships, aeroplanes); (2) being in open spaces (car parks, marketplaces, bridges); (3) being in enclosed places (shops, theatres, cinemas); (4) standing in a queue or being in a crowd; and (5) being outside the home alone. The examples are not exhaustive. The requirement of two situations is the main way to tell agoraphobia from a situational specific phobia, which is limited to one. Criterion B: the reason. The person fears or avoids the situations because of thoughts that escape might be difficult or help unavailable in the event of panic-like symptoms (any of the thirteen, such as dizziness, faintness or fear of dying) or other incapacitating or embarrassing symptoms. These include vomiting and bowel symptoms, a fear of falling in older adults, a fear of incontinence and, in children, a sense of being disoriented and lost. The reason is what separates agoraphobia from a phobia of the situation itself. A person afraid of flying because the plane might crash has a specific phobia; a person afraid of flying because she might panic and could not get off has agoraphobic fear. Criteria C and D: consistency and response. The situations almost always provoke fear or anxiety (someone anxious in a queue only once in five visits does not qualify), and they are actively avoided, require the presence of a companion, or are endured with intense fear. Avoidance can be behavioural (changing routes, taking a job close to home, having food delivered) or cognitive (getting through the situation by distraction), and the person may use safety behaviours such as sitting near exits. Criterion E: out of proportion. The fear must be out of proportion to the actual danger and to the sociocultural context. Not wanting to go out in a cyclone, or avoiding a deserted car park in a high-crime area at night, is not agoraphobia. Culture matters here in an important way. DSM-5-TR gives the example of societies in which it is customary for women not to leave the house alone; where that is the norm, staying at home is not a symptom. An Indian clinician must therefore ask whether a woman who never goes out alone is afraid, or is simply following what her family expects. Criteria F and G: persistence and impairment. The fear, anxiety or avoidance typically lasts 6 months or more, which excludes short-lived problems, and it causes clinically significant distress or impairment. Criteria H and I: other explanations. If a medical condition is present (inflammatory bowel disease, Parkinson's disease), the fear must be clearly excessive for it. And the picture must not be better explained by another mental disorder: by a situational specific phobia (one situation only), social anxiety disorder (social situations only, feared because of judgement), obsessive-compulsive disorder (avoidance driven by obsessions, such as fear of contamination), body dysmorphic disorder (avoidance because of perceived flaws in appearance), post-traumatic stress disorder (avoidance of trauma reminders only) or separation anxiety disorder (fear of separation from attachment figures). Nandini fears and avoids public transport, enclosed places, queues and crowds, and going out alone: four of the five situations. She fears them because she could not escape or get help if she panicked. She goes only with a companion, her fear is far beyond any real danger, it has lasted four years and it has shrunk her life. She has agoraphobia. She also has recurrent unexpected attacks and a lasting fear of them, so she has panic disorder too, and under DSM-5-TR she receives both diagnoses. At its most severe, agoraphobia makes a person completely housebound, dependent on others even for food and medicine. Barlow describes Mrs M., a 67-year-old woman who had suffered from panic disorder and agoraphobia for more than 30 years and had not left her second-floor flat for 20. Even parts of her flat had become unsafe: for 15 years she had not answered her own door because she was afraid to look into the hallway, and for 10 she had not entered the half of her kitchen that overlooked the back yard. Her daughter brought groceries once a week. When the evaluating psychologist arrived, he was the first person she had seen in three weeks; she offered him coffee and homemade biscuits, and she declined treatment. A happier example is the American television cook Paula Deen , whose interest in cooking, by Barlow's account, developed during the years when severe agoraphobia kept her at home. Demoralisation, depression and the misuse of alcohol and sedatives as self-medication are common in the housebound. Agoraphobia looks slightly different across the lifespan. In children the most feared situation is being outside the home alone, and the fear is of getting lost. In adults the fear is mostly of panic-like symptoms. In older adults the most feared situations are shops, queues and open spaces, and the commonest fear is of falling; about 10 percent of older adults with agoraphobia say their first episode came after 65. With an older person the clinician has to judge carefully whether the fear of falling is out of proportion to real frailty. Agoraphobia as a disorder in its own right: history, numbers and look-alikes For most of its history agoraphobia has been tied to panic, and the manuals have argued about which of the two comes first. Barlow's view, built on years of clinic work, is that most agoraphobic avoidance is simply a complication of severe unexpected panic attacks: if you have had attacks and fear another, you want to be in a safe place, or with a safe person, from which you can quickly get to a hospital or a bed. On that view agoraphobia is one way of coping with panic. Yet the avoidance, once learned, can become independent of the attacks. Mrs M. had not had an attack in years and was still housebound, because agoraphobic avoidance depends mostly on how strongly a person expects another attack, not on how many attacks he or she actually has. And epidemiological surveys, which find people in the community rather than in clinics, turned up a large group who have agoraphobia without ever having had a panic attack at all; Barlow notes that about half of the people with agoraphobia found in population surveys fit this description, though they are rarely seen in clinics. Some of them fear other unpredictable and embarrassing events: dizzy spells, loss of bladder or bowel control, falling. Those findings explain the change shown in Table 6.6. DSM-IV had a single combined disorder, panic disorder with agoraphobia, plus a residual category for agoraphobia without a history of panic disorder. DSM-5 made agoraphobia and panic disorder two independent diagnoses: agoraphobia is diagnosed irrespective of panic disorder, and a person who meets the criteria for both, like Nandini, receives both. Table 6.6 How the manuals have joined and separated panic and agoraphobia. Women are affected about twice as often as men; Barlow's clinic found that the more severe the agoraphobic avoidance, the higher the proportion of women (in his patients with panic disorder, 72 percent of those with mild agoraphobia were women, 81 percent with moderate and 89 percent with severe). He thinks the explanation is mainly cultural: it is more acceptable for women to admit fear and to avoid situations, while men are expected to "tough it out", and a large proportion of men with severe unexpected attacks cope instead by drinking heavily, which can hide the anxiety disorder behind an alcohol problem. Agoraphobia can occur in childhood, but its incidence peaks in late adolescence and early adulthood. Two-thirds of cases begin before 35, the mean age of onset is 21, and agoraphobia without preceding panic attacks or panic disorder begins later, at 25 to 29; there is a second rise in risk after 40. Panic attacks or panic disorder come before the agoraphobia in 30 percent of community cases and in more than 50 percent of clinical cases. The course is usually persistent and chronic: without treatment complete remission is rare (about 10 percent), and about a third of those who do remit relapse. About 90 percent of people with agoraphobia have another mental disorder, most often another anxiety disorder, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder or an alcohol use disorder, and about 15 percent report suicidal thoughts or behaviour. The theme is being trapped or helpless , not open space as such. 6.3 Specific Phobia, Social Anxiety Disorder and the Names of the Phobias Medium yield · 3 Qs John Madden (1936 to 2021) was one of the most famous figures in American sport, a championship-winning football coach who became a much-loved television commentator. His job meant covering a game in New York one Sunday and in San Francisco the next, a distance any other commentator would fly. Madden could not fly. He suffered from claustrophobia, and for years he crossed the country by train; later he travelled in a specially equipped private bus. As Barlow observes, he must have known that flying is the safest way to travel and that his fear was costing him time and money, and he even made fun of it in television advertisements. None of that knowledge made the fear go away. That combination, a fear that the sufferer may know is excessive but cannot argue away, which is reliably set off by one kind of thing and which reshapes a life around avoiding it, is the subject of this section. In panic disorder and agoraphobia (Section 6.2) the danger is felt to be inside the body. In the phobias it is felt to be outside: in a dog, a needle, a lift, or the eyes of other people. What makes a fear a phobia A phobia is a persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation: a fear that is out of proportion to the real danger, that is set off almost every time the person meets the object or situation, and that leads the person to avoid it or to endure it with dread. Each part of that sentence separates a phobia from something else. "Persistent" separates it from the passing fears that everyone has. "Out of proportion" separates it from a sensible fear (a fear of cobras in a field in Konkan in the monsoon is prudence, not phobia). "Almost every time" separates it from a fear that comes and goes. "Avoided or endured with dread" captures what makes it a problem. And "a specific object or situation" separates it from the free-floating worry of generalised anxiety disorder (Section 6.4), which attaches to almost anything. Examiners test the definition by offering things that are not phobias. A phobia is not a mild stress reaction : the ordinary upset that follows a bad event, or the more troublesome distress of an adjustment disorder (Chapter 7), is a response to a stressor and fades as the person adapts, whereas a phobia is a lasting fear of a particular stimulus. It is not a personality disorder , which is a pervasive, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behaviour that colours almost every area of life (Chapter 11); a phobia is circumscribed, and outside its territory the person may be quite untroubled. And it is not a temporary hallucination , which is a perception without a stimulus (Chapter 2); the phobic person perceives the spider or the lift perfectly accurately and is afraid of the real thing. A phobia is an anxiety disorder . (Phobia as a sign in the mental status examination is described in Book 2, Section 2.5.5.) Fears themselves are almost universal. In a classic community survey published in 1969, W. Stewart Agras and his colleagues asked people about intense fears and found that snakes headed the list, reported by about a quarter of the sample, followed by heights and flying; most such fears were far more common in women. Barlow's summary of later surveys is that few of the people who report intense fears qualify for a phobia, but that for roughly one person in eight a fear becomes severe enough at some point in life to earn the label. Children's fears are a special case, because many are a normal part of development (Section 6.1): infants fear loud noises and strangers, toddlers fear separation, and fears of animals and of the dark appear early and may last into the fourth or fifth year, with fears of monsters and imaginary creatures beginning around three. These fears are usually transient and only mildly impairing, and DSM-5-TR says plainly that such developmentally appropriate fears are not specific phobia. The DSM-5-TR criteria for specific phobia turn the definition into rules. Read them in groups. Criterion A: marked fear of a specific object or situation. The manual's examples are flying, heights, animals, receiving an injection and seeing blood. "Marked" means intense or severe. The feared thing is called the phobic stimulus . The fear may grow as the stimulus comes closer, may be felt in anticipation, and may take the form of a full or limited-symptom panic attack, which in this setting is an expected attack. In children the fear may be expressed by crying, tantrums, freezing or clinging rather than in words. Criterion B: almost always and at once. The stimulus almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety. Someone who is anxious on only one flight in five does not have a flying phobia, and the fear comes as soon as the stimulus is met, not after a delay. The intensity may still vary with circumstances (turbulence, the presence of others, how long the exposure lasts). Criterion C: avoidance or dread. The stimulus is actively avoided, or endured with intense fear. Avoidance can be obvious (a person who fears blood refusing to see a doctor) or subtle (a person who fears snakes refusing to look at pictures of anything snake-shaped), and people with long-standing phobias often arrange their lives so thoroughly around the fear (turning down a job that needs travel, moving to a place without the feared animal) that they no longer feel anxious day to day. Their avoidance itself then confirms the diagnosis. Criterion D: out of proportion. The fear is out of proportion to the actual danger and to the sociocultural context. People with specific phobia often recognise that their reactions are excessive, but they also tend to overestimate the danger, so the judgement is made by the clinician, not the patient. Context counts: a fear of the dark may be reasonable where there is ongoing violence. Criterion E: persistence. The fear, anxiety or avoidance is persistent, typically lasting 6 months or more. The rule separates a phobia from the transient fears that are so common, especially in children. "Typically" signals that the six months is a guide applied with clinical judgement, not a stopwatch. Criteria F and G: impairment and other explanations. There must be clinically significant distress or impairment, and the fear must not be better explained by another disorder: by agoraphobia (fear of panic-like symptoms in several situations), obsessive-compulsive disorder (fear tied to obsessions, such as fear of blood because of obsessional thoughts of HIV), post-traumatic stress disorder (reminders of a trauma), separation anxiety disorder (separation from attachment figures) or social anxiety disorder (fear of social scrutiny). DSM-5-TR also excludes avoidance confined to food (consider an eating disorder) and fear that grows out of a delusion (consider a psychotic disorder). Two changes from DSM-IV are worth knowing, because older books and many question banks still use the earlier wording. DSM-IV required that the person recognise that the fear was "excessive or unreasonable" (a requirement it waived for children); DSM-5 dropped this insight requirement and put the judgement of "out of proportion" in the clinician's hands, because the evidence showed that people with phobias tend to overestimate the danger and that older adults often put their fears down to ageing, so that relying on the patient's insight missed real cases. And DSM-IV applied its six-month duration only to people under 18; DSM-5 extended "typically 6 months" to all ages. The same two changes were made to social anxiety disorder. Finally, phobias seldom come singly. DSM-5-TR reports that the average person with specific phobia fears three objects or situations, and about three-quarters fear more than one. Each is diagnosed and coded separately: a person who fears thunderstorms and flying receives two diagnoses, specific phobia, natural environment type, and specific phobia, situational type. Exam trap A phobia is best described as a persistent irrational fear of a specific object or situation . It is not a mild stress reaction (ordinary or adjustment-level distress, Chapter 7), not a personality disorder (a pervasive trait pattern, Chapter 11) and not a temporary hallucination (a perceptual symptom, Chapter 2): it is an anxiety disorder . The DSM-5 duration for specific phobia is typically 6 months , not 1 week, 1 month or 3 months. The adult no longer has to recognise that the fear is excessive; the clinician judges it out of proportion. The five types of specific phobia Jack D. Maser once compiled a list of named phobias from medical dictionaries and other sources, and the entries under the letter "a" alone run from acarophobia (insects or mites) to autophobia (being alone). Barlow's verdict on such lists is that they have little or no value for the study of psychopathology. What does have value is the discovery, built into DSM-IV in 1994 (which also replaced the older name "simple phobia" with "specific phobia"), that phobias fall into a small number of types that differ in their age of onset, their physiology and the way they run in families. DSM-5-TR keeps five, recorded as specifiers and coded by the phobic stimulus (Table 6.8). The animal type covers spiders, insects, dogs, snakes, rats and mice, and the like. Such fears are common; they count as phobias only when the fear is far beyond ordinary distaste and the avoidance seriously interferes with life, as with Barlow's patients who could not read a magazine in case they turned a page and met a picture of a snake. The natural environment type covers heights, storms and water. These fears tend to cluster (a person who fears deep water is likely to fear storms too), and because each of these situations carries some real danger, some fear of them is adaptive. Barlow suggests that we may be biologically prepared to learn these fears easily, an idea, preparedness, taught in Section 6.8 (Book 1, Section 6.4.6). Animal and natural environment phobias usually begin early, at a peak age of about 7. The blood-injection-injury type covers needles and injections, invasive medical procedures, the sight of blood, and injury. It is physiologically unique, and the next subsection is devoted to it. The situational type covers aeroplanes, lifts, enclosed places, tunnels and driving. Madden's claustrophobia was situational. Situational phobias begin later than the other types, often from the mid-teens to the mid-twenties, much like panic disorder and agoraphobia, and for a time they were thought to be closely related to those disorders. The essential difference is that the person with a situational phobia has panic attacks only in or near the phobic situation and can relax completely when it is not in prospect, whereas the person with panic disorder may be struck anywhere. Situational phobias are also the type that most often brings people to clinics, probably because avoiding driving, flying or lifts is so hard to arrange in modern life. Finally, the other type collects phobias that fit nowhere else: fear of situations that might lead to choking or vomiting, fear of contracting an illness, and, in children, fear of loud sounds or of costumed characters such as clowns. Most phobias begin in childhood, but some can begin at any age after a frightening experience; a phobia of choking, for example, almost always follows a real near-choking episode. The first is between a situational phobia and agoraphobia, which share several situations (aeroplanes and lifts overlap with agoraphobia's "public transport" and "enclosed places"). DSM-5-TR gives two tests. One is the count: a person who fears only one of the agoraphobic situations has a specific phobia, situational type, whereas a person who fears, for example, aeroplanes, lifts and crowds, touching two of agoraphobia's five situations, is likely to have agoraphobia. The other is the reason: if the situation is feared because it might directly cause harm (the plane might crash, the lift cable might snap, the dog might bite), the diagnosis leans towards specific phobia; if it is feared because escape or help would be hard if panic struck, it leans towards agoraphobia. The second boundary is with panic disorder. People with a specific phobia may panic when they meet the phobic stimulus, but those attacks are expected; only if they also have unexpected attacks, and worry about them, is panic disorder added. Exam trap Know the type of every common phobia. Claustrophobia (enclosed spaces, lifts) and fear of flying are situational ; acrophobia (heights), fear of storms and fear of water are natural environment ; fear of needles, blood or injury is blood-injection-injury ; fear of choking or vomiting is other . Situational phobias begin later than the other types. One feared situation is a specific phobia; two or more of agoraphobia's five, feared because escape would be hard, is agoraphobia. Blood-injection-injury phobia: the phobia that makes people faint Farhan, nineteen, a first-year engineering student in Hyderabad, came to the college counsellor after an embarrassing morning. A blood test was required for his hostel medical. He had felt the familiar dread for a week, and as the needle went in he grew hot, then cold and sweaty; the room went grey and he slid off the chair. He came round on the floor with his legs raised and a nurse fanning him. It had happened before: at twelve, watching a cousin's cut being stitched; at fifteen, at a school vaccination drive, which he had avoided ever since by forging a note. He had not been to a dentist in six years despite a painful tooth, he skipped any film his friends warned was "bloody", and he dreaded the thought that a relative might one day need him in a hospital. "My father is the same," he said. "He cannot even watch the cricket when a player is bleeding." Farhan's story shows what makes the blood-injection-injury type unlike every other phobia. In almost all phobias, meeting the feared object produces a surge of sympathetic arousal: heart rate and blood pressure rise and stay up while the fear lasts. Many people with these phobias, and with panic attacks, say that they feel they are about to faint, but they almost never do, precisely because their blood pressure is rising, not falling. People with blood-injection-injury phobia show a different pattern, called a diphasic vasovagal response because it has two phases. In the first phase, the sight of blood or a needle produces a brief acceleration of heart rate and a rise in blood pressure. In the second, the body overcorrects: heart rate slows, the blood vessels widen and blood pressure drops sharply. Less blood reaches the brain, the person feels light-headed and queasy, vision greys, and he or she may faint. The faint is a vasovagal syncope ("syncope" means a swoon caused by low blood pressure in the head; "vasovagal" refers to the blood vessels and the vagus nerve, which slows the heart). Barlow suggests that the overcorrection comes from an overreactive sinoaortic baroreflex arc , the reflex that normally brings blood pressure back down after a sudden rise, and that the tendency to overcorrect is inherited. Figure 6.6 shows the difference schematically. feared object appears resting level Heart rate and blood pressure Time after exposure (schematic, not real data) faints Most phobias: a sustained rise (people feel faint but rarely faint) Blood-injection-injury: brief rise, sharp fall All other types of phobia Blood-injection-injury Figure 6.6 A schematic (not measured data) of the diphasic vasovagal response. In most phobias heart rate and blood pressure rise and stay raised during exposure; in blood-injection-injury phobia a brief rise is followed by a sharp fall below the resting level, and the person may faint. Other features follow from this unusual physiology. Blood-injection-injury phobia runs in families more strongly than any other phobia, which fits the idea that what is inherited is the strong vasovagal tendency; the phobia then develops as a fear of having the response (the family figures are given in Section 6.7). Unlike the other types, it affects women and men nearly equally, and its average age of onset is about 9 years. Yet the reflex is not the whole story: many people with a strong fainting tendency never become phobic, because they cope (some learn on their own to tense their muscles when they see blood), and some people with little fainting tendency develop the phobia anyway. The costs are out of all proportion to how trivial the phobia sounds. People with blood-injection-injury phobia are often reluctant to seek medical care even when they need it. They miss vaccinations, put off blood tests that would detect diabetes or anaemia, avoid the dentist until a tooth must be extracted, and refuse to donate blood. A pregnant woman with the phobia may dread the repeated blood tests and examinations of antenatal care, and some avoid them. In a country that depends on mass immunisation drives and on blood tests for screening, this matters. Key study: applied tension (Öst and Sterner, 1987) Ordinary exposure therapy has a problem with this phobia: a patient who faints during exposure learns nothing except that the feared thing makes him faint. The Swedish psychologist Lars-Göran Öst and Ulf Sterner described a solution in 1987 in Behaviour Research and Therapy , which they called applied tension . The patient learns to tense the large muscles of the arms, legs and trunk, holding the tension until a feeling of warmth rises in the face, then releasing it without relaxing completely, and repeating the cycle. Tensing the muscles quickly raises blood pressure, which counteracts the second, fainting phase of the vasovagal response. The patient also learns to recognise the very first signs of a fall in blood pressure and to apply the tension at once, and then practises it while looking at pictures of wounds, watching films of surgery and finally having blood taken, so that the exposure can be completed without fainting. The broader lesson is that a treatment built on the physiology of a particular phobia works better than a general one. Öst and his colleagues later showed that many specific phobias, blood phobia among them, can be treated in a single intensive session of about 2 to 6 hours of guided exposure, followed by practice at home (one of their trials, published in 2001, treated children and adolescents), and Barlow notes that after such treatment the vasovagal tendency itself lessens considerably. Exposure therapy as a method is taught in Book 2, Section 4.3. Exam trap Blood-injection-injury phobia shows a diphasic vasovagal response : a brief rise in heart rate and blood pressure, then a drop , and possibly fainting . In every other phobia, and in panic attacks, blood pressure rises and the person feels faint but almost never faints; so "fainting" in a question points to blood-injection-injury phobia. The treatment designed for it is applied tension (tensing, not relaxing, the muscles), because relaxation would lower blood pressure further. It runs in families more strongly than any other phobia, begins at about 9, and affects the sexes nearly equally. Who develops specific phobia, and how it runs Specific phobia is one of the most common of all mental disorders. In the United States the 12-month prevalence is about 8 to 12 percent; in Europe it is similar or somewhat lower (about 6 percent), and in Asian, African and Latin American countries it is generally 2 to 4 percent. Among children across countries the average is about 5 percent (range 3 to 9 percent); among adolescents aged 13 to 17 in the United States it reaches about 16 percent; among older people it falls to about 3 to 5 percent, perhaps because the fears fade to a level below the threshold. Women are affected about twice as often as men across the types, with the blood-injection-injury type the exception. (Barlow gives a more lopsided ratio of about 4 to 1; the DSM-5-TR figure of about 2 to 1 is the safer one to quote.) Specific phobia usually begins in early childhood, most cases before the age of 10, with a median age of onset between 7 and 11 and a mean of about 10; Barlow notes that its onset is earlier than that of any anxiety disorder except separation anxiety disorder. Phobias that begin in childhood often wax and wane during childhood and adolescence, but those that persist into adulthood rarely remit without treatment. How do they begin? Sometimes after a frightening event with the object (being bitten by a dog, being stuck in a lift); sometimes after watching someone else go through one (seeing someone drown); sometimes after an unexpected panic attack in the situation that will later be feared; sometimes after being told about danger (extensive news coverage of a plane crash). These correspond to Stanley Rachman's three pathways to fear (direct conditioning, vicarious learning and information), which are explained in Section 6.8. But many people simply cannot remember how their phobia began. Phobias are often dismissed as harmless, and DSM-5-TR's figures show why that is a mistake. People with specific phobia show impairment in work, relationships and quality of life comparable to people with other anxiety disorders, and the impairment grows with the number of things feared. Specific phobia is linked to suicidal thoughts and attempts; one large ten-year German study of young people aged 14 to 24 estimated that 30 percent of first suicide attempts were attributable to specific phobia. Because it begins so early, it is usually the first disorder in a person's history, and it raises the risk of later anxiety, depressive, substance-related and somatic symptom disorders and of personality disorders, particularly dependent personality disorder. In older people the most common phobias are of the natural environment and of falling, which can shrink mobility and independence. The biological and psychological causes of the phobias are taught in Sections 6.7 and 6.8, and their drug treatment (little needed, since exposure works so well) in Section 6.9. The names of the phobias Indian entrance papers love to ask for the name of a phobia, and the names look forbidding until you see how they are built. Almost all of them join a Greek word (occasionally a Latin one) for the feared thing to the Greek phobos , fear. Learn the root and the name decodes itself: algos is pain, so algophobia is the fear of pain; nosos is disease, so nosophobia is the fear of disease; kyon (genitive kynos ) is dog, so cynophobia is the fear of dogs; haima is blood, so haematophobia (also written hemophobia or haemophobia) is the fear of blood. The same roots run through ordinary medical words, which is the best way to remember them: analgesic (a painkiller) contains algos ; nosology (the classification of diseases) contains nosos ; haemoglobin and haemorrhage contain haima ; Acropolis , the "high city" of Athens, contains akros , high; thanatology (the study of death) contains thanatos .
