Agoraphobia is the one name in the list that DSM-5-TR uses as the name of a disorder, and its literal meaning, "fear of the marketplace", is itself examined; Subsection 6.2.6 explains why the real theme is being trapped rather than open space. Claustrophobia is the only common name with a Latin root, from claustrum , an enclosed place, the word that also gives "cloister". Aerophobia is built from aer , air, and older lists such as Maser's define it as a fear of draughts and air currents; in modern use it means fear of flying (aviophobia, from the Latin avis , bird, is the other name). Hydrophobia is the name the papers give for a fear of water, but you should know that in medicine hydrophobia is also the old name for rabies, in which attempts to drink set off painful spasms of the throat, so that the patient comes to dread water; modern writers often prefer aquaphobia for the phobia. Mysophobia , from mysos , uncleanness, was coined in 1879 by the American neurologist William Alexander Hammond (1828 to 1900) while describing a patient who washed the hands again and again; what Hammond was describing would today usually be called obsessive-compulsive disorder. That history is a warning. A fear of germs that comes with intrusive thoughts of contamination and with repetitive washing to neutralise them is obsessive-compulsive disorder (Section 6.5), not a phobia; a fear of dirt that is simply avoided, without obsessions or rituals, may be a specific phobia. Xenophobia today usually means hostility to foreigners, which is a social attitude (the Social Psychology book), not a psychiatric disorder; and the wary distress of an eight-month-old baby on meeting a stranger is normal stranger anxiety (Section 6.1), not a phobia at all. Other names you may meet are built the same way: ailurophobia (cats, Greek ailouros ), apiphobia (bees, Latin apis ) and autophobia (being alone, Greek autos , self). The clinical point is the one Barlow makes about Maser's list: these names are not diagnoses. A clinician never writes "trypanophobia" in a case record. DSM-5-TR asks only for the type , so the names are translated: trypanophobia and haematophobia become specific phobia, blood-injection-injury type; claustrophobia and aerophobia, situational type; acrophobia, astraphobia and hydrophobia, natural environment type; cynophobia, arachnophobia and ophidiophobia, animal type. Glossophobia is not a specific phobia at all, because the fear is of being judged while speaking; it is social anxiety disorder with the performance only specifier (subsection 6.3.6). And nosophobia, a fear of having or catching a disease, may be a specific phobia of the "other" type (fear of contracting an illness) or, when the person is preoccupied with already having a serious illness, illness anxiety disorder (Chapter 7). Exam trap The specific phobia of pain is algophobia ( algos , pain, as in analgesic). The distractors are other real names: nosophobia is fear of disease ( nosos , as in nosology), cynophobia fear of dogs ( kyon , kynos ) and haematophobia fear of blood ( haima , as in haemoglobin). Decode any unfamiliar name by its root. Agoraphobia literally means fear of the marketplace ; claustrophobia (Latin claustrum ) is enclosed spaces; acrophobia is heights; nyctophobia is darkness; astraphobia is thunder and lightning; mysophobia is dirt and germs; trypanophobia is needles; glossophobia is public speaking. Social anxiety disorder: the fear of scrutiny Prakash, twenty-three, is in the final year of an MSc in chemistry in Mysuru. He is a good student on paper, and he is in trouble. He has not given a single seminar this year; twice he reported sick on the day. In practical classes he cannot pour from a burette while the instructor watches, because his hands shake and he is sure everyone can see. He eats in his hostel room rather than the mess, because he cannot lift a glass of water steadily with people around him. His viva voce is in six weeks, and he has been rehearsing answers aloud every night, word for word. At home in his village it is worse in a different way. His parents have arranged a bride-viewing visit, and for a month he has been dreading the moment when he must sit in the girl's family's front room, hold a cup of tea in front of her father and uncles, and make conversation. "They will see my hand shaking. My voice will go. They will think I am weak, or that something is wrong with me, and my parents will be shamed." He remembers when it began: in Class 8 he was asked to read a passage aloud, stumbled, and the class laughed. Yet with his two closest friends, at his own pace, Prakash is relaxed and funny. Prakash has social anxiety disorder , the disorder called social phobia until DSM-5 renamed it. Its essence, in DSM-5-TR's words, is a marked fear or anxiety about social situations in which the person may be scrutinised by others. Notice the word: scrutiny . The person with social anxiety disorder does not fear an object, as in a specific phobia, or being trapped, as in agoraphobia. He fears the eyes of other people, and what they will conclude. The criteria again fall into groups. Criterion A: the situations. Marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations involving possible scrutiny. DSM-5-TR gives three families: social interactions (having a conversation, meeting unfamiliar people), being observed (eating or drinking in front of others), and performing in front of others (giving a speech). In children the anxiety must occur in peer settings and not just with adults, because many children are shy with adults in a way that is entirely normal. Criterion B: the feared outcome. The person fears that he or she will act in a way, or show anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated: that it will be humiliating or embarrassing, will lead to rejection, or will offend others. The feared symptoms are typically the visible ones (blushing, trembling, sweating, stumbling over words, staring). Each leads to its own avoidance: a person who fears trembling may avoid drinking, eating, writing or pointing in public; one who fears sweating may avoid shaking hands or eating spicy food; one who fears blushing may avoid bright lights and intimate topics. Blushing is the hallmark physical sign of the disorder. Some people, more often men, fear and avoid urinating in a public toilet when others are present, called paruresis or "shy bladder". Criteria C and D: consistency and response. The social situations almost always provoke fear (occasional nervousness does not count), and they are avoided or endured with intense fear. In children the fear may show as crying, tantrums, freezing, clinging, shrinking or failing to speak. Avoidance can be extensive (not going to parties, refusing school) or subtle: over-preparing a speech, as Prakash does, diverting attention to others, limiting eye contact, keeping the hands in the pockets. Anticipatory anxiety can begin weeks before the event. Criterion E: out of proportion. The fear is out of proportion to the actual threat of being negatively evaluated, and to the sociocultural context. If the person is actually being bullied, the anxiety may be realistic. Because people with the disorder overestimate the consequences of social situations, the clinician makes the judgement. Culture matters: in some cultures, behaviour that would look socially anxious elsewhere is the correct way to behave. In many Indian families a young person who lowers his eyes, speaks softly and says little in front of elders is showing respect, not symptoms. Criteria F and G: persistence and impairment. The fear typically lasts 6 months or more, which separates the disorder from the passing social fears of childhood and adolescence, and it must interfere significantly with routine, work or study, or relationships, or cause marked distress. DSM-5-TR's example is precise: a person who is afraid of public speaking does not have the disorder if speaking is never required at work or in class and the fear does not distress him, but if he avoids or is passed over for the job or course he really wants because of it, the impairment criterion is met. Criteria H, I and J: other explanations. The fear is not due to a substance or medical condition, not better explained by another mental disorder such as panic disorder, body dysmorphic disorder or autism spectrum disorder, and if a medical condition that might draw attention is present (Parkinson's disease, obesity, disfigurement from burns or injury), the fear is clearly unrelated to it or excessive. DSM-5-TR offers one specifier. Performance only is used when the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public. It suits musicians, dancers, actors, athletes and people whose work or study requires regular presentations, and it describes people who do not fear or avoid ordinary social situations at all. A young Bharatanatyam dancer who is relaxed and talkative at parties but trembles, feels sick and fears her memory will go blank before every performance fits this specifier; so does the student who is at ease in the canteen but cannot face the viva. Barlow gives sporting examples: professional baseball players who suddenly could not make a routine throw to first base when they had time to think about it, and the actress Scarlett Johansson, who stayed away from the Broadway stage for years because of performance anxiety. DSM-5 created this specifier in place of DSM-IV's "generalised" specifier, which had marked the opposite end, fear of most social situations. Glossophobia, the fear of public speaking (subsection 6.3.5), is the most common performance fear. Several associated features help recognise the disorder in an interview. People with social anxiety disorder may be unassertive or excessively submissive, may hold their bodies rigidly, avoid eye contact or speak very softly, and disclose little about themselves. They may choose jobs without social contact, live at home longer, and delay marriage. Many drink before a social event to steady themselves, and a few go on to an alcohol use disorder. Older adults with the disorder may fear that a tremor, a failing memory for names or a hearing problem will be noticed. Clinical link Social anxiety disorder is among the most under-treated of all disorders. DSM-5-TR reports that in high-income countries only about half of the people who have it ever seek treatment, and those who do typically wait 15 to 20 years. The disorder itself keeps people out of the clinic, because seeing a professional means meeting a stranger who will evaluate you. The treatments with good evidence are exposure (Book 2, Section 4.3), cognitive therapy built on the Clark and Wells model of social anxiety, which explains how self-focused attention and safety behaviours keep the fear alive (Book 2, Section 5.6.4, and Section 6.8 of this chapter), and social skills training where skills are genuinely lacking (Book 2, Section 4.7). The drugs, including the beta blockers used for performance anxiety, are compared in Section 6.9. Social anxiety disorder: who has it, how it runs, and what it is not The 12-month prevalence of social anxiety disorder in the United States is about 7 percent. Using the same interview, most of the rest of the world reports much lower figures, clustering around 0.5 to 2 percent, with a median of 2.3 percent in Europe; prevalence appears to be rising in the United States and in East Asian countries. Among young adolescents (13 to 17) the rate is roughly half the adult rate, and it falls after 65, to between 2 and 5 percent of older adults in North America, Europe and Australia. In the general population women have the disorder more often than men, with odds ratios between 1.5 and 2.2, and the gap is widest in adolescents and young adults. In clinical samples, however, the numbers of men and women are equal or men are slightly more numerous, probably because social expectations push men to seek help when the disorder blocks a career or marriage. (Barlow's text puts the sex ratio close to 50:50; DSM-5-TR's figures, which keep community and clinic samples apart, are the safer ones to quote.) The disorder begins early. The median age of onset in the United States is 13 years, and three-quarters of people with it date its onset to between 8 and 15. It may grow slowly out of childhood shyness or social inhibition, or it may follow a stressful or humiliating experience, such as being bullied or, like Prakash, being laughed at while reading aloud. A first onset in adulthood is relatively rare and usually follows a humiliating event or a change of role that brings new social demands (a promotion, marriage into a family of a different social standing). The course is variable, short and fluctuating for some, chronic for others, and among people who reach clinics it tends to be particularly persistent; DSM-5-TR notes that a fear of dating may fade after marriage and return after divorce. Social anxiety disorder commonly precedes the other disorders that accompany it: other anxiety disorders, major depressive disorder (chronic isolation can lead to depression) and substance use disorders, especially alcohol used as self-medication. It is frequently comorbid with avoidant personality disorder. Its consequences include leaving school early, lower employment, income and quality of life, fewer and less supportive friendships, and, particularly among men, remaining single. The roles of temperament (behavioural inhibition, studied by Jerome Kagan) and genes are taught in Section 6.7, and the evolutionary preparedness to fear angry and critical faces, with the cognitive model, in Section 6.8. Culture shapes the fear itself. In Japan and Korea a syndrome called taijin kyofusho ("fear of interpersonal relations") centres not on embarrassing oneself, as social anxiety disorder usually does, but on offending or making other people uncomfortable: the fear that one's gaze, one's blushing, one's facial expression or one's body odour is upsetting to others ("my gaze upsets people, so they look away and avoid me"). DSM-5-TR notes that the fear is sometimes held with delusional intensity, and that while many presentations meet the criteria for social anxiety disorder, others fit body dysmorphic disorder or delusional disorder. Barlow reports that among Japanese sufferers men outnumber women, by about 3 to 2. The form centred on body odour resembles olfactory reference disorder, which is described with the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders in Section 6.6, and the cultural syndromes in general are taught in Chapter 1. DSM-5-TR adds that in strongly collectivist cultures a fear of offending others may be the main fear even in people diagnosed with social anxiety disorder. Indian context Indian settings put social evaluation at the centre of many life events. The viva voce and the group discussion in admissions and job interviews, reading aloud or answering questions in class, the arranged-marriage "bride-viewing" or "girl-seeing" visit where a young man or woman is watched and assessed by a whole family, speaking at a family function, and even the morning school assembly can all be the situations a socially anxious person dreads. A clinician should keep two things apart: modesty, reticence and deference before elders, which are culturally expected and are not symptoms (Criterion E), and a fear of being judged that is out of proportion, is felt almost every time, and makes the person avoid or dread what he or she needs to do. Prakash, who has turned down two seminar slots and is planning to miss his own viva, has crossed that line. Because social anxiety is woven into so many other conditions, the differential diagnosis is examined heavily, and DSM-5-TR spends unusual care on it. The most important comparisons are set out in Table 6.10. Two need a further word. Ordinary shyness (social reticence) is a common personality trait and, by itself, is not pathological; some societies even value it. Only about 12 percent of people in the United States who call themselves shy meet the criteria for social anxiety disorder, and the diagnosis is made only when the shyness causes significant impairment and all the criteria are met. Avoidant personality disorder (Chapter 11) is the closest neighbour. It shows a broader pattern of avoidance, more impairment, a strongly and pervasively negative view of oneself, a sense that rejection means one is worthless, and a feeling of not fitting in that dates from early childhood. The two often occur together: social anxiety disorder is more often comorbid with avoidant personality disorder than with any other personality disorder, and avoidant personality disorder is more often comorbid with social anxiety disorder than with any other anxiety disorder. It is not fear of one object (specific phobia) or of being trapped (agoraphobia). Its duration, like that of specific phobia and agoraphobia, is typically 6 months , not 1 week, 1 month or 3 months. In children the anxiety must appear with peers , not only with adults. The only specifier is performance only (fear restricted to speaking or performing in public), which replaced DSM-IV's "generalised" specifier. She teaches mathematics at a girls' school in Nagpur and takes tuition classes at home in the evenings. She arrived at the psychiatry outpatient department of a medical college hospital holding a letter from her family physician: "Tension headaches, poor sleep, epigastric discomfort for two years. ECG, thyroid function and endoscopy normal. ?Anxiety. Kindly evaluate." When the psychologist asked what she worried about, she laughed. "What do I not worry about?" Then the list came out, one item tumbling over the next. Her husband rides his scooter on the ring road, and every evening, from half past six until she hears the gate, she pictures the trucks. Her daughter's Class 12 board examinations are four months away. The bank may raise the interest on their home loan. Her mother's sugar is not well controlled. She may have offended a neighbour by forgetting to invite her to a function. The milk might boil over while she checks the students' notebooks. "When one thing is settled, another one comes and sits in its place. I know most of it is useless. My husband says I borrow trouble from tomorrow. But I cannot switch it off." Her neck and shoulders, she said, feel "like stone"; she is tired by noon, snaps at her students and her daughter, loses the thread while marking papers, and lies awake going over the next day. She has never had a sudden attack of terror, she performs no rituals, and although she is weary she is not chiefly sad. "I have been a tension type since school," she said. "These last two years it is too much." Sunita has generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), the most ordinary looking of the anxiety disorders and, for most of the history of psychiatry, the hardest to pin down. A spider phobia has a spider; panic disorder has its attacks. GAD has no single object and no dramatic event. Its core is a mental activity that everyone engages in, worry, carried on too much, about too many things, for too long, and with too little control. This section first teaches GAD, from its history to its course, and then turns to two anxiety disorders that usually begin in childhood: separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism. The causes of all three are taught in Sections 6.7 and 6.8 and their drug treatment in Section 6.9; here the task is to recognise them and to tell them from their look-alikes. From free-floating anxiety to a diagnosis Chronic, diffuse anxiety is one of the oldest complaints in medicine. Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century physicians used the word pantophobia ("fear of everything") for patients who seemed afraid of all things at once, and the American neurologist George Miller Beard , who popularised neurasthenia from 1869 (a diagnosis taught in Chapter 7), listed "pantaphobia", a fear of everything, among its many forms. The decisive description came from Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939). In 1895 he carved an "anxiety neurosis" out of neurasthenia (Section 6.1 tells that story) and named as its central symptom anxious expectation : a constant readiness to expect the worst. His example could have come from Sunita's clinic. A woman who suffers from anxious expectation, he wrote, will think of pneumonia every time her husband coughs with a cold, and in her mind's eye will see his funeral go past. Freud described this state as a quantum of anxiety "in a freely floating state", ready to attach itself to any idea that came along, and from that phrase came the term free-floating anxiety : anxiety that is not bound to any particular object or situation but drifts from one concern to the next. For decades afterwards clinicians assumed, as Barlow and Durand put it, that people who were generally anxious had simply not yet focused their anxiety on anything specific. The first American manuals followed that view. DSM-I (1952) had an "anxiety reaction" for diffuse anxiety that was neither tied to particular situations, as in the phobic reactions, nor controlled by a particular defence, and DSM-II (1968) renamed it "anxiety neurosis", a single category that covered both chronic apprehension and sudden attacks. The split came with DSM-III in 1980. Partly because the attacks and the chronic anxiety responded differently to the antidepressant imipramine (Section 6.2 tells how Donald Klein's observation helped separate them), anxiety neurosis was divided into panic disorder and generalised anxiety disorder. GAD was born. It was a weak birth. DSM-III asked for only one month of generalised, persistent anxiety, with symptoms from three of four broad groups (motor tension, autonomic hyperactivity, apprehensive expectation, and vigilance and scanning). So loose a definition caught almost everyone who was anxious. In 1986 David H. Barlow and his colleagues pointed out that DSM-III's GAD was largely a residual diagnosis: patients with other anxiety disorders nearly always met its criteria too, so the label added little. They also made a suggestion that shaped everything that followed. There might be two kinds of "generalised anxiety": a residual kind, the apprehension that accompanies any anxiety disorder, and a qualitatively different syndrome of chronic worry that deserved its own name. The revisions moved steadily in that direction. DSM-III-R (1987) raised the duration to six months and put worry at the centre: "unrealistic or excessive anxiety and worry (apprehensive expectation) about two or more life circumstances", with at least six of eighteen listed symptoms. DSM-IV (1994) emphasised that the worry is hard to control, cut the eighteen symptoms to six (research had shown that the bodily profile of GAD differs from that of the other anxiety disorders, so most of the autonomic items of the older list, such as a racing heart, were dropped), required clinically significant distress or impairment, and absorbed the childhood diagnosis of overanxious disorder into GAD, which is why the modern criteria carry a note about children. DSM-5 (2013) changed almost nothing. A review led by Gavin Andrews and colleagues (2010) had proposed renaming the condition "generalised worry disorder" and adding a criterion for the behaviours that worry produces (avoidance, over-preparation, procrastination, reassurance seeking), and others argued that GAD is so close to major depression that both should be grouped as "distress disorders". Neither proposal was adopted, and DSM-5-TR (2022) keeps the DSM-IV definition. The lesson of this history is the one Barlow drew in 1986: what makes GAD a disorder in its own right is not anxiety in general but a particular way of worrying. Exam trap GAD as a named diagnosis dates from DSM-III (1980) , when anxiety neurosis was split into GAD and panic disorder. Its first duration rule was one month ; the six-month rule and the central place of worry date from DSM-III-R (1987) ; the six symptoms and the emphasis on uncontrollable worry from DSM-IV (1994) . "Free-floating anxiety" goes back to Freud's 1895 description of anxious expectation in anxiety neurosis. Do not credit Freud with the word neurosis itself, which was William Cullen's (Section 6.1). The criteria for generalised anxiety disorder, group by group The DSM-5-TR criteria make sense once you see that each one answers a question a sceptic would ask: everyone worries, so what makes this worry a disorder? The answers come in four groups: what the worry is like (criteria A and B), what comes with it (C), what it costs (D), and what else it might be (E and F). The worry itself (A and B). Criterion A asks for excessive anxiety and worry, which DSM-5-TR glosses as apprehensive expectation , occurring more days than not for at least six months, about a number of events or activities such as work or school performance. Each phrase does work. Thomas D. Borkovec and his colleagues in 1983 defined worry as a chain of thoughts and images, loaded with negative feeling and relatively uncontrollable, that represents an attempt at mental problem solving on an issue whose outcome is uncertain but might be bad. Notice that worry is mostly verbal ("What if the bus is late? Then I will miss the train. Then ...") and points to the future. "Excessive" means that the intensity, duration or frequency of the worry is out of proportion to the actual likelihood or impact of the feared event: Sunita's husband is a careful rider on a road he has used for twenty years, yet she pictures his death every evening. "More days than not" is a deliberate softening; the worry need not be present every single day, but it must be the usual state of affairs. "A number of events or activities" is what makes the disorder generalised: one dominant fear points to a different diagnosis. Criterion B adds that the person finds the worry difficult to control. This is the heart of the matter. People with GAD usually know they worry too much; what they cannot do is stop, put the worry aside when something more pressing comes up, or keep it from intruding on the task in front of them. The company the worry keeps (C). The anxiety and worry must come with at least three of six symptoms, at least some of them present more days than not over the same six months (Figure 6.7). The six are restlessness or feeling keyed up or on edge; being easily fatigued; difficulty concentrating or the mind going blank; irritability; muscle tension; and sleep disturbance (difficulty falling or staying asleep, or restless, unsatisfying sleep). Look at the list and you will see that it describes a mind and body held in a state of readiness for a threat that never quite arrives: the muscles braced, the attention divided, the temper short, the sleep shallow, and the person exhausted by the effort. Sunita had all six. For children only one of the six is required, a rule that Barlow's group tested in children and adolescents and found to work (Tracey, Chorpita, Douban and Barlow 1997). Excessive worry about many events, hard to control Restlessness, feeling keyed up or on edge Easily fatigued Difficulty concentrating, mind going blank Irritability Muscle tension Sleep disturbance: poor or restless sleep Three or more in adults, one in children; more days than not, for at least 6 months Figure 6.7 The shape of generalised anxiety disorder in DSM-5-TR. Worry that is excessive, spread across many events and hard to control sits at the hub; the six associated symptoms around it describe a body and mind held in readiness. Notice what is missing from the ring: a pounding heart and breathlessness, the signs of panic. The cost (D). The anxiety, worry or physical symptoms must cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning. This is the threshold that separates a worrier from a patient (the four Ds of abnormality are taught in Book 2, Section 1.6.5). Sunita was still teaching, but she was snapping at her students, losing her place in her marking and spending her evenings in dread; that was enough. The exclusions (E and F). Criterion E rules out anxiety that is the physiological effect of a substance or medication (heavy coffee drinking produces caffeine-induced anxiety disorder; withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines produces anxiety too, Chapter 10) or of another medical condition (DSM-5-TR names hyperthyroidism, and also pheochromocytoma, a hormone-secreting tumour of the adrenal gland). This is why Sunita's physician checked her thyroid before referring her (the medical mimics of anxiety are listed in Section 6.1). Criterion F rules out worry that belongs to another mental disorder. DSM-5-TR's list is long, but it follows one logic: in each case the worry has a single home. It may be worry about having panic attacks (panic disorder), about negative evaluation (social anxiety disorder), about contamination or other obsessions (obsessive-compulsive disorder), about separation from attachment figures (separation anxiety disorder), about reminders of a trauma (posttraumatic stress disorder), about gaining weight (anorexia nervosa), about physical complaints (somatic symptom disorder), about perceived flaws in appearance (body dysmorphic disorder), about having a serious illness (illness anxiety disorder), or about the content of delusions (schizophrenia or delusional disorder). GAD is what remains when the worry has no single home and wanders across the whole of life. Exam trap The DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR duration for GAD in adults is at least 6 months , more days than not. The wrong options all come from somewhere: 1 month was DSM-III's original GAD rule and is today the rule for panic disorder's period of concern and for selective mutism; 3 months is the window within which an adjustment disorder must begin after its stressor (Chapter 7); 12 months belongs to no anxiety disorder. The defining symptom of GAD is persistent, excessive worry that is hard to control. Mania and mood swings are mood symptoms (Chapter 5) and hallucinations are psychotic symptoms (Chapter 4); none is a criterion of GAD. Count carefully too: three of six symptoms in adults, but only one in children. What GAD worry is like, and how it differs from ordinary worry Ask people with GAD what they worry about and you will hear the ordinary business of life. DSM-5-TR lists job responsibilities, health and finances, the health of family members, misfortune to their children, and minor matters such as household chores or being late for appointments. The minor matters are the giveaway. When people with anxiety disorders were asked "Do you worry excessively about minor things?", every one of those with GAD said yes, against about half of those with other anxiety disorders (Barlow 2002, reported by Barlow and Durand), a difference large enough to be statistically significant. Large events quickly become the focus too, and the focus never stays put: as soon as one concern is settled another takes its place, which is exactly what Sunita meant when she said the next worry "comes and sits in its place". The content shifts with age, though the disorder itself looks much the same across the lifespan. Children and adolescents with GAD worry mainly about their competence and the quality of their performance at school or in sport, even when nobody is evaluating them; they may worry about being on time, or about catastrophes such as earthquakes or nuclear war. They tend to be over-conforming, perfectionistic and unsure of themselves, redo work that is not perfect, and seek reassurance again and again ("Ma, will I pass? Are you sure?"). Older adults worry most about health, and in the frail elderly a fear of falling may shrink daily life to a single room. Where, then, is the line between Sunita and every other mother in Nagpur who worries about a daughter's board examinations? DSM-5-TR draws it with three features, summarised in Table 6.11. First, GAD worries are excessive and interfere with functioning, whereas everyday worries feel manageable and can be put off when something more pressing arises. Second, GAD worries are more pervasive, pronounced and distressing, last longer, and often arise with no precipitating event; and the wider the range of life circumstances a person worries about, the more likely the diagnosis. Third, ordinary worries rarely come with physical symptoms such as restlessness and feeling keyed up. Table 6.11 Everyday worry and the worry of generalised anxiety disorder (after DSM-5-TR). Feature Everyday worry Worry in GAD Size In proportion to the real likelihood and impact of the event Excessive: out of proportion to the likelihood or impact Control Manageable; can be postponed when something more pressing comes up Hard to control; intrudes on the task in hand Range One or two live concerns Many areas of life, including minor matters; hops from topic to topic Trigger and duration Usually set off by a real event; fades when it is resolved Often no precipitant; more days than not for at least 6 months Body Seldom accompanied by physical symptoms Muscle tension, restlessness, fatigue, poor sleep Cost Little interference with work, study or relationships Clinically significant distress or impairment The bodily side of GAD holds a surprise. You might expect a person who worries all day to have a heart that races all day. It does not. Panic is a surge of the sympathetic nervous system: palpitations, sweating, trembling, breathlessness. GAD, by contrast, is marked by muscle tension, mental agitation, fatigue, irritability and poor sleep. When researchers measured how people respond to a stressor, those with GAD showed smaller responses than people with other anxiety disorders on most physiological measures, including heart rate, blood pressure, skin conductance and breathing rate (Borkovec and Hu 1990). For this reason they have been called autonomic restrictors (Barlow and colleagues 1996; Thayer, Friedman and Borkovec 1996). The one physiological measure that consistently separates people with GAD from non-anxious people is muscle tension: they are chronically tense. DSM-5-TR adds trembling, twitching, shakiness and aching muscles, sweating, nausea and diarrhoea, an exaggerated startle response, and frequent stress-related conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and headaches, while noting that racing heart, shortness of breath and dizziness are less prominent than in panic disorder. Why should worry go with restricted arousal but tense muscles? Borkovec's answer, that verbal worry is a way of avoiding the vivid images that would trigger real fear, is a theory of cause and is taught in Section 6.8. Culture shapes what the clinician first sees. DSM-5-TR notes that in some cultural contexts the bodily symptoms dominate the presentation and in others the cognitive ones do, and that the topics people worry about are culturally specific, so a clinician must judge excessiveness against what is usual in the person's setting. Sunita's route to the clinic, through two years of headaches, "gas" and sleeplessness taken to a general practitioner, is typical. Barlow and Durand report that only about 10 percent of patients at specialist anxiety clinics have GAD, against 30 to 50 percent with panic disorder, largely because people with GAD take their complaints to primary care doctors, where they are found in large numbers. Exam trap A question asks what the sufferer of GAD experiences, and the keyed answer is continued apprehension about unspecified things : free-floating apprehension that is not tied to one object or situation. Do not misread "unspecified" as "without content" (Sunita can list her worries); it means that no single object or theme defines the anxiety. The distractors each name another disorder. "Fear of fear" (Goldstein and Chambless 1978) is the fear of one's own bodily sensations in panic disorder and agoraphobia (Section 6.2). Continual flashbacks to past events are re-experiencing in PTSD (Chapter 7). A desire to check that the environment is safe is best read as the checking of OCD (Section 6.5), although it could also describe the hypervigilance of PTSD; either way it is not GAD, whose worry brings no ritual. Generalised anxiety disorder in ICD-10 and ICD-11 The two editions of the WHO classification handle GAD a little differently from DSM, and examiners like the differences. ICD-10 places generalised anxiety disorder (F41.1) among the "other anxiety disorders" (F41), next to panic disorder (F41.0) and mixed anxiety and depressive disorder (F41.2, taught in Chapter 5), and its category explicitly includes the older labels anxiety neurosis, anxiety reaction and anxiety state while excluding neurasthenia. ICD-10's clinical guidelines describe anxiety that is generalised and persistent and "free-floating", and ask for primary symptoms of anxiety on most days for at least several weeks at a time, and usually several months. The symptoms are grouped under three headings: apprehension (worries about future misfortunes, feeling on edge, difficulty concentrating), motor tension (restless fidgeting, tension headaches, trembling, inability to relax) and autonomic overactivity (light-headedness, sweating, a fast heart or fast breathing, epigastric discomfort, dizziness, dry mouth). ICD-10's separate research criteria are stricter: at least six months of prominent tension, worry and apprehension about everyday events, with at least four symptoms from a list of twenty-two, one of them autonomic. ICD-10 also did not allow the diagnosis when the full criteria for phobic anxiety, panic, obsessive-compulsive or hypochondriacal disorder were met. ICD-11 (code 6B00, in the grouping "anxiety or fear-related disorders") describes marked symptoms of anxiety that persist for at least several months, for more days than not, shown either as general apprehension (which it calls "free-floating anxiety") or as excessive worry about multiple everyday events, most often family, health, finances, and school or work. Worry about everyday events was thus added as an alternative to general apprehension. The accompanying symptoms (muscle tension or motor restlessness, sympathetic overactivity, nervousness, difficulty concentrating, irritability, sleep disturbance) are listed without a fixed count, the symptoms must cause significant distress or impairment, and, unlike ICD-10, ICD-11 allows GAD to be diagnosed alongside other mental disorders. Exam trap Only DSM-5-TR (and ICD-10's research criteria) fixes the duration of GAD at 6 months . The ICD-10 clinical guidelines say "at least several weeks at a time, and usually several months"; ICD-11 says " at least several months ", more days than not, with no fixed number of months and no fixed symptom count (the practice-mock explanation that says otherwise is flagged in Section 6.1). If a question asks for the DSM-5-TR minimum, the answer is 6 months; if it asks what ICD-11 requires, the answer is several months. Who develops generalised anxiety disorder, and what becomes of it DSM-5-TR gives a 12-month prevalence of 2.9 percent among adults and 0.9 percent among adolescents in the United States community; around the world the mean 12-month figure is 1.3 percent, with a range from 0.2 to 4.3 percent. Barlow and Durand, quoting the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, give 3.1 percent for a year and 5.7 percent for a lifetime. DSM-5-TR's lifetime figure is higher still, 9.0 percent, because it is a lifetime morbid risk : a projection of the proportion of people who will develop the disorder by the end of a normal lifespan, which counts the young people in a survey who have not yet reached the age of onset. (A lifetime prevalence, by contrast, counts only those who have had the disorder up to the day of the interview.) Women and girls are at least twice as likely as men and boys to have GAD; about two-thirds of the people with GAD in community surveys, and 55 to 60 percent of those presenting to clinics, are women. The 12-month prevalence among older adults, including people over 75, is 2.8 to 3.1 percent in the United States, Israel and Europe. People from high-income countries are more likely than those from low- and middle-income countries to report a lifetime history, and people of European descent meet the criteria more often than people of Asian and African descent, although the reasons are not clear. When does it start? DSM-5-TR gives a mean age at onset of 35 years in North America, later than any other anxiety disorder, and says the disorder rarely begins before adolescence; Barlow and Durand give a median of 31, from interview data. The two figures are not in conflict. A median is the midpoint of the ages at onset, whereas a mean is pulled upwards by the long tail of people whose GAD begins in middle or late life, so in a skewed distribution like this one the mean lies above the median; the two figures also come from different studies. A deeper puzzle is that Barlow and Durand describe GAD as having an earlier and more gradual onset than most anxiety disorders, which seems to contradict DSM-5-TR. The puzzle dissolves once you ask what is being dated. Many people with GAD, like Sunita, say they have felt anxious and nervous all their lives, and DSM-5-TR explains that excessive worry may begin early in life as an anxious temperament and only later reach the threshold of the disorder. The age at which the full criteria are first met is late; the age at which the person first remembers being a worrier is early (the temperament itself, and the genes behind it, are taught in Section 6.7). Once established, GAD is chronic. Its symptoms wax and wane across the lifespan, moving between full and subthreshold forms, and DSM-5-TR says that rates of full remission are very low. One study found only an 8 percent probability of becoming symptom-free after two years (Yonkers and colleagues 1996), and Bruce and colleagues (2005) found that twelve years after an episode began there was only a 58 percent chance of having recovered, with 45 percent of those who recovered relapsing later (both reported by Barlow and Durand). The earlier the onset, the more comorbidity and impairment. The cost is high: most adults with GAD outside institutions are moderately to seriously disabled, the disorder accounts for an estimated 110 million disability days a year in the United States, and it is linked to poorer work performance, heavier use of medical services and a raised risk of coronary disease. It is also linked to suicidal thoughts and behaviour even after other disorders are taken into account; in psychological autopsy studies GAD is the anxiety disorder most often diagnosed in people who died by suicide. In older adults the use of minor tranquillisers is strikingly high, and the benzodiazepines bring their own dangers of confusion, falls and hip fractures (Section 6.9). Pure GAD is the exception. People who meet its criteria are likely to have met, or to meet now, the criteria for other anxiety disorders and above all for major depression, and DSM-5-TR traces this overlap to a shared temperament of negative affectivity (neuroticism) and to shared genetic and environmental risk (the genetics are taught in Section 6.7). In women the comorbidity is mostly with other anxiety disorders and depression; in men it more often extends to substance use. The closeness of GAD and depression is why some researchers wanted to group them together as "distress disorders", and it is why both classifications offer a home for people with both kinds of symptoms below full threshold: ICD-10's mixed anxiety and depressive disorder (F41.2) and DSM-5-TR's "with anxious distress" specifier for depressive episodes, both taught in Chapter 5. Telling generalised anxiety disorder from its neighbours Because GAD is defined partly by what it is not, the differential diagnosis is half the work. Start with normal worry (Table 6.11). Then rule out the medical and substance causes (criterion E): an overactive thyroid, a pheochromocytoma, or simply eight cups of strong coffee a day. Then ask, for each worry, whether it has a single home in another disorder (criterion F). In social anxiety disorder the anticipatory anxiety is about upcoming situations in which the person will be watched or judged, whereas a person with GAD worries whether or not anyone is evaluating them. In separation anxiety disorder the worry is only about separation from attachment figures. In illness anxiety disorder the only fear is of having a serious illness oneself, whereas in GAD health is just one item on a long list. Panic attacks can occur in GAD, but attacks that are set off by worry do not make panic disorder; only unexpected attacks followed by persistent concern about them do (Section 6.2). Three neighbours need a closer look. The first is obsessive-compulsive disorder. GAD worries are about forthcoming real-life problems, and what is abnormal is their excess; OCD obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images, often odd or magical in content, that the person tries to neutralise, usually with a compulsion. The distinction is set out in full, along with depressive rumination and delusion, in Table 6.14 in Section 6.5. The second is depression. Depressive rumination dwells on the past (loss, failure, guilt) in a low mood, whereas GAD worry runs ahead into the future; when the worry is severe enough in a depressed person, both diagnoses may be given. The third is the stress-related group of Chapter 7. Anxiety is always present in posttraumatic stress disorder, and GAD is not diagnosed if the worry is better explained by PTSD; and an adjustment disorder with anxiety begins within three months of an identifiable stressor and does not persist more than six months after the stressor and its consequences end, whereas GAD needs no stressor and runs for years. Clinical link A useful interview question for suspected GAD is: "If this particular problem were solved tomorrow, would you stop worrying?" People with an adjustment problem say yes; people with GAD usually smile, as Sunita did, and say that something else would take its place. The treatments with the best evidence are cognitive behavioural therapy, applied relaxation (Book 2, Section 4.8.4) and metacognitive therapy (Book 2, Section 5.10.3), and the SSRIs and SNRIs among drugs (Section 6.9); much GAD is first treated in primary care, which is why it sits at the base of stepped-care models (Book 2, Section 5.11.5). Separation anxiety disorder Kunal is 8 and in Class 3 at an English-medium school in Kolkata. In the summer his grandmother, who had lived with the family since he was born, died after a short illness, and two months later his father was admitted to hospital for a heart procedure. His father is home and well now, but Kunal is not. For six weeks he has cried and clung to his mother every school morning, complaining of stomach ache and twice vomiting at the school gate; on Sundays he is perfectly well. When she goes to the market he follows her from room to room, or stands at the window until she returns. He has asked her a dozen times what would happen "if you also go to hospital". He will not sleep in his own bed and makes his way into his parents' bed every night, and twice he has woken screaming from a dream in which the house was on fire and he could not find her. His teacher reports that at school he asks to phone home, and the school counsellor has started to use a phrase the mother had not heard before: separation anxiety. Some anxiety about separation is a normal and healthy part of growing up. Around the first birthday infants begin to protest when a parent leaves and to be wary of strangers ( stranger anxiety ), and DSM-5-TR points out that these periods of heightened separation anxiety may actually indicate that a secure attachment relationship is developing (attachment theory is taught in the Developmental Psychology book). The fear normally fades through the preschool years as the child learns that the parent who leaves comes back. The disorder called separation anxiety disorder is the persistence or return of this fear beyond the age at which it is expected, and at a level that disrupts life: developmentally inappropriate and excessive fear or anxiety about separation from the people to whom the person is attached, the attachment figures . DSM-5-TR asks for at least three of eight signs. They fall naturally into three groups, set out in Table 6.12: distress and worry (distress at separation, worry about harm coming to the attachment figure, worry about some event that would separate them), avoidance (refusing to go out or to school, fearing being alone, refusing to sleep away from the attachment figure), and the signs that appear at night and in the body (nightmares about separation and physical complaints). Kunal shows seven of the eight. Table 6.12 The eight signs of separation anxiety disorder, grouped (at least three are needed). Repeated physical complaints when separation happens or is anticipated Headache, stomach ache, nausea, vomiting Palpitations, dizziness, feeling faint (rare in young children) The remaining criteria set the threshold. Criterion B asks that the fear, anxiety or avoidance last at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents (under 18) and typically 6 months or more in adults, the adult figure being a general guide applied with some flexibility. The short window for children is deliberate: a child who misses a month of school is already being harmed, and waiting six months would cost a school year. Criterion C asks for clinically significant distress or impairment. Criterion D rules out look-alikes: refusing to leave home because of an excessive resistance to change in autism spectrum disorder; delusions or hallucinations about separation in a psychotic disorder; refusing to go out without a trusted companion in agoraphobia, where the fear is of being trapped or helpless if panic strikes rather than of being away from a loved one; worries about ill health or harm coming to others that are only part of a wider pattern in GAD; and concerns about one's own illness in illness anxiety disorder. Two of the associated features are easy to mistake for something worse. Alone at night, young children with the disorder may report seeing people peering into their room or feeling eyes staring at them. These are not hallucinations: they are misperceptions of real stimuli, they occur only in particular situations such as the dark, and they vanish when the attachment figure is present. And when they are forced to separate, children may become angry or even aggressive towards the adult forcing them, which can look like oppositional defiance; DSM-5-TR advises diagnosing oppositional defiant disorder only when the defiance appears in situations that have nothing to do with separation. The most common and most costly consequence in childhood is school refusal , a child's persistent difficulty in attending school because of emotional distress. School refusal is a behaviour, not a diagnosis, and the clinician's job is to find out what the child fears. Barlow and Durand draw the classic distinction. In what used to be called school phobia the fear is of something at school (a teacher, a bully, a test, the toilets), and the child can leave the parent quite happily to go anywhere other than school; in separation anxiety the act of leaving the parent is what provokes the fear, wherever the child is going. DSM-5-TR adds two more possibilities: school avoidance driven by fear of being judged negatively, which points to social anxiety disorder (Section 6.3), and truancy in conduct disorder, where anxiety is not the reason and the child stays away from home rather than running back to it. Kunal, whose stomach aches vanished every Sunday and whose fear centred on his mother's safety, was a clear case of separation anxiety. Until DSM-5 the disorder lived among the "disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence", and DSM-IV required onset before age 18. Research forced a change. In an analysis of the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, M. Katherine Shear and her colleagues (2006) found that separation anxiety, if untreated, extended into adulthood in about 35 percent of cases, that about 6.6 percent of adults met the criteria at some point in their lives, and that in some people the disorder began in adulthood rather than continuing from childhood (reported by Barlow and Durand). The focus of the adult's anxiety is the same as the child's: that harm will befall loved ones during separation. Adults with the disorder are typically over-concerned about their children, spouses, parents and even pets, text or phone them throughout the day, may be unable to sleep in a hotel or to take a job that involves travel, and often reorganise their work to stay near their attachment figures. DSM-5 accordingly moved separation anxiety disorder into the anxiety disorders chapter and dropped the age limit, and it now stands first in that chapter, which is ordered by typical age at onset (Section 6.1). DSM-5-TR estimates the 6- to 12-month prevalence in children at about 4 percent (Barlow and Durand cite 4.1 percent from Shear's group), 1.6 percent among adolescents in the United States, and 0.9 to 1.9 percent among adults in the United States, with a mean of 1.0 percent across 18 countries. The disorder becomes less common from childhood through adolescence into adulthood. Toddler boys and girls are equally affected, school-age girls more often in community samples, and among adults women more often. Onset may be as early as the preschool years; the median age at onset reported by adults is late adolescence in high- and upper-middle-income countries and the mid-twenties in low- and lower-middle-income countries. Most adults describe a fluctuating course, yet the majority of children with the disorder are free of impairing anxiety disorders over their lifetimes. The disorder often follows a life stress, especially a loss: the death of a relative or a pet, an illness in the family, a change of school, parental divorce, a move, migration, or a disaster that separated the family, as Kunal's two losses did. Being bullied is a risk factor, and so is a history of parental overprotection and intrusiveness. The disorder runs in families and appears to be strongly heritable, and children with it are unusually sensitive to air enriched with carbon dioxide, a finding that links it to panic disorder; both findings are explained in Section 6.7. Indian context DSM-5-TR warns that cultures differ in how much separation they expect, and that separation anxiety disorder must be distinguished from the high value some communities place on interdependence among family members. In much of India adult children live with their parents until marriage and often after it, and a daily phone call to one's mother is unremarkable. Proximity is not the test. A 23-year-old who lives at home by choice is not disordered; a 23-year-old who has turned down a hard-won postgraduate seat in another city because she cannot bear a night away from her mother, and who phones home twenty times a day from her office in dread that something has happened, may be. The two classifications reflect the same history. ICD-10 placed "separation anxiety disorder of childhood" (F93.0) among the emotional disorders with onset specific to childhood, and DSM-5-TR still prints that code; ICD-11 (6B05) moved it, like DSM-5, into the anxiety or fear-related disorders and applies it across the lifespan. The psychological treatments, including cognitive behavioural programmes such as the Coping Cat and work with parents and schools on getting the child back into class, are taught in Book 2, Sections 10.3.2 and 10.4.2. Exam trap Separation anxiety disorder needs three of eight signs lasting at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents and typically 6 months or more in adults . Since DSM-5 it is an anxiety disorder (not a childhood disorder) and it can begin in adulthood ; an option saying "onset must be before 18" describes DSM-IV. School refusal is not itself a diagnosis: fear of leaving the parent points to separation anxiety, fear of being judged at school to social anxiety, and staying away from both school and home to conduct disorder. Selective mutism A five-year-old girl in an upper kindergarten class in Bengaluru has not said a single word at school in the eight months since term began. She is not a silent child. At home she chatters in Kannada and English with her parents and her older sister, sings along to film songs and argues about bedtime. But from the moment she reaches the school gate she falls silent. She answers her teacher by nodding, shaking her head or pointing; she joins in the action songs without singing; she will draw a picture of her family but will not name them. She does not speak even to her grandparents when they visit, or to the cousin she plays with happily. Her teacher first thought she did not understand English, but she follows every instruction, and her parents, who speak both languages at home, find the suggestion puzzling. At the parent-teacher meeting her mother said what she had been told by relatives: "She is just shy, she will grow out of it." She may, but what she has is selective mutism : a consistent failure to speak in specific social situations in which speech is expected, such as school, despite speaking in other situations, typically at home. The first description is usually credited to the German physician Adolf Kussmaul (1822 to 1902), who in 1877 called it aphasia voluntaria, voluntary loss of speech. In 1934 the Swiss child psychiatrist Moritz Tramer renamed it elective mutism , a term that, like Kussmaul's, implied that the child was choosing not to speak. ICD-10 kept that name (F94.0) and placed it among the "disorders of social functioning with onset specific to childhood and adolescence", describing a marked, emotionally determined selectivity in speaking. DSM-IV (1994) changed the word to "selective", to stress that the silence is tied to selected situations rather than chosen by the child, while still listing it among the childhood disorders. DSM-5 (2013) made the larger change of moving it into the anxiety disorders, and ICD-11 (6B06) did the same. The reason is the evidence that the silence is driven by anxiety, and above all social anxiety, rather than by defiance or a speech problem. The DSM-5-TR criteria are short, and each has a reason. Criterion A, consistent failure to speak where speech is expected despite speaking elsewhere, is the definition itself: the child has the capacity to speak and uses it, but not in certain settings. Criterion B asks that the silence interfere with education, work or social communication; teachers cannot assess reading, the child cannot ask for help with an assignment or to use the toilet, and peers tease or ignore her. Criterion C asks for at least one month , and adds that this month must not be limited to the first month of school , because many young children are quiet and watchful when they first start school and then settle. Criterion D excludes silence that comes from a lack of knowledge of, or comfort with, the language spoken in that setting. Criterion E excludes silence better explained by a communication disorder (DSM-5-TR names childhood-onset fluency disorder, or stuttering) and silence that occurs only during autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder. Children with selective mutism do not initiate speech or reply when spoken to, but many communicate in other ways: grunting, pointing, nodding, writing, or taking non-speaking parts in a school play. They are often excessively shy and afraid of social embarrassment, and may be clingy, negative, prone to tantrums or mildly oppositional, usually only in situations that demand speech. Their language skills are generally normal, though some have subtle receptive language difficulties within the normal range. In clinical settings they are almost always given an additional diagnosis of another anxiety disorder, most often social anxiety disorder. In one series of 50 children with selective mutism studied by Dummit and colleagues (1997), nearly all also met the criteria for social anxiety disorder (reported by Barlow and Durand). Separation anxiety disorder and specific phobia are the next most common companions, and in clinics selective mutism and autism are also often seen together. Selective mutism is rare. Point prevalence in clinic and school samples in the United States, Europe and Israel ranges from 0.03 to 1.9 percent, depending on the setting and the ages sampled; Barlow and Durand put the average at about 0.5 percent of children, with girls more often affected, although DSM-5-TR notes that some studies find an equal sex ratio. Onset is usually before the age of 5, but the disorder often comes to attention only at school entry, when the demands to speak and perform (reading aloud, answering in class) suddenly multiply. The longitudinal course is not well known. Many children appear to "outgrow" the mutism, but the social anxiety beneath it often remains. The temperamental risk factors are not well identified, but behavioural inhibition and negative affectivity may play a role, as may a parental history of shyness and social anxiety; socially inhibited parents may model reticence, and parents of these children have been described as more overprotective or controlling than other parents. Barlow and Durand note evidence that well-meaning parents may maintain the silence by readily stepping in to "do their talking for them". There is also some evidence of unusual auditory efferent activity during speaking, which might make the child's own voice sound strange to her. Children of families who have moved to a place where a different language is spoken run a higher risk, and this is where criterion D matters most. Many children pass through a silent period when they are learning a new language, listening and understanding before they dare to speak. That is not selective mutism. DSM-5-TR advises that the diagnosis may be warranted only if the child understands the new language adequately but still refuses to speak, in both languages, in several unfamiliar settings, and for a prolonged period. In India, where a child from a Bhojpuri-speaking home may start school in English or Kannada, this distinction is practical, not academic.
