The girl in the Bengaluru classroom is not being stubborn, and she is not simply shy. She is anxious, and the longer adults speak for her, the longer her silence is likely to last. Exam trap Selective mutism requires at least 1 month , not limited to the first month of school . In DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR it is an anxiety disorder , not a communication disorder and not a neurodevelopmental disorder; in DSM-IV it was a childhood disorder, and in ICD-10 it is "elective mutism" (F94.0). Its closest relative is social anxiety disorder , not autism and not defiance. Keep the three duration rules of this section apart: GAD 6 months ; separation anxiety disorder 4 weeks in children and typically 6 months in adults; selective mutism 1 month . 6.5 Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: The Clinical Picture High yield · 8 Qs Anjali is 24, a commerce graduate who lives with her parents and her younger brother in Indore. Three years ago, a few weeks after a neighbour's child was admitted to hospital with jaundice, a vegetable seller handed her change with what looked like wet hands. As she took the notes a thought struck her with the force of a blow: "There are germs on this money, and I will give jaundice to my brother." She washed her hands with soap ten times before she felt easier. Within a year the circle of "dirty" things had widened to all currency notes, the newspaper, the doorbell, footwear, the outer gate and anything that came in from the street. Now, whenever she returns home, she bathes for an hour and washes her clothes separately; she washes her hands forty or fifty times a day, counting twenty strokes on each finger and starting again from the beginning if anyone interrupts her; and she asks her mother over and over, "Did I touch the door? Are you sure my hands are clean?" The family has rebuilt its life around her fear. Her father changes his clothes on the verandah, her mother washes the vegetables three times in salt water, and nobody may sit on Anjali's bed in clothes worn outside. Her hands are raw and cracked, and a dermatologist treating her for "contact dermatitis" was the first to suggest that she see a psychiatrist. She left her job at a chartered accountant's office because she could not touch the files. On a bad day the washing, bathing, checking and asking take five or six hours. Sitting in the clinic, Anjali can almost laugh at it. "I know germs cannot jump from a note to my brother. Sitting here with you, I know it is nonsense. But once I have touched something, the feeling stays in my hands, like something sticky, and the thought keeps coming that if he falls ill it will be my fault. Washing is the only thing that makes it go away, for some time." In a household where bathing before entering the kitchen or the prayer room was part of daily life, the family at first took her washing for piety. Only when it began to swallow the day did they see it as an illness. Anjali has obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Barlow and Durand remark that contamination themes are highly prevalent in India, and as you will see later in this section, Indian clinical studies have repeatedly found fear of contamination to be the commonest obsession. This section teaches what OCD is, how it is diagnosed, how it varies and whom it strikes, and how to tell it from the many conditions that resemble it. Its causes are taught in Sections 6.7 and 6.8 and its treatment in Section 6.9. From the madness of doubt to a chapter of its own Doubting, washing and checking were recognised long before anyone called them a disorder, often as the scruples of the devout. The modern clinical history begins in France. In 1838 Jean-Étienne Dominique Esquirol (1772 to 1840) described a patient tormented by ideas she knew to be absurd but could not dismiss, and classed her condition as a monomania, a partial insanity in which reason is preserved outside a single area. Later French writers spoke of folie du doute , the "madness of doubt", and in 1875 Henri Legrand du Saulle drew the earlier descriptions together under the title of the madness of doubt "with delusion of touch": in one phrase, the two great forms of the disorder, doubting and checking on one hand, fear of contamination by touch on the other. In 1877 the German psychiatrist Carl Westphal (1833 to 1890), who had named agoraphobia six years earlier (Section 6.2.6), gave the classic definition of the Zwangsvorstellung, the "compelled idea" (the German word itself was already in use), and insisted that such ideas are not delusions: they force themselves into the mind of a person whose intelligence is intact and who recognises them as abnormal. According to a common account, British psychiatry translated the German term as "obsession" and American psychiatry as "compulsion", which is one reason the disorder came to carry both words. In 1903 Pierre Janet (1859 to 1947) published a large study of obsessions within a condition he called psychasthenia , a weakness of psychological energy, and gave a vivid account of the patients' tormenting "feeling of incompleteness", the sense that an act has not been done properly. You will meet that feeling again, under the name of "just right" experiences, in the modern criteria. Sigmund Freud's "obsessional neurosis", and his case of the Rat Man (1909), gave the disorder a psychoanalytic explanation that dominated the first half of the twentieth century; it is taught, with the defence mechanisms of isolation, undoing and reaction formation, in Section 6.8. The labels in the manuals followed: an "obsessive compulsive reaction" in DSM-I (1952), obsessive compulsive neurosis in DSM-II (1968), and from DSM-III (1980) to DSM-IV obsessive-compulsive disorder, listed among the anxiety disorders. ICD-10 placed it (F42) among the "neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders". DSM-5 (2013) gave OCD a chapter of its own, the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, shared with body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania and excoriation disorder, and ICD-11 (6B20) did the same; the reasons for the move are given in Section 6.1 and the related disorders are taught in Section 6.6. DSM-5-TR codes OCD as F42.2. Obsessions and compulsions defined Criterion A requires obsessions, compulsions or both, and defines each with two parts. The definitions are worth learning almost word for word, because examiners build their distractors from small changes to them. An obsession is defined by two features. First, it is a recurrent and persistent thought, urge or image that is experienced, at some time during the disturbance, as intrusive and unwanted, and that in most individuals causes marked anxiety or distress. Second, the person tries to ignore or suppress it, or to neutralise it with some other thought or action, that is, by performing a compulsion. Each phrase matters. "Thoughts, urges or images" covers the three forms the intrusion can take: a thought ("my hands are contaminated"), an image (a vivid picture of stabbing one's own child) or an urge (to shout an obscenity in a temple). "Intrusive and unwanted" means that the content arrives uninvited and is not welcome; DSM-5 chose "unwanted" in place of DSM-IV's "inappropriate", a word that implied a judgement which varies from culture to culture. "At some time during the disturbance" allows for people whose insight has faded: they may no longer see the thought as senseless, but at some point they experienced it as an intrusion. "In most individuals" allows for the minority who feel disgust or a nagging sense that something is incomplete rather than anxiety. And the second part, the attempt to ignore, suppress or neutralise, is the struggle that defines the experience: the obsession is fought. A compulsion is also defined by two features. First, it is a repetitive behaviour (hand washing, ordering, checking) or mental act (praying, counting, repeating words silently) that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly. Second, the behaviour or mental act is aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or distress, or at preventing some dreaded event or situation, yet it is either not connected in a realistic way with what it is meant to prevent or clearly excessive. Arranging the objects on a desk symmetrically to stop harm coming to one's mother is not realistically connected to her safety; showering for hours is clearly excessive. Barlow and Durand call compulsions "magical" for this reason: they may bear no logical relation to the obsession. Compulsions are often called rituals , because they must be done in a fixed way, a set number of times, in a set order, as Anjali's twenty strokes on each finger must be. DSM-5-TR adds a note that young children may not be able to say what their compulsions are for. Barlow and Durand describe an 8-year-old who each night had to undress, put on his pyjamas and turn down the covers in a slow, set sequence, three times over; he could give no reason, he simply had to. Most people with OCD have both obsessions and compulsions, and the two are usually linked by theme: thoughts of contamination go with washing, thoughts of harm with checking. The mental compulsion deserves special attention because it is invisible. A person who seems to have "pure obsessions" may be silently counting, praying, replacing a bad image with a good one or reviewing the day's events to make sure nothing terrible was done; these covert rituals neutralise just as hand washing does, and the clinician will miss them unless he asks. Three other behaviours surround the rituals. People with OCD avoid the people, places and things that trigger their obsessions: Anjali no longer handles money, and someone with contamination fears may stop using public toilets or eating in restaurants. They seek reassurance, which works as a ritual performed by someone else ("Are you sure my hands are clean?"). And they draw their families in. DSM-5-TR calls this involvement of family or friends in the rituals accommodation (clinicians usually say family accommodation ), and warns that it can worsen or maintain the symptoms and is an important target of treatment, especially in children. Anjali's father changing clothes on the verandah is accommodation; so is the mother who answers the same question for the fortieth time. Not everything that drives a ritual is fear. DSM-5-TR notes that up to 60 percent of people with OCD report sensory phenomena : physical sensations, "just right" feelings and feelings of incompleteness that come before the compulsion and are relieved only when things look, feel or sound exactly right. This is Janet's feeling of incompleteness, rediscovered a century later. Others report strong disgust rather than anxiety, and many hold characteristic beliefs: an inflated sense of responsibility for preventing harm, a tendency to overestimate threat, perfectionism and intolerance of uncertainty, and the belief that having a thought is as bad as acting on it. These beliefs are the raw material of the cognitive theories of OCD (Paul Salkovskis on responsibility, Stanley Rachman on thought-action fusion), which are taught in Section 6.8. One more point in the definition separates OCD from a whole family of "compulsive" behaviours. Compulsions are not done for pleasure. Performing one brings relief, a temporary drop in anxiety or distress, but never gratification. That is the difference between a compulsion and the acts of the impulse-control disorders such as kleptomania and pyromania (Chapter 11), the urges of the paraphilic disorders (Chapter 9), and so-called compulsive gambling, drinking or drug use (Chapter 10). In all of those, DSM-5-TR explains, the person usually enjoys the activity and wishes to resist it only because of its harmful consequences. ICD-10 made the same point in its own way: carrying out the act must not in itself be pleasurable, and simple relief of tension or anxiety does not count as pleasure. How obsessions and compulsions are recognised and recorded as signs in the mental status examination, and how they differ from phobias, preoccupations and overvalued ideas as items of descriptive psychopathology, is taught in Chapter 2 and in Book 2, Section 2.5.5. This section is concerned with the disorder. Criterion B: the cardinal feature If intrusive thoughts and repeated acts were enough for the diagnosis, almost everyone would qualify. Most people have occasional unwanted thoughts that are bizarre, violent or sexual, especially when bored; most people have gone back to check a lock they knew they had locked. The studies of intrusive thoughts in ordinary people, beginning with Rachman and de Silva in 1978, are told in Section 6.8; Barlow and Durand report one community survey in which 13 percent of people had moderate obsessions or compulsions that fell short of the disorder (Spinella 2005). Criterion B is what separates the disorder from this background. The obsessions or compulsions must be time-consuming (DSM-5-TR's example is more than 1 hour a day) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning. It is the cardinal feature of the diagnosis. Notice the word "or". A person who spends only forty minutes a day on rituals but is tormented by them, or has had to give up a job, still qualifies; so does someone who spends three hours a day on rituals and claims not to mind. The hour is an example, not a threshold to be timed with a stopwatch. DSM-5-TR describes the range: people with mild to moderate OCD spend 1 to 3 hours a day obsessing or performing compulsions, while others have nearly constant intrusive thoughts or compulsions that can be incapacitating. Anjali's five or six hours, her lost job and her damaged skin put her far beyond the threshold. Criterion C excludes symptoms that are the physiological effect of a substance or medication (stimulants can produce repetitive behaviour) or of another medical condition (DSM-5-TR has separate diagnoses for these, taught in Section 6.6, and the sudden childhood onset linked to infection, PANDAS, is taught in Section 6.7). Criterion D excludes symptoms better explained by another mental disorder, and its long list is the subject of Table 6.15 later in this section. Notice too what criterion A does not require. Unlike DSM-IV, DSM-5 no longer asks that the person recognise, at some point, that the obsessions or compulsions are excessive or unreasonable; that question is handled by the insight specifier instead. The WHO classifications measure the threshold differently. ICD-10 asks that obsessional symptoms or compulsive acts, or both, be present on most days for at least two successive weeks and be a source of distress or interference, and it adds four tests of the symptoms: they must be recognised as the person's own thoughts or impulses; at least one must still be resisted, even if unsuccessfully; carrying out the act must not in itself be pleasurable; and the thoughts, images or impulses must be unpleasantly repetitive. ICD-11 (6B20) drops the fixed duration and, like DSM-5, asks that the obsessions or compulsions be time-consuming (for example, more than an hour a day) or result in significant distress or impairment. Exam trap The cardinal DSM-5 feature of OCD is obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming (more than 1 hour a day) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment . Reject: " 6 hours a day " (an invented figure; even mild cases spend 1 to 3 hours); " 2 weeks of continuous symptoms " (DSM has no such rule; ICD-10 asks for symptoms on most days for 2 successive weeks, which is a different thing, and is not the DSM-5 answer); " only that obsessions are present " (presence alone is not enough, since nearly everyone has intrusive thoughts). In a cardinal-feature question, "persistent depressive symptoms" is persistent depressive disorder (Chapter 5), "a pervasive pattern of grandiosity and need for admiration" is narcissistic personality disorder (Chapter 11), and "recurrent unexpected panic attacks" is panic disorder (Section 6.2). A vignette of intrusive contamination thoughts with ritual hand washing for more than an hour a day is OCD , not GAD (realistic worries, no ritual), illness anxiety disorder (fear of having a disease, Chapter 7) or specific phobia (a circumscribed external object, avoided, with no ritual). Ego-dystonic: at war with one's own mind To understand how an obsession feels from the inside you need a pair of terms from psychoanalytic ego psychology that are now used throughout clinical psychology. Here "ego" means, roughly, a person's conscious sense of self: values, goals and self-image. Something is ego-syntonic (in tune with the ego) when it feels acceptable, consistent with who one is, perhaps even admirable. Something is ego-dystonic (out of tune with the ego) when it feels alien, unwanted and at odds with one's values and self-concept, something one wishes to be rid of. Obsessions are the textbook example of ego-dystonic experience, and they are ego-dystonic in a precise and rather strange way. The person recognises the thought as a product of his or her own mind. This is what separates an obsession from thought insertion in schizophrenia, where the person believes that the thought has been placed in the mind by some outside agency (Chapter 4). Yet the same person experiences the thought as foreign, as if it came from somewhere he or she does not recognise. A devout man is tormented by blasphemous phrases during prayer; a gentle new mother is horrified by images of dropping her baby from the balcony; Anjali, who loves her brother more than anyone, cannot stop the thought that she will make him ill. Notice the pattern. Obsessions fasten onto exactly what a person values most, which is why they are so distressing: the horror a gentle mother feels at the image of harming her baby is itself the measure of how foreign that image is to her. Barlow and Durand describe a young and deeply moral woman who stopped riding buses for fear that she would grab the crotch of a man sitting beside her; it was, they write, the last thing she would ever do, and that is precisely why the urge horrified her. Ego-dystonia should not be confused with insight, which is taught next. Ego-dystonia concerns how the person relates to the thought (unwanted, resisted, foreign to the self). Insight concerns whether the person believes that the feared consequence is real (will the house really burn down?). A man with poor insight who is fairly sure that disaster will follow an unchecked stove still hates the thought and the hours of checking. That is why an option describing someone "completely unaware that their obsessions are unreasonable" does not define ego-dystonia: it describes the far end of the insight scale. Exam trap Applied to obsessions, ego-dystonic means that the person experiences them as intrusive, unwanted and inconsistent with his or her self-concept . The distractors: experiencing the obsessions "as a core part of one's identity" is the opposite, ego-syntonic, which is how personality traits (including those of OCPD) are felt; "deriving pleasure from the thoughts" describes paraphilic fantasies or the gratification of impulse-control acts, never obsessions; "complete unawareness that the obsessions are unreasonable" is absent insight , a specifier, not ego-dystonia. In an OCD versus OCPD question, OCD obsessions and compulsions are ego-dystonic ; they are not "always reality-grounded" (OCD content is often odd or magical, which is how DSM-5-TR tells it from realistic GAD worry), and OCD is not "restricted to childhood" (mean onset 19.5 years, and it is usually chronic). The specifiers: insight and tics Rohit, 32, is an officer in a nationalised bank in Pune. Every morning before leaving for work he checks the knob of the gas stove, the regulator on the cylinder, the taps, the geyser switch and the lock of the main door, each a set number of times; twice a week he gets off the bus two stops along and goes back to check again, and he arrives late. His obsession is a vivid image of the building on fire and his neighbours' children trapped, all because of him. In the clinic he says, a little embarrassed, that "probably nothing would happen" if he checked only once. At six in the morning, alone in the flat, he is far less sure. DSM-IV asked that a person with OCD recognise, at some point, that the obsessions or compulsions were excessive or unreasonable, and offered a single "with poor insight" specifier. DSM-5 dropped the requirement and replaced it with a three-level insight specifier that records how far the person believes the beliefs behind the symptoms. DSM-5-TR illustrates it with a person who checks the stove 30 times (Figure 6.8). With good or fair insight , the person recognises that the OCD beliefs are definitely or probably not true, or that they may or may not be true: the house definitely will not, probably will not, or may or may not burn down if the stove is not checked 30 times. With poor insight , the person thinks the beliefs are probably true: the house will probably burn down. With absent insight/delusional beliefs , the person is completely convinced: the house will burn down. Many people have good or fair insight, some have poor insight, and a few, 4 percent or fewer, have absent insight. Insight can change within the same person over the course of the illness, and even, as Rohit shows, over the course of a day; and poorer insight has been linked to a worse long-term outcome. (The general grading of insight in a mental status examination is taught in Book 2, Section 2.6.9.) Increasing conviction that the OCD belief is true Good or fair insight "The house will not, or may or may not, burn down if I skip checking the stove 30 times." Belief seen as untrue, or only possibly true Poor insight "The house will probably burn down if I skip checking the stove 30 times." Belief thought probably true Absent insight / delusional beliefs "The house will burn down if I skip checking the stove 30 times." Completely convinced; 4 percent or fewer All three are diagnosed as OCD: absent insight does not make it a psychotic disorder Figure 6.8 The insight specifier of OCD, using DSM-5-TR's example of a person who checks the stove 30 times. What changes from left to right is how firmly the person believes the feared consequence, not whether the person has OCD. Insight can shift along this line within one person, from month to month or even within a day. The far right of the figure raises an obvious question. If a person is completely convinced that the house will burn down unless the stove is checked 30 times, is that not a delusion, and should the diagnosis not be a psychotic disorder? DSM-5-TR answers no. The person still has obsessions and compulsions, which is what distinguishes the condition from delusional disorder, and has none of the other features of schizophrenia, such as hallucinations or disorganised speech. People who warrant the "absent insight/delusional beliefs" specifier are diagnosed with OCD, not with a psychotic disorder. An additional psychotic diagnosis is given only if the person holds delusions whose content goes beyond the OCD (DSM-5-TR's example, from the related disorders, is a person with body dysmorphic disorder who is also convinced that his food has been poisoned). The same three-level specifier is used for body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding disorder (Section 6.6). ICD-11 uses a two-level version: "with fair to good insight" and "with poor to absent insight". The second specifier is tic-related : the person has a current or past history of a tic disorder. Up to 30 percent of people with OCD have a lifetime tic disorder, most often men whose OCD began in childhood. The specifier exists because this group differs from other people with OCD in the themes of its symptoms (Barlow and Durand note that the obsessions in tic-related OCD are almost always about symmetry), its comorbidity, its course and its pattern of family transmission. In children a triad of OCD, a tic disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder may be seen (tic disorders and Tourette's disorder are taught in Chapter 3). Tics and compulsions can look alike, so learn DSM-5-TR's distinction. A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic movement or vocalisation, such as eye blinking or throat clearing, often preceded by a premonitory sensory urge; a compulsion is usually more complex, is preceded by an obsession, and is aimed at neutralising it. Compulsions are voluntary acts, although the person feels driven to perform them, which is why "involuntary" is the wrong word for them. Exam trap OCD with absent insight/delusional beliefs is still diagnosed as OCD , not as delusional disorder or schizophrenia. The insight specifier has three levels in DSM-5-TR (good or fair; poor; absent/delusional), and the second specifier is tic-related . "With poor insight" was the only insight specifier in DSM-IV, and DSM-IV, unlike DSM-5, required that the person at some point recognise the symptoms as excessive or unreasonable. The symptom dimensions, and why hoarding is no longer one of them The content of obsessions varies endlessly from one person to the next, but it clusters. DSM-5-TR names four common symptom dimensions , each pairing a kind of obsession with a kind of compulsion (Figure 6.9). In the cleaning dimension, obsessions about contamination by germs, dirt, bodily fluids or "impure" things lead to washing and cleaning, as in Anjali's case. In the symmetry dimension, a need for things to be even, exact or "just right" leads to ordering, arranging, repeating and counting, and to touching or tapping objects a set number of times or evenly on both sides; the childhood game of not stepping on the cracks in the pavement is a harmless version of it, and the person with OCD may spend an hour lining up the objects on a table. The forbidden or taboo thoughts dimension includes aggressive, sexual and religious obsessions with related compulsions; religious obsessions about sin, blasphemy or ritual impurity, with repeated confession, prayer or purification, are often called scrupulosity . In the harm dimension, fears of harm to oneself or others lead to checking, as in Rohit's case. Statistical analyses of large samples (Bloch and colleagues 2008, reported by Barlow and Durand) found symmetry to be the largest factor, followed by forbidden thoughts, cleaning and hoarding. Each kind of obsession (left) tends to call up its own kind of compulsion (right), although most people have symptoms in more than one row. The bottom row, whose right-hand box has a heavier outline, is the old hoarding dimension: keeping things because of a typical obsession is still OCD, but primary hoarding is now a separate disorder. Three further facts about the dimensions are examined. First, most people have symptoms in more than one dimension; Anjali, for instance, also counts twenty strokes on each finger, a ritual more typical of the symmetry dimension. Second, the dimensions occur across cultures, are fairly stable over time in adults, and may involve different neural substrates. Third, their content tracks development and sex: harm obsessions (fears of death or illness striking oneself or loved ones) are commoner in children and adolescents than in adults, sexual and religious obsessions commoner in adolescents than in children, and women are more likely to have cleaning symptoms, men forbidden-thoughts and symmetry symptoms. What about hoarding? For decades it was treated as a form of OCD, and statistical studies like Bloch's still found it as a separate factor. DSM-IV listed hoarding as a criterion of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder and, at the same time, told clinicians to consider OCD when hoarding was extreme, so it was handled as a possible symptom of OCD as well; and DSM-5-TR's OCPD criteria still include being "unable to discard worn-out or worthless objects even when they have no sentimental value". But hoarding turned out to differ from OCD in important ways. Only about one in five people with hoarding disorder also meets the criteria for OCD (DSM-5-TR); the saving is usually purposeful and felt as reasonable rather than intrusive and unwanted; and whereas OCD waxes and wanes, hoarding tends to begin early and worsen with each passing decade (Barlow and Durand). So DSM-5 made hoarding disorder a separate diagnosis within the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (taught in Section 6.6). DSM-5-TR draws the line clearly. If a person keeps things because of a typical obsession (acquiring every object in a set to achieve a sense of completeness, or refusing to throw away old newspapers because they may contain information that could prevent a disaster), that accumulation is a compulsion and the diagnosis is OCD. Primary hoarding, the persistent difficulty in discarding possessions because of a perceived need to save them and distress at parting with them, is hoarding disorder. Exam trap Asked which is not a compulsive behaviour of OCD, choose hoarding . Tapping (a symmetry or "just right" ritual), washing (cleaning dimension) and checking (harm dimension) are textbook compulsions. Hoarding is now its own disorder in DSM-5, so it is not a compulsion "in this classic framing", which is how the question puts it. The nuance, if an interviewer pushes: DSM-IV listed hoarding as an OCPD criterion and advised considering OCD when it was extreme, OCPD still lists the inability to discard worthless objects, and saving that is driven by a true obsession is still diagnosed as OCD. Who develops OCD, and what course it takes DSM-5-TR gives a 12-month prevalence of 1.2 percent in the United States and similar figures internationally, 1.1 to 1.8 percent in countries as different as Canada, Germany, Taiwan, Korea and New Zealand; Barlow and Durand give lifetime estimates of 1.6 to 2.3 percent. These are the figures behind the textbook statement that OCD affects "1 to 2 percent" of people. Unlike most anxiety disorders, which affect women about twice as often as men, OCD is nearly evenly balanced: women are affected slightly more often in adulthood, but boys more often in childhood, because boys start earlier. The mean age at onset in the United States is 19.5 years (Barlow and Durand give a median of 19), and 25 percent of cases begin by age 14. Onset after 35 is unusual but does occur. Men begin earlier: nearly a quarter of men have their onset before age 10, whereas in girls onset is more typical in adolescence. Onset is usually gradual, although it can be acute (a sudden onset in childhood raises the question of an infection-related syndrome, Section 6.7). Untreated, the course is usually chronic, with symptoms that wax and wane; some people have an episodic course and a minority deteriorate. Remission without treatment is rare in adults: in one long follow-up only about 20 percent had remitted when they were re-examined 40 years later. Childhood onset can lead to a lifetime of OCD, yet about 40 percent of people whose OCD began in childhood or adolescence may remit by early adulthood. Two periods in a woman's life deserve mention. OCD can begin or worsen around childbirth, the peripartum period, often with aggressive obsessions such as intrusive thoughts of harming the infant that lead the mother to avoid the baby; and some women find that their symptoms worsen before menstruation. Key study: what Indian patients obsess about (1975 and 1988) In 1975 Salman Akhtar , Narendra Nath Wig and their colleagues published, in the British Journal of Psychiatry , a phenomenological analysis of 82 patients with obsessional neurosis seen at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh. They sorted the forms of obsession into doubts, obsessive thinking, fears, impulses and images, in that order of frequency, and found that the commonest content concerned dirt and contamination, followed by aggression, impersonal themes, religion and sex; they stressed that sociocultural factors shape what an obsession is about. A quarter of their patients had no compulsions, and those patients had the best outcome. Thirteen years later, S. Khanna and S. M. Channabasavanna at NIMHANS, Bengaluru, analysed 761 obsessions recorded from 410 patients over ten years and again found fear of contamination to be the single commonest theme. Both studies bear out Barlow and Durand's remark that contamination themes are highly prevalent in India. Culture shapes the content of OCD more than its structure. Barlow and Durand note that in Saudi Arabia and Egypt obsessions are mainly about religious practice, especially the Muslim emphasis on cleanliness, and that contamination themes are highly prevalent in India, yet studies from England, Hong Kong, India, Egypt, Japan, Norway and many other countries have found essentially similar types and proportions of obsessions and compulsions. DSM-5-TR agrees: the sex ratio, age at onset, comorbidity and symptom structure are similar around the world, while sexual obsessions may be reported less in some religious groups and violent obsessions more where urban violence is common. People also explain their symptoms differently, as physical, social, spiritual or supernatural in origin, and these explanations can shape both the rituals and the help that is sought. Anjali's family, who first read her bathing as devotion, is a small example; in India, as elsewhere, some patients first take their symptoms to religious or traditional healers. OCD is seldom alone. In the United States 76 percent of adults with OCD have had an anxiety disorder in their lifetime and 63 percent a depressive or bipolar disorder (41 percent major depression); impulse-control disorders (56 percent) and substance use disorders (39 percent) are also common. OCD usually begins later than most of the anxiety disorders that accompany it, but often comes before the depression. In one study of 214 treatment-seeking adults, 23 to 32 percent also had obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. Body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania and excoriation disorder are commoner than expected in people with OCD, and OCD is in turn much commoner than expected among people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder (about 12 percent), bipolar disorder, eating disorders, body dysmorphic disorder and Tourette's disorder, which is why a clinician who diagnoses any of these should ask about obsessions. The burden is heavy. Barlow and Durand call OCD "the devastating culmination of the anxiety disorders": among people with anxiety and related disorders, the one who needs admission is likely to have OCD, and the one referred for neurosurgery after every other treatment has failed probably does (Section 6.9). Quality of life is reduced across every domain. Harm obsessions can make relationships feel dangerous, symmetry obsessions can stop a student finishing an examination because the answer never looks right, contamination fears can keep a person away from hospitals or produce skin damage like Anjali's, and medicines themselves may be seen as contaminated. Some people impose rules on the whole family (no visitors, no outdoor shoes), and young people whose OCD began early may never achieve independence from their parents. Suicide is a real risk. DSM-5-TR reports a mean lifetime suicide attempt rate of 14.2 percent in clinical samples from many countries, lifetime suicidal ideation in 44.1 percent, and, in a Swedish national registry study of 36,788 people with OCD, a much raised risk of death by suicide (odds ratio 9.8) and of suicide attempt (odds ratio 5.5), even after other psychiatric disorders were taken into account. Severe OCD, the unacceptable-thoughts dimension and comorbid depression are among the predictors. Clinical link Because OCD is secret and shameful, people often wait years before telling anyone, and some first appear in a dermatology clinic with skin damaged by washing, in a general practice asking for "something for tension", or with a relative who complains about the hours spent in the bathroom. Ask directly and without embarrassment: "Some people get thoughts that they find upsetting and that keep coming back even though they try to push them away. Does that happen to you? Do you have to do anything again and again to feel all right?" Ask too about family accommodation, which treatment must address. The treatments of choice are exposure and response prevention (Book 2, Section 4.3.5), cognitive therapy built on Salkovskis' model (Book 2, Section 5.6.7) and the serotonergic drugs (Section 6.9). Obsession, worry, rumination or delusion? The differential diagnosis Repetitive thoughts and repetitive acts occur in many disorders, and much of the skill in diagnosing OCD lies in asking what kind of repetitive thought one is looking at. Table 6.14 compares the obsession with its six chief look-alikes. Three distinctions are examined most often. A GAD worry is usually about a real-life concern (money, health, the family), and what is abnormal is its excess; an obsession usually does not concern real-life problems, may be odd, irrational or magical in content, and is usually linked to a compulsion. Depressive rumination is mood-congruent brooding on loss, failure and guilt, not necessarily experienced as intrusive and not linked to compulsions. A delusion is a false, fixed belief that the person holds as simply true and does not resist (Chapter 4), whereas an obsession is resisted and usually recognised as excessive. Between the two lies the overvalued idea , a dominating, emotionally charged belief that the person holds with strong conviction and does not experience as senseless, such as the conviction of a disfigured nose in body dysmorphic disorder or of being fat in anorexia nervosa (Chapter 2 teaches the concept). Table 6.15 groups them. The common thread is simple: in OCD the repetition is driven by an intrusive, unwanted obsession and serves to neutralise it, whereas in each look-alike the repeated thought or act either has a narrower focus (appearance, possessions, hair, food, illness), brings pleasure (gambling, substances, paraphilic urges, impulsive acts), carries no neutralising purpose (tics, stereotypies, autistic routines), or belongs to another state of mind altogether (the guilt of depression, the thought insertion of psychosis). Rohit's branch manager, a man in his fifties, is admired for his thoroughness and disliked for almost everything else. He insists that every voucher be checked three times in his own fixed order, rewrites his juniors' reports until they miss their deadlines, will not delegate anything important, keeps every circular since 1998 in labelled files because "you never know", and has not taken his earned leave in years. His family complains that holidays with him feel like inspections. Asked whether any of this troubles him, he is puzzled: "Somebody in this branch has to do things properly." He has no intrusive thoughts that he fights, no rituals that relieve anxiety, and no wish to change. If he has a disorder, it is obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD). Despite the similar names, DSM-5-TR says, the two disorders are usually easy to tell apart: OCD is defined by true obsessions and compulsions, and OCPD is not. OCPD is an enduring and pervasive pattern, beginning by early adulthood and present across many contexts, of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness and efficiency; its criteria (preoccupation with details and rules, perfectionism that prevents completion, devotion to work over leisure, rigid scrupulousness about morals, inability to discard worthless objects, reluctance to delegate, miserliness, rigidity and stubbornness) are taught in Chapter 11. The decisive difference is how the person experiences the symptoms. OCD is ego-dystonic: Rohit hates his checking and wants to stop. OCPD is ego-syntonic : the manager's perfectionism feels to him like the right and rational way to live, and his rigidity often distresses the people around him more than it distresses him. Table 6.16 sets the two side by side. The two are separate categories in DSM-5-TR, one among the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders and one among the personality disorders, and they can coexist: when the criteria for both are met, both diagnoses are recorded. In DSM-5-TR, generalised anxiety disorder requires excessive anxiety and worry, more days than not, for at least in adults. Adults with GAD need three of six associated symptoms, but children need only . Because they show smaller heart rate, skin conductance and breathing responses to stress than people with panic, but chronic muscle tension, people with GAD have been called autonomic . ICD-11 asks that the symptoms of GAD persist for at least , more days than not. Separation anxiety disorder must last at least in children and adolescents, and typically 6 months or more in adults. Selective mutism must last at least 1 month, not limited to the first month of ; its closest companion disorder is social anxiety disorder. The cardinal feature of OCD is obsessions or compulsions that are time-consuming, for example more than a day, or that cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Obsessions are experienced as intrusive, unwanted and inconsistent with the self-concept; in other words they are ego- . A person with OCD who is completely convinced that the house will burn down unless the stove is checked 30 times receives the specifier "with absent insight/ beliefs" and is still diagnosed with OCD. In DSM-5, is no longer an OCD compulsion but a separate disorder, although obsessive-compulsive personality disorder still lists the inability to discard worthless objects. A college student in Delhi spends three hours a day examining her nose in every mirror, shop window and phone screen she passes. A retired clerk in Kolkata can no longer reach his bed, because the room is stacked to the ceiling with forty years of newspapers. A schoolgirl in Pune sits over her board-examination notes pulling out her eyebrows one hair at a time, until there are none left to pull. A nursing student in Bengaluru picks at a pimple on her cheek until it bleeds, then at the scab, then at the skin around it, until the small spot has become a scar. On the surface these four people have little in common: a worry about looks, a flat full of paper, a missing eyebrow, a wound. Yet when the American Psychiatric Association published DSM-5 in 2013 it placed all four problems in a single chapter, next to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and the World Health Organization's ICD-11 did much the same a few years later. Why should a worry about one's nose belong with a habit of pulling hair, and why should either belong with OCD? This section answers that question first and then takes the members of the family one at a time. A new family: why these disorders sit beside OCD Before 2013 the disorders in this section were scattered across the manual like relatives who had never met. OCD itself sat among the anxiety disorders from DSM-III (1980) to DSM-IV-TR, and in ICD-10 among the "neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders" (F40 to F48). Body dysmorphic disorder, the preoccupation with an imagined flaw in one's looks, had entered the American manual in 1980 only as an example of an atypical somatoform disorder, received its present name in DSM-III-R (1987), and was still listed among the somatoform disorders in DSM-IV, because its central feature is a preoccupation with the body. ICD-10 filed it under hypochondriacal disorder (F45.2), which is why DSM-5-TR, which prints ICD-10-CM codes, still gives body dysmorphic disorder the code F45.22: the number is a fossil of its old home. Hair pulling was one of DSM-IV's "impulse-control disorders not elsewhere classified", alongside kleptomania, pyromania, pathological gambling and intermittent explosive disorder, and in ICD-10 it sat with the "habit and impulse disorders" as F63.3, a code DSM-5-TR still uses. Hoarding had no category of its own at all: it was treated as a symptom of OCD and was one of the eight criteria for obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (an inability to discard worn-out or worthless objects even when they have no sentimental value, a criterion that survives in DSM-5-TR). Skin picking had no category either; excoriation disorder is new in DSM-5. DSM-5 gathered these strays into a new chapter, the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (OCRDs). In DSM-5-TR it contains OCD; body dysmorphic disorder; hoarding disorder; trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder); excoriation (skin-picking) disorder; substance/medication-induced obsessive-compulsive and related disorder; obsessive-compulsive and related disorder due to another medical condition; other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder; and unspecified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder. The chapter is placed immediately after the anxiety disorders, and DSM-5-TR says the sequence is deliberate: OCD remains closely related to anxiety, even though it no longer lives in the same chapter. What binds the family? DSM-5-TR answers in two parts. The first is a shared form of symptom: repetitive thoughts or behaviours . Some members (OCD, body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding disorder) are driven by a preoccupation, an obsession about contamination, a belief that one's nose is grotesque, a felt need to save things, and the person answers that preoccupation with repetitive behaviours or mental acts. Others (trichotillomania and excoriation disorder) are driven not by a thought but by an urge located in the body: recurrent body-focused repetitive behaviours (BFRBs), such as hair pulling and skin picking, together with repeated attempts to cut down or stop. The second part of the answer is evidence on what DSM calls diagnostic validators. The disorders occur together far more often than chance would predict: body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania and excoriation disorder are all commoner in people with OCD than in people without it, and trichotillomania and excoriation are commoner in the first-degree relatives of people with OCD. They tend to begin in childhood or adolescence and to run a chronic course. Several respond to the same treatments, drugs that block the reuptake of serotonin and therapies built on exposure (Section 6.9), and they appear to involve overlapping genes and overlapping brain circuits (Section 6.7). Grouping them has a practical point too: DSM-5-TR tells clinicians that a person who presents with one of these conditions should be screened for the others. The grouping is not a claim that the disorders are identical. DSM-5-TR is careful to say that there are important differences in validators and treatment across the chapter, and Barlow and Durand give examples: habit reversal, not exposure and response prevention, is the main psychological treatment for hair pulling and skin picking, and the treatments developed for hoarding have so far produced more modest results than those for OCD. Nor does every repetitive habit qualify. The chapter's disorders differ from normal preoccupations and rituals by being excessive or by persisting beyond the developmentally appropriate period. A four-year-old who insists that her bedtime story be read in exactly the same way every night, or a ten-year-old who collects every cricket card in a series, is behaving normally; the same rigidity at thirty, consuming hours and wrecking a marriage, is not. The disorders that have a cognitive core, OCD, body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding disorder, carry an insight specifier with three grades: good or fair insight, poor insight, and absent insight/delusional beliefs. Section 6.5 explains the specifier for OCD. The rule that matters here is that a person whose disorder-related belief is held with complete conviction is not given a second diagnosis of a psychotic disorder. A woman who is utterly certain that her nose is deformed has body dysmorphic disorder with absent insight, not delusional disorder. Only if her delusions spread beyond the disorder's own theme (DSM-5-TR's example is a person with body dysmorphic disorder who becomes convinced that her food is being poisoned) does a psychotic diagnosis come into play. Exam trap Know each disorder's old home , because papers set it as the wrong option. OCD was an anxiety disorder until DSM-5. Body dysmorphic disorder was a somatoform disorder in DSM-IV (and a form of hypochondriacal disorder in ICD-10). Trichotillomania was an impulse-control disorder in DSM-IV. Hoarding was a symptom of OCD and a criterion of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder . Excoriation disorder had no earlier category . In DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR all five are obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. Body dysmorphic disorder: the distress of imagined ugliness Zoya is nineteen and in her second year of a BA course in Delhi. She is, by any ordinary standard, a good-looking young woman. Zoya does not see it that way. For three years she has been convinced that her nose bends to the left, that its tip is "fat and ugly", and that the skin on her cheeks is dark and covered with pits. She checks her face in every reflecting surface she passes: mirrors, car windows, the back of a steel spoon, the front camera of her phone, which she opens perhaps fifty times a day. Before leaving home she spends an hour and a half applying and reapplying foundation, and she will not step out without it. Several times an hour she asks her mother, "Does my nose look crooked today?" Her mother says no; Zoya feels better for a few minutes and then asks again. On the metro she is sure that other passengers are glancing at her nose and whispering about it. She compares her face, feature by feature, with her classmates' and with the women on her phone, and she always loses. She has seen three dermatologists for what one of them called "mild acne", and she has begun to save money for an operation on her nose. Since the start of the term she has stopped going to college. Her family, at first amused and then exasperated, tells her that she is vain. She is not vain. She is miserable. Zoya has body dysmorphic disorder (BDD): a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that other people either cannot see or regard as slight. The condition was described in 1891 by the Italian psychiatrist Enrico Morselli (1852 to 1929), who called it dysmorphophobia (some sources date his first description to 1886). The word comes from Greek roots meaning, roughly, fear of misshapenness, and Barlow and Durand gloss it simply as "fear of ugliness". The name is misleading in one important way. A person with BDD is not afraid of becoming ugly, the way a person with a phobia is afraid of meeting a dog; she is convinced that she already is ugly. Because so many sufferers cannot accept, even for a moment, that their belief might be mistaken, the condition was for decades thought to be a psychotic delusional state. The modern understanding owes most to the American psychiatrist Katharine A. Phillips , whose 1991 paper described the disorder as the distress of "imagined ugliness" and whose research since then has shaped the DSM criteria. DSM-5-TR notes that the disorder was "formerly known as dysmorphophobia". The DSM-5-TR criteria have four parts, and each is there for a reason. First, there must be a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others. The word "preoccupation" means much more than dissatisfaction: the thoughts are intrusive, unwanted and hard to resist or control, and on average they occupy three to eight hours a day. The phrase "not observable or appear slight to others" is the heart of the diagnosis. A person with an obvious facial scar who worries about it does not have BDD; DSM-5-TR says explicitly that clearly noticeable defects are not diagnosed as BDD (an excessive, impairing preoccupation with a real and noticeable flaw is recorded as an "other specified" disorder, Section 6.6.6). Second, at some point during the disorder the person must have performed repetitive behaviours or mental acts in response to the appearance concerns. This criterion, added in DSM-5, is what makes BDD look like OCD: the mirror checking, grooming and reassurance seeking play the part that washing and checking play in OCD, and comparing one's appearance with other people's is the mental act that corresponds to a silent counting ritual. Third, the preoccupation must cause clinically significant distress or impairment; in practice, DSM-5-TR observes, usually both are present. Fourth, the preoccupation must not be better explained by concerns about body fat or weight in a person who meets criteria for an eating disorder. This last rule draws the border with anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa (Chapter 8): a young woman who believes she is fat and starves herself has an eating disorder, not BDD, although the two can coexist and then both are diagnosed. Any part of the body can become the focus, but the commonest targets are the skin (perceived acne, scars, lines, wrinkles, paleness), the hair (thinning hair, or too much body or facial hair) and the nose. In Phillips and colleagues' series of 200 patients (2005), 80 percent were concerned about their skin, 58 percent about their hair and 39 percent about their nose, and the average person was worried about five to seven body areas, not one. Some people are troubled by a perceived asymmetry, as Zoya is by the "bend" in her nose. The concerns range in intensity from looking "unattractive" or "not right" to looking "hideous" or "like a monster". The repetitive behaviours are varied, and DSM-5-TR's list repays careful reading because examiners draw on it. They include comparing one's appearance with that of others; repeatedly checking the perceived defect in mirrors and other reflecting surfaces, or examining it directly (some people do the opposite and avoid mirrors almost phobically); taking excessive "selfies"; excessive grooming (combing, styling, shaving, plucking or pulling hair); seeking reassurance; touching the disliked area to check it; excessive exercise or weightlifting; seeking cosmetic procedures; excessive tanning; repeatedly changing clothes; compulsive shopping for beauty products; and skin picking intended to improve the skin, which can itself cause damage, infection and scarring. Especially common is camouflaging : hiding the defect with make-up, a cap, a scarf, a hand held in front of the face, or hair arranged over the forehead. Notice the crucial difference from a habit that is enjoyed. These behaviours are not pleasurable; they are driven, time-consuming and hard to resist, and they often increase anxiety and low mood, because each glance in the mirror confirms the flaw. Zoya's checks do not reassure her. DSM-5-TR also describes a variant, body dysmorphic disorder by proxy , in which the preoccupation concerns flaws the person perceives in someone else's appearance, most often a spouse or partner. Many people with BDD have ideas of reference (or, at the extreme, delusions of reference): the belief that other people take special notice of them, stare at them or mock them because of the way they look, as Zoya believes of the passengers on the metro. The disorder goes with high anxiety, social anxiety and avoidance, depressed mood, high negative affectivity (neuroticism), rejection sensitivity, perfectionism and low self-esteem, and also with elevated hostility. Most sufferers are deeply ashamed, both of their appearance and of how much they think about it, and reluctant to tell anyone, which is why the disorder so often goes unrecognised. Laboratory studies add a striking detail: people with BDD tend to read neutral or ambiguous faces as negative or threatening, and they process what they see in a detailed, piece-by-piece way rather than taking in the whole. If you scrutinise your own nose as a collection of millimetre-sized features, it is easy to find something wrong with it. DSM-5-TR offers two specifiers. The first is muscle dysmorphia : preoccupation with the idea that one's body build is too small or insufficiently lean or muscular, the condition popularly called "bigorexia". It occurs almost exclusively in men and adolescent boys, whose bodies are normal-looking or even very muscular. Most diet, exercise or lift weights excessively, sometimes to the point of injuring themselves, and some take potentially dangerous anabolic-androgenic steroids and other substances to grow bigger. The specifier is used even when the person is also preoccupied with other body areas, which is often the case. The second specifier records insight into the BDD beliefs ("I look ugly", "I look deformed"): with good or fair insight (the person recognises that the beliefs are definitely or probably not true, or may or may not be true); with poor insight (the person thinks the beliefs are probably true); and with absent insight/delusional beliefs (the person is completely convinced that they are true). On average insight in BDD is poor, and one-third or more of sufferers currently hold their beliefs with delusional conviction. In Barlow and Durand's account, between 33 and 50 percent of the patients in two large clinical series were convinced that the defect was real, compared with about 10 percent of people with OCD who lack insight. Should such a convinced patient be called psychotic? Under DSM-IV, a person who held the belief with delusional intensity could be given a second diagnosis of delusional disorder, somatic type (Chapter 4). Research by Phillips and her colleagues (2006) then compared delusional and non-delusional patients and found no meaningful difference beyond the fact that the delusional group was more severely ill (and somewhat less educated). Later work by the same group (Phillips and colleagues 2010, cited by Barlow and Durand) showed that both groups responded equally well to the treatments that work for BDD, and that the delusional group did not respond to the drug treatments used for psychotic disorders. So DSM-5 gave all of them one diagnosis: body dysmorphic disorder, with the degree of insight recorded by the specifier. DSM-5-TR adds that the greater suicidality of the delusional group seems to be explained by its more severe symptoms rather than by the delusional conviction itself. Exam trap Despite its old name, dysmorphophobia, body dysmorphic disorder is not a phobia : the person is not afraid of becoming ugly but convinced of being ugly. A person who is completely convinced that the flaw is real receives body dysmorphic disorder with absent insight/delusional beliefs , not delusional disorder. A noticeable, real defect does not qualify (that is "body dysmorphic-like disorder with actual flaws", an other specified diagnosis). Muscle dysmorphia is a specifier of BDD, not an eating disorder. Body dysmorphic disorder: who, when, the cosmetic route and the look-alikes Because sufferers hide it, BDD was long thought to be rare. It is not. In a nationwide study of American adults the point prevalence was 2.4 percent (2.5 percent in women and 2.2 percent in men), and similar studies in other countries, such as Germany, have found 1.7 to 2.9 percent. That makes BDD at least as common as OCD. Clinical series vary in their sex ratio: 68.5 percent of Phillips's 200 patients were women, whereas a majority of a large Japanese series were men. DSM-5-TR concludes that men and women are more alike than different in their disliked body areas, repetitive behaviours, severity, suicidality and course, but that men are more likely to be preoccupied with their genitals, body build and thinning hair and more likely to misuse substances, while women are more likely to worry about weight, breasts, buttocks, legs, hips and excessive body hair and more likely to have a comorbid eating disorder. Among adolescents and college students the disorder is somewhat commoner in girls and young women. BDD is a disorder of adolescence. DSM-5-TR gives the mean age at onset as 16 to 17 years, the median as 15, and the most common age as 12 to 13; in two-thirds of sufferers it begins before 18. Milder, subclinical concerns usually appear around 12 or 13 and grow gradually into the full disorder, although some people experience an abrupt onset. Without treatment the course is usually chronic. Barlow and Durand describe a woman who had suffered for 71 years, since the age of nine, and a prospective study of 183 patients in which only 21 percent improved even somewhat over a year. Childhood neglect, abuse and trauma, and especially teasing, are commoner in the histories of people with BDD (the genetic findings are in Section 6.7). BDD is one of the most disabling disorders in this book. Almost everyone with it has impaired social and working life, from avoiding some gatherings to being completely housebound, and about 20 percent of young people with the disorder say they dropped out of school primarily because of it. In one study of 62 outpatients, their distress, impairment and quality of life were worse on several measures than those of patients with depression, diabetes or a recent heart attack. The risk of suicide is grave. A meta-analysis of 17 studies cited in DSM-5-TR found that people with BDD were about four times more likely to have had suicidal thoughts, and about 2.6 times more likely to have attempted suicide, than healthy controls and than people with eating disorders, OCD or any anxiety disorder. In two German population studies, suicidal thoughts were reported by 19 percent and 31 percent of people with BDD against about 3 percent of those without it. In three of the clinical series reported by Barlow and Durand, between 21 and 27.5 percent of patients had already attempted suicide. DSM-5-TR lists the ways BDD differs from OCD: poorer insight, more frequent depression and higher rates of suicidal ideation. Major depression is the commonest comorbid disorder, usually beginning after the BDD; social anxiety disorder, OCD and substance-related disorders (including anabolic steroid use in muscle dysmorphia) are also common. Where do people with BDD go for help? Not, as a rule, to a psychologist. They go to the people who can change the way they look. A majority receive cosmetic treatment, dermatological treatment and surgery most often, and DSM-5-TR's prevalence figures from these clinics are remarkable: BDD is found in 11 to 13 percent of dermatology patients, 13 to 15 percent of general cosmetic surgery patients and 20 percent of patients seeking rhinoplasty (an operation on the nose), as well as 11 percent of adults seeking jaw-correction surgery and 5 to 10 percent of adults seeking orthodontic or cosmetic dental work. The treatments rarely help. DSM-5-TR says that BDD responds poorly to cosmetic treatment and sometimes gets worse. In Barlow and Durand's summary of the research, people with BDD who have surgery seldom get the result they want: they return for more surgery on the same "defect" or shift their attention to a new one, and in one group of 50 people who sought surgery or a similar consultation, 81 percent were dissatisfied with the result. Some take legal action against their surgeons, and some become violent towards them. Key study: Veale and the patients who operated on themselves (2000) How desperate can the wish to change one's appearance become? The British psychiatrist David Veale collected information on 25 patients with BDD who had sought cosmetic surgery in the past. Nine of them, because they could not afford an operation or had been turned down, had tried to alter their appearance with their own hands, often with tragic results. A man who believed that the skin of his face was too "loose" used a staple gun on both sides of his face to pull it taut; the staples fell out after ten minutes, and he narrowly missed damaging his facial nerve. A woman preoccupied with the shape of her face filed down her teeth to change the line of her jaw. Another woman, who wanted liposuction but could not pay for it, cut her thighs with a knife and tried to squeeze out the fat. The study was small and descriptive, but its lesson is plain: the problem in BDD is not the nose or the skin, and changing the body does not cure it. DSM-5-TR confirms that "some individuals perform surgery on themselves". Clinical link Most people with BDD will never refer themselves to a psychologist, so the clinician who meets them is often a dermatologist, a cosmetic surgeon or a dentist. Liaison work with these clinics, and a few screening questions (How much time do you spend thinking about your appearance? What do you do about it? How has it affected your life?), can find patients before they undergo operations that will not help. When you see a client like Zoya, do not argue about whether her nose is crooked and do not offer endless reassurance, which works like another checking ritual. Focus instead on what the preoccupation is costing her, and always ask about suicidal thoughts. The treatments with evidence are cognitive-behavioural therapy built on exposure and response prevention (Book 2, Sections 4.3.5 and 5.6.7) and serotonin reuptake inhibitors (Section 6.9). What causes BDD is less well understood than what causes OCD. Psychoanalytic writers proposed that an unbearable unconscious conflict is displaced onto a body part, which becomes a safer target for the person's distress; there is little evidence for this, but it is worth knowing because displacement is usually taught as the defence of the phobias (Section 6.8). The genetic and brain evidence, much of it shared with OCD, is in Section 6.7. Culture shapes the form of the concern, though not the core of the disorder. DSM-5-TR notes that the gender ratio, the body areas of concern, the repetitive behaviours and the levels of distress are similar around the world, but that in collectivistic cultures such as Japan the fear may centre on offending other people with one's deformity, and that particular standards produce particular worries: eyelids in Japan, muscularity in Western countries. Traditional Japanese psychiatry recognises shubo-kyofu , "the phobia of a deformed body", a variant of taijin kyofusho that resembles BDD. In India, where advertisements have long sold creams that promise lighter skin, a wish for fairer skin is culturally ordinary and is not a disorder; what makes Zoya's concern about her "dark" skin part of BDD is the hours of preoccupation, the rituals, the distress and the fact that nobody else can see the flaw. BDD must also be told apart from koro , which DSM-5-TR describes as a culturally related condition, usually occurring in epidemics in South-East Asia, in which a man fears that his penis (or a woman that her labia, nipples or breasts) is shrinking or retracting into the body, often with a belief that death will follow. Koro is a fear of retraction and death, not a preoccupation with ugliness (Chapter 1 treats it, and its relative, dhat syndrome, among the cultural concepts of distress). Because BDD involves the body, anxiety and sometimes delusional conviction, it has many look-alikes, and examiners love to set them as distractors.
