Major depression can bring self-loathing about one's appearance, but it lacks the prominent preoccupation and rituals; and since depression so often follows BDD, the BDD should be diagnosed whenever its criteria are met. BDD is not diagnosed when the concern is discomfort with one's sex characteristics in gender dysphoria (Chapter 9), or when the belief is that one gives off a foul smell (olfactory reference disorder, Section 6.6.6). DSM-5-TR also contrasts BDD with body integrity dysphoria , a condition included in ICD-11 but not in DSM-5, in which a person persistently wants a healthy limb amputated, not because it looks ugly but because it feels as though it should not be there. Exam trap "Persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable to others" is body dysmorphic disorder . The distractors are all real disorders about the body: somatic symptom disorder (distressing symptoms), illness anxiety disorder (fear of a serious illness) and conversion disorder (unexplained neurological symptoms). In DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR, BDD is classified under obsessive-compulsive and related disorders , not under somatic symptom and related disorders, anxiety disorders or personality disorders. If an option says "somatoform disorders", it is the DSM-IV answer. Hoarding disorder Mahesh is a 64-year-old widower who retired from a clerk's post in the railways in Kolkata. His two-room flat holds what his daughter calls "forty years of paper": every newspaper he has bought since the early 1980s, tied in bundles that rise to the ceiling, together with old bills, wedding cards, calendars, plastic bags folded into other plastic bags, three broken table fans and a cupboard of shirts he has not worn in a decade. A narrow path leads from the door to a single chair, where he now sleeps, because his bed disappeared under the bundles years ago. The kitchen cannot be used; he eats out of packets. When Mahesh was in hospital two years ago his daughter hired two men and cleared half the flat. He wept when he came home, accused her of throwing away "important information", and within a year the space had filled again, partly with second-hand books he still buys every week from the pavement stalls of College Street. Neighbours complain about cockroaches and about the risk of fire, because stacks of paper lean against the old wiring. Mahesh does not think he has a problem. "Everything here is useful," he says. "One day I will sort it." Not long ago, Barlow and Durand recall, specialty anxiety clinics began to see patients like Mahesh, people who could not throw anything away, even a ten-year-old newspaper, for fear that they might urgently need it. At first the clinics assumed that this was a strange variant of OCD. It soon became clear that it was a major problem in its own right, and research led by the psychologists Randy O. Frost and Gail Steketee described its three main features: excessive acquisition of things, difficulty discarding them, and living amid excessive clutter and gross disorganisation. In 2013 DSM-5 made hoarding disorder a separate diagnosis. The DSM-5-TR criteria can be read as a series of answers to the question "Why isn't this just untidiness, poverty or a hobby?" Criterion A requires persistent difficulty discarding or parting with possessions, regardless of their actual value . "Persistent" rules out a temporary mess, such as the clutter that follows inheriting a relative's house; "discarding" covers throwing away, selling, giving away and recycling; and "regardless of their actual value" matters because people who hoard save valuable things too, often in piles mixed with worthless ones. Criterion B says why the person cannot discard: because of a perceived need to save the items and distress at the thought of parting with them. This criterion makes the saving intentional, and that is what separates hoarding disorder from the passive accumulation of objects seen, for example, in severe depression, dementia or schizophrenia, where possessions pile up because the person does not care or cannot manage, and removing them causes no distress. The reasons people give are the usefulness or beauty of the items, strong sentimental attachment, a sense of responsibility for the objects' fate, a horror of waste and a fear of losing important information. The commonest items saved are newspapers, magazines, clothing, bags, books, mail and papers, but virtually anything can be saved. Criterion C requires that the possessions congest and clutter active living areas and substantially compromise their intended use: the person cannot cook in the kitchen, sleep in the bed or sit in the chair. Here clutter has a technical meaning: a large group of usually unrelated or barely related objects piled together in a disorganised way in spaces designed for other purposes. The word "active" matters, because many people without the disorder have a cluttered attic, storeroom or garage; DSM looks at the rooms in which life is supposed to happen. The criterion ends with a clause written for cases like Mahesh's: if the living areas are uncluttered, it is only because third parties (family members, cleaners, local authorities) have intervened. A person whose home has been forcibly cleared still has hoarding disorder. Criterion D requires clinically significant distress or impairment, and DSM-5-TR adds "including maintaining a safe environment for self and others", because in hoarding the impairment often falls on the people around the hoarder. When insight is poor the person may report no distress at all, and the impairment is visible only to the family, until someone tries to clear the house, when distress is intense. The last two criteria are exclusions. Criterion E rules out hoarding that is the direct result of another medical condition: a brain injury, cerebrovascular disease, an infection of the brain such as herpes simplex encephalitis, surgery for a tumour, or Prader-Willi syndrome (a genetic disorder of chromosome 15 marked by an insatiable appetite, short stature and intellectual disability, in which hoarding and skin picking are common). Damage to the anterior ventromedial prefrontal and cingulate cortex is particularly associated with accumulating objects; in such patients the hoarding begins abruptly after the injury. Criterion F rules out hoarding better explained by another mental disorder: obsessions in OCD, decreased energy in major depression, delusions in schizophrenia, the cognitive deficits of a major neurocognitive disorder, or the restricted interests of autism spectrum disorder. Two specifiers complete the diagnosis. The first is excessive acquisition : the difficulty discarding is accompanied by excessive collecting, buying or stealing of items that are not needed or for which there is no space. About 80 to 90 percent of people with hoarding disorder show it. Excessive buying is the commonest form, followed by acquiring free items (leaflets, things other people have thrown out); stealing is less common. Barlow and Durand note that acquiring often brings pleasure, even euphoria, and may be a response to feeling low, the "retail therapy" of popular speech. Women tend to show more excessive acquisition, particularly buying, than men. The second specifier records insight, worded for hoarding: with good or fair insight (the person recognises that the hoarding-related beliefs and behaviours are problematic), with poor insight (the person is mostly convinced that they are not problematic, despite evidence to the contrary) and with absent insight/delusional beliefs (the person is completely convinced of this). Mahesh, who thinks that everything is useful and that nothing is wrong, has at best poor insight. People who hoard also tend to be indecisive (a trait their first-degree relatives share), perfectionistic, prone to procrastination and avoidance, distractible, and poor at planning and organising. Barlow and Durand add an extraordinarily strong emotional attachment to possessions, an exaggerated desire for control over them, and a striking difficulty deciding whether a possession is worth keeping, as though every object were equally valuable. A special group, animal hoarding , is defined by DSM-5-TR as the accumulation of a large number of animals together with a failure to provide minimal standards of nutrition, sanitation and veterinary care, and a failure to act on the animals' deteriorating condition (disease, starvation, even death) or on the environment (severe overcrowding, extremely unsanitary conditions). Newspaper reports describe homes occupied by one owner, often a middle-aged or elderly woman, and thirty or more animals, often cats, some of them dead. Many animal hoarders also hoard objects. Compared with object hoarding, animal hoarding involves more unsanitary conditions and even poorer insight: such people typically believe they are devoted carers. Where does hoarding end and collecting begin? A philatelist may own as many stamps as a hoarder owns newspapers. The difference, DSM-5-TR explains, is that normal collecting is organised and selective: the collector chooses, catalogues and displays, and the collection does not produce the clutter, distress or impairment of hoarding disorder. And why is hoarding not simply OCD? Barlow and Durand and DSM-5-TR give several reasons. In hoarding disorder there are no intrusive, unwanted obsessions that the saving is meant to neutralise; the urge to keep things feels natural, and the possessions are valued, sometimes loved. Acquisition can be pleasurable, whereas compulsions in OCD bring at most relief. The course differs: OCD tends to wax and wane, whereas hoarding begins early and gets worse with each passing decade, with few people reporting a waxing and waning course. And the results of treatment for hoarding have so far been more modest than those for OCD. Hoarding can occur within OCD, but then it looks different: it is driven by typical obsessions (fear of contamination or harm, or a feeling of incompleteness, such as a fear of losing one's identity unless every scrap of one's life is preserved), or by the wish to avoid onerous rituals (not throwing anything away to avoid endless washing). It is unwanted, distressing and never pleasurable, there is usually no excessive acquisition, and the hoarded items are more often bizarre (rubbish, rotten food, used nappies, nail clippings, even urine or faeces), which is very unusual in hoarding disorder. About 20 percent of people with hoarding disorder also meet criteria for OCD; when severe hoarding coexists with OCD but is independent of its obsessions, both disorders are diagnosed. Nationally representative figures for hoarding disorder do not yet exist, but community surveys in the United States and Europe put the point prevalence of clinically significant hoarding at 1.5 to 6 percent, and a meta-analysis of 12 studies in high-income countries found 2.5 percent, with no difference between the sexes. Clinical samples, by contrast, are mostly women. Hoarding is strongly tied to age. Symptoms may first appear around ages 15 to 19, start to interfere with daily functioning by the mid-twenties and cause clinically significant impairment by the mid-thirties; participants in clinical research are usually in their fifties, and Barlow and Durand put the average age at which people come for treatment at about 50, often after many years of hoarding and often living alone. In one population study in the Netherlands, hoarding symptoms were almost three times commoner in adults over 65 than in adults aged 30 to 40. About three-quarters of people with hoarding disorder also have a mood or anxiety disorder, most often major depression (30 to 50 percent), social anxiety disorder or generalised anxiety disorder, and these comorbid conditions are often the reason they consult, because people rarely volunteer their hoarding and clinicians rarely ask about it. The consequences reach well beyond the hoarder. Clutter impairs moving through the house, cooking, cleaning, washing and sleeping; appliances break and cannot be repaired because nobody can reach them; water and electricity may be cut off. In severe cases there is a real risk of fire, of falls (especially for elderly people) and of disease. Barlow and Durand cite a striking figure, which comes from one local data set: a ten-year review of residential fires by the Metropolitan Fire Brigade in Melbourne, Australia, found that fires in the homes of people who hoard made up only about 0.25 percent of residential fires but accounted for 24 percent of the preventable fire deaths (the figure is often quoted, as Barlow and Durand quote it, as 24 percent of all fire-related deaths, but it describes preventable deaths in one city). Families are strained, neighbours and local authorities are drawn in, and a substantial proportion of people with severe hoarding have faced eviction. Indian context In many Indian homes, keeping things is a virtue. Newspapers are stacked to be sold to the raddiwala, plastic bags and containers are washed and reused, and old clothes are passed down or turned into dusters. None of this is hoarding disorder. DSM-5-TR addresses exactly this situation: in cultures that place a high value on thrift and on storing possessions, the presence of distress and functional impairment should be the basis of the diagnosis. The test is not how much a family keeps but whether the keeping has defeated the use of the home and the safety of the people in it, as it has for Mahesh, who sleeps in a chair because his bed is buried. The available data from low- and middle-income countries suggest that the clinical features of hoarding are similar across cultures. Exam trap "Which one is not a compulsive behaviour in OCD: tapping, hoarding, washing or checking?" The answer is hoarding . Tapping, washing and checking are classic compulsions; hoarding has been a disorder in its own right since DSM-5, because it lacks intrusive obsessions, the possessions are valued rather than feared, and the course worsens with age. (Saving that is driven by OCD obsessions is diagnosed as OCD, but that is the exception.) Also know that an inability to discard worthless objects is a criterion of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder , and that collecting is organised and selective, while hoarding produces clutter and impairment. Trichotillomania and excoriation disorder: the body-focused repetitive behaviours Swati is fifteen and in Class 10 at a school in Pune. Her mother first noticed the bald patch on the crown of her head in the summer before the board examinations and took her to a dermatologist, sure that it was a disease of the scalp. It was not. Swati pulls out her hair. It happens mostly at night, at her desk, with her chemistry notes open in front of her, and on the bed when she is scrolling on her phone. Sometimes she does not notice that she is doing it until she sees a small heap of hairs on the page. At other times she feels an itchy, tingling sensation on her scalp and a building tension, and she searches with her fingers for a hair that feels coarse or "wrong", pulls it so that the root comes out whole, looks at it, rolls it between her fingers and bites off the root. For a moment she feels relief, almost pleasure; then she feels ashamed. Her eyebrows are almost gone, so she fills them in with a pencil, and she wears a broad hairband to cover the patch on her crown. She has stopped going to swimming classes. She has promised herself, and her mother, many times that she will stop. She has not been able to. Swati has trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder). The term was coined in 1889 by the French dermatologist François Henri Hallopeau (1842 to 1919) from Greek roots meaning hair ( thrix ), to pull ( tillein ) and madness ( mania ). The condition entered the American manual in DSM-III-R (1987), was classed in DSM-IV as an impulse-control disorder, and moved in DSM-5 to the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. DSM-5-TR's criteria are short. There must be (A) recurrent pulling out of one's own hair, resulting in hair loss; (B) repeated attempts to decrease or stop the pulling; (C) clinically significant distress or impairment; (D) no other medical condition, such as a skin disease, that accounts for the pulling or the hair loss; and (E) no other mental disorder that better explains it, such as attempts to improve a perceived flaw in appearance in BDD. Each criterion does a job. Criterion A requires hair loss, but DSM-5-TR notes that some people pull single hairs from all over a site, so that the loss is not clearly visible, and that many conceal it with make-up, scarves or wigs. Criterion B, the repeated attempts to stop, separates the disorder from a habit the person is content with, and it captures the sense of being out of control that makes the disorder so shaming. Criterion C counts as distress the feelings of loss of control, embarrassment and shame, and as impairment the avoidance of work, school and public situations, such as Swati's swimming class. Criterion D exists because many medical conditions cause hair loss without any pulling: alopecia areata, androgenic alopecia, telogen effluvium and several scarring conditions of the scalp. Most people with trichotillomania admit to pulling, but when they do not, a skin biopsy or dermoscopy of the scalp (trichoscopy) can settle the question, because pulled hair shows a characteristic pattern of reduced density and short, broken hairs of different lengths. Criterion E removes hair pulling that serves another disorder: the person with OCD who pulls hairs as part of a symmetry ritual, the person with BDD who plucks hairs that look ugly or asymmetrical, and the person with a psychosis who pulls hair in response to a delusion or a hallucination. The commonest sites are the scalp, the eyebrows and the eyelids (pulling eyelashes); less often the armpits, face, pubic area and perianal region. The sites may change over time. Pulling may come in brief episodes scattered through the day or in long sessions lasting hours, and the disorder may endure for months or years. It is often accompanied by rituals with the hair, of exactly the kind Swati performs: searching for a particular kind of hair (a specific texture or colour), trying to pull it out in a particular way (so that the root comes out intact), and examining it, rolling it between the fingers, pulling the strand between the teeth, biting it into pieces or swallowing it. Swallowing hair, trichophagia , can produce a trichobezoar , a ball of hair in the stomach or intestine that can cause anaemia, abdominal pain, vomiting, obstruction of the bowel and even perforation. Pain does not usually accompany pulling. Some people pull in a pattern that leaves nearly complete baldness except for a narrow fringe around the edges of the scalp, called tonsure trichotillomania after the shaved crown of a monk. Pulling rarely happens in front of anyone except immediate family members; some people also pull hair from other people, from pets or dolls, or from sweaters and carpets. The emotional sequence is what most clearly marks hair pulling off from an OCD compulsion. DSM-5-TR describes it in three steps: pulling may be triggered by anxiety or by boredom; it may be preceded by a rising sense of tension (either just before pulling or while trying to resist the urge); and it may lead to gratification, pleasure or relief. Some people report an "itch-like" or tingling sensation in the scalp that pulling relieves. Clinicians distinguish two styles. In focused pulling the person attends to the act, feels the tension beforehand and the relief afterwards; in automatic pulling the hand seems to pull on its own, while the person reads, watches television or lies in bed, without full awareness. Many people, like Swati, show both. Compare this with an OCD compulsion. The compulsion answers an obsession: a mother washes her hands because she fears she will infect her baby, and the washing brings relief from a feared consequence, never pleasure. Hair pulling answers no obsession and prevents no catastrophe; it is driven by an urge, a sensation or a mood, and it can feel good while it lasts. DSM-IV had actually required a rising tension before pulling and pleasure or relief afterwards. DSM-5 dropped both requirements, because research showed that a substantial number of people who pull do not experience the tension-relief sequence (Barlow and Durand). Trichotillomania is commoner than once believed. DSM-5-TR estimates its 12-month prevalence in adults and adolescents at 1 to 2 percent, and Barlow and Durand cite rates of 1 to 5 percent among college students. In clinical or self-identified samples women outnumber men by 10 to 1 or more, but the ratio may be closer to 2 to 1 in community samples, and in an online survey of more than 10,000 adults aged 18 to 69, representative of the American population, 1.7 percent reported current trichotillomania with no significant gender difference (1.8 percent of men and 1.7 percent of women). Among children, boys and girls are about equally represented. Hair pulling in infants is common and usually resolves; the disorder proper most often begins with, or just after, puberty. The course is chronic, with some waxing and waning if untreated, and symptoms may worsen before menstruation. A minority of people remit within a few years of onset without relapse. Most people with trichotillomania have at least one other body-focused repetitive behaviour (skin picking, nail biting, lip chewing), and the commonest comorbid disorders are major depression and excoriation disorder. Three more boundaries are worth knowing. Hair removal done purely for cosmetic reasons, such as plucking the eyebrows into shape, is not trichotillomania. Twisting and playing with the hair, or biting it rather than pulling it, does not qualify either. And a child with intellectual disability or autism who pulls hair along with head banging and hand biting, when frustrated or excited, is diagnosed with stereotypic movement disorder (Chapter 3) rather than trichotillomania. Stimulant drugs can worsen hair pulling, but they are rarely its main cause. Trichotillomania's twin is excoriation disorder (skin-picking disorder). Dermatologists had long described patients who picked their skin into wounds, under names such as neurotic or psychogenic excoriation, but DSM-5 was the first edition of the manual to give the problem its own diagnosis. The criteria follow the same pattern: (A) recurrent skin picking resulting in skin lesions; (B) repeated attempts to decrease or stop; (C) clinically significant distress or impairment; (D) not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance, such as cocaine, or to another medical condition, such as scabies (a mite infestation that causes intense itching and scratching); and (E) not better explained by another mental disorder: the delusions (such as a belief in parasites under the skin) or tactile hallucinations (formication, the feeling of insects crawling) of a psychotic disorder; attempts to improve a perceived flaw in BDD; stereotypies in stereotypic movement disorder; or the intention to harm oneself in non-suicidal self-injury. That last exclusion matters: a young person who cuts or burns herself to relieve unbearable feelings is injuring herself deliberately, whereas a person with excoriation disorder picks because of an urge and is distressed by the damage. The commonest sites are the face, the arms and the hands, though many people pick at several sites. They pick at healthy skin, at minor irregularities, at pimples or calluses, and at the scabs left by earlier picking, mostly with the fingernails but also with tweezers, pins or other objects, and they may rub, squeeze, lance or bite the skin as well. As with hair pulling, there may be rituals (searching for a particular kind of scab, examining it, playing with it, putting it in the mouth or swallowing it); there may be triggers of anxiety or boredom, rising tension and a sense of relief; and there are focused and automatic styles. The majority of people with the disorder spend at least an hour a day picking, thinking about picking and resisting the urge. The damage can be serious: scarring, infection that often needs antibiotics, occasionally surgery, and rarely a life-threatening complication. In the online survey of more than 10,000 American adults, 2.1 percent reported current and 3.1 percent lifetime excoriation disorder, and three-quarters or more of those affected in community samples are women. Picking usually begins in adolescence, around puberty, and often starts with a skin condition such as acne. When acne leads to picking that has taken on a life of its own, dermatologists speak of acne excoriée , and the clinical question is whether the picking has become independent of the skin condition. The course is chronic, with waxing and waning. Excoriation disorder must be told apart from dermatitis artefacta , the dermatologist's term for skin lesions that are presumably self-inflicted but that the patient denies producing. If there is evidence of deception, the diagnosis is malingering (when there is an external incentive) or factitious disorder (when there is none); in the absence of deception, and with repeated attempts to stop, excoriation disorder can be diagnosed. Washing compulsions in OCD can also damage the skin, and a person with BDD may pick at her skin to remove "imperfections"; in both cases the other disorder, not excoriation disorder, is diagnosed. People with Prader-Willi syndrome often begin picking their skin early in life, and their picking may meet the criteria for stereotypic movement disorder instead. Hair pulling and skin picking are the two named members of a larger group, the body-focused repetitive behaviours. DSM-5-TR records the others, such as nail biting, lip biting and cheek chewing, as "other body-focused repetitive behaviour disorder", one of its examples of other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder, when they are accompanied by repeated attempts to stop and cause significant distress or impairment. The psychological treatment with the best evidence for the whole group is habit reversal training, in which the person learns to notice the first movement of the hand and to substitute a competing response (Book 2, Section 4.9.1); the drug evidence is in Section 6.9. Exam trap Trichotillomania is no longer an impulse-control disorder : DSM-5 moved it to the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, and ICD-11 calls it a body-focused repetitive behaviour disorder. DSM-5 also removed DSM-IV's requirement of rising tension before pulling and relief afterwards. Hair pulling or skin picking aimed at fixing a perceived flaw is BDD , not trichotillomania or excoriation disorder; picking meant to hurt oneself is non-suicidal self-injury ; picking in response to delusional parasites belongs to a psychosis . Unlike OCD compulsions, body-focused repetitive behaviours are not triggered by obsessions . The rest of the family: other specified, substance-induced and medical forms, and ICD-11 Every DSM chapter ends with categories for presentations that do not fit its named disorders, and the OCRD chapter's examples are unusually interesting. DSM-5-TR uses other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder when the clinician wants to record why the criteria are not met, and lists seven examples: Body dysmorphic-like disorder with actual flaws : like BDD, except that the defects are clearly observable to others, yet the preoccupation with them is clearly excessive and impairing. Body dysmorphic-like disorder without repetitive behaviours : the person meets the criteria for BDD except that she has never performed repetitive behaviours or mental acts in response to the concern. Other body-focused repetitive behaviour disorder : nail biting, lip biting, cheek chewing and the like, with repeated attempts to stop and with distress or impairment. Obsessional jealousy : a non-delusional preoccupation with a partner's perceived infidelity, which may lead to repetitive behaviours or mental acts (checking the partner's phone, cross-questioning, replaying events) and which is not better explained by delusional disorder, jealous type, or by paranoid personality disorder. The person with obsessional jealousy can see that the suspicion may be unfounded but cannot stop checking; in delusional jealousy (Chapter 4) the infidelity is simply known to be true. Olfactory reference disorder (olfactory reference syndrome): a persistent preoccupation with the belief that one gives off a foul or offensive body odour that others cannot notice or notice only slightly, with repetitive and excessive behaviours such as checking for the odour, showering repeatedly, seeking reassurance and trying to camouflage the smell with perfumes. Traditional Japanese psychiatry knows it as jikoshu-kyofu , a variant of taijin kyofusho. Shubo-kyofu : the taijin kyofusho variant, met in Section 6.6.3, marked by an excessive fear of having a bodily deformity. Koro : which DSM-5-TR relates to dhat syndrome, an episode of sudden and intense anxiety that the penis (or the vulva and nipples) will recede into the body, possibly leading to death. Unspecified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder is used when the clinician chooses not to say why the criteria are not met, or lacks the information to say, for example in an emergency department. Two further categories mirror those found in every chapter of DSM-5-TR. In substance/medication-induced obsessive-compulsive and related disorder , obsessions, compulsions, hair pulling, skin picking or other OCRD symptoms predominate and develop during or soon after intoxication with, or withdrawal from, a substance, or after exposure to a medication. The substances DSM-5-TR names are stimulants, including cocaine and amphetamine-type drugs, together with heavy metals and toxins; its worked example is repetitive skin picking during intoxication in a man with a severe cocaine use disorder. The diagnosis is not made if the symptoms began before the substance use or persist for a substantial period (about a month) after intoxication or withdrawal ends, because then an independent disorder is more likely. The condition is very rare (Chapter 10 treats the substances). In obsessive-compulsive and related disorder due to another medical condition , the symptoms are the direct physiological consequence of an illness, shown by the history, examination or laboratory findings. DSM-5-TR's examples are instructive. Sydenham's chorea is the neurological manifestation of rheumatic fever, which itself follows infection with group A streptococcus (the bacterium of "strep throat"); alongside its involuntary, jerky movements it can produce obsessions, compulsions, inattention and emotional lability, and a child who presents with OCD-like symptoms of this kind receives this diagnosis. DSM-5-TR also discusses PANDAS and the broader PANS, sudden-onset childhood obsessions, compulsions or tics after an infection, which Section 6.7 explains. Damage to the striatum, from a cerebral infarction (a stroke) or Huntington's disease, can likewise produce OCRD symptoms. The diagnosis carries specifiers for the predominant symptom (OCD-like symptoms, appearance preoccupations, hoarding, hair pulling or skin picking), is coded F06.8, and should be suspected whenever symptoms begin acutely, begin unusually late in life or take an atypical form. The course follows that of the underlying illness. ICD-11, adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2019 and in use from 2022, has a grouping called obsessive-compulsive or related disorders that closely resembles DSM-5's, with three differences worth knowing. First, it gives olfactory reference disorder (6B22) full status as a named disorder, whereas DSM-5-TR mentions it only as an example of an other specified disorder. Second, it places hypochondriasis (health anxiety, 6B23) in this group, on the reasoning that, like OCD, it consists of a persistent preoccupation (with the possibility of having a serious illness) answered by repetitive behaviours such as checking the body and seeking reassurance; DSM-5-TR instead abolished hypochondriasis and replaced it with illness anxiety disorder and somatic symptom disorder, in a different chapter (Chapter 7). Third, ICD-11 names the urge-driven disorders as a group, the body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders (6B25), with trichotillomania and excoriation disorder as its two members. ICD-11 also cross-lists Tourette syndrome in this grouping, although Tourette syndrome itself is classified in the chapter on diseases of the nervous system (the tic disorders are taught in Chapter 3), and records symptoms caused by a medical condition as a "secondary obsessive-compulsive or related syndrome". One smaller difference: ICD-11's insight qualifier has two grades ("with fair to good insight" and "with poor to absent insight") where DSM-5-TR has three. Table 6.19 sets the two lists side by side. Koro (fear of genital retraction) and shubo-kyofu (fear of a deformed body) are cultural forms listed under other specified OCRD. 6.7 The Biology of Anxiety and Obsessions Medium yield · 2 Qs Two sisters grow up in the same house in Lucknow, eat the same food and go to the same school. One sails through her board examinations, sleeps well before interviews and shrugs off a near miss on the road. The other was a watchful, clinging baby, hid behind her mother's sari at every wedding, had her first panic attack at nineteen in a crowded bus and now cannot ride one alone. Why? Sections 6.2 to 6.6 described what the anxiety disorders and the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders look like. This section and the next ask what causes them. This section takes the biological evidence: the genes that run in families, the temperament that can be seen in a four-month-old, the chemical messengers that the anti-anxiety drugs act upon, and the brain circuits that sound the alarm. Section 6.8 takes the psychological evidence, conditioning, cognition and conflict, and joins the two in David Barlow's triple vulnerability theory. Keep one caution in mind throughout. Almost every biological finding in this field is a finding about vulnerability : something that makes a disorder more likely, not something that makes it inevitable. What runs in families: genes and a general tendency to be anxious The first question any biological theory must answer is whether a disorder runs in families, and the anxiety disorders clearly do. In family studies, investigators find people with a disorder (the probands), then interview their first-degree relatives (parents, siblings and children, who share on average half their genes) and compare the relatives' rates of illness with the rates among relatives of healthy people. Abby Fyer and her colleagues (1990), for example, found that about 31 percent of the first-degree relatives of people with a specific phobia also had a phobia, against 11 percent of the relatives of controls, and a later collaborative study with Barlow's centre replicated the finding (28 against 10 percent). Each type of phobia even seemed to "breed true": the relatives of a person with an animal phobia were most likely to fear animals. But families share kitchens and habits as well as genes. A child might learn to fear dogs simply by watching her mother scream at one. To separate genes from upbringing, researchers turn to twins, comparing identical (monozygotic) twins, who share all their genes, with fraternal (dizygotic) twins, who share about half. If identical twins are more alike in a disorder than fraternal twins, genes are probably at work, and the size of the difference yields an estimate of heritability , the proportion of the variation in a trait within a population that can be attributed to genetic differences between its members. First, every one of these disorders is moderately heritable, and none is wholly genetic. Second, and more surprising, the genes do not seem to be specific to the disorders. When the American psychiatric geneticist Kenneth S. Kendler and his colleagues (1995) analysed several disorders together in a large sample of twins, and when John Hettema and colleagues, with Kendler, returned to the question in 2005, they concluded that what is inherited is mostly a general tendency to become anxious rather than generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder or any other particular diagnosis. DSM-5-TR names this broad tendency in almost every risk-factor section of the anxiety chapter: negative affectivity (neuroticism), a stable disposition to experience negative emotions such as fear, worry, irritability and sadness easily and intensely. DSM-5-TR says that the genes for GAD overlap with those for negative affectivity and are shared with other anxiety and mood disorders, especially major depression, which is one reason why anxiety and depression so often occur in the same person and in the same family (Chapter 5). There are a few more specific contributions too. Barlow and Durand note that the tendency to panic runs in families with a genetic contribution somewhat different from that of general anxiety, and DSM-5-TR describes agoraphobia as the phobia most strongly tied to a genetic factor for "proneness to phobias". The clearest case of a specific inheritance is blood-injection-injury phobia, the fear that makes some people faint at the sight of blood or a needle (Section 6.3). Barlow and Durand report that as many as 60 percent of the first-degree relatives of people with this phobia share the reaction, at least to some degree, one of the highest rates of familial aggregation for any psychological disorder. What seems to be inherited is not the fear itself but an unusually strong vasovagal response: an overreaction of the baroreflex that normally corrects a sudden rise in blood pressure, so that the blood pressure drops too far and the person faints. The fear then grows around the possibility of fainting. Which genes are involved? Here the honest answer is disappointing. As with almost every emotional trait and psychological disorder, no single gene causes anxiety or panic. Barlow and Durand describe the vulnerability as coming from collections of genes in several regions of the chromosomes, each of small effect, and DSM-5-TR says of panic disorder that "multiple genes likely confer vulnerability", but that the exact genes and their functions remain unknown. Pinel's Biopsychology goes further: researchers have been unable to locate the genes for anxiety disorders definitively, and attention has shifted to the epigenetic mechanisms through which experience switches genes on and off. DSM-5-TR mentions one tantalising lead, that a high-expressing form of the gene for the enzyme monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) may be a risk factor for panic disorder in women only, but no single gene explains much. The genes, moreover, do not act alone. A genetic vulnerability, Barlow and Durand emphasise, does not cause anxiety or panic directly; stress and other events in the environment "turn on" the genes. DSM-5-TR gives an example in its account of social anxiety disorder: behavioural inhibition, the shy temperament described in the next subsection, is strongly genetically influenced, but the influence is subject to gene-environment interaction , because children high in behavioural inhibition are more susceptible to environmental influences such as socially anxious modelling by their parents. The same shy child may become a socially anxious adult if her parents avoid company and fret about what the neighbours think, and a merely reserved one if they gently and repeatedly encourage her to join in. Exam trap Heritability describes differences within a population , not the cause of one person's illness. A heritability of 61 percent for agoraphobia does not mean that 61 percent of your agoraphobia comes from your genes, nor that a heritable disorder cannot be treated. What is inherited in the anxiety disorders is mostly a general vulnerability (negative affectivity or neuroticism), not a specific disorder. The most familial phobia is blood-injection-injury , and the most familial form of OCD is the one that begins in childhood . Born shy: Jerome Kagan and behavioural inhibition If a general tendency to anxiety is inherited, it ought to be visible very early in life, long before a child could have learned to fear anything much. That is exactly what the Harvard developmental psychologist Jerome Kagan (1929 to 2021) set out to show. Kagan revived an idea as old as the Greek physician Galen, who sorted people into temperaments (his 1994 book was called Galen's Prophecy ). By temperament developmental psychologists mean the biologically based individual differences in emotional reactivity that appear in infancy and remain fairly stable. The temperament Kagan studied was behavioural inhibition : a tendency to become quiet, cautious, watchful, withdrawn and distressed in the face of unfamiliar people, objects and situations. Some toddlers walk into a room full of strangers and new toys and start playing; others stop, cling to their mother, fall silent and watch from a distance, sometimes for many minutes. Key study: Kagan and the high-reactive infants (1980s to 1999) Kagan and his colleague Nancy Snidman began with four-month-old babies. Each infant was shown a series of unfamiliar stimuli (moving mobiles, new voices, new smells) while the researchers recorded how much the baby thrashed its arms and legs and cried. About 20 percent of healthy infants were "high reactive": they became agitated and cried far more than the rest (Barlow and Durand describe them becoming agitated and crying at toys and other age-appropriate stimuli). The babies were then followed for years. The high reactors were much more likely than low reactors to be fearful and avoidant of unfamiliar events and people as toddlers, and they tended to show biological signs of an easily aroused nervous system: a more reactive heart, greater activation of the right frontal cortex on the EEG, and even a narrower facial skeleton. In their 1999 review, Kagan and Snidman reported that by adolescence about one-third of the high-reactive group showed signs of serious social anxiety. A companion study by Carl Schwartz, Snidman and Kagan (1999) followed 79 children who had been classified as inhibited or uninhibited in the second year of life; at 13, the inhibited group showed more generalised social anxiety, but not more specific fears, separation anxiety or performance anxiety. The conclusion was careful. Kagan and Snidman argued that the temperament should be seen as constraining the probability that a child will become fearless and spontaneous, not as determining an anxious personality: two-thirds of the high reactors did not develop serious social anxiety, and experience did much of the shaping. The criticisms are the usual ones for long follow-up studies: the samples were modest, mostly white and middle-class American children, and the many measures make chance findings possible. Later research has confirmed the main point. Barlow and Durand cite evidence that children with excessive behavioural inhibition are at increased risk of developing phobic behaviour, and DSM-5-TR lists behavioural inhibition as a temperamental risk factor for nearly every disorder in this chapter, from specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, agoraphobia and generalised anxiety disorder to OCD. Its strongest and most specific link is with social anxiety, which makes intuitive sense: a child who is distressed by strangers has many more occasions to learn that social life is threatening. Here, then, is part of the answer to the puzzle of the two sisters. The watchful, clinging baby probably began life with a more reactive alarm system, and what happened to her afterwards determined what it became. Exam trap Two famous ideas share the same words. Behavioural inhibition in Jerome Kagan's sense is a temperament of children: shyness and distress at the unfamiliar, visible by four months, that raises the risk of later social anxiety and phobias. The behavioural inhibition system of Jeffrey Gray is a brain circuit (Section 6.7.4) that produces anxiety and cautious checking for danger. If a question mentions infants, temperament or shyness, it is Kagan; if it mentions the septal-hippocampal system or a circuit, it is Gray. The chemistry of alarm: GABA, noradrenaline, serotonin and CRF Much of what we know about the chemistry of anxiety was discovered backwards. Pinel points out that current theories of the neural basis of the anxiety disorders rest heavily on the analysis of drug effects: a drug is found by accident to calm people, researchers work out what it does in the brain, and they then guess that anxiety must involve the system the drug acts on. That reasoning has a weakness that Barlow and Durand illustrate with aspirin: the fact that aspirin cures a headache does not mean that the headache was caused by a shortage of aspirin. With that caution, four systems have the strongest claims (Table 6.21). The first is the GABA-benzodiazepine system . Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter: when it binds to the GABA-A receptor , a channel opens and lets chloride ions into the neuron, making the neuron less likely to fire. The benzodiazepines, the family of drugs that includes chlordiazepoxide (Librium) and diazepam (Valium), act on this receptor; Pinel describes their behavioural effects as mediated by an agonistic action at GABA-A receptors. More precisely, they bind to their own site on the receptor complex and make GABA more effective, turning up the brain's natural brake. When specific binding sites for benzodiazepines were found in the brain in 1977, researchers wondered why the brain should have a receptor for a synthetic drug, and began to look for natural substances that might act on it. Two lines of evidence tie the system to anxiety. Drugs that act on the benzodiazepine site in the opposite direction, so-called inverse agonists , produce intense anxiety in animals and in human volunteers. And in a study by the British psychopharmacologist David J. Nutt and his colleagues (1990), an infusion of flumazenil, a drug that simply blocks the benzodiazepine site and has almost no effect in healthy people, provoked panic attacks in eight of ten patients with panic disorder and in none of ten controls, suggesting that the "set-point" of the receptor is altered in panic disorder. Barlow and Durand summarise the position: depleted levels of GABA are associated with increased anxiety, "although the relationship is not quite so direct." Pinel adds a caution about the animal research. The standard animal tests of anxiety (the elevated plus maze, in which rats choose between enclosed and exposed arms of a maze raised above the floor; the defensive-burying test; and the risk-assessment test) were all validated by showing that benzodiazepines reduce the measured anxiety. They may therefore be models of benzodiazepine-sensitive anxiety rather than of anxiety in general. The second system is noradrenaline. The locus coeruleus ("blue spot"), a small nucleus in the pons of the brain stem, is the main source of the brain's noradrenaline, and its fibres reach almost the whole forebrain. Barlow and Durand describe it as part of a circuit involved in emergency and alarm reactions that may be related to panic. The classic evidence comes from monkeys. In 1976 the American psychiatrist D. Eugene Redmond Jr. and his colleagues electrically stimulated the locus coeruleus of stump-tailed macaques and observed behaviour like that which the animals show when they are threatened. In humans, DSM-5-TR lists yohimbine, a drug that increases the firing of noradrenergic neurons by blocking the alpha-2 receptors that normally restrain them, among the agents that provoke panic attacks far more readily in people with panic disorder than in others. Clonidine, which acts on the same receptors in the opposite direction, quietens the locus coeruleus. The third system is serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT), made by the raphe nuclei of the brain stem and sent throughout the brain. Serotonin is best thought of as a modulator, a system that restrains and steadies other systems rather than producing anxiety or calm itself. The evidence again begins with treatment: the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) help most of the disorders in this chapter (Section 6.9). Jeffrey Gray and Neil McNaughton (1996) and the Brazilian researcher F. G. Graeff (1993) proposed that serotonin normally holds the brain's fight/flight system in check, so that a deficiency of serotonin activity releases it and makes panic more likely. The search for a "serotonin gene" has produced one famous lead: Klaus-Peter Lesch and his colleagues (1996) reported that a common variation in the gene for the serotonin transporter, the protein that SSRIs block, was associated with anxiety-related personality traits. The effect was small, and later studies have not been consistent. Serotonin's clearest role, as you will see, is in OCD. The fourth system is hormonal. Increasingly, Barlow and Durand note, attention has focused on corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF), the hormone with which the hypothalamus starts the body's main stress response. CRF activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis, which ends in the release of cortisol from the adrenal glands (the axis itself is described in Book 1, Section 11.8.4). But CRF also acts within the brain, on exactly the regions implicated in anxiety: the limbic system, particularly the hippocampus and the amygdala; the locus coeruleus; the prefrontal cortex; and the dopamine system. And it interacts with the other three systems, GABA, serotonin and noradrenaline. That is why many researchers now see the CRF system as central to the expression of both anxiety and depression, and why the genes that make it easier to switch on are a target of current research. The fear circuit: the amygdala, prefrontal control and Gray's two systems Chemicals act in places, and the places that matter most for anxiety lie in the limbic system, the ring of structures that, in Barlow and Durand's phrase, acts as a mediator between the brain stem and the cortex. The brain stem monitors changes in bodily functions and relays potential danger signals upward; the cortex evaluates what is seen and heard and sends its own danger signals down. At the centre of this traffic sits the amygdala , an almond-shaped cluster of nuclei deep in each temporal lobe. Figure 6.11 shows its connections in simplified form. Joseph LeDoux's research on the two routes by which a threat reaches the amygdala is taught in Book 1 (Section 11.4.5), and only one consequence of it is needed here. Sensory information travels from the thalamus to the amygdala by two roads: a fast, crude "low road" that goes directly from the thalamus to the amygdala, and a slower, more accurate "high road" that passes through the sensory cortex first. Because the low road bypasses the cortex, the amygdala can be set off by a threat before, or without, any conscious awareness of it. Imaging studies show the same thing in people: angry or fearful faces flashed too briefly to be consciously seen still activate the amygdala. This matters clinically. A panic attack that seems to come "out of the blue" may have had a trigger, a flicker of breathlessness, a faint smell, a glimpse of a crowded platform, that the person never consciously noticed. From the amygdala, signals go out to the structures that produce the bodily and behavioural side of fear: the hypothalamus, which releases CRF and starts the HPA axis; the locus coeruleus, which floods the forebrain with noradrenaline and raises arousal and vigilance; the central (periaqueductal) grey of the midbrain, which organises freezing and flight; and the brain stem nuclei that drive the heart and breathing. Meanwhile, the prefrontal cortex, especially its ventromedial part, sends signals back down to the amygdala that can damp its response: this is how a person learns that a once-dangerous dog is now safe, and how she talks herself down from a scare. Brain-imaging studies of anxiety disorders, Barlow and Durand report, now agree on a pattern: the limbic system, including the amygdala, is overly responsive to stimulation or new information (abnormal bottom-up processing ), while the controlling functions of the cortex that should down-regulate the hyperexcitable amygdala are deficient (abnormal top-down processing ). Pinel adds two refinements. Unlike depression, in which the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and amygdala appear to shrink, the anxiety disorders show no significant atrophy of these structures; the differences are differences of activity during emotional tasks. And each anxiety disorder seems to have its own pattern of functional connectivity between brain regions, so the "anxious brain" is not one brain but several. A threat reaches the amygdala by a fast low road from the thalamus and a slower high road through the cortex; the amygdala drives the hormonal, alarm, defensive and bodily outputs. In anxiety disorders the amygdala over-reacts and the prefrontal brake is weak. Is anxiety one state or two? The British neuropsychologist Jeffrey Alan Gray (1934 to 2004), working mostly with animals, argued that it is two, with two circuits (Gray 1982, 1985; Gray and McNaughton 1996; McNaughton and Gray 2000). The first, the behavioural inhibition system (BIS), runs from the septal and hippocampal area of the limbic system to the frontal cortex. It is activated by signals from the brain stem of unexpected events, such as sudden changes in bodily functioning that might mean danger, and by danger signals that descend from the cortex when we see something threatening; it receives a big boost from the amygdala. When it is activated, Barlow and Durand write, "our tendency is to freeze, experience anxiety, and apprehensively evaluate the situation to confirm that danger is present". In Gray's wider theory of personality the BIS responds to signals of punishment, of frustrated reward and of novelty, and people with a highly reactive BIS are anxiety-prone. The second circuit, the fight/flight system (FFS), identified by Gray and by Graeff, originates in the brain stem and travels through several structures, including the amygdala (in the temporal lobe), the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus and the central grey matter of the midbrain. When stimulated in animals it produces an immediate alarm-and-escape response that looks very much like panic in humans, and, as you saw, it may be held in check by serotonin.
