In the early 1960s the American psychiatrist Donald Klein, whose drug studies you met in Section 6.2 and whose theory of panic comes in the next subsection, found that the antidepressant imipramine stopped the sudden attacks of his anxious patients while leaving their chronic anticipatory anxiety largely untouched. In 1964 he published the result under the title "Delineation of two drug-responsive anxiety syndromes": if one drug could block panic without relieving anxiety, panic and anxiety were probably different states with different machinery. This "pharmacological dissection" helped persuade the authors of DSM-III (1980) to separate panic disorder from generalised anxiety, the division you met in Sections 6.2 and 6.4. Circuits are not fixed at birth. Barlow and Durand stress that factors in the environment can change the sensitivity of these circuits, making a person more or less susceptible to anxiety, and one study shows how ordinary such a factor can be. Jeffrey G. Johnson and his colleagues (2000), in the Children in the Community Study in New York State, interviewed 688 young people at an average age of 16 and again at an average age of 22. Heavy smoking in adolescence (20 or more cigarettes a day) predicted a far higher risk of anxiety disorders in early adulthood, even after the researchers had controlled for difficult childhood temperament, adolescent anxiety and depression, alcohol and drug use, and parental smoking and psychopathology: the odds of panic disorder were about 15 times higher, of generalised anxiety disorder about 5.5 times higher and of agoraphobia nearly 7 times higher. The reverse did not hold: anxious adolescents were no more likely than others to become heavy smokers. One explanation is that chronic exposure to nicotine, which itself produces bodily arousal, together with the breathing problems that smoking causes, increases biological vulnerability to anxiety and panic. DSM-5-TR now lists smoking as a risk factor for panic attacks and panic disorder. One of Johnson's co-authors was Donald Klein, and the link between breathing and panic was the centre of Klein's own theory. Exam trap In Gray's model the behavioural inhibition system (septal-hippocampal) produces anxiety and the fight/flight system (brain stem, amygdala, hypothalamus, central grey) produces panic . LeDoux's low road runs from the thalamus directly to the amygdala and is fast and unconscious; the high road passes through the cortex. The imaging pattern in anxiety disorders is too much bottom-up amygdala activity and too little top-down prefrontal control. A false alarm for suffocation: the biology of panic Ask people with panic disorder to describe their worst symptom and many will say that they could not breathe: a sudden air hunger, a smothering, a feeling that the next breath will not come. Ordinary fear, the fear of a man who meets a snake on the path, does not usually include a desperate shortage of breath. Why should panic? Donald F. Klein (1928 to 2019), the American psychiatrist whose imipramine studies had helped to define panic disorder, offered an answer in 1993 in a paper in Archives of General Psychiatry entitled "False suffocation alarms, spontaneous panics, and related conditions: an integrative hypothesis". Klein's suffocation false alarm theory begins with evolution. Suffocation is one of the oldest threats to life, and natural selection should have equipped us with a monitor that watches for its early signs, chiefly a rise in the level of carbon dioxide in the blood (and, Klein suggested, of lactate), and an alarm that fires when the monitor detects them. The alarm's output is exactly what a suffocating animal needs: sudden respiratory distress and air hunger, rapid breathing that blows off carbon dioxide, a surge of panic and an overwhelming urge to escape to open air. In most people the monitor fires only when there is real danger, as when someone is trapped in a smoke-filled room. Klein's proposal was that in panic disorder the monitor is oversensitive: its threshold is set too low, so that it "misfires" at small and harmless rises in carbon dioxide and sounds a false alarm. A spontaneous panic attack, on this view, is not a fear reaction gone wrong but a suffocation alarm going off when there is nothing to suffocate on. Klein argued that the idea could explain several puzzles: why breathlessness is so prominent in panic but not in other fears; why panic attacks can strike during relaxation and even sleep, when breathing slows and carbon dioxide rises; why panic is associated with lung disease; and why it is linked with childhood separation anxiety. Klein also suggested that the chronic over-breathing seen in many panic patients is not a cause of the attacks but an attempt to keep carbon dioxide below the alarm's threshold. Key study: provoking panic in the laboratory (1967 onwards) The theory rests on a long line of challenge studies , in which a substance is given to people with and without panic disorder to see who panics. The first classic was published by Ferris N. Pitts Jr. and James N. McClure Jr. in 1967 under the title "Lactate metabolism in anxiety neurosis": when they infused sodium lactate into patients with what was then called anxiety neurosis, most of the patients had an anxiety attack, while few of the healthy controls did. Later researchers found the same with carbon dioxide: breathing air enriched with carbon dioxide, whether a 5 to 7 percent mixture for several minutes or a single deep breath of a much stronger one, provokes attacks far more readily in people with panic disorder. DSM-5-TR lists the agents that provoke panic in panic disorder to a much greater extent than in other people: sodium lactate, caffeine, isoproterenol, yohimbine, carbon dioxide and cholecystokinin. It adds that people with panic disorder, and also children with separation anxiety disorder, show "particularly enhanced sensitivity to respiratory stimulation using CO2-enriched air", and that breathing disturbances such as asthma are associated with panic disorder in history, comorbidity and family history. This respiratory sensitivity is the part of the evidence that shows some specificity for panic disorder, just as Klein's theory predicts, although DSM-5-TR stresses that none of these tests is useful for diagnosis. The critique came from the psychologists. In 1989 William Sanderson, Ronald Rapee and David Barlow had 20 patients with panic disorder breathe 5.5 percent carbon dioxide for fifteen minutes. All were told that when a light in front of them was lit, they could reduce the carbon dioxide by turning a dial. For ten patients the light stayed on; for the other ten it never came on. In fact the dial did nothing, and everyone received the full mixture. Yet the patients who believed they had control reported fewer and milder panic symptoms, less anxiety and fewer catastrophic thoughts, and were significantly less likely to have a panic attack. The same chemical challenge, in other words, produced different amounts of panic depending on what the person believed. What should we conclude? The challenge studies show that people with panic disorder are unusually sensitive to changes in their own breathing and body chemistry, and Klein's theory gives that sensitivity an elegant evolutionary explanation. But the fact that so many chemically unrelated substances (lactate, caffeine, yohimbine, cholecystokinin, carbon dioxide) all provoke panic suggests that what they share may be the sensations they produce rather than a single chemical lesion, and the Sanderson experiment shows that the meaning a person gives to those sensations helps decide whether they end in panic. That is the starting point of David Clark's cognitive theory of panic, the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations, which Section 6.8 explains. The two accounts are not necessarily rivals: an oversensitive alarm may supply the sensations, and a catastrophic interpretation may turn them into an attack. Clinical link The challenge studies have a practical lesson. Before treating panic as purely psychological, make sure a physician has looked for medical conditions that produce similar sensations (thyroid disease, heart rhythm disorders, asthma and other lung disease), and ask about the client's caffeine intake and smoking, both of which raise the risk of attacks. The finding that harmless bodily sensations can be deliberately provoked is also the basis of interoceptive exposure in cognitive-behavioural treatment of panic, in which the client is helped to bring on breathlessness or dizziness on purpose and to learn that nothing terrible follows (Book 2, Sections 4.3 and 5.6.3). Exam trap "Suffocation alarm theories explain the clinical condition of" panic disorder . The distractors are unrelated conditions: Down syndrome is a chromosomal cause of intellectual disability (trisomy 21) and autism spectrum disorder a neurodevelopmental disorder (both in Chapter 3); delirium is an acute, fluctuating confusional state caused by a medical condition or a substance (Chapter 10). The theory is Donald Klein's (1993), not David Clark's: Klein's is a biological false alarm, Clark's a cognitive misinterpretation. The obsessive brain: serotonin and the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop The biology of OCD has its own story, and once again it began with a drug. In the 1960s and 1970s psychiatrists noticed that one tricyclic antidepressant, clomipramine, relieved obsessions and compulsions, while the other antidepressants of the day did little for them. Clomipramine differs from its relatives in one important way: it blocks the reuptake of serotonin much more powerfully. When the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors arrived, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine and the rest, they too helped OCD. The comparison that made the case was a direct one. In a double-blind crossover trial published in 1989, Henrietta Leonard, Susan Swedo, Judith Rapoport and their colleagues at the National Institute of Mental Health gave children and adolescents with OCD clomipramine and desipramine, a tricyclic that acts mainly on noradrenaline, in turn; clomipramine was clearly superior. The same group found the same contrast in trichotillomania (Swedo and colleagues 1989). Meanwhile the benzodiazepines, which act on the GABA system and help many anxiety disorders, did little for obsessions. These findings produced the serotonin hypothesis of OCD : the idea that the central serotonin (5-HT) system is disturbed in the disorder. Further evidence came from challenge studies of the kind used in panic. In 1987 Joseph Zohar , Thomas Insel and their colleagues gave patients with OCD and healthy controls a drug called m-chlorophenylpiperazine (mCPP), which stimulates serotonin receptors. In the patients, but not in the controls, it produced a temporary worsening of obsessions; and after a course of clomipramine treatment the patients' response to the same challenge was blunted (Zohar and colleagues 1988). The hypothesis has to be stated carefully, however. It is not simply that people with OCD lack serotonin, for if that were so, any drug that raised serotonin should work at once; in practice the serotonin reuptake inhibitors take weeks to help OCD and often need higher doses than in depression (Section 6.9). The better statement is that the serotonin system modulates the brain circuit that goes wrong in OCD, so that drugs acting on it can, over time, calm that circuit. And the aspirin caution applies here too: response to a drug does not prove what caused the disorder. Other transmitters play secondary parts. Dopamine is implicated because adding a low dose of an antipsychotic drug, which blocks dopamine, helps some patients who do not respond to a serotonin drug alone, especially those with tic-related OCD; glutamate, the brain's main excitatory transmitter and the working transmitter of the circuit described next, is the subject of much current research. Exam trap "Which biological system is implicated in obsessive-compulsive disorder?" The best single answer is the central serotonin (5-HT) system , because clomipramine and the SSRIs, which block serotonin reuptake, are the drugs that help OCD. GABA is the system of the anxiety disorders and of the benzodiazepines, which do little for obsessions. Glutamate and dopamine are implicated too, but secondarily (dopamine, for example, in antipsychotic augmentation for tic-related OCD), so they are not wrong in themselves; they are simply not the classic answer. Where in the brain does the trouble lie? Imaging studies have converged on a loop of connections known as the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit (CSTC circuit). DSM-5-TR names the orbitofrontal cortex (the underside of the frontal lobes, just above the eyes), the anterior cingulate cortex and the striatum as the regions most strongly implicated, with changes in frontolimbic, frontoparietal and cerebellar networks also reported. Barlow and Durand summarise the classic finding: although the size and structure of the brain are the same, people with OCD show increased activity in the orbital surface of the frontal cortex, increased activity in the cingulate gyrus and, to a lesser extent, in the caudate nucleus (part of the striatum), a circuit that runs from the orbital frontal cortex to parts of the thalamus. Activity in these regions is correlated, so that when one is active the others tend to be active too, and their pathways are rich in serotonin. A simple way to understand the loop is shown in Figure 6.12. The orbitofrontal cortex and the anterior cingulate act as an error detector: they generate a signal that "something is wrong" (the hands are dirty, the door is unlocked, the picture is crooked) and a feeling that something must be done about it. Normally, the striatum, and the caudate nucleus in particular, acts as a filter or gate. It lets through the signals that deserve action and suppresses the rest, so that a passing thought about germs on a doorknob is noticed and dismissed. In OCD the filter fails. The signal passes through the striatum undamped, the thalamus relays it back to the cortex, the cortex fires the alarm again, and the person is caught in a loop: the worry about contamination keeps returning, and the urge to wash will not switch off. The compulsion brings relief for a while, but because the loop has not been broken, the alarm soon sounds again. This is a model, not a photograph of the brain, but it explains why obsessions feel so insistent, and why they are experienced as foreign, sticky signals rather than as the person's own considered judgements. Trigger touching a doorknob Orbitofrontal cortex and anterior cingulate Signal: "something is wrong, act now" Striatum (caudate nucleus) Thalamus signal sent on filter fails: signal not damped looped back Urge to wash or check: compulsion, brief relief Serotonin pathways modulate this loop. In Baxter's 1992 PET study, patients who improved on fluoxetine or behaviour therapy showed lower right caudate activity. Figure 6.12 The cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop in OCD (schematic). The orbitofrontal cortex and anterior cingulate signal that something is wrong; the striatum fails to filter the signal; the thalamus loops it back to the cortex, and the alarm keeps sounding. A single case shows how much this region matters. Thomas Insel (1992) retold a case first reported by Paul Eslinger and Antonio Damasio (1985): a man who had been a successful accountant, husband and father of two had an operation to remove a brain tumour. He recovered well, and his intelligence test scores were as high as ever, but within a year his business had failed and his family had separated from him. He was spending his days in lengthy, uncontrollable rituals of washing, dressing and rearranging things in the single room where he lived. The area of his brain damaged by the surgery was a small part of the orbital frontal cortex. Insel himself urged caution. It is one case; other people with the same lesion might react differently; and the orbitofrontal cortex is implicated in other anxiety and emotional disorders, so damage there may raise negative emotion in general rather than cause OCD in particular. There is also the problem of direction. An overactive circuit might be the result of hours of obsessive thinking rather than its cause, just as a runner's brain looks different from a walker's because of the running. Key study: Baxter and the brain changed by behaviour therapy (1992) If the circuit causes the symptoms, then successful treatment, of any kind, should change the circuit. Lewis R. Baxter Jr. and his colleagues at the University of California, Los Angeles, tested this with positron emission tomography (PET), which measures how much glucose different brain regions are using. They scanned patients with OCD before and after treatment with either the SSRI fluoxetine or behaviour therapy (exposure and response prevention). In patients who responded to either treatment, the activity of the head of the right caudate nucleus fell significantly; in non-responders and in healthy controls it did not change. The paper's title made the point: "Caudate glucose metabolic rate changes with both drug and behavior therapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder." The same team replicated the finding with a new group of patients (Schwartz and colleagues 1996). The study, widely noted at the time, showed that a psychological treatment can change brain function as surely as a drug can, and that a brain difference is not proof that a disorder is "biological" in the sense of being beyond the reach of psychology. Its limits were the small samples and the fact that a change in the caudate after treatment still does not tell us what caused the disorder in the first place. When every other treatment has failed, some patients with severe OCD are offered neurosurgery or deep brain stimulation aimed at parts of this circuit; those treatments, and the Indian law that governs psychosurgery, are taught in Section 6.9. After a sore throat: PANDAS, tics and the biology of the related disorders Ajay was a cheerful seven-year-old in Chennai, in Class 2, with no history of worry. In the second week of January he had a fever and a sore throat; the paediatrician took a throat swab, which grew streptococcus, and prescribed an antibiotic. Within days of the fever settling, Ajay changed almost overnight. He began washing his hands dozens of times a day, until the skin cracked. He refused to touch his school bag because it "had germs", insisted on going back through every doorway he had walked through, and screamed if his mother left the room. His eyes began to blink hard and repeatedly, and he cleared his throat with a little grunt every few seconds. His handwriting, which had been neat, became a scrawl. His parents, frightened, took him back to the paediatrician, who referred him to a child psychiatrist. Over the next weeks the symptoms eased; months later, after another throat infection, they returned. Stories like Ajay's led Susan E. Swedo , an American researcher in paediatrics and neuropsychiatry, and her colleagues at the National Institute of Mental Health to propose a new syndrome. In 1998 they published a clinical description of their first 50 cases under the name PANDAS : paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections. They gave five working criteria: the presence of OCD and/or a tic disorder; onset before puberty; an episodic course, with abrupt onset and dramatic flare-ups; an association between the onset or flare-ups and infection with group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus; and associated neurological abnormalities, such as hyperactivity or jerky, choreiform movements during flare-ups. The mean age at onset in their sample was 6.3 years for tics and 7.4 years for OCD, and the onset was typically "acute and dramatic". Barlow and Durand list the features that set the PANDAS group apart from other children with OCD: they are more likely to be boys; their symptoms begin dramatically, often with a fever or sore throat; they have full remissions between episodes; their symptoms remit during antibiotic treatment; they show evidence of past streptococcal infections; and they are noticeably clumsy. The proposed mechanism borrowed from a disease that is not in doubt. Sydenham's chorea , the neurological form of rheumatic fever, is known to be caused by an autoimmune reaction: antibodies made against the streptococcus also attack the basal ganglia, the deep brain structures that include the striatum, producing involuntary movements and, often, obsessions and compulsions (Section 6.6.6). Swedo proposed that in PANDAS the same kind of misdirected immune attack on the basal ganglia, the very region at the heart of the CSTC circuit, produces OCD and tics without the other signs of rheumatic fever. The idea is attractive because it links a known infection, a known immune mechanism and a known brain circuit. It has also been intensely controversial. There is no laboratory test that confirms PANDAS; streptococcal throat infections are so common in schoolchildren that a link with any later symptom is easy to find by chance; studies of antibodies and of antibiotic treatment have given inconsistent results; and critics worry that the label is applied too readily. Barlow and Durand note that the prevalence of the condition has yet to be determined. Partly in response, Swedo, James Leckman and Noel Rose (2012) proposed a broader category, PANS , which DSM-5-TR spells out as paediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome: an abrupt, dramatic onset of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or severely restricted food intake, together with a range of other neuropsychiatric symptoms, whatever the trigger, because such acute onsets may follow many different infections or other insults. DSM-5-TR discusses both syndromes under obsessive-compulsive and related disorder due to another medical condition, and among the risk factors for OCD it notes that some children develop a sudden onset of obsessive-compulsive symptoms that has been associated with infectious agents and a post-infectious autoimmune syndrome. Whatever the final verdict, a child like Ajay, with an abrupt, dramatic onset of OCD and tics after an infection, needs a paediatric medical assessment as well as a psychological one. Ajay's tics point to a second biological thread. Tic disorders and OCD are closely linked (the tic disorders and Tourette's disorder are taught in Chapter 3). DSM-5-TR reports that up to 30 percent of people with OCD have a lifetime tic disorder, most commonly men whose OCD began in childhood, and that these people differ from others with OCD in the themes of their symptoms, their comorbidity, their course and the way the disorder runs in their families; a triad of OCD, tics and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder can also be seen in children. Barlow and Durand put the proportion of children and adolescents with OCD who have had a tic disorder at some point at 10 to 40 percent, and note that the obsessions in tic-related OCD are almost always about symmetry. This is why DSM-5 added the "tic-related" specifier to OCD (Section 6.5), and why tic-related OCD is the form in which the dopamine-blocking drugs are most useful. What of the other members of the OCRD family? Their biology is much less studied, but what there is points back towards OCD. Body dysmorphic disorder is commoner in the first-degree relatives of people with OCD; its heritability, 37 to 49 percent, reflects both a genetic vulnerability shared with OCD and influences specific to BDD; and one imaging study found abnormal brain functioning similar to that in OCD (Rauch and colleagues 2003, cited by Barlow and Durand). Hoarding is strongly familial, with about half its variability genetic and indecisiveness common in relatives; a study by David Tolin and colleagues (2012) found that, when deciding whether to keep or discard their own possessions, people with hoarding disorder showed abnormal activity in brain regions involved in judging the emotional significance of an object, unlike people with OCD; and, as Section 6.6.4 noted, damage to the ventromedial prefrontal and cingulate cortex can produce hoarding in people who never hoarded before. Trichotillomania and excoriation disorder are commoner in people with OCD and their first-degree relatives, and there is some evidence of a genetic vulnerability to each; in one study Stephan Züchner and his colleagues (2006) found rare mutations in a gene called SLITRK1 in a small number of people with trichotillomania. And the finding that clomipramine helped hair pulling more than desipramine did suggests that serotonin plays a part there too. Exam trap PANDAS (Susan Swedo and colleagues, 1998) stands for paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections: a sudden childhood onset of OCD or tics after a group A streptococcal infection, thought to be an autoimmune attack on the basal ganglia , on the model of Sydenham's chorea . PANS (2012) is paediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome, the broader category with any trigger; some textbooks, Barlow and Durand among them, expand it differently, but DSM-5-TR's "acute-onset" is the standard form. Finally, none of the evidence in this section makes anxiety or OCD purely biological : the heritabilities are moderate, temperament only shifts probabilities, and behaviour therapy changes the brain. Section 6.8's triple vulnerability theory brings the biological and psychological strands together. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first.
