Answers: (1) somatoform, (2) dysmorphophobia, (3) muscle dysmorphia, (4) active, (5) François Henri Hallopeau, (6) hypochondriasis (health anxiety), (7) four, (8) behavioural inhibition, (9) suffocation, (10) caudate. 6.8 Learning, Cognition and Conflict: Psychological Explanations High yield · 7 Qs Go back for a moment to the small boy in Vienna who would not go out into the street because a horse might bite him. Section 6.7 asked what Hans might have inherited: an anxious temperament, a jumpy alarm system, a brain that learns fear easily. That is only half the story. Two children with the same genes can grow up with very different fears, and the same child can lose a fear as quickly as he gained it. Something in experience and in thought decides which fear a vulnerable person develops, what it attaches to, and why it lasts long after any real danger has passed. Three traditions have tried to say what that something is. Learning theorists say the fear was learned and is kept alive by avoidance. Cognitive theorists say it lives in the way the person interprets danger, the body and his own mind. Psychodynamic theorists say it is a disguised expression of an inner conflict. This section takes each in turn, tests it against the evidence, and ends with the model that most researchers now use to tie the strands together: David Barlow's triple vulnerability theory. How these ideas are turned into therapy (exposure, cognitive therapy, psychoanalysis) is the business of Book 2; here they are explanations of cause. Fear as a learned response: conditioning and Mowrer's two-factor theory The behaviourists' starting point was a famous and ethically troubling experiment. In 1920 John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner showed an 11-month-old infant, Albert, a white rat; each time he reached for it, a steel bar was struck with a hammer behind his head. After a handful of pairings Albert cried and crawled away at the sight of the rat alone, and the fear spread to a rabbit, a dog and a fur coat. Book 1, Section 6.4.1 tells the story in full. For this chapter, what matters is the vocabulary it gave clinicians (Book 1, Section 6.2.2). The loud noise was an unconditioned stimulus (UCS): it produces fear without any learning. The startle and crying it produced was the unconditioned response (UCR), an unlearned reflex. The rat, once neutral, became a conditioned stimulus (CS), and the fear it now produced was a conditioned response (CR). Put a phobia into the same frame and it looks simple. A boy in Pune is bitten by a street dog (UCS), feels terror (UCR), and from then on the sight of any dog (CS) makes his heart race (CR). A phobia, on this view, is a conditioned emotional response that has spread from the original stimulus to everything that resembles it. There was an obvious problem, and it troubled learning theorists for years. Classical conditioning has a built-in cure. If a conditioned stimulus is presented again and again without the unconditioned stimulus, the conditioned response weakens and disappears; this is extinction . The boy meets dozens of dogs in the months after his bite, almost none of which bite him. By the laws of conditioning his fear should melt away. In real phobias it does not. People keep a fear of dogs, lifts or bridges for decades, even though the feared disaster almost never repeats itself. Why does extinction fail? The answer that became standard was given by the American learning theorist Orval Hobart Mowrer (1907 to 1982), usually cited as O. Hobart Mowrer. In 1947 he proposed that a phobia is built by two different kinds of learning working one after the other, an account known as the two-factor theory (or two-process theory). The first factor is classical conditioning: a neutral stimulus is paired with something frightening and becomes a conditioned stimulus for fear. The second factor is operant conditioning (Book 1, Section 6.5.5). Once the dog has become frightening, the boy learns to cross the road, to walk the long way to school, to stay indoors when the colony dogs are out. Each of these acts is followed by a fall in fear. A fall in an unpleasant state is a powerful reinforcer, and because the reinforcement comes from removing something aversive rather than adding something pleasant, it is negative reinforcement (Book 1, Section 6.5.3). The avoidance therefore grows stronger with every use. Here is the clever part. The very act that brings relief also stops extinction from happening. Extinction needs the person to meet the conditioned stimulus and stay with it long enough to discover that nothing terrible follows. The avoider never stays. He crosses the road before the dog is near, so he never learns that most dogs ignore passing boys, and the fear is preserved intact, ready for the next encounter. Mowrer went on, in 1948, to use the same logic to explain what he called the neurotic paradox : why people persist in self-defeating behaviour that costs them jobs, friendships and happiness. The answer is timing. The relief of avoidance is immediate and certain; its costs come later and are spread thin, and immediate consequences control behaviour far more strongly than delayed ones (Book 1, Section 6.9.7). Two kinds of avoidance learning are worth separating because they will matter in a moment. An escape response ends an aversive state that has already begun: the woman who is already in a crowded lift and gets out at the next floor. An avoidance response prevents the aversive state from beginning at all: the woman who takes the stairs. Both are negatively reinforced, and both protect the fear from extinction. Clinicians add a third, subtler family, the safety behaviours : actions taken inside a feared situation to prevent the feared catastrophe, such as gripping a handrail, sitting near the door of the cinema hall, carrying a bottle of water or a tablet, or going out only with a trusted companion. Because the catastrophe never happens, the person credits the safety behaviour rather than learning that the situation was safe (Book 2, Section 5.6.2). Exam trap "Two-factor theory" in a question on phobias or OCD means Mowrer's two-factor (two-process) theory of avoidance, 1947 : classical conditioning creates the fear, operant negative reinforcement of avoidance maintains it. Do not confuse it with Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer's two-factor theory of emotion (arousal plus a cognitive label, 1962) or with Frederick Herzberg's two-factor theory of job motivation. And avoidance is maintained by negative reinforcement (an unpleasant state is removed), not by punishment: punishment weakens behaviour, whereas negative reinforcement strengthens it. Compulsions as escape: the learning account of OCD Hema is a 27-year-old bank clerk in Coimbatore. Every working day she handles hundreds of currency notes that have passed, she cannot stop thinking, through countless unwashed hands. On a bad day the thought arrives each time she touches a bundle: "There are germs on this; I will carry them home to my father, who has diabetes, and he will fall ill because of me." Her anxiety climbs until she can bear it no longer. She goes to the washroom and scrubs her hands, fingers first, then palms, then wrists, always in the same order, until they feel clean; if she loses count she starts again. The relief is immediate. Twenty minutes later another bundle arrives, and so does the thought. At home she washes again before she can enter the kitchen, and her evening bath has grown to over an hour. Her hands are cracked and bleeding. Mowrer's two factors map onto Hema's day with uncomfortable precision. The thought of contamination, and the notes that trigger it, have become conditioned stimuli for anxiety (factor one). Washing ends the anxiety, and the relief negatively reinforces the washing (factor two). Because she always washes, she never discovers two things: that her anxiety would have subsided on its own if she had waited, and that her father would not have fallen ill. So the obsession returns at full strength and the ritual is needed again. In learning terms, a compulsion is simply an escape or avoidance response; washing after touching is escape, and washing in advance "just in case" before entering the kitchen is avoidance. Her refusal to touch the washroom door handle without a tissue is passive avoidance of the trigger, and it works the same way. Figure 6.13 sets the phobic loop and the obsessive-compulsive loop side by side, because they are the same machine fed with different material. This account made a prediction that could be tested in the laboratory, and in the late 1960s and 1970s a group at the Institute of Psychiatry in London set out to test it. If compulsions are escape responses, then contact with a feared contaminant should drive anxiety up, and carrying out the ritual should bring it down. Key study: contamination and washing (Hodgson and Rachman, 1972) Stanley Rachman (1934 to 2021), a South African-born psychologist who worked mainly on OCD and the other anxiety disorders, and his colleague R. J. Hodgson asked obsessional patients whose rituals were washing to touch an object they regarded as contaminated, and then measured their subjective discomfort and urge to wash. Touching the contaminant made the discomfort rise sharply; being allowed to wash then brought it down. The pattern was just what the two-factor theory predicted, and companion experiments soon extended the analysis to checking rituals (Röper, Rachman and Hodgson, 1973). A further study asked a different question: what happens if the patient touches the contaminant and does not wash? Rachman, Padmal de Silva and G. Röper (1976) found that the discomfort and the urge to wash declined by themselves, more slowly than after a ritual but just as surely. That finding is the scientific foundation of exposure and response prevention: if the ritual is blocked, the anxiety extinguishes (Book 2, Section 4.3.5). Now look closely at the words examiners use about compulsions, because two real questions turn on them. In Hema's case the conditioned stimulus is the contaminating thought or object: it comes first and signals anxiety. The washing is a response to that stimulus, so it cannot be a conditioned stimulus. An unconditioned response is an unlearned reflex, such as a startle at a loud noise, a flinch from a hot pan or salivation when food is in the mouth; Hema's elaborate, ordered, rule-bound washing is plainly learned, so it is not an unconditioned response. The washing is reinforced, but not positively: positive reinforcement adds something pleasant, and washing gives Hema no pleasure at all. It takes away distress, so it is negatively reinforced. Nor is a compulsion involuntary. Hema feels driven to wash and resists only with great difficulty, but she can delay the ritual, and in therapy she will learn to refrain from it; this is what separates a compulsion from a tic, which is sudden, rapid and largely involuntary (Chapter 3). Finally, "performance" is not a pattern of behaviour in learning theory at all; the word belongs to the distinction between learning something and showing it in performance, which is a different idea. The compulsive act, in the language of learning theory, is an escape (or avoidance) behaviour, a safety behaviour that works in the short run and keeps the disorder going in the long run. (a) Phobic avoidance Feared object or place (conditioned stimulus) Fear rises Escape or avoid it (leave, refuse, stay home) Fear falls: relief reinforces the avoidance never stays to learn it is safe Each escape brings relief, so avoidance grows; extinction never gets the chance to happen. (b) The OCD cycle Obsession (thought of germs) Anxiety rises Compulsion (washing, checking) Anxiety falls: relief reinforces the ritual the obsession returns The ritual ends the anxiety for now, so it is repeated; the belief that it was needed is never tested. Figure 6.13 Mowrer's two-factor theory at work. (a) Classical conditioning makes the object frightening; escaping it brings relief, which negatively reinforces avoidance and blocks extinction (the long arrow back). (b) The same loop in OCD: the compulsion removes the anxiety the obsession produced, so the ritual is strengthened and the obsession comes back. Clinical link Patients like Hema often say, "But the washing is the only thing that helps." The two-factor theory lets a clinician agree and then turn the point around: the washing helps for twenty minutes, and that is exactly why the thought keeps coming back. Drawing Figure 6.13(b) with the patient, using her own thoughts and rituals, is usually the first step in preparing her for exposure and response prevention, in which she touches the notes and does not wash, and watches the anxiety rise, peak and fall by itself (Book 2, Section 4.3.5). Exam trap A client washes to neutralise the anxiety of contamination thoughts: the washing is best seen as an avoidance response or safety behaviour (real paper, 2024). It is not a conditioned stimulus (the contaminating thought or object is the stimulus), not an unconditioned response (an unlearned reflex such as a startle) and not maintained by positive reinforcement (it removes distress; it adds nothing pleasant). In a second real question (IHBAS 2025), learning theory explains compulsive acts as patterns of escape behaviour. "Conditioning" is tempting and is defensible as the general mechanism (classical for the anxiety, operant for the ritual), but the question asks what pattern the acts show, and that pattern is escape from anxiety. "Involuntary" is wrong because compulsions can be delayed and resisted, unlike tics, and "performance" is not a learning-theory pattern of behaviour. Why every fright does not become a phobia: preparedness and the three pathways The two-factor theory explains why fears last. It is much less good at explaining how they start, and by the 1970s three awkward facts had piled up against the idea that every phobia begins with a frightening conditioning experience. The first awkward fact is that many people with phobias remember no frightening event at all. Section 6.3 noted that many cannot recall how the phobia began. Some may have forgotten, but it strains belief that the many adults with a lifelong fear of snakes, in countries where few of them have ever met a snake, were all bitten in childhood. The second fact runs the other way: many people who do have a frightening experience never become phobic. When the American psychologist Peter DiNardo and his colleagues (1988) studied people with a phobia of dogs and a matched group without one, about half of the phobics recalled a frightening encounter with a dog, usually a bite. So did about half of the non-phobic group. The same terrifying event had produced a phobia in some people and nothing lasting in others. Studies of people with a phobia of driving found the same pattern: only about half of those who could date the onset had had an accident or other real fright on the road (Munjack 1984, from Barlow). And Rachman, reviewing how British civilians coped with the repeated air raids of the Second World War, concluded that short-lived fear was common but "surprisingly few persistent phobic reactions emerged" (Rachman 1991, from Barlow). If conditioning were the whole story, the bombed cities should have been full of phobias. The third fact is the strangest. If any stimulus paired with pain can become a conditioned stimulus, phobias should be spread across all the dangerous things of modern life: electric sockets, cars, hammers, motorcycles, cigarettes. They are not. Phobias cluster around a short list of objects and situations, snakes, spiders, dogs, heights, deep water, darkness, blood and enclosed spaces, many of which harm very few people today. The American psychologist Martin Seligman (born 1942) proposed an explanation in a 1971 paper, "Phobias and preparedness". Through evolution, he argued, our species has become biologically prepared to learn fear of the objects and situations that threatened our ancestors. For an early human, a quick, lasting, unthinking fear of snakes, cliffs and strangers was worth having; a fear of flowers was not. Seligman's idea of preparedness (or prepared learning ) explains four features of phobias that ordinary conditioning does not: they are selective (they attach to some stimuli far more readily than others); they can be acquired in a single pairing or even without one; they resist extinction; and they are irrational in the sense that knowing the object is harmless does not dissolve them. You met the same principle in Book 1, Section 6.4.6, where John Garcia's rats learned in one trial to avoid a taste that was followed hours later by sickness. Preparedness has been tested directly. The Swedish psychologist Arne Öhman and his colleagues conditioned mild fear, measured by the skin conductance response, by pairing pictures with a mild electric shock. Fear conditioned to pictures of snakes and spiders resisted extinction far better than fear conditioned to pictures of flowers or mushrooms. In 1978 Öhman and Ulf Dimberg found the same for faces: a conditioned response to an angry face outlasted one to a happy or neutral face. We seem to be prepared to fear angry, rejecting faces as well as snakes, which is one reason preparedness is invoked for social anxiety disorder (Section 6.8.6). Key study: the monkeys who learned to fear snakes (Mineka and colleagues, 1984; Cook and Mineka, 1989) Rhesus monkeys born in the wild are afraid of snakes; monkeys born and raised in the laboratory are not. The American psychologist Susan Mineka and her colleagues let laboratory-reared monkeys watch wild-reared monkeys reacting fearfully to a snake. After watching, the observers had acquired an intense and lasting fear of snakes themselves (Mineka, Davidson, Cook and Keir, 1984). In 1989 Michael Cook and Mineka asked whether a monkey could learn to fear anything this way. They edited videotapes so that the same fearful model monkey appeared to be reacting either to toy snakes and a toy crocodile or to flowers and a toy rabbit. Observers who watched the fear directed at snakes and crocodiles learned it; observers who watched exactly the same fear directed at flowers and the rabbit learned nothing. The conclusion: fear can be learned by watching, and what is learned depends on what evolution has prepared the learner to fear. The usual caution applies: these are monkeys, and the human evidence is less direct. The second answer to the awkward facts came from Stanley Rachman, who in 1977 published a critical examination of the conditioning theory of fear and proposed that fears are acquired by three pathways . The first is direct conditioning , the classic route: the dog bite, the hours trapped in a lift, the choking episode (almost every person with a choking phobia has had a choking experience). The second is vicarious learning , or observational learning: acquiring a fear by watching someone else's fear or someone else's misfortune (Book 1, Section 6.8). The Swedish psychologist Lars-Göran Öst (1985) described an adolescent boy who sat in the waiting room of the school dentist, partly seeing and fully hearing his friend being treated. The friend jerked with pain, and the drill punctured his cheek. The boy in the waiting room ran out and developed a severe, long-lasting fear of dentistry, although nothing had happened to him. Closer to home, a child who has watched her mother scream and climb onto a chair every time a house lizard appears on the wall needs no bite to learn that lizards are terrifying. The third pathway is information transmission (instruction): being told, again and again, that something is dangerous. Öst described a woman with an extremely severe phobia of snakes who had never encountered one. All through childhood she had been warned about snakes in the long grass and made to wear high rubber boots, which she still wore even when walking down a city street. Rachman's three pathways do not replace conditioning; they widen it, and they explain why so many phobics cannot recall a frightening event: no event is needed. They still leave DiNardo's question unanswered. Why did half of the people bitten by dogs go on with their lives? David H. Barlow (born 1942), whose integrated model closes this section, answers with a distinction between three kinds of alarm. A true alarm is the fear response to real danger: the bite, the near-accident. A false alarm is the same intense fear when there is no danger at all: an unexpected panic attack, often during a period of stress. A learned alarm is a true or false alarm that has become conditioned to the cues present when it happened. Those cues can be external (the bus, the bridge, the cinema hall) or internal, such as a racing heart or a change in breathing. This last idea, that the body's own sensations can become conditioned stimuli, is called interoceptive conditioning , and it is central to modern learning accounts of panic (Bouton, Mineka and Barlow, 2001). The cues need not even be conscious: experiments with animals show that fear signals can travel from the senses to the amygdala without passing through the cortex, the seat of awareness (Section 6.7; Book 1, Section 11.4.5), which is why a person with panic disorder often cannot say what set off an attack. What turns an alarm into a disorder, Barlow argues, is not the alarm itself but whether the person develops anxiety about it happening again. The dog-bitten people who did not become phobic were those who did not start dreading the next dog (Section 6.8.11). Exam trap Preparedness is Martin Seligman's (1971) idea that evolution makes some fears easy to learn and hard to lose; do not attach it to Seligman's other famous idea, learned helplessness (a model of depression, Chapter 5), or credit it to Garcia, whose taste-aversion work is the classic animal example of prepared learning. Rachman's (1977) three pathways are direct conditioning, vicarious (observational) learning and information or instruction: three, not four, and "information" means being told, not "cognitive appraisal". Barlow's alarms come in three kinds: true (real danger), false (no danger) and learned (conditioned to cues). The anxious mind: overestimated danger, threat-hunting attention and catastrophic thinking Learning theory treats fear as something that happens to a person. Cognitive theory asks what the person is thinking while it happens. Its founding figure, Aaron Temkin Beck (1921 to 2021), argued that each emotional disorder has its own characteristic thought content: loss and failure in depression, danger in anxiety (Book 2, Section 5.3). In Anxiety Disorders and Phobias: A Cognitive Perspective (1985), written with Gary Emery and Ruth Greenberg, Beck described the anxious person as caught in a systematic error of appraisal. He overestimates the probability that something bad will happen, overestimates how bad it would be, underestimates his own ability to cope, and underestimates the help that others would give. Cognitive therapists later summarised this as an "anxiety equation", usually credited to the British psychologist Paul Salkovskis (1996; you will meet his model of OCD in Section 6.8.7): anxiety rises with the perceived probability and cost of the danger and falls with the perceived ability to cope and the perceived chance of rescue. Change any term in the equation and the anxiety changes. These appraisals are expressed through habitual distortions of thinking. Beck's full list belongs to Book 2, Section 5.3.4, but one of them, catastrophising (catastrophic thinking), is so central to anxiety that examiners ask about it directly. Catastrophising means expecting the worst possible outcome and treating it as both likely and unbearable. It usually takes the form of a chain, each link more terrible than the last. A postgraduate applicant waiting for his viva thinks: "If I fumble the first question, they will think I know nothing; I will lose the seat; I will have wasted my parents' money; I will never get into any programme; my life will be finished." Each step feels like a certainty, and the anxiety is driven by the last link, not the first. Table 6.23 sets catastrophising beside the three distortions that most often appear with it as wrong options. Table 6.23 Catastrophising and three distortions often set beside it in exam options (Beck's full list is in Book 2, Section 5.3.4). Thinking error What it means Example before a viva Most typical of Catastrophising (catastrophic thinking) Expecting the worst to happen and treating it as certain and unbearable "If I fumble one answer I will fail, lose the seat and shame my family" Anxiety: panic, GAD, health anxiety Dichotomous (all-or-nothing) thinking Sorting every experience into one of two extremes, wholly good or wholly bad "Either I top the list or I am a complete failure" Perfectionism, depression, personality disorders Selective abstraction (mental filter) Focusing on one negative detail and ignoring all the positive ones Remembering one examiner's frown and none of the nods Depression Personalisation Taking events personally, blaming oneself for things one did not cause "The examiner looked tired; I must have bored him" Depression, social anxiety Distorted thinking is not only a matter of conscious sentences. Anxious people also differ in what they notice, often before they are aware of noticing it. In the emotional Stroop task , words printed in coloured ink are flashed on a screen and the participant must name the ink colour as fast as possible while ignoring the word. If a word grabs attention because of its meaning, colour naming slows down. Colin MacLeod and Andrew Mathews (1991) presented threatening words for only 20 milliseconds, too briefly to be consciously read, and people with GAD were still slower than non-anxious people to name the colours of the threat words. In the dot-probe task (MacLeod, Mathews and Tata, 1986), a threatening and a neutral word appear together, one above the other, and then a dot replaces one of them; anxious participants detect the dot faster when it replaces the threat word, which shows that their attention was already there. This automatic pull towards threat is called attentional bias . It means that the anxious person lives in a world that really does look more dangerous, because the dangerous parts are the parts he sees. Exam trap "Catastrophic thinking is common to several anxiety disorders. The term describes:" the answer is worrying that the worst will always happen (RML 2021). The other options are other distortions: categorising experiences as extremely positive or extremely negative is dichotomous (all-or-nothing) thinking ; focusing on negative events and ignoring positive ones is selective abstraction (the mental filter); taking things very personally is personalisation . Catastrophising is about the future outcome ; the other three are about how the present is sorted, filtered or owned. Panic as a misreading of the body: Clark's model and anxiety sensitivity Nikhil is a 29-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru. Near the end of a product launch he had been sleeping four hours a night and drinking coffee all day. At two in the morning, at his desk, he felt his heart skip and then race. His uncle had died of a heart attack at 45. "This is it," he thought, "my heart is giving out." His chest tightened, he could not get his breath, his hands tingled, and the room seemed to move away from him. Certain he was dying, he woke his flatmate, who drove him to a hospital emergency department. The electrocardiogram was normal, and the doctor told him it was "only anxiety". He did not believe it. Over the next months he had several more attacks, began to check his pulse many times a day, gave up the gym and stopped climbing stairs quickly. Nothing about Nikhil's heart was abnormal; what was abnormal was what he made of it. The British clinical psychologist David M. Clark built this observation into the most influential psychological theory of panic. In "A cognitive approach to panic" (1986), Clark proposed that panic attacks result from the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations: perceiving normal or anxiety-produced sensations as signs of an immediate disaster. The sequence is a vicious circle (Figure 6.14). A trigger, which may be external (a crowded bus) or internal (a skipped beat after too much coffee, the breathlessness of a fast climb), is perceived as a threat. Perceived threat produces apprehension. Apprehension produces bodily sensations through the sympathetic nervous system: the heart pounds, breathing quickens, the head swims. If those sensations are interpreted catastrophically ("I am having a heart attack"), the perceived threat rises, apprehension increases, the sensations grow stronger, and each turn of the circle seems to confirm the catastrophe until the spiral peaks in a full panic attack. Clark described the typical pairings: palpitations read as a heart attack, breathlessness as suffocation, dizziness as fainting or losing control, and feelings of unreality as going mad. Trigger a racing heart Perceived threat Apprehension (anxiety) Body sensations (heart pounds) Catastrophic misinterpretation vicious circle the circle peaks Panic attack Typical misreadings Palpitations: "I am having a heart attack" Breathlessness: "I am going to suffocate" Dizziness: "I am going to faint" Feeling unreal: "I am going mad" (Clark 1986) Figure 6.14 David M. Clark's (1986) cognitive model of panic. A trigger, often a harmless bodily change, is perceived as a threat; apprehension produces more sensations; these are misinterpreted as a catastrophe, which raises the threat again, and the circle spirals up into a panic attack. On the right, the misreadings Clark described. Clark's model explains several puzzles at once. It explains "unexpected" attacks: they are not truly out of the blue but triggered by internal sensations the person barely noticed. It explains why people with panic disorder become hypervigilant about their bodies (Nikhil's pulse-checking): the more one monitors the heart, the more irregularities one finds. It explains the persistence of the disorder through safety behaviours: each time the heart attack fails to happen, Nikhil credits sitting down, or leaving the room, or the tablet in his pocket, and the belief survives. And it explains why the same laboratory challenge can provoke panic in one person and not another. Section 6.7 describes how inhaling carbon dioxide or receiving an infusion of sodium lactate sets off attacks in people with panic disorder far more readily than in others, the evidence for Donald Klein's suffocation false alarm theory. The cognitive reply is that the meaning of the sensations matters too. In the experiment of William Sanderson, Ronald Rapee and David Barlow (1989), told in Section 6.7.5, patients who wrongly believed they could turn down the carbon dioxide they were breathing had fewer catastrophic thoughts and significantly fewer panic attacks than patients given the same gas without that belief. Same gas, different belief, different outcome. The biological and cognitive theories are best seen as complementary: a sensitive alarm supplies the sensations, and the interpretation decides whether they spiral into panic. The therapy built on Clark's model, which teaches the patient to test his catastrophic interpretations, is described in Book 2, Section 5.6.3. Why do some people interpret bodily sensations catastrophically and others shrug them off? One answer is a trait. In 1985 the American psychologists Steven Reiss and Richard J. McNally introduced the idea of anxiety sensitivity : a lasting disposition to believe that the sensations of anxiety are harmful, that a racing heart may mean a heart attack, that a wave of anxiety may mean losing one's mind, that visible trembling will lead to humiliation. It is measured with the Anxiety Sensitivity Index (Reiss, Peterson, Gursky and McNally, 1986; Assessment book). People who score high are more likely to go on to have panic attacks, and DSM-5-TR lists anxiety sensitivity, alongside negative affectivity and behavioural inhibition, among the temperamental risk factors for panic attacks and panic disorder. Where does it come from? Barlow's group points to a specific psychological vulnerability learned in childhood. In a prospective study that followed more than a thousand young women aged 18 to 24 for about a year and a half, those with a history of physical illness who were anxious about their health went on to develop panic disorder rather than other anxiety disorders such as social phobia (Rudaz, Craske, Becker, Ledermann and Margraf, 2010). They had learned, it seems, that unexplained bodily sensations can be dangerous. Exam trap Four panic ideas, four authors, four years. Fear of fear : Alan Goldstein and Dianne Chambless, 1978 (a learned fear of the sensations of anxiety that develops after attacks, Section 6.2). Anxiety sensitivity : Steven Reiss and Richard McNally, 1985 (a lasting trait that predates attacks and predicts them). Catastrophic misinterpretation : David M. Clark, 1986 (what happens in the moment of an attack). Suffocation false alarm : Donald Klein, 1993 (a biological alarm that misfires, Section 6.7). Clark's model is cognitive, Klein's biological; neither is about GAD, whose worry is taught in the next subsection. Worry and scrutiny: cognitive models of GAD and social anxiety Section 6.4 described a curious finding about people with GAD: under stress their heart rate, blood pressure, skin conductance and breathing change less than those of people with panic disorder, so that they have been called autonomic restrictors, and yet they are chronically tense. The American psychologist Thomas D. Borkovec and his colleagues explained the paradox with an avoidance theory of worry (Borkovec, Alcaine and Behar, 2004). Worry, Borkovec noticed, is mostly verbal: an anxious stream of sentences about what might go wrong, with intense activity in the frontal lobes but little vivid imagery. Images of a threat (picturing the accident, the hospital, the funeral) produce strong emotion and strong bodily arousal; thinking about the same threat in words produces much less. By worrying in words, the person keeps the frightening images, and the arousal they would bring, at a distance. That small relief negatively reinforces worrying, exactly as escape reinforces a phobic's avoidance. The cost is the same too. Because the threat is never fully pictured and felt, it is never emotionally processed, the problems are never solved, and the worrier never adapts; he simply goes on worrying, with tight muscles and a restricted, inflexible autonomic system. On this view, worry does for the person with GAD what avoidance does for the person with a phobia. The British clinical psychologist Adrian Wells asked a different question: why does the person keep using a strategy that makes him miserable? His answer lies in metacognition , thinking about thinking. In Wells's metacognitive model of GAD (1995), people start with positive beliefs about worry: "Worrying helps me cope", "If I worry I will be prepared", "Worrying keeps bad things from happening." These beliefs lead them to use worry about everyday matters, which Wells calls Type 1 worry, as a way of coping. Over time a second set of beliefs develops, negative beliefs about worry itself: "My worrying is uncontrollable", "Worrying this much will make me ill or drive me mad." Now the person worries about his worrying. This Type 2 worry , or meta-worry, is in Wells's view what turns ordinary worry into GAD, and the person's attempts to control it (suppressing thoughts, seeking reassurance, avoiding the news) only feed it. The therapy built on the model is taught in Book 2, Section 5.10.3. A third account comes from the Canadian psychologist Michel Dugas and his colleagues at Laval University in Quebec. They proposed that the core of GAD is intolerance of uncertainty : a tendency to find uncertain situations unacceptable and threatening in themselves, whatever the actual odds of a bad outcome. For such a person, "I do not know for sure that my daughter's bus has arrived" feels almost as bad as "the bus has crashed". Worry is an attempt to remove the uncertainty by mentally rehearsing every possibility, and since the future is always uncertain, the worry never ends. In a preliminary test of their model, which also included positive beliefs about worry, poor problem orientation and cognitive avoidance, Dugas, Gagnon, Ladouceur and Freeston (1998) compared 24 patients with GAD and 20 non-clinical participants: intolerance of uncertainty was the factor that best separated the two groups, and the four variables together classified 82 percent of participants correctly. Intolerance of uncertainty is now recognised as a feature of other disorders too, including OCD. Social anxiety disorder has its own cognitive model, set out in 1995 by David M. Clark and Adrian Wells (Book 2, Section 5.6.4 explains the therapy built on it). Picture a young lecturer in Kolkata about to give her first departmental seminar. She believes she must always sound brilliant and that if she blushes people will think she is weak. As she stands up, she feels her face grow hot, and her attention turns inward. This self-focused attention is the heart of the model: instead of watching her audience, she watches herself, and she builds a picture of how she looks from how she feels. Because her face feels as if it is burning, she "sees" herself as scarlet and visibly shaking, an image of herself as others might see her, taken from an observer's perspective and treated as accurate. To get through, she uses safety behaviours: she avoids eye contact, reads from her notes, grips the lectern, says as little as possible in the discussion. These make her look aloof and stiff, which can provoke the very coolness she fears, and they stop her discovering that her blush was barely visible. Before the seminar she rehearsed every way it could go wrong (anticipatory processing); afterwards she replays it in a long "post-mortem", reviewing her performance through the same distorted self-image (post-event processing), so that the memory of the event is filed as another failure. Two further strands support this picture. Preparedness again: Öhman and Dimberg's angry faces (Section 6.8.3) suggest that we are prepared to fear signs of hostility and rejection, and socially anxious people recognise angry faces more quickly than others do (Mogg, Philippot and Bradley, 2004). And learning: in one Canadian sample, 92 percent of adults with social phobia reported severe teasing or bullying in childhood, against 35 to 50 percent of those with other anxiety disorders (McCabe and colleagues, 2003, from Barlow), though memories of this kind are retrospective self-reports and must be read with care. Exam trap Match the model to its author. Avoidance theory of worry : Thomas Borkovec (worry is verbal and damps the imagery and arousal of fear). Metacognitive model , with Type 2 worry (worry about worry): Adrian Wells. Intolerance of uncertainty : Michel Dugas and colleagues. Self-focused attention , the observer-perspective self-image and post-event processing: Clark and Wells's model of social anxiety (1995). Do not mix up Wells's metacognitive model of GAD with the Clark and Wells model of social anxiety, and do not give Borkovec's theory to panic: panic is Clark's 1986 model. Intrusions that feel dangerous: cognitive models of OCD Tara is 26, and six weeks ago she gave birth to her first child in Lucknow. One morning, as she was cutting vegetables with the baby lying on the bed beside her, a picture flashed into her mind of the knife plunging into the child. She was horrified. Since then the image has come back dozens of times a day. She has hidden every knife in the house, will not bathe the baby unless her mother-in-law is present, asks her husband again and again whether he thinks she is a bad mother, and repeats a prayer whenever the image appears "to cancel it". She has never had the slightest wish to hurt her daughter; the thought is so foreign to her that she fears she is going mad. DSM-5-TR notes that intrusive violent thoughts of harming the infant, leading to avoidance of the infant, are reported in OCD that begins or worsens in the peripartum period. Would a learning theorist or a cognitive theorist explain Tara better? The cognitive account begins with a surprising discovery. In 1978 Stanley Rachman and Padmal de Silva asked people with no psychiatric disorder whether they ever had unwanted, intrusive thoughts. Most did, and the content of their intrusions (harming a loved one, shouting an obscenity in a temple, a sudden doubt about whether the door was locked) resembled the obsessions of patients with OCD. What differed was how often the thoughts came, how intense and distressing they were, and how hard they were to dismiss. Parkinson and Rachman (1981) found that such intrusions become more frequent under stress. Unwanted thoughts, in other words, are a normal product of a normal mind. The question is why a few people cannot let them pass. The British clinical psychologist Paul M. Salkovskis gave the best-known answer in 1985. What turns an intrusion into an obsession, he argued, is the way it is appraised. The person with OCD interprets the intrusion as meaning that he is responsible for preventing harm to himself or others: "Because I had this thought, I must make sure it does not happen, and if it does it will be my fault." This inflated responsibility produces distress and drives neutralising : any action intended to cancel the thought or prevent the harm, whether a visible ritual (washing, checking), a mental act (a prayer, a counted sequence, a "good" thought to replace the bad one), or reassurance seeking. Neutralising brings brief relief, so it is reinforced; it also prevents the person learning that the harm would not have happened anyway; and it makes the thought seem more important, so it returns more often. Tara's hidden knives, her refusal to bathe the baby alone, her questions to her husband and her cancelling prayer are all neutralising. The therapy built on Salkovskis's model is taught in Book 2, Section 5.6.7. Rachman added a related idea, thought-action fusion : the belief that thinking about an act is the same as, or leads to, doing it. He and his colleagues distinguished two forms. In likelihood thought-action fusion, thinking about an event makes it more likely to happen ("If I picture my brother in an accident, he will have one"). In moral thought-action fusion, having an unacceptable thought is almost as wicked as acting on it; Barlow describes a patient who believed that thinking about abortion was morally equivalent to having one. Barlow also reports that it is the strength of a person's religious belief, not its type, that goes with thought-action fusion (Rassin and Koster, 2003) and with the severity of OCD (Steketee, Quay and White, 1991); most deeply religious people, of course, never develop OCD. Why not simply push the thought away? Because pushing makes it come back. In 1987 the social psychologist Daniel M. Wegner (1948 to 2013) and his colleagues asked students to talk aloud for five minutes about whatever came into their minds, while trying not to think of a white bear and ringing a bell whenever they did. They could not stop the bear from appearing. Afterwards, when they were allowed to think about white bears, they thought about them more than students who had been asked to think about white bears from the start. Wegner described this rebound of thought suppression in his book White Bears and Other Unwanted Thoughts (1989). For Tara, every effort to banish the image makes it more frequent, and its frequency seems to prove that it means something. DSM-5-TR sums up the cognitive research by noting that many people with OCD hold dysfunctional beliefs: an inflated sense of responsibility and a tendency to overestimate threat; perfectionism and intolerance of uncertainty; and over-importance of thoughts (for example, believing that having a forbidden thought is as bad as acting on it) together with the need to control thoughts. It adds an important caution: these beliefs are not specific to OCD. They raise the risk, but they are found in other anxiety disorders too, which is why they fit Barlow's idea of a specific psychological vulnerability (Section 6.8.11) rather than a sufficient cause. Exam trap Inflated responsibility and neutralising : Paul Salkovskis, 1985. Thought-action fusion : Stanley Rachman (likelihood and moral forms). Normal obsessions (most people have intrusive thoughts): Rachman and de Silva, 1978. Rebound after thought suppression (the white bear): Daniel Wegner, 1987. The cognitive models do not say that intrusive thoughts are abnormal; they say the appraisal of the thoughts is. And the DSM-5-TR beliefs list (responsibility, threat, perfectionism, uncertainty, importance and control of thoughts) is "not specific to OCD". Freud's two theories of anxiety Long before learning theory and cognitive science, Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) had made anxiety the central problem of psychopathology, and he answered it twice. His first theory came out of the "anxiety neurosis" he described in 1895 (Section 6.1). Freud noticed that many of his anxious patients had disturbed sexual lives, such as enforced abstinence or interrupted intercourse, and he proposed that sexual excitation that could not be discharged was transformed directly into anxiety. This is often called the transformed libido theory: anxiety as dammed-up sexual energy finding an outlet. On this view repression came first, and anxiety was its by-product. Thirty years later Freud turned the theory upside down. In Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety (1926; German Hemmung, Symptom und Angst ) he proposed that anxiety is a warning. The ego, the part of the mind that deals with reality, senses that a dangerous impulse from the id (a forbidden sexual or aggressive wish) is pressing towards consciousness or action, and it produces a small dose of anxiety as an alarm. This signal anxiety sets the defences going, so that the wish is pushed back or disguised before it can bring about the danger it threatens: punishment, loss of love, or the condemnation of one's own conscience. Freud now said explicitly that anxiety produces repression, not the other way round, and he distinguished signal anxiety from automatic anxiety, the overwhelming state of a helpless person flooded by excitation, the prototype of which is birth. He traced a developmental series of danger situations, from birth and the loss of the mother to castration and the disapproval of the superego, and he returned in the same book to Little Hans, now concluding that the motive force behind Hans's repression was fear of castration. Freud's classification of anxiety into realistic, neurotic and moral types belongs to the Personality book; the defence mechanisms in general are tabled in Book 1, Section 10.8.4, and their place in classical analysis is in Book 2, Sections 3.2.9 and 3.4.1. The signal theory gave every neurosis the same basic structure. A forbidden wish arouses signal anxiety; the ego defends; and when the defence partly fails, the result is a symptom, a compromise formation that both disguises the wish and expresses something of it. What distinguishes one neurosis from another, in this view, is which defences the ego relies on. Phobia, as you will see next, was built mainly on displacement; obsessional neurosis on isolation, undoing and reaction formation; hysteria on repression and conversion. Exam trap Signal anxiety belongs to Freud's second theory, Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety ( 1926 ): anxiety is the ego's warning of internal danger and it sets off the defences. The first theory (1890s, the anxiety neurosis of 1895) held that undischarged libido is transformed into anxiety. In the second theory anxiety causes repression; in the first, repression causes anxiety. William Cullen, not Freud, coined the word "neurosis" (1769, Section 6.1). Phobia and displacement: Little Hans as Freud read him The opening of this chapter told what happened to Hans: the fear of horses, the father who recorded everything, the single meeting with Freud. Here is what Freud made of it, because it remains the classic psychoanalytic account of how a phobia is formed and the source of a question that appears in almost every paper. Key study: Little Hans as Freud read him (Freud, 1909) Freud's reading ran as follows. Hans, at about five, was in the thick of the Oedipal phase: he loved his mother possessively, enjoyed being taken into her bed, and wished his father out of the way, especially when his father was away and he had his mother to himself. Those hostile wishes brought a terrible fear of the father's revenge, in the form of castration anxiety , a fear given substance by a real threat: when Hans was about three and a half, his mother had warned him that the doctor would cut off his "widdler" if he went on touching it. But the father was also loved, lived in the same flat and could not be avoided, so the fear could not stay attached to him. It was shifted onto horses. Freud pointed to the details that betrayed the disguise: Hans was especially frightened of horses with black around their mouths and of the blinkers in front of their eyes, which Freud linked to his father's moustache and spectacles, and the fear that a horse would bite him stood for the fear that his father would punish him. The horse that fell down in the street, in this reading, expressed his wish that his father would fall down and die. The phobia, Freud concluded, was a disguised, displaced expression of an Oedipal conflict, and it eased as Hans's father, on Freud's advice, explained matters to him and reassured him. The defence at the centre of this account is displacement : redirecting a feeling or impulse from the person or object that really arouses it onto a substitute that is safer. The everyday version is the clerk scolded by his manager who comes home and shouts at his younger brother. In a phobia the substitute has one extra advantage: it can be avoided. A boy cannot escape his father, but he can stay indoors and never see a horse. The phobia converts an inner danger, which follows you everywhere, into an outer one, which you can walk away from, and the price of the bargain is a shrunken life. Psychoanalysts gave displacement the same role in other conditions: in body dysmorphic disorder, for example, they proposed that an unbearable unconscious conflict is displaced onto a body part (Barlow; Section 6.6). Barlow's summary of Freud's view gives a further example of the phobic logic: a man's unconscious fear of being attacked and castrated may be consciously expressed as a fear of being bitten by a dog, even though he knows the dog is harmless. The critics were not slow. Freud built his case almost entirely from the reports of a father who was a devoted follower of his and who interpreted what his son said in Freud's terms, often by asking leading questions; Freud himself saw the boy only once. In 1960 Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997) and Stanley Rachman published a learning-theory critique of the case (Book 2, Section 4.1.3). They pointed out that Hans's fear began after he had seen a horse pulling a bus fall down in the street, an event that, as Hans himself said, gave him a great fright. A frightening event followed by fear of the thing involved, generalising to similar things (other horses, heavily loaded carts), is exactly what conditioning predicts, and the gradual fading of the fear as Hans went out again and grew older looked more like extinction than like insight. They found nothing in the record, they argued, that would count as scientific evidence for the Oedipal interpretation. Today a third reading sits beside these two: a sensitive, anxious temperament (Section 6.7) meeting a frightening event at a vulnerable age, which is Barlow's model in miniature (Section 6.8.11). A related psychodynamic idea has been tested more directly. Some analysts proposed that panic disorder and agoraphobia grow out of early separation and loss, so that the adult with agoraphobia, often dependent on a companion, is re-living a child's separation anxiety. Barlow's review of the evidence is blunt: despite some intriguing suggestions, little evidence indicates that people with panic disorder or agoraphobia experienced separation anxiety in childhood more often than people with other disorders or than people with no disorder (Barlow 2002; Thyer 1993). DSM-5-TR likewise notes that childhood separation anxiety may precede panic disorder but is not a consistent risk factor. Exam trap "Displacement is a defence mechanism typically seen in" phobias (IHBAS 2020). It is the defence of Little Hans: fear of the father displaced onto horses, which can be avoided. It is not the signature defence of hysteria (repression, with conversion of the conflict into a bodily symptom, Chapter 7), of OCD (isolation, undoing, reaction formation) or of depression (introjection and anger turned against the self, Chapter 5). Little Hans is a phobia case (1909); the Rat Man, published the same year, is the obsessional case. Obsessional neurosis: the Rat Man and the defences of OCD In October 1907 a young Viennese lawyer, now identified as Ernst Lanzer (1878 to 1914), came to Freud in a state of torment. For years he had been plagued by fears that something terrible would happen to the two people he loved most, his father and a lady he admired, and by impulses and prohibitions he could not resist. The crisis had come during army manoeuvres, when a fellow officer described a punishment said to be used in the East, in which a pot containing live rats was strapped to a prisoner's buttocks and the rats gnawed their way into his anus. At once the young man was seized by the idea that this was happening to the lady, and to his father, although his father had been dead for several years. To ward off the horror he had to perform protective acts and pronounce formulae, and he became entangled in an absurd, self-imposed vow about repaying a small debt that tortured him for days. Freud published the case in 1909 as "Notes upon a Case of Obsessional Neurosis" (in German, Zwangsneurose , which is why older books and Indian papers say "obsessive-compulsive neurosis"). The patient has been known ever since as the Rat Man. Freud claimed that the analysis had restored his mental health, and later lamented that he had been killed in the First World War. Scholars who compared Freud's surviving process notes with the published case, notably Patrick Mahony (1986), found that Freud implied a longer treatment than he gave (daily sessions for little more than three months, then irregular ones), presented some events out of their real order and overstated how complete the cure was. Freud's theory of obsessional neurosis, built on this case and refined over the next two decades, went like this. The obsessional person has met the conflicts of the Oedipal phase, but instead of dealing with them he has regressed to an earlier position, the anal stage of the second and third years, when the great issues were control, dirt and aggression, and when the child's battles over toilet training taught him both defiance and submission. The result is intense ambivalence : love and hatred for the same person, held at once. Hostile, often sadistic, wishes keep breaking through as obsessional thoughts (the rats gnawing into the father), and the ego fights them with a characteristic set of defences, which Freud described in 1926 and his daughter Anna Freud (1895 to 1982) listed in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936). Isolation of affect : the forbidden idea is allowed into consciousness, but its emotion is stripped away. This is why a person with OCD can describe a horrifying thought ("I might strangle my mother") in a flat, matter-of-fact voice; the thought stays, the feeling goes. Freud also described a second kind of isolation, in which a pause or ritual is inserted to cut the thought off from its connections. Undoing : performing an act, or thinking a thought, that symbolically cancels a previous forbidden thought or act, as if it had never happened. The Rat Man supplied the classic example. On the day his lady was to leave, he struck his foot against a stone in the road and felt obliged to move it aside, because her carriage would pass that way and might come to grief on it. A few minutes later it struck him as absurd, and he felt obliged to go back and put the stone back in the middle of the road. The second act undid the first: loving protection, then hostile cancellation. Washing after a "dirty" thought, saying a prayer to cancel a blasphemous one, or repeating an action until it has been done the "right" number of times are all undoing. Because the compulsion itself is an act of undoing, undoing is the defence most directly tied to compulsive rituals and is regarded as the most characteristic defence of obsessive-compulsive neurosis. Reaction formation : holding an unacceptable impulse in check by exaggerating its opposite. Scrupulous cleanliness guards against a wish to soil and be messy; excessive solicitude and kindness towards a person guards against hatred of him; rigid morality guards against forbidden desire. Freud had already described in 1908 an "anal character" marked by orderliness, parsimony and obstinacy, built largely on reaction formation; it is the ancestor of the modern idea of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (Chapter 11), not of OCD. Intellectualisation : dealing with an emotional conflict by thinking about it in abstract terms, so that feeling is replaced by reasoning. The person who cannot stop debating whether a thought counts as a sin, without ever feeling the guilt, is intellectualising. To these Freud added a style of thinking. People with obsessional neurosis, he observed, behave as if their thoughts could directly cause events in the world, so that a hostile thought is dangerous and must be cancelled. He called this omnipotence of thought , and in Totem and Taboo (1913) he said he had borrowed the phrase from a highly intelligent obsessional patient, the Rat Man. Its close relative, magical thinking , is the belief that a ritual (counting, touching, saying a word) can prevent a disaster with which it has no realistic connection. You will notice that this is the same observation that Rachman, eighty years later, called thought-action fusion (Section 6.8.7); the cognitive and psychodynamic traditions saw the same phenomenon and explained it differently. Notice what is missing from the list: repression. In Freud's account of hysteria, the forbidden idea is repressed, pushed out of consciousness altogether and forgotten, and its energy is converted into a bodily symptom such as a paralysed arm (Chapter 7). In obsessional neurosis the forbidden idea is not forgotten at all; it sits in consciousness, which is precisely what makes it an obsession. The defences work instead on its feeling (isolation), on its consequences (undoing) and on its direction (reaction formation). That is why repression is called the defence of hysteria and the answer to "which defence is not involved in OCD?". Its observations are often acute: the rituals of undoing, the flat voice of isolation, the magical quality of obsessional thinking are all real and recognisable. But its causal claims, in their classic form, are very hard to test and have found little support. There is no good evidence that people with OCD had distinctive toilet training, or that the content of obsessions reveals regressed anal-sadistic wishes, and helping a patient understand the supposed meaning of his symptoms rarely makes them go away. Exposure and response prevention, built on the learning account, and cognitive therapy, built on Salkovskis's model, have far stronger evidence (Section 6.9). The psychodynamic tradition survives in clinical vocabulary and in the examination hall, which is why you must know it well. Exam trap "The following defence mechanisms are used in OCD: (a) isolation (b) undoing (c) reaction formation (d) displacement" (RML 2024) is keyed (b) undoing , but notice the trap: isolation, undoing and reaction formation are all OCD defences , so three options are correct. The key picks undoing because it is the defence most directly tied to compulsive acts; only displacement (the defence of phobia) is wrong. If a paper allows several answers, choose (a), (b) and (c); if it demands one, choose undoing. Exam trap "Which defence mechanism is not involved in OCD?" Repression (IHBAS 2020): repression is the defence of hysteria, whereas in OCD the forbidden idea stays conscious and is isolated, undone or reversed. "The defence mechanism of undoing is typically seen in" obsessive-compulsive neurosis (Amity 2023), not in depression (introjection and anger turned inward), mania (which analysts read as a denial of depressive feelings, Melanie Klein's "manic defence") or schizophrenia (the psychotic defences of regression, projection and denial of reality). The Rat Man (1909) is the obsessional case; Little Hans (1909) the phobic one; and the anal character (1908) is the ancestor of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, not of OCD. Putting it together: Barlow's triple vulnerability theory Each of the theories in this section, and each in Section 6.7, explains part of the picture. Genes and temperament explain why anxiety runs in families but not which disorder appears. Conditioning explains how fears are learned and kept, but not why half of the people bitten by dogs stay fearless. Cognitive models explain how a misreading of the body or of a thought turns into panic or obsession, but not why some people misread and others do not. David H. Barlow, of the Center for Anxiety and Related Disorders at Boston University, has drawn these threads into a single account, the triple vulnerability theory (Barlow 2000, 2002; Barlow and colleagues 2013). It is a diathesis-stress model (Book 2, Section 1.7.10): three vulnerabilities, or diatheses, set the stage, and stressful life events trigger them. The first is a generalised biological vulnerability : an inherited tendency to be uptight, high-strung and neurobiologically over-reactive to the events of daily life. This is the negative affectivity or neuroticism of Section 6.7, the general anxious tendency that twin studies show is inherited, and it includes temperaments such as Jerome Kagan's behavioural inhibition. On its own it does not produce a disorder. The second is a generalised psychological vulnerability : a sense, built from early experience, that events are uncontrollable and unpredictable and that one may not be able to cope when things go wrong. Bruce F. Chorpita and Barlow (1998) traced it to parenting. Parents who respond to a child's needs in a positive and predictable way (attention when the child calls, food when hungry, comfort when hurt) teach the child that his actions have an effect on the world. Parents who provide a secure home base but let the child explore and meet manageable difficulties foster a healthy sense of control. Parents who are overprotective and intrusive, who "clear the way" so that the child never meets adversity, leave him without the experience of coping, and the sense of uncontrollability grows. A person with both generalised vulnerabilities is at risk of anxiety in general, and of depression too, which is one reason the two so often occur together. The third is a specific psychological vulnerability : learning, from early experience, that particular situations, objects or sensations are dangerous, even when they are not. A child whose parent is terrified of dogs, or constantly anxious about what the neighbours will think, may learn exactly that fear. This third vulnerability decides where the anxiety will be focused, and therefore which disorder develops. Figure 6.15 shows how the pieces fit. Stress, usually social and interpersonal (an examination, a marriage, a death, a job loss), activates the biological tendency, and the person may have a true alarm or a false alarm (an unexpected panic attack), which can become a learned alarm conditioned to internal or external cues. Whether this leads to a disorder depends on the generalised psychological vulnerability: if the person feels he cannot control or cope with such alarms, he develops anxious apprehension , a future-oriented state of tension, vigilance and dread focused on the possibility of the next one. The specific psychological vulnerability then fixes the focus of that apprehension. Push Nikhil's case through the model: an anxious temperament (biological), a lifelong sense that things could spin out of control (generalised psychological), an uncle's early death and a family that watched every twinge of the chest (specific: bodily sensations are dangerous), the stress of a product launch, and a false alarm at two in the morning. The result was not GAD or a dog phobia but panic disorder, with apprehension focused on his heart. Generalised biological vulnerability (inherited reactivity) Stressful life events Generalised psychological vulnerability (sense of no control) True, false and learned alarms Anxious apprehension (vigilance about future threat) Specific psychological vulnerability (what is dangerous) Focus of the apprehension Panic disorder body sensations Social anxiety being evaluated Specific phobia one object OCD own thoughts GAD everyday events Figure 6.15 Barlow's triple vulnerability theory (simplified from Barlow 2002). Stress acting on a generalised biological vulnerability produces alarms; a generalised psychological vulnerability turns them into anxious apprehension; the specific psychological vulnerability decides what the apprehension is about, and so which disorder develops. Barlow and his colleagues have drawn a version of the model for each disorder, and Table 6.25 sets them beside the other psychological theories of this section. For panic disorder (White and Barlow 2002), the specific vulnerability is the belief that unexplained bodily sensations are dangerous, and whether agoraphobia follows depends on cultural, social and practical factors and on the availability of safety signals such as a trusted companion. For specific phobia, a direct or vicarious experience, or simply information, teaches that one object or situation is dangerous, and inherited preparedness (and, for blood-injection-injury phobia, a vasovagal fainting tendency) makes some objects easier to fear. For social anxiety disorder, Barlow describes three routes: a person with the vulnerabilities may become anxious and self-focused under social stress even without an alarm; may have an unexpected panic attack in a social situation that becomes conditioned to social cues; or may suffer a real social trauma, such as the brutal teasing of early adolescence; in each case the specific vulnerability is having learned that social evaluation is dangerous. For OCD (Steketee and Barlow 2002), the specific vulnerability is having learned that certain thoughts are dangerous and unacceptable, as in thought-action fusion and inflated responsibility, so that apprehension is focused on recurring intrusive thoughts and rituals are used to neutralise them. GAD is the disorder in which the specific focus matters least: the generalised vulnerabilities and stress produce a diffuse anxious apprehension, carried by the worry process that Borkovec described.
