If the anxiety disorders and depression share the same two generalised vulnerabilities and differ mainly in the focus set by a specific one, then a person who has one disorder should often have another, and this is just what Brown and Barlow's large clinical studies found. Barlow's own treatment, the Unified Protocol, is built on the same logic, targeting the shared processes rather than each disorder separately (Book 2, Section 5.6.7). Exam trap The triple vulnerability theory is David H. Barlow's (2000, 2002). Its three vulnerabilities are a generalised biological vulnerability (inherited reactivity), a generalised psychological vulnerability (a sense of uncontrollability from early experience) and a specific psychological vulnerability (learning that particular things are dangerous); stressful life events are the trigger, not a fourth vulnerability. Do not substitute "social vulnerability" or "cognitive, emotional and behavioural vulnerabilities". Kagan's behavioural inhibition is a temperament that belongs inside the biological vulnerability; Gray's behavioural inhibition system is a brain circuit (Section 6.7). 6.9 Drug and Physical Treatments Lower yield · not asked yet Most people with an anxiety disorder who get any treatment at all get it first from a general physician, and in that setting the treatment is almost always a tablet. Barlow notes that primary care physicians are usually the first clinicians to see people with panic disorder and that psychological treatment is rarely available there. Nikhil's first stop (Section 6.8.5) was a hospital emergency department, and Section 6.2 notes that the first professional a person with a panic attack meets is usually a cardiologist or an emergency physician, not a psychologist. A clinical psychologist therefore needs to know the drugs his patients are taking: what they do, what they cannot do, what their side effects feel like, what happens when they are stopped, and how they interact with psychological treatment. This section teaches the drugs used for the anxiety disorders and the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, the surgical and stimulation treatments that are reserved for the most severe OCD, and the major trials that compared drugs with psychotherapy. The antidepressant classes and their pharmacology are taught in Chapter 5, Section 5.7; here the question is how they are used for these disorders. The psychotherapies are placed alongside the drugs at the end, with pointers to Book 2. How drugs and psychotherapy compare Three broad findings frame everything else. First, for most of these disorders, the short-term effects of an effective drug and of an effective psychological treatment are broadly similar. For GAD, Barlow summarises, psychological treatments give about the same benefit as drugs in the short term but are more effective in the long term. Second, gains made with drugs tend to last only as long as the drug is taken. About half of the patients with panic disorder who become panic-free on an antidepressant relapse once it is stopped, and the figure is close to 90 percent for those who stop a benzodiazepine, whereas gains made with cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) are more durable. Third, some drugs may weaken psychological treatment. Most studies, Barlow notes, suggest that drugs, particularly the benzodiazepines, can interfere with the effects of exposure-based therapy, perhaps because a person who faces his fear while sedated credits the tablet rather than learning that the situation is safe, so that the drug becomes one more safety signal. It follows, and the trials in Section 6.9.6 confirm, that combining a drug with CBT is not automatically better than either alone. None of this makes drugs unimportant. Drugs act faster in some patients, they are available where trained therapists are not, some patients prefer them, and for severe OCD, severe depression alongside anxiety, or a crisis, they may be essential. Pinel's verdict on the anxiolytics is a fair summary of the whole field: many drugs produce slight but statistically significant improvements in groups of patients, but many patients are not helped by them and many stop because of side effects. The art lies in matching the treatment to the person. The benzodiazepines Vikram is a 52-year-old cloth merchant in Surat. Six years ago, after his first panic attack, a family physician prescribed alprazolam "for the nerves". It worked within half an hour, and Vikram came to rely on it. Over the years the dose crept up, and he now takes it three times a day. If a dose is late he becomes shaky and sweaty, cannot sleep and feels the old panic rising, which convinces him that he cannot manage without it. His son has noticed that he is forgetful and slow at the accounts, and last winter he fell on the shop steps. His panic attacks have never really stopped. Vikram's drug belongs to the most famous family of anxiety drugs. Before them, physicians calmed anxious patients with bromides, alcohol and then the barbiturates, which were effective sedatives but dangerous in overdose and strongly habit-forming. In 1955 meprobamate, marketed as Miltown, arrived and is often described as the first blockbuster psychotropic drug in American history. Then, at the laboratories of the Swiss company Hoffmann-La Roche in Nutley, New Jersey, the chemist Leo Henryk Sternbach (1908 to 2005) produced the compound that became chlordiazepoxide, the first benzodiazepine , marketed as Librium in 1960; diazepam (Valium) followed in 1963. They were safer than the barbiturates and displaced them. By the 1970s, Barlow notes, Valium and Librium were among the most widely prescribed drugs in the world, and Pinel describes the benzodiazepines as the most widely prescribed psychoactive drugs, taken at any one time by about 5 percent of adult North Americans. Older books call them "minor tranquillisers", as opposed to the "major tranquillisers", the antipsychotics. The general term for a drug that reduces anxiety is an anxiolytic . How do they work? The main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain is GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid). One of its receptors, the GABA-A receptor , is an ion channel: when GABA binds, the channel opens, negatively charged chloride ions flow into the neuron, and the neuron becomes less likely to fire. Benzodiazepines bind to a separate site on the same receptor and make it respond more strongly to GABA; in Barlow's words, they make it easier for GABA molecules to attach to the receptors, so that the more benzodiazepine there is, the more GABA is attached and the calmer the person becomes, up to a point. Pinel describes them as GABA-A agonists; pharmacologists more precisely call them positive allosteric modulators, because they amplify GABA's effect rather than acting in its place. Since GABA inhibition runs through circuits all over the brain, the benzodiazepines have four main actions, and Pinel lists them as uses: they are anxiolytic, hypnotic (sleep-inducing), anticonvulsant and muscle relaxant. The family differs mainly in potency and in how long each drug stays in the body. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are long-acting; chlordiazepoxide is still widely used to manage alcohol withdrawal (Chapter 10). Alprazolam (Xanax) is a high-potency, short-acting drug that Barlow singles out as the benzodiazepine commonly used for panic disorder. Clonazepam is high-potency and longer-acting and is also used for panic; lorazepam is used for acute anxiety and, by injection, for prolonged seizures. Short-acting drugs wear off between doses, which is one reason people like Vikram feel rebound anxiety several times a day. Their proper place is narrow. There is wide agreement, Barlow writes, that the optimal use of benzodiazepines is short-term relief of anxiety during a temporary crisis or stressful event, such as a family emergency, prescribed until the crisis is resolved but for no more than a week or two. They are also used for acute, severe panic, for short-term insomnia and in alcohol withdrawal. Their problems are a long list, and every item on it is examined: Sedation and impaired performance. They impair cognitive and motor functioning: people are less alert at work or in class, and driving is impaired. Pinel adds ataxia (unsteadiness), tremor and nausea, and, for the hypnotic use, next-day drowsiness and a raised risk of traffic accidents. Falls. In older adults they are associated with falls and hip fractures, which is why prescribing them to the elderly is a particular worry (Section 6.4). Dependence and withdrawal. They produce both psychological and physical dependence. Stopping them, especially suddenly, brings a withdrawal reaction that includes rebound anxiety , the return of anxiety at a higher level than before treatment, and insomnia; after long use of high doses, abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures, which is why they are always tapered gradually. Danger in combination. Like alcohol, they are brain depressants; combined with alcohol or opioids, they can dangerously depress breathing. Cognitive effects of long use. Taken over a long period, benzodiazepines are associated with cognitive impairment (Deckersbach, Moshier, Tuschen-Caffier and Otto, 2011, from Barlow), and Pinel notes that chronic use as a hypnotic has been linked with reduced life expectancy. Interference with exposure therapy, as described in Section 6.9.1. The withdrawal problem was measured early. Abby Fyer and her colleagues (1987) tapered alprazolam in 17 patients with panic disorder at 10 percent of the starting dose every three days. Only four completed the withdrawal on schedule, in four to five weeks; during withdrawal 15 of the 17 had recurrent or increased panic attacks, and nine developed new withdrawal symptoms such as malaise, weakness, insomnia, a racing heart, light-headedness and dizziness. Findings like this (15 of 17 is 88 percent) lie behind the textbook figure that relapse is close to 90 percent when benzodiazepines are stopped. Yet the benzodiazepines remain the most widely used class of drugs for panic disorder in practice (Blanco and colleagues, 2004, from Barlow), and their use has continued to rise. They work quickly, patients feel the difference within an hour, and the costs come later. Two further points complete the picture. Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD: they may take the edge off the anxiety for a few hours, but they do not reduce obsessions or compulsions, which is one of the observations that set OCD apart from the anxiety disorders (Sections 6.1 and 6.7). And because they can be misused, DSM-5-TR includes them in the class of sedative, hypnotic or anxiolytic substances, whose use disorder, intoxication and withdrawal are taught in Chapter 10, where you will also meet flumazenil, a drug that blocks the benzodiazepine site and can reverse their effects. Clinical link Patients like Vikram are common in clinical practice, and the psychologist is often the person who explains why the tablet that "works" is part of the problem. Its fast relief negatively reinforces taking it, exactly as escape reinforces avoidance (Section 6.8.1), and the withdrawal symptoms between doses feel like proof that the anxiety is getting worse. A safe plan is made with the prescribing doctor: a slow, gradual taper over weeks to months, often while CBT for panic teaches the person to face the sensations that the drug has been suppressing. Never advise a patient to stop a benzodiazepine abruptly. Exam trap Benzodiazepines act by enhancing GABA at the GABA-A receptor ; they are anxiolytic, hypnotic, anticonvulsant and muscle relaxant. They are for short-term relief (a week or two), not first-line long-term treatment; for long-term treatment the first-line drugs are the SSRIs and SNRIs. They do not treat OCD . Alprazolam is the high-potency benzodiazepine associated with panic. "Minor tranquilliser" means an anxiolytic such as a benzodiazepine; "major tranquilliser" means an antipsychotic. Buspirone, pregabalin and the beta blockers The problems of the benzodiazepines drove a search for anxiolytics without sedation or dependence. The first to succeed was buspirone , a drug of the azapirone class approved in the United States in 1986 for generalised anxiety disorder. It does not act on the GABA-A receptor at all. Its main action is as a partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors : it stimulates them, but less strongly than serotonin itself, and it also has weak effects on dopamine receptors. Its profile is almost the mirror image of a benzodiazepine's. It causes little sedation and produces no significant dependence or withdrawal, so DSM-5-TR leaves it out of the sedative, hypnotic or anxiolytic class because it does not appear to be associated with significant misuse. But it has no immediate anxiolytic effect: its benefit appears only after two to four weeks of regular use. That means it cannot be taken "as needed" in a moment of panic, and a patient switched from a benzodiazepine may find it disappointing, since it neither gives the familiar rapid calm nor prevents benzodiazepine withdrawal. Its only established use among these disorders is GAD; it is not effective for panic disorder or the other anxiety disorders. Pregabalin is one of the newest drugs prescribed for anxiety disorders, and Pinel notes that it is particularly effective for GAD. It works neither on GABA receptors nor on serotonin but by modulating voltage-gated calcium channels, thus affecting calcium levels inside nerve cells and damping the release of excitatory neurotransmitters. It is licensed for GAD in Europe, though not in the United States. Its common side effects are dizziness and sleepiness, and it has a recognised potential for misuse. An older alternative still sometimes used for short-term relief of anxiety is hydroxyzine, an antihistamine whose calming effect comes largely from sedation. The beta blockers , such as propranolol (Inderal) and atenolol, work in the body rather than the brain. Adrenaline and noradrenaline act on beta-adrenergic receptors in the heart and muscles to produce the racing pulse and trembling hands of fear; beta blockers occupy those receptors and blunt these signs. They do nothing for the worry, the fear of evaluation or the catastrophic thought. Because a trembling bow or a shaking voice can wreck a single performance, beta blockers became popular with musicians, singers and public speakers, and clinicians long assumed they would treat social anxiety. The trials were disappointing. Michael R. Liebowitz and his colleagues (1992) gave 74 patients with social phobia eight weeks of double-blind, randomly assigned treatment with the MAOI phenelzine, the beta blocker atenolol or placebo: 64 percent responded to phenelzine, 30 percent to atenolol and 23 percent to placebo, and atenolol did not differ significantly from placebo. Samuel Turner, Deborah Beidel and Rolf Jacob (1994) found that flooding (intensive exposure) was consistently superior to placebo in 72 patients with social phobia, whereas atenolol was not. Beta blockers therefore keep a modest role for the bodily symptoms of occasional performance anxiety, and even there the controlled evidence is thin; they are not a treatment for social anxiety disorder as a whole. They are also unsuitable for some people: propranolol can provoke wheezing in asthma, and all of them slow the heart. Exam trap Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist for GAD : slow (two to four weeks), non-sedating, no dependence, useless "as needed" and not effective for panic or agoraphobia. Some Indian exam notes list "clomipramine, venlafaxine, buspirone" as the drug treatment of agoraphobia; the antidepressants belong on that list (Section 6.9.4), buspirone does not. Pregabalin acts on voltage-gated calcium channels and is used for GAD. Beta blockers (propranolol, atenolol) block the bodily signs of anxiety and are used before performances, but in controlled trials atenolol was no better than placebo for social anxiety disorder (Liebowitz and colleagues 1992; Turner, Beidel and Jacob 1994), whereas the MAOI phenelzine was clearly effective. Antidepressants: the first-line drugs for anxiety and obsessions It surprises many students that the first-line drugs for the anxiety disorders and OCD are called antidepressants. The name records the order in which their uses were discovered, not a claim that anxious people are secretly depressed, although the two conditions often coexist and Pinel points out that antidepressants are often effective against anxiety disorders and anxiolytics against depression. The classes, how they act on serotonin and noradrenaline, the lag of several weeks before they work, and their side-effect profiles are taught in Chapter 5, Section 5.7. The selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs: fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, fluvoxamine, citalopram, escitalopram) and the serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs: venlafaxine, duloxetine) are now the first choice across this chapter because they work for most of these disorders, they treat coexisting depression, and they do not produce the dependence of the benzodiazepines. What follows is disorder by disorder. Panic disorder and agoraphobia. The story begins with the tricyclic imipramine, whose ability to stop panic attacks while leaving anticipatory anxiety untouched led Donald Klein to separate panic from generalised anxiety (Section 6.2), and imipramine was the drug used in the great panic trial described in Section 6.9.6. Today, Barlow writes, the SSRIs are the indicated drugs for panic disorder on all available evidence, with the closely related SNRIs such as venlafaxine. About 60 percent of patients are free of panic as long as they stay on an effective drug, but 20 percent or more stop before treatment is complete, and about half relapse once the drug is stopped. The commonest reason for stopping is sexual dysfunction, which occurred in 75 percent or more of patients in Yves Lecrubier's studies. A special problem in panic is the start of treatment. People with panic disorder are acutely sensitive to bodily sensations, and in the first days an antidepressant can cause restlessness, insomnia and a rise in anxiety, which Pohl and his colleagues (1988) described as the jitteriness syndrome in panic patients treated with antidepressants. Read through Clark's model, a new jittery sensation is just the kind of thing a panic patient will misinterpret, so clinicians start with a low dose, raise it slowly and warn the patient in advance. Social anxiety disorder. Since 1999 the SSRIs paroxetine and sertraline and the SNRI venlafaxine have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for social anxiety disorder on the strength of placebo-controlled trials (Barlow). The older monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) phenelzine is also clearly effective: in Liebowitz's 1992 trial, 64 percent of patients responded to it against 23 percent on placebo. Because MAOIs require a strict low-tyramine diet to avoid a hypertensive crisis (Chapter 5, Section 5.7), they are now kept for patients who do not respond to the newer drugs. Generalised anxiety disorder. Benzodiazepines are the drugs most often prescribed for GAD and they give some short-term relief, but few studies have followed patients beyond eight weeks and the effect is modest. There is stronger evidence for antidepressants such as paroxetine and venlafaxine, which Barlow suggests may be the better choice; other SSRIs and SNRIs, such as escitalopram and duloxetine, are also widely used. Buspirone and pregabalin (Section 6.9.3) are the alternatives. Separation anxiety disorder and the anxious child. In a major trial with children and adolescents who had GAD, separation anxiety disorder or social phobia, CBT and the SSRI sertraline were each effective, and their combination was better still: 80 percent of children receiving both showed substantial improvement, against 24 percent on placebo (Walkup and colleagues, 2008, from Barlow). Notice that in this young group the combination did add something, unlike several adult trials in Section 6.9.6. The warning about antidepressants and suicidal thinking in young people is taught in Chapter 5. Obsessive-compulsive disorder. OCD is where the antidepressants are most distinctive, because only those that strongly block the reuptake of serotonin work. The first was clomipramine , a tricyclic antidepressant that is far more serotonergic than the other tricyclics; its benefit in OCD was first reported by the Spanish psychiatrists Fernández-Córdoba and López-Ibor in 1967, and in 1989 it became the first drug approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for OCD. The SSRIs (fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline, paroxetine) followed. Barlow summarises the evidence: clomipramine or the SSRIs benefit up to 60 percent of patients with OCD, with no particular advantage of one drug over another, but relapse often occurs when the drug is stopped. Three features of drug treatment in OCD differ from depression. The doses are usually higher: a meta-analysis of nine fixed-dose trials with 2,268 participants found that higher doses of SSRIs were more effective in OCD than low or medium doses, though more patients dropped out because of side effects (Bloch and colleagues, 2010). The trials must be longer: experts recommend at least three months at the highest tolerated dose before concluding that the drug is not enough and adding a second one (Bloch and colleagues, 2006). And even then the response is often partial: as many as half of patients given an adequate trial continue to have significant symptoms. That selective response to serotonergic drugs, together with the failure of benzodiazepines, is the foundation of the serotonin hypothesis of OCD taught in Section 6.7. Clomipramine's power has a price, the familiar tricyclic burden described in Chapter 5: anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, difficulty passing urine), sedation, weight gain, sexual dysfunction, effects on heart rhythm and danger in overdose. It also carries a higher risk of seizures than most other tricyclics, rising with dose. For these reasons the SSRIs are usually tried first and clomipramine kept for those who do not respond. Body dysmorphic disorder. Barlow notes that only two treatments for BDD have real evidence of effectiveness, and they are the same as for OCD: drugs that block the reuptake of serotonin and exposure-based CBT. Clomipramine (Anafranil) and fluvoxamine (Luvox) relieve at least some patients (Hadley, Kim, Priday and Hollander, 2006). In a controlled crossover trial, Eric Hollander and his colleagues (1999) found clomipramine significantly more effective than desipramine, a tricyclic that does not specifically block serotonin reuptake, even in patients whose BDD was of the delusional type; and in a placebo-controlled trial of fluoxetine, 53 percent responded well against 18 percent on placebo (Phillips, Albertini and Rasmussen, 2002). That even delusional BDD responds to serotonergic drugs is one reason DSM-5 keeps such patients in the OCD family rather than among the psychoses (Section 6.6). Cosmetic surgery is not a treatment. Hoarding disorder and the body-focused repetitive behaviours. Here drugs have least to offer. There is no established drug treatment for hoarding; the main approach is a specialised CBT that teaches people to assign different values to objects and to tolerate discarding them, and even its results are more modest than those achieved with OCD (Barlow). For trichotillomania and excoriation disorder the first-line treatment is psychological, habit reversal training (Book 2, Section 4.9.1). SSRIs hold some promise, particularly for trichotillomania (Chamberlain and colleagues, 2007), but the results have been mixed for excoriation (Grant and colleagues, 2012), both from Barlow. A newer candidate is N-acetylcysteine, an amino acid derivative that modulates the excitatory transmitter glutamate: in a 12-week double-blind trial with 50 adults with trichotillomania, it reduced hair pulling significantly more than placebo (Grant, Odlaug and Kim, 2009). Exam trap Clomipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant, not an SSRI, though it is the most serotonergic of the tricyclics; it was the first drug approved for OCD in the United States (1989). The SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line for long-term drug treatment of panic, social anxiety, GAD and OCD. OCD usually needs higher doses and longer trials than depression, and only serotonergic drugs help it; benzodiazepines do not. The MAOI phenelzine works for social anxiety disorder but needs the tyramine diet. Imipramine is the tricyclic of Klein's panic discovery. When the first drug is not enough: augmentation and D-cycloserine What happens when an adequate trial of a serotonergic drug leaves a person with OCD still ill? The best-studied step is augmentation : adding a second drug to the first rather than replacing it. In OCD the second drug is usually a low dose of an antipsychotic. Michael Bloch and his colleagues (2006) pooled nine double-blind trials involving 278 adults with OCD that had not responded to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Antipsychotic augmentation helped significantly, but only about one-third of these treatment-resistant patients showed a meaningful response. The evidence was clearest for haloperidol and risperidone, and patients with a coexisting tic disorder did particularly well. That last finding goes back to a trial by Christopher McDougle and his colleagues (1994), who added haloperidol or placebo for four weeks to the treatment of 34 patients who had not responded to fluvoxamine, comparing those with and without chronic tics. It fits the idea, taught in Section 6.7, that dopamine plays a secondary part in OCD, especially in its tic-related form (Chapter 3 teaches the tic disorders). The same review recommended at least three months of a serotonergic drug at the highest tolerated dose before augmentation, because a quarter of patients go on improving with the first drug alone. A very different idea has come from the laboratory study of extinction. Exposure therapy works, as Section 6.8 explained, because the person learns that the feared stimulus is safe; that new learning is a form of extinction, and extinction is an active learning process in the amygdala that depends on the excitatory transmitter glutamate acting at NMDA receptors. The neuroscientist Michael Davis and his colleagues at Emory University found that D-cycloserine , a partial agonist at the NMDA receptor (it acts at the receptor's glycine site and so boosts the receptor's response to glutamate), enhanced the extinction of conditioned fear in rats, so that fewer extinction trials were needed (Walker, Ressler, Lu and Davis, 2002). D-cycloserine is not new: it is an old antibiotic, used in India and elsewhere as a second-line drug for drug-resistant tuberculosis. In anxiety treatment it is used in a completely different way. It is given once, about an hour before an exposure session, and not taken on an ongoing basis, so that it can boost the learning that happens in that session. In double-blind trials it improved the results of CBT in panic disorder (Otto and colleagues, 2010) and in social anxiety disorder (Hofmann and colleagues, 2006), and a review by Hofmann, Sawyer and Asnaani (2012) summarised it as a promising augmentation strategy for CBT. A later and larger trial was more sobering: D-cycloserine made patients with social anxiety disorder improve 24 to 33 percent faster during a 12-week course of CBT, but by the end they were no more likely to respond or remit than those on placebo (Hofmann and colleagues, 2013). It seems, as Hofmann and his colleagues concluded, to start the treatment effect sooner rather than to make a full course of CBT more effective. Note what kind of drug it is: D-cycloserine is not an anxiolytic and does nothing for anxiety on its own; it is a learning enhancer that works only together with exposure. Exam trap In treatment-resistant OCD the usual augmenting drugs are antipsychotics (best evidence for haloperidol and risperidone), and they help about one patient in three, especially those with tics . D-cycloserine is a glutamate (NMDA) receptor enhancer and antibiotic given about an hour before exposure sessions to speed extinction learning ; it is an enhancer of CBT, not an anxiolytic, and it is not taken daily. The argument was finally put to the test in large randomised trials, which is why their results appear in examinations. The most influential was a panic trial sponsored by the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) in the United States. Key study: CBT, imipramine or both for panic disorder (Barlow, Gorman, Shear and Woods, 2000) In four anxiety research clinics between 1991 and 1998, 312 patients with panic disorder were randomly assigned, double-blind, to one of five conditions: imipramine alone; CBT alone; placebo alone; CBT plus imipramine; and CBT plus placebo, the last included to check whether any advantage of the combination came simply from taking a pill. Imipramine was used because the study began before the SSRIs were established for panic. Patients were treated weekly for three months, responders were seen monthly for six more months, and everyone was then followed for six months after treatment stopped. At the end of the first three months both imipramine and CBT were significantly better than placebo, with similar response rates (about 46 percent for imipramine and 49 percent for CBT, against 22 percent for placebo, on the main panic measure), and the combination was not significantly better than either. After the maintenance phase, the combination showed some advantage. The decisive result came six months after all treatment had ended: on the clinicians' global rating, the response rate was 41 percent for CBT plus placebo and 32 percent for CBT alone, but only 20 percent for imipramine alone and 26 percent for the combination, against 13 percent for placebo. Patients who had taken the drug, with or without CBT, had lost ground; those who had CBT without the drug kept most of their gains. The lesson: drug and psychological treatment work about equally well at first, combining them adds little, and CBT lasts. The same pattern appeared in OCD. Edna B. Foa and her colleagues (2005) randomly assigned 122 adults with OCD to intensive exposure and ritual prevention (four weeks of intensive sessions followed by eight weekly maintenance sessions), the tricyclic clomipramine (12 weeks, up to 250 mg a day), the two combined, or a pill placebo, at three centres chosen for their expertise in drugs, in exposure, or in both. All active treatments beat placebo. Among patients who completed treatment, 86 percent responded to exposure and ritual prevention alone, 79 percent to the combination, 48 percent to clomipramine alone and 10 percent to placebo. Exposure, with or without the drug, was superior to the drug alone, and adding the drug to exposure gave no further advantage; when the drug was withdrawn, relapse was high (Barlow). In social anxiety disorder, David Clark and his colleagues (2003) compared cognitive therapy, the SSRI fluoxetine plus instructions to seek out social situations (self-exposure), and placebo plus self-exposure. Both active treatments helped, but cognitive therapy was substantially better at every assessment, and its advantage held at a 12-month follow-up; in a separate Swedish trial (Mörtberg, Clark, Sundin and Åberg Wistedt, 2007), the gains of individual and of intensive group cognitive therapy for social phobia were not only kept but had grown further when patients were followed up five years later (Mörtberg, Clark and Bejerot, 2011). And Jonathan Davidson, Edna Foa, Jonathan Huppert and their colleagues (2004) found that CBT and fluoxetine were comparably effective for social anxiety disorder, while the combination was no better than either. Neurosurgery and deep brain stimulation for severe OCD A small number of people with OCD remain severely ill after years of every drug and of expert exposure and response prevention. They may spend most of their waking hours on rituals, be unable to work or leave the house, and be at serious risk of suicide. For them, two physical treatments are considered as a last resort. The first is neurosurgery. The word psychosurgery is still used, though Barlow calls it a misnomer: what is meant is neurosurgery for a psychological disorder. It carries the shadow of the prefrontal leucotomies of the 1930s to 1950s (Chapter 4), which destroyed large areas of brain in thousands of patients. Modern procedures are very different: small lesions placed precisely with stereotactic guidance in the circuits implicated in OCD (Section 6.7). In an anterior cingulotomy the lesion is made in the cingulate bundle, in the cingulate region above the corpus callosum. Michael A. Jenike and his colleagues (1991) reviewed the records of the patients with OCD who had undergone cingulotomy at Massachusetts General Hospital over 25 years, most of them extremely severe cases who had failed drug and psychological treatment. Using very conservative criteria, they estimated that at least 25 to 30 percent of the 33 patients benefited substantially; side effects included seizures, easily controlled, in 9 percent and transient mania in 6 percent, and six patients had died since surgery, four of them by suicide, a reminder of how severe the illness was. In an anterior capsulotomy the lesion is made in the front part of the internal capsule, interrupting fibres that link the frontal cortex and the thalamus. Christian Rück and his colleagues (2008) followed 25 consecutive Swedish patients for an average of almost 11 years after capsulotomy. Their mean score on the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Assessment book) fell from 34 to 18, and nine patients (about a third) were in remission; but only three of those nine had no adverse effects, and ten patients overall had significant problems with executive functioning, apathy or disinhibition, more often after high radiation doses or repeated operations. Barlow judges these results typical of the surgical procedures. The second is deep brain stimulation (DBS). Instead of destroying tissue, the surgeon passes thin electrodes through small holes drilled in the skull into a target deep in the brain and connects them to a pacemaker-like pulse generator implanted under the skin of the chest, which delivers continuous electrical stimulation. The usual target for OCD lies in the same circuit as capsulotomy, the ventral part of the anterior limb of the internal capsule and the adjoining ventral striatum, including the nucleus accumbens; a French trial stimulated the subthalamic nucleus instead (Mallet and colleagues, 2008). Its great advantages are that the stimulation can be adjusted and, if necessary, switched off: it is reversible. Barlow reports that its results are similar to those of the surgical procedures. In February 2009 the US Food and Drug Administration permitted its use for severe, treatment-resistant OCD under a humanitarian device exemption, a pathway for rare conditions that does not require full proof of effectiveness. The risks include those of any brain operation (bleeding, infection) and stimulation effects on mood. Both surgery and DBS remain treatments of last resort, offered only in specialised centres after careful assessment and alongside continued medication and therapy. Indian context Indian law treats psychosurgery as a special case. Under section 96 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, psychosurgery may not be performed as a treatment for mental illness unless the informed consent of the person on whom it is performed and the approval of the concerned Mental Health Review Board have both been obtained. The preceding section, 95, prohibits outright certain other procedures, including electroconvulsive therapy without anaesthesia and muscle relaxants, and chaining (Book 2, Section 1.10.7). Exam trap "Psychosurgery" means neurosurgery for a psychological disorder ; for OCD the procedures are cingulotomy (cingulate bundle; Jenike and colleagues 1991, about 30 percent of 33 patients helped substantially) and capsulotomy (anterior limb of the internal capsule; Rück and colleagues 2008, 9 of 25 in remission, most with adverse effects). Deep brain stimulation gives similar results but is adjustable and reversible. All are last resorts . In India, psychosurgery needs the person's own informed consent plus Mental Health Review Board approval (MHCA 2017, section 96). Where the psychotherapies fit For every disorder in this chapter there is a psychological treatment with evidence at least as good as that for any drug, and for several there is better evidence. How these therapies are actually carried out is taught in Book 2; Table 6.28 places them beside the first-line drugs so that you can see the whole treatment picture at once. For panic disorder and agoraphobia, the treatment of choice is CBT that combines cognitive therapy for catastrophic misinterpretations with interoceptive exposure (deliberately bringing on the feared sensations, by spinning in a chair or running on the spot, until they lose their power) and graded exposure to avoided situations; Barlow's panic control treatment is one version (Book 2, Sections 5.6.3 and 4.3), and breathing retraining is sometimes added (Book 2, Section 4.8.3). Specific phobia rarely needs drugs at all: exposure, which can be completed in a single session of a few hours, systematic desensitisation and participant modelling are highly effective (Book 2, Sections 4.2, 4.3 and 4.7.2), and blood-injection-injury phobia adds applied tension to prevent fainting (Section 6.3). Social anxiety disorder responds best to cognitive therapy based on the Clark and Wells model, with social skills training where skills are genuinely lacking (Book 2, Sections 5.6.4 and 4.7.5). GAD is treated with CBT, applied relaxation, metacognitive therapy and acceptance-based therapies (Book 2, Sections 4.8.4, 5.10.3 and 5.9). Separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism are treated with child-focused CBT and work with parents and schools (Book 2, Sections 10.3.2 and 10.4.2). For OCD, exposure and response prevention is the psychological treatment with the strongest evidence (Book 2, Section 4.3.5), and cognitive therapy aimed at inflated responsibility and the other beliefs of Section 6.8.7 is an effective alternative or addition (Book 2, Section 5.6.7). Thought stopping, once popular, is now discouraged, because suppressing a thought tends to make it rebound, as Wegner's white bears showed (Book 2, Section 4.9.4). BDD is treated with CBT that includes exposure and response prevention adapted to appearance concerns; cosmetic procedures are not a treatment and often lead to further operations (Section 6.6). Hoarding disorder has its own specialised CBT, and trichotillomania and excoriation disorder are treated with habit reversal training (Book 2, Section 4.9.1). Because these disorders share vulnerabilities and processes (Section 6.8.11), Barlow's group developed the Unified Protocol, a single transdiagnostic CBT for anxiety and related disorders (Book 2, Section 5.6.7), and services increasingly organise care in steps, starting with the least intensive effective treatment and stepping up when it fails (stepped care, Book 2, Section 5.11.5). The case of Little Hans, revisited Go back to the front door of the flat in Vienna, beyond which a boy of four and three-quarters would not go because a horse might bite him. You can now name what Hans had. His fear was intense, out of proportion to the danger, tied to one kind of animal and handled by avoidance; in DSM-5-TR terms it would be a specific phobia of the animal type (Section 6.3), not agoraphobia, because he stayed indoors to avoid horses, not because escape from the street might be difficult. Freud's reading (Section 6.8.9) made the horse a disguised father. The Oedipal fear of the father, who was loved and could not be avoided, was displaced onto horses, which could be; that is why displacement is still the answer when a paper asks which defence is typical of phobias, why Freud called phobias like this one anxiety hysteria (Section 6.1.3), and why in 1926 he returned to Hans to argue that fear of castration drove the repression (Section 6.8.8). Joseph Wolpe and Stanley Rachman's reading of 1960, also told in Section 6.8.9, needed none of this. Hans's fear began after he watched a bus horse fall and lie kicking in the street; a frightening event, followed by fear of the thing involved and its spread to other horses and to heavily loaded carts, is exactly what conditioning predicts (Section 6.8.1), and Mowrer's two-factor theory adds why staying indoors, rewarded by relief, would have kept the fear from extinguishing. Neither story on its own explains why Hans, and not every child in Vienna who saw a horse fall, became phobic. DiNardo found frightening encounters with dogs as often in people without a dog phobia as in people with one, and Rachman's three pathways (1977) allow a fear to be learned by watching or by being told, with no fright at all (Section 6.8.3). The modern answer is the third story of the opening, Barlow's triple vulnerability (Section 6.8.11): an inherited, reactive temperament of the kind Kagan found in high-reactive infants (Section 6.7.2), a sense that events are uncontrollable, and a specific lesson that this one thing is dangerous, brought together at a vulnerable age by a real fright. The ending fits as well. Phobias that begin in childhood often wax and wane (Section 6.3.4), and Hans's passed: the strapping youth of nineteen who called on Freud in 1922 was well and, having read his own case history, remembered nothing of it. A specific phobia today rarely needs a drug at all; exposure, the very contact with the feared thing that staying indoors prevented, is highly effective (Section 6.9.8). And the case Freud published beside his in 1909, the Rat Man, set out the other half of this chapter, the obsessions, together with the defences of isolation, undoing and reaction formation that still decide exam questions (Section 6.8.10), even though the classic causal claims of both case histories have found little support. Chapter summary 6.1 Fear, Anxiety and the Neuroses: Classifying the Anxiety Disorders. DSM-5-TR defines fear as the response to real or perceived imminent threat and anxiety as the anticipation of future threat. Either becomes a disorder when it is excessive, persists beyond the developmentally appropriate age, lasts (typically 6 months, less for two childhood disorders) and causes distress or impairment. William Cullen coined neurosis in 1769, Freud carved out anxiety neurosis in 1895, and DSM-III (1980), under Robert Spitzer, dropped the term. DSM-5 (2013) split the old group into anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, and trauma- and stressor-related disorders. ICD-10 keeps the neurotic block F40 to F48; ICD-11 has anxiety or fear-related disorders and asks for GAD symptoms over "at least several months". Comorbidity is the rule (Brown and colleagues, 2001), and anxiety caused by a substance or a medical illness is diagnosed separately. 6.2 Panic Attacks, Panic Disorder and Agoraphobia. A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes, with four or more of thirteen symptoms. Attacks may be expected or unexpected, and an attack is not itself a disorder: elsewhere it is recorded as a specifier. Donald Klein's imipramine studies (1959 to 1964) separated panic from anticipatory anxiety. Panic disorder needs recurrent unexpected attacks, at least one followed by a month or more of persistent concern or maladaptive change in behaviour; a single attack is not enough. Goldstein and Chambless (1978) traced its persistence to fear of fear, shown as anticipatory anxiety, interoceptive avoidance and safety behaviours. Agoraphobia, named by Westphal in 1871, is marked fear of two or more of five situations because escape might be difficult or help unavailable, typically for 6 months, and since DSM-5 it is diagnosed independently of panic disorder. 6.3 Specific Phobia, Social Anxiety Disorder and the Names of the Phobias. A phobia is a persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation, out of proportion to the danger, almost always provoked, and avoided or endured with dread; DSM-5-TR asks that it typically last 6 months, and the clinician judges it excessive. The five types are animal, natural environment, blood-injection-injury, situational and other. Blood-injection-injury phobia alone produces a diphasic vasovagal response with fainting, runs strongly in families and is treated with Öst and Sterner's applied tension (1987). Phobia names decode from their Greek roots: algophobia is fear of pain, nosophobia of disease, cynophobia of dogs, haematophobia of blood, and agoraphobia literally of the marketplace. Social anxiety disorder is fear of scrutiny and negative evaluation, typically for 6 months, with a performance-only specifier, a median onset of 13 and a cultural relative in taijin kyofusho. 6.4 Generalised Anxiety Disorder, Separation Anxiety Disorder and Selective Mutism. Generalised anxiety disorder grew from Freud's anxious expectation (1895); DSM-III (1980) named it with a one-month rule and DSM-III-R set six months. DSM-5-TR requires excessive, hard-to-control worry about a number of events, more days than not for at least 6 months, with three of six symptoms (restlessness, easy fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance; one in children). GAD is continued apprehension about unspecified things, not fear of fear, flashbacks or checking, and its sufferers are chronically tense autonomic restrictors. ICD-10's guidelines ask for several weeks, usually several months, and ICD-11 for at least several months. Separation anxiety disorder needs three of eight signs for 4 weeks in children or typically 6 months in adults, and can begin in adulthood; selective mutism (Kussmaul, 1877) needs 1 month, not the first month of school. 6.5 Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: The Clinical Picture. Esquirol, Westphal and Janet described obsessions long before DSM-5 gave OCD a chapter of its own. An obsession is a recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thought, urge or image that the person tries to ignore, suppress or neutralise; a compulsion is a repetitive behaviour or mental act performed to reduce anxiety or prevent a dreaded event, never for pleasure. The cardinal feature is that they take more than an hour a day or cause significant distress or impairment. Obsessions are ego-dystonic. Specifiers record insight (good or fair, poor, absent/delusional) and a tic history. Four symptom dimensions pair obsessions with compulsions, and hoarding is no longer one of them. Twelve-month prevalence is about 1.2 percent, mean onset 19.5 years, and contamination leads Indian series (Akhtar and Wig, 1975). Obsessions differ from worries, ruminations and delusions, and OCD from ego-syntonic obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. 6.6 Body Dysmorphic Disorder, Hoarding and the Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviours. DSM-5 gathered OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania and excoriation disorder, with substance-induced, medical and other specified forms, into the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. Body dysmorphic disorder, Morselli's dysmorphophobia (1891) and Phillips's "imagined ugliness", is preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others, with repetitive mirror checking, grooming, comparing or reassurance seeking. It has muscle dysmorphia and insight specifiers, usually begins in adolescence, carries a grave suicide risk, and is an obsessive-compulsive and related disorder, not a somatic symptom, anxiety or personality disorder. Hoarding disorder (Frost and Steketee) is persistent difficulty discarding possessions, whatever their value, until clutter blocks the use of living areas. Trichotillomania (Hallopeau, 1889) and excoriation disorder are body-focused repetitive behaviours. ICD-11 adds olfactory reference disorder and hypochondriasis to the group. 6.7 The Biology of Anxiety and Obsessions. Every disorder in this chapter is moderately heritable, but what is inherited is mostly a general tendency to anxiety (Kendler, 1995; Hettema, 2005); blood-injection-injury phobia is the most familial. Jerome Kagan and Nancy Snidman found about 20 percent of infants high reactive, and about a third of these socially anxious by adolescence. The GABA-benzodiazepine system, noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus, serotonin and CRF are implicated. The amygdala drives fear while the prefrontal cortex restrains it, and Jeffrey Gray separated a behavioural inhibition system (anxiety) from a fight/flight system (panic). Donald Klein's suffocation false alarm theory (1993) explains panic disorder as an oversensitive suffocation monitor, supported by lactate and carbon dioxide challenges. OCD is tied to the central serotonin system (clomipramine, the SSRIs, mCPP) and the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop (orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, caudate; Baxter, 1992), and PANDAS (Swedo, 1998) to streptococcal infection. 6.8 Learning, Cognition and Conflict: Psychological Explanations. Mowrer's two-factor theory (1947) holds that fear is acquired by classical conditioning and maintained because avoidance is negatively reinforced, which blocks extinction. Compulsions are escape or avoidance responses, as Hodgson and Rachman's washing experiments (1972) showed. Seligman's preparedness (1971) and Rachman's three pathways (1977) explain why phobias cluster on ancient dangers and need no frightening event. Beck traced anxiety to overestimated danger and catastrophising, worrying that the worst will happen. Clark (1986) explained panic as the catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations, Reiss and McNally described anxiety sensitivity, and Borkovec, Wells and Dugas modelled the worry of GAD. Salkovskis's inflated responsibility (1985) and Rachman's thought-action fusion explain obsessions. Freud's signal anxiety (1926) sets off the defences: displacement in phobia (Little Hans), and isolation, undoing and reaction formation, not repression, in OCD (the Rat Man). Barlow's triple vulnerability theory brings these strands together. 6.9 Drug and Physical Treatments. Drugs and psychological treatments work about equally well at first, but drug gains tend to last only while the drug is taken. The benzodiazepines (Sternbach's chlordiazepoxide, 1960) enhance GABA at the GABA-A receptor and act fast but bring sedation, falls, dependence and withdrawal, so they suit only short-term relief; they do not treat OCD. Buspirone, a 5-HT1A partial agonist, is slow and non-sedating and is used for GAD; beta blockers blunt the bodily signs but do not treat social anxiety disorder (Liebowitz, 1992). The SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line, and in OCD only strongly serotonergic drugs work, clomipramine first among them. Large trials in panic disorder (2000) and OCD (Foa, 2005) found the combination no better than psychological treatment alone. Cingulotomy, capsulotomy and deep brain stimulation are last resorts for severe OCD; in India, section 96 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 governs psychosurgery. From the past papers Someone diagnosed as suffering from Agoraphobia would be (JEMAS 2025) (a) hearing voices telling him or her to do certain things (b) feeling very nervous in an elevator (c) feeling very fearful of tall trees or buildings (d) feeling an irrational fear of public places Answer: (d) feeling an irrational fear of public places. Agoraphobia (Westphal, 1871; literally fear of the marketplace) is marked fear of two or more of five situations, public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, queues or crowds and being outside the home alone, because escape might be difficult or help unavailable if panic-like symptoms strike. Hearing voices is a psychotic symptom, nervousness in a lift on its own is claustrophobia (a situational specific phobia), and fear of tall trees or buildings is acrophobia (natural environment type). Panic disorder is where: (RML 2021) (a) An individual experiences a singular panic attack (b) There is excessive anxiety and worry about many different aspects of life (c) There is a fear of panicking in enclosed spaces (d) There are recurrent and unexpected panic attacks Answer: (d) There are recurrent and unexpected panic attacks. DSM-5-TR requires recurrent unexpected attacks, at least one followed by a month or more of persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour. A single attack is common and is not a disorder; worry about many aspects of life is generalised anxiety disorder; and a fear of panicking in enclosed spaces is a situational specific phobia, or agoraphobia if two or more of the five situations are feared. A phobia is best described as a: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Persistent irrational fear of a specific object or situation (b) Mild stress reaction (c) Personality disorder (d) Temporary hallucination Answer: (a) Persistent irrational fear of a specific object or situation. The fear is out of proportion to the real danger, is set off almost every time the object or situation is met, and is avoided or endured with dread; DSM-5-TR asks that it typically last 6 months. A mild stress reaction fades as the person adapts, a personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of traits, and a hallucination is a perceptual symptom, not a fear. The specific phobia of pain is known as: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Nosophobia (b) Algophobia (c) Cynophobia (d) Hematophobia Answer: (b) Algophobia. Algos is Greek for pain (as in analgesic) and phobos is fear. The distractors are real names for other fears: nosophobia is fear of disease (nosos, as in nosology), cynophobia fear of dogs (kyon, kynos) and haematophobia fear of blood (haima). Which of the following is a symptom of generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Mania (b) Persistent, excessive worry (c) Hallucinations (d) Mood swings Answer: (b) Persistent, excessive worry. GAD is defined by excessive anxiety and worry about a number of events, more days than not for at least 6 months, that the person finds hard to control, with three of six symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension and sleep disturbance. Mania and mood swings are mood symptoms (Chapter 5) and hallucinations are psychotic (Chapter 4); none is a criterion of GAD. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a pervasive condition in which the sufferer experiences: (IHBAS 2024) (a) Continued apprehension about unspecified things (b) Fear of fear (c) Continual flashbacks to past events (d) A desire to check that the environment is safe Answer: (a) Continued apprehension about unspecified things. The anxiety of GAD is free-floating: no single object or theme defines it, and the worry moves from topic to topic. Fear of fear (Goldstein and Chambless, 1978) belongs to panic disorder and agoraphobia, continual flashbacks are the re-experiencing of PTSD (Chapter 7), and a desire to check that the environment is safe is best read as the checking of OCD. Which one is NOT a compulsive behaviour in obsessive-compulsive disorder? (Amity 2023) (a) Tapping (b) Hoarding (c) Washing (d) Checking Answer: (b) Hoarding. Tapping (a symmetry or "just right" ritual), washing (the cleaning dimension) and checking (the harm dimension) are textbook compulsions. Hoarding has been a separate obsessive-compulsive and related disorder since DSM-5, because it lacks intrusive obsessions and the possessions are valued rather than feared; saving that is driven by a true obsession is still diagnosed as OCD, but that is the exception. Which of the following best describes the concept of "ego-dystonic" as it applies to obsessions in OCD? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) The individual experiences the obsessions as a core part of their identity (b) The individual experiences the obsessions as intrusive, unwanted, and inconsistent with their self-concept (c) The individual derives pleasure from the obsessive thoughts (d) The individual is completely unaware that their obsessions are unreasonable Answer: (b) intrusive, unwanted, and inconsistent with their self-concept. The person recognises the obsession as a product of his own mind yet feels it as alien and resists it. Feeling it as part of one's identity is ego-syntonic, the way OCPD traits are felt; pleasure belongs to paraphilic fantasies and impulse-control acts, never to obsessions; and complete unawareness that the obsessions are unreasonable is absent insight, a specifier, not ego-dystonia. Persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable to others is characteristic of which disorder? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Somatic Symptom Disorder (b) Body Dysmorphic Disorder (c) Illness Anxiety Disorder (d) Conversion Disorder Answer: (b) Body Dysmorphic Disorder. BDD, Morselli's dysmorphophobia (1891), is preoccupation with perceived flaws that are not observable or appear slight to others, with repetitive mirror checking, grooming, comparing or reassurance seeking, and DSM-5 placed it among the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. The distractors are real disorders about the body (Chapter 7): somatic symptom disorder is distress about bodily symptoms, illness anxiety disorder fear of having a serious illness, and conversion disorder unexplained neurological symptoms. Suffocation Alarm Theories explain the clinical condition of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Down Syndrome (b) Autistic Spectrum Disorder (c) Delirium (d) Panic Disorder Answer: (d) Panic Disorder. Donald Klein's suffocation false alarm theory (1993) proposes that people prone to panic have an oversensitive suffocation monitor that fires at harmless rises in carbon dioxide, which is why carbon dioxide and lactate challenges provoke attacks in them far more readily than in others. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) and autism spectrum disorder are neurodevelopmental (Chapter 3), and delirium is an acute, fluctuating confusional state (Chapter 10). A client with OCD washes their hands excessively to neutralize the anxiety caused by intrusive thoughts of contamination. This hand-washing behavior is BEST conceptualized as a(n): (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Conditioned stimulus (b) Unconditioned response (c) Avoidance response / Safety behavior (d) Operant behavior maintained by positive reinforcement Answer: (c) Avoidance response / Safety behavior. In Mowrer's two-factor theory applied to OCD, the contamination thought becomes a conditioned stimulus for anxiety, and washing, which brings relief, is an escape or avoidance response strengthened by negative reinforcement that also stops the person from learning that nothing bad would happen. It is not the conditioned stimulus (the thought or object is), not an unconditioned response (an unlearned reflex such as a startle), and not positively reinforced, because it removes distress rather than adding anything pleasant. From the perspective of learning theory 'compulsive acts' related to OCD are explained as patterns of ___________ behaviours. (IHBAS 2025) (a) Performance (b) Conditioning (c) Escape (d) Involuntary Answer: (c) Escape. The ritual ends the anxiety raised by the obsession, and the relief negatively reinforces it, as Hodgson and Rachman's washing experiments (1972) showed. "Conditioning" is defensible as the general mechanism but does not name the pattern the acts show; compulsions are not involuntary (they can be delayed and resisted, unlike tics), and "performance" is not a learning-theory pattern of behaviour. Catastrophic thinking is common to several anxiety disorders. The term describes: (RML 2021) (a) Categorising all experiences as either extremely positive or extremely negative (b) Focusing on negative events and ignoring positive ones (c) Worrying that the worst will always happen (d) Taking things very personally Answer: (c) Worrying that the worst will always happen. Catastrophising expects the worst possible outcome and treats it as likely and unbearable, usually as a chain of ever worse consequences; Beck made overestimated danger the core of anxiety. The other options are different distortions: dichotomous (all-or-nothing) thinking, selective abstraction (the mental filter) and personalisation. 'Displacement' is a defense mechanism typically seen in: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Hysteria (b) Phobias (c) Obsessive-compulsive disorder (d) Depression Answer: (b) Phobias. In Freud's reading of Little Hans (1909), the boy's fear of his father, whom he loved and could not avoid, was displaced onto horses, which he could avoid. Hysteria rests on repression and conversion, OCD on isolation, undoing and reaction formation, and depression, in the psychoanalytic account, on introjection and anger turned against the self. The following defense mechanisms are used in obsessive-compulsive disorder: (RML 2024) (a) Isolation (b) Undoing (c) Reaction formation (d) Displacement Answer: (b) Undoing, as keyed; but (a) and (c) are also correct. Undoing, an act that symbolically cancels a forbidden thought (the Rat Man moving a stone off the road and then putting it back), is the defence most directly tied to compulsive rituals, which is why the key picks it. Isolation of affect and reaction formation are OCD defences too, so only displacement, the defence of phobia, is wrong; if a paper allows several answers, choose (a), (b) and (c). Which of the following defense mechanisms is not involved in obsessive-compulsive disorder? (IHBAS 2020) (a) Reaction formation (b) Repression (c) Isolation (d) Undoing Answer: (b) Repression. Repression, which pushes the forbidden idea out of consciousness and turns its energy into a bodily symptom, is the defence of hysteria. In OCD the forbidden idea stays conscious: its feeling is isolated, it is cancelled by undoing, or it is held in check by its exaggerated opposite in reaction formation. The defence mechanism of Undoing is typically seen in: (Amity 2023) (a) Depression (b) Mania (c) Obsessive compulsive neurosis (d) Schizophrenia Answer: (c) Obsessive compulsive neurosis. Undoing is the hallmark defence of obsessional neurosis, and washing after a "dirty" thought or praying to cancel a blasphemous one are its everyday forms. Depression is linked with introjection and anger turned inward, mania with Melanie Klein's "manic defence" against depressive feelings, and schizophrenia with the psychotic defences of regression, projection and denial of reality. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The defences of OCD (Freud's obsessional neurosis, the Rat Man, 1909) are isolation of affect, undoing and reaction formation , with intellectualisation; undoing , an act that symbolically cancels a forbidden thought, is the most characteristic and is "typically seen in obsessive-compulsive neurosis". Repression is the defence of hysteria and is not involved in OCD. asked 3 times In learning theory (Mowrer's two-factor theory , 1947, applied to OCD) compulsive acts are escape or avoidance responses (safety behaviours) , maintained by negative reinforcement as anxiety falls; they are not conditioned stimuli, unconditioned responses, positively reinforced operants or involuntary acts. asked 2 times The cardinal DSM-5 feature of OCD : obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming (more than 1 hour a day) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment . Contamination thoughts with ritual washing for over an hour a day are OCD, not GAD, illness anxiety disorder or specific phobia. asked 3 times Ego-dystonic obsessions are experienced as intrusive, unwanted and inconsistent with one's self-concept , although recognised as one's own thoughts; not as part of one's identity (ego-syntonic), not as pleasurable, and not the same as lacking insight, which is a specifier. asked 2 times Body dysmorphic disorder : preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others , with repetitive mirror checking, grooming, comparing or reassurance seeking (Morselli's dysmorphophobia, 1891); not somatic symptom, illness anxiety or conversion disorder. asked 2 times Agoraphobia (Westphal, 1871; "fear of the marketplace") is an irrational fear of public places: marked fear of two or more of five situations (public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, queues or crowds, being outside the home alone) because escape might be difficult or help unavailable , typically for 6 months, diagnosed independently of panic disorder since DSM-5. A lift alone is claustrophobia; tall buildings, acrophobia. asked 2 times OCD versus OCPD : OCD has ego-dystonic intrusive obsessions and compulsions; obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is an ego-syntonic , pervasive pattern of perfectionism and control without true obsessions or compulsions . They are separate disorders that can coexist. asked 2 times GAD duration : DSM-5-TR requires excessive worry more days than not for at least 6 months in adults; ICD-11 asks for "at least several months" , not a fixed 6, and ICD-10's guidelines for several weeks, usually several months. asked 2 times A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes , with four or more of thirteen symptoms ; it is not itself a disorder and is recorded as a specifier in other disorders. asked 2 times The defining symptom of GAD is persistent, excessive, hard-to-control worry about many events, with three of six symptoms (restlessness, easy fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance; one in children). Mania, mood swings and hallucinations are not GAD symptoms. asked once GAD is continued apprehension about unspecified things (free-floating anxiety). Fear of fear (Goldstein and Chambless, 1978) belongs to panic disorder and agoraphobia, continual flashbacks to PTSD, and checking to OCD. asked once Panic disorder : recurrent unexpected panic attacks , at least one followed by 1 month or more of persistent concern or maladaptive change in behaviour; a single attack is not panic disorder. asked once Donald Klein's suffocation false alarm theory (1993) explains panic disorder : an oversensitive suffocation monitor fires at harmless rises in carbon dioxide (and lactate). It has nothing to do with Down syndrome, autism or delirium. asked once Catastrophic thinking (catastrophising) is worrying that the worst will always happen . All-or-nothing categorising is dichotomous thinking, focusing on negatives is selective abstraction, and taking things personally is personalisation. asked once Hoarding is not an OCD compulsion: since DSM-5 it is a separate obsessive-compulsive and related disorder. Tapping, washing and checking are compulsions. asked once Displacement is the defence typically seen in phobias : Little Hans's fear of his father displaced onto horses (Freud, 1909); not hysteria (repression), OCD or depression. asked once A phobia is a persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation , out of proportion to the danger and avoided or endured with dread; not a mild stress reaction, a personality disorder or a hallucination. asked once Algophobia is the fear of pain (algos); nosophobia is fear of disease, cynophobia of dogs and haematophobia of blood. asked once DSM-5 classifies body dysmorphic disorder under the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders , not under somatic symptom and related disorders (its somatoform home in DSM-IV), anxiety disorders or personality disorders. asked once Specific phobia needs fear typically lasting 6 months or more, as do social anxiety disorder and agoraphobia; panic disorder needs 1 month of worry, separation anxiety disorder 4 weeks in children, and selective mutism 1 month. asked once The biological system most implicated in OCD is the central serotonin (5-HT) system : clomipramine and the SSRIs help. GABA is the system of the anxiety disorders and the benzodiazepines; glutamate and dopamine are involved only secondarily. asked once
