Why should a clinical psychologist care about all three families? There are four good reasons. First, these disorders are common: DSM-5-TR calls insomnia disorder the most prevalent of all the sleep disorders, and the eating disorders begin mostly in adolescence and young adulthood, the very years in which young people sit in classrooms and counselling rooms. Second, they rarely travel alone. People with eating disorders often have depression, anxiety disorders or substance use; children who wet or soil often have behavioural or emotional problems as well; and DSM-5-TR reminds clinicians that sleep disorders are often accompanied by depression, anxiety and changes in thinking that have to be addressed in the same treatment plan. Third, some of them kill. Anorexia nervosa has one of the highest death rates of any mental disorder, from the medical effects of starvation and from suicide (Section 8.3.7), and untreated sleep apnoea puts a sleepy driver like Sudha's husband on the road. Fourth, sleep is a window onto the rest of mental health. DSM-5-TR states that persistent sleep disturbance, both insomnia and excessive sleepiness, is an established risk factor for the later development of mental illnesses, including substance use disorders, and of other medical conditions, and that it may be the first, prodromal sign of an episode of mental illness, which gives the clinician a chance to intervene before the full episode arrives. Clinical link Ask about eating, sleeping and toileting in every assessment, whatever the referral question. A student referred for "exam stress" who has stopped eating dinner, a man referred for irritability who sleeps four hours a night, and a child referred for "naughtiness" who soils at school are all common. Patients rarely volunteer these problems: anorexia nervosa is often denied, bulimic episodes are kept secret out of shame, bedwetting embarrasses the whole family, and a person with sleep apnoea usually has no idea that he stops breathing. Often, as with Sudha, the most useful informant is the person who shares the bed or the dinner table. What makes eating disordered Everybody's eating goes wrong sometimes. You skip lunch before an interview, overeat at a wedding, fast on a religious day, or live on biscuits and tea during board examinations. None of that is a disorder. So where is the line? DSM-5-TR draws it in one sentence. The feeding and eating disorders are characterised by a persistent disturbance of eating or eating-related behaviour that results in an altered consumption or absorption of food and that significantly impairs physical health or psychosocial functioning. Read that definition slowly, because each part of it rules something out. "Persistent" rules out the passing episode: the week of skipped meals before an examination, or a few days of poor appetite during an illness. "Eating-related behaviour" widens the net beyond what goes into the mouth, to the vomiting, the laxatives, the rituals and the hours of exercise that surround eating. "Altered consumption or absorption" tells you what the behaviour does: the person eats too little, too much or the wrong things, or eats and then gets rid of the food before the body can absorb it. And "significantly impairs physical health or psychosocial functioning" is the familiar clinical-significance rule that runs through the whole manual (Book 2, Section 1.6.5, the four Ds): a fussy eater who grows normally, enjoys school and eats happily with friends has no disorder, however strange her preferences. Within that definition DSM-5-TR gives full criteria for six disorders. Three of them, pica , rumination disorder and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), are disturbances of what or how a person eats, and none of them involves any concern about body weight or shape; they usually begin in childhood and are taught in Section 8.2. The other three, anorexia nervosa , bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder (BED), are the eating disorders in the everyday sense, organised around restriction, binges and, in the first two, an overvalued concern with weight and shape; they are taught in Sections 8.3 and 8.4. Presentations that cause real distress or impairment but do not fit any of the six are recorded as other specified or unspecified feeding or eating disorder (Section 8.4.7). One rule about these three main eating disorders is worth learning now, because it shapes every diagnosis in the rest of the chapter. The criteria for anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder form a mutually exclusive classification : during a single episode, only one of the three can be diagnosed. Why not simply diagnose two when a person has the features of both? DSM-5-TR gives the reason directly: despite many shared psychological and behavioural features, the three disorders differ substantially in their clinical course, their outcome and their treatment needs, so the clinician must decide which one is present. In practice the criteria themselves do the deciding. A woman who binges and makes herself vomit while she is at a significantly low weight has anorexia nervosa of the binge-eating/purging type, not anorexia plus bulimia, because low weight is asked about first; a man who binges but never compensates has binge-eating disorder, not bulimia (Section 8.4.6 sets out the full decision tree). Notice the words "during a single episode". Over a lifetime, a person can and often does move from one diagnosis to another, a movement called diagnostic crossover ; DSM-5-TR describes, for example, a minority of people whose bulimia nervosa later turns into anorexia nervosa (Section 8.4.4). DSM-5-TR adds a thoughtful paragraph about a resemblance that the newspapers often exaggerate. Some people with the disorders in this chapter describe their eating in the language of addiction: craving, loss of control, and compulsive eating that continues despite harm. The manual suggests that the resemblance may reflect the involvement of the same brain systems, those concerned with reward and with regulatory self-control, in both the eating disorders and the substance use disorders. But it is careful to add that the relative contributions of shared and distinct factors in the development and maintenance of eating and substance use disorders remain insufficiently understood. That caution matters, because food addiction is a popular idea and the subject of much research, but it is not a diagnosis in DSM-5-TR or in ICD-11. A clinician who hears "I am addicted to sweets" writes down the binge-eating pattern, if there is one, and diagnoses binge-eating disorder or bulimia nervosa by their own criteria. The last paragraph of DSM-5-TR's introduction answers a question that students often ask: if eating too little can be a mental disorder, why is eating too much not one? Why is obesity missing from the manual? Obesity is excess body fat, and it results from a long-term excess of energy taken in over energy used. DSM-5-TR leaves it out because a wide range of genetic, physiological, behavioural and environmental factors, varying from one person to the next, contributes to its development: it is a condition with many different causes, not a single pattern of disturbed behaviour and experience. (The usual adult definition, a body mass index of 30 or more, and Stanley Schachter's externality account of overeating are taught in Book 1, Section 10.9.4.) But leaving obesity out of the manual does not mean that psychology has nothing to say about it. DSM-5-TR lists robust associations between obesity and several mental disorders, among them binge-eating disorder, the depressive and bipolar disorders and schizophrenia; it notes that the side effects of some psychotropic drugs contribute importantly to the development of obesity; and it adds that obesity may itself be a risk factor for developing some mental disorders, such as depressive disorders. The relation between binge-eating disorder and obesity, which overlap but are not the same thing, is taken up in Section 8.4.5. Clinical link The weight gain caused by psychotropic drugs is not a cosmetic side effect. Some antipsychotics, olanzapine and clozapine above all, cause marked weight gain and rises in blood sugar and lipids (Section 4.10), and patients who gain weight on a drug often stop taking it. When a patient with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder starts such a drug, weight, waist and eating habits belong on the treatment plan from the first week, and an eating disorder history should be asked about before, not after, the weight starts to climb. Exam trap Obesity is not a mental disorder in DSM-5-TR, because it has many different genetic, physiological, behavioural and environmental causes; it is associated with binge-eating disorder, depressive and bipolar disorders and schizophrenia, but it is not itself a diagnosis. Only one of anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder can be diagnosed in a single episode , because they differ in course, outcome and treatment needs. And "food addiction" is not a diagnosis in either manual, however often the phrase is used. Self-starvation before anorexia nervosa Refusing food is very old. What has changed over the centuries is what people thought the refusal meant. In medieval Europe some deeply religious women ate almost nothing for years, and their contemporaries read the fasting as holiness. The best known is Catherine of Siena (1347 to 1380), the Italian mystic, later a saint, who lived for long periods on almost no food and who, even when churchmen pressed her to eat and she prayed to be able to eat like other people, still could not give up fasting. In 1985 the American historian Rudolph M. Bell gathered the lives of such women in a book called Holy Anorexia , and his title gave the phenomenon its name: holy anorexia , self-starvation in the service of religious devotion. Whether these women had anorexia nervosa in the modern sense is disputed, and with good reason. Some of them were tirelessly active and resisted every attempt to make them eat, which is strikingly familiar; but they starved, as far as anyone can tell, for God, for purity and for control over a body they regarded as sinful, not to be thin. In the nineteenth century the religious fasters were followed by the fasting girls , young women and girls who were said to live without any food at all and who drew crowds, journalists and doctors to their bedsides. Their stories often ended badly. Sarah Jacob (1857 to 1869), the "Welsh fasting girl", was a farmer's daughter from near Pencader in Carmarthenshire who was said to have eaten nothing for about two years. In December 1869 a team of four nurses was brought in to watch her day and night, to settle the matter. She died a little over a week after the watch began, and her parents were convicted of manslaughter. The fasting girls show how public and how powerful food refusal can be, but they are a story of claims and of spectacle; none of them was described as afraid of becoming fat. The first medical account of self-starvation as an illness, rather than a miracle, is usually credited to the London physician Richard Morton (1637 to 1698). His book on consumption, Phthisiologia , appeared in Latin in 1689 and in English in 1694. Most of it is about the wasting disease of the lungs that we now call tuberculosis, but Morton set aside a separate kind of wasting that he called nervous consumption , or "nervous atrophy", a wasting that he traced to the nerves rather than to the lungs. He described two patients. One was a girl, Mr Duke's daughter, who fell ill in 1684 in her eighteenth year and wasted until, in his words, she was "like a skeleton only clad with skin", with no fever and no cough; she died about three months after coming under his care. The other was a boy, the son of a minister, who at about sixteen fell gradually into "a total want of appetite", which Morton blamed on too much study; Morton advised him to give up his studies, ride in the country air and drink milk, and the boy recovered his health "in a great measure". A girl and a boy, then, at the very start of the medical story. Here is the point to carry forward. The modern diagnosis of anorexia nervosa is built around an intense fear of gaining weight and a disturbed experience of body shape (Section 8.3.2). That fear of fatness is not described in the saints, in the fasting girls or in Morton's patients, and, as you will see in the next subsection, neither Gull nor Lasègue described it either. It entered the clinical picture later, and it entered the DSM's diagnostic criteria only with DSM-III in 1980 (Table 8.1). Even today it is not universal. DSM-5-TR notes that the absence of an expressed intense fear of weight gain, sometimes called "fat phobia", appears to be relatively more common among patients in Asia, who more often explain their refusal to eat by a culturally sanctioned complaint such as discomfort in the stomach (Section 8.5.1 discusses culture in full, and Section 1.10.2 the debate over anorexia nervosa as a "Western culture-bound syndrome"). Exam trap The first medical description of anorexia-like wasting is usually credited to Richard Morton , in Phthisiologia (Latin 1689, English 1694), who called it nervous consumption ; the name anorexia nervosa came nearly two centuries later, from Gull. Holy anorexia is Rudolph Bell's term (1985) for the religious fasting of medieval women such as Catherine of Siena, and whether they had anorexia nervosa is disputed, because their motive was religious, not a fear of fatness. Gull, Lasègue and the naming of anorexia nervosa The disorder got its modern name in 1873, from two physicians working in two capitals at almost exactly the same moment. The first was William Withey Gull (1816 to 1890), a physician who had joined Guy's Hospital in London in 1837 and risen to become one of its leading physicians and teachers. By the 1870s he was among the most eminent doctors in Britain: in 1871 he was credited with saving the life of the Prince of Wales during an attack of typhoid, and he was made a baronet and one of Queen Victoria's physicians. In August 1868, in a long address on medicine to the British Medical Association meeting at Oxford, Gull had mentioned in passing a peculiar condition, occurring mostly in young women and marked by extreme emaciation, which he called apepsia hysterica , "hysterical indigestion". Apepsia means a failure of digestion, and the name shows that he still half suspected the stomach. Five years later he had changed his mind. On 24 October 1873 Gull read a paper to the Clinical Society of London, and it was printed in the Society's Transactions in 1874 under the title "Anorexia nervosa (apepsia hysterica, anorexia hysterica)". He gave the details of two patients, Miss A. and Miss B., "as fair examples of the whole", and added a third case sent to him by another doctor. Miss A. was seventeen when she was brought to him, and she had lost 33 pounds, more than a quarter of her weight. His published patients were all young women, emaciated and weak; he recorded amenorrhoea, and he noticed two things in the body that you will meet again in Section 8.3.5: the pulse was slow and the breathing was slow (in his last case, of 1888, he also recorded a low body temperature and cold, blue hands and feet). He noticed something else that surprised him. Starving as they were, his patients were restless and full of energy, constantly on the move. And he could find nothing wrong with their stomachs. "The want of appetite is, I believe, due to a morbid mental state," he wrote. He explained his choice of name with equal care: "We might call the state hysterical without committing ourselves to the etymological value of the word ... I prefer, however, the more general term 'nervosa', since the disease occurs in males as well as females, and is probably rather central than peripheral." The word hysteria comes from the Greek for the womb, and Gull, who had seen the illness in young men too, wanted a name that pointed to the nervous system instead. His advice on treatment has worn remarkably well. The patient's inclination, he insisted, "must be in no way consulted". He warned against the common advice to anxious parents, "let her do as she likes. Don't force food", saying that he had once thought it proper but that larger experience had shown him the danger of allowing the starvation to go on. Warmth and steady supplies of food would gradually restore the strength, and "the patients should be fed at regular intervals, and surrounded by persons who would have moral control over them; relations and friends being generally the worst attendants." Feeding as the first treatment, firm and caring control by others, and a wary eye on the family: all three are still debated in the treatment of anorexia nervosa today (Section 8.5.6, and Book 2, Sections 7.4.6 and 7.7.7, for the very different modern views of the family). In March 1888, less than two years before his death, Gull published in The Lancet one more case, Miss K. R., a girl of fourteen brought to him by a country doctor, illustrated with wood engravings made from photographs of the starved girl and of her recovery. The second physician was Ernest-Charles Lasègue (1816 to 1883) in Paris, whom you met in Chapter 2 as one of the two authors of folie à deux. In April 1873, six months before Gull's London paper, Lasègue published "De l'anorexie hystérique" in the Archives générales de médecine , the journal he edited, drawing on eight cases; an English translation appeared in a British medical journal the same year, although, as later scholars discovered, it left out some important passages. His name for the illness, anorexie hystérique (hysterical anorexia), kept the link with hysteria, and he described it only in women. What makes his paper remarkable is its psychology. Lasègue traced the illness through three stages, beginning with a gradual cutting down of food and a growing strictness about what could be eaten, and ending in severe emaciation. He described patients who insisted that they were well while those around them grew frantic, and he gave the family a central place in the story, writing about family interactions and parental attitudes as part of the illness itself. Put simply, Gull described the body and Lasègue described the family. Who came first? Gull is usually given a slight priority because of his brief mention of 1868. Lasègue, for his part, printed an immediate editorial reply in his journal after reading the report of Gull's London paper. A century later the Belgian psychiatrist Walter Vandereycken and his colleague Ron van Deth looked again at the documents and concluded, in 1989, that the two men's work was a remarkable but independent coincidence and that no clear priority can be established for either. Most textbooks therefore give the two joint credit. One more detail deserves notice. Neither Gull nor Lasègue described a patient who was afraid of becoming fat. Their patients refused food and kept on the move, but the fear of fatness that DSM-5-TR now places at the centre of the diagnosis is absent from both papers, a reminder that the picture of a disorder can change even while its name stays the same. Key study: Gull's paper to the Clinical Society of London (read 1873, printed 1874) The question. Why were some young women wasting away when no disease of the stomach, the lungs or the womb could be found? The method. Careful case histories followed over years: Miss A. and Miss B. in detail, with a third case in an addendum. The findings. Severe emaciation, amenorrhoea, slow pulse, slow breathing, restless overactivity and no organic disease; recovery with regular feeding under firm control. The conclusion. The loss of appetite comes from "a morbid mental state"; the illness is "nervosa" because it is central and occurs in males as well as females. The limits. A handful of patients, probably from wealthy families seen in private practice, no fear of fatness described, and a name, "anorexia", that misdescribes the illness, as the trap below explains. Exam trap Anorexia means "loss of appetite", but most people with anorexia nervosa are hungry; they restrict because they fear weight gain, not because they do not want food. The name is a historical accident. Gull (London) named it anorexia nervosa , in a paper read in October 1873 and printed in 1874; Lasègue (Paris) called it anorexie hystérique in April 1873. Hilde Bruch did not name it : she wrote about it a century later. And the first description of anorexia-like wasting is Morton's (1689), not Gull's. Hilde Bruch and the twentieth century For the first half of the twentieth century anorexia nervosa was often treated as a disease of the glands. In 1914 the German pathologist Morris Simmonds described fatal wasting caused by destruction of the pituitary gland, and in the 1920s and 1930s many patients with anorexia nervosa were misdiagnosed as having this pituitary disease and treated, without success, with pituitary extracts. For a generation the psychological view of Gull and Lasègue went out of fashion. The person who did most to bring it back, and to turn attention from the stomach and the glands to the person, was Hilde Bruch (1904 to 1984). Bruch was born in the small German town of Dülken, trained in medicine in Germany, and emigrated to the United States in 1934, after the Nazis had come to power. She worked first in New York, at Columbia University, where she studied obese children, and from 1964 she was professor of psychiatry at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston. In her work with young people who starved themselves she was struck by how little their illness had to do with appetite. In a paper of 1962 in Psychosomatic Medicine , "Perceptual and conceptual disturbances in anorexia nervosa", Bruch described what she saw. Her patients had a disturbance of body image "of delusional proportions": an emaciated girl would look in the mirror and see herself as too fat, and defend that perception fiercely (Section 2.10.3 examines body image in anorexia, and Section 2.5.6 why fatness in anorexia is classed as an overvalued idea). They also had trouble recognising the signals from their own bodies: they did not seem to read hunger, fullness or fatigue accurately, as if these sensations had never been properly learned. And underneath both, Bruch argued, lay a paralysing sense of ineffectiveness, a feeling of having no control over one's own life, against which control of the body became the one achievement that was truly one's own. Bruch's explanation of where those disturbances come from, in the early relationship between child and parent, is a theory of cause and is taught in Sections 8.5.2 and 8.5.3. What matters here is the historical shift: after Bruch, the core of the disorder was understood to lie in the person's experience of her body and herself, not in her stomach. She wrote two books that every student of the subject knows. Eating Disorders: Obesity, Anorexia Nervosa, and the Person Within (1973) was her full clinical account, and its subtitle, "the person within", announced her approach. The Golden Cage: The Enigma of Anorexia Nervosa , published by Harvard University Press in 1978, distilled the same experience for parents, patients and general readers, through vivid stories from her own case material, and it reached a very wide lay readership. Public awareness grew alongside the professional literature. One death in particular made the disorder known around the world. The American singer Karen Carpenter died on 4 February 1983, aged thirty-two, of heart failure attributed to the effects of anorexia nervosa, and the extensive news coverage taught millions of people that the illness can kill. By then researchers had also begun to notice how closely the eating disorders follow the values of a culture. Barlow and Durand go so far as to call anorexia nervosa, and particularly bulimia nervosa, "the most culturally specific psychological disorders yet identified", a claim weighed against the evidence in Section 8.5.1. Exam trap Hilde Bruch (1904 to 1984) wrote Eating Disorders: Obesity, Anorexia Nervosa, and the Person Within ( 1973 ) and The Golden Cage ( 1978 ), and in 1962 described the body-image disturbance "of delusional proportions". She did not name the disorder (Gull did, in 1873 to 1874) and she did not describe bulimia nervosa (Russell did, in 1979). "The Golden Cage" is Bruch; the "psychosomatic family" is Salvador Minuchin (Section 8.5.2). Bulimia and binge eating enter the manuals Eating far too much at one sitting is as old as feasting, and the word for it is old too: bulimia comes from the Greek for "ox hunger", a hunger big enough for an ox. Barlow and Durand note that clear cases of bulimic behaviour have been described for thousands of years, and, more surprisingly, that for hundreds of years most of the recorded cases were men. What is new is the idea that bingeing, together with the attempts to undo it, forms a distinct psychological disorder; Barlow and Durand date the recognition of bulimia nervosa as a disorder of its own to the 1970s. The road there had two stages. First the binge was noticed among people who were overweight, in the 1950s; then, in the 1970s, the binge followed by vomiting was noticed among young women who feared fatness, many of whom had once had anorexia nervosa. The first step was taken by the American psychiatrist Albert J. Stunkard (1922 to 2014), who spent most of his career at the University of Pennsylvania studying obesity. In 1955, with William Grace and Harold Wolff, he published in the American Journal of Medicine a description of the night eating syndrome , "a pattern of food intake among certain obese patients" who ate much of their day's food late in the evening and at night (its modern definition, as an example of other specified feeding or eating disorder, is in Section 8.4.7, and the different sleep-related eating disorder in Section 8.10.2). In 1959, in a paper called "Eating patterns and obesity" in the Psychiatric Quarterly , Stunkard described binge eating as a distinct pattern among some of his obese patients: eating very large amounts of food in a short time, followed by distress. Those patients were the forerunners of the binge-eating disorder that DSM-5 recognised more than half a century later. The second step came in the 1970s. In 1976 the American writer Marlene Boskind-Lodahl , writing from a feminist perspective, described young women caught in cycles of gorging and purging, and three years later, in London, the British psychiatrist Gerald Russell (1928 to 2018), then professor of psychiatry at the Royal Free Hospital and from 1979 at the Institute of Psychiatry and the Maudsley Hospital, gave the pattern the name that stuck. His paper in Psychological Medicine in 1979 was called "Bulimia nervosa: an ominous variant of anorexia nervosa", and it is the founding document of bulimia nervosa . The Key-study box tells it. Russell's sign, the marks on the knuckles of patients who make themselves vomit, is named after him and explained in Section 8.4.3, and his later work on family therapy for adolescent anorexia at the Maudsley is in Book 2, Section 7.7.7. Key study: Russell's thirty patients (1979) The question. What was wrong with the young women who kept their weight down not by starving but by overeating and then vomiting? The method. Russell selected thirty patients for a prospective study using two criteria: an irresistible urge to overeat, followed by self-induced vomiting or purging, and a morbid fear of becoming fat. The findings. Most had a previous history of anorexia nervosa, either obvious or "cryptic". Like patients with anorexia nervosa, they were determined to keep their weight below a threshold they set themselves, lower than their healthy weight before the illness. Unlike them, they tended to be heavier, more sexually active, more likely to menstruate regularly and to remain fertile. The vomiting and purging were dangerous, habit-forming and caused potassium loss; depression was often severe, with a high risk of suicide. The conclusion. A self-perpetuating vicious circle of overeating and vomiting, which treatment must interrupt while persuading the patient to accept a higher weight. Russell judged the outlook to be less favourable than in uncomplicated anorexia nervosa, hence "ominous". The legacy. DSM-III (1980) already listed a looser diagnosis called simply "bulimia"; DSM-III-R (1987) adopted Russell's name, bulimia nervosa, and with it the requirements of weight-control behaviour and of concern with shape and weight. The manuals then took over the story, and Table 8.1 follows it edition by edition; Figure 8.2 puts the whole history, from Morton to DSM-5-TR, on a single timeline. Read the table down each column and three trends stand out. The first is a move from description to rules. DSM-I (1952) and DSM-II (1968) gave only brief descriptions of disorders and no diagnostic criteria at all (Section 1.7). DSM-III (1980) gave anorexia nervosa five explicit criteria, among them an intense fear of becoming obese and a weight loss of at least 25 percent of original body weight, and it brought in a new diagnosis called simply "bulimia". The second trend is that the numbers were first added and then taken away. The 25 percent weight-loss rule became a weight at least 15 percent below what was expected (that is, below 85 percent) in DSM-III-R (1987) and DSM-IV (1994), and then DSM-5 (2013) dropped the percentage altogether in favour of a "significantly low" weight judged in context. Amenorrhoea, the absence of menstrual periods, became a criterion in DSM-III-R and was dropped in DSM-5, because it does not occur in every case and cannot apply at all to men, to girls before puberty or to women taking hormonal contraceptives (Section 8.3.3 tells that story in full). Bulimia had no frequency rule in DSM-III, required at least two binges a week for 3 months in DSM-III-R and DSM-IV, and needs only one a week for 3 months in DSM-5. The third trend is a gathering together. DSM-III-R kept the eating disorders in the section for disorders first evident in infancy, childhood or adolescence; DSM-IV gave anorexia and bulimia nervosa a chapter of their own but left pica, rumination disorder and feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood behind in the childhood chapter; and DSM-5 put all of them into one lifespan chapter, Feeding and Eating Disorders, replaced feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood with the broader avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, and promoted binge-eating disorder from the appendix to a full diagnosis. The other change in the last row deserves a sentence. Under DSM-IV, the leftover label eating disorder not otherwise specified (EDNOS) became the commonest eating disorder diagnosis in routine clinical practice, more common than anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, as Christopher Fairburn and Kristin Bohn pointed out in 2005 (Section 1.8.4). A residual category that outnumbers the main ones is a sign that the main categories are drawn too narrowly. DSM-5's lower thresholds, its new diagnoses and its other specified feeding or eating disorder (OSFED), which names the reason the presentation does not fit, were designed to shrink the leftover group (Section 8.4.7). DSM-5-TR (2022) kept the same set of disorders and revised the text, adding to anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder a section on their association with suicidal thoughts and behaviour. Where the disorders live in the manuals How the World Health Organization's two classifications are built, ICD-10 with its Chapter V of F codes and ICD-11 with its Chapter 6 of codes from 6A00 to 6E8Z, adopted in 2019 and in force from 1 January 2022, is explained in Sections 1.9.3 to 1.9.6. What this subsection adds is the address of every disorder in this chapter, and the two stories that the addresses tell. Table 8.2 is the master list. Its second column needs a word of explanation. DSM-5-TR prints the codes of ICD-10-CM, the clinical modification of ICD-10 that the United States uses for its health records, and the clinical modification often adds digits that the WHO's own ICD-10 does not have. That is why anorexia nervosa is F50.01 or F50.02 in DSM-5-TR but simply F50.0 in the WHO's ICD-10, and why pica carries two DSM-5-TR codes, F98.3 in children and F50.89 in adults: the American codes inherit the WHO's habit of filing childhood pica in a different block from adult eating problems. The WHO's ICD-10 split the feeding and eating problems between two blocks of Chapter V. Anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, with their "atypical" forms (F50.1 and F50.3) for incomplete pictures, sat in F50, within the block of behavioural syndromes associated with physiological disturbances and physical factors, alongside two codes for overeating and for vomiting associated with other psychological disturbances (F50.4 and F50.5) and a code for other eating disorders (F50.8) that held pica in adults and psychogenic loss of appetite. The feeding problems of young children, meanwhile, sat at the far end of the chapter, in the block of behavioural and emotional disorders with onset usually occurring in childhood and adolescence: feeding disorder of infancy and childhood (F98.2, which included rumination disorder of infancy) and pica of infancy and childhood (F98.3), next to nonorganic enuresis (F98.0) and nonorganic encopresis (F98.1). DSM-IV made the same split, as Table 8.1 showed. DSM-5 and ICD-11 abandoned it. Both now gather every feeding and eating disorder, whatever the age of the patient, into one family; in ICD-11 that family is the grouping of feeding or eating disorders, 6B80 to 6B85, which also brings in two diagnoses that ICD-10 never had, binge eating disorder (6B82) and avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (6B83), and renames rumination as rumination-regurgitation disorder (6B85). The elimination disorders, enuresis (6C00) and encopresis (6C01), get a small grouping of their own straight afterwards, instead of being two lines in a block of assorted childhood problems. The second story concerns sleep, and it is the more important one. ICD-10 divided the sleep disorders by their presumed cause. Its Chapter V held the nonorganic sleep disorders (F51), and the WHO's definition is explicit: the category includes only those sleep disorders in which emotional causes are considered to be a primary factor, and which are not due to identifiable physical disorders classified elsewhere. So F51 held nonorganic insomnia (F51.0), nonorganic hypersomnia (F51.1), nonorganic disorder of the sleep-wake schedule (F51.2), sleepwalking (F51.3), sleep terrors (F51.4) and nightmares (F51.5). Their "organic" counterparts lived in a different chapter altogether, Chapter VI, Diseases of the nervous system: disorders of initiating and maintaining sleep (G47.0), disorders of excessive somnolence (G47.1), disorders of the sleep-wake schedule (G47.2), sleep apnoea (G47.3), narcolepsy and cataplexy (G47.4) and other sleep disorders, including Kleine-Levin syndrome (G47.8); restless legs syndrome was filed among the extrapyramidal and movement disorders (G25.8). The trouble with this division is easy to see. The same complaint, a man who cannot sleep, had to be coded F51.0 or G47.0 according to whether the clinician judged its cause to be emotional or physical, and for most sleep disorders the honest answer is "both": worry keeps a person awake, and so do pain, apnoea and caffeine, often in the same person on the same night. It is the same objection that led DSM-IV to drop the old division between organic and functional mental disorders (Section 1.6.3). ICD-11 abolished the division by giving the sleep-wake disorders a chapter of their own, Chapter 7, outside the chapter of mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders and separate from the chapter on diseases of the nervous system. Its codes begin with 7A and 7B, and it has six groupings: insomnia disorders (chronic insomnia 7A00 and short-term insomnia 7A01), hypersomnolence disorders (narcolepsy 7A20, idiopathic hypersomnia 7A21, Kleine-Levin syndrome 7A22 and others), sleep-related breathing disorders (central sleep apnoeas 7A40, obstructive sleep apnoea 7A41, sleep-related hypoventilation or hypoxaemia disorders 7A42), circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders (7A60 to 7A65, including a jet lag type that DSM-5-TR does not have), sleep-related movement disorders (restless legs syndrome 7A80, periodic limb movement disorder 7A81 and others) and parasomnia disorders (disorders of arousal from non-REM sleep 7B00, parasomnias related to REM sleep 7B01 and other parasomnias 7B02). Figure 8.3 shows both reorganisations at a glance. DSM-5-TR, for its part, keeps the sleep-wake disorders inside the manual, because it is written for mental health and general medical clinicians who meet these complaints every day; but look at its codes in Table 8.2 and you can still see the ghost of the old split: insomnia, hypersomnolence, the NREM arousal disorders and nightmare disorder carry F codes, while narcolepsy, the breathing disorders, the circadian disorders, REM sleep behaviour disorder and restless legs syndrome carry G codes. How the sleep classifications developed, from DSM-III-R's dyssomnias and parasomnias to the sleep specialists' ICSD-3, is the subject of Section 8.7.3. A first look at who is affected Before the detailed sections, it helps to have a rough picture of who develops each disorder, because the pattern itself teaches something. Table 8.3 gathers, for every disorder of the chapter, the usual age at which it begins and how it is shared between the sexes; each disorder's own section gives the full prevalence figures and the reasons behind them. Three patterns stand out. The eating disorders, apart from the childhood feeding disorders, begin mostly in adolescence and young adulthood and are far commoner in girls and women: in two community studies in the United States, the lifetime prevalence of anorexia nervosa was about 0.9 to 1.42 percent among women against 0.12 to 0.3 percent among men. Binge-eating disorder is the least lopsided of the three, two to three times commoner in women, and ARFID is about equally common in boys and girls. The elimination disorders, by contrast, belong to childhood by definition and lean towards boys. And the sleep-wake disorders spread right across the lifespan, from the sleepwalking child to the sleep apnoea of middle age and the REM sleep behaviour disorder of older men, with a sex ratio that tilts one way for some disorders and the other way for others. Sudha's husband, a man in his forties, is exactly who obstructive sleep apnoea picks out; Shreya, a girl of seventeen, is exactly who anorexia nervosa picks out; and Varun, a boy of seven, is a very ordinary bedwetter. The reasons for those patterns, which are partly biological and partly social, are the business of Sections 8.3 to 8.10. That picture fits anorexia nervosa well, and Section 8.3 is devoted to it. But some of the oldest and, in their own way, most dangerous disturbances of eating have nothing to do with weight or shape at all. Think of a toddler who picks plaster off the wall and swallows it, an infant who brings up every feed and chews it again with apparent contentment, a boy who has eaten only three foods since the day he choked on a piece of apple. None of them wants to be thin. None of them is looking in a mirror. Yet each is eating in a way that can stunt growth, poison the body or, rarely, kill. This section is about these three disorders, which are usually grouped together as the feeding disorders : pica, rumination disorder and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder. You will learn what each one looks like, how DSM-5-TR (the text revision of the fifth edition of the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, 2022) defines it and why each rule is there, who develops it, and how a clinician tells it apart from the many conditions that resemble it. Feeding disorders across the life span What do the three have in common? Section 8.1.2 gave DSM-5-TR's definition of the whole family: a persistent disturbance of eating or eating-related behaviour that changes how food is consumed or absorbed and that significantly damages physical health or psychosocial functioning. Within that family, the feeding disorders are distinguished by what they lack. In each of them the disturbance concerns what a person eats (pica: things that are not food), what happens to food after it is swallowed (rumination disorder: it comes back up), or how much and how widely a person eats (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder: too little, or too narrow a range). What is missing is the disturbance in the experience of body weight or shape that defines anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa. A child with pica is not eating chalk to stay slim; a teenager with avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder may be painfully thin and wish she were not. Keep that negative definition in mind, because it is the single most useful fact in this section: when restriction happens without any fear of fatness, think of the feeding disorders before you think of anorexia. The three also share a history. In DSM-IV (1994) they lived in the chapter on disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence, under the heading "Feeding and Eating Disorders of Infancy or Early Childhood", which held pica, rumination disorder and a third diagnosis called feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood (a persistent failure to eat enough, with failure to gain weight or loss of weight, beginning before the age of 6). The adult eating disorders were in a separate chapter. That arrangement carried an unspoken message, that these were problems of babies and toddlers that children grew out of. Clinicians knew better. Adults with intellectual disability eat cloth and stones; adolescents and adults ruminate in secret; and many adults who have avoided whole classes of food since childhood never fit the old infant-centred criteria. DSM-5 (2013) therefore merged both groups into one lifespan chapter, "Feeding and Eating Disorders", rewrote the criteria so that they apply at any age, and replaced the infant feeding disorder with a much broader diagnosis, avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, which can be given to a toddler or to a 60-year-old (Section 8.1.6 tells this history edition by edition). The World Health Organization (WHO) made the same move later. Its ICD-10 (1992) kept the childhood problems among the disorders of childhood, as F98.2 (feeding disorder of infancy and childhood, which explicitly included rumination disorder of infancy) and F98.3 (pica of infancy and childhood), and filed pica in adults under F50.8, "other eating disorders". ICD-11 (in force from 2022) puts all six disorders in one block of the mental disorders chapter: 6B83 avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder, 6B84 pica and 6B85 rumination-regurgitation disorder sit next to anorexia nervosa (6B80), bulimia nervosa (6B81) and binge eating disorder (6B82). The third thing the feeding disorders share is a rule about other conditions, and it is worth understanding because examiners like to test it. All three are common in people who already have another diagnosis, above all autism spectrum disorder and intellectual developmental disorder (intellectual disability), which Chapter 3 teaches. A child with autism may eat only a handful of foods of one colour and texture; a man with severe intellectual disability may put everything he finds into his mouth. Should each of them receive a second diagnosis for the eating behaviour? If the answer were always yes, every feature of autism or intellectual disability would be counted twice, and the second label would add nothing that the first did not already say. If the answer were always no, a behaviour that is dangerous in its own right (a man who swallows batteries, a girl with autism whose diet has become so narrow that she is losing weight) would disappear inside the larger diagnosis and might never get its own treatment plan. DSM-5-TR solves the problem with one shared criterion, usually Criterion D: when the eating behaviour occurs in the context of another mental disorder or a medical condition, a separate diagnosis is given only if the behaviour is severe enough to warrant additional clinical attention , that is, more severe than the other condition usually produces and needing treatment of its own. The rule protects against both errors: it stops every symptom of a developmental disorder from becoming a second diagnosis, and it lets the clinician name the eating problem when it has become a target for treatment in its own right. Beyond that shared rule, the three differ in how they relate to the other eating disorders. Rumination disorder cannot be diagnosed if the regurgitation happens only during anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder or avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder cannot be diagnosed if the restriction happens only during anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, and it requires that there be no disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced. Pica's criteria contain no such exclusion, so pica can be diagnosed alongside another feeding or eating disorder when it needs attention in its own right. DSM-5 (2013) said so explicitly in its introduction to the chapter, stating that pica may be diagnosed in the presence of any other feeding or eating disorder; DSM-5-TR dropped that sentence but kept the criteria unchanged, and its text adds one exception: when non-food items such as tissue paper are eaten mainly to control weight, anorexia nervosa is the diagnosis (Section 8.2.2). None of the three has subtypes or severity ratings; each has a single specifier, in remission , for a person who once met the full criteria but has not done so for a sustained period.
