Pica Poonam is 24 and five months into her second pregnancy in a village in Madhya Pradesh. At the primary health centre the auxiliary nurse midwife notices that her haemoglobin is low and that she keeps rubbing her stomach. Gently questioned, Poonam admits that since her third month she has been breaking off pieces of the dried mud plaster on the courtyard wall, and pieces of an old earthen water pot, and chewing them several times a day. The smell of wet earth after the rain makes her mouth water. She eats them when her mother-in-law is not looking, because the older woman scolds her for it, and she has had painful constipation for weeks. "I know it is mud," she says, embarrassed. "But I want it more than food." Is this a mental disorder, a craving of pregnancy, or a custom? The answer depends on the criteria, so begin with the name. Pica is the Latin word for the magpie, a bird reputed to eat almost anything, and the disorder is the persistent eating of things that are not food. DSM-5-TR's criteria, in plain language, are four: A. Persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances for at least 1 month. The month separates a persistent pattern from a single episode, a dare or a passing experiment. B. The eating is inappropriate to the person's developmental level. Infants explore the world with their mouths and swallow some of what they mouth; that is normal. DSM-5-TR therefore suggests a minimum age of 2 years for the diagnosis. ICD-11 gives the reason in so many words: about 2 years is the developmental age at which a child is expected to tell edible from inedible things. C. The eating is not part of a culturally supported or socially normative practice. In some communities eating earth or clay is believed to have spiritual, medicinal or social value; when it does, it is not a disorder. D. If it occurs in the context of another mental disorder (intellectual developmental disorder, autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia) or a medical condition (including pregnancy), it is severe enough to warrant additional clinical attention. This is the shared rule of Section 8.2.1. Two words in Criterion A carry weight. "Non-nutritive" means the substance supplies little or no nourishment. "Non-food" was added in DSM-5 because some diet products, such as diet soft drinks and very low-calorie foods, are almost free of nutrients but are still foods, and eating them is not pica. Notice also what pica usually does not involve: there is typically no aversion to ordinary food. Poonam still eats her meals; she eats mud as well. ICD-11 draws the boundary slightly differently. Its pica includes non-food objects and materials (clay, soil, chalk, plaster, plastic, metal, paper) and also raw food ingredients eaten in large quantities, such as salt or corn flour, so a person who eats spoonfuls of raw flour can be given an ICD-11 diagnosis of pica but would not meet DSM-5-TR's "non-food" rule. What do people with pica eat? DSM-5-TR's list is a tour of the house and the yard: paper, soap, cloth, hair, string, wool, soil, chalk, talcum powder, paint, gum, metal, pebbles, charcoal or coal, ash, clay, starch and ice. The substances vary with age and with what is within reach. Several have their own names, all built on the Greek phagein , to eat: geophagia (from ge , earth) is eating earth, soil or clay, Poonam's form; pagophagia (from pagos , frost) is the compulsive eating of ice, the form most tightly linked with iron deficiency; amylophagia (from amylon , starch) is eating laundry starch or raw starch; trichophagia (from thrix , hair) is eating hair; lithophagia (from lithos , stone) is eating stones or pebbles; and coprophagia (from kopros , dung) is eating faeces. Swallowed hair cannot be digested, and over months it can collect in the stomach into a matted mass called a trichobezoar (a bezoar is any mass of undigested material trapped in the gut). A very large trichobezoar with a tail that extends from the stomach into the small intestine is called Rapunzel syndrome, after the fairy-tale girl with the long hair. That brings us to why pica matters. Often the first anyone hears of it is a medical emergency. DSM-5-TR lists the complications: mechanical bowel problems; intestinal obstruction , for example from a bezoar; intestinal perforation ; infections such as toxoplasmosis and toxocariasis (parasitic infections caught from soil or faeces contaminated by cats and dogs); and poisoning , above all lead poisoning in children who eat flakes of old lead-based paint. Plain abdominal X-rays, ultrasound and other scans can show an obstruction, and blood tests can measure lead or reveal an infection. Deficiencies of iron and zinc have often been reported in pica, but in many patients no specific biological abnormality is found. Depending on what is eaten, the course can be long and the disorder can be fatal. Clinical link: which came first, the craving or the deficiency? Pica and iron deficiency travel together so often that every patient with pica should have a blood count and an iron study. The direction of cause is still argued. On one view, iron deficiency produces the craving, perhaps through low iron in the brain; supporting it, ice craving in particular often stops soon after iron treatment begins. On the other view, pica produces the deficiency: clay and starch displace iron-rich food from the diet and may bind iron in the gut so that less is absorbed. Both may be true in different people, and some patients with pica have normal iron. The practical lesson does not depend on who is right: look for the deficiency, treat it, and see whether the craving goes. How common is pica? Good data are scarce. DSM-5-TR estimates that about 5 percent of school-age children show it. In pregnancy it is far commoner: roughly one-third of pregnant women engage in pica, especially women living with food insecurity (without reliable access to affordable, nutritious food), and a worldwide meta-analysis put the rate at 28 percent during pregnancy or the postpartum period . Pregnancy brings specific cravings, for chalk or ice for example, and here DSM-5-TR adds an important rule: the diagnosis is appropriate in pregnancy only when the cravings lead to eating non-food substances to an extent that poses medical risks. A pregnant woman who sucks an ice cube every evening does not have a mental disorder; Poonam, who is anaemic and constipated from daily clay eating, may. Lack of available food and vitamin deficiency are also associated with pica, which links it with poverty. Indian context Eating mud, chalk, slate pencils, ash or pieces of baked clay is familiar to Indian obstetricians and paediatricians, and it is often hidden out of embarrassment, so it is found only if someone asks. The question matters because anaemia is so common: in the fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019 to 2021), 52.2 percent of pregnant women aged 15 to 49 were anaemic (haemoglobin below 11.0 grams per decilitre). An antenatal history that includes "Do you eat anything that is not food, such as mud, chalk or ice?" costs nothing and can uncover both pica and the deficiency that may lie behind it. Pica can begin in childhood, adolescence or adulthood, but onset in childhood is most often reported. It occurs in otherwise normally developing children, whereas in adults it is more likely to appear in the context of intellectual developmental disorder or another mental disorder. The environmental risk factors DSM-5-TR names are neglect, lack of supervision and developmental delay : a toddler left alone for hours in a room with peeling paint is at risk in a way that a closely watched toddler is not. Pica occurs in both sexes. It can badly damage physical health, but it is rarely the sole cause of social impairment; when a person with pica is socially impaired, another disorder (autism, intellectual disability, schizophrenia) is usually responsible. Now return to Criterion C, because Poonam's case turns on it. DSM-5-TR warns in both directions. If earth eating is a culturally supported practice, such as clay taken as a remedy or as part of a religious observance with the approval of the community, it is not pica. But a behaviour that is common in a community is not therefore sanctioned by it, and DSM-5-TR says pica "should not be assumed to be socially normative without further evaluation". Poonam eats in secret, is scolded for it by her own family, and eats far more than anyone around her thinks proper; she has a craving, not a custom. Add the medical risk, and she meets the criteria for pica in pregnancy. Telling pica apart from its look-alikes depends on asking why the substance is eaten. Non-food eating occurs within other disorders, including autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia (where an object may be eaten because of a delusion) and Kleine-Levin syndrome, a rare disorder of recurrent excessive sleep with episodes of abnormal eating (Section 8.8.8); in each case pica is added only if the eating needs attention of its own. In anorexia nervosa some patients eat tissue paper to fill the stomach and blunt hunger; when non-food eating is mainly a means of weight control, anorexia nervosa is the diagnosis. In factitious disorder a person may deliberately swallow foreign objects to produce illness and gain the sick role (Book 3 Section 7.9); the element of deception distinguishes it. And some people swallow dangerous items such as pins, needles or knives as a form of non-suicidal self-injury or within a personality disorder (Chapter 11), where the act expresses distress rather than a craving. The disorders that most often accompany pica are autism spectrum disorder and intellectual developmental disorder, followed at a distance by schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Pica can also accompany trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) and excoriation (skin-picking) disorder, in which the pulled hair or picked skin is swallowed (Book 3 Section 6.6), and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, especially when that disorder has a strong sensory component. Whenever pica is known, the assessment should consider gastrointestinal complications, poisoning, infection and nutritional deficiency. Treatment therefore begins with the body. The physician checks haemoglobin, iron stores and zinc and corrects any deficiency; measures blood lead in a child who may have eaten paint, and removes the source; treats parasitic infection; and, if there is pain, vomiting or constipation, looks for an obstruction with an X-ray or ultrasound. A bezoar may need endoscopic or surgical removal. Then comes the behaviour. In children of normal development, supervision, safe surroundings and treatment of any deficiency are often enough. In intellectual disability and autism, where pica can be dangerous and persistent, behavioural programmes have the best support: enriching the environment so there are other things to do with the hands and mouth, blocking and interrupting attempts to eat non-food items, teaching the difference between edible and inedible things, and reinforcing alternative behaviour. Those methods are taught in Book 2, Sections 4.5 and 4.6. Poonam's treatment was simpler: iron tablets, advice on diet, a frank talk with her and her mother-in-law, and a follow-up visit at which she reported that the craving had faded. Exam trap Pica needs 1 month , not 3 months (3 months belongs to bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder). The suggested minimum age is 2 years , because mouthing objects is normal in infancy. Culturally sanctioned clay or earth eating is not pica, and in pregnancy pica is diagnosed only when the eating poses a medical risk. Pica can be fatal through obstruction or poisoning, but it is not "the most lethal eating disorder": that is anorexia nervosa (Section 8.3.7), so pica is a distractor in any question about mortality. Rumination disorder Kriti is 15 and in Class 10 in Pune. For about eight months, a few minutes after almost every meal, food has come back up into her mouth. It is not vomiting: there is no nausea, no heaving, no rush to the bathroom. The food simply rises, easily, and it tastes of what she has just eaten rather than of sour acid. At home she chews it again and swallows it. At school she spits it into a tissue behind her hand and pretends to cough, and she has stopped eating her tiffin there and skips breakfast on examination days so that nothing will come up in the hall. She has lost weight. Her gastroenterologist has found no disease of her stomach or oesophagus. "I do not decide to do it," she says. "It just happens, like a habit." Kriti has rumination disorder . The name comes from the Latin ruminare , to chew the cud: cows, buffaloes, sheep and goats are ruminants, animals that bring partly digested food back up from the stomach to chew it a second time. An older medical name for the human behaviour is merycism. DSM-5-TR's criteria are four: A. Repeated regurgitation of food over a period of at least 1 month. The regurgitated food may be re-chewed, re-swallowed or spat out. B. The regurgitation is not attributable to a gastrointestinal or other medical condition , such as gastro-oesophageal reflux or pyloric stenosis. C. It does not occur exclusively during anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder or avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder. D. If it occurs in the context of another mental disorder, such as intellectual developmental disorder or another neurodevelopmental disorder, it is severe enough to warrant additional clinical attention. The key word is regurgitation , the effortless return of swallowed food to the mouth, and it must be kept distinct from vomiting. Vomiting is a forceful reflex, usually preceded by nausea and accompanied by retching, that empties the stomach; it is unpleasant, and people try to avoid it. In rumination disorder, DSM-5-TR says, previously swallowed and perhaps partly digested food is brought up "without apparent nausea, involuntary retching, or disgust". Gastroenterologists, who call the adult form rumination syndrome, have shown how it happens: shortly after a meal the muscles of the abdominal wall contract, without the person being aware of it, squeezing the stomach so that its contents are pushed back up the oesophagus. The contraction is learned, not a disease of the gut, which is why the treatment that works best is behavioural. The behaviour must also be frequent: at least several times a week and typically every day. Many people with the disorder can be watched doing it during a consultation; in others the diagnosis rests on self-report or on reports from parents or carers. Adults and adolescents often describe it as habitual or outside their control, as Kriti does. Criterion B is there because the commonest cause of food coming back up is not psychological at all. In gastro-oesophageal reflux stomach acid and food leak back through a weak valve at the lower end of the oesophagus; in pyloric stenosis , a condition of young infants, the muscle at the outlet of the stomach thickens and causes forceful, projectile vomiting; in gastroparesis the stomach empties too slowly; in a hiatal hernia part of the stomach slides up through the diaphragm. In infants there is also Sandifer syndrome, in which reflux is accompanied by odd arching and twisting movements of the neck and back that can look very like the posture of an infant who ruminates. DSM-5-TR says these conditions can usually be ruled out by the history and by observation, though a gastroenterologist may need to run tests. Criterion C exists because people with anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa sometimes regurgitate and spit out food as a way of getting rid of calories; when that happens only within those disorders, the motive is weight control and the diagnosis is the eating disorder, not rumination. The picture in infants is distinctive. DSM-5-TR describes a characteristic position: the baby strains and arches the back with the head held back and makes sucking movements with the tongue, and seems to get satisfaction from the activity. Between episodes the infant may be irritable and hungry. Weight loss and failure to make the expected weight gains are common, and malnutrition can develop even though the infant seems hungry and takes large feeds, particularly when every feed is followed at once by regurgitation and the food is lost. Older children, adolescents and adults become malnourished mainly when they also restrict what they eat, and many do restrict, because the behaviour is socially unacceptable and they know it. They hide it by putting a hand over the mouth or coughing, avoid eating with others, and may skip meals before school or work, as Kriti skips breakfast before examinations. Rumination disorder was described first in people with intellectual disability, and it is still commonest there, but limited European data suggest that it may affect about 1 to 2 percent of grade-school children . It can begin at any age. In infants onset is usually between 3 and 12 months . In infants it often remits on its own, but its course can be long and it can cause medical emergencies such as severe malnutrition; it is potentially fatal, particularly in infancy. In older people it may be episodic or may continue until treated. DSM-5-TR notes something about its function: in infants, and in older people with intellectual developmental disorder or other neurodevelopmental disorders, regurgitation and rumination seem to be self-soothing or self-stimulating , in the same way as other repetitive behaviours such as head banging. That observation fits the environmental risk factors DSM-5-TR lists for infants and young children: lack of stimulation, neglect, stressful life situations and problems in the parent-child relationship . An infant left alone in a cot for long periods with little to look at or respond to may find in rumination the stimulation that the environment does not provide. The functional consequences follow from the malnutrition and the secrecy. In children, repeated loss of food can delay growth and harm development and learning. In older children, adolescents and adults, social life suffers most: meals are avoided, invitations refused, friendships narrowed. Rumination can accompany a medical condition or another mental disorder, such as generalised anxiety disorder; then, as in pica, the separate diagnosis is made only when the regurgitation is more severe than the other condition would explain and needs its own attention. ICD-11 calls the condition rumination-regurgitation disorder (6B85) and describes it a little differently. It speaks of the intentional and repeated bringing up of swallowed food, which may be re-chewed and re-swallowed or deliberately spat out "but not as in vomiting"; it requires the behaviour at least several times a week over at least several weeks; and it allows the diagnosis only in people who have reached a developmental age of at least 2 years. DSM-5-TR sets no minimum age, which is why an infant of 4 months can receive a DSM-5-TR diagnosis but not an ICD-11 one. In ICD-10, rumination was not a separate disorder at all: "rumination disorder of infancy" was included under F98.2, feeding disorder of infancy and childhood. Treatment starts by excluding gut disease. For older children, adolescents and adults, the treatment with the best support is behavioural. The person is taught diaphragmatic breathing , slow breathing from the diaphragm with the belly rising and the chest still, and practises it during and after meals. Breathing this way relaxes the abdominal wall, so it is physically incompatible with the abdominal contraction that pushes food up: a competing response , the same principle as in habit reversal for tics and nail biting (Book 2, Section 4.9.1). A systematic review of adult rumination syndrome published in 2019, which found 12 studies with 254 patients between them, concluded that diaphragmatic breathing had the strongest evidence and that baclofen, a drug that reduces the relaxations of the valve between oesophagus and stomach, had some, while judging the quality of all the evidence to be weak. In infants, treatment concentrates on nutrition and on the feeding relationship: helping the caregiver feed the baby calmly and responsively, holding and engaging the infant during and after feeds, and providing the stimulation that may have been missing. Kriti learned diaphragmatic breathing with a psychologist, practised it after every meal, and within a few weeks was eating her tiffin at school again. Exam trap Rumination disorder is the repeated regurgitation of food , which is re-chewed, re-swallowed or spat out, without nausea. It has nothing to do with rumination in the sense of repetitive brooding thought, the "chewing over" of worries or of one's sadness that maintains depression and anxiety (Book 3 Sections 5.6 and 6.5.8). Like pica, it needs only 1 month . If the regurgitation has a medical cause (reflux, pyloric stenosis) or occurs only within anorexia or bulimia as a way of disposing of calories, it is not rumination disorder. DSM-5-TR sets no minimum age; ICD-11 requires a developmental age of 2 years. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder Pranav is 10. Two years ago, at a family wedding, a piece of apple stuck in his throat; he could not breathe for a few terrifying seconds until an uncle thumped his back. Since then he has eaten only plain rice, curd and one brand of glucose biscuits. Rotis, dal with whole grains, fruit, anything with lumps or skin, he pushes away; if his mother insists, he gags. He is hungry, and he watches his younger sister eat with something like envy. "What if it gets stuck again?" he asks. His paediatrician's chart shows that he has fallen from the middle of his growth curve to well below it, and he has stopped going to birthday parties, because there will be food there that he cannot eat and children who will ask why. Pranav does not want to be thin. He wants to be big enough to bowl fast for his school team. Pranav has avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), the newest of the feeding disorders. DSM-5 (2013) created it to replace and extend DSM-IV's feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood, which had required onset before the age of 6, so that the diagnosis now reaches older children, adolescents and adults. The two adjectives in the name describe two patterns that often occur together: avoidant , refusing particular foods or kinds of food, and restrictive , eating too little overall. What makes it a disorder rather than a preference is what the eating does to the person. DSM-5-TR's criteria: A. An eating or feeding disturbance , for example an apparent lack of interest in eating or food, avoidance based on the sensory characteristics of food, or concern about aversive consequences of eating, associated with one or more of four consequences : significant weight loss, or, in children, failure to achieve the expected weight gain or faltering growth; significant nutritional deficiency; dependence on enteral feeding or oral nutritional supplements; marked interference with psychosocial functioning. B. The disturbance is not better explained by lack of available food or by an associated culturally sanctioned practice. C. It does not occur exclusively during anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, and there is no evidence of a disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced. D. It is not attributable to a concurrent medical condition and not better explained by another mental disorder ; if it occurs alongside one, its severity exceeds what that condition usually produces and warrants additional clinical attention. Look first at the four consequences in Criterion A, because they are what keep ordinary fussy eaters out of the diagnosis. Almost every child refuses some foods; almost every adult has foods he will not touch. The criteria do not ask whether someone is choosy but whether the choosiness has done harm, and they name four kinds of harm. Weight loss or faltering growth is a clinical judgement; a child who has not finished growing may not lose weight at all but may simply stop climbing along his expected curve, as Pranav has. Nutritional deficiency is established by asking what the person eats, examining him and doing blood tests, and it can be as serious as in anorexia nervosa: DSM-5-TR mentions hypothermia, bradycardia (a slow heart rate) and anaemia, and notes that in infants the malnutrition can threaten life. Dependence on enteral feeding or supplements means that the person cannot sustain an adequate intake without help. Enteral feeding is feeding directly into the gut through a tube, either a nasogastric tube passed through the nose into the stomach or a gastrostomy tube placed through the wall of the abdomen; DSM-5-TR's examples are an infant with failure to thrive who needs a nasogastric tube, a child with a neurodevelopmental disorder who lives on nutritionally complete supplement drinks, and a person who relies on tube feeding or complete oral supplements with no medical condition to explain it. Marked psychosocial interference means being unable to eat with others, attend school or work, or sustain relationships because of the eating problem, and DSM-5-TR adds that substantial disruption of family life can meet this criterion on its own: a home in which only a handful of foods may be cooked, or parents who drive across the city to one shop or one restaurant because their child will eat nothing else. Pranav meets two of the four: faltering growth and marked interference with social life. Criterion B removes two things that look like restriction but are not disorders. One is not having enough to eat: food insecurity and poverty explain a thin child far more often than any psychiatric diagnosis. The other is a culturally sanctioned practice. Religious fasting, such as a Navratri fast or the Ramadan fast from dawn to sunset, a family's lifelong vegetarianism, the Jain avoidance of root vegetables, and normal dieting are all excluded. Criterion C is the heart of the diagnosis. It says that ARFID is never diagnosed during anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, and that there must be no evidence of a disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced. A person who restricts because she feels fat, or because gaining weight would be a failure, does not have ARFID however strong her sensory dislikes. Criterion D, finally, applies the shared rule of Section 8.2.1 to medical and mental conditions, and it is discussed below with the differential diagnosis. DSM-5-TR describes three presentations, which are examples rather than formal subtypes, and many patients show more than one. The first is avoidance based on the sensory characteristics of food : extreme sensitivity to its appearance, colour, smell, texture, temperature or taste. Before DSM-5 this was described as restrictive eating, selective eating, choosy eating, perseverant eating, chronic food refusal and food neophobia (fear of new foods). Such a person may refuse every brand of a food but one, or be unable to bear the smell of food that others are eating; people with autism and its heightened sensory sensitivities often show the same behaviour. The second is concern about aversive consequences of eating : a conditioned negative response to food after, or in anticipation of, an aversive experience such as choking, a traumatic procedure involving the gut (DSM-5-TR's example is oesophagoscopy, a tube passed down the oesophagus) or repeated vomiting. This is classical conditioning at the dinner table (Book 1, Section 6.2): a frightening event becomes linked with the food or the act of swallowing, and eating itself comes to provoke fear. Older terms for this form are functional dysphagia (difficulty swallowing with no structural cause) and globus hystericus (the sensation of a lump in the throat). Pranav's is this form. The third is an apparent lack of interest in eating or food : the child who is never hungry, forgets to eat, or finds meals a boring interruption of play. Figure 8.4 shows how the three routes and the four consequences fit together. Three routes (examples) Criterion A: one or more Sensory sensitivity texture, smell, colour Lack of interest little appetite or drive Fear of consequences choking, vomiting, pain Avoids or restricts food intake 1 Weight loss or faltering growth 2 Nutritional deficiency 3 Tube feeding or supplements needed 4 Marked impairment of daily or family life Absent in ARFID: fear of fatness and any disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced (Criterion C) Also excluded (Criteria B and D): lack of food, cultural fasting, a medical cause Figure 8.4 How avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder is built. Any of three routes, often more than one, leads to avoidance or restriction; the diagnosis needs at least one of four consequences, and it requires the absence of the fear of fatness and body-image disturbance that define anorexia nervosa. The associated features change with age. Very young infants may refuse food, gag or vomit; infants and toddlers may not engage with the caregiver during feeding, or may not signal hunger, preferring other activities. In older children and adolescents food avoidance may come with more general emotional difficulties that do not meet the criteria for an anxiety, depressive or bipolar disorder, a pattern sometimes called food avoidance emotional disorder . In infants the feeding relationship matters a great deal. An infant with ARFID may be irritable and hard to console during feeds, or apathetic and withdrawn; a caregiver may present food in ways the infant cannot manage, or read the infant's refusal as aggression or rejection, and poor nutrition then makes the infant more irritable and the feeding harder still. If feeding and weight improve when someone else feeds the child, DSM-5-TR says, parental psychopathology, abuse or neglect should be suspected. How common is ARFID? Little is known. One Australian study found a frequency of 0.3 percent among people aged 15 or older . It is commoner in children and adolescents than in adults, and there may be a long delay between onset and the first consultation. Lack of interest in food usually begins in infancy or early childhood, and sensory avoidance in the first decade of life; both may persist into adulthood. Avoidance based on aversive consequences can begin at any age, often abruptly after a frightening event, as Pranav's did. The little long-term evidence suggests that sensory-based restriction is relatively stable, but that adults who still have it may function fairly normally. There is no good evidence that ARFID leads on to a later eating disorder , although in some people it precedes anorexia nervosa. Unlike anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, ARFID seems to be about equally common in boys and girls; when it occurs with autism spectrum disorder, boys predominate. Pregnancy can bring altered sensory sensitivities and food aversions, but these are not usually extreme enough to meet the criteria. DSM-5-TR groups the risk factors in its usual three headings. Temperamental : anxiety disorders, autism spectrum disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder all raise the risk. Environmental : anxiety in the family, and higher rates of feeding problems in the children of mothers with eating disorders. Genetic and physiological : a history of gastrointestinal conditions, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, vomiting and other medical problems. Similar presentations have been described in the United States, Canada, Australia, Europe, Japan and China. The disorders that most often accompany it are anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder and the neurodevelopmental disorders, specifically autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and intellectual developmental disorder. Restriction of food is a symptom of many conditions, so the differential diagnosis is long. DSM-5-TR's rule throughout is that ARFID can be diagnosed alongside another condition if all its criteria are met and the eating problem needs specific attention. Take the conditions in turn. Developmentally normal picky eating. Many toddlers and young children narrow the range of foods they will eat for a while; it usually resolves without treatment and causes none of the four consequences. It is not ARFID unless it becomes severe enough to cause nutritional failure or significant impairment. Anorexia nervosa. Both involve restriction and both can produce low weight. Anorexia nervosa adds the fear of gaining weight (or persistent behaviour that prevents gain) and a disturbed experience of weight and shape, which ARFID lacks, and the two are never diagnosed together. The line can be hard to draw in late childhood and early adolescence, and especially in a patient who denies any fear of fatness yet keeps doing things that prevent weight gain and does not see how dangerous her low weight is, a presentation sometimes called non-fat-phobic anorexia nervosa . DSM-5-TR advises looking at symptoms, course and family history and making the diagnosis over time. Specific phobia and other anxiety disorders. Specific phobia, other type, includes "situations that may lead to choking or vomiting" (Book 3 Section 6.3). When a fear of choking or vomiting has led to food avoidance and the eating problem becomes the main focus of clinical attention, ARFID is the better diagnosis. In social anxiety disorder a person may fear being watched while eating, which can also occur in ARFID. Autism spectrum disorder. Rigid eating and sensory sensitivity are common in autism but often do not cause the impairment ARFID requires; ARFID is added only when it does and needs treatment of its own. Obsessive-compulsive disorder. Restriction may follow preoccupations with food or ritualised eating; ARFID is added only when the eating is a major focus of treatment. Major depressive disorder. Appetite can fall so far that intake drops and weight is lost, but the restriction is of overall intake and it usually lifts as the mood recovers. Schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Odd eating, or avoidance of foods believed to be poisoned or contaminated, may follow from delusions. Paediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS). An abrupt, dramatic onset of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or severely restricted eating, with other neuropsychiatric symptoms, should raise this possibility (Book 3 Section 6.7). Acute onset, late onset or atypical symptoms are the warning signs. Reactive attachment disorder. A child's withdrawal from caregivers can disturb feeding (Book 3 Section 7.4); ARFID is added only if all its criteria are met and feeding is a primary focus. Factitious disorder, and factitious disorder imposed on another. Some people describe diets far more restrictive than the ones they actually eat in order to occupy the sick role, and some caregivers describe ARFID symptoms in a child, or induce failure to gain weight, in which case the caregiver receives the diagnosis (Book 3 Section 7.9). Medical conditions. Gastrointestinal disease, food allergies and intolerances, occult (hidden) cancers and many other illnesses reduce intake through vomiting, nausea, pain, diarrhoea or loss of appetite. ARFID requires that the disturbance go beyond what the physical symptoms explain; it may persist after a medical illness that triggered it has resolved. Because older people, patients after surgery and patients on chemotherapy often lose their appetite, ARFID is added for them only when the eating disturbance is itself a primary focus. Congenital and neurological conditions that impair chewing and swallowing can coexist with ARFID if all criteria are met. Table 8.5 condenses the four comparisons that matter most in practice. Feature ARFID Anorexia nervosa Picky eating Phobia of choking Why food is avoided Sensory dislike, no interest, or fear of a bad consequence To lose weight or avoid gaining it Preference, a passing phase Fear of choking or vomiting Fear of fatness, body-image disturbance Absent (Criterion C) Present, or behaviour that prevents gain Absent Absent Weight and nutrition May be very low; deficiency; supplements Significantly low weight Normal growth Usually normal unless avoidance widens Impairment One of four consequences required Marked, medical and social None of note Distress in the feared situation Usual onset Infancy or childhood; any age Adolescence or young adulthood Toddlers and young children Any age, often after an episode Diagnosis ARFID Anorexia nervosa; never also ARFID No disorder Specific phobia; ARFID if eating is the main focus Treatment begins, as with every disorder of this chapter that starves the body, with nutrition. The physician assesses weight and growth, checks for deficiencies, and restores intake, with nutritional supplements when the person can drink but not eat enough, and with tube feeding when oral intake cannot sustain life or growth. The psychological treatment designed specifically for the disorder is cognitive-behavioural therapy for ARFID (CBT-AR), developed by the American psychologists Jennifer J. Thomas and Kamryn T. Eddy and published as a manual in 2019. It is a modular, exposure-based treatment in four stages, built around the three routes of Figure 8.4: graded exposure to new tastes and textures for the sensory form, work on hunger cues and regular eating for the lack-of-interest form, and graded exposure to the feared food or the feared act of swallowing for the aversive form. It is intended for people aged 10 and older. The first evidence came from open trials, without a control group, which found it acceptable and promising; randomised controlled trials that include it have only recently begun to report, so its evidence base is still best described as preliminary. With younger children, therapists work through the parents, using family-based approaches adapted from the treatment of adolescent anorexia (Book 2, Section 10.4.7). No drug is approved for ARFID, and none has been shown in good trials to treat it; anxiety that accompanies it is treated in its own right. Pranav's treatment combined a dietitian's plan and supplement drinks to restart his growth with weekly sessions in which, mouthful by graded mouthful, he went from mashed banana to soft roti; a year later he was back on his growth curve and back at birthday parties. Exam trap ARFID is restriction without body-image concern or fear of fatness. A child who eats only a few foods and is falling off his growth curve has ARFID, not anorexia nervosa; a girl who restricts because she feels fat has anorexia nervosa, however strong her dislike of certain textures. ARFID replaced DSM-IV's feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood and can be diagnosed at any age . Selective eating without weight loss or any other of the four consequences is ordinary picky eating, not a disorder. And because ARFID involves too little eating, it is never the answer to a question about a patient who binges : in a stem describing recurrent binges with distress and no compensatory behaviour, the ARFID option is a distractor (the answer is binge-eating disorder, Section 8.4.5). 8.3 Anorexia Nervosa: Criteria, the Starving Body and the Course High yield · 7 Qs Of all the disorders in this chapter, anorexia nervosa is the one most likely to end a young life. It is also one of the most puzzling disorders in psychiatry. A person who is starving is normally consumed by hunger and will eat almost anything; the men of Minnesota in this chapter's opening talked and daydreamed about food. A person with anorexia nervosa is starving too, often far more severely, and yet she turns food away, counts every mouthful, and feels triumph rather than alarm as the scale goes down. This section describes the disorder as the clinician meets it: the three DSM-5-TR criteria and the reasoning behind each one, how the criteria have changed since DSM-IV and how ICD-10 and ICD-11 differ, the subtypes and the BMI severity ratings, what starvation does to every organ of the body and to the mind, who develops the disorder, how it runs and why it kills, and how it is told apart from the many other causes of weight loss. Why anorexia nervosa develops, and how it is treated, are the subject of Section 8.5. What anorexia nervosa is Anorexia nervosa is a disorder in which a person restricts the energy she takes in, relative to what her body needs, until her weight is significantly low for her age, sex, stage of development and physical health; she has an intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, or persistently behaves in ways that prevent weight gain, even though she is already underweight; and the way she experiences her body weight or shape is disturbed. The disorder was named twice in 1873, by Sir William Gull in London as anorexia nervosa and by Ernest-Charles Lasègue in Paris as anorexie hystérique (Section 8.1.4 tells the story). The name is a poor one. Anorexia , from the Greek an- (without) and orexis (appetite), means loss of appetite, and Barlow and Durand point out that this is an incorrect description because appetite often remains healthy. Most patients are hungry, at least some of the time; they control their hunger. The engine of the disorder is not a missing appetite but a fear of fatness and a relentless pursuit of thinness. Throughout this section the patient is called "she", because most patients are female, but the disorder occurs in boys and men too (Section 8.3.7). Malini is 16, in Class 11 at a school in Jaipur, and preparing for the medical entrance examination. She has always been top of her class. After a relative remarked on her weight, she began "eating healthy". Now she eats half a roti and some salad at dinner and little else, and she runs on the terrace at dawn before anyone else is awake. She wears loose kurtas, even in the heat. Several times a day she stands sideways in front of the mirror and checks her stomach. She weighs 39 kg and is 1.58 m tall, and she has not had a menstrual period for five months. Her parents have brought her to the clinic; she has come only because they insisted. "I am fine," she tells the psychologist calmly. "I just need to lose a little from my thighs." Every element of the definition is visible in those few lines. The restriction is there (half a roti and salad), and so are its methods (dieting and dawn exercise). The weight is significantly low, as Section 8.3.2 will show by calculation. The fear of fatness is not stated, but it is implied by everything she does, including the loose clothes and the mirror checks. And the disturbance in her experience of her body is in her own words: an emaciated girl who sees thighs that need to be smaller. Notice also two things that are typical. She did not come on her own, and she does not think she is ill. Remember Malini; she will be the worked example through the rest of this section. Exam trap Anorexia nervosa is primarily fear of gaining weight together with restriction of food intake , leading to a significantly low weight. The distractors each belong elsewhere. "Obsession with cleanliness" is the contamination theme of obsessive-compulsive disorder (Book 3 Section 6.5). "Repeated vomiting after bingeing" describes bulimia nervosa (Section 8.4), although vomiting can also occur in the binge-eating/purging type of anorexia. "Excessive exercise only" is one method of losing weight that many patients use; it is not the disorder. The three criteria, one by one DSM-5-TR says that anorexia nervosa has three essential features: persistent restriction of energy intake; intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behaviour that interferes with weight gain; and a disturbance in self-perceived weight or shape. Each is a criterion, and each is worded with care. Criterion A: restriction leading to a significantly low body weight. The criterion requires "restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to a significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health". Significantly low means "less than minimally normal" in adults and, in children and adolescents, "less than that minimally expected". Two features of the wording matter. First, the weight is low because of restriction; weight loss from cancer or tuberculosis does not count. Second, in a young person who is still growing, there may be no weight loss at all. A girl who stays at the same weight for two years while growing taller is getting thinner relative to what she should weigh, so failure to make the expected weight gain, or to keep to her developmental trajectory, meets the criterion. How does a clinician decide that a weight is significantly low? DSM-5-TR deliberately gives no single number, because normal weight differs between people, but it explains how to use the body mass index (BMI), which is weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres. The index was devised by the Belgian mathematician and statistician Adolphe Quetelet (1796 to 1874), which is why ICD-10 calls it "Quetelet's body-mass index"; the name "body mass index" was given to it in 1972 by Ancel Keys, the same physiologist who ran the Minnesota experiment. For adults, DSM-5-TR offers a set of guideposts: A BMI of 18.5 is the lower limit of normal weight used by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the WHO, so most adults at or above 18.5 would not be considered significantly underweight. A BMI below 17.0 indicates moderate or severe thinness by WHO's categories, so an adult below 17.0 is likely to be significantly underweight. An adult with a BMI between 17.0 and 18.5, or even slightly above 18.5 , may be judged significantly underweight if the clinical history or other physiological information supports it (a woman who has fallen from a BMI of 24 to 18.7 in four months, with a slow pulse and no periods, is an example). Adults with a BMI of 19.0 or more are not underweight by population standards and should not be diagnosed with anorexia nervosa; if everything else fits, the diagnosis to consider is other specified feeding or eating disorder, atypical anorexia nervosa (Section 8.4.7). For children and adolescents the clinician uses BMI-for-age percentiles , which compare a young person's BMI with those of others of the same age and sex. The CDC has used a BMI-for-age below the 5th percentile as suggesting underweight. A young person above that line may still be significantly underweight if she has failed to follow her expected growth trajectory, but one whose BMI is above the median (the 50th percentile) for her age should not be diagnosed with anorexia nervosa. Now apply this to Malini. Her BMI is 39 divided by 1.58 squared: 1.58 times 1.58 is 2.4964, and 39 divided by 2.4964 is about 15.6 . At 16 she is still an adolescent, so DSM-5-TR judges her by BMI-for-age percentiles, not by the adult signposts, and a BMI of 15.6 is well below the 5th percentile for a girl of her age. (ICD-10's guidelines allow the adult BMI from the age of 16, and on the adult scale 15.6 is also very low.) Criterion A is clearly met. Criterion B: fear of gaining weight, or behaviour that prevents gain. The criterion reads "intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, even though at a significantly low weight". The fear has a strange property: it is not relieved by losing weight. DSM-5-TR notes that the concern about gaining weight may actually increase as weight falls. Barlow and Durand describe the same thing from the patient's side: people with anorexia are never satisfied with their weight loss, staying the same weight from one day to the next causes panic, and only continued loss is acceptable. The second half of the criterion, "or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain", was added in DSM-5, and the reason is practical. Younger patients and some adults do not recognise or will not admit any fear of weight gain. Rather than leave them undiagnosed, DSM-5-TR allows the clinician to infer Criterion B from collateral history (what the family reports), from observation (food hidden in a napkin, exercise in secret), from physical and laboratory findings, or from the course of the illness (every gain followed by renewed restriction), as long as there is no other explanation for the low weight. The clause also helps with patients who explain their restriction by something other than fear of fatness, such as a feeling of fullness or stomach discomfort, a pattern DSM-5-TR describes as relatively more common in Asian populations (Section 8.5.1). Malini denies being afraid of anything; but her dawn running, her shrinking portions and her distress whenever her mother adds ghee to her dal tell the clinician what she does not say. Criterion C: a disturbed experience of weight and shape. This criterion has three alternatives, and any one is enough: a disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced; undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation; or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight. The first alternative takes two forms. Some patients feel fat all over. Others accept that they are thin but are still convinced that certain parts, particularly the abdomen, buttocks and thighs, are "too fat", which is Malini's form. To keep watch on those parts, patients weigh themselves often, measure their thighs or waist obsessively, and check the "fat" areas in the mirror, behaviours known as body checking . The second alternative concerns self-esteem: for these patients, weight and shape are not one part of self-worth but nearly all of it, so weight loss is experienced as an impressive achievement and a sign of extraordinary self-discipline, and weight gain as an unacceptable failure of self-control. The third alternative is about the danger: some patients can acknowledge that they are thin but do not grasp that a slow pulse, a falling blood pressure and missing periods mean their life is at risk. Three questions about Criterion C are taught in Chapter 2 of this book and need only a pointer here. Whether the body-image disturbance is a misperception of size or a matter of attitude and evaluation (the body-width estimation studies of Peter Slade and Gerald Russell in 1973, and the meta-analysis by Thomas F. Cash and E. A. Deagle in 1997 of 66 studies of perceptual and attitudinal body image) is discussed in Book 3 Section 2.10.3. The conviction of being too fat as an overvalued idea , a belief held with great emotional investment but short of a delusion, is in Section 2.5.6. And poor insight in anorexia nervosa, with the need to rely on informants, is in Section 2.10.4. A related idea from Section 2.1 is useful here: the disorder is largely ego-syntonic , felt by the patient as part of herself and in harmony with her goals. Barlow and Durand put the contrast with bulimia memorably: people with anorexia are proud of their diets and of their extraordinary control, whereas people with bulimia are ashamed of their eating and of their lack of control. That ego-syntonic quality explains how patients come to clinical attention. DSM-5-TR observes that it is rare for a person with anorexia nervosa to complain of weight loss as such. She is usually brought by her family after marked weight loss or failure to gain. When patients do seek help themselves, it is usually because of distress about the physical and psychological effects of starvation (feeling cold all the time, being unable to concentrate, sleeping badly), not about being thin. Many lack insight into the problem or deny it, so the clinician must gather the history of weight loss and the other features from family members or other sources. Malini meets all three criteria: A by her weight, B by inference from her behaviour, and C in at least two of its forms, her "fat" thighs and her calm failure to see any danger. Exam trap DSM-5-TR requires all three : (A) significantly low weight from restriction, (B) intense fear of weight gain or persistent behaviour that interferes with gain, and (C) a disturbed experience of weight or shape, undue influence of weight or shape on self-worth, or failure to recognise the seriousness of the low weight. It does not require a BMI below 17 "in all cases": DSM-5-TR sets no diagnostic BMI cut-off, and 17 is simply the boundary between mild and moderate severity. It does not require amenorrhoea, which DSM-5 dropped. It does not require purging, which defines a subtype, not the disorder. What changed from DSM-IV, and what ICD-10 and ICD-11 say Many of the questions you will meet about anorexia nervosa are really questions about which manual says what. The quickest way to master them is to see how the criteria changed and why. DSM-IV (1994) had four criteria. (A) A refusal to maintain body weight at or above a minimally normal weight for age and height, with the example of weight loss leading to a body weight less than 85 percent of that expected (or failure to gain weight during growth, leading to the same result). (B) Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though underweight. (C) A disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of weight or shape on self-evaluation, or denial of the seriousness of the current low body weight. (D) In post-menarcheal females, amenorrhoea, the absence of at least three consecutive menstrual cycles. The two subtypes were defined by what the person had "regularly" done "during the current episode". The DSM-5 work group, chaired by the American psychiatrist B. Timothy Walsh , made six changes, and each has a reason you can state in an interview. "Refusal" became "restriction of energy intake". The American Psychiatric Association's reason was that "refusal" implies intention on the part of the patient and is difficult to assess. Restriction describes what the person does without guessing at her motive. The 85 percent example was dropped. It looked precise but was not: "expected weight" can be calculated in several ways, and clinicians used different methods, so the same patient could be above 85 percent by one method and below it by another. In 2009 Jennifer J. Thomas, Christina A. Roberto and Kelly D. Brownell found 10 different methods in 99 published studies, and the share of a national sample that met the weight rule rose from 0.23 percent under the strictest method to 10.10 percent under the most lenient. DSM-5 replaced the example with clinical judgement, guided by the BMI signposts of Section 8.3.2, and moved BMI into the severity rating. "Or persistent behaviour that interferes with weight gain" was added to Criterion B , for the patients who will not or cannot report a fear. "Denial" became "persistent lack of recognition" of the seriousness of the low weight, a more neutral description of the same deficit. Amenorrhoea was removed. The reasons are taken up below. The subtypes now describe the last 3 months rather than the whole "current episode", and they speak of "recurrent" rather than "regular" behaviour, because patients so often move between subtypes (Section 8.3.4). DSM-5 also added the BMI-based severity ratings. The removal of amenorrhoea answers a question that examiners set often, so take it slowly. Amenorrhoea means the absence of menstrual periods. The word is Greek: a- (without), men (month) and rhoia (flow), so it is literally "no monthly flow". Primary amenorrhoea means that menstruation has never begun: the girl has not reached her menarche (her first period) at the expected age. Secondary amenorrhoea means that periods which had begun have stopped. Both occur in anorexia nervosa. In a girl whose illness begins before puberty, DSM-5-TR notes that menarche may be delayed, and ICD-10 spells out the consequence: if the onset is pre-pubertal, the sequence of pubertal events is delayed or even arrested, growth ceases, the breasts do not develop and there is a primary amenorrhoea. In an older girl like Malini, whose periods had been regular, the periods stop: secondary amenorrhoea. Why do they stop? Menstruation depends on a chain of hormones called the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis . The hypothalamus releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone; this signals the pituitary gland to release luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone; and these drive the ovaries (or, in males, the testes) to produce sex hormones and mature eggs or sperm. In starvation the hypothalamus turns the first link down. Less gonadotropin-releasing hormone means less luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone, which means little oestrogen and no ovulation, so periods stop. In males the same shutdown lowers testosterone, and sexual interest and potency fall. DSM-5-TR records the result in its laboratory findings: females have low serum oestrogen, males low serum testosterone. From an evolutionary point of view the shutdown makes sense: a famine is a bad time to begin a pregnancy, and the body suspends reproduction until food returns. Section 8.5 and Book 1 Section 10.9 say more about the hypothalamus in hunger. If amenorrhoea is so common and so meaningful, why was it dropped? There were two kinds of reason. The first was logical: a menstrual criterion cannot be applied to males, to girls who have not reached menarche or to women after the menopause, and it is hard to judge in women taking the contraceptive pill, whose withdrawal bleeds can look like periods (ICD-10 itself lists this as an "apparent exception"). The second was empirical, and it is the more important: patients who meet every other criterion but still menstruate turned out to be just as ill as those who do not. As Barlow and Durand put it, amenorrhoea can be an objective index of how severely food is restricted, but it is inconsistent, because it does not occur in all cases. The study in the box was one of those that settled the question. Key study: does losing your periods make you more ill? (Roberto and colleagues, 2008) Under DSM-IV, a woman who met every criterion for anorexia nervosa except amenorrhoea could not be diagnosed; she was placed in the residual category, eating disorder not otherwise specified. Was she really less ill? Christina A. Roberto , with Joanna Steinglass, Laurel Mayer, Evelyn Attia and B. Timothy Walsh, reviewed the charts of 240 consecutive patients admitted for inpatient treatment at the New York State Psychiatric Institute between 1993 and 2006, and compared those who had stopped menstruating with those who still menstruated. The two groups differed on only two measures, their lowest lifetime BMI and their BMI on admission, both lower in the amenorrhoeic group. They did not differ in age, duration of illness, number of previous admissions, BMI at discharge, scores for depression and anxiety, or the severity of their eating-disorder attitudes. The authors concluded that amenorrhoea mainly reflects weight and nutritional status and adds little diagnostic information. In a review the next year, Attia and Roberto (2009) suggested, as one option, that DSM-5 describe amenorrhoea as a frequent feature that may say something about clinical severity, but no longer treat it as a core criterion. That is exactly what DSM-5 did. So amenorrhoea is no longer a criterion, but it is still a finding . DSM-5-TR says that amenorrhoea is commonly present and "appears to be an indicator of physiological dysfunction"; it is usually a consequence of the weight loss, but in a minority of patients it actually comes first, before much weight has been lost. Whenever a question asks what amenorrhoea means, or whether it is found in anorexia nervosa, the answer is "absence of menstrual periods" and "yes, commonly". Only when a question asks what DSM-5 or DSM-5-TR requires is amenorrhoea the wrong answer. The two WHO systems take different approaches again. ICD-10's diagnostic guidelines for F50.0, anorexia nervosa, published in 1992, are the strictest of the four systems, because all five of its requirements must be met: Body weight maintained at least 15 percent below that expected (either lost or never achieved), or a BMI of 17.5 or less, the BMI being used from the age of 16; pre-pubertal patients may instead fail to make the expected weight gain. The weight loss is self-induced by avoiding "fattening foods"; one or more of self-induced vomiting, self-induced purging, excessive exercise, and appetite suppressants or diuretics may also be present (they are not required). Body-image distortion, in which a dread of fatness persists as an intrusive, overvalued idea and the patient imposes a low weight threshold on herself. A widespread endocrine disorder of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, shown in women as amenorrhoea and in men as loss of sexual interest and potency; there may also be raised growth hormone and cortisol, changes in the peripheral metabolism of thyroid hormone and abnormal insulin secretion. If onset is pre-pubertal, delayed or arrested puberty; with recovery puberty is often completed normally, but menarche is late. ICD-10 has no subtypes of anorexia nervosa. A patient who lacks one or more of the key features, such as amenorrhoea or significant weight loss, but otherwise presents a fairly typical picture, or who has all the features only to a mild degree, is coded F50.1, atypical anorexia nervosa. ICD-11 (6B80), in force from 2022, is closer to DSM-5-TR in spirit but keeps numbers. Its anorexia nervosa is characterised by significantly low body weight for height, age and developmental stage that is not due to another health condition or to lack of food, and it names the usual guide: a BMI below 18.5 in adults, or a BMI-for-age below the 5th percentile in children and adolescents. It adds a rule found in neither DSM nor ICD-10: rapid weight loss, for example of more than 20 percent of total body weight within 6 months, may replace the low-weight guideline. The low weight must be accompanied by a persistent pattern of behaviour that prevents the restoration of normal weight (restricting, purging, or raising energy expenditure by exercise), "typically associated with a fear of weight gain", so the fear is expected but not strictly required; and low weight or shape is central to the person's self-evaluation or is inaccurately perceived as normal or even excessive. Amenorrhoea is not required. ICD-11 then classifies by weight and by pattern: 6B80.0, anorexia nervosa with significantly low body weight (adult BMI between 18.5 and 14.0, or between the 5th and the 0.3rd percentile in the young); 6B80.1, with dangerously low body weight (adult BMI under 14.0, or under the 0.3rd percentile), a band ICD-11 links with a high risk of physical complications and greatly increased mortality; and 6B80.2, in recovery with normal body weight , for patients whose BMI has risen above 18.5 but who have not yet achieved a full and lasting recovery, the diagnosis being kept until healthy weight is maintained and weight-losing behaviour has stopped without treatment (for example for at least a year after intensive treatment ends). The first two each have a restricting pattern and a binge-purge pattern (6B80.00 and 6B80.01; 6B80.10 and 6B80.11). Table 8.6 puts the four systems side by side. Subtypes and severity Once the three criteria are met, DSM-5-TR asks the clinician to specify a subtype, and the rule for choosing it is narrow and precise. In the restricting type , during the last 3 months the person has not engaged in recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviour (self-induced vomiting, or misuse of laxatives, diuretics or enemas); weight loss is achieved primarily through dieting, fasting and/or excessive exercise. In the binge-eating/purging type , during the last 3 months the person has engaged in recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviour. Malini, who diets and runs but has never vomited or binged, has the restricting type. Read the binge-eating/purging definition again and notice the "or". Most people with this subtype who binge also purge, but some do not binge at all; they purge regularly after eating quite small amounts of food. Barlow and Durand add that, unlike people with bulimia nervosa, those with the binge-eating/purging type of anorexia tend to binge on relatively small amounts and to purge more consistently, in some cases every time they eat, and that roughly half of all people who meet the criteria for anorexia nervosa binge and purge. (What exactly counts as a binge is defined in Section 8.4.1.) Nalini, 22, shows the purging-only form. She weighs 45 kg at 1.65 m, a BMI of about 16.5. She eats a small breakfast and a small dinner and makes herself sick after each; she has never eaten a large amount in her life and is frightened of the idea. She has anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type, even though she never binges. Why limit the subtype to the last 3 months? Because the subtypes are not stable. DSM-5-TR says that crossover between them over the course of the disorder is not uncommon, so the subtype should describe current symptoms rather than the longitudinal course. The evidence came from follow-up studies. Kamryn T. Eddy and her colleagues (2002) followed 136 women with anorexia nervosa for 8 to 12 years and found that by the 8-year point 62 percent of those who began with the restricting type had crossed over to bingeing or purging, while the two subtypes differed little in severity of symptoms or in personality. Subtyping, they concluded, may describe a phase of the illness rather than two different illnesses. The subtypes are still worth recording, because they carry different risks. Compared with the restricting type, people with the binge-eating/purging type show higher rates of impulsivity and are more likely to misuse alcohol and other drugs; purging adds its own medical dangers, above all low potassium (Section 8.3.5); and obsessive-compulsive disorder is described especially in the restricting type. DSM-5-TR also provides two remission specifiers. In partial remission applies when, after the full criteria have been met, Criterion A (the low weight) has not been met for a sustained period but either Criterion B (the fear of weight gain or weight-preventing behaviour) or Criterion C (the disturbed experience of weight and shape) is still present. In full remission applies when none of the criteria has been met for a sustained period. The order matters clinically. Weight is usually the first thing to recover, because it can be restored by feeding; the fear of fatness and the overvaluation of shape recover much later, if at all. A young woman discharged from hospital at a healthy weight who still weighs herself ten times a day and panics at a second chapati is in partial remission, not recovered, and is at high risk of relapse. Finally comes severity. DSM-5-TR bases the minimum level of severity, for adults, on the current BMI, using ranges derived from the WHO's categories of thinness in adults; for children and adolescents the corresponding BMI percentiles are used. The four levels are: Mild: BMI 17 or more. Moderate: BMI 16 to 16.99. Severe: BMI 15 to 15.99. Extreme: BMI below 15. Two qualifications make the rating clinical rather than mechanical. The word "current" means that severity changes as weight changes: a patient admitted at a BMI of 14.5 (extreme) may be rated moderate a month later. And the level of severity may be increased to reflect clinical symptoms, the degree of functional disability and the need for supervision. A woman with a BMI of 17.3, which is formally mild, who faints in the bathroom, has a pulse in the thirties and cannot eat a meal without someone sitting beside her, can and should be rated as more severe. The BMI sets the floor, not the ceiling. Now the worked example, with one caution. Because Malini is 16, DSM-5-TR asks for her severity to be judged by her BMI-for-age percentile, not by the adult bands, which apply to adults only. The adult scale is used for her here simply to show how the bands work: her BMI of 15.6 would fall in the severe band (15 to 15.99), and on the percentile measure that DSM-5-TR actually applies to her she is well below the 5th percentile for her age, so her clinician rates her illness as severe. The top end of the ruler raises a question that clinicians meet more and more often. Mitali is 28. Over five months she has gone from 75 kg to 59 kg at a height of 1.62 m, a loss of more than a fifth of her body weight; her pulse is slow, her periods have stopped, she is terrified of regaining a gram and she weighs herself every hour. But her BMI is now about 22.5, well inside the normal range. Under DSM-5-TR she cannot be diagnosed with anorexia nervosa, because Criterion A requires a significantly low weight and adults at a BMI of 19 or more should not receive the diagnosis; she has atypical anorexia nervosa , one of the other specified feeding or eating disorders (Section 8.4.7), and she may be just as medically at risk. Under ICD-11 the answer could be different, because its rule that rapid loss of more than 20 percent of body weight within 6 months may replace the low-weight guideline could bring her within 6B80. The same patient, two manuals, two diagnoses: this is why examiners like to ask which system a number comes from. Exam trap The restricting type means no recurrent binge eating or purging during the last 3 months , with weight lost by dieting, fasting or excessive exercise. "Required compensatory vomiting", "binge-purge cycles within 3 months" and "required laxative use weekly" describe the binge-eating/purging type or nothing at all (DSM-5-TR sets no weekly frequency for purging in anorexia). "BMI below 17.5 only" is ICD-10's weight threshold, not a DSM subtype, and no DSM subtype is defined by BMI. "Selective eating without weight loss" is picky eating or ARFID (Section 8.2.4). The binge-eating/purging type does not require binges: purging after small meals is enough. And severity is rated by current BMI: mild 17 or more, moderate 16 to 16.99, severe 15 to 15.99, extreme below 15. The starving body When Malini's doctor examines her, he finds a resting pulse of 48 beats a minute, a low blood pressure, cold blue hands and a fine down of hair on her forearms and back. None of these findings is random. Almost every physical sign of anorexia nervosa follows from one idea: the body is defending itself against starvation. Faced with too little fuel, it cuts its spending. It slows the heart, lowers the temperature, turns down the thyroid hormone that sets the metabolic rate, switches off reproduction, and lets the bones and the blood-forming marrow run down. If you remember the phrase "slow and low", you can work out most of the findings for yourself, and, just as usefully, you can see at once which answer options point the wrong way. DSM-5-TR sums up the picture: the semistarvation of anorexia nervosa, and the purging that sometimes goes with it, can cause significant and potentially life-threatening medical conditions; the nutritional damage affects most major organ systems; and while most of the disturbances reverse with nutritional rehabilitation, some, including loss of bone mineral density, are often not completely reversible. What the clinician sees. The most remarkable finding on physical examination, DSM-5-TR says, is emaciation . Commonly there is also significant hypotension (low blood pressure), hypothermia (low body temperature) and bradycardia (a slow heart rate). Some patients develop lanugo , a fine, soft, downy body hair (the word is Latin, from lana , wool), which Barlow and Durand note on the limbs and cheeks; it is the same kind of hair that covers a foetus before birth. The skin is often dry and the hair and nails brittle, and the patient feels the cold when others do not. Some develop a yellowing of the skin associated with hypercarotenaemia , a raised level of carotene in the blood. Some develop peripheral oedema , swelling of the ankles and feet with fluid, especially during weight restoration or after stopping laxatives or diuretics, which frightens patients because it looks and feels like getting fat. Rarely, small pinpoint haemorrhages (petechiae) or bruises (ecchymoses), usually on the arms and legs, show a bleeding tendency. The patient's own complaints, when she makes any, are of amenorrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain, cold intolerance and lethargy, and also, paradoxically, of excess energy: many patients feel restless and driven rather than tired. The heart. Sinus bradycardia, a slow but otherwise normal rhythm, is common; it is the heart doing less work because there is less fuel to do it with. Rarely, there are arrhythmias, and in some patients there is significant prolongation of the QTc interval , the stretch of the electrocardiogram from the start of the ventricles' electrical activation to the end of their electrical recovery (repolarisation) after each beat, corrected for heart rate. A long QTc makes the heart vulnerable to a sudden, chaotic rhythm that can kill within minutes, and it is one reason deaths in anorexia nervosa can come without warning. The blood. The bone marrow, starved like the rest of the body, makes fewer cells. Leucopenia (a low white cell count) is common, with all types of white cell reduced but usually an apparent lymphocytosis (lymphocytes making up a larger share of a smaller total). Mild anaemia can occur, as can thrombocytopenia (low platelets) and, rarely, bleeding problems. On the blood chemistry, dehydration shows as a raised blood urea nitrogen. Hypercholesterolaemia , a raised cholesterol level, is common, which surprises students who expect everything to be low; liver enzymes may be raised; and low magnesium, zinc and phosphate, with a raised amylase, are occasionally found. The hormones. The thyroid tells the clearest story. The gland itself is healthy, and serum thyroxine (T4) is usually in the low-normal range. But T4 is mostly a precursor; the body converts it either into triiodothyronine (T3), the active hormone that sets the metabolic rate, or into reverse T3, an inactive form. In starvation the conversion shifts towards the inactive form, so T3 is decreased and reverse T3 is raised . This pattern, often called the low T3 syndrome or sick euthyroid syndrome, is not thyroid disease but another energy-saving manoeuvre, and giving thyroid hormone to "correct" it would be a mistake. It is the opposite of hyperthyroidism , in which an overactive gland raises T4 and T3 and produces weight loss with a fast pulse, heat intolerance and a high metabolic rate. Among the sex hormones, females have low oestrogen and males low testosterone, the result of the hypothalamic shutdown described in Section 8.3.3, and ICD-10 adds raised growth hormone and cortisol to the endocrine picture. Resting energy expenditure , the calories the body burns at rest, is often significantly reduced. The bones. Low bone mineral density, with areas of osteopenia (thinning of bone) or osteoporosis (thinning severe enough to make bones fragile), is often seen, and the risk of fracture is significantly raised. Low oestrogen and poor nutrition both drain the skeleton. This is the damage DSM-5-TR singles out as often not completely reversible, and it is especially serious because anorexia nervosa usually strikes in adolescence, the years in which much of the skeleton's lifetime store of bone is laid down. A girl who loses those years may carry fragile bones for life, even after full recovery. The brain. The electroencephalogram may show diffuse abnormalities reflecting a metabolic encephalopathy , a disturbance of brain function caused by significant fluid and electrolyte disturbances. Brain imaging shows that starvation itself shrinks the brain: as Barlow and Durand note, it induces loss of grey matter and hormonal dysregulation in the brain, changes that are reversible when normal weight is restored. The poor concentration, rigid thinking and preoccupation with food of the starving patient (Section 8.3.6) have a physical basis. What purging adds. Patients of the binge-eating/purging type carry a second set of findings, the same marks seen in bulimia nervosa. Self-induced vomiting loses stomach acid and potassium, causing metabolic alkalosis (a raised serum bicarbonate), hypochloraemia (low chloride) and hypokalaemia (low potassium); laxative misuse, which loses alkaline fluid from the bowel, can cause a mild metabolic acidosis . Potassium is essential to the electrical stability of the heart, so hypokalaemia in a patient whose heart is already slowed and whose QTc may be long is one of the most dangerous combinations in clinical psychiatry. Vomiting also enlarges the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands in front of the ears, which gives a puffy, round-cheeked face that contrasts oddly with the thin body; erodes the enamel of the teeth; and can leave scars or calluses on the back of the hand from repeated contact with the teeth while inducing vomiting, the mark known as Russell's sign (Section 8.4.3).
