Caffeine taken in low to moderate doses in the morning usually has no effect on night-time sleep, even in people with insomnia; it causes insomnia in proportion to how much is taken and how late, by blocking the adenosine that builds up sleep pressure during the day (Book 1, Section 5.6.3). The stimulants show the two faces of a single drug: insomnia during intoxication and sleepiness during withdrawal, when the multiple sleep latency test can show increased daytime sleepiness. Opioids are sedating at first, but tolerance soon brings complaints of insomnia, and because they depress breathing they worsen obstructive sleep apnoea and, especially in chronic use of long-acting opioids, produce central sleep apnoea. The newer hypnotics (ramelteon, low-dose doxepin and the orexin antagonist suvorexant) do not appear to carry significant abuse potential or major withdrawal syndromes, whereas short-acting benzodiazepines are the most likely to cause rebound insomnia (Section 8.7.6 treats the hypnotics). Smokers who smoke heavily may wake regularly at night with craving. Two groups are especially at risk and especially easy to miss. Adolescents and young adults who use cannabis or ecstasy may not seek help, so new insomnia in a teenager should prompt a careful, private question about drugs, and a parent's or teacher's report may help. Older people take more medicines, may put their poor sleep down to age and fail to report it, and people with dementia may be unable to report it at all, so a caregiver's account is essential. Sleep diaries kept for two weeks, actigraphy (a wrist-worn movement monitor) and, where needed, a drug screen help to confirm the diagnosis. The differential diagnosis turns on chronology. A sleep disturbance that began before any drug, or persists long after stopping it, points to an independent sleep disorder. People with a primary sleep problem often medicate it themselves (alcohol for insomnia is the classic example), and when the substance clearly makes the sleep problem worse, both diagnoses can be made. When the sleep disturbance is due to a medical condition and the medicine for it, the order of events decides: sleep problems that came with the illness, before any treatment, suggest insomnia disorder, hypersomnolence disorder or nightmare disorder "with [the medical condition]", whereas symptoms that appeared only after a particular medicine was started suggest the substance/medication-induced diagnosis. If the evidence cannot settle the matter, the diagnosis is unspecified sleep-wake disorder. That last diagnosis is one of six residual categories which, with the disorders of Sections 8.7 to 8.10, let a clinician place any sleep presentation. Other specified insomnia disorder (G47.09) is used when insomnia causes distress but does not meet the full criteria and the clinician records why, for example "short-term insomnia disorder" (less than 3 months) or insomnia "restricted to nonrestorative sleep". Unspecified insomnia disorder (G47.00) is used when the clinician does not specify the reason or lacks the information. Other specified hypersomnolence disorder (G47.19) covers presentations such as "brief-duration hypersomnolence", the example DSM-5-TR gives being Kleine-Levin syndrome (Section 8.8.8), and unspecified hypersomnolence disorder (G47.10) is its unspecified partner. Finally, other specified sleep-wake disorder (G47.8) covers presentations that fit none of the specific disorders and neither of the insomnia or hypersomnolence residual categories, with the reason recorded; DSM-5-TR's own example is "repeated arousals during REM sleep without polysomnography or history of Parkinson's disease or other synucleinopathy", the patient who seems to have RBD but cannot yet meet its Criterion D. Recurrent isolated sleep paralysis and exploding head syndrome, which have no DSM-5-TR category of their own, belong here when they are troublesome enough to diagnose. Unspecified sleep-wake disorder (G47.9) is used when the reason is not recorded or there is insufficient information. Remember To place a night-time event, ask four questions. When? First third (NREM arousal disorder, enuresis), last third (nightmare, RBD), the edges of sleep (sleep paralysis, sleep-related hallucinations, exploding head syndrome, hypnic jerks), or before sleep (restless legs). Awake afterwards? Confused and unreachable (NREM arousal) or at once alert (REM events, panic). Remembered? Nothing or a single image (NREM arousal), a whole story (nightmare, RBD), the fear but no dream (nocturnal panic). Moving? With eyes open and walking (sleepwalking), with eyes closed and fighting (RBD), only the legs and without knowing it (PLMD). Then check the medicines and drinks, because any of these patterns can be substance-induced. Exam trap A substance/medication-induced sleep disorder is diagnosed instead of intoxication or withdrawal only when the sleep symptoms predominate and need attention in their own right, and no separate substance use disorder diagnosis is coded. Its four types are insomnia , daytime sleepiness , parasomnia and mixed ; its onset specifiers are during intoxication, during withdrawal and after medication use. Symptoms that persist about a month after withdrawal ends point to an independent sleep disorder. Caffeine (F15.982) and tobacco (F17.208) have single codes. The men of the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, revisited Go back to the thirty-six conscientious objectors beneath the football stadium in Minneapolis and read their year again with this chapter in your hands. Almost every change in their bodies is on the list of Section 8.3.5. Their heart rate, body temperature and breathing fell, and some of them developed oedema of the limbs: the "slow and low" economy of the starving body, which a physician finds in anorexia nervosa as bradycardia, hypothermia and hypotension, with an oedema that frightens patients during weight restoration. Their minds followed the same script. They thought, talked and read about food, collected recipes, hoarded food-related things and grew depressed, irritable and withdrawn, with rising scores on the depression, hysteria and hypochondriasis scales of the MMPI. That is why DSM-5-TR warns that many of the depressive and obsessional features of anorexia nervosa may be secondary to semistarvation, why mood is assessed again once weight has been restored, and why obsessive-compulsive disorder is added only for obsessions unrelated to food, shape or weight (Section 8.3.6): Malini's recipe reading and the cakes she bakes and does not eat are the Minnesota men's preoccupation, not a second disorder. Even the ruler on which her severity is graded carries Keys's mark, because it was he who gave the body mass index its name in 1972 (Section 8.3.2). And many of the men said afterwards that the hardest part of the experiment was not the starvation but the rehabilitation. The hunger did not switch off when the food returned; some ate enormous meals, a few until they were sick. A body defending its weight resists a diet from within, which is why a rigid diet so often ends in a binge (Section 8.5.1), and feeding a starved person back to health, the problem Keys set out to solve, is still the first and most dangerous step in treating anorexia nervosa, now monitored day by day for the refeeding syndrome (Sections 8.3.5 and 8.5.6). The opening asked why the men of Minnesota longed for food, while a girl with anorexia nervosa refuses the food in front of her and a young woman with bulimia nervosa eats far more than she wants and then makes herself sick. The chapter's answer has three parts. The men longed for food because starvation raises the positive-incentive value of eating to enormous heights; for them, all food tasted good. A girl with anorexia nervosa is starving too, and often hungry, but her restriction is driven by an intense fear of gaining weight and by a self-worth measured in kilograms, the over-evaluation of eating, shape and weight and their control that Fairburn, Cooper and Shafran (2003) placed at the core of anorexia, bulimia and their atypical forms (Section 8.5.4); Pinel and Barnes add the hypothesis that meals in a starved body are unpleasant and produce conditioned taste aversions that lower the incentive value of food still further. A young woman with bulimia nervosa diets by rigid rules against her own physiology, so a broken rule releases a binge, and because her self-evaluation is unduly influenced by shape and weight (Criterion D, Section 8.4.2) she vomits to undo it, which prepares the next diet and the next binge. What the men never had was that over-evaluation: they had no wish to be thin, and their preoccupation with food was the work of hunger, not of a fear of fatness. Hunger supplies much of the psychology of an eating disorder, and dieting is its commonest first step; what turns starvation into anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa is the conviction that one's worth depends on one's shape and weight. Chapter summary 8.1 Eating, Elimination and Sleep: Three Families of Disorder and Their History. Feeding, voiding and sleeping are bodily functions every child must learn; their disorders fill DSM-5-TR's chapters 10, 11 and 12. A feeding or eating disorder is a persistent disturbance of eating or eating-related behaviour that alters the consumption or absorption of food and impairs health or functioning; anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder are mutually exclusive in a single episode, and obesity and food addiction are not diagnoses. Morton described nervous consumption (1689), Lasègue anorexie hystérique (April 1873) and Gull named anorexia nervosa (read 1873, printed 1874); Bruch turned attention to body image (The Golden Cage, 1978), Stunkard described night eating (1955) and binge eating (1959), and Russell named bulimia nervosa (1979). DSM-5 dropped amenorrhoea and set once a week for 3 months, and ICD-11 moved the sleep-wake disorders to their own Chapter 7. 8.2 Pica, Rumination Disorder and Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder. The feeding disorders lack the disturbance of weight or shape that defines anorexia and bulimia; since DSM-5 they apply at any age, and beside another disorder each is diagnosed only when severe enough to warrant additional clinical attention. Pica is the persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances for at least 1 month, inappropriate to developmental level (minimum age 2) and not culturally sanctioned; it goes with iron and zinc deficiency, pregnancy, intellectual disability and autism, and risks obstruction, bezoars and lead poisoning. Rumination disorder is repeated, effortless regurgitation for at least 1 month, treated with diaphragmatic breathing. ARFID, which replaced feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood, is sensory avoidance, lack of interest or fear of aversive consequences causing weight loss, deficiency, supplement dependence or psychosocial interference, without body-image disturbance; Thomas and Eddy's CBT-AR (2019) treats it. 8.3 Anorexia Nervosa: Criteria, the Starving Body and the Course. Anorexia nervosa needs restriction leading to a significantly low weight, intense fear of weight gain or persistent behaviour that interferes with gain, and a disturbed experience of weight or shape, undue influence of it on self-worth or failure to see the danger. DSM-5-TR sets no diagnostic BMI cut-off; the work group chaired by Walsh dropped DSM-IV's 85 percent example and amenorrhoea, which Roberto (2008) found added little. ICD-10 uses a BMI of 17.5 or less, ICD-11 below 18.5. The restricting type has no recurrent binge eating or purging in the last 3 months; severity runs from mild (17 or more) to extreme (below 15). The starving body is "slow and low": lanugo, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, low T3 and osteoporosis, with hypokalaemia from purging. Crude mortality, about 5 percent per decade, is the highest of the eating disorders. 8.4 Bulimia Nervosa, Binge-Eating Disorder and the Other Specified Eating Disorders. A binge is a definitely large amount eaten in a discrete period (usually under 2 hours) with loss of control. Bulimia nervosa adds recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviour (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, excessive exercise), both on average once a week for 3 months (twice a week in DSM-IV), with self-evaluation unduly influenced by shape and weight, outside episodes of anorexia. Weight is usually normal, so the clues are hypokalaemia, alkalosis, dental erosion, parotid swelling and Russell's sign, and crude mortality is nearly 2 percent per decade. Binge-eating disorder, a full diagnosis since DSM-5, needs three of five features, marked distress and no compensation. Weight, then binges, then compensation tell the three apart; they share body-image distortion, fear of fatness and psychological regulation of eating. Atypical anorexia, purging disorder and night eating syndrome are other specified forms. 8.5 Why Eating Disorders Develop and How They Are Treated. Eating disorders arise where several risks meet. The thin ideal harms when it is internalised (Thompson and Stice, 2001), as ballet students (Garner, 1987) and television in Fiji (Becker, 2002) show, while Sing Lee's non-fat-phobic patients (1993) show culture shaping the explanation. Dieting is the commonest first step: the Minnesota men showed that starvation itself produces many symptoms, and severe dieters were 18 times likelier to fall ill (Patton, 1999). Minuchin's psychosomatic family is no longer thought causal; perfectionism marks anorexia, impulsivity bulimia, and heritability is about half. Fairburn, Cooper and Shafran's transdiagnostic theory (2003) puts the over-evaluation of eating, shape and weight at the core. Weight is restored with monitored refeeding; no drug treats anorexia, fluoxetine (1996) helps bulimia and lisdexamfetamine (2015) binge-eating disorder. Family-based treatment comes first for adolescent anorexia, CBT for bulimia and binge eating. 8.6 Enuresis and Encopresis: The Elimination Disorders. Enuresis is the repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes, twice a week for 3 consecutive months or with significant distress or impairment, at a developmental age of at least 5; it is nocturnal only (monosymptomatic, the commonest), diurnal only or both, and primary or secondary. Bedwetting follows a mismatch of night urine output (low vasopressin, Rittig, 1989), bladder capacity and arousal, with strong heredity; most children outgrow it. The urine alarm (Mowrer and Mowrer, 1938) is first-line and durable; desmopressin works fast but relapse follows. Encopresis, Weissenberg's word (1926), is the repeated passage of faeces in inappropriate places, once a month for 3 months, from age 4; lack of bowel control is encopresis, not enuresis. Its commoner subtype, with constipation and overflow incontinence, follows the retentive cycle and is treated by disimpaction, maintenance laxatives and scheduled toileting without punishment. 8.7 Normal Sleep, the Sleep-Wake Disorders and Insomnia Disorder. Polysomnography (EEG, EOG and EMG) describes sleep continuity (sleep latency, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency) and architecture (REM latency; a sleep-onset REM period begins within 15 minutes), and the multiple sleep latency test measures sleepiness. Classification moved from DSM-III-R's dyssomnias and parasomnias to DSM-5-TR's ten groups, ICSD-3 (2014) and ICD-11's Chapter 7. Insomnia disorder is dissatisfaction with sleep, through difficulty initiating or maintaining it or early waking, on 3 nights a week for 3 months despite adequate opportunity, with daytime distress, and it is diagnosed alongside any coexisting disorder; about 10 percent of adults meet the criteria. Spielman's 3P model (1987), hyperarousal (Bonnet and Arand, 1995) and Harvey's cognitive model (2002) explain its persistence, and Dement's Mr B. shows iatrogenic insomnia. Hypnotics are for short-term use; CBT-I, with stimulus control (Bootzin, 1972), sleep restriction and Frankl's paradoxical intention, comes first. 8.8 Hypersomnolence Disorder, Narcolepsy and Kleine-Levin Syndrome. Sleepiness differs from fatigue; its commonest cause is insufficient sleep. Hypersomnolence disorder (idiopathic hypersomnia) is sleepiness despite at least 7 hours of main sleep, three times a week for 3 months, with long unrefreshing naps and sleep inertia. Narcolepsy, described by Westphal (1877) and named by Gélineau (1880), needs an irrepressible need to sleep three times a week for 3 months plus cataplexy, low hypocretin-1 or a short REM latency; its tetrad of sleep attacks, cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations is REM sleep out of place. Type 1 follows the loss of hypothalamic hypocretin (orexin) neurons (found 1998 to 2000), probably by autoimmunity in carriers of HLA DQB1*06:02. Cataplexy, an emotion-triggered loss of tone, is not catalepsy, the waxy flexibility of catatonia. Modafinil, antidepressants and sodium oxybate treat narcolepsy. Kleine-Levin syndrome is recurrent hypersomnia with hyperphagia and hypersexuality, mostly in adolescent males. 8.9 Breathing-Related and Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders. In obstructive sleep apnoea hypopnoea the upper airway collapses while breathing effort continues; it needs at least 5 obstructive events an hour with snoring or sleepiness, or 15 regardless of symptoms, and it picks out obese, middle-aged men. Dickens's fat boy gave the "Pickwickian" name, Gastaut recorded the apnoeas (1965), and Sullivan's CPAP (1981) remains the standard treatment, with psychological help for adherence; Udwadia's Mumbai study (2004) found the syndrome in 7.5 percent of men. In central sleep apnoea, including Cheyne-Stokes breathing and its opioid-related form, the drive to breathe fails, and sleep-related hypoventilation is shallow breathing with raised carbon dioxide. The circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders are the delayed sleep phase, advanced sleep phase, irregular, non-24-hour and shift work types; jet lag was dropped after DSM-IV. Timed bright light, melatonin, chronotherapy and forward-rotating shifts treat them. 8.10 Parasomnias, Restless Legs Syndrome and Substance-Induced Sleep Disorders. Parasomnias, which Mahowald and Schenck explained as state dissociation, are told apart by timing and recall. Sleepwalking (somnambulism) and sleep terrors (pavor nocturnus) are NREM sleep arousal disorders: incomplete awakenings from N3 in the first third of the night with amnesia, common in children and mostly outgrown, helped by scheduled awakenings (Durand and Mindell, 1999). Nightmare disorder arises from REM sleep late in the night, with rapid orientation and vivid recall; imagery rehearsal helps (Krakow, 2001). REM sleep behaviour disorder is dream enactment from loss of REM atonia, mostly in men over 50, and often heralds a synucleinopathy such as Parkinson's disease; clonazepam or melatonin treats it. Restless legs syndrome (Willis-Ekbom disease) is an evening urge to move the legs, relieved by movement and precipitated by iron deficiency. gaining weight and food restriction. DSM-5-TR defines anorexia nervosa by restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low weight, an intense fear of gaining weight (or behaviour that prevents gain) and a disturbed experience of weight or shape (Sections 8.3.1 and 8.3.2). Obsession with cleanliness is the contamination theme of obsessive-compulsive disorder, repeated vomiting after bingeing describes bulimia nervosa (although vomiting also occurs in anorexia's binge-eating/purging type), and excessive exercise is only one of the methods patients use to lose weight. Amenorrhea is Present in anorexia nervosa. This term means: (RML 2021) (a) An intense fear of weight gain. (b) Excessive exercise. (c) Absence of menstrual cycle. (d) Body-image distortion. Answer: (c) Absence of menstrual cycle. Amenorrhoea (a-, without; men, month; rhoia, flow) is the absence of menstrual periods, common in anorexia because starvation shuts down the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, although DSM-5 dropped it as a criterion (Section 8.3.3). Fear of weight gain, excessive exercise and body-image distortion are other features of the disorder, not the meaning of the word. Bulimia nervosa is characterised by recurrent binge eating and inappropriate use of compensatory behaviours. An example of compensatory behaviour is: (RML 2021) (a) Use of laxatives (b) Self-induced vomiting (c) Excessive exercising (d) All of the above Answer: (d) All of the above. Inappropriate compensatory behaviour is anything done to prevent weight gain after a binge: self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics or other medications, fasting and excessive exercise (Section 8.4.2). Vomiting and laxatives are purging, while exercise and fasting are compensatory without being purging, so every option is an example and none alone is the answer. Unlike people with anorexia, individuals with bulimia (RML 2022) (a) Often purge themselves to stay thin (b) Are obsessed with being too fat (c) Can do damage to their health (d) May appear normal in weight Answer: (d) May appear normal in weight. People with bulimia nervosa are typically of normal weight or overweight, which is the key difference from anorexia nervosa, defined by a significantly low weight (Sections 8.4.3 and 8.4.6). Purging to stay thin (in anorexia's binge-eating/purging type), an obsession with being too fat and damage to health occur in both disorders, so none of them is a difference. Which of the following symptoms do anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa have in common? (RML 2020) (a) distorted body image (b) intense fear of being fat (c) eating regulated by psychological and not physical processes (d) all of the above Answer: (d) all of the above. Both disorders involve a distorted body image, an intense fear of being fat, and eating governed by rules, fears, moods and judgements of self-worth rather than by hunger and fullness (Section 8.4.6). What separates them is body weight, not any of these three features, so picking a single option would miss the other two. A patient with anorexia nervosa has traits of: (RML 2024) (a) Perfectionism (b) Impulsivity (c) Avoidance (d) Dependence Answer: (a) Perfectionism. The personality most consistently linked with anorexia nervosa is over-controlled: perfectionism, with obsessionality, rigidity and anxiety (Section 8.5.3). Impulsivity is the trait of bulimia nervosa and of anorexia's binge-eating/purging type, while avoidance and dependence are the cores of avoidant and dependent personality disorders, which some patients show but which are not the characteristic traits. Lack of bowel control in children is known as: (RML 2024) (a) Encopresis (b) Analism (c) Enuresis (d) Anorexia Answer: (a) Encopresis. Encopresis is the repeated passage of faeces into inappropriate places, at least once a month for 3 months, at a developmental age of at least 4 (Sections 8.6.1 and 8.6.5). Enuresis is the same problem with urine (from age 5), anorexia is an eating disorder, and "analism" is not a recognised disorder in any manual, only bait built from Freud's anal stage. In narcolepsy, which of the following is most characteristically present? (IHBAS 2025) (a) Both cataplexy and catalepsy equally (b) Cataplexy: sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions (c) Neither cataplexy nor catalepsy (d) Catalepsy: maintenance of imposed posture with waxy flexibility Answer: (b) Cataplexy: sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions. Cataplexy, a brief, bilateral loss of muscle tone set off by emotion, above all laughter, with consciousness preserved, is the hallmark of narcolepsy type 1 and one of its diagnostic criteria (Sections 8.8.4 and 8.8.6). Catalepsy, a posture held with waxy flexibility, is a sign of catatonia, so "catalepsy", "both equally" and "neither" are all wrong. Which one of the following characterises somnambulism? (RML 2022) (a) Sitting, walking or performing complex behaviour while asleep (b) Extreme fear, agitation, screaming while asleep (c) Acting out nightmares (d) Uncomfortable sensations in the legs causing movement and loss of sleep Answer: (a) Sitting, walking or performing complex behaviour while asleep. Somnambulism (sleepwalking) is an NREM sleep arousal disorder: an incomplete awakening, usually from N3 in the first third of the night, with rising, walking or other complex behaviour, a blank stare and amnesia (Section 8.10.2). Extreme fear and screaming describe sleep terrors, acting out dreams describes REM sleep behaviour disorder, and uncomfortable leg sensations that force movement describe restless legs syndrome. Anorexia nervosa per DSM-5 requires: (practice mock) (a) Significantly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain or behaviours that interfere with weight gain, and disturbance in body image (b) BMI <17 in all cases (c) Amenorrhoea (still required) (d) Episodes of compensatory purging in all cases Answer: (a) Significantly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain or behaviours that interfere with weight gain, and disturbance in body image. These are DSM-5-TR's three criteria (Section 8.3.2). There is no diagnostic BMI cut-off (17 is only the line between mild and moderate severity), amenorrhoea was dropped in DSM-5, and purging defines the binge-eating/purging subtype, not the disorder. Anorexia nervosa, restricting subtype, is defined in DSM-5 by: (practice mock) (a) Required compensatory vomiting (b) No binge-eating or purging behaviours during the current 3-month episode; weight loss via dietary restriction, fasting, excessive exercise (c) Binge-purge cycles within 3 months (d) Required laxative use weekly Answer: (b) No binge-eating or purging behaviours during the current 3-month episode; weight loss via dietary restriction, fasting, excessive exercise. The restricting type means no recurrent binge eating or purging during the last 3 months, with weight lost by dieting, fasting or excessive exercise (Section 8.3.4). Vomiting, binge-purge cycles and laxatives describe the binge-eating/purging type, and DSM-5-TR sets no weekly frequency for purging in anorexia at all. Anorexia nervosa is associated with which medical finding? (practice mock) (a) Hyperthyroidism (b) Lanugo hair, bradycardia, hypokalaemia, amenorrhoea (c) Polyphagia (d) Hyperkalaemia and tachycardia Answer: (b) Lanugo hair, bradycardia, hypokalaemia, amenorrhoea. Starvation makes the body "slow and low": lanugo, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, amenorrhoea and, with purging, hypokalaemia (Section 8.3.5). Hyperthyroidism is wrong (T3 is low, with reverse T3 raised), polyphagia is wrong because the patient restricts, and hyperkalaemia and tachycardia both point the wrong way. Which is the most lethal eating disorder in terms of mortality rate? (practice mock) (a) Bulimia nervosa (b) Binge eating disorder (c) Anorexia nervosa (d) Pica Answer: (c) Anorexia nervosa. Anorexia nervosa has a crude mortality of about 5 percent per decade and a standardised mortality ratio of about 5.9 (Arcelus and colleagues, 2011), from medical complications such as arrhythmia and from suicide (Section 8.3.7). Bulimia nervosa's crude mortality is nearly 2 percent per decade, and binge-eating disorder and pica, though harmful, are not the most lethal. Bulimia nervosa per DSM-5 requires binge-purge episodes occurring on average at least: (practice mock) (a) Twice per week for 6 months (b) Once per week for 3 months (c) Once per day for 1 month (d) Three times per week for 1 month Answer: (b) Once per week for 3 months. DSM-5 lowered the threshold from twice a week (DSM-III-R and DSM-IV) to binges and compensation both at least once a week for 3 months (Sections 8.1.6 and 8.4.2). "Twice per week for 6 months" matches no edition (the 6 months was DSM-IV's provisional rule for binge-eating disorder), and the other two options are invented. DSM-5 criteria for Binge Eating Disorder require binge episodes to occur on average at least: (practice mock) (a) Once weekly for 6 months (b) Twice monthly for 1 month (c) Once weekly for 3 months (d) Once daily for a year Answer: (c) Once weekly for 3 months. Binge-eating disorder uses the same threshold as bulimia nervosa, binges on average at least once a week for 3 months (Section 8.4.5). "Once weekly for 6 months" borrows DSM-IV's provisional period (binges on 2 days a week for 6 months), and the other two options match no edition. A patient presents with episodes of binge eating ≥1/week for ≥3 months, without compensatory behaviours, with marked distress about the binges. The DSM-5 diagnosis is: (practice mock) (a) Binge-eating disorder (b) Bulimia nervosa (c) Anorexia nervosa, binge-purge subtype (d) Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder Answer: (a) Binge-eating disorder. Recurrent binges at least weekly for 3 months with marked distress and no compensatory behaviour is binge-eating disorder, a full diagnosis since DSM-5 (Section 8.4.5). Bulimia nervosa needs compensatory behaviour, the binge-eating/purging type of anorexia needs a significantly low weight, and ARFID is a disorder of eating too little, without binges and without concern about shape or weight. Anorexia nervosa is differentiated from bulimia nervosa primarily by: (practice mock) (a) Absence of body image disturbance in bulimia (b) Significantly low body weight in anorexia (c) Presence of compensatory behaviours only in anorexia (d) Absence of purging in anorexia Answer: (b) Significantly low body weight in anorexia. Significantly low body weight defines anorexia nervosa and takes precedence, whereas people with bulimia are usually of normal weight or overweight (Section 8.4.6). Body-image disturbance is present in both, compensatory behaviour occurs in both, and purging occurs in anorexia's binge-eating/purging type, so the other three options claim differences that do not exist. REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is characterised by: (practice mock) (a) Inability to enter any REM at all (b) Loss of REM atonia, causing patient to enact dream content (c) Bedwetting during N3 (d) Excessive daytime sleepiness without nocturnal symptoms Answer: (b) Loss of REM atonia, causing patient to enact dream content. In REM sleep behaviour disorder the normal paralysis of REM sleep fails, so the sleeper acts out his dreams and wakes alert with vivid recall, and the disorder often precedes a synucleinopathy such as Parkinson's disease (Section 8.10.4). The patient has plenty of REM sleep, bedwetting is enuresis (which is not tied to N3), and excessive daytime sleepiness without nocturnal symptoms describes hypersomnolence disorder. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Anorexia nervosa (DSM-5-TR) needs all three: restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight; intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behaviour that interferes with weight gain; and a disturbed experience of weight or shape, undue influence of weight or shape on self-evaluation, or failure to recognise the seriousness of the low weight. No BMI cut-off, amenorrhoea or purging is required. asked 3 times Low body weight, not purging, separates anorexia nervosa from bulimia nervosa: people with bulimia are usually of normal weight or overweight, and a person at a significantly low weight who binges and purges has anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type. asked 2 times Inappropriate compensatory behaviour in bulimia nervosa is self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics or other medications, fasting or excessive exercise; cycles of binge eating and compensation are bulimia nervosa, and binges without compensation are binge-eating disorder. asked 2 times Amenorrhoea means the absence of menstrual periods; it is common in anorexia nervosa, from the starvation shutdown of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, but it entered the criteria in DSM-III-R and was dropped in DSM-5. asked 2 times Enuresis is the repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes, at least twice a week for 3 consecutive months or with significant distress or impairment, at a developmental age of at least 5; night wetting clusters in the first third of the night but is not tied to N3 or any single stage. asked 2 times Bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder both need episodes on average at least once a week for 3 months (DSM-5); DSM-III-R and DSM-IV required twice a week for bulimia, and "6 months" comes only from DSM-IV's provisional criteria for binge-eating disorder. asked 2 times Anorexia nervosa, restricting type: no recurrent binge eating or purging during the last 3 months, with weight lost by dieting, fasting or excessive exercise; the binge-eating/purging type needs recurrent binges or purging, and purging after small meals is enough. asked 2 times ARFID is avoidance or restriction of food (sensory dislike, lack of interest or fear of aversive consequences) causing weight loss, deficiency, supplement dependence or psychosocial interference, with no disturbance of body weight or shape; selective eating without any of these consequences is ordinary picky eating. asked 2 times BMI numbers belong to different systems: DSM-5-TR rates adult severity as mild 17 or more, moderate 16 to 16.99, severe 15 to 15.99 and extreme below 15, with no diagnostic cut-off; ICD-10's threshold is a BMI of 17.5 or less; ICD-11's guide is below 18.5, with "dangerously low" below 14.0. asked 2 times Anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa share a distorted body image, an intense fear of being fat, and eating regulated by psychological rather than physiological processes. asked once Perfectionism, with obsessionality, rigidity and anxiety, is the characteristic trait of anorexia nervosa; impulsivity belongs to bulimia nervosa and to anorexia's binge-eating/purging type. asked once Lack of bowel control in a child is encopresis: repeated passage of faeces into inappropriate places, at least once a month for 3 months, at a developmental age of at least 4; the commoner subtype is with constipation and overflow incontinence. asked once Somnambulism (sleepwalking) is sitting up, walking or other complex behaviour during an incomplete awakening from NREM sleep (mostly N3) in the first third of the night, with a blank stare, difficulty waking and amnesia. asked once Sleep terrors (night terrors, pavor nocturnus) are abrupt arousals from N3 with a panicky scream, intense fear and autonomic arousal, little or no dream recall and amnesia; nightmares come from REM sleep later in the night, with full waking and vivid recall. asked once Restless legs syndrome (Willis-Ekbom disease) is an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, brought on by rest, relieved by movement and worse in the evening, at least three times a week for 3 months; iron deficiency is its most important precipitant. asked once Cataplexy, a sudden, brief, bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion (especially laughter) with consciousness preserved, is the most characteristic sign of narcolepsy; catalepsy, a posture held with waxy flexibility, belongs to catatonia. asked once The narcoleptic tetrad is sleep attacks, cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations (assembled by Yoss and Daly, 1957; narcolepsy named by Gélineau, 1880); narcolepsy type 1 follows the loss of hypothalamic hypocretin (orexin) neurons. asked once Binge-eating disorder, a full diagnosis only since DSM-5, is recurrent binges with three or more of five features (eating rapidly, until uncomfortably full, when not hungry, alone from embarrassment, with disgust or guilt afterwards), marked distress and no recurrent compensatory behaviour. asked once The medical findings of anorexia nervosa are "slow and low": lanugo, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, amenorrhoea, low T3 and, with purging, hypokalaemia; hyperthyroidism, polyphagia, hyperkalaemia and tachycardia are wrong-direction distractors. asked once Anorexia nervosa is the most lethal eating disorder: crude mortality about 5 percent per decade (bulimia nervosa nearly 2 percent) and a standardised mortality ratio of 5.86 (Arcelus and colleagues, 2011), from medical complications and suicide. asked once REM sleep behaviour disorder is the loss of normal REM atonia, so the sleeper acts out dreams and wakes alert with recall; about 75 percent of people with idiopathic RBD develop a synucleinopathy such as Parkinson's disease within 10 to 15 years. asked once Excessive sleepiness despite a main sleep of at least 7 hours, three times a week for 3 months, is hypersomnolence disorder (idiopathic hypersomnia), which never has cataplexy and whose long naps do not refresh. asked once Pica is the persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances for at least 1 month, inappropriate to developmental level (minimum age of 2 suggested) and not culturally sanctioned; it can kill through obstruction or poisoning but is not the most lethal eating disorder. asked once

Disorder: The Science of Sexuality and How the Manuals Classify It : distinguish sex, gender identity, gender role, sexual orientation and androgyny, trace sexology from Krafft-Ebing to Kinsey, and place every disorder of the chapter in DSM-5-TR, ICD-10 and ICD-11. 9.2 The Sexual Response Cycle: Models, Biology and What Disrupts It : compare the linear and circular models of sexual response, explain the nerves, blood vessels, hormones and transmitters behind arousal and orgasm, and show how anxiety, attention, relationships and culture disrupt them. 9.3 Sexual Dysfunctions I: The Shared Rules, and the Disorders of Desire, Arousal and Erection : apply the rules common to the DSM-5-TR sexual dysfunctions, estimate how common they are, and diagnose and treat female sexual interest/arousal disorder, male hypoactive sexual desire disorder and erectile disorder, including the PDE-5 inhibitors. 9.4 Sexual Dysfunctions II: Orgasm, Ejaculation, Pain and Substance-Induced Dysfunction : diagnose female orgasmic disorder, delayed and premature ejaculation, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder and substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction, explain their causes and match each to its drug and psychological treatments. 9.5 Paraphilias and Paraphilic Disorders: From Perversion to Disorder : define a paraphilia and a paraphilic disorder, trace the idea from Krafft-Ebing to DSM-5-TR, and explain how ICD-11 rebuilt the group around consent. 9.6 The Eight Paraphilic Disorders and the Other Paraphilias : diagnose the courtship, algolagnic and target-preference disorders by their focus, criteria and specifiers, and tell fetishism, transvestism and autogynephilia apart from the other named paraphilias. 9.7 Why Paraphilic Disorders Develop, and How They Are Assessed and Treated : evaluate conditioning, developmental and biological explanations of paraphilias, describe phallometric and actuarial assessment, and explain the psychological and hormonal treatments and their evidence. 9.8 Becoming Male or Female: Sexual Differentiation and Gender Identity : explain how chromosomes, gonads and hormones build male and female bodies, what the differences of sex development teach, and what the Reimer case shows about the origins of gender identity. 9.9 Gender Dysphoria and Gender Incongruence : trace the diagnosis from transsexualism to gender dysphoria and gender incongruence, apply the DSM-5-TR criteria for children and for adolescents and adults, and describe its course, causes, gender-affirming care and the Indian legal context. 9.10 Homosexuality: Pathologised and Depathologised : explain how homosexuality entered and left the DSM and the ICD, the evidence from Kinsey and Hooker that changed minds, what science now says about sexual orientation, and the Indian story from Section 377 to Navtej Singh Johar. Weightage. 9 of the 411 questions mapped in this book (2.2%) test this chapter, 8 of them from real past papers. 0 of its 10 sections are High yield. In Winnipeg, Canada, on 22 August 1965, Janet and Ron Reimer became the parents of identical twin boys, Bruce and Brian. When the babies were about six months old, the doctors found that both had phimosis, a foreskin too tight to be drawn back, and both were booked for circumcision, an ordinary operation. On 27 April 1966 Bruce, a baby of about eight months, went first. The doctor used an electrocautery device, an instrument that cuts by burning tissue with an electric current, and the current destroyed the baby's penis. Brian was never operated on; his phimosis cleared up by itself. The parents were told that there was no satisfactory way of surgically replacing what their son had lost. Early in 1967, after seeing him interviewed on Canadian television, the Reimers took Bruce to the Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore to meet John Money (1921 to 2006), a psychologist and sexologist famous for his work with children born with intersex conditions. Money believed that a child's sense of being a boy or a girl is not fixed at birth. It is learned, he argued, from the way the child is reared, and it firms up between about 18 months and 3 years of age. His advice followed from that belief. Bruce should be castrated and raised as a girl; an artificial vagina could be made later; and oestrogen given at puberty would feminise the body. After a great deal of anguish, the parents agreed. At 22 months Bruce's testes were removed, and Bruce became Brenda. The case looked like a perfect natural experiment, because Brenda had a genetically identical twin brother who was being raised as a boy: two children with the same genes and the same hormones before birth, reared as different sexes. Some saw it as the ultimate test of nature and nurture in the making of gender. Money described the case in Man and Woman, Boy and Girl , the book he published with Anke Ehrhardt in 1972, and again in a 1975 report written when the child was 9. "She", he reported, had developed as a typical girl, and he took the outcome as strong support for his social-learning theory of gender identity. For years the case was cited as evidence that gender identity is learned. Inside the Reimer home the story was very different. From an early age Brenda preferred boys' games and showed little interest in dolls or sewing. At four she refused to put on her mother's make-up and demanded to shave like her father; by seven she felt like a boy, tried to urinate standing up and sometimes went to the boys' lavatory. Teased by the other girls, she fought back and was expelled from school. When oestrogen treatment began at 12 she rebelled: she hated her developing breasts and refused to wear a bra. At 14 she told her parents that she was so miserable she was thinking of suicide, and on 14 March 1980 her father told her the truth. She decided to live as a boy and took the name David. In the words of one account, "all of a sudden everything clicked": for the first time he understood who and what he was. David later had testosterone treatment, a mastectomy and operations to construct a penis (phalloplasty). On 22 September 1990, at 25, he married Jane, and he adopted her three children. His early castration had permanently taken away his ability to father children of his own. The world learned what had really happened in 1997. In March of that year Milton Diamond, a sexologist at the University of Hawaii, and H. Keith Sigmundson, the psychiatrist who had once supervised the case, published a long-term follow-up, "Sex reassignment at birth: long-term review and clinical implications", in the Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine . The case had been known in medical writing by the pseudonym "John/Joan", and the follow-up reversed its lesson: the child had rejected the sex of rearing and had switched to living as a male. In December 1997 the journalist John Colapinto told the story in Rolling Stone , and in 2000 he expanded it into a book, As Nature Made Him: The Boy Who Was Raised as a Girl , which David helped to write "to save others from his experience". The scars never healed. In 2002 his twin brother died, and on 4 May 2004, amid several other losses, David Reimer died by suicide. He was 38. His life raises the questions at the heart of this chapter. What is the difference between a person's sex and a person's gender identity? Where does the sense of being a man or a woman come from, and can surgery, hormones and upbringing change it? When does a mismatch between body and identity count as a disorder, and who decides? And how do these questions differ from the problems of sexual response and of sexual interest that share this chapter with them? Sections 9.1, 9.8 and 9.9 take them up. Remember Bruce, who became Brenda and then David: you will return to him at the end of the chapter. 9.1 Sex, Gender and Disorder: The Science of Sexuality and How the Manuals Classify It Lower yield · 1 Q No other chapter of this book has had its borders redrawn as often as this one. Within living memory, the same psychiatric manuals have listed homosexuality as a disorder and then removed it, called a woman with little interest in sex "frigid" and then dropped the word, filed a person's sense of being a man or a woman beside fetishism and exhibitionism and then moved it out of the mental disorders altogether. Each change was argued over in journals, committees and, sometimes, the streets. To follow the rest of the chapter you need three things from this first section: a precise vocabulary for sex and gender, a sense of where the science of sexuality came from, and a map of where each disorder lives in DSM-5-TR, ICD-10 and ICD-11 and how it got there. Three families under one roof Picture the outpatient department of a large teaching hospital in an Indian city on an ordinary Tuesday morning. The sexual medicine clinic and the psychiatry clinic share a corridor, and four people are waiting to be seen. Chetan is 27 and has been married for four months. He is a confident man at work, but in the bedroom he ejaculates within seconds of entering his wife, every time, long before either of them wants him to. He now dreads each attempt; he has begun to make excuses to stay late at the office, and his wife has started to wonder whether he finds her unattractive. Ambika, 24, has been married for a year, and her marriage has never been consummated. She loves her husband and wants a child, but whenever intercourse is attempted her body tightens, she feels a wave of panic and penetration becomes impossible. Her mother-in-law has begun to ask pointed questions about grandchildren. Omkar, 34, has not come by choice. A magistrate's court has referred him for assessment after his second arrest for pressing himself against women in crowded buses, and his lawyer has told him that a report from the hospital may affect his sentence. He says he does not know why he keeps doing it. Trisha is 23. She was assigned male at birth, has lived as a woman for the last three years, and has come with a letter from her general practitioner asking for a psychological assessment before she starts hormone treatment. She is calm, articulate and tired of explaining herself. All four are, in a broad sense, "sexual" cases, and fifty years ago a psychiatrist might have filed them under a single heading. Look more closely, though, and you will see three quite different kinds of problem. Chetan and Ambika have problems of sexual function : the body's sexual response does not go the way the person wants it to. Each of them is attracted to an adult partner who wants the same thing they want; what fails is the response itself. These are the sexual dysfunctions , defined by DSM-5-TR as a group of disorders typically marked by a clinically significant disturbance in a person's ability to respond sexually or to experience sexual pleasure. Omkar's problem is of a different kind. His response works perfectly well; what is unusual is what arouses him, and the fact that acting on it involves people who have not consented. That is a problem of sexual interest and its consequences, and it belongs to the paraphilic disorders . Trisha's situation is not sexual at all. It concerns her gender identity , her sense of herself as a woman, and the distress that can arise when that identity does not match the sex recorded at birth and the body that came with it. The diagnosis for that distress, when it reaches clinical significance, is gender dysphoria . As Barlow and Durand put it, the condition "is not sexual but rather a disturbance in the person's sense of being a male or a female". The manuals have slowly come round to this view. As late as DSM-IV and its text revision, all three families still shared one chapter, "sexual and gender identity disorders". DSM-5 gave each its own: sexual dysfunctions became chapter 13 of Section II, gender dysphoria chapter 14, and the paraphilic disorders chapter 19, placed after the personality disorders near the end of the list (the full order of the twenty chapters is in Section 1.8.2). ICD-11 went further and moved two of the three families out of the mental disorders chapter altogether, as Section 9.1.6 explains. Figure 9.1 is the map of this chapter: the three families, the disorders in each, the sections of this chapter that teach them and the ICD-11 chapter in which each family now lives. Sexual dysfunctions DSM-5-TR chapter 13 Sections 9.2 to 9.4 Paraphilic disorders DSM-5-TR chapter 19 Sections 9.5 to 9.7 Gender dysphoria DSM-5-TR chapter 14 Sections 9.8 and 9.9 Delayed ejaculation Erectile disorder Female orgasmic disorder Female sexual interest/ arousal disorder Genito-pelvic pain/ penetration disorder Male hypoactive sexual desire disorder Premature (early) ejaculation Substance/medication- induced Courtship disorders Voyeuristic disorder Exhibitionistic disorder Frotteuristic disorder Pain and suffering Sexual masochism disorder Sexual sadism disorder Anomalous targets Pedophilic disorder Fetishistic disorder Transvestic disorder Other specified In children In adolescents and adults Other specified Unspecified Specifiers With a disorder/ difference of sex development Posttransition (adolescents and adults) A problem of identity, not of sexual response ICD-11 Chapter 17 HA00 to HA03, HA20 ICD-11 Chapter 6 6D30 to 6D3Z ICD-11 Chapter 17 HA60 and HA61 ICD-11 Chapter 6: mental disorders. Chapter 17: conditions related to sexual health. Figure 9.1 The map of this chapter. Each column is one DSM-5-TR family, with the sections of this chapter that teach it; the grey labels in the middle column are the three groups into which the paraphilic disorders fall (Section 9.6). Notice the bottom row: in ICD-11 only the paraphilic disorders remain among the mental disorders. Section 9.1 covers the ground all three share, and Section 9.10 tells the story of homosexuality, which is no longer a diagnosis anywhere. Why should a clinical psychologist care about this chapter? There are four good reasons. The first is that sexual problems are common and mostly hidden. Population surveys find that a large minority of adults report a sexual difficulty in any given year (the figures are in Section 9.3.2), yet very few raise it with a doctor, and fewer still with a psychologist. In India, where talking about sex is often difficult even between spouses, the silence is deeper; a man may visit a roadside "sex clinic" or buy a herbal tonic long before he tells anyone in a hospital. The second reason is that sexual problems rarely travel alone. They come with depression and anxiety, with marital conflict, with diabetes, heart disease and other physical illness, and with the medicines used to treat all of these, including many of the antidepressants and antipsychotics a psychologist's clients take every day (Sections 5.7.2 and 4.10.5). A clinician who never asks will never know, and the sexual history is a standard part of the personal history for exactly this reason (Book 2, Section 2.3.6, which notes that worry about semen loss is common among young Indian men). The third reason is forensic: courts, prisons and probation services refer men like Omkar for assessment, and the psychologist's report may affect a sentence or a decision about risk. The fourth is that more and more gender-diverse people like Trisha are seeking psychological assessment and support, and the clinician who meets them needs to know what the manuals now say, and why they changed. Clinical link Each of the four people in the waiting room needs a different kind of help. Chetan and Ambika need a careful sexual and medical history, a check for physical causes, and a treatment aimed at the response that has gone wrong (Sections 9.4.3 and 9.4.4). Omkar needs an assessment of what arouses him, of how often and how far he has acted on it, and of the risk he poses to others (Section 9.7). Trisha does not need anyone to change her identity; she needs an assessment of her gender history, of any distress she feels, of her mental health in general and of her readiness for the treatment she is asking for (Section 9.9). Putting them all in one box, as the older manuals did, would have led to the wrong question being asked of at least three of them. The vocabulary of sex and gender Before anything else, you need words that mean one thing each. This is harder than it sounds. In English the word "sex" means both being male or female and sexual activity; the word "gender" was borrowed from grammar in the twentieth century and has been used in a dozen ways since; and the vocabulary of gender identity has grown quickly in recent years. DSM-5-TR itself admits that the area "is highly controversial and has led to a proliferation of terms whose meanings vary over time and within and between disciplines". The sensible course is to learn the definitions the manual uses, because those are the ones the examiners use, and to notice what each term includes and leaves out. Start with the body. In DSM-5-TR, sex refers to the biological indicators of male and female, understood in relation to reproductive capacity: the sex chromosomes (usually XX or XY), the gonads (ovaries or testes), the sex hormones, and the internal and external genitalia. In most people these indicators line up with one another. In some they do not: a child may have XY chromosomes and testes but a body that cannot respond to testosterone, or genitals that are neither typically male nor typically female. These are the disorders of sex development (also called differences of sex development, DSDs, and once called intersex conditions), and Section 9.8.4 teaches them in full. For now notice only that "sex" is not one fact but a bundle of facts, which usually, but not always, agree. When a baby is born, somebody looks at the genitals and says "It's a boy" or "It's a girl". DSM-5-TR calls this gender assignment, and the result is the person's assigned gender , usually the birth-assigned gender. The manual notes that this used to be called "biological sex" and, more recently, "natal gender", and it has moved away from both terms. "Biological sex" suggests one simple biological fact, where in reality there are several indicators that can disagree; "natal" suggests that gender is fixed at birth. Calling it an assignment is more accurate, because it is a decision made by other people from one visible indicator, and the American Psychiatric Association described the change, in DSM-5-TR, as a move to more culturally sensitive language (so "natal male" became "individual assigned male at birth"). Assigned gender also covers assignments and reassignments made later in infancy or early childhood, usually in children with DSDs. Brenda, in the opening story, is the textbook case of these layers coming apart: her chromosomes and early hormones were male, her assigned gender after the age of 22 months was female, and her own sense of herself, as she grew up, was male. Gender , in DSM-5-TR, is the public, sociocultural and usually legally recognised lived role as a boy or a girl, a man or a woman, or another gender. Biology contributes to it, the manual says, but always in interaction with social and psychological factors. Gender identity is something more private: it is "a category of social identity", a person's identification of himself or herself as male, as female, as something in between (sometimes called gender fluid) or as something other than male or female (sometimes called gender neutral). Nobody can see another person's gender identity; you learn it by listening to what the person tells you about themselves. Trisha's gender identity is female, whatever is written on her birth certificate. Two further terms describe how gender is lived in public. A gender role is the set of behaviours, tasks and attitudes that a society expects of people of each gender. In many Indian households it is still taken for granted that the wife will cook and the husband will earn, and a man who stays at home while his wife runs a business may be teased by his relatives; in other families the same arrangement raises no eyebrows at all, and expectations shift from one generation to the next. Gender expression is the way a person presents gender to the world: dress, hair, name, voice, manner. A person's expression may follow the local gender role closely or not at all, and neither tells you for certain what the person's identity or orientation is. Behaviour that departs from the usual pattern for one's assigned gender is called gender-atypical or gender-nonconforming , and DSM-5-TR is careful to define it as atypical "in a statistical sense" for people of the same assigned gender "in a given society and historical era". The qualification matters. A girl in Mysuru who plays cricket with the boys and refuses to wear a frock is gender-nonconforming by the standards of some families today; a woman in trousers was gender-nonconforming in much of the world a century ago and is unremarkable now. Gender nonconformity is not a diagnosis and not the same thing as gender dysphoria. When a person's gender identity differs from the gender assigned at birth, the person is transgender ; DSM-5-TR uses the word for "the broad spectrum of individuals" whose identity differs in this way. A person whose gender is congruent with the birth-assigned gender is cisgender (the manual also gives "nontransgender"). An older word, transsexual , is described by DSM-5-TR as "a historic term" for a person who seeks, is undergoing or has undergone a social transition from male to female or female to male, which often but not always includes gender-affirming hormones or surgery. You will still meet it in older books and in ICD-10, whose diagnosis F64.0 is called "transsexualism". Gender identity is about who you are. Sexual orientation is about whom you are attracted to: the sex or gender of the people a person finds sexually and romantically attractive. People attracted mainly to the other sex are heterosexual, those attracted mainly to their own sex are homosexual (gay men and lesbian women), and those attracted to both are bisexual. People who feel little or no sexual attraction to anyone may describe themselves as asexual, and asexuality has an important place in DSM-5-TR: if a lifelong lack of sexual desire is better explained by the person's self-identification as asexual, the manual says, a diagnosis of female sexual interest/arousal disorder or of male hypoactive sexual desire disorder is not made (Section 9.3). Orientation and identity vary independently. As Pinel and Barnes put it, "sexual orientation, gender identity, and body type are sometimes unrelated": some transgender people are attracted to women, some to men and some to neither, and transition does not change that. The last term in this family is the one examiners like to slip in as a distractor. In the early 1970s most psychologists, and most personality tests, treated masculinity and femininity as the two ends of a single scale: the more masculine you were, the less feminine you had to be. The masculinity-femininity scale of the MMPI, for example, was scored that way. Sandra Lipsitz Bem (1944 to 2014), then at Stanford University, argued that this was a mistake. A person can be both assertive and gentle, both independent and affectionate. Masculinity and femininity, she proposed, are two separate dimensions, and a person who scores high on both is psychologically androgynous. Androgyny (from the Greek words for "man" and "woman") is therefore a blend of personality traits that the culture labels masculine and feminine. It describes personality, not the body, not gender identity and not sexual orientation, and it is not a disorder of any kind. Key study: Bem's measurement of psychological androgyny (1974) The question. Can masculinity and femininity be measured as two independent dimensions, so that a person can be high on both? The method. Bem built the Bem Sex Role Inventory , published in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology in 1974 under the title "The measurement of psychological androgyny". It has 60 personality adjectives: 20 judged more desirable for a man than a woman in American society of the time (such as self-reliant, assertive and willing to take risks), 20 judged more desirable for a woman (such as affectionate, gentle and sympathetic) and 20 neutral fillers. The person rates how true each adjective is of him or her on a 7-point scale, and masculinity and femininity are scored separately. The result. The two scores were largely independent of each other, and many people scored high on both. Bem and her colleagues then reported that androgynous people of both sexes behaved more flexibly: they showed "masculine" independence when pressed to conform and "feminine" nurturance when playing with a kitten, while strongly sex-typed people were low on one or both. The criticism. Later scoring split people into four groups: masculine, feminine, androgynous (high on both) and undifferentiated (low on both), a distinction drawn by Janet Taylor Spence and her colleagues. The claim that androgyny is the healthiest pattern did not survive well. When Bernard E. Whitley pooled 35 studies of sex role and self-esteem in a 1983 meta-analysis, the results best supported a "masculinity model": self-esteem rose with the masculine (assertive, instrumental) score, not with androgyny as such. The adjectives are also tied to one culture and one era. Bem herself moved on to gender schema theory (1981), the idea that sex-typed people process the world through a ready-made mental category of what is masculine and feminine; that theory belongs to the Developmental and Personality books, and the inventory as a test to the Assessment book.
