The distractors are each something else: a paraphilia concerns what arouses a person, a sexual dysfunction concerns the sexual response, and androgyny is a blend of masculine and feminine personality traits that Bem measured in 1974. Androgyny is never a diagnosis. The birth of sexology For most of European history, sexual behaviour was the business of the church and the courts. It was judged as sin or as crime, and the experts on it were priests and judges. In the second half of the nineteenth century that began to change. Doctors, and psychiatrists in particular, claimed sexual behaviour as a medical subject, and a new science of sexuality, sexology , was born. Its founders were few, and each is remembered for one big idea. You will meet their detailed contributions later in the chapter, where they belong; here you need to know who they were. The first and most influential was Richard von Krafft-Ebing (1840 to 1902), a German psychiatrist who held chairs of psychiatry at Strasbourg, Graz and finally Vienna. In 1886 he published Psychopathia Sexualis , a forensic reference book written for psychiatrists, physicians and judges who had to decide what to do with people brought before them for sexual offences. To keep it out of the hands of curious lay readers he gave it a scientific Latin title and wrote some passages in Latin. The book grew with every edition; the last that Krafft-Ebing prepared himself, the twelfth, held 238 case histories. Krafft-Ebing believed that the purpose of sexual desire was reproduction, so that any sexual behaviour that could not lead to reproduction was a perversion, and he explained most perversions as signs of an inherited "degeneration" of the nervous system, an idea he took from French psychiatry. He also gave medicine two of its lasting words. He coined masochism , the finding of sexual pleasure in being hurt or humiliated, from the name of the Austrian novelist Leopold von Sacher-Masoch (1836 to 1895), whose novel Venus in Furs (1870) describes a man who longs to be dominated by a woman. And he brought into medicine the word sadism , the finding of sexual pleasure in hurting others, named after the French writer the Marquis de Sade (1740 to 1814); "sadism" was already in use in French, so Krafft-Ebing turned it into a diagnosis rather than inventing it. Section 9.5.3 tells how his catalogue shaped every later list of paraphilias. Henry Havelock Ellis (1859 to 1939) was an English physician and writer who approached sex less as a court doctor and more as a naturalist. His Studies in the Psychology of Sex began to appear in 1897 and eventually ran to seven volumes, the last in 1928. The volume called Sexual Inversion , written with the poet and critic John Addington Symonds , appeared first in German in 1896 and in English in 1897; it was the first English medical textbook on homosexuality, and it did not treat homosexuality as a disease, a vice or a crime. A London bookseller was prosecuted for selling it. Ellis also wrote about "auto-erotism", and in 1920 he coined "eonism", after a famous eighteenth-century French cross-dresser, as his name for what others were calling transvestism. Ellis's ideas on homosexuality are taken further in Section 9.10.2. Magnus Hirschfeld (1868 to 1935) was a Berlin physician who combined research with campaigning. In 1897 he co-founded the Scientific-Humanitarian Committee to fight Paragraph 175, the German law that made sex between men a crime (Section 9.10.2). In Die Transvestiten (1910) he coined the word "transvestite" for people who wear the clothes of the other sex, and in 1923 he used the word "transsexual". On 6 July 1919 he opened the Institute for Sexual Science (Institut für Sexualwissenschaft) in Berlin, one of the first institutes of its kind, with a library, a clinic and a large practice with transgender patients; some of the earliest gender-affirming operations were carried out there (Section 9.9.1). On 6 May 1933, three months after the Nazis came to power, Nazi students stormed the institute and carried off its library, and its books were thrown on the fire in the Berlin book burning of 10 May 1933. Hirschfeld, who was Jewish and was then abroad, never returned to Germany; he died in exile in Nice in 1935. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) made his contribution in a single short book, Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905). Its first shock was the claim that sexuality does not begin at puberty but in infancy. Its second was that the young child's sexuality is "polymorphously perverse": not yet tied to the genitals or to any one kind of partner, it can take pleasure from many parts of the body and in many ways. The adult "perversions", in Freud's account, are what happens when development gets stuck at, or falls back to, one of these early childhood forms, so that the pervert is not a different kind of creature but an ordinary person whose development took a particular turn. Freud famously added that the neuroses are, so to say, the negative of the perversions: what the pervert acts out, the neurotic represses. The psychosexual stages that grew out of this book belong to the Personality book. The twentieth century brought counting and measuring. Alfred Charles Kinsey (1894 to 1956), a zoologist at Indiana University, set aside case histories of patients and asked thousands of ordinary volunteers, face to face, what they actually did. His two reports, Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953), and the criticism that his volunteers were not a representative sample, are told in Book 1, Section 10.9.6; his famous 0 to 6 scale and what it showed about homosexuality are taught in Section 9.10.3. Where Kinsey asked, the gynaecologist William Howell Masters (1915 to 2001) and his research partner Virginia Eshelman Johnson (1925 to 2013) watched: in Human Sexual Response (1966) they described the body's sexual response, recorded in the laboratory, as a cycle of four phases, and in Human Sexual Inadequacy (1970) they described how to treat its failures (Book 1, Section 10.9.6, and Book 2, Section 7.9; their model is the starting point of Section 9.2). Later surveys replaced Kinsey's volunteers with random samples of the population. The best known, the National Health and Social Life Survey, was carried out in 1992 by a team led by Edward Laumann at the University of Chicago and reported in The Social Organization of Sexuality (1994); what it found about how common sexual problems are is told in Section 9.3.2. India has its own long history of writing about desire. The best known text is the Kamasutra attributed to Vatsyayana , whose date is unknown; historians have placed it anywhere between about 400 BCE and 300 CE, most often in the early centuries of the Common Era. It is often mistaken for a manual of sexual positions, but it is a much broader guide to love, courtship, marriage and pleasure, treated as one of the legitimate aims of a good life. The colonial period brought a very different attitude: the Indian Penal Code of 1860 made "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" a crime under Section 377, a law whose story ends in the Supreme Court in 2018 (Section 9.10.8). Today, sexual medicine in India is shaped by both inheritances. Sexual clinics see far more men than women (Section 9.3.2), many of the men come with anxieties about semen loss and potency that are rooted in traditional beliefs about the body (dhat syndrome, Section 1.10.4), and the women who need help most often never come at all. Exam trap Krafft-Ebing wrote Psychopathia Sexualis ( 1886 ), not Ellis or Freud. He coined "masochism" (from Sacher-Masoch), but "sadism" (from de Sade) was already a French word that he turned into a diagnosis. Hirschfeld coined "transvestite" (1910) and founded the first Institute for Sexual Science (1919); Ellis coined "eonism" for the same behaviour. Freud's Three Essays date from 1905 . Keep the methods apart: Kinsey (1948, 1953) interviewed people about what they did; Masters and Johnson (1966) observed and recorded the body's response in the laboratory. What makes sexual behaviour a disorder Chapter 1 (Section 1.1) and Book 2 (Section 1.6, with the four Ds in Section 1.6.5) set out the criteria that clinicians use to decide what counts as abnormal: statistical rarity, the breaking of social norms, personal distress, impaired functioning and danger to oneself or others. Sexual behaviour is the hardest test of those criteria, and watching them strain here teaches you more about them than any definition. Take statistical rarity first. It fails in both directions. When Kinsey asked ordinary Americans what they did, he found that many behaviours that the law and the churches condemned, from masturbation to sex before marriage to same-sex experience, were common (Section 9.10.3); if rarity were the test, they could not be disorders, and yet the textbooks of the day treated several of them as exactly that. And the reverse holds too. A rare sexual interest, such as being aroused by a particular kind of shoe, may be enjoyed in private, with a willing partner, and harm nobody. Rarity alone tells you nothing about whether anything is wrong. Social norms fare no better, because they differ so much from one society to another. In the 1980s the anthropologist Gilbert Herdt described the Sambia of Papua New Guinea, among whom boys took part in ritual same-sex practices as part of their initiation into manhood and then, as young men, married and lived exclusively heterosexual lives. In about half of more than a hundred societies surveyed around the world, sex before marriage is accepted and even encouraged; in the other half it is forbidden. Within India itself, what is acceptable differs between communities, between cities and villages, and between grandparents and grandchildren. If breaking the local norm made a disorder, the same act would be healthy in one place and sick in another. History makes the same point. Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century doctors taught that masturbation caused physical decline and even insanity, and the belief survives in the fears about semen loss that bring young men to clinics in India today (Section 1.10.4). The words "nymphomania" and "frigidity" sound like relics, yet they were still printed as inclusion terms in the World Health Organization's ICD-10, under "excessive sexual drive" (F52.7, which also lists "satyriasis") and "lack or loss of sexual desire" (F52.0); neither survives as a diagnostic term in ICD-11. Medicine's idea of normal sexuality has moved with the moral climate of its time. Personal distress is more useful, and the manuals lean on it heavily: most sexual dysfunctions are diagnosed only when they cause clinically significant distress (Section 9.3.1). But distress has a trap of its own. A person may be distressed not because anything is wrong with them but because the people around them say there is. A gay man in a hostile family may hate his own orientation, and in 1980 DSM-III gave that distress a diagnosis, "ego-dystonic homosexuality"; the diagnosis was dropped in 1987 when critics pointed out that it medicalised the effects of stigma (Section 9.10.4, and Section 2.1.9 for the terms ego-syntonic and ego-dystonic). DSM-5-TR has learned the lesson: gender dysphoria, it says, "does not refer to distress related to stigma", which is a distinct, though possibly co-occurring, source of distress. That leaves harm and consent , and for sexual behaviour these turn out to be the decisive criteria. Omkar's problem is not that his interest is rare, or that his community disapproves of it, or even that he feels bad about it; it is that he acts on it with women who have not agreed and are frightened and humiliated by it. Harm to others, and the absence of consent, is what separates a paraphilic disorder from a harmless paraphilia in DSM-5-TR (Section 9.5.2), and it is the organising idea of the whole group of paraphilic disorders in ICD-11 (Section 9.5.4). The manuals now build these lessons into their definition of a mental disorder. DSM-5-TR's definition (Section 1.1.3) requires a dysfunction in the psychological, biological or developmental processes underlying mental functioning, and it adds that socially deviant behaviour, naming political, religious and sexual deviance as examples, and conflicts that are primarily between the individual and society are not mental disorders unless they result from such a dysfunction in the individual. Three of the biggest changes DSM-5 made in this chapter follow directly from that sentence. A paraphilia is not, by itself, a disorder; only a paraphilia that causes distress or impairment, or harm or risk of harm to others, is a paraphilic disorder (Section 9.5.2). A gender identity is not a disorder; only the clinically significant distress or impairment that may accompany incongruence is diagnosed (Section 9.9.2). And a sexual difficulty becomes a dysfunction only if it is persistent, happens on most occasions and causes distress, not because it falls short of somebody's idea of normal performance (Section 9.3.1). Indian context The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 writes the same principles into Indian law. Section 3(1) says that mental illness is to be determined according to nationally or internationally accepted medical standards, including the latest edition of the WHO's International Classification of Diseases, and section 3(3) says that mental illness shall not be determined on the basis of "non-conformity with moral, social, cultural, work or political values or religious beliefs prevailing in a person's community" (Book 2, Section 1.6.2). The Act also guarantees the right to mental health care without discrimination on the basis of "gender, sex, sexual orientation, religion, culture, caste" and other grounds (section 18(2)), and equal treatment with persons with physical illness, with "no discrimination on any basis including gender, sex, sexual orientation" (section 21(1)(a)). A clinician in India who treats a client's orientation or gender identity as an illness is out of step not only with the manuals but with the law. Exam trap Being gay, lesbian or bisexual, being transgender, or having an unusual sexual interest that harms nobody is not, by itself, a mental disorder in DSM-5-TR or ICD-11. What can be diagnosed is a persistent problem of sexual response with distress (a sexual dysfunction), an atypical interest that causes distress or impairment or harms or endangers others (a paraphilic disorder), or clinically significant distress or impairment linked to gender incongruence (gender dysphoria). Statistical rarity and social disapproval are never enough. From "sexual deviation" to three chapters: the DSM story The American manuals have reorganised this territory in almost every edition, and each reorganisation tells you what psychiatry thought sex and gender were at the time. Table 9.2 sets out the story edition by edition; the general history of the editions is in Sections 1.7.2 and 1.7.4, and the detailed histories of the paraphilias, of the gender diagnosis and of homosexuality are in Sections 9.5.3, 9.9.1 and 9.10.4. The first two editions had no chapter on sex at all. In DSM-I (1952) homosexuality and the other "sexual deviations" were listed as a form of sociopathic personality disturbance, the same family as antisocial behaviour. The message was that sexual variation was a defect of character, a failure to fit into society. Problems of sexual function hardly appeared: impotence and frigidity were mentioned only as psychophysiological reactions, physical complaints in which emotional factors were thought to play a part. DSM-II (1968) kept the same plan. It listed the sexual deviations (homosexuality, fetishism, pedophilia, transvestitism, exhibitionism, voyeurism, sadism and masochism, with "other" and "unspecified") among the "personality disorders and certain other non-psychotic mental disorders", and it mentioned dyspareunia (painful intercourse) and impotence only as examples of a psychophysiologic genito-urinary disorder "in which emotional factors play a causative role". After the American Psychiatric Association's decision of December 1973, the seventh printing of DSM-II in 1974 replaced homosexuality with "sexual orientation disturbance", a diagnosis for people distressed by their orientation (Section 9.10.4). Neither edition had any diagnosis for gender identity. DSM-III (1980) changed everything. For the first time, sexuality had a class of its own, the psychosexual disorders , divided into four groups. The first was the gender identity disorders: transsexualism, for adults, and gender identity disorder of childhood. The second was the paraphilias, the word now entering the DSM in place of "sexual deviation"; the list included fetishism, transvestism, zoophilia, pedophilia, exhibitionism, voyeurism, sexual masochism and sexual sadism. The third was the psychosexual dysfunctions, the first time problems of sexual response had a group of their own: inhibited sexual desire, inhibited sexual excitement, inhibited female orgasm, inhibited male orgasm, premature ejaculation, functional dyspareunia and functional vaginismus. Notice the logic of that list. It follows the phases of the sexual response cycle, desire, excitement and orgasm, with pain added at the end, the phases that Masters and Johnson and then Helen Singer Kaplan had described (Section 9.2.2); the dysfunctions have been sorted by the phase they disrupt ever since. The fourth group, "other psychosexual disorders", held ego-dystonic homosexuality, the successor of sexual orientation disturbance. DSM-III-R (1987) renamed the class "sexual disorders" (paraphilias and sexual dysfunctions) and moved the gender identity disorders out of it altogether, into the disorders usually first evident in infancy, childhood or adolescence, and added gender identity disorder of adolescence or adulthood, nontranssexual type. It dropped ego-dystonic homosexuality, added frotteurism to the paraphilias and stopped naming zoophilia as a separate paraphilia. It also renamed most of the dysfunctions: inhibited sexual desire was split into hypoactive sexual desire disorder and sexual aversion disorder, and inhibited sexual excitement became female sexual arousal disorder and male erectile disorder. DSM-IV (1994) and its text revision, DSM-IV-TR (2000), reunited the three families in one class, sexual and gender identity disorders . The dysfunctions were grouped by phase (desire, arousal, orgasm, pain); the orgasm disorders became female orgasmic disorder and male orgasmic disorder; and two new kinds of dysfunction, due to a general medical condition and substance-induced, were added. There were eight named paraphilias, with transvestism renamed transvestic fetishism. Transsexualism and gender identity disorder of childhood were merged into a single gender identity disorder, diagnosed in children or in adolescents or adults. DSM-5 (2013) broke the class into three chapters. Sexual dysfunctions (chapter 13) were rebuilt around the sexes: in women, the old desire and arousal disorders were merged into female sexual interest/arousal disorder, and vaginismus and dyspareunia into genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, both new in DSM-5; in men there were male hypoactive sexual desire disorder, erectile disorder, delayed ejaculation (the old male orgasmic disorder) and premature (early) ejaculation; sexual aversion disorder disappeared as a named disorder (DSM-5-TR now gives it only as an example of "other specified sexual dysfunction"); and most of the dysfunctions acquired explicit rules of duration and frequency (Section 9.3.1). Gender identity disorder became gender dysphoria (chapter 14), a change Section 9.9 explains. The paraphilias became the paraphilic disorders (chapter 19), with "disorder" added to each name (transvestic fetishism became transvestic disorder) and, most important of all, a formal distinction between a paraphilia and a paraphilic disorder (Section 9.5.2). DSM-5-TR (2022) kept the same chapters and, in substance, the same criteria and revised the text; in gender dysphoria (in the text and in the wording of the posttransition specifier) it replaced "desired gender" with "experienced gender", "cross-sex" hormones and procedures with "gender-affirming" ones, and "natal male" and "natal female" with "individual assigned male (or female) at birth". Because they are different kinds of problem, as the waiting room in Section 9.1.1 showed. Sexual dysfunctions are problems of response; paraphilic disorders are problems of interest and of the harm that acting on it may do; gender dysphoria is a problem of identity and the distress that may come with it. Barlow and Durand put the first point bluntly: paraphilic disorders "have little to do with sexual dysfunctions except for the fact that they both involve sexual behavior". The second point is more serious. Keeping gender identity disorder in the same class as fetishism and exhibitionism implied that being transgender was a kind of sexual deviation, a message that clinicians and transgender people alike had come to find both wrong and harmful. Giving gender dysphoria a chapter of its own, and placing it far from the paraphilic disorders, was a statement that it is not one. Exam trap DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR have three separate chapters : sexual dysfunctions (13), gender dysphoria (14) and paraphilic disorders (19). The paraphilic disorders chapter comes after the personality disorders , near the end of Section II, not next to the sexual dysfunctions. The one combined class, "sexual and gender identity disorders", belongs to DSM-IV and DSM-IV-TR ; DSM-III's class was "psychosexual disorders". The word paraphilia entered the DSM in 1980 ; DSM-I and DSM-II said "sexual deviation". There was no gender identity diagnosis at all before DSM-III. The ICD: from F52, F64, F65 and F66 to Chapter 17 The World Health Organization's classification tells a parallel story, and in the end a more radical one. How ICD-10 and ICD-11 are built, and when they came into use, is explained in Sections 1.9.4 to 1.9.6: ICD-10 was endorsed in 1990, and ICD-11 was adopted by the World Health Assembly in May 2019 and came into force on 1 January 2022. This subsection follows the sexual and gender diagnoses from one to the other, and it is one of the most examined pages in the chapter. ICD-10's Chapter V, the chapter of mental and behavioural disorders, spread them across four blocks. The first, F52 , was "sexual dysfunction, not caused by organic disorder or disease", and it sat among the behavioural syndromes associated with physiological disturbances (F50 to F59, beside the eating and sleep disorders). It held F52.0 lack or loss of sexual desire (which included "frigidity"), F52.1 sexual aversion and lack of sexual enjoyment, F52.2 failure of genital response (erectile failure in men, failure of lubrication in women), F52.3 orgasmic dysfunction, F52.4 premature ejaculation, F52.5 nonorganic vaginismus, F52.6 nonorganic dyspareunia, F52.7 excessive sexual drive, and the residual F52.8 and F52.9. The other three blocks sat among the disorders of adult personality and behaviour (F60 to F69). F64 , gender identity disorders, held F64.0 transsexualism, F64.1 dual-role transvestism (wearing the clothes of the other sex for part of one's life to enjoy temporary membership of it, without sexual arousal and without wanting a permanent change), F64.2 gender identity disorder of childhood, and F64.8 and F64.9. F65 , the disorders of sexual preference , held F65.0 fetishism, F65.1 fetishistic transvestism, F65.2 exhibitionism, F65.3 voyeurism, F65.4 paedophilia, F65.5 sadomasochism, F65.6 multiple disorders of sexual preference, F65.8 other disorders of sexual preference (among them obscene telephone calls, frotteurism and necrophilia) and F65.9. And F66 , "psychological and behavioural disorders associated with sexual development and orientation", held F66.0 sexual maturation disorder, F66.1 egodystonic sexual orientation , F66.2 sexual relationship disorder, and F66.8 and F66.9, under a note that "sexual orientation by itself is not to be regarded as a disorder" (Section 9.10.5 tells that story). Notice the words "not caused by organic disorder or disease". ICD-10 split every sexual dysfunction in two. If the cause was psychological, the problem was coded in Chapter V; if it was physical, it went to another chapter entirely, so that impotence of organic origin was N48.4, and organic dyspareunia and vaginismus were N94.1 and N94.2, in the chapter on diseases of the genitourinary system. The irony is that ICD-10's own definition of F52 admits that the split is artificial: "Sexual response is a psychosomatic process," it says, "and both psychological and somatic processes are usually involved in the causation of sexual dysfunction." Think of a 50-year-old man with diabetes who has had a few failures and now watches anxiously for the next one. His erectile problem is both organic and psychological, and forcing the clinician to choose one code for it distorts the picture. ICD-11 dissolved that split by creating a new chapter outside the mental disorders, Chapter 17, "Conditions related to sexual health" . Into it went three groups. The sexual dysfunctions are HA00 hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction; HA01 sexual arousal dysfunctions (HA01.0 female sexual arousal dysfunction and HA01.1 male erectile dysfunction); HA02 orgasmic dysfunctions (HA02.0 anorgasmia); HA03 ejaculatory dysfunctions (HA03.0 male early ejaculation and HA03.1 male delayed ejaculation); and HA0Y and HA0Z for other specified and unspecified dysfunctions. Each can be further coded as lifelong or acquired and as generalised or situational. The sexual pain disorders are HA20 sexual pain-penetration disorder, which replaces vaginismus and dyspareunia, with HA2Y and HA2Z. And gender incongruence is HA60 gender incongruence of adolescence or adulthood, HA61 gender incongruence of childhood and HA6Z unspecified (Section 9.9.1 teaches their definitions). The chapter ends with HA8Y and HA8Z for other and unspecified conditions related to sexual health. The cleverest part of the new chapter is a set of qualifiers, grouped under HA40, "aetiological considerations in sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders". Instead of forcing a choice between organic and nonorganic, ICD-11 lets the clinician add as many of these as apply to any dysfunction: HA40.0 associated with a medical condition, injury, or the effects of surgery or radiation treatment; HA40.1 associated with psychological or behavioural factors, including mental disorders; HA40.2 associated with use of psychoactive substance or medication; HA40.3 associated with lack of knowledge or experience; HA40.4 associated with relationship factors; and HA40.5 associated with cultural factors. The man with diabetes now receives one diagnosis, male erectile dysfunction, with two qualifiers, medical and psychological, which is a far truer description of his problem. ICD-11's definition of the sexual dysfunctions is also looser than DSM-5-TR's: the difficulty must occur frequently, though it may be absent on some occasions, must have been present for at least several months, and must cause clinically significant distress. DSM-5-TR, as Section 9.3.1 explains, asks for about 6 months and for the problem on about 75 to 100 percent of occasions. One family did not move. The paraphilic disorders stayed in Chapter 6, the mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, as codes 6D30 to 6D3Z: 6D30 exhibitionistic disorder, 6D31 voyeuristic disorder, 6D32 pedophilic disorder, 6D33 coercive sexual sadism disorder, 6D34 frotteuristic disorder, 6D35 other paraphilic disorder involving non-consenting individuals, 6D36 paraphilic disorder involving solitary behaviour or consenting individuals, and 6D3Z unspecified. Chapter 17 lists them only as a cross-reference to their home in Chapter 6. The group was rebuilt around consent: most of its categories concern arousal focused on people who have not consented or cannot consent, and Section 9.5.4 teaches it in detail. Several old categories disappeared altogether. The whole of F66, including egodystonic sexual orientation, was deleted. So were three disorders of sexual preference that involve only the person or consenting adults, fetishism (F65.0), fetishistic transvestism (F65.1) and sadomasochism (F65.5); such behaviour can now be coded only under 6D36, and only if it causes marked distress or a real risk of injury or death. Dual-role transvestism (F64.1) was deleted as well. And F52.7, "excessive sexual drive", has no place in Chapter 17. ICD-11 does have a category called compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (6C72), but it is defined differently, as a persistent failure to control intense, repetitive sexual impulses or urges, and it sits in Chapter 6 among the impulse control disorders, not among the sexual dysfunctions or the paraphilic disorders (Section 9.5.7). Why such a large reorganisation? Geoffrey Reed of the WHO and the members of its Working Group on Sexual Disorders and Sexual Health set out their reasons in World Psychiatry in 2016. The new chapter for the sexual dysfunctions was meant to be an integrated classification, "overcoming the mind/body separation that is inherent in ICD-10". Gender incongruence was moved out of the mental disorders because the double stigma of being both transgender and labelled mentally ill had contributed to legal insecurity, human rights violations and barriers to health care; but it was kept in the ICD, rather than deleted, because most health systems need a diagnosis before they will provide or pay for gender-affirming treatment (Section 1.9.6 makes the same point). The paraphilic group was redrawn to separate conditions that matter for public health and clinical psychopathology from those that "merely reflect private behaviour". And F66 was deleted because its categories had no evidence-based treatments, had attracted almost no research and in practice singled out people with same-sex orientation or gender nonconformity. Talking about sex: the clinician's stance Lavanya, 31, has been taking an antidepressant for three months. At her review she says the tablets "are not working" and she wants to stop them. Her mood, when the psychologist asks, is in fact much better. Only when she is asked, plainly and in the same tone as every other question, whether the medicine has affected her sex life does she say that she has not been able to reach orgasm since she started it, and that she was too embarrassed to mention it (Sections 9.4.5 and 5.7.2). Without that one question she would have stopped a treatment that was helping her, and nobody would have known why. Clients rarely raise sexual problems first. They are embarrassed, they do not know that the problem is relevant, or they fear being judged. The remedy is to ask routinely, as part of the personal history (Book 2, Section 2.3.6), in a neutral, matter-of-fact way that signals that any answer is acceptable. Annon's PLISSIT model (Book 2, Section 7.9.6) reminds the clinician that most people need only the first levels of help, permission to talk and limited information, and that specific suggestions and intensive therapy are needed by fewer. Use the client's own words for their body and their identity, and the name and pronouns they use. Do not assume that a client is heterosexual or that everyone is either a man or a woman: "Do you have a partner?" closes fewer doors than "Are you married?" (Book 2, Section 10.6.9). In India the interview often happens with a spouse or a parent in the room, and in a joint family privacy at home may be scarce; see the client alone for part of the session, and explain the limits of confidentiality before sensitive questions are asked. Two rules have no exceptions. Sexual contact between a therapist and a client is forbidden (Book 2, Sections 1.8 and 1.9, and the clinical link in Section 7.9.2). And if anything the client says suggests that a child may be at risk, the clinician's legal duty to report under the POCSO Act 2012 overrides confidentiality (Book 2, Section 10.6.5). A doctor who calls a man's blood pressure high is comparing it with a known normal range; a clinician who calls a woman's desire "hypoactive" or a man's ejaculation "premature" is comparing them with an idea of normal sexual response, whether or not the idea is stated. This section makes that idea explicit. It starts with the models of the response cycle that the diagnostic manuals have borrowed, and shows how each phase became the home of a family of disorders. It then goes inside the body, to the nerves, blood vessels, hormones and chemical messengers that produce desire, erection, lubrication and orgasm, because every drug treatment in Sections 9.3 and 9.4 acts on one of these links. After that it turns to the mind: the balance of excitation and inhibition, the anxious self-watching that Masters and Johnson called spectatoring, and the experiments in which David Barlow showed that anxiety is not quite the villain it was thought to be. It ends with the relationships, beliefs and cultures in which every sexual response is embedded, and with the instruments clinicians use to measure it. Why a model of normal response matters for diagnosis Picture a woman of 45, married for twenty years, who tells her doctor that she almost never finds herself thinking about sex or wanting it out of the blue. When her husband reaches for her, though, she is usually willing, and once they have begun she becomes aroused, enjoys it and is glad afterwards that they made love. Does she have a disorder of sexual desire? If normal sexual response is a sequence that must begin with a spontaneous feeling of wanting sex, then she lacks the first step, and a clinician could diagnose her. If normal response can begin with willingness and let desire arrive later, she is entirely ordinary. Nothing about her has changed between the two answers; only the model has. That is why the models matter. A sexual response cycle is a description of the sequence of bodily and mental changes that runs from the first stirring of interest, through arousal and orgasm, to the return to rest. Every sexual dysfunction is defined by comparison with such a sequence, and the manuals have taken their sequence from the researchers you will meet in a moment. From DSM-III (1980) onwards the American Psychiatric Association organised the sexual dysfunctions by the phase of the cycle each one disturbs, beginning with desire (Book 2, Section 7.9.5): disorders of desire, disorders of arousal, disorders of orgasm, and, outside the cycle, disorders of pain. The arrangement is tidy. Each phase can fail, and each way of failing gets a name. But tidiness rests on an assumption: that everyone passes through the same phases in the same order, so that a failure at one point can be cleanly separated from a failure at another. When researchers in the 1990s listened carefully to women in long relationships, the assumption began to look shaky. Many women said that desire came after arousal rather than before it, and in the clinic, women's problems of desire and of arousal proved very hard to tell apart. DSM-5 (2013) responded with the largest change in this chapter of the manual: for women it merged the old desire disorder and the old arousal disorder into a single diagnosis, female sexual interest/arousal disorder, while for men it kept desire and arousal as separate disorders (Sections 9.3.4 and 9.3.5). The choice of model therefore decides, quite literally, who receives a diagnosis and what it is called. Keep the woman of 45 in mind as you read the next two subsections; Section 9.3.4 returns to her kind of case. Masters and Johnson's four phases and Kaplan's desire phase The first model is the one you already know from Book 1, Section 10.9.6 and Book 2, Section 7.9.1, so it needs only a reminder here. William Howell Masters (1915 to 2001), a gynaecologist in St Louis, and his research partner Virginia Eshelman Johnson (1925 to 2013) recorded the bodily changes of 382 women and 312 men in the laboratory and published the results as Human Sexual Response (1966). They described four phases, the same in both sexes: excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution. Two physiological processes drive the whole sequence: vasocongestion , the swelling of tissues as blood flows into them faster than it can drain away, and myotonia , the build-up of muscle tension that is released in the rhythmic contractions of orgasm. After orgasm men pass through a refractory period , during which another erection or orgasm is not possible; women have none and can return to orgasm if stimulation continues. Thirteen years later Helen Singer Kaplan (1929 to 1995), a New York psychiatrist and psychologist who kept meeting patients whose bodies worked perfectly well but who simply did not want sex, published Disorders of Sexual Desire (1979). Her triphasic model put a desire phase first and reduced the cycle to three phases that can fail independently: desire, excitement and orgasm. The sequence the DSM adopted, desire, excitement, orgasm and resolution, joins the two models together. Book 2 draws the curves (Figure 7.14) and compares the two schools (Table 7.21); they are not redrawn here. What matters for this chapter is what each phase contributed to the classification, and Table 9.4 sets it out. The desire phase is the home of the disorders of low desire. The excitement phase, the phase of vasocongestion, is the home of the arousal disorders: failure of erection in men and failure of lubrication and swelling in women. The orgasm phase is the home of three different ways for orgasm to go wrong: too early, too late, or not at all. Notice the two empty rows. No disorder has ever been assigned to plateau, because a problem that appears at the plateau stage is experienced by the person either as a loss of arousal (the erection fades) or as a problem of orgasm (it comes too soon or not at all), so the plateau adds nothing that the other phases do not already capture. No disorder has been assigned to resolution either: the refractory period is normal physiology, not a disorder, however inconvenient it may be. Two further rows lie outside the cycle altogether. Pain during sex is not a phase; it can strike at any point, from the first attempt at penetration to the end of intercourse, which is why DSM-III-R and DSM-IV gave dyspareunia and vaginismus a group of their own, the sexual pain disorders, and why DSM-5-TR has one pain diagnosis, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (Section 9.4.4). And a drug, alcohol or illness can disturb any phase, so the substance-induced dysfunction belongs to every row at once (Section 9.4.5). ICD-11 follows the same logic in its own Chapter 17 (Section 9.1.6): HA00 for desire, HA01 for arousal, HA02 for orgasm, HA03 for ejaculation and HA20 for pain. Exam trap In DSM-5-TR, female sexual interest/arousal disorder spans two phases (desire and arousal), whereas in men desire and arousal stay separate (male hypoactive sexual desire disorder and erectile disorder). DSM-5-TR says so directly: "desire and arousal disorders have been retained as separate constructs in men". No disorder belongs to plateau or resolution , and the refractory period is normal. Pain is not a phase of the response cycle: genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder sits outside the cycle. Masters and Johnson's model has no desire phase; Kaplan's has no plateau or resolution. Rosemary Basson's circular model Both models you have just met are linear: they draw sexual response as a road that runs in one direction, from a starting point to an end point, with desire (in Kaplan's version) as the ignition that starts the engine. Rosemary Basson , a physician in the departments of psychiatry and of obstetrics and gynaecology at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, spent years listening to women in a sexual medicine clinic, and she noticed that many of them did not fit the road. Women in long relationships, in particular, described rarely or never feeling a spontaneous hunger for sex. Yet many of them had sex regularly, became aroused, enjoyed it and valued it. If the linear model was right, a large share of contented women had a desire disorder. Basson concluded that the model, not the women, was at fault. In "The female sexual response: a different model", published in the Journal of Sex and Marital Therapy in 2000, she proposed a cycle instead of a line. Her stated purpose was "to prevent diagnosing dysfunction when the response is simply different from the traditional human sex-response cycle", and also to define more clearly the women whose response really was disordered. Follow the cycle round, as Figure 9.3 draws it. It begins at a point Basson called sexual neutrality : the woman is not feeling desire, but she is not averse either, and she has reasons to be sexual that have little to do with lust. She may want to feel emotionally close to her partner, to express love, to please him or her, to share physical pleasure or to feel attractive and well. Because of those reasons she makes a choice to be receptive: she is willing to look for, and to focus her attention on, sexual stimuli, such as touch, words, a kiss, a setting free of interruptions. Those stimuli are processed in her mind, and whether they produce arousal depends on biological factors (fatigue, illness, hormones, medication) and psychological ones (distraction by the day's worries, feelings about the partner, past experiences, fear of being interrupted by the children or the in-laws). If the context is right, she becomes subjectively aroused; the word "subjectively" matters, because Basson meant the felt sense of being turned on, not merely the genital response. Now comes the step that reverses the linear model: arousal, once it is under way, triggers desire. Basson called this responsive desire , desire that arises in response to arousal during the sexual encounter, and contrasted it with the spontaneous desire of the linear models, the urge that appears beforehand, unprompted, as thoughts, fantasies and a conscious wish for sex. Desire and arousal then feed each other. Finally, if the experience is emotionally and physically satisfying (with or without orgasm, which Basson did not treat as the only measure of success), it deepens intimacy and strengthens the woman's reasons to begin again next time, and the circle closes. Spontaneous desire does not disappear from the model: it can still enter the cycle and add to it, and it tends to be more common early in a relationship. An everyday comparison helps. Many people at an Indian wedding have no wish at all to dance when the band strikes up. A cousin pulls them onto the floor, they go along to be sociable, the music and the crowd take hold, and ten minutes later they do not want to stop. The wanting came after the doing had begun. Nobody would call the reluctant dancer "hypoactive"; the desire was real, it was simply responsive. Basson's argument was that much of women's sexual desire works the same way, especially once the novelty of a new relationship has worn off, and that a model which counts only the spontaneous kind will mislabel normal women as disordered. Notice where desire sits in each panel: first in A, fourth in B. Why does this matter for diagnosis? Because DSM-5-TR has written Basson's insight into its rules. First, it states that a "desire discrepancy", a woman wanting sex less often than her partner does, is not enough for a diagnosis; somebody in every couple wants sex less than the other. Second, it notes that women "in relationships of longer duration are more likely to report engaging in sex despite no obvious feelings of sexual desire at the outset" than women in newer relationships: absence of spontaneous desire at the start is therefore treated as normal, not as a symptom. Third, what DSM-5-TR does treat as a sign of disorder is a lack of responsive desire: one of the six indicators of female sexual interest/arousal disorder is absent or reduced interest or arousal in response to any internal or external erotic cues, written, spoken or visual (Section 9.3.4). Fourth, the merger itself follows from the model. If desire can follow arousal and the two feed each other, then a disorder of "desire" and a disorder of "arousal" are not two separate breakdowns but two faces of one. DSM-5-TR records that its first indicator of the new disorder, reduced interest in sexual activity, "was previously the single criterion for hypoactive sexual desire disorder", and that women who have lost sexual desire "may be nine times more likely" also to have lost arousal. A woman like the one at the start of Section 9.2.1, whose desire is responsive and whose arousal and pleasure are intact, meets none of these markers and receives no diagnosis. How good is the model? It has had a deep influence on clinical practice, and its central observation, that many women in long relationships begin sexual encounters for reasons of intimacy rather than lust, matches what clinicians hear every day. When researchers tested it directly, though, the results were more mixed. In the Nurses' Sexuality Study, Sand and Fisher (2007) mailed questionnaires to a random sample of 580 registered nurses; 133 replied, and they were asked which of three short descriptions, of the Masters and Johnson, Kaplan and Basson models, best fitted their own experience. Roughly equal numbers chose each, and the women who chose Basson's model had significantly lower scores on the Female Sexual Function Index, a questionnaire of sexual functioning, than those who chose either linear model. An online survey of 404 women by the Australian psychologists Giles and McCabe (2009) found that a linear model fitted women both with and without sexual difficulties well, whereas the original circular model fitted neither group well until it was modified, after which it described women with sexual dysfunction better than women without. The likeliest reading of both studies is that women's sexual response is varied: some women's experience runs along the line, some round the circle, and the circle may describe especially well the women who come to clinics. Critics have added two cautions. The model is hard to test as a whole, because its steps (motives, attention, appraisal) are hard to measure separately. And it risks creating a new stereotype, that women's desire is responsive and men's spontaneous, when DSM-5-TR itself notes that men too "identify a variety of triggers for their sexual desire" and "describe a wide range of reasons" for choosing to have sex. A third caution is a clinical one: "willing to be receptive" means a free choice made for the woman's own reasons. A woman who has sex only because she believes it is her duty, or because refusing is not safe, is not illustrating responsive desire, and partner violence is an exclusion in every dysfunction diagnosis (Section 9.3.1). Exam trap The circular model with responsive desire is Rosemary Basson's (2000) . It is not Kaplan's (the triphasic model, desire, excitement and orgasm, 1979) and not Masters and Johnson's (four phases, excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution, 1966). In Basson's model responsive desire follows arousal; the cycle starts from sexual neutrality with motives such as wanting closeness. Lack of spontaneous desire is not by itself a dysfunction, and a desire discrepancy between partners is not enough for a diagnosis. The body in sexual response Every drug in this chapter, the tablets for erectile disorder, the antidepressants that delay ejaculation, the hormones and the medicines that damp desire, works by pulling on one link in a chain of nerves, blood vessels and chemical messengers. You cannot understand why a drug helps one dysfunction and causes another without knowing the chain, so this subsection follows it from the first touch to orgasm. Only what the disorders and their treatments need is taught here; the anatomy of the autonomic nervous system and of the reproductive organs belongs to the Physiological book. How an erection happens. An erection is a hydraulic event: it is produced by blood, not by muscle. Sexual stimulation reaches the spinal cord by two routes. Touch to the genitals sends signals into the lowest part of the cord, which can produce a reflex erection even when the brain is not involved (men with some spinal cord injuries keep these reflex erections). Erotic thoughts, sights and memories send signals down from the brain. Both routes converge on parasympathetic nerve fibres that leave the sacral spinal cord, at about the levels S2 to S4, and travel in the pelvic nerves to the penis. Their endings, and the cells lining the penis's blood vessels, release a small gaseous messenger, nitric oxide . Nitric oxide passes into the smooth muscle cells of the arteries and of the spongy erectile tissue, the two cylinders called the corpora cavernosa , and switches on an enzyme, guanylate cyclase, which manufactures a second messenger called cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). cGMP makes the smooth muscle relax. In the unaroused state that muscle is held contracted (by the sympathetic nerves), which keeps the arteries narrow and the spongy tissue empty; when it relaxes, the arteries widen and blood floods into the spaces of the erectile tissue. As the tissue swells inside its tough outer sheath, it squeezes shut the small veins that would normally drain it. This veno-occlusion traps the blood, the pressure inside rises, and the penis becomes rigid. The erection lasts as long as cGMP does. An enzyme called phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5) steadily breaks cGMP down; when the nitric oxide signal stops, PDE-5 wins, the muscle contracts again, the veins reopen and the blood drains away. Figure 9.4 draws the chain. Sexual stimulation (touch, erotic thoughts) Parasympathetic nerves (sacral cord, S2 to S4) Nitric oxide released (nerve endings, vessels) Guanylate cyclase makes cGMP Smooth muscle relaxes (arteries, spongy tissue) Blood floods in; veins squeezed shut Erection (lasts while cGMP lasts) PDE-5 breaks cGMP down: erection subsides PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) block this Nitrate drugs for angina also release nitric oxide. With a PDE-5 inhibitor, cGMP builds up in vessels everywhere: blood pressure can fall dangerously. Figure 9.4 The chemistry of erection. Read the top row left to right, the middle row right to left, then down to erection; the enzyme PDE-5 (bottom right) ends the erection by destroying cGMP, and PDE-5 inhibitors block that enzyme (the barred line). Notice what the drug cannot do: it slows the breakdown of cGMP but does not start its production, so without sexual stimulation (top left) there is no nitric oxide, no cGMP and nothing for the drug to protect. Two facts follow directly from the figure, and both are examined. First, a PDE-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil does not produce an erection by itself and does not increase desire. It protects cGMP from destruction, so it makes an erection easier to get and to keep, but only once sexual stimulation has set the nitric oxide signal going. Second, these drugs must never be combined with the nitrate drugs taken for angina (such as glyceryl trinitrate), because nitrates also work by releasing nitric oxide, this time in blood vessels throughout the body. With PDE-5 blocked, cGMP builds up in vessels everywhere, they all dilate at once, and blood pressure can fall dangerously. PDE-5 is also present in other blood vessels, which is why headache, flushing and a stuffy nose are common side effects; and sildenafil weakly blocks a related enzyme in the retina, which explains the brief blue tinge to vision that some men notice (the drugs themselves are taught in Section 9.3.6). The same vascular machinery works in women: during arousal the clitoris and labia engorge with blood, and fluid seeps through the swollen vaginal walls as lubrication (vasocongestion, Book 2, Section 7.9.1). Yet blood flow is rarely the limiting factor in women's arousal difficulties, which is one reason sildenafil disappointed when it was tried in women (Section 9.3.4). One more fact about erections turns out to be clinically priceless. Throughout life, from infancy to old age, men have erections during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, several times a night; Pinel notes that even babies have them, and that they are no more complete during dreams with sexual content than during other dreams. These nocturnal penile tumescence episodes owe nothing to desire, anxiety or a partner. A man who has firm erections in his sleep or on waking therefore has nerves and blood vessels that work, and if he cannot keep an erection with his partner, the likely cause is psychological. That logic underlies a laboratory test (Section 9.2.7) and the clinic's first question about erectile problems (Section 9.3.6). It also explains one physical cause that sleep can hide: in obstructive sleep apnoea, broken sleep and low oxygen are linked to erectile dysfunction (Book 3, Section 8.9.2). How ejaculation and orgasm happen. Ejaculation is not one event but two. In the first stage, emission , sympathetic nerves from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spinal cord (about T10 to L2) make the smooth muscle of the sperm ducts, seminal vesicles and prostate contract, moving semen into the back of the urethra, while the neck of the bladder closes so that semen cannot flow backwards. Once emission begins, a man feels that ejaculation can no longer be held back, the "point of no return" or ejaculatory inevitability; the stop-start technique for premature ejaculation works by learning to stop just before this point (Section 9.4.3). In the second stage, expulsion , rhythmic contractions of the bulbospongiosus and other pelvic floor muscles, driven by a somatic nerve (the pudendal nerve, from S2 to S4), propel the semen out. Orgasm is the intensely pleasurable experience that usually accompanies these contractions, and in women it consists of similar rhythmic contractions of the pelvic floor and the outer part of the vagina without emission. Orgasm and ejaculation are separable: after the prostate has been removed, for example, a man can still reach orgasm although no semen is emitted. Medical students remember the division of labour with the mnemonic "point and shoot": the parasympathetic system makes the penis point (erection), the sympathetic system makes it shoot (emission). The mnemonic simplifies, because expulsion is somatic, but it captures something important for this chapter. Erection needs calm parasympathetic activity, so a surge of sympathetic arousal, the bodily side of anxiety, works against it; emission is triggered by sympathetic activity, so the same surge can bring ejaculation on sooner. Barlow and Durand make the point for premature ejaculation: excessive sympathetic arousal may lower the threshold for ejaculation, and a man's anxiety about coming too quickly adds to that arousal and makes the problem worse. That is the physiology behind the close link between anxiety and premature ejaculation, taught fully in Section 9.4.3. Hormones. In men, testosterone is necessary for sexual desire. The classic evidence, told in Pinel's chapter on hormones and sex, comes from castration. Bremer (1959) reviewed 215 Norwegian men whose testes had been removed, about half of them sex offenders who had agreed to the operation to shorten their prison terms. About half became completely asexual within a few weeks; others quickly lost their erections but kept some sexual interest; a few went on having intercourse, less enthusiastically, for the duration of the study. The reverse experiment came from a single case: a First World War soldier who had been castrated by a shell fragment in 1918, at the age of 19, and who could not achieve an erection. In the first case report of testosterone replacement (described by de Kruif, 1945), his erections returned after the fifth injection. Two popular beliefs, however, are wrong. A man's level of desire does not track the amount of testosterone in his blood, and extra testosterone does not raise the desire of a healthy man: "sex drive and testosterone levels are uncorrelated in healthy men, and testosterone injections do not increase their sex drive" (Pinel). The experiment that shows why was done on guinea pigs by Grunt and Young (1952). They rated male guinea pigs as low, medium or high in sexual activity, castrated them all (their sexual behaviour fell to almost nothing), and then gave every animal the same large replacement dose of testosterone. Each returned to his own previous level, no higher. Above a threshold, more testosterone adds nothing, and DSM-5-TR says much the same for men's desire, suggesting a "critical threshold" below which testosterone matters and above which it has little effect. The clinical rule that follows, testosterone only for men whose levels are proven to be low, appears in Sections 9.3.5 and 9.3.6. In women the picture is less tidy. Removing the ovaries reduces sexual desire and fantasies, and in such women both oestradiol and testosterone supplements have restored desire and pleasure; but studies of testosterone or oestrogen after a natural menopause have been mixed, and some found an effect of testosterone only at unnaturally high doses. Pinel's summary is that both oestradiol and testosterone can influence female sexual behaviour, "at least in some cases". Women also differ from the females of most other mammals in being motivated to have sex when they are not fertile, so their sexuality is far less tightly tied to hormonal cycles. Hormones matter in one other, more mechanical way. After the menopause, falling oestrogen thins and dries the tissues of the vulva and vagina (vulvovaginal atrophy, now often called the genitourinary syndrome of menopause), which can make intercourse uncomfortable or painful and arousal and orgasm harder; DSM-5-TR lists it among the medical factors to rule out (Sections 9.3.4 and 9.4.4). Two further hormonal facts have direct drug consequences. A raised level of prolactin , the pituitary hormone that dopamine normally holds in check, suppresses desire and arousal in both sexes, partly by lowering sex hormone levels. That is why a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour can present as loss of desire or erectile failure, and why antipsychotic drugs that block dopamine and raise prolactin so often cause sexual side effects (Book 3, Sections 4.8.3 and 4.10.5; Section 9.4.5). And the huge doses of anabolic steroids taken by some bodybuilders do not improve sexual function: Pinel's answer is "an emphatic no". By negative feedback they shut down the pituitary hormones that drive the testes, so the testes shrink and fertility falls; in women they disrupt menstruation and masculinise the body. The distinction between the organising effects of hormones before birth and their activating effects in adulthood is taught in Book 1, Section 10.9.6 and applied to gender in Section 9.8.3; everything in this paragraph and the last concerns the activating effects. Brain chemistry. At the level the papers ask, three transmitters are enough. Dopamine , the transmitter of the brain's reward and wanting systems, broadly promotes sexual desire and arousal; drugs that boost dopamine can raise sexual interest, sometimes excessively, as in some patients with Parkinson's disease treated with dopamine agonists. Serotonin broadly inhibits sexual response, and most of all ejaculation and orgasm. That single fact explains two things that look contradictory: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a leading cause of delayed orgasm and ejaculation as a side effect (Section 9.4.5), and for exactly the same reason they are used to treat premature ejaculation (Section 9.4.3). Noradrenaline and the sympathetic system drive emission, as you saw above. Two drugs for women's low desire, flibanserin (on serotonin receptors) and bremelanotide (on melanocortin receptors), act on the brain rather than on blood flow (Section 9.3.4). DSM-5-TR also reports brain-imaging and genetic findings in lifelong premature ejaculation, which belong to Section 9.4.3. Table 9.5 gathers the biology of the phases with the drugs that act at each. Sildenafil and the other PDE-5 inhibitors block the breakdown of cGMP ; they do not create an erection without sexual stimulation and do not raise desire, and they are dangerous with nitrates . Erections in REM sleep point to a psychological cause of waking erectile failure. Testosterone is necessary for male desire, but extra testosterone does not raise desire in men with normal levels (Grunt and Young's guinea pigs). Serotonin inhibits ejaculation, which is why SSRIs both cause delayed ejaculation and treat premature ejaculation. Excitation, inhibition and anxiety: why arousal fails Here is the puzzle that the last subsection leaves. A man whose nerves and blood vessels are healthy has firm erections in his sleep, on waking and when he is alone, and yet he loses his erection every time he is with his partner. A woman who becomes aroused easily when she reads a novel feels nothing when her husband touches her. Nothing in the body has changed between the two situations. What has changed is the mind, and three ideas explain how: the clinical description of performance anxiety and spectatoring, Barlow's experiments showing that anxiety itself is not the culprit, and the dual control model, which explains why some people are far more vulnerable than others. Performance anxiety and spectatoring. In Human Sexual Inadequacy (1970) Masters and Johnson identified the force that keeps most sexual dysfunctions going, and Book 2, Section 7.9.2 tells the story of their treatment programme. Performance anxiety is the fear of failing sexually: of losing an erection, of not reaching orgasm, of coming too soon, of disappointing a partner. Its companion is spectatoring , their word for the way the anxious person mentally steps out of the experience and watches it, like a spectator in the stands, checking and judging instead of feeling. Picture a young husband who lost his erection once, on a night when he was exhausted and had drunk too much at a cousin's reception. The next time he and his wife are together, part of his mind is keeping watch: "Is it happening? Is it firm enough? It is going to fail again." Every ounce of attention spent on watching is attention taken away from the touch and the closeness that produce arousal, so the erection does fade, the fear is confirmed, and the next attempt begins with even more watching. Viktor Frankl had described the same trap as hyper-reflection, excessive attention to oneself that disrupts the very act attended to (Book 2, Section 6.5). Helen Singer Kaplan built the idea into her distinction between the immediate causes of a dysfunction (performance anxiety, spectatoring, a partner's demands, poor technique) and its remote causes in deeper personal and relationship conflict (Book 2, Section 7.9.5). For decades the lesson seemed simple: anxiety kills arousal. Masters and Johnson thought so, and so did Kaplan. Then a psychologist set out to test it. Barlow's experiments: anxiety is not the problem, attention is. David H. Barlow (born 1942), the American clinical psychologist better known for his work on panic and the anxiety disorders, ran a sexuality research laboratory at the State University of New York at Albany in the 1980s. Because he studied anxiety, he was well placed to ask whether anxiety really does what sex therapists assumed. His laboratory measured arousal in men directly, with a penile strain gauge (Section 9.2.7), and the answer it produced was a surprise. Key study: does anxiety reduce sexual arousal? (Barlow, Sakheim and Beck, 1983) Question. If performance anxiety causes sexual dysfunction, then making men anxious about their performance should reduce their arousal. Does it? Method. Young men without sexual problems watched erotic films while a strain gauge recorded their erections. Before the films each man received a harmless but somewhat painful electric shock to the forearm, so that later threats would be believed. Each man then watched films under three conditions: a control condition (relax, no chance of shock); a non-contingent threat (a 60 percent chance of a shock at some point during the film, whatever happened); and a contingent threat, designed to mimic performance anxiety (a 60 percent chance of a shock if his erection did not reach the average level reached by earlier participants). No shock was ever given during the films. Result. Both threats increased arousal compared with the control condition, and the contingent threat, the one that most resembled performance demand, increased it most of all. The paper's title says it plainly: "Anxiety increases sexual arousal". What happened next. In men with erectile dysfunction whose physical causes had been ruled out, the same kind of threat reduced arousal. A distraction experiment (Abrahamson and colleagues, 1985) had the opposite pattern: sexually functional men who had to listen to a story through earphones while watching an erotic film, knowing they would be questioned on it, became less aroused; men with dysfunction were not affected, as if they were already distracted by their own worries. Men with dysfunction also underreported their arousal: at the same measured erection, they said they were far less aroused than functional men did (Sakheim and colleagues, 1987). Criticism. These are laboratory analogues with young male volunteers, a shock is not the same as a partner's disappointment, and the strain gauge measures the genital response rather than the whole experience; but later studies with women, using vaginal photoplethysmography, found a broadly similar pattern. How can anxiety raise arousal in one man and lower it in another? Barlow's answer, published in 1986 as "Causes of sexual dysfunction: the role of anxiety and cognitive interference" in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology , was to break "performance anxiety" into three parts: physiological arousal, negative affect and, crucially, the direction of attention. Figure 9.5 shows the two loops he proposed. Both begin in the same place, a situation that demands sexual performance, such as a willing partner in bed. A sexually functional person meets that demand with positive feelings and expectations, a sense of being in control and an accurate sense of how aroused he or she is, and so attends to the erotic cues: the partner, the touch, the sensations. The autonomic arousal that follows (and anxiety adds to it) narrows and sharpens attention still further on those same cues, arousal rises, performance succeeds, and next time the person approaches sex more readily. A person with a dysfunction meets the same demand with negative feelings, an expectation of failure and a sense of having no control, and so attends to what Barlow called the "public consequences of not performing" ("I'll make a fool of myself", "she will think I'm useless") and to any sign that the response is failing. Here the rise in autonomic arousal sharpens attention on the threat instead of the erotic cues, arousal of the genitals falls, performance fails, and the failure confirms the fear, which feeds the next round and leads to avoidance. The same bodily arousal drives both loops; the difference is where it sends attention. That is why Barlow's name for the core problem is cognitive interference : the trouble is not anxiety as such but attention captured by non-erotic, threatening thoughts. Barlow and Durand note that this process applies to most sexual dysfunctions, which tend to occur together, but particularly to the arousal disorders.
