Both columns start from the same demand and contain the same rise in autonomic arousal. What differs is where attention goes: in the functional loop (left column, with its feedback arrow on the left edge) arousal sharpens attention on erotic cues, while in the dysfunctional loop (right column, feedback arrow on the right edge) it sharpens attention on the threat of failure, so each failure prepares the next. The model explains several clinical facts at once. It explains why simple reassurance ("relax, it will be fine") rarely works: the problem is not a lack of calm but a habit of attention. It explains why sensate focus, with its ban on intercourse (Book 2, Section 7.9.3), helps so many dysfunctions: when no performance is demanded there are no "public consequences" to attend to, and attention can return to sensation. And it explains why a drug that restores erections may not be enough for a very anxious man, whose attention to failure remains, a point taken up with the evidence in Section 9.3.6. The dual control model. Barlow's loops describe what happens in the moment. They do not explain why one man falls into the negative loop after a single bad night while another shrugs off ten. In 2000 John Bancroft and Erick Janssen , at the Kinsey Institute of Indiana University, offered an answer in a paper in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews , "The dual control model of male sexual response". The dual control model holds that whether sexual arousal occurs in a given situation depends on the balance between two separate systems in the brain: a sexual excitation system , which responds to sexually relevant stimuli and switches arousal on, and a sexual inhibition system , which responds to threats and switches it off. A car with an accelerator and a brake is the usual comparison: the car's speed depends on how hard each pedal is pressed, and a car can stand still either because nobody is pressing the accelerator or because somebody is standing on the brake. Inhibition is not a fault. From an evolutionary point of view it is useful to lose arousal when there is danger nearby. The key claim is that people differ, in a fairly stable, trait-like way, in how sensitive each system is. A person with a sensitive brake and a light accelerator is vulnerable to sexual dysfunction, especially under stress; a person with a sensitive accelerator and a weak brake may be more prone to sexual risk-taking. Bancroft and Janssen measured these propensities with a questionnaire, the Sexual Inhibition and Sexual Excitation Scales (SIS/SES; the instrument itself belongs to the Assessment book), which yields one excitation score and two inhibition scores. SIS1 measures inhibition due to the threat of performance failure (the brake pressed by worries such as "I may not be able to keep my erection"), and SIS2 measures inhibition due to the threat of performance consequences, external dangers such as being discovered, catching an infection, causing a pregnancy or hurting the relationship. In their paper they even predicted that men high on SIS2 would respond to psychological treatment, while men high on SIS1 would respond better to drugs. The idea has spread well beyond its origins in men: DSM-5-TR lists "differences in propensity for sexual excitation and sexual inhibition" among the risk factors for female sexual interest/arousal disorder, and suggests that one type of that disorder may rest on "overactivation of sexual inhibition" (Section 9.3.4). The three ideas fit together neatly. The dual control model says who is vulnerable, Barlow's model says what happens in the moment when the brake is pressed by worry, and spectatoring is what the experience feels like from the inside. Exam trap Anxiety does not always reduce sexual arousal: in sexually functional men it increased arousal (Barlow, Sakheim and Beck, 1983, "Anxiety increases sexual arousal"). In dysfunction the harm comes from cognitive interference , attention to failure and its consequences instead of to erotic cues (Barlow, 1986). Spectatoring and performance anxiety are Masters and Johnson's terms (1970); "hyper-reflection" is Frankl's. The dual control model (excitation versus inhibition, measured by the SIS/SES) is Bancroft and Janssen's (2000), not Barlow's or Basson's. Relationships, culture and beliefs Barlow's model explains how a dysfunction keeps itself going, but not where the negative feelings and the habit of watching for failure came from in the first place. For that we have to widen the lens from the person to the couple, the family and the culture. DSM-5-TR tells clinicians to weigh five groups of factors in every case (the list is given in Section 9.3.1); this subsection explains why the non-medical ones matter so much. The relationship. Sex is one of the few things people do that needs two willing participants, and it is exquisitely sensitive to how those two feel about each other. Barlow and Durand name a marked deterioration in the close relationship as the most common of the contributing factors: it is hard to feel desire for someone you have come to resent. Anger and contempt are incompatible with the positive feelings that start the functional loop in Figure 9.5. In a power struggle, sex easily becomes the arena where one partner withholds and the other demands, and each demand adds to the performance pressure on both. Poor communication matters in a more practical way: many people never tell their partner what kind of touch they like, so the stimulation they receive is not the stimulation that arouses them; one study found that women who did not reach orgasm reported discomfort in telling their partners what would help, such as direct clitoral stimulation (Kelly, Strassberg and Kircher, 1990). And a partner's own difficulty changes the other's experience: a wife whose husband always ejaculates within moments may gradually lose interest in sex that leaves her frustrated, and then it is she who is brought to the clinic with "low desire". That is why DSM-5-TR lists partner factors first, and why Masters and Johnson insisted that the couple, not the individual, is the patient. Scripts. The sociologist John Gagnon (1931 to 2016), who with William Simon introduced the idea in Sexual Conduct (1973), argued that human sexual behaviour is not simply driven by instinct but follows sexual scripts : culturally learned guides to what counts as sex, with whom, when, where, how it should begin and end, and what it means. Gagnon later helped to apply the idea in the large American survey published as The Social Organization of Sexuality (Laumann, Gagnon, Michael and Michaels, 1994). Scripts matter for dysfunction because a narrow script turns ordinary variation into failure. If the script says that sex means intercourse, that the man must lead and the woman must be passive, and that the act is over when he ejaculates, then a man with a softer erection has "failed", a woman who needs a different kind of stimulation is "frigid", and neither may ever discover the many other ways in which they could enjoy each other. A person who learns from the script that sex is dangerous, dirty or forbidden is more vulnerable still. Barlow and Durand note that such patterns are most evident in cultures with restrictive attitudes to sex, and that vaginismus, for example, is relatively rare in North America but considerably more common in Ireland and Turkey. Erotophobia and myths. The social psychologist Donn Byrne gave a name to one product of a restrictive upbringing: erotophobia , a negative cognitive and emotional set towards sexuality (its opposite is erotophilia), learned early from parents, religious authorities and others, which predicts sexual difficulties later in life (Byrne and Schulte, 1990). For people with this set, sexual cues come to be associated with negative feelings long before any sexual relationship begins, which is exactly the starting point of the dysfunctional loop. A related danger is sexual myths , confident but false beliefs about what normal sex is like. Bernie Zilbergeld , an American psychologist and one of the best-known writers on male sexuality, collected the myths that many men hold, among them that all touching should lead to sex, that sex is centred on a hard penis and what is done with it, that good sex is spontaneous and needs no talking or planning, and that real men do not have sexual problems (Zilbergeld, 1999; Book 2, Section 7.9.7 gives the myths most often met in Indian clinics). Do such beliefs actually matter? Baker and de Silva (1988) turned an earlier version of Zilbergeld's list into a questionnaire and gave it to sexually functional and dysfunctional men: the men with dysfunctions believed the myths significantly more strongly. A man who believes that a real man never has a problem cannot treat one soft erection as the normal event it is. Trauma, guilt and religion. Early sexual abuse leaves long shadows on sexual function. In the American national survey that Section 9.3.2 describes, Laumann and colleagues (1999) found that women who had been sexually touched by an adult before puberty, or forced into sexual contact, were about twice as likely to have orgasm problems as women who had not, and that men who had had sexual contact with an adult as children were more than three times as likely to have erectile dysfunction (trauma and its effects are taught in Book 3, Sections 7.2 and 7.3). DSM-5-TR's fourth group of factors, "cultural or religious factors", covers the quieter but more common influence of prohibitions against sexual activity or pleasure and the guilt they leave. A woman taught that sexual pleasure is shameful may find that arousal brings anxiety rather than delight; a man raised to see masturbation as sin may approach marriage already convinced that he has damaged himself. Indian context Two cultural patterns shape how sexual problems present in India, and both are taught elsewhere. Dhat syndrome, named by N. N. Wig in 1960, is distress attributed to the loss of semen, felt as weakness, fatigue and anxiety; DSM-5-TR treats it as a cultural explanation of distress and notes its links with erectile disorder and early ejaculation (Book 3, Section 1.10.4). Sexual myths, wall advertisements by self-styled sexologists, arranged marriages entered with little sex education, and unconsummated marriages are described in Book 2, Section 7.9.7. One study adds numbers. Verma, Khaitan and Singh (1998) reviewed 1,000 consecutive patients at the psychosexual clinic of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi: 71.3 percent complained of nocturnal emission ("night discharge"), 33.4 percent felt guilty about masturbation, and 30 percent worried that their penis was too small. The authors, as Barlow and Durand report, attribute this focus on semen to the culturally held belief that loss of semen causes depletion of physical and mental energy. Its findings on premature ejaculation and on how few women attended are given in Section 9.3.2. Age and illness. DSM-5-TR reminds clinicians that "aging and relationship duration may be associated with a normative decrease in sexual response": erections take longer and need more direct stimulation, lubrication lessens, and desire usually declines gently. None of this is a disorder. Nor does sex stop. In a national survey of older Americans, Stacy Tessler Lindau and colleagues (2007) found that 38.5 percent of men and 16.7 percent of women aged 75 to 85 had been sexually active with a partner in the previous year; the gap between the sexes probably reflects, among other things, that many older women no longer have a living partner. The declines that do occur are tied mostly to poorer health, reduced mobility, medication and the loss of a partner. Chronic illness affects sexual function directly (diabetes damages nerves and blood vessels, pelvic surgery and spinal injury cut nerve pathways, kidney disease and hormonal disorders disturb the endocrine system) and indirectly: a man who has had a heart attack may become so preoccupied with the fear that sex will strain his heart that he cannot become aroused even after his doctor has reassured him. The particular medical causes are taught with each disorder. Putting it together. Having reviewed the causes one by one, Barlow and Durand conclude that a sexual dysfunction is seldom caused only by psychological or only by physical factors; more often there is a subtle combination. Their own example is worth retelling in outline. A young man who is prone to anxiety and holds a few sexual myths (psychological and social factors) loses his erection one night after drinking, as many men do (a biological factor). He approaches the next encounter wondering whether it will happen again, and that worry sets the dysfunctional loop of Figure 9.5 in motion, whether or not he has had a drink. In the language of the biopsychosocial model and the four Ps (Book 3, Sections 1.3.3 and 1.3.5), anxiety-proneness and myths were predisposing, the alcohol was precipitating, and the anxious attention to failure, the avoidance and perhaps his partner's growing frustration are perpetuating. The treatment plan has to address all three, which is why so many of the treatments in Sections 9.3 and 9.4 combine a physical and a psychological method. Measuring sexual response in the laboratory and the clinic How does a clinician find out what is happening in a sexual response that takes place in private, at night, between two people? Barlow's group describe three parts to the assessment of sexual problems (Wiegel, Wincze and Barlow, 2002): an interview, supported by questionnaires; a medical evaluation; and, where available, psychophysiological measurement of arousal itself. The questionnaires belong to the Assessment book (two widely used ones are the International Index of Erectile Function for men and the Female Sexual Function Index for women), and taking a sexual history is taught in Book 2, Section 2.3.6. In Barlow's clinic the interview lasts about two hours, covers the relationship, physical health and other psychological problems as well as sex, uses the client's own everyday words rather than clinical terms, and includes the partner whenever possible. Questionnaires are given as well because many people will write down what they are not yet ready to say aloud. Measuring arousal directly. In men, erection can be recorded with a penile strain gauge , a thin, flexible loop placed around the shaft of the penis that registers changes in its circumference; the version used in so much sexuality research was developed in Barlow's own clinic (Barlow, Becker, Leitenberg and Agras, 1970). Measuring the penis's response to sexual stimuli is called penile plethysmography or phallometry, and it comes in two forms: circumferential, using the strain gauge, and volumetric, in which the penis sits inside a sealed cylinder that records changes in its volume, a more sensitive but more cumbersome method devised by Kurt Freund (whose work on paraphilias is taught in Section 9.7). Circumference is not the whole story: rigidity matters too, because a large erection without enough firmness is still inadequate for intercourse. The comparable device for women is the vaginal photoplethysmograph developed by James Geer and his colleagues (Geer, Morokoff and Greenwood, 1974). Smaller than a tampon, it is inserted by the woman herself; a light at its tip and two light-sensitive cells on its sides measure the light reflected back from the vaginal walls, which changes as blood flows into them during arousal. In a typical laboratory session the person watches an erotic film or listens to an erotic recording for a few minutes while the device records, and reports from moment to moment how aroused he or she feels. The comparison is often revealing: many people with psychologically caused dysfunctions become strongly aroused in the laboratory yet cannot become aroused with a partner. In women, however, the genital response and the feeling of being aroused often diverge, and DSM-5-TR notes that research with vaginal photoplethysmography has not found differences between women who do and do not report a lack of genital arousal. That is why female sexual interest/arousal disorder is diagnosed from the woman's own report, which DSM-5-TR says is sufficient (Section 9.3.4). Tests for physical causes. The other tests are aimed mainly at erectile problems, and DSM-5-TR lists them as its diagnostic markers. Nocturnal penile tumescence testing records erections during sleep, in a sleep laboratory or at home with a portable recorder; adequate erections in REM sleep suggest that the waking problem is psychological (Section 9.2.4). Doppler ultrasonography measures blood flow in the penile arteries, often after an injection of a vasoactive drug into the erectile tissue (the intracavernosal injection test: a good erection after the injection shows that the vessels can respond), and more invasive imaging can look for venous leakage. Nerve conduction studies of the pudendal nerve, and somatosensory evoked potentials, are used when nerve damage is suspected, as in diabetic neuropathy. Blood tests complete the picture: free or bioavailable testosterone, especially in men with diabetes, with low desire as well, or with no response to PDE-5 inhibitors; thyroid function; fasting glucose to detect undiagnosed diabetes; and serum lipids, because erectile disorder in men aged 40 and over predicts later coronary artery disease (Section 9.3.6). The same tools reappear in a different role when penile plethysmography is used to assess sexual interests in men with paraphilic disorders (Section 9.7.4). Exam trap The penile strain gauge (circumferential plethysmography) came from Barlow's clinic (1970); the volumetric method is Freund's; the vaginal photoplethysmograph is Geer's (1974) and measures light reflected from the vaginal walls. Good erections during REM sleep ( nocturnal penile tumescence ) point to a psychological cause of waking erectile failure. In women, genital measures do not separate those with and without arousal complaints, so self-report is enough for the diagnosis. 9.3 Sexual Dysfunctions I: The Shared Rules, and the Disorders of Desire, Arousal and Erection Lower yield · not asked yet DSM-5-TR's chapter on sexual dysfunctions contains eight specific disorders: delayed ejaculation, erectile disorder, female orgasmic disorder, female sexual interest/arousal disorder, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, male hypoactive sexual desire disorder, premature (early) ejaculation and substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction, together with other specified and unspecified sexual dysfunction for problems that fit none of them. All eight are built on one template, and examiners like nothing better than the places where a disorder breaks the template, so this section begins with the shared rules and the reason for each. It then asks how common sexual problems are and how a clinician assesses them, and teaches the three disorders of the first half of the response cycle: the two disorders of desire and arousal, one for women and one for men, and erectile disorder. Section 9.4 teaches the rest. What counts as a sexual dysfunction: the shared template DSM-5-TR describes the sexual dysfunctions as "a heterogeneous group of disorders that are typically characterized by a clinically significant disturbance in a person's ability to respond sexually or to experience sexual pleasure". Notice what the definition is about: the response cycle of Section 9.2, and the pleasure it brings. It says nothing about what or whom a person finds arousing (that is the territory of the paraphilias, Section 9.5) or about how a person experiences his or her gender (gender dysphoria, Section 9.9). That is why a person whose sense of gender does not match the body does not have a sexual dysfunction: that mismatch is gender dysphoria (Section 9.9). The word "heterogeneous" matters too: the disorders differ in cause, course and treatment, and one person can have several at once, a man with both erectile disorder and premature ejaculation, for example. When that happens, DSM-5-TR says that all of them should be diagnosed. Almost every disorder in the chapter then repeats four requirements, and each exists to rule something out. A duration of approximately 6 months. Sexual response is easily disturbed by fatigue, illness, bereavement, a new baby, a move, a quarrel or a new partner, and most such disturbances pass on their own. The 6-month rule keeps these passing reactions out of the diagnosis. The word "approximately" is deliberate: DSM-5-TR allows the clinician to judge persistence when the exact duration cannot be established. The problem on almost all or all occasions, approximately 75 to 100 percent. Occasional failure is normal. In a classic study, Ellen Frank and her colleagues (1978) gave questionnaires to 100 well-educated, happily married couples who were not seeking treatment; more than 80 percent described their marital and sexual relations as happy and satisfying, yet 40 percent of the men reported erectile or ejaculatory difficulties and 63 percent of the women reported difficulties with arousal or orgasm. Those difficulties did not spoil their overall satisfaction. A diagnostic rule that counted every occasional failure would turn most contented couples into patients. Clinically significant distress. Many people with a measurable sexual difficulty are not troubled by it. Bancroft, Loftus and Long (2003) surveyed a national sample of 987 American women who had been in a heterosexual relationship for at least 6 months. About 44 percent had at least one difficulty that would meet objective criteria for a problem, yet only 24.4 percent of the women reported marked distress about their sexual relationship or their own sexuality, and the best predictors of that distress were the woman's general emotional well-being and her emotional relationship with her partner during sex, not her lubrication or orgasm. A woman who rarely reaches orgasm and does not mind is not ill; the distress criterion protects her from being labelled. The exclusions (always Criterion D). The difficulty must not be better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, or be a consequence of "severe relationship distress, partner violence, or other stressors", and it must not be attributable to a substance or medication or to another medical condition. Each exclusion sends the case to a different diagnosis, as the hierarchy below explains. That is the template. Now the exceptions, which are where the marks are. Two disorders have no percentage of occasions at all and say only "persistent or recurrent": genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder and male hypoactive sexual desire disorder (desire is a state of mind, not something that can fail on a particular occasion). Female sexual interest/arousal disorder applies the 75 to 100 percent rule to only two of its six indicators, the two about pleasure and about genital or non-genital sensations during sexual activity. Premature ejaculation alone demands "at least 6 months", not "approximately". Substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction has no duration rule (it begins with the drug, and can begin within days) and grades severity by how often the problem occurs. Table 9.6 sets the eight side by side. Table 9.6 The shared template of the DSM-5-TR sexual dysfunctions and the exceptions to it. Sometimes a person does not become aroused or reach orgasm simply because the stimulation is not the kind that works for him or her, often because neither partner knows what effective stimulation is. DSM-5-TR says that in such cases "there may still be a need for care", in the form of education, but a sexual dysfunction is not diagnosed. A woman whose husband believes that a minute of kissing is enough preparation for intercourse does not have an arousal disorder. The subtypes. Every disorder except genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (which has only the first pair) and the substance-induced dysfunction (which records onset with the drug instead) uses two pairs of specifiers. Lifelong means the problem has been present since the person's first sexual experiences; acquired means it began after a period of relatively normal function. Generalised means it is not limited to certain kinds of stimulation, situations or partners; situational means it occurs only with certain kinds of stimulation, situations or partners. The first pair describes onset, the second describes context, and DSM-5-TR explains why they are worth recording: "the time of onset may indicate different etiologies and interventions". An erectile problem that is acquired and generalised in a 58-year-old smoker with diabetes suggests disease of the blood vessels; one that is lifelong and situational in a 25-year-old, who has good erections alone, suggests anxiety. Severity is rated mild, moderate or severe by the degree of distress, with the two exceptions already met: premature ejaculation is graded by time and the substance-induced disorder by the percentage of occasions. The five factors. Alongside the subtypes, DSM-5-TR asks the clinician to consider five groups of factors that may contribute to cause or treatment: (1) partner factors, such as the partner's own sexual problems or health; (2) relationship factors, such as poor communication or a difference in desire; (3) individual vulnerability factors (poor body image, a history of sexual or emotional abuse), psychiatric comorbidity (depression, anxiety) or stressors (job loss, bereavement); (4) cultural or religious factors, such as prohibitions against sexual activity or pleasure; and (5) medical factors relevant to prognosis, course or treatment. Section 9.2.6 explained why the first four matter; the medical factors are taught with each disorder. DSM-5-TR adds that ageing and the length of a relationship may bring a normal decrease in sexual response, which must not be mistaken for disorder. The hierarchy. What happens when something else explains the difficulty? DSM-5-TR gives four rules. If a nonsexual mental disorder such as depression, an anxiety disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder or a psychotic disorder mostly explains it, only that disorder is diagnosed. If a drug or substance explains it, the diagnosis is substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction. If another medical condition, such as peripheral neuropathy, fully explains it, the person does not receive a psychiatric diagnosis at all. And if severe relationship distress, partner violence or other major stressors explain it, no sexual dysfunction is diagnosed; instead a code for the relationship problem may be recorded, such as Z63.0, relationship distress with spouse or intimate partner. The last rule deserves a moment's thought. A woman who has no desire for a husband who hits her is not suffering from a sexual disorder; her lack of desire is an understandable response to violence, and calling it a dysfunction would locate the problem in the wrong person. In practice the causes are often tangled, and DSM-5-TR accepts that a sexual dysfunction can be diagnosed alongside a medical condition, another mental disorder or substance use when each contributes. Gender-diverse clients. DSM-5-TR adds a note for transgender, nonbinary and agender people. Despite their names, male hypoactive sexual desire disorder and female sexual interest/arousal disorder describe experiences that do not depend on a person's sex or gender, so either can be applied by clinical judgement. Diagnoses tied to reproductive anatomy (erectile disorder, premature and delayed ejaculation, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder) follow the person's current anatomy, not the sex assigned at birth. ICD-11 handles the same ground more loosely. Its Chapter 17 asks only that the difficulty occur frequently, though it may be absent on some occasions, that it has lasted at least several months and that it causes clinically significant distress, and instead of excluding medical and psychological causes it records them with the HA40 qualifiers (Section 9.1.6). The contrast reflects a difference of philosophy: DSM-5-TR asks whether the problem is a mental disorder, whereas ICD-11 treats the sexual dysfunctions as conditions of sexual health that usually have mixed causes. Exam trap The 6-month and 75 to 100 percent rules are not universal . No occasions percentage : genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder and male hypoactive sexual desire disorder. Only 2 of 6 items : female sexual interest/arousal disorder. "At least 6 months" : premature ejaculation. No duration rule : substance/medication-induced. Lifelong/acquired describes onset; generalised/situational describes context; genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder has only the first pair. A difficulty caused entirely by severe relationship distress or partner violence is not diagnosed as a sexual dysfunction (a Z code may be used instead), and one caused entirely by a medical condition receives no psychiatric diagnosis. A sexual dysfunction is a disturbance of sexual response or pleasure : when a question describes a person whose gender identity does not match the body, "sexual dysfunction" is the wrong option; the answer is gender identity disorder, now gender dysphoria (Section 9.9). How common: the surveys and the clinic Sexual problems are hidden problems, and for most of the twentieth century nobody knew how common they were. The landmark answer came from the sociologist Edward Laumann and his colleagues at the University of Chicago, who in 1992 interviewed a national probability sample of American adults, the National Health and Social Life Survey (the same survey reported more broadly in The Social Organization of Sexuality , Section 9.2.6). In a paper in the Journal of the American Medical Association on 10 February 1999, Laumann, Anthony Paik and Raymond Rosen analysed the answers of 1,749 women and 1,410 men aged 18 to 59 and reported that 43 percent of the women and 31 percent of the men had experienced a sexual dysfunction. The problems were more common in people with poor physical and emotional health and were strongly associated with unhappy sexual relationships and lower overall well-being. Table 9.7 gives the figures most often quoted. Table 9.7 Sexual problems among American adults aged 18 to 59 in the National Health and Social Life Survey (1992), as reported by Laumann, Paik and Rosen (1999) and Barlow and Durand. These are problems, not distressing disorders (see text). Problem Women Men Any sexual dysfunction 43 percent 31 percent Low sexual interest 22 percent 5 percent Arousal problems (women) 14 percent not applicable Premature ejaculation, the most common male problem not applicable 21 percent Erectile problems (rising steeply after 60) not applicable 5 percent Two lessons follow. First, the commonest problems were low desire in women and early ejaculation in men; erectile problems were uncommon in this sample only because it stopped at age 59, and they become far more common after 60 (Section 9.3.6). Second, these figures are far higher than the prevalence of the DSM disorders, because the survey counted problems lasting several months in the previous year without asking whether they caused distress. Section 9.3.1 explained why that matters: when distress is required, the numbers fall sharply. DSM-5-TR's own estimates show the gap. For example, fewer than 2 percent of men report clinically significant distress about low desire, against the 5 percent of the survey (Section 9.3.5), and only 1 to 3 percent of men meet the 1-minute definition of premature ejaculation, against the 21 percent who reported the problem (Section 9.4.3). People also rarely seek help: DSM-5-TR reports that only 10.5 percent of men with sexual problems in the previous year sought help. What about India? No national survey of the kind Laumann ran has been carried out, and no figure for the Indian population is given here. What exists are clinic studies, and the best known shows how skewed a clinic sample can be. Verma, Khaitan and Singh (1998) analysed 1,000 consecutive patients attending the psychosexual clinic of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi, published in the Archives of Sexual Behavior . Most were educated, middle-class men aged 21 to 30. The commonest complaints were premature ejaculation (77.6 percent) and nocturnal emission (71.3 percent); erectile dysfunction was a complaint of 23.6 percent. Only 36 women attended, and they came with their husbands. The figures say as much about who comes to a sexual clinic as about who has sexual problems. Young men attend with worries shaped by beliefs about semen (Section 9.2.6); many of their complaints, such as nocturnal emission, are not dysfunctions at all. Women with sexual difficulties more often go to a gynaecologist, presenting with pain or with "white discharge" and weakness, or never present at all (Book 2, Section 7.9.7), and Barlow and Durand suggest that the tiny number of women also reflects how little value is placed on women's sexual experience for religious and social reasons. A clinic sample is a window onto help-seeking, not onto the population. The diagnostic assessment The measures were described in Section 9.2.7; here is the order of questions a clinician works through, because each one maps onto a rule of the template. First, what exactly is the problem, in the client's own words, and which phase of the response does it affect: desire, arousal, orgasm, or pain? Second, is it lifelong or acquired? If acquired, what was happening in the person's life, health and medication when it began? Third, is it generalised or situational? The key questions are concrete: does it happen during masturbation, on waking, with another partner, on holiday, when the house is empty? Fourth, how often and for how long, and how much does it distress the person and the partner? Fifth, the five factors: the partner's own function and health, the state of the relationship (including, asked privately and safely, whether there is violence), past abuse, depression and anxiety, cultural and religious beliefs, and stressors. Sixth, the medical history: diabetes, blood pressure, heart disease, surgery, hormonal symptoms, the menopause, and every prescribed and unprescribed drug, alcohol and tobacco. Seventh, the partner's view, ideally from a joint and an individual interview, because the two accounts often differ. And finally, the client's goals: a couple who want a child, a man who wants to stop avoiding his wife and a woman who wants to feel desire again need different plans. The clues that separate physical from psychological causes of erectile problems are given in Section 9.3.6. Female sexual interest/arousal disorder Kamini, 38, teaches mathematics at a school in Pune. She has been married for fourteen years and has two children, aged 12 and 9. She comes to the clinic alone, a few weeks after her husband began sleeping in the other room "so as not to disturb her". "I never feel like it any more," she says. "I don't think about it, I never start anything, and when he reaches for me I pretend to be asleep. It isn't that I don't love him. Even in the early years I didn't always feel like it beforehand, but once we started I enjoyed it. Now I can't remember the last time." It has been like this for about two years, and she is distressed, for herself and because she fears what the separate rooms mean. The assessment fills in the picture. She teaches all day, coaches students in the evening, cooks, supervises homework and is rarely in bed before midnight. Her mother-in-law lives with them and the children's room shares a wall with theirs. Her husband initiates sex only very late at night, when she is exhausted, and with little touching beforehand. She sleeps adequately, still enjoys her work and her children and has no persistent low mood, so she does not have a depressive disorder; she takes no regular medicine, and her thyroid function and blood sugar are normal. The criteria. Female sexual interest/arousal disorder (DSM-5-TR code F52.22) is a lack of, or significant reduction in, sexual interest or arousal, shown by at least three of six indicators. The six fall naturally into two groups. Three concern interest and desire: (1) absent or reduced interest in sexual activity; (2) absent or reduced sexual or erotic thoughts or fantasies; and (3) no or reduced initiation of sexual activity, together with being typically unreceptive to a partner's attempts to initiate. Three concern arousal and response: (4) absent or reduced sexual excitement or pleasure during sexual activity on almost all or all (approximately 75 to 100 percent) occasions; (5) absent or reduced interest or arousal in response to any internal or external erotic cues, whether written, spoken or visual; and (6) absent or reduced genital or non-genital sensations during sexual activity on almost all or all occasions. The symptoms must have lasted approximately 6 months (Criterion B), must cause clinically significant distress (Criterion C), and must not be better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, by severe relationship distress (DSM-5-TR gives partner violence as its example) or other significant stressors, or by a substance, medication or another medical condition (Criterion D). The usual specifiers apply: lifelong or acquired, generalised or situational, and mild, moderate or severe distress. Why three of six, rather than a single essential symptom? Because, as DSM-5-TR puts it, there may be "different symptom profiles across women". In one woman the disorder shows itself as no interest in sex, no sexual thoughts and reluctance to start or respond; in another, as an inability to become excited, to respond to sexual stimuli with desire, or to feel the bodily signs of arousal. A polythetic rule (any three of six) captures both without forcing them into one mould. Kamini meets the first three indicators, which is enough; her report that she once enjoyed sex "once we started" also tells the clinician that her desire was always largely responsive, in Basson's sense, and that what has been lost is the context in which responsive desire could arise. Where the disorder came from. Until DSM-5, a woman like Kamini would have been diagnosed with hypoactive sexual desire disorder, and a woman who wanted sex but could not become aroused with female sexual arousal disorder (Table 9.4). DSM-5 merged the two, for the reasons given in Section 9.2.3: desire often follows arousal in women, the two problems usually occur together (women who have lost desire "may be nine times more likely" also to have lost arousal), and clinicians could not reliably tell them apart. The old desire diagnosis survives inside the new one as its first indicator, which DSM-5-TR says "was previously the single criterion for hypoactive sexual desire disorder". What the criteria do and do not count. Several details of the text prevent over-diagnosis. A "desire discrepancy", in which a woman wants sex less than her partner does, is not enough; the difficulty must be hers, not merely a difference between two people. Short-term changes in interest are common and often adaptive responses to life events, and they are not a disorder. Because low desire is often a lack of responsive desire (Section 9.2.3), the clinician must judge whether the stimulation and the context are adequate: if they are not, there may be a need for care but no diagnosis (Section 9.3.1). DSM-5-TR suggests that there may be at least two types of the disorder, one based on low sensitivity to sexual cues and one based on overactivation of sexual inhibition, the two pedals of the dual control model (Section 9.2.5). Because physiological measures of genital arousal do not distinguish women with arousal complaints from women without them (Section 9.2.7), the woman's own report of reduced genital or non-genital sensation is sufficient. And if a lifelong lack of desire is better explained by the woman's identification of herself as asexual, a person who experiences little or no sexual attraction, the diagnosis is not made (Section 9.1.2): asexuality is an orientation, not a dysfunction. How does Kamini fare against these rules? Her case is a good test. She meets three indicators for two years and is distressed, and she has no depressive disorder, no drug or medical cause, no partner violence and no relationship distress severe enough to explain her symptoms by itself. A clinician could reasonably diagnose female sexual interest/arousal disorder, acquired and generalised, with moderate distress. But the formulation matters more than the label. Her exhaustion, the lack of privacy, the timing and the brevity of her husband's approaches mean that the cycle in Figure 9.3 never gets started: there is no point at which she can choose to attend to sexual stimuli, and so no arousal from which desire could follow. A good plan works on the context, with the couple, before it reaches for anything else. How common. DSM-5-TR estimates that about 30 percent of women experience chronic low desire; about half of these report significant distress related to the partner, and about a quarter personal distress. Prevalence varies with age, culture, the duration of symptoms and above all whether distress is required: when it is, the estimates are markedly lower. Low desire becomes more common with age, but distress about it becomes less common. Reported rates of low desire range from 26 to 43 percent across world regions, and DSM-5-TR warns that such differences may partly reflect the measures used and how acceptable it is, in a given culture, for an unmarried, menopausal or widowed woman to report sexual activity at all; a woman's level of desire has to be judged against the norms of her own cultural group. DSM-5-TR finds no evidence that rates or expressions of the disorder differ between heterosexual and lesbian women. Risk and course. The risk factors DSM-5-TR names fall into the usual three groups. Temperamental: negative thoughts and attitudes about sexuality, a past history of mental disorder, and differences in the propensity for sexual excitation and inhibition. Environmental: relationship difficulties, the partner's own sexual functioning, and the woman's developmental history, including early relationships with caregivers and childhood stress. Genetic and physiological: medical conditions such as diabetes and thyroid dysfunction, and what DSM-5-TR calls "a strong influence of genetic factors on vulnerability to sexual problems in women". Women in longer relationships more often begin sex without feeling desire at the outset, and vaginal dryness in older women is related to age and the menopause; both are normal changes, not symptoms. The disorder commonly travels with other problems: difficulty with orgasm, pain during sex, depression, anxiety, thyroid disease, urinary incontinence, alcohol use and a history of sexual or physical abuse in adulthood. Differential diagnosis. The main alternatives follow the hierarchy of Section 9.3.1. Major depressive disorder, with its "markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all, or almost all, activities", may explain the lack of sexual interest, in which case only depression is diagnosed; this is why the clinician checked Kamini's mood, sleep and enjoyment of other things. A drug that coincides with the onset (antidepressants, antipsychotics and hormonal contraceptives are among those DSM-5-TR names) points to the substance-induced disorder (Section 9.4.5). Diabetes, thyroid disease, endothelial disease and disease of the central nervous system can explain it medically. Severe relationship distress or violence takes the case out of the sexual dysfunctions. Other sexual dysfunctions, by contrast, do not rule it out: chronic genital pain can lead to a lack of desire for painful sex, and lack of arousal can impair orgasm, so two or three diagnoses are common. Inadequate stimulation and transient, adaptive changes after a major life event complete the list. The ICD codes. ICD-10 recorded low desire as F52.0, lack or loss of sexual desire, and failure of lubrication as F52.2, failure of genital response. ICD-11 did not follow DSM-5's merger: in its Chapter 17, HA00 hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction (which can be given to either sex) and HA01.0 female sexual arousal dysfunction remain separate. A woman with Kamini's symptoms could therefore receive one DSM-5-TR diagnosis but, if both desire and arousal were affected, two ICD-11 codes. Treatment. Psychological treatment comes first, and its methods belong to Book 2: sex therapy built on education, sensate focus and communication (Book 2, Section 7.9), cognitive-behavioural and mindfulness-based approaches that train attention back to sensation, and couple therapy where the relationship is part of the problem (Book 2, Section 7.8). Barlow and Durand report that roughly 50 to 70 percent of people with low sexual desire benefit from sex therapy, at least initially. Physical causes are treated directly: depression is treated, any drug that may be responsible is reviewed (an SSRI might be switched to an antidepressant with fewer sexual side effects, such as bupropion, Section 9.4.5), and vaginal dryness after the menopause is treated with lubricants or local (vaginal) oestrogen. Two drugs have been approved in the United States specifically for low desire in women, and both act on the brain rather than on blood flow. Flibanserin (Addyi) was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on 18 August 2015 for premenopausal women with acquired, generalised hypoactive sexual desire disorder (the label kept the old DSM-IV name) not caused by a medical or psychiatric condition, relationship problems or a drug. Originally developed as an antidepressant, it stimulates serotonin 5-HT1A receptors and blocks 5-HT2A receptors, which is thought to reduce serotonin's braking effect on sexual response and free dopamine and noradrenaline in the frontal cortex. It is taken every day, at bedtime, and women who notice no improvement after eight weeks are advised to stop. Its benefit is modest: in the trials, women taking it had about half to one more satisfying sexual event a month than women taking placebo. Its main danger is severe low blood pressure and fainting, especially with alcohol, which earned it a boxed warning; in 2019 the FDA revised that warning so that, instead of avoiding alcohol altogether, women should wait at least 2 hours after one or two standard drinks before the bedtime dose, and skip the dose after three or more. Its approval came only after two earlier rejections, in 2010 and 2013, and after a vigorous advocacy campaign. Bremelanotide (Vyleesi), approved by the FDA on 21 June 2019 for the same group of women, works differently: it stimulates several melanocortin receptors in the brain (its label names the MC1 and MC4 subtypes as the most relevant at the doses used), although exactly how this raises desire is not known. It is injected under the skin of the abdomen or thigh at least 45 minutes before expected sexual activity, no more than once in 24 hours and no more than eight times a month, and its commonest side effect is nausea, reported by about 40 percent of women in the trials, with flushing and headache. Neither drug is approved for postmenopausal women or for men. Two other physical treatments are often asked about. Testosterone has been tried for low desire in postmenopausal women, and some studies find a benefit, but the evidence is mixed (Section 9.2.4) and no testosterone product is approved by the FDA for women. Sildenafil, which works so well for erections, was disappointing in women: in Barlow and Durand's account, one study found some improvement in postmenopausal women with arousal problems, but only in those whose desire was not reduced. The reason follows from Sections 9.2.4 and 9.2.7: in most women with these complaints, blood flow to the genitals is not what is missing. Clinical link: a pill for desire? Flibanserin was quickly nicknamed "the female Viagra", a label that is wrong twice over: sildenafil acts on blood vessels in the penis and works only once sexual stimulation is under way, whereas flibanserin is taken every day and acts on brain chemistry in the hope of creating desire. The debate around its approval revived an older critique. In 2000 the psychologist Leonore Tiefer and colleagues launched the "New View" campaign with a manifesto arguing that the DSM's phase model, based on Masters and Johnson's laboratory, was built around genital performance and fitted men better than women, and that women's sexual problems often arise from relationships, culture, money and power rather than from a faulty body; the collection A New View of Women's Sexual Problems followed in 2001. The lesson for a clinician is not that drugs are never useful, but that for a woman like Kamini the first questions are about exhaustion, privacy, the relationship and the kind of touch she receives. Exam trap Female sexual interest/arousal disorder needs 3 of 6 indicators, lasting about 6 months, with distress; the 75 to 100 percent rule applies only to the two indicators about pleasure and sensations during sex. It replaced DSM-IV's hypoactive sexual desire disorder (for women) and female sexual arousal disorder. A desire discrepancy is not enough, an asexual identity excludes the diagnosis, and self-report of reduced sensation is sufficient. ICD-11 keeps desire ( HA00 ) and female arousal ( HA01.0 ) separate. Flibanserin (2015) and bremelanotide (2019) act on the brain ; sildenafil acts on blood vessels and was disappointing in women. Male hypoactive sexual desire disorder Girish, 44, manages a bank branch in Lucknow. It is his wife who brings him, and she does most of the talking at first. For about a year, she says, he has shown no interest in sex at all; he never approaches her, turns away when she approaches him, and seems not to miss it. When the clinician sees Girish alone, he agrees. He rarely has a sexual thought or fantasy now, has no wish for sex, and feels guilty that his wife is unhappy. It began, he thinks, after he was passed over for promotion and moved to a smaller branch, which he still finds humiliating. He wakes most mornings with an erection. His blood tests, arranged by his physician, show normal testosterone, prolactin, thyroid function and blood sugar, and he takes no medicines. Is this depression, a relationship problem, a reaction to stress, or a sexual dysfunction? The criteria are designed to answer exactly that question. The criteria. Male hypoactive sexual desire disorder (DSM-5-TR code F52.0) is persistently or recurrently deficient or absent sexual or erotic thoughts or fantasies and desire for sexual activity (Criterion A). Both halves are required, a point DSM-5-TR makes explicitly, so a man who still has a rich fantasy life but no wish for sex with his partner does not meet it. The judgement of "deficient" is the clinician's, made in the light of factors that affect sexual functioning, such as the man's age and the general and sociocultural context of his life: a man of 75 is not expected to have the desire he had at 25. The symptoms must have lasted a minimum of approximately 6 months (Criterion B), must cause clinically significant distress (Criterion C), and must not be better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, by severe relationship distress or other significant stressors, or by a substance, medication or medical condition (Criterion D). The specifiers are the usual ones; there is no percentage of occasions (Table 9.6). DSM-5-TR gives an unusually clear reason for the duration rule: it is "meant to safeguard against making a diagnosis in cases in which a man's low sexual desire may represent a reactive but temporary response to adverse life conditions", and its examples are being fired from a job or a business failure. If the stressor and the low desire both persist beyond 6 months, the clinician must judge whether the diagnosis is appropriate. Several features of the text shape how the criteria are applied. As with women, a desire discrepancy, in which a man wants sex less than his partner does, is not sufficient. Many men with the disorder no longer initiate sex and are minimally receptive when their partner initiates, but because some men prefer their partner to take the lead, a lack of receptivity matters as much as a lack of initiation. Sexual activity, partnered sex or masturbation, may still occur despite low desire. And if the man's lifelong low desire is better explained by his identification as asexual, no diagnosis is made. How common. Estimates in representative samples range from 3 to 17 percent, depending on the country and the method. Desire problems are less common in younger men (3 to 14 percent at ages 16 to 24) than in older men (16 to 28 percent at ages 60 to 74). A persistent lack of interest lasting 6 months or more affects a smaller proportion, about 6 percent, and fewer than 2 percent of men report clinically significant distress about low desire, a clear illustration of how much the distress criterion narrows the field. Desire declines normally with age: in one set of figures DSM-5-TR cites, low desire rises from about 5.2 percent at age 27 to 18.5 percent at age 50. Across world regions, rates in men aged 40 to 80 range from 12.5 percent in Northern Europe to 28 percent in South-East Asia, which is the only figure for Asia that DSM-5-TR gives in this chapter. Low desire is also reported more often by gay men (19 percent) than by heterosexual men (9 percent). Risk. Mood and anxiety symptoms are strong predictors: up to half of men with a past history of psychiatric symptoms may have moderate or severe loss of desire, against only 15 percent of men without such a history. A man's feelings about himself, his sense of whether his partner desires him and his feeling of emotional connection all affect his desire, in either direction. Restrictive sexual attitudes and conservative beliefs are commonly associated with low desire, and so are a lack of erotic thoughts, worries about erection during sex and low confidence in erectile function. Environmental factors include alcohol use, a troubled relationship, reduced attraction to the partner, living in a long-term relationship, sexual boredom and work stress. Among physical factors, the endocrine disorders hyperprolactinaemia and hypogonadism (underactive testes with low testosterone) significantly reduce desire, and age is itself a risk factor. Whether men with low desire in general have abnormally low testosterone is unclear; DSM-5-TR suggests that there may be "a critical threshold" below which testosterone affects desire and above which it has little effect, exactly the pattern of Grunt and Young's guinea pigs (Section 9.2.4). Men are not women. DSM-5-TR states plainly that, in contrast to women, "desire and arousal disorders have been retained as separate constructs in men". Men on average report a higher intensity and frequency of desire than women, although desire and erectile function also overlap a great deal in men who seek help: persistent erectile failure can lead a man to lose interest in sex, and DSM-5-TR reports evidence that up to half of men with low desire also have erectile difficulties. The disorder is rarely the only sexual diagnosis: erectile disorder, delayed ejaculation and premature ejaculation are often present too, along with depression and endocrine problems. The presence of another dysfunction does not rule the diagnosis out. Differential diagnosis. The alternatives are the hierarchy of Section 9.3.1 applied to desire. Major depressive disorder, with its markedly diminished interest or pleasure in almost all activities, may explain the low desire, in which case only depression is diagnosed. A drug whose start coincides with the loss of desire points to the substance-induced disorder: SSRIs, antipsychotics that raise prolactin, opioids, finasteride and others (Section 9.4.5). Hypogonadism, diabetes, thyroid dysfunction and disease of the central nervous system can explain it medically. Severe relationship distress or other major stressors can explain it too. ICD-10 recorded the disorder as F52.0, lack or loss of sexual desire; ICD-11 uses HA00, hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction, the same code it gives to women. Back to Girish. His morning erections show that his erectile machinery works, and his normal blood tests make hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease and diabetes unlikely. The clinician's next task is to look for depression, carefully, because a humiliating setback at work is a classic trigger: does he still enjoy anything, how is his sleep and appetite, does he feel worthless, has he thought of death? If he meets the criteria for a major depressive episode, the diagnosis is depression and the low desire is one of its symptoms. If not, the clinician asks about the marriage: is there an old conflict that the demotion has exposed, and would the loss of desire be better explained by severe relationship distress? If neither depression nor a severe relationship problem explains the picture, and the low desire has lasted more than 6 months, distresses him and has persisted although the acute stress has passed, he meets the criteria for male hypoactive sexual desire disorder, acquired and probably generalised. Treatment. No drug is approved for low desire in men; flibanserin and bremelanotide are licensed only for premenopausal women. Treatment therefore means treating the cause. Testosterone replacement is given only when hypogonadism has been confirmed by blood tests, because, as Pinel stresses, extra testosterone does not raise desire in men whose levels are normal (Section 9.2.4). A raised prolactin is investigated for a pituitary tumour (a prolactinoma) and treated, usually with a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline, which mimics dopamine's natural brake on prolactin release. Drugs that may be responsible are reviewed with the prescriber, depression is treated, and the psychological work is couple-based: sex therapy, communication and the cognitive work on beliefs and performance worries described in Book 2, Section 7.9. Exam trap Male hypoactive sexual desire disorder needs both deficient sexual thoughts or fantasies and deficient desire for sexual activity, judged against the man's age and context , for about 6 months, with distress; there is no occasions percentage . The 6-month rule exists to exclude a temporary reaction to adversity, such as losing a job. In men, desire and arousal remain separate disorders. Fewer than 2 percent of men report distressing low desire. Testosterone helps only men with proven hypogonadism . An asexual identity excludes the diagnosis. Erectile disorder Two men sit in the same outpatient waiting room on the same morning with what looks like the same complaint. Hemant, 56, runs a hardware shop in Indore. He has had diabetes for twelve years and high blood pressure for eight, and he admits that he rarely checks his sugar and often forgets his tablets; he also smokes. Over the past three years his erections have weakened steadily, and now he cannot obtain a firm erection with his wife, on his own, or on waking; he cannot remember when he last woke with one. Aniruddh, 29, is a software engineer in Bengaluru. Eight months ago, on the first night he spent with his new partner, Pallavi, after a party at which he had drunk a good deal, he lost his erection. Since then it has happened every time they have tried, drunk or sober; he lies awake beforehand rehearsing the failure, and Pallavi has begun to wonder aloud whether he still finds her attractive. Yet he wakes most mornings with a firm erection and has normal erections when he masturbates. Both men are distressed, and both meet the criteria for the same disorder. By the end of this subsection you should be able to say why their causes, their tests and their treatment are entirely different. The criteria. Erectile disorder (DSM-5-TR code F52.21) requires at least one of three symptoms, experienced on almost all or all (approximately 75 to 100 percent) occasions of sexual activity: (1) marked difficulty in obtaining an erection during sexual activity; (2) marked difficulty in maintaining an erection until the completion of sexual activity; or (3) a marked decrease in erectile rigidity (Criterion A). The three options exist because men fail in different ways: some never become firm, some become firm and lose it, and some, like many older men, have erections that are present but too soft for penetration. The symptoms must have lasted approximately 6 months (Criterion B), must cause clinically significant distress (Criterion C), and must not be better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress or other significant stressors, or be attributable to a substance, medication or another medical condition (Criterion D). The specifiers are lifelong or acquired, generalised or situational, and mild, moderate or severe distress. In the language of Section 9.3.1, Hemant's disorder is acquired and generalised and Aniruddh's is acquired and situational. Words. DSM-5-TR is careful about terms, and the care is examinable. Erectile dysfunction is the widely used descriptive term, used in ICD-10 and in medicine generally, for difficulty getting and keeping an erection. Erectile disorder is the narrower DSM diagnostic category in which erectile dysfunction has persisted for at least about 6 months and causes distress. The older word impotence (and its female counterpart, "frigidity") has been abandoned: Barlow and Durand call both old and somewhat derogatory, and imprecise because they do not identify which phase of the response has failed. DSM-IV's name, "male erectile disorder", lost its first word in DSM-5. What it is like. DSM-5-TR describes men with erectile disorder as often having low self-esteem and self-confidence, a decreased sense of masculinity and depressed mood, with feelings of guilt, self-blame, failure and anger and a fear of disappointing their partner; fear and avoidance of sexual encounters may follow, and partners commonly report less sexual satisfaction and less desire of their own. Aniruddh's rehearsing of failure and Pallavi's question about attraction are both typical. DSM-5-TR lists the same five factors as for every dysfunction, with the medical ones spelt out (surgery such as transurethral resection of the prostate, hypogonadism, and neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis and diabetic neuropathy), and adds a sixth: the use of substances or medications. How common. Erectile problems rise steeply with age, particularly after 50. Internationally, DSM-5-TR estimates that erectile disorder affects about 13 to 21 percent of men aged 40 to 80: under 10 percent of men younger than 40, about 20 to 40 percent of men in their 60s and 50 to 75 percent of men over 70; in one Australian longitudinal study, 80 percent of men aged 70 and over had the disorder. The best-known study of ageing men, the Massachusetts Male Aging Study of 1,290 men aged 40 to 70 (Feldman and colleagues, 1994), found at least some degree of erectile impairment in 52 percent of the men overall, in about 40 percent of men at age 40 and in nearly 70 percent at age 70, and complete erectile failure tripled from 5 to 15 percent between those ages. The contrast with Laumann's 5 percent (Table 9.7) is mostly a matter of age and definition: Laumann's sample stopped at 59 and counted only clear problems, whereas the Massachusetts figures include mild impairment. At the other end of life, about 20 percent of young men in mostly Western studies feared erectile problems on their first sexual experience, and about 8 percent had problems that prevented penetration. Erectile problems are the commonest reason men seek sexual help: Barlow and Durand report that they account for half or more of the men referred to specialists for sexual problems. Course. Failure on the first attempt at intercourse is common and is linked to having sex with an unfamiliar partner, drugs or alcohol, not really wanting sex, and peer pressure; most such problems are thought to pass without treatment. Acquired erectile disorder, by contrast, is often associated with biological factors such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease and is likely to persist in most men. Lifelong erectile disorder is linked in clinical experience to psychological factors that are self-limiting or respond to psychological treatment. Distress about erectile problems is lower in older men than in younger ones. The medical links. Erectile disorder has the strongest physical ties of all the sexual dysfunctions, because an erection depends on healthy nerves, healthy blood vessels and adequate hormones all at once (Section 9.2.4). DSM-5-TR names age, smoking, lack of physical exercise, diabetes and decreased desire as risk factors for the acquired form. Diabetes is the classic physical cause, because it damages both the small nerves (neuropathy) and the blood vessels (vascular disease) on which erection depends; in the Massachusetts study, 28 percent of men with diabetes had complete erectile failure. Vascular disease works in two ways: arterial insufficiency, in which narrowed arteries cannot deliver enough blood, and venous leakage, in which blood drains away too quickly for an erection to be maintained, a failure of the veno-occlusion described in Section 9.2.4. Smoking is a risk in its own right: in a study of more than 4,000 male army veterans, cigarette smoking alone was associated with increased erectile dysfunction even after alcohol and vascular disease were allowed for (Mannino, Klevens and Flanders, 1994). Other medical causes include prostate surgery and radiotherapy, lower urinary tract symptoms from an enlarged prostate, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, hypogonadism, kidney disease and obstructive sleep apnoea, and many drugs: antihypertensives (Barlow and Durand single out the beta-blockers such as propranolol), antidepressants, antipsychotics, alcohol, nicotine and cocaine (Section 9.4.5). One medical link turns erectile disorder into a warning light. One widely cited explanation, the "artery size hypothesis" of the Italian cardiologist Piero Montorsi and his colleagues, is that the arteries of the penis are narrower than those of the heart, so the same amount of atherosclerotic plaque obstructs them sooner and the problem shows itself there first. Whatever the mechanism, DSM-5-TR states that erectile disorder in men aged 40 and over is predictive of future risk for coronary artery disease, which is why serum lipids are checked, and Barlow and Durand note the recommendation that men presenting with erectile dysfunction be screened for cardiovascular disease. A man like Hemant who comes for a sexual problem may be telling his doctor, without knowing it, that his heart is at risk. Clinical link: erectile disorder and depression DSM-5-TR reports that the risk of depression is significantly higher in men with erectile disorder, and markedly higher in the first year after onset. Among men treated for erectile disorder who were also depressed, raised rates of suicidal thoughts and behaviour have been observed; the men themselves blamed the erectile problem, though depression was probably also contributing. Elevated suicide rates in men with prostate cancer may be related in part to the erectile dysfunction caused by its treatment and the depression that follows. A clinician who sees a man for erectile problems should therefore ask about mood and suicidal thoughts, and a clinician treating a depressed man should ask about sexual function (suicide risk assessment is taught in Book 3, Chapter 5). Organic or psychogenic? The most difficult part of the diagnosis, DSM-5-TR says, is ruling out erectile problems that are fully explained by medical factors, because such cases receive no mental disorder diagnosis at all; and the distinction is usually unclear, because many cases have mixed biological and psychological causes. A problem is called organic when a physical cause (vascular, neurological, hormonal or drug-related) is responsible and psychogenic when psychological factors are. DSM-5-TR gives the clues, and Table 9.8 arranges them. Erectile dysfunction due to organic factors is generally generalised and gradual in onset, with one exception: a sudden onset after injury to the nerves of the genitals, as in spinal cord injury. Problems that are situational and inconsistent and that begin suddenly after a stressful life event are most often psychological, and an age under 40 also points to a psychological cause. Normal erections in sleep or on waking, or during masturbation, show that the physical machinery works. If the man is older than 40 to 50 or has other medical problems, medical causes, especially vascular disease, must be considered. And one warning cuts across the whole table: "the presence of an organic disease known to cause erectile problems does not confirm a causal relationship". A man with diabetes can develop erectile disorder in response to psychological stress, so a diagnosis of diabetes does not end the assessment. Hemant's problem began gradually, is generalised (it occurs with his wife, alone and on waking), and comes with uncontrolled diabetes, high blood pressure, smoking and an age over 50: every clue in the middle column. The likeliest cause is the combined vascular and nerve damage of diabetes and hypertension; his blood pressure tablets, if they are of a type that impairs erection, may be contributing. If the problem is fully explained by his medical condition, DSM-5-TR would give him no psychiatric diagnosis; in ICD-11 he would receive HA01.1 male erectile dysfunction with the qualifier HA40.0, associated with a medical condition. His workup includes fasting glucose, lipids, testosterone and a cardiovascular assessment. Aniruddh's problem began suddenly after a failure with a new partner and alcohol, is situational (it occurs only with Pallavi), spares his morning erections and masturbation, and he is under 40: every clue in the right-hand column. He is the young man of Section 9.2.6 made real, and Figure 9.5 shows exactly what keeps his problem going. He meets the criteria for erectile disorder, acquired and situational. Culture and sex. Rates of erectile disorder vary across countries, and DSM-5-TR is unsure how much of the variation reflects genuine differences and how much reflects how willing men are to report it. Cultural concern about appearing weak or less masculine, differing norms about whether erections should be expected to change with healthy ageing, and expectations about marriage, sexual performance, fertility and gender roles can all shape the anxieties that contribute to the disorder. DSM-5-TR's only regional details come from an online survey: concern about genital size in the United States and the Middle East, and fear of male infertility more often in the Middle East. It reports no Indian figure, and none is given here, although the pressures it describes (to perform on the wedding night, to produce a child soon after marriage) will be familiar from Book 2, Section 7.9.7. By definition the diagnosis is given only to men; distressing arousal difficulties in women belong to female sexual interest/arousal disorder. Differential diagnosis and comorbidity. Major depressive disorder and erectile disorder are closely associated; if the erectile problem is better explained by depression, erectile disorder is not diagnosed. A man with excessive expectations may in fact have normal erectile function, so the differential includes normal function judged against an unrealistic standard (an older man who expects the instant erections of his twenties, for instance). An onset that coincides with starting a drug and clears when it is stopped points to substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction. And a medical cause must be ruled out, as above. Erectile disorder often occurs with premature ejaculation and male hypoactive sexual desire disorder, with anxiety and depressive disorders, with posttraumatic stress disorder, with lower urinary tract symptoms of prostatic enlargement, and with dyslipidaemia, cardiovascular disease, hypogonadism, multiple sclerosis and diabetes. ICD-10 coded the nonorganic form as F52.2, failure of genital response; ICD-11 codes it as HA01.1, male erectile dysfunction, whatever the cause, with an HA40 qualifier to record the cause. Treatment: the drugs. Erectile disorder is the sexual dysfunction that drugs transformed. Sildenafil (Viagra) was approved by the FDA on 27 March 1998, and three more phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors followed: vardenafil (Levitra) on 19 August 2003, tadalafil (Cialis) on 21 November 2003 and avanafil (Stendra) on 27 April 2012. Section 9.2.4 explained how they work: they block PDE-5, the enzyme that destroys cGMP, so that the nitric oxide signal produced by sexual stimulation lasts longer and the erection is easier to obtain and keep. They do not create an erection without stimulation and they do not increase desire. They differ mainly in how long they last; tadalafil acts for up to about 36 hours, which frees couples from having to time sex around a tablet. In the clinical trials Barlow and Durand summarise, 50 to 80 percent of men had erections sufficient for intercourse on the drug, against about 30 percent on placebo. Common side effects follow from the presence of PDE-5 in other blood vessels: headache (reported by up to 30 percent of men in some studies, particularly at higher doses), flushing, indigestion and a stuffy nose, and, with sildenafil, a transient blue tinge to vision. The one absolute rule is never to combine them with nitrates: a nitrate should not be given within 24 hours of sildenafil, or within 48 hours of tadalafil, because of the risk of a dangerous fall in blood pressure. Generic sildenafil and tadalafil are cheap and widely sold in India, so many men try them before they see a doctor; the clinician's task is then to make sure the warning sign for heart disease has not been missed and that no nitrate is being taken. Restoring an erection is not the same as restoring a sex life. When Virag (1999) followed a large group of men treated with sildenafil, 61 percent had erections firm enough for intercourse, but only 32 percent rated the result good (an adequate erection and satisfaction of at least 7 on a 0 to 10 scale); 29 percent rated it fair and 39 percent unsatisfactory. Results are poorer in men who are particularly anxious about sex, and the great majority of men stop using the drug after a few months or a year. Bach, Barlow and Wincze (2004) therefore added cognitive-behavioural treatment to sildenafil, and couples reported greater satisfaction and more sexual activity with the combination than with the drug alone. The lesson echoes Barlow's model: a tablet can repair the hydraulics, but if attention stays fixed on the threat of failure, or the relationship is strained, the problem returns. Treatment: when the tablets fail or cannot be used. For men who do not respond to PDE-5 inhibitors or cannot take them, there are second-line physical treatments, summarised in Table 9.9. A man can learn to inject a drug that relaxes smooth muscle, such as papaverine or alprostadil (a prostaglandin, approved by the FDA for erectile dysfunction as Caverject on 6 July 1995), directly into the erectile tissue shortly before sex; because the drug acts on the muscle itself, it works even when nerves are damaged, producing an erection within about 15 minutes that lasts from 1 to 4 hours. Injections are somewhat painful and artificial, and half or more of men give them up after a short time; a prolonged, painful erection (priapism) is a rare emergency. Alprostadil can also be inserted into the urethra as a small pellet (MUSE, approved by the FDA on 19 November 1996), which avoids the needle but is less effective and is uncomfortable for some men. A vacuum erection device is a cylinder placed over the penis; a pump creates a vacuum that draws blood in, and a ring slipped onto the base of the penis traps it; 70 to 100 percent of users report satisfactory erections, although many find the device awkward. Finally, a penile prosthesis can be implanted surgically: either semi-rigid rods that are bent into position, or inflatable cylinders filled from a small pump implanted in the scrotum. Implants fall short of restoring earlier sexual function or guaranteeing satisfaction in most men, so they are now generally used only when other treatments have failed; they have been particularly useful for men whose prostate has been removed for cancer. Testosterone has only a negligible effect on erectile dysfunction in men with normal levels (Mann and colleagues, 1996) and is given only for proven hypogonadism, where it can also restore desire. For every man with an organic cause, the treatment also includes the cause itself: better control of diabetes and blood pressure, a change of antihypertensive drug if the present one impairs erection, stopping smoking, exercise and attention to lipids. These are taught in Book 2 and only their evidence is given here. Sensate focus and couple sex therapy (Book 2, Sections 7.9.2 and 7.9.3) remove the demand to perform that drives the negative loop of Figure 9.5. Masters and Johnson reported success close to 60 percent for the hardest cases, lifelong generalised erectile dysfunction, and later studies of sex therapy for erectile dysfunction report positive outcomes in as many as 60 to 70 percent of cases for at least several years, with some slipping afterwards. For Aniruddh, the plan is psychological: education about the effect of alcohol and anxiety on erection, a temporary ban on attempts at intercourse with graded sensate focus exercises with Pallavi, and cognitive work on his rehearsals of failure; a short course of a PDE-5 inhibitor can be added to give him a few successes that break the loop, provided the psychological work continues. For Hemant, the plan is medical first, with a PDE-5 inhibitor once a cardiovascular assessment has shown that sexual activity is safe and that he takes no nitrates, better control of his diabetes and blood pressure, and an invitation to his wife to take part, because their sexual life together, not only his erection, is what needs restoring. Exam trap Diabetes and vascular disease are the classic physical links of erectile disorder , not of premature ejaculation (which is most commonly associated with an anxiety state, Section 9.4.3). Erectile disorder needs 1 of 3 symptoms (obtaining, maintaining, rigidity) on 75 to 100 percent of occasions for about 6 months. Normal morning or nocturnal erections point to a psychological cause; a gradual, generalised problem after 50 points to an organic one, but a known disease does not prove the cause. Erectile disorder in men over 40 predicts coronary artery disease . Sildenafil needs sexual stimulation, does not raise desire and must never be combined with nitrates. The stop-start and squeeze techniques are for premature ejaculation , not for erectile disorder; sensate focus is the core psychological method for erectile disorder. "Impotence" is the rejected old term; "erectile dysfunction" is the descriptive term; "erectile disorder" is the DSM diagnosis. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks.
