In Laumann, Paik and Rosen's analysis (1999), percent of women and percent of men reported a sexual dysfunction. Firm erections during REM sleep, recorded by testing, point to a cause of erectile failure; the classic physical link of erectile disorder is . Answers: (1) resolution; desire, (2) neutrality; responsive, (3) parasympathetic; phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5), (4) increased; interference, (5) inhibition, (6) 75 to 100; 6, (7) male hypoactive sexual desire disorder, (8) 3; 6, (9) 43; 31, (10) nocturnal penile tumescence; psychological (psychogenic); diabetes (and vascular disease). 9.4 Sexual Dysfunctions II: Orgasm, Ejaculation, Pain and Substance-Induced Dysfunction Medium yield · 2 Qs Section 9.3 dealt with the first half of the sexual response: whether a person wants sex and whether the body becomes aroused. This section takes the second half and the problems that sit outside the cycle altogether. Three of the disorders concern the climax of the response, and they divide neatly by timing. In female orgasmic disorder and delayed ejaculation the climax comes too late or not at all; in premature (early) ejaculation it comes too soon. A fourth disorder, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder , is not a failure of any phase but a problem of pain, fear and muscular tension that makes penetration difficult or impossible. The fifth, substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction , can strike at any phase, and it matters to every clinician who sees a client on an antidepressant or an antipsychotic, because it is one of the commonest reasons people stop taking their tablets. The section ends by gathering every treatment for every sexual dysfunction into one table, so that you can see which psychological methods from Book 2 and which physical treatments from this book belong to which problem. Keep two things from Section 9.3.1 in mind as you read. First, every disorder here is diagnosed against the shared template: a problem that is persistent (usually about 6 months), frequent (usually on about 75 to 100 percent of occasions), distressing, and not better explained by another mental disorder, by severe relationship distress or partner violence, by a drug, or by a medical illness. Second, the template has exceptions, and several of them live in this section: premature ejaculation is graded by the clock rather than by distress, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder has no percentage of occasions and no generalised or situational specifier, and the substance-induced disorder has no 6-month rule at all. Examiners like exceptions, so they are flagged as we go. Female orgasmic disorder Namrata is 31, a pharmacist in Nagpur, married for six years to a man she describes as kind and patient. She comes to a women's health clinic with a question she has rehearsed for months and still cannot say directly: she has never had an orgasm, not with her husband and not alone. She enjoys closeness and sometimes feels aroused, but the feeling builds a little and then fades, "like a song that stops before the chorus". She grew up in a strict household where sex was never mentioned except as a danger, and she remembers an aunt telling her that pleasure "was for men, not for good girls". She has never touched herself deliberately; she has never told her husband what she likes because she does not know. For a year she has felt that something is wrong with her, and lately she has started avoiding intimacy so that the disappointment will not show. Namrata's problem is the one DSM-5-TR calls female orgasmic disorder . Its first criterion offers two routes. Either there is a marked delay in, marked infrequency of, or absence of orgasm , or there is markedly reduced intensity of orgasmic sensations : some women reach orgasm but feel it only faintly, and DSM-5-TR counts that as a dysfunction too. Either symptom must occur on almost all or all occasions of sexual activity (approximately 75 to 100 percent), in the situations where it occurs or, if it is generalised, in all of them. It must have lasted approximately 6 months, it must cause clinically significant distress, and it must not be better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, by severe relationship distress (DSM-5-TR names partner violence as its example) or other significant stressors, by a substance or medication, or by another medical condition. The specifiers are the usual pairs, lifelong or acquired and generalised or situational, and severity is rated by the degree of distress, mild, moderate or severe. There is also one specifier found nowhere else in the chapter: never experienced an orgasm under any situation . Namrata would carry it. It matters for treatment, because a woman who has never had an orgasm needs to learn how her body responds, whereas a woman who has lost a response she once had needs the clinician to find out what changed. Why does each rule exist? The 6-month and 75 to 100 percent rules separate a disorder from the ordinary variability of women's orgasm, which is far greater than men's. DSM-5-TR says that women show wide variability in the type and intensity of stimulation that brings orgasm, and that their descriptions of orgasm vary so much that it seems to be experienced in very different ways by different women and by the same woman on different occasions. The word "approximately" in the duration rule is deliberate: DSM-5-TR says it allows clinical judgement when a problem has not quite lasted 6 months. The distress rule exists because many women with infrequent orgasm are not troubled by it. DSM-5-TR is blunt about this: overall sexual satisfaction is not strongly correlated with orgasm, and many women report high satisfaction while rarely or never reaching orgasm. A difficulty that does not distress the woman who has it is a variation, not a disorder. Two further rules prevent false diagnoses, and both are favourite exam material. The first concerns intercourse. Many women need direct clitoral stimulation to reach orgasm, and only a relatively small proportion always reach orgasm during penile-vaginal intercourse. Barlow and Durand put a figure on it: only about 20 percent of women reliably have orgasms during intercourse (Graham, 2010; Lloyd, 2005). So DSM-5-TR states plainly that a woman who reaches orgasm through clitoral stimulation but not during intercourse does not meet the criteria . Her pattern is the commonest pattern there is. The second rule concerns stimulation. If the problem is the result of inadequate sexual stimulation (a partner who hurries, a couple who do not know what works), no diagnosis of female orgasmic disorder is made, although DSM-5-TR adds that care may still be needed. In Namrata's case the clinician must ask whether she has ever had the kind of stimulation that would bring most women to orgasm. If the answer is no, the first task is education, and the diagnosis waits. How common is the problem? The honest answer is that it depends on how you ask. DSM-5-TR reports that orgasm problems in premenopausal women range from 8 to 72 percent across studies, depending on age, culture, duration and severity, and warns that these figures ignore distress, so they count problems rather than disorders. About 10 percent of women internationally never experience orgasm in their lifetime. Barlow and Durand estimate that about 25 percent of women report significant difficulty reaching orgasm, that the problem is spread evenly across age groups, and that unmarried women were 1.5 times more likely to report it than married women. An inability to reach orgasm is, they add, the commonest complaint among women who seek therapy for sexual problems. DSM-5-TR also notes that reports of inability to reach orgasm vary over a twofold range across world regions, a reminder of how much culture shapes this experience. The course of orgasm in women differs from men's. A woman's first orgasm can occur at any time from before puberty to well into adulthood; women show a more variable age at first orgasm than men, and the proportion of women who have experienced orgasm rises with age, as they meet a wider variety of stimulation and learn more about their own bodies. Women are also more consistent in reaching orgasm through masturbation than with a partner. All of this is why lifelong orgasmic difficulty in a young woman with little sexual knowledge is often a problem of learning, and why the treatment that works best for it is, at heart, a teaching programme. The causes span every level of the biopsychosocial model (Book 3 Section 1.3.5). Among psychological factors DSM-5-TR names anxiety and worries about pregnancy, both of which pull attention away from sensation (the mechanism of Section 9.2.5). Environmental factors include relationship problems, physical and mental health, and sociocultural influences such as gender-role expectations and religious norms; DSM-5-TR adds that cultures which undervalue women's sexual satisfaction, or treat marital sex as a woman's duty rather than a pleasure, have lower rates of help-seeking. Namrata's upbringing, with its message that pleasure belongs to men, is a textbook example. Physiological factors include multiple sclerosis, damage to the pelvic nerves from radical hysterectomy, spinal cord injury, vulvovaginal atrophy (thinning and dryness of the vaginal tissues, which makes orgasm difficulties significantly more likely) and, above all in psychiatric practice, the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), which are known to delay or inhibit orgasm in women (Section 9.4.5). Menopausal status itself is not consistently linked to orgasm difficulty, and DSM-5-TR suggests there may be a significant genetic contribution to variation in women's orgasmic function. What has not been supported, it says, is any link between particular personality traits or forms of psychopathology and orgasmic dysfunction: the old psychoanalytic picture of the "frigid" woman with a characteristic personality has not survived the evidence. The differential diagnosis follows the template. If the difficulty is better explained by another mental disorder, such as major depression, female orgasmic disorder is not diagnosed. If it began with a drug and lifts when the drug is stopped or reduced, the diagnosis is substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction. If it is due to a medical condition such as multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury, or if severe relationship distress or partner violence explains it, female orgasmic disorder is not diagnosed either. By contrast, the presence of another sexual dysfunction does not rule it out: orgasm difficulties often co-occur with problems of interest and arousal (Section 9.3.4), and both can be diagnosed. In the manuals, DSM-5-TR prints the code F52.31; the WHO's ICD-10 placed orgasm problems of both sexes together under F52.3, orgasmic dysfunction ("orgasm either does not occur or is markedly delayed", including "inhibited orgasm (male) (female)"); and ICD-11 calls the condition anorgasmia , HA02.0, in Chapter 17. DSM-5-TR also notes that female orgasmic disorder is diagnosed only in women; distressing orgasm problems in men are considered under delayed ejaculation. Treatment is mainly psychological, and it is among the most successful in sex therapy. The method of choice for lifelong orgasmic disorder is directed masturbation , the graded programme of self-exploration and self-stimulation developed by Joseph LoPiccolo and W. Charles Lobitz in 1972 and set out for women themselves in Becoming Orgasmic (1976) by Julia Heiman , Leslie LoPiccolo and Joseph LoPiccolo; once a woman can reach orgasm alone, the learning is carried into the relationship, and the bridge manoeuvre helps carry it into intercourse. Kegel exercises are sometimes added to increase awareness of genital sensation. Book 2 Section 7.9.4 describes each technique step by step. The evidence is strong: summaries reviewed by Barlow and Durand suggest that 70 to 90 percent of women benefit, and that the gains are stable and even improve over time. On the physical side, the clinician looks for anything that blocks the response: an SSRI that might be changed (Section 9.4.5), vaginal atrophy that can be treated, a medical illness. There is no drug approved for female orgasmic disorder. For Namrata, the likely plan is education about anatomy and response, permission to explore her own body without guilt, directed masturbation, and then joint sessions in which she shows her husband what she has learned. Exam trap A woman who reaches orgasm with clitoral stimulation but not during intercourse does not have female orgasmic disorder; nor does a woman whose problem is due to inadequate stimulation . Criterion A has two routes: delay, infrequency or absence of orgasm, or markedly reduced intensity. The special specifier is "never experienced an orgasm under any situation". Severity is rated by distress , not by frequency. Personality traits are not an established cause. Codes: DSM-5-TR F52.31; ICD-10 F52.3 orgasmic dysfunction (for both sexes); ICD-11 HA02.0 anorgasmia . Treatment of lifelong cases: directed masturbation (LoPiccolo and Lobitz, 1972), not stop-start or squeeze. Delayed ejaculation Waseem is 35, a civil engineer in Hyderabad, and he did not come to see a psychologist. He and his wife came to a fertility clinic after four years of trying for a child, and it was only when the gynaecologist asked a direct question that the problem emerged: in their entire marriage Waseem has never ejaculated during intercourse. He can maintain an erection for a long time, sometimes until both of them are exhausted and sore, but the climax never comes. Alone, using his own hand and a firm, fast rhythm he has used since he was a teenager, he ejaculates without difficulty, and he does so almost every day. He has always been ashamed to say any of this, and his wife has begun to wonder whether he finds her unattractive. The fertility specialist, finding a normal semen sample, refers them on. Waseem has delayed ejaculation . DSM-5-TR's criteria require either a marked delay in ejaculation or a marked infrequency or absence of ejaculation , experienced on almost all or all (approximately 75 to 100 percent) occasions of partnered sexual activity, and, crucially, without the individual desiring delay . That last phrase separates a problem from a choice: a man who deliberately holds back has nothing to diagnose. The usual rules then follow: approximately 6 months, clinically significant distress, and no better explanation by a nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress or other stressors, a substance or medication, or a medical condition. The specifiers are lifelong or acquired and generalised or situational, and severity is rated by distress. The partnered activity can be manual, oral, coital or anal, so the diagnosis is not limited to intercourse with a woman, although most of the research has studied vaginal intercourse. DSM-5-TR notes that it is common for men with delayed ejaculation to ejaculate easily with self-stimulation but not with a partner, exactly Waseem's pattern, and that in heterosexual couples it is often the female partner's distress that brings the couple to treatment. The disorder has had several names, and the past papers offer one of them as a distractor, so learn them as a set. DSM-III (1980) and DSM-III-R (1987) called it inhibited male orgasm , the male partner of "inhibited female orgasm". DSM-IV (1994) renamed both, as male orgasmic disorder and female orgasmic disorder. DSM-5 (2013) replaced male orgasmic disorder with delayed ejaculation , which describes what actually happens; older clinical writing also called it retarded ejaculation. Whatever the name, the problem is the opposite of premature ejaculation: a climax that comes too late or never, rather than too soon. How long is too long? Here DSM-5-TR is candid. There is no consensus about what constitutes a reasonable time to reach orgasm, so "delay" has no precise boundary. Research on heterosexual couples has measured the intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT), the time from vaginal penetration to ejaculation, and found that for most men it lies between about 4 and 10 minutes. Nor is there a clear line between delayed ejaculation as a dysfunction and the slowing that comes with normal ageing. The diagnosis therefore rests on clinical judgement, taking account of the man's age, his medical and sexual history, the relationship and his patterns of stimulation, and DSM-5-TR warns that it should not be given if the clinician judges that the man's dissatisfaction is entirely due to unrealistic expectations. The clinical picture has some characteristic features. The man and his partner may describe prolonged thrusting to the point of exhaustion, genital discomfort or even injury before they give up, and some men begin to avoid sex altogether. Men with delayed ejaculation report less intercourse, more relationship distress, lower subjective arousal, anxiety about performance and more general health problems than other men. Three habits are associated with the disorder, and Waseem shows all of them: highly frequent masturbation , a masturbation technique that a partner cannot easily reproduce (unusual speed, pressure or method), and a marked gap between the fantasies used in masturbation and the reality of sex with a partner . The logic is simple: a man whose arousal has been trained for years to a very specific kind of stimulation may find that a partner's touch, however loving, simply does not reach the threshold. DSM-5-TR estimates the prevalence of delayed ejaculation at 1 to 5 percent in the United States and as high as 11 percent in some international studies, though different definitions make the figures hard to compare; one textbook estimate, from the American national survey, is about 8 percent of men (Laumann and colleagues, 1999, reported by Barlow and Durand). Men seldom seek help for it; Barlow and Durand suggest that many couples simply accommodate it, with the man reaching climax through other forms of stimulation. Prevalence rises with age. As men grow older they tend to show reduced ejaculatory volume, force and sensation and a longer refractory time, and age-related loss of fast-conducting sensory nerves and falling sex hormones may contribute. The causes run from the bedroom to the operating theatre. DSM-5-TR names depression and relationship dissatisfaction as the predominant psychosocial contributors, and notes that delayed ejaculation may be more common in severe major depressive disorder. Medically, anything that disrupts the sympathetic or somatic nerve supply to the genitals can delay or abolish ejaculation (Section 9.2.4 explains that emission depends on sympathetic nerves): radical prostatectomy for cancer, spinal cord injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis, pelvic surgery, severe diabetes (through diabetic neuropathy), epilepsy, hormonal abnormalities such as hypogonadism, sleep apnoea and bowel dysfunction. Drugs are a major cause: alpha-blockers that inhibit the adrenergic nerve supply to the ejaculatory system (tamsulosin, prescribed for an enlarged prostate, is DSM-5-TR's example), antihypertensives, antidepressants (especially the SSRIs), antipsychotics, alcohol, opioids and cannabis. When a drug is responsible, the diagnosis becomes substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction (Section 9.4.5). The differential diagnosis includes several urological conditions that a psychologist must know by name. In retrograde ejaculation the ejaculatory fluid travels backwards into the bladder instead of forwards out of the penis; the man feels orgasm but little or no semen appears, and Barlow and Durand note that this is almost always caused by drugs or a medical condition. In anejaculation there is no ejaculation at all, usually from hormonal, neurological or anatomical causes, and an ejaculatory duct obstruction blocks the outflow mechanically. The clinician must also separate ejaculation from orgasm. Ejaculation happens in the genitals; orgasm is primarily a subjective experience; the two usually occur together, but not always. A man who ejaculates normally but feels little or no pleasure has anhedonic ejaculation , which DSM-5-TR says is not coded as delayed ejaculation but as other specified (or unspecified) sexual dysfunction (Section 9.4.6). Delayed ejaculation matters beyond the bedroom: DSM-5-TR points out that it can contribute to difficulty conceiving and lead to extensive fertility investigations, because men rarely mention the problem unless a doctor asks directly, which is exactly what happened to Waseem. In the manuals, DSM-5-TR prints the code F52.32; ICD-10 placed the problem under F52.3, orgasmic dysfunction, shared with women; and ICD-11 calls it male delayed ejaculation , HA03.1, among the ejaculatory dysfunctions in Chapter 17. Treatment starts with the cause: review and if possible change any drug that inhibits ejaculation, treat depression, and investigate medical causes. Then comes retraining. The man is usually asked to reduce the frequency of masturbation, to change his technique so that it resembles what a partner can provide, and to bring his fantasies closer to his real sexual life; the couple work through sensate focus and sex therapy (Book 2 Sections 7.9.2 to 7.9.4) to reduce pressure and increase stimulation that works for both of them. Couple therapy addresses the hurt that has built up, such as Waseem's wife's fear that he does not desire her. No drug is approved for delayed ejaculation. Where conception is the urgent goal, the fertility team can help the couple conceive while the sexual problem is being treated. Exam trap Inhibited male orgasm (DSM-III and DSM-III-R) and male orgasmic disorder (DSM-IV) are old names for delayed ejaculation , the opposite of premature ejaculation; an option reading "inhibited male orgasm" in a question about stop-start and squeeze techniques is a distractor. The delay must occur without the man desiring it and in partnered activity; most men ejaculate after about 4 to 10 minutes of intercourse. Retrograde ejaculation (semen into the bladder) is a urological differential, not the same disorder; normal ejaculation without pleasure ( anhedonic ejaculation ) is coded as other specified sexual dysfunction. ICD-11: HA03.1 male delayed ejaculation. Premature (early) ejaculation Bhavesh is 26 and works in his family's diamond-polishing business in Surat. Four months ago he married in an arranged marriage, and he and his wife live with his parents and younger brother in a flat where every wall is thin. On every attempt at intercourse he ejaculates within about half a minute of penetration, sometimes before. He has started to dread bedtime, stays late at the workshop, and pretends to be asleep when he comes home. He has told no one in the family, but he has quietly bought two "power" capsules from an advertisement and has privately decided what the cause is: as a teenager he masturbated "too much", and he believes this weakened him. His wife has said nothing directly, but she seems hurt and withdrawn, and his mother has started dropping hints about grandchildren. DSM-5-TR calls Bhavesh's problem premature (early) ejaculation . Its first criterion is unique in the chapter because it contains a clock: a persistent or recurrent pattern of ejaculation during partnered sexual activity within approximately 1 minute following vaginal penetration and before the individual wishes it . Both halves count. A man who ejaculates at 50 seconds and is content does not have the disorder; neither does a man who ejaculates after 6 minutes and wishes he could last longer. A note adds that the diagnosis can be given for nonvaginal sexual activity, but no time criterion has been established for it; DSM-5-TR suggests that similar latencies are reasonable to assume for men who have sex with men. Criterion B requires the pattern to have been present for at least 6 months (note that the word "approximately" is missing here, unlike most of the chapter) and on almost all or all occasions (approximately 75 to 100 percent). Criterion C requires clinically significant distress and Criterion D the usual exclusions. The specifiers are lifelong or acquired and generalised or situational. Severity, unusually, is graded by time rather than distress: mild when ejaculation occurs within approximately 30 seconds to 1 minute of penetration, moderate within approximately 15 to 30 seconds, and severe before sexual activity, at its start or within approximately 15 seconds. At about half a minute, Bhavesh sits on the border of mild and moderate. Why does a psychiatric manual use a stopwatch? Because without one the diagnosis would have no edge. Before DSM-5 the criteria spoke only of ejaculation "with minimal sexual stimulation" and "before the person wishes it", which made almost any man with a worry eligible. The research measure is the intravaginal ejaculatory latency time you met in Section 9.4.2. In research, DSM-5-TR explains, it is usually measured by the partner with a stopwatch, which is hardly ideal in real life; in the clinic, the man's own estimate is accepted instead, because estimated and measured latencies are highly correlated as long as the latency is short. How short is short? For most men the latency is about 4 to 10 minutes, and the International Society for Sexual Medicine (ISSM) reports a median of about 5.4 minutes in multinational studies. DSM-5-TR adds a comment that is easy to misread: a 60-second latency, it says, was previously considered an appropriate cutoff for lifelong premature ejaculation, but "expert consensus now considers this latency time to be too brief and instead recommends a 120-second threshold". This is DSM-5-TR reporting the views of experts; its own criterion still says approximately 1 minute. The ISSM, whose second guideline panel met in Bangalore in April 2013, offered a unified definition of its own: lifelong premature ejaculation when ejaculation always or nearly always occurs before or within about 1 minute of vaginal penetration from the first sexual experience, and acquired premature ejaculation when there is a clinically significant reduction in latency, often to about 3 minutes or less, together with an inability to delay ejaculation and negative personal consequences such as distress or avoidance of intimacy. Figure 9.6 puts these numbers on one ruler. The WHO's ICD-10 had taken a different route altogether, defining premature ejaculation (F52.4) without any clock as "the inability to control ejaculation sufficiently for both partners to enjoy sexual interaction". Premature ejaculation comes in two forms, and they behave differently. Lifelong premature ejaculation begins with a man's first sexual experiences and persists; DSM-5-TR calls it relatively stable throughout life. Some young men ejaculate quickly in their first encounters and then gain control with experience, so it is the persistence of the problem beyond 6 months that makes the diagnosis. Acquired premature ejaculation develops after a period of normal latency, usually appears in or after the fourth decade of life, and is far less studied; DSM-5-TR links it to thyroid disease , prostatitis (inflammation of the prostate) and drug withdrawal , especially withdrawal from opioids. Two situations look like the disorder but are not. A man with a normal latency who simply wants to last longer has an ejaculatory concern that does not meet the criteria, and so does a man with episodic quick ejaculation, for example in the first encounter with a new partner, when a short latency is common or even normal. Both may be distressed, and both may benefit from reassurance and information; neither has a disorder. How common is it? It depends entirely on the definition. Internationally, DSM-5-TR reports that 8 to 30 percent of men across all ages report the problem, with prevalence rising with age: about 9 to 11 percent among men aged 18 to 30 in Switzerland and Turkey, and concern about ejaculating quickly in as many as 55 percent of American men in their fifties. Yet when premature ejaculation is defined strictly as ejaculation within about 1 minute of penetration, only 1 to 3 percent of men would be diagnosed, and the ISSM concludes that lifelong premature ejaculation, defined that way, is unlikely to exceed 4 percent of the general population. The gap between those numbers is the gap between worry and disorder. Even so, premature ejaculation is usually described as the most common male sexual dysfunction: in Laumann's American survey 21 percent of men reported it, and in an Indian sexuality clinic described by Barlow and Durand 77 percent of male patients complained of it (both surveys are discussed in Section 9.3.2). Clinic figures are inflated by who comes, but they show what Indian clinicians see every week. Now to the question the past papers ask directly: what is premature ejaculation most commonly associated with? The answer is anxiety . DSM-5-TR names the temperamental risk factor explicitly: premature ejaculation may be more common in men with anxiety disorders, especially social anxiety disorder , and it lists anxiety disorders among the conditions associated with the lifelong form. The physiology explains why (Section 9.2.4). Ejaculation, unlike erection, is driven partly by the sympathetic nervous system, the same system that anxiety activates. Barlow and Durand suggest that some men have a naturally low threshold for ejaculation, needing less stimulation and arousal to reach it, and that anxiety, by raising sympathetic arousal, lowers the threshold further. The result is a vicious circle you can see in Bhavesh: he worries that he will ejaculate quickly, the worry raises his arousal, he ejaculates even more quickly, and the failure feeds the next worry. Performance anxiety and spectatoring (Section 9.2.5) add to the loop by pulling his attention away from his own sensations, so that he never learns to recognise the moment before the point of no return. DSM-5-TR even notes a cultural version of this mechanism: reports of premature ejaculation were more common in arranged marriages, because of anxiety over family pressures and lack of premarital sexual experience. Bhavesh's thin walls, listening relatives and lack of experience are the anxieties DSM-5-TR has in mind. Anxiety is the answer for the exam; it is not the whole story for an interview. DSM-5-TR reports a moderate genetic contribution to lifelong premature ejaculation, associations with polymorphisms of the dopamine transporter and serotonin transporter genes, and positron emission tomography studies showing activation in the midbrain, including the ventral tegmental area, during ejaculation. The Dutch psychiatrist Marcel Waldinger proposed that men with lifelong premature ejaculation may have reduced serotonin signalling (specifically, hyposensitive 5-HT 2C receptors or hypersensitive 5-HT 1A receptors); since serotonin tends to delay ejaculation, low serotonergic tone would mean a lower ejaculatory threshold. That hypothesis explains why serotonin-enhancing drugs delay ejaculation, but the ISSM guideline cautions that serotonin dysregulation has been estimated to explain only a small share (2 to 5 percent) of premature ejaculation complaints in the general population. The balanced conclusion is that lifelong premature ejaculation sits on a biological threshold that anxiety can push lower, while most complaints are driven by anxiety, inexperience and expectation. Just as important are the causes that are not supported, because examiners offer them as options. Masturbation does not cause premature ejaculation. The belief that it does, and that semen loss drains a man's strength, is part of the cluster of beliefs behind dhat syndrome, which Book 3 Section 1.10.4 explains; for Bhavesh it is not a cause but an extra source of anxiety and guilt, and it has already sent him to buy useless capsules. Diabetes is the classic physical cause of erectile disorder, through damage to nerves and blood vessels (Section 9.3.6), not of premature ejaculation. And personality disorder has no special association with it: DSM-5-TR names no personality disorder among its risk factors or its comorbid conditions, which are anxiety disorders, erectile problems and, for the acquired form, prostatitis, thyroid disease and drug withdrawal (the personality disorders themselves are taught in Chapter 11). The phrase anxiety state in the question is simply the older name for a condition of pathological anxiety (ICD-9 grouped what are now the anxiety disorders under "anxiety states"), so it points to the same answer as DSM-5-TR's anxiety disorders. Premature ejaculation does have two important companions. It is often associated with erectile problems , and DSM-5-TR says it may be hard to tell which came first; the ISSM notes that a man worried about losing his erection may hurry to ejaculate before it fades, while anxiety can drive both problems. And it travels with anxiety disorders. Its consequences are real: lower self-esteem and confidence, a sense of lack of control, strain on the relationship and reduced satisfaction for the partner, and difficulty conceiving if ejaculation occurs before penetration. DSM-5-TR adds that single men are more bothered than partnered men, because the problem interferes with starting new relationships, and that elevated suicidal thinking has been seen in men treated for premature ejaculation with comorbid depression, though depression is likely to be a major contributor. In the manuals, DSM-5-TR and ICD-10 both use F52.4; ICD-11 calls it male early ejaculation , HA03.0. Treatment combines a behavioural programme, taught in Book 2, with drugs, taught here. The behavioural methods are old and well known. The stop-start technique was published by the American urologist James Semans in 1956 ("Premature ejaculation: a new approach", in the Southern Medical Journal ): stimulation stops just before the point of no return and resumes when the urge has passed, so that the man learns to recognise and control the sensations that precede ejaculation. Masters and Johnson modified it into the squeeze technique , in which the partner firmly squeezes the penis just below the head to make the urge subside, and a later variant, the basal squeeze , applies pressure at the base so it can be used during intercourse; Kegel exercises for the pelvic floor are sometimes added. Book 2 Section 7.9.4 describes them, and its Exam trap explains why Barlow and Durand credit Semans with "the squeeze technique": in an exam, pair stop-start with Semans (1956) and squeeze with Masters and Johnson. These methods work well at first, with 60 to 90 percent of men benefiting, but the gains fade, to about 25 percent after 3 years or more of follow-up (Barlow and Durand). That fading is the reason drugs and combined treatment have taken a larger place. The drugs exploit a side effect you will meet again in Section 9.4.5: serotonin-enhancing antidepressants delay ejaculation. The first drug to be licensed specifically for premature ejaculation was dapoxetine , a short-acting SSRI designed to be taken on demand , about 1 to 3 hours before expected sexual activity, rather than every day. In the two large American trials pooled by Pryor and colleagues in The Lancet in 2006, involving more than 2,600 men with moderate to severe premature ejaculation, dapoxetine at 30 or 60 milligrams raised the average stopwatch latency from under 1 minute at baseline to about 2.8 and 3.3 minutes after 12 weeks, against about 1.75 minutes on placebo, and it worked from the first dose; the commonest side effects were nausea, diarrhoea, headache and dizziness. The drug's regulatory history is a lesson in itself. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a "not approvable" letter in October 2005, and dapoxetine has never been approved in the United States; it was first approved in Sweden and Finland in early 2009, has since been approved in more than 50 countries, and is marketed in India. Before dapoxetine, and still today, doctors have used daily SSRIs such as paroxetine, sertraline, fluoxetine and citalopram, and the tricyclic clomipramine , all off-label (that is, prescribed for a use the drug is not licensed for). In a meta-analysis of drug trials, Waldinger and colleagues (2004) found paroxetine, clomipramine, sertraline and fluoxetine comparable overall when taken daily, with paroxetine producing the strongest delay. These drugs carry the usual antidepressant side effects, including reduced desire, and their effect lasts only while they are taken. A second approach works on the body's surface instead of the brain. Topical anaesthetics , creams, gels or sprays of lidocaine and prilocaine applied to the glans (the head of the penis) before intercourse, reduce its sensitivity and so delay the reflex; the ISSM calls this the oldest known drug treatment for premature ejaculation. A metered lidocaine-prilocaine spray was authorised in the European Union on 15 November 2013 and renamed Fortacin in 2014. The drawbacks are numbness of the penis and, unless a condom is used, numbness of the partner's genitals, with occasional loss of erection. Finally, the phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5) inhibitors such as sildenafil (Section 9.3.6) are not a treatment for premature ejaculation itself: the ISSM review found no robust evidence for them except in men who have premature ejaculation together with erectile dysfunction, where restoring a reliable erection removes the pressure to hurry. The off-label opioid painkiller tramadol has also been tried, but its risk of dependence limits it. Table 9.10 brings the options together. Table 9.10 Treatments for premature (early) ejaculation. The answer most sexual medicine clinics give is "both, in sequence". A drug can give quick relief and break the cycle of failure and dread; the behavioural programme, couple sessions and education give him lasting control and a way of talking to his wife. For Bhavesh the clinician would first correct the myth that masturbation has damaged him, explain the anxiety loop, involve his wife if he agrees, address the problem of privacy in a joint family, and then offer either an on-demand drug or the stop-start programme, or both. That combination of information, permission and specific suggestion is Annon's PLISSIT model at work (Book 2 Section 7.9.6). Exam trap The stop-start (Semans, 1956) and squeeze (Masters and Johnson) techniques treat premature ejaculation . They do not treat male erectile disorder (sensate focus and PDE-5 inhibitors, Section 9.3.6), inhibited male orgasm (the old name for delayed ejaculation, the opposite problem, Section 9.4.2) or vaginismus (graded dilators, Section 9.4.4). If an item credits Semans with the squeeze technique, it is following Barlow and Durand; if both names appear separately, pair stop-start with Semans. Premature ejaculation is most commonly associated with an anxiety state (DSM-5-TR: anxiety disorders, especially social anxiety disorder), not with masturbation (a myth that feeds dhat syndrome), not with diabetes mellitus (the classic link of erectile disorder) and not with personality disorder. In an interview, add that lifelong premature ejaculation also has a genetic and serotonergic side. DSM-5-TR: within about 1 minute , for at least 6 months , severity graded by time ; ICD-11 HA03.0 male early ejaculation. Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder Rupali is 25, a primary school teacher from a town near Kolhapur, married ten months to a man she chose with her family's blessing. She comes first to a gynaecologist, not a psychologist, and she comes because her mother-in-law has asked why there is no news of a baby. The marriage has never been consummated. Each time her husband tries, her body seems to close: her thighs press together, the muscles tighten, she feels a sharp burning pain at the entrance to the vagina and pushes him away, crying. She has never been able to use a tampon, and at 22 she fled from a doctor's room when an internal examination was suggested. She loves her husband, enjoys kissing and holding him, and becomes aroused; it is only penetration that she cannot bear. Now the gynaecologist wants to examine her, and she is terrified. Until 2013 Rupali would have been diagnosed with one of two disorders, or with both. The first, vaginismus , was the involuntary contraction of the muscles around the vagina that makes penetration painful or impossible (Barlow and Durand place the spasm in the outer third of the vagina, and note that it can occur during any attempted penetration, including a gynaecological examination or the insertion of a tampon). The second, dyspareunia , was pain during sexual intercourse. DSM-IV listed the two as separate "sexual pain disorders", and ICD-10 still lists them separately as F52.5, nonorganic vaginismus ("spasm of the pelvic floor muscles that surround the vagina, causing occlusion of the vaginal opening"), and F52.6, nonorganic dyspareunia, which, unlike DSM-5-TR's diagnosis, ICD-10 says can occur in both women and men. DSM-5 merged them into a single diagnosis, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder . The case for the merger was made by the McGill University psychologist Yitzchak Binik in two reviews in the Archives of Sexual Behavior in 2010. Vaginal spasm, he pointed out, had been treated as the defining feature of vaginismus for about 150 years, on the strength of expert clinical opinion, but the empirical research supported neither that definition nor the DSM-IV-TR distinction between vaginismus and dyspareunia. As Barlow and Durand put it, vaginismus and pain during intercourse overlap a great deal. Binik therefore proposed collapsing the two into a single diagnosis, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, defined by five dimensions: how often penetration succeeds, pain with penetration, fear of penetration or pain, pelvic floor muscle dysfunction, and medical comorbidity. DSM-5 adopted the name and the first four dimensions as its criteria. The criteria reflect those dimensions. Criterion A requires persistent or recurrent difficulty with one or more of four things: (1) vaginal penetration during intercourse; (2) marked vulvovaginal or pelvic pain during vaginal intercourse or attempts at penetration; (3) marked fear or anxiety about vulvovaginal or pelvic pain in anticipation of, during or as a result of vaginal penetration; and (4) marked tensing or tightening of the pelvic floor muscles during attempted vaginal penetration. The problem must have lasted approximately 6 months, must cause clinically significant distress, and must not be better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, by severe relationship distress (again with partner violence as the example) or other stressors, by a substance or medication, or by another medical condition. Notice three differences from the template, because each is a trap. There is no percentage of occasions ; the wording is simply "persistent or recurrent". There is no generalised or situational specifier ; only lifelong or acquired is specified. And severity, as for most of the chapter, is rated by distress. Why can one dimension be enough? DSM-5-TR's answer is practical: marked difficulty in any one of them is often enough to cause clinically significant distress. But it adds that all four should be assessed even when one is enough for the diagnosis, because they usually come together and each needs its own treatment. Each dimension has a range, and DSM-5-TR describes them carefully. Difficulty with penetration runs from total inability in every situation (intercourse, gynaecological examination, tampons) to easy penetration in one situation but not another; the commonest presentation is the woman who cannot have intercourse with her partner. Pain is described by place and kind: superficial pain at the entrance during penetration, or deep pelvic pain felt only with deeper penetration; pain that occurs only when provoked by intercourse or touch, or pain that is also spontaneous; pain described as burning, cutting, shooting or throbbing. It may last after intercourse and occur during urination, and it can usually be reproduced in a gynaecological examination. Its intensity, interestingly, is not closely related to how distressing or disabling it is. Fear is often a reasonable reaction to repeated pain and leads to avoidance; but in some women the fear does not seem related to pain at all, and DSM-5-TR compares it to a phobia whose object is penetration or the pain itself. Tensing of the pelvic floor ranges from a reflex-like spasm in response to attempted entry to a "normal" voluntary guarding against expected pain or fear; with guarding, penetration may be possible when the woman is relaxed. DSM-5-TR says that pelvic floor function is best assessed by a specialist gynaecologist or a pelvic floor physiotherapist. Rupali shows all four dimensions: penetration has never happened, it hurts, she fears it, and her muscles tighten. Two medical conditions are named in the text because they may be the primary cause. In vulvodynia there is chronic vulvar pain without an identifiable cause lasting at least 3 months; provoked vestibulodynia is a form of vulvodynia in which contact provokes pain at the vulvar vestibule, the area around the vaginal opening. Women with these conditions are usually distressed enough to meet the criteria for genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder as well. The disorder is frequently associated with low sexual interest (female sexual interest/arousal disorder), although desire is sometimes preserved in situations that do not involve penetration; with behavioural avoidance of sexual situations and of gynaecological examinations, a pattern DSM-5-TR compares to phobic avoidance; and with relationship problems. DSM-5-TR adds two observations that every clinician in India will recognise: it is common for women who have never achieved penetration to come for treatment only when they wish to conceive, and many women say that the symptoms diminish their feelings of femininity. How common is it? DSM-5-TR says the prevalence of the disorder itself is unknown, but about 10 to 28 percent of women of reproductive age in the United States report recurrent pain during intercourse, and the international range is 8 to 28 percent, varying by country. Difficulties with intercourse are a frequent reason for referral to sexual dysfunction clinics. Barlow and Durand give a best estimate of 6 percent of women for vaginismus (Bradford and Meston, 2011) and note that it is relatively rare in North America but considerably more common in Ireland and Turkey, countries with more restrictive attitudes to sex, a contrast that points to the role of culture. The course is hard to chart, because women usually seek help only after sexual problems have begun, so it can be difficult to say whether the problem is lifelong or acquired. The clinician's question is whether there has ever been a consistent period of successful intercourse without pain, fear or tension; if there has, the disorder is acquired. Earlier clues often exist: difficulty with or avoidance of tampons is an important predictor of later problems. Once symptoms have lasted about 6 months, spontaneous remission becomes less likely. Pain complaints peak in early adulthood and again around and after the menopause, and may increase after childbirth. The risk factors are many. Women with earlier mood or anxiety disorders are four times more likely to develop the disorder. Psychological processes keep it going: pain catastrophising (thinking about pain in an exaggerated, helpless, ruminating way), low confidence in managing pain, avoidance of pain and negative mood; and interpersonal factors such as insecure attachment, a partner's negative responses to the pain, and sexual motives that focus on avoiding conflict rather than seeking pleasure. Women with the disorder more often report a history of sexual or physical abuse, or fear of abuse, though many have no such history. Biological risks include previous vaginal infections (superficial pain often begins after infections and persists after they have cleared), early puberty, inflammation, early use of oral contraceptives, an increase and sensitisation of pain receptors in the vulva so that touch is felt as pain, low touch and pain thresholds, and abnormalities of the resting pelvic floor such as overactive muscles. Pain during tampon insertion, or inability to insert one, before any sexual contact is again singled out as an important risk factor. Culture shapes how the pain is lived and reported. DSM-5-TR describes the pressure of social narratives that put men's sexual desire and penetrative sex first and portray sex as easy and natural, and it notes that some women do not report pain at all but say instead that they are "unhappy in their marriages". The disorder is diagnosed only in women. DSM-5-TR acknowledges that men can have chronic pelvic pain (an estimated 2.2 to 9.7 percent worldwide), but says the research is not yet developed enough to extend the diagnosis to them; such men may receive other specified or unspecified sexual dysfunction. The differential diagnosis is where psychology and gynaecology must work together. Many women with the disorder also have a medical condition such as lichen sclerosus (a chronic inflammatory skin disease of the vulva), endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease or the genitourinary syndrome of menopause (dryness, irritation and thinning of the tissues as oestrogen falls). Treating the medical condition sometimes relieves the pain, but often it does not, and DSM-5-TR admits there is no reliable way to tell which came first. Some women may also meet criteria for somatic symptom disorder or for a specific phobia. The clinician must also check the adequacy of stimulation, since inadequate foreplay and arousal can themselves cause difficulty, pain and avoidance, and the partner's function, since a partner's erectile dysfunction or premature ejaculation may make penetration difficult; in such cases the diagnosis may not be appropriate. Comorbidity with other sexual problems, with relationship distress (usually because of the loss of intimacy rather than the pain alone), with other pelvic and reproductive disorders such as interstitial cystitis, constipation and irritable bowel syndrome, and with chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia is common. In the manuals, DSM-5-TR prints the code F52.6; ICD-10 separates nonorganic vaginismus (F52.5) and nonorganic dyspareunia (F52.6) from their organic forms, which it codes in the genitourinary chapter (N94.2 and N94.1); and ICD-11 merges them, as DSM-5 did, into sexual pain-penetration disorder , HA20, in Chapter 17. Treatment begins with a medical examination, done gently, with consent and with the woman in control, to look for infection, skin disease, endometriosis or atrophy; infections and skin conditions are treated, and the dryness and thinning of the genitourinary syndrome of menopause are usually treated with vaginal oestrogen. Then comes graded exposure. Within a sex therapy programme the woman, at her own pace and only when relaxed, inserts a series of graded vaginal dilators (or her own fingers), and later her partner does so under her guidance; Kegel exercises teach her that she can deliberately tighten and relax the pelvic floor. Book 2 Section 7.9.4 describes the method, and Barlow and Durand report that 80 to 100 percent of women overcome vaginismus with it, often in a relatively short time. Pelvic floor physiotherapy treats overactive muscles directly. Cognitive-behavioural therapy addresses the fear, the catastrophic thinking and the avoidance, and couple work addresses the partner's responses and the loss of intimacy. For Rupali, the first step is to postpone the feared examination until she has been given control over it, to explain what is happening in her body, and to bring her husband into the treatment. Indian context In Indian clinics this disorder often presents as an unconsummated marriage , sometimes months or years after the wedding, and often through a gynaecologist or an infertility clinic rather than a psychologist, because the family's question is about a baby, not about pain. Fear of the wedding night, frightening stories from relatives, no sex education, no privacy in a joint family, and the expectation that the bride will bleed all feed the fear and the tension; the husband's own anxiety, or an erectile problem that follows repeated failure, can join the loop. Book 2 Section 7.9.7 describes the presentation and the sex therapy approach; the point to add here is that the diagnosis belongs to the woman only when the difficulty is hers, so the clinician must assess both partners before deciding whose problem it is. Exam trap DSM-5 merged vaginismus and dyspareunia into genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder because the two could not be reliably distinguished (Binik, 2010). One of four dimensions is enough: penetration difficulty, pain, fear of pain, pelvic floor tensing. It has no 75 to 100 percent rule and no generalised/situational specifier (lifelong or acquired only). It is diagnosed only in women ; ICD-10's dyspareunia (F52.6) could be given to men. Tampon difficulty before sexual contact predicts it. Codes: DSM-5-TR F52.6; ICD-10 F52.5 vaginismus and F52.6 dyspareunia; ICD-11 HA20 sexual pain-penetration disorder (Chapter 17, not Chapter 6). Treatment: graded dilators (80 to 100 percent success), not the squeeze technique. Substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction Dhruv is 33, a bank officer in Pune, and three months ago his psychiatrist started him on sertraline for panic disorder. It has worked. The attacks that used to wake him at night have stopped, and he is travelling by train again. But within the first two weeks he noticed something he has not mentioned to anyone: he can no longer ejaculate. He becomes aroused and keeps his erection, but the climax does not come, and his wife has begun to ask what is wrong. He has read online that "these tablets ruin your sex life forever", and he is quietly planning to stop them before his next appointment. He tells all this to the clinical psychologist who is seeing him for cognitive-behavioural therapy, because she is the one person who asked. Dhruv has a problem that every psychiatric clinic sees daily. The diagnosis of substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction is made when a clinically significant disturbance in sexual function is predominant in the clinical picture (Criterion A); when there is evidence from the history, examination or laboratory findings both that it developed during or soon after intoxication with or withdrawal from a substance, or after starting, changing or stopping a medication, and that the substance or medication is capable of producing it (Criterion B); when it is not better explained by an independent sexual dysfunction (Criterion C), for example one that began before the substance was used or that persists for a substantial period, about a month, after acute withdrawal or severe intoxication has ended, or where there is a history of similar episodes unrelated to substances; when it does not occur only during a delirium (Criterion D); and when it causes clinically significant distress (Criterion E). A note adds that the diagnosis is made instead of a diagnosis of intoxication or withdrawal only when the sexual symptoms predominate and are severe enough to need clinical attention. The rules differ from the rest of the chapter in ways examiners exploit. There is no 6-month rule , because a drug effect can be recognised from its timing, and waiting 6 months would be pointless and harmful. Severity is graded by the percentage of occasions : mild when it occurs on 25 to 50 percent of occasions, moderate on 50 to 75 percent, and severe on 75 percent or more. Three onset specifiers record the timing: with onset during intoxication, with onset during withdrawal, and with onset after medication use (when the symptoms began at the start of a medication, with a change in its use, or during its withdrawal). The coding follows the substance. For alcohol the code is F10.181 with a mild alcohol use disorder, F10.281 with a moderate or severe one, and F10.981 with no use disorder (the fourth character, 1, 2 or 9, records the comorbid use disorder, which is not diagnosed separately); parallel codes exist for opioids (F11), sedatives, hypnotics or anxiolytics (F13), cocaine (F14), amphetamine-type and other stimulants (F15) and other or unknown substances (F19), and DSM-5-TR prints no row for cannabis. A prescribed medicine that fits none of these classes is coded under "other (or unknown) substance": DSM-5-TR's own example is F19.981 fluoxetine-induced sexual dysfunction . Dhruv's diagnosis would be recorded as F19.981 sertraline-induced sexual dysfunction, with onset after medication use, severe (he has the problem on every occasion). ICD-11 has no separate category for drug-induced sexual dysfunction in Chapter 17; instead the relevant dysfunction (for Dhruv, HA03.1 male delayed ejaculation) is given and the qualifier HA40.2, "associated with use of psychoactive substance or medication", is added. Which substances do it? DSM-5-TR names intoxication with alcohol, opioids, sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics, stimulants including cocaine, and other substances; withdrawal from alcohol, opioids, and sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics; and, among medications, antidepressants, antipsychotics and hormonal contraceptives. Table 9.11 sets out the main offenders. Two groups deserve a closer look because psychologists meet them daily. Antidepressants. About 25 to 80 percent of people taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors, tricyclics, serotonergic antidepressants (the SSRIs) and combined serotonergic-adrenergic antidepressants (the SNRIs) report sexual side effects, and the highest rates are with citalopram, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline and venlafaxine. Barlow and Durand note that estimates of up to 80 percent exist but that figures closer to 50 percent seem more reliable. The commonest effect is difficulty with orgasm or ejaculation in men and with arousal in women ; problems of desire and erection are less frequent. The effect occurs regardless of the level of depression, so it is a drug effect, not a symptom, and DSM-5-TR estimates that about 30 percent of the sexual complaints are clinically significant. Onset can be as early as 8 days after the first dose, as Dhruv found. About 30 percent of people with mild to moderate orgasm delay remit spontaneously within 6 months. In some cases SSRI-induced dysfunction persists after the drug is stopped, a condition the research literature calls post-SSRI sexual dysfunction. Bupropion, mirtazapine, nefazodone and vilazodone have lower rates. Book 3 Section 5.7.2 teaches the antidepressant classes and why bupropion, which acts on dopamine and noradrenaline rather than serotonin, spares sexual function; Section 6.9.4 reports Lecrubier's finding that sexual dysfunction occurred in 75 percent or more of patients treated for panic with antidepressants and was the commonest reason for stopping. Antipsychotics. About 50 percent of people taking antipsychotics have sexual side effects affecting desire, erection, lubrication, ejaculation or orgasm, with both typical and atypical drugs. Problems are less common with prolactin-sparing drugs and those that do not block dopamine receptors. The mechanism is the one Book 3 Section 4.8.3 described: blocking dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway releases the brake on prolactin, and a raised prolactin lowers sex hormones and desire. Section 4.10.5 ranks the antipsychotics by their effect on prolactin, high with risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride and low with aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine. DSM-5-TR says the effects of mood stabilisers are unclear, but lithium and the anticonvulsants, with the possible exception of lamotrigine, may reduce desire, and gabapentin may cause orgasm problems. Benzodiazepines may be linked to more erectile and orgasm problems, while none have been reported with buspirone. Among non-psychiatric medicines, cardiovascular, cytotoxic (anticancer), gastrointestinal and hormonal drugs are all associated with sexual problems; the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors finasteride and dutasteride, used for an enlarged prostate and for hair loss, may reduce erection, ejaculation and libido; and Barlow and Durand single out the beta-blocking antihypertensives such as propranolol. Illicit drugs are associated with low desire, erectile dysfunction and difficulty reaching orgasm, and the rates appear related to chronic use: about 60 to 70 percent among people who misuse heroin, higher than among users of amphetamine-type substances or MDMA (ecstasy). People on methadone maintenance often have sexual problems, but those on buprenorphine seldom report them. Premature ejaculation can appear when opioids are stopped (Section 9.4.3). Chronic nicotine use and chronic heavy drinking are associated with erectile problems, and their effects may take years to appear. Alcohol deserves its own paragraph, because almost everyone believes the opposite of the truth about it. At low and moderate doses alcohol reduces social inhibition, so people feel more like having sex and are more willing to ask for it. Physically, however, it is a central nervous system depressant, and erection and lubrication are harder to achieve when the nervous system is suppressed. Chronic heavy drinking can damage nerves, the liver and the testes, lowering testosterone and with it desire and arousal. Barlow and Durand point out that Shakespeare captured this dual effect four centuries ago, when the Porter in Macbeth says that drink "provokes the desire, but it takes away the performance". Fahrner (1987) found that 75 percent of male alcoholics had erectile dysfunction, low desire, or premature or delayed ejaculation. Cannabis is less clear: DSM-5-TR notes that, like alcohol, it is a central nervous system depressant and may be a risk factor for sexual dysfunction, but that it has also been suggested to improve satisfaction with orgasm, and Barlow and Durand suggest that any effect may be largely on attention. Cocaine produced sexual dysfunction in more than 60 percent of a large sample of users (Cocores and colleagues, 1988, reported by Barlow and Durand). Why should a psychologist care? DSM-5-TR names the main consequence: medication-induced sexual dysfunction leads to noncompliance , stopping medication or taking it irregularly, which in turn can make antidepressants fail. Dhruv is about to do exactly that, and if he stops sertraline abruptly he risks discontinuation symptoms and a return of panic. The first skill is simply to ask, because few patients volunteer the problem. The second is to know the differential diagnosis. Depressive, bipolar, anxiety and psychotic disorders themselves disturb sexual function, so it can be hard to tell whether a problem comes from the illness or from its treatment. DSM-5-TR gives the logic of proof: the diagnosis is usually made when there is a close link in time between starting or stopping the drug and the problem, and a clear diagnosis can be made when the problem appears after the drug is started, dissipates when it is stopped , and recurs when the same drug is reintroduced , the last step being called rechallenge . Problems that appear only after long use are much harder to attribute with certainty. In Dhruv's case the timing is clear: no ejaculatory problem before sertraline, onset within two weeks of starting it, and nothing else in his history to explain it. What can be done? The decisions are the prescriber's, but the psychologist should know the options well enough to encourage the client to raise them rather than act alone. The 2013 Cochrane review by Taylor and colleagues, which pooled 23 randomised trials with 1,886 participants, found that in men the PDE-5 inhibitors sildenafil and tadalafil improved antidepressant-induced erectile problems more than placebo, that adding bupropion at a higher dose showed benefit in some trials, that most other add-on drugs did not help, and, strikingly, that there were no randomised trials of switching to the currently available antidepressants with lower rates of sexual side effects, of psychological treatments or of "drug holidays" (stopping the drug briefly before sex). In practice, clinicians use a set of strategies whose logic follows from this section: waiting, since some early effects fade (about 30 percent of mild to moderate orgasm delays remit within 6 months); lowering the dose, if the illness allows; switching to a drug with a lower rate, such as bupropion or mirtazapine; adding a PDE-5 inhibitor for erectile problems; and, for antipsychotics, choosing a prolactin-sparing drug such as aripiprazole. Psychological support helps too: reassurance that the effect is usually reversible, sex therapy for the couple, and attention to the depression or anxiety that made the drug necessary. Dhruv's psychologist does not tell him to change his tablets; she tells him that his problem is common and treatable, that stopping on his own could bring the panic back, and that he should raise it with his psychiatrist, who has several options. Clinical link: ask before they stop Most clients will not mention a sexual side effect unless someone asks, and many will simply stop the tablet. A routine, matter-of-fact question at every review ("Some people on this medicine notice changes in their sex life, such as taking longer to climax or less interest. Has anything like that happened?") gives permission, the first level of Annon's PLISSIT model (Book 2 Section 7.9.6). It also protects the treatment: the client who reports the problem can be helped by the prescriber, while the client who hides it often relapses. Ask before starting the drug, too, so that a problem that was already there is not later blamed on the medicine. Exam trap Substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction has no 6-month rule ; severity is graded by occasions (mild 25 to 50, moderate 50 to 75, severe 75 percent or more); the onset specifiers are during intoxication, during withdrawal and after medication use . A medication is coded under "other (or unknown) substance", for example F19.981 fluoxetine-induced sexual dysfunction. Symptoms persisting for more than about 1 month after withdrawal or intoxication suggest an independent dysfunction. SSRIs mainly cause delayed orgasm or ejaculation in men and arousal problems in women; bupropion and mirtazapine have lower rates; antipsychotics act partly through prolactin . Alcohol "provokes the desire, but it takes away the performance" ( Macbeth ). Other specified and unspecified dysfunctions, and the treatment toolkit Not every sexual problem fits one of the seven named dysfunctions and the substance-induced category. When symptoms characteristic of a sexual dysfunction cause clinically significant distress but do not meet the full criteria for any specific disorder, DSM-5-TR offers two residual categories. The category of other specified sexual dysfunction (F52.8) is used when the clinician chooses to record the specific reason, and DSM-5-TR's own example is sexual aversion . Other examples from this chapter are anhedonic ejaculation, in which ejaculation is normal but brings no pleasure (Section 9.4.2), and genito-pelvic pain in men (Section 9.4.4). Unspecified sexual dysfunction (F52.9) is used when the clinician chooses not to give the reason or does not have enough information to be more specific. The example of sexual aversion has a history. DSM-III (1980) had a single disorder of desire, inhibited sexual desire. When DSM-III-R (1987) revised it, the committee divided it into two: hypoactive sexual desire disorder, a lack of interest in sex, and sexual aversion disorder , a phobic aversion to and avoidance of genital contact with a partner. DSM-IV kept both as "sexual desire disorders". DSM-5 dropped sexual aversion disorder as a separate diagnosis. Its patients now receive other specified sexual dysfunction, or, if the fear centres on penetration, they may meet the criteria for genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder. ICD-10 kept a related category, F52.1, sexual aversion and lack of sexual enjoyment, covering both the fearful avoidance of sex and the experience of normal response and orgasm without pleasure. That completes the sexual dysfunctions, and it is a good moment to stand back. Treatment of these disorders is divided between two books: the psychological methods are taught in Book 2, Clinical Psychology, Section 7.9, and the physical and drug treatments are taught in this chapter, in Section 9.3 for the disorders of desire, arousal and erection and in this section for the rest. Table 9.12 puts them side by side, disorder by disorder, so that you can match any treatment to its target.
