The psychological methods target the mechanisms you met in Section 9.2: sensate focus removes the demand to perform and so breaks the anxiety and spectatoring loop; stop-start, squeeze and dilators are forms of graded learning and exposure; directed masturbation is education by doing. The drugs target the body: they restore blood flow, delay a reflex, numb a surface or remove a chemical obstacle. Neither alone is usually enough. A tablet can restore an erection or delay an ejaculation, but it cannot remove the fear of failure, teach a couple to talk or repair a relationship that has been damaged by years of disappointment, which is why Bach, Barlow and Wincze (2004) found that adding cognitive-behavioural therapy to sildenafil increased couples' satisfaction and sexual activity (Section 9.3.6), and why so many men stop their tablets within months. Equally, sex therapy cannot reverse diabetic nerve damage or the effect of a drug. The best treatment for most clients is combined: a medical assessment, a drug where the body needs it, and psychological treatment for the anxiety, communication and relationship that surround the symptom. In India, where many people first take their worries to advertised "sexologists" and quacks, the first two levels of Annon's model, permission and limited information, meet most needs and undo much harm (Book 2 Section 7.9.7). Bhavesh needed to hear that masturbation had not damaged him; Namrata needed permission to explore her own body; Dhruv needed to know that his problem was a common, reversible drug effect. Only after that did specific techniques and drugs have their full effect. Exam trap Match each technique to its target: sensate focus for most dysfunctions, especially erectile disorder and low desire; stop-start and squeeze for premature ejaculation; directed masturbation and the bridge manoeuvre for female orgasmic disorder; graded dilators for vaginismus (genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder); PDE-5 inhibitors for erectile disorder; dapoxetine for premature ejaculation. "Sexual aversion" is DSM-5-TR's example of other specified sexual dysfunction (F52.8); sexual aversion disorder itself existed in DSM-III-R and DSM-IV only. Anhedonic ejaculation is other specified, not delayed ejaculation. 9.5 Paraphilias and Paraphilic Disorders: From Perversion to Disorder Lower yield · not asked yet The sexual dysfunctions are problems of response: the body does not do what the person wants it to do. This section turns to a different kind of question, about what a person wants in the first place. Some people are aroused by things most people are not: an object, a part of the body, an activity such as being bound, or a person who has not agreed to be involved. When is such an interest a disorder? The question is older than psychiatry, and the answers have swung widely. Nineteenth-century doctors called these interests "perversions" and treated almost any departure from intercourse aimed at reproduction as disease. Twentieth-century manuals listed them as "sexual deviations", and the second DSM put homosexuality at the head of the list. DSM-5 (2013) drew a new line: an unusual sexual interest is not, by itself, a mental disorder at all; it becomes one only when it causes distress or impairment, or when acting on it harms, or risks harming, others. ICD-11 went further and rebuilt the whole group around a single idea, consent. This section explains these ideas, traces how they developed, and asks who has paraphilias, how they relate to sexual crime, and where "hypersexuality" fits. Section 9.6 then describes the eight named disorders one by one, and Section 9.7 their causes, assessment and treatment. What a paraphilia is The word is Greek: para , beside, beyond or other than, and philia , love or attraction. Barlow and Durand gloss it as a strong attraction ( philia ) that is abnormal ( para ); the literal sense is a love that lies off to one side of the usual path. DSM-5-TR defines a paraphilia as "any intense and persistent sexual interest other than sexual interest in genital stimulation or preparatory fondling with phenotypically normal, physically mature, consenting human partners". The definition is worth reading slowly, because every phrase in it excludes something. "Intense and persistent" rules out the passing fantasy, the curiosity, the one-off experiment: a paraphilia is a lasting and powerful pattern, not a thought that crosses the mind. "Genital stimulation or preparatory fondling" describes, in clinical language, the ordinary repertoire of foreplay and intercourse; an interest outside it may be paraphilic. Then come four words that describe the usual partner, and each excludes a class of paraphilias. "Phenotypically normal" means having a body of typical appearance, so an intense interest in amputees as a class would count. "Physically mature" excludes children and young adolescents. "Consenting" excludes the unsuspecting stranger who is watched, the stranger to whom the genitals are exposed and the person who is rubbed against in a crowd. And "human" excludes animals, objects and corpses. Notice that the definition is built by exclusion: it does not list paraphilias, it defines what is not one and calls everything else paraphilic. Ray Blanchard, who chaired the group that wrote it, argued that defining paraphilia by exclusion, as anything that is not normophilic, was preferable to trying to define each unusual interest in turn. DSM-5 (2013) called interests inside the circle "normophilic"; DSM-5-TR (2022) uses the plainer word "nonparaphilic". Two refinements follow. First, "intense" is hard to apply to people who are very old or medically ill, who may have no intense sexual interests of any kind. For them DSM-5-TR offers an alternative test: a paraphilia is any sexual interest greater than or equal to the person's nonparaphilic sexual interests. Second, some paraphilias are better described as preferential than as intense: what marks them is not their strength but the fact that the person prefers them to ordinary sexual activity. DSM-5-TR then sorts paraphilias by what they are about. Some concern the person's erotic activities : intense and persistent interest in spanking, whipping, cutting, binding or strangulating another person, or an interest in such activities that equals or exceeds the interest in intercourse or its equivalent. Others concern the person's erotic targets : intense or preferential interest in children, corpses or amputees, in animals such as horses or dogs, or in inanimate objects such as shoes or articles made of rubber. A practical observation completes the picture: a person's pattern of paraphilic interests is often reflected in his or her choice of pornography, which is one reason clinicians and courts sometimes treat it as evidence. Section 9.6 shows how DSM-5-TR builds its two families of named disorders on this distinction between activities and targets. How many paraphilias are there? DSM-5-TR says that "many dozens" have been identified and named, and that almost any of them could rise to the level of a disorder through its consequences. Only eight are given their own criteria: voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual masochism, sexual sadism, pedophilic, fetishistic and transvestic disorder. DSM-5-TR gives two reasons for the choice. These eight are relatively common compared with the others, and some of them involve acts that, because they are noxious or potentially harmful to others, are crimes. Everything else, from necrophilia and zoophilia to obscene telephone calls, goes under other specified paraphilic disorder (Section 9.6.7). The eight, in other words, are not a natural kind; they are the paraphilias that most often come to the attention of clinics and courts. It helps to be clear about what a paraphilia is not . It is not a sexual orientation: sexual orientation concerns the sex or gender of the adults to whom a person is attracted (Section 9.1.2), and homosexuality, although once listed among the sexual deviations, is not a paraphilia (Section 9.10). It is not a gender identity: a person whose experienced gender differs from the gender assigned at birth has a question of identity, not of erotic interest, and gender dysphoria is a separate diagnosis (Section 9.9). It is not a sexual dysfunction, which concerns the response cycle. And it is not an obsession: the unwanted, horrifying sexual thoughts of obsessive-compulsive disorder are experienced as alien and are not arousing, whereas a paraphilic urge is arousing (Book 3 Sections 6.5.2 and 6.5.8). Exam trap A paraphilia is a pattern of sexual interest (what arouses a person), defined by exclusion from interest in genital stimulation or fondling with phenotypically normal, physically mature, consenting human partners. It is not a mismatch between gender identity and assigned sex (that is gender dysphoria or, in DSM-IV, gender identity disorder), not a sexual dysfunction and not androgyny. DSM-5-TR names eight paraphilic disorders because they are relatively common and some involve criminal acts, not because they are the only paraphilias; "many dozens" exist. "Normophilic" (DSM-5) and "nonparaphilic" (DSM-5-TR) mean the same thing. Interest is not disorder Consider three men. The first, aged 42, is being assessed for depression after losing his job. Asked routinely about his sexual life, he mentions, without embarrassment, that since adolescence he has been strongly aroused by women's high-heeled shoes; his wife knows, they include shoes in their sexual life by mutual agreement, and he has never been troubled by it. The second, aged 35, is referred because he has been arrested three times in a year for exposing his genitals to women at a bus stop; he insists that each occasion was an accident, that he was "only relieving himself", and that he has no sexual interest in it at all. The third, aged 28, comes to a clinic of his own accord because he is ashamed and frightened of recurrent sexual fantasies about being humiliated, avoids relationships because of them, and has begun to drink to push them away. Which of them has a mental disorder? Before 2013 the manuals blurred the answer. DSM-5 settled it with a distinction stated in one sentence: "A paraphilic disorder is a paraphilia that is currently causing distress or impairment to the individual or a paraphilia whose satisfaction has entailed personal harm, or risk of harm, to others." It then added the principle that governs the whole chapter: "A paraphilia is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for having a paraphilic disorder, and a paraphilia by itself does not necessarily justify or require clinical intervention." The first man has a paraphilia (a fetishistic interest) and no disorder. The second, if the clinician concludes that the exposures were sexually motivated, has a disorder despite his denials, because he has acted on the interest with nonconsenting strangers. The third has a disorder because his interest causes him distress and impairment, even though no one else has been involved. Every named paraphilic disorder in DSM-5-TR is built in two parts that mirror this sentence. Criterion A specifies the nature of the paraphilia: recurrent and intense sexual arousal from a particular focus, shown by fantasies, urges or behaviours, over a period of at least 6 months . The 6 months rule out transient interests, such as those that may appear during a stressful period or under the influence of a substance. Criterion B specifies the consequences. For the disorders that involve other people who have not consented (voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism and pedophilic disorder) it can be met in either of two ways: the person has acted on the urges with a nonconsenting person , or the urges or fantasies cause clinically significant distress or impairment (pedophilic disorder words it slightly differently: the person has acted on the urges, or they cause marked distress or interpersonal difficulty). For the disorders that need involve no victim (sexual masochism, fetishistic and transvestic disorder) only the second route exists: distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning. DSM-5-TR reserves the word "diagnosis" for people who meet both criteria. A person who meets Criterion A but not Criterion B, which might happen when a harmless paraphilia comes to light during treatment for something else, "may be said to have that paraphilia but not a paraphilic disorder". How can a clinician judge Criterion A when the person denies the interest? Each disorder's text in DSM-5-TR addresses this with the same procedure, which this book calls the ascertainment rule, after DSM-5-TR's phrase "ascertained as having". Disclosing individuals freely admit the interest. If they also report distress or psychosocial problems because of it, they can be diagnosed. If they report no distress (no anxiety, obsessions, guilt or shame about the impulses), are not impaired by the interest, and have psychiatric and legal histories showing that they do not act on it, they are said to be "ascertained as having" the sexual interest, but they should not be diagnosed. Nondisclosing individuals deny the interest, sometimes in the face of substantial objective evidence. A man who has repeatedly exposed himself to unsuspecting strangers on separate occasions but says each episode was accidental can still be diagnosed, because recurrent behaviour of this kind is itself evidence of the interest (meeting Criterion A) and simultaneously shows harm to others (meeting Criterion B). DSM-5-TR explains why it speaks of multiple victims on separate occasions: they increase confidence that the behaviour is driven by a paraphilia rather than by chance or opportunity. But multiple victims are sufficient, not necessary : fewer victims can satisfy the criterion if the person repeatedly targeted the same victim or if there is other evidence of a distinct interest, and the criteria can also be met if the person acknowledges intense interest. Notice that distress is not required when the person has acted on the urges with someone who did not consent. Two specifiers can be added to every named paraphilic disorder except pedophilic disorder. The specifier in a controlled environment applies mainly to people living in institutions or other settings, such as prisons or secure hospitals, where the opportunity to act on the urges is restricted, so that the absence of behaviour says little about the risk. The specifier in full remission applies when, for at least 5 years while living in an uncontrolled environment, the person has not acted on the urges with a nonconsenting person and has had no distress or impairment; for the disorders without victims (sexual masochism, fetishistic and transvestic disorder) the requirement is simply 5 years without distress or impairment. DSM-5-TR is careful to add that full remission says nothing about whether the paraphilia itself has gone: the interest "may still be present after behaviors and distress have remitted". Remission is of the disorder, not necessarily of the desire. Pedophilic disorder has neither specifier; instead it has its own (exclusive or nonexclusive type, the sex of the children to whom the person is attracted, and whether the behaviour is limited to incest: Section 9.6.4). Paraphilias rarely come alone. DSM-5-TR says it is not rare for a person to have two or more. Sometimes the connection is obvious (foot fetishism and shoe fetishism), sometimes it is not, and the combination may be coincidental or may reflect some general vulnerability in psychosexual development. Either way, separate diagnoses are given if more than one paraphilia is causing suffering to the person or harm to others. And because the diagnosis has two prongs, severity can be judged in two ways: by the strength of the paraphilic interest itself, or by the seriousness of its consequences, the latter measurable with ordinary scales of functioning and quality of life. Why did DSM-5 draw the line here? The DSM-5 Paraphilias Sub-Work Group was chaired by the sexologist Ray Blanchard (born 1945), within the Sexual and Gender Identity Disorders Work Group chaired by the psychologist Kenneth Zucker (born 1950). The change had two aims. The first was to stop labelling as mentally ill people whose unusual but harmless interests trouble no one, such as a man like the first in our three cases, or consenting adults who practise bondage and sadomasochistic sex together. Barlow and Durand explain that the change was made to accommodate the high prevalence of paraphilic-type fantasies among people without any mental disorder, citing the study by Ahlers and colleagues (2011) at the Charité hospital in Berlin: of 367 men aged 40 to 79 drawn from a community sample, 62.4 percent reported at least one paraphilia-associated pattern of sexual arousal, but only 1.7 percent said that it had caused them distress. If paraphilic fantasy alone were a disorder, most men would have one. The second aim was to keep a diagnosis for those who are harmed by their interests or who harm others. DSM-5 marked the change by retitling the chapter, from "Paraphilias" to "Paraphilic Disorders", and by adding the word "disorder" to every diagnosis: fetishism became fetishistic disorder, voyeurism voyeuristic disorder, and so on. The names without "disorder" now refer to the interest. The change was controversial, and Barlow and Durand set out both sides. Its advocates argued that a fantasy never acted on harms no one, and that pathologising a private mental life does more harm than good; on this view a person with a persistent interest in children who never acts on it and is not distressed has something abnormal, in the way that being very tall or very short is abnormal, but not a disorder. Its critics replied that it is hard to believe that someone with a strong and persistent arousal pattern of that kind would never act on it in any way, for example by looking at illegal material on the internet, and that doing so is itself harm. The debate goes back to the question Book 3 Section 1.1 asked about every mental disorder: whether a condition is a disorder because of what it is or because of what it does. Exam trap A paraphilia is not a disorder : it is necessary but not sufficient for one. A shoe fetish that troubles no one is a paraphilia; exposing oneself to unsuspecting strangers meets Criterion B even without distress , because the person has acted on the urges with nonconsenting people. Criterion A requires at least 6 months . A person who denies the interest can still be diagnosed on the evidence of repeated acts against several victims on separate occasions; multiple victims are sufficient but not necessary . "In full remission" needs 5 years in an uncontrolled environment and is not available for pedophilic disorder ; remission does not mean the interest has gone. DSM-5's work group on paraphilias was chaired by Ray Blanchard . From "perversion" to "paraphilia": the history For most of European history, unusual sexual behaviour was the business of priests and judges, not doctors: it was a sin or a crime, and "sodomy" covered almost any act not aimed at conception. In the second half of the nineteenth century physicians began to claim the territory, and the book that did most to make sexual behaviour a medical subject was Psychopathia Sexualis (1886) by the German-Austrian psychiatrist Richard von Krafft-Ebing (1840 to 1902), whose life is told in Section 9.1.3. Its subtitle, a clinical-forensic study , shows who it was written for: doctors and courts. Krafft-Ebing assumed that sexuality aimed at procreation was normal and that every other kind was a sign of disease, and he explained most of the conditions he described as the products of hereditary degeneration , a weakened nervous constitution passed down through families. His method was the case history, and the book grew through twelve German editions revised by Krafft-Ebing himself into a vast catalogue of cases of what he called perversion of the sexual instinct. Two of its words are still in use. He coined masochism from the name of the novelist Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, and he brought sadism , named after the Marquis de Sade, into medicine. The language of "perversion", with its moral overtones, dominated sexual medicine for the next half-century. A year later, in 1887, the French psychologist Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911), whom Book 1 Section 9.2 introduces as the father of intelligence testing, published an essay in the Revue philosophique , "Le fétichisme dans l'amour" ("Fetishism in love"), which gave the word fetishism its sexual sense. A fetish, in the anthropology of his day, was an object believed to have magical power (the word comes through French from the Portuguese feitiço , a spell); Binet used it for an erotic attachment to an object or a part of the body. His explanation was strikingly modern. He suggested that in certain vulnerable individuals an emotionally intense early experience in which the object happened to be present could fix the attachment by association , an idea that anticipates the conditioning theories of Section 9.7. Krafft-Ebing and the English physician Havelock Ellis also thought fetishism arose from associations, though they disagreed about the predisposition needed. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) gave the perversions a central place in his theory in Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905). His first essay sorted the "sexual aberrations" into deviations in respect of the sexual object (the person or thing desired) and deviations in respect of the sexual aim (the act desired), a division that anticipates DSM-5-TR's targets and activities. His central claim was that adult perversions are not alien to normal sexuality but are fixations at, or regressions to, components of the sexuality that every child passes through, and he famously described the neuroses as "the negative" of the perversions: what the pervert acts out, the neurotic represses. In a later essay, "Fetishism" (1927), he explained the fetish as a substitute that protects a man from castration anxiety. The psychosexual stages themselves belong to the Personality book; for this chapter the point is that Freud made the perversions part of the story of normal development rather than signs of degeneration. The word that replaced "perversion" came quietly. Coinage of paraphilia (German Paraphilie ) is credited to the Croatian-Austrian ethnographer and sexologist Friedrich Salomon Krauss (1859 to 1938) in 1903; the Viennese psychoanalyst Wilhelm Stekel (1868 to 1940) used it regularly in the 1920s; and John Money (1921 to 2006), the Johns Hopkins sexologist you met in the opening story, popularised it in the 1980s as a non-pejorative term for unusual sexual interests. It entered the DSM in 1980. The manuals then redrew the group edition by edition, and Table 9.13 summarises the changes. DSM-I (1952) had a single category, sexual deviation , placed under sociopathic personality disturbance alongside antisocial and dyssocial reaction, alcoholism and drug addiction. It had no coded subtypes: the clinician was simply to name the type of behaviour, and the manual's examples were homosexuality, transvestism, pedophilia, fetishism and sexual sadism (including rape, sexual assault and mutilation). DSM-II (1968) moved "sexual deviations" (code 302) to its group of personality disorders and certain other non-psychotic mental disorders and subdivided it: 302.0 homosexuality, 302.1 fetishism, 302.2 pedophilia, 302.3 transvestitism, 302.4 exhibitionism, 302.5 voyeurism, 302.6 sadism, 302.7 masochism, 302.8 other sexual deviation and 302.9 unspecified. Its definition is a window on the thinking of the time: the category was for individuals "whose sexual interests are directed primarily toward objects other than people of the opposite sex, toward sexual acts not usually associated with coitus, or toward coitus performed under bizarre circumstances as in necrophilia, pedophilia, sexual sadism, and fetishism", who "remain unable to substitute normal sexual behavior for them" even though many find their practices distasteful; and it was not to be used for people who performed such acts "because normal sexual objects are not available to them". The first clause made homosexuality a deviation by definition; Section 9.10 tells how it left the manual in 1973 and 1974. DSM-III (1980) introduced the word "paraphilias" for a group within its class of psychosexual disorders, with nine categories: fetishism, transvestism, zoophilia, pedophilia, exhibitionism, voyeurism, sexual masochism, sexual sadism and atypical paraphilia. DSM-III's fetishism also excluded arousal by body parts. DSM-III-R (1987) placed the paraphilias among the "sexual disorders", added frotteurism , renamed transvestism transvestic fetishism , moved zoophilia out of the named list into paraphilia not otherwise specified, and renamed atypical paraphilia paraphilia not otherwise specified; a proposed diagnosis of "paraphilic rapism" was rejected. DSM-IV (1994) and DSM-IV-TR (2000) kept the same eight named paraphilias (exhibitionism, fetishism, frotteurism, pedophilia, sexual masochism, sexual sadism, transvestic fetishism and voyeurism) within a chapter of "sexual and gender identity disorders", with paraphilia not otherwise specified for the rest; its examples included telephone scatologia (obscene telephone calls), necrophilia (corpses), partialism (an exclusive focus on a part of the body), zoophilia (animals), coprophilia (faeces), klismaphilia (enemas) and urophilia (urine). Transvestic fetishism could still be diagnosed only in heterosexual men, a restriction that went back to DSM-III's transvestism ("cross-dressing by a heterosexual male"). DSM-5 (2013) gave the group its own chapter, "Paraphilic Disorders", placed after the personality disorders (Book 3 Section 1.8.2), renamed all eight as disorders, introduced the paraphilia and paraphilic disorder distinction, folded partialism back into fetishistic disorder (DSM-5-TR notes that it had been subsumed in fetishism before DSM-III), and dropped DSM-IV's restriction of transvestic fetishism to heterosexual men. Two proposals were considered and not adopted: Blanchard's proposal to extend pedophilia to hebephilia , sexual attraction to children in early puberty, as a "pedohebephilic disorder", and a paraphilic coercive disorder for men aroused specifically by sexual coercion. The first is a steady narrowing of what counts as disorder: from a category so broad that it included every non-procreative interest and homosexuality, to a list of named interests, to a distinction between interests and disorders that leaves most people with unusual interests outside psychiatry altogether. The second is a shift in the criterion of disorder, away from the content of a desire (is it "normal"?) and towards its consequences (does it cause suffering, or harm someone who has not agreed?). ICD-11, as the next subsection shows, took the second trend to its conclusion. Exam trap The term paraphilia entered the DSM in DSM-III (1980) ; DSM-I and DSM-II said "sexual deviation(s)". DSM-I placed sexual deviation under sociopathic personality disturbance ; DSM-II listed homosexuality first among the sexual deviations. Frotteurism was added in DSM-III-R (1987) , when zoophilia lost its own code. Krafft-Ebing ( Psychopathia Sexualis , 1886) coined masochism and brought sadism into medicine; Binet (1887) gave fetishism its sexual meaning; Krauss (1903) coined "paraphilia"; Money popularised it. Freud's Three Essays (1905) treated perversions as fixations of infantile sexuality. Hebephilia was proposed for DSM-5 and not adopted. ICD-10 to ICD-11: a group rebuilt around consent The WHO's ICD-10 (1992) called the group disorders of sexual preference , F65, and noted that it included the paraphilias. Section 9.1.6 and Table 9.3 list its codes; what matters here is how it described them, because the descriptions show the older thinking. Fetishism (F65.0) was "reliance on some non-living object as a stimulus for sexual arousal and sexual gratification". Fetishistic transvestism (F65.1) was the wearing of clothes of the opposite sex principally to obtain sexual excitement, distinguished from the cross-dressing of transsexualism by its clear association with arousal and the strong wish to remove the clothes once arousal subsides. Exhibitionism (F65.2) and voyeurism (F65.3) were recurrent tendencies to expose the genitals to strangers or to watch people undressing or having sex without their knowledge. Paedophilia (F65.4) was "a sexual preference for children, boys or girls or both, usually of prepubertal or early pubertal age", a wider age range than DSM's. Sadomasochism (F65.5) was a single category, a preference for sexual activity involving the infliction of pain or humiliation, or bondage, called masochism in the recipient and sadism in the provider, with the remark that many people obtain excitement from both. F65.6 covered multiple disorders of sexual preference, noting that the commonest combination is fetishism, transvestism and sadomasochism, and F65.8 gathered the rest: obscene telephone calls, rubbing against people in crowded public places (frotteurism), sexual activity with animals, use of strangulation or anoxia to intensify sexual excitement, and necrophilia. What ICD-10 did not do was distinguish a harmless preference from a harmful one: the label described the content of the interest. ICD-11 (adopted by the World Health Assembly in May 2019 and in force from 1 January 2022) kept the group in Chapter 6, Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders, renamed it paraphilic disorders , and redefined it around consent. Its description reads: "Paraphilic disorders are characterised by persistent and intense patterns of atypical sexual arousal, manifested by sexual thoughts, fantasies, urges, or behaviours, the focus of which involves others whose age or status renders them unwilling or unable to consent and on which the person has acted or by which he or she is markedly distressed." The examples ICD-11 gives of people who cannot consent are prepubertal children, an unsuspecting person watched through a window and an animal. Six codes cover such disorders: 6D30 exhibitionistic disorder , 6D31 voyeuristic disorder , 6D32 pedophilic disorder , 6D33 coercive sexual sadism disorder , 6D34 frotteuristic disorder and 6D35 other paraphilic disorder involving non-consenting individuals , whose examples are arousal patterns involving corpses or animals. For every one of them the person must have acted on the arousal pattern or be markedly distressed by it. Then comes a seventh code for everything else. 6D36, paraphilic disorder involving solitary behaviour or consenting individuals , can be given for a persistent and intense pattern of atypical arousal involving consenting adults or solitary behaviour only if one of two conditions is met: either the person is markedly distressed by the nature of the arousal pattern , and the distress "is not simply a consequence of rejection or feared rejection of the arousal pattern by others"; or the behaviour involves a significant risk of injury or death to the person or to a partner, ICD-11's example being asphyxophilia , sexual arousal from restriction of breathing, which can kill by accident. The group ends with 6D3Z, paraphilic disorders, unspecified; there is no 6D3Y. ICD-11 then states the principle plainly: atypical patterns of sexual arousal that do not involve others whose age or status renders them unwilling or unable to consent, and that are not associated with marked distress or significant risk of injury or death, "are not considered to be Paraphilic Disorders". Notice the subtle difference from DSM-5-TR in that clause about distress. Under DSM-5-TR, the third man in Section 9.5.2, ashamed and frightened of his masochistic fantasies, meets Criterion B because his interest distresses him; DSM-5-TR counts guilt and shame as distress. ICD-11 asks a further question: is he distressed by the nature of the arousal pattern itself, or only because others reject it or because he fears they would? A man whose only suffering comes from his community's disapproval would not receive a diagnosis in ICD-11. The rule is the same one ICD-11 applies to compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (Section 9.5.7), and it carries the lesson of the history of homosexuality (Section 9.10): distress that comes from stigma is not evidence of a disorder in the person. The descriptions add several cautions. Paraphilic disorders should not be diagnosed in children and should be diagnosed only with utmost caution in adolescents, because sexual experimentation is typical in adolescence and sexual acts may occur impulsively or opportunistically rather than as part of a recurrent pattern. Many sexual crimes, ICD-11 says, involve behaviour that is not associated with a sustained underlying paraphilic arousal pattern; it may be transient, impulsive, opportunistic or related to intoxication, and in such cases a paraphilic disorder should not be diagnosed. Arrest, incarceration and impairment may follow, but they are not diagnostic requirements. And paraphilic disorders frequently co-occur with mood, anxiety and substance use disorders, and with one another. What did ICD-11 remove? The recommendations came from the WHO's Working Group on the Classification of Sexual Disorders and Sexual Health, and were set out by Richard Krueger , Geoffrey Reed, Michael First and their colleagues in the Archives of Sexual Behavior in 2017. The group recommended that the paraphilic disorders be "limited to disorders that involve sexual arousal patterns that focus on non-consenting others or are associated with substantial distress or direct risk of injury or death". Consistent with that framework, the ICD-10 categories of fetishism, fetishistic transvestism and sadomasochism were removed , and new categories were added: coercive sexual sadism disorder, frotteuristic disorder (until then hidden in F65.8), and the two "other" categories for non-consenting individuals and for solitary or consenting behaviour. The working group based its proposals on the WHO's role as a global public health agency and the ICD's function as a public health reporting tool. The practical meaning is that a consenting adult who enjoys a fetish, cross-dressing or sadomasochistic sex with a willing partner has no ICD-11 diagnosis at all, unless the pattern causes marked distress of the right kind or carries a serious risk of injury or death. Sadism survives only in its coercive form: ICD-11 says that coercive sexual sadism disorder "specifically excludes consensual sexual sadism and masochism". Why did the paraphilic disorders stay in Chapter 6 when the sexual dysfunctions and gender incongruence moved to the new Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health (Section 9.1.6)? The working group gave its reasons in the 2017 paper by Krueger and colleagues. It did consider moving the paraphilic disorders into the new chapter, because they are sexual in nature, but recommended keeping them in Chapter 6 for two reasons: they meet the general requirements for a mental disorder, and their status as mental disorders matters forensically, since legal processes such as civil commitment depend on it (Section 9.5.6). The other groups moved for reasons of their own: the sexual dysfunctions because ICD-10's split between "organic" and "non-organic" dysfunction did not fit the evidence, and gender incongruence because it is not regarded as a mental disorder, while keeping a code lets people obtain health care. The paraphilic disorders, as ICD-11 now defines them, are restricted to patterns of arousal and behaviour that harm or endanger others or cause the person marked distress, and their assessment and treatment are the business of mental health and forensic services. Who has paraphilias, and how common they are The first and most striking fact is sex. In clinics and courts, paraphilic disorders are overwhelmingly a male matter. DSM-5-TR says that voyeuristic disorder is very uncommon among women in clinical settings, that fetishistic disorder is "nearly exclusively reported in men" in clinical samples, and that people with sexual sadism disorder in forensic samples are almost exclusively men. Barlow and Durand note that paraphilic disorders were long thought to be absent in women, with the possible exception of sadomasochistic practices, and that current estimates suggest about 5 to 10 percent of sexual offenders are women. The gap narrows outside the clinic. For single voyeuristic acts the male to female ratio in surveys is about 2 to 1 or 3 to 1, and DSM-5-TR says the gender difference in fetishism is smaller for fantasy than for behaviour. So part of the male excess lies in who acts on interests and who comes to the attention of clinics and police; part may lie in development, and Section 9.7 examines the explanations. The second fact is that paraphilic interests are far commoner than paraphilic disorders. You have already met the Berlin study by Ahlers and colleagues (Section 9.5.2), in which most men reported at least one paraphilia-associated arousal pattern but very few were distressed by it. A national survey from Sweden makes the same point for behaviour, and because it sampled the general population rather than clinics or prisons it is the study most often cited on the question. Key study: exhibitionistic and voyeuristic behaviour in a Swedish national survey (Långström and Seto, 2006) The question. Almost everything known about exhibitionism and voyeurism came from men who had been arrested or referred for treatment. How common are these behaviours in ordinary people, and what goes with them? The method. Niklas Långström and Michael C. Seto analysed a national survey of sexuality and health in which 2,450 randomly selected Swedes aged 18 to 60 had been interviewed in 1996. The results. Seventy-six people (3.1 percent) reported at least one incident of being sexually aroused by exposing their genitals to a stranger, and 191 (7.7 percent) at least one incident of being sexually aroused by spying on others having sex. Both behaviours were associated with being male, with more psychological problems and lower life satisfaction, with greater alcohol and drug use, and with greater sexual interest and activity in general (more partners, more frequent masturbation, more use of pornography), and people who reported either were much more likely to report other atypical sexual behaviour, such as sadomasochism or cross-dressing. What it means, and its limits. Paraphilia-like behaviour is far from rare in the community and clusters with other sexual and psychological features, as clinical studies had suggested. But "at least one incident" of arousal is not a recurrent, intense pattern over 6 months, still less a disorder; the data are self-reported; and one country in one year may not generalise. Prevalence figures for each named disorder, including the large Quebec survey, are given in Section 9.6. The third fact concerns age. Paraphilic interests usually become apparent around puberty or in adolescence; DSM-5-TR says, for example, that men with voyeuristic disorder often first become aware of the interest during adolescence. The diagnosis is nevertheless held back until adulthood for most disorders (voyeuristic disorder requires the person to be at least 18), because adolescent sexual curiosity is normal and DSM-5-TR wants to avoid pathologising it, as ICD-11 does with its caution about adolescents. Once established, the interests are thought to be long-lasting, and Barlow and Durand write that paraphilic disorders run a chronic course and that recurrence is common; but the behaviour, the distress and the impairment can change over time, with life circumstances, psychiatric illness, hypersexuality and impulsivity, and DSM-5-TR notes that advancing age may be associated with decreasing paraphilic preferences and behaviour, as with other sexual preferences. When paraphilic behaviour appears for the first time late in life, the clinician should think first of a brain disorder (Book 3 Chapter 10, on the neurocognitive disorders). The fourth fact is that paraphilias cluster. Barlow and Durand write that their patients often present with two, three or more patterns, of which one is usually dominant. The classic study is by Gene G. Abel and his colleagues (1988), who collected self-reports, under an assurance of confidentiality, from 561 men with paraphilias who were not in prison. Contrary to the psychiatric literature of the time, which expected each man to have one kind of deviant behaviour, they found that most had experience with several different types, as many as ten, often crossing the lines of the victims' sex, age and family relationship. Confidentiality was the key to the finding, because men facing prosecution rarely admit more than they must. The clustering is why DSM-5-TR gives separate diagnoses for each paraphilia that causes suffering or harm, why ICD-10 had a category for multiple disorders of sexual preference, and why clinicians assessing one paraphilia ask about others (Section 9.7.4). The fifth fact is comorbidity. In a study of 120 consecutively assessed outpatient men with paraphilias or with nonparaphilic hypersexual behaviour, the American psychiatrist Martin P. Kafka (born 1947) and his colleague John Hennen (2002) found mood disorders in 71.6 percent (especially early-onset dysthymia), substance abuse in 40.8 percent (especially alcohol), anxiety disorders in 38.3 percent (especially social phobia) and, retrospectively diagnosed, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in 35.8 percent; ADHD was linked to conduct disorder, to having several paraphilias and to a higher chance of imprisonment. DSM-5-TR's comorbidity sections tell the same story: for exhibitionistic disorder, for instance, it lists depressive, bipolar, anxiety and substance use disorders, hypersexuality, ADHD, other paraphilic disorders and antisocial personality disorder. Finally, the differential diagnosis: people in a manic episode, with a major neurocognitive disorder, an intellectual developmental disorder, a personality change due to a medical condition, substance intoxication or schizophrenia may become sexually disinhibited and behave in ways that resemble a paraphilic disorder; DSM-5-TR says the diagnosis should not be made unless the behaviour also occurs outside such states. And in conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder, sexual offences occur among many other kinds of rule-breaking, usually without the specific paraphilic interest. Exam trap In the Swedish survey of Långström and Seto (2,450 adults; interviews in 1996, published 2006), 3.1 percent reported at least one incident of arousal from exposing themselves to a stranger and 7.7 percent from watching others have sex. Barlow and Durand print the first figure as "31%", a slip for 3.1 percent (the original reports 76 of 2,450 people); if an option offers 31 percent, it comes from that misprint. Women make up about 5 to 10 percent of sexual offenders. Abel and colleagues (1988) showed that many men with paraphilias have several , under assured confidentiality. Paraphilic behaviour appearing only during mania, intoxication or dementia is not diagnosed as a paraphilic disorder. Paraphilia, sexual offending and the law It is easy to assume that sexual offenders have paraphilias and that people with paraphilias are sexual offenders. Both assumptions are wrong, and a clinician who works with courts must keep the two categories apart. A sexual offence is a legal category, defined by a country's criminal law: what is an offence in one country, or one decade, may not be in another. A paraphilic disorder is a clinical category, defined by a pattern of arousal and its consequences. The two overlap, but less than people think. Consider rape. Barlow and Durand point out that it is not classified as a paraphilic disorder because most instances are better characterised as an assault by a man whose patterns of sexual arousal are not paraphilic; many rapists instead meet the criteria for antisocial personality disorder (Book 3 Chapter 11). Only a minority show a sadistic arousal pattern (Section 9.6.3). The same is true of offences against children: as many as 40 to 50 percent of men who sexually abuse children do not show pedophilic arousal patterns and do not meet criteria for pedophilic disorder; their offences are associated instead with antisocial, aggressive and opportunistic behaviour. ICD-11 makes the same point in its own words: many sexual crimes are not associated with a sustained paraphilic arousal pattern, and may be transient, impulsive, opportunistic or related to intoxication, in which case no paraphilic disorder should be diagnosed. The reverse is also true: many people with a paraphilic interest never offend. The best-known demonstration is the Prevention Project Dunkelfeld , begun in Berlin in June 2005. Dunkelfeld is German for the "dark field", the hidden figure of crimes that never come to light. The project ran a media campaign inviting people who are sexually attracted to children, who want help to control their urges and who are unknown to the legal authorities, to come forward for confidential treatment free of charge. More than a thousand people responded within its first few years. Its existence makes a point that the DSM-5 distinction depends on: there are people who have a paraphilic interest, who are distressed by it or afraid of acting on it, and who seek help before anyone is harmed. Section 9.6.4 describes pedophilic disorder and Section 9.7 the treatments. Why does DSM-5-TR insist that a paraphilia by itself does not justify or require clinical intervention? Partly to protect people with harmless interests, as Section 9.5.2 explained. But also because the diagnosis has legal force. In some countries, notably the United States, a diagnosed mental disorder is a precondition for the civil commitment of sexual offenders after they finish their prison sentences, under laws aimed at "sexually violent predators", and paraphilic diagnoses, including the contested "other specified paraphilic disorder, non-consent", have been used in such proceedings. DSM-5-TR's Cautionary Statement for Forensic Use of DSM-5 addresses this directly. It warns that the definition of mental disorder was written for clinicians and researchers rather than for courts, that a clinical diagnosis such as pedophilic disorder does not imply that a person meets a legal standard for mental illness, responsibility or disability, and that a particular diagnosis "does not imply a specific level of risk". A diagnosis describes a pattern; it does not, on its own, predict what a person will do. Risk is assessed with separate tools such as the Static-99 (Book 2 Section 10.9.5), and offender treatment is organised by the risk-need-responsivity model and the Good Lives Model (Book 2 Section 10.9.8). In India, the law that a clinician meets most often in this area is the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 , which defines a child as anyone under 18 years and creates a duty to report sexual offences against children; Book 2 Section 10.6.5 explains it and the clinician's reporting obligations. The general criminal law changed recently: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 , in force from 1 July 2024, replaced the Indian Penal Code of 1860, and it retains the earlier offences of rape, voyeurism, stalking and insulting the modesty of a woman, among others. Behaviours that a clinician might see as voyeuristic, exhibitionistic or frotteuristic can therefore also be crimes, whatever their diagnosis, and the person's legal situation will shape both the referral and the limits of confidentiality. Clinical link: the client who has not offended Occasionally a client discloses, often after weeks of building trust, an attraction he finds frightening and has never acted on. The clinical psychologist's tasks are to stay calm and non-judgemental, to assess what the interest is and whether there is any current risk to a particular person, especially a child, to explain clearly at the outset the limits of confidentiality (including the duty to report where a child is at risk, Book 2 Section 10.6.5), and to offer or refer for treatment. Treating such a client as an offender drives the problem underground; the Dunkelfeld project exists because help offered early, before anyone is harmed, is the most direct form of prevention. Exam trap A sexual offence is a legal category; a paraphilic disorder is a clinical one. Rape is not a paraphilic disorder: most rapists are not paraphilic, and many meet criteria for antisocial personality disorder . As many as 40 to 50 percent of men who sexually abuse children show no pedophilic arousal pattern, and many people with pedophilic interest never offend (the Dunkelfeld project, Berlin, 2005). DSM-5-TR's forensic caution: a diagnosis does not imply a legal standard or a specific level of risk. India: POCSO Act 2012 (a child is anyone under 18); the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024 . Hypersexuality and compulsive sexual behaviour One more problem of sexual interest needs a place, although it is not about what arouses a person but about how much and how uncontrollably. Clinicians have long seen people whose sexual behaviour, conventional in content, has become excessive, driven and damaging: hours each day of pornography or casual encounters, money spent, a marriage or a job lost, repeated failed attempts to stop. Older medicine had names for it, nymphomania in women and satyriasis in men, and ICD-10 kept them as inclusion terms under excessive sexual drive , F52.7, which, oddly, placed the problem among the sexual dysfunctions. The modern debate began with hypersexuality . Martin Kafka, whose comorbidity research you met in Section 9.5.5, studied men whose sexual behaviour was conventional in content but excessive in amount, which he called paraphilia-related disorders , and compared them with men with paraphilias. In a 2003 study with Hennen he found the two groups strikingly similar: both reported long periods, lasting on average about six years, of very high sexual activity, with a peak "total sexual outlet" (Kinsey's term for orgasms from all sources) of about 12 a week on average. In 2010, in the Archives of Sexual Behavior , Kafka proposed a new diagnosis for DSM-5, hypersexual disorder , a recurrent and intense pattern of sexual fantasies, urges and behaviour pursued to excess, despite consequences and often as a way of coping with low mood or stress. The DSM-5 Sexual and Gender Identity Disorders Work Group recommended it, but it was not adopted, and DSM-5-TR contains no such diagnosis. Proposals to recognise "sex addiction" have fared no better: DSM-5-TR says that "behavioral addictions" such as "sex addiction" are not included because there is insufficient peer-reviewed evidence to establish the diagnostic criteria and course descriptions needed to identify them as mental disorders, and its only behavioural addiction is gambling disorder (Book 3 Chapter 10). In DSM-5-TR, hypersexuality appears only as a feature of other conditions, notably in the comorbidity sections of several paraphilic disorders. ICD-11 took a different route. It created compulsive sexual behaviour disorder , 6C72, and placed it among the impulse control disorders of Chapter 6, next to pyromania and kleptomania, not among the paraphilic disorders and not among the addictions. ICD-11 describes it as "a persistent pattern of failure to control intense, repetitive sexual impulses or urges resulting in repetitive sexual behaviour". The pattern shows itself in one or more ways: repetitive sexual activity has become a central focus of the person's life, to the point of neglecting health, personal care or other interests, activities and responsibilities; the person has made numerous unsuccessful efforts to control or significantly reduce it; the behaviour continues despite adverse consequences, such as marital conflict, financial or legal problems or harm to health; and it continues even when it brings little or no satisfaction. The pattern must be present over an extended period, for example 6 months or more; it must not be better explained by another mental disorder, such as a manic episode, by a medical condition or by a substance; and it must cause marked distress or significant impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning. Then comes the clause that echoes the paraphilic disorders: "Distress that is entirely related to moral judgments and disapproval about sexual impulses, urges, or behaviours is not sufficient to meet this requirement." That last clause matters in practice. ICD-11 notes that the disorder may be expressed through sex with others, masturbation, pornography, cybersex, telephone sex and other repetitive sexual behaviour, and that people with it often turn to sexual behaviour in response to depression, anxiety, boredom, loneliness or other negative feelings. It also observes that people who judge their own sexual behaviour on religious or moral grounds, or who worry about others' disapproval, may describe themselves as "sex addicts" or call their behaviour "compulsive", and it asks the clinician to examine carefully whether that perception comes only from such judgements or whether impaired control and the other requirements are really present. People with a high sex drive who keep control of their behaviour and are not distressed or impaired should not be diagnosed, and nor should the high levels of sexual interest and masturbation that are common in adolescence. A young man from a conservative family who masturbates a few times a week and feels intense guilt about it does not have compulsive sexual behaviour disorder; he may need information and reassurance, and perhaps help with guilt, but not a diagnosis. In India, where the guilt that surrounds masturbation and semen loss is common (Book 3 Section 1.10.4), this distinction saves many young men from a label they do not need. The differential diagnosis includes mania, in which increased and reckless sexual activity is a classic symptom (Book 3 Chapter 5), and the effects of stimulant drugs (Book 3 Chapter 10); the impulse control disorders as a group are taught in Book 3 Chapter 11. Exam trap Compulsive sexual behaviour disorder is 6C72 , an impulse control disorder in ICD-11 Chapter 6 (with pyromania, kleptomania and intermittent explosive disorder). It is not a paraphilic disorder (the content of the behaviour is usually conventional), not classed as an addiction, and not in DSM-5-TR at all. It needs a persistent failure to control intense, repetitive sexual urges, over about 6 months or more, with marked distress or impairment; distress entirely due to moral judgements or disapproval does not count. Kafka's hypersexual disorder (2010) was proposed for DSM-5 and rejected . "Sex addiction" is a diagnosis in neither manual. ICD-10's F52.7 excessive sexual drive included nymphomania and satyriasis. A paraphilia is an intense and persistent sexual interest outside the ordinary range; a paraphilic disorder is a paraphilia that is now causing the person distress or impairment, or whose satisfaction has harmed someone else or put someone at risk of harm. Criterion A of every criteria set describes the interest, and Criterion B describes its consequences. This section runs eight particular interests through that machinery. Out of the "many dozens" of paraphilias that have been described, DSM-5-TR gives named criteria to only eight, and it explains the choice in one sentence: these eight are relatively common compared with the rest, and several of them involve acts that, because they are noxious or harmful to others, are crimes. Everything else goes into a residual category, other specified paraphilic disorder, which Section 9.6.7 explains. Before you meet the disorders one by one, it is worth seeing how DSM-5-TR arranges them, because the arrangement itself carries information that examiners like to test. The manual sorts the eight into two families, shown in Figure 9.9. The first family is defined by anomalous activity preferences : what the person wants to do. Within it, the courtship disorders are voyeuristic, exhibitionistic and frotteuristic disorder, so called because each resembles a distorted fragment of ordinary human courtship, which begins with looking, moves on to showing oneself and talking, and then to touching. Section 9.7.2 explains the theory behind that name. The algolagnic disorders (from the Greek algos , pain, and lagneia , lust) are sexual masochism disorder and sexual sadism disorder, in which the arousal is bound up with pain and suffering, received or inflicted. The second family is defined by anomalous target preferences : whom or what the interest is directed at. One is directed at other human beings, pedophilic disorder, and two are directed elsewhere, at objects or body parts (fetishistic disorder) and at the act of dressing in the clothes of the other sex (transvestic disorder). Unstarred disorders need distress or impairment, because no one else is harmed. Figure 9.9 How DSM-5-TR groups the eight named paraphilic disorders. Notice the two families (what the person wants to do, and whom or what the interest is aimed at) and notice which disorders carry a star: those are the ones in which another person can be a victim, and only they can be diagnosed on behaviour alone. Read the eight criteria sets side by side and a second pattern appears, which the stars in Figure 9.9 mark. Five of the disorders can involve another person who has not agreed: voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism and pedophilic disorder. Their Criterion B has two routes. The person either has acted on the urges with a nonconsenting person, or the urges and fantasies cause clinically significant distress or impairment (for pedophilic disorder the wording is "marked distress or interpersonal difficulty"). The other three, sexual masochism, fetishistic and transvestic disorder, involve no one who has not consented, so their Criterion B has only one route: distress or impairment. The logic is the logic of DSM-5 itself. A man who exposes himself to strangers on a platform has the disorder even if he says he feels perfectly happy, because someone else has been harmed; a man with a boot fetish who is content, and whose partner happily shares it, has a paraphilia and no disorder at all. Every set also requires that the interest has lasted at least 6 months. The specifiers "in a controlled environment" and "in full remission" (no acting on the urges and no distress or impairment for at least 5 years outside an institution), explained in Section 9.5.2, are available for seven of the eight; pedophilic disorder is the exception, for a reason Section 9.6.4 explains.
