The case of Bruce, Brenda and David Reimer, revisited Read the story of the Winnipeg twin again with this chapter in your hands. In the vocabulary of Section 9.1.2, Bruce's sex was male on every count that existed when he was born: XY chromosomes, an Sry gene that had built testes (Section 9.8.2), and the typical male hormones before birth whose permanent, organisational effects Section 9.8.3 describes. The accident of April 1966 took away his penis and the operation at 22 months took away his testes, but neither could undo what had happened before birth. Money's advice rested on the theory of Section 9.8.5: that a newborn is psychosexually open and that gender identity is written by rearing in the first two or three years. So Brenda was given the gender role of a girl, Money's own term from 1955 for everything a person says and does to show others that he or she is a boy or a girl: the name, the upbringing and, at 12, the oestrogen. What no one could give her was a girl's gender identity, the private sense of being male or female. She preferred boys' games, had little interest in dolls or sewing, felt like a boy by seven and hated her developing breasts, and when her father told her the truth at 14, "all of a sudden everything clicked". Diamond and Sigmundson's follow-up of 1997 turned the most famous proof that gender identity is learned into evidence against it, and Reiner and Gearhart's cloacal exstrophy series (2004) and the Dominican 5-alpha-reductase families (Section 9.8.4) showed that the case was no fluke: something established before birth, probably the action of androgens on the developing brain, pulls strongly towards a particular identity, and surgery, hormones and upbringing in the other direction often fail to override it. Girls with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, almost all of whom have a female identity, are the reminder that the rule is not simply "male hormones make a male identity". The opening also asked when a mismatch between body and identity counts as a disorder, and how these questions differ from the problems of sexual response and sexual interest. Brenda's childhood shows several of the indicators of Section 9.9.2 (a strong preference for the games of boys, a rejection of typically feminine toys and activities, a strong dislike of the sex characteristics that were developing), and her distress was unmistakable; but DSM-5-TR diagnoses the distress, not the identity, and ICD-11 has taken gender incongruence out of the mental disorders altogether, into Chapter 17 (Section 9.9.1). The chapter also warns against reading too much into one life. The child had been castrated, given hormones and raised in a family under extraordinary strain, and because David's identity matched his chromosomes, his gonads before castration and his prenatal hormones, his case says nothing directly about why a transgender person's identity differs from the sex assigned at birth. What can fairly be drawn is narrower: in both, a gender identity once formed resisted strong pressure from outside to change it. When David later had testosterone, a mastectomy and a phalloplasty, the same kinds of treatment that Section 9.9.6 describes as gender-affirming, his body was at last being changed to follow his identity instead of his identity being forced to follow his body, which is Pinel's conclusion: irrevocable treatments should await the emergence of the person's own gender identity. None of his suffering was a sexual dysfunction or a paraphilia. His problem was not with sexual response (Sections 9.2 to 9.4) or with what aroused him (Sections 9.5 to 9.7) but with being assigned a gender that was not his, which is why DSM-5 gave gender dysphoria a chapter of its own. Chapter summary 9.1 Sex, Gender and Disorder: The Science of Sexuality and How the Manuals Classify It. Three families share this chapter: sexual dysfunctions (problems of response), paraphilic disorders (problems of what arouses a person) and gender dysphoria (distress from a mismatch between gender identity and assigned gender). Sex is biological; gender identity is the inner sense of being male, female or another gender; gender role and gender expression are how gender is lived in public; sexual orientation is whom one is attracted to; and androgyny, which Bem measured in 1974, is never a diagnosis. Sexology began with Krafft-Ebing's Psychopathia Sexualis (1886), Ellis, Hirschfeld and Freud's Three Essays (1905), then Kinsey's interviews (1948, 1953) and Masters and Johnson's laboratory (1966). Rarity and social disapproval cannot define disorder; harm and consent decide. DSM-IV's single class became three DSM-5 chapters (13, 14 and 19), and ICD-11 moved the sexual dysfunctions, the sexual pain disorders and gender incongruence to Chapter 17, leaving only the paraphilic disorders in Chapter 6. 9.2 The Sexual Response Cycle: Models, Biology and What Disrupts It. Masters and Johnson (1966) described four phases, excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution, driven by vasocongestion and myotonia, with a refractory period in men; Kaplan (1979) put desire first in a triphasic model, and the DSM joined the two. No disorder belongs to plateau or resolution, and pain lies outside the cycle. Basson's circular model (2000) starts from sexual neutrality, with responsive desire that follows arousal. Erection is parasympathetic (nitric oxide, then cGMP, whose breakdown PDE-5 inhibitors block) and emission sympathetic; testosterone is necessary for male desire, prolactin suppresses desire and serotonin inhibits ejaculation. Barlow showed that anxiety can raise arousal in functional men (1983) and that dysfunction comes from cognitive interference (1986), and Bancroft and Janssen's dual control model (2000) balances excitation against inhibition. Relationships, sexual scripts, erotophobia and myths shape response, and nocturnal penile tumescence points to a psychological cause of waking erectile failure. 9.3 Sexual Dysfunctions I: The Shared Rules, and the Disorders of Desire, Arousal and Erection. DSM-5-TR's eight sexual dysfunctions share a template: a problem lasting about 6 months, on about 75 to 100 percent of occasions, with clinically significant distress, not better explained by another mental disorder, severe relationship distress, a substance or a medical condition, and specified as lifelong or acquired and generalised or situational; the exceptions are favourite questions. Laumann's 1992 survey found problems in 43 percent of women and 31 percent of men, mostly low desire in women and early ejaculation in men. Female sexual interest/arousal disorder (3 of 6 indicators) replaced DSM-IV's separate desire and arousal disorders in women, while male hypoactive sexual desire disorder keeps desire apart from arousal in men. Erectile disorder rises steeply with age, is linked to diabetes and vascular disease, predicts coronary artery disease and is treated with sensate focus and with sildenafil (1998) and the other PDE-5 inhibitors, never with nitrates. 9.4 Sexual Dysfunctions II: Orgasm, Ejaculation, Pain and Substance-Induced Dysfunction. A woman who reaches orgasm with clitoral stimulation but not in intercourse does not have female orgasmic disorder, which is treated by directed masturbation (LoPiccolo and Lobitz, 1972). Delayed ejaculation was inhibited male orgasm in DSM-III and male orgasmic disorder in DSM-IV. Premature (early) ejaculation, within about 1 minute of penetration for at least 6 months, is most commonly associated with anxiety, not with masturbation, diabetes or personality disorder, and is treated with Semans's stop-start (1956) and Masters and Johnson's squeeze techniques, dapoxetine, daily SSRIs and topical anaesthetics. DSM-5 merged vaginismus and dyspareunia into genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (Binik, 2010), treated with graded dilators. Substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction has no 6-month rule; SSRIs mainly delay orgasm and ejaculation, antipsychotics act partly through prolactin, and alcohol "provokes the desire, but it takes away the performance". Sexual aversion survives only as an example of other specified sexual dysfunction. 9.5 Paraphilias and Paraphilic Disorders: From Perversion to Disorder. A paraphilia is an intense and persistent sexual interest other than in genital stimulation or fondling with phenotypically normal, physically mature, consenting human partners. Since DSM-5, whose paraphilias group Ray Blanchard chaired, a paraphilia is necessary but not sufficient for a paraphilic disorder, which also needs current distress or impairment, or harm or risk of harm to others; Criterion A requires 6 months. Krafft-Ebing (1886) coined masochism, Binet (1887) gave fetishism its sexual meaning, Krauss (1903) coined "paraphilia" and Money popularised it, and the word entered the DSM in 1980. ICD-11 rebuilt the group around consent (6D30 to 6D3Z) and deleted fetishism, fetishistic transvestism and sadomasochism. The disorders are overwhelmingly male, interests are far commoner than disorders (Långström and Seto, 2006), paraphilias cluster (Abel, 1988), sexual offending is a legal rather than a clinical category, and compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (6C72) is an impulse control disorder. 9.6 The Eight Paraphilic Disorders and the Other Paraphilias. DSM-5-TR groups its eight named disorders by focus. The courtship disorders are voyeuristic (watching an unsuspecting person; the person must be at least 18), exhibitionistic (exposing one's genitals; no minimum age) and frotteuristic (touching or rubbing against a nonconsenting person). The algolagnic disorders are sexual masochism (being humiliated, beaten, bound or made to suffer, with an asphyxiophilia specifier) and sexual sadism (the suffering of another person). The target disorders are pedophilic (a prepubescent child, generally 13 or younger, with the person at least 16 and 5 years older), fetishistic (non-living objects or non-genital body parts) and transvestic, specified with fetishism or with autogynephilia, Blanchard's term (1989) for arousal by the image of oneself as a woman. Masochism, fetishism and transvestism need distress or impairment; the other five are also met by acting on a nonconsenting person. Necrophilia, zoophilia and telephone scatologia are among the other specified paraphilias. 9.7 Why Paraphilic Disorders Develop, and How They Are Assessed and Treated. Rachman (1966) conditioned weak, extinguishable arousal to a picture of women's boots, and masturbatory conditioning explains how early experiences are rehearsed in fantasy and reinforced by orgasm, but learning cannot explain who is susceptible. Money's lovemap (1986) and Freund's courtship disorder hypothesis (1983) are the developmental accounts. Castration (Bremer, 1959) and antiandrogens reduce the strength of sexual drive, never its direction; Cantor's group found lower IQ and non-right-handedness in pedophilia, and Kafka proposed a monoamine hypothesis (1997). Assessment uses penile plethysmography (Freund's method), viewing time and actuarial risk assessment; sexual recidivism averaged 13.4 percent (Hanson and Bussière, 1998). Cognitive-behavioural programmes with relapse prevention have mixed evidence (Marques, 2005). SSRIs suit milder cases, while cyproterone acetate, medroxyprogesterone acetate and GnRH agonists such as triptorelin (Rösler and Witztum, 1998) lower testosterone, and their effect is reversible. 9.8 Becoming Male or Female: Sexual Differentiation and Gender Identity. Male and female are not opposites (Pinel's "mamawawa"): both develop from a shared start through a series of switches. The Sry gene on the Y chromosome turns the primordial gonads into testes; testosterone builds the Wolffian ducts, Müllerian-inhibiting substance from the testes removes the Müllerian ducts, and dihydrotestosterone, made by 5-alpha-reductase, masculinises the external genitals, while female ducts develop without any ovarian hormone (Jost, 1947). Hormones have permanent organisational effects around birth and temporary activational effects from puberty (Phoenix and colleagues, 1959). Complete androgen insensitivity, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, Turner syndrome (45,X) and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) test the rules. Money held that gender identity is learned in the first years, but Diamond and Sigmundson's follow-up of the Reimer case (1997) and Reiner and Gearhart's cloacal exstrophy series (2004) showed that rearing often fails to override it. Gender identity firms up between about 18 months and 3 years. 9.9 Gender Dysphoria and Gender Incongruence. Hirschfeld coined "transvestite" (1910), and Benjamin's The Transsexual Phenomenon (1966) argued for changing the body. The diagnosis moved from transsexualism (DSM-III) through gender identity disorder (DSM-IV) to gender dysphoria (DSM-5), which diagnoses distress rather than identity, and to ICD-11's gender incongruence (HA60, HA61) in Chapter 17, which requires no distress. Children need 6 of 8 indicators, including a strong desire to be another gender; adolescents and adults need 2 of 6; both need 6 months and distress or impairment. No cause has been established. Gender nonconformity, transvestic disorder, body dysmorphic disorder and psychosis must be distinguished. Care includes psychological support, social transition, puberty suppression (the Dutch protocol), hormones and surgery, guided by WPATH's Standards of Care, Version 8 (2022), and debated since the Cass Review (2024). In India the NALSA judgment (2014) recognised a third gender, followed by the Transgender Persons Act (2019) and its 2026 amendment. 9.10 Homosexuality: Pathologised and Depathologised. Pathologisation is the classification of something as a mental disorder and depathologisation the removal of that classification; neither means changing orientation. Kertbeny coined "homosexual" (1868, in print 1869), Westphal made "contrary sexual feeling" a psychiatric matter (1870) and Krafft-Ebing called it degeneration, while Ellis and Freud, whose 1935 letter said it "cannot be classified as an illness", disagreed; Bieber's patient samples (1962) kept the sickness model alive. Kinsey's 0 to 6 scale and Hooker's blind judges (1957) broke it. The American Psychiatric Association's board removed homosexuality from DSM-II on 15 December 1973, and ego-dystonic homosexuality lasted until DSM-III-R (1987). ICD-10 (1990) dropped homosexuality but kept F66, which ICD-11 deleted. Twin studies, the fraternal birth order effect and LeVay's INAH-3 (1991) point to biological contributions, with no single gene. Conversion therapy is unethical, and in India Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, third gender, pathologisation, depathologisation, conversion therapy, medicalisation, hereditary degeneration, sexual inversion, Kinsey scale, sexual orientation disturbance, ego-dystonic homosexuality, sexual maturation disorder, sexual relationship disorder, fraternal birth order effect, maternal immune hypothesis, sexual fluidity, Section 377, reading down From the past papers The 'start-stop technique' and the 'squeeze technique' is useful in the treatment of: (RML 2024, real) (a) Male erectile disorder (b) Premature ejaculation (c) Inhibited male orgasm (d) Vaginismus Answer: (b) Premature ejaculation. Semans's stop-start technique (1956) and Masters and Johnson's squeeze technique teach the man to recognise and control the sensations before the point of no return (Section 9.4.3). Erectile disorder is treated with sensate focus and PDE-5 inhibitors, inhibited male orgasm is the DSM-III name for delayed ejaculation, the opposite problem (Section 9.4.2), and vaginismus is treated with graded dilators (Section 9.4.4). Premature ejaculation is most commonly associated with: (RML 2024, real) (a) Diabetes mellitus (b) Masturbation (c) Personality disorder (d) Anxiety state Answer: (d) Anxiety state. DSM-5-TR links premature ejaculation to anxiety disorders, especially social anxiety disorder, and anxiety raises the sympathetic arousal that partly drives ejaculation, so worry and early ejaculation feed each other; "anxiety state" is simply the older name (Section 9.4.3). Diabetes is the classic physical cause of erectile disorder, masturbation does not cause premature ejaculation (the belief belongs to dhat syndrome), and DSM-5-TR names no personality disorder among its risk factors. Autogynephilia is defined by: (RML 2022, real) (a) Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to prepubescent children (b) Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to thoughts, images, or thoughts about oneself as a woman (c) Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to oneself (d) Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to being humiliated Answer: (b) Recurrent, and intense sexual attraction to thoughts, images, or thoughts about oneself as a woman. Blanchard's term (1989), built from auto, gyne and philia, is in DSM-5-TR's words "a man's paraphilic tendency to be sexually aroused by the thought or image of himself as a woman", and it is a specifier of transvestic disorder (Section 9.6.6). Attraction to prepubescent children is pedophilia, to being humiliated is masochism, and attraction to oneself in general is not autogynephilia, which is specifically about the image of oneself as a woman. A condition characterised by recurrent intense sexually arousing fantasies and urges involving the use of an inanimate object to obtain sexual gratification: (Amity 2023, real) (a) Necrophilia (b) Fetishism (c) Frotteurism (d) Voyeurism Answer: (b) Fetishism. Fetishistic disorder is recurrent and intense arousal, for at least 6 months, from non-living objects or a highly specific focus on non-genital body parts, with distress or impairment (Section 9.6.5). Necrophilia needs a corpse and is an other specified paraphilia, frotteurism needs a nonconsenting person who is touched or rubbed against, and voyeurism needs an unsuspecting person who is watched. A condition in which a person's sexual identity does not match his or her physical gender: (Amity 2023, real) (a) Paraphilia (b) Gender identity disorder (c) Sexual dysfunction (d) Androgyny Answer: (b) Gender identity disorder. The loosely worded stem describes a mismatch between gender identity and assigned sex, which DSM-IV and ICD-10 called gender identity disorder, DSM-5 calls gender dysphoria and ICD-11 calls gender incongruence (Sections 9.1.2 and 9.9.1). A paraphilia concerns what arouses a person, a sexual dysfunction concerns the sexual response, and androgyny, which Bem measured in 1974, is a blend of masculine and feminine traits and never a diagnosis. In ICD-11, gender incongruence is placed in: (NIMHANS 2026 recall, real) (a) Chapter 6, Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders (b) Chapter 5, Endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases (c) Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health (d) Nowhere: it was removed from ICD-11 altogether Answer: (c) Chapter 17, Conditions related to sexual health. ICD-11, adopted in 2019 and in force from 1 January 2022, moved gender incongruence (HA60 and HA61) out of the mental disorders into the new Chapter 17, because being transgender is not a mental disorder but many transgender people need health care that health systems must code (Section 9.9.1). It is not in Chapter 6 or in Chapter 5, and it was not removed, since the code is what gives access to care. When gender incongruence moved out of the mental disorders chapter in ICD-11, which of these stayed in Chapter 6 (Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders)? (NIMHANS 2026 recall, real) (a) Sexual dysfunctions (b) Paraphilic disorders (c) Sexual pain disorders (d) Gender incongruence of childhood Answer: (b) Paraphilic disorders. Only the paraphilic disorders (6D30 to 6D3Z) stayed in Chapter 6, because they meet the general requirements for a mental disorder and their forensic use depends on that status (Sections 9.1.6 and 9.5.4). The sexual dysfunctions (HA00 to HA03), the sexual pain disorders (HA20) and gender incongruence of childhood (HA61), which is no more a mental disorder than the adult category, all went to Chapter 17. The DSM-5 (2013) diagnosis that corresponds to ICD-11 gender incongruence is: (NIMHANS 2026 recall, real) (a) Gender identity disorder (b) Transsexualism (c) Gender incongruence (d) Gender dysphoria Answer: (d) Gender dysphoria. DSM-5 renamed DSM-IV's gender identity disorder gender dysphoria, moving the focus from the identity to the distress, and it corresponds to ICD-11's gender incongruence (Section 9.9.1). Gender identity disorder is the DSM-IV name, transsexualism the DSM-III and ICD-10 (F64.0) name, and gender incongruence is ICD-11's own term, not a DSM diagnosis. Reports on the sexual behaviour of men were published by: (RINPAS 2019, real) (a) Sigmund Freud (b) Alfred Kinsey (c) Anna Freud (d) Karen Horney Answer: (b) Alfred Kinsey. Kinsey, a zoologist at Indiana University, interviewed thousands of ordinary volunteers face to face and published Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953) (Sections 9.1.3 and 9.10.3). Freud's Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905) is a theory of sexuality, not a survey, and Anna Freud and Karen Horney are psychoanalytic distractors. Masters and Johnson's sexual response cycle is distinct from Kaplan's model. Which of the following correctly reflects Masters and Johnson's sequence? (IHBAS 2025, real) (a) Excitement → Plateau → Orgasm → Resolution (b) Plateau → Excitement → Orgasm → Resolution (c) Excitement → Desire → Plateau → Orgasm → Refractory (d) Desire → Arousal → Plateau → Orgasm → Resolution Answer: (a) Excitement → Plateau → Orgasm → Resolution. Human Sexual Response (1966) described four phases, the same in both sexes, with a refractory period in men after orgasm (Section 9.2.2). Desire comes from Kaplan's triphasic model (1979), so options (c) and (d) borrow from her, plateau follows excitement rather than preceding it, and the refractory period is normal physiology within resolution, not a phase of its own. According to Masters and Johnson, following is the correct sequence of human sexual response: (RINPAS 2024, real) (a) Excitement-Orgasm-Plateau-Resolution (b) Excitement-Plateau-Orgasm-Resolution (c) Excitement-Arousal-Orgasm-Resolution (d) Arousal-Excitement-Orgasm-Resolution Answer: (b) Excitement-Plateau-Orgasm-Resolution. The plateau, in which arousal levels off at a high level, comes between excitement and orgasm, and resolution returns the body to the unaroused state (Section 9.2.2). Option (a) puts plateau after orgasm, and "arousal" is not one of the four Masters and Johnson phase names: excitement is the phase of arousal, driven by vasocongestion. Kegel exercises strengthen which part of the body? (NIMHANS 2026 recall, real) (a) The abdominal (core) muscles (b) The pelvic floor muscles (c) The lower back (lumbar) muscles (d) The gluteal (buttock) muscles Answer: (b) The pelvic floor muscles. Kegel exercises (1948) teach a person to tighten and relax the pelvic floor deliberately, and sex therapy adds them to directed masturbation for female orgasmic disorder, to the stop-start programme for premature ejaculation and to graded dilators for vaginismus (Sections 9.4.1, 9.4.3, 9.4.4 and 9.4.6). The abdominal, lumbar and gluteal muscles are not their target. The twenty-third pair of chromosomes is missing an X, turning into a syndrome characterised by a short, infertile female: (IHBAS 2020, real) (a) Down Syndrome (b) Asperger's Syndrome (c) Turner's Syndrome (d) Klinefelter's Syndrome Answer: (c) Turner's Syndrome. In Turner syndrome a girl has only one X chromosome (45,X); her ovaries fail to develop properly, so she is usually infertile, and she tends to be short (Section 9.8.4). Klinefelter syndrome is the opposite case, an extra X in a boy (47,XXY), while Down syndrome (trisomy 21) and Asperger's syndrome (now part of autism spectrum disorder) are not sex chromosome conditions (Chapter 3, Sections 3.3 and 3.5). A condition characterised by the karyotype 'XXY' with an extra X chromosome: (Amity 2023, real) (a) Down's Syndrome (b) Turner Syndrome (c) Klinefelter's syndrome (d) Transsexualism Answer: (c) Klinefelter's syndrome. In Klinefelter syndrome a boy has an extra X (47,XXY), with small testes and low testosterone, so he is usually infertile, and he is often tall (Section 9.8.4). Turner syndrome is a missing X in a girl (45,X), Down's syndrome is trisomy 21 (Chapter 3), and transsexualism is the old diagnostic name for a gender identity that differs from the assigned sex (DSM-III, ICD-10 F64.0), not a chromosome condition (Section 9.9.1). A male child presents with tall stature, small testes, and learning difficulties. Karyotype analysis shows an extra X chromosome. This condition is: (IHBAS 2025, real) (a) Klinefelter syndrome (b) Turner syndrome (c) Prader-Willi syndrome (d) Down syndrome Answer: (a) Klinefelter syndrome. An extra X in a boy who is tall with small testes is Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), which is often diagnosed only when a man seeks help for infertility (Section 9.8.4). Turner syndrome affects girls, who have one X, and Prader-Willi and Down syndromes are not sex chromosome conditions (Chapter 3, Section 3.3). Sex chromosome anomaly (XXY) results into the development of: (M.Phil Clinical Psychology Entrance Examination 2021, real) (a) Klinefelter's Syndrome (b) Turner Syndrome (c) Down Syndrome (d) Phenylketonuria Answer: (a) Klinefelter's Syndrome. The 47,XXY karyotype is Klinefelter syndrome: a male with an extra X, small testes and low testosterone (Section 9.8.4). Turner syndrome is 45,X, Down syndrome is trisomy 21, and phenylketonuria is an inborn error of metabolism (Chapter 3, Section 3.3); none of the three is an XXY anomaly. What do researchers mean by pathologization and depathologization of homosexuality? (Entrance Mock 2, practice) (a) None of the above (b) The classification of homosexuality as a mental disorder and the removal of this classification (c) The changing of sexual orientation from homosexual to heterosexual (d) The process of coming out as a gay or lesbian individual Answer: (b) The classification of homosexuality as a mental disorder and the removal of this classification. The DSM listed homosexuality until the American Psychiatric Association's Board of Trustees voted to remove it on 15 December 1973, and the WHO dropped it with ICD-10 in 1990 (Sections 9.10.1, 9.10.4 and 9.10.5). Changing orientation is conversion therapy, which is unethical and ineffective, coming out is disclosure, and "none of the above" is wrong because option (b) is exactly right. Weightage. 36 of the 411 questions mapped in this book (8.8%) test this chapter, 23 of them from real past papers. 2 of its 11 sections are High yield. Early in 1975 a new resident arrived at a home for the elderly near New York City. His transfer note was short and cryptic: "Helpless, demented, confused and disoriented." The neurologist who examined him, Oliver Sacks (1933 to 2015), found nothing of the kind on the surface. Jimmie G. was a handsome, healthy-looking man of forty-nine with a curly bush of grey hair, cheerful, friendly and warm. He talked with pleasure about his schooldays, his special fondness for mathematics and science, and above all the navy. He had been seventeen, just out of high school, when he was drafted in 1943, and he had served as an assistant radio operator on a submarine. He told these stories in vivid detail, and when he reached his navy days he slipped into the present tense, as if he were still living them. Then Sacks asked him what year it was. "Forty-five, man. What do you mean?" And how old was he? "Why, I guess I'm nineteen, Doc. I'll be twenty next birthday." Sacks then tried an experiment. He handed Jimmie a mirror and asked whether that was a nineteen-year-old looking out of it. Jimmie turned ashen and gripped the sides of his chair. "Jesus Christ," he whispered. "Christ, what's going on? What's happened to me? Is this a nightmare? Am I crazy? Is this a joke?" Sacks soothed him, led him to the window to watch some children playing baseball on a lovely spring day, and slipped out of the room, taking the mirror with him. Two minutes later he came back. Jimmie was still at the window, smiling at the game, and he greeted Sacks cheerfully as a doctor he had never met. When Sacks laid his watch, his tie and his glasses on the desk, covered them, and after a minute's chat asked what was under the cover, Jimmie remembered none of them, nor even that he had been asked to remember. On intelligence testing he did excellently, and he could become keenly involved in a game; what he could not do was keep anything new for more than a minute or so. A diary was tried. He kept it dutifully but could not recognise his own earlier entries, though he knew the handwriting was his. The navy records showed that Jimmie had stayed in the service until 1965 and had been perfectly competent then. The trouble began after he left. His drinking grew heavier in 1970, and around Christmas of that year, his brother understood, he had suddenly "blown his top", becoming deliriously excited and confused, and had been taken to Bellevue Hospital. Sacks's impression was Korsakoff's syndrome, the outcome of years of heavy drinking. Unsure what could be done, he wrote to the great Russian neuropsychologist Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977). "There are no prescriptions," Luria replied, "in a case like this. Do whatever your ingenuity and your heart suggest. There is little or no hope of any recovery in his memory. But a man does not consist of memory alone. He has feeling, will, sensibilities, moral being", matters, Luria went on, of which neuropsychology cannot speak. When Sacks asked the Sisters at the home whether they thought Jimmie had a soul, they told him: "Watch Jimmie in chapel, and judge for yourself." In chapel Jimmie was wholly held and absorbed, and as he took Holy Communion he seemed to have a continuity that his memory could not give him. He found something similar in the garden, where he took over some of the work and almost never lost his way. Sacks published the story as "The Lost Mariner" in The New York Review of Books in February 1984, by which time he had known Jimmie for nine years and his memory had not changed at all, and it became a chapter of The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat (1985). Think about what happened to Jimmie. One drug, taken for years, and a vitamin that the drinking starved his brain of, left a clever, competent man stranded in 1945, unable to carry a single new experience forward into the next minute. That journey is the subject of this chapter. It begins with what drugs are, how the manuals classify the trouble they cause, and why people come to depend on them; it moves through alcohol, the opioids, the stimulants and the other drugs, with their intoxications, their withdrawals and their treatments; and it ends with what happens when the brain that holds a life together breaks down, in delirium, in the dementias, and in disorders like Jimmie's. Remember Jimmie G.; you will return to him at the end of the chapter. 10.1 Drugs, Dependence and Addiction: The Vocabulary and the Manuals Medium yield · 4 Qs Few areas of psychiatry are as crowded with loaded words as this one. Drunkard, addict, junkie, abuser, charsi, bewda: every one of them carries a verdict about the person as well as a description of the behaviour. For most of history the heavy drinker was simply a sinner or a weakling, and the words reflected that. Science needs something different. A researcher comparing heroin users in Amritsar with heroin users in Glasgow, or a clinician deciding whether the man in front of her needs a brief word of advice or three weeks in hospital, needs terms that mean the same thing to everyone who uses them, and rules that say exactly when a pattern of use becomes a disorder. Much of the history of this field is the history of trying to find those words and those rules. This section builds the vocabulary from the ground up, and then shows how the three classifications that you will meet in practice and in examinations, ICD-10, DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, turn it into diagnoses. It ends with the behavioural addictions (gambling and gaming) and with the numbers: how many people in the world and in India use which drugs. The theories of why people become dependent are the business of Section 10.2; the individual drugs fill Sections 10.3 to 10.7. What counts as a drug, and the words for using one Start with the word drug. In pharmacology a drug is any chemical agent that alters the biochemical or physiological processes of the body: aspirin, insulin and an antibiotic are all drugs. In everyday Indian and English speech the word has narrowed to mean an illegal substance ("he got into drugs"). Psychology and psychiatry are interested in a particular group of drugs, those that act on the brain and so change how a person feels, thinks and behaves. A psychoactive substance is any substance that, once taken into the body, alters mood, cognition, perception, consciousness or behaviour by acting on the central nervous system. The biopsychologists John P. J. Pinel and Steven J. Barnes put it in one line: psychoactive drugs are drugs that influence subjective experience and behaviour by acting on the nervous system. To do that a substance must reach the brain, which in practice means it must cross the blood-brain barrier, the tightly packed lining of the brain's blood vessels that keeps most bloodborne chemicals out. Notice what the definition does not mention: legality, danger or medical use. Alcohol, nicotine and caffeine are psychoactive and legal; morphine, diazepam and methylphenidate are psychoactive and prescribed; heroin and cocaine are psychoactive and illegal. Pinel tells of the time he was invited to lecture a convention of high-school teachers on the dangers of drugs: the organisers first invited him to join them in a round of single-malt whisky, and he then gave his talk through a haze of cigarette smoke. The point of the story is that legal status says very little about safety: most drug laws were written in the early twentieth century, long before there was any research on the drugs they controlled. The word psychotropic overlaps with psychoactive, but in clinical use it usually refers to medicines prescribed to treat mental disorders, such as antidepressants and antipsychotics. These are psychoactive, yet most of them produce little pleasure and are rarely taken for their own sake, which is why they seldom appear among the drugs this chapter is about. When the manuals speak of a "substance", they mean three kinds of thing together: drugs of abuse, medications, and toxins such as solvents or insecticides. Psychoactive substances can be grouped by their main effect. Depressants slow the central nervous system: alcohol, the sedative-hypnotics (benzodiazepines and barbiturates) and most inhalants. Stimulants speed it up: cocaine, the amphetamines, and in milder form nicotine and caffeine. Opioids (opium, morphine, heroin and their relatives) relieve pain and produce a dreamy euphoria. Hallucinogens (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline) distort perception. Cannabis fits awkwardly, with sedative, euphoriant and mildly hallucinogenic effects. This simple scheme is a good first map, and many Indian textbooks use it, but it is crude: nicotine both calms and arouses, alcohol is a stimulant at low doses for many people, and ketamine and phencyclidine (PCP) do not fit any box. That is why the manuals list drug classes by name rather than by effect, as you will see in Section 10.1.5. Now the words for using. Substance use is simply taking a substance, whether a single experimental puff, a social drink at a wedding or a daily habit; use by itself is not a disorder. Misuse means use for a purpose or in a way that does not fit medical or legal guidelines, as when someone takes a relative's sleeping tablets, or swallows a whole bottle of codeine cough syrup for the high. Hazardous use (also called risky use) is a pattern that appreciably raises the risk of harm to the user or to others even though no harm has yet occurred: the man who drives home after five pegs every Saturday, or the student who drinks to the point of vomiting at every hostel party. Harmful use is use that has actually damaged physical or mental health, such as hepatitis from shared needles or a depressive episode brought on by heavy drinking. Finally, substance abuse is the American term that DSM-III (1980) and DSM-IV (1994) used for a maladaptive pattern of use causing problems but falling short of dependence. The World Health Organization (WHO) has long avoided the word "abuse", because it means different things to different people and carries a moral judgement, and DSM-5 dropped it as a diagnosis in 2013. Keep these four steps in mind (use, hazardous use, harmful use, dependence); the manuals are largely arguments about where to draw the lines between them. The word that everyone uses, addiction, has had the most turbulent career of all. It comes from the Latin addictus , a person bound over or handed over, originally a debtor surrendered to his creditor, and the image of a person enslaved to a habit has clung to it ever since. In the 1950s the WHO tried to separate "drug addiction" (compulsion, escalating doses, physical dependence, harm to the individual and society) from a milder "drug habituation" (desire without compulsion and without physical dependence). Nobody could apply the distinction consistently, and in 1964 the WHO Expert Committee on Addiction-Producing Drugs recommended that both terms be replaced by a single one, drug dependence . "Dependence" duly became the official word in the ICD and in DSM-III and DSM-IV. Addiction did not go away, however. It survived in everyday speech, in the names of hospitals, journals and professional bodies, and in neuroscience, and in 2013 DSM-5 brought it back into the title of its chapter, "Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders", partly so that the chapter could hold gambling disorder. Even so, DSM-5-TR says plainly that "drug addiction" is not used as a diagnostic term, because its definition is uncertain and its connotations are potentially negative; the official, more neutral diagnosis is substance use disorder. Exam trap "Psychoactive" means a drug that alters mood, cognition, perception and/or behaviour by acting on the brain. The distractors are word games. "A drug-induced hallucination" describes one possible effect of some psychoactive drugs (the hallucinogens), not the meaning of the word. "A particularly active psychopath" plays on psychopathy, a personality construct (Chapter 11). "The psychology of physical activity" is exercise and sport psychology. Also remember the year the WHO replaced "addiction" and "habituation" with "dependence": 1964. Intoxication, withdrawal and tolerance Three things can happen when a psychoactive substance meets a brain repeatedly: the brain is changed for a few hours (intoxication), it adapts so that the drug does less (tolerance), and once it has adapted it protests when the drug is taken away (withdrawal). These three ideas are the building blocks of every diagnosis that follows, so it is worth taking them slowly. Intoxication is a reversible, substance-specific syndrome caused by the recent intake of a substance. ICD-10 describes it as a transient condition following the intake of alcohol or another psychoactive substance, with disturbances of consciousness, cognition, perception, affect or behaviour. DSM-5-TR adds that for intoxication to count as a diagnosis there must be clinically significant problematic changes, such as belligerence, mood lability or impaired judgement, accompanied by the signs typical of that drug (slurred speech and an unsteady gait with alcohol, pinpoint pupils with opioids, dilated pupils and a racing heart with cocaine). The physiological sense of the word is wider than the diagnosis: a person whose heart races after three cups of strong filter coffee is, physiologically, intoxicated by caffeine, but if nothing else is wrong there is no disorder to diagnose. Intoxication is shaped by much more than the dose. The route matters (smoked or injected drugs reach the brain in seconds, swallowed ones in tens of minutes), so do tolerance, the person's expectations and the setting, and the same blood alcohol level can make one person merry and another aggressive. Intoxication usually ends when the drug is cleared, although some effects outlast it. DSM-5-TR does not recognise tobacco intoxication at all: nicotine at the doses smokers take does not produce a problematic syndrome of this kind. Withdrawal is the substance-specific syndrome that appears when a person who has used a substance heavily and for a long time stops or cuts down, so that its level in the blood and tissues falls. Its most useful property is that it is, roughly, the mirror image of the drug's acute effects. As Pinel points out, withdrawal from anticonvulsant drugs tends to cause convulsions and withdrawal from sleeping pills causes insomnia. A sedative such as alcohol leaves behind an over-excited brain (tremor, sweating, anxiety, insomnia, in severe cases seizures and delirium); a stimulant such as cocaine leaves behind an exhausted, slowed and miserable one; an opioid, which constricts the pupils, dries the secretions and constipates, leaves behind dilated pupils, running eyes and nose, and diarrhoea. How bad withdrawal is depends on the drug, on the size and duration of the doses, and on how fast the drug leaves the body. DSM-5-TR spells out the rule of half-life: within a drug class, short-acting substances are more likely to produce withdrawal, and withdrawal from them starts sooner and is more intense; long-acting substances produce withdrawal that starts later, lasts longer and is milder. That is why heroin withdrawal begins within hours and methadone withdrawal only after a day or more, and why a long-acting drug is used to ease people off a short-acting one. The danger also varies enormously. Withdrawal from alcohol, barbiturates and benzodiazepines can kill through seizures and delirium (Sections 10.3 and 10.7); withdrawal from opioids is wretched but rarely dangerous in a healthy adult (Section 10.5). Tolerance is a state of decreased sensitivity to a drug that develops as a result of exposure to it. It can be shown in two ways, and the manuals define it in both: a markedly increased amount of the substance is needed to achieve intoxication or the desired effect, or the same amount has a markedly diminished effect with continued use. Pinel's neat way of seeing this is as a shift of the dose-response curve , the graph of the size of a drug's effect at each dose, to the right (Figure 10.1). The young man whose first two pegs of whisky made him giddy now drinks half a bottle before he feels anything; the codeine syrup user who began with one bottle a week now needs three a day. Tolerance has more than one mechanism. In metabolic tolerance (also called dispositional or pharmacokinetic tolerance) less of the drug reaches its site of action, because the body breaks it down faster: chronic drinking and barbiturate use, for example, induce the liver enzymes that metabolise these drugs. In functional tolerance (pharmacodynamic tolerance) the same amount of drug reaches the brain, but the brain responds less, because receptors have become fewer or less sensitive or the cells' responses to them have been damped down. Pinel's verdict is that tolerance to psychoactive drugs is largely functional. A third, more surprising kind is behavioural tolerance , tolerance that depends on learning. In studies of contingent tolerance, rats given alcohol before each of a series of convulsive stimulations became almost completely tolerant to alcohol's anticonvulsant effect, while rats given exactly the same injections after each stimulation developed no tolerance at all: tolerance developed only to effects the animals actually experienced. In conditioned tolerance, tolerance is fully expressed only in the setting where the drug is usually taken, which turns out to explain some otherwise baffling overdose deaths; that story, and the conditioned compensatory responses behind it, belong to the learning theories in Section 10.2. Three further facts about tolerance matter clinically. First, tolerance can begin within a single session. Intoxication is greater while the blood alcohol level is rising than at the same level on the way down, so that a drinker can feel more sober two hours into an evening than his blood level warrants; this acute tolerance is often called the Mellanby effect. Second, tolerance develops to different effects of the same drug at different rates, a point DSM-5-TR makes with the example of tolerance to respiratory depression and to sedation developing at different speeds. Heroin users become tolerant to the euphoria faster than to the slowing of breathing, so chasing the old high pushes them steadily closer to a fatal dose. Third, tolerance is lost with abstinence, with deadly consequences for the person who returns to his old dose (see the Clinical link below). Do not confuse tolerance with ordinary differences in sensitivity: DSM-5-TR notes that some first-time drinkers show very little intoxication after three or four drinks while others of similar weight slur their speech. That inborn low sensitivity is not tolerance, although, as Section 10.2 shows, it predicts later alcohol problems. Cross-tolerance is tolerance to one drug that carries over to other drugs, usually drugs that act by the same mechanism. Alcohol, the barbiturates and the benzodiazepines all enhance the action of the inhibitory transmitter GABA at the GABA-A receptor, so a heavy drinker is tolerant to diazepam and phenobarbitone as well, and anaesthetists know that alcohol-dependent patients may need larger doses of sedatives and anaesthetics. Cross-tolerance also links the opioids with one another, and the classic hallucinogens LSD, psilocybin and mescaline with one another. It has an important practical consequence. Because a benzodiazepine can stand in for alcohol, a long-acting benzodiazepine such as chlordiazepoxide or diazepam is used to carry a person safely through alcohol withdrawal and then tapered off, the standard detoxification method described in Section 10.4. It also has a dangerous one: cross-tolerance does not stop the effects of two depressants from adding together, and alcohol or benzodiazepines taken with opioids is one of the commonest recipes for a fatal overdose (Section 10.7). The partner idea is cross-dependence : the ability of one drug to suppress the withdrawal syndrome produced by another and to maintain the physical dependence. Chlordiazepoxide prevents alcohol withdrawal; methadone and buprenorphine prevent heroin withdrawal; nicotine patches blunt the withdrawal of stopping cigarettes. Cross-tolerance and cross-dependence usually go together, and both rest on a shared mechanism of action. They are the pharmacological basis of detoxification and of substitution or maintenance treatment. Repeated doses do not always weaken a drug's effect. Sensitisation , also called reverse tolerance , is an increase in the effect of a drug with repeated, usually intermittent, use: the dose-response curve moves to the left. Pinel describes the experiment by Stephan Anagnostaras and Terry E. Robinson (1996), in which ten injections of amphetamine, one every three or four days, greatly increased amphetamine's power to activate the movement of rats, but only when the rats were injected and tested in the same environment as before. In people, repeated cocaine or amphetamine use can produce paranoia, psychosis or seizures at doses that once caused only euphoria, and a leading theory of addiction holds that drugs sensitise the brain's "wanting" system (incentive sensitisation, Section 10.2). Be aware that "reverse tolerance" is also used, loosely, for something quite different: the late-stage drinker whose liver is so damaged that it can no longer metabolise alcohol, so that a man who once drank a bottle now becomes drunk on two pegs. That is a loss of metabolic tolerance, not sensitisation of the brain. Table 10.1 sets the confusable terms side by side. Table 10.1 Five terms that examiners like to confuse. The weeks after release from prison and after discharge from a detoxification unit are the most dangerous time of all for a person with opioid dependence, because the brain's tolerance has faded while the memory of the old dose has not. Good discharge planning therefore includes warning the patient (and the family) about this, and, where available, continuing substitution treatment and supplying the overdose antidote naloxone (Section 10.5). Exam trap Cross-tolerance means that exposure to one drug produces tolerance to another (usually related) drug, so it reduces the person's sensitivity to that second drug. The keyed option in one paper, "exposure to one drug reduces/changes tolerance to other drugs", is loosely worded (strictly, exposure to one drug produces tolerance to the other), but it is the only option that describes cross-tolerance, so choose it. "No addiction to any drug" is a meaningless distractor, and "both" therefore fails too. Do not mix it up with cross-dependence (one drug relieves the other's withdrawal) or with sensitisation (the effect grows, the opposite of tolerance). Metabolic tolerance is the liver's doing, functional tolerance the brain's, and Pinel says tolerance to psychoactive drugs is largely functional. Dependence, addiction, craving and relapse Tolerance and withdrawal are two faces of the same adaptation. Pinel suggests that exposure to a drug produces compensatory changes in the nervous system that offset its effects, and those changes are the tolerance; when the drug is suddenly removed, the compensatory changes are left with nothing to offset, and they show themselves as withdrawal effects opposite to the drug's own. A person who suffers a withdrawal syndrome on stopping a drug is said to be physically dependent on it. Physical dependence (physiological dependence) is therefore the adapted state of the body that reveals itself in withdrawal. Psychological dependence is the older name for a compelling need to keep using a drug, for its pleasure or to escape discomfort, whether or not there is any physical withdrawal. For decades textbooks used this pair to rank drugs, saying for example that cocaine produced "only psychological dependence" because its withdrawal lacked the dramatic bodily signs of heroin or alcohol withdrawal. The distinction has worn badly. Every dependence is ultimately a change in the brain, cocaine does have a withdrawal syndrome (Section 10.6), and the drugs with the mildest bodily withdrawal include some of the hardest to give up. DSM-IV still let clinicians specify whether dependence was "with physiological dependence", but the modern manuals put far more weight on the behaviour than on the withdrawal. The most important point in this subsection is that physical dependence is not the same thing as addiction. A woman with cancer who has taken morphine for months will have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped suddenly; she is physically dependent, but she is not addicted, because she does not crave the drug, seek it compulsively or use it in harmful ways, and once her pain is gone she can be tapered off it without difficulty. A baby born to a mother maintained on methadone may need treatment for withdrawal in the first days of life, yet nobody would call the baby an addict. Conversely, a person can be thoroughly addicted with little physical withdrawal at all, as in gambling or binge cocaine use. Pinel defines addiction by the behaviour: addicted people are habitual drug users who continue to use a drug despite its adverse effects on their health and social life, and despite repeated efforts to stop. The heart of it is compulsion and loss of control, not withdrawal. Pinel adds the decisive piece of evidence. If addiction were simply a matter of avoiding withdrawal, it could be cured by keeping people in hospital for a week or two until the withdrawal had passed; in fact most addicted people return to the drug even after months of enforced abstinence. What drives that return? Part of the answer is craving , an intense desire or urge to use the drug. Craving can strike at any time, but it is most likely in the places, company and moods in which the drug used to be taken: the bar on the way home, the friend who always had a supply, the evening argument with the spouse. DSM-5-TR notes that craving involves classical conditioning and activates specific reward structures in the brain, and that clinicians often track it during treatment because a surge of craving can signal an impending relapse. A lapse is a single slip, one drink or one smoke after a period of abstinence; a relapse is a return to the old pattern of use. Whether a lapse becomes a relapse depends a great deal on how the person interprets it, which is the subject of relapse prevention (Book 2, Section 9.9.6). Because relapse is so common, many authorities describe substance dependence as a chronic, relapsing condition, more like diabetes or asthma than like a broken leg, to be managed over years rather than cured in a single admission. Real patients rarely confine themselves to one drug. Polysubstance use , the use of more than one substance either at the same time or in sequence, is the rule rather than the exception: most heavy drinkers also smoke or chew tobacco, many heroin users also take benzodiazepines, and some mix heroin and cocaine. DSM-IV once had a diagnosis of "polysubstance dependence" for people who met dependence criteria for a group of drugs without meeting them for any single one; DSM-5 abolished it, and DSM-5-TR asks clinicians to diagnose each substance use disorder separately, naming the specific drug ("severe heroin use disorder; moderate cocaine use disorder"). ICD-10 keeps a code (F19) for multiple drug use when it is impossible to say which drug contributes most, and ICD-11 has categories for multiple specified and for unknown substances. Behind all the modern definitions of dependence stands one short paper. The British psychiatrist Griffith Edwards (1928 to 2012) was born in India, trained at the Maudsley Hospital in London and in 1967 founded the Addiction Research Unit at its Institute of Psychiatry. While assessing patients for a series of alcohol research studies, he noticed that certain features kept turning up together. Key study: Edwards and Gross describe the alcohol dependence syndrome (1976) On 1 May 1976 Edwards and the American researcher Milton M. Gross published "Alcohol dependence: provisional description of a clinical syndrome" in the British Medical Journal . Instead of asking whether someone "was an alcoholic", they described a dependence syndrome , a cluster of related features that can be present to a greater or lesser degree, so that dependence has a range of severity. Its seven elements are: (1) narrowing of the drinking repertoire, so that the person drinks the same drink, in the same way, at the same times, whatever the day or the occasion; (2) salience of drink-seeking behaviour, as drinking takes priority over family, work, health and money; (3) increased tolerance to alcohol; (4) repeated withdrawal symptoms; (5) repeated relief or avoidance of withdrawal by further drinking, as with the morning "eye-opener"; (6) subjective awareness of a compulsion to drink, felt as loss of control or craving; and (7) reinstatement of the syndrome after abstinence, so that a dependent drinker who starts again returns to the full old pattern within days rather than months. Edwards and his colleagues also insisted that dependence should be kept separate from the physical, psychological and social damage that drinking causes (the alcohol-related problems or disabilities): a person can have serious problems without dependence, and dependence without many problems yet. That two-axis idea is why ICD-10 has separate categories for harmful use and for dependence. The syndrome was taken into ICD-9, DSM-III-R, ICD-10 and DSM-IV, and its elements are still recognisable in the DSM-5-TR criteria and in ICD-11's three features of dependence. The criticism is that the syndrome rested on clinical observation rather than measurement, and that how much of each element counts was left to clinical judgement; the American psychiatrist Marc Schuckit , reviewing its influence in 1995, noted that five of the seven elements (salience, tolerance, withdrawal, relief drinking and the sense of compulsion) are fairly easy to apply, but that the other two, narrowing of the repertoire and rapid reinstatement, are harder to define objectively. Here is what the syndrome looks like in a real life. Lalit is a 41-year-old medical representative in Lucknow. He began drinking beer with friends at weekends at 22. By his early thirties he was drinking whisky every evening, and over the next few years his drinking became fixed: the same brand, three or four large pegs, starting at the same hour whether it was a working day or a holiday (narrowing of the repertoire). Evenings with his children, his morning walks and much of his salary gave way to drinking (salience). Four pegs now do what one did in his twenties (tolerance). He wakes shaky, sweating and nauseous (withdrawal), and for a year he has kept a quarter bottle in his bag for a "small one" before his first doctor's visit of the day (relief drinking). He knows he cannot stop at two once he has started (compulsion). Last year, frightened by a liver test, he stopped completely for two months, then had "just one" at a cousin's wedding, and within a week he was back to his full evening quota and his morning drink (reinstatement). Lalit has every element of the dependence syndrome. You will meet him again in the next two subsections, because the clearest way to understand the manuals is to push one patient through all of them. Exam trap The dependence syndrome was described by Griffith Edwards and Milton Gross in 1976 ( British Medical Journal ), for alcohol; it is not Jellinek's disease concept (1960) or Kandel's gateway stages (1975), both of which are in Section 10.2. Physical dependence (a withdrawal syndrome on stopping) is not addiction: the cancer patient on morphine and the newborn of a mother on methadone are physically dependent but not addicted. A lapse is one slip; a relapse is a return to the old pattern. ICD-10: the F1 block and its clinical patterns The tenth revision of the WHO's International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10; its chapter on mental and behavioural disorders appeared with clinical descriptions in 1992) is still the system used in many Indian hospitals and in most Indian examination papers, and its way of handling substances is elegant. All the disorders sit in one block, F10 to F19, "Mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance use" (the place of the block in the ICD as a whole is described in Chapter 1, Section 1.9). Every code is built from two pieces of information. The third character names the substance (Table 10.2), and the fourth character, after the decimal point, names the clinical condition (Table 10.3). So F10.2 is alcohol dependence syndrome, F11.3 is opioid withdrawal state, and F12.5 is a psychotic disorder due to cannabis. Learn the two lists separately and you can build any code. Harmful use (F1x.1) is a pattern of use that is actually causing damage to health, physical (as in hepatitis from injecting) or mental (as in a depressive episode secondary to heavy drinking). ICD-10 attaches three careful rules to it. The damage must be real and clinically recognisable, not merely a risk. The fact that a pattern of use is disapproved of by the family or the culture, or has led to socially negative consequences such as an arrest or marital quarrels, is not by itself evidence of harmful use. And harmful use is not diagnosed if a dependence syndrome is present: dependence takes precedence. Notice what these rules exclude. A college student who has twice been arrested after drunken brawls, but whose health is unharmed, has no ICD-10 diagnosis of harmful use, although, as you will see, his recurrent legal problems would have qualified him for substance abuse in DSM-IV. The dependence syndrome (F1x.2) is ICD-10's version of Edwards and Gross. ICD-10 describes it as a cluster of physiological, behavioural and cognitive phenomena in which the use of a substance takes on a much higher priority for the person than other behaviours that once had greater value, and its central descriptive feature is the desire, often strong and sometimes overpowering, to take the drug. A definite diagnosis requires three or more of six features, experienced or shown at some time during the previous year: A strong desire or sense of compulsion to take the substance. Difficulty in controlling substance-taking behaviour: its onset, its termination, or the amount taken. A physiological withdrawal state when use is stopped or reduced, or use of the same or a closely related substance to relieve or avoid withdrawal. Evidence of tolerance. Progressive neglect of alternative pleasures or interests, with more and more time spent obtaining, taking or recovering from the substance. Persisting with use despite clear evidence of overtly harmful consequences, such as liver damage, depressed mood after heavy use, or drug-related impairment of thinking, when the person is, or could be expected to be, aware of the harm. ICD-10 also names the narrowing of the personal repertoire of use as a characteristic feature, a direct inheritance from Edwards and Gross. A fifth character then describes the person's current state: currently abstinent (F1x.20), abstinent but in a protected environment such as a hospital or prison (.21), on a clinically supervised maintenance or replacement regime such as methadone (.22), abstinent but taking aversive or blocking drugs such as disulfiram or naltrexone (.23), currently using (.24), with continuous use (.25), or with episodic use (.26, the old "dipsomania" of periodic binges). Lalit, drinking every evening and showing all six features, would be coded F10.24 (currently using) or, more precisely, F10.25 (continuous use). If he were admitted shaking after a seizure on his second dry day, the withdrawal would be coded as well (F10.31, withdrawal state with convulsions). The withdrawal state (F1x.3) and the withdrawal state with delirium (F1x.4) follow, and delirium tremens is the classic F10.4 (Section 10.3). The psychotic disorder (F1x.5) covers psychotic symptoms that arise during or soon after use and are not simply part of intoxication or withdrawal, such as alcoholic hallucinosis or amphetamine psychosis (Chapter 4, Section 4.5.6). The amnesic syndrome (F1x.6) is Korsakoff's syndrome, Jimmie G.'s disorder, taught in Section 10.11. The residual and late-onset category (F1x.7) collects lasting effects that persist beyond the period in which the drug could be acting directly: flashbacks after hallucinogens, lasting personality change, and dementia related to alcohol or other substances. Two codes outside the F1 block complete the ICD-10 picture. F55, "abuse of non-dependence-producing substances", covers the repeated, unjustified use of substances such as laxatives, analgesics, antacids, vitamins, steroids and herbal or folk remedies, which do not produce dependence of the F1 kind; it is the one place in ICD-10's chapter on mental and behavioural disorders where the word "abuse" appears in a diagnosis title. And pathological gambling is F63.0, not in the substance block at all but among the habit and impulse disorders (Section 10.1.7). One more source of confusion: the United States uses its own clinical modification, ICD-10-CM, in which the F1x.1 codes are relabelled "abuse" (F10.10 is "alcohol abuse, uncomplicated"), and DSM-5-TR codes a mild substance use disorder there. That is an American coding convenience. In the WHO's ICD-10, which Indian textbooks follow, F1x.1 is harmful use. Exam trap Asked which is NOT one of the ICD-10 patterns of disorder due to substance use, choose "drug abuse" . Acute intoxication (.0), harmful use (.1), dependence syndrome (.2), withdrawal state (.3) and withdrawal with delirium (.4) are ICD-10 categories; "abuse" was the DSM-III and DSM-IV category, and ICD-10's nearest term is harmful use. The dependence syndrome needs 3 of 6 features at some time in the previous year . Social disapproval, an arrest or a marital quarrel is not by itself evidence of harmful use. DSM: from abuse and dependence to substance use disorder The American manual took a long road to its present position. DSM-I (1952) listed alcoholism and drug addiction under "sociopathic personality disturbance", treating them as signs of a defective character, and DSM-II (1968) still placed them among the personality disorders and other non-psychotic conditions. DSM-III (1980) gave the substance disorders a class of their own and introduced the pair of diagnoses that ruled for the next three decades: substance abuse and substance dependence . DSM-III-R (1987) rebuilt dependence around the Edwards-Gross syndrome, and DSM-IV (1994) gave the pair its final shape. In DSM-IV, substance abuse required one or more of four problems within a 12-month period: recurrent use resulting in failure to fulfil major obligations at work, school or home; recurrent use in physically hazardous situations, such as driving while intoxicated; recurrent substance-related legal problems, such as arrests for disorderly conduct; and continued use despite persistent social or interpersonal problems caused or made worse by the substance. Abuse could be diagnosed only if the person had never met the criteria for dependence on that class of substance. Substance dependence required three or more of seven criteria in the same 12-month period: tolerance; withdrawal; taking the substance in larger amounts or for longer than intended; a persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down; a great deal of time spent obtaining, using or recovering; important activities given up or reduced; and continued use despite knowing that it was causing or worsening a physical or psychological problem. The clinician could add "with physiological dependence" if tolerance or withdrawal was present. The logic was that abuse was a milder, earlier stage and dependence the full disorder, with dependence trumping abuse in a hierarchy. Research gradually took that logic apart. The DSM-5 Substance-Related Disorders Work Group, whose analysis was published by Deborah S. Hasin , Charles P. O'Brien and colleagues in 2013, drew on studies of more than 200,000 participants and found several problems. Abuse was not reliably a stage on the way to dependence: many people developed dependence without ever meeting the abuse criteria. The abuse diagnosis was much less reliable than the dependence diagnosis. The one-criterion threshold for abuse meant that a single criterion, very often repeated drinking before driving, was enough for a diagnosis. At the same time it created diagnostic orphans , people who met two of the dependence criteria but none of the abuse criteria and therefore received no diagnosis at all, although they were often in more trouble than people diagnosed with abuse. Most tellingly, statistical analyses of how the criteria hang together showed that the abuse and dependence criteria were intermixed along a single dimension of severity rather than forming two separate disorders. The work group therefore recommended combining them into one disorder, dropping the legal problems criterion, adding craving, adding withdrawal syndromes for cannabis and caffeine, bringing the tobacco criteria into line with those for other substances, and moving gambling into the chapter. The result, in DSM-5 (2013) and unchanged in substance in DSM-5-TR (2022), is a single diagnosis. Substance use disorder is a problematic pattern of use of a substance leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, shown by at least two of eleven criteria occurring within a 12-month period. The manual itself groups the eleven into four families (Figure 10.2), and learning them as families is the easiest way to remember them. Pharmacological criteria (criteria 10 and 11): tolerance and withdrawal, defined as in Section 10.1.2. Withdrawal counts either as the characteristic withdrawal syndrome or as taking the substance (or a closely related one) to relieve or avoid withdrawal. Neither is necessary for the diagnosis. Withdrawal is not listed at all for phencyclidine, the other hallucinogens and inhalants, because significant withdrawal has not been documented for them, although DSM-5-TR notes that a past history of withdrawal generally goes with a more severe course. The threshold of two was chosen partly because it kept the overall prevalence close to that of DSM-IV abuse and dependence combined. Change over time can also be tracked through the frequency and amount of use (days of use a month, standard drinks a day). Two course specifiers describe recovery. Early remission means that, after the full criteria were once met, none of them has been met for at least 3 months but less than 12 months; sustained remission means that none has been met for 12 months or longer. In both, craving is the one criterion allowed to persist, a realistic concession, since craving can outlast years of abstinence. Two further specifiers describe circumstances. "In a controlled environment" is added when the person is in a setting where access to the substance is restricted, such as a closely supervised jail, a therapeutic community or a locked ward, because abstinence there says less about recovery. "On maintenance therapy" applies to opioid use disorder (a person stable on methadone or buprenorphine, or on the antagonist naltrexone) and to tobacco use disorder (a person on long-term nicotine replacement), as long as no criteria are met apart from tolerance to, or withdrawal from, the maintenance medicine. Return to Lalit and count. He drinks more than he means to once he starts (1); he has tried and failed to stop (2); his evenings and mornings are organised around drinking (3); he craves a drink at the end of a working day (4); he has been warned at work for missing appointments after heavy nights (5); his wife has threatened to leave over his drinking, and he still drinks (6); he has given up his walks and his children's school functions (7); he rides his scooter home after drinking (8); he continues despite an abnormal liver test (9); he is tolerant (10); and he has withdrawal and drinks to relieve it (11). Even if you are cautious and accept only seven of these, he has a severe alcohol use disorder, because six or more is severe. Under DSM-IV he would have had alcohol dependence with physiological dependence; under ICD-10, alcohol dependence syndrome (F10.2). One rule protects patients from a serious mistake. Symptoms of tolerance and withdrawal that occur during appropriate medical treatment with prescribed medicines, such as opioid painkillers, sedatives or stimulants, are specifically not counted towards a substance use disorder. DSM-5-TR explains why: the normal, expected tolerance and withdrawal of medical treatment have led to erroneous diagnoses of "addiction" when these were the only symptoms present. The rule does not mean that prescribed drugs can never be the object of a disorder. When compulsive, drug-seeking behaviour appears, the diagnosis can be made. Clinical link Deepa, a 52-year-old schoolteacher in Nagpur, was prescribed alprazolam by her family doctor after her husband died, and has taken 0.5 mg at night for six years. The tablet no longer helps her sleep as it once did, and when she ran out during a holiday she had two nights of rebound insomnia and jitteriness. On these facts alone, tolerance and withdrawal from a medicine taken as prescribed, she does not have a sedative use disorder, and labelling her an "addict" would be both wrong and harmful. The picture changes if she begins taking three tablets a night, obtains extra prescriptions from a second doctor without telling the first, and keeps taking them after a fall caused by drowsiness. Then she shows impaired control and risky use as well, and a diagnosis (recorded by the specific drug, as alprazolam use disorder) is justified. Her case is also a reminder that long-term benzodiazepine prescription is one of the commonest routes into dependence (Section 10.7). Alongside the use disorders, DSM-5-TR recognises the substance-induced disorders , a group that contains three things: substance intoxication, substance withdrawal, and the substance/medication-induced mental disorders . The last are syndromes that look like other mental disorders but are caused by the physiological effects of a substance on the brain, whether a drug of abuse, a medicine (corticosteroids are a well-known example) or a toxin such as an organophosphate insecticide. There are substance-induced psychotic, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, sleep, sexual, delirium and neurocognitive disorders, each described in its own chapter. They share a set of common features: the symptoms developed during or soon after intoxication, withdrawal or exposure to a medicine; the substance involved is capable of producing them; and they are not better explained by an independent mental disorder. Evidence of an independent disorder would be that the symptoms began before the substance use, or persisted for a substantial period, about a month, after acute withdrawal or severe intoxication ended. In general, sedating drugs (alcohol and the sedative-hypnotics) produce depressive syndromes during intoxication and anxiety during withdrawal, while stimulants produce psychotic and anxiety syndromes during intoxication and depression during withdrawal. This is why an alcohol-dependent patient who is depressed on admission is usually reassessed after a few weeks of abstinence before an independent depressive disorder is diagnosed (Section 10.3). Finally, DSM-5-TR organises all of this by drug, in ten classes. Its reason for ten is practical rather than pharmacological, and it admits that the classes "are not fully distinct". What the classes share, the manual says, is that all drugs taken in excess directly activate the brain's reward system, the circuit of Section 10.2. ICD-11: disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours The eleventh revision of the ICD was approved by the World Health Assembly in May 2019 and came into effect on 1 January 2022. Its mental disorders chapter (Chapter 6) contains a block called "Disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours", with two parts: disorders due to substance use, and disorders due to addictive behaviours (gambling and gaming, Section 10.1.7). The substance part keeps the ICD-10 idea of a substance code plus a clinical condition, but it updates the list of substances and redraws the boundary between harm and dependence. The list of substances grows from the nine specific classes of ICD-10 to fourteen (Table 10.6). The newcomers reflect what people around the world now actually take: synthetic cannabinoids (the laboratory-made "spice" products), synthetic cathinones (the "bath salts" related to the khat leaf chewed in East Africa and Yemen), MDMA and related drugs such as MDA, and dissociative drugs including ketamine and phencyclidine. Caffeine, which ICD-10 lumped with the other stimulants, gets its own code, and ICD-11 speaks of nicotine rather than tobacco and of volatile inhalants rather than volatile solvents. There are also categories for other specified substances (including medicines), for multiple specified substances, for unknown substances, and for non-psychoactive substances such as laxatives, growth hormone and erythropoietin, which can be harmful but produce no intoxication, dependence or withdrawal; this last category covers much of the ground of ICD-10's F55.
