Alcohol shows the pattern: 6C40.0 episode of harmful use, 6C40.1 harmful pattern of use, 6C40.2 dependence, 6C40.3 intoxication, 6C40.4 withdrawal, and then the alcohol-induced mental disorders (6C40.5 delirium, 6C40.6 psychotic disorder, and others such as mood and anxiety disorders). Three steps in this ladder are new or changed. The first is the episode of harmful use (often called a single episode of harmful use), a category ICD-10 did not have. It is a single episode of use that has damaged a person's physical or mental health, or has led to behaviour that harmed the health of others, in a person who has no known pattern of harmful use or dependence. The young man who, on his first big night of drinking, crashes his motorcycle and injures his pillion rider qualifies. The category exists so that emergency departments can record and respond to such episodes, which are an opportunity for brief intervention, without attaching a label of disorder to a first event. The second is the harmful pattern of use , the successor of ICD-10's harmful use: a pattern of use that has caused damage to the person's physical or mental health, or has resulted in behaviour leading to harm to the health of others. The pattern must be evident over at least 12 months if use is episodic, or at least one month if use is continuous (daily or almost daily), and it can be specified as episodic or continuous. Notice the new phrase in both definitions, harm to the health of others. ICD-10 counted only damage to the user; ICD-11 recognises that the drunk driver's victims, and the family of a violent drinker, are harmed by his use as well. The third is dependence itself. ICD-11 describes it as a disorder of regulation of substance use arising from repeated or continuous use, whose characteristic feature is a strong internal drive to use. ICD-10's six features are folded into three pairs, and a diagnosis needs at least two of the three: Impaired control over use, in its onset, level, circumstances or termination, often but not necessarily with a subjective sense of urge or craving. Increasing precedence of use over other aspects of life, so that use takes priority over other interests, daily activities, responsibilities, and health or personal care, and continues despite problems. Physiological features showing neuroadaptation: tolerance, withdrawal after stopping or reducing use, or repeated use to prevent or relieve withdrawal. The withdrawal must be the characteristic syndrome for that substance, not merely a hangover. The features are usually evident over at least 12 months, but dependence can be diagnosed sooner if use has been continuous (daily or almost daily) for at least three months. As in ICD-10, there is a hierarchy: dependence takes precedence over a harmful pattern of use, which takes precedence over a single episode. Lalit, with impaired control, drink taking precedence over his family and health, and tolerance and withdrawal, has all three features: ICD-11 alcohol dependence, 6C40.2. ICD-11 also reaches one step further down the ladder than any earlier manual. Hazardous use of a substance, a pattern that appreciably increases the risk of harmful physical or mental consequences for the user or others, but has not yet caused harm, is coded in Chapter 24, "Factors influencing health status or contact with health services", as hazardous alcohol use (QE10), hazardous drug use (QE11) and hazardous nicotine use (QE12). These are not mental disorders. They are risk factors, coded so that a primary-care doctor can record, and act on, the patient who drinks too much but has not yet come to harm. The same chapter has codes for hazardous gambling or betting (QE21) and hazardous gaming (QE22). Figure 10.3 puts the four classifications side by side. The new substance classes are synthetic cannabinoids, synthetic cathinones, MDMA, dissociative drugs and caffeine on its own. Behavioural addictions: gambling disorder and gaming disorder If addiction is defined by compulsion and loss of control rather than by a chemical, then there is no reason in principle why a behaviour should not be addictive. The phrase behavioural addiction is used for repetitive, rewarding behaviours that show the same core pattern as substance dependence: impaired control, increasing priority over the rest of life, continuation despite harm, and often something like tolerance (needing more of the behaviour for the same thrill) and withdrawal (restlessness and irritability when it is stopped). The obvious danger is that the idea can be stretched to anything people enjoy a great deal, from chocolate to cricket. The manuals have therefore admitted behavioural addictions one at a time, and only when the evidence was strong. The first to be admitted was gambling. Pathological gambling entered DSM-III in 1980 as an impulse-control disorder, and ICD-10 placed it among the habit and impulse disorders (F63.0), beside kleptomania and pyromania. DSM-5 renamed it gambling disorder and moved it into the addictions chapter, reflecting evidence that gambling activates reward systems similar to those activated by drugs and produces behavioural symptoms comparable to those of the substance use disorders. At the same time the threshold was lowered from five of ten criteria to four, and one criterion, committing illegal acts to finance gambling, was removed. Gambling disorder is the only behavioural addiction in the main text of DSM-5-TR. Its diagnosis requires persistent and recurrent problematic gambling leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, with four or more of nine features in a 12-month period: Needs to gamble with increasing amounts of money to achieve the desired excitement (the gambling equivalent of tolerance). Is restless or irritable when trying to cut down or stop (the equivalent of withdrawal). Has made repeated unsuccessful efforts to control, cut back or stop. Is often preoccupied with gambling: reliving past wins, planning the next bet, thinking of ways to get money for it. Often gambles when feeling distressed (helpless, guilty, anxious, depressed). After losing money, often returns another day to get even, which is called chasing losses . Lies to conceal the extent of the gambling. Has jeopardised or lost a significant relationship, job, or educational or career opportunity. Relies on others to provide money to relieve desperate financial situations caused by gambling (a "bailout"). The gambling must not be better explained by a manic episode, which can produce reckless betting of its own. The course can be specified as episodic or persistent, remission as early or sustained (using the same 3-month and 12-month rules as for substances), and severity as mild (4 to 5 criteria), moderate (6 to 7) or severe (8 to 9). Chasing is the hallmark: many gamblers chase a loss for an evening, but the person with gambling disorder chases frequently and for years, placing larger bets to win everything back at once. Preoccupation and chasing are the criteria most often endorsed in mild cases, and jeopardised relationships and bailouts mostly in severe ones. Distorted thinking is typical: superstitions, a sense of control over chance events ("I can feel when the card is coming"), and the belief that money is both the cause of and the cure for the person's problems. DSM-5-TR puts the past-year prevalence at about 0.2 to 0.3 percent of the general population of the United States, and notes one striking cause: gambling disorder can appear as a direct effect of the dopamine-boosting medicines used to treat Parkinson's disease, and such cases are still diagnosed as gambling disorder. Gambling in India has changed shape in the smartphone era. Satta, lotteries, card games at Diwali and betting on cricket matches have long existed, but online rummy, poker and real-money fantasy sports reached millions of young people within a few years, with the round-the-clock access, rapid repeat play and instant digital payments that make any gambling more dangerous. In August 2025 Parliament passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, which bans online money games (games played for money stakes, whether of skill, of chance or of both), their advertising, and the processing of payments for them by banks and payment systems, while promoting e-sports and online social games. The Act and its rules came into force on 1 May 2026. Gaming without money stakes is the second behavioural addiction, and here the two manuals part company. Consider Tenzin, a 20-year-old engineering student in Bengaluru who grew up in the Tibetan settlement at Bylakuppe. For the past fourteen months he has played an online multiplayer battle game for nine or ten hours a day, often until four in the morning. He misses most morning classes, has failed two semester papers, has stopped playing football, which he once loved, and lies to his parents about how long he plays. When his roommates switched off the router to make him study, he became so irritable and restless that he moved to a cyber cafe. He has tried several times to limit himself to two hours a day and has never managed more than three days. In DSM-5-TR, Tenzin's problem has a name but no official diagnosis. Internet gaming disorder sits in Section III, "Conditions for Further Study": its proposed criteria require five or more of nine features in 12 months (preoccupation, withdrawal symptoms such as irritability, anxiety or sadness when gaming is taken away, tolerance in the form of more and more time spent, unsuccessful attempts to control it, loss of other interests, continued excessive gaming despite knowing the problems, deceiving others about the amount, gaming to escape a negative mood, and jeopardising a relationship, job or education). The proposal covers only non-gambling internet games; internet gambling belongs to gambling disorder, and ordinary social media use, work on the computer and sexual websites are excluded. The DSM-5 work group reviewed more than 240 articles and found real similarities to gambling and substance disorders, but judged that the lack of a standard definition and of good natural-history data made it premature to make the condition official. ICD-11 took the step that DSM-5 did not. Gaming disorder (6C51) is a full diagnosis in the block of disorders due to addictive behaviours, alongside gambling disorder (6C50). It is a persistent or recurrent pattern of gaming, online or offline, with three features: impaired control over gaming (its onset, frequency, intensity, duration, termination and context); increasing priority given to gaming, to the extent that it takes precedence over other interests and daily activities; and continuation or escalation of gaming despite negative consequences. The pattern must cause marked distress or significant impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas, and it is normally evident over at least 12 months, although the period can be shortened if all the requirements are met and the symptoms are severe. It can be specified as predominantly online (6C51.0) or predominantly offline (6C51.1), and gambling disorder can be specified in the same way. Tenzin meets all of this: ICD-11 gaming disorder, predominantly online. The WHO stresses that only a small minority of people who play video games develop the disorder, and that, as with alcohol, hazardous gaming (QE22) can be recorded before it becomes a disorder. In India, the first dedicated clinic for problems with technology use, the Service for Healthy Use of Technology (SHUT) clinic at NIMHANS in Bengaluru, opened in 2014, and gaming is its commonest reason for referral. What about the other "addictions" of everyday speech: shopping, sex, exercise, work, food, the internet in general? DSM-5-TR says plainly that these are not included, because there is insufficient peer-reviewed evidence to establish diagnostic criteria and course descriptions. ICD-11 does recognise a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (6C72), a persistent failure to control intense, repetitive sexual impulses or urges, but it deliberately places it among the impulse control disorders, with pyromania, kleptomania and intermittent explosive disorder, not among the addictive behaviours (Chapter 11). How common: the world and India How many people use drugs? The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) publishes the best global estimates each year in its World Drug Report, and they deliberately leave out alcohol and tobacco. The 2026 report estimated that 331 million people used a drug at least once in 2024, about 6.2 percent of the world's population aged 15 to 64, up from 5.2 percent a decade earlier. Cannabis was by far the most widely used drug, with about 256 million users, followed by the opioids (63 million), the amphetamines (32 million), cocaine (25 million) and ecstasy (21 million). Treatment reaches only a small minority: about one in nine men and one in 23 women with a drug use disorder were in treatment. Alcohol and tobacco, which are legal almost everywhere, are used by far more people than all the illegal drugs together, and they do far more damage to health; their figures are given in Sections 10.3 and 10.6. For India, the key source is the report Magnitude of Substance Use in India , commissioned by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment and carried out between December 2017 and October 2018 by the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC) of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, in a team led by Atul Ambekar ; it was released in February 2019. The previous national survey, conducted with the UNODC in 2000 to 2001 and published in 2004, had interviewed only men and had given no state-level estimates. The 2018 survey combined two methods. A household survey covered the general population aged 10 to 75 in all 36 states and union territories: 200,111 households in 186 districts were visited and 473,569 people interviewed. Because household surveys miss most people who are dependent on illegal drugs, a second survey used respondent-driven sampling (each person interviewed recruits others from the same hidden population) to reach 72,642 people dependent on illicit drugs in 135 districts. The survey studied alcohol, cannabis, opioids, cocaine, amphetamine-type stimulants, sedatives, inhalants and hallucinogens; it did not study tobacco. Its main national findings are in Table 10.8. Alcohol was by a long way the most used substance (tobacco aside), then cannabis, then the opioids. Among the alcohol users, country liquor ("desi") and Indian Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) were each the main drink of about 30 percent, and roughly one in every three drinkers needed help for alcohol-related problems. Among the opioids, heroin had overtaken the traditional opium, and more people were dependent on heroin than on opium or pharmaceutical opioids. Inhalants, the glue, petrol and correction fluid that cost a few rupees, were the only substances more often used by children than by adults, and an estimated 4.6 lakh children needed help for inhalant use. Finally, the treatment gap was enormous: only about one in 38 people with alcohol dependence had received any treatment, and only about one in 180 had ever been admitted to hospital for it. The picture also varies enormously from one region to another. The states with the highest prevalence of alcohol use were Chhattisgarh, Tripura, Punjab, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa, and alcohol use disorders exceeded 10 percent of the population in Tripura, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, Chhattisgarh and Arunachal Pradesh. Cannabis use was above the national level in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Sikkim, Chhattisgarh and Delhi. More than half of all the people with opioid use disorders lived in a handful of states (Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Delhi and Andhra Pradesh), but as a proportion of the population the worst affected were the north-eastern states of Mizoram, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim and Manipur, together with Punjab, Haryana and Delhi. Punjab, on the heroin route from across the north-western border, and the north-east, close to the opium-producing region where Myanmar, Laos and Thailand meet and long troubled by injecting drug use and the HIV infection that spreads with shared needles, are the two regions most often discussed, but no part of the country is untouched. The National Mental Health Survey of India (2015 to 2016), carried out by NIMHANS among adults in twelve states, gives the psychiatric view. Mental and behavioural problems due to psychoactive substance use, including tobacco, affected about 22.4 percent of adults, making them the largest group of disorders in the survey. Tobacco use disorder (moderate and high dependence) alone affected about 20.9 percent, alcohol use disorder about 4.6 percent (9.1 percent of men and 0.5 percent of women) and illicit drug use disorders about 0.6 percent. Two lessons follow. Tobacco, which the 2019 survey did not measure, is the commonest substance problem of all in India (Section 10.6). And alcohol problems in India are concentrated overwhelmingly among men, which means that the burden falls, very often, on their wives and children. Indian context India's main drug law is the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985, which brought India's law into line with the United Nations drug conventions. It controls narcotic drugs (opium, poppy straw, coca, cannabis and their products) and listed psychotropic substances, and punishes their cultivation, production, possession, sale and transport, with penalties graded by quantity; consumption itself is an offence under Section 27. Section 64A offers immunity from prosecution to a person charged with consumption or possession of a small quantity who volunteers for de-addiction treatment, a recognition that dependence is a health problem as well as a crime. One quirk matters for exam questions about cannabis: the Act defines cannabis as charas (the resin, including hashish oil) and ganja (the flowering or fruiting tops, excluding the seeds and leaves when not accompanied by the tops). Bhang, made from the leaves, therefore falls outside the Act's definition, and its sale is regulated instead by state excise laws, which is why licensed bhang shops can operate in some states. Exam trap In the 2019 national survey (people aged 10 to 75, tobacco not studied) the order of current use was alcohol (14.6%), cannabis (2.8%), opioids (2.06%) ; among opioids, heroin led, then pharmaceutical opioids, then opium. Inhalants were the only class used more by children than adults. The survey was done by the NDDTC, AIIMS, New Delhi , for the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, not by NIMHANS, which ran the National Mental Health Survey (2015 to 2016). Answers: (1) psychoactive, (2) metabolic, (3) cross-tolerance, (4) cross-dependence, (5) Milton Gross, (6) harmful use, (7) moderate, (8) legal, (9) two, (10) addictive behaviours. 10.2 Why People Become Addicted: Reward, Learning, Genes and Personality Medium yield · 4 Qs Stand outside a liquor shop in any Indian town at seven in the evening and you are looking at the puzzle this section tries to solve. Most of the men in the queue will drink tonight, go to work tomorrow and never meet the criteria for a substance use disorder that Section 10.1 laid out. A few will. Some of those few began drinking at the same age, with the same friends and at the same weddings as the men who stayed out of trouble. Exposure to a drug is necessary for addiction, but it is nowhere near sufficient. So why do some users lose control while most do not? Why do they go on using when the drug no longer gives them much pleasure and is wrecking their lives? Why do they return to it after months of abstinence? And why do some drugs, tobacco above all, capture so many of the people who try them? Kuldeep is 36 and runs a tractor-repair workshop on the outskirts of Jalandhar. His father drank heavily, was jailed after a brawl when Kuldeep was ten and died of liver disease at 52. Kuldeep had his first drink at 14, from his uncles' bottle at a cousin's wedding, and liked it at once: "For the first time in my life I was not restless." By 18 he was drinking most evenings with the young men who gathered at the workshop after closing time, and by 22 he had been in two fights and had one police case against him. Today he drinks most of a bottle of country liquor every day. He has stopped many times, once for four months after a frightening talk with his doctor, but on the first evening he sat with his old friends at the workshop he "only had one", and within a week he was back to a bottle a day. "Doctor sahib," he says, "the first glass does nothing for me now. I drink so that my hands stop shaking and my mind stops troubling me." Every theory in this section claims a piece of Kuldeep. The disease model calls him an alcoholic who has lost control over drinking; the brain researcher points to a reward circuit that now wants alcohol more than it enjoys it; the learning theorist points to the workshop at closing time, a place that has become a signal for drink; the geneticist points to his father; the personality researcher points to the restless, novelty-seeking boy; the psychoanalyst points to his mouth; and the sociologist points to the cheap liquor, the friends and the culture of drinking around him. The section takes these explanations in roughly the order they appeared historically, and ends by fitting them together. From sin to sickness: the moral model and Jellinek's disease concept For most of history, heavy drinking was treated as a moral failing. In the moral model of addiction, the drunkard chooses to drink and could choose not to; drunkenness is a sin or a weakness of character, and the proper responses are blame, punishment and exhortation. The model still shapes how families, police and courts treat people with addictions, and it is one reason so many hide their problem until it is far advanced. In the nineteenth century the moral view drove the temperance movement , which began in Britain and the United States as a campaign for moderation and hardened into demands for total abstinence and then for prohibition by law. Its greatest victory was national Prohibition in the United States from 1920 to 1933, a period that cut drinking but also handed the liquor trade to organised crime. India had its own temperance tradition. Gandhi saw liquor as a scourge of the poor; picketing liquor shops was part of the Civil Disobedience movement of 1930, and the Constitution of India, in Article 47 of the Directive Principles of State Policy, directs the State to endeavour to bring about the prohibition of intoxicating drinks and harmful drugs except for medicinal purposes. Which states have tried prohibition, and with what results, is taken up in Section 10.3. Alongside the moralists, a few physicians had begun to call habitual drunkenness a disease. The American physician Benjamin Rush (1746 to 1813), a signer of the Declaration of Independence, described the habitual drinking of ardent spirits (distilled liquor) in 1784 as a progressive disease, and argued that the only cure was to give spirits up entirely. The Scottish naval physician Thomas Trotter treated drunkenness as a disease in his Essay on Drunkenness of 1804, and in 1849 the Swedish physician Magnus Huss coined the word "alcoholism" ( alcoholismus chronicus ) for the bodily damage done by long drinking. But the idea that alcoholism is a disease only became the dominant view in the twentieth century, and the man most responsible for it was a biostatistician, not a physician. Elvin Morton Jellinek (1890 to 1963), known to friends as "Bunky", worked at the Yale Center of Alcohol Studies and later for the World Health Organization. His first contribution was a description of the stages through which drinking problems were thought to progress. In 1945 the magazine of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA), the self-help fellowship of recovering alcoholics, circulated a questionnaire to members asking when each drinking problem had first appeared. Jellinek analysed just 98 replies, chosen from the small number returned, and published "Phases in the drinking history of alcoholics" in 1946. In 1952 he refined it into four phases of alcohol addiction : a prealcoholic phase of social drinking that increasingly serves to relieve tension; a prodromal phase announced by blackouts (which he called alcoholic palimpsests), secret drinking, gulping and guilt; a crucial phase marked by loss of control, in which any drink sets off a chain of drinking the person cannot stop; and a chronic phase of prolonged binges, moral and physical deterioration, impaired thinking, tremor and finally the admission of defeat. The U-shaped chart that still hangs on the walls of many de-addiction centres, a descent through these phases on the left and a climb back through recovery on the right, is called the Jellinek curve , but the recovery arm was added by the British psychiatrist Max Glatt in the 1950s, and Jellinek later distanced himself from the chart. Jellinek's great book, The Disease Concept of Alcoholism (1960), went further. Drawing on clinical reports from France, Britain, Germany and the United States, he argued that there was not one alcoholism but several, which he named with Greek letters and called "species". Table 10.9 sets them out. The key idea is that only two of them, gamma and delta, involve the bodily changes of true addiction (increased tissue tolerance, adaptation of cell metabolism and withdrawal symptoms), and Jellinek reserved the word disease for those two. They differ in the way control fails. The gamma alcoholic shows loss of control : he can stay dry for days or weeks, but once he starts drinking he cannot stop until he is drunk or ill. This was the type Jellinek found among AA members and in the spirit-drinking English-speaking countries, and it became the model of "the alcoholic" in the popular mind. The delta alcoholic shows the opposite failure, inability to abstain : he rarely gets drunk and can control how much he drinks on any one occasion, but he cannot go without alcohol for even a day or two without withdrawal. Jellinek's example was the French wine drinker who takes two or three litres of wine through the day, is seldom visibly intoxicated and has never had a sober day in years. Gamma alcoholism, in his account, grew mainly out of psychological vulnerability; delta out of social and economic custom. Table 10.9 Jellinek's species of alcoholism (1960). Because it moved the alcoholic from the jail to the hospital. If alcoholism is a disease, the alcoholic is a patient, not a sinner; he deserves treatment, hospitals can admit him and insurers can pay for him. The disease concept underpinned AA's teaching that the alcoholic is powerless over alcohol and must never drink again, and it helped persuade the medical profession to take addiction seriously. It also drew heavy fire. Jellinek's phases rested on 98 hand-picked questionnaires from one self-help group, filled in from memory; when Marc Schuckit and his colleagues studied 636 alcohol-dependent men in treatment in 1993, they did find a typical sequence (heavy drinking escalating in the late twenties, interference with work and family in the early thirties, then a sense of loss of control, then worsening social, job and physical problems in the mid to late thirties), but it was a general pattern reconstructed from the ages at which problems first appeared, not a fixed series of phases through which every drinker must pass. Loss of control, the heart of the gamma type, turned out to be less absolute than AA believed. In 1962 the British psychiatrist D. L. Davies reported that 7 of 93 men treated for alcohol addiction at the Maudsley Hospital had been drinking normally for years afterwards, and the experiments on expectancy described in Section 10.2.4 showed that alcoholics who were given alcohol without knowing it did not lose control at all. In 1988 the philosopher Herbert Fingarette attacked the whole idea in Heavy Drinking: The Myth of Alcoholism as a Disease , arguing that heavy drinking is a way of life, shaped by choices and circumstances, rather than a disease that strikes. The modern successor of Jellinek's view is the brain disease model , stated most famously by Alan Leshner , then director of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse, in a 1997 article in Science titled "Addiction is a brain disease, and it matters". Its evidence is the brain research described next. Its critics point out that most people with a substance use disorder recover, often without any treatment and often in their twenties as adult responsibilities arrive, which is not how most chronic brain diseases behave. Today's manuals sidestep the argument: DSM-5-TR speaks of substance use disorders graded by severity (Section 10.1), not of a disease with species. Exam trap Gamma means loss of control (cannot stop once started; the AA, Anglo-American type). Delta means inability to abstain (cannot go a day without, rarely drunk; the French wine type). Do not swap them. Alpha is psychological reliance without loss of control, beta is physical damage without dependence, and epsilon is periodic binge drinking (dipsomania). Some revision notes call epsilon "the most advanced" form; the species are types, not stages, and Jellinek thought too little was known about epsilon to describe it in detail. His phases (prealcoholic, prodromal, crucial, chronic; 1946 and 1952) are a different scheme from his species (1960). The disease concept book is 1960; the U-shaped "Jellinek curve" was completed by Max Glatt. The brain's reward circuit The first scientific theories of addiction were built on withdrawal. According to the physical-dependence theory of addiction, a person who has used a drug long enough to become physically dependent is trapped in a vicious circle: every attempt to cut down brings withdrawal, and withdrawal drives the person back to the drug. If that were the whole story, the cure would be simple. Take the person into hospital, withdraw the drug gradually until the withdrawal syndrome has passed, and send home someone who no longer needs it. Early treatment programmes did exactly that, and they failed. Almost every detoxified user returned to the drug soon after discharge. The theory had two further problems. Some of the most addictive drugs, cocaine and the amphetamines, produce only mild physical withdrawal; and many users live in a cycle of binges and enforced detoxification (a weekend binge, a dry week when the money runs out), which shows that clearing the body of the drug does not clear the mind of the wish for it. As John Pinel tells the story in his textbook of biopsychology, these failures pushed researchers in the 1970s and 1980s towards positive-incentive theories of addiction: people take drugs not mainly to escape withdrawal but to obtain the drug's anticipated pleasure, its positive-incentive value. If that is so, the place to look is the brain's machinery for pleasure, and that machinery had been found, by accident, twenty years earlier. In the early 1950s James Olds (1922 to 1976), a young American psychologist trained at Harvard, arrived as a postdoctoral fellow in the laboratory of Donald Olding Hebb (1904 to 1985) at McGill University in Montreal, where a graduate student, Peter Milner , was assigned to teach him how to implant electrodes in a rat's brain. Olds was aiming for the reticular formation of the midbrain, which was then thought to control arousal. He was new to the technique, and in his first rat the electrode ended up far forward of its target, near the septal area. When Olds switched on a weak current while the rat explored a table top, he noticed something odd: if the rat was stimulated when it happened to be in one corner, it kept coming back to that corner, and if he moved the stimulation to another spot, the rat moved its preference too. The stimulation was acting as a reward. Olds and Milner then put rats in a Skinner box in which pressing a lever delivered a brief pulse of current to the brain, and in 1954 they reported that rats would press, and press, for the stimulation alone. The phenomenon, intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS), turned out to be spectacular at some sites: rats would press a lever thousands of times an hour, stopping only when they were exhausted. The sites soon became known as "pleasure centres". Olds and Milner argued that they were the circuits that normally carry the pleasure of natural rewards such as food, water and sex, and mapping them became a research programme of its own. The map that emerged is centred on dopamine. The mesotelencephalic dopamine system is a set of dopamine-releasing neurons whose cell bodies lie in two small nuclei of the midbrain (mesencephalon) and whose axons project forward to the telencephalon (Figure 10.4). Neurons from the substantia nigra project mainly to the dorsal striatum (the caudate and putamen); this nigrostriatal pathway is the one that degenerates in Parkinson's disease (Section 10.10) and it is concerned with movement and with habits. Neurons from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) project to the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala, the hippocampus, the septum and, above all, the nucleus accumbens , the main part of the ventral striatum; this is the mesocorticolimbic pathway. Its two limbs are usually named separately: the mesolimbic dopamine pathway from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens and other limbic structures, and the mesocortical pathway from the VTA to the prefrontal cortex. (The same pathways reappear in the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia in Chapter 4, Section 4.8.) Self-stimulation rises when dopamine agonists are given and falls with dopamine antagonists, lesions of the mesocorticolimbic pathway disrupt it, and it is accompanied by dopamine release along the pathway. The pleasure centres were, for the most part, a dopamine circuit. Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area project to the nucleus accumbens (the ventral striatum), the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus; this mesolimbic and mesocortical system is where addictive drugs, directly or indirectly, converge. The prefrontal cortex and amygdala (and, not drawn, the hippocampus) feed back to the accumbens with glutamate. The nigrostriatal pathway to the dorsal striatum takes over as use becomes habitual. The cerebellum and brainstem nuclei are not part of the circuit. How do you show that a drug acts on this circuit? Laboratory work on addiction relies on two methods. In the drug self-administration paradigm , an animal presses a lever to inject a drug into its own bloodstream, or directly into one part of its brain, through an implanted tube; animals readily learn to self-administer almost every drug to which humans become addicted. In the conditioned place preference paradigm, an animal repeatedly receives a drug in one of two distinctive compartments of a box; later, drug-free, it is allowed to wander between them, and the time it chooses to spend in the drug-paired compartment measures how rewarding the drug was. Both methods pointed to the nucleus accumbens. Rats will self-administer addictive drugs straight into the accumbens; microinjections there produce a place preference; lesions of the accumbens or of the VTA block both effects; and self-administered drugs, like food and sex, raise the level of dopamine outside the cells of the accumbens. Key study: Di Chiara and Imperato's microdialysis experiment (1988) At the University of Cagliari in Sardinia, Gaetano Di Chiara and Assunta Imperato used brain microdialysis, a fine probe that samples the fluid between neurons, to measure dopamine in freely moving rats. They compared two dopamine targets: the nucleus accumbens (a limbic area) and the dorsal caudate (a motor area). Drugs that humans abuse (opiates, alcohol, nicotine, amphetamine and cocaine) all raised extracellular dopamine in both areas, but especially in the accumbens. Drugs with unpleasant effects (kappa opioid agonists) lowered dopamine, and drugs that people do not abuse (the antidepressant imipramine, the anticholinergic atropine and the antihistamine diphenhydramine) left it unchanged. The conclusion, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 1988, was that raising dopamine in the mesolimbic system might be a fundamental property shared by drugs of abuse, however different their chemistry. The drugs reach this common end by very different routes, which the drug sections of this chapter describe one by one. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of dopamine and the amphetamines force its release (Section 10.6). Nicotine excites VTA neurons directly through their nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Section 10.6). Opioids act indirectly: VTA dopamine neurons are held in check by inhibitory GABA neurons, and opioids silence those GABA neurons, releasing the brake (Section 10.5). Alcohol, the benzodiazepines and cannabis also raise accumbens dopamine indirectly, through GABA, opioid and cannabinoid systems (Sections 10.3 and 10.7). The convergence is real, but two cautions are needed. Other transmitters, including the endogenous opioids, serotonin, noradrenaline and glutamate, play their own parts in reward; and most of this research used stimulants. When heroin was studied as carefully, lesions of the mesocorticolimbic pathway and dopamine antagonists that disrupted cocaine self-administration did not disrupt heroin self-administration, so the "one dopamine pathway for all drugs" view is a useful approximation rather than a law. A deeper problem soon appeared. If dopamine simply meant pleasure, then addicted people should enjoy their drug more and more. They do not. Kuldeep's first glass "does nothing" for him, yet he wants it more than ever, and many heroin and cocaine users say the same: the drug has lost its magic but the craving has grown. The incentive-sensitisation theory of Terry Robinson and Kent Berridge (1993) explains this by separating two things that everyday language runs together. "Liking" is the pleasure actually felt when the drug is taken (its hedonic value). "Wanting" is the motivational pull of the drug and of everything that predicts it (its incentive salience, or positive-incentive value). Robinson and Berridge argued that mesolimbic dopamine carries wanting, not liking; liking depends on small "hedonic hotspots" that use opioids and other transmitters. With repeated use, in vulnerable people, the dopamine system becomes sensitised, more and more reactive to the drug and to the cues that signal it, while tolerance blunts the liking. The result is a person who craves intensely a drug he no longer much enjoys. The theory also explains why drug cues are so powerful: a stimulus that predicts a drug is enough on its own to trigger dopamine release in the accumbens, and the sensitised system turns that cue into an urge. And because sensitisation develops only in some users, it offers one answer to the question of why some people move from occasional to habitual use and others do not. A second change makes drug use automatic. Barry Everitt and Trevor Robbins of Cambridge summarised a decade of animal work in 2005 under the title "from actions to habits to compulsion". Early drug taking is a goal-directed action: the person drinks in order to get a valued outcome, and the behaviour depends on the ventral striatum. With long repetition, control shifts towards the dorsal striatum, the structure that stores stimulus-response habits. The behaviour is now triggered by its cues whether or not the outcome is still wanted, just as you reach for a light switch in a dark room without deciding to. When the habit persists even in the face of punishment, it has become compulsion, the state DSM-5-TR describes as continued use despite knowledge of harm. At the same time the brakes weaken. Brain imaging by Rita Goldstein and Nora Volkow showed that in addicted people the prefrontal cortex, especially the orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex, is underactive at rest yet overreacts to drug cues; they called the result impaired response inhibition and salience attribution (2002). Volkow's group also found reduced numbers of dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum of people addicted to cocaine, alcohol, methamphetamine and heroin, one reason why ordinary pleasures (food, sex, company, a good film) feel flat. This anhedonia persists long after the drug is stopped and pulls the abstinent user back. Are these brain differences caused by drugs, or were they there first? Probably both: in 2012 Karen Ersche and her colleagues found some of the same abnormalities in the non-using brothers and sisters of people dependent on stimulants, which suggests an inherited vulnerability that drug use then deepens. The third change is the darkest. From 1997 onwards George Koob and Michel Le Moal argued that repeated drug use does not only sensitise the reward system; it also recruits the brain's stress and "anti-reward" systems, centred on the extended amygdala and the stress hormone corticotropin-releasing factor. The person's resting mood is pushed downwards, so that between doses he feels anxious, irritable and joyless, a shifted set point they later called allostasis. Koob and Volkow (2010) then described addiction as a repeating three-stage cycle: binge and intoxication (driven by the basal ganglia), withdrawal and negative affect (the extended amygdala) and preoccupation and anticipation, or craving (the prefrontal cortex). The second stage is the neural version of the opponent-process theory you will meet in Section 10.2.3, and it explains Kuldeep's own account of why he drinks now: not for pleasure, but so that his hands stop shaking and his mind stops troubling him. Exam trap The circuit most consistently altered in substance use disorders is the mesolimbic dopamine system : the ventral tegmental area projecting to the nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum), with the prefrontal cortex. The distractors are real structures with other jobs. The cerebellar vermis coordinates the trunk and gait (it does shrink in heavy drinkers, giving a broad-based, staggering walk, but that is alcohol toxicity, not the shared circuit of addiction). The lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus relays vision from the retina to the visual cortex. The vestibular nuclei of the brainstem handle balance and the reflexes that keep the eyes steady when the head moves. Also note: dopamine signals wanting , not simply pleasure or liking (Robinson and Berridge), and habitual use shifts control from the ventral to the dorsal striatum (Everitt and Robbins). Learning: reinforcement, conditioning and the opponent process Long before anyone measured dopamine, learning theorists had their own answer to the puzzle of addiction: drug taking is learned behaviour, acquired and maintained by the same laws as any other. The reward circuit is, after all, the machinery of reinforcement. Seen through the lens of operant conditioning, a drug is a powerful reinforcer, and it reinforces in two ways. In positive reinforcement , a behaviour becomes more likely because it is followed by something pleasant: the rush of cocaine, the warmth of heroin, the relaxed talkativeness of the second drink. The evidence that drugs are positive reinforcers in their own right, apart from any social meaning, comes from animals. Rats and monkeys with a lever that delivers intravenous cocaine, amphetamine, opiates, alcohol or sedatives will learn to press it without any training beyond the drug itself. Given unlimited access, they can harm themselves badly. When Michael Bozarth and Roy Wise (1985) allowed rats to self-administer intravenous drugs around the clock for 30 days, the heroin rats kept grooming and kept their weight, but the cocaine rats took the drug in frenzied binges, stopped grooming, lost up to 47 percent of their body weight, and 90 percent of them died (against 36 percent of the heroin rats). In negative reinforcement , a behaviour becomes more likely because it removes or prevents something unpleasant. Aspirin is a negative reinforcer: you take it not because it makes you feel good but because it stops your headache. Many drugs relieve withdrawal, physical pain, anxiety, loneliness or low mood, and each relief strengthens the habit. Kuldeep's drink taken to stop his hands shaking is negative reinforcement in its plainest form. The most influential version of this idea for alcohol is the tension-reduction hypothesis , formally proposed by the American psychologist John Conger in 1956 on the basis of earlier animal work, including his own experiments in which alcohol reduced the fear-driven avoidance of animals placed in conflict. The hypothesis has two parts: alcohol reduces tension, and people therefore drink more when they are tense. Both parts turned out to be only partly true. Alcohol does calm some people in some situations at some doses, but at other doses and later in the drinking episode it increases anxiety, and many people drink most when they are happy and celebrating, not when they are stressed. The idea survives in a more specific form as the self-medication hypothesis (Section 10.2.7). One more operant principle explains why the long-term costs of drinking do so little to stop it. Reinforcement works best when it is immediate. The relief of a drink arrives in minutes; the cirrhosis, the lost job and the broken marriage arrive months or years later, uncertain and spread thin. People with addictions are especially prone to discount delayed consequences in favour of immediate ones, a pattern that laboratory choice tasks measure as steep delay discounting. Classical (Pavlovian) conditioning adds a second layer. Every time a drug is taken, the stimuli that reliably come just before it (the place, the time of day, the friends, the bottle, the syringe, even the person's own mood) are paired with the drug's effects, and they become conditioned stimuli. The American psychiatrist Abraham Wikler (1910 to 1981), working at the federal narcotics hospital in Lexington, Kentucky, noticed in 1948 that former opioid addicts who had been drug-free for months would begin to yawn and shed tears, signs of opioid withdrawal, when they talked about drugs in group therapy. He called this conditioned withdrawal and proposed that drug-related cues, through Pavlovian learning, come to evoke a withdrawal-like state and craving, which the person then relieves by using; because such conditioned responses fade slowly, the risk of relapse outlasts any detoxification. Clinical link: why Hamid relapsed on the way home Hamid, a 29-year-old tailor from Bhopal, had smoked and later injected "brown sugar" (impure heroin) for six years. He completed six weeks in a de-addiction ward, felt well and was sure that this time he was finished with the drug. On the walk home from the bus stand he passed the lane where he used to buy. Within a minute his eyes were watering, he was yawning, his stomach cramped and he felt "the same restlessness as the first day in the ward". By evening he had used. Nothing in his body had changed since that morning; what had changed was the place. The lane had become a conditioned stimulus for withdrawal and craving, exactly as Wikler described. This is why relapse prevention plans map a person's high-risk places, people and moods (Book 2, Section 9.9.6), and why the most dangerous moment for overdose is the first use after detoxification, when tolerance has faded but the habit has not (see the next paragraphs and Section 10.5). Conditioning also explains a strange feature of tolerance. Shepard Siegel , working at McMaster University in Canada, proposed that the body learns to anticipate a drug. If a drug lowers body temperature, slows the heart or depresses breathing, then the cues that regularly predict the drug come to elicit the opposite response in advance, a conditioned compensatory response that prepares the body for the drug's arrival and partly cancels its effect. Much of tolerance, on this view, is learned, and it should therefore be strongest in the usual setting. That is exactly what Siegel's group found. In one study (Crowell, Hinson and Siegel, 1981) rats received alcohol in a distinctive test room and saline in their colony room, or the reverse; tolerance to alcohol's temperature-lowering effect appeared only when the rats were tested in the room where they had always received alcohol. This situational specificity of tolerance has been shown many times, with many drugs. Key study: Siegel's heroin "overdose" rats (1982) Many heroin users found dead of an apparent overdose had taken no more than their usual dose. Siegel, Riley Hinson, Marvin Krank and Jane McCully asked whether the setting could be the missing factor. They built up heroin tolerance in rats with injections given in one distinctive environment, alternating with injections of a harmless sugar solution in another. Then every rat received a large dose of heroin (15 mg per kg). Of the tolerant rats given this dose in the familiar heroin environment, 32 percent died; of the equally tolerant rats given it in the environment that had been paired only with the sugar solution, 64 percent died; and of drug-naive control rats, 96 percent died. The same drug history, the same dose, and twice the death rate in an unfamiliar place, because the cues that triggered the protective compensatory response were missing. The study, published in Science in 1982, explains why users who inject in a new place, or in a hurry in an unusual way, are at special risk. The cues need not be external. Interoceptive stimuli, such as the thoughts and feelings of the drug-taking ritual or the first effects of the drug itself, can serve as conditioned stimuli too, which is why simply thinking about a drug can trigger craving. Conditioning also helps explain one of the most striking natural experiments in the history of addiction. When Lee Robins and her colleagues interviewed American soldiers who had left Vietnam in September 1971, almost half of the general sample had tried narcotics there and about 20 percent reported having been addicted to opiates; yet after they came home, their drug use and addiction fell back almost to pre-war levels (Robins, Helzer and Davis, 1975). Removed from the place, the companions, the boredom and the cheap pure heroin of Vietnam, most simply stopped (Section 10.5.6 tells the study in full). Finally, the pull of cues grows rather than fades during the first weeks of abstinence. In rats trained to self-administer cocaine, a drug-paired cue provokes few lever presses a day after withdrawal but many more a month or two later, a phenomenon called the incubation of craving . Pinel lists three triggers of relapse that research keeps confirming: stress, a single "priming" dose of the drug, and exposure to drug-associated cues. Cue exposure therapy, which presents the cues repeatedly without the drug so that the conditioned craving can extinguish, is described in Book 2, Section 9.9.6. The most elegant learning theory of addiction came from a teacher of James Olds. Richard Lester Solomon (1918 to 1995) of the University of Pennsylvania noticed that strong emotional states seem to set off their own opposites. With John Corbit he published the opponent-process theory of motivation, first applied to cigarette addiction (1973) and then set out in general form in the Psychological Review (1974); Solomon summarised it in 1980 under the subtitle "the costs of pleasure and the benefits of pain". The starting observation is a pattern of emotion that Solomon called the standard pattern of affective dynamics, with five features. When a strong stimulus begins, feeling rises quickly to a peak (State A). It then falls back a little to a steady level, even though the stimulus is still there. When the stimulus stops, feeling does not simply return to neutral: it swings past neutral into an opposite state (State B), the after-reaction, which reaches its own peak and then slowly decays back to baseline. In the laboratory Solomon saw it in dogs given a ten-second electric shock: the heart rate leapt, began to slow while the shock was still on, and after the shock dropped below its resting rate before slowly recovering. He found the same pattern in reports on military parachutists, who on their first jump were terrified during the free fall and, after landing, walked about stunned for a few minutes and then became talkative and elated. Solomon explained the pattern by two processes inside the nervous system. The a-process is the primary reaction to the stimulus: it starts quickly, follows the stimulus closely, stops quickly when the stimulus ends, and does not change with repetition. The a-process automatically arouses the b-process , an opponent reaction of the opposite emotional sign. The b-process is sluggish: slow to start, slow to build and slow to fade. What a person actually feels at any moment is the difference between the two, a minus b. Early on, a outweighs b, so the person feels State A; when the stimulus ends, the a-process vanishes at once while the b-process lingers, and the person feels State B. The crucial assumption is that the b-process is strengthened by use and weakened by disuse. Each time the stimulus is repeated, b starts sooner, grows larger and lasts longer, while a stays the same.
