After many doses (right) the a-process is unchanged, but the b-process has become larger, quicker and slower to fade: the high shrinks (tolerance) and the after-reaction becomes deep and long (withdrawal and craving). Apply this to a drug. Solomon's own example was opiates. With the first few doses, the user moves from a resting state to a rush and then euphoria, followed by a mild craving that soon passes. After many doses, the before-state is already craving, the drug produces only "contentment" (normality), and the after-reaction has become what Solomon called abstinence agony: the full withdrawal syndrome, intense and long-lasting. Two things have happened at once. The pleasure has shrunk, which is tolerance, and the misery after the drug has grown, which is withdrawal. The motive for taking the drug has shifted from positive reinforcement (getting the high) to negative reinforcement (escaping the low), and the one thing that ends the low fastest is another dose. That is the trap of "the hair of the dog that bit you", and it is Kuldeep's trap. The same mathematics runs in reverse for frightening experiences: the experienced parachutist feels eagerness before the jump, a thrill during it and exhilaration for hours afterwards, because his once-small b-process (relief and elation) has grown while the terror has habituated. Solomon thought love, grief, jogging, sauna bathing and many acquired tastes followed the same rule, and the theory remains one of the clearest accounts of how tolerance, withdrawal and craving arise together. The theory has limits. On its own it cannot explain why people relapse months or years after the b-process should have decayed through disuse. Here conditioning closes the gap: the b-process can itself be conditioned to drug cues, so that the lane, the workshop or the friends call up the opponent state (Wikler's conditioned withdrawal and Siegel's compensatory responses are both conditioned b-processes). And it says nothing about why one person is vulnerable and another is not, which is the business of genes and personality. Exam trap Negative reinforcement is not punishment. It strengthens behaviour by removing something unpleasant (drinking to stop withdrawal or anxiety); punishment weakens behaviour. In opponent-process theory the a-process is the fast, primary, unchanging reaction and the b-process is the slow opponent that grows with use; tolerance is the shrinking State A and withdrawal the enlarged State B. The authors are Solomon and Corbit (1974) ; do not confuse their theory with Ewald Hering's opponent-process theory of colour vision from the nineteenth century, which shares only the name and the idea of paired opposing processes. Siegel's conditioned compensatory response is opposite to the drug's effect, which is why tolerance is strongest, and overdose least likely, in the familiar setting. Thinking and social learning: expectancies, models, peers and the gateway Animals learn to take drugs without any beliefs about them, but people come to their first drink already full of beliefs. Long before an Indian boy tastes alcohol he has seen the film hero drink to forget a broken heart and the villain drink before a fight; he has seen uncles become loud and merry at weddings and his father become frightening at night. An alcohol expectancy is a belief about what alcohol will do to you: make you relaxed, sociable, witty, brave, sexually attractive, or angry. Children hold such beliefs years before they drink, learned from family, friends, films and advertising, and positive expectancies in early adolescence predict who starts drinking and who drinks more in the years that follow. Expectancies matter because they shape both the decision to drink and what drinking feels like. How can you separate what alcohol does from what people expect it to do? The answer was a clever design introduced by G. Alan Marlatt (1941 to 2011) and his colleagues Demming and Reid in 1973. They wanted to test the gamma alcoholic's "loss of control", the disease-model claim that a single drink triggers an uncontrollable craving for more. They recruited alcoholics and social drinkers for what was presented as a taste-rating task: each person was given three supposedly different drinks to compare on adjectives such as "sweet" and "strong", and the experimenters quietly measured how much was drunk. The drinks were vodka and tonic, chosen because tonic water hides the taste of vodka so well that people cannot tell reliably whether it is there. Crossing what people were told with what they actually received produced the four cells of the balanced-placebo design in Table 10.10. Table 10.10 The balanced-placebo design (Marlatt, Demming and Reid, 1973). How much people drank followed the row (what they believed), not the column (what was in the glass). What the person is told Actually given vodka and tonic Actually given tonic only "This is vodka and tonic" Drug plus expectancy (ordinary drinking) Expectancy alone (placebo) "This is plain tonic" Drug alone (hidden dose) Neither (control) The result was a blow to the loss-of-control idea. The amount people drank depended on what they had been told, not on what they had been given. Alcoholics who believed they were drinking vodka drank more, even when there was none in the glass; alcoholics who unknowingly received alcohol showed no runaway drinking at all. The same pattern held for social drinkers, though less strongly. A first drink does not, by its chemistry alone, set off the craving that the disease model described; what the drinker believes about that drink matters as much. (Pharmacology is not irrelevant, though: when Tim Stockwell and colleagues repeated the study in 1982, the alcohol itself did increase craving in severely dependent drinkers.) The balanced-placebo design became a standard tool of alcohol research, and later studies using it found that many of alcohol's social effects (feeling sociable, sexually aroused or aggressive) follow what people think they drank, whereas its effects on coordination and reaction time follow the alcohol itself. Marlatt went on to build a cognitive-behavioural model of relapse, including the abstinence violation effect , the "I've blown it, I may as well go all the way" reaction that turns a single slip into a full relapse; that model and the therapy built on it are described in Book 2, Section 9.9.6. Kuldeep's "only one" at the workshop, followed by a week of heavy drinking, is a textbook example. Expectancies are learned socially, and so is much of drinking itself. In the social learning theory of Albert Bandura (1925 to 2021), people learn by watching models, especially models who are similar, admired or rewarded. Marlatt showed the effect directly. In an experiment with B. D. Caudill (1975), male heavy social drinkers took part in a wine-tasting task alongside a confederate posing as another participant; when the confederate drank heavily, the real participants drank considerably more than when he drank lightly or was absent. In real life the most important models are parents and friends. Children of heavy-drinking parents see drinking as normal, learn their parents' expectancies and often have easier access to alcohol at home. Parents who are themselves using drugs also tend to supervise their children less, and poorly supervised adolescents drift towards friends who use. Peer use is one of the strongest predictors of adolescent substance use, through two processes: young people choose friends who share their habits (selection), and friends then shape one another (socialisation). For Kuldeep, the group at the workshop after closing time supplied all three: models, approval and a bottle. Social learning also tells you something about the order in which young people take up drugs, and that order is the basis of the most famous, and most misunderstood, idea in the epidemiology of drug use. Key study: Kandel's stages of adolescent drug use (1975) Denise Kandel , a sociologist and epidemiologist at Columbia University, followed random samples of New York State high-school students in two longitudinal surveys. She found that involvement with drugs moved through four stages in a regular order: (1) beer or wine, or both; (2) cigarettes or hard liquor (spirits); (3) marijuana; and (4) other illicit drugs such as LSD, amphetamines or heroin. The legal drugs were necessary intermediates between non-use and marijuana: 27 percent of students who both smoked and drank moved on to marijuana within a five to six month follow-up, against only 2 percent of those who had used no legal drug. Marijuana in turn was a crucial step towards other illicit drugs: 26 percent of marijuana users progressed to LSD, amphetamines or heroin, against 1 percent of non-users and 4 percent of users of legal drugs only. The same order held in every year of high school and in the year after, and students who cut down retreated through the stages in reverse. Kandel published these findings in Science in 1975. Kandel's sequence became the gateway hypothesis : the idea that using a "softer" drug opens the door to "harder" ones. Because so few heroin or cocaine users in her data had skipped the marijuana stage, marijuana became the drug most commonly cited as the gateway to hard drugs, and the phrase "gateway drug", popularised in the 1980s, became a slogan of drug policy. But notice what the data show. The first step on Kandel's ladder was not marijuana but alcohol and tobacco, and most people who use marijuana never go on to heroin or cocaine. A sequence is not a cause. The main alternative is the common liability model : the same underlying vulnerability (genes, impulsive temperament, troubled family, deviant friends, easy access) makes a young person likely to use any drug, and drugs are simply tried in order of their availability and social acceptability, cheapest and most legal first. The strongest evidence for this comes from comparing countries. When Louisa Degenhardt and her colleagues (2010) examined the order in which people began using alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and other illicit drugs in WHO World Mental Health Surveys from 17 countries, the order varied with how common each drug was locally, and people often broke the "normal" sequence where cannabis was easy to get; they concluded that the gateway pattern at least partly reflects shared causes rather than one drug causing the next. The causal version has not disappeared, however. In 2011 Kandel, her husband, the Nobel laureate neuroscientist Eric Kandel , and their colleagues reported that mice primed with nicotine showed a stronger response to cocaine, in behaviour and in gene expression in the striatum, than mice that were not, and in 2014 the Kandels argued that nicotine itself may act as a biological gateway. Exam trap Asked which drug is "most commonly cited" as the gateway to heroin or cocaine, answer marijuana (cannabis). The traps: alcohol and nicotine are in fact the first drugs in Kandel's sequence (beer or wine, then cigarettes or spirits), and the Kandels (2014) later argued for nicotine as a molecular gateway, but neither is the classic answer; ecstasy (MDMA, Section 10.6) is a later, "club" drug, not a gateway at all. Remember the order: beer or wine, cigarettes or hard liquor, marijuana, other illicit drugs. Kandel described a sequence ; whether it is causal is exactly what the common liability model disputes. Why some drugs capture more users than others Reena is 27 and works as a data analyst in Bengaluru. She smoked her first cigarette at 19, in her college hostel, and hated it: she coughed, felt dizzy and wondered why anyone bothered. But her friends smoked at the tea stall between lectures, and she began to join them, "only with friends, only at parties". Within a year she was smoking fifteen cigarettes a day. She has tried to quit four times; each attempt ended within a week, usually at the afternoon chai break with her team. In the same years she tried alcohol (she drinks a glass of wine perhaps once a month) and, once, cannabis at a party, which made her anxious and which she has never wanted again. Three drugs, three exposures, one addiction. Why tobacco? Drugs differ in their addictive liability , sometimes called their capture rate: the proportion of people who ever use a drug who go on to become dependent on it. The best-known estimate comes from the National Comorbidity Survey, a nationally representative American survey carried out between 1990 and 1992. James Anthony , Lynn Warner and Ronald Kessler (1994) took the 8,098 people aged 15 to 54 in the survey, found out which drugs each had ever used (outside medical use), and asked how many of the users had at some point met the criteria for dependence of the day (DSM-III-R). Table 10.11 gives the answer. Tobacco topped the list: almost one in three people who had ever smoked had become dependent, a higher proportion than for heroin, cocaine or alcohol, and more than three times the figure for cannabis. Table 10.11 The proportion of users who had ever become dependent on each drug, National Comorbidity Survey, United States, 1990 to 1992 (Anthony, Warner and Kessler, 1994). Drug Ever used (percent of population) Users who became dependent (percent) Tobacco 75.6 31.9 Heroin 1.5 23.1 (few users, so a wide margin of error) Cocaine 16.2 16.7 Alcohol 91.5 15.4 Stimulants (other than cocaine) 15.3 11.2 Sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics 12.7 9.2 Cannabis 46.3 9.1 Analgesics (opioid painkillers) 9.7 7.5 Psychedelics 10.6 4.9 Inhalants 6.8 3.7 A later and larger American survey told the same story with lifetime follow-up. Using the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions, Catalina Lopez-Quintero and her colleagues (2011) estimated the cumulative probability that a user would ever become dependent: 67.5 percent for nicotine, 22.7 percent for alcohol, 20.9 percent for cocaine and 8.9 percent for cannabis. Pinel's textbook gives the same figures, rounded: about 68 percent of people who experiment with smoking become addicted, against 23 percent for alcohol and 9 percent for marijuana. The same study adds a twist worth remembering: capture is not the same as speed. Among those who did become dependent, half the cases of cocaine and cannabis dependence had appeared within about 4 and 5 years of first use, against about 13 years for alcohol and 27 years for nicotine. Cocaine captures fewer of its users, but it captures them fast. Why should a legal drug that produces no intoxication be the most efficient trap of all? The answer lies in how the drug is delivered and how it fits into life. First, route and speed. Inhaled smoke carries nicotine from the lungs to the brain within seconds, and the faster a drug reaches the brain, the stronger its reinforcing effect; the same principle explains why smoked crack cocaine and injected heroin are more addictive than snorted cocaine or swallowed opium (Sections 10.5 and 10.6). Second, frequency. A smoker of twenty cigarettes a day, at roughly ten puffs a cigarette, delivers about two hundred small doses to the brain every day, and each puff is both a reinforcement and a conditioning trial that ties nicotine to tea, coffee, meals, the phone, the end of work and the company of friends. No heroin user gets two hundred doses a day. Third, nicotine is short-acting, so withdrawal (irritability, restlessness, poor concentration) begins within hours and every cigarette also relieves a little withdrawal: positive and negative reinforcement on every puff. Fourth, nicotine does not intoxicate. You can smoke while working, driving or studying, so use never has to stop. And fifth, tobacco is legal, cheap, sold at every pan shop and socially accepted almost everywhere. As Pinel puts it, can you think of any other psychoactive drug that people take almost continually, even while walking down the street? Pinel tells the story of one famous man who could not stop. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) used cocaine for about three years from 1884 and stopped in 1887, apparently without difficulty, yet he never gave up the twenty or so cigars he smoked every day, despite his physician's orders, cancer of the mouth and 33 operations on his jaw and palate. The man who could walk away from cocaine could not walk away from cigars; the Key study in Section 10.6.1 tells the whole story. Two qualifications keep this picture honest. Capture rates measure how often users become dependent, not how harmful or how intensely rewarding a single dose is. When David Nutt and his colleagues (2007) asked expert panels to rate drugs for their dependence potential, heroin (3.0 on a 0 to 3 scale) and cocaine (2.39) came above tobacco (2.21), which in turn came above alcohol (1.93) and cannabis (1.51). Heroin and cocaine are pharmacologically more compelling per dose; tobacco captures more of its users because of the five reasons above. And capture rates depend on context: they were measured mostly in Western samples, and a drug's liability changes with its price, purity, legal status and the way it is taken (Sections 10.5 and 10.6). Exam trap Which substance has the highest addictive liability, the largest proportion of users who become dependent? Nicotine (tobacco) : about a third of users in the National Comorbidity Survey (Anthony, Warner and Kessler, 1994) and about two thirds over a lifetime in NESARC (Lopez-Quintero and colleagues, 2011). Cocaine is the tempting wrong answer: it is more intensely rewarding per dose and dependence develops faster, but a smaller share of its users become dependent. Alcohol captures about one in seven to one in four of its users, and marijuana about one in ten. If a question asks instead which drug expert panels rate highest for dependence potential, the answer is heroin. Genes: families, adoptees, twins and inherited markers Kuldeep's father drank himself to death, and Kuldeep is drinking heavily. Is that inheritance or upbringing? Alcohol use disorder clearly runs in families: DSM-5-TR puts the risk at three to four times higher in the close relatives of a person with the disorder, highest for those with many affected relatives, close genetic ties and severe problems in the family. But families share homes, habits and liquor cabinets as well as genes, so family studies alone cannot separate the two. The tools that can are twin and adoption studies, whose logic is explained in Chapter 1, Section 1.4. For alcohol, the adoption studies came first. In Denmark, where national registers allowed adopted children to be traced back to their biological parents, the American psychiatrist Donald Goodwin and his Danish and American colleagues studied men who had been separated from their biological parents early in life and raised by unrelated adoptive families. In their 1973 report, 18 percent of the adopted-away sons of alcoholic biological parents had themselves become alcoholic, against 5 percent of adopted sons whose biological parents had no record of alcoholism. Being raised away from the alcoholic parent did not protect them. (In a later study by the same group, the adopted-away daughters of alcoholics did not show the same raised risk.) The most influential adoption study was Swedish. C. Robert Cloninger , an American psychiatrist at Washington University in St Louis, worked with the Swedish researchers Michael Bohman and Sören Sigvardsson on the records of all the children born to single mothers in Stockholm between 1930 and 1949 whose fathers were known and who had been adopted by non-relatives at an early age. Sweden kept unusually complete records of alcohol abuse, because people who drank to excess were registered with local temperance boards, and of treatment and crime. In 1981 Cloninger, Bohman and Sigvardsson reported their cross-fostering analysis of 862 adopted men. Alcoholism in a biological parent raised a son's risk; alcoholism in an adoptive parent did not. But the pattern of inheritance was not uniform, and they separated two forms of alcoholism with different causes (Table 10.12). Type I alcoholism , which they called milieu-limited, was the common form. The biological parents of these men had usually had mild, adult-onset alcohol problems without serious criminality, and the genetic predisposition expressed itself only when the adoptive environment also pushed (for example, when the adoptive father was an unskilled labourer); it was a joint product of genes and milieu, hence the name. A companion study of 913 adopted women found that their pattern of inheritance matched type I, so this form affects both sexes. Type II alcoholism , called male-limited, was less common but more strongly inherited. It ran in sons of biological fathers with severe alcoholism that had begun in adolescence, needed extensive treatment and went with serious criminality; the mothers were usually not alcoholic. Sons with this background were at high risk whatever kind of home they were raised in; the adoptive environment affected the severity of their drinking but not whether it appeared. In 1987 Cloninger linked the two types to personality and to clinical pictures. Type I alcoholics typically begin drinking heavily after the age of 25, drink in binges with loss of control, feel guilty and afraid about their drinking, and are anxious, cautious, emotionally dependent people (high in harm avoidance and reward dependence, low in novelty seeking) who drink to relieve anxiety. Type II alcoholics begin before 25, cannot abstain, often fight and get arrested when drinking, feel little guilt, and are impulsive, thrill-seeking and socially detached (high in novelty seeking, low in harm avoidance and reward dependence) who drink for euphoria. You will recognise Kuldeep: an alcoholic, violent father with a police record, drinking from 14, fights and a police case by 22, and a restless boy who felt calm for the first time with a drink in his hand. He is a type II picture. Table 10.12 Cloninger's type I and type II alcoholism (Cloninger, Bohman and Sigvardsson, 1981; Cloninger, 1987). The types are prototypes at the two ends of a continuum, not boxes into which every drinker fits. Feature Type I (milieu-limited) Type II (male-limited) Causes Genes plus environment; both needed Mainly genetic; environment affects severity only Sex Men and women Mainly men Frequency Common Less common Biological parents Mild, adult-onset alcohol abuse, little crime Father with severe, early, treated alcoholism and serious crime Usual age of onset After 25 Before 25 Typical drinking problem Loss of control and binges; problems worsen over time Inability to abstain; drinking with fighting and arrests Guilt and fear about drinking Frequent Infrequent Personality High harm avoidance and reward dependence, low novelty seeking High novelty seeking, low harm avoidance and reward dependence Drinks mainly to Relieve anxiety Get high (euphoria) The typology was criticised from the start. It was odd that type I covered both mild and severe abusers while type II covered moderate ones, and the "male-limited" label proved too strong, since some women fit the type II profile. A replication in Gothenburg, reported in 1996, confirmed both types in adopted men: the risk of severe type I alcoholism was raised about fourfold only when the genetic and the environmental risks were both present (11.4 percent against 3.0 percent), while the risk of type II alcoholism was raised about sixfold in sons with a type II genetic background, whatever their upbringing (10.7 percent against 2.0 percent). Other researchers found a similar divide by different routes: the American alcohol researcher Thomas Babor and colleagues (1992) used statistical clustering in treated alcoholics to separate a type A (later onset, fewer childhood risk factors, milder dependence, less psychopathology) from a type B (childhood risk factors, family history, early onset, severe dependence, use of other drugs and more psychopathology). The common message is that early-onset alcoholism with antisocial features is the more heritable and more severe form. Twin studies agree that genes matter a great deal. A meta-analysis of 12 twin studies and 5 adoption studies by Bradley Verhulst, Michael Neale and Kenneth Kendler (2015) put the heritability of alcohol use disorder at about 0.49, the same in men and women, with a modest contribution of shared family environment (about 0.10); DSM-5-TR gives the range as 40 to 60 percent of the variance in risk. Kendler's twin work has also shown that much of the genetic risk is shared across drugs: what is inherited is largely a general vulnerability to substance use disorders, not a gene for whisky or a gene for heroin. Heritability is not fate, though. The risk is spread across a great many genes, each of which, DSM-5-TR notes, explains only about 1 to 2 percent of it, and genes and environment interact: genetic effects on drinking are stronger when parents monitor their children poorly or when alcohol is easy to get. What exactly is inherited? Three kinds of answer have emerged. The first is the way the body handles alcohol. Alcohol is broken down to acetaldehyde, a toxic substance, and acetaldehyde is then broken down by the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2). A common variant of the ALDH2 gene, carried by roughly a third to a half of people of East Asian descent (some 540 million people, about 8 percent of the world's population) and almost absent elsewhere, produces an enzyme that barely works. When carriers drink, acetaldehyde builds up and they experience the alcohol flush reaction : a red, hot face, a racing heart, headache and nausea. Few people drink heavily through that, and carriers, especially those with two copies, are strongly protected against alcohol use disorder: in Japanese studies of several hundred alcoholics, people with two copies were almost never found. (Disulfiram, a drug used in treatment, works by producing the same reaction on purpose; Section 10.4.) Even this protection bends to culture. In Japan, as heavy drinking became more socially expected between 1979 and 1992, the protective effect of a single copy weakened, and more of the alcoholics treated at the end of that period carried the variant than at the start: a vivid example of genes and culture interacting. The second answer is how strongly a person feels alcohol. Low level of response to alcohol was discovered by Marc Schuckit in the San Diego Prospective Study. At about the age of 20, his group gave a standard dose of alcohol to 227 sons of alcoholics and 227 matched young men without such a family history, and measured how intoxicated they felt and how much their bodies swayed. About 40 percent of the sons of alcoholics, but fewer than 10 percent of the comparison men, showed a low response: they felt and showed surprisingly little effect. Almost a decade later, when the first half of the group was about 30, a low response at 20 predicted a fourfold greater likelihood of alcoholism in both groups; among the sons of alcoholics, 56 percent of those with a low response had developed alcoholism, against 14 percent of those with a high response (Schuckit, 1994). The likely mechanism is simple: a person who needs more drinks to feel the effect drinks more, more often, and the heavier drinking leads on to dependence. Note the direction carefully, because it is counter-intuitive: the risk marker is feeling less from alcohol, not more. The third answer is temperament, a restless, impulsive, novelty-seeking disposition that shows itself in childhood, long before the first drink; it belongs to the next subsection. (Researchers have also found a smaller P300 brain-wave response in the sons of alcoholics, but because the same finding appears in other disorders it is probably a general marker of vulnerability rather than a specific one.) Exam trap Type I (milieu-limited): later onset (after 25), both sexes, genes plus environment, loss of control, guilt, anxious and harm-avoidant. Type II (male-limited): early onset (before 25), mainly men, highly heritable from fathers with severe alcoholism and criminality, inability to abstain, fights and arrests, novelty seeking. Do not reverse them, and do not equate them with Jellinek's gamma and delta (Jellinek's types were clinical patterns; Cloninger's came from adoption records). Goodwin's Danish study found the raised risk in adopted-away sons . Schuckit's marker is a low response to alcohol. The ALDH2 flushing variant protects against alcohol use disorder. Heritability of alcohol use disorder is about 50 percent (40 to 60 percent). Personality, comorbidity and the psychodynamic view For much of the twentieth century clinicians spoke confidently of an addictive personality : immature, dependent, manipulative, unable to tolerate frustration, the kind of person who would become addicted to something sooner or later. The idea has not survived research. Its first problem is the direction of cause. The traits were described in people who were already addicted, and many of them (lying, manipulation, self-centredness) are what years of addiction do to anyone, because sustaining a habit that others disapprove of requires them. Its second problem is that when children are followed prospectively, no single personality predicts all addictions. What prospective research does find is a small number of traits that raise the risk, and they fall on two quite different paths. The first and stronger path runs through disinhibition. Children who are impulsive, restless, aggressive and poor at waiting for rewards are more likely to drink, smoke and use drugs early and to develop severe problems. Kenneth Sher and his colleagues (1991), comparing the children of alcoholics with other young people, called this behavioural undercontrol and showed that it was one of the routes by which risk passes from alcoholic parents to their children. It links substance use with childhood conduct problems, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (Chapter 3, Section 3.8) and antisocial personality disorder (Chapter 11) in what is now called the externalising spectrum; twin studies suggest that much of what these conditions share is inherited. DSM-5-TR notes that impulsivity raises the rates of all substance use disorders and of gambling disorder, and goes with earlier onset and greater severity. Closely related is sensation seeking , the need for varied, novel and intense experiences, studied by Marvin Zuckerman , and its cousin in Cloninger's 1987 theory, novelty seeking . Cloninger proposed three inherited dimensions of temperament, each tied to a transmitter: novelty seeking (dopamine), harm avoidance (serotonin) and reward dependence (noradrenaline); high novelty seeking marked his type II alcoholics, and his questionnaire is described in the Assessment book. Even rats show the pattern: animals that are more active in a novel environment, or that prefer sweetened water, are more likely to start self-administering cocaine. The second path runs through negative emotion: anxious, easily distressed, depressed people who use drugs to feel better. This is the path of Cloninger's type I drinker, and it brings us to comorbidity . Substance use disorders very often co-occur with depression, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and personality disorders. There are three ways such a link can arise, and in any one patient more than one may be at work. The drug may cause the other disorder: heavy drinking produces depression and anxiety that often clear within a few weeks of abstinence, which is why clinicians wait before diagnosing an independent depressive disorder in a drinker (Section 10.3). The other disorder may lead to drug use. Or a third factor, such as shared genes or childhood trauma, may cause both. The second possibility has a name. In the self-medication hypothesis , the Harvard psychiatrist Edward Khantzian (1985) argued, from clinical work with heroin and cocaine users, that people are predisposed to addiction because they suffer painful feelings and related psychiatric problems, and that their drug of choice is not random. It is chosen by the interaction between what the drug does and the feeling the person cannot bear. Opioid users, he wrote, prefer opiates for their powerful muting of disorganising rage and aggression; cocaine appeals because it relieves the distress of depression, hypomania and hyperactivity. Hamid, the young man from Bhopal, describes it exactly: his father beat him throughout his childhood, he grew into a man with a short fuse, and the first time he smoked brown sugar "the anger went quiet, for the first time in my life". The idea fits many clinical histories, and it explains why people with schizophrenia smoke so heavily (nicotine may ease some of their cognitive difficulties and their inability to feel pleasure). Its weakness is that in prospective studies the drug use often comes first, and the drugs usually worsen, in the long run, the very feelings they are taken to relieve. Khantzian's hypothesis is the modern heir of a much older tradition. Psychodynamic theories of addiction began with Freud, who thought addictions were rooted in the earliest stage of psychosexual development. In the oral stage, from birth to roughly 18 months, the infant's pleasure and its relationship with the world centre on the mouth: sucking, feeding and later biting. A child who is either frustrated or overindulged at this stage, Freud argued, becomes partly fixated there, leaving part of the libido invested in oral satisfactions. The adult with an oral fixation is dependent, passive and demanding, and seeks comfort through the mouth: eating, smoking, drinking, talking. In the Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905) Freud suggested that children in whom the pleasure of the lips remains unusually strong grow into adults with a strong motive for drinking and smoking. Earlier still, in a letter to his friend Wilhelm Fliess dated 22 December 1897, he had called masturbation the "primal addiction" and suggested that the other addictions, to alcohol, morphine and tobacco, arise as substitutes for it. His follower Karl Abraham (1877 to 1925) wrote on the psychological relations between sexuality and alcoholism in 1908, and the Hungarian-born analyst Sandor Rado (1890 to 1972) described addiction in 1933 as pharmacothymia , a disorder of mood in which a state of tense depression is relieved by the drug's elation, only to be followed by a deeper depression and a renewed need for the drug; read in modern terms, Rado had described the opponent process forty years before Solomon. Later analysts, Khantzian among them, moved away from libido and fixation and towards the idea that addiction is a failure to regulate feelings, self-esteem, relationships and self-care. How should you judge the psychodynamic view? The specific claim of oral fixation has little empirical support: there is no good evidence that the way an infant was fed predicts adult drinking, and the theory explains both too much and too little (any drinker can be called orally fixated after the fact). But the broader insight, that many people use drugs to manage feelings they cannot otherwise bear, has survived into the self-medication hypothesis, into the negative-reinforcement accounts of Section 10.2.3 and into the affect-regulation work of modern therapies (Book 2). Exam trap Freud linked alcohol dependence (and smoking and overeating) to fixation at the oral stage (birth to about 18 months; mouth; dependency). The distractors: anal fixation (about 18 months to 3 years; toilet training) gives the orderly, stingy, obstinate anal-retentive character, later linked to obsessional traits; phallic fixation (about 3 to 6 years; the Oedipus complex) is linked to vanity, recklessness and hysteria; latency (about 6 years to puberty) is a period of dormant sexual drives and is not a stage at which Freud placed fixations; and the genital stage (puberty onwards) is mature adult sexuality, the goal of development rather than a fixation point. Rado's term for drug addiction is pharmacothymia . The self-medication hypothesis is Khantzian's (1985). Culture, society and the biopsychosocial synthesis No one becomes dependent on a drug they cannot get, and no one drinks in a social vacuum. Society decides which drugs are legal, what they cost, where they are sold, who may use them, on which occasions and how much drunkenness is tolerated. DSM-5-TR's list of environmental risk factors for alcohol use disorder reads like a sociology syllabus: poverty and discrimination, unemployment, low education, cultural attitudes towards drinking and intoxication, the availability and price of alcohol, stress, heavy drinking among peers, exaggerated positive expectations of what alcohol will do, and poor ways of coping with stress. Of these, price and availability are the levers that public policy can pull most directly: when alcohol becomes cheaper or easier to buy, people drink more and suffer more harm, which is why taxes, licensing hours, the density of liquor outlets and the minimum drinking age matter (the Indian experience with prohibition is discussed in Section 10.3). Culture shapes not only how much people drink but what drinking does to them. In some societies wine or beer is part of family meals, children see adults drink moderately with food, and drunkenness is frowned upon; in others alcohol is kept apart from daily life, drunk mainly by men in groups, often in spirits and often with the explicit aim of getting drunk. The same quantity of alcohol produces different behaviour in different places. Barlow and Durand cite the finding that Poland and Finland, with relatively low alcohol consumption, had more drinking-related conflicts and arrests for drunkenness than the Netherlands with similar consumption, and one explanation is the expectancies discussed in Section 10.2.4: in one culture "drink makes me aggressive", in another "drink makes me sleepy". Culture can even override biology, as the Japanese experience with the protective ALDH2 variant showed. Indian context India's relationship with alcohol is deeply ambivalent. Many religious and social traditions disapprove of drinking, the Constitution's Article 47 asks the State to work towards prohibition, and most Indian women do not drink at all; yet among the men who do drink, drinking is often heavy, done in all-male groups, with cheap country liquor and with intoxication as the goal (Section 10.1 gives the survey figures, and Section 10.3 the pattern of drinking). Other substances carry cultural sanction of their own: bhang (cannabis) is drunk at Holi and offered at Shiva festivals, and offering paan, often with tobacco in it, is a traditional gesture of hospitality in many regions. A clinician assessing a client therefore needs to ask not only how much the person uses, but what that use means in the person's community: a glass of bhang at Holi and a bottle of liquor every evening sit in very different places in Indian life. The social environment matters for animals too. In standard self-administration studies a rat lives alone in a bare cage, where pressing a lever for a drug is the only interesting thing it can do. When rats are housed in groups, given enriched environments or offered other rewards, they are much less likely to take drugs. In the "Rat Park" studies of Bruce Alexander and his colleagues in Canada (1981), rats living in a large, comfortable colony with company and things to do drank much less morphine solution than rats kept in isolation (later attempts to repeat the result have been mixed). In a French study, given a choice between sweetened water and intravenous cocaine, only about 10 percent of rats preferred the cocaine. The lesson is not that drugs are harmless but that addiction flourishes where other rewards are scarce, and that treatment and prevention should add alternative rewards to people's lives: work, relationships, recognition, pleasure. The community reinforcement approach and contingency management, described in Sections 10.4 and 10.6 and in Book 2, are built on exactly this idea. Now step back. Each theory in this section is true of something, and none is true of everything. The most useful way to combine them is to notice that they answer different questions, because different causes act at different stages of a drug career (Figure 10.6). Whether a person tries a drug at all depends mostly on availability, price, family and peer models, expectancies and a curious, sensation-seeking temperament. Whether use becomes regular depends on the drug's rewarding power and how quickly and often it is delivered (Sections 10.2.2 and 10.2.5), on positive and negative reinforcement, on a low response to alcohol or an absent flushing reaction, and on a culture and peer group that support heavy use. Whether regular use becomes a disorder depends on incentive sensitisation, the slide from action to habit, weakening prefrontal control, the growing b-process of the opponent-process theory, and the stresses and lack of alternative rewards in the person's life. And whether a person who has stopped relapses depends on conditioned cues, stress, a single priming dose and the abstinence violation effect, set against the strength of the person's new life. This is the biopsychosocial model, introduced in Chapter 1, applied to addiction; it is also a version of the diathesis-stress idea, with genes and temperament supplying the diathesis and drugs, cues and circumstances supplying the stress. It is also the drug whose withdrawal can kill, a leading contributor to deaths on the roads, and the drug that starved Jimmie G.'s brain of a vitamin until his memory stopped working. DSM-5-TR estimates that alcohol use accounts for about 2.8 million deaths a year worldwide and that about 237 million men and 46 million women have an alcohol use disorder. No other substance combines so much ordinary social use with so much damage. (It is not, however, the drug that captures the largest share of the people who try it; that distinction belongs to nicotine, as Section 10.2 explains.) Because alcohol is legal and familiar, it is easy to forget that it is a drug in exactly the sense defined in Section 10.1: a psychoactive substance with a dose-response curve, tolerance, a withdrawal syndrome and a toxic dose. This section looks at it the way a pharmacologist, a physician and a psychiatrist would. It begins with what alcohol is and what the body does to it, moves to what it does to the brain at rising doses, and then follows the brain that has adapted to alcohol into withdrawal, where the most dramatic syndromes in this chapter (withdrawal seizures, alcoholic hallucinosis and delirium tremens) appear. It ends with the psychiatric and physical harm of years of heavy drinking, how problem drinking is recognised, and the place of alcohol in India. The theories of why some people become dependent and others do not are in Section 10.2; how alcohol use disorder is treated is the subject of Section 10.4. Ethanol, the standard drink and what the body does with alcohol The alcohol in every drink, from toddy to single malt, is the same molecule: ethanol (ethyl alcohol, C 2 H 5 OH). It is made when yeasts ferment the sugars in grain, fruit, palm sap, molasses or flowers. Fermentation stops when the alcohol reaches roughly 15 percent, because at that strength it kills the yeast, so beer, wine and toddy are all fairly weak. Stronger drinks (whisky, rum, brandy, vodka, arrack) are made by distillation, which boils off and concentrates the alcohol. Ethanol is not the only alcohol: methanol, used in industry, is a deadly poison, and you will meet it in the hooch tragedies of Section 10.3.9. Ethanol is a small molecule that dissolves in both water and fat. That simple chemistry explains much of what follows. It crosses every membrane in the body without needing a transporter, so it passes freely into the brain and across the placenta to the fetus, and it spreads evenly through the body's water. A person with more body water dilutes the same amount of alcohol more; a person with less body water (a smaller person, an older person, or a woman, who on average has more fat and less water than a man of the same weight) reaches a higher concentration from the same drink. Because drinks differ so much in strength, clinicians count alcohol in grams of pure ethanol, or in standard drinks. A standard drink is a conventional amount of pure alcohol used to compare drinks and to set safe-drinking advice. The World Health Organization (WHO), in the manual for its AUDIT questionnaire, uses 10 grams; DSM-5-TR describes a standard drink as about 10 to 12 grams; the United States uses 14 grams and the British "unit" is 8 grams. India has no official standard drink, so this book uses the WHO figure. The grams in any drink can be worked out from its volume and its strength: multiply the volume in millilitres by the percentage of alcohol by volume (divided by 100) and by 0.79, the density of ethanol. Table 10.14 does this for drinks you will hear about in an Indian clinic. Notice in particular the "quarter" (180 ml) of whisky, which many daily drinkers report as their usual amount: it contains about six standard drinks. A little alcohol is absorbed through the stomach wall, but most is absorbed from the small intestine, so anything that keeps the drink in the stomach slows absorption. On an empty stomach the blood level peaks roughly 30 to 90 minutes after drinking; a meal delays and flattens the peak, which is why the same two pegs feel very different before and after dinner. Some alcohol is broken down in the stomach wall and the liver before it ever reaches the general circulation, a process called first-pass metabolism ; women have less of the stomach enzyme involved, which is a second reason (DSM-5-TR lists it alongside body weight, fat and water) why women reach higher blood levels than men from the same drink. More than 90 percent of the alcohol is then metabolised by the liver; the small remainder leaves the body unchanged in breath, urine and sweat. The alcohol in the breath is in a fixed proportion to that in the blood, which is why a breath analyser can estimate the blood level. The liver's main route has two steps (Figure 10.7). First, the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) converts ethanol to acetaldehyde , a toxic and highly reactive chemical that causes flushing, nausea, a pounding heart and headache, and that damages tissues and DNA. Second, the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) converts acetaldehyde to acetate, which the body burns to carbon dioxide and water or turns into fat. Normally the second step is fast, so acetaldehyde never builds up. Two famous exceptions make this pathway a favourite of examiners. Many East Asian people carry a slow variant of the mitochondrial enzyme (ALDH2), so acetaldehyde accumulates and they flush, a reaction that protects them against alcohol use disorder (Section 10.2). And the drug disulfiram works by blocking ALDH deliberately, so that a drink produces the same unpleasant acetaldehyde reaction (Section 10.4.4). Acetaldehyde, the toxic middle product, normally never accumulates because the second step is fast; disulfiram and the slow ALDH2 variant both make it accumulate, and both make drinking unpleasant. Two further facts about this pathway matter clinically. Alcohol dehydrogenase becomes saturated at quite low blood levels, so the liver removes a roughly fixed amount of alcohol per hour however much is in the blood. Pharmacologists call this zero-order kinetics : elimination proceeds at a constant rate, not as a constant fraction. DSM-5-TR puts the rate at about one drink an hour, with the blood level falling by about 15 to 20 mg per 100 ml each hour. Black coffee, a cold shower or a walk in the night air do not speed it up; they produce a wide-awake drunk, not a sober one. Secondly, heavy drinkers recruit a second enzyme system in the liver, the microsomal ethanol-oxidising system (MEOS), whose main enzyme is cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1). Regular drinking induces it, so a heavy drinker clears alcohol somewhat faster than a non-drinker (one part of tolerance, Section 10.3.4). The same enzyme turns paracetamol into a liver-damaging product, which is why ordinary doses of paracetamol are more dangerous to a heavy drinker. The amount of alcohol in the blood is expressed as the blood alcohol concentration (BAC), usually in milligrams of ethanol per 100 millilitres of blood (mg per 100 ml, which is the same as mg per decilitre and is sometimes written "mg%"). A BAC of 80 mg per 100 ml is the same as 0.08 percent. In India, Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 makes it an offence to drive with more than 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood detected by a breath analyser (or another test); the limit in England and in most of the United States is 80. A useful approximation, worked out by the Swedish chemist Erik Widmark in 1932, estimates the peak BAC from the grams drunk divided by the body weight multiplied by the proportion of the body that is water (about 0.68 for men and 0.55 for women). Push a case through it. A 70 kg man finishes a quarter of whisky (61 g) over the evening. His peak BAC is about 100 × 61 ÷ (0.68 × 70), or roughly 128 mg per 100 ml, more than four times the Indian driving limit. At 15 mg per hour, it will take him about six and a half hours to fall below 30; if he stops drinking at midnight he is still over the limit at six in the morning, the "morning-after driver" whom traffic police catch every day. A 55 kg woman who drank the same quarter would peak at about 200, the level at which DSM-5-TR notes that most people without tolerance are severely intoxicated. The same arithmetic explains the DSM-5-TR rule of thumb that each standard drink raises the BAC by about 20 mg per 100 ml. Exam trap Alcohol is eliminated by zero-order kinetics : a roughly constant amount (about one drink, or 15 to 20 mg per 100 ml of BAC) per hour, not a constant percentage , and nothing the drinker does speeds it up. The pathway is ethanol to acetaldehyde (by alcohol dehydrogenase) to acetate (by aldehyde dehydrogenase ); the toxic product that causes flushing is acetaldehyde, not acetate. A "standard drink" is not one fixed amount: WHO uses 10 g, the United States 14 g, the British unit is 8 g, and India has no official definition. India's drink-driving limit is 30 mg per 100 ml, much lower than the 80 of England and most of the United States. How alcohol acts on the brain For most of the twentieth century pharmacologists thought alcohol worked like an anaesthetic gas, dissolving in the fatty membranes of neurons and making them sluggish. The theory explained why alcohol depresses everything at high doses, but not why some of its effects are so specific, or why benzodiazepines can stand in for it during withdrawal. From the 1980s onwards it became clear that alcohol acts on particular proteins in the membrane, and two of them carry most of the story: the main inhibitory receptor of the brain and one of the main excitatory ones. The brain's chief inhibitory neurotransmitter is gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). When GABA binds to the GABA-A receptor , a channel in the receptor opens and lets chloride ions flow into the neuron; the inside of the cell becomes more negative and the neuron becomes less likely to fire. You can think of GABA as the brain's brake. Alcohol does not bind where GABA binds. It binds at another site on the receptor complex and makes the channel respond more strongly when GABA arrives, so the brake works harder. A drug that acts like this is a positive allosteric modulator ("allosteric" means acting at another site). In ordinary exam language alcohol is called a GABA agonist, and functionally that is fair: its effect is to increase GABA's inhibition. Benzodiazepines and barbiturates act on the same receptor complex in the same way (barbiturates, at high doses, can even open the channel without GABA). This shared target is the reason alcohol, benzodiazepines and barbiturates show cross-tolerance and cross-dependence (Section 10.1), the reason a benzodiazepine can replace alcohol during detoxification (Section 10.4.3), and the reason that alcohol combined with sedative tablets is a common route to fatal overdose. The brain's chief excitatory neurotransmitter is glutamate, and one of its receptors, the NMDA receptor (named after N-methyl-D-aspartate, a chemical that activates it selectively), is the accelerator. Alcohol blocks it: it is an NMDA antagonist. The NMDA receptor is also essential for the strengthening of synapses that underlies new learning in the hippocampus, so its blockade is thought to explain why heavy drinking disrupts the laying down of new memories and produces blackouts (Section 10.3.3). So alcohol presses the brake and lifts the foot off the accelerator at the same time. Every depressant effect of drinking, from relaxation to coma, follows from that double action, and so, as you will see in Section 10.3.4, does the overexcited brain of withdrawal. Alcohol also acts on several other systems, and these explain its pleasures rather than its sedation. It increases the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, the common pathway of drug reward described in Section 10.2, partly because it triggers the release of the brain's own opioids (endorphins), which in turn release the brakes on dopamine neurons. That opioid link is the basis of naltrexone treatment (Section 10.4.5). Alcohol enhances the action of one serotonin receptor (the 5-HT 3 receptor) and raises serotonin release, and it affects glycine receptors, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and several ion channels. Barlow and Durand's textbook sums up the result: because alcohol affects so many neurotransmitter systems, we should not be surprised that its effects are so widespread and complex. Notice, though, the difference in status. The GABA-A and NMDA actions are direct and central; the dopamine, endorphin and serotonin effects are mostly downstream consequences or secondary targets. Exam trap "For which neurotransmitter is alcohol an agonist?" The answer is GABA : alcohol enhances inhibition at the GABA-A receptor (strictly, it is a positive allosteric modulator, the same family as benzodiazepines and barbiturates). Its second core action is to block the NMDA glutamate receptor , so if a question asks which receptor alcohol antagonises, the answer is NMDA. The distractors are not meaningless: alcohol does release endorphins and dopamine and does enhance one serotonin receptor, but it is not described as a serotonin , acetylcholine or endorphin agonist. Nicotine is the acetylcholine (nicotinic) agonist (Section 10.6); morphine and heroin are the opioid agonists (Section 10.5). Intoxication: from relaxed to comatose Watch the guests at a long wedding reception and you can see the whole dose-response curve of alcohol in one evening. Early on, the drinkers are warmer and more talkative than usual. A little later some are loud, a few are dancing who never dance, and one uncle is telling a story he would never tell sober. Later still, someone is slurring and swaying, someone has picked a quarrel over nothing, and someone is being helped to a car (where, one hopes, someone else is driving). Each stage corresponds roughly to a range of blood alcohol concentration, and each tells you something about how the drug acts. DSM-5-TR describes alcohol intoxication through four requirements, and each has a reason. There must be recent drinking. There must be clinically significant problematic changes in behaviour or psychological state that arise during or soon after drinking: inappropriate sexual or aggressive behaviour, swings of mood, impaired judgement. This requirement exists because having had a drink is not a disorder; the diagnosis is meant for intoxication that causes trouble. There must be at least one of six signs of a depressed nervous system: slurred speech, incoordination, an unsteady gait, nystagmus (jerky involuntary eye movements), impaired attention or memory, or stupor or coma. And the picture must not be better explained by something else. That last rule matters more in practice than any other. Low blood sugar, diabetic ketoacidosis, a head injury, cerebellar disease, multiple sclerosis and intoxication with sedative tablets can all look like drunkenness, and the drunk man in the casualty department who smells of alcohol and is "sleeping it off" is the classic person in whom a bleed inside the skull is missed. Partly because the first systems to be depressed are inhibitory ones. The frontal and social controls that normally hold behaviour in check are released before anything else is slowed, so the drinker is disinhibited , not stimulated. And partly because alcohol's effects are genuinely biphasic . DSM-5-TR notes that while blood levels are rising, the effects often reflect stimulation (talkativeness, a sense of well-being, a bright, expansive mood), whereas when levels are falling the drinker becomes progressively more depressed, withdrawn and cognitively impaired. The pleasant phase belongs to the rising limb of the blood alcohol curve and the unpleasant phase to the falling limb, which creates an obvious temptation: one more drink to get back to the rising limb. How can the same drug make one person aggressive, another tearful, a third generous and a fourth amorous? A strong answer was given by the social psychologist Claude M. Steele (born 1946) and Robert A. Josephs in a 1990 paper in American Psychologist called "Alcohol myopia: its prized and dangerous effects". Their idea of alcohol myopia is that alcohol narrows attention, like short sight, to the most salient cues of the moment, and leaves the drinker unable to process the more distant, abstract cues (consequences, rules, other people's feelings, tomorrow) that normally restrain behaviour. Steele and Josephs drew three conclusions. First, alcohol makes social behaviour more extreme by blocking a form of response conflict: a sober man who is insulted at a party feels the pull to hit back but is restrained by the thought of his job and his family; drunk, he sees only the insult. If the most salient cue happens to be a person asking for help, the same narrowing can make him unusually helpful. Secondly, the same process can inflate self-evaluation, which is why drinkers feel more attractive and capable than they are. Thirdly, alcohol myopia combined with a distracting activity reliably reduces anxiety and depression, because it becomes hard to attend to the thoughts that cause them; but a person who drinks alone with nothing to do but brood may feel worse. The theory explains the dangerous effects (violence, unsafe sex, drunk driving) and the prized ones, and it does so through what alcohol does to perception and thought rather than through a direct chemical "aggression effect" or through expectations alone. The role of expectations, studied with the balanced-placebo design, is described in Section 10.2. Heavy drinking can also wipe out memory for part of the evening. A blackout is amnesia for events that occurred during intoxication. It is not passing out: during a blackout the person was awake, talking, walking, perhaps driving, and to those around him he may not have seemed especially drunk. In 1969 the psychiatrists Donald W. Goodwin , J. Bruce Crane and Samuel Guze reviewed the subject and interviewed 100 hospitalised alcoholics about their blackouts, and they described two kinds. In an en bloc blackout a whole stretch of time, with a sharp beginning and end, is simply missing and cannot be recovered even with reminders. In a fragmentary blackout (sometimes called a grey-out) the memory has holes: islands of recollection remain, and reminders can bring back some of the rest. Blackouts reflect a failure to lay down new memories rather than a loss of memories already stored; the NMDA blockade described in Section 10.3.2 disrupts the hippocampal processes that consolidate new events. DSM-5-TR links them to high blood levels and perhaps to the speed with which the level rises, which is why gulping spirits on an empty stomach is the classic setting, and notes that women who drink heavily may be more vulnerable to them than men. Two rarer pictures complete the account of intoxication. The first is pathological intoxication , known in older texts by the Latin name mania a potu ("madness from drink"). ICD-10 lists it as a complication of acute intoxication (code F10.07) that applies only to alcohol: a sudden outburst of aggressive, often violent behaviour, quite unlike the person's sober character, after an amount of alcohol that would not intoxicate most people, usually followed by sleep and amnesia for the episode. DSM-III and DSM-III-R had a similar category (alcohol idiosyncratic intoxication), but DSM-IV dropped it, because the evidence that such a syndrome exists separately from ordinary drunken violence, epilepsy or other causes is thin. It is best regarded as a doubtful entity that is still examined because ICD-10 retains it. The second is acute alcohol poisoning , which is not rare at all. It follows the rapid drinking of large amounts, typically in drinking games, competitive "bottoms-up" sessions in hostels, or by a teenager drinking spirits for the first time, and it pushes the BAC into the range at which breathing slows and the gag reflex is lost. Death comes from respiratory depression, from inhaling vomit, from hypothermia, or from a fall in blood sugar (alcohol blocks the liver's production of glucose, a particular danger for children and the malnourished). The practical rules follow from the pharmacology: a person who cannot be roused is a medical emergency, not someone to be left to sleep it off; he should be placed on his side so that vomit drains out of the mouth, never left alone, and taken to hospital, where blood sugar is checked and corrected (with thiamine, Section 10.4.3) and other causes of coma, including head injury and sedative overdose, are looked for. Exam trap A blackout is amnesia for a period of intoxication during which the person was awake and acting; it is not fainting or passing out. En bloc blackouts are complete, with sharp edges, and unrecoverable; fragmentary ones are patchy, and cues can recover parts of them. Pathological intoxication (mania a potu, ICD-10 F10.07) means violent behaviour after a small amount of alcohol, out of keeping with the sober person; it is not simply heavy drunkenness, and modern DSM does not include it. And remember the biphasic rule: stimulation on the rising limb of the BAC curve, depression on the falling limb. Tolerance, neuroadaptation and kindling A man who has been drinking a quarter of whisky every night for ten years does not behave like the 70 kg man in Section 10.3.1 who drank the same quarter for the first time. He has developed tolerance, the need for markedly more of a drug to get the same effect, or a smaller effect from the same amount (Section 10.1). With alcohol, tolerance comes in several forms. A small part is metabolic: as you saw, regular drinking induces the liver's CYP2E1 system, so alcohol is cleared somewhat faster. But Pinel's textbook stresses that this increased metabolic efficiency contributes only slightly to overall alcohol tolerance; most alcohol tolerance is functional tolerance , a change in the brain itself so that the same blood level has less effect. There is even acute tolerance within a single drinking session: at the same blood level, a drinker is less impaired on the falling limb of the curve than he was on the rising limb, a finding known as the Mellanby effect after the British physiologist Edward Mellanby. Learned and situation-specific tolerance, the part played by conditioning, is described in Section 10.2. Because alcohol, benzodiazepines and barbiturates share a receptor, tolerance to one brings tolerance to the others (cross-tolerance, Section 10.1): heavy drinkers often need larger doses of sedatives and anaesthetics. Tolerance can also be lost. Late in a long drinking career, when the liver is failing or the brain has been damaged, some drinkers become drunk on far less than they used to drink. This late loss of tolerance is sometimes called reverse tolerance, but be careful with the term: Section 10.1 uses reverse tolerance for sensitisation, the increasing response to repeated doses of stimulants, and the two meanings should not be confused. What exactly changes in the brain? The answer, called neuroadaptation , is that the brain adjusts its own chemistry to cancel out a drug that is always present. Recall that alcohol strengthens the GABA brake and weakens the glutamate accelerator. A brain bathed in alcohol every day responds by making its GABA-A receptors fewer and less sensitive and by making more NMDA receptors, and the noradrenaline system of the brain stem, which drives arousal, sweating and a racing heart, becomes more active. With alcohol present these changes restore something close to normal function: that is tolerance. But the brain is now balanced only as long as the alcohol keeps coming (Figure 10.8). Take the alcohol away suddenly and the weakened brake and the strengthened accelerator are left unopposed. The result is a hyperexcitable nervous system: tremor, anxiety, sweating and a fast pulse first, then seizures and, at the extreme, delirium. This is why alcohol withdrawal is the mirror image of alcohol intoxication, and why it is relieved by alcohol itself or by a drug that acts on the same GABA-A receptor, such as a benzodiazepine. 1.
