In each panel the left bar is net GABA inhibition (the brake) and the right bar net glutamate excitation (the accelerator). The adapted brain of panel 2 is balanced only while alcohol is present; remove it and excitation wins. Even a single heavy evening produces a small version of this. Pinel's textbook describes the hangover as a withdrawal syndrome euphemistically named: headache, nausea, vomiting and tremor the morning after a single bout of drinking. Dehydration adds to it, because alcohol is a diuretic, and so do low blood sugar, acetaldehyde, poor sleep and the flavouring chemicals (congeners) in dark spirits. The hangover matters clinically because a drink relieves it. The morning drink taken to steady the hands, the "eye-opener", is relief drinking, one of the elements of the dependence syndrome described by Griffith Edwards and Milton Gross (Section 10.1), and it is one of the four CAGE questions you will meet in Section 10.3.8. Something else changes with each episode of withdrawal. In the late 1960s researchers discovered that if a weak electrical current is passed into a rat's amygdala once a day, at first nothing happens, but after many days the same weak current produces a full convulsion; the brain has been permanently sensitised. This phenomenon was called kindling , by analogy with the small sticks that light a fire. In 1978 the American psychiatrists James C. Ballenger and Robert M. Post proposed in the British Journal of Psychiatry that alcohol withdrawal works the same way. They reviewed evidence that the severity of withdrawal increases over years of drinking in a stepwise fashion, and argued that the overexcitement of each withdrawal kindles the brain a little further, so that a drinker whose early withdrawals were only the shakes may, years later, have seizures and delirium tremens. The kindling model fits a clinical observation that DSM-5-TR also records: people who have had more withdrawal episodes in the past have more severe withdrawal now. It also has a practical implication, which Section 10.4.3 takes up: every withdrawal should be treated properly, and repeated unsupervised "drying out" at home may be doing harm. Clinical link When you take a drinking history, ask about previous withdrawals, not just about drinking. "Have you ever had the shakes in the morning? Have you ever had a fit, or seen or heard things, when you stopped?" A history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens is the strongest single warning that the next withdrawal may be dangerous, and it is the main reason a patient is detoxified in hospital rather than at home. Exam trap Most alcohol tolerance is functional (pharmacodynamic) , a change in the brain, not metabolic ; the liver's faster clearance contributes only a little. Withdrawal is the mirror image of intoxication because of neuroadaptation: fewer and less sensitive GABA-A receptors, more NMDA receptors and an overactive noradrenaline system. The kindling model of increasingly severe withdrawals is Ballenger and Post (1978). And "reverse tolerance" has two meanings: sensitisation to stimulants (Section 10.1), and the late loss of tolerance in a drinker with a failing liver. The alcohol withdrawal syndrome: from the shakes to delirium tremens Jaswinder is 52, a long-distance truck driver from Ludhiana. He is admitted to the orthopaedic ward of a district hospital after his truck overturns on the highway, and the next morning a surgeon pins his broken thigh bone. Nobody asks about alcohol. On his second evening in hospital his hands tremble so much that he spills his tea, he is sweating, his pulse is 110 and he cannot sleep; the nurse puts it down to pain. On the third night, about sixty hours after his last drink, he is a different man. He pulls out his drip and tries to climb out of bed, shouting that he must unload the truck before the dhaba closes. He brushes furiously at his arms because, he says, ants are crawling all over him, and he points at small men in khaki uniforms climbing the bed rails. He does not know where he is or what day it is, and he cannot keep his attention on the doctor's questions for more than a few seconds. His temperature is 38.6 °C, his pulse 136, and he is drenched in sweat and shaking. During the next morning he is quieter and half-recognises his son, but by evening he is worse again. Only now does his wife tell the duty psychiatrist that he has drunk a 375 ml bottle of whisky (about thirteen standard drinks) every evening for fifteen years. Jaswinder has delirium tremens, and he is moved to the intensive care unit. For a long time doctors argued about what caused pictures like this. Some blamed malnutrition, some infection or head injury, and some the alcohol itself; delirium tremens often appeared when a drinker had stopped, but stopping was usually forced by an illness or injury that might have been the real cause. The question was settled by an experiment that could not be done today. Key study: Isbell and the experimental "rum fits" (1955) At the Addiction Research Center in Lexington, Kentucky, Harris Isbell (1910 to 1994) and his colleagues gave large amounts of alcohol to volunteers, former narcotic users at the centre. Of ten men who began, six were kept continuously and moderately intoxicated for between 48 and 87 days. Then the alcohol was stopped abruptly. All six developed tremor and weakness, two had convulsions, and four of the six developed hallucinations or delirium; one man's hallucinations included a shrunken, disembodied head whose eyes followed him and snakes coming up out of the floor. Because the seizures and delirium appeared only when the drinking stopped, after weeks of continuous intoxication had produced none, the study, published in 1955 as "An experimental study of the etiology of 'rum fits' and delirium tremens", showed that alcohol produces physical dependence and that withdrawal, not intoxication, precipitates seizures and delirium tremens. The criticism is ethical: volunteers were deliberately made dependent and then put through a withdrawal known to be dangerous, an experiment no ethics committee would approve today. Two years earlier, in 1953, the neurologists Maurice Victor and Raymond D. Adams had studied 226 men admitted to Boston City Hospital with alcohol-related illness, observing them from six to eight hours after their last drink until three or four days later. They described a spectrum that ran from mild tremor (the shakes or jitters) through seizures and hallucinations to delirium tremens, and they described the typical times at which each appeared. Their timetable, refined since, is the one clinicians still use. DSM-5-TR defines alcohol withdrawal by four requirements. There must have been heavy and prolonged drinking that has stopped or been cut down. Within several hours to a few days, at least two of eight signs must appear: autonomic hyperactivity (sweating, or a pulse over 100), increased hand tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient visual, tactile or auditory hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation, anxiety, and generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Read the list and you can see the hyperexcitable brain of Figure 10.8: everything on it is overactivity. The signs must cause distress or impairment, and they must not be better explained by another illness or by withdrawal from another drug (sedative withdrawal looks almost identical). The specifier "with perceptual disturbances" is used in the uncommon case in which hallucinations occur while the person knows they are not real (intact reality testing), or illusions occur without a delirium. DSM-5-TR also gives the timetable. Symptoms begin when the blood level falls sharply, within about 4 to 12 hours of the last drink; reflecting the fast metabolism of alcohol, they usually peak during the second day of abstinence and improve markedly by the fourth or fifth day. Fewer than 10 percent of people who develop withdrawal ever have dramatic symptoms (severe autonomic overactivity, marked tremor, delirium), and fewer than 3 percent have seizures. Withdrawal is more likely the more and the longer a person has drunk (DSM-5-TR says most people with the condition have been drinking more than about eight drinks a day for many days), is uncommon under the age of 30, and becomes more frequent and severe with age. Figure 10.9 lays out the four syndromes on this clock. Treat its windows as typical rather than fixed: different textbooks give slightly different hours (Pinel's, for example, places the onset of delirium tremens at three to five days), and individuals vary. Day 1 Day 2 (peak) Day 3 Day 4 Day 5 Minor withdrawal starts 6 to 24 h; tremor, sweating, insomnia Withdrawal seizures 12 to 48 h ("rum fits") Alcoholic hallucinosis 12 to 48 h; voices, clear mind Delirium tremens 48 to 72 h (up to 96 h) 0 24 48 72 96 120 Hours after the last drink Figure 10.9 The usual onset windows of the alcohol withdrawal syndromes. Minor withdrawal comes first and delirium tremens, the most dangerous, last; withdrawal as a whole peaks on day 2 and usually settles by day 4 or 5 (DSM-5-TR). Hours are typical, not fixed: sources differ by a few hours, and many people have only the first row. Minor withdrawal. Most people who go through withdrawal have only this stage, the shakes. Within the first day the hands (and sometimes the tongue and eyelids) develop a coarse tremor that is worse when the person tries to hold something; the drinker feels jittery and on edge, sweats, has a fast pulse and a raised blood pressure, loses his appetite, feels sick or vomits, and lies awake or sleeps fitfully with vivid dreams. He startles easily and is irritable and anxious. Brief illusions are common (a coat on a hook seems to move), and some people have fleeting hallucinations that they recognise as unreal. A drink abolishes all of it within minutes, which is exactly why a dependent drinker's first act of the day may be to drink. After the acute stage has passed, a milder protracted withdrawal may linger: DSM-5-TR notes that anxiety, insomnia and autonomic instability can persist at low intensity for 3 to 6 months, and these lingering symptoms are a common trigger of relapse (and the target of acamprosate, Section 10.4.5). Withdrawal seizures. Between about 12 and 48 hours after the last drink, a small minority have generalised tonic-clonic convulsions, which drinkers and older textbooks call rum fits . Usually there is a single seizure or a short burst of two or three. The risk is higher in people who have had withdrawal seizures before (the kindling of Section 10.3.4) and, DSM-5-TR notes, in people with epilepsy or a past severe head injury. A seizure that does not fit the pattern (one that is focal, that starts well after the second day, or that does not stop) should make the doctor look for another cause: a head injury with bleeding inside the skull, low blood sugar, low sodium, or meningitis. A withdrawal seizure is also a warning sign that the withdrawal is a severe one, and it calls for treatment, not just observation (Section 10.4.3). Alcoholic hallucinosis. Gopi, 46, a carpenter in Coimbatore, has drunk arrack heavily for twenty years. Two days after he stops drinking because of stomach pain, he begins to hear men's voices outside his window. They talk about him in the third person: "That drunkard is finished. Tonight we will come for him." They accuse him of stealing from his employer and say his wife has gone to the police. Gopi is terrified. He barricades the door and later runs to the neighbour's house to hide, and his family bring him to hospital. On examination he is fully alert. He knows the date, the place and the doctor's name, his attention is good, and he can give a coherent account of the voices, which he is quite sure are real. This is alcoholic hallucinosis , a term coined in 1900 by the German neuropsychiatrist Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905), the same Wernicke whose encephalopathy you will meet in Section 10.11. Its defining features are vivid hallucinations, mostly auditory and often threatening, accusing or insulting, occurring in clear consciousness, with orientation and attention intact. The voices frequently comment on the patient in the third person, and the patient may act on them in fear: barricading himself in, fleeing, calling the police, attacking the supposed persecutors, or attempting suicide. Delusions of persecution may grow out of the voices. It usually begins within about 12 to 48 hours of stopping or sharply reducing heavy drinking, though it can occur during continued drinking. In DSM-5-TR alcoholic hallucinosis is diagnosed as alcohol-induced psychotic disorder (with hallucinations); the manual notes that this usually occurs only after prolonged, heavy drinking in people with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder and that the hallucinations are generally auditory, and it estimates that alcohol-induced psychotic episodes are seen in fewer than 5 percent of people with alcohol use disorder. ICD-10 codes it within the psychotic disorders due to alcohol as F10.52, the predominantly hallucinatory form; the same F10.5 group includes alcoholic jealousy and alcoholic paranoia. Most episodes resolve within days to a few weeks of abstinence, and a minority persist for months. Because the picture can look exactly like paranoid schizophrenia, the distinction rests on the history: a long period of heavy drinking, onset when drinking stopped or fell, no earlier psychotic illness, and recovery with abstinence. Eugen Bleuler suspected that such cases were really schizophrenia released by alcohol, and the minority that become chronic keep that debate alive; substance-induced psychosis in general is discussed in Chapter 4, Section 4.5.6. Delirium tremens. The most dangerous withdrawal syndrome was named in 1813 by the English physician Thomas Sutton , who described it in his Tracts on Delirium Tremens and separated it from phrenitis, the delirium of fever and brain inflammation; the name means "trembling delirium". Delirium tremens (the DTs) is a delirium, a disturbance of consciousness and attention (Section 10.8 describes delirium in general), produced by alcohol withdrawal, and Jaswinder showed every part of it. Consciousness is clouded and fluctuates, worse at night; the patient is disoriented in time and place, cannot sustain attention, and misidentifies people and surroundings. Hallucinations are vivid and mainly visual and tactile: insects, snakes, rats and other animals, often moving, and sometimes tiny people or animals, the Lilliputian hallucinations named after the miniature inhabitants of Lilliput in Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels and famously described in 1909 by the French psychiatrist Raoul Leroy . The feeling of insects crawling on or under the skin is formication (from the Latin formica , ant), a tactile hallucination that is also typical of stimulant intoxication (Section 10.6 and Chapter 2, Section 2.3). Many patients act out their ordinary work, as Jaswinder tried to unload his truck, a picture called occupational delirium . Fear and agitation are marked, and patients are highly suggestible. Around the mental state is a storm of autonomic overactivity: coarse tremor, profuse sweating, fever, a racing pulse, raised blood pressure and complete sleeplessness, with the dehydration and loss of potassium and magnesium that follow. Delirium tremens usually begins about 48 to 72 hours after the last drink (the second or third day of abstinence), occasionally later, up to about 96 hours, and typically lasts two or three days, sometimes up to a week, often ending in a long, deep sleep. DSM-5-TR classes it as alcohol withdrawal delirium, one of the substance withdrawal deliriums in its neurocognitive disorders chapter, and ICD-10 as withdrawal state with delirium (F10.4). Fewer than one in ten people in withdrawal reach this stage, but it kills. Early studies reported death in as many as 15 percent of cases; with modern treatment deaths have become uncommon (the 2004 practice guideline of the American Society of Addiction Medicine cites recent series with a mortality of 0 to 1 percent, although textbooks often still quote a few percent). When death occurs it comes from cardiac arrhythmia, high fever, dehydration and electrolyte collapse, pneumonia and injuries. DSM-5-TR lists the predictors of severe withdrawal (a previous delirium or severe withdrawal, a low blood potassium, a low platelet count, and high systolic blood pressure) and warns that when withdrawal delirium develops, a clinically relevant medical condition is likely to be present as well: liver failure, pneumonia, gastrointestinal bleeding, the effects of a head injury, low blood sugar, an electrolyte imbalance or the aftermath of surgery. Jaswinder had one of these, a recent operation, and his doctors also had to rule out a head injury from the crash. Thiamine deficiency may also be present, and Wernicke's encephalopathy (Section 10.11) can hide inside the confusion of delirium tremens. Table 10.16 The four alcohol withdrawal syndromes compared. Clinical link Jaswinder's case is not unusual. DSM-5-TR warns that unanticipated alcohol withdrawal in hospitalised people whose alcohol use disorder has been overlooked adds to the risks and costs of their stay. Surgical, orthopaedic and medical wards are full of hidden drinkers, and their withdrawal typically appears on the second or third day after admission, just when an operation or injury seems to explain the confusion. Asking every newly admitted adult how much they drink, and asking a relative when the patient cannot answer, is one of the cheapest life-saving habits in medicine. Exam trap Do not mix up the two hallucinatory syndromes. Alcoholic hallucinosis : mainly auditory hallucinations (threatening voices) in clear consciousness , orientation intact, little autonomic disturbance, usually 12 to 48 hours after stopping. Delirium tremens : mainly visual and tactile hallucinations (animals, insects, Lilliputian people, formication) with clouded consciousness , disorientation, coarse tremor and severe autonomic overactivity, usually 48 to 72 hours after stopping, and potentially fatal. The order on the clock is tremor first, then seizures and hallucinosis, then delirium tremens. Thomas Sutton named delirium tremens (1813); Carl Wernicke named alcoholic hallucinosis (1900). Alcohol and the mind: depression, anxiety, jealousy, suicide and violence Sushila, 41, teaches mathematics at a school in Pune. After her mother died three years ago she began taking a glass of wine to help her sleep; now she drinks most of a 750 ml bottle of vodka over two or three nights, kept behind the saris in her cupboard. She comes to a psychiatrist complaining of depression, and on the face of it she has a major depressive episode: low mood most of the day, loss of interest in her classes, early waking, poor concentration, guilt, and the thought that her family would be better off without her. Only on careful questioning does the drinking emerge. Her psychiatrist does something that surprises her: after arranging detoxification and making sure she is safe, she decides to wait before prescribing an antidepressant. By the third week without alcohol Sushila is sleeping through the night, her mood has lifted and the thoughts of death have gone. She did have a depressive syndrome, but it was produced by the alcohol. Sushila's story illustrates the most important rule about the psychiatric syndromes that heavy drinking produces. DSM-5-TR describes a family of alcohol-induced mental disorders (alcohol-induced depressive, bipolar, anxiety, psychotic, sleep, sexual and neurocognitive disorders, each listed in the chapter of the disorder it resembles), diagnosed when the symptoms are severe enough to need attention in their own right. They look exactly like the independent disorders, and they can have the same grave consequences, including suicide attempts. What separates them is time. An independent disorder is more likely if the symptoms began before the heavy drinking or continue for more than a month after severe intoxication or withdrawal has ended; alcohol-induced disorders, in contrast, are likely to improve without specific treatment within days to weeks of stopping. The numbers show why this matters. DSM-5-TR estimates that about 40 percent of people with alcohol use disorder have a major depressive episode at some point in their lives, but that only about a third to a half of these are independent depressions occurring outside the context of intoxication. In practice, therefore, clinicians usually wait for two to four weeks of abstinence before diagnosing an independent depressive or anxiety disorder and starting long-term treatment for it, unless the depression is severe, the person is at high risk of suicide, or there is a clear history of depression before the drinking began. Anxiety follows the same logic. The overactive nervous system of withdrawal produces tremor, a racing heart, restlessness and panic attacks, and a person who drinks every evening goes through a small withdrawal every morning. Drinking also relieves anxiety in the short term, so people with social anxiety or panic may use alcohol as self-medication (Section 10.2 and Chapter 6), and the two problems can feed each other. Alcohol disturbs sleep too: it helps a person fall asleep, but as the blood level falls in the second half of the night sleep becomes fragmented and dream (REM) sleep rebounds, and insomnia often persists for months after stopping (Chapter 8, Section 8.10). Sexual function suffers in the way the porter in Shakespeare's Macbeth described: drink "provokes the desire, but it takes away the performance". Alcoholic hallucinosis, the commonest alcohol-induced psychotic disorder, was described in Section 10.3.5. One alcohol-related syndrome is notorious for its danger to other people. Morbid jealousy (pathological jealousy) is a preoccupation with a partner's supposed infidelity that is held on inadequate evidence and drives the person's behaviour. In 1955 the British psychiatrists John Todd and Kenneth Dewhurst called it the Othello syndrome , after Shakespeare's Moor, who murders his innocent wife Desdemona on the strength of a planted handkerchief. When it arises in a heavy drinker it is often called alcoholic jealousy , and ICD-10 lists it among the psychotic disorders due to alcohol (F10.5). The belief may be a true delusion or an overvalued idea. A 48-year-old mill worker becomes convinced that his wife is meeting a neighbour while he is at work; he checks her phone, inspects her clothes and bedsheets for stains, times her trips to the market, questions the children, follows her, and demands a confession, which (when a frightened wife finally gives a false one to stop the interrogation) only confirms his belief. Several things in a drinker's life feed the idea: alcohol-induced impotence, a wife who has understandably withdrawn from a drunken husband, and the suspicion and irritability of withdrawal. The jealousy does not always disappear with abstinence. It carries a real risk of assault and of homicide, so assessment always includes direct questions about threats, weapons and the partner's safety, and separation is sometimes the safest advice. Delusional jealousy as a feature of delusional disorder is taught in Chapter 4, Section 4.5. Alcohol is also tightly linked with suicide. DSM-5-TR summarises the evidence: both intoxication and chronic heavy drinking are associated with suicide; in a meta-analysis, acute alcohol use was associated with a nearly sevenfold increase in the risk of a suicide attempt compared with not drinking; and an international study of emergency departments in 17 countries found that each drink raised the risk of an attempt by about 30 percent. Intoxication removes the restraint that holds a suicidal impulse back (alcohol myopia again), chronic drinking brings depression, debt, job loss and broken relationships, and the combination of alcohol with sedative tablets is especially lethal. Violence follows a similar pattern. DSM-5-TR calls intoxication an important contributor to interpersonal violence and notes that severe alcohol use disorder, especially with antisocial personality disorder, is associated with criminal acts including homicide. In India, surveys of domestic violence consistently find a husband's heavy drinking among the strongest correlates of violence against his wife. Suicide risk assessment is taught in Chapter 5. Clinical link When a heavy drinker presents with depression, treat the safety first and the diagnosis second. Assess suicide risk at once, because intoxicated and recently detoxified drinkers are at high risk. Then, unless the depression is severe or clearly predates the drinking, review the mood after two to four weeks of abstinence before committing the person to an antidepressant. Many depressions will have lifted; the ones that have not are probably independent and need treatment in their own right. Exam trap The Othello syndrome (Todd and Dewhurst, 1955) is morbid jealousy, a delusion or overvalued idea that the partner is unfaithful ; in drinkers it is called alcoholic jealousy. Do not confuse it with erotomania (de Clérambault's syndrome, the delusion that someone, usually of higher status, is in love with the patient) or with the Capgras delusion (a familiar person has been replaced by an impostor). For alcohol-induced depression, DSM-5-TR's dividing line is about one month after stopping; clinically, wait two to four weeks of abstinence before diagnosing independent depression. The damage done to the body Pinel's textbook puts it bluntly: alcohol attacks almost every tissue in the body. It does so in three ways. It is directly toxic, and so is acetaldehyde; it displaces food and blocks the absorption of vitamins, especially thiamine and folate; and it causes accidents, falls and fights. Table 10.17 lists the main harms system by system. DSM-5-TR adds a sense of proportion: gastritis and ulcers are common, about 15 percent of people who drink heavily develop cirrhosis of the liver, pancreatitis or both, and mild high blood pressure is one of the most commonly associated conditions. Cirrhosis brings portal hypertension (oesophageal varices that can bleed, ascites) and hepatic encephalopathy (Section 10.8). Pinel calls cirrhosis the major cause of death among heavy drinkers Gut and pancreas Gastritis, ulcers, acute and chronic pancreatitis, malabsorption Chronic pancreatitis can cause diabetes; poor absorption deepens thiamine and folate deficiency Heart and circulation High blood pressure, cardiomyopathy, irregular heart rhythm, stroke Raised triglycerides and LDL cholesterol add to heart disease risk (DSM-5-TR) Nervous system Peripheral neuropathy; cerebellar degeneration; brain shrinkage and cognitive decline; Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome Neuropathy gives numb, burning feet and weakness; cerebellar damage gives a broad-based, unsteady gait. Rarer: Marchiafava-Bignami disease and central pontine myelinolysis Cancer Mouth, throat, oesophagus, stomach, liver, bowel, breast Pinel notes raised risk even at one or two drinks a day Blood and immunity Large red cells (raised MCV), anaemia, low platelets, lowered immunity Heavy drinkers are prone to pneumonia and tuberculosis Hormones and metabolism Low blood sugar; low testosterone, shrunken testes, erectile dysfunction; menstrual irregularity Alcohol blocks the liver's production of glucose, so a fasting drinker can become hypoglycaemic Pregnancy Miscarriage; fetal alcohol spectrum disorder No safe amount or time in pregnancy has been established (Chapter 3, Section 3.3.5) Two rare brain disorders appear in the table because examiners like them. Marchiafava-Bignami disease is a destruction of the myelin and nerve fibres of the corpus callosum, the great bridge between the two hemispheres. The Italian pathologists Ettore Marchiafava and Amico Bignami described it in 1903 in a drinker of Chianti red wine; it causes confusion, dementia and signs that the hemispheres have been disconnected, such as apraxia of one hand. Central pontine myelinolysis , described by Raymond Adams, Maurice Victor and Elliott Mancall in 1959 in alcoholic and malnourished patients, is a loss of myelin in the pons of the brain stem, causing paralysis of the limbs, difficulty swallowing and speaking, and sometimes a locked-in state; it is now known to follow correcting a low blood sodium too quickly, a common problem in drinkers. The most important alcohol-related brain disorder of all, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, belongs to Section 10.11, and the general shrinkage of the brain and alcohol-related dementia are also discussed there. Is a little alcohol good for you? For decades studies seemed to show a J-shaped curve: moderate drinkers had fewer heart attacks than abstainers, and some studies even suggested that moderate drinking protected the ageing brain. The finding has weakened under scrutiny. Many "abstainers" in such studies are former drinkers who stopped because they were already ill, which makes non-drinking look harmful; when studies correct for this, the protective effect largely disappears. Meanwhile the cancer risk starts at low levels of drinking, as Pinel notes. In 2023 the WHO's European office went so far as to state that no level of alcohol consumption is safe for health. For a clinician, the practical message is simpler: there is no medical reason to advise a non-drinker to start. Exam trap Match the alcohol-related brain disorders to their sites and causes. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome : thiamine deficiency; mammillary bodies and thalamus (Section 10.11). Marchiafava-Bignami disease : the corpus callosum (Italian red-wine drinkers, 1903). Central pontine myelinolysis : the pons , after over-rapid correction of low sodium. Cerebellar degeneration : the cerebellum (unsteady, broad-based gait). Hepatic encephalopathy : a delirium caused by liver failure, with a flapping tremor (asterixis). Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is taught in Chapter 3, not here. Spotting problem drinking: questions and blood tests Most people with alcohol problems are never asked about them, and those who are asked often minimise. Two kinds of tool help: short questionnaires and laboratory markers. Both belong in detail to the Assessment book; what follows is what a clinician needs to know to use and interpret them. The shortest questionnaire is the CAGE questionnaire , published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in 1984 by the psychiatrist John A. Ewing as "Detecting alcoholism: the CAGE questionnaire". Its name is a mnemonic for four questions: C ut down: Have you ever felt you should cut down on your drinking? A nnoyed: Have people annoyed you by criticising your drinking? G uilty: Have you ever felt bad or guilty about your drinking? E ye-opener: Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or get rid of a hangover? Two or more "yes" answers are usually taken as clinically significant. The CAGE asks about the whole of life rather than recent drinking and is good at picking up dependence, but it misses people whose drinking is risky without yet being dependent. For that the WHO developed the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT), first issued in 1989 and described in its development paper by John Saunders and colleagues in 1993. It has ten items: three about how much and how often the person drinks, three about signs of dependence, and four about harm. Scores range from 0 to 40, and a score of 8 or more usually indicates hazardous or harmful drinking. Its first three items alone form the AUDIT-C, a quick screen used in busy clinics. Blood tests add objective evidence, though DSM-5-TR stresses that they do not establish a diagnosis. The direct measure is the blood (or breath) alcohol concentration, which also reveals tolerance: a person who is talking normally at a BAC of 150 is a heavy drinker. Gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT), a liver enzyme, is a sensitive marker: DSM-5-TR notes that a modest elevation (above about 35 units) may be the only abnormal finding, and that at least 70 percent of people with a high GGT are persistent heavy drinkers. Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT), a form of an iron-carrying blood protein that rises with regular heavy drinking (levels of 20 units or more), is at least as sensitive and specific, and the two together are better than either alone. Because both fall towards normal within days to weeks of stopping, a rise during follow-up is a sign that drinking has resumed. The mean corpuscular volume (MCV), the average size of the red blood cells, rises because alcohol is toxic to the bone marrow; it helps to identify heavy drinkers but is a poor way to monitor abstinence, because red cells live for about four months and the MCV changes slowly. Newer tests detect breakdown products of alcohol itself, such as ethyl glucuronide in urine and phosphatidylethanol in blood, and can show recent drinking even after the alcohol has gone. Questionnaires, blood tests and a relative's account together give the most accurate picture. Exam trap CAGE stands for Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener (Ewing, 1984); the E is not "evening" or "excess". A score of 2 or more is significant. The AUDIT is the WHO's ten-item test (score 8 or more suggests hazardous drinking). Among blood markers, GGT and CDT return to normal within days to weeks and are good for monitoring; MCV changes slowly and is poor for monitoring. None of these tests makes the diagnosis on its own. Alcohol in India The national survey Magnitude of Substance Use in India, conducted in 2018 by the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC) of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences for the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment and released in 2019 (its design is described in Section 10.1), found that alcohol is the substance Indians use most. About 14.6 percent of people aged 10 to 75, roughly 16 crore people, were current users of alcohol, and use was 17 times commoner among men than women. About 5.2 percent of Indians, more than 5.7 crore people, were estimated to be affected by harmful or dependent drinking; in the report's words, every third alcohol user in India needs help for alcohol-related problems. The states with the highest prevalence of alcohol use were Chhattisgarh, Tripura, Punjab, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa, and those in which more than 10 percent of people had alcohol use disorders were Tripura, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, Chhattisgarh and Arunachal Pradesh. What do Indians drink? The same survey found that country liquor ("desi" liquor, a cheap distilled spirit made under government licence, of varying strength) and Indian-made foreign liquor (IMFL: whisky, rum, brandy and gin manufactured in India) were each the main drink of about 30 percent of drinkers. Beer and wine make up much of the rest, alongside a large world of traditional and local drinks: toddy (fermented palm sap) in the south and east, arrack (a distilled spirit), mahua liquor made from the flowers of the mahua tree in the tribal belt of central India, rice beers such as handia, and feni in Goa. Outside the licensed trade is illicitly distilled liquor, known as hooch , and it is responsible for the periodic tragedies in which dozens of people die after a single batch. The killer is usually methanol , industrial alcohol added to raise the strength or distilled by mistake. Methanol is metabolised by the same enzyme as ethanol, alcohol dehydrogenase, but its products are formaldehyde and formic acid, which cause severe acidosis of the blood and destroy the optic nerve; survivors may be left blind. The pharmacology of Section 10.3.1 explains the antidote. Alcohol dehydrogenase prefers ethanol to methanol, so giving ethanol (or fomepizole, a drug that blocks the enzyme) slows the conversion of methanol into its poisons while dialysis removes it. In June 2024 more than 60 people died in Kallakurichi district of Tamil Nadu after drinking methanol-laced illicit liquor; similar disasters have struck many states, including states where alcohol is banned. That last point brings in prohibition. Article 47 of the Constitution of India directs the State to endeavour to bring about the prohibition of intoxicating drinks except for medicinal purposes, and several states have tried. Gujarat has had prohibition since it was formed in 1960, Nagaland since 1989, and Bihar since April 2016; Mizoram's current prohibition law dates from 2019, and the Union Territory of Lakshadweep is also dry. Supporters point to reduced domestic violence and spending on drink; critics point to bootlegging, hooch deaths, the criminalisation of poor drinkers and the loss of revenue. For the clinician, the lesson of prohibition states is that a ban changes where and what people drink more reliably than whether they drink, and that the people who need treatment are still there. Indian context The figures above matter in interviews. Alcohol is the commonest substance used in India (about 14.6 percent of 10 to 75 year olds), every third user needs help, and men use it far more than women. Two practical consequences follow. First, an Indian clinical psychologist in almost any setting, a general hospital, a school, a family court, an industrial clinic, will meet alcohol problems every week, often presented as something else (marital conflict, depression, a child's school failure, domestic violence). Secondly, the treatment gap is enormous, as Section 10.4.8 shows. 10.4 Treating Alcohol Use Disorder: Detoxification, Drugs and Staying Sober Lower yield · 1 Q Treating a person with alcohol use disorder involves two quite different jobs, and confusing them is the commonest mistake in the field. The first is to get the person safely off alcohol: to manage a withdrawal that, as Section 10.3.5 showed, can produce seizures and a delirium that kills. That job takes about a week and is mainly medical. The second is to keep the person off alcohol, or at least out of harm, for the months and years afterwards, when craving, old habits, friends, stress and the shop on the way home all pull him back. That job is longer, harder and mainly psychological and social, although several drugs help with it. This section begins with what happens to people with alcohol use disorder over the course of their lives, with and without treatment, then follows the treatment ladder from a brief conversation in a clinic to detoxification in hospital, the drugs that help people stay stopped, the psychological treatments (which Book 2 teaches in full), the debate about whether the goal must be total abstinence, and finally the services that exist in India. The course of alcohol use disorder: who gets better? The popular picture of alcoholism is a steady slide: social drinking, heavier drinking, loss of control, and ruin, unless the drinker hits "rock bottom" and is saved. Section 10.2 describes how E. M. Jellinek's stages gave scientific form to this picture. The best evidence on what actually happens comes from studies that followed large groups of people for decades, and the most famous of them was conducted by the American psychiatrist George E. Vaillant (born 1934). Key study: Vaillant's natural history of alcoholism (1983) Vaillant drew on two groups of men followed since the 1940s: 268 Harvard undergraduates (the college sample) and 456 socially disadvantaged but non-delinquent boys from inner-city Boston, originally recruited as the comparison group of a study of delinquency (the core city sample). Because the men were studied prospectively, by repeated interviews, questionnaires and medical examinations, from adolescence onwards, Vaillant could see what drinkers were like before their drinking became a problem, something no study of patients in treatment can do. He published the first full analysis in The Natural History of Alcoholism (1983) and later follow-ups to age 70 and 80. At some point in their lives 20 percent of the college men and 31 percent of the core city men met criteria for alcohol abuse. Much of the anxiety, depression and instability seen in alcoholic men, Vaillant argued, was more often the result of years of drinking than its cause. By the age of 70, of the alcohol-dependent core city men who could be followed, 54 percent had died, 32 percent were abstinent, 1 percent were drinking in a controlled way and only 12 percent were still abusing alcohol. Alcohol abuse could persist for decades without either remitting or progressing to dependence; previous dependence and attendance at Alcoholics Anonymous were the two best predictors of sustained abstinence; once abstinence had lasted five years relapse was rare; and the men who managed a lasting return to controlled drinking were those who had had few symptoms of abuse. The criticism is that the samples were all men, all American and all born in the 1920s and early 1930s, so the findings may not apply to women or to other cultures and generations. Vaillant's results fit what DSM-5-TR says about the course of the disorder. It is variable, with periods of remission and relapse. A decision to stop, often in response to a crisis, is typically followed by weeks or more of abstinence, then by limited periods of controlled drinking; but once drinking resumes it is highly likely to escalate rapidly back to the old level. DSM-5-TR also corrects the gloomy stereotype. The disorder is often wrongly seen as intractable because the people clinicians meet in treatment have usually had many years of severe problems, but these most severe cases are only a minority, and the typical person with alcohol use disorder has a much more promising prognosis. Many people recover with no formal treatment at all, a process called natural recovery (or spontaneous remission); Barlow and Durand estimate that about 20 percent of people with severe alcohol dependence stop drinking on their own and do not develop problems again. Life events often trigger it: a health scare, a new relationship, a religious commitment, a new job, a child. Two lessons follow for treatment. First, the course is not fixed, so treatment is worth attempting at every stage, and the people who come to treatment are not a hopeless group. Secondly, relapse is part of the natural history, not proof of failure; a treatment plan should expect it and prepare for it, which is what relapse prevention does (Section 10.4.6). The treatment ladder and brief intervention Not every person whose drinking is a problem needs a de-addiction ward. Most clinicians now think of treatment as a ladder, matched to severity and stepped up if the lower rungs fail (an approach called stepped care). At the bottom are the large numbers of people whose drinking is hazardous (risky) or harmful without being severely dependent. For them the evidence supports a brief intervention : one to a few short conversations, often of 5 to 30 minutes, delivered by a general practitioner, nurse or counsellor in primary care, in an emergency department after an injury, or in a workplace clinic. Many brief interventions follow an outline that William R. Miller and his colleagues summarised with the acronym FRAMES : F eedback about the person's own risk (for example, his AUDIT score or his GGT result), emphasis on personal R esponsibility for change, clear A dvice to cut down or stop, a M enu of options for how to do it, an E mpathic style, and support for S elf-efficacy, the person's belief that he can succeed. Reviews of many trials show that brief interventions produce modest but real reductions in drinking among non-dependent drinkers, which, multiplied over a population, prevent a great deal of harm. They are not enough for severe dependence. Brief interventions borrow heavily from motivational interviewing and from the stages of change of the transtheoretical model, both of which are taught in Book 2, Section 6.9 (the stages in Section 6.9.6). Higher up the ladder are outpatient treatment for dependence (medication and psychological treatment while the person lives at home), detoxification (at home, as an outpatient, or in hospital), and residential rehabilitation followed by aftercare. How intensive should treatment be? Barlow and Durand summarise the evidence that outcomes after intensive residential programmes are often no better than after good outpatient care, which can cost a small fraction as much. Inpatient care is therefore kept for people who need it for safety: those with a history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, severe current withdrawal, serious physical or psychiatric illness (including suicidal risk and psychosis), dependence on sedatives as well as alcohol, pregnancy, very heavy daily drinking that starts in the morning, no one at home who can supervise, or previous failed attempts at outpatient detoxification. The sequence of psychological care that follows detoxification, from engagement through active treatment to aftercare, is described in Book 2, Section 9.9.5. Detoxification: getting safely through withdrawal Ravinder, 45, runs a hardware shop in Kanpur. For eight years he has drunk two quarters of whisky (360 ml, about twelve standard drinks) every day, and for the last two years his hands have shaken in the mornings until he has his first drink. Two years ago, during a pilgrimage on which he could not drink, he had a fit. He comes to the de-addiction clinic because his wife has threatened to leave after he fell asleep at the shop counter in front of customers. Because of his previous seizure, the team admits him. His last drink is at nine at night; by eight the next morning he is tremulous, sweating, anxious and nauseated, with a pulse of 108. How should he be detoxified? Detoxification (detox) is the medically supervised management of withdrawal. Its principle follows directly from the pharmacology of Sections 10.3.2 and 10.3.4. Ravinder's brain has adapted to a daily dose of a drug that enhances GABA-A inhibition. Stopping suddenly removes that support and leaves an overexcited brain. The answer is to replace alcohol with another drug that acts on the same GABA-A receptor, and then to withdraw that drug gradually over about a week, letting the brain readjust in small steps. The replacement works because of cross-tolerance and cross-dependence (Section 10.1): a benzodiazepine can suppress alcohol withdrawal because the two act on the same receptor complex. DSM-5-TR notes that the symptoms of alcohol withdrawal can be relieved by giving alcohol or benzodiazepines; alcohol itself is never used, because it is the problem and is toxic, but the benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice. A meta-analysis carried out by Michael F. Mayo-Smith for the American Society of Addiction Medicine in 1997 confirmed it: benzodiazepines reduce the severity of withdrawal and significantly reduce both delirium (by about 5 cases per 100 patients) and seizures (by about 8 per 100). Other drugs (beta-blockers, clonidine, carbamazepine) eased withdrawal symptoms, but the evidence was inadequate to show that they prevented delirium or seizures, and antipsychotics of the phenothiazine type were less effective than benzodiazepines at preventing both. Which benzodiazepine? The usual choices are the long-acting ones, chlordiazepoxide (the first benzodiazepine, synthesised by Leo Sternbach at the Hoffmann-La Roche company and marketed in 1960) and diazepam. Both are broken down into active products that themselves last for days, so the blood level falls smoothly as the dose is reduced, the drug in effect tapers itself, and protection against seizures is good. Their disadvantage is the same property: in a person whose liver is failing, or in an elderly patient, they can accumulate and cause oversedation. For such patients clinicians use lorazepam or oxazepam, which are cleared by a simple chemical step (glucuronidation) that a damaged liver can still manage, and have no long-lived active products. Table 10.18 compares them. Table 10.18 Benzodiazepines used in alcohol detoxification. Drug Duration of action Long-lived active products Typical use in detoxification Chlordiazepoxide Long Yes Standard oral choice for uncomplicated withdrawal; smooth taper Diazepam Long, fast onset Yes Oral or intravenous; loading doses; seizures and delirium tremens Lorazepam Intermediate No Liver disease, elderly patients; can be given by injection (also for seizures) Oxazepam Short No Liver disease, elderly patients; by mouth only How much, and on what schedule? There are three approaches. In a fixed-schedule regimen , the patient receives a set dose at set times (four times a day, for example) on day one, reduced step by step over five to ten days, with extra doses if symptoms break through. In a symptom-triggered regimen , nurses rate the withdrawal at regular intervals with the CIWA-Ar (Section 10.3.5), and a dose is given only when the score rises above a set threshold. In front-loading , large doses of a long-acting drug such as diazepam are given every hour or two until the patient is calm, after which the drug's long half-life carries him through. The symptom-triggered approach was tested in a classic trial. Key study: Saitz and symptom-triggered detoxification (1994) Richard Saitz and his colleagues, working in the detoxification unit of a Veterans Affairs medical centre in the United States, randomly assigned 101 patients admitted for alcohol withdrawal, in a double-blind trial, either to a standard fixed course of chlordiazepoxide four times daily (with extra doses as needed) or to chlordiazepoxide given only when a validated severity scale showed signs and symptoms of withdrawal. The median duration of treatment was 9 hours in the symptom-triggered group against 68 hours in the fixed-schedule group, and the total dose of chlordiazepoxide was 100 mg against 425 mg. There were no significant differences in the severity of withdrawal or in the number of seizures or cases of delirium tremens. The conclusion, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association , was that symptom-triggered therapy individualises treatment and gives less drug for a shorter time with equal safety. The limitation is in the patients: those with a history of seizures were excluded, and the method needs trained staff who check the patient regularly and patients who can describe their symptoms. Symptom-triggered treatment is therefore preferred where nurses can monitor closely. A fixed schedule is safer where monitoring is thin, for patients who cannot report their symptoms reliably, and for those, like Ravinder, with a history of seizures or delirium, in whom one does not wait for symptoms to appear. Ravinder receives a fixed reducing course of chlordiazepoxide over a week, with extra doses allowed. His symptoms peak on the second day, as Figure 10.9 predicts, he has no fit, and by the fifth day he is eating and sleeping. Benzodiazepines are not the whole of detoxification. Heavy drinkers are frequently short of thiamine (vitamin B1), and a brain short of thiamine can develop Wernicke's encephalopathy, the acute confusion, unsteadiness and eye-movement paralysis described in Section 10.11. Every patient in detoxification therefore receives thiamine, by injection when the risk is high (malnutrition, vomiting, any sign of Wernicke's encephalopathy), and, a rule every examiner knows, thiamine is given before glucose : the metabolism of glucose uses up thiamine, so a glucose drip given to a thiamine-depleted drinker can precipitate the encephalopathy. Fluids, a nourishing diet, other vitamins, and correction of low potassium, magnesium and sodium (slowly, because of central pontine myelinolysis, Section 10.3.7) complete the medical care, along with a calm, well-lit room, reassurance, and checks of pulse, blood pressure and temperature. Seizures and delirium tremens need specific treatment. A withdrawal seizure is treated with a benzodiazepine. In a trial in Boston emergency departments published in 1999, Gail D'Onofrio and her colleagues gave patients who had just had an alcohol-related seizure either 2 mg of lorazepam intravenously or salt water; 3 percent of the lorazepam group had a second seizure in the next six hours, against 24 percent of the placebo group. The anti-epileptic drug phenytoin, by contrast, does not prevent withdrawal seizures: in a 1989 placebo-controlled trial by Brian K. Alldredge and colleagues, 6 of 45 patients had a further seizure on phenytoin and 6 of 45 on placebo. The reason is that withdrawal seizures arise from a brain-wide state of overexcitement, not from an epileptic focus. Delirium tremens is a medical emergency, usually managed in an intensive care unit. The core is high doses of benzodiazepines (often intravenous diazepam or lorazepam) given until the patient is lightly sedated, with intravenous fluids, correction of electrolytes, thiamine, cooling of fever, and a search for the medical conditions that so often accompany it (infection, bleeding, head injury, low blood sugar). An antipsychotic such as haloperidol may be added for severe agitation or hallucinations, but only alongside adequate benzodiazepine, because antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and are less effective than benzodiazepines on their own. In the rare cases that do not respond, intensive care units use phenobarbital or anaesthetic drugs. Not everyone needs a hospital bed. People with mild to moderate withdrawal, no history of seizures or delirium, no serious illness and a responsible relative at home can be detoxified as outpatients or at home, with daily review and small supplies of medication (a benzodiazepine taken with alcohol is dangerous, so drinking must stop). Whatever the setting, the most important fact about detoxification is what it does not do. It makes stopping safe and bearable, but on its own it does almost nothing to prevent relapse. Book 2, Section 9.9.5 puts it bluntly: detoxification is the doorway to treatment, not treatment itself. When Ravinder is ready for discharge, the real question is how he will stay sober. Exam trap Alcohol detoxification uses long-acting benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) because of cross-tolerance at the GABA-A receptor; in liver disease or old age use lorazepam or oxazepam . Give thiamine before glucose . Symptom-triggered dosing with the CIWA-Ar gives less drug for a shorter time with equal safety (Saitz, 1994). Withdrawal seizures respond to benzodiazepines, not to phenytoin . Antipsychotics are only an add-on in delirium tremens, never the main treatment. And detoxification is not treatment: it does not prevent relapse. Disulfiram: the deterrent On the day of discharge Ravinder's wife asks the question families in every de-addiction clinic ask: is there a tablet that will make him hate alcohol? There is something close to it, and its discovery was an accident. In 1937 a physician working in the American rubber industry reported that workers exposed to certain sulphur compounds used in making rubber became ill when they drank alcohol. A decade later, in Copenhagen, the pharmacologists Jens Hald and Erik Jacobsen of the drug company Medicinalco were testing one of those compounds, tetraethylthiuram disulphide, as a possible treatment for intestinal worms, and, as pharmacologists then often did, they took it themselves. Both found that after taking it they had become strikingly sensitive to alcohol: an ordinary drink made them unwell. Working with the psychiatrist Oluf Martensen-Larsen, they tried the drug on patients with alcoholism, and in December 1948 they reported their findings in The Lancet under the title "A drug sensitizing the organism to ethyl alcohol". The drug, disulfiram , was sold as Antabuse ("anti-abuse"), and the United States Food and Drug Administration approved it in 1951. It was the first medicine for alcohol dependence, and for decades it was the only one. Disulfiram works on the second step of the pathway in Figure 10.7. Its breakdown products block aldehyde dehydrogenase irreversibly, so when a person taking it drinks, alcohol is converted to acetaldehyde as usual, but the acetaldehyde cannot be cleared and accumulates in the blood. Within minutes the disulfiram-ethanol reaction begins: the face and neck flush red and hot, the head throbs, the heart pounds and races, the person feels sick and vomits, sweats, becomes breathless and thirsty, and the blood pressure falls, with dizziness and sometimes fainting. The reaction usually lasts from half an hour to several hours, and its severity rises with the amount drunk. Severe reactions can include chest pain, irregular heart rhythm, heart failure, collapse, convulsions and, rarely, death. Because the enzyme is blocked irreversibly, the body must make new enzyme before alcohol is safe again, so a reaction can occur for up to about two weeks after the last tablet. For the same reason the first dose must not be taken until the person has been free of alcohol for at least 12 hours (many clinicians wait 24). The usual dose is a single tablet of about 250 mg each morning. How does a drug that does nothing to craving help people stay sober? Not, for most patients, by making them ill: most people taking disulfiram as prescribed never experience the reaction, because they do not drink. Disulfiram is a deterrent, and it works through the person's knowledge and fear of what would happen. Clinicians often describe its effect as changing the decision. Without it, a person recovering from dependence must decide not to drink many times every day, at every craving, every invitation, every passing liquor shop. With it, he has to make only one decision, once a day, in the morning when his resolve is strongest: will I take my tablet? Once it is taken, drinking is off the menu for the day. This also explains its great weakness. Barlow and Durand note that non-compliance is a major concern: a person who stops the tablets for a few days can drink again, and many who mean to drink simply stop taking it. Disulfiram therefore works best when someone else watches it being swallowed: a spouse, a parent, a pharmacist or a nurse, often under an explicit agreement made in therapy (behavioural couples therapy, Section 10.4.6, frequently builds a daily supervised dose into the contract). Supervision is the single most important determinant of whether disulfiram works. Key study: Does disulfiram work? Fuller (1986) and the De Sousa trials (2004 and 2005) In the largest blinded trial, Richard K. Fuller and colleagues in the United States Veterans Administration randomly assigned 605 men to 250 mg of disulfiram, to 1 mg (a dose too small to block the enzyme, but which still carried the threat of a reaction), or to no disulfiram; all received counselling. After a year there were no differences in total abstinence or time to first drink. Men on 250 mg who did drink reported fewer drinking days, and in every group the men who took their tablets faithfully were more likely to stay abstinent. The puzzle is in the design: in a blinded trial every patient fears the reaction, so the deterrent is spread across all groups. A 2014 meta-analysis of 22 trials by M. D. Skinner and colleagues found exactly this pattern: blinded trials showed no benefit, but open-label trials, in which patients know what they are taking, showed disulfiram superior to control conditions and to naltrexone and acamprosate. Two open trials from Mumbai by Avinash De Sousa and A. De Sousa, in alcohol-dependent men whose family members agreed to accompany them to follow-up, illustrate it. Against naltrexone over a year (2004), 86 percent of the men on disulfiram stayed abstinent against 44 percent on naltrexone, and relapse came later (at a mean of 119 days against 63). Against acamprosate over eight months (2005), the figures were 88 against 46 percent. In both trials, however, craving was lower on the comparison drug. The criticism of open trials is obvious: patients and doctors knew the treatment, and the men were a selected, well-supported group. Disulfiram has side effects of its own even without alcohol: drowsiness and fatigue, a metallic or garlic-like taste and bad breath, headache and skin rash. More serious but rare are inflammation of the liver (so liver tests are checked before and during treatment), damage to peripheral and optic nerves, and psychiatric effects. Disulfiram also blocks dopamine beta-hydroxylase, the enzyme that turns dopamine into noradrenaline, so dopamine levels rise; this can precipitate psychosis or worsen depression in vulnerable people, and it is why the drug has also been tried for cocaine dependence. It interacts with some other medicines, such as warfarin and phenytoin. It should not be given to people with coronary heart disease, heart failure or cardiomyopathy, uncontrolled high blood pressure or a past stroke (all of whom might not survive a severe reaction), psychosis, severe liver disease or pregnancy, to people at high risk of suicide or with marked impulsivity (who may drink deliberately), to those with cognitive impairment who cannot understand the risk, and to anyone who has not given fully informed consent. Patients must also be warned about hidden alcohol, because even small amounts can produce a reaction: cough syrups and "tonics", many Ayurvedic asavas and arishtas (which contain alcohol produced by fermentation during their preparation), some mouthwashes, aftershave and perfumes on the skin, vinegar, some sauces, and desserts made with liqueurs. Ravinder agrees to take disulfiram each morning in front of his wife, who has been taught what the reaction looks like; the team gives him a card to carry stating that he takes the drug, in case he is ever brought to a hospital unconscious. Clinical link Families in India sometimes ask for disulfiram tablets that they can crush into the patient's food without telling him. The answer must be no. A person who does not know he has taken disulfiram may drink heavily and suffer a severe, even fatal, reaction without anyone understanding why; and secret medication violates the patient's right to informed consent, which the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 makes explicit for people with mental illness, a term that, under Section 2(1)(s) of the Act, includes mental conditions associated with the abuse of alcohol and drugs. A family's desperation is real and deserves a response, but the response is to bring the family into treatment openly, not to drug the patient behind his back. Exam trap Disulfiram works because it inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde accumulates and drinking produces aversive symptoms (flushing, throbbing headache, nausea and vomiting, palpitations, a fall in blood pressure). It is a deterrent. Each wrong option in the usual question belongs to another treatment. "Reduces dopaminergic reward signalling in the nucleus accumbens" describes naltrexone , which blocks the opioid-driven release of dopamine. "Blocks NMDA receptors to reduce craving" is closest to acamprosate , which dampens glutamate (NMDA) overactivity. "Acts as a partial agonist at GABA-A receptors" describes none of the standard alcohol drugs: the drugs that act on the GABA-A receptor are the benzodiazepines used in detoxification (and alcohol itself), and they are positive allosteric modulators that strengthen GABA's own action, not partial agonists; baclofen is an agonist at a different GABA receptor, GABA-B. Disulfiram does not reduce craving, does not block opioid receptors and is not a GABA agonist. Naltrexone, acamprosate and the newer drugs Disulfiram makes drinking unpleasant. The drugs developed since the 1990s try to do something subtler: to make drinking less rewarding, or to quieten the craving that drives relapse. The first was an old drug put to a new use. Naltrexone is an opioid receptor antagonist, a drug that occupies the opioid receptors (mainly the mu receptor) and blocks them, originally developed to treat heroin dependence. Recall from Section 10.3.2 that part of alcohol's pleasure comes from the brain's own opioids: alcohol releases endorphins, which act on mu receptors and release dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. Researchers reasoned that blocking those receptors should blunt the reward of drinking. In 1992 two research groups, one in Philadelphia led by Joseph R. Volpicelli and one at Yale led by Stephanie S. O'Malley , published placebo-controlled trials in the same issue of the Archives of General Psychiatry showing that alcohol-dependent patients given naltrexone relapsed to heavy drinking less often than those given placebo. On the strength of these results the Food and Drug Administration approved naltrexone for alcohol dependence in 1994, and a once-a-month injectable form followed in 2006. What naltrexone does is easiest to see in a person who slips. A patient on naltrexone who takes a drink finds it less rewarding and feels less of the familiar pull to have another and another; a lapse is therefore less likely to turn into a full relapse. Naltrexone is consequently better at reducing heavy drinking than at producing total abstinence, and it can suit people whose goal is to cut down as well as those who want to stop. It is usually taken as a 50 mg tablet once a day. Its common side effects are nausea, headache, dizziness and tiredness. Its critical caution follows from its mechanism: because it blocks opioid receptors, it throws anyone who is physically dependent on opioids (heroin, morphine, tramadol, codeine cough syrups) into immediate withdrawal and blocks the pain relief of opioid analgesics, so patients must be opioid-free before starting and should carry a card saying they take it. Its use in opioid dependence itself is described in Section 10.5. It is avoided in acute hepatitis and liver failure, and liver tests are monitored. Acamprosate (calcium acetylhomotaurinate) works on the other side of the balance. A chemical relative of GABA and of the amino acid taurine, it is thought to dampen the excess glutamate activity at NMDA receptors that persists for months after detoxification, the neurochemical basis of the protracted withdrawal of Section 10.3.5, with its restlessness, poor sleep and anxiety that drive "relief" craving. Barlow and Durand note that the brain mechanisms of its effects are still not well understood. Acamprosate does not interact with alcohol and does not make drinking unpleasant; it is used to help people who have already stopped to stay stopped. It was first approved in France in 1989 and in the United States in 2004. It is taken as two 333 mg tablets three times a day by adults over about 60 kg, and its common side effect is diarrhoea. It has a pharmacological virtue that matters a great deal in heavy drinkers: it is not broken down by the liver but excreted unchanged by the kidneys. It can therefore be used in liver disease, but it must be avoided in severe kidney disease. In European trials it modestly increased the number of people who stayed abstinent; in the largest American trial, it did not. Key study: the COMBINE trial (2006) Which works better, naltrexone, acamprosate or a psychological treatment, and do they add up? The COMBINE study, led by Raymond F. Anton and funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, randomised 1,383 recently abstinent alcohol-dependent volunteers at 11 American centres between 2001 and 2004. For 16 weeks, eight groups received medical management (regular brief meetings with a health professional) with naltrexone, acamprosate, both, or placebos, with or without a combined behavioural intervention delivered by specialist therapists; a ninth group received the behavioural intervention with no pills at all. Drinking fell substantially in every group. Patients given naltrexone, the behavioural intervention, or both did better than those given placebo and medical management alone (for example, about 80 against 75 percent of days abstinent), and naltrexone reduced the risk of a heavy drinking day. Acamprosate showed no effect, alone or in any combination, and no combination beat naltrexone or the behavioural intervention alone. Strikingly, the group with the behavioural intervention but no pills did worse than the groups given placebo pills and medical management: simply taking a pill and seeing a professional regularly had a therapeutic effect. The conclusion, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association , was that naltrexone with medical management could be delivered in ordinary health-care settings. The criticisms are that the participants were motivated volunteers who were already abstinent, and that the acamprosate result contradicts many European trials, perhaps because the European patients were more severely dependent and had been abstinent longer. Several other drugs have entered practice more recently, and examiners now ask about them: Nalmefene is an opioid antagonist related to naltrexone. In 2013 the European Medicines Agency approved it for reducing alcohol consumption in dependent people who drink at high-risk levels but do not need immediate detoxification. It is taken "as needed", on days when the person expects to drink, one to two hours beforehand, so it fits a goal of cutting down rather than stopping. It is not approved for alcohol use disorder in the United States. Baclofen , a muscle relaxant used for spasticity, stimulates the GABA-B receptor (a different GABA receptor from the GABA-A target of alcohol and benzodiazepines). Its use for alcohol dependence was popularised by the French cardiologist Olivier Ameisen, who in 2005 described the suppression of his own alcohol dependence with high doses and in 2008 wrote a best-selling book about it, Le Dernier Verre ("The Last Glass"). After a wave of off-label prescribing, France allowed its use under a temporary recommendation in 2014 and in October 2018 became the first country to grant it a marketing authorisation for alcohol dependence, at doses up to 80 mg a day. Trial results are mixed; its risks include sedation, dangerous overdose, especially with alcohol, and withdrawal seizures if it is stopped suddenly. Because it is cleared mainly by the kidneys, it has been studied in patients with liver disease. Topiramate , an anticonvulsant that enhances GABA-A activity and blocks some glutamate receptors, reduced heavy drinking in a trial published in The Lancet in 2003 by Bankole A. Johnson and colleagues. It is used off-label (not formally licensed for this purpose); its side effects include tingling, slowed thinking and word-finding difficulty, weight loss and kidney stones. Gabapentin, another anticonvulsant, is also used off-label. Ondansetron , the anti-vomiting drug that blocks the 5-HT 3 serotonin receptor, reduced drinking in a trial by Johnson and colleagues in 2000, but only in people whose alcoholism had begun early in life, a finding that connects with the early-onset type of alcoholism described in Section 10.2. It remains experimental. Table 10.19 brings the relapse-prevention drugs together. Notice that choosing among them is mostly a matter of matching the drug's mechanism and route of elimination to the patient: whether the goal is abstinence or reduction, whether someone can supervise, whether the liver or the kidneys are damaged, and whether the person also uses opioids. Naltrexone : opioid antagonist (reduces the reward and craving; FDA 1994); never in someone using opioids. Acamprosate : glutamate and NMDA modulation (maintains abstinence); excreted by the kidneys, so usable in liver disease. Nalmefene : as-needed opioid antagonist for cutting down. Baclofen : GABA- B agonist. Benzodiazepines are for detoxification, not for long-term relapse prevention (they are themselves addictive and dangerous with alcohol). In the COMBINE trial naltrexone helped and acamprosate did not. The psychological treatments and mutual help Every drug in Table 10.19 works better with psychological treatment than without it. Barlow and Durand conclude that no biological treatment alone succeeds for most people, and the COMBINE trial found that even a placebo pill helped when it came with regular meetings with a professional. The psychological treatments for alcohol problems share four aims: to build and keep the motivation to change, to teach the skills of not drinking, to rearrange the person's life so that sobriety pays better than drinking, and to mobilise the support of family and peers. How each treatment is actually delivered is taught in Book 2; this subsection says what each one is and what the evidence shows for alcohol, and Table 10.20 summarises them. Motivational interviewing and motivational enhancement therapy. Ambivalence is the rule in alcohol problems: the drinker both wants to stop and wants to drink. Motivational interviewing, developed by William R. Miller in work with problem drinkers in the early 1980s and later with Stephen Rollnick, is a collaborative style of conversation that draws out the person's own reasons for change instead of confronting him. Motivational enhancement therapy (MET) is its structured, four-session form, built around personalised feedback from an assessment; in Project MATCH it did as well as twelve sessions of other treatments. Both are taught in Book 2, Section 6.9. Cognitive-behavioural coping skills and relapse prevention. Cognitive-behavioural treatment teaches the drinker to recognise the situations, moods and thoughts that trigger drinking, to refuse drinks, to manage craving and negative emotions, and to solve the problems that drinking used to numb. Its best-known branch is relapse prevention, set out by G. Alan Marlatt (1941 to 2011) and Judith Gordon in their book Relapse Prevention (1985). Marlatt distinguished a lapse (a single slip) from a relapse (a return to the old pattern), identified high-risk situations, and described the abstinence violation effect, the "I've blown it, so I may as well keep going" reaction that turns a lapse into a relapse. Relapse prevention is taught in Book 2, Section 9.9.6. A related technique, cue exposure, repeatedly exposes the person to the sight and smell of his drink without drinking, so that the conditioned craving described in Section 10.2 can extinguish; its results for alcohol have been modest. Aversion therapy. In the middle of the twentieth century some clinics tried to condition a distaste for alcohol by pairing drinks with nausea produced by an emetic drug, or with electric shocks; covert sensitisation, introduced by Joseph Cautela in 1966, pairs imagined drinking with imagined disgusting scenes. These methods are rarely used now. Do not confuse them with disulfiram, which works as a deterrent rather than by conditioning, since most people taking it never drink and so never experience the reaction. The community reinforcement approach and contingency management. In 1973 George M. Hunt and Nathan H. Azrin described the community reinforcement approach (CRA), which treats drinking as behaviour maintained by its rewards and sets out to make a sober life more rewarding: help with finding and keeping work, relationship counselling, new recreation and social activities, and training in the skills to enjoy them. Its family version, community reinforcement and family training, teaches relatives how to encourage a reluctant drinker into treatment. Contingency management rewards verified abstinence directly, typically with vouchers or small prizes; its strongest evidence comes from stimulant dependence, and its use for alcohol has been limited by the difficulty of proving abstinence, which breath tests and the newer urine markers of Section 10.3.8 are beginning to solve. Both are described in Book 2, Section 9.9.5. Couples and family treatment. Alcohol problems are family problems, and the family can be a powerful ally in treatment. In behavioural couples therapy , developed for alcohol problems by Timothy O'Farrell and William Fals-Stewart, the couple make a daily "sobriety contract" (often including a supervised disulfiram dose of the kind Ravinder takes), increase shared positive activities and learn to communicate without accusations; trials have found better drinking and relationship outcomes than with individual treatment alone. Relatives' own distress is addressed in family groups such as Al-Anon, founded in 1951 for the families and friends of alcoholics. Alcoholics Anonymous and twelve-step facilitation. The most widespread help of all is free and is not run by professionals. Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) was founded in Akron, Ohio, in 1935 by two men who had failed to stop drinking on their own: Bill Wilson (1895 to 1971), a New York stockbroker, and Robert Holbrook Smith (1879 to 1950), an Akron surgeon known as Dr Bob. Its programme, set out in the book Alcoholics Anonymous (the "Big Book", 1939), follows twelve steps that begin with admitting powerlessness over alcohol and include a moral inventory, making amends and carrying the message to other alcoholics. Members attend meetings, share their stories anonymously, and are guided by a sponsor, a member with longer sobriety. AA regards alcoholism as an illness that can be arrested by lifelong abstinence but never cured. Because members come and go anonymously it was long difficult to study, but the evidence has improved. Vaillant found that AA attendance was one of the two best predictors of sustained abstinence (Section 10.4.1), and a 2020 Cochrane review of 27 studies by John Kelly, Keith Humphreys and Marica Ferri concluded that manualised AA and twelve-step facilitation (TSF, a professional therapy that encourages active AA involvement) produced higher rates of continuous abstinence than other treatments such as cognitive-behavioural therapy, and performed about as well on other outcomes. Mutual-help groups are taught in Book 2, Section 7.11.7. Alternatives exist for people who do not want a spiritual or abstinence-based programme, such as SMART Recovery and Moderation Management. Therapeutic communities. A therapeutic community is a residential programme, lasting months, in which the community of residents and staff is itself the main instrument of treatment, with residents taking on graded responsibilities and confronting one another's behaviour. Therapeutic communities are used more for drug than for alcohol dependence; they are described in Book 2, Sections 7.11.8 and 9.9.7. Does it matter which of these treatments a person receives? The largest test of the question, Project MATCH (1997), randomly assigned 1,726 people with alcohol problems to cognitive-behavioural coping skills therapy, motivational enhancement therapy or twelve-step facilitation. All three groups improved substantially and about equally, and very few of the predicted "matches" between client characteristics and treatments appeared. The trial is described in Book 2, Section 8.8.2. Its message for this chapter is that well-delivered structured treatments for alcohol use disorder work about equally well, which makes it sensible to offer the one a person will actually attend, and to combine it with medication where medication fits.
