AA was founded in 1935 in Akron, Ohio, by Bill Wilson and Dr Bob Smith; it is a mutual-help group, not a therapeutic community and not a professional therapy (TSF is the professional therapy that links people to AA). The community reinforcement approach is Hunt and Azrin (1973); relapse prevention and the abstinence violation effect are Marlatt and Gordon (1985). Abstinence or controlled drinking? AA, and most treatment in India, insists that the only safe goal for a person with alcohol dependence is total, lifelong abstinence. Is that true? The question has caused one of the bitterest disputes in the history of clinical psychology. In 1962 D. L. Davies of the Maudsley Hospital in London reported that 7 of 93 men treated there for alcohol addiction had gone on to drink normally for years, a finding that contradicted the disease model's claim that one drink inevitably leads to loss of control. A decade later the issue became a scientific battle. Key study: the Sobells, Pendery and the controlled-drinking controversy (1973 to 1982) At Patton State Hospital in California, Mark B. Sobell and Linda C. Sobell gave hospitalised men with severe (physically dependent) alcohol dependence an individualised behaviour therapy of 17 sessions aimed at controlled drinking: they practised drinking moderately in a simulated bar, where drinking in an uncontrolled way was followed by an electric shock, received feedback from videotapes of their drunken behaviour, and learned to cope with situations that triggered heavy drinking. Compared with controls given conventional abstinence-oriented treatment, the controlled-drinking group did better; in the second year after treatment, as Barlow and Durand summarise it, the men in the controlled-drinking group were functioning well 85 percent of the time against 42 percent for the abstinence group. In 1982 Mary L. Pendery , Irving Maltzman and Louis Jolyon West published a re-examination in Science . Following the 20 men of the controlled-drinking group for about ten years, they reported that only one, who apparently had never had physical withdrawal symptoms, had maintained controlled drinking; eight had continued to drink excessively, six had become abstinent, four had died of alcohol-related causes and one was missing. The paper made headlines and the Sobells were accused of misrepresenting their results. Formal inquiries did not find misconduct, and the decisive criticism of the re-examination was methodological: it gave no comparable ten-year data on the abstinence group, so it could not show that controlled-drinking training had done worse than the usual treatment. The controversy had a lasting chilling effect on controlled-drinking research in the United States, while the approach remained widely accepted in Britain. Where does the debate stand now? Barlow and Durand summarise later research as showing that controlled drinking is at least as effective as abstinence as a goal, but that neither succeeds over the long term for most people with alcohol dependence, and Vaillant's data show who can drink moderately again: those whose problems were few and mild. Clinical practice therefore matches the goal to the person. Abstinence is the advice for people with severe dependence, liver disease or other alcohol-related organ damage (including the brain), pregnancy, a psychiatric illness that alcohol worsens, medication that interacts with alcohol, or repeated failures at moderation. A goal of reduced, controlled drinking is reasonable for people with hazardous or harmful drinking and milder disorders, and as a first step for people who will not yet accept abstinence. This is part of a wider philosophy called harm reduction : reducing the damage drinking does to the person and to others, even when the person is not ready to stop entirely. Nalmefene's European licence for reducing drinking, and naltrexone's effect on heavy drinking days, are its pharmacological expression. Exam trap The controlled-drinking study was by Mark and Linda Sobell (Patton State Hospital, early 1970s); the famous re-evaluation in Science (1982) was by Pendery, Maltzman and West , and its weakness was the lack of a comparable follow-up of the abstinence group. D. L. Davies (1962) first reported normal drinking in recovered alcohol addicts. Controlled drinking is a reasonable goal for less severe problems, not for severe dependence or alcohol-related organ damage. De-addiction care in India Whatever the treatment, it helps only the people who receive it, and in India very few do. The Magnitude of Substance Use in India survey (Section 10.3.9) found that only about one in 38 people with alcohol dependence reported getting any treatment, and only about one in 180 had ever received inpatient treatment or hospitalisation for an alcohol problem. Closing this gap is the main task of India's de-addiction services. Those services come from two ministries. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare runs the Drug De-Addiction Programme, under which de-addiction centres were set up in government hospitals. Its national resource centre is the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre of AIIMS, located at Ghaziabad near Delhi, which began in 1988 as the Drug Dependence Treatment Centre and was upgraded to a national centre, working from its Ghaziabad campus since 2003; it is also a WHO collaborating centre and coordinates Drug Treatment Clinics in government hospitals that offer outpatient care, including long-term medication. The Centre for Addiction Medicine at NIMHANS in Bengaluru is the other major national centre for treatment, training and research. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment funds the social side of treatment. In 2018 it launched the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR), with a roadmap to 2025, under which non-governmental Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts (IRCAs) are funded and Addiction Treatment Facilities are being set up in government hospitals with the NDDTC as coordinator; and on 15 August 2020 it launched the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan ("drug-free India campaign"), which began in 272 districts identified as most vulnerable. Alongside these are a large number of private de-addiction and "rehab" centres of very uneven quality, some of which have been exposed for locking up and beating residents (Book 2, Section 9.9.5). Because the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 includes conditions associated with alcohol and drug use within its definition of mental illness, people in all such centres have the Act's rights, including informed consent and freedom from chaining and cruel treatment. Indian de-addiction care has one feature that Western textbooks rarely describe: the family is usually present. Patients are typically brought by relatives, often stay in the ward with a family member, and return for follow-up with them, and Indian clinicians have learned to use this. Families are taught about withdrawal, relapse and the drugs (Ravinder's wife learned to supervise his disulfiram, and the De Sousa trials of Section 10.4.4 recruited only men whose relatives would accompany them); spouses' own distress, depression and exposure to violence are assessed and treated; and family members are helped to stop the patterns, from covering up absences at work to paying off liquor debts, that unwittingly keep the drinking going. Community-based camps, run by hospitals and voluntary organisations, have taken detoxification and follow-up to villages and workplaces where no clinic exists. Gopi, the carpenter with alcoholic hallucinosis from Section 10.3.5, shows the whole pathway. His voices faded within ten days on a short course of an antipsychotic and a benzodiazepine, under thiamine cover. Before discharge from the medical college's de-addiction ward, his wife and elder son joined a family session in which the team explained what had happened to him and what would help. He chose disulfiram, taken each morning in front of his son, attended a weekly relapse-prevention group for six months, and went back to work. A year later he had had one lapse, at a cousin's wedding, which he and his family recognised, discussed at the group and stopped. That is what success in this field usually looks like: not a single dramatic cure, but a lapse caught early. Indian context For interviews, know the institutions and the dates: the NDDTC of AIIMS (Ghaziabad; begun in 1988, national centre since 2003) under the Ministry of Health's Drug De-Addiction Programme; the NAPDDR (2018) and the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (launched 15 August 2020 in 272 districts) under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment; IRCAs run by non-governmental organisations; and the treatment gap of about one in 38 for alcohol dependence. The same molecule that lets a surgeon operate, a soldier survive a shattered leg and a woman with cancer die without agony can also take over a young man's life within a year and stop his breathing in a single evening. The biopsychologist John Pinel calls this their Jekyll-and-Hyde character: on the kindly side, the best painkillers medicine has ever had, and excellent treatments for cough and diarrhoea; on the other, a powerful capacity to produce addiction. In India this is not a distant problem. The national survey of 2019 found that about 2 percent of Indians aged 10 to 75 had used an opioid in the previous year, and that roughly 60 lakh people had an opioid use disorder (Section 10.5.6 gives the details). This section follows the family from the poppy field to the laboratory, explains how opioids act on the brain, describes what intoxication, overdose and withdrawal look like, and ends with the treatments, which are among the best supported by evidence anywhere in psychiatry. From the poppy to the pharmacy: a short history Opium is the dried milky latex of the opium poppy, Papaver somniferum , whose Latin name means "the poppy that brings sleep". When the petals have fallen, the farmer makes shallow cuts in the unripe green seed capsule in the late afternoon. A white sap oozes out, darkens and thickens overnight, and is scraped off the next morning as raw opium gum. The dried capsules left behind after the latex has been collected are poppy husk or poppy straw, known in north India as doda or post ; they still contain enough of the active chemicals to be crushed, soaked and drunk. The ripe seeds, the khus khus of Indian kitchens, contain only traces. People have used opium to relieve pain, bring sleep, stop diarrhoea and produce pleasure for more than four thousand years. In seventeenth-century England the physician Thomas Sydenham (1624 to 1689) popularised laudanum , a tincture of opium dissolved in alcohol, and for the next two hundred years laudanum and other opium mixtures were sold freely in Europe and North America. Labourers took them for aches, ladies for "nerves", and nursemaids spooned "soothing syrups" into crying babies. In 1821 the English writer Thomas De Quincey (1785 to 1859) published Confessions of an English Opium-Eater , first in a London magazine and then as a book. It was the first great first-person account of addiction, and its two halves, "the pleasures of opium" and "the pains of opium", describe a life that is still recognisable in any de-addiction ward: a glorious beginning, then years of dependence, tormenting dreams and failed attempts to stop. India sits near the centre of this history. In the late eighteenth century the British East India Company took control of opium production in Bengal and Bihar and turned it into one of the most profitable trades in the world: opium grown on the Gangetic plain was shipped to China and smuggled in, in exchange for tea and silver. When the Chinese government tried to stop the trade, Britain went to war. The First Opium War (1839 to 1842) ended with the Treaty of Nanking, which opened Chinese ports to British trade and handed Hong Kong to Britain, and a Second Opium War (1856 to 1860) followed. The opium factory that the Company's Benares Opium Agency opened at Ghazipur in 1820 is still working today as a government factory, alongside a second at Neemuch in Madhya Pradesh. India is now the only country in the world that legally produces opium gum: licensed farmers in selected tracts of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh grow the poppy under the supervision of the Central Bureau of Narcotics, and the gum is processed into morphine and codeine for medicine. The step that turned a plant into modern pharmacology came in 1804 (Pinel gives 1803; sources differ slightly), when Friedrich Wilhelm Adam Sertürner (1783 to 1841), a young pharmacist's assistant in Paderborn, Germany, extracted the main active ingredient of opium in pure form. He called it morphium , after Morpheus, the Greek god of dreams, because of the deep sleep it produced, and we know it as morphine . It was the first alkaloid to be isolated from a plant: an alkaloid is a nitrogen-containing compound made by a plant that has marked effects on animals (caffeine, nicotine, cocaine and atropine are others). The firm of Merck in Darmstadt began selling morphine commercially in 1827, and a second opium alkaloid, codeine, was isolated in 1832. Pure morphine could be given in an exact dose, and once the hypodermic syringe was developed in the 1850s it could be injected straight into the body, which made it act faster and more powerfully than opium ever had. Morphine was given freely to the wounded of the American Civil War (1861 to 1865), and a story later grew up that so many veterans were left addicted that morphine dependence became known as "the soldier's disease". Historians now regard the phrase and the size of that epidemic as largely legend, although the war was one of several reasons that opioid addiction rose so steeply in late nineteenth-century America. Then came heroin. In 1874 (Pinel gives 1870, but most sources give 1874) an English chemist working in London, C. R. Alder Wright (1844 to 1894), first made diacetylmorphine from morphine, but nobody took much notice. In August 1897 Felix Hoffmann (1868 to 1946), a chemist at the Bayer company in Elberfeld, Germany, made the same compound again, less than two weeks after he had made aspirin. From 1898 to 1910 Bayer sold it over the counter, under the trade name Heroin (from the German heroisch , "heroic" or "strong"), as a cough suppressant and as a supposedly non-addictive substitute for morphine. It was nothing of the kind. Adding the two acetyl groups makes the molecule far more fat-soluble, so it crosses the blood-brain barrier much faster than morphine; inside the brain it is converted back to morphine. Heroin is therefore a "fast morphine", and speed of arrival in the brain is one of the strongest predictors of how addictive a drug will be (Section 10.2). In the United States the Harrison Narcotics Act of 1914 restricted opium, coca and their derivatives, heroin among them, to sale on a doctor's prescription, apart from weak over-the-counter remedies. (Pinel writes that heroin was left out of the Act and that users switched to it, but the Act covered all opium "salts, derivatives, or preparations".) In 1924 Congress banned heroin's manufacture and import altogether, even for medical use. Exam trap Sertürner isolated morphine (about 1804), not heroin. Heroin (diacetylmorphine) was first made by C. R. Alder Wright in 1874 and marketed by Bayer from 1898 , ironically as a non-addictive cough medicine. Opium is the dried latex of the unripe capsule of Papaver somniferum ; poppy husk (doda) is the dried capsule, and poppy seeds contain only traces of the alkaloids. Thomas De Quincey's Confessions of an English Opium-Eater is 1821. The opioid family: natural, semi-synthetic, synthetic and endogenous Three overlapping words are used for these drugs, and examiners like to test them. An opiate , strictly, is one of the natural alkaloids of opium, such as morphine and codeine. An opioid is any substance, natural, semi-synthetic, synthetic or made by the body, that acts on the opioid receptors; it is the wider and now preferred term, and DSM-5-TR calls the whole class "opioids". Narcotic comes from the Greek narke , numbness, and once meant any drug that dulls the senses and brings sleep; today it is mainly a legal word. India's Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 (Section 10.1) counts coca leaf and cocaine as "narcotic drugs" along with opium and cannabis, even though cocaine is a stimulant, so "narcotic" is best avoided as a clinical term. Opium contains a couple of dozen alkaloids, and they fall into two chemical groups with very different effects. The first group, the phenanthrene alkaloids, act on the opioid receptors. Morphine is the most abundant, making up roughly 8 to 14 percent of the dry weight of opium; it is the standard against which every other opioid's strength is measured. Codeine is a much weaker relative, used for dry cough and mild pain. Codeine itself barely binds the receptor; it works because an enzyme in the liver (CYP2D6) converts a small part of each dose into morphine. People who inherit an inactive form of the enzyme get little relief from codeine, while "ultra-rapid metabolisers" turn it into morphine so fast that ordinary doses have caused dangerous breathing problems, especially in children, which is why many countries now restrict codeine for the young. Thebaine has little painkilling effect of its own and causes convulsions at high doses, but it is the raw material from which industry makes several important semi-synthetic drugs. The second group, the benzylisoquinoline alkaloids, do not act on opioid receptors at all, produce no euphoria and cause no dependence. Papaverine relaxes smooth muscle and widens blood vessels; it is used to relieve spasm of arteries and, injected into the penis, to treat erectile dysfunction (Chapter 9). Noscapine (once called narcotine, despite not being narcotic) suppresses cough and is found in cough remedies. So "natural opium alkaloid" does not mean "addictive": papaverine and noscapine are natural opium alkaloids that are neither. A semi-synthetic opioid is made in a laboratory by chemically modifying one of the natural alkaloids. Heroin is the classic example, made from morphine by adding two acetyl groups. Others are hydromorphone (from morphine), hydrocodone (from codeine or thebaine), oxycodone (from thebaine; first made in Germany in 1916 and, as the slow-release tablet OxyContin, at the centre of the North American crisis described in Section 10.5.6), buprenorphine (from thebaine, first made in 1966), and the opioid antagonists naloxone and naltrexone, which are also made from thebaine. A synthetic opioid is built from scratch in the laboratory and owes nothing to the poppy except its effects. Pethidine (meperidine in American texts) and methadone were both made in Germany in the late 1930s; methadone came from the chemists Gustav Ehrhart and Max Bockmühl at the IG Farben company in 1937. (You may read that its American brand name, Dolophine, honoured Adolf Hitler. That story is an urban myth; the name comes from the Latin dolor , pain, and finis , end.) Fentanyl was made by Paul Janssen (1926 to 2003) in Belgium around 1960; it is 50 to 100 times as potent as morphine, and its relative carfentanil, which vets use to sedate elephants and other large animals, is about 100 times more potent again. Tramadol is a weak synthetic opioid that also blocks the reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline; it can cause seizures and serotonin toxicity, it is misused in India and has been smuggled from India to countries where it is banned, and since April 2018 it has been controlled as a psychotropic substance under the NDPS Act. Tapentadol works in a similar double way. Loperamide, the familiar diarrhoea tablet, is a synthetic opioid that barely enters the brain at normal doses. The fourth member of the family is the body's own: the endogenous opioids , the endorphins, enkephalins and dynorphins described in the next subsection. Table 10.21 puts the family together. The answer is heroin , because it does not occur in the poppy: it is semi-synthetic , made by acetylating morphine. Every other option is natural. Morphine is the principal natural alkaloid and the reference opioid. Codeine is natural too (even though much medicinal codeine is in practice made from morphine, the molecule occurs naturally in opium). Papaverine is the option students wrongly reject: it is a genuine natural opium alkaloid, merely one that is not an opioid analgesic and causes no dependence. The same logic answers the twin question "which is not a natural alkaloid compound?": heroin. Do not confuse the classes the other way either: methadone and fentanyl are fully synthetic, not semi-synthetic, and buprenorphine is semi-synthetic (from thebaine). Receptors and what opioids do in the body By the early 1970s pharmacologists knew that opioids must act on some specific target in the nervous system. Tiny doses had huge effects; the effects depended on the exact three-dimensional shape of the molecule (a drug and its mirror image did not act alike); and the drug naloxone could reverse a heroin overdose within a minute or two, as though it were pushing the opioid off a site. But nobody had ever seen that site. The question was settled in 1973, and the way it was settled is one of the classic stories of neuroscience. Key study: finding the opiate receptor and the brain's own opioids (1973 to 1975) Candace Pert (1946 to 2013), a graduate student at Johns Hopkins University, and her supervisor Solomon Snyder (born 1938) made naloxone radioactive, mixed it with ground-up brain tissue, and washed away everything that was not firmly stuck. A small amount of radioactivity stayed bound, it could be displaced by opioids in proportion to their known strength as painkillers, and it was found in nervous tissue. They had found the opiate receptor, and they reported it in Science in March 1973; Eric Simon in New York and Lars Terenius in Sweden found it independently the same year. The discovery raised an obvious question: why would the human brain carry receptors for the sap of a poppy? The answer had to be that the brain makes its own opioid-like substances. In 1975 John Hughes and Hans Kosterlitz (1903 to 1996) at the University of Aberdeen extracted two small peptides from pig brain that acted like morphine and were blocked by naloxone. They named them enkephalins (from the Greek for "in the head"). Beta-endorphin and the dynorphins followed, and "endorphin", a contraction of "endogenous morphine", became the name for the whole group. The lesson for psychiatry is that addictive drugs work by hijacking systems the brain already has for its own purposes: here, for damping pain and stress and for signalling reward. There are three classical opioid receptors , named with Greek letters: mu, delta and kappa (a fourth, the nociceptin receptor, is a close cousin). All three are metabotropic receptors linked to inhibitory G proteins. When an opioid binds, the neuron's internal messenger cyclic AMP falls, potassium channels open and calcium channels close, so the neuron becomes harder to fire and releases less transmitter. Opioids are therefore, at the level of the single neuron, mostly inhibitory, and their effects depend on which neurons carry the receptors. The mu receptor is the one that matters most. Morphine, heroin, methadone and fentanyl are all mu agonists ("mu for morphine" is a useful memory hook), and beta-endorphin is its main natural ligand. Nearly everything an opioid does, good and bad, follows from where mu receptors sit: Pain relief. Mu receptors in the periaqueductal grey of the midbrain, in the brainstem and in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord block the transmission of pain signals. Opioids blunt the emotional sting of pain as well as its intensity; patients often say the pain is still there but no longer bothers them. Euphoria and reward. In the ventral tegmental area, mu receptors sit on GABA interneurons that normally hold the dopamine neurons in check. Opioids inhibit these brake cells, the dopamine neurons fire, and dopamine floods the nucleus accumbens; opioids also act directly in the accumbens. This is how opioids plug into the common reward circuit described in Section 10.2. Respiratory depression. Mu receptors in the breathing centres of the medulla make them less responsive to rising carbon dioxide, so breathing becomes slow and shallow. This is what kills in overdose. Pinpoint pupils. Opioids increase the activity of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, which drives the muscle that constricts the pupil, producing the tiny "pinpoint" pupils ( miosis ) that are the single most useful sign of opioid use. Cough suppression, nausea and constipation. Opioids depress the cough centre in the medulla (hence codeine linctus), stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone that causes vomiting, and slow the gut by acting on the nerve plexus in its wall (hence their use for diarrhoea, and the constipation that every long-term user knows). Hormonal and other effects. Opioids suppress the hormones that drive the gonads, reducing sex drive and disturbing menstruation; morphine releases histamine, causing itching and flushing; and opioids lower body temperature slightly. The kappa receptor, whose natural ligand is dynorphin, also relieves pain but produces dysphoria rather than euphoria, sometimes with perceptual distortions; the hallucinogen salvinorin A acts here. Delta receptors, the main target of the enkephalins, contribute to pain relief and mood. Two pharmacological facts explain much of what clinicians see. The first is that tolerance to opioids is uneven. With repeated use, tolerance develops quickly to the euphoria, the pain relief, the sedation and the nausea, and to some extent to the respiratory depression, although the evidence suggests that this last tolerance develops more slowly and is lost quickly when use stops. Almost no tolerance develops to the constriction of the pupils or to the constipation. That is why a man who has injected heroin daily for ten years still has pinpoint pupils and is still constipated, even though the "high" has long since faded. The second fact is the adaptation that produces physical dependence. Neurons exposed to an opioid day after day compensate for its inhibitory effect by turning up their internal machinery, especially the cyclic AMP system. This is clearest in the locus coeruleus, the brainstem nucleus that supplies most of the brain's noradrenaline: under the drug its neurons fire at a near-normal rate only because the compensating machinery is working hard against the opioid. Remove the drug, and the compensation is suddenly unopposed: the locus coeruleus fires furiously, and much of the opioid withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, sweating, racing heart, gooseflesh) is this noradrenergic storm. Tolerance, cross-tolerance and the difference between physical dependence and addiction are defined in Section 10.1; a cancer patient on regular morphine is physically dependent but not addicted, which is why DSM-5-TR does not count tolerance or withdrawal towards opioid use disorder when the drug is taken as prescribed. Exam trap The euphoria, analgesia, respiratory depression, miosis and constipation of morphine and heroin come mainly from the mu receptor; kappa (dynorphin) produces dysphoria. The opiate receptor was demonstrated by Pert and Snyder in 1973 ; the first endogenous opioids, the enkephalins , were isolated by Hughes and Kosterlitz in 1975 . Endorphins are the body's own opioid agonists ; naloxone is an antagonist . Little or no tolerance develops to miosis and constipation , so pinpoint pupils persist even in highly tolerant users. Intoxication and overdose Ask a person who injects heroin what the first seconds feel like and you will hear about the rush : a wave of warmth and intense pleasure that starts in the abdomen and spreads through the body, often compared to orgasm, which settles into a calm, drowsy, contented state in which nothing seems to matter. Smoking heroin from foil ("chasing the dragon") gives a slightly gentler version; swallowing opium or drinking poppy husk tea gives a slow, mild warmth without any rush at all. After the rush come the signs of intoxication. The person becomes drowsy and slips in and out of a light sleep, head dropping and jerking up again, which users call being "on the nod". Speech is slow and slurred, attention and memory are poor, and the person may scratch at the face and nose because of histamine release. The pupils are small, often pinpoint, even in a dim room. DSM-5-TR's criteria for opioid intoxication put that picture into a rule with three parts. There must be recent opioid use; there must be clinically significant behavioural or psychological change, typically an initial euphoria followed by apathy, dysphoria, slowing or agitation, and impaired judgement; and there must be pupillary constriction together with at least one of drowsiness or coma, slurred speech, or impaired attention or memory. The pupils are made a required sign because they are so reliable, and the manual adds one exception you should know: in a severe overdose the brain is starved of oxygen, and anoxia dilates the pupils, so a person close to death from an opioid can have wide pupils. The rule also excludes other explanations. Drunkenness and sedative intoxication can look much the same, but they do not shrink the pupils, and they do not respond to naloxone. An opioid overdose is intoxication that has gone far enough to stop the person breathing adequately. Its classic triad is unconsciousness (coma), pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression . Breathing slows to a few shallow breaths a minute, sometimes with a snoring or gurgling sound; the lips and fingertips turn blue (cyanosis); the pulse slows and the skin is cold and clammy; fluid may fill the lungs. Death comes from respiratory arrest, within minutes of a dose of fentanyl and usually within a few hours of heroin, which is why bystanders matter so much. Overdose rarely happens at random. It clusters in four situations. The first is loss of tolerance: after a few weeks without opioids, in a hospital, a de-addiction centre or a prison, a person's tolerance to the respiratory effect falls away, but the habit of taking the old dose does not, so the days after discharge or release are among the most dangerous in a user's life. The second is mixing: alcohol, benzodiazepines and other sedatives depress breathing by different mechanisms, and the combination with an opioid is far more lethal than either alone (Section 10.7). The third is unknown purity: street heroin is cut to an unknown degree, and when a batch is purer than usual, or has been cut with fentanyl, a familiar dose becomes a fatal one. The fourth is using alone, with nobody to call for help. The emergency treatment is naloxone , a pure opioid antagonist that binds the mu receptor more tightly than heroin or morphine, pushes them off and switches the receptor off. Given into a vein, into a muscle or as a nasal spray, it can restore breathing within minutes, and it is so safe that many countries put it in the hands of drug users, families and police. Three cautions go with it. Naloxone wears off faster than many opioids (its action often lasts only about an hour), so a person who wakes up can slip back into respiratory depression as the naloxone fades while the heroin, methadone or fentanyl is still present; anyone revived must be watched for several hours. Naloxone instantly throws a dependent person into withdrawal, so people often wake vomiting, shivering and angry. And naloxone reverses only the opioid part of a mixed overdose: it does nothing for alcohol or benzodiazepines. Manpreet, a 24-year-old from a village near Amritsar, had started smoking heroin ( chitta , as it is called in Punjab) on foil with friends at 19, and within two years was injecting it two or three times a day. After his mother sold her jewellery to pay for it, his family took him to a private de-addiction centre, where he was kept for six weeks without medication and discharged "clean". On the evening he came home he met an old friend, bought the amount he used to inject before admission and used it alone in a fields shed. His younger brother found him an hour later, unconscious, breathing perhaps four times a minute with a snoring sound, his lips blue and his pupils the size of pinheads. The ambulance crew gave naloxone, and within two minutes Manpreet was sitting up, retching, sweating and demanding to know why they had "ruined" his high. Two hours later he became drowsy again and needed a second dose. Every element of the overdose is there: the triad of coma, pinpoint pupils and slowed breathing; the loss of tolerance after six weeks of abstinence; using alone; the rapid response to naloxone; the precipitated withdrawal; and the second dip as the naloxone wore off. Exam trap Pinpoint pupils mean opioid intoxication (the only exception is anoxia in a severe overdose, which dilates them); dilated pupils mean opioid withdrawal, stimulant intoxication or hallucinogen intoxication. The overdose triad is coma, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression . Do not mix up the antagonists: naloxone is the short-acting emergency reversal agent; naltrexone is the long-acting antagonist taken to prevent relapse (Section 10.5.7); flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids (Section 10.7). The most dangerous moment is not the first use but the return to the old dose after a period of abstinence. Withdrawal: "cold turkey" Opioid withdrawal is one of the most recognisable syndromes in medicine, and it follows a simple rule that you met in Section 10.1: a withdrawal state is roughly the mirror image of the drug's acute effects. Opioids constrict the pupils, dry up secretions, slow the gut, relieve pain, calm, sedate and produce euphoria. Take them away from a body that has adapted to them, and the pupils dilate, the eyes and nose stream, the gut cramps and empties, every muscle aches, sleep vanishes, and the person feels restless, anxious and wretched. Once you know the effects, you can work out the withdrawal. The timing depends on the half-life of the drug, as Figure 10.10 shows. DSM-5-TR describes the usual course: most people dependent on a short-acting opioid such as heroin begin to have symptoms within 6 to 12 hours of the last dose; the acute symptoms peak within 1 to 3 days and subside gradually over 5 to 7 days. With longer-acting drugs such as methadone or buprenorphine, symptoms may take 2 to 4 days to emerge and last longer. Even after the acute phase has passed, a quieter "protracted" phase of anxiety, low mood, inability to enjoy anything, poor sleep and craving can continue for weeks or months, and it is this phase, not the dramatic first week, that drives many relapses. 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 Days since the last dose Severity of withdrawal (schematic) Heroin (short-acting) Methadone (long-acting) peak at 1 to 3 days later, milder, longer Low mood, insomnia and craving may linger for weeks (protracted) Figure 10.10 The time course of opioid withdrawal depends on the half-life of the drug (schematic, after the timings in DSM-5-TR). After a short-acting opioid such as heroin, symptoms begin within about 6 to 12 hours, peak in 1 to 3 days and fade over 5 to 7 days. After a long-acting opioid such as methadone they may take 2 to 4 days to appear, are milder at their peak and drag on much longer. In both, low mood, poor sleep and craving can persist for weeks. The first symptoms are subjective: anxiety, restlessness, irritability and an "achy" feeling, often in the back and legs. Then come yawning, watering eyes ( lacrimation ), a running nose ( rhinorrhoea ) and sweating. Many people fall into a fitful sleep for a few hours and wake worse. At the peak the original symptoms are joined by chills, shivering, piloerection (gooseflesh, the hairs standing on end), nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, dilated pupils, tremor, muscle pains and spasms, and fever in severe cases. The skin covered in goosebumps, which looks like a plucked bird, is the origin of the expression "going cold turkey " for stopping abruptly, and the involuntary kicking movements of the legs gave English "kicking the habit". DSM-5-TR's criteria for opioid withdrawal require either the cessation or reduction of heavy, prolonged use (several weeks or more) or the giving of an opioid antagonist after a period of use, followed within minutes to several days by at least three of nine signs: dysphoric mood; nausea or vomiting; muscle aches; lacrimation or rhinorrhoea; pupillary dilation, piloerection or sweating; diarrhoea; yawning; fever; and insomnia. The symptoms must cause significant distress or impairment and not be better explained by something else. The manual notes that piloerection and fever are seen mainly in severe withdrawal, which clinicians rarely see because dependent people usually find a dose before withdrawal gets that far. Withdrawal can be produced in two ways, and the second matters for treatment. Spontaneous withdrawal follows stopping the drug and builds over hours. Precipitated withdrawal is produced in minutes when an antagonist such as naloxone or naltrexone is given to someone dependent on opioids, or when buprenorphine, which binds more tightly than heroin but activates the receptor less (Section 10.5.7), displaces a full agonist. It is sudden and intense, which is why a revived overdose victim wakes in misery and why buprenorphine must be started only once withdrawal has already begun. How dangerous is opioid withdrawal? Far less than its reputation. The film image of the addict screaming and convulsing on the floor is misleading, and Pinel quotes the psychologist William McKim's verdict that even in its most severe form opioid withdrawal "is not as dangerous or terrifying as withdrawal from barbiturates or alcohol"; Pinel himself compares it to a bad case of the flu. Seizures are not part of the opioid withdrawal syndrome, delirium is rare (DSM-5-TR does allow a diagnosis of opioid withdrawal delirium, but it is uncommon), and in healthy adults the syndrome is very rarely fatal. The exceptions are worth knowing: severe vomiting and diarrhoea can dehydrate a frail or ill person; in pregnancy, withdrawal stresses the fetus, so pregnant women dependent on opioids are generally stabilised on methadone or buprenorphine rather than detoxified; and babies born to dependent mothers can develop a neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome of irritability, a high-pitched cry, tremor, poor feeding and diarrhoea in the days after birth. The real danger of withdrawal is indirect: it is a powerful reason to use again, and the person who gets through it has lost tolerance and is at high risk of overdose if he relapses, as Manpreet did. He had started, like many men in his area, to keep going through long days in the fields, and later took it "for strength" and to be sociable: opium was offered to guests at weddings in his village, as it had been in his father's time. When the licensed shops that sold poppy husk in Rajasthan closed at the end of March 2016 and he could not afford the black-market price, he came to the district hospital on the second day without it. He sat yawning repeatedly, his eyes and nose streaming, wiping his face with his turban cloth; his forearms were covered in gooseflesh although the ward was warm; he complained of cramps, loose motions six times since the night before, aching legs that would not keep still, and no sleep at all; his pupils were wide. He was sure he was going to die. The doctor reassured him that he would not, began a short course of buprenorphine with naloxone to relieve the symptoms, and talked with him and his son about whether he wanted to come off opioids altogether or to stay on a maintenance dose (Section 10.5.7). Bablu's withdrawal is textbook: spontaneous onset after the last dose, a peak on the second or third day, and nearly every sign in Table 10.22, from yawning and lacrimation to piloerection, diarrhoea and dilated pupils. Exam trap The signs that identify opioid withdrawal are yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, dilated pupils, piloerection, sweating, diarrhoea and muscle aches . Seizures and delirium are not features of uncomplicated opioid withdrawal; they point to alcohol or sedative withdrawal, which, unlike opioid withdrawal, can kill (Sections 10.3 and 10.7). DSM-5-TR itself uses the runny nose, streaming eyes and dilated pupils to tell opioid withdrawal from sedative withdrawal, whose anxiety and restlessness look similar. Heroin withdrawal starts in 6 to 12 hours and peaks at 1 to 3 days ; methadone withdrawal starts later (2 to 4 days) and lasts longer. "Cold turkey" comes from the gooseflesh, "kicking the habit" from the leg movements. Course, complications and the opioid epidemics How does opioid dependence usually unfold over a lifetime? The most surprising answer came from a war. In 1971 reports reached Washington that large numbers of American soldiers in Vietnam were using heroin, which there was cheap, pure and sold openly. The government feared that hundreds of thousands of addicted men were about to come home. It asked Lee Robins (1922 to 2009), a psychiatric epidemiologist at Washington University in St Louis, to find out what happened to them. Robins and her colleagues interviewed a representative sample of returning enlisted men, checked their accounts against urine tests and military records, and followed them up. About a third had used heroin in Vietnam and about one in five had had symptoms of dependence there. Yet in their first year back in the United States only about 1 percent became re-addicted, although about 10 percent tried heroin again (these are the figures as Wayne Hall and Megan Weier summarised them in 2016). DSM-5-TR sums up the same work by saying that over 90 percent of the soldiers who had become dependent in Vietnam stayed off opioids in the long term, although many later had problems with alcohol, amphetamines or suicidal thoughts. The study did not show that heroin is harmless. It showed how powerfully the environment controls drug use: the men left behind the cheap supply, the boredom and terror, the drug-using companions and every cue linked to using, and most of them simply stopped. The conditioning of craving and tolerance to places and cues is explained in Section 10.2. People who come to clinics in their home towns, where the cues and the supply never go away, tell a gloomier story. For them DSM-5-TR describes opioid use disorder as a condition that, once it needs treatment, often continues for many years, with brief periods of abstinence and long-term abstinence in only a minority. A 33-year follow-up of 86 people treated for injected heroin dependence in 1966 and 1967 in a small town in south-east England (Rathod, Addenbrooke and Rosenbach, 2005) found that 22 percent had died, about twice the rate expected, more than half of them from overdose; but 42 percent of the whole group had been abstinent for at least ten years, and another 10 percent were being maintained on methadone. So the natural history has two faces: high mortality, and a slow drift towards recovery among those who survive. Most of the physical harm of opioid dependence, oddly, does not come from the drug itself. Pinel points out that the direct effects of long-term use of pure opioids are surprisingly minor: constipation, small pupils, irregular periods and reduced sex drive. The great American surgeon William Stewart Halsted (1852 to 1922), one of the founders of the Johns Hopkins medical school, was secretly dependent on morphine for most of his brilliant career. The killers are overdose, the circumstances of illegal use and the needle. A person who injects street drugs never knows their strength or what they have been cut with, shares needles and syringes, and injects into ever smaller and more damaged veins. The results are abscesses and cellulitis at injection sites, infection of the heart valves (endocarditis), clots in deep veins, gangrene after accidental injection into an artery, and above all blood-borne infections: hepatitis B and C and the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In India the link between injecting and HIV was seen most starkly in Manipur and the other north-eastern states, where HIV spread rapidly among people injecting heroin from about 1990: reports that year described its prevalence among them rising from almost nil to about half within six months, and in the following years it spread to their sexual partners and to babies born to infected mothers. Add poverty, poor nutrition, crime to pay for the drug, imprisonment and violence, and the high mortality is easy to understand. DSM-5-TR also notes a raised risk of suicide, and it warns that an accidental overdose and a suicide attempt are different things that are easy to confuse. This analysis is the basis of harm reduction : policies and services that aim to reduce the damage drug use does, to the user and to others, without requiring the person to stop using first. Needle and syringe programmes give out sterile injecting equipment and collect used equipment, and they reduce HIV and hepatitis C transmission; opioid substitution treatment (Section 10.5.7) is itself one of the most effective harm-reduction measures; naloxone given to users and their families prevents overdose deaths; and some countries run supervised injection facilities. In 1994 Switzerland went further and opened clinics where long-term heroin users who had failed other treatments could receive pharmaceutical heroin from a doctor, as part of a package of medical and social care. The evaluations, which Pinel describes, found that most users gave up their criminal lifestyles and improved in health and social functioning, and similar trials followed in Germany, the Netherlands, Spain, Britain and Canada, where supervised heroin-assisted treatment proved more effective than methadone for this hard-to-treat group. The worst opioid epidemic of modern times began not in a back street but in doctors' surgeries. In the United States in the 1990s, pharmaceutical companies and medical bodies argued that pain was being undertreated and that addiction was rare when opioids were prescribed for pain. In 1996 Purdue Pharma launched OxyContin, a slow-release form of oxycodone, and marketed it as carrying a low risk of addiction; the company later pleaded guilty to federal criminal charges over its marketing and sale of the drug (in 2007, and again in 2020). Prescriptions soared, and DSM-5-TR describes what followed in three waves: until 2009 most overdose deaths involved prescribed opioids; from 2010, as prescribing was tightened, many dependent people turned to cheaper heroin and heroin deaths rose sharply; and from 2015 deaths from synthetic opioids other than methadone, mostly illicitly made fentanyl mixed into the heroin and counterfeit pill supply, outnumbered those from prescribed opioids. Deaths involving synthetic opioids in the United States rose from about 2,600 in 2011 to more than 70,000 in 2021. Canada went through the same waves. The epidemic is a lesson in how supply, marketing and medical fashion can create addiction on a mass scale, just as the opium trade did in nineteenth-century China. Indian context The national survey Magnitude of Substance Use in India (carried out by the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC), AIIMS, for the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, and released in 2019) found that 2.06 percent of Indians aged 10 to 75 were current users of opioids. Heroin was the most used (1.14 percent), followed by pharmaceutical opioids (0.96 percent) and opium (0.52 percent), and about 0.55 percent of Indians, roughly 60 lakh people, needed help for harmful use or dependence. More than half of them lived in a few large states: Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat. In proportion to population, the worst affected were the north-eastern states (Mizoram, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Manipur), together with Punjab, Haryana and Delhi. There were an estimated 8.5 lakh people who inject drugs, and the drugs they injected were almost all opioids (heroin and pharmaceutical opioids in equal shares). Only about one in 20 people dependent on illicit drugs had ever received inpatient treatment. The patterns are regional. In western Rajasthan, opium and poppy husk have a long ceremonial history: at weddings and other gatherings guests may be offered opium in the amal ceremony (called the riyan in Jaisalmer and Barmer), and many older men are dependent on daily doda. In Punjab, heroin, usually called chitta , has replaced the older opium and poppy husk among young men. In the north-east, heroin (sometimes as impure "brown sugar") arrives from Myanmar, on the route from the opium-growing Golden Triangle. Across the country pharmaceutical opioids are misused: codeine-containing cough syrups, tramadol (controlled under the NDPS Act since 2018), and injected buprenorphine, often mixed with the antihistamine pheniramine. Exam trap Lee Robins's Vietnam study found that most soldiers who became dependent on heroin in Vietnam stopped after coming home: the lesson is the power of environment and cues , not that heroin is non-addictive. Most medical harm in opioid dependence is indirect (overdose, infection from injecting, impurities, poverty) rather than direct toxicity. Harm reduction (needle and syringe programmes, opioid substitution, naloxone) does not require abstinence. In India, the most used opioid in the 2019 national survey was heroin , ahead of pharmaceutical opioids and opium. Treatment: detoxification, substitution and blockade Imagine three ways of helping Manpreet. You could take him off opioids altogether, as safely and comfortably as possible, and hope he stays off. You could replace the injected street heroin, which he must buy several times a day, with a legal, long-acting opioid taken by mouth once a day under supervision. Or you could give him a drug that blocks the opioid receptors, so that heroin no longer has any effect. These are the three medical strategies, detoxification , agonist maintenance and antagonist treatment , and each suits different people. All three work better with psychological and social support, and the most important practical lesson of the last fifty years is that the second one, unfashionable as it sounds, saves the most lives. Detoxification. Detoxification is the medically supervised management of withdrawal. The most comfortable method is to substitute an opioid and then reduce it: the person is stabilised on buprenorphine or methadone, and the dose is tapered over days to weeks. The alternative is to treat the withdrawal symptoms without an opioid. In 1978 Mark Gold , D. Eugene Redmond and Herbert Kleber (1934 to 2018) reported in The Lancet that clonidine, a blood-pressure drug, blocks acute opiate withdrawal symptoms. Clonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist: it stimulates the receptors that act as a brake on the locus coeruleus, and so calms the noradrenergic storm described in Section 10.5.3. It relieves sweating, gooseflesh, cramps, diarrhoea and anxiety, but helps less with aches, insomnia and craving, and it can drop the blood pressure. Lofexidine works the same way with less effect on blood pressure; it has been licensed in Britain since the 1990s and in the United States since 2018. Symptomatic medicines (loperamide for diarrhoea, an anti-emetic, simple painkillers) complete the regimen. The Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale guides dosing. Detoxification is safe and it is necessary for anyone who wants to be opioid-free, but on its own it rarely produces lasting abstinence. Most people relapse within weeks or months, and because detoxification removes tolerance, relapse after it carries a high risk of overdose: Manpreet's story is common. Detoxification is therefore best seen as the doorway into treatment, not the treatment itself (Book 2, Section 9.9.5). Key study: Dole and Nyswander's methadone maintenance (1965) In the early 1960s Vincent Dole (1913 to 2006), a specialist in metabolism at the Rockefeller Institute in New York, teamed up with the psychiatrist Marie Nyswander (1919 to 1986), who had years of experience treating heroin users and had concluded that conventional psychotherapy and detoxification almost always failed. Dole's hypothesis was that long-term heroin use produces a lasting metabolic change, so that the dependent person needs an opioid somewhat as a person with diabetes needs insulin. They admitted a small group of men with long histories of heroin dependence and many failed treatments to a hospital ward and gave them oral methadone in slowly rising doses, once a day. The results surprised them. On a stable daily dose the men stopped craving heroin, did not appear intoxicated, and when they were given heroin experimentally they felt little from it, because the cross-tolerance produced by methadone blocked its euphoria. Discharged to the community on daily methadone, most stayed off heroin, went back to work or school, and stopped committing crimes. They published the results in 1965 in the Journal of the American Medical Association as "A medical treatment for diacetylmorphine (heroin) addiction". Criticism came at once and has never quite stopped: methadone is itself an opioid and produces dependence, so critics said the patients had merely swapped one addiction for another; the metabolic theory has never been proved; and some methadone leaks onto the street. But in hundreds of later studies, methadone maintenance has kept people in treatment, reduced heroin use, crime and HIV transmission, and lowered death rates, and it became the model for all agonist treatment. Agonist maintenance with methadone. The logic of opioid substitution therapy (also called opioid agonist treatment or maintenance treatment) follows from pharmacology. Methadone is a full mu agonist, like heroin, but it differs in the ways that matter. It is taken by mouth, so there is no injection and no rush. It has a long half-life (about a day on average, though it varies widely between people), so a single daily dose keeps the level steady for 24 hours, with none of the cycle of highs and withdrawals that a heroin user goes through several times a day. And at an adequate dose its cross-tolerance blunts the effect of any heroin taken on top. The person's life no longer has to be organised around getting the next dose. Methadone has real dangers. Because it accumulates over the first days, the induction period is risky, and doses are started low and raised slowly; it prolongs the QT interval of the heart and can cause dangerous rhythm disturbances; combined with alcohol or benzodiazepines it can still stop breathing; and take-home doses can be diverted. For these reasons it is usually dispensed daily under supervision in a clinic, with take-home doses earned by stability. Agonist maintenance with buprenorphine. Buprenorphine , a semi-synthetic opioid made from thebaine, is a partial agonist at the mu receptor (it is also a kappa antagonist). Two of its properties make it unusual. It binds the mu receptor extremely tightly and comes off it slowly, so its action is long and it displaces other opioids; and because it can only partly activate the receptor, its effects rise with dose only up to a ceiling, as Figure 10.11 shows. The ceiling means enough opioid effect to prevent withdrawal and craving, but much less respiratory depression than a full agonist, so buprenorphine taken on its own is far safer in overdose than methadone or heroin (though not when mixed with sedatives or alcohol). The tight binding means that a dose given while a full agonist is still on the receptors pushes it off and replaces a large effect with a smaller one: precipitated withdrawal. Buprenorphine is therefore started only when the person is already in moderate withdrawal, usually at least 12 hours after the last heroin and longer after methadone. It is taken as a tablet or film under the tongue, often combined with naloxone in a ratio of four to one. Taken correctly, the naloxone is barely absorbed and does nothing; if the tablet is crushed and injected, the naloxone acts and precipitates withdrawal, which discourages injection. Monthly slow-release injections are now available in some countries. Buprenorphine has fewer side effects than methadone, but in trials in which the dose could be adjusted it kept fewer people in treatment than methadone did. 0 50 100 Dose (logarithmic scale) Opioid effect (percent of maximum) Effect at which breathing fails (schematic) ceiling effect Full agonist (heroin, methadone, fentanyl) Partial agonist (buprenorphine) Antagonist (naloxone, naltrexone) Figure 10.11 Full agonist, partial agonist and antagonist (schematic dose-response curves). A full agonist such as heroin, methadone or fentanyl produces more effect with every increase in dose, including more respiratory depression, until breathing fails. Buprenorphine, a partial agonist, binds the mu receptor even more tightly but can only switch it partly on, so its effect levels off at a ceiling: enough to prevent withdrawal and craving, far less likely to stop breathing when taken alone. An antagonist such as naloxone or naltrexone occupies the receptor and produces no effect at all, and it blocks the agonists. Antagonist treatment. Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid antagonist, taken by mouth daily or given as a monthly depot injection. While it is on board, heroin produces no euphoria and no respiratory depression, so using is pointless; naltrexone itself produces no high, no dependence and has no street value. Its weaknesses are practical. The person must be completely free of opioids for about 7 to 10 days before starting, or the first dose precipitates severe withdrawal, and many dependent people cannot get through that gap. Many stop taking the tablets once motivation dips, and if they then return to their old dose without tolerance they are at high risk of overdose. Naltrexone works best for people with strong reasons to stay abstinent and someone checking that they take it: doctors and nurses whose licence depends on it, or people on probation. The depot injection improves adherence. Naltrexone's use for alcohol dependence is described in Section 10.4. What the evidence shows. Systematic reviews of randomised trials (the Cochrane reviews led by Richard Mattick and colleagues) find that methadone maintenance keeps people in treatment and reduces heroin use far better than detoxification or treatment without medication, and that buprenorphine at adequate doses suppresses heroin use about as well, although flexible-dose buprenorphine retains fewer patients. The most important outcome is survival. In 2017 Luis Sordo and colleagues pooled cohort studies of more than 138,000 people treated with methadone or buprenorphine and found that the all-cause death rate was 11.3 per 1,000 person-years while people were on methadone and 36.1 after they left it, about a threefold difference; the corresponding figures for buprenorphine were 4.3 and 9.5. The two most dangerous periods were the first four weeks of methadone treatment and the weeks immediately after leaving either treatment. Agonist treatment also reduces injecting, HIV infection and crime, and both methadone and buprenorphine are on the World Health Organization's list of essential medicines. Medication works best alongside psychosocial help: contingency management (Book 2, Section 4.5.7), counselling and cognitive-behavioural therapy, family work, Narcotics Anonymous (Book 2, Section 7.11.7), relapse prevention (Book 2, Section 9.9.6) and therapeutic communities (Book 2, Section 9.9.7). Clinical link Families, and sometimes de-addiction staff, object that maintenance treatment "just swaps one addiction for another". A clinical psychologist should be able to answer that. The difference is between the compulsive use of a short-acting, injected, illegal drug of unknown strength, which organises the whole of a person's life and carries a high risk of death, and the supervised use of a long-acting oral medicine at a steady dose, which frees the person to work, look after children and engage in therapy. DSM-5-TR builds this into the diagnosis: a person who is taking methadone or buprenorphine and meets no criteria for opioid use disorder (apart from tolerance to and withdrawal from the medicine) is coded as being in remission, with the specifier on maintenance therapy . Pushing a stable patient to stop maintenance too soon is one of the commonest routes back to overdose. Exam trap Methadone is a full agonist (synthetic, oral, long-acting); buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a ceiling effect (semi-synthetic, sublingual, high affinity); naltrexone is a long-acting antagonist used after detoxification; naloxone is the short-acting antagonist for overdose, and it is added to buprenorphine tablets to deter injection. Clonidine and lofexidine are not opioids: they are alpha-2 adrenergic agonists that ease withdrawal. Methadone maintenance was introduced by Dole and Nyswander in 1965 . Starting buprenorphine too soon after heroin, or naltrexone before 7 to 10 opioid-free days, causes precipitated withdrawal . Detoxification alone is not an adequate treatment for opioid dependence. 10.6 Stimulants, Tobacco and Caffeine Lower yield · 1 Q Opioids slow the brain down; the drugs of this section speed it up. A stimulant is a drug whose main effect is a general increase in neural and behavioural activity: more alertness, energy and confidence, less need for food and sleep. The family runs from the cup of filter coffee that starts a working day in Chennai, through the bidi smoked at a roadside tea stall and the tablet a college student takes before an examination, to crack cocaine and crystal methamphetamine. They differ enormously in potency, and the way the drug reaches the brain matters as much as the drug itself: coca leaves chewed in the Andes and crack smoked in a pipe contain the same molecule. DSM-5-TR separates them into three classes, each with its own rules: stimulant-related disorders (cocaine and the amphetamine-type substances), tobacco-related disorders and caffeine-related disorders. This section takes them in that order, then looks at MDMA (ecstasy), which DSM-5-TR actually files among the hallucinogens, and at the synthetic cathinones. Cocaine: from the coca leaf to crack The coca shrub, Erythroxylum coca , grows on the eastern slopes of the Andes in Peru and Bolivia, and the peoples of the region have chewed its leaves for thousands of years, usually with a pinch of lime or plant ash that helps release the active alkaloid. Chewed leaf eases hunger, fatigue and the breathlessness of high altitude, and because the cocaine is absorbed slowly and in small amounts, it causes few problems; coca tea is still served to tourists arriving in La Paz. The trouble began when chemistry concentrated the leaf. In 1860 Albert Niemann (1834 to 1861), a young chemist at the University of Göttingen, described the purified alkaloid in his doctoral dissertation and named it cocaine, noting that it numbed his tongue. Within a few years cocaine was everywhere. From 1863 a Corsican chemist, Angelo Mariani, sold Vin Mariani, a Bordeaux wine steeped in coca leaves that was endorsed by a pope, and in 1886 an Atlanta pharmacist, John Pemberton, created Coca-Cola, whose original recipe contained coca extract. In the early 1900s the company switched to coca leaves from which the cocaine had been removed; its stimulant effect today comes from caffeine. Key study: Sigmund Freud, cocaine and cigars In 1884 Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939), then a young and ambitious neurologist in Vienna, read that a German army doctor had given cocaine to soldiers to help them endure manoeuvres. He obtained some, took it himself and was delighted. He pressed it on friends, colleagues and patients, sent some to his fiancée, and in July 1884 published "Über Coca" ("On coca"), an essay so enthusiastic about the drug that Pinel calls it a "song of praise". He even tried to cure his friend, the physiologist Ernst von Fleischl-Marxow, of morphine dependence by giving him cocaine; Fleischl became dependent on cocaine as well, developed a cocaine psychosis and died in 1891. Freud's colleague Carl Koller (1857 to 1944) took more careful notice of the numbing. In September 1884 a report of his experiments, read at the ophthalmological congress in Heidelberg, showed that a few drops of cocaine solution made the eye insensitive enough for surgery, and the age of local anaesthesia began. (The New York surgeon William Halsted developed cocaine nerve blocks in 1885 by experimenting on himself and became dependent on cocaine, and later on morphine.) As reports of cocaine dependence and psychosis accumulated, Freud was widely criticised. He stopped using cocaine around 1887 and seems to have had no difficulty doing so. His other drug was a different story. Freud smoked about 20 cigars a day. Told in 1894, at 38, to stop because of an irregular heartbeat, he managed seven weeks; once he stopped for fourteen months, and relapsed. In 1923, aged 67, he developed cancer of the mouth, and although he wrote that smoking had caused it, he kept smoking through attacks of chest pain whenever he smoked (tobacco angina) and through 33 operations by 1936, which cut away much of his upper jaw and palate and left him with an artificial prosthesis, so that he could swallow and speak only with difficulty. At 73, admitted to hospital for his heart, he stopped, and 23 days later he started again. He died in London in 1939, when his physician, at Freud's request, gave him the doses of morphine that ended the suffering of his incurable cancer. Pinel tells the story to make two points: nobody, however intelligent, is immune to addiction; and the drug that defeated Freud was not the dramatic, illegal one but tobacco. Cocaine comes in several forms, and the differences are mainly about speed. Coca leaves are soaked and treated to make a crude coca paste , which is purified into cocaine hydrochloride , the white powder usually meant by "cocaine". Because it is a salt, the powder dissolves in water and can be sniffed ("snorted") so that it is absorbed through the lining of the nose, or injected; but heat destroys it, so it cannot be smoked. The base form of cocaine, by contrast, vaporises when heated and can be smoked. Freebase and crack are smokeable base forms; crack, named after the crackling sound it makes when smoked, is the cheap, impure version that spread through American cities from the mid-1980s. Smoked cocaine reaches the brain within seconds, as fast as an injection, while snorted cocaine takes minutes and coca leaf much longer. The faster the rise in the brain, the more intense the high and the stronger the compulsion to repeat it, a rule explained in Section 10.2. Cocaine also has a short half-life of about an hour, so the high fades quickly and users redose again and again, often in binges that last until the money or the drug runs out. Cocaine has two actions that have nothing to do with pleasure but explain several of its dangers. It blocks sodium channels in nerve membranes, which is why it is a local anaesthetic (it was replaced in most medical uses by synthetic relatives such as procaine and lidocaine, whose names still end in its "-caine"); and it constricts blood vessels, which is why surgeons once used it to reduce bleeding in the nose and why chronic snorting can destroy the cartilage between the nostrils. The amphetamines, and how the stimulants act Amphetamine was first made in 1887 in Germany by the Romanian chemist Lazăr Edeleanu (1861 to 1941), who called it phenylisopropylamine and did not study its effects. In 1893 the Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi made methamphetamine from ephedrine, the active ingredient of the Chinese herb ma huang, and in 1919 Akira Ogata produced it in crystalline form. Amphetamine's effects on the body were rediscovered in 1927 by the American chemist Gordon Alles, who was looking for a substitute for ephedrine as an asthma treatment and tested it on himself, and in the early 1930s the firm Smith, Kline and French sold it as the Benzedrine inhaler for blocked noses. Users soon discovered that they could break open the inhaler and swallow the amphetamine-soaked paper strip inside. In the Second World War amphetamines were given to soldiers and pilots on both sides to keep them awake: German forces received millions of tablets of methamphetamine under the brand name Pervitin, and in Japan it was sold as Philopon, which after the war led to a large epidemic of methamphetamine use there. In the decades that followed, amphetamines were prescribed for slimming, for depression and as "pep pills". Today their main medical uses are attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy (Chapter 3, Section 3.8, describes the prescription stimulants for ADHD), but illicit methamphetamine, as tablets, powder or the smokeable crystals called "ice" or "crystal meth", is a major drug of misuse; Pinel notes that the amphetamine-type stimulants are now more widely misused worldwide than cocaine. DSM-5-TR's "amphetamine-type substances" include amphetamine, dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine, and also drugs with different structures but similar effects such as methylphenidate and modafinil, and the plant stimulant khat. How do these drugs act? Recall from Section 10.2 that after a dopamine neuron releases dopamine into the synapse, the signal is ended mainly by reuptake: a protein in the presynaptic membrane called the dopamine transporter pumps the dopamine back into the neuron. Similar transporters clear noradrenaline and serotonin. Cocaine and amphetamine both raise the level of these monoamines in the synapse, but in different ways. Cocaine is a reuptake blocker. It sits on the dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin transporters and jams them, so transmitter that the neuron releases stays in the synapse longer and at higher concentration. Cocaine therefore amplifies the neuron's own activity: its effect depends on the neuron firing. Amphetamine is a releaser. It is similar enough in shape to dopamine and noradrenaline to be carried into the nerve terminal by the transporters. Once inside, it disrupts the storage of transmitter in vesicles and makes the transporters run backwards, so dopamine and noradrenaline pour out into the synapse whether or not the neuron is firing. At high doses it also inhibits monoamine oxidase, the enzyme that breaks these transmitters down. Methamphetamine does the same, enters the brain more readily and lasts longer. In both cases the extra dopamine in the nucleus accumbens produces the euphoria and the drive to repeat, and the extra noradrenaline produces the "fight or flight" effects on the body: racing heart, raised blood pressure, dilated pupils, sweating and loss of appetite. Table 10.24 compares the two drugs. One more principle links them. Repeated doses produce tolerance to the euphoria, so users need more to get high, but they produce the opposite, sensitisation (reverse tolerance, defined in Section 10.1), to some other effects: repetitive movements, agitation and paranoia appear at lower doses after repeated binges.
