Stimulant intoxication and its physical dangers When injected or smoked, a stimulant produces an instant surge of well-being, confidence and euphoria. Users describe feeling clever, attractive, tireless and in control; they talk fast, laugh easily, make plans and feel no need to eat or sleep. With higher doses the pleasure acquires an edge: restlessness, irritability, anxiety, suspiciousness and hypervigilance, grinding of the teeth, and repetitive, pointless activity. DSM-5-TR's criteria for stimulant intoxication require recent use of an amphetamine-type substance, cocaine or another stimulant; clinically significant behavioural or psychological change (euphoria or blunted feeling, changes in sociability, hypervigilance, sensitivity to others, anxiety, tension or anger, stereotyped behaviour, impaired judgement); and at least two of nine physical signs. Those signs are tachycardia or bradycardia; pupillary dilation; raised or lowered blood pressure; sweating or chills; nausea or vomiting; weight loss; psychomotor agitation or retardation; muscular weakness, respiratory depression, chest pain or cardiac arrhythmias; and confusion, seizures, abnormal movements (dyskinesias, dystonias) or coma. Why does a list of stimulant effects include slowing of the heart, low blood pressure and psychomotor retardation? Because the picture depends on the dose, the person's tolerance and how long the use has gone on. The ordinary stimulant effects of a fresh dose are the common ones. The depressant-looking effects (sadness, slow pulse, low blood pressure, slowed movement) appear mainly with chronic high-dose use, when the person is exhausted and the transmitter stores are depleted. The specifier "with perceptual disturbances" is added when hallucinations occur with intact reality testing, or when there are illusions, in the absence of delirium. Stimulant intoxication can kill, and it kills in a different way from opioids. The surge of noradrenaline, together with cocaine's constriction of blood vessels, makes the heart work harder while narrowing the arteries that feed it, so heart attacks occur even in young people with normal coronary arteries; dangerous rhythm disturbances, strokes (both bleeding and blocked vessels) and tears in the wall of the aorta are other emergencies. Body temperature can climb dangerously (hyperthermia), especially in hot, crowded places, and severe toxicity brings convulsions, muscle breakdown, kidney failure and death. Combinations add their own dangers. Cocaine taken with alcohol produces a compound called cocaethylene in the liver, which is more toxic to the heart than either drug; cocaine injected with heroin (a "speedball") combines the cardiac risk of one with the respiratory risk of the other. Long-term methamphetamine users often lose weight, develop severe tooth decay and skin sores from picking, and show cognitive problems; Pinel notes that people who have used amphetamine or methamphetamine, but not cocaine, have a raised risk of later developing Parkinson's disease, although the evidence is correlational. There is no antidote like naloxone for stimulants. Emergency care is supportive: a calm, cool environment, benzodiazepines for agitation and seizures, cooling for hyperthermia and monitoring of the heart. Exam trap Pupils are dilated in stimulant intoxication (and in opioid withdrawal and hallucinogen intoxication); they are pinpoint in opioid intoxication. Stimulant intoxication kills mainly through the heart and brain (myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, stroke) and through hyperthermia and seizures , not through respiratory depression as with opioids. Cocaine plus alcohol forms cocaethylene . DSM-5-TR's list of intoxication signs includes bradycardia and low blood pressure as well as their opposites, because chronic high-dose use can produce depressant-like effects. Stimulant psychosis and formication In the early 1950s a puzzling group of patients began to appear in London hospitals. They were admitted with delusions of persecution and diagnosed as having paranoid schizophrenia, yet within days of admission their symptoms cleared and they went home. A young psychiatrist at the Maudsley Hospital, Philip Connell , suspected amphetamine, then freely available in tablets and inhalers. He developed a urine test to detect it and collected cases, and in 1958 he published the monograph Amphetamine Psychosis . Connell showed that amphetamine could produce a psychosis that was often indistinguishable from acute paranoid schizophrenia: persecutory delusions and ideas of reference, auditory and visual hallucinations, in a person who was usually fully alert and oriented (only a handful of his patients were disoriented). It occurred mainly in people taking large doses, and it usually settled within about a week of stopping. Doubters suggested that the drug had merely triggered schizophrenia in people already prone to it, so researchers tested the idea directly: in 1970 Burton Angrist and Samuel Gershon gave volunteers who had used amphetamine before, but had no history of psychosis, repeated doses of it under hospital supervision, and several developed paranoid psychoses. Stimulant psychosis became one of the main supports for the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia (Chapter 4, Section 4.8), and substance-induced psychotic disorder is described in Chapter 4, Section 4.5.6. The psychosis usually builds through a binge. Suspiciousness comes first: the user checks the window, peers through the curtains, believes the neighbours or the police are watching. Ideas of reference follow (a passing car, a remark on television, a cough in the next room are taken as signals), then frank persecutory delusions, often with jealousy, and hallucinations. DSM-5-TR describes paranoid ideation, auditory hallucinations in a clear sensorium and tactile hallucinations, which the person usually recognises as drug effects; visual hallucinations are common as well, as Connell had found. The person may be violent in what he believes is self-defence. Many show stereotypy , repetitive purposeless behaviour, and the Swedish psychiatrist Gösta Rylander, studying people who injected stimulants in Stockholm, described in 1972 what users called "punding": hours spent compulsively taking apart and reassembling radios and clocks, sorting objects or grooming. Cocaine psychosis is usually brief, lasting hours to days, because the drug is short-acting; amphetamine and methamphetamine psychoses last longer. Most clear within days to a week once the person stops and sleeps, although DSM-5-TR notes that cocaine-related disturbances can persist for up to a month, and a minority of people go on to develop a lasting psychotic illness. The tactile hallucinations deserve special attention because examiners ask about them. Formication (from the Latin formica , ant) is the false perception of insects crawling on or under the skin. Users of cocaine call them "cocaine bugs", and the French psychiatrist Valentin Magnan (1835 to 1916) described in 1889 how his cocaine-using patients felt foreign bodies, like fine sand or powder, moving beneath the skin, a symptom since called Magnan's sign . The sensation is so convincing that people scratch and dig at the skin with fingernails, needles or knives to get the "bugs" out, and arrive with excoriations and infected sores on their forearms and face. During intoxication many users recognise the sensations as drug effects, which is why DSM-5-TR's "perceptual disturbances" specifier refers to hallucinations with intact reality testing; when insight is lost, the sensations become part of a delusion of infestation. Formication is a sign (Chapter 2, Section 2.3) rather than a diagnosis, and it has a short list of usual causes: stimulant intoxication (cocaine and amphetamines), and withdrawal from alcohol (delirium tremens, Section 10.3) or from sedative-hypnotics (Section 10.7). It is also reported with nerve damage from diabetes or alcohol, around the menopause, and in delusional infestation (Ekbom's syndrome), where a person is fixedly convinced, without drugs, that parasites live in the skin. Satish, a 29-year-old events manager in Mumbai, was brought to the emergency department by his flatmate at four in the morning. For three days and nights he had been taking mephedrone ("MD") and then methamphetamine at a series of parties, and he had not slept. He was pacing, sweating and talking rapidly, convinced that the neighbours had hidden cameras in the ceiling fan and were sending what they filmed to a gang who planned to kill him. He kept looking at the door and said he could hear men whispering his name in the corridor. Every few seconds he rubbed his forearms, which were scratched raw: tiny insects, he said, were crawling under his skin, and he had tried to cut one out with a razor blade. His pupils were widely dilated, his pulse was 128 a minute, his blood pressure high and his temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. Yet he knew where he was, the date and the name of his flatmate, and he could count backwards without error. A urine test was positive for amphetamines. With a quiet room, intravenous fluids, a benzodiazepine for agitation and, for two days, a low dose of an antipsychotic, he slept for most of 36 hours. By the fourth day the voices and the insects had gone, and he was embarrassed about the cameras. His clear consciousness and intact orientation are what distinguish a stimulant psychosis from delirium (Section 10.8): the confusion, fluctuation and disorientation of delirium are absent, even though the hallucinations are vivid. How do you tell a stimulant psychosis from a first episode of schizophrenia? The clues are the history of a binge in the days before, prominent visual and tactile hallucinations (in schizophrenia hallucinations are mainly auditory), physical signs of stimulant use, a positive urine test, relatively preserved emotional expression with little thought disorder or negative symptoms, and above all rapid resolution within days of abstinence. If psychotic symptoms persist well beyond a month of abstinence, an independent psychotic disorder becomes much more likely. Exam trap Formication (tactile hallucinations of insects crawling on or under the skin) is most characteristic of stimulant intoxication (cocaine bugs, Magnan's sign) and of alcohol or sedative withdrawal , classically delirium tremens. The tempting wrong options do not produce it. Major depressive disorder with psychotic features produces mood-congruent delusions (guilt, ruin, disease) and, less often, accusing or derogatory voices, not crawling insects. Specific phobia is intense fear of an object or situation such as insects or spiders: the fear is of a real or anticipated stimulus, and there is no false perception at all. Generalised anxiety disorder is chronic, uncontrollable worry with tension, restlessness and fatigue; the tingling or numbness some anxious people feel comes from overbreathing and is not experienced as insects. Amphetamine psychosis resembles paranoid schizophrenia (Connell 1958) but occurs in clear consciousness and usually resolves within days to a week. The crash and stimulant withdrawal What goes up must come down, and with stimulants the coming down has its own name: the crash . After a binge the stores of dopamine and noradrenaline are depleted, the receptors have adapted to a flood that has suddenly stopped, and the person is left exhausted, flat and miserable. DSM-5-TR's criteria for stimulant withdrawal require the stopping or reduction of prolonged stimulant use, followed within a few hours to several days by dysphoric mood plus at least two of five physiological changes: fatigue; vivid, unpleasant dreams; insomnia or hypersomnia; increased appetite; and psychomotor retardation or agitation. Notice the mirror image again. Intoxication brought euphoria, energy, sleeplessness, loss of appetite and agitation; withdrawal brings dysphoria, fatigue, long heavy sleep, hunger and slowing. The manual adds that the heart rate often falls (bradycardia is a reliable sign), and that anhedonia and craving are common although they are not among the criteria. Physically, stimulant withdrawal is mild. There are no seizures, no delirium and no danger to life of the kind that alcohol or sedative withdrawal brings, and this is why the older literature called cocaine "psychologically" rather than "physically" addictive. The danger is psychological. The depressed mood can be intense enough to meet the criteria for a major depressive episode, it usually resolves within about a week, and DSM-5-TR singles out depressive symptoms with suicidal thoughts or behaviour as the most serious problem of the crash. A person crashing after a binge needs to be asked about suicide. Table 10.25 sets intoxication and withdrawal side by side. The most influential description of what happens after a cocaine binge came from Frank Gawin and Herbert Kleber at Yale. In 1986 they reported detailed longitudinal interviews with 30 chronic cocaine users and described a three-phase sequence of abstinence, shown in Figure 10.12. The first phase, the crash, begins within hours of the end of a binge and lasts up to about four days: agitation and depression give way to exhaustion, very long sleep and ravenous hunger, and during this phase craving is surprisingly low; the person wants sleep, not cocaine. The second phase, withdrawal proper, lasts for weeks (up to about ten in their account): mood is flat, energy is low and nothing gives pleasure, and against this joyless background craving returns, sharpened by memories of the high and by every reminder of using. This is when relapse is most likely. The third phase, extinction, is indefinite: mood returns to normal, but people, places, money, music or a glimpse of white powder can still trigger sudden, intense craving months or years later. Later studies of cocaine-dependent patients kept on a hospital or research ward, away from such cues (William Weddington and colleagues at the National Institute on Drug Abuse in 1990, following 12 men for 28 days, and Sally Satel and colleagues at Yale in 1991, following 22 patients for three weeks), found that mood distress and craving were worst at admission and then improved gradually and steadily, without a distinct crash or second phase, which suggests that much of the craving Gawin and Kleber saw in outpatients was driven by cues in the environment, exactly as conditioning theory predicts (Section 10.2). MDMA (ecstasy) and the synthetic cathinones MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine) is a ring-substituted amphetamine. It was first made by the German company Merck in 1912 as an intermediate in a chemical synthesis and then forgotten. In 1976 the American chemist Alexander Shulgin (1925 to 2014) made it again, noticed its unusual emotional effects and introduced it to a psychotherapist friend, and in the late 1970s and early 1980s some therapists in the United States used it to help patients talk about painful experiences. At the same time it spread into nightclubs and dance parties as "ecstasy", and in 1985 the United States banned it. It is usually taken as a tablet or as crystals ("Molly") at parties and festivals. MDMA works mainly as a releaser of serotonin : like amphetamine it enters nerve terminals through a transporter and reverses it, but it acts most strongly on the serotonin transporter, releasing large amounts of serotonin, with smaller effects on noradrenaline and dopamine; it also raises the hormone oxytocin. The result is a stimulant high with a distinctive emotional colour. Users feel euphoric, energetic and above all close to other people: warm, open, trusting and empathic. For this reason MDMA is called an empathogen or entactogen, and Pinel describes it as both a stimulant and an empathogen. DSM-5-TR, however, does not file MDMA with the stimulants. It lists MDMA among the hallucinogens, with mescaline in the chemical group called the phenylalkylamines, and notes that its effects come from both its hallucinogenic and its stimulant properties. A person with problems from MDMA is therefore diagnosed with other hallucinogen use disorder or other hallucinogen intoxication , never with a stimulant-related disorder, and the manual adds that ecstasy users have a higher risk of developing a hallucinogen use disorder than users of other hallucinogens. Because DSM-5-TR has no hallucinogen withdrawal diagnosis, there is no MDMA withdrawal diagnosis either, although many regular users report malaise, poor appetite, low, anxious or irritable mood, poor concentration and disturbed sleep after stopping. ICD-11, by contrast, gives MDMA and related drugs a category of their own (Table 10.27). The physical effects are those of an amphetamine: a fast heart, raised blood pressure, jaw clenching and teeth grinding, sweating and loss of appetite. The deaths that make the news come from a few specific dangers. The first is hyperthermia : MDMA raises body temperature, and hours of dancing in a hot, crowded venue can push it to levels that cause muscle breakdown, kidney failure, clotting failure and death. The second is hyponatraemia , a dangerous fall in blood sodium: MDMA makes the body release antidiuretic hormone and hold on to water, so a user who drinks large amounts of water to avoid overheating can dilute the blood sodium enough to make the brain swell, causing confusion, seizures and coma. The third is serotonin toxicity (serotonin syndrome), particularly when MDMA is combined with antidepressants, tramadol or other serotonergic drugs. Some users also describe a "midweek low", a few days of low mood and irritability after a weekend of use, attributed to depleted serotonin. Whether regular MDMA use permanently damages serotonin neurons has been argued for decades. High doses damage serotonergic axons in animals, and heavy users perform slightly worse on some memory tests, but Pinel notes that the effects in humans have often been small or hard to reproduce. The debate was not helped when an influential paper in Science in 2002, claiming that a typical recreational dose regimen caused severe damage to dopamine neurons in monkeys, was retracted in 2003 after the researchers discovered that the animals had been injected with methamphetamine from mislabelled bottles. Interest in MDMA as a therapeutic drug has returned. Trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder reported promising results, and since July 2023 Australia has allowed specially authorised psychiatrists to prescribe it for PTSD. In August 2024, however, the United States Food and Drug Administration declined to approve it, asking for further studies because of concerns about the design and conduct of the trials. Psychedelic-assisted therapy more generally is discussed in Section 10.7. The synthetic cathinones are relatives of cathinone, the stimulant in the leaves of the khat shrub ( Catha edulis ), which are chewed socially in Yemen and East Africa. Chemists have made dozens of synthetic versions, such as mephedrone, MDPV and alpha-PVP, sold as "legal highs" or, in North America, disguised as "bath salts". They act like amphetamines or cocaine and can cause severe agitation, paranoid psychosis, hyperthermia and death. In India mephedrone, known as "MD" or "meow meow", spread in Mumbai's party scene and was brought under the NDPS Act in February 2015; Satish's binge in Section 10.6.4 began with it. ICD-11 gives the synthetic cathinones a separate category; DSM-5-TR includes them among the stimulants. Exam trap MDMA (ecstasy) is a ring-substituted amphetamine that acts mainly by releasing serotonin ; it is an empathogen (entactogen). In DSM-5-TR it sits under other hallucinogen-related disorders , not stimulant-related disorders. Its specific dangers are hyperthermia, hyponatraemia and serotonin toxicity . The synthetic cathinones ("bath salts", mephedrone) are stimulants related to khat. Do not confuse MDMA with ketamine or PCP, which are dissociative NMDA antagonists (Section 10.7). Treating stimulant use disorder DSM-5-TR's stimulant use disorder uses the same eleven criteria as the other substance use disorders (Section 10.1), with one familiar note: tolerance and withdrawal do not count when the stimulant is taken as prescribed, for example for ADHD or narcolepsy. The manual adds that stimulant use disorder can develop very fast, sometimes within a week of starting to use. The disappointing fact about treatment is that, despite decades of trials, no medicine has yet been approved for treating cocaine or methamphetamine use disorder. Researchers have tried antidepressants to lift the crash, dopamine agonists to replace the missing dopamine, disulfiram, modafinil, topiramate and even vaccines that make antibodies against cocaine; none has proved reliably effective. The most encouraging trial so far was published in 2021 by Madhukar Trivedi and colleagues: in adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder, a combination of extended-release injectable naltrexone (every three weeks) and daily oral bupropion produced a response (at least three of four urine samples free of methamphetamine at the end of treatment) in 13.6 percent, compared with 2.5 percent on placebo. That is a real effect, but most patients did not respond. For now, the treatments with the strongest evidence are psychological, and the strongest of all came from a simple behavioural idea. Key study: Higgins's vouchers for cocaine-free urine (1991 to 1994) In the late 1980s cocaine dependence was considered almost untreatable in outpatients. Stephen Higgins and his colleagues at the University of Vermont reasoned that if drug use is behaviour maintained by its reinforcing consequences (Section 10.2), then a competing, immediate reinforcer for not using might change it. They combined the community reinforcement approach (which helps the person build a rewarding life without the drug: relationships, work, recreation) with contingency management : patients gave urine samples several times a week, and each cocaine-free sample earned a voucher that could be exchanged for goods in local shops, with the value rising for each consecutive clean sample and resetting after a positive one. After early reports in 1991 and 1993, they published a randomised trial in 1994 in which 40 cocaine-dependent adults received the community reinforcement treatment with or without the vouchers. In the voucher group 75 percent completed 24 weeks of treatment, against 40 percent without vouchers, and the average length of continuous cocaine abstinence confirmed by urine tests was 11.7 weeks against 6.0 weeks. Many later trials have confirmed that contingency management is one of the most effective treatments for stimulant use disorders. The criticisms are practical and moral: the effect fades when the incentives stop, the programme costs money, and many people dislike "paying people not to use drugs". The technique itself is described in Book 2, Section 4.5.7. Other psychological treatments with good evidence are cognitive-behavioural therapy focused on coping with craving and high-risk situations, the community reinforcement approach on its own, and structured outpatient programmes that combine these with family involvement and drug testing; mutual-help groups such as Narcotics Anonymous help many people stay abstinent (Book 2, Sections 7.11.7 and 9.9). Acute problems are treated as they arise: the crash with rest, food and attention to suicide risk, stimulant psychosis with a calm environment, benzodiazepines and, if needed, a short course of an antipsychotic. Stimulants are still uncommon in India compared with alcohol, cannabis and opioids. The 2019 national survey found current use of cocaine in 0.10 percent of Indians aged 10 to 75 and of amphetamine-type stimulants in 0.18 percent, among the lowest of all the substance categories. Use is concentrated in particular places and groups: cocaine among affluent party-goers in the big cities, mephedrone in Mumbai and other cities, and methamphetamine tablets ( yaba , a mixture of methamphetamine and caffeine) and crystal methamphetamine entering the north-eastern states from Myanmar. Exam trap There is no approved medication for cocaine or methamphetamine use disorder; there is no stimulant equivalent of methadone or naloxone. The best-supported treatment is contingency management (vouchers or prizes for drug-free urine), developed for cocaine by Stephen Higgins in the early 1990s, usually combined with the community reinforcement approach . Disulfiram's established use is for alcohol (Section 10.4), not stimulants. Tobacco and nicotine Tobacco, Nicotiana tabacum , is a plant of the Americas. Spanish and Portuguese sailors carried it to Europe in the sixteenth century, and its active alkaloid is named after Jean Nicot, the French ambassador in Lisbon who sent tobacco to the French court in 1560 and promoted it as a medicine. Portuguese traders brought it to India around the end of the sixteenth century, and within a few generations it was being smoked in hookahs and chillums, chewed with betel and lime, and later rolled into the bidi, a little tobacco wrapped in a tendu leaf. Freud's story in Section 10.6.1 already shows its power. Pinel puts the point another way: can you think of any other psychoactive drug that people take almost continuously, even while walking along the street? Nicotine acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors , ion channels that normally open in response to acetylcholine. The subtype most important for addiction, made of alpha4 and beta2 subunits, sits on dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area and on the nerve terminals that feed them; when nicotine opens these channels, the dopamine neurons fire and release dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, the same final common path that cocaine and heroin use (Section 10.2). Nicotine also releases noradrenaline, acetylcholine, serotonin and endorphins, which helps explain the smoker's paradox of feeling both more alert and more relaxed after a cigarette. Three features of the way nicotine is delivered make it extraordinarily addictive. Inhaled smoke carries nicotine from the lungs to the brain within about ten to twenty seconds, faster than an injection into an arm vein. Nicotine's half-life is short (about two hours), so smokers top up throughout the day. And each cigarette is about ten puffs, so a person who smokes twenty cigarettes a day gives the brain some two hundred separate doses, each paired with a cup of tea, the end of a meal, a work break, a phone call or a moment of stress, so that the whole fabric of daily life becomes a set of cues for smoking. Repeated exposure also changes the receptors themselves: they desensitise during the day (the first cigarette of the morning, after the receptors have recovered overnight, is usually the most satisfying) and they increase in number in smokers' brains. A non-smoker's first few cigarettes usually cause nausea, dizziness, coughing, sweating and sometimes vomiting; within days tolerance removes these effects, and the smoker reports feeling relaxed, alert and less hungry. That fast tolerance is part of why DSM-5-TR has no diagnosis of tobacco intoxication: in regular users clinically significant intoxication is very rare (ICD-10 does code acute intoxication with tobacco, and ICD-11 keeps a code for nicotine intoxication, which is seen mainly in naive users or after unusually large doses). DSM-5-TR's tobacco use disorder uses the standard eleven criteria for a substance use disorder, two or more within twelve months, with examples adapted to tobacco (smoking in bed as hazardous use; arguments about smoking as a social problem). Some criteria are rarely met: because tobacco is cheap, legal and does not intoxicate, few smokers spend much time getting it or recovering from it, and few fail in their work because of it. The criteria most often met are craving, unsuccessful efforts to cut down, use despite knowing the harm, tolerance and withdrawal. Markers of dependence include smoking within 30 minutes of waking, smoking daily, the number of cigarettes per day and waking at night to smoke; the Fagerström questionnaire built on such items belongs to the Assessment book. A person using nicotine replacement long term, who meets no other criteria, is in remission "on maintenance therapy". Tobacco withdrawal is the syndrome that every smoker who has tried to quit knows. DSM-5-TR requires daily use for at least several weeks, then an abrupt stop or reduction, followed within 24 hours by at least four of seven signs: irritability, frustration or anger; anxiety; difficulty concentrating; increased appetite; restlessness; depressed mood; and insomnia. It usually begins within 24 hours, peaks after two or three days and lasts two or three weeks. The heart rate falls by 5 to 12 beats a minute in the first few days, and weight rises by an average of 2 to 3 kilograms over the first year. About half of daily smokers who stop for two days or more have four or more symptoms, most commonly anxiety, irritability and difficulty concentrating. Craving is not one of the criteria, but it is almost universal and it is the main reason people fail. Notice that tobacco withdrawal, unlike alcohol withdrawal, contains no tremor, seizures or hallucinations, and unlike opioid withdrawal no streaming eyes or diarrhoea: it is a syndrome of mood, concentration and appetite. Thangam, a 52-year-old auto-rickshaw driver in Madurai, had smoked about twenty-five bidis a day since he was sixteen and also chewed tobacco with betel leaf after meals. When the doctor at the medical college told him that his breathlessness was chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, he threw away his bidis that evening. By the next afternoon he was snapping at passengers, could not sit still at the auto stand, kept losing track of fares, felt hungry all the time and lay awake most of the night; on the third day he felt low and tearful. On the fifth day, waiting at the tea stall where he had always smoked his mid-morning bidi, he borrowed one from another driver "just to calm down", and within a week he was back to twenty. His withdrawal had all the classic features (irritability, restlessness, poor concentration, increased appetite, insomnia, low mood), and his relapse shows how cues such as the tea stall drive craving long after the first days. On his second attempt he set a quit date with the hospital's tobacco cessation clinic, used a nicotine patch with nicotine gum for breakthrough cravings, and planned what he would do instead at the tea stall; at six months he was still not smoking. Why does any of this matter so much? Because tobacco kills more people than all the other drugs in this chapter together. In 1950 Richard Doll (1912 to 2005) and Austin Bradford Hill (1897 to 1991) reported in the British Medical Journal that patients with lung cancer in London hospitals were far more likely than matched patients without it to be smokers, and in 1951 they began following up about 34,000 male British doctors. After 40 years of this study, now known as the British Doctors Study, Doll, Richard Peto and colleagues concluded in 1994 that about half of all regular cigarette smokers are eventually killed by their habit. After 50 years (2004), men born between 1900 and 1930 who kept smoking cigarettes had died on average about ten years younger than lifelong non-smokers, but stopping at age 50 had halved the excess risk and stopping at 30 had avoided almost all of it. The World Health Organization's current estimate is that tobacco kills more than seven million people a year, and that second-hand smoke alone causes more than 1.6 million premature deaths; about 1.2 billion people use it, most of them in low- and middle-income countries. Smoking causes cancers of the lung, mouth, throat, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, kidney and bladder, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart attacks and strokes, and harms the fetus. Smokeless tobacco causes cancers of the mouth and oral precancerous conditions such as leukoplakia and oral submucous fibrosis. Pinel's most chilling illustration is Buerger's disease, a narrowing of the blood vessels of the legs seen mostly in male smokers, in which continued smoking leads to gangrene and amputation after amputation, and yet surgeons report patients smoking in their hospital beds after the second or third operation. Indian context The second Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS-2, 2016 to 2017) found that 28.6 percent of Indian adults aged 15 and over, about 26.7 crore people, used tobacco in some form, down from 34.6 percent in the first survey of 2009 to 2010. Use was 42.4 percent among men and 14.2 percent among women. India is unusual in that smokeless tobacco is used by more people (21.4 percent of adults) than smoked tobacco (10.7 percent). The smokeless products include khaini (tobacco rubbed with lime), gutka (tobacco with areca nut, lime and flavourings), zarda (flavoured tobacco chewed with betel), mawa, mishri and gul (roasted tobacco rubbed on the teeth and gums), and betel quid with tobacco; among smoked products, the bidi is more common than the cigarette. Women use tobacco mainly in smokeless forms. The main law is the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA), 2003, which bans smoking in public places, tobacco advertising, sale to anyone under 18 and sale within 100 yards of an educational institution, and requires health warnings on packs (pictorial warnings now cover most of the pack). Most states have banned gutka under food safety regulations since 2012, and the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019, bans e-cigarettes. The National Tobacco Control Programme runs tobacco cessation centres and a national quitline. Exam trap "Which substance has the highest addictive liability: marijuana, alcohol, nicotine (tobacco) or cocaine?" The answer is nicotine . Addictive liability (the capture rate) means the proportion of people who try a drug who go on to become dependent, and in the large American surveys that proportion is higher for tobacco than for any other drug. In the National Comorbidity Survey (Anthony, Warner and Kessler, 1994) about a third of everyone who had ever smoked had become dependent, against nearly a quarter of heroin users, about one in six cocaine users, about one in seven drinkers and fewer than one in ten users of cannabis; the later NESARC survey put the lifetime figure for nicotine at about two thirds (Section 10.2.5 and Table 10.11 give the full figures). Cocaine is the tempting option because it is more intensely rewarding per dose and animals will work hard for it, but a smaller share of people who try it become dependent. Alcohol is used by far more people but captures a smaller proportion of them, and marijuana has the lowest liability of the four. Nicotine wins because of its speed of delivery, the hundreds of doses a day, its legality and cheapness, and because it does not intoxicate, so it fits into every part of life. DSM-5-TR has tobacco use disorder and tobacco withdrawal but no tobacco intoxication . Helping people stop smoking Most smokers want to stop, and most attempts fail: Pinel notes that only about 20 percent of attempts to stop smoking succeed for two years or more, and attempts made without help do worse. The behavioural side of treatment (the five As of brief advice, setting a quit date, planning for high-risk situations, coping with cravings and relapse prevention) is described in Book 2, Section 9.4.4. Here we look at the medicines, which roughly double the chance of success and work best combined with behavioural support. Table 10.26 summarises them. Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) supplies nicotine without the tar, carbon monoxide and other toxins of smoke, and in a slower, steadier form that relieves withdrawal and craving without the rapid spike that makes smoking so reinforcing. It comes as chewing gum (chewed until the taste comes, then "parked" against the cheek so the nicotine is absorbed through the lining of the mouth), skin patches worn for 16 or 24 hours, lozenges, inhalators and sprays. Combining a patch, for a steady background level, with a short-acting form for breakthrough cravings works better than either alone. Bupropion , an antidepressant that blocks the reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline and also blocks nicotinic receptors, is started a week or two before the quit date; it reduces craving and the low mood of withdrawal, but it lowers the seizure threshold and must not be used by people with epilepsy, eating disorders or a risk of seizures from alcohol or sedative withdrawal. Varenicline , introduced in 2006, is the most effective single medicine. It is a partial agonist at the alpha4 beta2 nicotinic receptor, and its logic is exactly that of buprenorphine in Figure 10.11. Because it partly activates the receptor, it releases enough dopamine to ease withdrawal and craving; because it binds tightly and occupies the receptor, a cigarette smoked on top of it gives much less reward. Its common side effects are nausea and vivid dreams. Early reports of depression, agitation and suicidal thoughts led to a boxed warning in the United States, but the large EAGLES trial (2016), which included smokers with psychiatric illnesses, found no significant increase in moderate or severe neuropsychiatric adverse events with varenicline compared with placebo or the nicotine patch, and in December 2016 the warning was removed. Varenicline was modelled on cytisine , a plant alkaloid from the seeds of the laburnum tree that has been sold cheaply in Eastern Europe as a smoking aid since the 1960s. Trials published in 2011 by Robert West and colleagues (against placebo) and in 2014 by Natalie Walker and colleagues (against NRT) showed that cytisine works, and because it is so inexpensive it is attractive for countries like India; the World Health Organization's 2024 guideline on tobacco cessation recommends varenicline, NRT, bupropion and cytisine. Electronic cigarettes, first produced by the Chinese pharmacist Hon Lik in 2003, help some smokers to quit but also draw young people into nicotine use; India banned them in 2019. Two facts matter on a psychiatric ward. First, compounds in tobacco smoke (not the nicotine itself) speed up a liver enzyme that breaks down several psychiatric medicines, clozapine and olanzapine among them; when a patient stops smoking, for example on admission to a smoke-free ward, the blood levels of these drugs can rise sharply and cause toxicity, so doses may need to be reduced. Second, the irritability and restlessness of tobacco withdrawal can be mistaken for agitation, akathisia or alcohol withdrawal; DSM-5-TR notes that relief of the symptoms by nicotine confirms the diagnosis. Exam trap Varenicline is a partial agonist at the alpha4 beta2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (not an antagonist, and not a dopamine agonist); cytisine works the same way. Bupropion is an antidepressant that inhibits dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake and is contraindicated in epilepsy and eating disorders. Tobacco withdrawal requires four of seven signs within 24 hours ; it peaks at 2 to 3 days and lasts 2 to 3 weeks. Doll and Hill linked smoking to lung cancer in 1950 . Caffeine Caffeine is the most widely used psychoactive drug in the world. It is found in coffee, tea, cola drinks, energy drinks, chocolate, many cold and headache remedies and some slimming pills; a cup of brewed coffee typically contains roughly 100 milligrams, a cup of tea rather less than half that, and DSM-5-TR reports that American adults who use caffeine take about 280 milligrams a day on average. Because it is woven into daily rituals (the morning filter coffee, the office tea break), many people do not realise that they are physically dependent on it until they miss a dose. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors. Adenosine builds up in the brain during the hours of waking, and by acting on its receptors it inhibits the activity of many neurons and produces the growing pressure to sleep (Chapter 8). Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist : it occupies the receptors without activating them, so the "brake" of adenosine is released and the person feels alert, with faster reaction times and less fatigue. Through receptors that interact with dopamine receptors in the striatum it also has mild rewarding effects. Its half-life is about 4 to 6 hours; oral contraceptives slow its elimination and smoking speeds it up, so a heavy coffee drinker who stops smoking may find the same coffee suddenly making him jittery. DSM-5-TR recognises two caffeine diagnoses in its main text. Caffeine intoxication requires recent consumption of caffeine, typically a high dose well in excess of 250 milligrams, followed by five or more of twelve signs: restlessness, nervousness, excitement, insomnia, flushed face, diuresis (passing a lot of urine), gastrointestinal disturbance, muscle twitching, a rambling flow of thought and speech, tachycardia or cardiac arrhythmia, periods of inexhaustibility, and psychomotor agitation. The first seven can appear at quite modest doses in sensitive people such as children, the elderly and those not used to caffeine; the last five usually need more than a gram a day. Picture a postgraduate student who, in the week before an entrance examination, drinks six strong coffees and two energy drinks a day: he is wired and tremulous, his heart races, he cannot sleep, his stomach churns, he keeps running to the toilet and his thoughts tumble out faster than he can organise them. Caffeine intoxication can look like a panic attack, generalised anxiety, mania or amphetamine intoxication, and the timing of the symptoms in relation to caffeine is the clue. It usually clears within a day, but very large doses (5 to 10 grams, possible with caffeine tablets or powders) can be fatal. Caffeine withdrawal requires prolonged daily use, then an abrupt stop or reduction, followed within 24 hours by three or more of five signs: headache; marked fatigue or drowsiness; dysphoric or depressed mood or irritability; difficulty concentrating; and flu-like symptoms (nausea, vomiting, or muscle pain or stiffness). Headache is the hallmark: diffuse, throbbing and worse on movement. Symptoms usually begin 12 to 24 hours after the last dose, peak after one or two days and last two to nine days, although headaches can recur for up to three weeks, and they vanish within an hour of a cup of coffee. Withdrawal can follow even modest daily intake (about 100 milligrams), and it is often misread as the flu or a migraine: the "weekend headache" of the person who drinks coffee at work but sleeps late on Sunday, or the headache on a fasting day or before an operation when nothing may be taken by mouth. What DSM-5-TR does not have in its main text is a caffeine use disorder. Many caffeine users show tolerance and withdrawal, but the manual judged that there was not yet enough evidence that a full use disorder is clinically significant and common, so caffeine use disorder is listed in Section III as a condition for further study. Its proposed criteria deliberately set a higher bar than the other use disorders: the first three criteria (persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down, continued use despite knowing it is causing a physical or psychological problem, and withdrawal) must all be present, so that only cases of real clinical importance are labelled. ICD-11 similarly gives caffeine codes for harmful use, intoxication and withdrawal but no caffeine dependence. Caffeine can also induce an anxiety disorder or a sleep disorder (Chapter 6 and Chapter 8, Section 8.10). Alcohol and the opioids slow it down; cocaine, the amphetamines, nicotine and caffeine speed it up. The four groups in this section refuse to line up so neatly. Cannabis is the most widely used illegal drug in the world, yet in much of India it is also a legal festival drink, sold in licensed shops and stirred into milk at Holi. The hallucinogens change what a person sees, hears and feels while leaving him wide awake and alert, which is exactly what delirium does not do. The inhalants are not drugs at all in the ordinary sense: they are glue, petrol, paint thinner and the correction fluid in a schoolchild's pencil box. And the sedative-hypnotics are medicines, written on prescription pads by doctors for anxiety and sleeplessness, which turn out to be among the most dangerous drugs a person can stop taking. Two questions will run through the whole section. The first is what each drug does in the brain, and what intoxication with it actually looks like when the person is sitting in front of you. The second is what happens when a regular user stops, and whether that withdrawal can harm him. The answers to the second question cover the whole range, from "no recognised withdrawal at all" (the hallucinogens and the inhalants) to "withdrawal can kill" (the sedatives, like alcohol). At the end of the section, Table 10.31 sets all ten of the DSM-5-TR substance classes side by side, so that you can compare intoxication and withdrawal across the entire chapter at a glance. Cannabis: one plant, many preparations Cannabis is the hemp plant, Cannabis sativa (Pinel also lists Cannabis indica and Cannabis ruderalis as species). For thousands of years people have used it three ways at once: the fibres of its stem for rope and cloth, its seeds as food, and its leaves and flowers for their effects on the mind. Most of the psychoactive chemicals sit in a sticky resin that coats the flowering tops of the female plant, less in its leaves and almost none in its stalks and seeds. That single botanical fact explains the difference between the three preparations every Indian student has heard of, because each is made from a different part of the plant and so carries a different dose. Bhang is made from the dried leaves (and small stems and seeds) of the plant, ground with water into a green paste and then drunk in milk, in the spiced drink thandai or in lassi, or rolled into small balls and eaten. It is the mildest form and the one with the deepest roots in Indian religious life: it is associated with the god Shiva and drunk openly at Holi and Mahashivratri. Ganja is the dried flowering tops of the unpollinated female plant, the part richest in resin; it is smoked, often in a clay pipe (chillum) or rolled into a cigarette, and it is what Western writers call marijuana. Charas is the resin itself, rubbed off the flowering tops by hand and pressed into dark sticks or balls; it is the Indian equivalent of hashish , and it is the strongest of the three. Hashish oil, a solvent extract of the resin, is stronger still. Table 10.28 puts them in order. Table 10.28 The cannabis preparations, in rising order of potency. The first is potency. DSM-5-TR notes that the THC content of seized illegal cannabis has risen steadily over the past twenty years, and that legal products in some American states now reach about 20 percent in plant material and about 68 percent in concentrated extracts. A joint today is not the joint of the 1970s. The second is route. Smoked cannabis acts within minutes, so a user can stop when he feels the effect; cannabis eaten in food ("edibles") or drunk as bhang takes an hour or more to begin and lasts much longer, which is why first-time bhang drinkers at a Holi party so often take a second glass "because nothing is happening" and spend the evening terrified. Newer methods include vaping (heating the plant without burning it) and dabbing (heating a concentrated butane extract and inhaling it), both popular with young users. Key study: the Indian Hemp Drugs Commission (1893 to 1894) In 1893 members of the British House of Commons, worried by reports that ganja smoking was filling the lunatic asylums of Bengal, pressed the Government of India to act. The government appointed a seven-member commission, with W. Mackworth Young as its president, which began work on 3 July 1893 and was soon asked to cover the whole of India rather than Bengal alone. It travelled across the country and took evidence from almost 1,200 witnesses: doctors, officials, soldiers, cultivators, yogis and fakirs among them. It also visited the asylums to examine the cases blamed on hemp drugs. The report, completed in 1894, ran to more than 3,000 pages. Its central conclusion was that the moderate use of hemp drugs was "practically attended by no evil results at all", with no appreciable physical, mental or moral injury, whereas excessive use was harmful: it tended to weaken the constitution and "indicates and intensifies mental instability". The asylum visits helped to undermine the belief, common at the time, that ganja simply caused insanity. The commission remains one of the largest and earliest official inquiries into any drug, and its distinction between moderate and excessive use anticipates the modern idea that the harm of a drug depends on the pattern of use, not just on the drug. India's law still reflects this history. The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act of 1985 makes ganja and charas illegal, but its definition of cannabis leaves out the leaves and seeds when they are not accompanied by the flowering tops, so bhang falls outside it and is regulated by state excise laws instead (Section 10.1 explains the Act). The numbers are large. In the national survey Magnitude of Substance Use in India (2019), about 2.8 percent of Indians aged 10 to 75, roughly 3.1 crore people, had used a cannabis product in the previous year: about 2 percent bhang and about 1.2 percent ganja or charas. Exam trap Learn the three Indian preparations by the part of the plant: bhang = leaves (weakest, drunk), ganja = flowering tops (smoked; the same thing as marijuana), charas = resin (the same thing as hashish, strongest of the three). A favourite distractor swaps ganja and charas. A second trap is the law: bhang is outside the NDPS Act's definition of cannabis, ganja and charas are inside it. THC, the endocannabinoids and how cannabis acts For most of the twentieth century nobody knew which of the plant's many chemicals produced the "high". The answer came from the Israeli chemist Raphael Mechoulam and his colleague Yehiel Gaoni at the Weizmann Institute. Working with hashish seized by the Israeli police, they isolated the main active compound, worked out its structure and partly synthesised it, and published the result in the Journal of the American Chemical Society in 1964. The compound is delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). (Their paper called it delta-1-THC, under an older numbering system for the same molecule; you may see both names.) The plant contains more than 80 related chemicals, the cannabinoids , but THC is the one that produces intoxication and dependence. Knowing the molecule raised a deeper question. Drugs act by fitting receptors, and receptors exist because the brain makes its own chemical to fit them. Why would the human brain carry a receptor for a chemical from a plant? The receptor was found first. In 1988 a cannabinoid receptor was identified in the rat brain, and in 1990 it was cloned; it is now called the CB1 receptor . A second receptor, CB2 , found mainly on cells of the immune system, was cloned in 1993. Pinel points out that CB1 turned out to be one of the most common metabotropic receptors in the whole brain. Then, in 1992, Mechoulam's laboratory in Jerusalem, with William Devane and Lumír Hanuš , isolated from pig brain the brain's own chemical that binds the receptor. They named it anandamide , from the Sanskrit word ananda , bliss. A second such chemical, 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), was described in 1995. Together these are the endocannabinoids , and the receptors and enzymes that make and break them form the endocannabinoid system. The endocannabinoids work in an unusual direction. Most neurotransmitters travel forward, from the neuron that releases them to the one that receives them. Endocannabinoids are made on demand by the receiving neuron and travel backwards across the synapse to CB1 receptors on the sending terminal, where they turn down the release of other transmitters, both excitatory glutamate and inhibitory GABA. They are a brake that the receiving cell applies to its own input. THC hijacks that brake everywhere at once. The map of CB1 receptors, made around 1990, reads like a list of cannabis's effects: they are dense in the hippocampus (hence the impaired short-term memory), the basal ganglia and cerebellum (hence clumsiness and slowed reactions), the cortex (hence distorted thinking and time sense) and the hypothalamus (hence the hunger), and they are sparse in the brainstem centres that control breathing, which is one reason a fatal overdose of cannabis alone is virtually unknown. Like other drugs of abuse, THC also increases dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, indirectly, by quietening the GABA neurons that normally restrain the dopamine cells of the ventral tegmental area (Section 10.2 explains the reward circuit). One other cannabinoid deserves a line. Cannabidiol (CBD) is the second most abundant cannabinoid in many plants. It does not produce a high, it does not act like THC at CB1, and it may blunt some of THC's anxiety-provoking and psychosis-like effects. Cannabis bred for high THC usually contains little CBD, and that imbalance is one suggested reason why modern high-potency cannabis seems more likely to cause psychotic symptoms. Intoxication, use disorder and withdrawal Pinel quotes a 1972 American government commission's description of a usual "social" dose: initial restlessness and hilarity, then a dreamy, carefree relaxation, a sense that space and time have expanded, sharper touch, taste, smell and hearing, hunger with a craving for sweets, and subtle changes in the way thoughts form. To an onlooker, the commission added, the person might look no different at all. Higher doses tell a different story: short-term memory fails, the user loses the thread of a sentence, multistep tasks fall apart, and a sense of unreality, sensory distortion and paranoia can set in. The first-time user, or the user who has eaten far more than he meant to, may have a frank panic attack, convinced that his heart is about to stop or that he is going mad. DSM-5-TR's criteria for cannabis intoxication pull these observations into a rule. There must be recent use; problematic behavioural or psychological change during or shortly after it (impaired coordination, euphoria, anxiety, a sensation of slowed time, impaired judgement, social withdrawal); and at least two of four physical signs within two hours: conjunctival injection (red eyes), increased appetite, dry mouth and a fast heart rate. Notice what is not on the list. The pupils are not markedly changed, unlike opioid intoxication (pinpoint) or stimulant intoxication (dilated). Appetite goes up, whereas alcohol and sedatives usually reduce it, and DSM-5-TR uses exactly this difference, together with the nystagmus, ataxia and aggression that alcohol produces and cannabis usually does not, to tell the two intoxications apart. The specifier "with perceptual disturbances" is used when hallucinations occur with intact reality testing (the person knows the drug is responsible); if insight is lost, the diagnosis becomes a cannabis-induced psychotic disorder. Smoked cannabis acts within minutes and its effects last three to four hours; eaten cannabis takes a few hours to act and lasts longer. Because THC dissolves in fat, it is released slowly from body fat, so effects can linger or return for 12 to 24 hours and urine tests for its metabolite can stay positive for weeks in a heavy user. Can a drug with such gentle effects cause dependence? For decades many people, users and some doctors among them, said no. The evidence now says yes, though less often than with most other drugs. Pinel, citing a 2016 review, gives the proportion of users who become addicted as about 9 percent, against about 21 percent for cocaine, 23 percent for alcohol and 68 percent for tobacco; these are estimates of a user's lifetime chance of ever becoming dependent, a different measure from the proportions already dependent at interview in the National Comorbidity Survey (Table 10.11), which is why tobacco's figure there is lower, about a third, while cannabis stays at about 9 percent in both (Section 10.2 explains these "capture rates" and why tobacco tops the list on either measure). DSM-5-TR gives a higher figure, that 20 to 30 percent of cannabis users have symptoms consistent with a use disorder, mainly because it counts recent users rather than everyone who has ever tried the drug. Cannabis use disorder uses the same eleven criteria as every other substance use disorder (Section 10.1). Early onset, before about age 15, is one of the strongest predictors of later cannabis use disorder and of other substance and mental disorders in young adulthood. Heritable factors account for between 30 and 80 percent of the variance in risk, depending on the study. The decisive change came in 2013, when DSM-5 added cannabis withdrawal , which DSM-IV had not recognised. It follows the stopping of heavy and prolonged use, usually daily or almost daily for at least a few months, and requires three or more of seven features within about a week: irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty, including insomnia and disturbing dreams; decreased appetite or weight loss; restlessness; depressed mood; and at least one physical symptom causing real discomfort (abdominal pain, shakiness, sweating, fever, chills or headache). Onset is usually 24 to 48 hours after the last use, the symptoms peak within two to five days and they settle within one to two weeks, although poor sleep can persist longer. Unlike withdrawal from alcohol, sedatives or opioids, the emotional and behavioural symptoms are more prominent than the physical ones, and the syndrome is not dangerous. It matters clinically because it keeps people using: sleep difficulty is the withdrawal symptom most often linked to relapse. Push a case through these criteria. Chandan, 23, a final-year commerce student in Varanasi, began smoking ganja with friends at 16. By 22 he was smoking several chillums a day, starting soon after waking; evenings that began with "just one" often ended at dawn, and most of his day went in buying, smoking and sleeping off ganja. He had missed two semester examinations, given up the cricket he once played every evening and stopped visiting his friends from college, and his parents had found his stash twice; each time there was a bitter quarrel at home, and each time he promised to stop, and did not. He told the psychologist that he needed "almost double" what he used to smoke to feel anything. Before his final examinations he stopped completely. Two days later he could not sleep, his dreams were vivid and unpleasant, he had no appetite, he sweated at night and he shouted at his younger sister over nothing. On the fifth day he smoked again, "only to get some sleep". Count the criteria: larger amounts than intended, unsuccessful efforts to cut down, much time spent, failure in his role as a student, important activities given up, continued use despite family conflict, tolerance and withdrawal. That is eight of eleven, a severe cannabis use disorder, with cannabis withdrawal. Two longer-term consequences complete the clinical picture. The first is the amotivational syndrome , a term introduced by William McGlothlin and Louis Jolyon West in 1968 for the apathy, passivity, loss of ambition and poor school or work performance seen in some heavy, long-term users. DSM-5-TR still uses the label, describing reduced goal-directed activity and lowered self-efficacy, and notes that chronic use can produce a lack of motivation that resembles persistent depressive disorder. Whether it is a separate syndrome is doubtful: the same picture could be continuous intoxication, an underlying depression, or a personality that was unmotivated before the drug arrived. The second is the cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome , bouts of nausea and repeated vomiting in regular heavy users, which DSM-5-TR says is increasingly seen in emergency departments; many sufferers discover that long hot showers relieve it, and that odd habit is a clue to the diagnosis. Finally, the synthetic cannabinoids sold as "Spice" or "K2" (plant material sprayed with laboratory chemicals that act on CB1) are classed with cannabis in DSM-5-TR, but their potency is unpredictable and they can cause seizures, cardiac problems, psychosis and death. Exam trap Cannabis intoxication gives red eyes, hunger, dry mouth and a fast pulse , with no marked change in the pupils. Cannabis withdrawal exists in DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR (it was added in 2013), so an option saying that cannabis has no withdrawal syndrome is wrong; the classes with no withdrawal diagnosis are the hallucinogens (including phencyclidine) and the inhalants. THC was isolated by Mechoulam and Gaoni (1964); anandamide, the first endocannabinoid, was named from the Sanskrit for bliss (1992). The "amotivational syndrome" is the classic chronic cannabis picture, and its existence as a separate syndrome is disputed. Cannabis, psychosis, the adolescent brain and medical cannabis The most serious question about cannabis is whether it can cause a lasting psychotic illness. Three different things need to be kept apart. First, intoxication itself can bring paranoia and perceptual changes that fade as the drug wears off. Second, a heavy dose, especially of a potent preparation, can produce a cannabis-induced psychotic disorder , with delusions or hallucinations that outlast ordinary intoxication and need treatment in their own right. In India this was described long ago: in 1974 the psychiatrists Gurbakhsh Singh Chopra and J. W. Smith reported 200 in-patients who had developed serious psychiatric reactions after taking cannabis. Third, and most important, cannabis may raise the risk of schizophrenia itself in people who would not otherwise have developed it. The evidence for that third claim began with a Swedish cohort. In 1987 Sven Andréasson and colleagues followed 45,570 young men conscripted into the Swedish army and found that those who had used cannabis more than fifty times by the time of conscription, at 18 to 20, were six times more likely than non-users to be diagnosed with schizophrenia over the next fifteen years. When the same cohort was re-analysed in 2002 by Stanley Zammit and colleagues, with 27 years of follow-up and better control for other drugs and social factors, the excess risk for the heaviest users shrank to about threefold but did not disappear. More recently Marta Di Forti and colleagues compared 901 people with a first episode of psychosis with 1,237 controls across 11 sites in Europe and Brazil (published in 2019). Daily use of high-potency cannabis carried nearly five times the odds of psychosis, and they estimated, assuming the link is causal, that about 30 percent of new cases in London and about 50 percent in Amsterdam, where potent cannabis is easy to buy, could have been prevented if high-potency cannabis had not been available. DSM-5-TR summarises the field by saying that cannabis use in critical periods is consistently associated with a threefold increase in the risk of psychosis. Chapter 4, Section 4.7 places these findings within the wider causes of schizophrenia. Association, however, is not causation, and Pinel urges caution. People destined to develop schizophrenia might use cannabis to soothe early symptoms (self-medication), or a third factor, such as childhood abuse, which DSM-5-TR mentions, or shared genes, might raise the risk of both. The dose-response pattern, the sequence (use usually comes first) and the potency effect all favour a causal contribution, but the honest conclusion is that cannabis is one contributory cause among many, which matters most for young people with a family history of psychosis. The same caution applies to the adolescent brain. A study of the Dunedin birth cohort in New Zealand, published in 2012, found that people who used cannabis persistently from adolescence lost about eight IQ points between childhood and midlife; a critic, Ole Rogeberg , argued in 2013 that differences in social background could explain the result, the authors replied that they could not, and other cohorts have found that family background accounts for much of the gap. Pinel concludes that there is still no convincing direct evidence that cannabis causes brain damage, that the memory problems of heavy users largely fade within about 72 hours of stopping, and that hippocampal differences in users might have been present before use. What is not in dispute is that early, heavy use predicts worse outcomes, whatever the mechanism. Finally, the plant is also a source of medicines. Synthetic THC has been used for decades to reduce nausea and vomiting during cancer chemotherapy and to stimulate appetite in people with AIDS; a mouth spray containing THC and CBD (Sativex) was introduced in several countries in 2010 for the muscle spasticity of multiple sclerosis; and a purified CBD medicine (Epidiolex) was approved in the United States in 2018 for two severe childhood epilepsies. DSM-5-TR adds that when cannabis or a cannabinoid is taken as medically indicated, tolerance and withdrawal may occur but should not be the main basis for diagnosing a use disorder, exactly the rule that applies to prescribed opioids and benzodiazepines. Clinical link A young person who presents with a first psychotic episode should always be asked, specifically and without judgement, about cannabis: how often, what form (bhang, ganja, charas or something stronger), and since what age. The answer shapes the diagnosis (intoxication, a cannabis-induced psychotic disorder or a primary psychotic illness), the advice (continued use after a first episode predicts relapse) and the family work. Urine tests stay positive for weeks in heavy users, so a positive test proves use, not intoxication at the time of the symptoms. Exam trap The Swedish conscript study ( Andréasson and colleagues, 1987 ) found about a sixfold risk of schizophrenia in men who had used cannabis more than fifty times; better-controlled analyses and later studies put the risk at roughly threefold , highest with daily use of high-potency cannabis. These are associations: the papers may call cannabis "a risk factor" or "a contributory cause", never "the cause" of schizophrenia. A cannabis-induced psychotic disorder (symptoms tied to use, beyond ordinary intoxication) is a different diagnosis from schizophrenia. The hallucinogens: LSD, psilocybin and mescaline A hallucinogen is a drug whose main effect is to change perception, mood and thought while the user remains awake, alert and oriented. The name is a little misleading, because true hallucinations (perceptions with no outside object that the person takes to be real) are uncommon; what most users experience are intensified and distorted perceptions that they know are caused by the drug. Other names reflect other views of the same experience. "Psychotomimetic" (mimicking psychosis) was the 1950s research term, used when these drugs were studied as models of schizophrenia; "psychedelic" (mind-manifesting), coined by the British psychiatrist Humphry Osmond in the mid-1950s, reflects the hope that they could reveal the mind's hidden contents. DSM-5-TR groups the classic hallucinogens by chemistry: the phenylalkylamines (mescaline, and also MDMA, which DSM-5-TR places here), the indoleamines (psilocybin and its active product psilocin, from "magic mushrooms", and dimethyltryptamine or DMT), the ergolines (LSD and morning glory seeds) and a few plants such as Salvia divinorum and jimsonweed (a species of datura). Cannabis is deliberately excluded and has its own class, because its effects differ too much. Key study: Albert Hofmann and "Bicycle Day" (1938 to 1943) Albert Hofmann (1906 to 2008) was a chemist at the Sandoz pharmaceutical laboratories in Basel, Switzerland, working on compounds derived from ergot, a fungus that grows on rye. On 16 November 1938 he synthesised the twenty-fifth compound in a series of lysergic acid derivatives, lysergic acid diethylamide , LSD-25. Tests on animals showed nothing of interest, and it was shelved. Five years later, on 16 April 1943, he made it again and, while working, was overcome by restlessness, dizziness and a dreamlike state in which he saw an uninterrupted play of vivid images and colours; he suspected that a trace of the substance had been absorbed through his skin. Three days later, on 19 April 1943, he tested the idea on himself, deliberately swallowing 250 micrograms, a dose he believed tiny but which proved to be several times a strong dose. As the effects mounted he asked his assistant to take him home by bicycle (wartime restrictions limited the use of cars), and on the ride the world around him became distorted and threatening. He feared he was going mad or dying; by the next day he had recovered completely, with a sense of renewal. Users later named the anniversary "Bicycle Day". The conclusion was startling: a substance active in millionths of a gram could transform perception, emotion and the sense of self. Sandoz supplied LSD to psychiatrists for research from 1947, and its potency helped convince a generation of researchers that mental states have a chemical basis. The criticism is equally clear: a single self-experiment, however vivid, cannot separate drug from expectation, a point the idea of "set and setting" would later make. The other classic hallucinogens came from plants long used in religious ritual. Psilocybin, from mushrooms eaten in Mexican ceremonies, was isolated by Hofmann himself in 1958 from Psilocybe mexicana . Mescaline, from the peyote cactus of Mexico and the south-western United States ( Lophophora williamsii ), was isolated by the German chemist Arthur Heffter in 1897 and first synthesised in 1919; the novelist Aldous Huxley's account of taking it, The Doors of Perception (1954), introduced it to a wide public. Despite their different chemistry, these drugs act in the same way: they are agonists at the 5-HT2A receptor , a type of serotonin receptor dense in the cortex. The key evidence is that a drug blocking 5-HT2A receptors, ketanserin, abolished the psychological effects of psilocybin in volunteers in a 1998 study by Franz Vollenweider and colleagues. Their shared receptor also explains a neat example of cross-tolerance: tolerance to LSD develops within a few days of daily use, and a person tolerant to LSD is also tolerant to psilocybin and mescaline, but not to cannabis or amphetamine, which act on other systems. What is a "trip" like? With LSD the effects begin within about an hour and last eight to twelve hours; psilocybin's are shorter, DMT's (when smoked) only minutes. Colours become intense, surfaces seem to breathe or ripple, geometric patterns appear with the eyes closed, and objects leave trails as they move. Senses can cross, so that a sound is "seen" as colour; this is synaesthesia . Time slows or stops; the boundary between self and world can seem to dissolve (depersonalisation and derealisation); emotions swing from euphoria to fear, and many users describe experiences they regard as mystical. DSM-5-TR captures this in its criteria for hallucinogen intoxication (formally, other hallucinogen intoxication): recent use; problematic psychological change such as marked anxiety or depression, ideas of reference, fear of "losing one's mind", paranoid ideas or impaired judgement; perceptual changes occurring in a state of full wakefulness and alertness , such as intensified perception, depersonalisation, derealisation, illusions, hallucinations or synaesthesias; and at least two of seven physical signs: pupillary dilation, tachycardia, sweating, palpitations, blurring of vision, tremors and incoordination. The phrase about full wakefulness is the clinical key. A person in hallucinogen intoxication is not clouded, not disoriented and usually knows that the drug is responsible; a person whose perceptions are disturbed because consciousness itself is clouded has a delirium (Section 10.8). Whether a trip is pleasant or terrifying depends heavily on what the user brings to it and where he takes it. Timothy Leary (1920 to 1996), the Harvard psychologist whose psilocybin research ended with his departure from Harvard in 1963 and who became the best-known evangelist of LSD, popularised the phrase set and setting in 1961: "set" is the user's mindset (his expectations, mood and personality) and "setting" the physical and social surroundings. A frightened user in a chaotic setting is at risk of a bad trip , an acute panic with paranoid fears and the conviction that he will never come back to normal, during which accidents and dangerous behaviour can occur. The usual treatment is "talking down": a quiet room, a calm and reassuring companion who reminds him that the drug will wear off, and, if needed, a benzodiazepine. Two facts about the aftermath are examined often. First, DSM-5-TR includes no hallucinogen withdrawal syndrome, because a clinically significant one has not been consistently documented in humans; hallucinogen use disorder therefore has only ten applicable criteria, the withdrawal criterion being dropped. Hallucinogen use disorder is rare (about 0.1 percent of Americans aged 12 and over in a year), and the classic hallucinogens produce little compulsive use. Second, some users later re-experience the perceptual effects when sober. DSM-5-TR calls this hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD), the formal name for flashbacks : after the drug has gone, the person again sees geometric patterns, false movement at the edges of vision, flashes or intensification of colour, trails behind moving objects, after-images, halos, or objects that look too large (macropsia) or too small (micropsia). Reality testing is intact; he knows these are drug effects. The disturbances may be brief and episodic or nearly continuous, may last weeks, months or years, can be triggered by cannabis, alcohol, darkness or exercise, and occur mainly after LSD; DSM-5-TR gives an initial estimate of about 4.2 percent of hallucinogen users. Persisting psychosis after hallucinogens is uncommon, and a large American survey cited in DSM-5-TR found no evidence that lifetime psychedelic use was an independent risk factor for mental health problems or suicidal behaviour. That reassuring finding has fed a revival of research. After decades in which these drugs were banned and research stopped, controlled trials have tested psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression and MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder. Australia, from 1 July 2023, allowed specially authorised psychiatrists to prescribe psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression and MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration declined to approve MDMA-assisted therapy in August 2024, asking for further research; the developer was reported in August 2026 to have resubmitted its application without a new trial, and no decision has been announced. The developer of a synthetic psilocybin, COMP360, completed its application for treatment-resistant depression on 9 November 2026, and if it is approved it would be the first classic psychedelic medicine licensed there. Until then, these remain experimental treatments, given only with careful screening, preparation and supervision.
