There is no hallucinogen withdrawal in DSM-5-TR. "Flashbacks" are hallucinogen persisting perception disorder , with insight preserved. Cannabis is not a hallucinogen in DSM-5-TR, whereas MDMA is. Phencyclidine and ketamine: the dissociative drugs DSM-5-TR gives phencyclidine (PCP, "angel dust") and its relatives a separate category within the hallucinogen class, because they act quite differently. PCP was first made in 1926 and was developed in the 1950s as a surgical anaesthetic; it was abandoned for human use in the mid-1960s because so many patients woke from it agitated, deluded and irrational, and it appeared on the streets in the 1960s. Its gentler, shorter-acting relative ketamine , made in 1962, is still a widely used anaesthetic in human and veterinary medicine. Both are called dissociative anaesthetics : at low doses they produce a feeling of being separated from one's body and surroundings, and at high doses stupor and coma. Both block the NMDA receptor , the main receptor for the excitatory transmitter glutamate, by plugging its ion channel. Because PCP intoxication can reproduce both the positive and the negative symptoms of schizophrenia in healthy people, it is the basis of the glutamate hypothesis of schizophrenia (Chapter 4, Section 4.8). Phencyclidine intoxication is unlike the dreamy LSD trip. DSM-5-TR requires problematic behavioural change, such as belligerence, assaultiveness, impulsiveness, unpredictability, agitation and impaired judgement, and, within one hour, two or more of eight signs: vertical or horizontal nystagmus (jerking movements of the eyes), raised blood pressure or heart rate, numbness or reduced response to pain, ataxia, slurred speech (dysarthria), muscle rigidity, seizures or coma, and hyperacusis (sounds painfully loud). Picture a young man brought to an emergency department by police, sweating, rigid, staring with eyes that flick from side to side, convinced that the staff are attacking him, and apparently feeling nothing from the cuts on his hands. The combination of violence, nystagmus and insensitivity to pain is the signature that separates PCP from other hallucinogens and from stimulants. Because PCP users can switch suddenly to violence, "talking down" is less useful than it is for LSD; the person is nursed in a quiet, low-stimulation room and given a benzodiazepine, and doctors watch for dangerously high temperature, muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) and seizures. Its psychoactive effects last a few hours but it takes eight days or longer to leave the body, and in vulnerable people it can precipitate a psychotic episode resembling schizophrenia that lasts for weeks. As with the other hallucinogens, DSM-5-TR includes no PCP withdrawal, because withdrawal symptoms have not been clearly established in human users. Ketamine has a double life. As a street drug ("Special K") it is snorted at parties for its dissociation, and a large dose produces the frightening detached state users call the "K-hole"; heavy, long-term use can badly damage the bladder. As a medicine it is the most important new idea in the drug treatment of depression in decades: a single low dose can lift severe depression within hours, and DSM-5-TR notes its usefulness in major depressive disorder. A nasal spray of esketamine (one of its two mirror-image forms) was approved in the United States in 2019 for treatment-resistant depression, given under supervision because of its dissociative effects and its potential for misuse (Chapter 5, Section 5.7 discusses its place among the treatments for depression). Inhalants: the drugs in the household cupboard Walk through any large Indian railway station late at night and you may see children, some no older than ten, holding a handkerchief or a small plastic bag to their faces. Inside is a cloth soaked in correction fluid ("whitener"), the rubber solution used to mend cycle tubes and shoes, or petrol. These are inhalants : volatile chemicals whose vapour is breathed in for its intoxicating effect. DSM-5-TR's inhalant class covers the volatile hydrocarbons, such as toluene, found in glues, fuels, paints, paint thinners and similar products; gases that are not hydrocarbons, such as nitrous oxide ("laughing gas") and the amyl and butyl nitrites ("poppers"), are classed as "other substances" instead. Users sniff vapour straight from the container, "huff" it from a soaked rag held over the mouth and nose, or "bag" it from a plastic bag held over the face. Inhalants are cheap, legal, easy to hide and everywhere, which is why they are the drug of the very young and the very poor. In the Indian national survey of 2019 they were the only class of substance whose current use was higher among children and adolescents (1.17 percent) than among adults (0.58 percent), and DSM-5-TR notes that in low- and middle-income countries homeless children living on the streets have extensive inhalant problems, because of poverty, easy availability and the need to blunt hunger, cold and fear. Several Indian cities, Delhi among them, have restricted the sale of whiteners and thinners to minors. In America, calls to poison-control centres about deliberate inhalant misuse peak at age 14, and the disorder usually remits in early adulthood. Pharmacologically, most solvents behave like a very fast-acting alcohol: like alcohol they enhance GABA-A receptor function and block NMDA receptors. Because the vapour goes from lungs to brain in seconds and wears off within minutes to an hour, users take repeated breaths over hours to stay intoxicated. DSM-5-TR's criteria for inhalant intoxication require problematic behavioural change (belligerence, assaultiveness, apathy, impaired judgement) and two or more of thirteen signs that read like severe drunkenness: dizziness, nystagmus, incoordination, slurred speech, unsteady gait, lethargy, depressed reflexes, psychomotor retardation, tremor, generalised muscle weakness, blurred or double vision, stupor or coma, and euphoria. Users also describe hallucinations, headache and nausea. Clues that a youngster is using include the smell of solvent on breath or clothes, paint or glue on the face or hands, a rash around the nose and mouth ("glue-sniffer's rash"), and repeated episodes of apparent intoxication with negative results on standard urine drug screens, which do not detect inhalants. As with the hallucinogens, DSM-5-TR includes no inhalant withdrawal diagnosis, although some heavy users do report withdrawal-like symptoms. The real danger of inhalants is their toxicity. Acutely, any volatile hydrocarbon can cause sudden sniffing death : the solvent makes the heart muscle oversensitive to adrenaline, so that a fright or a burst of exertion (being chased by a policeman or a shopkeeper) triggers a fatal arrhythmia, even on a first occasion. People also die from suffocation inside a plastic bag, from inhaling vomit, from burns when fuel vapour ignites, and from accidents while intoxicated. Chronically, solvents dissolve the fatty myelin of the nervous system: long-term toluene users develop white-matter damage (leukoencephalopathy), cerebellar ataxia, brain atrophy and a dementia-like cognitive decline, and some solvents damage peripheral nerves, the liver, the kidneys and the bone marrow. DSM-5-TR adds that very frequent nitrous oxide users can develop spinal cord damage (subacute combined degeneration), nerve damage and psychosis; the gas inactivates vitamin B12, so the picture is that of B12 deficiency. Inhalant use disorder is strongly linked with conduct disorder, antisocial personality disorder, childhood maltreatment and the use of many other drugs. Indian context Inhalant use among street children in India is a problem of child welfare as much as of addiction. A child who sniffs whitener on a railway platform is usually also a child who has run away from violence at home, works for a few rupees a day and sleeps in the open. Treatment therefore means shelter, food, schooling and protection under child-welfare law as well as de-addiction care, and outreach workers from voluntary organisations, not hospitals, are often the first contact. The fact that inhalants are the one class used more by children than by adults in the national survey is a fact worth remembering for an interview. Exam trap Inhalant intoxication looks like alcohol intoxication (dizziness, nystagmus, slurred speech, unsteady gait, euphoria) but starts and ends within minutes. Standard urine drug screens miss inhalants. There is no inhalant withdrawal diagnosis in DSM-5-TR. Nitrous oxide and nitrites are "other substances", not inhalants, in DSM-5-TR. The acute killer is sudden sniffing death from cardiac arrhythmia. Sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics: barbiturates, benzodiazepines and the Z-drugs Three words describe what these drugs are prescribed for. A sedative calms, a hypnotic induces sleep and an anxiolytic relieves anxiety, and the same drug usually does all three, depending on the dose. DSM-5-TR puts them in one class, the sedative, hypnotic or anxiolytic substances, which includes the benzodiazepines, the benzodiazepine-like "Z-drugs" (zolpidem, zaleplon), the barbiturates, and older drugs such as methaqualone (barbiturate-like) and meprobamate (a carbamate). It notes two things about the class: like alcohol, these are brain depressants that produce intoxication and withdrawal very similar to those of alcohol, and they are available both on prescription and illegally. Buspirone, an anxiolytic that acts on serotonin receptors, is excluded because it is not associated with significant misuse. The barbiturates. Barbituric acid was first synthesised by the German chemist Adolf von Baeyer in 1864. In 1902 and 1903 Emil Fischer and Joseph von Mering made one of its derivatives, barbital, and found that it put dogs to sleep, and from 1904 it was sold as the sleeping pill Veronal; phenobarbital (Luminal) followed in 1912. For half a century the barbiturates were the standard treatment for anxiety and insomnia, and they were also the standard means of accidental and deliberate overdose: Marilyn Monroe's death in 1962 was among the many caused by barbiturates taken with other drugs. Their great defect is a narrow margin between the dose that sedates and the dose that stops breathing, made worse by the fact that tolerance develops to the sedative effect much faster than to the lethal effect. Barbiturates also speed up the liver enzymes that break down many other drugs, and withdrawal from them is the most dangerous of all sedative withdrawals. Today phenobarbital survives mainly as an anti-epileptic drug, which is still widely used for epilepsy in India because it is cheap, and short-acting barbiturates such as thiopental (thiopentone) are used to induce anaesthesia. The benzodiazepines. In the mid-1950s Leo Sternbach , a chemist at the Swiss company Hoffmann-La Roche, made a compound that sat untested on a shelf until, in 1957, routine animal screening revealed that it tamed animals without knocking them out. It was marketed in 1960 as chlordiazepoxide (Librium), and its simpler relative diazepam (Valium) followed in 1963. The benzodiazepines replaced the barbiturates almost completely and became, during the 1970s, among the most prescribed drugs in the world. They are used for anxiety, insomnia, alcohol withdrawal (Section 10.4), epileptic seizures and status epilepticus, muscle spasm, sedation before procedures and catatonia. All the drugs in this class, and alcohol too, act on the same receptor: the GABA-A receptor , a channel in the neuron's membrane that opens when the inhibitory transmitter GABA binds to it, letting negatively charged chloride ions flow into the cell and making it less likely to fire. The drugs bind to their own sites on the receptor, separate from GABA's site, and make GABA work better; they are positive allosteric modulators , often loosely called GABA agonists. The difference between the families lies in how they do it, and it explains their safety (Figure 10.13). Benzodiazepines make the channel open more often when GABA is present, but they cannot open it by themselves; because their effect depends on the brain's own GABA, it has a ceiling, and an overdose of a benzodiazepine alone is rarely fatal. Barbiturates make the channel stay open longer, and at high doses they open it directly, even without GABA; there is no ceiling, and breathing can stop. Alcohol also enhances GABA-A function, and in addition blocks the NMDA glutamate receptor (Section 10.3). GABA, the benzodiazepines, the barbiturates and alcohol each bind their own site on the GABA-A receptor, and each makes the chloride channel pass more current. Because they share this target they show cross-tolerance, and because their effects add they are dangerous in combination. The Z-drugs and GHB. Zolpidem, zopiclone (and its relative eszopiclone) and zaleplon were introduced as hypnotics that were chemically different from the benzodiazepines and, it was hoped, less habit-forming. In fact they bind the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor, and tolerance, dependence and withdrawal all occur. They can also cause complex sleep behaviours, such as sleepwalking, cooking or even driving while not fully awake, with no memory afterwards, which led the American regulator to add its strongest warning to their labels in 2019 (Chapter 8, Section 8.10 discusses drug-induced sleep disorders). Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a depressant that acts mainly at GABA-B receptors, is used medically for narcolepsy and illicitly as a club drug and in drug-facilitated sexual assault; its steep dose-response curve makes overdose easy and its withdrawal can be as severe as alcohol's. Intoxication and overdose. Sedative, hypnotic or anxiolytic intoxication is, in DSM-5-TR's words, a picture that may be identical to alcohol intoxication: problematic behavioural change (inappropriate sexual or aggressive behaviour, mood lability, impaired judgement) with one or more of slurred speech, incoordination, unsteady gait, nystagmus, impaired attention or memory, and stupor or coma. Without the smell of alcohol on the breath, only the history or a toxicology screen tells them apart. Memory impairment is prominent, usually an anterograde amnesia like an alcoholic blackout, which is one reason these drugs are used in drug-facilitated crime. In older people even prescribed doses cause confusion, falls and fractures, and DSM-5-TR warns that intoxication in an elderly person can resemble a progressive dementia. Overdose of a benzodiazepine alone is seldom fatal because of the ceiling effect; combined with alcohol or opioids it is a different matter, as Section 10.7.9 explains. Flumazenil , a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site, reverses benzodiazepine sedation within minutes, but it is used cautiously, because its effect is shorter than that of most benzodiazepines (so sedation can return) and because in a dependent person it can precipitate sudden withdrawal and seizures. Prescribed dependence. The benzodiazepines differ from almost every other drug in this chapter in one way: most dependent users never set out to get high. DSM-5-TR describes two routes into the disorder. The commoner begins with young people who use these drugs socially, often alongside alcohol, opioids or stimulants (to "come down" from cocaine, for example, or to "boost" methadone). The second begins in a doctor's surgery, with a prescription for anxiety or sleeplessness, and continues as the dose creeps up, the patient justifies each increase by the original symptoms, and he begins to collect prescriptions from several doctors. By the 1980s the scale of this problem was clear in Britain, where research by the psychopharmacologist Malcolm Lader and the clinician Heather Ashton documented withdrawal in long-term patients on ordinary doses, and in 1988 the British Committee on Safety of Medicines advised that benzodiazepines be prescribed for anxiety or insomnia only for two to four weeks. DSM-5-TR is careful about such patients: when a benzodiazepine is prescribed for a proper medical reason and taken as prescribed, tolerance and withdrawal do not count towards a use disorder, which is diagnosed only if the other criteria are also met. Simran, 46, a school administrator in Chandigarh, was prescribed alprazolam 0.25 milligrams at night when she could not sleep after her husband's heart attack. Six years later she was taking 2 milligrams a day in four doses, obtained from two doctors and a chemist who did not ask for a prescription, and she felt anxious and shaky an hour or two before each dose was due. On a family trip to Shimla she ran out. By the next evening she was trembling, sweating and unable to sleep; ordinary sounds seemed painfully loud, the light hurt her eyes, she had a metallic taste in her mouth and she felt strangely unreal, "as if I was watching myself in a film". On the second day she had a generalised seizure in the hotel lobby. Notice the features of benzodiazepine withdrawal that go beyond the anxiety she was first treated for: perceptual hypersensitivity, depersonalisation and, most dangerous, a seizure. Her short-acting drug, taken several times a day, had given her a small withdrawal between every dose, and stopping it abruptly produced a severe one within a day. Indian context In the national survey of 2019, about 1.08 percent of Indians aged 10 to 75 (about 1.18 crore people) were current non-medical users of sedatives, that is, taking them without a prescription or not as prescribed, which is easy where chemists sell benzodiazepines over the counter. Barbiturates have a second, legal history in India: thiopental ("sodium pentothal") was used by investigating agencies for "narcoanalysis", in the belief that a drugged suspect would tell the truth. In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) the Supreme Court held that narcoanalysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests carried out without the person's consent violate the constitutional protection against self-incrimination and the right to personal liberty; statements made under the drug are unreliable as well as coerced. Exam trap Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of GABA-A channel opening and need GABA to work (hence a ceiling and a wide safety margin alone); barbiturates increase the duration of opening and at high doses open the channel directly (hence the narrow margin). Both are positive allosteric modulators, loosely "GABA agonists"; neither acts on serotonin, dopamine or opioid receptors. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, naloxone reverses opioids; neither reverses the other. Buspirone is an anxiolytic but not a sedative-hypnotic of abuse in DSM-5-TR. Cross-tolerance in practice, and the withdrawal that can kill Section 10.1 defined cross-tolerance : tolerance to one drug that extends to other drugs, usually of the same class or acting on the same target. The sedatives are where the idea earns its keep. A man who drinks a bottle of whisky a day is tolerant not only to alcohol but also to the benzodiazepines and barbiturates, because all three act on the GABA-A receptor; anaesthetists know that heavy drinkers need more of many anaesthetic and sedative drugs. The hallucinogens give a second example (tolerance to LSD carries over to psilocybin and mescaline, all three acting at 5-HT2A), and the opioids a third (Section 10.5). Cross-tolerance is usually incomplete: the second drug is weakened, not abolished. Its partner, cross-dependence , is the ability of one drug to suppress the withdrawal syndrome of another. These two facts are the whole logic of substitution and tapering : replace a dangerous or short-acting drug with a long-acting drug of the same family, stabilise the patient, then reduce the long-acting drug slowly. That is why alcohol withdrawal is treated with chlordiazepoxide or diazepam (Section 10.4), why a person dependent on alprazolam is switched to diazepam before tapering, why phenobarbital can be used to withdraw a person from barbiturates, and why methadone can replace heroin (Section 10.5). Cross-tolerance has a deadly side. Tolerance to the sedative and pleasurable effects of these drugs develops much faster than tolerance to their depressant effect on the brainstem, which controls breathing; DSM-5-TR spells this out. A tolerant user who keeps raising his dose to feel the effect is narrowing, without knowing it, the gap between the dose that pleases him and the dose that stops his breathing. Add a second depressant and the effects combine. With alcohol and barbiturates the combination acts on the same receptor; with opioids it acts through a different receptor (the mu opioid receptor) on the same breathing centres, so there is no cross-tolerance to protect the user and the effects simply add. DSM-5-TR notes that benzodiazepines, safe on their own, are particularly dangerous with opioids and alcohol, and in 2016 the American regulator placed its strongest warning on both opioids and benzodiazepines after deaths involving the two together nearly tripled between 2004 and 2011. Many deaths labelled "heroin overdose" turn out, on toxicology, to involve alcohol or benzodiazepines as well. The withdrawal is the mirror image of the drug. Long exposure to a drug that enhances inhibition makes the brain adapt by reducing its GABA-A sensitivity and increasing its excitatory glutamate activity. Remove the drug suddenly and the brain is left with weak brakes and a strong accelerator. Sedative, hypnotic or anxiolytic withdrawal in DSM-5-TR follows the cessation of, or reduction in, prolonged use, and requires two or more of eight features within several hours to a few days: autonomic hyperactivity (sweating, a pulse over 100), hand tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient visual, tactile or auditory hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation, anxiety and grand mal seizures. This is almost word for word the list for alcohol withdrawal, and for the same reason. DSM-5-TR adds that a grand mal seizure may occur in perhaps 20 to 30 percent of people undergoing untreated withdrawal, and that withdrawal can progress to a life-threatening withdrawal delirium , with clouded consciousness and hallucinations, which is then diagnosed instead (Section 10.8). The risk rises with dose and duration: withdrawal has been reported after as little as 15 milligrams of diazepam a day for several months, is more likely to be clinically important at about 40 milligrams, and is more likely to bring seizures or delirium at doses around 100 milligrams. Lingering anxiety, poor sleep and low mood can persist at a lower level for months and are easily mistaken for a returning anxiety disorder. The timing depends on the drug's half-life (Figure 10.14). After drugs whose action lasts about ten hours or less, such as lorazepam, oxazepam or temazepam, symptoms begin within six to eight hours as blood levels fall, peak on the second day and improve markedly by the fourth or fifth. After a long-acting drug such as diazepam, symptoms may not appear for more than a week, peak in the second week and ease in the third or fourth. A patient who stops diazepam on Monday and feels well on Friday has not escaped withdrawal; it has not started yet. After a short-acting drug it starts within hours and peaks on the second day; after diazepam it may not start for a week and peaks in the second week. The practical rules follow directly. A person who has taken a sedative-hypnotic regularly for more than a few weeks should never stop it suddenly. The usual approach is to switch a short-acting drug to an equivalent dose of a long-acting one (usually diazepam), then reduce the dose gradually over weeks or, after years of use, months, more slowly towards the end, while helping the person manage the insomnia and anxiety that return (cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is taught in Book 2, Section 9.4.3). Seizures and withdrawal delirium are medical emergencies treated with benzodiazepines themselves. Simran was admitted, switched to diazepam and tapered over five months; she later said that the hardest part was not the drug but learning to sleep without it. Exam trap Cross-tolerance means that tolerance to one drug extends to another, so exposure to the first reduces the effect of the second; the papers' wording, "exposure to one drug reduces or changes tolerance to other drugs", is a loose way of saying this, and it is the option to choose. It does not mean "no addiction to any drug". The classic group is alcohol, benzodiazepines and barbiturates , which share the GABA-A receptor; it is the basis of benzodiazepine detoxification. Do not confuse it with cross-dependence (one drug suppresses the other's withdrawal) or with sensitisation (reverse tolerance, an increasing effect). Of all the withdrawal syndromes, only those of alcohol and the sedative-hypnotics regularly bring seizures and a delirium that can kill; opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely dangerous in a healthy adult. The ten classes side by side You have now met every class of substance in DSM-5-TR. Before the chapter turns from what drugs do to the brain to what happens when the brain itself fails, it is worth seeing them together, because the examiners' favourite questions are comparisons: which drug gives pinpoint pupils, which gives nystagmus, which has no withdrawal, which withdrawal can kill. Table 10.31 summarises what Sections 10.3 to 10.7 have taught, using DSM-5-TR's criteria. (Hallucinogens are one class with two parts, phencyclidine and the other hallucinogens, which is why the table has eleven rows for ten classes.) Three patterns are worth carrying away. First, withdrawal is usually the mirror image of intoxication: the sedating drugs leave an agitated, sleepless, trembling brain behind; the stimulants leave a slowed, sleepy, hungry, dysphoric one; opioid withdrawal reverses opioid intoxication sign by sign, from small pupils to large ones and from constipation to diarrhoea. Second, only the depressants acting on GABA-A, alcohol and the sedative-hypnotics, have a withdrawal that is regularly dangerous to life. Third, three classes have a gap in their diagnoses: caffeine has no use disorder in the main text (caffeine use disorder is a condition for further study), tobacco has no intoxication diagnosis, and the hallucinogens (including phencyclidine) and the inhalants have no withdrawal diagnosis. Withdrawal that can kill belongs to alcohol and the sedative-hypnotics. 10.8 From Organic Brain Syndrome to Neurocognitive Disorder: The Cognitive Domains and Delirium High yield · 8 Qs So far this chapter has been about what people do to their brains with drugs. The rest of it is about what happens when the brain itself begins to fail, whether suddenly, because of an infection, an operation or a drug, or slowly, over years, because of a degenerative disease. These are the disorders psychiatry used to call "organic", and they are the one group in the whole classification whose cause can usually be found, measured and sometimes cured. This section lays the foundations for the rest of the chapter. It explains how the names changed, defines the six cognitive domains on which modern diagnosis rests, sorts out the old vocabulary of dementia, amnesia, aphasia, apraxia and agnosia, and then teaches the commonest and most dangerous of these disorders, the one a psychologist in a general hospital will see every week: delirium. Sections 10.9 to 10.11 then take up the dementias and the amnesic syndromes one by one. From "organic" to "neurocognitive": the history of a name For most of the twentieth century psychiatry divided mental disorders into two great families. Organic mental disorders were those with a demonstrable physical disease of the brain or body behind them: the dementias, delirium, the amnesic syndromes and the psychiatric pictures produced by brain injury, epilepsy, infection or hormones. Functional disorders were those in which no such disease could be found: schizophrenia, the mood disorders and the neuroses, disorders of how the mind "functioned" rather than of its machinery (Chapter 1 and Chapter 2, Section 2.1 trace the origins of the split). The division was useful at the bedside, because it reminded clinicians to look for a treatable physical cause, but it rested on a false assumption: that "functional" disorders have no biological basis. Twin studies, brain imaging and the discovery of drugs that act on specific transmitters made that assumption untenable, and the word "organic" came to imply, wrongly, that schizophrenia or depression were somehow not disorders of the brain. The American manuals show the change step by step. DSM-I (1952) spoke of acute and chronic brain disorders, roughly the reversible and the irreversible; DSM-II (1968) of organic brain syndromes; DSM-III (1980) and DSM-III-R (1987) of organic mental syndromes and disorders, a large category that also held organic mood, anxiety, delusional and personality syndromes. DSM-IV (1994) dropped the word "organic" altogether. It kept delirium, dementia and the amnestic disorders together in a chapter called "Delirium, Dementia, and Amnestic and Other Cognitive Disorders", because impaired cognition is their main feature, and moved the organic mood, anxiety and psychotic syndromes into the chapters for mood, anxiety and psychosis, as disorders "due to a general medical condition". DSM-5 (2013) renamed the chapter neurocognitive disorders (NCDs). It kept delirium , but replaced "dementia" and "amnestic disorder" with two new syndromes of different severity, major neurocognitive disorder and mild neurocognitive disorder , each of which is then labelled by its cause. DSM-5-TR (2022) keeps this scheme and stresses two defining points: the primary problem is cognitive, and it is acquired , a decline from a level the person once reached, which separates NCDs from intellectual disability and the other neurodevelopmental disorders (Chapter 3). The word "dementia" is still allowed, for continuity, in the subtypes where it is customary. ICD-10 (1992), which Indian hospitals still widely use, kept the older name for its block F00 to F09: organic, including symptomatic, mental disorders . "Organic" here means that the syndrome can be attributed to an independently diagnosable disease of the brain; "symptomatic" means that the brain is affected secondarily, by a disease elsewhere in the body, such as a fever, kidney failure or a hormone disorder. Table 10.32 lists the block. Two details are favourites with examiners. First, the amnesic syndrome and delirium caused by alcohol and other drugs are not coded here but in the substance block: Korsakoff's syndrome from alcohol is F10.6 and delirium tremens is F10.4 (Section 10.1), which is why F04 and F05 carry the words "not induced by alcohol and other psychoactive substances". Its Chapter 6 has a block of neurocognitive disorders containing delirium (6D70), mild neurocognitive disorder (6D71), amnestic disorder (6D72) and dementia (6D80 to 6D8Z, with separate codes for dementia due to Alzheimer disease, cerebrovascular disease, Lewy body disease, frontotemporal dementia, dementia due to psychoactive substances, and dementia due to diseases classified elsewhere). Notice one difference that DSM-5-TR itself points out: ICD-10, ICD-11 and the old DSM-IV require several cognitive deficits for a diagnosis of dementia, whereas DSM-5's major NCD can be diagnosed when only one domain is substantially impaired. A person with a pure, severe memory disorder therefore has an amnestic disorder in ICD-11 but a major NCD in DSM-5-TR. Exam trap DSM-5 replaced "dementia" and "amnestic disorder" with major and mild neurocognitive disorder and kept "delirium" ; it did not abolish delirium or rename it. DSM-IV, not DSM-5, was the edition that dropped the word "organic". ICD-10's F00 to F09 are the "organic, including symptomatic" disorders; delirium is F05 , but delirium tremens is F10.4 and alcoholic Korsakoff's syndrome F10.6 . In DSM-5-TR one impaired domain is enough for major NCD, so a pure amnesia counts. The six cognitive domains, and major versus mild neurocognitive disorder "Dementia" once meant, in practice, memory loss plus something else. The trouble with that definition is that some brain diseases begin elsewhere. Frontotemporal degeneration usually starts with a change in personality and social conduct while memory is still good; some strokes destroy language and leave everything else intact; a man recovering from a head injury may remember perfectly well but be unable to plan a day. DSM-5 therefore built its definitions on six cognitive domains , broad families of mental ability that can be impaired independently and tested separately (Table 10.33). The least familiar domain, and the newest to diagnostic manuals, is social cognition , the ability to read other people's emotions and intentions, added because its loss is the earliest sign of the behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia (Section 10.10). The tests themselves belong to the Assessment book; the table names typical bedside tasks only so that you can picture what each domain means. Table 10.33 The six DSM-5-TR cognitive domains. Major neurocognitive disorder requires evidence of significant decline from a previous level in one or more domains, based on two kinds of evidence together: concern on the part of the person, someone who knows him well or the clinician, and a substantial impairment on standardised neuropsychological testing or, failing that, another quantified clinical assessment. The deficits must interfere with independence in everyday activities: at a minimum, the person needs help with complex instrumental activities of daily living such as paying bills or managing medicines. They must not occur only during a delirium, and must not be better explained by another mental disorder such as major depression or schizophrenia. Mild neurocognitive disorder has the same structure, with a modest decline, a modest impairment on testing, and preserved independence, although the person now needs greater effort, compensatory strategies or accommodation (lists, reminders, a son who checks the bank statement) to manage. DSM-5-TR gives rough testing guides: in major NCD, performance typically falls two or more standard deviations below appropriate norms (the third percentile or below); in mild NCD, between one and two standard deviations below (between the third and sixteenth percentiles). Each rule has a reason. Concern and objective testing are both required because each alone misleads: a retired professor may still score in the normal range while clearly declining from his own high baseline, whereas a test score alone may label as impaired an elderly woman who never went to school and was never good at the tasks (which is why culturally appropriate norms and Indian adaptations of the tests matter). The independence criterion is what separates major from mild, and it is a functional, not a test-score, judgement. The exclusion of delirium matters because delirium also impairs cognition, but temporarily; an NCD can only be diagnosed when the person's consciousness is clear. And the exclusion of depression and schizophrenia protects the patient whose poor concentration is part of a treatable mood disorder (depressive "pseudodementia", Section 10.11). Major NCD is then rated by severity: mild (difficulties with instrumental activities such as housework or managing money), moderate (difficulties with basic activities such as feeding and dressing) or severe (fully dependent), and specified as with or without behavioural disturbance (psychotic symptoms, mood disturbance, agitation, apathy). Finally, the clinician names the cause: Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal degeneration, Lewy body disease, vascular disease, traumatic brain injury, a substance or medication, HIV infection, prion disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, another medical condition, multiple causes or an unspecified cause. Sections 10.9 to 10.11 teach them. Mild NCD overlaps closely with the older research idea of mild cognitive impairment (Section 10.9). Exam trap The six domains are complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor function and social cognition ; "intelligence", "personality" and "orientation" are not on the list. Major and mild NCD differ in the size of the decline and, decisively, in whether it costs the person independence in everyday activities. Major NCD roughly corresponds to the old "dementia". Severity of major NCD (mild, moderate, severe) is a different thing from mild NCD. Naming the deficit: dementia, amnesia, aphasia, apraxia and agnosia Long before DSM-5's domains, neurology had a precise vocabulary for what goes wrong when the brain is damaged, and the examiners still test it as a matching exercise. Each word names a failure of one kind of function, and each tells you, roughly, where to look. Most of them begin with the Greek "a-", meaning "without". Dementia (from the Latin for "out of one's mind") is an acquired, usually progressive, global decline of intellect: memory, but also abstraction (the ability to form concepts and grasp general principles, tested by asking what a proverb means or how an orange and a banana are alike), judgement, reasoning, language and personality, all in clear consciousness. When a question asks which disorder chiefly affects abstraction, the answer is dementia, because abstraction is the highest-level function and the one a global decline erodes. Amnesia is a selective disorder of memory with other functions relatively intact: anterograde amnesia for new learning, retrograde amnesia for what was learned before the onset (Chapter 2, Section 2.7.2 sets out the forms; Section 10.11 the amnesic syndromes). Aphasia is an acquired disorder of language, the ability to produce and understand words and sentences, caused by brain damage. It is not a disorder of articulation: a person with slurred but grammatical speech has dysarthria , a motor problem. The classical types, named after the patients that founded the subject, are set out in Table 10.35. Paul Broca described in 1861 a man who could say little except "tan" but understood much of what was said to him; Carl Wernicke described in 1874 patients who spoke fluently but meaninglessly and could not understand speech. Three related "a-words" complete the symbolic functions. Alexia is an acquired loss of the ability to read, agraphia of the ability to write, and acalculia of the ability to calculate (a term coined by the Swedish neurologist Salomon Henschen); they differ from the developmental dyslexia and dyscalculia of Chapter 3 because they are lost, not never acquired. Acalculia and agraphia appear together with finger agnosia (inability to name or identify one's own fingers) and right-left confusion in Gerstmann syndrome , the classic sign of damage to the dominant parietal lobe. Apraxia is the inability to carry out skilled, purposeful, learned movements, although the person has the strength, sensation and coordination to perform them and understands what is asked; its modern study began with the German neurologist Hugo Liepmann in 1900. Asked to show how he would comb his hair, the patient with ideomotor apraxia waves the hand vaguely or uses his fingers as the comb, although he may comb his hair perfectly well when he picks up a real comb in the morning. In ideational apraxia the plan of a sequence is lost: he puts the tea leaves in the cup before boiling the water, or tries to strike the matchbox with the candle. Constructional apraxia is difficulty drawing or assembling (copying a cube or a clock face), and dressing apraxia difficulty putting clothes on the right way round. Apraxia is what the papers mean by a disorder of "motor skills". Agnosia is a failure of recognition despite intact sensation: the eyes, ears and skin work, but the brain cannot attach meaning to what they report. The word was coined by Sigmund Freud in his book on aphasia in 1891, and a year earlier the German neurologist Heinrich Lissauer had proposed that visual recognition could fail in two ways: in apperceptive agnosia the person cannot put the parts of what he sees together into a whole (he cannot copy a drawing), whereas in associative agnosia he can copy the drawing perfectly but still does not know what it is. Special forms include prosopagnosia , the inability to recognise familiar faces (a man who knows his wife only by her voice), named by Joachim Bodamer in 1947; auditory agnosia for sounds; tactile agnosia or astereognosis , inability to recognise an object such as a key placed in the hand with the eyes closed; and simultanagnosia, the inability to see more than one object of a scene at a time. Closely related is anosognosia , unawareness of one's own deficit, named by Joseph Babinski in 1914 for patients who denied that their paralysed left side was paralysed. And do not confuse Wernicke's aphasia (a language disorder, 1874) with Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency, 1881, Section 10.11): same Carl Wernicke, two different disorders. Delirium: an old word for acute brain failure Begin with a patient. Vimal, 72, a retired railway station master from Lucknow, had coronary bypass surgery on a Monday. He had diabetes, wore a hearing aid (left at home in the rush to hospital) and, his daughter admitted, had been "a little forgetful" for a year. On Tuesday, in the cardiac intensive care unit, he was quiet and drowsy, and the nurses thought he was simply resting. On Wednesday night he became a different man. He pulled at his drip and his chest drain, tried to climb over the bed rails, and picked repeatedly at the bedsheet as though gathering something from it. He was sure he was back at his old station and kept telling the nurses that the 6.15 to Kanpur was late and that the signals must be checked; at one point he pointed in fear at "the men on the ceiling". He could not say what day it was. Asked to name the months of the year backwards, he managed "December, November" and then drifted into a story about a train. By Thursday afternoon he was calm, apologetic and almost himself, then worse again after dark. Vimal had delirium , and everything about him is typical: an elderly, already vulnerable brain; a major physical insult; an onset over a day or two; a picture that swings between drowsy and agitated and is worst at night; attention so poor that a simple sequence cannot be held; disorientation; misperceptions and frightening visual hallucinations; and even the habit of acting out his old occupation, which clinicians call an occupational delirium . It is also typical that his first, quiet day was missed. The syndrome is one of the oldest in medicine. The Hippocratic writers described two forms of mental disturbance in fever: phrenitis , a wild, sleepless frenzy, and lethargus , a dull, drowsy inertia. These are recognisably the hyperactive and hypoactive deliria of today. The Roman writer Celsus, in the first century AD, introduced the word delirium for the mental disorder that could follow fever or head injury. It comes from the Latin de lira , "out of the furrow": the image is of a ploughman whose plough has left the straight line of the furrow, a mind that has gone off its track. Over the centuries the same syndrome acquired many other names (acute confusional state, acute brain syndrome, acute organic reaction, toxic psychosis, metabolic encephalopathy, "ICU psychosis", "post-operative psychosis"), which made it seem like many disorders when it was one. In the second half of the twentieth century the Canadian psychiatrist Zbigniew Lipowski did more than anyone to argue that all these were a single syndrome, best called delirium, and he is usually credited with dividing it by motor activity into hyperactive and hypoactive forms. He also gave it a memorable alternative description: acute brain failure , a counterpart to acute heart failure or acute kidney failure. The comparison is apt. Just as a failing heart shows itself in breathlessness whatever has damaged it, a brain in acute failure shows itself in delirium whatever the cause, and the cause is almost always outside psychiatry. Key study: Engel and Romano, "a syndrome of cerebral insufficiency" (1959) In the 1940s and 1950s the American physicians George L. Engel and John Romano asked whether the confusion of seriously ill medical patients was a psychological reaction to illness or a direct sign of a brain that was not working. They recorded the electroencephalogram (EEG) of delirious patients while they assessed their awareness and cognition, and repeated the recordings as the patients' conditions changed. They also observed what happened when blood glucose, oxygen levels or acid-base balance were altered, or certain drugs were given. The result was consistent: delirium went with slowing of the background rhythm of the EEG, the degree of slowing tracked the degree of impaired awareness, and both reversed together when the underlying disturbance was corrected. In their 1959 paper they called delirium "a syndrome of cerebral insufficiency", a general failure of brain metabolism measurable by EEG slowing, whatever its cause. The paper became a classic of neuropsychiatry and was reprinted in full in 2004. Its limitation is that a slowed EEG can still fall within the normal range in mild delirium, so a single recording without a baseline for comparison may miss it. Section 2.2.3 of Chapter 2 sets out the DSM-5-TR criteria for delirium and what clouding of consciousness feels like from the inside; here is the logic of them, in brief. The core is a disturbance of attention and awareness : the patient cannot direct, focus, sustain or shift attention, questions must be repeated, and he is pulled away by every passing distraction. Attention is chosen as the core rather than memory because it is what fails first and most consistently when consciousness is clouded, and because a brain that cannot attend cannot be tested on anything else. The disturbance develops over a short period , usually hours to a few days, represents a change from the person's usual state, and fluctuates during the day, often worsening in the evening and at night when the orienting cues of daylight, visitors and ward routine fall away, which nurses call sundowning . There is an additional cognitive disturbance : memory (especially recent memory), orientation (to time first, then place), language (rambling, incoherent speech and poor comprehension), visuospatial ability or perception. The picture must not be better explained by an existing NCD and must not occur in coma, because a patient too deeply unconscious to respond cannot be said to be inattentive. And there must be evidence of a physical cause : a medical condition, intoxication or withdrawal, a medication, a toxin, or several of these. Around this core lies the rest of the picture. The sleep-wake cycle is disturbed in almost every case, sometimes completely reversed, so that the patient dozes by day and is awake and agitated at night. Perceptual disturbances range from misinterpretations (a coat on a hook becomes a man standing in the corner) and illusions to vivid hallucinations, which are typically visual and often of people or small animals; delusions, when present, are fleeting, poorly organised and usually persecutory, built on the misperceptions of the moment. Emotion is unstable, with fear, irritability, anger, tearfulness, euphoria or apathy and rapid shifts between them. Afterwards the patient usually remembers little or nothing of the episode, because information that is never attended to is never stored. ICD-10 (F05) describes the same syndrome as an "etiologically nonspecific organic cerebral syndrome" with concurrent disturbances of consciousness and attention, perception, thinking, memory, psychomotor behaviour, emotion and the sleep-wake schedule, transient and of fluctuating intensity, with most cases recovering within four weeks or less, although a fluctuating delirium lasting up to six months is not uncommon (for example, in chronic liver disease or cancer). DSM-5-TR asks the clinician to specify the course, acute (hours or days) or persistent (weeks or months), and the cause: substance intoxication delirium , substance withdrawal delirium (the commonest being alcohol withdrawal delirium, or delirium tremens, taught in Section 10.3), medication-induced delirium , delirium due to another medical condition, or delirium due to multiple causes. A delirium-like state that falls short of the full criteria can be recorded as subsyndromal delirium. Exam trap The cardinal feature of delirium is a disturbance of attention and awareness (clouded consciousness), not memory loss, hallucinations or agitation. Its onset is acute and its course fluctuating , typically worse at night (sundowning). "Acute confusional state" and "acute brain failure" are other names for delirium; delirium tremens is one cause-specific form of it, alcohol withdrawal delirium (Section 10.3). The word was introduced by Celsus , and the Hippocratic phrenitis and lethargus foreshadow the hyperactive and hypoactive types. At the bedside: the three motor types, the motor signs and the EEG DSM-5-TR asks the clinician to specify the level of psychomotor activity, and the distinction matters because it decides whether the delirium is noticed. In hyperactive delirium , which Vimal showed on Wednesday night, the patient is restless, agitated and emotionally labile, pulls out lines, tries to leave the bed or the ward and refuses care; this form is often linked to drug withdrawal and medication side effects. In hypoactive delirium , which he showed on Tuesday, the patient is slow, sluggish and lethargic, sometimes nearly stuporous, lies still and says little. DSM-5-TR notes that this quiet form may be the more frequent in older adults, that it is often unrecognised in emergency departments and hospitals, and that it is commoner in women, whereas men more often show agitation; it is regularly mistaken for depression or for "tiredness after the operation". In delirium of mixed level of activity the patient's activity is normal although attention and awareness are disturbed, or it swings rapidly between the two states. Delirium is a disorder of the whole brain, and the body shows it. Several motor signs are characteristic, and any or all of them may occur. Asterixis , the "flapping tremor": when the patient holds his arms out with the wrists bent back and fingers spread, the hands repeatedly drop forward and jerk back up, like a bird's wings. It is not a true tremor but a series of brief lapses of muscle tone (negative myoclonus). It was described in 1949 by the American neurologists Raymond Adams and Joseph Foley in patients with liver failure, and it is a sign of metabolic delirium: hepatic encephalopathy, kidney failure, carbon dioxide retention in lung disease, and drug toxicity. Multifocal myoclonus : sudden, brief, shock-like jerks of different muscles in different parts of the body, again typical of metabolic and toxic causes such as kidney failure. Tremor : often coarse and irregular, and most marked in withdrawal states such as delirium tremens. Carphologia and floccillation : aimless picking at the bedclothes, as though plucking threads or bits of fluff from them, which is what Vimal was doing. The words come from the Greek karphos , a straw or twig, and the Latin floccus , a tuft of wool, and the sign has been regarded as an ominous one since ancient medicine. Changes in tone and reflexes : increased tone or rigidity, brisk reflexes and sometimes an upgoing plantar response, all reflecting widespread disturbance of brain function rather than a single lesion. Slurred speech (dysarthria) and clumsiness, and, very sensitively, disturbed handwriting: a delirious patient asked to write a sentence often produces untidy, misspelt, poorly organised writing even when his speech seems almost normal. Autonomic signs (a fast pulse, sweating, flushing, fever, raised blood pressure) are prominent in withdrawal and in anticholinergic delirium. None of these signs is found in a functional psychosis such as schizophrenia, which is why a careful physical examination is part of every psychiatric assessment of an acutely confused patient. The electroencephalogram confirms what Engel and Romano found. DSM-5-TR describes generalised, irregular slowing into the theta range as the usual finding in delirium, with fast activity occasionally seen instead, for example in some cases of alcohol withdrawal delirium (and the fast beta rhythms produced by benzodiazepines can also appear). The EEG is useful in three situations: to distinguish delirium from a functional psychosis or a severe depression, in which the EEG is normal; to detect non-convulsive seizures, a treatable cause of confusion that otherwise looks like delirium; and to follow recovery. Its limitation is the one Engel and Romano noted: without a baseline, mild slowing may still look "normal". Exam trap A question listing asterixis, multifocal myoclonus, carphologia and tone and reflex abnormalities as motor signs of delirium wants the answer "all of the above" : every one can occur, and tremor and dysarthria can be added to the list. Carphologia (picking at the bedclothes) is not a tic, a compulsion or a catatonic sign. The hypoactive type is the one most often missed and mistaken for depression. The EEG in delirium shows diffuse slowing ; fast activity is the exception (some alcohol withdrawal delirium). A normal EEG argues against delirium and for a functional disorder. Why delirium happens: causes, vulnerability and the surgical ward The single most important fact about delirium is that it always has a physical cause, and usually more than one. Early in the twentieth century the German psychiatrist Karl Bonhoeffer pointed out that the brain has only a limited repertoire of responses to physical illness, so that very different causes (a fever, a poison, kidney failure, a head injury) produce the same "exogenous" reaction. Delirium is the commonest of those reactions. The picture tells you that the brain is failing, not why; the why has to be found by history, examination and tests. Table 10.36 groups the common causes. A popular memory aid lists them as "I WATCH DEATH": infection, withdrawal, acute metabolic disturbance, trauma, central nervous system disease, hypoxia, deficiencies, endocrine disorders, acute vascular events, toxins or drugs, and heavy metals. Table 10.36 The common causes of delirium, grouped. Group Examples Infection Urinary and chest infections in the elderly, septicaemia, malaria, typhoid, meningitis and encephalitis, HIV Drugs: intoxication and side effects Anticholinergic drugs (including some bladder, antiparkinsonian and older antidepressant drugs), opioids, benzodiazepines and other sedatives, steroids, lithium toxicity, digoxin; datura poisoning; several drugs at once Drugs: withdrawal Alcohol (delirium tremens, Section 10.3), benzodiazepines, barbiturates and other sedatives (Section 10.7) Metabolic and electrolyte disturbance Low or high blood sugar, low sodium, high calcium, dehydration, kidney failure (uraemia), liver failure Lack of oxygen Heart failure, pneumonia, chronic lung disease, anaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning Brain disease and injury Head injury, stroke, epileptic seizures and the post-ictal state, brain tumour, raised intracranial pressure Endocrine and deficiency states Thyroid and adrenal disorders; thiamine deficiency (Wernicke's encephalopathy, Section 10.11); vitamin B12 deficiency Surgery and intensive care The post-operative state, especially after heart and hip surgery; sleep deprivation, immobility and sedation in intensive care Simple, overlooked causes Urinary retention, severe constipation, uncontrolled pain, a missing hearing aid or spectacles Why do so many causes produce the same picture? The answer is still incomplete, but three mechanisms stand out. The first is a shortage of acetylcholine , the transmitter on which attention and arousal depend. Drugs that block acetylcholine reliably produce delirium, the drug physostigmine, which boosts acetylcholine, can reverse such a delirium, and the cholinergic losses of Alzheimer's disease (Section 10.9) help explain why people with dementia become delirious so easily. (DSM-5-TR adds a note of caution: in a meta-analysis, anticholinergic drug use was not confirmed as a validated predictor of delirium, so it is one cause among many, not the whole story.) The second is a relative excess of dopamine , which is why dopamine-enhancing drugs can provoke delirium and dopamine-blocking antipsychotics can calm its agitation. The third is inflammation : infections and major surgery release inflammatory chemicals that cross into the brain and disturb its function. Whatever the route, the final common pathway is a widespread failure of the brain's metabolism, which is exactly what Engel and Romano's slowed EEG was recording. Indian context A classic Indian cause of anticholinergic delirium is datura (dhatura), whose seeds contain atropine and scopolamine (hyoscine). It is sometimes eaten by accident or in ritual preparations, and Indian forensic reports describe travellers on trains and buses who were offered sweets or "prasad" laced with datura and robbed while they were stupefied. The patient is agitated and hallucinating, with the textbook signs that medical students learn as "hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter": fever, dry skin and mouth, flushing, widely dilated pupils with blurred vision, and delirium, often with a full bladder and a racing pulse. Who becomes delirious depends on two things at once, a balance first set out by Sharon Inouye and Peter Charpentier in 1996. Predisposing factors make a brain vulnerable: old age, an existing dementia or mild NCD, poor vision or hearing, severe illness, functional dependence, depression, a past stroke and heavy drinking, with male sex an added risk in DSM-5-TR's list. Precipitating factors are the insults that tip it over: an infection, a new drug, an operation, dehydration, a urinary catheter, physical restraint, a sleepless night on a noisy ward. The two trade off against each other. A very vulnerable patient, an 88-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease and cataracts, may become delirious after a single sleeping tablet or a mild urinary infection; a robust young man needs a large insult, such as severe burns or septicaemia. Children with high fevers also become delirious easily. Pre-existing brain disease is the strongest predisposing factor of all; as many as half of people with dementia have at least one episode of delirium. The numbers in hospital are large, and they climb with the seriousness of the setting. DSM-5-TR gives a community prevalence of only 1 to 2 percent, but 8 to 17 percent among older people arriving in North American emergency departments, 18 to 35 percent at the time of admission to hospital, 11 to 51 percent of older people after an operation, up to 81 percent of patients in intensive care, and up to 88 percent of people with a terminal illness in their last days. Surgery on the heart is especially likely to cause it. A 2024 meta-analysis of 106 studies put the pooled incidence after open cardiac surgery at about 23 percent, with very wide variation between studies that depended partly on the patients and partly on which screening tool was used to look for delirium. The reasons are easy to see in Vimal's case: his age and his vulnerable brain, the heart-lung bypass machine (which can send tiny emboli to the brain, lower its blood flow and trigger inflammation), long anaesthesia, opioid painkillers, sleep deprivation in intensive care, and the vascular disease that made the operation necessary in the first place. Depression and anxiety are also common after heart surgery, but they develop more slowly, over weeks, and are not the acute syndrome of the first days after the operation; schizophrenia is not caused by surgery at all. The older term post-cardiotomy delirium recognises how familiar this picture is. Exam trap The commonest psychiatric syndrome after cardiac surgery , and after surgery in older people generally, is delirium , not depression, anxiety or schizophrenia. Depression after a heart attack or bypass is common and important (Book 2, Section 9.3 covers it under health psychology), but delirium is commoner, earlier and more dangerous. Delirium always has a physical cause ; "psychological stress" alone is never the answer. Course, outcome and management Delirium is usually short. DSM-5-TR says that in hospital it lasts about a week, although some symptoms often persist after discharge, and most people recover fully, with or without treatment, especially if they are not elderly. But "usually reversible" does not mean "harmless". Delirium can progress to stupor, coma, seizures or death if its cause is not found and treated, and it is a marker of how ill the patient is: as many as 38 to 41 percent of hospitalised people with delirium die within a year, the risk being greatest in those with cancer and other serious illness. Older people who become delirious are more likely to lose function, to need institutional care and to develop dementia, and there is increasing evidence that an episode of delirium can be followed by long-term cognitive decline, especially in people who already had some impairment. Sometimes delirium unmasks a dementia that was already developing: six months after his operation Vimal's daughter noticed that his memory was clearly worse than before, and he was later found to have an early Alzheimer's disease. Management rests on four principles. Find and treat the cause. This is the only treatment that cures. It means a full history (including from the family), a review of every drug the patient takes, a physical examination and investigations for infection, metabolic disturbance and hypoxia. In alcohol withdrawal it means benzodiazepines and thiamine (Sections 10.4 and 10.11); in anticholinergic delirium, stopping the drug. Support the brain while it recovers. Keep the patient oriented with a visible clock and calendar, a window, explanations repeated as often as needed and the same nurses where possible; restore spectacles and hearing aids; let a family member stay; keep the room lit and active by day and quiet and dim at night; get the patient out of bed and walking; ensure fluids and food; remove catheters and lines that are not essential; and avoid physical restraint, which increases agitation, injury and the length of the delirium. Review and reduce drugs. Stop or reduce anticholinergic, sedative and other drugs that can cause delirium, and avoid starting new ones casually. Use drugs for symptoms only when necessary. When agitation, fear or hallucinations put the patient or others at risk, a low dose of an antipsychotic such as haloperidol is used for the shortest possible time. It calms; it does not cure. In the large MIND-USA trial in intensive care, published in 2018 by Timothy Girard and colleagues, neither haloperidol nor ziprasidone shortened delirium or improved survival compared with placebo. Benzodiazepines are avoided, because they worsen confusion and prolong delirium, with one crucial exception: in delirium caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal they are the treatment, because they replace the missing drug (Section 10.7.9). Key study: preventing delirium, the Hospital Elder Life Program (1999) If so much delirium is precipitated by the hospital itself, can it be prevented? Sharon Inouye and colleagues at Yale tested this with 852 patients aged 70 or over admitted to a general medical service. Patients on one unit received a multicomponent programme aimed at six risk factors: cognitive impairment (orientation and stimulating activities), sleep deprivation (a non-drug sleep routine of warm milk or herbal tea, relaxation music and back massage, and a quiet ward at night), immobility (early walking), poor vision (spectacles, large-print materials), poor hearing (hearing aids, removing ear wax) and dehydration. They were compared with matched patients receiving usual care. Delirium developed in 9.9 percent of the intervention group against 15.0 percent of the usual-care group, a reduction of about a third (matched odds ratio 0.60), and the total number of days spent delirious also fell. The conclusion was that a substantial part of delirium in hospital is preventable with simple, non-drug measures delivered by staff and trained volunteers. The study's limitation is that the groups were matched rather than randomised, and the programme reduced new episodes rather than making established delirium go away faster. It became the basis of the Hospital Elder Life Program now used in many countries. Screening is part of prevention. The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), introduced by Inouye and colleagues in 1990, lets a trained nurse or doctor diagnose delirium at the bedside in a few minutes from four features: an acute onset and fluctuating course, and inattention, together with either disorganised thinking or an altered level of consciousness (the Assessment book describes it). Clinical link Psychologists in general hospitals are often the people who recognise delirium, because they are called to see "depression", "behavioural problems" or "a difficult patient". Three things make the psychologist's contribution distinctive. First, cognitive screening that tests attention (digit span, months backwards), not just memory. Second, work with the family, who are frightened by a parent who does not recognise them and often fear that the change is permanent; explaining that delirium is usually temporary, and involving them in reorientation, helps both patient and family. Third, follow-up: many intensive care survivors have vivid, frightening memories of their delirious hallucinations, which can feed anxiety and post-traumatic symptoms months later, and a patient who has been delirious needs his cognition checked again once he has recovered. Exam trap Delirium is usually reversible but it is not benign: it signals serious physical illness and carries a high mortality (up to about 40 percent within a year of a hospital diagnosis). The treatment is to find and treat the cause ; antipsychotics only calm distress or danger, and benzodiazepines worsen most deliria , except delirium due to alcohol or sedative withdrawal, where they are the treatment of choice. Physical restraint makes delirium worse, not safer. Delirium or dementia? In an elderly patient who is confused, the commonest question is whether the confusion is delirium, dementia or both, and DSM-5-TR calls this the most common differential diagnostic problem in the whole area. The answer matters enormously: delirium is a medical emergency with a cause to be found, whereas dementia is a chronic condition to be planned for, and a delirium mistaken for "just his dementia getting worse" may be a pneumonia left untreated. The two differ most clearly in time and in consciousness (Figure 10.15). Delirium begins over hours or days and fluctuates through each day, with attention and awareness disturbed from the start; dementia begins insidiously, over months or years, progresses slowly and steadily, and leaves consciousness and attention clear until its late stages. First, the two often coexist. The single strongest risk factor for delirium is an existing dementia, and on an elderly medical ward a delirium superimposed on dementia (ICD-10's F05.1) is the commonest situation of all; the clue is a sudden, recent worsening on top of a slow decline, and DSM-5-TR advises that when both are present, the delirium is treated first. Second, hallucinations, delusions, disorientation and memory loss occur in both disorders, so none of them separates the two; neither does age, because both are commonest in the elderly. Third, some dementias imitate delirium. NCD with Lewy bodies (Section 10.10) has marked fluctuations in attention and alertness and vivid visual hallucinations, so a fluctuating course alone does not prove delirium. And a depression in an older person can look like dementia (pseudodementia, Section 10.11), which Table 10.37 does not cover. The examiners return again and again to one question in different words: what is the most reliable way to tell delirium from dementia? The answer is always the same cluster: acute onset, a fluctuating course and a disturbance of attention and consciousness in delirium, against memory impairment in clear consciousness, with an insidious onset and a progressive course , in dementia. Exam trap The distractors in delirium-versus-dementia questions follow a few patterns, all wrong. "Hallucinations (or delusions) occur only in delirium" or "only in dementia": they occur in both . "Memory impairment only in delirium" or "memory loss is greater in delirium": memory is impaired in both, and progressive memory loss is the hallmark of dementia. "Onset gradual in delirium, acute in dementia": this is reversed . "Reversibility only in dementia" or "dementia is always reversible": it is delirium that is usually reversible. "Delirium occurs only in young patients" or "older age at onset": both are commonest in the elderly. "Confabulation" points to Korsakoff's syndrome (Section 10.11), and "aphasia and apraxia as early features" to Alzheimer's disease (Section 10.9). The right answer is acute onset, fluctuation and disturbed attention or consciousness in delirium, versus impaired memory with clear consciousness in dementia. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks.
