A neurocognitive disorder is an acquired decline from a person's own earlier level in one or more of six cognitive domains; it is major when the decline costs the person independence in everyday life and mild when it does not. Notice what that frame leaves out: it says nothing about why the decline happened. A stroke, a tumour, a vitamin deficiency, a virus, a blow to the head and a slow, silent pile-up of abnormal proteins can all produce the same picture of a person who forgets, gets lost and can no longer manage money. So once a clinician has decided that a neurocognitive disorder is present, the next question is always about cause, and DSM-5-TR builds that question into the diagnosis itself: you do not diagnose "major neurocognitive disorder" and stop, you diagnose "major neurocognitive disorder due to" something. By far the commonest answer to that question is Alzheimer's disease. It is the prototype against which every other dementia is described ("more stepwise than Alzheimer's", "memory better preserved than in Alzheimer's"), so it has to be learned first and learned well. Its story begins with one woman in Frankfurt at the start of the twentieth century. Auguste D. and the disease that took Alzheimer's name In 1901 Alois Alzheimer (1864 to 1915) was a senior physician at the municipal asylum in Frankfurt am Main. He was a psychiatrist who was also a skilled microscopist: with his friend and lifelong collaborator Franz Nissl (1860 to 1919), whose stain for nerve cells is still used, he spent years studying slices of the brains of patients who had died on the wards, hoping to find the physical lesion behind each kind of madness. That ambition was the programme of German psychiatry at the time. The patient who made his name arrived in November of that year. Key study: Auguste Deter (1901 to 1906) Auguste Deter (1850 to 1906), the wife of a railway clerk, was admitted to the Frankfurt asylum on 25 November 1901, aged 51. Since the spring she had become irrationally jealous of her husband, then forgetful; she hid things, could no longer cook, lost her way in her own flat and sometimes screamed that someone was going to kill her. Alzheimer interviewed her the next day. Asked her name, she said "Auguste"; asked her husband's name, she again said "Auguste". When he asked her to write her name she began, lost the thread, and said what became the most quoted sentence in the history of dementia: "I have lost myself" (in German, roughly "I have, so to speak, lost myself"). Alzheimer moved to Kraepelin's clinic in Munich but kept track of her. When she died on 8 April 1906, of septicaemia from infected bedsores, her brain was sent to him. Using a new silver stain he found two abnormalities: clumps of a strange material scattered between the neurons (the plaques) and thick, tangled bundles of fibrils inside them (the tangles), along with marked shrinkage of the cortex. He presented the case at a meeting of south-west German psychiatrists in Tübingen in November 1906, where it drew little interest, and published it in 1907 as "On a peculiar disease of the cerebral cortex". Her case file was then lost for almost ninety years until psychiatrists at the Frankfurt university clinic, led by Konrad Maurer , found it in the mid-1990s (accounts give 1995 or 1996) and published it in The Lancet in 1997. Re-examination of her preserved brain sections confirmed plaques and tangles without significant vascular disease. A 2013 report that she carried a presenilin 1 mutation could not be replicated the following year. Alzheimer did not claim to have found a new disease; he claimed to have shown that a dementia could be explained by visible changes in the cortex. The name came from his chief, Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926), who in the eighth edition of his textbook of psychiatry (1910) used the term "Alzheimer's disease" for this kind of case. Because Auguste had fallen ill in her early fifties, Kraepelin classed the condition as a presenile dementia , one beginning before old age. The far commoner mental decline of the very old was called senile dementia and was widely assumed to be a different thing, the result of hardening of the arteries or simply of wear and tear. For most of the twentieth century, then, "Alzheimer's disease" meant a rare illness of the middle-aged. Two pieces of evidence changed that. In Newcastle in 1968, Gary Blessed , Bernard Tomlinson and Martin Roth tested elderly people in life and then counted plaques in their brains after death; the more plaques, the worse the dementia had been, and the brains of most elderly people with "senile dementia" showed exactly the changes Alzheimer had described. Then in 1976 the American neurologist Robert Katzman (1925 to 2008) argued in an editorial that presenile Alzheimer's disease and senile dementia were one and the same disease, divided only by an arbitrary birthday, and that, counted properly, it was one of the major killers of old people. That argument won. Today Alzheimer's disease is understood to be a single disease that can begin at any adult age, with a rare early-onset form and a common late-onset form, and the age of 65 survives only as a coding convenience (ICD-10 still separates F00.0, dementia in Alzheimer's disease with early onset, before 65, from F00.1, with late onset). Two older words are worth pinning down because they still appear as options. "Senile dementia" is a description, not a diagnosis: it means only "dementia beginning in old age" and says nothing about cause, so it could be Alzheimer's, vascular or anything else. Cerebral atrophy is also a description: it means shrinkage of the brain, with wider sulci and larger ventricles, and it is seen on scans in Alzheimer's disease, in many other dementias, after chronic heavy drinking and, to a modest degree, in normal ageing. Neither term names a disease with its own mechanism, and that is why neither can be the best answer when a paper asks which disease is linked to a specific chemical deficit. Exam trap "Which condition is related to a deficiency of acetylcholine in the brain?" The answer is Alzheimer's disease , because its defining chemical lesion is the loss of the cholinergic neurons of the basal forebrain (Section 10.9.4). "Senile dementia" and "atrophy" are descriptive labels that cover many causes, and Korsakoff's syndrome is a disorder of thiamine deficiency, usually caused by chronic drinking, that damages the mammillary bodies and thalamus (Section 10.11); Alzheimer's disease is not caused by alcohol. Dates: Auguste admitted 1901; Alzheimer's lecture 1906 and paper 1907; Kraepelin's naming 1910. If an option says "first described in 1906" or "in 1907", both refer to the same case. How common it is, and who gets it The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 57 million people were living with dementia in 2021, with nearly 10 million new cases every year and more than 60 percent of all cases in low- and middle-income countries such as India. Dementia is now the fifth leading cause of death in the world, and in 2019 it cost economies an estimated 1.3 trillion US dollars, much of it in unpaid care by families. Alzheimer's disease is the commonest single cause: WHO puts its share at 60 to 70 percent of cases, and DSM-5-TR gives a range from about 60 percent to over 90 percent depending on the setting and the criteria used. The range is wide because many old people have more than one kind of pathology, so "pure" figures depend on how mixed cases are counted. The strongest risk factor, by a wide margin, is age. Alzheimer's disease is rare before 60, and after 65 the prevalence of dementia roughly doubles with every five years of age; a well-known meta-analysis by Anthony Jorm and colleagues in 1987 put the doubling time at about five years. DSM-5-TR quotes American figures that make the point: dementia due to Alzheimer's disease is found in 11 percent of people aged 65 and over and in 32 percent of those aged 85 and over, and 81 percent of all people with the disease are 75 or older. Onset is usually between 70 and 89. Early-onset cases, beginning in the forties or fifties, are uncommon and are often, though not always, caused by single-gene mutations (Section 10.9.5). More women than men have the disease, partly because women live longer; whether women also have a higher age-specific risk is less certain, since European studies have found a higher incidence in women and most North American studies have not. Indian context The first large rural study, the Indo-US study in Ballabgarh, Haryana ( Vijay Chandra , Mary Ganguli and colleagues, 1998), screened 5,126 people aged 55 and over and found strikingly low rates: dementia in 1.36 percent and Alzheimer's disease in 1.07 percent of those aged 65 and over, far below Western figures. Possible reasons include fewer people surviving into the highest-risk ages, different risk factors, and under-detection where forgetfulness in the old is taken as natural (in Hindi an old person who has become forgetful may be said to have "turned sixty", sathiya gaye ). The nationwide Longitudinal Ageing Study in India's dementia sub-study (LASI-DAD; Jinkook Lee and colleagues, 2023) gave a much higher national estimate: 7.4 percent of Indians aged 60 and over, about 8.8 million people, with large differences between states. Almost all of this care is given at home by families, usually women, with little formal support. The course: from forgetting to dependence The two words that define the course of Alzheimer's disease are insidious and gradual . Insidious means that nobody can say when it began: families date the onset to a wedding at which the person repeated the same story three times, or to a bill that went unpaid, but on questioning the changes had been creeping in for a year or more. Gradual means that the decline is steady, without the sudden drops of a stroke and without extended plateaus; DSM-5-TR builds this into the criteria. The disease runs to death, which comes on average about ten years after diagnosis (DSM-5-TR), sometimes as long as twenty, most often from aspiration pneumonia in a person who can no longer swallow safely. Pinel describes the illness in three phases. In the preclinical stage the brain is already accumulating plaques and tangles but the person has no symptoms at all; studies of families with dominant mutations suggest that this silent phase lasts a decade or two. In the prodromal stage there is mild cognitive impairment, noticeable to the person and to careful tests but not yet disabling (Section 10.9.8). Then comes the dementia stage, which clinicians usually divide into early (mild), middle (moderate) and late (severe), as in Table 10.38. Push a case through the stages and the pattern becomes clear. Rajinder is a 68-year-old retired headmaster in Ludhiana who for forty years kept the school accounts in his head. His wife first noticed that he asked the same questions again and again ("Is Pinky coming on Sunday?" five times in an afternoon), that he forgot conversations held the day before, and that he had started leaving notes all over the house. He laughed it off as age. Over the next two years he began to hunt for words, calling a spoon "the thing for eating dal" (circumlocution), lost his way driving home from the gurdwara he had attended for decades, and could no longer work out the change at the market. He insisted that the servant was stealing the money he had in fact hidden himself. Dressing became a puzzle: he put his kurta on inside out and could not work out the buttons, although his arms and fingers were perfectly strong. His speech remained fluent and polite, his walking was normal and there was no tremor, and on no day was he suddenly worse. This is the IHBAS 2025 vignette in living form: progressive memory impairment, then language difficulty and visuospatial deficits, with insidious onset and gradual progression. Look at the order in which things went. The first casualty is episodic memory for recent events, the memory of what happened to me yesterday, because the damage starts in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus that lay down new memories. Old memories of school, marriage and the partition stories of his parents are kept far longer, a pattern described in 1881 by the French psychologist Théodule Ribot (1839 to 1916) and known as Ribot's law : in a progressive dementia the most recent memories are lost first and the oldest last. Semantic memory (knowledge of words and facts) fades later, and procedural memory (skills such as cycling or tying a turban) lasts longest of all. As the disease spreads into the temporal and parietal association cortex, Indian teaching summarises the middle stage as the "four As": amnesia , aphasia (word-finding difficulty and empty, roundabout speech at first, with comprehension failing later), apraxia (inability to carry out skilled purposeful movements such as dressing or using a comb, despite normal strength) and agnosia (failure to recognise objects or faces despite normal sight). Visuospatial and executive skills fail alongside them, and orientation goes first for time, then for place, and only very late for person. Section 10.8 defined each of these deficits and matched it to the function it affects. DSM-5-TR stresses that neuropsychiatric symptoms are almost universal (in one American sample 98 percent of patients developed them within five years), that more than half of people who develop dementia begin with them, and that they are often more distressing to families than the memory loss itself. The umbrella term for them is behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD). In the mild stage they are mostly depression, irritability and apathy; in the moderate stage delusions (classically that misplaced belongings have been stolen), misidentifications (the reflection in the mirror is a stranger; the house is not really his house), agitation, aggression and wandering; and many patients become more confused and restless in the late afternoon and evening, the phenomenon called sundowning . Hallucinations occur but are less prominent than in Lewy body disease (Section 10.10.4). Late in the illness come gait disturbance, difficulty swallowing, incontinence, myoclonus and seizures. Strikingly, the motor system is spared until late: the primary motor and sensory cortex and the basal ganglia are among the last regions the disease reaches, which is why a person with moderate Alzheimer's disease can walk briskly out of the house and get lost. That preserved movement is one of the most useful clues separating Alzheimer's disease from the subcortical dementias of Section 10.10.10. DSM-5-TR also notes a moderate risk of suicide that persists even many years after the diagnosis, so mood and suicidal thinking need to be asked about throughout the illness. Alongside the typical amnestic picture there are less common presentations that begin elsewhere: a visuospatial form (posterior cortical atrophy, in which a person cannot read, judge distances or find objects in plain view while memory is relatively spared), a language form (logopenic aphasia, with halting, word-searching speech) and a dysexecutive or behavioural form. They are worth knowing because they are often misdiagnosed, and because the logopenic form is easily confused with the language variants of frontotemporal disorder (Section 10.10.3). Exam trap "A progressive neurodegenerative disorder with memory impairment, language difficulties and visuospatial deficits, insidious onset and gradual progression" is Alzheimer's disease . Each distractor has a different signature: Lewy body dementia fluctuates and brings well-formed visual hallucinations and parkinsonism; vascular dementia begins abruptly and worsens in steps with focal neurological signs; frontotemporal dementia starts younger with personality change or a language disorder while memory and visuospatial skills are relatively spared. The key words to match are "memory first" and "smooth decline". Memory loss with confabulation and nystagmus in a heavy drinker is not Alzheimer's disease but Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (Section 10.11). What goes wrong in the brain Look at the brain of a person who has died of Alzheimer's disease and the first thing you notice is that it is shrunken: the gyri are thin, the sulci gape, the ventricles are enlarged to fill the lost space, and the hippocampus and the rest of the medial temporal lobe are worst affected, with the temporal and parietal association cortex close behind. The primary motor, sensory and visual areas look relatively normal, which fits the clinical picture you have just met. Under the microscope Pinel lists the three defining features: neurofibrillary tangles , threadlike tangles of tau protein inside the cytoplasm of neurons; amyloid plaques , clumps outside the neurons made of degenerating nerve terminals around a core of a protein called beta-amyloid , which is present in healthy brains only in small amounts; and loss of neurons. Tau is a protein that normally stabilises the microtubules, the internal scaffolding and transport tracks of the axon. In Alzheimer's disease it becomes hyperphosphorylated (it carries too many phosphate groups), lets go of the microtubules and aggregates into the paired filaments that make up the tangles, and the neuron's transport system collapses. Which of these lesions matters most for symptoms? Plaques, it turns out, correlate only loosely with how demented a person was in life; tangles correlate better, and the loss of synapses correlates best of all, as Robert Terry and colleagues showed in 1991. The spread of the tangles also explains the order of the symptoms. In 1991 Heiko Braak and Eva Braak , examining 83 brains from people with and without dementia, showed that tangles appear in a predictable sequence that can be divided into six Braak stages : in stages I and II they are confined to the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, the gateway to the hippocampus, and the person has no symptoms; in stages III and IV they fill the limbic system, including the hippocampus, and memory begins to fail; in stages V and VI they flood the association cortex of the neocortex and the person is demented. Memory goes first because the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus are hit first. The cholinergic hypothesis. The first chemical theory of the disease came from a simple measurement. In 1976 Peter Davies and A. J. F. Maloney , in Edinburgh, reported in The Lancet a selective loss of the enzyme that makes acetylcholine (choline acetyltransferase) in the cortex and hippocampus of patients with Alzheimer's disease; other neurotransmitter systems were much less affected. Where were the missing cholinergic neurons? The cortex gets most of its acetylcholine from a small group of large neurons in the basal forebrain, just above the hypothalamus, called the nucleus basalis of Meynert after the Viennese anatomist Theodor Meynert (1833 to 1892). In 1981 and 1982 Peter Whitehouse and colleagues at Johns Hopkins showed that these neurons are severely depleted in Alzheimer's disease. Meanwhile drugs that block acetylcholine receptors, such as scopolamine, had been shown to impair memory in healthy young volunteers in a way that resembled ageing. In 1982 Raymond Bartus and colleagues pulled these findings together in Science as the cholinergic hypothesis : the memory loss of Alzheimer's disease (and some of the memory loss of ageing) is caused by the failure of the basal forebrain cholinergic system. That hypothesis led directly to the first drugs for the disease, the cholinesterase inhibitors (Section 10.9.7). Pinel's verdict is the modern one: acetylcholine depletion from basal forebrain damage contributes to Alzheimer's amnesia, but it is clearly not the only factor, because the damage is diffuse and reaches the medial temporal lobes and the prefrontal cortex as well. That is also why the drugs built on it help only modestly. Exam trap Match each transmitter to the disorder in which its loss is the textbook lesion. Acetylcholine : Alzheimer's disease (nucleus basalis of Meynert). Dopamine : Parkinson's disease (substantia nigra to striatum); dopamine excess in the mesolimbic pathway is the classical hypothesis of positive psychotic symptoms (Chapter 4, Section 4.8). GABA : Huntington's disease destroys the GABA-releasing neurons of the striatum; low GABA function is also linked to anxiety and epilepsy. Serotonin and noradrenaline : the monoamine hypothesis of depression (Chapter 5). Glutamate is the excitotoxic villain targeted by memantine, not a transmitter that is deficient. The amyloid cascade hypothesis. The second and now dominant theory begins with the plaque. In 1984 George Glenner and Caine Wong isolated beta-amyloid and worked out its sequence. It turned out to be a fragment of a much larger membrane protein, the amyloid precursor protein (APP), whose gene lies on chromosome 21. APP is normally cut by enzymes called secretases. When it is cut first by beta-secretase and then by gamma-secretase (an enzyme complex whose working core is a protein called presenilin), the product is beta-amyloid, and one form of it, 42 amino acids long, is especially sticky: it clumps into small soluble aggregates called oligomers and eventually into plaques. In 1991 Alison Goate , working in John Hardy 's group in London, found the first mutation in the APP gene in a family with early-onset Alzheimer's disease. In 1992 Hardy and Gerald Higgins set out the amyloid cascade hypothesis in a short paper in Science : the accumulation of beta-amyloid is the first event, and everything else (tau tangles, inflammation, synapse loss, neuron death and dementia) follows from it (Figure 10.17). Read the centre column from top to bottom: in this view beta-amyloid is the first domino and tau tangles, synapse loss and neuron death follow. The genes in the top two boxes (APP, presenilins) cause early-onset familial disease; APOE e4 (right) raises the risk of the common late-onset form. The case for the hypothesis is strong. Every mutation known to cause early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease alters the production or stickiness of beta-amyloid. People with Down syndrome, who carry a third copy of chromosome 21 and hence of the APP gene, make extra beta-amyloid and almost all develop plaques and tangles by the age of 40. And in 2012 a rare variant of the APP gene that reduces beta-amyloid production was found in Iceland to protect against the disease, a natural experiment pointing in the same direction. The case against is also strong, and Pinel spells it out. Many elderly people carry heavy loads of plaques without any dementia (the "high-plaque normals"). Plaque load tracks symptoms poorly. And in the decade before the 2020s one anti-amyloid drug after another cleared plaques or lowered amyloid in animals and then failed in patients. The modern position is a softened cascade: beta-amyloid (probably the soluble oligomers rather than the plaques) is an early and necessary trigger, but tau is the agent that does the damage, and inflammation by the brain's immune cells, the microglia, and vascular disease shape how fast it happens. Pinel also describes the newer pathogenic spread hypothesis : misfolded tau or beta-amyloid "seeds" the misfolding of normal copies of the protein, which then spread from neuron to neuron along connected pathways, much as prions do (Section 10.10.7). That idea fits the orderly Braak sequence remarkably well. Exam trap Plaques are outside neurons and made of beta-amyloid ; tangles are inside neurons and made of hyperphosphorylated tau . Do not swap them. The pathology starts in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus (medial temporal lobe), not in the frontal lobe (frontotemporal disorder), the substantia nigra (Parkinson's) or the caudate (Huntington's). Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein) and Pick bodies (tau) belong to other diseases (Section 10.10). Genes, risk and reserve Alzheimer's disease comes in two genetic forms. The rare early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait: a child of an affected parent has a one-in-two chance of carrying the mutation, and a carrier will almost certainly develop the disease, often in the forties or fifties. Three genes are responsible, and they map neatly onto the cascade in Figure 10.17: APP on chromosome 21 (the first found, in 1991), presenilin 1 (PSEN1) on chromosome 14 (1995, the commonest of the three) and presenilin 2 (PSEN2) on chromosome 1 (also 1995). DSM-5-TR summarises them as the rare Mendelian mutations on chromosomes 1, 14 and 21. Familial early-onset disease is rare, and Pinel notes that these mutations contribute little (about 1 percent) to the common late-onset form; they matter far more for what they have taught about mechanism than for the number of patients. The common late-onset form is not inherited in that simple way, but it is still strongly genetic: DSM-5-TR puts the genetic share of the risk at 60 to 80 percent, spread across more than 45 risk genes of small effect and one of large effect. That one is the gene for apolipoprotein E (APOE), a cholesterol-carrying protein, on chromosome 19. The gene comes in three common forms (alleles), e2, e3 and e4. In 1993 a group at Duke University led by Allen Roses showed that the e4 allele is overrepresented in late-onset Alzheimer's disease. Carrying one copy raises the risk roughly threefold, and carrying two copies raises it much more (estimates range from about eight to fifteen times, depending on the study and the population), while also bringing onset forward by several years. The e2 allele is mildly protective. APOE e4 appears to bind beta-amyloid and slow its clearance from the brain, encouraging plaques. But e4 is a risk factor, not a cause: many carriers, even some with two copies, live to great age without dementia, and many patients carry no e4 at all. DSM-5-TR is therefore clear that APOE testing is not a diagnostic test; and it notes that the strength of the e4 effect differs between ethnic groups. Down syndrome is the third genetic route. Because people with Down syndrome have three copies of chromosome 21, they have three copies of the APP gene; Pinel reports that by the age of 40 almost all have numerous plaques and tangles, and by 60 about two-thirds have developed dementia. The Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, an international panel led by Gill Livingston , has tried three times to estimate how much dementia could in principle be prevented. In 2017 it named nine modifiable risk factors accounting for about 35 percent of dementia; in 2020 it named twelve, accounting for about 40 percent; and in its 2024 report it named fourteen, accounting for nearly half. Grouped by stage of life, the fourteen are: in early life, less education; in midlife, hearing loss, high LDL cholesterol, depression, traumatic brain injury, physical inactivity, diabetes, smoking, high blood pressure, obesity and excessive alcohol; and in later life, social isolation, air pollution and untreated loss of vision (the two factors added in 2024 were high LDL cholesterol and vision loss). These figures concern dementia of all causes, not Alzheimer's disease alone, and they assume that associations found in observational studies are causal, which is the main criticism of them. Still, their message is a hopeful one: a large share of dementia may be postponed by things a society can change. Why should schooling protect a brain against plaques? The best answer is the idea of cognitive reserve , developed especially by Yaakov Stern : education, mentally demanding work and a rich mental life build extra neural capacity and more flexible ways of using it, so that more damage must accumulate before symptoms show. Barlow and Durand describe the telling consequence. Better-educated people develop symptoms later, but once symptoms appear they decline faster, which suggests that education does not stop the disease but buys a period of normal functioning while the pathology quietly advances. In India a clinic-based study from Hyderabad ( Suvarna Alladi and colleagues, 2013) found that people who spoke two languages developed dementia about four and a half years later than those who spoke one, another possible source of reserve. Key study: the Nun Study (Snowdon and colleagues, 1996) The epidemiologist David Snowdon studied elderly American nuns of the School Sisters of Notre Dame, women who had lived remarkably similar lives (no smoking, similar diet, housing and work), which removes many of the confounds that plague studies of ordinary populations. The sisters agreed to yearly cognitive testing and to donate their brains. Snowdon's team found the short autobiographies that 93 of them had written as young women joining the order, at an average age of 22, and scored each for idea density , the number of distinct ideas packed into every ten words. About 58 years later, the sisters whose youthful writing had been low in idea density scored worse on cognitive tests; and among the 14 who had died and been examined at autopsy, Alzheimer's disease was found in all of those with low idea density and in none of those with high idea density. The criticism is the size of the autopsy sample, and whether low idea density was a cause (less reserve) or a very early sign of a brain already vulnerable. The study also found sisters whose brains were full of plaques and tangles but who had shown little dementia in life, which is the reserve idea in its purest form. Exam trap APOE is on chromosome 19 ; APP is on 21 ; presenilin 1 on 14 ; presenilin 2 on 1 . APOE e4 is a susceptibility gene for late-onset disease, not a cause of early-onset familial disease and not a diagnostic test. Early Alzheimer's in Down syndrome is explained by the extra APP gene on the extra chromosome 21. Huntington's disease (chromosome 4) is the textbook single-gene dementia, not Alzheimer's. Making the diagnosis For most of the twentieth century a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease in life was a matter of probability, confirmed only by the microscope after death. It is still made mainly at the bedside, by establishing three things. First, that there is a neurocognitive disorder: a history of decline taken from someone who knows the person well (patients with Alzheimer's disease often underestimate their problems), a mental state examination, and cognitive testing. The brief screening tests are taught in the Assessment book: the Mini-Mental State Examination ( Marshal Folstein , Susan Folstein and Paul McHugh, 1975), a 30-point test of orientation, registration, attention, recall, language and copying; the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA; Ziad Nasreddine and colleagues, 2005), more sensitive to mild impairment; and Indian adaptations for people with little schooling, such as the Hindi Mental State Examination. Second, that the pattern fits Alzheimer's disease: insidious onset, memory first, steady progression. Third, that nothing else explains it better, which is why every patient needs a physical and neurological examination, blood tests for the treatable mimics (thyroid function, vitamin B12, syphilis serology, HIV where relevant, glucose, electrolytes, liver and kidney function) and usually a brain scan (Section 10.10.9). DSM-5-TR turns this reasoning into criteria, and it is worth understanding why each rule is there. The general criteria for major or mild neurocognitive disorder must be met (Section 10.8). The onset must be insidious and the progression gradual, in at least one cognitive domain for mild disorder and at least two for major disorder; this excludes the sudden onset of stroke and the acute onset of delirium. The clinician must then grade the certainty. Probable Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed if there is evidence of a causative gene mutation (from genetic testing or family history), or, for major disorder, if all three of the following are present: clear decline in learning and memory and in at least one other domain; a steadily progressive decline without extended plateaus; and no evidence of a mixed cause, such as cerebrovascular disease or another neurodegenerative disease. Otherwise the diagnosis is possible Alzheimer's disease. For mild neurocognitive disorder the bar is higher: without a known mutation only "possible" is allowed, because at the mild stage it is not yet certain that the deficits will progress. Finally the disturbance must not be better explained by cerebrovascular disease, another neurodegenerative disease, a substance, or another mental or medical disorder. A specifier records whether behavioural disturbance is present. ICD-10 codes the same condition as F00 (with F00.0 early onset, F00.1 late onset and F00.2 atypical or mixed), and ICD-11 as 6D80, dementia due to Alzheimer disease. Technology is steadily turning "probable" into something closer to certain. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy and, just as important, rules out tumours, subdural haematomas, strokes and hydrocephalus. Positron emission tomography (PET) with a glucose tracer shows reduced metabolism in the temporal and parietal lobes. Amyloid PET and tau PET make the plaques and tangles visible in a living person, and the cerebrospinal fluid of a patient with Alzheimer's disease shows low beta-amyloid 42 (because it is trapped in plaques) and raised total tau and phosphorylated tau (released from dying neurons). DSM-5-TR predicted that blood tests would follow, and they have: plasma measures of phosphorylated tau now detect Alzheimer pathology with useful accuracy, and in May 2025 the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the first blood test to help diagnose it. These biomarkers have pushed some researchers to define Alzheimer's disease biologically, by the presence of amyloid and tau whether or not there are symptoms, a move that remains controversial because many people with positive biomarkers never become demented. The differential diagnosis of an older person with failing memory runs through the rest of this chapter: delirium, which is acute and fluctuating with disturbed attention (Section 10.8); depression presenting as dementia, the "pseudodementia" of Section 10.11; the other neurocognitive disorders of Section 10.10; the medical causes of Section 10.11; and, at the mildest end, normal ageing (Section 10.9.8). Mixed cases are common in the very old, and when Alzheimer's disease and vascular disease both contribute DSM-5-TR asks for both diagnoses (or for neurocognitive disorder due to multiple etiologies). Exam trap The definitive diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease has traditionally been neuropathological (plaques and tangles at autopsy or biopsy); clinical criteria give "probable" or "possible". A normal CT scan does not exclude Alzheimer's disease, and a scan showing atrophy does not prove it. The MMSE and MoCA screen for impairment; they do not diagnose its cause. Treatment: what the drugs can and cannot do There is no cure for Alzheimer's disease, and every treatment available today either eases symptoms for a while or slows the decline a little. The first class of drugs grew straight out of the cholinergic hypothesis. If the cholinergic neurons are dying, the acetylcholine that the survivors release can be made to last longer by blocking the enzyme that breaks it down in the synapse, acetylcholinesterase. The cholinesterase inhibitors do exactly that. The first, tacrine, was approved in the United States in 1993 but caused liver damage and fell out of use. It was followed by donepezil (1996), rivastigmine (which also blocks a second enzyme, butyrylcholinesterase, and is available as a skin patch) and galantamine (originally derived from the snowdrop plant). They are used in mild to moderate disease (donepezil in severe disease as well) and, as you will see, in Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease dementia. Their benefit is real but modest: on average a small improvement or a temporary halt on cognitive scales, small gains in daily function and behaviour, and then the decline resumes, because the drugs do nothing to the disease process. Their side effects are those of extra acetylcholine: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, loss of appetite and weight, slowing of the heart and fainting, muscle cramps and vivid dreams. The second class acts on glutamate. Excessive stimulation of the NMDA type of glutamate receptor is thought to damage neurons (excitotoxicity), and memantine , a low-affinity NMDA receptor antagonist, dampens that over-activity without blocking the normal signals needed for learning. It is used in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease, alone or together with a cholinesterase inhibitor, and is generally well tolerated (dizziness, headache, constipation, sometimes confusion). Like the cholinesterase inhibitors, it treats symptoms only. The third class is new, and it is the first that attacks the disease itself: monoclonal antibodies that bind beta-amyloid and help the brain's immune cells clear it. The story has had three acts. Aducanumab received accelerated approval from the FDA in June 2021, on the strength of its ability to remove amyloid rather than clear evidence of clinical benefit; the decision was fiercely criticised, other regulators refused it, and its maker discontinued it in 2024. Lecanemab followed (FDA approval in 2023): in its main trial, in about 1,800 people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease, it slowed decline on a dementia rating scale by about 27 percent over 18 months, roughly half a point on an 18-point scale. Donanemab was approved by the FDA in 2024, after a trial in which decline was about 35 percent slower over about a year and a half. The price of these benefits is a side effect called amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA): swelling of the brain (oedema) and tiny bleeds (microhaemorrhages) seen on MRI. They are usually silent but occasionally cause confusion, seizures or death, and they are most frequent in people with two copies of APOE e4; in the donanemab trial ARIA was seen in 36.8 percent of treated patients against 14.9 percent on placebo. So the drugs are given only in the early stages, only to people whose amyloid has been confirmed by PET or cerebrospinal fluid, by repeated intravenous infusion, with scheduled MRI scans. As of late 2026, as far as can be verified, regulators remain divided. In the European Union lecanemab was authorised in April 2025 and donanemab in September 2025, both restricted to people with one or no copy of APOE e4 because of the ARIA risk. In the United Kingdom the medicines regulator approved both in 2024, but the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence ruled in 2025 that their modest benefit did not justify their cost for routine National Health Service use; the manufacturers' appeals succeeded on several procedural points in early 2026, and the decision was sent back to NICE's committee to reconsider. In India the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) approved donanemab in November 2025 and it was launched in May 2026, and lecanemab was launched in India in 2026 after CDSCO authorisation. Against this, a Cochrane systematic review published in April 2026, pooling 17 trials with more than 20,000 participants, judged the effect of anti-amyloid antibodies on cognition and dementia severity to be trivial and confirmed the raised risk of ARIA; its critics, including the manufacturers, objected that it pooled failed drugs with the two that succeeded. For the examination, remember four things: they remove amyloid; they slow early disease modestly; ARIA is their main danger, especially in APOE e4 homozygotes; and they have no place in moderate or severe dementia. When a person with dementia becomes agitated, aggressive or sleepless, the first step is to look for a cause: pain, constipation, a urinary infection, a new drug, delirium, hunger, boredom or a frightening environment. Non-drug approaches come first (a predictable routine, daylight and activity, simple calm communication, and training for carers), and they are taught in Book 2, Section 10.7.4 on agitation and wandering. Depression is treated with an antidepressant such as sertraline or citalopram; drugs with anticholinergic effects (older tricyclics, many antihistamines and bladder drugs) and benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls and are avoided. Antipsychotics help severe agitation or distressing psychosis a little, but they increase the risk of stroke and death in people with dementia, a danger the FDA has warned about since 2005, so they are used only when there is real risk, at low dose and for as short a time as possible; in 2023 the FDA approved brexpiprazole specifically for agitation in Alzheimer's dementia. Psychological and social approaches to the person (cognitive stimulation, reality orientation, reminiscence and validation therapy) are in Book 2, Section 10.7.3, and support for the family caregiver, whose own health suffers badly, is in Book 2, Section 10.7.2. Clinical link Diagnosis early in the disease is also the moment for planning while the person can still decide: who will manage money and property, whether driving should stop, and what treatment the person would or would not want later. In India the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 allows an adult to make an advance directive about mental health care and to appoint a nominated representative; capacity must be judged for each decision, and a person with mild dementia often retains it for many of them. The family is nearly always the care system, so a clinical psychologist's work with a patient with Alzheimer's disease is usually also work with the spouse, son or daughter-in-law who provides the care. Exam trap Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are symptomatic treatments; they do not stop the disease. Memantine is an NMDA antagonist , not a cholinergic drug. Only the anti-amyloid antibodies remove the pathology, and only in early disease. Antipsychotics in dementia carry a raised risk of stroke and death , and in Lewy body dementia they can be catastrophic (Section 10.10.4). Normal ageing, mild cognitive impairment and mild neurocognitive disorder Every older person forgets names, and every forgetful older person who reads about Alzheimer's disease wonders whether it has begun. Where does normal ageing end? Normal ageing slows the speed of processing and makes retrieval less efficient: names come to mind later, the reason for entering a room is momentarily lost, and new learning takes more repetitions. But the information is not lost. Cues and recognition bring it back, new things can still be learned, and everyday life goes on unimpaired. In 1962 the Canadian psychiatrist V. A. Kral drew the distinction that clinicians still use, between benign senescent forgetfulness , in which a person forgets details of an experience but remembers the experience itself and knows that he is forgetting, and a "malignant" forgetfulness in which whole recent events vanish, which often led on to dementia. In 1999 Ronald Petersen and colleagues at the Mayo Clinic gave the in-between state a name and a definition that stuck. They compared 76 people with what they called mild cognitive impairment (MCI) with 234 healthy older people and 106 patients with mild Alzheimer's disease. People with MCI complained of poor memory (ideally confirmed by someone who knew them), had memory test scores clearly below what was expected for their age and education, but had otherwise normal general cognition and essentially normal daily activities, and were not demented. Followed over time, they declined faster than the healthy controls but more slowly than the patients with Alzheimer's disease: they were, in effect, in between. In Petersen's clinic samples about 10 to 15 percent of people with MCI progressed to dementia each year, against about 1 to 2 percent of healthy older people. Petersen later divided MCI into amnestic MCI, in which memory is the main problem and which usually leads to Alzheimer's disease, and non-amnestic MCI, affecting language, attention or executive or visuospatial function, which more often leads to frontotemporal, Lewy body or vascular disease. Not everyone with MCI gets worse: a sizeable share, especially in community rather than clinic samples, stays stable or returns to normal, often because the impairment was caused by depression, medication, poor sleep or a medical illness. That is the reason MCI is never treated as a diagnosis of early dementia. DSM-5 absorbed this concept into mild neurocognitive disorder : a modest decline from a previous level in one or more cognitive domains, shown by concern from the person, an informant or the clinician and by test performance typically between one and two standard deviations below the norm (Section 10.8), with independence in everyday activities preserved, although the person may need more effort, compensatory strategies or accommodation. It is broader than MCI, since it covers mild decline of any cause (mild neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease, to vascular disease, to traumatic brain injury and so on), and it is the stage at which DSM-5-TR allows only "possible" Alzheimer's disease without a known mutation. ICD-10 had a rough equivalent in F06.7, mild cognitive disorder, and ICD-11 lists mild neurocognitive disorder alongside dementia. A still earlier state, subjective cognitive decline , describes people who feel their memory is worse but perform normally on tests; their risk of later decline is slightly raised, but many are simply anxious or depressed. The honest answer is: look for and treat anything reversible, treat vascular risk factors and hearing loss, encourage exercise and mental and social activity, review medicines, and follow the person up. Exam trap Mild cognitive impairment (Petersen, 1999) and DSM-5's mild neurocognitive disorder are not dementia : the defining difference is that independence in daily activities is preserved . The usual quoted conversion rate is 10 to 15 percent per year (against 1 to 2 percent in healthy older people), so most people with MCI have not become demented after a year, and some return to normal. Benign senescent forgetfulness (Kral, 1962) is normal ageing, not MCI. 10.10 The Other Neurocognitive Disorders Medium yield · 3 Qs Alzheimer's disease accounts for perhaps half to two-thirds of dementia; the rest is a crowd of other causes, and the papers love to make you tell them apart. DSM-5-TR lists the named causes after "major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to": Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal degeneration, Lewy body disease, vascular disease, traumatic brain injury, substance or medication use, HIV infection, prion disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, another medical condition, multiple etiologies, and unspecified. You will not remember them as a list. You will remember them as patterns, by asking five questions of every patient. How did it start, suddenly or creeping? How has it moved since, steadily, in steps, up and down from day to day, or frighteningly fast? What failed first: memory, behaviour, language or attention? Are there signs in the body, such as a tremor, a jerk, a weak arm or a stiff walk? And how old was the person when it began? Each disorder in this section has its own answers to those five questions, and Table 10.45 at the end lines them up. First, though, one word that the papers use as a trap. What makes a disease neurodegenerative A neurodegenerative disease is one in which neurons progressively lose their structure and function and die, usually in a characteristic set of brain regions and usually because a particular protein misfolds and accumulates. The person does not recover between bad patches; the disease moves only one way. The diseases are now often grouped by the protein that accumulates: beta-amyloid and tau in Alzheimer's disease; tau or a protein called TDP-43 in frontotemporal degeneration; alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia and multiple system atrophy (together called the synucleinopathies); mutant huntingtin in Huntington's disease; the prion protein in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease; and, in most cases, TDP-43 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The pathogenic spread hypothesis that you met in Section 10.9.4 proposes that in all of them a misfolded protein seeds the misfolding of its normal neighbours and spreads along connected pathways. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), described by the French neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot (1825 to 1893) in 1869 and known in America as Lou Gehrig's disease after the baseball player it killed, is the main motor neuron disease: the upper and lower motor neurons degenerate, producing weakness, wasting, twitching of muscles (fasciculations) and stiffness, until the muscles of breathing fail, usually within a few years. Its sufferers were long thought to keep their minds intact, and many do, but a substantial minority develop behavioural and cognitive change, and some develop full frontotemporal dementia; the two diseases share pathology (TDP-43) and a common gene, as Section 10.10.3 explains. Now look at two diseases that are not neurodegenerative. Epilepsy , Pinel explains, is diagnosed in people whose seizures are repeatedly generated by their own chronic brain dysfunction; about 0.8 percent of people are diagnosed with it at some point. Its defining feature is not the death of neurons but paroxysms: sudden bursts of excessive, synchronous firing (seen as spikes on the electroencephalogram) that begin and end, with the brain often working normally in between. Many cases arise from faults at inhibitory synapses. A very prolonged seizure can damage the brain, through the hypoxia that accompanies it, and epilepsy can complicate neurodegenerative diseases, but epilepsy itself is a disorder of excitability, not of progressive neuronal loss. Its psychiatric syndromes are taught in Section 10.11. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive disease that attacks the myelin of axons in the central nervous system. It is usually regarded as an autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks myelin as if it were foreign; it begins typically in early adulthood, is commoner in women and in people who grew up in cold climates, and in most patients runs a relapsing and remitting course before becoming steadily progressive. Visual disturbance, weakness, numbness, tremor and ataxia are its common signs, and some patients develop cognitive slowing and emotional change. Pinel notes that neurons are damaged in MS even without demyelination, so it has a degenerative component; but it is classified as an inflammatory demyelinating disease, not as a neurodegenerative one. A stroke, similarly, is a vascular injury, sudden rather than progressive, which leads us to the second commonest cause of dementia. Exam trap "Which is NOT a neurodegenerative disorder: Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, epilepsy, Huntington's?" The answer is epilepsy , a paroxysmal disorder of neuronal firing. Neurodegenerative: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's, frontotemporal degeneration, Lewy body disease, ALS, progressive supranuclear palsy, prion disease. Multiple sclerosis is an inflammatory demyelinating (autoimmune) disease and is the next-best "not neurodegenerative" answer. Neither MS nor schizophrenia is the disorder of severe memory loss and confusion caused by chronic drinking: that is Korsakoff's syndrome (Section 10.11). Vascular neurocognitive disorder For the first half of the twentieth century the usual explanation for the confusion of old age was "hardening of the arteries": narrowed vessels were supposed to starve the whole brain slowly of blood, producing arteriosclerotic dementia . In 1974 the neurologist Vladimir Hachinski , with Niels Lassen and John Marshall , argued in The Lancet that this picture was wrong. Measurements of cerebral blood flow showed that blood flow falls in dementia because brain tissue has died, not the other way round; what destroys the brain is not a slow starvation but the cumulative damage of many strokes, large and small. They called the result multi-infarct dementia , and their idea explains why vascular dementia so often behaves differently from Alzheimer's disease. A year later Hachinski's group published a bedside checklist, the Hachinski Ischaemic Score, that weights the features of a vascular cause: abrupt onset, stepwise deterioration, a fluctuating course, nocturnal confusion, relative preservation of personality, depression, bodily complaints, emotional incontinence, a history of high blood pressure, a history of strokes, signs of atherosclerosis elsewhere, and focal neurological symptoms and signs. A total of 7 or more suggests a vascular cause and 4 or less a degenerative one (the scale itself belongs to the Assessment book). Today the broader term vascular neurocognitive disorder covers every way in which disease of the blood vessels can damage cognition. Here is what that looks like. Shyam is a 71-year-old cloth merchant in Kanpur with high blood pressure that he treats only when he remembers, diabetes and a forty-year bidi habit. Two years ago his right hand went weak for a day and recovered; nobody thought much of it. Eight months ago, after what his son calls "a turn", he became muddled and slow, and he has never quite returned to his old self. Since then there has been another sudden worsening, after which he began to walk with small shuffling steps and to leak urine. His family describe good days and bad days. He is slow to answer, has lost interest in the shop and weeps at sentimental television scenes and then laughs a moment later, but he knows that his memory is not what it was and is upset about it. His memory is patchy rather than uniformly poor: he recalls the cricket scores perfectly while forgetting that his daughter visited. On examination his speech is slightly slurred, the reflexes on his right side are brisk and his right plantar response is extensor. An MRI scan shows several small deep infarcts (lacunes) and widespread damage to the white matter. Every feature in that history points to a vascular cause. The onset was abrupt, linked in time to a vascular event. The course went down in steps, with plateaus and even partial recovery in between (the dashed line of Figure 10.16). The deficits were patchy, sometimes called "islands" of preserved function, because they depend on where the infarcts happened to fall. Personality and insight were relatively preserved, unlike in Alzheimer's or frontotemporal disease. And there were focal neurological signs. Emotional lability of the kind Shyam shows (sudden crying or laughing out of proportion to feeling, sometimes called pseudobulbar affect or emotional incontinence) is typical of damage to the pathways between the cortex and the brainstem. Depression and apathy are very common; late-onset depression with slowing and poor executive function in an older person with small vessel disease has been called "vascular depression" (Chapter 5). DSM-5-TR's criteria for major or mild vascular neurocognitive disorder capture this reasoning. The criteria for a neurocognitive disorder must be met. The clinical features must be consistent with a vascular cause, shown either by an onset of cognitive deficits linked in time to one or more cerebrovascular events, or by a decline that is most prominent in complex attention (including processing speed) and frontal-executive function, the signature of small vessel disease. There must be evidence of cerebrovascular disease, from history, examination or neuroimaging, sufficient to account for the deficits. And the picture must not be better explained by another brain or systemic disease. The diagnosis is probable if imaging shows significant tissue damage from cerebrovascular disease, or the syndrome is clearly linked in time to documented strokes, or there is both clinical and genetic evidence; otherwise it is possible . As a rough guide, DSM-5-TR says that a single stroke or extensive white matter disease is usually enough for mild vascular neurocognitive disorder, whereas major disorder generally needs two or more strokes, a strategically placed stroke, or white matter disease combined with one or more lacunes. The clinical forms differ with the size and site of the damage. Multi-infarct (cortical) vascular dementia follows repeated strokes in the territories of larger arteries and produces the classic stepwise course with aphasia, neglect or other cortical signs depending on the territories hit. A strategic infarct is a single stroke in a critical place, such as the thalamus, the angular gyrus or the basal forebrain, which can produce dementia on its own. Post-stroke neurocognitive disorder appears immediately after a stroke; DSM-5-TR notes that 20 to 30 percent of people are diagnosed with dementia within three months of a stroke. And subcortical ischaemic vascular disease , or small vessel disease, follows the narrowing of the tiny penetrating arteries that supply the white matter, basal ganglia and thalamus, usually in people with long-standing high blood pressure or diabetes. Its extreme form was described in 1894 by the Swiss-born psychiatrist Otto Binswanger (1852 to 1929), professor at Jena in Germany, as a slowly progressive dementia with severe damage to the white matter beneath the cortex; it is known as Binswanger's disease or subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy. Small vessel disease produces a slower, more gradual decline than multi-infarct dementia, with slowed thinking, apathy, executive failure, a shuffling gait and urinary problems, and it can look very much like Alzheimer's disease or like normal pressure hydrocephalus (Section 10.10.9). A rare hereditary form, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL), caused by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene on chromosome 19, brings migraine, strokes and dementia to people in their forties and fifties. Leakage from vessels whose walls are infiltrated by amyloid (cerebral amyloid angiopathy) causes haemorrhages and is another vascular route to dementia. Vascular disease is the second commonest cause of neurocognitive disorder after Alzheimer's disease. Its prevalence rises steeply after 65 and its risk factors are simply those of stroke: high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, obesity, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation and other sources of emboli. DSM-5-TR notes higher rates among African Americans, Mexican Americans and South Asian Americans than among non-Latinx White Americans, possibly because of their higher rates of diabetes and cardiovascular disease, which makes vascular cognitive impairment a large and largely preventable problem in India. In the very old, pure vascular dementia is less common than mixed dementia , in which Alzheimer pathology and vascular damage add together; when both contribute, both diagnoses are made. Treatment is above all prevention of the next stroke: control of blood pressure and diabetes, stopping smoking, antiplatelet drugs or anticoagulation where indicated, statins, exercise, and rehabilitation of the deficits already present. Cholinesterase inhibitors give at best a small benefit. Exam trap Vascular dementia: abrupt onset, stepwise course, patchy deficits, focal neurological signs, relatively preserved personality and insight, vascular risk factors . Alzheimer's: insidious onset and smooth decline, no focal signs early. Multi-infarct dementia was named by Hachinski and colleagues (1974); Binswanger's disease (1894) is the subcortical, small vessel form. Vascular dementia does not explain confabulation and nystagmus in a heavy drinker; that is Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (Section 10.11). Frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder In 1892 Arnold Pick (1851 to 1924), professor of psychiatry in Prague, described a patient with behavioural change and a progressive loss of language whose brain showed shrinkage that was confined, asymmetrically, to the left temporal lobe. The point of his report was that a degenerative dementia need not be global: atrophy limited to one lobe could produce symptoms limited to that lobe's functions. Pick reported further cases over the next years, some with marked frontal atrophy and disinhibited behaviour. In 1911 Alzheimer described what Pick had not seen, the microscopic signature of many of these brains: dense, round, silver-staining inclusions inside the neurons, now called Pick bodies and known to be made of tau, together with swollen, "ballooned" neurons. For decades the whole syndrome was called Pick's disease . Today the clinical syndrome is called frontotemporal dementia (DSM-5-TR: frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder), the underlying pathology frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and "Pick's disease" is reserved for the subtype with Pick bodies. ICD-10 coded the condition as F02.0, dementia in Pick's disease; ICD-11 has a separate category, 6D83, frontotemporal dementia. Frontotemporal dementia is a disease of the middle-aged. DSM-5-TR says that it most commonly presents in the fifties (the range runs from the twenties to the eighties), that it is a common cause of dementia beginning before 65, and that only 20 to 25 percent of cases begin after 65. It accounts for about 5 percent of all dementia in unselected autopsy series. It runs faster than Alzheimer's disease, with a median survival of 6 to 11 years from the first symptoms. It is strongly familial: about 40 percent of patients have a family history of early-onset dementia and about 10 percent show autosomal dominant inheritance. The main genes are MAPT, which codes for tau, and GRN (progranulin), both on chromosome 17, and C9orf72 on chromosome 9, an expanded repeat in which, discovered in 2011, is the commonest genetic cause both of frontotemporal dementia and of ALS. That shared gene, and the shared protein TDP-43, explain why some patients have both diseases. Under the microscope about 40 percent of cases show tau inclusions (Pick's disease among them), about half show TDP-43, and a small remainder show another protein, FUS. The commonest presentation, in about 60 percent of cases, is the behavioural variant. Balwinder is a 54-year-old bank officer in Amritsar whose wife brought him to the psychiatric outpatient department. Over eighteen months the careful, rather formal man she married had become tactless and crude. He made sexual remarks to women customers, told jokes at a funeral and helped himself to food from other people's plates at a wedding. He spent a large part of their savings on lottery tickets. He now eats whole boxes of jalebis at a sitting and has put on ten kilograms. When his mother was admitted to hospital he showed no concern and asked when dinner would be ready. He insists on walking the same route to the gurdwara at exactly the same time each day and has filled a cupboard with old newspapers. He was suspended from work and is entirely unbothered by it. A doctor had diagnosed mania, but he had never been elated, he slept normally and lithium did nothing. Strikingly, he still remembers appointments, finds his way about the city without difficulty and scores 27 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination. An MRI scan shows atrophy of both frontal lobes and of the front of the temporal lobes. DSM-5-TR's criteria explain every part of that story. The disorder must have an insidious onset and gradual progression. For the behavioural variant there must be three or more of five behavioural symptoms: disinhibition (socially inappropriate words and acts, impulsivity, loss of manners); apathy or inertia ; loss of sympathy or empathy (coldness towards family that is quite unlike the person); perseverative, stereotyped or compulsive and ritualistic behaviour (repeated routes, hoarding, counting, fixed routines); and hyperorality and dietary changes (craving sweets, overeating, putting non-food objects in the mouth). There must also be a prominent decline in social cognition or executive ability. And, crucially, learning and memory and perceptual-motor function must be relatively spared : the frontal and anterior temporal lobes are damaged, but the hippocampus and the parietal lobes are not, at least at first. Insight is usually lost early, which is why the patient rarely comes on his own, and the first referral is often to a psychiatrist, because the picture can be mistaken for mania, depression, schizophrenia, a late-onset personality disorder or an ordinary midlife crisis. The diagnosis is probable if a causative mutation is found or if imaging shows disproportionate frontal or temporal involvement; otherwise it is possible. The other presentation is the language variant, a form of primary progressive aphasia , the syndrome that the neurologist Marsel Mesulam described in 1982 as a slowly progressive loss of language without, for a long time, a general dementia. In the semantic variant , linked to atrophy of the anterior temporal lobes (usually more on the left), the person loses the meanings of words and eventually of objects: speech remains fluent and grammatical but grows empty, nouns are replaced by "thing", and the patient may ask "What is a tiger?" on being told about one. In the nonfluent or agrammatic variant , linked to atrophy of the left posterior frontal lobe and insula, speech becomes slow, effortful and halting, with grammatical errors and distorted sounds, while the understanding of single words is preserved. A third form, logopenic progressive aphasia, with word-finding pauses and difficulty repeating sentences, is usually caused by Alzheimer pathology rather than frontotemporal degeneration (Section 10.9.3). Frontotemporal degeneration also overlaps with two parkinsonian tau diseases, progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration (Section 10.10.5), and with motor neuron disease. There is no disease-modifying treatment. Cholinesterase inhibitors do not help, because the cholinergic system is relatively intact, and they can make behaviour worse. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and trazodone can reduce disinhibition, compulsions and overeating; antipsychotics are used sparingly. Most of the work is with the family: explaining that the coldness and the rudeness are symptoms, protecting money and property early (as Balwinder's lottery spending shows), managing access to food, and supporting carers who are often still bringing up children and paying a mortgage. Clinical link A marked change of personality or conduct beginning for the first time in a person in his fifties, without a past psychiatric history, should make you think of a brain disease, frontotemporal dementia above all, before you settle on a primary psychiatric diagnosis. The clues are loss of insight, loss of empathy, new compulsions and a sweet tooth, with memory and orientation still good. Ordinary bedside cognitive screening tests can be almost normal; tests of executive function and social cognition, a careful history from the family, and frontal and temporal atrophy on a scan make the diagnosis. Exam trap Frontotemporal dementia: younger onset (often the fifties) , personality and behaviour change or language loss first , memory and visuospatial skills relatively spared , insight lost early. Alzheimer's: older onset, memory first, social graces long preserved. Pick's disease (Arnold Pick, 1892; Pick bodies described by Alzheimer, 1911) is a frontotemporal tauopathy, not an alcohol-related or amnesic disorder, so it is wrong whenever the stem describes a heavy drinker with memory loss and confabulation. Logopenic aphasia points to Alzheimer pathology, not frontotemporal degeneration. Neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies In 1912 the young German neurologist Friedrich Heinrich Lewy (1885 to 1950), working in Alzheimer's laboratory in Munich, described round inclusions inside neurons deep in the brains of patients who had died with Parkinson's disease; a few years later they were named Lewy bodies after him, and they are now known to be clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein. For half a century they were regarded as a sign of Parkinson's disease. Then in 1976 the Japanese psychiatrist Kenji Kosaka described a patient with dementia whose Lewy bodies were scattered through the cerebral cortex, and in the following years he and others showed that this was not a rarity. In the 1990s an international consortium led by Ian McKeith of Newcastle agreed consensus criteria (first published in 1996, revised in 2005 and most recently in 2017) for what they named dementia with Lewy bodies , the condition DSM-5-TR calls major or mild neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies. When the American actor Robin Williams died in 2014, the autopsy found diffuse Lewy body disease, and his widow's account of his last confused, frightened year did much to make the disease known. Paramjit is a 74-year-old retired nurse in Chandigarh. For a year she has seen children sitting quietly on the end of her bed and a man in a turban standing beside the almirah; she can describe their clothes in detail, they never speak, and on some days she knows they are not real. Her cognition swings dramatically: on a good morning she does the newspaper crossword, but on bad days she stares into space for long periods, is drowsy at noon and talks in a muddled way, so that her family twice took her to hospital fearing a stroke, and both times no cause was found. Her husband says that for years before any of this she shouted, kicked and punched in her sleep as if fighting someone. She now walks slowly with small steps, her face has become expressionless, and she has had several falls and two faints on standing up. When a doctor prescribed haloperidol for the hallucinations she became rigid, could not swallow and was admitted to hospital. Her memory for recent events is surprisingly good on her good days, but she cannot copy a drawing of two overlapping pentagons. Paramjit's story contains the whole of DSM-5-TR's criteria. The disorder has an insidious onset and gradual progression, and its diagnosis rests on core and suggestive features. The three core features are: fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness (so marked that it can resemble a delirium, as in her two hospital visits); recurrent visual hallucinations that are well formed and detailed (people, children and animals are typical, often silent, and the patient may have some insight into them); and spontaneous features of parkinsonism (slowness, rigidity, a shuffling gait; tremor is less prominent than in Parkinson's disease) beginning after the cognitive decline. The two suggestive features are REM sleep behaviour disorder , the acting out of dreams because the normal paralysis of REM sleep is lost (Chapter 8, Section 8.10.4), which can precede the dementia by many years; and severe neuroleptic sensitivity . A probable diagnosis needs two core features, or one suggestive feature with at least one core feature; a possible diagnosis needs one core feature, or one or more suggestive features. McKeith's 2017 revision differs slightly, and you should know both: it lists four core features (fluctuation, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism), moves severe sensitivity to antipsychotics into a list of supportive features, and adds indicative biomarkers: reduced uptake of a dopamine transporter tracer in the basal ganglia on a SPECT or PET scan, reduced uptake on a cardiac scan (MIBG myocardial scintigraphy) showing loss of the heart's sympathetic nerves, and sleep-laboratory confirmation of REM sleep without the normal muscle paralysis. The cognitive profile differs from Alzheimer's disease in a way that helps at the bedside. Attention, executive function and visuoperceptual ability (copying figures, judging shapes and distances) are affected early and severely, while memory and learning are relatively better preserved early on, and the hippocampi look relatively normal on an MRI scan. Associated features listed by DSM-5-TR include repeated falls, faints and brief episodes of unresponsiveness, autonomic failure (a fall in blood pressure on standing, constipation, urinary incontinence), excessive daytime sleepiness, reduced sense of smell (hyposmia), hallucinations in other senses, delusions, depression, anxiety and apathy. The disorder usually begins in the mid-seventies, is perhaps commoner in men, and progresses to death in an average of about 5.5 to 7.7 years after cognitive decline begins. In community studies it accounts for about 4 percent of dementia and in clinic studies about 7.5 percent, although Lewy bodies are found at autopsy in 20 to 35 percent of dementia cases, often alongside Alzheimer pathology. Neuroleptic sensitivity deserves its own paragraph because it kills. In 1992 McKeith and colleagues reported in the British Medical Journal that patients with this form of dementia who were given antipsychotic drugs often reacted catastrophically: sudden severe parkinsonism, rigidity, immobility, worsening confusion, falls and inability to swallow, sometimes resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with a marked rise in mortality. DSM-5-TR says that up to 50 percent of patients have severe sensitivity, so antipsychotics, especially older high-potency drugs such as haloperidol, must be avoided or used with extreme caution. The good news is that Lewy body dementia has an even greater cholinergic deficit than Alzheimer's disease, and cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine, donepezil) often help more than they do in Alzheimer's, improving attention, fluctuations and even hallucinations. Levodopa can ease the parkinsonism but may worsen the hallucinations, so the doses are a balancing act; melatonin or clonazepam help the REM sleep behaviour disorder; and falls and low blood pressure need practical management. Exam trap Lewy body dementia is most characteristically associated with recurrent, well-formed visual hallucinations , not auditory ones (prominent auditory hallucinations suggest schizophrenia or a mood disorder). Aphasia belongs to Alzheimer's disease and the language variants of frontotemporal dementia. Loss of smell does occur, but only as a supportive, non-specific feature shared with Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. The other two hallmarks are fluctuating attention and alertness and parkinsonism , plus REM sleep behaviour disorder and severe sensitivity to antipsychotics . Parkinson's disease and its neurocognitive disorder In 1817 the London surgeon and apothecary James Parkinson (1755 to 1824) published An Essay on the Shaking Palsy , describing six people with "involuntary tremulous motion" and a stooped, hurrying gait, with "the senses and intellects being uninjured". The last phrase turned out to be wrong for many patients, which is why the disease belongs in this section. Pinel describes Parkinson's disease as a movement disorder of middle and old age affecting 1 to 2 percent of people over 65, slightly more often men. Its four motor signs are a tremor that is most marked at rest and disappears during voluntary movement and sleep (the "pill-rolling" tremor of the fingers), muscular rigidity, slowness and difficulty initiating movement (bradykinesia), and, later, unstable posture, together with a mask-like face. Sleep disturbance, loss of the sense of smell and depression can precede the motor signs by up to a decade. The core lesion is the degeneration of the dopamine-releasing neurons of the substantia nigra that project along the nigrostriatal pathway to the striatum, and the surviving neurons contain Lewy bodies of alpha-synuclein. Levodopa, the precursor from which the brain makes dopamine, relieves the symptoms for some years before its benefits fade and its side effects (involuntary movements) grow; dopamine agonists and, when drugs fail, deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus are the next steps. The motor system and the drugs belong to the Physiological book; here the interest is in the mind. Parkinson's disease is full of psychiatry. Depression, anxiety and apathy are common and often precede the diagnosis. Psychosis, usually visual hallucinations or a sense that someone is present, appears as the disease advances, often provoked by the dopaminergic drugs themselves, and must be treated without the antipsychotics that block dopamine (quetiapine or clozapine at low dose, or pimavanserin, a drug acting on serotonin receptors). And dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole cause impulse control disorders in a substantial minority of patients: pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality and binge eating appear in previously careful people and vanish when the drug is reduced. That observation is one of the strongest pieces of human evidence for the role of dopamine in the reward circuit (Section 10.2) and in gambling disorder (Section 10.1). Cognitive decline is common. Pinel reports that most patients who live more than ten years after diagnosis develop dementia, and DSM-5-TR that as many as 80 percent eventually do; among those not demented, a quarter have mild neurocognitive disorder. The profile is that of a subcortical dementia (Section 10.10.10): slowed thinking, poor attention and executive function, visuospatial difficulty and trouble retrieving memories, with language relatively intact. DSM-5-TR's criteria for neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson's disease require that the disturbance occurs in the setting of established Parkinson's disease and has an insidious onset and gradual progression; it is probable when there is no evidence of a mixed cause and the Parkinson's disease clearly came first, and possible when only one of those holds. Rivastigmine and donepezil help, and antipsychotic sensitivity is a danger here too. Since Parkinson's disease dementia and Lewy body dementia share the same protein, the same Lewy bodies and many of the same symptoms, what separates them? Only the order of events, captured in the one-year rule of the Lewy body consensus criteria (Figure 10.18). If parkinsonism has been present for at least a year before dementia develops, the diagnosis is neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson's disease. If dementia comes first, or at the same time, or within a year of the onset of parkinsonism, or without parkinsonism at all, the diagnosis is Lewy body dementia. DSM-5-TR notes that the Parkinson's disease experts allow cognitive decline to precede the motor diagnosis, so within that twelve-month overlap the clinician may choose either; outside it, both sets of experts agree. The rule is a convention, not a law of nature: many neurologists regard the two as points on a single spectrum of Lewy body disease. ICD-11 builds the same rule into its definition of dementia due to Lewy body disease.
