Top: in neurocognitive disorder due to Parkinson's disease the movement disorder has been present for at least a year before dementia appears. Bottom: in neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies dementia comes first, or with parkinsonism, or within a year of it, often with fluctuations, visual hallucinations and REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD). Three other degenerative parkinsonian disorders bring cognitive change and are worth one line each. Progressive supranuclear palsy (a tauopathy) causes a palsy of vertical gaze, a stiff upright posture, early backward falls, slowed thinking and executive dysfunction; it was through this disease that the idea of a "subcortical dementia" became established (Section 10.10.10). Corticobasal degeneration (also a tauopathy) causes asymmetrical rigidity, apraxia of one limb and the "alien limb" that seems to act on its own. Multiple system atrophy (a synucleinopathy) causes parkinsonism with early, severe autonomic failure, and cognition is relatively spared. Finally, remember that antipsychotic drugs themselves cause parkinsonism, which must not be mistaken for a degenerative disease. Exam trap Parkinson's disease is the loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra (Lewy bodies of alpha-synuclein), not an acetylcholine disease, although its dementia adds a cholinergic deficit. One-year rule : parkinsonism at least a year before dementia means Parkinson's disease dementia; dementia before, with or within a year of parkinsonism means Lewy body dementia. Parkinson's disease is not caused by alcohol and does not produce the profound amnesia of Korsakoff's syndrome. James Parkinson (1817) wrote that the intellect was "uninjured"; he was wrong for most long-surviving patients. Huntington's disease In 1872 a young general practitioner from East Hampton on Long Island, George Huntington (1850 to 1916), still in his early twenties, published a short paper called "On Chorea". His father and grandfather had been doctors in the same district and had watched the same families for decades, and Huntington described a "hereditary chorea" with three marked peculiarities: its hereditary nature, a tendency to insanity and suicide, and its appearance as a grave disease only in adult life. He also noticed that it never skipped a generation: if a child of an affected parent escaped it, that child's descendants were free of it too. In those few lines he described an autosomal dominant disease decades before anyone knew what a gene was. The disease was long called Huntington's chorea, from the Greek word for dance, after its writhing, dance-like movements; it is now called Huntington's disease because the movements are only one part of it. Pinel calls it a progressive motor disorder that, unlike Parkinson's disease, is rare, has a simple genetic basis and is always associated with severe dementia. The first sign is often fidgetiness. As it advances, rapid, complex, jerky movements of whole limbs take over; the person cannot keep the tongue out or keep a steady grip (the grip squeezes and relaxes, "milkmaid's grip"), speech becomes slurred, swallowing fails and the gait becomes lurching and unstable. Late in the course chorea may give way to rigidity and slowness. But DSM-5-TR stresses that the psychiatric and cognitive changes often come first, by a decade or more: irritability, anxiety, depressed mood, apathy, disinhibition, impulsivity, obsessive-compulsive symptoms and, more rarely, psychosis. The cognitive decline begins with executive functions (speed, organisation, planning), with memory retrieval affected more than storage, and it follows the subcortical pattern of Section 10.10.10. The risk of suicide is markedly raised, both before and after the movements begin; in a large European cohort the commonest causes of death were pneumonia (19.5 percent), other infections (6.9 percent) and suicide (6.6 percent). Symptoms most often begin between 35 and 45, and death follows about 10 to 20 years after diagnosis. Scans show atrophy of the caudate nucleus and putamen, so that the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles balloon outwards. The American folk singer Woody Guthrie, who died of the disease in 1967, is its most famous victim. The genetics are as simple as Huntington guessed. The disease is caused by a single dominant mutation in the gene for a protein called huntingtin ( HTT ), on the short arm of chromosome 4 . The mutation is a trinucleotide repeat expansion : a stretch of the gene in which the three DNA letters C-A-G are repeated, coding for a run of the amino acid glutamine. Most people have fewer than 27 repeats. Repeats of 27 to 35 do not cause disease but are unstable and can expand when passed on; 36 to 39 repeats cause the disease in some carriers, usually late in life; and DSM-5-TR states that 40 or more repeats are invariably associated with the disease. The longer the repeat, the earlier the onset. Because the repeat tends to lengthen as it passes down the generations, especially through the father's sperm, the disease tends to begin earlier in each generation, a phenomenon called anticipation ; the juvenile form, beginning before 20 and often inherited from the father, has very long repeats and brings rigidity, slowness, dystonia and seizures rather than chorea. The expanded huntingtin protein is, in Pinel's word, "stickier" than normal, clumps inside cells and is toxic, killing first the GABA-releasing medium spiny neurons of the striatum and later neurons throughout the brain. Each child of an affected parent has a 50 percent chance of inheriting the mutation; and because symptoms do not begin until about 40, after the peak reproductive years, the gene has stayed in the population. Key study: Nancy Wexler and the villages of Lake Maracaibo (1979 to 1993) In 1968 the mother of Nancy Wexler , a young American psychologist, was diagnosed with Huntington's disease, the illness that also took three of her mother's brothers and her grandfather; Nancy and her sister each faced a one-in-two risk. Their father founded a foundation to fund research, and from 1979 Wexler led expeditions to villages on the shores of Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, where an extraordinary number of people were affected: an extended family of thousands, descended from one ancestor, in which the disease was everywhere. Year after year the team recorded the family tree and collected blood samples. Using DNA from this pedigree and an American family, James Gusella and colleagues found in 1983 a genetic marker close to the gene, on chromosome 4, one of the first disease genes to be located in this way. A further ten years of collaborative work by the Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group identified the gene itself and its expanded CAG repeat in 1993. The study is a model of how a single, carefully documented family can reveal a gene; its criticism is mainly ethical, about what researchers owed the poor villagers whose blood made the discovery possible. In 2020 Wexler disclosed that she herself had the disease. The discovery of the gene created one of the hardest decisions in medicine. A simple blood test can now tell a healthy 25-year-old whether he will develop an incurable disease in middle age. Pinel puts the question to the reader: would you want to know? International guidelines for predictive genetic testing require counselling before and after the test, a period to reflect, the right of the at-risk person not to know, no testing of children for an adult-onset disease, and care when a test on one person will reveal the status of another (a positive result in a young adult whose at-risk parent has never been tested reveals that the parent, too, carries the gene). Only a minority of people at risk choose to be tested. The advantages are real: those who test negative are freed of fear, those who test positive can plan, and couples can use prenatal or preimplantation testing. There is still no treatment that slows the disease. The chorea can be reduced with drugs that deplete dopamine stores, such as tetrabenazine (which can worsen depression), or with antipsychotics; depression, irritability and obsessional symptoms are treated in the usual ways; and physiotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy and support for the family carry the rest. The papers test Huntington's disease against three other genetic conditions taught in Chapter 3, Section 3.3. Table 10.42 sets them side by side, and one confusion is worth naming: the gene for phenylketonuria lies on chromosome 12, and notes that put Huntington's disease on chromosome 12 have mixed the two up. Both Huntington's and fragile X show anticipation, so "repeat expansion" alone does not decide; the repeat (CAG versus CGG), the chromosome (4 versus X) and the inheritance (dominant versus X-linked) do. Huntington's disease destroys the caudate and its GABA neurons; it is not an alcohol-related amnesia. Prion disease Some dementias move so fast that families can watch the decline week by week. The fastest are the prion diseases , which are unlike any other disease in medicine because they are transmissible yet contain no genetic material at all. Their agent is a prion , a name coined in 1982 by the American neurologist Stanley Prusiner for a "proteinaceous infectious particle": an abnormally folded form of a normal protein found on nerve cell membranes, the prion protein, encoded by the PRNP gene. The misfolded form converts normal prion protein into copies of itself, which clump, kill neurons and leave the brain full of tiny holes, like a sponge; hence the older name, the spongiform encephalopathies. Prions resist ordinary sterilisation, which is why some cases have been passed on by surgery. Prusiner, whose idea was ridiculed for years, received the Nobel Prize in 1997. The commonest human prion disease is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), named after the German neurologists Hans Gerhard Creutzfeldt (1885 to 1964) and Alfons Maria Jakob (1884 to 1931), who described cases in 1920 and 1921. DSM-5-TR describes the forms. Sporadic CJD, the great majority, arises spontaneously at a rate of about one or two cases per million people per year, with a peak age of about 67. Genetic forms, up to 15 percent of cases, are caused by autosomal dominant mutations of PRNP and include familial CJD, Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome and fatal familial insomnia (a disease of the thalamus that destroys sleep). Acquired forms have followed corneal transplants, grafts of dura mater, contaminated neurosurgical instruments and injections of growth hormone and gonadotropin extracted from human pituitary glands. The typical picture begins with weeks of vague fatigue, anxiety, poor sleep or appetite and poor concentration; then comes a rapidly progressive dementia, often reaching the major level within a few months, with myoclonus (sudden shock-like jerks, often provoked by a startle), ataxia, visual disturbance and other abnormal movements, ending in a mute, immobile state and death, usually within a year. The diagnostic clues are a characteristic electroencephalogram showing periodic sharp, often triphasic, synchronous discharges at about 0.5 to 2 per second; bright signals in the cortex and deep grey matter on diffusion-weighted MRI, the most sensitive test; raised 14-3-3 protein and tau in the cerebrospinal fluid; and a highly specific test called real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC), which amplifies tiny amounts of the abnormal prion. Confirmation still requires brain tissue. There is no treatment. In the mid-1990s a new form appeared in the United Kingdom. Variant CJD struck young people, often in their teens and twenties, began with psychiatric symptoms (low mood, withdrawal, anxiety) and painful sensations before the dementia and the jerks, and ran a longer course. It was traced to eating beef from cattle with bovine spongiform encephalopathy, "mad cow disease", which had spread through British herds fed on the processed remains of other animals; a few cases were later transmitted by blood transfusion. The prion had crossed from one species to another. Key study: Gajdusek and kuru (1957 to 1976) In 1957 the American physician Daniel Carleton Gajdusek (1923 to 2008) and the local medical officer Vincent Zigas described kuru , a fatal disease of trembling, staggering and dementia among the Fore people of the eastern highlands of Papua New Guinea; in the Fore language the word means to shiver or tremble. It killed mainly women and children. Anthropologists working with the Fore pointed to the explanation: at mortuary feasts, as a mark of respect, women and young children ate the bodies of dead relatives, including the brain. In 1966 Gajdusek and his colleagues transmitted kuru to chimpanzees by injecting brain tissue from patients, proving that a degenerative brain disease could be infectious, with an incubation period of years. When the feasts stopped, in the late 1950s, kuru slowly disappeared, although cases continued to appear for decades in people exposed as children, showing how long the incubation could be. Gajdusek shared the 1976 Nobel Prize. He believed the agent was a "slow virus"; Prusiner's prion theory later explained what it actually was. Exam trap Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: rapidly progressive dementia (weeks to months) with myoclonus and periodic sharp-wave complexes on the EEG ; death usually within a year. "Mad cow disease" (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) caused variant CJD in young people, not the sporadic form. Kuru: the Fore of Papua New Guinea, Gajdusek (Nobel 1976); prions: Prusiner (Nobel 1997). CJD is not the answer for an alcohol-related amnesia with confabulation. HIV infection, brain injury and substances HIV. The human immunodeficiency virus enters the brain early in infection, carried by infected white blood cells, and infects the brain's macrophages and microglia rather than neurons; the damage comes from the inflammation and toxic products that follow. Before effective treatment, many people with AIDS developed a severe dementia, described in 1986 by Bradford Navia , Richard Price and colleagues as the AIDS dementia complex. Since antiretroviral therapy became widely available, severe dementia has become uncommon and milder impairment common. A consensus meeting at Frascati in 2007 divided HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders into three levels: asymptomatic neurocognitive impairment (abnormal test scores without functional impairment), mild neurocognitive disorder, and HIV-associated dementia. DSM-5-TR reports that a third to over half of people with HIV show some neurocognitive disturbance, but that most of this is asymptomatic; of those with a disturbance, about a quarter meet criteria for mild disorder and typically fewer than 5 percent for major disorder. The pattern is typically subcortical: slowed processing, poor executive function and demanding attention, difficulty learning new information with better recall of what has been learned, apathy, and motor slowing and clumsiness, while aphasia is uncommon. DSM-5-TR's criteria require documented HIV infection and exclusion of other causes, especially the opportunistic brain infections (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy) and lymphoma, which must be treated in their own right. Antiretroviral therapy is the treatment. Traumatic brain injury. A blow to the head, or any force that moves the brain violently inside the skull, can damage it diffusely by stretching and shearing axons and focally by bruising (contusion) and bleeding; Pinel describes the closed-head injury in which the brain strikes the skull on the side opposite the blow. In India the commonest causes are road traffic accidents, especially on two-wheelers without helmets, and falls, which matter most in the elderly. DSM-5-TR's criteria for neurocognitive disorder due to traumatic brain injury require evidence of a traumatic brain injury with one or more of loss of consciousness, post-traumatic amnesia, disorientation and confusion, or neurological signs; and the neurocognitive disorder must appear immediately after the injury, or immediately after consciousness returns, and persist beyond the acute period. That timing rule separates it from a dementia that merely happens to follow an old injury. The severity of the injury is graded from the duration of unconsciousness, the duration of post-traumatic amnesia and the Glasgow Coma Scale score: roughly, mild injury means unconsciousness of 30 minutes or less, post-traumatic amnesia of a day or less and a score of 13 to 15; severe injury means unconsciousness of a day or more, post-traumatic amnesia of a week or more and a score of 3 to 8. The usual deficits are in complex attention, processing speed, memory, executive function and social cognition, often with irritability, apathy or disinhibited personality change (the frontal lobe syndromes of Section 10.11). Recovery after mild injury is usually complete within 3 to 12 months; after moderate and severe injury it continues for months or years but is often incomplete. The memory gaps around the injury, retrograde for the moments before it and anterograde for the period of confusion after it, are described in Book 1, Section 7.10. Many people have persistent symptoms after a mild injury: headache, dizziness, fatigue, irritability, poor concentration and memory, insomnia and intolerance of noise and alcohol. ICD-10 called this postconcussional syndrome (F07.2). DSM-5-TR is cautious about it: when symptoms persist after a mild injury it asks the clinician to consider depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, substance use, poor sleep and pessimistic expectations of recovery, and to diagnose a neurocognitive disorder only if the problems persist after those have been treated. Repeated injuries are a different matter. In 1928 the American pathologist Harrison Martland described boxers who had become "punch drunk": slowed, unsteady, tremulous and forgetful after years of blows, a condition later called dementia pugilistica. In 2005 the pathologist Bennet Omalu described the same kind of damage in the brain of a retired American football player, and the condition is now called chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE): a tau disease, with tangles clustered around small blood vessels at the depths of the cortical folds, causing mood change, impulsivity, aggression, suicidality, memory loss and parkinsonism. Pinel tells the case of the footballer Junior Seau, who shot himself in 2012 and whose brain met the criteria. CTE can be confirmed only after death, and figures such as its presence in 110 of 111 donated brains of professional American football players (Jesse Mez and colleagues, 2017) come from brains donated because families were worried, so they exaggerate its frequency. Substances and medicines. DSM-5-TR's substance or medication-induced neurocognitive disorder is a decline that persists beyond the usual duration of intoxication and acute withdrawal, caused by a substance capable of producing it. Alcohol is by far the commonest culprit, producing both alcohol-related dementia and the amnesia of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which Section 10.11 teaches. Sedatives, hypnotics and anxiolytics, inhalants (Section 10.7) and some other drugs can also do it, and in the elderly a heavy load of anticholinergic medicines can produce an apparent dementia that lifts when the drugs are stopped. Some improvement with sustained abstinence is the rule. Exam trap HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder follows a subcortical pattern (slowing, apathy, poor retrieval, motor clumsiness, little aphasia). For neurocognitive disorder due to traumatic brain injury, DSM-5-TR requires the disorder to appear immediately after the injury (or after consciousness returns) and to persist. "Punch drunk" (Martland, 1928), dementia pugilistica and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (Omalu, 2005) describe the damage of repeated head blows, a tau disease confirmed only at autopsy. The dementias that can be reversed Every dementia work-up is, first of all, a search for a cause that can be treated, and the reason is not that such causes are common but that missing one is a disaster. In a 2003 review of studies of people being investigated for dementia, the geriatrician A. Mark Clarfield found that about 9 percent had a potentially reversible cause, but that only about 0.6 percent actually recovered fully or partly after treatment. Those few patients are the point of the blood tests and the scan. The dementia that most rewards recognition is normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), described in 1965 by the Colombian neurosurgeon Salomón Hakim and the American neurologist Raymond Adams . The ventricles of the brain enlarge, although the pressure of the cerebrospinal fluid measured at lumbar puncture is normal, and they stretch the fibres that run around them. The result is a triad that students remember as "wet, wobbly and wacky": a disturbance of gait, usually first (a broad-based, shuffling walk in which the feet seem stuck to the floor, a "magnetic" gait); urinary urgency and incontinence; and a subcortical dementia of slowness, apathy and inattention. It may follow a subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis or head injury, but in older people it usually has no known cause. Imaging shows ventricles enlarged out of proportion to any atrophy; removing some cerebrospinal fluid by lumbar puncture (a tap test) temporarily improves the walking; and a shunt that drains fluid from the ventricles into the abdomen can bring lasting improvement, best for the gait and least for the dementia, and best when the condition is treated early. A chronic subdural haematoma is a slowly enlarging collection of blood between the brain and its covering, usually after a minor fall that the patient may have forgotten; it is commonest in the elderly, in heavy drinkers and in people taking anticoagulants, it causes headache, drowsiness and confusion that fluctuate (and so can mimic both dementia and delirium), and it is cured by draining it. Wilson's disease , described by Samuel Alexander Kinnier Wilson (1878 to 1937) in 1912, is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism in which copper accumulates in the liver and the basal ganglia; it presents in adolescents and young adults with liver disease, tremor, rigidity, dysarthria and psychiatric symptoms (mood change, irritability, psychosis) that are easily mistaken for a primary mental illness, and the brownish ring of copper in the cornea (the Kayser-Fleischer ring) gives it away. Treated early with drugs that remove copper, it can be halted. Exam trap Normal pressure hydrocephalus: gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and dementia (Hakim and Adams, 1965), with enlarged ventricles and normal cerebrospinal fluid pressure; treated with a shunt . Do not confuse its triad with Wernicke's (confusion, ataxia, eye signs) or with the parkinsonian signs of Lewy body disease. "Reversible" does not mean "common": truly reversed dementia is rare, which is exactly why it must be searched for. Cortical and subcortical dementia, and the whole picture By now you will have noticed that the dementias fall into two families. Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia damage the cerebral cortex and its "instruments": language, skilled movement, recognition and the storage of new memories. Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, small vessel vascular disease, HIV and normal pressure hydrocephalus damage the structures beneath the cortex (the basal ganglia, the thalamus, the brainstem nuclei and the white matter connections) and slow the whole machine down instead. In 1974 Martin Albert , Robert Feldman and Anne Willis described patients with progressive supranuclear palsy whose dementia consisted of forgetfulness, slowed thinking, apathy or depression and an impaired ability to use what they knew, without aphasia, apraxia or agnosia, and called it a subcortical dementia . In 1975 Paul McHugh and Marshal Folstein described the same pattern in Huntington's disease, and in the 1980s Jeffrey Cummings and others set it against the cortical dementia of Alzheimer's disease and Pick's disease. The distinction rests on a simple idea. The cortex holds the instruments; the subcortical circuits, linking the basal ganglia and thalamus with the frontal lobes, supply speed, motivation and the ability to retrieve and use what is stored. Damage the instruments and the person cannot speak, use objects or learn; damage the circuits and the person can still do all those things, but slowly, without initiative, and without being able to pull out on demand what he knows. The memory difference is the most useful single test. In a cortical dementia new information is never properly stored, so recall is poor, recognition is also poor, and giving cues does not help. In a subcortical dementia information is stored but cannot be retrieved efficiently, so free recall is poor but recognition is much better and cues help. Table 10.44 sets out the contrast. As early as 1986 Peter Whitehouse pointed out that Alzheimer's disease destroys subcortical nuclei too (the nucleus basalis of Meynert, which you met in Section 10.9.4, is one of them), that the "subcortical" diseases eventually reach the cortex, and that the two patterns overlap so much that they describe tendencies rather than separate classes. Lewy body dementia, with its cortical visuospatial deficits and its subcortical slowing and parkinsonism, is the obvious mixed case. Most clinicians therefore now speak of a predominantly cortical or a predominantly frontal-subcortical pattern. The contrast nonetheless remains a powerful bedside tool and a favourite of examiners. Section 10.9.1 explained the older descriptive terms "senile dementia" (dementia beginning in old age, of any cause) and "cerebral atrophy" (shrinkage of the brain, seen in many conditions); neither is a disease in its own right. This last section sits where those two meet, and then widens the view. It begins with a vitamin. Thiamine costs almost nothing, yet a brain starved of it for a few weeks can lose, within days, the machinery that turns experience into lasting memory; Jimmie G., whose story opened this chapter, is the most famous example. The section then turns to two kinds of impostor. The first is depression in an older person, which can look so like dementia that it was given a name of its own, pseudodementia. The second is physical illness: a tumour that pours out cortisol, a sluggish thyroid gland, a spirochaete, an antibody against the brain's own receptors, any of which can produce depression, anxiety, mania, psychosis or a change of personality that looks exactly like a "functional" psychiatric disorder. One lesson ties these together, and every clinician has to learn it early: before you decide that a mind is ill, make sure that the body is not. Thiamine and the starving brain Why should a vitamin matter to memory? Ask most people what heavy drinking does to the brain and they will tell you a story about poison. The most dramatic damage that alcohol does to memory is, surprisingly, mostly a story about food. Thiamine , or vitamin B1, is a water-soluble vitamin found in whole grains, pulses, nuts, yeast and meat. The body cannot make it and keeps only a small reserve, enough for about two to three weeks. Inside the cell it is converted into thiamine pyrophosphate (also called thiamine diphosphate), a helper molecule, or coenzyme, for three enzymes at the centre of energy metabolism. Two of them work in the main line of energy production: pyruvate dehydrogenase carries the products of glucose breakdown into the citric acid (Krebs) cycle, where most of a cell's energy is made, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase drives one of the steps of that cycle itself. The third, transketolase , runs a side pathway that supplies the raw materials for nucleic acids and helps cells defend themselves against oxidative damage. Now picture a neuron. It burns almost nothing but glucose, and it cannot store fuel. Take thiamine away and the neuron becomes a car with a full tank and a broken fuel pump: the glucose is there, but it cannot be burned. Energy production fails, lactic acid builds up, cells swell, and the first to die are the small, busy clusters of neurons packed around the fluid-filled spaces in the middle of the brain, the third ventricle, the cerebral aqueduct of the midbrain and the floor of the fourth ventricle. Hold on to that geography; every symptom in the next few pages follows from it. The disease of thiamine lack was known long before the vitamin. In the 1890s Christiaan Eijkman (1858 to 1930), a Dutch army doctor working in Java, noticed that chickens fed on polished white rice developed a paralysis very like the human disease beriberi, and that rice with its bran left on prevented it. The protective factor in the bran turned out to be thiamine, and Eijkman shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1929. Beriberi is thiamine deficiency of the peripheral nerves and the heart; the brain disease came to be recognised as its cerebral form. When H. E. de Wardener and B. Lennox reported 52 cases of the brain disease that they had seen in a prisoner-of-war hospital in Singapore, among men held by the Japanese on a diet made up largely of polished rice, they called their 1947 paper "Cerebral beriberi". Why are heavy drinkers in particular so exposed? There are four reasons, and they add up. First, a person who drinks heavily takes a large part of his daily calories as alcohol, which contains no vitamins at all, and he often eats little else. Second, alcohol interferes with the absorption of thiamine from the gut, so even the thiamine he does eat is poorly taken up. Third, a fatty or cirrhotic liver stores less of it and converts less of it into its active form. Fourth, drinkers often vomit, have diarrhoea or go through bouts of near starvation. John P. J. Pinel uses this disorder to illustrate what he calls converging operations. Because the syndrome is common in heavy drinkers, it was first thought to be a direct toxic effect of alcohol. That interpretation was overturned by evidence of different kinds (case studies of patients, comparisons of heavy drinkers with abstainers, and controlled experiments on animals) that converged on the same answer: the syndrome turned up in malnourished people who drank little or no alcohol, and rats made thiamine-deficient developed memory deficits and patterns of brain damage like those of heavy drinkers. Alcohol is not wholly innocent, though: it speeds up the damage in thiamine-deficient rats, so it probably adds some direct toxicity of its own. That still leaves a puzzle. Most heavy drinkers never develop the syndrome, so why do some? In 1977 John P. Blass and Gary E. Gibson grew skin cells from four patients with the syndrome and found that their transketolase gripped thiamine pyrophosphate far less tightly than the enzyme in healthy people's cells (it needed roughly twelve times as much of the coenzyme to work at half speed), and that the abnormality persisted when the cells were grown with plenty of thiamine and no alcohol. The fault was inborn. A person with such an enzyme would be perfectly well on a normal diet but unusually vulnerable when drinking and poor eating cut his thiamine supply. DSM-5-TR lists this genetic transketolase abnormality, together with poor nutrition, as a risk factor. Heavy drinking is the commonest route, but not the only one. Carl Wernicke's own first series, as you will see in a moment, included a young woman whose deficiency came from persistent vomiting, not from drink. Thiamine deficiency also follows the severe vomiting of pregnancy (hyperemesis gravidarum), weight-loss (bariatric) surgery on the stomach, starvation and anorexia nervosa (Chapter 8), prolonged vomiting from any cause, cancer and its chemotherapy, kidney dialysis, AIDS and long periods of intravenous feeding without added vitamins. In 2003 an outbreak struck infants in Israel who had been fed a soy-based formula that lacked thiamine. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is therefore best understood as a nutritional disease to which heavy drinkers are especially exposed, not simply as a poisoning by alcohol. Exam trap Korsakoff's syndrome and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome are caused by deficiency of thiamine, vitamin B1 , classically in chronic alcoholism (MET Mock 5; Biopsych and Testing paper). Know what each distractor causes. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia, damage to the spinal cord (subacute combined degeneration) and nerves, depression and a reversible dementia (Section 10.11.9). Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia (soft bones) in adults. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects in the unborn child and low mood. Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency causes pellagra, with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. Hypoxia (lack of oxygen) damages the hippocampus and can cause amnesia, but it is not the cause of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Lead poisoning causes encephalopathy and lasting cognitive loss in children, and anaemia, abdominal colic and wrist drop in adults. B1 is thiamine; B12 is cobalamin. Do not swap them. Wernicke's encephalopathy: an emergency hiding in plain sight In 1881 Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905), the German neurologist whose name you already know from the receptive aphasia he had described seven years earlier, published part of his textbook of brain diseases, the Lehrbuch der Gehirnkrankheiten . In it he described three patients: two men with alcoholism, aged 33 and 36, and a woman of 20 who had swallowed sulphuric acid and then developed persistent vomiting. All three became confused and drowsy, could not move their eyes properly and walked unsteadily. All three died, and at autopsy Wernicke found tiny pinpoint haemorrhages in the grey matter around the third and fourth ventricles and the aqueduct. He believed he was looking at an inflammation and called it polioencephalitis haemorrhagica superior ("polio" is Greek for grey, the same root as in poliomyelitis). Its real cause, thiamine deficiency, was not established until the 1930s and 1940s. The disorder is now called Wernicke's encephalopathy : an acute disorder of the brain caused by thiamine deficiency and marked by confusion, abnormal eye movements and an unsteady gait. Those three signs became the textbook triad, and each is worth seeing clearly. The first is a change in mental state, usually a global confusional state. The patient is apathetic, drowsy and inattentive; he cannot follow a conversation, does not know where he is or what day it is, and without treatment may sink into stupor and coma. The second is ophthalmoplegia , weakness or paralysis of the muscles that move the eyes. Most often the lateral rectus muscles of both eyes are weak, so the eyes cannot turn outwards (DSM-5-TR describes it as a lateral gaze paralysis), and the patient may complain of double vision. It is almost always accompanied by nystagmus , an involuntary rhythmic jerking of the eyes, usually from side to side when the patient looks sideways. The third is ataxia , unsteadiness of stance and gait: the patient stands with his feet wide apart, sways and lurches, and cannot walk heel to toe, while his arms may be relatively spared. Many patients also have numb, weak legs and absent ankle reflexes from the peripheral neuropathy that so often accompanies heavy drinking. Key study: Harper's autopsies (1983 and 1986) How often is Wernicke's encephalopathy missed? The Australian neuropathologist Clive Harper answered the question from the other end, by examining brains after death. In a nine-year series of autopsies in Western Australia he found the characteristic lesions in 2.8 percent of all the brains examined, yet only 20 percent of his 131 cases had been diagnosed during life, and 83 percent of the lesions were old, chronic ones. In 1986 Harper, M. Giles and R. Finlay-Jones went back to the hospital notes of 131 cases proved at autopsy: only 16 percent had had the full triad recorded, and 19 percent had had no documented sign at all. The conclusion changed practice. If you wait for all three signs, you will miss most cases. Harper suggested that many patients reach the chronic stage through repeated small episodes of deficiency that nobody notices. Clinicians now use looser rules. In 1997 D. Caine, Harper and their colleagues in Sydney proposed that a heavy drinker should be diagnosed with Wernicke's encephalopathy if he shows any two of four signs: a history of dietary deficiency, eye signs, signs of cerebellar dysfunction (unsteadiness, poor coordination), and either an altered mental state or mild memory impairment. The European Federation of Neurological Societies adopted these criteria in its guideline of 2010, and added a blunt piece of advice: suspect the disorder in any condition that can lead to thiamine deficiency, whether or not the patient drinks. Each sign maps onto a site of damage, as Figure 10.19 shows. The lesions are symmetrical and lie close to the midline, in the tissue that lines the third and fourth ventricles and the aqueduct. The eye signs come from damage to the brainstem nuclei that control eye movements (the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nuclei) and to the vestibular nuclei, around the floor of the fourth ventricle. The ataxia comes from damage to the upper part of the cerebellar vermis, the midline strip of the cerebellum that keeps the trunk balanced, together with the vestibular damage. The confusion, and later the memory loss, come from damage in the diencephalon: to the mammillary bodies , two small rounded swellings on the underside of the hypothalamus that are affected in almost every case, and to the medial thalamus, especially the dorsomedial nucleus of the thalamus (also called the mediodorsal nucleus). The grey matter around the aqueduct, the periaqueductal grey , is often affected too. In the acute stage these regions are swollen and speckled with small haemorrhages; in the chronic stage the mammillary bodies shrink. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can show symmetrical changes in exactly these places and supports the diagnosis, but a normal scan does not rule it out. The lesions of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome cluster around the midline: the mammillary bodies and the dorsomedial and anterior nuclei of the thalamus (linked to memory and confusion), the periaqueductal grey and the eye-movement nuclei of the brainstem (ophthalmoplegia and nystagmus), and the upper cerebellar vermis (ataxia). Notice that the hippocampus, the structure lost in Henry Molaison, is not the main site of damage: Korsakoff's amnesia is a diencephalic amnesia. Wernicke's encephalopathy is a medical emergency, and it is one of the few emergencies in neuropsychiatry with a cheap, safe and effective treatment: thiamine, given by injection (intravenously or intramuscularly), in high doses, at once. The 2010 European guideline recommends 200 mg three times a day, preferably intravenously, given before any carbohydrate and continued until the signs stop improving. Tablets are not enough, because a drinker's gut absorbs thiamine poorly and the brain needs it now. The response can be dramatic. The eye-movement palsies often begin to improve within hours, so quickly that the improvement itself helps confirm the diagnosis; the ataxia and the confusion recover more slowly, over days and weeks. Left untreated, the patient may slide into stupor, coma and death, and many survivors, in some series most of them, are left with Korsakoff's syndrome. You will often read that glucose must never be given before thiamine. The reasoning is sound. Thiamine is needed to burn glucose, so a large glucose load (an intravenous drip of dextrose, for example) can use up the last of a patient's thiamine and tip a borderline deficiency into Wernicke's encephalopathy. The evidence, however, is thinner than the slogan suggests. When E. Schabelman and D. Kuo reviewed the literature in 2012, they found 19 relevant papers, none of them better than case reports or series. Their advice reflects current practice: a patient with low blood sugar must never be left without glucose while someone looks for thiamine, because hypoglycaemia itself damages the brain; give thiamine at the same time or straight afterwards, and never keep an at-risk patient on glucose drips for long without it. Clinical link This is why thiamine is part of every alcohol detoxification regimen (Section 10.4), and why many units give it by injection to every malnourished drinker on admission instead of waiting for signs. In a 2001 report, set out as guidelines for emergency departments in 2002, the Royal College of Physicians of London advised that drinkers who may be poorly nourished should be given B vitamins by injection at the outset in emergency departments, especially when drunkenness hides the clinical signs. The same vigilance applies outside psychiatry: to the woman with hyperemesis gravidarum, to the patient after bariatric surgery (the European guideline advises checking thiamine for at least six months afterwards), and to anyone being refed after starvation. A few rupees' worth of vitamin given in time can prevent a lifetime of amnesia. Exam trap Wernicke's triad is confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia (with nystagmus). Amnesia, confabulation and apathy belong to Korsakoff's syndrome. Wernicke's encephalopathy is acute and largely reversible with thiamine; Korsakoff's syndrome is chronic and largely irreversible. The full triad is present in only a minority (16 percent in Harper's autopsy series), so "all three signs are needed for the diagnosis" is false. Finally, do not confuse Wernicke's encephalopathy (1881, thiamine deficiency) with Wernicke's aphasia (1874, a fluent receptive aphasia from damage to the left superior temporal gyrus): the same man described both. Korsakoff's syndrome: a memory that cannot hold Six years after Wernicke's description, a Moscow psychiatrist began to describe the other half of the story. Sergei Sergeievich Korsakoff (1854 to 1900) took his doctorate in 1887 with a thesis on alcoholic paralysis, and in a series of papers from 1887 to about 1891, in Russian, French and German, he described a peculiar mental disorder that accompanied polyneuritis (disease of many peripheral nerves at once). He saw it in about thirty heavy drinkers and in fourteen patients whose illness had nothing to do with alcohol, and he called it polyneuritic psychosis, or cerebropathia psychica toxaemica. What struck him was the memory. His patients, he wrote, promptly forgot what had just happened, yet remembered the events of the years before their illness. He noticed abnormal eye movements in some of them but did not stress them; the link with Wernicke's cases was made by others. The eponym is usually credited to the German psychiatrist Friedrich Jolly, who in 1897 proposed that the disorder be named after Korsakoff (sources differ on his exact wording). Today Korsakoff's syndrome (also called Korsakoff's psychosis, or Korsakoff's amnesic syndrome) means a chronic disorder of memory, caused by thiamine deficiency and seen most often in heavy drinkers, in which the ability to learn new information is severely impaired while alertness, immediate memory and general intelligence are relatively preserved. Notice the old word "psychosis": in the nineteenth century it meant any serious mental disorder, not hallucinations and delusions. Babu, a 47-year-old lorry driver from Salem, had drunk arrack every evening for twenty years and had eaten almost nothing for a month when his wife brought him to the district hospital, confused, staggering and seeing double. The duty doctor found nystagmus and weakness of outward gaze in both eyes and gave intravenous thiamine at once; within two days his eyes moved normally, though his walking improved much more slowly. By the third week the fog had lifted, and the ward team could see what was left. Babu was alert, polite and chatty. He could repeat seven digits forwards without a mistake, and he still played cards as shrewdly as ever. But he could not recall the doctor's name five minutes after hearing it for the fourth time, greeted the same nurse each morning as if they had never met, and when asked what he had done that morning said that he had driven a load of turmeric to Erode and stopped for a meal on the way. He had not left the ward in three weeks. He thought the year was 2016 and that his married daughter was still at school. Asked about his memory, he said it was perfectly good. Babu shows almost every feature of the syndrome. The core is anterograde amnesia , the inability to form new lasting memories of events and facts after the illness begins. DSM-5-TR describes the alcohol-induced amnestic-confabulatory (Korsakoff's) type as an impairment of recent memory out of proportion to any other cognitive problem, with severe difficulty learning new information and rapid forgetting. Information gets in (Babu can repeat seven digits), but it does not stay: a few minutes later, once his attention has moved on, it has gone. Patients ask the same question over and over, cannot learn the way to the toilet in a new ward, and do not recognise people they see every day. The second feature is retrograde amnesia , the loss of memories formed before the illness. In Korsakoff's syndrome it is patchy and often extensive, sometimes reaching back decades, and it has a temporal gradient : the most recent years are lost most completely, while memories of childhood and youth are relatively spared. In 1979 Marilyn S. Albert , Nelson Butters and J. Levin tested eleven patients with alcoholic Korsakoff's syndrome using photographs of famous faces from different decades, questions about famous people and events, and a multiple-choice questionnaire. The patients had a marked retrograde amnesia with a steep gradient, and because the researchers had included items of both passing and lasting fame, they could show that the gradient was not simply an artefact of older items being easier. The pattern had been predicted a century before. In 1881 the French psychologist Théodule Ribot (1839 to 1916) argued that memory dissolves in the reverse of the order in which it was built, the newest and least consolidated memories going first and the oldest last; this is Ribot's law . Pinel adds that anterograde amnesia dominates in the early stages, and that the retrograde loss can deepen as the disorder progresses, eventually stretching back into childhood. The third feature is the one that makes Korsakoff's syndrome unforgettable to anyone who has seen it. Confabulation is the production of false memories, often fluent and plausible, to fill the gaps in memory, without any intention to deceive (Chapter 2, Section 2.7.5 describes it as a sign). Babu's trip to Erode is an example. In 1987 the British neuropsychiatrist Michael D. Kopelman distinguished two types. Provoked confabulation appears in answer to a question that probes memory ("What did you do this morning?"). It is common, and Kopelman argued that it may be a normal response to a faulty memory, because healthy people make similar errors when asked to recall a story after a very long delay. Spontaneous confabulation pours out unprompted, can be fantastic (the patient describes his meeting with a film star last week) and is sometimes acted upon. Kopelman suggested that it appears when frontal-lobe dysfunction is added to an organic amnesia, so that the patient can no longer check and reject the false memories his brain throws up. Confabulation tends to be most florid in the early weeks of the illness and to fade as the syndrome becomes chronic. Several other features sit around these three. Patients are disoriented, especially in time: they lose track of the date and of how long they have been in hospital. They are apathetic, with little initiative or spontaneous interest, and seem emotionally bland. They usually lack insight, denying that anything is wrong with their memory, as Babu did. Many also show the effects of frontal damage: poor planning, difficulty shifting from one way of thinking to another, and an unusual vulnerability to interference, so that material learned earlier intrudes into what they are trying to learn now. In its advanced stages, Pinel notes, the disorder brings sensory and motor problems, extreme confusion and personality change, and a risk of death from liver, gut or heart disease. Just as important, for diagnosis and for the exam, is what Korsakoff's syndrome leaves alone. Consciousness is clear: unlike the patient with Wernicke's encephalopathy or delirium, the Korsakoff patient is alert and attentive. Immediate memory, the span of what can be held in mind for a few seconds (tested with the digit span), is normal or nearly so. General intelligence, as measured by tests of knowledge and reasoning acquired long ago, is largely preserved, and so are language and old skills: Babu still plays cards, and other patients have kept up chess, carpentry or music. Most remarkably, some kinds of new learning survive. Patients can learn motor skills such as mirror drawing, they show priming (a word seen once is completed more readily later, although they do not remember having seen it), and they can be conditioned. The first and most famous demonstration came from Geneva. Key study: Claparède's pin (1911) The Swiss psychologist Édouard Claparède (1873 to 1940) studied a woman with Korsakoff's syndrome at the Bel-Air asylum in Geneva. She was 47 when he first tested her in 1906, and her illness had begun around 1900. She could name the capitals of Europe and do mental arithmetic, but after five years in the asylum she did not know where she was, did not recognise the doctors she saw every day or the nurse who had looked after her for six months, and forgot a story read to her within three minutes. To see whether an emotional experience would last longer, Claparède hid a pin between his fingers and pricked her hand as he shook it. A few minutes later she had forgotten the prick. Yet when he reached for her hand again, she pulled it back without knowing why. Pressed for a reason, she asked, "Is there perhaps a pin hidden in your hand?", and explained, "Sometimes pins are hidden in people's hands." She never recognised the idea as a memory. Claparède published the case in 1911, and it remains one of the first demonstrations of what is now called implicit memory: learning that shows itself in behaviour without conscious recollection (Book 1, Section 7.5 sets out the explicit and implicit memory systems). Exam trap In Korsakoff's syndrome the amnesia is mainly anterograde , with a temporally graded retrograde amnesia that can be profound (older memories are kept better than recent ones). Consciousness is clear , immediate memory (digit span) and general intelligence are relatively preserved , and implicit and procedural memory survive. Confabulation is not lying : there is no intent to deceive, which separates it from malingering. "Korsakoff's psychosis" does not mean that the patient hallucinates; "psychosis" is the old general word for a serious mental illness. So when a paper asks which illness caused by long-term alcohol use "often involves profound retrograde amnesia" (RML 2024), the answer is Korsakoff's psychosis. One disease in two stages, and where the damage lies For almost a century Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's syndrome were described in different books, one as a neurological emergency and the other as a psychiatric curiosity. The study that joined them for good came from the American neurologists Maurice Victor , Raymond D. Adams and George H. Collins, who in 1971 published a monograph based on 245 patients, 82 of whom had been examined after death. They followed patients from the acute illness onwards and found that the two disorders were stages of one disease. Most drinkers who survived Wernicke's encephalopathy were left, as their confusion cleared, with Korsakoff's amnesia, and the brains of patients with Korsakoff's syndrome showed the same lesions as those with Wernicke's encephalopathy, only older. The combined term Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome therefore names a single disorder of thiamine deficiency with an acute phase (Wernicke's encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia and eye signs) and a chronic phase (Korsakoff's syndrome: amnesia and confabulation in clear consciousness). Figure 10.20 shows how the one turns into the other in a treated patient such as Babu. After thiamine is started: the order in which signs change (schematic, time not to scale) Thiamine started Eye-muscle palsy often improves within hours to days Nystagmus improves more slowly; may persist Ataxia improves over days to weeks; often incomplete Global confusion clears over days to weeks Korsakoff amnesia masked by confusion revealed as confusion lifts; lasting Hours to days Days to weeks Weeks to months and beyond Outcome: partial recovery of memory is the rule; full recovery is the exception Figure 10.20 Wernicke's encephalopathy turning into Korsakoff's syndrome in a treated drinker (schematic, following the clinical course described by Victor, Adams and Collins). The eye signs respond first, often within hours; ataxia and confusion recover more slowly. As the confusion clears, the amnesia it had hidden comes into view, and that is the part that lasts. Not every patient passes visibly through the first stage. Some arrive at Korsakoff's syndrome with no recorded episode of Wernicke's encephalopathy, and Harper's finding that most lesions at autopsy were old ones suggests why: repeated small episodes of deficiency, each too mild to be noticed, can add up to the chronic disorder. That is one more reason to give thiamine to every at-risk drinker instead of waiting for signs. Which lesion causes the amnesia? Compare Korsakoff's syndrome with the amnesia of Henry Molaison (H.M.), whose medial temporal lobes, including most of both hippocampi, were removed by surgery in 1953 (Book 1, Section 7.10). Both men lost the ability to form new explicit memories, but their damage lay in different places. Korsakoff's amnesia is a diencephalic amnesia , caused by damage to the medial diencephalon (the medial thalamus, and the hypothalamus with its mammillary bodies) rather than to the medial temporal lobe. Pinel points out that the damage in Korsakoff's syndrome is diffuse, reaching the neocortex, the cerebellum and other structures (some studies include the hippocampus, although neuron counts described below found it intact), so that no single lesion can be blamed with certainty; but the mediodorsal (dorsomedial) nuclei of the thalamus are damaged in almost every patient, and the mammillary bodies nearly as often. Converging evidence comes from rare patients with damage confined to the same region. The best known is N.A., a radar technician in the United States Air Force whose roommate, playing with a fencing foil behind his chair, accidentally stabbed him up the right nostril; the foil passed through the thin bone at the base of the skull into his brain. N.A. was left with a lasting anterograde amnesia, first described by Hans-Lukas Teuber , Brenda Milner and H. G. Vaughan in 1968, and an MRI scan taken in the late 1980s showed extensive medial diencephalic damage, including the mediodorsal nuclei and the mammillary bodies. More recent work has sharpened the picture. In 2000 A. Harding, G. Halliday and their colleagues in Sydney counted neurons in the brains of drinkers who had had Wernicke's encephalopathy, with and without Korsakoff's amnesia. Neuron loss in the mammillary bodies and the mediodorsal thalamus was substantial in both groups, the amnesic and the non-amnesic alike; only loss in the anterior nuclei of the thalamus consistently separated the patients with Korsakoff's syndrome, and the hippocampus was unaffected. Why should the anterior thalamus matter so much? Because it is a relay in a loop that links the hippocampus to the rest of the memory system. In 1937 James Papez (1883 to 1958) traced a circuit that runs from the hippocampus through the fornix to the mammillary bodies, from there through the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, then to the cingulate cortex and back to the hippocampus. Papez thought that the circuit served emotion; it is now known to matter more for memory (Book 1, Chapter 11). The Papez circuit explains why lesions in quite different places, the hippocampus in H.M., the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus in Korsakoff's syndrome, the fornix in rare surgical cases, all produce amnesia: break the loop anywhere and new memories are not laid down. The mediodorsal nucleus belongs to a second loop, with the prefrontal cortex, and its damage probably adds the frontal features of the syndrome: the poor organisation of memory, the vulnerability to interference and perhaps the failure to check confabulations. What becomes of patients like Babu? Thiamine and abstinence stop the damage from getting worse, but the amnesia itself recovers only partly, and slowly. In the long follow-up by Victor and his colleagues, partial recovery was the rule: only about a fifth to a quarter of patients recovered fully, roughly a quarter did not improve at all, and improvement, when it came, crept on over many months. Pinel puts it soberly: thiamine limits further damage and often brings slight improvement, but the brain dysfunction already acquired is mostly irreversible. Care therefore has two aims. The first is to prevent further damage, with complete abstinence (helped by the treatments in Section 10.4), a proper diet and continued vitamins. The second is to help the person live with the memory that remains. Because implicit and procedural memory are relatively spared, patients learn best by doing the same thing in the same way, many times over, in an unchanging environment, with diaries, labelled cupboards, phone alarms and a fixed daily routine. Trial-and-error learning is avoided, because a patient who cannot remember his mistakes will learn them implicitly and repeat them; errorless learning , in which the correct response is supplied before the patient has a chance to guess wrongly, works better (Book 2, Section 9.9.3). Many patients cannot live independently again, and in India that care usually falls on the family. The manuals file the syndrome in different places, and the papers occasionally ask where. ICD-10 codes the Korsakoff stage in drinkers as F10.6, the alcohol-induced amnesic syndrome (one of the clinical patterns of Section 10.1), and codes Wernicke's encephalopathy itself among the vitamin deficiencies, as E51.2, a form of thiamine deficiency; Korsakoff's syndrome without alcohol goes under F04, the organic amnesic syndrome. DSM-5 abolished the separate category of amnestic disorder, so DSM-5-TR calls the condition alcohol-induced major neurocognitive disorder, amnestic-confabulatory type, adding "persistent" when it lasts; a man like Babu, with severe alcohol use disorder, would be coded F10.26. ICD-11 goes furthest towards the biology. It codes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome under vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency (5B5A.1, with Wernicke encephalopathy as 5B5A.10 and Korsakoff syndrome as 5B5A.11), in its chapter on endocrine, nutritional or metabolic diseases, and explicitly excludes both from 6D72.10, amnestic disorder due to use of alcohol, a category reserved for memory impairment caused by alcohol itself. Exam trap Anterograde amnesia with confabulation after bilateral damage to the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus is Korsakoff's syndrome (MET Mock 3). Each distractor has its own lesion. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion disease with spongiform change in the cortex and deep grey matter, and a dementia that progresses over months with myoclonus. Pick's disease is a frontotemporal degeneration: shrunken frontal and temporal lobes, Pick bodies, and early change of personality or language with memory relatively spared. Huntington's chorea is an inherited degeneration of the caudate nucleus with chorea, depression and a subcortical dementia (Section 10.10 teaches all three). And the hippocampus is H.M.'s lesion, not Korsakoff's: the alcoholic amnesia is diencephalic. Telling the alcoholic amnesia from its look-alikes The papers test this topic mostly with one vignette in several costumes, so it is worth pushing it through slowly, as a worked example. A man with a long history of heavy drinking presents with severe memory deficits, confabulation and nystagmus. Which diagnosis fits (Real PYQ 2024; NIMHANS Mock 1)? Take each option in turn and ask what it would predict. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Every finding points here. Nystagmus is a Wernicke sign, from damage around the floor of the fourth ventricle; severe memory loss with confabulation is the Korsakoff stage; chronic drinking is the setting in which thiamine deficiency develops. An eye sign together with an amnesia in a drinker is the signature of the whole syndrome, its acute and chronic phases overlapping. This is the answer. Alzheimer's disease. Memory loss, yes, but it comes on insidiously over years, usually after 65, and spreads to language (aphasia), skilled movement (apraxia) and visuospatial ability. There are no eye-movement signs, confabulation is not its hallmark, and drinking does not cause it (Section 10.9). Vascular dementia. The course is sudden or stepwise, following strokes, with patchy deficits, focal neurological signs (weakness of one side, a lost half of the visual field, slurred speech) and vascular risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes (Section 10.10). A brainstem stroke can cause nystagmus, but it would not explain an amnesia with confabulation in a heavy drinker. Frontotemporal dementia. The early picture is a change of personality (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive or tactless behaviour) or a progressive loss of language, typically beginning between about 45 and 65, with memory relatively spared at first. Nystagmus has no place in it (Section 10.10). The other questions on the topic change the distractors but not the logic: when chronic drinking and a disorder of memory appear together in the stem, the answer is Korsakoff's syndrome. Asked which illness caused by long-term alcohol use often involves profound retrograde amnesia (RML 2024), you choose Korsakoff's psychosis over Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease. Parkinson's disease is a disorder of movement, caused by the loss of the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra, with tremor at rest, rigidity and slowness of movement; dementia, if it comes, comes late. Huntington's disease is an inherited, autosomal dominant degeneration of the caudate nucleus with chorea, depression and a subcortical dementia. Neither has anything to do with drinking. Asked which amnesic disorder chronic alcoholism may cause (RML 2021), you choose Korsakoff's syndrome over Alzheimer's, Pick's and Parkinson's diseases; Pick's disease, the classic frontotemporal dementia, spares memory early. Asked which neuropsychological disorder is marked by severe memory impairment and confusion and often caused by chronic alcohol abuse (IHBAS 2024), you choose Korsakoff's syndrome over schizophrenia, Huntington's disease and multiple sclerosis. Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder of hallucinations, delusions, disorganisation and negative symptoms (Chapter 4); it brings real cognitive deficits, but it is not an amnesic syndrome and alcohol does not cause it. Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease in which patches of the myelin sheath in the brain and spinal cord are inflamed and destroyed, usually beginning in young adults with episodes of blurred vision, numbness or weakness that come and go; depression and slowed thinking are common in it, but it is not caused by alcohol. (Strictly, the "confusion" in that stem belongs to the Wernicke stage and the memory loss to the Korsakoff stage, but the papers use "Korsakoff's syndrome" for the whole.) In the clinic the look-alikes are wider than the exam's options, and Table 10.46 lines them up. Two come straight from Section 10.3. Delirium tremens, the most severe stage of alcohol withdrawal, also brings confusion and memory failure in a drinker, but it begins two or three days after the last drink, with clouded consciousness, tremor, sweating, fever, a racing pulse and vivid hallucinations, and it is over within days; Korsakoff's syndrome is quiet, alert and lasting. An alcoholic blackout is amnesia only for a period of intoxication, and memory works normally once the person is sober. Two others come from elsewhere: transient global amnesia, described below, and dissociative amnesia (Chapter 7, Section 7.5), in which a person loses autobiographical memory, sometimes even his sense of who he is, after psychological trauma or stress, while his ability to learn new information is intact. That is almost the reverse of the Korsakoff pattern. Table 10.46 Korsakoff's syndrome and the conditions it is confused with. Many long-term drinkers develop a slower, broader decline, called alcohol-related dementia when it is severe, in which memory, attention, planning and problem solving all suffer and there is no dense, isolated amnesia; DSM-5-TR names it alcohol-induced major neurocognitive disorder, nonamnestic-confabulatory type. Brain scans of people with chronic alcohol use disorder frequently show cortical thinning, loss of white matter and enlarged sulci and ventricles, and Pinel notes that the commonest finding, even in heavy drinkers without Korsakoff's syndrome, is a general loss of cortical white and grey matter. British clinicians use the umbrella term alcohol-related brain damage for the whole range, because most patients have a mixture: some thiamine damage, some direct toxicity, some head injury, some liver disease, some vascular disease. The hopeful finding is that much of this damage is reversible. In 1978 P. L. Carlen and his colleagues scanned eight chronic drinkers repeatedly with computed tomography; the four who stayed abstinent and improved in function showed partial reversal of their cerebral atrophy, while those who kept drinking did not. DSM-5-TR adds that about 30 to 40 percent of people with alcohol use disorder have a mild neurocognitive disorder in the first two months of abstinence, that substantial or even complete recovery is common in those who achieve stable abstinence before the age of 50, and that the impairment is most likely to become permanent in those who go on drinking past 50. Whether alcohol on its own, without thiamine deficiency, can cause a true dementia is still argued; that stopping drinking is the treatment is not. Korsakoff's syndrome is the commonest example of a wider group. An amnestic syndrome (or amnesic syndrome) is a disorder in which memory is impaired out of proportion to every other cognitive function, in clear consciousness. ICD-10 defines its organic amnesic syndrome (F04, or F10.6 when alcohol is the cause) by three requirements: a prominent impairment of recent memory, with both anterograde and retrograde amnesia; a history or evidence of injury to or disease of the brain, especially one affecting the diencephalon or the medial temporal lobes on both sides; and the absence of any defect in immediate recall (the digit span), of any disturbance of attention or consciousness, and of global intellectual impairment. Confabulation, lack of insight and apathy often accompany it but are not required. Each exclusion has a purpose: a defect of attention or consciousness would make the diagnosis delirium (Section 10.8), and a global intellectual decline would make it dementia. ICD-11 keeps the category as amnestic disorder (6D72). DSM-5, as Section 10.8 explained, folded it into major or mild neurocognitive disorder, because a major neurocognitive disorder can now be diagnosed when only one cognitive domain is significantly impaired. The causes of an amnestic syndrome fall into two families, matching the two parts of the memory circuit. Damage to the medial temporal lobes and hippocampi on both sides can come from surgery, as in H.M.; from herpes simplex encephalitis, a viral infection with a liking for the temporal lobes, which destroyed the memory of the musician Clive Wearing in 1985 (his story opens Book 1, Chapter 7); and from lack of oxygen. Pinel tells the case of R.B., who at 52 suffered a period of ischaemia when the pump circulating his blood broke down during heart bypass surgery. He was left amnesic, and after his death in 1983 the damage was found to be largely confined to one strip of the hippocampus, the CA1 field, whose neurons are exceptionally sensitive to the loss of oxygen. Damage to the diencephalon comes from thiamine deficiency, from strokes of the thalamus, from tumours in the region of the third ventricle and from penetrating injuries like N.A.'s. Head injury can damage both, and adds a period of post-traumatic amnesia after the blow. One amnesia is frightening to watch but harmless. In transient global amnesia , a syndrome named by C. Miller Fisher and the same Raymond Adams, an otherwise healthy middle-aged or older adult suddenly becomes unable to lay down new memories. He knows who he is and can still drive or cook, but he asks the same questions again and again ("What are we doing here? What day is it?"), because each answer vanishes within minutes, and he has a patchy retrograde amnesia for the preceding days or weeks. The attack typically lasts four to six hours and then clears, leaving only a gap for the episode itself, and it seldom recurs. Attacks are often set off by physical exertion, a plunge into cold water, sexual intercourse or emotional stress. Pinel describes it as perhaps the strongest evidence that damage to the hippocampus alone can cause amnesia: small abnormalities have been found on MRI in the CA1 field, appearing some hours after the attack begins and usually gone ten days later, a time course that suggests a brief ischaemia. Exam trap When the stem combines chronic drinking with a disorder of memory , choose Korsakoff's syndrome, or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome when an eye sign or ataxia is mentioned. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's, Pick's and Creutzfeldt-Jakob diseases, vascular and frontotemporal dementia, schizophrenia and multiple sclerosis are not caused by drinking. Within the alcohol family, separate Korsakoff's syndrome (clear consciousness, lasting) from delirium tremens (clouded consciousness, autonomic storm, days) and from a blackout (amnesia only for the drinking episode). And separate organic amnesia (new learning lost, identity kept) from dissociative amnesia (personal past and sometimes identity lost, new learning intact). Pseudodementia: when depression looks like dementia Mani, a 68-year-old retired postmaster from Thanjavur, came to the memory clinic on his own initiative, his son trailing behind him. "My brain is finished, doctor," he said. "I forget everything. I think I am getting Alzheimer's." The trouble had begun about two months earlier, fairly suddenly, after a heart attack had left him frightened and housebound. He had stopped reading the newspaper, which he said he could no longer follow, slept badly and woke at four every morning, had lost five kilograms, and felt that he had become a burden on his son. On a bedside cognitive test he scored poorly, but the pattern was odd. To many questions he simply said, "I don't know, I can't," and gave up; when the psychologist encouraged him and gave him time, he got several of them right. He remembered recent events about as well, or as badly, as distant ones, and he described in detail the hospital stay he insisted he had forgotten. He had had a severe depression at 52. Eight weeks after he started an antidepressant his mood had lifted, he was reading again, and his test score was back in the normal range. Mani shows a picture that has puzzled and misled clinicians for more than a century: an older person whose depression looks like dementia. Pseudodementia is cognitive impairment that resembles dementia but is caused by a psychiatric disorder, most often depression, and that improves when the psychiatric disorder is treated. The phenomenon was known in the late nineteenth century as "melancholic dementia". The word itself (in German, Pseudodemenz ) is often credited to Carl Wernicke, but it never appears in his published writings; the earliest printed use that historians have traced is by his student Georg Stertz in 1910, who applied it to a psychogenic state after trauma. Its modern meaning comes from the psychiatrist Leslie Gordon Kiloh , whose paper "Pseudo-dementia" appeared in Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica in 1961. Kiloh had noticed patients who had been labelled demented and then recovered when their psychiatric illness was treated, and he meant the word to describe a clinical presentation, not a diagnosis: "pseudodementia" tells you what the patient looks like, and you still have to find out what he has. Others disliked the prefix, because the cognitive impairment is perfectly real. Marshal F. Folstein and Paul R. McHugh preferred the dementia syndrome of depression (1978), and modern writers also speak of depression-related cognitive impairment. Why should depression damage thinking at all? Because depression is not only a disorder of mood. It slows thought and movement (psychomotor retardation), narrows attention, drains the effort that learning demands and weakens the executive functions that organise memory. A depressed person encodes new information shallowly, his attention turned inwards on his own misery, and he retrieves poorly whenever retrieval takes effort. That is why the memory of a depressed patient often improves sharply when he is given cues or a recognition format (choosing the right answer from a list), whereas in Alzheimer's disease the information was never properly stored, so cues and recognition help much less. DSM-5-TR describes the overlap directly: in older people with depression, memory difficulties may be the chief complaint and may be mistaken for early dementia ("pseudodementia"), and when the depressive episode is successfully treated the memory problems often fully abate. In 1979 the American psychiatrist Charles E. Wells listed the clinical features that help separate pseudodementia from dementia. His list, refined by later writers, is the basis of Table 10.47, and it repays careful reading, because nearly every row turns on a single idea: the depressed patient emphasises his failures, while the patient with dementia hides them.
