Then the patients were followed for longer, and an awkward truth emerged. Key study: when pseudodementia turns into dementia (1989 to 2019) In Canada, V. A. Kral and O. B. Emery treated 44 older patients (mean age 76.5) for depressive pseudodementia; when the depression cleared, their cognition returned to its previous level. They then retested the patients every six months for 4 to 18 years, 8 years on average. By the end, 39 of the 44 (89 percent) had developed a dementia of the Alzheimer type. In 1993 George S. Alexopoulos and his colleagues in New York followed 57 older inpatients with major depression for almost three years on average: irreversible dementia developed in 43 percent of those whose depression had come with a "reversible dementia", against 12 percent of those with depression alone, a risk nearly five times higher. In 2019 Michael Connors, L. Quinto and Henry Brodaty pooled 18 follow-up studies covering 284 patients with pseudodementia: a third (33 percent) went on to irreversible dementia, about half (53 percent) no longer met criteria for dementia, and the rest were lost to follow-up. The lesson is double. Pseudodementia is real and often treatable, but in older people it can also be the first sign of a dementing illness, so the patient who recovers must still be followed up. DSM-5-TR makes the same point in its account of major depression: in some individuals, particularly elderly persons, a major depressive episode may be the first presentation of an irreversible dementia. Depression in late life is now seen as both a risk factor for dementia and, in some people, its earliest symptom, which is why the old question "depression or dementia?" so often turns out to have the answer "both". Depression is also by far the commonest cause of pseudodementia, but not the only one. In the pooled sample of Connors and his colleagues, 238 of the 284 patients were depressed, while 18 had conversion disorder, 14 a psychosis and 11 bipolar disorder. A rarer and more theatrical form is the Ganser syndrome , described by Sigbert Ganser in 1898 among prisoners awaiting trial, in which the person gives approximate answers : asked how many legs a cow has, he says three; asked the colour of snow, he says black. The answers show that he knows the right answer well enough to miss it. The syndrome is now classed with the dissociative disorders (Chapter 7). Clinical link Never accept a diagnosis of dementia in an older person until depression has been looked for and, if it is present, treated. The cost of missing it is high: a person written off with an untreatable label when he had a treatable illness, and a depression left to deepen, with all its risk of suicide. The bedside clues are those in Table 10.47; the tests used to measure cognition and late-life depression are covered in the Assessment book, and the treatment of late-life depression, with antidepressants and, when it is severe, electroconvulsive therapy, in Chapter 5. When the patient improves, book the follow-up anyway. Exam trap The common cause of pseudodementia is depression (RML 2024). Each distractor fails for its own reason. Schizophrenia brings real cognitive deficits and, in old age, a chronic impoverished picture, but it is not the common cause of a reversible, dementia-like state. Mania can make a patient so distractible that he seems disoriented, and a few such cases are reported, but they are rare. Hypochondriasis (now illness anxiety disorder or somatic symptom disorder, Chapter 7) may bring constant worry about memory, but tested memory is normal: worry without impairment is the opposite of pseudodementia. And remember the two classic contrasts: the depressed patient complains and says "I don't know"; the patient with dementia conceals and gives near misses. When the body makes the mind ill Pseudodementia is a psychiatric illness disguised as a brain disease. The rest of this section deals with the opposite disguise: a bodily disease that presents as a psychiatric illness. The brain is an organ of the body, bathed in its hormones, fed by its blood and exposed to its infections and antibodies, so almost any disease of the body can disturb mood, thinking and behaviour. Older psychiatry called such conditions organic, because they had a known physical cause, and set them against the functional disorders, which had none; Section 10.8 explained why DSM-IV dropped the word "organic" and DSM-5 kept it out. The idea survives in the terms secondary mental syndrome and mental disorder due to another medical condition : a psychiatric syndrome judged, on the evidence, to be the direct physiological consequence of a medical illness. The stakes are high. DSM-5-TR estimates that about 60 percent of older people who develop a psychosis for the first time have a medical cause for it. All three manuals provide for these syndromes. ICD-10 places them in F06, other mental disorders due to brain damage and dysfunction and to physical disease (among them organic hallucinosis, F06.0; organic catatonic disorder, F06.1; organic delusional disorder, F06.2; organic mood disorders, F06.3; and organic anxiety disorder, F06.4), and in F07, personality and behavioural disorders due to brain disease, damage and dysfunction (organic personality disorder, F07.0; postencephalitic syndrome, F07.1; and postconcussional syndrome, F07.2). ICD-11 groups them as secondary mental or behavioural syndromes associated with disorders or diseases classified elsewhere (6E60 to 6E6Z), which include secondary psychotic, mood, anxiety and neurocognitive syndromes and secondary personality change, always coded alongside the medical disease. DSM-5-TR does not gather them into one chapter. Instead, each chapter carries its own version: psychotic disorder, catatonic disorder, bipolar and related disorder, depressive disorder, anxiety disorder and obsessive-compulsive and related disorder due to another medical condition, personality change due to another medical condition, and neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition. The DSM-5-TR diagnoses share one template, and each rule in it exists to prevent a particular mistake. First, the psychiatric syndrome must be prominent: depressed mood, anxiety or panic, hallucinations or delusions, a change of personality. Second, there must be evidence from the history, the physical examination or laboratory findings that the syndrome is the direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition; suspicion is not enough, and the disease has to be found. Third, the syndrome must not be better explained by another mental disorder. The commonest trap here is adjustment disorder: a woman who becomes miserable and anxious after being told she has cancer is reacting psychologically to the meaning of her illness, and that is not a disorder "due to" the cancer. DSM-5-TR adds that anxiety due to a medical condition often has a prominent physical component, such as breathlessness, while the person with an adjustment disorder is especially distressed about what the illness means. Fourth, the syndrome must not occur only during a delirium, which would simply be diagnosed as delirium (Section 10.8). Fifth, it must cause clinically significant distress or impairment. When the cause is a drug rather than a disease (a steroid tablet, interferon injections, a street drug), the diagnosis becomes a substance/medication-induced disorder instead. How do you decide that a disease is the cause and not a coincidence? DSM-5-TR admits that there are no infallible rules, but it offers three considerations, set out in Figure 10.21. The first is biological plausibility: a medical condition must be present that is known to be able to produce the syndrome through a physiological mechanism (a severe generalised infection, lupus, porphyria, temporal lobe epilepsy, an overactive thyroid). The second is temporality: the psychiatric syndrome begins, worsens and improves along with the medical disease, and DSM-5-TR calls this the strongest evidence of all. The third is typicality, or rather atypicality: features that would be unusual in the primary psychiatric disorder, such as a first episode at an unusual age, no family history, or hallucinations that are visual, tactile or olfactory instead of auditory. DSM-5-TR notes, for example, that olfactory hallucinations suggest temporal lobe epilepsy. The three considerations are the ones DSM-5-TR offers: biological plausibility, temporality and atypical features. None is proof on its own, and the diagnosis still requires that drugs, delirium and a psychological reaction to illness be ruled out. In practice every new psychiatric presentation deserves a physical examination and a few basic investigations, and some deserve many. The warning signs that should make you look harder are a first episode after middle age with no previous history; a sudden onset; any disturbance of consciousness, attention or orientation; visual, tactile or olfactory hallucinations; seizures, headache, abnormal movements or other neurological signs; physical changes such as weight loss, fever or an altered appearance; and a poor response to treatment that usually works. The investigations follow from the suspicion: a blood count, blood sugar, electrolytes and calcium, liver and kidney function, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, tests for syphilis and HIV, and, where indicated, brain imaging, an electroencephalogram (EEG) or examination of the cerebrospinal fluid. Ordering them is the doctor's job, but a clinical psychologist who notices the warning signs and asks "has he been examined?" can save a patient years of the wrong treatment. Exam trap A mental disorder "due to another medical condition" needs evidence of a direct physiological cause (history, examination or laboratory findings). A psychological reaction to being ill is an adjustment disorder ; a syndrome caused by a drug or medication is substance/medication-induced ; a syndrome that occurs only during a delirium is coded as delirium . "Organic" is the ICD-10 word (F06, F07); "secondary" is the ICD-11 word (6E6); "due to another medical condition" is the DSM-5-TR phrase. Hormones and the mind: the endocrine disorders Gurpreet, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Ludhiana, had been treated for depression for a year with two different antidepressants and was no better. She slept badly, cried easily, snapped at her pupils, could not concentrate on the lessons she prepared, and said she felt "like a stranger in my own body". That phrase made her new psychiatrist look at her body. She had put on twelve kilograms, almost all of it on her face and trunk, while her arms and legs had grown thin; her face had become round and flushed; there were broad purple stretch marks on her abdomen; she bruised easily; and her blood pressure and blood sugar, normal two years earlier, were now high. Her cortisol levels were raised, and an MRI scan showed a small tumour of the pituitary gland. Six months after it was removed, her mood had lifted without any change in her antidepressant. Cushing's syndrome is the result of prolonged exposure to too much cortisol, the main glucocorticoid hormone of the adrenal cortex. Its commonest cause by far is treatment with corticosteroid drugs; its commonest natural cause is Cushing's disease , a small pituitary tumour that secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and drives the adrenal glands to overproduce cortisol, as in Gurpreet. The American neurosurgeon Harvey Cushing (1869 to 1939) described the syndrome in 1932 from twelve cases drawn from his own practice and the published literature, and noted "emotional disturbances" among its features from the start. The psychiatric picture is dominated by depression. Major depression affects more than half of patients with active disease (about 50 to 81 percent across the studies reviewed by Rosario Pivonello and colleagues in 2015), and it is typically irritable and anxious, with insomnia, poor concentration and emotional lability. Anxiety and panic are common, and about two thirds of patients have cognitive impairment, especially of memory and concentration, which fits the shrinkage of the hippocampus, a structure dense with cortisol receptors, seen on their scans. Mania or hypomania occurs in a minority (reported rates vary widely), and psychosis is uncommon. The depression is often an early sign of the disease, and it tends to lift when the cortisol excess is corrected, by surgery or by drugs that block cortisol production such as metyrapone and ketoconazole, more reliably than with antidepressants, although some symptoms and some loss of brain volume can persist after cure. Corticosteroid drugs such as prednisolone and dexamethasone produce a slightly different picture, because the dose is often high and starts suddenly. In the first days of treatment the commonest effects are euphoria, insomnia and restlessness, and some patients become hypomanic or manic; with long-term use depression becomes more common, and stopping steroids abruptly can bring fatigue and low mood. The risk climbs steeply with the dose. In a classic 1972 survey of 676 patients by the Boston Collaborative Drug Surveillance Program, psychiatric reactions occurred in 1.3 percent of those taking 40 mg of prednisone a day or less, 4.6 percent of those taking 41 to 80 mg, and 18.4 percent of those taking more than 80 mg. Strictly these are substance/medication-induced disorders, a distinction that matters for coding but not for the patient. The opposite disorder, too little cortisol, was described by the London physician Thomas Addison (1793 to 1860) in 1855. In Addison's disease the adrenal cortex is destroyed, most often by an autoimmune process and, where tuberculosis is common, as in India, still often by tuberculosis. It comes on slowly, and its early symptoms are easy to mistake for depression or even anorexia nervosa: fatigue, weakness, apathy, low mood, irritability, poor appetite and weight loss. The clues are physical: low blood pressure with dizziness on standing, a craving for salt, and darkening of the skin, especially in the creases of the palms, in scars and inside the mouth. Untreated, an infection or injury can tip the patient into an adrenal crisis, with collapse and delirium. The thyroid gland sets the pace of the body's metabolism, and the mind keeps time with it. In hypothyroidism , an underactive thyroid, everything slows: thinking, speech and movement grow sluggish, memory and concentration fail, and the patient feels tired, cold, constipated and low. The skin is dry, the hair coarse and thin, the voice hoarse, the face puffy, and weight goes up. In older people the result can look exactly like dementia, and hypothyroidism is one of the reversible causes that must be excluded before dementia is diagnosed (Section 10.10). Depression is the commonest psychiatric picture, and DSM-5-TR names hypothyroidism, together with Cushing's syndrome, as the endocrine conditions most closely associated with depression. In severe, untreated cases a psychosis can develop, with paranoid delusions, hallucinations and confusion. In 1949 the London physician Richard Asher (1912 to 1969), who two years later named Munchausen syndrome, described fourteen such patients in the British Medical Journal under the title "Myxoedematous madness", and the phrase myxoedema madness has stuck (myxoedema is the old name for severe hypothyroidism, from the swollen, waterlogged look of the skin). His message was that a treatable cause was hiding behind the madness. Lithium, the mood stabiliser, can itself cause hypothyroidism (Chapter 5), which is why thyroid function is checked in people who take it. In hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis, most often from Graves' disease) the pace quickens. The patient is anxious, restless, irritable and unable to sit still, sleeps poorly, has a fine tremor and a racing or irregular heart, sweats, cannot bear the heat, and loses weight in spite of a large appetite. The picture is easily mistaken for generalised anxiety disorder or panic disorder, and occasionally for mania; the clues are the weight loss with a good appetite, the heat intolerance and, in Graves' disease, staring, protruding eyes. In older people, hyperthyroidism can instead produce an "apathetic" picture of fatigue, withdrawal and low mood that passes for depression. Three more endocrine disorders complete Table 10.48. In hyperparathyroidism an overactive parathyroid gland raises the calcium in the blood, and hypercalcaemia causes fatigue, depression, poor concentration and, when severe, psychosis or delirium, along with kidney stones, bone pain and abdominal pain, summed up by generations of medical students as "stones, bones, groans and psychic moans". A phaeochromocytoma is a rare tumour, usually of the adrenal medulla, that releases adrenaline and noradrenaline in bursts; each burst brings a pounding headache, sweating, palpitations, tremor, pallor and a sense of dread with a sharp rise in blood pressure, so like a panic attack that DSM-5-TR uses anxiety disorder due to this tumour as its coding example. And hypoglycaemia, from an insulin-secreting tumour of the pancreas or, far more often, from too much insulin in a person with diabetes, causes episodes of anxiety, sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion and strange behaviour that end within minutes of taking sugar. In 2013 A. G. Unnikrishnan and colleagues tested 5,360 adults in eight cities (Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi, Goa, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad and Kolkata) and found hypothyroidism in 10.95 percent, about one adult in ten; for nearly a third of them (3.47 percent of the whole sample) it had never been detected. Anyone assessing low mood, fatigue or memory complaints in an Indian clinic, especially in a woman or an older adult, should make sure the thyroid has been tested. Exam trap Cushing's syndrome most commonly produces depression, with anxiety and cognitive impairment, and occasionally psychosis (MET Mock 2). "Mania only" is wrong: mania occurs, more often with steroid drugs than with the natural disease, but depression is far commoner. Catatonia (stupor, mutism, posturing, negativism; Chapter 4) can be caused by medical illness, classically by encephalitis such as anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, but it is not the typical picture of Cushing's. A selective loss of smell points elsewhere: to head injury, to a tumour under the frontal lobes, and to the early stages of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases. Do not swap Cushing's (too much cortisol) with Addison's (too little: apathy, fatigue and low mood with low blood pressure and darkened skin). Deficiencies, infections and immune attacks on the brain Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) comes only from foods of animal origin, which matters in a country where many people are lifelong vegetarians. Deficiency, from a vegetarian diet, from pernicious anaemia (an autoimmune failure to absorb the vitamin), from stomach surgery or from long-term use of drugs such as metformin, damages the blood, the spinal cord, the peripheral nerves and the brain. The blood shows a megaloblastic anaemia, with large, immature red cells. The spinal cord suffers subacute combined degeneration , in which the tracts that carry position and vibration sense and the motor tracts degenerate together, so the patient becomes numb, unsteady in the dark and weak. The mind suffers fatigue, irritability, depression, slowed thinking, a reversible dementia and occasionally a psychosis with paranoid delusions and hallucinations, which A. D. Smith called "megaloblastic madness" in 1960. Two clinical points matter most. The neuropsychiatric damage can come before the anaemia, or without it, so a normal blood count does not rule out B12 deficiency; and the damage becomes permanent if treatment with B12 injections is delayed. Folate deficiency, from a poor diet, heavy drinking or drugs such as phenytoin and methotrexate, also causes a megaloblastic anaemia and is associated with depression; in pregnancy it causes neural tube defects in the baby. Pellagra , the deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3), is remembered by its three Ds: dermatitis (a rough, darkened rash on sun-exposed skin, often in a band around the neck), diarrhoea and dementia, with a fourth D, death, if it is not treated. Early on the mental changes are depression, anxiety, irritability and insomnia; later come confusion, delirium and dementia. Pellagra was epidemic in the maize-eating American South until Joseph Goldberger (1874 to 1929) of the United States Public Health Service showed, from 1914 onwards, that it was caused by diet and not by infection. In India it was found among people who lived on jowar (sorghum), and in 1960 Coluthur Gopalan and S. G. Srikantia, working in Hyderabad, proposed that an excess of the amino acid leucine in jowar was partly to blame. Today it is seen mainly in heavy drinkers, in people with malabsorption, and in patients taking the anti-tuberculosis drug isoniazid. DSM-5-TR lists deficiencies of thiamine and niacin among the nutritional causes of neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition. Of all the medical causes of mental illness, one has the most remarkable history. In the nineteenth century the asylums of Europe and America were crowded with patients suffering from general paresis of the insane (general paralysis, or GPI). It began, often in middle age, with a change of personality and poor judgement, sometimes with wildly grandiose delusions (the patient announced that he was a millionaire or an emperor), although a simple, progressive dementia and depression were in fact the commoner pictures. It went on to paralysis and death within a few years. A classic sign was the Argyll Robertson pupil : small, irregular pupils that constrict when the eyes focus on a near object but not when a light is shone into them. The cause, syphilis, was long suspected and long disputed. Key study: from Bayle to the Nobel Prize (1822 to 1927) In 1822 the French physician Antoine-Laurent Bayle (1799 to 1858) described general paralysis as a distinct disease with a characteristic inflammation of the membranes covering the brain. Ninety years later, in 1913, Hideyo Noguchi (1876 to 1928) and J. W. Moore, working at the Rockefeller Institute and a New York state hospital, demonstrated the syphilis spirochaete, Treponema pallidum , in the brains of patients who had died of general paralysis. For the first time a major mental illness had a proven physical cause: a germ. Treatment came from an odd observation, that patients sometimes improved after a fever. In 1917 the Viennese psychiatrist Julius Wagner-Jauregg (1857 to 1940) deliberately infected patients with malaria, letting the fever attack the heat-sensitive spirochaete before curing the malaria with quinine, and many improved. This malaria therapy won him the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1927, the first awarded to a psychiatrist. Penicillin, from the 1940s, made it obsolete. Neurosyphilis has not vanished. It can still present as depression, mania, psychosis or dementia, which is why a blood test for syphilis remains part of the investigation of a new dementia or a late-onset psychosis. The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) also enters the brain early. Section 10.10 describes HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder; in addition, depression is the commonest psychiatric problem in people living with HIV, mania can appear late in the illness, opportunistic infections of the brain can cause delirium and psychosis, and some antiretroviral drugs, efavirenz in particular, cause vivid dreams, insomnia and low mood. Herpes simplex encephalitis attacks the temporal lobes, as it did in Clive Wearing, leaving a dense amnesia and sometimes a change of personality, and other infections common in India, tuberculous meningitis, Japanese encephalitis and cerebral malaria among them, can leave lasting cognitive and behavioural change (ICD-10's postencephalitic syndrome, F07.1). Wilson's disease, an inherited disorder of copper metabolism described by Samuel Alexander Kinnier Wilson in 1912, deserves a line of its own: it can present in adolescence or early adulthood with a change of personality, mood disorder or psychosis, sometimes before the tremor and liver disease are obvious, and the golden-brown Kayser-Fleischer ring at the edge of the cornea gives it away. The immune system can also turn on the brain. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease, commoner in women and usually beginning in young adulthood, in which antibodies attack the skin, joints, kidneys, blood and brain. When it involves the nervous system (neuropsychiatric lupus) it can cause headache, seizures, strokes, cognitive impairment, depression, anxiety, delirium and psychosis. Two things complicate the picture: the high-dose steroids that control lupus can themselves cause mania, depression or psychosis, and a painful, disfiguring chronic illness brings its own psychological burden. The clues are the butterfly rash across the cheeks, joint pains, mouth ulcers, kidney disease and a positive antinuclear antibody test. The newest member of this family was discovered in 2007, and it has changed how psychiatrists think about a first psychosis in a young person. Josep Dalmau and his colleagues in Philadelphia described twelve women, aged 14 to 44, who developed prominent psychiatric symptoms, then memory loss, seizures, abnormal involuntary movements of the face and limbs (dyskinesias), instability of pulse, blood pressure and breathing, and a falling level of consciousness that often needed a ventilator. All had antibodies in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid against the NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) glutamate receptor, and eleven had a teratoma of the ovary, a tumour that contained nerve tissue carrying the same receptor: the immune response against the tumour had turned against the brain. After the tumour was removed and immunotherapy given, eight of the nine patients so treated improved or recovered fully. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is now known to be one of the commonest autoimmune encephalitides. Most patients are young women; many are first seen by a psychiatrist, with agitation, paranoia, hallucinations, mood change or catatonia, before the neurological signs appear; and the illness responds to treatment. A young person with a first psychosis who also has seizures, abnormal movements, catatonia, autonomic instability or an unusually severe reaction to antipsychotic drugs should be tested for it. The American journalist Susannah Cahalan told her own story of the illness in the memoir Brain on Fire . Table 10.49 gathers these conditions, with the neurological ones of Section 10.11.10. Epilepsy, brain injury and the organic personality Epilepsy, a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, is not itself a mental disorder (nor, as Section 10.10 stressed, a neurodegenerative one), but its ties to psychiatry are old and close. Its psychiatric symptoms are described by their timing in relation to the seizures. Ictal symptoms are part of the seizure itself. A focal seizure beginning in the temporal lobe may open with a rising feeling in the stomach, sudden fear, a dreamy state, déjà vu (the feeling that a new experience has happened before) or jamais vu, depersonalisation, or a brief and often unpleasant hallucination of smell or taste, such as burning rubber, before awareness clouds and automatisms such as lip-smacking and fumbling begin. Because such attacks are brief, stereotyped and come out of the blue, they can be mistaken for panic attacks or dissociation. Postictal psychosis is the commonest of the epileptic psychoses, seen in 2 to 7.8 percent of people with epilepsy according to DSM-5-TR. Typically, after a cluster of seizures and a clear interval of hours to a few days, the patient develops delusions, hallucinations and often a disturbance of mood, which last days to weeks. Interictal psychosis occurs between seizures and is not tied to them in time. In 1963 Eliot Slater, A. W. Beard and E. Glithero described these "schizophrenia-like psychoses of epilepsy", which usually arise after many years of temporal lobe epilepsy and resemble paranoid schizophrenia, although emotional warmth tends to be better preserved. Depression, anxiety and suicide are all commoner in people with epilepsy than in the general population, and some antiepileptic drugs add mood and behavioural side effects of their own. A more controversial idea is that of an interictal personality. In 1975 Stephen G. Waxman and Norman Geschwind (1926 to 1984) described a distinctive pattern of behaviour between seizures in many people with temporal lobe epilepsy: altered sexual behaviour (usually reduced interest), intense religiosity, and a tendency to write and draw extensively, sometimes compulsively (hypergraphia). Later accounts added "viscosity", a sticky, long-winded, over-detailed way of talking that makes conversations hard to end. The Geschwind syndrome (the interictal behaviour syndrome) is often quoted, but controlled studies disagree about how specific it is, and it should never be used to stereotype people with epilepsy. A brain tumour can present to a psychiatrist long before it presents to a neurologist, especially when it grows slowly in a "silent" region. Tumours of the frontal lobes (a meningioma growing beneath them is the classic example) cause apathy, disinhibition, poor judgement and a change of personality that can pass for depression, mania or simple bad behaviour, and such a tumour may also destroy the sense of smell. Temporal lobe tumours cause seizures, psychosis and mood change, and tumours near the third ventricle cause amnesia. The warning signs are a new headache that is worse in the morning, vomiting, seizures, focal neurological signs, and a psychiatric illness that does not fit its usual pattern. Head injury brings post-traumatic amnesia; the postconcussional syndrome (ICD-10 F07.2), in which headache, dizziness, fatigue, irritability, poor concentration and memory, insomnia and a reduced tolerance of stress follow a head injury; and, when the frontal and temporal lobes are bruised, a lasting change of personality (Section 10.10 covers traumatic brain injury as a neurocognitive disorder). Stroke brings depression to many survivors; DSM-5-TR notes that depression beginning within days of a stroke is most strongly linked to left frontal lesions, and that the depressive episodes after stroke last 9 to 11 months on average. When brain disease changes a person's character, families say the same thing in every language: "He is not the same man." DSM-5-TR uses almost those words, noting that the person is often described by others as "not himself". ICD-10 calls the condition organic personality disorder (F07.0): a significant change in a person's habitual pattern of behaviour, especially in the expression of emotions, needs and impulses, caused by disease, damage or dysfunction of the brain. Its features include a reduced ability to persevere with goal-directed activity; emotional lability, shallow and unwarranted cheerfulness, or irritability with brief outbursts of anger; apathy; the expression of needs and impulses without regard for consequences or social convention (crude jokes, sexual remarks, overeating, neglect of hygiene); suspiciousness; and changes in the rate and flow of speech. ICD-10 includes the frontal lobe syndrome under this heading. DSM-5-TR's equivalent is personality change due to another medical condition , also coded F07.0: a persistent personality disturbance that is a change from the person's previous pattern (in children, a marked deviation from normal development lasting at least a year), with evidence that a medical condition caused it. It is specified by its predominant feature as the labile, disinhibited, aggressive, apathetic, paranoid, other, combined or unspecified type. The diagnosis is not given when the change is a psychological reaction (a man who becomes dependent on his wife after a head injury because he needs her help) or when it occurs only during a delirium. And unlike the personality disorders of Chapter 11, which are lifelong patterns visible by early adulthood, a personality change due to a medical condition has a definite onset after an illness or injury; ICD-11 calls it secondary personality change. Frontal lobe damage is the classic cause, and it comes in three broad forms, because the prefrontal cortex is not one region but several, each joined in a loop with the basal ganglia and thalamus. Jeffrey L. Cummings, describing these frontal-subcortical circuits in 1993, matched three of them to three behavioural syndromes (Table 10.50). Damage to the orbitofrontal cortex, on the underside of the frontal lobes above the eyes, produces the disinhibited syndrome: the patient is impulsive, tactless, socially inappropriate and emotionally shallow, with a facetious, punning humour that German neurologists called Witzelsucht (joking addiction) and a silly euphoria once called moria . Damage to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex produces the dysexecutive syndrome : the patient cannot plan, organise, shift strategy or think abstractly, and keeps repeating the same response (perseveration), although his memory and intelligence scores may be normal. Damage to the medial frontal cortex and anterior cingulate produces the apathetic syndrome: the patient lacks drive and spontaneity, speaks and moves little and shows no interest in anything ( abulia , a loss of will), and in the extreme lies awake and silent, following people with his eyes, a state called akinetic mutism . The frontal lobe syndrome is the general name for these pictures, which in practice often overlap. Table 10.50 The three frontal lobe syndromes. On 13 September 1848 Phineas Gage (1823 to 1860), a railway construction foreman in Vermont, was tamping explosive powder into a hole in rock when it went off and drove the iron rod, more than a metre long, up through his left cheek and out of the top of his head, destroying much of his left frontal lobe. He survived. His physician, John Martyn Harlow (1819 to 1907), reported in 1868 that the efficient, capable foreman had become fitful, irreverent, profane, impatient of advice and unable to carry through his plans, so that his friends said he was "no longer Gage". The details have been argued over (the historian Malcolm Macmillan showed that many later accounts exaggerated the change, and that Gage later worked for years as a stagecoach driver in Chile), but the case remains the first clear evidence that the frontal lobes govern personality and social conduct. Book 1 and the Physiological book tell it in full; for this chapter, Gage is simply the first well-documented personality change due to another medical condition. Exam trap Organic personality disorder (ICD-10 F07.0) and personality change due to another medical condition (DSM-5-TR) are a change from a previous personality caused by brain disease, not a lifelong personality disorder (Chapter 11). Orbitofrontal damage disinhibits (Witzelsucht, moria); dorsolateral damage disorganises (the dysexecutive syndrome); medial frontal damage demotivates (apathy, abulia, akinetic mutism). Postictal psychosis is the commonest epileptic psychosis; olfactory hallucinations point to temporal lobe epilepsy; and epilepsy itself is neither a mental disorder nor neurodegenerative. The case of Jimmie G., revisited Read Jimmie's story again with Section 10.11 open beside it. Everything Sacks found fits Korsakoff's syndrome: a chronic disorder of memory, caused by thiamine deficiency and seen most often in heavy drinkers, in which the ability to learn new information is severely impaired while alertness, immediate memory and general intelligence are relatively preserved. The core was anterograde amnesia. Information got in but did not stay: the watch, the tie and the glasses under the cover were gone after a minute's chat, the doctor who had shown him the mirror was a stranger two minutes later, and the diary entries in his own handwriting were unrecognisable. Behind it lay a retrograde amnesia with the temporal gradient that Albert, Butters and Levin measured in 1979 and that Ribot's law predicts: his schooldays, his mathematics and his submarine were vivid, but the twenty years of navy service that followed, up to 1965, were gone, so that in 1975 he was sure the year was 1945 and that he was nineteen. What the syndrome leaves alone, he kept. He was alert, warm and attentive, he did excellently on intelligence testing and he could become keenly involved in a game. That is why the word "demented" on his transfer note was wrong: Korsakoff's syndrome is an amnestic syndrome, memory impaired out of proportion to every other cognitive function in clear consciousness, not the global intellectual decline of dementia or the clouded attention of delirium (Sections 10.8 and 10.11.5). The chapter also explains how a clever, competent man came to this. Heavy drinking starves the brain of thiamine in four ways at once (alcohol brings calories without vitamins, cuts absorption from the gut, weakens the liver's store and comes with vomiting and bouts of near starvation), and the neurons that die first lie around the third and fourth ventricles, in the mammillary bodies and the dorsomedial thalamus, so that his was a diencephalic amnesia, not the hippocampal amnesia of Henry Molaison. His sudden illness around Christmas 1970, when he became deliriously excited and confused, fits the course that Victor, Adams and Collins described in 1971, in which the confusion of the acute stage clears to reveal the amnesia it had hidden, although, as Harper's autopsies suggest, many patients reach the chronic stage through repeated small episodes of deficiency that nobody notices. Sacks's nine years of observation, in which Jimmie's memory did not change at all, match Pinel's verdict that thiamine limits further damage but that the dysfunction already acquired is mostly irreversible. Luria's reply anticipated the second aim of care in Section 10.11.4, helping the person to live with the memory that remains. In the garden, where Jimmie took over some of the work and almost never lost his way, he showed the kind of learning that Korsakoff's syndrome spares, the implicit and procedural learning that Claparède's pin first revealed and that grows best by doing the same thing in the same place many times over; in chapel, wholly held and absorbed, he showed what Luria meant. A man does not consist of memory alone. But the cheapest lesson of the case is the one in the Clinical link of Section 10.11.2: a few rupees' worth of thiamine, given in time, can prevent a lifetime of amnesia. Chapter summary 10.1 Drugs, Dependence and Addiction: The Vocabulary and the Manuals. A psychoactive substance alters mood, cognition, perception or behaviour by acting on the brain; use, misuse, hazardous use and harmful use are different things. Intoxication, withdrawal (the mirror image of the drug's effect) and tolerance (metabolic or functional) are the building blocks. Cross-tolerance among alcohol, barbiturates and benzodiazepines is the basis of benzodiazepine detoxification, cross-dependence lets one drug suppress another's withdrawal, sensitisation is reverse tolerance, and physical dependence is not addiction. Edwards and Gross described the alcohol dependence syndrome in 1976. ICD-10's F10 to F19 block runs from .0 acute intoxication to .7 residual and late-onset psychotic disorder, with no "drug abuse". DSM-5 merged abuse and dependence into substance use disorder (2 or more of 11 criteria; mild, moderate, severe; craving added, legal problems dropped). ICD-11 adds the episode of harmful use and places gambling and gaming disorder among the addictive behaviours. In India, alcohol leads, then cannabis and opioids. 10.2 Why People Become Addicted: Reward, Learning, Genes and Personality. Rush and Trotter called habitual drunkenness a disease, Huss coined "alcoholism" (1849), and Jellinek's The Disease Concept of Alcoholism (1960) named five species, of which gamma (loss of control) and delta (inability to abstain) were diseases. Olds and Milner found intracranial self-stimulation (1954), and Di Chiara and Imperato (1988) showed that abused drugs raise dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, the target of the mesolimbic pathway from the ventral tegmental area. Robinson and Berridge separated wanting from liking. Positive and negative reinforcement, Wikler's conditioned withdrawal, Siegel's conditioned tolerance and Solomon and Corbit's opponent process explain much of relapse. Marlatt's balanced-placebo design exposed the power of expectancy, and Kandel's stages (1975) made marijuana the classic gateway. Tobacco captures the largest share of its users. Cloninger described type I and type II alcoholism, heritability is about half, and Khantzian's self-medication hypothesis and Freud's oral fixation complete the picture. 10.3 Alcohol: The Drug, Intoxication, Withdrawal and the Damage Done. The liver turns ethanol into acetaldehyde (alcohol dehydrogenase) and then acetate (aldehyde dehydrogenase) at a roughly constant rate of about one drink an hour. Alcohol is a GABA-A positive modulator, functionally an agonist, and an NMDA antagonist; Steele and Josephs's alcohol myopia explains its varied effects on behaviour. Tolerance is mostly functional, and repeated withdrawals kindle worse ones (Ballenger and Post, 1978). Isbell's "rum fits" (1955) proved that stopping causes withdrawal: tremor from 6 to 24 hours, seizures and alcoholic hallucinosis (mainly auditory, in clear consciousness) at 12 to 48 hours, and delirium tremens, named by Sutton in 1813, at 48 to 72 hours, with clouded consciousness, visual and tactile hallucinations, formication and autonomic overactivity. Heavy drinking also brings depression, morbid jealousy (the Othello syndrome), suicide and damage to almost every organ. The CAGE and AUDIT detect problem drinking, and alcohol is the substance Indians use most. 10.4 Treating Alcohol Use Disorder: Detoxification, Drugs and Staying Sober. Vaillant's natural history (1983) showed a variable course, frequent natural recovery and few relapses after five years of abstinence. Detoxification uses long-acting benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam), relying on cross-tolerance, or lorazepam and oxazepam in liver disease and old age, with thiamine before glucose; Saitz (1994) showed that symptom-triggered dosing with the CIWA-Ar uses less drug, and lorazepam, not phenytoin, prevents repeat withdrawal seizures. Disulfiram, discovered by Hald and Jacobsen (1948), inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase so that acetaldehyde accumulates and drinking brings flushing, nausea and palpitations. Naltrexone, an opioid antagonist, blunts the reward of drinking, and acamprosate modulates glutamate, though it showed no effect in COMBINE (2006). Motivational interviewing, relapse prevention, the community reinforcement approach and Alcoholics Anonymous (founded 1935) work about equally well, as Project MATCH found, and the Sobells' controlled-drinking study was challenged by Pendery and colleagues in 1982. 10.5 Opioids: From Opium to Heroin, and Their Treatment. Opium is the dried latex of Papaver somniferum. Sydenham popularised laudanum, De Quincey wrote the first great account of addiction (1821), Sertürner isolated morphine (about 1804), and heroin was first made by Alder Wright (1874) and sold by Bayer from 1898. Morphine, codeine, thebaine, papaverine and noscapine are natural alkaloids; heroin (diacetylmorphine) is semi-synthetic, made from morphine; methadone, pethidine, fentanyl and tramadol are synthetic. Pert and Snyder found the opiate receptor (1973), and the mu receptor carries euphoria, analgesia, respiratory depression and miosis. Overdose is coma, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression, reversed by naloxone. Withdrawal, the mirror image, brings yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, dilated pupils, piloerection, diarrhoea and aches, but is far less dangerous than alcohol or barbiturate withdrawal. Robins's Vietnam study showed how strongly environment controls use. Treatment combines detoxification (clonidine), Dole and Nyswander's methadone maintenance (1965), the partial agonist buprenorphine and the antagonist naltrexone. 10.6 Stimulants, Tobacco and Caffeine. Niemann named cocaine in 1860; Freud praised it in "Über Coca" (1884) and Koller made it a local anaesthetic, but the drug Freud could not give up was tobacco. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline and amphetamines force their release, and smoked crack and freebase reach the brain fastest. Intoxication brings euphoria and dilated pupils; Connell (1958) showed that amphetamine psychosis can be indistinguishable from paranoid schizophrenia, and formication ("cocaine bugs", Magnan's sign) is its hallmark. Gawin and Kleber (1986) described crash, withdrawal and extinction. MDMA releases serotonin and counts in DSM-5-TR as a hallucinogen. No medicine is approved for stimulant use disorder, and Higgins's vouchers work best. Nicotine acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, Doll and Hill linked smoking to lung cancer, and varenicline, a partial agonist, is the most effective single medicine for stopping. Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors; DSM-5-TR has no caffeine use disorder. 10.7 Cannabis, Hallucinogens, Inhalants and the Sedative-Hypnotics. Cannabis comes as bhang (leaves), ganja (flowering tops, marijuana) and charas (resin, hashish), and the Indian Hemp Drugs Commission (1893 to 1894) found moderate use practically harmless. Mechoulam and Gaoni identified THC (1964), and anandamide followed in 1992. Intoxication brings red eyes, hunger and a fast pulse; DSM-5 added cannabis withdrawal in 2013; McGlothlin and West named the amotivational syndrome (1968); and Andréasson's Swedish conscripts (1987) began the evidence linking heavy use to psychosis. Hofmann synthesised LSD in 1938 and found its effects in 1943; the classic hallucinogens act at 5-HT2A receptors, depend on set and setting and can leave hallucinogen persisting perception disorder. Phencyclidine and ketamine block the NMDA receptor, and inhalants are the drug of the very young and poor. Benzodiazepines increase the frequency and barbiturates the duration of GABA-A channel opening; cross-tolerance makes mixtures with alcohol dangerous, and sedative withdrawal can kill. 10.8 From Organic Brain Syndrome to Neurocognitive Disorder: The Cognitive Domains and Delirium. The old split between organic and functional disorders ended when DSM-IV dropped "organic", and DSM-5 replaced dementia and amnestic disorder with major and mild neurocognitive disorder, keeping delirium; ICD-10 keeps F00 to F09. DSM-5-TR assesses six domains: complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor function and social cognition. Classical deficits pair with functions: dementia with abstraction, amnesia with memory, aphasia, alexia and acalculia with language, apraxia with skilled movement, agnosia with recognition. Delirium, Lipowski's acute brain failure, is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, worse at night, hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed, with asterixis, multifocal myoclonus, carphologia and diffuse EEG slowing (Engel and Romano, 1959). It always has a physical cause, arises from predisposing and precipitating factors (Inouye), is the commonest psychiatric syndrome after cardiac surgery and differs from dementia by its acute onset, fluctuation and clouded attention. 10.9 Alzheimer's Disease and Mild Neurocognitive Disorder. Alzheimer described the plaques and tangles of Auguste Deter, admitted in 1901 at 51, in 1906; Kraepelin named the disease in 1910, and Katzman (1976) argued that presenile and senile forms are one disease. The course is insidious and gradual: episodic memory first, then language, praxis and visuospatial skill. Beta-amyloid plaques outside neurons and tau tangles inside them spread through the Braak stages from the entorhinal cortex, and the loss of the cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert grounds the cholinergic hypothesis, while Hardy and Higgins proposed the amyloid cascade (1992). APP, presenilin 1 and 2 cause early-onset familial disease, Down syndrome brings it early, and APOE e4 raises late-onset risk; cognitive reserve (the Nun Study) delays symptoms. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine ease symptoms, anti-amyloid antibodies slow early disease modestly, and Petersen's mild cognitive impairment (1999) became mild neurocognitive disorder. 10.10 The Other Neurocognitive Disorders. Neurodegenerative diseases kill neurons progressively as misfolded proteins accumulate; epilepsy is not one, and multiple sclerosis is demyelinating. Vascular neurocognitive disorder, the second commonest, has an abrupt, stepwise course with focal signs (Hachinski's multi-infarct dementia; Binswanger's disease). Frontotemporal disorder (Pick, 1892) begins younger with personality change, disinhibition or progressive aphasia and spares memory early. Lewy body disorder brings fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder and dangerous neuroleptic sensitivity, and the one-year rule separates it from Parkinson's disease dementia. Huntington's disease (1872) is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion on chromosome 4 with chorea, caudate atrophy and subcortical dementia; Wexler's Lake Maracaibo families led to the gene (1993). Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rapid prion dementia with myoclonus (Prusiner; Gajdusek's kuru). HIV, brain injury, substances and reversible causes such as normal pressure hydrocephalus complete the list, and the dementias divide into cortical and subcortical. 10.11 Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome, Pseudodementia and Mental Disorders Due to Medical Illness. Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, to which heavy drinkers are especially exposed, damages the neurons around the third and fourth ventricles. Wernicke's encephalopathy (1881) is an acute emergency of confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia with nystagmus, complete in only 16 percent of Harper's autopsy cases and treated with injected thiamine. Korsakoff's syndrome is a chronic amnesia in clear consciousness: severe anterograde and temporally graded retrograde amnesia, confabulation and apathy, with digit span, intelligence and implicit memory (Claparède's pin) spared. Victor, Adams and Collins (1971) showed the two are stages of one disease, with lesions of the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus. Kiloh (1961) gave pseudodementia its modern meaning: depression mimicking dementia, separated by Wells's features, though it can herald true dementia. Cushing's syndrome mainly causes depression and hypothyroidism "myxoedema madness"; B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, lupus, anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, epilepsy and frontal damage (Phineas Gage) complete the medical causes. From the past papers The term psychoactive refers to: (RML 2021) (a) A drug-induced hallucination (b) A particularly active psychopath (c) A drug that alters mood, cognition and/or behaviour (d) The psychology of physical activity Answer: (c) A drug that alters mood, cognition and/or behaviour. A psychoactive substance is any substance that alters mood, cognition, perception, consciousness or behaviour by acting on the central nervous system, which in practice means it must reach the brain (Section 10.1.1). A hallucination is only one possible effect of some such drugs, "active psychopath" is a play on the personality construct of Chapter 11, and the psychology of physical activity is exercise and sport psychology. Cross tolerance is: (Amity 2023) (a) No addiction to any drug (b) Exposure to one drug reduces/changes tolerance to other drugs (c) Both a and b (d) None of the above Answer: (b) Exposure to one drug reduces/changes tolerance to other drugs. Cross-tolerance is tolerance to one drug that carries over to other drugs acting by the same mechanism, as among alcohol, the barbiturates and the benzodiazepines at the GABA-A receptor, which is why chlordiazepoxide can cover alcohol withdrawal (Sections 10.1.2 and 10.7.9). The keyed wording is loose (strictly, exposure to one drug produces tolerance to the other), but it is the only option that describes cross-tolerance; "no addiction to any drug" is meaningless, so (c) fails as well. Substance use disorder has the following patterns EXCEPT: (Amity 2023) (a) Acute intoxication and withdrawal (b) Dependence syndrome (c) Harmful use (d) Drug abuse Answer: (d) Drug abuse. ICD-10's F1 block codes acute intoxication (.0), harmful use (.1), dependence syndrome (.2), withdrawal state (.3) and withdrawal state with delirium (.4), so the first three options are all genuine patterns (Section 10.1.4). "Abuse" was the DSM-III and DSM-IV category, which DSM-5 merged with dependence into substance use disorder; ICD-10's nearest term is harmful use. In the "Gateway Theory" of substance use, which drug is most commonly cited as the primary "gateway" that leads to the use of harder substances like heroin or cocaine? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Alcohol (b) Nicotine (c) Marijuana (d) Ecstasy Answer: (c) Marijuana. In Denise Kandel's sequence (1975), beer or wine came first, then cigarettes or spirits, then marijuana, then other illicit drugs, so marijuana is the stage just before heroin and cocaine and the drug most often cited as the gateway (Section 10.2.4). Alcohol and nicotine come first in the sequence, and the Kandels later argued for nicotine as a biological gateway, but neither is the classic answer; ecstasy is a later club drug, not a gateway at all. Which of the following substances is generally considered to have the highest addictive liability and potential for dependence based on epidemiological and neuropharmacological data? (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Marijuana (b) Alcohol (c) Nicotine (Tobacco) (d) Cocaine Answer: (c) Nicotine (Tobacco). Addictive liability is the proportion of users who become dependent: about a third of everyone who had ever smoked in the National Comorbidity Survey (Anthony, Warner and Kessler, 1994), and about two thirds over a lifetime in NESARC (Lopez-Quintero and colleagues, 2011), more than for any other drug (Section 10.2.5). Cocaine is the tempting option because it is more rewarding per dose and captures its users faster, but a smaller share of them; alcohol captures about one in seven to one in four of its users and marijuana about one in ten. Sigmund Freud stated that alcohol-dependent individuals had fixation in: (RML 2022) (a) Anal stage (b) Oral stage (c) Genital stage (d) Latency stage Answer: (b) Oral stage. Freud linked alcohol dependence, smoking and overeating to fixation at the oral stage, from birth to about 18 months, when pleasure and dependency centre on the mouth (Section 10.2.7). Anal fixation gives the orderly, stingy, obstinate character; latency is a period of dormant drives at which Freud placed no fixations; and the genital stage is mature adult sexuality, the goal of development rather than a fixation point. For which of the following neurotransmitter is Alcohol an agonist? (RML 2022) (a) Serotonin (b) Acetylcholine (c) GABA (d) Endorphins Answer: (c) GABA. Alcohol enhances inhibition at the GABA-A receptor (strictly, it is a positive allosteric modulator, like the benzodiazepines and barbiturates), and its second core action is to block the NMDA glutamate receptor (Section 10.3.2). It does release endorphins and dopamine and enhances one serotonin receptor, but it is not described as a serotonin, acetylcholine or endorphin agonist; nicotine is the acetylcholine (nicotinic) agonist. Which of the following substances is NOT a natural alkaloid compound? (Amity 2023) (a) Morphine (b) Heroin (c) Codeine (d) Papaverine Answer: (b) Heroin. Heroin (diacetylmorphine) does not occur in the poppy: it is semi-synthetic, made by acetylating morphine, and was first made by C. R. Alder Wright in 1874 (Sections 10.5.1 and 10.5.2). Morphine and codeine are natural opium alkaloids, and papaverine, the option students wrongly reject, is a genuine natural alkaloid that simply is not an opioid analgesic. The twin question in the same paper, "which is NOT a natural alkaloid of opium?", has the same answer. Which cognitive disorder is correctly matched with its primary function affected: Dementia, Amnesia, Aphasia, Apraxia? (RML 2025) (a) Dementia - Abstraction; Amnesia - Memory; Aphasia - Language; Apraxia - Motor skills (b) Dementia - Memory; Amnesia - Language; Aphasia - Motor skills; Apraxia - Abstraction (c) Dementia - Motor skills; Amnesia - Memory; Aphasia - Abstraction; Apraxia - Language (d) Dementia - Language; Amnesia - Motor skills; Aphasia - Memory; Apraxia - Abstraction Answer: (a) Dementia - Abstraction; Amnesia - Memory; Aphasia - Language; Apraxia - Motor skills. Dementia is a global decline of intellect that includes abstraction and judgement, amnesia is a disorder of memory, aphasia (with alexia and acalculia) is a disorder of language and symbolic function, and apraxia is the loss of skilled, purposeful movement (Section 10.8.3, Table 10.34). Every wrong option merely shuffles these fixed pairs, and the matching question in the same paper (abstraction, memory, language and motor skills against dementia, amnesia, aphasia and apraxia) uses the same pairs. In Delirium, the motor symptoms may include: i) Asterixis, ii) Multifocal myoclonus, iii) Carphologia, iv) Tone and reflex abnormalities. (Amity 2023) (a) Only ii & iv are correct (b) Only i & iii are correct (c) Only iv is correct (d) All are correct Answer: (d) All are correct. Delirium is a disorder of the whole brain, and its motor signs include asterixis (the flapping tremor of metabolic delirium), multifocal myoclonus, tremor, carphologia (picking at the bedclothes) and changes in tone and reflexes (Section 10.8.5). Any option that leaves one of them out is wrong. Which of the following psychiatric illness is most common after cardiac surgery? (RML 2024) (a) Schizophrenia (b) Delirium (c) Anxiety (d) Depression Answer: (b) Delirium. Delirium is the commonest psychiatric syndrome after cardiac surgery, with a pooled incidence of about 23 percent after open heart surgery, because age, bypass, long anaesthesia, opioids and sleepless nights in intensive care all strike a vulnerable brain at once (Section 10.8.6). Depression and anxiety are also common after heart surgery, but they develop more slowly, over weeks, and schizophrenia is not caused by surgery at all. A key of distinguishing feature of dementia versus delirium is: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Delusions in dementia but not delirium (b) Onset gradual in delirium versus acute in dementia (c) Hallucinations in dementia but not delirium (d) Impaired memory in dementia versus fluctuating consciousness in delirium Answer: (d) Impaired memory in dementia versus fluctuating consciousness in delirium. The cardinal distinction is a fluctuating disturbance of consciousness and attention in delirium against impaired memory with clear consciousness in dementia (Section 10.8.8, Table 10.37). Delusions and hallucinations occur in both, and the onset is acute in delirium and gradual in dementia, the reverse of option (b). A progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by memory impairment, language difficulties, and visuospatial deficits, with an insidious onset and gradual progression, is: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Lewy Body Dementia (b) Vascular Dementia (c) Alzheimer's Disease (d) Frontotemporal Dementia Answer: (c) Alzheimer's Disease. Memory first, then language (aphasia) and visuospatial deficits, with an insidious onset and a smooth, gradual decline, is the signature of Alzheimer's disease (Section 10.9.3). Lewy body dementia fluctuates and brings visual hallucinations and parkinsonism, vascular dementia begins abruptly and worsens in steps with focal signs, and frontotemporal dementia starts younger with personality change or language loss while memory and visuospatial skills are relatively spared. Which of the following condition is related to the deficiency of acetylcholine in the brain? (RML 2022) (a) Senile dementia (b) Atrophy (c) Alzheimer's disease (d) Korsakoff's syndrome Answer: (c) Alzheimer's disease. The defining chemical lesion of Alzheimer's disease is the loss of the cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert, the basis of the cholinergic hypothesis (Bartus, 1982) and of the cholinesterase inhibitors (Sections 10.9.1 and 10.9.4). "Senile dementia" and "atrophy" are descriptions that cover many causes, and Korsakoff's syndrome is a disorder of thiamine deficiency that damages the mammillary bodies and thalamus. Which of the following neurological conditions is NOT classified as a neurodegenerative disorder? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Parkinson's disease (b) Alzheimer's disease (c) Epilepsy (d) Huntington's disease Answer: (c) Epilepsy. In a neurodegenerative disease neurons progressively lose their structure and function and die, usually as a particular protein misfolds and accumulates, and Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and Huntington's diseases are all of this kind (Section 10.10.1). Epilepsy is a paroxysmal disorder of neuronal firing, recurrent seizures generated by chronic brain dysfunction, not a progressive loss of neurons. Lewy body dementia is most characteristically associated with: (IHBAS 2025) (a) Aphasia (b) Auditory hallucinations (c) Visual hallucinations (d) Olfactory loss Answer: (c) Visual hallucinations. Recurrent, well-formed visual hallucinations are a core feature of neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies, alongside fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism (Section 10.10.4). Prominent auditory hallucinations suggest schizophrenia or a mood disorder, aphasia belongs to Alzheimer's disease and the language variants of frontotemporal dementia, and loss of smell is only a supportive, non-specific feature shared with Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases. A patient presents with severe memory deficits, confabulation, and nystagmus, with a history of chronic alcohol use. This clinical picture is classic for: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Alzheimer's Disease (b) Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome (c) Vascular Dementia (d) Frontotemporal Dementia Answer: (b) Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome. Nystagmus is a Wernicke sign, severe memory loss with confabulation is the Korsakoff stage, and chronic drinking is the setting of thiamine deficiency, so the whole picture is Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (Section 10.11.5). Alzheimer's disease has no eye signs and is not caused by drinking, vascular dementia is sudden or stepwise with focal signs, and frontotemporal dementia begins with personality or language change. Which neuropsychological disorder is characterised by severe memory impairment and confusion, often caused by chronic alcohol abuse? (IHBAS 2024) (a) Schizophrenia (b) Korsakoff's syndrome (c) Huntington's disease (d) Multiple sclerosis Answer: (b) Korsakoff's syndrome. When chronic drinking and a disorder of memory appear together in the stem, the answer is Korsakoff's syndrome (strictly, the confusion belongs to the Wernicke stage, but the papers use the name for the whole; Section 10.11.5). Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder, not an amnesic syndrome, Huntington's disease is an inherited degeneration of the caudate nucleus, and multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease; none is caused by alcohol. Chronic alcoholism may result in which amnesic disorder? (RML 2021) (a) Korsakoff's syndrome (b) Alzheimer's disease (c) Pick's disease (d) Parkinson's disease Answer: (a) Korsakoff's syndrome. Korsakoff's syndrome, a chronic amnesia caused by thiamine deficiency in heavy drinkers, is the amnesic syndrome of chronic alcoholism, coded F10.6 in ICD-10 (Sections 10.11.3 to 10.11.5). Alzheimer's disease is not caused by alcohol, Pick's disease, the classic frontotemporal dementia, spares memory early, and Parkinson's disease is a disorder of movement caused by loss of the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra. Which of the following illnesses caused by a long term abuse of alcohol often involves profound retrograde amnesia? (RML 2024) (a) Alzheimer's disease (b) Parkinson's disease (c) Huntington's disease (d) Korsakoff's psychosis Answer: (d) Korsakoff's psychosis. Besides its anterograde amnesia, Korsakoff's syndrome brings a patchy and often extensive retrograde amnesia, sometimes reaching back decades, with a temporal gradient in which recent years are lost most completely (Albert, Butters and Levin, 1979); "psychosis" here is the nineteenth-century word for any serious mental disorder (Section 10.11.3). Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases are not caused by drinking. Which of the following disorder is a common cause of pseudodementia? (RML 2024) (a) Schizophrenia (b) Mania (c) Depression (d) Hypochondriasis Answer: (c) Depression. Pseudodementia, given its modern meaning by Leslie Kiloh in 1961, is cognitive impairment that resembles dementia but is caused by a psychiatric disorder, most often depression, and improves when that disorder is treated (Section 10.11.6). Schizophrenia brings real cognitive deficits but is not the common cause of a reversible, dementia-like state, mania only rarely mimics dementia, and in hypochondriasis the worry about memory comes with normal tested memory. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Korsakoff's syndrome (Korsakoff's psychosis; Sergei Korsakoff, from 1887) is the amnesic disorder of chronic alcoholism: severe anterograde amnesia, a temporally graded and often profound retrograde amnesia, confabulation and apathy, in clear consciousness with digit span and general intelligence preserved; ICD-10 codes it F10.6. asked 3 times Delirium versus dementia : delirium has an acute onset (hours to days), a fluctuating course and a disturbance of attention and awareness (clouded consciousness), and is usually reversible; dementia has an insidious onset, a progressive course and impaired memory with clear consciousness. Hallucinations and delusions occur in both. asked 4 times Dementia chiefly affects abstraction (a global decline), amnesia memory, aphasia (with alexia and acalculia) language, and apraxia skilled purposeful movement (motor skills); agnosia is a failure of recognition. asked 2 times Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is not a natural alkaloid of opium: it is semi-synthetic, made by acetylating morphine (C. R. Alder Wright, 1874). Morphine, codeine, thebaine, papaverine and noscapine are natural; methadone, pethidine, fentanyl and tramadol are synthetic. asked 2 times Severe memory loss, confabulation and nystagmus in a chronic drinker is Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome : Wernicke's encephalopathy (Carl Wernicke, 1881) is the acute stage of confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia with nystagmus, and Korsakoff's syndrome the chronic amnesic stage (Victor, Adams and Collins, 1971, showed they are one disease). asked 2 times Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is caused by deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1) , classically in chronic alcoholism; not vitamin B12 (cobalamin), vitamin D, folate, hypoxia or lead. It is treated at once with high-dose thiamine by injection. asked 2 times A psychoactive substance is a drug that alters mood, cognition, perception or behaviour by acting on the central nervous system. asked once Cross-tolerance : tolerance to one drug extends to other drugs acting by the same mechanism, as among alcohol, barbiturates and benzodiazepines at the GABA-A receptor; it is the basis of benzodiazepine detoxification for alcohol withdrawal. asked once The ICD-10 patterns of F10 to F19 are .0 acute intoxication, .1 harmful use, .2 dependence syndrome, .3 withdrawal state, .4 withdrawal state with delirium, .5 psychotic disorder, .6 amnesic syndrome and .7 residual and late-onset psychotic disorder; "drug abuse" is not one of them (it was a DSM-III and DSM-IV category). asked once In the gateway hypothesis , built on Denise Kandel's stages (1975: beer or wine, cigarettes or spirits, marijuana, other illicit drugs), marijuana is the drug most commonly cited as the gateway to heroin and cocaine, although alcohol and tobacco come first. asked once Nicotine (tobacco) has the highest addictive liability: about a third of all who had ever smoked had become dependent in the National Comorbidity Survey (Anthony, Warner and Kessler, 1994), and about two thirds over a lifetime in NESARC (Lopez-Quintero and colleagues, 2011). asked once Sigmund Freud held that alcohol-dependent people are fixated at the oral stage (birth to about 18 months). asked once Alcohol is a GABA-A agonist (strictly a positive allosteric modulator, like the benzodiazepines and barbiturates) and an NMDA glutamate antagonist; it is not a serotonin, acetylcholine or endorphin agonist. asked once The motor signs of delirium include asterixis (flapping tremor), multifocal myoclonus, tremor, carphologia (picking at the bedclothes) and abnormalities of tone and reflexes: all can occur. asked once Delirium is the commonest psychiatric syndrome after cardiac surgery (a pooled incidence of about 23 percent after open heart surgery). asked once Alzheimer's disease has an insidious onset and gradual progression: episodic memory loss first, then language difficulty (aphasia), apraxia and visuospatial deficits, with amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the brain. asked once Acetylcholine deficiency is the chemical lesion of Alzheimer's disease : loss of the cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert (the cholinergic hypothesis), hence the cholinesterase inhibitors. asked once Epilepsy is not a neurodegenerative disorder (it is a paroxysmal disorder of neuronal firing); Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases, frontotemporal degeneration and ALS are. asked once Neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies : recurrent, well-formed visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder and severe sensitivity to antipsychotics. asked once The common cause of pseudodementia is depression (Leslie Kiloh, 1961): fairly abrupt onset, "I don't know" answers, the patient complains of poor memory, and cognition improves when the depression is treated. asked once Korsakoff's amnesia is diencephalic: bilateral damage to the mammillary bodies and the dorsomedial (mediodorsal) nucleus of the thalamus, not H.M.'s hippocampus. asked once Formication , tactile hallucinations of insects crawling on or under the skin, is most characteristic of stimulant intoxication ("cocaine bugs", Magnan's sign) and of alcohol or sedative withdrawal (delirium tremens). asked once ICD-11 places gaming disorder (6C51), with gambling disorder (6C50), under disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours;
