Exam trap Which is NOT a borderline criterion? "Marked aggression toward animals or persistent rule-breaking before age 15" is conduct disorder, the childhood precursor of antisocial personality disorder (Sections 11.5 and 11.9); frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, recurrent self-harm and identity disturbance are criteria 1, 5 and 3. In the Amity 2023 item, "regular and predictable changes in mood" is keyed as not a cardinal feature, because borderline mood is reactive and unpredictable; but the option "eccentric behaviour marked by oddities in thinking and communication" is not a borderline feature either: it is schizotypal personality disorder (Section 11.2.6). The remaining two options, a lack of a well-defined and stable self-image and an enduring pattern of unstable relationships, are criteria 3 and 2. Two options are strictly correct. Mark the keyed mood option, the direct inversion of criterion 6, and remember why the other is also wrong. Paranoid ideation in borderline personality disorder is only transient and stress-related (criterion 9); pervasive suspiciousness is paranoid personality disorder. Who receives the diagnosis, and what it costs How common is borderline personality disorder? The answer depends on where you look and how you count. DSM-5-TR gives three community figures: 1.4 percent in a probability subsample of the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, 5.9 percent in the much larger National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions, and a median of 2.7 percent across seven epidemiological studies, six of them American (the 2013 edition of DSM-5 gave a median of 1.6 percent, so you will meet both figures). Barlow and Durand settle on about 1 to 2 percent of the general population. In clinical settings the disorder is far more concentrated: about 6 percent of patients in primary care, about 10 percent of people seen in outpatient mental health clinics and about 20 percent of psychiatric inpatients. Those clinical figures explain why the disorder seems so common to clinicians: people with it use services heavily, especially in crises. Is it a disorder of women? In clinical samples, yes, by a wide margin; older editions of the DSM put the proportion of women at about three-quarters. But DSM-5-TR now states plainly that community samples show no difference in prevalence between men and women, and suggests that the clinical excess reflects greater help-seeking by women. Men may also be diverted elsewhere: the clinical characteristics are similar in the two sexes, but men and boys show more externalising behaviour (anger, fights, substance use), which brings them to prisons and addiction services, while women and girls show more internalising behaviour, which brings them to mental health clinics. Diagnostic bias plays a part too. In a study by Leslie Morey and Enrique Ochoa (1989), 291 mental health professionals described a patient with a personality disorder they had recently seen, gave their diagnosis and listed the symptoms; when the diagnoses were checked against the clinicians' own symptom reports, patients who were female, white or poor had been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder more often than the criteria warranted. At what age? Borderline personality disorder was long regarded as a disorder of adults, but in treatment settings adolescents as young as 12 or 13 can meet the full criteria. A personality disorder can be diagnosed under 18 if the features have lasted at least a year (Section 11.1), and borderline personality disorder is the one most often diagnosed in this way; antisocial personality disorder is the only one that can never be diagnosed under 18. Natasha's pattern, by her mother's account, began at about fifteen. The disorder seldom travels alone. DSM-5-TR lists as common companions the depressive and bipolar disorders, substance use disorders, anxiety disorders (panic disorder and social anxiety disorder in particular), eating disorders (notably bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder), post-traumatic stress disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, as well as other personality disorders. In the American national survey, up to two-thirds of people with the disorder had at least one substance use disorder, and Barlow and Durand note that almost a quarter of people with bulimia also have borderline personality disorder. These overlaps matter because each makes the other harder to treat, and because, as Section 11.3.6 shows, some of them are also its chief mimics. The gravest cost is death. Older editions of the manual put the proportion of people with the disorder who die by suicide at 8 to 10 percent. DSM-5-TR reports more recent prospective data: in a sample of hospitalised patients followed for 24 years, around 6 percent died by suicide, against 1.4 percent of a comparison group with other personality disorders. Barlow and Durand also give about 6 percent. Suicide is most likely in people with co-occurring depressive or substance use disorders, and impulsive and antisocial behaviour raise the risk further. The same manual adds a sobering correction to the usual focus on suicide: in people with borderline personality disorder, deaths from other causes, accidents and illness, are more than twice as common as deaths by suicide. And it gives one hopeful number: in a ten-year follow-up, the proportion of patients making suicide attempts fell from 79 percent to 13 percent. What that decline says about the course of the disorder is the subject of Section 11.4. The wider consequences are what one would expect from the criteria: repeated job losses, interrupted education, separations and divorces, and physical damage from self-injury and failed suicide attempts. The childhood histories of people with the disorder more often include physical and sexual abuse, neglect, hostile conflict and early parental loss; whether and how these cause the disorder is again a question for Section 11.4. Finally, culture. DSM-5-TR says that the borderline pattern has been identified in many settings around the world, but it warns that some social contexts (heavy demands for self-affirmation and acceptance, ambiguous or conflictual relations with authority, marked uncertainty during adaptation to a new setting) can produce impulsivity, emotional instability, explosive behaviour and dissociation that look borderline but are transient reactions. It adds that features such as the number of sexual partners, shifting between relationships or substance use must be judged against cultural norms. A clinician in India should be especially careful with the first and the last: what counts as a reckless relationship or a "shifting" sexual life differs sharply between a metropolitan hostel and a small town, and a young woman who defies her family's choice of husband is not, by that fact alone, showing an unstable identity. Clinical link Treat every act of self-harm in a person with borderline personality disorder as a reason for a careful suicide risk assessment, not as "attention-seeking". Ask directly about intent, method, lethality, rescue and what has changed; look for the risk factors that raise the danger (a co-occurring depressive episode, substance use, impulsive and antisocial behaviour, recent loss, discharge from hospital). Chapter 5, Sections 5.8 and 5.9 teach suicide risk and prevention; Book 2, Section 2.7 teaches the risk interview; dialectical behaviour therapy, which was built for exactly this group, is in Book 2, Section 5.8. Borderline or bipolar? Mood that moves by the hour The most consequential mistake in diagnosing borderline personality disorder is to confuse it with a mood disorder, in either direction. A person with borderline personality disorder whose moods change several times a day may be told that she has "rapid-cycling bipolar disorder" and be given a mood stabiliser that does little for her; a person with bipolar II disorder whose hypomanias have been missed may be told that she is "just borderline" and be denied a treatment that would help. The two can also coexist, and DSM-5-TR says that when the criteria for both are met, both should be diagnosed. So how does one tell them apart? Figure 11.6 shows the essential difference, which is a difference of time. Top panel, the borderline mood line: in borderline personality disorder a mildly low baseline is broken by plunges into despair, anger or panic that follow events in relationships and pass within hours; a reunion brings brief relief, not elation. Bottom panel, the bipolar mood line: in bipolar I disorder a manic episode and a depressive episode each last weeks, arise without needing a trigger, and are separated by a return to normal mood. Note the different time scales. Five questions separate the two, and they are worth asking in this order. How long does a mood state last? Borderline shifts last hours, rarely more than a few days; a manic episode lasts at least a week, a hypomanic episode at least four days and a major depressive episode at least two weeks (Chapter 5, Sections 5.1 and 5.4). What sets it off? Borderline shifts are reactive, triggered by events in relationships, often small ones; bipolar episodes may follow stress or lost sleep but often arise on their own and then run a course independent of what happens. What is the mood? Borderline mood moves among anxiety, anger, despair and emptiness; sustained elation, grandiosity, a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts and increased goal-directed energy belong to mania and hypomania, not to borderline personality disorder. What happens in between? In bipolar disorder there are usually periods of normal mood between episodes; in borderline personality disorder the background is a chronic dysphoria with no clean return to well-being. Is it a trait or an episode? Borderline instability is how the person has been since adolescence, in all relationships; bipolar episodes are changes from the person's usual self, with a recognisable beginning and end. Apply the questions to Natasha. Her moods last hours; they follow messages from her boyfriend and her professor; they are despair and fury, never days of elation; she has never gone without sleep full of energy; and the pattern has been there since she was fifteen. The diagnosis is borderline personality disorder. Had her mother reported that at nineteen Natasha had spent a week barely sleeping, talking incessantly, planning to start three businesses and spending her savings on them, a bipolar disorder would also have to be considered, and perhaps both diagnoses given. The same logic applies to depression. Borderline personality disorder very often coexists with major depressive disorder, and a depressive episode can make almost anyone look unstable, empty and hopeless for a few weeks. DSM-5-TR therefore warns against giving an additional diagnosis of borderline personality disorder on the strength of a cross-sectional presentation alone, during a depressive or bipolar episode, without having documented that the pattern began early and has lasted long. A personality disorder is diagnosed from a life history, not from a single interview on a bad day. Exam trap Borderline mood is reactive, brief (hours) and interpersonally triggered ; bipolar episodes are sustained (days to weeks) , often autonomous, and include elation, grandiosity and a decreased need for sleep. "Regular and predictable changes in mood" fits neither borderline personality disorder nor most bipolar disorder; it is the textbook wrong option for borderline personality disorder. Mood that swings several times a day in response to events points towards borderline personality disorder, not towards rapid-cycling bipolar disorder (which counts at least four whole episodes in a year). Both can be diagnosed together. Borderline or another personality disorder? Most examination questions on borderline personality disorder are really questions about its neighbours. The stem describes one disorder; the options describe four. Learning the neighbours is therefore half the work, and DSM-5-TR's own differential diagnosis gives the key distinction for each. Histrionic personality disorder shares attention-seeking, manipulative behaviour and rapidly shifting emotions with borderline personality disorder. The manual says that borderline personality disorder is distinguished by self-destructiveness, angry disruptions in close relationships, and chronic feelings of deep emptiness and loneliness. The histrionic person wants an audience; the borderline person wants not to be left. Dependent personality disorder shares the fear of abandonment, and this is the pair most likely to be confused. The difference lies in the response. When a relationship is threatened, the person with borderline personality disorder reacts with emptiness, rage and demands; the person with dependent personality disorder reacts with increasing appeasement and submissiveness and, if the relationship ends, urgently seeks a replacement who will provide care and support. The dependent person's relationships are also clinging but not stormy, and her identity, though built around being looked after, is not unstable. Narcissistic and paranoid personality disorders share the angry reaction to minor slights. What distinguishes them from borderline personality disorder, in the manual's words, is the relative stability of the self-image and the relative lack of physical self-destructiveness, repeated impulsivity and profound abandonment concerns. The narcissistic person's self is grandiose and stable, however fragile beneath; the borderline person's self is unstable and often bad. Antisocial personality disorder shares manipulation, but the goal differs: the antisocial person manipulates for profit, power or some other material gratification, the borderline person to gain the concern of carers. Schizotypal personality disorder shares paranoid ideas and illusions, but in borderline personality disorder these are more transient, more interpersonally reactive and more responsive to external structure. When the criteria for more than one personality disorder are met, all are diagnosed, and borderline personality disorder co-occurs with each of these. Exam trap Decode the option phrases before you answer. "Detachment and social withdrawal" or "detachment from social relationships and restricted emotion": schizoid. "Social inhibition, fear of rejection, desire for acceptance" : avoidant. "Eccentric beliefs and odd speech without psychosis" : schizotypal. "Paranoid ideation" as the main feature: paranoid. "Obsessive perfectionism" : obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. "Pervasive grandiosity and lack of empathy" : narcissistic. "Excessive attention-seeking, emotional volatility, dramatic behaviour" : histrionic. "Disregard for others' rights, manipulative behaviour" or "manipulation, lack of remorse, irresponsibility": antisocial. "Unstable relationships, impulsive behaviour, fear of abandonment" , "emotional instability and impulsivity", "instability in relationships, self-image and affect with marked impulsivity", and a vignette of idealising and devaluing, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, an unstable self-image and recurrent self-harm: borderline , every time. Borderline, trauma, conduct and the adolescent Four further boundaries come up again and again, two in adults and two in the young. Complex post-traumatic stress disorder. ICD-11's complex PTSD (Chapter 7, Section 7.2.8) adds to the PTSD core three disturbances in self-organisation: affect dysregulation, a persistently negative self-concept and difficulty in relationships. Since many people with borderline personality disorder report childhood trauma, the overlap is large. Chapter 7 gives the distinction: in borderline personality disorder the self-image is unstable and shifting, relationships are clung to and fought over, and repeated self-harm and suicidal behaviour are central; in complex PTSD the self-image is stable and stably negative ("I am worthless"), the person tends to avoid closeness rather than cling to it, and repeated self-harm is not a defining feature (self-destructive behaviour may appear only as one example of affect dysregulation). Trauma is required for complex PTSD but not for borderline personality disorder. A latent class analysis by Marylène Cloitre and her colleagues (2014) found that the two diagnoses picked out largely different groups of patients; they can coexist, and the distinction matters because the treatments differ. Dissociative identity disorder and the other mimics in adults. Borderline personality disorder shares identity disturbance and stress-related dissociation with dissociative identity disorder, but it has no distinct alternate identities and no amnesia between them (Chapter 7, Section 7.6). Separation anxiety disorder in adults shares the fear of losing loved ones, but DSM-5-TR notes that problems of identity, self-direction, interpersonal functioning and impulsivity are central only to borderline personality disorder. Substance use can produce every one of the criteria during intoxication or withdrawal, so the pattern must be seen outside those states. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder shares impulsivity, but begins in childhood with inattention and restlessness and lacks the abandonment fears and identity disturbance; the two often coexist. And a personality change due to another medical condition, after a head injury, for instance, is a change from an earlier, different personality, not a pattern since adolescence. The adolescent and the identity problem. Adolescence is a time of trying on identities, intense friendships and passionate moods, and DSM-5-TR warns that adolescents and young adults with an identity problem , especially when substance use is added, may transiently display behaviour that misleadingly suggests borderline personality disorder. The manual describes such periods as marked by emotional instability, existential dilemmas, uncertainty, anxiety-provoking choices, conflicts about sexual orientation and competing social pressures to decide on a career. An identity problem is tied to a developmental phase and is not a mental disorder. The distinction depends on pervasiveness and duration: Natasha's instability has lasted eight years and shows in every part of her life, which is why the one-year rule for diagnosing a personality disorder under 18 exists. Conduct disorder. Here a practice question asks which feature most reliably distinguishes borderline personality disorder from conduct disorder, and the answer it keys is the right one in spirit: borderline personality disorder is a pattern of instability of identity and affect and fear of abandonment, while conduct disorder is a repetitive and persistent pattern of violating the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate rules, through aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious violations of rules (Section 11.9). Its wrong options are easy to dismiss once the disorders are understood. The two are not identical conditions. Conduct disorder does not "always become" borderline personality disorder; in most young people it remits by adulthood, and when it does persist the adult outcome is antisocial personality disorder, which requires conduct disorder before 15 (Section 11.5), not borderline personality disorder. And neither disorder is "exclusively biological" or "exclusively environmental": both arise from genes acting with adverse environments (Sections 11.4 and 11.9). The keyed answer's ages, however, are a simplification that you should not repeat in a viva. Borderline personality disorder can be diagnosed in adolescents whose features have lasted a year, and conduct disorder can be diagnosed in a person of 18 or older if the criteria for antisocial personality disorder are not met; what truly separates the two is the content of the pattern, not the age of the patient. A list of criteria tells you what to look for, but it does not tell you why a person who longs to be close to others keeps destroying the very relationships she depends on, why her picture of the people around her flips so suddenly from rescuer to betrayer, or what happens to her over the following ten or twenty years. Those are the questions of this section. We begin inside the mind, with the defences that psychoanalysts placed at the centre of the disorder; move to the four modern accounts of where it comes from (psychodynamic, biosocial, attachment and biological); and end with what happens over time and what helps. Keep one person in mind as you read. Rhea is 24 and works at the front desk of a large hotel in Bengaluru. She was brought to a general hospital's emergency department at two in the morning after cutting her forearm, the third time in a year, when her boyfriend did not answer her calls after an argument. In her first session with the clinical psychologist the next week she said, with tears in her eyes, "You are the first person who has ever really listened to me." Three weeks later the psychologist had to move an appointment by a day. That evening Rhea sent a message: "You are exactly like everyone else. You never cared about me. I don't know why I bothered." Those two sentences, a few weeks apart, contain the defence that psychoanalysts consider the signature of the disorder. Splitting: the defence at the centre A defence mechanism is an unconscious mental operation that protects a person from anxiety, shame or other painful feeling by altering her awareness of a wish, a feeling, a fact or a relationship. Sigmund Freud described the first of them; his daughter Anna Freud catalogued them in 1936; and George Eman Vaillant ranked them from immature to mature in 1977 (Book 2, Sections 1.7.3 and 3.4.1 teach all three). What matters here is that defences differ not only in what they do but in how much of the mind they require. Some, such as repression, need a fairly well-integrated self that can push one wish out of awareness while keeping the rest of experience intact. Others work at a more primitive level, before such integration has been achieved. Borderline personality disorder is the disorder of the primitive defences, and the chief of them is splitting. The idea comes from the Viennese-born British analyst Melanie Klein (1882 to 1960), whose theory of the infant mind is taught in Book 2, Section 3.4.4. Klein argued that a baby cannot at first grasp that the mother who feeds and soothes is the same person as the mother who keeps it waiting. It therefore experiences two separate mothers, a wholly good one and a wholly bad one, and keeps them apart so that its rage at the bad one cannot spoil the good. This way of organising experience she called the paranoid-schizoid position. Around the middle of the first year the infant begins to see that the two are one whole person, whom it both loves and hates, and enters the depressive position, which brings the capacity for ambivalence and concern. Klein described the mechanism that keeps the good and bad images apart, splitting, most fully in 1946 in "Notes on some schizoid mechanisms", the same paper that introduced projective identification, which you will meet in the next subsection. Otto F. Kernberg (born 1928) took the concept from Klein and made it the hallmark of what he called borderline personality organisation (described in 1967; Section 11.3 traced this history, and Book 2, Section 3.4.7 teaches the model in full). Splitting , in Kernberg's sense, is the active keeping apart of contradictory images of the self and of other people, so that each person is experienced as all good or all bad and the two images are never brought together into a single realistic picture. The motive, on his account, is protective: the person's loving images of herself and others are fragile, and her hostile images are so charged with aggression that if the two met, the good would be destroyed. Keeping them in separate compartments keeps something good alive, at the cost of never seeing anyone, herself included, as a whole. Listen to how it sounds. The idealised figure is not merely liked; she is "the only one who understands me". When that person disappoints, even slightly, she does not become a good person who made a mistake; she becomes someone who "never cared". The switch is total, and while one image is active the other seems to have no emotional reality at all. If you remind Rhea, on the evening of her angry message, that she called you the first person who ever listened, she may agree that she said it, but the memory carries no weight: "That was before I knew what you were really like." Splitting applies to the self as well. Rhea describes herself on good days as "a completely different person, confident, I can do anything", and on bad days as "rotten inside, evil, I deserve to be hurt", with nothing in between. This rapid alternation of all-good and all-bad images is what drives two of the criteria listed in Section 11.3, the unstable, intense relationships that swing between idealisation and devaluation and the identity disturbance. Splitting must be told apart from two ordinary experiences. The first is ambivalence , holding loving and angry feelings about the same person at the same time ("I'm furious with my mother, and I love her"). Ambivalence is the mature achievement that splitting prevents. The second is ordinary disappointment. Everyone revises their opinion of people; what marks splitting is that the revision is sudden, total and reversible, that it happens to the same people again and again, and that the previous view is not modified but simply switched off. Notice too that splitting, unlike repression, does not hide anything from awareness. Both images are conscious; they are simply never present at the same moment. That is the key to why it is classed as primitive, and to the examiners' favourite question about the disorder. Clinical link Splitting does not stay inside the patient. On a ward or in a team, a patient with borderline personality disorder may idealise one nurse or doctor and denigrate another, and the staff, each seeing only their own half, can begin to quarrel about the patient: one group argues that she is being treated harshly, the other that she is manipulating everyone. This is called staff splitting . The British psychoanalyst Tom Main described how a hospital staff became divided and exhausted over certain patients in a 1957 paper, "The ailment". The remedy is regular team discussion in which every member's view is pooled, so that the team, unlike the patient, holds the good and bad pictures together. Dialectical behaviour therapy builds this in as the weekly consultation team (Book 2, Section 5.8). Exam trap "Borderline personality disorder is most characteristically associated with which primary defence mechanism?" The answer is splitting (Real PYQ 2025; RML 2024). The distractors are real defences that belong elsewhere: repression is the core defence of the neurotic level, sublimation is a mature defence, rationalisation is a disavowing defence used by everyone, regression is a general retreat to earlier ways of functioning under stress, and undoing is the obsessional defence of cancelling one act with another. Splitting goes with Klein (who described it in the infant mind) and Kernberg (who made it the hallmark of borderline organisation). Do not confuse splitting with the Bleulerian "splitting" of mental functions in schizophrenia (Chapter 4), which has nothing to do with all-good and all-bad images. The other primitive defences, and the ones that are not the answer Kernberg described splitting as the centre of a cluster of defences that support it, all of which distort the person's images of self and others rather than hiding a wish from awareness. The most important, and the hardest to grasp, is projective identification , another of Klein's 1946 concepts. In ordinary projection a person attributes his own unacceptable feeling to someone else and then disowns it: the man who is attracted to a colleague accuses her of flirting with him. Projective identification goes further in three ways. The person places an intolerable feeling in another person; she stays emotionally connected to the feeling she has placed there, so she fears and tries to control the other person; and, by the way she behaves, she pressures the other person into actually feeling or acting out what has been projected. It is an interpersonal event, not only a private fantasy. Here is how it happened with Rhea. In the fourth session, furious but unable to own her fury, she accused the psychologist of being irritated with her ("I can see it in your face; you want to get rid of me"). When the psychologist calmly denied it, Rhea became more contemptuous, mocked her qualifications and refused to answer questions, until the psychologist did begin to feel exasperated and a little hostile. At that point Rhea said, almost with relief, "See? You do hate me." The anger had been Rhea's; by the end of the hour it was also, genuinely, the therapist's. This is why therapists who work with borderline patients pay close attention to their own reactions (their countertransference, Book 2, Section 3.3): a sudden, uncharacteristic wish to punish, rescue or get rid of a patient is often information about what the patient cannot bear to feel. The remaining primitive defences are easier. Primitive idealisation exaggerates the goodness and power of another person so that he becomes a perfect protector against a world full of bad figures; it is not admiration but a desperate need for someone who cannot fail. Its inevitable partner is devaluation : when the idealised figure disappoints, he is dropped as worthless, which also protects the person from envying him or depending on him. Omnipotence and omnipotent control describe the patient's sense of magical power over others, who are treated as extensions of herself and must be controlled completely (the ten messages in an hour, the demand that the therapist be reachable at any time). Primitive denial , in Kernberg's special sense, is the mental partner of splitting: the person knows perfectly well that she felt the opposite about someone yesterday, but the knowledge has no emotional force and cannot soften what she feels today. Why, then, are the other famous defences not the answer when an examiner asks about borderline personality disorder? The clearest way to see it is to place every defence on a ladder (Figure 11.7). The ladder shown is the seven-level Defensive Functioning Scale that DSM-IV (1994) printed in its appendix of proposals for further study; Vaillant's four levels (psychotic, immature, neurotic and mature) compress the same idea. The mature defences at the top deal with conflict while keeping reality and feeling largely intact. One step down, the neurotic defences keep a threatening wish or memory out of awareness. Lower still come the defences that distort the image of self and others, and the defences of action and of psychosis at the bottom. Splitting and projective identification sit on the "major image-distorting" rung, below the defences of ordinary neurotic people and above those of psychosis, which is exactly where Kernberg placed borderline organisation: between neurosis and psychosis. more mature: reality and feeling largely intact 1 High adaptive sublimation, suppression, altruism, humour 2 Mental inhibitions repression, undoing, reaction formation, isolation 3 Minor image-distorting idealisation, devaluation, omnipotence 4 Disavowal denial, projection, rationalisation 5 Major image-distorting splitting, projective identification 6 Action acting out, passive aggression, apathetic withdrawal 7 Dysregulation delusional projection, psychotic denial, distortion more primitive: images of self and others, or reality itself, distorted regression: a slide down under stress Figure 11.7 Where the defences sit, after the Defensive Functioning Scale of DSM-IV. Splitting and projective identification (thick outline) lie on the major image-distorting level, below the neurotic and disavowing defences that the distractors name. Regression is not a rung but a movement down the ladder. Now take the distractors one at a time (Table 11.10). Repression , the oldest of Freud's defences, keeps an unacceptable wish, feeling or memory out of consciousness, as when a woman cannot recall how angry she was with her father in the months before he died. It requires a self integrated enough to bury one part of experience while the rest carries on, and Kernberg made it the central defence of the neurotic level of organisation, the opposite pole to splitting. Sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued activity (aggression into competitive sport or surgery, sexual curiosity into art or science) and is one of the mature defences. Rationalisation supplies plausible, acceptable reasons for behaviour whose real motive is unacceptable ("I didn't study because the syllabus was unfair anyway"); everyone uses it, it belongs to the disavowal level, and it is typical of no particular disorder. Regression is a return, under stress, to the ways of behaving of an earlier stage of development: the five-year-old who starts wetting the bed again when a baby brother arrives, or the competent adult who becomes demanding and childlike in a hospital bed. Borderline patients can regress, sometimes dramatically (DSM-5-TR mentions patients who regress severely just after a discussion of how well therapy is going), but regression is a general movement, not the disorder's characteristic defence. Undoing is an act that symbolically cancels an earlier unacceptable thought or act, such as repeatedly touching wood after wishing someone dead, or bringing flowers after an insult; it is the classic defence of obsessional neurosis and sits with repression on the neurotic level. Splitting is the answer to both. If a question asks which defence is also typical of borderline personality disorder, look for projective identification , primitive idealisation , devaluation , omnipotence or primitive denial . Do not confuse projective identification with simple projection : in projection the feeling is attributed to someone else and disowned; in projective identification the person stays connected to it and induces the other person to feel it. Projection on its own is the characteristic defence of paranoid personality (Section 11.2), not of borderline personality. Psychodynamic accounts: conflict or deficit? Why would a person come to rely on splitting long after childhood? The psychodynamic answers fall into two families. A conflict model says that the patient has the capacities a healthy adult has, but that intense, unmanageable feelings (above all aggression) force her to use defences that distort her picture of herself and others. A deficit model says that something needed for normal development was never supplied, so a psychological capacity is simply missing. Kernberg's theory is the great example of the first; Heinz Kohut's and Gerald Adler's are examples of the second. The difference matters, because it decides what the therapist does: a conflict is interpreted, a deficit is repaired. Kernberg's account, introduced in Section 11.3 as a level of personality organisation, is also a theory of cause. He traced borderline organisation to an excess of early aggression, arising either from the child's constitution (an inborn temperament prone to intense negative feeling) or from severe early frustration, neglect or abuse. A child flooded with rage cannot afford to bring her loving and hating images of the same mother together, because the hate would overwhelm the love; so she keeps them apart, and the splitting that Klein thought normal in infancy persists into adult life. Integration never happens, and identity remains diffuse: the adult self is a collection of contradictory part-images rather than a whole. Note that Kernberg's "borderline personality organisation" is broader than DSM's borderline personality disorder: it includes most of the severe personality disorders, among them narcissistic, antisocial and paranoid personality. His treatment, transference-focused psychotherapy, follows directly from the theory: the split images are allowed to appear in the relationship with the therapist and are clarified, confronted and interpreted until they can be integrated (Book 2, Section 3.4.7; its trials are weighed in Book 2, Section 3.11.7). Heinz Kohut (1913 to 1981) founded self psychology , taught in full in Book 2, Section 3.5.1. On his account a child's self becomes firm and continuous only if two needs are met by the people around it, whom he called selfobjects: the need for mirroring , a parent's delighted reflection of the child's worth (the gleam in the mother's eye when the toddler shows off a scribble), and the need for an idealising relationship, a calm, strong parent whose strength the child can borrow. When both fail chronically, the self is left without structure. It is prone to fragmentation (the frightening sense of falling apart), to depletion (an emptiness and deadness), and to rage at the smallest slight. Kohut built the theory to explain the narcissistic personality disorders, and Section 11.6 compares his view of narcissism with Kernberg's. Later clinicians found that it describes borderline experience well too, above all the chronic emptiness and the sense of being nobody, which is why a question about a client who feels "no one" and "empty inside" expects Kohut's answer. The Boston analysts Gerald Adler and Dan H. Buie proposed a second deficit model in a 1979 paper, "Aloneness and borderline psychopathology". They started from the intense, painful aloneness their borderline patients described, a feeling of being utterly alone in the world even when people who cared for them existed. They explained it with a developmental idea borrowed from Jean Piaget 's work on object permanence: by about the end of the second year, most children can call up a comforting image of an absent mother and be soothed by it (evocative memory). Borderline patients, they argued, achieved this capacity only tenuously, after inconsistent care during the toddler's struggle to separate from the mother ( Margaret Mahler 's rapprochement subphase, Book 2, Section 3.4.6), and lose it under stress. When the therapist goes on leave or a partner fails to reply, the patient cannot summon an inner image of someone who cares, and the panic of utter aloneness follows. The theory makes sense of the frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, of the comfort some patients take in a transitional object (a photograph, a soft toy, a voice message replayed), and of the treatment advice that followed from it: be reliably available, prepare the patient for absences, and let her hold on to something of the therapist while the therapist is away. The American psychiatrist John G. Gunderson, whose diagnostic work you met in Section 11.3, reached a similar conclusion in 1996, describing intolerance of aloneness as a core deficit of the disorder. Exam trap A 2024 paper describes a client who feels she is "no one", is "empty inside", fears abandonment and has intense, unstable relationships, and asks what "psychoanalytic object relations theory" blames. The keyed answer, a failure in parental mirroring and idealising, leading to a fragmented self , is strictly Kohut's self psychology , not object relations theory. The two schools are close relatives (both study how early relationships build the self, and many textbooks group them), so choose it, but know the difference: object relations theory proper means Klein, Fairbairn, Winnicott and Kernberg, with their internalised images of self and others (Book 2, Section 3.4.3). The other options are classical Freudian answers: fixation at the oral stage (the psychosexual explanation of dependency, depression and addiction), an unresolved Oedipus complex with castration anxiety (the classical account of neurosis) and harsh superego demands with constant guilt (Freud's account of melancholia and obsessional neurosis, the "Guilty Man" Kohut contrasted with his "Tragic Man"). Linehan's biosocial theory The most influential modern theory of the disorder came not from psychoanalysis but from behaviour therapy. Marsha M. Linehan (1943 to 2026) set out to treat chronically suicidal women at the University of Washington, failed with standard behaviour therapy, and built dialectical behaviour therapy on a theory she published in 1993. Book 2, Section 5.8.2 teaches the theory as the foundation of the therapy; here the question is what it says about the disorder. Linehan's biosocial theory holds that borderline personality disorder is, at root, a disorder of the emotion regulation system. It arises from a transaction, over many years, between a child who is biologically vulnerable to intense emotion and an environment that invalidates her emotional experience. The biological half is emotional vulnerability , which has three parts: high sensitivity (a low threshold, so that a cool tone of voice or a late reply sets off an emotion other people would hardly notice), high reactivity (once triggered, the emotion is extreme and disorganises thinking and action) and a slow return to baseline (the emotion lasts, so that the next trigger arrives before the last one has faded). Linehan's own image is that such people are like patients with third-degree burns over most of the body: they have no emotional skin. The social half is the invalidating environment , a family or setting that responds to the child's account of her inner experience as wrong, exaggerated or unimportant. It dismisses or punishes emotional expression ("Stop crying, it's nothing"), it ignores ordinary distress but responds to extreme distress, so that the child learns that only extremes work, and it makes problems look easier to solve than they are ("If you really wanted to, you would just stop"). Abuse is a severe form of invalidation, but the theory does not require it: an ordinary, well-meaning family can be a poor fit for an unusually sensitive child. The word that matters is transaction . Biology and environment do not simply add together; each changes the other over time (Figure 11.8). A highly reactive infant is hard to soothe; exhausted parents become dismissive; dismissal makes her more distressed; her escalating distress provokes more dismissal, and only her most extreme displays get a response. By adolescence she has learned neither to name her emotions, nor to trust them as valid, nor to soothe them, and she swings between suppressing them (invalidating herself as her family did) and displaying them in extreme forms. Self-harm, on this view, is not "attention-seeking" but a learned way of escaping unbearable emotion: cutting brings rapid relief, so it is negatively reinforced each time it works. Rhea said exactly this: "When I cut, the noise in my head stops." In 2009 Sheila E. Crowell , Theodore P. Beauchaine and Linehan extended the model developmentally, adding trait impulsivity in childhood as a second inherited vulnerability that the invalidating environment can shape into the full disorder. Child: emotional vulnerability high sensitivity, intense reactions, slow return Cries intensely, is slow to settle Tantrums over small things Escalates until someone responds Cuts herself: brief relief "Stop crying, it's nothing" Only extremes get a response "You are making a fuss again" "Just seeking attention" provokes shapes Environment: invalidation feelings dismissed, punished or heeded only at extremes infancy early childhood school years adolescence Outcome: pervasive emotion dysregulation She never learns to name, trust or soothe her own feelings, and swings between suppressing them and extreme displays that finally get a response. Figure 11.8 Linehan's biosocial theory as a transaction over time. Each reaction of a sensitive child provokes an invalidating response (downward arrows), and each response shapes her next, more extreme reaction (diagonal arrows), until emotion dysregulation is established. Neither side alone is enough; the escalating exchange is the cause. How good is the evidence? The emotional half is well supported: people with the disorder report more intense and more variable negative emotions than other people in daily diary studies, and imaging studies (Section 11.4.6) show an overreactive emotional brain. The social half is harder to test, because "invalidation" is usually measured by asking adults to remember their childhoods, and memories coloured by the disorder itself are not neutral evidence. An exploratory study at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru, by J. Alafia and M. Manjula (2020), compared 34 adults with the disorder with matched controls and found more reported emotional abuse and physical punishment in the patients' childhoods, with emotional abuse and negative affect together accounting for 68.4 percent of the variation in their difficulties with emotion regulation: the pattern the theory predicts, in an Indian sample, although with the same reliance on recall. The theory's greatest strength is clinical. It is a no-blame account that families can accept, and every module of dialectical behaviour therapy was built to repair one part of the dysregulation it describes. Exam trap Linehan's theory is biosocial : emotional vulnerability × an invalidating environment , transacting over time, producing emotion dysregulation . Do not confuse it with George Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977), a general framework for all illness (Chapter 1, Section 1.3), or with the general diathesis-stress model. Key words that signal Linehan: "invalidating", "emotion dysregulation", "no emotional skin", "transaction". Key words that signal Kernberg: "splitting", "identity diffusion", "aggression". Key words that signal Kohut: "mirroring", "idealising", "fragmented self". Key words that signal Fonagy and Bateman (next): "mentalising", "reflective function", "psychic equivalence". Attachment and mentalisation Notice how many of the borderline criteria are about closeness: frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, relationships that swing between idealisation and devaluation, anger when a partner or caregiver seems neglectful, paranoid or dissociative episodes "most frequently in response to a real or imagined abandonment", as DSM-5-TR puts it. It was natural to ask whether the disorder grows out of disturbed early attachment, the bond between a child and her caregivers whose study John Bowlby began (Book 2, Section 3.5.5). Researchers have answered with the Adult Attachment Interview, which classifies the way adults talk about their own childhood attachments (Book 2, Section 3.5.6). In 2004 Agrawal, Gunderson and their colleagues reviewed 13 studies of borderline patients that had used the Adult Attachment Interview or other attachment measures. Every study found a strong association between the disorder and insecure attachment, and the most characteristic types were unresolved (disorganised talk about loss or trauma), preoccupied (entangled, angry or anxious absorption in past relationships) and fearful. In each of these types, the reviewers noted, the person longs for intimacy while dreading dependence and rejection, which is the borderline dilemma in a sentence. Peter Fonagy (born 1952) and the British psychiatrist Anthony W. Bateman turned this finding into a theory of the disorder (taught in Book 2, Section 3.5.7, with the treatment it produced). Their key concept is mentalisation , the capacity to understand one's own and other people's behaviour in terms of mental states: feelings, wishes, beliefs and intentions. A child learns to mentalise, they argued, by finding her own mind reflected in the mind of an attuned caregiver, and secure attachment is its natural training ground. In borderline personality disorder the capacity is fragile, and it collapses precisely when the attachment system is switched on hardest: in a quarrel with a partner, at a hint of rejection, in the therapist's absence. When mentalising fails, older, prementalising ways of experiencing the mind take over. In psychic equivalence a feeling is taken as fact ("I feel you hate me, so you do"); in the teleological mode only physical action counts as evidence of a mental state ("If you cared, you would have answered within a minute"), and self-harm may become a way of making invisible pain visible; in the pretend mode thoughts float free of feeling, as in fluent therapy talk that changes nothing. On Saturday night Rhea did not think "he may be asleep, or angry, or his phone may be dead". She knew, with the certainty of psychic equivalence, that he had left her, and she cut. Mentalisation theory is a deficit model, closer to Kohut and to Adler than to Kernberg, and it has two strengths. It links the disorder to a well-developed body of developmental research, and it explains why the symptoms come and go with relationships rather than appearing at random. Its weakness is the one shared by every attachment account: insecure attachment is common in many disorders and in many healthy people, so it can be at most one ingredient among several. Mentalisation (Fonagy and Bateman) is understanding behaviour in terms of mental states; it is not mindfulness , which is non-judgemental attention to the present moment. The three prementalising modes are psychic equivalence , the teleological mode and the pretend mode . Adler and Buie's "aloneness" and Kohut's "fragmented self" are deficit models; Kernberg's is a conflict model. Trauma, genes and the brain For many years one cause dominated public and clinical discussion of the disorder: childhood abuse. The argument rested on studies like the one in the Key-study box, and it was put most forcefully by the American psychiatrist Judith Lewis Herman , whose book Trauma and Recovery (1992) proposed that prolonged, repeated trauma produces a "complex" form of posttraumatic stress disorder, and that many women diagnosed with borderline personality disorder are better understood as survivors of such trauma. The idea has had lasting influence: ICD-11 now includes complex PTSD as a diagnosis in its own right, and telling it apart from borderline personality disorder is a skill taught in Section 11.3 and in Chapter 7. But how strong is the evidence that abuse causes the disorder? Key study: from recalled abuse to documented abuse (Herman 1989; Widom 2009) The retrospective study. In 1989 Herman, J. Christopher Perry and Bessel van der Kolk interviewed 55 patients in depth about major childhood trauma: 21 with borderline personality disorder, 11 with borderline traits and 23 with closely related diagnoses. Of the borderline patients, 81 percent reported such trauma: physical abuse (71 percent), sexual abuse (68 percent) and witnessing serious domestic violence (62 percent). Abuse histories were less common in those with borderline traits and least common in the other patients. The association looked strong, but the design could not show cause: the sample was small, and the trauma was recalled by adults years after the events. The prospective study. Cathy Spatz Widom , Czaja and Joel Paris (2009) started at the other end. They took 500 people whose physical abuse, sexual abuse or neglect in childhood had been documented by courts decades earlier, and 396 demographically similar people without such records, and assessed them for the disorder in adulthood. Significantly more of the abused and neglected group met the criteria, but the risk was clearest for physical abuse and neglect, and it ran partly through other problems in their lives: a parent with alcohol or drug problems, unemployment, leaving school early, drug abuse, depression and PTSD. Conclusion: childhood maltreatment does raise the risk, but through many pathways, and it is neither necessary nor sufficient. That is now the consensus, and DSM-5-TR states it directly: high rates of reported childhood abuse and neglect are found in the disorder, but sexual abuse is neither necessary nor sufficient, and its higher rates in inpatients than in outpatients suggest that it predicts the severity of the disorder as much as the disorder itself. Many people with the disorder report no abuse at all, and most abused children never develop it. Abuse is best seen as one powerful form of the invalidating environment, acting on a child who is already vulnerable. What makes a child vulnerable? Part of the answer is genetic. DSM-5-TR reports that the disorder is about five times more common in the first-degree relatives of people with it than in the general population, and that their relatives also have more substance use, anxiety, depressive and bipolar disorders and antisocial personality disorder. Family studies cannot separate genes from shared upbringing, so twin studies are needed (Chapter 1, Section 1.4). In a Norwegian study of 92 identical and 129 fraternal twin pairs interviewed with a structured diagnostic interview, Svenn Torgersen and his colleagues (2000) estimated the heritability of borderline personality disorder at 0.69, though they warned that their sample was modest and the specific disorders rare. A much larger questionnaire study by Distel and colleagues (2008), covering 5,496 twins in the Netherlands, Belgium and Australia, put the heritability of borderline features at 42 percent in both sexes and in all three countries, with the remaining 58 percent due to environmental influences unique to each twin rather than to the family the twins shared. A fair summary is that genes account for roughly 40 to 70 percent of the variation, depending on the study. What is inherited is probably not the disorder itself but traits beneath it, above all emotional reactivity and impulsivity, which is exactly what the biosocial theory assumed. Those traits have a recognisable brain signature (the anatomy belongs to the Physiological book; only the essentials are given here). In one of the first imaging studies, Donegan and colleagues at Yale (2003) showed pictures of faces to 15 patients with the disorder and 15 controls in a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanner. The patients' left amygdala, the structure that detects threat and generates negative emotion, responded more strongly to emotional faces; and when interviewed afterwards, some patients said they had found even the neutral faces threatening or hard to read. Later studies have repeatedly found the same two-part picture: an overreactive limbic system, centred on the amygdala, and weaker regulation from the prefrontal cortex (especially the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal regions), which normally damps emotion and holds back impulsive action. Low activity of the neurotransmitter serotonin has been linked to impulsive aggression and suicidal behaviour in this and other disorders, which is one reason serotonin-acting drugs were tried (Section 11.4.8). None of these findings is a diagnostic test, and none shows that the brain differences came first rather than developing with the disorder. Exam trap "Childhood sexual abuse causes borderline personality disorder" is the tempting overstatement. The correct answer is that abuse and neglect are common in the histories of people with the disorder and raise the risk , but are neither necessary nor sufficient (DSM-5-TR says this of sexual abuse; the prospective studies show the same for maltreatment in general). The heritability of borderline personality disorder is substantial, about 40 to 70 percent in twin studies, and DSM-5-TR says the disorder is about five times commoner in first-degree relatives. The brain picture is amygdala hyperreactivity with weaker prefrontal control , not a lesion. The course: better than anyone expected For most of the twentieth century, borderline personality disorder was thought to be close to a life sentence. A personality disorder is by definition enduring, the patients were among the most troubled in any service, and clinicians who met the same people in crisis year after year concluded that they never changed. The trouble with that impression is that clinicians mostly see the patients who are still ill; those who get better stop coming. Only a prospective study, which follows a whole group from the start and keeps counting, can say what really happens. Two such studies, both begun in the 1990s, transformed the picture. Key study: the McLean and CLPS follow-ups (2003 to 2012) The McLean Study of Adult Development. Mary C. Zanarini and her colleagues at McLean Hospital near Boston recruited 290 inpatients who met two sets of criteria for borderline personality disorder (DSM-III-R and the Revised Diagnostic Interview for Borderlines), with 72 inpatients who had other personality disorders as a comparison group, and reinterviewed them every two years. At six years (2003), 34.5 percent met the criteria for remission at two years, 49.4 percent at four years and 68.6 percent at six years, and only 5.9 percent of those who remitted relapsed. Impulsive symptoms such as self-harm resolved fastest; affective symptoms such as anger, emptiness and dysphoria were the most chronic. At ten years (2010), 93 percent had had a remission lasting at least two years and 86 percent one lasting at least four; of those with a four-year remission only 15 percent had a recurrence. But only 50 percent had achieved recovery , defined as remission together with good social and vocational functioning, and a third of those lost it again. At sixteen years (2012), remission had reached 78 to 99 percent, depending on how long it had to last, while recovery reached only 40 to 60 percent. The Collaborative Longitudinal Personality Disorders Study (CLPS). John Gunderson, Andrew E. Skodol and colleagues followed treatment-seeking patients aged 18 to 45 from 19 clinical settings in four cities of the north-eastern United States: 175 with borderline personality disorder, 312 with Cluster C disorders and 95 with major depression but no personality disorder. Over ten years (2011), 85 percent of the borderline patients remitted and only 12 percent relapsed, a lower relapse rate than in major depression. Social functioning, however, remained severely impaired and improved only modestly. Conclusion: the symptoms of the disorder usually remit and rarely return; a satisfying working and social life is much harder to win. Criticism: remission was defined by falling below the diagnostic threshold, so a "remitted" patient may still be quite unwell, and most patients were receiving treatment, so the studies describe treated rather than natural course. DSM-5-TR now summarises the same evidence: stable remissions lasting one to eight years are very common; impulsive symptoms remit most rapidly and affective symptoms much more slowly; and recovery, symptomatic remission with good psychosocial functioning, is harder to achieve and less stable, with failure to recover linked to living on disability benefits and to poor physical health. The pattern makes sense of the theories above. The behaviours that define the diagnosis (self-harm, impulsive acts, frantic crises) are what fade first, partly through treatment and partly through ordinary maturation, while the underlying temperament, an emotional sensitivity and a lonely, empty sense of self, changes slowly. For Rhea and her family, this is the most useful single fact in this chapter: the disorder is not a life sentence, and most people with it will one day no longer meet its criteria. For her clinicians, the lesson is that treatment must aim beyond the absence of crises, towards work, friendship and a life worth living. Section 11.3 gives the figures for suicide, which remains the gravest risk along the way. Exam trap "Borderline personality disorder is chronic and does not improve" is false. In the McLean study 93 percent had a two-year remission within ten years, and in CLPS 85 percent remitted, with low relapse rates. What lags is recovery of social and vocational functioning (about half at ten years). Of the symptoms, impulsive ones remit fastest and affective ones (anger, emptiness, dysphoria) slowest. The McLean Study of Adult Development is Zanarini's; CLPS is the multi-site study led by Gunderson and Skodol. Treatment Treatment of borderline personality disorder rests on one principle that every guideline repeats: psychological treatment comes first, and medication plays a supporting role at most. The specialised psychotherapies are taught in Book 2, so here they need only be named, placed and weighed. Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT), Linehan's treatment, combines weekly individual therapy, a weekly skills group (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness), telephone coaching in crises and a consultation team for the therapists; it has more randomised trials than any other therapy for the disorder and its clearest effect is on self-harm and suicide attempts (Book 2, Section 5.8). Mentalisation-based treatment (MBT), Bateman and Fonagy's, combines individual and group sessions over about eighteen months to strengthen mentalising (Book 2, Section 3.5.7). Transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP), Kernberg's, works twice weekly within a firm treatment contract to integrate the split images (Book 2, Section 3.4.7). Schema therapy , developed by Jeffrey Young , works on early maladaptive schemas and the rapidly shifting schema modes of borderline patients, and in a Dutch trial in 2006 it outperformed TFP (Book 2, Section 5.7). Two less intensive options complete the list. STEPPS (Systems Training for Emotional Predictability and Problem Solving), from Nancee Blum , Donald W. Black and colleagues at the University of Iowa, is a 20-week manual-based group programme that adds cognitive-behavioural skills training to the patient's usual care and teaches family members and friends how to respond. Good psychiatric management (also called general psychiatric management), developed by Gunderson, is a structured, less intensive generalist approach built on case management, psychoeducation about the disorder and realistic goals; in a Toronto trial in 2009 it did as well as DBT. What do the trials show overall? The 2020 Cochrane review found that disorder-specific psychotherapies reduce the severity of the disorder compared with usual treatment, with DBT and MBT the most studied, but rated much of the evidence as low in certainty; and none of the specialised therapies is clearly better than the others (Book 2, Section 3.11.7 weighs the trials). The more striking lesson is that well-organised generalist care also does surprisingly well. What the successful treatments share is a clear structure, a coherent model that patient and clinician both understand, a consistent team, steady attention to the relationship, and active work on self-harm. The NICE guideline for England and Wales (2009) added a warning that matches this lesson: brief psychological interventions of less than three months should not be used specifically for the disorder. Medication is a different story. No drug is licensed for borderline personality disorder itself. In 2001 the American Psychiatric Association's practice guideline recommended a symptom-targeted approach: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for affective dysregulation and impulsive behaviour, low-dose antipsychotics for the transient paranoid and dissociative symptoms, and mood stabilisers as additions. That advice has not survived: the APA's revised guideline of 2024 found no evidence that any drug treats the core symptoms, and suggests only short-term use aimed at a specific, measurable target symptom, alongside psychotherapy. Larger and better trials have been disappointing (Table 11.12). The 2010 Cochrane review found some benefit on particular symptoms for second-generation antipsychotics and mood stabilisers, but the trials were small and short. When a well-powered British trial tested the mood stabiliser lamotrigine in 276 patients ( Mike Crawford and colleagues, 2018), it was no better than placebo at one year on borderline symptoms or on any other outcome. The 2022 Cochrane update, with 18 more trials than the 2010 version, concluded that no medication seems effective in treating the core pathology of the disorder. NICE was blunt even in 2009: drug treatment should not be used specifically for the disorder or for its individual symptoms (repeated self-harm, emotional instability, risk-taking, transient psychotic symptoms); antipsychotics should not be used for medium- or long-term treatment; drugs may be used for coexisting conditions such as major depression; and in a crisis a sedative may be used cautiously for no longer than a week. Polypharmacy is common and dangerous: a patient who has been given a new drug at each crisis may end up on four or five, with weight gain, sedation and a large supply of tablets for an overdose. And every prescription carries a message. A patient told that her distress is a chemical problem to be fixed by a tablet may lose the sense that she can learn to manage it herself, which is the central aim of the psychological treatments. Crises and self-harm are where treatment is most often won or lost. The guideline approach is to plan ahead with the patient: a written crisis plan saying what she will do, whom she will call and what the service will offer; brief, goal-directed hospital admission only when risk cannot be managed in the community, with its length and purpose agreed in advance; and a calm, non-judgemental response to self-harm that treats it as a behaviour with functions to be understood, not as manipulation. Long, open-ended admissions tend to backfire, because they remove the patient from the life she has to learn to manage and can reward escalation. Clinical link Patients with this disorder provoke strong reactions in clinicians: the wish to rescue during idealisation, hurt and anger during devaluation, and exhaustion when crises repeat. These reactions are the ordinary consequences of splitting and projective identification, and acting on them (becoming the patient's special saviour, or quietly discharging her as "manipulative") repeats her history of unpredictable care. The protections are a clear treatment frame agreed at the start, consistent limits explained rather than imposed, and regular supervision or a consultation team. Avoid the word "attention-seeking" in notes and conversations: it is inaccurate (the behaviour usually regulates unbearable emotion) and it predicts worse care. Exam trap The first-line treatment of borderline personality disorder is psychological , not pharmacological. No drug is licensed for the disorder; NICE (2009) advised that drugs should not be used specifically for it or for its individual symptoms, that antipsychotics should not be used for medium- or long-term treatment, and that a sedative in a crisis should be used for no longer than a week. Match the therapy to its developer: DBT , Linehan; MBT , Bateman and Fonagy; TFP , Kernberg (with Clarkin and Yeomans); schema therapy , Young; STEPPS , Blum and Black; good psychiatric management , Gunderson. Borderline personality disorder in India Most Indian hospitals still record the disorder under ICD-10, as emotionally unstable personality disorder, borderline type (F60.31), and research on it in India is thin. A 2020 review by Choudhary and Gupta concluded that Indian research rests on a few case reports and small samples, and argued that culture shapes all three of the disorder's core domains, emotion, relationships and the self. Indian clinicians must judge, for example, whether a young woman's conflict with her family over a relationship or a career reflects a disorder of identity or a clash between her own choices and family expectations, and whether outbursts of anger in a crowded joint family are a fixed pattern or a reaction to a situation. Screening studies give large numbers, but they must be read carefully: in a 2019 survey of 500 medical and engineering students in Manipal, 15.2 percent scored above the cut-off on a self-report screening questionnaire for the disorder, a figure that reflects the screen's low threshold rather than the true rate of the diagnosed disorder. In practice the disorder usually reaches services through self-harm. A young person is brought to a general hospital emergency department after cutting or an overdose, often following a quarrel with a partner or parents, and the psychiatric consultation that follows is the first chance to recognise the pattern behind the act. Since the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (section 115), a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and is not to be tried and punished, and the government has a duty to provide care, treatment and rehabilitation (Chapter 5 covers suicide in India). Men are recognised less often. Mihir, a 27-year-old sales executive, was brought by his parents for "anger and drinking"; only on careful history did the pattern emerge of terror of being left, rapid idealisation and hatred of girlfriends, impulsive spending and repeated cutting of his thighs, hidden from his family. Attitudes of professionals matter too: a 2025 survey of 189 mental health staff in Jammu and Kashmir found that attitudes to patients with the disorder varied by profession, with psychology and nursing interns the most positive and psychiatrists the least. Full DBT or MBT programmes need a trained team and many hours of staff time each week, which few public services anywhere can provide, so most Indian patients receive generalist care; this is one reason the good results of structured generalist treatments such as good psychiatric management matter so much in low-resource settings. Indian context In Indian families, invalidation often comes in loving, ordinary words: "Don't cry, people will see", "What is there to be sad about?", "Just adjust" (Book 2, Section 5.8.2). Involving the family is usually essential, because most young adults live with their parents and depend on them for treatment. Psychoeducation that presents the disorder as a problem of emotional sensitivity and learnable skills, rather than as bad character or "drama", reduces blame on both sides and makes the family an ally of treatment. 11.5 Antisocial Personality Disorder and Psychopathy Medium yield · 4 Qs Jayant is 29, well dressed, relaxed and courteous. He has been referred by a magistrate's court in Nagpur for a psychological assessment after his third arrest for cheating: over two years he persuaded several retired schoolteachers to hand over their savings for flats in a housing project that did not exist, using two different names. He shakes the psychologist's hand warmly, compliments her on her office and explains, in fluent and plausible detail, that he has "always been misunderstood". The victims, he says, "wanted easy money; I only gave them a story, and anyway they will get some of it back." His work history is a list of jobs left after a few weeks. He has been in several fights, has two convictions for drunken, reckless driving and owes money to almost everyone he knows. His mother, interviewed separately, adds what he left out: he stole from her purse at nine, was suspended from school at twelve for bullying and threatening younger boys, regularly skipped school from the age of eleven, set fire to a neighbour's haystack at thirteen "to see it burn", and twice ran away from home overnight at fourteen. Asked how he feels about the teachers, Jayant says, "Of course I feel bad," in exactly the tone he used to praise the office. Is Jayant bad, or is he ill? The question is older than psychiatry, and the answers given to it over two centuries explain why there are now two overlapping concepts, antisocial personality disorder and psychopathy, and why examiners keep asking you to tell them apart. Madness without delusion: Pinel, Rush and Prichard At the end of the eighteenth century, madness meant a disorder of the intellect: delusions, hallucinations, confused reasoning. Philippe Pinel (1745 to 1826), the French physician remembered for unchaining patients at the Bicêtre and the Salpêtrière (Book 2, Section 1.3), found that this definition did not fit some of the men in his care. In his Traité médico-philosophique sur l'aliénation mentale (1801) he wrote that he had shared the view of the English philosopher John Locke that insanity is inseparable from disordered reasoning, until at the Bicêtre he was "not a little surprised" to find patients who showed no disturbance of understanding but were dominated by "a kind of instinct of fury, as if only their affective faculties had been damaged". He called the condition manie sans délire , mania without delirium or, as it is often translated, mania without delusion (in French, délire means a disorder of the intellect, not only delirium in the modern sense). His first example is a story you will not forget. A single child was brought up by a weak and indulgent mother who gave in to every whim. As he grew older his impulses grew stronger; anyone who opposed him was attacked, and if a dog, a sheep or a horse annoyed him, he had it killed on the spot. At fairs he lost his temper and came home covered in blood. Yet when calm he was full of good sense: as an adult he ran a large estate competently, fulfilled his duties in society and was known for his charity to the poor. Lawsuits and payments of damages had been the only consequences of his violence until one day a woman swore at him and he threw her down a well. At his trial, witnesses described his long history of rages, and he was sentenced to confinement in the asylum at the Bicêtre. Notice what Pinel was describing, and what he was not. His next case was a mechanic who suffered attacks of bloodthirsty fury, warned his beloved wife to flee before one of them, was "full of remorse" and tried to kill himself with a cobbler's knife. Manie sans délire was therefore a broad category of impulsive, emotional violence with intact reasoning, not specifically the remorseless, callous person we now call a psychopath. Its importance is that it was the first medical claim that a person could be disordered in emotion and conduct while sane in intellect. The idea spread on both sides of the Atlantic. In the United States Benjamin Rush (1746 to 1813), in his Medical Inquiries and Observations upon the Diseases of the Mind (1812), described people whose moral faculties alone seemed deranged. In England James Cowles Prichard (1786 to 1848) gave the condition its lasting name in A Treatise on Insanity and Other Disorders Affecting the Mind (1835). Moral insanity , he wrote, is "madness consisting in a morbid perversion of the natural feelings, affections, inclinations, temper, habits, moral dispositions, and natural impulses, without any remarkable disorder or defect of the intellect or knowing and reasoning faculties, and particularly without any insane illusion or hallucination". The word "moral" needs care. In Prichard's day it meant emotional and dispositional as much as ethical, the same sense as in Pinel's "moral treatment", and his category was wide enough to include what we would now call mood disorders and eccentricity. Only gradually did "moral insanity" narrow towards the lack of conscience. It had little effect in the courts, where the M'Naghten rules of 1843 tied the insanity defence to a defect of reason that moral insanity, by definition, lacked (Book 2, Section 10.9.3). Two more strands complete the nineteenth-century picture. The Italian physician Cesare Lombroso (1835 to 1909) argued in L'uomo delinquente (1876) that some criminals are "born criminals", evolutionary throwbacks recognisable by physical stigmata such as a sloping forehead or large jaw; the theory did not survive careful measurement, but it fixed the idea of a constitutional criminal type. And in German psychiatry the word "psychopathic" took on a meaning very different from today's. Julius Koch's "psychopathic inferiorities" (1891), Emil Kraepelin's psychopathic personalities and Kurt Schneider's Psychopathic Personalities (1923) used "psychopathic" for abnormal personality of every kind, the depressive, insecure and asthenic as well as the callous; Section 11.1 tells that history. When you meet "psychopathic" in a text before about 1940, read it as "personality disordered", not as "psychopath" in Cleckley's sense. Exam trap Match the term to its author and year. Moral insanity as a named diagnosis: Prichard, 1835 (not Pinel; Rush and others had written of derangement of the moral faculties earlier, in a looser sense). Born criminal : Lombroso, 1876 .
