Can coexist: both are then recorded 23 to 32 percent of one treated OCD sample had OCPD The two can occur together. When the criteria for both are met, DSM-5-TR says both diagnoses should be recorded, and in one American study of 214 treatment-seeking adults with OCD, comorbid OCPD was found in 23 to 32 percent of them over the course of follow-up. But DSM-5-TR also notes that the majority of people with OCD do not have a pattern that meets criteria for OCPD, and Barlow and Durand describe OCPD as only distantly related to OCD. The shared name misleads more than it informs. Exam trap Compared with OCD, OCPD is ego-syntonic with limited insight . Reject the distractors one by one. " Ego-dystonic and accompanied by significant insight " describes OCD (with good or fair insight), the reverse of OCPD. " Only present during manic episodes " is wrong for any personality disorder, which is an enduring pattern, not an episode; a manic person's expansive overactivity is not OCPD. " Acute in onset and rapidly remitting " contradicts the definition of every personality disorder: stable, long-standing and beginning by adolescence or early adulthood. And do not let the shared name fool you: OCPD has no true obsessions or compulsions , and when both disorders are present, both are diagnosed. Cluster C compared: does it hold together, and what helps? Table 11.24 brings the three anxious or fearful disorders together, with the fear at the centre of each, the strategy each uses against it and what that strategy costs, the ICD-10 name, and the look-alike it is most often confused with. Table 11.24 The Cluster C personality disorders (PD) compared. Disorder (criteria) Core fear Strategy and its cost ICD-10 name Main look-alike Avoidant (4 of 7) Rejection, humiliation, being found inadequate Withdraws until sure of acceptance; loneliness and a narrowed life Anxious (avoidant), F60.6 Schizoid PD (no wish for people); social anxiety disorder Dependent (5 of 8) Being left to care for oneself Clings and submits; loses initiative, may tolerate mistreatment Dependent, F60.7 Borderline PD (rage, not appeasement); histrionic PD Obsessive-compulsive (4 of 8) Error, disorder, losing control Controls tasks, people, money; loses flexibility and efficiency Anankastic, F60.5 OCD (true obsessions, ego-dystonic); narcissistic perfectionism Read across the rows and the family resemblance is clear: in each disorder anxiety drives a strategy that brings short-term relief and long-term cost. But is the resemblance more than skin deep? The best test comes from the Norwegian twin studies. In 2007 Ted Reichborn-Kjennerud and his colleagues, Kendler and Torgersen among them, interviewed 1,386 young adult twin pairs from the Norwegian Institute of Public Health Twin Panel and measured the three Cluster C disorders as dimensions, by counting criteria. The heritability of each was modest, between 27 and 35 percent, and for dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder much lower than the small earlier study had suggested; there was no effect of shared family environment. A common genetic factor accounted for 83 percent of the genetic variance in avoidant personality disorder and 48 percent in dependent personality disorder, but only 15 percent in OCPD. OCPD, the authors concluded, is largely distinct in its causes from the other two, and the DSM-IV Cluster C construct is not supported in its present form. A year later Kendler's broader analysis of all ten disorders found that genetic risk does not follow the A, B and C clusters at all, although environmental risk largely does, with one telling exception: the environmental factors behind OCPD grouped with those of Cluster B. Avoidant personality disorder, meanwhile, shared a genetic factor with schizoid personality disorder that looked like introversion. So the "anxious or fearful" label describes how these people appear, not a shared cause, which is one of the arguments Section 11.8 uses for abandoning categories altogether. In DSM-5's Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD), avoidant and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder survive among the six retained types while dependent personality disorder does not, and in ICD-11 only OCPD has a direct descendant, the anankastia trait domain. Treatment for Cluster C is better studied than for most personality disorders, and the news is reasonably good. The psychological treatments themselves belong to Book 2: cognitive and cognitive behavioural therapy in Book 2, Chapter 5 (with the Clark and Wells model of social anxiety in Book 2, Section 5.6.4), and schema therapy in Book 2, Section 5.7. What matters here is what the trials show. Key study: dynamic versus cognitive therapy for Cluster C (Svartberg, Stiles and Seltzer, 2004) Martin Svartberg and his colleagues in Norway randomly assigned 50 outpatients who had one or more Cluster C personality disorders, and no other personality disorder, to 40 weekly sessions of either short-term dynamic psychotherapy or cognitive therapy. Most also had anxiety or depressive disorders. The therapists were experienced full-time clinicians following manuals under supervision, and symptoms, interpersonal problems and core personality pathology were measured repeatedly during treatment and over two years afterwards. Both groups improved significantly on every measure, and kept improving after treatment ended. There were no significant differences between the two therapies at any point. Two years after treatment, 54 percent of the dynamic therapy patients and 42 percent of the cognitive therapy patients had recovered symptomatically, and about 40 percent in both groups had recovered in interpersonal problems and personality functioning. The authors concluded that both therapies have a place, and that factors other than the type of therapy may better predict who does well. The limitation is size: with 50 patients, a modest real difference between the therapies could have been missed. For avoidant personality disorder specifically, a Dutch trial by Paul M. G. Emmelkamp and colleagues (2006) randomly assigned 62 patients to 20 weekly sessions of brief dynamic therapy, 20 weekly sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy, or a waiting list. Cognitive behavioural therapy did better than both the waiting list and brief dynamic therapy on several measures, and the gains were maintained at follow-up; brief dynamic therapy did no better than waiting. Because avoidant personality disorder and social anxiety disorder overlap so heavily, the same exposure-based and cognitive methods are used for both, and the strength of the therapeutic alliance appears to be an important predictor of success. The largest trial was of schema therapy. Lotte L. M. Bamelis , Arnoud Arntz and their colleagues (2014) treated 323 patients with Cluster C, paranoid, histrionic or narcissistic personality disorder in twelve Dutch mental health institutes, assigning them to 50 sessions of schema therapy, to treatment as usual, or to clarification-oriented psychotherapy. Three years after treatment began, judged by interviewers who did not know which treatment each patient had received, significantly more of the schema therapy patients had recovered from their personality disorder than in either other group. They also dropped out less often than patients given treatment as usual, and at follow-up had less depression and better general and social functioning. Results did not differ by diagnosis. Drugs play a smaller part. No medicine is approved for any personality disorder as such. When avoidant personality disorder occurs with social anxiety disorder, clinicians use the medicines that work for social anxiety, chiefly the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) (Chapter 6, Section 6.9.4), but trials in avoidant personality disorder itself are few and have not established a drug treatment for it. For dependent personality disorder and OCPD, medication is used, if at all, for an accompanying depression or anxiety disorder; the evidence for any drug acting on OCPD itself is thin, which is one more practical reason not to confuse it with OCD, where SSRIs are a first-line treatment. Clinical link Each Cluster C pattern recreates itself in the therapy room. The dependent client is the "ideal patient": punctual, grateful, eager to be told what to do, and that very eagerness defeats the goal of greater independence. The therapist must resist becoming the new caretaker and hand decisions back to the client a little at a time. The avoidant client watches the therapist's face for disapproval and may silently drop out after one session that felt critical, so the alliance must be built carefully and checked openly ("Was there anything today that felt uncomfortable?"). The obsessive-compulsive client may argue over the details of the treatment plan, intellectualise rather than feel, and do homework so thoroughly that it is never finished; the work is often to practise "good enough". Exam trap Cluster C is anxious or fearful : avoidant (4 of 7), dependent (5 of 8) and obsessive-compulsive (4 of 8). It once had a fourth member, passive-aggressive personality disorder (DSM-III and DSM-III-R), moved to an appendix as "negativistic" in DSM-IV. The ICD-10 names are anxious (avoidant) F60.6, dependent F60.7 and anankastic F60.5. Twin studies show OCPD to be largely distinct in its causes from avoidant and dependent PD, so the cluster is descriptive, not causal. In the DSM-5 Alternative Model, avoidant and obsessive-compulsive PD are retained; dependent PD is not. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Antisocial, borderline, histrionic and narcissistic personality disorders form Cluster , described as dramatic, emotional or erratic. A style of speech that is excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail is a criterion of personality disorder. The DSM-5 core triad of narcissistic personality disorder is grandiosity, need for admiration and lack of . People with narcissistic personality disorder often have some cognitive empathy but lack empathy. Gabbard (1989) described two subtypes of narcissistic personality disorder, the oblivious and the . In ICD-10, narcissistic personality disorder has no code of its own and is listed by name under F60.8, other personality disorders. Brummelman and colleagues (2015) found that narcissism in children was predicted by parental , not by a lack of parental warmth. The avoidant person wants relationships but fears rejection; the person has little wish for relationships at all. Faced with abandonment, the borderline person reacts with emptiness and rage, whereas the dependent person reacts with and urgently seeks a replacement relationship. Freud's anal character (1908) was orderly, parsimonious and obstinate; people with OCPD are primarily motivated by a need for , and their traits are ego-syntonic. Answers: (1) B, (2) histrionic, (3) empathy, (4) emotional (affective), (5) hypervigilant, (6) specific, (7) overvaluation, (8) schizoid, (9) appeasement (submissiveness), (10) control. 11.8 The Newer Models: Dimensions, ICD-11 and the DSM-5 Alternative Model Lower yield · not asked yet Meet Manish. He is 31, an accountant in a Pune firm, and he has come to the outpatient department because his third serious relationship in five years has just ended and he has started punching the wall of his rented room at night. Over three long interviews his clinician gathers a clear picture. His moods swing within hours, usually after something a colleague or a girlfriend has said; he flares into rages he regrets; he describes a hollow feeling "like a room with no furniture". He is also deeply suspicious: he is sure that his manager is quietly building a case against him, he reads insults into harmless remarks, and he still has not forgiven a cousin for something said at a wedding in 2019. And he keeps to himself, avoiding the office lunch group because he expects to be laughed at, although he would like to belong. Now try to give Manish one of the ten diagnoses you have met in this chapter. He meets four of the nine borderline criteria (Section 11.3), one short of the five required. He meets three of the seven paranoid criteria (Section 11.2), one short of four. He meets three of the seven avoidant criteria (Section 11.7), again one short. Under the rules of DSM-5-TR Section II he has no specific personality disorder at all. Yet he is plainly unwell, his problems have shaped his whole adult life, and they are costing him his relationships and perhaps his job. The best the manual can offer him is "other specified personality disorder", a label that tells the next clinician almost nothing about what Manish is like. Manish is not a rare case. He is the typical case, and the newer models of personality disorder were built for people like him. This section explains why so many researchers lost faith in the ten categories, what the dimensional alternative is, and how the two newest systems, the ICD-11 classification that has been official since 2022 and the Alternative Model printed in Section III of DSM-5, describe personality pathology instead. By the end you will be able to diagnose Manish three different ways, and you will see that the three answers are telling the same story in different languages. What is wrong with ten boxes Section 1.6.4 set out the general case against purely categorical diagnosis: no zones of rarity between disorders, too much comorbidity, too many "other" and "unspecified" diagnoses, and so on. The personality disorders are where every one of those problems is at its worst, and it is worth seeing exactly how. The ten Section II categories were carried over almost unchanged from DSM-IV, and DSM-5-TR itself admits, in the opening pages of its alternative model, that "symptoms meeting criteria for a specific personality disorder frequently also meet criteria for other personality disorders" and that the residual diagnosis "is often the correct (but mostly uninformative) diagnosis". The first problem is artificial comorbidity . A patient who meets the criteria for one personality disorder very often meets them for a second or a third. That is not because people collect personality disorders the way some people collect illnesses. It is because the criteria sets overlap (suspiciousness appears in paranoid, schizotypal and, as stress-related paranoid ideation, borderline personality disorder; social withdrawal appears in schizoid, schizotypal and avoidant personality disorder), and because a few broad traits, above all a tendency to strong negative emotion, run through many of the categories at once. When one underlying dimension is sliced into several named boxes, a person high on that dimension lands in several boxes. The comorbidity is produced by the classification, not by the patient. The second problem is heterogeneity within a single diagnosis. Borderline personality disorder needs any five of nine criteria. Work out the arithmetic: there are 126 ways of choosing exactly five of nine criteria, 84 ways of choosing six, 36 of seven, 9 of eight and 1 of all nine, a total of 256 different combinations that all earn the same label. Two patients can share the diagnosis while sharing only one criterion: one may meet criteria 1 to 5, the other criteria 5 to 9. If you were told only that a new patient "has borderline personality disorder", you would not know whether to expect self-harm, dissociation, frantic clinging or explosive anger. The third problem is arbitrary thresholds . Why five borderline criteria and not four or six? Why four of seven for paranoid personality disorder? The cut-offs were set by committees, not discovered in nature, and nothing special happens to a person between criterion four and criterion five. Manish, with four borderline features, is no less impaired than a patient with five; studies that treat the criteria as a simple count generally find that the count predicts impairment and outcome better than the yes-or-no diagnosis does. A category treats a person one criterion below the line exactly like a person with no features at all. The fourth problem follows from the first three. Because real patients so often have a mixture of features, or fall just short of several thresholds, the residual category becomes one of the busiest in the chapter. In 2004 Roel Verheul and Thomas A. Widiger pooled 51 studies of the DSM-IV diagnosis "personality disorder not otherwise specified" (PD NOS, the forerunner of today's other specified and unspecified personality disorder). In studies using structured interviews it ranked third among all the personality disorder diagnoses, and in studies relying on ordinary clinical interviews it was often the single commonest. When the most frequent answer a classification gives is "none of the above", the classification is not carving nature at its joints. Several further weaknesses complete the case. Unstructured clinical diagnosis of personality disorders agrees poorly from one clinician to the next; structured interviews such as the SCID-5-PD and the International Personality Disorder Examination (Assessment book) agree better but take hours. The diagnoses are less stable than the definition (a pattern "stable and of long duration") promises: Section 11.4 shows that most patients with borderline personality disorder slip below the threshold within a few years, often by losing one or two criteria, while the underlying traits and the problems in work and relationships change much more slowly. And the three clusters, which Section 11.1 uses to organise the chapter, are by DSM-5-TR's own account useful for teaching but "not consistently validated": disorders from different clusters co-occur all the time. It is ICD-11 , not DSM-5-TR, that made a dimensional model official. There is no Cluster D, and the clusters themselves are described by the manual as having "serious limitations". "Personality disorder not otherwise specified" was the DSM-IV name; DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR replaced it with other specified and unspecified personality disorder . The dimensional alternative: personality disorder as normal personality taken to an extreme If the boxes do not fit, what should replace them? DSM-5-TR states the alternative in one sentence. The categorical perspective holds that personality disorders are "qualitatively distinct clinical syndromes"; the dimensional perspective holds that they are "maladaptive variants of personality traits that merge imperceptibly into normality and into one another". On this view nobody simply has or lacks a personality disorder, any more than anybody simply has or lacks height. Everyone sits somewhere on a set of continuous trait dimensions, and what we call a personality disorder is a position far out on one or more of them, combined with the rigidity and the damage to self and relationships that the general definition in Section 11.1 describes. Figure 11.13 shows the idea. number of people Section II cut-off (for example, five of nine criteria) A B low average high ICD-11 grades the same continuum: no personality disorder difficulty mild moderate severe Horizontal axis: severity of personality pathology. Figure 11.13 One continuum, one arbitrary cut. The shaded tail is everyone a categorical rule calls disordered. Persons A and B differ by a whisker, yet the rule calls B disordered and A well. A dimensional system keeps the information: ICD-11 places both people on a graded scale of severity instead of a yes-or-no line. Which dimensions? The obvious candidate was the most thoroughly replicated description of normal personality, the five-factor model (the "Big Five": neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness and conscientiousness), whose history and measurement belong to the Personality book. In 1994 Widiger and Paul T. Costa Jr. argued in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology that the personality disorders could be understood as extreme and maladaptive positions on these same five dimensions, and in the same year Costa and Widiger edited a book of studies testing the claim. The idea was elegant: instead of a separate science of abnormal personality, there would be one science of personality, with the disorders as its far ends. Does the evidence support it? In 2004 the Australian psychologists L. M. Saulsman and A. C. Page pooled 15 independent samples in which people had been measured on both the five factors and the ten DSM-IV personality disorders. Two findings came out. First, each disorder had a five-factor profile that was "meaningful and predictable" from its criteria: avoidant personality disorder was high in neuroticism and low in extraversion, obsessive-compulsive personality disorder high in conscientiousness, and so on. Second, the most consistent thread running through many of the disorders was high neuroticism and low agreeableness, with extraversion "a more discriminating dimension" because it pointed in opposite directions for different disorders (low in schizoid and avoidant patients, high in histrionic ones). That second finding is exactly what you would predict if artificial comorbidity is real: many personality disorders share a high-neuroticism, low-agreeableness core, so they overlap. Some researchers argued that a model of normal personality would miss the clinically important extremes, and built their dimensions from personality pathology itself. The psychiatrist W. John Livesley, working in Vancouver, collected the features clinicians use to describe personality disorders and reduced them statistically to a self-report questionnaire, the Dimensional Assessment of Personality Pathology -Basic Questionnaire (DAPP-BQ: 290 items, 18 lower-order traits), whose items group into four higher-order factors: emotional dysregulation, dissocial behaviour, inhibitedness and compulsivity. Other groups produced the Personality Psychopathology Five (PSY-5), scored from the MMPI-2, and several more (all of them Assessment book material). The striking thing is how similar the answers are. Again and again the same four or five broad dimensions come out: a tendency to intense negative emotion, a tendency to withdraw from people, a tendency to be callous and antagonistic, a tendency to act without restraint, and (in some models) a tendency to rigid control or to odd thinking. Hold on to that list; you are about to see it reappear, under slightly different names, in ICD-11 and in DSM-5's alternative model. At the broadest level still, the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) places these personality dimensions inside spectra that cover all mental disorders (Section 1.6.4). A dimensional description has clear advantages. It keeps information that a cut-off throws away (Manish's four borderline features are recorded, not discarded); it describes every patient, so there is no residual category; ratings on a continuum are more reliable than yes-or-no judgements; it explains comorbidity instead of multiplying it; and it links the disorders to a large research literature on the genetics and development of normal traits (the broad traits are substantially heritable, Section 11.1). Its disadvantages are practical. Clinicians think and talk in syndromes; "high negative affectivity, moderate detachment" is harder to say across a ward round than "borderline". Decades of treatment research, including all the trials of dialectical behaviour therapy and mentalisation-based treatment (Section 11.4), were done with patients selected by category. And courts, insurers and health services want a name. The two newest systems are attempts to keep the advantages while softening the disadvantages. Exam trap The Big Five (neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness) describe normal personality; DSM-5's five pathological domains (negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, psychoticism) are their maladaptive variants , not the same list under new names. The five-factor account of personality disorders is associated with Widiger and Costa (1994). Livesley's instrument is the DAPP-BQ, with four higher-order factors (emotional dysregulation, dissocial behaviour, inhibitedness, compulsivity). The dimensional view says personality disorders "merge imperceptibly into normality and into one another"; the categorical view says they are "qualitatively distinct clinical syndromes". ICD-11: one personality disorder, graded by severity The World Health Organization took the bolder step. ICD-10 had listed eight specific personality disorders (F60.0 to F60.7, from paranoid to dependent, Section 11.1), and in practice they were used very unevenly: two of them, emotionally unstable personality disorder and dissocial personality disorder, were recorded far more often than the rest, and the overlap among the types produced the artificial comorbidity described in Section 11.8.1. The working group that WHO set up to revise the personality disorders for ICD-11 was chaired by the British psychiatrist Peter Tyrer , and in 2011 Tyrer, Michael Crawford, Roger Mulder and their colleagues published the case for a complete reclassification. Its central argument is one that DSM-5-TR itself now concedes in its alternative model: "Generalized severity may be the most important single predictor of concurrent and prospective dysfunction in assessing personality psychopathology." If what matters most for prognosis and treatment is how severe a person's personality problems are, the classification should ask that question first, and treat the style of the problems as a secondary description. That is the shape of the ICD-11 classification, which the World Health Assembly adopted in 2019 and which came into effect on 1 January 2022 (Section 1.9). The ten types are gone. In their place is a single diagnosis, personality disorder (6D10), which the clinician makes in three steps: first decide whether the general requirements are met, then grade the severity, and then, if it helps, describe the style with trait qualifiers. The general requirements will feel familiar from Section 11.1, but read them closely, because they differ from DSM-5-TR in instructive ways. There must be an enduring disturbance in the functioning of aspects of the self (identity, self-worth, the accuracy of one's view of oneself, self-direction) and/or interpersonal dysfunction (the ability to develop and maintain close and mutually satisfying relationships, to understand other people's perspectives and to manage conflict). The disturbance must have persisted over an extended period of time, which the guidelines illustrate as 2 years or more. It shows itself in patterns of cognition, emotional experience, emotional expression and behaviour that are maladaptive (for example, inflexible or poorly regulated), and it appears across a range of personal and social situations rather than in one relationship or one role. The patterns must not be developmentally appropriate and must not be explained primarily by social or cultural factors, "including socio-political conflict", a clause that protects, for example, a young man whose mistrust and hostility grew up in a region of armed conflict. They must not be due to a substance or medication, or be better explained by another mental, neurological or medical condition. And they must cause substantial distress or significant impairment. Notice what is missing. ICD-11 does not require the pattern to have begun in adolescence or early adulthood, as DSM-5-TR does. Its guidelines say that personality disorder usually shows itself first in childhood or adolescence, but that it is only "relatively" stable after young adulthood: a person with a personality disorder at 25 may no longer have one at 50, and a person who never had one may develop one later in life, sometimes when the loss of a spouse, a job or a supportive family removes the scaffolding that had compensated for a fragile personality. Notice, too, that the ICD-11 definition is built around the self and relationships, the same two pillars as Criterion A of DSM-5's alternative model, which you will meet in Section 11.8.5. Once the general requirements are met, the clinician grades severity. ICD-11 judges severity from four things: how widely and deeply the functioning of the self is disturbed; how widely and deeply relationships are disturbed across contexts (romantic, family, work, friendship); how pervasive, severe and chronic the emotional, cognitive and behavioural manifestations are (including how accurately the person appraises situations under stress, and whether intense emotion leads to self-harm or violence); and how much distress and impairment all this causes. Level (code) Areas of personality functioning affected Relationships and roles Harm to self or others Personality difficulty (QE50.7) Pronounced traits that cause problems only intermittently or at low intensity, for example under stress; present for at least about 2 years Not severe enough to cause notable disruption of work, friendships or intimate relationships Not expected Mild personality disorder (6D10.0) Some areas but not others (for example, self-direction disturbed while identity and self-worth are intact); may not be apparent in some contexts Problems in many relationships or roles, but some relationships maintained and some roles carried out Typically not substantial Moderate personality disorder (6D10.1) Multiple areas (identity, intimacy, control of impulses), though some are less affected Marked problems in most relationships; most social and occupational roles compromised to some degree Sometimes Severe personality disorder (6D10.2) Severe disturbance of the self (no sense of who one is, or a self so rigid that life shrinks; self-contempt, grandiosity or marked eccentricity); most if not all areas Virtually all relationships seriously affected; ability or willingness to perform roles absent or severely compromised Often There is also a code for personality disorder, severity unspecified (6D10.Z). The lowest step deserves a sentence. Personality difficulty describes pronounced personality traits that cause some trouble, perhaps only when the person is under strain, without reaching the level of a disorder. It is coded as QE50.7 in Chapter 24 of ICD-11 (factors influencing health status or contact with health services), not in the mental disorders chapter at all: ICD-11 records it as a reason for clinical attention, not as an illness. Its existence is itself a dimensional statement. The line between a difficult personality and a disordered one is drawn on a continuum, and ICD-11 gives a name to the zone just below the line, the zone Person A occupies in Figure 11.13. Exam trap ICD-11 has one personality disorder diagnosis (6D10) graded mild, moderate or severe ; there are three severity grades of disorder, not four or five. Personality difficulty (QE50.7) is not a mental disorder ; it is coded outside Chapter 6. ICD-11 asks for a disturbance lasting 2 years or more and, unlike DSM-5-TR, sets no age of onset . The model was developed by the WHO working group chaired by Peter Tyrer ; it is ICD-11's official system, not a research appendix. The ICD-11 trait domains and the borderline pattern Severity says how much; the trait domain qualifiers say what kind. ICD-11 offers five, each coded under 6D11 ("prominent personality traits or patterns"). They are optional, the clinician may record as many as are prominent, and they may be attached to personality difficulty as well as to personality disorder. Each describes an enduring disposition, not a symptom: Negative affectivity (6D11.0): a tendency to experience a broad range of negative emotions with a frequency and intensity out of proportion to the situation. It covers anxiety, anger, worry, fear, vulnerability, hostility, shame, depression, pessimism, guilt, low self-esteem and mistrustfulness. Once upset, such a person has great difficulty regaining composure. Detachment (6D11.1): a tendency to keep interpersonal distance (social detachment: avoiding social contact, few friends, avoidance of intimacy) and emotional distance (emotional detachment: reserve, aloofness, limited emotional expression and experience). Such a person may deliberately seek out work that involves no dealings with others. Dissociality (6D11.2): disregard for the rights and feelings of others, with two components. Self-centredness covers entitlement, grandiosity, expecting admiration and attention seeking; lack of empathy covers being deceptive, manipulative, exploitative, ruthless, mean, callous and physically aggressive, sometimes taking pleasure in others' suffering. Notice that this one domain absorbs much of what Section II divides between antisocial and narcissistic personality disorder. Disinhibition (6D11.3): a tendency to act rashly on immediate external or internal stimuli (sensations, emotions, thoughts) without considering the consequences: impulsivity, distractibility, irresponsibility, recklessness and lack of planning, seen in reckless driving, dangerous sports, substance use, gambling and unplanned sex. Anankastia (6D11.4): a narrow focus on one's own rigid standard of perfection and of right and wrong, and on controlling one's own and other people's behaviour, and situations, to make them conform. It has two parts: perfectionism (concern with rules, details, hyper-scheduling, orderliness, neatness) and emotional and behavioural constraint (rigid control of emotional expression, stubbornness, risk avoidance, perseveration, deliberateness). The name comes from the Greek ananke , necessity or compulsion, and survives from ICD-10's anankastic personality disorder, the ICD name for obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (Section 11.7). The person who stubbornly redoes a colleague's work because it falls short of his standards is the typical example. One domain is conspicuously absent. There is no trait qualifier for odd, eccentric or psychotic-like thinking, and no schizotypal personality disorder anywhere in the ICD-11 personality chapter. ICD-11, like ICD-10 before it, classifies schizotypal disorder (6A22) with schizophrenia and the other primary psychotic disorders (Sections 4.5.8 and 11.2). Where a person's personality disturbance includes transient psychotic-like beliefs or perceptions, or marked eccentricity, ICD-11 counts these towards the severity rating rather than treating them as a separate trait, which echoes Kernberg's old idea (Section 11.4) that impaired reality testing marks the most severe level of personality organisation. The sixth qualifier is a compromise, and it is honest to call it one. The original ICD-11 proposal had no place for borderline personality disorder at all. Many clinicians and researchers objected: borderline personality disorder has by far the largest research literature of any personality disorder, specific psychological treatments have been tested on it (Section 11.4), and in many health systems the label opens the door to those treatments. WHO therefore added the borderline pattern qualifier (6D11.5), which may be applied when the personality disturbance is characterised by a pervasive pattern of instability of relationships, self-image and affects, with marked impulsivity, shown by five or more of nine features that closely follow the DSM criteria taught in Section 11.3 (frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, unstable intense relationships, identity disturbance, self-damaging impulsivity, recurrent self-harm, affective instability, chronic emptiness, intense anger, and transient dissociative or psychotic-like features under high emotional arousal). The inclusion is often described as a "pragmatic compromise". Critics have argued that the pattern adds little, since borderline features are largely captured by high negative affectivity combined with disinhibition and dissociality, and some studies find borderline criteria hard to separate from negative affectivity at all. The essential decisions are the first two (is there a personality disorder, and how severe is it?); the trait qualifiers and the borderline pattern describe its style and are optional. There is no psychoticism domain: schizotypal disorder is classified with the psychoses. Now return to Manish. Does he meet the general requirements? Yes: his self-image and his relationships have been disturbed for well over 2 years, across work, family and romance, and the disturbance is costing him dearly. How severe? Several areas are affected (his sense of self, his close relationships and his control of anger), he has marked problems in most relationships, his work is suffering, and his anger has led to some harm (the wall, and very nearly a colleague), but some areas are less affected: he works competently and keeps one old school friendship. That is moderate personality disorder, 6D10.1. Which traits are prominent? His mood swings, rages, emptiness, low self-worth and mistrust all fall under negative affectivity (6D11.0), and his avoidance of the lunch group and of new friendships falls under detachment (6D11.1). The borderline pattern qualifier does not apply, because he shows only four of its nine features. So ICD-11's description of Manish is "moderate personality disorder with prominent negative affectivity and detachment": a short phrase that tells the next clinician more than "other specified personality disorder" ever could. Clinical link The ICD-11 model was designed partly for clinics like a busy Indian psychiatry outpatient department, where a full structured interview for ten personality disorders is rarely possible. The first two questions (is there a personality disorder, and how severe is it?) can be answered from a good history and an informant in a few minutes, and the severity grade carries most of the practical information: it guides how intensive treatment needs to be, how closely risk must be watched, and what the prognosis is. The trait qualifiers then point towards what to work on: emotion regulation for negative affectivity, engagement and trust for detachment, consequences and empathy for dissociality, impulse control for disinhibition, flexibility for anankastia. Exam trap The five ICD-11 trait domains are negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition and anankastia . Dissociality and anankastia are ICD-11 words; antagonism and psychoticism are DSM-5 Alternative Model words. ICD-11 has no psychoticism domain and no schizotypal personality disorder : schizotypal disorder is 6A22, in the schizophrenia block. The borderline pattern is a qualifier (6D11.5), not a separate personality disorder diagnosis, and it needs five or more of nine features. "Anankastic" in ICD-10 (F60.5) means obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, not OCD. The DSM-5 Alternative Model I: Criterion A, the level of personality functioning Section 1.8.5 introduced the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD) in a paragraph. Here is the full model, and the story of how it came to be printed at the back of the manual rather than in the front. The DSM-5 Personality and Personality Disorders Work Group, chaired by Andrew E. Skodol with John M. Oldham as co-chair and Robert F. Krueger coordinating the text, set out to replace the DSM-IV categories with a model built on impairment and traits. Its first draft, posted on the DSM-5 website in February 2010, proposed deleting five of the ten personality disorders (paranoid, schizoid, histrionic, dependent and narcissistic). The deletion of narcissistic personality disorder provoked a storm of protest, and a revised draft in June 2011 reinstated it. The arguments continued inside and outside the work group, two of whose members, Livesley and Verheul, resigned in 2012. Finally, in December 2012, the Board of Trustees of the American Psychiatric Association decided to keep the DSM-IV categories, virtually unchanged, as the official diagnoses in Section II and to print the work group's model in Section III as an alternative, "to preserve continuity with current clinical practice, while also introducing an alternative approach". DSM-5-TR (2022) kept that arrangement and describes the result as a hybrid dimensional-categorical model . The model rests on seven general criteria, A to G. The essential two are Criterion A , moderate or greater impairment in personality (self and interpersonal) functioning, and Criterion B , one or more pathological personality traits. Criteria C to G then repeat, in new words, the familiar conditions of Section 11.1: the impairment and traits are relatively inflexible and pervasive across situations (C) and relatively stable over time, with onset traceable to at least adolescence or early adulthood (D); they are not better explained by another mental disorder (E), not solely due to a substance or another medical condition such as severe head injury (F), and not better understood as normal for the person's developmental stage or sociocultural environment (G). Criterion A is the heart of the model, because the work group regarded disturbances of the self and of relationships as "the core of personality psychopathology". It is rated with the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (LPFS), developed by Donna S. Bender , Leslie C. Morey and Skodol and published in 2011. The scale has four elements, two for the self and two for relationships: Identity : experiencing oneself as a unique person with clear boundaries between self and others; stable self-esteem and accurate self-appraisal; the capacity to experience and regulate a full range of emotions. Self-direction : pursuing coherent and meaningful short-term and life goals; using constructive and prosocial internal standards of behaviour; being able to reflect productively on oneself. Empathy : understanding and appreciating other people's experiences and motives; tolerating differing perspectives; understanding the effects of one's own behaviour on others. Intimacy : the depth and duration of connection with others; the desire and capacity for closeness; mutual regard shown in the way one behaves towards people. For each element the scale describes five levels: 0, little or no impairment (healthy, adaptive functioning); 1, some impairment; 2, moderate impairment; 3, severe impairment; and 4, extreme impairment. The clinician chooses the level that best captures the person's overall current functioning. A personality disorder requires at least level 2, moderate impairment . The manual explains that this threshold was chosen on evidence: in the work group's studies (Morey and colleagues, 2011) the moderate level was the point that best allowed clinicians to identify personality disorder pathology accurately and efficiently. The level also carries information beyond the diagnosis. Greater impairment predicts having more than one personality disorder, or one of the typically more severe ones, and the scale can be used on its own as a global index of personality functioning, even in someone with no personality disorder. Look at what the four elements describe and you will see why the AMPD and ICD-11 are close cousins. Identity and self-direction are ICD-11's "functioning of aspects of the self"; empathy and intimacy are its "interpersonal dysfunction". Both systems have concluded, from the same research, that a single dimension of personality functioning (how integrated a person's sense of self is and how capable they are of real relationships) carries most of what clinicians need to know about severity. Psychodynamic readers will recognise an old idea in modern dress: Kernberg's levels of personality organisation (Section 11.4) also ranked people by the integration of their identity and the quality of their relationships. Exam trap Criterion A of the AMPD has two areas and four elements : self (identity, self-direction) and interpersonal (empathy, intimacy). The LPFS runs from level 0 (little or no impairment) to level 4 (extreme impairment) , five levels in all, and a disorder needs moderate impairment, level 2, or worse . Do not confuse the LPFS levels with ICD-11's grades: ICD-11 has personality difficulty plus mild, moderate and severe disorder. The AMPD is in Section III of DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR; it was placed there by the APA Board of Trustees in December 2012 . The DSM-5 Alternative Model II: Criterion B, the pathological traits, and the six types Criterion B describes the style of a person's personality pathology in terms of pathological personality traits . The manual defines a trait as a tendency to feel, perceive, behave and think in relatively consistent ways across time and situations; it is not the same as a single act (one impulsive purchase does not make a person impulsive) or a symptom (symptoms such as poor concentration come and go with episodes of illness, whereas traits are relatively stable). Traits are arranged in a hierarchy. Broad traits are called trait domains ; narrower traits that tend to occur together within a domain are called trait facets . The AMPD has five domains containing 25 facets. Each domain is a pole of a dimension whose healthy opposite the manual names in brackets, and the manual states plainly that the five are "maladaptive variants of the five domains" of the five-factor model: Negative affectivity (versus emotional stability): frequent and intense experience of a wide range of negative emotions (anxiety, depression, guilt and shame, worry, anger) and their behavioural and interpersonal expressions, such as self-harm and dependency. Detachment (versus extraversion): avoidance of socioemotional experience, both withdrawal from people (from casual daily contact to intimate relationships) and restricted emotional experience and expression, especially a limited capacity for pleasure. Antagonism (versus agreeableness): behaviour that puts the person at odds with others, including an exaggerated sense of self-importance with an expectation of special treatment, and a callous antipathy towards others, both unaware of their needs and ready to use them. Disinhibition (versus conscientiousness): an orientation towards immediate gratification, so that behaviour is driven by current thoughts, feelings and stimuli without regard for past learning or future consequences. Psychoticism (versus lucidity): a wide range of culturally incongruent odd, eccentric or unusual behaviours and cognitions, both in process (perception, dissociation) and in content (beliefs). Table 11.28 lists the 25 facets under their domains. Three details repay attention. Some facets belong to two domains: hostility sits in both negative affectivity and antagonism, and depressivity and suspiciousness are defined under detachment but also contribute to negative affectivity. Restricted affectivity is defined under detachment and appears under negative affectivity only as a "lack of" facet, pointing the opposite way. And rigid perfectionism is listed under disinhibition as a "lack of" facet: it is the extreme opposite pole of disinhibition, too much conscientiousness rather than too little. That is how the AMPD represents what ICD-11 calls anankastia. Table 11.28 The five trait domains and 25 trait facets of the DSM-5 Alternative Model (DSM-5-TR Section III). The manual compares the clinical use of the trait model to the review of systems in general medicine: whatever the presenting complaint, review all five domains, lest an important area be missed. From Criteria A and B the model derives six specific personality disorders, the six for which the work group judged the evidence of validity and clinical usefulness strongest. The AMPD's narcissistic personality disorder is defined around variable and vulnerable self-esteem, with grandiosity that may be overt or covert, which brings the vulnerable narcissism described in Section 11.6 into the definition. And the antisocial type carries a specifier, with psychopathic features , for the variant often called primary psychopathy (Section 11.5): low anxiousness and low withdrawal combined with high attention seeking, so that a bold, socially dominant and stress-immune style masks the antisocial behaviour. This is the AMPD's way of recording psychopathy; it is not the same thing as the "with limited prosocial emotions" specifier of conduct disorder (Section 11.9.4). Everyone who meets the general criteria but does not match one of the six types receives personality disorder, trait specified (PD-TS). The diagnosis needs moderate or greater impairment in at least two of the four elements of personality functioning and one or more pathological trait domains or facets, and the person's particular traits are always recorded, so that each PD-TS diagnosis is in effect a personal profile. Paranoid, schizoid, histrionic and dependent personality disorder, the four Section II types that did not survive as named types, are represented by PD-TS with the relevant traits (for example, suspiciousness and hostility for a paranoid style, withdrawal and restricted affectivity for a schizoid one, attention seeking and emotional lability for a histrionic one, submissiveness and separation insecurity for a dependent one). The PD-TS diagnosis does the job that "other specified personality disorder" fails to do: it says exactly what is wrong. Push Manish through the model one last time. Criterion A: his sense of self is unstable and empty (identity), and his close relationships are intense, conflicted and short-lived (intimacy), so he has moderate impairment in two of the four elements, level 2 on the LPFS. Criterion B: the PID-5 and the interview show elevated emotional lability, anxiousness, depressivity and hostility, together with suspiciousness and withdrawal. Now check the type rules. For the AMPD borderline type he needs four of seven traits, one of them impulsivity, risk taking or hostility: emotional lability, anxiousness, depressivity and hostility make four, and hostility is among them. So, although Section II gave him no specific diagnosis, the alternative model diagnoses borderline personality disorder , and the clinician adds the traits not required for it (suspiciousness, withdrawal) as specifiers. The example is a useful warning as well as a demonstration. The two DSM models were designed to identify roughly the same people, but they reach their verdicts by different routes, and in individual patients they can disagree. Exam trap The AMPD has 5 trait domains and 25 facets , and keeps six types: antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive and schizotypal . The four that became PD-TS are paranoid, schizoid, histrionic and dependent (a favourite "which is not retained" option). Everyone else gets personality disorder, trait specified . The domains are negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition and psychoticism . The PID-5 measures the traits; the LPFS rates Criterion A. Narcissistic personality disorder was dropped in the 2010 draft but restored in 2011 , so it is one of the six. Three systems side by side You can now line up the three systems that a clinician in India may meet on a single day: DSM-5-TR Section II in a research paper, ICD-10 or ICD-11 on the hospital case sheet, and the AMPD in a journal article or a training programme. Their great strength is that they rest on the research of the previous thirty years rather than on the clinical traditions of the previous century. The five broad domains turn up again and again, in many countries, whether researchers start from normal personality, from personality pathology or from the PID-5. DSM-5-TR itself accepts that general severity may be the best single predictor of how a person will fare. And both systems remove the residual category: nobody falls outside them. Their weaknesses are practical and political. The AMPD is complicated: two criteria, four elements, five levels, five domains, 25 facets and six rule-sets. WHO, while noting that ICD-11's model is conceptually close to it, judged the AMPD "too complicated for implementation in most clinical settings around the world", which is one reason ICD-11 has no facets. Critics of both systems point out that the line between "impairment in functioning" and "pathological traits" is hard to draw (is chronic emptiness a disturbance of identity or a facet of depressivity?), that clinicians are unfamiliar with the new language, and that abandoning the named types cuts the link with decades of treatment research, which is exactly why ICD-11 kept a borderline pattern and the AMPD kept six types. The likely future is a period in which both languages are spoken, and the clinician who can translate between them, as you have just done for Manish, is the one who understands personality disorder best. Exam trap A 2021 paper asked: "Personality disorders are stable long-term conditions which can affect an individual's (a) cognition, (b) mood, (c) interpersonal functioning, (d) all of the above." The answer is (d) all of the above , and every system in this section agrees. DSM-5-TR Section II requires the pattern in two or more of cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning and impulse control (Section 11.1); ICD-11 requires it in patterns of cognition, emotional experience, emotional expression and behaviour, with disturbance of the self and/or relationships; the AMPD rates the self and interpersonal functioning and traits that span emotion, thought and behaviour. Matching pairs to learn: negative affectivity, detachment and disinhibition appear in both manuals; antagonism (AMPD) corresponds to dissociality (ICD-11); psychoticism is AMPD only; anankastia is ICD-11 only. 11.9 Oppositional Defiant and Conduct Disorders Lower yield · 2 Qs It is a Saturday morning at a child guidance clinic in a large Indian city, and three new families are waiting. Veer is seven. His mother says he "simply will not listen": he argues about everything, throws a tantrum whenever the tablet is taken away, blames his little sister for whatever goes wrong and drives his class teacher to distraction by humming when she asks for silence. Daksh is twelve and has been sent by his school after a series of fights, the last one with a cricket bat; neighbours say he has hurt stray dogs, and his father admits, with a mixture of anger and fear, that he has never once seen the boy sorry. Falguni is fifteen. Until last year she was a quiet, ordinary student; then she fell in with an older group, began lying about where she was, took money from her aunt's purse and twice ran away overnight. All three children are in trouble with the adults around them, and a hurried clinician might give them all the same label, "behaviour problem". This section shows why they almost certainly have three different conditions: oppositional defiant disorder for Veer, conduct disorder of childhood onset with limited prosocial emotions for Daksh, and conduct disorder of adolescent onset for Falguni. It also shows why that matters, because the three diagnoses carry very different prospects for the adults these children will become. The section ends where Section 11.5 began, at the door of antisocial personality disorder. The disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders: why these sit together DSM-5 (2013) created a new chapter, disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders , and DSM-5-TR keeps it. The manual defines the family by a shared problem and a shared consequence. The problem is poor self-control of emotions and behaviour. Many disorders involve that, so the defining feature is the consequence: in these disorders the failures of control show themselves in behaviour that violates the rights of others (aggression, destruction of property) or brings the person into significant conflict with social norms or authority figures. The chapter contains oppositional defiant disorder, intermittent explosive disorder, conduct disorder, antisocial personality disorder (whose criteria are printed in the personality chapter but listed here as well, because it is the adult end of the same externalising spectrum), pyromania, kleptomania, and other specified and unspecified disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorder for impairing presentations that miss the thresholds. The disorders differ in the balance between the two kinds of self-control. At one end, the criteria for conduct disorder are almost entirely about behaviour: acts that violate other people's rights or major social rules, which may or may not spring from poorly controlled emotion (some of the coldest aggression in the chapter comes from constricted, not excessive, emotion). At the other end, intermittent explosive disorder is almost entirely about emotion: outbursts of anger out of all proportion to the provocation. Oppositional defiant disorder sits between them, with criteria shared between emotion (anger and irritability) and behaviour (argumentativeness and defiance). Pyromania and kleptomania are different again: poor control over one specific act, fire setting or stealing, that relieves inner tension. Intermittent explosive disorder, pyromania and kleptomania are taught in Section 11.10; this section takes oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder. The chapter's members share more than a definition. They are all commoner in boys and men, they usually begin in childhood or adolescence (conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder almost never begin in adulthood), and they are linked, in the manual's words, to "a common externalizing spectrum associated with the personality dimensions of disinhibition and negative emotionality", and inversely with constraint and agreeableness. Those are the very dimensions you met in Section 11.8, and they explain why these disorders co-occur so often with one another, with substance use disorders and with antisocial personality disorder. The manual also adds a warning that runs through everything that follows. Almost every symptom in this chapter (a tantrum, a lie, a fight, a night out without permission) is something ordinary children and teenagers do from time to time. What makes it a symptom is its frequency, persistence, spread across situations and the impairment it causes, judged against what is normal for the child's age, gender and culture. The history of the names is short but examined. DSM-III (1980) introduced conduct disorder, divided into four subtypes by two dimensions (undersocialised or socialised, aggressive or nonaggressive), and a milder condition called oppositional disorder; DSM-III-R (1987) renamed it oppositional defiant disorder. DSM-IV (1994) replaced the four subtypes with the childhood-onset and adolescent-onset types still used today, and placed both disorders with ADHD among the "attention-deficit and disruptive behavior disorders" of childhood. DSM-5 moved them into the new chapter alongside the old impulse-control disorders and added the "with limited prosocial emotions" specifier. ICD-10's "socialised" and "unsocialised" conduct disorders (Section 11.9.8) preserve the DSM-III idea. Exam trap The DSM-5-TR chapter "Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders" contains oppositional defiant disorder, intermittent explosive disorder, conduct disorder, antisocial personality disorder (listed in two chapters), pyromania, kleptomania and the other specified and unspecified categories. It does not contain ADHD (a neurodevelopmental disorder, Section 3.7), disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (a depressive disorder, Section 5.3.2), gambling disorder (now with the addictions, Section 10.1.7) or trichotillomania (obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, Section 6.6.5). Conduct disorder is the most behavioural member, intermittent explosive disorder the most emotional , and oppositional defiant disorder lies between. Oppositional defiant disorder Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) is a frequent and persistent pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behaviour, or vindictiveness, lasting at least 6 months and shown by at least four symptoms from any of three groups, during interaction with at least one person who is not a sibling. The eight symptoms are worth learning in their groups, because the groups have different futures. Angry or irritable mood : often loses temper; is often touchy or easily annoyed; is often angry and resentful. Argumentative or defiant behaviour : often argues with authority figures (for a child or adolescent, with adults); often actively defies or refuses to comply with requests from authority figures or with rules; often deliberately annoys others; often blames others for his or her own mistakes or misbehaviour. Vindictiveness : has been spiteful or vindictive at least twice within the past 6 months. Every rule in the criteria has a reason. The sibling rule exists because squabbling, provoking and refusing are so common between brothers and sisters that they would make the diagnosis meaningless; the pattern must show with a parent, a teacher, a peer or some other person. The word "often" is given a number, because every child sometimes loses his temper. For children under 5 the behaviour should occur on most days for at least 6 months; from age 5 onwards, at least once a week for at least 6 months (vindictiveness has its own rule of twice in 6 months). Even then the clinician must ask whether the frequency and intensity are outside the range normal for the child's developmental level, gender and culture: weekly tantrums are common in preschool children, but daily tantrums occur in only about 10 percent of them. The behaviour must also cause distress to the child or to the people around him, or impair his social, educational or other functioning. And it must not occur only during a psychotic, substance use, depressive or bipolar disorder, and must not meet the criteria for disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, which takes precedence. Severity is graded not by the number of symptoms but by how far the pattern has spread. Mild means the symptoms are confined to one setting (home, school, work or peers); moderate , some symptoms in at least two settings; severe , some symptoms in three or more. The manual's logic is that pervasiveness is the best indicator of severity, and it adds a useful clinical observation: many children with ODD show their symptoms only at home and only with family members, and because the behaviour is most visible with adults the child knows well, it may not appear at all during the clinic interview. A charming, polite seven-year-old in the consulting room tells you nothing either way. Veer shows how the criteria work. Over the past year, two or three times a week, he has lost his temper when told to stop playing (symptom 1); he is touchy and quick to take offence (2); he argues with his parents and teacher (4); he refuses homework instructions "because nobody can tell me what to do" (5); he hums to annoy his teacher (6); he blames his sister for everything (7); and twice in the past 6 months he took revenge on a classmate who had reported him, once by spreading a story that got the boy scolded (8). That is seven symptoms, well over four, lasting more than 6 months, at least weekly, at home and at school, with adults who are not his siblings, and causing real trouble in both places: ODD, moderate. Notice, too, what Veer does not do. He does not hit people, hurt animals, destroy property, steal or run away; those belong to conduct disorder. Between his outbursts he is a cheerful boy, which matters for the next distinction. And children with ODD typically do not see themselves as angry or defiant at all; like Veer, they explain that the demands made of them are unreasonable. Oppositional defiant disorder is common. The manual gives a cross-national prevalence of 1 to 11 percent, with an average of about 3.3 percent; before adolescence it is somewhat commoner in boys (about 1.6 to 1), a difference not consistently found in adolescents and adults. The first symptoms usually appear in the preschool years and rarely later than early adolescence. Its future is the most important fact about it, and it divides along the symptom groups. Most children with ODD never develop conduct disorder, although ODD often precedes conduct disorder, especially the childhood-onset type. The defiant, argumentative and vindictive symptoms carry most of the risk of conduct disorder; the angry and irritable mood symptoms carry most of the risk of later anxiety and depressive disorders, even without conduct disorder. Adults who had persistent ODD as children have more troubled relationships, less education and more workplace stress. ODD is also associated with an increased risk of suicide attempts, even after other disorders are allowed for. The diagnosis depends on telling ODD apart from its many look-alikes, set out in Table 11.32. Three deserve a sentence each. A child with ADHD may also fail to do what he is told, but he fails because the task demands sustained attention or sitting still, not because he resents being told; the two disorders often coexist, and both can then be diagnosed (Section 3.7.5). A child with disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (Section 5.3.2) has severe temper outbursts, on average three or more times a week, and a persistently irritable or angry mood between them, nearly every day; such a child usually meets the ODD criteria too, but when DMDD is diagnosed ODD is not, even if all its criteria are met. That is why Veer's good humour between outbursts is diagnostically important. And conduct disorder, as you will see next, involves aggression to people or animals, destruction of property, theft or deceit, which ODD does not; yet ODD can be at least as impairing, and when a child meets the criteria for both, DSM-5-TR allows both diagnoses (DSM-IV did not). If the criteria for DMDD are met, ODD is not diagnosed. Most children with ODD do not go on to conduct disorder. Conduct disorder: the fifteen criteria Conduct disorder (CD) is a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour in which the basic rights of others, or major age-appropriate social norms or rules, are violated. The two halves of that definition matter. "The basic rights of others" covers what the child does to people, animals and property; "major age-appropriate norms" covers the rules that a child of that age is expected to keep, such as coming home at night and going to school. The pattern is shown by at least three of 15 criteria in the past 12 months, with at least one present in the past 6 months, from any of four groups (Table 11.33). The behaviour must cause clinically significant impairment in social, academic or occupational functioning. And if the person is 18 or older, the criteria for antisocial personality disorder must not be met; conduct disorder can be diagnosed in an adult, though onset after 16 is rare, but once the adult pattern of antisocial personality disorder is present that diagnosis replaces it.
