Some begin with "often" (bullies, initiates fights, lies, stays out, is truant): they describe repeated behaviour, because one fight or one lie means little. Others begin with "has" (has used a weapon, has been cruel, has stolen while confronting a victim, has forced someone into sex, has set fires, has broken in): these are acts serious enough that a single occurrence in the past year counts. The two rules with an age, staying out at night and truancy, must have begun before age 13 , because a 16-year-old who comes home late or misses lectures is breaking rules that are far less "age-appropriate" than an 11-year-old doing the same. And running away counts only if it happened at least twice overnight, or once for a long period, and not if the child was fleeing abuse: a girl who runs from a beating is protecting herself, not violating a norm. Falguni shows the criteria applied. In the past year she has repeatedly lied to her parents and relatives to obtain money (criterion 11), stolen a substantial sum from her aunt's purse when no one was looking (12), and run away overnight twice (14), the last time three months ago. That is three criteria in 12 months with at least one in the past 6, and her schooling and family life are badly impaired: conduct disorder. She has also been bunking school, but that began when she was 14, so it does not count towards criterion 15. Nothing in her history suggests conduct problems before the age of 10, a fact that the next subsection shows to be the most important thing about her. The manual grades severity by both the number of problems and the harm done. Mild : few if any problems beyond those needed for the diagnosis, causing relatively minor harm (lying, truancy, staying out late, other rule breaking). Moderate : intermediate in number and effect (stealing without confronting a victim, vandalism). Severe : many problems beyond those required, or problems that cause considerable harm (forced sex, physical cruelty, use of a weapon, stealing while confronting a victim, breaking and entering). Falguni's stealing makes her moderate; Daksh's cruelty and the cricket bat make him severe. Conduct disorder is common and costly. In the United States and other largely high-income countries the one-year prevalence ranges from 2 percent to more than 10 percent, with a median of 4 percent; one American survey found a lifetime prevalence of 12.0 percent in men and 7.1 percent in women. Rates rise from childhood into adolescence, and few children with impairing conduct disorder receive any treatment. The disorder looks different in the two sexes. Boys more often fight, steal, vandalise and get into trouble for school discipline; girls more often lie, are truant, run away, and are drawn into prostitution; both use relational aggression (harming another person's friendships and reputation), but girls show much less physical aggression. Substance misuse is a common associated feature, particularly in adolescent girls. Suicidal thoughts, attempts and suicide are more frequent than expected; a ten-year Taiwanese follow-up found that adolescents with conduct disorder made more suicide attempts even after mood, anxiety and substance use disorders were allowed for. The functional costs (suspension and expulsion, injuries, early pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections, police contact) may carry into poorer health in midlife. Exam trap Conduct disorder needs three or more of 15 criteria in the past 12 months , at least one in the past 6 months , from four groups: aggression to people and animals (7 criteria), destruction of property (2), deceitfulness or theft (3) and serious violations of rules (3). Staying out at night and truancy count only if they began before 13 . Fire setting with intent to cause serious damage is a conduct disorder criterion (destruction of property); pyromania is a separate disorder of fire setting for gratification or relief, and is not diagnosed when conduct disorder better explains the fires (Section 11.10). Conduct disorder can be diagnosed at 18 or over, but only if the criteria for antisocial personality disorder are not met. Two specifiers that predict the future: age at onset and limited prosocial emotions Of all the facts a clinician can gather about a child with conduct disorder, the age at which the problems began is one of the most informative, and DSM-5-TR builds it into the diagnosis as three subtypes. In the childhood-onset type the child showed at least one symptom of conduct disorder before the age of 10. In the adolescent-onset type no symptom appeared before 10. The unspecified onset type is used when the history is too thin to say. Either onset type can be mild, moderate or severe. The two onset types describe two different kinds of child. Children with the childhood-onset type are usually boys, often had oppositional defiant disorder in early childhood, usually meet the full criteria before puberty, are more physically aggressive, have disturbed relationships with other children, and very often have ADHD or another neurodevelopmental difficulty as well. Their families more often show the risk factors described in Section 11.9.6, and they are much more likely to carry the disorder into adulthood, with criminal behaviour, substance use and antisocial personality disorder. Children with the adolescent-onset type have more ordinary peer relationships, even if they misbehave in company, and most of them, especially those with fewer and milder problems, settle into adequate social and working lives as adults. Daksh, whose fights and cruelty to animals began when he was eight, has the childhood-onset type. Falguni, who was an ordinary student until fourteen, has the adolescent-onset type. If you had to bet on which of them will be in serious trouble at thirty, the onset type tells you where to put your money; Section 11.9.5 explains why. The second specifier is newer, and it is the most examined fact in this section. It grew out of a line of research led by the American psychologist Paul J. Frick , who later served as text coordinator of the DSM-5 work group on ADHD and the disruptive behaviour disorders and as section editor for this chapter of DSM-5-TR. Frick and his colleagues showed that within the large and varied group of children with serious conduct problems there is a smaller group marked by what they called callous-unemotional traits : a lack of guilt and empathy, a cold and shallow emotional life, and indifference to how well they do. These children resemble adult psychopaths in miniature (Section 11.5). DSM-5 turned the idea into the specifier with limited prosocial emotions . To qualify, the child must have shown at least two of the following four characteristics persistently over at least 12 months, in more than one relationship and setting: Lack of remorse or guilt. The child does not feel bad or guilty after doing something wrong and shows a general lack of concern about the consequences of his actions. Remorse expressed only when caught or facing punishment does not count. Callous lack of empathy. The child disregards and is unconcerned about other people's feelings; he is described as cold and uncaring, and seems more concerned about what his actions do to himself than about the harm they do to others. Unconcerned about performance. The child does not care about doing poorly at school, at work or in other important activities, does not make the effort needed even when expectations are clear, and typically blames others for poor results. Shallow or deficient affect. The child does not express feelings to others, or does so only in ways that seem shallow, insincere or superficial (emotions switched "on" and "off" quickly, or actions contradicting the emotion shown), or uses emotional displays for gain, to manipulate or intimidate. Every word of the specifier guards against a mistake. "Persistently over at least 12 months" and "in multiple relationships and settings" rule out a child who is cold to one disliked teacher or unrepentant after one incident; the specifier describes the child's typical way of relating, not an occasional state. And because children with these traits rarely admit to them in an interview, the manual insists on multiple sources of information: besides the child, people who have known him over long periods and in different settings, such as parents, teachers, relatives and peers. Daksh qualifies. His father has never seen genuine remorse ("he says sorry only when he is caught, and then he smiles"), teachers describe him as cold, he does not care about failing his examinations, and his tears, when they come, appear and vanish as needed. That is four of the four characteristics, at home and at school, for well over a year. Why does the specifier matter? The manual lists the reasons. Only a minority of children with conduct disorder qualify for it; in one study by Kahn, Frick and colleagues (2012), between 10 and 50 percent of youth with conduct disorder met the threshold, depending on the sample and on who was reporting. Those who do qualify are more likely to have the childhood-onset type and a severe rating, and more likely to show aggression that is planned for gain (instrumental aggression) rather than the hot-headed, reactive aggression of a frustrated child. Other features travel with them: thrill seeking, fearlessness and insensitivity to punishment. And their disorder is more likely to persist. Treatment research points the same way. In 2005 David J. Hawes and Mark R. Dadds followed 56 young boys (average age about six) through a 10-week behavioural parent-training programme. Boys with high callous-unemotional traits had more severe conduct problems to begin with and did worse at 6-month follow-up, even after the severity of their problems was allowed for; they responded less to time-out and showed less emotional reaction to it. Punishment, it seems, teaches these children less, which fits the fearlessness account of adult psychopathy that Section 11.5 develops from Lykken's work. Clinical link Assessing the specifier is a lesson in interviewing children. A twelve-year-old who has learned that adults want to hear "I am sorry" will say it; the question is whether he says it only when cornered, and whether his behaviour changes. Ask the parent, the class teacher and, where possible, the grandmother or the tuition teacher who sees the child in another setting: "When he hurts someone, what does he do next? Does he ever seem upset about it when no one is watching?" Record exactly who said what. A child who is distressed and guilty after his fights, however frequent, does not have limited prosocial emotions, and the distinction changes both the treatment plan and what you tell the family about the future. Exam trap In DSM-5-TR, "with limited prosocial emotions" is a specifier for conduct disorder only : not for antisocial personality disorder (whose Section III version has its own specifier, "with psychopathic features", Section 11.8.6), not for oppositional defiant disorder and not for intermittent explosive disorder. Its four characteristics are lack of remorse or guilt, callous lack of empathy, unconcern about performance, and shallow or deficient affect ; two or more are needed, for 12 months , in more than one relationship or setting. Wrong options in the papers include "hyperactivity and inattention" (that is ADHD), "comorbid major depression" and "onset before age 5" (no such rule; the onset types turn on age 10). Childhood-onset type means at least one symptom before age 10 . Two traps from other sources: some textbooks (Barlow and Durand among them) give the DSM-5 specifier as "with a callous-unemotional presentation", and the DSM-5 drafts proposed "with significant callous-unemotional traits", whereas the published manual says "with limited prosocial emotions"; and in ICD-11 the limited prosocial emotions qualifier can be applied to both conduct-dissocial disorder and oppositional defiant disorder (Section 11.9.8). A question that names DSM-5 or DSM-5-TR wants conduct disorder. Two paths through adolescence: Moffitt's developmental taxonomy Why should the age at onset matter so much? The most influential answer came from the American psychologist Terrie E. Moffitt (born 1955), in a 1993 paper in Psychological Review titled "Adolescence-limited and life-course-persistent antisocial behavior: a developmental taxonomy". Moffitt began with a puzzle that had troubled criminologists for decades. On the one hand, antisocial behaviour is remarkably continuous: the aggressive five-year-old is far more likely than his classmates to be the delinquent fifteen-year-old and the violent thirty-year-old. On the other hand, antisocial behaviour is remarkably common in adolescence: its prevalence rises almost tenfold during the teenage years and then falls away sharply in early adulthood, the famous age-crime curve. If antisocial behaviour is a stable trait, why do so many teenagers who were never troublesome as children suddenly start, and then just as suddenly stop? Moffitt's answer was that the puzzle dissolves once you see that "delinquents" are two different groups of people who happen to look alike for a few years. The first is a small group whose antisocial behaviour begins in early childhood and persists at every stage of life, changing only its form: biting and hitting at four, shoplifting and truancy at ten, selling drugs and stealing cars at sixteen, robbery and fraud at twenty-two, and violence towards a partner and children at thirty. She called this life-course-persistent antisocial behaviour . Its roots, she argued, are neuropsychological problems present early in life (difficulties with verbal ability and with executive functions such as self-control, often with a difficult temperament and hyperactivity), which meet and are magnified by a criminogenic environment: parents who are themselves struggling, harsh or inconsistent discipline, poverty. A difficult infant provokes coercive parenting, which makes the child more difficult; each failure (at school, with peers) narrows the options for the next stage, so the problems accumulate and become, in her words, a pathological personality. The second group is much larger. Its members had ordinary childhoods and begin offending around puberty. Moffitt called this adolescence-limited antisocial behaviour . Her explanation is one of the most quoted ideas in developmental psychology: the maturity gap . Modern teenagers are biologically adult years before society allows them adult privileges (money, independence, sex, respect), and the life-course-persistent youths around them seem to have exactly these things. So ordinary teenagers imitate them, a process Moffitt called social mimicry: smoking, drinking, vandalism and minor theft become ways of announcing that one is grown up. On this view adolescence-limited delinquency is normative and even adaptive, and it fades when adult roles (a job, a marriage, a home) offer the real thing. It fades, that is, unless the teenager is caught in one of the snares that can trap an adolescence-limited youth in antisocial behaviour: a criminal record, an addiction, dropping out of school, an early pregnancy. Key study: the Dunedin cohort and the two paths (1993 to 2008) The test bed for Moffitt's theory was the Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study, which follows 1,037 people born between April 1972 and March 1973 in the New Zealand city of Dunedin, a study founded by Phil Silva and assessed repeatedly from age 3 into middle age with remarkably few drop-outs. Moffitt and her husband and colleague Avshalom Caspi sorted the cohort's delinquents by the age at which their problems began. In 2001 they reported that the childhood-onset group had the predicted childhood risks (inadequate parenting, neurocognitive problems, difficult temperament and behaviour problems) and the adolescent-onset group did not; the male to female ratio was about 10 to 1 for childhood-onset delinquency but only about 1.5 to 1 for adolescent onset. At age 26 (2002) the childhood-onset men were the most impaired on every measure: psychopathic traits, mental health problems, substance dependence, financial and work problems, and drug-related and violent crime, including violence against women and children. The adolescent-onset men were less extreme, but they were not in the clear: they still showed impulsive traits, substance problems, financial difficulties and property offences. A third group, aggressive as children but not very delinquent as teenagers, became anxious, depressed, isolated low-level offenders. By age 32 (Candice Odgers and colleagues, 2008) four trajectories could be seen in both sexes, and life-course-persistent women, like the men, had serious problems with violence, mental and physical health and money. Criticism: the data show more than two groups, so "taxonomy" is a simplification; adolescence-limited offending is less benign and less limited than the name implies; and onset age is a marker of risk, not destiny. The theory maps neatly onto the DSM onset types. The childhood-onset type of conduct disorder is, roughly, the clinical face of the life-course-persistent path, and the adolescent-onset type of the adolescence-limited path, which is why DSM-5-TR says the childhood-onset type predicts a worse prognosis. Moffitt herself sat on the DSM-5 work group for ADHD and the disruptive behaviour disorders. For the clinician the lesson is practical: a history taken carefully back to early childhood (school reports, an old teacher's memory, a grandmother's account of the toddler years) can matter more than the details of the latest incident. Exam trap Terrie Moffitt (1993) proposed life-course-persistent versus adolescence-limited antisocial behaviour, using the Dunedin (New Zealand) study; not Patterson (coercive family process), not Robins (follow-up of St Louis child guidance clinic children) and not Frick (callous-unemotional traits). Life-course-persistent: rare , begins in early childhood , rooted in neuropsychological deficits plus adverse environments , mostly male, persists. Adolescence-limited: common , begins at puberty , explained by the maturity gap and social mimicry , sex ratio nearer equal, usually desists unless caught in snares . Why some children develop conduct disorder: genes, bodies, families and peers No single cause produces conduct disorder. What the research shows instead is a set of risk factors, biological, psychological, family and social, which add up and interact, and which are both more common and more severe in children with the childhood-onset type. It helps to take them in the order in which they come into a child's life. Genes. Conduct disorder runs in families, and twin and adoption studies show that this is partly genetic. Risk rises when a biological or adoptive parent or a sibling has conduct disorder (the adoptive parent is a reminder that families also pass on environments), and the disorder is more common in the children of biological parents with severe alcohol use disorder, depressive and bipolar disorders, schizophrenia, ADHD or conduct disorder. In 2002 Soo Hyun Rhee and Irwin Waldman pooled 51 twin and adoption studies of antisocial behaviour. In their best-fitting model, additive genetic influences accounted for 32 percent of the variation, non-additive genetic influences for 9 percent, the shared environment (what siblings in one family have in common) for 16 percent, and the non-shared environment (experiences unique to each child) for 43 percent. Genes and environment, in other words, each matter a great deal. Genetic influence appears stronger for the aggressive symptoms than for rule breaking, and a family history is particularly typical of the childhood-onset type. The best-known gene-environment interaction in psychiatry, between a variant of the MAOA gene and childhood maltreatment in the Dunedin cohort (Caspi and colleagues, 2002), is told as a Key study in Chapter 1 (Section 1.5) and recalled in Section 11.5. Temperament, intelligence and the body. A difficult, undercontrolled temperament in infancy and lower than average intelligence, especially verbal intelligence, predict later conduct disorder; these are exactly the early neuropsychological problems at the root of Moffitt's life-course-persistent path. Two physiological findings are unusually robust. A slower resting heart rate has been reliably found in children with conduct disorder, and DSM-5-TR notes that this marker is not characteristic of any other mental disorder; reduced autonomic fear conditioning, especially low skin conductance responses, is also well documented. Brain-imaging studies consistently find structural and functional differences in the circuits that regulate and process emotion, particularly the connections between the ventral prefrontal cortex and the amygdala. None of these findings is diagnostic, and none can be used to identify an individual child. What they mean (a fearless, under-aroused child who learns little from punishment and seeks stimulation) is the subject of the fearlessness and stimulation-seeking theories of antisocial personality in Section 11.5. Families and the coercive cycle. The family-level risk factors listed by DSM-5-TR read like a catalogue of childhood adversity: parental rejection and neglect, inconsistent child-rearing, harsh discipline, physical or sexual abuse, lack of supervision, early institutional living, frequent changes of caregiver, large family size, parental criminality and parental substance use disorders. The most detailed account of how parenting and a child's behaviour shape each other came from Gerald R. Patterson (1926 to 2016) and his colleagues at the Oregon Social Learning Center, who spent years observing aggressive children and their families at home, recording every exchange. In his 1982 book Coercive Family Process Patterson described what he called the coercive family process . Picture it in an ordinary Indian flat. A mother tells her eight-year-old to switch off the television and do his homework. He ignores her. She repeats the instruction more loudly; he whines and argues; she shouts; he screams, kicks the sofa and calls her names. At last, exhausted and embarrassed in front of the neighbours, she gives up and walks into the kitchen. Peace returns. Both have learned something. The boy has learned, by negative reinforcement, that escalating his aversive behaviour makes the demand go away. The mother has learned, also by negative reinforcement, that giving in makes the screaming stop. Each partner's behaviour is rewarded by the other, so the cycle repeats and escalates: the child learns that the louder he fights the more often he wins, and the parent learns that the only way to "win" is to withdraw all demands, or to explode in turn. Add poor monitoring of where the child is and what he is doing, parental depression and low involvement, and the pattern is maintained. Patterson and his colleagues (Patterson, DeBaryshe and Ramsey, 1989) traced what happens next. A child trained in coercion at home carries it to school, where his aggression and defiance bring academic failure and rejection by ordinary classmates in middle childhood. Rejected children drift together, and by late childhood and adolescence the child has committed himself to a deviant peer group, which supplies the models, opportunities and approval for delinquency. That sequence, home to school to peers, is the early-starter path, and it is the social half of Moffitt's life-course-persistent theory. Its practical corollary is parent management training (Section 11.9.9), which teaches parents to break the cycle. How the child reads the world. The American psychologist Kenneth A. Dodge studied what happens inside an aggressive child's head in the moment before he hits. In his social information-processing studies, aggressive children shown an ambiguous provocation (a classmate's ball strikes them from behind, a drink is spilled on their work) were much more likely than other children to conclude that it was done on purpose, and then to retaliate. This hostile attribution bias , which DSM-5-TR describes in its account of conduct disorder, makes aggression feel justified to the child: he believes he is only defending himself. Dodge and John Coie (1987) also distinguished reactive aggression , hot-headed retaliation to perceived threat, which goes with hostile attributions, from proactive aggression , cool and planned use of force to get something, which is closer to the instrumental aggression of children with limited prosocial emotions. Peers, neighbourhood and culture. At the community level the risk factors are peer rejection, membership of a delinquent peer group, neighbourhood disadvantage and exposure to violence. Co-occurring ADHD and substance use make persistence more likely. Two cautions about culture complete the picture. Disruptive behaviour can be near normal in some settings, such as very threatening, high-crime areas or war zones, and the diagnosis should not be applied to a child whose behaviour is an adaptation to such a place. And DSM-5-TR warns that in youth from marginalised groups, anger and resistance in reaction to discrimination can be misdiagnosed as conduct disorder by an uninformed clinician; an Indian clinician should hold the same caution about children who face discrimination by caste, religion or class. On the other side of the ledger, first-generation immigrants and refugees often have fewer conduct problems than their peers, despite their adversities. Exam trap The coercive family process (negative reinforcement of child aggression and parental giving-in) is Gerald Patterson's (1982), not Moffitt's or Bandura's. The hostile attribution bias is Kenneth Dodge's . A slower resting heart rate is the most reliable physiological marker of conduct disorder and, according to DSM-5-TR, is not characteristic of any other mental disorder ; but no biological finding is diagnostic. Rhee and Waldman's meta-analysis put genetic influences on antisocial behaviour at roughly 40 percent (32 additive plus 9 non-additive), with environment accounting for the rest. Course and outcome: the road to antisocial personality The single most hopeful fact about conduct disorder is in the manual: in a majority of individuals the disorder remits by adulthood. Many people with conduct disorder, especially those with the adolescent-onset type and those with few and milder symptoms, achieve adequate social and occupational adjustment as adults. The childhood-onset type predicts a worse prognosis, with a higher risk of criminal behaviour, persisting conduct problems and substance-related disorders; persistence is also more likely with limited prosocial emotions, co-occurring ADHD and substance use. The order in which symptoms appear tells part of the story. The first to emerge tend to be the less serious (lying, shoplifting) and the last the most severe (rape, theft while confronting a victim), and physically aggressive symptoms are commoner in childhood while nonaggressive ones become commoner in adolescence; a child who shows the most damaging behaviours early has the worst outlook. The developmental chain that runs through this chapter therefore links three diagnoses, but only for a minority at each step. Oppositional defiant disorder often precedes the childhood-onset type of conduct disorder, yet most children with ODD never develop conduct disorder. Conduct disorder is the necessary precursor of antisocial personality disorder, yet most children with conduct disorder never become antisocial adults. Lee Robins, whose follow-up of the St Louis child guidance clinic children opens this chapter, summarised the paradox in 1978: adult antisocial behaviour virtually requires childhood antisocial behaviour, yet most antisocial children do not grow up to be antisocial adults. DSM-5-TR writes the first half of that finding into its rules. Antisocial personality disorder (Section 11.5) can be diagnosed only in a person at least 18 years old who has shown evidence of conduct disorder with onset before the age of 15, and the pervasive pattern of disregard for others' rights must have been present since age 15. When a person with conduct disorder reaches adulthood and the aggression, destruction, deceit and rule breaking continue at work and at home, including violence towards partners and children, the diagnosis moves from conduct disorder to antisocial personality disorder. Antisocial personality is not the only adult outcome. People who had conduct disorder are at increased risk of mood disorders, anxiety disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder, impulse-control disorders, psychotic disorders, somatic symptom disorders and substance-related disorders, and of the social consequences of a disrupted youth: incomplete education, unstable work, early parenthood and poor health in midlife. The Dunedin data showed that this is true of women as well as men: by 32, women on the life-course-persistent path had serious problems with violence, mental and physical health and money, just as the men did, although fewer women follow that path. One distinction that the papers like to test does not belong to this chain at all. Conduct disorder in childhood leads, in those whom it follows into adulthood, to antisocial personality disorder, not to borderline personality disorder; how the two differ (a youthful pattern of rule violation and aggression versus an adult pattern of unstable identity, affect and relationships with fear of abandonment) is taught in Section 11.3. Exam trap The majority of children with conduct disorder remit by adulthood, and most do not develop antisocial personality disorder; the childhood-onset type and limited prosocial emotions predict persistence. The link runs one way in the rules: antisocial personality disorder needs evidence of conduct disorder with onset before 15 and an age of at least 18 (Section 11.5 sets out the age traps). Childhood conduct disorder leads to antisocial , not borderline, personality disorder; a mock-paper question that contrasts the two wants "borderline personality disorder is an adult pattern of identity and affective instability with fear of abandonment; conduct disorder is diagnosed in youth and centres on rule-violating, aggressive behaviour" (Section 11.3). Conduct disorders in ICD-10 and ICD-11 ICD-10 classified the conduct disorders (F91) among the behavioural and emotional disorders with onset usually in childhood and adolescence (F90 to F98). Its general description is a repetitive and persistent pattern of dissocial, aggressive or defiant conduct, more severe than ordinary childish mischief or adolescent rebelliousness, lasting 6 months or longer. Its subtypes were organised not by age of onset but by the setting and the child's social integration, the idea DSM-III had used. Conduct disorder confined to the family context (F91.0) is antisocial behaviour shown entirely, or almost entirely, at home or towards members of the household. Unsocialised conduct disorder (F91.1) combines persistent dissocial or aggressive behaviour with a pervasive abnormality in the child's relationships with other children: he is not integrated into any peer group and is isolated or rejected. Socialised conduct disorder (F91.2) occurs in a child who is generally well integrated into a peer group, often a group of delinquent friends. Oppositional defiant disorder (F91.3) was placed inside the conduct disorders as their mildest form, characteristically seen in children below the age of about 9 or 10 years, with defiant, disobedient, provocative behaviour but without severe dissocial or aggressive acts. ICD-10 also offered a mixed disorder of conduct and emotions (F92), for conduct disorder combined with marked depression (F92.0, depressive conduct disorder) or other emotional symptoms such as anxiety (F92.8), and hyperkinetic conduct disorder (F90.1) for children who meet the criteria for both hyperkinetic disorder and conduct disorder. ICD-11 places these conditions in a block called disruptive behaviour or dissocial disorders. Oppositional defiant disorder (6C90) is divided into ODD with chronic irritability-anger (6C90.0) and without it (6C90.1). The irritability qualifier is ICD-11's answer to the problem DSM-5 solved with disruptive mood dysregulation disorder: ICD-11 has no DMDD, and records the persistently irritable, angry child as ODD with chronic irritability-anger instead (Section 5.3.2). Conduct disorder becomes conduct-dissocial disorder (6C91), with a childhood-onset type (6C91.0, features before adolescence, for example before age 10) and an adolescent-onset type (6C91.1). And ICD-11 attaches its own limited prosocial emotions qualifier, describing what are sometimes called callous and unemotional traits, to both disorders: each ODD and conduct-dissocial code can be completed as "with limited prosocial emotions" or "with typical prosocial emotions" (6C91.00, for instance, is childhood-onset conduct-dissocial disorder with limited prosocial emotions). Treatment, and conduct disorder in Indian law The treatments with the best evidence for oppositional defiant and conduct disorders are psychological, and they are taught in Book 2; here, what each is and where the evidence stands. Parent management training , which grew directly out of Patterson's work, teaches parents to give clear instructions, attend to and reward good behaviour, ignore minor provocations, use brief non-violent consequences such as time-out consistently, and supervise their children, so breaking the coercive cycle; it is the best-supported treatment for younger children with ODD and conduct problems (Book 2, Sections 4.10.4 and 10.3.5). For school-age children, problem-solving skills training , developed by Alan E. Kazdin , and anger-management programmes such as John E. Lochman 's Coping Power teach the child to stop, read social situations without a hostile bias, generate alternatives and weigh consequences, directly targeting the processing errors Dodge described (Book 2, Section 10.3.4). For serious adolescent offenders, multisystemic therapy , developed by Scott W. Henggeler and colleagues, is an intensive home- and community-based treatment that works on the young person's family, school, peers and neighbourhood at once. Book 2, Section 10.4.4 brings these together for oppositional and conduct problems. Two general findings run through the research: the younger the child, the better the response, and children with limited prosocial emotions respond less well to standard programmes, especially to their punishment components. A third is a warning: grouping antisocial adolescents together for treatment can make them worse, because the group teaches and rewards deviance (Thomas Dishion and colleagues described such iatrogenic peer effects in 1999). No medicine treats conduct disorder itself. The nearest thing to an approval is narrow: in the United Kingdom and Europe risperidone is licensed only for the short-term treatment (up to 6 weeks) of persistent aggression in conduct disorder in children from 5 years and adolescents with below-average intellectual functioning. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline on antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders in children and young people (CG158, 2013) advises against using drugs for the routine management of behaviour problems. It allows the antipsychotic risperidone to be considered for the short-term management of severely aggressive behaviour, in young people with explosive anger and severe emotional dysregulation, when psychosocial interventions have failed, after a full assessment and baseline physical investigations, with regular monitoring of effect and side effects. Those side effects are the familiar ones of second-generation antipsychotics (Section 4.10): weight gain and metabolic changes, raised prolactin, sedation, and less often movement disorders, which is why the guideline asks for height and weight to be plotted on a growth chart. When ADHD coexists, as it so often does in the childhood-onset type, treating the ADHD according to its own guidance, with methylphenidate or atomoxetine (Section 3.8), often reduces the conduct problems as well. Mood stabilisers have been tried for aggression, but the evidence is weaker. Indian context In India, a person under 18 who is alleged or found to have committed an offence is a child in conflict with law under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, which received presidential assent on 31 December 2015 and came into force on 15 January 2016. Such children are dealt with by a Juvenile Justice Board, not an ordinary criminal court, and the emphasis is on care, rehabilitation and reintegration. The Act's most debated change followed public anger over the December 2012 Delhi gang rape, in which one accused was a few months short of 18. Under Section 15, when a child who has completed 16 years is alleged to have committed a heinous offence (one carrying a minimum punishment of seven years' imprisonment or more), the Board must make a preliminary assessment of the child's mental and physical capacity to commit the offence, ability to understand its consequences and the circumstances in which it was committed, and it may take the assistance of experienced psychologists, psycho-social workers or other experts. On that assessment the case may be transferred to a Children's Court and the child tried as an adult. The Supreme Court has stressed that this is a delicate task needing expertise (Barun Chandra Thakur versus Master Bholu, 2022), and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights issued guidelines for it in 2023. Clinical psychologists are therefore increasingly asked to assess adolescents with conduct problems for the courts (Book 2, Section 10.9). Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. Criterion A of the Alternative Model requires at least level 2, impairment, on the Level of Personality Functioning Scale. Answers: (1) severe, (2) difficulty, (3) anankastia, (4) antagonism, (5) moderate, (6) dependent, (7) four, (8) 10, (9) conduct disorder, (10) adolescence-limited. 11.10 Impulse-Control Disorders: Intermittent Explosive Disorder, Pyromania and Kleptomania Medium yield · 2 Qs Most people know the moment. A car cuts across you on the flyover and for a second you want to lean on the horn and shout something unprintable. A box of sweets sits unattended on a colleague's desk and your hand drifts towards it. You stand by the bonfire on Lohri night and feel an odd pull to throw on one more stick, just to watch the flames leap. For nearly everyone the moment passes. Something like a brake engages, the urge is weighed against what it would cost, and the urge loses. This section is about people in whom, again and again, the urge wins: the man whose rage at a trivial slight ends in a broken door or a bleeding stranger, the young man who sets fires because fire itself thrills him, and the woman who steals lipsticks she could easily afford and then throws them away. Their acts look like crimes, and many of them end in court, yet the motive that drives ordinary crime, gain, is missing. What drives them instead is the question of this section. Section 11.9 explained why DSM-5-TR places these three conditions in one chapter with oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder. Here you will go further: first what an impulse-control disorder is and how the idea grew out of the "monomanias" of nineteenth-century Paris, then each of the three disorders in turn, and finally the wider family of impulse disorders as ICD-10 and ICD-11 draw it, including the two conditions that have left the family (gambling and hair pulling) and the one that ICD-11 has added (compulsive sexual behaviour disorder). The failure to resist: what an impulse-control disorder is Begin with the word. An impulse is a sudden urge to act, felt before there has been time to think the act through. The tendency to act on such urges is impulsivity . A widely used definition, from the American psychiatrist F. Gerard Moeller , the psychologist Ernest S. Barratt and their colleagues in 2001, calls it "a predisposition toward rapid, unplanned reactions to internal or external stimuli without regard to the negative consequences of these reactions" to the person or to others. Everybody has some impulsivity, and a little of it is useful: a person who never acts without a week of deliberation misses every chance that comes and goes quickly. Too much of it runs through half of psychiatry. You have met it in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (Chapter 3), in the reckless spending and sexual behaviour of mania (Chapter 5), in the binges of bulimia nervosa (Chapter 8) and in the substance use disorders (Chapter 10), and in this chapter it is one of the nine criteria of borderline personality disorder and one of the seven of antisocial personality disorder. Impulse control is even one of the four areas in which the general definition of a personality disorder can show itself (Section 11.1). Impulsivity is not one thing. In 2001 the psychologists Stephen P. Whiteside and Donald R. Lynam analysed the many questionnaires that claim to measure it and found four separable tendencies: urgency (acting rashly when gripped by strong feeling), lack of premeditation (acting without thinking ahead), lack of perseverance (abandoning tasks that have become boring) and sensation seeking (craving excitement and novelty). The disorders in this section draw on different parts of that mixture. The man who explodes at a minor provocation shows urgency in its purest form. The fire setter who is fascinated by flames, fire engines and the crowd that gathers looks much more like a sensation seeker. The shoplifter who could easily have paid is caught by an urge she cannot explain even to herself. What, then, turns an impulse into a disorder? DSM-IV (1994) gave the classic answer. The essential feature of an impulse-control disorder , it said, is "the failure to resist an impulse, drive, or temptation to perform an act that is harmful to the person or to others". For most of these disorders, it went on, the person feels an increasing sense of tension or arousal before the act, experiences pleasure, gratification or relief while committing it, and afterwards may or may not feel regret, self-reproach or guilt. That sequence, drawn in Figure 11.16, is the impulse cycle . Learn it stage by stage, because most examination questions about these disorders are really questions about where in the cycle a symptom belongs. 1 Urge and rising tension trigger: stress, boredom, a cue 2 Failure to resist: the act steals, sets a fire, explodes 3 Pleasure, gratification or relief, during the act 4 Afterwards regret, guilt, shame, or none the urge returns tension falls Tension or arousal over time high low time tension builds act act relief The line shows tension: it drops at each act and then builds again. Figure 11.16 The impulse cycle. Tension builds, the act discharges it with pleasure or relief, regret (if any) comes afterwards, and the urge returns. The relief arrives at once and the cost arrives late, which is why the cycle keeps turning. Look at what each stage contributes. The first is the urge, usually set off by something quite ordinary: boredom, a quarrel, a lonely evening, the sight of an open display counter. The tension builds, sometimes over minutes and sometimes over days, and the person may fight it. In the second stage the fight is lost. The third stage is the reason the cycle repeats. The act brings pleasure (a thrill, a "high") or relief (the tension drops away), and often both. In the language of learning theory, which Book 1 teaches, the pleasure is positive reinforcement and the removal of an unpleasant state of tension is negative reinforcement, and an act that is reinforced at once becomes more likely next time. The fourth stage, regret, comes too late to compete: a punishment that arrives hours later, or only when the police arrive months later, suppresses a behaviour far less than a reward that arrives in the same second. Then the tension begins to build again. Notice also how the act feels while it is happening. At that moment it is wanted; the person is not fighting it but welcoming it. Clinicians say the act is ego-syntonic at the time it is done, even if the person condemns it bitterly afterwards. This is the sharpest difference between an impulsive act and a compulsion, the repetitive act of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD; Chapter 6, Section 6.5.2). A compulsion is driven by dread, not desire. The woman who washes her hands forty times does so to undo the contamination she fears, and the washing relieves anxiety but never gives pleasure; she experiences it as alien and senseless, that is, ego-dystonic (Section 6.5.4). In the 1990s the American psychiatrist Eric Hollander and his colleagues proposed that the disorders of repetitive behaviour could be arranged along a single dimension. At the compulsive end people overestimate harm and act to avoid it; at the impulsive end they underestimate harm and act to obtain pleasure or arousal. OCD sits at one end. Pyromania, kleptomania, pathological gambling and explosive outbursts sit towards the other. Hair pulling, which can be pleasurable and yet is fought against, sits in between, a middle position that fits with its later move out of the impulse-control disorders, as the next subsection explains. DSM-5-TR still requires the rise of tension before the act and the pleasure or relief that follows it for pyromania and kleptomania; those two criteria are the heart of both diagnoses. It does not require them for intermittent explosive disorder, which is defined by the outbursts themselves, although many people with that disorder describe their outbursts as attacks or spells in which pressure builds, bursts and drains away, leaving remorse behind. And when DSM-5 rehoused trichotillomania it dropped the tension and relief criteria altogether, because a substantial number of people who pull their hair do not experience that sequence (Section 6.6.5). Exam trap The impulse cycle is tension or arousal before the act, then pleasure, gratification or relief during it, then (sometimes) regret . Anxiety relief without pleasure, in response to an obsession, is the mark of a compulsion , not an impulse. "Ego-syntonic at the time of the act" describes the impulse-control disorders; "ego-dystonic" describes OCD. The rising tension and the relief are formal criteria for pyromania and kleptomania , not for intermittent explosive disorder, and DSM-5 removed them from trichotillomania. From monomania to a chapter of its own: the history and the classification The idea that a person might be driven to one particular harmful act while remaining sane in every other respect is a child of the early nineteenth century. Philippe Pinel had already described patients whose behaviour was violently disordered without any delusion, his manie sans délire (Section 11.5 tells that story). His pupil Jean-Étienne Dominique Esquirol (1772 to 1840) went further with the concept of monomania , a partial insanity confined to one sphere of the mind while the rest stays intact. Among its forms was an "instinctive" monomania, in which the will is driven to acts that reason condemns, and French physicians began to give each such impulse its own name, built from a Greek root and the word mania. In 1816 the Swiss physician André Matthey described thieves who stole things they did not need and called the condition klopémanie , stealing madness. In 1833 Charles Chrétien Henri Marc (1771 to 1841; some French sources date his death to January 1840), a Paris physician and a leading figure in French legal medicine, published a long medico-legal study of monomanie incendiaire (incendiary monomania) and used the word pyromanie , pyromania, from the Greek pyr , fire. And in 1838 Esquirol and Marc renamed Matthey's condition kleptomanie , from the Greek kleptein , to steal. The English word kleptomania comes from them. These names were made in the courtroom as much as in the clinic, and that origin explains the suspicion that has followed them ever since. If a farmhand who set fire to a barn was suffering from incendiary monomania, he was ill rather than wicked, and could not justly be hanged. Critics answered that nobody can tell an impulse that could not be resisted from one that simply was not resisted, the same objection that later dogged the "irresistible impulse" test of insanity (Book 2, Section 10.9.3). The psychiatrist Jeffrey L. Geller and his colleagues, in a 1986 history of pyromania in America, traced how the diagnosis rose in the era of moral insanity in the 1840s, when it was called a monomania, an impulsive mania or an instinctive mania; faded once physicians began to argue that there could be diseased brains but not diseased minds, so that fire setting without a brain lesion became a moral failing to be punished; and returned with psychoanalysis between the 1920s and the 1950s, when it was explained as an irresistible impulse, an obsession or a "urethral-erotic" character trait. That last phrase goes back to Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939), who in a footnote to Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) speculated that primitive man could tame fire only after he had renounced the pleasure of putting it out by urinating on it. The theory linked fire setting with bedwetting for decades; there has never been good evidence for it. The great German classifier Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926) gathered the impulsive acts into a single chapter on "impulsive insanity" ( das impulsive Irresein ) in the eighth edition of his textbook, published between 1909 and 1915. Its common forms were impulsive fire setting, stealing, poisoning, child killing and running up debts. His descriptions tell you as much about his society as about his patients. Impulsive fire setting, he wrote, was mostly a disorder of inexperienced young women, predisposed by low intelligence, a parent's alcoholism or a "hysterical" make-up, and placed in positions of dependence they were trying to escape; impulsive theft, especially from the new department stores, was a weakness of otherwise respectable women, worst during menstruation. The young Karl Jaspers (1883 to 1969), later famous for his General Psychopathology , wrote his doctoral dissertation, published in 1909 as Heimweh und Verbrechen (Homesickness and Crime), on the link between homesickness and impulsive crimes, especially among young servant girls. Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) carried Kraepelin's category into his own textbook, which is one reason his name turns up as a distractor in questions about kleptomania. Notice the pattern. Until well into the twentieth century both pyromania and kleptomania were imagined as disorders of women, explained by the womb, menstruation and the menopause, and the department-store "lady thief" was a stock figure in the newspapers of Paris, London and New York, with sceptics complaining that kleptomania was simply an excuse for wealthy women caught shoplifting. Today kleptomania is still diagnosed more often in women, but fire setting is far commoner in men. The American manuals took a long time to settle the family. DSM-I (1952) mentioned kleptomania only as a supplementary term, not a formal diagnosis, and DSM-II (1968) left it out altogether. The explosive outbursts lived for two editions among the personality disorders: in DSM-I as the "aggressive type" of passive-aggressive personality, and in DSM-II as "explosive personality". DSM-III (1980) created a group called "disorders of impulse control not elsewhere classified", whose members included pathological gambling, kleptomania, pyromania and intermittent explosive disorder, the first time the explosive outbursts had been a disorder in their own right rather than a type of personality. The phrase "not elsewhere classified" mattered: problems of impulse control that belonged to another group (substance use, paraphilias, binge eating, the impulsivity of a personality disorder) stayed where they were, and the new group took only the orphans. DSM-III-R (1987) added trichotillomania, and DSM-IV (1994) kept the five disorders plus "impulse-control disorder not otherwise specified". DSM-5 (2013) broke the group up. Pathological gambling, renamed gambling disorder, moved to the chapter on substance-related and addictive disorders, because gambling activates the brain's reward systems much as drugs do and produces symptoms like those of the substance use disorders (Chapter 10, Section 10.1.7). Trichotillomania moved to the new obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, because it runs in families with OCD, co-occurs with it and responds to some of the same treatments (Chapter 6, Section 6.6.5). The three that remained, intermittent explosive disorder, pyromania and kleptomania, joined oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder (which is listed in both places) in a new chapter, "Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders". Section 11.9 explains why. In one sentence: all the disorders in that chapter are failures of emotional and behavioural self-control that violate the rights of others or bring the person into conflict with society's norms. Within it, DSM-5-TR places intermittent explosive disorder at the "emotion" end (poorly controlled anger), conduct disorder at the "behaviour" end, and describes pyromania and kleptomania as poor control over one specific behaviour, fire setting or stealing, that relieves inner tension. Even the codes tell the story. DSM-5-TR prints ICD-10-CM codes, and intermittent explosive disorder (F63.81), pyromania (F63.1) and kleptomania (F63.2) still carry numbers from ICD-10's block of habit and impulse disorders, F63, which Section 11.10.8 describes. Exam trap Who named what: Matthey , klopémanie (1816); Marc , pyromanie (1833); Esquirol and Marc , kleptomanie (1838); Esquirol , monomania; Kraepelin , impulsive insanity (eighth edition, 1909 to 1915). The DSM-IV "impulse-control disorders not elsewhere classified" were five: intermittent explosive disorder, kleptomania, pyromania, pathological gambling and trichotillomania. In DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR only the first three remain impulse-control disorders, in the chapter "Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders"; gambling is an addictive disorder and trichotillomania an obsessive-compulsive and related disorder. An option that still lists gambling or hair pulling as a DSM-5 impulse-control disorder is out of date. Intermittent explosive disorder: the clinical picture Uday is 29 and works as a software tester in Hyderabad. His wife calls him "the gentlest man in the world, ninety-nine percent of the time". The other one percent has cost him dearly. In the past four months he has screamed abuse at a delivery boy who rang the bell twice, hurled his phone onto the sofa when a video call froze, and shouted at his mother until she wept because she had put too much salt in the dal. These verbal storms come two or three times a week; each blows up in seconds and blows out within a quarter of an hour. Twice in the past year the storm was worse. After an argument about money he kicked in the panel of a cupboard door, and last month, when an auto-rickshaw driver refused to go by the meter, he grabbed the man by the collar and split his lip. Afterwards Uday is ashamed. "It is as if something switches on," he says. "I feel it boiling up, and then I am watching myself do it. Afterwards I am drained, and then I feel sick with myself." He is sober when it happens, he is not depressed, he has never had a head injury, and he gains nothing from the outbursts except a cupboard to repair, a police complaint and a frightened family. Uday has intermittent explosive disorder (IED): recurrent behavioural outbursts that represent a failure to control aggressive impulses. The word intermittent is chosen with care. Between outbursts the person's mood and behaviour may be quite unremarkable, and that is one of the things that separates IED from the conditions it resembles. DSM-5-TR's criteria can be learned in three groups. What the outbursts must look like (Criterion A). There are two routes, and either is enough (Figure 11.17). The first is frequent and relatively mild: verbal aggression (temper tantrums, tirades, verbal arguments or fights) or physical aggression towards property, animals or other people that causes no damage and no injury, occurring twice a week on average for 3 months. Uday's shouting meets this route. The second is infrequent and severe: three outbursts within 12 months that damage or destroy property or that injure an animal or a person. Uday's cupboard and the driver's lip make two; he does not yet meet the second route, and does not need to. DSM-5-TR notes that many people show both patterns, with milder outbursts in between occasional destructive ones. The value of the damaged object does not matter; smashing a cheap plastic chair counts. A1: verbal, or physical without damage or injury twice a week on average, for 3 months (12 weeks shown) or A2: damage to property, or injury to a person or animal three such outbursts within 12 months (12 months shown) Plus all of these: B far out of proportion C impulsive, not planned D distress or impairment E aged 6 or older F no better explanation A typical outburst: sudden, over within 30 minutes, after a minor provocation. Dots: outbursts without damage or injury. Squares: damaging or injurious outbursts. Figure 11.17 The two routes to Criterion A of intermittent explosive disorder: frequent outbursts that harm nothing, or a few that do. Either route counts only when the outbursts are also disproportionate, unplanned, impairing, in a person aged at least 6, and not better explained by something else. What makes the outbursts disordered (Criteria B, C and D). The aggression must be grossly out of proportion to the provocation or to any stressor that set it off (Criterion B): a salty dal, a doorbell rung twice. It must not be premeditated, that is, it is impulsive or anger-based, and it must not be committed to achieve some tangible objective such as money, power or intimidation (Criterion C). And it must cause marked distress, impair the person's work or relationships, or bring financial or legal consequences (Criterion D). Criterion C is the one that does the most work, because it separates two kinds of aggression that psychologists have long distinguished. The first, reactive aggression , also called hostile or affective aggression, is hot: a furious response to a perceived provocation or threat. The second, proactive aggression , also called instrumental aggression, is cold: aggression used as a tool to obtain something. The developmental psychologist Kenneth A. Dodge (Section 11.9), who studied both in aggressive children in the 1980s, showed that reactively aggressive children tend to read hostile intent into ambiguous situations (a push in the queue is taken as an attack), the hostile attribution bias. IED is a disorder of reactive aggression. The bully who threatens a classmate for his lunch money is showing proactive aggression, and that belongs with conduct disorder (Section 11.9). Who can receive the diagnosis (Criteria E and F). The person must be at least 6 years old, or at an equivalent developmental level, because tantrums are normal in small children (Criterion E). The outbursts must not be better explained by another mental disorder (major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, a psychotic disorder, antisocial or borderline personality disorder), must not be the result of a medical condition such as head trauma or Alzheimer's disease, and must not be the effect of a drug or medication (Criterion F). In children and adolescents aged 6 to 18, aggression that is part of an adjustment disorder does not count. A note to the criteria adds that IED can be diagnosed in addition to ADHD, conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder or autism spectrum disorder when the outbursts go beyond what is usual in those disorders and need attention in their own right. DSM-5-TR describes the typical outburst exactly as Uday experiences it: a rapid onset with little or no warning, a duration of less than 30 minutes, and a trigger that is usually a minor provocation by someone close, a spouse, a parent, a colleague. Depressive, anxiety and substance use disorders often accompany IED, but they usually begin later than the outbursts. These criteria are new. DSM-IV demanded "several discrete episodes" of failure to resist aggressive impulses that resulted in serious assault or destruction of property, so a man who only shouted, however often and however destructively for his family, could not qualify. DSM-5 widened the diagnosis to include verbal aggression and non-damaging physical aggression, and added the frequency thresholds. The changes followed research criteria first published in 1998, and later revised, by the American psychiatrist Emil F. Coccaro and his colleagues, which, Coccaro argued in 2012, identified people with higher levels of aggression, impulsivity, family history of aggression and biological markers of aggression better than the DSM-IV criteria did. Barlow and Durand note the controversy that has always surrounded the diagnosis: critics fear that a general category for aggressive behaviour could be offered as an insanity defence for any violent crime. How common is it? Far commoner than was believed when DSM-III introduced it as a rare disorder. In the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, a household survey of 9,282 American adults carried out between 2001 and 2003, Ronald C. Kessler , Coccaro and their colleagues (2006) found that 7.3 percent met DSM-IV criteria at some point in life and 3.9 percent in the past year. The average person with IED had had 43 attacks in a lifetime, causing about 1,359 dollars of property damage, and there were 180 injuries for every 100 cases; the average age at onset was 14; and although most had at some time been treated for some emotional or substance problem, only 28.8 percent had ever been treated for their anger. Surveys that define the disorder differently give different figures, and DSM-5-TR gives a 1-year prevalence of about 2.6 percent in the United States and a lifetime prevalence of 4.0 percent. The disorder is commoner in people younger than about 35 to 40 than in those over 50, and in people with a high-school education or less; some studies find it commoner in men and boys and others find no difference. Lower rates in parts of Asia and the Middle East, says DSM-5-TR, may mean that such behaviour is less often present, or simply that it is less often reported when people are asked; a clinician anywhere, India included, has to ask about outbursts directly, because patients and families tend to call them temper rather than illness. The outbursts usually begin in late childhood or adolescence and rarely start for the first time after 40. The course is chronic and persistent over many years, sometimes episodic, with stretches of frequent outbursts. The costs are what you would expect: lost friends, broken marriages, demotion and dismissal, the price of what was smashed, civil suits and criminal charges. The risk of suicide is real too. In one study of 1,460 research volunteers, people with IED who also had posttraumatic stress disorder had a lifetime rate of suicide attempts of 41 percent. Because angry outbursts occur in so many conditions, the diagnosis is largely a matter of exclusion, and Table 11.36 sets out the look-alikes. Two are worth spelling out. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (Chapter 5, Section 5.3.2) also has severe temper outbursts, but between them the child's mood is persistently irritable or angry most of the day, nearly every day; it must begin before age 10 and cannot be diagnosed for the first time after 18; and the two diagnoses are never given together. Borderline and antisocial personality disorders both bring outbursts, but as one part of a much wider pattern, and DSM-5-TR notes that the level of impulsive aggression in them is lower than in IED. Popular culture has a name for one look-alike, amok, the Malay pattern of brooding after an insult followed by a violent rampage, which Chapter 1 (Section 1.10.5) describes among the cultural syndromes. The two routes are twice a week on average for 3 months (no damage or injury) or three damaging or injurious outbursts in 12 months . The minimum age is 6 , so "IED is diagnosed only in adults" is wrong, and no comorbid mood disorder is required. The outbursts are not premeditated and gain the person nothing tangible; planned, instrumental aggression points to conduct disorder or antisocial personality disorder. The specifier "with limited prosocial emotions" belongs to conduct disorder only , never to IED (Section 11.9). Intermittent explosive disorder: causes and treatment Why does the brake fail? The oldest and best-supported biological answer concerns serotonin, and it began with a study of men in prison. Key study: Linnoila and the impulsive offenders (1983) A joint American and Finnish team led by Markku Linnoila and Matti Virkkunen asked whether violent men differ in their brain chemistry, and whether it matters how they were violent. They studied 36 violent offenders and divided them by the nature of their crimes: some had acted impulsively, in a sudden rage, and others had premeditated their acts. In each man they measured, by lumbar puncture, the monoamines and their breakdown products in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), including 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the main breakdown product of serotonin and an index of how much serotonin the brain is turning over. The impulsive offenders had relatively low CSF 5-HIAA; the premeditating offenders did not. The other monoamines did not differ between the groups, and the lowest levels of all were in impulsive offenders who had also attempted suicide. The authors concluded that low CSF 5-HIAA may be a marker of impulsivity rather than of violence as such. The sample was small and entirely male, and later research found the link between serotonin and aggression weaker and more complicated than the early studies suggested, but the distinction it drew, between hot impulsive aggression and cold planned aggression, became the backbone of the modern IED diagnosis. The same idea of a failed brake shows up in brain imaging. DSM-5-TR summarises the findings: serotonergic abnormalities, both globally and in particular regions of the limbic system (the anterior cingulate cortex) and the orbitofrontal cortex; greater responses of the amygdala to angry faces during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in people with IED than in healthy people; and reduced volume of grey matter in several frontolimbic regions, which correlates with measures of aggression, although these differences are not always found. Put simply, the amygdala raises the alarm too loudly at signs of threat or insult, and the orbitofrontal and cingulate cortex, which normally weigh the alarm against its social consequences, damp it too weakly. You will recognise the pattern from Phineas Gage, whose damaged orbitofrontal cortex turned a reliable foreman into a man given to profanity and outbursts (the Physiological book tells his story). The genes contribute: first-degree relatives of people with IED are at increased risk, and twin studies show a substantial genetic influence on impulsive aggression. So does experience. People who suffered physical and emotional trauma in the first 20 years of life are at increased risk, and in some refugee populations long displacement from home and separation from family are risk factors too. Psychologically, people with IED share the hostile attribution bias of reactively aggressive children: an ambiguous remark or an accidental jostle is read as a deliberate insult, and the anger that follows feels to them entirely justified. Treatment combines psychological and drug approaches, although for a long time there were almost no controlled trials of either. The first randomised trial of psychotherapy was reported in 2008 by Michael S. McCloskey , Coccaro and their colleagues in Chicago. They assigned 45 adults with IED to 12 weeks of group cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), individual CBT, or a waiting list. The therapy, adapted from an anger-management programme by the psychologist Jerry L. Deffenbacher , combined relaxation training, cognitive restructuring of hostile thoughts and rehearsal of coping skills. Group and individual therapy did about equally well, and both reduced aggression, anger, hostile thinking and depressive symptoms and improved anger control, with large effects that were maintained at the 3-month follow-up. These programmes descend from the anger-control version of stress inoculation training developed by Raymond W. Novaco in the 1970s (Book 2, Section 5.5.2 explains stress inoculation). In practice the person learns to notice the early bodily signs of rising anger, to identify the triggers and the hostile interpretations that feed it, to leave the situation before the explosion, to relax, and to rehearse other responses. On the drug side, the serotonin story led naturally to the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). In a double-blind trial in which 100 people with IED were randomly given fluoxetine or a placebo (Coccaro, Lee and Kavoussi, 2009), fluoxetine produced a sustained reduction in aggression and irritability that was visible by the second week, and it did so whether or not the person was depressed or anxious, so it was not working simply as an antidepressant. Yet only 46 percent of those given fluoxetine reached full or partial remission of their outbursts. Smaller trials have tested anticonvulsant mood stabilisers with mixed results, and no medicine is approved specifically for IED. Two practical points complete the picture: alcohol and other drugs that release inhibition make outbursts more likely and should be cut down or stopped, and where children or a partner are at risk, safety comes before any treatment plan. Clinical link Many people who seek help for IED are sent by a frightened family or by a court, and many describe their outbursts in the passive voice: "it just happened", "something switched on". The diagnosis explains a pattern, but it does not remove responsibility, and a clinician who treats IED must still ask about violence at home, about children who witness it, and about weapons. Criterion C is also a useful clinical check: if the "explosions" happen only at home, never in front of the boss, and reliably get the person his way, they are not as impulsive as they look. Exam trap Low CSF 5-HIAA (the serotonin metabolite) was found in impulsive violent offenders but not in premeditating ones (Linnoila and colleagues, 1983): it marks impulsivity, not violence in general. The brain picture of IED is an over-reactive amygdala with weak orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate control. Fluoxetine reduces impulsive aggression, but fewer than half of patients remit; CBT for anger has the best psychological evidence. Pyromania: fire setting for its own sake Mukund is 20, a second-year polytechnic student in Nagpur. His father has brought him to the outpatient department because the police have found him, for the third time, standing beside a burning heap of tyres and scrap behind a warehouse. He did not run; he was watching. Over two years, he admits, he has set perhaps fifteen fires: piles of dry leaves and rubbish, an abandoned shed, the dry grass along the railway line in May. He plans them, carrying a small bottle of kerosene and a lighter in his bag for days and waiting for an evening when the wind is right. For hours beforehand he feels "tight and restless, like the night before a result". When the flames catch, the tightness melts into an excitement he struggles to describe: "It is the most alive I ever feel." He stays to watch the fire engines arrive, knows which fire station will answer a call from each part of the city, and has twice applied to train as a fireman. He has never set a fire for money, to hurt anyone or to get back at anyone; he feels guilty afterwards about the shed, and frightened that one day someone will be inside. He was sober each time, he has never had a manic episode, and apart from the fires he does not lie, steal or fight, and he was not a troublesome child. Mukund has pyromania . The criteria fall into three groups. First, the act and the feelings around it: deliberate and purposeful fire setting on more than one occasion (Criterion A); tension or affective arousal before the act (Criterion B); fascination with, interest in, curiosity about or attraction to fire and its situational contexts, its paraphernalia, uses and consequences (Criterion C); and pleasure, gratification or relief when setting fires or when witnessing or taking part in their aftermath (Criterion D). Second, what the fire must not be for (Criterion E): monetary gain, the expression of a sociopolitical ideology, the concealment of a crime, the expression of anger or vengeance, the improvement of one's living circumstances (a tenant who burns a flat to be rehoused), a response to a delusion or a hallucination, or the result of impaired judgement in major neurocognitive disorder, intellectual disability or intoxication. Third, a rule of precedence (Criterion F): the fire setting must not be better explained by conduct disorder, a manic episode or antisocial personality disorder. Read the criteria as a funnel. A and E together say that the fire must be deliberate yet serve no outside purpose; B, C and D say what it serves instead, an inner state of tension, fascination and release. DSM-5-TR adds associated features that make the picture vivid. People with pyromania are often regular "watchers" at fires in their neighbourhood, may set off false alarms, and take pleasure in the institutions, equipment and personnel of firefighting; some spend time at the fire station, set fires in order to be associated with the fire service, or even become firefighters. They may make considerable advance preparation before starting a fire, and they may be indifferent to the damage and danger to life, or take satisfaction from the destruction. That point about preparation matters for the examination. An impulse-control disorder is not defined by how quickly the act follows the urge; it is defined by the person's failure to resist the urge at all. Mukund's urge is impulsive, but his fires are planned. ICD-11 describes pyromania (6C70) in almost the same words, as a recurrent failure to control strong impulses to set fires in the absence of an apparent motive, with mounting tension, persistent fascination with fire and pleasure, excitement, relief or gratification during and after the act. Its list of motives that rule the diagnosis out adds one that DSM-5-TR mentions only in its differential diagnosis: setting a fire to attract attention or recognition, as in the person who lights a fire in order to "discover" it and be the hero who raised the alarm. How common is pyromania? Probably very rare, and this is the most important fact about it. Fire setting itself is not rare. In one population sample, DSM-5-TR reports, the lifetime prevalence of fire-setting behaviour was 1.0 to 1.1 percent, 1.7 percent in men and 0.4 percent in women. But most fire setters do not have pyromania, as one careful Finnish study showed. Key study: Looking for pyromania (Lindberg and colleagues, 2005) Nina Lindberg , Virkkunen and their colleagues at the University of Helsinki reviewed the records and forensic psychiatric reports of all 90 men with repeated arson who had been referred for pretrial psychiatric assessment at the Helsinki University Hospital Department of Forensic Psychiatry between 1973 and 1993. If pyromania exists anywhere, it should exist among repeat arsonists. The commonest diagnoses were personality disorders, psychoses and intellectual disability, often with alcoholism, and 68 percent had been intoxicated during the index fire. Men with psychosis or intellectual disability tended to be "pure" arsonists, guilty of nothing but fires, whereas those with personality disorders committed many kinds of crime and arson was just one of them. Only three of the 90 (3.3 percent) met the criteria for pyromania. The authors concluded that, as defined, pyromania is an extremely rare phenomenon, and they questioned whether intoxication should automatically exclude it, since so many repeat fire setters drink. The figures from clinics are similar: in an American study of adults hospitalised for psychiatric reasons, 3.4 percent met the full criteria for current pyromania. And in the largest clinical description of people with the disorder, Jon E. Grant and Suck Won Kim (2007) at the University of Minnesota interviewed 21 adults and adolescents with lifetime pyromania. Their average age at onset was 18.1 years; 18 of the 21 reported urges to set fires; on average they set a fire every 5.9 weeks; much of their fire setting did not reach the legal threshold of arson; 61.9 percent had a current mood disorder and 47.6 percent another impulse-control disorder. Ten of the 21 were women, which fits DSM-5-TR's caution: fire setting is commoner in men, but whether this holds for pyromania itself is unknown. DSM-5-TR suggests late adolescence as the typical age at onset; incidents come and go episodically; and the long-term course is unknown. The comorbid conditions are substance use disorders, gambling disorder, depressive and bipolar disorders and other disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders. The commonest fire setters of all are children and adolescents: in the United States more than 40 percent of those arrested for arson are younger than 18. Yet pyromania in childhood appears to be rare. Juvenile fire setting usually belongs to conduct disorder, ADHD or an adjustment disorder, or is simply developmental experimentation with matches and lighters. Compare Mukund with Wasim, a 14-year-old in Surat who set fire to a neighbour's scooter after the neighbour complained about him to his father. Wasim also fights at school, steals from shops, lies his way out of trouble and stays out all night. His fire was revenge, and it is one item in a broad pattern of violating other people's rights. It counts towards conduct disorder, whose criterion of deliberate fire setting with the intention of causing serious damage is taught in Section 11.9, and Criterion F forbids a separate diagnosis of pyromania.
