Pyromania is what is left when accident, outside motive, psychosis, intoxication, impaired judgement and the broader antisocial disorders have all been ruled out, and tension, fascination and pleasure are present. What causes pyromania is almost unknown, because so few people have it that research has had to study fire setters in general. The research that Barlow and Durand review has examined family histories of fire setting and the comorbid antisocial personality disorder and alcoholism of arsonists. The serotonin story reappears here too. In 1987 Virkkunen, Linnoila and their colleagues compared 20 imprisoned arsonists with 20 habitually violent offenders and 10 healthy volunteers and found significantly lower CSF levels of 5-HIAA, and of a breakdown product of noradrenaline, in the arsonists; and the lower an arsonist's blood sugar fell in a glucose tolerance test, the more severe his fire setting had been. The authors read both findings as signs of poor impulse control. Treatment is generally cognitive-behavioural: the person learns to recognise the signals that start the urge and practises ways of coping with it without fire. For children, programmes of fire-safety education and work with the family are the usual first step. None of these has been tested in controlled trials of people with pyromania itself. Clinical link In 1963 the psychiatrist John M. Macdonald , in a paper called "The threat to kill", mentioned in passing that childhood fire setting, cruelty to animals and bedwetting turned up in the histories of some of the patients he had studied who had threatened to kill. The "Macdonald triad" became a fixture of crime fiction as a predictor of adult violence, but research has not supported it, and Macdonald's own later follow-up did not find the association he had suggested. A child who sets fires deserves a careful assessment, for conduct disorder, ADHD, abuse or neglect, and a family in crisis, not a label as a future murderer. Exam trap The hallmark difference: pyromania is deliberate, purposeful fire setting, often prepared in advance, for the gratification or relief that fire itself brings ; intermittent explosive disorder is impulsive aggression grossly out of proportion to the trigger . Fire set for money, revenge, ideology, concealment of a crime, a better home, or (in ICD-11) attention is not pyromania; nor is fire set in psychosis, intoxication, dementia or intellectual disability. A teenager's fire setting within a pattern of antisocial behaviour counts towards conduct disorder (Section 11.9). Pyromania has no minimum or maximum age, but it is very rare in childhood and typically begins in late adolescence; older books say it is "mostly male", while DSM-5-TR says fire setting is commoner in men and the sex ratio of pyromania itself is unknown. Kleptomania: stealing what one does not need Abhay is 38, a respected lecturer in commerce at a college in Kochi, married and well paid. For about eight years he has been stealing from supermarkets and stationery shops: a packet of gel pens, a keychain, a tube of lip balm, a pack of batteries. He never takes anything expensive and never anything he needs. Most of it ends up in a locked drawer in his staffroom cupboard, and some he drops in a bin on the way home. "When I see it on the shelf, something starts," he says. "My heart races, my palms sweat, I tell myself no, and the more I say no the worse it gets. When it is in my pocket there is a rush, a release. Then on the road home I feel disgusted with myself." He has tried avoiding the shops, dropping money into a shop's charity box to make up for what he took, and once creeping back to return the things to the shelf. Last month a store manager caught him with a bar of chocolate worth forty rupees in his pocket and three thousand rupees in his wallet. He was let off with a warning, and he has not told his wife. Abhay has kleptomania . He is unusual in one way, because most people seen in clinics with the disorder are women, and typical in every other. The DSM-5-TR criteria are short. There must be a recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their monetary value (Criterion A); an increasing sense of tension immediately before the theft (Criterion B); and pleasure, gratification or relief at the time of committing it (Criterion C). The stealing must not be done to express anger or vengeance, and not in response to a delusion or a hallucination (Criterion D), and it must not be better explained by conduct disorder, a manic episode or antisocial personality disorder (Criterion E). Notice how closely B and C copy the impulse cycle of Figure 11.16, and how Criterion A is worded. It does not say the objects are worthless. It says they are not stolen because they are needed or valuable; the value is simply not the point. The clinical features follow from that. The objects are usually of little value to the person, who could have afforded them, and they are often given away or thrown away, occasionally hoarded or secretly returned. People with kleptomania generally avoid stealing when arrest is immediately likely (they do not steal in full view of a police officer), but they do not usually preplan the thefts or fully weigh the chance of being caught, and they steal alone, without help from or collaboration with anyone else. They know that the act is wrong and senseless, they usually try to resist it, and they frequently fear arrest and feel depressed or guilty afterwards. ICD-11 describes kleptomania (6C71) in the same terms, as a recurrent failure to control strong impulses to steal objects in the absence of an apparent motive, with mounting tension beforehand and pleasure, excitement, relief or gratification during and immediately after the theft, and it adds a coding note that the diagnosis is not given separately when stealing occurs within conduct-dissocial disorder or a manic episode. Kleptomania is rare. DSM-5-TR puts its prevalence in the general population of the United States at about 0.3 to 0.6 percent, and among people arrested for shoplifting in the United States and Canada at about 4 to 24 percent; women outnumber men by about three to one. Studies of psychiatric patients find it more often than you might expect: in the survey of 204 consecutively admitted adult inpatients by Grant and his colleagues (2005), 7.8 percent had current kleptomania, the second commonest impulse problem after compulsive buying. The age at onset varies, but the disorder often begins in adolescence, and it can begin in childhood, in adulthood or, rarely, late in life. Three courses have been described: sporadic, with brief episodes and long remissions; episodic, with long periods of stealing and periods of remission; and chronic, with some fluctuation. The disorder may continue for years despite repeated convictions. Its comorbid companions are compulsive buying, depressive and bipolar disorders (especially major depression), anxiety disorders, eating disorders (particularly bulimia nervosa), personality disorders, substance use disorders (especially alcohol use disorder) and other impulse-control disorders. First-degree relatives have higher rates of alcohol use disorder than the general population, and kleptomania is associated with an increased risk of suicide attempts. The main differential diagnosis is ordinary theft, and Table 11.37 sets them apart. Ordinary theft, whether planned or impulsive, is deliberate and motivated by the usefulness or the money value of the object; some adolescents also steal on a dare, as an act of rebellion or as a rite of passage. Kleptomania is rare, whereas shoplifting is relatively common, so most shoplifters do not have it. In malingering, a person caught stealing may claim the symptoms of kleptomania to escape prosecution. In antisocial personality disorder and conduct disorder, the theft is part of a general pattern of antisocial behaviour. And stealing that occurs during a manic episode, in response to delusions or hallucinations, or in a major neurocognitive disorder belongs to that condition; when respectable people begin to shoplift for the first time in middle or late life, a clinician should think of a dementia (Chapter 10). Section 11.10.2 told its history; the box that follows turns it into the answer, and teaches the distractors that the question sets beside it. Exam trap "The term kleptomania was given by" Marc (Charles Chrétien Henri Marc, with Jean-Étienne Esquirol, 1838), the keyed and correct answer; Matthey's earlier word was klopémanie (1816). The distractors are famous for other words. Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) coined schizophrenia (1908 to 1911) and the terms ambivalence and autism (Chapter 4); he did not name kleptomania, and simply carried Kraepelin's "impulsive insanity" into his textbook. Enrico Morselli (1852 to 1929) named dysmorphophobia in 1891, the fear of ugliness now called body dysmorphic disorder (Chapter 6). Alistair Munro described monosymptomatic hypochondriacal psychosis in a series of papers in the 1970s and 1980s: a single, encapsulated hypochondriacal delusion, such as the conviction of being infested by parasites or of giving off a foul smell, which he found often responded to the antipsychotic pimozide. A second trap: the objects in kleptomania need not be worthless; they are simply not stolen for their use or their value . And unlike the fire setter, the person with kleptomania usually does not plan the theft and always steals alone . Kleptomania: explanations and treatment Why would anyone steal what they do not want? The psychoanalysts gave the first answers, reading the stolen object as a symbol: a substitute for love that was missing, compensation for a loss, an act with a hidden sexual meaning. Such accounts are hard to test, and they have faded. Two modern ideas have more support. The first treats the theft as a way of regulating mood. Kleptomania is strongly comorbid with mood disorders, and some writers have called it an "antidepressant" behaviour, an act that briefly lifts an unpleasant feeling (Barlow and Durand cite Fishbain, 1987). The second idea treats kleptomania as close kin to the addictions. The urge to steal behaves like a craving: it is set off by cues (the open counter, the crowded aisle), it builds, it is relieved by the act, and the act brings a "rush". People with kleptomania score high on measures of impulsivity, reflecting their difficulty in weighing the immediate gratification of stealing against its long-term costs of arrest and shame (Grant and Kim, 2002). DSM-5-TR notes that the neurotransmitter pathways involved in the behavioural addictions, serotonin, dopamine and the brain's own opioids, appear to play a part in kleptomania as well, and one small imaging study found abnormalities in the white matter of the inferior frontal regions, areas associated with decision making. The addiction idea led directly to the best-tested treatment. Key study: naltrexone for kleptomania (Grant, Kim and Odlaug, 2009) Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors, and in alcohol dependence it is thought to blunt the "high" that drinking brings (Chapter 10, Section 10.4). If the rush of stealing also runs through the brain's opioid system, Jon Grant, Suck Won Kim and Brian L. Odlaug at the University of Minnesota reasoned, naltrexone should weaken the urge to steal. They randomly assigned 25 adults with kleptomania to naltrexone (50 to 150 mg a day) or a placebo for 8 weeks, under double-blind conditions, and 23 of them completed the trial. Those on naltrexone showed significantly greater reductions in the urge to steal, in actual stealing and in overall severity than those on placebo; the mean effective dose was about 117 mg a day, and the drug was well tolerated. Before it, as the authors pointed out, kleptomania had no empirically validated treatment at all. Its limits are clear: it was small and short, and at doses above those used for alcohol the liver has to be monitored. The serotonin reuptake inhibitors have a weaker record. Several case series and open trials reported improvement, but in the most informative study ( Lorrin M. Koran and colleagues at Stanford, 2007, with 24 patients), 79 percent improved on open-label escitalopram, and when the responders were then randomly switched to placebo or kept on the drug, relapse was about as common on escitalopram (43 percent) as on placebo (50 percent); the SSRI added nothing that could be shown. No medicine is approved for kleptomania. Psychological treatment is cognitive-behavioural, and most of the evidence comes from case reports. The classic technique is covert sensitisation , in which the person imagines the build-up to a theft and then imagines vividly its worst consequences, being caught, handcuffed and named in the newspaper, so that the urge becomes linked with aversion rather than relief (Book 2, Section 4.4.3 explains the method). Imaginal desensitisation, exposure to the shop with the urge resisted, and the relapse-prevention methods of addiction treatment (Chapter 10) are also used. As Grant and Odlaug pointed out in 2008, there have been no controlled trials of any psychotherapy for kleptomania. Indian context Fire setting and theft are crimes in India as everywhere, and a diagnosis of pyromania or kleptomania does not by itself excuse them. The insanity defence, now section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly section 84 of the Indian Penal Code), protects only a person who, because of unsoundness of mind, was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law (Book 2, Section 10.9.4). People with kleptomania, by definition, know that the act is wrong; Indian law, unlike some American states, has no "irresistible impulse" test. The diagnosis matters instead for treatment, for how families and employers respond, and sometimes in sentencing. You now have the three disorders side by side, and Table 11.38 sets them out in the form that questions most often take: what is done, what precedes it, what follows it, whether it is planned, and what rules it out. A thief who steals out of anger or revenge, or a manic patient who walks out of a shop with goods, does not have kleptomania, and the knowledge that stealing is wrong, which people with kleptomania have, is exactly why the diagnosis does not make out an insanity defence in Indian law. The wider family: habit and impulse disorders in ICD-10, impulse control disorders in ICD-11 The two international classifications draw the family differently from DSM-5-TR, and the differences are tested. ICD-10 (1992) placed the impulse disorders among the "disorders of adult personality and behaviour" (F60 to F69), in a block called habit and impulse disorders (F63). Its definition is worth reading slowly, because it is unusually honest. These are disorders characterised by "repeated acts that have no clear rational motivation, cannot be controlled, and generally harm the patient's own interests and those of other people", which the patient reports are associated with impulses to act; their cause is not understood, and they are grouped together "because of broad descriptive similarities, not because they are known to share any other important features". Habitual excessive use of alcohol or drugs, and impulse and habit disorders of sexual behaviour, are excluded. The block contains pathological gambling (F63.0), pathological fire-setting [pyromania] (F63.1), pathological stealing [kleptomania] (F63.2), trichotillomania (F63.3), other habit and impulse disorders (F63.8) and an unspecified category (F63.9). Intermittent explosive disorder has no code of its own in ICD-10; it is listed as an inclusion term under F63.8. Notice ICD-10's own names. Its definition of pathological fire-setting speaks of multiple acts or attempts at setting fire to property without apparent motive, a persistent preoccupation with fire, tension before and intense excitement after, and it excludes fire setting by an adult with dissocial personality disorder, in conduct disorder, in intoxication, in organic mental disorders and in schizophrenia. Its pathological stealing excludes stealing in a depressive disorder. ICD-11 (2022) rebuilt the block. Its impulse control disorders (6C70 to 6C7Z) are "characterised by the repeated failure to resist an impulse, drive, or urge to perform an act that is rewarding to the person, at least in the short-term, despite consequences such as longer-term harm either to the individual or to others, marked distress about the behaviour pattern, or significant impairment" in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning. Read that definition beside DSM-IV's: the key new word is "rewarding". The block has four named members, pyromania (6C70), kleptomania (6C71), compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (6C72) and intermittent explosive disorder (6C73), with other specified (6C7Y) and unspecified (6C7Z) categories. ICD-11's intermittent explosive disorder is described without DSM-5-TR's frequency thresholds, as repeated brief episodes of verbal or physical aggression or destruction of property, grossly out of proportion to the provocation, that are not part of a pattern of chronic anger and irritability (such as oppositional defiant disorder) and that cause significant impairment. Equally important is what ICD-11 sends elsewhere, with a "coded elsewhere" note. Gambling disorder (6C50) and gaming disorder (6C51) are disorders due to addictive behaviours (Chapter 10, Section 10.1.7). Trichotillomania and excoriation disorder are body-focused repetitive behaviour disorders (6B25) in the obsessive-compulsive group (Chapter 6, Section 6.6.5). Oppositional defiant disorder (6C90) and conduct-dissocial disorder (6C91) form a separate block of disruptive behaviour or dissocial disorders; unlike DSM-5-TR, ICD-11 does not put them in the same block as the impulse disorders. And ICD-11 has a category for impulse symptoms that are the direct physiological effect of a medical condition, secondary impulse control syndrome (6E66): prominent stealing, fire setting, aggressive outbursts, compulsive sexual behaviour or excessive gambling judged to be the direct result of a health condition outside the mental disorders, such as a brain injury or a neurological disease, and recorded alongside that condition. How directly brain chemistry can produce such behaviour is shown by the dopamine-boosting medicines used for Parkinson's disease, which can set off pathological gambling (Section 10.1.7) and other impulsive behaviour in people who never had it before. The newcomer is compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (6C72): a persistent pattern of failure to control intense, repetitive sexual impulses or urges, resulting in repetitive sexual behaviour that has become a central focus of life, that the person has repeatedly and unsuccessfully tried to reduce, and that continues despite adverse consequences and even when it brings little satisfaction, over an extended period (for example 6 months or more), with marked distress or impairment. Distress that comes entirely from moral judgements and disapproval of sexual impulses or behaviour does not count. ICD-11 deliberately placed it among the impulse control disorders, not among the paraphilic disorders (its content is usually conventional) and not among the addictive behaviours. DSM-5-TR has no such diagnosis: the proposal for a "hypersexual disorder" made for DSM-5 by Martin Kafka in 2010 was not adopted. Chapter 9, Section 9.5.7 tells this story in full. One more urge has knocked at the door of both manuals without being let in: compulsive buying , repeated and uncontrollable shopping that leads to distress, debt and family conflict. Kraepelin described it in his textbook under the name oniomania (buying mania), Bleuler described it after him, and it is common: a 2004 American telephone survey of 2,513 adults put its point prevalence at 5.8 percent, and in the inpatient study by Grant and his colleagues it was the commonest impulse problem of all (9.3 percent). In 1994 Susan L. McElroy and her colleagues described 20 compulsive buyers; 19 of them had a lifetime diagnosis of a major mood disorder, and the authors proposed operational criteria so that the condition could be studied as a disorder in its own right. It is still not a diagnosis with its own code and criteria in either manual. DSM-5-TR mentions compulsive buying only as a frequent companion of kleptomania; ICD-11 lists "compulsive buying-shopping disorder" as an example under other specified impulse control disorders (6C7Y), so that is where it is coded, although some researchers argue that it belongs with the addictive behaviours instead. The case of the St Louis children, revisited Read Lee Robins's results again with this chapter behind you, and each of them now has a name. The adults she called sociopathic personalities are what DSM-5-TR calls antisocial personality disorder (Section 11.5): a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, counted from age 15 and shown by three or more of seven features. Those features are behavioural because DSM-III (1980) built them, as Robins had built her nineteen areas of life, from things that can be checked: arrests, fights, debts, abandoned jobs. Her finding that not one sociopathic adult had reached adulthood without marked antisocial behaviour in childhood became the rule that the adult diagnosis needs evidence of conduct disorder with onset before 15, in a person at least 18 years old. And her best predictor, the number and variety of a child's antisocial acts rather than any single one of them, is the logic of the conduct disorder criteria (Section 11.9): three or more of fifteen, drawn from four groups, with severity graded by the number of problems and the harm done. The other half of her paradox, that most antisocial children do not become antisocial adults, is the subject of Sections 11.9.4 to 11.9.7. In a majority of children conduct disorder remits by adulthood. What predicts that it will not is exactly what a clinic file can record: problems that began early (the childhood-onset type, with a symptom before 10), callous-unemotional traits (the specifier with limited prosocial emotions), and what Terrie Moffitt (1993) called the life-course-persistent path, rare and rooted in neuropsychological deficits and adverse environments, as against the far commoner antisocial behaviour that is limited to adolescence. The St Louis children also illustrate the general definition with which the chapter began (Section 11.1): a personality disorder is not an episode but an enduring pattern that can be traced back at least to adolescence. The files that were about to be destroyed held the childhood half of hundreds of adult lives, and Robins's achievement was to see that a personality disorder can only be understood across the whole of a life. Chapter summary 11.1 What a Personality Disorder Is. A personality disorder is an enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from the expectations of the person's culture in two or more of four areas (cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning and impulse control), is inflexible and pervasive, stable and long-standing with onset by adolescence or early adulthood, and causes distress or impairment; its traits are usually ego-syntonic. Under 18 the features must have lasted a year, and antisocial personality disorder is never diagnosed before 18. The idea runs from Pinel's manie sans délire (1801) and Prichard's moral insanity (1835) through Schneider (1923) to Freud's anal character and Reich's character armour; DSM-III (1980) placed the disorders on Axis II. DSM-5-TR has ten disorders in three clusters, A (odd or eccentric), B (dramatic, emotional or erratic) and C (anxious or fearful), with no Cluster D. The median prevalence is 10.5 percent, and Torgersen's twins gave a heritability of .60. 11.2 Cluster A: Paranoid, Schizoid and Schizotypal Personality Disorders. The odd or eccentric disorders share social distance and a kinship with schizophrenia. Paranoid personality disorder (four of seven criteria) is pervasive distrust and suspiciousness without delusional conviction; Cameron's paranoid pseudo-community (1943) and Lemert's corrective (1962) show how suspicion creates real enemies. Schizoid personality disorder (four of seven) is detachment from social relationships with restricted emotional expression: the schizoid person does not want closeness, the avoidant person wants it but fears rejection, a split Millon brought into DSM-III. Schizotypal personality disorder (five of nine) adds acute discomfort in close relationships, ideas of reference, magical thinking, odd speech and eccentric behaviour. Rado's schizotype (1953), Meehl's schizotaxia, schizotypy and schizophrenia (1962) and the Danish adoption studies of Kety, Rosenthal and Wender placed it in the schizophrenia spectrum, which is why ICD-10 and ICD-11 class it with schizophrenia (F21, 6A22). 11.3 Borderline Personality Disorder I: The Clinical Picture. Borderline personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, with marked impulsivity, shown by five or more of nine criteria: frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, relationships swinging between idealisation and devaluation, identity disturbance, self-damaging impulsivity, recurrent suicidal behaviour or self-mutilation, affective instability from marked reactivity of mood, chronic emptiness, intense anger, and transient stress-related paranoid ideation or dissociation. Stern named the "border line" group (1938), Kernberg described borderline personality organisation (1967), Grinker made the first empirical study (1968), and Gunderson and Singer (1975) and Spitzer, Endicott and Gibbon (1979) led to the DSM-III criteria. It is diagnosed more often in women in clinical samples, though not in the community, and carries a real suicide risk. Its mood shifts within hours, unlike bipolar episodes, and it must be told apart from the other Cluster B disorders, complex PTSD, an adolescent identity problem and conduct disorder. 11.4 Borderline Personality Disorder II: Defences, Causes, Course and Treatment. Splitting, the keeping apart of all-good and all-bad images of self and others, comes from Klein and is the defence Kernberg placed at the centre of borderline organisation, supported by projective identification, primitive idealisation, devaluation, omnipotence and primitive denial; in a ward it appears as staff splitting (Main, 1957). Repression, sublimation, rationalisation, regression and undoing are not the borderline answer. Kernberg's conflict model contrasts with the deficit models of Kohut (failed mirroring and idealising, a fragmented self) and of Adler and Buie (aloneness). Linehan's biosocial theory (1993) has emotional vulnerability transacting with an invalidating environment; Fonagy and Bateman trace the disorder to failed mentalisation. Abuse raises the risk but is neither necessary nor sufficient. The McLean and CLPS follow-ups showed that most patients remit. Psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, TFP, schema therapy, STEPPS, good psychiatric management) comes first; no drug is licensed for the disorder. 11.5 Antisocial Personality Disorder and Psychopathy. Antisocial personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others since age 15, shown by three or more of seven features (unlawful acts, deceitfulness, impulsivity, aggression, recklessness, irresponsibility, lack of remorse), in a person at least 18 with evidence of conduct disorder before 15. The concept runs from Pinel and Prichard to Cleckley's The Mask of Sanity (1941) and Robert Hare's PCL-R (1991, 20 items, two factors and four facets), the instrument Cleckley never built. DSM-III's behavioural criteria drew on Robins; ICD-10 calls the disorder dissocial. Psychopathy and the disorder overlap without coinciding; Karpman separated primary from secondary psychopaths, and Patrick and colleagues proposed the triarchic model. Lykken's fearlessness (1957), Raine's underarousal, Eysenck's poor conditioning and Cadoret's gene-environment interaction explain it. It is about three times commoner in men, often fades by about 40, and is no insanity defence in Indian law. 11.6 Histrionic and Narcissistic Personality Disorders. Histrionic personality disorder descends from hysteria: Chodoff and Lyons (1958) separated the personality from conversion, and DSM-III made "histrionic" official. Its core is excessive emotionality and attention seeking (five of eight), with seductive behaviour, shallow, rapidly shifting emotion, impressionistic speech, suggestibility and relationships seen as more intimate than they are; Kaplan (1983) and Ford and Widiger (1989) raised the question of sex bias. Narcissistic personality disorder takes its name from Narcissus through Ellis, Näcke and Freud (1914), and Kohut named it (1968). Its core triad is grandiosity, need for admiration and lack of empathy (five of nine); Gabbard and Wink separated grandiose from vulnerable narcissism. Kohut read it as a deficit to be met with empathy, Kernberg as a pathological grandiose self to be confronted. Asking what each person wants from others separates the Cluster B disorders: the admiration seeker who is emotional and seductive, not grandiose, is histrionic. 11.7 Cluster C: Avoidant, Dependent and Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorders. In each anxious or fearful disorder a strategy against fear brings short-term relief and long-term cost. Avoidant personality disorder (four of seven) is social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation: the person wants relationships but fears rejection, unlike the indifferent schizoid, and may share a continuum with social anxiety disorder. Dependent personality disorder (five of eight) is an excessive need to be taken care of, with submissive, clinging behaviour and fear of separation; Bornstein linked it to overprotective and authoritarian parenting, and Neki and Roland warned against reading Indian family closeness as disorder. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (four of eight) is preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and control at the expense of flexibility, openness and efficiency, driven by a need for control and descended from Freud's anal character. Unlike OCD it is ego-syntonic with limited insight. Cluster C responds reasonably well to psychotherapy (Svartberg, Emmelkamp, Bamelis). 11.8 The Newer Models: Dimensions, ICD-11 and the DSM-5 Alternative Model. Ten categorical boxes produce artificial comorbidity, heterogeneity within a diagnosis, arbitrary thresholds and a crowded residual category (Verheul and Widiger, 2004), and Widiger and Costa (1994) recast the disorders as extremes of the five-factor model. ICD-11, in effect from 1 January 2022 and built by the working group Tyrer chaired, abolished the types: one personality disorder (6D10) graded mild, moderate or severe, with personality difficulty below it, five trait domain qualifiers (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) and a borderline pattern qualifier. The DSM-5 Alternative Model, kept in Section III, rates Criterion A, the level of personality functioning (identity, self-direction, empathy, intimacy), from 0 to 4, and Criterion B, five pathological trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, psychoticism) with 25 facets, and retains six types: antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive and schizotypal. 11.9 Oppositional Defiant and Conduct Disorders. DSM-5 created the chapter of disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders, problems of emotional and behavioural self-control. Oppositional defiant disorder is angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behaviour or vindictiveness, four or more symptoms for at least 6 months, graded by the number of settings. Conduct disorder is a repetitive and persistent violation of others' basic rights or major age-appropriate norms: three or more of 15 criteria in 12 months, from four groups (aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, serious violations of rules). The childhood-onset type (a symptom before 10) predicts persistence, and the specifier with limited prosocial emotions, built on Frick's callous-unemotional traits, belongs to conduct disorder alone. Moffitt (1993) separated life-course-persistent from adolescence-limited antisocial behaviour; Patterson's coercive family process and Dodge's hostile attribution bias explain part of the cause. Most children remit, but adult antisocial personality requires conduct disorder before 15. 11.10 Impulse-Control Disorders: Intermittent Explosive Disorder, Pyromania and Kleptomania. An impulse-control disorder is a failure to resist an urge to a harmful act, often following the impulse cycle: tension, then pleasure, gratification or relief, then sometimes regret. The names grew from monomania: Matthey's klopémanie (1816), Marc's pyromanie (1833) and Esquirol and Marc's kleptomanie (1838). Intermittent explosive disorder is recurrent impulsive verbal or physical aggression grossly out of proportion to the provocation, from age 6, linked to low serotonin (Linnoila, 1983) and treated with anger-focused CBT and fluoxetine. Pyromania is deliberate, purposeful fire setting on more than one occasion for its own gratification, not for money, revenge or ideology, and is very rare. Kleptomania is stealing objects not needed for personal use or their value, with tension before and relief after; only naltrexone has a positive controlled trial. From the past papers Personality disorders are stable long-term conditions which can affect an individual's: (RML 2021, real) (a) Cognition (b) Mood (c) Interpersonal functioning (d) All of the above Answer: (d) All of the above. The general definition requires the enduring pattern to show in two or more of four areas: cognition, affectivity (mood and emotion), interpersonal functioning and impulse control (Section 11.1.2). Choosing (c) alone treats personality disorders as relationship problems only, and choosing (a) or (b) alone forgets that the definition spans all four areas. Identify the 'odd one out' from the groups: (Amity 2023, real) (a) Paranoid personality disorder (b) Schizoid personality disorder (c) Schizotypal personality disorder (d) Borderline personality disorder Answer: (d) Borderline personality disorder. Paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal personality disorder make up Cluster A, the odd or eccentric cluster; borderline belongs to Cluster B, the dramatic, emotional or erratic cluster (Sections 11.1.4 and 11.2.1). Schizotypal is the option that might tempt, because ICD-10 and ICD-11 class it with schizophrenia, but in DSM-5-TR it is a Cluster A personality disorder. DSM-5 groups the personality disorders into three clusters. Which cluster is described as the 'dramatic, emotional, or erratic' cluster and includes antisocial, borderline, histrionic, and narcissistic personality disorders? (Flight Mock 100, practice) (a) Cluster A (b) Cluster B (c) Cluster C (d) Cluster D Answer: (b) Cluster B. Cluster A is odd or eccentric (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal) and Cluster C anxious or fearful (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive). There is no Cluster D, although it appears as an option in almost every question on the clusters (Section 11.1.4). Which of the following is NOT a Cluster A personality disorder? (MET Mock 1, practice) (a) Paranoid personality disorder (b) Avoidant personality disorder (c) Schizotypal personality disorder (d) Schizoid personality disorder Answer: (b) Avoidant personality disorder. Avoidant personality disorder is Cluster C, anxious or fearful (Section 11.7.1). The avoidant person ends up as isolated as the schizoid person, which is the bait, but wants relationships and avoids them for fear of rejection, while the schizoid person does not want them at all (Section 11.2.5). Borderline personality disorder is primarily characterised by (JEMAS 2025, real) (a) Detachment and social withdrawal (b) Emotional instability and impulsivity (c) Obsessive perfectionism (d) Paranoid ideation Answer: (b) Emotional instability and impulsivity. DSM-5-TR defines borderline personality disorder as a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, with marked impulsivity (Section 11.3.2). Detachment and social withdrawal describe schizoid personality disorder, obsessive perfectionism describes OCPD, and paranoid ideation as the main feature is paranoid personality disorder; in borderline personality disorder paranoid ideation is only transient and stress-related (criterion 9). Which of the following disorders often involves identity disturbance and fear of abandonment? (IHBAS 2025, real) (a) Schizoid personality disorder (b) Histrionic personality disorder (c) Borderline personality disorder (d) Antisocial personality disorder Answer: (c) Borderline personality disorder. Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment and identity disturbance, a markedly and persistently unstable self-image, are criteria 1 and 3 of borderline personality disorder (Section 11.3.3). The schizoid person is indifferent to relationships; the histrionic person seeks attention, but identity disturbance, emptiness and self-harm are not histrionic criteria; and the antisocial person disregards others' rights rather than fearing their loss. Which of the following is NOT considered a cardinal feature of Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)? (Amity 2023, real) (a) Lack of a well-defined and stable self-image (b) Regular and predictable changes in mood (c) Eccentric behaviour marked by oddities in thinking and communication (d) Enduring pattern of instability in relationships Answer: (b) Regular and predictable changes in mood (keyed). Borderline mood is reactive and unpredictable, shifting within hours in response to events (criterion 6), so "regular and predictable" is the direct inversion of a criterion (Section 11.3.4). But (c) is not a borderline feature either: eccentric behaviour with oddities of thinking and communication is schizotypal personality disorder (Section 11.2.6). Two options are strictly correct; mark the keyed (b) and know why (c) is also wrong. Options (a) and (d) are criteria 3 and 2. Borderline personality disorder requires how many of nine criteria for diagnosis? (MET Mock 2, practice) (a) 3 (b) 4 (c) 5 (d) 6 Answer: (c) 5. Five or more of the nine criteria are needed (Section 11.3.2). The distractors are other disorders' thresholds: 3 (of 7) is antisocial, and 4 is paranoid, schizoid and avoidant (of 7) and obsessive-compulsive (of 8); no personality disorder needs 6. Which of the following is a core feature of Borderline Personality Disorder that is NOT typically a defining feature of Narcissistic Personality Disorder? (Real PYQ 2024, real) (a) Grandiose sense of self-importance (b) Pervasive instability in interpersonal relationships and self-image (c) Need for excessive admiration (d) Belief that one is "special" and can only be understood by other high-status people Answer: (b) Pervasive instability in interpersonal relationships and self-image. Instability of relationships and self-image is the core of borderline personality disorder (Section 11.3.7). Options (a), (c) and (d) are all among the nine criteria of narcissistic personality disorder (Section 11.6.5), so they define the narcissist, not the borderline patient. Borderline Personality Disorder is most characteristically associated with which primary defense mechanism? (Real PYQ 2025, real) (a) Repression (b) Splitting (c) Sublimation (d) Rationalization Answer: (b) Splitting. Splitting, the keeping apart of all-good and all-bad images of self and others, comes from Melanie Klein and was placed at the centre of borderline personality organisation by Otto Kernberg; it explains the swing between idealisation and devaluation (Section 11.4.1). Repression is the core defence of the neurotic level, sublimation is a mature defence and rationalisation is a defence everyone uses; none of them is the primitive defence of the borderline level. Which of the following defense mechanism is seen in patients with borderline personality disorder? (RML 2024, real) (a) Splitting (b) Regression (c) Undoing (d) Sublimation Answer: (a) Splitting. The same answer with new distractors (Sections 11.4.1 and 11.4.2); the defences that accompany splitting in borderline personality disorder are projective identification, primitive idealisation, devaluation, omnipotence and primitive denial. Regression is a general retreat to earlier ways of functioning under stress, undoing is the obsessional defence of cancelling one act with another, and sublimation is mature. A client tells you that they are "no one" and feels "empty inside." They report chronic fears of abandonment and have a history of intense, unstable relationships. According to psychoanalytic object relations theory, this pathology of the self is most likely a result of: (Real PYQ 2024, real) (a) Fixation at the oral stage of psychosexual development (b) A failure in parental mirroring and idealizing, leading to a fragmented self (c) Unresolved Oedipal complex and castration anxiety (d) Harsh superego demands leading to constant guilt Answer: (b) A failure in parental mirroring and idealizing, leading to a fragmented self. The vignette is borderline, and the keyed answer is Heinz Kohut's: without a parent's mirroring and a parent to idealise, the child's self never becomes cohesive and stays fragmented and empty (Section 11.4.3). Strictly this is self psychology, a close relative of object relations theory (Klein, Fairbairn, Winnicott and Kernberg), so choose it but know the difference. The other options are classical Freudian accounts: oral fixation of dependency, depression and addiction, the Oedipus complex of neurosis, and the harsh superego of melancholia and obsessional neurosis. Dialectical Behaviour Therapy is indicated for the treatment of: (IHBAS 2020, real) (a) Anxiety Disorders (b) Borderline Personality Disorder (c) Acute and Transient Psychotic Disorder (d) Post-traumatic Stress Disorder Answer: (b) Borderline Personality Disorder. Marsha Linehan built dialectical behaviour therapy while treating chronically suicidal women, on her biosocial theory of borderline personality disorder (1993); it combines individual therapy, a skills group (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness), telephone coaching and a consultation team, has more randomised trials than any other therapy for the disorder, and works most clearly on self-harm and suicide attempts (Section 11.4.8; Book 2, Section 5.8). Anxiety disorders, acute and transient psychotic disorder and PTSD belong to Chapters 6, 4 and 7, each with its own first-line treatment; DBT was not built for any of them. Which personality disorder is marked by manipulation, lack of remorse, and irresponsibility? (RML 2025, real) (a) Borderline personality disorder (b) Antisocial personality disorder (c) Dependent personality disorder (d) Narcissistic personality disorder Answer: (b) Antisocial personality disorder. Deceitfulness and manipulation, consistent irresponsibility and lack of remorse are three of the seven antisocial criteria, of which three are needed (Section 11.5.4). The borderline person may manipulate, but for nurturance and out of fear of abandonment; the dependent person is submissive and clinging; the narcissist exploits others for admiration but is not characteristically impulsive, aggressive or deceitful. Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before what age, and requires evidence of conduct disorder before what age? (MET Mock 2, practice) (a) Diagnosed before 16; CD before 12 (b) Diagnosed at or after 18; evidence of CD before age 15 (c) Diagnosed before 18; CD before 15 (d) Diagnosed only after 21 Answer: (b) Diagnosed at or after 18; evidence of CD before age 15. The person must be at least 18 and must have shown conduct disorder with onset before 15, and the pattern of disregard for others' rights is counted from 15 (Section 11.5.4, Figure 11.9). There is no rule about 12, 16 or 21, and a person under 18 with the pattern receives a diagnosis of conduct disorder instead. The PCL-R (Psychopathy Checklist-Revised) was developed by: (Biopsych + Testing paper, practice) (a) Hervey Cleckley alone, 1941 (b) Aaron Beck (c) Robert Hare (d) Hans Eysenck Answer: (c) Robert Hare. Robert D. Hare built the Psychopathy Checklist (1980) and the PCL-R (1991): 20 items scored 0, 1 or 2, maximum 40, usual cut-off 30, building on Cleckley's description (Section 11.5.6). Cleckley wrote The Mask of Sanity (1941) with its sixteen characteristics but built no checklist; Beck is cognitive therapy and the Beck Depression Inventory; Eysenck is the PEN model and an arousal theory of crime. A client reports a persistent pattern of seeking admiration, but their behavior is characterized by excessive emotionality, attention-seeking, and seductive behavior, rather than grandiosity. This presentation is more characteristic of: (Real PYQ 2024, real) (a) Narcissistic Personality Disorder (b) Histrionic Personality Disorder (c) Borderline Personality Disorder (d) Dependent Personality Disorder Answer: (b) Histrionic Personality Disorder. Excessive emotionality and attention seeking, with seductive or provocative behaviour, is the definition of histrionic personality disorder (five of eight criteria, Section 11.6.2). Grandiosity is the mark of the narcissist, so an admiration seeker without it is histrionic (Section 11.6.8); borderline personality disorder would need instability, abandonment fears or self-harm, and dependent personality disorder submissiveness and clinging. Individuals with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder are primarily motivated by a need for which of the following? (RML 2022, real) (a) Efficiency (b) Achievement (c) Control (d) Autonomy Answer: (c) Control. DSM-5-TR defines OCPD as a preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and mental and interpersonal control at the expense of flexibility, openness and efficiency (Section 11.7.5). Efficiency is what the disorder sacrifices; achievement suffers because perfectionism stops tasks being finished (working for admiration is closer to narcissism); and autonomy is bait from Erikson's second stage, which matches Freud's anal stage, but the person with OCPD is bound by rules, not seeking freedom. Compared to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is characterised by symptoms that are typically: (PYQ Mock 2, practice) (a) Ego-dystonic and accompanied by significant insight (b) Ego-syntonic with limited insight (c) Only present during manic episodes (d) Acute in onset and rapidly remitting Answer: (b) Ego-syntonic with limited insight. In OCPD the rules, the perfectionism and the need for control feel right and part of the self, and there are no true obsessions or compulsions; in OCD the obsessions are intrusive and ego-dystonic (Section 11.7.6). Option (a) describes OCD, and (c) and (d) contradict the definition of every personality disorder, an enduring pattern that begins by adolescence or early adulthood. The DSM-5-TR specifier 'with limited prosocial emotions' is applied to which diagnosis? (PYQ Mock 2, practice) (a) Antisocial personality disorder (b) Conduct disorder (c) Oppositional defiant disorder (d) Intermittent explosive disorder Answer: (b) Conduct disorder. The specifier belongs to conduct disorder only: two or more of lack of remorse or guilt, callous lack of empathy, unconcern about performance and shallow or deficient affect, persistently for at least 12 months in more than one relationship or setting (Section 11.9.4). Antisocial personality disorder is the tempting answer, but its Section III counterpart is a different specifier, "with psychopathic features"; oppositional defiant and intermittent explosive disorder have no such specifier. The hallmark difference between pyromania and intermittent explosive disorder (IED) is: (PYQ Mock 2, practice) (a) IED involves only verbal aggression, never physical (b) Pyromania involves planned, deliberate fire-setting for gratification; IED involves impulsive aggression disproportionate to the trigger (c) Pyromania is diagnosed only in adolescents; IED only in adults (d) Both require a comorbid mood disorder Answer: (b). Pyromania is deliberate, purposeful fire setting on more than one occasion, often prepared in advance, with tension before and pleasure, gratification or relief after; IED is recurrent impulsive aggression grossly out of proportion to the provocation (Sections 11.10.3 and 11.10.5). IED aggression may be verbal or physical and can be diagnosed from age 6, pyromania has no age limit, and neither needs a comorbid mood disorder. The term 'kleptomania' was given by: (RML 2024, real) (a) Marc (b) Bleuler (c) Munro (d) Morselli Answer: (a) Marc. Charles Chrétien Henri Marc, with Jean-Étienne Esquirol, renamed André Matthey's klopémanie (1816) as kleptomanie in 1838; Marc had already coined pyromanie in 1833 (Sections 11.10.2 and 11.10.6). Eugen Bleuler coined schizophrenia, ambivalence and autism; Alistair Munro described monosymptomatic hypochondriacal psychosis; Enrico Morselli named dysmorphophobia (1891). High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. Borderline personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image and affects, with marked impulsivity, beginning by early adulthood; not detachment (schizoid), obsessive perfectionism (OCPD), pervasive paranoid ideation (paranoid) or grandiosity (narcissistic). asked 4 times There are three clusters and no Cluster D : A, odd or eccentric (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal); B, dramatic, emotional or erratic (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic); C, anxious or fearful (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive). So borderline is the odd one out among the Cluster A disorders, and avoidant is Cluster C, not A. asked 4 times The nine borderline criteria : frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment; unstable, intense relationships alternating between idealisation and devaluation; identity disturbance; impulsivity in at least two self-damaging areas; recurrent suicidal behaviour or self-mutilation; affective instability from marked reactivity of mood; chronic emptiness; intense anger; transient stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociation. asked 3 times Splitting (self and others seen as all good or all bad) is the characteristic defence of borderline personality disorder: Melanie Klein's idea, placed at the centre of borderline personality organisation by Otto Kernberg (1967). asked 2 times Not the borderline defence: repression (the neurotic level), sublimation (mature), rationalisation (used by everyone), regression (a general retreat under stress), undoing (obsessional). The companions of splitting are projective identification, primitive idealisation, devaluation, omnipotence and primitive denial. asked 2 times Histrionic personality disorder : excessive emotionality and attention seeking (five of eight), with seductive or provocative behaviour, shallow, rapidly shifting emotion, impressionistic speech and suggestibility. The admiration seeker who is emotional and seductive rather than grandiose is histrionic, not narcissistic. asked 2 times A personality disorder shows in two or more of four areas, cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning and impulse control, so it can affect cognition, mood and interpersonal functioning alike ("all of the above"). asked once Borderline mood is reactive and unpredictable, shifting within hours (criterion 6, affective instability due to marked reactivity of mood): "regular and predictable changes in mood" is not a borderline feature, and eccentric behaviour with odd thinking and communication is schizotypal. asked once What borderline has that narcissistic lacks is pervasive instability of relationships and self-image ; grandiosity, need for admiration and the belief in being special and understood only by high-status people are narcissistic criteria. asked once Heinz Kohut 's self psychology: failure of parental mirroring and idealising leaves a fragmented, empty self (the keyed answer to the "no one, empty inside" vignette, which the paper calls object relations theory); object relations theory proper is Klein, Fairbairn, Winnicott and Kernberg. asked once Dialectical behaviour therapy (Marsha Linehan, on her biosocial theory of 1993: emotional vulnerability transacting with an invalidating environment) is the treatment indicated for borderline personality disorder; its clearest effect is on self-harm and suicide attempts. asked once Antisocial personality disorder : deceitfulness and manipulation, consistent irresponsibility and lack of remorse are three of its seven criteria (three or more needed). asked once OCPD is a preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and mental and interpersonal control at the expense of flexibility, openness and efficiency; its motive is a need for control , not efficiency, achievement or autonomy. asked once The term kleptomania was given by Charles Chrétien Henri Marc with Jean-Étienne Esquirol (kleptomanie, 1838); Matthey's earlier word was klopémanie (1816), and Marc also coined pyromanie (1833). asked once The kleptomania distractors: Bleuler coined schizophrenia, ambivalence and autism; Morselli named dysmorphophobia (1891); Munro described monosymptomatic hypochondriacal psychosis. asked once Antisocial personality disorder needs an age of at least 18, evidence of conduct disorder with onset before 15, and a pattern of disregard for others' rights since 15 (not 12, 16 or 21). asked 2 times The DSM-5 core triad of narcissistic personality disorder is grandiosity, need for admiration and lack of empathy (five of nine criteria). asked 2 times "With limited prosocial emotions" is a specifier for conduct disorder only (not antisocial personality, oppositional defiant or intermittent explosive disorder): two or more of lack of remorse or guilt, callous lack of empathy, unconcern about performance and shallow or deficient affect, for at least 12 months, in more than one relationship or setting. asked 2 times Borderline personality disorder versus conduct disorder : identity and affective instability with fear of abandonment versus rule violation and aggression (cruelty to animals, serious rule breaking). Conduct disorder before 15 is the precursor of antisocial, not borderline, personality disorder. asked 2 times Thresholds: borderline 5 of 9 ; antisocial 3 of 7; paranoid, schizoid and avoidant 4 of 7; obsessive-compulsive 4 of 8; schizotypal and narcissistic 5 of 9; histrionic and dependent 5 of 8; none needs 6. asked once Compared with OCD, OCPD is ego-syntonic with limited insight and has no true obsessions or compulsions; OCD is ego-dystonic. asked once The PCL-R was developed by Robert D.
