Her items ask how often each feeling is true of a student in general, so her scale is meant to measure trait anxiety, and a two-week retest is exactly the right check: a good trait scale should rank the students in much the same order a fortnight later. Had she written "Right now I feel tense", she would have been measuring a state, and a two-week retest would have punished her scale for doing its job. The first question to ask about any retest coefficient, then, is not "Is it high?" but "Should it be high, given what the test measures and how long the interval was?" Exam trap "Test-retest reliability is most appropriate for ..." The answer is stable trait measures : constructs expected to stay stable over the retest interval, such as intelligence and personality. The other options fail for different reasons. Measures of a rapidly changing state (current mood, state anxiety) are the classic wrong answer, because real change lowers the coefficient and would make a good state measure look bad. Single-item measures only is wrong because of the word "only": retesting is in fact one of the few ways to estimate the reliability of a single item (internal consistency needs several items to compare), but the method is in no way restricted to single items. Open-ended interviews only is wrong because the first worry with open-ended material is whether scorers agree (inter-rater reliability, Section 3.6), and again because of "only". In another version of the question, " there is no opportunity to administer twice " rules test-retest out completely, since the method needs two administrations, and " there is only one rater " is irrelevant: the number of raters concerns scorer reliability, not stability over time (one rater re-scoring the same protocols later gives intra-rater reliability, Section 3.6). Clinical link In therapy, change is the point. A client's score on a measure of current anxious or depressive symptoms is supposed to fall if the treatment works, so a low correlation between the scores of a treated group before and after therapy says nothing about the measure's reliability. The clinician's question is a different one: is this client's drop of, say, 8 points larger than the bouncing about that measurement error alone would produce? Answering it needs the standard error of measurement and the standard error of the difference between two scores, which Section 3.7 teaches. A trait measure behaves differently. If a client's score on a measure of a stable personality trait changes sharply over a fortnight, suspicion falls first on the testing (a hurried administration, misunderstood instructions, or a change in how the client wished to appear) before any conclusion is drawn about the person. How stable are intelligence and personality over a lifetime? A retest over a few weeks asks a question about the test. A retest over decades asks a question about the person. When the interval is long enough for real change to happen, the correlation between two testings stops being a reliability coefficient in the ordinary sense and becomes a measure of how stable the attribute itself is: how far people keep their places relative to one another as they grow up and grow old. Two lines of research give a sense of the numbers, and they are worth knowing because they show why intelligence and personality are treated as traits. Key study: the Scottish children of 1932, retested at 77 (Deary and colleagues, 2000) On 1 June 1932, almost every child born in 1921 and attending school in Scotland sat the same group intelligence test, the Moray House Test, as part of the Scottish Mental Survey. The score records survived. In 1998, Ian Deary , Lawrence Whalley and their colleagues traced 101 of those children, by then 77 years old, and gave them the identical test again; a group of them sat it on 1 June 1998, 66 years to the day after the first sitting. The correlation between the scores at 11 and at 77 was 0.63, and 0.73 after a statistical correction for the fact that the people retested were a less varied group than the whole cohort (restriction of range, Section 3.8). Across almost a whole lifetime, then, the rank order of intelligence held up remarkably well, though not perfectly: there was room for some people to rise and others to fall. The study was published in the journal Intelligence in 2000. Personality shows a similar but more gradual picture. In 2000 Brent Roberts and Wendy DelVecchio combined 152 longitudinal studies, containing more than 3,000 retest coefficients for personality traits measured several years apart, in a meta-analysis published in Psychological Bulletin . Rank-order consistency rose steadily with age: from about 0.31 in childhood to about 0.54 in the college years, about 0.64 at age 30, and a plateau of about 0.74 between the ages of 50 and 70. Personality, in other words, becomes more stable as people mature. Neither set of figures is a reliability coefficient for any particular test, since each mixes measurement error with genuine change over years. But they tell a test user what to expect over a few weeks: because the traits themselves barely move in so short a time, a good intelligence or personality test should give a high coefficient of stability, and a low one points to the test. The same retest logic is applied to clinical judgements. A diagnosis can be checked for stability by having patients interviewed twice, a short time apart, and asking how often the second interview gives the same diagnosis; Book 2, Section 2.10.5 describes how the field trials of the diagnostic manuals did this, and Book 3, Section 1.6.6 discusses what the results mean for the reliability of psychiatric diagnosis. Behavioural ratings by observers can be retested in the same way, although for them the first question is usually whether two observers agree (Book 2, Section 2.8.7). Telling test-retest apart from its neighbours Because the methods of estimating reliability differ from one another in only one or two ingredients (how many forms, how many occasions, how many scorers, what is correlated with what), they are easy to confuse with each other and with the different kinds of validity. Table 3.7 lists the descriptions you are most likely to find set beside "the same test given twice to the same people", says what each one actually describes, and points to where this book teaches it. Predictive validity also involves two sets of scores collected at two times, which is why it is such a tempting distractor. But in a predictive validity study the second set of scores comes from a different measure, a criterion such as later examination marks or performance in a job, and the question is whether the test forecasts it. Two final points place test-retest among the other methods. First, it is one of the methods that work for a speed test (a test of easy items under a tight time limit), for which splitting a single timed sitting gives a spuriously high coefficient; Section 3.4 explains why. Second, it is one of the few methods available for a single-item measure, such as a one-question rating of life satisfaction, because there are no other items to compare that one item with. Its blind spot, content sampling error, is the reason the next method was invented. Exam trap A test-retest coefficient is most appropriate for assessing stability of scores over time . "Internal consistency of items" is Cronbach's alpha or KR-20 (Section 3.5); "inter-rater agreement" is kappa or the intraclass correlation (Section 3.6); "equivalence of two parallel forms" is the alternate-forms coefficient of equivalence (Section 3.3); "correlating the test with a future criterion" is predictive validity (Chapter 4); and "item response theory" is a model of item responses, not a reliability design. If a stem says "the same test ... the same people ... on two occasions ... correlated", the answer is test-retest reliability, and the coefficient is the coefficient of stability, not of equivalence. Construct and content validity, often offered beside it, concern what a test measures, not whether it measures consistently. 3.3 Alternate and Parallel Forms: Equivalence Lower yield · not asked yet Komal is a clinical psychologist in the memory clinic of a hospital in Mysuru. A retired schoolteacher in his late sixties has been referred because his family has noticed that he forgets conversations, and among other tasks Komal tests his memory with a list of 15 words that she reads aloud and he then recalls. She will need to test him again in six months to see whether his memory is holding steady or declining. If she reads him the same 15 words, part of whatever he recalls the second time may be memory of the test itself, which is exactly the thing that is not supposed to count. So she needs a second list: different words, but just as hard as the first, measuring the same thing on the same scale, so that a change in his score means a change in the man rather than a change in the list. How such a second version is built, how you check that it really is interchangeable with the first, and what the correlation between the two versions tells you about reliability are the subjects of this section. They lead to a second kind of reliability coefficient, the coefficient of equivalence, and to a third, the strictest of all. Why one form is not always enough Section 3.2 ended with the blind spot of the retest design: because the same items are used twice, the luck of which items were chosen is repeated and counted as true score. That is a measurement problem, and it is one reason for building a second form. There are also practical reasons why test users want a second version of a test, and historically these came first. The four commonest are the following. Retesting without memory for the items. When a person must be tested twice, to follow a child's development, a patient's recovery or decline, or the effect of a drug, a second form removes the problem of remembered items (though not, as you will see, every carry-over effect). Measuring change before and after treatment. Outcome research in clinical psychology compares scores before and after therapy, and a client who has seen the items once may answer differently the second time simply because of that first exposure. Alternate forms reduce this source of contamination. Make-up and repeat examinations. A student who missed an examination through illness, or who must sit it again, cannot fairly be given the paper that classmates have already seen and discussed. Security in large-scale testing. When thousands of candidates sit an examination in several sessions or places, a single paper would leak. Indian board examinations, for example, commonly print several sets of each question paper, built to the same pattern of chapters, marks and question types, so that different candidates answer different questions. Each set is meant to be an equivalent form of the others. In every one of these uses, the second form is valuable only if it is interchangeable with the first: a person's score should not depend on which form he or she happened to receive. How interchangeable is interchangeable enough? Psychometricians answer at two levels of strictness. Parallel forms in the strict sense, alternate forms in the practical sense The strict answer comes straight from the classical model of Section 3.1. Two forms are parallel forms in the classical sense when every person has the same true score on both and the two forms have equal error variances. Put more plainly, the two forms measure exactly the same thing, on the same scale, with the same precision; they differ only in the random errors that happen to fall on each. Section 3.1 showed the most important consequence: the correlation between two truly parallel forms equals the reliability of either one. That is why giving two parallel forms and correlating them is a legitimate way to estimate reliability: in classical theory it is the most direct estimate there is. The definition sounds abstract, because nobody can see true scores. But it has consequences that can be checked with ordinary statistics. If two forms give everyone the same true score, they must have the same mean in any group of people. If they also have equal error variances, they must have the same standard deviation, since true variance plus an equal amount of error variance gives an equal observed variance. And because both forms carry the same true score with the same amount of error, each must correlate equally with any third measure, whether another test or a criterion such as examination marks. Harold Gulliksen (1903 to 1996), in his Theory of Mental Tests (1950), turned these consequences into a statistical criterion for parallel tests: equal means, equal variances and equal intercorrelations, checked with significance tests so that the small differences that always arise from sampling are not mistaken for real ones. He also insisted on a psychological criterion: the forms must contain items dealing with the same subject matter, in the same format and with the same kind of instructions, so that they are parallel as far as psychological judgment can tell. Statistics can tell you that two forms behave alike; only their content can tell you that they behave alike for the right reason. Strict parallelism is an ideal that real forms can only approach, and psychometricians later named some looser relationships that are useful in their own right. In Statistical Theories of Mental Test Scores (1968), Frederic Lord and Melvin Novick described tau-equivalent forms (tau, τ, is the Greek letter used for the true score), which give every person the same true score but may differ in their error variances, so that one form is noisier than the other; and essentially tau-equivalent forms, whose true scores differ only by a constant, as if one form simply added two points to everyone's score. In 1971 Karl Jöreskog named the loosest useful relationship: congeneric forms measure the same attribute but may do so on different scales and with different precision. These distinctions matter most for coefficient alpha, which assumes that the items are at least essentially tau-equivalent, as Section 3.5 explains. For a test developer building two forms, the practical message is simpler: aim at strict parallelism, check how close you came, and report it. In everyday use a looser standard applies. Two versions of a test built independently from the same blueprint are called alternate forms (also equivalent forms or comparable forms). The blueprint is the table of specifications , which fixes the content areas and the proportion of items in each, and the forms also share the number of items, the item formats, the range and spread of difficulty, the instructions, the time limit and the scoring. Alternate forms aim at parallelism without claiming to have reached it. Most writers use "parallel forms reliability", "alternate forms reliability" and "equivalent forms reliability" interchangeably for the method of correlating two forms, and you may do the same, as long as you remember that "parallel" in its strict sense is the stronger claim. A. K. Singh's textbook, for example, reproduces the practical criteria for equivalent forms listed by Frank S. Freeman (1898 to 1986) in his Theory and Practice of Psychological Testing (third edition, 1962). Table 3.8 summarises them beside Gulliksen's statistical checks. Table 3.8 What makes two forms parallel: the classical definition and the practical criteria for alternate forms (after Gulliksen, 1950, and Freeman, 1962). Requirement Strictly parallel forms Alternate (equivalent) forms True scores Identical for every person Intended to be the same Error variance Equal Similar Means and standard deviations Equal Equal or nearly so Content Same subject matter, same item format Same blueprint: content areas and proportions Items Different items, same properties Same number, format, difficulty range and spread, and homogeneity Administration Identical Same instructions, time limit and mode Correlation with other measures Equal Similar Exam trap Parallel forms must match in means, variances (standard deviations), content and format , and they should correlate equally with other measures. Covering the same topic is not enough: two forms with the same content but different difficulty will give different means and may rank people differently. Nor are two forms parallel just because they correlate highly with each other. Two forms that correlate 0.90 but differ by five points in their means are closely related tests, not interchangeable ones: a person's score would still depend on which form was taken. Building and checking two forms How does a test developer actually produce two forms that come close to the ideal? The standard method starts with more items than either form needs. Suppose Akash, who sets examinations for a coaching institute, wants two 30-item forms of an arithmetic reasoning test for Class 8 pupils. He writes an item pool of about 80 items to a single blueprint, tries them out on a sample of pupils, and runs an item analysis (Chapter 2): for each item he finds its difficulty (the proportion of pupils who answer it correctly) and its discrimination (how well it separates pupils who do well on the test as a whole from those who do badly). He discards the weak items and then pairs the survivors: two fraction items of about the same difficulty and discrimination, two percentage items, two time-and-distance items, and so on. Within each matched pair, a coin toss decides which item goes to Form A and which to Form B. The result is two forms that match item for item in content, difficulty and discrimination, which is about as close to parallel as careful construction can get. Construction is a promise; the data are the proof. Akash gives both forms to 120 pupils at a single sitting and compares them. Form A has a mean of 18.4 and a standard deviation of 5.0; Form B has a mean of 18.1 and a standard deviation of 5.2; and the two forms correlate 0.86. Is that close enough? The means differ by 18.4 − 18.1 = 0.3 of a mark, which is 0.3 / 5.0 = 0.06 of a standard deviation, far too small to matter for any practical decision. The standard deviations differ by only 0.2, so the spreads are almost the same. And the correlation of 0.86 says that the two forms rank the pupils in very nearly the same order. Had the means differed by 3 marks, Form B would have been clearly harder, and a pupil's mark would have depended partly on the luck of which form he or she received. With significance tests (Gulliksen's statistical criterion; the Research Methodology book teaches the tests themselves), Akash can check formally whether differences as small as his could be accidents of sampling. What if two forms turn out not quite equal? Rather than throw one away, test developers often turn to equating : converting scores on one form to the scale of the other, so that a converted score means the same level of performance whichever form was taken. Two methods are common. In linear equating , a score on Form B is converted to the Form A score that lies the same number of standard deviations from the Form A mean. In words: find how far the Form B score is from the Form B mean, counted in Form B standard deviations; then go the same distance from the Form A mean, counted in Form A standard deviations. As a formula: Equated Form A score = M A + (SD A / SD B ) × (X B − M B ) Here X B is the score obtained on Form B, M A and M B are the means of the two forms, and SD A and SD B are their standard deviations, all found in the same group of people or in groups known to be equivalent. Suppose two forms of a final examination came out with a Form A mean of 30 and standard deviation of 8, and a Form B mean of 26 and standard deviation of 6, so that Form B was harder and its scores less spread out. A student who scored 32 on Form B stood (32 − 26) / 6 = 6 / 6 = 1.0 standard deviation above the Form B mean. The Form A score that stands 1.0 standard deviation above the Form A mean is 30 + 1.0 × 8 = 38. So 32 on the harder Form B is worth 38 on Form A. In equipercentile equating , scores with the same percentile rank on the two forms are treated as equal (if 32 on Form B and 38 on Form A both have a percentile rank of 84, they are declared equivalent), which also corrects for differences in the shapes of the two score distributions. Percentile ranks and standard scores are taught in Chapter 5, and large testing programmes use more elaborate designs. Notice, though, what equating can and cannot do. It can remove a difference in difficulty and spread. It cannot remove a difference in what the two forms measure, or in how reliably they measure it; those have to be got right when the items are written. Indian context Large Indian entrance examinations meet the alternate-forms problem on a vast scale. When the National Testing Agency (NTA) holds the Joint Entrance Examination (JEE) Main in several shifts over several days, each shift answers a different question paper, and no team of paper setters can make the papers exactly equal in difficulty. The NTA's answer is a normalisation procedure based on percentile scores. Each candidate's raw marks are converted into a percentile within that candidate's own shift (the percentage of candidates in the shift who scored at or below that candidate), and candidates are then compared on these percentiles rather than on raw marks. The logic is that of equipercentile equating, and it rests on one assumption: that the candidates allotted to the different shifts are, on average, equally able, so that a candidate at the 95th percentile of a hard shift has done as well as one at the 95th percentile of an easy shift. The coefficient of equivalence and the coefficient of stability and equivalence Once two forms exist, there are two ways to give them, and the choice changes what the resulting correlation means. Figure 3.6 sets the two designs beside the test-retest design of Section 3.2. 1. Test-retest: coefficient of stability Form A interval Form A occasion 1 occasion 2 Shows: time sampling error Hidden: content sampling error (the same items both times) 2. Two forms, one sitting: coefficient of equivalence Form A Form B same day, back to back Shows: content sampling error Hidden: time sampling error (one occasion only) 3. Two forms, two occasions: coefficient of stability and equivalence Form A interval Form B occasion 1 occasion 2 Shows: time and content sampling error together (usually the lowest coefficient) Figure 3.6 Three designs and the errors each one lets in. Retesting with the same form shows time sampling error but hides content sampling error; two forms at one sitting do the opposite; two forms on two occasions let both in, which is why the coefficient of stability and equivalence is the strictest estimate. In designs 2 and 3, half the group takes Form B first (counterbalancing). In the first alternate-forms design, the same group takes Form A and then Form B at a single sitting, one straight after the other, perhaps with a short break. The correlation between the two forms is the coefficient of equivalence . Because both forms are taken on the same occasion, the person's state, the hall and the day are the same for both, so time sampling error has almost no chance to appear. What does differ between the forms is the items. A pupil who happens to find the Form A fraction items easy and the Form B fraction items awkward will score differently on the two forms, and that difference lowers the correlation. The coefficient of equivalence therefore measures content sampling error, the very error that the retest design could not see. Akash's 0.86 is a coefficient of equivalence: it says that about 86 percent of the score differences among his pupils would survive a change of items, and about 14 percent depend on which particular items each form happened to contain. In the second design, the group takes Form A on one occasion and Form B after an interval, perhaps a few weeks. The correlation is the coefficient of stability and equivalence , sometimes called delayed alternate-forms reliability. Now both kinds of error have a chance to lower the correlation: the items differ (content sampling) and so does the occasion (time sampling). A person can score differently because the second form suits them less well, or because they are tired on the second day, or both. Because this design lets in more sources of error than any other classical design, it is the most demanding test of a score's consistency, and it usually gives the lowest coefficient of all the classical methods. It is also the most realistic estimate whenever scores will be compared across occasions and forms, which is exactly how tests like Komal's memory lists are used: the patient is tested on different days with different versions. Giving two forms in sequence creates an order problem. Suppose every pupil took Form A first and Form B second. Any fatigue, boredom or warming up produced by the first form would fall entirely on the second, and a difference between the forms' means would be impossible to interpret: is Form B harder, or were the pupils simply tired by the time they reached it? The standard remedy is counterbalancing : half the group, chosen at random, takes Form A first and Form B second, and the other half takes Form B first and Form A second. Order effects then fall equally on both forms, and the two influences can be separated. A small example shows how. Suppose Form B is really 1 mark harder than Form A, and tiredness lowers whichever form comes second by another mark. Without counterbalancing, pupils taking A first and B second would score, say, 20 on A and 18 on B, and Form B would look 2 marks harder when it is really only 1 mark harder. With counterbalancing, the other half (B first) would score 19 on B (1 mark for difficulty, no tiredness) and 19 on A (no difficulty penalty, 1 mark of tiredness). Averaging over both halves, Form A's mean is (20 + 19) / 2 = 19.5 and Form B's is (18 + 19) / 2 = 18.5: a difference of exactly 1 mark, the true difference in difficulty. And comparing each form taken first with the same form taken second (20 against 19 for A, 19 against 18 for B) recovers the 1-mark order effect. Counterbalancing does not abolish order effects. It spreads them evenly, so that they cannot masquerade as a difference between the forms. Having coefficients from more than one design also allows a rough piece of book-keeping on where the error comes from. In a second sample of Class 8 pupils, Akash gives Form A, waits six weeks, and then gives Form B: this time the forms correlate 0.76, the coefficient of stability and equivalence. Treat each coefficient, as Section 3.1 taught, as the proportion of score variance that is consistent, so that one minus the coefficient is the proportion that is error. Then: Error from content sampling alone (two forms, one sitting) is about 1 − 0.86 = 0.14, or 14 percent of the variance. Error from content and time sampling together (two forms, two occasions) is about 1 − 0.76 = 0.24, or 24 percent. So the share due to time sampling is about 0.24 − 0.14 = 0.10, or 10 percent, which is the same as 0.86 − 0.76. Of the 24 percent of the variance that is error when pupils are compared across both forms and occasions, about 14 points come from the items and about 10 from the occasion. This is only a rough accounting: it assumes that the error sources simply add up and that the two samples of pupils are comparable. Generalizability theory (Section 3.9) does the same job properly, estimating every source of error at once with analysis of variance. But the rough version already shows why the coefficient of stability and equivalence must be the lowest: it is the only classical design that charges the test for both kinds of error at once. Remember Error variance from content sampling ≈ 1 − r eq Error variance from content and time sampling together ≈ 1 − r se Error variance from time sampling ≈ r eq − r se Here r eq is the coefficient of equivalence (two forms, one sitting) and r se is the coefficient of stability and equivalence (two forms, two occasions), each read as a proportion of variance. Because more error enters the second design, r se is normally the lower of the two. Exam trap Match each design to its coefficient and its error. Same form, two occasions : coefficient of stability; time sampling error. Two forms, one sitting : coefficient of equivalence; content sampling error. Two forms, two occasions : coefficient of stability and equivalence; both errors, so usually the lowest estimate. A stem that speaks of "the equivalence of two parallel forms" is describing alternate-forms reliability, not test-retest; a stem that describes "the same scale given again two weeks later" is test-retest, not parallel forms, because no second form is involved. Strengths, weaknesses and tests published in alternate forms The great strength of alternate forms is that they remove the most damaging carry-over effect of a retest, memory for particular items, while still allowing a person to be tested more than once. They let the developer estimate content sampling error directly. A second form is also useful in itself, for retesting, make-up examinations and test security, quite apart from any reliability study. And alternate forms are especially valuable for speed tests, for which splitting a single timed sitting gives a misleadingly high coefficient (Section 3.4). The weaknesses are just as real. Building a genuinely parallel second form roughly doubles the work of test construction, since every item must in effect be written, tried out and analysed twice, and even then complete equivalence is rarely, if ever, achieved. Practice effects are reduced but not removed: a person who has done one form has learned the instructions, the format, the pace and often the strategy that the items call for, and that learning carries over to the other form. A child who has once worked out how matrix puzzles "work" is better at the next one, whatever its particular pattern. When the two forms are given at one sitting, fatigue and boredom can lower scores on whichever form comes second, which is why counterbalancing matters. And for some kinds of test, true alternate forms are almost impossible to build: a short test whose few items are each unique in what they demand cannot easily be duplicated. When a patient is assessed repeatedly (before and after surgery for epilepsy, during treatment with a drug, or every six months to follow a possible dementia), alternate forms protect the scores from remembered items. But they do not make repeated testing free of practice. Patients still become familiar with the tasks, the room and the examiner, and many show small gains on retesting even with new items, gains that can hide a real decline. Good practice is to use alternate forms where they exist, to know the size of the practice effect reported for the test, and to judge whether a change is real with the standard error of the difference between two scores (Section 3.7), not by eye. From two forms to two halves Alternate forms solve the content sampling problem, but at a price: two forms to build and, usually, two administrations to arrange. Can the same information be had more cheaply? Look again at Akash's construction method. He wrote matched pairs of items and sent one member of each pair to Form A and the other to Form B. Suppose that, instead of printing two booklets, he printed all 60 items in one booklet with the two members of each pair next to each other, gave it once, and scored the odd-numbered and the even-numbered items separately. Each half would contain one member of every pair. He would have two short "forms" from a single sitting. That is the idea of split-half reliability: one administration, two halves treated as if they were miniature parallel forms. It inherits the coefficient of equivalence's strength (it detects content sampling error) and its weakness (it says nothing about stability over time), and it brings a new problem of its own. Each half is only half as long as the real test, and a shorter test is a less reliable one, so the correlation between the halves underestimates the reliability of the whole. Section 3.4 explains how Charles Spearman and William Brown corrected for that in 1910. Exam trap Do not confuse parallel forms reliability with split-half reliability . Parallel (alternate) forms reliability correlates two complete, separately built versions of a test, given as two administrations, at one sitting or with an interval. Split-half reliability correlates two halves of a single form from a single administration, and the half-test correlation must then be stepped up with the Spearman-Brown formula because each half is short. The two halves are a miniature version of parallel forms, which is why the methods resemble each other; but an option describing "two forms of a test given to the same group" is parallel forms, and one describing "correlating two halves of a single test" is split-half. Neither is Cronbach's alpha, which in effect averages over all the possible ways of splitting the items into halves and is an index of internal consistency (Section 3.5). The test-retest design detects sampling error, which arises from differences between occasions. Because the same items are used both times, test-retest reliability cannot detect sampling error. Too short an interval between testings the test-retest coefficient, because memory and practice carry over. Test-retest reliability is appropriate for stable , such as intelligence and personality, but not for rapidly changing states such as current mood. If every person's score rises by exactly 4 points on the retest, the coefficient of stability changes by . Two alternate forms given at a single sitting yield the coefficient of . Giving half the group Form A first and the other half Form B first is called . Form A has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10; Form B has a mean of 45 and a standard deviation of 5. By linear equating, a score of 55 on Form B is equivalent to on Form A. Two forms correlate 0.85 when given at one sitting and 0.75 when given six weeks apart. The share of score variance due to time sampling error is roughly . Answers: (1) stability, (2) time, (3) content (item), (4) inflates (raises), (5) traits, (6) nothing, zero (a change that is the same for everyone leaves a correlation unchanged), (7) equivalence, (8) counterbalancing, (9) 70 (the Form B score is (55 − 45) / 5 = 2 standard deviations above the Form B mean, and 50 + 2 × 10 = 70), (10) 0.10, or 10 percent (content sampling error is 1 − 0.85 = 0.15, content and time together are 1 − 0.75 = 0.25, so time sampling is 0.25 − 0.15 = 0.10). 3.4 Split-Half Reliability and the Spearman-Brown Prophecy Formula High yield · 16 Qs The two methods you met in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 share an awkward requirement: the same people must be tested twice. Test-retest reliability needs a second session days or weeks after the first, and alternate forms need a second form that somebody has had to write, try out and match to the first. Both cost time and money. Both lose people who do not turn up the second time. And both leave room for things to happen in between: students learn, patients recover, and memories of the first sitting linger. So test developers have long asked a tempting question. Can we estimate reliability from a single sitting, with a single form? The first answer, and still one of the most examined ideas in psychometrics, was to cut the test in two. This section explains how to cut it, why the correlation between the two halves must then be corrected with the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula, how the same formula predicts what happens when any test is made longer or shorter, which formulas avoid the correction altogether, and the one kind of test for which cutting in two gives a badly wrong answer. One sitting, two halves The logic of split-half reliability is simple. Give the test once. Then, instead of scoring each person once, score each person twice: once on one half of the items and once on the other half. Every person now has two scores, and the two sets of scores are correlated across the whole group. (The correlation coefficient, Pearson's r, is a number between −1 and +1 that shows how closely two sets of scores rise and fall together; the Research Methodology book teaches it in full.) If the two halves measure the same thing, people who do well on one half will do well on the other, and the correlation will be high. Look at what this design really does. The two halves are, in effect, two short alternate forms of the test, printed in one booklet and taken at one sitting. In the language of Section 3.3, a split-half correlation is a coefficient of equivalence for two miniature forms given back to back. Because both halves are taken at the same time, nothing can change between them: there is no interval in which to learn, forget, recover or fall ill, so time-sampling error cannot enter the estimate. What does differ between the halves is the particular items each one contains. A student who happens to know the words that landed in one half but not those in the other will score unevenly, and that is exactly the content-sampling (item-sampling) error of Section 3.1. Split-half reliability therefore tells you how consistently a test measures across different samples of items. That is why it is counted as the oldest member of the family of internal consistency methods that Section 3.5 completes. Rohini, whose Verbal Reasoning Test (VRT) you have followed since Section 3.1, did exactly this with her 40-item test. After her 200 Class 12 students had taken it, she scored each answer sheet twice: once for the 20 odd-numbered items (items 1, 3, 5 and so on up to 39) and once for the 20 even-numbered items (2, 4, 6 and so on up to 40). The odd-item scores and the even-item scores correlated 0.70. Hold on to that number. It is not yet the reliability of her test, and the next three subsections explain why not and what to do about it. The attractions of the method are plain. It needs one administration, one form and no second appointment. Nobody can remember answers from an earlier sitting, because there is no earlier sitting. Nobody drops out between sessions, and the conditions of testing (the hall, the noise, the invigilator, the time of day) are identical for both halves. For a developer like Rohini, who had to travel to four colleges to test her students, these are not small advantages. But the method's simplicity hides a decision that is not simple at all: which items go into which half? Dividing the test: first and second halves, odd-even and matched halves The most obvious way to divide a 40-item test is to put items 1 to 20 in one half and items 21 to 40 in the other. This first-half and second-half split is almost always a bad idea, for four reasons. First, most ability tests arrange their items from easy to hard, so the first half would be the easy half and the second half the hard one; the halves would have different means and different spreads, and would even tap slightly different levels of the ability. Second, people change during a sitting. Some need a few items to warm up and settle their nerves, and most grow tired, bored or careless towards the end, so the second half catches more fatigue than the first. Third, if time is tight, some people never reach the last items at all, and their second-half score partly measures speed rather than ability. Fourth, many tests group their items by content (all the analogies together, then all the vocabulary items), so the two halves would sample different content. Each of these effects pushes a person's two half-scores apart for reasons that have nothing to do with how consistent the items are, and the correlation comes out too low. The standard remedy is the odd-even split : the odd-numbered items form one half and the even-numbered items the other. Because the items alternate, each half receives an easy item for every easy item in the other half, an early item for every early item and a late item for every late item. Warm-up, fatigue and rising difficulty are now shared almost equally between the halves, so they no longer drive the two scores apart. This is why the odd-even split is the one textbooks recommend and the one used most often. One practical refinement matters: items that belong together, such as five questions on the same reading passage or several items built on one diagram, should go into the same half as a block. Such items share something (familiarity with that passage, say) that would otherwise inflate the correlation between the halves. The most careful developers go a step further and build matched random halves . They first use the item statistics from a tryout, chiefly each item's difficulty (the proportion of people who pass it) and its discrimination (how well it separates high scorers from low scorers; Chapter 2 explains both), to arrange the items into pairs that are as alike as possible in difficulty and content. Then, for each pair, chance (a coin, or a table of random numbers) decides which member goes to half A and which to half B. The result is two halves matched in difficulty and content by design, not by the accident of how the items happened to be numbered. Even the most carefully matched split is only one of a very large number of possible splits. A test of just 10 items can be divided into two halves of five items in 126 different ways, and each way gives a slightly different correlation. Which one is "the" split-half reliability? There is no single answer. This arbitrariness is the weakness that led G. Frederic Kuder, Marion Richardson and later Lee Cronbach to the coefficients of Section 3.5, which in effect average over every possible split. For now the practical lesson is the one examiners like to test: the hard part of split-half reliability is not the arithmetic but the division of the test into two halves that are nearly equivalent. Exam trap The major challenge of split-half reliability is dividing the test into two nearly equivalent halves . Computing the Spearman-Brown step-up is one line of arithmetic, so that option is bait. Giving the same test twice with an interval is the burden of test-retest reliability (Section 3.2), and giving two forms is the burden of alternate forms (Section 3.3); split-half was invented precisely to avoid both. And remember which split is the poor one: first half against second half. Odd-even is the usual split. Why half a test underestimates the whole Rohini's halves correlate 0.70. Why can she not simply report 0.70 as the reliability of the VRT? Because 0.70 describes the consistency of two 20-item tests, and the test her students will actually take has 40 items. Common sense already tells you that a longer test is a more dependable measure than a shorter one. Imagine judging a batsman's form from a single ball: one lucky edge or one unplayable delivery decides everything. Judge him over an over and the luck starts to even out; judge him over a whole innings and you learn a great deal about his real ability. A test item is one ball. Every item carries a little of the person's true ability and a little luck: a word they happened to read last week, a careless slip, a lucky guess. The more items you add up, the more the luck cancels out and the more the true ability shows through. This is the domain-sampling idea of Section 3.1: a longer test is a bigger sample from the universe of possible items, so it represents a person's standing in that universe more faithfully. You can see exactly how much a test gains from being doubled if you follow the true part and the error part of the score separately, using the model of Section 3.1: observed score = true score + error (X = T + E). Suppose each half of a test has an observed-score variance of 6, of which 3.6 is true-score variance and 2.4 is error variance. (Variance is the average squared distance of the scores from their mean, a measure of how spread out they are; the Research Methodology book teaches it in full.) The reliability of each half is the share of its variance that is true: 3.6 / 6 = 0.60. Because the two halves are parallel, this is also the correlation you would find between them; Section 3.1 explains why the correlation between two parallel tests equals the reliability of each. Now add the two halves together to make the full test, and watch what happens to each part of the score. The true parts add up in step. Each person has the same true score on both halves, because parallel halves measure the same thing equally well. So the true part of the full score is simply twice the true part of one half. Doubling every number in a set doubles every distance from the mean, and since variance is built from squared distances, doubling multiplies the variance by four (2 × 2): 4 × 3.6 = 14.4. The error parts only partly add up. The errors on the two halves are independent: being lucky on half A makes you no more likely to be lucky on half B. For some people the two errors point the same way; for others they point in opposite directions and cancel. When two independent quantities are added, their variances simply add: 2.4 + 2.4 = 4.8. That is only twice the error variance of one half, not four times. The full test therefore has a true variance of 14.4, an error variance of 4.8 and an observed variance of 14.4 + 4.8 = 19.2. Its reliability is 14.4 / 19.2 = 0.75. Doubling the test has raised its reliability from 0.60 to 0.75, and the reason is now in plain view: when a test is lengthened, its true variance grows faster (here four times) than its error variance (here two times), so the true share of the total rises. Keep these numbers in mind (half variances of 6, a full-test variance of 19.2 and an error variance of 4.8); you will meet them again in Hrithik's data later in this section. The Spearman-Brown prophecy formula The formula that turns a half-test correlation into a whole-test reliability was published in 1910, in the same issue of the British Journal of Psychology (volume 3), by two men who reached it separately. One was Charles Spearman, whose true-score model you met in Section 3.1 and whose theory of general intelligence, g, is told in Book 1, Section 9.4. His paper, "Correlation calculated from faulty data", continued the project he had begun in 1904: working out how errors in psychological measurements (the "faulty data" of his title) distort the correlations between them. The other was William Brown (1881 to 1952), a young British psychologist whose paper, "Some experimental results in the correlation of mental abilities", grew out of his doctoral research on the use of correlation in psychology. Brown was no disciple of Spearman. His doctoral thesis criticised parts of Spearman's 1904 work on correlation, Spearman's 1910 paper in turn criticised Brown's, and for some years Brown questioned whether Spearman's evidence really proved a general factor. Historians describe the two as rivals rather than partners, even though their papers sit back to back in the journal and the formula carries both their names. Brown went on to a distinguished career at Oxford, where he was Wilde Reader in Mental Philosophy from 1921 and became the first director of the university's Institute of Experimental Psychology when it opened in 1936. The word "prophecy" in the formula's usual name describes what it does: it foretells the reliability of a test that nobody has yet given, whether that is the full-length test made by putting two halves together or a test lengthened or shortened by any amount. For the split-half case the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula is short. In words: the reliability of the whole test equals twice the correlation between the halves, divided by one plus that correlation. Using it is called stepping up the half-test correlation, and the result is often reported as the corrected or stepped-up split-half coefficient. Remember The Spearman-Brown formula for split halves: r full = 2r half / (1 + r half ) where r half is the correlation between the two half-test scores (the reliability of a test half as long) and r full is the estimated reliability of the whole, full-length test. Rohini's VRT shows the formula at work. Her odd and even halves correlate 0.70, so r half = 0.70. Step 1, the top line: 2 × 0.70 = 1.40. Step 2, the bottom line: 1 + 0.70 = 1.70. Step 3, divide: 1.40 / 1.70 = 0.8235, which rounds to 0.82 at two decimal places. So the split-half reliability of the 40-item VRT is 0.82. Read it as Section 3.1 taught you to read any reliability coefficient, directly and without squaring: about 82 percent of the variance in students' total scores reflects true differences in verbal reasoning, as sampled by items of this kind, and about 18 percent reflects the luck of which items a student happened to meet. The commonest examination version uses halves that correlate 0.60. Step 1: 2 × 0.60 = 1.20. Step 2: 1 + 0.60 = 1.60. Step 3: 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75. This is exactly the 0.75 you reached in the last subsection by adding up true and error variances, which is reassuring: the formula is nothing more than that bookkeeping done in one line. Running a few more values through it shows a pattern. Halves correlating 0.30 step up to 0.46, 0.50 to 0.67, 0.60 to 0.75, 0.70 to 0.82, 0.80 to 0.89 and 0.90 to 0.95. The stepped-up value is always higher than the half-test correlation (unless that correlation is exactly 0 or 1), it never exceeds 1, and the boost is largest for middling correlations and smallest for those already near 1. Exam trap "Odd and even halves correlate .60; the full-test reliability is?" The answer is .75 (1.20 / 1.60). The other options are traps with a story: .60 forgets that the half correlation describes a half-length test; .30 halves it instead of stepping it up; .36 squares it (squaring belongs to ordinary correlations, never to reliability coefficients, Section 3.1); .82 is the step-up of .70, not .60; and .80 has no route to it at all. Quick check: the stepped-up value must lie between the half correlation and 1. Making a test longer or shorter Spearman and Brown's insight works for any change of length, not just for doubling. Call the change the length factor , n: the new number of items divided by the present number of items. A test lengthened from 20 to 60 items has n = 60 / 20 = 3; a test cut from 40 to 20 items has n = 20 / 40 = 0.5. Then the general form of the formula predicts the reliability of the new test from the reliability of the present one. Remember The general Spearman-Brown formula: r new = n r / [1 + (n − 1) r] where r is the reliability of the present test, n is the length factor (new length divided by present length; many books call it k) and r new is the predicted reliability of the lengthened or shortened test. With n = 2 it becomes the split-half formula, 2r / (1 + r). The added or removed items must be parallel to the existing ones. Where does this come from? Exactly the bookkeeping of the doubled test. Make a test n times as long with parallel items and its true variance is multiplied by n × n, because the true parts add up in step, while its error variance is multiplied only by n, because independent errors partly cancel. If you write the new reliability as new true variance over new total variance and divide the top and bottom by the old total variance, the formula above drops out. You do not need to reproduce that algebra in an examination, but you should be able to say in words why lengthening helps: true score accumulates faster than error. Take a test with a reliability of 0.50 that is made three times as long with parallel items, so n = 3. Step 1, the top line: n × r = 3 × 0.50 = 1.50. Step 2, the bottom line: (n − 1) × r = 2 × 0.50 = 1.00, and 1 + 1.00 = 2.00. Step 3, divide: 1.50 / 2.00 = 0.75. Tripling the test raises its reliability from 0.50 to 0.75. Notice what it does not do: it does not triple the reliability. Three times 0.50 would be 1.50, an impossible value for a coefficient that cannot exceed 1, and an option of 1.00 in a multiple-choice question is there to catch exactly that straight multiplication. An option of 0.83 is the answer to a different question: it is what five times the length would give (2.50 / 3.00). An option of 0.60 credits the tripled test with too small a gain: it is less than merely doubling the test would give (1.00 / 1.50 = 0.67). The formula works just as well in reverse, and here it gives a warning. Devansh works for a test publisher in Delhi and has been asked to produce a 20-item short form of a 60-item vocabulary test whose reliability is 0.90, because schools complain that the long version takes too much time. The length factor is n = 20 / 60, one third (0.333). Step 1: n × r = (1/3) × 0.90 = 0.30. Step 2: n − 1 = −2/3, so (n − 1) × r = (−2/3) × 0.90 = −0.60, and 1 + (−0.60) = 0.40. Step 3: 0.30 / 0.40 = 0.75. Cutting the test to a third of its length drops its predicted reliability from 0.90 to 0.75. That may be acceptable for comparing classrooms in a research project, but, as Section 3.8 explains, it is too low for decisions about a single child. The commonest examination version is the half-length short form: a test with a reliability of 0.80 cut to half its length, so n = 0.5. Step 1: 0.5 × 0.80 = 0.40. Step 2: (0.5 − 1) × 0.80 = −0.40, and 1 − 0.40 = 0.60. Step 3: 0.40 / 0.60 = 0.667, or 0.67. You can check it by running it backwards: stepping 0.667 up with n = 2 gives 1.333 / 1.667 = 0.80, the reliability you started with. The tempting wrong answers are 0.40 (simply halving the coefficient), 0.89 (doubling the test instead of halving it) and 0.80 (assuming that length makes no difference). Clinical link Clinicians are always short of time, and short forms are everywhere: brief versions of long personality inventories (Chapter 9), short forms of the Wechsler intelligence scales built from a few subtests (Chapter 6), one-page screening questionnaires. The Spearman-Brown formula tells you the price before you pay it. A lower reliability means a wider band of error around each person's score (Section 3.7 shows how to compute it), so a short form can screen a group but should not, on its own, decide a diagnosis or a placement. Lengthening has a price too: a 200-item questionnaire may tire a depressed or elderly patient so badly that the last items are answered carelessly, which breaks the formula's assumption that every added item is answered as well as the first ones. Solving for the length Test developers usually meet the formula the other way round. They know the reliability of their tryout version and the reliability they want, and they need to know how much longer the test must become. Rearranging the general formula to solve for n gives the answer directly. Remember The length needed to reach a target reliability: n = r target (1 − r) / [r (1 − r target )] where r is the present reliability, r target is the reliability you want and n is how many times longer the test must be (with parallel items). Multiply n by the present number of items to get the number of items needed, and always round up. The classic problem: a test has a reliability of 0.60; how many times longer must it be made to reach 0.90? Step 1, the top line: r target × (1 − r) = 0.90 × (1 − 0.60) = 0.90 × 0.40 = 0.36. Step 2, the bottom line: r × (1 − r target ) = 0.60 × (1 − 0.90) = 0.60 × 0.10 = 0.06. Step 3, divide: 0.36 / 0.06 = 6. The test must be made six times as long. Always check by putting the answer back into the general formula: 6 × 0.60 = 3.60 on top; 1 + (5 × 0.60) = 1 + 3.00 = 4.00 underneath; 3.60 / 4.00 = 0.90. If the original test had 20 items, the new one needs 6 × 20 = 120 items, that is, 100 new items all parallel to the first 20. The wrong options in such a question are worth working too: three times the length gives only 1.80 / 2.20 = 0.82, one and a half times gives 0.90 / 1.30 = 0.69, and nine times gives 5.40 / 5.80 = 0.93, more than is needed. The size of the answer carries a lesson of its own: a short screening tool with a reliability around 0.60 cannot be pushed to the 0.90 needed for decisions about individuals by adding a handful of items. It needs better items, not just more of them. A smaller, more realistic case shows why you must round up. Sanya, a clinical psychology trainee in Chandigarh, has written a 10-item questionnaire on sleep problems among college students. Its reliability in a pilot study is 0.70, and she wants 0.80 for her research. Step 1: 0.80 × (1 − 0.70) = 0.80 × 0.30 = 0.24. Step 2: 0.70 × (1 − 0.80) = 0.70 × 0.20 = 0.14. Step 3: 0.24 / 0.14 = 1.714. Her questionnaire must be about 1.71 times as long: 1.714 × 10 = 17.1 items. Items come in whole numbers, so she rounds up to 18, which means writing 8 new items like the first 10. Rounding down to 17 would fall just short: with n = 1.7 the formula gives 1.19 / 1.49 = 0.799. The first, for its split-half use, is that the two halves are parallel tests in the classical sense of Section 3.1: each person has the same true score on both halves, and the halves have equal error variances. In data you can see this as halves with equal means and equal variances that measure the same content. Only then is the correlation between the halves a fair estimate of the reliability of each half, which is what the formula needs as its starting point. When one half is harder than the other, so that its scores bunch near the floor, or when one half simply has a much larger spread of scores, the halves are not parallel, and once their spreads differ the stepped-up value comes out too high; the next subsection shows by how much. The second assumption, for its lengthening use, is that the new items are parallel to the old ones: the same content, the same range of difficulty and the same quality, so that each new item correlates with the others as strongly as the old items do. Add twenty easy general-knowledge questions to a verbal reasoning test and the prophecy fails, because the new items measure something else. The third is that the people answer the new items under the same conditions and in the same frame of mind as the old ones: a test made six times longer may bring fatigue, boredom and careless responding that the formula knows nothing about. The fourth is that the prediction applies to the same kind of group in which the present reliability was found; Section 3.8 shows how a coefficient changes when the group is more or less varied. Exam trap The Spearman-Brown correction of a split-half coefficient is accurate only when the two halves are parallel: equal means and equal variances, measuring the same content . Halves that differ in difficulty violate the assumption (they do not help by "widening the range"). Halves scored by two different examiners bring in scorer error, the subject of inter-rater reliability (Section 3.6). Halves given on two different days bring in time-sampling error, which turns the design into a kind of test-retest or alternate-forms study (Sections 3.2 and 3.3). It is just as important to know what the formula does not do, because examiners build their wrong options from the other famous formulas of this chapter. The Spearman-Brown formula does one job in two guises: it estimates full-test reliability from a split-half correlation, and it predicts reliability when the length of a test changes. It does not estimate agreement between raters on categorical judgements; that is Cohen's kappa (Section 3.6). (A cousin of the idea does appear there: averaging several raters' scores raises reliability much as adding items does, but measuring how far two raters agree is a different job.) It does not correct a validity coefficient for the unreliability of the test and the criterion; that is the correction for attenuation (Section 3.8), which is easy to confuse because Spearman devised it too, in 1904. It cannot rescue a speed test from a single sitting (Section 3.4.9 below explains why). It does not predict validity: lengthening a test does raise its validity as well, but more slowly, and that needs a different formula (Chapter 4). And it says nothing about factor structure, which is found by factor analysis (Book 1, Section 9.4), or about effect sizes in an analysis of covariance, which belong to the Research Methodology book. Exam trap By the Spearman-Brown formula, reliability is improved by increasing the number of parallel items . Decreasing the number of items lowers it (n below 1). Making items more ambiguous adds random error, so it lowers reliability. Reducing the sample size does not change the size of the coefficient in any predictable way; it only makes the estimate less trustworthy. And when a question asks what the formula predicts, the answer is the reliability of a test whose length is changed by a factor n (or k) , not the validity of a new test, not an effect size in ANCOVA and not the factor structure of the WAIS. Formulas that need no step-up: Rulon, Flanagan and Guttman The split-half procedure as Spearman and Brown left it has two steps (correlate the halves, then step up the correlation) and one fragile assumption (equal variances in the two halves). In the late 1930s two American psychometricians found a way to go straight from the two half-scores to the reliability of the whole test, without assuming equal variances. The first route was published by Phillip Justin Rulon (1900 to 1968), a psychometrician at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, in a 1939 paper in the Harvard Educational Review titled "A simplified procedure for determining the reliability of a test by split-halves". Rulon's idea is beautifully direct. If the two halves measure the same true score, then a person's two half-scores can differ only because of error. So, for every person, subtract one half-score from the other to get a difference score, d. The spread of these differences across the group tells you how much error there is. In fact the variance of the differences is an estimate of the error variance of the whole test. You can see why from X = T + E. Write a person's half-scores as T + E A and T + E B . Their difference is E A − E B , because the true scores cancel, and their sum, the total score, has the error part E A + E B . When two errors are independent, subtracting them spreads the result exactly as much as adding them does, so the variance of the differences equals the error variance of the totals. Now recall the definition of reliability from Section 3.1: it is the proportion of observed variance that is not error, r = 1 − σ 2 E / σ 2 X . Put the variance of the differences in place of the error variance and you have Rulon's formula . Remember Rulon's formula (1939): r = 1 − σ 2 d / σ 2 X where σ 2 d is the variance of the differences between each person's two half-scores and σ 2 X is the variance of the total scores. The result is already the reliability of the full-length test: there is no Spearman-Brown step afterwards. The second route belongs to John Clemans Flanagan (1906 to 1996), better remembered for the critical incident technique and for Project TALENT, a vast survey of American high-school students begun in 1960. The formula credited to him, usually dated to his 1937 paper in the Journal of Educational Psychology , uses the variances of the two halves instead of the variance of their differences. The Flanagan formula is r = 2[1 − (σ 2 a + σ 2 b ) / σ 2 X ], where σ 2 a and σ 2 b are the variances of the two halves and σ 2 X is the variance of the totals. The logic is this. The variance of a total is the two half variances plus twice the part the halves share (their covariance, the amount by which they rise and fall together). Subtract the two half variances from the total variance and what is left is twice the shared part, the consistent core of the test. Flanagan expresses that leftover as a proportion of the total variance and doubles it. Louis Guttman (1916 to 1987), the Guttman of the cumulative attitude scale among the attitude measures of Chapter 8, reached the same expression in a 1945 paper in Psychometrika , "A basis for analyzing test-retest reliability", as the fourth of six lower bounds to reliability that he derived, his lambda 4 (λ 4 ). That is why the same formula is called the Flanagan formula, Guttman's split-half coefficient or simply lambda 4. And because Rulon's and Flanagan's formulas always give exactly the same number (they are two algebraic forms of one quantity), many books speak of the Flanagan-Rulon formula. Remember The Flanagan formula (1937), also Guttman's λ 4 (1945): r = 2 [1 − (σ 2 a + σ 2 b ) / σ 2 X ] where σ 2 a and σ 2 b are the variances of the two half-scores and σ 2 X is the variance of the total scores. It always equals Rulon's coefficient, and needs no step-up. A small data set lets you work all three formulas side by side. Hrithik, a school counsellor in Bhopal, gave a 36-item numerical ability test to ten Class 9 students. (A real tryout needs hundreds of students; ten keep every step visible.) He scored the 18 odd-numbered items as half A and the 18 even-numbered items as half B, and for each student worked out the difference d = A − B and the total X = A + B. Table 3.13 shows his results. Now the three formulas. Rulon: σ 2 d / σ 2 X = 4.8 / 19.2 = 0.25, so r = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. Flanagan: σ 2 a + σ 2 b = 6.0 + 6.0 = 12.0; 12.0 / 19.2 = 0.625; 1 − 0.625 = 0.375; and 2 × 0.375 = 0.75. Spearman-Brown: first find the correlation between the halves. The shared part (the covariance) is half of what is left when the half variances are taken from the total variance: (19.2 − 12.0) / 2 = 3.6. Dividing by the product of the two standard deviations (√6 × √6 = 6) gives r half = 3.6 / 6 = 0.60. Stepping up: 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75. All three agree on 0.75. Notice also that Hrithik's data contain the very numbers of Section 3.4.3: half variances of 6, a total variance of 19.2 and, in the variance of the differences, an error variance of 4.8. Rulon's difference scores really are the error of the test made visible. Why bother with Rulon and Flanagan, then, if Spearman-Brown gave the same answer? Because it gave the same answer only because Hrithik's two halves happened to have equal variances (6 and 6). When the half variances differ, Spearman-Brown parts company with the other two. Suppose a test is split into first and second halves and the second half is so hard that most students score near zero on it: the easier half has a variance of 16 (a standard deviation of 4), the harder half a variance of only 4 (a standard deviation of 2), and the halves correlate 0.50. Their shared part is 0.50 × 4 × 2 = 4. The total variance is 16 + 4 + (2 × 4) = 28, and the variance of the differences is 16 + 4 − (2 × 4) = 12. Rulon gives 1 − 12 / 28 = 1 − 0.43 = 0.57. Flanagan gives 2 × [1 − (16 + 4) / 28] = 2 × (1 − 0.714) = 2 × 0.286 = 0.57. Spearman-Brown, blind to the unequal variances, steps 0.50 up to 1.00 / 1.50 = 0.67, an overestimate of 0.10. The rule is general: for halves that correlate positively, as the halves of any sensible test do, the Spearman-Brown value is never lower than the Flanagan-Rulon value, and the two are equal only when the two halves have equal variances. (For the algebraically minded: Flanagan's coefficient can be written as 4 times the covariance divided by σ 2 a + σ 2 b + 2 times the covariance, and Spearman-Brown's as the same thing with 2σ a σ b in place of σ 2 a + σ 2 b ; since σ 2 a + σ 2 b is never smaller than 2σ a σ b , and equals it only when σ a = σ b , the rule follows.) Exam trap Rulon's formula estimates split-half reliability from the variance of the differences between the two half-scores, relative to the total-score variance . The correlation between two administrations of one test is test-retest reliability (Section 3.2); the correlation between the halves stepped up with Spearman-Brown is the very procedure Rulon made unnecessary; and the proportion of examinees passing each item is item difficulty, p, the raw material of KR-20 (Section 3.5). In the numerical versions, every wrong option has a story. With variances 4 and 20: .20 forgets to subtract from 1, .89 wrongly steps .80 up with Spearman-Brown (1.60 / 1.80), and .96 squares the ratio. With standard deviations 3 and 6: .50 plugs the SDs in unsquared (1 − 3 / 6), .25 is the error share, and .86 wrongly steps .75 up (1.50 / 1.75). Square SDs first; never step up a Rulon or Flanagan result. Speed tests, power tests and the split that fails Every method in this section so far quietly assumes something about how a test is taken: that each person has a fair chance to attempt every item, so that the score reflects which items they can answer. That is true of some tests and false of others, and the difference decides whether splitting works at all. Psychologists describe it with two ideal types. A pure speed test consists of items so easy that anyone would answer every one of them correctly given enough time (crossing out every letter "a" on a page of print, or deciding whether two strings of numbers are identical), set under a time limit so tight that nobody finishes. Since almost nobody makes errors, the score is simply the number of items done, and differences between people are differences in speed. A pure power test is the opposite: its items rise in difficulty until some are too hard for almost anyone, and the time limit is generous enough that nearly everyone attempts every item they are able to. The score shows how far up the ladder of difficulty a person can climb. A mathematics paper with ample time is close to a power test; a clerical checking test is close to a speed test. Most real tests lie somewhere between, and the degree to which scores on a test depend on the rate of working rather than on the level reached is called its speededness . Now try an odd-even split on a pure speed test. Ranjit, an industrial psychologist in Kolkata, uses a 100-item clerical speed test to help a bank select clerks. Each item shows two long numbers, and the candidate marks whether they are identical; the time limit is ten minutes, and almost nobody makes a mistake. A candidate who reaches item 34 has answered items 1 to 34 correctly and nothing beyond, so her odd-item score is 17 (items 1, 3 and so on up to 33) and her even-item score is also 17 (items 2, 4 and so on up to 34). A candidate who reaches item 47 scores 24 odd and 23 even; one who reaches item 81 scores 41 odd and 40 even. Every candidate's two half-scores are equal or differ by one, whatever kind of day the candidate was having. When Ranjit correlated the odd and even scores of ten candidates, he got 0.998, and Spearman-Brown stepped it up to 1.00: apparently a perfectly reliable test. It is nothing of the sort. The consistency was manufactured by the scoring. The two halves are not two independent samples of the candidate's speed; they are two halves of a single count of how far the candidate got, so they must agree. In a speed test the items are all alike, so content-sampling error, the only error a split from one sitting can detect, hardly exists. The real error lies in the rate of working: a slow minute, a moment of distraction, a stiff wrist, a bad night's sleep. A single timed sitting cannot see that error, because whatever slows a candidate down slows both halves together. The left panel of Figure 3.9 shows the result: every point lies on, or one point away from, the line of equal scores. The same objection applies to KR-20 and coefficient alpha computed from one timed sitting (Section 3.5): every unreached item counts as wrong in every subset of items, so they too come out spuriously high. Harold Gulliksen (1903 to 1996) analysed the problem formally in a 1950 paper, "The reliability of speeded tests". Splitting into a first half and a second half is no cure either: whether a person even gets into the second half depends on speed, so those halves are not parallel. So how should the reliability of a speed test be estimated? The answer given in the standard textbooks, such as Psychological Testing by Anne Anastasi (1908 to 2001), is to make sure the two scores come from separately timed performances. Test-retest reliability (Section 3.2) does this by testing on two occasions, and alternate forms (Section 3.3) by giving two separately timed forms. If a split-half estimate is wanted, the test must be split by time, not by scoring: print the two halves separately and give each as a test of its own with half the time limit, the method of separately timed halves . Now how far a candidate gets on half A does not fix her score on half B, and a slow five minutes costs her on one half only. Ranjit did this with the same ten candidates, giving the odd items and the even items as two five-minute tests. The two half-scores correlated 0.76 (the right panel of Figure 3.9), and because each half is half the length of the full test, he stepped this up with Spearman-Brown: 2 × 0.76 = 1.52; 1 + 0.76 = 1.76; 1.52 / 1.76 = 0.86. That is an honest reliability, high as speed tests usually are, but not the impossible perfection of the single-sitting split. Indian textbooks such as A.K. Singh's Tests, Measurements and Research Methods in Behavioural Sciences also describe a quarter method: the total time is divided into four equal quarters, the work done in the first and fourth quarters forms one half-score and the work done in the second and third forms the other (so that warm-up and fatigue are balanced), and Rulon's formula is applied. Why Test-retest Yes Two full timed sittings; each score is its own performance Alternate forms Yes Two separately timed forms Separately timed halves, stepped up with Spearman-Brown Yes Progress on one half cannot fix the score on the other Odd-even split from one timed sitting No: the least appropriate Halves equal by construction, so r is near 1.00 and spurious KR-20 or alpha from one timed sitting No Unreached items count as wrong everywhere, inflating the estimate Clinical link You can see this rule at work in the technical data of the Wechsler intelligence scales (Chapter 6). The fourth edition of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV), for example, reports split-half reliabilities for all its subtests except the speeded ones (Coding, Symbol Search and Cancellation), for which it uses test-retest coefficients instead, because a split of a speeded subtest from one sitting would be spuriously high. When you read any test manual, check which method produced each coefficient before you trust it. The same reasoning explains why the odd-even method suits some kinds of test and not others. It is most appropriate for power tests, where everyone has time to attempt every item they can and the odd and even items are two fair samples of the same ability. It is least appropriate for speed tests, for the reason you have just seen. It is also awkward for projective tests such as the Rorschach inkblots (Chapter 10): their ten cards are each different, a person's free responses cannot be divided into two equivalent halves, and the reliability question that matters most for them is whether two scorers agree (Section 3.6). And many neuropsychological tests (Chapter 11) consist of a single task, such as connecting numbered circles against the clock or copying a complex figure, often timed, which cannot sensibly be cut into two matching halves; their reliability is usually estimated by retesting or with alternate forms. Exam trap The odd-even method is most appropriate for power tests , not for speed, projective or neuropsychological tests. For a pure speed test, the least appropriate estimate is an odd-even split-half from a single timed sitting ; test-retest, alternate forms and two separately timed halves are all acceptable. If a clerical speed test must be split, the acceptable procedure is to time the two halves separately, correlate them and step up with Spearman-Brown . Scoring odd and even items from one sitting and stepping up is the trap, and so are Cronbach's alpha and KR-20 from the single sitting, which are inflated in the same way. Spearman-Brown cannot rescue the single sitting: stepping up a spurious correlation only gives a bigger spurious number. What one sitting cannot tell you One limitation is shared by every method in this section (split-half with Spearman-Brown, Rulon, Flanagan and Guttman) and by KR-20 and alpha in Section 3.5. They all rest on a single administration, so the only error they can see is content-sampling error, the luck of which items a person met. Anything that affects the whole sitting, such as a fever, a sleepless night, a quarrel at breakfast or an unusually good mood, lifts or lowers both halves together, and these methods quietly count it as true-score variance. That is why a single-sitting coefficient is often a little higher than a test-retest coefficient for the same test, and why it says nothing at all about whether a person would obtain the same score next month. The choice of method should follow the question you need answered. If the scores will be used to compare people across time or to predict the future, you need evidence of stability from retesting (Section 3.2). If you need to know whether the items of a test hang together as samples of one ability, a single-sitting method answers it, and the next section shows how to do so without the arbitrariness of choosing one split.
