Invented example + Synthesised Two or more, related; at least one has form demand "Two children pulling a kite string" o Ordinary One with form demand (or several, unrelated) "A temple bell" v/+ Vague-synthesised Two or more, related; none has form demand "Smoke rising from a fire" v Vague One without form demand (or several, unrelated) "A splash of paint" Developmental quality is claimed to reflect the quality of a person's information processing: synthesised responses suggest a mind that analyses and integrates, a predominance of vague ones a mind that settles for global, undifferentiated impressions, as young children and some people with serious disorders often do. Neither Klopfer's nor Beck's system had a separate developmental quality code; the nearest relative in Beck's system was his Z score for organisational activity, which the Comprehensive System also kept (described below with the special scores). Exam trap Developmental quality and form quality are independent . DQ asks how the percept is organised; form quality asks how well it fits the blot. A response can be beautifully synthesised and still fit badly (W+ with minus form quality), or simple and accurate (Wo with ordinary form quality). And "v" means vague , not "very good"; "+" in DQ means synthesised, which is a different "+" from the elaborated form quality "+" described below. Determinants I: form and movement The determinant is the heart of Rorschach coding and the hardest part to learn. The question it answers is: which features of the blot made it look like that, to this person? A blot offers only a few kinds of raw material. It has a shape. It has colour, or the blackness, greyness and whiteness of the ink. It has shading, the variations of light and dark within the ink. And it has nothing that actually moves, although many people see movement in it. Rorschach's book of 1921 coded only form, movement and colour. He began to score shading himself, with the symbol (C) for chiaroscuro, in his last paper, a lecture of 1922 published after his death in 1923, and his successors then worked out the separate shading codes as they studied what people did with the light and dark tones (Section 10.3 tells how the printing of the plates put the shading there). The Comprehensive System uses 24 determinant symbols, grouped into nine families, all collected in Table 10.13 below, after the shading codes. The coder finds them in the person's own words, mostly in the inquiry: "it's the shape", "they are dancing", "because it is red", "it looks furry". Start with the simplest. A pure form response , coded F , is one determined by the shape or outline of the blot alone. Vaishali, a trainee clinical psychologist in a hospital psychology department, shows an invented black blot to her client Chirag. He says, "A maple leaf." In the inquiry she asks what made it look like a maple leaf, and he answers, "Just the shape: the pointed edges here, and this is the stalk." Nothing about colour, shading or movement enters, so the determinant is F. Form is the most common determinant in almost every record. Note one rule at once: F is coded only when nothing else contributes. If colour, shading or movement also played a part, the form is carried inside another code (FC, FT and so on) or is taken for granted (movement responses assume form), and F is not written separately. F is therefore never part of a combination of determinants. Pure form answers are traditionally read as handling the blot in a matter-of-fact, impersonal way, with feeling and fantasy kept out; a record made almost entirely of F is read as a narrowed, economising style, which Section 10.5 measures with the ratio called Lambda. Movement was among Rorschach's most original ideas. The blots are motionless ink, yet many people see figures running, dancing, fighting or bowing, and Rorschach believed that this "kinaesthetic" seeing came from inside the perceiver. The Comprehensive System codes three kinds of movement, according to who or what is moving. A human movement response , coded M , is scored when the person describes human activity: "two women dancing", "a man bending to tie his shoe", "two old men arguing", and also quiet human states such as sitting, thinking or looking. M is coded as well when an animal or a fictional character is described doing something only humans do: "two rabbits riding a scooter" and "two crows chatting over tea" are M, not animal movement, because neither rabbits nor crows do such things. Rorschach linked M to the inner life: imagination, the capacity to put oneself in another's place, and the ability to delay action and think instead. That is why human movement sits on one side of his experience type, which Section 10.5 explains. An animal movement response , coded FM , is scored when an animal does something natural to its kind: "a frog leaping", "two dogs fighting", "a bird perched on a branch". The code was introduced by Klopfer; Beck refused to treat animal movement as a determinant at all and coded such answers by their form, one of the clearest differences between the two classical systems. FM is traditionally read as a sign of basic urges and need states, pressing for attention but less integrated into thought than M. An inanimate movement response , coded m (a small m), is scored when the movement belongs to objects or natural forces: "a flag fluttering in the wind", "a waterfall pouring down", "an explosion", and also objects held in tension, such as "a coat hanging on a hook" or "a rope pulled tight". The code goes back to Zygmunt Piotrowski (1904 to 1985), and Klopfer took it up. It is read as a sign of situational stress, a feeling of being pushed by forces outside one's control. Each movement code also carries a small letter showing whether the movement is active or passive movement : a for active, p for passive, often printed as superscripts (M a , FM p ) and written on the line simply as Ma or FMp. Running, fighting, dancing and lifting are active. Sitting, sleeping, standing, looking and, by convention, talking are passive. When one response contains both, the code is written a-p. "Two women dancing" is Ma; "a bird perched on a branch" is FMp; "a flag fluttering" is ma. Exam trap A response determined by the shape of the blot alone, with no colour or movement, is F , pure form (2024 paper): not FC (form plus colour), not M (human movement), not C (pure colour). M is human movement only , not "any movement": FM is animal movement, m is inanimate movement. But an animal doing something only people do ("two rabbits riding a scooter") is coded M, and an object under tension ("a coat hanging on a hook") is coded m. F is never combined with another determinant. Determinants II: chromatic and achromatic colour Five of the ten cards carry colour (Section 10.3), and the colour codes ask two questions about every response to a coloured area. Did the colour contribute to the percept? And if it did, which led the way, the shape or the colour? The answer places the response on a short ladder that runs from form-dominant to colour-dominant, shown in Figure 10.9. A form-colour response , coded FC , is one in which form comes first and colour is added to elaborate or identify the object. Shown an invented blot with a green patch, Chirag says, "A green parrot: here is its beak, here are its wings, and it's green, like a parrot." The parrot needs a definite shape, the shape is there, and the green confirms it. A colour-form response , coded CF , reverses the order: colour leads and form is vague and secondary. "Fire: all this red and orange, roughly the shape of flames here." Fire has no fixed shape; the colour carries the percept and the shape is only loosely used. A pure colour response , coded C , uses colour with no form at all: "Blood, because it's red." Asked where, Chirag points vaguely at the red patch; asked what made it look like blood, he says only that it is red. There is no shape in the answer, so the code is C. If he had said, "A splash of blood, red, and spread out at the edges the way a splash spreads", the shape would have entered in a loose way, and the code would be CF. The fourth chromatic code is not on the ladder at all. In colour naming , coded Cn , the person simply names the colours as if that were the answer: "Red. And this is green. And blue." No object is seen; the colour is reported instead of interpreted. An exclamation such as "What lovely colours!" is not Cn, because the person is commenting, not answering. Cn is very rare in ordinary records and has traditionally been associated with serious disorganisation or brain damage, a piece of lore with little modern research behind it. form decides colour decides F pure form: shape alone "A maple leaf: see the pointed edges." claimed: feeling kept out FC form first, colour added "A green parrot: here is its beak, and it is green." claimed: feeling well controlled CF colour first, shape vague "Fire: all this red and orange, flames, roughly." claimed: feeling less restrained C colour alone, no shape at all "Blood, because it is red." claimed: impulsive discharge Cn (colour naming): "Red. And that is green." The colours are named as the answer; no object is seen, so Cn stands outside the continuum. Figure 10.9 The form-colour continuum. Read it from left to right: as colour takes over from form, the traditional reading moves from emotion kept out (F), through well-modulated emotion (FC) and less restrained emotion (CF), to impulsive discharge (C). These readings are interpretive lore inherited from Rorschach; Sections 10.5 and 10.10 say how much of it has held up. Rorschach linked colour to emotion, and the ladder carries that idea. Responses in which form controls colour (FC) were read as feeling that is felt but kept in hand; colour that overrides form (CF) as feeling that is less restrained; colour with no form at all (C) as emotion discharged without control. In one of the specimen records printed in his book, Rorschach described the person's feelings as lively but stabilised by "good affective adaptability" (in a recent English translation), and the evidence he pointed to was two FC responses. How the three codes are weighted and summed, and set against human movement, is the business of Section 10.5. Black, white and grey can also be used as colours, and the Comprehensive System codes this achromatic colour response with the symbol C' (read "C prime"), in the same three steps. "A black crow: here is its beak and its tail, and it's black" is FC' , form first. "A dark storm cloud, all black" is C'F , the blackness leading and the shape vague. "Coal, because it's black" is C' , achromatic colour alone, a rare response. Rorschach's own book had no separate code for black and white used as colours; Klopfer introduced one, and the Comprehensive System kept it. Achromatic colour is traditionally read as painful feeling that is held in rather than expressed. The line between C' and the shading codes below is drawn by what the person uses: C' when the blackness, greyness or whiteness itself is named as a colour, a shading code when the variations of light and dark are used. One more colour phenomenon has its own code, but not as a determinant. Sometimes a person sees chromatic colour in an area that has none: "a pretty purple flower" on an all-black blot. This colour projection is recorded with the special score CP (described below), and the determinants are coded from whatever else the person used. Exam trap "This is a blood stain because it's red", with no reference to shape, is C , pure colour (2024 paper). It is not FC (a clear shape with colour added) or CF (colour first, shape vague but present), and it is not Cn, which merely names the colours ("red, green") without seeing anything. Remember too that the prime matters: C' is achromatic (black, white, grey), not chromatic. Colour seen on a black area is not a colour determinant at all but the special score CP. Determinants III: shading, form dimension, pairs, reflections and blends The ink of the blots is not flat. Within the black, the grey and the colours there are gradations, lighter and darker zones that can suggest a surface, a depth or a haze, and people use them in three different ways. The Comprehensive System gives each its own family, and each family has the same three steps as the colour codes: form first, shading first, or shading alone. A texture response , coded with T , is one in which the shading is felt as a surface to touch: soft, furry, rough, silky, wet, cold. "A woollen shawl: here is the fringe, and the shading makes it look soft and fuzzy" is FT , the shape of the shawl leading. "Something soft, like cotton wool" is TF , the softness leading and the shape vague. "Velvet, from the shading", with no shape at all, is a pure T , which is rare. In most records the form-first FT is by far the commonest of the three. A vista response , coded with V , is one in which the shading is seen as depth or distance. "A well seen from above; the darker middle is deeper down" is FV ; "a deep valley, the shading going down and down" is VF ; "depth, just depth" is a pure V . A diffuse shading response , coded with Y , uses the light and dark in a general way that is neither touch nor depth. "A shirt with dirty patches; the darker parts are the dirt" is FY ; "smoke, lighter here, darker there" is YF ; "darkness" or "fog" is a pure Y . Here the older systems disagreed most. Klopfer used a small c for texture, K and k for diffuse shading (K for shading seen as a three-dimensional haze, k for shading seen as a flat projection such as an X-ray or a map) and FK for vista. Beck used T for texture, V for vista and Y for diffuse shading, and these are the letters Exner adopted. The traditional readings, all of them claims to be tested in Section 10.10, are that texture reflects a need for closeness and contact, vista a painful kind of self-examination, and diffuse shading a sense of helplessness under stress. Depth can also come from shape alone. A form dimension response , coded FD , is one in which the person sees perspective or distance from the size and outline of the blot areas, with no use of shading: "a man lying on his back with his feet towards us; the feet look big because they are nearer". FD was a new category in the Comprehensive System. The difference from FV is the source of the depth: shading for FV, shape and size for FD. Two more codes exploit the symmetry of the blots. A pair response is scored when the person reports two identical objects, one on each side of the midline, relying on the symmetry: "two crabs, one on each side". It is written (2) in the tables and simply 2 in the code string, after the form quality. A reflection response is scored when one side is seen as the mirror image or reflection of the other: "a tiger at the river's edge, and this half is its reflection in the water" is Fr , form first; "trees and clouds reflected in a lake, all hazy" is rF , the reflection leading and the shape vague. A reflection is never also coded as a pair, because the second object is not a second object, only an image of the first. Beck had scored reflections as vista and Klopfer as FK; the Comprehensive System gave them a category of their own, and Section 10.5 shows how pairs and reflections are combined in an index of self-focus. Finally, many good responses use more than one feature of the blot. A response with two or more determinants is a blend , and the codes are joined by full stops. "Two women in red saris, dancing and holding hands" is Ma.FC: human movement, active, plus form-colour. "Two puppies curled up asleep; they look soft and furry here" is FMp.FT: animal movement, passive, plus form-texture. Each determinant in a blend is counted separately when the codes are tallied, and the number of blends in a record is itself read as a sign of psychological complexity (Section 10.5). Texture (T) is shading felt as touch, not "tension"; tension in objects ("a coat hanging on a hook") is inanimate movement, m. Form quality: how well does the percept fit the blot? A response can be organised with great energy, use form, colour and movement together, and still be wrong. Chirag looks at an invented blot with two small hooks at the top and nothing else crab-like about it, and says, "A crab; these are the claws." The claws fit, more or less. The rest of the crab is simply not there. The form quality (FQ) code records how well the object a person reports matches the contours of the area they used. It is the one point in coding at which the coder judges the match between the inner impression and the outer stimulus, and for that reason it is the main Rorschach index of reality testing : the capacity to perceive the world as others perceive it, and to check one's impressions against what is actually there. The Comprehensive System uses four form quality codes, attached to the end of the determinants, and a fifth possibility, none; Table 10.14 sets them beside their older equivalents. Ordinary (o) : a common answer, in which the general features of the object are easy to see in the area used. Whether an answer counts as ordinary is not left to the coder's taste; the system's form quality tables list, area by area, the objects reported often enough in large samples of records, and in the Comprehensive System good form is above all a matter of how often an answer occurs. "A moth" for a whole blot shaped like one is Wo Fo. Ordinary-elaborated (+) (called superior-overelaborated in Exner's 1993 edition): an ordinary answer described with unusual precision, in a way that improves the fit rather than straining it. "A woman dancing: her arms raised here, the edge of her sari flaring out here, and her hair tied in a knot at the top." It is uncommon, and a coder should not give it simply because an answer is long. Unusual (u) : an infrequent answer whose contours nevertheless fit, so that an observer can see it quickly and easily once it is pointed out. "Two puppies curled up together" for a small rounded area might be u: few people say it, but it is not a distortion. Minus (−) : a distorted, arbitrary or unrealistic use of form, in which the person imposes contours that are not there or ignores the contours that are. Chirag's crab is F−. None : a response with no form in it at all (pure C, C', T, V or Y, and Cn) receives no form quality code, and is counted as "none". Code Name Rule Older systems + Ordinary-elaborated Ordinary fit, described with unusual, fitting detail Good form, F+ o Ordinary Common answer; contours easily seen Good form, F+ u Unusual Rare answer; contours fit and are easily seen Often F+; a good original − Minus Distorted, arbitrary; form imposed or ignored Poor form, F− none (no code) No form used at all Not rated Form quality is the oldest idea in Rorschach scoring. Rorschach marked each pure form response either F+ (good) or F− (poor), judging it against the answers of his normal subjects and his own sense of the fit, and the F+ percentage , the share of pure form responses that are good, was one of the first ratios Rorschach himself calculated. In one specimen record in his book he counted 12 good forms among 14 pure-form responses and wrote the result as 86 per cent. Beck tied the plus and minus judgements to frequency tables drawn from normal records; Klopfer replaced the simple plus and minus with a graded form level rating that also gave credit for elaboration; and the Comprehensive System extended the judgement from pure F responses to every response that uses form, and split "good" into ordinary, elaborated and unusual. Once each response has its form quality code, a few simple percentages summarise the whole record. Remember X+% = (number of responses with form quality + or o) ÷ R × 100 X−% = (number of responses with form quality −) ÷ R × 100 XA% = (number of responses with form quality +, o or u) ÷ R × 100 F+% = (pure F responses with form quality + or o) ÷ (all pure F responses) × 100 R is the total number of responses in the record. X+% is the share of conventional, good fits; X−% the share of distorted fits; XA% ("form appropriate") the share of all acceptable fits, conventional or unusual; F+% the old Rorschach ratio, restricted to pure form answers. In the Comprehensive System these are usually written as proportions (.50) rather than percentages (50%); the two mean the same thing. Work through Chirag's record. He gave R = 20 responses. Vaishali's form quality codes came out as follows: 1 response coded +, 9 coded o, 5 coded u, 4 coded −, and 1 with no form (a pure C). Check that they add up: 1 + 9 + 5 + 4 + 1 = 20. Good. For X+%, add the + and o responses: 1 + 9 = 10. Divide by R: 10 ÷ 20 = 0.50. Multiply by 100: X+% = 50%. For X−%, take the minus responses: 4 ÷ 20 = 0.20, so X−% = 20%. For XA%, add the +, o and u responses: 1 + 9 + 5 = 15, and 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75, so XA% = 75%. Notice that the pure C response counts in R, the denominator, but in none of the numerators, because it has no form quality at all. Finally, for F+%: 8 of Chirag's responses were pure F, and of those, 5 were coded o and none +, while 1 was u and 2 were minus. So F+% = 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625; rounded to two decimal places, .63, or 63%. In plain words: half of Chirag's percepts are the conventional ones most people would see, another quarter are unusual but fit the blot, and one in five does not fit the blot at all. One minus answer in five is well above the average in Exner's own adult norms, though less striking against several later international samples, and it is the kind of figure that sends a careful clinician back to the record: are the four minus answers bunched on the coloured cards, as if strong feeling disturbed his perception, or scattered through the record with odd wording, which would suggest something more pervasive? But it is a hypothesis, not a finding. Section 10.5 shows how form quality enters the Structural Summary and the Perceptual-Thinking Index, and Section 10.10 explains why the answer to "is 20 per cent high?" depends on which normative sample you compare with. Clinical link Form quality is where the Rorschach comes closest to a perceptual test, and the reviews summarised in Section 10.10 found the perceptual accuracy and thought disorder variables among the best supported in the whole test. But the tables that define "ordinary" were built mostly from Western records, and samples from many countries produce lower form quality on them. A percept that is common and well fitting in an Indian setting (a kalash, a temple lamp, a Kathakali face) may not appear in the table at all; the coder must then extrapolate from similar objects that are listed, and an answer that resembles nothing on the list will usually be coded u at best. A good coder judges the fit, not the familiarity, and a careful interpreter remembers that a lower X+% in a person from a different culture may partly reflect the table rather than the person. Exam trap Form quality is the index of reality testing ; colour is read for emotion, location for organisational approach. Minus means a poor fit, not unpleasant content or "minus marks". u is unusual but acceptable, not "unacceptable". A formless response (pure C) has no form quality; it is not coded minus. X+% counts + and o; X−% counts minus; both are divided by all responses, R. And the confabulatory DW almost always carries poor form quality, which is why it is read as impaired reality testing (IHBAS 2020). Content, popular and original responses Only now, after location, organisation, determinants and fit, does coding turn to the question a lay person would ask first: what did the person see? The content code names the category of the object. The later editions of the Comprehensive System use 27 content codes, set out in Table 10.15, the last of which, Idiographic (Id), takes anything the other 26 do not cover. When a response contains more than one kind of object, every content is coded, separated by commas, with the main one first: "two women in red saris" is H,Cg, human and clothing. Brackets mark the unreal: (H) is a whole human figure that is fictional or mythological, such as a ghost, a fairy, a demon or a cartoon character, and (A) and (Ad) do the same for animals. Rorschach's own specimen records used only a handful of headings (human, human detail, animal, animal detail, plant, object and the like), each later system drew up its own list of a different length, and even the letters differed: anatomy is An in Beck's system and the Comprehensive System but At in Klopfer's. Content is the part of the code most open to interpretation by symbol, and also the part on which the traditional readings are least secure. Human contents are read as a sign of interest in people, and their absence as a sign of poor interpersonal orientation, a reading Section 10.5 explains; anatomy and X-ray contents are read as signs of concern with the body. A popular response , coded P , is a particular answer, to a particular area of a particular card, that is given so often that it marks the most conventional way of seeing that blot. In the Comprehensive System a response is popular if it occurs at least once in every three records in the normative samples, and the system lists 13 of them; P is written after the contents in the code string. The 13 are not reproduced in this book, card by card or in any other way, because a person who knew them in advance could game the test, which is part of the case for test security made in Book 2, Section 1.9.6. Populars are read as a measure of conventional perception: a record with very few suggests a person who does not see what most people see, and a record crowded with them a person clinging to the obvious. Because populars exist only for the real cards, the invented responses in this section never receive a P. The older systems also coded the opposite pole. An original response , coded O , was an answer so rare that, by Rorschach's own rule in Psychodiagnostik , it turned up only about once in a hundred records. Originals were split by their fit: O+ for a rare answer that fits well, read as a sign of creativity, and O− for a rare answer that fits badly, read as a sign of bizarre or idiosyncratic thinking. Coders found originals very hard to agree on, because whether an answer is rare depends on how many records the coder has seen. The Comprehensive System has no O code at all. A rare answer that fits is coded u for form quality, and a rare answer that does not fit is coded minus, so the two halves of the old O live on inside form quality. Exam trap P is popular, O is original : P is frequent (at least one record in three in the Comprehensive System, which lists 13 populars), O is rare and was dropped by the Comprehensive System. H is a real whole human, Hd a part of one, (H) a fictional or mythological one; Hx is human experience, an emotion or sensation, not a human figure. And content is what was seen, never why it was seen: "a red butterfly" is an animal content with form-colour determinants. Special scores and the Z score The last slot of the code string records features that have nothing to do with which part of the blot was used, and everything to do with how the person thinks and speaks about it. These are the special scores . The most important group, six cognitive special scores, records cognitive slippage : lapses in the logic or language of a response, from the kind of slip anyone makes when tired to the strange fusions of the most disordered thinking. The six descend from the deviant verbalisations catalogued by David Rapaport (1911 to 1960) and his colleagues in Diagnostic Psychological Testing (1945 to 1946), who described fabulised combinations, contaminations and autistic logic as signs of disordered thinking. Four of the six (DV, INCOM, DR and FABCOM) are coded at Level 1, a mild slip, or Level 2, a severe or bizarre one; ALOG and CONTAM have a single level. Section 10.5 shows how the six are weighted and summed (WSum6), and how they enter the Perceptual-Thinking Index. Further special scores record perseveration (PSV, the same answer repeated rigidly), confabulation (CONFAB, the old DW: one detail generalised to a larger area or the whole blot, usually with minus form quality) and features of content: abstract or symbolic content (AB), aggressive movement (AG), cooperative movement (COP), morbid content (MOR, damaged objects or a sad, gloomy quality), personalised answers that lean on the person's own experience (PER), and the colour projection (CP) met earlier. In the later editions every response with human content or human movement is also classified as a good or poor human representation (GHR or PHR), by a set of rules that uses the other codes of the response. The Z score , for organisational activity, was Beck's idea, and the Comprehensive System kept it. A Z value is given whenever a response organises the blot in a meaningful way: a whole response (unless it is vague), separate details brought into a relationship, whether they are next to each other or far apart, or white space integrated with the ink. The value is read from a table for each card, higher where organising the blot is harder. The values are summed, and the sum is compared with what would be expected for that number of organised responses; Section 10.5 explains the result, Zd, and what it is claimed to show about how efficiently a person scans a complex field. Exam trap INCOM versus FABCOM : an incongruous combination is impossible features inside one object ("a parrot with four legs"); a fabulised combination is an impossible relationship between two objects ("two rabbits riding a scooter", which is also coded M because rabbits do not ride). CONTAM , two percepts fused into one, is the most severe of the six. CP is colour seen where there is none; it is a special score, not a colour determinant. In front of you are twenty short lines of letters and symbols, one for each thing the person saw, and every line is correct. You still know almost nothing about the person. "W+ M a .FCo H" tells you that one response used the whole blot, saw people in action and used colour in a controlled way, but a single line is like a single word torn out of a letter. The meaning lies in how the lines add up: how many of the responses used the whole blot, how often movement appeared compared with colour, how many percepts fitted the blot and how many did not, whether people appeared at all. This is the step at which the Rorschach stops being a list of percepts and becomes a portrait, and it is also the step on which Hermann Rorschach's followers argued most fiercely. Who decides which numbers matter, and what they mean? The answer changed three times in a hundred years, and the story of those changes is the story of the scoring systems, from the rival American schools of Samuel Beck and Bruno Klopfer to John Exner's Comprehensive System and its successor, the Rorschach Performance Assessment System (R-PAS). From codes to a profile: the sequence of scores and the Structural Summary Start with what you already have. Section 10.4 taught you to turn each response into a code string, and this section uses only a handful of those codes. For location , W is the whole blot, D a common detail, Dd an unusual detail, and S, white space, is always added to one of the others (WS, DS). Developmental quality grades how the percept is put together: + for synthesised (separate parts related to each other), o for ordinary, v for vague, v/+ for vague parts brought together. The determinants are F (form alone); M, FM and m (human, animal and inanimate movement, each marked a for active or p for passive); the colour codes FC, CF, C and Cn (form-colour, colour-form, pure colour and colour naming); C' for achromatic colour; T, V and Y for texture, vista and diffuse shading; FD for form dimension; (2) for a pair and Fr or rF for a reflection; and a dot joins two determinants in a blend , as in M.FC. Form quality is + (unusually well fitted), o (ordinary), u (unusual but acceptable) or minus (a poor fit). Content codes name what was seen: H a whole human, (H) a fictional or mythical human, Hd a human part, A and Ad an animal and an animal part, An anatomy, Bt botany, Cg clothing, Na nature and so on. P marks a popular response. So an invented response, "two dancers lifting a lantern between them, and their skirts are red", might be coded W+ M a .FCo (2) H, Cg. The first thing a scorer in the Comprehensive System does with these strings is write them out in order as the sequence of scores : one line per response, card by card, giving the card number, the response number, the location and developmental quality, the determinants, the form quality, any pair, the contents, a P if it is popular, an organisational score and any special scores (the codes for odd verbalisations and faulty logic that Section 10.4 introduced). Why keep the order instead of going straight to totals? Because some of the most interesting information is sequential. A person whose form quality is good on the black and grey cards but collapses every time colour appears, or whose responses grow shorter and vaguer as the test goes on, shows something no total can show. The sequence is the raw record of how the person met each blot, one after another. Then come the totals. The Structural Summary is the page on which the codes are counted and combined, and it has two halves. The upper section is simple bookkeeping: frequencies. How many W, D and Dd responses were there, and how many involved white space? How many were synthesised, ordinary or vague? How many times did each determinant appear (a blend such as M.FC counts once for M and once for FC, and the blends are also listed separately)? How many responses had each level of form quality, and each kind of content? How many populars, and how many special scores? The lower section turns those counts into ratios, percentages and derived scores, grouped into clusters that each address one area of functioning: a core section (with the number of responses, R, Lambda and the Experience Balance, all taught below), and clusters for ideation (thinking), affect (feelings), mediation (how accurately the person perceives), processing (how much effort the person puts into taking in information), interpersonal perception and self-perception. At the foot of the page sit the constellations , indices that add up several signs at once to flag a specific problem, such as the Depression Index; you will meet them in Section 10.5.6. Notice that the first five steps are bookkeeping that two trained scorers should agree on; judgement enters only at the last step, and there it works on the whole configuration, not on single scores. Why go to all this trouble instead of reading each response for what it seems to say? Because the founding idea of the scored Rorschach is that no single sign means anything on its own. One pure colour response may be a moment of playfulness; five of them, with poor form quality and few form-dominant colour responses, begin to say something about how the person handles feeling. Interpretation therefore works on the configuration , the pattern of many scores together, and each score is read against norms: the values found in samples of non-patients of similar age (what norms are and how they are built is the subject of Chapter 5; whether the Rorschach's norms were sound is argued in Section 10.10). Exner made this into a fixed routine. His interpretive "search strategy" checks a list of key variables in order, and the first one that is positive decides which cluster is read first; if the index of disordered perception and thinking is raised, for example, the interpreter begins with the clusters for thinking and perceptual accuracy. Every conclusion is then treated as a hypothesis to be checked against the history, the interview and the other tests, which is the posture this chapter recommends for every projective technique. The very first number on the page is R, the total number of responses, and it is read first as a check on whether the record can be interpreted at all. Rorschach himself was unimpressed by it; in the English translation of Psychodiagnostik he concludes that "the study of the number of answers reveals nothing characteristic in the different groups of cases". Later systematisers took it more seriously, if only because so many other scores rise and fall with it: a person who gives 40 responses has more chances to produce a minus form or a texture response than a person who gives 12. A. K. Singh's Indian textbook gives the normal ranges the older authorities proposed: 15 to 30 for Rorschach, 20 to 45 for Klopfer and 17 to 27 for Exner in 1974. Exner later fixed a floor: a Comprehensive System record with fewer than 14 responses is treated as of doubtful validity, and the examiner asks the person to take the test again straight away, giving more answers this time (Section 10.3 describes the administration). Very short records are read as possible guardedness, depression, low ability or organic impairment; very long ones as an inability to stop, a striving to impress or, at the extreme, the flooding of disordered thinking. Notice what is missing from the Structural Summary: there is no IQ score anywhere on it. The Comprehensive System codes location, determinants, form quality, content, populars and special scores, and none of its ratios is a measure of intelligence (Section 10.4 makes the same point about the codes). Location, form quality and content: what the main scores are claimed to mean Each family of codes has a traditional reading, built up from Rorschach's own observations and the clinical experience of his successors, and in the Comprehensive System partly tested against research. As you read the claims below, keep two questions in mind: what is the logic linking the score to the trait, and how good is the evidence that the link is real? The first question is answered here. The second is answered in Section 10.10, and the short version is that the scores for perceptual accuracy and disordered thinking have the strongest support, while many of the others rest more on tradition than on data. Location: how the person takes in a complex field. Every blot is a cluttered field of shapes, and the person must decide how much of it to use. A whole response (W) is the most demanding choice, because the person has to hold the entire blot in mind and make it into one thing. Rorschach linked a good supply of well-formed W responses to intelligence and to an abstract, synthesising turn of mind, and the link with intelligence turned out to be modest. In the Comprehensive System the reading is more careful. Many W responses, especially synthesised ones (W+, in which separate parts are related to one another, "two people leaning over a fire"), are taken to show organisational activity , the effort and drive to pull a complex field together into a meaningful whole. Exner measures this partly with Zf, the number of responses that earn an organisational score (a score for organising the blot, which Exner took from Samuel Beck), and partly with two ratios: the Economy Index, W : D : Dd, which shows how the person spreads attention between the whole, the obvious parts and the odd corners, and the Aspirational Index, W : M, which compares organising effort with the human movement responses that are taken to show resources for using it. Indian textbooks quote an expected adult W : D ratio of about 1 : 2 (A. K. Singh, citing Exner's 1974 volume): most people, most of the time, take the obvious parts. The quality of the W matters as much as the number. Many synthesised W responses suggest ambition and effort; many vague W responses ("some kind of map", "a cloud") suggest an easy, global, unanalysed way of taking things in, which in an adult is read as immature or careless processing. The other locations are read against W. D responses, the common details, show a practical, economical person who deals with what is obvious; a record built almost entirely of D suggests someone who plays safe and avoids the effort of integration. Dd responses, the unusual details, are expected to be few (Singh gives about 5 to 8 per cent of responses in normal adults); many of them suggest a person who fixes on small or odd parts of a situation, read either as perfectionistic, obsessional care or as idiosyncratic perception. White space responses (S) have had the most argued reading of all. Rorschach, Beck and Rapaport took them as a sign of negativism or opposition, the person reversing figure and ground; Klopfer read a moderate number as healthy self-assertion; the Comprehensive System treats a large number as a sign of anger or resentment. Here the research is mixed, which is a good example of why each sign is a hypothesis. Form quality: reality testing. If location tells you how the person approaches the field, form quality tells you whether what the person saw is actually there. A response whose shape fits the outline of the area used, the way most people would see it, has good form; a response that ignores or violates the outline ("a man's face" for an area with no face-like shape at all) has minus form. Form quality is therefore the Rorschach's main index of reality testing , the ability to perceive the world as it is and to tell one's own ideas from what is out there. The Comprehensive System puts it into three percentages, each worked out the same way: count the responses with a given level of form quality, divide by R, and (if you like) multiply by 100. X+% , conventional form, is the share of all responses with + or o form quality. XA% , form appropriate, is the share with +, o or u form quality, that is, every response that fits the blot whether or not it is common. X−% , distorted form, is the share with minus form quality. In Exner's 1993 adult reference tables the average X+% was .79 and the average X−% .07, so about four responses in five were conventional and fewer than one in ten distorted (in 2001 James Wood and colleagues, pooling independent samples of non-patients, found X+% much lower and X−% much higher than these figures, a story for Section 10.10). A high X−% is the classic sign of psychotic perception: the person sees what is driven by inner preoccupation rather than by the stimulus, and minus human movement responses (M−) are taken as especially serious. A very high X+% has its own, quieter meaning: a person who sees only what everybody sees, conventional to the point of rigidity. The confabulated whole: one detail becomes everything. Rorschach noticed that some people saw a small part of the blot clearly and then, on the strength of that part alone, named the whole blot, paying little attention to the rest of it. In an invented example: "It's a bicycle, because of this little round wheel in the corner", where the wheel fits but the rest of the blot looks nothing like a bicycle. He scored such an answer not W but DW, meaning a whole arrived at from a detail, and he called it a confabulated whole response (A. K. Singh's table adds the rarer DdW, from an unusual detail, and the confabulated detail DdD; Section 10.4 gives the codes). The word is the one neurologists use for patients with Korsakoff's syndrome (Book 3 describes the amnestic disorders), who fill gaps in memory with confident inventions, and the parallel is apt. Why should a DW say anything about reality testing? Because the person has let one fragment of evidence override everything else in the stimulus, and has done so without noticing the misfit. That is exactly what impaired reality testing means: the conclusion is no longer checked against the data. Rorschach reported such answers in people of low intelligence, in organic, epileptic and schizophrenic patients, in whom the grasp of form is unclear, and in some normal subjects, and most later Rorschach workers treated a clear DW as pathological. A. K. Singh reports that Beck was the dissenter, arguing that some confabulatory answers came from bright normal adults; the general reading, and the one examiners want, is impairment in reality testing. Content: what the person sees, and who. Content is the most intuitive family of scores and, in the Comprehensive System, the least weighted on its own. The scores that matter most are the human contents. Human responses (H), and above all whole, real human figures, are taken to show interpersonal orientation : an interest in other people and a capacity to understand them as whole, real beings. The total of human contents, SumH (H + (H) + Hd + (Hd)), shows how much the person thinks about people at all; the number of pure H responses shows how far they are seen as complete, real people rather than as parts (Hd) or as fictions and caricatures ((H), (Hd)). In Exner's 1993 adult tables non-patients gave on average a little over three pure H responses, and fewer than two pure H responses in a record of ordinary length counts as a warning sign. So when a record contains no human responses at all, the reading is poor interpersonal orientation : little interest in or understanding of people, a person whose inner world is not populated by others. The other contents have their own traditional readings: many anatomy and X-ray responses (An, Xy) suggest preoccupation with the body; a high share of animal content is read as stereotyped, unimaginative thinking; food responses (Fd) as dependency; blood (Bl) and explosions as poorly controlled affect or aggression. Finally, the popular responses (P), the dozen or so percepts given by a large share of people, show how far the person sees the world the conventional way; Exner's 1993 adults gave on average about six or seven. Few populars suggest a person out of step with ordinary perception, many a cautious conformist. Exam trap Know which score answers which question. Many good W responses (Comprehensive System) = organisational and integrative effort , the drive to synthesise. Reality testing is read from form quality (X−%, XA%), not from location; emotional reactivity from the colour responses and the Affective Ratio (Afr, responses to the three all-coloured last cards divided by responses to the first seven); impulse control from the balance of form-dominant to colour-dominant colour (FC : CF + C) and the stress scores taught in Section 10.5.4. So in IHBAS-style items: confabulatory (DW) responses = impaired reality testing , not "extreme lack of empathy" (empathy is read, if at all, from the human movement and human content scores), not "regressed ego" (a psychoanalytic notion of falling back to earlier, more primitive modes of functioning, which psychoanalytic Rorschach workers read from the overall pattern of a record rather than from this one sign) and not "cognitive immaturity" (vague, unintegrated responses, DQ v, are the sign of immature processing). Absence of human responses = poor interpersonal orientation , not apathy (which would be read from a short, constricted record with few movement or colour responses), not "lack of empathy" (too narrow: the score is about interest in and understanding of people in general), and therefore not "all of the above". Movement, colour and style: the Experience Balance and Lambda Of everything Rorschach left behind, the idea his successors kept most faithfully is a ratio between two kinds of response. Rorschach noticed that people who saw many human figures in movement (M) seemed to live much of their lives inside their own heads: in his list, more creative, with more "inner life", stable feelings and "more intensive than extensive rapport" with others, a few deep ties rather than many light ones. People who gave many colour responses seemed to live outward: more adaptable to reality, with labile feelings and "more extensive than intensive rapport", reaching out to many people and to the world. He called the balance between the two a person's Erlebnistypus , German for "experience type", the characteristic way a person experiences life. A person in whom M predominated was introversive, one in whom colour predominated was extratensive, and one with both present in about equal, large amounts he called ambiequal. If both were nearly absent, he called the type coarctated (from the Latin for "narrowed"; the English translation spells it coartated), and he found it in pedants, in depressed moods and in some long-standing psychoses; if both were present in abundance, the type was dilated. Rorschach was careful about one word, and so should you be. He insisted that the M-type person "must not be said to be introverted, but described as capable of introversion, or introversive", because for him introversion was a mobile capacity, not a fixed trait, and a rigid, fixed introversion was pathological. His "introversive" is also not Carl Jung's introvert, and not the low scorer on Hans Eysenck's extraversion scale. An introversive person in the Rorschach sense may be warm and sociable; what defines the style is that problems are worked out in thought before they are acted on. To compare M with colour, Rorschach needed a way of counting colour responses that recognised that they are not all alike. A form-colour response, in which shape leads and colour only adds to it ("a red butterfly"), shows feeling under the control of form; a pure colour response ("blood, because it is red") shows feeling with no control at all. He solved the problem with weights, and the Comprehensive System kept them exactly. In words: give each FC response half a point, each CF response one point and each pure C response one and a half points, and add them up. Colour naming (Cn), simply listing the colours, gets no weight at all, because it is not a response to the blot as something seen. The total is the weighted sum of colour , WSumC. Remember WSumC = (0.5 × FC) + (1.0 × CF) + (1.5 × C) FC, CF and C are the numbers of form-colour, colour-form and pure colour responses; Cn is not counted. EB = M : WSumC EA = M + WSumC EB is the Experience Balance , M the number of human movement responses; EA, Experience Actual , is their sum. John Exner renamed Rorschach's Erlebnistypus the Experience Balance, EB, and wrote it as the ratio M : WSumC, with human movement on the left and weighted colour on the right. Only M goes on the left. Animal movement (FM) and inanimate movement (m) are not part of the EB; they go, with the achromatic and shading responses, into a separate ratio that Section 10.5.4 uses. Add the two sides of the EB and you get Experience Actual, EA, which Exner read as the person's available resources: the amount of organised thinking and feeling the person can bring to bear on life. How large must the difference be before a person counts as having a style? A difference of half a point means nothing, so Exner set rules. When EA is between 4.0 and 10.0, one side of the EB must exceed the other by at least 2.0 points; when EA is greater than 10.0, by at least 2.5 points, because with more responses a bigger gap is needed to mean the same thing. If M is larger by that margin the person is introversive; if WSumC is larger, extratensive; if neither side is larger by the margin, the person is ambitent , Exner's name for Rorschach's ambiequal type. And when EA is below 4.0 there is simply too little movement and colour to judge, and no style is assigned; nor is one assigned when either side of the EB is zero. Exner's descriptions of the three styles are claims built on his research programme. The introversive style belongs to a person who prefers to delay action, think the alternatives through and rely on inner evaluation; the extratensive style to one who merges feeling with thinking, tests ideas by trying them out and learns from the results. Neither is healthier than the other; they are two different ways of solving problems. The ambitent, by contrast, has no consistent preference, and in one of Exner's problem-solving studies ambitents took longer, repeated more operations and made more errors than either of the styled groups, so Exner, unlike Rorschach, did not see the ambitent as the more flexible person. Try the rules on two invented records. Esha, a 24-year-old, gives 22 responses with 2 M, 2 FC, 3 CF and 1 pure C. Her WSumC is (0.5 × 2) + (1.0 × 3) + (1.5 × 1) = 1.0 + 3.0 + 1.5 = 5.5. Her EB is 2 : 5.5 and her EA is 2 + 5.5 = 7.5, inside the 4.0 to 10.0 band, so she needs a gap of 2.0. Eight of her responses are pure form, so her Lambda is 8 ÷ (22 − 8) = 8 ÷ 14 = .57, well under 1.0, and nothing overrides the EB. The gap is 5.5 − 2 = 3.5, on the colour side, so her style is extratensive. A record with 4 M and a WSumC of 3.5, by contrast, also has an EA of 7.5, but the gap is only 0.5, so that person is ambitent. There is one more number that can overrule the EB, and it is about the responses that have no movement or colour at all. Lambda (written L, after the Greek letter) compares the pure form responses with all the rest. In words: count the responses whose only determinant is F, then divide that number by the number of responses that have any other determinant. As a formula: Remember Lambda = F ÷ (R − F) F is the number of pure form responses and R the total number of responses, so R − F is the number of responses with at least one other determinant. Do not confuse it with F%, which is F ÷ R. Why compare pure form with the rest? A pure F response is the most economical answer possible: the person attends to shape and nothing else, ignoring colour, shading and the movement a figure might suggest. Everybody gives some, and Exner's 1993 adult tables put the average Lambda at about .58, so a typical person gives a little over one pure form response for every two richer ones. A person with a high Lambda , 1.0 or more (Exner's rule is "greater than .99"), gives at least as many pure form answers as all the others put together. Exner read this as an avoidant style : a habit of narrowing and simplifying the field, economising on effort, dealing with complexity by not looking at it. It can be efficient, and it can also miss a great deal. In the fourth edition of his first volume (2003) Exner treated high Lambda as a style in its own right that takes precedence over the EB, so a high-Lambda person with an introversive EB is described as avoidant-introversive. Very low Lambda suggests the opposite problem: a person who cannot leave any complexity alone and gets caught up in every shade and colour. A high Lambda also has an innocent explanation that the examiner must rule out first: a guarded person who wants to give nothing away will produce a short record full of pure form answers. Take a third invented record. Nirmal, seen for a court-ordered assessment, gives only 15 responses, of which 11 are pure form; the other four are 1 M, 2 FC and 1 FM. His Lambda is 11 ÷ (15 − 11) = 11 ÷ 4 = 2.75, nearly three times the cut-off: a high-Lambda, avoidant record. His EB is 1 : 1.0 (two FC at half a point each), and his EA is 2.0, below 4.0, so no EB style can be assigned anyway. Figure 10.11 places Esha and Nirmal, and Brinda from the next subsection, on one map. Exam trap EB is M : WSumC , human movement against weighted colour; it is not M against FM, and FM and m belong elsewhere. The weights are 0.5 for FC, 1.0 for CF and 1.5 for C ; Cn gets none. Lambda is F ÷ (R − F) , not F ÷ R (that is F%). Rorschach's introversive is not Jung's or Eysenck's introvert: it is a problem-solving style, not shyness. "Ambiequal" is Rorschach's word and "ambitent" Exner's for the same middle type, and "coarctated" means both M and colour are nearly absent. Brinda's record is of ordinary length and gives the examiner plenty to work with, which suggests she was not guarded during the test. She puts real effort into making sense of things as a whole: two responses in five use the whole blot, more than the one in three that the usual W : D ratio of 1 : 2 implies, and half of those are well-organised syntheses, so she is an ambitious, effortful organiser, perhaps one who finds it hard to settle for a quick, partial answer. Clinical link A Rorschach report never says "Brinda is introversive and has good reality testing" as if these were measured facts like her height. It says what the record suggests and how far the other evidence agrees: "Her Rorschach suggests a reflective style that prefers to think problems through before acting, consistent with her own account of long deliberation; there were no signs of perceptual distortion or disordered thinking." Writing findings as tested hypotheses protects the client from over-reading, and it protects the report from the vague, flattering statements that fit everybody (the Barnum effect, Book 2, Section 2.9.9). And no diagnosis is ever made from the Rorschach alone. Exam trap The arithmetic slips examiners like: count a blend's determinants separately (M.FC adds one to M and one to FC); leave Cn out of WSumC; divide F by R − F , not by R, for Lambda; check Lambda before EB , because a Lambda over .99 means the avoidant style comes first; and check EA before naming a style, because the gap needed is 2.0 when EA is 4.0 to 10.0, 2.5 when EA is over 10.0, and no style is called when EA is under 4.0. X+% counts + and o; XA% adds u; X−% counts minus alone. After Rorschach: five American schools Everything in the last four subsections presupposes that somebody has settled which codes exist, how each is defined and what each ratio means. For fifty years nobody had. Hermann Rorschach died in April 1922, months after Psychodiagnostik appeared, and he left a method still under construction: a handful of codes, a theory of experience type and a last paper on applying the test, published after his death by his colleague Emil Oberholzer . The method crossed the Atlantic with the American psychiatrist David M. Levy , usually credited with bringing it to the United States in the mid-1920s, and there it was taken up by several energetic people who never agreed on how to use it. By the 1950s there were five American systems, and they were different enough that a "Rorschach" given in Chicago and one given in Los Angeles were not quite the same test. Figure 10.12 lays out the century. Era 1: the test and its arrival in America (1921 to 1930) 1921 Rorschach: Psychodiagnostik; dies 1922, no full scoring system mid-1920s David Levy brings the test to the United States 1930 Beck: the first American research paper on the test Era 2: rival schools (1936 to 1961) 1936 Klopfer founds the Rorschach Research Exchange 1937 Beck: Introduction to the Rorschach Method; Piotrowski: organic signs 1942 Klopfer and Kelley: The Rorschach Technique 1945 to 1946 Rapaport, Gill and Schafer: Diagnostic Psychological Testing 1954 Schafer: Psychoanalytic Interpretation in Rorschach Testing 1957 Piotrowski: Perceptanalysis 1961 Holtzman and colleagues: the Holtzman Inkblot Technique Era 3: one system, then its successor (1969 to 2011) 1969 Exner: The Rorschach Systems compares the five schools 1974 Exner: The Rorschach: A Comprehensive System, volume 1 2000 Perceptual-Thinking Index replaces the Schizophrenia Index 2003 Comprehensive System, volume 1, fourth edition 2006 Exner dies; the system is frozen 2011 Meyer and colleagues: the R-PAS manual Figure 10.12 A century of reading the Rorschach. Notice the three eras: a method left unfinished by its author, a long period of rival American schools, and then Exner's single Comprehensive System and, after his death, the R-PAS. The Holtzman (1961) is a different set of blots, not a scoring system for Rorschach's. The first and the most rigorous of the five was Samuel Jacob Beck (1896 to 1980). Beck, who also studied the method in Zurich with Oberholzer, wrote the first American research paper on the test in 1930, took his doctorate at Columbia University in 1932, and set out his method in Introduction to the Rorschach Method (1937), followed from 1944 by the volumes of Rorschach's Test . His instinct was the psychometrician's. A detail area counted as a common D only if it was used often in real records; a form was good only if it matched the forms that normal people saw there, which meant building frequency tables; and organising activity was scored with numbers, the Z score that Exner later took over. Beck distrusted anything that depended on the scorer's intuition, and he did not hide it. The intuition he distrusted belonged above all to Bruno Klopfer (1900 to 1971). Klopfer, who had a doctorate from Munich, left Germany in 1933 as a Jew, spent a year in Zurich, where he first met the test, and reached Columbia University, where he worked for a time with the anthropologist Franz Boas. He taught Rorschach seminars, and in 1936 he founded the Rorschach Research Exchange , the journal that became the Journal of Projective Techniques and, in 1971, the Journal of Personality Assessment . With the psychiatrist Douglas M. Kelley, the Nuremberg examiner of this chapter's opening, he wrote The Rorschach Technique (1942), a manual from which a generation of clinicians learned the test. Klopfer's approach was phenomenological and clinical: he wanted the scoring to capture the experience behind a response, so he multiplied the codes (separate symbols for animal movement and for the kinds of shading, and a separate scoring of achromatic colour), rated the level of form on a scale rather than as simply good or bad, added testing the limits to the administration (Section 10.3), and summarised a record in a bar chart of its determinants that he called the psychogram. To Beck, many of these innovations were unreliable additions with no normative base, and the two men criticised each other's methods in print from the late 1930s. The quarrel split American Rorschach work into camps that lasted for decades. Between them stood Marguerite Rosenberg Hertz (1899 to 1992), who took her doctorate at Western Reserve University in Cleveland in 1932 and taught there from 1938 to 1970. Her system leaned, like Beck's, on carefully compiled frequency tables for judging form, but she was open to some of Klopfer's ideas, and she is often described as the person who tried to keep the two camps talking; she was a founding member, and in 1940 to 1941 president, of the society that is now the Society for Personality Assessment. Zygmunt A. Piotrowski (1904 to 1985), born in Poland, made his name in 1937 with a list of ten Rorschach signs of organic brain disease, the "organic signs", and later set out his own system in Perceptanalysis (1957). Several codes in today's systems are his: A. K. Singh credits him with the symbol m for inanimate movement and the symbol Cn for colour naming (both 1936), and he was among the first to try to computerise Rorschach interpretation in the 1950s and 1960s. The fifth school came from psychoanalysis. David Rapaport (1911 to 1960), a Hungarian-born psychologist, worked at the Menninger Clinic in Topeka, Kansas, with Merton Gill and Roy Schafer (1922 to 2018), and their two-volume Diagnostic Psychological Testing (1945 to 1946) did two new things. It treated the Rorschach as one test in a battery, read alongside the Wechsler-Bellevue, word association and the TAT, and it read the results through psychoanalytic ego psychology, asking what each response showed about the ego's ways of thinking, defending and adapting. Its most lasting gift was a careful catalogue of deviant verbalisations , the odd, illogical or bizarre ways some patients talk about what they see (a "fabulised combination" that merges two percepts impossibly, a "contamination" that fuses two ideas into one), which is the ancestor of the Comprehensive System's special scores for disordered thinking. Rapaport's group also differed in method, preferring an inquiry after each card instead of after all ten. Schafer carried the approach further in Psychoanalytic Interpretation in Rorschach Testing (1954), a classic of thematic reading. Exam trap The recognised Rorschach scoring systems are those of Beck, Klopfer, Hertz, Piotrowski, Rapaport and Schafer , then Exner's Comprehensive System and R-PAS . There is no "Murray system" : Henry Murray gave us the Thematic Apperception Test (Section 10.6), not a way of scoring inkblots. Pair the names with their signatures: Beck, the empiricist with frequency tables and the Z score; Klopfer, the clinician with the Rorschach Research Exchange, the psychogram and testing the limits; Piotrowski, the organic signs and Perceptanalysis ; Rapaport, Gill and Schafer, the Menninger test battery and deviant verbalisations. Exner's Comprehensive System By the 1960s the Rorschach was one of the most widely used tests in American clinics and also, scientifically, a mess. Research findings from one school could not be checked by another, because the scores were not defined the same way; the same response could be coded differently in different systems, and many clinicians used no formal scoring at all. John E. Exner Jr. (1928 to 2006) set out to sort it out. Born in Syracuse, New York, he took his doctorate in clinical psychology at Cornell University in 1958, knew Beck, Klopfer and Hertz personally, and spent the rest of his career on the test, later directing his Rorschach Workshops in Asheville, North Carolina. His solution was not to found a sixth school but to build one system out of the best-supported parts of the existing five. Key study: Exner compares the five systems (1969 to 1974) The question. Were the five American systems five versions of one test, or five different tests? The method. In The Rorschach Systems (1969) Exner laid the systems side by side and traced how each had developed, comparing them with each other and with Rorschach's own scoring. In 1972, with D. E. Exner, he surveyed practising clinicians on how they actually used the test ("How clinicians use the Rorschach", Journal of Personality Assessment ). The result. The systems overlapped far less than their shared name suggested, and in practice many clinicians scored loosely or not at all, often mixing elements of different systems with their own preferences. The conclusion. In The Rorschach: A Comprehensive System , volume 1 (1974), Exner kept an element from any of the older systems only if it could be scored reliably by different examiners (the .85 agreement hurdle of Chapter 3, Section 3.6.9) and had research evidence behind it, standardised the administration, and collected norms. The criticism. Critics later argued that the system's norms made healthy adults look disturbed and that many of its variables had weak validity; that argument belongs to Section 10.10. The Comprehensive System (CS) soon became the dominant way of giving, scoring and reading the Rorschach, in America and far beyond. Its parts will now be familiar. The administration is fixed: the person and examiner sit side by side, the instruction is simply "What might this be?", every word is recorded, and the inquiry follows the response phase (Section 10.3 gives the details). The codes take their area definitions from Beck, borrow freely from the others (animal movement and achromatic colour from Klopfer, inanimate movement from Piotrowski, the special scores from Rapaport's deviant verbalisations) and are defined in a single manual with tables of common areas and of form quality. The codes are added into the sequence of scores and the Structural Summary, and the summary is read against normative tables. Later, as Exner's research accumulated, came the rule that a record must have at least 14 responses, the interpretive search strategy, and the constellations. A constellation works like a checklist. Each one lists a set of conditions on the Structural Summary, and the index is positive when enough of them are met; the Suicide Constellation, S-CON, for example, has 12 conditions and is positive when 8 or more are present. The idea is that no single sign is trusted, but a cluster of signs that each, on their own, slightly raise a risk may together point to it. Table 10.21 lists them. The best known change came in 2000, when Exner replaced the Schizophrenia Index (SCZI) with the Perceptual-Thinking Index (PTI), designed to measure disordered perception and thinking more accurately, under a name that no longer suggests that a positive score is a diagnosis. The first volume reached its fourth edition in 2003. Exner died of leukaemia in 2006, and the system was then frozen: about two years later his heirs decided that it would not be developed further, which is part of the reason a successor was built. It is a system for scoring the Rorschach : not the MMPI (an objective inventory with its own scales, Chapter 9), not the TAT (scored through need and press or through systems such as McClelland's, Section 10.6) and not the Wechsler scales (Chapter 6). It scores location, determinants, form quality, content, populars and special scores and builds a Structural Summary, but it gives no IQ score . The PTI is the renamed and revised SCZI, so an older paper may call it the "schizophrenia index"; S-CON is the suicide constellation, DEPI depression, CDI coping deficit, HVI hypervigilance and OBS obsessive style. After Exner: R-PAS, and Holtzman's different answer Even before Exner died, the people closest to his research had begun to see three problems that a frozen system could not fix. The first was evidence: a long series of critiques had argued that many Comprehensive System variables had little validity, and a large meta-analysis of the system's variables led by Joni Mihura (published in 2013 and discussed in Section 10.10) would later sort the well-supported variables from the poorly supported ones. The second was the norms, which in independent samples made ordinary adults look disturbed. The third was R itself. Because the person decides how many responses to give, records vary enormously in length, from the minimum of 14 to 40 or more, and many scores rise and fall with length; Gregory Meyer showed in 1993 that R was significantly related to 26 of the 29 count-based criteria of the constellations. A long record has more chances to produce every kind of sign, so the same person could look healthier or sicker depending on how talkative they were that day. The answer was the Rorschach Performance Assessment System (R-PAS), whose manual appeared in 2011, written by Gregory J. Meyer , Donald J. Viglione , Joni L. Mihura , Robert E. Erard and Philip Erdberg ; four of the five had sat on Exner's Rorschach Research Council, and the fifth, Erard, was a forensic psychologist. It uses the same ten cards and much of the same coding, but it changes three things. First, it controls R with R-Optimized administration . Before the first card the examiner asks the person to give "two, or maybe three" responses to each card. If the person gives only one, the examiner prompts for another, reminding them of the request (and accepts one if no more comes); if the person gives four, the examiner pulls the card, reminding them of the request and moving on to the next card. Studies comparing the two administrations found that R-PAS raises R slightly and, more importantly, makes it much less variable, with little effect on most other scores. Second, R-PAS keeps only variables with research support, and lays them out on two profile pages, Page 1 for the variables with the strongest support and Page 2 for those with less, each page grouped into the same five domains: administration behaviours and observations; engagement and cognitive processing; perception and thinking problems; stress and distress; and self and other representation. Lambda, whose statistical properties made it awkward to analyse, gives way to F%, pure form divided by R. Third, every score is reported against an international reference sample of adult records gathered in the United States, Europe, Israel, Argentina and Brazil, as a standard score with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 and as a percentile (Chapter 5 explains both). Exner did not write R-PAS, which appeared five years after his death, although the R-PAS developers list him among the contributors of the American records in its reference data. Long before either system, an American psychologist had asked a more radical question: if the Rorschach's statistical problems come from the test itself, why not build a better test? Wayne H. Holtzman (1923 to 2019), who worked at the University of Texas at Austin from 1949 to 1993, and his colleagues Joseph S. Thorpe , Jon D. Swartz and E. Wayne Herron published the Holtzman Inkblot Technique (HIT) in Inkblot Perception and Personality (1961). It has two parallel forms, A and B, of 45 inkblots each, with two practice blots common to both forms. Some blots are chromatic and some achromatic, and unlike Rorschach's they vary in how symmetrical they are. The crucial rule is that the person gives only one response to each blot , followed at once by a brief standardised inquiry. That single rule removes the problem R-PAS later attacked with prompts and pulls: every record has the same number of responses, so scores can be compared directly from person to person. Responses are scored on 22 variables, many of them borrowed from the Rorschach literature (location, form appropriateness, colour, shading, movement and so on), with norms. Because there are two equivalent forms, the HIT can do what the Rorschach never could, give a true alternate-form reliability coefficient (Chapter 3, Section 3.3 explains parallel forms), and it can even be given to groups. It was widely praised by psychometricians and much less widely used by clinicians, who stayed with the familiar ten cards. In Lindzey's scheme it is, like the Rorschach, an association technique (Section 10.2). Table 10.22 gathers every system in this section, from Rorschach's own unfinished scheme to the HIT.
