past papers Which of these projective tests uses the perception of inkblots to assess respondent's personality types? (RML 2020) (a) Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (b) Thematic Apperception Test (c) Myers-Briggs Type Indicator Test (d) Rorschach Test Answer: (d) Rorschach Test. Hermann Rorschach's ten cards (1921) are the only inkblots among the options (Section 10.3.3). The MMPI is a true-false self-report inventory and the MBTI a forced-choice questionnaire that sorts people into Jungian "types", so neither uses a picture of any kind; the word "types" in the stem is bait for the MBTI. The TAT uses pictures of people in ambiguous scenes, not inkblots. Projective tests claim to reveal information about: (RML 2020) (a) intellectual attainment (b) unconscious processes (c) parenting style (d) career aptitude Answer: (b) unconscious processes. The central claim, which follows from the projective hypothesis, is that the response to an ambiguous stimulus reveals needs, wishes, fears and conflicts of which the person is unaware (Section 10.1.6). Intellectual attainment is measured by achievement tests, parenting style by questionnaires and by observing families, and career aptitude by aptitude batteries and interest inventories. What is Rorschach's projective test designed to measure? (RML 2021) (a) Unconscious intentions. (b) Dreams (c) Conscious desires. (d) Brain size Answer: (a) Unconscious intentions. In the projective tradition the Rorschach gives a person room to reveal unconscious needs, conflicts and intentions that he would not or could not report directly (Section 10.3.3). It is not a way of analysing dreams; conscious desires are what an inventory asks about; and it is not a test of brain structure. Which is not a projective test (RML 2021) (a) Word association test (b) Rorschach's ink lot test (c) Thematic apperception test (d) Sentence completion test Answer: keyed (a) Word association test, but the key is wrong: by the standard classification all four are projective. Word association is a founding member of Lindzey's association family, named beside the Rorschach, and Galton's word association of 1879 is usually called the first projective technique; Jung made it clinical with complex indicators (Section 10.2.5). The Rorschach is an association technique, the TAT a construction technique and sentence completion a completion technique. Learn word association as projective; mark (a) only if this exact item reappears, because that is the paper's known key. If an option names a genuine objective inventory (MMPI-2, 16PF, NEO-PI-R) or the Controlled Oral Word Association Test, a fluency test, that option is the answer. How many Rorschach cards are coloured? (RML 2022) (a) 10 (b) 5 (c) 3 (d) 4 Answer: (b) 5. Two cards (II and III) are black and grey with red, and three (VIII, IX and X) are fully multicoloured, so five carry colour; the other five (I, IV, V, VI and VII) are achromatic (Section 10.3.4). "3" counts only the multicoloured cards, and "10" and "4" are simply wrong. Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) is based on which technique of psychological testing? (RML 2022) (a) Expressive technique (b) Construction technique (c) Association technique (d) Completion technique Answer: (b) Construction technique. In Gardner Lindzey's classification (1959; the families are his, not Frank's) the TAT is the model construction technique: the person builds a new and elaborate product, a story with a past, a present and an outcome (Section 10.2.2). Association asks for the first word or percept (the Rorschach), completion for finishing a supplied stem or frame (sentence completion, the P-F Study), and expression for a free production whose manner is studied (drawings, play). Who developed the House-tree-person test? (RML 2022) (a) John Buck (b) Aaron T.Beck (c) David D. Burns (d) Karen Machover Answer: (a) John Buck. John N. Buck set out the House-Tree-Person in 1948: an achromatic (pencil) phase and then a chromatic (crayon) phase, each followed by the post-drawing interrogation (Section 10.9.2). Aaron T. Beck founded cognitive therapy and wrote the Beck Depression Inventory, David D. Burns wrote the self-help book Feeling Good , and Karen Machover devised the Draw-a-Person (1949). The following statements about the Rorschach inkblot test are correct EXCEPT: (RML 2022) (a) It was introduced in 1921 by Swiss psychiatrist Hermann Rorschach. (b) It is a projective method of psychological testing. (c) Its function is to assess cognition and personality of the person and to diagnosis certain psychological conditions. (d) It employs 12 inkblots in which a person is asked to describe what he or she sees in them. Answer: (d). The test has ten cards, not 12 (Section 10.3.4). The other three statements are true: Psychodiagnostik appeared in 1921, the test is the classic projective method, and it is used to assess cognition and personality and to help diagnose psychological conditions, especially psychosis (Section 10.3.3). Which of the following is an association technique of psychological testing? (RML 2022) (a) Sentence completion test (b) Rorschach inkblot test (c) Thematic apperception test (d) Draw-a-person test Answer: (b) Rorschach inkblot test. Association techniques ask for the first word, image or percept a stimulus calls up, and the Rorschach is the founding member of the family (Section 10.2.2). Sentence completion is a completion technique, the TAT a construction technique and the Draw-a-Person an expression technique. Which testing method uses ambiguous stimuli to uncover unconscious thoughts? (RML 2025) (a) Projective tests (b) Personality inventories (c) Standardized intelligence tests (d) Observation (direct) tests Answer: (a) Projective tests. This is the projective hypothesis in one line: an ambiguous, unstructured stimulus makes the person supply the structure, revealing what he could not or would not say (Section 10.1.3). Personality inventories use clear items with fixed answers and a key, intelligence tests present structured problems with correct answers, and direct observation records behaviour itself with no test stimulus at all (Section 10.1.6). What types of cards are included in the Rorschach test? (RML 2025) (a) Only black and white cards (b) Only colored cards (c) Five black and white and five multi-colored cards (d) Ten multi-colored cards Answer: (c), the keyed option, but its wording is loose. The five-five split is right and (c) is the only option with it; "only black and white", "only coloured" and "ten multicoloured" are all false. Strictly, the five achromatic cards (I, IV, V, VI, VII) are black and grey, and of the five chromatic cards only three (VIII, IX, X) are fully multicoloured, while two (II, III) are black and red (Section 10.3.4). Choose (c), and know the exact composition: 5 achromatic, 2 black and red, 3 multicoloured. What is the main purpose of the Rorschach inkblot test? (RML 2025) (a) To diagnose physical illness (b) To measure thought disorder and identify mental illness through perception of inkblots (c) To assess intelligence quotient (d) To evaluate memory recall Answer: (b). Rorschach's own clinical interest centred on schizophrenia, and the test is still used as one source of evidence on thought processes, thought disorder and psychopathology, especially psychosis (Section 10.3.3); form quality and the thought-disorder scores are its best-supported variables (Section 10.10.4). It is not a test of physical illness or of memory, and no system turns a Rorschach record into an IQ. What is the Enquiry Phase in the Rorschach test? (RML 2025) (a) Phase where the cards are randomly shuffled (b) Phase involving detailed discussion and clarification of each response without leading answers (c) Initial exposure to inkblots without recording responses (d) Phase that involves scoring the responses only Answer: (b). After all ten cards the examiner reads each response back and asks, in essence, only "Where is it?" and "What makes it look like that?", following the person's own key words without leading questions, to establish location and determinants (Section 10.3.6). The cards are always shown in the fixed order I to X, every word is recorded verbatim from Card I onwards, and coding is done afterwards, away from the client. Who developed the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) and in which decade? (RML 2025) (a) Sigmund Freud in the 1920s (b) Henry A. Murray and Christiana D. Morgan in the 1930s (c) Carl Jung in the 1940s (d) B.F. Skinner in the 1950s Answer: (b). Christiana D. Morgan (the paper's "Christina" is a misspelling) and Henry A. Murray of the Harvard Psychological Clinic published the TAT in 1935, with the final set and Murray's manual in 1943 (Section 10.6.1). Freud devised no picture test, Jung's test was word association (1904 to 1910), and Skinner was studying operant conditioning. How many picture cards are usually used in a typical TAT assessment session? (RML 2025) (a) 1 to 3 cards (b) 5 to 12 cards (c) 20 to 31 cards (d) Over 50 cards Answer: (b) 5 to 12 cards. The full set has 31 cards (30 pictures and the blank card 16), and Murray gave one person 20 in two sessions of ten, but clinicians today select about 5 to 12 cards for a single session, 8 to 12 being the figure most often quoted (Section 10.6.2). One to three is too few for a theme to recur, 20 to 31 describes the whole kit, never one sitting, and no version has over 50. What is the main purpose of analyzing the stories a participant tells during the TAT? (RML 2025) (a) To measure IQ (b) To reveal unconscious thoughts, conflicts, and motivations (c) To assess vocabulary skills (d) To test memory retention Answer: (b). The stories are read through the hero, his needs, the press, the thema and the outcome for needs and conflicts the person may not be able or willing to report (Sections 10.6.3 and 10.6.6). Murray's instruction calls the test "a test of imagination, one form of intelligence" only as a disguise; a long, fluent story is not scored as IQ or vocabulary, and the examiner does not test memory for the pictures. Which is a key difference between the TAT and the Rorschach Inkblot Test? (RML 2025) (a) TAT uses ambiguous social scenes with characters; Rorschach uses symmetrical inkblots (b) TAT measures IQ; Rorschach measures personality (c) TAT requires yes/no answers; Rorschach requires storytelling (d) Both tests are identical in method and purpose Answer: (a). The TAT shows recognisable people in ambiguous situations and asks for stories; the Rorschach shows symmetrical inkblots and asks for percepts (Section 10.6.6). Both are personality techniques, neither asks for yes or no answers (those belong to inventories), option (c) also puts the storytelling in the wrong test, and the two differ at every step of method and purpose. What is the main advantage of projective tests, like the Rorschach inkblot test? (RML 2025) (a) They allow people to use defence mechanisms of projection (b) They avoid self-report biases (c) They have superior re-test reliability (d) They provide numerical quantitative data Answer: (b) They avoid self-report biases. Because the purpose is disguised and there are no right answers, social desirability, faking and defensiveness have less to work with (Section 10.1.7). Option (a) twists the theory: the test is meant to see past defences, and the projection it relies on is everyday perception, not a defence handed to the client. Superior retest reliability and numerical data are strengths of objective inventories; projective retest figures are modest (Section 10.10.2). Remember too that informed people can still fake (Albert, Fox and Kahn, 1980). Confabulatory responses on Rorschach Psychodiagnostics are indicative of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Impairment in reality testing (b) Extreme lack of empathy (c) Regressed ego (d) Cognitive immaturity Answer: (a) Impairment in reality testing. A confabulated whole response (DW) seizes on one detail and stretches the percept over the whole blot without checking the fit, so the conclusion is no longer tested against the stimulus; it almost always carries poor form quality, and the later Comprehensive System codes it W with minus form quality and the special score CONFAB (Sections 10.4.2 and 10.5.2). Empathy is read, if at all, from human movement and human content; "regressed ego" is a psychoanalytic reading of a whole record, not of this one sign; cognitive immaturity shows in vague (DQ v) responses. Absence of 'Human' Response on Rorschach Psychodiagnostics Test indicates: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Apathy (b) Poor interpersonal orientation (c) Lack of empathy (d) All the above Answer: (b) Poor interpersonal orientation. Human contents, above all whole, real human figures (pure H), are taken to show interest in and understanding of people, so a record with none is read as poor interpersonal orientation (Section 10.5.2). Apathy would be read from a short, constricted record with few movement or colour responses, and "lack of empathy" is too narrow, so "all the above" fails as well. Identify the correct option for Projective tests of Personality: i) Rorschach & TAT, ii) Eysenck Personality Questionnaire, iii) 16 PF, iv) MCMI-III. (Amity 2023) (a) Both i and ii (b) Only i (c) i, ii and iv (d) None Answer: (b) Only i. The Rorschach and the TAT present ambiguous stimuli and leave the response open; the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire, the 16PF and the MCMI-III are objective inventories with fixed items, fixed answers and a scoring key (Section 10.1.6 and Table 10.3). The Rorschach Inkblot Test has: (Amity 2023) (a) 3 chromatic and 7 achromatic cards (b) 5 chromatic and 5 achromatic cards (c) 10 inkblots and 1 blank card (d) 3 achromatic and 7 chromatic cards Answer: (b) 5 chromatic and 5 achromatic cards. Cards I, IV, V, VI and VII are achromatic; II and III add red and VIII, IX and X are multicoloured, so five are chromatic (Section 10.3.4). "3 chromatic and 7 achromatic" forgets that the red of Cards II and III is a hue, "3 achromatic and 7 chromatic" is wrong twice over, and the blank card belongs to the TAT (card 16), not the Rorschach. In the Rorschach Inkblot Test, a response that is determined primarily by the shape or form of the blot, with little consideration for color or movement, is scored as: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) FC (Form-Color) (b) F (Form) (c) M (Human Movement) (d) C (Pure Color) Answer: (b) F (Form). A pure form response is determined by the shape or outline of the blot alone, and F is coded only when nothing else contributes (Section 10.4.4). FC is form with colour added, M is human movement, and C is colour with no form at all. A clinician is interested in understanding a client's characteristic way of thinking, feeling, and behaving in close relationships, by having them tell stories about ambiguous pictures. The MOST appropriate test to administer would be the: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) Rorschach Inkblot Test (b) Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) (c) Sentence Completion Test (d) Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) Answer: (b) Thematic Apperception Test (TAT). Only the TAT asks for stories about pictures of people, and with a relationship-focused scoring system such as Westen's SCORS it is the standard choice (Section 10.6.6). The Rorschach uses inkblots and asks for percepts, sentence completion uses written stems with no pictures, and the MMPI is a true-false inventory with neither pictures nor stories. In the Rorschach Inkblot Test, a response that is determined primarily by the chromatic color of the blot (for example, "this is a blood stain because it's red") is scored as: (Real PYQ 2024) (a) FC (Form-Color) (b) CF (Color-Form) (c) C (Pure Color) (d) Cn (Color Naming) Answer: (c) C (Pure Color). Colour with no reference to shape is pure colour (Section 10.4.5). FC has a clear shape with colour added, CF has colour leading with a vague shape still present, and Cn merely names the colours ("red, green") without seeing anything. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The Rorschach has ten symmetrical cards (not 12, 15 or 20, and no blank card): five achromatic (I, IV, V, VI, VII), two black and red (II, III) and three multicoloured (VIII, IX, X), so five chromatic and five achromatic. asked 5 times The Rorschach is the inkblot test (not the MMPI, MBTI or TAT): it assesses personality and thought processes, helps measure thought disorder and identify mental illness, and in the projective tradition reveals unconscious intentions; it does not measure IQ, memory, dreams, physical illness or brain size. asked 4 times Projective versus objective : the Rorschach and the TAT are projective; the 16PF, MMPI-2, NEO-PI-R, EPQ, MBTI and MCMI-III are objective self-report inventories. The TAT is a projective personality test, not an objective, achievement, intelligence or neuropsychological test. asked 4 times The projective hypothesis : faced with an ambiguous, unstructured stimulus, a person imposes his own structure and so reveals needs, conflicts and unconscious processes. Projective tests claim to reveal unconscious processes, not intellectual attainment, parenting style or career aptitude; Lawrence K. Frank named "projective methods" in 1939. asked twice Lindzey's five families (1959) : the TAT is construction and the Rorschach association; sentence completion and the Rosenzweig P-F Study are completion, the Szondi is choice or ordering, and the drawings are expression. asked twice The TAT's theory : Murray's need-press theory of psychogenic needs and environmental press, and the assumption that people project their needs and conflicts onto ambiguous pictures; not personal constructs (Kelly), operant conditioning (Skinner), cognitive distortions (Beck) or a single general intelligence factor. asked 3 times Hermann Rorschach (1884 to 1922), a Swiss psychiatrist, published Psychodiagnostik with its ten cards in 1921; Exner wrote the Comprehensive System, Murray the TAT and Jung the word association test. asked twice The TAT was published by Christiana D. Morgan and Henry A. Murray of the Harvard Psychological Clinic in 1935 (the 1930s), with the final set and Murray's manual in 1943; not Freud, Jung, Skinner, Rorschach, Exner or Bellak. asked twice For a client's ways of thinking, feeling and behaving in close relationships, through stories about ambiguous pictures , the test of choice is the TAT, not the Rorschach, sentence completion or the MMPI. asked twice Exner's Comprehensive System (John E. Exner Jr, 1974), built from the best-supported parts of the five American systems, is the major scoring system for the Rorschach, not for the MMPI, the TAT or the Wechsler scales, and not Beck's, Klopfer's or Piotrowski's. asked twice There is no "Murray system" for the Rorschach: the recognised systems are those of Beck, Klopfer, Hertz, Piotrowski, and Rapaport and Schafer, then Exner's Comprehensive System and R-PAS (Meyer and colleagues, 2011). asked twice Word association is projective : it is a founding member of Lindzey's association family, and Galton's word association (1879) is usually called the first projective technique. RML 2021 keyed it "not projective"; by the standard classification word association, the Rorschach, the TAT and sentence completion are all projective. asked once House-Tree-Person : John N. Buck, 1948; an achromatic (pencil) then a chromatic (crayon) phase, each followed by the post-drawing interrogation; not Aaron Beck, David Burns or Karen Machover. asked once The inquiry (enquiry) phase follows the response phase: each response is read back and clarified for location and determinants without leading questions; the cards are never shuffled, and coding comes afterwards. asked once TAT cards : 31 in the set (30 pictures and blank card 16); Murray gave one person 20 in two sessions of ten; a typical session today uses about 5 to 12 selected cards. asked once The purpose of analysing TAT stories is to reveal unconscious thoughts, conflicts and motives, not IQ, vocabulary or memory. asked once TAT versus Rorschach : the TAT uses ambiguous social scenes with characters and asks for stories; the Rorschach uses symmetrical inkblots and asks for percepts. asked once The main advantage of projective tests is that they avoid self-report biases (social desirability, faking, defensiveness); not "they let people use the defence of projection", not superior retest reliability, not numerical data. asked once Confabulatory (DW) responses , one detail generalised to the whole blot, indicate impaired reality testing; not lack of empathy, regressed ego or cognitive immaturity. asked once Absence of human (H) responses indicates poor interpersonal orientation; not apathy, not simply lack of empathy, and so not "all the above". asked once F, pure form : a response determined by the shape of the blot alone, with no colour or movement; not FC, M or C. asked once C, pure colour : a response determined by chromatic colour alone ("blood, because it's red"); FC is form-colour, CF colour-form and Cn colour naming. asked once The Comprehensive System gives no IQ score : it codes location (W, D, Dd, S), developmental quality, determinants, form quality, content, populars, organisational activity (Z) and special scores. asked once Many W responses in the Comprehensive System show organisational and integrative effort; reality testing is read from form quality, emotional reactivity from the colour responses. asked once Draw-a-Person (Karen Machover, 1949), used projectively, rests on the body-image hypothesis: the drawing reflects the person's self-concept and unconscious attitudes, not fine motor skill alone, academic achievement or specific lesions. asked once Children's Apperception Test (Leopold and Sonya Bellak, 1949): 10 cards of animals in human situations, for children of about 3 to 10; the CAT-H (1965) uses human figures and the CAT-S (1952) is a supplement. asked once Rosenzweig Picture-Frustration Study (Saul Rosenzweig, 1945): 24 cartoon frames with an empty speech balloon for the frustrated person, scored for direction (extrapunitive, intropunitive, impunitive) and type (obstacle-dominance, ego-defence, need-persistence). asked once

Chapter 11 Neuropsychological Assessment and Clinical Rating Scales In this chapter 11.1 What Neuropsychological Assessment Is: Questions, Domains, Approaches and Premorbid Ability : explain what neuropsychological assessment asks, which domains it tests, the battery and flexible approaches, and how premorbid ability and decline are estimated. 11.2 The Fixed Batteries: Halstead-Reitan and Luria-Nebraska : describe the tests of the Halstead-Reitan and Luria-Nebraska batteries, how they are scored, and what each is used for. 11.3 Indian Neuropsychological Tools: The NIMHANS Battery, the PGI Battery and the PGI Memory Scale : describe the main Indian batteries and memory scale, who built them, and what their tests measure. 11.4 Memory Tests: The Wechsler Memory Scale, Digit Span and the Learning Tests : explain how memory is tested, from digit span to the Wechsler Memory Scale and the verbal and visual learning tests. 11.5 Visuomotor and Visuospatial Tests: The Bender-Gestalt, the Benton Tests and Constructional Tasks : explain the Bender-Gestalt Test and the other visuomotor, visuospatial and body-schema tests, and what errors on them suggest. 11.6 Executive Function, Attention, Concept Formation and Language Tests : explain the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, the Trail Making Test and the other tests of executive function, attention, abstract thinking and language. 11.7 Bedside Screening and Staging: The MMSE, MoCA, Glasgow Coma Scale and Dementia Ratings : explain the brief cognitive screens, the Glasgow Coma Scale and the dementia staging scales, with their scoring and cut-offs. 11.8 Clinical Rating Scales I: Principles, Depression, Anxiety and OCD : explain how rating scales are built and used, self-report versus clinician-rated, and the main depression, anxiety and OCD scales with their scoring. 11.9 Clinical Rating Scales II: Psychosis, Mania, Substance Use, Children, Disability and Forensic Use : explain the main scales for psychosis, mania, substance use, children, global functioning and disability, and psychopathy, and choose the right scale for a question. Weightage. 40 of the 148 questions mapped in this book (27.0%) test this chapter, 11 of them from real past papers. 2 of its 9 sections are High yield. In 1935 a young psychologist named Ward Campbell Halstead (1908 to 1968, the year most reference works give; the Library of Congress record has 1969) arrived at the University of Chicago as a National Research Fellow, fresh from a doctorate at Northwestern University. He set out to study people whose brains had been injured, many of them patients of the university's neurosurgeons, among them people who had lost part of a frontal lobe in an operation to remove a tumour. Halstead's laboratory for this work was one of the first of its kind in North America, and he began in an unusual way. Before he built a single test, he spent many hours watching and talking with brain-injured people as they went about the ordinary business of their lives, and he became convinced that the intelligence tests of the day missed much of what such people had lost: a person could lose a large part of the frontal lobes in surgery, he pointed out, without a large fall in IQ. Whatever these people had lost, the IQ test was not measuring it. Halstead called the missing quality biological intelligence , the adaptive abilities that depend directly on the health of the brain, as distinct from the school-taught knowledge that intelligence tests sample so well. He built tasks to capture it, gave them to patients and to healthy people, and in 1947 published the results in Brain and Intelligence: A Quantitative Study of the Frontal Lobes , where a factor analysis of his tests yielded four factors that together made up biological intelligence. His most important student was Ralph M. Reitan (1922 to 2014), who met Halstead in 1945, while working as a psychologist with brain-injured soldiers at an army hospital in Illinois. Halstead encouraged him to apply to graduate school and took him into the laboratory as a research assistant; it was there that Reitan learned how to test, and he completed his doctorate at Chicago in 1950. In 1951 he moved to the Indiana University Medical Center in Indianapolis and founded a neuropsychology laboratory of his own. Its battery of tests took one to one and a half days to give, and by the beginning of 1959 the laboratory had tested about 2,000 patients. In 1955, in the Archives of Neurology and Psychiatry , Reitan reported the study that made Halstead's tests famous. He compared 50 patients with brain damage and 50 people with no evidence of it, matched in pairs for race ("colour", in the language of the day), sex, age and education, so that both groups averaged about 32 years of age and about 11.6 years of schooling. On Halstead's summary score, the Impairment Index, not one of the brain-damaged patients did better than his or her matched partner, and at the best cut-off the index misclassified only 4 per cent of the patients and 14 per cent of the controls. Not every test passed: two measures based on Halstead's flicker-fusion test did not separate the groups to a significant degree, and the flicker test was later dropped from the battery. Reitan became best known for something more daring. At Halstead's suggestion he made a habit of interpreting test results blind : from the scores alone, without seeing the patient or knowing the medical findings, he wrote down whether the brain was damaged, on which side, roughly where, and what kind of process was likely to be at work. Only then did he compare his conclusions with what the neurologists, the neurosurgeons and the pathologists had found, and study his mistakes. A report his laboratory issued in January 1959 prints a series of such cases, each in the same order: the scores, Reitan's report signed with his initials, a comment on the reasoning, and finally the neurological and neurosurgical summary. For one 42-year-old man he wrote that the left hemisphere was working worse than the right and that the pattern fitted a fairly large tumour lying mainly in the left temporal lobe and reaching forward towards the frontal lobe; his strongest clue was the man's difficulty with language. The surgeons who operated found a fast-growing tumour, a glioblastoma, in the left frontal and temporal region. The report printed the misses too. For a 57-year-old man Reitan placed the trouble in the right temporal region but judged it slow or static, perhaps the after-effects of an old head injury; the man had a tumour of an unusually slow-growing kind, and the laboratory's comment admitted that it could not change its conclusion after the fact and must accept the case "as an important illustration of the limitations of our procedures". Within twenty years of that report, the computerised tomography (CT) scanner, and later magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), could show a tumour or a stroke directly, and nobody now needs a psychologist to say on which side of the head a lesion lies. Yet neuropsychological testing did not disappear; it grew. A scan shows the brain's structure, but it cannot show what a person can still remember, plan, say or do, and those are the questions that patients, families, doctors and courts actually ask. Hold on to Halstead's laboratory and Reitan's blind reports, because they contain this chapter's central lesson: behaviour on carefully chosen tasks can tell you a surprising amount about the brain. The chapter asks which tasks, how they are scored, and against what standard. It then turns to the clinician's rating scales, which answer a different kind of question: not "where is the damage?" but "how ill is this person, and are they getting better?" Remember Halstead and Reitan; you will return to them at the end of the chapter. 11.1 What Neuropsychological Assessment Is: Questions, Domains, Approaches and Premorbid Ability Medium yield · 4 Qs Suppose a neurologist sends you a patient with a one-line note: "Kindly do a neuropsychological assessment." What exactly are you being asked to do? Not to give a test, because no single test answers anything useful about a brain. A neuropsychological assessment is an inquiry. It starts from a question, samples a set of abilities chosen to answer it, reads the resulting scores by rules that Halstead's successors worked out over decades, and judges them against a standard: either what healthy people of the same age and background achieve, or what this particular person could do before the illness began. This section takes those pieces in turn. It begins with what neuropsychology is and what an assessment is for, moves to the abilities that are tested and the history of how the field learned to test them, sets out the three ways of building an assessment and Reitan's four ways of reading one, and then turns to the hardest question of all: how much has this person lost, when nobody tested them before they fell ill? It ends with two questions that every report must face, whether the person was giving their best effort and whether "organic or functional?" is still the right thing to ask, and then walks one patient from the referral note to the final report. Brain, behaviour and the referral question Neuropsychology is the study of the relationship between the brain and behaviour. "Behaviour" here has its broadest meaning: remembering, speaking, perceiving, planning, moving and feeling all count, because all of them depend on the brain. Clinical neuropsychology applies this knowledge to people whose brains have been affected by injury or disease (Book 2, Section 10.9.9 describes the specialty and the settings it works in). Its central tool is the neuropsychological assessment : the systematic measurement of a person's cognitive abilities and behaviour with standardised tests, interpreted together with the history, the clinician's observations and the medical findings, in order to answer a question about how the brain is working and what that means for the person's life. Why should a test of behaviour tell you anything about a brain? Because each ability depends on particular brain systems. Damage to a system lowers the abilities that depend on it and leaves the others alone, so the pattern of strengths and weaknesses carries information that a single score cannot. That was Halstead's and Reitan's wager, and the opening of this chapter shows how far it could be pushed. But a test measures behaviour, and behaviour depends on much more than the brain. A person who is tired, frightened, depressed, half-deaf, short-sighted without her glasses, tested in a language she does not use at home, or hoping to look more impaired than she is will also score badly. Every interpretation therefore weighs the brain against these other explanations, and much of this section is about how that is done. Every assessment begins with a referral question : the question, usually asked by someone else, that the assessment exists to answer. A psychiatrist asks whether an older man's forgetfulness is early dementia or the effect of depression. A neurosurgeon asks which abilities a planned operation might put at risk. A rehabilitation team asks whether a woman who had a head injury in a road accident can go back to running her shop. A school asks why a bright boy with epilepsy cannot keep up in class; a court asks whether a man accused of a crime can follow his own trial. A good referral question names the decision that hangs on the answer. A vague one ("assess cognition") has to be turned into a useful one, usually by a conversation with the person who sent it, because the question decides which tests are given, how long the assessment takes and what the report must say. Figure 11.1 sets out the path from the question to the report; Section 11.1.10 walks one patient along it. 1 The question what decision depends on it? 2 History interview and informant, records 3 Choose tests the domains the question needs 4 Testing standard way; watch the process 5 Scoring against norms and premorbid level 6 Interpreting pattern, history and other findings 7 Report and feedback, recommendations 8 Review retest to measure change next round Throughout: check vision, hearing, mood, effort and medication Figure 11.1 The neuropsychological assessment as a process. Read the top row from left to right and the bottom row from right to left. Notice that testing is only one step of eight: the question at the start decides everything that follows, and the upward arrow labelled "next round" shows that a later retest, compared with this one, can itself answer a new question. The questions that reach a neuropsychologist fall into a handful of families, and between them they define what the assessment is for: Detecting and describing impairment. Is there a cognitive impairment at all, and if so, which abilities are affected, how badly, and which are spared? John Pinel and Steven Barnes, in their biopsychology textbook, point out that testing helps most where brain imaging, the electroencephalogram (EEG) and the neurological examination have proved equivocal, as they often are after a mild head injury or early in a degenerative disease. Differential diagnosis. Which of several conditions best explains what is seen? The classic case is an older person with poor memory and low mood, who may have early dementia, a depression that is impairing concentration (the "pseudodementia" of Book 3, Section 10.11.6), or both. Others are delirium versus dementia (Book 3, Section 10.8.8), one kind of dementia versus another, and the lasting effects of alcohol. Localisation. Which part of the brain is likely to be affected? This was the great purpose of Reitan's era, and the next paragraph explains why it has shrunk. A baseline for measuring change. A first assessment becomes the yardstick for later ones: after surgery, during a course of electroconvulsive therapy, through the slow course of a dementia or a drug trial, or in recovery from a head injury. Because people improve on tests simply by having taken them before (Chapter 3, Section 3.2.3 explains this practice effect), a later score must rise or fall by more than practice and measurement error alone would produce; the reliable change index of Chapter 3, Section 3.7.6 is built for exactly this. Planning rehabilitation and care. A clear map of what is lost and what remains tells the team what to retrain, what to work around with diaries and alarms, and what the family should expect (Book 2, Section 9.9 describes neuropsychological rehabilitation). Capacity and fitness. Can this person consent to treatment, manage money, make a will, drive, return to a demanding job, or follow a trial? The tests do not answer these questions on their own, but they supply much of the evidence on which the people who must answer them rely. Medico-legal and disability work. Claims for compensation after road accidents and injuries at work, and the certification of disability (Section 11.9 and Book 2, Section 9.9.8), depend on a documented, defensible account of what has been lost. Localisation deserves its own word, because it is the purpose that changed most. In the 1950s a neurologist who suspected a tumour had only crude and often unpleasant ways of looking inside the head: X-rays of the skull, the EEG, angiography (X-rays after dye is injected into the arteries of the neck) and pneumoencephalography, in which air was introduced into the spaces of the brain so that they would show on an X-ray. Reitan's 1959 case reports mention both of the last two. Against that background, a battery of tests that could say "left hemisphere, probably temporal, probably a fast-growing lesion" was a genuine diagnostic tool. CT, introduced in the early 1970s, and MRI, which entered hospitals in the 1980s, took most of that job away. Neuropsychological assessment still contributes to localisation where structure and function part company, as when the scan is normal after a mild head injury or in the earliest stage of a degenerative disease, and in planning epilepsy surgery, where the team must know which abilities the tissue to be removed supports. But its main business today is description: not where the damage is, but what it does to the person. Clinical link Capacity is a legal judgement, not a test score. In India the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (Section 4) says that every person, including a person with mental illness, is deemed to have the capacity to make mental healthcare and treatment decisions if he or she has the ability to understand the information relevant to the decision, or to appreciate any reasonably foreseeable consequence of a decision or of not deciding, or to communicate the decision by speech, expression, gesture or any other means (the Act joins the three abilities with "or"). The information must be given in simple language the person understands, or in sign language or visual aids, and a decision that others perceive as inappropriate or wrong does not, by itself, mean that the person lacks capacity. A neuropsychologist's findings on comprehension, memory, reasoning and judgement are evidence for each of those abilities, so a good report says what the person can and cannot understand, retain and weigh, in words a doctor or magistrate can use. Exam trap Neuropsychological assessment measures how the brain is working through behaviour: its purposes are detection and description of impairment, differential diagnosis, localisation, a baseline for change, rehabilitation planning, capacity and medico-legal work. It is not personality assessment, vocational guidance, projective testing or the measurement of attachment, which is why "neuropsychological assessment" is the answer whenever a paper asks what the Halstead-Reitan battery is for (Section 11.2). And if an item asks for the main purpose today , prefer describing the pattern of deficits and its consequences over localisation, which imaging now does better. What is tested: the domains of cognition A neuropsychologist does not test "the brain" or "intelligence" in general. The abilities that brain damage can impair are grouped into cognitive domains : families of related abilities that can be lost independently of one another and can therefore be tested separately. A stroke can destroy speech and leave memory intact; a head injury can leave a man able to remember everything and unable to plan his day. The usual list runs from the most basic abilities to the most complex, and the order matters, because a person who fails an early item on the list cannot be fairly tested on the later ones (Book 2, Section 2.6.1 makes the same point about the bedside examination). Orientation and level of consciousness come first. Is the person awake and alert, and does she know who she is, where she is and what the date is? Orientation is the person's awareness of time, place and person. A drowsy or disoriented patient will fail every later test for that reason alone, so these are checked before anything else (Book 2, Section 2.6.2 describes the levels of consciousness, and Section 11.7 the Glasgow Coma Scale that grades them). Attention and concentration come next: the ability to take in a certain amount at once (attention span), to keep the mind on a task over time (sustained attention, or vigilance), to pick out what matters and ignore the rest (selective attention) and to share attention between two tasks (divided attention). Repeating strings of digits, crossing out every target letter on a page and pressing a key whenever a target appears on a screen are typical tasks (Sections 11.4 and 11.6). Closely tied to attention is processing speed , the speed with which a person carries out simple mental work, such as copying symbols that match digits against the clock. Slowing is one of the commonest effects of almost any brain disorder, but it is also produced by ageing, depression and sedative drugs, so it is sensitive without being specific. Memory is the domain most often complained of. The neuropsychologist separates learning new material from keeping it over a delay and from getting it back out, verbal material from visual, free recall from recognition, and new learning from memory for the remote past (Section 11.4, and the PGI Memory Scale in Section 11.3). Language covers naming objects, the fluency and grammar of speech, understanding what is said, repeating, reading and writing (Section 11.6 gives the tests; the aphasias themselves are in Book 3, Section 10.8.3). Visuospatial skill is the perception of shape, position, distance and direction, and constructional ability is the capacity to put parts together into a whole, as in copying a drawing or building a pattern from blocks (Section 11.5, and block design in Chapter 6). Executive functions are the higher-order control processes that plan, start, stop, switch, monitor and adjust behaviour towards a goal, together with abstract reasoning and the formation of concepts; they depend especially on the frontal lobes and their connections, and they are the abilities that most often decide whether a person can live independently (Section 11.6). Motor and sensory function covers the speed, strength and dexterity of each hand and the perception of touch on each side of the body, which matter less for their own sake than for what a difference between the two sides reveals (Section 11.1.5 below, and Sections 11.2 and 11.5). Two further things are always estimated, though they are not domains of the same kind. One is general intellectual ability, now and before the illness, because every other score is judged against it (Chapter 6 teaches the intelligence tests, and Section 11.1.7 below the estimation of the earlier level). The other is the context: the person's mood, behaviour and effort. Depression and anxiety lower scores on attention, speed and memory, which is why neuropsychologists routinely add a mood inventory such as the Beck Depression Inventory to their tests (Section 11.8), and an assessment that ignored whether the person was trying would be worthless (Section 11.1.9). If you have read Book 3, you will recognise the same territory in a different arrangement: DSM-5-TR builds its neurocognitive disorders on six domains, complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor function and social cognition (Book 3, Section 10.8.2). "Perceptual-motor" gathers the visuospatial and constructional abilities, and social cognition , the ability to recognise other people's emotions and infer their intentions, is the newest member of either list. Table 11.1 is the map of the whole chapter: each domain, what it means, the tests you will meet for it and where they are taught. Table 11.1 The domains of a neuropsychological assessment and the tests taught in this chapter. Domain What it means Typical tests Taught in Orientation and consciousness Alertness; knowing person, place and time Glasgow Coma Scale; orientation items of the brief screens 11.7 Attention and concentration Span, sustained, selective and divided attention Digit span forward; cancellation tasks; Continuous Performance Test 11.4, 11.6 Processing speed Speed of simple mental work Digit symbol substitution; Trail Making Part A; reaction time tasks 11.6, Chapter 6 Memory Learning, keeping and retrieving, verbal and visual Wechsler Memory Scale; Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test; PGI Memory Scale 11.4, 11.3 Language Naming, fluency, comprehension, repetition, reading, writing Boston Naming Test; Token Test; verbal fluency; aphasia batteries 11.6 Visuospatial and constructional Perceiving space and form; copying and assembling Bender-Gestalt; Judgment of Line Orientation; complex figure copy 11.5 Executive functions Planning, switching, inhibition, abstraction, monitoring Wisconsin Card Sorting Test; Trail Making Part B; Stroop; Tower of London 11.6 Motor and sensory Speed, strength and touch on each side of the body Finger Tapping; grip strength; Tactual Performance Test; Finger Localization 11.2, 11.5 General and premorbid ability Intellectual level now, and before the illness Wechsler intelligence scales; reading tests such as the NART Chapter 6, 11.1.7 Global screening A quick overview of several domains MMSE; MoCA; Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination III 11.7 Context: mood and effort What else may be lowering the scores Depression and anxiety scales; performance validity tests 11.8, 11.1.9 Notice what every entry in the table has in common. Each is an ability : something a person can do well or badly, quickly or slowly, and that depends on the working of particular brain systems. That is the test for whether something can be a neuropsychological domain. An opinion fails it at once. What a person believes about politics, prefers in music or thinks of her employer has no right answer and no speed, and it is measured, when it is measured at all, by the attitude and opinion scales of Chapter 8. The same is true of a person's "reaction" in the everyday sense of how she feels about something. Neither is a domain, and no neuropsychological test is designed to assess either. Exam trap Asked which of language, memory, executive functioning and opinion is not assessed by neuropsychological tests (RML 2025), answer opinion: an attitude, not a brain-dependent ability. Asked which set of domains neuropsychological tests assess, choose language, memory and executive functioning ; every other option in that RML 2025 item contains "opinion" or "reaction", neither of which is a domain. One caution for next year's paper: reaction time is measured, as an index of processing speed and attention, so do not reject an option that says "reaction time" or "processing speed" on the strength of this item. From the localisers to the process approach: a short history The idea that a careful study of what a patient can and cannot do reveals where the brain is damaged is older than psychology's tests. In 1861 the French physician Paul Broca (1824 to 1880) showed at autopsy that a patient who had lost almost all speech had damage in the left inferior frontal region, and in 1874 the German neurologist Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) described a different loss, of the understanding of speech, after damage further back in the left temporal lobe (Book 1, Section 8.9.6 tells both stories). These localisers established the principle on which all of neuropsychology rests, the localisation of function : particular abilities depend on particular parts of the brain. What they could not supply was a way of measuring those abilities in a living patient, reliably, against a standard. A first challenge to simple localisation came from Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965), a German neurologist who studied soldiers with brain wounds after the First World War. Goldstein argued that brain damage changes the whole person's way of meeting the world, not just one isolated skill. His patients had lost what he called the abstract attitude , the ability to think about what is merely possible, to group things by a category, to shift from one point of view to another and to grasp what is common to different things, and were left with the concrete attitude , bound to the immediate, visible situation. To take an invented illustration of the kind of loss he described: such a patient may drink from a glass of water perfectly well when he is thirsty, yet be unable to pretend to drink from an empty glass when asked to, because the pretence requires him to step outside the concrete situation. The sorting tests he built with Martin Scheerer to assess this loss are taught in Section 11.6. For several decades after the 1930s, the question that psychiatrists put to clinical psychologists was blunt: is this patient "organic" (suffering from a disease of the brain) or "functional" (suffering from a psychiatric illness with no visible brain disease)? The psychologist answered with a single test of organicity , the supposed general effect of brain damage, such as the copying test of Lauretta Bender (1938) or the design-memory test of Arthur Benton (1946), both taught in Sections 11.5 and 11.4. Pinel and Barnes call this the single-test approach , and they explain why it failed: no single test could be sensitive to all the varied effects that brain damage can have, because brain damage is not one thing. A stroke in the right parietal lobe and a tumour in the left frontal lobe produce entirely different pictures, and a test that catches one may miss the other. The failure of single tests produced the batteries. Halstead and Reitan's battery (the opening of this chapter, and Section 11.2) gave every patient the same broad set of tests, scored against cut-offs, and by the 1960s this standardised-battery approach dominated North American neuropsychology. Pinel and Barnes add its limitation: such batteries separate neurological patients from healthy people well, but separate neurological patients from psychiatric patients much less well. In Moscow, meanwhile, Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977) had developed a very different method, much of it from his work with soldiers wounded in the head during the Second World War (you met one of his patients, Zasetsky, in Book 2, Chapter 9). Luria saw every complex act, writing a word for example, as a functional system : a chain of links, each supported by a different region of the brain, all of which must work for the act to succeed. A lesion breaks one link, and the act then fails in a characteristic way that depends on which link is broken. So Luria did not count right answers against norms. He set the patient a task, watched exactly how it went wrong, changed the task to test his guess, and reasoned from the kind of failure to the broken link, a method called syndrome analysis . He also grouped the brain into three functional units: one for regulating arousal and waking (the brainstem and its connections), one for receiving, analysing and storing information (the rear of the cortex: occipital, temporal and parietal lobes), and one for programming, regulating and checking activity (the frontal lobes). His methods appear in Higher Cortical Functions in Man (English edition 1966) and The Working Brain (1973), and their later standardisation as the Luria-Nebraska battery is described in Section 11.2. Pinel and Barnes credit Luria and his Soviet colleagues with the customised, flexible approach that spread to American research centres from the 1960s and now predominates in both the laboratory and the clinic. Two American women gave the modern field its textbook and its method. Muriel Deutsch Lezak (1927 to 2021) published Neuropsychological Assessment in 1976, a book that, in its later editions written with colleagues, is still the standard reference of the field; it taught a generation to treat the assessment as the testing of hypotheses about a particular patient rather than the administration of a fixed list. Edith Kaplan (1924 to 2009), working at the Boston Veterans Administration Hospital, developed the Boston process approach , which shares Luria's interest in how a patient fails but builds it into standardised, scorable tests (Section 11.1.4). Exam trap Match the person to the idea. Broca (1861) and Wernicke (1874): localisation of language. Goldstein : abstract versus concrete attitude, and sorting tests with Scheerer. Halstead : biological intelligence (1947). Reitan : validated and extended Halstead's battery, blind interpretation, the four methods of inference. Luria : functional systems, three functional units, qualitative syndrome analysis. Lezak : the textbook Neuropsychological Assessment (1976). Kaplan : the Boston process approach. A favourite confusion is to credit the process approach to Luria: Luria's method was qualitative and Soviet; the process approach is Kaplan's, American, and built into standardised tests. Three ways to build an assessment: fixed, flexible and process The history leaves three ways of building an assessment, and every neuropsychologist works with some mixture of them. They differ in a simple question: who decides which tests the patient receives, and what is recorded about the answers? In the fixed battery approach the answer is the battery itself. Every patient receives the same comprehensive set of tests, in the same way, scored against norms or cut-offs, often with a summary index such as Halstead's Impairment Index. The Halstead-Reitan and Luria-Nebraska batteries are the two classic fixed batteries (Section 11.2). The strengths are real. Nothing is missed because the examiner did not think to look for it; every patient's record can be compared with every other's, and with the same patient's record a year later; the large bodies of data collected with the same tests make research possible; and a fixed procedure is easy to defend in court, because nobody can say that the examiner chose tests to suit a conclusion. The weaknesses are equally plain. A full fixed battery takes many hours (Reitan's own battery took a day or more), it tires and sometimes distresses patients, it includes tests that the referral question does not need, and it may lack the tests that the question does need. In the flexible battery approach, also called the hypothesis-testing approach , the clinician decides. A core set of tests is given to every patient to survey the main domains, and further tests are then chosen to fit the referral question and the first results. If the core tests show a memory problem, the clinician adds tests that can tell whether the trouble lies in learning, in keeping or in retrieving; if they show slowness and poor switching, tests of executive function follow. This is what Pinel and Barnes call the customised-test-battery approach, and it is how most clinicians now work; the NIMHANS battery, for example, is usually used as a set of domain-based tests from which the clinician selects (Section 11.3). It is efficient and tailored, and it can use the newest tests built on modern theories of memory and attention. But it depends heavily on the clinician's skill, it makes patients harder to compare with one another because each has had a different set of tests, and it carries a quiet danger: a clinician who forms a hypothesis early may choose only the tests likely to confirm it. The process approach of Edith Kaplan and her Boston colleagues adds a third question: not only whether the patient got the answer right, but how he or she got there. The examiner records the order in which a drawing was made, the kinds of errors, the strategies used, the time taken over each item and the self-corrections, and may add steps such as offering a multiple-choice version of an item that the patient failed to answer freely, to see whether the knowledge is there but cannot be retrieved. Kaplan's group built this thinking into standardised tests, among them the WAIS-R as a Neuropsychological Instrument (1991), the California Verbal Learning Test (Section 11.4) and the Delis-Kaplan Executive Function System (2001). A worked example shows why "how" matters. Imagine two invented patients who each copy the same complex line drawing and each earn exactly the same score, say 20 out of a possible 36. The first drew it piece by piece, getting many small details right but losing the overall shape, so that the parts never quite fitted together; this fragmented, piecemeal style is common after damage to the right hemisphere. The second drew the outline correctly at once but left out many of the internal details; a simplified copy with an intact overall shape is more typical of damage to the left hemisphere. The score says the two patients are equal. The process says they have different problems, different likely lesions and different needs in rehabilitation. The price of such richness is that observations of process are harder to score reliably and to norm than a simple total, and they take longer. In practice the three approaches blend: most clinicians give a flexible selection of standardised tests and watch the process as they go. Table 11.2 compares them. Do not be thrown by the irony that the Luria-Nebraska is a fixed , standardised battery although Luria's own method was flexible and qualitative: Charles Golden and his colleagues standardised Luria's tasks, as Section 11.2 explains. And remember the one-sentence summary of the process approach: two patients with the same score may have failed for different reasons. Reading a profile: Reitan's four methods of inference Once the scores are in, how does a clinician reason from them to the brain? Reitan's answer, refined over decades of blind interpretation, was that no single kind of evidence is enough. He taught four methods of inference , each asking a different question of the same record, and insisted that they be used together, because each catches mistakes that the others make. 1. Level of performance. The first question is simply whether each score is worse than it should be. The level of performance method compares a score with a cut-off or with norms for healthy people. It is the most obvious method and the bluntest. Reitan's own 1955 data show why. With a cut-off at 51 or more errors, Halstead's Category Test (Section 11.2) misclassified 16 per cent of the brain-damaged patients and 18 per cent of the controls, far worse than the Impairment Index, which pooled the levels of many tests. Low scores have many causes besides brain damage, among them little schooling, depression, old age and poor effort, and some people with brain damage still score within normal limits on any one test. 2. Pattern of performance. The second question is how the scores relate to one another. The pattern of performance method looks at the shape of the profile: which abilities are relatively low and which relatively high, compared with the person's own other scores. A pattern can point where a level cannot. Fatigue, low education or a general illness tends to lower everything a little; a lesion tends to lower some abilities much more than others. Reitan's laboratory listed many such patterns as working hypotheses; one was that an outstandingly low score on the block-design subtest of the Wechsler scale, against otherwise even scores, suggested damage in the right parietal region. 3. Pathognomonic signs. The third question is whether the record contains any error that healthy people almost never make. A pathognomonic sign is a finding so rarely seen without the condition that its presence alone is strong evidence for it. Reitan's chief example was dysphasia, a disturbance of language: his laboratory stated that dysphasic symptoms, when present, provide a valid basis for inferring brain damage, and in his blind reports a definite dysphasia took precedence over every other indicator in placing a lesion in the left hemisphere. Others are a constructional dyspraxia , the inability to copy even a simple shape, and sensory suppression , in which a person feels a touch on either hand alone but, when both hands are touched at the same moment, reports only one. The method has a built-in asymmetry that you must remember: the presence of a sign is strong evidence, but its absence proves very little, and Reitan's own case reports include a mislocalised lesion that he blamed on leaning too heavily on a sign that was missing. 4. Right-left comparisons. The fourth question uses a fact of anatomy: each cerebral hemisphere controls movement on, and receives touch from, the opposite side of the body. A right-left comparison sets the two sides of the body against each other on the same task: tapping speed, grip strength, the time to complete a form board blindfolded, the recognition of touches and of numbers traced on the fingertips. Because each person serves as his own control, the comparison works even when norms are doubtful. A common rule of thumb in Reitan's tradition is that the preferred hand taps about 10 per cent faster than the other; a much larger difference, or a reversal, points to the hemisphere opposite the weaker side. Now push one invented record through all four methods, as Reitan might have done with nothing but the scores in front of him. Omesh is a 41-year-old right-handed draughtsman with 14 years of education, referred after two seizures. His invented results are these. Level. Omesh makes 78 errors on the Category Test, well past the 1955 cut-off of 51 or more, and his Impairment Index is 0.7 (about seven of every ten core scores in the impaired range; Section 11.2 explains the index). Conclusion: something is wrong, but the level says nothing about where. Pattern. His vocabulary and verbal reasoning scores are in the high average range, as his education would predict, but his scores for copying drawings and building block patterns are far below the rest. A general cause such as fatigue or low schooling would have pulled everything down; this pattern singles out visuospatial and constructional abilities, which points towards the right hemisphere, especially its rear part. Pathognomonic signs. He names, repeats, reads and writes without error, so there is no dysphasia (which, remember, proves little). But his copy of a simple geometric shape is broken and lopsided, with sides that fail to meet, a constructional dyspraxia; and when both hands are touched at once he repeatedly reports only the right, although he feels single touches on the left hand perfectly well, a suppression on the left side. Right-left comparison. He taps 50 times in 10 seconds with his right hand and 34 times with his left. By the 10 per cent rule the left hand should manage about 50 − (10 per cent of 50) = 50 − 5 = 45 taps, so it is 45 − 34 = 11 taps short, and 11 ÷ 45 = 0.244, about 24 per cent below expectation. On the form board he takes 7.5 minutes with his right hand and then 9.0 minutes with his left. Because the left hand works second, on the same board, it normally benefits from the practice and finishes faster; Omesh's left hand was 1.5 minutes slower instead. The level says the brain is not working normally; the pattern, the signs and the right-left comparisons all point to the right hemisphere; and the constructional dyspraxia and the tactile suppression suggest that the rear part of it, around the parietal lobe, is most affected. In right-left comparisons the brain is contralateral : a slow or insensitive left hand implicates the right hemisphere. And "pathognomonic" means a sign whose presence nearly settles the matter, which is why its absence settles nothing. Compared with whom? Normative and individual standards A score means nothing on its own. Thirty-four taps, 78 errors or a memory score of 100 become informative only when they are compared with something, and Lezak's textbook names the two standards that a neuropsychologist can use. The normative comparison standard compares the person with a large group of healthy people of the same age, and often of the same education and sex: the norms of Chapter 5. This is a nomothetic comparison, from the Greek for "law-giving", the study of what holds for people in general; the philosopher Wilhelm Windelband (1848 to 1915) coined the pair of terms in 1894, and Gordon Allport (1897 to 1967) brought them into psychology in 1937. The individual comparison standard compares the person's present performance with his or her own earlier level of ability, the premorbid level ("before the illness"). This is an idiographic comparison, the study of the individual case. A third, related idea you have already used: comparing a person's scores with one another, as the pattern method did for Omesh, is an ipsative comparison , from the Latin ipse , "self". Which standard is right? It depends on the ability. Some abilities are shared by almost every healthy adult, whatever his or her intelligence or schooling: knowing the year, naming a pen, copying a simple shape, recognising a familiar face. For these the normative standard is enough, because failure is abnormal in anyone. Other abilities vary widely among healthy people, among them vocabulary, reasoning, arithmetic and the amount that can be learned from one hearing of a list. For these, an average score can mean very different things in different people. Ujwala , an invented example, shows the difference. She is a 54-year-old chartered accountant in Pune, a partner in her firm, who has started to make mistakes at work and to forget what clients told her the week before. On a memory test her standard score is 100, exactly the average for women of her age (standard scores with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 are explained in Chapter 5). By the normative standard she is normal. But everything known about her past (Section 11.1.7 shows how it is estimated) places her premorbid level at about 117. By the individual standard she has lost about 17 points, more than one standard deviation, and for a person of her ability an average memory is a decline. Figure 11.3 draws the two verdicts side by side. The error can run the other way as well: a man with four years of schooling may score below the average of norms built on better-educated people without having lost anything at all, which is why Indian batteries are normed separately by education (Section 11.3). Whether a gap of 17 points is larger than measurement error alone would produce is a question for the standard error of the difference (Chapter 3, Section 3.7.6).
