Both rows use the scale at the bottom. Against the norms for her age Ujwala's memory score of 100 sits in the middle of the average range; against her own estimated premorbid level of about 117 it is a fall of 17 points, more than one standard deviation. In practice a good report uses both standards and says which it is using. The normative standard protects against calling ordinary scores abnormal; the individual standard protects against missing a real loss in an able person. The individual standard has one obvious difficulty: it needs an estimate of a level that nobody measured. That difficulty is the subject of the next subsection. Exam trap An RML 2025 item asks what the " ideometric approach " in neuropsychological assessment primarily focuses on. The term is not standard: you will not find it in Lezak or the other major textbooks, and it is probably a garbling of idiographic . The item uses it for the individual comparison standard, so answer (a) evaluating the patient's premorbid functioning and current status . Option (b), quantitative analysis of standardised test scores, is psychometric scoring, which every approach uses and which is not a standard of comparison. Option (c), comparison with normative population data, is the normative (nomothetic) standard, the opposite of what is asked. Option (d), emotional and psychological well-being, is mood assessment (Section 11.8), not a way of judging cognitive scores. Estimating premorbid ability: demographics, best performance, hold tests and reading Very few people are given a neuropsychological assessment before they fall ill. Occasionally there is a record of the earlier level: school marks, board examination results, a university degree, a selection test taken for a job or for the armed forces, or an assessment done years before for some other reason. When such records exist they are gold, though they rarely measure the same abilities as today's tests. Most of the time the earlier level has to be estimated, and over the past eighty years neuropsychologists have devised four main families of methods. Each has a typical way of going wrong, so a careful clinician uses more than one and looks for agreement. Premorbid ability is the level of intellectual and cognitive ability a person had before the onset of the illness or injury, and estimating it is what makes the individual comparison standard possible. Demographic estimates. The simplest method uses what is known about the person's life. Years of education and the kind of work a person did are strongly related to measured intelligence, so an estimate can be made from them, either informally ("a chartered accountant who qualified at the first attempt was very probably of high average ability or above") or with a regression equation. A widely used equation of this kind for American adults was published by Barona, Reynolds and Chastain in 1984 for the WAIS-R; it combines age, sex, race, education, occupation and region of residence. The great advantage of a demographic estimate is that illness cannot touch it: a stroke does not change how many years a person spent in school. Its weaknesses follow from its nature. Equations of this kind pull every estimate towards the middle of the range, so they underestimate the most able people and overestimate the least able; they describe what is typical of a group, not what was true of this person; and they are built on particular populations, so an equation made in the United States says little about a person educated in a Kannada-medium village school. For Ujwala, with a commerce degree and the chartered accountancy qualification (about 17 years of education in all) and a career as a partner in a firm, an informal demographic estimate would be about 115. The best-performance method. Lezak described a second method: take the person's best current scores as the best guide to the earlier level. The reasoning is that brain damage can lower an ability but almost never raises one, so the highest scores in the record are the ones least affected. Ujwala's best score is on vocabulary, a scaled score of 15. Scaled scores have a mean of 10 and a standard deviation of 3 (Chapter 6), so 15 lies (15 − 10) ÷ 3 = 5 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.67 standard deviations above the mean, which on the familiar scale with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 is 100 + (1.67 × 15) ≈ 100 + 25 = 125. The method's weakness is that it overestimates. Healthy people are not equally good at everything: their scores scatter, and anyone's single best score is, by definition, the luckiest point in the record. A best-performance estimate of 125 is probably a little too high for Ujwala, and the method is most useful as an upper limit. Hold and don't-hold tests. The third method belongs to David Wechsler (1896 to 1981), and it is the one examiners ask about by name. Wechsler noticed, while building the age norms of his Wechsler-Bellevue scale (Book 1, Section 9.3.2), that some abilities decline much more slowly with age than others. Knowledge of general information and of word meanings holds up well; the ability to copy symbols quickly against the clock, or to repeat long strings of digits, falls away much faster. He reasoned that the abilities that resist ageing might also be the ones that resist the "deteriorative process" of brain disease and prolonged mental illness, so that a person's scores on them would preserve his earlier level, and that a comparison of the two kinds of subtest would therefore show how much he had lost. Wechsler set out this differential-test-score method in the third edition of The Measurement of Adult Intelligence (1944). The subtests that resist decline he called hold tests ; those that decline he called don't-hold tests . Taking care to balance verbal and performance subtests in each group, he listed Information, Comprehension, Object Assembly, Picture Completion and Vocabulary as hold tests, and Digit Span, Arithmetic, Digit Symbol, Block Design and Similarities as don't-hold tests. When he revised the method for the WAIS in The Measurement and Appraisal of Adult Intelligence (1958), the four hold tests were Vocabulary, Information, Object Assembly and Picture Completion, and the four don't-hold tests Digit Span, Similarities, Digit Symbol and Block Design: these are the lists to learn. Remember: Wechsler's deterioration index Deterioration index = (Hold − Don't Hold) ÷ Hold , usually multiplied by 100 to give a percentage loss. Hold is the sum of the scaled scores on the hold tests (Vocabulary, Information, Object Assembly, Picture Completion) and Don't Hold the sum on the don't-hold tests (Digit Span, Similarities, Digit Symbol, Block Design). Wechsler also gave the ratio form, Don't Hold ÷ Hold × 100, which in 1944 he called the deterioration quotient ; the two carry the same information, because the quotient is simply 100 minus the percentage loss. In the 1958 WAIS book he gave the name deterioration quotient to the percentage-loss formula itself, and most textbooks now use the two names for the same thing. In 1944 he suggested that a loss more than 10 per cent greater than the normal loss for the person's age indicates possible deterioration, and more than 20 per cent greater definite deterioration. For the WAIS, whose age-corrected scores already allow for normal ageing, he judged a loss of more than about 15 to 20 per cent significant. Work it through for Ujwala, with invented scaled scores that are already corrected for her age (the WAIS version of the method works with age-corrected scores, so the normal decline with age has been allowed for before the comparison is made). Her hold tests: Vocabulary 15, Information 14, Picture Completion 13 and Object Assembly 12, so Hold = 15 + 14 + 13 + 12 = 54. Her don't-hold tests: Digit Span 10, Similarities 12, Digit Symbol 8 and Block Design 9, so Don't Hold = 10 + 12 + 8 + 9 = 39. Then: Deterioration index = (54 − 39) ÷ 54 = 15 ÷ 54 = 0.2778, which multiplied by 100 is 27.8 per cent (rounded to one decimal place). The quotient form gives 39 ÷ 54 × 100 = 72.2, the same result seen from the other side (100 − 27.8 = 72.2). In plain words: Ujwala's scores on the abilities that usually resist illness are about 28 per cent higher than her scores on the abilities that usually give way, a gap beyond Wechsler's 20 per cent mark for definite deterioration. Taken alone, the index would say that she has lost a good deal of her former efficiency. Why, then, is the method now mostly of historical interest? Because both of its assumptions are shaky. The hold tests are not immune: vocabulary and general information do fall as a dementia advances, so the index underestimates loss in exactly the patients who have lost most. And the don't-hold tests fall for many reasons besides brain disease: anxiety, depression, slowness, fatigue, poor effort and little schooling all lower digit span, speeded coding and block design. Reitan tested the method against his own and found that Halstead's Impairment Index separated brain-damaged patients from controls far better than any Wechsler measure, the hold tests, the don't-hold tests and Wechsler's deterioration ratio included; and in 1984 Dano Leli and Susan Filskov, opening a study in the Journal of Clinical Psychology , summed up four decades of work: none of the deterioration formulas and ratios of that era, Wechsler's 1958 index included, had been shown empirically to be useful. What the index really measures is a fall in mental efficiency from any cause. That is not a defect for the purpose Wechsler intended: he wrote that the method would be most useful in organic brain cases but could also be applied in schizophrenia, and to appraise the effects of shock treatment, which is why the examiners' phrasing, the impact of brain or psychiatric illness on cognitive and intellectual ability, is a fair description of it. Reading tests: the National Adult Reading Test. The fourth method is the most successful, and it comes from a clever observation about reading. English is full of irregular words , words whose pronunciation cannot be worked out from their spelling by the ordinary rules: "yacht" and "colonel" are the examples Book 1 uses (Section 8.9.6) to explain the dual-route model of reading, and a reader can only say them correctly if he already knows them as whole words. So the ability to read irregular words aloud is really a test of vocabulary, built up over a lifetime of reading and closely related to general intelligence. Better still, it is an old, overlearned skill that requires no new learning, no speed and almost no reasoning, so it survives the early stages of a dementia when memory and reasoning are already failing. Key study: Nelson and O'Connell and the reading test that dementia spares (1978) The question. The British psychologist Hazel E. Nelson had shown with her colleague McKenna in 1975 that current reading ability was useful in assessing dementia. Could a reading test be designed specifically to estimate the intelligence a patient had before the dementia began? The method. With her colleague O'Connell she built a new test of 50 words chosen to assess familiarity with words rather than the ability to decode them phonetically: each word was irregular enough that intelligent guesswork alone would not produce the right pronunciation. They gave it to patients with cortical atrophy (shrinkage of the brain's outer layer, as in dementia) and to a control group. The result. The test predicted intelligence more accurately than the best word-reading list then available, the Schonell Graded Word Reading Test, and the patients' reading of the words did not seem to be significantly affected by the dementing process. The conclusion. The reading score could provide an accurate estimate of premorbid intelligence in such patients ( Cortex , 1978, where it was called the New Adult Reading Test). The sequel. Nelson's manual of 1982 renamed it the National Adult Reading Test (NART), and it became one of the most widely used premorbid estimates and the model for later reading tests. The NART is scored by counting the words read wrongly, and the error count is turned into an estimate with a regression equation. Nelson's 1982 equation for the Full Scale IQ of the original WAIS is: Predicted Full Scale IQ = 127.7 − (0.826 × number of errors) Here 127.7 is the IQ predicted for a person who makes no errors, and 0.826 is the number of IQ points the estimate falls for each word read wrongly. Suppose, in an invented exercise, that Ujwala reads aloud a list of 50 irregular English words and makes 13 errors. Then 0.826 × 13 = 10.738, and 127.7 − 10.738 = 116.962, which rounds to an estimated premorbid IQ of 117. Like any regression estimate it is a band rather than a point: the published standard error of estimate for this equation is between 7 and 8 IQ points, so the honest statement is "about 117, give or take 7 or 8 points". (The arithmetic is real but the application is not: Nelson's equation was built on a sample of British adults tested with the original WAIS, and it would need fresh validation before it could be trusted for an Indian accountant.) The reading method has clear limits. It assumes that the person is fluent in the language of the test; it is invalid in a person who is dyslexic, aphasic or cannot see the words; and once a dementia is moderate or severe, reading declines too, so the estimate falls with it. It also shares the tendency of all regression estimates to pull extreme people towards the middle. Successors include the revised NART of Nelson and Willison (1991), North American versions, and the Wechsler Test of Adult Reading (2001) and Test of Premorbid Functioning (2009), which were normed together with the Wechsler scales so that reading can predict them directly. Many clinicians now combine a reading score with demographic information in a single equation, getting the stability of the one and the individuality of the other. For Ujwala the methods agree well: about 115 from her history, about 117 from reading, 125 as an upper limit from her best score, and a deterioration index pointing to a substantial fall in efficiency. A clinician would report her premorbid level as "high average, about 117", the figure used in Figure 11.3. Table 11.4 sets the methods side by side. An English irregular-word test assumes a fluency in English that many Indian adults do not have, and it cannot simply be translated: Indian scripts such as Kannada and Devanagari are written in aksharas that are read much more regularly than English spelling (Book 1, Section 8.9.6), so they offer few "irregular words" to test. Years of schooling also mean very different things in different schools, and American demographic equations do not transfer. Indian clinicians therefore lean on norms stratified by age and education (Section 11.3), on school and examination records where they exist, on the person's work history and on the accounts of family members. Exam trap "The impact of psychiatric illness on one's cognitive and intellectual abilities can be estimated on the basis of..." (IHBAS 2020): the answer is the deterioration quotient (also called the deterioration index or mental deterioration index), Wechsler's comparison of hold and don't-hold subtests. The distractors come from other fields. A mediation index is a statistic from mediation analysis, which asks whether a third variable carries the effect of a cause on an outcome (the Research Methodology book). The sense of coherence is Aaron Antonovsky 's (1923 to 1994) idea, from his work on salutogenesis, of a person's sense that life is comprehensible, manageable and meaningful (Book 1, Section 11.10.3): a predictor of health, not a measure of cognitive loss. A theory of mind index would concern social cognition, the ability to infer other people's beliefs and intentions (the Developmental Psychology book), and estimates nothing about intellectual decline. Learn the two lists too: hold, Vocabulary, Information, Object Assembly, Picture Completion ; don't hold, Digit Span, Similarities, Digit Symbol, Block Design . Organic or functional? An old question reframed For much of the twentieth century the commonest referral to a psychologist in a psychiatric hospital asked, in effect, "organic or functional?" Was the patient's trouble caused by a demonstrable disease of the brain, or was it a "functional" disorder such as schizophrenia, depression or a neurosis, in which no such disease could be found? Book 3, Section 10.8.1 tells the history of the two words and of their retirement from the diagnostic manuals. Here the point is why the question, put that way, could not be answered by tests. There are three reasons. The first you have already met: brain damage is not one thing, so there is no single "organic" pattern for a test to detect, which is why the single tests of organicity failed. The second is that the functional disorders themselves impair performance. People with schizophrenia have real and often substantial cognitive deficits in attention, memory and executive function; depression slows thinking and weakens effortful memory; anxiety disrupts attention. A low score on a test sensitive to brain damage can therefore come from an illness that the old scheme called functional, which is exactly why, as Pinel and Barnes note, the batteries that separate neurological patients from healthy people so well separate them from psychiatric patients much less well. The third is that the premise behind the dichotomy is false. Schizophrenia and the mood disorders are disorders of the brain too, as twin studies, imaging and the drugs that treat them show, and a person can have both kinds of trouble at once: a depressed man can also be in the earliest stage of Alzheimer's disease, and a heavy drinker may also have had a head injury. So the modern question is framed differently. Instead of a yes-or-no verdict, the neuropsychologist describes the profile of abilities, asks whether it matches a recognised pattern (a severe, isolated loss of new learning; a frontal pattern of poor planning and switching; a lateralised pattern like Omesh's), asks how much of it is explained by mood, effort, medication, education or the testing conditions, and states what it means for the person's daily life. "Is he organic?" becomes "Is his pattern of memory loss the kind seen in Alzheimer's disease, the kind seen in depression, or a mixture, and what should be done next?" That question can be answered, and Section 11.1.10 answers it for one patient. Exam trap If a paper asks what the early single tests such as the Bender-Gestalt (1938) and the Benton Visual Retention Test (1946) were used for, the answer is screening for organic brain damage ("organicity"), as distinct from functional psychiatric illness. If it asks why the single-test approach failed, the answer is that brain damage is not a unitary condition : different lesions produce different deficits, and psychiatric illnesses also lower test scores. Is the person doing their best? Effort and performance validity An ability test measures what a person can do only if he or she is trying to do it. Every score in a neuropsychological report rests on that assumption, and in some settings it cannot be taken for granted. Fatigue, pain, depression and plain lack of interest can all reduce effort; so can a wish to appear more impaired than one is, in order to win compensation after an accident, to obtain a disability benefit or to escape a criminal charge. The deliberate production or gross exaggeration of symptoms for an external reward is malingering , which DSM-5-TR treats as a condition that may be a focus of clinical attention rather than as a mental disorder (Book 3, Section 7.9.6). Neuropsychologists therefore build checks on effort into their assessments. A performance validity test checks whether a person's effort on ability tests was adequate; a symptom validity test checks whether the symptoms a person reports are exaggerated, as the validity scales of the MMPI-2 do for questionnaires (Chapter 9). Performance validity tests work by one of two kinds of logic. The first is a test that looks difficult but is in fact easy, so easy that people with genuine brain injury usually pass it. The best known is the Test of Memory Malingering (TOMM) of Tom N. Tombaugh (1996). The person is shown 50 line drawings of everyday objects one at a time and then, for each, a pair of drawings, and must point to the one seen before; there are two such learning trials and an optional retention trial later. Despite its name it is not really a test of memory, because the task is far easier than it seems. Scoring below 45 out of 50 on the second trial, that is, making more than five errors, is the usual sign that effort was inadequate, a level that patients with real head injuries rarely fall below. The second kind of logic is more powerful, and it rests on simple probability. In a test where every item offers two choices, a person who knows nothing and merely guesses will be right about half the time. On 50 two-choice items, pure guessing gives about 50 × 0.5 = 25 correct. A person who scores far below 25 is doing worse than chance, and the only way to do worse than chance is to know the right answer and choose the other one. How far below is far enough? For pure guessing on 50 items the standard deviation of the score is √(50 × 0.5 × 0.5) = √12.5 ≈ 3.54 (this formula for the spread of chance scores, the binomial distribution, is taught in the Research Methodology book). A score of 15 is 25 − 15 = 10 points below the chance level, and 10 ÷ 3.54 ≈ 2.83 standard deviations below it. The exact probability of guessing one's way to 15 or fewer is about 0.0033, roughly 3 chances in 1,000. A score that low is very hard to explain except as deliberate. This is below-chance performance , and on a forced-choice test (one in which the person must choose an answer on every item) it is the strongest evidence of feigning that testing can provide. Exam trap A score at chance means the person got nothing right beyond guessing, which can happen in genuine severe impairment such as advanced dementia; a score below chance means the person must have known the answers to avoid them. Failing a performance validity test shows that the other scores cannot be trusted; it does not by itself prove malingering, which is a clinical judgement that weighs the test results together with the incentive, the history and the consistency of the person's behaviour. And the TOMM, despite its name, measures effort, not memory. From referral to report: one assessment, step by step Everything in this section comes together in a single assessment. Follow Vipul , an invented patient, along the eight steps of Figure 11.1. Step 1: the question. Vipul is a 67-year-old retired headmaster from Dharwad. His wife died ten months ago. His son brings him to a psychiatrist because for about eight months Vipul has been forgetting conversations, asking the same question twice in an evening and leaving the newspaper unread; he sleeps badly and has lost weight. The psychiatrist's note asks: "Early dementia or depression?" A short telephone call turns this into the real question. The psychiatrist needs to know whether to treat a depression first and wait, or to tell the family to plan for a dementia; the son, who now handles the household money, wants to know whether his father can still look after his own pension and bank account. Step 2: history. The interview with Vipul, and separately with his son as informant, establishes that Vipul has about 16 years of education, taught English and mathematics for decades and ran a school for twenty years. There is no history of head injury, stroke or heavy drinking. The physician's blood tests for thyroid function and vitamin B12 are normal, and the MRI report describes changes usual for his age. One detail matters: a sleeping tablet of the benzodiazepine type was started three months ago, and drugs of this kind can slow thinking and weaken memory. Step 3: choosing the tests. The question decides the selection. Orientation and a brief screen come first; then attention and processing speed; then memory, with a word-list test that separates free recall, recall after a delay and recognition, because that comparison is the most useful single clue in telling depression from Alzheimer's disease (Section 11.4 explains why); then naming and verbal fluency, copying and clock drawing, and two tests of executive function. A depression scale for older adults is added (Section 11.8), along with a performance validity check and a premorbid estimate from his education, his career and his reading. Step 4: testing. Vipul is tested over two mornings of about ninety minutes each, wearing his reading glasses and his hearing aid, and in English and Kannada as he prefers. The examiner notes, as the process approach would want, that he answers slowly, says "I can't" quickly and often does better when gently encouraged to try again. Step 5: scoring. Against age and education norms, his attention and speed scores are in the low average range and his verbal fluency is low. His free recall of the word list is poor, but when he is given the words to recognise he picks out nearly all of them, and he forgets little between the immediate and the delayed trials. Naming and copying are normal. His depression score is well into the depressed range, and he passes the performance validity check. His premorbid level is estimated as high average, so against his own past the falls in speed and free recall are larger than the norms alone suggest. Step 6: interpretation. The pattern is one of slowness and of difficulty getting information out rather than of failing to store it: when recognition removes the need for effortful retrieval, his memory is close to normal. That pattern fits the cognitive effects of depression, perhaps added to by the sleeping tablet, better than the pattern of early Alzheimer's disease, in which newly learned material is typically lost over a delay and recognition does not rescue it (Section 11.4, and Book 3, Section 10.11.6 on pseudodementia). It is not proof, because depression in later life is sometimes the first sign of a dementia, and the report says so. Step 7: report and feedback. The written report answers the two questions in plain words. It recommends treating the depression, reviewing the sleeping tablet with his doctor, and retesting in about six months. On the money question, it notes that Vipul understood and could explain his pension and bank arrangements, and suggests that he continue to manage them with his son's help for now. The neuropsychologist also explains the findings to Vipul and his son in person. Step 8: review. Six months later, with his mood much improved, Vipul is retested. If his scores have risen by more than practice and measurement error would explain (the reliable change index of Chapter 3, Section 3.7.6), the depression account is supported; if they have stayed low or fallen despite a better mood, the team must think again about an early dementia. Either way, the first assessment has done its job as a baseline. Clinical link The feedback session is part of the assessment, not an afterthought. Patients and families come wanting to know "Is it dementia?", "Will he get worse?" and "What can we do?", and a report full of percentiles answers none of these. A good feedback session describes strengths before weaknesses, explains what the results mean for everyday life (for Vipul, that his memory is likely to improve as his mood lifts, and that lists and routines will help in the meantime), is honest about uncertainty, and checks that the family has understood. Interviewers for clinical psychology programmes often ask how you would give difficult results; this is the shape of a good answer. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Neuropsychology is the study of the relationship between the brain and . The question that names the decision an assessment must inform is the question. Halstead called the brain-dependent adaptive abilities that IQ tests missed intelligence. The approach of Edith Kaplan that records how a patient reaches an answer is the Boston approach. Reitan's four methods of inference are level of performance, pattern of performance, signs and right-left comparisons. A right-handed man taps 60 times in 10 seconds with his right hand. By the 10 per cent rule, his left hand should tap about times. Comparing a patient's current scores with her own estimated earlier level uses the comparison standard. In the WAIS version of Wechsler's method, Vocabulary, Information, Object Assembly and Picture Completion are the tests. A patient's hold tests sum to 60 and his don't-hold tests to 48. His deterioration index is per cent. On a test of 50 two-choice items, pure guessing gives about correct, so a score of 12 is below-chance performance. Answers: (1) behaviour; (2) referral; (3) biological; (4) process; (5) pathognomonic; (6) 54 (10 per cent of 60 is 6, and 60 − 6 = 54); (7) individual; (8) hold; (9) 20 ((60 − 48) ÷ 60 = 12 ÷ 60 = 0.20, that is, 20 per cent); (10) 25 (50 × 0.5). 11.2 The Fixed Batteries: Halstead-Reitan and Luria-Nebraska Medium yield · 5 Qs Suppose you were asked to build, from nothing, a set of tasks that could tell a doctor whether a person's brain was damaged, without opening the skull and without a scanner. Which tasks would you choose? You would want some that are easy for healthy people and hard for injured ones. You would want to test many abilities, because damage in different places breaks different things. You would want each task given in exactly the same way to every person, so that scores could be compared, and you would want some tasks that can be done with the right hand and the left hand separately, because each side of the body is run by the opposite side of the brain. Two famous answers to this problem dominated the second half of the twentieth century. The first grew out of the laboratory of Ward Halstead in Chicago and the decades of work of his student Ralph Reitan, whose story opens this chapter. The second began with the bedside methods of the Russian neuropsychologist Alexander Luria and was turned into a standardised battery in Nebraska. Both are fixed batteries in the sense explained in Section 11.1: every patient receives the same tests, in the same order and the same way, and the scores are compared with the same norms. This section takes each battery apart test by test (what the person does, what the examiner scores, and what a poor score tends to mean), then shows how the scores are summarised, what each battery is good for, and why both drew fierce criticism. From "biological intelligence" to a clinical battery The opening of this chapter told how Ward C. Halstead set out to measure what he called biological intelligence , and how Ralph M. Reitan (1922 to 2014) tested his measures against patients and controls and learned to read a profile of scores almost like an X-ray. That story is not repeated here. What matters for this section is what the two men left behind. Halstead meant something different from the intelligence measured by Binet-type tests (Chapter 6). An IQ test asks how much a person knows and how well they reason compared with others of the same age; Halstead wanted to measure the brain's basic capacity to adapt, to grasp a new principle, to organise information from the senses and to act on it, a capacity he believed depended heavily on the frontal lobes. His book Brain and Intelligence: A Quantitative Study of the Frontal Lobes (1947) described more than two dozen procedures as possible "quantitative indicators" of this biological intelligence. The theory about the frontal lobes has not survived well; what survived is the observation that several of his tests are very sensitive to brain damage of many kinds. Reitan's contribution was to turn a research collection into a clinical instrument. Working at Indiana University in Indianapolis, he kept the measures that best separated brain-damaged patients from controls, dropped those that did not, and added tests of his own: the Trail Making Test, an aphasia screening test, a sensory-perceptual examination, a test of grip strength and an examination of which hand, eye and foot the person prefers. The result is the Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery (often abbreviated HRNB or HRB). With Deborah Wolfson he set out its theory and interpretation in a manual first published in 1985 (second edition 1993). The adult battery is meant for people aged 15 and over. Two children's versions exist: the Halstead Neuropsychological Test Battery for Older Children, for ages 9 to 14, and the Reitan-Indiana Neuropsychological Test Battery for Children, for ages 5 to 8, with shorter or simpler forms of the adult tests. In routine practice an intelligence scale (the WAIS, Chapter 6) and a personality inventory (the MMPI, Chapter 9) are almost always given alongside the battery as allied procedures ; they help the interpretation, but they are not part of the battery itself. A test battery is simply a set of separate tests given together, each yielding its own score, chosen so that together they sample the abilities you care about. Figure 11.4 shows the Halstead-Reitan battery grouped by what each test mainly measures. Notice two things before you read on. First, the battery is heavy on doing things with the hands, against the clock: placing blocks, tapping, drawing lines between circles. Second, several tests are done with each hand separately, which is what allows the battery to compare the two sides of the body. Both features will matter when we come to its strengths and weaknesses. Exam trap Halstead built the tests and the idea of biological intelligence (1947); Reitan validated them, added Trail Making, the aphasia screening test and the sensory-perceptual examination, and turned the set into a clinical battery. The WAIS and the MMPI are often given with the battery, but an option that says the battery "is the WAIS plus the MMPI" is wrong: they are allied procedures, not its tests. Halstead's core tests, one by one The Category Test. Picture the original apparatus. The person sits in front of a small screen on which a picture is projected: a few geometric figures, lines or shapes. Below the screen is a panel with four keys numbered 1 to 4. The instruction is simply that each picture suggests one of the numbers, and the task is to press the right one. Nobody says what the rule is. If the answer is right a pleasant bell rings; if it is wrong a buzzer sounds. That is the only help the person ever gets. Within each subtest one principle holds throughout, and the person who works it out can answer every remaining item correctly. To see the idea, take an invented item (not one from the test): if a card showed three small circles and the hidden rule were "count the shapes", the answer would be 3, and a person who discovered the rule from a few bells and buzzers could then apply it to every new card. The adult test has 208 items in seven subtests ; Halstead's original version was longer. The principle changes from one subtest to the next, so the person must also give up an old rule and look for a new one, and the seventh subtest mixes items from the earlier ones to see whether the principles have been remembered. The score is simply the number of errors . Because projectors and keys are awkward, booklet and computer versions are now common, and children's versions are shorter (168 items for older children and 80 for young children). What does the Category Test measure? It is the battery's test of abstract reasoning and concept formation : noticing what several different pictures have in common, forming a hypothesis, testing it against feedback and changing it when it fails. It needs sustained attention and learning from experience too. It is often described as the single most sensitive test in the battery to brain damage in general, which also tells you its weakness: because so many kinds of damage raise the error count, a poor score says little about where the damage is. It is also long, about an hour for most adults and longer for a severely impaired patient. You will meet a close cousin in Section 11.6: the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test also asks the person to discover an unstated rule from "right" and "wrong" and to shift when the rule changes. The Tactual Performance Test. This test borrowed a much older piece of equipment, the form board, a wooden board with cut-out spaces into which shaped blocks (a star, a cross, a triangle and so on) must be fitted. The French physician Edouard Seguin (1812 to 1880) had used such boards to train children with intellectual disability, and Henry Herbert Goddard (1866 to 1957) later used one as a timed test, which is why it is often called the Seguin-Goddard form board. Halstead's change was the blindfold. The person is blindfolded before ever seeing the board, and then places the ten blocks of the adult board (six for children under 15) into their spaces, first using only the preferred hand, then only the other hand, and finally both hands together; each trial is timed. Then the board and blocks are hidden, the blindfold is removed, and the person is asked, without having been warned in advance, to draw the board from memory, showing the shapes in their correct places. Three scores come out of this one test, and all three count in the Impairment Index. Total time is the sum of the three trials. Memory is the number of shapes drawn correctly. Localisation is the number of shapes drawn in roughly the right position on the board. Because the person did not know they would be asked to draw the board, the memory and localisation scores measure incidental memory , what was learned without any intention to learn. The test as a whole draws on touch and the sense of limb position, fine movement, spatial problem solving and learning across trials. It also gives a right-left comparison. The second trial is normally quicker than the first, because the person has already explored the board, and the third is quicker still. If the trial with the non-preferred hand is no faster, or is slower, than the trial with the preferred hand, that hand's performance is relatively poor, and the hemisphere on the opposite side becomes a suspect. The Seashore Rhythm Test. Carl Emil Seashore (1866 to 1949), a psychologist at the University of Iowa, built tests of musical talent early in the twentieth century, and Halstead took one of them for his battery. The person hears 30 pairs of short rhythmic patterns of beats, presented from a recording in three sets of ten, and marks each pair "same" or "different". The score is the number correct (often converted to a ranked score). The task sounds musical, but it is mainly a test of sustained auditory attention and concentration together with the perception of non-verbal sound patterns: the pairs come one after another at a steady pace, and a person whose attention drifts for a few seconds simply misses items. Poor scores occur with damage on either side of the brain, so the test is not a good pointer to one hemisphere. The Speech-Sounds Perception Test. Here the person hears 60 spoken nonsense words, each built around an "ee" sound, and for each one marks, from a short row of printed spellings, the spelling that matches what was heard. The score is the number of errors. The test needs sustained attention, accurate hearing of speech sounds, and the ability to match a heard sound to letters on a page. That last requirement is worth noticing: a person who reads poorly, or who has had little schooling in the Roman alphabet, can fail it for reasons that have nothing to do with the brain. Section 11.3 returns to this problem. The Finger Tapping Test (also called the Finger Oscillation Test). The person rests the hand flat and taps a small key, attached to a mechanical or electronic counter, with the index finger as fast as possible for ten seconds. Trials are repeated with each hand (until five consecutive trials fall within five taps of one another, usually five to ten trials per hand) and those five are averaged. This is a test of simple fine motor speed , and it is the battery's classic lateralising test, meaning a test that can suggest which side of the brain is affected. In right-handed people the preferred hand is normally about 10 per cent faster than the other. If the preferred hand is no faster than the other, or a hand is much slower than expected, the motor areas of the opposite hemisphere become a suspect, provided nothing is wrong with the hand itself. The Trail Making Test , which Reitan took from the Army Individual Test Battery of 1944 and added to the battery, asks the person to draw a line connecting numbered circles in order (Part A) and then circles that alternate between numbers and letters (Part B), as quickly as possible. It is taught in full, with its scoring, in Section 11.6. Table 11.5 brings the tests of the battery together. The BDI and the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HAM-D) are depression rating scales (Section 11.8); the Bender-Gestalt is a single visuomotor copying test (Section 11.5), not this battery. The Rorschach is a projective personality test (Chapter 10) and is never part of the Halstead-Reitan, so in an "all EXCEPT" item it is the odd one out. Do not confuse the Tactual Performance Test (blindfolded form board, Halstead) with the Benton tests (Section 11.5) or with the Kohs Block Design test of Bhatia's battery (Chapter 6). The tests Reitan added: language, the senses, strength and handedness Halstead's tests are good at detecting that something is wrong, but they say little about language or about simple sensation, two areas where damage to one side of the brain leaves very clear marks. Reitan filled these gaps with short examinations that a neurologist would recognise. The Reitan-Indiana Aphasia Screening Test is Reitan's modification of the Halstead-Wepman Aphasia Screening Test, which Halstead had published with Joseph Wepman in 1949. In a few minutes the person is asked to name common objects from drawings, to spell, read and write short words, to repeat words and phrases, to do simple arithmetic, to follow simple instructions and to copy a few simple geometric shapes. The test is not scored by adding up a total. Instead each failure is noted as a sign of a specific deficit: an inability to name an object is a sign of dysnomia, a gross spelling or writing failure a sign of dysgraphia, a badly distorted copy of a shape a sign of constructional difficulty, and so on. This is the "pathognomonic sign" method of inference described in Section 11.1: a few such errors are rare in healthy adults, so even one or two carry weight. The aphasias themselves are described in Book 1, Section 8.9.6 and Book 3, Section 10.8.3. The Reitan-Klove Sensory-Perceptual Examination , developed by Reitan with the Norwegian neuropsychologist Hallgrim Klove , tests touch, hearing and vision on each side of the body. Its most important part is double simultaneous stimulation . The examiner touches the person's right hand, then the left, then both at once (and does the same with sounds near each ear and with small movements in each half of the visual field). Many patients with damage to one hemisphere, particularly the parietal lobe, report a single touch on either side correctly but, when both sides are touched together, report only the touch on the side opposite the healthy hemisphere. The stimulus on the other side is said to be extinguished , or suppressed. The examination also asks the person, with eyes closed, to say which finger has been touched (failure suggests finger agnosia ), to identify numbers traced on the fingertips, and to recognise small shapes placed in the palm by touch alone. Grip strength is measured with a hand dynamometer, a spring device with a dial that the person squeezes as hard as possible, in alternating trials with each hand. As with tapping, the preferred hand is normally somewhat stronger. The Lateral Dominance Examination records which hand the person uses for writing and other everyday actions, which eye they use to sight through a tube, and which foot they kick with. It may look trivial, but every right-left comparison in the battery depends on it: a left hand that is slower than the right means something quite different in a left-handed person. Clinical link The right-left comparisons are the most direct link between the battery and the anatomy of the brain, because the motor and sensory pathways cross. A clear pattern (the left hand slower at tapping, weaker in grip and clumsier on the Tactual Performance Test, with extinction of touches on the left) points towards the right hemisphere. But before you write "right hemisphere dysfunction" in a report, look at the hands and ask about them. An old fracture of the wrist, arthritis, a nerve injury or a plaster cast slows a hand without any help from the brain, and a good examiner rules these out first. This is one reason why Reitan insisted on combining several methods of inference (Section 11.1) rather than trusting a single score. Exam trap The aphasia screening test is the Reitan-Indiana (from the Halstead-Wepman test of 1949); the sensory examination is the Reitan-Klove . Extinction on double simultaneous stimulation is a sensory-perceptual finding, not a memory or attention test score. The test that "shows whether a person makes more errors on one side of the body" in a past item is Benton's Finger Localization Test (Section 11.5), but the same logic runs through the whole Halstead-Reitan: tapping, grip, the Tactual Performance Test and the sensory examination all compare the two sides. Summarising the battery: the Halstead Impairment Index and its successors A full Halstead-Reitan examination yields dozens of numbers. How do you turn them into an answer to the first question a referring doctor asks, "Is this brain impaired or not?" Halstead's answer was the simplest summary imaginable. For each of his key scores he set a cut-off, the point beyond which healthy people rarely fall; then he counted how many of the patient's scores lay beyond their cut-offs, and expressed the count as a proportion. This proportion is the Halstead Impairment Index . Halstead's original index was built from ten scores. Two of his measures, a critical flicker fusion test (the rate at which a flickering light appears to become steady, which gave two scores) and a test of time sense, added little and were dropped, which leaves the seven scores used today: the Category Test, the three Tactual Performance Test scores (total time, memory and localisation), the Seashore Rhythm Test, the Speech-Sounds Perception Test and the Finger Tapping Test (preferred hand). Remember Halstead Impairment Index = (number of the seven core scores in the impaired range) ÷ 7 The numerator is how many of the seven scores fall beyond their cut-offs; 7 is the number of scores counted. The index runs from 0.0 (no score impaired) to 1.0 (all seven impaired) and is reported to one decimal place. By the traditional rule, an index of 0.5 or more suggests brain damage, and some guides treat 0.4 as borderline. Some reference works add a severity grading (one gives 0.0 to 0.2 normal, 0.3 to 0.4 mild, 0.5 to 0.7 moderate and 0.8 to 1.0 severe impairment), but such gradings vary from source to source; the figure to remember is the 0.5 cut-off. Let us push a case through the formula. Ehsan is a 48-year-old bank officer (an invented case) who was hurt in a road accident eight months ago. His CT scan showed bruising of the brain at the time, and he has now gone back to work but says he cannot follow new procedures, gets lost in his files and tires by midday. His employer's insurer and his own lawyer both want to know whether there is lasting impairment, and his doctor wants to plan his return to work. Table 11.6 shows his seven index scores. The cut-off for each score is printed in the battery's manual (for the Category Test, for example, Reitan's cut-off was about 50 errors); the last column simply records whether each of Ehsan's scores lies beyond it. Table 11.6 Ehsan's seven Impairment Index scores (an invented case). Score Ehsan's result Beyond the cut-off? Category Test errors 88 errors Yes (impaired) Tactual Performance Test, total time 26.4 minutes for the three trials Yes (impaired) Tactual Performance Test, memory 4 shapes drawn Yes (impaired) Tactual Performance Test, localisation 1 shape correctly placed Yes (impaired) Seashore Rhythm Test 27 of 30 correct No Speech-Sounds Perception Test 5 errors No Finger Tapping, preferred hand 53 taps in 10 seconds No Step 1: count the impaired scores. The Category Test and all three Tactual Performance Test scores are beyond their cut-offs, so the count is 1 + 3 = 4. Step 2: divide by the number of scores counted, which is 7. So the index is 4 ÷ 7 = 0.5714. Step 3: round to one decimal place, as the index is always reported: 0.5714 becomes 0.6 . Step 4: interpret. An index of 0.6 is above the traditional cut-off of 0.5, so by this rule Ehsan's performance is in the impaired range, and in the severity grading quoted above it would fall in the moderate band. Now look at the pattern, not just the level. His simple attention to sounds (Rhythm), his perception of speech sounds and his motor speed are intact; what has failed is the Category Test and the Tactual Performance Test, the two tests that demand working out a new problem with no instructions, learning as you go, and remembering what you never meant to learn. That pattern fits his complaint (he cannot follow new procedures) far better than a single number does, and it tells the rehabilitation team what to work on. Suppose instead that three of the seven scores had been impaired. Then the index would be 3 ÷ 7 = 0.4286, which rounds to 0.4: below the cut-off of 0.5, but in the zone that some guides call borderline. Notice what this means for a person with only seven scores. Each impaired score moves the index by 1 ÷ 7, about 0.14, so a single test on a bad day can carry a patient across the cut-off. That is one reason why no experienced neuropsychologist interprets the index alone. The index answers one question (how much?) and leaves others open. It cannot tell you where the damage is, what kind it is, when it happened or what caused it; two patients with the same index of 0.6 may have failed completely different tests. Later summary scores tried to do better. The Average Impairment Rating , from Elbert W. Russell , Charles Neuringer and Gerald Goldstein 's book Assessment of Brain Damage: A Neuropsychological Key Approach (1970), rates each of a set of the battery's scores (including the Digit Symbol subtest of the Wechsler scale) on a short scale running from normal to severely impaired and averages the ratings, so it reflects how badly each test was failed, not just whether it was. Reitan's own later General Neuropsychological Deficit Scale rates 42 of the battery's variables for how far each departs from normal and adds the ratings; in Reitan's bands a total up to 25 is normal, 26 to 40 mild, 41 to 67 moderate and 68 or more severe impairment. For all three summary scores, a higher number means more impairment. A deeper problem was that the original cut-offs were the same for everyone. A score that is ordinary for a 75-year-old with five years of schooling may be a clear sign of damage in a 25-year-old engineer, because performance on almost every test falls with age and rises with education. Robert K. Heaton , Igor Grant and Charles G. Matthews addressed this in Comprehensive Norms for an Extended Halstead-Reitan Battery (1991), which converts each raw score into a demographically corrected T score : a standard score with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10, computed against healthy people of the same age, education and sex (Chapter 5 explains T scores). A revision in 2004 by Heaton and colleagues provided separate norms for African American and Caucasian adults. With demographically corrected scores, a T score below about 40 (one standard deviation below the mean of comparable people) is commonly read as impaired. Section 11.3.1 shows what goes wrong when such norms are borrowed for a population they were not built on. Exam trap The Halstead Impairment Index is a proportion from 0 to 1, not a T score, a percentage of items or an IQ. The traditional cut-off is 0.5 (about four of the seven scores impaired). The seven scores are the Category Test, the three Tactual Performance Test scores, Rhythm, Speech-Sounds and Tapping; Trail Making, the aphasia screening test and the sensory examination are interpreted separately and are not in the index. On the index, the Average Impairment Rating, the General Neuropsychological Deficit Scale and the Luria-Nebraska T scores, a high number is bad ; on Heaton's T scores, as on IQ, a low number is bad. What the Halstead-Reitan is for, and what it costs Put plainly, the Halstead-Reitan battery is used for comprehensive neuropsychological assessment : to find out whether a person's brain is working normally, and if not, how severely and in what pattern it is impaired. In Reitan's hands it was also used to suggest whether damage was on the left, on the right or on both sides, whether it was focal or diffuse, and whether it was recent or long-standing. Before CT and MRI, that localising purpose was a large part of the battery's value; imaging now shows the lesion directly, and the battery's main uses have shifted to the questions a scan cannot answer (Section 11.1): how is the person actually functioning, which abilities are spared, has there been change since the last assessment, and what does this mean for work, driving, independent living or a legal claim. Its long, standardised and well-documented procedure has made it particularly popular in medico-legal and research settings, where an assessment may be scrutinised by the other side. Its strengths follow directly from its design. Because every patient takes the same tests, scores can be compared across patients, across clinics and across decades, and an enormous research literature has accumulated on what different patterns mean. The battery samples many abilities, so it is unlikely to miss a major deficit in the areas it covers. Its right-left comparisons give it genuine lateralising power. And with the large demographically corrected norms of Heaton and colleagues, a raw score can be judged against people like the patient. Its weaknesses are just as real. The first is time. A full battery with its allied procedures usually takes most of a day, commonly quoted at five to eight hours, which is exhausting for a patient who is already ill, expensive for the family or the health service, and impossible for someone who cannot sit for long. The second is content. The battery is heavily loaded with motor and speed demands (placing blocks, tapping, drawing lines against the clock), so slow, elderly or physically disabled people can look impaired for reasons that have little to do with cognition; and apart from the incidental memory scores of the Tactual Performance Test it contains no proper test of memory, which is why clinicians add the Wechsler Memory Scale or a word-list learning test (Section 11.4). The third is the logic of a fixed battery itself: it gives every patient tests they may not need, and it may still miss the one specific deficit that matters for this patient. The fourth concerns what it can discriminate. As the biopsychologist John Pinel notes, standardised batteries of this kind separate neurological patients from healthy people well, but they are much less good at separating neurological patients from psychiatric ones, whose attention, motivation and speed are often affected too. These criticisms are why most clinicians today prefer the flexible and process approaches described in Section 11.1, using individual Halstead-Reitan tests (Trail Making, Finger Tapping, the Category Test) inside a battery chosen for the referral question. Exam trap If an item asks what the Halstead-Reitan battery is used for, the answer is neuropsychological assessment : a broad range of cognitive, sensory and motor functions sampled to detect and localise brain dysfunction and estimate its severity. Each wrong option names a different kind of test taught elsewhere: personality assessment measures enduring traits and styles (inventories such as the MMPI and 16PF, Chapter 9); vocational testing means aptitude and interest measures used to guide careers, such as the Differential Aptitude Tests or the Strong inventory (Chapter 8); projective testing , of adults or of children, uses ambiguous stimuli such as inkblots or pictures (the Rorschach, the TAT, the Children's Apperception Test, Chapter 10); attachment style is assessed by observation and interview methods such as the Strange Situation and the Adult Attachment Interview, not by a neuropsychological battery; and a self-report depression screen is a questionnaire such as the BDI (Section 11.8). Luria's method turned into a battery: the Luria-Nebraska The second fixed battery has a stranger history, because it was built from the work of a man who did not believe in fixed batteries. Alexander Romanovich Luria (1902 to 1977), the Russian neuropsychologist whose theory of functional systems is outlined in Section 11.1, examined patients at the bedside with a large repertoire of small tasks: tapping a rhythm back to the examiner, copying a sequence of hand positions, repeating words and sentences, reading, writing, doing sums, recalling short stories, solving problems. He did not add up scores or compare them with norms. He watched exactly how each patient failed, chose the next task to test his hypothesis about which link in a functional system was broken, and built up a picture of the syndrome. It was a brilliant method in the hands of someone with Luria's experience, and almost impossible to teach to anyone else from his books. The first step towards a battery was taken by the Danish psychologist Anne-Lise Christensen , who set down Luria's bedside methods in English in Luria's Neuropsychological Investigation (1975), published as a text with a manual and a set of test cards. Christensen's version kept Luria's spirit: the examiner was still expected to choose tasks and to interpret qualitatively. The second step was taken at the University of Nebraska by Charles J. Golden , Thomas A. Hammeke and Arnold D. Purisch . They took the items in Christensen's compilation, fixed the way each was to be given, laid down how each was to be scored, grouped the items into scales and collected norms. Their first validity study appeared in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology in 1978, and the published test and manual followed in 1980. The result is the Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery (LNNB). The original form, Form I, has 269 items grouped into eleven clinical scales , listed in Table 11.7. Each item is scored 0, 1 or 2 : 0 for normal performance, 1 for borderline and 2 for clearly abnormal. Some items are scored for both speed and accuracy. The item scores on a scale are added to give the raw scale score, and the raw score is converted into a T score (mean 50, standard deviation 10) from the manual's tables. Here the T score runs the opposite way from most tests you know: a higher T score means more impairment , because the raw score counts errors. The whole battery takes about two and a half hours, often quoted as two to three, which was one of its main selling points against the Halstead-Reitan. Scale Abbreviation What its items sample C1 Motor Mot Simple and complex hand movements, copying positions and sequences, drawing, oral movements C2 Rhythm Rhy Judging and reproducing tones and rhythmic patterns C3 Tactile Tac Touch on each hand, position sense, recognising shapes and figures by touch C4 Visual Vis Recognising objects and pictures, visual-spatial judgement C5 Receptive Speech Rec Hearing speech sounds, understanding words, sentences and grammar C6 Expressive Speech Exp Repeating, naming, producing speech C7 Writing Wri Copying and writing letters, words and phrases C8 Reading Rea Reading letters, words and sentences C9 Arithmetic Ari Reading and writing numbers, simple calculation C10 Memory Mem Learning and recalling words, pictures and short material C11 Intellectual Processes Int Understanding pictures and stories, reasoning, problem solving How do you decide whether a T score is "high"? Not with a single fixed line, because older and less-educated people make more errors on many of these items even when their brains are healthy. The manual instead provides a critical level , a T score computed from the person's age and years of education; older people and people with less schooling are allowed a higher T score before a scale is counted as abnormal. The manual's decision rules then count how many clinical scales lie above the critical level: the more of them there are, the stronger the evidence of brain dysfunction (rules of thumb of two, or three, scales are both used). Beyond the clinical scales the battery provides summary scales , including a Pathognomonic scale made of items that people without brain damage seldom fail, Left Hemisphere and Right Hemisphere scales built from the motor and tactile items done with the right and with the left side of the body, and scales for the overall elevation of the profile and the level of impairment; and localisation scales intended to point to the frontal, sensorimotor, parietal-occipital and temporal regions of each hemisphere. The figure of "fourteen scales" that you will meet in some notes counts the eleven clinical scales plus the Pathognomonic, Left Hemisphere and Right Hemisphere scales. Work through an invented profile. Juhi is a 40-year-old schoolteacher with twelve years of schooling and a two-year teacher's diploma who had a stroke four months ago and has been referred by a rehabilitation unit. Take one scale first. Suppose that on the Expressive Speech scale she scores 2 on five items, 1 on four items and 0 on all the rest. Her raw score is (5 × 2) + (4 × 1) + 0 = 10 + 4 = 14. The examiner looks up 14 in the manual's table for that scale and reads off a T score; in our invented example it is 71. Doing the same for all eleven scales gives the profile in Figure 11.5. For Juhi's age and education, suppose the critical level works out at a T score of 60 (an invented value for the example). Now count: Receptive Speech (66), Expressive Speech (71), Writing (68), Reading (64) and Memory (67) are above 60, so five scales lie above the critical level. That is well past any of the usual rules, so the profile indicates brain dysfunction. The pattern is the interesting part: the elevated scales are the language scales and a memory scale that uses words, while motor, tactile and visual scales sit close to the normal mean of 50. In Luria's terms that points to the left hemisphere, which fits a left-sided stroke. Hold on to that interpretation for a moment, though, because the battery's critics would ask a pointed question about it. Remember that on this battery a high T score is bad. Two later versions complete the family. Form II (1985) has 279 items; the extra items form a twelfth clinical scale, Intermediate Memory, which asks about material presented earlier in the session. And a children's revision, the Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery: Children's Revision (Golden, 1987), adapted the battery for children aged 8 to 12. In India, the Luria-Nebraska was the model for the Hindi battery developed at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, described in Section 11.3.6. Exam trap Alexander Luria did not write the Luria-Nebraska. The chain is Luria (the bedside methods) to Christensen (compiled them, 1975) to Golden, Hammeke and Purisch (standardised and scored them at Nebraska, 1978; manual 1980). Form I has 269 items in 11 clinical scales ; Form II has 279 and adds Intermediate Memory. Items are scored 0, 1 or 2, and a high T score means impairment . "Rhythm" appears in both batteries (the Seashore Rhythm Test of the Halstead-Reitan and the C2 Rhythm scale of the Luria-Nebraska), so read the option carefully. And although Luria's own method was flexible and qualitative, the Luria-Nebraska is a fixed battery: an answer explanation that calls it "the flexible battery" is wrong. The Luria-Nebraska controversy, and the two batteries compared Few tests have been attacked as fiercely, or as soon, as the Luria-Nebraska. The pointed question about Juhi's profile is the heart of the attack. Her five elevated scales have names that suggest five different abilities, but every one of them depends on understanding and producing language: the instructions for the memory items are spoken, the writing and reading items need letters, and even many "intellectual" items are given in words. A single problem, an aphasia from a left-hemisphere stroke, could raise all five together. If so, the profile is not five findings but one, and a clinician who read the scale names literally ("memory impaired, reading impaired, writing impaired") would be misled. Key study: the Luria-Nebraska controversy (1980 to 1983) In 1980 the neuropsychologist Kenneth M. Adams published a critique in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology with the blunt title "In search of Luria's battery: A false start". He argued that the battery had been put into clinical use before its development and validation could support it, and that the early validation studies were not strong enough to justify the claims made for it. Golden replied in the same issue. In 1981 Paul A. Spiers reviewed the dispute under the title "Have they come to praise Luria or to bury him? The Luria-Nebraska battery controversy", questioning whether a scored, fixed set of items could capture a method whose whole point was flexible, qualitative observation. In 1983 Dean Delis and Edith Kaplan, the founder of the process approach (Section 11.1), added "Hazards of a standardized neuropsychological test with low content validity": the scales' names, they argued, imply functions that the items do not measure purely, because the same item can be failed for many different reasons. The defenders replied that the battery was never meant to replace Luria's method, only to give clinicians a standardised, reasonably brief examination with norms, and that validity evidence was accumulating. The debate taught the whole field a lesson that applies to every battery in this chapter: a scale's name is a hypothesis about what it measures, not a guarantee. So how do the two batteries compare in practice? When Gerald Goldstein and Carolyn Shelly compared them in 1984, as Barlow and Durand summarise the study, the Halstead-Reitan and the Luria-Nebraska were about equally good at detecting brain damage, each classifying roughly 80 per cent of cases correctly. That figure is a good reminder of what "fixed battery" accuracy means: impressively better than chance, but still wrong in about one case in five, which is why neither battery is used on its own to make a diagnosis. The Halstead-Reitan is empirical and American (tests kept because they separated patients from controls), long, and summarised by the Impairment Index ; the Luria-Nebraska is Luria's theory-driven methods given American norms , shorter, and summarised by T scores against a critical level . If an option says the Luria-Nebraska "takes longer than the Halstead-Reitan" or "was standardised by Luria", it is wrong. And neither battery is a personality, projective or vocational test. 11.3 Indian Neuropsychological Tools: The NIMHANS Battery, the PGI Battery and the PGI Memory Scale Lower yield · not asked yet Imagine giving the Speech-Sounds Perception Test of Section 11.2.2 to a 60-year-old farmer from a village in Mandya district who left school after two years, speaks only Kannada and has never held a test booklet. He will make a great many errors. Is his brain damaged? You cannot tell, because the test asks him to match spoken English-style nonsense words to Roman spellings, something his brain was never trained to do. The same problem appears, less dramatically, in almost every test built in America or Europe: in the words chosen for a memory list, in the pictures chosen for a naming test, in the alphabet used in Trail Making Part B, and above all in the norms, the scores of healthy people against which a patient's score is judged. This section asks why Indian clinicians built their own tools and what they built. It describes the three you are most likely to meet in an Indian clinic or an Indian question paper (the NIMHANS Neuropsychology Battery from Bengaluru, and the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction and the PGI Memory Scale from Chandigarh) and then the newer Indian batteries that sit beside them. Why India needed its own tools A raw score on a test means nothing until it is compared with the scores of a normative sample , a group of healthy people tested in the same way (Chapter 5 explains norms and standard scores in full). Norms built in one population can be used in another only if the two are alike in the things that affect scores on that test. For neuropsychological tests those things are age, education, literacy, language and familiarity with being tested, and on every one of them India differs from the populations on which the classic tests were normed, and differs enormously within itself. Education and literacy come first. Healthy people with more schooling do better on almost every cognitive test, and the effect is largest exactly where Indian samples are most varied: among people with little or no schooling. As early as 1980 Dwarka Pershad and S. K. Verma of the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER) in Chandigarh reported, in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry , tentative education-wise norms for several tests built or standardised in their department, including the verbal section of an adult intelligence scale, the PGI Memory Scale and proverb and similarity tests, for adults aged 16 to 50. The mean scores of the different educational groups differed markedly, and they concluded that norms must be reported separately for different levels of education. Even years of schooling are an imperfect guide in India, as a 2017 review of cognitive testing in Indian adults by A. P. Porrselvi and V. Shankar pointed out: schools and curricula vary widely, and many older people who completed school have since lost the reading, writing, drawing and arithmetic skills they learned there because their lives have not needed them, a state the authors call functional illiteracy. Language is the second difficulty. A verbal test translated into another language is, strictly speaking, a new test: the words in a memory list differ in how common, how long and how familiar they are, and a reading or spelling task depends on the script. Tests that use the Roman alphabet, such as Trail Making Part B with its sequence 1-A-2-B, cannot be given fairly to a person who does not read it; the Colour Trails Test (Louis D'Elia and colleagues, 1996), which replaces the letters with two colours, was designed for exactly this problem and is the version used in the NIMHANS battery (Section 11.6 teaches both). Familiarity with testing is the third. The same 2017 review noted that many Indian adults have little experience of psychological tests and treat them like a school examination, which brings test anxiety, and that a social pressure of "scoring the highest" makes some people reluctant to attempt tasks such as drawing or recall unless they are sure of doing well. Content is the fourth: a picture of an object that is common in Iowa may be unknown in Assam. How much difference does the norm group make? A striking answer comes from a study outside India. In 2021 a team led by A. Morlett Paredes gave the Halstead Category Test (Section 11.2.2) to 252 healthy native Spanish speakers living in the United States-Mexico border region. When their scores were judged against published, demographically adjusted norms for English-speaking non-Hispanic White Americans, 48 per cent of these healthy people were classified as impaired; against the norms for Black Americans, 27 per cent were. Now do the arithmetic. The impairment rule used was a T score below 40, one standard deviation below the mean, and by definition only about 16 per cent of a healthy group falls below that line. So 48 per cent is 48 ÷ 16 = 3 times what the norms promise: borrowed norms made healthy people look brain-damaged three times as often as they should. That is the risk an Indian clinician runs by scoring an Indian patient against American tables. Indian clinicians responded in two ways. One was to take widely used Western tests, adapt their content and instructions, and collect fresh norms on Indian samples broken down by age, sex and education; this is the approach of the NIMHANS batteries. The other was to assemble a battery from tests that had already been built or adapted in India, and to derive a single rating of overall dysfunction from them; this is the approach of the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction. Both are described below, and Book 2, Section 2.6.1 shows where they fit in clinical work: the bedside examination of cognition screens, and these batteries measure. Exam trap The reason for Indian norms is not that Indians "score lower"; it is that education, literacy, language and test familiarity change scores in healthy people, so a borrowed cut-off misclassifies healthy people as impaired (a false positive). Education is the variable the Indian test-builders stressed most: Pershad and Verma's 1980 paper and every Indian battery report norms by education level. The NIMHANS Neuropsychology Battery for adults The National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru has the longest tradition of neuropsychological testing in India. Its first battery was described by C. R. Mukundan and V. N. Murthy in a paper presented at NIMHANS in 1979 on lateralising and localising cerebral lesions with a battery of neuropsychological tests. It was a "lobe function" battery built on Luria's principles of the localisation and lateralisation of higher mental functions (Section 11.1), with about 20 tests, several of them adapted Western tests and one an indigenous delayed-response test of working memory. A review of Indian cognitive testing in 2017 called it the earliest neuropsychological test battery developed in India. The battery in use today is the NIMHANS Neuropsychology Battery , whose manual, NIMHANS Neuropsychology Battery-2004 Manual , was written by Shobini L. Rao , D. K. Subbakrishna and K. Gopukumar and published by NIMHANS in 2004. (You will see it called both the "Neuropsychology" and the "Neuropsychological" Battery; they are the same.) It consists of 19 widely used Western tests that were adapted and standardised for Indian adults, with norms for ages 16 to 65. Unlike the Halstead-Reitan, it has no single summary index. Each test is tied to a particular cognitive function and, where the research allows, to a brain region: tests of planning and set-shifting to the prefrontal cortex, verbal learning tests traditionally to the left temporal lobe, the complex figure to right-hemisphere visuospatial memory, and so on. The clinician chooses the tests that the referral question calls for, so in practice it is used as a flexible, domain-based battery (Section 11.1), not a fixed one. Table 11.9 groups the tests you will most often see reported from the battery by the domain each assesses. Most are taught in their own sections of this chapter; here you need to know what each is for and where it sits. Two are taught nowhere else in this chapter. The Digit Vigilance Test is a page densely packed with rows of digits on which the person crosses out two target digits as fast as possible; the score is the time taken together with the omissions (targets missed) and commissions (other digits crossed out), and it measures sustained attention . The Triads Test measures divided attention : the person must respond to words that the examiner reads out in groups of three while, at the same time, identifying digits that the examiner traces on the person's hand, so that attention has to be split between two streams of information at once.
