The battery's norms are what make it Indian, so it is worth seeing how they were built. As the battery's users describe them, healthy volunteers were tested in every combination of three levels of education (illiterate; school, 1st to 10th standard; and college, 11th standard and above), three age bands (young adults 16 to 30, middle-aged adults 31 to 50, and older adults 51 to 65) and both sexes, with 30 volunteers in each combination. That gives 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 groups, and 18 × 30 = 540 people in all. For every score of every test, the manual gives percentile norms within each of the 18 groups: the percentage of comparable healthy people who scored at or below a given level. The usual cut-off is the 15th percentile , close to one standard deviation below the mean (which strictly corresponds to about the 16th percentile): a score that fewer than 15 per cent of comparable healthy people would obtain is read as a deficit in that function. Follow one score through the tables. Juhi, the schoolteacher of Section 11.2.6 (an invented case), is 40, female and has twelve years of schooling plus a diploma, so she belongs in the group of women aged 31 to 50 with education of 11th standard and above. On the Digit Vigilance Test she takes 690 seconds. For a timed test, a longer time is a worse score, so the cut-off is a time: suppose (invented figures, not the manual's) that the 15th-percentile time for her group is 600 seconds. Step 1: compare. Her 690 seconds is slower than 600 seconds. Step 2: translate. Slower than the 15th-percentile time means that fewer than 15 per cent of comparable healthy women were as slow, so her score falls below the 15th percentile. Step 3: conclude. Juhi has a deficit in sustained attention, which fits her complaint that she loses her place when marking a pile of answer scripts. Now suppose an older woman of 58 with eight years of schooling also took 690 seconds. She belongs in a different group, and if (again invented) that group's 15th-percentile time were 840 seconds, her identical 690 seconds would be faster than the cut-off and would count as normal. The same raw score is a deficit for one person and normal for another, which is the whole point of stratified norms. Published studies show how widely the battery is used: to measure outcome in cognitive retraining after head injury and in schizophrenia (Book 2, Section 9.9 describes cognitive retraining), to profile patients with epilepsy, bipolar disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder, and to follow patients after brain surgery. In such studies raw scores are typically converted to percentiles from the battery's age-, sex- and education-matched tables, and a score below the 15th percentile is classed as impaired in that domain. Clinical link In awake brain surgery, a tumour near the language or motor areas is removed while the patient is conscious, so that the surgeons can check from moment to moment that the patient can still speak, understand and move. NIMHANS clinicians have described how a clinical neuropsychologist prepares such a patient: a detailed assessment a few days before surgery, typically with tests from the NIMHANS Neuropsychology Battery normed for Indian age, education and sex, sets a baseline; the same functions are then checked during the operation, with the aim of preserving the patient's existing level of functioning. Here the battery is doing exactly what Section 11.1 said modern neuropsychology is for: not finding the lesion, which the scan has already found, but measuring what the patient can do and protecting it. Exam trap NIMHANS battery = Bengaluru; Rao, Subbakrishna and Gopukumar; 2004 manual; 19 tests; adults 16 to 65; percentile norms by age, sex and education; 15th percentile cut-off; domain-based, with no single index. It uses the Colour Trails Test, not the alphabet-based Trail Making Part B. It was built on Luria's principles of localisation and lateralisation, but it is not a translation of the Luria-Nebraska (the Hindi version of the Luria-Nebraska is the AIIMS battery, Section 11.3.6). Do not confuse it with the NIMHANS battery for specific learning disability used in disability certification (Book 2, Section 9.9.8), which is a different instrument. The NIMHANS batteries for children and for older adults Children are not small adults, neuropsychologically speaking. Their abilities are still developing, at different rates for different functions, so a child's score must be compared with children of the same age, and a test that suits a 40-year-old may be meaningless at seven. The NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery for Children was developed by Bhoomika R. Kar , Shobini L. Rao, B. A. Chandramouli and K. Thennarasu, with a manual dated 2004, and has norms for ages 5 to 15. It has been validated on children with brain injury. In a study published in 2011 the same authors used the battery to chart the growth of neuropsychological functions in 400 healthy children from three schools in Bangalore city, at eleven age levels from 5 to 15. The tests reported in that study show how the adult domains were adapted for children: the Finger Tapping Test for motor speed; a Colour Cancellation Test for visual scanning and sustained attention and the Colour Trails Test for focused attention; the Design Fluency Test, the Porteus Maze Test for planning and foresight, and verbal and visual N-back tasks for working memory, as tests of executive function; the Motor-Free Visual Perception Test, a picture completion test and a block design test for visuoperceptual, visuoconceptual and visuoconstructive ability; the Token Test for verbal comprehension; and Rey's Auditory Verbal Learning Test and a Memory for Designs Test for verbal and visual learning and memory. The Indian Psychiatric Society's 2025 guidelines on autism also list the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test and a phonemic fluency test among the children's battery's tests. Chapter 7 describes developmental assessment more broadly. At the other end of life, the NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery for Elderly (NNB-E) was developed for Indian older adults aged 55 to 80, a group in whom the main question is often whether memory complaints mark the beginning of dementia. In a preliminary report of its clinical validity in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 2013, Ravikesh Tripathi and his colleagues found that patients with Alzheimer's disease performed significantly worse than healthy older people on every test, memory and non-memory alike, but that tests of episodic and semantic memory were particularly good at telling the two groups apart. Scores on the battery's subtests rose with scores on the Hindi Mental State Examination and fell as ratings on the Clinical Dementia Rating and the Everyday Abilities Scale for India rose, which is the pattern you would expect if all of them measure the same decline. Section 11.7 teaches the Hindi Mental State Examination and the Clinical Dementia Rating. Exam trap Three NIMHANS neuropsychological batteries, three age ranges: adults 16 to 65 (Rao and colleagues, 2004), children 5 to 15 (Kar and colleagues, 2004) and elderly 55 to 80 (NNB-E; validity reported by Tripathi and colleagues, 2013). The children's battery is associated with Bhoomika Kar ; the adult battery with Shobini Rao . The PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction In Chandigarh, the psychiatry department of PGIMER faced a practical question in the 1970s. Patients were referred to its psychology section with a single request: is there brain pathology here or not? This was the old "organic versus functional" question that Section 11.1 describes, and no single test answered it well. The psychologists already had several tests built or adapted in their own department, including a memory scale, verbal and performance tests of intelligence and tests of perception and visuomotor copying. Could they be combined into one judgement? Key study: screening for organic brain dysfunction at PGIMER (1984) Dwarka Pershad, S. K. Verma, S. Malhotra and S. Prabhakar reported in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 1984 on 180 adult patients, aged 20 to 50, who had been referred to the psychology section between 1976 and 1980 for differential diagnosis of brain pathology, and in whom at least two of three cognitive functions (intelligence, memory and perceptuo-motor ability) had been tested and a clinical diagnosis had later been reached from follow-up and other evidence. They rescored nineteen psychological test variables to reduce the effects of age and education. For each variable they drew the frequency distributions separately for patients with and without brain damage, and plotted them as cumulative curves (ogives) to find the score that separated the two groups best. Each score was then converted into a rating, with 0 for average performance and higher ratings for lower scores, and the ratings were combined. The combined rating identified about two thirds of the organic patients correctly among these difficult-to-diagnose cases. Two thirds may sound modest, but these were the cases that clinicians had found hard; the study turned a collection of separate tests into a single, reproducible rating, and that rating is the core of the PGI battery. The battery that grew from this work is the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction (PGI-BBD), whose handbook by Pershad and Verma was published by the National Psychological Corporation, Agra, in 1990. It is administered in Hindi, and it combines five tests : The PGI Memory Scale (Section 11.3.5), which contributes ten scores, one for each of its subtests. A short form of C. M. Bhatia 's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (Bhatia's short scale), consisting of the Kohs Block Design test and Alexander's Pass-Along test, which contributes two scores. Bhatia's full battery, built for Indians who cannot read, is described in Chapter 6. The Verbal Adult Intelligence Scale (VAIS), a Hindi verbal intelligence scale whose four subtests carry Wechsler names ( Information, Digit Span, Arithmetic and Comprehension ); the VAIS contributes five scores. The Nahor-Benson Test of perceptual acuity, eight cards of which five each carry a design to be copied and three carry instructions to draw an object; it is read as a test of visual acuity and depth perception, and it contributes one score. The Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test , nine designs to be copied (Section 11.5), which contributes one score. Add the contributions: 10 + 2 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 19, the same nineteen variables as the 1984 study. Each raw score is looked up in the handbook's tables, which allow for age and education, and converted into a dysfunction rating from 0 to 3; the 19 ratings are then added to give a total. Since each of the 19 ratings can be at most 3, the highest possible total is 19 × 3 = 57. Studies using the battery report its bands as follows. Remember PGI-BBD total dysfunction rating = sum of the 19 ratings (each 0 to 3), so the total runs from 0 to 19 × 3 = 57. Bands: 0 to 19 no impairment; 20 to 38 slight impairment; 39 to 57 severe impairment. Higher means more dysfunction. The norms are for adults, usually given as 20 to 59 years (one Indian guideline gives 20 to 50), and the full battery takes about 90 to 120 minutes. Return to Ehsan from Section 11.2.4 and suppose that, instead of the Halstead-Reitan, he had been assessed in Hindi with the PGI-BBD. His invented ratings (Figure 11.6) are: on the ten memory scores, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 2 and 1; on the two performance scores, 3 and 3; on the five verbal scores, 0, 1, 1, 0 and 1; on the Nahor-Benson, 2; and on the Bender, 3. Step 1: add within each test. Memory: 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 10. Performance: 3 + 3 = 6. Verbal: 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 3. Nahor-Benson: 2. Bender: 3. Step 2: add the five subtotals: 10 + 6 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 24. Step 3: place the total in its band. 24 lies between 20 and 38, so the battery rates Ehsan as having slight impairment . Step 4: look at where the ratings came from, just as you did with his Halstead-Reitan profile. His verbal intelligence scores are almost untouched (3 out of a possible 15), while the block design and pass-along tests, which demand working out a new spatial problem against the clock, earned the maximum rating of 3 each, and the two copying tests are also affected. The two batteries, built on different continents from different tests, tell the same story about Ehsan: old verbal knowledge preserved, new problem-solving and visuospatial work impaired. PGI Memory Scale 10 scores Bhatia's short scale 2 scores Verbal Adult Intelligence Scale, 5 scores Nahor-Benson Test 1 score Bender-Gestalt Test 1 score 19 scores, each converted (handbook tables, by age and education) into a dysfunction rating of 0 to 3 Total rating = sum of 19 ratings (0 to 57) No impairment, 0 to 19 Slight, 20 to 38 Severe, 39 to 57 0 57 Ehsan (invented): 24 Figure 11.6 How the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction turns five tests into one number. Notice that the PGI Memory Scale supplies more than half of the 19 ratings, so memory weighs heavily in the total, and that the total is read against three bands; Ehsan's invented total of 24 falls in the slight-impairment band. What is the PGI-BBD good for? It answers the screening question it was built for, "is there brain dysfunction, and roughly how much?", in a language and with tests suited to Hindi-speaking North Indian adults, and in about two hours rather than a day. It remains in use in Indian hospitals and in Indian research on alcohol and opioid dependence, depression and the cognitive after-effects of COVID-19, and it is listed among the tools for assessing cognition after head injury (see the Indian context box below). Its limits follow from the same design. A single total says little about which functions are affected (although, as with Ehsan, the pattern of ratings helps); the battery contains no real test of executive function, which the NIMHANS battery covers well; and its tests and norms are decades old. Exam trap PGI-BBD = PGIMER, Chandigarh (not NIMHANS, Bengaluru); Pershad and Verma; handbook 1990. Its five tests are the PGI Memory Scale, Bhatia's short scale (Kohs Block Design and Alexander's Pass-Along), the Verbal Adult Intelligence Scale, the Nahor-Benson Test and the Bender-Gestalt : 19 scores, total rating 0 to 57. The perceptual test is Nahor-Benson , not Benton (Arthur Benton's tests are in Sections 11.4 and 11.5). In a "which is NOT part of the PGI-BBD" item, the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, the Tower of London and the Halstead Category Test are the outsiders. Note that it contains the Bender, and that the memory scale is part of the battery as well as a test in its own right. The PGI Memory Scale Memory complaints are among the commonest reasons for referral to a clinical psychologist, and in the 1970s Indian clinicians had no memory test built for their patients. The Wechsler Memory Scale (Section 11.4) existed, but its stories, word pairs and designs had been built and normed in the United States. Dwarka Pershad and N. N. Wig of PGIMER described "a battery of simple tests of memory for use in India" in the journal Neurology India in 1976, published a normative study on elderly people in 1977 and reported its reliability and validity in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 1978. The PGI Memory Scale (PGIMS) is usually dated to 1977. It is given in Hindi, it uses simple material that people with limited education can manage, and its norms are for adults aged 20 to 45, broken down by age and education. The scale has ten subtests , set out in Table 11.10 with the maximum score of each as commonly reported (record forms in circulation differ slightly, so check the maxima on the form you are using). The table describes each subtest in general terms; the actual questions and lists are in the test materials and are not reproduced here. Table 11.10 The ten subtests of the PGI Memory Scale (Pershad and Wig). No. Subtest What it samples (in general terms) Maximum 1 Remote memory Questions about events of the person's distant past 6 2 Recent memory Questions about recent events and the present day 5 3 Mental balance Overlearned sequences under control: counting backwards, serial subtraction 9 4 Attention and concentration Digit span forward and backward 15 5 Delayed recall Recall of a list of words after a delay 10 6 Immediate recall Repeating sentences of increasing length at once 12 7 Retention for similar pairs Learning pairs of words that belong together in meaning 5 8 Retention for dissimilar pairs Learning pairs of unrelated words 15 9 Visual retention Drawing simple designs from memory after a brief exposure 13 10 Recognition Picking out objects or pictures shown earlier from a larger set 10 Read the list as a map of memory, using the distinctions taught in Section 11.4 and in Book 1, Sections 7.3.4 and 7.3.6. Subtests 3 and 4 test attention, span and mental control rather than storage: mental balance is the old clinical name for running an overlearned sequence under deliberate control, and has nothing to do with emotional balance. Subtest 6 tests immediate verbal memory. Subtests 5, 7, 8 and 9 test what clinicians most often need to know about, the learning and retention of new material, verbal and visual. Subtest 10 tests recognition, which is easier than free recall and can show that material was stored even when it cannot be recalled. Subtests 1 and 2 test memory for the distant and the recent past. The pair of paired-associate subtests is particularly neat. A pair of words that already belong together can be remembered by leaning on what the person already knows; a pair of unrelated words must be bound together from scratch. A person whose new learning is impaired often manages the related pairs reasonably and fails the unrelated ones badly. How good is the scale? Later Indian reviews, summarising the original reports, give test-retest reliabilities of 0.69 to 0.85 for the individual subtests, and Pershad and Wig's 1978 paper reported evidence of the scale's validity as well as its reliability (Chapter 3 explains test-retest reliability; Chapter 4, validity). One limitation shows up in research: healthy people, and many patients, score at or near the maximum on the easy subtests (remote memory, recent memory and mental balance), a ceiling effect that makes those subtests insensitive to mild impairment. One Indian study of schizophrenia dropped those three subtests from its analysis for exactly this reason. Each subtest score is judged against the norms for the person's age and education group. A clear way to see how far a score lies from the norm is to turn it into a z score : the distance of the score from the norm group's mean, measured in standard deviations (Chapter 5 teaches standard scores in full). Remember z = (X − M) ÷ SD X is the person's score on the subtest, M the mean of the norm group, and SD the standard deviation of the norm group. A z of 0 is exactly average; −1 is one standard deviation below average. Conventions vary, but a score more than about 1.5 to 2 standard deviations below the mean is commonly read as a deficit. Bela is a 42-year-old nurse in Chandigarh with 14 years of education (an invented case). Three months ago she had a viral infection of the brain, encephalitis, from which she has physically recovered, but her colleagues say she asks the same questions again and again and forgets what she was told at the morning handover. Table 11.11 shows her PGI Memory Scale scores against invented norms for her group (the real norm tables are in the handbook). Work two rows by hand. Delayed recall: X = 3, M = 8.6, SD = 1.6, so z = (3 − 8.6) ÷ 1.6 = −5.6 ÷ 1.6 = −3.50. Remote memory: X = 6, M = 5.8, SD = 0.5, so z = (6 − 5.8) ÷ 0.5 = 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = +0.40. The other rows are worked the same way and rounded to two decimal places. Subtest Bela's score Norm mean Norm SD z Remote memory 6 5.8 0.5 +0.40 Recent memory 3 4.6 0.6 −2.67 Mental balance 7 7.5 1.4 −0.36 Attention and concentration 10 10.5 1.8 −0.28 Delayed recall 3 8.6 1.6 −3.50 Immediate recall 10 10.4 1.3 −0.31 Similar pairs 4 4.7 0.5 −1.40 Dissimilar pairs 5 11.5 2.2 −2.95 Visual retention 7 11.4 1.6 −2.75 Recognition 8 9.4 0.8 −1.75 Now read the profile. Bela's total is 6 + 3 + 7 + 10 + 3 + 10 + 4 + 5 + 7 + 8 = 63, but, as with every total in this chapter, the pattern matters more than the sum. Her attention span, her mental control, her immediate repetition of sentences and her memory for the distant past are all within about half a standard deviation of the mean: she can take information in and hold it for a few seconds, and her old memories are intact. What has failed is everything that requires new material to be stored and kept: delayed recall (z = −3.50), learning unrelated word pairs (−2.95), retaining designs (−2.75) and memory for recent events (−2.67). Related pairs (−1.40) are much better than unrelated pairs, because existing knowledge carries her part of the way. Both verbal and visual new learning are affected, which suggests damage on both sides of the brain rather than one. And her recognition (−1.75) is clearly better than her free recall (−3.50), a sign that some of what she cannot recall has been stored and could be prompted. Taken together, this is the profile of an anterograde amnesia, a failure to lay down new memories with old ones spared, which fits an encephalitis that has damaged the memory structures of the temporal lobes (Book 3, Section 10.8.3 describes the amnestic disorders; Section 11.4 explains how recall and recognition are used to separate problems of storage from problems of retrieval). The profile also tells the team what will help: written handover notes and a fixed routine will work far better for Bela than asking her to try harder to remember. Exam trap PGI Memory Scale = Pershad and Wig (not Pershad and Verma), PGIMER, 1977; 10 subtests. Learn them as five pairs: remote and recent memory; mental balance and attention-concentration; delayed and immediate recall; retention for similar and for dissimilar pairs; visual retention and recognition. "Mental balance" is mental control (counting backwards, serial tasks), not an emotional measure. The scale is part of the PGI-BBD as well as a test on its own. It is not the Wechsler Memory Scale and has no "memory quotient" index structure like the WMS-IV (Section 11.4). Other Indian tools, and choosing among them Two further batteries complete the picture. The AIIMS Comprehensive Neuropsychological Battery in Hindi (adult form) was developed at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, by S. Gupta, S. K. Khandelwal, P. N. Tandon and their colleagues, and published in the Journal of Personality and Clinical Studies in 2000. It is the Indian descendant of the Luria-Nebraska (Section 11.2.6): 160 items divided into ten basic scales (motor, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, reading, writing, arithmetic, memory and intellectual processes) and four secondary scales (left hemisphere, right hemisphere, pathognomonic and a total score), with norms for ages 15 to 80. If you compare its basic scales with Table 11.7, you will see that it keeps ten of the Luria-Nebraska's eleven clinical scales and has no separate rhythm scale. The newest addition is the ICMR Neurocognitive Tool Box (ICMR-NCTB), developed by a consortium under the Indian Council of Medical Research to standardise the diagnosis of dementia across India's linguistic and educational diversity; its design was published in 2020 and its validation in 2021, in five languages (Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam), with tests of attention and executive function, episodic memory, language and visuospatial function. Several other Indian adaptations are taught where their topic belongs. Mary Ganguli's Hindi Mental State Examination (1995), an adaptation of the Mini-Mental State Examination for illiterate rural older people, is in Section 11.7. Savita Malhotra's Childhood Psychopathology Measurement Schedule, an Indian rating scale for children's behaviour problems from PGIMER, is in Section 11.9. The answer follows from the question, just as Section 11.1 said. If a Hindi-speaking adult is referred with the old question, "is there any brain dysfunction, and how much?", and a single rating is wanted quickly, the PGI-BBD was built for that. If the question is "which functions are impaired, and which are spared?", as it is when planning rehabilitation, measuring change after cognitive retraining or preparing for brain surgery, the domain-by-domain profile of the NIMHANS battery, with its age-, sex- and education-matched percentiles, is the better tool; the NIMHANS children's battery answers the same question for a child of 5 to 15. If the complaint is memory, the PGI Memory Scale on its own takes far less time than either battery. If an older person may be developing dementia, the NNB-E or the ICMR-NCTB, which were built for that question, are better than a general battery. And whichever battery is used, the clinician still asks of every score the question this section began with: compared with whom? Indian context These tools are not museum pieces. The Indian Psychiatric Society's clinical practice guidelines published in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 2025 list the PGI-BBD, the PGI Memory Scale, the NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery, the AIIMS battery and the ICMR-NCTB among the tools for assessing cognitive impairment after traumatic brain injury, and the guidelines on alcohol use disorder list the NIMHANS, AIIMS, ICMR and PGI batteries alongside the Luria-Nebraska and the Halstead-Reitan. The same alcohol guidelines describe a brief cognitive screen for alcohol use disorder built from three tests of the NIMHANS battery (finger tapping, the N-back and the Auditory Verbal Learning Test). The tools were built where they are still most used: the NIMHANS batteries in Bengaluru, the PGI tests in Chandigarh and the AIIMS battery in New Delhi. Exam trap Indian syllabi (the RML and IHBAS syllabi among them) name these tools, and the questions usually test the pairing of tool, author and institution: NIMHANS battery, Rao, Bengaluru ; PGI-BBD, Pershad and Verma, Chandigarh ; PGI Memory Scale, Pershad and Wig, Chandigarh ; AIIMS battery, Hindi, based on the Luria-Nebraska, New Delhi . Two other traps: the Hindi Mental State Examination is a screening test (Section 11.7), not a battery; and an option that calls the NIMHANS battery "a Hindi adaptation of the Luria-Nebraska" has confused it with the AIIMS battery. N. Wig, 10. 11.4 Memory Tests: The Wechsler Memory Scale, Digit Span and the Learning Tests Lower yield · 3 Qs "Doctor, she keeps forgetting." Few complaints bring more people to a clinic, and few are vaguer. The daughter who says it may mean that her mother repeats the same question five times in an hour, or loses her spectacles, or cannot recall what she cooked yesterday, or has started to confuse the names of her grandchildren, or cannot follow a television serial any more. Each of these is a failure of something people call memory, but they are not failures of the same thing. A clinician who simply writes "memory poor" in the notes has said almost nothing. Is the trouble in taking information in, in keeping it, or in getting it back out? Is it worse for words or for pictures? Does it affect what was learned this morning, or what was learned forty years ago as well? Is it really memory at all, or is the mother simply not attending, or too depressed to try? A memory test is a way of answering these questions under controlled conditions. It puts known material into the person at a known moment and asks for it back at chosen moments afterwards, so that the examiner knows exactly what was offered, when, and how much came back. Everything else in this section is a variation on that plan: a few digits asked for at once, a list of words offered five times, a story asked for after half an hour, a drawing copied and then drawn again from memory. The theory of memory itself, the stores, the working memory model and the kinds of forgetting, is taught in Book 1, Chapter 7, and the disorders of memory, the amnesias and dementias, in Book 3, Sections 2.7 and 10.8.3. This section is about the tests: what each one asks, how it is scored, and how a pattern of scores is read. What a memory examination asks Start with the three processes that every account of memory recognises (Book 1, Section 7.1.1). Getting information in is encoding , keeping it over time is storage , and getting it back out when it is needed is retrieval . A person can fail at any of the three, and the remedy, the diagnosis and the advice to the family differ for each. The art of memory testing is to arrange the moments of a test so that each process shows itself separately. Clinicians and cognitive psychologists use slightly different words for the same territory, and you need both vocabularies. At the bedside (Book 2, Section 2.6.5) memory is divided by how long ago the material was learned. The first, immediate memory , is the reproduction of material within seconds of hearing or seeing it; recent memory covers the last few minutes, hours and days; remote memory covers months and years. Cognitive psychology divides memory by the stores and systems involved: short-term memory, working memory and long-term memory, which divides in turn into episodic, semantic and procedural memory (Book 1, Sections 7.2 and 7.5). The two vocabularies do not map neatly onto each other. When a neuropsychologist reads a list of fifteen words and asks for them back at once, she calls the result "immediate recall", yet fifteen words are far more than short-term memory can hold, so much of what comes back has already been carried into long-term memory. "Immediate" in a test manual means "asked for straight away", not "held in the short-term store". With those words in hand, the moments of a typical memory examination fall into place, and Figure 11.7 sets them out. The examiner first presents the material: a list of words, a short story, a set of word pairs or a design. She then asks for it back at once. If the person cannot reproduce even a short sequence immediately, the problem is one of attention or registration, and there is no point in asking whether the material was stored, because it never got in. If the material is offered several times, the examiner can watch learning happen: a healthy person recalls more on each trial, and the rise across trials is the learning curve . Next comes something to interfere: a second list, or other tasks. Then, after a delay of about twenty to thirty minutes filled with other tests so that the person cannot rehearse, comes delayed recall , the best single measure of whether new material has been retained. Last comes a recognition trial, in which the person is shown the studied items mixed with new ones and asked which were on the list. Recognition is easier than recall because the item itself acts as a cue (Book 1, Section 7.1.3), and the contrast between the two is one of the most useful comparisons in the whole of neuropsychology: if a person cannot recall the words but can recognise them, they were stored and the problem lies in retrieval; if he cannot even recognise them, they were never stored. One memory test, six moments: what each one measures time 0 seconds a few minutes minutes 20 to 30 min after delay Present material Immediate recall Repeated trials Interference Delayed recall Recognition words, story or design span and registration learning curve proactive and retroactive retention (storage) storage or retrieval? Alongside: working memory (digits backward) holds and rearranges material. Separately: remote memory for the personal and public past, months or years old. Figure 11.7 The moments of a memory examination. Notice that each moment answers a different question: recall seconds later shows registration, repeated trials show learning, an interfering task and a filled delay show how well material was kept, and recognition shows whether material that cannot be recalled was stored at all. Two more distinctions complete the map. The first is between kinds of material. Verbal memory (words, stories, word pairs) and visual memory (designs, faces, locations) can fail separately, and the classic finding behind this is that people who had the left temporal lobe removed for epilepsy lost more verbal memory while those who lost the right temporal lobe lost more memory for designs and faces. A deficit confined to one kind of material is a material-specific memory deficit, and it is the reason every good battery tests both. The second is between new learning and old memories. Failure to lay down new memories after an illness or injury is anterograde amnesia; loss of memories laid down before it is retrograde amnesia (Book 1, Section 7.10.1). Almost every test in this section measures new learning, which is what most illnesses damage first; remote memory needs its own tests (Section 11.4.7). Table 11.13 brings the kinds of memory together with the tasks that test them. Table 11.13 The kinds of memory a clinician tests, and how. "Recent memory" at the bedside (minutes to days) is long-term memory for recent events. Recognition is easier than recall; good recognition with poor recall points to a retrieval problem, poor recognition to a storage problem. Digit span forward and backward The oldest memory test in the clinic is also the simplest. The examiner says a string of digits and the person says them back. Joseph Jacobs measured span in this way in 1887 (Book 1, Section 7.2.3), Alfred Binet put the repetition of digits into his intelligence scale, and David Wechsler made it a subtest of his adult and school-age intelligence scales and of his original memory scale. A test that has lasted well over a century must be doing something useful. What exactly is it measuring? First, the procedure, because the details matter. In digit span forward the examiner reads the digits at a steady rate of about one per second, in an even voice, without grouping them the way people group a telephone number, and the person repeats them in the same order. The strings start short and grow by one digit at a time, and there are two different strings at each length. Testing stops when the person fails both strings of the same length. In digit span backward the person hears a new set of strings and must say each one in reverse: hearing 7, 2, 9 he must say 9, 2, 7. The fourth edition of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (2008) added a third task, digit sequencing, in which the person repeats the digits in ascending order, so that hearing 7, 2, 9 he says 2, 7, 9. Two numbers come out of each task. The longest span is the length of the longest string the person repeated correctly on at least one of its two trials. The points are simply the number of trials passed. Wechsler's scales add the points across the tasks into a raw score and convert it into a scaled score against age norms (Chapter 5 explains scaled scores). Work through an invented record to see how the counting goes. Neel is a 24-year-old postgraduate student who volunteered as a healthy comparison subject in a hospital study. His performance is set out in Table 11.14. Table 11.14 Neel's digit span (an invented record). Two strings are given at each length; one point for each string repeated correctly. Forward, longest span: the longest length at which Neel passed at least one trial is 7 (he failed the first string of seven digits but passed the second). His forward span is therefore 7. Forward, points: 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 8. Backward, longest span: he passed at least one trial at length 5 (the second one) but neither at length 6, so his backward span is 5. Backward, points: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 6. Total points for the two tasks: 8 + 6 = 14. Forward span minus backward span: 7 − 5 = 2. How do these numbers compare with other adults? Most adults of average education repeat six or seven digits forward and four or five backward, backward span is usually one or two digits shorter than forward span, and a forward span below five is usually abnormal (Book 2, Section 2.6.4, gives the same bedside figures). Neel's 7 forward and 5 backward, two apart, are ordinary healthy values. Note that span depends on schooling, on hearing and on language: digit names that take longer to say give a shorter span (Book 1, Section 7.3.2), so a person tested in a language other than his own, or compared with norms collected in another language, can look worse than he is. Now to what the two tasks measure, which is what the papers ask. Repeating digits in the order heard requires the person to attend to the string, register it and hold it for a few seconds: it measures immediate attention span , the capacity of the short-term store that George Miller put at about seven items (Book 1, Section 7.2.3). Repeating them backwards requires all of that and more. The person must hold the string while he works on it, reading it off from the end, keeping his place and suppressing the urge to say it the way it came in. Holding and manipulating information at the same time is exactly what Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch meant by working memory (Book 1, Sections 7.3.4 and 7.3.6), and backward span is the classic clinical test of it. Digit sequencing is a second working memory task of the same kind, and Letter-Number Sequencing in the Wechsler scales (hear "7, C, 2, A", say "2, 7, A, C") is a third. There is a visual counterpart too. In the Corsi block-tapping test , devised by Philip Corsi at McGill University in 1972, the examiner taps a sequence on blocks scattered on a board and the person taps the same sequence back, which gives a visuospatial span. What do span scores tell a clinician? Three things, mainly. A short forward span tells you that attention and registration are impaired, as they are in delirium, in severe anxiety, in acute intoxication and in many people who are simply exhausted or unwilling, and it warns you that every later memory test will be hard to interpret, because material that never got in cannot be stored. A normal forward span alongside very poor delayed recall is the signature of the classic amnesic syndrome: the patient H.M. could repeat digits normally yet could not learn a new list (Book 1, Section 7.2.6). A disproportionately poor backward span points to a weakness of working memory and executive control, common after frontal and diffuse brain injury, in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and in schizophrenia. What span does not tell you is anything about long-term retention, about memory for events or about skills. An impossibly low span in a person who chats fluently is itself informative, because it can be a sign of poor effort; Section 11.1 explains how effort is checked. Clinical link Span is fragile in exactly the people a psychiatric clinician sees most. An anxious student at a viva, a man three days into alcohol withdrawal and a woman with a high fever can all show a forward span of four. Before concluding that memory is impaired, check that the person can hear you, is not delirious (Book 3, Section 10.8.8), understands the language of testing and is trying. Repeat the test later in the session if anxiety seems to be the cause: anxious span improves with reassurance; the span of a damaged brain does not. Exam trap Backward digit span measures working memory (a real 2025 paper asked exactly this), because the digits must be held and manipulated at once. Forward span measures immediate attention span (short-term memory). The wrong options are all real memory systems tested in other ways: long-term memory is tested by delayed recall after a filled delay of 20 to 30 minutes (Section 11.4.4); sensory memory , the brief iconic or echoic trace lasting a fraction of a second to a few seconds, is studied with laboratory methods such as Sperling's partial report (Book 1, Section 7.2.2), not with spoken digits; procedural memory , memory for skills, is tested by learning a motor task such as mirror drawing, which H.M. learned without remembering the practice (Book 1, Sections 7.5.1 and 7.10.2). Amnesic patients can have a normal digit span, which is exactly why span is not a test of long-term memory. The Wechsler Memory Scale Digit span tells you whether material gets in. It cannot tell you whether a story heard ten minutes ago is still there, or whether a design is remembered as well as a sentence. For that a clinician needs a battery of memory tests built on the same plan and standardised on the same people, and the most widely used one is the work of David Wechsler (1896 to 1981). Wechsler, the chief psychologist at Bellevue Hospital in New York, had published the Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale in 1939 (Book 1, Section 9.3.2; Chapter 6). In 1945 he published "A standardized memory scale for clinical use" in the Journal of Psychology : a short memory examination that any trained psychologist could give in the same way, so that the memory of one patient could be compared with that of others and with the same patient's intelligence. The original Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) had seven subtests, which you should know by type rather than by item. Personal and Current Information asked simple questions about the person's own life and about well-known public facts. Orientation asked about time and place. Mental Control asked for overlearned sequences under pressure, such as counting backwards or running through the alphabet. Logical Memory read two short stories aloud and asked the person to retell each at once, scoring the number of ideas recalled. Memory Span was digits forward and backward. Visual Reproduction showed simple geometric designs for a few seconds and asked the person to draw them from memory. Associate Learning read pairs of words, some easy because the words belonged together and some hard because they did not, and then gave the first word of each pair and asked for the second, over three trials. The raw points were added, an age correction was added to the total, and a table converted the result into a memory quotient (MQ) on the same scale as the Wechsler-Bellevue IQ. The point of that design was comparison: if a patient's MQ fell far below his IQ, his memory was worse than his general ability would predict. An alternate form, Form II, followed in 1946 (by C. P. Stone, J. Girdner and R. Albrecht) so that a patient could be retested without simply remembering the stories; why alternate forms help is explained in Chapter 3, Section 3.3. The 1945 scale was used for four decades, and its weaknesses taught the field a great deal. All of its recall was immediate, so it could not detect the rapid forgetting over half an hour that is the hallmark of the amnesic syndrome. Its single MQ mixed true memory with orientation, attention and general knowledge, so two patients with the same MQ could have quite different problems. It was almost entirely verbal, which made it blind to many right-hemisphere disorders, and its norms came from a small sample. Clinicians patched it first: in 1975 Elbert Russell added a recall of the stories and designs after a delay of about thirty minutes. Then the publisher rebuilt it, four times over, and Table 11.15 traces the editions. Table 11.15 The Wechsler Memory Scale from 1945 to the WMS-5. It was standardised together with the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition, on about 1,400 adults in the United States, which means that a person's memory scores and intelligence scores come from the same norms and can be compared directly. There are two batteries. The Adult battery, for ages 16 to 69, has six core subtests and an optional screen. The Older Adult battery, for ages 65 to 90, leaves out two of the visual subtests to keep testing short. (For people aged 65 to 69 the examiner may use either.) Most subtests come in two parts: part I is the immediate recall, and part II is the recall of the same material after a delay of 20 to 30 minutes, usually followed by a recognition trial. The Auditory Memory index combines the two verbal subtests, Logical Memory and Verbal Paired Associates, parts I and II. The Visual Memory index combines Designs and Visual Reproduction, parts I and II. The Visual Working Memory index combines Spatial Addition and Symbol Span. The Immediate Memory index takes the four part I scores, and the Delayed Memory index the four part II scores. So the same subtest scores are cut two ways, by kind of material (auditory against visual) and by time (immediate against delayed), and the two cuts answer the two questions the clinician most wants answered: is memory worse for words or for designs, and is the trouble in learning or in keeping? Notice what is missing. The WMS-III had a Working Memory index built on an auditory task (letter-number sequencing) and a visual one (spatial span); the WMS-IV dropped the auditory working memory task, because the WAIS-IV already measures auditory working memory with digit span and arithmetic, and kept only visual working memory, now measured by two new subtests. And because the Older Adult battery omits Designs and Spatial Addition, it reports only four indices, with no Visual Working Memory index at all. Each subtest gives a scaled score with a mean of 10 and a standard deviation of 3, and each index an index score with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, the same metric as an IQ (Chapter 5 teaches standard scores in full). To read an index score, turn it into a distance from the mean in standard deviation units, a z score. Remember How far an index score lies from the average: z = (index score − 100) / 15 where 100 is the mean of the index scores in the norm group of the person's age, 15 is their standard deviation, and z is the number of standard deviations the person stands above (positive) or below (negative) that mean. Urvi is an invented 71-year-old retired schoolteacher whose family noticed over the past year that she asks the same questions again and again. She is given the Older Adult battery. Her General Ability Index from the WAIS-IV, which reflects reasoning rather than memory, is 102. Her WMS-IV indices are Auditory Memory 78, Visual Memory 74, Immediate Memory 82 and Delayed Memory 70. Delayed Memory: z = (70 − 100) / 15 = −30 / 15 = −2.00. On the normal curve about 2 people in 100 score this low or lower (the exact table value is 2.3 percent), so the score is at about the 2nd percentile. Immediate Memory: z = (82 − 100) / 15 = −18 / 15 = −1.20, about the 12th percentile (table value 11.5 percent, rounded to the nearest whole percentile). The gap between general ability and delayed memory: 102 − 70 = 32 points, a little more than two standard deviations (32 / 15 = 2.13). What does this mean in plain words? Urvi reasons like an average woman of her age, but she keeps new material far worse than her reasoning predicts, and she loses more over the delay than she fails to take in at first (her delayed score is 12 points below her immediate score). A memory deficit out of proportion to general ability, worst after a delay, is the pattern of a disorder of storage such as early Alzheimer's disease, although no single test makes that diagnosis (Book 3, Section 10.9.6). Whether a gap between two scores is larger than measurement error alone would produce is a question for the standard error of the difference (Chapter 3, Section 3.7.6); the WMS-IV manual supplies tables for exactly these comparisons, which is one reason the co-norming with the WAIS-IV matters. Exam trap The WMS-IV (and the WMS-5) indices are Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory, Immediate Memory and Delayed Memory . The lures each come from somewhere real. Verbal IQ and Performance IQ were the summary scores of the old Wechsler intelligence scales up to the WAIS-III; the WAIS-IV replaced them with four indices (Chapter 6). Crystallised and fluid intelligence are Raymond Cattell's and John Horn's broad abilities, a theory of intelligence (Chapter 6). "Attention, concentration and vigilance only" borrows the WMS-R's Attention/Concentration index; vigilance is measured by continuous performance tests (Section 11.6). Mechanical Reasoning is a subtest of the Differential Aptitude Tests of George Bennett, Harold Seashore and Alexander Wesman (1947), an aptitude battery (Chapter 8). An index called plain "Working Memory" belonged to the WMS-III. Only the 1945 scale gave a memory quotient. Learning a list: the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test Batteries like the WMS give a broad survey. When the question is specifically how a person learns, and where learning breaks down, many clinicians turn to a list of words read again and again. The idea goes back to Geneva. Édouard Claparède (1873 to 1940) used a list of fifteen words, read once, as a memory test. His student André Rey (1906 to 1965) turned it into a learning test by reading the list five times and asking for recall after each reading, and he and the workers who adapted his test added an interfering list, a delayed recall and a recognition trial. Rey's version is usually cited from his book of 1958 (some sources give 1964, so expect either date); an English version appeared in 1959, and Muriel Lezak's textbook made it standard in the English-speaking world. Today it is called the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (Rey AVLT or RAVLT), and a version of it is part of the NIMHANS battery, with Indian norms (Section 11.3). The procedure follows the moments of Figure 11.7 almost exactly. The examiner reads List A, fifteen common nouns that have nothing to do with one another, at about one word per second, and asks the person to say as many as he can, in any order. This is Trial I. The whole list is read again, and the person again recalls all he can, including the words he gave before: Trial II. And so on to Trial V. The examiner writes down every word in the order given, and notes repetitions and intrusions (words that were never on the list). Next comes List B, fifteen new words read once and recalled once. Then, without hearing List A again, the person is asked for List A: Trial VI. After a delay of 20 to 30 minutes, filled with tests that are not verbal so that he cannot rehearse, he is asked for List A once more: Trial VII. Last comes a recognition trial, in which the List A words are mixed with others and the person picks out the ones he heard (the formats differ: a printed list of words, or a short story that contains them). Healthy young adults usually recall about six or seven words on Trial I and about twelve or thirteen by Trial V; older adults recall fewer, and people with more schooling more, which is why the norms are given by age and education. The power of the test lies in the comparisons it allows, and each comparison has a simple formula. Learn them in words first. Remember The main Rey AVLT indices (I to VII are the words recalled on each trial, B the words recalled from List B): Total learning = I + II + III + IV + V (out of 75) Learning over trials = V − I Proactive interference ratio = B / I Retention after interference = (VI / V) × 100 Retention after delay = (VII / V) × 100 Corrected recognition = hits − false positives where a hit is a List A word correctly recognised and a false positive (false alarm) is a word wrongly claimed to have been on List A. Total learning says how much was learned overall; V − I says how much the person gained by repetition; B / I compares a fresh list heard once (B) with the first hearing of List A (I), so a ratio well below 1 means the first list is getting in the way of the new one; the two retention percentages say how much of what had been learned by Trial V survived the interfering list and the delay. Set the three records side by side and the test starts to talk. Neel's curve is the healthy shape: a good first trial, a steep rise, a small dip after the interfering list and almost no loss over the delay. Urvi shows the pattern of a storage deficit . She learns little however often the list is read, she loses what she has learned when another list intervenes and over a delay, and recognition does not rescue her, because the words were never laid down in a lasting form; her many false positives show that she cannot even tell which words are familiar. Rapid forgetting with poor recognition is the mark of damage to the medial temporal lobe memory system, and it is typical of Alzheimer's disease and of the amnesic syndromes. Mridul is different. His learning is slow and his free recall poor, but what he learned by Trial V he keeps: there is no further loss between Trial VI and the delayed Trial VII (7 and 7), and when the words are put in front of him he recognises 14 of the 15. The words were stored; he has trouble getting them out. This is a retrieval deficit , the pattern seen when the frontal and subcortical systems that organise effortful search are not working well: in depression, in Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases, in subcortical vascular disease and, to a milder degree, in normal ageing. A few further details complete the reading. A very low Trial I with a normal rise afterwards suggests a problem of attention or initial encoding rather than of storage. Many intrusions and repetitions suggest poor monitoring of one's own recall, common after frontal damage and in Korsakoff's syndrome. And the serial position of the words recalled matters: healthy people recall words from the start (primacy) and the end (recency) of the list best, while patients with amnesia keep the recency effect, which depends on the short-term store, and lose the primacy effect, which depends on transfer to long-term memory (Book 1, Section 7.2.6). Clinical link Mridul's complaint is one of the commonest referrals in a psychiatric hospital: is this depression or the beginning of dementia? Depressed patients often complain bitterly of poor memory, try little, answer "I don't know", and recall poorly; but they usually recognise well and do not forget over a delay, and they get better as the depression lifts. When depression produces a picture that looks like dementia it is called pseudodementia (Book 3, Section 10.11.6). The recall versus recognition contrast of a list-learning test is one of the most useful pieces of evidence for telling the two apart, but it is evidence, not a verdict: depression and early dementia can coexist, and depression in late life is sometimes the first sign of a dementing illness, so a retest after treatment is wise. Exam trap Rey AVLT = 15 unrelated words, 5 trials, then List B, then recall of List A (VI), then delayed recall after 20 to 30 minutes (VII), then recognition . Keep the two interferences straight with the rule from Book 1, Section 7.8.2: pro active means old disrupts new, so poor recall of List B because of List A is proactive interference; retro active means new disrupts old, so the drop from Trial V to Trial VI caused by List B is retroactive interference. Poor recall with good recognition is a retrieval deficit; poor recall with poor recognition is a storage deficit. Rey is also the Rey of the complex figure (Section 11.4.6). The California Verbal Learning Test and how people organise what they learn Rey's words were chosen to have nothing in common, so the only way to learn them is by rote. Real memory rarely works like that. When you go to the market with a mental list, you probably group the items without trying: the vegetables together, the spices together, the things for the puja together. Groups make a list easier to learn and easier to search, and whether a person spontaneously finds the groups says a good deal about the brain systems that organise memory. That insight, and Edith Kaplan's broader conviction that the way a person fails matters as much as the score (the process approach, Section 11.1), lie behind the California Verbal Learning Test (CVLT) of Dean C. Delis , Joel Kramer, Edith Kaplan and Beth Ober (1987). The CVLT is built like the Rey test but with one crucial change: its list is a shopping list. Sixteen words are read, four from each of four categories, mixed so that no two words from the same category come one after another. As in the Rey test there are five learning trials, then an interfering second list, then recall of the first list straight away (short-delay free recall) and with the category names given as cues (short-delay cued recall), then free and cued recall again after about twenty minutes, and finally recognition. The second edition (CVLT-II, 2000) and the third (CVLT-3, 2017) kept the plan, and a children's version (CVLT-C, 1994) uses a shorter list. Because the categories are known, the examiner can score not only how many words come back but how they come back. The central process score is clustering. In semantic clustering the person recalls words from the same category together, which shows that he has noticed the structure of the list and is using it, an active strategy that depends on the frontal lobes. In serial clustering he recalls the words in the order he heard them, a passive strategy that leans on the sequence of input. A simplified way to see the difference is to count, in a recall, the adjacent pairs of words that come from the same category, and divide by the number of adjacent pairs (one fewer than the number of words recalled). Suppose two invented people each recall eight words, and we write F for fruit, T for tool, C for clothing and S for spice. The first recalls F, F, F, T, T, C, C, S. Of his seven adjacent pairs, four join two words of the same category (his three fruits make two such pairs, his two tools one and his two clothes one), so his index is 4 / 7 = 0.571, or 57 percent to the nearest whole percent. The second recalls the words in the order heard, F, T, C, S, F, T, C, S; none of her seven adjacent pairs is from the same category, so her index is 0 / 7 = 0. Both recalled eight words, but only the first used the structure of the list. (The published test uses a more refined formula that also corrects for the clustering expected by chance.) The cued recall trials add a second process comparison. If a person recalls few words freely but many more when given the category names, the words were stored and the cues have helped him search for them, a retrieval pattern like Mridul's. If cues add little, the words were not stored. With these scores the CVLT became a tool for distinguishing patterns of memory disorder: patients with Alzheimer's disease, for example, forget rapidly and make many intrusions, while patients with Huntington's disease retrieve poorly but recognise and benefit from cues much better. Exam trap Rey AVLT: 15 unrelated words , so no strategy but rote. CVLT (Delis, Kramer, Kaplan and Ober, 1987): 16 words in 4 categories (a shopping list), so it can measure semantic clustering , cued recall and intrusions. Edith Kaplan's name on the CVLT links it to the process approach. Visual memory: the Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure and the Benton Visual Retention Test Words are easy to rehearse silently, so a person with a weak memory system can sometimes prop up his verbal scores by talking to himself. Designs that cannot easily be named are harder to prop up, which is why visual memory tests use abstract figures. Two are classics. The first again comes from André Rey. In 1941, in a paper on the psychological examination of people with traumatic brain injury, he introduced a complicated abstract line drawing: a large rectangle crossed by diagonals and midlines, with many smaller details inside it and attached to its sides. The drawing is meaningless, so it cannot be remembered as a picture of something, and it is complicated, so it cannot be copied well without a plan. In 1944 his colleague Paul-Alexandre Osterrieth standardised its administration and scoring, and the test has carried both names ever since: the Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure (ROCF, or simply "the Rey figure"). The figure itself is protected test material; the description above is all you need. Key study: Osterrieth standardises the Rey figure (1944) Osterrieth asked a developmental question: how do people of different ages go about copying a figure too complex to take in at a glance? He gave the copy task to about 230 children and 60 adults and watched not only how accurate each copy was but in what order it was drawn. He sorted the copying procedures into a small number of types, from building the whole drawing on the big central rectangle and fitting the details to it, through drawing the outline first or assembling the details one beside another, down to a mere scribble. Young children mostly pieced details together; with age the approach became organised around the main structure, and most adults began with the large rectangle. He also divided the figure into 18 scoring units. The conclusion still guides practice: a copy shows how a person perceives and plans, so it must be judged before the recall is read as a memory score. Later workers added qualitative scoring systems for exactly this planning, because the 18-unit score alone says nothing about how the copy was made. Administration has three stages. The person first copies the figure with it in full view, and the examiner times the copy and records the order in which the parts are drawn (in the process approach, by handing over pencils of different colours at intervals, so that the sequence can be read later). Then, without warning, the figure is taken away and the person draws it from memory, a few minutes later (immediate recall) and again after about 30 minutes (delayed recall). John and Kelly Meyers's version (1995) adds a recognition trial. Each drawing is scored on Osterrieth's 18 units: a unit earns 2 points if it is correct and correctly placed, 1 point if it is correct but misplaced or distorted but well placed, half a point if it is distorted and misplaced but still recognisable, and nothing if it is missing or unrecognisable. The maximum is 18 × 2 = 36. Because the copy and the recall are scored on the same scale, a simple percentage tells you how much of what was drawn was remembered. Remember Complex figure score and retention: Score = (units scoring 2 × 2) + (units scoring 1 × 1) + (units scoring 0.5 × 0.5) , out of 36 Percentage retained = (delayed recall score / copy score) × 100 where the copy score shows what the person was able to perceive and construct with the figure in view, and the delayed recall score what remained after about 30 minutes. Return to Urvi. On the copy, 13 units earn 2 points, 3 units earn 1 point, 2 units earn half a point and none earns nothing (13 + 3 + 2 + 0 = 18 units, so every unit is accounted for). Her copy score is (13 × 2) + (3 × 1) + (2 × 0.5) = 26 + 3 + 1 = 30 out of 36, a reasonable copy for her age. Her delayed recall earns 8 points. Percentage retained = (8 / 30) × 100 = 0.2667 × 100 = 26.67, which rounds to 27 percent. Because her copy is adequate, her poor recall cannot be blamed on poor seeing or poor drawing: it is a genuine failure of visual memory, which fits her low WMS-IV Visual Memory index and her verbal storage pattern on the Rey AVLT. Contrast two other invented patients. A man with damage to the right parietal lobe produces a fragmented copy that loses the overall shape and leaves out details on the left; his recall will be poor too, but it cannot be read as a memory failure, because the figure was never properly perceived. A woman with frontal damage copies the details accurately but piece by piece, with no overall plan, and then recalls very little, because a disorganised copy is a poorly encoded one. The same recall score of 8 means three different things in the three patients, and only the copy tells you which. The second classic is the work of Arthur Lester Benton (1909 to 2006), whose other tests you will meet in Section 11.5. During the Second World War Benton served as a psychologist in the United States Navy, and at the San Diego Naval Hospital he examined servicemen with penetrating brain wounds alongside the neurologist Morris Bender (a different Bender from the one in Section 11.5). Out of that work came a short test of memory for designs, described in 1945 and published as the Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) in 1946. Its fifth edition, revised by Abigail Benton Sivan, appeared in the early 1990s. The BVRT is a set of cards, each showing one or more simple geometric figures; most designs have two large figures and one small figure off to one side. There are three equivalent forms, called C, D and E, of ten designs each, so that a patient can be retested before and after treatment without simply remembering the first set (Chapter 3, Section 3.3). There are also four ways of giving it, labelled Administrations A to D. In Administration A, the standard one, each card is shown for 10 seconds and then removed, and the person draws it from memory at once. In B the exposure is only 5 seconds. In C the person copies the design with the card in view, so there is no memory demand at all. In D the card is shown for 10 seconds and the person waits 15 seconds before drawing. Two scores are kept: the number of designs reproduced correctly (0 to 10) and an error score, with each error classed as an omission, a distortion, a perseveration (repeating a figure from an earlier design), a rotation, a misplacement or an error of size. The manual gives the expected number correct by age and estimated intelligence, so a score well below expectation suggests impairment. Two features make the BVRT more useful than it looks. The small peripheral figures are sensitive to unilateral neglect: a patient who consistently leaves out the small figure when it is on the left is ignoring the left side of space (Section 11.5.7). And comparing Administration C with Administration A separates two quite different failures. A person who copies well but draws poorly from memory has a visual memory problem; a person who cannot even copy has a problem of perception or construction, and his memory cannot be judged from this test at all. That is the same logic as the Rey figure's copy, and it is the single most important rule for reading any visual memory test: check the copy before you read the recall . Exam trap Benton (1946) = visual retention : ten designs drawn from memory, Forms C, D and E, Administrations A to D (C is the copy condition). Bender (1938) = visual-motor copying of nine designs (Section 11.5). The letters are a favourite trick: the forms are C, D, E; the administrations are A, B, C, D. Rey-Osterrieth: Rey devised the figure (1941), Osterrieth standardised it (1944); 18 units × 2 points = 36; copy, then immediate and delayed recall. Everyday and remote memory, and choosing a memory test A woman can score poorly on a word list and still run her kitchen; a man can score in the average range on every subtest of the WMS-IV and still forget to take his tablets, miss his appointments and get lost on the way back from the market. Laboratory-style tests sample memory under ideal, quiet, one-to-one conditions, and they say little about the memory demands of ordinary life, especially prospective memory , remembering to do something in the future (Book 1, Section 7.5.5). Barbara A. Wilson , a British neuropsychologist who worked for decades in brain injury rehabilitation, built the Rivermead Behavioural Memory Test (1985) with Janet Cockburn and Alan Baddeley to close that gap. Its tasks imitate everyday demands: remembering the name of a person shown in a photograph, remembering where a belonging of the person's was hidden and asking for it back at the end, remembering to ask about an appointment when an alarm sounds, remembering a short route around the room and a message to deliver on the way, and recognising pictures and faces. Because it measures the memory problems people actually report, it is used mainly to plan and evaluate rehabilitation (Book 2, Section 9.9). Remote memory needs different tests again, because the examiner did not present the material and must check the answers against someone who knows. The Autobiographical Memory Interview of Michael Kopelman, Barbara Wilson and Alan Baddeley (1989) asks about personal facts (the names of schools and teachers, addresses) and about specific remembered incidents from childhood, early adult life and recent years, and checks them with relatives. Tests of public events and famous faces ask about well-known happenings and people of different decades, and they must be built locally: a question about an Indian election or a Bollywood star of the 1970s means something in Delhi that it would not mean in Denver. In many amnesic patients such tests show a temporal gradient, with the oldest memories best preserved (Book 1, Section 7.10.1). Two more tools complete the kit. Elizabeth Warrington's Recognition Memory Test (1984) has a words half and a faces half, each a forced choice between a studied item and a new one, so it compares verbal and visual memory directly with a recognition format. And in India the PGI Memory Scale of Dwarka Pershad and N. N. Wig (1977), with its ten subtests and Indian norms, is often the first memory test given to an adult; Section 11.3 teaches it. Effort tests are built to look like memory tests. The Test of Memory Malingering is explained in Section 11.1. Rey's own 15-item test works the same way: fifteen simple characters, arranged in five rows of three that follow obvious patterns, are shown for ten seconds and then drawn from memory. The patterns make the task far easier than it looks, so most people with genuine memory loss reproduce most of the items, and a score below about nine has traditionally raised a question about effort rather than memory. How does a clinician choose among all these? By the referral question, as always. "Is there a memory problem at all, and how bad?" calls for a broad standardised battery such as the WMS-IV or, in India, the PGI Memory Scale. "Is this a storage or a retrieval problem?" calls for a list-learning test with delayed recall and recognition, the Rey AVLT or the CVLT. "Is it worse for words or for pictures?" calls for matched verbal and visual tests, the auditory and visual indices of the WMS-IV, or a word list against the Rey figure. "Can he manage at home, and is rehabilitation helping?" calls for the Rivermead. "Is he trying?" calls for an effort test. Table 11.18 summarises the tests of this section.
