A test of everyday memory is the Rivermead, not the WMS. 11.5 Visuomotor and Visuospatial Tests: The Bender-Gestalt, the Benton Tests and Constructional Tasks Medium yield · 6 Qs Ask a healthy adult to copy a simple drawing, a few dots and lines, and the request seems almost insulting. Yet copying is one of the most demanding things you ask of a brain in a clinic. The eyes must register the lines; the visual system must turn them into a shape and see how its parts relate; something must judge where each part sits, at what angle and how far from the next; something else must plan where on the page to begin; and the hand must be steered, stroke by stroke, under the constant guidance of the eyes. A failure at any of these links spoils the copy, which is why copying tasks were among the first tests of brain damage and why, for half a century, the most popular of them, the Bender-Gestalt, was one of the most widely used psychological tests in the world. This section teaches that test in full, then the shorter, sharper tests of Arthur Benton that isolate single links of the chain, and finally the constructional and neglect tasks that complete a clinician's visual kit. What visuomotor, visuospatial and constructional tests ask Four words recur in this area and the papers use them loosely, so fix them now. The first, visuoperception , is the recognition and discrimination of what is seen: telling one shape, one face or one object from another. The second, visuospatial ability, is the judgement of where things are: their position, direction, orientation and distance, and their relations to one another and to the viewer, including the ability to attend to both halves of space. The third, visuoconstruction (constructional ability), is putting parts together to make a whole, by drawing or by assembling blocks or sticks; its loss after brain damage is constructional apraxia , the difficulty in copying a cube or a clock face described in Book 3, Section 10.8.3. The fourth, visual-motor integration , is the coordination of what is seen with fine movements of the hand, the hand-eye coordination that copying, handwriting and threading a needle all need. The first two are about seeing; the last two are about doing what one sees. Why separate them? Because the same bad copy can come from very different places, and the treatment and the prognosis differ. Damage to the back of the right hemisphere, especially the parietal lobe, tends to wreck the overall shape: the drawing is fragmented, parts are scattered or misplaced, the spatial relations between them are lost, and the left side is often left out altogether. Damage to the left hemisphere tends to leave the overall outline recognisable but simplified, with details missing and the drawing slow and laboured. Damage to the frontal lobes spoils planning: the person starts in the wrong place, runs out of room, repeats elements he has already drawn. Diffuse disorders such as dementia and delirium degrade every element. And a person with poor eyesight, a tremor, an injured hand or very little schooling will copy badly with an entirely healthy brain. So a careful examiner never stops at "the copy is poor". She asks which link failed, and she has tests designed to answer that: matching tasks that need perception but no drawing (Benton's Judgment of Line Orientation and Facial Recognition tests, Section 11.5.6), simple motor tasks that need drawing but little perception, and the copy conditions of memory tests that need drawing but no memory (Administration C of the Benton Visual Retention Test, Section 11.4.6). Education deserves a special word in India. A woman who has never been to school and has rarely held a pencil may copy a diamond as a lopsided circle and draw overlapping shapes side by side, and an examiner who reads that as brain damage will be badly wrong. Copying tests are more sensitive to schooling than many people realise, so the norms must match the person's education, and matching tasks, which ask only that the person point, are fairer to people who cannot write. Chapter 5 explains why norms collected on one population can mislead when applied to another, and Section 11.3 describes Indian batteries normed by education. Exam trap Visuoperceptual = what is it? (shapes, faces). Visuospatial = where is it? (position, angle, the two sides of space). Visuoconstructional = can he put it together? (drawing, blocks); its loss is constructional apraxia . Visual-motor integration = can the hand do what the eye sees? The Bender is a test of visual-motor integration; Benton's Judgment of Line Orientation is a pure visuospatial test with no drawing at all. The Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test: Lauretta Bender's nine designs There is a fine irony in the life of the woman who built the most famous test of visual-motor maturity. Lauretta Bender (1897 to 1987), born in Butte, Montana, had to repeat the first grade at school and was thought to be intellectually slow, largely because she reversed her letters. She proved an able student after all, took degrees at the University of Chicago and a medical degree at the State University of Iowa in 1926, and trained in neuropathology under Samuel Orton, the pioneer of research on reading disability. In 1930 she joined the psychiatric staff of Bellevue Hospital in New York, and from 1934 she headed its children's psychiatric division. She described herself as a psychiatrist and neurologist, not a psychologist, and much of her career was spent with severely disturbed children. Bender's test grew out of Gestalt psychology. In 1923 Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) had published his study of the laws by which the visual system groups elements into wholes, proximity, similarity, continuity and the rest, illustrated with simple patterns of dots, lines and curves (Book 1, Sections 2.3.4 and 4.2.3). Bender took several of Wertheimer's patterns, modified some, put each on a card and asked her patients to copy them. She first tried them with adult psychiatric patients, including mute patients with schizophrenia, and then with children. Her reasoning was that copying a design is not a mechanical tracing of lines but a reconstruction of a perceived whole, a "gestalt", by the integrated action of perception and movement, and that this integrative capacity matures with age. Young children reproduce designs as primitive loops and circles; with age they come to handle the relation of figure to background, the boundaries of forms and vertical lines, and then crossing lines, slanting lines and angles, a later level of maturation that usually appears at about six to eight years. Her monograph, A Visual Motor Gestalt Test and Its Clinical Use (1938), was published by the American Orthopsychiatric Association, and presented the test as a way of evaluating the maturation of visual-motor gestalt function in children of about 4 to 11 years. She believed that immature or "primitive" copies in older children could signal childhood schizophrenia, brain damage or learning difficulties. The Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (BVMGT, the "Bender-Gestalt" or simply "the Bender") consists of nine cards , an introductory design labelled Figure A and eight more labelled Figures 1 to 8 . The designs are built from dots, small circles, lines, curves and angles, some joined and some overlapping; they are protected test material and are not shown in this book. Administration is simple. The person sits at a table with a pencil and blank paper. The cards are shown one at a time in a fixed order, starting with Figure A, and the person is asked to copy each design as well as he can; the card stays in view while he copies. There is no time limit, and rulers and other aids are not allowed. The whole test usually takes about five to ten minutes. The examiner watches as carefully as she scores. Does the person count the dots or work by eye? Does he turn the card or the paper to make a design easier? Does he plan the page or crowd the designs into one corner? Does he notice his errors and correct them, or rush on? Is he frustrated, impulsive, painstaking? Over the years examiners added variations that Bender's original did not have. In a recall phase, after all the copies are done, the cards are put away and the person is asked to draw as many designs as he can from memory, which adds a measure of visual memory. In a brief-exposure version each card is shown for only a few seconds and then drawn from memory. The designs can be projected on a screen for group testing in schools. Max Hutt added phases for projective use, in which the person elaborates the designs and says what they remind him of (Chapter 10, Section 10.9.4). And in 1966 Arthur Canter introduced the Background Interference Procedure : the person copies the designs once on plain paper and once on paper printed with a mesh of intersecting wavy lines. The idea was that a damaged brain finds it harder than a healthy one to pick out a figure from a distracting background, so the copies of brain-damaged patients should deteriorate more on the busy paper. Some studies found that it did improve detection of brain damage over the standard procedure; others found it of limited use as a screen. In India the Bender is part of the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction (Section 11.3) and remains one of the commonest tests in clinical psychology departments. Exam trap Bender = Lauretta Bender, 1938 , a child psychiatrist at Bellevue (a woman, and not a psychologist). Nine cards: Figure A and Figures 1 to 8 . The designs were adapted from Max Wertheimer's 1923 Gestalt grouping patterns; the test is named after Gestalt perception, not Gestalt therapy. The original test is copying only: the recall phase, the background interference procedure (Canter, 1966) and Hutt's projective phases came later. Scoring the Bender: Pascal and Suttell, Hutt, Lacks and Koppitz Bender herself judged copies clinically, by comparing them with the designs typical of children of each age. That made her test depend on the experience of the examiner, and for the next forty years psychologists built scoring systems that would let two examiners reach the same score from the same drawings (scorer reliability is the subject of Chapter 3, Section 3.6). Four of them are worth knowing, and Table 11.19 sets them out with the later systems. For adults, Gerald R. Pascal and Barbara J. Suttell published The Bender-Gestalt Test: Quantification and Validity for Adults (1951). They listed, design by design, the many ways a copy can deviate from the model, weighted each deviation, added them up and converted the total into a standard score, with higher scores meaning more deviant copies; their conversion tables were for adults. Max L. Hutt , who trained army psychologists during the Second World War and circulated a guide to the Bender in 1945, published The Clinical Use of the Revised Bender-Gestalt Test with Gerald Briskin in 1960. Hutt and Briskin picked out a set of errors they regarded as the essential signs of brain damage, and they also read copies projectively, a use taught in Chapter 10, Section 10.9.4. In 1984 Patricia Lacks turned the Hutt-Briskin signs into a brief screening system for adults, Bender Gestalt Screening for Brain Dysfunction : twelve kinds of error, each scored present or absent, with five or more errors suggesting brain dysfunction. Studies of the Lacks system found it useful in some populations and a much poorer basis for screening in others. The system that came to dominate, especially in schools, was built for children by Elizabeth Munsterberg Koppitz , an American school psychologist. In The Bender Gestalt Test for Young Children (1963, often cited by the 1964 date of the book) she published the Developmental Bender Scoring System , normed on children of about 5 to 10, and in a second volume (1975) she reviewed a decade of research and extended the norms to age 11. The system has 30 scoring items , each a specific error on a specific design, scored 1 if present and 0 if absent, so the total error score runs from 0 to 30 and a higher score means a less mature copy. Every item belongs to one of four types of error, and these four are what the papers ask about. A distortion of shape: the shape is misformed. Angles are lost or added, a figure is badly out of proportion, or one kind of element is replaced by another (dots drawn as small circles, for example). A rotation : the design, or part of it, is turned through 45 degrees or more from its proper orientation; turning the card and copying it in the turned position counts too. An integration difficulty: the parts are not put together into the whole. Parts that should meet are left apart, overlap when they should only touch, or a design that should be closed is left open or falls apart into pieces. A perseveration : a pattern is continued beyond what the model shows (many more dots, columns or curves than the design has). Some other scoring systems also count a feature of one design carried over into the next as perseveration. Figure 11.9 shows the four types on invented shapes. Notice that each error is a failure of a different part of the copying process: distortion of the shape itself, rotation of its orientation, integration of its parts into a whole, and perseveration, the failure to stop. Chanda is a Class 2 pupil aged 7 years 2 months, referred by her teacher because her handwriting is untidy and she is slow to copy from the blackboard, although she answers well in class. Chanda makes one standard deviation more errors than the average 7-year-old. On the normal curve about 84 percent of children score at or below +1.00, so she makes more errors than roughly 84 percent of children her age; put the other way, her performance is at about the 16th percentile. Age equivalent: her 9 errors fall between the 6-year mean (10) and the 7-year mean (6). Age equivalent = 6 + [(10 − 9) / (10 − 6)] × (7 − 6) = 6 + (1 / 4) × 1 = 6 + 0.25 = 6.25 years, which is about 6 years 3 months (0.25 of a year is 3 months). In plain words, Chanda copies like a child about a year younger than she is. That is a finding, not a diagnosis. Koppitz herself stressed that a high error score shows immaturity of visual-motor integration, which can come from many sources: a problem of vision, of fine motor control, of attention, of general intellectual development, of schooling, or simply a slower rate of development that will catch up. The next steps for Chanda are an eye test, a test that separates visual perception from motor coordination (the Beery tests of Section 11.5.7), observation of her attention in class, and, if questions remain, an intelligence test (Chapter 6). Koppitz also listed a separate set of "emotional indicators" in children's Bender copies, such as heavy reworking of lines or a confused order on the page; like her emotional indicators in human figure drawings they are taught in Chapter 10, Section 10.9.4, and they are viewed sceptically. Koppitz died in the early 1980s, and her system was later revised by Cecil Reynolds as the Koppitz-2 (2007), with new norms on about 3,600 people aged 5 to 85 and over and separate scoring for ages 5 to 7 and 8 upwards. Exam trap Koppitz (1963) = developmental scoring of the Bender for children , 30 items, four error types: distortion, rotation, integration, perseveration ; a higher score means more errors and a less mature copy. Pascal and Suttell (1951) = adults. Hutt = the Bender read projectively (and, with Briskin, signs of brain damage). Lacks (1984) = a 12-error adult screen, 5 or more errors suggesting brain dysfunction. Koppitz also built the 1968 emotional indicators for human figure drawings (Chapter 10). The Bender-Gestalt II By the 1990s the Bender was showing its age. Its designs were too easy for adults, so a healthy adult made almost no errors and the test could detect only fairly marked problems (a ceiling effect); they were too hard for very young children; its norms were old; and its users scored it in half a dozen incompatible ways. A revision was prepared by Gary G. Brannigan and Scott L. Decker , who published the Bender-Gestalt II (Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test, Second Edition) in 2003. The Bender-Gestalt II keeps Bender's nine designs and adds seven new ones, sixteen in all. Four of the new designs are easier and are used only with young children, from 4 years to 7 years 11 months; three are harder and are used only from 8 years upwards. So a young child copies 13 designs (the original 9 plus the 4 easy ones) and an older child or adult 12 (the 9 plus the 3 hard ones). The test was normed on about 4,000 people in the United States, aged from 4 to 85 years and over. It has two phases. In the Copy phase the person copies each design with the card in view, as in the original. In the Recall phase, which follows without warning, he draws as many of the designs as he can from memory, which gives a measure of visual-motor memory. Two short supplemental tests help locate the cause of a poor copy: a Motor test, which needs drawing but very little perception, and a Perception test, which needs perception but no drawing, the person simply pointing to the design that matches. A poor copy with a normal Perception test points to the motor side of the chain; a poor copy with a poor Perception test points to the perceptual side. The copy and recall take about five to ten minutes, the supplemental tests about five more. Scoring uses Brannigan's Global Scoring System . Instead of hunting for specific errors, the scorer rates each drawing as a whole on a five-point scale, from 0 (a scribble, or no resemblance to the design) to 4 (a nearly perfect copy). The ratings are added, and the totals for Copy and for Recall are converted, by age, into standard scores (on the familiar scale with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15) and percentile ranks. The arithmetic of the raw score is easy. Because each design is rated 0 to 4, the maximum raw Copy score is 13 × 4 = 52 for a young child and 12 × 4 = 48 for anyone aged 8 or more. Suppose an invented 45-year-old man is tested after a head injury and his twelve copies are rated 4, 4, 3, 4, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, 3 and 2. His raw Copy score is 4 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 37 out of 48, which is 37 / 48 = 0.771, or 77 percent of the maximum. Whether 37 is low for a man of his age is not something the percentage can tell you; only the norm table in the manual, which turns raw scores into standard scores for each age group, can say how unusual it is. The authors chose the global system for its reliability and validity in their studies and because it is quick and easy to use. Exam trap Original Bender (1938) = 9 cards , copy only. Bender-Gestalt II (Brannigan and Decker, 2003 ) = 16 designs (13 given below age 8, 12 from age 8), ages 4 to 85 and over , a Copy phase and a Recall phase, supplemental Motor and Perception tests, and the Global Scoring System (each drawing 0 to 4). If a question says the Bender-Gestalt II uses 9 figures, it has confused it with the original. What the Bender measures, and what it does not Take stock of what the evidence of seventy years says. The Bender is above all a test of visual-motor integration : the ability to perceive a design and reproduce it by hand. In children it is a measure of the development of that ability, which is why school psychologists used it for decades to judge readiness for school and to investigate children who struggle with handwriting and copying. In adults it is a brief screen for organic brain dysfunction , the old term for damage to or disease of the brain itself: brain-damaged patients as a group make more errors than healthy people, and a copy full of rotations, fragmentations and perseverations should prompt a fuller neuropsychological examination. That is the answer every paper wants: the Bender assesses visual-motor integration and screens for neurological (organic) impairment and for developmental immaturity. The limits are just as important, and they explain why expert opinion turned against using it alone. First, it does not localise. As Barlow and Durand's abnormal psychology textbook puts it, the Bender can raise a suspicion of brain dysfunction when a child's errors exceed the number expected for her age, but it cannot tell you the nature or the location of the problem. Second, it is not specific. Errors arise from brain damage, but also from intellectual disability, from a low developmental level (a mental age below the age at which children normally copy the designs well), from learning disorders, from poor vision or motor control, from lack of schooling, from inattention and from emotional disturbance; a high error score says that something is wrong with copying, not what. Third, healthy adults make so few errors that only marked impairment shows. Fourth, the test was used for decades to answer the question "organic or functional?" with a single score, as if brain damage were one thing that any sensitive test would detect. Section 11.1 explains why that question has been abandoned: brain damage is many different things, and a single test of one function will miss most of them. Bender's early hopes that the test would identify schizophrenia did not survive research either, and the projective reading of copies for personality has little support (Chapter 10, Section 10.9.4). From the 1960s to the early 1990s the Bender was among the five tests most used by practitioners; a later Delphi poll of experts on discredited psychological tests placed its use as a test of neuropsychological impairment among the most discredited. The fair conclusion is that the Bender is a quick, pleasant, non-verbal screen of one function, useful as one part of a battery and as an ice-breaker with a child, but never a diagnosis on its own. The papers test this from the other side, with a list of things the Bender might be thought to measure. Clinical link A teacher's referral like Chanda's is common in child guidance clinics. The Bender, or the Beery tests of Section 11.5.7, can show that a child's copying is immature, and the supplemental motor and perception tasks can show which half of the skill is weak, which matters for an occupational therapist planning help with handwriting. But a slow, untidy copier may also be a child with a specific learning disorder, with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, with poor eyesight or with a borderline intellectual level (Book 3, Chapter 3 describes these conditions), and the copying test cannot choose among them. It opens the enquiry; it does not close it. The Benton tests: finger localization, line orientation, faces and right-left orientation The Bender asks a person to do one complicated thing and then tries to work out what went wrong. Arthur Benton, whom you met as the author of the Visual Retention Test (Section 11.4.6), preferred the opposite strategy: many short tests, each aimed as narrowly as possible at a single function, each standardised with norms corrected for age and education, so that a failure could be read precisely. After the war Benton taught at the University of Louisville from 1946 and then at the University of Iowa from 1948, where he became professor of psychology and neurology in 1958 and built a laboratory that trained a generation of neuropsychologists. In 1983, with Kerry deS. Hamsher, Nils R. Varney and Otfried Spreen, he published Contributions to Neuropsychological Assessment: A Clinical Manual , which gathered about a dozen of these tests in one place. Four of them belong in this section. The first is the one the papers ask about. Your sense of your own body includes a map of your fingers, so precise that you can tell, with your eyes shut, which finger has been touched. Loss of that ability is finger agnosia , a disorder of the body schema (Book 3, Section 2.10.3) and one of the four signs of Gerstmann's syndrome after damage to the dominant parietal lobe (Book 3, Section 10.8.3). Benton studied it with Bertram Cohen in 1955, alongside right-left discrimination, in normal and brain-injured adults, and the Finger Localization Test grew from that work. It has three parts. In the first, the person's hand rests in full view; the examiner touches the tip of one finger with the point of a pencil, and the person names the finger or points to it on an outline drawing of a hand (pointing lets people who cannot name fingers, such as some patients with aphasia, take the test). In the second, the hand is hidden behind a screen and single fingers are touched. In the third, the hand is hidden and two fingers are touched at once, and the person must identify both. Each part is given to each hand, ten trials per hand per part, sixty trials in all, and the score is the number correct for each hand separately. Why score the hands separately? Because touch from each hand is analysed mainly in the parietal lobe of the opposite hemisphere. If a person makes consistently more errors on one hand than on the other, the most likely explanation is damage to the hemisphere opposite that hand. Errors on both hands equally have a different meaning: they are seen after damage to the left (dominant) parietal lobe, often together with aphasia and the other Gerstmann signs, and after more widespread brain disease. One precondition must be checked first. The test assumes that the person can feel each touch. If sensation itself is lost on one hand, the failure is sensory, not a failure of finger localisation, so the examiner first confirms that every touch is felt. Remember Scoring a side difference: Percentage correct for a hand = (correct trials on that hand / trials given to that hand) × 100 Asymmetry = correct on the better hand − correct on the worse hand where each hand receives 30 of the 60 trials. A large asymmetry points to the hemisphere opposite the worse hand; equal errors on both hands point to dominant-hemisphere or diffuse damage. Here is an invented record. A 60-year-old man is tested two weeks after a stroke. He feels every touch on both hands. On his right hand he gets 29 of 30 trials correct; on his left hand, 19 of 30. Right hand: (29 / 30) × 100 = 0.9667 × 100 = 96.67, about 97 percent. Left hand: (19 / 30) × 100 = 0.6333 × 100 = 63.33, about 63 percent. Asymmetry: 29 − 19 = 10 trials, a gap of about 33 percentage points (96.67 − 63.33 = 33.33). Errors: 30 − 29 = 1 on the right hand; 30 − 19 = 11 on the left. He makes consistently more errors on the left hand, with touch sensation intact, so the test points to damage in the right hemisphere, probably the parietal lobe. On its own that is a hypothesis; Section 11.5.7 shows how a second test, line bisection, can support it, which is exactly Reitan's method of right-left comparison described in Section 11.1. Exam trap "Which test can show that an examinee consistently makes more errors on one side of the body than the other?" The answer is Benton's Finger Localization Test , because it scores each hand separately and touch from each hand goes to the opposite hemisphere. The distractors are all attention tests, and attention is not tested side by side: the Continuous Performance Test (H. Enger Rosvold and colleagues, 1956) measures sustained attention through omissions and commissions over a long run of stimuli; a sustained attention test is the general name for such vigilance tasks (Book 1, Section 5.4.6); the Test of Everyday Attention (Ian Robertson and colleagues, 1994) measures sustained, selective and switching attention through everyday tasks. Section 11.6 teaches all three. The sensory-perceptual examination of the Halstead-Reitan battery (Section 11.2) uses the same right-left logic. The second Benton test isolates visuospatial judgement more purely than any copying task can. In the Judgment of Line Orientation test (Benton, Varney and Hamsher, 1978) the person sees two short lines set at different angles and, below them, a fan of eleven numbered lines arranged in a semicircle, 18 degrees apart. He says which two lines of the fan have the same orientations as the pair above. After five practice items come 30 test items, and an item counts as correct only if both lines are identified, so scores run from 0 to 30. Two forms, H and V, contain the same items in different orders. Because the person only has to say or point to numbers, the test needs no drawing, very little movement and very little language, so a poor score cannot be blamed on a clumsy hand. It was developed to detect dysfunction of the right hemisphere, and patients with damage at the back of the right hemisphere do worst on it. The third, the Facial Recognition Test (Benton and Van Allen, 1968), asks the person to match photographs of unfamiliar faces. In the first items he picks, from six photographs, the one identical to a target face; in later items he must pick three photographs of the target person taken from different angles or under different lighting. The long form (22 items) is scored out of 54, and a 13-item short form, scored out of 27, can be converted to the long-form scale. It is most impaired after damage to the back of the right hemisphere. Note what it does not test: recognition of familiar people. Some people who cannot recognise their own relatives by face (prosopagnosia) pass it by matching features slowly and carefully, so a normal score does not rule out a problem with face recognition in daily life. The fourth, Right-Left Orientation , gives a series of commands. Some concern the person's own body ("show me your left hand", "touch your right ear with your left hand"); others concern the examiner, sitting opposite ("point to my left eye"), which requires the person to reverse left and right in imagination. Errors on his own body suggest left-hemisphere damage, especially with aphasia, and are part of Gerstmann's syndrome; errors only when the examiner's body must be mentally reversed suggest a spatial difficulty. The other tests of Benton's manual include Temporal Orientation, Visual Form Discrimination (matching complex designs that differ in small details, some of them at the edges, so neglect shows up), Three-Dimensional Block Construction, Tactile Form Perception, Pantomime Recognition, Serial Digit Learning, Phoneme Discrimination and Motor Impersistence; his verbal fluency test, the Controlled Oral Word Association test, is taught in Section 11.6. Constructional tasks, tests of neglect and the Beery VMI Drawing is only one way of constructing. In block design tasks the person arranges coloured cubes to copy a pattern, the method Samuel Kohs introduced and David Wechsler took into his scales as the Block Design subtest (Chapter 6); Kohs's blocks are also part of Bhatia's battery of performance tests in India (Chapter 6). How a person fails at block design is as telling as how a person fails at copying. Patients with right-hemisphere damage tend to break the overall square, laying blocks in a line or a jumble; patients with left-hemisphere damage tend to keep the square outline but get the details of the pattern inside it wrong. Benton's Three-Dimensional Block Construction asks for models built in depth. Stick construction , copying a pattern of matchsticks laid on the table, needs no pencil at all, which makes it useful for people who have rarely written. Drawing to command and to copy (a cube, a house, a flower) completes the set, and the most informative drawing of all, the clock, is taught with the bedside screens in Section 11.7. Among the disorders these tasks reveal, unilateral neglect is the most striking: a failure to notice, attend to or respond to things on the side of space opposite a brain lesion, even though the eyes and the limbs on that side work. It is commoner and more severe after damage to the right parietal lobe, so it is usually the left side that is neglected. At the bedside such a patient eats only the right half of his plate, shaves only the right side of his face and bumps into door frames on his left (Book 3, Section 2.10.3, describes it with the disorders of body experience). Several simple tests measure it. In line bisection the person marks the middle of horizontal lines printed across a page (a version standardised by Thomas Schenkenberg and colleagues in 1980). A patient with left neglect treats the line as if it began further to the right than it does, so his mark falls to the right of the true centre. Remember Line bisection deviation: Percentage deviation = [(position of the mark − true midpoint) / (half the length of the line)] × 100 where positions are measured from the left end of the line, a positive value means the mark is to the right of centre and a negative value to the left, and half the length of the line is the largest possible error on one side. The man with the left-hand finger localisation errors bisects a line 200 millimetres long. The true midpoint is 100 millimetres from the left end; his mark is 136 millimetres from the left end. The deviation is 136 − 100 = +36 millimetres, to the right. Half the length of the line is 200 / 2 = 100 millimetres. Percentage deviation = (36 / 100) × 100 = 36 percent to the right. Healthy people usually place the mark within a few millimetres of the centre, often slightly to the left of it, so his large rightward error is evidence of left neglect, and it fits the right-hemisphere hypothesis raised by his finger localisation scores. Two tests of different functions pointing to the same hemisphere are far more convincing than either alone. In cancellation tests the person crosses out every target on a page: every short line scattered across a sheet, in Martin Albert's line-crossing test (1973), or every star among words and letters, or every bell among other small pictures. A patient with left neglect leaves the targets on the left uncrossed. Drawings show neglect too: asked to draw a flower or a clock, the patient crowds all the petals or numbers onto the right half. Because paper tests and daily life do not always agree, Barbara Wilson, Janet Cockburn and Peter Halligan built the Behavioural Inattention Test (1987), which adds everyday tasks such as reading a menu, telling the time, sorting coins and dialling a telephone to the paper-and-pencil ones. The small peripheral figures of the Benton Visual Retention Test (Section 11.4.6) catch neglect as well. Two more tests complete the kit. The Hooper Visual Organization Test (1958) shows thirty line drawings of common objects that have been cut into pieces and scattered, and the person says what each would be if the pieces were put together, a test of visual synthesis that needs no drawing. And for children, the main alternative to the Bender is the Beery VMI , the Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration of Keith E. Beery and Norman A. Buktenica , first published in 1967 and in its sixth edition (with Natasha Beery) in 2010, for ages 2 to 100 in its full form. The child copies geometric forms of increasing difficulty printed in a booklet, and two supplemental tests, Visual Perception and Motor Coordination, separate the two halves of the skill, exactly the question raised by Chanda's Bender. The tests of Sections 11.2 to 11.5 would find little wrong with him, because they ask what a person can do when the examiner sets the task, times it and says when to stop. His problem lies somewhere else: in the controls that choose a goal, plan the steps, start the work, notice when it is going wrong and change course. Such patients are real (you will meet one of them in Section 11.6.8), and they are the reason neuropsychologists built a separate family of tests for the brain's "management". This section teaches that family and three neighbours that are examined alongside it. The executive tests come first: the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, the most widely used of them, then the Trail Making Test, the Stroop test, the tower tests and the fluency tests, and finally the newer tests that try to capture executive failure in everyday life. Then come the tests of attention, which executive tests depend on; the tests of concept formation, which clinical psychologists have used since the 1940s to examine disordered thinking in schizophrenia; and the language tests used to describe an aphasia. For each test you will learn what the person does, what is scored, what the score means and what it does not mean. What executive functions are, and why they are hard to test The executive functions are the higher-order control processes that let a person set a goal, organise behaviour towards it, start and keep it going, inhibit actions that do not serve it, monitor the result and change strategy when the situation changes. The word "executive" is borrowed from management: memory, language, perception and movement are the departments of a company, and the executive functions are the managers who decide what the departments should do, in what order and when to stop. A person can have every department intact and still fail, if the management is gone. The clinical definition most quoted in neuropsychology comes from Muriel Lezak , whose textbook is introduced in Section 11.1. In a 1982 paper titled "The problem of assessing executive functions", in the International Journal of Psychology , and in later editions of her textbook, she divided executive functioning into four components. Volition (called goal formulation in the 1982 paper) is the capacity for intentional behaviour: forming a goal and the motivation to act on it. Planning is identifying and organising the steps needed to reach the goal. Purposive action is starting, maintaining, switching and stopping the sequence of actions the plan requires. Effective performance is monitoring the result and correcting it. Lezak's point was that each component can fail on its own: an apathetic patient has no volition, a disorganised one cannot plan, a perseverating one cannot switch, and a careless one cannot check. Experimental psychology has broken the executive into parts in a different way. Book 1, Section 7.3.4 describes the central executive of the working memory model and the work of Akira Miyake and colleagues (2000), who found three related but separable executive functions in healthy adults: inhibition of unwanted responses, shifting between tasks or mental sets, and updating the contents of working memory. Clinicians add three more that matter at the bedside. Planning is working out a sequence of moves before making them. Fluency , in this sense, is generating many responses from memory under a rule and against the clock. Abstraction, or concept formation, is finding the general principle behind particular examples. The classic answer is the frontal lobes, and in particular the prefrontal cortex , the part of the frontal lobe in front of the motor and premotor areas. Three broad regions are usually distinguished. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, on the upper outer surface, is linked with organising, shifting, working memory and abstract reasoning. The orbitofrontal and ventromedial cortex, on the underside and the midline, is linked with social conduct, emotional control and decisions about reward and risk. The medial frontal cortex with the anterior cingulate is linked with starting behaviour and monitoring errors. Damage to each produces a recognisable frontal syndrome (disorganised, disinhibited or apathetic), which Book 3, Section 10.11.10 describes. But "executive" names a function and "frontal" names a place, and the two are not the same thing. The prefrontal cortex works through loops with the basal ganglia, the thalamus, the parietal lobes and even the cerebellum: in 1998 Jeremy Schmahmann and Janet Sherman described the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome, in which disease confined to the cerebellum impaired planning, set-shifting, verbal fluency and abstract reasoning. Executive deficits are also found in schizophrenia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), obsessive-compulsive disorder, autism, depression and the dementias. A poor executive score therefore says "the management is failing", not "the damage is in the frontal lobe". Why are these functions so hard to test? There are four reasons, and you will meet each of them again. The first is the paradox Lezak pointed out: a testing session is the most structured hour of a patient's week. The examiner chooses the task, explains it, says when to begin, keeps the patient on track and says when to stop, so the examiner is supplying exactly the planning and control that the test is meant to measure. A patient may do well in the clinic and fall apart at home. The second is the task impurity problem, Miyake's term for the fact that every executive task also needs non-executive abilities: the Trail Making Test needs vision and hand speed, the Stroop needs reading and colour vision, fluency needs vocabulary. A low score can come from any of them, which is why so many executive scores are differences or ratios that try to remove the basic ability (you will compute three of them below). The third is novelty: an executive test works best the first time, when the problem is new; on a second attempt the patient may remember the solution, and the task has become a routine one that no longer needs the executive. That is one reason retest reliabilities for these tests are modest (Chapter 3, Section 3.8 lists the other things that lower reliability). The fourth is ecological validity , the extent to which a test score predicts how a person functions in everyday life; Section 11.6.8 shows that it can be surprisingly low. Exam trap Match each executive test to its main component: the WCST measures set-shifting and cognitive flexibility, the Stroop measures response inhibition, the Tower of London measures planning, verbal fluency measures generation, Trail Making Part B measures switching, and backward digit span and the N-back measure working memory. A question asking for "the test of planning" wants a tower test, not the WCST. And "executive" is not a synonym for "frontal": damage elsewhere, and many psychiatric disorders, can lower executive scores. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test: from a learning experiment to a frontal-lobe test The most widely used test of executive function began life as an experiment on learning in healthy students. Its roots go back to the German neurologists of the 1920s. Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965) and his colleague Adhémar Gelb , studying soldiers with brain injuries in Frankfurt after the First World War, noticed that many could sort objects by one property, colour for example, but could not switch to sorting the same objects by another property when asked. One of their circle, Egon Weigl , described a simple colour-form sorting test for this purpose in 1927: a few cut-out shapes in several colours, which the patient sorts first one way and then the other. Section 11.6.10 returns to Goldstein's ideas. Two decades later, at the University of Wisconsin, the experimental psychologist David A. Grant and his colleague Esta A. Berg turned Weigl's idea into a card-sorting task that could be scored objectively. Their 1948 paper in the Journal of Experimental Psychology has a title that tells you what they were interested in: "A behavioral analysis of degree of reinforcement and ease of shifting to new responses in a Weigl-type card-sorting problem". In the same year Berg published "A simple objective technique for measuring flexibility in thinking" in the Journal of General Psychology . Their question was about learning, not about brains: when a response has been rewarded with "right" many times, how easily can a person abandon it once it starts to be called "wrong"? The neuropsychologist Bryan Kolb , in a tribute to Brenda Milner published in 2022, notes that Grant designed the task as a human counterpart of the reversal problems that Harry Harlow, also at Wisconsin, was giving to monkeys. It was Milner who took the task to Montreal and made it a test of the frontal lobes, in the study told in Section 11.6.4. The test was standardised for clinical use by Robert K. Heaton , whose manual appeared in 1981 and was revised and expanded in 1993 (by Heaton, Gordon Chelune, Jack Talley, Gary Kay and Glenn Curtiss), with norms from about six and a half to 89 years, corrected for age and education. A short form using a single deck, the WCST-64, followed in 2000, and computer versions are now common. The materials are simple. In front of the person the examiner lays four stimulus cards (key cards). Each card shows one, two, three or four copies of a single symbol, and the four key cards differ from each other in three ways at once: in the colour of the symbols, in their form (shape) and in their number. The person is then handed a pack of 128 response cards , made up of two decks of 64, each showing a combination of one colour, one form and one number. The instruction is to place each response card below whichever key card the person thinks it goes with. The examiner says nothing about how to match the cards: after each card the only feedback is "right" or "wrong". The examiner has a rule in mind, and in Heaton's procedure the first rule is colour. Once the person has matched ten cards in a row correctly, the rule changes without warning, to form, and after the next ten correct in a row to number, and then the cycle repeats (colour, form, number). The test ends when the person has completed six categories or has used all 128 cards. Figure 11.10 shows the logic with invented cards. Four key cards (invented for this book) Card 1: one orange moon Card 2: two purple hearts Card 3: three green diamonds Card 4: four blue squares Response card: two orange squares If the rule is colour: it goes under card 1 (orange) If the rule is number: it goes under card 2 (two) If the rule is form: it goes under card 4 (squares) Card 3 shares nothing with it Invented cards in the style of the test; the real cards are not reproduced. Figure 11.10 The logic of the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, shown with invented cards. Each response card can be matched to different key cards by colour, form or number, so the person has to discover from "right" and "wrong" which rule the examiner is using, and must notice when it silently changes. Why is such a simple task so revealing? Because it makes three separate demands, and a person can fail any of them. First, the person must form a concept from feedback alone: nobody says "sort by colour", so the rule has to be inferred from a run of "rights" and "wrongs". That is abstraction. Second, once found, the rule must be kept in mind and applied card after card, even when a card would also fit another key card. That is maintenance of set. Third, when the "wrongs" begin, the person must give up the rule that has just been rewarded ten times, and search for another. That is set-shifting, and it is the demand the test is famous for. The two great ways of failing are opposites. A person who cannot let go keeps sorting by the old rule despite being told "wrong" again and again. A person who cannot hold on finds the rule, gets several cards right, and then drifts away from it for no reason. The scores in the next subsection are designed to tell these failures apart. Set-shifting , also called cognitive flexibility , is the ability to disengage from one mental set (a rule, a strategy or a way of seeing a problem) and engage another when the situation demands it. In daily life it is what lets you take another route when the road is closed, or change your explanation to a pupil who has not understood the first one. Its failure is what clinicians see as rigidity, and on the WCST as perseveration. Exam trap The WCST was devised by David Grant and Esta Berg in 1948, not by Robert Heaton (who wrote the clinical manual, 1981 and 1993) or Brenda Milner (who showed its link with frontal lesions, 1963). It uses four stimulus cards and 128 response cards; the rule changes without warning after ten consecutive correct sorts, in the order colour, form, number; and the test ends after six categories or 128 cards. Some Indian notes give 60 or 64 cards: the standard test has 128, in two decks of 64, and the one-deck WCST-64 is a short form. The task descends from Weigl's colour-form sorting test, which is why Grant and Berg called it a "Weigl-type" problem. Scoring the WCST: perseveration and the other scores The central idea in WCST scoring is perseveration : the continued repetition of a response, or a way of responding, after it has stopped being appropriate. On the card test it means going on sorting by a rule after the feedback has started to say "wrong". Heaton's manual makes the idea exact through the perseverated-to principle , the rule that the person is clinging to. In the simplest case, and in the worked example below, that is the rule that used to be right: after ten correct sorts by colour, the rule becomes form, and colour becomes the perseverated-to principle. A perseverative response is any response that matches the perseverated-to principle. Most such responses are wrong, but not all, because some response cards match a key card on two dimensions at once: a card that matches by both colour and form is "right" under the form rule, and yet it is still consistent with the old colour rule. So the manual distinguishes the perseverative response (which may be right or wrong) from the perseverative error , a perseverative response that is also wrong. The perseverative error count is the score most clinicians look at first. Remember Perseverative error = a response that is wrong under the current rule and matches the rule the person is clinging to (usually the previous correct one). Percentage of perseverative errors = (perseverative errors ÷ trials administered) × 100 Here "trials administered" is the number of cards the person sorted (at most 128). Converting a count into a percentage allows a person who sorted 128 cards to be compared with one who finished in 80. The other scores describe the rest of the performance. Table 11.24 lists them. Two need a word of explanation. Failure to maintain set is counted when a person makes an error after a run of five or more consecutive correct responses but before completing the category: the person had found the rule and then lost it. That is the opposite of perseveration, and points towards distractibility or a working memory lapse rather than rigidity. Conceptual level responses are correct responses that occur in runs of three or more in a row; the reasoning is that a run of three correct sorts is unlikely by chance and shows that the person has grasped the concept. The raw scores are converted, using the manual's tables, into standard scores (mean 100, standard deviation 15), T scores and percentiles corrected for age and years of education, so that a 70-year-old with eight years of schooling is compared with similar people and not with university students (Chapter 5 explains standard scores and norms). His wife says he "gets stuck": he repeats the same suggestion in family discussions long after it has been turned down. Table 11.25 is an invented excerpt of twenty trials from his test, using the invented key cards of Figure 11.10 (card 1 one orange moon, card 2 two purple hearts, card 3 three green diamonds, card 4 four blue squares).
