Take the options one at a time. The Beck Depression Inventory is a self-report inventory: the patient reads each group of statements and circles the one that fits. The Beck Anxiety Inventory, from the same group of authors, is also self-report: the patient rates how much each symptom has bothered her. The Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale is completed by a trained clinician after an interview, so it is the clinician-rated one. Option (d) would be right only if both (b) and (c) were clinician-rated; since (b) is self-report, (d) is wrong. The answer is (c). A useful rule of thumb, with exceptions you will meet in Section 11.9, is that scales called "inventory" or "questionnaire" are self-reports and scales called "rating scale" (the Hamilton scales, the Montgomery-Åsberg) are clinician-rated; the word "questionnaire" in the question's stem is loose usage, since a clinician-rated scale is not really a questionnaire at all. Exam trap All the Beck inventories you meet here (depression, anxiety, hopelessness) are self-report ; both Hamilton scales (anxiety 1959, depression 1960) are clinician-rated . So "both the Beck Anxiety Inventory and the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale are clinician-rated" is false. The one Beck instrument of this section that is clinician-rated is the 1979 Scale for Suicide Ideation, which is an interview; its 1991 successor, the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation, is a self-report. The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale is clinician-rated too, although self-report versions have since been made. How a scale is built: items, anchors, time frames, totals, bands and cut-offs Open any rating scale and you will find the same parts. Each item covers one symptom (low mood, sleep, guilt, worry) or one aspect of a symptom (the time obsessions take, the distress they cause). Each item offers a set of response options, and the format of those options comes in a few standard kinds. In a Likert-type response format , named after Rensis Likert (1903 to 1981), whose 1932 method of attitude measurement summed people's ratings of agreement with a set of statements (Chapter 8 teaches the Likert scale as an attitude scale), each item is answered on an ordered set of five or so options, such as "not at all, several days, more than half the days, nearly every day" (the frequency format of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7) or "not at all, mildly, moderately, severely" (the intensity format of the Beck Anxiety Inventory). In a dichotomous format each item is simply yes or no, or true or false, as on the Geriatric Depression Scale and the Beck Hopelessness Scale; this is easier for elderly or ill patients but gives less information per item. In a graded-statement format , the one the Beck Depression Inventory made famous, each item is a group of four statements describing the same symptom at increasing severity, and the patient picks the statement that fits. And in a visual analogue scale the patient marks a point on a line, traditionally 100 millimetres long, whose ends are labelled with the extremes ("no anxiety at all", "the worst anxiety I can imagine"); the score is the distance from the left end in millimetres, from 0 to 100. For a clinician-rated scale the response options are anchors (or anchor points): written descriptions attached to each score that tell the rater exactly what a 0, a 1 or a 3 looks like. A scale whose points carry only bare labels such as "mild" and "severe" leaves each rater to decide for himself what "severe" means, and two raters will disagree. A scale whose points carry concrete descriptions ("wakes most nights and takes more than an hour to fall asleep again") makes them agree. The quality of the anchors is the single biggest influence on inter-rater reliability , the agreement between two raters scoring the same interview, which Chapter 3, Section 3.6 teaches with its statistics (kappa and the intraclass correlation). Figure 11.16 shows an invented anchored item and how its rating becomes part of a total. Invented item: Sleep Time frame: the past 7 days 0 Sleeps as usual 1 A little less; not troubled by it 2 Wakes most nights; slow to resume 3 Under four hours most nights 4 Hardly sleeps at all The rater picks the anchor that fits best Item score = 2 each item is scored 0 to 4 Add up all 10 items so the total runs from 0 to 40 Read the total against severity bands or a cut-off Repeat later to track change Figure 11.16 The anatomy of a clinician-rated item (invented for illustration, not taken from any published scale). Notice the three things that make ratings comparable: a stated time frame, a written anchor for every score, and a fixed rule (here, adding ten items) for turning item scores into a total that is read against bands. Every scale also states a time frame : the period the ratings refer to. The Beck Depression Inventory-II asks about the past two weeks, including today; the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 also ask about the past two weeks; the Hamilton scales and the Yale-Brown scale are usually rated for the past week; some mania ratings use the past 48 hours (Section 11.9). The time frame is not a detail. A rating of "how you feel today" swings with the weather of the day, while a two-week window matches the duration that the diagnostic criteria for a depressive episode require; a scale used to track weekly change in therapy cannot use a window longer than a week or two without each rating overlapping the last. Next comes the total. On most scales it is a simple sum of the item scores, and the possible range follows from the number of items and the range of each item. This little piece of arithmetic is worth doing every time, because examiners love to ask for ranges. Remember Lowest possible total = number of items × lowest item score. Highest possible total = number of items × highest item score (when all items share one range). So 21 items scored 0 to 3 give 0 to 63 (21 × 3 = 63); 10 items scored 0 to 4 give 0 to 40; 20 items scored 1 to 4 give 20 to 80, not 0 to 80, because the lowest score on each item is 1. When items have different ranges, add the item maxima one by one: Hamilton's 17-item depression scale has nine items scored 0 to 4 and eight scored 0 to 2, so its maximum is 9 × 4 + 8 × 2 = 36 + 16 = 52, not 17 × 4 = 68. Some scales deliberately word half their items in the healthy direction ("I enjoy the things I used to do") and half in the ill direction ("I feel downhearted"). They do this to catch acquiescence , the tendency of some respondents to agree with whatever they are asked (Chapter 2 teaches it among the response biases). An item worded in the healthy direction is a reverse-keyed item : before adding up, its score is turned round, so that agreeing with "I enjoy things" counts as health, not illness. For an item scored from a lowest value to a highest value, the rule is: Remember Reversed score = (highest item score + lowest item score) − raw score For an item scored 1 to 4, the reversed score is 5 − raw; for an item scored 0 to 3, it is 3 − raw. Worked example. Kirti, a trainee clinical psychologist in a district hospital outpatient department, is scoring a self-rating depression form whose 20 items are each answered 1 ("a little of the time") to 4 ("most of the time"), with ten items worded positively; this is the design of William Zung's scale, met again in Section 11.8.7, but the patient's answers here are invented. On the ten negatively worded items the patient's answers add up to 27. On the ten positive items her raw answers are 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1. Step 1: reverse each one with 5 − raw: the answers 1 become 4 and the answers 2 become 3, giving 4, 3, 4, 4, 3, 4, 4, 3, 4, 4. Step 2: add them: seven 4s make 28 and three 3s make 9, so the reversed total is 28 + 9 = 37. Step 3: add the two halves: 27 + 37 = 64. The total of 64 lies in the possible range 20 to 80. Had Kirti forgotten to reverse, she would have added 13 instead of 37 and reported 40, a score that makes a fairly depressed woman look nearly well. Reversal mistakes are among the commonest scoring errors in practice, which is why scoring templates and computer scoring exist. Finally, the total has to be interpreted. There are two ways of doing this. A severity band divides the range into labelled segments (minimal, mild, moderate, severe), so that a total can be described in words in a report. A cut-off score is a single point chosen so that people at or above it are treated as probable cases: on the PHQ-9 the usual cut-off is 10. Both are conventions set by the scale's authors or later researchers, usually by comparing scores with the diagnoses of clinicians who interviewed the same people, and choosing the point that best balances sensitivity (the proportion of true cases the cut-off catches) against specificity (the proportion of non-cases it correctly passes). When Kurt Kroenke and his colleagues checked the PHQ-9 against interviews by mental health professionals in 580 patients, a score of 10 or more caught 88 percent of the people with major depression and correctly passed 88 percent of those without it. Chapter 4 teaches sensitivity, specificity and how cut-offs are chosen; for now, notice that a different cut-off would have traded one kind of error for the other, and that bands are agreed conventions, not facts of nature. That is why different sources sometimes print different bands for the same scale, and why a careful report names the bands it used. Norms, the score distributions of reference groups that let you say "higher than 90 percent of outpatients", are a further aid, taught in Chapter 5. Exam trap Do the range arithmetic before you choose an option. A scale whose items start at 1 cannot have a minimum of 0 (the Zung scale runs 20 to 80; the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory's two halves each run 20 to 80). A scale with mixed item ranges cannot be "items × 4" (the 17-item Hamilton depression scale tops out at 52, not 68). And "Likert scale" names a response format and an attitude-scaling method (Rensis Likert, 1932), not a clinical test: many clinical scales use Likert-type options, but "a Likert scale" is never the name of a depression or neuropsychological instrument. What makes a good scale: reliability, validity and sensitivity to change A rating scale is judged by the same standards as any psychological measure, and Chapters 3 and 4 teach those standards in full. Here the question is what each standard means for a symptom scale in particular. Reliability comes first. For a self-report scale the usual evidence is internal consistency, most often Cronbach's alpha (Chapter 3, Section 3.5): do the items hang together as measures of one thing? For a clinician-rated scale the crucial evidence is inter-rater reliability (Chapter 3, Section 3.6): if two trained clinicians watch the same interview, do they give the same total? When Wayne Goodman and his colleagues introduced the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale in 1989, their reliability study had four raters score 40 patients with OCD, and agreement on the total and on each of the ten items was excellent; that study, more than anything else, is why the scale became the standard. Test-retest reliability (Chapter 3, Section 3.2) is checked over a short interval of days, not months, because a symptom scale is supposed to change when the patient changes: a low correlation between a depression score in January and one in June says more about the course of depression than about the scale (Chapter 3, Section 3.2.4 makes this point about states and traits). Validity asks whether the scale measures what it claims to (Chapter 4). Content validity asks whether the items cover the symptoms of the disorder: the Beck Depression Inventory was rewritten in 1996 partly so that its items matched the DSM-IV criteria for a depressive episode, and the PHQ-9's nine items simply are those nine criteria. Convergent validity asks whether the scale correlates with other measures of the same thing (a new depression scale should correlate with the Hamilton scale), and discriminant validity asks whether it correlates less with measures of different things: the Beck Anxiety Inventory was built specifically to overlap as little as possible with depression, and the Yale-Brown scale's total correlates only weakly with depression and anxiety ratings in OCD patients who are not markedly depressed. Criterion validity, for a screening scale, is the comparison with an interviewer's diagnosis that produced the PHQ-9's sensitivity and specificity figures above. The third standard is the one that makes a clinical scale clinical. A scale's sensitivity to change (also called responsiveness) is its ability to move when the patient genuinely improves or worsens. A scale can be reliable and valid as a snapshot of severity and still be sluggish as a measure of change, if its items cover symptoms that change slowly or that a treatment does not touch. For a drug trial, a sluggish scale is expensive: it hides real effects, so the trial needs more patients to show them. Key study: building a scale to be sensitive to change (Montgomery and Åsberg, 1979) The question. By the 1970s the Hamilton depression scale was the standard outcome measure in antidepressant trials, but it was criticised as heavy with bodily symptoms, some of which the drugs' own side effects could produce, and as slow to show change. Could a scale be built on purpose to detect change? The method. Stuart Montgomery in England and Marie Åsberg in Sweden started from a long 65-item psychopathology scale (the Comprehensive Psychopathological Rating Scale) rated on 54 English and 52 Swedish patients, and picked out the 17 symptoms most common in depressive illness. They then followed 64 patients through trials of four different antidepressants and kept the 10 items that changed most with treatment and correlated best with overall change. The result. The new 10-item scale had high agreement between raters, correlated well with the Hamilton scale (so it measured the same thing), and separated responders from non-responders better than the Hamilton scale did. The conclusion. Selecting items for responsiveness produces a scale that needs fewer patients to show a drug's effect, which the authors pointed out had ethical as well as practical value. The criticism. A scale chosen for what changed with antidepressants may suit drug trials better than psychological treatments or very different patient groups. How much change counts? Three yardsticks are used, and they answer different questions. The first is percentage change from the starting score: Remember Percentage reduction = (baseline score − follow-up score) ÷ baseline score × 100 Baseline is the score before treatment; follow-up is the score at the later rating. Following the consensus definitions that Ellen Frank's task force proposed in 1991 (Book 3, Section 5.7.1), and the conventions of the trials since, a response in depression is usually a fall of at least 50 percent on a scale such as Hamilton's, and remission is reaching a score low enough to count as essentially well, commonly 7 or less on the 17-item Hamilton scale (the threshold the task force suggested). Worked example. Charvi, a 27-year-old bank clerk in Pune, starts treatment for a depressive episode; her clinician's Hamilton rating at the first visit is 26. At week 8 it is 12. Step 1: the fall is 26 − 12 = 14 points. Step 2: divide by the baseline: 14 ÷ 26 = 0.538. Step 3: multiply by 100: 53.8 percent, which rounds to 54 percent. Since 54 percent is more than 50 percent, Charvi has responded; but since 12 is well above 7, she has not remitted, and treatment should continue toward full recovery. A patient who starts at 40 and falls to 20 has also responded (50 percent) while remaining very ill, which is why trials report both response and remission. The second yardstick asks whether a change is bigger than the scale's own measurement error. Neil Jacobson and Paula Truax's reliable change index , taught with a worked example in Chapter 3, Section 3.7.6, divides the change by the standard error of the difference; a value beyond 1.96 means the change is unlikely to be measurement error alone. The third asks whether the change matters to the patient. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID), a term introduced by Roman Jaeschke , Joel Singer and Gordon Guyatt in 1989, is the smallest change in score that patients perceive as beneficial and that would make a clinician change the management; in their studies it was about half a point per item on seven-point scales. A change can be statistically reliable yet too small to matter, or large enough to matter yet within the error of an unreliable scale, so the three yardsticks are used together. Two last properties complete the list. A scale has a floor effect when many people score at or near its lowest possible value, so it cannot distinguish among the mildly ill, and a ceiling effect when many score at or near the top, so it cannot show that a very ill patient has become worse. A scale built for hospitalised melancholic patients may show a floor effect in a college counselling centre, and a brief screen may show a ceiling effect on an inpatient ward. And a total score assumes that the items measure one underlying thing. When factor analysis (taught in the Research Methodology book) shows that a scale's items fall into several separate clusters, as it does for Hamilton's depression scale, the total mixes different things, and researchers have proposed shorter "core" subscales that measure the central mood symptoms more cleanly. Exam trap The Montgomery-Åsberg scale (1979) is the depression scale designed for sensitivity to change , by keeping the 10 items that moved most with antidepressant treatment. Response (usually a fall of 50 percent or more) is not remission (a score low enough to be essentially well, for example 7 or less on the 17-item Hamilton scale): a patient can respond and still be ill. The minimal clinically important difference (Jaeschke, Singer and Guyatt, 1989) is about what matters to patients; the reliable change index (Jacobson and Truax, 1991) is about measurement error. Do not swap them. Errors that raters make Whenever a person, rather than a scoring key, decides the score, the person becomes part of the measuring instrument, and people bring their own systematic errors with them. Chapter 3, Section 3.6 explains how agreement between raters is measured and noted these errors in one line each. This is the place to understand them, because clinical ratings are where they do their damage. Key study: Thorndike and the halo (1920) Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949) examined ratings that had real consequences: official ratings of army officers and aviation cadets by their superior officers in the United States Army, used to decide salaries and promotions, and, in an earlier study of 1915, ratings of employees of two large industrial corporations. The officers had been rated separately on qualities such as physique, intelligence, leadership and character. These are different qualities, and in reality they are only modestly related, yet the ratings correlated with each other too highly and too evenly: even physique correlated about 0.3 to 0.4 with intelligence and leadership. Thorndike concluded that the raters could not treat each quality on its own; a general impression of the man suffused every separate judgement, like a halo. His paper, "A constant error in psychological ratings" in the Journal of Applied Psychology (1920), gave the error its name. The lesson for clinicians is uncomfortable: the more a rater likes, or dislikes, a patient overall, the more every item drifts in the same direction. The halo effect , then, is the error in which an overall impression, or one striking attribute, colours the ratings of other, separate attributes. It can run either way: a negative halo (sometimes called the horns effect) drags every rating down. In symptom rating it has a particular form that an RML paper (2024) asked about: when a patient's anxiety improves markedly, the rater may also record an improvement in her depression, although her depression has not changed. The striking improvement in one symptom spreads, as a halo, to the rating of another, and the right answer to "the improvement in anxiety may sometimes spuriously improve depression; this is called..." is the halo effect, not a ceiling effect (a scale too short at the top to register change), a Hawthorne effect (people changing because they know they are being studied) or a therapeutic effect (a real improvement). Several other errors were catalogued in the classic psychometrics textbooks, notably Joy Paul Guilford 's (1897 to 1987) Psychometric Methods , first published in 1936. A leniency error (or generosity error) is a rater's constant tendency to rate too favourably; its mirror image, the severity error , is a constant tendency to rate too harshly. On a symptom scale "favourable" means "less ill", so a clinician who is fond of a patient, or who hopes his treatment is working, may rate symptoms as milder than they are. The reverse pressure exists too, and trial methodologists warn about it: in drug trials that admit patients only above a threshold score, raters may nudge entry scores upward (so-called baseline score inflation), so that the patients then appear to improve partly because their first scores were inflated. A central tendency error is the avoidance of the extremes of the scale: the rater, unsure, gives everyone a 1 or a 2 on a 0 to 4 item, so that differences between patients shrink. A logical error is rating two attributes alike because the rater believes, as a matter of his own theory, that they go together: he rates a patient who sleeps badly as anxious, because "poor sleepers are anxious people", without asking about anxiety. The difference from halo is the source: halo comes from a general impression of the person, a logical error from the rater's beliefs about which symptoms belong together. A contrast error is rating a person against an inappropriate standard, either the previous patient (a moderately depressed patient seen after a profoundly depressed one looks mild) or the rater himself. A proximity error is rating items alike because they sit next to each other on the form. Expectancy is a further, separate danger: a rater who knows which patients are receiving the active drug sees what he expects, which is why trials use blind raters who do not know the treatment. And rater drift is the slow wandering of a rater's standards away from the anchors over months of use, which repeated calibration corrects. Concrete anchors leave less room for impressions. A semi-structured interview guide, which gives the rater suggested questions in a fixed order but lets him follow up, makes raters gather the same evidence before they rate: Janet Williams published such a guide for the Hamilton depression scale in 1988, and the Yale-Brown scale has always come with one. Training on videotaped interviews, with each trainee's ratings compared against expert ratings until they agree, deals with leniency, severity and central tendency. Blind raters deal with expectancy. Hamilton himself suggested that two clinicians should rate each interview independently and that their ratings be combined, which, as Chapter 3, Section 3.6 shows, makes the combined rating more reliable than either alone. Exam trap Halo (Edward Thorndike, 1920) is the error in which one global impression or one attribute colours the ratings of others; it is the answer to "the improvement in anxiety may spuriously improve depression" (RML 2024) and to "judging an individual on the basis of one single attribute" (IHBAS 2024). It is not a logical error (the rater's belief that two traits go together), a central tendency error (rating everyone average), a contrast error (rating relative to the last person or to oneself) or a similarity error (favouring people like the rater). Leniency and severity are constant errors: they shift everyone the same way. The Beck Depression Inventory In the late 1950s Aaron Temkin Beck (1921 to 2021), a psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, was trying to test a psychoanalytic idea about depression, and he needed a way of measuring how depressed his patients were that did not depend on one psychiatrist's impression. (The research led him away from psychoanalysis to cognitive therapy, whose story Book 2, Chapter 5 tells.) In 1961, with C. H. Ward, M. Mendelson, J. Mock and J. Erbaugh, he published "An inventory for measuring depression" in the Archives of General Psychiatry . The items were not taken from a theory or a textbook. Beck chose them from his clinical observations: the attitudes and symptoms that depressed patients often described and that other psychiatric patients rarely did. Each became a group of statements describing the same symptom at increasing severity, from its absence to its extreme, and in the first version an interviewer read each group aloud while the patient followed on her own copy and chose the statement that fitted. The Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) became the most widely used self-report measure of depression in the world. It has had three main forms. The 1961 original was revised during the 1970s at Beck's Center for Cognitive Therapy as the BDI-IA (copyrighted in 1978 and published in 1979 in Beck's Cognitive Therapy of Depression ), with simpler wording, fully self-administered, and asking about the past week, including today. In 1996 Beck, Robert Steer and Gregory Brown published the BDI-II , rewritten so that the items matched the DSM-IV criteria for a major depressive episode. Four items that dealt with weight loss, body image, bodily preoccupation and difficulty working were dropped; four on agitation, worthlessness, difficulty concentrating and loss of energy were added; the sleep and appetite items now allow for an increase as well as a decrease, because depression can make people sleep and eat more as well as less; and the time frame was lengthened to the past two weeks, including today, to match the two-week duration in the diagnostic criteria. The BDI-II is meant for ages 13 to 80, takes five to ten minutes, and is published, under copyright, by Pearson (formerly The Psychological Corporation). Like every copyrighted test in this book, its items are not reproduced here: in general terms, they cover the cognitive and emotional symptoms of depression (sadness, pessimism, a sense of failure, loss of pleasure, guilt, self-dislike and self-criticism, suicidal thoughts, crying, indecisiveness, worthlessness) and its bodily and vegetative symptoms (agitation, loss of energy, sleep, appetite, concentration, tiredness and loss of interest in sex). Factor analyses usually find two clusters, a cognitive-affective one and a somatic one. Scoring is simple, which is part of the inventory's appeal. Each of the 21 items is scored 0, 1, 2 or 3 according to the statement chosen; if the patient finds that several statements in a group fit equally well, the instructions ask her to choose the highest. The total is the sum of the 21 item scores, so it runs from 0 (21 × 0) to 63 (21 × 3). The BDI-II manual divides that range into four bands, which Figure 11.17 draws to scale. Remember: BDI-II 21 items, each 0 to 3, for the past two weeks including today; total 0 to 63. 0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate, 29 to 63 severe (Beck, Steer and Brown, 1996). Self-report, ages 13 to 80. Worked example. Charvi, the bank clerk whose Hamilton ratings you followed in Section 11.8.4, also completes the BDI-II at her first visit. Her item scores, in order from item 1 to item 21, are invented for this example (the item content is not shown): 2, 1, 1, 3, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0. Step 1: rather than adding 21 numbers in a row, where slips are easy, count how many times each score appears. There is one 3 (item 4). There are five 2s (items 1, 7, 12, 15 and 16). There are four 0s (items 6, 9, 18 and 21). That leaves 21 − 1 − 5 − 4 = 11 items scored 1. Step 2: multiply and add: 1 × 3 = 3; 5 × 2 = 10; 11 × 1 = 11; 4 × 0 = 0; and 3 + 10 + 11 + 0 = 24. Step 3: check the count of items: 1 + 5 + 11 + 4 = 21, so none has been missed. Step 4: place the total in a band. Since 24 is at least 20 and no more than 28, Charvi's score falls in the moderate band. Step 5: look at the single items as well as the total. Her item 9 (a 0 here, invented) would in a real record be checked first, because on the BDI-II that item concerns suicidal thoughts and any score above 0 calls for a risk assessment (Book 2, Section 2.7.2). Interpreted in plain words: by her own account, Charvi has a moderate level of depressive symptoms, with her highest ratings on a few items rather than mild complaints spread evenly, a pattern her therapist would explore. Charvi at intake: 24 Week 8: 12 Minimal Mild Moderate Severe 0 to 13 14 to 19 20 to 28 29 to 63 Fall of 12 points = 50 percent Total score, 0 to 63 Bands from the BDI-II manual (Beck, Steer and Brown, 1996); scores invented Figure 11.17 The BDI-II bands drawn to scale on the 0 to 63 range. Notice how unequal they are: the mild band covers only six scores (14 to 19) and the severe band covers 35, so a few points' change near the bottom of the range can move a patient across two labels, while large changes within the severe band leave the label unchanged. Eight weeks later Charvi scores 12. The fall is 24 − 12 = 12 points, and 12 ÷ 24 = 0.50, a reduction of exactly 50 percent; her score has moved from the moderate band into the minimal band. Is the change larger than measurement error? Using the illustrative figures of Chapter 3, Section 3.7.6 (a depression inventory with a standard deviation of 8 and a reliability of 0.88), a fall of about 7.7 points or more is needed before chance can be set aside; Charvi's 12 points clears that bar. Her self-report and her clinician's Hamilton rating tell the same story here. When they do not, the clinician asks why: has the patient learned what the clinician hopes to hear, or does she feel better than she looks? Four of this chapter's questions turn on the BDI, and each rewards the facts above. The first (NIMHANS practice mock) describes a 35-year-old with two months of persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, weight loss, insomnia, worthlessness and poor concentration, and asks which assessment would be most appropriate to evaluate her symptoms further. The Beck Depression Inventory is right: the picture is of a depressive episode, and the BDI quantifies its severity in ten minutes and gives a baseline against which treatment can be judged. The Rorschach Inkblot Test is a projective technique for personality and perceptual-cognitive functioning (Chapter 10); its Comprehensive System even has a Depression Index (Chapter 10, Section 10.5), but it is long, needs expert scoring and is not the instrument for measuring a depressive episode. The MMPI is a broad personality and psychopathology inventory of several hundred items (Chapter 9); its depression scale is one of ten clinical scales, so it is far less direct. The WAIS measures intelligence (Chapter 6), which is not the question here. Note what the BDI does not do in this case: it does not confirm the diagnosis (a clinical interview against the criteria does that), and it does not replace asking her directly about suicidal thoughts. The second (MET mock) asks how the BDI-II measures severity. Option (a), "21 items rated 0 to 3 corresponding to symptoms over the past two weeks", is exactly right. Option (b), "31 items rated 0 to 4", matches no Beck scale. Option (c), "10 items rated 0 to 10", sounds like a short clinician scale, but the 10-item Montgomery-Åsberg scale rates each item 0 to 6, not 0 to 10. Option (d), "1 item rated 0 to 100", describes a single global rating, such as a visual analogue scale of mood or the old 0 to 100 Global Assessment of Functioning (Section 11.9), not an inventory. The third and fourth (MET mocks) ask for the bands. The conventional BDI-II bands are 0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate and 29 to 63 severe, so the band that flags "moderate" depression is 20 to 28; 14 to 19 is mild, 0 to 13 minimal and 29 to 63 severe. The distractor bands in the other options are worth a moment. "0 to 9 minimal" is the opening of the older BDI's bands: for the 1961 and 1978 versions the commonly cited bands, the Center for Cognitive Therapy guidelines reported in Beck, Steer and Garbin's 1988 review of the inventory, are 0 to 9 none or minimal, 10 to 18 mild to moderate, 19 to 29 moderate to severe and 30 to 63 severe (other sources print slightly different cut-offs), so a question about the BDI-II should not be answered with them. A set ending at 40 cannot belong to a scale whose maximum is 63; 40 is the Yale-Brown maximum. A three-band split of 0 to 20 minimal, 21 to 40 moderate and 41 to 60 severe is simply invented: it has no mild band and stops at 60, three points short of the BDI-II's maximum. And bands of five points such as 0 to 5, 6 to 10 and 11 to 15 belong to no Beck scale; the PHQ-9's thresholds, which step up by five (5, 10, 15, 20), are the likeliest source of the confusion. Exam trap: the BDI keyed as a neuropsychological test (RML 2025) RML 2025 asked "Which of the following tests is typically used for neuropsychological assessment?" with the options Beck Depression Inventory, Likert Scale, 16 Personality Factor Questionnaire and Peabody Individual Achievement Test, and keyed the Beck Depression Inventory . The BDI is not a neuropsychological test: it is a self-report inventory of depressive symptoms and tests no brain function. It earns its place in a neuropsychological assessment because neuropsychologists routinely add a mood measure: depression lowers effort, speed and memory on tests, and severe depression in an older adult can even mimic dementia (Book 3, Section 10.11.6). The other three options are further off. A Likert scale is a response format and an attitude-scaling method (Rensis Likert, 1932; Chapter 8), not a test at all. The 16PF is Raymond Cattell's personality inventory (Chapter 9). The Peabody Individual Achievement Test (Lloyd Dunn and Frederick Markwardt, 1970) is an individually given test of school achievement (Chapter 8); achievement tests can enter a neuropsychological work-up, for example when a learning disability is in question, but not as the typical example. In the examination, choose the BDI as keyed, knowing that the defensible reason is "the mood measure that a neuropsychological battery commonly includes", not "a test of brain function". Clinical link: depression scales in neurological and medical patients When a neuropsychologist gives the BDI-II to a patient after a head injury, a stroke or in multiple sclerosis, the somatic items need care: fatigue, poor concentration, poor sleep and loss of energy may come from the brain illness itself, not from depression, and inflate the total. Clinicians therefore look at the cognitive-affective items separately, or use a scale that leaves out bodily symptoms: Beck's seven-item BDI-FastScreen for medical patients, or the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (Section 11.8.7), which was designed for this problem. The reverse error matters too: an apathetic patient with frontal damage may report little distress on any self-report, and a clinician's rating and the family's account are needed. Indian context A self-report inventory assumes that the patient can read the form in a language she thinks in. In many Indian clinics the clinician reads the items aloud and records the answers, which turns a self-report into an interviewer-administered scale (as the 1961 BDI originally was); the report should say so. A translation should be one that has been checked, not one improvised at the desk, because a word chosen for "guilt" or "worthless" can shift an item's meaning. Many patients in Indian primary care first describe depression in bodily terms (aches, weakness, poor sleep), so the somatic items carry a heavy load and a mainly cognitive scale can under-read their distress. Brief scales are also used to select patients for Indian trials: the PREMIUM trial of lay-counsellor treatment in Goa enrolled adults with PHQ-9 scores above 14 (Book 2, Section 5.11.5). Exam trap BDI-II: 21 items, 0 to 3, two weeks, 0 to 63, 1996, Beck, Steer and Brown, self-report ; moderate is 20 to 28 . The BDI and the Beck Anxiety Inventory both have 21 items and a 0 to 63 range, so questions swap them. And two different Becks appear in this book: Aaron T. Beck (depression inventory, cognitive therapy) and Samuel J. Beck , whose Rorschach scoring system is in Chapter 10, Section 10.5. Other depression scales: Hamilton, Montgomery-Åsberg, Zung, PHQ-9 and the rest Max Hamilton (1912 to 1988) was born in Offenbach in Germany, came to Britain as a small child, trained in medicine at University College Hospital in London, began his psychiatric training at the Maudsley Hospital and finished it at University College Hospital, and spent most of his career at the University of Leeds, where he became professor of psychiatry in 1963. He was unusual among the psychiatrists of his time for his command of statistics and measurement. His "A rating scale for depression", published in the Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry in 1960, set out what the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HAM-D, also abbreviated HRSD or HDRS) was for, and its limits. It was meant for patients already diagnosed with a depressive illness, to quantify how severe it was; it was not a diagnostic or screening instrument. The ratings were to be based on a clinical interview, and Hamilton wrote that the scale's value depended entirely on the skill of the interviewer. The 1960 scale had 21 items, but Hamilton advised that only the first 17 be added into the total: the last four (diurnal variation, depersonalisation and derealisation, paranoid symptoms and obsessional symptoms) describe the kind of depression rather than its severity. His 1967 revision kept the 17-item total, and the 17-item version (HAM-D17) is still the one meant when a trial reports "the Hamilton". Its items are a mixture of the psychological symptoms of depression (low mood, guilt, suicidal ideas, loss of interest in work and activities, psychic anxiety, slowing and agitation, insight) and a large share of bodily ones (three separate items for difficulty falling asleep, waking in the night and waking early, plus appetite, weight loss, bodily anxiety, general physical symptoms, sexual symptoms and hypochondriasis). Nine items are scored 0 to 4 and eight are scored 0 to 2, which is why the total runs from 0 to 52 (the arithmetic is in Section 11.8.3). The time frame is usually the past week. Bands vary between sources; one commonly used set is 0 to 7 normal, 8 to 13 mild, 14 to 18 moderate, 19 to 22 severe and 23 or more very severe, while an empirical study by Mark Zimmerman and colleagues (2013), which compared scores with clinicians' global severity ratings in 627 outpatients, placed the boundaries at 8 to 16 mild, 17 to 23 moderate and 24 or more severe. Whatever the bands, 7 or less is the usual definition of remission. Why has a 1960 scale lasted so long? Because so many trials used it that every new trial had to use it too, so that results could be compared, and because a clinician's rating catches the slowing, agitation and bodily changes of severe depression that a self-report can miss. Its weaknesses are just as well known. The heavy bodily content reflects the hospitalised, melancholic patients of the 1950s; it means that side effects of a drug (or the sleep-inducing effect of a sedating antidepressant) can move the score; some items have poor agreement between raters; and the items do not measure one single thing. A 2004 review by Michael Bagby and colleagues in the American Journal of Psychiatry asked, in its title, whether the "gold standard" had become "a lead weight". Structured interview guides, such as Janet Williams's of 1988, improved its reliability. Book 2, Section 5.4.3 shows the Hamilton and Beck scales in use side by side in cognitive therapy research. The Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), whose construction was the key study of Section 11.8.4, was published by Stuart Montgomery and Marie Åsberg in the British Journal of Psychiatry in 1979. It is clinician-rated, with 10 items covering sadness as the patient reports it and as the rater sees it, inner tension, sleep, appetite, concentration, lassitude, inability to feel, pessimistic thoughts and suicidal thoughts. Each item is scored 0 to 6, with written anchors at 0, 2, 4 and 6 and the odd numbers for ratings in between, so the total runs from 0 to 10 × 6 = 60. Only one item, the sadness the rater observes, rests on observation alone. Because it has fewer bodily items than the Hamilton scale and was selected for change, it is favoured in antidepressant trials. Its bands also vary between sources. Another early and widely used self-report scale for depression came from William W. K. Zung of Duke University, whose Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) appeared in the Archives of General Psychiatry in 1965. Its 20 statements cover the emotional, physiological and psychological symptoms of depression, and the patient rates each for how much of the time it applies, from "a little of the time" (1) to "most of the time" (4). Half the statements are worded in the healthy direction to guard against acquiescence, so half are reverse-scored, exactly as in Kirti's worked example in Section 11.8.3. The raw total therefore runs from 20 to 80, and Zung converted it to an index out of 100: Remember SDS index = raw score ÷ 80 × 100 The raw score is the sum of the 20 items after reversing the positive ones; 80 is the highest possible raw score. The index runs from 25 (a raw score of 20) to 100. For the patient in Kirti's example, whose raw total was 64, the index is 64 ÷ 80 = 0.80, and 0.80 × 100 = 80. A raw score of 20, the lowest possible, gives 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25, which is why the index can never be 0. Zung also built a matching Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (1971). The scale you will most often see in a general hospital or a primary health centre today is the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) of Kurt Kroenke , Robert Spitzer (1932 to 2015, the psychiatrist who led the making of DSM-III) and Janet Williams , published in 2001. It is the depression module of the Patient Health Questionnaire, a self-report version of an earlier interview for primary care called PRIME-MD. Its nine items are simply the nine DSM-IV criteria for a major depressive episode, and the patient rates how often each has bothered her over the past two weeks: not at all (0), several days (1), more than half the days (2), nearly every day (3). The total runs from 0 to 27. In the validation study, 6,000 patients in primary-care and obstetrics clinics completed it; scores of 5, 10, 15 and 20 marked the thresholds of mild, moderate, moderately severe and severe depression; and a score of 10 or more, checked against interviews of 580 patients, had a sensitivity and a specificity of 88 percent each for major depression. The ninth item asks about thoughts of death or self-harm and, whatever the total, a positive answer must be followed by a direct risk assessment. Its first two items, low mood and loss of interest, form the even shorter PHQ-2 screen. Because it is short, free to use and tied to the diagnostic criteria, it is the measure that stepped-care services use session by session (Book 2, Section 5.11.5). Remember: PHQ-9 9 items, each 0 to 3, past two weeks; total 0 to 27. 0 to 4 minimal, 5 to 9 mild, 10 to 14 moderate, 15 to 19 moderately severe, 20 to 27 severe; 10 or more is the usual screening cut-off. Worked example. Gunjan, a 41-year-old schoolteacher, fills in the PHQ-9 at a primary health centre because she has been sleeping badly and feeling tense for three months. Her invented item ratings are 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0. Adding: 1 + 2 = 3; 3 + 1 = 4; 4 + 2 = 6; 6 + 1 = 7; 7 + 1 = 8; 8 + 1 = 9; and the two zeros add nothing, so the total is 9. That lies in the mild band (5 to 9) and below the screening cut-off of 10, and her ninth item is 0. In plain words: she has some depressive symptoms, but not a probable major depressive episode. Section 11.8.8 shows what her anxiety scale says. Several other depression scales are named in the papers, and each has one thing worth knowing. The Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) of Jerome Yesavage and colleagues (in the Journal of Psychiatric Research , in a volume dated 1982 to 1983, so you will see it cited under both years, most often 1983) was built for older adults: the authors gave 100 candidate questions to normal and depressed elderly people and kept the 30 that correlated best with the total. Every item is answered yes or no, which suits frail or mildly impaired older people, and the final scale contains almost no bodily symptoms, an advantage because aches, poor sleep and low energy are common in old age from physical illness alone. A 15-item short form followed in 1986. For people with dementia, who may not be able to answer questions about their own mood reliably, the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia of George Alexopoulos and colleagues (1988) has a clinician rate the patient from interviews with a carer as well as the patient. The Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) of A. S. Zigmond and R. P. Snaith (1983) was designed for patients attending general hospital medical clinics: 14 self-report items, seven for anxiety and seven for depression, each 0 to 3, so each subscale runs 0 to 21, with 8 to 10 read as borderline and 11 or more as a probable case; like the GDS it leaves out bodily symptoms, so that physical illness does not inflate the scores. For children, Maria Kovacs adapted the BDI into the Children's Depression Inventory, for ages 7 to 17. Two Beck scales concern suicide risk rather than depression as such, and Book 2, Section 2.7.2 places them in the assessment of risk. The Beck Hopelessness Scale (Aaron Beck, Arlene Weissman, David Lester and Larry Trexler, 1974) has 20 true-or-false statements about the future, scored 0 to 20; the follow-up studies in which hopelessness predicted eventual suicide better than depression did are told in Book 3, Section 5.9.3. The Scale for Suicide Ideation (Beck, Maria Kovacs and Arlene Weissman, 1979) is a clinician-rated interview of 19 items, each 0 to 2 (a total of 0 to 38), that measures how intense and specific a person's current suicidal thinking is; its self-report version, the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation, followed in 1991. Exam trap HAM-D : Hamilton 1960, clinician-rated, 17 scored items (21 in the 1960 form), 0 to 52, for patients already diagnosed. MADRS : 1979, clinician-rated, 10 items 0 to 6, 0 to 60, built for sensitivity to change. Zung SDS : 1965, self-report, 20 items 1 to 4, raw 20 to 80 (never 0). PHQ-9 : 2001, self-report, 9 DSM criteria, 0 to 27, cut-off 10. Two "GDS" scales exist: the Geriatric Depression Scale (Yesavage, 30 yes or no items) and the Global Deterioration Scale (Barry Reisberg, 1982, seven stages of dementia, Section 11.7). The Beck Hopelessness Scale is the Beck scale that is true or false , with 20 items, not 21. Anxiety scales: Hamilton, Beck, GAD-7, Spielberger and the Fear Survey Schedule Hamilton's first scale was for anxiety. "The assessment of anxiety states by rating", in the British Journal of Medical Psychology in 1959, introduced the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A, also HARS), and its logic is the same as the depression scale's a year later: a clinician, after an interview, rates the severity of anxiety in a patient already known to have an anxiety state; it is not a diagnostic or screening test. It has 14 items, each rated 0 (not present) to 4 (very severe), so the total runs from 0 to 14 × 4 = 56. The items fall into two halves. The psychic items cover the mental side of anxiety (anxious mood, tension, fears, poor sleep, poor concentration, low mood) and the patient's behaviour at the interview; the somatic items go through the body system by system (muscles, senses, heart, breathing, gut, urinary and sexual function, and other autonomic signs). That heavy bodily content is both its strength (it captures the physical misery of anxiety) and its weakness: it does not separate anxiety well from depression or from physical illness, and a patient with a thyroid or heart condition scores high for reasons that are not psychological. As with the depression scale, bands vary from source to source. Nearly thirty years later Beck's group built the self-report partner. Aaron Beck, Norman Epstein and their colleagues described the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology in 1988. Their stated aim was an anxiety measure that overlapped as little as possible with depression, the known failing of the older anxiety scales. The patient rates how much each of 21 symptoms has bothered her during the past week, including today (the wording of the record form in the 1993 manual), from not at all (0) to severely (3); the total therefore runs from 0 to 63, the same range as the BDI-II. The 1993 manual's bands are 0 to 7 minimal, 8 to 15 mild, 16 to 25 moderate and 26 to 63 severe. Most of its items describe bodily arousal of the kind seen in a panic attack, involving the heart, breathing, balance and skin sensations, and a few describe frightening thoughts of catastrophe or loss of control. Its critics point out that this makes it a better measure of panic-like arousal than of the worry of generalised anxiety. The GAD-7 , the Generalized Anxiety Disorder seven-item scale, is the PHQ-9's anxiety partner, by Robert Spitzer, Kurt Kroenke, Janet Williams and Bernd Löwe (2006). It was tested on 2,740 adults in 15 primary-care clinics in the United States, 965 of whom were then interviewed by mental health professionals. Its seven items ask how often, over the past two weeks, the patient has been bothered by the core symptoms of generalised anxiety (nervousness, uncontrollable worry, restlessness, irritability and the like), each scored 0 to 3 on the same frequency options as the PHQ-9, so the total runs from 0 to 21. Scores of 5, 10 and 15 mark mild, moderate and severe anxiety; a cut-off of 10 gave a sensitivity of 89 percent and a specificity of 82 percent for generalised anxiety disorder, and later work showed that it also picks up panic disorder, social anxiety disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder reasonably well. Its first two items form the GAD-2. Worked example. Gunjan, whose PHQ-9 total was 9, also completes the GAD-7. Her invented item ratings are 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2. Adding: 3 + 2 + 3 = 8, and four 2s make 8 more, so the total is 8 + 8 = 16. Since 16 is 15 or more, she falls in the severe band, well above the cut-off of 10. Put the two scales together and the picture is clear: severe anxiety with mild depressive symptoms, a pattern that points the clinician towards a careful assessment for generalised anxiety disorder (Book 3, Chapter 6) rather than a depressive episode. Her clinician also rates her on the HAM-A at interview. If the clinician's rating is much lower than her self-report, it is worth asking why: some patients feel far more than they show. The State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) of Charles Donald Spielberger (1927 to 2013), with Richard Gorsuch and Robert Lushene, rests on a distinction Spielberger made central to anxiety research. The first, state anxiety , is a temporary condition, the tension and apprehension a person feels right now, which rises before an examination or a surgical operation and falls afterwards. The second, trait anxiety , is a stable disposition, the person's general tendency to respond to many situations with anxiety. The STAI measures both with two separate 20-item halves, one asking how the person feels "right now" and the other how she "generally" feels, each item rated 1 to 4 and some reverse-keyed, so each half runs from 20 to 80. The first form (Form X) appeared in 1970 and the revised Form Y in 1983. It is a research workhorse in studies of stress, surgery and test anxiety more than a clinical severity scale. It should not be confused with the older Taylor Manifest Anxiety Scale (Janet Taylor, 1953), whose items were drawn from the MMPI. The Fear Survey Schedule (FSS) of Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997) and Peter J. Lang (1964) is different in kind from all of these. It is not a severity scale for a disorder but a list of common feared objects and situations (animals, heights, injections, criticism, being alone and many more), each of which the patient rates on a five-point scale from "not at all" to "very much". Wolpe used it to find out what a client feared before building the anxiety hierarchy for systematic desensitisation; its best-known later edition, the FSS-III, lists 108 items. Within the hierarchy itself each situation is rated on Wolpe's 0 to 100 subjective units of distress scale (SUDS), which is not a standardised scale at all but the client's own moment-to-moment rating; Book 2, Section 4.2.3 teaches both in their therapeutic setting. Specific anxiety disorders also have scales of their own, which you need only recognise: the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (Michael Liebowitz, 1987), the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (Katherine Shear and colleagues, 1997), the Penn State Worry Questionnaire (1990) for generalised worry, and, for post-traumatic stress disorder, the clinician-rated Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS, 1995) and the self-report PTSD Checklist (now the PCL-5). Exam trap HAM-A : Hamilton 1959 (a year before the depression scale), clinician-rated , 14 items 0 to 4, total 0 to 56 . BAI : Beck 1988 , self-report , 21 items 0 to 3, total 0 to 63 , mostly bodily symptoms, built to separate anxiety from depression. GAD-7 : 2006, 0 to 21, cut-off 10. The STAI is Spielberger's (state versus trait), not Taylor's. The Fear Survey Schedule (Wolpe and Lang, 1964) lists feared stimuli; the 0 to 100 SUDS (Wolpe) rates hierarchy items. And the PCL-5 (PTSD Checklist) is not the PCL-R (Robert Hare's Psychopathy Checklist-Revised, Section 11.9). The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale Before 1989, the scales for obsessive-compulsive disorder mostly counted symptoms. The Leyton Obsessional Inventory (John Cooper, 1970) and the Maudsley Obsessional-Compulsive Inventory (Ray Hodgson and Stanley Rachman, 1977), for example, asked which of a long list of obsessional symptoms a person had. That works as a description, but as a measure of severity it fails in an obvious way. A man with one devastating obsession about harming his child, which fills his day and keeps him from going home, would score lower than a woman with a dozen mild habits of checking and tidying that cost her a few minutes a day. And OCD comes in so many forms (contamination and washing, doubt and checking, symmetry and ordering, forbidden aggressive, sexual or religious thoughts, hoarding) that a list of contents favours whichever forms the list happens to contain. Wayne Goodman , with Lawrence Price, Steven Rasmussen, Carolyn Mazure and their colleagues at Yale University and Brown University, set out to remedy this. In two papers in the Archives of General Psychiatry in 1989 they described the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS), designed to measure the severity of OCD in a way that is not influenced by the type of obsessions or compulsions present. The trick is to separate two questions: what are your symptoms, and how bad are they? The Y-BOCS is a clinician-rated semi-structured interview in two parts. The first part is the symptom checklist : the clinician goes through several dozen examples of obsessions and compulsions, grouped by theme (aggressive, contamination, sexual, hoarding, religious, symmetry, bodily and miscellaneous obsessions; cleaning, checking, repeating, counting, ordering, hoarding and miscellaneous compulsions), to identify the patient's own target symptoms, past and current. The checklist is not scored into the total. Its job is to make sure that the clinician and the patient know exactly which symptoms the severity ratings are about. The second part is the 10-item severity scale. The same five questions are asked twice, first about the obsessions taken together and then about the compulsions taken together, for the past week. The five dimensions are: Time occupied by the symptoms, anchored by how many hours of the day they take up. Interference : how much the symptoms get in the way of work, study, social life and family life. Distress : how much anxiety or upset the obsessions cause, or how anxious the patient becomes if prevented from carrying out the compulsions. Resistance : how much effort the patient makes to resist the obsessions or compulsions. Control : how much success the patient has in stopping or diverting them. Each item is rated from 0 (no symptoms) to 4 (extreme), so the obsession subtotal (items 1 to 5) runs from 0 to 20, the compulsion subtotal (items 6 to 10) from 0 to 20, and the total from 0 to 40. Further items (insight, avoidance, indecisiveness and others) are rated for clinical description but are not added into the total. One item needs care. Resistance is scored for the effort made, not for its success, and effort counts as health: a patient who always tries to resist scores 0 on that item, and one who gives in completely without trying scores 4. Success is captured separately by the control item. So a high resistance score means little resistance, which is the opposite of what the word suggests. Remember: Y-BOCS Goodman and colleagues, 1989; clinician-rated semi-structured interview. Checklist (not scored), then 10 severity items: 5 for obsessions, 5 for compulsions, each rating time, interference, distress, resistance and control from 0 to 4. Subtotals 0 to 20; total 0 to 40. Conventional bands: 0 to 7 subclinical, 8 to 15 mild, 16 to 23 moderate, 24 to 31 severe, 32 to 40 extreme. Those bands are widely printed with the scale, but they do not come from the 1989 papers, and a large study published in 2022, drawing on data from more than 5,000 people, derived somewhat different benchmarks; treat the bands as a convention for describing a score. Drug trials have commonly required a total of 16 or more for entry. Change is judged by the definitions an international expert consensus led by David Mataix-Cols proposed in 2016: a response is a fall of at least 35 percent on the Y-BOCS together with a clinician's global rating of "much" or "very much" improved; a fall of 25 to 35 percent is a partial response; and remission is a score of 12 or less together with a clinician's global rating of no more than borderline illness, in each case lasting at least a week. (The clinician's global ratings, the Clinical Global Impression scales, are in Section 11.9.) Worked example. Elina, a 29-year-old architect in Hyderabad, has feared contamination since her second year at college. She spends three to four hours a day washing, avoids public transport and has nearly stopped visiting friends. Her clinician's invented ratings at the first assessment are shown in Figure 11.18. Obsessions: time 3, interference 2, distress 3, resistance 1 (she still tries hard to push the thoughts away), control 3. Step 1, the obsession subtotal: 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 12. Compulsions: time 3, interference 3, distress 3 (she becomes very anxious if she is stopped from washing), resistance 3 (she rarely tries to resist the urge), control 3. Step 2, the compulsion subtotal: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15. Step 3, the total: 12 + 15 = 27. Step 4, the band: 27 lies between 24 and 31, the severe band. After twelve weeks of exposure and response prevention her total is 15. Step 5, the change: 27 − 15 = 12 points, and 12 ÷ 27 = 0.444, a reduction of about 44 percent (rounded to the nearest whole percent). Step 6, interpretation: 44 percent is more than 35 percent, so if her clinician also rates her much improved, she meets the consensus definition of a response; but 15 is above 12, so she is not in remission, and her score now sits at the top of the mild band. In plain words: Elina's OCD has gone from severe to mild, a real and worthwhile improvement, with work still to do. Notice that the same five dimensions are rated twice, once for obsessions and once for compulsions, so the content of the symptoms (washing, checking, intrusive thoughts) never enters the score; and that on the resistance column a low number means the patient is trying hard to resist. Book 3, Section 6.9.7 gives a real example of the scale at work: in a long follow-up of Swedish patients with severe, treatment-resistant OCD who underwent capsulotomy, the mean Y-BOCS score fell from 34 to 18. You can now read those numbers: 34 is in the extreme band and 18 in the moderate band, and the fall of 16 points is 16 ÷ 34 = 0.47, a reduction of about 47 percent, which is large by any standard, although, as that section explains, it came at a price in adverse effects. The scale has two important relatives. The Children's Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (CY-BOCS) of Lawrence Scahill and colleagues (1997), including Goodman, keeps the same checklist-then-ten-items design in simpler language and combines what the child and the parents report; it was validated on 65 children and adolescents aged 8 to 17. The Y-BOCS-II of Eric Storch, Goodman and colleagues (2010) rescored each item from 0 to 5 (so its total runs to 50), built avoidance into the ratings and replaced the resistance item. Self-report versions of the Y-BOCS also exist, but the classic scale, and the one examinations mean, is the 1989 clinician-rated interview. Its authors also showed in their second 1989 paper that its total fell when patients improved on the drug fluvoxamine in a placebo-controlled trial, evidence of the sensitivity to change that makes it the standard outcome measure in OCD trials. Three of this chapter's questions ask simply what the Y-BOCS measures, and every option is worth a sentence because each wrong option has a scale of its own. Asked what the Y-BOCS assesses the severity of (MET mock), the options are schizophrenia symptoms, obsessive-compulsive disorder, depression and PTSD; the answer is OCD. Schizophrenia symptoms are rated with the PANSS or the BPRS (Section 11.9), depression with the BDI-II, Hamilton or Montgomery-Åsberg scales (Sections 11.8.6 and 11.8.7), and PTSD with the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale or the PTSD Checklist (Section 11.8.8). Asked what the Y-BOCS rates (a testing paper), the options are severity of suicidal ideation, depression severity only, hallucination frequency, and the severity of OCD across 10 items, five for obsessions and five for compulsions, each 0 to 4, on time, interference, distress, resistance and control. The last is right, and is a complete description of the severity scale. Suicidal ideation is rated with Beck's Scale for Suicide Ideation (Section 11.8.7); hallucinations with the hallucination items of the positive-symptom scales (Section 11.9). And IHBAS 2025 asked "Y-BOCS is a scale for: depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, OCD", and the answer is OCD; the mania of bipolar disorder is rated with the Young Mania Rating Scale (Section 11.9). Exam trap The Y-BOCS (Goodman, 1989 , Yale and Brown universities) rates OCD severity , never depression, mania, schizophrenia, PTSD, hallucinations or suicidal ideation. It is clinician-rated ; 10 scored items (5 + 5) on time, interference, distress, resistance and control , each 0 to 4 , total 0 to 40 ; the symptom checklist is not scored. On resistance, more effort means a lower score. The children's version is the CY-BOCS (Scahill, 1997). A 35 percent fall is the consensus "response"; 12 or less is "remission". Nobody knows better than you how hopeless you feel at three in the morning, and a self-report inventory simply asks you. This section deals with the situations in which that witness is unreliable, unavailable or interested in the outcome. A man with schizophrenia may not know that his beliefs are unusual, and he cannot see his own flattened face. A woman in a manic episode feels better than she has ever felt and sees nothing to report. A heavy drinker minimises. A seven-year-old cannot fill in a questionnaire about her own attention. A disability board needs a number that will stand up in a government office, and a court wants to know whether a prisoner is dangerous, while the prisoner has every reason to look harmless. Each of these problems has produced its own family of scales. Read them with one question held steadily in mind (who supplies the information, and what does the design do about that person's blind spots?) and a long list of acronyms turns into a handful of ideas. The section takes the scales in that order: psychosis (Sections 11.9.1 to 11.9.3), mania (11.9.4), the broad screens for distress (11.9.5), substance use (11.9.6), global functioning and disability (11.9.7), children (11.9.8), and two special settings, the weeks after childbirth (11.9.9) and the prison (11.9.10). It ends by showing you how to choose a scale for a referral question (11.9.11), with two tables that pull the whole chapter together (11.9.12). The principles every rating scale shares, such as anchors, time frames, cut-offs, rater errors and the difference between self-report and clinician rating, were taught in Section 11.8 and are not repeated here; the reliability ideas behind them are in Chapter 3, especially inter-rater agreement in Section 3.6 and the standard error of measurement in Section 3.7. Rating psychosis: from the BPRS to the PANSS How do you put a number on a delusion? For most of the history of psychiatry nobody needed to. Case notes said that a patient was "improved" or "unchanged", and the doctor who wrote the note was the only judge. Then chlorpromazine arrived in the early 1950s (Book 3, Section 4.10), followed by a stream of new drugs that had to be compared with placebo and with each other. A drug trial cannot run on "improved". It needs a number that two raters will agree on, that moves when the patient changes, and that can be averaged across a hundred patients in a dozen hospitals. The psychosis rating scales are the answer to that need, and their history is a history of making the number more trustworthy. The first answer that lasted was the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) of John E. Overall and Donald R. Gorham (the Gorham of the Proverbs Test in Section 11.6.10), published in Psychological Reports in 1962. As the name says, its virtue was brevity. Overall and Gorham picked out, from factor analyses of longer inpatient rating scales, sixteen symptom areas that between them described most of what psychiatrists saw on the wards, and they asked the rater to judge each one after a short interview. Two more items, excitement and disorientation, were added in the 1960s, and the 18-item form is the one an exam means by "the BPRS". Notice how the items get their information. Some are rated from what the patient says during the interview (worry about his body, anxiety, guilt, low mood), and others from what the rater sees (emotional withdrawal, tension, odd mannerisms and postures, blunted affect, slowed movement). That split between reported and observed items runs through every psychosis scale, because a patient with psychosis can tell you about his fears but cannot tell you that his face no longer moves. Each item is rated on a seven-point scale, from 1 (not present) to 7 (extremely severe), so the 18-item total runs from 18 to 126. Some centres score the same seven levels from 0 to 6, which gives a range of 0 to 108; always check which convention a paper or a question is using. The BPRS had one serious weakness, and it teaches a lesson about all rating scales. The original form gave each level only a word ("mild", "moderate", "severe") and no description of what that level looks like. Each rater therefore carried a private picture of "moderately severe suspiciousness", and two psychiatrists who had not trained together could rate the same patient two or three points apart. The remedy is the anchor , a written description of the behaviour that earns each score (Section 11.8 introduced anchored items). In 1986 David Lukoff , Keith H. Nuechterlein and Joseph Ventura published an expanded 24-item version, the BPRS-E, with a manual that anchors every level of every item, and inter-rater agreement rose accordingly. Chapter 3, Section 3.6 explains how such agreement is measured, with the intraclass correlation for ratings like these. By the early 1980s the question in schizophrenia research had changed. Timothy Crow had proposed in 1980 that positive and negative symptoms reflected two different disease processes, and Nancy C. Andreasen had begun to measure them separately (Book 3, Section 4.3.6 tells that story; it is not repeated here). The results of positive-negative research were inconsistent, and part of the reason was measurement: different studies used different scales, and those scales gave positive and negative symptoms unequal weight. In 1987 Stanley R. Kay , Abraham Fiszbein and Lewis A. Opler published, in the Schizophrenia Bulletin , a scale designed to fix exactly that problem: the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). They built it from two established rating systems, the 18 items of the BPRS and 12 items of the Psychopathology Rating Schedule, and they arranged the 30 items so that positive and negative symptoms had equal representation and could be compared with each other and with overall severity. They described it as an operationalised, drug-sensitive instrument. The PANSS has three scales. The positive scale has 7 items covering delusional and suspicious thinking, hallucinations, disorganised thinking, grandiosity, excitement and hostility. The negative scale has 7 items covering blunted affect, emotional and social withdrawal, poor rapport with the interviewer, lack of spontaneity and flow in conversation, stereotyped thinking and difficulty in abstract thinking. The general psychopathology scale has 16 items covering everything else a person with schizophrenia may show: anxiety, guilt, depression, bodily concern, tension, odd movements and postures, disorientation, poor attention, lack of judgement and insight, poor impulse control and so on. That makes 7 + 7 + 16 = 30 items. A fourth score, the composite scale , is simply the positive total minus the negative total: a positive number means the positive syndrome predominates, a negative number the negative syndrome. It was meant for the "typological" use the authors had in mind, sorting patients by which syndrome dominates. Every item is rated from 1 to 7, and this is the feature that matters most. Each of the seven levels has a written anchor: 1 is absent, 2 minimal, 3 mild, 4 moderate, 5 moderate severe, 6 severe and 7 extreme, and for each item the manual says what the patient must show to earn each level. The rating usually covers the past week. The information comes from three sources: a semi-structured interview of about 30 to 40 minutes (the Structured Clinical Interview for the PANSS, or SCI-PANSS), the rater's observation of the patient during that interview, and reports from family members or ward staff about behaviour the interviewer cannot see, such as how the patient spends the day or whether he talks to anyone on the ward. A clinician who rates the PANSS from a five-minute ward round, without the interview or the informants, is not using the PANSS. Remember PANSS ranges. Each item scores 1 (absent) to 7 (extreme), so the lowest possible score on any scale is the number of its items. Positive scale: 7 items, range 7 to 49. Negative scale: 7 items, range 7 to 49. General psychopathology scale: 16 items, range 16 to 112. Total: 30 items, range 30 to 210. Composite scale = Positive − Negative, range −42 (7 − 49) to +42 (49 − 7). Kay, Fiszbein and Opler standardised the scale on 101 patients with schizophrenia and reported that the four scales were normally distributed and reliable, and later studies confirmed good inter-rater agreement among trained raters. The PANSS became the standard outcome measure in antipsychotic drug trials, which is why its scores fill the research literature. When researchers factor-analysed large sets of PANSS ratings, however, the items did not fall neatly into the three published scales. They fell better into five factors (positive, negative, disorganised, excited and depressed), a finding that Book 3, Section 4.3.6 describes. For exam purposes the published structure is still 7, 7 and 16. Exam trap BPRS: Overall and Gorham, 1962; 18 items in the standard form (16 in the original, 24 in Lukoff, Nuechterlein and Ventura's expanded BPRS-E); each 1 to 7, total 18 to 126 (or 0 to 108 when scored 0 to 6). PANSS: Kay, Fiszbein and Opler, 1987; built from the 18 BPRS items plus 12 from the Psychopathology Rating Schedule, so the PANSS contains the BPRS. Its 30 items are 7 positive, 7 negative and 16 general, each 1 to 7, so the total runs from 30 to 210 and can never be 0; the composite is positive minus negative. Two placements surprise people: "difficulty in abstract thinking" is a negative item, and "lack of judgement and insight" a general one. Reading a PANSS score: a worked example, response and remission Tanuj, 27, is admitted to a psychiatric ward in Lucknow during his second episode of schizophrenia. He believes that the neighbours are filming him through the ceiling fan, hears two voices commenting on what he does, speaks in loosely connected sentences and has threatened his brother. He has also become withdrawn over the past year, and his face moves little. A trained psychologist rates him on the PANSS after a SCI-PANSS interview and a talk with his mother. The invented ratings are as follows. Positive items: 6, 5, 6, 4, 3, 6, 4. Sum: 6 + 5 = 11; 11 + 6 = 17; 17 + 4 = 21; 21 + 3 = 24; 24 + 6 = 30; 30 + 4 = 34. Positive total = 34 (out of a possible 7 to 49). Negative items: 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 3, 2. Sum: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8; 8 + 3 = 11; 11 + 2 = 13; 13 + 3 = 16; 16 + 2 = 18. Negative total = 18 (out of 7 to 49). General psychopathology: the 16 ratings add up to 48 (an average of 48 ÷ 16 = 3, "mild", per item). His total is 34 + 18 + 48 = 100. His composite score is 34 − 18 = +16, so the positive syndrome clearly predominates. What does a total of 100 mean? A number on a 30-to-210 scale tells a clinician very little until it is tied to something clinically familiar, and that tie was made by one of the most useful studies in this field. Key study: What does the PANSS mean? (Leucht and colleagues, 2005) Drug trials had long reported that a medicine produced, say, a 20 percent or a 50 percent fall in PANSS scores, but nobody could say what such numbers meant to a patient. Stefan Leucht of the Technical University of Munich, with John Kane and other colleagues, pooled the baseline and follow-up ratings of 4,091 patients with acute exacerbations of schizophrenia from seven trials of olanzapine or amisulpride. In those trials each patient had been rated on the PANSS and, at the same visit, on the Clinical Global Impression (CGI, Section 11.9.7), the clinician's one-line judgement of how ill the patient is and how much he has improved. The team used equipercentile linking : they lined up the two distributions and found the PANSS score that sat at the same percentile as each CGI category. A PANSS total of about 58 corresponded to "mildly ill", about 75 to "moderately ill", about 95 to "markedly ill" and about 116 to "severely ill". A CGI rating of "minimally improved" went with a mean PANSS reduction of about 19 to 28 percent (depending on the week of treatment), and "much improved" with about 40 to 53 percent. The conclusion: the popular 20 percent response criterion captures only minimal improvement, while a 50 percent reduction marks clinically substantial change. The limitation is the sample: these were acutely ill patients in drug trials, and the links may differ for chronic outpatients. By those anchors Tanuj, at 100, sits between "markedly" and "severely" ill. Six weeks after starting a new antipsychotic he is rated again: positive 15, negative 15 and general 34, a total of 15 + 15 + 34 = 64, close to "mildly ill". How much has he improved? The obvious calculation is the fall (100 − 64 = 36 points) divided by the starting score (100), which gives 36 percent. That calculation is wrong, and the reason is worth understanding, because it applies to every scale whose items start at 1. A percentage change only makes sense when zero means "none of the thing being measured". On the PANSS, a patient with no symptoms at all scores 1 on every item, which is 30, not 0. The first 30 points of the scale can never be lost, so dividing by the raw score treats them as illness that could have improved. In 2010 Obermeier and colleagues, writing in the Schizophrenia Bulletin under the title "Should the PANSS be rescaled?", showed that this habit distorts response rates and can even change the significance of treatment effects, and that the correct method is to subtract 30 from every score before calculating a percentage. (Their suggested alternative was to score each item 0 to 6, which builds the subtraction in.) Remember Percentage improvement on the PANSS = (baseline total − follow-up total) ÷ (baseline total − 30) × 100 Here 30 is the score of a patient with no symptoms (30 items × the minimum rating of 1). On a scale that starts at 0, such as the Young Mania Rating Scale, nothing is subtracted. For Tanuj: the fall is 100 − 64 = 36 points. The part of his baseline score that was real illness is 100 − 30 = 70 points. His improvement is 36 ÷ 70 = 0.514, or about 51 percent (rounded to the nearest whole number). Now look at what the two methods do to a decision. Many trials define response as a 50 percent reduction. By the naive method Tanuj improved by 36 percent and is a non-responder; by the correct method he improved by 51 percent and is a responder. Same patient, same ratings, opposite conclusions. Figure 11.19 shows the scale's structure and why the floor matters.
