Measured from zero (upper bar), Tanuj's invented fall from 100 to 64 looks like 36 percent; measured from the true floor of 30 (lower bar), it is 51 percent, enough to count as a 50 percent response. One more yardstick deserves a sentence. A large reduction is not the same thing as being well. In 2005 a working group led by Nancy Andreasen proposed standard criteria for symptomatic remission in schizophrenia that do not depend on change at all: eight core PANSS items (covering delusions, unusual thought content, hallucinations, disorganised thinking, mannerisms and posturing, blunted affect, social withdrawal and lack of spontaneity) must all be rated mild or better, that is 3 or less, and must stay there for at least six months. A response criterion asks "how far has he come?"; a remission criterion asks "where is he now, and has he stayed there?". Tanuj at week 6 may have responded, but he cannot yet be in remission, because six months have not passed. Exam trap Percentage change on the PANSS must subtract the floor: (baseline − follow-up) ÷ (baseline − 30). The same rule applies to the 18-item BPRS scored 1 to 7, whose floor is 18, not 30. Using the raw baseline understates improvement. By Leucht and colleagues' 2005 linking, a PANSS total of about 58 means mildly ill, 75 moderately, 95 markedly and 116 severely ill; a 20 percent reduction corresponds only to minimal improvement and a 50 percent reduction to much improvement. Response is a change criterion; remission (Andreasen and colleagues, 2005) is a state criterion: eight core items all at 3 (mild) or less, held for at least six months. Andreasen's SANS and SAPS, and the scales that followed While the PANSS packed both syndromes into one interview, Nancy Andreasen (born 1938), at the University of Iowa, had already built a separate, more detailed instrument for each. Her Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS) was first reported in 1982, with a manual in 1983, and its companion, the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS), followed in 1984. Book 3, Section 4.3.6 explains why she wanted them; here the interest is in how they measure. The SANS has 25 items grouped into five symptom complexes: affective flattening or blunting, alogia, avolition-apathy, anhedonia-asociality, and attention (20 symptom items plus one global rating for each complex). The SAPS has 34 items in four: hallucinations, delusions, bizarre behaviour and positive formal thought disorder (30 symptom items plus four global ratings). Both rate each item from 0 (none) to 5 (severe), so, unlike the PANSS, a zero really does mean absent. Their great strength is detail: the SAPS, for example, rates about a dozen kinds of delusion separately, where the PANSS has one delusions item, and the SANS breaks blunted affect into separate observations of facial expression, gesture, eye contact and vocal inflection. Each symptom complex in both scales ends with a global rating , the rater's overall judgement of that complex, which is not simply the sum or average of the item ratings above it. This creates a choice that confuses readers of the research: some studies report the sum of all the item ratings, and others the sum of the five (or four) global ratings. The two are not interchangeable, so a SANS score of 15 means one thing in a paper that sums globals (a maximum of 25) and something quite different in one that sums items (a maximum of 100 for the 20 symptom items, or 125 if the globals are counted too). The SANS also shows how a measure can carry a theory that later research rejects. Andreasen included attention among the negative symptoms. Factor analyses kept finding that inattention goes with disorganisation and cognitive impairment rather than with blunted affect and loss of drive, and a consensus conference on negative symptoms held by the United States National Institute of Mental Health and its MATRICS initiative (its statement was published in 2006) concluded that the negative symptoms proper are five: blunted affect, alogia, asociality, anhedonia and avolition. Two newer scales were built to that blueprint and dropped attention: the 13-item Brief Negative Symptom Scale of Brian Kirkpatrick and colleagues (2011) and the 13-item Clinical Assessment Interview for Negative Symptoms of Ann Kring and colleagues (2013), whose items fall into an expression scale and a motivation and pleasure scale. Both also separate what a patient shows in expression from what he experiences inside, such as the pleasure he anticipates or the drive he feels, because a person may look flat and yet feel a great deal. Finally, two neighbouring needs have their own instruments, and they matter because exam options borrow them. Depression is common in schizophrenia but hard to rate, because negative symptoms and the slowing caused by antipsychotics look like depression. The Calgary Depression Scale for Schizophrenia of Donald Addington, Jean Addington and B. Schissel (1990) was built for exactly this problem: its authors selected, from the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression and the Present State Examination, the items that best measured depression in 50 acutely ill patients with schizophrenia, leaving out items that overlap with negative symptoms and drug side effects. The first report had 11 items; the final scale has nine, each rated 0 to 3, so its total runs from 0 to 27. Cognitive impairment, the third great domain of schizophrenia, is measured not by any symptom rating but by neuropsychological tests, and for drug trials a standard set of them was agreed in 2008 as the MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery (MATRICS stands for Measurement and Treatment Research to Improve Cognition in Schizophrenia), which samples seven cognitive domains with ten tests of the kinds taught in Sections 11.4 and 11.6. The answer is symptom severity in schizophrenia, on three scales (positive, negative, general psychopathology) with 30 items, each 1 to 7. It does not assess personality disorders (those need a personality disorder interview such as the SCID-5-PD or IPDE, Book 2, Section 2.1.4). It is not a depression severity scale, even though one of its 16 general items is depression (use the BDI or HAM-D of Section 11.8, or the Calgary scale in schizophrenia). It does not measure cognitive impairment, even though it has items on attention and abstract thinking (use tests, such as the MoCA of Section 11.7 or the MATRICS battery). SANS: 25 items in five complexes (affective flattening, alogia, avolition-apathy, anhedonia-asociality, attention); SAPS: 34 items in four (hallucinations, delusions, bizarre behaviour, positive formal thought disorder); both rated 0 to 5, both Nancy Andreasen (1982 to 1984), not Kay and not Crow (Crow proposed Types I and II, not a scale). "Attention" as a negative symptom domain is a favourite odd one out, and the newer negative symptom scales (BNSS, CAINS) dropped it. Rating mania: the Young Mania Rating Scale Mania poses the self-report problem in its purest form. A woman in a manic episode may not have slept for three nights, may have spent her family's savings and may be shouting down the ward corridor, and if you hand her a questionnaire she will tell you, quite sincerely, that she has never felt better. Loss of insight is part of the illness (Book 3, Chapter 5 describes it), so a scale that relies on her own account will report the least illness precisely when there is the most. Mania therefore had to be rated by an observer, and the scale that became the standard was built in deliberate imitation of the Hamilton depression scale of Section 11.8. In 1978 Robert C. Young , with J. T. Biggs, V. E. Ziegler and D. A. Meyer, published "A rating scale for mania: reliability, validity and sensitivity" in the British Journal of Psychiatry . The Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) has 11 items, rated by a clinician after an interview, covering the core features of mania: elevated mood, increased activity and energy, sexual interest, sleep, irritability, the rate and amount of speech, disordered language and thought, the content of thought (grandiose or persecutory ideas), disruptive or aggressive behaviour, appearance, and insight. The rating draws on the patient's own account of the previous 48 hours together with what the rater observes during the interview. The short time frame is deliberate: mania changes from day to day, and a week-long window, like the PANSS's, would blur the change a drug trial needs to see. The YMRS has one unusual design feature that you must know. Seven of the eleven items are rated from 0 to 4, but the other four (irritability, speech, thought content, and disruptive or aggressive behaviour) are rated from 0 to 8. These four carry double weight, and the authors explained why: they compensate for the poor cooperation of severely ill patients. A patient who is too irritable or distractible to answer questions about sleep or sexual interest can still be rated, from observation alone, on how irritable, pressured, grandiose and disruptive she is, and the double weighting makes sure that these observable items dominate the total in exactly those patients. The arithmetic follows directly. Remember YMRS maximum = (7 items × 4) + (4 items × 8) = 28 + 32 = 60. The minimum is 0, so the range is 0 to 60. Young and his colleagues reported that two independent clinicians agreed closely, with a correlation of 0.93 for the total score and 0.66 to 0.92 for individual items. The YMRS correlated highly with an independent global rating and with two other mania scales, its score predicted the number of days the patient would go on to spend in hospital, and it distinguished patients before and after two weeks of treatment, which is the property a drug trial needs most. There are no official severity bands. By convention, many drug trials admit patients with a score of 20 or more and count a score of 12 or less as remission, while some use a stricter remission threshold of 8 or less. Here is the scale at work. Laxmi, 34, a schoolteacher with bipolar I disorder, is admitted in a manic episode. The invented ratings on the seven ordinary items are: elevated mood 3, activity and energy 3, sexual interest 2, sleep 3, language and thought disorder 2, appearance 1 and insight 3, which add to 3 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 17. On the four double-weighted items she is rated irritability 6, speech 6, thought content 4 and disruptive behaviour 2, which add to 6 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 18. Her total is 17 + 18 = 35, well above the usual threshold for entering a trial. Ten days after starting lithium and an antipsychotic she is rated again: the seven ordinary items now add to 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 2 = 6, and the four double-weighted items to 2 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 6, for a total of 12. She has fallen 35 − 12 = 23 points. Because the YMRS starts at 0, the ordinary percentage is correct here, unlike the PANSS: 23 ÷ 35 = 0.657, a reduction of about 66 percent (rounded). She meets the standard remission threshold of 12 or less, but not the stricter one of 8 or less, so her psychiatrist would continue to watch closely before calling the episode over. Two other tools complete the picture, and they do different jobs from the YMRS. Self-report mania scales exist, such as Edward Altman's five-item Altman Self-Rating Mania Scale (1997), and they are useful for patients with milder hypomania and good insight, but they share the blind spot described above. The bigger clinical problem runs the other way: many people with bipolar disorder first seek help when they are depressed, and if nobody asks about past highs, they may be treated with an antidepressant alone. Screening questionnaires for a history of bipolarity were built for that problem. The Mood Disorder Questionnaire of Robert Hirschfeld and colleagues (2000) asks 13 yes-or-no questions about past manic symptoms, followed by two questions on whether several of them happened during the same period and how much trouble they caused; in its validation study with 198 patients from mood-disorder clinics, a score of 7 or more gave a sensitivity of 0.73 and a specificity of 0.90 against a structured diagnostic interview (Chapter 4 explains sensitivity and specificity). The Hypomania Checklist (HCL-32) of Jules Angst and colleagues does the same job with 32 items. Neither rates current severity; both ask "has this person ever been high?". Clinical link In mania the family is often the best informant. A patient may deny that she has slept little or spent heavily, while her husband can describe the last two nights in detail. The YMRS is anchored in the patient's account and the interview, but raters commonly check that account against what relatives and nurses have seen, and on an Indian ward the relatives who stay with the patient are an unusually rich source. Record who told you what: if the YMRS is repeated later with a different informant, part of any change may be a change of witness, not of illness. Exam trap YMRS: Robert Young and colleagues, 1978, 11 items, clinician-rated, previous 48 hours, four items (irritability, speech, thought content, disruptive or aggressive behaviour) double-weighted 0 to 8, total 0 to 60. Do not confuse it with the MADRS of Section 11.8, which also runs from 0 to 60 but has 10 items rated 0 to 6 and measures depression. Do not confuse Robert Young with Jeffrey Young, whose Young Schema Questionnaire belongs to schema therapy. And the Mood Disorder Questionnaire (13 items, 7 or more positive) screens for a history of bipolar disorder; it does not rate how manic someone is today. Watch the names, too: the Altman Self-Rating Mania Scale is a "rating scale" that the patient completes himself, and the Psychopathy Checklist of Section 11.9.10 is a "checklist" scored by a trained clinician, two exceptions to the naming rule of thumb in Section 11.8.2. Screening for distress: the General Health Questionnaire and the SCL-90-R Every scale so far assumes that you already know what is wrong: you would not rate a PANSS on a man without psychosis. But most people with a mental disorder are never seen by a psychiatrist. They sit in the waiting rooms of general practitioners and primary health centres, complaining of headaches, poor sleep or tiredness, and their doctors miss a large share of them. In the late 1960s the British psychiatrist David P. Goldberg , working at the Institute of Psychiatry in London, set out to build a questionnaire that a patient could complete in a few minutes in such a waiting room and that would pick out the people most likely to have what he called non-psychotic psychiatric disorder: the common anxiety and depressive conditions. The result was the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ), published in 1972 in his monograph The Detection of Psychiatric Illness by Questionnaire . Goldberg's central design decision explains both the GHQ's strength and its weakness. Each item asks whether the person has recently experienced a particular symptom or behaviour, and the four answers are graded relative to the person's usual state, from something like "better than usual" or "not at all", through "same as usual" or "no more than usual", to "less than usual" or "rather more than usual", and finally "much less than usual" or "much more than usual" (the wording depends on whether the item describes something healthy or a symptom). The GHQ is therefore a detector of change: it is designed to catch a recent break in a person's normal functioning, not to describe lifelong traits. That is exactly what a screen in primary care needs, because a recent onset is what brings the patient in. Its weakness is the mirror image. A woman who has been anxious and miserable for ten years may truthfully answer "no more than usual" to every question, and the questionnaire will call her well. The GHQ comes in several lengths. The original had 60 items; shorter forms followed with 30, 28, 20 and 12 items. The 28-item form, the GHQ-28 of Goldberg and Valerie Hillier (1979), was derived by factor analysis of questionnaires completed in primary care and is the only common version with subscales: four of them, seven items each, called somatic symptoms, anxiety and insomnia, social dysfunction and severe depression. The 12-item GHQ-12 gives a single score and became the most widely used screen of its kind in the world. How much is lost by shortening it? In a World Health Organization study of psychological disorders in general health care, Goldberg and his colleagues (1997) compared the GHQ-12 with the GHQ-28 in 5,438 patients interviewed in 15 centres in many countries. Both versions worked well, with an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.88 (ranging from 0.83 to 0.95 across centres); the GHQ had been translated into ten further languages and worked almost as well in them; it was no less efficient in developing countries; and age, sex and education made no significant difference to its validity. (The area under the curve is explained in Chapter 4: 0.5 means guessing and 1.0 perfect discrimination.) The GHQ also illustrates something Chapter 1 says in general: the same answers can be scored in more than one way, and the scoring must suit the purpose. There are three common methods. In GHQ scoring , the two "healthy" answers score 0 and the two "unhealthy" answers score 1 (often written 0-0-1-1), so the GHQ-12 runs from 0 to 12; this is the method for deciding whether someone is a probable case, because it ignores the difference between a person who habitually ticks extreme answers and one who habitually ticks moderate ones. In Likert scoring , the four answers score 0, 1, 2 and 3, so the GHQ-12 runs from 0 to 36; this spreads people out more and suits research on severity. And in the C-GHQ (chronic) scoring proposed by M. E. Goodchild and P. Duncan-Jones in 1985, the answer "no more than usual" to an item describing a symptom is scored as 1 rather than 0, on the argument that a person who reports the symptom as "usual" may be chronically ill rather than healthy. They found that the revised scoring predicted caseness better and was more stable on repeated measurement. Work through two invented respondents to see what the methods do. The GHQ-12 has six items worded in a positive direction (about coping or enjoying things) and six worded in a negative direction (about strain or unhappiness). Suppose a clinic in Mysuru has chosen, from a local validation study, a threshold of 2/3 on GHQ scoring, so that 3 or more marks a probable case. The first respondent gives four answers in the healthiest column, three in the second, three in the third and two in the most unhealthy column. GHQ scoring counts only the third and fourth columns: 3 + 2 = 5, a probable case. Likert scoring gives (4 × 0) + (3 × 1) + (3 × 2) + (2 × 3) = 0 + 3 + 6 + 6 = 15 out of 36. The second respondent ticks the second column, "same as usual" or "no more than usual", on all twelve items. GHQ scoring gives 0: not a case. Likert scoring gives 12 × 1 = 12. C-GHQ scoring gives 1 for each of the six negatively worded items answered "no more than usual" and 0 for the six positive ones, a total of 6, double the clinic's threshold of 3 (a service that adopts chronic scoring should validate its own, higher threshold, because every respondent scores more under it). If this second person has in fact been depressed for years, only the chronic scoring has noticed. Indian context The GHQ was among the first Western screens to be standardised in India. S. Gautam, M. Nijhawan and P. Kamal published a Hindi version in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 1987, translated into everyday language and checked by back-translation; its split-half reliability was tested on 500 psychiatric outpatients and 500 people from the general population, and it separated them sharply (mean scores of 30.64 in the patients against 4.9 in the comparison group). The GHQ-12 has since been used in many Indian community and primary-care surveys. Because thresholds depend on the setting and the population, an Indian study should report which scoring method and which threshold it used, and preferably justify the threshold against a clinical interview. A second screen built for such settings is the World Health Organization's Self-Reporting Questionnaire (SRQ-20), twenty yes-or-no questions about non-psychotic symptoms, which grew out of the questionnaire used in the WHO's study of mental disorders in primary health care in four developing countries (Colombia, India, the Philippines and Sudan). In that study (T. W. Harding and colleagues, 1980, with the Indian psychiatrists R. Srinivasa Murthy and N. N. Wig among the authors), 13.9 percent of 1,624 primary-care attenders had a psychiatric disorder, most presented with a bodily complaint such as headache or weakness, and the health workers recognised only about a third of them: the very gap that screening questionnaires exist to close. The GHQ answers "is this person probably a case?" with a single number. Sometimes a clinician wants a profile instead: which kinds of distress, and how much of each? The most widely used self-report profile of current symptoms is the Symptom Checklist-90-Revised (SCL-90-R) of Leonard R. Derogatis . It grew out of the older Hopkins Symptom Checklist; Derogatis, R. S. Lipman and L. Covi described the 90-item SCL-90 in 1973 as "an outpatient psychiatric rating scale", and the revised form, the SCL-90-R, followed in the 1970s, with later editions of its manual. The respondent rates how much each of 90 problems has distressed or bothered him during the past seven days, including today, on a five-point scale from 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely). The 90 items are scored on nine primary symptom dimensions : somatisation, obsessive-compulsive, interpersonal sensitivity, depression, anxiety, hostility, phobic anxiety, paranoid ideation and psychoticism. Seven further items (about appetite, sleep, thoughts of death, guilt and the like) belong to no dimension but are counted in the totals. On top of the profile sit three global indices , and they are best learned through their formulas. Remember Global Severity Index: GSI = (sum of all 90 item ratings) ÷ 90 Positive Symptom Total: PST = the number of items rated above 0 Positive Symptom Distress Index: PSDI = (sum of all 90 item ratings) ÷ PST The GSI is the average distress per item across the whole checklist; the PST counts how many different symptoms the person reports; the PSDI is the average intensity of the symptoms he does report. Suppose an invented outpatient's 90 ratings add up to 117, and 45 of the items are rated above 0. Then GSI = 117 ÷ 90 = 1.30; PST = 45; PSDI = 117 ÷ 45 = 2.60. In words: he reports half the symptoms on the list, and the ones he reports bother him, on average, between "moderately" (2) and "quite a bit" (3). Now imagine a second person with exactly the same sum of 117 spread thinly over 90 endorsed items: her GSI is also 1.30, but her PST is 90 and her PSDI is 117 ÷ 90 = 1.30. Same overall severity, very different pattern: he has fewer, intense complaints; she ticks every item at a low level. Derogatis suggested that the PSDI also says something about response style, whether a person tends to amplify or play down distress, which is why it is worth looking at alongside the GSI. Raw scores are converted to T-scores (mean 50, standard deviation 10; Chapter 5 explains them) against the norm group that fits the person: adult non-patients, psychiatric outpatients, psychiatric inpatients or adolescents. The manual's rule for "caseness" is a GSI T-score of 63 or more, or T-scores of 63 or more on any two of the primary dimensions. A T of 63 is 1.3 standard deviations above the mean, roughly the top tenth of the comparison group. One caution matters more than any other. Many factor-analytic studies have failed to recover the nine dimensions cleanly; the dimensions correlate highly with each other, and much of the variance reflects a single general distress factor. The GSI is therefore the most trustworthy SCL-90-R score, and a profile with "elevated paranoid ideation" should not be read as evidence of paranoia without an interview. A 53-item short form with the same nine dimensions, the Brief Symptom Inventory (Derogatis and N. Melisaratos, 1983), is often used when time is short. Exam trap The GHQ (David Goldberg, 1972) screens for non-psychotic psychiatric disorder, the common anxiety and depressive conditions, in community and primary-care settings; it does not diagnose, and it is not a psychosis screen. It asks about recent change from the usual state, so it can miss chronic illness (the C-GHQ scoring of Goodchild and Duncan-Jones, 1985, was devised for that). Versions: 60, 30, 28, 20, 12 items; only the GHQ-28 (Goldberg and Hillier, 1979) has the four subscales (somatic symptoms, anxiety and insomnia, social dysfunction, severe depression). "GHQ scoring" means 0-0-1-1, Likert scoring 0-1-2-3. The SCL-90-R (Leonard Derogatis) has 90 items rated 0 to 4 for the past seven days, nine primary symptom dimensions and three global indices (GSI, PST, PSDI); its short form, the BSI, has 53 items. Do not confuse its nine dimensions with the MMPI's ten clinical scales (Chapter 9), and do not call it a projective or a personality test: it measures current symptomatic distress. Substance use: screening, dependence and withdrawal Mayank, 42, a clerk in a cooperative bank, sees his general practitioner about burning pain in his stomach. Over the next month he will meet three different alcohol instruments, and each will answer a different question. At the first visit the doctor needs to know whether his drinking is a problem at all. If it is, the de-addiction team needs to know how dependent he is, because that decides whether he can stop at home or needs admission. And if he is admitted, the nurses need to know, every few hours, how severe his withdrawal is right now. These are three different constructs, and each has its own time frame: lifetime or past year for a screen, a recent period of heavy drinking for dependence, and the present moment for withdrawal. The commonest error with substance scales is to use one built for one of these jobs to answer another. The clinical side of these tools is taught elsewhere: the AUDIT, its risk zones and brief interventions in Book 2, Section 9.4.5; the CAGE questions and the blood markers of heavy drinking in Book 3, Section 10.3.8; and the use of the CIWA-Ar in detoxification in Book 3, Sections 10.3.5 and 10.4.3. What follows is the measurement side. Screening. The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) of the World Health Organization (1989; validation study by John B. Saunders, Thomas F. Babor and colleagues, 1993) has ten items in three groups: consumption (items 1 to 3), dependence (items 4 to 6) and harm (items 7 to 10). Its scoring has a detail that students miss. Items 1 to 8 have five answer options scored 0 to 4, but items 9 and 10, about injury and about other people's concern, have only three options, scored 0, 2 and 4 (no; yes, but not in the past year; yes, during the past year). The maximum is still 10 × 4 = 40. The first three items alone form the AUDIT-C (consumption), scored 0 to 12, which K. Bush and colleagues (1998) showed to be at least as good as the full AUDIT at detecting heavy drinking in male primary-care patients (though slightly weaker at detecting abuse or dependence); in men a score of 4 or more is the usual positive screen, and lower thresholds are often used for women. The full AUDIT's usual threshold of 8 also varies by setting, and some guidelines lower it for women and older adults, who reach harmful levels at lower intakes. Mayank's invented answers run: consumption items 4, 2 and 3; dependence items 2, 1 and 1; harm items 2, 1, 0 and 4. His consumption subtotal (which is also his AUDIT-C) is 4 + 2 + 3 = 9; his dependence subtotal 2 + 1 + 1 = 4; his harm subtotal 2 + 1 + 0 + 4 = 7. His total is 9 + 4 + 7 = 20, which falls in the highest WHO zone, possible dependence calling for specialist assessment (Book 2, Table 9.5). Notice that the subtotals carry information the total hides: a man with 20 points mostly from consumption is a heavy drinker who may not yet be dependent, while a man with the same total weighted towards the dependence items probably needs supervised withdrawal. The four-item CAGE questionnaire is older and shorter, and its history is a small lesson in how names attach to tests. John A. Ewing devised it around 1968; it was first validated in print by D. Mayfield, G. McLeod and P. Hall in the American Journal of Psychiatry in 1974; and Ewing's own 1984 paper in the Journal of the American Medical Association made it famous. Two or more positive answers count as a positive screen. Its measurement limits follow from its wording: every question asks whether something has ever happened, so a man who stopped drinking ten years ago still screens positive and the score cannot fall with recovery; and its questions pick up dependence far better than they pick up the risky but not yet dependent drinking that the AUDIT was designed to catch. The Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test (MAST) of Melvin L. Selzer (1971) is a longer lifetime screen of 25 yes-or-no questions about the social, legal, occupational and medical consequences of drinking, with weighted items (some answers count more than others); in Selzer's original scoring a total of 5 or more indicated alcoholism. Shorter forms include the 13-item Short MAST. For drugs other than alcohol, Harvey Skinner's Drug Abuse Screening Test (DAST, 1982) asks 28 self-report questions about the consequences of drug use (internal consistency 0.92 in its first clinical sample of 256 clients), and a 10-item short form is common. The WHO's ASSIST (Alcohol, Smoking and Substance Involvement Screening Test, 2002) asks the same short set of questions about each of tobacco, alcohol and the main classes of other drugs, so that one interview screens for all of them; India was one of the countries in which it was first tested. Severity of dependence. A screen says "probably a problem"; it does not say how dependent someone is. The Severity of Alcohol Dependence Questionnaire (SADQ) of Tim Stockwell, Ray Hodgson, Griffith Edwards, Colin Taylor and Howard Rankin (1979), from the Addiction Research Unit in London, was built on Griffith Edwards and Milton Gross's 1976 description of the alcohol dependence syndrome (Book 3, Chapter 10). The drinker thinks of a recent, typical period of heavy drinking and answers 20 questions in five groups of four: physical withdrawal symptoms, emotional withdrawal symptoms, drinking to relieve withdrawal, typical daily consumption, and how quickly withdrawal returns when drinking restarts after a period of abstinence. Each item is scored 0 to 3, so the total runs from 0 to 60, and the conventional bands are below 16 mild, 16 to 30 moderate and 31 or more severe dependence. The bands have a practical use: a person with severe dependence is at higher risk of complicated withdrawal, and many services use a high SADQ score as one reason to advise admission rather than withdrawal at home. Withdrawal right now. Mayank's SADQ is 34, and he is admitted. Withdrawal is a state that changes by the hour, so it needs a measure that can be repeated quickly and that responds to every change. The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised (CIWA-Ar) of John T. Sullivan, Karen Sykora, Joseph Schneiderman, Claudio Naranjo and Edward Sellers (1989), from the Addiction Research Foundation in Toronto, shortened an earlier 15-item version to ten items that a nurse can rate in a few minutes. Nine items (nausea and vomiting, tremor, sweating, anxiety, agitation, and tactile, auditory and visual disturbances, and headache) are rated 0 to 7, and the tenth, orientation and clouding of consciousness, is rated 0 to 4. Remember CIWA-Ar maximum = (9 items × 7) + (1 item × 4) = 63 + 4 = 67. At eight in the morning, a day after his last drink, the nurse rates Mayank: nausea 2, tremor 3, sweating 2, anxiety 3, agitation 2, tactile disturbances 1, auditory 0, visual 0, headache 2 and orientation 0. His score is 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 15. After a dose of a benzodiazepine the noon rating is 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1 and 0, a total of 6. In typical hospital protocols a score below about 8 to 10 calls for observation only, a score in the teens for medication, and a score above about 15 to 20 marks severe withdrawal with a raised risk of seizures and delirium, though each unit sets its own thresholds. In a symptom-triggered regimen (Book 3, Section 10.4.3) the 8 a.m. score of 15 earns a dose and the noon score of 6 does not. Three measurement points complete the picture. First, the CIWA-Ar depends on the patient being able to describe his nausea, itching or anxiety, so it fails exactly where withdrawal is most dangerous: in a patient who is already delirious, sedated or unable to communicate. Second, several items (anxiety, headache, sweating) are not specific to alcohol withdrawal; a patient anxious about losing his job, or one with a fever, will score points that are not withdrawal at all, which is why the scale is used only after the diagnosis of withdrawal has been made. Third, other substances have their own withdrawal scales built the same way, the best known being the 11-item Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) of Donald Wesson and Walter Ling (2003), used, for example, to decide when an opioid-dependent patient is far enough into withdrawal to start buprenorphine safely. Nicotine. In 1978 the Swedish researcher Karl-Olov Fagerström published an eight-item Fagerström Tolerance Questionnaire. When Todd Heatherton, Lynn Kozlowski, Richard Frecker and Fagerström examined it in 254 smokers (1991), two items, about the nicotine rating of the brand and about inhaling, were unrelated to biochemical measures of how heavily people smoked and were the main source of its psychometric weaknesses. They dropped them, rescored the items on time to the first cigarette of the day and number of cigarettes per day, and produced the six-item Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND), scored 0 to 10. The two strongest items alone, time to first cigarette and cigarettes per day, form the Heaviness of Smoking Index. This is a neat example of item analysis (Chapter 2) improving a test by removing items that measured nothing. Indian context Scales built for cigarettes fit India poorly. In the second Global Adult Tobacco Survey of India (2016 to 2017), 28.6 percent of adults used tobacco, but only 10.7 percent smoked, while 21.4 percent used smokeless tobacco such as khaini, gutkha or betel quid with tobacco. Questions about "cigarettes per day" mean little to such users, which is why adaptations of the Fagerström test for smokeless tobacco have been developed and why the WHO's ASSIST, which asks about tobacco in any form, is often preferred in Indian primary care. A withdrawal scale cannot diagnose dependence, and a screen cannot tell you how much medication to give. Global functioning and disability: the CGI, the GAF, WHODAS 2.0 and IDEAS Every scale so far counts symptoms. But a patient and his family rarely care about the symptom count for its own sake. They care about two broader things: how ill is he, all things considered, and what can he still do? The first question is answered by global ratings, the second by measures of functioning and disability, and the two are easy to confuse because both often come out as a single number. The simplest rating in psychiatry is the Clinical Global Impression (CGI), published by William Guy in 1976 in the ECDEU Assessment Manual for Psychopharmacology , the collection of standard scales prepared for the drug-evaluation programme (the Early Clinical Drug Evaluation Unit) of the United States National Institute of Mental Health. It has two main parts. The CGI-Severity (CGI-S) asks the clinician to rate how ill the patient is at this moment, judged against his total clinical experience with this particular kind of patient. The CGI-Improvement (CGI-I) asks how much the patient has changed since the start of treatment. Both are single items rated on seven points (Table 11.39); a score of 0 means "not assessed". A third part, the efficacy index, crosses four levels of therapeutic effect with four levels of side effects to judge whether a treatment's benefit outweighs its cost. Table 11.39 The two Clinical Global Impression ratings (Guy, 1976). Score CGI-Severity: how ill now? CGI-Improvement: how changed since baseline? 1 Normal, not at all ill Very much improved 2 Borderline mentally ill Much improved 3 Mildly ill Minimally improved 4 Moderately ill No change 5 Markedly ill Minimally worse 6 Severely ill Much worse 7 Among the most extremely ill patients Very much worse Look at how the two columns differ, because exam questions turn on it. On the severity scale a higher number is worse throughout. On the improvement scale 4 is the middle ("no change"), numbers below 4 are improvement and numbers above 4 are deterioration. The usual definition of a treatment responder in a drug trial is a CGI-I of 1 or 2. Why use such a crude instrument alongside a 30-item PANSS? Because the CGI is the clinician's bottom line in plain language, and that is exactly what made it useful to Leucht and colleagues in the key study of Section 11.9.2: a PANSS total means something to a clinician once it is linked to "markedly ill". For Tanuj, a baseline PANSS of 100 sits close to the PANSS value of about 95 that corresponds to "markedly ill", and his psychiatrist rates him CGI-S 5; at week 6, with a corrected PANSS reduction of 51 percent, she rates him CGI-I 2, much improved. The weakness of the CGI is the weakness of any single global judgement: it depends on the rater's frame of reference ("compared with the patients I usually see"), so a psychiatrist in a busy government hospital and one in a private clinic for mild anxiety may rate the same patient differently. It works best when the same rater makes all the ratings. The Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) scale, the 0 to 100 rating that formed Axis V of DSM-III-R and DSM-IV, is taught in Book 3, Section 1.7.5, with its bands and the rule that the rater takes the worse of symptoms and functioning; Book 3, Section 1.7.6 records that DSM-5 dropped it. The measurement reason is worth stating. DSM-5 (2013) gave as its reasons the scale's "conceptual lack of clarity", because its descriptions mixed symptoms, suicide risk and disability, and its "questionable psychometrics in routine practice". A single number that mixes two constructs cannot be interpreted: a GAF of 45 may mean a man who functions well but has serious suicidal thoughts, or a man with mild symptoms who cannot hold a job, and those two need different help. One answer, already in DSM-IV's appendix, was the Social and Occupational Functioning Assessment Scale (SOFAS), which rates functioning alone. For children the equivalent of the old global scale is the Children's Global Assessment Scale (CGAS) of David Shaffer and colleagues (1983), an adaptation of the adult Global Assessment Scale rated from 1 to 100, which they found reliable between raters and over time. DSM-5's replacement was a measure built on an entirely different model. The World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0), described by T. Bedirhan Üstün and colleagues in 2010, is based on the WHO's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, so it measures disability in the same way whatever its cause, a stroke, arthritis or schizophrenia. It covers six domains of life: understanding and communicating (cognition), getting around (mobility), self-care, getting along with people, life activities (household and work or school), and participation in society. The full version has 36 items and the short version 12; each comes in self-administered, interviewer-administered and proxy forms (the proxy form is completed by a relative when the person cannot answer, for example in dementia). Every item asks how much difficulty the person has had in the past 30 days and is answered on five levels: none (1), mild (2), moderate (3), severe (4) and extreme or cannot do (5). In the development studies, which included more than 65,000 respondents in many countries, it showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.86), very high test-retest reliability (an intraclass correlation of 0.98), a stable factor structure and good sensitivity to change. WHODAS 2.0 can be scored in three ways, and they illustrate a choice Chapter 2 discusses in general. In simple scoring the 36 item scores are added, giving 36 to 180; this needs no computer and suits a busy clinic. In item-response-theory scoring , a computer weights each item and each level of difficulty differently and converts the result to a metric from 0 (no disability) to 100 (full disability), which can be compared with population norms. And DSM-5-TR recommends a third, very practical method: average scores , in which each domain's raw total is divided by its number of items, so that every result reads directly on the 1-to-5 scale of none, mild, moderate, severe and extreme. Remember WHODAS 2.0 average domain score = raw domain score ÷ number of items in the domain Average general disability score = raw total ÷ 36. Both read on the item scale: 1 none, 2 mild, 3 moderate, 4 severe, 5 extreme. DSM-5-TR warns that if 10 or more of the 36 items are unanswered, the overall scores may not be helpful. Six months after her manic episode Laxmi, who has returned to teaching, completes the 36-item self-administered form. Her invented raw domain totals are: understanding and communicating 12 (6 items), getting around 5 (5 items), self-care 4 (4 items), getting along with people 15 (5 items), life activities 24 (8 items) and participation 20 (8 items). Her simple total is 12 + 5 + 4 + 15 + 24 + 20 = 80, out of a possible 36 to 180. Her average general disability score is 80 ÷ 36 = 2.22, which rounds to 2, mild. The domain averages tell a sharper story: understanding 12 ÷ 6 = 2.0 (mild), getting around 5 ÷ 5 = 1.0 (none), self-care 4 ÷ 4 = 1.0 (none), getting along 15 ÷ 5 = 3.0 (moderate), life activities 24 ÷ 8 = 3.0 (moderate) and participation 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 (between mild and moderate). The overall "mild" hides two moderate problems, in relationships and at work, which are precisely where her rehabilitation should aim. In India, however, the instrument that decides legal entitlement for disability caused by mental illness is not WHODAS but the Indian Disability Evaluation and Assessment Scale (IDEAS), developed by the Rehabilitation Committee of the Indian Psychiatric Society and adopted for certification by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment in 2002. Book 2, Section 9.9.8 teaches its use in full: a psychiatrist, interviewing the person and the family, rates four areas (self-care, interpersonal activities, communication and understanding, and work) from 0 to 4 each, adds a score of 1 to 4 for the duration of illness, and converts the global total of 0 to 20 into a grade and a percentage (Book 2, Table 9.17). Here the interest is in IDEAS as a measurement, and three features stand out. First, the global score is not purely a measure of disability. The duration score (1 for less than two years of illness up to 4 for more than ten) adds as much as 4 points that have nothing to do with how the person functions today, so two people with identical current functioning can receive different grades because one has been ill longer. That is a policy decision (it favours certifying chronic rather than temporary disability), not a psychometric one, and you should be able to say so in an interview. The duration rule just described is that of the version gazetted in 2002, which Book 2 teaches; the revised guidelines of March 2024 instead score the months of illness in the preceding two years, which ties the score to recent illness rather than to the whole history, although, as Indian commentators have noted, it still measures illness rather than functioning. Second, the scale's most important boundary sits between a global score of 6 (mild, below 40 percent) and 7 (moderate, 40 percent or more), because 40 percent is the "benchmark disability" that unlocks most legal benefits. At a legal cut-off, a one-point disagreement between two raters on any single area changes a person's entitlements, so the reliability of ratings near the cut-off matters far more than the reliability of the scale on average; Chapter 3, Section 3.7 shows how the standard error of measurement turns a single score into a band, and how that band can straddle a cut-off. Third, its validity has been studied against other measures: in a study at PGIMER, Chandigarh, of 178 patients with schizophrenia in remission (S. Sahoo, S. Grover and colleagues, 2017), all four IDEAS area scores and the total correlated significantly with the GAF and with a social and occupational functioning scale, and 84.8 percent of these patients had disability above 40 percent. Comparisons of IDEAS with WHODAS 2.0 have also been published, a natural question now that DSM-5 recommends the WHO's instrument. Exam trap CGI (Guy, 1976): CGI-S rates current severity from 1 (normal) to 7 (among the most extremely ill); CGI-I rates change from baseline from 1 (very much improved) through 4 (no change) to 7 (very much worse); a responder is usually CGI-I 1 or 2. GAF: 0 to 100, Axis V of DSM-III-R and DSM-IV, dropped by DSM-5 and replaced by WHODAS 2.0 (WHO; 36 or 12 items; six domains; past 30 days; items 1 to 5). In India, disability from mental illness is certified with IDEAS (Indian Psychiatric Society, 2002), not WHODAS. A trap from the IHBAS 2024 paper: asked for "the Indian tool to assess the severity and disability of children with autism", the answer is ISAA, the Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (Book 2, Section 9.9.8). The other options are not Indian disability tools for autism: the CGAS rates a child's overall functioning from 1 to 100, the CBCL rates general behaviour problems (Section 11.9.8), and the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) is the American scale of Eric Schopler and colleagues (1980). The paper keyed CARS; Book 2, Section 9.9.8 explains why ISAA is the correct fact and how to handle the IHBAS key. Rating children: the CBCL, the Conners scales, the SDQ and the CPMS Riddhi, 9, is referred by her school in Chandigarh because she "does not concentrate" and has fallen behind in mathematics. Who should you ask about her? A nine-year-old can tell you some things about how she feels, but she cannot rate her own attention against that of other girls her age. Her mother sees her at home, in the mornings and evenings; her class teacher sees her for six hours a day among thirty other children. Book 2, Section 10.1.4 showed how poorly such informants agree with each other, and why: children behave differently in different settings, so each informant sees a different slice of the child. Child rating scales are built around that fact. They come in parallel forms for parents, teachers and older children, and each form is normed separately, so that a mother's rating is compared with other mothers' ratings and a teacher's with other teachers'. Two further distinctions organise the field. A broad-band scale surveys the whole range of emotional and behavioural problems, while a narrow-band scale concentrates on one area, such as ADHD. And a scale can be empirically based , with its scales derived by factor analysis of how problems actually cluster in children (a "bottom-up" approach), or built "top-down" from the diagnostic criteria of DSM or ICD. The best-known broad-band, empirically based system is that of Thomas M. Achenbach at the University of Vermont. In factor analyses of children's psychiatric problems in the 1960s, Achenbach found that most problems fall into two broad groupings, which he called internalising (problems directed inward, such as anxiety, sadness, withdrawal and bodily complaints) and externalising (problems directed outward, such as aggression and rule-breaking). The distinction is now used throughout child psychology. His Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), completed by a parent, was published with a manual co-written with Craig Edelbrock in 1983 and became the core of the Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessment (ASEBA). The school-age forms in use today (Achenbach and Leslie Rescorla, 2001) are the CBCL/6-18 for parents, the Teacher's Report Form (TRF) and the Youth Self-Report (YSR) for ages 11 to 18; preschool forms cover ages 1½ to 5. On the school-age parent form, more than a hundred problem items (118 specific problems and two open-ended items, printed as 113 numbered questions because one question has eight parts) are each rated 0 (not true), 1 (somewhat or sometimes true) or 2 (very true or often true) for the past six months, and separate competence items cover activities, social life and school. The problem items are scored on eight syndrome scales : anxious/depressed, withdrawn/depressed, somatic complaints, social problems, thought problems, attention problems, rule-breaking behaviour and aggressive behaviour. The first three add up to the Internalising score and the last two to the Externalising score; social, thought and attention problems belong to neither but count in the Total Problems score. A set of DSM-oriented scales, regrouping the same items by diagnostic criteria, was added later, so the CBCL now offers both bottom-up and top-down views of one set of answers. Raw scores are converted to T-scores using norms for the child's sex, age range and informant. On the syndrome scales, T-scores of 65 to 69 (roughly the 93rd to 97th percentiles) are in the borderline clinical range and 70 or above in the clinical range ; the broad Internalising, Externalising and Total Problems scores use lower cut-offs, with 60 to 63 (roughly the 84th to 90th percentiles) counting as borderline and 64 and above as clinical. Why percentile cut-offs rather than "two standard deviations"? Because problem scores are strongly skewed: most children have few problems, so a symmetric bell curve does not describe them, and the manual's T-scores are anchored to percentiles of the actual distribution (Chapter 5 explains normalised standard scores). Riddhi's mother completes the CBCL and her class teacher the TRF. Their invented T-scores are plotted in Figure 11.20. Her mother's ratings reach the borderline range for anxious/depressed (68) and somatic complaints (66): she describes stomach aches on school mornings and worry about tests. Her teacher's ratings are unremarkable except for attention problems, at 74, in the clinical range: Riddhi stares out of the window, leaves work unfinished and loses track of instructions. Her mother rates attention problems at 63, raised but below the borderline range. Neither informant is wrong. Attention problems show most where sustained attention is demanded, in the classroom; anxiety and stomach aches show most where the child is about to face school, at home in the morning. The two profiles together generate the clinical questions: is this ADHD, predominantly inattentive, with secondary anxiety; is it anxiety that disrupts concentration; or is a specific learning disorder in mathematics producing both? A rating scale cannot settle that, but it tells you where to look next: a narrow-band ADHD scale from both informants, cognitive and attention tests (Sections 11.4 and 11.6), an educational assessment and an interview with Riddhi herself. 50 55 60 65 70 75 80 T-score 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 Syndrome scale (numbers explained in the key) clinical range Key to scales 1 Anxious/depressed 2 Withdrawn/depressed 3 Somatic complaints 4 Social problems 5 Thought problems 6 Attention problems 7 Rule-breaking 8 Aggression mother (CBCL) teacher (TRF) clinical: 70 and up borderline: 65 to 69 Figure 11.20 Riddhi's invented CBCL syndrome profile as rated by her mother (line with filled circles) and her teacher (line with open squares). The mother's ratings rise into the borderline range on anxious/depressed and somatic complaints; the teacher's rise into the clinical range only on attention problems. Disagreement between informants is expected, and it is information about where the problem shows. Where the CBCL is broad, the scales of C. Keith Conners (1933 to 2017) are the classic narrow-band instrument for ADHD and its neighbours. Conners published a teacher rating scale in 1969, "for use in drug studies with children", because the stimulant trials of the time needed a way to measure change in classroom behaviour, and a parent scale followed. The scales were revised several times (the Conners' Rating Scales-Revised in 1997, the Conners 3 in 2008 and the Conners 4 in 2022) and now come in parent, teacher and self-report forms, the last for older children and adolescents. They yield T-scores, against age and sex norms, for inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, and related areas such as learning problems, executive functioning, defiance and aggression, and peer relations, together with scales that follow the DSM criteria for ADHD, oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder. A T-score of 70, two standard deviations above the mean of the norm group, marks a very elevated rating. Do not confuse these rating scales with the Conners Continuous Performance Test, a computerised attention task by the same author (Section 11.6). Other ADHD rating scales, such as the Vanderbilt scales of Mark Wolraich, are listed in Book 3, Section 3.1.5. A shorter broad-band screen, now used worldwide, is the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) of the British child psychiatrist Robert Goodman (1997). Its 25 items fall into five scales of five items each: emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity-inattention, peer relationship problems and prosocial behaviour. Each item is scored 0, 1 or 2, so each scale runs from 0 to 10, and the first four scales add up to a total difficulties score of 0 to 40; the prosocial scale is kept separate, because it measures a strength. Goodman designed a single form that parents and teachers both complete, which he hoped would raise their agreement, and in his first study of 403 children from dental and psychiatric clinics the SDQ discriminated between the two groups as well as the longer Rutter questionnaires it was meant to replace. A self-report version exists for adolescents, and because the questionnaire is free to use, translations exist in many languages, including Indian ones. India has its own broad-band instrument, and it is a standard exam answer. The Childhood Psychopathology Measurement Schedule (CPMS) was developed at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh, by Savita Malhotra , V. K. Varma, S. K. Verma and Anil Malhotra, from Savita Malhotra's doctoral work of 1984, and published in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 1988. It is an Indian adaptation of the Child Behavior Checklist, standardised on Indian children of both sexes aged 4 to 14, and used in Hindi and English. It has 75 items, each marked yes or no by a parent or other informant, and it yields a total score for overall psychopathology and scores on eight factorially derived syndromes: low intelligence with behaviour problems, conduct disorder, anxiety, depression, psychotic symptoms, special symptoms, physical illness with emotional problems, and somatisation. A total above about 10 is commonly taken to mark significant psychopathology. Its authors proposed it as a screening instrument for population surveys and as a research tool, and Indian studies of children with chronic physical illness and surveys of schoolchildren have used it in exactly those ways. The same team built a companion temperament schedule. Instruments for autism (CARS, ISAA, the M-CHAT) and for adaptive behaviour (the Vineland scales) are taught in Chapter 7, with the Indian certification rules in Book 2, Section 9.9.8. After childbirth: the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale Why would the weeks after childbirth need their own depression scale, when Section 11.8 already offers the BDI and the PHQ-9? Think about what a general depression scale asks. Several of its items concern the body: tiredness, poor sleep, changes in appetite and weight, loss of sexual interest. Almost every mother of a six-week-old baby is exhausted, sleeps in fragments and eats at odd hours, depressed or not. A general scale therefore gives many healthy new mothers points for symptoms that are simply part of caring for a baby, and the result is a flood of false positives. The obvious remedy is a scale that leaves those items out, and that is what a team in Edinburgh built. Key study: Building a postnatal screen (Cox, Holden and Sagovsky, 1987) The psychiatrist John L. Cox , with Jeni M. Holden and Ruth Sagovsky , set out to give health visitors and community health workers a short questionnaire that mothers would accept and that would pick out those with postnatal depression. After extensive pilot interviews with mothers, they wrote ten items about mood, enjoyment, self-blame, anxiety, panic, feeling overwhelmed, unhappiness, tearfulness and thoughts of self-harm, and deliberately avoided items about bodily symptoms that are normal after delivery. They then validated the scale on 84 mothers, comparing their scores with diagnoses made by the Research Diagnostic Criteria from Goldberg's Standardised Psychiatric Interview. The scale showed satisfactory sensitivity and specificity, could be completed in about five minutes, was simple to score, and was sensitive to change in the severity of depression over time. They published the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) in the British Journal of Psychiatry in 1987. Each EPDS item has four answers scored 0 to 3, with some items reverse-scored so that the mother cannot simply tick the same column throughout, and she answers for the past seven days. The total therefore runs from 0 to 30. Cox and his colleagues proposed two thresholds, and the reason for having two is a lesson in screening. A threshold of 12/13 (13 or more) marks probable depression and keeps false positives low; a lower threshold of 9/10 (10 or more) catches more of the depressed mothers at the price of more false alarms, which suits a first-stage screen in primary care where a positive result only means "see the doctor". Chapter 4 explains this trade between sensitivity and specificity. A large meta-analysis of individual participants' data pooled from many countries (Brooke Levis and colleagues, 2020) later found that a threshold of 11 or more balanced sensitivity and specificity best, while 13 or more was less sensitive but more specific. The scale is now also used during pregnancy, and it has been validated in fathers and in many languages, including Indian ones; each validation tends to find its own best threshold, which is why a clinic should use one established for its own population. One item is treated differently from all the others. The last question asks about thoughts of harming oneself, and any score above 0 on it calls for a same-day assessment of risk, whatever the total. A total score is an average judgement; a single answer about self-harm is a fact that must be acted on. Nupura, 26, is seen at a primary health centre near Pune six weeks after the birth of her first child. She completes a translated EPDS. Her invented item scores are 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1 and 0. Adding them: 2 + 1 = 3; 3 + 2 = 5; 5 + 2 = 7; 7 + 1 = 8; 8 + 2 = 10; 10 + 1 = 11; 11 + 2 = 13; 13 + 1 = 14; 14 + 0 = 14. Her total of 14 is above both thresholds, so she is a probable case and is referred for a clinical interview, which is what will decide whether she has a depressive episode. Now change one detail. Suppose instead that her total had been 8, below both thresholds, but that she had scored 1 on the self-harm item. The total says "probably not depressed"; the single item says "assess today". The item wins. Exam trap EPDS: Cox, Holden and Sagovsky, 1987; 10 items, each 0 to 3, total 0 to 30; past seven days; self-report; a screen, not a diagnosis. Its defining design feature is that it avoids the bodily symptoms that are normal after childbirth. Thresholds: 12/13 for probable depression, 9/10 for a more sensitive first screen. A positive answer on the self-harm item needs immediate assessment regardless of the total. Do not confuse the EPDS with the Geriatric Depression Scale (Section 11.8), which solves a similar problem for older adults by using simple yes-or-no items and few bodily symptoms. In the forensic setting: the PCL-R as a measurement Forensic assessment is the setting in which the person being assessed has the strongest reasons to shape the result. A man facing a parole board does not report his lack of remorse. That single fact explains most of the design of the instrument that dominates forensic psychology, the Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R) of Robert D. Hare (born 1934). Book 3, Section 11.5.6 tells its history, from Hervey Cleckley 's (1903 to 1984) portrait of the psychopath in The Mask of Sanity (1941) to Hare's 22-item Psychopathy Checklist of 1980, the 20-item PCL-R of 1991 and its second edition of 2003, and it sets out the two factors and four facets with their content. This subsection takes the PCL-R as a piece of measurement. How it is scored. A trained rater scores each of the 20 items 0 (does not apply), 1 (applies to some extent) or 2 (definitely applies), so totals run from 0 to 40. The information comes from two sources: a semi-structured interview, and a review of the person's files (police records, court papers, prison and hospital notes) and, where possible, interviews with people who know him. The file review is not optional. Because many of the traits being rated (pathological lying, conning, lack of remorse, shallow affect) are exactly the traits that distort a self-account, the PCL-R should not be scored from an interview alone; when the interview and the files conflict, the documented record weighs heavily. Research ratings are sometimes made from files alone when the files are rich, but never from the interview alone. Missing information and prorating. Files are often incomplete, so the manual allows a rater to omit an item for which there is not enough information, up to a maximum of five items, and to prorate the total, that is, to scale it up to what it would be on 20 items. Remember Prorated PCL-R total = (sum of the scored items ÷ number of items scored) × 20 No more than five items may be omitted; with more missing information the total cannot be trusted. Take an invented prisoner whose files say nothing about two items, so 18 items are scored, and suppose those 18 items add up to 25. His prorated total is (25 ÷ 18) × 20 = 1.389 × 20 = 27.8, which rounds to 28. Is he "a psychopath" by the usual North American cut-off of 30? Here the reliability ideas of Chapter 3 earn their keep. Every score carries error, and Chapter 3, Section 3.7 shows how the standard error of measurement (SEM) turns a single score into a band. Suppose, for the sake of the example, that the SEM of a single rater's PCL-R total is 3 points (an assumed figure, chosen to make the arithmetic clear). A 95 percent band is the score plus or minus 1.96 SEM: 28 ± (1.96 × 3) = 28 ± 5.9, which runs from about 22 to about 34. The band straddles 30. The honest conclusion is not "he is not a psychopath" but "his true score could lie on either side of the cut-off", and a court should hear exactly that. Key study: Are forensic experts biased by the side that retained them? (Murrie and colleagues, 2013) In research studies trained PCL-R raters agree closely. Yet in real trials, experts called by the prosecution and by the defence often report strikingly different scores for the same offender. Is that because they see different files, or because the side that pays them shapes their judgement? Daniel C. Murrie , Marcus Boccaccini and their colleagues designed an experiment to find out. They recruited more than a hundred experienced forensic psychologists and psychiatrists through a two-day workshop, and 108 of them were then paid to review and score the same set of offender case files as a consultation. The experts were deceived about one thing: some were told that they had been retained by the prosecution and others by the defence. They scored each offender on two widely used instruments, the PCL-R and the Static-99R, a risk scale for sexual offenders. Experts who believed they were working for the prosecution gave higher risk scores to the same offenders than those who believed they were working for the defence, with effect sizes (Cohen's d) as large as 0.85. The gap was larger on the PCL-R, whose items demand judgement, than on the more mechanical Static-99R, which is scored largely from documented facts. The authors, writing in Psychological Science , called this an allegiance effect , and they noted that it appeared in some experts, not all. The lesson for measurement is that inter-rater reliability measured in a research team does not guarantee reliability in an adversarial setting: the rater's situation is a source of error in its own right. The family of instruments. Because the full PCL-R takes several hours of interview and file review, a 12-item Psychopathy Checklist: Screening Version (PCL:SV), scored 0 to 24, was published in 1995 by Stephen Hart, David Cox and Hare for use in civil psychiatric and other settings, and a 20-item youth version (PCL:YV) by Adelle Forth, David Kosson and Hare (2003) adapts the items for adolescents, whose personalities are still forming, which makes the label especially risky (Book 3, Section 11.5.6). Self-report questionnaires of psychopathic traits also exist, such as the Psychopathic Personality Inventory of Scott Lilienfeld and Brian Andrews (1996); they are cheap and useful in research with ordinary adults, but in forensic settings they face the obvious problem that the people they are meant to detect are skilled at managing impressions. Note, finally, what the PCL-R is not. It measures a personality construct; it is not in itself a violence risk assessment, although its scores predict reoffending (Book 3, Section 11.5.6 describes the evidence) and it appears as one item in structured risk instruments. Exam trap "The PCL-R was developed by..." Robert Hare (PCL 1980; PCL-R 1991; second edition 2003). Not Hervey Cleckley alone in 1941: Cleckley described the psychopath in The Mask of Sanity and listed his features, but he built no rating scale. Not Aaron Beck (cognitive therapy, the BDI of Section 11.8) and not Hans Eysenck (the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire and the PEN model, Chapter 9). Measurement facts: 20 items, each 0, 1 or 2, total 0 to 40, rated by a trained clinician from a semi-structured interview plus file review, with at most five items omitted and the total prorated; cut-off 30 in North America (25 is often used in Britain and Europe). PCL:SV has 12 items (0 to 24); PCL:YV is the youth version. Choosing a scale: three referral questions You have now met several dozen instruments in this chapter, and a referral letter never says "please administer the PANSS". It asks a question: is he getting better, does she have ADHD, is he fit to be released, can she get a disability certificate? Choosing the instrument is a skill in its own right, and it rests on a short sequence of questions that the rest of this book has prepared you to ask. Figure 11.21 sets them out. Figure 11.21 A decision path for choosing a rating scale. Begin with the decision the score must inform, which narrows the field to one family of instruments; then the four checks (informant, time frame, norms, reliability at the cut-off) pick the instrument within the family. Note that diagnosis belongs to interviews, not to rating scales. Two kinds of instrument mentioned in the figure are not rating scales at all, and they mark the edges of this chapter. If the question is "which disorder does he have?", the tool is a structured diagnostic interview , such as the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM (SCID-5), the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry with its Present State Examination, or the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI); Book 2, Section 2.1.4 teaches them. A rating scale presupposes the diagnosis and measures how much. And if the question is how much stress a person has been exposed to, the tool is a life-events scale, such as Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (1967), taught in Book 1, Section 11.9.1; it measures events, not symptoms. With those boundaries in place, here are three invented referrals worked through the figure. Referral 1: "Is Tanuj responding to clozapine?" The decision is about severity and change in a known diagnosis of schizophrenia, so the family is the clinician-rated psychosis scales. The informant problem points to a scale that combines interview, observation and family report, because Tanuj's own account of his voices is incomplete and he cannot report his blunted affect. The time frame is the past week, and the rating must be repeated at fixed intervals. The PANSS fits, with a CGI alongside to translate the number into clinical language. Two further details follow from Sections 11.9.1 and 11.9.2: the same trained rater should make every rating if possible (rater differences would otherwise masquerade as change), and the percentage improvement must be calculated after subtracting 30. A GHQ-12 would be useless (it screens for non-psychotic disorder), and so would a BDI-II, unless the specific question were whether he has become depressed, in which case the Calgary scale is the better choice. Referral 2: "Does Riddhi have ADHD?" This is a diagnostic question, and no rating scale can answer it alone. But scales are an essential part of the answer, because the diagnosis requires symptoms in two or more settings, and only informants from those settings can supply them. The path therefore runs: a broad-band scale first, the CBCL from her mother and the TRF from her teacher, to see the whole range of problems (as Figure 11.20 showed, anxiety may be part of the picture); then a narrow-band ADHD scale such as the Conners from both; then tests of attention and executive function (Section 11.6) and an educational assessment for a possible learning disorder, and finally a clinical interview that brings it all together. For a Hindi-speaking family in north India, the CPMS offers Indian norms. Throughout, the scores are read with the expectation that the informants will disagree, and the disagreement itself is information. Referral 3: "Can Laxmi get a disability certificate?" Two years after the episode described in Section 11.9.4, and after two further episodes, Laxmi has lost her teaching post. She has now had bipolar I disorder for nine years, with poor recovery between episodes, and her family asks about a disability certificate. The decision is legal, in India, for a mental illness, so the instrument is fixed by law: IDEAS, rated by the certifying psychiatrist (Book 2, Section 9.9.8 gives the procedure). Suppose the invented ratings are self-care 0, interpersonal activities 2, communication and understanding 1 and work 2, which add to 0 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 5, and that her nine years of illness earn a duration score of 3 (six to ten years, by the 2002 rule of Book 2, Section 9.9.8; under the 2024 guidelines the duration score would instead count her months of illness in the past two years). Her global score is 5 + 3 = 8, in the moderate band of 40 to 70 percent, above the 40 percent benchmark. Now apply the fourth check of Figure 11.21. If a second rater scored her interpersonal activities 1 instead of 2, her global score would be 7, still moderate; but if that rater also scored work 1, it would be 6, mild, below the benchmark. A disagreement of one point on each of two areas separates entitlement from no entitlement. That is why the rating must rest on a careful interview with Laxmi and her family, with the evidence for each rating written down. Her earlier WHODAS 2.0 profile from Section 11.9.7, or a new one, is useful clinical information about where she needs rehabilitation, but it is not the instrument the certifying authority uses. Remember To choose a scale, name the decision first (screen, diagnose, rate severity and change, measure disability, assess forensic risk), then check the informant, the time frame, the norms and language, and the reliability at the cut-off that matters. Rating scales measure how much; diagnostic interviews decide which disorder. Exam trap "Which of these is a diagnostic instrument?" The SCID-5, the MINI and the SCAN (with the Present State Examination) are structured diagnostic interviews; the PANSS, YMRS, HAM-D, BDI-II and Y-BOCS are severity scales; the GHQ, AUDIT, EPDS and MoCA are screens. A positive screen means "assess further", never "diagnosis made". The Social Readjustment Rating Scale of Holmes and Rahe (1967) measures life events, not symptoms. And when an item asks for "the Indian tool", check the purpose: IDEAS certifies disability in mental illness, ISAA in autism, and the CPMS rates childhood psychopathology.
