Halstead's laboratory, revisited Go back to Chicago and Indianapolis with what this chapter has taught. Halstead's conviction that the intelligence tests of his day missed what brain-injured people had lost is the reason a neuropsychological assessment samples separate domains rather than one general ability (Section 11.1.2), and his tasks survive in the battery of Section 11.2: the Category Test for abstract reasoning and concept formation, the blindfolded Tactual Performance Test, the Seashore Rhythm and Speech-Sounds Perception Tests and Finger Tapping, joined by Reitan's Trail Making Test, aphasia screening test and sensory-perceptual examination. Reitan's 1955 study made its case with the Impairment Index, the proportion of the seven core scores in the impaired range, and the index's two kinds of mistake, 4 per cent of the patients and 14 per cent of the controls misclassified, are what Section 11.7.1 calls false negatives and false positives. By matching his two groups for age and education, Reitan respected a lesson that Heaton and his colleagues later built into every score with their demographically corrected norms (1991), and the same lesson, that schooling, language and test familiarity change the scores of healthy people, is why India built its own tools: the NIMHANS Neuropsychology Battery, the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction and the PGI Memory Scale (Section 11.3). His blind reports are the four methods of inference of Section 11.1.5 at work. For the 42-year-old man his strongest clue was the difficulty with language, the kind of sign, dysphasia, that in his blind reports took precedence over every other indicator in placing a lesion in the left hemisphere; and the printed miss, a slow-growing tumour that the scores made look like the static after-effect of an old injury, shows what a profile read from scores alone cannot settle. What changed after 1959 was the question, not the logic. Once CT and MRI could show a lesion directly, localisation lost its central place, and the hypothesis-testing approach that Lezak taught and Edith Kaplan's Boston process approach (Sections 11.1.3 and 11.1.4) asked instead what a person can still remember, plan, say or do, and how he fails: the memory tests of Section 11.4, the Bender and Benton tests of Section 11.5 and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Trail Making Test and Stroop of Section 11.6 are chosen to answer that question. Reitan's battery took one to one and a half days; the MMSE and MoCA of Section 11.7 take ten minutes or so, and a positive result means only "assess further". The rating scales of Sections 11.8 and 11.9 answer the other question the opening promised, not "where is the damage?" but "how ill is this person, and are they getting better?", and they carry Reitan's lesson into a new setting: a number means something only against a stated standard, and only when the rater who produces it is trained, anchored and checked. Halstead began by watching brain-injured people go about the ordinary business of their lives; the patient of Section 11.6.8 who passes the tests and fails at life shows that the field is still learning the lesson he started with. Chapter summary 11.1 What Neuropsychological Assessment Is: Questions, Domains, Approaches and Premorbid Ability. Neuropsychology studies the relationship between brain and behaviour, and every assessment answers a referral question: detecting impairment, differential diagnosis, localisation, a baseline for change, rehabilitation, capacity or medico-legal work. It tests abilities grouped into domains (orientation, attention, processing speed, memory, language, visuospatial and constructional skill, executive functions, motor and sensory function), never opinions. Broca and Wernicke founded localisation, Goldstein described the abstract attitude, single tests of organicity failed, Luria analysed functional systems, and Lezak (1976) and Kaplan's process approach shaped modern practice beside the fixed and flexible batteries. Reitan read profiles by level, pattern, pathognomonic signs and right-left comparisons. Scores are judged against norms (nomothetic) or against the person's premorbid level (idiographic; RML's "ideometric"), estimated from demographics, best performance, Wechsler's hold and don't-hold tests (the deterioration quotient) and Nelson's NART. Performance validity tests check effort. 11.2 The Fixed Batteries: Halstead-Reitan and Luria-Nebraska. Reitan turned Halstead's tests into the Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery, with the WAIS and MMPI as allied procedures, not parts of it. At its core are the Category Test (abstract reasoning and concept formation), the blindfolded Tactual Performance Test (time, memory and localisation scores), the Seashore Rhythm and Speech-Sounds Perception Tests and Finger Tapping; Reitan added the Trail Making Test, the Reitan-Indiana Aphasia Screening Test, the Reitan-Klove Sensory-Perceptual Examination, grip strength and lateral dominance. The Halstead Impairment Index is the proportion of seven core scores impaired, 0.5 or more suggesting impairment; Heaton's demographically corrected T scores (1991) replaced fixed cut-offs. It serves comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, never personality, projective or vocational testing, and excludes the Rorschach. The Luria-Nebraska ran from Luria through Christensen (1975) to Golden, Hammeke and Purisch (1978, 1980): Form I has 269 items in 11 clinical scales. Critics attacked it, but the two batteries proved about equally accurate. 11.3 Indian Neuropsychological Tools: The NIMHANS Battery, the PGI Battery and the PGI Memory Scale. Indian norms are needed because education, literacy, language and test familiarity change the scores of healthy people, so borrowed cut-offs misclassify them. The NIMHANS Neuropsychology Battery (Rao, Subbakrishna and Gopukumar, 2004) adapts 19 Western tests for adults aged 16 to 65, with percentile norms by age, sex and education and no single index; it uses the Colour Trails Test, the WCST, the Stroop, the Tower of London, fluency, verbal learning and a complex figure. Kar and colleagues built the children's battery (5 to 15), and the NNB-E serves older adults. At PGIMER, Pershad and Verma's PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction combines the PGI Memory Scale, Bhatia's short scale, the Verbal Adult Intelligence Scale, the Nahor-Benson Test and the Bender-Gestalt into 19 ratings totalling 0 to 57. Pershad and Wig's PGI Memory Scale (1977) has ten subtests. The AIIMS battery is a Hindi Luria-Nebraska. 11.4 Memory Tests: The Wechsler Memory Scale, Digit Span and the Learning Tests. A memory examination separates encoding, storage and retrieval, immediate from delayed recall, recall from recognition and verbal from visual material. Digit span forward measures immediate attention span; backward span measures working memory, not long-term, sensory or procedural memory. Wechsler's Memory Scale (1945) gave a single memory quotient; the WMS-IV (2009) gives five indices: Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory, Immediate Memory and Delayed Memory. André Rey's Auditory Verbal Learning Test reads 15 unrelated words over five trials, then an interference list, a delayed recall and a recognition trial, separating proactive from retroactive interference and storage from retrieval deficits; the California Verbal Learning Test (Delis and colleagues, 1987) adds categories and so semantic clustering. Rey's complex figure, standardised by Osterrieth (1944), is copied and then recalled, Benton's Visual Retention Test (1946) has ten designs, and Wilson's Rivermead (1985) samples everyday memory. 11.5 Visuomotor and Visuospatial Tests: The Bender-Gestalt, the Benton Tests and Constructional Tasks. Visuoperception, visuospatial judgement, construction and visual-motor integration are separate skills, and schooling affects them all. Lauretta Bender's Visual Motor Gestalt Test (1938) asks for copies of nine designs, Figure A and 1 to 8, adapted from Max Wertheimer's Gestalt patterns. Pascal and Suttell (1951) scored adults, Hutt read copies projectively, Lacks (1984) built a twelve-error screen, and Koppitz (1963) scored children for distortion, rotation, integration and perseveration. Brannigan and Decker's Bender-Gestalt II (2003) has 16 designs. The Bender assesses visual-motor integration and screens for organic impairment and developmental immaturity, not personality, depression, schizophrenia, ADHD, reading or premorbid intelligence. Benton's Finger Localization Test scores each hand separately, so consistently more errors on one side point to the opposite hemisphere; his line orientation, facial recognition and right-left tests isolate single functions. Line bisection and cancellation reveal neglect, and the Beery VMI serves children. 11.6 Executive Function, Attention, Concept Formation and Language Tests. Executive functions set goals, plan, inhibit, monitor and shift strategy, and depend heavily on the prefrontal cortex. Grant and Berg's Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (1948), standardised by Heaton, has four key cards and 128 response cards sorted by colour, form or number under unannounced rule changes; perseverative errors are its signature score. Milner (1963) tied it to dorsolateral prefrontal damage, though other damage can lower it too. The Trail Making Test (1944) contrasts Part A (attention and speed) with Part B (set-shifting) and helps assess inattention in ADHD; the Colour Trails Test avoids the alphabet. Stroop interference tests inhibition, Shallice's Tower of London (1982) planning, and fluency generation. Patient EVR showed why ecological validity matters. The Continuous Performance Test (1956) and the Test of Everyday Attention (1994) test attention, Goldstein and Scheerer's Object Sorting Test (1941) thought disorder, and the Boston Naming Test, Token Test, BDAE and WAB language. 11.7 Bedside Screening and Staging: The MMSE, MoCA, Glasgow Coma Scale and Dementia Ratings. A screen picks out who needs full assessment; sensitivity, specificity and predictive values describe its accuracy, and a positive result means "assess further". The MMSE (Folstein, Folstein and McHugh, 1975) is scored out of 30 with a 23/24 cut-off and screens for and tracks global cognitive impairment and dementia, but it has a ceiling, depends on schooling and has no executive tasks. Ganguli's Hindi Mental State Examination (1995) adapted it for rural elders without schooling. Nasreddine's MoCA (2005), also out of 30 with 26 and above normal, adds executive tasks and clock drawing and is more sensitive to mild cognitive impairment. Addenbrooke's examination has 100 points; the clock and Mini-Cog are briefer. Teasdale and Jennett's Glasgow Coma Scale (1974) rates consciousness from 3 to 15, 8 or below severe. The CAM detects delirium, and the CDR, Reisberg's Global Deterioration Scale and the Hachinski score stage and type dementia. 11.8 Clinical Rating Scales I: Principles, Depression, Anxiety and OCD. A rating scale measures how much, where a diagnostic interview decides whether. Scales are self-report, clinician-rated or informant-rated: the Beck inventories are self-report and the Hamilton scales clinician-rated. Anchors, time frames and item ranges fix the totals, bands and cut-offs, and a good scale is reliable, valid and sensitive to change. Raters make halo (Thorndike, 1920), leniency, central tendency, logical and contrast errors. Beck's Depression Inventory (1961; BDI-II 1996) has 21 self-report items rated 0 to 3 for two weeks: 0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate, 29 to 63 severe; neuropsychologists add it as a mood measure, but it is not a neuropsychological test. Other depression scales are the HAM-D (1960), MADRS (1979), Zung (1965) and PHQ-9 (2001); anxiety scales include the HAM-A (1959), BAI (1988), GAD-7 and STAI. Goodman's Y-BOCS (1989) rates OCD severity on 10 items, 0 to 40. 11.9 Clinical Rating Scales II: Psychosis, Mania, Substance Use, Children, Disability and Forensic Use. Psychosis is rated by clinicians: Overall and Gorham's BPRS (1962) and Kay, Fiszbein and Opler's PANSS (1987), whose 30 items (7 positive, 7 negative, 16 general), each 1 to 7, measure symptom severity in schizophrenia; percentage change must subtract its floor of 30. Andreasen's SANS and SAPS rate the two syndromes in detail, and Young's scale (1978) rates mania. Goldberg's GHQ (1972) screens for non-psychotic disorder and Derogatis's SCL-90-R profiles distress. AUDIT and CAGE screen drinking, the SADQ rates dependence and the CIWA-Ar withdrawal. The CGI (Guy, 1976), the GAF, WHODAS 2.0 and India's IDEAS rate global functioning and disability. Achenbach's CBCL, the Conners scales, Goodman's SDQ and Malhotra's CPMS rate children, and the EPDS (Cox and colleagues, 1987) screens mothers after childbirth.
