Psychopathy Checklist-Revised, prorate, allegiance effect, structured diagnostic interview From the past papers Which of these is NOT typically assessed by neuropsychological tests? (RML 2025) (a) Opinion (b) Language (c) Memory (d) Executive functioning Answer: (a) Opinion. Neuropsychological tests measure abilities that depend on particular brain systems, grouped into domains: orientation and consciousness, attention, processing speed, memory, language, visuospatial and constructional skill, executive functions, and motor and sensory function (Section 11.1.2 and Table 11.1). An opinion is an attitude with no better or worse level of performance, so it is the outsider; language, memory and executive functioning are three of the core domains. Which domains are assessed by neuropsychological tests? (RML 2025) (a) Language, Memory, Executive Functioning (b) Opinion, Language, Reaction (c) Memory, Reaction, Opinion (d) Executive Functioning, Opinion, Reaction Answer: (a) Language, Memory, Executive Functioning. All three are domains of cognition (Section 11.1.2). Every other option contains "opinion" or "reaction", and neither is a domain. Do not over-learn the item, though: reaction time is measured, as an index of processing speed and attention, so an option that says "reaction time" or "processing speed" in a future paper may be right. In neuropsychological assessments, the Ideometric Approach primarily focuses on: (RML 2025) (a) Evaluating patient's premorbid functioning and current status (b) Quantitative analysis of standardized test scores (c) Comparison with normative population data (d) Assessment of emotional and psychological well-being Answer: (a), the keyed option, but "ideometric" is not a standard term. It appears in no major textbook and is probably a garbling of idiographic; the item uses it for Lezak's individual comparison standard, which compares the person's present scores with his or her own estimated premorbid level (Section 11.1.6). Option (c) is the opposite standard, the normative (nomothetic) comparison; (b) is psychometric scoring, which every approach uses and which is not a standard of comparison; (d) is mood assessment (Section 11.8). Impact of psychiatric illness on one's cognitive and intellectual abilities can be estimated on the basis of: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Deterioration quotient (b) Mediation index (c) Sense of coherence index (d) Theory of Mind index Answer: (a) Deterioration quotient. David Wechsler compared the hold tests (Vocabulary, Information, Object Assembly, Picture Completion), which resist brain disease and prolonged mental illness, with the don't-hold tests (Digit Span, Similarities, Digit Symbol, Block Design), which give way; the gap estimates the loss (Section 11.1.7). A mediation index is a statistic from mediation analysis, the sense of coherence is Aaron Antonovsky's predictor of health, and a theory of mind index would concern social cognition; none estimates intellectual decline. The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery is primarily designed to: (RML Practice 1, practice mock) (a) Screen for depression using self-report items (b) Assess a broad range of cognitive functions to detect and localize brain dysfunction (c) Measure vocational aptitude (d) Assess attachment style Answer: (b). The battery samples a broad range of cognitive, sensory and motor functions to detect brain dysfunction, estimate its severity and, in Reitan's hands, suggest its side and site (Section 11.2.5). A self-report depression screen is a questionnaire such as the BDI (Section 11.8), vocational aptitude is measured by aptitude batteries such as the Differential Aptitude Tests (Chapter 8), and attachment style by the Strange Situation and the Adult Attachment Interview. The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery includes all of the following EXCEPT: (MET Mock 3, practice mock) (a) Category Test (b) Tactual Performance Test (c) Trail Making Test (d) Rorschach Inkblot Test Answer: (d) Rorschach Inkblot Test. The Rorschach is a projective personality technique (Chapter 10) and is never part of the battery. The Category Test (abstract reasoning and concept formation) and the blindfolded Tactual Performance Test are Halstead's own tests, and the Trail Making Test, taken from the Army Individual Test Battery of 1944, was added by Reitan (Section 11.2.2). The backward digit span test, where participants must repeat a sequence of numbers in reverse order, is primarily used to assess which type of memory system? (Real PYQ 2025) (a) Long-term memory (b) Working memory (c) Sensory memory (d) Procedural memory Answer: (b) Working memory. Reversing the string means holding the digits and manipulating them at once, which is what Baddeley and Hitch meant by working memory; forward span measures immediate attention span (Section 11.4.2). Long-term memory is tested by delayed recall after a filled delay, sensory memory by laboratory methods such as Sperling's partial report, and procedural memory by learning a skill such as mirror drawing; amnesic patients can have a normal span. The Wechsler Memory Scale-IV (WMS-IV) yields which primary indices? (MET Mock 4, practice mock) (a) Verbal IQ and Performance IQ (b) Crystallised + Fluid Intelligence only (c) Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory, Immediate Memory, Delayed Memory (d) Attention, Concentration, and Vigilance only Answer: (c). These are the five WMS-IV indices (2009), kept in the WMS-5 (Section 11.4.3). Verbal and Performance IQ were the summary scores of the old Wechsler intelligence scales, crystallised and fluid intelligence are Cattell and Horn's broad abilities (Chapter 6), and "attention, concentration and vigilance" borrows the WMS-R's Attention/Concentration index; vigilance belongs to continuous performance tests. The Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test is primarily used to assess: (RML Practice 1, practice mock) (a) Verbal intelligence (b) Visual-motor integration and possible neurological impairment (c) Unconscious sexual conflicts (d) Vocational interests Answer: (b). Lauretta Bender's test (1938) asks the person to copy nine designs adapted from Max Wertheimer's Gestalt patterns; it measures visual-motor integration and screens for organic impairment in adults and for developmental immaturity in children (Section 11.5.5). Copying needs no words, so it says nothing about verbal intelligence; unconscious conflicts are the business of projective techniques (Chapter 10), and Hutt's projective reading of the Bender is secondary; vocational interests are measured by interest inventories (Chapter 8). Which test can diagnose if an examinee consistently makes more errors on one side of the body than the other? (Entrance Mock 1, practice mock) (a) Finger Localization Test (b) Continuous Performance Test (c) Sustained Attention Test (d) The Test of Everyday Attention Answer: (a) Finger Localization Test. Arthur Benton's test scores each hand separately, and touch from each hand is analysed mainly in the parietal lobe of the opposite hemisphere, so consistently more errors on one hand point to damage on the other side of the brain (Section 11.5.6). The other three measure attention, which is not tested side by side: the Continuous Performance Test (Rosvold and colleagues, 1956) sustained attention, "sustained attention tests" vigilance in general, and the Test of Everyday Attention (Robertson and colleagues, 1994) several kinds of attention through everyday tasks. One of the most widely used tests to assess executive functioning: (Amity 2023) (a) Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (b) Minnesota Number Ordering Test (c) Manhattan Card Sorting Test (d) None of the above Answer: (a) Wisconsin Card Sorting Test. David Grant and Esta Berg's card-sorting task (1948), standardised clinically by Robert Heaton, is the most widely used test of executive function, measuring set-shifting and cognitive flexibility (Sections 11.6.2 and 11.6.4). The "Minnesota Number Ordering Test" and the "Manhattan Card Sorting Test" do not exist, so "none of the above" is wrong too; do not confuse them with real look-alikes such as the Minnesota Rate of Manipulation Test (manual dexterity) or Nelson's Modified Card Sorting Test. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) is most sensitive to dysfunction of which region? (Biopsych + Testing paper, practice mock) (a) Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (set-shifting, response to changing rules) (b) Primary motor cortex (c) Hippocampus (d) Cerebellum Answer: (a) Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Brenda Milner (1963) found card sorting impaired after dorsolateral frontal excisions but not after orbitofrontal or temporal ones, and Demakis's meta-analysis (2003) found the frontal deficit largest after dorsolateral damage, although damage outside the frontal lobes can also lower the score (Section 11.6.4). The hippocampus serves memory, the primary motor cortex movement (tested by finger tapping) and the cerebellum coordination. Trail Making Test helps to assess ______ in children with ADHD. (IHBAS 2020) (a) Inattention (b) Social Skills (c) Impulsivity (d) Over-activity Answer: (a) Inattention. A child with ADHD loses the place, skips circles, makes sequencing errors and takes longer, especially on Part B, where attention must switch between numbers and letters (Section 11.6.5). Social skills are judged from observation and informants, over-activity is a classroom behaviour recorded on rating scales such as the Conners scales, and impulsivity, for which the test has no score, is better shown by the commission errors of a continuous performance test. Disorder in thinking can be effectively assessed by: (IHBAS 2020) (a) Rorschach Psychodiagnostics (b) Thematic Apperception Test (c) Bender Gestalt Test (d) Object Sorting Test Answer: (d) Object Sorting Test. Goldstein and Scheerer's test (1941), brought into clinical psychology by David Rapaport, asks the person to group everyday objects and explain why, and so examines concept formation directly: peculiar, fabulated and overinclusive sorts are the signs of disordered thinking (Section 11.6.10). The Rorschach shows thought disorder only indirectly, through its special scores and the Perceptual-Thinking Index; the TAT taps needs and themes in stories (Chapter 10); the Bender measures visual-motor integration. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) is primarily used to: (MET Mock 5, practice mock) (a) Diagnose specific personality disorders (b) Measure depression severity (c) Assess intelligence quotient (d) Screen for and track global cognitive impairment / dementia (out of 30) Answer: (d). The MMSE of Folstein, Folstein and McHugh (1975) is a 30-point bedside screen, with a cut-off of 23/24, for detecting and following global cognitive impairment, especially dementia (Section 11.7.2). Personality disorders are assessed by structured interviews and inventories, depression severity by scales such as the BDI and the Hamilton scale (although depression can lower an MMSE score), and an IQ needs a full intelligence test such as the Wechsler scales. The MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) differs from the MMSE in that MoCA: (Biopsych + Testing paper, practice mock) (a) Tests only language, not memory (b) Has greater sensitivity for mild cognitive impairment, includes executive function and clock-drawing, and is freely scored out of 30 with ≤25 as a screening cut-off (c) Is administered only by neurologists (d) Is much shorter (5 min versus 30 min) Answer: (b), with one correction. Nasreddine's MoCA (2005) adds executive and visuospatial tasks, clock drawing and a harder five-word recall, and in its validation study it caught 90 percent of people with mild cognitive impairment against 18 percent for the MMSE; 26 and above is normal, so "25 or below" is the same cut-off (Section 11.7.4). "Freely" describes only its early years: since 2019 its use has been tied to the publisher's training and certification. Delayed recall carries 5 of its 30 points, it was designed for first-line doctors, and both tests take about ten minutes. Which aspect of cognitive function is assessed by the Glasgow Coma Scale? (Entrance Mock 1, practice mock) (a) Consciousness (b) Attention (c) Memory (d) Intelligence Answer: (a) Consciousness. Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett's scale (1974) rates the level of consciousness from eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6), a total of 3 to 15, with 8 or below meaning severe injury or coma (Section 11.7.6). Attention is tested with forward digit span, continuous performance and cancellation tasks, memory with the Wechsler Memory Scale and learning tests, and intelligence with the Wechsler intelligence scales. Which of the following is a clinician-rated questionnaire? (RML 2022) (a) Beck Depression Inventory (b) Beck Anxiety Inventory (c) Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (d) Both b and c Answer: (c) Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. Max Hamilton's scale (1959) is completed by a trained clinician after an interview (Section 11.8.2). The Beck Depression Inventory and the Beck Anxiety Inventory are both self-report, so (a) is wrong and (d), which needs both (b) and (c) to be clinician-rated, is wrong too. A useful rule: "inventory" and "questionnaire" usually mean self-report, "rating scale" usually means clinician-rated. Which of the following tests is typically used for neuropsychological assessment? (RML 2025) (a) Beck Depression Inventory (b) Likert Scale (c) 16 Personality Factor Questionnaire (d) Peabody Individual Achievement Test Answer: keyed (a) Beck Depression Inventory, but the key needs a caution: the BDI is not a neuropsychological test. It is Aaron Beck's self-report inventory of depressive symptoms and tests no brain function; it earns a place in a neuropsychological assessment only because neuropsychologists routinely add a mood measure, since depression lowers effort, speed and memory and can even mimic dementia (Section 11.8.6). A Likert scale is a response format and attitude-scaling method (Chapter 8), the 16PF is Cattell's personality inventory (Chapter 9), and the Peabody Individual Achievement Test measures school achievement (Chapter 8). Choose (a) as keyed, for the reason given. A 35-year-old presents with persistent sadness, anhedonia, weight loss, insomnia, worthlessness, and concentration difficulties for 2 months. Which assessment would be MOST appropriate to further evaluate her symptoms? (NIMHANS Mock 1, practice mock) (a) Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) (b) Rorschach Inkblot Test (c) Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) (d) Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) Answer: (a) Beck Depression Inventory. The picture is a depressive episode, and the BDI quantifies its severity in about ten minutes and gives a baseline for judging treatment, though it does not confirm the diagnosis (Section 11.8.6). The Rorschach is a long projective technique needing expert scoring (Chapter 10), the MMPI a broad inventory whose depression scale is one of ten (Chapter 9), and the WAIS measures intelligence (Chapter 6). BDI-II severity bands are conventionally: (MET Mock 4, practice mock) (a) 0-13 minimal, 14-19 mild, 20-28 moderate, 29-63 severe (b) 0-5 minimal, 6-10 mild, 11-15 moderate, 16+ severe (c) 0-9 minimal, 10-15 mild, 16-23 moderate, 24-40 severe (d) 0-20 minimal, 21-40 moderate, 41-60 severe Answer: (a). The BDI-II (Beck, Steer and Brown, 1996) has 21 items scored 0 to 3 for the past two weeks, a total of 0 to 63, with the manual's bands 0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate and 29 to 63 severe (Section 11.8.6). Option (c) opens with the older BDI's "0 to 9 minimal" and ends at 40, the Yale-Brown maximum, which a scale running to 63 cannot do; (d) has no mild band and stops at 60; and the five-point steps of (b) belong to no Beck scale. Y-BOCS is a scale for : (IHBAS 2025) (a) Depression (b) Bipolar disorder (c) Schizophrenia (d) OCD Answer: (d) OCD. Wayne Goodman and colleagues' Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (1989) is a clinician-rated measure of OCD severity: 10 items, five for obsessions and five for compulsions, rating time, interference, distress, resistance and control from 0 to 4, a total of 0 to 40 (Section 11.8.9). Depression is rated with the BDI-II, Hamilton or Montgomery-Åsberg scales, the mania of bipolar disorder with the Young Mania Rating Scale, and schizophrenia with the PANSS or the BPRS. The PANSS (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale) is used to assess: (Biopsych + Testing paper, practice mock) (a) Personality disorders (b) Depression severity (c) Cognitive impairment (d) Symptom severity in schizophrenia, with separate positive, negative, and general psychopathology subscales (30 items) Answer: (d). Kay, Fiszbein and Opler's PANSS (1987) has 7 positive, 7 negative and 16 general psychopathology items, each rated 1 to 7, so its total runs from 30 to 210 (Section 11.9.1). Personality disorders need a personality disorder interview; one general item is depression, but depression severity is rated with the BDI or the Hamilton scale (or the Calgary scale in schizophrenia); and cognitive impairment needs tests such as the MoCA, even though the PANSS has items on attention and abstract thinking (Section 11.9.3). The PCL-R (Psychopathy Checklist-Revised) was developed by: (Biopsych + Testing paper, practice mock) (a) Hervey Cleckley alone, 1941 (b) Aaron Beck (c) Robert Hare (d) Hans Eysenck Answer: (c) Robert Hare. Hare built the Psychopathy Checklist (1980) and the 20-item PCL-R (1991; second edition 2003), each item scored 0, 1 or 2 by a trained rater from interview and file review, a total of 0 to 40 (Section 11.9.10). Cleckley described the psychopath in The Mask of Sanity (1941) but built no rating scale; Beck built the BDI and cognitive therapy; Eysenck built the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire. High-yield sheet The facts this chapter's questions ask most, most-asked first. Last read before the exam. The Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (Lauretta Bender, 1938; nine designs, Figure A and 1 to 8, adapted from Max Wertheimer's Gestalt patterns) assesses visual-motor integration and screens for organic (neurological) impairment and developmental immaturity; not personality, depression, schizophrenia, ADHD, reading, verbal intelligence or premorbid intelligence. The Bender-Gestalt II (Brannigan and Decker, 2003) has 16 designs. asked 5 times The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (David Grant and Esta Berg, 1948; Heaton's clinical manual, 1981) is the most widely used test of executive function: set-shifting, cognitive flexibility and abstract reasoning, with perseverative errors its signature score; not memory, language, reading or mood. The "Minnesota Number Ordering Test" and "Manhattan Card Sorting Test" do not exist. asked 4 times The Y-BOCS (Wayne Goodman and colleagues, 1989) is a clinician-rated scale of OCD severity, not depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, PTSD, hallucinations or suicidal ideation: 10 items (5 for obsessions, 5 for compulsions) rating time, interference, distress, resistance and control, each 0 to 4, total 0 to 40. asked 3 times Neuropsychological tests assess brain-dependent abilities : language, memory and executive functioning, with orientation, attention, processing speed, visuospatial, motor and sensory function. Opinion and "reaction" are not domains (though reaction time is measured as an index of processing speed). asked twice The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Battery (Ward Halstead, 1947; Ralph Reitan) is used for comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, sampling a broad range of functions to detect and localise brain dysfunction; not personality, vocational, projective or attachment assessment, and not a self-report depression screen. asked 3 times BDI-II (Beck, Steer and Brown, 1996): 21 self-report items, each 0 to 3, for the past two weeks, total 0 to 63; 0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate, 29 to 63 severe. asked 3 times The WCST is most sensitive to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex dysfunction (Brenda Milner, 1963), not the hippocampus, primary motor cortex or cerebellum, although damage outside the frontal lobes can also lower the score. asked 3 times The Halstead-Reitan tests are the Category Test, the Tactual Performance Test, the Seashore Rhythm Test, the Speech-Sounds Perception Test, Finger Tapping and the Trail Making Test, with the Reitan-Indiana Aphasia Screening Test and the Reitan-Klove Sensory-Perceptual Examination; the Rorschach, the BDI, the HAM-D and the Bender are not in it, and the WAIS and MMPI are allied procedures. A Halstead Impairment Index of 0.5 or more suggests impairment. asked twice WMS-IV (2009): five indices, Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory, Immediate Memory and Delayed Memory; not Verbal and Performance IQ, crystallised and fluid intelligence, or Mechanical Reasoning (a Differential Aptitude Tests subtest). Only the 1945 scale gave a memory quotient. asked twice Backward digit span measures working memory , because the digits must be held and manipulated at once; forward span measures immediate attention span; neither measures long-term, sensory or procedural memory. asked once The "ideometric approach" (RML 2025; not a standard term, probably a garbling of idiographic) is the individual comparison standard: evaluating the patient's premorbid functioning against current status, as opposed to the normative (nomothetic) comparison with population data. asked once Wechsler's deterioration quotient (deterioration index) estimates the impact of brain or psychiatric illness on cognitive and intellectual abilities from hold tests (Vocabulary, Information, Object Assembly, Picture Completion) against don't-hold tests (Digit Span, Similarities, Digit Symbol, Block Design); not a mediation index, sense of coherence (Antonovsky) or theory of mind index. asked once Thought disorder is assessed most effectively by the Object Sorting Test (Kurt Goldstein and Martin Scheerer, 1941; brought into clinical use by David Rapaport), which examines concept formation directly; not the Rorschach, the TAT or the Bender. asked once The Trail Making Test (Army Individual Test Battery, 1944; adopted by Reitan) helps assess inattention in children with ADHD; Part A measures attention and speed, Part B set-shifting; it does not measure social skills, over-activity or, as such, impulsivity. asked once Clinician-rated versus self-report : the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (1959) and the Hamilton depression scale (1960) are clinician-rated; the Beck Depression and Beck Anxiety Inventories are self-report, so "both the BAI and the HAM-A" is wrong. asked once The BDI is not a neuropsychological test : RML 2025 keyed it as "typically used for neuropsychological assessment" because neuropsychologists add a mood measure; choose it as keyed, knowing that a Likert scale is a response format, the 16PF a personality inventory and the Peabody Individual Achievement Test an achievement test. asked once Glasgow Coma Scale (Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett, 1974) assesses the level of consciousness: eye opening 1 to 4, verbal 1 to 5, motor 1 to 6, total 3 to 15, 8 or below severe; not attention, memory or intelligence. asked once Benton's Finger Localization Test shows whether an examinee consistently makes more errors on one side of the body than the other, pointing to the opposite hemisphere; the Continuous Performance Test, sustained attention tests and the Test of Everyday Attention measure attention, not side differences. asked once MMSE (Marshal Folstein, Susan Folstein and Paul McHugh, 1975): out of 30, cut-off 23/24; screens for and tracks global cognitive impairment and dementia; not personality disorders, depression severity or IQ, and it has no clock drawing. asked once MoCA (Ziad Nasreddine and colleagues, 2005): out of 30, 26 and above normal, one point added for 12 or fewer years of education; adds executive tasks and clock drawing and is more sensitive than the MMSE to mild cognitive impairment; it takes about as long as the MMSE and is not reserved for neurologists. asked once PANSS (Stanley Kay, Abraham Fiszbein and Lewis Opler, 1987): 30 items (7 positive, 7 negative, 16 general psychopathology), each 1 to 7, total 30 to 210; rates symptom severity in schizophrenia, not personality disorders, depression severity or cognitive impairment. asked once The PCL-R was developed by Robert Hare (PCL 1980; PCL-R 1991): 20 items scored 0 to 2, total 0 to 40, building on Hervey Cleckley's The Mask of Sanity (1941); not Cleckley alone, Beck or Eysenck. asked once For a depressive presentation (two months of sadness, anhedonia, weight loss, insomnia, worthlessness and poor concentration), the instrument to evaluate it further is the Beck Depression Inventory, not the Rorschach, the MMPI or the WAIS. asked once

title: Master Guide for Clinical Psychology — Amit Panwar
text: Master Guide for Clinical Psychology — Amit Panwar A cheat-map of exactly what the MPhil / MA Clinical Psychology entrances test, lifted straight from Amit Panwar's Master Guide for Clinical Psychology and folded in clean. Four parts: the exam pattern analysis (what CIP, IHBAS, RML and NIMHANS hammer every year, plus the questions that actually repeat), an A–Z terminology glossary , 24 named therapies with founder + key concepts + techniques, and 25 landmark experiments with who/when/where/what. Read it once for the map, then drill the glossary and experiments cold. Source Amit Panwar, Master Guide for Clinical Psychology (Power Within Psychology). Transcribed verbatim; only obvious scan slips were cleaned. Marketing/contact pages dropped. Two of the experiments (Harry Harlow's monkeys, the Darley "Good Samaritan / bystander" pair) appear twice in the original numbering — both kept as the guide lists them. In this guide Exam pattern analysis & repeated questions Why revising UGC-NET JRF papers pays off A–Z terminology glossary 24 important therapies (founder · concepts · techniques) 25 landmark experiments (who · year · where · what) 1. Exam pattern analysis: what actually gets tested Admission into CIP Ranchi, IHBAS, RML and NIMHANS (for MA/MPhil, PGDCP/PDCP, PsyD and PhD Clinical Psychology) is competitive, but the entrances recur in shape. The structure across institutes is similar: MCQs dominate , covering theoretical concepts, psychological tools, research methods, psychotherapies and clinical diagnosis. 1.1 Sections that show up Area What they ask General Psychology Classical theories — Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, B. F. Skinner, Albert Bandura; cognition, memory, sensation, perception, learning. Clinical Psychology Disorders, diagnosis, defense mechanisms, therapeutic approaches. Psychological Testing & Assessment Intelligence (Binet, Wechsler, Bhatia Battery, Performance tests), personality, projective tests; test construction. Psychotherapy & Counselling CBT, DBT, psychodynamic, client-centred; applied / case-based. Research Methods & Statistics Design, hypothesis testing, ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, factor analysis. Developmental Psychology Lifespan, stage theories, attachment. Biopsychology Brain anatomy and its link to psychological function. 1.2 Commonly asked topics, with real stems A. General & Clinical Psychology. Foundational theories of Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, B. F. Skinner, Bandura come up constantly. "Psychoanalytic theory about human personality was proposed by?" (CIP) "Insight learning is studied by?" (CIP) B. Psychometric Testing & Intelligence. Binet, Wechsler, Bhatia Battery / Performance tests — components and Indian-context applications. "The prototype of the modern intelligence test was developed by?" (CIP) "Bhatia Battery of Performance Test includes which test?" (CET) Key tip Go deep on test theory and application; drill test-construction concepts ( reliability, validity ) — they're commonly tested. C. Research Methodology & Statistics. Design, hypothesis testing, and stats. Know ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, factor analysis cold. "Degrees of freedom in a chi-square 3×4 table?" (CIP) "What is Cronbach's Alpha used for?" (RML) D. Clinical Diagnosis & Disorders. DSM-5 criteria, especially schizophrenia, OCD, PTSD, depression; defense mechanisms; therapy approaches. "Which defense mechanism is most common in Borderline Personality Disorder?" (RINPAS) "Which therapy focuses on changing negative thought patterns?" — CBT (CIP) E. Neuropsychology & Biopsychology. Brain structures — hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, hypothalamus — and their functions. "Which structure allows communication between the hemispheres?" (RINPAS) "What is the role of the hippocampus in memory?" (NIMHANS) F. Therapies & Treatment Approaches. CBT, DBT, psychodynamic, client-centred — and applying them. "Functional Analysis is considered under which therapy?" (RINPAS) 1.3 Repeated questions across exams (use this to sharpen the mocks) Many items recur near-verbatim across papers. These are the highest-value drills. Theme Repeated stem Seen in Psychological theories "What are the basic types of defense mechanisms according to Freud?" (Id/Ego/Superego, displacement, repression) IHBAS, CIP, RML MPhil Psychometric tests "Which intelligence test includes the Pattern Drawing Test?" CET, RML Neuropsychology "Damage to the hippocampus affects?" RINPAS, NIMHANS, IHBAS Clinical disorders "Which disorder is characterised by repetitive intrusive thoughts?" (OCD) IHBAS, NIMHANS Defense + BPD "Which defense mechanism is most commonly associated with borderline personality disorder?" IHBAS, CIP, NIMHANS (first via UGC-NET) 1.4 Strategy for cracking the MPhil entrances Focus on core areas: master psychoanalytic, behavioural and cognitive theories; DSM-5 categories, criteria and treatments for common disorders; brain anatomy tied to cognition and memory. Practise previous-year papers: they expose recurring themes and question patterns — drill MCQs on the Bhatia Battery, CBT techniques and brain functions. Master psychometrics & research: intelligence tests, methodology and statistical tools are tested heavily; command of them is a real edge. Stay current: DSM-5 revisions and emerging trends in psychotherapy and neuropsychology. Time management: front-load high-yield topics (research methods, clinical disorders, brain functions); revise and take timed mocks to build speed and accuracy. 2. Why revising UGC-NET JRF papers pays off One of the strongest levers for these entrances: revise UGC-NET JRF papers. The overlap with MPhil Clinical Psychology entrances is large and well-documented. High overlap of topics & questions. Clinical and abnormal psychology (schizophrenia, OCD, personality disorders and their DSM-5 criteria), psychoanalytic theory and research methodology all recur in both. "What are the key diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia?" turns up across UGC-NET, GATE and MPhil papers. Theorist items — e.g. "Which theorist proposed the collective unconscious?" — appear in MPhil exams after first showing in UGC-NET JRF. Strong focus on research methods & statistics. ANOVA, t-tests, chi-square, validity and reliability are repeated. "Degrees of freedom in a chi-square 3×4 table?" appears across UGC-NET and GATE with slight variations in MPhil papers. Psychometric & intelligence tests. WAIS, Binet, and the Bhatia Battery are frequent. "Bhatia Battery of Performance Test includes which test?" has appeared across CIP Ranchi, UGC-NET and GATE — high repetition. Direct repeats in MPhil exams. Items on cognitive distortions, memory systems and CBT techniques carry over from UGC-NET into IHBAS, CIP and NIMHANS papers (e.g. shortlisting rounds). High-utility shared topics. Neuropsychology (hippocampus, amygdala, neurotransmitters; serotonin in depression), cognitive psychology and clinical diagnostics overlap heavily across UGC-NET JRF, GATE and MPhil. Bottom line UGC-NET JRF papers cover the same foundational topics and carry repeated questions and terminology. Folding them into your practice strengthens concepts, drills the repeats, and lifts your odds across the board. 3. A–Z terminology glossary Quick definitions for the key terms the guide flags. Searchable — type any term in the library search and this entry surfaces. A Agraphia The partial or complete inability to write, usually caused by brain damage. Aphasia Partial or complete loss of the ability to speak or comprehend language, typically caused by brain injury or neurological conditions. Aphonia The inability to produce vocal sounds due to damage to the larynx or related structures. Apraxia A disorder where an individual struggles to produce normal movement or speech despite intact muscles and comprehension. Anorexia Nervosa An eating disorder marked by an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted body image, leading to extreme restriction of food intake. Amygdala A structure in the brain's limbic system involved in emotion regulation, particularly fear and aggression. Anterograde Amnesia The inability to form new memories following brain damage, with preserved recall of past events. Attachment Theory Developed by John Bowlby; explains how early relationships with caregivers shape emotional bonds, with types such as secure, anxious and avoidant. Attention Span The length of time an individual can concentrate on a task without becoming distracted. Autosome Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome, carrying genetic information unrelated to sex determination. B Behavioural Theories Theories such as classical and operant conditioning that explain learning through associations, reinforcements and punishments (Ivan Pavlov, B. F. Skinner). Borderline Personality Disorder A disorder of unstable moods, relationships and behaviour, often marked by impulsive actions and intense fears of abandonment. Broca's Area A frontal-lobe region responsible for speech production; damage results in Broca's aphasia. Brute Force A problem-solving strategy that tries all possible solutions until the correct one is found. C Catharsis The release of pent-up emotions and psychological tension through expression, resulting in emotional relief. Chi-Square Test A statistical test used to examine the association between two categorical variables. Chunking A memory strategy where information is grouped into larger, meaningful units, making it easier to recall. Classical Conditioning Learning where a neutral stimulus becomes associated with a meaningful one, eliciting a conditioned response (Ivan Pavlov). Client-Centred Therapy A humanistic approach by Carl Rogers emphasising unconditional positive regard, empathy and client autonomy. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) A widely used therapy focused on altering negative thought patterns and behaviours to treat psychological disorders. Cognitive Dissonance The discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs or behaviours, motivating people to reduce the inconsistency (Leon Festinger). Cognitive Distortions Irrational thought patterns (all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising) that lead to emotional distress (CBT framework). Cognitive Psychology The study of mental processes like memory, problem-solving, perception and decision-making. Conformity The tendency to change behaviour or beliefs to align with group norms, often under social pressure. D Defense Mechanisms Unconscious strategies that protect the ego — e.g. repression, displacement, projection (Sigmund Freud). Degrees of Freedom (df) The number of values free to vary when calculating a statistic. Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) An offshoot of CBT by Marsha Linehan, aimed at borderline personality disorder via mindfulness and emotion regulation. Displacement A defense mechanism where negative emotions are redirected from the original source to a less threatening target. Down's Syndrome (Trisomy 21) A congenital condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, leading to developmental and intellectual delays. E EEG (Electroencephalogram) A method for recording electrical activity in the brain using electrodes on the scalp. Extinction In classical conditioning, the weakening and disappearance of a conditioned response when the CS is no longer paired with the US. Eclectic Therapy An approach combining elements from different therapeutic techniques to best meet the client's needs. Empiricism The belief that knowledge comes primarily from sensory experience and observable evidence. Epigenetics The study of how environmental factors influence gene expression without changing the DNA sequence. Ethnocentrism Viewing one's own culture as superior and judging other cultures by its standards. F Factor Analysis A statistical method to identify underlying relationships between variables, often used in psychometrics. Flashbulb Memory Vivid, detailed memories of significant, emotionally charged events, often resistant to decay. G Gate Control Theory A theory of pain perception: a neural "gate" in the spinal cord modulates pain by controlling signal flow to the brain. Gene A unit of heredity composed of DNA carrying genetic information that influences traits and characteristics. Genotype The genetic makeup of an individual, including dominant and recessive genes. Groupthink A phenomenon where group members prioritise consensus over critical thinking, leading to poor decisions. H Halo Effect A general impression of a person (positive or negative) influencing judgements about their other, unrelated traits. Hallucinations Sensory perceptions occurring without external stimuli, common in psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. Hippocampus A brain structure crucial for forming new memories, particularly long-term memory processing. House-Tree-Person Test A projective test in which individuals draw a house, tree and person to assess personality traits. Hypothesis A testable prediction made by researchers, usually formed before an experiment. I Illusion A misperception or distortion of a sensory experience where perception does not match reality. Implicit Memory Memory that influences behaviour unconsciously, without intentional retrieval (e.g. procedural memory, riding a bike). Insight Learning A problem-solving process where understanding arises suddenly (Wolfgang Köhler's chimpanzee experiments). Insight-Oriented Therapy Psychotherapy aimed at helping clients gain awareness of unconscious thoughts, emotions and behaviours. Internal Locus of Control The belief that one controls one's own life events and outcomes, vs. external factors like luck or fate. J Just Noticeable Difference (JND) The smallest change in sensory stimulation a person can detect 50% of the time. Just-World Hypothesis A bias where people believe the world is fair, assuming individuals get what they deserve even in misfortune. K Klüver-Bucy Syndrome A disorder from temporal-lobe and amygdala damage, causing hypersexuality, visual agnosia and reduced fear responses. Klinefelter Syndrome (XXY) A genetic condition in males caused by an extra X chromosome, leading to developmental delays and specific physical traits. L Lateralisation of Brain Function Certain mental processes are specialised to the left or right hemisphere (e.g. language is typically left-hemisphere). Learned Helplessness Feeling unable to control or change a situation after repeated failure, leading to passivity and depression. Limbic System Brain structures regulating emotion, memory and motivation — includes hippocampus, amygdala and hypothalamus. Linguistic Relativity Hypothesis (Sapir-Whorf) Language influences thought and perception; speakers of different languages may experience the world differently. M Memory Systems The categorisation of memory into short-term, long-term and working memory, with subtypes like episodic and semantic. Null Hypothesis A statistical hypothesis stating there is no effect or difference; the baseline assumption in hypothesis testing. N Narcolepsy A sleep disorder of excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep attacks, often with muscle weakness (cataplexy). Neurotransmitters Chemical messengers across synapses — e.g. serotonin (mood), dopamine (reward), GABA (inhibitory). Neuroplasticity The brain's ability to reorganise and form new neural connections, especially after injury or during learning. Nomothetic Approach Seeking general laws that apply to all individuals (vs. the idiographic focus on the unique individual). Nurture Assumption The hypothesis that development is largely shaped by environment (nurture) rather than genetics (nature). O Object Permanence Understanding that objects continue to exist when unseen — Jean Piaget's sensorimotor stage. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) Intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours (compulsions) performed to reduce anxiety. Operant Conditioning B. F. Skinner's theory of how behaviour is shaped by consequences, through reinforcement and punishment. Overgeneralisation A cognitive distortion: applying a single event or experience to an entire range of situations. P Phenotype The observable traits of an individual, influenced by both genetics and environment. Premack Principle In operant conditioning, high-probability behaviours reinforce low-probability ones ("games after homework"). Priming Exposure to one stimulus influences the response to a later stimulus, often outside conscious awareness. Projection A defense mechanism: attributing one's own unacceptable thoughts or motives to another person. Prosocial Behaviour Voluntary behaviour aimed at helping others, motivated by empathy or social norms. Psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud's approach exploring unconscious thoughts and desires via free association and dream analysis. R Reinforcement In operant conditioning, increasing a behaviour by adding a positive outcome (positive) or removing an aversive stimulus (negative). Reciprocal Determinism Albert Bandura's view that behaviour, environment and cognition all influence one another bidirectionally. Regression to the Mean Extreme data points tend to move closer to the average on subsequent measurements. Regression Analysis A statistical method to predict the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables. Reliability The consistency of a test or measure in producing stable, repeatable results (e.g. test-retest reliability). Retrograde Amnesia The inability to recall memories formed before the onset of amnesia. S Scaffolding In Lev Vygotsky's theory, support from more knowledgeable others that helps a learner reach a higher level of understanding. Schemas Mental frameworks used to organise and interpret information, shaping perception and memory. Schizophrenia A severe disorder with hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech and impaired functioning. Short-Term Memory (STM) Temporary storage lasting ~15–30 seconds, with limited capacity. Social Learning Theory Albert Bandura's view that learning occurs through observation, imitation and modelling, with reinforcement and punishment. Somatoform Disorders Disorders with physical symptoms lacking a medical cause — e.g. conversion disorder, hypochondriasis. Standardisation Establishing uniform procedures for administering and scoring tests to ensure consistency across situations. Stereotypes Oversimplified, generalised beliefs about groups of people, often based on race, gender or ethnicity. Stroop Test Naming the ink colour of a word, hardest when the word names a different colour (e.g. "red" printed in blue). T Temperament Biologically based tendencies to feel or act a certain way, present from early childhood; the foundation of personality. Transference In psychotherapy, clients projecting feelings and attitudes from past relationships onto the therapist. Transactional Analysis Eric Berne's theory examining interactions (transactions) based on Parent, Adult and Child ego states. T-Test A test comparing the means of two groups to see whether the difference is statistically significant. Turner Syndrome (XO) A condition in females from partial or complete absence of one X chromosome, with delayed development and infertility. U Unconditional Positive Regard Carl Rogers' term for a therapist's non-judgemental acceptance and support of a client, regardless of what they say or do. Unconscious Motivation Desires, urges or thoughts that influence behaviour but exist outside conscious awareness (Freudian). Universal Emotions Per Paul Ekman, basic emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger and fear are recognised and expressed similarly across all human cultures. V Validity The degree to which a test measures what it is supposed to. Types: construct, criterion and content validity. Variable Ratio Schedule A reinforcement schedule rewarding behaviour after an unpredictable number of responses, giving high response rates (e.g. gambling). Visual Agnosia A disorder where a person can see but cannot recognise or interpret visual information, due to brain damage. W Working Memory Short-term memory that actively holds and manipulates information; crucial for reasoning, learning and comprehension. Wernicke's Area A region involved in language comprehension; damage causes Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but nonsensical speech). X Xenophobia An irrational fear or dislike of people from other countries or cultures. X-Linked Disorders Genetic disorders from mutations on the X chromosome, often affecting males more severely (e.g. colour blindness, haemophilia). Y Yerkes-Dodson Law Performance improves with arousal up to a point, after which further arousal hinders performance. Youth Bulge A demographic phenomenon where a large share of a population is young, often linked to social instability. Z Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) Lev Vygotsky's gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can achieve with guidance or collaboration. Zeigarnik Effect The tendency to remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed ones — tension aids memory. 4. 24 important therapies Founder · key concepts · techniques for each. NIMHANS/MET love "Therapy X was founded by?" and "Technique Y belongs to which therapy?" — drill both directions. Therapy Founder Key concepts Techniques 1. Animal-Assisted Therapy (AAT) No single founder (various psychologists & animal therapists) Uses animals (dogs, horses) to improve emotional well-being, enhance cognition and reduce stress; used for PTSD, anxiety, depression. Structured interaction with animals to build rapport and reduce anxiety. 2. Attachment Therapy Based on John Bowlby's attachment theory Building and repairing attachment bonds, often in children with trauma, neglect or inconsistent caregiving. Activities to build trust and strengthen the caregiver–child relationship. 3. Bibliotherapy No specific individual (used as an adjunct) Reading material that relates to the person's struggle to support healing and growth. Reading and discussing books, poetry or essays that give insight. 4. Cognitive Analytic Therapy (CAT) Anthony Ryle (1980s) Integrates cognitive and analytic approaches to understand problematic patterns of thinking, feeling and relating. Mapping behaviour patterns, identifying maladaptive thinking, reformulation letters to build insight. 5. Coherence Therapy Bruce Ecker & Laurel Hulley Symptoms arise from learned emotional responses; therapy uncovers and resolves them. Emotional uncovering, experiential work, creating moments of change. 6. Dance Movement Therapy (DMT) Marian Chace and other dance therapists (1940s) Movement as a form of expression to enhance emotional, cognitive and physical well-being. Movement exploration, body mirroring, expressive dance. 7. Developmental Needs Meeting Strategy (DNMS) Shirley Jean Schmidt Unmet childhood developmental needs drive adult emotional and psychological issues. Healing attachment wounds by meeting unmet developmental needs. 8. Dramatherapy Influenced by Jacob L. Moreno & Peter Slade Drama and theatre techniques to facilitate emotional expression, self-awareness and conflict resolution. Role-play, improvisation, storytelling, guided imagery. 9. EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation & Reprocessing) Francine Shapiro (1987) Treats trauma by processing distressing memories and reducing their impact; client recalls trauma while focusing on bilateral stimuli. Eye movements, bilateral tapping, cognitive restructuring of traumatic memories. 10. Functional Analytic Psychotherapy (FAP) Robert Kohlenberg & Mavis Tsai Uses the therapeutic relationship to change problematic interpersonal behaviours as they emerge in session. Reinforcing adaptive behaviour in the relationship, in-vivo exposure, emotional validation. 11. Hypnotherapy Modern form attributed to Milton Erickson (roots in Franz Mesmer, 18th c.) Hypnosis to create focused attention, heightened suggestibility and deep relaxation; used for phobias, addictions, chronic pain. Trance induction, suggestion therapy. 12. Integral Therapy Ken Wilber Integral theory integrating multiple perspectives — internal/external, individual/collective — into a holistic whole. Working across four quadrants to create a holistic approach to therapy and development. 13. Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP) Habib Davanloo Active therapy to overcome resistance and access repressed emotions; tackles deep-rooted problems in a short time. Emotionally focused interventions, unlocking the unconscious, working through defenses. 14. Logotherapy Viktor Frankl Existential therapy centred on finding meaning in life, even amid suffering; humans are driven by a "will to meaning." Socratic dialogue, dereflection, paradoxical intention. 15. Metacognitive Therapy Adrian Wells Modifies dysfunctional metacognitive beliefs that maintain anxiety and depression. Detachment from thought processes, attention training, challenging metacognitive beliefs. 16. Multimodal Therapy (MMT) Arnold Lazarus Evaluates seven dimensions of personality — the BASIC ID: Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal relationships, Drugs/biology. Tailored interventions for each modality based on the person's specific needs. 17. Narrative Therapy Michael White & David Epston Sees people as separate from their problems; clients "re-author" their lives with empowering narratives. Externalising problems, identifying unique outcomes, re-authoring personal stories. 18. Play Therapy Virginia Axline & Carl Rogers (influences) Play as a medium for children to express emotions, resolve conflicts and process difficult experiences. Sand tray, role-playing, art-based activities, storytelling. 19. Positive Psychotherapy Nossrat Peseschkian Emphasises inherent capacities for growth and healing; focuses on strengths rather than pathology. Balancing techniques, active goal-setting, identifying personal strengths. 20. Rational Living Therapy (RLT) Aldo R. Pucci A cognitive-behavioural approach building on REBT to replace irrational beliefs with more logical ones. Cognitive restructuring, disputing irrational beliefs, a rational-living plan. 21. Reality Therapy William Glasser Based on choice theory: clients take control of their lives by making better choices; emphasises personal responsibility and the present. Action planning, focusing on current behaviour, exploring new choices. 22. Sexual Identity Therapy No single founder Addresses sexual orientation, identity and gender identity in a supportive, affirming way. Exploratory discussion, psychoeducation, supportive counselling. 23. Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT) Steve de Shazer & Insoo Kim Berg Short-term, goal-oriented; finds solutions in the present rather than dwelling on past problems. Miracle question, scaling questions, identifying exceptions. 24. Structural Family Therapy Salvador Minuchin Looks at family hierarchies, boundaries and subsystems and how they shape individual behaviour and mental health. Joining, restructuring family interactions, boundary setting. 5. 25 landmark experiments The classic studies, with who ran them, when, where and what they showed. The entrances ask these as "Experiment X was conducted by?" and "Which study demonstrated effect Y?". Experiment Conducted by Year Where What it showed 1. Hawthorne Studies Elton Mayo 1924–1932 Western Electric, Hawthorne Works, Chicago Productivity rose when workers knew they were observed — the Hawthorne effect . 2. Little Albert Experiment John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner 1920 Johns Hopkins University A baby was classically conditioned to fear a white rat; fear generalised to similar stimuli. Now a landmark in research ethics. 3. Halo Effect Experiment Edward Thorndike 1920 Case Western University A positive impression of one quality (e.g. attractiveness) led people to overestimate other qualities. 4. The Monster Study Wendell Johnson 1939 University of Iowa Attempted to induce stuttering in orphan children through negative speech therapy — one of the most unethical studies in psychology. 5. Robbers Cave Experiment Muzafer Sherif 1954 Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma Intergroup conflict arises between groups and is resolved through superordinate goals . 6. Asch Conformity Experiment Solomon Asch 1951 Swarthmore College Participants conformed to clearly wrong answers given by a group — the power of social pressure. 7. Cognitive Dissonance Experiment Leon Festinger 1957 Stanford University Discomfort when behaviour conflicts with belief; participants justified their behaviour by changing their beliefs. 8. Harlow's Monkey Experiment Harry Harlow 1961 University of Wisconsin-Madison Infant monkeys preferred a cloth "mother" (comfort) over a wire one (food) — contact comfort drives attachment. 9. Fantz Looking Chamber Experiment Robert Fantz 1961 Case Western Reserve University Infants preferred looking at human faces over patterns — innate visual preferences. 10. Bobo Doll Experiment Albert Bandura 1961 Stanford University Children who watched an adult act aggressively toward a doll imitated it — observational / social learning. 11. Milgram Obedience Experiment Stanley Milgram 1961 Yale University Participants administered what they believed were painful shocks when told to by an authority — obedience over morality. 12. Schachter & Singer Experiment on Emotion Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer 1962 Columbia University Supported the two-factor theory of emotion (arousal + cognitive labelling); participants misattributed arousal based on others' behaviour. 13. Ainsworth Strange Situation Mary Ainsworth 1969 Johns Hopkins University Assessed infant attachment via reaction to a caregiver's absence/return; three styles — secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant. 14. Split-Brain Experiment Roger Sperry 1968 California Institute of Technology Studied severed-corpus-callosum patients; showed the two hemispheres have specialised functions (Nobel Prize). 15. The Good Samaritan Experiment John Darley & C. Daniel Batson 1973 Princeton University Situational factors (being in a hurry) drove helping more than values — even among theology students. 16. Stanford Prison Experiment Philip Zimbardo 1971 Stanford University A simulated prison showed the extreme psychological effects of perceived power; guards turned abusive, prisoners traumatised — ended early. 17. Marshmallow Test Walter Mischel 1972 Stanford University A longitudinal study of delayed gratification in children; those who waited for a larger reward had better later outcomes. 18. Bystander Effect (Good Samaritan study) John Darley & Bibb Latané 1968 Columbia University People are less likely to help in distress when others are present — responsibility is diffused. 19. Ross's False Consensus Effect Study Lee Ross 1977 Stanford University People overestimate how much others share their beliefs, attitudes and behaviours — the false consensus effect . 20. Selective Attention (The Invisible Gorilla) Daniel Simons & Christopher Chabris 1999 Harvard University Counting basketball passes, many viewers missed a gorilla walking through — inattentional blindness . 21. Car Crash Experiment Elizabeth Loftus & John Palmer 1974 University of California, Irvine The misinformation effect : question wording ("smashed" vs "hit") altered recalled speed of the cars. 22. A Class Divided Jane Elliott 1968 Riceville, Iowa After MLK's assassination, Elliott split her class by eye colour, treating one group as superior then reversing it — showing prejudice is arbitrary and damaging. 23. Learned Helplessness Experiment Martin Seligman 1967 University of Pennsylvania Dogs given unavoidable shocks stopped trying to escape even when they could — learned helplessness , a model for depression. 24. Surrogate Mother Experiment (Harlow's monkeys) Harry Harlow 1961 University of Wisconsin-Madison Monkeys offered a wire mother (food) and a cloth mother (comfort) chose comfort — contact comfort over feeding. 25. Visual Cliff Experiment Eleanor Gibson & Richard Walk 1960 Cornell University Infants placed on a glass surface over an apparent drop avoided the "cliff" — depth perception develops early.

title: High-Yield Gap Closer (PYQ-targeted)
text: High-Yield Gap Closer (PYQ-targeted) Thirty-four clusters the PYQ audit flagged as missing or too thin across the books you actually revise from, now on a full deep re-pass : every cluster rebuilt against the textbook with the mechanism, the full contrast tables, worked PYQ-style stems, and the exact trap the examiner builds on. Part A = the 16-cluster PYQ-coverage audit (every university's paper re-read). Part B = the NIMHANS PhD paper of 30 May 2026, every recalled topic (1 to 18, 28 to 31, incl. the Heschl set) folded into its own cluster. Part C = two more clusters from the scanned university papers. Each section still leads with the single most testable fact so it still crams as fast as it reads deep. Deep re-pass: 2026-05-30. How to use it. Two speeds in one page. Fast: read the lead line and the red trap box in each section, those are the exact things that get tested, and use the tables for the "which one is it?" items. Deep: the prose and worked stems under each are there to actually learn the topic cold. If you only have 30 minutes, do clusters 1 (Indian tests), 2 (which test), 4 (correlation types) and 5 (MH law), they are the densest mark-savers. Jump to: 1. Indian intelligence/developmental tests 2. Which statistical test? 3. Nonparametric tests 4. Special correlation types 5. Indian mental-health law 6. Neuropsych batteries 7. Amnesia & memory disorders 8. IRT / Rasch 9. Item analysis formulae 10. Sampling methods 11. Defense mechanisms (levels) 12. Emotion theories 13. ICD-11 changes 14. Projective scoring depth 15. Reinforcement schedules 16. Reliability & validity types Part B (NIMHANS paper, 30 May 2026): B1. Family therapy B2. Suicide (Durkheim) B3. CGI/PANSS B4. AUDIT B5. RAVLT B6. Levodopa B7. GCS B8. NMHS % B9. Functional hallucination B10. WASI B11. Attunement/Floortime B12. R² B13. Gazette tests B14. Prevention levels B15. Heschl's gyrus B16. Schizoid/schizotypal 1. Indian intelligence & developmental tests Lead fact: Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (C. M. Bhatia, 1955) is the classic Indian non-verbal/performance IQ test, standardised on Indian children, useful for the illiterate and the hearing-impaired. Its 5 subtests are the single most-asked Indian-test item: Koh's Block Design, Alexander's Pass-Along, Pattern Drawing, Immediate Memory (for digits), Picture Construction. The decisive distinction an examiner tests here is what the score is called and what it measures . There are three different quotients in this cluster and they are not interchangeable: a true intelligence test yields an IQ (via Mental Age, MA), an adaptive/social measure yields a Social Quotient (SQ) , and a developmental screen yields a Developmental Quotient (DQ) . Always read the stem for the output word ("IQ" vs "social age" vs "developmental quotient") and the data source (does the child perform a task, or does a parent/informant report?). That single read usually disambiguates the whole question. The three quotients (do not mix them up) Quotient Formula What it taps Typical test IQ (Intelligence Quotient) IQ = MA / CA × 100 (ratio IQ); modern tests use deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15) Cognitive ability (reasoning, problem-solving) Binet-Kamat, MISIC, Bhatia, Draw-A-Man, Kohs SQ (Social Quotient) SQ = SA / CA × 100 Adaptive / social maturity (self-help, self-direction), NOT cognition VSMS DQ (Developmental Quotient) DQ = developmental age / CA × 100 Milestone attainment across motor, adaptive, language, personal-social Gesell, DST (Bharat Raj) The Indian tests in detail Test Author / Indian adapter & year Yields Age range Subtests / key facts Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests C. M. Bhatia, 1955 (standardised in U.P.) Non-verbal (performance) IQ ~11 to 16 yrs (often used as an adult performance screen too) 5 subtests: Koh's Block Design, Alexander's Pass-Along, Pattern Drawing, Immediate Memory (digits, forward and reverse), Picture Construction. For illiterate / language-barrier / deaf clients. India's most-used performance test. MISIC: Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children Arthur J. Malin, 1969 (Nagpur). Indian adaptation of WISC Verbal IQ + Performance IQ → Full-Scale IQ (deviation IQ) 6 to 15 yrs Indianised WISC. 11 subtests (6 verbal, 5 performance). Verbal: Information, Comprehension, Arithmetic, Similarities, Vocabulary, Digit Span. Performance: Picture Completion, Block Design, Object Assembly, Coding, Mazes. The standard Indian child IQ test alongside Binet-Kamat. Binet-Kamat Test (BKT) C. H. Kamat, 1934 (revised 1967). Indian adaptation of Stanford-Binet Mental Age & IQ (ratio IQ, age-scale) ~3 to 22 yrs Verbal-loaded, age-scale format with items grouped by age level. Adapted for Kannada/Marathi-speaking children. Gives a Mental Age like the original Binet. Heavily language-dependent. Seguin Form Board (SFB) Édouard Séguin (original, 19th c.); Indian norms by Bhatia and others Visuo-motor speed; a quick non-verbal performance/IQ screen ~3 to 10 yrs (esp. preschool / suspected intellectual disability) Child fits 10 wooden shapes into matching slots; best (shortest) time of 3 trials = score. Quick non-verbal screen; also used to assess eye-hand coordination and to give a rough MA estimate. VSMS: Vineland Social Maturity Scale Edgar Doll (original, 1935); Indian adaptation by A. J. Malin (1965, Nagpur) Social Age (SA) & Social Quotient (SQ) , adaptive behaviour, NOT IQ Birth to 15 yrs (Indian adaptation) Informant-based (parent/caregiver interview). 8 domains: self-help general, self-help eating, self-help dressing, self-direction, occupation, communication, locomotion, socialisation. Core tool in intellectual disability assessment. Draw-A-Man Test (DAMT) Florence Goodenough (1926); revised Goodenough-Harris (1963); Indian adaptation by Pramila Pathak Non-verbal MA → IQ ~3 to 15 yrs Score = number of scorable details in a human-figure drawing → MA → IQ. Culture-fair, quick, non-verbal. Goodenough-Harris adds a Draw-A-Woman and self-drawing. Koh's Block Design S. C. Kohs (1920); used within Bhatia's Battery in India Non-verbal abstract reasoning, spatial/perceptual organisation ~5 yrs to adult Reproduce printed designs with coloured cubes. A subtest of Bhatia's Battery and the conceptual ancestor of WAIS/WISC Block Design. DST: Developmental Screening Test Bharat Raj (1977, NIMHANS / Mysore) Developmental Quotient (DQ) and developmental age Birth to 15 yrs A quick screening tool to estimate developmental level when a full IQ test is impractical (very young or severely disabled). Informant + observation based. Indian developmental screen of choice. Gesell Developmental Schedule Arnold Gesell (Yale) Developmental age → DQ ~4 weeks to 6 yrs (infancy/early childhood) Four areas: motor, adaptive, language, personal-social. Classic infant developmental schedule; used where standard IQ tests cannot be applied. NIMHANS Index / SLD Index NIMHANS, Bangalore Profile of specific learning disability (reading/writing/spelling/arithmetic), not an IQ School-age children Used after an IQ test has ruled out intellectual disability. Identifies dyslexia/dysgraphia/dyscalculia patterns. Notified for SLD certification. IQ test vs adaptive measure vs developmental screen Category Tests Data source Output True intelligence (IQ) tests Binet-Kamat, MISIC, Bhatia, Draw-A-Man, Kohs, Seguin (rough) Child performs tasks MA → IQ Adaptive-behaviour measure VSMS Informant interview (parent) SA → SQ Developmental screens Gesell, DST (Bharat Raj) Observation + informant Developmental age → DQ Worked PYQ-style examples Stem: "A clinician assesses a 7-year-old by interviewing the mother about the child's self-help, communication and socialisation, then computes a quotient. Which test?" → VSMS (informant interview + social domains → SQ). It is NOT an IQ test even though it gives a "quotient." Stem: "A deaf, non-literate 13-year-old needs an intelligence estimate. Best test?" → Bhatia's Battery (performance / non-verbal, designed for illiterate and hearing-impaired). Binet-Kamat and MISIC's verbal half would be invalid. Stem: "Indian adaptation of the WISC for children is the ___." → MISIC (Malin). "Indian adaptation of the Stanford-Binet is the ___." → Binet-Kamat (Kamat). Stem: "Child fits ten wooden shapes into a board; the best of three trials is timed." → Seguin Form Board. Stem: "Quick estimate of a developmental quotient in an infant who cannot do a standard IQ test." → Gesell schedule (or DST / Bharat Raj in the Indian context). Trap / compare: VSMS measures SOCIAL maturity (Social Quotient), NOT IQ. If a stem says "adaptive behaviour / social age / informant interview," it is VSMS, not an intelligence test. MISIC = adapted WISC (Malin); Binet-Kamat = adapted Stanford-Binet (Kamat). Don't swap them. Bhatia's Battery and Draw-A-Man are performance / non-verbal (good for illiterate/deaf); Binet-Kamat and MISIC's verbal half need language. Trap (quotients): IQ comes from MA (cognition), SQ from SA (adaptive, VSMS), DQ from developmental age (Gesell / DST). A "quotient" alone does not mean intelligence. DST = Developmental Screening Test (Bharat Raj) , NOT a learning-disability test; the NIMHANS Index is the SLD tool. Trap (Seguin vs Form Board "of intelligence"): Seguin is primarily a visuo-motor/form-board speed task scored by best-of-3 time; treat it as a quick non-verbal screen, not a full IQ battery like Bhatia's. Hooks: " Mal in did the two Indian standards ( MISIC = WISC, and the Indian VSMS )." " Kamat = Binet" (both K/B verbal age-scales). Seguin = form board , best-of-3-trials. Goodenough = Draw-A-Man . D ST + G esell = D evelopmental quotient (the "D" tests). V SMS = V ineland = social/adaptive (the odd one out: a quotient that isn't IQ). 2. Which statistical test do I choose? Lead logic: three questions decide it, in order: (1) What is the level of measurement of the outcome (DV)? nominal/categorical → chi-square family; ordinal → nonparametric; interval/ratio & normal → parametric. (2) How many groups/conditions? 1, 2, or 3+. (3) Are the groups independent or paired (repeated/matched)? Those three answers point to exactly one test. A fourth question, "relationship vs difference?" , splits off the correlation/regression family from the group-comparison family. Every "which test" PYQ is really asking you to run a small decision tree. The examiner buries the answer in the wording: the scale of the outcome (a score, a rank, or a category), the number of groups or conditions, and whether the same people are measured more than once (paired/repeated/matched) or different people make up each group (independent). Get those three facts out of the stem and the test is forced. Step 1: level of measurement of the outcome Nominal/categorical (counts in categories: passed/failed, M/F, blood group): chi-square family, McNemar, Cochran's Q, Fisher's exact, logistic regression. Ordinal (ranks, Likert single items, 0 to 10 pain ratings treated as order only): nonparametric tests on ranks (Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman, Spearman, Kendall). Interval/ratio AND assumptions met (a genuine numeric score that is roughly normal with equal variances): the parametric tests (t-tests, ANOVA, Pearson, regression). If the score is interval but assumptions fail, you drop down to the matching nonparametric test (see cluster 3). Master decision table Situation Parametric (interval, normal) Nonparametric (ordinal / non-normal) Categorical (nominal) 1 group vs a known/population value One-sample t-test (σ unknown); z-test (σ known) Wilcoxon signed-rank (vs a median) Chi-square goodness-of-fit; binomial test 2 independent groups Independent (unpaired) t-test Mann-Whitney U (= Wilcoxon rank-sum) Chi-square test of independence; Fisher's exact (small n / expected <5) 2 paired / repeated / matched Paired (related) t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank McNemar's test (2×2 before-after) 3+ independent groups One-way ANOVA (then post-hoc) Kruskal-Wallis H Chi-square (r × c table) 3+ paired / repeated measures Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test Cochran's Q (dichotomous, 3+ conditions) 2+ IVs / factors at once Factorial (two-way) ANOVA; tests main effects + interaction (no simple classic equivalent) Log-linear analysis Control for a covariate ANCOVA (rank ANCOVA, rare in PYQs) Mantel-Haenszel (stratified) Relationship between 2 continuous variables Pearson r; simple linear regression Spearman's rho; Kendall's tau (see correlation types, cluster 4) Predict outcome from several predictors Multiple regression (continuous DV) (ordinal/robust regression) Logistic regression (binary DV) Assumptions of the parametric tests (why you would drop to nonparametric) The parametric tests buy their extra power by assuming things about the data. If a stem says the assumption is violated, the answer flips to the nonparametric counterpart. The three that examiners test are: Assumption What it means Checked by / violated when Which tests it applies to Normality The DV (or the residuals / the sampling distribution of the mean) is normally distributed in each group. Shapiro-Wilk, Kolmogorov-Smirnov; skew/kurtosis; Q-Q plot. Violated by skew, small n, outliers. t-tests, ANOVA, Pearson r, regression Homogeneity of variance (homoscedasticity) Groups have roughly equal variances; in regression, residual scatter is constant across X. Levene's test (most common), Bartlett's, Hartley's F-max. If significant, variances differ. Independent t-test, ANOVA (use Welch's correction if violated) Independence of observations Each data point is unrelated to the others (no clustering, one score per person per cell). By design, not a test; violated by repeated measures wrongly treated as independent, or nested data. All parametric tests; the hardest to fix (needs RM-ANOVA / mixed models) Additional assumptions the examiner may name: interval/ratio level of the DV, linearity (Pearson, regression), and for ANOVA the same normality + equal-variance logic extended to all groups. The Central Limit Theorem rescues normality when n is large (the sampling distribution of the mean becomes normal even if the raw data are not), which is why parametric tests are often defended on big samples. The F = t² relationship Key identity: a one-way ANOVA on exactly 2 groups gives the same p-value as an independent t-test, because F = t² (with 1 df in the numerator). ANOVA is the generalisation of the t-test to 3+ groups; the t-test is the special 2-group case. So "compare two groups, normal data" can be answered by either, and an F of, say, 9.0 from a 2-group design corresponds to t = 3.0. Why ANOVA, not many t-tests (and post-hoc tests) With 3+ groups you do not run multiple t-tests, because each test carries a 5% Type I error and running many inflates the familywise error rate (the chance of at least one false positive climbs well above 5%). ANOVA's omnibus F asks one question: "is there any difference among the means?" If F is significant, F only tells you that a difference exists, not which pairs differ. To locate the pairs you run a post-hoc test , which controls the familywise error: Post-hoc test Character Pick when Tukey's HSD All pairwise comparisons, equal n, good balance of power and error control Default for "compare every pair after a significant ANOVA," equal group sizes Bonferroni Divides alpha by the number of comparisons (alpha/k); simple, very conservative Few planned comparisons; you want a strict, easily-justified correction Scheffe The most conservative; allows any/complex contrasts, not just pairs Unequal n, exploratory or complex contrasts; least powerful but most flexible Other names that may appear: Newman-Keuls and Duncan (more liberal, more power, weaker error control), Games-Howell (when variances are unequal), Dunnett (comparing several treatments to a single control only). Planned (a priori) contrasts are decided before data collection and need no post-hoc penalty; post-hoc (unplanned) comparisons do. One-tailed vs two-tailed A two-tailed test asks "is there a difference in either direction?" (H1: μ1 ≠ μ2) and splits alpha across both tails (2.5% each at α = .05). A one-tailed (directional) test asks "is it specifically greater (or less )?" (H1: μ1 > μ2) and puts the whole 5% in one tail, making it easier to reach significance in that predicted direction but unable to detect an effect the other way. Use one-tailed only when a directional hypothesis is justified before seeing the data; default and safest answer in exams is two-tailed . Worked examples (the way PYQs phrase them) "Compare mean anxiety scores of a therapy group vs a control group (scores normal)." → 2 independent groups, interval, normal → independent t-test . "Same patients' depression scores before and after treatment, scores normal." → 2 paired, interval → paired t-test (Wilcoxon signed-rank if ordinal/skewed). "Mean reaction time across four drug-dose groups." → 3+ independent, interval → one-way ANOVA ; if significant, Tukey to find which doses differ. "Median pain rating (ordinal 0 to 10) across three hospitals." → 3+ independent, ordinal → Kruskal-Wallis . "Same 20 subjects rate three drugs for drowsiness (ranked)." → 3+ paired, ordinal → Friedman . "Association between gender (M/F) and passed/failed ." → both nominal → chi-square test of independence (Fisher's exact if cells are tiny). " Before vs after an ad campaign, each person says yes/no to buying." → 2 paired, nominal → McNemar's test . "Rank-correlate class rank with exam rank ." → two ordinal → Spearman's rho . "Effect of drug (yes/no) AND therapy (yes/no) on a normal score, including their interaction ." → 2 factors → two-way (factorial) ANOVA . "Compare two groups but controlling for baseline IQ ." → covariate present → ANCOVA . Trap: "Repeated / matched / before-after / same subjects" → paired test (paired t, Wilcoxon signed-rank, RM-ANOVA, Friedman, McNemar). "Two/more different groups of people" → independent (independent t, Mann-Whitney, one-way ANOVA, chi-square). The examiner hides this in one word: same vs different participants. Trap: ANOVA on 2 groups = t-test, because F = t². Don't pick "ANOVA" over "t-test" just because the wording sounds fancier; with exactly two groups they are the same test and either answer's logic must match the option list. Trap: a significant omnibus ANOVA does NOT tell you which groups differ; that needs a post-hoc test. And running many t-tests instead of one ANOVA inflates the familywise Type I error, which is exactly why post-hoc corrections (Tukey/Bonferroni/Scheffe) exist. Trap: chi-square needs frequencies/counts , not means or percentages fed in directly. If a stem gives you category counts, it is the chi-square family; if it gives you a mean score, it is t/ANOVA territory. Hook: " Scale, number, pairing. " Ask the outcome's scale (category / rank / score), the number of groups (1, 2, 3+), and same-vs-different people. Then: 2 groups normal = t, 3+ = ANOVA (F = t²), ordinal = its rank twin, categories = chi-square. 3. Nonparametric tests (selection & when to use) Lead fact: use a nonparametric test when (a) data are ordinal/ranked or nominal , or (b) the DV is interval but assumptions of the parametric test fail (non-normal distribution, small n, heterogeneity of variance, or many outliers). They work on ranks, signs, or frequencies, not means , so they make no assumption about the shape of the population distribution ("distribution-free"), and they are robust to outliers, at the cost of some statistical power. Why and when to go nonparametric Parametric tests (t, ANOVA, Pearson) assume an interval/ratio DV that is normally distributed with roughly equal variances and independent observations. A nonparametric test is the correct choice whenever those props are knocked away: Ordinal data: ranks or single Likert items carry order but not equal intervals, so a "mean" is not strictly meaningful; rank-based tests are appropriate. Nominal data: counts in categories have no order at all → chi-square family. Non-normal distribution: strong skew or a known non-normal shape that the Central Limit Theorem cannot rescue. Small samples: with small n you cannot verify normality and the CLT does not help, so a distribution-free test is safer. Outliers / heavy tails: ranks compress extreme values, so a few outliers cannot drag the result the way they drag a mean. Heterogeneity of variance: when groups have very unequal spread. How they work and the power cost Most nonparametric tests replace the raw scores with ranks (or with the bare sign of a difference) and then ask whether the ranks are distributed differently than chance would predict. Because they throw away information about the exact distances between scores, they are typically less powerful than their parametric twin when the parametric assumptions actually hold (the Mann-Whitney has roughly 95% of the t-test's power, i.e. a small efficiency loss). But when assumptions are violated, the nonparametric test can be more powerful and is the valid one. Trade-off summary: less power, fewer assumptions, more robustness.
