And " sign test = direction only, signed-rank = direction + size." 4. Special correlation types Lead fact: the coefficient is chosen by the types of the two variables . Two continuous & linear → Pearson r. Two ranks → Spearman/Kendall. One continuous + one true dichotomy → point-biserial . Two true dichotomies → phi (φ). One continuous + one artificial dichotomy → biserial ; two artificial dichotomies → tetrachoric . That true-vs-artificial line is the single best-answer trap. The underlying logic: true vs artificial dichotomy A correlation coefficient is just an index of how two variables co-vary; the "special" coefficients are all ways of handling variables that are not both clean continuous measures. The decisive question for the dichotomous cases is whether the two-category split is true (genuine) or artificial : True / genuine dichotomy: the variable is naturally two-valued, with no continuum underneath. Examples: alive/dead, male/female, pregnant/not, smoker/non-smoker by definition. Artificial dichotomy: there is a real underlying continuum that has been chopped into two categories. Examples: pass/fail (from a continuous score split at a cut-off), "high vs low anxiety," "tall vs short." The biserial and tetrachoric coefficients exist to estimate what the correlation would have been had we not thrown away the continuum , so they tend to be a bit larger than the matched point-biserial/phi. Variable-type → coefficient matrix Coefficient Variable types Use when / notes Pearson r (product-moment) Two continuous (interval/ratio), linear The default; both variables roughly normal and linearly related. Sign = direction, magnitude (0 to 1) = strength. Spearman's rho (ρ) Two ordinal (ranked), or non-normal continuous Monotonic relationship; it is literally Pearson r computed on the ranks. Kendall's tau (τ) Two ordinal (ranked) Based on concordant vs discordant pairs ; preferred for small samples or many tied ranks. Usually numerically smaller than rho. Point-biserial (r pb ) One continuous + one TRUE dichotomy e.g. exam score × pass/fail or M/F. Mathematically Pearson r on a 0/1 coding. Used in item analysis (item right/wrong × total score). Biserial (r b ) One continuous + one ARTIFICIAL dichotomy e.g. score × "high vs low" where the split is arbitrary on an underlying continuum. Estimates the r if the dichotomy were left continuous; can exceed 1.0. Phi (φ) Two TRUE dichotomies (2 × 2) e.g. smoker/non-smoker × disease/no-disease. Pearson r on two 0/1 variables; linked to chi-square: φ = √(χ²/N). Tetrachoric (r tet ) Two ARTIFICIAL dichotomies (both underlying continua) The 2×2 analogue of biserial: both variables are really continuous and normal but recorded as yes/no. Partial correlation Two continuous, controlling for a third X with Y after the effect of Z is removed from both X and Y ("holding Z constant"). Part / semipartial correlation Two continuous, Z removed from one only Z's effect is removed from the predictor (or Y) only, not both. Used to gauge a predictor's unique contribution in regression. Multiple correlation (R) One DV + several predictors Correlation between the observed DV and the values predicted by the whole set of predictors. Ranges 0 to 1; R² = variance explained (see cluster B12). Eta (η) / correlation ratio Two variables, nonlinear / curvilinear relationship Indexes the strength of a curved association that Pearson r would underestimate; η ≥ |r|. Used in ANOVA as η² (effect size). Interpreting r, and the link to R² For any of these, the sign gives direction (positive = move together, negative = inversely) and the absolute value (0 to 1) gives strength. Squaring it gives the coefficient of determination, r² , the proportion of variance shared between the two variables. So r = 0.60 means r² = 0.36, i.e. 36% of the variance in one variable is accounted for by the other (this is the bivariate version of the R² in cluster B12). Note that a moderate-looking r explains a much smaller share of variance once squared (r = .30 → only 9%). Point-biserial in item analysis, and attenuation Item discrimination: the point-biserial between an item (scored 0/1, right/wrong) and total test score tells you how well that item separates high from low scorers. A low or negative r pb flags a bad item. Range restriction: if the sample's spread on a variable is narrowed (e.g. only high scorers were selected), the observed correlation is attenuated (shrunk) toward zero. Classic case: validity coefficients look low when computed only on already-selected employees/students. Attenuation due to unreliability: measurement error in either variable also pulls the observed correlation below the true correlation; the "correction for attenuation" formula estimates what r would be with perfectly reliable measures. Worked examples "Correlate IQ score with gender (M/F) ." → continuous × true dichotomy → point-biserial . "Correlate test score with a median-split 'high vs low motivation'." → continuous × artificial dichotomy → biserial . "Relate smoking (yes/no) to lung disease (yes/no) , both genuine." → true × true → phi (and φ = √(χ²/N)). "Two yes/no items each splitting an underlying trait." → artificial × artificial → tetrachoric . "Relation of study hours to marks, removing the effect of IQ from both ." → partial correlation . "How strong is the U-shaped link between arousal and performance?" → nonlinear → eta (correlation ratio) , not Pearson r. Trap matrix (memorise): continuous × TRUE dichotomy → point-biserial ; continuous × ARTIFICIAL dichotomy → biserial ; TRUE × TRUE dichotomy → phi ; ARTIFICIAL × ARTIFICIAL → tetrachoric . Rule of thumb: "biserial-family = at least one ARTIFICIAL dichotomy (an underlying continuum); point-biserial/phi = TRUE/genuine dichotomy." Trap: partial vs part (semipartial). Partial removes the third variable from both X and Y; part/semipartial removes it from only one . "Holding Z constant for both" = partial; "unique contribution of one predictor" = semipartial. Trap: Pearson vs eta. A near-zero Pearson r does not mean "no relationship"; it means no linear relationship. For a curved (e.g. inverted-U) pattern use eta / the correlation ratio . Pearson assumes linearity. Trap: phi (φ) and the point/biserial coefficients are still just correlations on a 2×2 or 0/1 coding , not chi-square itself; but φ is derived from chi-square (φ = √(χ²/N)), so a chi-square stem asking for "strength of association in a 2×2" points to phi. Indian mental-health law & regulatory bodies Lead fact: the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (passed 2017, came into force July 2018 ) repealed the Mental Health Act 1987 . It is rights-based and aligned to the UN CRPD , effectively decriminalised attempted suicide (Section 115: a person attempting suicide is presumed to have severe stress and shall not be tried/punished, overriding IPC 309 in practice), and introduced the Advance Directive and Nominated Representative . Keep three statutes apart: MHCA 2017 = treatment & rights of the mentally ill ; RPwD 2016 = rights/benefits of persons with disability ; RCI Act 1992 = who is licensed to practise (a clinical psychologist must be RCI-registered with a CRR number ). Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (MHCA): key provisions Repealed the Mental Health Act 1987; shifts from a custodial model to a rights-based, patient-centred framework consistent with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) , which India ratified in 2007. Definition of "mental illness": a substantial disorder of thinking, mood, perception, orientation or memory that grossly impairs judgement, behaviour, capacity to recognise reality or ability to meet the ordinary demands of life; includes mental conditions associated with the abuse of alcohol and drugs, but excludes mental retardation/intellectual disability (i.e. arrested or incomplete development of mind, which is covered instead under RPwD). Decriminalised suicide (Sec 115): any person who attempts suicide is presumed, unless proven otherwise, to be under severe stress and shall not be prosecuted or punished ; the government has a duty to provide care, treatment and rehabilitation. This effectively neutralises IPC 309. Right to access mental healthcare run or funded by government, plus rights to community living, dignity, confidentiality, legal aid, information, and protection from cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment . Advance Directive (AD): a person may state in advance how they wish (or do not wish) to be treated for mental illness, and may appoint their representative. It operates when the person ceases to have capacity. Nominated Representative (NR): a person nominated to support and take decisions on behalf of the patient; if none is named, the Act specifies an order of default (e.g. relative, caregiver) and the NR is appointed accordingly. Mental Health Review Boards (MHRBs): quasi-judicial bodies that review advance directives, registrations of admissions, complaints, and protect rights. They replaced the old magistrate/judicial-route reception orders of the 1987 Act. Central Mental Health Authority (CMHA) and State Mental Health Authorities (SMHAs): register and supervise mental-health establishments and maintain registers of professionals. ECT & restraint rules: unmodified ECT is banned (ECT only with muscle relaxants and anaesthesia); ECT is not permitted for minors except with the MHRB's prior permission (and informed consent of the guardian). Sterilisation as a treatment for mental illness is prohibited; chained restraint is prohibited ; seclusion and physical restraint are tightly regulated and only when necessary to prevent imminent harm. Capacity & supported decision-making: the Act presumes capacity to make mental-healthcare decisions and adopts a supported (not substituted) decision-making model; capacity is defined functionally (ability to understand information, appreciate consequences and communicate a decision). RPwD Act, 2016 (Rights of Persons with Disabilities) Repealed the Persons with Disabilities (PwD) Act 1995; enacted to give effect to the UN CRPD. Expanded the recognised disabilities from 7 to 21 conditions , including mental illness, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, specific learning disabilities , cerebral palsy, blindness/low vision, deaf/hard of hearing, locomotor disability, muscular dystrophy, chronic neurological conditions, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's, haemophilia, thalassaemia, sickle-cell disease, acid-attack victims, and multiple disabilities. Benchmark disability = 40% or more of a specified disability (as certified); this is the threshold that unlocks reservations and benefits. Reservation: 4% in government jobs and 5% in higher-education institutions for persons with benchmark disabilities; plus accessibility mandates, guardianship provisions and penalties for discrimination. RCI Act, 1992 (Rehabilitation Council of India) Statutory body that regulates the training and registration of rehabilitation professionals, including Clinical Psychologists . Maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register (CRR) ; a clinical psychologist needs RCI registration (a CRR number ) to practise legally, and practising without registration is a punishable offence . Prescribes and recognises minimum standards of education, including the M.Phil in Clinical Psychology as the qualifying degree for registration as a clinical psychologist. Policy / regulatory context National Mental Health Programme (NMHP): launched 1982 to ensure availability and accessibility of minimum mental-health care; its field arm is the District Mental Health Programme (DMHP, started 1996) under the Bellary model. This is a programme/policy , not a statute, so do not confuse it with the MHCA. NTA (National Testing Agency): the autonomous body that conducts national entrance examinations; relevant as the conducting/regulatory body for entrance tests, distinct from RCI which governs the right to practise. Trap (three Acts): if a stem mentions " 40% / benchmark / reservation / 21 conditions / repealed 1995 " it is RPwD 2016 . " Advance directive / nominated representative / decriminalised suicide / review board / repealed 1987 / unmodified ECT banned " is MHCA 2017 . " CRR number / register to practise / recognises M.Phil Clinical Psychology " is RCI 1992 . The overlap the examiner exploits: MHCA and RPwD both repealed an older 1987/1995 law and both flow from the CRPD , but one is about illness & treatment and the other about disability rights/benefits . Finer traps: Mental retardation/intellectual disability is excluded from MHCA's definition of mental illness but is a recognised disability under RPwD . The 1987 Act used magistrates/judicial reception orders ; the 2017 Act uses Mental Health Review Boards instead. NMHP/DMHP is a programme (1982/1996) , not an Act. Do not attribute licensing to MHCA: practice rights belong to the RCI . Hook: " MHCA = my care (advance directive, nominated rep, no-prosecution suicide, review boards). RPwD = rights & reservation (21 conditions, 40% benchmark). RCI = right to practise (CRR). Repeals: 2017 buries 1987, 2016 buries 1995, 1992 stands alone. " 6. Neuropsychological test batteries Lead fact: the PGI Memory Scale (Pershad & Wig, 1977; PGIMER Chandigarh) is the standard Indian memory battery with 10 subtests . It is the most-asked Indian neuropsych instrument. The other high-yield axis is " which function does each test isolate? ", frontal/executive vs memory vs visuomotor vs attention. Neuropsychological testing maps behaviour onto brain systems. The examiner wants you to attach each test to the function it isolates and, by extension, the region/system implicated. The big conceptual debate is fixed vs flexible batteries: a fixed battery (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska) administers a standard set to every patient (good for comparability, screening, forensic defensibility, but long and not hypothesis-driven), whereas a flexible / process approach (the Boston process tradition, and how the NIMHANS battery is often used) selects tests to test a specific hypothesis about the patient (efficient and targeted, but less standardised across patients). Amnesia types & memory disorders Lead fact: the whole topic is anchored to one reference point, the moment of injury. Anterograde = cannot form NEW memories AFTER the event (the clock runs forward, the past is intact). Retrograde = loss of OLD memories from BEFORE the event (the clock runs backward into the past). H.M. is the classic anterograde case (bilateral medial temporal lobe / hippocampus removed for epilepsy). Most real organic amnesias are mixed but anterograde-dominant; pure retrograde amnesia is rare and raises suspicion of a functional (psychogenic) cause. The underlying logic the examiner tests: the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe are needed to consolidate new declarative memories, but once a memory is fully consolidated it is stored in distributed neocortex . So damaging that consolidation machinery wipes out the ability to lay down new traces (anterograde) and the not-yet-consolidated recent past (a graded retrograde loss), while old, well-consolidated memories survive. This single mechanism explains both Ribot's gradient and why H.M. kept his childhood but not his afternoon. Anterograde amnesia Retrograde amnesia What is lost New memories cannot be formed after the event Old memories from before the event are gone Time direction Forward from the injury Backward from the injury Memory type hit New declarative (episodic + semantic); procedural usually spared Mostly episodic/autobiographical; graded by recency Classic case / cause H.M.; Korsakoff's; hippocampal / medial temporal damage Head trauma, ECT; often follows Ribot's gradient Typical exam tag "Can't make new memories" "Forgot the past / who they were" Ribot's Law and the temporal gradient Ribot's Law (Théodule Ribot, 1881): in retrograde amnesia, recent memories are lost first and most severely; older, remote memories are most resistant. This is the temporal (Ribot) gradient , summarised as " last in, first out ." The reason: remote memories have had more time to consolidate into neocortex and no longer depend on the damaged hippocampus. A flat (non-graded) retrograde loss, where even childhood is gone but new learning is fine, points away from organic amnesia and toward a dissociative/functional picture. Korsakoff's syndrome and the Wernicke-Korsakoff complex Cause: chronic thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency , classically from alcoholism (also severe malnutrition, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery). Thiamine is a cofactor for glucose metabolism, so deprived diencephalic neurons die. Lesion sites: the mammillary bodies and the dorsomedial (mediodorsal) nucleus of the thalamus ; this is the prototype diencephalic amnesia . Clinical picture: dense anterograde amnesia (plus a graded retrograde component) with prominent confabulation (fabricated answers filling memory gaps, without intent to lie) and poor insight. Wernicke's encephalopathy is the acute, reversible phase that precedes/accompanies it. Its classic triad : confusion (global encephalopathy) + ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus (eye-movement palsy) + ataxia (gait). Treat emergently with thiamine before glucose (giving glucose first can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's). Untreated Wernicke's can progress to the chronic, largely irreversible Korsakoff psychosis : hence Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome . The other named amnesias Transient Global Amnesia (TGA): sudden, temporary, self-limiting episode of dense anterograde (and some retrograde) amnesia lasting a few hours, with characteristic repetitive questioning ("where am I? what are we doing?"). Personal identity is preserved and there is no focal neurology; it resolves fully within 24 hours and rarely recurs. Dissociative (psychogenic) amnesia: memory loss from psychological trauma, not organic injury ; typically a loss of autobiographical / personal identity information, often selective for the traumatic event, and reversible. A DSM-5 dissociative disorder; dissociative fugue (sudden travel with identity loss) is a specifier. This is the key organic-vs-functional split: functional amnesia spares new learning but loses the personal past, often flat rather than graded. Source amnesia: the information is retained but its source/context is lost (you know the fact but not where or when you learned it). Tied to frontal-lobe function and prominent in ageing and frontal damage; underlies "cryptomnesia" (unintentional plagiarism). Infantile (childhood) amnesia: the normal inability of adults to recall events from roughly the first 3 to 4 years of life , attributed to immature hippocampal/prefrontal consolidation and lack of an autobiographical "self" framework. The landmark cases H.M. (Henry Molaison): underwent bilateral medial temporal lobectomy (hippocampus + nearby structures) by William Scoville for intractable epilepsy. Result: severe anterograde amnesia and graded retrograde loss, but intact procedural learning (improved at the mirror-drawing task across days while denying ever having done it). Studied for decades by Brenda Milner ; the proof that declarative and procedural (non-declarative) memory are separate systems , and that the medial temporal lobe is for declarative memory. Clive Wearing: herpes simplex encephalitis destroyed his hippocampi, leaving perhaps the most extreme combined anterograde + retrograde amnesia (a memory span of seconds, repeated "first awakening"), yet he retained procedural skill, still playing and conducting music. K.C. (Kent Cochrane): motorcycle head injury; a striking dissociation in which episodic memory (personal re-experienced events) was lost but semantic memory (facts, general knowledge) was preserved, key evidence for Tulving's episodic/semantic distinction.
